summary.en: Crossing the worlds with his magic gem, King Mandhatar comes to Uttarakuru, whose inhabitants need neither plough nor sow: from the wishing-trees they gather rice un Planted and clothe themselves in garments that grow ready upon the boughs.
summary.zh: 曼陀多王攜神寶遊歷諸界，至北俱盧洲；其人不耕不種：如意樹自生稻米，枝頭自垂衣裳，取之而已。

sensitivity.note: Buddhist narrative preserved in the Tibetan canon (Kah-gyur); presented as a mythic corpus text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: garland-like trees of various colours planted on one side of Sumeru. Having remarked them, he asked the Yaksha Divaukasa what were these garland-like trees of various colours. "O king, these are the wishing-trees of the inhabitants of Uttarakuru. The inhabitants of Uttarakuru clothe themselves with garments from the wishing-trees." [...] "O chieftains, those are the wishing-trees that bear the garments with which the inhabitants of Uttarakuru clothe themselves. Ye also, when ye have arrived there, will clothe yourselves with garments from off the wishing-trees."
passages.zh: 須彌山一側生長著種種顏色的花鬘樹。他注意到這些樹後，便問藥叉提婆迦沙這些種種顏色的花鬘樹是什麼。「大王，這些是北俱盧洲居民所擁有的如意樹。北俱盧洲的居民以如意樹所生的衣裳為衣。」……「首領們，那些就是如意樹，生有北俱盧洲居民用以蔽體的衣裳。你們到了那裡，也將以如意樹上的衣裳為衣。」

title.en: Glooskap and Malsum, the Twin Brothers
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普與狼弟馬爾蘇姆

region.en: Nova Scotia / Gaspe peninsula, Wabanaki country
region.zh: 瓦巴納基之地：新斯科舍／加斯佩半島

period: Micmac oral tradition; recorded 1884 (Leland)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'Of Glooskap's Birth, and of his Brother Malsum the Wolf'

summary.en: The good Glooskap and his evil twin Malsum the Wolf, who burst through their mother's side and killed her, exchange the secrets of their lives; the Wolf, betrayed and betrayed again, smites his brother with pine and owl-feather in vain — until a fern-root, learned from the Beaver, proves his bane.
summary.zh: 善神格魯斯卡普與惡弟狼馬爾蘇姆乃孿生；弟破母肋而出，弒其母。兄弟互換命門之秘：狼以松根、鴞羽擊兄而皆不驗——終自河貍處洩出「蕨根」之秘，格魯斯卡普一擊而斃之。

sensitivity.note: Wabanaki oral tradition recorded from named Indian narrators; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Wabanaki/Algonquian communities.

passages.text: Now the great lord Glooskap, who was worshiped in after-days by all the Wabanaki, or children of light, was a twin with a brother. As he was good, this brother, whose name was Malsumsis, or Wolf the younger, was bad. Before they were born, the babes consulted to consider how they had best enter the world. And Glooskap said, "I will be born as others are." But the evil Malsumsis thought himself too great to be brought forth in such a manner, and declared that he would burst through his mother's side. And as they planned it so it came to pass. Glooskap as first came quietly to light, while Malsumsis kept his word, killing his mother.
passages.zh: 如今，偉大的主格盧斯卡普，日後為所有瓦巴納基人、即光明之子所崇拜，與一位兄弟是雙生子。由於他善良，這位名叫馬爾蘇姆西斯、即小狼的兄弟卻是邪惡的。在他們出生之前，這兩個胎兒商議，考慮他們最好如何進入這世界。格盧斯卡普說：「我要像其他人那樣出生。」但邪惡的馬爾蘇姆西斯自以為太偉大，不屑以這種方式被生出，便宣告他要從母親的脅側破出。他們如此謀劃，事情便如此應驗。格盧斯卡普先安然見了天日，而馬爾蘇姆西斯則履行了他的話，殺死了母親。

passages.text: It came to pass in after-days that Kwah-beet-a-sis, the son of the Great Beaver, or, as others say, Miko the Squirrel, or else the evil which was in himself, tempted Malsumsis to kill Glooskap; for in those days all men were wicked. So taking his bow he shot Ko-ko-khas the Owl, and with one of his feathers he struck Glooskap while sleeping. [...] Therefore Glooskap arose in sorrow and in anger, took a fern-root, sought Malsumsis in the deep, dark forest, and smote him so that he fell down dead.
passages.zh: 日後，大狸的兒子夸比塔西斯，或如他人所說，松鼠米科，又或是他自身內在的邪惡，誘使馬爾蘇姆西斯去殺格盧斯卡普；因為在那個時代，所有的人都邪惡。於是他拿起弓，射下貓頭鷹科科卡斯，並用牠的一根羽毛，趁格盧斯卡普熟睡時擊打他。……因此，格盧斯卡普滿懷悲傷與憤怒起身，取來一根蕨根，在幽深黑暗的森林中尋見馬爾蘇姆西斯，將他擊倒而死。

title.en: Glooskap Makes Man of the Ash Tree
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普以梣樹造人

region.en: Maine / Nova Scotia, Wabanaki country
region.zh: 瓦巴納基之地：緬因／新斯科舍

period: Passamaquoddy oral tradition; recorded 1884 (Leland)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How Glooskap made the Elves and Fairies, and then Man of an Ash Tree'

summary.en: Glooskap came first into the land next to sunrise: he shot his arrows into the basket-trees, the Ash, and the first Indians came out of the bark; then, finding the animals he had made too strong, he questioned Moose, Squirrel, and Bear, and made each smaller — or banished them — according to their answers.
summary.zh: 格魯斯卡普初至日出之地；彎弓射梣樹，樹皮中湧出最初之印第安人。又見所造之獸過強，乃問麋、松鼠、白熊：「遇人則何為？」聽其答而各縮其形，或逐之遠方。

sensitivity.note: Wabanaki oral tradition recorded from named Indian narrators; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Wabanaki/Algonquian communities.

passages.text: Glooskap came first of all into this country, into Nova Scotia, Maine, Canada, into the land of the Wabanaki, next to sunrise. There were no Indians here then (only wild Indians very far to the west). First born were the Mikumwess, the Oonabgemessuk, the small Elves, little men, dwellers in rocks. And in this way he made Man: He took his bow and arrows and shot at trees, the basket-trees, the Ash. Then Indians came out of the bark of the Ash-trees. [...] Glooskap made all the animals. He made them at first very large. [...] Then he said to the Squirrel, who was of the size of a Wolf, "What would you do if you should meet an Indian?" And the Squirrel answered, "I would scratch down trees on him." Then Glooskap said, "You also are too strong," and he made him little. [...] So he questioned all the beasts, changing their size or allotting their lives according to their answers.
passages.zh: 格盧斯卡普最先來到這片土地，來到新斯科舍、緬因、加拿大，來到瓦巴納基人的土地，即迎向日出之處。那時這裡還沒有印第安人（只有極西之處的野印第安人）。最先出生的是米庫姆維斯、烏納布格梅蘇克、小精靈、小人，棲居於岩石之中。他就這樣造了人：他拿起弓與箭，射向樹木，即籃樹，即梣樹。於是印第安人便從梣樹的樹皮中走了出來。……格盧斯卡普造了所有的動物。他起初把牠們造得非常大。……然後他對那時有狼一般大小的松鼠說：「你若遇見一個印第安人，會怎麼做？」松鼠答道：「我會抓下樹木砸在他身上。」於是格盧斯卡普說：「你也太強壯了。」便把他變小。……於是他逐一詢問所有野獸，依牠們的回答改變其大小或分派其壽命。

title.en: Sky Woman and the Good Mind, the Bad Mind
title.zh: 天女與善心惡心

region.en: Onondaga country, New York, USA
region.zh: 紐約州奧農達加之地

period: Iroquois tradition as written by David Cusick (Tuscarora), 1827/1848; quoted in Leland, 1884

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations (1848), as quoted in Leland, Algonquin Legends of New England

summary.en: David Cusick's Iroquois account: a pregnant woman of the upper world descends and is received on the turtle; her twin sons, the Good Mind and the Bad Mind, break into the dark world — the Good makes the sun and moon of their mother's head and body, creates creeks, animals, and two breathing figures of dust, while the Bad raises mountains and falls to spite him.
summary.zh: 卡西克所記易洛魁神話：上界孕婦下墜，落於龜背；孿生二子善心與惡心破腹而出，入黑暗世界。善心以母之顱造日、以身造月，作川流動物，又以土塑男女二像吹以生氣；惡心則造高山飛瀑以相抗。

sensitivity.note: Iroquois tradition as written down by a Tuscarora author in 1827/1848; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Haudenosaunee communities.

passages.text: There was a woman who was with child, with twins. She descended from the higher world, and was received on the turtle. While she was in the distress of travail, one of the infants in her womb was moved by an evil desire, and determined to pass out under the side of the parent's arm, and the other infant endeavored in vain to prevent his design. They entered the dark world by compulsion, and their mother expired in a few minutes. One of them possessed a gentle disposition, and was named Enigorio, the Good Mind. The other possessed an insolence of character, and was called Enigonhahetgea; that is, the Bad Mind. [...] The Good Mind, determined to prosecute his design, began the work of creation. Of his mother's head he made the sun, of her body the moon. After he had made creeks and rivers, animals and fishes, he formed two images of the dust of the ground in his own likeness, male and female, and by his breathing into their nostrils he gave them living souls
passages.zh: 有一個懷著雙胞胎的婦人。她從較高的世界降下，被承接在龜上。當她身處分娩的苦痛之中時，她腹中兩個嬰兒之一受邪惡的慾望所驅使，決意從母親腋下的一側鑽出，另一個嬰兒則徒勞地試圖阻止他的圖謀。他們被迫進入黑暗的世界，而他們的母親在幾分鐘內便氣絕身亡。其中一個生性溫和，名叫埃尼戈里奧，即善心。另一個性情傲慢無禮，名叫埃尼戈納赫特格亞，也就是惡心。……善心決意推行他的計畫，開始了創造之工。他用母親的頭造了太陽，用她的身體造了月亮。他造出溪流與江河、走獸與魚類之後，又照自己的形貌，用地上的塵土造了兩個形像，一男一女，並向他們的鼻孔吹氣，賜給他們活的靈魂。

title.en: The Children Throw the Sleeping Sun into the Sky
title.zh: 孩童擲睡日上天

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍山

period: Bushman (San) oral tradition; recorded 1873-1879 (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Children are sent to throw the sleeping Sun into the Sky'

summary.en: The Sun lies sleeping with his armpit shining on the ground; an old woman sends the children to seize him together and throw him up into the sky, telling him to stand fast and travel hot — so the Sun became the Sun which dries the Bushman rice as he passes along above.
summary.zh: 太陽熟睡，腋下光芒照地；老嫗遣孩童共執而舉擲於天，囑其站定而行、熾熱如常——太陽遂為今日之太陽，行於天上，曝乾桑人之米。

sensitivity.note: San (|Xam Bushman) oral tradition dictated to Bleek and Lloyd by named narrators; presented as an archival record of 19th-century recordings, not as permission to speak for San communities.

passages.text: they waited for him (the Sun), they went to sit down. They arose, going on, they stealthily approached him, they stood still, they looked at him, they went forward; they stealthily reached him, they took hold of him, they all took hold of him together, lifted him up, they raised him, while he felt hot. Then, they threw him up, while he felt hot; they spoke to him, while he felt hot: "O Sun! thou must altogether stand fast, thou must go along, thou must stand fast, while thou art hot."
passages.zh: 他們等候他（太陽），便前去坐下。他們起身前行，悄悄接近他，站定不動，注視著他，又向前走去；他們悄悄來到他身旁，抓住他，眾人一齊抓住他，把他舉起，將他抬高，而他當時正感灼熱。於是，他們趁他灼熱之際把他拋了上去；他們趁他灼熱之際對他說：「哦，太陽啊！你務必全然堅定不移，你務必一路前行，你務必堅定不移，當你灼熱之時。」

passages.text: The old woman said to the children: "O children going yonder! ye must tell him, that, he must altogether become the Sun, that he may go forward, while he feels that he is altogether the Sun, which is hot; therefore, the Bushman rice becomes dry, while he is hot, passing along in the sky; he is hot, while he stands above in the sky."
passages.zh: 老婦人對孩子們說：「哦，往那邊去的孩子們啊！你們務必告訴他，他務必全然成為太陽，好讓他一路前行，當他感到自己全然是那灼熱的太陽之時；因此，當他灼熱地行經天空時，叢林人之米便會乾枯；當他高懸於天空之上時，他便是灼熱的。」

title.en: The Moon and the Origin of Death
title.zh: 月亮與死亡之起源

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍山

period: Bushman (San) oral tradition; recorded 1873-1879 (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Origin of Death'

summary.en: The Moon meant mankind to be like himself: dying, and then coming again living back; but the Hare contradicted him, declaring his mother utterly dead — and the Moon, enraged, struck his mouth and cursed the people to die altogether and vanish away, while the hare ever after bears the scar.
summary.zh: 月神本欲人類如己：死而復生；野兔逆其言，堅稱其母已真死。月神怒擊其口而咒人類：「爾等必盡死而滅」，兔唇之疤由此而來——死亡自此常駐人間。

sensitivity.note: San (|Xam Bushman) oral tradition dictated to Bleek and Lloyd by named narrators; presented as an archival record of 19th-century recordings, not as permission to speak for San communities.

passages.text: Therefore, the Moon spoke, he said: Ye who are people, ye shall, when ye die, altogether dying vanish away. For, I said, that, ye should, when ye died, ye should again arise, ye should not altogether die. For, I, when I am dead, I again living return. I had intended, that, ye who are men, ye should also resemble me [...] The hare, when I intended to tell him about it, -- while I felt that I knew that the hare's mother had not really died, for, she slept, -- the hare was the one who said to me, that his mother did not sleep; for, his mother had altogether died. These were the things that I became angry about
passages.zh: 因此，月亮開口說道：你們這些為人者，你們死時，必全然死去而消逝無蹤。因為我曾說過，你們死時，應當再度復起，不應全然死去。因為我死之後，仍會再度活著歸來。我本打算讓你們這些為人者，也像我一樣……當我打算把這件事告訴野兔時——當時我自覺知道野兔的母親其實並未真正死去，因為她只是睡著了——野兔卻是那個對我說他母親沒有睡的人；因為他母親已全然死去。正是這些事令我發怒。

passages.text: And the Moon became angry about it, that the hare spoke thus, while he did not assent to him (the Moon). And he hit with his fist, cleaving the hare's mouth; and while he hit the hare's mouth with his fist, he exclaimed: "This person, his mouth which is here, his mouth shall altogether be like this, even when he is a hare; he shall always bear a scar on his mouth..."
passages.zh: 月亮為此發怒，因為野兔如此說話，卻不肯順從他（月亮）。他用拳頭一擊，劈裂了野兔的嘴；當他用拳頭擊打野兔的嘴時，他喊道：「這人，他這裡的嘴，他的嘴必全然變成這樣，即使他身為野兔也是如此；他的嘴上將永遠帶著一道疤痕……」

title.en: The Mantis Feigns Death as a Hartebeest
title.zh: 螳螂詐死為麋羚

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍山

period: Bushman (San) oral tradition; recorded 1873-1879 (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Mantis assumes the form of a Hartebeest'

summary.en: |Kaggen the Mantis, the trickster of the early race, cheats the children by feigning death as a dead hartebeest; they joyfully skin him with stone knives — until his skin snatches itself free, and the dismembered flesh springs together again, joining itself piece by piece to the living Mantis.
summary.zh: 早期之民的詭計者——螳螂|卡根——化身死麋羚詐騙孩童；孩童歡然以石刀剝皮——皮忽自脫手而遁，碎肉相尋，節節復接，螳螂復活如初。

sensitivity.note: San (|Xam Bushman) oral tradition dictated to Bleek and Lloyd by named narrators; presented as an archival record of 19th-century recordings, not as permission to speak for San communities.

passages.text: The Mantis is one who cheated the children, by becoming a hartebeest, by resembling a dead hartebeest. He feigning death lay in front of the children, when the children went to seek gambroo [...] The children perceived him, when he had laid himself stretched out, while his horns were turned backwards. The children then said to each other: "It is a hartebeest that yonder lies; it is dead." The children jumped for joy (saying): "Our hartebeest! we shall eat great meat." They broke off stone knives by striking (one stone against another), they skinned the Mantis. The skin of the Mantis snatched itself quickly out of the children's hands.
passages.zh: 螳螂就是那個欺騙孩子們的傢伙，他變成一隻麋羚，裝作一隻死去的麋羚。他裝死躺在孩子們面前，當時孩子們正前去尋找甘布魯……孩子們察覺到了他，當時他伸展開身子躺著，雙角向後翻轉。孩子們於是彼此說道：「那邊躺著的是一隻麋羚；它死了。」孩子們歡呼雀躍（說道）：「我們的麋羚！我們要吃大塊的肉了。」他們敲擊（一塊石頭擊向另一塊）打製出石刀，剝下了螳螂的皮。螳螂的皮迅速從孩子們手中掙脫而去。

passages.text: Her sisters let fall the flesh of the Mantis. The flesh of the Mantis sprang together, it quickly joined itself to the lower part of the Mantis's back. The head of the Mantis quickly joined (itself) upon the top of the neck of the Mantis. [...] The shoulder blade of the Mantis ran forward, it joined itself on to the ribs of the Mantis.
passages.zh: 她的姊妹們讓螳螂的肉落了下來。螳螂的肉重新聚攏，迅速接合到螳螂背部下方。螳螂的頭迅速接合在螳螂頸項的上端。[……]螳螂的肩胛骨向前奔去，接合到螳螂的肋骨上。

title.en: Kua Fu Chases the Sun; Xingtian Dances with Shield and Axe
title.zh: 夸父逐日；刑天舞干戚

region.en: Mythic northwest China (Shanhaijing)
region.zh: 神話西北中國（山海經）

period: Shanhaijing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing (Classic of Mountains and Seas), original Chinese text (Guo Pu recension): Kua Fu in 'Haiwai Bei Jing', Xingtian in 'Haixi Jing'

summary.en: Two defiant figures of the Shanhaijing: Kua Fu races the sun, drinks the rivers dry, and dies of thirst, his staff becoming a peach grove; and the headless Xingtian, slain by the Yellow Emperor, makes his nipples his eyes and navel a mouth, dancing forever with shield and battle-axe.
summary.zh: 《山海經》兩位抗爭者：夸父與日逐走，飲盡河渭，道渴而死，棄杖化為鄧林；刑天與帝爭神，帝斷其首，乃以乳為目、以臍為口，操干戚而舞，永不止息。

sensitivity.note: Mythic corpus entry based on classical Chinese sources without a public-domain English translation; passages are condensed paraphrases referenced to modern scholarship. Living cultural heritage of China. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Kua Fu raced with the sun. As he followed it toward Yu Valley, he drank the Yellow River and the Wei River dry; when he turned north to seek the waters of the Great Marsh, he died of thirst on the way. The staff he carried fell to the ground and grew into a peach grove, and the wind and rain feed it still.
passages.zh: [節縮改述]夸父與太陽競逐。他追隨太陽奔向禺谷，飲乾了黃河與渭水；當他轉向北去尋求大澤之水時，途中渴死。他所持的手杖落在地上，化為一片桃林，風雨至今仍滋養著它。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Xingtian fought the Yellow Emperor for divine supremacy; the Emperor cut off his head and buried it on Changyang Mountain. Headless, Xingtian made his nipples his eyes and his navel a mouth, and he dances still, wielding his shield and battle-axe.
passages.zh: [節縮改述]刑天與黃帝爭奪神位；黃帝斬下他的頭，葬於常羊山。刑天雖無頭，卻以乳為眼、以臍為口，至今仍揮舞著盾與斧而舞。

title.en: Susanoo Slays the Eight-Forked Serpent
title.zh: 須佐之男斬八岐大蛇

region.en: Izumo, Japan
region.zh: 日本出雲

period: Kojiki, 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain, 1882)

source.archive: Wikisource (reference; Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain)
source.work: Kojiki, sections XVIII-XIX: The Eight-Forked Serpent and the Palace of Suga (trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain)

summary.en: Exiled for his ravages, His-Impetuous-Male-Augustness comes to Izumo where the eight-forked serpent of Koshi has devoured seven daughters of an aged couple; he brews eight-fold strong sake, and when the serpent dips each head into a vat and lies drunk, he cuts it apart, finding the sword Kusanagi in its tail.
summary.zh: 暴虐之神須佐之男被逐出高天原，至出雲，遇高志之八岐大蛇——蛇已吞食老夫婦七女。乃釀八醞之酒置於八槽；大蛇垂八首入槽而醉，須佐之男拔劍斬之，於蛇尾中得草薙劍，並娶倖存之櫛名田比賣為妻。

sensitivity.note: Ancient court myth of Japan (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of Chamberlain's public-domain translation. Presented as a comparative-mythology text.

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] His-Impetuous-Male-Augustness, expelled from the Plain of High Heaven, came to the upper reaches of the River Hi in Izumo, and found an old man and an old woman weeping, with a young girl between them. They told him the eight-forked serpent of Koshi, with a body spanning eight valleys and eight hills, its eyes like winter cherries, had each year devoured one of their daughters, until only Kushinada-hime remained.
passages.zh: [節縮改述]素盞嗚尊被逐出高天原，來到出雲國肥河上游，見一老夫與一老婦哭泣，中間立著一名少女。他們告訴他，越之八岐大蛇身跨八谷八岡，雙眼如冬櫻，每年吞食他們一個女兒，直到只剩下櫛名田比賣。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Susanoo bade them brew strong sake of eight-fold brewings, and set it in eight vats. The serpent came, dipping a head into each vat, and drank until it was drunk; then Susanoo, drawing the sword ten-grasps long, cut the serpent apart till the blood flowed out — and in the middle of its tail he found a great sword, which he presented to the Sun Goddess, named the Herb-Quelling-Blade of the Great Deity.
passages.zh: [節縮改述]素盞嗚尊命他們釀造八次蒸餾的烈酒，盛於八個大甕之中。大蛇來了，將八個頭各探入一甕，飲至醉倒；於是素盞嗚尊拔出十握之劍，將大蛇斬開，血流而出——他在蛇尾之中發現一柄大刀，便獻給太陽女神，名為大神之草薙劍。

title.en: The First Sunrise of the Popol Vuh
title.zh: 波波爾烏之初日

region.en: Chichicastenango, Guatemala
region.zh: 瓜地馬拉奇奇卡斯德南哥

period: Popol Vuh, c. 1554-58 (copy of older traditions)

source.work: H. H. Bancroft, The Native Races of the Pacific States, vol. III: Myths and Languages (1875), Quiche chapter retelling the Popol Vuh

summary.en: Before the dawn of the present sun, the first men of wood were destroyed; the true people — made of yellow and white maize dough — gathered at the place of raising their faces to await the first light. The morning star came forth, and the sun shown like a white flash of lightning, drying the face of the earth, as the ancestors sang the raising of the heart of the sky.
summary.zh: 太陽未昇之世，木人已滅；真民——黃白玉米所塑——齊聚「仰面之地」以待初光。晨星先出，太陽如白電乍現，烘乾大地之面；先祖遂歌詠天心之高舉。

sensitivity.note: K'iche' Maya mythic corpus (Popol Vuh); passages are condensed paraphrases of the council-book's narrative. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] When the true people had been fashioned from yellow and white maize by the Creator and the Maker, they could see to the ends of the earth, and they gave thanks on the surface of the earth; but the gods dimmed their eyes as a man dims a mirror when he breathes on it, so that they might see only what was near.
passages.zh: [節縮改述]當造物者與塑造者用黃、白玉米造出真正的人類之後，他們能望見大地的盡頭，並在大地之上獻上感恩；但眾神使他們的眼目黯淡，如同人對著鏡子呵氣使其朦朧一般，好讓他們只看見近處的事物。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] They waited there in the dark, holding the hearts of their hearts, until the great star came forth before the sun, and then the sun itself shown like a white ray of lightning, turning the faces of the carved images of the animals of old to stone, while the true people watched the sun's face rise, and the sky and the earth were glad.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 他們在黑暗中等待，懷抱著心中之心，直到那顆巨星先於太陽出現，接著太陽本身如白色閃電般照耀，將古老動物雕刻圖像的面孔化為石頭，而真正的人們望著太陽的臉升起，天與地皆歡喜。

title.en: The Birth of Huitzilopochtli at Coatepec
title.zh: 維齊洛波奇特利誕於蛇山

region.en: Coatepec (mythic: Mexico City region)
region.zh: 蛇山（神話地：今墨西哥城一帶）

period: Florentine Codex (Sahagun, c. 1578-80) and related codex traditions

source.work: H. H. Bancroft, The Native Races of the Pacific States, vol. III: Myths and Languages (1875), Aztec chapter (after Clavigero's version of the Sahagun tradition)

summary.en: Coatlicue, sweeping on the hill of Coatepec, conceives from a ball of humming-bird feathers; her daughter Coyolxauhqui rallies the four hundred stars to slay her, but at the moment of her death the young Huitzilopochtli springs from her womb in full war-gear, and with the fire-serpent he dismembers his sister and routs the stars of night.
summary.zh: 科阿特利庫埃於蛇山掃地，懷羽球而孕；其女科約爾沙赫吉聚四百星辰欲弒之。臨難之際，青年維齊洛波奇特利全副武裝自母腹躍出，持火蛇斬其姊，肢解其身，逐散夜之群星。

sensitivity.note: Aztec (Mexica) codical tradition; passages are condensed paraphrases referencing the Florentine Codex. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] While Coatlicue swept the temple hill of Coatepec, a ball of humming-bird feathers descended upon her, and she gathered it into her bosom; when she sought it again it was gone, and she had conceived a child. Her daughter Coyolxauhqui, shamed by the pregnancy, stirred the four hundred of the southern stars to slay their mother.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 當科亞特利庫埃在科阿特佩克清掃神廟山丘時，一團蜂鳥羽毛從天而降落在她身上，她將其拾起收入懷中；當她再次尋找時，羽毛已消失無蹤，而她已受孕懷了一個孩子。她的女兒科約爾沙烏基為這懷孕感到羞恥，煽動南方星辰四百眾去殺害她們的母親。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] At the moment the attackers reached the summit, Coatlicue gave birth to Huitzilopochtli, arrayed in shield, brand, and feather crest, with a face of blue stripes. He slew Coyolxauhqui with the fire-serpent, cut her pieces rolling down the hill, and put her mother's enemies to flight in all directions — and the mother's heart was made glad by her son.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 就在攻擊者抵達山頂的那一刻，科亞特利庫埃生下了維齊洛波奇特利，他身披盾牌、火矛與羽冠，臉上有藍色條紋。他以火蛇殺死科約爾沙烏基，將她切成碎塊滾落山丘，並將母親的敵人驅散至四面八方——母親的心因她的兒子而歡喜。

title.en: Sventovit of Arkona and the White Horse
title.zh: 斯文托維特與白馬神諭

region.en: Arkona, Rugen island (Baltic coast)
region.zh: 波羅的海呂根島阿科納

period: 12th-13th c. Danish/German chronicles (Saxo, Book XIV; Helmold of Bosau)

source.work: Jan Machal, 'Slavic Mythology', in The Mythology of All Races, vol. III (1918), Part II ch. I 'Svantovit'

summary.en: On the cliff of Arkona stood the great temple of Sventovit, god of the Rani, served by a horse kept for the god: each year the priests set the white horse's hoof against three pairs of spears to divine war or peace; victory in battle belonged to whoever took the omens with the horn of mead, and the god's quadruple horn was filled each year with wine.
summary.zh: 阿科納崖上立蘭尼人之大神斯文托維特聖殿；殿中養神馬為占：歲首祭司以神馬之蹄踏三重並置之雙矛，以卜戰和。出征者執蜜酒之角以受吉兆；神之四角蜜酒歲滿則傾而再斟。

sensitivity.note: Pre-Christian Slavic tradition surviving only through Christian chronicles (Saxo, Helmold, the Russian Primary Chronicle); passages are condensed paraphrases of the chroniclers' accounts — reconstruction status should be treated with care. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] On the cliff of Arkona on the isle of Rügen rose the wooden temple of Sventovit, with its one great door and carved inner chamber, hung with purple and crowded with the horns of princes. The god's image held a drinking-horn each year refilled with mead, and a white horse was kept in the enclosure; only the priest might feed and ride it.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 在呂根島阿爾科納的懸崖上，矗立著斯文托維特的木造神廟，有一扇大門與雕刻的內室，懸掛著紫色布幔，擠滿了王公們的號角。神像手持一隻飲酒角，每年重新注滿蜂蜜酒，圍欄中飼養著一匹白馬；唯有祭司可以餵養並騎乘牠。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Before a war the priests set three rows of crossed spears, led the horse over them, and if it stepped first with the right foot the venture was blessed; the horse was also run at dawn through triple spear-lines each year. The people said the god rode his horse at night against their enemies, and his oracle decided war, peace, seed-time and harvest.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 戰爭之前，祭司會排列三排交叉的長矛，牽馬跨越其上，若馬先踏出右腳，則此行蒙受祝福；每年黎明時，馬也會被牽著跑過三重矛線。人們說神在夜間騎著牠的馬對抗敵人，而祂的神諭決定戰爭、和平、播種時節與收穫。

title.en: Svarog and Dazhbog, the Heavenly Father and Sun Prince
title.zh: 斯瓦羅格與達日博格：天父與日君

region.en: Kyiv (Rus' capital), Ukraine
region.zh: 基輔（羅斯之都，烏克蘭）

period: Russian Primary Chronicle, year 980 CE entry (later compilations)

source.work: Jan Machal, 'Slavic Mythology', in The Mythology of All Races, vol. III (1918), on Svarog, Dazhbog and Svarozic, and the Deities of the Pagan Russians

summary.en: The chronicle's heathen pantheon of Prince Vladimir lists Dazhbog among the idols of the Kyiv hill; the scholia to an Old Russian translation of John Malalas makes Svarog the heavenly smith-father who reigned in the age of tools, and his son Dazhbog 'the Sun' who reigned after him — giving fire and light to the Rus' people.
summary.zh: 編年史載弗拉基米爾王於基輔山丘所立神像中有達日博格；古俄譯約翰·馬拉拉斯史書之邊注則謂：天匠斯瓦羅格治器物之世，其子「日」達日博格繼之為君——賜火與光於羅斯之民。

sensitivity.note: Pre-Christian Slavic tradition surviving through chronicle references and later scholia; passages are condensed paraphrases — reconstruction status should be treated with care. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] When Prince Vladimir ruled in Kyiv he set idols on the hill: Perun of wood with silver head, and Hors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl and Mokosh. The people sacrificed to them, calling their sons and daughters to the hill, and the heathen gods of the old Russians were honored with offerings.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 當弗拉基米爾大公統治基輔時，他在山丘上設立神像：木製的佩倫有著銀製頭顱，還有霍爾斯、達日博格、斯特里博格、西馬爾格爾與莫科什。人們向它們獻祭，將兒女召喚至山丘，古俄羅斯的異教諸神以祭品受到尊崇。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] In the scholia appended to the Old Russian translation of the Chronicle of John Malalas, the heavenly smith Svarog is said to have reigned in Egypt in the days when tongs and hammers first fell from heaven; and after him his son, called Dazhbog, 'the giving lord,' ruled as the Sun — for the heathen named the Sun the son of Svarog, who gives warmth and light to all the world.
passages.zh: [節錄改寫] 在《約翰·馬拉拉斯編年史》古俄譯本所附的註疏中，據說天界的鐵匠斯瓦羅格曾在鐵鉗與鐵鎚初從天而降的那些日子裡統治埃及；在他之後，他的兒子——名為達日博格，意即「賜予之主」——以太陽的身分統治——因為異教徒稱太陽為斯瓦羅格之子，祂賜予全世界溫暖與光明。

title.en: Jumong, Born of Light and River
title.zh: 朱蒙：光與河之子

region.en: East Buyeo (Manchuria/Korean borderland)
region.zh: 東扶餘（滿洲／朝鮮邊境）

period: Samguk Sagi (1145) and Samguk Yusa (1281)

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, vol. 1 (1905), Ko-gu-ryu chapter (Chu-mong legend)

summary.en: Habaek's daughter Yuhwa, impregnated by sunlight, lays an egg in leather that a boy of wondrous speech breaks forth from in seven days; pursued by the princes of Buyeo, Jumong warns the river, and fish and turtles rise to bridge the water under him — he crosses, founds Goguryeo, and is the Heavenly King of the East.
summary.zh: 河伯之女柳花感日光而孕，產一卵於革囊；七日卵中出一語奇之童。扶餘王子欲害之，朱蒙告於河：魚鱉浮而為橋，履之而渡——遂東至紇升骨城，建高句麗，是為東明聖王。

sensitivity.note: Foundational myth recorded in Korea's oldest court chronicles; passages are condensed paraphrases of the Samguk Sagi/Yusa narratives. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] The daughter of the river god Habaek, called Yuhwa, was carried off by the heavenly king and made pregnant by a ray of sunlight; her father, shamed, shut her in a leather sack and threw it into the river, where it floated to a king's court. The child hatched from an egg, and the king raised the boy, named Jumong, a master bowman.
passages.zh: [節錄改寫] 河神河伯之女，名為柳花，被天王擄去，因一縷陽光而受孕；她的父親羞憤之下，將她關進皮囊，投入河中，皮囊漂流至一位國王的宮廷。孩子自蛋中孵化，國王將這名為朱蒙的男孩撫養長大，成為一名神射手。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] When the princes of Buyeo plotted against him, Jumong fled to the great river and, striking the water with his bow, cried that he was the grandson of Heaven and the River; fish and turtles rose in shoals to make a bridge of their backs. He crossed over the crossing of them, the bridge sank behind, and he came to the hill of Holbon and made his capital, calling his kingdom Goguryeo.
passages.zh: [節錄改寫] 當扶餘的王子們圖謀害他時，朱蒙逃至大江，以弓擊水，高呼自己是天與河之孫；魚與龜成群浮起，以背脊架成一座橋。他從牠們的背上渡過，橋隨即在身後沉沒，他來到忽本山岡，建都於此，稱其國為高句麗。

title.en: Suro of Gaya Born from Six Golden Eggs
title.zh: 首露王與六金卵

region.en: Gimhae (Gaya confederacy), Korea
region.zh: 朝鮮金海（伽倻）

period: Samguk Yusa (1281), 'Garak-gukgi' (Records of Garak)

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, vol. 1 (1905), Kingdom of Ka-rak section

summary.en: The six elders of Gujiguk prayed without rest for a king; a voice from heaven promised to send one, and nine chiefs sailed out to find a ship bearing a red banner and a red sail moored on the sand — from six golden eggs came six boys, the firstborn Suro king of Geumgwan Gaya, and the five other kings of the Gaya states.
summary.zh: 龜旨國九干晝夜祈禱求王；天音許之，遣九長老出海尋訪——果見赤帆赤旗之船泊於龜旨峰下沙灘。船中六金卵化為六童，長者首露為金海伽倻之王，餘五卵為五伽倻列國之君。

sensitivity.note: Foundational myth recorded in the Samguk Yusa; passages are condensed paraphrases of the Garak records. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] The chiefs of the nine villages of Gujiguk gathered on the peak of Kui-ji (Turtle Peak) and prayed day and night for a king to rule them; a voice from heaven answered that it would send down a ruler, and told them to wash, pound the earth, and set out wine and food before looking out on the sea.
passages.zh: [節錄改寫] 龜旨國九村的族長們聚集於龜旨峰上，日夜祈禱，求一位君王來統治他們；一個來自天上的聲音回答說，將遣下一位統治者，並吩咐他們沐浴、搗地，擺出酒食，然後眺望大海。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] They sailed out and found a ship moored by the sandhill, flying a red banner and red sail; in it were six golden eggs which turned into beautiful boys. The first to be born they named Suro, and he became the king of Geumgwan Gaya; his five brothers became the kings of the other Gaya states, and the queen who came to him, Heo Hwang-ok, arrived likewise from a far land by sea.
passages.zh: [節錄改寫] 他們出海，發現一艘船停泊在沙丘旁，船上飄揚著紅旗與紅帆；船中有六枚金蛋，化為俊美的男孩。最先出生的，他們命名為首露，他成為金官伽倻的國王；他的五個兄弟成為其他伽倻諸國的國王，而前來嫁給他的王后許黃玉，同樣是從遠方經海路而來。

title.en: The Kumulipo: Life from the Deep Darkness
title.zh: 庫木里波：幽暗深處的生命

region.en: Hawai'i (chant homeland)
region.zh: 夏威夷（頌歌之地）

period: Kumulipo chant, committed to writing c. 18th-19th c.; trans. Queen Liliuokalani, 1897

source.archive: Internet Archive (reference; Kumulipo, trans. Queen Liliuokalani)
source.work: The Kumulipo, a Hawaiian creation chant, trans. Queen Lili'uokalani (1897)

summary.en: The Kumulipo, the Hawaiian chant of genealogy, opens in the deep darkness of Po: in the first age the coral polyp is born, then the fish of the sea and the creeping things; night and day, dark and light follow one another, generation after generation, until the ages of the gods give way to the ages of men — the chiefly line born from darkness into light.
summary.zh: 庫木里波為夏威夷系譜頌歌：起於暗夜「坡」之深處——第一紀珊瑚蟲出生，繼而海魚、蠕行之物；夜與晝相代，一代復一代，直至神紀讓於人紀——酋長世系自幽暗生於光明。

sensitivity.note: Hawaiian genealogical chant recorded in the 18th-19th century and translated by Queen Lili'uokalani (1897); passages are condensed paraphrases. Living tradition of Hawai'i — presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Native Hawaiian communities.

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] In the first age of the Kumulipo, born was the coral polyp in the sea, born the worm that creeps, born the shellfish and the swarming things; born in the sea the fish, and on the land the man. Night began, night ended: the deep darkness of Po brought forth, and the light of day followed after.
passages.zh: [節錄改寫] 在《庫穆利波》的第一個時代，海中生出了珊瑚蟲，生出了爬行的蠕蟲，生出了貝類與成群蠕動之物；海中生出了魚，陸上生出了人。夜開始了，夜結束了：波之深暗孕育而出，白晝之光隨後而至。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Age followed upon age, the dark with the dark giving birth to the finned and the creeping, until the age was born of the woman and the man; the chant runs down the generations of the gods to the generations of the chiefs, for the child of chiefly blood is born from the deep darkness into the world of light.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 世代相繼，黑暗與黑暗交合，生出有鰭之物與爬行之物，直到那世代由女人與男人所生；此頌歌自諸神的世代一路傳下，直至首領的世代，因為首領血脈之子乃從幽深黑暗中誕生，進入光明之世。

title.en: Hina, the Sky-Mother of Hawaiian Chants
title.zh: 希娜：夏威夷頌歌中的天母

region.en: Waimea / Kohala, Hawai'i
region.zh: 夏威夷威美亞／科哈拉

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; recorded 19th c. (Fornander Collection)

source.archive: Internet Archive (reference; Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Antiquities)
source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Antiquities and Folk-lore: Hina and Māui narratives

summary.en: In the Fornander chants, Hina the mother of Māui dwells in the moon, beating her tapa cloth; her son Māui the demigod snares the sun on Haleakala with ropes plaited by her hands, forcing it to slow its journey so the days might be long enough for men to dry their kapa and cook their food.
summary.zh: 弗南德爾歌集所載：毛伊之母希娜居月中，晝夜擣樹皮布；其子半神毛伊以母所編之繩於哈萊亞卡拉縛日，迫其緩行——庶使白晝延長，民得曝布炊食。

sensitivity.note: Hawaiian oral tradition recorded in the 19th century; passages are condensed paraphrases of the Fornander Collection narratives. Living tradition of Hawai'i — presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Native Hawaiian communities.

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Hina, the woman of the moon, beat her kapa cloth under the full moon's light, and her strokes were the thunder; her sons were the small Māui of many wonders, who fished islands from the sea with the hook manaiakalani, the fishhook of the great land.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 月之女希娜在滿月的光輝下捶打她的卡帕布，她的捶擊聲便是雷鳴；她的兒子們是行諸多奇蹟的小毛伊，以馬奈阿卡拉尼——那大地的魚鉤——從海中釣起島嶼。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Because the days were too short for the work of men, Māui took the ropes his mother had plaited, climbed to the crater of the great mountain, and laid snares upon the sun's rays as they broke over the rim; the sun cried out and promised to travel slowly across the sky forever — and thus the days grew long for all the people.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 因為白晝對人的勞作而言太過短促，毛伊便取來母親所編的繩索，攀上大山的火山口，趁太陽的光芒破出山緣之際，在其上佈下羅網；太陽高聲呼喊，許諾永遠緩緩行過天空——於是眾人的白晝便變長了。

title.en: Inanna's Descent to the Netherworld
title.zh: 伊南娜下冥府

region.en: Uruk, Sumer, Iraq
region.zh: 蘇美烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Sumerian cuneiform text, c. 1900-1600 BCE

source.work: Lewis Spence, Myths & Legends of Babylonia & Assyria (1916), 'The Descent of Ishtar into Hades'

summary.en: The goddess Inanna abandons her temples to descend to the netherworld and seize the seat of her sister Ereshkigal; stripped of one power at each of seven gates, she stands naked before the throne and is struck dead — until wise Enki creates two sexless beings who win her corpse and revive her with the food and water of life, and galla demons demand she give a substitute to go free.
summary.zh: 女神伊南娜棄其七廟而降冥府，欲奪姊埃雷什基伽勒之位；過七門，一門除一力，至御前裸然而立，遂遭誅——智神恩基造二無性之人，媚於冥后而得屍，以生命之食水活之；冥界群魔隨之索替死者。

sensitivity.note: Sumerian mythic text; passages are condensed paraphrases referenced to the ETCSL scholarly translation. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] From the great heaven she set her mind on the great below: the holy priestess Inanna abandoned her temples of heaven and earth and went down to the netherworld. At each of the seven gates of the land of no return, the keeper removed from her a garment of her power, until she stood naked before Ereshkigal on the throne, and the judges of the underworld fixed on her the eye of death.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 她自偉大的天上將心思轉向偉大的地下：聖潔的女祭司伊南娜捨棄她天上與地上的神廟，下到冥界。在無歸之地的七道門前，每一道門的守門者都從她身上取下一件代表她權能的衣物，直到她赤身站在寶座上的埃列什基伽勒面前，冥界的判官們便將死亡之眼定在她身上。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Her minister Ninshubur pleaded at the temples until Enki, the god of wisdom, made from the dirt of his nails two sexless creatures who slipped into the underworld, sympathized with the mourning queen, and won the corpse; they sprinkled it with the food and water of life, and Inanna rose. But the galla demons rose at her side, and she went from city to city mourning, until she found her husband Dumuzi on his throne and set the demons upon him.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 她的臣宰寧舒布爾在神廟前再三懇求，直到智慧之神恩基用指甲中的泥土造出兩個無性別的生物，潛入冥界，對哀悼的女王表示同情，並贏得屍身；他們將生命之食與生命之水灑於其上，伊南娜便起身了。但伽拉惡魔也隨她而起，她從一城到一城哀悼，直到她在寶座上找到丈夫杜穆濟，便將惡魔們引向他。

title.en: The Wayang Cycle: Rama in Java
title.zh: 哇揚戲：爪哇的羅摩

region.en: Yogyakarta, Java, Indonesia
region.zh: 印尼爪哇日惹

period: Old Javanese Ramayana (kakawin, c. 9th c. CE) and wayang tradition

source.work: W. Basil Worsfold, A Visit to Java (1893), chs. XII-XIV (Hindu Javanese literature; the wayang)

summary.en: The Indian epic arrived early in Java, where the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin retold Rama's war against the giant-king Rawana, and the wayang shadow theatre made Rama, his monkey ally Hanuman, and the ten-faced Rawana the fixed figures of a nightly shadow-myth that Javanese courts have treated as sacred genealogy.
summary.zh: 印度史詩早傳爪哇：古爪哇《羅摩衍那》頌詩重述羅摩征討十面巨靈王拉瓦納之戰；哇揚皮影戲遂以羅摩、神猴哈奴曼與十首拉瓦納為夜夜搬演之定角，爪哇歷朝視為神聖譜系。

sensitivity.note: Javanese adaptation of the Ramayana tradition; passages are condensed paraphrases referencing the kakawin and wayang scholarship. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Rama of Ayodhya, exiled with his wife Sinta, lost her to the giant-king Rawana of Alengka, who carried her over the sea to his island city; with the monkey general Hanuman and the army of the monkeys, Rama built a bridge across the water, burned the city's gate, and killed Rawana and his host to take back his wife.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 阿逾陀的羅摩與妻子辛塔一同流放，卻失去了她——阿楞卡的巨人之王羅瓦那將她帶過大海，擄至他的島城；羅摩與猴將哈奴曼及猴軍一同在水中築起橋樑，燒毀城門，誅殺羅瓦那及其部眾，奪回妻子。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] The court poets of Java rendered the war in the kakawin, and the dalang (puppet-master) of the wayang kulit performs it by lamplight to this day: the dalang is considered to sanctify the audience as he speaks the gods' parts, and the story is told as both legend and royal genealogy, for Javanese kings claimed descent from Rama's line.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 爪哇的宮廷詩人在 kakawin 中鋪陳這場戰爭，而 wayang kulit 的 dalang（操偶師）至今仍在燈光下演出此劇：人們認為 dalang 在念誦諸神台詞時，能令觀眾蒙受聖化；這個故事既是傳說，也是王室譜系，因為爪哇諸王皆自稱是羅摩世系的後裔。

title.en: Sang Sapurba Descends from the Hill of Light
title.zh: 山格山普巴：自光山而下

region.en: Bukit Siguntang, Palembang, Sumatra, Indonesia
region.zh: 印尼蘇門答臘巴鄰旁西貢塘山

period: Malay Annals (Sulalat al-Salatin), 17th c. compilation of older legends; trans. Leyden, 1821

source.archive: Internet Archive (reference; The Malay Annals, trans. John Leyden)
source.work: Malay Annals (Sulalat al-Salatin), trans. John Leyden (1821): the descent of Sang Sapurba

summary.en: The Malay Annals open the line of the Malayan kings at the hill of Siguntang-gunung above Palembang, where the divine Raja Sang Sapurba appeared in the age of Pandai-pandai, showing himself to be of the race of the kings of the world; his princely greatness was first shown when he drew the wondrous sword from the river and wed the king's daughter — from his descent the Malay royal lines are traced.
summary.zh: 《馬來紀年》以巴鄰旁上方西貢塘山為馬來諸王之始：神君山格山普巴顯聖於班代時代，示其為世界列王之裔；其「王者之德」初現於拔劍出水、迎娶公主之事——馬來蘇丹世系由此而開。

sensitivity.note: Malay royal myth recorded in the Sulalat al-Salatin; passages are condensed paraphrases of Leyden's 1821 public-domain translation. Presented as a comparative-mythology text.

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] At the foot of the hill of Siguntang-gunung, on the banks of the river of Palembang, the people of the age of Pandai-pandai beheld a prince of divine aspect descend from the hill, washing in the water; the king gave him his daughter, and because he wore the signs of the race of the kings of the world he was called Sang Sapurba, the great prince of descent.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 在錫根唐山（Siguntang-gunung）山腳下、巴鄰旁河（Palembang）畔，潘代潘代（Pandai-pandai）時代的人們看見一位容顏如神的王子從山上降下，在水中沐浴；國王將女兒許配給他，又因他身上帶著世間諸王族裔的標記，他便被稱為 Sang Sapurba，意即出身高貴的偉大王子。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] When he drew from the river the wonderful sword that appeared on the water's surface, the greatness of his soul was made manifest, and the people took him for their king; the line of the Malay kings of Minangkabau, of Singapore, and of Melaka is traced in the Annals to this descent from the hill of light.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 當他從河中抽出那柄浮現於水面的神劍時，他靈魂的偉大便顯露無遺，人們遂奉他為王；《馬來紀年》將米南加保、新加坡與馬六甲諸馬來王室的世系，都追溯至這位自光明之山降下的先祖。

title.en: Dewi Sri and the Rice That Rises from the Body
title.zh: 德維斯里：身化稻米

region.en: East Java, Indonesia
region.zh: 印尼東爪哇

period: Javanese-Sundanese rice mythology, older than the Hindu period

source.work: J. G. Frazer, The S. of the Corn and of the Wild (The Golden Bough pt. V, vol. I, 1912), East-Indian rice-ceremony section

summary.en: The rice-goddess of Java and Bali: in the Sundanese cycle the heavenly maiden Pohaci Sanghyang Asri, hounded by desire she cannot answer, is buried by the gods — and from her head the coconut springs, from her lips the betel, from her body the rice that feeds the world; her serpent-consort, the god of the field, protects the seed.
summary.zh: 爪哇與巴厘之稻神：巽他神話中天上仙女波哈奇桑揚阿斯里因無法回應之情所困，眾神葬之——頭生椰子，唇生蔞葉，身化稻米以養萬民；其蛇伴田神護種於田。

sensitivity.note: Javanese and Sundanese agricultural myth; passages are condensed paraphrases of the rice-goddess cycles. Living cultural heritage of Indonesia. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Pohaci Sanghyang Asri, the maiden of heaven, was so beautiful that all the gods desired her; because she could not answer their desire without breaking her virtue, the gods in sorrow killed her and buried her body in the earth so that something good might come of her death.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 天之少女 Pohaci Sanghyang Asri 美貌絕倫，眾神皆愛慕她；由於她若不毀壞自身貞潔便無法回應眾神的欲求，眾神在悲傷中將她殺死，並把她的身體埋入土中，好讓她的死能結出善果。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] From her head grew the coconut-palm, from her lips the betel-vine, from her eyes the many kinds of spice, from her body the rice that gives life to the world; the serpent that guarded the fields became her consort, and the rice goddess Dewi Sri is worshipped still in the planting and harvest of Java and Bali.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 她的頭長出椰子樹，她的唇長出檳榔藤，她的眼睛長出種種香料，她的身體長出滋養世界的稻米；守護田地的蛇成為她的配偶，稻之女神 Dewi Sri 至今仍在爪哇與峇里的播種與收穫時節受到崇祀。

title.en: Dievs, Saule, and the Celestial Wedding of the Dainas
title.zh: 笛維斯、紹蕾與達伊納天婚

region.en: Latvia (Livland and Kurzeme)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（利夫蘭與庫爾蘭）

period: Dainas (Latvian folk songs) collected from the 19th c.

source.work: Encyclopaedia Britannica 11th ed. (1911), 'Lithuanians and Letts'

summary.en: The Latvian dainas sing a sky-court of gods: Dievs the Father of the sky, Saule the Sun-mother whose daughters wash her gold in the sea, Meness the Moon who loves the sun's daughter — the celestial wedding of the sun's daughter is the great daina theme, with the bathers, the weavers, and the mourners of the gods below.
summary.zh: 拉脫維亞達伊納短歌唱天上神廷：天父笛維斯、日母紹蕾（其女於海中洗金）、月神梅內斯戀日女——太陽女兒之天婚為達伊納之要題；神之浴者、織者與哭喪者皆在其間。

sensitivity.note: Baltic mythic corpus of the dainas (folk songs with mythic content); passages are condensed paraphrases — reconstruction status of the deity list should be treated with care. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] In the dainas Dievs the sky-father rides in the longest autumn nights to see the green fields, and rings the silver bell; Saule the sun-mother drives her chariot across the hill of the sky, and her daughters wash her golden girdle in the sea at evening.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 在 dainas 中，天父 Dievs 於最漫長的秋夜策馬巡行，察看翠綠的田野，並搖響銀鈴；太陽之母 Saule 駕著她的車輦越過天丘，她的女兒們則在傍晚於海中洗滌她的黃金腰帶。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] The great wedding of the dainas is the wedding of the sun's daughter: Meness the moon, or Auseklis the morning star, rides to the bridal hill; the guests sit at the table of the celestial stone, and the Latvian singers made of this sky-wedding the image of their own year — light and dark, sowing and harvest.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 戴納歌謠中最盛大的婚禮，是太陽之女的婚禮：月神梅涅斯，或晨星奧塞克利斯，騎馬前往新娘的山丘；賓客們坐在天上石桌旁，而拉脫維亞的歌者把這場天界婚禮化為自身一年的寫照——光明與黑暗、播種與收穫。

title.en: Lacplesis, the Bear-Slayer of Latvia
title.zh: 熊殺者拉奇普萊西斯

region.en: Latvia (Kurzeme and the Daugava)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（庫爾茲梅與道加瓦河）

period: Latvian national epic (Andrejs Pumpurs, 1888) built on folk myth

source.work: Andrejs Pumpurs, Lacplesis (1888), Latvian original of the national epic

summary.en: The folk layers of the Latvian epic: Lacplesis, born of a bear-woman, slays the monstrous bear that devours the land's herds, wears its ears as his mark, and defends the Latvian shore against the Black Knight — the folk song figures of the bear-son and the hero of the Daugava gathered into a national myth of freedom.
summary.zh: 拉脫維亞史詩之民間層：拉奇普萊西斯為熊母所生，誅食畜之怪熊，以其耳為記；守道加瓦河岸而抗黑騎士——民間歌謠中熊子與河上英雄之形象，匯為民族自由之神話。

sensitivity.note: Latvian epic built on folk mythic material; passages are condensed paraphrases — the epic is a 19th-century literary construction on folk songs and its content is treated as mythic corpus. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Lacplesis was the son of a bear and a human mother, and grew in the forests of Kurzeme, strong beyond all men; when the monstrous bear laid waste the herds of the people, he fought it in its den and strangled it, wearing its torn ears upon his head — hence his name, the Bear-Slayer.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 拉奇普雷西斯是熊與人類母親所生之子，在庫爾澤梅的森林中長大，力氣勝過所有人；當那頭巨熊毀壞了人們的畜群，他在熊穴中與之搏鬥並將其扼死，把撕下的熊耳戴在頭上——因此得名「屠熊者」。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] By the Daugava he met the Black Knight who ruled the river with fire and iron; in the folk layers the hero was promised to the land until the day he should be cast into the river by the Black Knight — and the singers said the Latvian nation would rise when Lacplesis should wake again from the river's bed.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 他在道加瓦河畔遇見以火與鐵統治河流的黑騎士；在民間傳說層面，這位英雄被許諾給這片土地，直到他被黑騎士投入河中的那一天——而歌者們說，當拉奇普雷西斯再度從河床中醒來時，拉脫維亞民族將會崛起。

title.en: Jurate and Kastytis: The Amber Palace of the Sea
title.zh: 尤拉特與卡斯蒂蒂斯：海上琥珀宮

region.en: Baltic sea coast (Palanga), Lithuania
region.zh: 立陶宛波羅的海海岸（帕蘭加）

period: Lithuanian folk legend recorded from the 19th c.

source.work: Ludwik Adam Jucewicz, Wspomnienia Zmudzi (1842), 'Krolowa morza Baltyckiego' (Queen of the Baltic Sea)

summary.en: Jurate, the goddess who ruled the Baltic sea from an amber palace, took pity on the fisherman Kastytis whose nets the waves tore, and loved him; Perkunas, the thunder-god, wrecked the amber palace with a lightning bolt for her betrayal of the sea — and the pieces of the palace still wash up as amber on the shore of Palanga.
summary.zh: 海上女神尤拉特居琥珀宮而統波羅的海；憫漁人卡斯蒂蒂斯網破之苦而相愛。雷神佩爾庫納斯怒其背海之約，以雷火轟碎琥珀宮——帕蘭加海岸至今猶拾宮殿之碎屑，是為琥珀。

sensitivity.note: Lithuanian folk legend; passages are condensed paraphrases — reconstruction status of Baltic myth should be treated with care. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Jurate the sea-maiden ruled the deep in a palace built of amber under the Baltic waves; when the fisherman Kastytis dared to fish in her waters and his nets were cut by her servants, she rose in anger to chide him — and finding him fair, took him to the amber palace and loved him.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 海之少女尤拉特統治著波羅的海波濤之下以琥珀築成的宮殿深處；當漁夫卡斯提提斯膽敢在她的水域捕魚、漁網被她的僕從割破時，她憤怒地升起斥責他——卻發現他容貌俊美，便將他帶入琥珀宮殿並愛上了他。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Perkunas the thunder-god, keeper of order among the gods, came in fury at the goddess's love for a mortal; his lightning broke the amber palace and struck Kastytis dead in its ruins. The sea keeps Jurate bound to the wreck, and the fishermen of Palanga gather the little pieces of the palace that the waves still cast up, which men call amber.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 雷神佩爾庫納斯是眾神之間秩序的守護者，因這位女神愛上凡人而盛怒而來；他的閃電擊碎了琥珀宮殿，並在廢墟中將卡斯提提斯擊死。大海使尤拉特被束縛於殘骸之上，而帕蘭加的漁夫們收集海浪至今仍沖上岸的宮殿碎片，人們稱之為琥珀。

title.en: Baal and the Sea-Dragon Yam
title.zh: 巴力與海龍雅姆

region.en: Ugarit (Ras Shamra), Syria
region.zh: 敘利亞烏加里特（拉斯沙姆拉）

period: Ugaritic tablets (CTA 2), c. 14th-13th c. BCE

source.work: Walter G. Williams, The Ras Shamra Inscriptions and Their Significance for the History of Hebrew Religion (1934), summary of the Baal epics

summary.en: Yam, the tyrant Sea, commands the assembly of the gods to surrender Baal; crafty Kothar makes Baal two clubs that leap from his hand and split the tyrant — but the singers warn that the dragon Lotan, the wriggling seven-headed serpent, is not utterly slain, for Mot will one day swallow the storm-god in his turn.
summary.zh: 暴君海神雅姆迫眾神廷交出巴力；巧匠科塔爾為巴力鑄雙棍，躍出手而擊碎暴君——然歌者言：盤繞之七首巨龍羅坦未嘗盡誅，死神莫特他日必反噬風雨之神。

sensitivity.note: Ugaritic mythic tablets excavated from 1929; NO public-domain English translation exists, so passages are clearly-labeled condensed paraphrases of the tablet narrative (referenced to modern scholarly translations). [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Yam the sea-tyrant sent to the divine assembly his demand that the gods deliver Baal to him, and the gods hid beneath their thrones; Astarte reproved them, and the craftsman Kothar wa-Khasis forged for Baal two Clubs which he named. The Club leapt from Baal's hand and smote Yam on the skull, and the tyrant Sea collapsed — and Baal reigned in his place.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 海之暴君雅姆向諸神議會傳達他的要求：眾神須將巴力交給他，眾神便躲到自己的寶座之下；阿斯塔特責備他們，而工匠科塔爾·瓦·哈西斯為巴力鍛造了兩根棍棒，並為它們命名。棍棒從巴力手中躍出，擊中雅姆的頭顱，暴君海便倒下了——巴力遂取而代之，君臨其位。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] The singers warned: when you smite Lotan, the fleeing serpent, take his everlasting dominion from him — for Lotan the wriggling serpent, the seven-headed dragon, would rise again; and the day would come when Death himself, Mot, would swallow the storm-god who had conquered the Sea.
passages.zh: [精簡意譯] 歌者警告說：當你擊殺那逃遁的蛇羅坦時，要奪去他永恆的統治權——因為那蜿蜒的蛇羅坦，那七頭巨龍，必將再度興起；終有一日，死亡本身莫特將吞下那位曾征服海洋的風暴之神。

title.en: Baal Swallowed by Mot, and Restored
title.zh: 巴力入莫特之口而復生

region.en: Ugarit (Ras Shamra), Syria
region.zh: 敘利亞烏加里特（拉斯沙姆拉）

period: Ugaritic tablets (CTA 5-6), c. 14th-13th c. BCE

source.work: Walter G. Williams, The Ras Shamra Inscriptions and Their Significance for the History of Hebrew Religion (1934), the first and second 'Alein Baal' epics

summary.en: Death, Mot, swallows Baal — the rains fail and the earth withers; his sister Anat finds the corpse, grinds Death in the sieve of her winnowing-fan, and the sun-goddess Shapash carries Baal back; seven years the devourer of the world lies crushed — and when Mot returns, the two are parted only by the terror of Shapash.
summary.zh: 死神莫特吞噬巴力——雨澤斷絕，大地枯槁；其妹阿娜特尋得其屍，以揚穀之篩碎磨死神，日神沙帕什負巴力而歸；滅世之口被碾凡七年——莫特復來時，唯畏日神之威而二神相分。

sensitivity.note: Ugaritic mythic tablets; NO public-domain English translation exists, so passages are clearly-labeled condensed paraphrases of the tablet narrative (referenced to modern scholarly translations). [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Mot the devourer invited Baal to come down into his house, the pit of the heart of the earth; Baal went, and Death swallowed him. With the storm-god in the grave, the rains ceased, the fields withered, and the earth lay dry; El grieved on his throne that Baal was perished like a dead man from the earth.
passages.zh: [精簡意譯] 吞噬者莫特邀巴力下到他的屋中，即大地核心的深坑；巴力去了，死亡便吞下了他。風暴之神既入墳墓，雨水止息，田野枯萎，大地乾涸；埃爾在他的寶座上哀傷，因巴力如死人一般從地上滅絕了。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Anat came down and found the body; she seized Death her brother, split him with the sword, winnowed him with the fan, burned him with fire, and ground him like grain for the birds. Then Shapash the sun-goddess lifted Baal from the pit and set him on his throne — and the rains returned; when Mot rose again seven years later, the terror of Shapash kept the two gods apart, and Baal's reign over the wet winds of the sky was secure.
passages.zh: [精簡意譯] 阿娜特下來，尋見了屍身；她抓住她的兄弟死亡，以劍劈開他，以簸箕簸揚他，以火焚燒他，又將他磨如穀粒，供鳥啄食。隨後，太陽女神沙帕什從坑中舉起巴力，安置他於寶座之上——雨水便復返；七年之後莫特再起時，沙帕什的威懾使二神分隔，巴力對天空濕風的統治遂得穩固。

title.en: Danel and the Murdered Hero Aqhat
title.zh: 但以理族長丹尼爾與被害英雄阿卡特

region.en: Ugarit (Ras Shamra), Syria
region.zh: 敘利亞烏加里特（拉斯沙姆拉）

period: Ugaritic tablets (CTA 17-19), c. 14th-13th c. BCE

source.work: James A. Montgomery, 'The Danel Text', Journal of the American Oriental Society, vol. 56 (1936), pp. 440-445

summary.en: The righteous king Danel, childless for seven years, prays and is granted a son, Aqhat — whom the craftsman Kothar equips with a wondrous bow; the goddess Anat covets the bow, and when the boy refuses to sell or give it, she slays him on the wings of the wind — and the birds of heaven bury the hero, while his sister Pughat takes up the avenger's place.
summary.zh: 義王丹尼爾無子七年，禱而得子阿卡特；巧匠科塔爾為其造神弓。女神阿娜特欲得此弓，少年拒售與贈，遂遭女神弒於風翼之上——天上群鳥葬英雄；其妹普珥特執報仇之職。

sensitivity.note: Ugaritic mythic tablets; NO public-domain English translation exists, so passages are clearly-labeled condensed paraphrases of the tablet narrative (referenced to modern scholarly translations). [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Danel the righteous ruler of the assembly offered food to the gods and clothed the holy ones; seven years he had no son. On the seventh day Baal heard and moved El, and the god blessed the king: a son should be born to his house — and the child Aqhat was born to him, fed on the milk of the assemblies of the holy ones.
passages.zh: [精簡意譯] 會眾的正義統治者達內爾向諸神獻食，為聖者們供衣；七年之久他沒有兒子。到了第七日，巴力聽見了，並打動了埃爾，神便祝福這位君王：他的家必得生一子——孩子阿迦特遂為他所生，以聖者會眾之乳哺育。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Kothar the smith made the boy a bow of wonderful craft; Anat the huntress desired it, offering silver and gold, then the gift of immortality itself, but Aqhat refused her, saying the bow was for a warrior and not for a goddess to carry. In fury she cast him from the wings of the wind, and he became as a piece of the clouds; the eagle of the sky carried the tale to the grieving king, and his sister Pughat dressed as a man to take vengeance at the feasts of the murderer.
passages.zh: [精簡意譯] 工匠科塔爾以奇妙技藝為這男孩造了一張弓；女獵手阿娜特覬覦此弓，先獻銀與金，繼而獻上不朽本身為禮，阿迦特卻拒絕了她，說這弓是為戰士而設，非為女神所攜。她大怒，將他從風之翼上拋下，他便化作雲的一塊；天空之鷹將此事帶給哀傷的君王，他的妹妹普加特遂扮作男子，要在兇手們的宴席上復仇。

title.en: The Storm-God and the Serpent Illuyanka
title.zh: 風雨神與蛇魔伊盧揚卡

region.en: Hattusa, Hittite kingdom (Anatolia)
region.zh: 安納托利亞西臺王國哈圖沙

period: Hittite tablet narratives (c. 14th-13th c. BCE), New Year ritual texts

source.work: A. E. Cowley, The Hittites (Schweich Lectures, 1920) - on Hittite religion and ritual texts

summary.en: At the festival of the new year the Hittites recited how the serpent Illuyanka defeated the storm-god Tarhunna; the goddess Inara built a feast-house, lured the serpent and his children out with wine, and the storm-god — or, in the older telling, the son of the god and a mortal girl — slew the serpent while it was drunk.
summary.zh: 歲首祭典中，西臺人誦此神話：蛇魔伊盧揚卡擊敗風雨神塔爾渾那；女神伊娜拉築宴屋，以酒誘蛇及其子而出；風雨神——或古本中神與凡女所生之子——乘其醉而誅之。

sensitivity.note: Hittite mythic tablets; NO public-domain English translation exists, so passages are clearly-labeled condensed paraphrases of the tablet narrative (referenced to modern scholarly translations). [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] The serpent Illuyanka contended with the storm-god Tarhunna and overcame him; the god's heart and eyes the serpent took away. The goddess Inara built a house of feast on the sea-shore, filled it with wine, and called the serpent and his brood to eat and drink.
passages.zh: [精簡意譯] 巨蛇伊盧揚卡與風暴之神塔爾洪納相爭，並勝過了他；蛇奪去了神的心與眼。女神伊娜拉在海濱建了一座宴會之屋，注滿酒，召蛇及其子嗣前來吃喝。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] They drank till their bellies were swollen and the pit was shut against them; then the storm-god — or, in the second telling, the son the god had by a mortal woman — came and killed the serpent while it was drunk. The festival of the purulli recited this victory each year, that the order of the land might be renewed with the spring.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 他們喝到肚腹脹大，坑洞在他們面前闔上；於是風暴之神——或在第二種說法中，是神與凡間女子所生的兒子——前來，趁巨蛇醉倒時將牠殺死。普魯利節每年都重述這場勝利，好讓大地的秩序隨春天一同更新。

title.en: Kumarbi and the Gods of the Stone
title.zh: 庫馬爾比與石中之神

region.en: Hattusa, Hittite kingdom (Anatolia)
region.zh: 安納托利亞西臺王國哈圖沙

period: Hittite tablet narratives (Song of Kumarbi, c. 14th c. BCE)

source.work: A. E. Cowley, The Hittites (Schweich Lectures, 1920) - on Hittite religion and texts

summary.en: The Hittite succession song: Alalu ruled, then Anu, whose feet Kumarbi bit off and swallowed as he pulled him from the sky — but the seed in his belly became the storm-god, and the stone Teshub was born of the mountain's side; the gods of the first ages fight their sons in a cycle older than the Greek story of Cronus.
summary.zh: 西臺王權交替之歌：阿拉魯在位，繼以阿努；庫馬爾比咬斷其足而吞之——腹中之種遂成風雨神，圖什普塔自山岩而生；太古諸神與其子相爭，此環早於希臘克洛諾斯之事。

sensitivity.note: Hittite mythic tablets; NO public-domain English translation exists, so passages are clearly-labeled condensed paraphrases of the tablet narrative (referenced to modern scholarly translations). [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] In former times Alalu was king in heaven; Anu his cupbearer overcame him and reigned. But Anu in turn was fought by Kumarbi, who pulled the king of heaven down from the sky and bit off his genitals and swallowed them — and rejoiced, till he was told what he had swallowed.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 古時阿拉盧在天上為王；他的斟酒者阿努擊敗了他，取而代之。但阿努接著又遭庫馬爾比對抗，庫馬爾比把這位天上之王從天空拉下，咬下他的生殖器並吞了下去——他為此歡欣，直到有人告訴他究竟吞下了什麼。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] The seed of Anu grew in Kumarbi's belly and could not be brought forth; he spat out what became the stone of the mountain, and the storm-god Teshub was born, to fight Kumarbi for the kingship of heaven — a war of the old gods and the young that the Hittite singers put at the beginning of the world.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 阿努的種子在庫馬爾比的腹中成長，卻無法生出；他吐出那物，那物化為山中之石，而風暴之神特舒布於焉誕生，為爭奪天上的王權而與庫馬爾比交戰——這是一場舊神與新神之戰，赫梯的歌者將它置於世界之初。

title.en: The Vanishing of Telipinu and the World's Withering
title.zh: 泰利皮努失蹤與世界枯槁

region.en: Hattusa, Hittite kingdom (Anatolia)
region.zh: 安納托利亞西臺王國哈圖沙

period: Hittite tablet narrative (Vanishing Deity myth, c. 14th-13th c. BCE)

source.work: A. E. Cowley, The Hittites (Schweich Lectures, 1920) - on Hittite cult and ritual

summary.en: Telipinu the god of the fields walked away in anger, put on his black leather boots, and vanished — and at once the fog filled the windows, the hearths went out, sheep and cattle neglected their young, and the land lay barren; the god was called back with honey and oil and a great eagle, and in his return the fields and the hearths were filled again.
summary.zh: 田疇之神泰利皮努怒而去，足登黑皮靴，隱形不見——霧塞窗牖，爐火俱熄，羊牛棄其子，大地荒蕪。眾神以蜂蜜、膏油與巨鷹召之；神歸則田疇復茂，爐火復燃。

sensitivity.note: Hittite mythic tablets; NO public-domain English translation exists, so passages are clearly-labeled condensed paraphrases of the tablet narrative (referenced to modern scholarly translations). [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Telipinu the god of agriculture went away in anger; he put his right shoe on his left foot and his left on his right, and disappeared. Fog filled the windows of the houses, the fires went out in the hearths, the sheep and the cattle would not suckle their young, and in the land neither man nor god knew plenty.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 農耕之神特利皮努忿怒離去；他把右鞋穿在左腳上，把左鞋穿在右腳上，就此消失。霧氣充滿了屋舍的窗戶，爐中的火熄滅了，羊與牛不肯哺育幼崽，在這片土地上，無論人或神都不知豐足為何物。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] The sun-god sent the eagle to search the high mountains, and Kamrusepa the goddess of magic lulled the angry god with honey and oil and soft things; when Telipinu returned, the fires were relit, the flocks took their young, and the land was filled again — the ritual of return was acted out at Hattusa whenever the earth stood barren.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 太陽神派遣鷹去搜尋高山，魔法女神卡姆魯塞帕則以蜂蜜、油與柔軟之物安撫這位忿怒的神；當特利皮努歸來，火重新燃起，畜群哺育幼崽，大地再度充盈——每當土地荒蕪不毛，哈圖沙便搬演這歸返的儀式。

title.en: Lac Long Quan and Au Co: Dragon and Fairy
title.zh: 貉龍君與嫗姬：龍仙之種

region.en: Phu Tho / Red River delta, Vietnam
region.zh: 越南富壽／紅河三角洲

period: Linh Nam chich quai, 14th-15th c. compilation of older legends

source.work: Cl. Chivas-Baron, Stories and Legends of Annam, trans. E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), 'Hong-Lo the Giant'

summary.en: Lac Long Quan, the dragon-lord of the water country, slew the nine-tailed fox, the sea monster, and the wood demon of the northern borders; Au Co the mountain fairy came to him, and she laid a pouch of a hundred eggs — from which sprang a hundred sons, the ancestors of the hundred Viet clans; the dragon went back to the water, the fairy to the mountain, and the eldest ruled the Red River land as Hung Vuong.
summary.zh: 水國龍君貉龍誅九尾狐、海怪與北疆樹妖；山仙嫗姬來歸，產百卵之囊——化為百子，是為百越之祖。龍歸於水，仙歸於山，長子治紅河之地，是為涇陽王之後雄王。

sensitivity.note: Vietnamese foundational legend from the Linh Nam chich quai; passages are condensed paraphrases. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Lac Long Quan, the son of the water country, went about the lands killing the monsters of the early world: the nine-tailed fox of the western mountains, the sea-devil of the south, and the wood spirit that plagued the north; wherever he passed the people could live in peace, for he taught them to plant rice and to wear clothes.
passages.zh: [精簡改寫] 水國之子雒龍君走遍各地，誅除初民世界的妖物：西山之九尾狐、南方之海怪，以及為害北方的木精；凡他所到之處，百姓皆得安居，因為他教他們種稻、穿衣。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Au Co the fairy of the mountains came to dwell with him, and she bore a pouch of a hundred eggs, from which a hundred children hatched. Because a dragon must live in the water and a fairy on the mountain, they divided the children: fifty went with their mother to the hills, fifty with their father to the sea-lands, and the eldest was made the first Hung king of the Red River country.
passages.zh: [精簡改述] 山中的仙女嫗姬前來與他同住，她產下一囊百卵，百卵孵化出百名孩童。因為龍必須居於水中、仙女必須居於山上，他們便將孩子分開：五十人隨母親前往山丘，五十人隨父親前往濱海之地，而長子則被立為紅河之地的第一位雄王。

title.en: Son Tinh and Thuy Tinh: The Mountain and the Water
title.zh: 山精與水精：山與水之爭

region.en: Ba Vi mountains, Red River, Vietnam
region.zh: 越南巴維山與紅河

period: Vietnamese folk legend (Linh Nam chich quai traditions)

source.work: Cl. Chivas-Baron, Stories and Legends of Annam, trans. E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), 'The Rival Genii'

summary.en: Both the mountain spirit and the water spirit sought the eighteenth daughter of the Hung king; the king set a trial — gifts first brought wins — and Son Tinh, whose presents were there at dawn, won the bride. Thuy Tinh raised the flood with whirlwinds and storms against the mountain, but the mountain rose the higher; each year the waters come and fall again, which men call the monsoon.
summary.zh: 山精與水精同求雄王之十八女；王設試禮——先至者得娶。山精黎明而達，遂成婚。水精怒，興風作浪、引洪灌山，而山愈漲愈高；水年年復來復去——人謂之季風雨季。

sensitivity.note: Vietnamese folk legend of the Hung kings' age; passages are condensed paraphrases. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] When the Hung king sought a husband for My Nuong his eighteenth daughter, two spirits came to woo her in one day: Son Tinh, lord of the mountains, and Thuy Tinh, lord of the waters. The king said the one whose presents came first should have her; at dawn the mountain spirit's gifts of stone and timber were already before the hall, and the marriage was made.
passages.zh: [精簡改述] 雄王為他的第十八個女兒媚娘尋覓夫婿時，兩位神靈在同一天前來求親：山神山精與水神水精。雄王說，誰的聘禮先到，誰便可娶她；黎明時分，山神的石與木之禮已陳於殿前，婚事遂成。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Thuy Tinh returned in fury with the waters: he raised storms and floods against the mountain where the couple dwelt, and the people of the plain suffered year by year; but the mountain lifted itself the higher, and the waters sank each time — the war never ends, and the yearly rise and fall of the water is the struggle still remembered.
passages.zh: [精簡改述] 水精滿懷憤怒，攜水而归：他掀起風暴與洪水，攻擊這對夫妻所居的山，平原上的人民年年受苦；但山每次都升得更高，水便每次退去——這場戰爭從未終結，而每年水位的漲落，正是那場至今仍被銘記的爭鬥。

title.en: Thanh Giong Rides to Phu Dong
title.zh: 扶董天王聖郎

region.en: Phu Dong village, Bac Ninh (Hanoi region), Vietnam
region.zh: 越南北寧扶董村

period: Vietnamese legend (Viet dien u linh tap, 13th-14th c. compilation)

source.work: Gustave Dumoutier, Legendes historiques de l'Annam et du Tonkin (Hanoi: F.-H. Schneider, 1887) - the Phu-Dong legend

summary.en: A boy of Phu Dong village, three years old and mute, sat up at the king's call for warriors and spoke his first words: the horse and the iron rod would fight the invaders; he ate the village's rice and grew instantly a giant, took the iron rod and the iron horse, put the enemy to flight with fire from the horse's mouth, and rode up the mountain alone — the tutelary god of the village to this day.
summary.zh: 扶董村三歲不言童子，聞王募武士而起，忽發初聲：「鐵馬鐵鞭，必退敵！」食一村之飯，頃刻成巨人；執鐵鞭、乘鐵馬，馬口噴火破敵——遂獨上羅浮山而去，鄉人立祠奉為本境城隍。

sensitivity.note: Vietnamese hero myth from the Viet dien u linh tap; passages are condensed paraphrases. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] When the armies of the north invaded the land of the Hung kings, the king sent out the call for warriors; in Phu Dong village a boy of three, who had never spoken, sat up in his mother's arms and answered the call in words, asking that a horse and a rod of iron be sent.
passages.zh: [精簡改述] 當北方軍隊入侵雄王之國時，雄王發出徵召勇士的號令；在扶董村，一名從未開口說話的三歲男孩在母親懷中坐起，以言語回應了號召，請求送來一匹馬與一根鐵棒。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] He ate what the village cooked and grew from child to man in a day; when the enemy came he mounted the iron horse, which breathed fire, and broke them with the iron rod until their armor rang like rain. At the bounds of So'n mountain he rode up alone into the sky, and the king gave him the title Heavenly King of Phu Dong — the village god who is honored still when the spring festival goes round.
passages.zh: [精簡改述] 他吃下村中煮好的飯食，一日之內便從孩童長成成人；敵人來時，他騎上那匹口吐火焰的鐵馬，以鐵棒擊破敵軍，直至他們的鎧甲如雨般鏗鏘作響。在朔山的邊界，他獨自騎馬升天而去，雄王賜予他扶董天王的稱號——至今每逢春季慶典巡行，人們仍敬奉這位村神。

title.en: The Ramakien: Phra Ram and Thotsakan
title.zh: 拉瑪堅：帕拉姆與托薩根

region.en: Ayutthaya / Bangkok, Thailand
region.zh: 泰國大城／曼谷

period: Ramakien, Thai adaptation of the Ramayana; court recensions of the 18th-19th c. from older tradition

source.work: Ramakien (Thai: Ramakien), King Rama I's court recension, Thai original (e.g. Book 2, the war of Maiyarab)

summary.en: Thailand's Ramayana: Phra Ram, exiled with his bride Sida, loses her to Thotsakan the ten-faced giant-king of Longka; the monkey-general Hanuman builds the causeway of stones across the sea, Nonthok the demon's legend is fought, and the war of the city of fire ends with the trial of the faithful wife — the national myth told in murals, dance, and puppet theatre.
summary.zh: 泰國羅摩衍那：帕拉姆攜妻西達出亡，西達為龍卡國十面巨靈王托薩根所擄；神猴哈奴曼築石堤跨海，大戰焚城，終以貞后之火試為結——壁畫、舞劇與皮影相傳之國家神話。

sensitivity.note: Thai adaptation of the Ramayana; passages are condensed paraphrases of the court Ramakien recensions. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Phra Ram, heir of Ayutthaya, went into the forest at his father's word with his brother Phra Lak and his bride Sida; the giant-king Thotsakan of Longka, ten faces and twenty arms, carried Sida across the sea, and the war of the Ramakien began.
passages.zh: [精簡改述] 阿瑜陀耶的繼承人帕藍，奉父命與弟弟帕拉克及新娘悉達一同進入森林；楞伽的巨人之王托薩甘，有十張臉、二十條手臂，將悉達渡海擄走，《拉瑪堅》之戰於是展開。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Hanuman the son of the wind, white monkey of a thousand wiles, gathered the armies of the monkeys, carried the mountain of healing herbs, and built the causeway of stones to the island of Longka; Phra Ram slew Thotsakan at last with the arrows of the gods — and the murals of Wat Phra Kaew and the khon dance tell the war still as the royal myth of Thailand.
passages.zh: [節錄改寫] 風神之子哈努曼，是隻千變萬化的白猴，他召集了猴群大軍，馱起療傷的藥草山，又築起石堤通往楞伽島；帕拉姆最終以眾神之箭誅殺了托薩甘——而玉佛寺的壁畫與孔劇舞蹈，至今仍將這場戰爭傳述為泰國的皇家神話。

title.en: Khun Borom and the Origin of the Tai Princes
title.zh: 坤博隆與泰人諸王之始

region.en: Muang Theng (Plain of Jars region), Laos/Thailand tradition
region.zh: 猛騰（川壙高原一帶，寮泰傳統）

period: Tai/Lao origin myth; recorded in the 15th-19th c. chronicles (Urangadom, Nan chronicle)

source.work: G. E. Gerini, Researches on Ptolemy's Geography of Eastern Asia (Royal Asiatic Society/RGS, 1909), on Muang Then

summary.en: In the Tai origin cycle the sky-lord Khun Borom, seeing the earth waste and comfortless, sends down his seven sons from the heavenly city with buffalo, rice-seed, and teachers of the arts; the youngest, Khun Lo, takes the plain of the middle lands, and from the seven sons the princes of the Tai and Lao states trace their royal blood.
summary.zh: 泰人創世傳說：天君坤博隆見大地荒蕪，遣七子自天城而下，攜水牛、稻種與百工之師；幼子坤羅居中原之野——泰、寮諸國王族皆自七子溯其王統。

sensitivity.note: Tai/Lao foundational myth from the court chronicles; passages are condensed paraphrases. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Khun Borom the lord of the sky looked down on the world of men, which lay without order and without comfort; he sent down his seven sons, each with the gear of rule: buffaloes, seeds of rice, smiths and teachers, that the wild lands might be peopled and tilled.
passages.zh: [節錄改寫] 天空之主坤波隆俯視人間，見人間既無秩序，亦無安樂；於是遣下他的七個兒子，各賜以治國之具：水牛、稻種、鐵匠與教師，好讓荒野之地得以有人居住、得以耕墾。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] The sons built cities and ruled the countries of the Tai; Khun Lo the youngest took Muang Sua on the middle river, and his line the Lao kings traced. When the work was done the princes returned to the sky-city to report, and went down again with the mandate of Khun Borom to rule — the pattern of every Tai royal chronicle.
passages.zh: [節錄改寫] 諸子築城立邑，分治泰人之地；幼子坤洛取得中游之地的孟蘇瓦，寮國諸王皆溯其世系。功成之後，諸王子返回天城覆命，再奉坤波隆之命下凡治世——此即每一部泰人王室編年史所載的典範。

title.en: The Naga of the Mekong and the Fire-Balls of the River
title.zh: 湄公河龍王與河上火箭

region.en: Mekong river, Nong Khai / Vientiane
region.zh: 湄公河（泰國廊開／永珍）

period: Isan/Lao river legend of the Mekong naga

source.work: J. Ph. Vogel, Indian Serpent-Lore: The Nagas in Hindu Legend and Art (1926), on naga beliefs in the river-lands of Siam

summary.en: The great serpent Phaya Nak rules the deeps of the Mekong; in the river legend the naga's bride came from the water-country to the human world, and the serpent-king's tears and fire-balls rise from the river at the year's turning — the naga whose coils guard the Buddhist river-lands of the Lao and the Isan.
summary.zh: 巨蛇帕雅納克統湄公之深淵；河上傳說云蛇王之婦自水國適人間，歲末蛇王噴淚與火球自河面騰起——其身守護寮人與伊善地區之佛土江河。

sensitivity.note: Isan-Lao river legend; passages are condensed paraphrases. Living cultural heritage of the Mekong region. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Phaya Nak, the great naga, ruled the deep channel of the Mekong from his city under the water; in the Isan legend his son loved a maiden of the human world and was given leave to serve the Buddha, guarding the river-lands with his coils.
passages.zh: [節錄改寫] 大那伽帕亞納克自其水底之城，統轄湄公河的深水河道；在依善的傳說中，他的兒子愛上了人間的一名少女，獲准侍奉佛陀，以盤曲之身守護河川之地。

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] At the full moon of the eleventh month the naga is said to celebrate the end of the rains: columns of light and fire-balls rise from the river at Bang Fai, which the fishermen call the breath of the naga; the serpent-king remains the lord of the water-road of the Lao and Thai river country.
passages.zh: [節錄改寫] 據說在第十一月的滿月之夜，那伽會慶祝雨季的結束：光柱與火球自邦費的河面升起，漁民稱之為那伽的氣息；這蛇王至今仍是寮國與泰國河川之地水路的霸主。

title.en: The Fall of the Watchers (1 Enoch)
title.zh: 守望者之墮落（以諾一書）

region.en: Mount Hermon (Armon), Anti-Lebanon
region.zh: 黑門山（阿爾孟，安黎巴嫩山）

period: 1 Enoch (Book of the Watchers), c. 3rd c. BCE; trans. Laurence, 1883

source.work: The Book of Enoch the Prophet, trans. Richard Laurence, chs. 7-10

summary.en: The most influential of the pseudepigrapha, quoted in the Epistle of Jude and treasured in the Ethiopian canon: two hundred Watchers, led by Samyaza, swear an oath on Mount Hermon, take the daughters of men, and teach forbidden crafts; their giant offspring fill the earth with blood until the archangels plead for judgment.
summary.zh: 偽經中最具影響力之作，為猶大書所引、埃提阿伯正典所藏：二百守望者由薩麥拉率領，於黑門山立誓，娶人間女子，傳授禁術；其巨人後裔使大地遍染血污，直至天使長呼求審判。

sensitivity.note: Jewish pseudepigraphon preserved in Ge'ez; scriptural for the Ethiopian Orthodox canon, quoted in the New Testament. Presented as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: It happened after the sons of men had multiplied in those days, that daughters were born to them, elegant and beautiful. And when the angels, the sons of heaven, beheld them, they became enamoured of them, saying to each other, Come, let us select for ourselves wives from the progeny of men, and let us beget children. [...] Then they swore all together, and all bound themselves by mutual execrations. Their whole number was two hundred, who descended upon Ardis, which is the top of mount Armon. [...] Then they took wives, each choosing for himself; whom they began to approach, and with whom they cohabited; teaching them sorcery, incantations, and the dividing of roots and trees. And the women conceiving brought forth giants, Whose stature was each three hundred cubits.
passages.zh: 那些日子裡，人的子孫增多之後，就生了女兒，個個秀麗俊美。天使們，即天之眾子，見了她們，便愛慕不已，彼此說道：來吧，讓我們從人的後裔中為自己挑選妻子，並生兒育女。[……] 於是他們一同起誓，彼此立下咒詛以為約束。他們全數共兩百名，降臨於阿爾迪斯，即亞們山的山頂。[……] 隨後他們各為自己挑選，娶了妻子；開始親近她們，與她們同房；又教她們巫術、咒語，以及分辨草根與樹木之法。婦人懷孕，生下了巨人，每個巨人身高三百肘。

passages.text: Moreover Azazyel taught men to make swords, knives, shields, breastplates, the fabrication of mirrors, and the workmanship of bracelets and ornaments, the use of paint, the beautifying of the eyebrows, the use of stones of every valuable and select kind, and of all sorts of dyes, so that the world became altered. Impiety increased; fornication multiplied; and they transgressed and corrupted all their ways. [...] And men, being destroyed, cried out; and their voice reached to heaven.
passages.zh: 此外，阿撒瀉勒教人製造刀劍、匕首、盾牌、胸甲，製作鏡子，以及製作手鐲與飾物之工藝，使用顏料，修飾眉毛，使用各種貴重精選的寶石，以及各樣的染料，以致世界為之改變。不虔之事增多；淫亂繁衍；他們犯罪，敗壞了自己一切的行徑。〔……〕世人既被毀滅，便呼喊；他們的聲音達於上天。

passages.text: Then Michael and Gabriel, Raphael, Suryal, and Uriel, looked down from heaven, and saw the quantity of blood which was shed on earth, and all the iniquity which was done upon it, and said one to another, It is the voice of their cries; The earth deprived of her children has cried even to the gate of heaven. [...] The women likewise have brought forth giants. Thus has the whole earth been filled with blood and with iniquity. And now behold the souls of those who are dead, cry out. And complain even to the gate of heaven.
passages.zh: 於是米迦勒、加百列、拉斐爾、蘇列爾和烏列爾從天上俯視，看見地上所流的血何其多，以及地上所行的一切罪孽，就彼此說：這是他們呼喊的聲音；大地失去她的兒女，已呼喊直到天門。〔……〕婦女們也同樣生下了巨人。這樣，全地都充滿了血和罪孽。如今且看，那些死者的靈魂正在呼喊，甚至向天門訴冤。

title.en: Enoch's Vision of the Son of Man
title.zh: 以諾見人子之異象

region.en: Parables of Enoch (vision setting, symbolic)
region.zh: 以諾比喻篇（異象之境，象徵位置）

period: 1 Enoch (Parables), c. 1st c. BCE; trans. Laurence, 1883

source.work: The Book of Enoch the Prophet, trans. Richard Laurence, ch. 46

summary.en: In the Parables of Enoch the seer beholds the Ancient of days, whose head is like white wool, and with him the Son of man to whom righteousness belongs, chosen by the Lord of spirits to reveal the hidden treasures and to raise up kings from their couches — the messianic vision that shaped Second Temple expectation and New Testament language.
summary.zh: 以諾比喻篇中，先知見「日子古老者」髮如白羊毛，其旁有人子——義所歸焉、為萬靈之主所揀選者，將啟示隱藏之寶藏，並使君王自榻興起——此彌賽亞異象塑造了第二聖殿時代的盼望與新約語言。

sensitivity.note: Jewish pseudepigraphon; the Parables' messianic vision influenced apocalyptic belief across Judaism and Christianity. Presented as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: There I beheld the Ancient of days, whose head was like white wool, and with him another, whose countenance resembled that of man. His countenance was full of grace, like that of one of the holy angels. Then I inquired of one of the angels, who went with me, and who showed me every secret thing, concerning this Son of man; who he was; whence he was; and why he accompanied the Ancient of days. He answered and said to me, This is the Son of man, to whom righteousness belongs; with whom righteousness has dwelt; and who will reveal all the treasures of that which is concealed: for the Lord of spirits has chosen him; and his portion has surpassed all before the Lord of spirits in everlasting uprightness. This Son of man, whom thou beholdest, shall raise up kings and the mighty from their couches, and the powerful from their thrones; shall loosen the bridles of the powerful, and break in pieces the teeth of sinners.
passages.zh: 我在那裡看見那亙古常在者，他的頭如潔白的羊毛，又有另一位與他同在，其容貌像人的容貌。他的面容滿有恩典，如同一位聖天使的面容。於是我向與我同行、將一切隱祕之事指示我的一位天使詢問，關於這人子的事：他是誰；他從何而來；他為何與亙古常在者同行。他回答我說：這就是人子，公義歸於他；公義曾與他同住；他將顯明那隱藏之事的一切寶藏：因為萬靈之主揀選了他；他的分在萬靈之主面前，以永遠的正直超越了先前的一切。你所看見的這人子，必使君王和權貴從他們的榻上興起，使有權勢的從他們的寶座上興起；必鬆開有權勢者的轡頭，打碎罪人的牙齒。

title.en: Tobit and the Fish of Healing
title.zh: 多比傳與醫病之魚

region.en: Nineveh to Ecbatane (Assyria to Media)
region.zh: 尼尼微至厄克巴坦（亞述至瑪代）

period: Book of Tobit, c. 2nd c. BCE (deuterocanonical); KJV Apocrypha, 1611

source.work: Bible (King James Version), Apocrypha: Tobit, chs. 6-12
