summary.en: Blinded for burying the dead, Tobit sends his son to Media with the angel Raphael in disguise; a fish of the Tigris, caught at the angel's word, supplies the heart and liver whose smoke binds the demon Asmodeus and the gall that heals Tobit's eyes — the deuterocanonical book beloved for its angelology and its teaching on almsgiving.
summary.zh: 多比因埋葬死者而目盲，遣子多比亞往瑪代；拉斐爾天使假伴同行，於底格里斯河捕魚——魚心肝之煙驅逐惡魔阿斯摩太，魚膽醫愈多比之目。此次經典以天使論與施捨教訓聞名。

sensitivity.note: Deuterocanonical/Apocryphal book — canonical for Catholic and Orthodox traditions, apocryphal in Protestantism. Presented as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: And when the young man went down to wash himself, a fish leaped out of the river, and would have devoured him. Then the angel said unto him, Take the fish. And the young man laid hold of the fish, and drew it to land. [...] And he said unto him, Touching the heart and the liver, if a devil or an evil spirit trouble any, we must make a smoke thereof before the man or the woman, and the party shall be no more vexed. As for the gall, it is good to anoint a man that hath whiteness in his eyes, and he shall be healed.
passages.zh: 當那少年下去洗身的時候，有一條魚從河裡跳出來，想要吞吃他。於是天使對他說：抓住那條魚。那少年便抓住那魚，把它拉到岸上。〔……〕他又對他說：至於心與肝，若有魔鬼或惡靈困擾任何人，我們就必須在人面前把這些燒出煙來，那人便不再受困擾。至於膽，則宜於塗抹眼中有白翳的人，他就必得醫治。

passages.text: And when they had supped, they brought Tobias in unto her. And as he went, he remembered the words of Raphael, and took the ashes of the perfumes, and put the heart and the liver of the fish thereupon, and made a smoke therewith. The which smell when the evil spirit had smelled, he fled into the utmost parts of Egypt, and the angel bound him.
passages.zh: 他們用過晚餐之後，就把多比雅帶到她那裡。他進去的時候，想起了拉斐爾的話，就取來香料的灰，把魚的心和肝放在其上，燒出煙來。那惡靈聞到這氣味，就逃往埃及極遠之地，天使便把他捆綁了。

passages.text: I am Raphael, one of the seven holy angels, which present the prayers of the saints, and which go in and out before the glory of the Holy One. [...] For not of any favour of mine, but by the will of our God I came; wherefore praise him for ever.
passages.zh: 我是拉斐爾，是那七位聖天使之一，他們呈獻聖徒的祈禱，並在聖者的榮耀前出入。〔……〕因為我來，不是出於我任何的情面，乃是因我們神的旨意；所以你們要永遠讚美他。

title.en: Mattathias and the Rededication of the Altar
title.zh: 瑪他提亞與祭壇之重新奉獻

region.en: Modin and Jerusalem, Judea
region.zh: 猶太地摩丁與耶路撒冷

period: 1 Maccabees, c. 2nd-1st c. BCE (deuterocanonical); KJV Apocrypha, 1611

source.work: Bible (King James Version), Apocrypha: 1 Maccabees, chs. 2-4

summary.en: The book that records the Maccabean revolt: Antiochus Epiphanes profanes the temple, Mattathias refuses the king's commandment — 'We will not hearken to the king's words, to go from our religion' — and after Judas Maccabeus overthrows the king's host, the sanctuary is cleansed and the altar dedicated anew for eight days, the origin of the feast of Hanukkah.
summary.zh: 記載瑪加伯起義之經卷：安提阿古·伊皮法尼褻瀆聖殿；瑪他提亞拒王命——「不聽王言，不棄祖教」；猶大·瑪加伯破敵之後，潔淨聖所，重新奉獻祭壇八日——修殿節（光明節）之緣起。

sensitivity.note: Deuterocanonical/Apocryphal book — canonical for Catholic and Orthodox traditions, historically foundational for the Jewish feast of Hanukkah. Presented as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Then Mattathias answered and spake with a loud voice, Though all the nations that are under the king's dominion obey him, and fall away every one from the religion of their fathers, and give consent to his commandments: Yet will I and my sons and my brethren walk in the covenant of our fathers. God forbid that we should forsake the law and the ordinances. We will not hearken to the king's words, to go from our religion, either on the right hand, or the left.
passages.zh: 於是瑪他提亞回答，高聲說：縱然所有在國王統治下的列國都聽從他，各人都背離自己祖先的宗教，同意他的命令；然而我和我的兒子並我的弟兄，仍要遵行我們祖先的約。我們絕不可離棄律法和典章。我們不聽國王的話，無論偏右或偏左，都不離開我們的宗教。

passages.text: Then said Judas to the men that were with him, Fear ye not their multitude, neither be ye afraid of their assault. Remember how our fathers were delivered in the Red sea, when Pharaoh pursued them with an army. [...] For the victory of battle standeth not in the multitude of an host; but strength cometh from heaven.
passages.zh: 於是猶大對跟隨他的人說：不要懼怕他們人多，也不要怕他們的攻擊。要記念我們的祖先在紅海怎樣蒙拯救，那時法老率軍追趕他們。〔……〕因為戰爭的勝利不在乎軍隊的眾多，力量乃是從天上來的。

passages.text: Now on the five and twentieth day of the ninth month, which is called the month Casleu, in the hundred forty and eighth year, they rose up betimes in the morning, And offered sacrifice according to the law upon the new altar of burnt offerings, which they had made. Look, at what time and what day the heathen had profaned it, even in that was it dedicated with songs, and citherns, and harps, and cymbals. [...] And so they kept the dedication of the altar eight days, and offered burnt offerings with gladness, and sacrificed the sacrifice of deliverance and praise.
passages.zh: 如今在第九月，就是稱為基斯流月的二十五日，即一百四十八年，他們清早起來，照律法在他們所造的新燔祭壇上獻祭。看哪，外邦人在何時何日褻瀆了這壇，就在那時那日，這壇以詩歌、琴、瑟和鈸奉獻了。〔……〕於是他們守獻壇之禮八日，歡歡喜喜地獻上燔祭，又獻上得救與讚美的祭。

title.en: Dante's Inferno: The Gate and the Lovers
title.zh: 但丁《神曲·地獄篇》：冥門與情人

region.en: Florence / a dark wood (vision-setting), Italy
region.zh: 義大利佛羅倫斯／幽暗森林（異象之境）

period: Divine Comedy, c. 1308-1320; trans. Henry Francis Cary, 1805-14

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Hell (Inferno), Cantos 1, 3, 5

summary.en: Dante's pilgrimage through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise — the poem that shaped the Western imagination of the afterlife: lost in a dark wood at mid-life, he passes the gate whose doomful lines end 'All hope abandon ye who enter here,' and hears the lovers Francesca and Paolo tell how the book of Lancelot betrayed them to their love.
summary.zh: 但丁遊歷地獄、煉獄與天堂——塑造西方死後想像之詩：半生迷途於幽暗森林，過地獄之門（門上銘文云：「入此門者，當捨棄一切希望」），聞弗蘭切斯卡與保羅情人敘述蘭斯洛特之書如何使其墮入情網。

sensitivity.note: Influential Christian literary-religious imagination (not scripture); presented as a comparative text alongside underworld-journey narratives — a scholarly framing.

passages.text: In the midway of this our mortal life, I found me in a gloomy wood, astray Gone from the path direct: and e'en to tell It were no easy task, how savage wild That forest, how robust and rough its growth, Which to remember only, my dismay Renews, in bitterness not far from death.
passages.zh: 在我們這凡塵生命的半途中，我發現自己置身於一片幽暗的森林，迷失了正路：而要述說那森林是何等荒蠻，其林木何等茁壯粗野，也絕非易事；單是回想，我的驚惶便重新湧起，那苦澀與死亡相去不遠。

passages.text: "Through me you pass into the city of woe: Through me you pass into eternal pain: Through me among the people lost for aye. Justice the founder of my fabric mov'd: To rear me was the task of power divine, Supremest wisdom, and primeval love. Before me things create were none, save things Eternal, and eternal I endure. "All hope abandon ye who enter here."
passages.zh: 「經由我，你們進入苦難之城：經由我，你們進入永恆的痛苦：經由我，你們進入永遠沉淪的眾生之中。公義推動了我的建造者：建立我乃是神聖權能、至高智慧與太初之愛的任務。在我之前，除了永恆之物，別無受造之物，而我也永恆長存。「凡進入此處者，當捨棄一切希望。」

passages.text: "Love, that in gentle heart is quickly learnt, Entangled him by that fair form, from me Ta'en in such cruel sort, as grieves me still: Love, that denial takes from none belov'd, Caught me with pleasing him so passing well, That, as thou see'st, he yet deserts me not. Love brought us to one death: Caina waits The soul, who spilt our life." [...] "No greater grief than to remember days Of joy, when mis'ry is at hand! [...] The book and writer both Were love's purveyors. In its leaves that day We read no more."
passages.zh: 「愛，在溫柔的心中很快就被領會，因那美麗的形體而使他纏綿，那形體從我這裡被奪去，方式如此殘酷，至今仍令我悲傷：愛，從不寬恕被愛者，因我如此極度地取悅於他而將我捕獲，以致如你所見，他至今仍不離棄我。愛使我們同赴一死：該隱環等待著那奪去我們生命者的靈魂。」〔……〕「沒有比在苦難臨近之時，回想歡樂的日子更大的悲傷了！〔……〕那書與寫書的人都是愛的媒介。那一天，我們在書頁中不再讀下去了。」

title.en: Milton's Paradise Lost: The Fall of the Rebel Angels
title.zh: 彌爾頓《失樂園》：叛天使之墮落

region.en: Heaven / Pandemonium (vision-setting)
region.zh: 天堂／萬魔殿（異象之境）

period: Paradise Lost, 1667

source.work: Paradise Lost, John Milton, Book I

summary.en: Milton's epic of the fall — 'to justify the ways of God to men' — opens with Satan and his legions hurled from heaven through nine days' space into a dungeon of darkness visible; waking on the burning lake, the Arch-fiend rallies his fallen host and builds Pandemonium, resolving on 'war, then, war, open or understood.'
summary.zh: 彌爾頓之史詩——「辯明上帝待人之道」——敘撒旦與其黨羽九日九夜自天墮落，墜入「可見之黑暗」深淵；於火湖醒來，召集墮落天使，建萬魔殿，立誓「戰爭——明戰或暗戰，勢不可免」。

sensitivity.note: Influential Christian literary-religious imagination (not scripture); the epic paraphrases the apocryphal angelologies of Enoch and shaped Protestant imagination. Presented as a comparative text.

passages.text: Of Man's first disobedience, and the fruit Of that forbidden tree whose mortal taste Brought death into the World, and all our woe, With loss of Eden, till one greater Man Restore us, and regain the blissful seat, Sing, Heavenly Muse [...] That, to the height of this great argument, I may assert Eternal Providence, And justify the ways of God to men.
passages.zh: 論及人類最初的違命，以及那禁樹的果實——其致命的滋味將死亡帶入世界，並帶來我們一切的苦難，使我們失去伊甸園，直到一位更偉大的人類使我們復原，並重獲那蒙福的居所。歌唱吧，天上的繆思……使我得以達到這偉大論題的高度，宣揚永恆的天意，並向世人證明上帝之道的正當。

passages.text: Th' infernal Serpent; he it was whose guile, Stirred up with envy and revenge, deceived The mother of mankind [...] Him the Almighty Power Hurled headlong flaming from th' ethereal sky, With hideous ruin and combustion, down To bottomless perdition, there to dwell In adamantine chains and penal fire, Who durst defy th' Omnipotent to arms.
passages.zh: 那地獄的蛇；正是他，以嫉妒與復仇所激起的詭詐，欺騙了人類的母親……全能的力量將他從以太的天空中烈焰般地猛然擲下，伴隨著可怕的毀滅與焚燒，墜入無底的滅亡，在那裡以金剛石般的鎖鏈與懲罰之火居住——他竟敢以武力挑戰全能者。

passages.text: A dungeon horrible, on all sides round, As one great furnace flamed; yet from those flames No light; but rather darkness visible Served only to discover sights of woe [...] Here at least We shall be free; th' Almighty hath not built Here for his envy, will not drive us hence: Here we may reign secure; and, in my choice, To reign is worth ambition, though in Hell: Better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven.
passages.zh: 一座可怕的地牢，四周環繞，如同一座巨大的熔爐燃燒著；然而從那些火焰中並無光亮；反倒是可見的黑暗，僅足以顯露苦難的景象……至少在此處我們將得自由；全能者並非為他的嫉妒而建造此地，不會將我們驅逐出去：在此我們可以安然稱王；而依我之選擇，稱王值得雄心，即便在地獄之中：在地獄稱王勝於在天堂為僕。

title.en: The Song of the Reed (Masnavi of Rumi)
title.zh: 蘆笛之歌（魯米《瑪斯納維》）

region.en: Konya, Anatolia (Rumi's whirling home)
region.zh: 安納托利亞科尼亞（魯米旋轉祈禱之家）

period: Masnavi, Book 1, c. 1258-1273; trans. E. H. Whinfield (abridged), 1887

source.work: Masnavi I Ma'navi, trans. E. H. Whinfield, Book I Prologue

summary.en: The Masnavi — the Sufi 'Qur'an in the Persian tongue,' read for eight centuries across the Muslim world — opens with the reed-flute cut from its osier bed, wailing for its home: the soul torn from the Source, whose fire of love is the physician of pride, the confidant of all unhappy lovers.
summary.zh: 《瑪斯納維》——蘇菲「波斯語之古蘭經」，八百年來穆斯林世界誦讀不絕——以蘆笛自葦床剪斷、哀鳴思鄉為喻：靈魂離其本源，愛之火乃傲慢之醫、苦戀者之知己。

sensitivity.note: Influential Sufi literature of Islam (not scripture); presented as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: HEARKEN to the reed-flute, how it complains, Lamenting its banishment from its home: "Ever since they tore me from my osier bed, My plaintive notes have moved men and women to tears. I burst my breast, striving to give vent to sighs, And to express the pangs of my yearning for my home. He who abides far away from his home Is ever longing for the day he shall return. [...] My secrets are not alien from my plaintive notes, Yet they are not manifest to the sensual eye and ear. Body is not veiled from soul, neither soul from body, Yet no man hath ever seen a soul." This plaint of the flute is fire, not mere air. Let him who lacks this fire be accounted dead! 'Tis the fire of love that inspires the flute, 'Tis the ferment of love that possesses the wine.
passages.zh: 傾聽蘆笛，它如何訴怨，哀嘆自己被逐離故鄉：「自從他們將我從柳叢中扯下，我的哀音便使男男女女落淚。我撕裂胸膛，竭力吐出嘆息，表達我對故鄉的渴慕之痛。凡遠離故鄉而居者，總是渴望著歸返之日。[……]我的秘密並不異於我的哀音，然而它們並不顯露於感官之眼與耳。身體並不對靈魂隱藏，靈魂也不對身體隱藏，然而從沒有人見過靈魂。」這笛的哀訴是火，不只是空氣。讓那缺乏這火的人被算為死人！是愛之火激發了蘆笛，是愛的醞釀佔據了酒。

passages.text: The pitcher of the desire of the covetous never fills, The oyster-shell fills not with pearls till it is content; Only he whose garment is rent by the violence of love Is wholly pure from covetousness and sin. Hail to thee, then, O LOVE, sweet madness! Thou who healest all our infirmities! Who art the physician of our pride and self-conceit! Who art our Plato and our Galen! Love exalts our earthly bodies to heaven, And makes the very hills to dance with joy!
passages.zh: 貪婪者慾望之罐永不滿盈，牡蠣殼直到滿足才裝滿珍珠；唯有那因愛的猛烈而衣裳撕裂之人，才完全純淨，免於貪婪與罪。那麼，向你致敬，噢，愛，甜美的瘋狂！你醫治我們一切軟弱！你是我們驕傲與自負的醫師！你是我們的柏拉圖與我們的蓋倫！愛將我們塵世的身軀提升至天，並使群山也歡欣起舞！

title.en: The Cosmic Egg and the Sleep of Vishnu (Vishnu Purana)
title.zh: 宇宙之卵與毗濕奴之眠（毗濕奴往世書）

region.en: Kurukshetra (narrative frame), India
region.zh: 印度庫魯克謝特拉（敘述之地）

period: Vishnu Purana, c. 1st millennium CE; trans. H. H. Wilson, 1840

source.work: The Vishnu Purana, trans. H. H. Wilson, Book I, chs. 1-2

summary.en: The Purana that Wilson called the most authentic of the eighteen: the world was produced from Vishnu, exists in him, and he is the world; the elements combine to form the vast egg that is the abode of Vishnu in the form of Brahma — and at the close of each kalpa, as Rudra, he swallows up the universe and reposes on the serpent-couch, to create again.
summary.zh: 威爾遜譽為十八往世書中最可信者：世界自毗濕奴而生、存於其中，彼即世界；諸元素結合成大卵，乃毗濕奴現梵天之身而居之——每一劫末，彼現為魯陀羅吞滅宇宙，偃臥巨蛇之榻，而後再造。

sensitivity.note: Influential Puranic cosmology of Hinduism; presented as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The world was produced from Vishnu: it exists in him: he is the cause of its continuance and cessation; he is the world. [...] Who can describe him who is not to be apprehended by the senses: who is the best of all things; the supreme soul, self-existent: who is devoid of all the distinguishing characteristics of complexion, caste, or the like; and is exempt from bulk, vicissitude, death, or decay: who is always, and alone: who exists everywhere, and in whom all things here exist; and who is, thence, named Vasudeva? [...] He is Brahma, Supreme, lord, eternal, unborn, imperishable, undecaying; of one essence; ever pure, as free from defects. He, that Brahma, was all things; comprehending in his own nature the indiscrete and discrete.
passages.zh: 世界由毗濕奴產生：它存在於他之中：他是其延續與終止之因；他就是世界。[……]誰能描述那不可由感官領會者：那為萬物之最善者；那至尊的靈魂，自存者：那遠離膚色、種姓等一切可區別之特徵者；那免於體積、變遷、死亡或衰敗者：那永遠且獨一者：那遍存於一切處，而此間萬物皆存於其中者；並因此名為婆藪天者？[……]他是梵，至尊、主、永恆、未生、不滅、不衰；一體之本质；永遠純淨，毫無瑕疵。那梵，曾是一切事物；於其自身本性中涵攝未分者與已分者。

passages.text: Having combined, therefore, with one another, they assumed, through their mutual association, the character of one mass of entire unity; and, from the direction of spirit, with the acquiescence of the indiscrete Principle, Intellect and the rest, to the gross elements inclusive, formed an egg, which gradually expanded like a bubble of water. This vast egg, O sage, compounded of the elements, and resting on the waters, was the excellent natural abode of Vishnu in the form of Brahma [...] In that egg, O Brahman, were the continents and seas and mountains, the planets and divisions of the universe, the gods, the demons, and mankind.
passages.zh: 因此，它們彼此結合之後，藉由相互的聯屬，便形成了全然一體的一團之性質；並且，從精神的方向，在不分別之原理的默許下，從智性及其餘諸者，一直到粗大的元素為止，形成了一個卵，這卵漸漸地膨脹，如同水中的氣泡一般。這巨大的卵，哦，聖者啊，由諸元素所構成，並安息於水上，乃是毗濕奴以梵天之形所居的絕妙天然住處。[……] 在那卵中，哦，婆羅門啊，有諸大陸、諸海與諸山，有諸行星與宇宙的諸分區，有諸神、諸魔與人類。

passages.text: Vishnu, with the quality of goodness, and of immeasurable power, preserves created things through successive ages, until the close of the period termed a Kalpa; when the same mighty deity, Janardana, invested with the quality of darkness, assumes the awful form of Rudra, and swallows up the universe. Having thus devoured all things, and converted the world into one vast ocean, the Supreme reposes upon his mighty serpent-couch amidst the deep: he awakes after a season, and, again, as Brahma, becomes the author of creation.
passages.zh: 毗濕奴以其善性與無量之力，歷經相繼的諸時代，護持所造之物，直到稱為一劫的時期終結；此時，同一位大能之神賈納爾達那，披覆著暗性，化為樓陀羅的可畏之形，吞噬宇宙。如此吞盡一切，並將世界化為一片浩瀚之海後，至尊者便安息於其大蛇之床上，處於深海之中：過了一段時日，他醒來，又再度作為梵天，成為創造的作者。

title.en: The Vision of Arda Viraf: Bridge, Damsel, and Hell
title.zh: 阿爾達·維拉夫之異象：橋、少女與地獄

region.en: Fars, Sasanian Persia (vision of the spirit realm)
region.zh: 薩珊波斯法爾斯（靈界異象）

period: Arda Viraf Namak, Sasanian-era Pahlavi text; trans. Haug (with West), 1872

source.work: The Book of Arda Viraf, trans. Martin Haug (1872), chs. 4-5, 17-18

summary.en: The Zoroastrian Dante four centuries before Dante: chosen by lot after a council of the priests, Viraf drinks the narcotic of Vishtasp and his soul crosses the Chinwad bridge — where his own religion and deeds meet him 'in the graceful form of a damsel' — beholds the reward of the pious in Garothman and the many torments of hell, and returns to report truly.
summary.zh: 早但丁四百年之祆教《神曲》：祭司議會抽籤選中維拉夫，飲維什塔斯普之迷藥，其靈魂渡欽瓦特橋——其宗教與善行化為「婀娜少女」相迎——得見伽羅斯曼中義人之報與地獄諸刑，歸而如實稟告。

sensitivity.note: Zoroastrian religious vision literature of great influence on Parsi devotion (and famously compared with Dante); presented as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Taking the first footstep with the good thought, and the second footstep with the good word, and the third footstep with the good deed, I came up to the Chinwad bridge, the very wide and strong and created by Ohrmazd. [...] And there stood before him his own religion and his own deeds, in the graceful form of a damsel, as a beautiful appearance [...] And the soul of the pious asked that damsel thus: 'Who art thou? [...] To him replied she who was his own religion and his own deeds, thus: 'I am thy actions, O youth of good thoughts, of good words, of good deeds, of good religion. It is on account of thy will and actions that I am as great and good and sweet-scented and triumphant and undistressed as appears to thee.
passages.zh: 以善念邁出第一步，以善言邁出第二步，以善行邁出第三步，我來到了欽瓦德橋，那橋極為寬闊、堅固，由歐爾馬茲德所造。[……] 而在他面前，站著他自己的宗教與他自己的諸行，以一位少女的優雅形貌，作為美麗的容顏 [……] 而那虔信者的靈魂如此問那少女：『你是誰？[……]』那作為他自身宗教與自身諸行者，如此回答他：『我就是你的諸行，哦，善念、善言、善行、善教的青年啊。正因你的意志與諸行，我才如你所見的這般偉大、良善、芬芳、得勝而無憂。』

passages.text: And afterward, Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, took hold of my hand, so that I went on unhurt. In that manner, I beheld cold and heat, drought and stench, to such a degree as I never saw, nor heard of, in the world. And when I went farther, I also saw the greedy jaws of hell, like the most frightful pit, descending in a very narrow and fearful place; in darkness so gloomy that it is necessary to hold by the hand [...] and when three days and nights have elapsed he says thus: 'The nine thousand years are completed, and they will not release me!'
passages.zh: 此後，虔信的斯羅什與天使阿達爾握住我的手，使我安然前行。就這樣，我見到了寒冷與炎熱、乾旱與惡臭，其程度之甚，是我在世間從未見過、也從未聽聞的。而當我走得更遠，我也見到了地獄貪婪的巨口，如同最可怖的深坑，向下延伸至一處極為狹窄而可怖之地；那裡的黑暗如此陰沉，以至於必須彼此牽手而行 [……] 而當三日三夜過去，他便如此說道：『九千年已滿，他們仍不會釋放我！』

passages.text: And I saw the darkest hell, which is pernicious, dreadful, terrible, very painful, mischievous and foul-smelling. And after further observation, it appeared to me as a pit, to the bottom of which, a thousand cubits would not reach [...] and as many as the hairs on the mane of a horse, so close and many in number, the souls of the wicked stand, but they see not and hear no sound, one from the other; everyone thinks thus: 'I am alone'.
passages.zh: 而我見到了最黑暗的地獄，那地獄有害、可怖、可怕、極其痛苦、惡毒而惡臭。再經進一步觀察，它在我看來如同一口深坑，其底深達千肘亦不能及 [……] 而惡人的靈魂站立著，其數目之稠密眾多，如同馬鬃上的毛髮；但他們彼此看不見，也聽不見對方的聲音；每個人都如此想：『我是孤獨的。』

title.en: Theogony: Creation from Chaos and the Fall of Cronos
title.zh: 神譜：混沌創世與克羅諾斯之傾覆

region.en: Greece (Boeotia)
region.zh: 希臘（維奧蒂亞）

period: c. 700 BCE (Hesiod, trans. Evelyn-White 1914)

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. H. G. Evelyn-White, Loeb Classical Library 57 (1914), lines 116-149

summary.en: Hesiod's Theogony opens the Greek cosmos with Chaos, from which came Gaia, Tartarus, and Eros. Gaia then bears Ouranos (Heaven), and their union produces the Titans, including Cronos, who hates his father.
summary.zh: 赫西俄德《神譜》以混沌開篇，混沌之中先有大地該亞、深淵塔爾塔羅斯與愛神厄洛斯；該亞再生天空烏拉諾斯，二神結合而生克羅諾斯等泰坦諸神。

sensitivity.note: Coordinates placed at Ascra in Boeotia, Hesiod's home village, as a symbolic inland anchor (the cosmogony has no geographic setting). Quoted from a standard public-domain academic translation as comparative mythology scholarship, not as any religious truth claim. [Merged 2026-11-11: the entry 'greek-theogony-succession' (same Evelyn-White Theogony, succession myth and Titanomachy) was folded in as passage 3; its opening passage duplicated passage 1 and was dropped, and the duplicate entry removed. Sacred-kingship and storm-thunder motifs come from the folded material.]

passages.text: Verily at the first Chaos came to be, but next wide-bosomed Earth, the ever-sure foundations of all the deathless ones who hold the peaks of snowy Olympus, and dim Tartarus in the depth of the wide-pathed Earth, and Eros (Love), fairest among the deathless gods, who unnerves the limbs and overcomes the mind and wise counsels of all gods and all men within them. From Chaos came forth Erebus and black Night; but of Night were born Aether and Day, whom she conceived and bare from union in love with Erebus. And Earth first bare starry Heaven, equal to herself, to cover her on every side, and to be an ever-sure abiding-place for the blessed gods.
passages.zh: 誠然，最初出現了混沌，其次則是寬胸的大地，那是一切不死者——那些居於積雪奧林帕斯諸峰者——永遠穩固的根基，以及位於寬闊道路的大地深處的幽暗塔爾塔羅斯，還有厄洛斯（愛），他在不死諸神中最為美麗，他使肢體鬆軟，並在一切神與一切人的胸中征服其心智與明智的謀慮。從混沌生出了厄瑞玻斯與黑色的夜；而從夜生出了埃忒爾與白日，她與厄瑞玻斯在愛中結合而孕育並生下了他們。而大地首先生出了繁星點點的蒼天，與她自己相等，以便從各方覆蓋她，並成為蒙福諸神永遠穩固的居所。

passages.text: But afterwards she lay with Heaven and bare deep-swirling Oceanus, Coeus and Crius and Hyperion and Iapetus, Theia and Rhea, Themis and Mnemosyne and gold-crowned Phoebe and lovely Tethys. After them was born Cronos the wily, youngest and most terrible of her children, and he hated his lusty sire.
passages.zh: 但後來她與天結合，生下了深渦流轉的俄刻阿諾斯、科俄斯與克里俄斯、許佩里翁與伊阿佩托斯、忒亞與瑞亞、忒彌斯與謨涅摩緒涅、戴金冠的福柏與可愛的忒堤斯。在他們之後出生的是狡黠的克洛諾斯，他是她子女中最年幼、最可怖的一個，他憎恨他那情慾旺盛的父親。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Theogony 453-506: Rhea, cheated of each child, hands Kronos a swaddled stone, which he swallows whole; the infant Zeus is smuggled to a Cretan cave, grows to strength, and forces his father to disgorge his swallowed siblings — the stone last of all. Not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《神譜》453-506行節縮改述：瑞亞每生一子便被騙走，於是她把一塊裹著襁褓的石頭交給克洛諾斯，他一口吞了下去；嬰兒宙斯則被偷偷送到克里特的一座洞穴中，長大成人後，迫使父親吐出他所吞下的眾兄弟姐妹——那塊石頭是最後吐出的。非逐字照錄。

title.en: Isis and the Secret Name of Ra
title.zh: 伊希斯與拉的秘名

region.en: Egypt (Heliopolis)
region.zh: 埃及（赫利奧波利斯）

period: c. 1300-1100 BCE (Ramesside Turin Papyrus; Budge, Legends of the Gods, 1912)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg (eBook #9411; Sacred Texts returned HTTP 403)
source.work: Legends of the Gods: The Egyptian Texts, ed. and trans. E. A. Wallis Budge (London, 1912), ch. III, 'The Legend of Ra and the Snake-bite'

summary.en: In this Egyptian legend, Isis seeks Ra's hidden name, in which his very existence and power are bound up. She fashions a venomous serpent to wound the aging sun god, and only by surrendering his secret name can Ra be healed, transferring his power to Isis.
summary.zh: 在這則埃及傳說中，伊西斯謀求太陽神拉的秘名——其生命與神力之所繫。她鑄成毒蛇使年邁的拉受傷，拉為求痊癒只得獻出秘名，權柄遂歸伊西斯所有。

sensitivity.note: The story follows Ra's daily journey through Egypt, so coordinates are placed at Heliopolis (ancient Anu), Ra's chief cult city, as an approximate anchor. Ancient Egyptian religious text quoted for comparative scholarship; Budge's 1912 wording is dated in style but is the cited public-domain source, presented without religious truth claims.

passages.text: she decided that she could only obtain the power she wanted if she possessed the knowledge of the secret name of Ra, in which his very existence was bound up. Ra guarded this name most jealously, for he knew that if he revealed it to any being he would henceforth be at that being's mercy. Isis saw that it was impossible to make Ra declare his name to her by ordinary methods, and she therefore thought out the following plan. It was well known in Egypt and the Sudan at a very early period that if a magician obtained some portion of a person's body, e.g., a hair, a paring of a nail, a fragment of skin, or a portion of some efflux from the body, spells could be used upon them which would have the effect of causing grievous harm to that person.
passages.zh: 她認定，唯有掌握拉之祕名的知識，她才能獲得她想要的力量，因為拉的存在本身即繫於此名。拉對這名字守護得極其嚴密，因為他知道，一旦向任何生靈洩露此名，他從此便將任其擺佈。伊西斯看出，用尋常方法不可能讓拉向她說出自己的名字，於是便想出了以下的計策。早在極古的時代，埃及與蘇丹便已眾所周知：巫師若能取得某人身體的某一部分，例如一根頭髮、一片指甲屑、一小塊皮膚，或該人身體排出的某種分泌物，便可對之施以咒語，而其效力將使該人遭受嚴重傷害。

passages.text: Then Isis said to him with guile, "Divine Father, tell me thy name, for he who uttereth his own name shall live." Thereupon Ra proceeded to enumerate the various things that he had done, and to describe his creative acts, and ended his speech to Isis by saying, that he was Khepera in the morning, Ra at noon, and Temu in the evening. Apparently he thought that the naming of these three great names would satisfy Isis, and that she would immediately pronounce a word of power and stop the pain in his body, which, during his speech, had become more acute. Isis, however, was not deceived, and she knew well that Ra had not declared to her his hidden name; this she told him, and she begged him once again to tell her his name.
passages.zh: 於是伊西斯以詭詐對他說：「神聖的父啊，請告訴我你的名字，因為說出自己名字的人必得存活。」拉於是開始一一列舉他所做過的種種事蹟，描述他的創造之功，並在對伊西斯說話的末尾說道：他早晨是凱佩拉，正午是拉，傍晚是特穆。顯然他以為，說出這三個偉大的名字便足以令伊西斯滿意，以為她會立刻念出一句有法力之言，止住他身上的疼痛——那疼痛在他說話期間已變得更加劇烈。然而伊西斯並未受騙，她很清楚拉並未向她宣告他那隱藏的名字；她把這話告訴了他，並再次懇求他告訴她自己的名字。

title.en: The Weighing of the Heart
title.zh: 稱量心臟（亡靈書）

region.en: Egypt (Thebes)
region.zh: 埃及（底比斯）

period: c. 1550-1292 BCE (New Kingdom funerary spells; Budge, 1920)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg (eBook #7145; Sacred Texts returned HTTP 403)
source.work: The Book of the Dead, ed. E. A. Wallis Budge (1920), ch. CXXV, the Judgment Hall and Negative Confession

summary.en: Chapter 125 of the Book of the Dead places the deceased in the Hall of Maati, where his heart is weighed before Osiris. Addressing the Forty-Two gods, he recites the Negative Confession, declaring innocence of a catalogue of sins before the Great Scales and the Eater of the Dead.
summary.zh: 《亡靈書》第一二五咒將亡者置於瑪阿特之廳，其心臟須在奧西里斯面前受稱量。亡者向四十二神逐條背誦「否定懺悔」，在審判大天秤與亡者吞噬者面前宣告無罪。

sensitivity.note: Category reclassified from religious to myth at the editor's direction: Chapter 125 is canonical funerary scripture, but its core is a narrative of the underworld Hall of Maati — Osiris, the Forty-Two assessors, the devourer of hearts — which this project reads as a myth of judgment rather than a scripture narrative; the interpretive division (README) is noted here. Classed religious rather than myth was the initial call because Chapter 125 is a funerary script used by worshippers. Coordinates are a neutral inland point at Thebes (Luxor), the source of the Papyrus of Ani, since the judgment occurs in the mythic Hall of Maati. Egyptian funerary text quoted for comparative scholarship on ancient afterlife beliefs, not as religious truth claims; Budge's 1920 translation is dated but is the cited public-domain source.

passages.text: When the deceased had repeated the magical names of the doors of the Hall, he entered it and saw these gods arranged in two rows, twenty-one on each side of the Hall. At the end, near Osiris, were the Great Scales, under the charge of Anpu (Anubis), and the monster Amemit, the Eater of the Dead, i.e., of the hearts of the wicked who were condemned in the Judgment of Osiris. The deceased advanced along the Hall and, addressing each of the Forty-Two gods by his name, declared that he had not committed a certain sin, thus: "O Usekh-nemmit, comer forth from Anu, I have not committed sin. O Fenti, comer forth from Khemenu, I have not robbed. O Neha-hau, comer forth from Re-stau, I have not killed men. O Neba, comer forth in retreating, I have not plundered the property of God.
passages.zh: 亡者念誦完廳堂諸門的魔法之名後，便走進廳堂，看見這些神祇分列兩排，廳堂兩側各二十一位。在盡頭、靠近奧西里斯之處，是那巨大的天平，由安普（阿努比斯）掌管，還有怪物阿米特，即亡者吞噬者，也就是吞噬那些在奧西里斯審判中被定罪之惡人心臟的怪物。亡者沿著廳堂前行，逐一以名字稱呼那四十二位神祇，聲明自己未曾犯下某項罪過，如此說道：「哦，烏塞赫-涅姆米特，自阿努而出者，我未曾犯罪。哦，芬提，自赫墨努而出者，我未曾搶劫。哦，涅哈-豪，自瑞斯塔烏而出者，我未曾殺人。哦，涅巴，於退卻中而出者，我未曾掠奪神之財物。」

passages.text: Homage to thee, O Great God, Lord of Maati, I have come to thee, O my Lord, that I may behold thy beneficence. I know thee, and I know thy name, and the names of the Forty-Two who live with thee in the Hall of Maati, who keep ward over sinners, and feed upon their blood on the day of estimating characters before Un-Nefer ... Behold, I have come to thee, and I have brought maat (i.e., truth, integrity) to thee. I have destroyed sin for thee. I have not sinned against men. I have not oppressed [my] kinsfolk. I have done no wrong in the place of truth.
passages.zh: 向你致敬，哦，偉大的神，瑪阿提之主，我來到你面前，哦，我的主，願我能得見你的恩澤。我認識你，我知道你的名字，也知道與你同住在瑪阿提廳堂中的那四十二位的名字，他們看守罪人，在烏恩-涅費爾面前評判品性之日以他們的血為食……看哪，我已來到你面前，我已將瑪阿特（即真理、正直）帶到你面前。我已為你消滅了罪惡。我未曾得罪於人。我未曾壓迫[我的]親族。我未曾在真理之地行任何不義。

title.en: Gilgamesh, Enkidu and Humbaba
title.zh: 吉爾伽美什、恩奇都與洪巴巴

region.en: Cedar Forest (Mount Lebanon range) and Uruk
region.zh: 雪松林（黎巴嫩山區）與烏魯克

period: Sumerian/Babylonian epic, recorded c. 2100-1200 BCE (Spence 1916)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Babylonia & Assyria, by Lewis Spence (1916), eBook #45137

summary.en: Gilgamesh and his companion Eabani (Enkidu) plan an expedition against Khumbaba, the terrifying guardian appointed by Bel over the Forest of Cedars. The heroes seek the blessing of Shamash through Gilgamesh's mother before entering the forest, where they slay the monster.
summary.zh: 吉爾伽美什與摯友恩奇都遠征貝勒所任命的雪松林守護巨怪洪巴巴；臨行前二人託祭司之母向太陽神沙瑪什祈求庇佑，終於林中誅殺怪物。

sensitivity.note: Coordinates placed in the cedar-bearing Mount Lebanon range, the customary identification of the epic's mythic Cedar Forest. Spence's 1916 text is a retelling (one step removed from the tablets) using period transliterations (Khumbaba, Eabani), so passages are clearly-labeled condensed recounts in the template's terms; the combat belongs to heroic legend rather than temple cult, so it is classed as myth.

passages.text: The old priestess advises her son and his friend how to proceed, and after they have gone we see her alone in the temple, her hands raised to the sun-god, invoking his blessing on Gilgamesh: "Why hast thou troubled the heart of my son Gilgamesh? Thou hast laid thy hand upon him, and he goeth away, on a far journey to the dwelling of Khumbaba; he entereth into a combat (whose issue) he knoweth not; he followeth a road unknown to him. Till he arrive and till he return, till he reach the Forest of Cedars, till he hath slain the terrible Khumbaba and rid the land of all the evil that thou hatest, till the day of his return -- let Aya, thy betrothed, thy splendour, recall him to thee."
passages.zh: 年邁的女祭司囑咐她的兒子與他的友人該如何前行；待他們離去後，我們見她獨自留在神殿中，雙手高舉向太陽神，祈求祂賜福給吉爾伽美什：「你為何擾動我兒吉爾伽美什的心？你已將手按在他身上，他便離去，踏上遙遠的旅程，前往胡姆巴巴的居所；他投入一場他不知結局的戰鬥；他行走在一條他所不識的路上。直到他抵達、直到他歸來，直到他抵達雪松林，直到他殺死可怕的胡姆巴巴，並從這地除去一切你所憎惡的邪惡，直到他歸來之日——願阿雅，你的未婚妻、你的榮光，將他喚回你身邊。」

passages.text: Khumbaba, whom Bel had appointed to guard the cedar (_i.e._, one particular cedar which appears to be of greater height and sanctity than the others), is a creature of most terrifying aspect, the very presence of whom in the forest makes those who enter it grow weak and impotent. As the heroes draw near Eabani complains that his hands are feeble and his arms without strength, but Gilgamesh speaks words of encouragement to him.
passages.zh: 胡姆巴巴是貝爾指派守護那棵雪松的（即一棵似乎比其餘更高大、更神聖的雪松），其形貌極為可怖，單是牠在林中出現，便使進入林中的人變得虛弱無力。當兩位英雄走近時，埃阿巴尼抱怨他的雙手軟弱、兩臂無力，但吉爾伽美什對他說出鼓勵的話。

title.en: Etana and the Eagle
title.zh: 伊塔那與神鷹

region.en: Kish, Babylonia
region.zh: 巴比倫尼亞基什城邦

period: Old Babylonian Akkadian legend, tablets from c. 1800-1100 BCE (Jastrow 1898)

source.work: The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria, by Morris Jastrow, Jr. (1898), eBook #20758

summary.en: The shepherd-king Etana, whose wife cannot deliver the child she has conceived, appeals to Shamash for the 'plant of birth.' Carried on the eagle's pinions, he ascends gate after gate toward the heaven of Anu until, flying too high, eagle and rider are hurled back to earth.
summary.zh: 牧者之王伊塔那因妻子難產，向沙瑪什祈求「生育之草」；他乘神鷹之翼層層昇上安努天門，終因飛得太高而與鷹一同墜回大地。

sensitivity.note: Coordinates placed at Kish (Tell al-Uhaymir), the traditional seat of Etana's royal line in the Sumerian King List. Bracketed footnote numbers from Jastrow's text have been removed; his 1898 rendering reconstructs the legend from then-known fragments, exemplifying early comparative philology before later tablet finds altered some readings.

passages.text: Etana's wife is in distress because she is unable to bring to the world a child which she has conceived. Etana appeals to Shamash. Through the mediation of the priests he has offered sacrifices, and he now prays to Shamash to show him the "plant of birth." The oracles have completed my sacrifices, They have completed my free-will offerings to the gods. O Lord, let thy mouth command, And give me the plant of birth, Reveal to me the plant of birth, Bring forth the fruit, grant me an offspring.
passages.zh: 埃塔納的妻子因無法將她所懷的孩子帶到世上而憂苦。埃塔納向沙馬什求助。藉著祭司們的居中轉達，他已獻上祭品，如今他向沙馬什祈禱，求祂向他顯示「生育之草」。神諭已完成了我的祭獻，它們已完成了我們對眾神的自由意願供品。哦，主啊，願你的口發出命令，賜我生育之草，向我揭示生育之草，結出果實，賜我一個子嗣。

passages.text: Etana obeys, and thus, securely attached to the eagle, begins the daring journey. They fly for the space of a double hour, when The eagle addresses Etana: Look, my friend, how the earth appears; Look at the sea and at its side, the house of wisdom; The earth appears as a mountain, the sea has become a pool (?). A second double hour he (i.e., the eagle) carried him on high. The eagle spoke to Etana: Look, my friend, how the earth appears; The sea is a mere belt (?) around the earth. A third double hour he carried him on high. The eagle spoke to Etana: Look, my friend, how the earth appears; The sea is a mere gardener's ditch.
passages.zh: 埃塔納聽從了，於是緊緊依附著鷹，開始了這大膽的旅程。他們飛行了兩個時辰的工夫，這時鷹對埃塔納說：看哪，我的朋友，大地是什麼模樣；看看那海，以及海旁那智慧之屋；大地看起來像一座山，海已變成一個水池（？）。第二個兩個時辰，牠（即那鷹）將他帶到高處。鷹對埃塔納說：看哪，我的朋友，大地是什麼模樣；海不過是環繞大地的一條腰帶（？）。第三個兩個時辰，牠將他帶到高處。鷹對埃塔納說：看哪，我的朋友，大地是什麼模樣；海不過是園丁的一條溝渠。

title.en: The Salmon of Knowledge
title.zh: 智慧鮭魚

region.en: River Boyne, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭博因河

period: Irish Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tales; retold in Lady Augusta Gregory's Gods and Fighting Men (1904)

source.work: Gods and Fighting Men, by Lady Augusta Gregory (1904), eBook #14465

summary.en: The poet Finegas waits seven years on the River Boyne for the salmon of knowledge, foretold to grant all wisdom to whoever eats it. His pupil Finn, roasting the fish, burns his thumb and sucks it, tasting the salmon first; Finegas gives him the whole fish, and Finn gains the wisdom of the nine hazels.
summary.zh: 詩人菲尼加斯守候博因河七年，只待預言中食之可獲全智的智慧鮭魚；弟子芬恩烤魚時燙傷拇指，吮指之際先嚐其味，菲尼加斯遂將全魚相讓，芬恩因此得自海底靈井旁九株智慧榛樹的知識。

sensitivity.note: Coordinates placed on the River Boyne near Slane, where Finegas kept watch by the water for the salmon of knowledge. Lady Gregory's stylised 'Kiltartanese' English deliberately mirrors Irish oral idiom; the tale belongs to Fenian heroic lore but is classed as myth per the project scheme, presented as comparative scholarship.

passages.text: And then he said farewell to Crimall, and went on to learn poetry from Finegas, a poet that was living at the Boinn, for the poets thought it was always on the brink of water poetry was revealed to them. And he did not give him his own name, but he took the name of Deimne. Seven years, now, Finegas had stopped at the Boinn, watching the salmon, for it was in the prophecy that he would eat the salmon of knowledge that would come there, and that he would have all knowledge after. And when at the last the salmon of knowledge came, he brought it to where Finn was, and bade him to roast it, but he bade him not to eat any of it.
passages.zh: 然後他向克里馬爾告別，前去向居住在博因河畔的詩人芬尼加斯學習詩藝，因為詩人們認為詩藝總是在水邊向他們顯現。他沒有告訴他自己的本名，而是取了戴姆內這個名字。如今芬尼加斯已在博因河畔停留了七年，守望著那鮭魚，因為預言說他將吃到那條會來到那裡的知識之鮭，之後他便會擁有全部的知識。當最後那條知識之鮭來到時，他將牠帶到芬恩所在之處，吩咐他烤牠，但吩咐他不可吃牠的任何一點。

passages.text: And when Finn brought him the salmon after a while he said: "Did you eat any of it at all, boy?" "I did not," said Finn; "but I burned my thumb putting down a blister that rose on the skin, and after doing that, I put my thumb in my mouth." "What is your name, boy?" said Finegas. "Deimne," said he. "It is not, but it is Finn your name is, and it is to you and not to myself the salmon was given in the prophecy." With that he gave Finn the whole of the salmon, and from that time Finn had the knowledge that came from the nuts of the nine hazels of wisdom that grow beside the well that is below the sea.
passages.zh: 過了一會兒，當芬恩將鮭魚帶給他時，他說：「孩子，你可有吃過牠一點？」「我沒有，」芬恩說；「但我放下皮膚上冒起的一個水泡時燙傷了我的拇指，做完之後，我把拇指放進嘴裡。」「孩子，你叫什麼名字？」芬尼加斯說。「戴姆內，」他說。「不是的，你的名字是芬恩，預言中那鮭魚是賜給你，而不是給我的。」說罷，他將整條鮭魚給了芬恩，從那時起，芬恩便擁有了來自生長在海下之井旁那九棵智慧榛樹的果實的知識。

title.en: The Children of Lir
title.zh: 里爾的孩子們

region.en: Killarney lakes region, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭基拉尼湖區

period: Old Irish saga of the Tuatha De Danann cycle, retold in Joseph Jacobs' More Celtic Fairy Tales (1894)

source.work: More Celtic Fairy Tales, ed. Joseph Jacobs (1894), eBook #34453 (Stephens' Irish Fairy Tales, 1920, was checked and does not include this tale)

summary.en: Oifa (Aoife), consumed by jealousy of her sister's children, strikes the four children of Lir with a Druid's wand, transforming them into four perfectly white swans. Doomed to wander the lakes and streams of Erin for nine hundred years, they retain their speech and a plaintive music unmatched in the world.
summary.zh: 因嫉恨而心生惡念的艾伊芙，以德魯伊魔杖將里爾的四名子女化為四隻純白天鵝，令其在愛爾蘭諸湖諸川漂流九百年；天鵝們保有人言，其哀婉歌聲世間無雙。

sensitivity.note: Coordinates placed at Lough Leane, Killarney, the customary identification of the lake where Aoife's spell was cast. The 900-year swan exile is one of the 'three sorrows of story-telling' and involves harm to children by a foster-mother; framed here for comparative scholarship.

passages.text: Then she would have raised a sword herself to kill and destroy the children, but her own womanhood and her weakness prevented her; so she drove the children of Lir into the lake to bathe, and they did as Oifa told them. As soon as they were upon the lake she struck them with a Druid's wand of spells and wizardry and put them into the forms of four beautiful, perfectly white swans, and she sang this song over them: "Out with you upon the wild waves, children of the king! Henceforth your cries shall be with the flocks of birds."
passages.zh: 那時她本想親自舉劍殺害並毀滅這些孩子，但她自身的婦人之身與柔弱阻止了她；於是她把李爾的孩子們趕進湖裡沐浴，他們便照奧伊芙所吩咐的做了。他們一入湖中，她便以一根施咒行法的德魯伊法杖擊打他們，將他們變成四隻美麗、純白無瑕的天鵝，並在他們上方唱起這首歌：「去吧，國王的孩子們，到狂野的波濤上去！從今以後，你們的哀鳴將與群鳥同聲。」

passages.text: Oifa laughed and said: "Never shall ye be free until the woman from the south be united to the man from the north, until Lairgnen of Connaught wed Deoch of Munster; nor shall any have power to bring you out of these forms. Nine hundred years shall you wander over the lakes and streams of Erin. This only I will grant unto you: that you retain your own speech, and there shall be no music in the world equal to yours, the plaintive music you shall sing."
passages.zh: 奧伊芙大笑說道：「你們永遠不得自由，直到南方的女子與北方的男子結合，直到康諾特的萊爾格嫩娶了芒斯特的黛奧赫；也無人能有力量使你們脫離這些形貌。你們將在愛琳的湖泊與溪流上漂泊九百年。我只賜予你們這一件事：你們得以保留自己的言語，世上再無音樂能與你們的歌聲相比，那將是你們所唱的哀怨之樂。」

title.en: Baba Yaga and the Little Girl with the Kind Heart
title.zh: 芭芭雅嘎與善良的小女孩

region.en: Russia (forest village, central Russia)
region.zh: 俄羅斯（中央俄羅斯森林村莊）

period: retold 1916 (Ransome)

source.work: Old Peter's Russian Tales, told by Arthur Ransome (1916), tale 'Baba Yaga and the Little Girl with the Kind Heart', eBook #16981

summary.en: A kind stepdaughter is sent into the forest to the witch Baba Yaga. Kindness to the gate, dog, cat, and birch wins their help, and she escapes from the hut on hen's legs, flinging down a towel that becomes a river and a comb that becomes a deep forest to hold off Baba Yaga chasing in her flying mortar.
summary.zh: 善良的女孩被狠心的繼母送到森林女巫芭芭雅嘎處，幸得行善相助脫逃：先後丟下化為大河的毛巾和化為密林的木梳，擋住駕石臼飛追而來的鐵齒女巫，平安返家。

sensitivity.note: Coordinates point to central European Russia, the broadly named setting of Ransome's collection, since the tale's forest is symbolic. Ransome retells for children 'from memory' from Afanasyev-type published collections and frames the tale through the narrator Old Peter, so passages are verbatim from his 1916 telling; a European literary folktale with no sacred or restricted subject matter.

passages.text: "And her hut?" said Vanya. He had often heard about it before, but he wanted to hear about it again. "She lives in a little hut which stands on hen's legs. Sometimes it faces the forest, sometimes it faces the path, and sometimes it walks solemnly about. But in some of the stories she lives in another kind of hut, with a railing of tall sticks, and a skull on each stick. And all night long fire glows in the skulls and fades as the dawn rises."
passages.zh: 「那她的屋子呢？」萬尼亞說。他從前常聽說過那屋子，但他想再聽一遍。「她住在一間立於雞腳上的小屋裡。有時它面向森林，有時它面向小路，有時它莊嚴地四處走動。但在有些故事裡，她住在另一種屋子裡，圍著高高的木樁欄杆，每根木樁上都有一個骷髏頭。整夜火光在骷髏頭中閃爍，隨著黎明升起而漸漸熄滅。」

passages.text: Baba Yaga gnashed at them with her iron teeth. Then she jumped into the mortar and sat down. She drove it along with the pestle, and swept up her tracks with a besom, and flew off in pursuit of the little girl. The little girl ran and ran. She put her ear to the ground and listened. Bang, bang, bangety bang! she could hear Baba Yaga beating the mortar with the pestle. Baba Yaga was quite close. There she was, beating with the pestle and sweeping with the besom, coming along the road. As quickly as she could, the little girl took out the towel and threw it on the ground. And the towel grew bigger and bigger, and wetter and wetter, and there was a deep, broad river between Baba Yaga and the little girl.
passages.zh: 芭芭雅嘎用她的鐵牙朝他們咬牙切齒。接著她跳進臼裡坐下。她用杵推著臼前行，又用掃帚掃去自己的足跡，飛也似地追趕那小女孩。小女孩跑啊跑。她把耳朵貼在地上傾聽。砰，砰，砰砰砰！她聽得見芭芭雅嘎用杵敲打著臼。芭芭雅嘎已經很近了。她就在那裡，一邊用杵敲打、一邊用掃帚清掃，沿著路趕來。小女孩盡可能快地取出毛巾，把它扔在地上。毛巾越變越大，越變越濕，於是在芭芭雅嘎與小女孩之間出現了一條又深又寬的河。

title.en: The Coming of Men, a Long, Long While Ago
title.zh: 很久很久以前，人類的來臨

region.en: East Greenland (Ammassalik district)
region.zh: 東格陵蘭（安馬沙利克一帶）

period: collected 1921 (Rasmussen)

source.work: Eskimo Folk-Tales, collected by Knud Rasmussen, ed. and trans. W. J. Alexander Worster (1921), eBook #28932

summary.en: The earth fell down from the sky long ago, and children came out of the willow bushes. Men who could not die became too many, so a mighty flood from the sea drowned many of them; then two old women agreed that light and death should both come to the world — and when men die they go up into the sky to become brightly shining things.
summary.zh: 遠古時大地自天而降，孩童從柳叢中出生；不識死亡的人類過多，海上滔天洪水淹沒許多人。兩位老婦議定光與死並至，自此人死後升上天際，化為光芒閃亮的太陽、月亮和星辰。

sensitivity.note: A creation tale, not tied to one place; coordinates mark Ammassalik, East Greenland, the district where parts of the volume's material was collected. No restricted (sacral/ceremonial) content was collected; the tale is a published folk narrative version from a 1921 public-domain collection, not ceremonial knowledge.

passages.text: A long, long time ago, when the earth was to be made, it fell down from the sky. Earth, hills and stones, all fell down from the sky, and thus the earth was made. And then, when the earth was made, came men. It is said that they came forth out of the earth. Little children came out of the earth. They came forth from among the willow bushes, all covered with willow leaves. And there they lay among the little bushes: lay and kicked, for they could not even crawl. And they got their food from the earth.
passages.zh: 很久很久以前，在大地將要被造出來的時候，它從天上落了下來。大地、山丘與石頭，全都從天上落了下來，大地便這樣造成了。然後，大地造成之後，人來了。據說他們是從大地裡出來的。小孩子從大地裡出來。他們從柳樹叢中出來，渾身覆滿柳葉。他們就躺在那裡的小灌木之間：躺著踢蹬，因為他們甚至還不會爬。他們從大地獲得食物。

passages.text: But these men who did not know how to die, they grew to be too many, and crowded the earth. And then there came a mighty flood from the sea. Many were drowned, and men grew fewer. We can still see marks of that great flood, on the high hill-tops, where mussel shells may often be found. And now that men had begun to be fewer, two old women began to speak thus: "Better to be without day, if thus we may be without death," said the one. "No; let us have both light and death," said the other. And when the old woman had spoken these words, it was as she had wished. Light came, and death.
passages.zh: 但這些不懂得死亡的人繁衍得太多，擠滿了大地。於是從海上來了一場巨大的洪水。許多人被淹死，人便變少了。我們至今仍能在高高的山頂上看到那場大洪水的痕跡，那裡常可找到貽貝的殼。而既然人已開始變少，兩個老婦人便這樣說了起來：「若這樣便能沒有死亡，那不如沒有白晝。」一個說。「不；讓我們既有光明又有死亡吧。」另一個說。那老婦人說了這些話之後，事情便如她所願。光明來了，死亡也來了。

title.en: How Pele Came to Hawaii
title.zh: 火神佩蕾如何來到夏威夷

region.en: Hawaiian Islands (Kilauea, Hawaii Island)
region.zh: 夏威夷群島（夏威夷島基拉韋厄火山）

period: retold 1916 (Westervelt)

source.work: Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, collected and retold by W. D. Westervelt (1916), eBook #66516

summary.en: The fire-goddess Pele and her family are driven across the ocean by the vengeance of her sea-goddess sister. Wherever Pele strikes her magic pa-oa, a fire-pit opens, but the sea drowns her fires on island after island until she settles in Kilauea; even after her body is broken in battle, her spirit lives on in the volcanic smoke of Mauna Loa.
summary.zh: 火神佩蕾一家遭其姊、海神追復仇而流亡海上；佩蕾以魔鏟處處掘火坑，屢被海水撲熄，最後在基拉韋厄安身。即使肉身被毀，其神魂仍化作火山口的煙火，永為火山火神。

sensitivity.note: Coordinates mark the Kilauea fire-pit, the permanent home Pele digs and occupies at the end of her epic journey. Drawn from a 1916 published retelling by a non-Hawaiian collector; Westervelt's spellings and interpretations are of his era and do not represent present-day kumu teachings, and no restricted content was collected.

passages.text: When Pele came to the island Hawaii, she first stopped at a place called Ke-ahi-a-laka in the district of Puna. From this place she began her inland journey toward the mountains. As she passed on her way there grew within her an intense desire to go at once and see Ai-laau, the god to whom Kilauea belonged, and find a resting-place with him as the end of her journey. She came up, but Ai-laau was not in his house. Of a truth he had made himself thoroughly lost. He had vanished because he knew that this one coming toward him was Pele. He had seen her toiling down by the sea at Ke-ahi-a-laka. Trembling dread and heavy fear overpowered him. He ran away and was entirely lost. When Pele came to that pit she laid out the plan for her abiding home, beginning at once to dig up the foundations. She dug day and night and found that this place fulfilled all her desires. Therefore, she fastened herself tight to Hawaii for all time.
passages.zh: 當佩蕾來到夏威夷島時，她首先在普納區一個名叫凱阿希阿拉卡的地方停下。她從此地開始了她向群山進發的內陸旅程。當她一路前行時，心中生出一股強烈的渴望，想要立刻前去見基拉韋厄所屬的神艾拉奧，並在他那裡找到一處安歇之地，作為她旅程的終點。她來到了那裡，但艾拉奧不在他的屋中。他確實已將自己徹底藏匿起來。他之所以消失，是因為他知道這個朝他而來的人正是佩蕾。他早已看見她在凱阿希阿拉卡的海邊辛苦跋涉。顫抖的恐懼與沉重的畏懼壓倒了他。他逃走了，消失得無影無蹤。當佩蕾來到那個坑洞時，她為自己長久的居所定下了規劃，立刻開始挖掘地基。她日夜挖掘，發現這個地方滿足了她所有的願望。因此，她將自己牢牢地繫於夏威夷，直到永遠。

passages.text: The battle was fought by the two sisters hand to hand. The conflict lasted for a long time along the western slope of the mountain Hale-a-ka-la. Na-maka-o-ka-hai tore the body of Pele and broke her lava bones into great pieces which lie to this day along the seacoast of the district called Kahiki-nui. The masses of broken lava are called Na-iwi-o-Pele (The bones of Pele). Pele was thought to be dead and was sorely mourned by the remaining brothers and sisters. Na-maka-o-ka-hai went off toward Nuu-mea-lani rejoicing in the destruction of her hated enemy. By and by she looked back over the wide seas. The high mountains of the island Hawaii, snow covered, lay in the distance. But over the side of the mountain known as Mauna Loa she saw the uhane, the spirit form of Pele in clouds of volcanic smoke tinged red from the flames of raging fire-pits below. She passed on to Nuu-mea-lani, knowing that she could never again overcome the spirit of Pele, the goddess of fire.
passages.zh: 這場戰鬥由兩姐妹親手交鋒。衝突沿著哈萊阿卡拉山的西坡持續了很長時間。娜瑪卡歐卡海撕碎了佩蕾的身體，將她的熔岩骨骼擊成巨大的碎片，這些碎片至今仍散落在名為卡希基努伊區的海岸邊。那些破碎的熔岩塊被稱為「納伊維歐佩蕾」（佩蕾之骨）。佩蕾被認為已死，其餘的兄弟姐妹為她悲痛不已。娜瑪卡歐卡海因毀滅了她所憎恨的敵人而歡欣鼓舞，朝努烏梅亞拉尼而去。不久之後，她回頭眺望廣闊的海洋。夏威夷島的高山覆蓋著白雪，矗立在遠方。但在那座名為冒納羅亞的山的一側，她看見了烏哈內——佩蕾的靈體形態，隱現於火山煙霧之中，被下方熊熊燃燒的火坑映得通紅。她繼續前往努烏梅亞拉尼，心知自己再也無法戰勝佩蕾的靈魂——那位火焰女神。

title.en: The Creation Story (Tagalog)
title.zh: 創世故事（他加祿人）

region.en: Luzon, Philippines (Tagalog lowlands)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋島（他加祿族低地）

period: recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Philippine Folk Tales, compiled and annotated by Mabel Cook Cole (1916), eBook #12814

summary.en: In the beginning there was no land, only the sea and the sky with a kite flying between. The bird stirs up the sea until the sky showers islands upon it; then a bamboo born of the married breezes splits open to release the first man and woman, whose scattered, hiding children become the ancestors of the different peoples.
summary.zh: 太初無陸地，只有海與天，其間飛著一隻鳶；海鳥攪動海水，天便降下許多島嶼鎮住大海。其後風與風成婚生出一竿竹子，竹中迸出世界第一對男女；其後裔因躲避父母責打而四散，從此分化為酋長、奴隸與各族之人。

sensitivity.note: A creation-dawn story of the Tagalog lowlands, pinned to Manila Bay on Luzon as the ethnic heartland. The verbatim text carries period racial labels from the 1916 edition, quoted unmodified for documentary accuracy; Cole's footnote marks that later tellers adapted the ending to name known peoples. Bracketed footnote markers [154]/[155] and one printer's typo ('stea' for 'sea', in the Gutenberg text) have been removed/corrected.

passages.text: When the world first began there was no land, but only the sea and the sky, and between them was a kite. One day the bird which had nowhere to light grew tired of flying about, so she stirred up the sea until it threw its waters against the sky. The sky, in order to restrain the sea, showered upon it many islands until it could no longer rise, but ran back and forth. Then the sky ordered the kite to light on one of the islands to build her nest, and to leave the sea and the sky in peace.
passages.zh: 世界初創之時，沒有陸地，只有海洋與天空，而在它們之間有一隻鳶。有一天，那隻無處可棲的鳥兒厭倦了四處飛翔，於是攪動海水，直到海水拍打向天空。天空為了約束海洋，向它降下許多島嶼，直到它再也無法升起，只能來回奔流。於是天空命令鳶棲息在其中一座島上築巢，讓海洋與天空歸於安寧。

passages.text: Many children were born to the couple, and from them came all the different races of people. After a while the parents grew very tired of having so many idle and useless children around, and they wished to be rid of them, but they knew of no place to send them to. Time went on and the children became so numerous that the parents enjoyed no peace. One day, in desperation, the father seized a stick and began beating them on all sides. This so frightened the children that they fled in different directions, seeking hidden rooms in the house -- some concealed themselves in the walls, some ran outside, while others hid in the fireplace, and several fled to the sea. Now it happened that those who went into the hidden rooms of the house later became the chiefs of the Islands; and those who concealed themselves in the walls became slaves. Those who ran outside were free men; and those who hid in the fireplace became negroes; while those who fled to the sea were gone many years, and when their children came back they were the white people.
passages.zh: 這對夫妻生了許多孩子，所有不同的種族都源自他們。過了一段時間，父母對身邊有這麼多懶散無用的孩子感到十分厭倦，他們希望能擺脫這些孩子，卻不知道該把他們送到何處。時光流逝，孩子們變得如此眾多，以致父母不得安寧。有一天，父親在絕望中抓起一根棍子，開始向四面八方抽打他們。這把孩子們嚇得四散奔逃，在屋中尋找隱蔽的房間——有些藏在牆壁裡，有些跑到外面，還有些躲在壁爐中，另有幾個逃向大海。後來，那些進入屋中隱蔽房間的人成了群島的首領；那些藏在牆壁裡的人成了奴隸。那些跑到外面的人是自由人；那些躲在壁爐中的人成了黑人；而那些逃向大海的人多年不見蹤影，當他們的孩子歸來時，他們便是白人。

title.en: The Birth of Athena
title.zh: 雅典娜的誕生

region.en: Athens (Acropolis, Attica), Greece
region.zh: 雅典衛城（阿提卡，希臘）

period: retold 1893, rev. 1921 (Guerber, Myths of Greece and Rome)

source.work: H. A. Guerber, 'Myths of Greece and Rome' (1893/1921), eBook #39250

summary.en: Suffering agonizing head pains, Zeus orders his son Hephaestus to cleave his skull open, and Athena springs out full-grown and armed for war. Later she wins the naming of Athens over Poseidon by raising the olive tree.
summary.zh: 宙斯頭痛難忍，命兒子赫菲斯托斯以斧劈開其顱骨，全副武裝的雅典娜躍然而出。其後她以橄欖樹擊敗波塞冬，贏得為雅典城命名的權利。

sensitivity.note: All passages are condensed paraphrases of Guerber's retelling in the collector's own words. Myth plus aition: the birth explains Athena's cult, and the olive contest explains the city's name; coordinates point to the Acropolis of Athens. Source caveat: Guerber uses Latinized names (Jupiter, Vulcan, Minerva, Neptune) and the most popular version; the Homeric Hymn to Athena differs (birth by the river Triton, no axe).

passages.text: Even the deathless gods could suffer pain. Zeus was one day seized with a splitting headache so severe that he summoned the gods of Olympus and begged them for relief. Every remedy failed, even those proposed by Apollo, the divine physician. Unable to bear the torment longer, Zeus commanded his son Hephaestus — the lame smith-god — to split his skull open with an axe. The smith obeyed, and in that instant Athena (whom the Romans called Minerva) leaped out of her father's head, full-grown, glinting in shining armor, spear raised, singing a shout of victory. The assembled gods drew back in alarm, and a mighty trembling over land and sea bore witness that a great new divinity had arrived.
passages.zh: 即便是永生的神祇也會遭受痛苦。有一天，宙斯突發劇烈的頭痛，痛得他召集奧林匹斯眾神，懇求他們設法緩解。一切療法都無效，甚至連神醫阿波羅所提議的也不例外。宙斯再也無法忍受這般折磨，便命令他的兒子赫菲斯托斯——那位跛足的鍛造之神——用斧頭劈開他的頭顱。鐵匠遵命而行，就在那一瞬間，雅典娜（羅馬人稱她為密涅瓦）從她父親的頭中躍出，已然成年，身披閃耀的鎧甲，高舉長矛，唱出勝利的吶喊。聚集的眾神驚恐地退後，大地與海洋劇烈震顫，見證一位偉大的新神已然降臨。

passages.text: The newborn goddess came to preside over wisdom, skill, and peaceful warfare. Soon afterward a Phoenician named Cecrops founded a fine city in Attica, and the gods contended for the honor of naming it. Eventually only Athena and Poseidon remained, so Zeus declared that whoever gave the city's people the most useful gift would win. Poseidon struck the rock and a splendid horse sprang out, drawing cries of amazement; the onlookers mocked Athena's quieter offering, an olive tree. But when she explained how wood, fruit, and leaves of the olive all serve humankind, and that it stands for peace and prosperity rather than war, the judges granted her the city. She named it Athens in her own honor, and the Athenians worshipped her as their guardian goddess, with the great Parthenon raised to her on their citadel.
passages.zh: 這位新生的女神前來主宰智慧、技藝與和平的戰爭。不久之後，一位名叫刻克洛普斯的腓尼基人在阿提卡建立了一座美好的城邦，眾神爭奪為它命名的榮譽。最終只剩下雅典娜與波塞冬，於是宙斯宣布，誰能賜予該城人民最有用的禮物，誰便獲勝。波塞冬擊打岩石，一匹駿馬躍然而出，引來驚嘆之聲；旁觀者嘲笑雅典娜較為平淡的贈禮——一棵橄欖樹。但當她解釋橄欖樹的木材、果實與葉子如何皆有益於人類，且它象徵和平與繁榮而非戰爭時，評判者便將這座城判給了她。她以自己的名義將其命名為雅典，雅典人尊她為守護女神，並在他們的衛城上為她建起了宏偉的帕德嫩神廟。

title.en: The Judgment of Paris
title.zh: 帕里斯的裁判

region.en: Mount Ida near Troy, Anatolia
region.zh: 特洛伊附近的伊達山（安納托利亞）

period: retold 1855 (Bulfinch, The Age of Fable, rev. E. E. Hale)

source.work: Thomas Bulfinch, 'Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable' (1855), eBook #3327

summary.en: Left off the guest list at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, the goddess of Discord tosses a golden apple inscribed for the most beautiful. Zeus hands judgment to the shepherd Paris, who chooses Venus — carrying Helen to Troy and sparking the Trojan War.
summary.zh: 婚禮上未曾獲邀的爭執女神在佩琉斯與忒提斯的婚宴擲下金蘋果，宙斯把裁判交給牧人帕里斯；他選擇維納斯，並將海倫帶回特洛伊，遂爆發特洛伊戰爭。

sensitivity.note: All passages are condensed paraphrases of Bulfinch in the collector's own words. The Peleus–Thetis wedding anchors the divine-marriage motif; Bulfinch follows the Roman naming (Juno, Minerva, Venus) and his golden-apple telling is a 19th-century synthesis rather than Hesiod. Coordinates point to Mount Ida (39.70, 26.66) where the judgment occurs; the wedding itself is at Pelion in Thessaly, so one anchor covers the tale.

passages.text: At the wedding feast of Peleus and Thetis every god had been invited except Eris, the goddess of Discord. Furious at being excluded, she caused a golden apple to appear among the guests, engraved with the words "for the most beautiful." Juno, Minerva, and Venus each claimed it as her prize, and Zeus, unwilling to be dragged into so delicate a dispute, sent the three goddesses to settle their own quarrel on Mount Ida near Troy, where a young shepherd named Paris tended his flocks. Each tried to bribe him: Juno offered power and dominion, Minerva glory in war, and Venus promised the most beautiful woman alive as his wife.
passages.zh: 在珀琉斯與忒提斯的婚宴上，眾神皆受邀，唯有紛爭女神厄里斯未獲邀請。她因被排除在外而大怒，便使一顆金蘋果出現在賓客之間，上面刻著「獻給最美者」的字樣。朱諾、密涅瓦與維納斯皆聲稱此蘋果應歸自己，而宙斯不願捲入如此微妙的爭執，便打發三位女神前往特洛伊附近的伊達山，自行了結這場爭端；那裡有一位名叫帕里斯的年輕牧人正在放牧羊群。三位女神各自試圖賄賂他：朱諾許以權力與統治，密涅瓦許以戰爭中的榮耀，維納斯則承諾將世上最美的女子許配給他為妻。

passages.text: Paris judged in Venus's favor and handed her the golden apple, gaining her favor but making perpetual enemies of the other two goddesses. Venus later guided Paris across the sea to Greece, where he was received hospitably by Menelaus, king of Sparta. Venus had destined Helen, Menelaus' wife and the most beautiful woman in the world, to belong to Paris; during the king's absence Paris persuaded her to flee with him to Troy. The Greek princes had sworn an oath to defend the marriage of whoever won Helen's hand, so when Menelaus called upon them they mounted a great expedition to reclaim her — the Trojan War of Homer's epics.
passages.zh: 帕里斯判定維納斯勝出，將金蘋果交給她，因而贏得她的眷顧，卻使另外兩位女神與他結下永久的仇怨。維納斯後來引導帕里斯渡海前往希臘，他在那裡受到斯巴達國王墨涅拉俄斯的殷勤款待。維納斯早已註定，墨涅拉俄斯之妻、世上最美的女子海倫應歸帕里斯所有；趁國王不在之際，帕里斯說服海倫隨他逃往特洛伊。希臘諸王子曾立誓捍衛那贏得海倫芳心者的婚姻，因此當墨涅拉俄斯向他們求援時，他們便發起一場浩大的遠征以奪回海倫——這便是荷馬史詩中的特洛伊戰爭。

title.en: Cuchulain's Boyhood Deeds
title.zh: 庫丘林的少年事蹟

region.en: Emain Macha (Navan Fort), Ulster, Ireland
region.zh: 埃馬因馬哈（納文堡，阿爾斯特，愛爾蘭）

period: retold 1909 (Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain the Hound of Ulster)

source.work: Eleanor Hull, 'Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster' (1909), ch. III-IV, eBook #52963

summary.en: The boy Setanta runs to Emain Macha at four years old, beats the whole boy-corps at their own game and withstands their assault, and takes the King's protection. Later he kills the smith Culain's giant guard-hound on his way to a feast and pledges himself as its replacement, earning the name Cuchulain, 'the Hound of Culain.'
summary.zh: 四歲的塞坦塔獨自奔至埃馬因馬哈，曲棍技壓整支少年兵團，奮力擋下圍攻，由國王親自庇護。其後赴宴途中殺死鐵匠庫倫的巨犬，自願替補其職，從而得名庫丘林——「庫倫之犬」。

sensitivity.note: All passages are condensed paraphrases of chapters III-IV of Hull's retelling in the collector's own words. Coordinates point to Emain Macha / Navan Fort (54.3446, -6.6946), the royal seat of Ulster. Source caveat: Hull (1909) is an English retelling that re-arranges and prunes the Irish originals (her own admission); the heroic-fury description ('hero-fury', hair crowned with light) follows her version of the twelfth-century texts.

passages.text: Not yet past four years old, the boy heard tales of the boy-corps of King Conor at Emain Macha and could not be held back. Arming himself with a brass hurley and a ball of silver, a toy javelin and a toy spear, he ran the long road north-west over the Slieve Fuad Mountains, driving ball, hurley, and spears before him in an unbroken game. Without asking anyone's leave he dived into the midst of the hundred and fifty princes' sons, caught the ball between his legs, and drove it home to the goal. When the corps attacked the unknown intruder with their spears, hurleys and balls all at once, he parried every throw — and then his 'hero-fury' seized him: his hair rose and seemed crowned with fire, he grew taller in furious contortion, and, springing like a young lion, he stretched fifty of the boys on the ground before the King stopped him at the chessboard and granted the newcomer protection under his own name.
passages.zh: 這男孩還不滿四歲，便聽聞康納王在艾明馬夏的少年軍團之事，再也按捺不住。他為自己配上一根黃銅曲棍與一顆銀球、一支玩具標槍與一柄玩具長矛，便沿著漫長的道路向西北奔越斯利夫富阿德山脈，一路將球、曲棍與長矛驅趕於前，玩著一場不曾中斷的球戲。他不問任何人許可，便一頭衝進那一百五十名王子之子的行列之中，將球夾在兩腿之間，一路驅球攻入球門。當軍團眾人以長矛、曲棍與球一齊攻擊這名陌生的闖入者時，他擋下了每一次投擲——接著，他的「英雄之怒」攫住了他：他的頭髮豎起，彷彿頂戴火焰之冠，他在狂怒的扭曲中身形漸長，又像一頭幼獅般躍起，將五十名男孩打倒在地，直到國王在棋盤旁制止了他，並以自己的名義賜予這名新來者庇護。

passages.text: Some time later the smith Culain prepared a feast for the King, warning that his grounds held no room for a great company. The King, lingering fascinated by the boy's games, left the child behind to finish a ball-game and forgot him; and Culain, told that the company was complete, loosed his great watch-dog, brought from Spain, with the strength of a hundred hounds, to guard the district. Setanta, following the chariot-trails of the royal party, came to the fort alone with club and ball. The mastiff charged open-jawed; the boy flung his ball down its throat, caught the choking beast's head in his hands, and dashed it against the pillars of the door until it lay dead. When the grieving smith lamented the loss of his defense and safeguard, the boy promised to rear a new whelp of that breed — and meanwhile to serve as Culain's own hound in defense of his cattle and house. "Then your name shall no longer be Setanta," the assembly cried, "but Cu-Chulain, the Hound of Culain!"
passages.zh: 過了些時日，鐵匠庫蘭為國王備下盛宴，並告誡說他的場地容不下大批人馬。國王因著迷於男孩的遊戲而流連不去，便留下這孩子玩完一場球戲，卻把他忘了；而庫蘭聽聞賓客已齊，便解開他那頭從西班牙帶回、擁有百犬之力的巨大看門犬，令其守衛此地。塞坦塔循著王室隊伍的車轍而來，獨自帶著棍棒與球來到堡壘。那猛犬張口撲來；男孩將球擲入牠的喉嚨，雙手抓住這頭噎住的猛獸的頭，猛力撞向門柱，直到牠倒地而死。當悲痛的鐵匠哀嘆失去了他的防衛與守護時，男孩承諾要撫養一頭該品種的新幼犬——同時在此期間，親自充當庫蘭的看門犬，守護他的牲畜與家宅。「那麼你的名字便不再是塞坦塔，」眾人高呼，「而是庫呼蘭——庫蘭之犬！」

title.en: Sigurd Slaying Fafnir
title.zh: 西格德屠龍

region.en: Gnita Heath (Rhineland), Germanic North
region.zh: 格尼塔荒原（萊茵地區，北歐傳說地）

period: Saga c. 12th-13th c.; tr. William Morris & Eirikr Magnusson (1888)

source.work: The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga), tr. William Morris & Eirikr Magnusson (1888), ch. XIII-XVIII, eBook #1152

summary.en: The smith Regin tells Sigurd of the cursed gold of Andvari, which turned the smith's brother Fafnir into a great dragon brooding on its hoard. Sigurd slays the dragon from a hidden pit, roasts its heart, and tastes its blood — gaining the understanding of bird-speech, which warns him to slay his treacherous tutor.
summary.zh: 鐵匠雷金向西格德講述安德瓦里的詛咒黃金——正是這份黃金使其兄法夫尼爾化為盤踞寶藏的巨龍。西格德於隱蔽坑洞中一劍誅龍，烤食其心、啖其血而通鳥語，鳥言警其誅殺反噬的親師，遂得寶藏。

sensitivity.note: All passages are condensed paraphrases of the Morris/Magnusson translation, chapters XIII-XVIII, in the collector's own words; the birds' counsel and Odin's disguise as an old bearded man follow the saga. Saga version, not the Poetic Edda; coordinates are a neutral spot in the Rhineland, the unnamed 'Gnita-heath' of the Germanic legend-cycle.

passages.text: Regin, the smith who fostered him, told Sigurd the tale of his family: Hreidmar and his three sons — the smith Regin, the mighty Fafnir, and Otter the fisher — lived alongside the gods. When Odin, Hoenir, and Loki slew Otter in his beast-shape, Hreidmar demanded as ransom an otter-skin's weight of gold, forcing Odin to extort the whole hoard of the dwarf Andvari, whom Loki robbed of his magic ring. The dwarf cursed the gold, dooming it to destroy every owner; the doom soon fell, for Fafnir killed their father for the treasure and, transformed into a great dragon of malice and greed, brooded over his gold on the heath, while Regin nursed his claim on the next generation — the fostered hero Sigurd, son of Sigmund, owner of the reforged sword Gram.
passages.zh: 撫養他長大的鐵匠雷金，向齊格魯德講述了他的家族故事：赫瑞德瑪與他的三個兒子——鐵匠雷金、強悍的法夫納，以及漁夫奧特——與眾神比鄰而居。當奧丁、海尼爾與洛基將化為獸形的奧特殺死後，赫瑞德瑪要求以一張水獺皮所能容納的黃金作為贖金，迫使奧丁強奪矮人安德瓦里的全部寶藏，洛基更從他手中奪走了那枚魔法戒指。那矮人詛咒了這批黃金，註定它將毀滅每一位擁有者；這厄運不久便應驗了，因為法夫納為這批財寶殺死了他們的父親，並化身為一頭充滿惡意與貪婪的巨龍，在荒原上守著他的黃金，而雷金則將自己的主張寄望於下一代——那受他撫養的英雄齊格魯德，即齊格蒙德之子，重鑄之劍格拉姆的持有者。

passages.text: On the heath Sigurd saw the track of the worm marvellously great; Regin, shaking in fear, showed him where to dig. As Sigurd dug, an old bearded man appeared, advised him to make many pits for the running blood, then vanished — Odin in disguise. When the dragon crept down to drink, shaking the earth and snorting venom before him, Sigurd thrust his sword Gram up under Fafnir's left shoulder to the hilt. The dying worm lashed out with head and tail, smashing all that stood before him, and warned Sigurd: the same gold he had owned would be Sigurd's bane too. Regin bade the victor roast Fafnir's heart for him; tasting the dragon's blood on his finger, Sigurd Suddenly understood the speech of birds, and the wood-peckers' chatter warned him that Regin meant to beguile him — so he took the gold, struck off Regin's head, and rode on toward Hindfell, where the fire slept.
passages.zh: 在荒原上，齊格魯德看見那巨蛇的蹤跡大得驚人；雷金嚇得發抖，指點他在何處挖掘。齊格魯德挖掘之時，一位蓄著鬍鬚的老者出現，建議他多挖幾個坑以承接奔流的鮮血，隨後便消失了——那是奧丁的化身。當巨龍爬下來飲水，震動大地、口吐毒液於身前時，齊格魯德將他的劍格拉姆自法夫納的左肩下直刺至劍柄。垂死的巨蛇以頭與尾猛烈甩擊，擊碎了身前的一切，並警告齊格魯德：牠曾擁有的同一批黃金，也將成為齊格魯德的禍根。雷金吩咐這位勝者為他烤炙法夫納的心臟；齊格魯德的手指沾嘗到龍血，忽然聽懂了鳥語，啄木鳥的啁啾警告他雷金意圖欺瞞他——於是他取走黃金，砍下雷金的頭，繼續策馬前往辛德菲爾，那火焰沉睡之地。

title.en: Yi, the Divine Archer, and the False Suns
title.zh: 后羿射落偽日

region.en: Tung-t'ing Lake region, China
region.zh: 洞庭湖一帶（中國）

period: told of the reign of Yao (c. 2346 BCE) as dated by tradition; retold 1922 (Werner, Myths and Legends of China, ch. VI)

source.work: E. T. C. Werner, 'Myths and Legends of China' (1922), ch. VI 'Myths of Thunder, Lightning, Wind, and Rain' — 'The Divine Archer', eBook #15250

summary.en: Under the emperor Yao, the marvel archer Ch'ih-chiang Tzu-yü is renamed Shên I, the Divine Archer, and sent against the calamities ravaging the land — storms, floods, a thousand-foot serpent and giant boars, and ten burning suns. He tames the wind-spirit Fei Lien, shoots down the nine suns born of fire-blowing birds, wins the water-spirit's sister Hêng O as wife, and is canonized as Pacifier of the Country.
summary.zh: 帝堯在位時，異士赤將子輿獲賜名神羿，奉命討平肆虐大地之災禍——狂風、洪水、千尺巨蛇與大野豬，以及天上的十個毒日。他降服風神飛廉，射落妖鳥吹成之九個偽日，娶水神之妹嫦娥，受封「定國侯」。

sensitivity.note: All passages are condensed paraphrases of Werner's chapter VI in the collector's own words. Werner (1922) renders a composite Chinese legend-cycle drawn from the Feng shên yen i and related works; in his version the archer (Shên I / Yi) shoots down nine suns created by fire-blowing birds rather than nine of ten true suns, and the same cycle includes his marriage to Hêng O and the pill of immortality — motif 'sun-capture' hence covers the ten-sun excess and 'quest-immortality' the immortality-pill episode in this culture-hero cycle. Coordinates mark the Tung-t'ing Lake region, tied to the serpent episode.

passages.text: In the twelfth year of the reign of the Emperor Yao — dated by tradition to 2346 BCE — the emperor met in the streets of Huai-yang a man bearing a bow bound with red cloth. He was Ch'ih-chiang Tzu-yü, who claimed to be a skilful archer able to fly on the wings of the wind. To test him, Yao ordered an arrow shot at a pine on a neighbouring mountain: an arrow transfixed the tree, and the bowman soared up the current of air to fetch it back. Named Shên I, 'the Divine Archer,' and attached to the imperial suite, he helped face the calamities then laying waste the land: ten suns burnt up the crops, storms uprooted trees and overturned houses, floods covered the country, a serpent a thousand feet long devoured people near the Tung-t'ing Lake, and boars of enormous size ravaged the east.
passages.zh: 帝堯在位第十二年——傳統上定為公元前二三六四年——帝於淮陽街市遇一持弓之人，弓以紅布纏束。其人名赤將子輿，自稱善射，能乘風之翼而飛。堯欲試之，命其射鄰山一松：箭貫其樹，射者遂乘氣流騰空取箭而返。其人名為神羿，號「神射」，隸於帝側，助帝應對其時荼毒大地之諸災：十日並出，焦灼禾稼；暴風拔木傾屋；洪水淹沒國土；洞庭湖濱有長千尺之巨蛇吞噬生民；又有碩大無朋之野彘肆虐東方。

passages.text: Studying the storms from Mount Ch'ing Ch'iu, Shên I found they poured out of the sack of Fei Lien, Spirit of the Wind, whose blows he mastered — Fei Lien sued for mercy and swore friendship, and the tempests ceased. Then, discovering nine extraordinary birds on three neighbouring peaks of the Hsi Ho blowing out fire that made nine new suns in the sky, he shot nine arrows in succession, pierced the birds, and watched the false suns dissolve into red clouds; the nine arrows stood fast in nine red stones on the mountains. He slew the Tung-t'ing serpent with an arrow in its left eye, trapped and killed the monstrous boars, married Hêng O the sister of Ho Po the water-spirit, and for these exploits the emperor Yao canonized him with the title Marquis Pacifier of the Country.
passages.zh: 神羿登青丘之山察風，見風自風神飛廉之囊中傾瀉而出，遂制服其吹噓之勢——飛廉乞哀，誓結友誼，暴風乃止。其後，羿於西河相鄰三峰之上發現九隻異鳥，鼓翼吐火，於天上化成九輪新日；羿連發九箭，貫穿諸鳥，眼看偽日消散為紅雲；九箭牢牢插於山上九塊紅石之中。羿以一箭射中洞庭巨蛇左目而殺之，又設陷捕殺巨彘，並娶水神河伯之妹嫦娥為妻；以是諸功，帝堯封之為「平國侯」。

title.en: The Wives of Shiva: Sati, Uma, and Parvati
title.zh: 濕婆之妻：薩蒂、烏瑪與帕爾瓦蒂

region.en: Mount Kailasa, Himalayas; Daksha's sacrifice-house, the Ganges plain
region.zh: 凱拉薩山（喜馬拉雅）；祭祀罪火場（恆河平原）

period: Puranic synthesis, c. 500-1000 CE; retold 1913 (Donald A. Mackenzie, Indian Myth and Legend, ch. VIII)

source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, 'Indian Myth and Legend' (1913), ch. VIII 'Divinities of the Epic Period', eBook #47228

summary.en: Shiva's brides reflect his many aspects: Sati, the ideal of wifely devotion, dies on her father's sacrificial fire when her husband is slighted; reborn as Uma and as Parvati, she wins Shiva again and bears him Ganesa and Kartikeya. The love god Kamadeva, rousing the widowed god, is burned to ashes by the flame of Shiva's third eye.
summary.zh: 濕婆的伴侶映照其多面：薩蒂在父親祭祀之際受辱殉火，死後化身烏瑪與帕爾瓦蒂，再度贏得濕婆，生下智慧神象鼻與戰神韋馱。試以愛神箭激醒鰥居之神的迦摩天，遂被濕婆第三眼之火燒成灰燼。

sensitivity.note: All passages are condensed paraphrases of Mackenzie's chapter VIII in the collector's own words. A Puranic synthesis rather than one scripture; Mackenzie (1913) serves as a secondary PD compilation and his naming follows period conventions (Sivá, Parvati, Himavat omitted). Coordinates mark Mount Kailasa, Shiva's dwelling per Mackenzie, a mythic Himalayan site. The widows' self-immolation (sati) is reported as a named historical custom in the source and treated here as mythic-historical, not endorsed.

passages.text: Shiva's complex character is mirrored in the many forms his bride assumes. As Sati she is the ideal of the devoted wife: when her father, the sage Daksha, slighted her spouse at the sacrifice, the goddess cast herself onto the sacrificial fire — and the widows who later died on their husbands' funeral pyres were called Sati in imitation of the faithful goddess. Sati, however, was reborn as Uma, 'Light,' the impersonation of divine wisdom; as Amvika she was Rudra's sister and counterpart; and as Parvati, another form of the same goddess, she endured Shiva's taunt about her dark skin, retired to austerities, and so regained a golden complexion. One Varaha Purana myth makes the three goddess-forms — white Saraswati, red Lakshmi, and black Parvati — originally a single goddess, divided into shapes representing Past, Present, and Future.
passages.zh: 濕婆性格之繁複，映現於其新娘所化之諸多形貌。身為薩蒂，她是貞婦之典範：其父仙人達剎於祭祀中輕慢其夫，女神遂投身祭火——後世殉夫自焚之寡婦，皆仿此忠貞女神而稱薩蒂。然薩蒂轉世為烏瑪，意為「光明」，乃神聖智慧之化身；為安毗迦時，她是樓陀羅之妹與對應者；為波哩婆提時，即同一女神之另一形貌，她忍受濕婆譏其膚色黝黑，退而苦修，遂復得金色之膚。一則《筏羅訶往世書》神話謂三女神形貌——白之娑羅室伐底、紅之吉祥天女、黑之波哩婆提——本為一女神，分化為象徵過去、現在、未來之三形。

passages.text: Two more tales wreathe the divine marriage. After Sati's death the sorrowing Shiva was wounded by Kamadeva, the love god — son of Vishnu and Lakshmi, who shoots flowery arrows and whose wife Rati symbolizes Spring; a flame darted from Shiva's third eye burned Kamadeva to ashes. Of the god's own children, Ganesa, the four-armed elephant-headed god of wisdom and good fortune, invoked at the beginning of books, houses and journeys, is a son of Shiva and Parvati — a Purana tells how the cursed gaze of Saturn decapitated the infant, and Vishnu, flying on Garuda, replaced the head with that of Indra's elephant; the son Kartikeya is the celestial general and slayer of demons.
passages.zh: 另有二則故事縈繞此神聖婚姻。薩蒂死後，悲傷之濕婆為愛神伽摩所傷——伽摩乃毗濕奴與吉祥天女之子，射花箭，其妻羅蒂象徵春天；一道火焰自濕婆第三眼迸出，將伽摩焚為灰燼。神之親子中，象首四臂之伽內什乃智慧與福運之神，於書卷、屋宅、行旅之始受祈請，為濕婆與波哩婆提之子——一則往世書述土星之詛咒目光如何斬落嬰兒首級，毗濕奴乘迦樓羅飛至，以因陀羅大象之首易之；其子室建陀則為天軍統帥、誅魔者。

title.en: The Chinvat Bridge Judgment
title.zh: 欽瓦特橋的審判

region.en: Persia (symbolic: the unseen world beyond the bridge)
region.zh: 波斯（象徵：橋彼岸之幽冥世界）

period: Avestan c. 1000-600 BCE, Pahlavi accounts 8th-9th c. CE; Dhalla ed. 1914

source.work: M. N. Dhalla, 'Zoroastrian Theology' (1914), ch. XIX 'Death and Beyond'

summary.en: In Zoroastrian teaching the soul lingers three days and nights beside the corpse, then journeys to the unseen world, where its own conscience appears as a beautiful maiden (for the good) or a taunting hag (for the wicked). Every soul must cross the Chinvat Bridge of Judgment: the righteous pass with spirit-guard dogs' help into a four-tiered heaven, while the wicked fall into a four-tiered hell of poisonous food and endless darkness.
summary.zh: 瑣羅亞斯德教認為，亡魂死後三晝夜停留屍旁，隨即啟程前往幽冥之境：義人的良心化身絕美少女相迎，惡人則受醜嫗嘲弄。一切靈魂皆須渡過審判之橋——欽瓦特橋：義人得靈犬相助進入四重天國，惡人則墮入以毒物為食、黑暗無底的四層地獄。

sensitivity.note: All passages are condensed, fully paraphrased retellings of Dhalla's chapter XIX in the collector's own words. Source caveat: the planned primary source (SBE Vol. 5, 'Pahlavi Texts Part I', tr. E. W. West, 1880) was inaccessible (sacred-texts.com returns 403), so Dhalla's 1914 PD scholarly synthesis was substituted; it is secondary, so exact Pahlavi chapter attributions are less precise. Category 'religious': scriptural/doctrinal eschatology rather than folk narrative. Coordinates are symbolic — the Chinvat Bridge is an otherworldly location, placed inland at Yazd, a historic centre of surviving Zoroastrianism.

passages.text: In Zoroastrian thought, death is a trial no one escapes: even legendary heroes like Yima fell to Astovidhotu, the demon of death. After the body dies, the soul remains near it for three days and nights, retracing the deeds of its lifetime. The soul of a righteous person sits by the spot where the head once rested, chanting sacred hymns and feeling joy as great as all the living world combined, while the soul of a wicked person sits near the skull in bewildered dread and suffering as great as all the living world combined. At the fourth dawn the journey into the unseen world begins. The righteous soul travels amid a sweet south wind, and then meets its own daena — religious conscience appearing as a damsel of unmatched beauty — who reveals that she is simply the embodiment of its own good thoughts, words, and deeds. Helpers such as Sraosha and Rashnu escort such a soul on its way. The wicked walk a dreadful path in a foul north wind and, in the Pahlavi accounts, are confronted by their conscience in the shape of an ugly old hag mocking the wicked life they led.
passages.zh: 瑣羅亞斯德教思想中，死亡乃無人能免之試煉：即如伊瑪等傳奇英雄，亦為死亡之魔阿斯托維達圖所制。肉身既死，靈魂留於其側三晝夜，回顧生平諸行。善人之靈魂坐於昔日頭部所安之處，誦神聖讚歌，感受之喜樂等同於全體生靈之總和；惡人之靈魂則坐於顱骨之旁，惶惑恐懼，所受之苦亦等同於全體生靈之總和。第四日黎明，赴幽冥之旅程開始。善人之靈魂行於芬芳南風之中，繼而遇其自身之達埃娜——宗教良知化為絕世美貌之少女——少女示其不過為其人善念、善言、善行之化身。斯勞沙與拉什努等助者護送此靈魂前行。惡人則行於污穢北風中之可怖道路，據巴列維文獻所載，其良知化為醜陋老嫗，嘲諷其生前所行之惡。

passages.text: Every soul, good or bad, must pass over the Chinvat Bridge before entering the world beyond, for it stands as the crossing point of judgment. Spirit hounds are stationed at the bridge; they lend aid to devout souls, while the wicked find none. Whoever recites the Ahuna Vairya prayer in full faith is enabled by Ahura Mazda to cross and reach the best existence, the best righteousness, and the best lights; a true priest is one whose wise teaching leaves a person easy of conscience at the bridge, whereas anyone who mistreats dogs in life finds the way barred. Paradise has four levels — Good Thought, Good Word, Good Deed, and highest of all Garonmana, the abode of endless light — where the archangel Vohu Manah greets the newcomers and celestial food, embroidered robes, and golden thrones are provided. Hell likewise has four depths, ending in endless, stinking darkness, where Angra Mainyu feeds souls the foulest food amid the mockery of the infernal rabble.
passages.zh: 一切靈魂，無論善惡，皆須跨越欽瓦特橋，方能入於彼世，蓋此橋乃審判之渡口。橋畔有靈犬守衛；彼等助虔誠之靈魂，而惡人則無所依。凡以全信誦阿胡納·瓦伊里亞祈禱文者，阿胡拉·馬茲達使之得渡，抵達最善之存在、最善之正義、最善之光明；真祭司者，其智慧教誨使人於橋上良心安泰，反之，凡生前虐待犬隻者，則見道路受阻。天堂有四層——善念、善言、善行，其最上者為加羅曼納，無盡光明之居所——大天使沃胡·馬納於此迎候新來者，並備天界之食、錦繡之袍與黃金之座。地獄亦有四重深淵，終於無盡惡臭之黑暗，安格拉·曼紐於此以最穢之物飼養靈魂，並受地獄群魔之嘲弄。

title.en: Adam and Eve, the Forbidden Fruit, and Expulsion from Eden
title.zh: 亞當與夏娃的墮落（創世記二至三章）

region.en: The Garden of Eden (symbolic)
region.zh: 伊甸園（象徵性）

period: Genesis, c. 6th-5th c. BCE; KJV 1611 (Project Gutenberg eBook #8001)

source.work: The Bible, King James version, Book 1: Genesis, chapters 2-3, eBook #8001

summary.en: God forms the first man from dust and sets him in a garden in Eden, forbidding him to eat from the tree of knowledge of good and evil. The serpent persuades the woman that the fruit brings knowledge rather than death; she and her husband eat, are punished with hardship and mortality, and are driven out of Eden, with a flaming sword set to guard the tree of life.
summary.zh: 上帝以塵土造出第一個人，安置在伊甸園中，囑咐他不可吃分辨善惡樹的果子。蛇哄騙女人說果子不會致死，反能開眼如神；她與丈夫吃了，因而受勞苦與死亡的刑罰，被逐出伊甸園，園東有天使與火焰之劍把守生命樹的通路。

sensitivity.note: Passages are condensed paraphrased retellings of the KJV Genesis 2-3 narrative in the collector's own words. The KJV is presented strictly as a public-domain comparative text, not as religious truth. Category 'religious' (canonical scripture + taboo-and-transgression narrative); motifs chosen for the dust-formed Adam and the forbidden-fruit transgression. Coordinates mark a neutral inland spot in southern Mesopotamia, the traditional association for Eden — the location is symbolic, not a verified site.

passages.text: In the second chapter of Genesis the Lord God, having formed a man from the dust of the ground, plants a garden eastward in Eden, full of trees pleasant to see and fit for food, with the tree of life and the tree of knowledge of good and evil standing in it. He settles the man there to dress and keep it, warning that he may eat freely of every tree but one: the tree of knowledge, whose fruit brings death on the very day it is eaten. Since it is not good for the man to be alone, God brings every living creature to him to be named, then casts him into a deep sleep, builds a woman out of a rib taken from his side, and the man joyfully recognizes her as bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh.
passages.zh: 在《創世記》第二章中，主神用地上的塵土造了人之後，在伊甸的東邊栽種了一座園子，園中滿是悅人眼目、適合作食物的樹木，又有生命樹和分別善惡的樹立在園中。祂將那人安置在那裡，要他耕種看守；並警告他，園中各樣樹上的果子都可以隨意吃，唯獨那一棵不可吃，就是分別善惡的樹，其果子在吃的那一日便帶來死亡。因為那人獨居不好，神就把各樣活物帶到他面前讓他命名，然後使他沉睡，從他肋旁取出一根肋骨造成一個女人，那人便歡喜地認出她是自己骨中的骨、肉中的肉。

passages.text: In Genesis 3 the serpent, subtler than every beast of the field, undermines the prohibition: eating will not kill the woman, he insists, but will open her eyes so that she becomes as a god, knowing good and evil. Seeing that the fruit is good for food, lovely to look at, and a path to wisdom, she takes and eats, and gives some to her husband, who eats too. Their eyes are opened, they sew fig leaves into coverings, and they hide among the trees when they hear the Lord God walking in the garden. Judgment follows: the serpent is doomed to crawl and eat dust; the woman is sentenced to sorrowful childbirth under her husband's rule; the man is cursed through a ground that will yield thorns and thistles only under the sweat of his face until he returns to dust. God clothes them in animal skins and drives them out to the east of Eden, where a cherub and a turning, flaming sword seal off the way back to the tree of life.
passages.zh: 在《創世記》第三章中，那蛇比田野一切的活物更狡猾，它動搖了那條禁令：它堅稱，吃了不會使女人死，反倒會叫她眼睛明亮，使她如同神一樣，能知道善惡。女人見那果子好作食物、悅人眼目，又是通往智慧的途徑，就摘下吃了，又給她的丈夫一些，他也吃了。他們的眼睛明亮了，便用無花果樹的葉子為自己編作遮身的衣物；當他們聽見主神在園中行走，就藏在樹木中間。審判隨之而來：那蛇被註定要爬行、吃土；女人被判在丈夫的管轄之下受生產之苦；男人則因土地受咒詛，地必長出荊棘和蒺藜，他必汗流滿面才得糊口，直到歸回塵土。神用獸皮給他們做衣服，把他們趕出伊甸的東邊，那裡有基路伯和四面轉動發火焰的劍，把守著回生命樹的道路。

title.en: The Prodigal Son
title.zh: 浪子回頭的比喻（路加福音十五章）

region.en: Judea (setting of Jesus' teaching)
region.zh: 猶太（耶穌講道之地）

period: Gospel of Luke, c. 80-110 CE; KJV 1611 (Project Gutenberg eBook #8042)

source.work: The Bible, King James version, Book 42: Luke, chapter 15, eBook #8042

summary.en: Jesus tells of a younger son who demands his inheritance, squanders it in a distant country, and returns ruined and repentant, resolving to beg forgiveness. His father runs to meet him, restores him with robe, ring, and a feast, and answers the resentful elder brother that this son who was dead is alive again.
summary.zh: 耶穌講述：小兒子分得家產，遠走他鄉揮霍殆盡，淪為豬倌窮困潦倒，醒悟後回家認罪悔過。父親遠遠望見便奔上前擁抱親吻，為他披袍戴戒、設宴慶祝，並對心生妒忌的長兄說，這兄弟是死而復生、失而復得的孩子。

sensitivity.note: Passages are a paraphrase of the KJV narrative in the collector's own words. Interpretive points: the KJV is treated as a public-domain comparative text only, not as religious truth.
