Category 'religious' since it is a canonical scripture teaching story; motif 'parable-teaching' reflects the genre. The parable never names a place, so the coordinates are symbolic, on a neutral inland spot near Jerusalem.

passages.text: Jesus tells of a man with two sons. The younger asks for his share of the family property, and having received it, journeys into a far country where he wastes all his money in reckless, riotous living. When a great famine grips the land he falls into poverty and takes a job feeding pigs on a local farm; so hungry is he that he would gladly have filled his belly with the husks the swine eat, and no one gives him anything. Coming to his senses at last, he recalls that even his father's hired servants have bread enough and to spare, while he is starving. He resolves to get up, go home, confess that he has sinned against heaven and against his father, and ask to be taken in, no longer as a son, but as one of the hired servants.
passages.zh: 耶穌講到一個人，他有兩個兒子。小兒子要求分得家產中他應得的一份，得到之後，就往遠方去了，在那裡放蕩揮霍，耗盡了所有的錢財。當大饑荒籠罩那地，他陷入貧困，只得在當地一個農場裡找了一份餵豬的活；他餓得恨不得拿豬所吃的豆莢充飢，卻沒有人給他什麼。他終於醒悟過來，想起他父親的雇工尚且糧食充足有餘，而他自己卻要餓死。他決意起來，回家去，承認自己得罪了天，又得罪了父親，求被收留，不再當兒子，而當一個雇工。

passages.text: While the young man is still a long way off, his father sees him, is moved with compassion, runs to meet him, and falls on his neck with kisses. The son makes his confession, admitting he is no longer worthy to be called a son, but before he can even ask to be made a servant, the father orders his best robe, a ring for his hand, shoes for his feet, and a feast on the fattened calf, declaring that this son of his was dead and is alive again, was lost and is found. The elder brother, who has served faithfully for years without ever receiving so much as a feast with his friends, refuses to come in and complains at the celebration. His father answers gently that everything the household owns has always been his, but rejoicing is right, because the boy's brother was dead and is alive again, was lost and is found.
passages.zh: 那年輕人還離得遠的時候，他父親就看見了他，動了慈心，跑去迎接他，摟著他的頸項連連親吻。兒子作了認罪，承認自己不再配稱為兒子，但他還沒來得及求被當作雇工，父親就吩咐拿上好的袍子、手上的戒指、腳上的鞋，並宰了肥牛犢擺設筵席，宣告他這個兒子是死而復活、失而又得的。那大兒子多年忠心服事，卻連與朋友一同歡宴一次也不曾得著，他拒絕進去，對這慶祝滿懷怨言。他父親溫和地回答說，家中所有的一切向來都是他的，但歡喜快樂原是應當的，因為他這個兄弟是死而復活、失而又得的。

title.en: The Miracles of Saint Bridget of Kildare
title.zh: 聖布里吉德（基爾代爾）的奇蹟

region.en: Kildare, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭基爾代爾

period: Saint's life from 7th c. CE hagiography onward; Baring-Gould, 'Lives of the Saints' (1897, Gutenberg eBook #45604)

source.work: S. Baring-Gould, 'The Lives of the Saints', vol. 2 (February), chapter 'S. Bridget', eBook #45604

summary.en: Baring-Gould recounts the legends of Bridget of Kildare: a wonder-marked birth on a threshold, lavish charity, the founding of her famous double monastery under an oak at Kildare, and miracles such as a cloak thrown over a sunbeam, a spared wolf, and sight restored to a blind nun. Before her death she foretells it, having earlier related a prophetic vision explained by Saint Patrick.
summary.zh: 巴林-古爾德敘述基爾代爾的布里吉德：門檻上誕生的靈異預兆、極度慷慨的童年、在基爾代爾橡樹下建立的修道院，以及斗篷懸擋日光柱、贈狼救農、復明盲修女等奇蹟。她預告自己的死期，此前亦向聖派屈克講出「白田被黑衣耕者翻掘」的異夢，被解為愛爾蘭未來的異端之亂。

sensitivity.note: Passages are condensed paraphrases written in the collector's own words; Baring-Gould's sentences were not reproduced verbatim. Category 'religious': hagiography (devotional saint-life). Edition caveat: this is the revised 16-volume 1897 edition; the legend source list concedes Bridget's surviving lives are late compositions of uneven reliability, and the cloak-expanding-over-land miracle is not in this edition, so only miracles actually present in this chapter are drawn on. Coordinates point to Kildare town, the account's concrete setting.

passages.text: The legend says Bridget is born on a doorway's threshold, fulfilling a court augury heard before her confinement: happy is the child born neither in the house nor out of it. Her mother, the nobleman Dubtach's slave-girl, has been sold to a bard, but with the bargain that the child is returned to her father; and when the infant is delivered on the threshold, a pitcher of warm milk falls and pours itself over her. Growing up, she gives every beggar whatever he asks, until her exasperated father takes her to the king's court to sell her as too expensive to keep — and when she hands even the royal sword to a beggar, the king refuses to buy a girl ready to give away the king himself. To escape an unwanted suitor she prays for disfigurement and loses an eye; veiled as a nun, she kisses the dry altar-wood, which turns green, and her beauty is restored.
passages.zh: 傳說布麗姬出生在門檻上，應驗了她臨產前所聽到的一句宮廷預言：生於屋內屋外皆非之地的孩子有福了。她的母親是貴族杜布塔赫的女奴，已被賣給一位吟遊詩人，但附有條件，要把孩子交還給她的父親；當嬰兒在門檻上誕生時，一壺溫熱的牛奶傾倒下來，澆在她身上。她長大後，凡乞丐所求，她無不施予，直到她那忍無可忍的父親把她帶到王宮，要把她賣掉，因為養她太費錢了——而當她甚至把王室的寶劍也交給一個乞丐時，國王便拒絕買下一個隨時準備把國王本人也送出去的姑娘。為了逃避一個她不想要的求婚者，她祈求毀損自己的容貌，因而失去了一隻眼睛；她蒙著面紗作了修女，親吻了乾枯的祭壇木，那木頭竟轉為青綠，她的美貌也恢復了。

passages.text: Bridget founds her cell under a great oak at Kildare — 'the cell of the oak' — which grows into a famed double community of monks and nuns in a church divided into three parts. The chapter is crowded with wonders: her priestly charioteer preaching while a loose horse runs free; stolen cows carrying the thieves' tied clothes back to her convent gates; her cloak, thrown in haste over a sunbeam she has mistaken for a beam, holding the ray standing there until midnight; a live wolf delivered into her chariot and offered to the king in place of the one a rustic has killed, sparing the man's life; and the blind nun Dara, whom Bridget heals of darkness only to be asked to shut her eyes again, since a world so visible leaves God less visible to the soul. Bridget relates a vision before Saint Patrick of a white-harvest field torn up by black ploughmen and sowers scattering tares, which Patrick interprets as future false teaching in Ireland. She foretells the hour of her own death, dies on February 1, 525, and her convent keeps its perpetual fire — the 'House of Fire' — burning down to 1220.
passages.zh: 布麗姬在基爾代爾一棵大橡樹下建立了她的居所——「橡樹之廬」——那裡發展成一座著名的修士與修女雙重團體，其教堂分為三部分。這一章充滿了奇蹟：她那駕車的祭司車夫在講道，而一匹脫韁的馬自由奔跑；被偷的牛群馱著盜賊捆綁的衣物回到她修院的門口；她匆忙之間把斗篷扔在一道她誤以為是橫樑的陽光上，那斗篷竟托住光線，直到午夜仍立在那裡；一頭活狼被送進她的車中，代替一個鄉下人殺死的狼獻給國王，保全了那人的性命；還有盲眼的修女達拉，布麗姬治好了她的黑暗，她卻只求再閉上眼睛，因為一個如此可見的世界，反使神對靈魂不那麼可見了。布麗姬在聖派翠克面前講述了一個異象：一片白色收成的田地，被黑色的耕夫翻掘，撒種的人散播著稗子；派翠克將此解釋為愛爾蘭未來虛假的教導。她預言了自己死亡的時刻，於五二五年二月一日去世，她的修院守護著那不滅之火——「火之屋」——一直燃燒到一二二〇年。

title.en: Cheung Puk-chang, the Seer
title.zh: 崔卜鎮：先知與神通

region.en: Joseon Korea (Seoul; Bird Pass, Kyongsang Province)
region.zh: 朝鮮王朝（首爾；慶尚道鳥嶺）

period: tale collected by Im Bang (1640-1718); English ed. James S. Gale, 'Korean Folk Tales' (1913, Gutenberg eBook #51002)

source.work: Im Pang & Yi Ryuk, tr. James S. Gale, 'Korean Folk Tales: Imps, Ghosts and Fairies' (1913), Tale IV: 'Cheung Puk-chang, the Seer', eBook #51002

summary.en: Cheung Puk-chang is born a marvel of knowledge who needs no study, instantly mastering books, foreign tongues, and the speech of birds and beasts. Loochooan envoys arrive carrying a prophecy that names the day and hour they will meet a Holy Man, and it is fulfilled in him; he also displays distant vision, correctly reporting how a servant is faring far away on his journey.
summary.zh: 崔卜鎮天生異稟，書過目成誦，通天文、醫術、卜算與鳥獸之語。琉球使節攜預言書赴京尋訪「聖人」，其字句在崔卜鎮身上應驗而拜倒；他又能遙視千里，正確指出僕人行踪與遭遇，日期細節日後全部核實。

sensitivity.note: Passages are condensed paraphrases of Gale's translation in the collector's own words; none of Gale's sentences are reproduced verbatim. Category 'myth': a folk wonder-tale of supernatural sight and fulfilled prophecy rather than scripture (per the project genre split). Coordinates use Seoul, where the tale's opening events occur; its farthest episode is at Bird Pass, Kyongsang Province. The Gutenberg text pairs a scholarly historical preamble with each tale; both parts informed the summary.

passages.text: Cheung Puk-chang is a wonder from his earliest years: he needs only to glance through a book once to recite it word for word, and without any study he becomes a master of astronomy, medicine, fortune-telling, music, mathematics, and geomancy. He understands the calls of birds and the voices of beasts, and when he travels with his envoy father to Peking he picks up the language of any strange people after hearing it a single time, astonishing Koreans, Chinese, and foreigners alike. Envoys from Loochoo carry a horoscope-based prophecy in a little book naming the exact year, day, hour, and place they will meet a Holy Man; tracing one envoy station after another, they find him, are struck down with awe, prostrate themselves before him, and are taught at last the Book of Changes in their own tongue. Some call him 'The Mystery.'
passages.zh: 張福昌自幼便是奇才：他只需將書瀏覽一遍，便能一字不差地背誦出來，而且不經任何學習便精通天文、醫術、占卜、音樂、算學與堪輿之術。他能聽懂鳥鳴與獸語，當他跟隨身為使臣的父親前往北京時，任何陌生民族的語言，他只要聽過一次便能學會，令朝鮮人、中國人與外國人同樣驚嘆。琉球的使臣帶著一本小書，書中載有依星象而作的預言，寫明他們將在某年、某日、某時、某地遇見一位聖人；他們循著一個又一個驛站追尋，終於找到了他，驚愕萬分，匍匐在他面前，最後還以本國語言受教《易經》。有人稱他為「神祕者」。

passages.text: One day Cheung Puk-chang calls on his aunt, worried because the servant she sent to do harvest work in Yong-nam County is overdue, and she fears he has met thieves or fire. Puk-chang offers to tell her how matters stand, and gazing off toward the far south he reports that the man is just crossing Bird Pass in Mun-kyong County, Kyong-sang Province — and at that very moment is being beaten by a passing gentleman, since he rode by without dismounting while the official was eating his meal at the top of the hill. The aunt laughs the whole thing off as a joke, but she marks the date on the wall. When the servant arrives on exactly the recorded day, he confirms everything: he was seized by the gentleman's servants, pulled from his horse, and beaten about the face with their straw shoes, precisely as Puk-chang had said.
passages.zh: 有一天，張福昌去探望他的姑母，姑母正憂心忡忡，因為她派往嶺南郡收割的僕人逾期未歸，她擔心他遇上了盜賊或火災。福昌說他能道出事情的原委，便朝遙遠的南方望去，回報說那人正經過慶尚道聞慶郡的鳥嶺——而就在那一刻，他正被一位路過的士紳毆打，因為那位官員在山頂用餐時，他騎馬經過卻未下馬。姑母一笑置之，只當是玩笑，卻在牆上記下了日期。當僕人恰好在所記的那一天抵達時，他證實了一切：他被那位士紳的僕人抓住，拉下馬來，用草鞋打他的臉，與福昌所說的絲毫不差。

title.en: Fuji, the Never-Dying Mountain
title.zh: 富士：不死之山

region.en: Mount Fuji, Japan (plain of Suruga)
region.zh: 日本富士山（駿河平原）

period: populary legends; F. Hadland Davis, 'Myths & Legends of Japan' (1912, Gutenberg eBook #45723), ch. IX 'Legends of Mount Fuji'

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, 'Myths & Legends of Japan' (1912), ch. IX 'Legends of Mount Fuji', eBook #45723

summary.en: Davis's chapter ties Fuji to immortality and apotheosis: the moon-maiden Kaguya commanded that the elixir of life be burned on its peak, and a Chinese emperor who climbs in hope of it dies smiling at the summit. The mountain itself rose in a single night before the woodman Visu; and a goddess of Fuji, a white-clad maiden, healed Yosoji's plague-stricken mother before being carried back to the peak by a cloud.
summary.zh: 戴維斯筆下，富士山與不死傳說相連：輝夜姬命人在峰頂焚燬長生不老藥；中國皇帝登山求藥，卻在山巔含笑而逝；此山一夜拔地而起，出現於樵夫斐素眼前，故稱「不死山」；白衣少女（富士女神）指路取靈泉救瘟疫病母，救人後自化彩雲澨被雲帶回峰頂。

sensitivity.note: Passages are condensed paraphrases of Davis's chapter IX in the collector's own words. Interpretive points: filed as 'myth' (folk legend of a sacred landscape); motifs — Fuji as hallowed peak (sacred-place), the elixir quest (quest-immortality), the cloud-borne apparition of the Goddess of Fuji (theophany). Edition caveat: Davis (1912) is a popular reteller whose versions blend several traditions, and the Kaguya episode is cross-referenced from his chapter III; the passages draw only on chapter IX material. Coordinates are the real Mount Fuji summit area, since the geography here is concrete.

passages.text: Fuji is sacred terrain: pilgrims have climbed it for hundreds of years, its crater was once an active volcano, and its very name is linked with the Aino fire-goddess. Legend even crowns the mountain with the prize of immortality. In the bamboo-cutter romance, the court commanded by the moon-maiden Lady Kaguya ascends Fuji to burn the elixir of life, along with a scroll, upon the peak. The mountain's fame reaches an emperor of China; when he learns that Fuji came into being in a single night, he reasons that so marvelous a mount must yield the elixir of life itself. He gathers handsome youths and maidens and sails to Japan, where the junks ride through a roaring storm before Fuji's white splendour rises before them. Forming his company in procession, the gold-robed emperor walks hour after hour at their head over soft snow, until, eager to be the first to drink, he runs ahead — and his people find him lying on his back, a smile on his face. He has indeed found life eternal, but by way of death.
passages.zh: 富士是聖地：數百年來朝聖者攀登此山，其火山口曾是活火山，山名本身也與愛努人的火之女神相連。傳說甚至將不死之藥的獎賞加冕於此山。在《竹取物語》中，受月宮少女輝夜姬所命的朝廷隊伍登上富士，在山頂焚燒不死之藥與一卷文書。此山之名遠播至中國的一位皇帝；當他得知富士在一夜之間形成，便推斷如此神奇的山必定蘊藏不死之藥本身。他召集俊美的青年男女，揚帆航向日本，船隊在呼嘯的風暴中前行，富士的白色壯麗景象終於在他們眼前升起。他將隨從排成行列，身披金袍的皇帝在他們前頭走了一小時又一小時，踏過鬆軟的積雪，直到急於搶先飲下，他跑到了前頭——而他的臣民發現他仰面躺著，臉上帶著微笑。他確實尋得了永生，卻是藉由死亡之途。

passages.text: How Fuji rose: a giant woodman named Visu lives with his family on the then-barren plain of Suruga. One night, as he is about to fall asleep, a sound more terrifying than any thunder comes out of the ground beneath him; fearing an earthquake, he snatches up the younger children and rushes out, to see a great mountain erupting in tongues of flame and dense smoke where there was only flat plain before — a peak that has run unseen under the earth for two hundred miles and leapt up in a single night. Spellbound, Visu watches dawn dress the mountain in opal, and names it Fuji-yama, the Never-Dying Mountain, its seeming eternity giving rise to the old belief in an elixir hidden upon it.
passages.zh: 富士如何升起：一位名叫維蘇的巨人樵夫與家人住在當時荒蕪的駿河平原上。一天夜裡，他正要入睡，腳下的大地傳出一聲比任何雷鳴都更可怕的聲音；他害怕是地震，便抓起年幼的孩子衝了出去，只見原本平坦的平原上，一座大山正噴發著火舌與濃煙——一座在地底潛行兩百英里、無人得見的山峰，竟在一夜之間躍起。維蘇著了魔似地看著黎明以蛋白石之色為山披上衣裳，便將它命名為富士山，即「不死之山」，它看似永恆，遂生出山中藏有不死之藥的古老信仰。

passages.text: Another tale casts the mountain as a living healer: Yosoji, whose mother is dying of smallpox, is sent by the magician Kamo Yamakiko to fetch water from Fuji's south-west slope; a lady in white guides him to the stream by the shrine of the God of Long Breath. After five visits his mother and many villagers are cured; but when Yosoji returns to give thanks the shrine has dried up, and the maiden — she is the Goddess of Fuji — refuses all thanks, swings her camellia branch into the air to summon a cloud from the sacred peak, and lets it carry her home.
passages.zh: 另一個傳說將此山描繪成活的醫者：陽素子的母親正因天花而垂危，術士加茂山彥命他前往富士西南坡取水；一位白衣女子引他來到長息神祠旁的小溪。經過五次造訪，他的母親與許多村民都痊癒了；但當陽素子回來致謝時，神祠已經乾涸，而那位少女——她正是富士女神——拒絕一切謝意，將她的山茶枝向空中一揮，從聖峰召來一朵雲，讓它載她回家。

title.en: Coyote and the Dragon; Coyote in the Buffalo Country
title.zh: 郊狼與惡龍；水牛之地的郊狼

region.en: Columbia Plateau (Nez Perce and Flathead homelands, Idaho-Montana)
region.zh: 哥倫比亞高原（內茲珀斯人與弗拉特黑德人故地，愛達荷—蒙大拿）

period: collected from Plateau narrators; retold 1910 (Katharine Berry Judson, Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest)

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), 'Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest', A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'Coyote and the Dragon' (Nez Perce) and 'Coyote in the Buffalo Country' (Flathead)

summary.en: Two Coyote trickster tales from the Columbia Plateau. Coyote drags the sun down on a chain of arrows and hides it in a river, luring a light-fearing man-eating dragon into daylight where he can kill it; and in the buffalo country he defeats the greedy chief Bear, loses the herds through his own misrule, and finally out-tricks Wolf's revenge party.
summary.zh: 兩則哥倫比亞高原郊狼故事：郊狼以箭鏈拉下太陽藏入河中，誘出懼光的食人怪龍並趁其目盲殺之；另在水牛之地以計除掉霸占獵物的酋長熊，卻因自家作法失去獸群，最終以更狡猾的詭計擊敗前來復仇的狼群。

sensitivity.note: Passages are condensed paraphrases of two Plateau Coyote tales as retold in Katharine Berry Judson's Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest (1910), in the collector's own words. The intended 'Coyote and the Rolling Rock' could not be verified in a successfully fetched public-domain collection, so two canonical Plateau trickster tales from the same verified PD source are substituted ('Coyote and the Dragon', Nez Perce; 'Coyote in the Buffalo Country', Flathead), with tradition kept as 'plateau'. Category 'myth': trickster-etiological folk narratives, not liturgy; Judson's preface states that ceremonial and coarse content was excluded from her selection. No restricted ceremonial content was collected; only published folk-narrative versions are used. Coordinates mark the Nez Perce homeland as a regional reference only, not a story site.

passages.text: A man-eating dragon lived in a cave in the Willamette Valley, slipping out each night to seize and devour the people, who lived in fear of it. Coyote, the shrewdest and most cunning of all the animals, resolved to help them. Knowing the monster could not endure daylight, he climbed a mountain when the sun stood high and shot one arrow into the sun, then another into the end of the first, and another still, until a chain of arrows stretched from sky to earth. He pulled hard and dragged the sun down, hiding it in the Willamette River. Thinking night had come, the dragon crept out to attack the people; Coyote then broke the chain, the sun leapt back into the sky, and the blinded monster was killed. When white settlers later carried off the creature's great bones, the storytellers said, evil would come of it.
passages.zh: 一隻食人的巨龍住在威拉米特谷的一個洞穴裡，每夜溜出來抓人吞食，人們生活在對牠的恐懼之中。郊狼是所有動物中最機敏、最狡猾的，決心幫助他們。牠知道這怪物受不了日光，便在太陽高懸時爬上一座山，朝太陽射出一箭，又朝第一支箭的末端射出一箭，再射一箭，直到一連串箭矢從天連到地。牠用力一拉，把太陽拖了下來，藏在威拉米特河裡。巨龍以為黑夜已至，便悄悄爬出來攻擊人們；郊狼隨即打斷鎖鏈，太陽躍回天空，雙目失明的怪物被殺死了。說故事的人說，日後當白人拓荒者運走這生物的巨大骨骸時，邪惡將由此而生。

passages.text: Starving after his travels, Coyote heard Eagle mock that the buffalo country was closed to so poor a creature. Determined to prove otherwise, he walked fifteen days to a great camp near the falls, where the unpopular chief Bear kept the fat and good meat of every buffalo kill for himself. Coyote killed a buffalo and, playing host, wrapped a red-hot stone in fat and fed it to Bear, killing him; the grateful people made Coyote chief. Because the slain Bear had been a powerful medicine-man who had willed the herds to remain, all the buffalo vanished once Coyote ruled. Fleeing in shame, Coyote played dead on a trail, was thrown among a traveller's meat, and gorged himself; he then tricked Wolf into trying the same ruse, and the suspicious man clubbed Wolf nearly to death. Wolf gathered Bear and Mole for revenge, but Coyote, dressed like a great chief and aided by Cat and Dog, killed them all.
passages.zh: 郊狼在旅途中饥肠辘辘，听见老鹰讥笑说，水牛之乡对如此穷困的生灵是关闭的。他决心证明并非如此，便走了十五天，来到瀑布附近的一座大营地，那里不受欢迎的首领熊把每一头被杀水牛的肥美肉都据为己有。郊狼杀了一头水牛，做东道主，把一块烧红的石头裹在脂肪里喂给熊吃，将他杀死；感激的人们便拥立郊狼为首领。因为被杀的熊曾是一位强大的巫医，曾以意志令兽群留下，所以郊狼一统治，所有水牛都消失了。郊狼羞愧地逃走，在小路上装死，被扔进一位旅人的肉堆里，大吃一顿；随后他又诱骗狼尝试同样的伎俩，多疑的那人把狼打得几乎丧命。狼召集熊和鼹鼠复仇，但郊狼打扮成大首领，在猫和狗的帮助下，把他们全部杀死。

title.en: Loki Cuts Sif's Hair: Loki's Wager with the Dwarfs
title.zh: 洛基剪斷西芙的頭髮：與矮人的賭注

region.en: Asgard - mythic Scandinavia (neutral marker, central Sweden)
region.zh: 阿斯加德——神話中的斯堪地那維亞（座標為瑞典中部的中性標記）

period: Prose Edda c. 1220 CE; trans. Rasmus B. Anderson (1879)

source.work: Snorri Sturluson, 'The Younger Edda' (Prose Edda), tr. Rasmus B. Anderson (1879), Skáldskaparmál: 'Loke's Wager with the Dwarfs', eBook #18947

summary.en: Loki's mischief and amends: after craftily cutting off Sif's hair, he saves himself from Thor's wrath by having dwarfs forge living hair of gold, the ship Skidbladnir, and Odin's spear. He then bets his head that Brok and Sindri can match those gifts, and though the fly-tormented Brok falters once, the boar Gullinbursti, the ring Draupnir, and the hammer Mjolnir are produced — with the hammer judged the best treasure.
summary.zh: 洛基的惡作劇與補償：他偷剪西芙金髮，為免雷神之怒，讓矮人打造可生長的黃金髮、神船斯希布拉尼爾與奧丁長槍；又以自己的頭打賭布洛克兄弟的手藝，忍受化身蒼蠅的洛基干擾，鍛出黃金野豬、德羅普尼爾指環與雷神之鎚妙爾尼爾，眾神裁定鐵鎚為最上品。

sensitivity.note: Passages are condensed paraphrases of the Skáldskaparmál section 'Loke's Wager with the Dwarfs' as rendered in Anderson's 1879 public-domain translation, in the collector's own words. Classified as 'myth': mythological narrative from Snorri's thirteenth-century handbook of poetics, not a devotional text. Coordinates are a neutral inland-Scandinavia marker because Asgard is a mythic locus rather than a real place. The fly that torments Brok is identified as Loki in disguise, and the account closes on the gifts and the gods' judgment rather than on Loki's later punishment.

passages.text: Loki, in a mean prank, craftily cut off all of Sif's hair. When Thor discovered it, he seized the trickster and would have broken every bone in his body; Loki saved himself by swearing an oath that the dark elves would forge for Sif golden hair that would grow like natural hair. He went to the dwarf brothers called Ivald's sons, who in their smithy made three treasures: the golden hair for Sif, which would grow as soon as it touched her head; the ship Skidbladnir, which always found a fair wind wherever its owner wished to sail and could be folded like a napkin and carried in a pocket; and Odin's spear Gungnir, which would never miss its mark.
passages.zh: 洛基出于恶意的恶作剧，狡猾地剪掉了希芙所有的头发。托尔发现后，抓住这个诡计之神，几乎要打断他全身的骨头；洛基发誓说，黑暗精灵会为希芙锻造出如同天然头发般生长的金发，以此自救。他去找被称为伊瓦尔迪之子的矮人兄弟，他们在锻炉里造出三件宝物：给希芙的金发，一碰到她的头就会生长；船斯基德布拉德尼尔，无论主人想驶向何处，它总能遇到顺风，还能像餐巾一样折叠起来放进口袋；以及奥丁的矛冈格尼尔，它从不失手。

passages.text: Loki then staked his own head with the dwarf Brok on a bet that Brok's brother Sindri could not forge three treasures equally fine. While Sindri worked the furnace, a fly — Loki in disguise — stung Brok, who worked the bellows: first his hand, then his neck, and at last between his eyes, where blood ran down and blurred his sight so that for a single instant he let go the bellows. From the forge came the golden-bristled boar Gullinbursti, which runs through air and sea and lights the darkest night; the ring Draupnir, which every ninth night drips eight new rings of equal weight; and the hammer Mjolnir, which never misses, always returns to the hand, and shrinks small enough to hide in one's bosom, its only flaw a rather short handle. The gods judged the hammer the best of all the treasures and the dwarf the winner of the wager.
passages.zh: 洛基随后与矮人布洛克打赌，以自己的头颅作赌注，说布洛克的兄弟辛德里无法锻造出同样精美的三件宝物。辛德里在炉前工作时，一只苍蝇——乔装的洛基——叮咬操作风箱的布洛克：先是他的手，然后是脖子，最后是两眼之间，血直流下来模糊了他的视线，使他有一瞬间松开了风箱。从锻炉里出来了金鬃野猪古林伯斯提，它奔跑于空中和海上，照亮最黑暗的夜晚；戒指德劳普尼尔，每第九夜滴出八枚同等重量的新戒指；以及锤子姆约尔尼尔，它从不失手，总能回到手中，还能缩小到足以藏在怀里，唯一的缺陷是柄稍短。众神判定锤子是所有宝物中最好的，矮人赢得了赌注。

title.en: Anansi Outwits Tiger: Tying Tiger and the Sheep-skin Suit
title.zh: 阿南西戲勝老虎：縛虎與羊皮套裝

region.en: Jamaica - Mandeville and surrounding country districts
region.zh: 牙買加——曼德維爾及其周邊鄉村地區

period: recorded 1919/1921 from Jamaican storytellers; published 1924 (Beckwith, Jamaica Anansi Stories)

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories', Memoirs of the American Folk-Lore Society vol. XVII (1924) — 'Tying Tiger: The Fish-basket' and 'Tiger's Sheep-skin Suit' (both told by George Parkes of Mandeville)

summary.en: Jamaican spider stories taken down by Martha Warren Beckwith from named storytellers. Anansi repays Tiger for robbing his magically caught fish by tying the dozing bully to a tree with his own hair, leaving him to a hunter; and in a second tale he frames the same Tiger, dressed in a sheepskin suit, for the sheep thefts Anansi himself committed, winning the reward and the master's daughter.
summary.zh: 貝克威思從牙買加說書人筆錄的蜘蛛故事：阿南西的魚獲被老虎強奪後，趁其打盹以長髮將其縛在樹上，任由獵人處置；另一則中他又把偷羊罪行設計到身穿羊皮套裝的老虎身上，老虎被定罪，阿南西贏得賞金與主人的女兒。

sensitivity.note: Passages are condensed paraphrases of Beckwith's transcribed tales 'Tying Tiger: The Fish-basket' and 'Tiger's Sheep-skin Suit' (both narrated by George Parkes of Mandeville), with the vernacular rendered into standard modern English in the collector's own words; no sentences are copied verbatim and no incidents are invented. Category 'myth' (folk narrative): Beckwith identifies Anansi as the culture hero of the Gold Coast remembered in Jamaican wake-night entertainment; these are social amusement tales, not restricted ceremonial or obeah material — the sorcery 'Old Stories' matter was avoided in favor of plain animal trickster tales. The remembered 'Anansi wins all the stories' theme is represented through the trickster-defeats-Tiger contests in this verified source. Coordinates mark Mandeville, Jamaica, where these variants were recorded.

passages.text: In a season of hunger, the spider Anansi went to the sea-shore with pot and basket, made a fire, and commanded the fish by magic — big fish come, little fish go, then the reverse — until pot and basket were full. He cooked and ate his fill, but on the road home he met the bully Tiger, who demanded the basket and ate every fish, spitting out the bones that Anansi humbly gnawed while murmuring about his wasted labor. Anansi began at once to scheme. Praising a wayside fruit tree, he coaxed Tiger beneath it, then offered to pick the lice from Tiger's long head-hair, and while Tiger dozed Anansi lashed the hair round the trunk, tying him fast like a hog. Anansi danced away singing of it, and a hunter who found the trapped Tiger killed him.
passages.zh: 在一个饥荒的季节，蜘蛛阿南西带着锅和篮子来到海边，生起火，用魔法命令鱼群——大鱼来，小鱼去，然后又反过来——直到锅和篮子都装满了。他煮了鱼，吃饱了，但在回家的路上遇到了恶霸老虎，老虎索要篮子，吃光了所有的鱼，吐出骨头，阿南西谦卑地啃着骨头，低声抱怨自己白费了力气。阿南西立刻开始谋划。他称赞路边的一棵果树，把老虎诱到树下，然后提出为老虎长长的头发捉虱子，趁老虎打盹时，阿南西把头发缠在树干上，像捆猪一样把他牢牢绑住。阿南西跳着舞唱着这件事离开了，一个猎人发现了被困的老虎，把他杀死了。

passages.text: Hired to mind Mr. Mighty's flock of two thousand sheep, Anansi stole them one by one until only a single animal remained. His master promised his best daughter and two hundred pounds to whoever could explain how the sheep were lost, and Anansi, who could fiddle, proposed a ball. He dressed his friend Tiger from cap to boots in a sheepskin suit, telling him that when the music sang 'Mister Mighty lost him sheep — it stands like a Tiger thief,' the song mocked some other Tiger from far country. Anansi then played the tune himself, denounced the sheepskin-clad musician as the very thief who had skinned the sheep to clothe himself, and Tiger, seized and convicted, drew ten years in prison, while Anansi collected the money and the daughter in marriage.
passages.zh: 阿南西受雇照看 mighty 先生的两千只羊群，他一只一只地偷，直到只剩下一只动物。他的主人许诺，谁能解释羊群是如何丢失的，就把最好的女儿和两百英镑给他，会拉小提琴的阿南西提议举办一场舞会。他把朋友老虎从头到脚打扮成羊皮套装，告诉他说，当音乐唱起“ mighty 先生丢了他的羊——它站得像老虎贼”时，这首歌是在嘲笑远方某个别的老虎。然后阿南西亲自演奏这首曲子，谴责那个穿羊皮的乐手正是剥了羊皮来给自己穿的贼，老虎被抓住并定罪，坐了十年牢，而阿南西则收下了钱，娶了那个女儿。

title.en: How the Tinguian Learned to Plant
title.zh: 丁桂安人如何學會耕種

region.en: Abra Province, northwestern Luzon, Philippines (Tinguian homeland)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋島西北部阿布拉省（丁桂安人故地）

period: collected c. 1903-1908 among the Tinguian; published 1916 (Cole, Philippine Folk Tales)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole (comp.), 'Philippine Folk Tales', A.C. McClurg, 1916 — Group I (Tinguian): 'How the Tinguian Learned to Plant', eBook #12814

summary.en: A Tinguian origin story of agriculture and healing. The sky spirit Kaboniyan, sent by the Great Spirit Kadaklan, enters the ailing woman Dayapan as she bathes at a spring, gives her rice and sugar-cane, and teaches her planting, harvest, storage and the Sayung ceremony; because the dog then kills the ceremonial cock, some of the sick will die while others recover, and rice-planting passes from her to the people.
summary.zh: 丁桂安人的農耕起源故事：天神卡達克蘭見族人飢病無醫，派使者卡博尼揚下凡，在病了七年的婦人達雅潘沐浴時進入她體內，賜予稻米與甘蔗，教導種植、收貯與Sayung治病儀式；因狗殺雞的徵兆，從此有人病癒有人死亡，耕種之法由達雅潘代代相傳。

sensitivity.note: Passages are condensed paraphrases of 'How the Tinguian Learned to Plant' as retold by Mabel Cook Cole in Philippine Folk Tales (1916), in the compiler's own words; nothing quoted verbatim and no elements added. Category 'myth' rather than 'religious': although the tale narrates the spirit-granted origin of the Sayung healing ceremony and rice-planting, it is a short folk etiological narrative as published for general readers; the rite is named and framed only, not described in operational detail, and no restricted ceremonial knowledge is reproduced. Coordinates mark the Abra river valley of northwestern Luzon, the Tinguian homeland, as a regional reference.

passages.text: In the very old times the Tinguian knew nothing of planting or harvest, gathering only wild forest foods and fish, and they had no way to cure sickness caused by the evil spirits, so many died who might have lived. Kadaklan, the Great Spirit who dwells in the sky, saw their hunger and sickness and sent his servant Kaboniyan down to teach them. In Caalang lived Dayapan, a woman who had been ill for seven years; bathing one day at the spring, she felt a spirit enter her body, bringing rice and sugar-cane. He told her to plant them, to reap and store the rice in a granary, to press the cane, and to hold the ceremony called Sayung, promising she would be well; and entering her again as she planted, the spirit showed her exactly what to do.
passages.zh: 在非常古老的时代，廷吉安人不懂种植或收获，只采集野生的森林食物和鱼，他们也没有办法治愈恶灵引起的疾病，所以许多本可以活下来的人死了。住在天空中的大神卡达克兰看到他们的饥饿和疾病，便派他的仆人卡博尼扬下凡教导他们。在卡阿朗住着达亚潘，一个病了七年的女人；有一天她在泉边洗澡，感到一个精灵进入她的身体，带来了稻米和甘蔗。他告诉她种植它们，收割稻米并储存在粮仓里，压榨甘蔗，并举行称为萨永的仪式，承诺她会痊愈；当她种植时，精灵再次进入她的身体，准确地告诉她该怎么做。

passages.text: When Dayapan had reaped the first rice and cane, she made the Sayung ceremony as the spirit directed, and when it was finished and her sickness gone, he told her to bathe in the river, tying a dog and a cock near the water as a sign that the rite was complete. While she bathed, the dog killed and ate the cock. Dayapan wept until Kaboniyan came and explained the omen: had the cock lived, no person would die when the ceremony was made, but now some of the sick would recover and some would die. She called the people together and taught them everything the spirit had shown her; seeing that she was healed, they believed, and ever since the Tinguian have planted rice and cane each year, while Dayapan treated the sick as she had been taught.
passages.zh: 當達雅潘收割了第一批稻米與甘蔗之後，她便遵照神靈的指示舉行了薩尤恩儀式；儀式完成、她的病也痊癒之後，神靈吩咐她到河裡沐浴，並在河邊綁上一隻狗和一隻公雞，作為儀式圓滿完成的標記。就在她沐浴的時候，那隻狗咬死了公雞並將牠吃掉。達雅潘哭泣不止，直到卡博尼揚前來，向她解釋這個徵兆：倘若公雞還活著，那麼舉行儀式之後便不會有人死去；但如今，患病者之中有些人會康復，有些人則會死去。她召集了眾人，將神靈向她顯現的一切教導他們；眾人見她已然痊癒，便都信服了。自此以後，廷吉安人年年種植稻米與甘蔗，而達雅潘則依照所受的教導為病人治病。

title.en: When the Ravens Could Speak (with The Raven and the Goose)
title.zh: 當渡鴉還會說話時（附：渡鴉與鵝）

region.en: South-East Greenland (Angmagssalik/Ammassalik district)
region.zh: 格陵蘭東南部（昂馬沙利克地區）

period: collected by Knud Rasmussen; published 1921 (Gyldendal), English by W. J. A. Worster

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (ed.), 'Eskimo Folk-Tales', rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster, Gyldendal, 1921 — 'When the Ravens could speak' and 'The Raven and the Goose' (South-East Greenland tales; eBook #28932)

summary.en: Two very short Greenlandic pourquoi tales from Rasmussen's collection. Ravens once could talk, but always said the opposite of what they meant, until an old man magically took their speech away, leaving only shrieking; in the companion tale the raven's rude impatience while being painted by the goose leaves it black all over.
summary.zh: 兩則格陵蘭短篇起源故事：渡鴉曾能說話，總是口是心非，被怒老人設法收回說話之能，從此只會嘶啞啼叫；姊妹篇中，渡鴉嫌棄鵝為其鳥羽畫上的花紋，激怒的鵝索性將其潑成一身黑，這便是渡鴉烏黑羽毛的由來。

sensitivity.note: Passages are condensed paraphrases of two short tales from Knud Rasmussen's Eskimo Folk-Tales (1921), rendered into English by W. J. A. Worster, in the collector's own words. Because 'When the Ravens could speak' is only a few lines long, a second passage is drawn, as permitted, from the same verified public-domain book ('The Raven and the Goose', same source region); the book's notes place both tales among the South-East Greenland stories. Category 'myth' (folk narrative): brief etiological entertainments of the winter story-telling repertoire, not ceremonial or shamanic material. Coordinates mark the Angmagssalik (Ammassalik) district of East Greenland, the named source region.

passages.text: Once, long ago, the ravens could talk — but their words carried the opposite of their meaning. Whenever they wished to thank someone, they spoke abuse, so that everything they said was the reverse of what they meant, a whole speech of lies. One day, the story goes, an old man came and, by magical means, took their power of speech away altogether, and since that time ravens can do nothing but shriek. Yet their nature was not changed along with their language: the storyteller adds that ravens remain to this day an ill-tempered, lying, thieving lot of birds.
passages.zh: 很久以前，渡鴉曾經會說話——但牠們的話語所表達的意思，總是與其本意相反。每當牠們想向某人道謝，說出口的卻是辱罵，因此牠們所說的一切都與心中所想相反，整段話盡是謊言。據說有一天，一位老人前來，以法術將牠們說話的能力徹底奪走，從那時起，渡鴉便只會尖叫。然而牠們的本性並未隨著語言的喪失而改變：講述故事的人補充說，渡鴉至今仍是一群脾氣暴躁、愛說謊、愛偷竊的鳥。

passages.text: A second short tale explains the raven's color. In the days when all the birds were receiving their colours and the patterns of their coats, the raven and the goose met and agreed to paint one another. The raven went first, giving the goose a fine black coat with a pleasing white pattern showing between, and the goose found it very beautiful. But when the goose began painting the raven a coat exactly like its own, the raven fell into a rage, declaring the pattern frightfully ugly; and the goose, offended by all this fuss, simply splashed the raven black all over. That, says the teller, is why the raven is so dull and black in colour.
passages.zh: 另一則簡短的故事解釋了渡鴉的顏色。在那個眾鳥各自領受顏色與羽毛花紋的日子裡，渡鴉與鵝相遇，相約彼此為對方上色。渡鴉先動手，為鵝塗上一身漂亮的黑色羽毛，其間點綴著悅目的白色花紋，鵝覺得這身羽毛美極了。但當鵝開始為渡鴉塗上與自己一模一樣的羽毛時，渡鴉勃然大怒，直說這花紋醜得可怕；鵝被這番大驚小怪惹惱了，索性把渡鴉全身塗成一片漆黑。講述者說，這就是渡鴉顏色如此黯淡烏黑的原因。

title.en: Demeter and Persephone: The Homeric Hymn to Demeter and the Eleusinian Mysteries
title.zh: 得墨忒耳與珀耳塞福涅：德墨忒耳頌歌與厄琉息斯秘儀

region.en: Eleusis, Attica, Greece
region.zh: 希臘阿提卡厄琉息斯

period: Homeric Hymn 2 composed 7th-6th c. BCE; principal MS: Leiden, University Library 33 H (15th c.); Eleusinian cult attested c. 750-550 BCE onward

source.archive: Center for Hellenic Studies / Perseus Digital Library
source.work: Homeric Hymns 2 (To Demeter), trans. H. G. Evelyn-White, Loeb, 1914; ed. N. J. Richardson, Oxford 1974

summary.en: Persephone is seized by Hades with Zeus's consent; her mother Demeter halts all growth until Zeus negotiates a two-thirds/one-third division of the year; the goddess founds the Eleusinian Mysteries, whose initiates were promised a better lot after death.
summary.zh: 哈得斯得宙斯默許擄走珀耳塞福涅；得墨忒耳憤而令五穀不生，宙斯遂斡旋，女兒一年三分之二在世、三分之一居冥府；女神創立厄琉息斯秘儀，許入儀者身後得福。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cult text; the Eleusinian Mysteries' secret rituale is lost — only public literary versions survive. Nothing restricted is reproduced. [Merged 2026-11-11: the entry 'hymn-demeter' (Homeric Hymn 2, trans. Evelyn-White 1914, Theoi Classical Texts Library, https://www.theoi.com/Text/HomericHymns1.html — verbatim passages on the rape of Persephone and the reunion with Demeter) was folded in as passages 3-4 and the duplicate entry removed; motif world-renewal comes from the folded material.]

passages.text: I begin to sing of rich-haired Demeter, awful goddess — of her and her slim-ankled daughter, whom Aidoneus rapt away, given to him by all-seeing Zeus the loud-thunderer. Condensed paraphrase of Hymn 371-394: Hades secretly gives Persephone a pomegranate seed to eat, binding her to return; Zeus dispatches Rhea, and mother and daughter are reconciled — one third of the year below with her dark lord, two thirds above with her mother and the other immortals. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hymn 371-394; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 我開始歌頌濃髮的狄蜜特，令人敬畏的女神——歌頌她與她那纖細腳踝的女兒，那女兒被艾多紐斯擄走，是那無所不見、雷聲隆隆的宙斯將她許配給他的。第三七一至三九四行頌歌的濃縮意譯：哈迪斯暗中給波瑟芬妮一顆石榴籽吃下，使她受縛而必須歸返；宙斯派遣瑞亞前去，母女二人於是和解——一年之中有三分之一在地下與她那黑暗的夫君同住，三分之二在地上與她的母親及其他不朽神祇同住。此非逐字翻譯。

passages.text: He caught her up reluctant on his golden car and bare her away lamenting. Then she cried out shrilly with her voice, calling upon her father, the Son of Cronos, who is most high and excellent. But no one, either of the deathless gods or of mortal men, heard her voice, nor yet the olive-trees bearing rich fruit: only tender-hearted Hecate, bright-coiffed, the daughter of Persaeus, heard the girl from her cave, and the lord Helios, Hyperion's bright son, as she cried to her father, the Son of Cronos. But he was sitting aloof, apart from the gods, in his temple where many pray, and receiving sweet offerings from mortal men. So he, that Son of Cronos, of many names, who is Ruler of Many and Host of Many, was bearing her away by leave of Zeus on his immortal chariot — his own brother's child and all unwilling.
passages.zh: 他將不情願的她抱上金色的車輦，帶著悲泣的她離去。於是她高聲尖叫，呼喚她的父親，那至高至卓越的克洛諾斯之子。然而無論是不死的眾神，還是凡間的人類，都沒有聽見她的聲音，就連結滿豐碩果實的橄欖樹也沒有聽見：唯有溫柔心腸、頭飾明亮的赫卡忒，即珀耳塞斯之女，從她的洞穴中聽見了這少女的呼喊；以及那光輝的赫利俄斯，許佩里翁的明亮之子，也聽見了她向父親克洛諾斯之子的呼喚。但他卻遠離眾神，獨坐在他那眾人祈禱的廟宇之中，接受凡人獻上的甜美祭品。於是，那克洛諾斯之子、擁有眾多稱號者、那統治眾多亡魂並款待眾多賓客者，便奉宙斯之許可，駕著他不朽的車輦將她擄走——她是他親兄弟的女兒，而且全然不情願。

passages.text: But while Demeter was still holding her dear child in her arms, her heart suddenly misgave her for some snare, so that she feared greatly and ceased fondling her daughter and asked of her at once: "My child, tell me, surely you have not tasted any food while you were below? Speak out and hide nothing, but let us both know. For if you have not, you shall come back from loathly Hades and live with me and your father, the dark-clouded Son of Cronos and be honoured by all the deathless gods; but if you have tasted food, you must go back again beneath the secret places of the earth, there to dwell a third part of the seasons every year: yet for the two parts you shall be with me and the other deathless gods.
passages.zh: 然而，正當狄蜜特仍將她親愛的孩子抱在懷中時，她心中忽然起了疑慮，覺得其中有詐，於是萬分恐懼，不再撫弄女兒，立刻問她道：「我的孩子，告訴我，你在下界時當真沒有吃過任何食物嗎？說出來，什麼都不要隱瞞，好讓我們兩人都明白。因為你若沒有吃過，你便能從可憎的哈迪斯那裡歸來，與我和你的父親，那烏雲籠罩的克洛諾斯之子同住，並受所有不死神祇的尊崇；但你若吃過食物，就必須再度回到大地的幽秘深處，每年有三分之一的時節住在那裡；而其餘三分之二的時節，你將與我及其他不死的神祇同在。」

canonical_translation: H. G. Evelyn-White, Homeric Hymns, Loeb 57 (1914); scholarly translation in Helene P. Foley, The Homeric Hymn to Demeter (Princeton, 1994)

narrative.en:
The Hymn (495 dactylic lines) is the fullest continuous Greek narrative of abduction, grief, and negotiated return.

THE ABDUCTION. Persephone, daughter of Demeter, is playing with the daughters of Okeanos, gathering flowers — roses, crocuses, violets, iris, hyacinth — on the Nysian plain. Earth, at Zeus's secret instruction, produces a marvelous narcissus as a snare. As the girl reaches for it, the earth opens; Hades bursts out on his deathless horses, seizes her, and carries her wailing down through the gates of the west. She cries to her father and to the immortals, but no voice heeds her except Hekate's, who hears from her cave with torches lit, and Helios, who sees all and later tells Demeter the truth: the abduction was not the kidnapper's plan alone but Zeus's gift to his brother.

THE GRIEF. For nine days Demeter wanders with flaming torches, neither eating nor washing. Hekate runs to meet her, but can only tell what she heard. From Helios Demeter learns the full crime; furious at the gods, she withdraws from Olympos and comes to Eleusis in the guise of an old woman, sitting in sorrow by the 'maiden's well' (the Parthenion). The daughters of Keleos, lord of Eleusis, find her and lead her to their mother Metaneira; the disguised goddess nurses the infant Demophoon, secretly anointing him with ambrosia and burning away his mortality in the hearth at night — she would make him ageless, a god. Metaneira, spying at night, screams and breaks the ritual: the child cannot now be immortal. Demeter reveals herself, demands a temple and altar at Eleusis, and withdraws her rites.

THE FAMINE. In wrath against Zeus, Demeter 'who brings the seasons' destroys the year's seed; the oxen drag useless ploughs; the whole race of men would have perished of famine, and the gods would have lost their honours and sacrifices. Zeus sends Iris, then one by one all the gods, bearing gifts; Demeter will not lift the curse until she sees her daughter with her own eyes. Zeus therefore sends Hermes to Hades, who agrees — but smilingly, as Persephone is about to ascend, gives her a pomegranate seed to eat, 'secretly and deliberately', so that she must return to him for a third of each year.

THE SETTLEMENT AND END. Mother and daughter embrace; Demeter, learning of the seed, accepts the arrangement. Through the stern command of Rhea, sent down from Olympos by Zeus, the goddesses are reconciled: Persephone spends two-thirds of the revolving year with her mother and the immortals, one-third below; the earth's increase returns, and Demeter restores abundance to the ploughlands. She then returns to Olympos, but first she calls the princes of Eleusis — Triptolemos, Diokles, Eumolpos, and Keleos — and shows them her rites, 'awful mysteries which none may transgress, pry into, or utter; for deep awe of the gods checks the voice'. Blessed is the mortal who has seen them, the Hymn ends: the initiate shares a better lot below; the uninitiated, dying, gets the opposite.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative is the charter myth of the Eleusinian Mysteries, the panhellenic cult whose initiates (from across the Greek world, including slaves and women) swore ritual secrecy; it structures the women's Thesmophoria festival at Athens (which re-enacted fasts and used pig-offerings aitiologically); it explains the agricultural year as a mother-daughter rhythm; it gives Greek marriage its anthropological image — a daughter 'abducted' with paternal consent into the husband's house; and, uniquely among public Greek texts, it attaches eschatological reward to initiatory knowledge. The secret dramatization at Eleusis (reconstructed from archaeology and later Christian polemic) is lost and must not be confounded with the Hymn.
narrative.zh: 珀耳塞福涅與大洋女兒們在尼薩原野採花，大地按宙斯密令生出奇妙水仙為餌；哈得斯裂地而出，攜女入冥，唯赫卡忒聞聲、赫利俄斯見事。得墨忒耳執火炬遍尋九日，怒離奧林波斯，化身老嫗至厄琉息斯王家，哺乳嬰兒得謨福翁，欲以夜火焚其凡性；母后撞破，女神現真身，命建廟。遂降饑饉，牲祭絕於諸神。宙斯屢遣使不得，乃命赫爾墨斯赴冥府；哈得斯微笑授石榴籽一粒，女遂須每年歸冥三月。瑞亞降旨和解：女居上界三分之二，下界三分之一；五穀復生。女神召厄琉息斯諸王子，授以『不可窺、不可傳』之奧儀；入儀者身後得福，未入者不然。秘儀儀程今已失傳，文獻所存僅此公開敘事。

functions: Charter myth of the Eleusinian Mysteries (initiatory secrecy and afterlife promise)
Aitia for the Thesmophoria and the agricultural cycle
Cultural model of marriage-as-abduction under paternal consent
Rare public Greek eschatology: differential fate of initiates and non-initiates

variants.name: Orphic version (Zagreus-Dionysos and Persephone's line)
variants.text_tradition: Orphic fragments (e.g. OF 58, 299 Bernabe); Derveni Papyrus; late antique Neoplatonist citations
variants.summary: In Orphic theology Persephone mates with Zeus and bears Dionysos Zagreus, who is dismembered by Titans; humankind, born from the Titans' ashes, carries both Titanic guilt and Dionysian essence — a descent-and-restoration soteriology rather than a seasonal myth.

variants.name: Arcadian 'Despoina' cult (Lykosoura)
variants.text_tradition: Pausanias, Description of Greece 8.37-38 (2nd c. CE)
variants.summary: A closely parallel mystery cult of Demeter and an unnamed daughter ('Despoina', 'the Mistress') with Artemis and Anytos; the child of Demeter and Poseidon in horse-form. Shows the Eleusinian story is one local, panhellenized form of a wider family of mother-daughter mysteries.

variants.name: Sicilian and South Italian versions
variants.text_tradition: Pindar, fragments; Diodorus Siculus 5.2-5; coin iconography of Enna
variants.summary: Persephone is carried off near Enna/Henna in Sicily's lake meadow, and the island claims the rape and the foundation of cult; Diodorus (himself Sicilian) renders the myth as an allegory of the grain cycle. Underwrites strong Sicilian/Italian mystery cults of Persephone and Dionysos.

variants.name: Thesmophoria liturgical narrative
variants.text_tradition: Athenian women's festival (attested by scholia to Lucian, Dialogue of the Courtesans 2.1; Aristophanes, Thesmophoriazusae)
variants.summary: The women's festival preserves the ritual sequence the Hymn reflects — fasting, obscenity (iambe's jokes), piglets thrown into pits whose rot is mixed with seed-corn — narratively reorganized as Demeter's search, grief, and restoration.

Principal MS: Leiden, Universiteitsbibliotheek 33 H, 15th c. Standard edition: N. J. Richardson, The Homeric Hymn to Demeter, Oxford 1974.

title.en: Heracles: Madness, the Twelve Labors, and Apotheosis
title.zh: 赫拉克勒斯：瘋癲、十二勞役與成神

region.en: Tiryns / Mycenae, Argolid, Greece (symbolic pin for the pan-Hellenic cycle)
region.zh: 希臘阿爾戈利斯提任斯／邁錫尼（泛希臘神話圈象徵性定位）

period: Cycle attested from 8th-7th c. BCE epics; coherent prose retelling in Apollodorus' Bibliotheca 2.4.12-2.7.7 (1st-2nd c. CE; principal MS: Laurentianus 66, 4, 14th c.)

source.work: Apollodorus, The Library 2.4-2.7 (trans. J. G. Frazer, Loeb 121, 1921)

summary.en: Driven mad by Hera, Heracles kills his own family; to expiate, he serves Eurystheus and performs twelve labors — lion, hydra, hind, boar, stables, birds, bull, mares, belt, cattle, apples, Cerberus — then dies on Oeta's pyre and is taken up to Olympos.
summary.zh: 赫拉所遣瘋癲之下，赫拉克勒斯手刃親族；為贖罪服侍歐律斯透斯，歷十二勞役——獅、蛇、鹿、豬、牛廄、鳥、牛、母馬、腰帶、牛群、金蘋果、三頭犬——終於俄塔山火中成神。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary material; classification 'myth' (not 'religious') because Heracles' cult-cycle narrative circulated as heroic legend; note reasoning per README. [Merged 2026-11-11: the earlier entry 'heracles-labors' (Bulfinch, The Age of Fable, 1855, Project Gutenberg eBook #3327 — condensed paraphrase of the Nemean lion and Lernaean hydra labors) was folded in as passages 3-4 and the duplicate entry removed.]

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Apollodorus 2.4.12-2.5.1: Hera sends a madness in which Heracles hurls his children (and Megara's) into the fire; when the fit passes, he seeks purification from Delphi, where the Pythia renames him 'Glory of Hera' (Herakles) and orders him to serve Eurystheus for twelve years and perform whatever labors he is commanded. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Apollodorus 2.4.12-2.5.1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿波羅多洛斯《書庫》2.4.12–2.5.1 之節縮改述：赫拉降下瘋狂，使赫拉克勒斯將自己的孩子（以及墨伽拉的孩子）擲入火中；待狂亂平息，他前往德爾斐尋求潔淨，皮媞亞在那裡為他改名為「赫拉之榮耀」（赫拉克勒斯），並命他為歐律斯透斯服役十二年，執行所吩咐的一切苦役。非逐字引文。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Apollodorus 2.6.2-2.7.7: to fetch the golden apples of the Hesperides Heracles holds up the sky for Atlas, who fetches the fruit; to bring the hound Cerberus up from Hades he wrestles the shade of Meleager and frees Theseus, then presents the dog to the terrified Eurystheus, who returns it to the underworld. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Apollodorus 2.6.2-2.7.7; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿波羅多洛斯《書庫》2.6.2–2.7.7 之節縮改述：為取得赫斯珀里得斯的金蘋果，赫拉克勒斯替阿特拉斯撐起天空，由阿特拉斯前去摘取果實；為從冥界帶回地獄犬刻耳柏洛斯，他與墨勒阿革洛斯的亡魂搏鬥，並釋放了忒修斯，隨後將那犬帶到驚恐萬分的歐律斯透斯面前，歐律斯透斯又將其送回冥界。非逐字引文。

passages.text: Heracles, born to Zeus and the mortal woman Alcmene, drew the lasting hostility of Zeus's wife, who persecuted him from the cradle onward. Through her contrivance he was placed under the authority of his cousin Eurystheus and made to obey whatever that cousin commanded — a chained series of desperate feats the later ages counted as the twelve labors. The first task was to strip the skin from a monstrous lion that was ravaging the valley of Nemea. When club blows and arrows proved useless against the beast's hide, Heracles closed with it and throttled it with his bare hands. He then brought the whole carcass back on his shoulders; Eurystheus, so shaken by this proof of the hero's strength, ordered that future reports be delivered outside the town walls.
passages.zh: 赫拉克勒斯為宙斯與凡人女子阿爾克墨涅所生，自搖籃時起便招致宙斯之妻的持久敵意，屢遭其迫害。經她設計，他被置於表兄歐律斯透斯的權柄之下，須聽從這位表兄的一切命令——那是一連串身陷枷鎖般的絕望功業，後世稱之為十二項苦役。第一項任務是剝下一頭蹂躪涅墨亞谷地的巨獅之皮。當棍棒與箭矢對那野獸的皮毫無作用時，赫拉克勒斯與之近身相搏，徒手將其扼死。隨後他將整具屍體扛在肩上帶回；歐律斯透斯見此英雄神力之證，驚懼不已，遂下令日後一切稟報皆須在城牆之外呈遞。

passages.text: The next commission was to destroy the Hydra, which laid waste the countryside of Argos from its lair in a swamp near the well of Amymone. The creature had nine heads, and the middle one could not be killed; its defense was self-renewal, for with every head Heracles cut away, two sprang up in its place. The task became possible only through teamwork — his faithful servant Iolaus burned away each severed stump so no new heads could rise, and the one immortal head was finally buried beneath a massive rock. Even this victory brought him no lasting peace; harder labors, from the Augean stables to the golden apples of the Hesperides, still lay ahead.
passages.zh: 下一項委派是消滅九頭蛇許德拉，牠盤踞在阿密摩涅泉附近的沼澤中，禍害阿爾戈斯的鄉野。此物有九個頭，中央那顆無法殺死；其防禦在於自我再生，因為赫拉克勒斯每砍去一個頭，原處便生出兩個。唯有憑藉協力，此任務方得完成——他忠實的僕從伊俄拉俄斯燒灼每一個被砍斷的殘頸，使新頭無法再生，而那顆不死的頭最終被埋於一塊巨石之下。即便有此勝利，他也未得長久安寧；更艱難的苦役，從奧革阿斯牛圈到赫斯珀里得斯的金蘋果，仍在前方等待。

canonical_translation: J. G. Frazer, Apollodorus: The Library, Loeb 121-122 (1921)

narrative.en:
BEGINNING. Zeus fathers Herakles on Alkmene while impersonating her husband Amphitryon; Hera, jealous from birth, sends two serpents to strangle the infant, who strangles them instead. Herakles marries Megara, daughter of King Kreon of Thebes, and has children. Hera now strikes him with madness (as dramatized in Euripides' Herakles): in the fit he kills Megara and his sons, and some accounts add his brother Iphikles' children. When sanity returns, the seer, priestess at Delphi (the Pythia), and oracle together impose expiation: he must go to Tiryns, call himself by the name 'Herakles' ('Glory of Hera' — the etymology records the goddess's paradoxical ownership of the hero), and serve the king Eurystheus for twelve years, performing whatever labors are commanded, after which he will become immortal.

THE TWELVE LABORS. (1) The Nemean lion, invulnerable to iron, he strangles and wears its skin; Eurystheus thereafter hides in a bronze jar. (2) The Lernaean hydra, whose heads regrow when cut — with his nephew Iolaos he burns each neck-stump, buries the immortal head under a rock, and dips his arrows in the gall; Eurystheus disallows the labor because of the helper. (3) The Ceryneian hind with golden horns, sacred to Artemis, chased for a year and taken alive. (4) The Erymanthian boar, driven into deep snow and carried back alive. (5) The stables of Augeias, cleaned in a day by diverting the rivers Alpheios and Peneios — denied payment, he sacked Elis; this labor too was disallowed (he demanded wages). (6) The Stymphalian birds, bronze-feathered, driven from the marsh by Athena's rattle and shot down. (7) The Cretan bull, father (by Pasiphae) of the Minotaur, brought alive to Eurystheus and released to wander Marathon. (8) The man-eating mares of Diomedes of Thrace, fed their master to tame them. (9) The war-belt of the Amazon queen Hippolyte — taken (in most versions) after a treacherous brawl. (10) The cattle of the three-bodied Geryon at the far west, past the Pillars he sets up (Gibraltar/Ceuta), driving the herd home through Italy, where cattle-thieves and giants are killed along the way. (11) The golden apples of the Hesperides in Atlas' garden: he holds the sky while Atlas fetches them, tricks the Titan into taking the burden back, and brings the apples to Eurystheus, who returns them to the Hesperides; on the way he frees the chained Prometheus (whose advice steers the episode). (12) Kerberos: he descends at Taenarum, learns courtesy from the shades (Meleager's story of Atalanta; the freeing of Theseus, who is stuck fast), wrestles the hound with bare hands, and brings it up — Eurystheus leaps into his jar, and the hound goes back below.

AFTERMATH AND END. Freed labors, Herakles continues parerga: rescues Hesione at Troy, sacks Pylos, fights the river-god Acheloos for Deianira, and crosses the world in chains of service to Omphale at Sardis. Deianira, jealous, heedlessly sends him a robe soaked in the centaur Nessos' poisoned blood (as Sophocles' Trachiniae dramatizes); it burns his flesh. He builds his own pyre on Mount Oita, and Philoktetes lights it for the reward of the bow. The mortal part burns away; the divine part ascends: Hera reconciles (in late versions by nursing him), and Herakles marries Hebe on Olympos, while the image of the dead hero is worshipped in temples as Herakles the god (Heraikles). Eurystheus, outlived, is defeated by the Herakleidai, his descendants' return aition for the Dorian settlements.

FUNCTIONS. The cycle makes Herakles the panhellenic culture-hero: monster-slayer who clears land, sea, and the edges of the world for colonization (his routes map Greek trade to Gades, the Pontos, and Africa); founder of the Olympic games and of royal genealogies (the Herakleidai); the paradigmatic human who by toil (ponoi) wins immortality — the ideological bridge between mortal suffering and divine reward, ritually echoed at his shrines and in sympotic song.
narrative.zh: 宙斯化形近阿爾克墨涅而生赫拉克勒斯；赫拉自襁褓即遣蛇加害，後遣瘋癲使英雄殺妻兒。得諭示：往提任斯服歐律斯透斯十二年，行其所命之勞役，方可成神。遂歷十二役：一扼涅墨亞獅；二焚九頭蛇許德拉；三獲刻呂涅亞金角鹿；四擒厄律曼托斯野豬；五一日清奧革阿斯牛廄；六驅斯廷法利斯怪鳥；七縛克里特公牛；八馴色雷斯食人馬；九取亞馬孫女王腰帶；十驅革律翁紅牛過西極；十一代阿特拉斯擎天取赫斯珀里得斯金蘋果；十二自塔納隆下冥府擒三頭犬刻耳柏洛斯。後因涅索斯毒血之衣，於俄塔山自焚；凡軀燼滅，神性升天，娶赫柏，受享廟祀。此圈將英雄塑為清辟妖獸、開疆拓土之文化英雄，兼奧林匹亞賽會創立者、多利安諸王族始祖，並示『以勞致不死者』之範型。

functions: Panhellenic culture-hero cycle: clearing the world of monsters and aitiologizing colonization routes
Founding myth for the Olympic games and Dorian royal genealogies (Herakleidai)
Paradigm of mortal toil rewarded with immortality; ideology of expiation after pollution

variants.summary: The earliest fixed twelve-labor sequence, cited (Pausanias 9.11.2) as the reason the labors are now counted twelve; survives only in fragments, so the sequence is partly reconstructed from citation.

variants.name: Sophocles, Trachiniae
variants.summary: Retells the ending through Deianira's tragedy: the Nessos robe, Heracles' agony on Oita, and the apotheosis left offstage — foregrounding human error rather than divine plan.

variants.name: Euripides, Herakles
variants.summary: Places the madness-murder after the labors (reversing the chronological order of the prose tradition) and emphasizes Theseus' role in restoring the broken hero — an ethics-of-friendship recasting.

variants.name: Scythian version (Herodotus 4.8-10)
variants.summary: In the Scythian aition Herakles herds Geryon's cattle through the northern steppe, fathers Skythes on a half-serpent local goddess, and the triple sons' bow-test founds the Skythian royal line — a colonizing appropriation of the Greek cycle.

title.en: Bereshit: The Creation of the World and the Garden of Eden (Genesis 1-3)
title.zh: 創世記：世界之造與伊甸園

region.en: Jerusalem (symbolic pin for the Judean scribal tradition)
region.zh: 耶路撒冷（猶太書寫傳統象徵性定位）

period: Composite text: Priestly account (6th-5th c. BCE), Eden narrative (perhaps 10th-9th c. BCE, 'J'); Hebrew Bible stabilized c. 3rd c. BCE-1st c. CE; principal MS: Leningrad Codex B19a, 1008 CE

source.work: Genesis 1:1-3:24, Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia; English: Jewish Publication Society Tanakh 1917

summary.en: Two intertwined accounts: the Priestly seven-day creation by divine speech culminating in the Sabbath, and the Eden narrative of the human of dust, the garden, the tree of knowledge, the serpent, and the expulsion that founds human mortality and toil.
summary.zh: 兩敘事交織：祭司典七日以言造世、以安息日作結；伊甸園敘述摶土之人、知識樹、蛇與逐出——人類勞碌與有死之由來。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Treated with respect: divine names handled per Jewish convention (the Tetragrammaton is not pronounced; the English renders it 'the LORD'). No liturgical or restricted material is reproduced.

passages.text: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. Now the earth was unformed and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep; and the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters. And God said: 'Let there be light.' And there was light.
passages.zh: 起初，神創造天地。那時大地混沌空虛，黑暗籠罩深淵的表面；神的靈運行在水面上。神說：「要有光。」就有了光。

passages.text: And the LORD God said: 'Behold, the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil; and now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever.' Therefore the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken.
passages.zh: 主神說：「看哪，那人已與我們相似，能知善惡；如今恐怕他伸手又摘生命樹的果子吃，就永遠活著。」於是主神打發他離開伊甸園，去耕種他所出自的土地。

canonical_translation: Jewish Publication Society Tanakh (1917), public domain

narrative.en:
The book of Genesis opens with two successively layered creation narratives that Jewish and Christian tradition have read as one continuous story.

ACCOUNT ONE: SEVEN DAYS (PRIESTLY SOURCE, GEN 1:1-2:4a). Before the world there are 'the deep' (tehom) and a waste-and-void earth (tohu va-bohu) swept by a divine wind/spirit — a primordial state of undifferentiated waters rather than a battle. God creates entirely by speech in seven liturgical days. Day one: light, separated from darkness and named Day and Night. Day two: a firmament (raqia) dividing waters above from waters below, named Heaven. Day three: waters gathered so dry land appears (named Earth and Seas), and the earth brings forth vegetation. Day four: the great lights — sun, moon, stars — to rule day and night and mark sacred times. Day five: swarms of living creatures in sea and air, blessed 'be fruitful and multiply'. Day six: land animals, and finally humanity — male and female together — made 'in the image and likeness of God' (selem u-demut) and given dominion over the creatures and seed-bearing plants for food. Day seven: God rests from all the work, blesses the seventh day and sanctifies it — the institution of the Sabbath and the theological signature of the Priestly telling. The account closes with the formula that these are 'the generations of the heavens and of the earth when they were created'.

ACCOUNT TWO: EDEN (GEN 2:4b-3:24). A second, older narrative begins with the day the LORD God (YHWH-Elohim) made earth and heaven: no plant yet grew, for there was no rain and no man to till the ground. God forms the human (ha-adam) from dust of the ground (adamah) — a deliberate wordplay — breathes into his nostrils the breath of life, and plants a garden in Eden watered by four rivers. The human is placed there 'to till it and to keep it', permitted every tree except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, 'for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die'. God then observes 'it is not good that the man should be alone'; the animals are named (no helper found among them), and God casts a deep sleep, takes one side/rib, and builds the woman. The man's exclamation ('bone of my bones, flesh of my flesh') grounds the narrative's closing comment on marriage, and the pair stand 'naked and not ashamed'.

THE TRANSGRESSION. The serpent, 'more subtle than any beast of the field', asks the woman whether God forbade all the trees; she answers that even touching the forbidden tree means death. The serpent denies the death, promises godlike knowledge, and she eats, giving fruit to her husband. Their eyes open; they sew fig leaves. When they hear God walking in the garden's breeze they hide; questioned, the man blames the woman, the woman the serpent. The judgments are spoken in order: the serpent is cursed to crawl and eat dust, with an enmity announced between its seed and the woman's; the woman gets pain in childbirth and a husband who 'shall rule over thee'; the man gets the cursed ground, thorns, thistles, and bread by the sweat of his face. God clothes them in coats of skins — the first act of mercy — and expels them 'lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and live for ever'. East of Eden, cherubim and a flaming sword turn every way 'to keep the way of the tree of life'. The narrative flows into the birth of Cain and Abel (4:1-16), where the pattern of fraternal violence continues.

FUNCTIONS. The Priestly day-structure sanctifies the Sabbath as creation's climax — the core of Jewish liturgical time; the Eden story aitiologizes human mortality, agricultural toil, the pain of childbirth, the snake's form, and shame; the whole sequence, read in the synagogue from the fall festival cycle onward, grounds Israel's theology of an ordered, spoken creation without combat myth (contrast Enuma Elish, where the sea-goddess is slain).
narrative.zh: 祭司典七日造世：以言創造，光、穹蒼、陸地草木、日月星辰、海空生物、陸獸與人（按神形像造，男與女），第七日安息祝聖。伊甸敘事：耶和華神摶土造人，吹生氣成活魂；置園使耕守，惟知識樹之果不可食。亞當無配，神取其肋骨造夏娃，二人赤身不羞。蛇誘之食，二人目明知羞；神問罪，蛇受咒伏行，女受產痛，男受地詛與汗面糊口；神以皮衣蔽之，恐其復摘生命樹，遂逐出伊甸，遣基路伯與火焰劍守樹。全文功能：安息日之立、人類有死勞碌之釋義、以及與巴比倫爭戰型創世神話對照之『以言造世』神學。

functions: Institution of the Sabbath as liturgical re-enactment of creation's seventh day
Aitia for mortality, toil, childbirth pain, and the serpent's posture
Theological demythologization: creation by word, without combat with the sea
Torah-cycle reading in the synagogue (Bereshit section, annual lectionary)

variants.name: Priestly vs. 'J' doublets
variants.summary: The two accounts differ in divine name, method (speech vs. crafting and breathing), sequence (plants-animal-human vs. human-animals-woman), and setting (world-ocean vs. rainless steppe); source-critical scholarship (Wellhausen onward) reads them as independently composed traditions joined by redactors.

variants.name: Babylonian Enuma Elish parallel
variants.text_tradition: Seven Tablets of Creation (c. 18th-12th c. BCE)
variants.summary: Marduk defeats the sea-dragon Tiamat and builds cosmos from her halves; humanity is made from a rebel god's blood to serve the gods. Genesis shares motifs (waters, firmament-divide, rest of the deity) but removes combat and divine servitude — the sea becomes tehom, 'the deep', an inanimate mass.

variants.name: Combat-myth remnants in poetry
variants.summary: Israelite poetry preserves older dismemberment imagery: God 'breaks the heads of the dragons (tanninim) on the waters' and 'smites Rahab'; later Hebrew literature retains the sea-battle as liturgical metaphor while the Genesis prose account excludes it.

variants.name: Second Temple expansions
variants.text_tradition: 1 Enoch 6-16 (Book of Watchers); Jubilees 2-3 (2nd c. BCE); b. Sanhedrin 38b (rabbinic)
variants.summary: Genesis 6:1-4's 'sons of God' are expanded into the Watchers' descent; Jubilees numbers the days and gives Eden a cultic geography; rabbinic midrash adds the two Adams, the angels' creation debate, and the serpent's role. The MT consonantal text is unchanged in all three.

title.en: The Flood of Noah and the First Covenant (Genesis 6-9)
title.zh: 挪亞洪水與首立之約（創世記六至九章）

region.en: Mount Ararat region (traditional landing; symbolic pin)
region.zh: 亞拉臘山地區（傳統停靠地；象徵性定位）

period: Composite: 'J' flood source and Priestly source joined in exilic/post-exilic redaction; text stabilized c. 5th c. BCE; principal MS: Leningrad Codex B19a, 1008 CE

source.work: Genesis 6:5-9:29, Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia; English: JPS Tanakh 1917

summary.en: Human corruption moves God to un-create the world by water; Noah builds the ark, the flood drowns all flesh, and upon the dry land's return God binds an unconditional covenant sealed by the rainbow, founding the renewed human order under the Noachide rules.
summary.zh: 人類敗壞，神以洪水滅世；挪亞造方舟攜生靈得存；地乾之後，神以虹為記立約，並以挪亞七誡重啟人間秩序。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition; quoted from public-domain JPS 1917 with standard conventions (Tetragrammaton rendered 'the LORD').

passages.text: I do set My bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between Me and the earth. And it shall come to pass, when I bring clouds over the earth, and the bow is seen in the cloud, that I will remember My covenant, which is between Me and you and every living creature of all flesh; and the waters shall no more become a flood to destroy all flesh.
passages.zh: 我把虹放在雲彩中，這就可作我與地立約的記號了。我使雲彩蓋地的時候，必有虹現在雲彩中，我便記念我與你們和各樣有血肉的活物所立的約；水就再不氾濫、毀壞一切有血肉的物了。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Genesis 7-8: Noah enters the ark with his household and the animals; rain falls forty days and forty nights while the deeps of the great abyss are broken open; the waters prevail fifteen cubits above the mountains, then subside in dated stages until the twenty-seventh day of the second month, when the earth is dry and Noah leads the creatures out. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Genesis 7-8; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《創世記》第七至八章的濃縮意譯：挪亞帶著家眷和牲畜進入方舟；大雨降了四十晝夜，大深淵的泉源都裂開了；水勢比山高過十五肘，隨後按著所記的日期逐步消退，直到二月二十七日，地就乾了，挪亞便領著眾活物出來。非逐字照錄。

canonical_translation: Jewish Publication Society Tanakh (1917), public domain

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: THE DECREE. The sons of God have taken the daughters of men; giants (Nephilim) are in the land; and 'God saw that the wickedness of man was great, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually', so that God 'repents' having made humanity and resolves to destroy 'man, beast, creeping thing, and fowl'. One exception: 'Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD', a righteous man, 'perfect in his generations', who 'walked with God'. God announces the decree — 'The end of all flesh is come before Me... behold, I will destroy them with the earth' — and commands Noah to build a tebah (ark) of gopher wood, pitched (kaphar) within and without, three hundred cubits long, with rooms, a window, and a door in its side; into it all flesh shall come 'to keep them alive' — the Priestly text specifies one pair of every kind, the older source seven pairs of clean animals and one pair of unclean, a distinction needed for Noah's later sacrifice.

MIDDLE: THE DELUGE. 'In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, the seventeenth day of the month' the fountains of the great deep are broken and the windows of heaven opened; rain falls forty days and nights (the older narrative), while the Priestly text tracks the waters rising fifteen cubits over the mountains and prevailing one hundred and fifty days. 'All in whose nostrils was the breath of life... died'; only Noah and those with him remain. The waters subside by dated stages (the ark grounding on Ararat in the seventh month; mountain tops seen in the tenth; the earth dry in the six hundred and first year, twenty-seventh day of the second month). Noah tests the waters first with a raven, then three times with a dove — returning with nothing, then with a freshly plucked olive leaf, then not at all. The double bird test (raven/dove) belongs to the older narrative, the precise calendar to the Priestly; the redactor interlaces both.

END: COVENANT AND RENEWAL. Noah builds an altar and offers burnt offerings of every clean beast and fowl; the LORD smells 'a sweet savour' and vows in his heart: 'I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake... neither will I again smite any more every thing living, as I have done. While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease' (8:21-22). God now blesses Noah and his sons: 'Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth'; animals fear humanity; meat is permitted but blood forbidden — 'whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed, for in the image of God made he man' (9:6). God establishes His covenant (berit) — unconditional, 'with you, and with your seed after you, and with every living creature' — signed by the bow (qeshet) in the cloud: the warrior's weapon hung up, never again to destroy all flesh by flood.

CLOSING EPISODE. Noah plants a vineyard, drinks, lies uncovered in his tent; Ham 'sees his father's nakedness' and reports it; Shem and Japhet cover him walking backward. Waking, Noah curses Canaan, Ham's son, to servitude to Shem and Japhet — the narrative aition grounding the Israelite view of Canaanite peoples and, in the redacted genealogy of ch. 10-11, the table of nations from which Abram will be called.

FUNCTIONS. In Jewish liturgical life the flood section is read annually in the Torah cycle; the Noachide rules (blood prohibition, and in rabbinic expansion seven commands for the children of Noah) become the covenantal frame for humanity at large; the rainbow covenant is the archetype of biblical covenant theology; and the narrative's precise dates regulate a Priestly theology of sacred time. Theologically it re-sets creation — a de-creation and re-creation — with covenant, not combat, subduing the waters.
narrative.zh: 世人敗壞，神命挪亞造歌斐木方舟，內外施松香；潔畜七對、不潔一對俱入舟。二月十七日，深淵泉源裂，天窗洞開，大雨四十晝夜，水漲過山十五肘；凡有生氣者皆滅。水勢漸消：七月十七日舟擱亞拉臘山，十月見山頂，挪亞先放烏鴉，再三放鴿，第三次銜回新橄欖葉，遂知地乾。出舟後築壇獻潔牲為燔祭，耶和華聞馨香，誓言不再因人咒詛地，四時寒暑晝夜永不停息。遂賜福挪亞眾子，准食肉而禁血，凡流人血者必被人流；又立永約，以虹為記，不再以洪水滅凡有血肉者。末尾葡萄園一章釋迦南族受咒之由。功能：會堂年讀經課、挪亞七誡之普世約框架、彩虹約為聖約神學原型。

functions: Annual synagogue Torah-cycle reading (Noah section of Bereshit)
Archetype of covenant theology; rainbow as divine self-binding
Noachide rules as the covenantal frame for humanity as a whole
Priestly sacred calendar: dated stages regulating the flood narrative

variants.name: Source-critical doublets ('J' vs. Priestly)
variants.summary: Two flood narratives differ in animal counts (7 pairs vs. 1 pair), duration (40 days vs. 150+ days), divine name, and motive (sweet savour vs. covenant); the redactor interleaved them verse by verse, a key case of classical source criticism.

variants.name: Old Babylonian Atrahasis
variants.text_tradition: Old Babylonian tablets (c. 17th c. BCE), scribe Ipiq-Aya
variants.summary: The flood is sent to stop human overpopulation/noise, not corruption; the survivor Atrahasis is granted immortality; population-control measures end the story. Shares the ark-announcement formula ('wall, listen'), the sealed boat, and the bird tests.

variants.name: Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh, Tablet XI
variants.summary: Utnapishtim retells the flood to Gilgamesh as a embedded narrative: secret warning through a reed wall, cube-ark, seven days of storm, gods 'gathered like flies', Enlil's rage and blessing. Near-verbatim parallel to Genesis' boat instructions; the raven episode is identical.

variants.name: Sumerian Ziusudra flood
variants.text_tradition: Fragment Nippur tablet Ni 9625 (Old Babylonian copy of Sumerian poem)
variants.summary: The earliest attested Mesopotamian flood: Ziusudra, a pious king, is warned in a dream, rides out the deluge, and is granted eternal life in Dilmun; heavily fragmentary and reconstructed by scholarly restoration.

variants.name: Quranic Nuh narrative
variants.summary: Noah (Nuh) preaches to his people for 950 years; one son refuses the ark and drowns; the arc of prophetic warning replaces covenant legislation. Cross-tradition comparandum for the Islamic corpus.

title.en: Yetziat Mitzrayim: Oppression, Signs, Plagues, and the Sea (Exodus 1-15)
title.zh: 出埃及記：壓迫、神蹟、十災與過海（出埃及記一至十五章）

region.en: Jebel Musa, Sinai (traditional pin for Horeb/Sinai; symbolic)
region.zh: 西奈山傳統地點（象徵性定位）

period: Composite narrative (oldest strata 10th-8th c. BCE; Priestly redaction exilic; final form 5th c. BCE); principal MS: Leningrad Codex B19a, 1008 CE

summary.en: Israel's children are enslaved; Moses is drawn from the Nile, called at the burning bush, and sent back to confront Pharaoh; ten plagues break Pharaoh's resistance, the Passover is instituted, and the sea splits so Israel crosses dry-shod — the founding liberation narrative of Judaism, commemorated every Pesach.
summary.zh: 以色列人為奴；摩西自尼羅河被撈起，於焚而不毀之荊棘蒙召；十災迫法老釋放；逾越節設立，海水分開，以色列人行乾地而過——猶太教之根本解放敘事，年年於逾越節重述。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition, retold ritually at the Passover Seder (Haggadah). The Haggadah's rabbinic liturgy is protected material — only the biblical text from public-domain JPS 1917 is quoted.

passages.text: And God said unto Moses: 'I AM THAT I AM'; and He said: 'Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel: I AM hath sent me unto you.' Condensed paraphrase of Exodus 14:21-25: Moses stretches his hand over the sea; the LORD drives the water back by a strong east wind all night, and the children of Israel go through on dry ground, the waters a wall on right and left. Pharaoh's chariots pursue; at the morning watch the LORD looks through the pillar of fire and cloud, clogs the wheels, and the sea returns upon the army. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Exodus 14; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 神對摩西說：「我是自有永有的」；又說：「你要對以色列人這樣說：『那自有的打發我到你們這裡來。』」《出埃及記》第十四章二十一至二十五節的濃縮意譯：摩西向海伸杖；耶和華用強烈的東風，一夜之間使水退去，以色列人便走乾地過去，水在他們左右作了牆垣。法老的戰車追來；到了晨更的時候，耶和華從火柱雲柱中觀看，使車輪脫落，海水便回流淹沒了軍兵。非逐字照錄。

canonical_translation: Jewish Publication Society Tanakh (1917), public domain

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: OPPRESSION AND THE DRAWN CHILD. The sons of Israel multiply in Egypt until 'a new king' who 'knew not Joseph' enslaves them with rigor. Pharaoh orders the Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah to kill every boy; they fear God and defy him, and God 'made them houses'. Pharaoh commands all Egyptians to cast every son into the Nile. A Levite woman hides her son three months, sets him in an ark (tebah — the same word as Noah's) of bulrushes among the reeds; Pharaoh's daughter draws him out and names him Moshe, 'because I drew him out of the water' (Hebrew mashah). Raised at court, Moses kills an Egyptian overseer striking a Hebrew brother, flees to Midian, marries Zipporah daughter of Jethro, and shepherds.

THE CALL. At Horeb, 'the mountain of God', the angel of the LORD appears 'in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush', which burns without being consumed. God announces: 'I have surely seen the affliction of my people... and am come down to deliver them', sending Moses to Pharaoh and naming the goal — 'bring forth my people... out of that place unto a good and large land'. Asked His name, God answers 'Ehyeh asher Ehyeh' — 'I AM THAT I AM' — 'Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel: I AM hath sent me unto you', and gives the Tetragrammaton as the name of remembrance. Lacking eloquence, Moses is given his brother Aaron as mouth, and a tripartite mission: gather the elders, perform signs (rod to serpent, leprous hand, water to blood), and demand, 'Let us go, we pray thee, three days' journey into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God'.

THE HARDENING AND THE PLAGUES. Pharaoh answers by increasing the brick-quota. The redactional refrain follows — sometimes 'Pharaoh hardened his heart', sometimes 'the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart' — through escalating signs and plagues in which each Egyptian god-figure is defeated: blood (all water), frogs, lice/gnats (also called kinnim), swarms of flies, pestilence on cattle, boils and blains, hail with fire running on the ground, locusts, darkness 'which may be felt'; the fourth plague on begins to separate Goshen (Israel spared). Moses is God's 'god to Pharaoh' and Aaron his prophet; the rod, the outstretched hand, and the fixed set-times structure each plague.

PASSOVER AND THE TENTH PLAGUE. The month is inaugurated ('this month shall be unto you the beginning of months'); each household takes a lamb without blemish, kills it at twilight on the fourteenth day, marks doorposts with blood, eats it roasted with unleavened bread (matzot) and bitter herbs 'with loins girded, shoes on feet, staff in hand' — 'it is the LORD's passover (pesach)'. At midnight the LORD smites all the firstborn of Egypt 'from the firstborn of Pharaoh... unto the firstborn of the captive... and all the firstborn of cattle', while the destroyer passes over the blood-marked houses. Pharaoh sends them out; the Israelites 'borrow' Egyptian jewels at the peoples' favor, and unleavened cakes are baked 'because they were thrust out of Egypt, and could not tarry'. The festival statute is given: seven days of matzot, 'in the first month, at even, ye shall eat unleavened bread, until the one and twentieth day of the month at even', and 'thou shalt tell thy son in that day, saying: It is because of that which the LORD did for me when I came forth out of Egypt'.

THE SEA. God leads them not by the Philistine road but 'by the way of the wilderness', in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night. Encamped by the sea at Pi-hahiroth, they are trapped as Pharaoh repents and pursues with six hundred chariots; the people cry out, Moses answers, 'Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD'. The angel and cloud move behind them; Moses stretches his hand over the sea, and 'the LORD caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all that night' (the Priestly note); Israel crosses on dry ground, walls of water right and left. At the morning watch the LORD 'looked through the pillar of fire and of the cloud' upon the Egyptian host, took off their chariot wheels, and the returning waters covered 'the chariots, and the horsemen, and all the host of Pharaoh'.

THE SONG. Israel's answer is the Song of the Sea (Exod 15:1-18), among the oldest Hebrew poems: 'I will sing unto the LORD, for He is highly exalted; the horse and his rider hath He thrown into the sea. My strength and song is the LORD... The LORD is my strength and might; He is become my salvation; this is my God, and I will glorify Him... Thy right hand, O LORD, dasheth in pieces the enemy... Thou in Thy love hast led the people whom Thou hast redeemed; Thou hast guided them in Thy strength unto Thy holy habitation... The LORD shall reign for ever and ever.' Miriam the prophetess, Aaron's sister, takes a timbrel, and all the women answer her in dance and refrain. The column then moves into the wilderness — bitter waters sweetened at Marah, quails and manna given (ch. 16), water from the rock at Rephidim — en route to the mountain where the covenant will be made.

FUNCTIONS. This is Israel's foundational redemption narrative: the mandated household retelling ('thou shalt tell thy son') structures the Passover Seder and the Haggadah; the manna legislation grounds the Sabbath (double portion on the sixth day); the Song of the Sea entered early liturgy; and the exodus became the central hermeneutic of liberation — invoked in seder liturgy 'in every generation one must see himself as if he came out of Egypt', in rabbinic tradition, and in later emancipation movements worldwide.
narrative.zh: 新王不識約瑟，苦役以色列人，又命溺殺男嬰；利未婦人匿子三月，置蒲草箱於河畔，法老之女撈起，名之摩西。摩西殺埃及人後逃米甸牧羊；至何烈山，耶和華使者於火焰荊棘中顯現，宣示眷顧降救；摩西問名，得『我就是我』之答。返埃及後，亞倫為口，屢以杖行神蹟；法老心硬，遂有血、蛙、蝨、蠅、疫、瘡、雹、蝗、暗諸災，末災之前設逾越節禮：取無殘疾羔羊，血塗門楣，腰束手杖急食無酵餅苦菜。正月十四日夜，埃及一切長子盡亡，法老逐以色列人出；行至海邊，追兵六百戰車至；摩西伸杖，東風使海退，以色列人行乾地，埃及軍覆沒。遂有海之歌：『我要向耶和華歌唱，因祂大大戰勝，將馬和騎馬的投在海中。』米利暗擊鼓應和。其後瑪拉苦水變甜、鵪鶉嗎哪降下，往西奈山而去。功能：逾越節家述『當日要告訴你的兒子』、嗎哪立法立安息日、海之歌入禮儀，並為後世解放釋義之根本範型。

functions: Mandated intergenerational retelling: charter of the Passover Seder and Haggadah
Sabbath grounding via manna legislation (Exod 16)
Song of the Sea as early liturgical poem; Miriam's dance as women's ritual leadership
Master-hermeneutic of liberation in Jewish (and later universal) emancipation discourse

variants.name: Samaritan Pentateuch readings
variants.text_tradition: Samarran Torah (Ms. Abisha tradition; standard edition A. von Gall)
variants.summary: The Samaritan text harmonizes the hardening refrains toward divine causation and adjusts the tenth plague and the P festival calendrics; significant for tracking the literary development of the plagues narrative.

variants.name: Septuagint (Greek) version
variants.summary: Renders tebah as kibotos and pesach as pascha; famously reads the 430 years of sojourning as 'in Egypt and in Canaan' (Exod 12:40 LXX) against the MT, and supplies the 'hand of the Lord' formula where the MT varies — the version through which early Christian seder-influence flows.

variants.name: Song of the Sea as independent poetic tradition
variants.text_tradition: Exod 15:1-18 (and Miriam's refrain 15:21); parallels in Judges 5
variants.summary: Meter and archaic language argue for an older victory hymn incorporated into the prose narrative; Miriam's one-line antiphon (15:21) implies a separate performance tradition in which women led the refrain.

variants.name: Deuteronomic credo recensions
variants.summary: Compressed liturgical cretelling ('My father was a wandering Aramean...') for first-fruits recitation — evidence that the exodus narrative functioned as a fixed ritual script already in the First Temple period.

variants.name: Quranic Musa narratives
variants.summary: Pharaoh is named Fir'aun; the sorcerers submit at the staff miracle; Pharaoh's drowning ends with God preserving his body 'as a sign'. Key comparandum for the Islamic corpus (separate record planned).
