title.en: Obatala, Oduduwa, and the Creation of Ile-Ife
title.zh: 奧巴塔拉、奧杜杜瓦與伊費創世

region.en: Ile-Ife, Osun State, Nigeria
region.zh: 尼日利亞奧孫州伊雷-伊費

period: Oral tradition; recorded ethnographically c. 1938 onward (Bascom field recordings); Ifa odu corpus transmitted orally for centuries (UNESCO Intangible Heritage 2008)

source.archive: William Bascom, Ifa Divination: Communication between Gods and Men in West Africa (Bloomington, 1969)
source.work: Ile-Ife creation narratives (Obatala/Oduduwa traditions) recorded by William Bascom and Yoruba scholars; Wande Abimbola, Ifa: An Exposition of Ifa Literary Corpus (Ibadan, 1976)

license: Paraphrase summaries only; underlying oral texts are community heritage and are not reproduced verbatim

summary.en: Olodumare sends Obatala down from heaven on a chain with sand, a hen, and a palm kernel; drunk on palm wine, he sleeps, and Oduduwa completes the work, pouring the sand that becomes Ile-Ife — 'where the day broke' — the navel of the Yoruba world and the origin of its kings; Obatala is given the molding of human bodies from clay.
summary.zh: 至高神奧洛杜馬雷遣奧巴塔拉沿鐵鍊降世，攜沙、雞與棕櫚仁；奧巴塔拉因棕櫚酒醉眠，奧杜杜瓦代之傾沙成陸，成為伊費——『破曉之地』、約魯巴世界之臍與諸王之源；奧巴塔拉則受命以土塑人身。

sensitivity.note: Not excluded: this record contains paraphrase summaries only, built from published scholarship (Bascom 1969; Abimbola 1976). Some Ifa odu verses and royal Ife narratives ARE initiate-restricted and are not reproduced; see sensitivity_guidance and sensitivity_flag (living_tradition_high).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Ife tradition as published by Bascom (1969) and Abimbola (1976): Olodumare, the supreme being, sends Obatala from heaven on a chain, carrying a snail-shell of loose earth, a five-toed hen, and a palm kernel; Obatala first consults Ifa (the odu prescribed the offerings), pours the earth on the primordial waters, and the hen scratches it outward until land spreads — where the spread stops, hills rise; he plants the palm kernel and names the place Ife. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Ife tradition as published by Bascom (1969) and Abimbola (1976); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 根據 Bascom（1969）與 Abimbola（1976）所出版的伊費傳統之濃縮改寫：至高存在奧洛杜馬雷從天上用一條鎖鏈派遣奧巴塔拉下凡，他帶著一隻裝有鬆散泥土的蝸牛殼、一隻五趾母雞與一顆棕櫚仁；奧巴塔拉先請教伊法（odu 規定了祭品），將泥土倒在原初之水面上，母雞將其向外刨開，直到陸地蔓延開來——在蔓延停止之處，山丘升起；他種下棕櫚仁，並將此地命名為伊費。非逐字引用。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Obatala/Oduduwa episode as published by Bascom (1969): Obatala, on arriving, drinks palm wine (breaking his taboo for the mission) and sleeps; Oduduwa takes the materials and completes the pouring and spreading; the brothers dispute precedence, and Olodumare assigns Obatala the molding of human bodies from clay — whose imperfect forms (hunchbacks, cripples) explain human difference and Obatala's protective care for the deformed. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Obatala/Oduduwa episode as published by Bascom (1969); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 根據 Bascom（1969）所出版的奧巴塔拉／奧杜杜瓦插曲之濃縮改寫：奧巴塔拉抵達後飲下棕櫚酒（為此使命破了自己的禁忌）並睡去；奧杜杜瓦取走材料，完成傾倒與鋪展；兄弟二人爭論誰為長，奧洛杜馬雷將以黏土塑造人體的職責分派給奧巴塔拉——其不完美的形體（駝背者、跛足者）解釋了人類的差異，以及奧巴塔拉對畸形者的保護性關懷。非逐字引用。

language: Yoruba (oral, tonal; Ifa chants in recitative style)
canonical_translation: Published scholarly paraphrases (Bascom 1969; Abimbola 1976); no canonical written text exists — the tradition is oral and variant

narrative.en:
The Ife creation narrative is not a single text but a family of oral traditions, recited in Ifa divination verses (odu) and in royal praise-poetry, with regional and political variants. The summary below follows the published scholarly paraphrases and flags the contested points.

BEGINNING: THE DESCENT. In the beginning there is only sky (orun) and the watery waste (aye) below, over which Olodumare (Olorun, the owner/sky-being) rules. Olodumare determines to create solid land and chooses Obatala, the first orisha of the royal line, to do it: first, Obatala must consult Ifa, the divination system of Orunmila, whose odu prescribe the offerings (the divination myth itself is thereby the charter of Ifa's primacy). Obatala descends from heaven on a long chain, carrying a snail-shell of loose earth, a five-toed hen, and a palm kernel. Arriving over the waters, he pours the earth into a heap; the hen scratches and scatters it outward in every direction until it forms land — where the spreading stopped, hills remain (the aition of Ife's topography). Obatala plants the palm kernel (from which the palm tree grows, source of wine, oil, and many uses) and names the place Ile-Ife — 'the house of spreading' or, in the common gloss, 'the place where the day broke' (ibere aye), the spot where the world's light first shone.

MIDDLE: THE DRUNKEN SLEEP AND ODUDUWA. Obatala, having accomplished the work, drinks palm wine — in some tellings to celebrate, in others seduced by the tree he planted — and breaks the taboo of his mission. He sleeps. Oduduwa (in Ife tradition a brother or fellow-divine agent; in Oyo royal tradition, the ancestor-sultan who completed creation) takes the snail-shell and the hen, completes the pouring, and claims the work: 'I have created the earth.' On waking, Obatala is humiliated; the brothers dispute precedence, and Olodumare intervenes: Oduduwa's act stands — the earth is his — and the earth's kingship descends through him (the Ooni of Ife and, in Oyo versions, the Alaafin claim descent); Obatala is consoled with a different office: the molding of human bodies.

END: THE MOLDING OF HUMANKIND. Obatala, at the hill of Ife (in some tellings at a house of clay), molds human figures from earth — each one different, some hunchbacked, some crippled, some blind — and Olodumare breathes life into them. The deformed bodies are Obatala's work and therefore under his protection: the tradition aitiologizes both human difference and the Orisha's care for the disabled, and grounds Obatala's cult taboos (no palm wine; white cloth, purity, coolness — Obatala is the orisha of white chalk, of calm heads and clear judgment). Ile-Ife remains the sacred origin-point: 'Ife is where the work of creation was done' — the origin of humanity and the source from which kingship radiated to the Yoruba kingdoms (Oyo, Benin's dynasty in some tellings, Ketu, Sabe) — and the Ooni of Ife is acknowledged as spiritual head of the Yoruba world.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative is the charter of Yoruba kingship (the Ife-centered royal genealogies), of Ifa's divinatory primacy (the odu consulted before the descent), of Obatala's cult (white cloth, palm-wine taboo, care for the deformed), and of Ile-Ife's sacred geography (topography aitiologized; the Ooni's primacy). It is also the ground on which 19th-20th century 'Yoruba' identity was built — the ethnonym itself is a modern back-formation, and the narrative's political variants map real inter-kingdom rivalries (Ife vs. Oyo vs. Benin).
narrative.zh: 太初唯有天界與下方水域。奧洛杜馬雷遣奧巴塔拉沿鐵鍊降世，先諮詢伊法占卜（奧杜經文定祭品）：攜蝸牛殼之沙、五趾雞與棕櫚仁；傾沙於水，雞抓而四散，陸地遂成，丘留於散處；植棕櫚仁，名其地伊費——『破曉之地』。奧巴塔拉因棕櫚酒破戒而眠；奧杜杜瓦代之傾沙、完成造陸，兄弟爭先，奧洛杜馬雷裁定：地歸奧杜杜瓦，王權沿其後裔（伊費之奧尼、奧約之阿拉芬皆有宣稱）；奧巴塔拉受命以土塑人，形體或有殘缺，皆其所造而受其護佑——釋人類之異與其白布、禁酒、護殘之祭儀。伊費遂為神聖起源之地與約魯巴王權之放射中心。功能：王權憲章、伊法占卜至上之證、奧巴塔拉祭儀之根、伊費地理之釋義。

functions: Charter of Yoruba kingship: Ife as origin-point and the Ooni's spiritual primacy
Ifa divination's primacy: the odu consulted before creation itself
Obatala's cult: white cloth, palm-wine taboo, and care for the deformed
Ethnogenesis: the narrative's political variants map Ife-Oyo-Benin rivalries

variants.name: Ife version (Obatala first, Oduduwa completes)
variants.text_tradition: Ile-Ife royal and Ifa tradition (recorded Bascom 1969; Abimbola 1976)
variants.summary: Obatala descends, drinks, and sleeps; Oduduwa completes the work and is given the earth; Obatala is given the molding of humans. The Ooni of Ife is the world's spiritual head.

variants.name: Oyo version (Oduduwa as founder-ancestor)
variants.text_tradition: Alaafin's court traditions (recorded in Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, 1921, from 19th c. Oyo accounts)
variants.summary: Oduduwa is the first king of Ife and father of the dynasties; Obatala's role is reduced or omitted — the Oyo imperial claim to legitimacy, politically motivated against Ife's primacy.

variants.name: Benin version (Eweka line)
variants.text_tradition: Benin royal tradition (recorded in Jacob Egharevba, A Short History of Benin, 1934)
variants.summary: Oduduwa's son Oranmiyan (Eweka) founds the Benin dynasty — the story radiates Ife's kingship outward and grounds Benin's own legitimacy claims.

variants.name: Ifa odu recitations (Oduduwa/Obatala in divination verses)
variants.text_tradition: Ifa corpus (256 odu, oral, sung); Bascom 1969 records verses with named informants and odù names
variants.summary: The creation narrative appears inside divination verses as the moral-mythic warrant for divination's fees and sacrifices — the same story functions as ritual charter rather than origin-tale; some odu are initiate-restricted and not published.

title.en: Maui of Aotearoa: The Snared Sun, the Fished Island, and Hine-nui-te-po
title.zh: 毛利之毛伊：縛日、釣島與夜之女神

region.en: Te Ika-a-Maui (North Island), Aotearoa New Zealand
region.zh: 紐西蘭北島（『毛伊之魚』）

period: Oral tradition; recorded in Sir George Grey's Polynesian Mythology (Auckland, 1855) from named Te Arawa informants incl. Wiremu Maihi Te Rangikaheke

source.archive: NZETC (Victoria University of Wellington) / Internet Archive (Grey 1855)
source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race (Auckland, 1855); Margaret Orbell, The Illustrated Encyclopedia of Maori Myth and Legend (Christchurch, 1995)

license: Grey 1855 public domain; Orbell 1995 quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Maui-tikitiki-a-Taranga, last-born and mocked, snares the sun with ropes to slow its race; fishes up the North Island with a hook of ancestral jawbone and his own blood; steals fire's secret from Mahuika; and finally, seeking immortality, enters the sleeping giantess of death, Hine-nui-te-po — the birds laugh, she wakes, and death remains in the world.
summary.zh: 幼子毛伊遭兄嘲弄，以繩縛日使其慢行；以祖顎骨之鉤、自血為餌，釣起北島；自火神瑪胡伊卡處竊得火種之秘；末欲求不死，潛入睡臥之死亡巨女希紐伊特波——雀鳥輕笑，巨女驚醒，人類自此有死。

sensitivity.note: Living Maori tradition (matauranga Maori). Grey 1855 is a colonial-era collection of named Te Arawa informants, published with attribution; contemporary iwi and Maori scholarship (Orbell) is prioritized. Some narratives are tapu in context; only published paraphrases are reproduced.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Grey (1855), 'Maui and the Sun': Maui says to his brothers: 'Let us snare the sun, that he may not travel so fast'; they twist ropes of flax, and when the sun rises from his pit, Maui beats him with the enchanted jawbone of Murirangawhenua until he promises to go slowly — hence the long days of summer. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Grey (1855), 'Maui and the Sun'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 根據格雷（1855）〈毛伊與太陽〉之濃縮改寫：毛伊對他的兄弟們說：「讓我們套住太陽，使他不能走得那麼快」；他們搓編亞麻繩，當太陽從他的坑中升起時，毛伊以穆里蘭加威努亞的魔法顎骨擊打他，直到他承諾緩慢而行——因此夏季白晝漫長。非逐字引用。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Grey (1855), 'Maui and Hine-nui-te-po': Maui says: 'Let us seek death or life; if she sleeps, I will enter her body and pass through it, and death shall have no power.' The little birds (tiwaiwaka, fantail) laugh at his approach and wake her; the thighs close, and Maui is killed — hence death came into the world, and no man has escaped it since. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Grey (1855), 'Maui and Hine-nui-te-po'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 根據格雷（1855）〈毛伊與希內努伊特波〉之濃縮改寫：毛伊說：「讓我們去尋求死亡或生命；若她睡著，我將進入她的身體並穿過它，死亡便無能為力。」小鳥（tiwaiwaka，扇尾鶲）在他接近時發笑並喚醒了她；雙腿合攏，毛伊被殺——因此死亡進入世界，自此無人逃脫。非逐字引用。

canonical_translation: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, 1855 (public domain); Margaret Orbell, Maori Myth and Legend, 1995 (modern Maori-authored synthesis)

narrative.en:
The Maori Maui cycle is the best-documented Polynesian variant of a figure known across the Pacific (Hawaiian, Samoan, Tongan, Tahitian). The fullest early record is Sir George Grey's Polynesian Mythology (1855), assembled from named Te Arawa informants, above all Wiremu Maihi Te Rangikaheke — a relatively well-provenanced colonial collection, flagged as such.

BEGINNING: THE LAST-BORN. Taranga, mother of five, casts her last-born into the sea at birth wrapped in a knot of her hair (topknot); the sea-ancestor Tama-nui-ki-te-Rangi finds and raises him. When Maui comes to his mother's village he finds four older brothers who mock the newcomer; his mother sends him to them as 'Maui-tikitiki-a-Taranga' ('Maui of the topknot of Taranga'), and the brothers, grudging, take him fishing — where he outperforms them all, and reveals his powers of transformation (he turns into birds, dogs, fish at will).

THE SNARING OF THE SUN. The days are too short: the sun (Te Ra) races across the sky so fast that food cannot be cooked and work cannot be done. Maui says to his brothers: 'Let us snare the sun, that he may go more slowly.' They twist great ropes of flax (the source says of the white-flowered flax) and noose them into nets; they build a fortress of clay (to hide behind), and at dawn, when the sun rises from his pit, Maui rises in his enchanted jawbone (the jawbone of his ancestor Murirangawhenua, which he has taken without leave) and beats the sun's face until the sun cries out — 'you will kill me!' — and promises to go slowly: 'hence the long days of summer'.

THE FISHING UP OF TE IKA. Maui tells his brothers to sail far out to sea ('do not look back, do not speak of your own doings'); he strikes his nose and smears his blood (his own sacred blood, tapu) on the jawbone-hook; he baits it and casts. The hook catches on the house of Tonganui, the great fish under the sea — and Maui hauls up the North Island, Te Ika-a-Maui ('the fish of Maui'), while his brothers, disobeying, carve at the catch with their adzes (greedy for food), cutting the valleys and ridges into the land. The South Island is Maui's canoe (Te Waka-a-Maui), and Stewart Island its anchor-stone — the entire cartography of Aotearoa hangs on this narrative. (In some tellings the giant fish is Tonganui, the grandson of Tangaroa, god of the sea.)

THE FIRE QUEST. Maui puts out all the fires of his village (in punishment for a slight, or by accident while the family are out); his mother sends him to Mahuika, the fire-goddess, ancestress of fire. He pretends his fires went out by chance; Mahuika, generous, plucks one of her fingernails (each finger a flame) and gives it; Maui, trickster, returns again and again with excuses ('the wind blew it out') until Mahuika, furious, throws her last fingernail at him — the world catches fire; Maui transforms himself into a hawk and flees (the land scorches behind him: Grey notes the burnt country of the story), and calls on his ancestors — Rangi the sky sends floods of rain, and the sea (Tangaroa) puts out the fire, while Maui turns himself into a mu (a bird) or (in some tellings) into a kaka hawk. All fire is extinguished except what Mahuika's flames had hidden in the kaikomako and tōtara trees — whence Maui teaches humanity to kindle fire by friction (hika: the fire-drill, kaikomako wood), the aition of Polynesian fire-making.

END: HINE-NUI-TE-PO. Maui has made the sun slow, the islands fished, fire kindled — the last enemy is death itself. He sees Hine-nui-te-po ('Great Woman of Night'), the giantess who guards the passage of the dead (her eyes are greenstone, her hair kelp, her mouth a shark's jaws); Maui says to the birds with him: 'If she sleeps I will enter her body, pass through it, and come out by her mouth — then death will not hold men, and mankind will be immortal.' The little tiwaiwaka (fantail) — in some tellings the riroriro (grey warbler) — laughs at the sight, and Hine-nui-te-po wakes and crushes Maui between her thighs; he dies, the first man to die by the great night. 'Hence', Grey's text concludes, 'death came into the world, and no man has escaped it since.' The culture-hero who defeated every obstacle is defeated by death — the aition of human mortality.

FUNCTIONS. The cycle aitiologizes Aotearoa's geography (Te Ika-a-Maui, Te Waka-a-Maui), the sun's pace, fire-by-friction, and human mortality; Maui-tikitiki is the trickster-culture-hero whose transformations teach that form is negotiable; the narratives are taught on the marae, in kapa haka, and in kōhanga reo as part of matauranga Maori, and the figure's name is claimed for canoes, landmarks, and institutions (e.g. 'Maui's dolphin').
narrative.zh: 毛伊乃塔蘭加之幼子，生而棄海，為祖先塔瑪努伊基特蘭吉所育；歸家為兄所嘲。初縛日：以亞麻繩結網，黎明時伏於土壘，持祖顎骨之力棒擊日面，日求饒而許緩行——夏日遂長。次釣島：以自血祭祖顎骨之鉤，深入遠洋，釣起北島『毛伊之魚』；兄違命以斧削之，遂成山谷；南島為其舟、斯圖爾特島為其錨石。再竊火：毛伊滅村中火，母遣其赴火神瑪胡伊卡；屢以藉口索火，神怒擲最後指甲，大地焚燒；毛伊化鷹而遁，祖先遣雨滅火；火種藏於卡伊科馬科與圖塔拉木中，毛伊遂教人鑽木取火。末求不死：見死亡巨女希紐伊特波，欲入睡臥之軀而穿過，令死亡失其權；雀鳥輕笑而驚醒巨女，巨女合股夾斃之——『死亡自茲入世，無人得免』。功能：新西蘭地理之釋義、日行之序、取火之由、人類有死之解；毛伊為毛利知識體系中之詭計英雄。

functions: Aitia of Aotearoa's geography: Te Ika-a-Maui, Te Waka-a-Maui, Stewart Island's anchor-stone
Aitia of the sun's pace and of fire-by-friction (kaikomako and tōtara trees)
Explanation of human mortality: the hero who defeated everything defeated by death
Living matauranga Maori: taught on marae, in kapa haka and kōhanga reo

variants.name: Hawaiian Maui
variants.text_tradition: Hawaiian oral tradition (recorded in 19th-20th c. collections, e.g. Fornander, Nathaniel Emerson)
variants.summary: Hina is the mother; Maui snares the sun at Haleakala to lengthen the day for Hina's kapa-making; steals the secret of fire from the 'alae hen; fishes up islands with a magic hook; dies in a failed quest for immortality. Separate record planned.

variants.name: Samoan Ti'iti'i (Maui-Ti'iti'i)
variants.text_tradition: Samoan oral tradition (recorded in Fraser, Pratt collections, 19th c.)
variants.summary: Ti'iti'i tricks the earthquake-god Mafuie's fire, breaking one of his arms — fire belongs to humankind thereafter; variants give him the fishing-up of islands and the slowing of the sun. Separate record planned.

variants.name: Tongan Maui Kisikisi
variants.text_tradition: Tongan oral tradition (recorded in Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, 1924)
variants.summary: Maui Kisikisi fishes up the islands (Tonga as the fish), snares the sun with a noose of ropes, and seeks immortality from Hikule'o — the Tongan chain of the same Polynesian cycle.

variants.name: Tahitian and Tuamotuan Maui
variants.text_tradition: Tahitian/Tuamotuan oral tradition (recorded in Henry, Ancient Tahiti, 1928; Stimson, 1930s)
variants.summary: Maui-taha and related forms fish up islands and capture the sun; the Tuamotuan corpus preserves genealogical Maui poems tying the hero to deep Polynesian whakapapa traditions.

primary_sources.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race
primary_sources.citation: Auckland 1855 (public domain; NZETC digital edition). Chapters: 'Maui and the Sun', 'Maui and Hine-nui-te-po', 'Maui and the Fish' (Te Ika-a-Maui), 'Maui and Mahuika' (fire). Sources: named Te Arawa informants, esp. Wiremu Maihi Te Rangikaheke (Te Arawa tohunga), 1849-1853 Grey papers.

secondary_sources.work: Margaret Orbell, The Illustrated Encyclopedia of Maori Myth and Legend
secondary_sources.citation: Orbell 1995, Christchurch: Canterbury University Press — Maori-authored synthesis of the Maui corpus with source attributions.

secondary_sources.work: Edward Robert Tregear, The Maori-Polynesian Comparative Dictionary
secondary_sources.citation: Tregear 1891, Wellington (public domain) — Polynesian comparison of the Maui cycle's names and motifs.

secondary_sources.work: Te Ahukaramu Charles Royal (ed.), The Woven Universe: Selected Writings of Rev. Maori Marsden
secondary_sources.citation: Royal 2003, Otaki: Te Wananga-o-Raukawa — contemporary Maori scholarship on matauranga Maori and the Maui cycle's living function.

source_urls.description: New Zealand Electronic Text Collection (Victoria University of Wellington) — Grey, Polynesian Mythology (1855) digital edition
Internet Archive — scans of Grey 1855 (public domain)

sensitivity_guidance: Grey 1855 is a colonial-era collection; it is flagged (not excluded) because it names its Te Arawa informants (esp. Wiremu Maihi Te Rangikaheke) and remains the standard public-domain text. Prefer contemporary Maori sources (Orbell; Royal) in scholarly citation; some Maui narratives are tapu in ceremonial contexts — published paraphrase only, no verbatim re-publication of restricted material.

title.en: The Passion and Resurrection of Jesus Christ
title.zh: 基督受難與復活

region.en: Jerusalem, Judaea
region.zh: 猶太耶路撒冷

period: Composition: Mark c. 70 CE, Matthew/Luke c. 80-90 CE, John c. 90-110 CE; principal MSS: Codex Sinaiticus (British Library Add MS 43725) and Codex Vaticanus, 4th c.; papyri P52, P75 (2nd-3rd c.)

source.archive: Sefaria / Bible Gateway (KJV) / Codex Sinaiticus online
source.work: Mark 14-16; Matthew 26-28; Luke 22-24; John 18-21; 1 Corinthians 11:23-26 (English: King James Version, 1611, public domain)

summary.en: Jesus shares a last supper with his disciples, is betrayed by Judas, tried before Pilate, crucified at Golgotha, buried in a rock tomb; on the third day women find the tomb empty and the risen Lord appears to his followers — the founding narrative of Christian faith, ritually re-enacted in Eucharist and Holy Week.
summary.zh: 耶穌與門徒共進晚餐，遭猶大出賣，於彼拉多前受審，被釘於各各他，葬於石墓；第三日婦女見墓空，復活之主向門徒顯現——此為基督教信仰之根本敘事，於聖餐與聖週禮儀中年年重演。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition; quoted from public-domain KJV.

passages.text: And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me. Likewise also the cup after supper, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you. And he saith unto them, Be not affrighted: Ye seek Jesus of Nazareth, which was crucified: he is risen; he is not here: behold the place where they laid him.
passages.zh: 又拿起餅來，祝謝了，就擘開，遞給他們，說：這是我的身體，為你們捨的，你們也應當如此行，為的是記念我。飯後也照樣拿起杯來，說：這杯是用我血所立的新約，是為你們流出來的。他又對他們說：不要驚恐！你們尋找那釘十字架的拿撒勒人耶穌，他已經復活了，不在這裡。請看安放他的地方。

canonical_translation: King James Version (1611), public domain; modern critical text: Novum Testamentum Graece (Nestle-Aland 28)

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: THE LAST SUPPER. Jesus enters Jerusalem acclaimed as king on an ass's colt; he eats the Passover meal with the Twelve, predicts his betrayal, and institutes the Eucharist — bread broken 'this is my body', the cup 'this is the new testament in my blood' (the earliest written witness, Paul's 1 Corinthians 11:23-26, preserves the tradition within twenty years of the event). Judas Iscariot has already sold him for thirty pieces of silver; at the supper Jesus identifies him: 'that thou doest, do quickly'. In Gethsemane Jesus prays in agony — 'O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me' — while the disciples sleep; Judas arrives with an armed crowd and betrays him with a kiss. Peter three times denies knowing him before the cock crows; Jesus is tried by night before the high priest, condemned for blasphemy ('Again the high priest asked him... Art thou the Christ?... Jesus said: I am'), and delivered to the Roman procurator Pontius Pilate.

MIDDLE: TRIAL AND CRUCIFIXION. Pilate, finding no fault, tries to release him — even offering the customary Passover pardon — but the crowd chooses Barabbas; Jesus is scourged, crowned with plaited thorns, mocked in purple, and crucified at Golgotha between two thieves, with the titulus 'The King of the Jews'. Darkness covers the land from the sixth to the ninth hour; at the end Jesus cries 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' (Mark 15:34, quoting Psalm 22), gives up the ghost, and the temple veil is torn in two from top to bottom. A centurion confesses: 'Truly this man was the Son of God.' Joseph of Arimathaea buries him in a new rock tomb sealed with a great stone; in Matthew the priests set a watch.

END: THE EMPTY TOMB AND APPEARANCES. On the first day of the week, women come to anoint the body: the stone is rolled back, a young man in white (or in John, the risen Jesus himself) announces: 'He is risen; he is not here.' Mark's gospel — our oldest — ends abruptly at 16:8, the women fleeing in fear and telling no one (verses 16:9-20 are a later addition absent from the oldest manuscripts); Matthew has the risen Christ commission the Eleven on a Galilee mountain ('Go ye therefore, and teach all nations'); Luke adds the Emmaus road, where the risen Lord is known 'in breaking of bread'; John gives Mary Magdalene in the garden ('Touch me not') and the doubting Thomas — 'Reach hither thy finger... be not faithless, but believing'. The forty days of appearances close with the Ascension (Luke 24, Acts 1).

VARIANTS AND RECEPTION. The four passion narratives differ in detail (Matthew: earthquake, saints rising; Luke: Herod, penitent thief; John: seamless robe, water and blood, 'It is finished'); theological interpretation ranged from ransom ('a ransom for many') to sacrifice (Hebrews) to Christus victor. Ritual: the narrative structures the Christian liturgical year — Palm Sunday, Maundy Thursday (foot-washing), Good Friday, the Easter Vigil — and the Eucharist re-presents the Last Supper in every celebration; pilgrimage to Jerusalem's Holy Sepulchre from the 4th century onward.
narrative.zh: 始於榮入聖城；逾越節晚餐中設立聖餐，預言出賣；客西馬尼園禱告後被拿，彼得三度不認主，公會夜審定罪。彼拉多查無罪狀仍判釘刑：受鞭、冠荊、紫袍受辱，於各各他釘於二盜之間，罪狀牌書『猶太人的王』；遍地黑暗，最後呼喊詩篇之言，殿幔裂開，百夫長認信。亞利馬太人約瑟葬之於石墓。七日首日清晨，婦女至墓，石已輥開：『他復活了，不在這裡。』馬可於十六章八節戛然而止（九至二十節為後加）；馬太載加利利大使命，路加載以馬忤斯路上於擘餅時被認出，約翰載抹大拉的馬利亞與多馬觸摸傷痕。四十日顯現後升天。禮儀：聖週與復活節守夜禮重演此敘事，聖餐每主日重現晚餐。

functions: Founding narrative of Christian faith and creeds (died, buried, raised on the third day)
Eucharist: ritual re-presentation of the Last Supper in every liturgy
Liturgical year structure: Holy Week, Easter Vigil, Ascension
Jerusalem pilgrimage: Holy Sepulchre from the 4th c. CE

variants.name: Mark (oldest gospel)
variants.text_tradition: c. 70 CE; ends abruptly at 16:8 in Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus
variants.summary: The starkest telling: no birth narrative, no post-resurrection appearances before the longer ending; emphasis on the cry of dereliction and the fear of the women.

variants.name: Matthew and Luke (redacted versions)
variants.summary: Matthew adds the guards, the earthquake, and the Galilee commission; Luke adds Herod's trial, the penitent thief, Emmaus, and the Ascension — both soften Mark's abruptness.

variants.name: John (theological version)
variants.summary: Jesus carries his own cross, gives his mother to the Beloved Disciple, speaks the seven last words; resurrection appearances merge recognition with faith ('blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed').

variants.name: Non-canonical Gospel of Peter (2nd c.)
variants.summary: The cross itself speaks and walks from the tomb; a giant risen Jesus and a walking cross are witnessed by Roman soldiers — an early independent variant showing the range of second-century retellings.

primary_sources.work: Mark 14-16 (with parallels Matthew 26-28, Luke 22-24, John 18-21; 1 Cor 11:23-26)
primary_sources.citation: Novum Testamentum Graece (NA28); English KJV 1611. Key MSS: Codex Sinaiticus (BL Add MS 43725), Codex Vaticanus, P75.

secondary_sources.work: Raymond E. Brown, The Death of the Messiah
secondary_sources.citation: Brown 1994, New York: Doubleday (Anchor Bible Reference) — the standard commentary on the passion narratives and their differences.

secondary_sources.work: Adela Yarbro Collins and John J. Collins, King and Messiah as Son of God
secondary_sources.citation: Yarbro Collins 2008, Grand Rapids: Eerdmans — royal-Davidic framing of the passion title 'King of the Jews'.

source_urls.description: Codex Sinaiticus online facsimile (British Library) — Mark 14-16, earliest witness to the abrupt ending

sensitivity_guidance: Canonical scripture of a living faith: cite by chapter/verse from established editions; avoid casual remixing; be aware of Jewish-Christian polemical history of the passion narrative when excerpting trial scenes.

title.en: The Creation of Adam and the Fall of Iblis (Quran)
title.zh: 阿丹之造與易卜劣廝之墮（古蘭經）

region.en: Mecca / Medina (recitation contexts; symbolic pin)
region.zh: 麥加／麥地那（誦經語境；象徵性定位）

period: Quran revealed c. 610-632 CE; canonical rasm fixed under Uthman (c. 650 CE); earliest MSS: Sanaa palimpsest, Codex Parisino-petropolitanus (1st c. AH); tafsir tradition from al-Tabari (d. 923 CE)

source.work: Quran 2:30-39; 7:11-25; 15:26-48; 20:115-127; 38:71-85 (Arabic text; English: E. H. Palmer, The Qur'an, Sacred Books of the East vol. 6, Oxford 1880)

license: Arabic text public domain; Palmer 1880 translation public domain

summary.en: God creates Adam from clay, teaches him the names of all things, and the angels bow — all but Iblis, who refuses ('I am better than he') and is cast down until the Day of Judgment; Adam and his wife dwell in the Garden, approach the forbidden tree through Satan's whispering, and are sent down to earth, where revealed words teach them repentance.
summary.zh: 真主以黏土造阿丹，教以萬物之名，天使皆拜——惟易卜劣廝拒拜（『我比他尊貴』），遂被逐，待至審判日；阿丹夫婦居園中，受魔鬼唆使近禁樹，被降於大地，得啟示之言而悔悟。

sensitivity.note: The Quran is the literal word of God in Arabic; translations are interpretations. Only public-domain translations are quoted, with the Arabic source as primary.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Quran 2:30-33 (Palmer 1880 translation): The Lord says to the angels, 'I am going to place in the earth a successor'; they ask whether he will place one who will do evil there while they praise God; He teaches Adam the names of all things and calls the angels to name them — 'did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and of the earth?' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Quran 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《古蘭經》2:30-33 的濃縮意譯（帕爾默 1880 年譯本）：主對眾天使說：「我將在大地上安置一位繼任者」；他們問，祂是否會安置一個在大地上作惡的人，而他們卻讚頌真主；祂教亞當萬物的名稱，並召眾天使說出這些名稱——「我不是告訴過你們，我知道天地間的奧秘嗎？」非逐字引文。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Quran 7:11-18: God commands the angels to bow before Adam; all bow except Iblis, who says 'I am better than he: Thou hast created me from fire and him from clay.' God casts him down: 'Get out of it, despised, driven away'; Iblis obtains respite until the Day of Judgment, vowing to lie in wait for Adam's children. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Quran 7; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《古蘭經》7:11-18 的濃縮意譯：真主命令眾天使向亞當叩拜；除易卜劣廝外，眾天使皆叩拜，易卜劣廝說：「我比他優越：你用火造化了我，卻用泥造化了他。」真主將他貶斥：「你從這裡出去吧，你是卑賤的、被驅逐的」；易卜劣廝獲准緩刑至復生日，並發誓要潛伏窺伺亞當的子孫。非逐字引文。

canonical_translation: E. H. Palmer, The Qur'an, Sacred Books of the East vol. 6, Oxford 1880 (public domain); modern: Sahih International, Abdel Haleem (copyright)

narrative.en:
The Quran retells the Adam story not as one continuous sura but as a cycle of episodes spread across Meccan and Medinan revelations, each re-focusing the tale on obedience, knowledge, and the enmity of Iblis.

THE CREATION AND THE NAMES. God announces to the angels: 'I am going to place in the earth a khalifa (successor/viceroy)' (2:30). The angels object — will this creature 'do evil therein and shed blood, while we celebrate thy praise?' God's answer is an act of teaching: He 'taught Adam the names, all of them' (2:31) — the names of all things, the gift of language and knowledge no angel possesses — and when the angels fail the test, God calls Adam to recite them: 'Did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and of the earth?' (2:33). Adam is created from sounding clay (salsal), from mud kneaded (15:26); in the tafsir tradition (al-Tabari, citing Ibn Abbas) the clay is gathered from every earth — white, black, red, sweet, bitter — so that Adam's children will be of every kind.

THE REFUSAL OF IBLIS. God commands the angels to prostrate before Adam. All bow except Iblis — 'he refused and was arrogant, and was of the disbelievers' (2:34). His reason: 'I am better than he: Thou hast created me from fire and him from clay' (7:12). The refusal is the Quran's primal sin: pride of substance over obedience. God casts him out — 'Get thee down from it, despised and driven away' (7:18) — and Iblis obtains respite until the Day of Judgment, on which he vows to 'lie in wait for them upon thy straight path' (7:16), to tempt Adam's children 'from before them, behind them, from their right and from their left'. God grants the respite: 'over my servants thou shalt have no power' except those who follow him (15:42-43).

THE GARDEN AND THE TREE. Adam dwells with his spouse in the Garden, eating freely 'wherever ye will' — but not 'this tree', approached lest they 'be of the unjust doers' (2:35). Satan (al-Shaytan, Iblis) whispers that the tree is 'the tree of eternity' (20:120), that eating will make them angels or immortal; the two eat, 'and their shame became apparent to them, and they began to stitch upon themselves leaves of the garden' (7:22). Unlike the biblical telling, the Quran distributes the transgression to both (the couple, not the wife alone), and the serpent plays no speaking role: the tempter is Iblis himself. Both are stripped, both descend.

THE DESCENT AND THE WORDS OF REPENTANCE. The fall is answered by mercy: 'Adam received words from his Lord, and He turned toward him, for He is the Relenting, the Compassionate' (2:37) — in the tafsir tradition, the words are those of sura 7:23 ('Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves') or a divine prayer of repentance. Adam is set down on earth 'a dwelling and a provision' (2:36) — the human condition as exile-with-mercy, not inherited guilt: 'no soul shall bear the burden of another' (6:164). The episode closes with the promise of guidance ('there shall surely come to you guidance from me; whoso followeth my guidance, no fear shall be on them') — prophecy itself is the sequel to the fall.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds Islamic theology of human nature (fitra — no original sin), the protocol of angels' obedience, the taxonomy of pride (takabbur) as the first sin, and the ritual of repentance (tawba); it is recited at weddings and funerals in various regions and is the anchor for the Muslim etiquette of resisting satanic whispering (isti'adha before recitation).
narrative.zh: 古蘭經以多處經文重述阿丹之事：真主告眾天使將於大地設『代治者』；天使問將置造惡流血者乎；真主教阿丹萬物之名，天使不能名。真主命天使拜阿丹，易卜劣廝自恃火造優於土造而拒拜，遂被逐，求緩刑至審判日，誓誘惑阿丹子孫。阿丹夫婦居園中得食園果，惟近禁樹勿為；魔鬼唆言此樹致永生，二人食之，羞恥乃現，以園葉蔽身。真主降諭：阿丹獲主之數言而蒙饒恕——無原罪之世，人各負其責。夫婦降於大地為居所與給養，啟示隨之而至：循主之引導者無懼。功能：人性本淨之義、天使順服之儀、傲慢為首罪、悔悟之禮。

functions: Theology of fitra: human nature untainted by original sin
Pride of substance (fire vs. clay) as the first sin — Iblis' refusal
Ritual: isti'adha (seeking refuge from Satan) before recitation; repentance (tawba)
Charter of knowledge: Adam taught 'the names' grounds human epistemic dignity

variants.name: al-Tabari's tafsir (Isra'iliyyat material)
variants.text_tradition: Jami' al-bayan fi ta'wil al-Quran (d. 923 CE); trans. Cooper/Brinner (copyright)
variants.summary: Collects the early exegetical expansions: the clay gathered from the four corners, the hollow Adam left standing while angels feared it, Iblis' entry into the Garden 'in the mouth of the serpent' — traditions inherited from Jewish-Christian sources, weighed critically by Muslim exegetes.

variants.name: Biblical Genesis parallel
variants.summary: Shares the Garden, the tree, the leaf-clothing; differs in the serpent (silent or absent in the Quran), the wife's role (both eat), and the fall (exile-with-mercy rather than inherited curse).

variants.name: Sufi readings (Ibn Arabi and later)
variants.summary: Ibn Arabi reads Iblis' refusal as the lover's exclusive devotion (he would bow to none but God), making the episode a parable of the tension between pure love and revealed command.

variants.name: Popular hagiography (Stories of the Prophets)
variants.summary: Expands into full narrative lore: the four clays, Adam's size (60 cubits), the naming of all things, and the children born after the descent — the story-book Adam that shaped vernacular Islam across Asia.

primary_sources.citation: 2:30-39; 7:11-25; 15:26-48; 20:115-127; 38:71-85. Canonical Uthmanic rasm; earliest MSS: Codex Parisino-petropolitanus (BNF arabe 328), Sanaa palimpsest. English: E. H. Palmer, SBE vol. 6, Oxford 1880 (public domain).

secondary_sources.work: Fazlur Rahman, Major Themes of the Quran
secondary_sources.citation: Rahman 1980, Minneapolis: Bibliotheca Islamica — theological reading of the Adam-Iblis cycle and fitra.

secondary_sources.work: Andrew Rippin (ed.), The Blackwell Companion to the Quran
secondary_sources.citation: Rippin 2006, Oxford: Blackwell — chapters on tafsir and the Isra'iliyyat problem.

title.en: The Buddha's Awakening and Great Passing Away
title.zh: 佛陀之成正覺與大般涅槃

region.en: Bodh Gaya and Kushinara (Kushinagar), India
region.zh: 印度菩提伽耶與拘屍那揭羅

period: Canonical texts c. 4th-2nd c. BCE (oral transmission); written Pali canon in Sri Lanka 1st c. BCE; principal MS tradition: Pali script MSS, e.g. Brunet? (PTS editions); Mahaparinibbana Sutta (DN 16)

source.archive: Internet Sacred Texts Archive (Rhys Davids translations) / SuttaCentral.net
source.work: Majjhima Nikaya 26 (Ariyapariyesana Sutta); Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta), trans. T. W. Rhys Davids, Dialogues of the Buddha, PTS, 1899-1921

summary.en: The ascetic Siddhattha leaves his palace, studies under two teachers, rejects their paths, and attains awakening under the Bodhi tree; forty-five years of teaching later, he dies at Kushinagar between two sala trees, is cremated like a world-monarch, and his relics are divided into eight portions — nirvana beyond rebirth.
summary.zh: 悉達多太子捨家出家，從二師學而棄其道，於菩提樹下成正覺；說法四十五載，於拘屍那揭羅雙娑羅樹間大般涅槃，以轉輪王法焚身，舍利分作八份——此為解脫輪迴之涅槃敘事。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Pali canon); Vesak and relic cults treat these sites as sacred.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of MN 26: The ascetic Siddhattha, having studied under Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta and found their attainments short of the deathless, recalls the bliss of the first meditation he knew as a child under the rose-apple tree: 'Might this be the path to awakening?' and, taking solid food, sits down to strive. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of MN 26; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《中部》第 26 經的濃縮意譯：苦行者悉達多曾師從阿羅邏迦羅摩與鬱陀迦羅摩子修學，發覺他們的成就仍未達不死之境，於是回想起幼時在閻浮樹下所體驗的初禪之樂：「這或許就是通往覺悟之道？」他於是食用堅實的食物，坐下精勤修習。非逐字引文。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of DN 16: The Buddha lies between two sala trees at Kusinara; the twin trees flower out of season and celestial music sounds; he tells Ananda: 'It may be that ye think... the Master is gone. But thus should ye think: the Doctrine and the Discipline he has made known — that is your Master when I am gone.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of DN 16; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《長部》第 16 經的濃縮意譯：佛陀在拘尸那羅的兩棵娑羅樹之間臥下；雙樹非時開花，天樂奏鳴；他告訴阿難：「你們或許會想……導師已離去。但你們應當這樣想：他所宣示的法與律——那就是我離去後你們的導師。」非逐字引文。

canonical_translation: T. W. Rhys Davids, Dialogues of the Buddha (PTS, 1899-1921, public domain); modern: Bhikkhu Bodhi (copyright)

narrative.en:
The two canonical poles of the Buddha's biography — the night of awakening and the great passing — bracket forty-five years of ministry and together constitute the charter narrative of the Buddhist path.

THE GOING FORTH. The Pali canon tells the renunciation briefly (MN 26, MN 36), expanding it in the commentarial Nidanakatha. Prince Siddhattha Gotama of the Sakyans, son of Suddhodana, lives a palace life of the three mansions until the sight of the four signs — an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a renunciate — convicts him of aging, sickness, and death. He leaves Kapilavatthu by night, casts off his hair, and dons ochre robes; his son is born that same night and he names him Rahula, 'the fetter' — and leaves anyway: 'A fetter has been born.'

THE SEARCH AND THE AWAKENING. He studies first under Alara Kalama (attaining the 'sphere of nothingness'), then Uddaka Ramaputta (the 'sphere of neither perception nor non-perception') — and rejects both: 'This doctrine does not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace... to nirvana.' He joins the five ascetics at Uruvela and undertakes extreme austerities for six years, to the point of skeleton-like self-mortification, and rejects this too, recalling the spontaneous bliss of the first meditation he had known as a child under the rose-apple tree — 'might this be the path to awakening?' — and takes milk-rice offered by the village girl Sujata. Seated on a mat of grass under the Bodhi tree (pipphali), he makes the vow not to rise until liberation. Mara, the tempter, challenges his seat-right: 'Who is thy witness?' — the Buddha touches the earth, and the earth goddess (in the later account) roars in witness. Mara's armies of desire, aversion, and doubt are defeated; through the three watches of the night the Buddha attains the three knowledges — his own former lives, the passing and arising of all beings according to karma, and the destruction of the cankers (asava) — 'birth is destroyed... this is the last birth; there is now no renewed existence'. The awakening formulas of dependent arising (paticca-samuppada) are recited three times in the canonical account.

THE MINISTRY AND THE GREAT PASSING. He teaches for forty-five years (his first sermon at Sarnath, 'the wheel of dhamma', sets the path rolling). At eighty, on his final journey, he is poisoned by Cunda the smith's 'pig's delight' (sukara-maddava) — he foretells it, takes on the suffering, and walks to Kusinara. There, between two sala trees, he lies on his right side 'like a lion': the trees flower out of season and celestial music honors him; his disciple Subhadda becomes the last convert. Ananda grieves; the Buddha consoles him ('all that is dear is subject to change') and lays down the succession: 'the Doctrine and the Discipline... that is your Master when I am gone' (DN 16). He asks the assembly three times whether any has a doubt — silence. 'Now then, monks, I say to you: all conditioned things are subject to decay. Strive on with diligence!' (vayadhamma samkhara, appamadena sampadetha) — and he passes from the fourth meditation to nirvana without remainder (anupadisesa-nibbana). The Mallas cremate him with royal rites like a world-monarch; the relics are claimed by eight kingdoms and divided into eight portions (a war of relics is averted by the brahmin Drona), each enshrined in a stupa — the aition of the stupa cult.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds the Buddhist analysis of suffering and liberation (the four signs as the problem; the awakening as the solution), the middle way between indulgence and self-torment (the milk-rice episode), the sanctity of the sites (Bodh Gaya, Kusinagar — among the eight great pilgrimage places), Vesak (the full-moon festival of birth, awakening, and passing), and the relic-stupa economy that structures Buddhist devotional space; the succession formula grounds the sangha's authority in dhamma-vinaya rather than a living teacher.
narrative.zh: 悉達多太子因四門遊觀見老病死與沙門，捨家夜遁，剃髮披衣，名子羅睺羅為『繫縛』。先從阿羅邏迦蘭學無所有處定，從鬱陀迦羅摩子學非想非非想定，皆棄之，言其道不至涅槃；六年苦行形同枯骨，亦棄之，憶幼時閻浮樹下初禪之樂，受牧羊女乳糜，於畢缽羅樹下敷草而坐，誓不證無上正覺不起。魔羅譏其座位無證，佛觸地為證，魔軍潰敗；夜三時得三明：宿命、天眼見眾生業報流轉、漏盡——『生已盡，梵行已立，所做已辦，不受後有』。說法四十五年，初轉法輪於鹿野苑。八十歲末行，受鐵匠純陀供養而中毒，行至拘屍那揭羅，於雙娑羅樹間右脅如獅子臥；樹非時開花，天樂供養；化度末化者須跋陀羅；阿難憂泣，佛慰之：『諸行無常，法與律為汝等師。』三問眾無疑，末誡：『諸行無常，精進勿懈！』入第四禪而般涅槃。諸末羅以轉輪王法焚身，舍利八分起塔供養——塔制之緣起。功能：苦與解脫之釋義、中道之範、八大聖地朝聖、衛塞節、以及僧團依法不依人之憲章。

functions: Charter of the middle way: rejection of both palace indulgence and mortification
Pilgrimage geography: Bodh Gaya, Kusinagar among the eight great sites; Vesak festival
Stupa cult: relic division into eight portions grounds devotional architecture
Sangha authority: dhamma-vinaya as the Master after the passing

variants.name: Nidanakatha (commentarial biography)
variants.text_tradition: Introductory narrative of the Jataka commentary (Buddhaghosa, 5th c. CE)
variants.summary: Supplies the palace drama the canon omits: the four signs, Yasodhara, Kanthaka the horse, the gate-gods lifting the prince over the city — the biography most people know, transmitted as comment rather than sutta.

variants.name: Sarvastivada/Lalitavistara tradition
variants.summary: A hagiographic expansion (Buddha's birth from his mother's side, the seven steps, mara's daughters) that fed Mahayana devotional art from Gandhara to Dunhuang; the awakening is a cosmic event witnessed by all beings.

variants.name: Mahaparinibbana doublet verses
variants.summary: The passing-away sutta preserves older verse doublets (e.g. the 'earthquake' verses) whose repetitions betray a centuries-long oral transmission before the 1st-c. BCE writing down in Sri Lanka.

title.en: The Transformations of Lord Lao: Laozi's Hagiography in Daoist Tradition
title.zh: 太上老君變化紀：道教老子聖傳

region.en: Louguan (Louguantai), Shaanxi, China (the western pass; symbolic pin)
region.zh: 中國陝西樓觀台（西出函谷關；象徵性定位）

period: Hagiographic strata: Shiji 63 (c. 90 BCE); Laozi bianhua jing (Scripture of the Transformations of Laozi, Dunhuang MS, 6th-9th c. CE); Shenxian zhuan (c. 4th c. CE)

source.archive: Internet Sacred Texts Archive (Dao De Jing translations) / Daozang (DZ 1412 etc.)
source.work: Laozi bianhua jing (Scripture of the Transformations of Lord Lao, DZ 1412?); Sima Qian, Shiji 63; Ge Hong, Shenxian zhuan (trans. R. F. Campany, To Live as Long as Heaven and Earth, 2002)

license: Ancient texts public domain; Campany 2002 quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The Dao itself takes embodied form: Laozi is born of a plum tree under his mother's left armpit after eighty-one years in the womb, serves as Zhou court archivist, transmits the five-thousand-character scripture to Yin Xi at the western pass, and through eight incarnations teaches the world until the Daoist empire of the Tang crowns him 'August Emperor of the Mysterious Origin'.
summary.zh: 大道化身：老君自母左腋下李樹而出，懷胎八十一年；為周守藏室之史，於函谷關授關令尹喜五千言；歷八十一變教化世間，至唐代李氏尊為『太上玄元皇帝』。

sensitivity.note: Daoist scriptural canon (Daozang) is sacred to a living tradition; these hagiographic narratives are public liturgical culture. Ordination-restricted liturgies are not reproduced.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Shiji 63 (Sima Qian, c. 90 BCE): Laozi was a man of Quren village in Li township of Ku county in Chu; he served the Zhou court as archivist; seeing the decline of Zhou, he departed westward; at the pass, the keeper Yin Xi asked him to write a book — Laozi composed a work in two parts, on the Way and its power, five thousand characters and more, and went off; no one knows where he died. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Shiji 63 (Sima Qian, c. 90 BCE); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《史記》卷六十三（司馬遷，約公元前 90 年）的濃縮意譯：老子是楚國苦縣厲鄉曲仁里人；他在周朝擔任守藏室之史；見周室衰微，便西行離去；至關口，關令尹喜請他著書——老子於是著書上下兩篇，論道及其德，五千餘言，而後離去；無人知其終於何處。非逐字引文。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Laozi bianhua jing: Lord Lao declares: 'I have no fixed form; in response to beings I transform.' He lists his embodiments — in the age of the Three Kings and Five Emperors as teacher of rulers, as personal savior in each dynasty — and foretells the age when Li Hong, the 'heir of the Dao', will descend to gather the elect and bring the world of Great Peace. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Laozi bianhua jing; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《老子變化經》的濃縮意譯：老君宣告：「我沒有固定的形貌；隨眾生而變化。」他列舉自己的化身——在三皇五帝之世為帝王之師，在每個朝代作為個人的救度者——並預言李弘這位「道的繼承者」將降世，聚集選民，帶來太平之世。非逐字引文。

canonical_translation: Primary texts public domain; scholarly translations: Livia Kohn (The Taoist Experience, 1993; God of the Dao, 2000) and R. F. Campany (2002) — quoted only as summary

narrative.en:
Daoism did not merely preserve a philosopher: it developed a full hagiography in which the historical Laozi (traditionally Li Er, court archivist of Zhou, 6th-4th c. BCE) is an incarnation of the Dao itself — Lord Lao (Taishang Laojun), second in the Daoist trinity after the Celestial Worthy and before the Celestial Master.

THE HISTORICAL SKELETON. Sima Qian's Shiji 63 (c. 90 BCE) gives the oldest account: Laozi of Chu served as archivist of the Zhou archives; seeing Zhou's decline, he departed west; at the pass, the keeper Yin Xi begged him to write; Laozi composed the two-part 'Way and Power' text of over five thousand characters and vanished, 'no one knows where he died'. Confucius' legendary visit ('a dragon... I cannot know') is attached; Sima Qian already notes rival claims (Lao Laizi; the Daoist Grand Historian of Duke Xian) — the ambiguity that later hagiography resolved by making multiplicity essential: the sage has no single body.

THE MIRACULOUS BIOGRAPHY. The Shenxian zhuan (Ge Hong, c. 4th c.) and the Laozi bianhua jing build the deity: Laozi's mother, pregnant for eighty-one years, gives birth from her left armpit under a plum tree (li — his surname); the infant walks immediately, points to the plum tree, and has white hair and long ears ('Laozi' — 'Old Child'). He serves the declining Zhou; the world decays around him; he rides a green ox west, and at the Hangu Pass Yin Xi — himself a visionary who reads the breath of the east as 'purple vapor from ten thousand li, a sage coming' — receives the five thousand characters of the Daode jing and the transmission of the Dao. Laozi's later career is a trajectory of epiphanies: at Louguan (the 'Look-at-the-Terrace' hermitage founded on the spot), he reveals the Xisheng jing ('Scripture of Western Ascension'); in the Zhang Lu tradition, Lord Lao descends in 142 CE to Mount Heming and consecrates Zhang Daoling as Celestial Master, founding organized Daoism — the hagiographic hinge between philosopher and church.

THE TRANSFORMATIONS AND THE MESSIANIC END. The bianhua tradition lists Lord Lao's cyclic incarnations: in every age of the Three Kings and Five Emperors he appears as teacher and regenerator of rulers; under the Shang and Zhou he descends as savior 'nine times nine' — the scripture says he 'was never born, yet manifests birth; never dies, yet manifests passing'. The eschatological horizon is Li Hong (the 'heir'), the future Lord Lao who will descend at the world's crisis to gather the righteous and establish Great Peace (taiping) — a millenarian expectation that repeatedly ignited Daoist uprisings across the medieval period. The imperial cult completed the arc: the Tang dynasty (Li family, 618-907) claimed Laozi as ancestor, erecting steles at Louguan and conferring the title 'August Emperor of the Mysterious Origin' (Taishang Xuanyuan Huangdi, 666 CE) — the sage becomes the empire's ancestor-god, and his cult at Louguan, Wudang, and the Baiyun guan anchors Daoist liturgy to this day.

FUNCTIONS. The hagiography grounds Daoist liturgy (the Three Pure Ones' throne; the audience with Lord Lao in jiao offerings), legitimizes the lineage (Zhang Daoling's revelation; the Louguan tradition), aitiologizes the Daode jing as revealed scripture rather than composed book, and structures Daoist messianism (Li Hong; taiping).
narrative.zh: 太史公《史記》卷六十三記老子為楚苦縣厲鄉曲仁里人，周守藏室之史，見周衰西去，關令尹喜強而著書上下篇言道德之意五千餘言，莫知所終。後世道教聖傳層累：老君自母左腋生於李樹之下，懷胎八十一年，生而能行，白髮長耳，號『老子』；騎青牛西出函谷，紫氣東來，尹喜讀氣知聖人至，受五千言並受道訣；於樓觀說《西昇經》；漢安元年鶴鳴山降授張道陵天師之職，開教立治。《老子變化經》（敦煌本）言老君『隨時感化』，三皇五帝之世為帝王之師，商周以降九九化身，救度世人；末世將降李弘，收種民致太平。唐李氏尊為祖，封『太上玄元皇帝』，樓觀立碑。功能：齋醮科儀之供奉、道統之根、五千言為天啟之經、李弘彌賽亞主義。

functions: Legitimation of the Daoist lineage: Zhang Daoling's revelation at Mount Heming
Aition of the Daode jing as revealed scripture (five thousand characters at the pass)
Liturgical anchor: Lord Lao's throne in jiao offerings and the Three Pure Ones
Daoist messianism: Li Hong and the expectation of Great Peace (taiping)

variants.name: Shiji 63 (historiographic version)
variants.text_tradition: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian, c. 90 BCE
variants.summary: The sober oldest account, already noting rival identities (Lao Laizi; Zhou Grand Historian Tan) — later hagiography turns this very multiplicity into proof of the Dao's bodiless transformations.

variants.name: Laozi bianhua jing (Dunhuang recension)
variants.text_tradition: Dunhuang MS S.2295; scripture 6th-9th c. CE
variants.summary: First-person apocalypse: Lord Lao lists his incarnations 'nine times nine' and foretells Li Hong's descent; recovered at Dunhuang, it shows the messianic strand in full.

variants.name: Xisheng jing (Western Ascension)
variants.text_tradition: Scripture of Western Ascension, Louguan tradition, 5th-6th c.
variants.summary: Laozi's discourse to Yin Xi after crossing the pass — the 'westernization' strand (huahu) later used to claim Laozi taught the Buddha, a polemic that shaped Sino-Buddhist debate.

variants.name: Tang imperial cult
variants.text_tradition: Imperial steles at Louguan (e.g. 626, 666 CE); Daozang liturgies
variants.summary: The Li family claims Laozi as ancestor; imperial jiao sacrifices crown the sage as 'August Emperor' — the hagiography becomes state religion, with steles and images across the empire.

title.en: Papa Legba: Keeper of the Crossroads in Fon and Afro-Atlantic Vodou
title.zh: 雷格巴老爹：豐族與非裔大西洋巫毒中的十字路口守門神

region.en: Dahomey (Benin) and Haiti (diaspora; symbolic pin at Port-au-Prince)
region.zh: 達荷美（貝寧）與海地（離散地；象徵性定位於太子港）

period: Fon narratives recorded 1931 fieldwork (Herskovits, published 1938); Haitian Vodou attested from 18th c. onwards; recording traditions (Verrettes? plaine du Nord) 20th c.

source.work: Legba narratives recorded by Melville J. Herskovits, Dahomey: An Ancient West African Kingdom (New York, 1938); Alfred Metraux, Voodoo in Haiti (Paris 1958/New York 1959); Karen McCarthy Brown, Mama Lola: A Vodou Priestess in Brooklyn (Berkeley, 1991)

license: Paraphrase summaries only; underlying oral/liturgical texts are living tradition and are not reproduced verbatim

summary.en: Legba, the old man with the staff, guards every gate, road, and crossroads: the lwa cannot be reached without his key, the messages of the living cannot pass without his word; tricked by his own cleverness in Dahomey, enthroned as first-served in Haiti — the divine gatekeeper whose opening ritual (priye Legba) begins every Vodou ceremony.
summary.zh: 雷格巴拄杖老人，守一切門、路與十字路口：無其鑰則羅亞不至，無其言則生者之訊不通；在達荷美因巧智受騙，在海地為首奉之神——每場巫毒儀式以『雷格巴開門』之禱開始。

sensitivity.note: Not excluded: record is built from published scholarly paraphrase only. Some Vodou/Santeria liturgical songs, veve drawings, and initiation knowledge ARE restricted (oungan/asogwe levels) and are not reproduced; see sensitivity_guidance.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Fon narrative recorded by Herskovits (1938): Legba, youngest son of Mawu-Lisa, is set over the gates and the market road; he alone goes freely between the world of the gods and the world of men, carrying messages in both directions — and exploits the privilege, reporting each side's words to the other in altered form, until the old mother Mawu confirms his office: no one may come to the gods except through him. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Fon narrative recorded by Herskovits (1938); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 赫斯科維茨（1938）所記豐族敘事的濃縮改述：萊格巴是馬烏-麗莎最小的兒子，被派掌管門戶與市場之路；唯有他能自由往來於諸神的世界與凡人的世界之間，雙向傳遞訊息——並利用這項特權，將雙方的話語加以變造後轉告對方，直到老母親馬烏確認了他的職分：任何人若非經由他，皆不得前來謁見諸神。非逐字引述。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Haitian ritual sequence described by Metraux (1959) and McCarthy Brown (1991): A Vodou service opens with the priye Legba at the poteau-mitan (center pole) and the drawn veve of the crossroads; the celebrant salutes Legba as old man, gatekeeper, opener of the way — 'pay for the gate, open the road' — before any other lwa may arrive. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Haitian ritual sequence described by Metraux (1959) and McCarthy Brown (1991); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 梅特羅（1959）與麥卡錫·布朗（1991）所述海地儀式程序的濃縮改述：一場伏都儀式以在中央柱（poteau-mitan）前誦念萊格巴祈禱文、並繪出十字路口的維維（veve）圖案揭開序幕；主祭者向萊格巴致敬，稱他為老者、守門者、開路者——「為門付費，開闢道路」——此後其他洛阿（lwa）方能降臨。非逐字引述。

canonical_translation: No written canon; scholarly paraphrases (Herskovits 1938; Metraux 1959; McCarthy Brown 1991) are the published record

narrative.en:
Legba is the portmanteau god of the crossroads: a Fon (Dahomean) deity carried across the Middle Passage and enthroned in Haitian Vodou (and in cognate forms across the Afro-Atlantic world, from Brazilian Candomble Exu to Cuban Eleggua in Lucumi practice — cognate but distinct traditions).

THE FON ORIGIN: MESSENGER AND TRICKSTER. In the Dahomean narratives recorded by Herskovits in 1931 fieldwork, Mawu (the moon-mother, with Lisa her sun-twin) apportions the world among her children; Legba, the youngest and most wayward, receives no province — instead he is set over the gates, the roads, and the market crossroads, the in-between spaces. He alone travels freely between aye (the world of humans) and the world of the gods, and he makes the office his own: carrying messages up and down, he alters them for his own amusement — telling the gods that humans mock them, telling humans that the gods demand impossible fees — profiting in goats and palm wine from both sides of the gate. In the best-known episode, Legba's deception is discovered when Mawu (or in some tellings the hunter-god's households) sets a test; humiliated, Legba hides in a grass roof, and the fires of the gods' anger burn the grass house around him — but he survives through trickery, and the office stands: the mother confirms that nothing comes to the gods and nothing leaves them except through Legba. The narrative aitiologizes the ritual fact that all Fon and Vodou addresses begin with Legba's salutation.

THE HAITIAN THRONE: FIRST SERVED. In Haitian Vodou, Papa Legba (Legba Atibon) stands at the head of the lwa: the old man in rags with a straw hat, a crutch or machete, followed by a small white dog, smoking a pipe, guarding the crossroads at dawn. He is ritually first: no Vodou ceremony opens without the priye Legba, spoken at the poteau-mitan with the drawn veve (ritual flag/drawing) of the crossroads, saluting him as gatekeeper and 'opener of the way' — the lwa cannot descend to mount their servants until Legba has opened the gate between worlds. He is also the humblest of the great lwa — a beggar at the gate, poor and old — so that the highest threshold is kept by the least: a theological pole against pride, and a social image of the enslaved who kept their gods at the gates of the masters' world.

FUNCTIONS. Legba's narrative grounds Vodou ritual grammar (the priye and veve of the crossroads; the peristyle's center-pole as axis), the ethics of the marginal (gatekeeper as beggar), and the historical memory of the Middle Passage — the god of gates carried through the gate of slavery. His Fon stories aitiologize the market as cosmological meeting-place and the messenger's monopoly as both blessing and danger.

PROVENANCE NOTE. Key printed sources (Herskovits 1938) are colonial-era ethnography; contemporary community scholars (McCarthy Brown's partnership with Mama Lola/Alourdes, 1980s-90s; Gerdès Fleurant's ritual music studies) are preferred. Initiation-restricted liturgies (asogwe knowledge; secret society materials) are not represented here and are not reproduced.
narrative.zh: 豐族敘事（赫斯科維茨1931年田野）：瑪烏-麗莎分封諸子，幼子雷格巴無所封，得守門、路與市集路口，獨自在神人兩界間往來傳話；他篡改兩界之訊以取利，事發受辱，藏身草頂屋，神怒之火焚屋而不死；母神遂定其職：凡欲至神前者必經雷格巴。海地巫毒：雷格巴·阿蒂邦為羅亞之首，襤褸老者，草帽、杖、煙斗，隨一小白犬，守黎明之十字路口；每場儀式必先於中柱行『雷格巴之禱』、畫路口之韋韋旗，稱其『開路者』——羅亞降臨前必先請其開門。他同時是最卑微之神：守最高門檻者形同乞丐，釋奴隸神學之義。功能：巫毒儀式語法（開門禱與韋韋）、邊緣者倫理、以及穿越奴役之門的神話記憶。

functions: Ritual grammar: priye Legba opens every Vodou ceremony; veve of the crossroads
Cosmology of the in-between: market and crossroads as meeting of worlds
Ethics of the marginal: the highest gate kept by the humblest god
Middle Passage memory: the Fon gatekeeper enthroned in diaspora

title.en: The Bundahishn: Ohrmazd's Creation and Ahriman's Assault
title.zh: 《創世紀》：阿胡拉·馬茲達創世與阿赫里曼之侵

region.en: Sasanian Persia (symbolic pin at Fars province)
region.zh: 薩珊波斯（象徵性定位於法爾斯省）

period: Pahlavi cosmological compendium, Sasanian strata c. 4th-6th c. CE, copied 9th-11th c.; principal MS: Indian Bundahishn (Bombay) and Iranian Bundahishn (Copenhagen MS)

source.archive: Internet Sacred Texts Archive (West, SBE vol. 5, 1880)
source.work: Bundahishn chs. 1-4, 34 (Pahlavi); trans. E. W. West, Pahlavi Texts Part I, Sacred Books of the East vol. 5, Oxford 1880

summary.en: Ohrmazd creates the good creation in six stages — sky, water, earth, plants, animals, man (Gayomart) — and the seven Amesha Spentas; Ahriman bursts up from the darkness to destroy it; Ohrmazd recites the Ahuna Vairya, drives him back, and seals the attack for nine thousand years, fixing history as a battle the good creation will win.
summary.zh: 阿胡拉·馬茲達以六段造善世——天、水、地、植物、動物、原人伽約馬特——並七大天使；阿赫里曼自黑暗突起毀世；馬茲達誦阿胡納·瓦里亞經文擊退之，封其侵擾九千年——歷史遂為善必勝之戰。

sensitivity.note: Scripture of a living tradition (Zoroastrian/Parsi); the Yasna liturgy is sacred and is not reproduced; Bundahishn cosmology is a public Pahlavi text.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bundahishn 1 (West 1880): 'Ohrmazd is in the light on high, Ahriman in the abyss of darkness below... both are limited and unlimited... between them is the void, in which their meeting shall occur.' Ohrmazd creates the creation spiritually first, then materially, in six stages. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Bundahishn 1 (West 1880); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《班達希申》第一章（韋斯特，1880）的濃縮改述：「歐爾馬茲德居於高處的光明之中，阿里曼則在下方黑暗的深淵……兩者皆有限亦無限……他們之間是虛空，他們的相遇將在其中發生。」歐爾馬茲德先以精神的方式創造了受造界，繼而以物質的方式創造，共分六個階段。非逐字引述。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bundahishn 3-4: Ohrmazd recites the Ahuna Vairya prayer, twenty-one words matching the twenty-one books of the scripture; Ahriman, seeing the creation, is confounded, and for three thousand years lies fettered; he then bursts up through the earth's middle and defiles the waters, the earth, the fire, and the plants; Gayomart and the unique ox are slain — from the ox's body spring the plants and animals, from Gayomart's body the first human couple. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Bundahishn 3-4; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《班達希申》第三至四章的濃縮改述：歐爾馬茲德誦念阿胡那·瓦伊里亞祈禱文，共二十一個詞，對應經典的二十一卷；阿里曼見到這受造界，驚惶失措，被束縛達三千年之久；其後他衝破大地的中央，汙染了水、大地、火與植物；伽約馬特與獨一無二的原牛被殺——從原牛的身軀生出植物與動物，從伽約馬特的身軀生出第一對人類男女。非逐字引述。

canonical_translation: E. W. West, Pahlavi Texts Part I (Bundahis), SBE vol. 5, Oxford 1880 (public domain); modern: B. T. Anklesaria, Zand-Akasih (1956, copyright)

narrative.en:
The Bundahishn ('Primal Creation') is the Zoroastrian book of cosmogony, cosmology, and apocalypse — a Sasanian-era Pahlavi compendium preserving a theology whose oldest layers are the Gathas of Zarathustra.

BEGINNING: THE TWO SPIRITS. Ohrmazd (Ahura Mazda) dwells in endless light on high; Ahriman (Angra Mainyu) in the abyss of darkness below; between them stretches the void in which they will meet. Ohrmazd 'is in knowledge, goodness, and light'; Ahriman in 'stinging venom and darkness' — and their knowledge runs backward and forward nine thousand years. Ohrmazd creates first spiritually (menog, the 'thought-state'): the sky, water, earth, plants, animals, and man — six creations in six stages, each guarded by one of the seven Amesha Spentas (Vohu Manah, Asha Vahishta, Khshathra Vairya, Spenta Armaiti, Haurvatat, Ameretat, with Ohrmazd/Spena? as the seventh) — then materially (getig), clothing each creation in body. The cosmology is numerically ordered: 3,000 years of spiritual creation; Ahriman bound; the final 3,000 years of the mixed state; and the last 3,000 under the Saviors.

MIDDLE: THE ASSAULT. Ahriman, seeing the good creation in the light, is confounded by its perfection and by Ohrmazd's recitation of the Ahuna Vairya — twenty-one words whose power binds him; he lies fettered for three thousand years. Then, roused by the spirit Jeh (the whore-demon), he rises, bursting up through the middle of the earth: he defiles the water with salt, corrupts the fire with smoke, sows noxious creatures (khrafstra) in the plants, and brings disease, decay, and death into the animals. He reaches up to the sky's dome and enters creation through it; the sky is cracked, and the battle of history begins. Gayomart, the primal man, and the unique ox (Gopatshah? the Uniquely-created Ox) are slain by Ahriman's assault — but their deaths are productive: from the ox's body spring fifty-five kinds of grain and twelve kinds of medicinal plants, and from its seed, purified in the moon, the pairs of animals; from Gayomart's body, purified in the sun, grows the rivas plant from which Mashya and Mashyana, the first human couple, arise. Death itself is thus revealed as transformed fertility: the assault of evil becomes the field of its own defeat.

END: THE SEALED BATTLE. Ohrmazd binds the assault: 'the creatures of Ahriman... he placed in the earth' — and Ahriman is sealed back through the hole by which he came, while Ohrmazd sets the celestial spheres in motion — 12,000 years apportioned among the four ages, with the sun's path, the stars' stations (the 6,488? the fixed and wandering stars), and the mountains as fortresses (the earth's mountains are 'the garners' that hold back the waters). Time is now the arena: history runs as a battle in which every act of righteousness (asha) strengthens the good creation and every sin feeds Ahriman, until the final renovation (Frashokereti — Bundahishn 34, cross-referenced).

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds Zoroastrian dualist ethics (every deed affects the cosmic battle), the ritual duties (protecting the good creations — water, fire, earth, cattle — from pollution), the priestly calendar (the 12,000-year scheme and the Saviors), and the eschatology of the molten river; it is recited and taught in Parsi and Irani communities, and its imagery structured Sasanian royal art (the rock reliefs of the investiture).
narrative.zh: 《創世紀》（班達希申）開篇：奧爾馬茲德居高處光明中，阿赫里曼居下界黑暗深淵，其間為鴻溝；二者皆知前後九千年之事。馬茲達先以『默界』（menog）創造六段——天、水、地、植物、動物、原人——由七大天使各守其一，後賦以『實界』（getig）之體。阿赫里曼見善世完美而懼，為阿胡納·瓦里亞二十一字所縛，囚三千年；後經女魔耶赫所激，破地而出：使水鹹、火生煙、於植物中播毒蟲，以病老死入獸界；原人伽約馬特與獨牛被殺——然牛身出五十五種穀物與十二種藥草，牛種經月淨而生百獸之偶；伽約馬特之身經日淨而生瑞瓦斯植物，從中生初人夫婦馬希亞與馬希亞娜。馬茲達封閉邪侵之路，立天球之運行，分歷史為四紀一萬二千年：善惡之戰即歷史，凡義行皆壯善世，凡罪皆飼惡靈，直至末世淨化之河。功能：善惡二元倫理、護善四物之祭儀、祭司曆法、以及薩珊王家藝術之意象。

functions: Dualist ethics: every deed as engagement in the cosmic battle
Ritual duties: protecting the good creations (water, fire, earth, cattle) from pollution
Priestly calendar: 12,000-year scheme with the Saviors (Saoshyants)
Royal iconography: Sasanian investiture reliefs echo the cosmic order
