title.en: Pangu Opens Heaven and Earth: The Cosmogony of the Primal Giant
title.zh: 盤古開天闢地

region.en: Nanyang, Henan (Pangu Mountain shrine; symbolic pin)
region.zh: 中國河南盤古山（象徵性定位）

period: First recorded by Xu Zheng, Sanwu liji (3rd c. CE; text lost, fragments preserved in Yiwen Leiju, 7th c.); cult attested Tang-Song onward

source.archive: Internet Sacred Texts Archive (Werner, Myths and Legends of China, 1922) / Project Gutenberg
source.work: Xu Zheng, Sanwu liji (fragments in Yiwen Leiju); trans. Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction (Baltimore, 1993); E. T. C. Werner, Myths and Legends of China, London 1922

license: Werner 1922 public domain; Birrell 1993 quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Heaven and earth begin as an egg-like chaos in which the giant Pangu grows for eighteen thousand years; when he wakes he splits the light and heavy, and each day the sky rises ten feet and the earth thickens ten feet while he stands between them; at his death his body becomes the world — breath the winds, eyes the sun and moon, blood the rivers — and the mites on his flesh become the peoples.
summary.zh: 太初如雞卵之混沌，盤古生其中，萬八千歲而醒；陽清為天，陰濁為地，天日高一丈，地日厚一丈，盤古居中長成；其死也，氣為風雲，聲為雷霆，左眼為日，右眼為月，血液為江河，肢為五嶽——身上諸蟲受風所感化為黎民。

sensitivity.note: Heritage narrative; living folk cult at Pangu shrines treats it as sacred geography.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Xu Zheng, Sanwu liji (as preserved in fragments): Heaven and earth were together like the inside of an egg; Pangu was born within; after eighteen thousand years the clear and light rose to become heaven, the heavy and turbid settled to become earth, and Pangu stood between, growing ten feet a day as heaven rose and earth thickened ten feet a day — for another eighteen thousand years. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Xu Zheng, Sanwu liji (as preserved in fragments); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 徐整《三五歷記》（以殘篇保存）的濃縮改述：天地渾沌如同雞蛋的內部；盤古生於其中；經過一萬八千年，清而輕者上升成為天，重而濁者下沉成為地，盤古立於其間，天每日升高一丈、地每日增厚一丈，盤古亦每日長高一丈——如此又過了一萬八千年。非逐字引述。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the death catalogue (Sanwu liji fragments): At his death, his breath became the winds and clouds, his voice the thunder, his left eye the sun and right eye the moon, his four limbs and body the four poles and five mountains, his blood the rivers, his veins the roads, his flesh the fields, his hair and beard the stars, his skin and body-hair plants and trees, his teeth and bones metals and stones, his marrow pearls and jade, his sweat the rain — and the mites on his body, touched by the wind, became the black-haired people. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the death catalogue (Sanwu liji fragments); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 化生清單（《三五歷記》殘篇）的濃縮改述：他死之時，氣息化為風雲，聲音化為雷霆，左眼化為太陽、右眼化為月亮，四肢與身軀化為四極與五嶽，血液化為江河，筋脈化為道路，肌肉化為田土，頭髮與鬍鬚化為星辰，皮膚與體毛化為草木，牙齒與骨骼化為金石，骨髓化為珠玉，汗水化為雨露——而他身上的蟲豸，經風吹拂，化為黑髮的人民。非逐字引述。

canonical_translation: Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction, Johns Hopkins, 1993 (copyright); E. T. C. Werner, Myths and Legends of China, 1922 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Pangu is China's best-known cosmogonic figure, though a latecomer to the textual record: the story first appears in a 3rd-century CE encyclopedia, at a time when Daoist cosmology and Indian Buddhist creation stories circulated at court, and it became the dominant folk cosmogony of imperial and modern China.

BEGINNING: THE EGG OF CHAOS. Heaven and earth were once joined without shape or boundary, undifferentiated like the inside of a hen's egg (hundun, the primal murk). Within this chaos the primal being Pangu was born and grew — asleep for eighteen thousand years in the dark. When he woke, he could not endure the confinement; he took up a chisel and mallet (or, in other tellings, stretched his limbs) and split the chaos: the clear, light qi rose and became heaven; the heavy, turbid qi sank and became earth.

MIDDLE: THE STANDING GIANT. Fearing that heaven and earth would close again, Pangu stood between them, his head holding up the sky, his feet planted on the earth — and he grew with them: each day heaven rose ten feet, the earth thickened ten feet, and Pangu grew ten feet taller, for another eighteen thousand years, until the poles were fixed at their proper distance and the giant had become taller than any being could measure.

END: THE DEATH THAT IS THE WORLD. Exhausted, Pangu died — and his death is the creation's second act: his last breath became the winds and clouds; his voice, the rolling thunder; his left eye the sun, his right eye the moon; his four limbs and trunk became the four poles and the Five Mountains; his blood the rivers, his veins the roads of the land, his flesh the fields and soil; his hair and beard the stars of heaven, his skin and body-hair the grasses and trees; his teeth and bones metals and rocks, his marrow pearls and jade, his sweat the rain and dew that nourishes all. The mites and lice that lived on his flesh, touched by the wind, became the black-haired people — human beings born not from a god's design but from the body of the one who made the world possible.

AFTERMATH AND FUNCTION. The Sanwu liji continues with the Three Sovereigns who follow Pangu (Heaven, Earth, Man), grounding dynastic succession in cosmic succession; Pangu's cult centers (Pangu Mountain in Henan; shrines across the south; the Yao and Zhuang Pangu traditions of Guangdong/Guangxi) treat him as local ancestor. The myth's functions: it aitiologizes topography (mountains as limbs, rivers as blood — a body-map of China), establishes the cosmos as organism rather than artifact, and, in the modern era, became the centerpiece of Chinese national myth-history (Pangu statues, the Pangu Era of textbooks).

COMPARATIVE NOTE. Scholars have long compared Pangu to the dismembered-cosmos figures of other traditions (Ymir in Norse myth; Purusha in the Rigveda's Purusha Sukta; Manu in Indo-Iranian texts) and debated South Asian influence on the 3rd-century story (the giant from the cosmic egg), while Chinese folk tradition holds him indigenous. The record keeps both positions open.
narrative.zh: 盤古之名首見於三國吳徐整《三五曆紀》，其時佛教創世說與道教宇宙論並行，而盤古遂為後世民間創世之主。太初天地混沌如雞子，盤古生其中，萬八千歲；覺而惡其困，執鑿開混沌：陽清為天，陰濁為地；恐復合，以身居中，頭托天、足踏地，天日高一丈、地日厚一丈、盤古日長一丈，又一萬八千歲，天地極深而極固。後盤古力竭而死：氣成風雲，聲為雷霆，左眼為日右眼為月，四肢五體為四極五嶽，血液為江河，筋脈為地理，肌肉為田土，髮髭為星辰，皮毛為草木，齒骨為金石，精髓為珠玉，汗流為雨澤；身上諸蟲感風化為黎民——人非神所設計，乃開天者之身所遺。續以三皇承之，王朝承宇宙之序。功能：地形之釋義（山為肢、河為血——中國之地圖即身體圖）、宇宙為有機體、及現代民族神話之核心（盤古紀元）。比較：與北歐尤彌爾、吠陀原人普魯沙結構平行，學界有印度影響說，民間則自認本土。

functions: Topographical aition: mountains as limbs, rivers as blood — the body-map of the land
Cosmos as organism: creation as growth and death rather than craft
Succession template: the Three Sovereigns and dynastic order follow cosmic order
Modern national myth-history: Pangu statues and the 'Pangu Era' of textbooks

variants.name: Xu Zheng's Sanwu liji (3rd c. CE)
variants.text_tradition: Text lost; fragments preserved in the Yiwen Leiju encyclopedia (7th c.) and Taiping Yulan
variants.summary: The earliest telling: the egg-chaos, the eighteen-thousand-year growth, the ten-foot-a-day measure, and the full death-catalogue; no chisel — Pangu splits chaos by growing.

variants.name: Wu Yueneng? 'Pangu Kai Tiandi' folk versions (Henan/Shandong)
variants.text_tradition: 20th-c. oral recordings at Pangu Mountain (Nanyang) and folk storytellers
variants.summary: Folk tellings add the chisel-and-mallet, the sister-spouse motif (Pangu and his sister repopulate the world, with smoke-sign divination), and local shrine genealogies — the living folk stratum.

variants.name: South Asian parallel (Purusha/Manu hypothesis)
variants.summary: The dismembered-cosmos structure parallels the Vedic Purusha, and the cosmic egg parallels Brahmanda; scholars debate transmission via Buddhist India in the Han-Song interval versus independent development.

variants.name: Pangu in Yao and Zhuang traditions
variants.text_tradition: Guangdong/Guangxi minority narratives; Pan Hu figure
variants.summary: Southern minority traditions entwine Pangu with Pan Hu (the dog-ancestor of the Yao), a distinct but etymologically tangled figure — caution against conflating them is standard in scholarship.

primary_sources.citation: 3rd c. CE; fragments in Ouyang Xun (ed.), Yiwen Leiju, ch. 1 (7th c.) and Taiping Yulan; English in Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction, Baltimore 1993, pp. 25-28 (copyright; quoted as summary only).

secondary_sources.work: Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction
secondary_sources.citation: Birrell 1993, Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press — annotated translations and the dating debate.

secondary_sources.work: Derk Bodde, 'Myths of Ancient China'
secondary_sources.citation: Bodde 1961, in Mythologies of the Ancient World (ed. S. N. Kramer), New York: Doubleday — the South Asian influence argument.

source_urls.description: Project Gutenberg — E. T. C. Werner, Myths and Legends of China (1922, public domain)

title.en: Izanagi and Izanami: The Stirring of the Islands and the Land of Yomi
title.zh: 伊邪那岐與伊邪那美：淤能碁呂島與黃泉國

region.en: Onogoro Island / Awaji, Seto Inland Sea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瀨戶內海淤能碁呂島／淡路島（象徵性定位）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (principal MS: Shinpukuji-bon, 1371 copy); Nihon Shoki 720 CE

source.work: Kojiki, Book 1, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain, A Translation of the 'Ko-ji-ki', Kobe, 1882 (public domain)

summary.en: The divine pair Izanagi and Izanami stir the primordial brine with the jeweled spear to raise Onogoro island, marry with a circuit of the celestial pillar, and beget the islands of Japan and the gods; when Izanami dies bearing the fire-god, Izanagi follows her to Yomi, breaks the taboo of looking, flees her putrefying corpse, seals the land of the dead with a boulder, and purifies himself — begetting Amaterasu, Tsukuyomi, and Susanoo.
summary.zh: 伊邪那岐與伊邪那美以天沼矛攪滄海，滴鹹成淤能碁呂島；繞天柱成婚，生大八洲與諸神；火神焚母而死，伊邪那岐赴黃泉，破『勿視』之禁，見腐屍而逃，以大石封黃泉比良坂，於日向橘小戶之阿波岐原祓禊，遂生天照、月讀、須佐之男。

sensitivity.note: Living Shinto tradition; the imperial mythology's modern political history (State Shinto, 1868-1945) should be handled critically.

passages.text: Chamberlain translation (Kojiki 1.3): 'So the two Deities, standing on the Floating Bridge of Heaven, pushed down the jewel-spear with a churning-churning, and lingered? and when they had churned the brine till it went curdle-curdle, and drew [the spear] up, the brine that dripped down from the end of the spear was piled up and became an island. This is the island of Onogoro.' (Close to Chamberlain's wording; quoted as public-domain translation.)
passages.zh: 張伯倫譯本（《古事記》1.3）：「於是二神立於天之浮橋之上，以攪攪之勢推下瓊矛，而久留之乎？及攪拌鹽水直至凝凝然，乃拔矛而上，自矛尖滴落之鹽水積聚成島。此即淤能碁呂島。」（近於張伯倫之措辭；引作公有領域譯本。）

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Kojiki 1.8-9 (Chamberlain, public domain source): At Yomi's gate Izanagi breaks the tooth of his left comb and lights it; he sees his wife's body crawling with maggots and the eight thunder-deities on it; fleeing, he casts his headdress (grapes), his comb (bamboo shoots), and peaches to delay the pursuit; at the pass he plugs it with a boulder of a thousand men — and the pair exchange threats: she will strangle a thousand a day, he will build fifteen hundred birthing-huts. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Kojiki 1.8-9 (Chamberlain, public domain source); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《古事記》1.8-9之節縮意譯（張伯倫，公有領域來源）：於黃泉之門，伊邪那岐折其左櫛之齒而燃之；見其妻之身蛆蟲蠕動，八雷神附於其上；逃遁之際，擲其頭飾（葡萄）、其櫛（竹筍）及桃子以阻追兵；至坡道處，以千人之巨石塞之——而二人互放狠話：她將日縊千人，他將日建一千五百產屋。非逐字照錄。

canonical_translation: Basil Hall Chamberlain, A Translation of the 'Ko-ji-ki', Kobe 1882 (public domain); W. G. Aston, Nihongi, 1896 (public domain); modern: Donald Philippi, Kojiki, Tokyo 1968 (copyright)

narrative.en:
The Kojiki (712 CE) opens the age of gods with the first stirrings of creation and the first death — a narrative whose movements structure Shinto purity practice to this day.

BEGINNING: THE STIRRING. When heaven and earth first parted, three gods came into being, and the seven generations of the age of gods followed; the last pair, Izanagi ('He Who Invites') and Izanami ('She Who Invites'), stand on the Floating Bridge of Heaven with the jeweled spear Ame-no-nuboko. They churn the sea beneath ('churning-churning'); lifting the spear, the brine drips from its point and piles into the island Onogoro. Descending, they erect the Heavenly Pillar (Ame-no-mihashira) and circle it in the marriage rite: she greets him first — 'how lovely a young man!' — and he answers her greeting. The children of this first union are deformed: the leech-child Hiruko, set adrift in a reed boat, and Awashima. They return and ask the Heavenly Deities the cause; the gods divine it — the woman spoke first. They repeat the rite with the man first, and the union is made right.

MIDDLE: THE BIRTH OF THE ISLANDS AND OF DEATH. Izanami now bears the islands of Japan — Awaji, Shikoku, Oki, Kyushu, Iki, Tsushima, Sado, and Yamato ('the fairest land') — and then the gods of sea, wind, mountains, trees, and plains. Last she bears the fire-god Kagutsuchi; his flames burn her genitals, and she sickens — her vomit, excrement, and urine each begetting gods — and she dies. Izanagi, raging, cuts Kagutsuchi in pieces with his ten-grasp sword, and from the blood and the severed parts spring gods (including Takemikazuchi). Grieving, Izanagi follows his wife to Yomi, the land of roots and darkness.

THE TABOO AND THE FLIGHT. Izanami greets him: 'Why hast thou come?... I have eaten of the hearth of Yomi' — too late to return. She retires to consult the gods of the land, forbidding him to look; Izanagi waits, then breaks a tooth from his comb and lights it — and sees the horror: her body crawling with maggots, the eight Thunder-deities lodged on it. He flees; Izanami's shame turns to fury: 'Thou hast brought shame on me!' She sends the hags of Yomi (yomotsu-shikome), then the eight thunder-gods and the warriors of Yomi. Izanagi delays them by casting his black headdress (which becomes grapes), his comb (bamboo shoots), and plucking three peaches to strike at the pursuers — the peaches he names saviors of humanity. At the foot of the Even Pass of Yomi (Yomotsu-hirasaka), he plucks three peaches from a tree and hurls them; the pursuers fall back, and the pass he blocks with a boulder that would take a thousand men to move. From either side of the rock the couple speaks their last: Izanami threatens to strangle a thousand people of his land each day; Izanagi answers he will have fifteen hundred birthing-huts built each day — death and birth locked in ratio. She is proclaimed Yomotsu-Ookami, the great goddess of the dead.

END: THE PURIFICATION AND THE THREE NOBLE CHILDREN. Pollution-clad, Izanagi performs the first great purification (misogi) at Awajihara (Tachibana no Odo) in Himuka: casting his clothes and staff into the water begets gods of each garment; washing his left eye begets Amaterasu-Omikami (Heaven-Illuminating Great Deity), his right eye Tsukuyomi (Moon), his nose Susanoo (Storm). 'Rejoicing, he divides his treasures': Amaterasu receives the High Plain of Heaven with the necklace, Tsukuyomi the night, Susanoo the seas — and Susanoo wails for his mother until his beard reaches his chest, laying waste to the lands. Izanagi expels him — and the next cycle begins. The narrative grounds Shinto purity (kegara? kegare and harae): death is pollution, water purification, and the sun's lineage the world's light.
narrative.zh: 天地下分之初，神世七代之末生伊邪那岐、伊邪那美二神。二神立於天浮橋，以天沼矛攪滄海，提起時矛尖滴鹹積為淤能碁呂島；下島立天之御柱，繞柱成婚：妹先言『好男子』，遂生水蛭子，棄於蘆舟；歸問天神，知女先言之故；男先言，復生大八洲（淡路、四國、隱岐、九州、壹岐、對馬、佐渡、大和）與海山風木諸神。末生火神迦具土，焚母陰而病，吐泄亦化神，遂死。伊邪那岐怒斬火神為五段，血與斷部化神。悲而赴黃泉；伊邪那美言已食黃泉灶火之食，不得歸，囑勿視；伊邪那岐折左鬢櫛齒燃火照之，見屍蛆蠕、八雷神附，驚逃。妻怒曰『辱我』，遣黃泉醜女、八雷神、黃泉軍追之；丟鬢飾化葡萄、櫛化筍、擲桃退敵；至黃泉比良坂取桃三枚投之，以千人所引大石塞坂。隔石互誓：妻日殺千人，夫日立千五百產室——生死相抵。妻為黃泉大神。穢甚，遂於日向橘小戶阿波岐原祓禊：濯左眼生天照大御神、右眼生月讀、鼻生須佐之男，分寶而命之；須佐之男啼欲見母，毀山川，被逐——次一神話由此而始。功能：穢與祓之禮、死為穢之釋義、日光之世系。

functions: Grounding of Shinto purity practice: kegare (pollution) and harae (purification)
Aition of death as pollution and of the birth/death ratio in the world
Charter of the solar lineage: Amaterasu's birth from the left eye
Political theology: the imperial genealogy descends from this cosmogony

variants.name: Nihon Shoki version (720 CE)
variants.text_tradition: Nihon Shoki, Book 1, trans. W. G. Aston, 1896 (public domain)
variants.summary: The official chronicle's parallel telling with multiple textual variants appended (itself quoting 'one writing' versions), softer in tone (no maggot catalogue) and ordered for courtly legitimation.

variants.name: Kojiki's Shinpukuji-bon manuscript
variants.summary: The oldest surviving full manuscript of the 712 text, the base of modern critical editions; earlier Kojiki quotations survive in the Kokki? and Kogo Shui (807).

variants.name: Local Yomi traditions
variants.text_tradition: Yomotsu-hirasaka (Higashiizumo, Shimane) shrine traditions; Yomi cult sites
variants.summary: The Even Pass of Yomi is localized in Shimane prefecture, where the boulder (chigaeshi-no-oka) is a cult site — the myth as sacred geography maintained by living shrines.

primary_sources.citation: Chs. 1.3-1.9 (stirring, marriage, births, fire-god, Yomi, purification). MS: Shinpukuji-bon (1371 copy). Translations: B. H. Chamberlain, Kobe 1882 (public domain); D. Philippi, Tokyo 1968 (copyright).

secondary_sources.work: Gary L. Ebersole, Ritual Poetry and the Politics of Death in Early Japan
secondary_sources.citation: Ebersole 1989, Princeton: Princeton University Press — the Yomi narrative's ritual and political poetics.

secondary_sources.work: Michael Ashkenazi, Handbook of Japanese Mythology
secondary_sources.citation: Ashkenazi 2003, Santa Barbara: ABC-CLIO — reference synthesis of Kojiki/Nihongi variants.

source_urls.description: Internet Sacred Texts Archive — Chamberlain's Kojiki translation (1882, public domain)

sensitivity_guidance: Living Shinto tradition and imperial mythology: cite Kojiki by chapter; handle the 1868-1945 State Shinto use of this material critically in commentary; shrine sites in Shimane maintain active cults of the Yomi narrative.

title.en: Enki and Ninhursag: The Paradise of Dilmun and the Eight Healing Goddesses
title.zh: 恩基與寧胡爾薩格：迪爾蒙樂園與八位癒合女神

region.en: Nippur, Iraq (tablet findspot; Dilmun traditionally identified with Bahrain)
region.zh: 伊拉克尼普爾（泥板出土地；迪爾蒙傳統上比定為巴林）

period: Old Babylonian copies (c. 1750-1600 BCE) of earlier Sumerian poems; principal tablets: Nippur finds (e.g. Ni-series), University of Pennsylvania Museum

source.work: Enki and Ninhursag (ETCSL 1.1.1), trans. Jeremy Black et al., Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature, Oxford, 1998-2006

license: Open access with attribution (ETCSL); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: In the pure land of Dilmun, where nothing is sick and no crow caws, Enki waters the earth; the mother-goddess Ninhursag bears him a line of goddesses, and when Enki eats eight plants she has grown, eight of his organs sicken — until the fox wins her return, and she gives birth to eight healing deities, among them Ninti, Lady of the Rib.
summary.zh: 純淨之邦迪爾蒙，無病無疾、無鴉啼無獅噬；恩基灌水其地；母神寧胡爾薩格為之生女神一系；恩基竊食其八草，八臟俱病；狐智請回母神，母神遂生八位癒合之神，其中有寧提——『肋骨之女』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary text of a dead tradition.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of ETCSL 1.1.1, lines 1-30: The land Dilmun is pure, the land Dilmun is clean... In Dilmun the raven utters no cry, the lion kills not, the wolf snatches not the lamb... its sicknesses are not — for Enki has blessed it: 'may the city drink healthful waters'. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of ETCSL 1.1.1, lines 1-30; not verbatim.
passages.zh: ETCSL 1.1.1第1-30行之節縮意譯：迪爾蒙之地潔淨，迪爾蒙之地純淨……於迪爾蒙，烏鴉不啼，獅不殺戮，狼不攫羔……其地無疾——因恩基已賜福之：「願此城飲康健之水。」非逐字照錄。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of ETCSL 1.1.1 (ending): Eight plants have sprung up; Enki eats them one by one in the marsh; Ninhursag curses him: 'until thou art dead, I shall not look upon thee with life-giving eye'; eight of his organs fail — until the fox offers to bring her back; she returns, seats him by her vulva, and for each ailing part bears a deity: 'for my rib — Ninti, the Lady of the rib.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of ETCSL 1.1.1 (ending); not verbatim.
passages.zh: ETCSL 1.1.1（結尾）之節縮意譯：八株植物萌生；恩基於沼澤中逐一食之；寧胡爾薩格詛咒之：「直至汝死，我必不以賦生之目視汝」；其八處器官衰竭——直至狐狸自請將其請回；她歸來，令其坐於其陰部之側，為每一患病之部位各生一神：「為我之肋骨——寧提，肋骨之女主。」非逐字照錄。

language: Sumerian (emegir; literary dialect with Emesal laments)
canonical_translation: ETCSL translation (Black et al., Oxford, open access); scholarly: Attinger's French edition (copyright)

narrative.en:
The Sumerian paradise narrative — Eden's oldest Near Eastern relative — combines a creation-blessing, a genealogy of goddesses born from desire, and a sickness-and-healing plot whose rib pun was noted by every generation of Genesis scholars.

DILMUN: THE PURE LAND. Dilmun, a land traditionally identified with Bahrain or the eastern shore, is blessed before it is real: 'In Dilmun the raven utters no cry... the lion kills not... no one says: my eyes are sick... no one says: my head is sick.' But it lacks one thing — fresh water. Ninhursag, the mother-goddess ('Lady of the Mountain'), asks Enki, lord of the waters, for the gift; he answers: 'May the city of Dilmun drink healthful waters' — and Enki, god of the sweet water (abzu), brings the Tigris and Euphrates to her: he mates with her in the marsh, and his seed pours into her womb. She bears nine days, and Ninsar ('Lady Green Herb', the plant-goddess) is born.

THE CHAIN OF BIRTHS. The narrative repeats: Ninsar grows lush in the reed-beds; Enki desires her and lies with her; she bears Ninkurra ('Lady of the Pasture'); Enki lies with her; she bears Uttu, 'the Lady of Plants' — the spider-weaver of the vegetable world. Ninhursag, angered, warns Uttu and removes Enki's seed from her; Uttu asks for fruit, and Enki, with the gardener's help, fills her with apples, cucumbers, and grapes — the seed falls into the earth, and from it eight plants sprout in the marsh.

THE EATING AND THE SICKNESS. Enki, walking the marsh with his vizier Isimud, sees the eight plants and eats them, one by one — his steward warns each time, 'My lord, the plant!' — he eats. Ninhursag, furious ('was he to eat them all?'), curses him: she will not look on him with the life-giving eye until he is dead, and she vanishes. Eight of Enki's organs sicken one by one — jaw, tooth, mouth, hand, rib, foot, side, head — and the great gods sit helpless: 'the fox said to Enlil: shall I bring her? I know her place' — the fox, for a reward, fetches Ninhursag from the mountain; she returns, seats Enki by her vulva, and asks each part: 'my jaw aches... my tooth aches... my rib aches' — and for each she bears a deity to heal it: Abu for the plants? (Abu, Nintul, Ninsutu, Ninkasi — Lady Beer — Dazimua, Ninki, Nanshe? and Ningiri? — the canonical list includes Ninti, 'Lady of the Rib' or 'Lady of the Leaf' (ti = both), the pun that later readers compared to Eve, 'mother of all living', built from a rib).

END: THE BLESSING OF SUMER. Healed, Enki blesses his recovered organs and assigns them cults — Urim, Nippur, Eridu, Meluhha — and the poem ends with the goddess's praise: Ninhursag, 'who has given birth to all the gods', is exalted. The paradise episode of Dilmun (pure, watered, painless) becomes the scriptural prototype of the garden-of-god narratives of the Near East.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds the theology of water (Enki's blessing makes paradise), the horticultural economy (goddesses as plants; healing as childbirth), and the medical ideology of healing deities born from sickness; its rib-leaf pun entered the comparative literature of Genesis; and its Dilmun frames the Persian Gulf as a trade paradise in Sumerian economy.
narrative.zh: 迪爾蒙為純淨之邦：鴉不啼、獅不噬、無病無疾，惟缺淡水。寧胡爾薩格請恩基灌水，恩基許之，於沼地交合，九日生寧薩爾（綠草女神）；恩基復與寧薩爾合，生寧庫拉；再生烏圖（植物女神）。寧胡爾薩格怒而告烏圖避之；烏圖求果，恩基以蘋果、黃瓜、葡萄誘之；種子落地，沼中生八草。恩基與侍臣伊西姆得行沼上，侍臣每草皆勸『主，草也！』而恩基一一食之。寧胡爾薩格大怒詛之：『不與汝生命之眼，至死方休』，遂隱。恩基八臟次第病——頜、齒、口、手、肋、足、脅、首——眾神束手。狐言『能請其歸』，受賞請回母神；母神歸，使恩基坐己陰之前，逐一問病，逐病生一神以癒之：頜生阿布、齒生寧圖勒、口生寧蘇圖、手生寧卡西（啤酒女神）、肋生寧提（『肋骨之女』；ti 兼『肋』『葉』之音，與夏娃『眾生之母』之雙關為比較文學經典）、足生達茲木阿、脅生寧基、首生寧吉利。癒後恩基賜福諸器而封其祀——烏爾、尼普爾、埃利都、梅魯哈。母神『生眾神者』受頌。功能：水之創世論、園藝經濟之女神系、病而愈之醫學神學、以及近東樂園敘事之原型。

functions: Prototype of Near Eastern paradise narratives (pure land, watered, painless)
Theology of water: Enki's blessing as the making of paradise
Medical ideology: healing deities born from diseased organs
Gulf economy: Dilmun as the trade-paradise of Sumerian commerce

variants.name: Genesis 2-4 parallel
variants.summary: Shares the garden, the curse-on-eating, the sickness of the body, and — famously — the rib woman ('Ninti'/'Eve, mother of all living'); the pun (Sumerian ti = 'rib' and 'leaf') is the classic comparandum.

variants.name: Enki and the World Order (ETCSL 1.1.3)
variants.summary: A companion poem in which Enki, healed and enthroned, assigns offices to every deity and land — the administrative sequel to the paradise narrative.

variants.name: Dilmun in later Mesopotamian and Gulf texts
variants.text_tradition: Administrative and epic references (Gilgamesh XI's Dilmun; Persian Gulf trade archives)

title.en: The Baal Cycle: Yam, the Palace, and the Defeat of Mot
title.zh: 巴力神話圈：雅姆、神殿與死亡之敗

region.en: Ras Shamra (Ugarit), Syria
region.zh: 敘利亞拉斯沙姆拉（烏加里特）

period: Tablets excavated 1929-; composition c. 14th-13th c. BCE; principal tablets RS 2.014 etc. (Louvre AO 17.094 series; National Museum of Damascus)

source.work: Baal Cycle, KTU 1.1-1.6 (CTU 1.1-1.6); English: J. C. L. Gibson, Canaanite Myths and Legends, Edinburgh 1978; Dennis Pardee, Stories from Ancient Canaan, 2nd ed., Atlanta 2018

license: Cuneiform text public domain; modern translations quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Baal, the storm-god, defeats the sea-king Yam with two magic clubs, wins a palace on Mount Saphon after the widow-goddess Asherah intervenes, and is swallowed by Mot, lord of death; Anat kills Mot — splitting, burning, grinding, and sowing him — and Baal returns; the two powers meet in seven-year combat until Shapash the sun separates them.
summary.zh: 風暴神巴力以雙魔杖誅海王雅姆，經寡婦女神阿瑟拉說情得蘇鳳山神殿；後為死神摩特所吞；阿娜特誅摩特——以刀分之、以火焚之、以磨研之、於田播之——巴力遂歸；二神七年之戰，以太陽神沙帕什居中調停。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary text of a dead tradition; significant for biblical scholarship.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of KTU 1.2.iv: Kothar-wa-Hasis names the clubs — 'Yagrush (Chaser): chase Yam... Ayamur (Scatter): scatter Yam'; the clubs fly, and Yam falls; Baal proclaims: 'I have surely smitten Yam, the beloved of El... surely Baal reigns!' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of KTU 1.2.iv; not verbatim.
passages.zh: KTU 1.2.iv之節縮意譯：科塔爾-瓦-哈西斯為棍棒命名——「雅格魯什（追逐者）：追逐雅姆……阿亞穆爾（驅散者）：驅散雅姆」；棍棒飛出，雅姆倒下；巴力宣告：「我確已擊殺雅姆，埃爾之寵兒……巴力確已為王！」非逐字照錄。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of KTU 1.6.ii: Anat seizes Divine Mot: 'with a blade she split him, with a winnowing-fork she burned him, with millstones she ground him, in the field she sowed him — the birds ate his remains.' El dreams that Baal lives; Baal returns to his palace; Mot, restored, claims the fight again — and Shapash parts them. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of KTU 1.6.ii; not verbatim.
passages.zh: KTU 1.6.ii之節縮意譯：阿娜特擒住神性之莫特：「以刃劈之，以簸箕焚之，以磨石磨之，於田中播之——飛鳥食其遺骸。」埃爾夢見巴力尚存；巴力歸其宮殿；莫特復原，再索一戰——沙帕什將二者分開。非逐字照錄。

canonical_translation: J. C. L. Gibson, Canaanite Myths and Legends, Edinburgh 1978 (copyright); Dennis Pardee, Stories from Ancient Canaan, 2nd ed., Louisville 2018 (copyright) — quoted as summary only

narrative.en:
The Baal Cycle — six tablets found at Ugarit (Ras Shamra, Syria) in 1929-31 — is the fullest Canaanite narrative and the essential comparandum for biblical storm-theology.

TABLET 1-2: BAAL VERSUS YAM. The sea-king Yam (Sea, 'Prince Yam, the beloved of El') tyrannizes the divine assembly and demands Baal delivered as his slave. The gods cower; even El counsels compliance. Baal seizes weapons and would kill the messengers in the assembly; Asherah, the mother of the gods, intervenes — 'why do you kill the messengers?' — and pledges to secure Baal's freedom by persuading El to concede Yam's kingship in exchange for a palace? (In KTU 1.1, Asherah promises Yam gifts, including a palace, if he lets Baal live.) The craftsman-god Kothar-wa-Hasis forges two clubs and names them as spells: 'Yagrush (Chaser): chase Yam!' — the club flies and fails; 'Ayamur (Scatter): scatter Yam!' — Yam falls dead at Baal's feet. Baal proclaims his reign: 'surely Baal reigns over the gods'; Yam's scattered body is threshed (in some readings the sea's fishing aition: 'fish are his tribute').

TABLET 3: ANAT'S VENGEANCE. Anat, Baal's sister, the virgin warrior, slaughters the men of the towns who wronged her guests (the gruesome interlude), and exchanges messages with Baal about her powers ('I have a word of the tree, the whisper of the stone... which no man knows'); Baal promises to reveal the secret if she brings word of the? — Anat, pacified, proposes the palace project.

TABLET 4: THE PALACE ON SAPHON. Baal has no house like the other gods; Asherah goes to El, walks across his? and secures the grant: 'A house for Baal like his brothers' — Kothar builds on Mount Saphon with cedars from Lebanon and gold, silver, lapis. Kothar offers to install windows: Baal refuses — through a window Yam's agents (or demons) would come; he promises? finally concedes; windows are opened, and storm passes through them ('Baal opened windows in the house, a rift in the clouds') — the aition of the rain through the clouds. Baal celebrates, and the hymn of his triumph: 'Baal's word is secret? ' He copulates with a heifer (in some tellings his own? as bull), begets Magar ('the Victory') — and visits Mot.

TABLET 5: MOT SWALLOWS BAAL. Mot, lord of death ('Divine Mot'), sits in the pit, his throat from earth to heaven ('one lip to the earth, one lip to the heaven'); Baal comes at his summons and is swallowed whole: 'Baal is dead... what will the people do?' El, on his throne, dreams; the rains stop; the world dries (the death of the storm-god is the death of rain). Anat buries Baal on Saphon, slaughters Mot's son? (in KTU 1.5, she 'seizes the son of Asherah? ' — she cuts Mot's? the rite: she kills 'Divine Mot's heir'? — standard reading: she buries Baal, slays his killers?), and mourns with Shapash, the sun-goddess, who collects the pieces.

TABLET 6: THE DEATH OF MOT AND THE RETURN. Athtar, 'the Morning Star', takes Baal's empty throne — but he is too small for it ('his head did not reach its top'). Anat finds Mot, seizes him, and performs the ritual execution: 'with a blade she split him, with a winnowing-fork she burned him, with millstones she ground him, in the field she sowed him — the birds ate his remains' — the farmer-god's death sown like seed. Seven years pass (in some tellings seven years of famine? the text: after seven years, Mot returns alive, complaining that he was slain 'as if a kid? '); El dreams that Baal lives; Baal returns, defeats the restored Mot in seven-year combat ('as Baal seized Mot... the two? '), until Shapash, the sun, intervenes: 'how can you fight the Word of the Strongest? Mot, hear: Baal has thy word? — the sun parts them, and the cycle closes with Baal restored and El's blessing.

FUNCTIONS. The cycle is the theology of the year: rain (Baal) versus drought (Mot) versus chaos-sea (Yam); it grounds Ugaritic kingship ideology (the palace of Saphon mirrors the royal temple), the cult of the ancestors and of Baal-Hadad at Ugarit, and — through biblical polemic (Baal and Asherah in Hosea, Elijah on Carmel) — the very vocabulary in which Hebrew monotheism defined itself.
narrative.zh: 巴力神話圈六板：海王雅姆暴虐神會，索巴力為奴；諸神懾服，阿瑟拉說情；工匠神科塔爾鑄雙杖，念咒而投：『追趕者，追雅姆！』『驅散者，碎雅姆！』雅姆斃，巴力稱王。阿娜特屠城雪恥，與兄論神力之秘。寡婦阿瑟拉往說埃爾，巴力得蘇鳳山建殿：黎巴嫩雪松、金銀青金；科塔爾欲開窗，巴力初拒，終許之——雲隙降雨之緣起。巴力化牛與牝牛合，生『勝利』。後赴死亡之主摩特之召，被其吞噬：其喉自地至天；巴力既亡，雨絕地枯。阿娜特葬巴力於蘇鳳山，與日神沙帕什同哀。星辰阿塔爾攝位而身小不能登。阿娜特擒摩特，以刀分之、以簸箕焚之、以磨研之、於田播之、飛鳥食之——死神如種被播。七年後摩特復生索戰，埃爾夢巴力猶存；巴力歸，與摩特七年之鬥，日神沙帕什止之：『汝安能與至強者之言爭？』巴力復位，埃爾賜福而終。功能：雨旱海三力之年環神學、王權神學（蘇鳳山殿即王廟之影）、以及希伯來聖經巴力論戰之詞彙源。

functions: Theology of the year: rain (Baal) vs. drought (Mot) vs. chaos-sea (Yam)
Royal ideology: the palace of Saphon mirrors Ugarit's temple-kingship
Aititions of weather: windows of the palace as rain through cloud-rifts
Biblical polemic: the Baal vocabulary against which Hebrew monotheism defined itself

variants.name: Hebrew Bible's Baal polemic
variants.summary: Israelite scripture absorbs and inverts the Baal cycle: the storm-theophany vocabulary of Psalm 29 is near-Baalic, while Elijah's contest reworks the rain-battle into monotheist polemic.

variants.name: The Amarna and Phoenician survivals
variants.text_tradition: Amarna letters (14th c. BCE); Philo of Byblos (1st-2nd c. CE)
variants.summary: Baal/Hadad appears in Egyptian archive letters; Philo's Phoenician History preserves a Hellenized cosmogony (Elioun, Ouranos, El/Kronos) derived from the same Canaanite mythic stratum.

variants.text_tradition: RS 2.014; RS 3.364; successive joins (Herder CTUA 1978; KTU 1976; CTU 2003)
variants.summary: The cycle survives in joins and lacunae; the standard editions reconstruct sequences that remain under scholarly revision (Smith 1994/2009) — a reconstructed text by definition.

title.en: The Song of Ullikummi: Kumarbi's Stone Giant and the Storm-god's War
title.zh: 烏利庫米之歌：庫馬爾比之石巨與風暴神之戰

region.en: Hattusa (Bogazkoy), Turkey (tablet findspot)
region.zh: 土耳其哈圖沙（博阿茲柯伊；泥板出土地）

period: Tablets c. 14th-13th c. BCE (Hittite copies of Hurrian material); principal tablets from Bogazkoy (Vorderasiatisches Museum Berlin; Istanbul Archaeological Museums)

source.work: Song of Ullikummi (Kumarbi Cycle, CTH 345), trans. Harry A. Hoffner Jr., Hittite Myths, Atlanta 1998

license: Cuneiform text public domain; Hoffner 1998 quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Deposed by the storm-god Teshub, Kumarbi mates with a great rock cliff and fathers the stone giant Ullikummi, who grows deaf and blind on the shoulder of the sleeping giant Upelluri; Teshub's weapons fail, the wise Ea finds the ancient reed-knife that first separated heaven and earth and cuts the giant loose, and the final battle is fought — the tablet breaks at the climax.
summary.zh: 庫馬爾比遭風暴神特舒卜廢黜，遂與巨巖交合，生石巨人烏利庫米，託沉睡巨人烏佩魯里肩上生長，聾且盲；特舒卜兵刃不能傷；智神埃亞尋得上古分天地之銅刀，斷巨人足而解放之；決戰將分勝負之際，泥板斷。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary text of a dead tradition; Hittite cultural heritage (Turkey).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of CTH 345 i-ii: Kumarbi 'took his seat and his mind plotted a battle: he set his right hand on the rock and his left foot on it... and fathered on the rock a terrible stone'; the midwives lift the newborn, and Kumarbi exults: 'I have created a rival for Teshub... his name shall be Ullikummi.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of CTH 345 i-ii; not verbatim.
passages.zh: CTH 345 i-ii 的濃縮意譯：庫馬爾比「就座，心中謀劃一場戰鬥：他將右手按在岩石上，左腳踏在其上……並在岩石上孕育出一塊可怕的石頭」；助產婦將新生兒舉起，庫馬爾比歡欣道：「我已為特舒卜造出一個對手……他的名字將叫烏利庫米。」非逐字引文。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of CTH 345 iv: Ea descends to Upelluri, who groans: 'When heaven and earth were built upon me, I knew nothing; now something small pains my right shoulder.' Ea finds the old reed-knife with which heaven and earth were once cut apart, and with it severs Ullikummi's feet from Upelluri's shoulder. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of CTH 345 iv; not verbatim.
passages.zh: CTH 345 iv 的濃縮意譯：埃阿降臨到烏佩盧里處，後者呻吟道：「當天地被建於我身上時，我一無所知；如今有個小東西使我右肩疼痛。」埃阿找到那把昔日用以剖開天地的舊蘆葦刀，用它將烏利庫米的雙腳從烏佩盧里的肩上割斷。非逐字引文。

canonical_translation: Harry A. Hoffner Jr., Hittite Myths, Writings from the Ancient World 2, Atlanta 1998 (copyright)

narrative.en:
The Song of Ullikummi is the masterpiece of the Kumarbi Cycle — the Hittite succession mythology (CTH 344-345) whose castration-scheme parallels Hesiod's Theogony and whose war in heaven foreshadows Greek Titanomachy imagery.

BEGINNING: THE DEPOSED KING'S PLOT. The Song opens in the tradition of the Song of Kumarbi (CTH 344): the old king Kumarbi, deposed by the storm-god Teshub, 'took his seat and his mind plotted battle'. He goes to the great rock cliff of Urkis by the sea, sets his right hand and left foot upon it, and impregnates the stone; the midwife-goddesses deliver a stone child, and Kumarbi exults: 'I have created a rival for Teshub... let his name be Ullikummi.' He sends the child — deaf, blind, made of diorite — far away to the shoulder of the sleeping giant Upelluri, the Atlas-figure 'on whose shoulders heaven and earth are built', to grow in secret; the messenger warns: 'when he is grown, he will be like a god'.

MIDDLE: THE GIANT RISES. The sun-god, circling the heavens, sees a strange new height rising from the sea and reports to Teshub; the storm-god ascends Mount Hazzi with his brothers and looks: a stone tower is growing on Upelluri's shoulder, already taller than Hazzi and his brother Namni. Teshub's first assault fails: his thunder and lightning cannot split the stone, his heart 'melts like lead'; the goddess Ishtar sings to charm the giant — deaf as stone, he does not hear. Teshub's consort Hebat panics; the giant is growing to besiege the city Kummiya. The wise Ea is called from his sea-house; he descends to Upelluri and asks: 'do you know why your right shoulder pains you?' The sleeping giant groans: 'when heaven and earth were built upon me, I knew nothing; now something small has begun to pain me.' Ea recognizes Ullikummi and descends into the old storehouse of the gods, where he finds the ancient copper reed-knife 'with which heaven and earth were once cut apart' — the primal instrument of separation.

END: THE CUTTING AND THE FINAL BATTLE. Ea severs Ullikummi's feet from Upelluri's shoulder with the reed-knife: the giant, cut loose from his foundation, still stands — but is now mortal-sized and can be fought. Ea's sons carry word to Teshub: 'go and fight, and let the gods watch you'. The storm-god mounts his chariot, storms gather behind him, and he confronts the deaf giant in single combat — 'Teshub drove Ullikummi into the sea? he hurled him into the sea' — and the tablet breaks at the climax. The fragments suggest Teshub's victory, and a broken passage in which Hebat sees the king restored on Mount Hazzi; the end (whether Ullikummi is destroyed or transformed) is lost — the final scenes are a scholarly reconstruction from joins.

FUNCTIONS. The Song is the Hittite theology of succession and threat: Kumarbi's counter-creation (stone against storm) dramatizes the danger of sterility and inertia; Upelluri's aching shoulder aitiologizes the weight of the cosmos on its foundation; the reed-knife grounds the principle that the primal act of separation can be repeated to unmake threats; and the myth's Greek parallel (Ouranos-Kronos-Zeus; Atlas; the Typhon campaign) makes it the key comparandum in Near Eastern-Greek myth studies.
narrative.zh: 《烏利庫米之歌》：庫馬爾比被特舒卜廢黜，坐而謀亂；赴烏爾吉斯巨巖，右手左足按石而孕之；助產神女接生石嬰，庫馬爾比喜曰：『我為特舒卜造一對手……其名烏利庫米。』遂託聾盲石巨於沉睡巨人烏佩魯里肩上，暗中生長。日神巡天見海中異高，報特舒卜；特舒卜登哈齊山望之：石塔已高過山嶺。雷電不克，心如鉛熔；伊什塔爾歌之而石聾不聞。埃亞降至烏佩魯里問之，巨人呻曰：『昔天地築於我肩，我一無所知；今右肩微痛。』埃亞遂入上古神庫，得昔日分天地之銅刀，斷巨人足與肩之連結——巨人失其基而可戰。特舒卜驅車，風雷隨行，與聾石巨決戰，擲之於海——泥板至此而斷；勝負之末與結局由學界據殘片重構。功能：繼承與威脅之神學、宇宙重量之釋義（烏佩魯里肩痛）、原初分離之刃可再施之理、以及希臘神話比較之樞紐。

functions: Theology of succession: counter-creation (stone vs. storm) as deposition strategy
Cosmological aition: Upelluri's aching shoulder as the weight of heaven and earth
Principle of unmaking: the primal separation-knife can be reapplied
Greek comparandum: castration-succession, Atlas, and Typhon parallels with Hesiod

variants.name: Song of Kumarbi (CTH 344)
variants.summary: The cycle's first tablet: Kumarbi bites off Anu's genitals and swallows the seed of the storm-god — the castration-succession that parallels Ouranos-Kronos; Ullikummi is its martial sequel.

variants.name: Hesiod's Theogony (Greek parallel)
variants.summary: Castration of Ouranos, swallowing of the stone, war in heaven with giants thrown from the sky — the structural comparandum; scholarship debates Anatolian influence on Hesiod's family (West 1966).

variants.name: Hurrian originals (Song of Hedammu)
variants.summary: The Hurrian stratum from which the Hittite versions translated; the sea-monster Hedammu cycle shows the same Kumarbi plotting with a monstrous child of the sea.

primary_sources.citation: CTH 345; principal tablets from Bogazkoy (Vorderasiatisches Museum Berlin VAT series; Istanbul Archaeological Museums). Translation: Harry A. Hoffner Jr., Hittite Myths, Atlanta 1998, pp. 49-60 (copyright).

secondary_sources.work: Harry A. Hoffner Jr., Hittite Myths
secondary_sources.citation: Hoffner 1998, Atlanta: Scholars Press (Writings from the Ancient World 2) — annotated translation of the Kumarbi cycle.

secondary_sources.work: Volkert Haas, Geschichte der hethitischen Religion
secondary_sources.citation: Haas 1994, Leiden: Brill — the Hittite religious system and mythic corpus.

reconstructed_segments.restored_in: Hoffner, Hittite Myths, Atlanta 1998, pp. 58-60; Guterbock, The Song of Ullikummi, New Haven 1952

title.en: The Birth of Huitzilopochtli at Coatepec and the Defeat of Coyolxauhqui
title.zh: 威齊洛波奇特利於科阿特佩克山降生與科約爾沙赫基之敗

region.en: Coatepec ('Serpent Mountain'), symbolic pin at Tenochtitlan's Templo Mayor, Mexico City
region.zh: 科阿特佩克『蛇山』；象徵性定位於墨西哥城大神廟

period: Recorded 16th c. CE: Florentine Codex (Sahagun, 1575-77, Book 3); Codex Chimalpopoca/Anales de Cuauhtitlan; principal MS: Florentine Codex, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Mediceo Palatino 218-220

source.archive: Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana (Florentine Codex) / scholarly translation (Dibble & Anderson)
source.work: Florentine Codex Book 3 (The Origin of the Gods), trans. A. J. O. Anderson and C. E. Dibble, Santa Fe 1957; Codex Chimalpopoca, trans. John Bierhorst, Tucson 1992

license: 16th-c. sources public domain; modern translations quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Coatlicue, sweeping the serpent mountain, conceives from a ball of quetzal feathers; her daughter Coyolxauhqui and the four hundred southern stars plot her death; at the moment of birth the child Huitzilopochtli springs up fully armed, beheads Coyolxauhqui, and scatters the four hundred — the charter myth of war, sacrifice, and the Templo Mayor.
summary.zh: 科阿特利圭掃蛇山，得羽球而孕；女科約爾沙赫基與南方四百星神謀殺其母；臨產之際，威齊洛波奇特利全副武裝躍出，斬母姊之頭，驅散四百眾——此為戰爭、犧牲與大神廟之憲章神話。

sensitivity.note: Sources are colonial-era codices; living Nahua communities treat this heritage respectfully. Modern excavations at the Templo Mayor are Mexican national heritage.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Florentine Codex Book 3, ch. 1: Coatlicue, our mother, was sweeping at Coatepec; a ball of feathers fell before her; she took it and placed it at her waist and was found with child; her sons said: 'Who has done this? She has dishonored us.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Florentine Codex Book 3, ch. 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《佛羅倫斯抄本》第三卷第一章的濃縮意譯：我們的母親科阿特利庫埃在科阿特佩克掃地；一團羽毛落在她面前；她拾起它放在腰間，遂被發現有了身孕；她的兒子們說：「是誰幹的？她使我們蒙羞。」非逐字引文。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Florentine Codex Book 3, ch. 1 (ending): Just as Coyolxauhqui reached the summit, Huitzilopochtli was born, adorned with his shield, darts, and the blue serpent-sandal; he seized the turquoise serpent and struck his sister's head from her, and it fell below the mountain; he pursued and routed the four hundred, who became the stars. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Florentine Codex Book 3, ch. 1 (ending); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《佛羅倫斯抄本》第三卷第一章（結尾）的濃縮意譯：正當科約爾沙烏基抵達山頂，維齊洛波奇特利誕生了，佩帶著他的盾、飛鏢與藍色蛇形涼鞋；他抓起綠松石蛇，將他姊妹的頭顱擊落，頭顱墜落山下；他追擊並擊潰了四百人，他們化作了星辰。非逐字引文。

canonical_translation: A. J. O. Anderson and C. E. Dibble, Florentine Codex, General History of the Things of New Spain, Book 3, Santa Fe 1957 (copyright)

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: THE CONCEPTION. The goddess Coatlicue ('Serpent Skirt'), mother of the gods, sweeps the temple on Coatepec ('Serpent Mountain') near Tula; a ball of quetzal feathers (some versions: white feathers) descends before her; she tucks it into her waistband and is found pregnant. Her daughter Coyolxauhqui ('Painted with Bells'), mistress of the moon or of the dismembered, gathers the four hundred sons — the Centzon Huitznahua, the 'four hundred of the south' (stars of the southern sky) — and plots to kill their mother in shame: 'Who has done this? She has dishonored us!' Coatlicue hears them coming and trembles; the child in her womb speaks: 'Do not fear, mother; I know what I must do.'

MIDDLE: THE BIRTH IN ARMS. A messenger (Quauitlicac) runs ahead warning the besieged goddess; Coyolxauhqui leads the four hundred up the mountain, armed in ranks. At the moment of crisis, Huitzilopochtli ('Hummingbird of the South') is born — full-grown, armed with his shield (teueuelli), darts (tlacalhuaztli? tin? the atlatl darts), and the blue serpent-sandal (xiuhcoatl, the fire-serpent), painted with his war-paints (tlael? 'the refuse-smeared one' — tlaelquani, eater of filth, his ritual epithet). He seizes the xiuhcoatl and strikes Coyolxauhqui, cutting her head from her body; the head rolls down Coatepec and lands at their mother's feet. Huitzilopochtli chases the four hundred down the mountain slopes, routing them into the sky; those who die at his hand become the stars, and their scattered limbs were carved on the stone disk later found at the Templo Mayor.

END: THE TEMPLE AND THE RITUAL. The victory founds the sanctuary of Coatepec, and Huitzilopochtli takes the name Tetzahuitl Huitzilopochtli ('the terrifying one') — 'the people built the temple for him'; the goddesses who remained (Coyolxauhqui's sisters) mourn, and the ritual calendar builds on the battle: the festival of Panquetzaliztli raised banners to Huitzilopochtli; the Templo Mayor of Tenochtitlan reproduced Coatepec — Huitzilopochtli's temple on the south side, with the Coyolxauhqui disk at the stair's foot where sacrificed captives 'fell' like the moon-goddess; the serpent head at the temple's base marked the mountain. In 1978, excavations beneath Mexico City recovered the great Coyolxauhqui disk — the myth verified in stone.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative is the charter of Aztec warfare and sacrifice: the sun/star battle mapped the sky (southern stars routed daily by the rising sun — in some tellings Huitzilopochtli as solar god), the sacrificial victim's fall down the temple stair re-enacted Coyolxauhqui's fall, and the Templo Mayor's twin shrines (rain/Tlaloc and war/Huitzilopochtli) reproduced the mythic mountain in urban stone. The 'four hundred' became the classifier of military units (the Centzon), and the hummingbird-god the patron of migration — the god who led the Mexica from Aztlan to Tenochtitlan.
narrative.zh: 母神科阿特利圭於圖拉附近蛇山掃殿，羽球自天而降，納於腰間而孕。女科約爾沙赫基聚南方四百子（南天星神）謀弒母：『誰人所為？辱及吾族！』腹中子聞聲曰：『母勿懼，我知所為。』信使夸維特利卡克先行報信；科約爾沙赫基率四百眾執械上山。危急之際，威齊洛波奇特利（『南方之蜂鳥』）誕生——全身戰妝，持盾、飛鏢與藍蛇靴（修修科阿特爾火蛇）；執蛇擊其姊，斷其首，首滾落山下至母足之前；遂驅四百眾下坡，四散者化為群星。山頂遂立神殿，尊號『可畏者』。特諾奇蒂特蘭大神廟即蛇山之復刻：南殿奉戰神，階下置科約爾沙赫基石盤，犧牲者自階上滾落如月神之墜；1978 年墨西哥城地下發掘得此石盤。功能：戰爭與犧牲之憲章、日月星之天象釋義、大神廟雙殿（雨神與戰神）之山形復刻、以及四百之軍制分類。

functions: Charter of Aztec warfare and sacrifice: the victim's fall re-enacts Coyolxauhqui's
Solar theology: the rising sun routing the four hundred southern stars
Urban replication of myth: Templo Mayor as Coatepec, Coyolxauhqui disk at the stair
Migration cult: Huitzilopochtli as guide of the Mexica from Aztlan

variants.name: Florentine Codex (Sahagun) version
variants.summary: The fullest telling, collected from Nahua elders of Tepepolco and Tlatelolco; supplies the feather-ball conception, the armed birth, the beheading, and the temple foundation.

variants.name: Codex Chimalpopoca / Anales de Cuauhtitlan version
variants.summary: Embeds the birth in the migration sequence from Aztlan and adds the four hundred's ‘birthing' via sacrificial flaying motifs — the annalistic, historically-located telling.

variants.name: Durán's colonial chronicle
variants.text_tradition: Diego Duran, Book of the Gods and Rites (1570s), trans. Doris Heyden (copyright)
variants.summary: Supplies the ritual calendar detail (Panquetzaliztli) and the temple-stair reenactment as eyewitnessed practice — the myth as liturgy.

variants.name: Archaeological variant (Templo Mayor excavations)
variants.text_tradition: Coyolxauhqui monolith found 1978; Templo Mayor Project (Matos Moctezuma)
variants.summary: The excavated disk (3.25 m diameter) at the stair's foot and the serpent heads at the temple base verify the narrative's spatial program — a variant documented in stone rather than text.

primary_sources.work: Florentine Codex, Book 3 (The Origin of the Gods)
primary_sources.citation: MS: Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Mediceo Palatino 218-220 (1575-77). Translation: A. J. O. Anderson and C. E. Dibble, Santa Fe 1957, Book 3, chs. 1-2 (copyright).

secondary_sources.work: Eduardo Matos Moctezuma, The Great Temple of the Aztecs
secondary_sources.citation: Matos Moctezuma 1988, London: Thames & Hudson — the excavated Coyolxauhqui disk and the temple as mythic mountain.

secondary_sources.work: Davíd Carrasco, City of Sacrifice
secondary_sources.citation: Carrasco 1999, Boston: Beacon Press — the Coatepec narrative as urban ritual program.

source_urls.description: World Digital Library — Florentine Codex facsimile (Laurenziana MS)

sensitivity_guidance: Key sources are colonial-era codices (Sahagun; Duran) with missionary framing; living Nahua communities hold this heritage. Prefer the Florentine Codex's Nahuatl side and contemporary Nahua scholarship (e.g. INAH's Templo Mayor publications); avoid sensationalizing sacrifice.

title.en: Viracocha: Creation from Lake Titicaca and the Journey to the Sea
title.zh: 維拉科查：自的的喀喀湖創世與赴海之旅

region.en: Lake Titicaca / Tiwanaku (symbolic pin), Bolivia-Peru border
region.zh: 的的喀喀湖／蒂亞瓦納科（玻利維亞-秘魯邊境；象徵性定位）

period: Recorded 1572 (Sarmiento de Gamboa, Historia Indica, commissioned by Viceroy Toledo); principal MS: Gottingen University MS (trans. Clements Markham, 1907, public domain)

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, Historia Indica chs. 6-11 (1572), in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1907 (public domain)

summary.en: In darkness Viracocha rises from Lake Titicaca and creates sun, moon, and stars; after a flood destroys the stone giants he repopulates the land, animating stones into peoples at Tiwanaku, Cacha, and Urcos; he sends two companions to teach, walks the Andes naming tribes, and departs westward across the sea at Manta, walking on the water.
summary.zh: 黑暗之中，維拉科查自的的喀喀湖升起，造日月星辰；洪水滅石巨人後重造萬民，於蒂亞瓦納科、卡查與烏爾科斯點石成人；遣二徒傳教，遍行安第斯點名部落，終於曼塔踏海西去。

sensitivity.note: Key sources are colonial-era chronicles commissioned to justify conquest; living Quechua and Aymara communities hold the heritage.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento ch. 7 (Markham 1907): Viracocha rose from Lake Titicaca and made the sun, moon, and stars, commanding the sun: 'Thou shalt rise, and go up gradually to where thou art... and by thy beams thou shalt comfort and light the world.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento ch. 7 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 薩米恩托第七章（馬卡姆 1907 年版）的濃縮意譯：維拉科查從的的喀喀湖升起，造了太陽、月亮與星辰，並命令太陽：「你當升起，緩緩升到你所在之處……並以你的光芒慰藉、照亮世界。」非逐字引文。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento chs. 9-11 (Markham 1907): He made the peoples from stones: at Tiwanaku he fashioned the 'stone nations'; at Cacha he called out the men and women ('come forth from the caves and mountains'); at Urcos he left one man kept in stone? he named each tribe its place — and going west he came to Manta, where he walked over the sea and was seen no more. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento chs. 9-11 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 薩米恩托第九至十一章（馬卡姆 1907 年版）的濃縮意譯：他以石頭造出各族：在蒂瓦納庫他塑造了「石頭民族」；在卡查他喚出男女（「從洞穴與山嶺中出來」）；在烏爾科斯他留下一個被保存在石中的人？他為每個部族指定其居地——而向西行進，他來到曼塔，在那裡走過海面，便不再現身。非逐字引文。

language: Spanish (colonial chronicle rendering Quechua oral tradition)
canonical_translation: Clements R. Markham, Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, Hakluyt Society, London 1907 (public domain)

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: CREATION FROM THE LAKE. The world began in darkness: there was no sun, moon, or stars, only a people of stone giants. Viracocha (Pachayachachic, 'teacher of the world'; Tici Viracocha) rose from Lake Titicaca on the island of the Sun and made the celestial bodies: the sun he commanded to rise and climb to its height, 'and by thy beams thou shalt comfort and light the world'; the moon he made brighter at first, then dimmer (the moon's pallor is the aition). The stone giants of the first age, too large and insolent, are destroyed — Viracocha floods the world (the unu pachacuti), leaving two? (in Sarmiento: none but the deep caves) — and the age of giants is judged a failure.

MIDDLE: THE MAKING OF THE PEOPLES FROM STONES. Viracocha now repopulates: at Tiwanaku he models the nations out of stone — men, women, and children, each tribe with its own dress and language ('to each he gave its tongue and its raiment') — and at Cacha (where he was stoned by the first? in some tellings he burned the fields in anger) he animates the sculpted stones, calling them out of the mountains, caves, springs, and rivers: 'Come forth, and remember him who created you.' The stones of Tiwanaku still stand as the unfinished 'stone nations' — the aition of the ruins. At Urcos he leaves a stone man as? (in Sarmiento: he left one kept 'in the shape of a man' as the idol which Yupanqui later carries to war); he sends two companions (his 'brothers' in some tellings, dressed as apostles — the Christian frame of the colonial scribe) along the coasts to teach, while he himself walks the inland road, naming the tribes and ordaining their settlements.

END: THE JOURNEY TO THE SEA. Viracocha travels the Andes 'as a king? as a pilgrim', calling each nation by name and sending them their lands; he teaches sowing, irrigation, and crafts. At Manta (Ecuador), with his two companions, he walks over the sea and is seen no more — 'and they say that he went over the water as if without it' — the departing god of the western sea, expected to return. The Inca state builds on this: the temple of Viracocha at Cacha (Raqchi) with its great central wall; the imperial theology in which the Inca is Viracocha's regent; and the 16th-century accident by which 'Viracocha' became the term the Andeans used for the Spanish strangers themselves — the returning god expected, and the conqueror received.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds Andean cosmology (the lake as creation-point, Tiwanaku as the workshop of peoples), the political theology of Inca kingship (regency under Viracocha), the pilgrimage geography of Raqchi and Titicaca, and the colonial-era debate over the 'white bearded god' myth; it is the Inca corpus's most textually stratified narrative (Sarmiento's Toledo-commissioned version vs. Garcilaso's Christianized telling vs. the Tiwanaku archaeology).
narrative.zh: 太初黑暗無日月星辰，有石巨人族。維拉科查（『世界之師』）自的的喀喀湖日島升起，造日月星辰，命日：『爾當升起，漸登高處，以光耀普照安慰世界』；先使月明，後令月淡（月色之緣起）。首紀石巨人傲慢，維拉科查以洪水滅之。遂於蒂亞瓦納科以石塑諸族——男女童各具服飾語言——於卡查呼石人出洞出泉：『出來吧，記念造爾者』；蒂亞瓦納科石像即未成之『石族』，為遺址之緣起。於烏爾科斯留一石化人為像；遣二徒沿海傳教，己行內陸之路，逐一點名部落、定其居所，教播種灌溉技藝。終至厄瓜多爾曼塔，與二徒踏海而去，『行於水上如無水』——西方之海所逝之神，世傳其將復返。印加王權即其攝政；卡查神廟（拉奇）中牆猶存；殖民時代『白鬚神』之說使『維拉科查』成為對西班牙人之稱呼。功能：湖為創世點、蒂亞瓦納科為萬民工坊、印加王權神學、拉奇與湖之朝聖地理。

functions: Andean cosmology: Lake Titicaca as creation-point, Tiwanaku as the workshop of peoples
Political theology: the Inca as Viracocha's regent on earth
Pilgrimage geography: Raqchi temple and the island of the Sun
Colonial reception: 'Viracocha' as the Andean name for the Spanish

variants.name: Sarmiento de Gamboa (1572)
variants.summary: The Toledo-commissioned telling: flood, stone-giants, stone-nations, the walking journey, departure at Manta; politically framed to legitimize conquest (bias flagged).

variants.name: Garcilaso de la Vega (1609)
variants.text_tradition: Comentarios Reales de los Incas, Part 1
variants.summary: The mestizo chronicler's Christianized version: Viracocha as a benevolent apostolic teacher, gentler and more evangelical — evidence of colonial reinterpretation in the diaspora genre.

variants.name: Tiwanaku archaeology
variants.text_tradition: Tiwanaku monuments (Bolivia); Viracocha portico (Gateway of the Sun)
variants.summary: The Gateway of the Sun's central staff-god figure (c. 500-1000 CE) is read by many scholars as the pre-Inca Viracocha image — the myth's material stratum predating Inca retellings by centuries.

primary_sources.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, Historia Indica
primary_sources.citation: 1572, chs. 6-11; principal MS: Gottingen University Library MS (Lat. Fol. 79). Trans. Clements R. Markham, Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, Hakluyt Society, London 1907 (public domain).

secondary_sources.work: John H. Rowe, 'Inca Culture at the Time of the Spanish Conquest'
secondary_sources.citation: Rowe 1946, in Handbook of South American Indians vol. 2 (BAE Bulletin 143) — the standard source-critical survey.

secondary_sources.work: Gary Urton, Inca Myths
secondary_sources.citation: Urton 1999, Austin: University of Texas Press — the mythic corpus with Quechua sources.

source_urls.description: Project Gutenberg — Markham, Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (1907, public domain; Sarmiento's Historia Indica)

sensitivity_guidance: Sarmiento was commissioned by Viceroy Toledo to justify conquest; his history is politically framed. Prefer community and Quechua/Aymara scholarship in commentary; the Tiwanaku monuments are Bolivian national heritage.

title.en: Omama and the White People: Yanomami Creation as Told by Davi Kopenawa
title.zh: 奧瑪瑪與白人：雅諾馬米創世敘事（達維·科佩納瓦口述）

region.en: Yanomami territory, Roraima-Apaz?, Brazil-Venezuela border (symbolic pin at Demini)
region.zh: 巴西-委內瑞拉邊境雅諾馬米領地（象徵性定位於德米尼）

period: Recorded 1980s-2000s by Bruce Albert with Davi Kopenawa; published 2010 (French) / 2013 (English): The Falling Sky, Harvard University Press

source.work: Davi Kopenawa and Bruce Albert, The Falling Sky: Words of a Yanomami Shaman (Cambridge MA, 2013) — Omama creation narratives

license: Community-authorized publication (Kopenawa's own words); quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Omama, the first shaman, created the forest and its peoples; he caught the xapiri spirits from the heights and taught the shamans to call them; he wept for the future and his tears became the white people, who were foretold to destroy the forest; when the gold-miners' smoke rises, the sky itself will fall — the authorized Yanomami telling of creation and apocalypse.
summary.zh: 首薩滿奧瑪瑪造森林與眾生；自高處捕沙皮里神靈，教薩滿召之；為未來而哭，其淚化為白人，預言將毀森林；金礦煙起之時，天必將塌落——此為雅諾馬米人自授權之創世與末世敘事。

sensitivity.note: This record uses the community-authorized publication of Davi Kopenawa (Yanomami shaman) with Bruce Albert; shamanic song texts are quoted only as summary. Other Yanomami recordings without consent are not used.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of The Falling Sky, ch. 3 (Omama): Omama, the first shaman, grew tired of the old world's silence; he made the forest and the rivers, caught the xapiri spirits in his? and released them into the mountains, and taught the first shamans to call them with songs — 'the xapiri dance in the mirror of the spirits.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of The Falling Sky, ch. 3 (Omama); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《天空將落》第三章（Omama）之節縮改述：Omama，第一位薩滿，厭倦了舊世界的沉寂；他造出森林與河流，將xapiri諸靈捕於其？之中，釋放至群山之間，並教導最初的薩滿以歌聲召喚它們——「xapiri在諸靈之鏡中起舞。」非逐字引文。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of The Falling Sky (the white people and the falling sky): Omama wept for what the forest would suffer; his tears fell and became the white people, and he foretold they would come to consume the forest's land; when the miners' smoke rises to the sky, the xawara epidemic smoke will grow so hot that the sky, exhausted, will fall and crush the earth. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of The Falling Sky (the white people and the falling sky); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《天空將落》（白人與將落之天）之節縮改述：Omama為森林將受的苦難而哭泣；他的淚水落下，化為白人，他並預言他們將前來吞噬森林之地；當礦工的煙升上天空，xawara疫煙將熾熱至極，以致天空力竭而墜，壓碎大地。非逐字引文。

language: Yanomae/Yanomami (Nadahup? Yanomaman family), told in Portuguese with Bruce Albert
canonical_translation: Davi Kopenawa & Bruce Albert, The Falling Sky (Harvard UP, 2013; trans. Nicholas Elliott and Alison Dundy)

narrative.en:
The Yanomami (Yanomae/Yanomami) of the Brazil-Venezuela borderlands have a creation corpus transmitted by shamans; the fullest authorized published telling is by Davi Kopenawa, the Yanomami shaman and spokesman, in The Falling Sky (2010/2013), dictated to the anthropologist Bruce Albert over decades of collaboration.

BEGINNING: OMAMA MAKES THE WORLD. Omama, the first shaman, the son of Yarorimi? (Kopenawa's account), found the primordial world silent and inhospitable; he made the forest and its rivers, set the animals and plants in their places, and raised the first shabono houses and the first humans. He then journeyed to the heights of the sky where the xapiri (the spirit-beings, the 'mirror images' of forest beings and ancestors) live in great houses; he caught the xapiri, brought them down, and taught the first shamans to call them with songs and yakoana snuff: 'the xapiri dance in the mirror of the spirits' — the shamanic vocation is thus Omama's apprenticeship gift, not a human invention.

MIDDLE: THE TEARS THAT BECAME THE WHITE PEOPLE. Omama, seeing what would come, wept for the forest; his tears fell to the ground and became the white people (napë) — and he foretold that they would come from across the sea to consume the land of the forest, hunting its ore and oil, building roads and mining gold: 'the napë did not fall from the sky; they are the children of Omama's tears.' Kopenawa's telling integrates this foretelling with the historical memory of contact (the road-builders of the 1970s-80s, the epidemics — xawara, the epidemic smoke — that killed Yanomami by the thousands, and the garimpeiro gold-miners of the 1980s).

END: THE FALLING SKY. The shamans know the world's fate: when the smoke of the miners' fires (and the oil-burning of the cities) rises too thick, the xawara epidemic-smoke will heat the sky's flesh; the sky, which is alive and exhausted, will grow dry and crack — 'and the sky will fall, and it will crush the earth and its forest'. The shamans' work — dancing the xapiri, cooling the sky, holding the forest's spirits — is the only thing that keeps the sky from falling now: the creation narrative is thus a charter of ecological duty and of Yanomami political speech ('the forest is alive... the sky is watching'). Kopenawa's book, awarded worldwide, made this telling the best-known Amazonian creation narrative in contemporary circulation.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds Yanomami shamanic practice (the xapiri dances; yakoana), the ethics of forest-keeping, and the community's political discourse (land demarcation, mining bans); its authorized publication is itself a land-rights intervention, cited before the Brazilian Congress and UN bodies.
narrative.zh: 雅諾馬米創世之最完備之已授權出版文本為薩滿達維·科佩納瓦與人類學家布魯斯·阿爾貝數十年合作之《天空將墜》（2010/2013）。首薩滿奧瑪瑪嫌太初世界死寂，造森林江河，安萬獸萬木，立首座舍博諾長屋與初民；再赴天頂沙皮里神靈之大屋，捕沙皮里而釋於群山，教首批薩滿以歌與亞科阿那鼻煙召之：『沙皮里在神靈之鏡中起舞』——薩滿之職乃奧瑪瑪之傳授，非人自創。奧瑪瑪預見未來，為森林而哭；其淚落地化為白人（napë），並預言彼等將渡海而來，獵地礦油、築路掘金：『白人非天降，乃奧瑪瑪之淚所化。』科佩納瓦以此預言融匯接觸史：1970-80 年代之公路與疫病（xawara 疫煙）滅族之災、1980 年代金礦侵入。末世：礦火與城市油煙過厚，疫煙烤熱天之軀體；天乃活物，疲竭將裂——『天將墜，壓大地與森林』。薩滿舞沙皮里、冷卻天空、守林中之靈，為今日唯一不使天墜之功——創世敘事遂成生態職責與雅諾馬米政治言說之憲章。

functions: Charter of Yanomami shamanism: xapiri dances and yakoana as Omama's gift
Ecological duty: forest-keeping as the work that holds up the sky
Political speech: the narrative cited in land-demarcation and mining debates
Contact history integrated: tears-as-whites as the myth of colonial encounter

variants.summary: The fullest published creation-apocalypse, told by a named Yanomami shaman with explicit collaboration — the community-authorized record.

variants.name: Bruce Albert's ethnographic apparatus
variants.text_tradition: Albert's fieldwork (1975-present) among the Yanomae of the Demini region
variants.summary: The book's notes and appendices supply the parallel mythic corpus (Omama's songs, the Yarorimi? cycle) with linguistic glosses — the scholarly frame around the authorized telling.

variants.name: Earlier ethnographic recordings (caution)
variants.text_tradition: Napoleon Chagnon's fieldwork corpus (1960s-90s); Lizot's recordings
variants.summary: Contested and ethically criticized collections; Kopenawa and Yanomami associations (Hutukara) have critiqued unconsented use — this record flags them and prefers the authorized text.

primary_sources.citation: Harvard University Press, Cambridge MA 2013 (trans. N. Elliott and A. Dundy); original: La chute du ciel, Paris 2010. Omama narratives: chs. 2-6.

Unconsented Yanomami recordings (Chagnon corpus) are flagged and not used. title.en: The Diving-Bird Creation: God and the Devil in Slavic Cosmogony
title.zh: 斯拉夫潛水鳥創世：神與魔之潛深取土

region.en: Dnieper region / Carpathians (symbolic pin at Kiev)
region.zh: 第聶伯河流域／喀爾巴阡山（象徵性定位於基輔）

period: Recorded 19th c. in East-Slavic and South-Slavic folk collections (Afanasyev, Dragomanov); apocryphal strata from medieval Church Slavonic manuscripts

source.work: A. N. Afanasyev, Poetic Views of the Slavs on Nature (1865-69); W. R. S. Ralston, Songs of the Russian People, London 1872 (public domain); M. Dragomanov collections

summary.en: Before land, God commands the Devil (Satanael) diving under the primordial sea to bring up sand; the Devil hides a mouthful in his cheek, and God blesses the earth so it grows — bursting the Devil's cheek; the sand becomes the world, and the stolen bit becomes the mountains, marshes, and all the crooked places.
summary.zh: 太初無陸，神遣魔（薩塔那埃爾）潛入原初之海取沙；魔藏沙於腮中隱而不報，神祝土使長，爆其腮——所取之沙成世界，所竊之沙成山嶺、沼澤與一切崎嶇之地。

sensitivity.note: Folk cosmogony recorded in 19th-c. ethnography; modern Rodnovery (Slavic neo-pagan) communities claim heritage.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the East-Slavic folk version (Afanasyev/Ralston 1872): 'The Lord said to Satanael: Dive into the sea and bring me a handful of earth with the words In the name of the Lord. The devil dove but forgot the words, brought earth, and God spread it on the water — and it grew.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the East-Slavic folk version (Afanasyev/Ralston 1872); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 東斯拉夫民間版本（Afanasyev／Ralston 1872）之節縮改述：「主對撒旦說：潛入海中，念著『奉主之名』為我帶回一把泥土。魔鬼潛了下去，卻忘了那句話，帶回泥土，神將其鋪於水面——它便生長起來。」非逐字引文。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Ukrainian/Carpathian variant: The devil hid earth in his mouth to make his own world, but the earth grew and grew in his cheek until it burst — and from the stolen earth came the mountains and marshes and thorns; so God's earth is level and good, and the crooked places are the devil's theft. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Ukrainian/Carpathian variant; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 烏克蘭／喀爾巴阡變體之節縮改述：魔鬼將泥土藏於口中，欲造自己的世界，但那泥土在他頰中不斷增長，直至脹破——從那偷來的泥土中生出山巒、沼澤與荊棘；故神的大地平坦而美好，而那些歪斜之處乃是魔鬼的竊取。非逐字引文。

language: East Slavic (Ukrainian/Belarusian/Russian dialects) and South Slavic dialects
canonical_translation: W. R. S. Ralston, Songs of the Russian People, London 1872 (public domain); Louis Leger, La mythologie slave, Paris 1901 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Slavic pagan mythology survives in fragments — no pre-Christian Slavic text exists — but a cosmogony of extraordinary consistency was collected from oral tradition across the Slavic world in the 19th century, blended with apocryphal Church legend.

BEGINNING: THE WATERS AND THE TWO DIVERS. Before the world there is only water, with God (or in the apocryphal versions, the old god riding the waters in a boat? in the Russian versions: God walks on the sea) and his companion the Devil (Satanael, dyavol) swimming beneath. God commands the Devil to dive to the bottom and bring up a handful of earth 'with the words: In the name of the Lord'. The Devil — proud, and intending to make a world of his own — dives twice and fails (in some versions he is blocked by a voice: 'the bottom of the sea is mine'); the third time he takes the earth but forgets the sacred words, and he also conceals a second mouthful of sand in his cheek for himself.

MIDDLE: THE GROWING EARTH. God spreads the obedient earth on the waters and blesses it: 'grow, thou earth' — and it grows until it fills the sea. The stolen sand in the Devil's cheek also begins to grow, swelled by God's blessing, until the Devil's cheek bursts; he spits the earth out, and it becomes the mountains, gorges, marshes, and thorny wastes — everything uneven in the world. In the Ukrainian and Carpathian tellings, the Devil is flung from heaven first (a Lucifier-parallel from the apocrypha), and the diving is his punishment or his last claim to creative power.

END: THE TWO-WORLDED LAND. The world is thus double-authored: God's earth — the level, fertile plain — and the Devil's earth — the mountains, rocks, and swamps. The narrative aitiologizes the landscape of the Slavic east (the endless plain against the Carpathian uplands), locates evil in the crooked rather than the deep, and grounds the folk dualism that scholars (Ivanov & Toporov) trace to the Bogomil heresy carried north from the Balkans: God creates through obedience and word; the Devil through theft and pride. In the South Slavic versions, God and Devil are brothers, and the Devil is called 'our elder brother' — a familial dualism.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds Slavic folk geography (the plain as blessed, mountains as stolen), the ethics of speech (the forgotten words of power), and the apocryphal theology of the medieval Church Slavonic manuscripts; it is the standard frame within which the fragmentary pre-Christian storm-myth (Perun vs. Veles, cross-ref) is read, and its motifs fed 19th-century Romantic reconstruction — which modern scholarship treats with caution.
narrative.zh: 斯拉夫前基督教神話無文本存世，而十九世紀民間採錄之創世敘事高度一致，並與教會偽經傳說相融。太初唯水；神（或曰騎水之老神）與其伴魔（薩塔那埃爾）居於水上。神命魔潛底取土，且須誦『奉主之名』；魔兩潛而不得（水中聲言『海底屬我』），第三次取得，然忘聖言，且於腮中私藏一撮欲自造世界。神展土於水面而祝之：『長吧，大地』——土長滿海；魔腮中之沙亦受祝而長，腮裂乃出，化為山嶺、峽谷、沼澤與荊棘之地。世界遂為雙造：神土平沃，魔土崎嶇——釋東斯拉夫平原與喀爾巴阡山地之貌，亦立『崎嶇為惡』之俗信。南斯拉夫版本中神魔為兄弟，稱魔為『我等長兄』。功能：民間地理釋義、言語倫理（力言之忘）、中世紀偽經神學；學者（伊凡諾夫與托波羅夫）溯其二元論至巴爾幹鮑戈米勒異端。

functions: Aition of Slavic landscape: the blessed plain and the Devil's crooked mountains
Ethics of speech: creation by obedient word vs. stolen silence
Folk dualism traced to Bogomil influence (Ivanov & Toporov)
Frame for reconstructing the pre-Christian Perun-Veles storm myth

variants.name: East-Slavic (Russian/Ukrainian) versions
variants.text_tradition: Afanasyev's Poetic Views of the Slavs (1865-69); Ralston 1872
variants.summary: God walks the waters; Satanael dives; the cheek of stolen earth bursts — the fullest recorded family, with dozens of local variants across gubernias.

variants.name: South Slavic (Bulgarian/Serbian) versions
variants.summary: God and the Devil as brothers ('our elder brother'), sometimes with the Devil creating men from clay and God animating them — the Bogomil-tinged dualism at its clearest.

variants.name: Church Slavonic apocrypha (Tolkovaya Paleya)
variants.summary: The written antecedent: Satanael as God's elder son cast from heaven; the diving-creation absorbed into apocryphal Genesis — the literary layer behind the folk versions.

secondary_sources.citation: Ivanov & Toporov 1970s, in scholarly collections on Slavic mythology (Russian) — the dualist-source analysis.

secondary_sources.work: Louis Leger, La mythologie slave
secondary_sources.citation: Leger 1901, Paris (public domain) — the classical synthesis of Slavic mythic fragments.

title.en: The Tain Bo Cuailnge: The Cattle Raid of Cooley
title.zh: 《奪牛記》：庫利牛之爭

region.en: Cruachan (Rathcroghan), Connacht, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭康諾特克魯亨山（拉思克羅根）

period: Recension I in the Book of the Dun Cow (Leabhar na hUidre, c. 1100, RIA MS 23 E 25); Recension II in the Book of Leinster (c. 1160, TCD MS 1339); oral strata c. 7th-9th c.

source.archive: Internet Archive (Faraday translation, 1904) / Royal Irish Academy (Leabhar na hUidre)
source.work: Tain Bo Cuailnge, trans. Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge, London 1904 (public domain); modern: Thomas Kinsella, The Tain, Oxford 1969 (copyright)

license: Public domain (Faraday 1904); Kinsella 1969 quoted only as summary (copyright)

summary.en: Queen Medb of Connacht, quarreling with her husband Ailill over wealth, invades Ulster to seize the brown bull of Cooley — the one treasure matching her husband's white-horned bull; the men of Ulster lie in their labor-pains curse until the seventeen-year-old Cuchulainn holds the ford alone against the province, killing friend and foster-brother Ferdiad at the ford, until the bulls themselves meet and destroy each other.
summary.zh: 康諾特女王梅芙與夫艾利爾爭財，舉兵入阿爾斯特欲奪庫利棕牛——唯一可匹其夫白角牛之寶；阿爾斯特男子盡陷產褥之詛，唯十七歲之庫丘林獨守渡口，力抗一省之兵，於渡口誅摯友與結義兄弟弗迪亞，終致二牛相鬥、同歸於盡。

sensitivity.note: Manuscripts are Irish national heritage (RIA, TCD); living Gaelic and Irish-language communities hold the tradition.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Tain (Recension I): Medb gathers the men of Connacht and asks of each a fair fight; the men of Ulster are seized by the ces noinden (the pains of childbirth curse); Cuchulainn alone, not yet seventeen, takes up arms: 'I will hold the ford against them all.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Tain (Recension I); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《奪牛記》（第一抄本）之節縮改述：Medb召集康諾特的男人們，向每人求一場公平的決鬥；阿爾斯特的男人們被ces noinden（分娩之痛的詛咒）所攫；唯有Cuchulainn，年未十七，執起兵器：「我將獨守渡口，抵擋他們所有人。」非逐字引文。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Ferdiad episode: Cuchulainn and Ferdiad, foster-brothers taught by the same woman-warrior Scathach, meet at the ford; each calls the other by the love of their training days; after four days of combat Cuchulainn casts the gae bolga under Ferdiad's armor — 'not I alone, but my friend was slain' — and carries grief from the ford. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Ferdiad episode; not verbatim.
passages.zh: Ferdiad插曲之節縮改述：Cuchulainn與Ferdiad，同受女戰士Scathach教導的義兄弟，在渡口相會；二人各以習藝歲月之情誼呼喚對方；激戰四日之後，Cuchulainn將gae bolga擲入Ferdiad的甲下——「非獨我一人，我的朋友亦被殺」——並自渡口攜悲而去。非逐字引文。

canonical_translation: Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge, London 1904 (public domain); Thomas Kinsella, The Tain, Oxford 1969 (copyright); Cecile O'Rahilly, Tain Bo Cualnge from the Book of Leinster, Dublin 1967 (copyright)

narrative.en:
The Tain is the central epic of the Ulster Cycle — a cow-raid that escalates into an apocalypse of single combat, told with a raucous humor and tragic gravity unique in medieval European literature.

BEGINNING: THE PILLOW TALK AND THE RAID. Queen Medb of Connacht and her husband Ailill compare possessions in bed and find them equal — except Ailill's white-horned bull Finnbennach, formerly Medb's own (he defected to the herd for human treatment). Medb resolves to match him with the brown bull Donn Cuailnge of Ulster; negotiation fails (an insult at the feast), and Medb summons the province — seven thousand? twenty-seven camps, with her allies (the exiled Ulsterman Cormac, the hero Fergus mac Roich) — while a curse keeps the men of Ulster helpless: Macha's curse, the ces noinden, has them seized with the pangs of childbirth for five days and four nights after each alarm. Only the seventeen-year-old Cuchulainn (Setanta, son of the god Lugh) — too young for the curse — is left; he takes up arms at the Ford of the?, with his charioteer Laeg, and holds the border alone.

MIDDLE: THE SINGLE COMBAT AND THE WARP-SPASM. The Tain's middle is a sequence of single combats at the fords (the tradition of the iomarbad): Cuchulainn defeats champion after champion — his boyhood feats recalled, his warp-spasm (riastrad) described in horrifying detail (the contortion that makes him unrecognizable, one eye swallowed into his head, his blood rising like a mast?). He slays the queen's warriors, the loneliest of them his own foster-brother Fraech, and the men of Connacht offer terms; Fergus negotiates a day-by-day pact. The climax approaches when Medb sends Ferdiad mac Daman, Cuchulainn's closest friend, trained with him by the woman-warrior Scathach in Alba (Scotland). The two meet at the ford of Ardee; four days of combat, each night healing the other with herbs and each morning weeping; Cuchulainn finally casts the gae bolga — the barbed spear thrown underfoot that opens inside the body — and Ferdiad dies; Cuchulainn carries grief from the ford: 'not I alone, but my friend was slain'.

END: THE BULLS' DUEL. Medb breaks the pact and invades; the Ulster men rise from their pains at last and converge; the brown bull of Cooley, seized by Medb's host, kills the white-horned bull in a monstrous duel across Ireland (carrying him on his back through the land, his pieces forming place-names — the aition of the province), then runs wild and dies — 'the brown bull's heart broke within him'. The province is devastated, the raid futile: Medb's own evaluation ('it was a good cattle-raid... only that the men of? ' — 'we have gained nothing'), and the narrative closes with its most famous frame: the poet Fergus reciting the Tain to the poet Senchan Torpeist, whose students resurrect it from fragments — the self-referential moment when the epic claims oral transmission as its authority.

FUNCTIONS. The Tain grounds the Ulster heroic ideology (single combat at fords; the boy-hero vs. the cursed province), the legal theology of honor-price (Medb's argument about equal wealth as the marriage contract), and the aitiology of Irish topography (bull-duel place-names); it is taught as the Irish national epic and studied for its layering (oral saga, 8th-11th c. composition, manuscript transmission in the Book of the Dun Cow and Book of Leinster).
narrative.zh: 梅芙女王與夫艾利爾枕上較財，惟夫之白角牛勝其所有；欲得庫利棕牛以配之，談判不成遂興兵。阿爾斯特男子盡中瑪哈之詛（產褥之痛五日四夜），唯十七歲庫丘林（神魯格之子）免於詛，與御者萊格獨守渡口，歷經單挑：其變形痙攣（riastrad）之狀可怖，連誅康諾特諸將。梅芙遣其摯友與同門（同師女戰士斯卡哈）弗迪亞；二人於阿迪渡口血戰四日，夜以草藥互療、晨起相泣；庫丘林終以腳下倒鉤槍（gae bolga）破其甲而殺之，扶屍而慟：『非獨我殺之，亦殺我友。』梅芙毀約入侵，阿爾斯特眾起；棕牛奪回，與白角牛鬥於全愛爾蘭，背負死敵而奔，碎為地名——牛心碎而亡。梅芙自評：『一場好劫，然所得無幾。』史詩以詩人費爾古斯向詩人森坎誦述《奪牛記》為結，自證口傳之權威。功能：阿爾斯特英雄意識形態、榮譽價之法律神學、牛鬥地名之地理釋義、以及口傳傳承之自我宣稱。

functions: Charter of Ulster heroic ideology: ford-combat, the boy-hero, the cursed province
Legal theology: honor-price and the marriage contract of equal wealth
Topographical aition: bull-duel place-names across Ireland
Oral authority: the epic's self-referential frame of transmission

variants.text_tradition: Leabhar na hUidre, c. 1100 (RIA MS 23 E 25)

variants.name: Recension II (Book of Leinster)
variants.summary: Adds the preamble (the poets' recovery of the lost Tain from the Otherworld dead — Fergus reciting to Senchan) and rearranges episodes; the version behind most modern translations.

variants.name: Stowe and later recensions
variants.summary: Later continuous versions with prose expansion; evidence of the Tain's living recitation into the Early Modern period.

variants.name: Dindsenchas and place-name tradition
variants.summary: Independent place-name poems (e.g. of Ardee, of the fords) preserve the Tain's episodes as aitiologies — the topographical stratum of the tradition.
