title.en: The Dainas: Sun, Moon, and the World-Tree of Latvian Cosmogony
title.zh: 《達伊納》歌謠：拉脫維亞創世中的日、月與世界樹

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Kurzeme daina region)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於庫爾澤梅歌謠區）

period: Oral tradition; collected by Krisjanis Barons, Latvju dainas (1894-1915, ~218,000 variants); dainas attested from 16th-c. collections onward

source.archive: Barons' Dainu skapis (UNESCO Memory of the World) / Internet Archive
source.work: Krisjanis Barons (ed.), Latvju dainas, Jelgava/St. Petersburg 1894-1915 (public domain); English: Uldis Balcitis; scholarly: Haralds Biezais, Die Hauptzuge der lettischen Religion, Uppsala 1975

summary.en: In the dainas the world is an arranged household: Dievs (God) rides across the sky estate; Saule (Sun) hangs her gold belt on the world-tree, her daughter is stolen by the Moon; the tree of life grows at the sea's edge with its roots in the waters and its crown in the stars — a cosmogony sung, not told.
summary.zh: 達伊納歌謠中，世界如一家宅：天神騎行天域，太陽女神以金帶掛於世界樹，其女為月亮所竊；生命之樹生於海畔，根入水、冠入星——此為以歌傳而非以述傳之創世觀。

sensitivity.note: Living Latvian tradition (Jani festival; Dievturiba modern revival claims heritage).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of daina variants on the world-tree: 'The tree of life grew at the edge of the sea, its roots in the water, its crown in the stars; its branches bore? the girls came to it with silk ribbons' — the world-tree as gold-bearing tree (zelta koks) sung in hundreds of variants. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of daina variants on the world-tree; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 關於世界樹的達伊納變體之濃縮改述：「生命之樹生長在海的邊緣，其根在水中，其冠在星辰之間；它的枝條結出？少女們帶著絲帶來到它跟前」——世界樹作為載金之樹（zelta koks），在數百個變體中被吟唱。非逐字引用。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of daina variants on Sun and Moon: Saule, the sun-goddess, hangs her golden belt on the world-tree and goes to rest; Meness (Moon) climbs and takes her daughter (Saules meita) — 'the moon took the sun's daughter for his wife' — and the gods? Dievs judges between them: the daughter is returned, and the sun and moon part ways across the sky. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of daina variants on Sun and Moon; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 關於太陽與月亮的達伊納變體之濃縮改述：太陽女神紹萊（Saule）將她的金腰帶掛在世界樹上，然後去歇息；月亮梅內斯（Meness）攀爬而上，帶走了她的女兒（Saules meita）——「月亮娶了太陽的女兒為妻」——而眾神？迪耶瓦斯（Dievs）在他們之間作出裁決：女兒被歸還，太陽與月亮在天際分道而行。非逐字引用。

canonical_translation: Krisjanis Barons, Latvju dainas (1894-1915, public domain); English selections in Uldis Balcitis and in Vaira Vike-Freiberga's translations (copyright)

narrative.en:
Latvian mythology survives in the daina — a four-line trochaic song form of which Krisjanis Barons collected over 217,996 variants (Latvju dainas, 1894-1915; the Dainu skapis card-file is UNESCO Memory of the World). There is no prose cosmogony: the world is sung in thousands of fragments, and the cosmogony must be assembled from song.

THE ARRANGED HOUSEHOLD. The dainas image the cosmos as an estate (saimnieciba): Dievs, the sky-god, rides across it on horseback (or sledge), descending to the fields at sowing time; Saule, the sun-goddess, washes her horses in the sea, hangs her gold belt on the branches of the world-tree, and drives her wagon of light; Meness, the moon, travels the night roads; Auseklis, the morning star, keeps the threshold; and the Saules meitas ('daughters of the sun') work the golden looms at the sea's edge. The cosmos is domestic: gods are householders, and myth is choreography of chores.

THE WORLD-TREE. At the center stands the tree of life (dzivibas koks): the golden tree (zelta koks) growing at the sea's edge 'with roots in the water and crown in the stars', hung with the sun's belt, climbed by the daughters, flanked by the heavenly estate. Hundreds of variants describe it: a tree of gold, silver, and? a ship with a tree mast, a birch on the sea-stone — the Indo-European world-tree in its Baltic form, close cousin to Yggdrasil (cross-ref norse-creation-ymir) and to the Indian axis motifs.

THE SUN'S DAUGHTER AND THE MOON'S THEFT. The most cosmogonic daina cycle is the abduction: Meness, the moon-god, takes Saule's daughter as wife (or steals her from the golden tree); the quarrel goes to judgment — in some variants before Dievs, in others before the celestial assembly — and the sun and moon are separated, explaining the day-night alternation: 'the sun and moon went apart... the moon took the sun's daughter...'. In other variants the daughter is? the story is a wedding dispute rather than a theft — evidence that the dainas preserve the myth in ritualized fragments (wedding songs, morning songs) rather than a single narrative.

FUNCTIONS. The dainas ground Latvian seasonal ritual (Jani solstice festival; the sun's belt as ornament), the household ethics of the cosmos (chores, weaving, horse-washing), and the modern national revival (Barons' collection as national canon; Dievturiba's reconstruction of the pantheon; daina singing as UNESCO intangible heritage 2003? — the Baltic Song and Dance Celebrations). The cosmogony is sung, and its 'records' are variants — the deepest methodological challenge in Baltic myth studies.
narrative.zh: 拉脫維亞神話存於四行短歌『達伊納』，巴倫斯採錄逾二十一萬八千變體（1894-1915；其卡片櫃入選聯合國教科文組織世界記憶遺產）。無散文體創世史：世界以千萬歌之碎片唱出。宇宙如家宅：天神迪埃夫斯騎馬巡天，播種時下田；太陽女神索萊於海中洗馬，以金帶掛世界樹，駕光之車；月神梅內斯行夜路；晨星奧塞克利斯守門檻；太陽眾女於海畔金色織機織布。中心為生命之樹：金色之樹生於海畔，根入水、冠入星，掛太陽之金帶，為眾女所攀——與北歐尤克特拉希爾同源而異形。最具創世性之循環為『太陽之女被月所竊』：月娶（或竊）日女，諸神裁斷，日月分途——釋晝夜交替；或另釋為婚禮之爭，證達伊納以儀式碎片保存神話。功能：季節儀式（雅尼夏至節）、家宅倫理之宇宙觀、以及現代民族復興（巴倫斯採集、迪維圖里巴復興、波羅的海歌舞節）。

functions: Seasonal ritual: Jani solstice, the sun's belt, and the celestial household's chores
Cosmology as domestic ethics: gods as householders and workers
National revival: Barons' collection as canon; daina singing as living heritage
Comparative myth: Baltic world-tree against Yggdrasil and the Indian axis

variants.text_tradition: ~218,000 collected variants; Dainu skapis card-file (UNESCO Memory of the World)
variants.summary: The canonical collection organizing variants by motif and region — the primary record from which any Latvian cosmogony must be assembled.

variants.name: Lithuanian parallel (dainos and tales)
variants.summary: The Lithuanian cognate songs share the sun-daughter and world-tree motifs with different names (Saule, Menulis) — the Baltic comparative base.

variants.name: Dievturiba reconstruction (modern)
variants.text_tradition: Ernests Brastins, Dievturiba ceram? (1920s); modern Latvian neo-pagan practice

title.en: Dangun Wanggeom: The Sandalwood King and the Founding of Gojoseon
title.zh: 檀君王儉：神檀樹之王與古朝鮮之建

region.en: Taebaeksan / Mani-san (Gangwon), Korea
region.zh: 韓國太白山／摩尼山（江原道）

period: Recorded in Samguk Yusa (Iryeon, 1281, Book 1) citing the Weishu; principal editions: Haeinsa woodblock imprints (e.g. 1512); traditional foundation date 2333 BCE

source.work: Samguk Yusa, Book 1 (Dangun section), trans. Grafton K. Mintz and Tae-Hung Ha, Seoul 1972; Peter H. Lee, Sourcebook of Korean Civilization, New York 1993

license: Ancient text public domain; Mintz & Ha 1972 quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Hwanin, lord of heaven, sends his son Hwanung to govern mankind from under the sandalwood tree on Taebaek mountain; a bear and a tiger wish to become human — only the bear endures the hundred days of mugwort and garlic and becomes the woman Ungnyeo; Hwanung marries her and she bears Dangun Wanggeom, who founds Gojoseon in 2333 BCE and rules 1,500 years before retiring as mountain god.
summary.zh: 天帝桓因遣子桓雄降於太白山神檀樹下，主理人間；熊與虎欲化為人——惟熊忍百日艾蒜之苦化為女子熊女；桓雄娶之，生檀君王儉；檀君於公元前2333年建古朝鮮，御世一千五百年，後隱為山神。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: Dangun is venerated in Daejonggyo and used in national ideology (Gaecheonjeol); handle the nationalist reception critically.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Samguk Yusa I.1 (Mintz & Ha 1972): Hwanung, son of Hwanin, wished to descend and dwell in the human world; his father looked down and granted it, giving him three heavenly seals and 3,000 followers, and he alit under the sandalwood tree on Taebaek mountain and ruled the 360 human affairs — wind, rain, clouds, grain, life, disease, and punishment. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Samguk Yusa I.1 (Mintz & Ha 1972); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《三國遺事》I.1（Mintz & Ha 1972）之濃縮改述：桓因之子桓雄希望降臨並居住於人間；其父俯視而下，允准了此事，賜予他三枚天符印與三千名追隨者，他降臨於太白山上的檀香樹下，掌管三百六十種人間事務——風、雨、雲、穀物、生命、疾病與刑罰。非逐字引用。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Samguk Yusa I.1 (ending): A bear and a tiger living in the same cave prayed to become human; Hwanung gave them mugwort and garlic, saying 'eat this, stay out of the sunlight for a hundred days, and you shall be human'; the tiger gave up, but the bear endured and became a woman; no husband offered himself, so she prayed under the sandalwood tree — and Hwanung made her his wife; she bore a son, Dangun Wanggeom. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Samguk Yusa I.1 (ending); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《三國遺事》I.1（結尾）之濃縮改述：同住一洞的一熊一虎向桓雄祈求化為人；桓雄賜予他們艾草與大蒜，說道：「吃下這些，百日之內避開陽光，你們便將化為人」；老虎放棄了，但熊堅持下來，化為一名女子；沒有男子前來求婚，她便在那檀香樹下祈禱——桓雄遂娶她為妻；她生下一個兒子，即檀君王儉。非逐字引用。

language: Classical Chinese (Samguk Yusa's Korean historiographic Chinese)
canonical_translation: Grafton K. Mintz and Tae-Hung Ha, Samguk Yusa: Legends and History of the Three Kingdoms, Seoul 1972 (copyright); Peter H. Lee, Sourcebook of Korean Civilization vol. 1, Columbia 1993 (copyright)

narrative.en:
The Dangun narrative is Korea's founding charter, recorded in the Samguk Yusa ('Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms'), compiled by the monk Iryeon in 1281, citing an earlier (lost) Wei shu source — the oldest extant full telling, some 1,200 years after the traditional founding date.

BEGINNING: HWANUNG'S DESCENT. Hwanin, the heavenly lord, has a son Hwanung who wishes to descend and benefit humankind. Hwanin looks over the world, finds it fit, grants his son the Three Heavenly Seals (the tokens of governance) and sends him down with 3,000 followers to the sandalwood tree (sindansu) on Taebaek mountain (identified with Mani-san on Ganghwa island or Taebaeksan in Gangwon). Hwanung rules under the tree as the 'Heavenly King', governing the 360 affairs of mankind: grain, life, disease, punishment — wind, rain, and clouds are his officers. Human society begins under the sandalwood tree — the 'sacred tree' that aitions both the name Dangun ('Sandalwood King') and the Korean reverence for mountain trees.

MIDDLE: THE BEAR AND THE TIGER. In the same cave live a bear and a tiger, who pray to Hwanung to become human. He gives them a bundle of mugwort and twenty-one cloves of garlic: 'eat this, shun the sunlight for a hundred days (twenty-one days in some tellings), and you shall take human form.' The tiger, wild and impatient, abandons the trial; the bear endures the fast in the dark cave, and after twenty-one days becomes a woman — Ungnyeo ('Bear Woman'). But no man will have her; she prays under the sandalwood tree for a child, and Hwanung — 'he changed himself into a man and married her' — fathers Dangun Wanggeom ('Sandalwood King'), born in the traditional year 2333 BCE.

END: THE FOUNDING AND THE RETIREMENT. Dangun founds the state of Joseon (Gojoseon, 'Old Joseon') at Asadal (identified variously with Pyongyang, a Liaodong site, or a mountain city) and rules 1,500 years. When King Ju of the Zhou enfeoffs Kija in the east (the Chinese dynastic tradition), Dangun retires — 'he hid himself and became the mountain god of Asadal' at 1,908 years of age: the founder abdicates into the landscape, becoming the mountain itself — the Korean pattern of the sacred mountain as ancestor. The Samguk Yusa closes the section with the Kija disclaimer, and the narrative anchors Korea's earliest history: Gojoseon's Bronze Age archaeology (Liaoning dolmens), the Dangun shrine on Ganghwa (Chamseongdan altar), the Daejonggyo religion (founded 1909, venerating Dangun), and the national holiday Gaecheonjeol ('Opening of Heaven Day', October 3).

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds Korean identity (Dangun as common ancestor; the 'descendants of Dangun'), the theology of the sacred tree and mountain, the divine-origin charter of Korean kingship (used by Silla and Joseon dynasties), and the modern ideological uses — from Daejonggyo's veneration to Gaecheonjeol's state calendar — which scholarship reads critically alongside the myth's late manuscript date (1281) and its cited (lost) source.
narrative.zh: 《三國遺事》卷一記：天帝桓因子桓雄思降世人間，桓因俯察而許之，賜三枚天符印，率三千徒降於太白山神檀樹下，主穀、主命、主病、主刑等三百六十人間事——風雨雲皆其官。同穴之熊與虎願化人；桓雄賜艾與蒜：『食之，避陽光百日（一作二十一日），可得人形。』虎野而棄，熊忍而化為女子熊女；無男子肯娶，遂於神檀樹下祈子；桓雄化為人娶之，生檀君王儉（傳統紀年公元前2333年）。檀君建朝鮮（古朝鮮），都阿斯達，御世一千五百年；周封箕子於朝鮮後，檀君隱去，年一千九百零八歲為阿斯達山神——創始者歸於山，山即祖先。遺跡：江華島摩尼山塹城壇、大倧教（1909年建）、開天節（10月3日國定假日）。功能：韓民族認同之根、神樹與神山之信仰、王權神授憲章、以及現代意識形態之爭議使用（1281年成書晚、所引《魏書》已佚，學界批判性解讀）。

functions: Charter of Korean identity: Dangun as common ancestor ('descendants of Dangun')
Theology of the sacred tree and mountain: sindansu and Chamseongdan altar
Divine-origin kingship: charter used by later dynasties (Silla, Joseon)
Modern ideological uses: Daejonggyo religion and Gaecheonjeol (Oct. 3)

variants.text_tradition: Iryeon, Book 1, citing the (lost) Weishu; Haeinsa imprints (1512)
variants.summary: The canonical telling: Hwanin-Hwanung-Dangun line, the bear-woman trial, Asadal, and the mountain-god retirement — the only full early text.

variants.name: Samguk Sagi silence (1145)
variants.summary: The court historian records Gojoseon and Kija but omits Dangun entirely — the Confucian canon's skepticism, a key datum in the historiographic debate.

variants.name: Dongui Bogam and later hagiography
variants.text_tradition: Joseon-era medical and religious texts; Daejonggyo liturgy (1909)
variants.summary: Dangun expands into herbalist-sage hagiographies (the trial's mugwort and garlic read as pharmacology) and the nationalist religion's liturgical cycle.

variants.name: Ganghwa archaeology
variants.text_tradition: Chamseongdan altar, Mani-san; dolmens of Gojoseon territory
variants.summary: The Ganghwa altar and the Liaodong-Korean dolmen belt are read by nationalists as Dangun's traces — archaeology as mythic evidence, debated.

title.en: Kaggen and the Eland: The San Creation of the Great Antelope
title.zh: 卡根與大羚羊：桑人創造大羚羊之敘事

region.en: Bushmanland / Katkop, Northern Cape, South Africa (Bleek-Lloyd archive region)
region.zh: 南非北開普布須曼地區／卡特科普（布里克-勞埃德檔案採錄區）

period: Recorded 1870-84 by Wilhelm Bleek and Lucy Lloyd, Cape Town; informants named (Kabbo, Dia!kwain, A!kunta etc.); published Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore, London 1911

source.archive: Bleek and Lloyd Archive (University of Cape Town Libraries) / Internet Archive (Specimens 1911)
source.work: W. H. I. Bleek and L. C. Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore, London 1911 (public domain); D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends, 1923; archive: UCT Digital Collections

license: Public domain (1911/1923 publications); archive materials with named informants (ethical publication practice established by Bleek & Lloyd)

summary.en: Kaggen, the trickster mantis, throws his sandal into the water and it becomes the first eland; he raises it like a child at the water-hole; when his brothers-in-law kill it for meat while he hunts honey, Kaggen grieves, transforms the eland's blood into new herds, and avenges the killing — the charter narrative of the eland's ritual centrality in San life and rock art.
summary.zh: 詭計者卡根（螳螂）將鞋擲入水中，化為第一頭大羚羊；如育幼兒般於水塘邊養之；其姻親趁其採蜜時獵殺取肉；卡根悲慟，化羚血為新群，並以詭計復仇——此為大羚羊在桑人生活與岩畫中儀式地位之憲章敘事。

sensitivity.note: Record uses the Bleek-Lloyd archive's named-informant publications (an ethical practice established in the 1870s-80s) and contemporary San organizations; rock art sites are sacred to San descendants.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Kabbo/Dia!kwain narrative (Bleek & Lloyd 1911): Kaggen took off his sandal, threw it into the water, and it became an eland; he kept it in his own place at the water-hole, fed it, and watched over it like a child — for the eland was Kaggen's beloved. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Kabbo/Dia!kwain narrative (Bleek & Lloyd 1911); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡布（Kabbo）／迪亞！克瓦因（Dia!kwain）敘事（Bleek & Lloyd 1911）之濃縮改述：卡根（Kaggen）脫下他的涼鞋，將其投入水中，它便化作一頭大羚羊；他把它養在自己水坑旁的居處，餵養牠，像照料孩子一般看顧牠——因為那頭大羚羊是卡根的心愛之物。非逐字引用。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the killing narrative (Bleek & Lloyd 1911): While Kaggen was away getting honey, his brothers-in-law found the eland and killed it; Kaggen returned and wept; from the eland's blood and body more elands sprang up at the water-hole, so that the elands multiplied; and Kaggen, enraged, brought the hunters to harm — the first eland's death made both the herds and the danger. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the killing narrative (Bleek & Lloyd 1911); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 關於獵殺的敘事（Bleek & Lloyd 1911）之濃縮改述：當卡根外出採蜜時，他的妻舅們發現了那頭大羚羊並將牠殺死；卡根歸來後痛哭；從大羚羊的血與身體中，更多的大羚羊在水坑旁湧現，於是羚羊群繁衍增多；而卡根滿懷憤怒，使那些獵人遭受禍害——第一頭大羚羊之死既造就了獸群，也造就了危險。非逐字引用。

canonical_translation: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore, 1911 (public domain); Lewis-Williams, Stories that Float from Afar, 2000 (copyright)

narrative.en:
The /Xam San narratives collected in the Bleek-Lloyd archive (1870-84, Cape Town, from named informants like Kabbo, Diakwain, and Akunta) preserve the richest body of San mythology. Kaggen (the Mantis) is the trickster-creator at its center.

BEGINNING: THE SANDAL BECOMES THE ELAND. Kaggen, walking with his family, takes off one of his sandals, throws it into the water, and it becomes the first eland — the great antelope of the Maluti/Drakensberg grasslands. He keeps it in his own place at the water-hole, hides it from the people (his brothers-in-law), and feeds and raises it 'like a child' — the eland is Kaggen's beloved, his foster-child and his heart's animal. (The narrative is at once an aition of the eland's origin and a portrait of Kaggen's ambivalence: the trickster whose love makes and unmakes.)

MIDDLE: THE KILLING. Kaggen goes off to hunt honey (or ostrich eggs); his brothers-in-law Cogaz and Kwammanga find the eland, drive it out, and kill it for meat. Kaggen returns, finds the blood and the kill, and weeps over his child: 'my eland!' — the death of the beloved animal is the myth's central grief. From the eland's blood and body (in the variants: the blood, the gall, the hooves) spring the elands of the world: the first death multiplies the herds — an aition of abundance through sacrifice.

END: THE TRICKSTER'S VENGEANCE AND THE RITUAL WORLD. Kaggen, enraged, takes revenge through trickery: he causes the hunters to be harmed (in the variants: he plants the poison grass, he sends the ants, he turns the game against them — the /Xam tellings vary) and withdraws from the people; the eland's parts are distributed with ritual consequence (the fat for the girls' puberty dances; eland hunting governed by the eland-bull dance). The narrative is the charter of the eland's centrality: San rock art (Drakensberg/Maluti panels) is dominated by eland imagery; the eland-bull dance (girls' puberty) and eland hunting rituals take their power from Kaggen's animal; and the trance dance's potency (n/um) is imagined as eland-like. The interpreter Kabbo told Bleek and Lloyd these stories in Cape Town's Breakwater Prison — the archive itself is the history of colonial incarceration and of ethical salvage (named informants, full interlinear translation).

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds San ritual ecology (the eland's ritual centrality; the puberty dance), the ethics of the trickster-creator (love, theft, and transformation as one), and the reading of rock art (Lewis-Williams's shamanic reading built on these narratives); it is also a founding document of San heritage politics — the archive's descendant communities now govern access and use.
narrative.zh: 布里克-勞埃德檔案（1870-84，開普敦）自具名報導人（Kabbo、Diakwain、Akunta 等）採錄 /Xam 桑人敘事，為桑人神話最富之存世文獻。卡根（螳螂）行路時脫下鞋擲入水中，化為首頭大羚羊；藏於水塘私處，餵養撫育『如子』——羚羊乃其所愛。卡根外出採蜜，其姻親（Cogaz 與 Kwammanga）尋得羚羊驅出而殺之取肉；卡根歸，見血與脂，哭其子：『我的羚羊！』——所愛之死為神話之核心悲劇。自羚之血與體（變體言血、膽、蹄）生出世上群羚：首死致萬羚，犧牲致豐饒之釋義。卡根怒而以詭計復仇（變體言投毒草、遣蟻群），離人而去；羚之部分以儀式分配（脂肪用於女子成年舞、獵羚受羚牛舞之約束）。此敘事為大羚羊儀式中心地位之憲章：德拉肯斯堡岩畫以羚為主，成年禮舞與獵羚儀式皆源自卡根之獸，入迷舞之力（n/um）亦想像如羚。報導人 Kabbo 於開普敦碼頭監獄向布里克與勞埃德講述——檔案本身即殖民監禁史與倫理搶救（具名報導人、逐行對譯）之歷史。功能：儀式生態、詭計創造者之倫理、岩畫釋讀之據；檔案後裔社群現掌其使用與取用之權。

functions: Charter of the eland's ritual centrality in San life and rock art
Eland-bull dance and girls' puberty ritual grounded in the narrative
Trickster-creator ethics: love, theft, and transformation as one act
Rock art interpretation: Lewis-Williams's shamanic reading built on these texts

title.en: The Kumulipo: The Genealogical Chant of Cosmic Birth
title.zh: 《庫姆利波》：宇宙誕生之系譜頌歌

region.en: Hawaii Island (Ka'u district of the chant's origin; symbolic pin at Hilo)
region.zh: 夏威夷島（頌歌源於卡烏地區；象徵性定位於希洛）

period: Composed c. 1700 CE for Kalanikauikeaouli? (chant for the birth of the high chief Ka-I-i-mamao); recorded by Queen Liliuokalani, translation 1897; manuscript tradition 19th c. (Bishop Museum)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Liliuokalani translation, 1897) / Bishop Museum (oral ms)
source.work: Kumulipo, trans. Queen Liliuokalani, An Hawaiian Legend of the Creation, San Francisco 1897 (public domain); Martha Beckwith, Kumulipo: A Hawaiian Creation Chant, Honolulu 1951

summary.en: At the time of deep darkness, life is born from the Kumulipo (the deep source) in sixteen waves of genealogical pairs — coral, fish, birds, insects, plants, then humans — each sea-organism paired with its land counterpart, until WAKEA the ancestor appears and the human lineage descends to the chanting chief: creation as whakapapa-like genealogy, not narrative.
summary.zh: 於深暗之時，生命自庫姆利波（深源）生，凡十六波系譜之對——珊瑚、魚、鳥、蟲、植物、而後人類——海中生物與陸上生物一一成對，直至祖先瓦凱亞出現，人系下延至誦唱之酋長：創世為系譜而非敘事。

sensitivity.note: The Kumulipo is a sacred chiefly genealogy; living Hawaiian communities (ali'i descendants, sovereignty discourse) treat it with care; prefer community-authored scholarship.

passages.text: Liliuokalani translation (1897), opening lines (public domain): 'When the light of day was dim, and the night of Kumulipo was being born; when the light of day was dim, and the night of Pō'ele was being born... of the Pola'i, of the Ha'ele? of the deep darknesses, the Po was born.'
passages.zh: 莉莉烏歐卡拉尼譯本（1897年），開篇數行（公有領域）：「當白晝之光昏暗，庫穆利波的夜正被誕生；當白晝之光昏暗，波耶列的夜正被誕生……波拉伊的、哈耶列的？屬於深沉黑暗的，波被誕生了。」

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the first wā (Beckwith 1951 base): Born of the night, the coral polyp; born of the night, the small fry that swim in the sea's shallows; born of the night, the echinoderm? and on land its pair — each sea creature paired with a land creature through seven wā, until the fourth? until men are born of the night and Wakea's line begins. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the first wā (Beckwith 1951 base); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第一瓦（wā）的濃縮意譯（貝克威斯1951年底本）：生自夜者，珊瑚蟲；生自夜者，游於海中淺灘的小魚；生自夜者，棘皮動物？及其陸上之配對——每一海中生物皆與一陸上生物配對，歷經七個瓦，直到第四個？直到人類生自夜，瓦凱亞的血脈開始。非逐字照錄。

canonical_translation: Queen Liliuokalani, An Hawaiian Legend of the Creation, 1897 (public domain); Martha Beckwith, Kumulipo: A Hawaiian Creation Chant, Honolulu 1951 (copyright)

narrative.en:
The Kumulipo is the royal cosmogonic chant of Hawaii — over 2,000 lines of genealogical verse chanted at the birth of the high chief Ka-I-i-mamao (c. 1700) to graft his lineage onto the origin of all things. It is a cosmogony as genealogy: the world is not made but born, in sixteen wā (waves/generations), each verse pairing a sea-being with its land twin.

THE SIXTEEN WAVES. The chant opens in the time of Po, the deep darkness: 'When the light of day was dim, and the night of Kumulipo was being born...' — creation begins in seven darknesses (Kumulipo, Pō'ele, Pō'eli...), the deep source out of which life emerges. The first wā brings the coral polyp and the small fry of the shallows; the second the fish of the deep; each sea-being born 'of the night' is paired with its land counterpart — the sea pig with the land pig, the sea banana with the land banana, the sea taro with the land taro — the paired taxonomy by which Hawaiian thought classifies the world. Through the wā life rises: fish, birds, insects, reptiles? plants; then in the middle wā the age of humans begins — humans born of the night in successive generations — and in the final waves the great ancestral figures appear: Wakea ('sky-father') and Papa ('earth-mother'), the divine siblings whose union founds the human line, and the chiefly line descends — through Kāne? through the generations of chiefs — until the chant arrives at Ka-I-i-mamao himself: the newborn chief is the latest born of all things, his mana continuous with the coral polyp.

FUNCTIONS. The Kumulipo grounds Hawaiian chiefly legitimacy (the newborn chief's genealogy is the cosmos), the ecology of pairing (land-sea reciprocity — the fishpond and the garden as ritual twins), the kapu system's logic (Wakea and Papa's family laws — the 'Ulu? the breadfruit child episode — ground gender and eating taboos), and the modern sovereignty discourse (Liliuokalani's 1897 translation, made while deposed, is itself a political act: the nation's genealogy against annexation). It is chanted in hula hālau, taught in Hawaiian immersion schools, and cited in land claims; its sixteen waves are recited at the Makahiki new year and at royal commemorations, keeping the genealogy itself a living liturgy.

PROVENANCE. The chant was recorded in the 19th century (Bishop Museum manuscript tradition; the Liliuokalani translation made in exile); Beckwith's 1951 edition is the scholarly base. Prefer contemporary Hawaiian scholarship (e.g. Puakea Nogelmeier's Awaiaulu projects; Ku'ulei Higashi Kanaehe? — community-authored work) in citation.
narrative.zh: 《庫姆利波》為夏威夷王族宇宙頌歌，凡二千餘行，於約1700年高酋 Ka-I-i-mamao 誕生時誦唱，將其世系接於萬物之源。創世為系譜：世界非造而是生，凡十六波（wā），每節海中生物與陸上生物成對。頌歌啟於波之深暗：『當晝光漸暗，庫姆利波之夜誕生時……』——生命自七重黑暗之深源生出。第一波生珊瑚蟲與淺灘小魚；第二波生深海之魚；凡夜中所生之海中物皆與陸上物成對——海中之豬配陸上之豬、海中蕉配陸上蕉、海芋配陸芋——此即夏威夷思想分類世界之對偶法。歷波而上：魚、鳥、蟲、植物；至中波而人類之紀始；末波出現大祖瓦凱亞（天父）與帕帕（地母），其兄妹之結合開人系；酋長世系下延至新生酋長本人——酋長為萬物中最晚生者，其瑪那與珊瑚蟲相續。功能：酋長合法性之根基、海陸互惠之生態觀、卡普制度之邏輯（瓦凱亞與帕帕之家法釋性別與飲食禁忌）、以及現代主權論述（利留卡拉尼女王於被廢之年譯之，為抵抗兼併之政治行為）。

functions: Charter of chiefly legitimacy: the newborn chief's genealogy is the cosmos
Ecology of pairing: land-sea reciprocity as ritual taxonomy
Kapu logic: Wakea and Papa's family laws ground gender and eating taboos
Sovereignty discourse: Liliuokalani's 1897 translation as political act

title.en: Ti'iti'i and the Earthquake God: The Samoan Theft of Fire
title.zh: 蒂伊蒂伊與地震之神：薩摩亞盜火記

region.en: Savai'i, Samoa (the volcano Mafuie's domain)
region.zh: 薩摩亞薩瓦伊島（地震之神馬富耶之域）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 19th c. (George Turner, Samoa a Hundred Years Ago, London 1884; John B. Stair, Old Samoa, 1897)

source.work: George Turner, Samoa a Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, London 1884 (public domain); John B. Stair, Old Samoa, London 1897 (public domain)

summary.en: Ti'iti'i, son of the woman Talanga, descends to the underworld to demand fire from the earthquake-god Mafuie; beaten, he returns, catches Mafuie's tail in a crack, and fights him; he breaks off one of Mafuie's arms, the source of earthquakes, and carries the firesticks to mankind — the Samoan variant of the Maui fire-theft cycle.
summary.zh: 蒂伊蒂伊（塔蘭加之子）下冥府向地震神馬富耶索火；被擊而返，夾其尾於石縫而鬥；折斷馬富耶致地震之一臂，攜取火之木歸於人類——此為毛伊盜火圈之薩摩亞變體。

sensitivity.note: Living Samoan tradition (fa'asamoa); recordings are 19th-c. missionary-era collections — flagged.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Turner (1884): Talanga told her son Ti'iti'i that Mafuie kept fire in the underworld; Ti'iti'i went down, demanded fire, was beaten, came back with a broken arm — and his mother said: 'go again, and catch him by the tail when the earthquake shakes the ground.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Turner (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 特納（1884年）的濃縮意譯：塔蘭加告訴她的兒子蒂伊蒂伊，馬富伊埃把火藏在地下世界；蒂伊蒂伊下去了，索求火，遭毆打，帶著斷臂回來——他的母親說：「再去一次，當地動搖撼大地時，抓住他的尾巴。」非逐字照錄。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Turner (1884) (ending): Ti'iti'i caught Mafuie by the tail and held him in a crack of rock; they fought, and Ti'iti'i broke off one of Mafuie's arms — 'wherefore earthquakes are less violent than of old' — and Mafuie surrendered the firesticks; Ti'iti'i carried them up, and fire belonged to mankind. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Turner (1884) (ending); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 特納（1884年）的濃縮意譯（結尾）：蒂伊蒂伊抓住馬富伊埃的尾巴，把他制在岩石的裂縫中；他們搏鬥，蒂伊蒂伊折斷了馬富伊埃的一條手臂——「因此地震比往昔較為緩和」——馬富伊埃交出了取火木棒；蒂伊蒂伊把它們帶了上去，火便歸於人類。非逐字照錄。

language: Samoan (Gagana Samoa; recorded in English translation)
canonical_translation: George Turner, Samoa a Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, London 1884 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The Samoan fire-theft is the western Polynesian variant of the Māui cycle (cross-ref maori-maui) — with a distinct hero and a distinct cosmology of earthquake.

BEGINNING: THE MOTHER'S INSTRUCTION. In Savai'i, fire is the secret of the earthquake-god Mafuie, who keeps it in the underworld (his domain is the volcano region of Savai'i, the Saleaula? the volcanic district). Talanga, the mortal woman married to the gods, tells her son Ti'iti'i ('the smashed? the striker') that men eat their food raw because Mafuie hoards fire: 'go down and get fire for us.'

MIDDLE: THE FIGHT WITH MAFUIE. Ti'iti'i descends to the underworld and demands fire; Mafuie refuses — fire is the gods' — and beats the youth. Ti'iti'i returns broken-armed to his mother, who gives him the strategy of the trickster: 'Mafuie's tail is his strength; when the earthquake shakes, catch him by the tail.' Ti'iti'i goes down again, and when the ground quakes he seizes Mafuie by the tail and holds him fast in a crack of rock; the two wrestle until Ti'iti'i breaks off one of Mafuie's arms — the arm with which Mafuie shook the earth — 'and hence earthquakes are less violent than they were of old' (the aition of Samoa's lessened quakes, tied to Savai'i's volcanism).

END: FIRE FOR MANKIND. Defeated, Mafuie surrenders the firesticks (the ritual fire-plough of Polynesian fire-making); Ti'iti'i carries them up to the world of men, and from that day mankind cooks its food and kindles fire — the western-Polynesian answer to the Maui-Mahuika tale (in the Māori telling the hero is Maui, the fire-keeper the goddess Mahuika; in Samoa the fire-keeper is male and the loss is an arm). The narrative's twins (Talanga's family) and the volcano geography root it in Samoan chiefly genealogy and the geology of Savai'i.

COMPARATIVE AND FUNCTIONAL NOTE. Set beside the Maori telling (Maui against the fire-goddess Mahuika, whose fingernails are flames) and the Hawaiian telling (Maui snaring the sun on Haleakala; the alae hen guarding fire), the Samoan variant shows the cycle's grammar: a young hero of double descent, a fire-keeper of the chthonic world, a trick to break the monopoly, and an aition written into the landscape. In Samoa the aition is geological — the broken arm of Mafuie explains why quakes gentled — and the firesticks ground the ritual fire-plough (the si? the 'tili aila) that Turner describes as still practiced. The narrative is told in chiefly oratory (fa'alupega) contexts where Savai'i's descent lines claim the tale; Turner's missionary collection preserved it in English at the cost of its liturgical setting — a caution this record flags.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative aitiologizes fire-by-friction (the firesticks), the diminished violence of Samoan earthquakes, and the geography of Savai'i's volcanic district; it structures the Samoan trickster-hero cycle and the chiefly genealogies that claim descent from Talanga's line; and it is the standard Samoan comparandum in Polynesian myth studies (Turner's 1884 collection being the missionary-era base text — flagged).
narrative.zh: 薩摩亞盜火記為毛伊圈之西玻里尼西亞變體。薩瓦伊島上，火為地震神馬富耶之秘藏於冥府；凡女塔蘭加告其子蒂伊蒂伊：世人食生食，因馬富耶吝火——『去為我們取火來。』蒂伊蒂伊下冥府索火，馬富耶拒而擊之；蒂伊蒂伊斷臂而歸，母授詭計：『地震搖動時，抓其尾。』再下，乘地震之際夾其尾於石縫，相搏至折斷馬富耶致震之一臂——『故地震較古時為輕』（薩瓦伊火山地震減弱之釋義）。馬富耶降，交出取火之木；蒂伊蒂伊攜火上界，人類自茲熟食取火——與毛利本中英雄為毛伊、守火者為女神瑪胡伊卡相對，薩摩亞版守火者為男、所失者為臂。功能：鑽木取火之釋義、地震減弱之釋義、薩瓦伊火山地理之敘事化、以及酋長世系（塔蘭加之後）之憲章。

Aition of diminished Samoan earthquakes: Mafuie's broken arm
Geography of Savai'i's volcanic district mythologized
Polynesian comparative hero-cycle (Samoan variant of the Maui fire-theft)

title.en: Qat of the Banks Islands: The Culture Hero of Vanuatu
title.zh: 班克斯群島之卡特：瓦努阿圖文化英雄

region.en: Banks Islands (Gaua/Mota), Vanuatu
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島（高阿島／莫塔島）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore, Oxford 1891 (public domain)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore, Oxford 1891 (public domain), chs. on Qat and Mota narratives

summary.en: Qat, born of a stone and raised by his mother's brothers, creates the islands, men, and pigs, kills the night with a joke, teaches the Suqe graded society, and departs in a canoe said to return — the great culture hero of the northern Vanuatu archipelago.
summary.zh: 卡特效生於石、由母舅養大；造島嶼、人類與豬，以戲言終結長夜，創立蘇蓋等級會社，後乘獨木舟而去，傳言將返——此為瓦努阿圖北部群島之大文化英雄。

sensitivity.note: Record uses the 1891 Codrington collection (missionary-era; flagged); living Vanuatu communities (kastom movement) hold the heritage.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Codrington (1891), Qat narratives: Qat was born of a stone, which split? he emerged as a boy; his mother's brothers raised him; he made pigs, made men? he carved wooden figures and beat drums until the wood opened and living men stepped out — 'thus men came.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Codrington (1891), Qat narratives; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 科德林頓（1891年）的濃縮意譯，卡特（Qat）諸敘事：卡特生自一塊石頭，石頭裂開了？他以男孩之身出現；他母親的兄弟們將他撫養長大；他造了豬，造了人？他雕刻木像並擊鼓，直到木頭裂開，活人走了出來——「人便是這樣來的。」非逐字照錄。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Codrington (1891) (the night): In the beginning night was long, longer than the day; Qat bought? he took a cock from the Night-man (Qong? Qat's brother), waited for the dawn-cock's crow, and killed the Night-man — 'so the night became short, as it now is.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Codrington (1891) (the night); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 科德林頓（1891年）的濃縮意譯（夜）：起初夜很長，比白晝更長；卡特買了？他從夜之人（瓊？卡特的兄弟）那裡取得一隻公雞，等候報曉公雞的啼鳴，並殺死了夜之人——「於是夜變短了，正如現今一樣。」非逐字照錄。

language: Mota (Banks Islands language), recorded in English
canonical_translation: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, Oxford 1891 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Qat (Qat) is the culture hero of the Banks Islands (northern Vanuatu), recorded by the missionary-anthropologist R. H. Codrington in the 1880s-90s — the fullest Melanesian hero corpus in print.

BEGINNING: THE STONE-BORN BOY. Qat was born of a stone (in some tellings of the great rock of Gaua); his mother's brothers raised him. From boyhood he shows the maker's power: he makes pigs from? he goes about creating — islands of the archipelago, the reef, the forest.

MIDDLE: THE MAKING OF MEN AND PIGS. The great creative acts: Qat carves figures of wood (or dris? of dracaena wood), beats drums beside them until the wood splits and living men and women step out — 'thus men came into the world'; he makes pigs, coconuts, and gardens; he teaches the Suqe, the graded men's society (the pig-killing grade system that organizes Banks-Islands status) — culture is Qat's curriculum. His brothers (or shadow-rivals, the Qat-qaravu? the eleven brothers including Qat the trickster) parody his works — making bad men? bad pigs — and Qat must undo or outdo them (the Melanesian theme of defective creativity).

END: THE KILLING OF THE NIGHT AND THE DEPARTURE. Night (Qong? the long night) originally lasted longer than day; Qat goes to the Night-man (his brother in some tellings), buys a cock? waits hidden until the dawn-cock crows, and slays the Night-man — 'and so night became short, as now it is' — the aition of day and night's balance. Qat then departs: he sails away in a canoe for the horizon, and the Mota tradition says he went to? that he will return — the departed hero whose return is hoped (Codrington records the missionary-era debate: Qat identified with the returning Christ by some converts, and with the departed ancestral power by others). In the Torres Islands? the adjacent traditions, Qat's mother? the variants across the Banks group differ on his relations and his wives (the Ro Leiq? the Ambae? — the neighboring island traditions have their own heroes, Tagaro of the New Hebrides? cross-ref tagaro-sea).

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds the Suqe graded society (pig-killing ranks as Qat's institution), the aition of day/night, the creative ethics of Melanesian culture heroes (making by carving and drum-beat; parody and defective twins), and the kastom movement's hero canon in modern Vanuatu; Codrington's collection remains the printed base (missionary-era, flagged), with contemporary Vanuatu Cultural Centre fieldwork (kastom narratives recorded in Bislama and Mota) as the living source.
narrative.zh: 卡特（Qat）為瓦努阿圖北部班克斯群島之文化英雄，柯德林頓（1880-90年代）採錄之敘事為印刷文獻中之美拉尼西亞英雄敘事最富者。卡特自大石而生（一說生於高阿島巨巖），由母舅養大；自幼即顯造物之力：造群島、礁、林。其大功：刻木為像，擊鼓於側，木裂而活人步出——『人由此而來』；造豬、椰、園圃；創立蘇蓋男子等級會社（殺豬進階之制度）——文化即卡特之課程。其諸兄（或影響之對手）仿其作而皆劣（美拉尼西亞『殘缺創造』之題）。太初夜長於晝；卡特至夜之主人（一說其兄）處，候晨雞初啼而殺之——『故夜短如今日』（晝夜之釋義）。後卡特乘獨木舟駛向海平線而去，莫塔島傳統言其將返——柯德林頓記錄了宣教時代之爭：歸化者或以卡特擬復臨之基督，或以其為先祖之力。功能：蘇蓋等級會社之創立、晝夜釋義、美拉尼西亞文化英雄之創造倫理（刻木擊鼓而造人）、以及現代瓦努阿圖『卡斯通』運動之英雄正典。

title.en: Hainuwele: The Coconut Girl and the DEMA Creation of the Kei Islands
title.zh: 海努韋萊：椰子之女與凱伊群島之德瑪創世

region.en: Kei Islands, Maluku, Indonesia
region.zh: 印尼馬魯古群島凱伊群島

period: Recorded 1937-38 by Ad. E. Jensen (Frobenius Institute expedition); published Jensen, Hainuwele, Frankfurt 1939

source.archive: Frobenius Institute (Jensen expedition materials) / scholarly editions
source.work: Adolf E. Jensen, Hainuwele: Volkserzahlungen von der Malaiischen Grossen Inselkette, Frankfurt 1939; the dema corpus (recordings with named informants in the expedition notebooks)

license: Jensen 1939 quoted only as summary (copyright); underlying dema narratives are community heritage — paraphrase only

summary.en: Ameta, hunting wild pigs, finds a coconut in a boar's tusk; a girl, Hainuwele, grows from it in three days bearing valuables in her palms; at the maro dance the men crowd around her until she sinks into the ground; Ameta digs up her body and cuts it into pieces, which, buried, become the clans' food-plants — the dema myth of culture rising from murder.
summary.zh: 阿梅塔獵野豬，於豬牙中得椰子；三日期間椰中生出女孩海努韋萊，掌中藏寶；瑪羅舞會上眾男擁擠相擠，少女陷入地中；阿梅塔掘其屍，碎而埋之，化為各氏族之食用植物——此為『德瑪』神話：文化自謀殺中生。

sensitivity.note: Record uses the 1937-39 Jensen expedition materials (colonial-era; flagged); Kei and Maluku communities hold the heritage — paraphrase only.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Jensen-recorded narrative: Ameta the hunter was tracking a wild pig; his spear? the boar's tusk held a coconut; he brought it home and put it in a basket; after three days a girl came out — Hainuwele — and in the hollows of her palms she bore dishware? gold? valuables for the household. Not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the maro dance (Jensen 1939): At the nine-day maro dance the men danced in a circle around Hainuwele, who stood at the center; each night the circle pressed closer; on the ninth night she sank into the ground; Ameta dug her up and, following a spirit's? instruction, cut her body into pieces and buried them; from the pieces grew the plants — the yams, coconuts, and tubers that feed the clans. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the maro dance (Jensen 1939); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 根據馬羅舞（簡森，1939年）的濃縮改寫：在為期九天的馬羅舞中，男人們圍著站在中央的海努維勒繞圈起舞；每一夜，圈子都逼得更近；到了第九夜，她沉入地下；阿梅塔把她挖了出來，並遵照一位精靈？的指示，將她的身體切成碎塊埋下；從這些碎塊中長出了植物——滋養各氏族的薯蕷、椰子和塊莖。非逐字引用。

language: Kei (Veveu Evav? Kei language), recorded in German
canonical_translation: Jensen 1939 (German, copyright); English summaries in Jensen's Myth and Cult among Primitive Peoples (1963, copyright)

narrative.en:
Hainuwele is the best-known dema myth — the 'dema' (ancestral-deity) narratives of Maluku recorded by the Frobenius Institute expedition of 1937-38 under Adolf E. Jensen — in which the world's culture rises from the killing of a primordial being.

BEGINNING: THE COCONUT IN THE TUSK. Ameta, the hunter of the Kei Islands, was tracking a wild pig; the boar's tusk held a coconut — an object unknown in the land. He brought it home and put it in a basket; after three days a girl emerged from the coconut: Hainuwele, 'the coconut branch? the coconut girl'. In the hollows of her palms she bore valuables — porcelain dishes? gold? gongs and gift-goods — for the household: she is the source of wealth.

MIDDLE: THE MARO DANCE AND THE SINKING. At the great maro dance (the nine-night exchange festival), Hainuwele stood at the center of the dancing circle, giving gifts from her palms. Each night the men pressed closer around her; on the ninth night, the circle closed — the men crowded around her 'like the? like? ' — and she sank into the ground and was gone. (In the variants, the men's greed for her gifts is the cause; the dema's death is collective.)

END: THE PIECES THAT BECAME FOOD. Ameta dug her up and, instructed by a spirit (or following the custom), cut her body into pieces and buried them at the dance ground. From the buried pieces grew the plants: yams, taro, coconuts, tubers — each piece a food, distributed among the clans (each clan's staple from a different part). Jensen's theory: the dema narratives encode the theology that human culture (agriculture, ritual, death) rises from the primordial murder of the dema-being — killing is the price of sustenance, and ritual (the maro dance, the funeral) re-enacts it. The corpus of dema myths around Hainuwele (the Maro dance cycle, the Watumas? the primordial sisters) frames the Kei understanding of death, planting, and exchange.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds Kei agriculture (clans' staple plants from the dema's body), the maro festival (gift-exchange as re-enactment), the theology of death (burial as planting), and the comparative typology of dismembered-culture myths (Purusha, Ymir — with the distinction that the dema is killed collectively and produces not the cosmos but the food system). Provenance: the Jensen expedition (1937-39, Dutch East Indies) recorded with named informants in the notebooks; colonial-era — flagged; contemporary Maluku scholarship (e.g. Kei community publications) is preferred.
narrative.zh: 海努韋萊為馬魯古『德瑪』（祖靈神）神話之最著名者，1937-38 年弗羅貝尼烏斯研究所遠征隊（詹森主持）採錄。獵人阿梅塔追野豬，於豬牙中得椰子——此物前所未有；帶回家置於籃中，三日後椰中生出女孩海努韋萊；其掌紋中藏寶物（瓷器、金、鑼與禮品），為家宅之財源。九夜瑪羅交換節之舞會上，海努韋萊立於舞圈中央施贈；夜夜眾男逼近，第九夜圍擠——少女陷入地中而失（變體言因眾男貪其贈禮；德瑪之死屬集體）。阿梅塔掘其屍，依神諭（或依俗）碎而埋於舞場；埋處生出薯蕷、芋、椰、塊莖——每一片成一種食物，分歸各氏族（各氏族之主食自不同部位）。詹森之論：德瑪神話之神學即人類文化（農耕、儀式、死亡）自原始謀殺中生——殺戮為取食之代價，儀式（瑪羅舞、葬禮）即其重演。凱伊人圍繞海努韋萊之德瑪敘事群（瑪羅舞循環、原始姊妹瓦圖瑪斯等）構成其對死亡、種植與交換之理解。功能：氏族主食之釋義、瑪羅節之憲章、葬為種之死亡神學、以及碎身造物神話比較類型（普魯沙、尤彌爾——惟德瑪為集體所殺、所產非宇宙而為食物體系）。

Theology of death: burial as planting; the funeral as planting rite

title.en: Bathala Maykapal: The Tagalog Creation and the Three Rivals
title.zh: 巴哈拉·馬伊卡帕爾：他加祿創世與三神之爭

region.en: Luzon (Tagalog region; symbolic pin at Manila)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋島他加祿地區（象徵性定位於馬尼拉）

period: Recorded early 20th c.: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales, Chicago 1916 (public domain); Fay-Cooper Cole, The Tinguian, Chicago 1922

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales, Chicago 1916 (public domain), 'The Creation' and 'The Battle of the? ' Tagalog sections; Fay-Cooper Cole, The Tinguian, 1922

summary.en: Bathala Maykapal, ruler of the sky, wars with Aman Sinaya of the sea and Amihan of the northeast wind; Amihan, tiring of the battle, flies between them, and the sky-god's thrown rock and the sea-goddess's islands meet — the Philippine archipelago is born, and from a bamboo stalk the first man and woman emerge.
summary.zh: 天神巴哈拉·馬伊卡帕爾與海神阿曼·西納亞及東北風之神阿米漢相爭；阿米漢厭戰，飛於二者之間；天神擲石、海神起島，相遇成群島——菲律賓由是而生；竹節中走出最初之男女。

sensitivity.note: Record uses the 1916 Cole collection (American colonial-era; flagged); Philippine IPRA law (1997) vests community intellectual rights over indigenous knowledge.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Cole (1916), 'The Creation' (Tagalog): Bathala of the sky, Aman Sinaya of the sea, and Amihan of the northeast wind quarreled; Bathala threw great rocks at the sea-goddess, and she raised great waves; Amihan, weary of the war, flew between them — the rocks fell where she passed and became islands. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cole (1916), 'The Creation' (Tagalog); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 根據科爾（1916年）〈創世〉（他加祿語）的濃縮改寫：天空的巴塔拉、海洋的阿曼·西納亞與東北風的阿米漢起了爭執；巴塔拉向海之女神投擲巨石，而她掀起巨浪；阿米漢厭倦了這場爭戰，飛到二者之間——巨石落在她飛過之處，化為島嶼。非逐字引用。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Cole (1916) (the bamboo): A bamboo stalk grew by the shore? it grew tall and divided; the first man, Malakas ('strong'), came out of one half, and the first woman, Maganda ('beautiful'), out of the other — and from their children are the peoples of the islands. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cole (1916) (the bamboo); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 根據科爾（1916年）（竹子）的濃縮改寫：岸邊？長出了一株竹子，它長得高大並分為兩半；第一個男人馬拉卡斯（「強壯」）從一半中走出，第一個女人瑪甘達（「美麗」）從另一半中走出——島上各民族皆出自他們的子孫。非逐字引用。

canonical_translation: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales, Chicago 1916 (public domain); Damiana L. Eugenio, Philippine Folk Literature: The Myths, Quezon City 1993 (copyright)

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: THE THREE POWERS. The Tagalog creation narrative recorded by Cole (1916) begins with three primordial powers: Bathala Maykapal ('Maker' Bathala), ruler of the sky; Aman Sinaya, goddess of the sea; and Amihan, the bird-shaped deity of the northeast wind. The sky and the sea warred: Bathala hurled great rocks at the sea-goddess; she answered with towering waves; the battle shook the world.

MIDDLE: THE WIND BETWEEN. Amihan, the northeast wind, weary of the eternal battle, flew between the two antagonists — and where the wind passed, Bathala's thrown rocks could not fall into the sea but struck the shallow waters and stood as islands: 'and thus were the islands of the Philippines formed.' The peace-making wind is the aition of the archipelago — seven thousand islands as projectiles arrested mid-fall.

END: THE BAMBOO AND THE FIRST COUPLE. On one of the islands a bamboo stalk grew tall; it split, and from one half came the first man Malakas ('Strong') and from the other the first woman Maganda ('Beautiful'); they married and bore children — in the fuller folk telling the children scatter (the blind? the shy ones hide in the house walls — ancestors of the hidden peoples; the wanderers go to sea — ancestors of? ), grounding the diversity of Philippine peoples. Bathala remains the supreme sky-father (the term 'Bathala' itself became the Tagalog word for God in Christian translation), the ancestral pantheon's head, whose helpers (the anito? the katutubong anito) mediate between him and the people.

RITUAL WORLD. Bathala's worship in the pre-colonial Tagalog world was mediated by the babaylan (priestesses, often women or feminized men) who offered to the anito — carved ancestral spirits housed in the household and the fields; the diwata of the groves and the? the river spirits received offerings of rice wine, betel, and first-fruits at the village pag-aanito rites. The narrative's three powers map onto this ritual division: the sky-father above, the sea beneath the fisher's world, the wind of the monsoon that opens and closes the sailing year — the agricultural and maritime calendar of Luzon written as divine politics. The bamboo couple grounds the household itself: the first house, the first fire, the division of labor between Malakas and Maganda as the folk explanation of marriage custom. Under Spanish rule the name Bathala transferred to the Christian God (the Doctrina Christiana of 1593 uses Bathala for Deus), making the creation narrative the hinge between the old anito religion and Philippine Catholicism — one reason the story remains the country's most recognizable myth.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds Tagalog cosmology (sky-sea duality settled by wind), the aition of the archipelago (islands as thrown rocks), the bamboo-couple origin of humanity, and the term 'Bathala' as the theological bridge to colonial Christianity; it is the best-known Philippine myth nationally (school textbooks), collected in the American colonial era (Cole 1916 — flagged) and re-collected by Eugenio's Philippine Folk Literature series.
narrative.zh: 他加祿創世（科爾1916年採錄）：太初有三神——天神巴哈拉·馬伊卡帕爾、海神阿曼·西納亞、東北風神阿米漢。天海相戰：巴哈拉擲巨石，海神起巨浪，世界震動。阿米漢厭於永戰，飛於二者之間——風過之處，天神所擲之石不得落海深處，立於淺水而成島嶼：『菲律賓群島由是而成』——七千島即半途受阻之飛石。其中一島生巨竹，竹裂，上半出首男馬拉卡斯（『強』），下半出首女馬甘達（『美』）；結為夫婦生子，子孫分散（躲於牆內者為隱匿族群之祖、漂於海上者為航海者之祖），釋菲島民族之多樣。巴哈拉為最高天父（Bathala 一詞後成他加祿語中『神』之稱，為基督教譯名之橋）。功能：天海二元經風而和之宇宙觀、群島飛石釋義、竹節男女之人類起源、以及國家教科書中之民族敘事。

Bamboo-couple origin: Malakas and Maganda as national first ancestors
Theological bridge: 'Bathala' as the Tagalog name of God in Christian translation
National school-canon: the best-known Philippine creation narrative

title.en: Lac Long Quan and Au Co: The Dragon and the Fairy of a Hundred Eggs
title.zh: 貉龍君與嫗姬：龍父仙母百卵之裔

region.en: Phu Tho province (Hung Temple sanctuary; symbolic pin)
region.zh: 越南富壽省雄王廟（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded in Linh Nam chich quai (14th c.); Dai Viet su ky toan thu (Ngo Si Lien, 1479); Hung Temple cycle living ritual

summary.en: Lac Long Quan, the dragon lord of the waters, clears the land of monsters, marries the mountain fairy Au Co, who lays a sac of a hundred eggs; fifty children follow the father to the sea, fifty the mother to the mountains; the eldest becomes Hung Vuong, first of the Hồng Bàng kings — the charter of the Vietnamese people (children of dragon and fairy).
summary.zh: 水澤之龍君貉龍君掃除妖魔，娶山仙嫗姬；嫗姬產卵百枚；五十子隨父入海，五十子隨母上山；長子為雄王，開鴻龐氏——越南人『龍子仙孫』之憲章。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: the Hung Kings' festival (national holiday) and the Hung Temple cult; nationalist ideology uses the narrative — handle critically.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Linh Nam chich quai narrative: Lac Long Quan, son of the dragon Kinh Duong Vuong, rid the land of the fish-monster Ngu Tinh, the nine-tailed fox Ho Tinh, and the tree demon Moc Tinh; he married the mountain fairy Au Co, who laid a sac of a hundred eggs, from which a hundred sons hatched. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Linh Nam chich quai narrative; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 根據《嶺南摭怪》敘事的濃縮改寫：龍君涇陽王之子的雒龍君，為這片土地除去了魚怪魚精、九尾狐狐精與樹妖木精；他娶了山間仙女嫗姬，她產下一囊百卵，百名兒子自卵中孵出。非逐字引用。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the division (Toan thu 1479): The dragon lord said: 'I am of the dragon line, thou of the fairy line; water and mountain differ' — and they divided the hundred sons: fifty with the father to the deeps, fifty with the mother to the highlands; the eldest was crowned Hung Vuong at Phong Chau, and the country named Van Lang. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the division (Toan thu 1479); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 根據分治（《全書》，1479年）的濃縮改寫：龍君說道：「我屬龍族，汝屬仙族；水與山不同」——於是他們將百名兒子分開：五十人隨父親往深水，五十人隨母親往高地；長子於峰州受封為雄王，國號定為文郎。非逐字引用。

canonical_translation: Scholarly summaries via Taylor 1983 and Vietnamese editions (copyright); ancient texts public domain

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: THE MONSTER-SLAYER. Lac Long Quan ('Dragon Lord of Lac'), son of Kinh Duong Vuong (the water-line of the South Sea dragon), roams the land and clears it of its monsters: the fish-monster Ngu Tinh of the sea (slain with? driven out with nets and rams? — the variants give his three monster-battles: Ngu Tinh the fish, Ho Tinh the nine-tailed fox of the mountains, Moc Tinh the tree demon of the forests), founding the order of the settled world.

MIDDLE: THE MARRIAGE AND THE HUNDRED EGGS. Lac Long Quan marries Au Co, the mountain fairy descended from the highlands; she lays a sac of a hundred eggs, from which hatch a hundred sons — the first Vietnamese. But the dragon of the waters and the fairy of the mountains cannot dwell together: 'I am of the dragon line, you are of the fairy; water and mountain differ; we cannot be forever joined.'

END: THE DIVISION AND THE HUNG KINGS. They divide the children: fifty follow the father into the sea-country (the coastal and riverine Lowlands — the Lac peoples), fifty follow the mother into the highlands (the mountain peoples); the eldest son is crowned Hung Vuong at Phong Chau (Phu Tho), founding the Hong Bang dynasty and the kingdom Van Lang — the first Vietnamese state. The narrative is the charter of Vietnamese identity: 'con Rong chau Tien' (children of Dragon, grandchildren of Fairy) — the unity of lowland and highland, water and mountain, in one descent; it is ritually grounded at the Hung Temple sanctuary (Phu Tho), where the Hung Kings' Festival (10th day of the 3rd lunar month, national holiday) renews the covenant; the national symbol (the dragon of Hanoi's? the descending-dragon Ha Long Bay aition is attached to the same dragon-line).

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds Vietnamese ethnic charter (dragon-fairy descent), the lowland-highland political synthesis (the fifty-fifty division), the Hung Temple cult (national pilgrimage), and the historiographic construction of antiquity (Toan thu 1479's editorial framing against Chinese 'Kija? ' claims — the Vietnamese response to Korea-style foundation legends). Scholarship (Taylor 1983) reads the cycle as 15th-century state ideology projected onto prehistoric materials — the record keeps both the mythic and the historiographic frames.

RITUAL AND RECEPTION. The Hung Temple sanctuary on Nghia Linh mountain (Phu Tho) holds the Hung Kings' Festival each year on the tenth day of the third lunar month — a national holiday since 2007 — when processions climb the 225 steps to the Upper Temple, offering chung and giay cakes (the square and round rice cakes of the Lang Lieu legend, the same dynasty's culinary charter). The Hung Kings' worship was inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list (2012) as 'belief? a belief of the Vietnamese people'. In the modern state the narrative is taught as the first lesson of national history, and its fifty-fifty division is invoked in highland-lowland policy discourse; the dragon of the descent descends further in Hanoi's Thang Long ('ascending dragon') aition and Ha Long Bay's pearl-islands — one dragon-line, three geographies.
narrative.zh: 貉龍君為涇陽王（南海龍系）之子，遍行國土驅除三妖：海中魚精吳精、山中九尾狐狐精、林中樹妖木精，立定居之世。後娶山仙嫗姬；嫗姬產卵百枚，孵出百子——越南人之始祖。然龍屬水、仙屬山，二者難久居：『我為龍種，爾為仙種，水土不同，難合久居。』遂分百子：五十隨父入海居低地（貉人），五十隨母上山居高土；長子立於峰州為雄王，開鴻龐之世，國號文郎——越南第一國。此為越南民族認同之憲章：『龍子仙孫』——低地與高地、水與山之一系同源；富壽雄王廟為其聖地，雄王祭（三月初十，國定假日）年年更新盟約；下龍灣『龍降』之釋義亦屬同龍系。功能：民族族源憲章、低地高地政治綜合（五五之分）、雄王廟朝聖、以及1479年《大越史記全書》之國家意識形態建構（Taylor 1983 之批判讀法——十五世紀國家意識形態投射於史前素材）。

title.en: The Ramakien: Phra Ram in the Bangkok Recension
title.zh: 《拉瑪堅》：曼谷本之帕拉瑪

region.en: Bangkok (Wat Phra Kaew murals; symbolic pin)
region.zh: 泰國曼谷玉佛寺壁畫（象徵性定位）

period: Rama I recension completed 1797 (Bangkok); Wat Phra Kaew mural program 1782-1809; khon masked dance-drama court tradition

source.archive: Wat Phra Kaew murals / scholarly studies

summary.en: The Thai Ramayana: Phra Ram, exiled with Nang Sida and Phra Lak, loses Sida to the ten-faced demon king Thotsakan of Longka; with the monkey armies and Hanuman's leaps, he builds the bridge, destroys Thotsakan, and returns to rule Ayodhya — the Thai royal recension that legitimates the Chakri dynasty.
summary.zh: 泰版羅摩衍那：帕拉瑪與娘子西達、帕拉剋流放；西達為十面魔王托沙坎擄至楞伽；得猴兵與哈努曼之助，跨海建橋、誅托沙坎，歸阿逾陀而王——此為確認卻克里王朝正統之王家抄本。

sensitivity.note: The Ramakien is royal heritage (Chakri dynasty; kings titled Rama); khon performance is living court art.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Ramakien (Rama I recension): Phra Ram, exiled to the forest with Nang Sida and Phra Lak, loses Sida when the demon Marit? Mareet transforms into a golden deer; Thotsakan, the ten-faced king of Longka, seizes her; the dying bird? the vulture? Sida drops her ornaments to mark the trail. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Ramakien (Rama I recension); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《拉瑪堅》（拉瑪一世本）的濃縮改寫：帕拉姆與娜西達、帕拉克一同被流放至森林，當惡魔瑪里特化為金鹿時，他失去了西達；朗卡的十面王托薩甘擄走了她；垂死的鳥？禿鷲？西達丟下她的飾物以標記蹤跡。非逐字引用。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Ramakien (the bridge and the war): Hanuman builds the causeway to Longka; the monkey armies storm the city; Thotsakan's brother Kumphakan is roused from sleep to devour armies; Indrajit's? the demon prince's illusions nearly break them; Phra Ram at last slays Thotsakan with the great bow, and Sida's fidelity is proven by fire. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Ramakien (the bridge and the war); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《拉瑪堅》（橋樑與戰爭）的濃縮改寫：哈努曼建造通往朗卡的堤道；猴軍猛攻該城；托薩甘的兄弟昆帕甘從睡夢中被喚醒以吞噬軍隊；因陀羅耆特？惡魔王子的幻術幾乎擊潰他們；帕拉姆最終以巨弓殺死托薩甘，西達的貞潔由火證明。非逐字引用。

canonical_translation: Thai text (Rama I recension, 1797; public domain); scholarship: Klaus Wenk's Ramakien studies (copyright); English summaries via Reynolds & Reynolds 1982 (copyright)

narrative.en:
The Ramakien is Thailand's national Ramayana, recast from the Sanskrit epic through Khmer and Mon intermediaries and finalized in the Bangkok recension completed by King Rama I in 1797 — the founding cultural act of the new Chakri dynasty, whose kings take the regnal name Rama.

THE THAI TELLING. Phra Ram (Rama) of Ayodhya (Thai: Ayutthaya), son of King Thotsarot (Dasharatha) by Nang Kaosuriya, is exiled fourteen years when Nang Kaiyakesi (Kaikeyi) claims her boons; he departs with his wife Nang Sida (Sita) and brother Phra Lak (Lakshmana). In the forest of? at Khao? the demon Mareet transforms into a golden deer; Sida's demand and Phra Lak's reluctant departure let Thotsakan (Ravana), the ten-faced, twenty-armed demon king of Longka (Lanka), abduct her — pulling up the whole hut with the earth; the vulture Satabut (Jatayu) fights him dying. Phra Ram allies with the monkey kings Sukhrip (Sugriva) and the white monkey Hanuman — son of the wind, son of? his jaw? his tail of fire burns Longka after his capture (the Thai scene of Hanuman's burning tail). The monkey army builds the stone causeway to Longka (the aition of the Adamman? of the string of islands — the 'bridge' still named in Thai geography); the war rages: Kumphakan (Kumbhakarna), roused from his six-month sleep, devours armies before falling to Phra Ram's arrows; the demon prince Intharachit (Indrajit) conjures illusory Sidas and nearly breaks the siege; Phra Lak and the? are healed by the? — the Thai version multiplies the magical battles. At the last, Phra Ram faces Thotsakan: the demon's ten heads regrow as they fall, until the great bow Brahmastra? the arrow of? Phra Ram's arrow — the bow given by Phra Isuan (Shiva) — severs the head that cannot regrow, and Thotsakan falls; his brother Wiroon? Vibhishan (Thai: Phra Wiroon? Piphek) is crowned. Sida's fidelity is proven by fire (the Thai fire ordeal — she survives, and the couple return in the flying chariot Pul? the Pali? the pushpaka); the Khmer? the Bangkok recension ends with the ideal kingship of Phra Ram at Ayutthaya.

FUNCTIONS. The Ramakien is the charter of Thai kingship: Rama I's recension legitimated the new dynasty (kings named Rama I-X); the Wat Phra Kaew mural program (1782-1809) walls the royal temple with 178 scenes of the story — the king walks the myth daily; the khon masked dance-drama enacts it at court festivals; and Hanuman is the comic sacred center of Thai popular culture (statues, amulets, kickboxing gyms). The Thai recension localizes: place-names, costume, the Buddhist karmic frame (Thotsakan's virtue acknowledged; his green? his color-coding), and the royal theology of the devaraja.
narrative.zh: 《拉瑪堅》為泰國之羅摩衍那，經高棉與孟人中介，於1797年由拉瑪一世定稿——新卻克里王朝立國之文化大典，歷代國王皆號『拉瑪』。帕拉瑪（羅摩）遭後母凱伊雅凱西索諾而流放十四年，攜娘子西達與弟帕拉剋入林；魔馬里特化金鹿誘之，十面二十臂之楞伽魔王托沙坎連屋帶地擄走西達；神鷹薩塔布特力戰而死。帕拉瑪結盟猴王蘇格里與白猴哈努曼（風神之子）；哈努曼被擒，火尾燒楞伽城；猴軍壘石跨海建橋（泰地群島之釋義）。戰爭層疊：睡六個月方醒之魔將坤帕坎吞食軍旅而亡；魔子因塔拉吉特幻化西達亂敵；最後帕拉瑪以濕婆所賜神弓之箭斬托沙坎不能復生之首；弟皮佩克受封。西達過火驗貞，夫婦乘飛車歸國，帕拉瑪行理想之治。功能：泰王權之憲章（拉瑪一世至十世之號）、玉佛寺178幅壁畫環繞王寺、孔劇於宮廷節慶演出、哈努曼為泰國大眾文化之聖喜中心。

title.en: Sky Woman on the Turtle's Back: The Haudenosaunee Creation
title.zh: 天女踏龜背：豪德諾索尼創世

region.en: Onondaga territory, central New York (symbolic pin at Onondaga Nation)
region.zh: 美國紐約州中部奧農達加領地（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded 1828 (David Cusick, Tuscarora author, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations) and 1899-1900s (J. N. B. Hewitt, Iroquoian Cosmology, BAE, with named Onondaga informant Simeon Gibson)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Lewiston NY 1828 (public domain); J. N. B. Hewitt, Iroquoian Cosmology, BAE-R 21, Washington 1903 (public domain)

summary.en: Sky Woman falls from the upper world through the uprooted tree of light; waterfowl catch her and the Great Turtle offers his back; the muskrat dives and dies bringing up earth, which grows into the world; she bears a daughter, and the daughter's twin sons — Sapling the Good Mind and Flint the crooked one — make the living world, ending in a duel that fixes death and flint in the land.
summary.zh: 天女自上界經被連根拔起之光樹墜落；水禽接之，大龜獻背；麝鼠潛水致死而得土，土生為世界；天女生女，其孿生子——善心之樹苗與心術不正之火石——造萬物，末以決鬥定死亡與燧石之由來。

sensitivity.note: Record uses Indigenous-authored (Cusick 1828) and named-informant (Hewitt/Gibson) public-domain sources; Haudenosaunee protocols govern ceremonial knowledge — some condolence chants are restricted and are not represented.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Cusick (1828): The woman (Ataensic? Sky Woman) fell from the upper world through the hole of the uprooted tree; a tortoise volunteered his back; the beaver, the? the muskrat diving brought up earth in his claws and died of the effort — 'the tortoise took the earth and strewed it on his back, and the world grew.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cusick (1828); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 庫西克（1828）的濃縮改寫：那女人（阿塔恩西克？天空女）從上界經由被連根拔起的樹洞跌落；一隻烏龜自願獻出牠的背；河狸、那？那潛水的麝鼠以爪帶上泥土，並因這番努力而死——「烏龜取來泥土，撒在牠的背上，世界便生長了。」非逐字引用。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the twin-sons episode (Cusick 1828; Hewitt 1903): The daughter bore twin sons; the crooked-minded one (Tawiskaron/Flint) killed their mother at birth, and she was buried — from her body grew the corn, the squash, and the tobacco; the Good Mind (Sapling) made the rivers run both ways, the crooked one made them rapids; at last they fought, and Flint was driven from the world — his blood became the flint stones. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the twin-sons episode (Cusick 1828; Hewitt 1903); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 雙生子插曲（庫西克 1828；休伊特 1903）的濃縮改寫：那女兒生下雙生子；心術不正的那一個（塔維斯卡隆／燧石）在她們的母親分娩時殺了她，她被埋葬——從她的身體長出玉米、南瓜和菸草；善心（幼樹）使河流雙向流動，那歪斜的一個使它們成為急流；最後他們爭鬥，燧石被逐出世界——他的血化為燧石。非逐字引用。

language: Mohawk-Onondaga (recorded in English; Cusick via Tuscarora English)
canonical_translation: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, 1828 (public domain, Indigenous-authored); J. N. B. Hewitt, Iroquoian Cosmology, BAE-R 21, 1903 (public domain)

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: THE FALL THROUGH THE TREE. In the upper world, a woman (Ataensic / Sky Woman) dreams of the Tree of Light at the world's root; when her husband uproots it (or she falls through its hole in the tellings), she falls toward the dark lower world of endless water. The waterfowl (swans or geese) rise and catch her on their backs — in the Hewitt recording, the ducks? the loons pass her from bird to bird; the Great Turtle offers his broad back as a resting place. The creatures of the water dive for earth: the beaver fails, the? fails, and the little muskrat dives deepest, stays longest, and rises dead with a handful of earth in his claws — honored ever after. The Turtle takes the earth and strews it on his back: it grows and grows until it is the island world — Turtle Island, North America.

MIDDLE: THE DAUGHTER AND THE TWINS. Sky Woman bears a daughter (in the Cusick telling, the mother of the twins), who is courted by two spirit-suitors (the turtle? in Hewitt, Sapling and Flint court her in dream); she bears twin sons. The left-handed twin — Flint, the crooked-minded one (Tawiskaron) — kills their mother at birth (born through her side), and she is buried; from her body grow the sustenance plants: corn, beans, squash, and tobacco (the Three Sisters and the ceremonial fourth). The grandmother (Sky Woman) favors Flint; the Good Mind (Okwiraseh / Sapling) creates the good world: straight navigable rivers, the sun and moon of the sky (in some tellings he raises the grandmother's head as the moon), the useful animals; Flint counter-creates: rapids and waterfalls where the rivers should run smooth, thorns, monsters, mountains, and winter.

END: THE DUEL OF THE TWINS. The brothers finally duel (in Cusick: with reed decoys? the contest of creations ends in battle); Sapling wins — Flint is driven from the world (in the tellings: imprisoned under a mountain; banished to the night world; or killed, his blood becoming the flint stones that ring the land). Sapling establishes the world as it is: mortals, death (fixed as the human lot in some tellings), the hunting covenant, and the Good Message that follows. The narrative grounds the Haudenosaunee world: Turtle Island as geography, the Three Sisters agriculture, the moral dualism of creation (the good maker and the crooked counter-maker), and the flint beds of the Mohawk valley as Flint's blood.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds Haudenosaunee cosmology and geography (Turtle Island), the agricultural rites (Three Sisters; the midwinter ceremony honors the twins), the ethics of dual creation (good and crooked as principles, not absolute good and evil — a point scholarship stresses against missionary readings), and the political theology of the Longhouse (the creation is recited in the Condolence and Code ceremonies — the restricted parts are not represented here).
narrative.zh: 上界女子（阿塔恩西剋／天女）夢見世界之根處的光之樹；樹被連根拔起（或她自樹洞墜落），天女墜向永暗之水下世界。水禽（天鵝或雁）接住她；大龜獻出寬背；水中諸獸潛水取土——海狸不成、麝鼠潛得最深最久，力竭而死，爪中握土——永受尊崇。大龜取土撒於背上，土生長成為島嶼世界——龜島即北美。天女生女；女孕孿生子：左撇子之火石（塔維斯卡隆，心術不正者）出生時穿母脅而弒母；葬處生出玉米、豆、南瓜與菸草（三姊妹與第四種儀式作物）。祖母偏袒火石；善心者（樹苗）造善世：直而可行之河、日月、有用之獸；火石反造：湍流瀑布、荊棘、怪獸、山嶺與寒冬。兄弟終以蘆葦傀儡之計決鬥；善心者勝——火石被驅離世界（一說封於山下、一說殺之，其血化為環地之燧石）。善心者立今世：凡人、死亡之定命、狩獵之約與隨後之善訊。功能：豪德諾索尼宇宙觀與地理（龜島）、三姊妹農耕之禮、善與曲之二元創造倫理（非善惡絕對論——學界對宣教式解讀之修正）、以及長屋之政治神學（哀悼與法典儀式誦其創世——受限部分不入此檔）。

functions: Geographic charter: Turtle Island as the continent's origin
Agricultural rites: the Three Sisters and the mother's burial-gifts
Ethics of dual creation: good and crooked makers (not absolute good/evil)
Longhouse liturgy: the creation recited in Condolence and Code ceremonies

title.en: Rustam's Seven Trials: The Shahnameh's Hero of Zabulistan
title.zh: 魯斯坦七難：《列王紀》之扎布勒斯坦英雄

region.en: Zabulistan / Sistan, Iran-Afghanistan border
region.zh: 伊朗-阿富汗邊境扎布勒斯坦／錫斯坦

period: Shahnameh completed 1010 CE (Ferdowsi); principal MS: Florence 3281 (1217 CE); trans. Warner & Warner, The Shahnama of Firdausi, London 1905-25 (public domain)

source.work: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh (Book of Kings), Haft Khan-e Rustam (Seven Trials of Rustam) and Rustam-o Sohrab; trans. Arthur and Edmond Warner, London 1905-25 (public domain)

summary.en: Rustam, son of Zal and the simurgh's ward, rides Rakhsh through the Seven Trials — lion, desert, dragon, witch, unquenchable torches, the white demon, and the demon-king's brother — to free King Kay Kavus from the white demon of Mazandaran; the same hero later slays, unknowing, his own son Sohrab — the tragic masterpiece of the Iranian epic.
summary.zh: 魯斯坦（扎勒之子、西摩爾格所育）騎拉赫什歷七難——獅、荒漠、巨龍、妖婦、不滅之炬、白魔與魔君之弟——救馬贊達朗白魔所囚之卡烏斯王；後同一英雄不自知而手刃親子蘇赫拉布——伊朗史詩之悲劇絕唱。

sensitivity.note: National epic of Iran; shahnameh-khani recitation is living practice.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Haft Khan (Warner 1905-25): Rustam rode through the night; a lion sprang, and Rakhsh? he slew it; the desert parched him; the dragon rose from the pool, and Rakhsh kicked its head — twice Rustam slept and twice his horse saved him; the witch's? the white demon's cave was his seventh gate. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Haft Khan (Warner 1905-25); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 七關（華納 1905-25）的濃縮改寫：魯斯塔姆連夜騎行；一頭獅子躍出，拉赫什？他殺了牠；沙漠使他乾渴；巨龍從池中升起，拉赫什踢牠的頭——魯斯塔姆睡了兩次，他的馬救了牠兩次；女巫的？白魔的洞穴是他的第七道門。非逐字引用。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Rustam-o Sohrab: Sohrab, Rustam's son raised in Turan, seeks his father with an army; they meet in armor unknown to each other and fight three days; Rustam casts him and stabs him; the dying youth reveals his arm-seal — 'I am Sohrab, son of Rustam' — and the father's cry rends the field. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rustam-o Sohrab; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《魯斯塔姆與索赫拉布》的濃縮改寫：索赫拉布，魯斯塔姆在圖蘭撫養長大的兒子，率軍尋找他的父親；他們身披彼此不相識的鎧甲相遇，激戰三日；魯斯塔姆將他摔倒並刺傷他；垂死的青年露出他的臂印——「我是索赫拉布，魯斯塔姆之子」——父親的哭喊撕裂了戰場。非逐字引用。

canonical_translation: Arthur G. and Edmond Warner, The Shahnama of Firdausi, 9 vols., London 1905-25 (public domain); modern: Dick Davis, The Shahnameh (copyright)

narrative.en:
The Haft Khan-e Rustam ('Seven Trials of Rustam') and Rustam-o Sohrab are the twin masterpieces of the Shahnameh (completed 1010 CE by Ferdowsi of Tus) — the Persian national epic's heroic and tragic poles.

BEGINNING: THE HERO OF ZABUL. Rustam is son of Zal, the white-haired child cast out on Mount Alborz and raised by the simurgh (the wise bird — cross-ref zal-simurgh), and of Rudaba of Kabul. He grows to superhuman strength; his horse is Rakhsh, the flame-red stallion of Sistan (won from a herd by a kick that killed the challenger? by taming). When King Kay Kavus marches on Mazandaran and is captured — bound in the white demon's fortress, his army blinded? maddened by the demon's blackness — only Rustam can pass the seven stages of Mazandaran: 'the path is dark, and none has returned.'

MIDDLE: THE SEVEN TRIALS. Rustam rides in his tiger-skin through the seven: (1) the desert of thirst, where he slays a lion that springs on sleeping Rakhsh; (2) the sunless waste, where he finds? a spring and a wineshop? the shepherd? — the trials vary by recension, but the canonical seven: lion; desert; the dragon of the pool (Rakhsh kicks its head while Rustam sleeps — the horse saves the hero twice, the theme of the silent companion); the witch of the garden (who reveals herself as a hag — he strikes her down with a shout? with the? 'the witch became a black cat? ' she crumbles); the unquenchable torches of the? (the demon city of Arzhang — he? the vine-torch? Rustam quenches the unquenchable by tearing a vine? by? ); the banquet of Olad? the chieftain Olad converted; and (7) the white demon himself — the simurgh's feather given by Zal guides him (Zal had? the simurgh instructs: burn the feather, and I will come); Rustam sleeps on the demon's breast? he grapples the white demon (whose wail 'I am? ' fills the mountain), cuts out his liver? beheads him, and frees the blinded king — the army's eyes are healed with the demon's blood? with the simurgh's leaf. Mazandaran's tribute flows to Iran.

END: SOHRAB AND THE TRAGIC CLOSE. Years later, in Turan, Sohrab — Rustam's son by the princess Tahmineh of Samangan, raised fatherless — marches on Iran to find his father. Rustam, not knowing his son, meets him in single combat, three days of wrestling on the field between the hosts; on the third day Rustam casts him, and — fearing a sorcerer's trick ('none can cast me but Rustam? ') — stabs him. The dying youth opens his armor: the arm-seal (the seal Rustam gave Tahmineh) — 'I am Sohrab, son of Rustam.' The father's lament rends the epic: he begs for the? the healing feather of the simurgh comes, binding the wound but not the fate; Sohrab dies with the words that he had? 'I came to seek my father... my heart? ' — and Rustam carries the grief to his grave, cursing? vowing? the two buried in one? Sohrab laid in? the coffin of? — the tragedy that seals the epic's theme: the hero's strength destroys what it loves.

FUNCTIONS. The Shahnameh grounds Persian national identity (Ferdowsi's 'I revived? I have revived the? the Persian tongue through verse'), the ideal of javanmardi (heroic manliness), the recitation tradition (shahnameh-khani in coffeehouses; the naqqal storytellers of Iran, UNESCO-listed 2011), and the political theology of kingship (Kay Kavus's failure vs. Rustam's loyalty); the Sohrab episode is among the most performed in opera, film, and drama across Iran and the diaspora.
narrative.zh: 《魯斯坦七難》與《魯斯坦與蘇赫拉布》為菲爾多西《列王紀》（1010年成書）之英雄與悲劇雙璧。魯斯坦為扎勒（棄於阿爾白茲山、由西摩爾格神鳥養育——見扎勒條）與喀布爾之魯達貝之子；力大無匹，坐騎為錫斯坦火焰紅駒拉赫什。卡烏斯王征馬贊達朗被白魔所囚，唯魯斯坦能過七關：一誅夜撲之獅；二越焦渴荒漠；三魔龍自池起，魯斯坦兩度酣睡，拉赫什兩度踢首救主（無言夥伴之題）；四識妖婦（現形為老嫗而碎）；五滅不滅之炬（阿爾詹格魔城）；六收服酋長奧拉德；七與白魔決——扎勒所藏西摩爾格之羽為號，燒羽則神鳥自天而降授策；魯斯坦搏白魔、斬其首，救出盲王，魔血? 神鳥之葉癒眾軍之目；馬贊達朗貢賦歸伊朗。多年後，圖蘭之蘇赫拉布（魯斯坦與薩曼甘公主塔赫米內之子，無父而養）率軍尋父；魯斯坦不識其子，與之三日角力；第三日擲之，懼妖術而刺之；垂死之子啟甲露臂印——『我乃蘇赫拉布，魯斯坦之子』。父之慟哭裂史詩：求西摩爾格之癒羽，縛傷而不縛命；蘇赫拉布言『我來尋父……』而逝。功能：波斯民族認同（菲爾多西以詩復興波斯語）、賈萬瑪爾迪（英雄氣）之理想、說書傳統（咖啡館之沙赫納梅誦、納卡勒說書人，2011年入選非遺）、以及王權政治神學（卡烏斯之敗與魯斯坦之忠）。

functions: Persian national identity: Ferdowsi's defense of the Persian tongue
Javanmardi ideal: heroic manliness and loyalty to kingship
Living recitation: shahnameh-khani and naqqal storytelling (UNESCO 2011)
Tragic ethics: strength destroying what it loves (Sohrab)

title.en: The Monkey and the Rock Ogress: The Tibetan Origin Narrative
title.zh: 獼猴與羅剎女：藏族起源敘事

region.en: Tsurpu valley / Potala hill, Lhasa, Tibet (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西藏拉薩頗章布山（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded in the Mani Kabum (12th c.) and the rGyal rabs gsal ba'i me long (Clear Mirror, 1368); the monkey cave (Tsupu? Tsekhorong) is a pilgrimage site

source.archive: Scholarly translations (Taylor & Yuthok 1996) / Library of Congress Tibetan collections
source.work: rGyal rabs gsal ba'i me long (The Clear Mirror of Royal Genealogy, 1368), trans. McComas Taylor and P. Yuthok, The Clear Mirror, Delhi 1996; Maṇi bka' 'bum (12th c.)

license: Ancient texts public domain; Taylor & Yuthok 1996 quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Avalokiteshvara sends a monkey to meditate in a Tibetan rock cave; the rock ogress Senmo demands him in marriage, threatening to wed a demon and slay ten thousand beings; with the bodhisattva's and Tara's consent the monkey weds her; their six children, tailless and speechless, are fed barley by Avalokiteshvara — losing tails, gaining speech, they become the Tibetans.
summary.zh: 觀世音菩薩遣獼猴至西藏巖洞修行；羅剎女森魔逼婚，揚言若不允則嫁魔並殺萬生靈；得菩薩與度母允許，獼猴娶之；六子無尾無語，菩薩賜青稞養之——尾漸失、語漸生，遂為藏族之祖。

sensitivity.note: Living Buddhist tradition; the monkey cave (near Tsurpu / at Potala hill) is a pilgrimage site; no esoteric (initiation-restricted) material reproduced.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Clear Mirror (Taylor & Yuthok 1996): The bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara looked upon Tibet — 'a land of darkness? of wilderness where no? ' — and sent a monkey (his emanation) to meditate in a cave at Tsekhorong? in the rocky valley; the monkey took his vows and sat. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Clear Mirror (Taylor & Yuthok 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《明鏡》節述（Taylor & Yuthok 1996）：觀世音菩薩俯視西藏——「一片黑暗之地？一片無人煙的荒野？」——遂遣一猴（其化身）於岩谷中澤廓瓏？之洞穴修行；此猴受戒而坐。非逐字引文。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Clear Mirror (the ogress and the six children): The rock ogress came to the monkey and demanded marriage; he refused — he was a vowed celibate; she threatened: 'if you will not have me, I will wed a demon, bear ten thousand demon children, and devour all beings of Tibet'; the monkey asked Avalokiteshvara and Tara, who blessed the marriage; their six children, each of a different? complexion, were tailless and could not speak — fed on barley, they lost their tails and gained the power of speech. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Clear Mirror (the ogress and the six children); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《明鏡》節述（岩羅剎女與六子）：岩羅剎女來到猴前，要求與之成婚；猴拒絕——他乃受戒守貞者；她威脅道：「你若不肯接納我，我便嫁與妖魔，生一萬魔子，吞噬西藏一切眾生」；猴遂請示觀世音菩薩與度母，二尊賜福允婚；其所生六子，膚色各異？，皆無尾而不能言語——以青稞為食後，尾脫而能言。非逐字引文。

canonical_translation: McComas Taylor and P. Yuthok, The Clear Mirror: A Perspective of Life, Politics and Culture During the Early Tibetan Empire, Delhi 1996 (copyright)

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: THE COMPASSIONATE MANDATE. The origin narrative opens with Avalokiteshvara (Chenrezig), the bodhisattva of compassion, looking upon Tibet: a land of wilderness and snow, empty of the dharma, whose beings 'had no? ' — he sends a monkey, his own emanation, to meditate in a rock cave in the valley (the cave is sited at Tsupu? near Tsurpu, or by the Potala hill — the pilgrimage tradition marks it). The monkey takes his vows and sits.

MIDDLE: THE OGRESS AND THE MARRIAGE OF COMPASSION. The rock ogress (brag srin mo, Senmo) — a demoness of the cliffs — comes to the cave and demands the monkey in marriage. He refuses: he is a celibate votary. She threatens: 'if you will not wed me, I will take a demon for my husband; I will bear ten thousand little demons and devour every being in Tibet.' The monkey, torn between his vows and the ogress' threat to all living things, asks Avalokiteshvara and the goddess Tara; both consent — the bodhisattva's compassion outweighs the vow. The monkey marries the ogress, and she bears six children — each of a different complexion and disposition (the aition of Tibetan clan diversity).

END: THE BARLEY AND THE SPEECH. The six children are tailless and speechless — neither monkey nor demon. The monkey, hungry to raise them, returns to Avalokiteshvara, who gives barley seed from the heavens? from the? the monkey sows the first barley in the valley — the aition of Tibetan agriculture (tsampa, the roasted barley flour, as the national food). Fed on barley, the children's tails wither and their speech opens; they become the ancestors of the Tibetans — the six clans descending from the six children. The narrative binds Buddhist cosmology to national origin: Tibetans are born of compassion (the bodhisattva's monkey) wedded to the wild (the ogress of the cliffs) — the theology of Tibet's conversion, in which Chenrezig is the special protector and the Dalai Lama his emanation. The monkey-year festival (every twelfth year) draws pilgrims to the cave circuit, and the Potala hill itself — where the cave is sited in Lhasa traditions — is named for the bodhisattva's mountain (Potalaka); the origin narrative, the palace, and the protector-deity form one continuous theology of place.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds Tibetan clan genealogy (the six clans), the aition of agriculture (the first barley), the pilgrimage geography of the monkey cave, and the political theology of Avalokiteshvara's protection (the Dalai Lama as emanation); it is retold in school texts, temple murals, and the festivals of the monkey year (the monkey-year circumambulation of Tsurpu? of the sacred sites).
narrative.zh: 起源敘事始於觀世音菩薩（Chenrezig）垂視西藏：荒野雪嶺、無法無糧，遂遣自身化身之獼猴往巖洞修行（洞址在粗樸寺附近或頗章布山——朝聖傳統標定）。獼猴受戒而坐。羅剎女（巖魔女森魔）至洞前逼婚；獼猴以梵行拒之；魔女威脅：『若不娶我，我將嫁魔，生萬魔子，盡食西藏眾生。』獼猴兩難，問觀音與度母；二聖允之——慈悲重於戒。遂婚，生六子，膚色性情各異（藏族氏族多樣之釋義）。六子無尾無語，非猴非魔；獼猴復求菩薩，得青稞種，於谷中播下第一把青稞——西藏農耕之釋義（糌粑為國食）。以青稞為食，子尾漸禿、語言漸開，遂為藏人六氏族之祖。敘事將佛教宇宙論繫於民族起源：藏人生於慈悲（菩薩之猴）與荒野（巖之魔女）之結合——即西藏弘教之神學，觀音為殊勝護主、達賴喇嘛為其化身。功能：六氏族系譜、青稞農耕釋義、獼猴洞朝聖地理、以及觀音護佑之政治神學。

functions: Genealogy of the six Tibetan clans from the six children
Aition of agriculture: the first barley and the national food (tsampa)
Pilgrimage geography: the monkey cave site and monkey-year festivals
Political theology: Avalokiteshvara as Tibet's protector; the Dalai Lama as emanation

variants.name: Mani Kabum version (12th c.)
variants.text_tradition: Maṇi bka' 'bum (treasure-cycle attributed to the dharma-king Songtsen Gampo's period)
variants.summary: The earliest fuller telling: the ogress' threat, Avalokiteshvara's and Tara's consent, and the barley miracle — embedded in the Songtsen Gampo hagiography.

variants.name: Clear Mirror version (1368)
variants.text_tradition: rGyal rabs gsal ba'i me long; trans. Taylor & Yuthok 1996
