region.en: Parnassus & river Peneus (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 帕爾納索斯與珀紐斯河（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 8 CE (Latin; Riley translation 1851)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)
source.work: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book I (Fable XII)

summary.en: Mocked by Cupid for boasting of his Python kill, Apollo is shot with love's gold arrow over Daphne, the river-god Peneus' daughter — while Daphne, who has begged her father for perpetual virginity like Diana's, takes the blunted lead dart in her heart instead. She flees; her running makes her more beautiful; and at the brink of her father's river she is changed into the laurel, which Apollo, holding its leaves, adopts as his tree of triumph and of song.
summary.zh: 阿波羅因誇耀誅殺巨蟒遭庫皮德嘲諷：愛神以金箭射他，令其愛上河神珀紐斯之女達芙妮；而祈求父親賜她永葆處子之身的達芙妮卻中了鈍鉛之箭，見其追來便逃。貌美而奔，愈奔愈麗；她抵河畔呼救，父親把她化為月桂。阿波羅滿懷憐愛地攬住枝葉，將月桂定為凱旋與詩歌之樹。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Apollo, flush from his slaying of the Python — the vast serpent that had covered the acres of a plain with its pestilential body — saw Cupid bending a bow, and mocked the boy: gallant arms, he said, belonged on his own shoulders; the child could keep to his torch and its small fires. 'Let your bow shoot everything, Phoebus,' Cupid answered; 'my bow shall shoot you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses I (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿波羅剛誅殺巨蟒皮同——那條以疫病之軀覆蓋平原畝地的巨蛇——便看見邱比特正在彎弓，於是嘲弄這男孩：他說，英勇的臂膀當屬於他自己的肩頭；孩子只管守著他的火炬與那微小的火焰。「讓你的弓射盡萬物吧，福玻斯，」邱比特答道；「我的弓將射中你。」

passages.text: Cupid then drew two arrows of different workmanship: the one that kindles love was gold, bright and sharp-pointed; the one that repelled it was lead, blunt of tip. With the golden head he struck Apollo through the marrow, and with the leaden dart he pierced Daphne, the daughter of the river Peneus — his first love and her fated refusal. She had begged her father to grant her perpetual virginity, as Diana had been granted it, and was off in the wild places, rival of Phoebe, when the wound took hold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses I (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 邱比特隨即取出兩支工藝不同的箭：點燃愛情的那支是金的，明亮而尖銳；驅逐愛情的那支是鉛的，箭頭鈍拙。他以金箭頭射穿阿波羅的骨髓，又以鉛鏢刺中達芙妮——河神珀紐斯之女——他的初戀與她命定的拒絕。她曾懇求父親賜她永恆的童貞，如同黛安娜所蒙賜者，並在傷痛發作之際，正身處荒野之地，與福柏爭勝。

passages.text: The god burst into flame at the sight of her and pursued: as the stubble burns at the hedge torch's touch, so he burned in a fruitless passion, and his own oracles failed him even as he ran behind her, calling her back with promises that he was no enemy, that he was lord of Delphi and of the lyre, and that no herbs of his healing arts — here his confession — could ever cure love.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses I (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這位神祇一見她便燃起烈焰，奮力追逐：正如殘梗遇籬邊火炬之觸而燃燒，他亦在無果的熱情中焚燒，而當他奔隨其後、以種種承諾喚她回頭——說他並非敵人，說他是德爾菲與豎琴之主，又說他醫術中的任何藥草——在此他坦承——都永遠無法治癒愛情——他自己的神諭竟也失了靈。

passages.text: The winds, let loose against her flight, spread her garments and committed her small shame upon the air; and the light wind streaming behind her made her look lovelier as she ran. Ovid compares the pair, god and girl, to a greyhound and the hare at the open field: the one striving for a grip, the other for her safety. When Apollo was about to seize her, the nymph, come at last to the brink of her father's river, prayed to the water of Peneus
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses I (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 陣陣狂風鬆脫開來，迎著她的奔逃吹拂，掀開她的衣裳，把她那小小的羞怯散播到空中；而她身後流過的微風，使她奔跑時顯得更加秀美。奧維德把這一對——神與少女——比作曠野上的獵犬與野兔：一個奮力要抓住，另一個則為自身安全而奔逃。當阿波羅即將抓住她時，這位寧芙終於來到父親河流的岸邊，向珀紐斯的水祈禱。

passages.text: Her prayer was scarcely ended. A sluggish numbness closed over her body; her soft breast was enclosed in thin bark; her hair grew into green leaves; her arms became branches, and her feet, staying on the soil, were roots; her face was hidden in the spreading crown. Phoebus loved her still; and, with his hand on the trunk, he felt the heart beat beneath the bark, and prophesied: the laurel, alone of trees, should now be his — his when triumphs shone about the caps of victors, his at Rome's joyful gate-tops — and as evergreen, faithful to the wreath of victory, remain his for ever.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses I (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她的祈禱幾乎還未說完。一陣遲滯的麻木闔上她的身體；她柔軟的胸膛被薄薄的樹皮包覆；她的頭髮長成綠葉；她的雙臂化作樹枝，而她的雙腳停留在泥土上，成了樹根；她的面容隱沒在舒展的樹冠之中。福玻斯依然愛她；他將手按在樹幹上，感到樹皮之下心跳的搏動，於是預言道：月桂，唯有此樹，從今以後將屬於他——當勝利的榮耀閃耀於勝利者的頭盔之上時，它屬於他；在羅馬歡欣的門楣之上，它屬於他——而作為常青之樹，忠於勝利的冠冕，它將永遠屬於他。

title.en: Narcissus and Echo
title.zh: 納喀索斯與厄科

region.en: Helicon & Thespia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 赫利孔與忒斯庇亞（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 8 CE (Latin; Riley translation 1851)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)
source.work: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book III (Narcissus & Echo)

summary.en: Blind Tiresias, asked by Liriope whether her boy Narcissus would live to old age, answers only: 'if he never know himself.' The boy scorns all lovers; the nymph Echo, robbed of her full voice by Juno and able only to repeat the last words told her, pines away in longing for him till nothing is left of her but the sound; and Narcissus, seeing himself in the spring at Thespia, wastes where he kneels, saying the immortal words 'I am undone' — and a flower grows where he dies.
summary.zh: 利里俄珀請盲先知提瑞西阿斯問其子納喀索斯壽命，先知只答：「若他不認識自己。」美少年拒絕所有愛慕者；寧芙厄科因赫拉之怒只能尾音學舌，愛而不得，消瘦至只剩聲音。納喀索斯於忒斯庇亞泉水中瞥見自身倒影，誤為幽靈之愛，跪於泉邊耗盡自己，只留一句「唉——」而亡；其葬身處，長出一朵以他名字命名的花。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The seer Tiresias, blind and double-gifted, had once answered Jupiter and Juno's famous question about pleasure with the judgment that a man had nine times more pleasure in the love of woman than she had. Juno called the answer a lie. And it was Tiresias, the same, whom the nymph Liriope, when she bore the beautiful Narcissus, consulted about her son's life: would he live to see old age? The answer she got was strange, and it kept its shape: 'if he never know himself, he shall have a long life.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses III (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那位雙目失明卻有雙重天賦的預言者提瑞西阿斯，曾以這樣的判斷回答朱庇特與朱諾關於歡愉的著名問題：男人在女人的愛中所得的歡愉，比女人所得到的多九倍。朱諾說這答案是謊言。而正是這位提瑞西阿斯，當寧芙利里俄珀生下俊美的納西瑟斯時，曾就她兒子的性命向他求問：他能否活到看見老年？她所得的答案很奇怪，而且始終保持原樣：「若他永不認識自己，他將得享長壽。」

passages.text: Narcissus at sixteen might pass for a boy or a man: many youths and many girls desired him, and he was proud to no one of them. One of these admirers was the nymph Echo, who had lost to Juno's punishment the whole force of her voice — for Juno had found her chatting with the nymphs while Jove dallied among them — and could now only reply in others' words. Still she loved him: she followed him in the woods and spoke back at him from behind the trees, and, when she offered herself, was turned down in the same echo-words she had used.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses III (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 納西瑟斯十六歲時，既可被當作少年，也可被當作男子：許多青年和許多少女都愛慕他，而他對他們之中任何一人都不屑一顧。這些仰慕者之一便是寧芙厄科，她因朱諾的懲罰而失去了聲音的全部力量——因為朱諾發現她正與眾寧芙閒談，而朱庇特則在她們之間尋歡——如今她只能以他人的話語作答。她仍然愛他：她在林中跟隨他，從樹後向他回話；而當她主動獻身時，卻被她自己所慣用的、同樣的迴聲之語拒絕了。

passages.text: Scorned by him, she hid her deep grief in hollow glens and never more addressed herself with any face but shunned the light, and, growing gaunt with sorrow, faded altogether; her body's substance, they say, turned to stone, and only her voice stayed, nimble still among the rocks and caves, ready to repeat the last word as it always did, in answer to all who called her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses III (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 被他輕蔑之後，她將深沉的悲傷藏進幽深的峽谷，從此不再以任何面容示人，只避開天光；她因憂傷而日漸消瘦，終於完全消逝；他們說，她身體的實質化作了石頭，唯有她的聲音留存下來，仍舊在岩石與洞穴之間靈活敏捷，隨時準備複述最後一個字，一如往常，回應所有呼喚她的人。

passages.text: And Narcissus, worn faint elsewhere by many suitors, came one noon to a spring in whose fresh waters no shepherd had ever carried his flocks, and lay down upon the grass to drink. As he stooped, he saw his own form returned from the water and fell in love with a bodiless face: not knowing that what he sought was himself, he admired all he saw in it. Everything he praised was in him, and he was taken in by being taken in; his own eye had deceived him, his own body fired him. Ovid tells that while he tried to clasp the river, and wept over the return'd face of the water withdrawing, his own tears fell instead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses III (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 而納西瑟斯，在別處被眾多追求者弄得疲憊不堪，某日正午來到一處泉水，那清冽的水中從未有牧人趕過羊群，他躺在草地上飲水。當他俯身時，他看見自己的形貌從水中映回，便愛上了一張沒有軀體的面容：他不知道自己所追求的正是他自己，卻欽羨著他在其中所見的一切。他所讚美的一切都在他自己身上，而他因被迷惑而受迷惑；他自己的眼睛欺騙了他，他自己的身體點燃了他。奧維德講述道，當他試圖擁抱河水，並為水中退去的面容而哭泣時，落下的卻是他自己的淚水。

passages.text: He sat by the water until the whole desire had dried him up. At his death Echo grieved with him, and the shades in their hopelessness kept their word: he was his own death at last. When his relations leant over the bier to find a body, there was only a spring-side flower, its leaves white-cupped round a saffron heart; and the flower that grew there after his death took his name and grows there still: the narcissus, that narrows everything it sees on sight, and has no voice of its own.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses III (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他坐在水邊，直到整個慾望將他耗乾。他死時，回聲與他一同悲傷，而那些無望的幽魂也守住了他們的諾言：他最終成了自己的死因。當他的親人俯身於靈床之上，想尋回他的軀體時，那裡只有一朵水畔之花，花瓣潔白如杯，環繞著番紅色的花心；而他死後在那裡長出的花，取了他的名字，至今仍生長在那裡：那喀索斯，凡它一見之物皆為之收窄，而它自己卻沒有聲音。

title.en: Phaethon and the Chariot of the Sun
title.zh: 法厄同與太陽車

region.en: Palace of the Sun (mythic geography)
region.zh: 日宮（神話地理）

period: Composed c. 8 CE (Latin; Riley translation 1851)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)
source.work: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book II (Fable I-II)

summary.en: Taunted that his father is no god, the boy Phaethon goes to the Sun's palace for a recognition — and wrings from his father a promise sworn on the Styx. Against every warning, he mounts the chariot of the sun; the horses bolt; the world burns, Africa's skin is seared black, the Ethiopians bleached and the Po dried. Earth herself appeals to Jupiter, and a bolt from the all-father hurls the boy into the river Eridanus; and the daughters of Heliades, sisters of the dead, still weep amber tears on its banks.
summary.zh: 法厄同因被人嘲其父非神，赴日宮求證，並迫使父親以斯提克斯河起誓允諾。他無視勸阻執意駕太陽車，神馬失控亂奔：大地乾裂燃燒，非洲人被烤黑，埃塞俄比亞人曬白，波河乾涸，夜空失燭。大地女神哀求宙斯，宙斯以雷霆擊中少年，法厄同墜入波河；其姊妹淚化琥珀，至今凝在河岸的楊樹梢上。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Epaphus, son of Io, taunted Phaethon with the claim that his shining father was no god at all. The boy went burning to his mother Clymene, then eastward to the palace of the Sun — its columns of gold and jewelled light — where Phoebus, father, recognised his son, and swore, upon the Styx itself, to grant whatever the boy should ask.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊俄之子厄帕福斯譏諷法厄同，聲稱他那光輝的父親根本不是神。這少年滿懷怒火地去找母親克呂墨涅，隨後又東行至太陽的宮殿——那裡有黃金的柱子和寶石般的光芒——在那裡，父親福玻斯認出了自己的兒子，並以斯堤克斯河本身起誓，必將賜予這少年所求的一切。

passages.text: Phaethon asked for the reins. The father's face changed even as he listened: he knew what he had promised. He begged the boy away from it, warned him of the steepness of the sky-road, of the horses that never take a driver, of the constellations that would tear him from the yoke and hurl him down: 'my own child, take some other wish; this wish is not for kings, nor mortals even — not from me. The gods themselves could not hold it.' But the boy, having gripped the reins, would not give up his father's oath.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 法厄同求的是韁繩。父親聽著的當兒，臉色就變了：他知道自己許下了什麼。他懇求少年放棄此念，警告他天路何等陡峭，警告他那些從不容人駕馭的馬匹，警告他那些會將他從軛上扯下、將他拋落的星辰：『我的親生孩子，換一個願望吧；這個願望不是國王所能求的，甚至不是凡人所能求的——更不是從我這裡。眾神自己也承受不住它。』但那少年既已握住韁繩，便不肯放棄父親的誓言。

passages.text: At dawn the gates of the east open, and the Hours bring forth the horses, full of fire and trembling strength. The father, trembling himself, anoints his son's face with a protecting ointment, and tells him — too late — to spare the whip and hold the reins tightly, and follow the ruts of wheels gone before him; the road runs between the Wain of Bootes and the Wain of the Little Bear; keep midway, Phaethon, and on neither side depart too far.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 黎明時分，東方之門開啟，時序女神牽出馬匹，滿身是火，力量顫動。父親自己也顫抖著，用防護的油膏塗抹兒子的臉，並——為時已晚地——告訴他要少用鞭子，緊緊握住韁繩，沿著前車的輪轍前行；道路介於牧夫之車與小熊之車之間；法厄同，居於中間，兩邊都不要偏離太遠。

passages.text: The horses felt the hand of a stranger, lighter by an age than their master's, and ran away: the poles broke their hames, the ribbons were wasted in the sky, and the sun-chariot heavy no longer with its master hurtled on. Phaethon, from the zenith looking down upon lands too far beneath him, grew pale with fear. The world burned; Africa dried black its people; the cloud-rivers were driven backward and fire gushed from the cracked earth; Atlas groaned beneath the glowing weight of a sky tormented. And the sea drew in; the rivers that burned streamed away into hollows. At the last the Earth, half buried in the fire, cried out that she could not endure it, and appealed to Jupiter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬匹感到一隻陌生人的手，比它們的主人輕了一個世代，便奔逃而去：轅木折斷了軛繩，韁繩在天上白白浪費，太陽戰車不再因主人而沉重，疾馳向前。法厄同從天頂俯瞰腳下過於遙遠的大地，因恐懼而面色蒼白。世界燃燒起來；非洲將它的人民曬得焦黑；雲河被驅趕倒退，火焰從裂開的大地中噴湧而出；阿特拉斯在備受折磨的天空那灼熱的重量下呻吟。海水退縮；燃燒的河流流散進窪地之中。最後，半埋於火中的大地呼喊說她再也無法忍受，並向朱庇特求助。

passages.text: Jupiter drew the bolt to his ear and hurled it: Phaethon, in flames and clouded with smoke, was hurled headlong from the top of the sky and fell for the whole day's space, into the Eridanus. The daughters of the Sun, the Heliades, and Cycnus too bleached for his joy beside the dead man, buried their griefs in the river of their ancestor: the mother of Cycnus had changed her joy to a swan that hates the heavens; and the sisters still stand upon its banks, men say, as poplar-trees, weeping amber tears. The father of the dead boy hid his face with clouds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 朱庇特將雷霆拉至耳邊，擲了出去：法厄同身陷火焰、被煙霧籠罩，從天頂被猛然拋下，墜落了整整一日的路程，落入厄里達諾斯河。太陽的女兒們，赫利阿得斯姊妹，還有那因他的歡樂而變得蒼白的庫克諾斯，在死者身旁將他們的悲傷埋葬於祖先的河中：庫克諾斯的母親已將她的歡樂化作一隻憎恨天空的天鵝；而姊妹們，人們說，至今仍立於河岸之上，化作白楊樹，流著琥珀的眼淚。那死去少年的父親以雲霧遮住了自己的臉。

title.en: Pyramus and Thisbe
title.zh: 皮拉摩斯與提斯柏

region.en: Babylon (as told by the Roman poet)
region.zh: 巴比倫（羅馬詩人所記）

period: Composed c. 8 CE (Latin; Riley translation 1851)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)
source.work: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book IV (Pyramus & Thisbe)

summary.en: Two households in Babylon live under one roof, and the wall has a crack, and through the crack two lovers talk. They arrange a runaway tryst at Ninus' tomb under the mulberry; Thisbe comes first, sees a lioness, and drops her veil in the flight; Pyramus, arriving to find the bloodied veil, believes her dead and kills himself under the tree; Thisbe returns, finds him dying, and dies on the same steel; the berries of the mulberry — white till that hour — turn to that deep stain, and the wall, forever after, bears only their joint memorial.
summary.zh: 巴比倫同一院牆內的兩家世代相仇，而牆細縫成了兩人的私語孔。相約於尼努斯王墓旁的桑樹下私奔；提斯柏先到，見一頭母獅現身，逃遁時掉了面紗；皮拉摩斯來時只見染血面紗，誤以為她已葬於獅口，遂在樹下自刎。提斯柏返回，見愛人垂死，亦自盡於同一把短劍。桑樹自那刻起，白果變成紫黑之色，成為二人的紀念。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Pyramus was the most beautiful of youths; Thisbe, of maidens, the loveliest in the east. Ninus' city was theirs, and their houses, joined together by one wall. They fell in love through that same wall of theirs by breath and gesture; and where there was no crack nor passage for the sight or ear of each other in that wall, the wall had, between the rafters and lightly as a dove, along its top, a narrow cleft. And they kept up their careful talk each night through it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses IV (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 皮拉摩斯是青年中最俊美的；提斯柏则是东方少女中最可爱的。尼努斯之城属于他们，他们的宅邸由同一道墙相连。他们正是隔着这道共有的墙，以气息与手势相爱；在那道墙上，凡目光或耳朵无法相通之处，墙在椽木之间、轻如鸽子般，沿墙顶有一道狭窄的裂缝。他们每夜便透过它细细交谈。

passages.text: Because their families would not let the marriage happen, they swore a tryst. They named the place in Ninus' city where, under the great tree that bore white mulberries, the tomb of Ninus lay; they whispered for the shining moon and stole out of their houses like ghosts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses IV (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 因两家不许婚事成真，他们便立誓相会。他们约定在尼努斯城中那株结白色桑葚的大树下、尼努斯之墓所在之处相会；他们对着明月低语，像幽灵一般溜出家门。

passages.text: Thisbe came first — veiled — and sat under the tree out of the moonlight, when a lioness came up to drink from a smooth spring near the tomb. Thisbe fled. Her veil fell in the grass in her running, and as she hid, the lioness, finding the garment on its path, snatched it up and made the fabric blood: she had torn at some kill before coming to the pool.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses IV (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 提斯柏先到——蒙着面纱——坐在月光之外的树下，这时一头母狮走来，到墓旁一泓平滑的泉水边饮水。提斯柏逃走了。奔跑间她的面纱落在草中，而她躲藏之时，母狮在路上发现那件衣物，便将它叼起，使布料染上血色：它来池边之前曾撕咬过猎物。

passages.text: Pyramus, late in coming, saw the deep prints of a wild beast shift upon the plain; and, in the moon's light, came upon the bloodied veil. He knew the garment of the one he loved and had lost her; and under the mulberry — his body trembling — drew out a short knife and pierced himself, saying practically over his own blood the doom of the lovers who had waited their whole lives in flowers that could not hold them. He knelt where his blood fell on the tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses IV (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 皮拉摩斯来迟了，看见平原上野兽深深的足迹，又在月光下撞见那染血的面纱。他认出那是他所爱之人的衣物，便知已失去了她；在桑树下——他身体颤抖——他抽出短刀刺入自身，几乎是在自己的血上说出那对恋人的命运，他们一生都在无法容纳他们的花中等待。他跪倒在他的血洒落树上的地方。

passages.text: Thisbe came back, afraid and not yet knowing what had happened, and saw him dead under the tree, the veil beside him in the blood. She would not go more slowly than he had done: she fell upon the same blade over him, wept him in the dark, and prayed that they, so joined in life, might share at least one tomb. The berries of the mulberry — white till that hour — ever after bore the deep purple of their blood: the gods granted the prayer, and changed that tree's fruit for the memory of two who loved too truly for their households to allow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses IV (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 提斯柏回来了，心怀恐惧，尚不知发生了何事，却见他死在树下，面纱就在他身旁的血中。她不愿比他慢一步：她扑向那同一把刀，伏在他身上，在黑暗中为他哭泣，并祈求他们既在生时如此相连，至少能共有一墓。桑树的果实——直到那一刻还是白色——从此便带着他们血液的深紫色：诸神应允了这祈祷，为纪念那两个爱得太真、以致两家都不容的恋人，改变了那树的果实。

title.en: Hesiod's Bones
title.zh: 赫西俄德的遺骨

region.en: Orchomenus & Naupactus (symbolic pins)
region.zh: 俄爾科墨努斯與瑙帕克托斯（象徵性定位）

period: Written c. 2nd century CE (Shilleto/Bohn translation; G. B. 68680)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 68680 (A. R. Shilleto, trans.)
source.work: Pausanias, Description of Greece IX.38

summary.en: A plague on men and cattle struck Orchomenus, and Delphi's oracle prescribed a strange cure: fetch the bones of the poet Hesiod from Naupactus. Guided onward by the promise that a crow would show the place, the messengers found a crow sitting on a stone by the road, and within its hollow the poet's bones, with elegiac verses cut on the stone. The poet of 'the half is more than the whole' came home to history by a riddling service of the god.
summary.zh: 瘟疫襲擊俄爾科墨努斯，德爾菲神諭開出奇方：到瑙帕克托斯取回詩人赫西俄德的遺骨。信使再問何處可尋，神諭允諾一隻烏鴉將指引他們；果然路旁一石上有烏鴉佇立，石中即詩人遺骨，石上還刻有哀歌頌其身世與榮譽。詩人喊出「半勝於全」的名句，其遺骨卻以神諭之謎才得以還鄉。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: A pestilence was destroying men and cattle alike at Orchomenus, until the town sent messengers out to Delphi. The Pythian priestess returned them a strange prescription: carry home the bones of Hesiod from Naupactus, and the plague would cease. The messengers asked where in Naupactus such bones were to be found, and the priestess answered that a crow would show them the way. On the road they spied a stone by the wayside, and on it a crow at rest; they rolled the stone aside, and in a hollow of it they came upon the bones of the poet, exactly where the oracle had promised.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.38 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一场瘟疫在俄耳科墨诺斯同时毁灭人畜，直到城中派人前往德尔斐。皮提亚女祭司给了他们一个奇怪的处方：从瑙帕克托斯把赫西俄德的遗骨带回家，瘟疫便会停止。使者问在瑙帕克托斯何处能找到这样的遗骨，女祭司回答说一只乌鸦会为他们指路。他们在路上瞥见路边有一块石头，石上歇着一只乌鸦；他们把石头滚到一旁，在石中的凹处发现了诗人的遗骨，恰在神谕所许诺之处。

passages.text: And on the stone itself elegiac verses were cut, telling the story of his grave: his fatherland had been the poor village of Ascra, but after his death the horse-taming Minyans took his remains, and judged by the test of wisdom, the fame of the poet was suprème in all Greece.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.38 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 而在那石上刻有哀歌体的诗句，讲述其坟墓之事：他的故土本是贫瘠的阿斯卡拉村，然其死后，驯马的弥倪埃人取走了他的遗骸，并以智慧的考验为判，认定这位诗人的声名冠绝全希腊。

passages.text: Pausanias saw the tomb of Hesiod standing at Orchomenus beside the treasury of Minyas — the poet of 'the half is more than the whole' and of the steep road to virtue, come home by way of a riddle from the oracle. It is one of the extraordinary accounts in his Book of relics and their medicine: the authority of a poet measured, after death, by a crow on a stone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.38 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 保萨尼阿斯见到赫西俄德的坟墓立于俄耳科墨诺斯，紧邻弥倪阿斯的宝库——这位吟唱「一半多于全部」、吟唱通往德行之陡峭道路的诗人，经由神谕的一道谜语而得以归乡。这是其《遗物及其药方》一书中非凡的记载之一：一位诗人的权威，于死后由石上的一只乌鸦来裁断。

title.en: The Kings of Arcadia: Lycaon, Callisto, and the She-Bear
title.zh: 阿卡迪亞王族：呂卡翁、卡利斯托與母熊

region.en: Mount Lycaeus, Arcadia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿卡迪亞呂卡厄斯山（象徵性定位）

period: Written c. 2nd century CE (Shilleto/Bohn translation; G. B. 68680)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 68680 (A. R. Shilleto, trans.)
source.work: Pausanias, Description of Greece VIII.2-4

summary.en: Pausanias numbers the ages of Arcadia by its wicked kings: Lycaon, who founded Lycosura and the Lycaea, set a living child upon the altar of Zeus Lycaeus and was turned into a wolf for it; the dynasty kept wolf-men across generations. His daughter Callisto, loved by Zeus, is turned into a she-bear by Hera's doing, shot by Artemis, redeemed as a constellation, and her son Arcas inherits the land and gives it its name.
summary.zh: 阿卡迪亞之王呂卡翁建呂科索拉城、立呂卡厄亞慶典，卻把活人孩童放上宙斯祭壇焚祭，隨即化為狼；其王族歷代皆有狼化傳說。其女卡利斯托因與宙斯交而遭赫拉嫉妒，被變為母熊、遭阿爾忒彌斯射殺；宙斯遣赫爾墨斯救出其腹中之子，並把母熊化為大熊座；其子阿耳卡斯承繼城邦，並為其土地命名。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Lycaon, son of Pelasgus, did greater things than his father: he founded the town Lycosura on the mountain of Lycaeus and gave his name to Zeus Lycaeus, instituting the festival of the Lycaea in his honour. Pausanias places this era alongside Cecrops in Athens — an age when men still rose to the tables of the gods, so that honour or wrath were handed out face to face.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 8.2 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 佩拉斯戈斯之子吕卡翁所行之事较其父更为宏大：他在吕凯俄斯山上建起吕科苏拉城，以自己的名字为宙斯·吕凯俄斯命名，并为其设立吕凯亚节庆。保萨尼阿斯将这一时代与雅典的刻克洛普斯并列——那是一个人类仍能登上诸神餐桌的时代，故而荣宠或震怒皆是当面施予。

passages.text: Then came the division between east and west: Cecrops ruled that only baked cakes should be offered in sacrifice, and called Zeus supreme; but Lycaon laid a living child on the altar and cut its throat. He was a wolf the moment the sacrifice was done. Pausanias says plainly that this is one of the few stories of divine transformation he can easily credit, because the age in which it was set was an age when the gods still walked with mortal men, and punished wickedness openly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 8.2 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 其后便有了东西之分：刻克洛普斯规定献祭只可用烘烤过的饼，并称宙斯为至高；而吕卡翁却将一名活生生的孩童置于祭坛之上，割断其咽喉。献祭方毕，他便化为狼。保萨尼阿斯直言，这是他所易于采信的少数神变故事之一，因为此事所处的时代，正是诸神仍与凡人同行、公然惩罚邪恶的时代。

passages.text: In the third age after Pelasgus, Arcas, son of Lycaon and Callisto, took power. He named the whole land from his own people, calling its inhabitants Arcadians. And Callisto's story is the darker thread of the family: Zeus had loved her, and Hera, when she found it out, turned her into a she-bear; Artemis shot her to please Hera; and Zeus ordered Hermes to redeem her from the ruin his own guile had brought on her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 8.3 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在佩拉斯戈斯之后的第三代，吕卡翁与卡利斯托之子阿尔卡斯掌权。他以自己族人的名字为整片土地命名，称其居民为阿卡迪亚人。而卡利斯托的故事则是这个家族中更为阴暗的一线：宙斯曾爱恋于她，赫拉察觉之后将她变为一头母熊；阿尔忒弥斯为取悦赫拉而将她射杀；宙斯则命赫尔墨斯将她从他自己的诡计所招致的毁灭中救赎出来。

passages.text: Hermes carried the child of her womb away — the boy Arcas — and the mother, in her own form, was set among the stars as the constellation called the Great Bear, the one Homer names on Odysseus' voyage home. And the Arcadians still showed Pausanias her tomb: a high mound of earth set with trees, surmounted by a little sanctuary of Artemis called 'the Most Beautiful.' Arcas later ruled the land and gave it the name the Greeks would keep: Arcadia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 8.3 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 赫尔墨斯将她腹中的孩子——男孩阿尔卡斯——带走了，而母亲则以其本来的形貌被安置于群星之间，成为名为大熊座的星座，即荷马在奥德修斯归乡航程中所提及的那一个。阿卡迪亚人仍向保萨尼阿斯展示她的坟墓：一座高耸的土丘，其上植有树木，顶端立着一座小小的阿尔忒弥斯圣所，名为「至美者」。阿尔卡斯后来统治了这片土地，并赋予它希腊人将长久沿用的名字：阿卡迪亚。

title.en: Menestratus and the Dragon of Thespia
title.zh: 墨涅斯特拉圖斯與忒斯庇亞巨龍

region.en: Thespia, Boeotia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波厄提亞忒斯庇亞（象徵性定位）

period: Written c. 2nd century CE (Shilleto/Bohn translation; G. B. 68680)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 68680 (A. R. Shilleto, trans.)
source.work: Pausanias, Description of Greece IX.26

summary.en: A dragon infested the town of Thespia until Zeus required a boy as sacrifice, drawn annually by lot. When the lot fell on Cleostratus, his lover Menestratus forged a bronze breastplate hooked on every plate, put it on the doomed boy, and sent him cheerfully to his death — for though he would perish he would also destroy the monster. It is why, Pausanias says, Zeus was thereafter Soter (Saviour) in that city.
summary.zh: 忒斯庇亞城遭巨龍為害，宙斯命每年抽籤獻一少年。當籤落在克勒俄斯特拉托斯身上，其爱人墨涅斯特拉圖斯為他打製滿鉤銅胸甲，親載少年赴死：少年雖會喪命，也必能以內鉤殺死巨龍。鮑桑尼亞斯說，此後該城尊稱宙斯為「救主」。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The town of Thespia told Pausanias its tale at the shrine of Zeus Soter: a dragon had once overrun the place, so Zeus's assent came to yearly sacrifice. Each year one boy was chosen by lot and given to be devoured, until none could stand the land but drove the sons out of their homes and left their fields unworked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias 9.26 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 忒斯庇亞城在宙斯·索忒爾的神殿裡向保薩尼亞斯講述了它的傳說：一條巨龍曾肆虐此地，於是經宙斯允准，每年都要獻祭。每年抽籤選出一名男孩，交出去供其吞食，直到無人能忍受這片土地，紛紛把兒子們逐出家門，任田地荒蕪。

passages.text: When the lot fell, for its last offering, upon a youth named Cleostratus, his lover Menestratus went to work. He hammered bronze plates into a breastplate and bent a hook into each of the plates, then cloaked the young man in it; the bolts of the dragon would be forced to take their barbing from those hooks. Cleostratus, armoured and resigned, was sent to the dragon willingly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias 9.26 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當抽籤落到一位名叫克萊奧斯特拉托斯的青年身上，作為最後一次獻祭時，他的愛人墨涅斯特拉托斯動手了。他將青銅板錘打成一副胸甲，又在每塊板上彎出一個鉤子，然後把它披在青年身上；巨龍的利齒勢必得從那些鉤子上取得倒刺。克萊奧斯特拉托斯披甲在身，聽天由命，心甘情願地被送去見巨龍。

passages.text: The sacrifice turned into the kill. Cleostratus knew he would die, even as — on the usual arrangement of his death — he tore through the monster's belly, and took the dragon with him. The names they decorated the young man's tomb, and the custom of giving boys to the dragon ended.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias 9.26 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 獻祭變成了誅殺。克萊奧斯特拉托斯知道自己必死，即便如此——按照他死亡慣常的安排——他撕穿了怪物的腹部，與巨龍同歸於盡。人們把他們的名字刻在青年的墳墓上，將男孩獻給巨龍的習俗就此終結。

passages.text: In bronze at Thespia, Pausanias spied the boy and his lover standing near Zeus's statue: Menestratus in gold-plated armour, offering the sacrifice for others' protection. And that is why, he comments, Zeus was thereafter styled Soter — that he devised again, in a spirit of comradeship, one more facing in the pattern of the freely given life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias 9.26 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在忒斯庇亞的青銅像中，保薩尼亞斯瞥見那男孩與他的愛人立在宙斯神像旁：墨涅斯特拉托斯身披鍍金鎧甲，為保護他人而獻上犧牲。他評論道，正因如此，宙斯此後被尊稱為索忒爾——因為他又一次本著同志情誼，在自願獻出生命的模式中添上了新的一面。

title.en: Pausanias' Sphinx: A Boeotian Version
title.zh: 鮑桑尼亞斯的斯芬克斯：波厄提亞版本

region.en: Mount near Onchestus, Boeotia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波厄提亞翁開斯托斯附近山丘（象徵性定位）

period: Written c. 2nd century CE (Shilleto/Bohn translation; G. B. 68680)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 68680 (A. R. Shilleto, trans.)
source.work: Pausanias, Description of Greece IX.26

summary.en: Pausanias records a rationalized Boeotian variant of the Sphinx: not a riddling monster on a rock but a seafaring pirate with a band, headquartered on a Boeotian mountain where she questioned the men she captured; and she was, some said, Laius' own illegitimate daughter, who used the Delphic oracle secretly learned from her father as her test of royal blood — a secret Oedipus, learning it in a dream, turned against and defeated her with armed men from Corinth.
summary.zh: 鮑桑尼亞斯記下波厄提亞地區另一版斯芬克斯：非山頂石怪，而是一夥海盜頭目，以海路劫掠、以安忒冬港為基地、以翁開斯托斯附近的山為巢穴，劫往來行人；傳言她更是拉伊俄斯王私生之女，靠其父告知的德爾菲祕諭考驗各位嫡皇子是否為王室血統，答不上便處死；俄狄浦斯則夢中得知該神諭，率科任托斯軍士 一戰將其殲滅。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Just past the sanctuary of the Cabiri the track climbed to a Boeotian hill, and a folk-story of the district told Pausanias the Sphinx had made her headquarters there — not a riddle-monster on a rock but a raider with a fleet, who cruised the sea as a pirate, made her port at Anthedon, and used the mountain for her robberies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.26 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 剛過卡比里聖所，小徑便攀升至一座玻俄提亞的山丘，當地的一則民間故事告訴保薩尼亞斯，斯芬克斯曾在此安營紮寨——不是岩石上出謎題的怪物，而是一位率領艦隊的劫掠者，她像海盜一樣在海上游弋，以安忒冬為港口，並利用這座山進行搶劫。

passages.text: She captured men on the road and, in the ruin of them, questioned them. Oedipus did not come to her with a riddle at all in the local version but with an armed force from Corinth, and she was routed by the column and the numbers he brought, leaving behind him the ordinary Boeotian memory of a killed pirate captain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.26 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她在路上擄走行人，並在將他們毀掉之際盤問他們。在當地版本中，俄狄浦斯根本不是帶著謎題來找她的，而是率領一支來自科林斯的武裝力量前來，她被他帶來的隊伍與人數擊潰，身後只留下玻俄提亞人對一位被殺海盜首領的尋常記憶。

passages.text: Other locals gave Pausanias a family twist: the Sphinx was the illegitimate daughter of Laius, and Laius, from fatherly goodwill, had told her the Delphic oracle given to Cadmus, a secret which only the kings of Thebes were entitled to know. Whenever a claimant brother came to her about the succession she demanded the oracle's wording; if they answered, they were sons of Laius and true claimants of the blood royal; if they failed, she condemned them to death as doubtful usurpers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.26 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 另一些當地人則向保薩尼亞斯講述了一個家族版本：斯芬克斯是拉伊俄斯的私生女，而拉伊俄斯出於為父的慈愛，將德爾斐神諭告知卡德摩斯一事透露給了她，這是一項唯有底比斯諸王才有權知曉的秘密。每當有自稱兄弟之人前來向她詢問繼承之事，她便要求對方說出神諭的內容；若他們答得出，便是拉伊俄斯之子、王族血統的真正繼承者；若答不出，她便以可疑的篡位者之罪將他們處死。

passages.text: And Oedipus, in this telling, defeated her not by luck at riddles but by having the same secret: he learnt the Delphic oracle in a dream, recognized what she was testing, and met her with a superior force. The Sphinx's rock is one of those Greek sites that Pausanias reports almost as a tour guide — an old story with a map on it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.26 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 而在這一說法中，俄狄浦斯擊敗她並非憑藉猜謎的運氣，而是因為掌握了同樣的秘密：他在夢中得知了德爾斐神諭，識破了她所考驗的究竟是什麼，並以更勝一籌的力量與她交鋒。斯芬克斯的岩石是保薩尼亞斯幾乎以導遊口吻記述的眾多希臘遺跡之一——一個附有地圖的古老故事。

title.en: Trophonius and the Treasury of Orchomenus
title.zh: 特羅福紐斯與俄爾科墨努斯寶庫

region.en: Orchomenus, Boeotia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波厄提亞俄爾科墨努斯（象徵性定位）

period: Written c. 2nd century CE (Shilleto/Bohn translation; G. B. 68680)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 68680 (A. R. Shilleto, trans.)
source.work: Pausanias, Description of Greece IX.37

summary.en: The master-builders Trophonius and Agamedes constructed the Delphic temple of Apollo and then the treasure-house of Hyrieus with one stone they could secretly slide out from outside; the hidden robbery was Hamacious, and Hyrieus, reading his keys intact and his coffers empty, set a trap. Agamedes was caught, and Trophonius cut off his brother's head to silence him; the earth opened at Lebadea and swallowed Trophonius, and the underground became the Chthonic oracle that still gave its answers from beneath the earth.
summary.zh: 工匠兄弟特羅福紐斯與阿伽墨得斯先後建成德爾菲阿波羅神殿與希利俄斯的藏寶庫：庫中留置可從庫外滑開的石頭 routinely 竊財；財主見鎖完好而寶金日減，逐置陷阻。阿伽墨得斯被陷，特羅福紐斯唯恐洩密，竟斬其兄首級；地開裂，在勒巴底亞的聖林將他吞下。當地立其貼點，成了深受希臘人信賴的「冥間神諭」。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Erginus, king of the Minyans at Orchomenus, went out to Delphi in old age, after his war with Heracles, and the Pythian priestess told him to put a new top on the old plough — a young wife. Trophonius and Agamedes were born to him; and though Pausanias adds that Trophonius was in truth Apollo's son, the two boys grew into the best temple-builders of their age.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.37 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 俄耳科墨諾斯地方彌倪亞人的國王厄耳癸諾斯，在與赫拉克勒斯交戰之後，於晚年前往德爾斐，皮提亞女祭司囑他為舊犁換上新犁頭——即娶一位年輕的妻子。特洛福尼俄斯與阿伽墨得斯便由此而生；儘管保薩尼亞斯補充說，特洛福尼俄斯實為阿波羅之子，這兩個男孩仍成長為他們那個時代最出色的神廟建造者。

passages.text: They raised the temple of Apollo at Delphi itself; and then the treasury of Hyrieus. In the stone wall they set a single movable block, a door that could be slid out from outside. Year by year the two brothers opened it at night and carried away their employer's wealth, and the keys and seals the owner found untampered with left him at a loss, for he saw his money going and no thief in evidence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.37 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們建造了德爾斐的阿波羅神廟本身；隨後又建造了許里俄斯的寶庫。他們在石牆中安放了一塊可移動的石塊，一道能從外面抽出的暗門。年復一年，兩兄弟在夜間打開它，運走雇主的財富，而主人發現鑰匙與封印皆未被動過，因而困惑不已，因為他眼見錢財流失，卻不見竊賊的蹤影。

passages.text: So Hyrieus set traps where his coffers kept their darkness. Agamedes entered first and was caught fast; and Trophonius, afraid that if his brother were seen alive he would name him beside him, cut off Agamedes' head and carried it away. In the morning the corpse stood alone in the dark of the treasury; the town was never the wiser about the culprit who lay dead among the stolen wealth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.37 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是許里俄斯在寶庫幽暗之處設下陷阱。阿伽墨得斯先進去，被牢牢困住；特洛福尼俄斯唯恐兄長若被活捉便會供出自己，便砍下阿伽墨得斯的頭顱帶走。翌日清晨，屍體獨自立在寶庫的黑暗中；全城始終未能查明那個死在贓財之中的罪犯究竟是誰。

passages.text: But the earth, Pausanias reports, opened under Trophonius and swallowed him whole, in the grove of Lebadea; and there a hollow in the ground marks the spot. Deep in that grove, in fact, still give their answers: men go down the dark hole to consult him, and come back remembering things they are sworn to silence about. The architect who dived under a temple built into the earth was turned into the Chthonic oracle of all Greece.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.37 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而據保薩尼亞斯記述，大地在特洛福尼俄斯腳下裂開，將他整個吞沒，地點在勒巴狄亞的聖林中；那裡地面上有一處凹陷標記著該地。事實上，在那片聖林深處，至今仍有人作出回答：人們下到那黑暗的洞穴中向他求問，歸來時卻記得一些他們發誓保密之事。那位潛入建於地下的神廟的建築師，就此變成了全希臘的冥界神諭。

title.en: Heracles and the Apples of the Hesperides
title.zh: 赫拉克勒斯與赫斯珀里得斯金蘋果

region.en: Mount Atlas to the Hyperboreans (mythic geography)
region.zh: 阿特拉斯山至極北之地（神話地理）

period: Compiled c. 1st-2nd century CE (attrib. Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), §§ 2.5.10-2.5.11

summary.en: Eurystheus, rejecting the labour of Augeas' cattle and of the hydra, sends Heracles as an eleventh labour to fetch golden apples of the Hesperides from among the Hyperboreans. The tree is guarded by an immortal dragon with many heads; and, to find it, Heracles wrestles Antaeus, foils Busiris' sacrilege, who is to offer strangers to Zeus, and — at the edge of the world — meets Atlas, who agrees to fetch the apples for him if Heracles will carry the sky. Atlas wishes to be rid of heaven forever, but Heracles, by a trick, loads the weight back on him and departs with the fruit.
summary.zh: 尤里斯透斯以第十一項勞役遣赫拉克勒斯赴極北的赫斯珀里得斯取金蘋果：果樹由百頭不死之龍看守。沿途他摔死巨安泰俄斯（觸地即增力之神子）、逃過埃及王布西里斯的人祭 punt；至世界之邊時，擎天者阿特拉斯願替他取果，但要赫拉克勒斯替他扛天。赫拉克勒斯以計重歸其肩，帶果返還。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The eleventh labour was invented because Eurystheus refused to acknowledge the hydra and the cattle of Augeas at all: he bade Heracles fetch golden apples from the garden of the Hesperides. These apples had not been laid in Libya, as some said, but in the land of the Hesperides themselves, on the slopes of Mount Atlas among the far-off Hyperboreans; Earth had presented them to Zeus at his marriage with Hera, and they grew guarded by an immortal dragon with a hundred heads, child of Typhon and Echidna, that spoke with many sorts of voices.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, 2.5.11 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第十一項勞役之所以被編派出來，是因為歐律斯透斯根本不承認九頭蛇與奧革阿斯的牛群：他命赫拉克勒斯去赫斯珀里得斯的花園取回金蘋果。有人說這些蘋果存放在利比亞，其實不然，它們就在赫斯珀里得斯姊妹自己的土地上，位於阿特拉斯山的山坡間，居於遙遠的許珀玻瑞俄伊人之中；大地曾在宙斯與赫拉成婚時將它們贈予宙斯，並由一條長著一百個頭的不死巨龍看守，那是堤豐與厄喀德那的孩子，能發出各種各樣的聲音。

passages.text: On the journey he came to the river Echedalus, and a king Cycnus, son of Ares, challenged him to a single combat; but a thunderbolt thrown between them parted the men. He went on foot through Illyria, and by the river Eridanus found the nymphs who were daughters of Zeus and Themis; they told him where Nereus, the Old Man of the Sea, kept his knowledge, and Heracles seized the seer as he slept and held him fast, though he changed himself into every kind of shape, until he had told where the apples and the Hesperides were to be found.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, 2.5.11 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 途中他來到厄刻達羅斯河，阿瑞斯之子、國王庫克諾斯向他挑戰，要與他單打獨鬥；但一道雷電擲在兩人之間，將他們分開。他徒步穿越伊利里亞，在厄里達諾斯河畔遇見宙斯與忒彌斯所生的寧芙們；她們告訴他海中老人涅柔斯把知識藏在何處，赫拉克勒斯趁那先知熟睡時將他擒住，緊緊抱住不放，儘管他變幻成各種形貌，直到他說出蘋果與赫斯珀里得斯所在之處。

passages.text: Traversing Libya, he came upon Antaeus, son of Poseidon, who forced all strangers to wrestle and killed them; for when he was on the earth his mother's earth, he grew stronger. Heracles hugged him, lifted him clear of the ground, and broke him; for held off the earth he could not wax strong. Traversing Egypt, he met Busiris, who in expiation of a nine years' drought sacrificed strangers at the altar of Zeus; and Heracles was seized himself, put on the altar, but burst his bonds, slew Busiris and his son Amphidamas, and went on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, 2.5.11 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 穿越利比亞時，他遇上了波塞冬之子安泰俄斯，此人強迫所有外鄉人與他角力並將他們殺死；因為他身在他母親的大地之上時，力氣便會增長。赫拉克勒斯將他緊緊抱住，舉離地面，把他折斷；因為一旦離開大地，他便無法再增長力氣。穿越埃及時，他遇見布西里斯，此人為贖九年乾旱之罪，在宙斯的祭壇上獻祭外鄉人；赫拉克勒斯自己也被捉住，放上祭壇，但他掙斷了繩索，殺了布西里斯及其子安菲達瑪斯，繼續前行。

passages.text: At the ends of the earth he received a goblet from the Sun, crossed by it to the other side of the world-stream, and, on the Caucasus, shot down with his bow the eagle that was eating the liver of Prometheus and set the fire-stealer free, accepting, so that Heracles should not be hounded by Zeus, the substitution of Chiron, who consented to die in his stead; and Prometheus told him not to go to the garden himself, but to send Atlas, after relieving him of the sphere.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, 2.5.11 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在大地的盡頭，他從太陽那裡得到一隻杯，乘著它渡過世界之流到達彼岸，並在高加索以弓箭射下那隻啄食普羅米修斯肝臟的鷹，釋放了這位盜火者，並接受了喀戎自願代他赴死的替換，好讓赫拉克勒斯不致被宙斯追逼；普羅米修斯告訴他不要親自前往花園，而應先替阿特拉斯卸下天球，再派他去。

passages.text: So he relieved Atlas of his great weight, while Atlas went and plucked three golden apples from the Hesperides. But he did not want to carry the sphere again, and when he had once been free of it, wished never to take it up; so he said he would take the apples to Eurystheus himself. Heracles agreed, on a plan suggested by Prometheus; he asked Atlas to hold up the sky just long enough for a pad to be put on his head: the request seemed easy, Atlas laid down his burden, and Heracles slipped out from beneath the weight and made away with the golden apples.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library, 2.5.11 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是赫拉克勒斯替阿特拉斯卸下那沉重的負擔，阿特拉斯便前去從赫斯珀里得斯那裡摘下三顆金蘋果。但阿特拉斯不願再扛天球，一旦擺脫了它，便希望永遠不必再舉起它；於是他說要親自把蘋果送去給歐律斯透斯。赫拉克勒斯依普羅米修斯所獻之計應允了；他請阿特拉斯暫且再撐一下天空，好讓他在頭上墊一塊襯墊：這請求看似容易，阿特拉斯便放下負擔，赫拉克勒斯卻從重壓之下溜了出來，帶著金蘋果離去。

title.en: Asclepius: The Healer Who Raised the Dead
title.zh: 阿斯克勒庇俄斯：起死回生的醫者

region.en: Thessaly to Epidaurus (mythic geography)
region.zh: 色薩利至厄庇道魯斯（神話地理）

period: Compiled c. 1st-2nd century CE (attrib. Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), §§ 3.10.3-3.10.4

summary.en: Coronis, seduced by Apollo and unfaithful to him with Ischys the Arcadian, is shot by the god, who is told by his raven; the raven, once white, is cursed black. Apollo snatches the living child from his mother's pyre and gives him to Chiron, the wise centaur, who brings him up in the arts of hunting and of healing. Athena gives him the two-sided blood of the Gorgon, and Asclepius, using the blood from the right-side vein, raises the dead — Hippolytus, Tyndareus, Hymenaeus, Glaucus — until Zeus, fearing that men might never die, hurls a thunderbolt at him. Apollo avenges him by slaying the Cyclopes, thunder-smiths of Zeus; and Asclepius thereafter settles among men as a god of healing, worshipped at Epidaurus with its snake-garden and shrine of miracle cures.
summary.zh: 科羅尼斯被阿波羅所愛、卻另屬伊斯基斯；白烏鴉告密，神怒而殺之，並咒烏鴉永世為黑。阿波羅自焚屍中把嬰孩取回，交人馬喀戎撫育，教他醫術與獵術。雅典娜賜他戈耳貢雙側之血：左血為毒、右血能起死回生，希波呂托斯等多人因此還陽。宙斯恐凡人習得醫術而不再死亡，以雷霆擊之；阿波羅憤而射殺鑄雷的獨眼巨人，賴母親勒托求情，被罰作阿德墨托斯的僕役一年。後世尊其為醫神，厄庇道魯斯聖域香火最盛。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Apollo loved Coronis, daughter of Phlegyas, and she, against her father's judgment, preferred another man, Ischys, brother of Caeneus. A raven brought tidings of her infidelity to the god, and Apollo, in his anger, cursed the raven that had once been white and made it black for ever; and he killed Coronis for her unfaithfulness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.10.3 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿波羅愛上了佛勒古阿斯之女科洛尼斯，而她卻不顧父親的判斷，選擇了另一個男人，即卡紐斯之兄伊斯庫斯。一隻渡鴉將她不忠的消息帶給這位神，阿波羅在憤怒中詛咒了那隻原本雪白的渡鴉，使它永遠變黑；又因科洛尼斯的不忠而將她殺死。

passages.text: But when she was burning on the pyre, he snatched the living child from the fire, and went with him to Chiron the centaur, who brought him up and taught him the arts of healing and of hunting. And so Asclepius became such a surgeon as the world had never seen, and carried the art to such a pitch that he not only prevented some from dying but even raised up the dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.10.3 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但當她在火葬堆上燃燒時，他從火中奪走了那活著的孩子，帶著他去見半人馬喀戎，喀戎將他撫養長大，並教他醫術與狩獵之藝。於是阿斯克勒庇俄斯成了世間前所未見的外科醫者，並將這門技藝推至如此境地，不僅使一些人免於死亡，甚至還讓死者復生。

passages.text: The power was a gift of Athena, who gave him the blood that had flowed from the veins of the Gorgon when Perseus cut off her head: the blood that came from the veins on the left side he kept for the bane of mankind, and the blood from the right side for salvation; and with it he raised up the dead. Hippolytus, Tyndareus, Hymenaeus, and Glaucus the son of Minos are among those named in the old tellings as restored to life by him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.10.3 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這股力量是雅典娜的贈禮，她將珀耳修斯砍下戈耳工頭顱時從其血管中流出的血賜給了他：來自左側血管的血，他留作人類的禍害；來自右側的血，則用於拯救；他以此使死者復生。希波呂托斯、廷達瑞俄斯、許墨奈俄斯，以及彌諾斯之子格勞科斯，都是古老傳說中被他復活的人。

passages.text: But Zeus, fearing that men might learn the art of healing from him and come to the rescue of one another for ever, hurled a thunderbolt at Asclepius and struck him dead. Apollo, enraged at the death of his son, slew the Cyclopes who had forged the thunderbolt for the king of gods; and Zeus would have hurled his own son to Tartarus, but at the intercession of Latona he instead ordered Apollo to serve a mortal man: the god went as a thrall to Admetus for a year.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.10.4 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但宙斯擔心人類會從他那裡學會醫術，從此互相拯救、永無止境，便向阿斯克勒庇俄斯擲出雷霆，將他擊死。阿波羅因兒子之死而震怒，殺死了為眾神之王鍛造雷霆的庫克洛普斯；宙斯本欲將自己的兒子打入塔爾塔羅斯，但因拉托娜的求情，改命阿波羅去服侍一個凡人：這位神祇以奴僕之身服侍阿德墨托斯一年。

passages.text: But the art of healing survived its maker. Asclepius came to be honoured as a god of medicine; his temples stood in many parts of the Greek world, and above all at the great shrine of Epidaurus, where the sick came in pilgrimage, slept a night within the god's precinct, and waited in their dreams for the miracle of the cure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.10.4 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但醫術卻比它的創造者更為長存。阿斯克勒庇俄斯逐漸被尊為醫藥之神；他的神廟遍佈希臘世界的許多地方，尤其是在埃皮達魯斯的大聖所，病人前來朝聖，在神域內睡上一夜，於夢中等待治癒的奇蹟。

title.en: The Cadmean Vixen and the Dog That Could Not Be Outrun
title.zh: 卡德摩斯母狐與永不失足的獵犬

region.en: Thebes (Cadmea) (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 底比斯卡德美亞（象徵性定位）

period: Compiled c. 1st-2nd century CE (attrib. Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), §§ 2.4.6-2.4.7

summary.en: To win back his wife Alcmena, Amphitryon must first rid the Cadmea of a fated vixen no man could catch; every month a son of the Thebans was thrown to it as sacrifice. He called in Cephalus of Athens with the hound Laelaps — a dog destined to catch whatever it pursued — a gift, some say, from Minos. The two fated creatures were set against each other, and Zeus, resolving the paradox, turned them both into stone.
summary.zh: 安菲特律翁欲贖回妻子阿爾克墨涅，先得除掉卡德美亞無人可擒的天命母狐，底比斯人每月以城內一子獻祭。他請來雅典的刻法羅斯，助其神犬拉埃拉普斯——命定能追上一切獵物（或說米諾斯所贈）。兩種天命相遇，宙斯以石化二者收場，化解矛盾。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Amphitryon, exiled from Tiryns for the killing of Electryon and now a suppliant at Thebes, had promised Alcmena that he would redeem her brothers and she would marry him. He fell accordingly on the Teleboans; but Creon, king of Thebes, agreed to help on a condition: first Amphitryon must rid the citadel of a monstrous vixen that ravaged the Cadmea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 2.4.6 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 安菲特律翁因殺死厄勒克特律翁而被逐出提林斯，如今在忒拜為求庇者，他曾向阿爾克墨涅承諾，他將為她的兄弟們報仇，而她便會嫁給他。於是他便進攻忒勒波伊人；但忒拜國王克瑞翁同意相助，卻附有一個條件：安菲特律翁必須先為衛城除去一頭蹂躪卡德摩斯的怪異母狐。

passages.text: This was no ordinary beast: fate had decreed that nobody should catch it. Thebes, at its mercy, sacrificed to it a son of one of the citizens every month, so it would not carry off many more; yet the beast's ravages continued.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 2.4.6-2.4.7 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這絕非尋常野獸：命運已註定無人能捕獲牠。忒拜任其宰割，每月獻上一位公民之子給牠，以免牠擄走更多；然而這野獸的肆虐仍未停止。

passages.text: So Amphitryon went to Cephalus, son of Deioneus, at Athens, and persuaded him, in return for a share of the Teleboan spoils, to bring to the chase a marvellous dog — Laelaps — which men said Procris had brought from Crete as a gift of Minos; for that dog was destined to catch whatever it pursued.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 2.4.7 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是安菲特律翁前往雅典，去找狄俄纽斯之子刻法羅斯，以分得一部分忒勒玻亞人的戰利品為條件，說服他帶一頭神奇的獵犬——拉伊拉普斯——一同出獵；人們說這頭獵犬是普洛克里斯從克里特帶回來的，是彌諾斯所贈的禮物；因為這頭獵犬註定要捕獲牠所追逐的一切。

passages.text: When the hound was set upon the vixen, two inevitabilities met: the dog that must catch, and the fox that must not be caught. Zeus, to end the paradox, turned both of them to stone — the fox and the hound — and so Amphitryon, freed of the constraint, went on with his allies Cephalus, Panopeus, Heleus and Creon to ravage the islands of the Taphians and take the revenge for Alcmena's brothers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 2.4.7 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當獵犬被放去追那頭雌狐時，兩種不可避免之事相遇了：那頭必須捕獲的獵犬，與那頭必須不被捕獲的狐狸。宙斯為終結這悖論，把牠們雙雙化為石頭——那狐狸與那獵犬——於是安菲特律翁擺脫了這桎梏，便與他的盟友刻法羅斯、帕諾佩烏斯、赫勒烏斯和克瑞翁一同前去蹂躪塔菲俄斯人的島嶼，為阿爾克墨涅的兄弟們報仇。

title.en: Comaetho and the Golden Lock
title.zh: 科瑪厄托與金髮

region.en: Taphos, Ionian islands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 塔福斯島（伊奧尼亞群島，象徵性定位）

period: Compiled c. 1st-2nd century CE (attrib. Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), §§ 2.4.5-2.4.7

summary.en: The Taphian king Pterelaus was made unconquerable by a single purple-golden lock of hair that Poseidon had given him; while it lived on his head, not even Amphitryon could take Taphos. But his daughter Comaetho fell in love with the besieger, pulled out her father's lock, and he died on the spot; Amphitryon subdued all the islands, slew Comaetho for her treachery, and carried the spoils back to Thebes to lay them before Alcmena on the night before Heracles' own birth.
summary.zh: 塔福斯王普忒勒勞斯因波塞頓所賜的一根金紫色髮而近乎不死；髮存則城不可破。其女科瑪厄托愛上圍城的安菲特律翁，趁夜拔下父親金髮，普忒勒勞斯立即身亡。安菲特律翁遂蕩平群島，卻因她的背叛而誅之；戰利品被攜回底比斯，在赫拉克勒斯誕生前夜獻上阿爾克墨涅。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Amphitryon, the exiled lord of Tiryns and the son-in-law of Electryon's house, had promised to avenge Alcmena's brothers who had been killed by the Taphians. Creon of Thebes had helped him rid the Cadmea of the vixen; and, with allies from Attica, Phocis, Argos and Thebes, Amphitryon set out against the islands of the Taphians.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 2.4.7 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 安菲特律翁，這位被逐出提林斯的君主、厄勒克特律翁家族的婿，曾許諾要為阿爾克墨涅那些被塔菲俄斯人所殺的兄弟報仇。底比斯的克瑞翁曾助他清除卡德墨亞的雌狐；於是安菲特律翁帶著來自阿提卡、福基斯、阿爾戈斯和底比斯的盟友，出發攻打塔菲俄斯人的島嶼。

passages.text: But while Pterelaus, king of the Taphians, lived, the able Amphitryon could not take the island. For Poseidon, in the tradition, had given Pterelaus one golden-purple lock of hair which made him unconquerable while it remained rooted in his head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 2.4.7 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而只要塔菲俄斯人的國王普忒瑞拉俄斯還活著，能幹的安菲特律翁便無法攻下這座島。因為據傳說，波塞冬曾賜給普忒瑞拉俄斯一綹金紫色的頭髮，只要它仍長在他頭上，他便不可戰勝。

passages.text: It was Comaetho, his own daughter, who undid him. In love with Amphitryon, she pulled the golden lock from her father's head as she kept watch over him; Pterelaus died at once, and Amphitryon subdued all the islands in a single stroke.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 2.4.7 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 毀掉他的，正是他自己的女兒科邁托。她愛上了安菲特律翁，趁著看守父親之際，從他頭上拔下了那綹金髮；普忒瑞拉俄斯當即死去，安菲特律翁一舉便征服了所有的島嶼。

passages.text: The victor did not spare the daughter: he slew Comaetho for her treachery to her own house, carried the spoils back to Thebes, and made over the islands to his allies Cephalus and Heleus, who founded cities named after themselves and dwelt in them. And when Amphitryon came home in glory, it was the night before the birth of Heracles, the child the god Zeus had fathered in Amphitryon's own bed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 2.4.7 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這位勝利者並未饒過那個女兒：他因科邁托背叛自己的家族而殺了她，把戰利品帶回底比斯，並將那些島嶼轉交給他的盟友刻法羅斯和赫勒烏斯，他們各自建立了以自己命名的城邦並居住其中。而當安菲特律翁榮歸故里時，正是赫拉克勒斯誕生的前夜——那孩子是宙斯神在安菲特律翁自己的床上所生的。

title.en: Icarius and the First Wine
title.zh: 伊卡里俄斯與第一杯酒

region.en: Attica, deme Icaria (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿提卡伊卡里亞村（象徵性定位）

period: Compiled c. 1st-2nd century CE (attrib. Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), § 3.14.7

summary.en: When Dionysus came to Attica, Icarius welcomed him and received from the god the gift of the vine and knowledge of winemaking — the first draught of wine in Greece. But the shepherds to whom he served the new beverage drank unwatered and strong, and, thinking themselves bewitched, killed him. His daughter Erigone, searching for her father, was led to the body by his faithful dog Maera; she mourned over him and hanged herself.
summary.zh: 酒神來到阿提卡，伊卡里俄斯接待他，得神所贈葡萄藤並習得釀酒之法——希臘的第一杯酒。他將新酒分給牧人；牧人無水摻悶暢飲，自覺中邪，竟將此人殺害。其女厄里戈涅尋父，忠犬邁拉引至屍旁；她哀悼父親，自縊而亡。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: When Dionysus came to Attica, he was received by Icarius, an Athenian of the deme Icaria; the god gave him a branch of a vine and taught him the whole art of making wine. Icarius, wishing to share the new boon with men, went out to some shepherds and served them the juice. They drank it copiously without watering, for the pleasure of it; and when the strength of the wine worked upon them, they made sure they had been bewitched by the giver.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.14.7 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當狄俄尼索斯來到阿提卡時，他受到伊卡里俄斯的接待，此人是阿提卡伊卡里亞德莫的雅典人；這位神賜給他一根葡萄藤的枝條，並教會他釀酒的整套技藝。伊卡里俄斯想與人分享這份新的恩惠，便出去找了一些牧羊人，把汁液端給他們。他們因為覺得美味，便不摻水地大量飲用；當酒力在他們身上發作時，他們確信自己是被那送酒的人施了巫術。

passages.text: So they killed the man who had brought them present delight. By daylight they understood the truth and buried him; but the boon-giver of Dionysus lay under the earth unheard, and his daughter Erigone went out to search for him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.14.7 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他們殺死了那個給他們帶來眼前歡愉的人。天亮時他們明白了真相，便將他埋葬；但狄俄尼索斯的這份恩惠卻默默無聞地躺在地下，他的女兒厄里戈涅便出去尋找他。

passages.text: His faithful dog Maera, which had attended him in life, led her to the body; and Erigone bewailed her father and hanged herself. So the gift that was meant to be joy came first to Attica as a tale of blood — the first wine in Greece and the first death for the pouring of it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 3.14.7 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他那忠實的狗邁拉，曾在他生前陪伴他，領她找到了屍體；厄里戈涅為父親哀哭，然後自縊而死。於是這本該帶來歡樂的禮物，最初卻以一個血的故事來到阿提卡——希臘的第一杯酒，以及為斟出這杯酒而發生的第一樁死亡。

title.en: Sisyphus, Founder of Corinth, and His Punishment
title.zh: 西敘福斯：科林斯建城者與其懲罰

region.en: Corinth (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科林斯（象徵性定位）

period: Compiled c. 1st-2nd century CE (attrib. Apollodorus; Frazer translation 1921)

source.work: Apollodorus, Library, trans. J. G. Frazer (1921), § 1.9.3

summary.en: Sisyphus, son of Aeolus, founded Ephyra, which is now called Corinth, and married Merope, daughter of Atlas; his house went on through Glaucus to Bellerophon the rider of Pegasus. But for betraying to Asopus the secret of Zeus's theft of Aegina, he is punished in Hades: he rolls a stone with hands and head to heave it over the crest, and push it as he will, it rebounds backwards — the mythic picture of self-defeating cleverness forever rolled round again.
summary.zh: 埃俄羅斯之子西敘福斯建立埃菲拉——即今之科林斯——娶阿特拉斯之女墨洛珀為妻；其家經格勞科斯傳至騎天馬的柏勒洛豐。但因把宙斯誘拐埃癸娜之祕密告訴追女的科任托斯王阿索波斯，他被判入冥府：日日以手與頭推巨石上山，石至頂即回滾、永不休止——自我打擊的智者、無休止重複的懲罰典範。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Sisyphus, son of Aeolus, founded Ephyra, which in later ages men called Corinth, and married Merope, one of Atlas's daughters. He had a son Glaucus, and Glaucus had by Eurymede a son Bellerophon, who would one day slay the fire-breathing Chimera; so royal wisdom ran in the family.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 1.9.3 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 埃俄羅斯之子西緒福斯建立了厄費拉，後世之人稱之為科林斯，並娶了阿特拉斯的女兒之一墨洛珀。他有一個兒子格勞科斯，格勞科斯與歐律墨得生下一個兒子柏勒洛豐，此人日後將殺死吐火的喀邁拉；可見王者的智慧在這個家族中世代相傳。

passages.text: But the founder of Corinth also came to an infamous end in the world below. Zeus had secretly carried off Aegina, daughter of the river-god Asopus; and Sisyphus, knowing where she had gone, betrayed the secret to Asopus while the god of the river was still seeking for her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 1.9.3 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但科林斯的建立者在冥界也落得一個聲名狼藉的下場。宙斯曾暗中擄走河神阿索波斯的女兒埃癸娜；西緒福斯知道她去了何處，便在河神仍在尋找她時，把這個秘密洩露給了阿索波斯。

passages.text: The punishment in Hades endures to this telling: he rolls a stone with his hands and with his head, in the effort to heave it over the crest of the hill; but push as he will, it rebounds backward. And so, in the land of the dead, the man who had built a city that survives to this day, and knew the trick of gods, is held under the weight that he cannot finish lifting — rolling the same stone forever, from hill to fountain and back again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Apollodorus, Library 1.9.3 (Frazer 1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 哈得斯中的懲罰流傳至今：他用雙手和頭顱滾動一塊石頭，竭力要把它推上山頂；但不論他怎樣使勁，石頭總是向後滾落。於是，在亡者之地，那個曾建起一座至今猶存的城市、又懂得諸神詭計的人，被壓在他無法完成舉起的重負之下——永遠滾著同一塊石頭，從山丘到泉邊，再從泉邊回到山丘。

title.en: The Birth of Bacchus (Dionysus)
title.zh: 酒神巴克斯的誕生

region.en: Thebes (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 底比斯（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 8 CE (Latin; Riley translation 1851)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)
source.work: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book III (Fables IV-V)

summary.en: Juno, in the disguise of Semele's old nurse Beroe, teaches the daughter of Cadmus to demand of her lover Jupiter the form he wears for Juno in bed. Bound by an oath on the Styx, Jupiter comes in full thunder; Semele, consumed, burns in his embrace; the fetus, however, is rescued, sewn into the father's own thigh to complete the months, and born again. Ino, his aunt, raises him in secret, then the Nysean nymphs in their caves, with milk; and thus the god is twice-born under the still-living mother Cytherea's care.
summary.zh: 朱諾化作塞墨勒的乳母柏瑞厄，教她向情人宙斯索其擁抱朱諾時的威嚴原形。宙斯以斯提克斯河立誓、無法食言，遂全副雷霆下界；塞墨勒在人間婚禮的嫁妝中焚燬；胎兒取自母腹縫入父親大腿補足孕期，二次誕生。姨母伊諾祕密撫養，後由尼薩山寧芙藏於洞窟以乳哺育——酒神由此兩生。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Among the descendants of Agenor, Jove doted now on the Phoenician maiden, Europa; then on Aegina; and then, in turn, he doted on Semele, the daughter of Cadmus, who was cared for with a fond mother, and desired nothing of this. Juno, nursing her grudge against a mortal woman who dared above her rank, put on the shape of Beroe — Semele's Epidaurian nurse — so the two talked and joked of their lover together, and Juno, singing, told her: has he often so far stretched his love as, for instance, a god? and does he swear so faithfully as the nature of a lover allows?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses III, Fable IV (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在阿革諾耳的後裔之中，朱庇特先是鍾情於腓尼基少女歐羅巴；接著是埃癸娜；然後又輪到塞墨勒，即卡德摩斯之女，她由慈愛的母親照料，對此別無所求。朱諾對這個膽敢逾越自身身分的凡人女子心懷怨恨，便化作貝羅厄——塞墨勒那位厄庇道洛斯的乳母——的模樣，於是兩人一同談笑她們的情人，朱諾唱著歌對她說：他是否常常把愛伸展到這般地步，譬如像個神那樣？他是否發誓發得如此忠誠，如同情人的天性所容許的那般？

passages.text: For proof, the nurse taught the girl to demand of him that, if he was indeed Jove, he would come to her in the ensigns and state of royalty, the majesty he wore for Juno herself. The daughter of Cadmus innocently asked the boon, saying nothing; and Jupiter, as he ever could for a mortal, granted her the request before it was made; and swore, for the more belief, by the Styx, the dread river of the underworld that all gods fear to break.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses III, Fable IV (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 為了證明，乳母教這少女向他要求：倘若他真是朱庇特，就讓他以王者的標誌與威儀、以他為朱諾本人所披戴的那份尊嚴來見她。卡德摩斯之女天真地求了這恩惠，並未多言；而朱庇特，一如他對凡人向來所能的那樣，在她開口之前便已應允了她的請求；並且為了更取信於人，他以斯堤克斯河起誓，那是眾神都懼怕違背的冥界可怖之河。

passages.text: Overjoyed at her misfortune, she said: 'present thyself as Juno is wont to embrace thee.' The god groaned: he could not unsay his oath. So he mounted the skies, drew thick clouds around himself, and added rain and mixed winds, thunders, and the inevitable thunderbolt. He put on the least of his many fires, the second thunder, which the Cyclops had forged with less anger in it; but her mortal body could not endure the ethereal blaze: she burned amid her own nuptial presents, the dowry of a bride who had married a god.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses III, Fable V (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她因自己的不幸而欣喜若狂，說道：『就以朱諾慣常擁抱你的那副模樣現身吧。』神呻吟了一聲：他無法收回自己的誓言。於是他登上天際，在自己周圍聚起濃厚的雲層，又添上雨水與交錯的風、雷霆，以及那不可避免的霹靂。他披上自己眾多火焰中最微弱的一種，即第二等的雷火，那是庫克洛普斯懷著較少怒氣所鍛造的那一道；但她凡人的軀體承受不住那以太的烈焰：她在自己的新婚禮物之間焚毀，那是一位嫁給了神的女子所帶來的嫁妝。

passages.text: The infant, as yet unformed, was snatched from the womb of his mother, and — if we can believe it — sewn into the thigh of his father, where he completed the months he should have spent in the womb. His aunt Ino nursed him secretly in his first cradle; after her, the Nysean Nymphs concealed him in their caves and gave him the nourishment of milk. So the god grew, twice-born, under the care of nurses and the watch of heaven: and in due time all Thebes knew him for the son of the thunderer, who before all others came back living from the tomb of his mother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses III, Fable V (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那尚未成形的嬰兒從母親的腹中被奪出，並且——倘若我們能相信的話——被縫進他父親的大腿，在那裡補足了他本該在母腹中度過的月數。他的姨母伊諾在他的第一個搖籃裡暗中哺育他；在她之後，尼薩的寧芙們把他藏在她們的洞穴中，以乳汁餵養他。這神就這樣長大，兩度出生，在乳母們的照料與上天的看顧之下：及至時候滿足，全底比斯都認他為那位雷霆之神的兒子，他先於所有其他人，從母親的墳墓中活著歸來。

title.en: The Making of the World (Ovid's Creation)
title.zh: 世界的造成（奧維德創世記）

region.en: Universal cosmos (mythic geography)
region.zh: 宇宙全體（神話地理）

period: Composed c. 8 CE (Latin; Riley translation 1851)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)
source.work: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book I (Fables I-II)

summary.en: Ovid opens his poem with the separation of the whole mass into land, sea, air and the passions proper to each; the four winds are given their settlements, the stars to shine, the living kinds to their elements; and then man is made — whether of the divine seed of the Creator, or of the earth tempered with rain — by Prometheus, and set upright to look at the heavens.
summary.zh: 奧維德的《變形記》以混沌劈開開篇：天、地、海、氣，各自成形，四風安座，星辰起光；諸靈各歸其界。最後造人：或由造物主之神性元素鍛成，或由普羅米修斯以雨水調和泥土塑就；直立人身，仰首望天。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Before sea and land and the encircling sky, the face of the whole world was one — they call it Chaos: a rough unordered mass of things, nothing alive except a sluggish weight of matter heaped together. Not yet was the sun's light divided from the earth, nor the moon's from the sun; not yet did the earth hang balanced by its own weight around its own sky. From this one mass, some Power divided the parts: the god (or kindlier nature) cut it up, separated the earth from the sky and the watery waves from the earth, and distinguished the ethereal heavens from the grosser air.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses I, Fable I (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在海洋、陸地與環繞的天空之前，整個世界的面貌渾然一體——他們稱之為卡俄斯：一堆粗糙無序的雜物，除了遲滯堆積的物質之重，別無活物。太陽的光尚未與大地分開，月亮的光也尚未與太陽分開；大地尚未憑自身重量懸於自己的天空而保持平衡。從這一團混沌之中，某種力量劃分了各部分：那位神（或更仁慈的自然）將其切開，使大地與天空分離，使水波與大地分離，並使以太的諸天與較粗濁的氣區分開來。

passages.text: Each element received its proper place, and none can be removed whence it has been placed; each contains one life of its own. Fire, the lightest, went up to the heaven; the air came next; earth sank lower, drawn down by its weight; and water hung beneath it, the lowest of all. This one Provider — whoever he was — ordered the universe with form and regularity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses I, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 每一元素各得其應在之處，無一能被移離其所安置之地；各含其自身的一種生命。火最輕，升上天際；氣次之；土因重量被向下牽引而沉得更低；水則懸於其下，為萬物之最低。這唯一的安排者——無論他是誰——以形式與秩序安排了宇宙。

passages.text: He made the globe in even measure, poured the sea round the shores, added springs and pools and lakes, bounded the rivers as they leapt down; extended the plains, sunk the valleys, clothed the woods; raised the cragged mountains; and clime upon clime, two heavens upon either side overhung them. Over these he hung the air with its vapours and clouds and terrifying thunders and the winds that quarrel with each other even still, so hardly kept from rending the world asunder.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses I, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他按均等的尺度造出圓球，把海洋傾注於海岸四周，添上泉源、水池與湖泊，為奔流而下的河川劃定界限；鋪展平原，凹陷山谷，覆以林木；隆起崎嶇的山巒；又將一層層的氣候、兩重天宇分懸於兩側，覆罩其上。在這之上，他懸起空氣，連同其中的蒸氣、雲霧、可怖的雷霆，以及至今仍彼此爭鬥的諸風——它們好不容易才被制止，不至於將世界撕裂。

passages.text: Then the stars, which had lain hid beneath the mass of Chaos, began to glow through the whole sphere of the heavens: the stars of the gods to the heavens; the waters fell to the fishes; the earth yielded the beasts; and the yielding air yielded the birds. An animal more holy than these, and fitted to command the rest, was still wanting: and then Man was made — whether by the Artificer of the world himself from the divine seed, or by Prometheus, son of Iapetus, who tempered the new-made earth with rainwater and shaped it after the image of the gods; and for the first time lifted up his face to behold the heavens and the stars. Thus that which had been lately rude earth, and without form, took on the shape of Man, till then unknown to all the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses I, Fable II (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是，那些原本潛藏於混沌之中的星辰，開始在整個天穹中閃耀：眾神的星辰歸於天宇；水歸於魚；大地獻出野獸；柔順的空氣獻出飛鳥。然而，仍缺少一種比這些更為神聖、適於統御其餘萬物的生靈：於是，人便被造了出來——或是由世界之工匠親手以神聖的種子所造，或是由伊阿珀托斯之子普羅米修斯所造，他將新造的泥土與雨水調和，依眾神的形象加以塑造；人首次抬起臉來，仰望天宇與星辰。於是，那不久前還是粗陋的泥土、毫無形狀之物，便化作了人的形貌——這形貌在此之前，為整個世界所未知。

title.en: Latona and the Lycian Peasants
title.zh: 勒托與呂基亞農夫：青蛙之由來

region.en: Lycia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 呂基亞（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 8 CE (Latin; Riley translation 1851)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)
source.work: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book VI (Fables III-IV)

summary.en: Driven by Juno across the world, heavy with her twins and parched with a Lycian sun, Latona comes to a pool to drink — and the peasants working the rushes bar her, then muddy the water with their feet for spite. She renounces begging: 'may you live for ever in that pool.' Their limbs sink, their necks swell, their mouths gape in abuse — and they are frogs forever, keeping their spite under water. She calls, still, the peasants who told the tale — and still their frogs croak from the same pool, at the altar black with ash, in the Lycian valley — the altar where the people say Latona herself bore her twins.
summary.zh: 被朱諾二十一國追索、懷孕雙胎、烈日中日曬渴的勒托至池邊欲飲，凡夫俗子竟下腳把水踩渾不許她喝。女神怒而求討：'願你們永世住在池中！'她體態漸沉、脖項粗大、口吐污水之呪罵聲永不得休——化為青蛙。呂基亞山谷中至今仍有一座灰燼黑成的古祭壇，人們說那是勒托產雙胎之處。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: There is an old altar in a Lycian valley, black with the ash of sacrifices, standing in a modest pool hedged about with quivering reeds. A native guide told Ovid's narrator its story as he passed: 'there is no mountain-divinity for this altar. She claims it for herself whom royal Juno banished from the world — whom the wandering Delos, still swimming like a light island, scarcely received at her prayers.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VI, Fable III (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 呂基亞的一處山谷中有一座古老的祭壇，被獻祭的灰燼染得漆黑，立於一泓淺池之中，四周環繞著顫動的蘆葦。一位當地嚮導在奧維德的敘述者經過時，向他講述了這祭壇的來歷：『這座祭壇並無哪位山神所有。它屬於那位被王后朱諾逐出世界的女神——那位漂泊的得洛斯島，當時仍如一座輕盈的島嶼般漂浮不定，在她的祈求之下才勉強收留了她。』

passages.text: By that palm, on that island, Latona brought forth in pain her twins, Apollo and Diana, against Juno's spite; and now, after all her wanderings, she was again on the hot Lycian road, carrying her two young children in her arms, worn out with sun, and parched with thirst, when she saw a lake of clear water in the bottom of the valley, and some countryfolk in it, gathering osiers and rushes and sedge.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VI, Fable III (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 就在那島上、那棵棕櫚樹旁，拉托娜違逆朱諾的惡意，在痛苦中誕下了她的雙生子阿波羅與狄安娜；如今，在歷經種種漂泊之後，她又踏上了呂基亞炎熱的道路，懷中抱著兩個年幼的孩子，被烈日曬得疲憊不堪，口渴難耐，這時她望見山谷底部有一泓清澈的池水，池中有幾個鄉民正在採集柳枝、燈心草與莎草。

passages.text: She knelt on the ground for a draught: the peasants barred her. Their answer was a stream of abuse and threats, and then — this is the brutality they could not keep from their hands — they stirred up the soft mud from the bottom with their feet and made the clean water filthy against her. Her thirst went out of her with her anger; no more did the daughter of Coeus supplicate the wretches, nor hold back words a goddess should have to speak: she raised her voice to heaven and said, 'Live in that pool for ever.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VI, Fable III (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她跪在地上想飲一口水：那些農人卻攔住了她。他們的回答是一連串的辱罵與威脅，接著——這便是他們雙手按捺不住的粗暴之舉——他們用腳攪起池底的軟泥，把清澈的水攪得污濁，使她無法飲用。她的怒氣隨口渴一同湧出；科俄斯之女不再向這些惡徒哀求，也不再克制一位女神本該說出的話語：她揚聲向天說道：『就讓你們永遠住在那池水裡吧。』

passages.text: Her wish came to pass on them all. They delighted then to go under the water, and sometimes to plunge their whole bodies in the pool; now they lifted their heads to the surface, now swam on the top; they would sit on the bank for a moment and leap back in the cold stream. Still, under the green water, they kept up their scandalous tongues in insults they could not stay from, and their voices grew hoarse with the shouting, and their bloated necks swelled out with their abuse. And their backs closed into one plane with their heads; their necks looked cut off; the green of their backs spread over them, and their bellies, the largest part of them, went white: they were frogs, brand-new, leaping in the muddy water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VI, Fable III (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她的心願在他們所有人身上應驗了。他們如今樂於潛入水下，時而將整個身子沒入池中；時而把頭探出水面，時而在水面上游動；他們會在岸邊坐上片刻，又跳回冰冷的溪流之中。然而，在碧綠的水下，他們仍不停用那些戒不掉的辱罵搬弄是非，他們的聲音因叫嚷而變得沙啞，他們鼓脹的脖子因咒罵而膨大。他們的背與頭連成一個平面；脖子看上去像是被切斷了；背上的綠色蔓延全身，而他們身上最大的部分——肚子——則泛著白色：他們成了青蛙，嶄新的青蛙，在泥濘的水中跳躍。

passages.text: And at the altar Ovid's local guide whispered 'Be thou propitious' — for it had become the place of the goddess herself: the Letoön, where villagers came to offer and the sacredness of the pool and the frogs to be taken as a sign. The croaking frogs thus descend from one old myth: of those who denied water to the mother of gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VI, Fable III, with Riley's explanation of the etiological tradition (1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在祭壇前，奧維德的當地嚮導低聲說道：「願你降福」——因為這裡已成為女神本人的所在：勒托翁，村民前來獻祭，而池水與青蛙的神聖性則被視為一種徵兆。因此，鳴叫的青蛙源自一則古老神話：那些拒絕給眾神之母水喝的人。

title.en: Tereus, Philomela, and the Language of the Web
title.zh: 特柔斯、菲羅墨拉與織上文字

region.en: Daulia, Phocis (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 福基斯道利亞（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 8 CE (Latin; Riley translation 1851)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 21765 (H. T. Riley, trans.)
source.work: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book VI (Fables V-VI)

summary.en: Tereus, king of Thrace, wed to Progne and conquering for Athens her father Pandion's war, takes the younger sister Philomela home in disguise; ravishes her in the wood, and, for fear of discovery, cuts out her tongue. Robbed of speech, she weaves the crime into a cloth and sends it by hand to her sister; Progne reads it in her halls, then, with the boy Itys led to the slaughter, takes her revenge: she cooks her own child to serve at Tereus' table. At Daulia in Phocis the gods change all three into birds: the husband a hoopoe with a warrior's crest, Progne a swallow, and Philomela a nightingale, singing for ever of what was done to her speechless tongue.
summary.zh: 色雷斯王特柔斯娶普洛克涅為妻，因此協助雅典王潘狄翁作戰。他以探親為名接走菲羅墨拉，在林中施暴，並割其舌以防事發——啞女斐無法言語但巧於織技：她把罪行織成一匹布，囑僕人送至宮中。普洛克涅見之，抱回幼子伊提斯的屍首，終以復仇之宴上體肉奉夫。三人於道利亞化為鳥：特柔斯為戴羽冠之戴勝、普洛克涅為燕、菲羅墨拉為夜鶯，其歌聲永訴無舌之苦。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; the story contains graphic violence; presented as ancient material without endorsement.

passages.text: Pandion, king of Athens, had made a good marriage: his daughter Progne to Tereus, the great warrior of Thrace, son of Mars, by whose aid Pandion drove off his enemies. Their wedding was celebrated without omen; the Furies sat on the roof, and the owl — a boding bird of the night — haunted the bridal chamber: ill omens that came true. Itys was their son, and for five autumns the couple lived in harmony.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VI, Fable V (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 雅典國王潘狄翁結了一門好親事：將女兒普洛克涅嫁給了色雷斯偉大的戰士、瑪爾斯之子忒柔斯，潘狄翁藉助他的力量驅退了敵人。他們的婚禮在沒有吉兆的情況下舉行；復仇女神坐在屋頂上，而貓頭鷹——夜間的不祥之鳥——縈繞於新房：這些凶兆後來都應驗了。伊提斯是他們的兒子，這對夫婦和諧地共度了五個秋天。

passages.text: Then Progne begged her sister Philomela, left in Athens, to visit her in Thrace; and Tereus, loaded with gifts, sailed back for her himself. Seeing the girl, he was inflamed, and all the way framed the dark plan of violence. He tricked Pandion's consent under flattery, shipped her over the sea, and, within a frame of woods, deceived her into the wilds: seized, deflowered, and — when in hatred she gave him the tongue — silenced literally, in silence, and hidden in a stone structure, with a slave girl to keep her alone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VI, Fable V (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 後來普洛克涅懇求留在雅典的妹妹菲洛墨拉來色雷斯探望她；忒柔斯滿載禮物，親自乘船回去接她。一見到這姑娘，他便慾火中燒，一路上謀劃著暴力的陰暗計劃。他以諂媚之詞騙得潘狄翁的同意，用船將她載過大海，又在一片樹林之中將她騙入荒野：抓住她，玷污了她，而當她滿懷憎恨地要向他說出實情時——他竟以沉默的方式使她真正地沉默，並將她藏在一座石造建築中，派一名女奴單獨看守她。

passages.text: But the girl, having no voice, had memory, and she had a craft: she wove the story into a fabric, and sent it by servant to Progne. Progne, reading her sister's wrongs — the proof on the cloth before her — said nothing out loud: the festival of Bacchus, from one of the house-wombs, was coming. And it was then the plan she formed: revenge at her own home, over wine, with her sister present at the table.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VI, Fable V (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但這姑娘雖無聲音，卻有記憶，而且她有一門手藝：她將這故事織入一塊布中，派僕人送給普洛克涅。普洛克涅讀到妹妹的冤屈——證據就在她眼前的布上——沒有出聲：酒神節即將來臨，從家中某個女人的腹中而來。正是在那時，她定下了計劃：在自己家中復仇，藉著酒，讓妹妹也在席間。

passages.text: With Itys — her own son — she finished Tereus' homecoming: the banquet she placed before him was his boy. At the table Tereus called for his son, and in response she cried, 'You have him within.' He raged for his weapon; and the three of them sprang from the house in flight, prophesying in bird-language. Tereus was changed into a hoopoe with a crest of soldier's feathers; Progne into the swallow, red-breasted beneath the eaves; Philomela into the nightingale, still announcing with her notes the crime done to her tongue.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VI, Fable VI (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她以伊提斯——她自己的兒子——了結了忒柔斯的歸家：她擺在他面前的宴席就是他的男孩。席間忒柔斯呼喚他的兒子，而她回應道：「他就在你體內。」他狂怒地尋找武器；他們三人從屋中躍出逃亡，以鳥語預言。忒柔斯被變成戴著士兵羽毛冠的戴勝；普洛克涅變成燕子，在屋簷下胸脯通紅；菲洛墨拉變成夜鶯，仍以她的鳴聲宣告那加於她舌頭的罪行。

passages.text: In Daulis, and the country all about, the names of that bird became the names of the story: the swallow that never sings after that night, the nightingale always wailing, and the hoopoe with the head-dress of the ravisher. And so the love-songs of nightingales in the midsummer of Thessaly were understood, in this telling, to be the voice of the girl whose tongue a king took from her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ovid, Metamorphoses VI, Fable VI (Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在道利斯及周圍一帶，那鳥兒的名字成了這故事的名字：那夜之後再不放聲歌唱的燕子，永遠哀鳴的夜鶯，以及頭戴掠奪者冠飾的戴勝。於是，在這一說法中，忒薩利仲夏時節夜鶯的情歌，被理解為那位被國王割去舌頭的姑娘的聲音。

title.en: Actaeon's Spectre at Orchomenus
title.zh: 阿克泰翁的鬼影：俄爾科墨努斯的祭祀起源

region.en: Orchomenus, Boeotia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波厄提亞俄爾科墨努斯（象徵性定位）

period: Written c. 2nd century CE (Shilleto/Bohn translation; G. B. 68680)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 68680 (A. R. Shilleto, trans.)
source.work: Pausanias, Description of Greece IX.38

summary.en: At Orchomenus a spectre in the shape of Actaeon was said to sit upon a certain stone and work harm on the land; the Delphic oracle prescribed that whatever remains of Actaeon could be found be buried, and a bronze copy of the spectre be attached with iron to the stone; and Pausanias says he himself saw it, and that the town offers him funeral rites every year. A short story: the origin of a local cult, and a folk-memory of the hunter who had seen Artemis at her bath and died for it.
summary.zh: 俄爾科墨努斯傳言有一位阿克泰翁形貌的鬼影盤坐某巨石之上、為害鄉土；德爾菲神諭指示：把能找到的阿克泰翁遺骨掩埋，並以青銅仿其鬼形鐵釘於石。鮑桑尼亞斯親眼見之，並說此城每年為鬼影舉行喪祭。短小故事背後，是有關獵手阿克泰翁因偷看阿爾忒彌斯沐浴而亡之地方祭祀起源。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The men of Orchomenus had a tradition that a spectre, having the shape of Actaeon, sat upon a certain stone and injured their land: blights, they said, would strike down their crops wherever the spectre sat. They sent to Delphi, and the oracle's answer prescribed two acts at once: bury in the ground whatever remains of Actaeon they could find, and make a bronze copy of the spectre and fasten it with iron to the stone on which it sat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.38 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 俄耳科墨诺斯人有一则相传的说法：有一个形貌如阿克泰翁的幽灵，坐在某块石头上，祸害他们的土地；他们说，幽灵坐在哪里，哪里便有枯萎病侵袭他们的庄稼。他们派人去德尔斐求问，神谕的答复同时规定了两种做法：把他们所能找到的阿克泰翁遗骸尽数埋入土中，并照那幽灵的形貌铸一尊铜像，用铁钉固定在它曾坐过的那块石头上。

passages.text: Pausanias says he himself saw the bronze figure fixed upon the stone; and that to this day the people of Orchomenus perform funeral rites to Actaeon every year. The name behind it is old: Actaeon the hunter, who in the familiar telling came upon Artemis at her bath and was changed into a stag and torn apart by his own hounds. Here, in Pausanias' quieter version, his lingering presence is the cause of an annual rite — a daimon of the fields propitiated with an offering every year at harvest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.38 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 保萨尼阿斯说，他亲眼见过那尊固定在石头上的铜像；又说直到今日，俄耳科墨诺斯人每年仍为阿克泰翁举行丧葬之礼。其背后的名字由来已久：猎人阿克泰翁，在人们熟知的说法里，他撞见阿尔忒弥斯沐浴，被变成一头鹿，又被自己的猎犬撕碎。而在这里，在保萨尼阿斯较为平和的版本中，他残存不去的身影成了一年一度仪式的起因——一位田野的精灵，每年收获时节以祭品加以安抚。

title.en: Hippocrene, the Spring Struck from the Rock
title.zh: 希波克瑞涅：馬蹄踏石出泉

region.en: Mount Helicon (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 赫利孔山（象徵性定位）

period: Written c. 2nd century CE (Shilleto/Bohn translation; G. B. 68680)

source.archive: Project Gutenberg eBook 68680 (A. R. Shilleto, trans.)
source.work: Pausanias, Description of Greece IX.31

summary.en: Twenty stades above Thebes' valley lies the grove of the Muses on Helicon, and beyond it Hippocrene — the Horse's Spring, gushing, the Boeotians said, where the hoof of Bellerophon's Pegasus struck the earth. Around it Pausanias found a museum-country of relics: the oldest tripod won by Hesiod at Chalcis, a leaden plate said to be written with The Works and Days in a poet's own hand, and the Mouseia festival where Thespians — with games to the Muses and to Eros both — still contest in song and sport.
summary.zh: 赫利孔山繆斯聖林內有赫西俄德在卡爾基斯詩賽奪得的古銅鼎；山上二十斯塔德處是希波克瑞涅泉——傳為柏勒洛豐的天馬一蹄踏石而出。泉畔曾見一近乎朽盡的鉛板，傳為詩人手書《勞作與時日》；忒斯庇亞人在聖林舉行繆斯節慶，設詩歌與體育競技，亦每年祭愛神厄若斯。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: At Helicon there are several tripods, of which the oldest, Pausanias notes, is the one they say Hesiod received at Chalcis by the Euripus for a victory in song — the very tripod the poet himself tells of in his verse. Around the grove the people live and till; and the Thespians hold there a festival of the Muses with games not only of music but of athletes; and another also to Eros — the famous deity of the Thespians.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.31 (Shilleto); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 赫利孔山上有好几只三足鼎，保萨尼阿斯指出，其中最古老的一只，据说是赫西俄德在欧里波斯海峡畔的卡尔基斯因诗歌比赛获胜而得到的——正是诗人本人在其诗篇中提及的那只三足鼎。圣林四周，人们居住耕作；忒斯庇亚人则在那里举办缪斯节，不仅有音乐比赛，还有竞技比赛；另有一个节日献给厄洛斯——忒斯庇亚人所崇奉的著名神明。

passages.text: And twenty stades upstream from the sacred grove, going up from it, you reach Hippocrene — the Horse's Spring.
