But as soon as she was ready to bring forth the gleaming-eyed goddess Athena, then the crafty father deceived her with flattering words, and swallowed her down into his own belly; for Earth and starry Heaven had given him counsel — that this would come to pass, lest some other deathless holder of the thunder should come to be king in Zeus's place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 886-900 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 如今，宙斯王娶墨提斯為第一位妻子，她所知勝過所有神明與凡人。但就在她即將誕下明眸女神雅典娜之際，這位狡黠的父親便以諂媚之言欺騙了她，將她吞入自己的腹中；因為大地與繁星點點的天空曾給他諫言——此事必將發生，以免另有某位不死者、另一位雷霆的執掌者，取代宙斯而為王。

passages.text: For the two elders had prophesied what children Metis would bear: first the bright-eyed maiden who would be her father's equal in strength and wisdom; then a son, the rash king of gods and men. To forestall this, Zeus swallowed Metis while the child was on the point of being born, so that the goddess might counsel him in the sitter's own heart, and teach him the good from the evil deed and counsel his charity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 886-900 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 因為這兩位長者曾預言墨提斯將生下何等子女：先是那位明眸的少女，她將在力量與智慧上與其父相當；繼而是一個兒子，那魯莽的眾神與凡人之王。為防患於未然，宙斯便在孩子即將出生之際吞下了墨提斯，好讓這位女神在他自己的心中為他諫言，教他分辨善行與惡行，並為他的仁厚進言。

title.en: The Making of the Sun, Moon and Dawn
title.zh: 日月晨光的誕生

region.en: Mount Olympus side-paths (mythic geography)
region.zh: 奧林波斯東面山道（神話地理）

period: Composed c. 700 BCE (Evelyn-White translation 1914)

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 371-376

summary.en: The shining lights of the sky are born of a single marriage of the older gods: Theia, Radiant Titaness of the shining eye, weds Hyperion, and their children are three — Helios who lights the world for gods and for men, Selene the round and bright-collared moon, and Eos, Dawn, whose Palinodes are for every morning's return of all mortals and immortals on the earth.
summary.zh: 日月晨光同屬一族：發光眼睛的提坦女忒亞嫁給許珀里翁，生下三子——普照神人的赫利俄斯（太陽）、頭戴圓冠的塞勒涅（月）、及每日為神人「再開晨光」的厄俄斯（黎明）。奧維德《變形記》中亦有此系統：法厄同為太陽神之子，其遭遇將是不太理想的冒險，代危性的神請他握韁、不可逞其父之私人之力。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Now again to Hyperion wed Theia, element of brightness, and bare to him great children — Helios the Sun, and Selene the Moon, and Eos, the early-born Dawn — who shines upon all that dwell on the earth, and on the deathless gods who hold the wide heaven above.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 371-376 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 如今，忒亞——光明之元素——又嫁與許佩里翁，為他生下偉大的子女——太陽神赫利俄斯、月神塞勒涅，以及早生的黎明女神厄俄斯——她照耀著一切居住於大地之上者，也照耀著那些執掌上方遼闊天空的不死神明。

passages.text: The poem follows the family's own paths: from Eos in her love with Astraeus came the great winds — clearing Zephyrus, swift Boreas, and sultry Notus — and after them Heosphoros, the morning star, and every shining star that graces the heavens. In Ovid's later Roman account, Phaethon is set in this same family lineage — the Sun irradiates the lineage but his son insists on the reins, driven to ruin, and the celestial body takes the road of flood and fire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 371-383, with Ovid II. (Evelyn-White 1914; Riley 1851); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 詩篇循著這一家族自身的脈絡展開：厄俄斯與阿斯特賴俄斯相戀，由此生出了諸位大風——清朗的西風之神澤菲羅斯、迅疾的北風之神玻瑞阿斯，以及悶熱的南風之神諾托斯——其後又有晨星之神赫俄斯福羅斯，以及一切點綴天穹的閃耀星辰。在奧維德後來的羅馬記載中，法厄同被置於這同一家族世系之中——太陽照亮了這世系，其子卻執意要掌馭韁繩，終致毀滅，而天體則走上了洪水與烈火之路。

title.en: Ginnungagap: From the Yawning Void to the First Life
title.zh: 金倫加鴻溝：從鴻蒙初開到最初的生命

region.en: Ginnungagap (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland - provenance of Codex Regius)
region.zh: 金倫加鴻溝（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利——《雷吉烏斯抄本》產地）

period: Prose Edda c. 1220-1230, using older eddic material; MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to (c. 1300-1325), Codex Upsaliensis DG 11, Codex Trajectinus

source.work: Snorri Sturluson, Edda: Gylfaginning chs. 1-5, trans. A. G. Brodeur (1916); critical ed. Anthony Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Before earth, sky or sea there was only Ginnungagap, the yawning void. North lay Niflheim, whose eleven venom rivers froze into rime; south lay Muspell, a burning world no outsider could endure. Where the two met, rime dropped into the gap and quickened into the giant Ymir; the thawing drops next shaped a cow, Audhumla, whose milk fed the giant while she licked salt stones until Buri came forth. The myth explains the primal polarity of ice and fire and the accidental, multi-generational birth of the gods.
summary.zh: 天地海尚未存在時，唯有張開的金倫加鴻溝。北面尼福爾海姆的十一條毒河凍成霜雪，南面是無人能居的火焰之國穆斯貝爾海姆。冰火交會處，霜雪落入鴻溝化為活物，霜巨人尤彌爾由此而生；融冰之滴復凝成母牛歐德姆布拉，其乳哺育巨人，牛舌舔舐鹽石三日而舔出布里。神話解釋了冰與火的二元原初，以及諸神經數代偶然降生的譜系。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain); consulted against Anthony Faulkes, Edda, London 1987

narrative.en:
Snorri's cosmogony begins with an admission of learned ignorance: it was the beginning of the world - and then immediately qualifies it. Before anything was made there was that which had always been, Niflheim, the mist-world, and in its center Hvergelmir, the roaring well from which the eleven rivers called Elivagar pour forth. The rivers carried with them the venom that flows from the spring, and as they ran farther from their source the current hardened into ice; the poison settled in the flow and froze with it. Far to the south, at the world's rim, lay Muspell, bright and hot, fenced with fire and given to no outsider to enter, guarded by Surtr with his flaming sword.

Between these two worlds spread Ginnungagap, the 'yawning gap', a void with no floor and no sky. The doctrine of the myth is that creation is a condensation, not a command. Nothing spoke the world into being; instead the warm air of Muspell met the frozen rime of Niflheim at the lip of the gap, and where they met the ice softened and dripped. By the heat that quickened the drops, the rime took the form of a living thing, and that form was the giant Ymir, whom the rime-giants acknowledge as their sire. He was not born of father or mother in any human sense: he is the oldest being, grown from the collision of opposites, sweating giants from his own left arm while from his paired feet a son was engendered.

The second birth is just as accidental and just as generative. The thawing drops formed another creature, a cow named Audhumla, whose milk is the first sustenance in the cosmos: she feeds Ymir from her four rivers of milk, and she in turn feeds on the salt of the ice-stones. Licking the salty blocks she brings forth on the first day a man's hair; on the second, his head; on the third, an entire man, Buri. Buri's son Bor marries Bestla, daughter of the giant Bolthorn, and their sons - Odin, Vili and Ve - are the first gods, beings who carry both the fire of Muspell's line and the descent of the rime-giants.

The myth's cultural function is to establish the cosmic economy on which all later Norse myth runs: the world is made of antagonistic elements held in unstable balance; giants are the elder race with a birthright claim; gods exist as a younger, mixed lineage that must seize order rather than inherit it; and nourishment - a cow, salt, milk - underlies even divine existence. Snorri, writing as a Christian and a learned Icelander, frames all this as the doctrine that 'heathen men' held; the myth also serves his pedagogy in Gylfaginning, where King Gylfi is walked through the void as a first lesson before the illusion of Asgard dissolves.

Later eschatology feeds back into this cosmogony: at Ragnarok the fire of Surtr returns and the venom rivers of the deep past are renewed in punishment, so that the end of the world replays its own raw materials in reverse.

functions: Cosmogonic doctrine of a pre-created material void rather than creation by word or will
Establishes the ice-fire polarity that organizes the whole Norse cosmos
Legitimates the giants as an elder race and the gods as a younger mixed lineage
Learned-Christian frame: Snorri presents heathen cosmology as the doctrine of a vanished system

variants.name: Voluspa (Poetic Edda)
variants.text_tradition: Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270s (poem c. 900-1000 CE)
variants.summary: The sibyl's opening is spare: in earliest days there was no sand, no sea, no cool waves, no earth, no sky, only a single gaping void - a minimal cosmos without Snorri's named worlds, rivers or cow.

variants.name: Vafthrudnismal (Poetic Edda)
variants.summary: In the wisdom contest the giant confirms that before the ages Ymir existed in the void, and names Muspell as the fire-world whose people ride to Ragnarok - eddic source for Snorri's geography.

variants.name: Gylfaginning frame (Prose Edda, chs. 1-2)
variants.summary: Snorri first surveys what learned men say about the world's age (an epitome of Christian chronology) and only then lets the three enthroned figures teach the heathen doctrine - a double bookkeeping of biblical and pagan time.

primary_sources.citation: Chs. 1-5 (Niflheim, Hvergelmir, Elivagar, Muspell, Surtr, the quickening of Ymir and Audhumla, Buri). Critical edition: Anthony Faulkes, Edda, London 1987. MSS: Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to; Codex Upsaliensis DG 11; Codex Trajectinus. English: Brodeur 1916.

Stanza 3 (the bare void). Principal MS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to; Hauksbok variants. Critical edition: Ursula Dronke, The Poetic Edda vol. II, Oxford 1997; public-domain English: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923.

secondary_sources.work: Margaret Clunies Ross, Prolonged Echoes: Old Norse Myths in Medieval Northern Society, vol. 1
secondary_sources.citation: Clunies Ross 1994, Odense: Odense University Press - on the antagonistic-element economy of Norse cosmogony.

secondary_sources.work: Rudolf Simek, Dictionary of Northern Mythology (trans. Angela Hall)
secondary_sources.citation: Simek 1993, Cambridge: D. S. Brewer - entries 'Ginnungagap', 'Niflheim', 'Muspell' synthesizing the manuscript evidence.

secondary_sources.work: Ursula Dronke, The Poetic Edda, vol. II: Mythological Poems
secondary_sources.citation: Dronke 1997, Oxford: Clarendon Press - critical edition and commentary of Voluspa.

source_urls.description: handrit.is catalogue - Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to and related Edda manuscripts

sensitivity.note: Historical literary corpus; claimed as heritage by modern heathen communities, but nothing restricted is reproduced.

passages.text: There was nothing, they said, before the making of the earth: no sand above, no sea below, no grass or air; only that vast opening, Ginnungagap, which had no bottom on any side. North of it lay the mist-world and its roaring spring, from whose rivers the rime spread and froze with the venom that flowed in the water; and the venom froze with the ice and dripped into the gap.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning chs. 3-4 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們說，在大地造成之前，什麼也沒有：上無沙，下無海，無草亦無空氣；唯有那巨大的裂口——金倫加鴻溝，它無論哪一面都沒有底。其北面是霧之國及其轟鳴的泉眼，霜從那裡的眾河漫延開來，隨著水中流淌的毒液一同凍結；毒液與冰一同凍結，滴入那鴻溝之中。

passages.text: Southward at the world's rim was the burning world, Muspell, fenced with fire and given to no man to enter. Where the heat of Muspell touched the frozen rime at the lip of the gap, the ice began to melt and drip; and the drops, quickened by the heat, took the form of a living thing - and that form was Ymir, from whom the rime-giants count their race.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning chs. 4-5 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在世界邊緣的南方，是那燃燒的世界穆斯貝爾，以火焰為籬圍繞，不許任何人進入。當穆斯貝爾的熱氣觸及鴻溝邊緣的冰霜時，冰便開始融化滴落；那些被熱氣催活的滴液，化為一個活物的形狀——那形狀便是尤米爾，霜巨人便從他數算自己的族裔。

passages.text: The melting drops next formed a cow, Audhumla, and from her udders flowed the rivers of milk with which the giant was fed; and the cow herself fed by licking the salt of the ice-stones, and the first day she licked there came up a man's hair, and the second day a head, and the third day the whole man was come forth, and he was called Buri.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 5 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 融化的滴液接著化成一頭母牛，奧德姆拉，從她的乳房流出餵養巨人的奶河；母牛自己則以舔食冰石上的鹽為食，她舔食的第一天，便有一人的頭髮冒出，第二天冒出頭顱，第三天整個人便出來了，他名叫布里。

title.en: Bergelmir's Raft: The Flood That Made the Rime-Giants
title.zh: 貝格爾米爾之筏：造就霜巨人的洪水

region.en: Jotunheimr (symbolic pin at Jotunheimen, Norway)
region.zh: 約頓海姆（象徵性定位於挪威尤通黑門山）

period: Vafthrudnismal c. 900-1000 CE; Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; principal MS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to (c. 1270s)

source.work: Vafthrudnismal st. 35; Snorri Sturluson, Gylfaginning ch. 7; critical ed. Ursula Dronke (Poetic Edda II, 1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: When Odin, Vili and Ve slew Ymir, so much blood rushed from the giant's wounds that all his kin drowned in it - the first flood of the world. Only one household escaped: Bergelmir with his wife climbed onto a wooden trough (ludr) and floated the deluge, and from the two of them descend all the rime-giants. A Norse counterpart to Deucalion and the biblical flood, the story explains why the giants survived to menace the gods, and makes the enemies of order itself a remnant people saved by water at the making of the world.
summary.zh: 奧丁、維利與偉誅殺尤彌爾時，巨人血湧成滔天洪水，淹沒其族人——此為世上第一場洪水。唯有貝格爾米爾夫婦登上木臼（ludr）漂於洪水之上，倖免於難，其後代即所有霜巨人。此神話與丟卡利翁及聖經洪水平行，既解釋巨人何以存續以威脅諸神，亦使秩序的仇敵成為在世界誕生之際由水救起的孑遺之族。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
The making of the world is inseparable from an act of drowning. In Vafthrudnismal - a wisdom-contest in which Odin wagers his head against the ancient giant Vafthrudnir - Odin asks the oldest question he knows: whence came Aurgelmir's kin, the rime-giants? The giant answers that the eldest of years is Bergelmir, and that when Ymir was slain, the one 'on the ludr' floated the waters of the deluge; on the ludr - the trough or mill-vat, the timber of a primitive mill - Bergelmir and his wife went forth, and from them are all the giants come.

Snorri turns the fragment into narrative. The blood of Ymir poured out so abundantly that it flooded everything: his sons Odin, Vili and Ve had no purpose in it other than the making of the world, and the flood was a by-product of the killing - the first catastrophe was collateral damage of the first act of order. Only Bergelmir and his wife climbed into the ludr and were saved; Snorri adds pointedly that from them a new race of giants is come, wherefore it is said in the old songs that the giants are a very ancient race - older in lineage than the gods themselves even though younger in the world.

The tale carries a dense set of cultural functions. It establishes a Germanic flood myth parallel to Deucalion and Pyrrha in Greece and to the deluge of Genesis and Mesopotamian literature - a theme motif-collectors codified as A1010, the world-flood and the surviving pair. It explains the structure of Norse enmity: the giants are not an original evil but a survivor-population, refugees of a cosmic crime committed by the gods, which grounds the moral ambiguity of the entire myth-world. And it defines the giants genealogically as a people - 'from them are come' - so that the war between gods and giants is framed as an ethnic myth of two nations, not a battle of good and evil.

Scholars have debated the meaning of the ludr: a mill-trough (Vafthrudnismal elsewhere places Bergelmir's mill in Jotunheim), a cradle-like boat, or a raft; all readings keep the paradox that the ark of the giants' salvation is a humble domestic implement of wood. Vafthrudnismal's phrasing also makes Bergelmir 'the eldest of years', a being as primordial as Ymir himself, so that the flood-remnant is nearly as old as the cosmos. Snorri's use of the poem is so close that his Gylfaginning paragraph is effectively a prose translation of st. 35 - a rare window into how the learned Icelandic compilers mined eddic verse for narrative.

The flood is never allowed its full closure: giants will fill the world again until Ragnarok, when the deluge's logic returns - the sea rising, the sun darkening, the survivors once more reduced to a pair. The myth thus forms a bracket around Norse time: from a flood at creation to a drowning at the end, with the remnant-pair the constant of both.

functions: Aition of the giants as a survivor-people saved from the first flood
Norse analog of the universal flood myth (A1010), parallel to Deucalion and Genesis
Frames god-giant enmity as ethnic and historical rather than moral
Documents Snorri's method: prose narrative mined from eddic verse

variants.name: Vafthrudnismal st. 35 (Poetic Edda)
variants.summary: The authoritative eddic version: in the wisdom contest Bergelmir is named the eldest of years, the one on whose ludr the deluge floated, from whom all giants descend - six lines only, no drowning scene, no motive for the flood.

variants.name: Gylfaginning ch. 7 (Prose Edda)
variants.summary: Snorri's expansion: the blood-flood, the escape of the single household, and the genealogical conclusion; adds the explanation that heathen men believed the giants an ancient race.

variants.name: Greek parallel: Deucalion and Pyrrha
variants.summary: Zeus's flood destroys the bronze race; one pious couple survives in a chest and repopulates the earth - the structural twin of the Norse remnant-pair, though repopulation, not enemy-ancestry, is the Greek point.

Ch. 7 (the slaying of Ymir and the blood-flood; Bergelmir and his wife on the ludr). Critical ed. Faulkes 1987; English: Brodeur 1916.

passages.text: Odin asked the giant the oldest of questions: whence came Aurgelmir's kin, the rime-giants, that are so many? And the giant answered that the eldest of years was Bergelmir, when Ymir was slain; the one on the ludr went aboard, they floated the deluge, and from them the giants are come again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vafthrudnismal st. 35 (Bellows 1923); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧丁向巨人問了最古老的問題：奧格爾米爾的親族，那些為數眾多的霜巨人，是從何而來？巨人回答說，在尤米爾被殺之時，最年長者是貝格爾米爾；那一位登上盧德爾，他們漂浮於洪水之上，巨人便又從他們而來。

passages.text: So much blood flowed from Ymir's wounds that with it they drowned all the race of the giants, save one household only: Bergelmir and his wife went up upon the ludr and were saved from the deluge, and from them is come a new race of giants - wherefore it is said in the old songs that the giants are a very ancient people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 7 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從尤米爾的傷口流出如此多的血，他們以此淹沒了所有巨人族裔，只除了一戶人家：貝格爾米爾與他的妻子登上盧德爾，得免於洪水，新的巨人族裔便從他們而來——因此古歌中說，巨人是極其古老的民族。

title.en: Ask and Embla: The First Humans Made from Trees
title.zh: 阿斯克與恩布拉：以樹木造最初的凡人

region.en: Midgard shore (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 米德加爾特海岸（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Voluspa st. 17-18, c. 900-1000 CE; Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to and GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Voluspa st. 17-18; Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 9; critical ed. Ursula Dronke (Poetic Edda II, 1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Walking on the sea-shore, three gods find two trees, driftwood - an ash and an elm - and make from them the first man and woman. Odin gives them spirit and breath, Hoenir gives sense and motion, Lodurr gives warmth, colour and good looks. Named Ask (Ash) and Embla, they become the ancestors of humankind within the walls of Midgard. The tripartite gift is the Norse doctrine of what a human being is: breath, mind, and living warmth, each a divine loan.
summary.zh: 三神行於海灘，得二木——梣木與榆木——遂造最初的男人與女人。奧丁賜予氣息與靈魂，海尼爾賜予知覺與舉止，洛德爾賜予溫熱、血色與容儀。二木得名阿斯克與恩布拉，在米德加爾特的城牆之內繁衍人類。三分之賜正是北歐對「人」的界定：呼吸、心智與生命之熱，皆是諸神的借貸。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
Voluspa compresses the whole doctrine of human origin into two stanzas. The gods - 'the mighty and loving' - dwelt in their halls in bliss and lacked nothing, till there came to them three mighty ones, kind and wise, out of that host - and three gods went to the sea-shore and found there two trees, without strength, without fate-spirit (orloglauss). Odin gave them ond, breath and spirit; Hoenir gave them odr, sense and the power of motion; Lodurr gave them la and litr godr, warmth of blood and fair colouring. The trees become Ask and Embla - ash and elm, or on one disputed reading 'horse and vine' - and humanity begins.

Snorri retells the scene in Gylfaginning with the names fixed as Odin, Vili and Ve: the three sons of Bor were walking along the sea-strand and found two trees and took from them the man and his wife; Odin gave them life and spirit, Vili gave wit and feeling, Ve gave countenance, speech, hearing and sight, and they clothed them. The gifts divide differently between tellings - breath/warmth, mind/motion, colour/speech-senses - which shows that the poem's doctrine mattered more than the exact inventory: a human is assembled from three divine gifts and lives only while all three are loaned.

The myth's deepest resonance is its parallel to the Christian creation of Adam from clay, a resemblance so exact that some scholars have argued for Christian influence on the poem's final form, while others see an old Germanic doctrine of tree-birth. Either way, the choice of material is decisive: humans are not made from the giants' flesh (that is the earth itself) but from trees, living wood standing at the boundary of the rooted and the walking; the Norse imagination later multiplies tree-imagery - the family as a trunk, the person's fate as a wood, Yggdrasil as the world's tree of which each ash is a kinsman.

Culturally the record explains three things. First, human equality before the gods: the first couple receive identical gifts, and no class mythology (unlike Rigspula) is attached to their creation. Second, the fragility of personhood: because the self is three loans, death can be narrated as the gifts going back - breath to Odin, wit to Hoenir. Third, the name of the human race: men are 'of Ask and Embla', an ethnic aition as tight as any founding legend. In Voluspa the episode sits between the golden age and the arrival of the Norns, so that the first humans are born into a world already scheduled for fate - they are given breath, motion and warmth, but not orlog, and fate must come to them from the three maidens under the tree.

The record is also a hinge for the motif atlas: the Greek clay-humans (Prometheus molding men) and the Norse tree-humans (gods finding wood) are the two European answers to the same question - what material deserves to be animated into humankind.

functions: Aition of human origin: the species named for its founding material (ash and elm)
Doctrine of the tripartite self: breath, mind, and living colour as divine gifts
Boundary myth: humans are made of living wood, kin to the world-tree
Liminal setting: creation on the sea-shore, the edge between chaos and order

passages.text: The mighty and loving gods dwelt in their halls in happiness; they lacked nothing, till there came to them three mighty ones, kind and wise, out of that host. They went to the sea-shore and found two trees, without strength, without fate, without breath.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Voluspa st. 17 (Bellows 1923); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 強大而慈愛的神祇幸福地居於他們的殿堂；他們一無所缺，直到那神族中有三位強大、仁慈而智慧者來到他們那裡。他們走到海邊，發現兩棵樹，沒有力量，沒有命運，沒有氣息。

passages.text: Odin gave them breath and spirit; Hoenir gave them sense and motion; Lodurr gave them warmth of blood and goodly colour. The ash became a man named Ask, the elm a woman named Embla, and from the two of them, within walls of Midgard, is humankind descended.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Voluspa st. 18 (Bellows 1923); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧丁賜予他們氣息與精神；海尼爾賜予他們知覺與行動；洛德爾賜予他們血的溫熱與美好的色澤。那梣樹成了名為阿斯克的男人，那榆樹成了名為恩布拉的女人，人類便從他們二人，在中庭的牆垣之內繁衍而來。

passages.text: The sons of Bor, walking by the sea-strand, found two trees and shaped from them a man and a wife: Odin gave life and spirit, Vili gave wit and feeling, Ve gave countenance, speech, hearing and sight, and they clothed the pair; the man they named Ask and the woman Embla, and from them is the race of men come.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 9 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 波爾的兒子們沿海岸行走，發現兩棵樹，便從中塑造出一男一女：奧丁賜予生命與精神，維利賜予智慧與情感，維賜予容貌、言語、聽覺與視覺，並為這對男女穿上衣服；男子命名為阿斯克，女子命名為恩布拉，人類的種族即由他們而來。

title.en: The Dvergatal: Dwarfs from the Maggots of Ymir's Flesh
title.zh: 矮人譜：尤彌爾腐肉中的蛆蟲所化

region.en: Dwarven realms in rock and earth (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 岩土中的矮人之境（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Voluspa Dvergatal st. 9-16, c. 900-1000 CE; Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Voluspa st. 9-16 (Dvergatal); Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 14; critical ed. Ursula Dronke (1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: While the gods sat on their high seats in the golden age, dwarfs came into being: the gods took counsel where to place them, for they had quickened in Ymir's dead flesh like maggots, and were given human shape and made their homes in earth and rock. The Dvergatal catalogs some seventy dwarf names - Modsognir, Durin, Gandalf, Thorin, Gimli - many of which became personal names of real Scandinavians and, much later, characters in modern fantasy.
summary.zh: 諸神端坐於黃金時代的高座之際，矮人悄然誕生：諸神商議該將矮人安置於何處——矮人乃尤彌爾屍身腐肉中之蛆蟲所化，得賦人形，居於大地與岩穴。所謂「矮人譜」羅列約七十個矮人名——莫德索格尼爾、都林、甘道夫、索林、金靂——其中許多後來成為斯堪的納維亞真實人名，千百年後又成為現代奇幻作品中的人物。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
The Dvergatal - the 'catalog of dwarfs' - is a strange intrusion in Voluspa: a list-poem of names inserted between the golden age of the gods and the prophecy of the world's end. Its frame is brief. In the golden age, when the gods played at tables and lacked nothing, there came from the host a third race: dwarfs of Modsognir's kinship, made - or, on the prose version, born - under Dvalin. The compilers' prose in the Codex Regius asks why, and answers with a doctrine: the gods, sitting in judgment, took counsel where the dwarfs should be placed, for they had been born in Ymir's flesh 'like maggots' and were quickening in it; the gods gave them human shape and understanding, and they made their home in the earth and the rocks.

Then follows the catalog itself: Durin and Modsognir as chiefs, Gandalf, Vindalf, Thorin, Fili, Kili, Fundin, Nali, Hepti, Vili, Hanar, Sviur, Frar, Hornbori, Fraeg and Loni, Aurvang, Jari, Eikinskjaldi, Ginnar - some seventy names, many of them transparent nicknames ('Gimli' = fire, 'Thorin' = daring, 'Gandalf' = wand-elf). Snorri, who normally expands, here does the opposite: he copies the catalog almost verbatim into Gylfaginning, adding only the frame of maggots-in-flesh and the assignment of the dwarfs to stone.

The cultural logic is a double etiology. First, a cosmological aition: dwarfs are the decomposers of the primordial corpse, the third order of being that arises from Ymir's body after the earth (his flesh) is made - so dwarfs are literally autochthonous, born of the world's own substance, and their art of working metal in the earth is the craft of the world's flesh. Second, a social aition: the catalog reads like a name-book of Norse smiths, and many names in it are attested as real human names in runic inscriptions and sagas; naming a child after a dwarf was thought to pass on dwarf-luck in craft and wealth. The Dvergatal is thus a bridge between mythic and historical name-giving - evidence that the eddic poets saw dwarf-names as inheritable human names.

Later reception is spectacular. The catalog supplied Tolkien with the names of Gandalf, Thorin, Fili, Kili, Dwalin, Bifur, Bofur, Bombur, Gimli and more - he lifted them wholesale from the Dvergatal in his Old Norse reading, and modern fantasy dwarves are, at one remove, the maggots of Ymir. For a critical digital history of the myth database, the record documents how a one-thousand-year-old list-poem continues to generate characters.

Scholars treat the Dvergatal as a late insertion - its verse style differs from the surrounding poem, and the Hauksbok version places it differently - but even as a foreign body it had to be accommodated: the sibyl could not prophesy the end of the world without first cataloguing everything the world contained.

functions: Cosmological aition: dwarfs as the third order of being, born of Ymir's decaying flesh
Explains dwarfs' autochthony and their craft in metal, earth and stone
Name-book linking mythic names to historical Scandinavian personal names
Late-medieval and modern afterlife: Tolkien's dwarves drawn from the catalog

passages.zh: 於是眾神前往他們的審判座，高位諸神召開議會，詢問矮人應被安置何處——因為他們生於尤米爾的肉體之中，在那裡如蛆蟲般蠕動甦醒，諸神賜予他們人類的智慧與形貌，儘管他們居於大地與石頭之中。

passages.note: Paraphrase of Voluspa st. 10-16, Dvergatal (Bellows 1923); not verbatim.

title.en: The Norns: Fate at the Well Beneath the Tree
title.zh: 命運三女神：世界樹下泉水旁的命定者

region.en: The Well of Urd beneath Yggdrasil (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 尤克特拉希爾樹下的兀兒德之泉（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Voluspa st. 20, c. 900-1000 CE; Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Voluspa st. 20; Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 15; critical ed. Dronke (1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: After the gods give the first humans their gifts, three mighty maidens come from that host to a hall beneath the tree: Urd (what is), Verdandi (what is becoming) and Skuld (the debt still owed). They cut law-staves, carve, and choose lives; they water Yggdrasil daily with clay from the well so its bark stays white; and they assign to every person the life they are to live. The Norse doctrine of fate is thus a legal one: law is cut and carved, and even the gods are bound by what the maidens choose.
summary.zh: 諸神賜予最初人類神賜之後，三位威嚴少女自其族中降臨樹下之廳：兀兒德（已成之事）、薇兒丹蒂（正在成就之事）與詩蔻蒂（尚欠之事）。她們鐫刻法律木籤，裁斷眾生之命；又每日以泉水沃泥澆灌世界樹，使樹皮常白。北歐命運觀帶有法律色彩：命運如律法般被鐫刻，而諸神亦受三女神之裁斷所束縛。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
The Norns enter Voluspa at the precise moment the world becomes populated: lawless they were born until three came - until three mighty maidens, mighty in wisdom, came from that host to a hall beneath the tree, and their names were Urd and Verdandi and Skuld. There they took up the lives assigned, they cut law-staves, they carved, they chose; they spoke the law, the judgments of men, and pronounced the fates. Everything that follows - war, the death of Baldr, Ragnarok - happens under their cut staves.

Snorri's chapter does for the Norns what it does for every doctrine: it systematizes. The maidens dwell by the well of Urd under the tree; they water the tree daily from the well with clay that lies about it, so that its bark remains white against the Ash's wounds; and the dew from it falls into the valley as honey. Besides the three Norns there are many others, Snorri adds, good and bad, kin of elves and dwarfs, who give to every man his life: the good are of the race of gods, the bad of the race of the giants - so that each person's lot is assigned at birth by a committee of fate-workers whose quality depends on which race their norn belongs to. He even names where the three great ones come from: from the hot springs of the Sun, of the Moon, and of Night, blending astrology into folklore.

The cultural function is to naturalize fate as jurisprudence. In Norse law-culture, judgments were spoken from a stone, staves were cut as legal instruments, and debt (skuld is literally 'shall' or 'debt') defined the future; the Norns are the cosmos's law-court. Their names - what is, what is becoming, and the debt owed - are a temporal triad. No myth claims they can be bargained with: Odin himself dies at Ragnarok on a fate cut before Baldr ever dreamt. The record is thus the anchor of the Norse doctrine that even gods are inside fate, not above it.

The motif chain runs from the Norns to the Greek Moirai (Clotho, Lachesis, Atropos) and beyond, and the well itself joins the cosmological geography: Urd's well is where the gods hold their daily court - the thing-stead of the universe - and where Odin pawns his eye at its sister well, Mimir's. Fate, water and law are one system under the tree.

functions: Doctrine of fate: life assigned at birth, law cut and carved
Legal imagination: Norns as a cosmic court speaking judgments from under the tree
Temporal triad of what-is, what-is-becoming, and what-is-owed; no bargain with fate is possible, even for gods
Geographic anchor: Urd's well as the daily assembly-place of the gods

passages.text: Lawless they were born, until there came three mighty maidens, mighty in wisdom, from out of that host, to a hall beneath the tree: one was named Urd, the second Verdandi, and the third Skuld. They took up the lives assigned, they cut law-staves, they carved and chose, they spoke the law and the judgments of men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Voluspa st. 20 (Bellows 1923); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她們生而無律法，直到三位強大的少女從那群體中走出，她們智慧強大，來到樹下的一座廳堂：一位名為烏爾德，第二位名為薇爾丹蒂，第三位名為斯庫爾德。她們掌管被分配的生命，她們刻劃律法之杖，她們雕鏤與選擇，她們宣說律法與人間的裁決。

passages.text: Beside Urd's well the three maidens pour water and clay over the Ash every day, so that its bark never rots; the dew that falls from the tree into the valley men call honey. And besides these there are many other Norns, good and bad, kin to elves and to dwarfs, who give to each person at birth the life they are to live.

passages.zh: 在烏爾德之井旁，三位少女每日將水與泥土澆灌於那棵白蠟樹上，使其樹皮永不腐爛；從樹上落入山谷的露水，人們稱之為蜜。除此之外，還有許多其他的諾恩，有善有惡，與精靈和矮人同族，她們在每個人出生時賜予其將要度過的生命。

title.en: The Golden Age of the Gods: Shrines, Forges and Games Before the Ruin
title.zh: 諸神的黃金時代：神殿、鍛爐與遊戲，及其傾覆之前

region.en: Idavoll, the meeting-plain of the gods (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 伊達平原——諸神的集會之地（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Voluspa st. 7-8, 25, c. 900-1000 CE; principal MS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to

source.work: Voluspa st. 7-8, 25; critical ed. Ursula Dronke (1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: In the first days the gods met on the plain of Idavoll and founded temples and high places, laid forges and made tools, played at tables, and lacked nothing - gold was counted wealth enough, until three giant-maidens came out of Jotunheim with burdens of that too-precious metal. The passage is a lost-age myth and, simultaneously, a template: at the world's renewal the surviving gods will find again on the same plain the golden game-pieces in the grass.
summary.zh: 太初之時，諸神會於伊達平原，建神殿與高座，置鍛爐、製工具，擲骰對弈，一無所缺——彼時黃金只被稱作足夠的財富，直到三位巨人族少女自約頓海姆而來，帶著那過分貴重的金屬。此段既是失落時代的神話，也是一個模板：世界更新之日，倖存諸神將在伊達平原的草間重新拾起黃金棋子。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Voluspa's golden age is six short lines with an architecture of institutions. The gods went to their judgment-seats, the holy gods held council on the plain of Idavoll, and there they founded temples and high places - shrines; with tools, tongs and forges they laid; they made wealth, smithied ore, shaped tongs and made tools; and at tables they played at chess, gleeful, they lacked nothing - no gold, till there came three giant-maidens, mighty-mighty, out of Jotunheim.

The passage compresses a whole cultural program: religion (temples and high seats), law (judgment-seats, councils), technology (forges, tools, smithied wealth), and leisure (the board-game). Its grammar of origin matches Greek accounts of the Olympian order after the Titanomachy - the founding of divine society is told as the founding of institutions. What ruins the age is not a fall from virtue but an import: gold, arriving in the hands of three giant-women, becomes the metal of greed and later the subject of the Andvari curse and the whole Niflung cycle; gold is the first transgression of the gods' economy.

The golden age functions as a temporal anchor in a myth-cycle that knows decline: it is the positive pole against which the first war (the Aesir-Vanir war), the killing of Baldr, and Ragnarok are measured. And in a uniquely Norse move, the age is scheduled for restoration: at the renewal after Ragnarok, the surviving gods again find on Idavoll the wondrous golden game-pieces in the grass - the same chess-pieces of the first age lying where the old world fell. The plain of Idavoll is thus both the site of the first founding and of the second, a palindrome of institutional memory.

For the motif database the record demonstrates a structural rule of Norse myth: institutions are founded by council, and ruins are remembered as recoverable board-games. No other European corpus makes its paradise a meeting-place where law and craft are invented, then lost, then refound with the selfsame objects.

The gold-maidens' link completes the doctrine: the three giant-women arriving 'with burdens of gold' connect the golden age's end to the whole Niflung-cycle - the metal that ends paradise becomes the curse-metal of the heroic corpus, the first import the gods' economy cannot digest. And the restoration-template completes the record: at the renewal the surviving gods find again the golden game-pieces 'in the grass' on Idavoll - the same plain, the same objects - so the golden age is not lost but stored, recoverable by literal rediscovery. The record thus anchors the lost-age family: paradise as a meeting-place where law and craft are invented, lost and refound with the selfsame game-pieces.

functions: Founding myth of divine institutions: temples, law-courts, forges, leisure
Decline-myth engine: the arrival of giant-women and gold begins the economy of greed
Restoration template: post-Ragnarok renewal on the same plain with the same game-pieces
Temporal anchor for measuring all later mythic decline

passages.text: The gods went to their judgment-seats, the high and holy gods held council, and founded temples and high places; they laid forges and made tools, smithied ore, shaped tongs; at tables they played gleefully, they lacked nothing - they had gold until there came three giant-maidens, mighty, out of Jotunheim. And after the world's burning the gods will meet again on Idavoll and find there, wonder of wonders, the golden game-pieces of the first age lying in the grass, which in the elder days they had possessed.

title.en: Mundilfari's Children: How the Sun and Moon Were Set in Their Courses
title.zh: 蒙迪爾法利之子：日月如何被置於天軌

region.en: The courses of the sky (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 天空的軌道（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Voluspa st. 5, c. 900-1000 CE; Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Voluspa st. 5; Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 12; critical ed. Dronke (1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: A man named Mundilfari had two children so fair he dared call the son Mani (Moon) and the daughter Sol (Sun). For that presumption the gods took both children and set them to drive the actual sun and moon across the sky in horse-drawn chariots - horses with frost-manes whose sweat is the morning dew, pursued by wolves who will one day catch them. Cosmic order is thus installed by punishment: arrogance supplies the personnel of time.
summary.zh: 蒙迪爾法利有子女二人，貌美非凡，竟敢稱其子為「月」（瑪尼）、其女為「日」（索爾）。諸神因這僭越，奪走二子，令其駕馭真正的日與月，驅馬車橫越天際——馬鬃凝霜，汗水滴成清晨的露水，並有狼群窮追不捨，終有一日將吞日食月。宇宙秩序由此以懲罰方式確立：傲慢為時間提供了役使之人。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
The sun and moon exist twice in Norse myth: once as the physical lights whose paths the gods laid out from Muspell's sparks, and once as persons - named Sol and Mani, children of the man Mundilfari. The doctrine joins both in one story of punishment. Mundilfari named his children after the great lights, and for that presumption the children were taken up into the sky: Sol drives the horses of the sun, the horses that draw the chariot of day, and Mani steers the moon and governs its waxing and waning.

The machinery is lovingly specified in Gylfaginning: the sun-horses are Arvakr (Early-Waker) and Alsvith (All-Strong), and to spare the horses the shield Svalinn is set before the sun - were it loosed, land and sea would burn. From the horses' manes falls the frost that is the morning dew. The moon-horses are Hrimfaxi (Rime-Mane), who brings the night's frost from his bit, and his son Skinfaxi (Shining-Mane), whose light wakes men to work. Behind both chariots run the wolves Skoll, who pursues the sun, and Hati, who goes before the moon - and of them the sibyl prophesies that one day, feasting on the blood of doomed men, they will swallow the lights, the first sign of Ragnarok.

The myth is thus a triple aition: of the daily path of the sun (a punished girl driving a chariot), of the dew and frost (the sweat and rime of the horses), and of eclipses and the world's end (the wolves forever closing). Voluspa has only the kernel - the sun, sister of the moon, out of the south; her right hand o'er the horse of heaven - a fragment some editors read as an eclipse omen; Snorri supplies the names, the presumptuous father, and the machinery. Time, in the Norse system, is not impersonal: it is labor performed by an exiled family under threat, a mythology of clocks driven by a household punished into service.

The motif's kinship with the Greek chariots of Helios and Selene is evident, and with the world-sun myths of the atlas generally: everywhere the sun is a person in a vehicle; only in the Norse case is the driver the punished child of a father's vanity, and her pursuer an apocalyptic wolf.

The machinery's completion-document (Gylfaginning's named horses, Arvakr and Alsvith for the sun; Skinfaxi for the moon's day) shows the doctrine's systematization: Snorri's catechism assembled the machinery from the eddic fragments, and the wolves' genealogy (Fenrir's kin in the iron-wood) links the punishment-family to the doom-animals - the sun-driver and her pursuers are one household's tragedy. And the comparative frame completes the record: the Greek Helios and Selene drive the same sky without the punishment-frame; only the Norse driver is a punished child, and her pursuer an apocalyptic wolf. The record thus anchors the sun-in-vehicle family: time as labor performed by an exiled family.

functions: Aition of the daily courses of sun and moon and of dew, frost and night
Punishment narrative: hybris (naming children after cosmic powers) conscripts the family into time-keeping
Eschatological hook: the pursuing wolves carry the prophecy of eclipse and Ragnarok
Personification doctrine: the lights are persons employed by the gods

passages.zh: 有一人名喚蒙迪爾法利，他有兩個孩子生得極為俊美，於是他把女孩喚作索爾，男孩喚作瑪尼；眾神因這份僭妄而震怒，便奪走這兩個孩子，將他們安置於天上，命他們驅策拉動太陽與月亮、使其繞行世界的馬匹。

From the horses' manes falls the frost called the rime of the manes, which is the morning dew. Before the moon runs a wolf, and behind the sun another, and of the one the sibyl said that he would in the end swallow the moon.

passages.zh: 太陽由兩匹馬拉動，以冷卻其炎熱，並有一面盾牌置於其前，名為斯瓦林；此盾若被解開，陸地與海洋都將焚燒。從馬的鬃毛間落下名為「鬃毛之霜」的寒霜，那便是晨露。月亮之前有一匹狼奔馳，太陽之後另有一匹，女先知曾說，那後者終將吞下月亮。

title.en: Day and Night as Horsemen: Dagr, Nott and the Calendar of the North
title.zh: 騎馬的晝與夜：達格、諾特與北方的曆法

region.en: Courses of day and night over Midgard (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 環繞人間的晝夜之軌（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Vafthrudnismal st. 12-14, 25; Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Vafthrudnismal st. 12-14, 25; Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 13; critical ed. Dronke (1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Night is a person: Nott, daughter of the giant Narfi, born dark like her kin, first married and bore Audr, then Annar (mother of Earth), then Delling of the light-elves, whose son Dagr is Day, bright as his father's people. The gods gave both riders horses - Nott a horse whose bit-frost makes the morning dew, Dagr a shining steed whose mane lights the sky - and they ride around the world each day. The myth is a calendar aition: it names who drives the daily cycle and preserves the northern custom of reckoning time by nights rather than days.
summary.zh: 夜亦有其人格：諾特乃巨人納爾菲之女，生來如其族般黝黑；她先後三嫁，誕下奧德，再嫁安納爾而生出大地，最後嫁與光精靈一族之德靈，其子達格便是白晝，明亮如其父族。諸神賜予二騎者馬匹——諾特的馬以咬鐵凝霜，滴作清晨之露；達格的駿馬鬃毛發亮，照亮整片天穹——二者每日環繞世界奔馳。此神話是一則曆法起源故事：它確立了誰有資格驅動晝夜之輪，也保留了北方民族以夜計日的傳統。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
The oldest layer is a riddle-answer. In Vafthrudnismal Odin asks whence came Nott and her kin, and the giant answers: Nott was born first to Narfi; she was given to three husbands - Audr, Annar, and Delling - and with Delling, of the race of the light-elves, she bore Dagr, Day; night and her son were given horses by the gods, that they might ride round the world: she is Hrimfaxi, whose bit-frost wets the earth in morning-dew, and he is Skinfaxi, whose shining mane raises light both north and south.

Snorri expands the genealogy into a social map. Nott first married the man Naglfari, with whom she had Audr; then Annar, a giant, whose daughter Jord - Earth - is Odin's consort and Thor's mother; then Dellingr, of the race of the light-elves, whose son Dagr is as fair and bright as his father's people. The All-father took Nott and her son Dagr, gave them fine horses and set them in the sky, to ride round the world in every twenty-four hours - she first with the horse Frostmouth, drops from whose bit make the morning-dew, he after with Shining-man.

The record is thus the Norse calendar story par excellence: it explains the diurnal cycle by a household - a widow of three marriages whose children are Earth, Day, and the first Audr (a name meaning 'wealth', elsewhere the name of a king's line). It encodes the hierarchy of light: night is elder and giant-born, day younger and elf-lit, and the world is governed from the family up. And it preserves the deep northern time-reckoning: Scandinavians counted by nights ('a hundred nights and a hundred more'), so a myth of a night-rider leading the cycle is the calendar's mythic self-portrait.

The social content has been read as proto-ethnological: Nott's successive husbands mark the passage from the age of darkness (giant kin) to the age of light (elf/god kin), a genealogy of transition from the old world to the new that Vafthrudnismal elsewhere makes its business - the whole poem is a quiz on what will remain after Ragnarok. In the riddle-contest frame, Dagr's answer (Delling is Day's father, Nott his mother) is one of the cosmological facts that must survive the end of the world: day and night are meant to outlast the gods.

The nights-reckoning completes the record: Scandinavians counted time by nights ('a hundred nights and a hundred more' - the sagas' dating-formula), so a myth of a night-rider leading the cycle is the calendar's self-portrait - the deep northern custom documented as cosmology. And the family's social map completes the record: Nott's three marriages (Naglfari, Annar, Dellingr) produce the wealth-name (Audr), the earth (Jord, mother of Thor) and the day (Dagr) - the diurnal cycle explained as a widow's household, night elder and giant-born, day younger and elf-lit. The record thus anchors the calendar-story family: the day-cycle driven by an exiled family under punishment.

functions: Aition of the daily cycle of day and night and of the morning dew
Genealogy of transition from giant-kin darkness to elf-kin light
Calendar doctrine: the world reckoned in nights, led by a night-rider
Riddle-cosmology: day/night facts are certified as surviving Ragnarok

passages.zh: 最先，諾特為巨人納爾菲所生；她曾三度出嫁，先嫁給納格爾法利，再嫁給安納爾，她與安納爾所生的女兒便是約德，即大地；第三任丈夫是光明精靈一族的德林，他們所生的兒子便是達格，他與父親的族人一般俊美明亮。

passages.text: The All-father took Nott and Dagr her son, gave them two horses and set them in the sky to ride round the world in every twenty-four hours. She rides first with the horse called Frostmouth, and drops from its bit each morning are the dew; and after her rides Day with Shining-man, whose mane gleams from his crest and lights both heaven and earth.

passages.zh: 眾父之父帶走了諾特與她的兒子達格，賜予他們兩匹馬，將他們安置於天上，命他們每二十四小時繞行世界一周。她先行，騎著名為「霜口」的馬，每日清晨自其銜鐵滴落的便是露水；在她之後，白日騎著「耀鬃」而行，那馬的鬃毛自其頸脊閃耀光芒，照亮了天與地。

title.en: The First War in the World: Aesir, Vanir and the Origin of Divine Society
title.zh: 世間第一場戰爭：阿薩神族與華納神族，及神界秩序的起源

region.en: The walls of Asgard (symbolic pin at Gamla Uppsala, Sweden)
region.zh: 阿斯加德城牆（象徵性定位於瑞典舊烏普薩拉）

period: Voluspa st. 21-26, c. 900-1000 CE; Ynglinga saga c. 1225; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, AM 41 4to (Kringla)

source.work: Voluspa st. 21-26; Snorri, Ynglinga saga chs. 1-4; critical ed. Dronke (1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Laing 1844); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The first war in the world began when the witch-woman Gullveig was burned three times and reborn three times in Odin's hall, and the Vanir - whom the wise gods had cheated of their pledge, Freyja - broke the peace. Shield against spear, the war staled to a stalemate, and the two divine nations made peace by spitting into a vat: from the mingled spittle was made Kvasir, wisest of all, and hostages Njord, Freyr and Freyja came to live among the Aesir. The war explains why the Norse pantheon has two houses, why sacrifice and magic are split between them, and why the gods' counsel, Mimir, paid for the treaty with his head.
summary.zh: 世間第一場戰爭源於女巫古爾維格——她在奧丁的大廳被焚燒三次，又三次重生；被「睿智諸神」以人質芙蕾雅欺瞞的華納族遂背棄誓約。盾與矛相抗，戰事膠著，兩個神族最終以唾液匯入巨甕締結和平：混合的唾液誕生了全智的克瓦希爾，而人質尼奧德及其子女則前來阿薩神族定居。這場戰爭解釋了北歐神譜何以有兩個家族、祭祀與魔法何以分屬兩族，以及諸神的謀主密米爾何以為條約付出首級。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Ynglinga saga via Laing 1844

narrative.en:
The opening of Voluspa's war-fragment is a trial: she remembers the first war in the world, when Gullveig they pierced with spears and burned thrice - thrice burned, thrice reborn, ever anew she lives. Her name, Gold-drink or Gold-drunkenness, marks what the war was about; the sibyl then names her Heid, a witch in every house they saw her, teaching seid, the magic of prophecy, always delighting in evil. Then the war proper: the Vanir, whom the wise gods had overreached with oaths, broke their pledges - for Freyja had been given as a pledge and came back cheated, says Loki in Lokasenna, who claims he was there when it happened.

The prose tradition, Ynglinga saga, makes the casus belli explicit: Odin, leader of the Aesir in their Asiatic migration, cast his spear over the Vanir and began the first war. The Vanir defended their land so fiercely that the Aesir could not prevail, and peace was made on these terms: each side spat into a vat, and the mingled spittle - because no lie can come from it - was shaped into a man, Kvasir, wisest of all; and as hostages the Vanir sent Njord with Freyr and Freyja, while the Aesir sent Hoenir and Mimir to the Vanir. The exchange turns sour: Hoenir is handsome but dependent, answering every question 'let others decide', so the Vanir, discovering they were cheated, cut off Mimir's head and sent it back. Odin embalmed it with herbs, sang spells over it, and thereby gained the head that counsels him - wisdom preserved from an act of diplomatic atrocity.

The myth's cultural functions are heavy. It explains the composite pantheon: two houses, one of sky- and war-gods (Aesir) and one of sea-, wealth- and fertility-powers (Vanir), merged after an ethnic war - the mythic memory, some scholars think, of an actual merger of cults. It founds the ritual economy: hostageship and oath-fines, the spitting vat as the origin of the peace-oath, and Freyja's arrival as the introduction of seid magic into Asgard (the Vanir hostages bring the arts of prosperity and prophecy; the Aesir bring spear-luck). And it seeds the mead of poetry, for Kvasir, born of the peace, is killed by dwarfs whose brewing of his blood becomes the mead Odin will steal - the first war's peace-child turns into the very substance of skaldic art.

The war-fragment also preserves a motif of medieval politics: hostage-exchange as institution. In saga Iceland and viking Scandinavia, peace was sealed by fosterage and hostages; the myth casts the gods in the same legal forms, so that the divine order is literally a treaty, not a family tree alone.

functions: Aition of the composite pantheon: two divine nations merged by treaty
Origin of the ritual economy: oaths, hostages, and the spitting-vat peace
Introduction of seid magic and fertility cult into the Aesir's order
Seeds the Kvasir-mead myth: the peace-child becomes the origin of poetry

passages.text: She remembers the first war in the world, when they stabbed Gullveig with spears and burned her thrice in the hall of the High One: thrice they burned her, thrice she was reborn, over and over she lives - and wherever they saw her, she was a witch called Heid, a seer in every house, and she delighted always in evil.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Voluspa st. 21-22 (Bellows 1923); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她記得世間的第一場戰爭，那時他們以長矛刺向古爾薇格，並在高者之廳中三度將她焚燒：三度焚燒她，三度她重生，一次又一次她存活下來——而無論他們在何處見到她，她都是名為海德的巫女，家家戶戶中的先知，而她始終以邪惡為樂。

passages.text: Then the wise gods broke their oaths with the Vanir, and the shield-sundering war began; spear against shield they strove till the war was worn out. At last they made peace in this way: each side spat into a vat, and from the mingled spittle they shaped a man, wisest of all, whose name was Kvasir.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Voluspa st. 24-25 and Ynglinga saga ch. 4 (Bellows; Laing); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是睿智的眾神與華納神族毀棄了誓約，破盾之戰就此展開；矛對盾，他們爭戰直至戰事耗盡。最終他們以此方式締結和平：雙方各向一器中吐唾沫，並以混合的唾沫塑造出一人，此人為眾生中最睿智者，名為克瓦希爾。

passages.text: As hostages the Vanir sent to the Aesir Njord the Wealthy with his son Freyr and his daughter Freyja; the Aesir sent to the Vanir Hoenir and Mimir. But Hoenir, handsome and strong though he was, answered every question 'let others counsel'; the Vanir saw that they had been cheated, and they took Mimir and cut off his head and sent it to Odin, who preserved it with herbs and spells - and from it he won true counsel in every matter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ynglinga saga chs. 3-4 (Laing 1844); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 華納神族作為人質，將富有的尼約德連同其子弗雷與其女芙蕾雅送往阿薩神族；阿薩神族則將霍尼爾與密米爾送往華納神族。然而霍尼爾雖俊美強壯，對每個問題卻都答以「讓別人來出主意」；華納神族見自己受了騙，便抓住密米爾，砍下他的頭顱送往奧丁處，奧丁以草藥與咒語保存其頭——自此他藉此頭顱於萬事中獲得真確的謀議。

title.en: Kvasir and the Mead of Poetry: How Skaldic Art Was Made
title.zh: 克瓦希爾與詩之蜜酒：吟遊詩藝的起源

region.en: Hnitbjorg and Suttungr's halls (symbolic pin at Gamla Uppsala, Sweden)
region.zh: 尼特山與蘇頓巨人諸廳（象徵性定位於瑞典舊烏普薩拉）

period: Skaldskaparmal c. 1220-1230 (older mythic material); principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to, Codex Trajectinus

source.work: Snorri Sturluson, Edda: Skaldskaparmal prologue and ch. 1 (the mead of poetry); critical ed. Anthony Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: From the peace between two divine nations came Kvasir, wisest of all beings; the dwarfs Fjalar and Galar killed him and brewed his blood, mixed with honey, into the mead that makes anyone who drinks it a poet or scholar. The mead passes through murder and theft - to the giant Suttungr, whose daughter Gunnlod guards it in a mountain - until Odin, taking every shape from serpent to eagle, drinks it dry in three draughts and spits it out over the world, giving poetry to the gods and to men who can master the gift.
summary.zh: 兩神族締和的產物克瓦希爾，是全智的存在；矮人法亞拉與加拉謀殺了他，將其血混合蜂蜜釀成「使人飲之成為詩人或學者」的蜜酒。此酒幾經謀殺與竊奪——輾轉落入巨人蘇頓之手，其女貢恩洛德守於山中——直到奧丁化身蛇與鷹，三口飲盡，再噴灑世間，將詩藝賜予諸神及能承此天賦之人。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain); consulted against Faulkes 1987

narrative.en:
The myth of the mead is the Norse aition of poetry - and it is built entirely out of murder, theft and diplomacy. At the settlement of the Aesir-Vanir war, both sides spat into a vat, and from the mingled spittle they made Kvasir, a man so wise no question could be asked that he could not answer. He traveled the world teaching knowledge, until two dwarfs, Fjalar and Galar, invited him home and murdered him, letting his blood run into two vessels, the kettle Odroerir ('stirrer of inspiration') and the bowls Son and Bodn; they mixed his blood with honey, and the drink formed was such that whoever drank of it became a skald or scholar - the mead of poetry.

The dwarfs compounded crime: they invited the giant Gillingr and his wife and drowned the one and crushed the other under a rolling millstone, and when Gillingr's son Suttungr came for vengeance they gave him the mead as weregild. Suttungr hid it in the mountain Hnitbjorg and set his daughter Gunnlod to guard it - poetry as a giant's treasure under a woman's watch. Odin, learning this, worked his way through the whole chain of exchange. Under the name Bolverk ('worker of evil') he hired himself to Suttungr's brother Baugi for a summer's labor, and demanded as wages one drink of the mead; he bored the mountain through with the auger Rati, turned himself into a serpent, wriggled through, and for three nights was Gunnlod's lover; then he drank all three vessels dry in three draughts, turned into an eagle and flew - pursued by Suttungr in eagle shape - until the gods, seeing him, set out bowls in the enclosure of Asgard. Odin vomited the mead into them (a little he had voided backward, and that is the 'poetaster's share' - the bad poetry given to anyone), and gave the mead to the gods and to men skilled in poetry.

The doctrine packed into this fable is that poetry is not invention but substance: a liquid distilled from the blood of the wisest being, seasoned with honey, hoarded, and finally distributed by the god who owns everything worth having. The chain of possession - gods, dwarfs, giants, god again - is the myth's map of who owns cultural goods: the dwarfs make, the giants hoard, the Aesir circulate. And its ethic is candor about art's cost: every link is bought with a corpse, a seduction or a fraud, so that the skaldic poet sings with full knowledge of what his art was bought with.

Snorri's prologue to Skaldskaparmal makes the use explicit: this is why poetry and scholarship are called Odin's property and find, and why the technical language of kennings - 'Odin's gift', 'Gunnlod's liquor', 'dwarf's drink' - is the working apparatus of skaldic verse. The mead myth is at once an origin myth for a cultural institution (the court poet's craft) and a charter for the social hierarchy of knowledge in thirteenth-century Iceland.

functions: Aition of poetry and scholarship: art as a substance distilled from a murdered sage
Map of cultural exchange: dwarfs make, giants hoard, gods circulate knowledge
Charter of skaldic practice: kennings for poetry cite this myth's chain of possession
Ethic of art's cost: every link bought with murder, seduction or fraud

passages.text: Fjalar and Galar invited Kvasir to their home and killed him, letting his blood flow into the kettle Odroerir and the two bowls Son and Bodn; they mixed honey with the blood, and the drink that came of it was such that whoever drank of it became a skald or a man of knowledge - the mead they called that, and it makes a poet of everyone who partakes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 1 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 法亞拉與加拉邀克瓦希爾至其家中，將他殺害，任其鮮血流注入大釜奧德羅埃里爾以及「子」與「博德恩」兩隻缽中；他們將蜂蜜摻入血中，由此釀成的飲料，凡飲之者皆成為吟遊詩人或博學之士——他們稱之為蜜酒，凡沾唇者皆成詩人。

passages.text: Under the name Bolverk Odin served Baugi the giant for a summer, and took as wages one drink of the mead; he bored the mountain with the auger Rati, became a worm and crept through, and lay three nights by Gunnlod the warden - then he drank all the mead in three draughts, became an eagle and flew, with Suttungr in eagle shape hard after him, till the gods had set out bowls in Asgard's field and he emptied the mead into them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 1 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧丁化名波爾維克，為巨人鮑吉做工一整個夏天，議定以飲一口蜜酒為酬；他以鑽具拉提鑽穿山岩，化為一條蟲蠕行而入，在女守衛岡洛德身旁躺了三夜——隨後他分三口飲盡全部蜜酒，化為鷹飛去，蘇圖恩格亦化鷹形緊追其後，直至眾神在阿斯嘉特的田野上擺好缽器，他將蜜酒盡傾其中。

passages.text: What Odin voided of the mead behind him as he flew, anyone took who wished - and that is the poetaster's part; but the mead he had brought to Asgard he gave to the gods, and to men who are skilled in the craft of poetry, so that poetry is called Odin's property and Odin's find, and drink of Odin, and Gunnlod's liquor, and dwarf's drink.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 1 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧丁飛行時自身後排出的蜜酒，任誰願意便可取用——那便是劣等詩人的部分；但他帶回阿斯嘉特的蜜酒，則贈予眾神，以及精於詩藝的人們，因此詩歌被稱為奧丁的財產、奧丁的發現、奧丁的飲料、岡洛德的酒液，以及侏儒的飲品。

title.en: Rigspula: How Heimdall Fathered the Three Estates
title.zh: 里格詩篇：海姆達爾如何誕下三個階層

region.en: Farmsteads of a Norse land (symbolic pin at Skagafjordur, Iceland)
region.zh: 北歐農莊地帶（象徵性定位於冰島斯卡加峽灣）

period: Rigspula c. 10th-13th century CE (with debated Christian-era additions); sole MS Codex Wormianus AM 242 fol. (c. 1350)

source.work: Rigspula (Rigsthula), prose prologue and st. 1-46; commentary in Dronke (Poetic Edda II, 1997) and Simek (1993)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The god Heimdall, traveling under the name Rig ('king'), visits three households in turn - the hovel of Great-Grandfather (Ai) and Great-Grandmother (Edda), the farmhouse of Grandfather (Afi) and Grandmother (Amma), and the hall of Father (Fadir) and Mother (Modir) - and lies in the middle of each bed. Nine months later each wife bears a child: Thrall, the swarthy laborer, whose children carry servant names; Karl, the freeman farmer, whose children carry farmer names; and Jarl, the noble, whose children carry noble names - and whose youngest son Kon reads the runes and is called Konung, king. The poem is the Norse aition of social class: the three estates are three children of the same god, and the name of kingship itself descends from the poem's closing riddle.
summary.zh: 海姆達爾神化名「里格」（王）巡行，先後造訪三戶人家——曾祖父與曾祖母的陋室、祖父與祖母的農舍、父親與母親的廳堂——並各睡於床中。九個月後，三婦各誕一子：奴隸者，黝黑皺縮的勞役之人，其子孫皆僕役之名；自由農卡爾，其子孫乃體面農人之名；貴族雅爾，其子孫皆貴族之名，而其幼子康能誦如尼文，被稱為「康努恩格」——即王。此詩是北歐的階層起源神話：三個階層同為一位神所生，「王」之名亦出自詩篇結尾之謎。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); consulted against Dronke 1997

narrative.en:
Rigspula is a myth of origin for the whole social order, told as a travelogue of hospitality. A god - one they say was Heimdall, wisest of gods - walks along the sea-strand to a dwelling and calls himself Rig. In the first house the door was open; he went in, and the fire was on the floor, and the man and wife, Great-grandfather and Great-grandmother, fed him with heavy coarse bread, broth of goats, and meat boiled in broth. He lay between them three nights, and nine months later the wife bore a boy, sprinkled with water, named Thrall: swarthy, rough-skinned, crooked-nosed, with a broad back and knotted hands. He grew, took to binding bast and carrying loads, and married a woman with scarred heels; their children are named like servants - Byr, Bomber, Swarthy, Lusty, Fat-leg, Crooked, Cinder - the kinds of slaves.

Rig went on to a well-built farmhouse. The couple, Grandfather and Grandmother, fed him boiled veal and wheaten bread, wine in cups, and he stayed three nights. Their son is Karl - ruddy, bright-eyed, like a little snake - who breaks oxen, builds barns, makes carts and ploughs; his children wear linen, keep dogs and horses, and carry the names of free farmers. And Rig went on to the hall: Father and Mother, silk-bedecked, served him bread of wheat white as snow, wine, venison and birds; their son is Jarl, blond, brilliant-eyed, a warrior in the woods, lord of rings and shields, whose children are noble names. Jarl's youngest is Kon the young, who learns the runes, outflies birds, stills the sea, quenches fire, and understands the speech of birds; a crow tells him to fight, and he wins - and from his name comes Konung, king.

The cultural work is dense. Class is biological and divine at once: all three estates descend from the same god through women of different housekeeping, so hierarchy is an accident of the bed, not of merit or blood pollution - each class carries its own dignity, each its own names. The sprinkling with water (ausa vatni) at birth is a real rite attested in the sagas, here written into cosmic origin. And the poem's frame is a name-book: the lists of children's names are the same name-collections used by real families, giving each estate a life of its own names. Its last stanza is famous for its pun - the rune-riddle that 'Kon' plus the final rune spells Konung - and scholars have argued whether the poem's ending is Christian-era flattery of a king or a genuine mythic close.

For the database the record is a comparative hinge: the Norse three-estate origin myth answers the Greek Prometheus' distribution of skills to humans and the Hindu varna-myth, but with an erotic, biological mechanism - a god siring a nation by sleeping with three housewives - that is unique to the north.

The name-book doctrine completes the record: each estate's children carry their own set of names (the servants' nicknames, the farmers' respectable names, the nobles' ring-giving names), and many are attested as real Scandinavian personal names in runic inscriptions - the mythic catalog doubling as a name-book used by actual families. And the Konung-riddle completes the record: the young king's name plus the final rune spells 'king' - the poem's closing pun debated as either native myth or Christian-era flattery, the corpus's most famous textual crux. The record thus anchors the class-origin family: the estates as three children of one god, distinctive in the erotic mechanism and the name-inheritance.

functions: Aition of the three estates: thrall, freeman, noble - one god as common ancestor
Name-book doctrine: each class inherits its own set of personal names
Legitimates real rites: sprinkling with water at birth written into cosmic origin
Etymology of kingship: Konung derived from the poem's concluding riddle

passages.text: Heimdall walked along the sea-strand and came to a dwelling; the door was open, the fire on the floor, and an old couple at work - Great-grandfather with a bundle of bast, Great-grandmother with her kerchief askew. Rig gave them his name, sat between them, and stayed three nights; nine months later the woman bore a boy swarthy and rough, and they sprinkled him with water and named him Thrall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigspula st. 1-9 (Bellows 1923); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 海姆達爾沿著海灘行走，來到一處居所；門敞開著，火在地板上，一對老夫婦正在勞作——曾祖父手持一捆韌皮，曾祖母頭巾歪斜。里格向他們道出自己的名字，坐於二人之間，停留了三夜；九個月後，那婦人生下一名黝黑粗陋的男孩，他們為他灑水命名，稱他為瑟爾。

passages.text: Rig went on to a well-built house; the couple there, Grandfather and Grandmother, fed him veal and wheaten bread and wine in cups. Their son Karl was ruddy and bright-eyed, and broke oxen and made ploughs and houses; his children kept horses and dogs and wore linen - and Rig passed on to the third hall, where Father and Mother served him wheaten bread white as snow, and their son Jarl was blond and brilliant-eyed, a maker of shields and knots of rings.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigspula st. 10-32 (Bellows 1923); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 里格繼續前行，來到一幢建造精良的房屋；那裡的夫婦，即祖父與祖母，以犢肉、麥餅與杯中之酒款待他。他們的兒子卡爾面色紅潤、目光明亮，能馴牛、製犁、造屋；他的子孫飼養馬匹與犬隻，身著亞麻——里格又前往第三座廳堂，那裡父親與母親以潔白如雪的麥餅款待他，他們的兒子雅爾金髮燦爛、目光炯炯，是盾牌與指環之結的製造者。

passages.text: Jarl's youngest son Kon learned the runes, and could still the sea, quench fire, and understand the speech of birds; a crow told him of a battle to be won, and he went and won it - and from his name is come the name Konung, which is king; so the poem ends with the riddle of his name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigspula st. 40-46 (Bellows 1923); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 雅爾最小的兒子康恩學會了盧恩符文，能平息大海、熄滅火焰，並聽懂鳥語；一隻烏鴉告訴他一場必勝的戰役，他便前去贏得了它——而從他的名字衍生出「Konung」這個稱號，意即國王；因此這首詩以他名字之謎作結。

title.en: Odin's Sacrifice: Nine Nights on the Tree and the Winning of the Runes
title.zh: 奧丁的獻祭：懸於樹上九夜而得如尼文

region.en: Yggdrasil, the World-Tree (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 世界樹尤克特拉希爾（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Havamal st. 138-145, c. 900-1000 CE; principal MS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to (c. 1270s)

source.work: Havamal st. 138-145; critical ed. Ursula Dronke (Poetic Edda II, 1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: In his own voice Odin tells how he hung on a windswept tree nine full nights, wounded with a spear and given to himself, to himself; none brought him bread or drink; he looked down, took up the runes, screaming, and fell back from the tree. The myth is the origin of runic writing and magic: the alphabet is won by a god's self-sacrifice on the gallows-tree, and with the runes come eighteen songs of power - healing, binding, blunting weapons, quenching fire, warding sorcery - and a closing taboo: Odin will teach the eighteenth song to no man or woman, only to a dead horse the king was going to bring back to life.
summary.zh: 奧丁親述：他懸於迎風之樹整整九夜，被矛所刺，將自己獻祭給自己；無人賜他麵包或酒漿；他俯身向下，拾取如尼文，長嘯而落回樹下。此即如尼文字與魔法之起源：字母經由神在絞刑之樹上的自我犧牲而贏得。隨如尼文而來的是十八首咒歌——療傷、束縛、鈍化兵刃、熄火、抵禦巫術——最後是禁忌：第十八首咒歌，奧丁不肯傳授於人，而是傳給一匹國王欲復活之死馬。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); consulted against Dronke 1997

narrative.en:
The myth of the runes is told by Odin in the first person, in the stern voice of a man remembering his own initiation: I know that I hung on a windswept tree nine long nights, wounded with a spear, given to Odin, myself to myself; on that tree of which no man knows from what root it rises. He had no bread and no horn of drink; he peered downward, took up the runes - screaming I took them, and I fell back from there - and then, from the sons of men happy, glad of harvest, grew I, and wise; word from word gave me word, deed from deed gave me deed.

The passage is the origin myth of the runic alphabet and, with it, of magic: the letters are not invented but won, and the price is a god's voluntary death-shape. The theological shock is the reflexive formula - 'myself to myself' - Odin sacrifices Odin, offering and offering-place in one; scholars have long compared the Christian crucifixion and debated influence in either direction, but the Norse myth's own logic is that of an exchange: the god gives the highest thing he has (his own life-suspension) and receives in exchange the highest thing the cosmos has (the runes, the script that names everything).

Then follow the eighteen songs. Their contents are a pharmacopoeia of magic: help in sorrow and pain; the charm that heals wounds; the spell that blunts a foe's weapons; the fetter-snare for the tongue; the counterspell that breaks fetters; the throwing that stops a spear in flight; the fire-song that quenches flame; the charm that turns hatred away; the stilling of storms at sea; the banishing of witches from their horses; the ward against sorcery; the raising of the dead to answer questions; the winning of a maiden's love; and the eighteenth that is never taught to anyone - that I shall tell to no man or woman but to that dead horse which the king was going to bring back to life. The joke closes the sequence: the eighteenth song is resurrection, and Odin has practiced it only on a horse.

The cultural function is to make writing sacred. Runic inscriptions were cut for memorials, ownership, curses and prayer, and - per this myth - are a gift that runs down from Odin's self-sacrifice: the letter-forms themselves are a wound on wood. The taboo of the last song is the myth's moral: the highest magic is hoarded by its inventor, and the anecdote of the dead horse turns the doctrine of resurrection into a barb at the expense of kings. In database terms, this is the Norse 'theft of fire' - the civilizing gift that Prometheus stole is here not stolen but self-sacrificed, and its vocabulary is not flame but letter.

The rune-won doctrine's ritual context completes the record: the self-hanging on the tree is the initiation-rite's mythic form (the ordeal-hanging documented in Germanic practice), and the reflexive formula ('myself to myself') makes Odin both offer and offering-place - the sacrifice's grammar stated in one clause. And the eighteen songs' catalog completes the record: the practical pharmacopoeia of galdr (healing, binding, blunting, quenching, warding, waking the dead) with the eighteenth (resurrection) withheld - the myth's moral: the highest magic hoarded by its inventor, and the dead-horse joke as the doctrine's barb. The record thus anchors the sacred-writing family: the alphabet won by a god's self-sacrifice, the letters as wounds on wood.

functions: Origin myth of the runic alphabet as a gift won by self-sacrifice
Doctrine of magic: eighteen songs cataloging the practical pharmacopoeia of galdr
Reflexive sacrifice: the god offers himself to himself, making writing a divine wound
Closing taboo: the eighteenth (resurrection) song withheld from humans

They gave me neither bread nor horn of drink; I peered downward, took up the runes, screaming I took them, and fell back from there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Havamal st. 138-139 (Bellows 1923); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 我知道我懸掛在風吹的樹上，整整九夜，被長矛刺傷，獻給奧丁，自己獻給自己；在那棵樹上，無人知道它的根從何處生長。他們既不給我麵包，也不給我飲用的角杯；我向下窺視，拾起盧恩符文，我尖叫著拾起它們，然後從那裡跌落。

passages.text: Thence I grew happy, glad of harvest, and wise; word from word gave me word, deed from deed gave me deed. Then follow the songs: one helps in all sorrow; one stills the wave; one blunts the sword; one breaks fetters; one wards sorcery; one stops a spear in flight; one raises the dead - and the eighteenth I shall tell to no man or woman, but to the dead horse the king was going to bring back to life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Havamal st. 140-145 (Bellows 1923); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從此我變得快樂，為收穫而歡欣，且充滿智慧；話語從話語中給我話語，行為從行為中給我行為。接著是那些歌謠：一首在一切悲傷中助人；一首平息波浪；一首使劍變鈍；一首斷開枷鎖；一首抵禦巫術；一首阻止飛行的長矛；一首喚起死者——而第十八首我將不告訴任何男人或女人，只告訴那匹國王打算使之復活的死馬。

title.en: Midgard and the World-Serpent: Building the Enclosure of Men
title.zh: 米德加爾特與世界之蛇：人類圍牆的建立

region.en: The encircling ocean of Midgard (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 環繞米德加爾特的大洋（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230 (older material); Voluspa st. 4; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Snorri, Gylfaginning chs. 7-8, 34; Voluspa st. 4; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916; Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: To defend the new world from the giants, the gods raised a wall around the middle of Ymir's eyebrows - the enclosure called Midgard - and beyond it the sea, whose edge the gods gave to the lands. Into that encircling ocean Odin cast Loki's monstrous middle child, the serpent Jormungand, which grew so vast that, lying in the ring of the sea, it gripped its own tail. The record is a double aition: of the coastlines of the inhabited world and of the apocalyptic serpent that will one day release its tail and poison the sky.
summary.zh: 為防範巨人，諸神在尤彌爾眉毛中部築起圍牆——這道圍欄名為米德加爾特——牆外是大海，諸神把海岸賜給陸地。奧丁將洛基的怪物次子、巨蛇耶夢加得拋入環繞的大洋之中，蛇身長得如此巨大，以至盤於海環之上時竟能咬住自己的尾巴。此記錄是雙重起源故事：既解釋人類所居世界的海岸線，也解釋終有一日鬆開尾巴、毒化天空的末日之蛇。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The building of Midgard is described in Gylfaginning as urban planning of cosmic scale. After the gods slew Ymir and made the earth from his flesh, the sea from his blood and the sky from his skull, they took his eyebrows - the fringe of hair above the great corpse's eyes - and made of them the fortress-wall of the middle world, and called the enclosure Midgard, 'middle enclosure'. Beyond the wall they gave the lands to men, and the sea's edge to the shore-peoples; outside lies Utgard, the out-yard, where the giants live. The world of men is thus literally an eyebrow of the primordial corpse - a thin defensive fringe between two hostile zones.

Then Odin conscripted the enemy's own offspring as the outer defense. Loki's three monstrous children - the wolf Fenrir, the serpent Jormungand and the girl Hel - had been brought before the gods in Asgard, and prophecy said they would cause great harm. Odin threw the serpent into the encircling ocean, where it grew so vast that, lying in the ring of all lands, it gripped its own tail. The World-Serpent thus became the mythic geometry of the ocean itself: the sea is a serpent, and every shore is the edge of its body.

The cultural functions are cartographic and eschatological at once. Midgard's wall explains why the inhabited world is an island-ring with hostile beyonds; the serpent explains the sea's unity (it has one body) and its menace (one bite poisons everything). The image is concentric: hearth, wall, shore, sea, serpent's scales, tail - the last linking back to the first, since the tail is in the serpent's own mouth. And the myth sets up the two signature encounters of Norse myth: Thor's fishing trip, when he hooks the serpent's head (the eye of the ocean glares into the fisher's), and the final battle at Ragnarok, when the tail releases and the serpent rises, and Thor kills it and dies of its venom after nine steps.

Voluspa's opening cosmology carries the same architecture in compressed form: the sun and moon were set on their courses, the ground was green, and then the sibyl sees the Yggdrasil of fate and the genders of men - the middle world already fenced, already fated. The record anchors the motif 'world-serpent' (A-code world-encircling reptile) that the atlas tracks from Jormungand to Leviathan to the rainbow serpent of Australia: the ocean as an animal that has swallowed the world's edge.

functions: Cartographic aition: the inhabited world as an enclosure (eyebrow of Ymir) ringed by hostile beyonds
Explains the sea as a single living body encircling all lands
Sets up Thor's fishing exploit and the apocalyptic release of the serpent at Ragnarok
Anchors the world-serpent motif family across world mythologies
