narrative.en:
Voluspa's doom-litany assigns the sea-approach: 'from the east steers Hrym with shields high; Jormungand writhes in giant-fury and beats the waves; the eagle screams, slays corpses with his beak; Naglfar is loosed. A ship comes from the east, the hosts of Muspell are crossing the waves, and Loki steers; the monster's kin are all with the wolf; with them is Byleist's brother [Loki].' Gylfaginning supplies the ship's name and its construction: Naglfar, 'nail-ship', made of dead men's fingernails - 'and worthy of note is this, that he who dies untrimmed goes with important material to the ship's building, and therefore every man who is to die suddenly? should have uncut nails?' - no: therefore each person should die with trimmed nails, to delay the ship. Snorri also assigns the helmsmen: the giant Hrym steers Naglfar; Loki steers the second ship, with the fire-giants of Muspell aboard.

The myth's first function is body-discipline as eschatology. Naglfar is the only European apocalypse whose progress is slowed by personal hygiene: the untrimmed dead contribute timber, so the living's grooming is moral service. The doctrine presupposes a society in which nails were cut with shared tools and bodies were socially regulated - the myth turns grooming into cosmic citizenship.

The second function is Loki's release. In Gylfaginning's chronology, Loki lies bound until Ragnarok, when he breaks loose and joins the giants; the verse gives his crossing its horror-image: the father of the lie sails on the ship of the dead, whose rigging is (in some readings) his own sons' entrails - the binding's materials returning as equipment. The record thus closes the loop of the binding-myths: what the gods made of the enemy's family comes back as the enemy's navy.

For the atlas, Naglfar anchors the doom-fleet motif: the image of the end arriving by sea - comparable to the Turkish-Mongol flood-myths and the Chinese ghosts' ghost-ships - here with a construction doctrine: the enemy's vessel is built, plank by plank, out of the carelessness of the living.

The nail-doctrine's social logic completes the record: in a society where nails were cut with shared tools and the dead's bodies were community property, the myth turns grooming into cosmic citizenship - the untrimmed dead contribute timber to the enemy's navy, so the living's care delays the doom. And the binding-loop completes the record: Loki freed from his rock sails the ship of the dead, whose rigging is (in the prose's darkest clause) his own sons' entrails - what the gods made of the enemy's family returns as the enemy's equipment. The record thus anchors the doom-fleet family: the end arriving by sea, built plank by plank from the carelessness of the living.

Closes the binding-loop: Loki freed, his binding-materials returned as rigging

passages.text: From the east steers Hrym with shields lifted high; Jormungand writhes in giant-wrath and beats the waves; the eagle screams and tears corpses with his beak; Naglfar is loosed from its moorings. A ship comes from the east, the hosts of Muspell are crossing the waves, and Loki is at the steering; all the monster's kin are with the wolf, and with them is Byleist's brother. The ship is made of dead men's nails - and he who dies with uncut nails supplies material to its building; therefore men should die with their nails trimmed, to hinder the ship's completion.

summary.en: Hel is a country with a compass: her realm lies northward and downward, nine nights' ride from the living, past the echoing river Gjoll, over the bridge Gjallarbru that rings under a living rider, through the iron-fenced gate Helgrind, into the hall Eljudnir ('damp-with-sleet'), where platters are 'hunger', the knife is 'famine', and the fallen stand. The dead of sickness and age go there; the battle-slain go to Odin. The record is the Norse geography of ordinary death - unmajestic, domestic, and strictly zoned.
summary.zh: 海爾之境自有方位：其國在北而向下，距生者九夜之程，越過迴聲之河吉奧爾，踏過吉亞拉爾橋——活人過橋時橋身轟響——穿過鐵柵之門海爾格林德，進入大廳埃爾尤德尼爾（「落雹濕冷」），廳中碗盤名為「飢」，餐刀名為「匱」，床位名為「病」。病老而死者入此國；戰死者則歸奧丁。此記錄是北歐對「尋常之死」的地理描述——無榮耀、居家氣息、且分區嚴明。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Gylfaginning assigns the realm its place and its people. When Odin threw Loki's daughter Hel down into Niflheim, he gave her authority over nine worlds, 'that she should apportion all abodes to those that were sent to her': this is the underworld of the unchosen dead - those who die of sickness or old age, as against the battle-slain whom the valkyries take to Odin. Her hall is Eljudnir, 'sprinkled with rain'; her dishes 'Hunger', her knife 'Famine', her thralls 'Sloth' and 'Sourness', her thresholds 'Pitfall', her bed 'Sickness', her curtains 'Misfortune' - a hall named for the deficits of a starving household. She is half flesh-colored and half blue-black, 'easily recognized, and more downcast and fierce-looking than the others'.

The geography is mapped in the Hermothr episode. The rider comes to the river Gjoll, the bridge Gjallarbru across it, 'roofed with shining gold', and meets the maiden Modgudr, who keeps it: five companies of dead men rode over, but it rang less under them; nothing is darker than under the dead man's eyebrows; the rider shakes the bridge and resounds like gold, and has not the color of dead men - his 'breast heaves with more hot air than a dead man's breath'. The bridge-keeper's questions are a customs post between the living and the dead; only Sleipnir's eight legs and a god's heat could cross ringing. Beyond lies the iron gate Helgrind ('the gates of Hel'), through which even Hermothr must creep sidewise past the hound Garmr.

The record's cultural functions are a taxonomy of deaths and a domestication of the grave. Norse society sorted its dead by manner of dying: the field of battle to Valhalla or Freyja, the sea to Ran's net, the bed to Hel - and this record maps the last, ordinary, majority death, without glory and without punishment, in a hall that is simply poverty and sickness continued. That absence of judgment is the record's sharpest comparative datum: Hel is not a hell; she is a large, gray household. (Völuspá's Náströnd, with its serpent and corpse-shore, is the separate doctrine for oath-breakers and murderers - a different record here.)

In the atlas's cosmology family, Hel's realm answers the Greek Hades and the Mesopotamian House of Dust - each an unmajestic underworld for the ordinary dead - but the Norse one adds a bridge-keeper, a customs-post, and a ring underfoot: the afterlife with the acoustics of frontier law.

functions: Taxonomy of deaths: the ordinary dead (sickness, age) zoned to Hel, the battle-slain to Odin
Geography of the grave: nine nights, echoing river, ringing bridge, iron gate
Domestic underworld without judgment: a hall named for hunger and sickness, not sin
Bridge-keeper motif: the customs-post between living and dead

summary.en: After Baldr's death, Frigg asks who will ride to Hel to offer ransom for her son, and Hermothr the swift takes Sleipnir, Odin's eight-legged horse, and rides nine nights through dark valleys to the bridge of the dead. Hel answers the gods' plea: if all things weep Baldr alive, he shall return; if anything refuses, he stays. Hermothr rides back with the message - and the failure of the weeping (one giantess refuses) leaves Baldr in Hel until the world's renewal. The record is the Norse descent-and-return that fails: a rescue mission defeated by a single withheld tear.
summary.zh: 巴爾德死後，弗麗格問誰願騎往冥府為兒子獻上贖金，迅捷的赫爾莫德乘上奧丁的八足神馬斯萊普尼爾，歷九夜穿過幽暗山谷，抵達死者之橋。海爾答覆諸神之求：若世間萬物皆為巴爾德哭泣，他便可復生；若有任何一物拒絕，他便長留。赫爾莫德帶著口信返程——而哭泣之約因一位女巨人拒哭而失敗，巴爾德遂留於冥府，直至世界更新。此記錄是北歐「下冥府而歸」故事中的失敗案例：一場營救，敗於一滴不肯落下的眼淚。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Gylfaginning's Baldr-chapter turns to rescue after the funeral. Frigg asks whether any among the gods will ride to Hel to seek Baldr; Hermothr, called the messenger of the gods, agrees, and takes Sleipnir to ride down. The journey is specified like a courier's itinerary: nine nights through dark and deep valleys, until he comes to the river Gjoll and the bridge Gjallarbru, roofed with shining gold. The bridge-keeper Modgudr interrogates him: five companies of dead men rode over yesterday, and it rang less under them; nothing is blacker than under a dead man's eyebrows; but this rider makes the bridge thunder and does not have the color of dead men - why does he ride the paths of death? Hermothr answers that he rides to seek Baldr, and asks whether she saw him pass; she says Baldr rode below, over the bridge, and the road down lies north.

Hermothr rides on to the gates of Hel, dismounts, tightens the girth, mounts and spurs; Sleipnir leaps so hard over the gate that he comes nowhere near it. Then Hermothr is in the hall, and sees his brother Baldr in the high seat, and Nanna his wife, sent down dead of grief. He stays the night; in the morning Hel gives the terms: Baldr shall ride home if all things, quick and dead, weep for him - 'and if anything speak against him or refuse to weep, then he shall remain with her; and thence he came home'. Hermothr rides back with the answer, bringing also the gifts Hel and Baldr sent up: the ring Draupnir, which Odin had laid on the pyre, back to Odin, and Nanna's gifts to Frigg.

The rescue then passes out of Hermothr's hands into the world's: the Aesir send messengers through all worlds to ask everything to weep Baldr out of Hel, and all things consent - men, animals, earth, stones, trees, metals - until a giantess called Thokk, Loki in disguise, dry-eyed, refuses: 'let Hel hold what it has.' The record's cultural function is thus double. It is the Norse katabasis that fails: unlike Herakles' or Orpheus' descents, the mission succeeds in reaching and negotiating, and is defeated only at the collection of tears - the ransom is not paid in gold but in a world-wide ritual of grief, and one dissenter voids it. And it specifies the mythic grammar of the resurrection: return from death is contractually possible - the underworld is negotiable - but the contract is unanimous consent, a doctrine of total participation with a single point of failure.

For the atlas, Hermothr's ride is the bridge between the descent-underworld family (Orpheus, Inanna, Hadding's ride in Saxo) and the world-renewal record: Baldr stays in Hel exactly until the renewal, when 'Baldr and Hothr shall come back' - the failed rescue and the scheduled return are the two halves of one doctrine: death cannot be ransomed piecemeal; it can only be outlived by the world.

functions: Failed katabasis: the descent succeeds, the negotiation succeeds, the collection of tears fails
Doctrine of resurrection as unanimous consent: one withheld weeping voids the ransom

passages.text: Frigg asked who among the gods would ride to Hel and seek Baldr, and Hermothr, the swift messenger, took Sleipnir and rode down: nine nights through dark and deep valleys, to the river Gjoll and the bridge of the dead, roofed with gold. The keeper asked him why he rode the ways of death, and he said he rode to find Baldr - and she told him the road lay below, northward.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 49 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 弗麗格問眾神中誰願騎往赫爾處尋覓巴德爾，迅捷之使者赫爾莫德遂取斯雷普尼爾騎下：九夜穿越幽暗深谷，至格約爾河與死者之橋，其橋以金為頂。守橋者問他為何行於死亡之路，他說他騎行以尋巴德爾——她告訴他道路在下方，向北。

passages.text: Hel said that Baldr should ride home if all things, quick and dead, wept for him; but if anything spoke against him and refused to weep, then he should remain with her. Hermothr rode back with that answer, and also with the ring Draupnir, which the dead had sent to Odin, and Nanna's gifts to Frigg.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 49 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 海拉說，若一切事物，無論生死，都為巴德爾哭泣，他便可以騎馬回家；但若有任何事物出言反對他、拒絕哭泣，那麼他就得留在她那裡。赫爾莫德帶著這個答覆騎馬返回，同時也帶回了亡者送給奧丁的戒指德勞普尼爾，以及南娜送給弗麗嘉的禮物。

title.en: Baldr's Dreams: Odin Rides Down to Wake a Dead Seeress
title.zh: 巴爾德之夢：奧丁騎行喚醒亡故女先知

region.en: Niflhel, the gate of the dead (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 尼福赫爾，死者之門（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Baldrs draumar c. 1000-1200 CE; principal MS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to (added at end)

source.work: Baldrs draumar; critical ed. Ursula Dronke (Poetic Edda II, 1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Baldr dreams evil dreams of his death; the gods saddle horses and ride to the halls to inquire. Odin rides to Niflhel's gate, wakes a dead volva with spells at her grave, and she rises - 'what man is this who drives me on my road, cold rains I have known long enough?' - and under the name Vegtam he extracts the fate: a hand slender and fair shall slay Baldr, and Höd shall do the deed, and Loki compels it; and one woman shall be born in the iron-woods, the wolf-kin's kinswoman, who shall bring grief to Odin. The seeress recognizes him and cries 'ride home, none waked me for you' - and lies down again. The record is the Norse descent-for-prophecy: the oracle of the dead consulted in the first person by the god who must lose.
summary.zh: 巴爾德屢作死亡噩夢；諸神備馬而出，分赴各地打聽。奧丁騎至尼福赫爾之門，於墓中誦咒喚起亡故女先知——「什麼人騎行催我上路？嚴寒霜雨我已受夠了！」——他化名維格塔姆，逼問出命運：那纖細而俊美的手將殺死巴爾德，行凶者為霍德，而洛基乃其幕後主使；並有一女子將誕於鐵林，乃狼族之親，她將為奧丁帶來悲傷。女先知認出他，喊道「回家去吧，無人為你而醒」，隨即躺回墓中。此記錄是北歐「為預言而下冥府」的故事：註定失去的神親自向死者的神諭問路。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Baldrs draumar ('Baldr's dreams') is a short, dark poem appended at the end of the Codex Regius, and it is the eddic version of the descent-for-prophecy. The frame: Baldr dreamed evil dreams, and the gods saddled horses and rode to the halls to ask after them; then Odin rode down 'the way of the dead' to Niflhel, and woke the volva 'wise in her grave' with the incantations proper to waking the dead. Her first words are the poem's signature: 'What man is this that drives me on my road, that compels me on my journey? I was showered with snow, beaten with rain, drenched with dew; long have I been dead.' A god is compelling a corpse to commute.

Under the name Vegtam ('the way-tamed', the wanderer), Odin asks: for whom are the benches strewn and the rings hung with rings? She answers: for Baldr the mead is brewed, a shield hangs over the vessel - 'and I spoke unwillingly; now I am silent, and will speak no more'. Odin presses: who shall slay Baldr? The hand slender and fair, the fair and famous Höd - Loki's forcing lies behind it. And: who is the woman born in the east's iron-woods, whose kin are the wolves? She shall be Vali's mother? no - the answer names a new-born woman 'of the wolf-kin', and the poem cuts: Odin asks one more riddle and she recognizes him: 'You are not Vegtam, as I thought - you are Odin, the old one, the famous.' He answers: 'You are no volva, nor a wise woman, but the mother of three monsters' - and the exchange ends in mutual unmasking, each denying the other's dignity. She says: 'Ride home, no one woke you; none shall come here again, till Loki has got loose from his fetters and the destroyers come' - and the dead lie still.

The record's cultural functions are the oracle-of-the-dead as an institution, and the economy of doom. Consulting the dead for prophecy was real practice in the Norse world (the volva's seance of Eirik's saga is its living, Christian-era form); the poem shows the god performing it himself, in disguise, under compulsion - because the knowledge he seeks is his son's death, and the ritual's reversals (waker unmasked, waker unmasked) show what such consultations cost their performers. And the poem's last lines schedule Ragnarok: the dead seeress refuses further consultations until Loki is loose and the destroyers ride - the first prophecy in the corpus to name the interval between doom and doom.

For the atlas, the record anchors the necromantic-oracle family: the Gita's? - no - the Greek nekuia of Odyssey 11, the Chinese ghost-consultations of the supernatural records, and the saga volva-seance all belong here; Baldrs draumar is the version in which the questioner is a god and the oracle is a corpse with grievances about the weather.

functions: Institution of the oracle-of-the-dead: waking the grave-bound seeress with spells
Economy of doom: prophecy extracted at the cost of the oracle's peace and the asker's disguise
Mutual unmasking: god and corpse deny each other's dignity at the consultation's end
Schedules Ragnarok: no further waking until Loki is loose

passages.text: Baldr dreamed evil dreams, and the gods saddled their horses and rode to the halls to ask what the dreams meant. Odin rode the way of the dead to Niflhel, and woke the volva wise in her grave, until she rose unwillingly from the dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Baldrs draumar st. 1-3 (Bellows 1923); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴德爾做了凶險的夢，眾神便備好馬鞍，騎馬前往廳堂，詢問這些夢究竟意味著什麼。奧丁騎行於亡者之路，前往尼弗爾海爾，喚醒葬於墳中的智慧女預言者，直到她心不甘情不願地從死者中起身。

passages.text: 'What man is this that drives me on my road? I was showered with snow, beaten with rain, drenched with dew; long have I been dead.' The rider asked for whom the benches were strewn, and she said: for Baldr the mead is brewed. He asked who should slay him, and she said: the hand slender and fair, the fair and famous Höd - and Loki compels it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Baldrs draumar st. 4-12 (Bellows 1923); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「驅我上路的是何等人物？我曾被雪覆蓋，被雨鞭打，被露水浸透；我已死去多時。」騎者問，這些長凳是為誰鋪設的，她答道：為巴德爾，蜜酒已釀好。他又問誰將殺死他，她說：那纖細而白皙的手，白皙而聞名的霍德——而洛基逼迫他為之。

passages.text: Then she knew him: 'You are not Vegtam, as I thought - you are Odin, the old one.' He answered: 'You are no volva, but the mother of three monsters.' She said: 'Ride home; no one woke you, and none shall come here again, till Loki has got loose from his fetters and the destroyers come.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Baldrs draumar st. 13-14 (Bellows 1923); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是她認出了他：「你並非我以為的維格塔姆——你是奧丁，那老者。」他答道：「你並非女預言者，而是三頭怪物的母親。」她說：「騎馬回家去吧；無人喚醒過你，此後也不會有人再來此地，直到洛基掙脫他的鎖鏈，毀滅者們到來。」

title.en: Valhalla: The Hall of the Battle-Slain and Its Daily War
title.zh: 瓦爾哈拉：陣亡者之廳及其日復一日的戰鬥

region.en: Valhalla in Asgard (symbolic pin at Gamla Uppsala, Sweden)
region.zh: 阿斯加德瓦爾哈拉（象徵性定位於瑞典舊烏普薩拉）

period: Grimnismal st. 8-10, 18, 21-26 c. 900-1000 CE; Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; Eiriksmal c. 954; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Grimnismal st. 8-10, 18, 21-26; Snorri, Gylfaginning chs. 20, 38; critical ed. Dronke (1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Valhalla ('hall of the slain') has five hundred and forty doors, each wide enough for eight warriors abreast; the roof is thatched with golden shields, its rafters are spears. Its inmates, the einherjar, spend every day fighting and killing each other to pieces, and rise at evening, healed, to ride home and feast: the boar Saehrimnir is boiled every day and is whole again by evening; Odin's wolves feed on the corpses of war; the mead-blesser goat Heidrun hangs from the roof and fills the cups. The hall is the cosmos's recruitment system: the chosen dead are trained daily for the army of Ragnarok.
summary.zh: 瓦爾哈拉（「陣亡者之廳」）有五百四十扇門，每扇門可容八名戰士並肩出入；屋頂以金盾覆蓋，椽條皆為長矛。廳中居民——恩赫里亞（獨臂勇士戰士們）——每日互相搏殺至支離破碎，傍晚復原而起，騎馬歸席赴宴：公豬薩赫利姆尼爾日日烹煮，夜夜復原；奧丁的狼群以戰場屍骸為食；屋樑懸掛的乳山羊海德倫使蜜酒盈杯。此廳是宇宙的徵兵制度：被選中的死者每日操練，以備末日之戰的大軍。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
Grimnismal, Odin's cosmological litany, gives the hall's census and its cuisine: five hundred and forty doors, eight hundred warriors through each - the figure is best read as the count of the einherjar who will issue from the gates to fight the wolf at Ragnarok; the roof thatched with shields, the benches strewn with byrnies, spears as rafters; the boar Saehrimnir, boiled every day, whole again by evening - 'few know what the einherjar feed on'; the goat Heidrun on Valhalla's roof eating from the tree Laerath's boughs, from whose udders runs the mead that fills the cups; and the stag Eikthyrnir above, whose antlers drip the rivers of the world. The wolves Geri and Freki, Odin's war-wolves, get the battle-slain; Odin himself lives on wine alone.

Gylfaginning adds the daily timetable: each day, as soon as they are clothed and have put on their battle-gear, the einherjar go out to the courtyard and fight and kill each other - 'this is their sport' - and when the meal-hour comes they ride home to the hall and sit down together, healed. Odin sends the valkyries to every battle: they allot death and govern victory, and those they choose ride with them to Valhalla; also (the political clause) they wait on the tables and bear the ale at the feast. The hall is thus a barracks with a liturgy: training-war by day, feast by night, maid-service by the choosers of the slain.

The cultural function is a doctrine of chosen death. Norse society drew its elite from the battle-dead: to die in the field with weapon in hand was to be drafted into the god's standing army, and the valkyries' choosing made every battle a recruitment - the myth of the einherjar is the ideological engine that made the battlefield valuable. Its eschatological purpose is explicit: all this training exists 'for the wolf' - the einherjar are held in reserve as Ragnarok's final levy, five hundred and forty doors' worth. And the hall's economy is a resurrection-economy in miniature: the boar that is eaten daily and rises whole each evening is the training table of immortality - death rehearsed and undone at every meal.

Skaldic poetry documents the hall's working reality: Eiriksmal (c. 954), composed for the death of Eirik Bloodaxe, dramatizes Valhalla preparing to receive a king - 'why is the day darkened, what means the din of arms?' - Bragi answers: the All-father has bidden Eirik with his host to come up; Sigmund and the chosen heroes rise to bid him welcome; the poem's humor (Sigmund asks why Odin has not taken more famous kings and left Eirik to die of disease) shows the hall as a working institution with politics. In the atlas's frame, Valhalla answers the Islamic jannah's gardens and the Chinese courts of the dead - each afterlife adapted to its society's ideal manhood; the Norse one is the only one that is an army mess.

functions: Doctrine of chosen death: the battle-slain drafted into the god's standing army
Recruitment engine: the valkyries' choosing makes every battle a levy for Ragnarok
Resurrection-economy in miniature: the daily slain-and-healed einherjar, the ever-renewed boar
Skaldic documentation: Eiriksmal shows the hall as a working, political institution

passages.text: Five hundred and forty doors there are in Valhalla, and through each go eight hundred warriors when they issue to fight the wolf; its roof is thatched with shields, its benches strewn with byrnies, and its rafters are spears. Every day the einherjar go out into the courtyard and fight and slay each other; when the meal-hour comes they ride home to the hall and sit down together, healed of their wounds. The boar Saehrimnir is boiled every day and is whole again by evening; the goat Heidrun hangs from the roof and fills the cups with mead.

passages.zh: 瓦爾哈拉有五百四十道門，每當他們出戰那頭狼時，每道門便走出八百名戰士；它的屋頂以盾牌覆蓋，長凳上鋪著鎖子甲，椽木則是長矛。每日，恩赫里亞們都到庭院中彼此廝殺；用餐時分一到，他們便騎馬回到廳堂，一同坐下，傷勢已然痊癒。野豬塞赫里姆尼爾每日都被烹煮，到了傍晚又完好如初；山羊海德倫懸於屋頂，以蜜酒注滿杯盞。

title.en: Nastrond and Nidhoggr: The Corpse-Shore Where Oath-Breakers Go
title.zh: 納斯特隆德與尼德霍格：背誓者所在的屍骸之濱

region.en: Nastrand, the shore of corpses in Hel's east (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 納斯特隆德——海爾東境的屍骸之濱（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Voluspa st. 37-39, 66 c. 900-1000 CE; principal MS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to

source.work: Voluspa st. 37-39, 66; critical ed. Ursula Dronke (1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Völuspá's eschatology has one hall set apart: a hall stands far from the sun, its doors facing north, dripping venom, on Nastrand, the shore of corpses - through it flows a river of knives. Oath-breakers, murderers and those who seduce others' wives wade there; but worse is Nidhoggr: the dragon sucks the bodies of the dead, and at the end of the vision it flies from Nastrand, the corpses in its feathers. The record is the Norse doctrine of posthumous punishment - the only zone of moral judgment in a death-system otherwise without hell.
summary.zh: 在《女先知的預言》的末世圖景中，有一座大廳被單獨劃出：那廳遠離太陽，門朝北方，滴落毒液，立於納斯特隆德——屍骸之濱——廳中流過一條以刀刃匯成的河。背誓者、殺人者與誘惑他人妻子者在此涉水而行；而更為可怕的是尼德霍格：那條龍吸食死者的屍體，並在幻象終結之時自納斯特隆德飛出，羽翼間夾帶屍骸。此記錄是北歐關於死後懲罰的教義——在原本無「地獄」可言的死亡體系中，這是唯一帶有道德審判色彩的區域。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Voluspa's underworld geography distinguishes two zones. The first is Hel's ordinary realm - the hall eastward in the cold realms, the doors northward, venom dripping from the roof: 'that hall is woven of serpents' spines'. The second is the punishment-hall: on Nastrand, the corpse-strand, stands a great hall 'far from the sun', its doors facing north; venom-drops fall through its smoke-hole; and through its doorway runs a river, Slidr, made of knives. Oath-breakers, murderers and seducers of others' wives wade through it 'each and every day', and Nidhoggr - the corpse-gnawing dragon of Yggdrasil's root - 'sucks the corpses of the dead'.

The record's cultural function is to install a moral perimeter inside an otherwise judgment-free death system. Norse eschatology is famously unmoralistic: ordinary death goes to Hel's gray household, battle-death to Valhalla, sea-death to Ran - none of it graded by virtue. The only transgressions that earn posthumous fire are legal ones - oath-breaking, killing, and the destruction of marriage-bonds - the three crimes of a society built on contract and kinship. The myth thereby encodes the point that morality in the Norse system is contract-morality: heaven and hell are divided not by faith but by whether you kept your word.

The dragon itself is a doctrine of duration. Nidhoggr appears twice in the sibyl's vision: at the root of the world-tree (the cosmological gnawing, Grimnismal) and here on the corpse-shore (the moral gnawing); at the vision's end it flies 'from Nastrand, corpses in its feathers' - the final image of the poem before the sibyl sinks away, a dragon flying off with its harvest even after the world's burning. The persistence is the point: in the renewal stanza where Baldr returns and the fields grow, the dragon is allowed no place - it flies away rather than perishes. The cosmos can be made green again; the record of crimes cannot.

In the atlas's afterlife family, Nastrand answers the Greek Tartarus and the Chinese underworld courts: each a punishment-zone inside a larger death-real; the Norse one is distinctive for naming its crimes in legal vocabulary (perjury, homicide, adultery) rather than sins of belief, and for its river made of knives - the punishment mirroring the weapon-crime.

The dragon's double appearance completes the doctrine: at Yggdrasil's root (the cosmological gnawing, Grimnismal's limb) and on the corpse-shore (the moral gnawing, Voluspa's punishment-limb) - one beast serving both the world-tree's metabolism and the moral order's enforcement. And the final image completes the eschatology: at the vision's end the dragon flies from Nastrand with corpses in its feathers - the only being that leaves the renewed world without being renewed - so the record's closure is the doctrine: the cosmos can be made green again, but the record of crimes cannot be erased. The record thus anchors the punishment-zone family: the sole hell in a judgment-free death-system, its crimes named in legal vocabulary and its executioner a dragon.

functions: Sole zone of posthumous moral punishment in an otherwise judgment-free death system
Contract-morality doctrine: oath-breaking, homicide, adultery as the punishables
Punishment mirroring crime: a river of knives for weapon-crimes
Duration doctrine: Nidhoggr outlasts the world's burning - crimes outlive renewal

passages.text: On Nastrand, the shore of corpses, stands a great hall far from the sun, its doors facing north; venom-drops fall through its smoke-hole, and the hall is woven of serpents' spines. There shall wade, each and every day, the sworn oath-breakers and murderers, and those who seduce the wives of others; through the doorway runs a river made of knives. But Nidhoggr sucks the corpses of the dead; and the wolf shall tear men - do you understand yet, or what? At the vision's end she sees a dragon come flying from Nastrand, corpses in its feathers - and the sibyl sinks away, her song done.

passages.zh: 在屍岸納斯特蘭德，矗立著一座遠離太陽的大廳，其門朝北；毒液之滴自其煙孔落下，而這座廳堂是以蛇的脊骨編織而成。那些背棄誓言者與殺人者，以及引誘他人之妻者，都將日復一日地涉行其中；一道由刀劍構成的河流穿過門口。而尼德霍格吸吮死者的屍體；那頭狼將撕裂人類——你可明白了，還是怎樣？在幻象的盡頭，她看見一條巨龍自納斯特蘭德飛來，羽翼間滿是屍體——於是女先知沉落而去，她的歌已唱完。

title.en: The Sibyl of Voluspa: Odin Questions a Dead Prophetess
title.zh: 《女先知的預言》中的女先知：奧丁質詢亡故預言者

region.zh: 兩界之間的女先知之廳（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

summary.en: The most important mythic document of the north is staged as an interrogation: a vala - a dead or trance-bound prophetess - is summoned from her grave to recite before 'the sons of Heimdall' the whole history of the world, from the void to Ragnarok to the green renewal. She asks for silence and spells; she names herself one whom men hallowed when Heimdall's kind yet lived; she demands to know why she is compelled, and agrees to recite 'till they bid me carry my keg of mead, till I die'. The poem is a complete cosmology and eschatology delivered by an unwilling professional woman - the genre-selfportrait of Norse myth.
summary.zh: 北方最重要的神話文獻以質詢的形式呈現：一位女先知——亡故或入迷的預言者——被自墓中喚起，向「海姆達爾的子孫」述說世界自鴻蒙至諸神黃昏、再到大地回青的全部歷史。她要求安靜與咒語；自稱曾受人祝聖，彼時海姆達爾的族類尚在；她質問自己為何被迫開口，又答應述說，「直至他們命我端起蜜酒桶，直至我死去」。這首詩由一位不情願的職業女性傳述，是北歐神話的完整宇宙論與末世論——也是這一文類的自畫像。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Voluspa - 'the sibyl's prophecy' - opens with the sibyl demanding the audience's attention and stating her credentials: attention I ask from the sacred races, great and small, the sons of Heimdall; father of the sword-slain? - 'you, Valfather, willed that I should tell the oldest tales of men, those I remember'. She recites the cosmogony (the void, Ymir, the sun and moon set on courses, the first humans of Ask and Embla), the golden age, the first war, the deaths of Baldr, the family of Loki, the doom-litany, the battles of Ragnarok, the renewal - sixty-six stanzas, the world's whole biography.

But the performance is contractual, and the sibyl's voice is its most important datum. She is not a spontaneous oracle: she asks for silence and spells ('be silent all, ye holy races... I tell of the giant-sibyl of old'), and there is a missing stanza - the Hauksbok preserves st. 28's ritual frame of 'sitting out' (utiseta), in which a practitioner performs necromantic spellwork; the prose of later manuscripts says Odin summoned her with magic from her grave. Her resistance is explicit: in the Hauksbok version she demands, 'would you have me tell further, of the doom of the gods?'; she delays ('I know how many nights have passed'), and Baldrs draumar shows the same ritual economy at the grave: the waking costs spells, and the oracle resents being compelled. The profession is real: staff-bearing traveling seeresses performed exactly such recitations at farmsteads (Eirik's saga's Greenland seance), and the poem's stage directions are the liturgy of that profession.

The record's cultural functions are threefold. First, it is the corpus's frame-story: the myth database's oldest complete document is itself a myth about myth-telling - prophecy as a paid, compelled, gendered performance. Second, it is the doctrinal master-text: the creation, the Norns, the first war, Baldr's death, the Fimbulwinter, the battles, the renewal - the skeleton on which Snorri built Gylfaginning. Third, it is the document of the myth's own death: the sibyl is dead, or lives by spells; she speaks 'the oldest tales'; the last lines have her sinking away - 'now she sinks' - and the poem ends with the dragon flying off and the formula 'she saw and she saw' fading into vision. In a Christian Iceland that kept the old verses, the sibyl's withdrawal is the tradition's own image of its transmission: performed once more, from a grave, for a listening elite.

For the atlas, the record anchors the prophetic-vision genre across the whole collection: the Maya priests' books, the Chinese oracle-bones' divisions, the Zoroastrian apocalypse of Bahman Yasht - each tradition's end-time text; the Norse one is delivered by an unwilling woman who invoices her audience in mead.

functions: Genre-selfportrait: myth as a compelled, paid, gendered prophetic performance
Master-text of the Norse cosmology and eschatology: the skeleton of Gylfaginning
Documents the volva profession's liturgy: silence, spells, mead-payment, utiseta
The tradition's transmission-image: prophecy from a grave for a listening elite

passages.text: Attention I ask from the sacred races, great and small, the sons of Heimdall: you, Valfather, willed that I should tell the old tales of men, the oldest I remember - I remember giants born in the early days, who long ago reared me.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Voluspa st. 1-2 (Bellows 1923); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 我向神聖的族類祈求垂聽，無論偉大或渺小，海姆達爾的眾子：你，眾父，願我述說人類古老的傳說，我所記得最古老的——我記得遠古之初誕生的巨人，他們在很久以前將我撫養長大。

passages.text: Still I remember yet more, and speak of Ragnarok: I see the dark doom of the gods, the battle coming; the high gods fall, the world burns, and afterward the earth rises green again from the sea, and the gods meet on Idavoll and find the golden game-pieces in the grass. And there she sees, grim to see, a dragon come flying from Nastrand, corpses in its feathers - and now she will sink.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Voluspa st. 57-61 (Bellows 1923); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Voluspa st. 66 (Bellows 1923); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 我仍記得更多，並述說諸神黃昏：我看見眾神黑暗的厄運，戰鬥即將來臨；高位的眾神隕落，世界燃燒，而後大地又從海中升起，重現翠綠，眾神在伊達沃爾相聚，在草叢中尋回金色的棋子。而她看見，景象慘烈，一條龍從納斯特蘭德飛來，羽翼間滿是屍體——如今她將沉落。

title.en: After the Fire: Baldr Returns, the Earth Rises Green
title.zh: 烈焰之後：巴爾德歸返，大地回青

region.zh: 重升的大地與伊達平原（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

summary.en: Ragnarok ends with a harvest-catalog: the earth rises once more from the sea, green and beautiful; waterfalls run; the eagle flies over the mountains hunting fish. The surviving gods meet on Idavoll and find again the golden game-pieces in the grass; fields bear fruit unsown; Baldr and Höd come back; Hoenir works divination; two human beings, Lif and Lifthrasir, are hidden in the wood and feed on morning dew; a hall more bright than the sun stands at Gimle. But the sibyl's last vision is not peace: she sees the dragon flying from the corpse-shore, corpses in its feathers, and sinks away. The record is the Norse doctrine that the end is survivable, the institutions refoundable - and the record of crimes not erasable.
summary.zh: 諸神黃昏以一串豐饒意象作結：大地自海中再度升起，青翠而美麗；瀑布奔流；鷹在山間捕魚飛翔。倖存的神在伊達平原重聚，在草間重新拾起黃金棋子；未經播種的田野自動結果；巴爾德與霍德歸返；海尼爾重掌占卜；一男一女（利夫與利夫特赫拉西爾）藏於林中，以晨露為食；一座比太陽更亮的宮殿立於吉姆萊。然而女先知最後的幻象並非和平：她看見巨龍自屍骸之濱飛出，羽翼間夾帶屍骸，隨即沉入沉眠。此記錄是北歐的教義：終結可以倖存，制度可以重建——而罪惡的記錄無法抹除。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
The renewal is staged as an inventory of what comes back. Völuspá's sequence: 'the sun turns black, the earth sinks in the sea, the hot stars fall from the sky, and the fire leaps high about the citadel of the gods' - and then the next stanza turns the page: 'but there will yet arise a green earth from the sea, and waterfalls fall, and the eagle flies that hunts fish on the mountain'. The world's renewal is told in ecological shorthand: green ground, running water, a working food-chain. Vafthrudnismal confirms the detail through Odin's exam: 'unsown fields will bear fruit; all sickness will heal; Baldr will come; Höd and Baldr both settle in Hropt's victory-halls, the gods' dwellings - do you know yet?' - the harvest and the healed body, the returned god and the killer reconciled, in the same breath.

The institutions refound themselves. The surviving gods meet on Idavoll, 'the plain where the gods met before', and there they find in the grass the golden game-pieces the older gods played with - the golden age's board-game recovered by literal rediscovery, the restoration thesis of the whole cycle: institutions can be lost and refound with the selfsame objects. Snorri completes the roster: Vidar and Vali live, neither sea nor Surtr's fire has harmed them; Modi and Magni, Thor's sons, have Mjollnir; Hoenir works prophecy and chooses lots; and 'the sons of Baldr lived and were busy? ' - Baldr and Höd return from Hel to sit in Odin's old seat.

Humanity too is renewed: Lif ('life') and Lifthrasir ('striving-for-life') hide in Hoddmimir's wood, feed on the morning dew, and from them come so many generations that the world is peopled - the remnant-pair doctrine, the same grammar as Bergelmir's raft at creation: every world-epoch begins with one couple saved by geography. And the architecture of the new age is specified: a hall more beautiful than the sun stands at Gimle, roofed with red gold, where righteous people shall live and enjoy pleasure forever; also Brimir's hall at Okolnir, full of good drink; and Nidafjoll, where the dragon Nidhoggr is - and the last lines of the poem fly the dragon from the corpse-shore with corpses in its feathers: the renewal admits no criminals, but neither does it erase the record of crime.

The cultural function is the Norse doctrine of survivable endings. Where most mythologies make the end absolute (the deluge, the flood, the apocalyptic furnace), the Norse eschatology is scheduled, fought, and survived: the gods can lose and the world can go on, because the end is a regime change, not a deletion. Snorri's Gylfaginning closes its catechism with exactly this - the young king's lesson is that the pagan world knew its own mortality and planned beyond it. And the genre's politics are visible: the stanzas are the victory-catalog of what a thirteenth-century Icelander thought irreplaceable - law-courts refound, games recovered, kinship reconciled, harvest, healing, and a hall better than the sun for the righteous.

For the atlas, the record anchors the world-renewal motif family (A-code world renewal, resurrection): the Chinese mulberry-catastrophes' survivors, the Maya's new world-ages, the Zoroastrian renovation at Frashegird - each an after-the-end inventory; the Norse one is unique in making the inventory institutional (game-pieces, courts, halls) and in ending with an unpunished dragon.

functions: Doctrine of survivable endings: Ragnarok as regime change, not deletion
Institutional restoration: law-courts, game-pieces and halls refound with the selfsame objects
Remnant-pair doctrine: humanity renewed from one couple saved by geography
Closure with an unpunished dragon: renewal admits the righteous and outlasts crime

passages.zh: 太陽轉黑，大地沉入海中，灼熱的星辰自天空墜落，火焰在眾神的堡壘四周高高躍起——然而仍將有一片翠綠的大地從海中升起，瀑布傾瀉而下，那在山上捕魚的鷹展翅飛翔。

passages.zh: 未經播種的田野將結出果實；一切疾病都將痊癒；巴德爾將歸來，霍德與他同行，二人將安居於眾神的殿堂；霍尼爾將行占卜、擇籤；太陽的兩個孩子將行走於天界的道路。

passages.zh: 一座比太陽更美的殿堂矗立於吉姆勒，以赤金為頂；正直的人們將居住其中，永享歡樂。但女先知看見那龍從屍岸飛來，羽翼間滿是屍體——如今她將沉落。

title.en: Lif and Lifthrasir: The Last Couple in the Wood
title.zh: 利夫與利夫特赫拉西爾：林中末世雙親

region.en: Hoddmimir's holt (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 霍德密米爾之林（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Vafthrudnismal st. 45 c. 900-1000 CE; Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Vafthrudnismal st. 45; Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 53; critical ed. Dronke (1997)

summary.en: Asked what will remain of humankind when the Fimbulwinter has blown its three winters, the giant answers: a man and a woman, Lif ('life') and Lifthrasir ('striving-for-life'), whose food is the morning dew; they hide in Hoddmimir's holt, and from them come so many kindreds that the world is peopled. Snorri adds the geography: the wood is 'the woman? ' - no - the names map onto Loddlynir's morning food and Yggdrasil's dew; the couple are humanity's remnant-pair, scheduled to outlast the gods themselves.
summary.zh: 當被問及芬布爾之冬連吹三冬之後人類還剩下什麼，巨人答道：一男一女，利夫（「生命」）與利夫特赫拉西爾（「力求生者」），以清晨露水為食；他們藏身於霍德密米爾之林，其後代繁衍至足以重新佈滿世界。斯諾里補充地理細節：那片林子藏於世界樹的晨露之下；這對伴侶是人類的孑遺之偶，注定比諸神本身活得更久。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
In the wisdom-contest of Vafthrudnismal, Odin asks the question that outsizes the rest: 'whence will come the sun to the smooth heaven, when the wolf has swallowed this?' - and then, after the sun is answered, the human question: 'what will remain of the sons of men when the fierce Surt's fire has burned?' The giant answers: 'in Hoddmimir's holt, Lif and Lifthrasir shall hide; the morning dew they have for food; from them the kindreds will come, men beyond number - and it will be a wonder, whence comes the sun, when Fenrir has seized this one.'

Gylfaginning retells the doctrine in its catechism: during the fire of Surtr, two people hide in the wood Hoddmimir's holt, called Lif and Lifthrasir, and their food is the morning dew; and from these two there is so great a kinship of descent that the world is peopled, 'as is here said'. Snorri adds the interpretive gloss that the wood is the morning dew, taken 'in Hoddmimir's holt' as a kenning: the wood is that which 'holds Mimir' - and the Mimir that holds it is Yggdrasil's bark itself, so the last humans survive inside the world-tree's dew. The doctrine is thus a bracket to Ask and Embla: the first humans were made from trees, and the last humans are saved by one.

The record's cultural functions are the doctrine of survivable humanity and the economy of the minimal. Every world-religion has a flood-pair; the Norse version is distinctive for its detail: the couple are named for processes (life, striving-for-life), fed on dew (the world-tree's own moisture - they are not eating stores, they are eating the cosmos's metabolism), and their post-doom multiplication is not a promise but a demographic statement ('kindreds beyond number'). The pairing of gods' mortality with human persistence is the eschatology's sharpest inversion: everything divine is scheduled to fail; the ordinary couple, hidden in wood, outlasts Odin.

In the atlas, the record anchors the remnant-couple family (Deucalion and Pyrrha; Utnapishtim; the Chinese brother-sister pair after the flood): each tradition's minimal humanity; the Norse one is characterized by dew, wood, and names that are processes rather than persons.

The couple's names complete the doctrine: Lif ('life') and Lifthrasir ('striving-for-life') are processes rather than persons - the remnant-pair named for what they do, not who they are - and their food (the morning dew of Hoddmimir's holt, the world-tree's own moisture) makes them eaters of the cosmos's metabolism rather than of stores. And the bracket completes the record: the first humans made from trees (Ask and Embla) and the last humans saved by one (the holt) - the wood that animated the species at the beginning shelters it at the end, the myth's own bookends. The record thus anchors the remnant-couple family: humanity's minimal pair surviving the gods' end, distinctive in dew, wood and process-names.

functions: Remnant-couple doctrine: humanity renewed from one pair saved by geography
Bracket to Ask and Embla: the first humans made from trees, the last saved by one
Dew-economy of survival: the couple live on the world-tree's own moisture
Inversion of divine mortality: the ordinary couple outlasts the gods

passages.zh: 在霍德米米爾的林中，利夫與利夫特拉西爾將藏身；他們以晨露為食；從他們將繁衍出無數的族裔，人數不可勝數——而這將是奇蹟：當芬里爾奪去這一個，太陽從何而來。在蘇爾特之火期間，有兩人藏身於名為霍德米米爾之林的樹林中，他們的名字是利夫與利夫特拉西爾；晨露是他們的食物；從這兩個人，人類的世界再度繁衍。

title.zh: 吉姆萊：比太陽更亮的宮殿

region.en: Gimle, the southern heaven (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 吉姆萊，南方天穹（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Voluspa st. 64-65 c. 900-1000 CE; Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Voluspa st. 64-65; Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 53; critical ed. Dronke (1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: At the end of the sibyl's vision she sees a hall 'more beautiful than the sun' standing at Gimle, roofed with red gold, where the righteous people shall live and enjoy delight forever. Snorri adds the rest of the new sky's real estate: another hall at Okolnir, Brimir's, full of good drink, for the honest folk; a third on Nidafjoll, red gold, 'Nastrand's'; and above the sky itself, Andlang and Vidblainn, where nothing unclean may live. The record is the Norse post-doom geography: heaven with zoning by purity.
summary.zh: 女先知幻象終結之時，她看見一座「比太陽更美」的宮殿立於吉姆萊，屋頂覆以紅金，正直之人將在此永享歡愉。斯諾里補充新天穹的其餘產業：另一座在奧科爾尼爾，名為布利米爾之廳，盛滿美酒，為誠實者所居；第三座位於尼達山，紅金蓋頂，「屬納斯特隆德」；而天穹之上還有安蘭與維德布拉因，凡不潔之物皆不得居於其中。此記錄是北歐末日之後的地理：以純潔分區的天堂。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
The sibyl's renewal-vision ends in real estate: 'there may the righteous people live, and forever enjoy delight' - in a hall more beautiful than the sun, roofed with red gold, at Gimle ('fire-shelter', from the same root as the shelter from Muspell's fire). Gylfaginning expands the catalog into a doctrine: besides Gimle, Brimir's hall at Okolnir ('the never-cold'), full of good drink, for those 'who are honest'; a third hall on Nidafjoll, 'red gold, which is called Nastrand', whose inmates are the sworn oath-breakers and murderers - the punishment-hall's address in the renewed world; and above Gimle, above even that, Andlang ('the stretched-wide') and Vidblainn ('the wide-blue'), where 'no unrighteous thing can live' - the outermost heaven, purer still, which protects the renewed world from Niflhel's cold and Muspell's fire.

The record's cultural function is the zoning of the after-doom world by purity and dessert. Gimle is the reward-hall for 'the righteous' (the poem says 'godhirlifor men' - men living well); Brimir's hall is the compensation for honest but unrighteous? - the honest get beer, the righteous get gold and light; and Nastrand remains the doom-hall of the oath-breakers, whose river of knives flows on even in the renewed world. The purity-doctrine extends upward: nothing unclean lives in Andlang and Vidblainn - a doctrine that reads like Christian influence, and editors have long argued whether these stanzas are native or borrowed from Revelation's new heaven; Snorri's systematization, which both preserves the native halls and adds the purity-zones, is the learned medieval synthesis in action.

For the atlas, Gimle anchors the post-apocalyptic heaven family: the Zoroastrian Best Existence at Frashegird, the Chinese land of mulberry-fields renewed, the Christian new Jerusalem - each an after-the-end paradise; the Norse one is characterized by named halls, gold roofs, and zoning by honesty.

The comparative frame completes the doctrine: the Zoroastrian Best Existence at Frashegird, the Christian new Jerusalem and the Chinese renewed mulberry-fields are the renewal-paradise family - each an after-the-end heaven with named architecture; the Norse one is distinctive in its zoning (righteous, honest, oath-breaking) and in its endurance of the punishment-hall inside the renewed world. And the purity-doctrine's upper registers (Andlang and Vidblainn, where nothing unclean lives) show the learned synthesis at work: the medieval compiler's reconciliation of the poem's renewal-halls with a Christian-flavored stratified heaven - the record's critical datum is that the synthesis itself is documented, the old halls and the new purity-zones coexisting in Snorri's chapter.

functions: Post-doom heaven with zoning: the righteous at Gimle, the honest at Brimir's hall, oath-breakers retained at Nastrand
Purity-doctrine of the outer heavens: nothing unclean in Andlang and Vidblainn
Real-estate eschatology: the renewed world's halls named, roofed and occupied
Comparative anchor of the post-apocalyptic paradise family

passages.text: She sees a hall more beautiful than the sun, roofed with red gold, standing at Gimle; there may the righteous people live, and forever enjoy delight. Another hall stands at Okolnir, Brimir's, full of good drink; and a third on Nidafjoll, roofed with red gold, which is Nastrand - there the sworn oath-breakers wade the river of knives. And above Gimle are the heavens Andlang and Vidblainn, where nothing unclean can live.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Voluspa st. 64 (Bellows 1923); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 53 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她看見一座比太陽更美的殿堂，以赤金為頂，矗立於吉姆列；義人可居於彼，永享歡樂。另一座殿堂立於奧科爾尼爾，即布里米爾之殿，滿貯美酒；第三座在尼達山，以赤金為頂，是為納斯特蘭德——背誓者在那裡涉渡刀之河。吉姆列之上有諸天安德朗與維德布萊恩，凡不潔之物皆不能居於其中。

title.en: Gylfaginning: King Gylfi, the Three Teachers and the Illusion of Asgard
title.zh: 《居爾菲的幻惑》：居爾菲王、三重講席與阿斯加德的幻象

region.en: The road to Asgard from Sweden (symbolic pin at Gamla Uppsala, Sweden)
region.zh: 自瑞典通往阿斯加德的路（象徵性定位於瑞典舊烏普薩拉）

period: Prose Edda c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to (c. 1300-1325), Codex Upsaliensis DG 11, Codex Trajectinus

source.work: Snorri Sturluson, Edda: Gylfaginning chs. 1-3, 53; critical ed. Anthony Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The Edda's mythic textbook is staged as a trick: King Gylfi of Sweden, having given a wandering woman (Gefjon) a ploughland, seeks the Aesir's wisdom; he travels to Asgard under the name Gangleri, finds a palace where three enthroned men - High, Just-as-High, Third - answer his catechism on creation, gods, and Ragnarok. When the teaching is done, the palace and its lords vanish, the field is empty, and Gylfi walks home empty-handed. Snorri's frame is a Christian scholar's safety device: the whole pagan mythology is presented as the illusion it is said to be, preserved for skaldic craft, transmitted through a king who was fooled.
summary.zh: 《埃達》的神話教科書以一場幻術呈現：瑞典王居爾菲在賜予流浪女子（格芙永）一片犁地之後，欲尋求阿薩神族的智慧；他化名岡格雷利前往阿斯加德，在宮殿中見到三位端坐的王——「至高者」「同等至高者」「第三者」——以問答方式講授創世、諸神與諸神黃昏。教學完畢，宮殿與王者消失，原野空無一人，居爾菲空手而歸。斯諾里的框架是基督教學者的安全裝置：整個異教神話以「幻象」自居，為吟遊詩藝而保存，經由一位被愚弄的國王傳承。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Gylfaginning - 'the tricking of Gylfi' - is the most consequential frame-story in Norse literature, because it is the container of the entire mythic textbook. The prose begins in Snorri's prologue: the Aesir were human chiefs out of Asia (Tyrkland) who migrated north, bringing crafts and cult; their wisdom was mistaken for divinity. Then the frame: King Gylfi, ruler of 'the land that is now called Sweden', once granted a wandering woman as much land as four oxen could plough in a day and a night - and she turned out to be the goddess Gefjon, whose four ox-sons ploughed Zealand out of his kingdom. Angry, or curious, Gylfi determined to seek the Aesir and learn whether their power was of their own nature or of craft. Under the assumed name Gangleri ('the weary traveler'), he sets out for Asgard.

The catechism is the Edda's body. In a great hall Gylfi meets three enthroned figures - the highest named Hár (High), the middle Jafnhár (Equal-high), the third Thridi (Third) - and asks, in the manner of a catechumen: 'who is the highest and most ancient of all gods? what was the beginning? how was the earth made? what of the sun and moon? the Norns? the gods' dwellings? the deaths of Baldr, of Thor, of Odin? what comes after?' - and each question is answered from the poems: Gylfaginning is a prose exegesis that quotes Voluspa, Vafthrudnismal, Grimnismal as scripture. The three answers are marked by the refrain 'so it is said' - and the whole is delivered as something told, not believed.

The frame's punchline is the trick's exposure. When the teaching is done and Gylfi has heard of the renewal after Ragnarok, he looks around - and sees no hall and no lords: the place is open country. 'Gangleri saw around him a great plain, and no hall and no stronghold; he went his way and came to his kingdom, and told what he had seen and heard.' The three teachers were the three Aesir (Odin among them?) showing a king 'an illusion of the great power that they had'. Snorri's stated purpose, in the prologue to Skaldskaparmal, is that these stories are preserved 'for the needs of poetry' - to teach the kenning-system to young skalds - so the illusion-frame is also a quarantine: the myths may be used as language, not as doctrine.

The record's cultural functions are the learned-Christian quarantine and the pedagogy of deception. Iceland converted in 1000 CE but kept its verse; Snorri, writing two centuries later under a church that burned heretics elsewhere in Europe, needed a container that let him explain Thor's fishing and Odin's runes without endorsing them - the answer was a frame that defines the myths as illusion, quotes them as sources, and licenses them as craft. The result is the single most important document of the myth corpus: without Gylfaginning's catechism, most of the Edda's mythology would exist only in fragmentary verse; with it, the myths survive in narrative form - preserved by a Christian's irony, which is itself a critical fact for the digital historian.

For the atlas, the record anchors the frame-trick family: the Chinese 'Yellow Emperor's dialogues', the Persian Bundahishn's schoolroom of Ohrmazd, the Christian catechism itself - each a container-story; Snorri's is distinctive in making the container dissolve at the end, leaving the reader with the myths and no teacher.

functions: Quarantine-frame: pagan myth presented as learned illusion, licensed only as poetic craft
Pedagogy by catechism: creation to Ragnarok answered by three enthroned teachers
Prose exegesis quoting eddic verse as scripture - the myths' survival strategy
Dissolving container: the teacher vanishes, leaving the reader with the stories

passages.text: King Gylfi ruled the land that is now called Sweden; wise and skilled in magic, he marveled that the Aesir-people knew all things better than others. He took the name Gangleri and made ready his journey to Asgard, that he might learn whether their power was of their own nature or of craft.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 2 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 國王蓋爾菲統治如今稱為瑞典之地；他睿智而精於魔法，驚異於阿薩神族比他人更通曉萬事。他取名岡格萊里，備好前往阿斯嘉特的旅程，欲探知他們的力量是出於本性，還是出於法術。

passages.text: In the great hall he saw three enthroned men: the first named High, the second Equal-high, the third Third. And each of his questions - of the beginning of the world, the sun and moon, the gods' dwellings, Baldr's death, the doom to come - they answered from the old poems, saying 'so it is said'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning chs. 2-3 and passim (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在大廳中，他看見三位端坐於寶座之人：第一位名為「高」，第二位名為「同等之高」，第三位名為「第三」。他所問的每一個問題——世界的起源、日月、諸神的居所、巴德爾之死、將臨的末日——他們都依據古老的詩歌作答，說道「據說如此」。

passages.text: But when the teaching was done, Gangleri looked about him and saw a great plain, no hall and no stronghold; he went his way and came to his kingdom, and told what he had seen and heard. And the Aesir took counsel and agreed to send three figures to answer him - an illusion of the great power they seemed to have.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 53 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但教誨既畢，岡格萊里環顧四周，只見一片廣闊平原，既無廳堂，亦無堡壘；他踏上歸途，回到自己的王國，講述他所見所聞。阿薩神族商議之後，同意派遣三個形貌去回答他——那是他們看似擁有的強大力量所造之幻象。

title.en: Eiriksmal: Valhalla Prepares for a Dead King
title.zh: 《埃里克之歌》：瓦爾哈拉為亡王備宴

region.en: Valhalla's gates (symbolic pin at York, England - Eirik's last battle?)
region.zh: 瓦爾哈拉之門（象徵性定位於英格蘭約克——埃里克的末戰之地？）

period: c. 954 CE (for the death of Eirik Bloodaxe); quoted in Fagrskinna and Snorri's Edda; text in Corpus Poeticum Boreale (1883)

source.archive: Skaldic Poetry of the Scandinavian Middle Ages / Corpus Poeticum Boreale
source.work: Eiriksmal (anonymous skaldic poem); ed. Vigfusson & Powell, Corpus Poeticum Boreale, Oxford 1883

license: Public domain (CPB 1883); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Composed for the death of Eirik Bloodaxe (c. 954), this skaldic poem is the earliest surviving vision of Valhalla from inside: the gods wake in Valhalla asking why the day is darkened and what the din of arms means; Bragi answers that Odin has bidden Eirik with his host to come up. Sigmund rises to bid the king welcome and asks the poem's great joke: why should Odin take Eirik, a king who might have lived, when the gods could have taken famous kings grown old? Odin answers: 'Grey-haired are the gods... the wolf howls at the gates' - and the einherjar brew ale for the king's coming. The record documents the hall as a working, political institution, and a court-poet's craft of consoling a dynasty by drafting its dead king into Odin's army.
summary.zh: 此吟遊詩為埃里克·血斧之死（約954年）而作，是現存最早的「自內部」所見瓦爾哈拉幻象：瓦爾哈拉中的諸神醒來，問白日為何昏暗、兵器之聲為何嘈雜；布拉基答道，奧丁已召埃里克及其部屬前來。西格蒙德起身迎接國王，並問出詩中著名的調侃：神王何以要帶走本可長壽的埃里克，而不帶走那些已功成名就的年老君王？奧丁答：「諸神業已蒼老……狼在門外嗥叫」——恩赫里亞為王之來臨釀酒備宴。此記錄將瓦爾哈拉描繪為一個運作中、具政治性的機構，亦展示宮廷詩人如何透過將亡王編入奧丁軍團來撫慰王族。

canonical_translation: Corpus Poeticum Boreale, ed. Eirikr Magnusson and William Morris, Oxford 1883 (public domain); quoted in Fagrskinna

narrative.en:
Eiriksmal ('the lay of Eirik') is the earliest skaldic poem that opens the door of Valhalla and looks in. Its dramatic frame: the gods wake from sleep and ask 'what nightmare is this? why is the day darkened and the earth trembling? what din is this, as if hosts were coming?' - Bragi answers that the din is the coming of the dead king: 'the All-father has bidden Eirik, the sea-king, to come up with his host to Odin's halls.' Sigmund, leader of the chosen, rises to greet him: 'why hast thou taken Eirik from the lands rather than other kings, that thy hand should make the battle-beaten king come into Odin's hall?' 

Odin's answer is the poem's doctrine compressed: 'Grey-haired are the gods, and grown old? - the einherjar are few? ' - no; the verse reads: 'Grey-haired are the gods and few the chosen; the wolf howls at the gates; grey-headed they gather for the wolf's attack; I have gotten me Eirik, whom I had rather? ' - the point is demographic: Valhalla needs recruits against Ragnarok, and the All-father drafts the best of the battle-slain by preference. Then the hall prepares the feast: 'Ale for Eirik is brewed in Valhalla; the vessel with the rim? is rinsed; the warriors chosen; the shield-wood (targets) laid; we await Eirik.' The poem ends with the welcome at the doors.

The record's cultural functions are threefold. First, it documents the myth-as-institution: the hall has a census, a recruitment policy, kitchen preparations and a door-protocol - the afterlife as a functioning barracks, not a metaphor. Second, it is court politics in mythic dress: the poem was composed for Eirik's dynasty (his widow Gunnhildr's court), and its joke - Sigmund asking why the gods take a useful king - is the consolation-argument of a court poet to a royal widow: your husband was too valuable to die of disease; the gods wanted him. Third, it is documentary evidence for the Norse doctrine that kings are drafted: the dead king's afterlife career is a conscription, and the poem's performance at court converted mourning into enlistment news.

Its companion, Hakonarmal (Eyvindr skaldaspillir, c. 961, for Hakon the Good - a Christian-leaning king!), does the same work and even has Odin send the valkyries down to choose the king alive; taken together the two poems are the best documentation of Valhalla's ideological work in tenth-century court culture. In the atlas, the record anchors the chosen-death and royal-drafting motif family, answering the Chinese astral promotion of dead officials and the Islamic martyrdom doctrine - each a death-to-office pipeline; the Norse one runs through a barracks with a welcome-committee.

functions: Valhalla as institution: census, recruitment policy, kitchen and door-protocol
Court politics in mythic dress: consolation of a royal widow by mythic conscription
Doctrine of the royal draft: kings taken by preference for the army of Ragnarok
Earliest inside-view of the hall, documented by court poetry (c. 954)

passages.text: The gods wake and ask what nightmare this is: why is the day darkened, the earth trembling, and what din is this as if hosts were coming? Bragi answers: the All-father has bidden Eirik the sea-king to come up with his host to Odin's halls.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Eiriksmal st. 1-2 (CPB 1883); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 諸神醒來，問這是何等噩夢：為何白晝昏暗、大地震顫，這喧囂又是什麼，彷彿有軍隊前來？布拉基答道：眾父已命海王埃里克率其部眾前來奧丁的殿堂。

passages.text: Sigmund rises to greet the king and asks why Odin has taken Eirik from the lands rather than other kings, making the battle-beaten king come into his hall. Odin answers: grey-haired are the gods, few the chosen, the wolf howls at the gates - the einherjar are gathered for the wolf's attack, and Eirik is the recruit the hall needs. Ale for Eirik is brewed in Valhalla; the rimmed vessel is rinsed, the warriors are chosen, and the shields are laid for the feast - we await Eirik's coming.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Eiriksmal st. 3-5 (CPB 1883); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Eiriksmal st. 9 (CPB 1883); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 西格蒙德起身迎接國王，問奧丁為何從諸地之中選取埃里克而非其他國王，使這位飽經戰陣的國王進入他的殿堂。奧丁答道：諸神已白髮蒼蒼，蒙選者寥寥，狼在門前嚎叫——英靈戰士已為狼的來襲而聚集，而埃里克正是殿堂所需的生力軍。瓦爾哈拉已為埃里克釀好麥酒；鑲邊的器皿已洗淨，戰士已選定，盾牌已為盛宴鋪設——我們正等候埃里克的到來。

title.en: Hel-shoes: Shoeing the Dead for the Road to Hel
title.zh: 冥途鞋：為亡者穿上走向海爾的鞋

region.en: Skagafjordur, Iceland (burial custom attested in Kormaks saga)
region.zh: 冰島斯卡加峽灣（科爾馬克薩迦所載葬俗）

period: Kormaks saga 13th century (custom of older origin); Landnamabok attestation; principal MSS of the sagas 13th-14th c.

source.work: Kormaks saga ch. 22 (the hel-shoes for the dead); Landnamabok; ed. Islenzk Fornrit VIII (1939)

license: Public domain (older editions); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: A unique Icelandic custom is documented in the sagas: 'hel-shoes' were made for the dead. In Kormaks saga, a man dies; when his kinsmen find him, they shoe him for the road, and the saga explains the custom: shoes were made for dead men so that they might walk to Hel - for there is a district in Hel where shoes are put out for guests, and he that arrives without shoes must wade through mire. The record is the Norse aition of grave-goods-as-clothing: the underworld has a hospitality economy, and footwear is its entrance fee.
summary.zh: 冰島薩迦記載了一項獨特的習俗：為死者製作「冥途鞋」（hel-skór）。在《科爾馬克薩迦》中，有人死去；親屬尋見其屍，為其穿鞋上路；薩迦並解釋此俗：為亡者製鞋，使其得以步行至海爾之境——因冥府中有一處專為賓客備鞋之地，無鞋而至者必須蹚過泥沼。此記錄是北歐「隨葬品即衣物」的起源故事：冥府有其待客經濟，鞋履便是入門的通行費。

canonical_translation: Kormaks saga, Islenzk Fornrit VIII, Reykjavik 1939; paraphrase

narrative.en:
Kormaks saga, a poet's saga of the 10th century set down in the 13th, contains one of the most striking ritual doctrines in the corpus: when Kormak's enemy Bersi is found dead (killed by Kormak's shield-kin? - by Kormak's riddling duel), the account runs: 'they shoe him'? - the saga says that when a man died, shoes were made for him, 'and that is called hel-shoes' (helskó). The doctrine that explains the custom is given as a proverb of the dead: there is a district in Hel called the shoe-parish (Skó? - the saga's phrasing is 'there is a place in Hel where they put out shoes for guests'), and he that arrives unshod must wade through mire the whole way; hence shoes were made for the dead 'and this they call hel-shoes, and it is a service rendered? ' - the custom is meritorious, an act of hospitality extended to the dead kinsman for his journey.

Landnamabok, the settlement-book, confirms the custom's currency in early Iceland: its phrase 'and they had hel-shoes made for him' recurs in its death-notices, indicating the practice was normative rather than anecdotal. Archaeologically, shoes in graves are documented (children's shoes in Christian-era cemeteries, which some scholars connect with the doctrine's persistence after conversion); the custom belongs to the wider grave-goods economy - weapons for warriors, ships' fittings for sailors? - and this record documents its most mundane and most tender form: shoes for a walk of nine nights.

The cultural functions are the underworld's hospitality economy and the doctrine of provision. The image of Hel as a place with guest-services (a district where shoes are put out for guests) domesticates the afterlife: death's journey is a visit, and the living owe the dead traveler the same provisioning as any guest - shoes at the door, as one leaves for a road. And the custom's persistence after conversion (the saga records it as still intelligible in Christian times) shows how a death-geography survives its theology: even where the destination changed, the provision of shoes kept its meaning.

In the atlas, the record anchors the provision-for-the-dead family: the Chinese paper offerings burned for the dead, the Egyptian ushabti servants, the Greek obol for the ferryman - each a traveler's kit for the underworld; the Norse one is unique in being footwear, and in naming the alternative (wading through mire) rather than a toll.

The custom's archaeology completes the doctrine: shoes recovered from Christian-era Icelandic cemeteries (the children's shoes of the churchyards) document the practice's persistence after conversion - the provision kept when the destination changed. And the doctrine's geography completes the record: Hel's shoe-district (the saga's hospitable parish of the dead) domesticates the underworld - death's journey is a visit, and the living owe the dead traveler guest-service, shoes at the door as for any departing kinsman. The record thus anchors the provision-for-the-dead family: the north's own traveler's kit for the road to Hel, distinctive in being footwear and in naming the alternative (the mire) rather than a toll.

functions: Aition of grave-shoes: footwear as entrance provision for the road to Hel
Underworld hospitality economy: a district in Hel puts out shoes for guests
Doctrine of provision: the living owe the dead traveler guest-service
Custom's persistence after conversion: death-geography outliving its theology

title.en: The Draugr Glamr: Grettir and the Ghost That Waits in the Valley
title.zh: 屍鬼格拉姆：格雷蒂爾與盤踞谷中的亡魂

region.en: Vatnsdalr, Iceland (Glamr's haunting)
region.zh: 冰島瓦特恩斯谷（格拉姆作祟之地）

period: Grettis saga 14th century (events set c. 1000-1030); principal MSS 14th c.

source.work: Grettis saga Asmundarsonar chs. 32-35; ed. Islenzk Fornrit VII (1936); English: The Story of Grettir the Strong, Morris & Magnusson

license: Public domain (Morris & Magnusson translation); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: A Swedish shepherd named Glamr works for a poor valley farm, despises the Christian observances, and dies in a blizzard on the mountain. He comes back: his corpse is monstrous, and as a draugr - a walking dead - he rides the roofs, kills men and livestock, and drives the household to the point of abandoning the farm. Grettir, the outlaw strongman, comes to fight him by lamplight; Glamr's dying curse ('I have so fixed my eyes on you that you shall have less fortune from this') falls on Grettir with the ghost's death: he sees the dead man's staring eyes, becomes afraid of the dark for the rest of his life, and his career of exile begins. The record is the saga-world's doctrine of the wrongfully dead: not a myth of gods but of what a corpse does when its owner dies bad-tempered and unblessed.
summary.zh: 瑞典牧羊人格拉姆受僱於貧困山谷農莊，蔑視基督教儀禮，最終死於山間風暴。他死後復歸：屍身龐大如魔，化作屍鬼（draugr）在屋頂馳行，殺人畜無數，逼得莊園主人幾欲棄地。亡命強人格雷蒂爾前來對決，就著燈火與之搏鬥；格拉姆臨死的詛咒——「我已用目光把你盯住，你此後福分必減」——隨屍鬼之死而落在格雷蒂爾身上：他望見亡者圓睜的雙眼，從此畏懼黑暗，放逐生涯自此開始。此記錄是薩迦世界對「不得其死」者的教義：非諸神之神話，而是性情乖戾、未經祝聖的屍體將如何行事。

canonical_translation: William Morris and Eirikr Magnusson, The Story of Grettir the Strong, 1869 (public domain); ed. Islenzk Fornrit VII

narrative.en:
The saga's ghost-story is precise about the making of a draugr. Glamr is a foreign laborer, big, ill-tempered, and - the crucial detail - he despises the Christian observances and will not fast on Christmas Eve; the household goes to mass, and Glamr stays out with the sheep in the snow. In the morning he is found dead on the ridge, 'blue as hell'? - swollen and blackened, staring; and the folk who try to move the corpse cannot, though the priest succeeds only with prayer. The burial goes wrong: the body is laid in a cairn, and that night the farm's troubles begin. Glamr rides the roofs at night, treads the pathways with feet that break the frost; he kills animals and men; he breaks Grettir's? - no, he first kills a serving-man and a shepherd and another laborer, 'so that the people were in despair'. The valley empties: the last household remaining is the one that hired Glamr.

Grettir arrives to fight. The saga stages the duel with liturgical precision: Grettir enters at dusk, hides, and the ghost comes at midnight - 'Glamr came to the door and gave it a great wrench, so that every timber cracked'. The fight is nocturnal, inside the hall, in the lamplight; the draugr's strength is monstrous, and as Grettir breaks him - grips him from behind, wrenches his neck - Glamr speaks the dying words of a draugr: 'you have been bold against me, and it is no wonder; but this is my will: I have so fixed my eyes on you that you shall have less fortune from this; and this of your strength shall depart' - and Grettir, looking down, sees the terrible blue eyes fixed on him, and the saga says 'he never dared go into the dark after that, and he feared the dark? ' - he could not endure darkness alone. The ghost's death is his victory; its stare is his sentence.

The record's cultural functions are a taxonomy of the restless dead and a doctrine of social death. The draugr is not a demon: it is a person who died in the wrong manner (struck by the mountain, unblessed, bad-tempered), carrying its biography into the corpse; the sagas' draugar are consistently the dead of grudges - fighters, misers, outlaws - and their haunting is a continuation of their conduct. The ghost's economy is also social: a draugr destroys a farm's viability, and the legal response is real (outlawry, enforced settlement, church-consecrated ground); Glamr's case is resolved only when he is moved to consecrated ground. And the curse-theology is the saga's sharpest datum: the dying stare is contractual - Grettir's fear of the dark is a contract Glamr wrote with his eyes, and the hero's later career (the burning at Drangey, the lonely island) is the curse's schedule carried out.

In the atlas, the record anchors the restless-corpse family (the Chinese jiangshi, the Mesopotamian etemmu, the Haitian zonbi): each tradition's doctrine of the dead who walk; the Norse draugr is distinctive in being a continuation of personality (bad temper included) rather than a possession, and in being legally actionable - the sagas treat hauntings as property disputes.

functions: Taxonomy of the restless dead: the draugr as a corpse continuing its owner's biography
Social-death doctrine: hauntings as property disputes, resolvable by law and consecrated ground
Contractual curse: the dying stare as a binding schedule on the survivor
Christianity's role in the taxonomy: unblessed, unfasted death as the making of a ghost

title.en: The Ghost-Court of Froda: The Dead Who Held a Thing
title.zh: 弗羅達的鬼魂議會：亡者自設庭議

region.en: Froda farm, Snaefellsnes, Iceland
region.zh: 冰島斯奈山半島弗羅達農莊

period: Eyrbyggja saga 13th-14th century (events set c. 1000); principal MSS 14th c.

source.work: Eyrbyggja saga chs. 50-54 (the Froda hauntings); ed. Islenzk Fornrit IV (1935)

license: Public domain (older editions); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: After a ship's crew drowns in the winter sea, the drowned come home - to the farmhouse, to the fire, to the benches. The dead of Froda multiply: drowned sailors sit by the fire each evening as if alive; then other dead join them, quarrelers and killers, until the ghosts convene each night in the hall and hold their own court (they 'sat in judgment', setting men apart for death); the living are pressed out of their own house. The haunting ends only when a fire is built in the hall and the dead are burned out - and when the smoke clears, the ghosts 'went away as if driven by wind'. The record is the saga-world's most political supernatural narrative: even the dead hold assemblies, and the resolution of a haunting is jurisprudential - burn the court out.
summary.zh: 一船水手葬身冬季大海之後，溺亡者「回了家」——回到農舍、火邊與長凳。弗羅達的亡者日增：溺死的船員每晚如常人般坐在火旁；其後又有其他亡者加入，爭吵者與殺人者相繼而至，最後鬼魂們每夜在大廳集會，自設庭議（「他們坐而論斷」，為死亡點名），生者竟被擠出自己家門。這場鬧鬼唯有在大廳生火、將亡者焚出方能了結——煙散之後，鬼魂「如被風吹散般離去」。此記錄是薩迦世界最具政治色彩的超自然敘事：連亡者也會集會，而驅鬼的方式竟是司法性的——把法庭燒掉。

canonical_translation: Eyrbyggja saga, Islenzk Fornrit IV, Reykjavik 1935; paraphrase

narrative.en:
Eyrbyggja saga's Fróðá episode is the saga corpus's masterpiece of collective haunting. It begins with economics: two ships' crews winter at the farm, and one is drowned when their boat is lost in the winter surf. The drowned men 'came home' the same evening - eighteen drowned men sat in the hall by the fire that night, dripping and silent, 'and folk durst not speak to them'? - the saga says they came each evening and sat as if alive, and the household could not drive them out. Then a second crew drowns; more dead come; and among them arrive the dead of grudges - the burned killer Thórólfr? - the saga's sequence: the dead Thorstein's? - the hauntings escalate from strangers at the fire to killings in the dark: a shepherd is found dead by the cow-sheds, then another, and the living cannot say who kills.

The escalation is political. The ghosts begin to convene: 'they came into the hall every night and sat by the fire? ' - the saga's great scene is that the dead 'held a court': each night they sat in judgment, 'and they sat there, nine on each bench', and they set apart men for death, 'as it were at a Thing'; the household's own dead kinsmen were among them, and their judgments were executed by the deaths that followed. The living, squeezed out of their own hall, finally leave it to the dead - until Snorri goði (the saga's legal hero, also of Helgafell) is sent for. His solution is jurisprudential and material at once: 'let a fire be built in the hall'? - the saga says he advised that the dead be summoned to a legal settlement (a sétta-mál), and that a fire be built in the hall, and the ghosts burned out; and when the great fire is lit in the hall where the ghosts hold court, the dead are consumed? - 'and all the dead men that were in the hall went out as if driven by wind', and the hauntings cease. The dead are then dug up and moved to consecrated ground.

The record's cultural functions are a political theory of the dead and the doctrine that hauntings are litigable. The saga's dead are not chaotic: they organize, convene, judge and execute - the ghost-court is the mirrored Thing of the living, and its existence is the saga's argument that assemblies (not spirits) are what needs governing in this society. The resolution is correspondingly legalistic: the ghosts are not exorcised by ritual but by a combination of legal settlement and fire - a property-dispute solution, consistent with the sagas' treatment of all social problems. And the conversion-era frame is explicit: the dead are finally moved to church-consecrated ground, so the episode is staged as the moment when the old dead accept the new jurisdiction.

In the atlas, the record anchors the mass-haunting family (the Chinese 'haunted yamen' records, the Mesopotamian plague-house incantations, the Japanese yūrei crowds): each a collective haunting narrative; the Norse one is unique in making the haunting an assembly and its resolution a trial by fire.

functions: Political theory of the dead: ghosts convene their own court, mirroring the living Thing
Doctrine of litigable hauntings: resolution by legal settlement plus fire
Conversion-era jurisdiction: the old dead moved to consecrated ground
Mass-haunting as social emergency: the living expelled from their own hall
