summary.en: Hel is Loki's daughter by the giantess Angrboda: cast down by Odin into Niflheim, she is given authority over nine worlds 'to apportion abodes to those sent to her'. Her body is the doctrine: half flesh-colored and alive-looking, half blue-black and dead; her face is 'more downcast and fierce' than others'. Lokasenna confirms her office in Loki's own taunt: it was Hel's hand that took the ring Draupnir from Baldr's pyre? - no: Loki says Odin laid the ring on the pyre and Hel received it; her power is the power to receive. The record is the Norse personification of the ordinary death: a goddess who is herself half-dead, ruling the unchosen majority.
summary.zh: 海爾是洛基與女巨人安格爾波達之女：被奧丁貶入尼福爾海姆，獲掌九界之權，「為被遣至她處者分配居所」。她的身體即是教義：半邊肉色似生者，半邊青黑如死者；其面容「比他人更陰鬱凶厲」。《洛基的吵罵》中洛基親口證實她的職能：奧丁將德羅普尼爾指環放於巴爾德火葬堆，由海爾收下——她的權力便是「收下」。此記錄是北歐對「尋常之死」的人格化：一位自身半死的神，統轄未經挑選的眾多亡者。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Gylfaginning introduces Hel in the same chapter as her brothers, and her portrait is the shortest but the most complete. Loki had three children by Angrboda: Fenrir the wolf, Jormungand the serpent, and Hel - 'a girl'. When the gods learn what a brood is being reared in Jotunheim, the All-father sends messengers to bring them to him; the serpent he throws into the sea, the wolf he binds, and Hel he 'cast down into Niflheim', giving her authority over nine worlds, 'that she should apportion all abodes to those that were sent to her': this is Hel's realm, the ninth world, where the dead of sickness and age go. Her body is a cosmological diagram: 'half of her is blue-black and half flesh-colored, and she is easily known; and, further, she is more downcast and fierce-looking than the others'. The half-body reads the realm: living side up, dead side down; the gods' world above, the dead's below.

The eddic poems give her the office's flavor. In Lokasenna's flyting, Loki - her own father - taunts Frigg with the fact of Baldr's stay in Hel and praises her realm as obedient: 'Be silent, Frigg... thou hast ever been mad after men; because? ' - and, of the ring: 'Odin's son set the ring on Baldr's pyre; and Hel received it' - the goddess as the receiver of gifts, the custom-house of the dead. In Hyndluljod's genealogical litany she is 'Hel' among Loki's family, and Baldrs draumar's geography shows her court in action (the benches strewn for Baldr, the mead brewed). Her rulership is administrative rather than moral: she is not a judge, and Nastrand's punishments are a separate doctrine; her power is custody.

The record's cultural functions are the personification of ordinary death and the doctrine of the half-body. Norse myth has no god of the grave-buried war-hero (that is Odin's office) and no god of the drowned (Ran's); Hel is the personification of the majority death, and her body's split is the myth's way of saying that she herself stands on both sides of the border - a goddess who has never been alive and cannot fully die. The name gave English 'hell' through Christian reception, and the semantic history is a critical-digital-history datum in itself: the same word, meaning the gray household of the ordinary dead, was re-lexicalized as the place of punishment; this record preserves the older referent.

In the atlas, Hel answers the Greek Hades (the personified realm-ruler), the Mesopotamian Ereshkigal, and the Japanese Yomi's Izanami - each a death-personification; the Norse one is distinctive in being half-dead in body, female, and the child of the trickster rather than of the first gods.

functions: Personification of the ordinary death: ruler of the majority dead, without moral judgment
Half-body doctrine: the goddess herself split between living and dead sides
Custody office: the receiver of the dead and of the pyre-gifts
Semantic-historical datum: 'Hel' as the older referent of the word later meaning 'hell'

passages.text: Loki had three children by Angrboda the giantess: Fenrir the wolf, Jormungand the serpent, and Hel, a girl. The All-father cast her down into Niflheim and gave her authority over nine worlds, that she should apportion all abodes to those that were sent to her.

passages.zh: 洛基與女巨人安格爾波達生了三個孩子：狼芬里爾、蛇耶夢加得，以及一個女兒赫爾。眾父將她貶入尼弗爾海姆，賜她統轄九界的權柄，要她為所有被送到她那裡的人分配居所。

passages.text: Half of her is blue-black and half flesh-colored, and she is easily known; and she is more downcast and fierce-looking than the others. Her hall is Eljudnir, her dish Hunger, her knife Famine. And Loki, her own father, confirms her office at the flyting: 'Odin's son set the ring Draupnir on Baldr's pyre, and Hel received it' - the receiver of the dead and of the pyre-gifts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 34 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Lokasenna st. 32-33 (Bellows 1923); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她一半是藍黑色，一半是肉色，很容易辨認；她比其他人更為陰鬱，面容也更為兇惡。她的廳堂名為埃琉德尼爾，她的盤子是「飢餓」，她的刀是「饑荒」。而她的生父洛基在嘲諷之爭中確認了她的職司：「奧丁之子將德羅普尼爾戒指置於巴德爾的葬火堆上，海拉收下了它」——她是亡者與葬火贈禮的收受者。

title.en: Thokk's Refusal: The One Dry Eye That Kept Baldr in Hel
title.zh: 索克的拒絕：唯一乾涸的眼睛，讓巴爾德長留冥府

region.zh: 普世哭泣與約頓海姆一處洞穴（象徵性定位於挪威尤通黑門山）

summary.en: To ransom Baldr from Hel, the gods send messengers through all worlds asking everything to weep him alive: men, animals, earth, stones, trees, metals - all consent. Only in a cave sits a giantess who names herself Thokk ('thanks'), dry-eyed, and refuses: 'Neither quick nor dead needed I Baldr's weeping? - let Hel hold what it has.' And she is Loki in disguise. One refusal voids the unanimous contract, and Baldr stays in Hel until the world's renewal. The record is the Norse doctrine that resurrection requires total participation: a single withholding defeats a universe's grief.
summary.zh: 為將巴爾德從海爾手中贖回，諸神遣使遍歷諸界，請求萬物為之哭泣：人類、鳥獸、大地、石頭、樹木、金屬——無不應允。唯有一洞穴中坐著一位自稱「索克」（「謝意」）的女巨人，眼中無淚，拒絕哭泣：「無論生死，我不需要巴爾德的眼淚——讓海爾留著她已有的吧。」而她正是喬裝的洛基。一個拒絕便作廢了全體一致的契約，巴爾德遂長留冥府，直至世界更新。此記錄是北歐的教義：復生需要全體參與——一滴不肯落下的眼淚，足以擊敗整個宇宙的悲傷。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The weeping-transaction is the myth's most legalistic scene. After Hermothr returns with Hel's terms - Baldr shall ride home if all things weep for him - the Aesir send messengers 'through all the world' to bid everything weep Baldr out of Hel: 'and all things did - men and every living creature, and the earth, and the stones, and the trees, and all metals, just as you will have seen these things weep when they come from frost into heat'. The list is the myth's phenomenology of thaw: dew on stones, sap in trees, moisture on metal - the world's own weeping, cosmic and material. The doctrine beneath it is that resurrection is a unanimity-contract: the underworld releases only what the whole cosmos mourns.

The contract's one dissent is the myth's sharp end. The messengers 'came at last to a certain giantess, who called herself Thokk', sitting in a cave; she refuses: 'Thokk will weep dry tears for Baldr's burial; neither quick nor dead got I any joy of him? - let Hel hold what it has.' Snorri then unmasks her: 'men believe that this same Thokk was Loki, Lopt's son, who has most? ' - no: 'who all? ' - the text: 'and men believe that she who refused was Loki himself'. The giantess's name is a pun - thokk, 'thanks', as if the refusal were a courtesy - and the disguise is the trickster's signature: the cosmos's unanimous grief defeated by a cross-dressing father's courtesy.

The record's cultural functions are the unanimity-doctrine of resurrection and the trickster's veto. Where most mythologies make death's reversal a matter of ritual or heroism, the Norse makes it a matter of total assent - a social contract with a death-clause; and the myth's history of its failure is a portrait of the trickster as the one agent able to withhold consent: gods, stones, trees and metals all weep, but the father who engineered the death wears a woman's shape and declines. The record also closes Baldr's arc: he stays in Hel 'until the renewal', when 'Baldr and Höd shall come back' - the failed ransom and the scheduled return are one doctrine: death cannot be bought back piecemeal; it can only be outlived.

In the atlas, the record anchors the withheld-consent family: the Greek Orpheus' glance, the Inanna-returns-with-a-substitute doctrine, the Japanese Izanagi's turn back - each a resurrection defeated at a single exit-condition; the Norse one is distinctive in locating the failure not in the rescued or the rescuer but in the universe's one dissenter.

functions: Unanimity-doctrine of resurrection: release requires the whole cosmos's weeping
Phenomenology of thaw: the world's own moisture as the weeping
Trickster's veto: one disguised refusal defeats universal grief
Closes Baldr's arc: failed ransom, scheduled return at the renewal

passages.zh: 諸神派遣使者走遍全世界，要求萬物為巴德爾哀哭，將他從海拉那裡贖回；萬物皆哭——男人與一切生靈、大地、石頭、樹木以及所有金屬，正如你可以看見這些東西從嚴寒進入溫暖時會流淚一樣。

passages.text: But at last they came to a giantess who called herself Thokk, sitting in a cave; she refused: 'Thokk will weep dry tears for Baldr's burial; let Hel hold what it has.' And men believe that this Thokk was Loki himself, who has done the greatest evil among gods and men.

passages.zh: 但最後他們來到一位自稱索克的女巨人面前，她坐在一個洞穴裡；她拒絕了：「索克將為巴德爾的葬禮哭出乾眼淚；讓海拉留住她所有的。」人們相信這索克就是洛基本人，他在諸神與人類之間犯下了最大的惡行。

title.en: The Forging of Mjollnir: Loki, the Fly and the Dwarf-Brothers
title.zh: 妙爾尼爾的鍛造：洛基、蒼蠅與矮人兄弟

region.en: The dwarf forges under the earth (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 地下的矮人鍛爐（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Skaldskaparmal c. 1220-1230 (older mythic material); principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to, Codex Trajectinus

source.work: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 2-3 (the treasures of the gods); critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: To replace the hair Loki cut from Sif, the dwarf sons of Ivaldi forge golden hair, the ring Draupnir and the ship Skidbladnir; Loki then bets his head that the brothers Brokkr and Eitri cannot forge better. At their forge a fly - Loki in disguise - stings the smith's hands and neck to spoil the work; on the third attempt the fly stings the eyelid, blood runs, and Eitri draws out the hammer Mjollnir with a short handle. At the judgment the gods rule that the hammer is best of all - it can be small in the shirt, it never misses, it returns to the hand - and the dwarf moves to behead Loki, whose neck (no part of the head) is saved by a deus ex stitch: the gods cut the holes to enlarge the neck. The record is the aition of the god of thunder's signature weapon and of the dwarf-gift economy.
summary.zh: 為補償洛基剪掉的西芙金髮，伊瓦爾迪之子矮人鍛出金髮、指環德羅普尼爾與神船斯基德布拉德尼爾；洛基隨即以自己的頭顱打賭，說矮人兄弟布洛克與埃特里鍛不出更好的寶物。在鍛爐旁，一隻蒼蠅——喬裝的洛基——蜇刺鍛工的手與頸以毀其工；第三次時蒼蠅蜇其眼瞼，血流不止，埃特里仍抽出短柄的雷錘妙爾尼爾。諸神裁定雷錘為至寶——可縮小藏於衣內、出手必中、擲出必回——矮人便要斬洛基之頭，而諸神以「頸非頭」的縫線詭計保下其性命。此記錄是雷神標誌性兵器的起源故事，也是矮人贈禮經濟的呈現。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Skaldskaparmal's treasure-chapter is one of the myth-world's wittiest industrial narratives. Loki has cut off all of Sif's hair in malice; Thor seizes him; and the price of the neck is a commission: the dwarf sons of Ivaldi will forge hair of real gold that grows like living hair, and, carried away, also the ship Skidbladnir, which always finds fair wind, and the ring Draupnir, which drops eight rings of itself every ninth night. Loki, wanting to win more, goes to the brothers Brokkr and Eitri and stakes his head that they cannot forge better treasures.

The forge-scene is a contest of endurance. Eitri sets a pigskin in the forge and bids Brokkr blow, 'and not stop until he has taken out of the forge what he had put there'; a fly comes and stings Brokkr's arm, and he blows on regardless; what comes out is the boar Gullinbursti with golden bristles. Then gold goes into the forge, and the fly stings Brokkr's neck, twice as hard, and he blows on; out comes the ring Draupnir. Then iron, and the fly - Loki in the shape of a gadfly - stings Brokkr's eyelid, and when the blood runs down into his eye and he cannot see, he drops the bellows for a moment 'just to brush the fly away' - and what comes out of the forge is the hammer Mjollnir, whose one flaw is the short handle.

The judgment at Asgard formalizes the myth's doctrine. Odin rules: the hammer is the best of all treasures - 'for it is small and can be hidden in the shirt, and it never misses its mark, and it returns to the hand that throws it' - and the sun withers and rock splits at its stroke. Brokkr moves to collect the stake: the head of Loki. Loki consents - to the head - but the dwarf may take no more than the head: so Loki says his neck belongs to him, and the dwarf, denied the knife-path, sews up Loki's lips instead. The gods' economy thus runs on technical theft, wagers and loophole law - and the thunder-god's weapon is forged with a wound in its maker's eye, which is why the world's most reliable weapon has one flaw.

The cultural functions are the divine toolkit's genealogy and the doctrine of flaws. Each god's signature object (Sif's hair, Draupnir, the ship, the boar, the hammer) is a dwarf-gift with a story, and the kenning-system cites them; Mjollnir's short handle is the myth-world's admission that even perfect weapons are accidents of interrupted labor. And Loki's role - the saboteur whose sabotage produces the world's best weapon - is the trickster as quality-control: the fly in the forge is the reason the hammer has a handle too short to be perfect and too true to fail.

In the atlas, the record anchors the forge-gift family (the Greek Hephaestus' works, the Chinese Gan-Jiang and Mo-Ye swords): each a divine weapon with a maker's wound; the Norse one is distinctive in being won by a wager between two dwarf-brother workshops.

functions: Aition of Mjollnir's form: short handle from a saboteur's interruption of the smith
Doctrine of flaws: the world's best weapon is an accident of interrupted labor
Dwarf-gift economy: each god's signature object cited by the kenning-system
Trickster as quality-control: Loki's sabotage produces the best treasure

passages.text: Loki wagered his head that the dwarf-brothers could forge nothing better than the sons of Ivaldi's treasures; at their forge a fly stung Brokkr's arm, then his neck, and he blew on regardless; on the third round the fly stung his eyelid, and blood ran into his eye, and he let go the bellows but a moment - and out of the forge came the hammer Mjollnir, with its handle short.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 2-3 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 洛基以他的頭顱打賭，說那對矮人兄弟鍛造不出比伊瓦爾迪之子們的寶物更好的東西；在他們的鍛爐旁，一隻蒼蠅叮了布洛克的胳膊，接著又叮了他的脖子，他仍照樣鼓風；到第三輪時，蒼蠅叮了他的眼皮，血流進他的眼睛，他只不過鬆手放開風箱一瞬間——鍛爐裡便產出了錘子妙爾尼爾，它的柄很短。

passages.text: The gods judged: the hammer is best of all treasures, for it is small and may be hidden in the shirt, it never misses its mark, and it returns to the hand that throws it; and at its stroke the sun withers and the rock splits. Then Brokkr claimed Loki's head; but Loki said his neck belonged to him, and the dwarf sewed up his lips instead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 3 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 諸神評判：這錘子是所有寶物中最好的，因為它小巧，可以藏在襯衫裡，它從不偏離目標，而且會回到投擲者的手中；它一擊之下，太陽為之萎縮，岩石為之迸裂。於是布洛克索要洛基的頭；但洛基說他的脖子屬於他自己，那矮人便縫合了他的嘴唇。

title.en: Thrymskvida: Thor Dressed as a Bride
title.zh: 《特呂姆之歌》：扮作新娘的索爾

region.en: Thrym's hall in Jotunheim (symbolic pin at Jotunheimen, Norway)
region.zh: 約頓海姆特呂姆之廳（象徵性定位於挪威尤通黑門山）

period: Thrymskvida c. 900-1000 CE; principal MS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to; also preserved in the Edda MS

source.work: Thrymskvida (complete poem); critical ed. Ursula Dronke (Poetic Edda II, 1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The giant Thrym has stolen Thor's hammer and will return it only for Freyja as his bride. Freyja's rage breaks the hall's floors; Heimdall proposes the counter-disguise: Thor dressed as the bride, Loki as the maid of honor. The wedding proceeds against accumulating comedy - Thor eats an ox and eight salmon (the bride eats? the maid explains: eight nights' fasting), drinks three casks, glares when Thrym lifts the veil to kiss her - and at the crucial moment the hammer is laid in the bride's lap to hallow the wedding by Thor's rite; Thor seizes it, kills the groom, the bride's kin and the old sister who begged a gift. The record is the myth's greatest comedy and its doctrine of ritual disguise: the most masculine god saves the world dressed as a woman, because marriage rites are society's most hallowed border.
summary.zh: 巨人特呂姆偷走了索爾的雷錘，並宣稱只有將芙蕾雅許配為妻才會歸還。芙蕾雅的怒火震裂了大廳的地板；海姆達爾獻計反喬裝：索爾扮作新娘，洛基扮作伴娘。婚禮在笑料不斷中推進——新娘一口吃下一頭牛、八條鮭魚（伴娘解釋：八日未進食），豪飲三桶蜜酒，特呂姆掀起面紗欲吻時，新娘眼中雷光如電——而在關鍵時刻，雷錘被放在新娘膝上，以索爾之禮為婚禮祝聖；索爾一把抓住錘柄，擊殺新郎、新娘親族與那位乞求禮物的老姐妹。此記錄是神話中最偉大的喜劇，亦是「儀式喬裝」的教義：最陽剛之神以女裝救世，因為婚禮正是社會最神聖的邊界。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Thrymskvida is the myth corpus's comedy of cross-dressing, and it is also one of its tightest plot-engines. The theft: Thor wakes to find his hammer gone; Loki borrows Freyja's feather-dress, flies to Jotunheim, and Thrym tells him plainly: the hammer lies eight leagues under the earth, 'and no one shall bring it back to Thor unless he bring me Freyja for a wife'. The ransom rejected: Freyja's fury is the poem's great scene - 'then burst Freyja's wrath, and she threw the necklace Brisings from her, so that the floors of the halls trembled, and the great Brising-necklace broke'; no god or goddess will go disguised as her.

The plan and its costume: Heimdall, 'wisest of gods', proposes that Thor go as the bride, with the necklace, keys, woman's clothes, and head-dress; Loki as the maid-servant. Thor's objection - 'the Aesir will call me unmanly if I go as a bride' - is answered by Loki with the poem's logic: 'be silent, Thor, unless the giants settle in the gods' courts'. The costume is completed with a grinding stone? - a millstone under the bridal veil, for shoulders (the poem: 'his eyes burned fiercely? ' - the stone was laid under his woman's-garment, 'and he had a look of rage').

The wedding's comedy is the doctrine. The bridal party arrives at Thrym's hall; the feast begins; the bride eats at evening one ox, eight salmon, all the dainties for women, and drinks three casks of mead - Thrym marvels ('I never saw a bride bite harder, nor a maiden drink more mead'), and the maid's explanation - 'eight nights before coming here, Freyja ate nothing, so eager was she for the wedding' - is the ritual lie that feeds the disguise. Thrym lifts the veil to kiss the bride and leaps back the length of the hall: fire burns in the bride's eyes. The maid explains: she has not slept for eight nights, so hot is her longing for the wedding. Then the sister of the giant begs gifts - 'bring rings of red gold to thy sister' - and Thrym orders the hammer brought in to hallow the bride 'by Thor's rite': 'lay the hammer in the maiden's lap, and hallow us both by the hand of Var'. At that word the thunder-god laughs in his heart? - the poem: 'the heart laughed in Thor's breast when the hard-hearted one knew the hammer', he seizes it first and kills Thrym, then the whole giant-kin, and the old sister who had asked for rings 'she? ' - the poem: he struck her also who begged the wedding-gift, 'and got a blow instead of coin'.

The cultural functions are the ritual-disguise doctrine and the border-theology of marriage. The myth locates society's holiest transaction - marriage, with its ring, veil, feast and bride-price - on the frontier with the giants, and shows that the frontier can be crossed by the gender-disguise of the strongest god: the marriage rite is so hallowed that even a god must enter it in costume. And the poem's Var-doctrine (the goddess of betrothal vows) means the wedding is legally binding: Thrym's hall is a lawful wedding-feast, and the bride's weapon is lawful too. Its reception: the poem is the myth corpus's most parodied and performed text (17th-20th-century ballads, Wagner, Marvel), and its comedy's core - the god of thunder in a bridal veil - has never stopped working.

For the atlas, the record anchors the ritual-disguise family (the Greek Achilles on Skyros, the Chinese Mulan cycle, the Irish Cuchulainn's compulsion into womanhood): each a hero in women's clothes; only the Norse one saves the world by it.

functions: Ritual-disguise doctrine: the marriage rite as society's holiest, most crossable border
Gender-comedy as theology: the most masculine god saves the world in a bridal veil
Legal frame: the wedding under Var's vow makes the feast lawful - and the weapon lawful
The myth's greatest comedy: plotted theft, angry goddess, wedding sabotage

passages.text: Thrym the giant said the hammer lay eight leagues under the earth, and no one should bring it back to Thor unless he brought him Freyja for a wife. Freyja's wrath burst forth: she threw the necklace of the Brisings from her, so that the floors of the halls trembled, and the great necklace broke.

passages.zh: 巨人特里姆說錘子埋在地下八里格深處，誰也不能把它帶回給索爾，除非他為他帶來芙蕾雅作妻子。芙蕾雅的怒火爆發了：她扯下布里辛格項鍊，甩了出去，以至於廳堂的地板都為之震顫，那條大項鍊斷裂了。

passages.text: Thor went as the bride, with the necklace and keys and woman's clothes, a millstone under the bridal veil; Loki went as the maid. At the feast the bride ate an ox and eight salmon and drank three casks of mead; the maid explained that Freyja had eaten nothing for eight nights, so eager was she for the wedding.

passages.zh: 索爾裝扮成新娘，戴著項鍊、鑰匙，身穿女子衣裳，婚紗下藏著一塊磨石；洛基則扮作侍女。婚宴上，新娘吃了一頭牛、八條鮭魚，還喝了三桶蜂蜜酒；侍女解釋說，芙蕾雅已八夜未進食，只因她太渴望這場婚禮了。

passages.text: Thrym lifted the veil to kiss the bride and leapt back the length of the hall: fire burned in her eyes. Then he bade the hammer be laid in the maiden's lap, to hallow them both by Var's rite; the heart laughed in Thor's breast when he knew the hammer, and he first slew Thrym, then all the giant-kin, and her also who had begged the wedding-gift - she got a blow instead of coin.

passages.zh: 斯里姆掀開頭紗要親吻新娘，卻向後跳開整整一個廳堂的距離：她的眼中燃著火。於是他吩咐把錘子放在新娘膝上，以瓦爾的儀式為兩人祝聖；索爾認出那錘子時，胸膛裡的心笑了起來，他先殺了斯里姆，又殺盡所有巨人族類，連那個討要婚禮贈禮的也一併殺了——她得到的是一記重擊，而非錢幣。

title.en: Thor and Hrungnir: The Duel with the Stone Giant
title.zh: 索爾大戰石巨人赫朗格尼爾

summary.en: The giant Hrungnir, drunk on Odin's mead, boasts he will carry Valhalla off to Jotunheim and drink all the Aesir's ale; cornered at Griots? - at the duel-ground, he faces Thor with a whetstone and a heart of stone. Thor's hammer meets the whetstone in the air; the stone shatters, one splinter sticks in Thor's head, and the hammer crushes the giant's stone skull. The fallen giant's leg pins Thor until his three-year-old son Magni heaves it off; a sorceress' clay giant, Mokkurkalfi, melts in terror at the thunder-god's approach. The duel leaves Thor with a whetstone in his skull and the aition of the quern-hone in every valley: Hrungnir's shattered stone is why the landscape is full of the giant's broken weapons.
summary.zh: 巨人赫朗格尼爾在奧丁處醉飲後誇口，要將瓦爾哈拉整座搬到約頓海姆，喝盡阿薩神族的美酒；被迫應戰的他在決戰平原上以磨石為盾、以石為心面對索爾。雷錘在空中與磨石相撞，磨石碎裂，一片碎石嵌進索爾頭顱，雷錘則擊碎巨人的石頭腦袋。倒下的巨人以其腿壓住索爾，直至三歲的兒子曼尼將其掀開；女巫所製的黏土巨人莫庫卡爾菲在雷神逼近時嚇得融化。這場決鬥讓索爾頭中留下一枚磨石碎片，也解釋了為何山谷間遍布碎裂的磨石——那正是巨人被打碎的兵器。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain); Haustlong via Corpus Poeticum Boreale 1883

narrative.en:
The duel begins as a guest's impertinence. Hrungnir, the strongest of giants, is invited into Asgard as Odin's guest, drinks himself mad on the god's mead, and boasts: he will carry off Valhalla to Jotunheim, empty the Aesir's ale-cellar, and carry off Freyja and Sif for his housewives. The gods call Thor from the east; Hrungnir, armed in stone - 'his head and heart were of stone, hard as any rock' - demands single combat at the frontier, 'for it would have been a disgrace if Thor had come upon him unprepared'.

The duel is myth's staged physics. The giants, fearing the result, make a clay man nine leagues tall - Mokkurkalfi ('mist-calf'), with a mare's heart, which trembles so at Thor's thunder that it wets itself and hides. Hrungnir stands with his whetstone raised; Thor casts the hammer; the whetstone and the hammer meet in the air, and the stone breaks - 'part fell to the earth, whence come all flint-rocks? ' - Snorri's aition: the shards of Hrungnir's whetstone are the world's flint. One splinter sticks in Thor's head; the hammer strikes the giant's stone skull and shatters it; and as Hrungnir falls, 'his leg came over Thor's neck, and he was pinned'. All the giants could not lift the leg; Thor's son Magni, three winters old, lifts it, saying: 'had I been older, I would have shaken the giant off with my fist' - the earliest exploit of the god who will inherit the hammer.

The wound's sequel is the myth's medical-ritual coda: the sorceress Groa, wife of the rune-wight Aurvandil, comes to sing healing-charms over Thor's head, and the whetstone begins to loosen; Thor, delighted, tells her that her husband is alive - carried homeward in a basket from Jotunheim, one toe frozen and knocked off into the sky to be a star (Aurvandil's Toe) - and at the good news Groa forgets her charms, 'so that the whetstone never came out'. Thor's headache is permanent: the fragment is why thunder-god statues? - the doctrine: the stone in the head is the myth's explanation of the god's essential vulnerability, and Groa's interrupted charm is the aition of half-cured wounds.

The skaldic evidence: Thjodolfr of Hvinir's Haustlong (c. 900), a shield-poem, narrates the duel in kennings - 'the stony-hearted one' whose skull the hammer broke - centuries before Snorri, evidencing the myth's court currency. And the cultural functions: the duel formalizes the god-giant warfare as single combat at the frontier; the whetstone-in-the-head is the aition of flint and of the god's wound; and Mokkurkalfi's mare-heart is the myth's satire of manufactured armies. In the atlas, the duel answers the Greek Heracles-Geryon combats and the Chinese Yi's archery duels: each a frontier single-combat with geological aftermath.

functions: Aition of flint: Hrungnir's shattered whetstone as the world's flint-rocks
Doctrine of the god's wound: the whetstone in Thor's skull, permanently half-cured
Frontier single-combat: god-giant warfare formalized as a duel at the border
Skaldic documentation: Haustlong (c. 900) evidences the myth centuries before Snorri

passages.zh: 赫倫格尼爾喝奧丁的蜂蜜酒喝得發狂，誇口說要把瓦爾哈拉搬到約頓海姆，喝光阿薩神族的麥酒，還要娶芙蕾雅和希芙為妻。索爾從東方歸來，決鬥定在邊境舉行；那巨人的頭和心都是石頭做的，堅硬如任何岩石。

passages.text: Thor cast the hammer and Hrungnir raised the whetstone; the two met in the air, and the stone broke - part fell to the earth, whence come all flint-rocks - and one splinter stuck fast in Thor's head; but the hammer crushed the giant's stone skull. As Hrungnir fell, his leg came over Thor's neck, and none could lift it till Magni, three winters old, came and shook it off.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 9 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 索爾擲出錘子，赫倫格尼爾舉起磨刀石；兩者在空中相撞，石頭碎裂——一部分落在地上，所有燧石便由此而來——一片碎片則牢牢嵌進索爾的頭裡；但錘子砸碎了巨人那石造的頭顱。赫倫格尼爾倒下時，他的腿壓在索爾的脖子上，無人能搬動，直到三歲的馬格尼前來把它掀開。

passages.text: Groa the sorceress sang charms to loosen the whetstone in Thor's head; but when he told her that her husband Aurvandil lived - his frozen toe knocked off into the sky to be a star - she was so glad that she forgot the rest of the charm, and the stone never came out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 9 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 女巫格蘿亞唱起咒歌，要鬆開索爾頭中的磨刀石；但當他告訴她，她的丈夫奧爾萬迪爾還活著——他凍僵的腳趾被拋上天空，成了一顆星——她高興得忘了其餘的咒語，那石頭便再也沒有出來。

title.en: Thor's Fishing: The Ox-Head Bait and the World-Serpent's Eye
title.zh: 索爾垂釣：牛頭為餌與世界之蛇之眼

summary.en: The best-attested exploit in Norse skaldic art: Thor rows out with the giant Hymir, baits the hook with the head of Hymir's best ox, and fishes the World-Serpent off the bottom of the sea. The serpent's head comes over the gunwale, venom dripping, eyes glaring; Thor reaches for the hammer to kill it, and the terrified giant cuts the line; the serpent sinks, struck once on the crown. Snorri adds the doctrine: it is from that blow that the serpent's mark? - no, the monster still lives with the scar, and Thor's fury has its reason: the fishing is the rehearsal of Ragnarok's final duel. Skaldic verse from the 9th century (Bragi, Eysteinn) documents the scene on shields and in lausavisur centuries before the Edda poems.
summary.zh: 這是北歐吟遊詩歌中記載最完備的神蹟：索爾與巨人希米爾出海，以希米爾最好的牛頭為餌，自海底釣起世界之蛇。蛇頭越過船舷，毒液滴落，雙眼圓睜；索爾伸手取錘欲誅之，嚇壞的巨人卻割斷了釣線；巨蛇沉入海底，頭頂留下的一道傷痕。斯諾里補充：此傷至今未癒，怪物仍活著——這一釣正是諸神黃昏最終決戰的預演。早在《埃達》詩歌成文數世紀之前，9世紀的吟遊詩（布拉基的《拉格納之盾》、艾斯泰因的獨立詩句）便已在盾面上記載了這一場景。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); skaldic texts via Corpus Poeticum Boreale 1883

narrative.en:
The fishing-myth is the myth corpus's best-attested narrative, because it lives in three media at once: eddic verse, skaldic shield-poetry and prose doctrine. The eddic version (Hymiskvida) sets the trip inside the kettle-quest: to test the god's appetite, the giant Hymir rows out with the ox-head bait to his deep-sea fishing grounds, 'where he was wont to sit and angle for halibut'; Thor rows on 'past the giants' lands' to the deeps where the serpent lies. The bite is cosmic: 'the line goes taut, the boat heaves? ' - the poem: 'the hook caught the monster, the girdle of all lands below' - and Thor's pull is such that his feet go through the boat's boards to the sea-bottom. The serpent's head comes up over the gunwale 'with venom dripping from its jaws'; Thor reaches for the hammer to kill it - and Hymir, 'pale with terror, cut the line', and the serpent sank away with a blow on its head.

The skaldic attestations are the myth's oldest witnesses. Bragi Boddason's Ragnarsdrapa (9th c.), a shield-poem for Ragnar Lodbrok, describes a shield-picture of the fishing: Thor 'angry? ' - the verses: 'the enemy of the Midgard-serpent'? - Bragi's kennings name the god as 'the tester of the serpent's jaw? ' and the giant's line-cut; and Eysteinn Valdason's lausavisur (10th c.) devote three stanzas to the scene: 'the splendid god? with the ox-head's hook lifted the girdle of the earth'. The images on actual Viking-age stones and cross-slabs (Altuna stone, Gosforth) show the scene carved - the myth documented in four media, which makes it the corpus's strongest case for a pan-Scandinavian mythic iconography.

Snorri's doctrine adds the eschatological freight: the blow Thor struck the serpent's crown is the wound that does not heal, and at Ragnarok the two will meet again - Thor's fishing is the rehearsal of his death-duel, when the tail releases and the venom comes. The ox-head bait is the myth's economy of the frontier: the god fishes with the giant's own property (the ox of the giant's herd, killed at the giant's table), so the exploit is theft upon theft - the kettle, the fish, the ox - all hauled from the borderlands to feed the gods' feast.

Cultural functions: the sea as the serpent's body (the world's girdle, hooked from below); the fishing as rehearsal of doom (the wound that never closes); and the four-media documentation (eddic, skaldic, iconographic, prose) that makes this the myth corpus's strongest cross-media record. In the atlas, the fishing answers the Chinese Nezha's sea-battles and the Greek Heracles' Triton episodes: each a hero versus the sea's monster; only the Norse one is an angling contest with the world's edge.

functions: Sea-as-serpent doctrine: the world's girdle hooked from below
Rehearsal of Ragnarok: the unhealed wound schedules the final duel
Frontier economy: the exploit is theft upon theft (ox, fish, kettle) from the giants
Four-media documentation: eddic, skaldic, iconographic, prose - the corpus's strongest cross-media record

passages.text: Thor took the head of Hymir's best ox for bait, and rowed with him past the giants' lands to the deeps where the World-Serpent lies. He cast the hook, and the line grew taut; the hook caught the girdle of all lands below, and the god's feet went through the boat's boards to the sea-bottom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hymiskvida st. 17-22 (Bellows 1923); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 索爾取了希米爾最好那頭牛的頭作餌，與他一同划船，經過巨人的領地，來到世界巨蛇潛伏的深海。他拋下魚鉤，釣線繃緊；鉤子鉤住了底下環繞一切陸地的腰帶，神的雙腳竟踩穿船板，直抵海底。

passages.text: The serpent's head came up over the gunwale, venom dripping from its jaws; Thor reached for the hammer to kill it - but Hymir, pale with terror, cut the line, and the monster sank away with a blow on its crown. Skalds carved the scene on shields and stones, and Snorri says the wound does not close until Ragnarok, when serpent and god meet again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hymiskvida st. 23-26, skaldic verses and Gylfaginning ch. 45 (Bellows; CPB; Brodeur); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蛇頭探出船舷之上，毒液自其顎間滴落；索爾伸手取錘欲殺之——但希米爾驚恐得面色蒼白，割斷了釣線，那巨獸頭頂挨了一擊，便沉入海中而去。吟唱詩人將此情景刻於盾牌與石上，斯諾里則言，此傷口直到諸神黃昏、蛇與神再度相遇之時方會癒合。

title.en: Thor and Geirrod: The Thorsdrapa and the Brokendown River
title.zh: 索爾大戰蓋爾羅德：《索爾頌》與碎裂之河

region.en: Geirrod's hall across the Vimur river (symbolic pin at Jotunheimen, Norway)
region.zh: 維穆爾河對岸的蓋爾羅德之廳（象徵性定位於挪威尤通黑門山）

period: Thorsdrapa (Eilifr Godrunarson, c. 10th c.); Skaldskaparmal c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Eilifr Godrunarson, Thorsdrapa; Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 10 (the story of Thorsdrapa); ed. Vigfusson & Powell, CPB 1883

license: Public domain (CPB 1883; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The most violent exploit in skaldic art: Loki, forced by Geirrod's capture of him, decoys Thor into the giant's land without hammer, belt or gloves; the giantess Grid lends the god her belt of strength, iron gloves and staff. At the Vimur river - swollen by the witch's incantations - Thor wades with the staff, 'and they say that the river rose highest at his shoulders', and he finds a stone and hurls it: 'and that stone stayed the stream, as if a rock had been set there' - the aition of a boulder-stopped river. In the hall, Geirrod's iron-hot wedge? - the giant hurls a molten iron wedge with tongs; Thor catches it in his iron gloves and hurls it back through pillar and giant. The skaldic Thorsdrapa, the corpus's most violent poem, tells the same with blood-drinking kennings.
summary.zh: 這是吟遊詩歌中最暴烈的神蹟：洛基被蓋爾羅德擒獲後受迫誘騙索爾——不帶錘、不帶腰帶與鐵手套——深入巨人之地；女巨人格里德借予雷神神力腰帶、鐵手套與木杖。在維穆爾河畔——河水因女巫咒語而暴漲——索爾執杖涉水，「據說河水最高漲至他的肩頭」；他拾起一塊巨石擲出：「那石頭便攔住了水流，如同天然巨岩立於河中」——這是巨石攔河的起源故事。在廳中，巨人以鐵鉗擲出熾熱的鐵楔；索爾以鐵手套接住，反擲回去，貫穿石柱與巨人。吟遊詩《索爾頌》——歌謠中最暴烈的作品——以嗜血的隱喻講述同一故事。

canonical_translation: Corpus Poeticum Boreale, ed. Vigfusson & Powell, Oxford 1883 (public domain); Skaldskaparmal via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
The tale's frame is a deception within a deception. Geirrod the giant captures Loki (in hawk-shape) and releases him only on his oath to bring Thor to the hall without his hammer or his strength-girdle; Loki decoys the god with a lying tale of hospitality. The journey is armed by a third party: the giantess Grid, mother of Vidar, warns Thor and lends him her belt of strength, her iron gloves and her staff Gridarvolr.

The river-crossing is the poem's physics-set-piece. The witch Gjalp, Geirrod's daughter, stands astride the Vimur and raises the water with incantations; Thor wades with the staff, 'and they say that the river rose highest at his shoulders'; he finds a stone in the riverbed and casts it, 'and that stone stayed the stream, as if a rock had been set there' - Snorri's aition for a river dammed by a thrown boulder - and then he wades out and grips a mountain-berry? - the prose: he seizes a rowan-tree (the famous 'Thor's salvation' of the rowan) and climbs out; whence the kenning that the rowan is 'Thor's salvation'. In the hall, the tests turn physical: Gjalp, hidden under Thor's chair, presses it up with her knees; the god breaks her back by seating himself hard. Geirrod, seeing the god's fury, hurls a wedge of molten iron with tongs; Thor catches it in the iron gloves and hurls it back 'so that it passed through the pillar and through Geirrod and through the wall, and so out? ' - and the giant's daughters, fleeing, are crushed.

The skaldic poem Thorsdrapa by Eilifr Godrunarson (10th c.) is the myth's oldest and most violent telling - so violent that the Edda-MSS preserve it 'because it is hard to understand? ' - Snorri says he quotes it 'because it is excellent and? ' - the prose says he includes it for its art. The poem's kennings drink blood: Geirrod's hall is 'the wolf-feeding hall? ', the wedge 'the reddening? iron of the giant', Thor 'the breaker of Geirrod's brain-pan'. Snorri retells it to explain the poem's obscure diction - the prose retelling exists for the verse, a case-study of the myth corpus's transmission: skaldic difficulty generating prose narrative.

The record's cultural functions are the river-as-attack doctrine (the frontier's waters weaponized by witchcraft, dammed by a god) and the counter-throw doctrine (the god defeats the giant's technology with the giant's own weapon, caught and returned). And the rowan-tree doctrine ('Thor's salvation') is an aition of folk botanical belief - the rowan's protective reputation in Scandinavian farm-culture descends from this river-crossing. In the atlas, the record anchors the duel-by-technology family: the Chinese Yi's archery, the Greek Heracles' poisoning? - no: the atlas frame is the hero armed by borrowed gear (Grid's belt answers the Greek Athena's aegis-loans), and the myth's weapons are industrial: molten iron against iron gloves.

functions: River-as-attack doctrine: frontier waters weaponized by witchcraft, dammed by a thrown boulder
Counter-throw doctrine: the giant's molten iron caught in iron gloves and returned
Aition of the rowan: 'Thor's salvation' as the tree's protective reputation in farm-culture
Transmission case-study: a violent skaldic poem generating its own prose retelling

passages.text: Geirrod captured Loki in hawk-shape and released him only on his oath to bring Thor without hammer or girdle; but the giantess Grid warned the god and lent him her belt of strength, her iron gloves and her staff. At the Vimur, swollen by the witch's incantations, Thor waded with the staff, and the river rose to his shoulders; he found a stone in the riverbed and hurled it, and the stone stayed the stream as if a rock had been set there. In the hall, Geirrod hurled a wedge of molten iron with tongs; Thor caught it in the iron gloves and hurled it back through the pillar and through the giant.

passages.zh: 蓋爾羅德擒住了化為鷹形的洛基，僅以洛基立誓將不帶錘與力帶地引索爾前來為條件才放了他；然而女巨人葛莉德警告了這位神祇，並借予他自己的力量腰帶、鐵手套與手杖。在因女巫咒語而暴漲的維穆爾河中，索爾拄著手杖涉水而行，河水漲至他的肩頭；他在河床中尋得一塊石頭並將其擲出，那石頭竟擋住了水流，彷彿有巨石立於該處。在大廳中，蓋爾羅德以火鉗擲出一塊熔鐵楔；索爾以鐵手套接住，又將其擲回，穿透了石柱，也穿透了那巨人。

title.en: The Utgard Contests: Drinking the Sea, Wrestling Old Age
title.zh: 烏特加德競賽：飲盡滄海、力戰暮年

region.en: Utgard, the giants' stronghold (symbolic pin at Jotunheimen, Norway)
region.zh: 巨人要塞烏特加德（象徵性定位於挪威尤通黑門山）

period: Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230 (older mythic material); principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to, Codex Upsaliensis

source.work: Snorri, Gylfaginning chs. 44-47; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Thor, Loki and Thjalfi travel to the stronghold of Utgard-Loki and are set three contests. Thor must drain a drinking-horn (it is the sea, and he lowers it visibly), lift a grey cat (it is the Midgard-Serpent, and he raises one paw off the ground), and wrestle an old woman (she is Elli, Old Age itself, and he is forced to one knee). Thjalfi races a thought; Loki eats against fire itself. When the trickster-king reveals the illusions, he adds the cruelest doctrine of all: the giants had meant to kill them at the first tests - Skrymir's iron gloves were the mountain-range of the world, and the wrestling-match 'would never have been? ' - no man could stand before Old Age. The record is the Norse doctrine that strength has absolute rivals: the sea, the earth, and time.
summary.zh: 索爾、洛基與蒂亞爾菲前往烏特加德·洛基的要塞，被迫接受三項競賽。索爾須飲乾一隻號角（那是海洋，而他確實讓水位明顯下降），舉起一隻灰貓（那是環繞世界的大蛇，他抬起了它的一隻爪），並與一位老嫗角力（她是「暮年」本身，他只能單膝跪地）。蒂亞爾菲賽跑的對手是「思想」；洛基與火焰比賽吞食。當詭計之王揭穿幻象後，還補上一句最殘酷的教義：巨人們本想在第一輪就殺死他們——斯克利米爾的鐵手套原是世界的山脈，而那場角力「無人能敵」，因為無人能戰勝暮年。此記錄是北歐的教義：力量自有其絕對對手——海洋、大地與時間。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Gylfaginning's greatest adventure is a doctrine about the limits of strength, told as a tournament of illusions. Thor, Loki and the boy Thjalfi travel east into Jotunheim and spend a night in a vast hall - in the morning it is a glove: Skrymir's glove, the giant sleeping beside it. Skrymir travels with them, and his snoring, his stride and his food-sack test Thor three times on the road; each hammer-blow lands, and Skrymir only asks whether a leaf, an acorn or a bird has fallen on his head. At Utgard, the king sets the contests: Thjalfi races against Hugi (thought, unbeatable); Loki eats against Logi (fire, which consumes the trough, the bones and the table itself); and Thor must drink from a horn 'thought short by many' - and he drinks three deep draughts that lower the sea around the shore visibly; then lifts a cat off the ground with one paw - and the cat is Jormungand, arched, one foot raised; then wrestles the old nurse Elli - Old Age - and is brought to one knee.

The revelation is the myth's philosophy. Utgard-Loki confesses: 'I brought forth spells against you'; the horn was the sea; the cat was the Midgard-Serpent; Elli was Old Age, 'which no man can stand before, though he live to the world's end'. And the cruelest clause: 'I had purposed, had I known? ' - the text: 'had we known you were so mighty, you would never have come into the stronghold; for we had meant to destroy you with the first tests' - the giants' welcome was an execution, and the illusions were mercy. Then the giant offers to show Thor his match: two men who will fight him - 'and they were? ' - no one appears; the stronghold and its king vanish, 'and no castle and no king were to be seen'. Thor raises the hammer to strike and cannot find them; the record ends with the god swindled by geography.

The cultural functions are the doctrine of strength's absolute rivals and the theology of the borderline. In the Norse system, Thor's strength is the gods' insurance; the Utgard episode teaches what the insurance does not cover: the sea (drinkable only visibly), the earth's circumference (liftable only by a paw), and time (wrestled to one knee). It is a humility-doctrine delivered as comedy - the myth of a strongman beaten by the world's dimensions - and its politics are pointed: the giants' stronghold wins by wit and illusion, the same weapons Loki uses, so the frontier is shown as contestable by intelligence rather than muscle. And the wrestling-with-Old-Age is the myth-world's most precise existential statement: 'no man can stand before Old Age' - the sentence the whole Edda is written to prove.

For the atlas, the record anchors the impossible-contest family (the Greek labors' impossible tasks, the Chinese Sun Wukong's contests with Buddha's palm): each a hero tested by cosmic scale; the Norse one is unique in setting the tests against natural absolutes - sea, serpent, age - and in admitting defeat on the record.

functions: Doctrine of strength's absolute rivals: sea, serpent and Old Age
Humility-theology as comedy: the strongman beaten by the world's dimensions
Frontier politics: the giants win by illusion and intelligence, not muscle
Existential formula: no man can stand before Old Age

passages.text: Thor was set to drink from a horn thought short by many; three deep draughts he took, and the sea around the shore fell visibly. Then he was set to lift a grey cat from the ground; he raised one paw, and the cat arched its back - it was the Midgard-Serpent, the girdle of the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 46 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 索爾被命以一隻許多人以為甚淺的角杯飲酒；他深深飲了三口，岸邊周圍的海水便明顯下降。接著他又被命將一隻灰貓從地上舉起；他抬起了一隻貓爪，那貓便弓起了背——那正是米德加德巨蛇，環繞世界的腰帶。

passages.text: Then Thor wrestled with the old nurse Elli, and was brought to one knee. The king revealed all: the horn was the sea, the cat the Midgard-Serpent, and Elli was Old Age, which no man can stand before, though he live to the world's end. The stronghold and its king then vanished, and no castle and no king were to be seen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 46-47 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隨後索爾與老乳母艾莉角力，被逼得單膝跪地。國王揭示了一切：那角杯是海，那貓是米德加德巨蛇，而艾莉乃是老年，無人能與之抗衡，縱使他活到世界盡頭亦然。那座堡壘與其國王隨即消失，再也見不到任何城堡與任何國王。

title.en: Idunn's Apples: The Gods' Youth and the Eagle's Bargain
title.zh: 伊登的蘋果：諸神的青春與巨鷹的交易

region.en: Asgard's orchard and Thjazi's eyrie (symbolic pin at Gamla Uppsala, Sweden)
region.zh: 阿斯加德果園與夏茲之巢（象徵性定位於瑞典舊烏普薩拉）

period: Haustlong (Thjodolfr of Hvinir, c. 900); Skaldskaparmal c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Thjodolfr of Hvinir, Haustlong; Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 1-2; ed. Vigfusson & Powell, CPB 1883

license: Public domain (CPB 1883; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The gods' immortality is a produce-supply: Idunn the keeper keeps in her box the apples the gods bite when they feel age coming, and they grow young again. Loki, pressed by the eagle-shaped giant Thjazi, lures Idunn out of Asgard with a lie about apples better than hers - and the eagle carries her off. The gods age visibly; forced, Loki borrows Freyja's falcon-shape, flies to Thjazi's hall, turns Idunn into a nut and carries her back - pursued by the giant as an eagle; the Aesir set fire to the wood-shavings at the wall, and the burning eagle's wings drop him, and Thor kills him. The record is the aition of the gods' dependency on an orchard and the first dividend of the Skadi-feud: her father killed, she comes armed to Asgard.
summary.zh: 諸神的長生原來是一門農產品供應：看守者伊登在匣中保管那些蘋果，諸神感覺衰老將至時便咬上一口，重獲青春。洛基被化為巨鷹的巨人夏茲所迫，以謊言（外頭有更甜的蘋果）誘騙伊登離開阿斯加德——巨鷹遂將她擄走。諸神的容顏迅速衰老；被逼無奈，洛基借來芙蕾雅的游隼羽衣，飛至夏茲大廳，將伊登變作一顆核桃帶回——巨鷹窮追不捨；阿薩神族在牆邊點燃刨花，燒著鷹翼的巨人墜落，索爾隨即將其誅殺。此記錄既解釋了諸神對一座果園的依賴，也開啟了斯卡蒂世仇的序幕：父親被誅，她持械前來問罪。

canonical_translation: Corpus Poeticum Boreale, ed. Vigfusson & Powell, Oxford 1883 (public domain); Skaldskaparmal via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
Skaldskaparmal opens its treasure-chapters with a myth of divine logistics. Idunn, wife of Bragi the skald-god, 'keeps in her box those apples which the gods shall bite of when they begin to grow old; and then they all become young again, and so it shall be even unto the day of Ragnarok'. The supply-chain's weakness is Loki: the giant Thjazi (in eagle-shape) catches him in the flesh-pot trick? - the episode: Odin, Hoenir and Loki cook an ox in the wood; the eagle demands his share; Loki strikes the eagle with the staff, and the staff sticks to the eagle and Loki to the staff, and the eagle flies off with him, offering release only on his oath: he must bring Idunn out of Asgard with her apples.

The abduction is engineered by a lie: Loki tells Idunn that he has found apples better than hers, and she should come and compare; out in the wood, Thjazi in eagle-shape snatches her and flies to Thrymheimr. The gods age visibly - 'their beards? ' - the prose: 'the gods began to grow old' at council, asking where Idunn was gone; Loki confesses under threat of death and borrows Freyja's falcon-shape. The rescue is the myth's flight-comedy: Loki flies to Thrymheimr, finds Idunn alone, turns her into a nut, carries her in his claws and flies home 'with all his might'; the eagle pursues; the Aesir, seeing the flight, gather wood-shavings at the wall and set fire to them; the falcon clears the wall; the eagle, wings alight, drops, and Thor kills him inside the enclosure.

The aftermath founds a dynasty of feud: Thjazi's daughter Skadi comes armed to Asgard to demand atonement, and gets it - a husband (Njord, by feet-choice) and her father's eyes set as stars. The skaldic evidence: Thjodolfr's Haustlong (c. 900), a shield-poem, narrates the whole episode in kennings - Idunn's box, the eagle's claws, the burning wings - centuries before Snorri, and Snorri retells it to gloss the poem.

Cultural functions: the doctrine that divine immortality is agricultural (the gods' youth depends on an orchard and a keeper); the negotiation-with-hostage grammar (the eagle's oath extracted from a captured trickster); and the shapeshifting-rescue (nut, falcon, eagle). In the atlas, the record anchors the rejuvenation-produce family (the Greek ambrosia, the Chinese peaches of immortality, the Inca coca of the gods? - the frame is fruit-of-life myths): each an immortality-crop guarded by a keeper; the Norse one is distinctive in being portable, in a box, in a woman's keeping, and stealable by oath.

functions: Aition of divine youth: the gods' immortality as an orchard-supply with a keeper
Hostage-oath grammar: the eagle's release price extracted from a captured trickster
Shapeshifting-rescue: nut, falcon and eagle in the flight home
Feud-origination: Skadi's armed arrival and her settlement found the Njord-marriage

passages.text: Idunn keeps in her box the apples which the gods bite when they begin to grow old; then they all become young again, and so it shall be even unto the day of Ragnarok. The eagle-shaped giant Thjazi forced Loki by oath to bring her out of Asgard, and snatched her away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 1-2 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊登在她的箱中保存著蘋果，眾神開始衰老時便咬食之；於是他們又全都恢復年輕，如此直至諸神黃昏之日亦然。鷹形的巨人夏基以誓言逼迫洛基將她帶出阿斯加德，並將她擄走。

passages.text: The gods began to grow old; Loki confessed and borrowed Freyja's falcon-shape. He flew to Thrymheimr, turned Idunn into a nut, and carried her home in his claws, the eagle pursuing; the Aesir fired the wood-shavings at the wall, the burning eagle dropped, and Thor killed him inside the enclosure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 2 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 眾神開始衰老；洛基坦承了此事，並借來芙蕾雅的鷹形。他飛往斯里姆海姆，將伊登變成一顆堅果，以爪將她帶回家，那鷹在後追趕；諸神將刨木花點燃擲向牆垣，燃燒的鷹墜落，索爾在圍欄內將牠殺死。

title.en: Njord and Skadi: A Marriage of Sea and Mountain, Settled by Feet
title.zh: 尼奧德與斯卡蒂：以雙腳擇定的山海聯姻

region.en: Noatun by the sea and Thrymheim in the mountains (symbolic pin at Lofoten, Norway)
region.zh: 海邊的諾阿頓與山中的特呂姆海姆（象徵性定位於挪威羅弗敦）

period: Skaldskaparmal c. 1220-1230 (older material); Grimnismal st. 11, 15; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to, GKS 2365 4to

source.work: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 3; Grimnismal st. 11, 15; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916; Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: When the Aesir kill her father Thjazi, the giantess Skadi comes armed to Asgard for atonement. The settlement: she shall choose a husband from among the gods - by his feet. She picks the cleanest pair, believing them Baldr's; they are Njord's, and the marriage is made with the condition that each shall dwell nine nights in the other's home. The sea-hall deafens her with gulls; the mountain-hall wakes him with wolves; the compromise fails - and the myth of the failed divine marriage is also the aition of the shoreline's ecology: the place where sea-birds and wolves meet is the negotiated border between two households.
summary.zh: 阿薩神族誅殺其父夏茲後，女巨人斯卡蒂持械前來阿斯加德要求償付。和解條件是：她可從神族中自選一位丈夫——但只能看腳。她挑中雙足最潔淨者，以為是巴爾德，實則是尼奧德。婚約附加條款：夫妻須輪流在對方家中各住九夜。海邊大廳的海鳥鳴聲令她徹夜難眠；山中大廳的狼嚎又吵醒了海神。妥協失敗——而這則「失敗的神聖聯姻」神話，同時也是海岸線生態的起源故事：海鳥與狼群相遇之地，正是兩戶人家談判出的邊界。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The myth begins as a legal action. Skadi - 'the shining bride of the gods'? - the giantess, in helmet and byrnie and weapons of war, comes to Asgard to demand atonement for her father Thjazi, killed in the burning of the eagle. The Aesir offer compensation: she shall choose a husband from among them - 'but she shall choose by the feet only, and see nothing else of the man'. She finds one pair of feet passing fair and says: 'him I choose; little do I expect? ' - the text: 'there is little blemish, Baldr should be faultless in form' - and it is Njord of Noatun. The settlement also obliges the gods to make her laugh - Loki's trick (a goat's bait on his own beard, the rope tied to his testicles and to the goat's) does it - and to set her father's eyes as stars in the sky, which Odin does: 'the greatest memorials? ' - the two eyes thrown into the heaven as stars.

The marriage's terms are the myth's experimental clause: each shall dwell nine nights in the other's home. At Noatun, the sea-hall, the gulls' cries wake her: 'evil birds wake me that fly from the sea; every morning the gull wakes me'. At Thrymheim, the mountain-hall, the wolves' howls wake him: 'sick? ' - the prose: 'the wolves' howling wakes him, sick? ' - 'I was waked by the howling of wolves, he said? ' - the poem Grimnismal supplies the speeches in st. 11 and 15: each spouse testifies against the other's home. Neither can sleep in the other's world; the marriage dissolves by experiment, and Skadi returns to Thrymheim 'and abides there? ' - the text: 'she went up? ' - Snorri: 'Skadi then went up on the mountain and abode in Thrymheim, and often rides? ' - she keeps to the mountains, hunting on snowshoes with bow, and is called the snowshoe-goddess (ondurdís).

The record's cultural functions are the doctrine of habitat-marriage and the aition of the shore's ecology. The myth formalizes an observation about two landscapes - sea-shore and mountain - that cannot be inhabited by the other's household; the failed marriage is the boundary-negotiation of two ecological regimes, and the shoreline (where gull-cries and wolf-howls meet) is the myth's map of the compromise-point. And the feet-choice is the myth-world's theory of mate-selection: beauty is judged by its least poetic part, and the chooser guesses wrong - the doctrine that marriage by appearance mistakes its partner. Grimnismal's verse-argument (each spouse's testimony) is the poem's own trial-record, and Snorri's prose adds the judicial frame (atonement, choice, compensation, laugh-payment) that makes the whole episode read like a legal settlement of a feud.

In the atlas, the record anchors the divine-marriage family (Zeus-Hera's institution, the Izanagi-Izanami separation): each a marriage myth; the Norse one is distinctive in being failed by design - an experiment in cohabitation whose result is geography: the sea stays with the sea-folk, the mountain with the ski-goddess, and the boundary is the beach.

functions: Habitat-marriage doctrine: sea and mountain households cannot cohabit - the failed experiment maps the shoreline's ecology
Legal frame: the marriage as atonement, with feet-choice, laugh-payment and star-compensation
Mate-selection theory: beauty judged by feet, and the chooser guesses wrong
Skadi's office: the snowshoe-goddess of the mountains, bow and snowshoe as her cult-gear

passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 3 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 斯卡蒂戴著頭盔、穿著鎧甲、帶著兵器來到阿斯嘉特，為她的父親要求賠償。諸神提出讓她從他們之中挑選一位丈夫，但只能憑腳來挑選；她發現一雙腳十分俊美，便說：「我選他。」——那正是諾歐通的尼約德。

passages.text: The marriage's terms were that each should dwell nine nights in the other's home. At the sea-hall the gulls' cries woke Skadi; at the mountain-hall the wolves' howling woke Njord. Neither could sleep in the other's world, and Skadi went up on the mountain and abode in Thrymheim, hunting on snowshoes - the snowshoe-goddess.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 3 and Grimnismal st. 11, 15 (Brodeur; Bellows); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這樁婚事的條件是，兩人各自在對方家中住上九夜。在海邊的廳堂裡，海鷗的啼叫吵醒了斯卡蒂；在山中的廳堂裡，狼群的嚎叫吵醒了尼約德。兩人都無法在對方的世界裡安睡，於是斯卡蒂上山，住在斯里姆海姆，穿著雪鞋打獵——人稱雪鞋女神。

title.en: Freyr of the Swedes: The God-King, Beli and the Mound at Uppsala
title.zh: 瑞典人的弗雷：神王、貝利與烏普薩拉的墳丘

region.en: Gamla Uppsala, Sweden (temple and royal mounds)
region.zh: 瑞典舊烏普薩拉（神廟與王家墳丘）

period: Ynglinga saga c. 1225 (older material); Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; Adam of Bremen, Gesta c. 1070s; principal MSS AM 41 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Snorri, Ynglinga saga chs. 10-12; Gylfaginning ch. 37; Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis 4.26-27

license: Public domain (Laing 1844; Brodeur 1916); Adam of Bremen passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Freyr, the Vanir hostage, becomes the first king of the Swedes and the god of their wealth: under his reign come the peace-froth? - the 'Frodi-peace'? - good seasons and peace. When he weds the giantess Gerd, he pledges his sword and later slays the giant Beli with a stag's antler, bare-handed. At his death his body is laid in a great mound at Uppsala, and the Swedes, still prospering, believe the god still alive beneath the barrow - offerings continue; the mound-cult of a buried god-king. Adam of Bremen, writing in the 1070s, saw the temple: Thor enthroned in the center, Wodan and Fricco (Freyr) with the enormous phallus on either side, sacrifices of nine males of every species hanging in the sacred grove. The record is the best-documented cult in the Norse corpus: god as king, king as buried god.
summary.zh: 華納人質弗雷成為瑞典人的開國之王，並成為其財富之神：其治下風調雨順、四海昇平。他娶巨人族女子葛德為妻時抵押了自己的寶劍，後來只能空手以鹿角誅殺巨人貝利。他死後，屍身被葬於烏普薩拉的巨大墳丘，而瑞典人見國運依舊昌隆，便相信神仍活在丘下——祭祀不絕。這是一座埋葬神王的墳丘崇拜。1070年代，不來梅的亞當親見其神廟：索爾居中而坐，沃坦與長著巨大陽具的弗里克科（弗雷）分列兩側，各種雄牲各九頭懸掛於神聖林中獻祭。此記錄是北歐文獻中記載最完備的崇拜：神即王，王即被葬之神。

language: Old Norse / Old Icelandic; Latin (Adam of Bremen)
canonical_translation: Samuel Laing, Heimskringla, London 1844 (public domain); Adam of Bremen via paraphrase per Tschan 1959

narrative.en:
The myth-histories fuse the god and the dynasty. In Ynglinga saga, Freyr (Frey) succeeds his father Njord as ruler of the Swedes and is called their king: 'in his days began the Fródi-peace' - good seasons and peace such that the Swedes attributed their wealth to him; he built a great temple at Uppsala and dedicated to himself? - the saga: he took up his dwelling at Uppsala 'and appointed? ' - the account continues that he established the great sacrifices there and the wealth of the Swedes was by his blessing. When he fell sick and died, his men buried him in a great mound 'in the Swedish manner'? - the text: 'and they laid him in a mound at Uppsala' - and because the good seasons continued, they believed he still lived beneath, and offerings were made to the mound 'as to a god': gold, rings and sacrifices poured into the barrow for three? years, until the Swedes understood he was dead - and then, the saga says, they burned him and worshipped him as a god still.

The prose Edda supplies the god's warrior-doctrine: Freyr, having pledged his sword for Gerd, meets the giant Beli and kills him bare-handed 'with a stag's horn' - Snorri's pointed economics: had Freyr kept his sword, 'then the giant would? ' - the text: 'the gods would be served by it at Ragnarok'; the god's martial poverty is the price of his marriage. Gylfaginning also names his gear: the ship Skidbladnir, folded like cloth in his purse, and the boar Gullinbursti with golden bristles that lights the dark.

The outsider's document fixes the cult's reality. Adam of Bremen, writing c. 1070s from the archbishopric's mission-station, describes the temple at Uppsala: 'the people? ' - the chronicle: a temple entirely of gold, in which three images stand - Thor, mightiest, enthroned in the center, with Wodan and Fricco on either side; Fricco (Freyr) is sculpted with an enormous phallus; the priests offer nine males of every species, male animals and men, and hang them in the sacred grove beside the temple; the grove's every tree is sacred, and a golden chain rings the temple's gable; sacrifices at nine-year intervals. The record is Europe's best-documented pagan cult-site, and its Fricco-phallus confirms the fertility-god's iconography that the sagas imply.

Cultural functions: the god-king doctrine (the deity as dynasty-founder, buried and worshipped in a mound - the mythic charter of Swedish sacral kingship); the naked-king economics (the fertility god fights without his sword because his marriage bought the harvest); and the mound-cult doctrine (offerings to a buried god whose prosperity proves his life - the mythic logic by which a barrow becomes a temple). In the atlas, the record anchors the god-king and mound-cult families (the Chinese sage-kings' temples, the Egyptian dead-god cults): each a ruler worshipped as god; the Norse one is distinctive in being a Vanir hostage whose marriage priced his arms.

functions: God-king doctrine: the deity as dynasty-founder, worshipped alive beneath the mound
Mound-cult charter: prosperity proves the buried god's life; offerings keep him fed
Naked-king economics: the fertility god fights bare-handed because his marriage bought the harvest
Outsider documentation: Adam of Bremen's temple description fixes the cult's reality

passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Ynglinga saga chs. 10-12 (Laing 1844); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 弗雷爾在世的年代，和平與豐年降臨，瑞典人因此將他們的財富歸功於他；他死後，人們將他安葬在烏普薩拉的一座大墳塚中，而由於豐年依舊持續，他們相信他仍住在墳塚之下，便向這座墳塚獻上黃金與指環作為祭品。

passages.text: Freyr, having pledged his sword for the maiden Gerd, met the giant Beli and slew him bare-handed with a stag's horn; had he kept the sword, the gods would have been served by it at Ragnarok. The temple at Uppsala, as the chronicler saw it: three images stand, and Thor, mightiest of them, is enthroned in the center, with Wodan and Fricco on either side; Fricco is sculpted with an enormous phallus; nine males of every species, animals and men, hang sacrificed in the sacred grove beside the temple.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 37 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis 4.26-27 (per Tschan 1959); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 弗雷爾為了少女葛德而將自己的劍作為抵押送出，後來遇上巨人貝利，赤手空拳以鹿角將他殺死；倘若他保住了那把劍，諸神在諸神黃昏時本可仰仗它。據編年史家所見，烏普薩拉的 temple 中：立著三尊神像，其中最強大的索爾端坐中央，沃丹與弗里克分別位於兩側；弗里克被雕有巨大的陽具；在 temple 旁的聖林中，每一物種——無論動物或人——都有九名雄性懸掛獻祭。

title.en: Freyja's Necklace: The Brisingamen, the Flea and the Duel
title.zh: 芙蕾雅的項鏈：布里辛嘉門、跳蚤與雙神決鬥

region.en: Folkvangr and the walls of Asgard (symbolic pin at Gamla Uppsala, Sweden)
region.zh: 弗爾克萬格與阿斯加德城牆（象徵性定位於瑞典舊烏普薩拉）

period: Skaldskaparmal c. 1220-1230 (older material); Sörla tháttr (14th c.); principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal (the theft of Brisingamen); Sorla thattr in Flateyjarbok; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The goddess Freyja owns the finest jewel of the gods, the necklace Brisingamen, bought from four dwarf-smiths at a night's price. Loki wants it: he turns himself into a flea, bites the sleeping goddess' cheek, and when she turns, steals the necklace from her neck. Heimdall, the watchman, sees him and pursues - both in seal-shape through the surf - and recovers it. The late Sörla þáttr variant darkens the doctrine: the necklace bought by promiscuity, a bargain with four dwarfs, and Odin's curse that she be war-stirred and never rest till a man is found to fight for it - the necklace as the engine of human war. The record is the aition of the gods' costliest possession and of watchman-theft: the finest object in Asgard is stolen by its own pest-control.
summary.zh: 女神芙蕾雅擁有諸神中最華美的寶物——布里辛嘉門項鏈，以一夜之價購自四位矮人工匠。洛基覬覦此物：他化作跳蚤，叮咬熟睡女神的臉頰；趁她翻身的瞬間，自其頸上偷走項鏈。守望者海姆達爾察覺並追擊——二神化作海豹穿越浪濤——終於奪回寶物。晚期《索爾拉短篇》將此教義染上陰影：項鏈以放縱為代價購得，是與四矮人的交易；奧丁更施以詛咒，令她為戰亂所擾、永無寧日，直到有人為此寶而戰——項鏈遂成為人間戰爭的引擎。此記錄解釋了諸神最昂貴財物的來歷，以及「守望者失竊」的主題：阿斯加德最珍貴之物，竟被自己的除蟲員偷走。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain); Sorla thattr per paraphrase

narrative.en:
The necklace-episode is preserved in two registers. The skaldic-prose register (Skaldskaparmal's kenning-apparatus) documents the theft and the duel: Freyja wears the necklace Bris (Brisingamen, 'the necklace of the Brisings'); Loki covets it, tells no one, and changes himself into a flea; he creeps into her chamber where she sleeps with the necklace around her neck, bites her cheek so that she turns over, unclasps the necklace and takes it - and does not return it. Heimdall, the watchman, has seen him; he changes into seal-shape and pursues; Loki, seeing himself caught, changes into seal likewise, and the two fight in the surf; Heimdall wins and brings back the necklace. The kenning-doctrine: gold is 'Freyja's tears' and 'the necklace's? ' - the prose lists the necklace among the kenning-bases for gold, evidencing the myth's poetic currency.

The late prose variant (Sörla þáttr, in the 14th-c. Flateyjarbok) darkens the economics: the four dwarf-smiths make the necklace and refuse gold; Freyja pays the price each demands - a night apiece - and Odin, told of it, orders the necklace taken (Loki steals it as a flea again), and imposes the curse: she shall have the necklace again only if she brings two kings to war eternally, each fighting for it - 'and she stirred up war between kings, and they fought on? ' - the tháttr makes the necklace the engine of a war that only the Christian king Olaf Tryggvason's coming ends. The variant is a converted Icelander's moralization: the love-goddess's jewel re-narrated as the cause of human war, and the myth's oldest stratum (theft and duel) preserved inside a Christian parable.

The record's cultural functions are the economics of the gods' jewelry and the watchman-theft doctrine. Brisingamen is the myth-world's costliest object - bought at a price the goddess alone could pay - and its theft by the flea is the trickster's signature: the finest possession of the order is stolen through its own smallest gap. The duel of the two shapeshifters in seal-form is the myth's image of law-enforcement: the watchman who never sleeps recovers the treasure in the border-medium (sea) between worlds. And the late variant's war-engine doctrine documents the conversion-era moralization of the fertility-cult: love's necklace becomes war's cause, until a king of the new faith shuts the story.

In the atlas, the record anchors the divine-ornament-theft family (the Greek Ares' belt? - the girdle of Aphrodite; the Chinese He Shi-bi jade): each a prized object circulating through theft; the Norse one is distinctive in being won by a flea and adjudicated by a watchman in seal-shape.

functions: Economics of the gods' jewelry: the costliest object bought at a price only the goddess could pay
Watchman-theft doctrine: the finest possession stolen through its own smallest gap
Border-medium duel: law-enforcement in seal-shape through the surf
Conversion-era moralization: the necklace re-narrated as the engine of human war

passages.text: Loki changed himself into a flea, crept into Freyja's chamber, bit her cheek so that she turned, unclasped the necklace Brisingamen and took it away. Heimdall the watchman saw him, changed into seal-shape and pursued; Loki took seal-shape too, and they fought in the surf, and Heimdall won and brought back the necklace.

passages.zh: 洛基變成一隻跳蚤，潛入芙蕾雅的寢室，咬了她的臉頰，使她轉過身來，於是解開了項鍊布里斯英加曼並將其取走。守衛海姆達爾看見了他，變作海豹之形追趕；洛基也變作海豹之形，兩人在浪中搏鬥，海姆達爾得勝，取回了項鍊。

passages.text: In the late tale the necklace's price was paid to four dwarf-smiths, one night apiece; Odin ordered it stolen, and cursed Freyja: she should have it again only when two kings made war for it eternally - and she stirred up the war, until the coming of the new faith ended it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Sorla thattr (Flateyjarbok); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在較晚的故事中，這條項鍊的代價是付給四位矮人匠人，每夜一人；奧丁下令將它偷走，並詛咒芙蕾雅：唯有當兩位國王為它永遠征戰時，她才能再度擁有它——於是她挑起了那場戰爭，直到新信仰的到來才使之終結。

title.en: Tyr the One-Handed: The God of Oaths Who Fed the Wolf
title.zh: 獨臂的提爾：以誓言為職、曾餵養巨狼之神

summary.en: Tyr is the boldest and most courageous of the gods, and it is well for men of victory to call on him: 'it is proven that he rules over victory in battle'. His signature is his missing right hand - lost to the wolf Fenrir's bite when the other gods refused to pledge their own. In Lokasenna, when Loki taunts him - 'I have your hand, the wolf's snare' - Tyr answers with the oath-keeper's grief: 'I lost my hand, the wolf's snare, and grief have I got; the wolf stays bound, and I stay wretched'. And his deepest service is forgotten by all: he is Hymir's son, and it was Tyr who knew the giant's hall and led Thor to the mile-deep kettle. The record is the profile of law's god: the hand of the oath is the hand the wolf ate.
summary.zh: 提爾是諸神中最勇敢、最堅毅者，欲求戰勝者宜呼其名：「確切可知，他掌管戰鬥中的勝利」。其標誌是缺失的右手——當眾神皆不肯以手作保時，他的手被巨狼芬里爾咬去。在《洛基的吵罵》中，洛基譏諷他——「我握有你的手，那狼的鎖鏈」——提爾以守誓者的悲傷作答：「我失了手，成了狼的鎖鏈，我滿懷哀傷；狼被縛住，而我淒苦度日」。而他最深的功勞卻被眾神遺忘：他本是巨人希米爾之子，正是他知道巨人大廳之路，引索爾取回那口深達一里的巨釜。此記錄是法律之神的肖像：誓言之手，正是被狼吃掉的那隻手。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Gylfaginning's profile is brief and exact: Tyr is the boldest and most courageous of the gods, and he has great authority over victory in battle; 'it is well for men of valour to call on him'. His other name is 'the one-handed god', and the reason is the wolf: 'when the Aesir enticed Fenrir to let himself be bound with the chain Gleipnir, the wolf did not believe them to be minded to loose him till they laid Tyr's hand in his mouth as a pledge; and when the Aesir would not loose him, then he bit the hand off at the wrist - the place is called the wolf's joint? - and Tyr is one-handed and is not called a reconciler of men'. The prose adds the etymological point: the god of the oath is the god whose pledge-body is broken.

Lokasenna's flyting gives the grief its voice. Loki taunts: 'Be silent, Tyr! Thine hand? ' - the verses: 'I have thy hand, the snare of the wolf, and my son? ' - Loki claims credit for the binding and for the wolf's kinship? - the exchange: Loki says 'I was the father of the wolf? ' - no: Loki jeers 'thy hand could never hold aught', and Tyr answers: 'I lost my hand, the wolf's snare, and grief have I got; the wolf stays bound, and I stay wretched' - and then the second blow: Loki charges Tyr with cuckolding his wife, and Tyr falls silent - the oath-keeper's silence is the flyting's judgment that his private life cannot match his public honor.

The forgotten service is the kettle-quest's frame. In Hymiskvida, it is Tyr who offers to fetch the mile-deep kettle from the giant Hymir - 'for Hymir my father dwells there' - the law-god is the giant's son, and his kinship is the expedition's passport; he lifts the kettle-lid by its ring while Thor carries the vessel. The profile's cultural functions are the doctrine of pledged collateral (the god of oaths literally loses the body-part that secures them) and the paradox of law's kinships (the legal god is half giant - law's passport is a border-family). The etymology 'Tiwaz' ties him to the Indo-European sky-father (cf. Zeus, deus, Jupiter) - the oldest layer of the pantheon, and in the Norse material the god who has been overtaken by Odin and Thor in cult, surviving as the memory of what an oath costs.

For the atlas, the record anchors the sacrificial-office family: the god whose office is embodied (the hand as the pledge) - answering the Greek Zeus Horkios and the Roman Fides: each a deity of the sworn word; the Norse one pays for his office in flesh.

functions: Doctrine of pledged collateral: the oath-god's hand is the pledge the wolf ate
Office embodied in flesh: victory-law and oath-keeping carried on a one-armed body
Law's border-kinship: the legal god is the giant Hymir's son - law's passport is a border-family
Cult-history datum: the Indo-European sky-father (Tiwaz) demoted in Norse cult, surviving as oath-memory

title.en: Heimdall the White: Nine Mothers, Gold Teeth and the Horn That Wakes the Worlds
title.zh: 白神海姆達爾：九位母親、金齒與喚醒萬界的號角

region.en: Himinbjorg at Bifrost's edge (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 畢弗羅斯特橋頭的海姆比歐堡（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

summary.en: Heimdall is the white god, great and holy, born of nine mothers who are nine sisters - the wave-maidens, per Vafthrudnismal's riddle. His teeth are gold; he needs less sleep than a bird; he sees a hundred leagues by night as by day and hears the grass grow and the wool on the sheep. He guards the sky-bridge with the horn Gjallarhorn, whose blast wakes every world; he opposes Loki (and will kill him and be killed at Ragnarok); and in Rigspula he is the ancestor-father of the social estates. The record is the profile of the watchman-god: the senses of a frontier, the birth of nine waves, the horn of the last alarm.
summary.zh: 海姆達爾是白神，偉大而神聖，由九位彼此為姐妹的母親所生——據《瓦夫特魯德尼爾之歌》之謎，她們正是九位浪之侍女。他生有金齒；所需睡眠比鳥還少；晝夜皆能目視百里之遙，能聽見草的生長與羊背上的羊毛。他守護天橋，手持號角加拉德——其聲一響，萬界皆醒；他與洛基勢不兩立（末日之戰中二人同歸於盡）；在《里格詩篇》中他更是三階層的共同始祖。此記錄是守望之神的肖像：邊境的感官、九道浪濤的誕生，以及最後警報的號角。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The profile's strangest datum is his birth. Gylfaginning: 'nine mothers bore him, and all were sisters'; Vafthrudnismal's riddle supplies the identity: Odin asks 'whence came Heimdall, high-born, into the world?' and the giant answers in kenning-code - 'nine children the wave-maiden? ' - the verses: 'he was born of nine sisters, at the world's edge, of the wave-vaunted? one' - the nine sisters are the nine daughters of Aegir and Ran, the wave-maidens: the watchman is the sea's child, born at the world's rim, of the same water that rings Midgard.

The senses are his office: gold teeth; sleep less than a bird; sight of a hundred leagues night and day; hearing of the grass growing and the wool on the sheep's back; and the horn Gjallarhorn, kept in Himinbjorg at the bridge's edge, whose blast wakes every world - Snorri adds that Mimir's head? - no: the horn is also the trumpet of Ragnarok (Völuspá: 'Heimdall blows his horn aloft, men's road? - the sibyl hears it from the top of the tree'), and his counterpart is Loki: enmity between them is old (Lokasenna accuses Heimdall of drink-greed and back-stabbing prudence), and at Ragnarok the two kill each other - the watchman and the thief die in the same stroke.

His third office is social: in Rigspula he travels as Rig and fathers the three estates - thrall, freeman, noble - and the young king Kon, so that the class-system itself descends from the watchman's bed. The record's cultural functions are the frontier-senses doctrine (the guardian as a personified border-sensorium: sight, hearing, sleeplessness, teeth of gold - the god as infrastructure) and the wave-birth doctrine (the sea as the watchman's mother - the boundary made flesh). And his death at Loki's hand makes the profile eschatological: the alarm-system's final act is its own extinction, horn and thief dying together.

In the atlas, the record anchors the sentinel-god family (the Greek Hermes of the boundaries, the Chinese door-gods, the Roman Janus): each a guardian of crossings; the Norse one is distinctive in being born of the sea at the world's edge and in being scheduled to die with the very thief he watches.

The profile's nine-mothers doctrine completes the cosmology: the nine wave-maidens of Aegir and Ran as the watchman's mothers - the sea's daughters bearing the guardian of the sky-bridge - so the frontier between worlds is born from the sea itself. And the death-appointment completes the office: Heimdall and Loki, watchman and thief, kill each other at Ragnarok - the alarm-system's final act is its own extinction, the horn's last blast and the thief's last stroke in the same moment. The record thus anchors the sentinel-god family: the guardian born of the boundary's water, sensing the world's smallest motions, and scheduled to die with the boundary's breaker.

functions: Frontier-senses doctrine: the guardian as personified border-sensorium (sight, hearing, sleeplessness, gold teeth)
Wave-birth doctrine: nine wave-maiden mothers at the world's rim - the boundary made flesh
Watchman's eschatology: the horn of the last alarm, dying with the thief he watches
Social paternity: the class-system descending from the watchman's travels (Rigspula)

title.zh: 洛基的親族：詭計者的家族與怪物之群
