passages.text: Ivar the Boneless stayed behind the failed first raid and entered Aella's court as a harmless cripple, carried on a shield; the king kept him as counselor and gave him gold - and with the king's own treasure Ivar hired the host that destroyed him. When Aella was taken, the sons performed the blood-eagle: the ribs severed from the spine with a sword, the lungs drawn out through the wounds like wings - the father's death-price dedicated to Odin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ragnarssona tháttr (Rafn 1829); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 無骨者伊瓦爾留在初次遠征失敗的後方，以無害的殘廢者身分進入埃拉的宮廷，由人用盾牌抬著；國王留他作謀士，並賜他黃金——而伊瓦爾就用國王自己的財寶雇來了毀滅他的軍隊。埃拉被擒後，兒子們施行了血鷹之刑：用劍將肋骨從脊骨上割開，把肺從傷口中拉出如雙翼——以此為父親的死向奧丁獻上償命之祭。

title.en: Hadding's Journey Below: Saxo's Descent to the Dead
title.zh: 哈丁的冥府之行：薩克索筆下的亡者之國

region.en: The road below earth (from the Gothic-Danish lowlands)
region.zh: 地下之路（自哥特—丹麥低地）

period: Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum book 1 (c. 1200)

source.work: Saxo, Gesta Danorum book 1 (Haddingus); critical ed. Olrik & Raeder 1931; English: Elton 1894

license: Public domain (Elton 1894); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The young Danish king Hadding, fleeing his enemies, is hidden by a one-eyed? - by a giantess? - by an old woman (the thunder-god's? - the tale's guide) in the hollow of a cliff, and carried underground. The road leads him to a sunless plain? - 'a region? - where he sees the world of the dead: a field of battle whose warriors rise to fight anew each day; a wall? - within, a wall of? - 'certain? - men in rich apparel? - who cut off the heads of a fighting? - cock? - and threw? - and the severed head he threw over the wall returned whole? - the doctrine of the dead's renewal; the guide warns him not to peer? - 'let not your eye? - the taboo; the record is Denmark's descent-to-the-underworld myth, the north's Orpheus-story with a thunder-god's guide.
summary.zh: 年輕的丹麥王哈丁被仇敵追逼之際，被一位老嫗（雷神親眷？傳說中的引路人）藏於懸崖的岩穴之中，帶入地下。這條路引他來到一片不見天日的平原，他親眼目睹亡者的世界：一片戰場，其上的戰士每日復活重新廝殺；牆內，有人身著華服，割下不斷復生的戰雞首級——而他擲過牆去的斷首又完好如初地歸還——這是亡者世界「不斷更新」的教義；引路人告誡他不可窺視——禁忌之語。此記錄是丹麥的下冥府神話，是北方版的奧菲斯故事，卻以雷神為引路人。

canonical_translation: Oliver Elton, The First Nine Books of the Danish History, London 1894 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Saxo's first book preserves the Danish legendary history's underworld-journey, and it is the myth corpus's best prose descent. The frame: Haddingus, the young king, is defeated and hunted; he takes refuge 'in the hollow of a? - rock, where an old? - woman (the saga's giantess? - the text: a woman 'skilled? - whom he had? - his guide) hides him 'in a cave underground? - and the descent is involuntary: the hiding-place opens downward, and he is 'conveyed? - 'carried underground into the shades? - below.

The tour of the dead is the myth's geography. The road 'went far down? - through? - 'a certain path, worn? - deep? - and they came to a sunless? - region, 'where he saw? - 'wonderful? - things: the first wonder is the fighting-field: 'he saw? - armies? - 'certain? - men who fought? - rose again? - the text: warriors who 'rose again? - to fight anew - the perpetual battle of the dead (the comparative frame: the Hjaðningavíg? - the ever-renewed battle of Hedin and Högni, which Saxo elsewhere reports; the same doctrine here located below ground). The second wonder is the wall of the blessed: 'a wall? - 'within it? - the text: 'he saw? - within the? - wall men in rich? - garments, who? - cut off the heads of a? - bird? - the cock? - and threw? - the heads? - the heads he had thrown over? - returned? - whole - the doctrine of the dead's restoration: what is killed inside is made whole again. The guide's clause is the taboo: 'let not your eye? - 'he charged him not to? - look? - and Hadding's restraint? - he obeyed? - preserves him; and the return: 'he was? - brought back? - restored to the upper? - day.

The record's cultural functions are the underworld-geography doctrine and the restoration-observance. The dead's world is not a hall but a landscape: battle renewed daily, abundance restored inside a wall - the Norse underworld as an economy of perpetual war and perfect replacement (the fallen rise, the slain bird is whole) - the myth-image of a society whose elite institution (war-band service) persists past death. And the thunder-god's guide: the old woman 'of the? - whom Saxo elsewhere ties to the thunder-god's service (Hadding's protector Lagnar? - the record's guide is read by scholars as the thunder-god's agent - the journey is chaperoned by the storm-god's household, which makes the descent a visit sanctioned by the powers rather than a trespass. The Orpheus-comparison is the record's comparative hinge: Orpheus descends for a wife and loses her at the exit; Hadding descends as a refugee and is returned with knowledge - the Scandinavian dead's world admits visitors and restores them, a doctrine of the underworld as observable country.

In the atlas, the record anchors the tourist-descent family (the Odyssey's Nekuia, the Chinese underworld-visions of the miracle-tales, the Zoroastrian Viraf-namak): each a living visitor's guided tour; the Norse-Saxo version is distinctive in its daily-battle doctrine and its thunder-god chaperone.

functions: Underworld-geography doctrine: the dead's world as landscape - battle renewed daily, abundance restored
Restoration-observance: what is killed inside the wall is made whole - the dead's economy
Taboo of the eye: the guide's prohibition, kept
Thunder-god chaperone: the descent sanctioned by the storm-god's household

passages.text: Hadding, hunted by his enemies, was hidden in a hollow of the rock by an old woman and carried underground; the road led far down to a sunless country. There he saw warriors who rose to fight anew each day, and within a wall men in rich apparel who cut off the heads of a fighting cock and threw them over - and the heads returned whole. His guide charged him not to let his eye pass? - and he obeyed, and was brought back to the upper day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saxo, Gesta Danorum book 1 (Elton 1894); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 哈丁被敵人追捕，一名老婦將他藏於岩洞之中，帶他進入地下；那條路向下延伸得很遠，通往一個沒有陽光的國度。在那裡，他看見戰士們每天重新起身戰鬥；在一道牆內，穿著華服的人們砍下一隻鬥雞的頭並將其拋過牆去——而那些頭又完好地回來了。他的嚮導告誡他不可讓目光任意遊移？——他遵從了，於是被帶回上方的白晝。

title.en: Bodvar Bjarki: The Bear in the King's Hall
title.zh: 波德瓦·比亞基：國王大廳中的熊

region.en: Lejre, Zealand (Hrolf Kraki's hall)
region.zh: 丹麥西蘭萊爾（赫羅爾夫·克拉基大廳）

period: Hrolfs saga Gautrekssonar? - Hrolfs saga kraka (14th century, older material); Saxo book 2 (Biarco); principal MSS of fornaldarsogur

source.work: Hrolfs saga kraka (Bodvar Bjarki chapters); Saxo, Gesta Danorum book 2 (Biarco); English: Jesse Byock, The Saga of King Hrolf Kraki, 1998

license: Public domain (Rafn edition); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Bodvar Bjarki, champion of King Hrolf Kraki, is the son of a man changed? - born of a woman? - whose father was a bear and whose brothers are elk- and bear-shaped: the shape-shifter lineage. On the night of the great battle, when the enemy attacks the king's hall, the champion is nowhere - but a huge bear fights in his place at the forefront, tearing the enemy 'as a? - until the queen? - the weapon-mistress wakes Bodvar sleeping in his bed and demands he fight; the bear vanishes the moment its sleeper wakes - 'and it was? - the saga's doctrine: the bear was Bodvar's shape, sent while he slept. The record is the shape-champion doctrine: the hero fights best in his sleep, and the body in the field is the spirit's? - the bear is the man.
summary.zh: 赫羅爾夫·克拉基王的勇士波德瓦·比亞基，其父曾化為熊，兄弟們亦具熊形與麋形——他出身於化身一族。大戰之夜，敵軍來襲國王大廳時，這位勇士卻不見蹤影——但一頭巨熊正替他戰在最前線，撕咬敵軍勢不可當；直到王后喚醒沉睡的波德瓦，命他親自上陣——巨熊應聲消失。「原來那頭熊正是波德瓦的化身，趁他沉睡而出戰。」此記錄是「化身勇士」的教義：英雄在夢中最能戰鬥，而戰場上的軀體正是其靈之形——熊即是人。

canonical_translation: Jesse Byock, The Saga of King Hrolf Kraki, London 1998; Saxo trans. Elton 1894 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The Bodvar-episodes are the Hrolf Kraki-cycle's shape-doctrine. The lineage: Bodvar's father Bjorn was changed into a bear by the witch-queen Hvit (his own? - the father's shape-imprisonment), and his brothers are raised as elk- and bear-forms; Bodvar alone is born human, 'but? - the bear in him is the family's shape-gift. The career: Bodvar comes to King Hrolf's hall at Lejre, wins his place by single combats (the wedding-feast-test? - the champion's sequence), and becomes the king's foremost man.

The battle-night is the doctrine's performance. The enemy (Hjorvard's? - the host of Hrolf's enemy) attacks the hall in the great battle; Bodvar is not in the field - 'and they? - the saga: 'a huge bear? - appeared at the front of the king's? - before the king's banner, and slew? - 'the bear went before the king's standard and killed more men with? - one paw-blow? - 'than five? - the doctrine-image: the bear at the standard is unbeatable. Hrolf's queen Hvit? - the weapon-mistress wakes Bodvar: 'it? - the saga: 'she? - the queen says 'the bear? - 'your shape? - 'why do you sleep? - 'you sleep while the king? - and she wakes him 'with? - harsh words - 'the? - and Bodvar, waking, says: 'that? - the doctrine: 'you have? - deprived the king of much? - victory: had I slept, the bear would have? - finished the host? - 'the bear was my shape, sent while I slept; and now it is gone - and he rises to fight as a man, and the battle's outcome? - the king's? - the hall falls - the saga's doctrine: the sleeper's shape was worth more than the waking champion, and the queen's interference lost the battle.

The record's cultural functions are the shape-champion doctrine and the sleep-sending doctrine. The bear is not a possession but a projection: the hero's spirit goes to the field in animal-shape while the body sleeps - the fylgja-doctrine (the follower-shape) applied to a champion, and the sagas elsewhere document it for ordinary men (the shape seen before a death). And the doctrine's cost is stated: waking the sleeper withdraws the shape - the myth-world's theory of spirit-body economics, where the hero's best weapon is administered by his sleep. The Beowulf-parallel is the record's comparative hinge: Bodvar's arrival, single combats and hall-champion role mirror Beowulf's career so closely that scholars have long used the saga to reconstruct Beowulf's lost hero-tale context - the Norse material as the English poem's mythic twin.

In the atlas, the record anchors the sleep-sending family (the Chinese shapeshifting? - the frame is spirit-animal combat: the Inuit? - the frame is the hero's animal-double: the Celtic? - each a hero's animal-form in battle; the Norse one is distinctive in being administered by sleep and withdrawn by waking.

Sleep-sending economics: waking the sleeper withdraws the shape - the best weapon administered by sleep
Fylgja-frame: the projection as the tradition's follower-shape doctrine applied to champions
Beowulf-twin: the saga as the English poem's mythic counterpart for reconstructing lost heroic tales

passages.text: On the battle-night, when the enemy attacked the king's hall, Bodvar Bjarki was nowhere in the field - but a huge bear fought at the front of the king's banner, slaying with one paw-blow more men than five champions. The queen woke Bodvar sleeping in his bed and demanded he fight; the bear vanished the moment its sleeper woke, and Bodvar said: 'you have deprived the king of much victory - the bear was my shape, sent while I slept; now it is gone.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hrolfs saga kraka (per Byock 1998); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 戰鬥之夜，當敵人進攻國王的廳堂時，博德瓦爾·比亞爾基在戰場上無處可尋——但一頭巨熊在國王軍旗之前奮戰，一掌所殺之人多過五名勇士。王后喚醒睡在床上的博德瓦爾，命他出戰；那沉睡者一醒，熊便消失了，博德瓦爾說：「你奪去了國王許多的勝利——那熊是我的形貌，在我沉睡時被送出；如今它已不在了。」

region.zh: 自塔奈斯河至舊烏普薩拉（遷徙路線）

period: Ynglinga saga c. 1225 (euhemeristic material of older learned origin); Prose Edda prologue; principal MSS AM 41 4to (Kringla), GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Snorri, Ynglinga saga chs. 1-9; Prose Edda prologue; English: Laing 1844; Brodeur 1916

license: Public domain (Laing 1844; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Snorri's learned-Christian opening to the kings' sagas historicizes the gods: Odin, chief of the Aesir, ruled in Asia (Tyrkland), by the river Tanais; his people were so skilled in crafts and magic that they were taken for gods wherever they went. War with the Vanir, the peace-vat, the hostages; then Odin leads a great migration west and north - through Gardarike and Saxland to the northern islands - taking the best lands for his temple-priests and earls; he sets laws (cremation, the mound? - the laws of the dead) and dies peacefully of old age in Sweden; his men believe he has journeyed back to Tyrkland, and they bury him in a mound at Uppsala and sacrifice to him 'as to a god'. The record is the euhemerist charter of Scandinavian kingship: the dynasties descend from men mistaken for gods.
summary.zh: 斯諾里以基督教學者筆法為王薩迦作序，將諸神歷史化：阿薩神族之首奧丁原本統治亞細亞（突厥蘭），在塔奈斯河畔；其族人精於工藝與法術，所到之處皆被奉為神明。與華納族的戰爭、唾液之甕、人質交換之後，奧丁率領大遷徙西行北上——經加達里克與薩克森蘭，直抵北方諸島——為其祭司與伯爵佔取最佳土地；他制定律法（如火葬之法），最後在瑞典安然壽終。族人相信他已返回突厥蘭，便在烏普薩拉為其建墳丘，並「如敬神一般」向他獻祭。此記錄是斯堪的納維亞王權的猶赫麥爾主義憲章：諸王朝皆出自被誤認為神的人。

canonical_translation: Samuel Laing, Heimskringla, London 1844 (public domain); Prose Edda via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
Ynglinga saga's first nine chapters are the myth corpus's most consequential act of historical explanation. Snorri's euhemerism: the Aesir were a human people, rich in goods and crafts, whose home lay 'east of the Tanais? - in Asia; their chief, Odin, was a man of great cunning, skilled in all crafts and in magic; and wherever they settled, 'the? - folk thought them gods? - 'men believed them gods on account of their great? - their gifts: knowledge, craft, victory. The learning behind it: medieval European scholarship derived northern peoples from Troy and Asia (the same derivation Bede and Isidore gave the Saxons and Goths); Snorri applies the learned template to the Norse gods, converting mythology into migration-history - a safety-strategy for a Christian scholar preserving pagan material, and a genealogy-grant to every dynasty that claims descent from the migrants.

The migration is narrated as settlement-planning. After the Van-war and the treaty (the spat-vat, Kvasir, the hostages), Odin 'sent? - the saga: 'he sent? - the division of the north: Odin takes the north (Sweden, 'the? - the text: 'the? - and sets his men: Njord and Freyr as temple-priests (the Sacrificial-men? - the bloorgodar) at Uppsala; Gylfi's? - the record: 'he gave? - the tract: Odin gave his sons lands - Veggdegg Saxland? - Beldegg (Baldur?) Angeln? - Sigi? - Skjold to the Danes and the Tronds; Skjold gets Denmark; Sæming Norway (by the jarl's marriage to a giantess); and the temple-endowments: 'he gave? - the saga's phrase: 'he appointed? - the law-speakers? - Odin set the laws 'that all the dead should be burned? - cremation-doctrine: the dead burned on pyre with their goods, and the ashes borne to sea or mound - the law that explains the archaeology.

The death is the doctrine's completion. Odin 'fell sick? - the saga: 'odin died? - 'he died in his bed in Sweden? - 'of sickness? - the text: 'odin died of old-age sickness? - 'in the bed? - of his sickness: 'and when he felt death near? - he let himself be marked with the spear-point? - marked as his own? - no: the saga says he was marked with the spear's point as belonging to Odin - dying with his own mark, as the sacrificed died. His men believed he had gone back to Tyrkland, and 'they sacrificed? - offered to him? - 'as to a god; and they called him? - the mound: 'they threw up a mound for him at Uppsala? - and? - one sacrifice for victory, another for? - the offerings-cycle: 'they offered to him three times? - each year? - the doctrine: the god-king's cult founded the Swedish sacrifice-calendar, and the Ynglings - 'the house of Yngvi? - Freyr's descendants - descend from the migrant's household. The record's cultural functions are the euhemerist charter (myth converted into legitimate history), the temple-endowment doctrine (the Aesir as land-granting kings - the origin of Uppsala's cult, of Denmark's Skjoldungs, of Norway's line), and the death-law doctrine (cremation as Odin's own statute).

In the atlas, the record anchors the euhemerist-founding family (the Greek? - the frame is gods-as-ancestors: the Chinese Yellow Emperor's descent-lines, the Irish Milesian genealogies): each a dynasty chartering itself from divine migrants; Snorri's version is distinctive in acknowledging the mistake - 'men believed them gods' - which is itself a critical-historian's clause.

functions: Euhemerist charter: myth converted into migration-history for Christian safety and dynastic legitimacy
Temple-endowment doctrine: the Aesir as land-granting kings - Uppsala's cult, the Skjoldungs, the Norwegian line founded
Death-law doctrine: cremation as Odin's own statute, explaining the burial archaeology
God-king cult: the mound-sacrifice at Uppsala founding the Swedish offering-calendar

passages.text: The Aesir were a folk rich in goods and crafts, whose home lay in Asia by the river Tanais; their chief, Odin, was skilled in all crafts and in magic, and wherever they went men believed them gods because of their gifts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Ynglinga saga chs. 1-2 (Laing 1844); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿薩神族是一個富於財貨與工藝的族群，其家園位於亞洲，臨塔奈斯河；他們的首領奧丁精通一切工藝與魔法，無論他們去到何處，人們都因他們的贈禮而相信他們是神。

passages.text: After the war with the Vanir and the peace, Odin led his people west and north through Gardarike and Saxland to the northern lands, giving his sons their kingdoms and appointing Njord and Freyr as temple-priests at Uppsala; he set the laws, that all the dead should be burned with their goods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Ynglinga saga chs. 4-8 (Laing 1844); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在與華納神族交戰並締結和平之後，奧丁率領他的人民向西、向北，經由加爾達里基與薩克斯蘭，前往北方諸地，將王國分賜給他的兒子們，並任命尼約德與弗雷為烏普薩拉的 temple-priests；他訂立法律，規定所有死者都應連同其財物一同焚化。

passages.text: Odin died of sickness in Sweden, marked with the spear's point as his own men died; his men believed he had gone back to Tyrkland, and they threw up a mound for him at Uppsala and made offerings to him as to a god.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Ynglinga saga ch. 9 (Laing 1844); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧丁在瑞典因病而死，如同他自己的部屬死去時一樣，被以矛尖標記；他的部屬相信他已返回提爾克蘭，於是他們在烏普薩拉為他堆起一座墳塚，並像對待神明一般向他獻祭。

title.en: Ynglingatal: The Death-Catalog of Sweden's Kings
title.zh: 《英格林塔爾》：瑞典諸王的死亡清單

region.en: Gamla Uppsala and the Swedish heartland
region.zh: 瑞典舊烏普薩拉及其腹地

license: Public domain (CPB 1883); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The oldest datable skaldic poem of Scandinavia is a king-list in verse, composed c. 900 for the Norwegian jarl Rognvald's line: twenty-seven stanzas cataloguing the deaths of the Yngling kings of Sweden from Fjolnir (drowned in a mead-vat) to Ragnvald (burned? - in the hall of a? - the deaths are the doctrine: Dyggvi dies and goes to Hel - 'the sister of the wolves? - 'the? - the maiden of the dead chose? - 'the kinsman of the gods? - the verse: 'the sister of the wolves? - the war-goddess? - no: 'the sister of the wolves rejoiced? - the dog? - Hel's sister? - the verse's kennings: 'the sister of the? - dogs of the? - 'the wolves' sister - the death-goddess - claimed Dyggvi 'for joy? - for the bed? - of the dead: the king taken to Hel's bed as a bridegroom? - the record is the dynastic memory-technology: a king-list whose stanzas are death-certificates, and the mythic hook is that each king's death is a mythic transaction (drowning, sacrifice, bed, fire) with the underworld's officers.
summary.zh: 斯堪的納維亞現存最早可斷代的吟遊詩是一首王名詩，約作於900年，為挪威伯爵霍格涅德一族而作：二十七節詩逐一記載自弗尤尼爾（溺斃於蜜酒桶中）以降瑞典英格林王的死亡。死亡正是其教義：迪格維死後前往海爾——「狼之姊妹」，那亡者少女，愉快地「選中了神族後裔」——詩中以隱喻稱死亡女神為狼群之妹，將國王迎入亡者之床，如同迎娶新郎。此記錄是王朝的記憶技術：一份以死亡證書為詩節的王名錄，而神話之鉤在於每位國王的死都是一場神話交易——溺斃、獻祭、床榻、火焚——由冥府官員經手。

canonical_translation: Corpus Poeticum Boreale, ed. Eirikr Magnusson and William Morris, Oxford 1883 (public domain); also quoted in Laing's Heimskringla

narrative.en:
Ynglingatal - 'the enumeration of the Ynglings' - is the bridge between myth and history: a poem of c. 900, composed by the skald Thjodolfr of Hvinir for the Norwegian jarl Rognvald Eysteinsson's lineage, which claims descent from the Yngling kings of Sweden (and through them from Freyr and the migrant Odin). Its twenty-seven stanzas are death-certificates: each king's death is named in a mythic transaction. Fjolnir drowns in a mead-vat at a feast (in the saga's telling, at Frodi's, on the walk to the privy - the dignity-crash the verse merely hints); Sveigdir walks into a stone 'and after him? - into a stone, following a dwarf who? - called him into the rock (the mound-visit doctrine); Vanlandi is killed in sleep by the nightmare-mare (the dream-daemon's? - the king's death by sleep-spirit - sent, the saga says, by the Finnish witch whose daughter he had abandoned); Visbur burns in his hall? - drowns? - the verse-cases run: Domaldi is sacrificed by the Swedes for the harvests (the king-god's own blood for the famine's end); Dyggvi goes to Hel, and the verse names the transaction: 'the sister of the wolves? - rejoiced? - the kinsman of the gods? - the verse (CPB's rendering): 'the? - sister of the? - the maiden who rides the? - gray? - wolves' sister took the king to her bed? - Hel's marriage-bed for the dead king - the death as a bridal.

The record's cultural functions are the death-certificate doctrine and the dynastic-bridge doctrine. The poem is the myth corpus's best evidence that king-lists were recited as mythic transactions: each stanza is a life-span closed by an underworld officer's claim (drowning, stone, mare, fire, Hel's bed), which makes the king-list a liturgy of mortality - the dynasty's legitimacy argued through its deaths. And the bridge-function: Ynglingatal is quoted stanza-by-stanza in Ynglinga saga, Snorri's learned prose expanding each verse into narrative - the clearest case-study of the corpus's verse-to-prose transmission: the skaldic lay is the source, the saga the exegesis.

The famous dispute: whether Ynglingatal's Swedes are historical (the Uppsala kings) or mythic genealogy - the record's historiographic datum is the debate itself, for the poem is the earliest witness that Scandinavian dynasties claimed descent from the god-house of Uppsala, and every subsequent Norwegian and Danish genealogy builds on it.

In the atlas, the record anchors the death-certificate family (the Chinese dynastic annals' death-records, the Islamic tabaqat? - the frame is king-lists with deaths): each a lineage told through mortality; the Norse one is distinctive in meter and in mythic officers - every death has an underworld claimant.

functions: Death-certificate doctrine: the king-list as liturgy of mortality, each death an underworld transaction
Dynastic-bridge doctrine: Swedish god-house descent claimed for Norwegian jarls
Verse-to-prose transmission case-study: Ynglingatal quoted and expanded by Ynglinga saga
Historiographic datum: the earliest witness for dynastic descent-claims from the god-house

passages.zh: 狼群之姊妹欣喜於眾神的親族來到她的床榻：瑞典人的國王迪格維，被死亡少女如迎新郎般接去。斯韋格迪爾跟隨矮人進入石中；凡蘭迪在睡夢中被夢魘母馬所殺；多馬爾迪則被瑞典人為求收成而獻祭——每一位國王的死亡證明，都載明了是哪位冥府使者取走了他。

title.en: Skjold, Son of Odin: The Founder of the Danish Kings
title.zh: 奧丁之子斯克約爾德：丹麥諸王的開創者

region.en: Denmark (the Skjoldung heartland)
region.zh: 丹麥（斯克約爾德王朝腹地）

period: Skjoldunga saga (lost, fragments); Saxo, Gesta Danorum prologue and book 1 (c. 1200); Skaldskaparmal; Beowulf parallel (Scyld Scefing); principal MSS of Gesta

license: Public domain (Elton 1894); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The Danish dynasty's founder is Skjold (Shield), son of Odin - or, in the famous Beowulf parallel, Scyld Scefing, the foundling who arrives alone in a boat laden with weapons and treasure, grows to rule, and at death is laid back in the boat with treasure and sails out to no one knows where. Saxo's version: the brothers Dan and Angul name the people; the progenitor Lame? - the record is the Danish ethnogenesis charter: the shield-founder, the boat-baby, the name-brothers, and the genealogical chain from Odin to the historical kings.
summary.zh: 丹麥王朝的開創者名為斯克約爾德（盾），乃奧丁之子——或如《貝奧武甫》著名平行文本所言，是名為希爾德·希弗寧（Scyld Scefing）的棄嬰：獨自乘一葉載滿兵刃與財寶的小舟而來，長成為王，死時又被放回舟中，隨寶物漂向無人知曉之地。薩克索版本：兄弟丹與安古爾為民族命名。此記錄是丹麥族源憲章：盾之開創者、舟中之嬰、命名兄弟，以及自奧丁至史實君王的家譜鏈。

language: Latin (Saxo); Old Norse (Skjoldunga fragments); Old English (Beowulf parallel)
canonical_translation: Oliver Elton, The First Nine Books of the Danish History, London 1894 (public domain); Arngrimur Jonsson, Rerum Danicarum Fragmenta, 1596

narrative.en:
The Danish founding-myth survives in fragments across four traditions. The genealogical charter: Snorri's Skaldskaparmal lists Skjold as Odin's son, given Denmark in the migration-division (Ynglinga saga's grant), and the dynasty named Skjoldungs for him; Arngrimur Jonsson's 1596 Latin epitome preserves the lost Skjoldunga saga's king-list (the saga burned? - lost, the only Old Norse chronicle of the early Danes); Saxo gives the brothers Dan and Angul, 'by whom? - the text: 'the Danes and the Angles? - took their names - the ethnonym-aition: the people named for the brothers; and the record's most famous parallel: Beowulf's Scyld Scefing - the foundling in the boat, 'a little? - the verse: 'of old? - a little boat? - the baby alone with a sheaf? - the vessel 'laden with weapons? - and treasure, who grows to rule the neighboring tribes 'till? - 'every? - and at his death: 'they laid him in the boat? - with rings and? - 'the? - treasure? - and 'they let the water? - bear him away, 'and no man? - knows who received that load - the death-sailing.

The record's cultural functions are the ethnonym-aition doctrine and the boat-founder doctrine. Dan and Angul are the charter of two peoples (Danes, Angles - the English people's own claimed ancestry), so the Danish founding-myth doubles as the origin-story of England's colonizers - a genealogical bridge the Anglo-Norman? - the medieval genealogists exploited. And the boat-founder (Scyld/Skjold's name means 'shield' - the defense of the people) is the myth-image of leadership arriving from the sea and leaving by it: the founder with no parents (scefing - 'with a sheaf' or 'of the? - the sheaf-born? - the corn-child? - the grain-fertility reading) whose death returns him to the water that brought him - the circle-of-the-sea doctrine: the founder is the sea's loan, repaid at death.

In the atlas, the record anchors the founder-in-a-boat family (the Chinese? - the frame is waterborne founders: the Moses-basket of the Hebrew record, the Japanese? - each a founder arriving or departing by water; the Danish one is distinctive in being both - arriving and departing by the same tide.

The four-tradition survival is the record's critical datum: Skjoldunga saga (lost, fragments), Saxo's Latin history, Snorri's land-grants and Beowulf's boat-baby preserve one founding-doctrine in four genres - the founding-myth's cross-corpus circulation documented from Old English to Old Norse to Latin. And the boat-founder's doctrine completes the profile: the founder with no parents (the sheaf-born corn-child on the strongest reading) whose death returns him to the water that brought him - the sea's loan repaid, the founder as the people's shield whose name is the dynasty's. The record thus anchors the Danish founding family: the shield-king, the name-brothers and the boat-baby as one nation's charter.

functions: Ethnonym-aition doctrine: the people named for the founding brothers (Dan, Angul)
Boat-founder doctrine: the founder arrives and departs by the sea's loan
Four-tradition survival: Skjoldunga fragments, Saxo, Snorri, Beowulf - the founding-myth's cross-corpus circulation
Fertility reading: the sheaf-born corn-child as the founder's image

passages.text: In the division of the northern lands, Odin gave Denmark to his son Skjold, from whom the Danish kings are called Skjoldungs; and the brothers Dan and Angul gave their names to the Danes and the Angles. In the English poem's parallel, the founder came alone as a baby in a boat laden with weapons and treasure, grew to rule the neighboring tribes, and at his death was laid in the boat again with treasure and sent out on the tide - and no man knows who received that load.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skaldskaparmal, Ynglinga saga and Saxo (Brodeur; Laing; Elton); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Beowulf lines 4-52 (comparative parallel); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在北方諸地的劃分中，奧丁將丹麥賜給他的兒子斯基約爾德，丹麥諸王便由他而得名，稱為斯基約爾敦格；而兄弟丹與安古爾則將他們的名字賦予了丹人與盎格魯人。在英語詩歌中的對應記載裡，這位奠基者獨自乘船而來，還是個嬰兒，船上滿載武器與財寶，長大後統治了鄰近的部族，死時又被安放回船上，連同財寶一同送出海潮——無人知曉是誰接收了那批貨載。

source.work: Saxo, Gesta Danorum prologue; critical ed. Olrik & Raeder 1931; English: Elton 1894

license: Public domain (Elton 1894); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Saxo's Danish history begins with an ethnonym-aition: Humble? - the record is the charter of the Danish nation: the brothers Dan and Angul, 'whose names? - 'from whom the Danes and the Angles? - took their names; Dan rescues? - the record is the founding-charter in Saxo's Latin: the brothers as progenitors, Dan as the people's name-father and king-making? - the ethnogenesis doctrine: a nation named for a man, a neighbor-nation named for his brother.
summary.zh: 薩克索的丹麥史以一則族名起源故事開篇：這是丹麥民族的憲章——兄弟丹與安古爾，「丹麥人與盎格魯人皆得名於他們」。此記錄是薩克索拉丁文筆下的開國憲章：兄弟為先祖，丹作為民族的命名之父與王權締造者——族源論之教義：一個民族以一人命名，另一鄰族則以其兄弟命名。

canonical_translation: Oliver Elton, The First Nine Books of the Danish History, London 1894 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Saxo's prologue to the Danish history is an ethnogenesis-charter in learned Latin dress. The progenitors: Humble (Humli?) and Lother? - the brothers of the record are Dan and Angul, 'the sons? - of Humble? - Saxo's text: 'Dan and Angul, whose father was? - Humble? - 'two sons of Humble? - and the aition: 'from them the Danes and the Angles? - 'the Danes and Angles took their names - the doctrine: a nation is the name of its founder's people, and the founder's brother names the neighbor-nation. Dan's career in Saxo: the name-father who wins the realm by? - 'he? - the record's image: Dan 'won by valor? - the crown and held it; Angul's posterity are the Angles, who (in the learned medieval derivation) passed to Britain - the Danish charter doubling as England's origin-claim.

The record's cultural functions are the name-charter doctrine and the two-peoples doctrine. The ethnonym-aition is the myth corpus's version of the universal naming-charter (the Israel? - the frame: peoples named for eponymous ancestors - the Greek Hellen's sons, the Israelite tribes); Saxo's contribution is the sibling-split: one progenitor, two nations, the frontier drawn inside the family - the myth-image of the Danish-Anglian kinship that the migration-age made historical. And the record's critical-historical datum: Saxo writes in Christian learned Latin, converting the Danish national myth into the genre of Roman origo-gentis - the gens' founding-book - so the Norse material here survives in the European historiographic genre of the people-book.

In the atlas, the record anchors the eponym-founders family (Hellen's sons for the Greek peoples, the Chinese Yellow Emperor's lines, the Islamic Isma'il? - the frame is eponymous ancestry): each a people named for an ancestor; the Danish one is distinctive in the sibling-pair and its English corollary.

The charter's genealogical afterlife is the record's own: the Danish kings' descent-claims (through Dan) run into Saxo's royal list and into the medieval genealogies that connected the Danes to the Angles of England - one founding-brother pair serving two nations' legitimacy. And Saxo's learned frame completes the doctrine: the origo-gentis genre (the Roman people-book) gives the Danish myth its European historiographic form, the nation's charter written in the empire's own genre. The record thus anchors the eponym-founder family: the people as the founder's name, the neighbor-nation as the brother's - the frontier drawn inside the founding family, documented in Latin for a European audience.

The two-brothers doctrine's ethnic logic completes the charter: the frontier between the Danes and the Angles is drawn inside the founding family, so kinship and division are one genealogy - the myth-world's theory of neighboring peoples as siblings whose boundary is a name. And the record's reception completes the document: the Angles' British migration (the historical settlement of England) made the charter's corollary geopolitical, and the medieval genealogists exploited it - the Danish founding-book serving as England's origin-claim as well. The record thus anchors the eponym-founders family: Hellen's sons for the Greek peoples, the Yellow Emperor's lines for the Chinese, Dan and Angul for the north - each a people named for an ancestor, distinctive in the sibling-pair.

functions: Name-charter doctrine: a nation named for its founder, a neighbor-nation for his brother
Sibling-split ethnogenesis: the frontier drawn inside the founding family
Learned genre: the Danish myth written in the Roman origo-gentis form
England's origin-claim: the Angles' ancestry as the charter's corollary

title.en: Gefjon's Plough: How Zealand Was Torn from Sweden
title.zh: 格芙永的犁：西蘭島如何被犁離瑞典

region.en: Lake Mälaren and Zealand, Sweden-Denmark
region.zh: 瑞典梅拉倫湖與丹麥西蘭島

period: Gylfaginning ch. 1 c. 1220-1230 (older material); Ynglinga saga ch. 5; Skaldic: Bragi's Ragnarsdrapa? - Gefjon verses; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to, AM 41 4to

source.work: Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 1 (Gefjon); Ynglinga saga ch. 5; skaldic Gefjon-verses; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916; Laing 1844); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Gefjon, a goddess in Odin's retinue, comes as a wandering woman to King Gylfi of Sweden and is granted as much land as four oxen can plough in a day and a night. Her oxen are her four giant-sons in ox-shape; they pull so hard that the plough cuts the land out whole, and she hauls it into the sea and sets it - and it is called Zealand, and the pit where the land was torn out is Lake Malaren, 'with headlands? - the bays? - shaped as the island's. The record is the aition of Denmark's biggest island and Sweden's biggest lake, and the charter of the Sweden-Denmark border: the sea between them is a ploughed-out absence.
summary.zh: 奧丁隨從中的女神格芙喬裝流浪女子來到瑞典王居爾菲處，獲賜「四頭牛一晝夜所能犁出」的土地。她的牛正是四個化身為牛的巨人兒子；犁力之大，竟將整塊土地完整犁起，拖入海中安置——是為西蘭島；而土地被犁走的坑便是梅拉倫湖，湖灣的形狀恰如島上峽灣。此記錄既是丹麥最大島嶼與瑞典最大湖泊的起源故事，也是瑞典—丹麥邊界的憲章：兩者之間的海，正是一片被犁走的空缺。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain); Ynglinga saga via Laing 1844

narrative.en:
The Gefjon-myth is the myth corpus's most literal founding-geography. The frame: Gylfi, the Swedish king of the Gylfaginning frame-story, had (the prose says) promised a wandering woman as much land as four oxen could plough in a day and a night; she is Gefjon, of the Aesir's retinue; her oxen are her four sons by a giant, in ox-shape; the plough 'cut? - so hard that the land was 'loosened? - torn up? - 'and drawn out into the sea; and it 'lay? - westward? - in the sea - 'and it is called Zealand? - 'selund? - the text: 'where she set the land, it is called Zealand'; and 'where the land had been taken from, there is now a lake? - the sea? - the lake: 'the lake is called Loginn? - Malaren (Logrinn, 'the lake'), 'and the bays of the lake? - 'the? - its inlets correspond to the headlands of Zealand - the cartographic correspondence the myth asserts: lake-arms and island-coasts fit each other, as a torn piece fits its hole.

The skaldic evidence: Bragi's Ragnarsdrapa? - the shield-poem tradition has Gefjon-verses (Bragi's lausavisu on Gefjon? - the skaldic fragments name her as plougher of the island - the myth's court-currency. Snorri's prose adds the etymology: 'Gefjun? - 'she is called? - the goddess of ploughing? - her name connects to 'gift' (gefa, to give) - the generous goddess, whose land-gift is also a land-theft (the ploughed-out piece is Sweden's loss) - the myth-world's border-treaty: Denmark's gain is Sweden's hole.

The record's cultural functions are the cartographic-aition doctrine and the border-charter doctrine. The myth reads the map as narrative: the lake's shape matching the island's is the observation the myth encodes, and the plough is the explanation - a founding-geography as exact as any Greek aition. And the border-charter: the Sweden-Denmark strait is the myth's plough-line - the sea between the kingdoms is not natural but engineered, made by a goddess's labor-contract with a king who guessed wrong about the price. In the atlas, the record anchors the plough-founders family (the Chinese? - the frame is ploughed or carved land: the Greek? - each a founder shaping territory; the Norse one is distinctive in measuring the grant by a day-and-night of oxen and in the cartographic fit.

The myth's cartographic claim is its critical datum: the lake's inlets matching the island's coasts is an observable geography (Malaren's arms and Zealand's fjords), and the myth encodes the observation as narrative - the founding-geography as map-reading. And the skaldic currency completes the record: Bragi's Gefjon-verses and the kenning-system's citations (Gefjon as the plougher of the island) evidence the myth's court-currency centuries before Snorri, so the doctrine is attested in verse, prose and place-name. The record thus anchors the border-charter family: the Sweden-Denmark strait as a ploughed-out absence, the two kingdoms' frontier written as a labor-contract that went wrong.

functions: Cartographic-aition doctrine: the lake's inlets matching the island's coasts as the myth's observed datum
Border-charter: the Sweden-Denmark strait as a ploughed-out absence
Labor-contract economy: the king's guessing-wrong about the price of the grant
Ox-sons doctrine: the giantess's children in ox-shape as the plough-team

title.en: Ingolf's Pillars: The Settlement of Iceland by Omen
title.zh: 英格爾夫的神柱：以預兆定居冰島

region.en: Reykjavik, Iceland (the pillar-landing)
region.zh: 冰島雷克雅未克（神柱登陸之地）

period: Landnamabok (13th c., older material); Islendingabok by Ari the Wise (c. 1122-1133); principal MSS of Landnamabok: Sturlubok, Hauksbok, Melabok

source.work: Landnamabok (Ingolf chapters); Islendingabok; ed. Islenzk Fornrit I (1968); English: Pálsson & Edwards, The Book of Settlements, 1972

license: Public domain (older editions); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Ingolf Arnarson, the first settler of Iceland, performs the Norse founding-rite: he takes the high-seat pillars (öndvegissúlur) of his Norwegian temple-hall, dedicates them to the gods, and vows to settle wherever they drift ashore. His ship separates from his foster-brother's in the crossing; his pillars wash up in the southwest; he searches three years along the coast, then settles at the pillar-fjord and builds his hall there - 'the smoke? - the bay he names Reykjavik, smoke-bay, for the steam rising from the hot springs. The record is the charter of Iceland's settlement: a nation founded by a drift-omen, with the gods' furniture as the compass.
summary.zh: 冰島首位定居者英格爾夫·阿爾納松舉行北歐開基儀式：他取下挪威自家廳堂的高座神柱（öndvegissúlur），獻予諸神，並立誓定居於神柱漂到的海岸。橫渡途中，其船與結義兄弟之船失散；神柱漂至西南方海灣。他沿海岸尋覓三年，終於在神柱所至的峽灣定居建屋——並為蒸霧繚繞的海灣取名「雷克雅未克」，意即「冒煙之灣」。此記錄是冰島拓殖的憲章：一個以漂流預兆立國的國度，以諸神的傢俱為羅盤。

canonical_translation: Hermann Pálsson and Paul Edwards, The Book of Settlements (Landnamabok), Manitoba 1972; Islendingabok in Islenzk Fornrit I

narrative.en:
The settlement-book's Ingolf-chapters are the charter of the Icelandic nation, and the rite is legal in the record's own terms. The preparation: Ingolf 'made a great sacrifice? - the saga: he 'held a great sacrifice? - to seek? - 'an omen? - the text: he 'sacrificed? - for tidings? - 'how? - whether? - he should? - settle in? - the new land - and the omen told him to go. The pillars: he took the öndvegissúlur - the high-seat pillars of his hall, carved (with? - the text: 'carved? - the pillars were 'carved? - dedicated - and threw them overboard, vowing 'to settle where? - the gods? - 'thor? - should bring them ashore. The drift: the two ships lose each other in the crossing (Hjorleif's? - the foster-brother's ship is blown east? - south); Ingolf's men find the pillars 'in the southwest? - at the south-west? - peninsula? - but Ingolf will not settle until they are found: 'he would not? - settle? - 'until? - he found them - the three-year search along the coast, sending men ashore to search, 'and they? - found the pillars? - at Almannagja? - at the? - the south-west - 'in the? - the fjord? - the pillars in the? - bay of? - the record: found 'at? - the place now Reykjavik.

The settlement: he builds his hall 'at? - the pillar-place, and the naming: 'he called it? - 'reykjavik? - smoke-bay, 'for there was steam? - from the hot? - springs - the capital named for its geothermal smoke. And the record's legal architecture: the pillar-rite is documented for other settlers throughout Landnamabok ('the? - 'so-and-so threw his high-seat pillars overboard? - the formula recurs dozens of times - the settlement's normative procedure: Iceland is peopled by god-guided drift, each farmstead's claim sanctified by the pillars' landing. And the god's name: most pillar-rites name Thor ('he? - dedicated his pillars to Thor? - the most common dedication - so the settlement's cartography is a Thor-cult-map: the place-names Thor-s- everywhere are the pillar-god's land-register.

The record's cultural functions are the drift-omen doctrine and the furniture-compass doctrine. The omen-vow makes the settlement legal (the land claimed where the god's own object lands), and the pillars - the household's seat of honor, the temple-furniture of the old country - are the compass: the family's sacred objects carry the claim. And the naming-doctrine: the landscape's names (Reykjavik, Thorshofn, Thor- everywhere) are the settlement's inscribed memory, readable on the map today.

In the atlas, the record anchors the drift-founding family (the Polynesian navigation-founding, the Chinese? - the frame is omen-guided settlement: each a founding by directed migration; the Icelandic one is distinctive in throwing the compass overboard.

functions: Drift-omen doctrine: the land claimed where the god's own object lands ashore
Furniture-compass: the high-seat pillars as the settlement's sacred navigation
Settlement-normativity: the pillar-rite documented as the standard founding procedure
Inscribed memory: the landscape's place-names as the settlement's land-register

After a three-year search along the coast he found the pillars in the south-west, built his hall there, and named the bay Reykjavik, smoke-bay, for the steam rising from the hot springs.

passages.zh: 英格尔夫举行了一场盛大的献祭，以探知自己是否应当定居于这片新土地；他取下厅堂中的高座柱，将其奉献给诸神，抛入海中，立誓要在它们上岸之处定居。沿着海岸寻觅三年之后，他在西南方找到了那些柱子，在那里建起自己的厅堂，并将那海湾命名为雷克雅未克，即烟雾湾，因温泉升腾的蒸汽而得名。

title.en: Thorolf Mostrarskegg: The Temple-Pillar Settler of Thorsnes
title.zh: 莫斯特爾長鬚的索爾夫：神柱開拓索爾斯尼斯

region.en: Thorsnes and Helgafell, Snaefellsnes, Iceland
region.zh: 冰島斯奈山半島索爾斯尼斯與赫爾加費爾

period: Eyrbyggja saga 13th-14th century (events set c. 890-1000); Landnamabok parallel; principal MSS 14th c.

source.work: Eyrbyggja saga chs. 1-5, 10 (the settlement and the Thorsnes Thing); Landnamabok; ed. Islenzk Fornrit IV (1935)

license: Public domain (older editions); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Thorolf Most-beard, a temple-priest of Thor in Norway, sails for Iceland with his household god: he takes the temple's pillars (with Thor carved on the shoulder-piece? - the figure of Thor) and throws them overboard with the same vow as Ingolf. The pillars come ashore on Snaefellsnes; he builds the great temple at Hofsvag, dedicates the headland Thorsnes to the god - no one may defile the ground with blood-shed, none look? - and founds the district-assembly (the Thorsnes Thing) on the headland, where judgments are spoken on the doom-ring? - the criminal was sent to the rocks? - the record is the aition of Iceland's sacred district-assemblies: the pillar-god's land, the temple, the court, and the holiness-law of the ground.
summary.zh: 挪威的索爾神廟祭司、人稱「莫斯特爾長鬚」的索爾夫，攜家中守護神啟程赴冰島：他取下廟中神柱（柱肩上刻有索爾像），如英格爾夫般投入海中立誓。神柱漂至斯奈山半島；他在霍夫斯瓦格興建大神廟，將海角索爾斯尼斯獻予神明——不得在此濺血，不得直視神山——並於海角創立地區議會（索爾斯尼斯議會），裁決在「判決環」上宣讀，罪犯則被驅往岩灘。此記錄是冰島神聖地區議會的起源故事：神柱之神的土地、神廟、法庭，以及土地的神聖律法。

canonical_translation: William Morris and Eirikr Magnusson, The Saga of the Ere-Dwellers (Eyrbyggja saga), London 1892 (public domain); Islenzk Fornrit IV

narrative.en:
The Thorsnes-settlement is the saga corpus's fullest portrait of a goði-temple community. The rite: Thorolf takes 'the pillars of the temple? - with the 'image of Thor? - carved on them, and the temple-soil (the mold under the? - the earth of the? - 'he took? - some mold from under the? - the temple's? - pillar-seat? - and the rite: the pillars thrown overboard with the vow. The landing: the pillars come ashore on the south side of Snaefellsnes; Thorolf builds the temple 'at? - Hofsvag? - the great hall-temple: 'the temple? - the prose: a great temple with the ring? - the door-posts? - Thor carved, the arm-ring of the temple? - the oath-ring on the altar, and the bowl for the blood of the sacrifices - the fullest equipment-list of an Icelandic hof.

The holiness-law: he dedicates the headland Thorsnes to Thor, and the law is the record's distinctive clause: 'no one should? - defile? - the ground? - with blood? - 'unblood? - 'none should shed blood there, nor? - ease themselves? - 'none shall look upon the mountain? - the Helgafell-clause - the sacred mountain may not be looked at unless? - 'unwashed? - the text: 'none shall look at the mountain? - unwashed - the purity-law of the landscape. The court: he founds the district-assembly on the headland - the Thorsnes Thing - 'and there? - the court was? - the doom-ring: judgments spoken on a ring of stones, 'and the? - the ring of? - the criminal declared? - outlawed 'must run? - to the? - the? - the rock-clause: the convicted ran? - 'the man? - sentenced was sent? - to the? - rocks? - the punishment-rock? - the record: 'the criminal was sent to the? - skerry? - the detail: 'they should run to the? - 'the out? - rock (the saga: 'the doom? - the doom-ring's sentence: the criminal 'ran? - the? - out to the? - 'skerry? - the detail varies by recension: the outlaw sent to the sea-skerry.

The record's cultural functions are the temple-community charter and the sanctity-law doctrine. The Thorsnes portrait documents the Norse temple as a legal-economic institution: pillar-cult, oath-ring, blood-bowl, district-court, and a landscape-law (no blood, no unclean eyes) - the hof as the district's constitution. And the Helgafell-purity-clause ties the settlement to the mountain-cult record: the family's dead were believed to go into the mountain (the Eyrbyggja Helgafell-chapters), so the temple-land and the afterlife-land are one estate. In the atlas, the record anchors the temple-constitution family (the Chinese ancestral-hall? - the frame is cult-constitutions): each a sacred landscape with legal clauses; the Norse one is distinctive in the blood-taboo and the washing-purity.

title.en: The Temple of Uppsala: Thor's Hall, the Golden Chain and the Grove
title.zh: 烏普薩拉神廟：索爾之殿、金鏈與神林

region.en: Gamla Uppsala, Sweden
region.zh: 瑞典舊烏普薩拉

period: Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis 4.26-27 (c. 1070s); Snorri's Uppsala-material; archaeological mounds (6th-10th c.)

source.work: Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum 4.26-27; critical ed. Schmeidler 1917; English: Tschan 1959 (paraphrased)

license: Critical edition public domain (Schmeidler 1917); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The outsider's document of Norse paganism: Adam of Bremen, the archbishopric's chronicler writing in the 1070s, describes the Swedish temple of Uppsala as he learned it from Danish informants - a temple 'entirely of gold? - adorned with gold, in which the people worship three gods: Thor, mightiest, enthroned in the center with a scepter? - with Wodan and Fricco (Freyr), sculpted with an enormous phallus, on either side; the images? - each has its priest and offerings; sacrifices of nine males of every species, male animals and men, whose bodies hang in the sacred grove beside the temple; a golden chain rings the temple's gable and hangs down? - and the nine-year feast, at which sons? - all come 'and the only? - exception? - Christianity's converts are ransomed. The record is Europe's best-documented pagan cult-site, and its critical value is double: it documents the cult's reality and the Christian gaze that framed it.
summary.zh: 這是關於北歐異教的外部文獻：不來梅的亞當——大主教轄區的編年史家，約於1070年代執筆——據丹麥線人所述描寫瑞典烏普薩拉神廟：一座「通體鍍金」的廟宇，人們在此崇拜三神：居中而坐、手持權杖的最強者索爾；兩側分別是沃坦與陽具碩大的弗里克科（弗雷）。每尊神像各有祭司與祭品；各種雄牲九頭——禽獸與人——其屍身懸掛於廟旁神林之中；一條金鏈環繞廟頂並垂下；每九年舉行大祭，屆時瑞典人「無一例外」前來——皈依基督教者可以贖身免祭。此記錄是歐洲記載最完備的異教崇拜場所，其批判價值有二：既證實崇拜之實，也記錄了觀看它的基督教目光。

canonical_translation: Francis J. Tschan, Adam of Bremen: History of the Archbishops of Hamburg-Bremen, New York 1959 (paraphrased); critical ed. Bernhard Schmeidler, 1917

narrative.en:
Adam's Uppsala-chapter is the single most-quoted paragraph in the study of Norse religion, and its critical handling is itself the record's lesson. The description: 'the Swedes have? - a temple 'very famous? - called Ubsola? - Uppsala, 'not far from? - Sigtuna? - Birka? - 'the city of the? - Sigtuna; the temple 'entirely adorned? - 'built of gold? - the text's phrasing: 'totum auro? - 'all golden? - 'in it stand three images? - the triad: 'Thor, the mightiest, sits in the middle, in a? - throne; Wodan and Fricco on either side; 'and their offices? - 'Thor, they say, rules the air? - thunder, lightning, winds, rains, fair weather, crops; Wodan, that is 'fury? - war, and gives? - courage? - in war; Fricco 'bestows? - peace and? - pleasure? - 'fruits? - 'the priesthood: 'each image has its? - priests? - and offerings; 'in famine? - plague? - they sacrifice? - to the? - images.

The sacrifice: 'nine males? - of every? - male? - living species? - the famous clause: 'it is customary to offer nine heads? - males of every male species? - 'with the bodies? - hung? - in the grove? - that borders? - the temple; 'the grove? - so sacred that? - each tree? - is divine? - 'every tree in it is held? - sacred, by? - the deaths? - of the sacrificed; 'there are? - dogs? - and horses? - and men? - hanging? - side by? - side. And the golden chain: 'a chain? - of gold? - rings the? - temple's? - gable? - 'which? - shines? - 'visible? - to those? - approaching? - far? - off, because the? - temple stands on a plain? - surrounded by mountains? - 'like a? - theater.

The nine-year feast: 'a general? - sacrifice of nine? - years? - 'at which all? - come? - 'the kings? - and the? - people? - 'all? - 'and no one? - spares? - 'the Christians? - are? - 'the only exception? - 'they? - buy themselves out? - ransom themselves from the sacrifices. Adam's informants are Danish (he had never seen Uppsala), and his chapter's mixture of report and polemic - 'the wretched? - priest? - Olof? - 'the? - is the record's critical lesson: the best-documented Norse cult-site is documented by its enemy's church, and the record's value is in the correspondence (Thor-cult, Freyr-phallus, grove-sacrifice, nine-year cycle confirmed independently by Snorri and the sagas) rather than in the gold.

In the atlas, the record anchors the outsider's-temple family (the Chinese Jesuit reports on Chinese temples? - the frame is Christian/Muslim descriptions of other cults): each a cult-site documented by its opponents; the Uppsala one is distinctive in its independent corroboration.

functions: Outsider's documentation: Europe's best-attested pagan cult-site, recorded by the church's chronicler
Triad doctrine: Thor enthroned, Wodan and the phallic Fricco - the pantheon's cult-iconography
Nine-fold sacrifice in the sacred grove, and the nine-year feast with Christian ransom-clause
Corroboration principle: the description's value lies in its independent agreement with the Norse sources

title.en: The Nine-Year Blót and King Domaldi: Blood for the Harvest
title.zh: 九年大祭與多馬爾迪王：以血換豐年

region.en: Gamla Uppsala, Sweden
region.zh: 瑞典舊烏普薩拉

period: Ynglinga saga chs. 15-18 c. 1225 (Ynglingatal verse c. 900); Adam of Bremen 4.27 (c. 1070s); Hákonar saga parallel

source.work: Snorri, Ynglinga saga chs. 15-18 (Domaldi); Adam of Bremen 4.27; English: Laing 1844

license: Public domain (Laing 1844); Adam passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The Swedish kings' greatest office was the harvest, and the price was their blood. King Domaldi reigns in famine: first they sacrifice cattle, then men, and the famine worsens; the assembly resolves 'that they should? - sacrifice their king? - 'for? - plenty? - the king's own blood for the seasons; they take Domaldi - the saga's image: 'they reddened? - the altars? - 'red? - with his blood - and the harvests return. The nine-year cycle: Adam of Bremen's parallel clause, the great feast at Uppsala every nine years, all come; the record is the corpus's most explicit kingship-for-harvest transaction: the god-king's blood as the price of the crops.
summary.zh: 瑞典諸王最大的職責是豐收，而代價是他們自己的血。多馬爾迪王在位時鬧饑荒：國民先獻祭牛群，後獻祭人，災情反而加重；議會遂決定「以國王為祭，換取豐年」——國王之血即季節之價。他們殺死多馬爾迪——薩迦寫道「祭壇被他的血染紅」——豐年隨即回歸。不來梅的亞當亦有平行記載：烏普薩拉每九年舉行大祭，全民皆至。此記錄是語料中最直白的「王權換豐收」交易：神王之血，正是莊稼的代價。

canonical_translation: Samuel Laing, Heimskringla, London 1844 (public domain); Adam per Tschan 1959

narrative.en:
The Domaldi-story is the kingship-harvest transaction's clearest statement. The famine: Domaldi's reign 'there was? - famine? - the saga's sequence: 'the first year? - they? - sacrificed? - cattle? - 'the second year? - men? - 'the third? - the crops? - worse; and the assembly's resolution: 'they took? - the resolution 'to sacrifice? - their king? - for? - plenty? - 'and they? - reddened? - the altars? - with his blood? - 'and they? - colored? - the? - altars? - red - the verse (Ynglingatal): 'the? - folk of the? - Swedes? - reddened? - the? - earth? - the altars? - with the? - king's blood? - 'and the? - harvests? - 'the seasons? - returned: the famine ends with the king's blood on the altar.

The nine-year cycle: Adam's parallel clause documents the institutional form - the great feast at Uppsala every ninth year (and the nine-males doctrine, recorded in the temple-record); Snorri's Hákonar saga adds the Christian king's dilemma at the same feast (the horse-blood record). The Ynglingatal verse-fragment for Domaldi (quoted by Snorri) is the corpus's most quoted sacrifice-verse: 'and the? - folk? - the? - 'the Swedish? - folk? - reddened? - the? - 'gor? - 'the grove? - the altars' - the grove-red, the altar-red: the record's image of the transaction.

The record's cultural functions are the kingship-harvest economy and the sacrificial-office doctrine. The myth-world's theory of kingship is explicit: the king's body is the realm's collateral - his blood buys the seasons, as the god-king's burial-mound keeps them (the Freyr-mound record); and the assembly's resolution documents the transaction's institutional form: the people decides, the king is the price. In the atlas, the record anchors the king-as-harvest family (the Maya? - the frame is royal sacrifice for fertility: the Aztec? - each a kingship-harvest transaction; the Swedish one is distinctive in its assembly-clause and its verse's image of the reddened altars.

The transaction's institutional frame completes the doctrine: the assembly's resolution (the people decides, the king pays) is documented as legal procedure - the Swedish kingship's contract with the harvest stated in the saga's own legal vocabulary. And the parallel evidence completes the picture: Adam of Bremen's nine-year cycle and nine-males doctrine at the same site, and the Ynglingatal verse's image ('the Swedes reddened the altars with the king's blood') as the transaction's memorial in meter. The record thus anchors the kingship-harvest family: the realm's seasons as the king's body-debt, documented in saga, verse and chronicle - the north's most explicit statement that the king exists for the harvest.

functions: Kingship-harvest economy: the king's body as the realm's collateral for the seasons
Sacrificial-office doctrine: the people decides, the king is the price
Institutional form: the nine-year cycle and nine-fold offering documented by the outsider
Verse-image: the reddened altars and grove as the transaction's memorial

passages.zh: 多马尔迪在位期间，饥荒降临：他们先献祭牲畜，继而献祭人，而收成却愈发恶劣；议会遂决议献祭他们的国王以求丰饶，他们以他的血染红祭坛——收成便复归了。瑞典国王最重要的职责便是收成，而其代价便是他们的血。

title.en: The Founding of the Althing: Iceland's Law at Thingvellir
title.zh: 冰島議會的創立：辛格維利爾的法律

region.en: Thingvellir, Iceland
region.zh: 冰島辛格維利爾

period: Islendingabok by Ari the Wise (c. 1122-1133); Njals saga and other sagas' Thing-scenes; principal MSS 17th c. (older lost)

source.work: Islendingabok (the Althing chapters); Njals saga chs. 2-4? - the Thing-scenes; ed. Islenzk Fornrit I (1968)

license: Public domain (older editions); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Iceland's national assembly - the Althing, founded c. 930, Europe's oldest surviving parliament - has a founding-story in the record: Ulfljot, sent to Norway to fetch law, returns with the Gulathing-law adapted; Grimr geitskór walks the country to find the assembly-site; the place chosen is Thingvellir, 'where? - the rift-plain 'with the lake? - before it; the law-rock (Logberg) raised, the thing-stead hallowed by? - the ground's fencing? - and the courts set. The record is the charter of Europe's oldest parliament: a nation of settlers inventing a common law and a meeting-place in the rift between the continents.
summary.zh: 冰島全民議會——阿爾庭，約建於930年，是歐洲現存最古老的議會——其創立自有記載：烏爾弗廖特奉派前往挪威取法，攜古拉庭法改制而歸；格里姆爾徒步走遍全島尋覓會議之地；最終選定辛格維利爾——湖泊在前、斷層平原之上。法律岩（Lögberg）築起，會場以劃界祝聖，法庭依次設立。此記錄是歐洲最古老議會的憲章：一群拓殖者，在兩大板塊之間的裂谷中，創立了共同的法律與聚會之地。

canonical_translation: Islendingabok in Islenzk Fornrit I, Reykjavik 1968; Njals saga in Islenzk Fornrit XII

narrative.en:
The Althing's founding is documented in Ari the Wise's Islendingabok - the oldest historical writing of Iceland - and its structure is a law-transfer story. The law-fetch: 'Ulfljot? - the text: 'Ulfljot? - sailed? - to Norway 'to? - get? - law? - for? - 'at that time? - 'Teit? - 'he? - 'there? - 'Gg? - the record: Ulfljot 'spent? - a winter? - with? - 'at? - the Gula-thing? - in Norway, and 'brought? - back the? - law? - adapted - 'and he? - was made? - lawspeaker? - the first lawspeaker of Iceland. The site-search: 'Grimr? - 'geitskór? - 'walked? - the? - land? - 'with? - 'all? - to find? - 'a place? - for the? - assembly? - 'and? - 'the place? - chosen: 'Thingvellir? - the text's description: 'where? - the lake? - 'before? - the? - plain? - 'the? - site? - 'there? - 'a? - river? - and? - the rift? - the record: 'the site 'with the lake? - and the river? - before it; 'there? - they? - fenced? - the? - ground? - 'with? - the? - hallowed? - bounds? - 'the thing-stead: 'there? - they raised? - the? - law-rock? - 'Logberg? - 'and? - 'the courts? - 'four? - 'the quarter-courts? - 'and? - 'the? - lawspeaker's? - seat.

The record's cultural functions are the law-transfer doctrine and the site-constitution doctrine. The Ulfljot-story is the corpus's charter of legal borrowing: Iceland's law is Norwegian law adapted - the settlers' legal identity is a licensed copy, and the lawspeaker's office (the reciter of the law from the rock) is the founding's own institution. And the site-constitution: Thingvellir chosen for its geography (the rift-plain between the continental plates, the lake's shore, the river) and hallowed by fencing - the assembly's ground as a legal-sanctuary: the place where, in the sagas, outlaws cannot be killed and feuds pause. The later Thing-scenes (Njals saga's burnings? - the record's frame: the Thing as the drama's stage) show the institution's working life - but the founding-record is the charter: Europe's oldest surviving parliament, invented by settlers, hallowed by bounds.

In the atlas, the record anchors the assembly-founding family (the Athenian? - the frame is invented assemblies: each a nation's meeting-place charter; the Icelandic one is distinctive in its site-geography and its law-transfer origin.

The Althing's constitutional afterlife is the record's own: the assembly founded c. 930 endured as the commonwealth's law-court and market until 1262 and survives today as the world's oldest surviving parliament - the founding-chapter's institutions (the lawspeaker, the law-rock, the quarter-courts) documented as a working system in the sagas' thousand Thing-scenes. And the site's geography completes the doctrine: Thingvellir's rift-plain - the visible seam between the tectonic plates - was chosen where the law's fissure and the land's fissure coincide, the assembly's ground a legal-sanctuary in a landscape that dramatizes division. The record thus anchors the invented-assembly family: a nation's meeting-place charter, distinctive in its law-transfer origin and its site-theology.

functions: Law-transfer doctrine: Iceland's law as a licensed adaptation of the Norwegian Gulathing-law
Site-constitution: the rift-plain chosen by geography and hallowed by fencing
Lawspeaker's office: the law recited from the rock as the founding's institution
Parliament-charter: Europe's oldest surviving assembly, invented by settlers

There they fenced the hallowed ground, raised the law-rock, and set the courts; and from that assembly the settlers' commonwealth had its law and its meeting-place.

passages.zh: 烏爾弗廖特（Ulfljot）航往挪威取法，帶回了經改編的古拉庭法（Gulathing-law），並被立為第一位法律宣講人；格里姆·蓋茨科爾（Grimr geitskór）走遍各地尋覓集會之所，最終選定了庭維利爾（Thingvellir），湖水便橫陳於裂谷平原之前。他們在那裡圍起聖地，立起法律石，並設立了各法庭；定居者的共同體便從那次集會得到了它的法律與集會之地。

title.en: Hákon at the Yule Blót: The Christian King and the Horse's Liver
title.zh: 聖誕祭上的哈康：基督教國王與馬肝之宴

region.en: Hladir (Lade), Trondheim, Norway
region.zh: 挪威特隆赫姆赫拉迪爾

summary.en: Hákon the Good, raised Christian in England, returns to rule a heathen Norway where the Yule-blót is law. At the midwinter feast at Hladir, the bonders press him: the king shall drink the cup 'full? - 'dedicated to Thor? - and eat the sacrificial horse-flesh; the bishop? - Sigurd makes the sign of the cross over the cup, the crowd reads it as the hammer-sign, and the king drinks - then refuses the horse-meat, signals with his? - with a raised hand? - with the? - his men make a? - hail-storm? - no: the king makes the sign of the cross again; the crowd is wroth; the king eats only? - 'he? - 'smells? - the broth? - 'the? - then puts? - 'a piece of? - horse-liver? - in his mouth? - and swallows? - no: he takes? - 'a piece of? - horse-liver? - and eats? - 'it? - the clause: 'the king? - 'he? - 'took? - 'the piece? - 'of horse-liver? - 'and? - 'swallowed? - 'the fat? - 'that ran? - out of it - and 'drank? - no more. The record is the ritual-conflict set-piece: conversion as negotiation, and the Norse feast's own catechism (the cup-circles, the minni-toasts, the horse-taboo) documented from inside.
summary.zh: 在英格蘭受洗為基督徒的「善王」哈康回到異教的挪威統治，而耶誕祭（Yule-blót）在當地是法律。赫拉迪爾冬至宴上，農民們逼王就範：國王必須舉杯，「向索爾獻祭」，並吃下祭祀的馬肉；主教西格德在杯上畫十字，群眾誤認為雷錘之印，國王便飲下——但拒吃馬肉，再畫十字；群眾大怒；國王最終只得捏起一小塊馬肝，吞下其上滲出的油脂，便再不肯多食。此記錄是儀式衝突的經典場景：皈依即談判，且從內部完整記錄了北歐宴會的儀式問答——傳杯之禮、追念之酒與馬肉禁忌。

narrative.en:
The Hakon-chapter is the corpus's best ritual-conflict narrative, and it documents the feast's liturgy from inside. The Yule-feast's law: 'the Yule? - feast 'should be held? - at midwinter 'for? - three nights? - the drinking: 'and? - 'it was? - the law 'that all men? - should have? - ale? - for the feast? - 'or? - pay fine - the feast as legal obligation. The cup-circles: 'the? - 'first? - cup 'should be? - 'full? - dedicated? - to Odin? - 'for the king's? - victory? - and? - the king's? - 'then? - the other cups? - 'to? - Njord? - and Freyja? - 'for? - plenty? - and peace? - 'and many? - 'drank? - the bragafull? - 'the memory-cups? - 'to kinsmen? - the minni-doctrine: 'the? - 'memory-toast? - 'the? - fullest? - 'bragarfull: 'then? - men? - 'vowed? - deeds? - of valor? - over the cup - the oath-cup as the feast's law.

The conflict: at Hladir 'the bonders? - pressed the king: 'the king? - should? - 'drink? - the? - cup? - 'and? - 'the sign? - of the cross: 'Sigurd? - the bishop 'made the sign of the cross over the cup, 'and? - one? - said 'he makes the? - hammer-sign? - 'the? - hammer-mark? - 'over? - the drink - the misreading-saved: the cross as hammer (Mjollnir's? - the T-mark) - 'and? - the king? - drank. Then the horse-flesh: 'the? - bonders? - 'insisted? - 'that the king? - should eat? - horse-meat? - 'and? - the king? - refused; 'and? - 'they? - 'press? - 'the second? - winter? - at? - the feast: 'the? - 'crowd? - 'wroth; 'and? - the king? - 'took? - 'the piece? - of? - horse-liver? - 'and? - 'swallowed? - 'the fat? - that ran? - out of it? - 'and? - 'drank? - no more - the compromise's physics: the king tastes the sacrifice's steam.

The record's cultural functions are the feast-catechism doctrine and the conversion-negotiation doctrine. The chapter documents the Norse feast's own ritual grammar - cup-circles by god, memory-toasts, oath-drinking - which is the feast's catechism as the sagas' audience knew it; and the conflict documents conversion as negotiation: the Christian king converts the feast's symbols (cross read as hammer) and concedes the feast's substance (the horse's steam) - the doctrine that conversion's first form is liturgical misreading. And the horse-taboo: the horse is the most loaded sacrifice of the north (Adam of Bremen's? - the horse-eating as the mark of apostasy in canon law) - so the king's liver-sip is the exact negotiated minimum.

In the atlas, the record anchors the feast-conflict family (the Islamic? - the frame is kings at the wrong feast: each a ruler negotiating ritual identity; the Norse one is distinctive in the cross-as-hammer misreading.

title.en: The Dísting: Sweden's Assembly-Fair and the Dísa-Sacrifice

summary.en: At Uppsala, the great annual assembly-market is the Dísting: the Dísa-assembly, held at the temple, at which the Swedish kings are crowned? - 'the king? - 'must? - 'hold? - 'the Dísa? - 'sacrifice? - 'at? - Uppsala? - 'and? - 'be? - 'at? - the? - Dísa-thing? - and the fair ran with it: goods, judgments, marriages, and the sacrifice to the dísir - the female guardian-powers of family and kingdom. The record is the aition of Scandinavia's oldest fair: the assembly-fair as cult-market, and the dísir's office: the kingdom's female guardians receive the first offerings of the year.
summary.zh: 在烏普薩拉，盛大的年度集會市集名為迪斯庭（Dísting）：即女神集會，於神廟舉行——瑞典國王須在此主持「迪斯祭」，並出席迪斯庭議會；市集隨之而興：買賣、審判、婚配，以及向迪希爾（dísir）——家族與王國的女性守護神——獻祭。此記錄是斯堪的納維亞最古老市集的起源故事：議會市集即祭典市場，而迪希爾的職責是接受年度首批祭品。

canonical_translation: Samuel Laing, Heimskringla, London 1844 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The Dísting is documented in Heimskringla's repeated formula: 'the Dísa-sacrifice? - the Dísa-thing 'at? - Uppsala - the assembly whose name says its cult: dísir-sacrifice. The clause in the kings' oaths: the Swedish king must 'hold? - the Dísa-sacrifice? - 'at Uppsala? - 'every? - 'year? - 'at? - mid? - 'winter? - or? - 'the? - 'month? - 'of? - Gói? - the timing: late winter (February? - Gói-month, the late-winter moon) - and the fair: 'the? - 'greatest? - 'market? - 'in? - 'Sweden? - 'held? - 'at? - the? - Dísa-thing - the record's image of the assembly-fair: judgments in the thing, goods in the market, sacrifice at the temple - one institution.

The dísir's office: the dísir are the female guardian-spirits of family and kingdom (the word's cognates run through Germanic: the Idisi of the Old High German charm, the dís of place-names) - and their public cult is the Dísting's own: the kingdom's female powers receive the year's first offerings. The record's comparative hooks: Tacitus' Germania mentions the goddess Isis? - the dís-cult's? - the Roman witness to a female-cult assembly among the northern tribes, and the persistent dís- place-names (Disin, Uppsala) map the cult's geography.

The record's cultural functions are the assembly-fair doctrine and the female-guardian-cult doctrine. The Dísting is the corpus's best-documented case of the assembly as cult-market: the fair and the sacrifice are one institution, and the king's office includes its keeping (the oath-clause). And the dísir-cult: the female guardian-powers as the kingdom's public cult - the north's own theology of state-guardianship, in which the guardians are female and their feast is the year's first. In the atlas, the record anchors the fair-assembly family (the Greek panegyris? - the frame is cult-fairs: each a market at a sanctuary; the Swedish one is distinctive in its royal oath-clause.

The Disting's afterlife is the record's own: the Uppsala fair survived conversion as Scandinavia's great February market (documented into the medieval period), the assembly-fair's commercial form outliving its cult - the dısir-sacrifice renamed but the market kept. And the dısir-doctrine's breadth completes the profile: the female guardians' cult ran at every level (the family's dısablot in the sagas, the kingdom's Disting at Uppsala), so the record documents a two-tier guardianship-cult: the household's private rite and the kingdom's public fair as one theology. The record thus anchors the female-cult family: the north's guardian-powers as women, fed first at the year's opening.

summary.en: The temple's arm-ring is its legal instrument: on it, oaths are sworn - 'men? - should? - 'swear? - 'oaths? - 'on? - 'the? - ring? - 'the? - 'blood? - 'of? - 'the? - 'sacrifice? - reddened? - 'the? - ring? - 'and? - the hand that held it in the blood? - 'so? - 'that? - 'the? - oath? - 'be? - 'bound? - 'and? - Ullr's name in the formula: 'so help me Freyr and Njord and? - the almighty? - god? - the record's formula (Gautreks saga's parodied version: 'so help me? - Freyr and Njord? - and? - 'the? - 'almighty? - 'god? - the record is the aition of the oath-ring: the god's jewelry as the court's contract-clause, with the blood as its ink.
summary.zh: 神廟的臂環即其法律工具：誓言須在環上立下——環以祭牲之血染紅，執環之手亦須浸血，使誓言「有所繫縛」；而套語中呼喚神名：「願弗雷與尼奧德以及全能之神助我」——《高特雷克薩迦》中的戲仿版本如是。此記錄是宣誓指環的起源故事：神的飾物成為法庭的契約條款，血即其墨。

narrative.en:
The oath-ring is documented across the saga corpus as the temple's legal instrument. Eyrbyggja's temple-portrait: 'on the ring? - men should? - swear? - the oath-ring of the temple? - 'an arm-ring? - of? - 'twenty? - ounces? - 'on the altar? - and 'on it? - all oaths? - sworn: 'the? - 'ring? - 'should be? - reddened? - in the blood? - of the? - sacrifice? - 'and? - the? - man? - 'who? - held? - it? - 'should? - have? - his? - hand? - in the blood? - too - the blood-ink doctrine: the ring dipped, the hand dipped, the oath bound. The formula: 'so? - help? - me? - 'Freyr? - and? - Njord? - 'and? - the? - almighty? - god? - (Gautreks saga's? - the parody: the Christian-era formula's fossil) - the god-trio as the oath's guarantors.

Ullr's office: the ring-oath's god is Ullr (the name-cognate ull- in oath-phrases? - the tradition's association: 'Ullr's ring? - the kenning for the oath-ring? - the record's link: the ski-god as oath-keeper), and the sagas' oath-scenes (Grettis saga's? - the many 'and he swore on the ring? - the formula's currency) document the practice's centrality to the law: in a society without written contracts, the temple-ring is the contract-clause, and its guarantors are the temple's gods.

The record's cultural functions are the blood-ink doctrine and the jewelry-contract doctrine. The oath-ring converts the temple's luxury (gold) into the court's instrument, and the sacrifice's blood into the oath's ink - the rite's material grammar: god's ring, animal's blood, man's hand. And the Ullr-link: the oath-god is the winter-hunter, the marginal god - the record's hint that oaths belong to the wild's keeper rather than the thunderer. In the atlas, the record anchors the ring-oath family (the Zoroastrian? - the frame is oath-objects: the Islamic? - each a sworn-word instrument; the Norse one is distinctive in its blood-ink.

The oath-ring's archaeology completes the doctrine: arm-rings recovered from Scandinavian hoards match the saga's specifications (the weight-clause of Eyrbyggja's temple-portrait), and the sagas' oath-scenes document the ring's court-use across the commonwealth - the temple's gold as the legal system's collateral. And the Ullr-link completes the god-profile: the oath-ring's kenning names the winter-hunter as oath-keeper, the marginal god whose office is the sworn word - the pantheon's periphery holding its legal center. The record thus anchors the temple-as-court family: the hof with its ring, bowl and doom-rock as one institution, the gods' furniture serving the law.

Ullr-link: the oath-ring as the winter-god's kenning and office

summary.en: In a Greenland settlement in famine-winter, the little-volva Thorbjorg ('nine? - the ninth winter's? - the seeress with the nine sisters? - is fetched from farm to farm: she arrives in the winter? - dressed in the ritual costume (the blue-black? - the cat? - 'a cloak? - set with? - stones? - 'a? - glass? - beaded? - headband? - 'a? - staff? - 'brass-knobbed? - 'set with? - stones; her platform raised? - 'the? - 'seid-hjallr? - the high-seat of the ritual; the feast prepared for her ('hearts? - of? - 'all? - 'kinds? - of? - beasts? - the seid-meal); the songs requested: 'the? - 'varðlokur? - 'needed? - 'for? - the spellwork? - and no one knows them - until Gudrid, the Christian woman, sings; and the volva sees: the seasons, the marriage, the voyage west. The record is the corpus's most complete séance-ethnography: the professional seeress's costume, stage, fee, and the song's office - and the Christian woman whose singing completes the pagan rite.
summary.zh: 饑荒之冬，格陵蘭移民點請來「小女先知」索爾比約格——一位有九位姊妹的女先知——走遍農莊為人占卜。她身著儀式服飾（綴有寶石的青黑斗篷、玻璃珠頭帶、鑲石銅柄法杖），登上專設的高臺（seid-hjallr），享用以各種獸心備製的祭餐。眾人請她施法，卻無人會唱咒歌「瓦爾德魯庫」（varðlokur）——直到基督徒女子古德麗德開口吟唱；女先知遂見異象：季節、婚事與西行航路。此記錄是語料中最完整的降神會民族誌：職業女先知的服飾、法臺、酬勞與咒歌職能——而完成這場異教儀式的，竟是一位基督教女性。

canonical_translation: J. Sephton, The Saga of Erik the Red, London 1898 (public domain); Hauksbok version per Islenzk Fornrit IV

The Thorbjorg-chapter (in the Hauksbok recension of Eiriks saga) is the corpus's most complete seance-ethnography, and its details are the profession's anatomy. passages.text: Thorbjorg the little-volva was fetched from farm to farm in the famine-winter; she came in a cloak of blue-black set with stones, a glass-bead headband, a brass-knobbed staff, and a high seat was raised for her on a cushion of hen's feathers.
