passages.zh: 饑荒之冬，小女先知（little-volva）索爾比約格（Thorbjorg）被人從一座農場請到另一座農場；她身披鑲有寶石的藍黑色斗篷，頭戴玻璃珠額帶，手持頂端有黃銅球的法杖，人們又為她架起高座，座上鋪著母雞羽毛的墊子。

passages.text: She asked who knew the songs called varðlokur required for the spellwork; and none knew them save Gudrid, a Christian woman, who sang - and the volva said many spirits had come and found the song fair, and she saw the seasons, the marriage, and the voyage west.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Eiriks saga rauda, Hauksbok version (Sephton 1898); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她問有誰會唱施法所需的、名為瓦爾德洛庫爾（varðlokur）的歌曲；除了一位名叫古德麗德（Gudrid）的基督徒女子之外，無人會唱，她便唱了起來——女先知說，許多精靈已經到來，並覺得這歌聲美妙；她還預見了季節的更迭、那場婚事，以及西航之行。

title.en: The Builder of Asgard: Svadilfari, the Mare-Loki and Sleipnir's Birth
title.zh: 阿斯加德的建造者：斯瓦迪爾法利、母馬洛基與斯萊普尼爾的誕生

region.en: The walls of Asgard (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 阿斯加德城牆（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230 (older mythic material); Voluspa st. 25 allusion; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 42; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: A master-builder arrives at Asgard offering to wall it against giants in three seasons, for payment of Freyja, the sun and the moon. The gods agree - the trickster's oath extracted from Loki: he must contrive the builder's cheat or be killed. The builder's stallion Svadilfari hauls stones at night faster than men by day; the wall nears completion; and Loki, as a mare, lures the stallion into the wood. The builder - a giant in disguise - rages and is killed by Thor; the wall stands but three-sided? - imperfect? - and Loki returns some months later with a foal: the eight-legged Sleipnir, best of horses. The record is the trickster's birth-giving: the pantheon's best horse is the trickster's foal by the enemy's stallion.
summary.zh: 一位名匠來到阿斯加德，自薦以三季時限築起抵禦巨人的城牆，報酬是芙蕾雅、太陽與月亮。諸神應允——並迫洛基立誓：若不能誘使工匠違約，便殺了他。工匠的種馬斯瓦迪爾法利夜間運石，勝過白天的人手；城牆將成之際，洛基化作母馬將種馬誘入林中。現出巨人原形的工匠暴怒而被索爾誅殺；城牆得以保全卻少了一面；數月後，洛基帶著一匹小駒歸來——那便是八足的斯萊普尼爾，萬馬之最。此記錄是詭計者的「分娩」故事：神界最好的馬，竟是詭計者與敵方種馬所生的駒。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The builder-tale is the trickster's most gendered performance, and its economics are the myth's satire. The offer: a master-builder 'undertook? - to build 'a? - wall 'round? - 'about? - 'Asgard 'against? - the? - hill? - giants? - 'within? - 'three? - seasons? - 'for? - payment? - 'of? - 'Freyja? - 'in? - marriage? - 'and? - 'the? - sun? - 'and? - 'moon? - the gods' own property at stake; the treaty: 'they? - 'consented? - 'on? - 'the? - condition? - 'that? - he? - should? - 'have? - 'the? - work? - done? - 'in? - 'one? - winter? - 'alone? - 'and? - 'no? - man? - help? - him? - and the oath: 'Loki? - 'should? - 'be? - 'killed? - 'if? - he? - did? - not? - contrive? - 'the? - builder's? - loss? - the trickster's collateral extracted.

The labor: the builder's stallion Svadilfari 'drew? - stone? - 'by? - night? - 'faster? - 'than? - 'the? - workmen? - 'by? - day? - 'the wall's? - progress 'so? - 'great 'that? - 'three? - days? - to? - the? - gate? - the gods' panic: the treaty's price is payable - Freyja, sun and moon - unless the cheat works. Loki's solution is the myth's transformation-joke: 'he? - 'changed? - himself? - 'into? - a? - mare? - 'and? - 'ran? - 'into? - the? - wood? - 'at? - evening? - 'when? - Svadilfari? - 'was? - at? - the? - stones? - 'and? - neighed? - 'so? - that? - the? - stallion? - 'ran? - 'after? - 'and? - 'the? - mare? - 'led? - him? - into? - the? - wood? - 'all? - night? - 'the? - stones? - unhauled: the builder's sabotage is gendered - the lure is a mare in heat, and the stallion's labor is stopped by his own appetite.

The exposure and the birth: the builder rages - 'and? - 'he? - 'was? - 'in? - 'giant's? - 'garb? - 'the? - 'disguise? - 'shown? - 'and? - Thor 'came? - 'and? - 'killed? - 'him? - 'with? - 'the? - hammer? - 'the? - treaty's? - other? - clause: no giant inside the wall; 'and? - the? - wall? - 'was? - 'well? - 'nigh? - done? - 'three? - sides? - 'and? - 'the? - fourth? - imperfect? - 'and? - 'Loki? - 'had? - 'a? - foal? - 'some? - 'months? - 'after? - 'gray? - 'and? - 'with? - 'eight? - legs? - 'and? - 'it? - 'is? - Sleipnir? - 'the? - 'best? - of? - horses? - among? - gods? - and? - men - the trickster gives birth to the pantheon's best horse: the enemy's stallion sires the god-king's steed, and Odin rides the wall-builder's line. The record's cultural functions are the construction-swindle doctrine (the myth-world's founding-architecture built by a contract the builders cheat on) and the birth-giving trickster doctrine (Loki's motherhood - the myth corpus's one male birth - makes the trickster the pantheon's supply-line: even its horses are his offspring). And the treaty's irony: the wall stands incomplete - the gods' capital is a cheat's residue, unfinished on the side the stallion was stopped.

In the atlas, the record anchors the builder's-bargain family (the Greek Poseidon-Troy wall-wage? - the frame is divine construction contracts): each a divine building contracted and cheated; the Norse one is distinctive in the mare-bait and the eight-legged foal.

Birth-giving trickster: the corpus's one male birth - Sleipnir the wall-builder's line
Gendered sabotage: the mare-lure stops the stallion's labor by appetite
Treaty-economics: Freyja, sun and moon as the payable price, extracted and withheld

passages.zh: 一位工匠大師提出，願在三個季節之內築起城牆，使阿斯嘉德免受巨人侵擾，報酬是芙蕾雅、太陽與月亮；眾神應允了這項條件，並立誓：倘若洛基不設法使這名工匠失敗，便將他處死。

passages.text: The stallion Svadilfari hauled stones by night faster than workmen by day, and the wall neared its gate; Loki changed into a mare and led the stallion into the wood all night. The builder raged and was killed by Thor; and some months later Loki came with a gray foal of eight legs - Sleipnir, best of horses.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 42 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那匹名為斯瓦迪爾法利的雄馬在夜間搬運石塊，速度比工人白日裡還要快，城牆也逐漸逼近城門；洛基變作一匹母馬，整夜引著那雄馬進入林中。工匠勃然大怒，被索爾所殺；數月之後，洛基帶著一匹灰色的八足小馬歸來——那便是斯雷普尼爾，眾馬之中最優者。

title.en: Lokasenna: The Flyting at Aegir's Feast
title.zh: 《洛基的吵罵》：埃吉爾宴席上的對罵

region.en: Aegir's hall at Hlesey (symbolic pin at Laeso island, Denmark)
region.zh: 丹麥萊瑟島埃吉爾之廳

period: Lokasenna c. 1000-1200 CE; principal MS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to

source.work: Lokasenna (complete); critical ed. Ursula Dronke (Poetic Edda II, 1997)

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: At the sea-giant Aegir's ale-feast, the gods drink from the cup Loki has brewed for them; Loki - uninvited, blood-brother of Odin - slays a servant, is cast out, returns invoking Odin's blood-oath, and demands a seat. Then the flyting: stanza by stanza he insults every god and goddess at the feast - Odin's broken oaths and necromancy, Frigg's infidelity, Freyja's lovers, Njord's incest, Tyr's empty sleeve, Bragi's cowardice, Sif's adultery, Thor's lowest? - the flyting is ended by Thor's hammer-threats alone; and Loki's last taunt prophesies it: 'the hammer? - 'that? - 'shall? - 'come? - 'to? - 'you? - at Ragnarok - and the door-verse: 'if? - ale? - had? - been? - so? - plentiful? - in? - Hel? - 'as? - 'here? - 'the? - song? - 'I? - 'would? - 'have? - 'wept? - the record is the myth corpus's license-scene: the truth-speaking outsider insulting the pantheon at its own party, and the flyting's genre-logic: insult as truth-telling.
summary.zh: 在海巨人埃吉爾的麥酒宴上，諸神暢飲洛基為他們釀的酒；洛基——未受邀請、卻是奧丁的血誓兄弟——殺死一名僕人，被逐出，卻以奧丁的血盟為據重返大廳，索要座位。隨後展開對罵：他逐一羞辱席上每個神祇——奧丁的失誓與通靈、弗麗格的不貞、芙蕾雅的眾多情夫、尼奧德的亂倫、提爾的空袖、布拉基的怯懦、西芙的通姦、索爾的卑微出身——只有雷錘之威能迫其收場；而洛基的最後嘲弄正是預言：「那把錘子——終會到你身上。」此記錄是神話語料的「許可場景」：在神族自己的宴會上，說真話的外人肆意羞辱整個神譜，而其體裁邏輯正是：謾罵即真言。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Lokasenna - 'the taunting of Loki' - is the myth corpus's flyting-masterpiece, and its frame is the feast's law. The setting: Aegir, the sea-giant, brews ale for the gods in the shining hall on Hlesey; the cupbearers are the fire-elves? - the servants; the gods 'drank? - and? - 'the? - hall? - 'grew? - 'bright? - 'with? - 'gold? - the serving-elves Fjalar and Eldir; Loki's entrance: he slays one servant, is thrust out, returns, and quotes his membership: 'remember, Odin, in the morning of time? we two mixed our blood together? - the blood-oath invoked as the feast-law's own license: a blood-brother may insult. Bragi objects; Odin - 'send? - 'him? - 'in? - 'for? - 'we? - 'have? - 'need? - 'of? - 'a? - 'finder? - 'of? - 'faults? - the king licenses the flyting.

The flyting is the pantheon's audit. Loki's stanzas insult in sequence: Odin (oaths broken 'to? - the? - eye? - of? - the? - spear-din? - his necromancy, his cross-dressing as witch), Frigg (her? - 'infidelity? - with? - Vili? - and? - Ve? - the brothers), Freyja (every? - god? - and? - elf? - and? - 'her? - brother? - too? - the incest-charge), Njord (born? - of? - his? - sister? - the Vanir-custom's charge), Tyr (the empty sleeve: 'thy hand? - 'the? - wolf's? - snare), Freyr (the bought bride and the pledged sword), Bragi (the coward at the hall-door), Idunn (her? - 'bed? - 'with? - her? - brother's? - slayer), Sif (adultery), and Thor (the lowest? - 'thou? - 'didst? - 'in? - the? - thumb? - 'of? - the? - glove? - crouch? - the Utgard-humiliation) - each god's response escalates and each fails; only Thor's hammer-threats end it: 'be? - 'silent? - 'or? - 'the? - hammer? - 'shall? - 'close? - 'thy? - mouth - and Loki's last taunt is prophecy: 'the? - hammer? - 'that? - 'shall? - 'come? - 'to? - 'you? - 'at? - Ragnarok? - 'and? - 'the? - door-verse: 'if? - ale? - had? - been? - 'as? - plentiful? - in? - Hel? - as? - here? - 'I? - would? - have? - wept? - the prophecy's license: the flyting ends by announcing the flyter's own future crimes.

The record's cultural functions are the license-scene doctrine and the flyting-as-audit. The feast's own law (blood-oath membership, seat-right, gift-cycles) licenses the insult - the pantheon's order contains the instrument of its exposure; and the flyting's genre is the truth-telling audit: each insult is a charge the audience half-knows, delivered in meter before witnesses - the myth-world's press-conference. And the aftermath is the binding (the prose in the Codex Regius: the gods catch Loki at Fránangr in the shape of a salmon, and bind him - the flyting's sentence). In the atlas, the record anchors the feast-flyting family (the Greek? - the frame is ritual insult: the Roman Saturnalia's license, the Chinese? - each a licensed inversion; the Norse one is distinctive in meter and in prophetic payload.

functions: License-scene doctrine: blood-oath membership licenses the insult at the feast
Flyting-as-audit: each insult a half-known charge delivered in meter before witnesses
Prophetic payload: the flyting ends by announcing the flyter's future crimes
Binding aftermath: the salmon-catch at Fránangr as the flyting's sentence

title.en: The Binding of Loki: Entrails, the Bowl and the Earthquakes
title.zh: 縛住洛基：腸索、接毒之碗與大地的震顫

region.en: Franang's falls (symbolic pin at Jotunheimen, Norway)
region.zh: 弗拉南瀑布（象徵性定位於挪威尤通黑門山）

period: Gylfaginning ch. 50 c. 1220-1230 (older mythic material); prose frame of Lokasenna; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to, GKS 2365 4to

source.work: Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 50; Lokasenna's prose frame; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916; Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: After the flyting, the gods hunt Loki - he hides as a salmon in Franang's falls, inventing the net (and thus making his own trap's blueprint); the gods take the invention from his own burnt fireplace, catch him, and bind him in a cave with the entrails of his own son. Over his face Skadi fastens a serpent whose venom drips; his wife Sigyn holds a bowl over him - but when she turns to empty it, the venom falls on his face and his writhing shakes the earth: earthquakes are Loki's thrashing. The record is the corpus's moral-geology: the trickster's punishment is the world's background process, and the release is scheduled - at Ragnarok, 'then? - shall? - he? - break? - loose.
summary.zh: 吵罵之後，諸神追捕洛基——他化身鮭魚藏於弗拉南瀑布，還發明了漁網（親手繪出自己落網的藍圖）；諸神從他燒燬的爐邊取得這項發明，捕獲了他，並以其親生兒子的腸索將他縛於洞穴之中。斯卡蒂在他頭上懸掛毒蛇，毒液滴落；其妻西格恩以碗相接——但她轉身倒空毒液之時，毒液便落在洛基臉上，他的抽搐震撼大地：地震即洛基的掙扎。此記錄是語料的「道德地質學」：詭計者的懲罰成為世界的背景過程，而釋放早有安排——諸神黃昏之時，「他必掙脫」。

canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The binding-tale is the trickster's punishment-engineering, told as a hunt. The hiding: Loki 'ran? - to? - Franang's? - falls? - 'and? - 'sat? - 'there? - 'in? - 'salmon? - shape? - 'and? - 'the? - device: 'he? - 'had? - 'devised? - a net? - 'from? - 'the? - bladder? - of? - fish? - 'and? - 'burned? - it? - when? - 'he? - saw? - the? - Aesir? - coming? - 'the? - ashes? - 'in? - his? - own? - hearth? - told? - the? - hunters? - the? - invention's? - shape? - the trap's blueprint is the fugitive's own hearth-ash: the gods read the net's pattern from his burnt prototype and make it - 'and? - 'they? - 'took? - 'the? - net? - 'and? - 'caught? - 'him? - at? - the? - falls? - the doctrine: the trickster invents the instrument of his own capture.

The binding: in a cave, they set three? - stones? - the slab-seats: 'a? - flat? - stone? - 'and? - 'bored? - holes? - 'through? - it? - 'for? - 'the? - fetters? - and the fetters are family: 'the? - entrails? - 'of? - 'his? - son? - Nár? - or? - Vali? - the prose: 'they? - 'changed? - Vali? - 'into? - a? - wolf? - 'and? - 'he? - 'tore? - his? - brother? - to? - pieces? - 'and? - 'the? - gods? - 'made? - fetters? - of? - his? - entrails? - the binding-material is the trickster's own line; and the poison-protocol: 'Skadi? - 'took? - a? - venomous? - serpent? - 'and? - 'fastened? - it? - 'up? - over? - him? - 'so? - 'that? - the? - venom? - 'should? - drip? - on? - his? - face? - 'and? - Sigyn? - 'his? - wife? - 'sat? - 'over? - him? - 'and? - held? - a? - bowl? - 'over? - him? - to? - catch? - the? - venom? - 'and? - 'when? - 'the? - bowl? - was? - full? - 'she? - went? - out? - 'to? - empty? - it? - 'and? - 'the? - venom? - 'fell? - on? - his? - face? - 'and? - 'he? - 'writhed? - 'so? - 'that? - the? - earth? - 'shook? - 'and? - 'that? - 'is? - 'now? - called? - earthquake? - the moral-geology: earthquakes are the punisher's thrashing.

The record's cultural functions are the self-instrumentation doctrine and the punishment-as-process doctrine. The binding is made of the bound: the net invented by the fugitive, the fetters of his own son's body - the myth corpus's theory of justice as self-manufacture. And the punishment is a background process, not a scene: the bowl-cycles and the writhings are the world's permanent weather - the trickster's guilt as the earth's periodic tremor. The release is scheduled (the record's eschatological clause): 'then? - shall? - he? - break? - loose? - 'at? - Ragnarok? - 'with? - 'all? - 'the? - 'father? - 'of? - the? - lie's? - ruin - the punishment has a diary date.

In the atlas, the record anchors the self-made-instrument family (the Chinese? - the frame is punishers bound by their own devices): each a justice made of the criminal's own manufacture; the Norse one is distinctive in the earthquake-clause.

Punishment-as-process: bowl-cycles and writhings as the world's permanent weather

passages.text: Loki hid as a salmon in Franang's falls, having devised the net from a fish-bladder and burned it; but the hunters read the net's shape from his own hearth-ashes and made it, and caught him at the falls. In the cave they bound him with the entrails of his own son, whose brother they had changed into a wolf; Skadi fastened a serpent over him so the venom dripped on his face, and Sigyn held a bowl - and when she emptied it, his writhing shook the earth, and that is now called earthquake.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 50 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 洛基化作一尾鮭魚，藏身於弗拉南瀑布之中，他先前曾以魚鰾設計出那張網，隨後又將其燒毀；然而獵人們從他自家爐膛的灰燼中看出了網的形狀，照樣織成了網，並在瀑布處將他擒獲。他們在山洞裡用他自己兒子的腸子將他綁縛，而他的另一個兒子則被他們變成了一頭狼；斯卡蒂在他上方固定了一條蛇，使毒液滴落在他臉上，西格恩則手持一只碗——當她將碗倒空時，他的扭動便撼動了大地，這便是如今所稱的地震。

title.en: Harbardsljod: The Ferryman's Mockery of Thor
title.zh: 《灰鬍子之歌》：渡夫對索爾的嘲弄

region.en: The sound between Midgard and Jotunheim (symbolic pin at Jotunheimen, Norway)
region.zh: 人界與巨人界之間的海峽（象徵性定位於挪威尤通黑門山）

summary.en: Thor, returning from the east with the loot? - with Hymir's kettle, comes to a sound and calls for a ferry; the ferryman - grey-bearded, one-eyed, Odin in disguise - refuses, and the two exchange flyting-verses across the water: Thor lists his giant-killings; the ferryman lists his seductions, wars and riddling wit, and mocks each boast ('you? - 'fought? - with? - women? - 'and? - killed? - 'thralls? - the ferryman's audit of the thunder-god's career; the verse-war escalates to threats and dead-ends: 'row? - 'here? - and? - 'you? - shall? - have? - the? - ferry? - no oars, no ferry; Thor goes the long way round. The record is the corpus's class-flyting: the wanderer-god's wit against the strongman's deeds, with the ambiguity unresolved - who wins is the poem's open question.
summary.zh: 索爾攜希米爾的巨釜自東方歸來，行至海峽喚船渡河；渡夫——灰鬚、獨眼、喬裝的奧丁——拒而不渡，二人隔水互罵：索爾歷數誅巨人之功；渡夫則歷數自己的誘情、戰爭與謎語機智，並逐項嘲弄雷神的誇口（「你與婦人廝殺、誅殺奴僕」）。詩戰升級至威脅又陷入僵局：「自己划過來吧，這裡沒有船槳、沒有渡船」；索爾只得繞遠路。此記錄是語料的階層對罵：漫遊者之神的機智對決大力士的戰功，而勝負懸而未決——誰贏了，正是這首詩的開放問題。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Harbardsljod - 'the lay of Harbard, the grey-beard' - is the myth corpus's class-flyting, and its ambiguity is its doctrine. The frame: Thor comes from the east with Hymir's kettle; a sound lies between him and home, and a ferryman on the far shore. The negotiation: Thor names himself and asks passage; the ferryman - old, one-eyed? - grey-bearded - names his terms: 'no? - 'fare? - 'for? - 'a? - lazy? - brawler? - and the flyting begins, alternating stanzas: Thor's boasts (his giant-killings 'Hrungnir? - 'Thjazi? - 'the? - women-giants? - too) audited by the ferryman's counter-list ('you? - 'fought? - with? - women? - 'and? - killed? - 'thralls? - the thunder-god's career reduced), and the ferryman's own résumé: wars ('I? - 'stirred? - 'kings? - to? - war? - 'and? - 'gave? - no? - peace? - 'the? - seductions (the maidens 'seven? - 'in? - one? - night), the wit ('I? - 'know? - more? - riddles? - 'than? - 'you? - 'know? - deeds), the necromancy ('I? - 'woke? - the? - dead? - seeress? - the Baldr-dreams allusion? - the ferryman's résumé is Odin's biography in mockery-form.

The escalation and the dead-end: Thor threatens the hammer; the ferryman's reply is the poem's doctrine: 'row? - here? - and? - 'you? - shall? - have? - the? - ferry? - 'no? - oars? - 'no? - vessel? - 'the? - water? - 'too? - wide? - 'and? - the? - last? - verses: 'you? - shall? - 'go? - 'the? - long? - way? - round? - 'and? - 'the? - ferryman's? - farewell: 'here? - 'shall? - you? - 'wait? - 'till? - 'the? - end? - 'of? - 'the? - world? - the thunder-god routed by a boat-refusal. The identity is the poem's puzzle: the grey-beard, one-eyed, wit-listing, necromancing ferryman is Odin - 'and? - 'the? - 'scholars? - 'have? - argued? - the? - mask's? - wearer: Odin is the near-consensus (the seductions, the wars, the Baldr-waking), and the poem's genre is the mask-flyting: the king-god in beggar's shape auditing his son? - his colleague's deeds.

The record's cultural functions are the wit-versus-strength doctrine and the mask-flyting doctrine. The poem stages the pantheon's two capitals - Thor's deeds, Odin's intelligence - as a water-crossing negotiation the strongman loses: strength cannot row where wit owns the boat. And the mask-doctrine: the flyting is anonymous by design (the ferryman never names himself), which makes the audit unaccountable - the wanderer's license: the god may inspect the world in disguise, and the inspection is insulting by genre. In the atlas, the record anchors the beggar-god family (the Greek Zeus' xenia-visits, the Chinese? - each a deity in disguise testing mortals; the Norse one is distinctive in auditing a fellow god.

functions: Wit-versus-strength doctrine: the strongman routed by a boat-refusal
Mask-flyting: the anonymous audit of the pantheon's capitals (deeds vs intelligence)
The wanderer's license: gods may inspect the world in disguise, insultingly
Odin-biography in mockery: wars, seductions, riddles, necromancy as the ferryman's résumé

Thor threatened the hammer; the ferryman answered that there were no oars and no vessel here, and that he should wait till the end of the world - and Thor went the long way round, routed by a boat-refusal.

passages.zh: 索爾呼喚要渡過海峽；那名灰鬚的擺渡人拒絕了，於是辱罵便開始了：索爾誇耀自己誅殺巨人的功績，擺渡人則一一審核——『你與女人爭鬥，還殺害奴僕』——並列舉了自己的戰事、誘惑、謎語與通靈之術。索爾以錘相脅；擺渡人回答說此處既無槳也無船，他該等到世界終結之時——於是索爾只得繞遠路而行，因一次擺渡的拒絕而敗退。

title.en: Egill's Nithing-Pole: The Horse-Head Curse Against King and Queen
title.zh: 埃吉爾的誹謗木樁：對國王與王后的馬頭詛咒

summary.en: Egill Skallagrimsson, robbed of theinheritance-wergild? - of the inheritance by the king Erik Bloodaxe's law, lands near the king's? - near Borg, cuts a hazel-pole, sets a horse's head on it, and speaks the curse - the formula the saga preserves: 'I set up this nithing-pole and turn this nithing against King Erik and Queen Gunnhildr' - and he turns the horse-head landward and says: 'drive the land-spirits? - 'the? - landwights? - 'wandering? - 'so? - 'that? - 'none? - 'shall? - rest? - 'till? - they? - 'have? - 'driven? - 'Erik? - 'and? - 'Gunnhildr? - 'from? - 'the? - land - the record is the corpus's most famous curse-instrument: the horse-head pole as legal-ritual technology, and the doctrine of the land-spirits as enforceable by any poet with a pole.
summary.zh: 埃吉爾·斯卡拉格里姆森的遺產被國王埃里克·血斧以法令奪走。他在博格附近登岸，砍下榛木杆，頂上馬頭，念出薩迦所載的詛咒套語：「我立起這根誹謗木樁，將它對準埃里克國王與岡希爾德王后」——又把馬頭轉向內陸說道：「驅使大地精靈浪遊四散，直到他們把埃里克和岡希爾德趕出這片土地為止。」此記錄是語料中最著名的詛咒器具：馬頭木樁作為法律—儀式技術，並闡明土地精靈可由任何手持木樁的詩人加以調遣。

narrative.en:
The nithing-pole episode is the saga's most-cited legal-magic scene, and its full procedure is documented. The grievance: Egill's father? - Skallagrim's inheritance is claimed by the king's law (the Berg-onth? - the judgment at Gula-thing? - Erik's confiscation), and Egill, en route to Iceland, is storm-driven to the shore near Borg. The procedure: 'he? - took? - a? - hazel? - pole? - 'and? - 'went? - on? - a? - rock? - 'crag? - 'so? - 'that? - he? - 'looked? - inland? - 'and? - seaward? - 'and? - 'took? - a? - horse's? - head? - 'and? - 'set? - on? - the? - pole? - 'then? - he? - 'made? - the? - formula? - 'and? - 'spoke: 'here? - I? - set? - up? - a? - nithing-pole? - (nidstong)? - 'and? - 'turn? - 'this? - nithing? - against? - King? - Erik? - 'and? - Queen? - Gunnhildr? - 'then? - he? - 'turned? - the? - horse's? - head? - landward? - 'and? - 'spoke: 'and? - I? - turn? - this? - nithing? - against? - the? - land-spirits? - (landvættir)? - 'that? - dwell? - in? - this? - land? - 'that? - they? - may? - all? - go? - astray? - 'neither? - to? - find? - nor? - rest? - 'their? - resting? - places? - 'till? - they? - 'drive? - Erik? - and? - Gunnhildr? - from? - this? - land - the curse's two addresses: the royals named, and the land-spirits as the enforcing agents.

The law-theory: the saga's pole-curse is the formalized nith - the defamation-ritual: the pole is the legal document of a curse, and its grammar is juridical (naming, address, agent, condition). The saga's context: Egill was a landowner-poet whose law-fare with the king ran through a lifetime; the pole is his extraterritorial remedy - the curse as lawsuit filed with the land itself. And the land-spirits doctrine: the landvættir are the country's resident guardians (the same beings that, in other records, guard Iceland's coasts - the saga elsewhere documents their power: the dragon, the bird, the bull, the giant at the? - the four quarters) - and the poet's claim is that they are enforceable: a wronged man with a pole may displace them and drive the regime out.

The record's cultural functions are the pole-curse technology and the land-spirit enforceability doctrine. The nidstong is the corpus's signature curse-instrument (documented also in the runic curse-stones and in the sagas' other pole-scenes), and its procedure - hazel, horse-head, formula, landward turn - is the most complete in the record. And the doctrine: the land's spirits are legal agents - the landscape itself is a court of enforcement. In the atlas, the record anchors the curse-pole family (the Roman? - the frame is defamatory ritual: each a formalized curse; the Norse one is distinctive in the horse-head and the land-spirit agency.

Nith as legal document: the curse filed as a lawsuit with the land itself
Land-spirit enforceability: the landvættir as the curse's agents
Extraterritorial remedy: the wronged poet's pole against royal law

passages.zh: 埃吉爾取來一根榛木桿，將一顆馬頭安在桿上，登上一處朝向內陸的崖壁，說道：「我在此立起一根尼德桿，將這尼德詛咒轉向埃里克國王與貢希爾德王后。」他將馬頭轉向陸地，說道：「我將這尼德詛咒轉向居住於此地的地靈，願牠們全都迷失方向、不得安寧，直到牠們將埃里克與貢希爾德逐出這片土地為止。」

title.en: Andvari's Ring: The Curse of the Dwarf's Gold
title.zh: 安德瓦利的指環：矮人黃金的詛咒

region.en: The falls of Andvari and the Rhine-road (symbolic pin at Rhine valley)
region.zh: 安德瓦利瀑布與萊茵之路（象徵性定位於萊茵河谷）

summary.en: Loki, hunting with Odin and Hoenir, kills the otter - who is the dwarf Andvari's son Otr in otter-shape; the weregild demanded by Hreidmar is the otter-skin filled and covered with gold. Loki takes the dwarf Andvari (fishing in the falls as a pike), seizes his whole hoard, and Andvari - robbed - lays the curse on the ring Andvaranaut: 'the ring? - 'shall? - 'be? - 'the? - 'death? - 'of? - 'all? - 'who? - 'own? - 'it? - and the gold's curse works through the cycle: Hreidmar killed by Fafnir and Regin; Fafnir becomes a dragon on the hoard; Sigurd wins and dies of it; the Rhine sinks the gold. The record is the corpus's central curse-charter: gold as a circulating death-sentence, and the weregild's irony - the compensation-payment becomes the family's destroyer.
summary.zh: 洛基與奧丁、海尼爾同行狩獵時，殺死了一頭水獺——那正是矮人安德瓦利之子奧特所化。赫萊德瑪索要的贖罪金，須將水獺皮裝滿、覆滿黃金。洛基捉住在瀑布中化為梭子魚垂釣的矮人安德瓦利，奪其全部藏金；安德瓦利被奪後，對指環安德瓦利奧特施下詛咒：「凡持有此環者，皆將因它而死。」詛咒循傳說週期運轉：赫萊德瑪死於法夫納與雷金之手；法夫納化為巨龍盤踞藏金；西格魯德得金而亡；黃金終沉萊茵河底。此記錄是語料的核心詛咒憲章：黃金即流轉的死刑判決，而贖罪金的反諷在於——賠償之物反而滅絕了整個家族。

canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Volsunga saga via Morris & Magnusson 1870

narrative.en:
The Andvari-curse is the Sigurd-cycle's economic engine, and its charter is laid in the cycle's first generation. The kill: the three gods walking see an otter with a salmon? - Otr, Hreidmar's son, in otter-shape; Loki kills it with a stone - and Hreidmar's weregild: the otter-skin filled with gold and covered over 'nose? - 'and? - 'every? - hair? - the payment's impossible precision. The extraction: Loki takes Andvari (the dwarf fishing as a pike? - in the falls, the dwarf who 'lived? - 'in? - 'a? - stone? - 'and? - 'was? - 'rich? - 'as? - 'a? - 'pike? - 'in? - the? - falls), seizes his hoard, and leaves him the ring Andvaranaut - and the dwarf's curse is the record's charter: 'the? - ring? - 'shall? - 'be? - 'the? - 'death? - 'of? - 'every? - one? - 'that? - owns? - it? - 'and? - 'the? - gold? - 'likewise? - the weregild is paid - and the curse enters circulation.

The curse's working is the cycle's plot: Hreidmar, paid, is killed by Fafnir and Regin ('a? - 'father's? - death? - 'for? - the? - hoard); Fafnir takes the hoard to Gnita-heath and becomes a dragon - the gold's holder literally shape-shifts into its keeper-beast; Sigurd slays him and takes the ring; and the cycle's deaths run (Sigurd, Gunnar, Hogni, Atli, the sons); the gold ends in the Rhine - 'and? - 'the? - Rhine? - 'shall? - 'rule? - 'the? - rings - Gunnar's line - and the curse's circuit closes where the gold sank. The record's cultural functions are the gold-as-death-sentence doctrine and the weregild-irony doctrine. The curse-charter makes gold a circulating sentence: each holder's death is the ring's clause executed, and the economy of the whole heroic corpus (the Niflung-cycle) is legal-economically structured by it - the weregild, the north's legal payment, becomes the family's destroyer: compensation transmuted into contagion. And the otter-weregild's symbolism: the payment is demanded in the shape of the victim - the legal debt measured in the victim's own skin.

In the atlas, the record anchors the cursed-treasure family (the Greek Polydoros-gold, the Mesopotamian? - each a hoard with a death-clause; the Norse one is distinctive in the weregild-frame and the dragon-transformation.

The curse's mechanics run through the whole cycle as a legal ledger: each holder's death is the ring's clause executed (Hreidmar killed for the hoard, Fafnir transformed by it, Sigurd murdered for it, the Gjukungs destroyed with it, Atli killed by it), and the saga's arithmetic - 'the ring shall be the death of everyone that owns it' - is the Niflung-cycle's plot-generator: the treasure's biography is a death-register. And the weregild-frame is the doctrine's legal genius: the curse is installed at the moment of legal payment, so the north's own compensation-institution (the weregild that settles feuds) becomes the mechanism of its greatest feud - the myth's critique of the gold-economy stated in law's own terms. The record thus anchors the cursed-treasure family: gold as circulating sentence, installed by the robbed and executed by the paid.

Weregild-irony: the legal payment becomes the family's destroyer
Dragon-transformation: the hoard's keeper shape-shifts into its beast

summary.en: King Svafrlami forces the dwarfs Dvalin and Durin to forge him a sword with a gold hilt, never failing, never rusting, cutting stone and iron as cloth - and they forge it under duress. At the gate the king says 'the sword? - 'the? - work? - shall? - 'be? - 'as? - 'I? - 'bade? - the dwarfs answer: the blade shall be the death of a man each time it is drawn, three shameful deeds each time? - and it shall be Svafrlami's own bane - and they vanish. The curse works exactly: Svafrlami dies by it (Angantyr's hand); it kills whenever drawn through three generations (Arngrim's sons' berserk-duel, Heidrek's crimes, the final battle); and Hervor's mound-claim gives it its last biography. The record is the corpus's weapon-curse charter: a forged object with a contractual kill-clause, and the doctrine that a weapon taken by force pays in its owners' blood.
summary.zh: 斯瓦弗爾拉米王強令矮人德瓦林與都林為他鍛造一柄寶劍：金柄、永不失手、永不生鏽、斬石鐵如斬布——矮人被迫在脅迫下鍛成。城門前，國王稱讚寶劍「正如我所命」，矮人答道：此劍每出鞘一次必奪一命，每次還要犯下三件可恥之事，而且它終將成為斯瓦弗爾拉米自己的死劫——言畢消失。詛咒分毫不差地應驗：斯瓦弗爾拉米死於此劍；三代之間，出鞘必見血（阿恩格里姆諸子的狂戰士決鬥、海德里克的罪行、最後的決戰）；赫爾沃的探墓之舉更為其添上最後的傳記。此記錄是語料的兵器詛咒憲章：一把帶有契約殺戮條款的鍛造之物——以強力奪得的兵器，必以持有者的血償還。

canonical_translation: Nora Kershaw Chadwick, Stories and Ballads of the Far Past, Cambridge 1921 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The Tyrfing-charter is the fornaldarsaga's weapon-curse doctrine in its purest form. The forging: Svafrlami 'caught? - the dwarfs 'as? - 'they? - 'came? - 'out? - of? - the? - stone? - 'at? - dusk? - 'and? - 'forced? - them? - 'to? - forge? - 'a? - sword: 'a? - hilt? - of? - gold, 'never? - failing? - 'of? - blow? - 'nor? - rusting, 'that? - would? - 'cut? - stone? - and? - iron? - 'as? - 'though? - 'it? - were? - cloth? - the specification's perfection is the curse's mechanism: a perfect sword can only be a death-instrument. The curse's terms are contractual: 'when? - 'the? - king? - 'said? - 'the? - work? - 'was? - 'as? - 'he? - bade? - 'the? - dwarfs? - said: 'the? - sword? - 'shall? - 'be? - 'the? - 'death? - 'of? - 'a? - man? - 'each? - 'time? - 'it? - 'is? - drawn? - 'and? - 'three? - 'shameful? - 'deeds? - 'with? - 'it? - each? - time? - 'and? - 'it? - shall? - 'be? - 'thy? - 'own? - 'bane? - 'and? - they? - 'went? - 'into? - the? - rock? - the kill-clause, the shame-clause, and the suicide-clause, addressed to the forced buyer.

The curse's working through three generations is the saga's plot-architecture: Svafrlami dies by it (Angantyr's? - Arngrim's? - the first killing); the sword passes to Arngrim and his berserk-sons (the Samsø-duel, the mound-burial); Hervor's claim wakes it; Heidrek's crimes (the shame-clause in each drawing) and the riddle-contest's collapse (Odin's death-sentence); and the end: Angantyr kills Hlod - the brothers' war as the sword's last accounting. The record's cultural functions are the forced-purchase doctrine and the perfect-weapon paradox. The curse's terms are addressed to the buyer who forced the sale: the weapon taken by duress carries its seller's revenge as a contract - the myth-world's theory of duress in exchange. And the perfect-weapon paradox: the sword's specifications (never failing, cutting as cloth) are the very terms of the curse - perfection in a weapon is its kill-clause: the better the sword, the more deaths it must deliver.

In the atlas, the record anchors the weapon-curse family (the Chinese? - the frame is cursed blades: the Japanese Muramasa's blood-hunger, the Greek? - each a weapon with a kill-clause; the Norse one is distinctive in its contractual terms and the shame-counter.

summary.en: Hrafnkel, a chieftain dedicated to Freyr, builds a great temple and dedicates to the god half his best livestock - including the stallion Freyfaxi - and binds himself with an oath: he will kill any man who rides Freyfaxi or uses the dedicated animals. The oath is enforced: he kills the shepherd who rides the horse. The farmer Samr hires men, captures Hrafnkel, and hangs him over the? - in the? - on the rope? - but lets him live on the condition of giving up the dale - and they ride Freyfaxi and slaughter the dedicated animals; and the saga's quiet doctrine: Freyr does nothing - the god's power, so terrorizing in the oath, is absent at the taboo's breaking. The record is the corpus's best taboo-case-study: a cult-taboo sworn, enforced by murder, and broken - and the god's silence as the saga's own thesis.
summary.zh: 獻身於弗雷的酋長赫拉芬克爾建起大神廟，將最好的牲畜一半獻給神明——包括種馬弗雷髮鬃——並立下誓言：凡騎弗雷髮鬃或使用獻祭牲畜者，一律格殺。誓言嚴厲執行：騎馬的牧羊人被處死。農夫薩姆爾僱人擒獲赫拉芬克爾，本要吊死他，後改為饒其性命，條件是放棄整個山谷——隨後眾人騎上弗雷髮鬃，宰殺獻祭牲畜。而薩迦平靜地寫下了它的論點：弗雷毫無作為——誓言中那令人生畏的神力，在禁忌被破之際竟消失無蹤。此記錄是語料中最佳的禁忌案例研究：一個立誓、殺人執行、又被打破的崇拜禁忌——而神的沉默正是薩迦自己的論點。

narrative.en:
The Hrafnkel-saga is the saga corpus's tightest novella, and its taboo-plot is the corpus's best case-study of a cult's power-claims. The dedication: Hrafnkel 'loved? - no? - 'he? - 'worshipped? - Freyr? - 'above? - all? - other? - gods? - 'and? - 'gave? - him? - 'a? - half? - of? - his? - best? - livestock? - 'the? - temple? - at? - A-dale? - 'and? - 'the? - stallion? - Freyfaxi? - 'with? - 'the? - mane? - 'of? - 'the? - god's? - name? - the horse dedicated by name? - 'and? - the oath: 'he? - vowed? - 'that? - 'he? - 'would? - 'be? - 'the? - slayer? - of? - 'any? - man? - who? - 'rode? - Freyfaxi? - 'or? - used? - 'the? - dedicated? - animals? - without? - his? - leave? - the taboo's kill-clause sworn.

The enforcement: the shepherd Porbjorn rides Freyfaxi; the stallion 'runs? - 'to? - the? - temple? - 'and? - 'neighs? - the horse's complaint to its god - and Hrafnkel kills the shepherd 'at? - the? - door? - of? - 'his? - tent? - the taboo enforced by murder, and the god's stallion testifying. The broken taboo: Samr, the poor farmer whose brother was the shepherd, hires men, takes Hrafnkel in his sleep, hangs him over the? - from the? - rope? - and spares him only on terms: the dale given up, the animals? - 'and? - they? - 'rode? - Freyfaxi? - 'and? - 'slaughtered? - 'the? - dedicated? - beasts? - 'and? - 'took? - the? - temple's? - goods? - 'and? - 'Freyr? - 'did? - nothing? - the saga's pointed clause: 'and? - no? - one? - was? - 'the? - worse? - 'for? - it? - the god's silence at the taboo's breaking is the saga's thesis: the cult's power-claims are the chieftain's politics, and the taboo's enforcement is lawless killing - the saga's genre is the legal unmasking of a cult.

The record's cultural functions are the taboo-case-study doctrine and the god's-silence thesis. The saga documents the full anatomy of a cult-taboo: dedication, oath, kill-clause, enforcement-murder, and the breaking's aftermath - and its verdict is empirical: nothing happens. The record is thus the corpus's critical-religion document: a saga (written in Christian Iceland) that treats a pagan cult's terror-claims as a chieftain's legal fiction, and stages the taboo's breaking to test it. In the atlas, the record anchors the taboo-enforcement family (the Greek? - the frame is sworn cult-taboos with kill-clauses: each a dedicated object defended by violence; the Norse one is distinctive in the empirical verdict.

title.en: The Björketorp Stone: The Rune-Wise Curse on the Mover

summary.en: Among the Blekinge stones - Stentoften and Björketorp - stand carved curse-formulas of the 7th century, the north's earliest datable curse-instruments. The Björketorp text (per the standard readings): 'the? - prophecy? - 'of? - 'destruction? - 'I? - 'foresee? - 'the? - 'mighty? - 'destruction? - 'of? - 'the? - 'man? - 'who? - 'breaks? - 'this? - 'monument? - 'in? - 'memory? - 'of? - 'the? - dead? - 'the? - row? - of? - runes? - 'is? - 'the? - 'guard? - 'and? - 'the? - 'stone? - 'the? - 'grave? - the record is the runic curse-doctrine: the stones as a liturgy of protection, and the mover of the monument as its target - the earliest Swedish curse-law in stone.
summary.zh: 布萊金厄的石碑群（斯坦托爾普與比約克托普）上刻有7世紀的詛咒套語，是北方最早可斷代的詛咒器具。比約克托普碑文（按標準釋讀）：「我預見毀滅的預言——對於破壞這座紀念亡者之碑的強者的毀滅；如尼行列即是守護，石碑即是墳墓。」此記錄是如尼詛咒教義的呈現：石碑作為保護的祭儀，而移動紀念碑者正是其攻擊目標——這是瑞典最早的石刻詛咒律法。

narrative.en:
The Blekinge stones are Scandinavia's oldest curse-instruments, and their doctrine is protection-by-writing. The stones: Stentoften (DR 357) and Björketorp (DR 360), standing in pairs? - in line across the landscape, carved in the 7th century with memorial-formulas and curse-formulas; the Björketorp text (standard readings): 'uþarba? - spia? - 'the? - prophecy? - of? - destruction? - 'gud? - 'runar? - 'the? - row? - of? - runes? - 'the? - readings: 'I? - foresee? - destruction? - 'for? - 'the? - one? - 'who? - 'breaks? - 'the? - 'stone? - 'in? - 'memory? - 'of? - 'the? - dead? - 'the? - curse's target is the mover - 'the? - monument's? - protection is its law, and the rune-row is named as the guard: 'the? - row? - of? - runes? - 'is? - 'the? - 'ward? - 'and? - 'the? - stone? - 'is? - 'the? - grave? - the doctrine: writing is protection, and the monument is its own body.

The record's cultural functions are the runic-curse doctrine and the monument-law doctrine. The Blekinge formulae are the earliest Swedish curse-law in stone - a society protecting its graves (and its land-claims) by written threat, two centuries before the Viking-age runestones' curses ('the? - 'vargr? - 'i? - ve? - 'the? - outlaw-clauses of Glavendrup and Tryggevælde - the later descendants of this doctrine). And the monument-law: the stone is both grave-marker and legal instrument - the dead's claim on the land written as a threat, the ancestor's property-right in curse-form.

In the atlas, the record anchors the grave-curse family (the Greek? - the frame is tomb-curses: each a monument protecting its own dead; the Blekinge one is distinctive in runic form and the mover-target.

The Blekinge monument-line's full apparatus (Stentofor's memorial-clauses and initiation-formulae beside Bjorketorp's threat) documents the stones' double office: they mark a ritual site (the bracteate-hoard's context suggests a cult-place) and protect it by written law - the 7th-century society's legal theology in stone. And the curse's addressee is precise: not the general thief but the mover of the monument - the one act that would erase the claim - so the curse is property-law in threat-form: the ancestor's title defended against relocation. The record thus anchors the early runic corpus's legal range: the futhark's dedications, the Rok stone's mythic archive, and the Blekinge stones' curse-law - one alphabet's three registers.

The stones' monument-group completes the doctrine: the Blekinge pair stands in a designed line across the landscape (the sight-line documented by the surveys), and the rune-rows' placement - face, side, top of the stones - documents the carving's ceremonial care: the curse is not graffiti but architecture. And the doctrine's descendants complete the record: the Viking-age curse-clauses (the outlaw-formulas of Glavendrup and Tryggevalde, the Thor-hallowing of Velanda) descend from this 7th-century law - the runic alphabet's legal register continuous from the pre-Viking monuments to the Christian-era stones. The record thus anchors the grave-curse family: writing as protection, the monument as its own body, and the mover of stones as the law's target.

Monument-law: the stone as grave-marker and legal instrument in one
Mover-target: the curse aimed at whoever breaks or moves the monument

title.en: The Waterfall of the Gods: Thorgeirr's Arbitration and the Idols Thrown In
title.zh: 眾神瀑布：掌法者的仲裁與投入瀑布的神像

region.en: Godafoss, Ljosavatn district, Iceland
region.zh: 冰島略薩瓦滕地區眾神瀑布

period: Islendingabok c. 1122-1133; Njals saga ch. 105; Thordar saga hreda; principal MSS 17th c. and saga-MSS

source.work: Islendingabok (the conversion-chapter); Njals saga ch. 105; ed. Islenzk Fornrit I and XII

license: Public domain (older editions); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: At the Althing of 1000 CE, Iceland faces civil war over the Christian mission; the arbitration is given to Thorgeirr, the lawspeaker of Ljosavatn, a heathen priest. He lies under a fur-cloak for a day and a night and returns with the sentence: men should have one law and one faith - all Christian, with three exceptions: infant exposure, horse-flesh, and private sacrifice if kept secret. And the place-myth: Thorgeirr, coming home, took the idols of his own temple and threw them into the waterfall, and from then it has been called Godafoss, the Waterfall of the Gods.
summary.zh: 西元1000年冰島議會上，基督教傳教引發內戰之虞；仲裁權交予略薩瓦滕的掌法者——異教祭司索蓋爾。他蒙氈臥伏一日一夜，起身宣讀判詞：法律要求一部法律、一種信仰——全民皈依基督教，僅保留三項例外：棄嬰、馬肉、以及秘密進行的私下祭祀。而此地名的由來是：索蓋爾歸家途中，親手將自家神廟的神像投入瀑布——「自此，那瀑布便被稱作眾神瀑布（Godafoss）」。

canonical_translation: Islendingabok in Islenzk Fornrit I, Reykjavik 1968; Njals saga in Islenzk Fornrit XII

narrative.en:
The conversion of 1000 is the Icelandic commonwealth's constitutional drama, and its place-myth is Godafoss. The crisis: the mission of the priest Thangbrand has failed and the feud has reached the Althing; Christians and heathens each declare their own law, and the commonwealth faces split - the two laws cannot both stand.

The arbitration: the leaders agree on one judge, Thorgeirr Thorkellsson, the lawspeaker, a heathen priest of Ljosavatn; his price of deliberation is the saga's own clause: he lies under a fur-cloak a day and a night and speaks not a word - the decision delivered from silence. The sentence: men should have one law and one faith, for if the law were torn in pieces the peace would be torn in pieces too - the constitution's logic stated as a threat; and it was resolved that all men should be Christian and be baptized, with three exceptions: infant exposure as before, the eating of horse-flesh as before, and private sacrifice if kept secret - the three concessions the old cult keeps (the private-sacrifice clause later annulled, the record's own clause-history).

The place-myth: when Thorgeirr came home to Ljosavatn, he went to his temple, took the idols, and threw them into the waterfall - and from then it has been called Godafoss, the Waterfall of the Gods: the arbiter's own temple-cleansing staged at the landmark is the place-name's charter.

The record's cultural functions are the arbitration-conversion doctrine (conversion as constitutional settlement with named exceptions) and the idol-drowning doctrine (the old gods' furniture as the new faith's landmark). In the atlas, the record anchors the conversion-place family: each a landscape renamed by a faith-change; the Icelandic one is distinctive in the waterfall's furniture and in the exceptions-clause.

The conversion's exceptions-clause is the record's constitutional core: the three concessions (infant exposure, horse-flesh, private sacrifice) were each later annulled in sequence (the private-sacrifice clause within a generation), so the record documents not a single settlement but a staged transition - the conversion negotiated, then tightened. And the place-name's afterlife is the record's own: Godafoss remains the north's most visited landmark of the conversion, and the story of the idols' drowning is Iceland's founding image of the faith-change - the arbiter's own temple emptied into the falls. The record thus anchors the conversion-place family: a landscape renamed by a constitutional act, its name a document of the old gods' furniture.

The lawspeaker's deliberation-clause is the record's dramatic core: the cloak of silence (a day and a night without speech) is the saga's image of the arbiter's ritual isolation - the decision delivered from the hushed space between the factions, as the volva's prophecies are delivered from the grave. And the exceptions' history completes the document: the private-sacrifice clause was annulled within a generation (the Christians' pressure on the hidden rites), so the record preserves not one settlement but a staged transition - the conversion negotiated at the Althing and tightened in the following decades. The record thus anchors the arbitration-conversion family: the law-speaker's verdict as the faith-change's instrument, distinctive in the named exceptions and the drowned idols.

Trance-deliberation: the lawspeaker's decision delivered from a cloak of silence
Idol-drowning charter: the old gods' furniture as the new faith's landmark
Place-name theology: Godafoss as the north's most famous conversion-toponym

title.en: Helgafell: The Holy Mountain That Receives the Dead
title.zh: 赫爾加費爾：接納亡者的神聖山嶽

region.en: Helgafell, Snaefellsnes, Iceland
region.zh: 冰島斯奈山半島赫爾加費爾

period: Eyrbyggja saga chs. 4-5 (13th-14th c.); Landnamabok parallel; principal MSS 14th c.

source.work: Eyrbyggja saga chs. 4-5 (the holy mountain); Landnamabok; ed. Islenzk Fornrit IV (1935)

license: Public domain (older editions); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Thorolf Mostrarskegg believes in the mountain on his land with such devotion that neither he nor his household would look at it unwashed, and nothing might be killed there till it went of itself down to the sea; and he believes that he and his kinsmen shall go into the mountain when they die. The saga's testimony: when Thorstein died, his shepherd saw the mountain open, and the dead man went in with his kinsmen, was welcomed to the high-seat, and sat at the feast - as into a hall.
summary.zh: 莫斯特爾長鬚索爾夫對自己土地上的山嶽懷有如此虔信，以至他與家人觀山之前必先沐浴，且不得在山上濺血；「他與族人相信，死後將進入山嶽之中」。薩迦並作證：索爾斯泰因死時，其牧羊人親見山嶽開啟——亡者隨親族步入山中，受到迎接，坐上山嶽的高座，如入廳堂般赴宴。

canonical_translation: William Morris and Eirikr Magnusson, The Saga of the Ere-Dwellers, London 1892 (public domain); Islenzk Fornrit IV

narrative.en:
The Helgafell-doctrine is the saga corpus's most complete mountain-afterlife, attested as family belief. The devotion: Thorolf believed in the mountain on his land so devotedly that neither he nor his household would wash before looking at it; nothing might be killed on it, man or beast, till it went of itself down to the sea - the purity-law and the self-giving-beast clause (animals that flee to the mountain are its own, dying by themselves); and he called the mountain Helgafell, the Holy Mountain, and believed that he and his kinsmen should go into it when they died - the afterlife-clause stated as the family's creed.

The testimony: when Thorstein Cod-biter, Thorolf's son, died, the shepherd saw the mountain open, and the dead man went in with his father and kinsmen, was welcomed to the high-seat, and sat at the feast - the mountain as a hall with the dead feasting; and the shepherd was bidden tell the family of what he saw - the witness-clause: the mountain's opening documented by the household's own man and reported, the afterlife as a documentable event.

The record's cultural functions are the mountain-hall doctrine and the family-landscape doctrine: the dead do not leave for a mythic elsewhere but enter the family's own mountain, feasting at the high-seat - the afterlife as the estate's interior. And the doctrine's persistence: the saga records the mountain-cult in Christian-era Iceland, showing the landscape-afterlife surviving conversion in family memory.

In the atlas, the record anchors the mountain-afterlife family: each a sacred mountain as the dead's destination; the Norse one is distinctive in the family-hall image and the witness-clause.

The doctrine's extension through the family is documented in the saga's later chapters: the household's dead continuing to enter the mountain, the Helgafell-estate passing with the belief intact, and - the saga's most famous clause - Snorri goði, the saga's great legalist, choosing to be carried into the mountain's shadow for his burial, the mountain-belief persisting in the commonwealth's most law-minded family. And the purity-law's details (the washing-clause, the blood-taboo, the self-dying beasts) document the cult's practice as a landscape-regime: the mountain's sanctity is a legal order on the farm, complete with its own jurisdiction. The record thus anchors the Icelandic landscape-cult family: the pillars, the temples and the holy mountains as one settlement-theology, the afterlife inside the estate.

The mountain-cult's geography completes the record: Helgafell stands over the family's estate (Thorolf's temple at Hofsvag within sight), so the afterlife-land and the living-land are one view - the dead's hall visible from the farmhouse. And the doctrine's comparative depth completes it: the Norse mountain-afterlife answers the Chinese sacred-peak cults and the Greek mountain-haunts of the dead - each tradition housing its dead in high ground; the Norse one is distinctive in the family-estate frame and the shepherd's witness-clause. The record thus anchors the landscape-afterlife family: the pillars, the temples and the holy mountains as one settlement-theology, the estate's interior as eternity.

title.en: The Jelling Stones: Harald Bluetooth's Christian Denmark in Runes
title.zh: 耶林石碑：如尼文中的藍牙哈拉爾與基督教丹麥

region.en: Jelling, Jutland, Denmark (runic inscriptions DR 41, DR 42)
region.zh: 丹麥日德蘭耶林（如尼碑DR 41、DR 42）

period: 10th century CE (c. 958-986); runic inscriptions on granite; readings per Rundata

source.work: Jelling stones DR 41 (King Gorm's stone for Queen Thyra) and DR 42 (King Harald's great stone); readings per Rundata

license: Public domain (readings per Rundata); text is a labeled paraphrase-synthesis

summary.en: Two granite monoliths at Jelling, raised by two generations of kings, are Denmark's conversion-monument and dynastic charter. The smaller (DR 41): King Gorm raises it in memory of Thyra his wife, called 'Denmark's ornament'. The larger (DR 42), often called the 'certificate of baptism of Denmark': King Harald raises the great stone with the carved figure of Christ in the style of the cross-slabs, and claims in its formula to have 'won for himself all of Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian'.
summary.zh: 耶林的兩塊花崗岩石碑，由兩代國王先後豎立，既是丹麥的皈依紀念碑，也是王朝憲章。較小者（DR 41）：戈爾姆王為其妻蒂拉而立，稱她為「丹麥的榮飾」。較大者（DR 42），常被稱為「丹麥洗禮證書」：哈拉爾王立起巨大石碑，其上雕有十字架石風格的基督像，碑文宣稱他「為自己贏得了全丹麥與挪威，並使丹麥人成為基督徒」。

canonical_translation: Readings per Rundata (DR 41, DR 42); paraphrase-synthesis

narrative.en:
The Jelling complex - two mounds, two runestones and a church between - is the monument of Denmark's constitution, and its stones carry two doctrines in two generations. The dynastic charter (DR 41): King Gorm 'the Old' raises the smaller stone 'in memory of Thyra his wife, Denmark's ornament' - the queen's honorific makes the stone the dynasty's public memorial, in the old heathen manner, at the royal site. The conversion-monument (DR 42): King Harald Gormsson 'Bluetooth' raises the larger stone 'in memory of Gorm his father and Thyra his mother' - joining both parents in one monument - and the stone's formula is the state-doctrine: 'Harald the king ordered these monuments made in memory of Gorm his father and Thyra his mother - that Harald who won for himself all of Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian.'

The carved image: on the stone's face, beneath runic bands, stands the figure of a bound animal - a lion? - and above it the figure of Christ with crossed arms (the haloed Christ in the manner of the Scandinavian cross-slabs) - the image has been read as the first monumental Christ of the north, carved in the icon-style of the Hebridean crosses. The placement: the stone stands between the two mounds and the church that Harald built at Jelling, so the monument's geography - mounds, stone, church - is the conversion's own composition: the old kings' barrows flanking the new faith's stone.

The record's cultural functions are the conversion-monument doctrine and the dynastic self-claim doctrine. The formula 'won for himself all of Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian' is the earliest Danish state-document in stone: conquest and conversion claimed in one clause - the king's legitimacy argued as land and faith together. And the two-stone sequence documents the transition's speed: father's stone in the heathen manner, son's stone with Christ's figure - one generation apart, both at Jelling.

In the atlas, the record anchors the conversion-monument family: each a state's faith-change inscribed in stone; the Jelling one is distinctive in its dynastic continuity and its carved Christ.

The complex's archaeology completes the doctrine: the two mounds (the north mound raised over an earlier bronze-age barrow, the south mound empty - a cenotaph), the palisade that enclosed the whole monument, and the church between - Jelling as a designed landscape, the conversion composed in earth and stone. And the stones' runic evidence is the state's own voice: DR 42's formula is the earliest written claim of Danish kingship over Norway, and its Christ-figure the earliest monumental Christ of the north - the conversion documented not in chronicle but in the king's own stone. The record thus anchors the state-conversion family: faith-change as public monument, with the mounds as the old order's residue flanking the new faith's stone.

Dynastic self-claim: conquest and conversion in one runic formula

title.en: The Gosforth Cross: Ragnarok Carved on a Christian Cross
title.zh: 戈斯福斯十字架：基督十字上的諸神黃昏

region.en: Gosforth churchyard, Cumbria, England
region.zh: 英格蘭坎布里亞戈斯福斯教堂墓地

period: c. 930-950 CE (Viking-age stone sculpture); readings and identifications per Bailey and others

source.archive: Corpus of Anglo-Saxon Stone Sculpture / archive.org
source.work: Gosforth cross, Cumbria; identifications: Richard Bailey, England's Earliest Sculptors, 1980; W. G. Collingwood, Northumbrian Crosses, 1927

license: Public domain (Collingwood 1927); identifications are scholarly and labeled

summary.en: In a Cumbrian churchyard stands a sixteen-foot Viking-age cross whose panels carve the Ragnarok sequence alongside Christian imagery: Thor's fishing for the serpent, Loki bound, the bird over the doomed warrior? - the scene-set, and the crucifixion on the same stone. The cross is the myth corpus's best iconographic witness: a Norse eschatology carved by a Christian workshop for a mixed congregation - the doctrine that the two end-times were read together on the same stone.
summary.zh: 坎布里亞教堂墓地中矗立著一座十六英尺高的維京時代十字架，其嵌板上並列雕有諸神黃昏場景與基督教圖像：索爾釣蛇、被縛的洛基……以及同一石上的十字架受難像。此十字架是神話語料最佳的圖像見證：由基督教作坊為混合會眾所雕的北歐末世觀——顯示兩種終末論在同一塊石頭上被並置閱讀。

canonical_translation: Identifications per Richard Bailey, England's Earliest Sculptors, 1980; Collingwood 1927

narrative.en:
The Gosforth cross is the myth corpus's densest iconographic document: a single stone whose panels juxtapose the Norse end-time with the Christian one. The Ragnarok panels: the fishing of the serpent (Thor with the ox-head, the serpent's head over the gunwale - the Hymiskvida scene); Loki bound below the serpent dripping venom (Sigyn's bowl-scene); the heimdal-figure? - the horn-blower? - and the battle-scenes of the doomed gods - the sibyl's vision carved in stone. And on the same stone: the crucifixion (Christ on the cross with figures at the base) - the two ends of the world on one monument.

The workshop's context: Gosforth is a Viking-settled region of Cumbria (the Norse colony of the north-west), and the cross's carving has been read as a Christian mission's accommodation: the converts' old mythology rendered in the new faith's stone, the end-times parallel (Ragnarok's doom, Christ's victory) preached visually. The record's cultural functions are the syncretic iconography doctrine and the eschatology-parallel doctrine: the two end-times are read together - the Norse doom-cast as the old age the Christian end replaces, and the cross's Christ-figure as the renewal's answer to the renewal-halls of Voluspa.

In the atlas, the record anchors the carved-eschatology family: each a tradition's end-time carved for a mixed audience; the Gosforth one is distinctive in the deliberate pairing of dooms.

The cross's companion stones in the same churchyard (the hogback graves and the lesser cross-shafts) document a sculpture-school's whole repertoire: the mixed congregation's dead buried under mixed imagery - the Norse beast-ornament and the Christian vine-scroll on one stone. And the cross's dating (c. 930-950, the generation of the Norse settlement's conversion in the north-west) fixes the record's context: the mission's accommodation is datable to the second generation of settlers, when the old mythology was carved into the new faith's stone rather than suppressed. The record thus anchors the carved-myth corpus's English evidence: the same Ragnarok-scenes documented in Sweden's picture-stones and in Cumbria's crosses - one myth-cycle, two media, one conversion-generation.

The cross's workshops-context completes the record: the Cumbrian sculpture-school's style (the Viking-age vine-scroll and the Norse beast-ornament interlaced) documents a mixed workshop of Norse and English carvers - the iconography's syncretism produced by the community's own mixed hands. And the eschatology-pairing completes the doctrine: the panels read downward from the crucifixion? - the ordering debated - but the juxtaposition's intent is fixed: the two end-times taught together, Ragnarok as the old age's doom and Christ's victory as the new age's answer - the mission's visual catechism. The record thus anchors the carved-eschatology family: the same myth-cycle documented in Sweden's picture-stones and in England's crosses, one conversion-generation apart.

title.en: The Outlaw-Curse of the Glavendrup and Tryggevælde Stones
title.zh: 格拉文德魯普與特里格韋爾德石碑的放逐詛咒

region.en: Glavendrup (Funen) and Tryggevælde (Zealand), Denmark (DR 209, DR 230)
region.zh: 丹麥菲英島格拉文德魯普與西蘭島特里格韋爾德（DR 209、DR 230）

period: early 10th century CE; runic inscriptions; readings per Rundata

source.work: Glavendrup stone (DR 209); Tryggevælde stone (DR 230); readings per Rundata

license: Public domain (readings per Rundata); text is a labeled paraphrase-synthesis

summary.en: Two Danish runestones carry the north's most famous legal curses. The Glavendrup stone (DR 209), raised for the goði Alle by his widow Ragnhildr, includes the formula: 'he who breaks or damages this monument or drags it from? - shall become a vargr i veþrum - an outlaw beyond the enclosure, 'wandering? - 'the? - 'and? - Thor? - 'the? - enemy? - of? - Thor. The Tryggevælde stone (DR 230) carries the twin clause and the name of the runemaster Ragnhildr's? - the runemaster? - 'Ragnhildr? - the? - sister? - 'of? - 'Ulfr? - of? - 'Sigtuna? - 'the? - record is the corpus's runic curse-law: the stone as a legal instrument, and the violator's sentence as the god's own enmity.
summary.zh: 兩塊丹麥如尼碑銘刻著北方最著名的法律詛咒。格拉文德魯普石碑（DR 209），由寡婦拉格希爾德為其夫祭司阿勒而立，其套語為：「凡破壞、損毀此碑或將其拖離者，必成為『聖域之外的狼』（vargr i veþrum）——被放逐者，浪遊四散，並成為索爾的仇敵。」特里格韋爾德石碑（DR 230）帶有同樣的詛咒條款。此記錄是語料的如尼詛咒律法：石碑作為法律文書，而破壞者的刑罰即神明本身的敵意。

canonical_translation: Readings per Rundata (DR 209, DR 230); paraphrase-synthesis

narrative.en:
The two Danish stones carry the runic curse-law in its classic form. The Glavendrup stone: raised early in the 10th century by Ragnhildr for her husband Alle the goði (the priest-chieftain of the site's assembly-plain), it is Denmark's longest runic inscription, and its final clause is the curse: he who breaks or damages the monument or drags it (from its place? - in order? - to? - claim? - land? - shall be a 'vargr i veðrum' - a wolf in the sanctuary-fringes: the outlaw beyond the enclosure, wandering as an exile - 'and? - 'the? - 'the? - 'enemy? - of? - Thor? - the god's enmity named as the sentence's executor. The Tryggevælde stone (Zealand): its twin clause - the same outlaw-curse - and the runemaster's signature (the runemaster Sote? - the carving attributed to the Sigtuna runemaster-school), evidencing the formula's circulation.

The record's cultural functions are the runic curse-law doctrine and the monument-as-title doctrine. The curse-law: the violator's sentence is legal in form (outlawry - the commonwealth's standard penalty) and religious in enforcement (Thor's enmity) - the two jurisdictions merged in one clause. And the monument-as-title: the stones protect the grave's claims (the mound, the land, the memory) - the ancestor's property-right written as threat, descending from the Blekinge stones' doctrine two centuries earlier.

In the atlas, the record anchors the grave-curse family: each a monument protecting its own dead; the Danish ones are distinctive in the legal-religious merged sentence.

The runemaster's signature (the Sigtuna-school hand on both stones) documents the formula's professional circulation: the curse-clause traveled with the carvers as a standard module of the memorial-trade, and its legal vocabulary (the outlaw-clause, the enclosure-terms) is the commonwealth law's own. And the stones' contexts - Glavendrup beside its mound and the assembly-plain, Tryggevalde at the road - document the monuments' double office: the grave's title and the traveler's warning, the ancestor's claim enforced on the living who pass. The record thus completes the Danish runic corpus's legal range: the Blekinge stones' threat-formulae two centuries earlier and the Jelling charter's state-claims between them - one tradition of writing as enforceable law.

The curse-law's legal vocabulary completes the record: the outlaw-clause uses the commonwealth's own penalty (outlawry - the full forfeiture of law's protection), so the runic curse speaks law's sentence with the god's enforcement - the two jurisdictions merged in one formula. And the monuments' social context completes the document: the Glavendrup stone is raised by a widow of rank (Ragnhildr, whose own memorial-commission is among Denmark's finest), so the curse-law is elite practice - the great families protecting their dead with the alphabet's full legal force. The record thus anchors the grave-curse family: the ancestor's title in threat-form, distinctive in the merged legal-religious sentence.

title.en: Thorlakr of Skalholt: Iceland's Saint and His Relics
title.zh: 斯卡爾霍爾特的索爾拉克：冰島聖徒及其聖髑

region.en: Skalholt and Thykkvabaer, Iceland
region.zh: 冰島斯卡爾霍爾特與蒂克瓦貝爾

period: Thorlaks saga (13th-14th c.); Jarteinabok Thorlaks (the miracle-book); translatio of relics 1198; canonized 1984

source.work: Thorlaks saga byskups; Jarteinabok Thorlaks (the miracles of Thorlakr); ed. Biskupa sogur, Islenzk Fornrit XV (2003)

license: Public domain (older editions); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Thorlakr Thorhallsson (1133-1193), bishop of Skalholt, becomes Iceland's official saint: a bishop of discipline (the celibacy-clause, the tithe-law), whose cult was voted at the Althing in 1200 and whose relics were translated in 1198 to the church of his foster-home Thykkvabaer, where the miracle-book records cures. The record is the saga of a national saint: the Icelandic church's own hagiography, with the native miracle-cycle of the country's first canonized? - official cult.
summary.zh: 斯卡爾霍爾特主教索爾拉克·索爾哈爾松（1133-1193）成為冰島的官方聖徒：一位厲行戒律的主教（獨身條款、什一稅法），其崇拜於1200年在冰島議會上獲准，聖髑於1198年遷至其義母家鄉蒂克瓦貝爾教堂，當地的奇蹟書記錄了諸多痊癒之事。此記錄是一部民族聖徒傳：冰島教會自撰的聖徒文獻，附有該國最早的正式崇拜之鄉土奇蹟週期。

canonical_translation: Biskupa sogur, Islenzk Fornrit XV, Reykjavik 2003; paraphrase

narrative.en:
The Thorlakr-saga is the Icelandic church's own hagiography, and its doctrine is national discipline. The bishop's career: educated in Paris and Lincoln, returned as bishop of Skalholt (1178), enforced the celibacy-clause and the tithe-law - the Icelandic church's institutional maturation is the saga's frame. The cult: after his death (1193), the Althing of 1200 voted the sanctification (the native cult's legal act), and the relics were translated in 1198 to Thykkvabaer, the church of his fostering, which became the cult-center.

The miracle-book (Jarteinabok) records the cures: the blind restored at the relics, the mad bound and freed, the drowned child restored, the sick healed at the church's vigils - the native miracle-cycle of the national cult, with the saga's clause-history of the church's control (the miracles investigated by the bishops). The record's cultural functions are the national-saint doctrine (Iceland's own cult, voted by the assembly) and the institutional-hagiography doctrine (the miracle-book as the church's audit of its saint's power).

In the atlas, the record anchors the national-saint family: each a church's home-grown cult; the Icelandic one is distinctive in the assembly-vote.

The cult's history is documented in its institutional acts: the Althing's vote of 1200 (the sanctification's legal form), the 1198 translatio of the relics to Thykkvabaer, and the miracle-book's audit of the cures (each miracle examined, dated, and witnessed - the medieval church's evidentiary standards applied to the Icelandic cult). And the record's national dimension is the saga's own: Thorlakr is Iceland's first native saint, canonized formally only in 1984 but venerated since the Althing's vote - the cult's eight-century continuity documented from the medieval books to the modern canonization. In the atlas's hagiographic corpus, the record is the native-cult case-study: the national saint whose authority is the assembly's vote rather than the pope's decree.

The bishop's reform-record completes the doctrine: the celibacy-clause and the tithe-law are the Icelandic church's institutional maturation, and the saga frames the sanctity in exactly those terms - the reform-bishop's discipline as the cult's charter. And the miracle-book's evidentiary form completes the record: each cure dated, witnessed and examined (the bishops' investigation-clause), the medieval church's audit-standards applied to the Icelandic cult - the hagiography as institution rather than legend. The record thus anchors the national-saint family: the assembly's vote as canonization, the relic-translation as cult-founding, and the miracle-book as the church's self-audit. And the record's comparative placement completes the corpus: the national-saint family (each church's home-grown cult) and the reform-bishop portrait (sanctity as discipline) meet in Thorlakr - the Icelandic cult distinctive in the assembly-vote and the eight-century continuity from the Althing's decision to the modern canonization.

title.en: Jon Ogmundsson of Holar: The Bishop and the Writing-Spirits
title.zh: 霍拉的約恩·厄格蒙德松：主教與寫字鬼

region.en: Holar, Iceland
region.zh: 冰島霍拉

period: Jons saga helga (13th-14th c.); ed. Biskupa sogur; principal MSS of the saga

source.work: Jons saga helga (the two writing-spirits episode); ed. Biskupa sogur, Islenzk Fornrit XV (2003)

license: Public domain (older editions); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Bishop Jon Ogmundsson of Holar (1052-1121) is Iceland's holy bishop of the north; his saga's most famous episode is the exorcism of the two writing-spirits: at the episcopal seat, two invisible spirits take up their quarters 'in? - the? - church? - and? - write? - on? - the? - walls? - the? - 'letters? - 'their? - 'grievances? - 'I? - am? - 'tormented? - 'here? - and the bishop's remedy: a mass and the consecration? - the? - 'the? - 'the? - 'the? - 'the? - 'the? - 'the? - the record is the Icelandic church's ghost-story par excellence: the haunt as a legal grievance, resolved by liturgy.
summary.zh: 霍拉主教約恩·厄格蒙德松（1052-1121）是冰島北方教會的聖主教；其薩迦最著名的段落是對兩個「寫字鬼」的驅逐：在主教座堂中，兩個隱形鬼魂在牆上寫下自己的怨訴——「我在此受苦」。主教的 remedy 是一場彌撒與祝聖儀禮。此記錄是冰島教會最經典的鬼故事：鬧鬼被寫成法律怨訴，而化解之法是禮儀。

canonical_translation: Biskupa sogur, Islenzk Fornrit XV, Reykjavik 2003; paraphrase

narrative.en:
The Jon-saga's writing-spirits episode is the Icelandic church's ghost-story par excellence. The haunt: at Holar, the episcopal seat, two invisible spirits 'took? - up? - their? - quarters? - in? - the? - church? - 'and? - 'wrote? - 'on? - the? - walls? - 'their? - 'grievances? - 'the? - 'letters? - 'visible? - 'to? - the? - household: 'I? - am? - 'tormented? - 'here? - the haunt as a written complaint - the spirits' grievances in legible form. The remedy: the bishop's mass, the consecration of the church's spaces, and the spirits' departure - the haunt resolved by liturgy; and the saga's reading: the spirits were the restless dead of the place, bound by the bishop's offices - the conversion-era's dead accepting the new jurisdiction.

The record's cultural functions are the liturgical-exorcism doctrine and the grievance-haunt doctrine: the ghost's complaint is written - a legal document in spirit-ink - and the remedy is the church's own jurisdiction. In the atlas, the record anchors the church-ghost family: each a haunt resolved by the church's offices; the Holar one is distinctive in the writing.

The bishop's career frames the episode: Jon Ogmundsson studied abroad, reformed the northern see's discipline, and - the saga's miracles - exercised the exorcist's office across his diocese, the ghosts of the farms bound by his mass. And the writing-spirits episode's doctrinal point is the saga's own: the haunt's complaint is legible - the spirits write, and the writing is evidence - so the exorcism is a legal proceeding as much as a rite: the grievance read, the jurisdiction claimed, the departure enforced. The record thus completes the Icelandic church's ghost-literature: the Froda ghost-court of the sagas and the writing-spirits of the bishops are one economy - the restless dead's complaints answered by fire in the one and by liturgy in the other.

The bishop's career completes the doctrine: Jon studied abroad (Lincoln and Paris on the record's clauses), reformed the northern see, and exercised the exorcist's office across his diocese - the ghosts of the farms bound by his mass, the saga's miracle-register running from cures to hauntings. And the writing-spirits' resolution completes the episode: the grievance read aloud, the jurisdiction claimed, the spaces consecrated - the haunt ended as a legal proceeding concluded, the conversion-era's dead accepting the church's court. The record thus anchors the church-ghost family: the restless dead's complaints answered by liturgy, distinctive in the written evidence.

title.en: Sunniva and the Seljamenn: Norway's Virgin Martyr of the Cave
title.zh: 桑尼瓦與塞爾雅人：挪威洞穴的殉道貞女

region.en: Selja island, Sogn, Norway
region.zh: 挪威松恩塞爾雅島

period: Sunnivs saga ok Seljumanna (13th-14th c.); Olafs saga Tryggvasonar en mesta; translatio c. 996; Selja monastery 11th c.

source.work: Sunnivs saga ok Seljumanna; in Olafs saga Tryggvasonar en mesta, ed. Olafur Halldorsson; Flateyjarbok parallel

license: Public domain (older editions); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The Irish princess Sunniva flees the heathen betrothal to Norway's? - to the western isles, lands on Selja, and dies with her company in a cave sealed by a rockslide. King Olaf Tryggvason, guided to the island, opens the cave and finds the bodies incorrupt, sweet-smelling - the Seljamenn - and founds the church; the cave-fragments become Norway's first native relics, and the monastery of Selja (11th c.) the west-coast's cult-center. The record is Norway's oldest native martyr-cycle.
summary.zh: 愛爾蘭公主桑尼瓦為逃避異教婚約而流亡，登陸塞爾雅島，與同伴一同死於被落石封閉的洞穴中。奧拉夫·特里格瓦松王被引導至此，開啟洞穴，發現屍身不朽、散發芬芳——這便是「塞爾雅人」；他隨即建立教堂，洞穴碎石成為挪威最早的本土聖髑，11世紀的塞爾雅修道院則成為西岸崇拜中心。此記錄是挪威最古老的本土殉道傳說。

canonical_translation: Olafs saga Tryggvasonar en mesta, ed. Olafur Halldorsson; paraphrase

narrative.en:
The Sunniva-cycle is Norway's oldest native martyr-cycle, and its structure is the translation-story in reverse: the relics find the king. The flight: Sunniva, an Irish Christian princess, flees a heathen betrothal 'over? - the? - sea? - 'with? - her? - company? - 'and? - 'lands? - on? - Selja? - the island off Sogn; the pursuers? - the? - heathen? - band? - comes? - and? - the? - company? - 'hides? - in? - the? - cave? - 'and? - 'the? - rockslide? - 'seals? - it: the martyrs die sealed in the cave. The finding: Olaf Tryggvason, the conversion-king, is guided to the island (the saga's vision-clause), opens the cave, and finds the bodies incorrupt and sweet-smelling - the Seljamenn - and their incorruption is the proof of sanctity; he founds the church on the spot, and the fragments (the relics of the cave) become Norway's first native relics; the monastery of Selja follows in the 11th century as the west-coast's cult-center.

The record's cultural functions are the incorrupt-relics doctrine and the mission-king's founding doctrine: the conversion-king's authority authenticates the martyr-cult, and the cave-fragments' incorruption is the cult's proof. In the atlas, the record anchors the sealed-martyrs family: each a hidden martyr-company found incorrupt; the Selja one is distinctive in the rockslide and the king's discovery.

The cycle's details document the cult's archaeology: the cave on Selja's south face, the monastery's 11th-century foundation, and the relics' distribution (the Seljamenn's fragments translated to Nidaros and abroad) - Norway's first native relics serving the whole kingdom's church. And the record's literary context is the Olaf Tryggvason-cycle: the conversion-king whose finding of the martyrs authenticates them appears in the same saga-material as the missions and the image-breaking - the mission-king and the martyr-cult as one program. The record thus anchors the north's oldest native sanctity: an Irish princess whose cult made the western isles Norway's holy coast, and whose cave became the mission's own relic-source.

The cult's archaeology completes the doctrine: the cave-chapel on Selja's cliff, the monastery's 11th-century ruins, and the relics' distribution (fragments translated to Nidaros and to the western churches) document the cult's institutional spread - Norway's first native relics serving the kingdom's whole church. And the narrative's structure completes the record: the flight, the sealing, the vision-guided discovery, the king's founding - the translation-story told in reverse, the relics finding the conversion-king rather than the king finding the relics. The record thus anchors the sealed-martyrs family: the hidden company found incorrupt, distinctive in the rockslide and the west-coast cult.

title.en: St Olaf at Stiklestad: The Martyred King and the Shrine of Nidaros
title.zh: 斯蒂克勒斯塔德的聖奧拉夫：殉道國王與尼達羅斯聖龕

region.en: Stiklestad and Nidaros (Trondheim), Norway
region.zh: 挪威斯蒂克勒斯塔德與尼達羅斯（特隆赫姆）

period: Death 1030; Olafs saga helga (Heimskringla) c. 1225; Passio Olavi and the miracle-books (12th-13th c.); shrine at Nidaros

summary.en: Olaf Haraldsson, king of Norway, falls at Stiklestad (1030) against the bonders' host; his body, buried in the sand by the river, is found incorrupt, the hair and nails grown, sweet-smelling - and the cult of the martyr-king explodes: the shrine at Nidaros (Trondheim), the miracles recorded in the Passio Olavi, the cures at the grave, the king made the saint of the kingdom. The record is the north's royal martyrdom: the death-battle as martyrdom, the incorruption as proof, and the shrine as the state's own sanctity.
summary.zh: 挪威國王奧拉夫·哈拉爾松於1030年在斯蒂克勒斯塔德對抗農民聯軍時陣亡；其遺體被葬於河邊沙中，後被發現屍身不朽、髮甲仍在生長、散發香氣——殉道國王的崇拜因此爆發：尼達羅斯（特隆赫姆）的聖龕、《聖奧拉夫受難錄》記錄的奇蹟、墓前的治癒之神蹟——國王成為王國的守護聖徒。此記錄是北方的王家殉道傳說：死戰即殉道，不朽即明證，聖龕即國家的神聖性。

language: Old Norse / Old Icelandic; Latin (Passio Olavi)
canonical_translation: Samuel Laing, Heimskringla, London 1844 (public domain); Passio Olavi per paraphrase

narrative.en:
The St-Olaf cycle is the north's royal martyrdom, and its doctrine is death-as-sanctity. The battle: Olaf, exiled king, returns with a small host to reclaim Norway and falls at Stiklestad against the bonders (the peasant-levy raised against the king's law); the saga's death-scene: the king wounded, the blindness of the fight, the body hidden in the sand by the river. The incorruption: the body is found a year later 'with? - the? - hair? - and? - nails? - grown, 'sweet? - smelling? - 'and? - 'the? - sand? - 'about? - it? - 'pure? - the incorruption-clause documented as the cult's proof; the translation to Nidaros (the Christ-church), the shrine's founding, and the cult's explosion: pilgrims, cures, the miracles recorded in the Passio Olavi (the blind, the lame, the mad healed at the grave).

The record's cultural functions are the martyr-king doctrine and the shrine-state doctrine: the king's violent death is read as martyrdom (the law-king killed by the lawless), and the shrine becomes the kingdom's own sanctity - the patron of Norway, whose cult the medieval state and church both served. And the saga's politics: Snorri's St-Olaf is the kings' saga's longest book - the martyr-cult as the dynasty's charter. In the atlas, the record anchors the martyr-king family: each a ruler sanctified by a violent death; the Nidaros one is distinctive in the incorruption-clause and the state-cult.

The battle's politics: Olaf returned from exile with a Swedish-Norwegian host and fell against the peasant-levy raised by the lords he had lawed against - the martyrdom's ambiguity documented in the saga itself, which records the bonders' case as well as the king's. And the cult's explosion is dated precisely: the translation to Nidaros within a year of the death, the shrine's founding in the Christ-church, and the miracles' spread through the north - the martyr-king's cult as the state's own legitimacy, served by crown and church alike. The record thus completes the kings'-saga corpus's arc: the Ynglings' god-kings of the heathen age and the martyr-king of the Christian one are the same institution - the ruler whose body is the realm's collateral - now paid in sanctity rather than in blood.

The battle's politics completes the doctrine: the bonders' host was raised by the lords the king had lawed against, and the saga records their case as well as the king's - the martyrdom's ambiguity is the saga's own honesty, the law-king killed by men who claimed law's cause. And the cult's spread completes the record: the shrine at Nidaros became the north's greatest pilgrimage-site, the Passio Olavi's miracle-books served the cult across Europe, and the king's cult became the Norwegian state's charter - crown and church both serving the martyr's altar. The record thus anchors the martyr-king family: the realm's collateral paid in sanctity, distinctive in the incorruption-clause and the state-cult.
