title.en: Yayati's Bargain with Old Age
title.zh: 耶耶提與衰老的交易

region.en: Pratishthana on the Ganges, Yayati's capital (symbolic pin near Prayagraj)
region.zh: 恆河畔耶耶提都城缽哩沙陀那（象徵性定位近般遮羅闍）

period: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Sharmishtha Upaparva), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Adi Parva, the story of Yayati

summary.en: Cursed by his father-in-law to age before his time, the emperor Yayati begs each of his sons to trade him their youth. Four sons of Devayani refuse; his youngest, born of the servant Sharmishtha, agrees - and Yayati spends a thousand years of borrowed youth chasing pleasure, only to discover that desire is never satisfied by feeding it. He returns the youth, renounces the throne, and goes into the forest.
summary.zh: 耶耶提遭岳父之詛提前衰老，乞求諸子與之交易青春。德瓦亞尼所生四子皆拒；侍女沙爾蜜什陀所生之幼子應允——耶耶提以借來的千年青春追逐歡樂，終悟欲望愈餵愈飽不得。他歸還青春、放棄王位、入林而去。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (epic recitation; katha retellings). Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Devayani, daughter of the sage Shukra, married King Yayati in anger at the princess Sharmishtha; Sharmishtha followed her as a servant and bore Yayati secret sons. When Shukra learned of the union, his curse fell: Yayati would pass into old age, untimely, deprived of his pleasures in the prime of life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Yayati episode (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 仙人舒克拉之女提婆衍尼因對公主莎米什塔懷怒，而嫁與國王耶亞提；莎米什塔以侍女身分隨她而去，並為耶亞提生下私生子。舒克拉得知此事後，其詛咒降下：耶亞提將未老先衰，於壯年之際被剝奪一切享樂。

passages.text: Old age came upon the emperor like a guest he could not turn away. He went to his sons, each in turn: take my old age upon you, he said, and give me your youth, that I may enjoy the world a while longer and then hand it back. Four sons of Devayani refused - who would take a spent man's years for their own spring? Only Puru, the youngest, son of the servant, said: take it, father; I will bear your age and stand by your word.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Yayati episode (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 老年如一位無法辭退的客人，降臨於這位帝王身上。他依次走到每個兒子面前，說道：請承受我的老年，把你的青春給我，讓我再享樂世間一段時日，然後再歸還。提婆衍尼的四個兒子都拒絕了——誰願以自己之青春年華，換取一個衰朽之人的殘年？唯有最小的兒子布魯，即侍女之子，說道：父親，請拿去；我願承受您的老年，並守您的諾言。

passages.text: With Puru's youth upon him Yayati resumed the pleasures of the senses - the gardens, the women, the hunts, the feasts - a thousand years of it, and every appetite only grew the more it was fed. At last he understood: desire is like fire; it is never satisfied by fuel. 'There is no end to desire,' he said; 'he who feeds it starves by feeding.' He gave Puru back his youth, declared Puru heir - disinheriting the elder line - and went to the forest with nothing, eating leaves, desiring nothing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Yayati episode (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有了布魯的青春加身，耶亞提重又沉溺於感官之樂——園林、美人、狩獵、宴飲——如此過了千年，而每一種慾望越是餵養，便越是增長。終於他領悟了：慾望如火，燃料永不能使其滿足。「慾望無有止境，」他說；「餵養它的人，正因餵養而飢餓。」他將青春歸還布魯，立布魯為繼承人——廢黜了長子一系——然後一無所有地走入森林，食葉維生，無所欲求。

canonical_translation: Kisari Mohan Ganguli, The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, 1883-96 (public domain); modern: J. A. B. van Buitenen, The Mahabharata, vol. 1, University of Chicago Press, 1973

narrative.en:
The story of Yayati, told in the Adi Parva as part of the genealogy of kings, is the Mahabharata's sharpest fable about desire - and the charter myth of the Puru dynasty, the line from which the epic's own Bharata kings descend.

The tangle begins in a household war. Devayani, daughter of the preceptor Shukra, is humiliated by the Asura princess Sharmishtha and thrown into a well; Yayati rescues her; she marries him on condition that Sharmishtha be given to her as a servant. But Sharmishtha, in the palace as a maid, is soon secretly Yayati's mistress too, and bears him sons. When Shukra learns of it, his curse is precise and domestic: Yayati shall pass into untimely old age, cheated of his pleasures at their height.

The curse is also the experiment. Old age arrives, and Yayati - not yet done with the world - goes to his sons with the strangest request in the epic: give me your youth and carry my old age; I will enjoy the world a while and return what I borrow. The four sons of Devayani refuse, with the eldest speaking for them: what wise man would trade his springtime for another's winter? Only Puru, the youngest, son of the servant Sharmishtha - the unprivileged son - consents: 'take it, father; I will bear your age and stand by your word.'

So armed, Yayati re-enters the world's pleasures for a thousand years - the text lingers on the inventory: gardens, women, hunting, wine, festivity. And the experiment's result is the story's entire point: a thousand years of feeding desire leaves it hungrier, not quieter. Yayati's conclusion is spoken like a scientist closing his notebook: desire is a fire that no fuel satisfies; 'he who feeds it starves by feeding'; there is no end of wanting, only an end of the wanting man. He returns Puru's youth, makes Puru his heir - disinheriting the elder sons and founding the line of Puru that leads, in the epic's genealogy, to Bharata and to the Pandavas themselves - and walks into the forest owning nothing, 'desiring nothing, eating leaves and fruit'. The curse thus becomes a cure: the father-in-law's punishment delivers the hero to renunciation by the longest possible route.

Function: the story is recited as a teaching fable on craving (the epic's own frame commentary calls it the story of how even a thousand years of indulgence teaches only one sentence) and as a legitimation myth - the youngest servant-born son becomes the dynasty's founder because he alone paid his father's debt. In later retellings (Purana versions; Marathi and modern novel treatments, e.g. Vishnu Sakharam Khandekar's Yayati), the emphasis shifts between the erotic fable and the dynastic politics - the servant queen's line displacing the high-born one, a troubling undercurrent the epic leaves unresolved.
narrative.zh: 耶耶提的故事見於阿底篇王統之中，是摩訶婆羅多關於欲望最鋒利的寓言——也是補魯王朝的創建神話，史詩自身的婆羅多王族即出此系。家庭之戰開其端：仙人尸 訶之女德瓦亞尼受阿修羅公主沙爾蜜什陀之辱而墮井；耶耶提救之；她以沙爾蜜什陀為婢為條件嫁之。然沙爾蜜什陀居宮為婢，旋為耶耶提之秘密情人，生子數人。尸訶得知，其詛精確而家常：耶耶提將提前衰老，於歡樂正盛時被剝奪。詛咒亦即實驗。衰老降臨，耶耶提——未厭於世——向諸子提出史詩中最奇異的請求：予我青春而代我衰老；我將稍享世界而歸還所借。德瓦亞尼四子皆拒，長子代言：孰以己之春換他人之冬？唯侍女之子、最幼者補魯應允：『取之，父；我代父老，守父之言。』耶耶提遂攜補魯之青春重入感官之樂千年——經文細列清單：園林、婦女、田獵、酒宴——而實驗之果即故事全部之義：餵養欲望千年，欲望愈餵愈飢。耶耶提之結論如科學家合上筆記：欲望如火，燃料不能滿之；『餵它者因餵而餓』；欲無盡處，唯有欲者之盡。他歸還補魯之青春，立補魯為嗣——廢長支而建補魯之系，於史詩王統中直達婆羅多與般度諸子——且空手入林，『無所欲，食葉與果』。詛咒遂成療法：岳父之懲罰以最長之路將英雄送至出離。功能：此篇被誦為貪求之教寓言（史詩自註：縱千年之縱慾，所學僅一句），亦為正統神話——侍女所生之幼子因其獨償父債而成王朝之祖。後世重述（往世書；馬拉提語與現代小說，如坎德卡之《耶耶提》）於情欲寓言與王朝政治之間擺動——婢后之支取代嫡支，史詩留下未解的暗流。

functions: Teaching fable on desire: a thousand years of indulgence proves appetite unquenchable
Legitimation myth of the Puru-Bharata dynasty (the servant's son as founder)
Charter of renunciation as the end of the pleasure-path
Genealogical bridge from the gods' era to the epic's own royal line

variants.name: Vishnu Purana version
variants.summary: Condenses the epic telling into dynastic annals, keeping the youth-exchange and Puru's succession; the erotic frame is trimmed to genealogy.

variants.name: Khandekar's Yayati (Marathi, 1959)
variants.summary: Retells the myth from Sharmishtha's and Devayani's perspectives, expanding the women's interiority and making the curse a psychological tragedy rather than a fable.

variants.name: Katha retellings (Puranas and vernacular)
variants.summary: The story circulates as a stand-alone parable in Purana digests and oral katha, often with the moral stated explicitly: the man fed by all the world's pleasures died desiring.

primary_sources.citation: Critical edition, BORI Poona, Adi Parva; English: Ganguli 1883-96 (public domain), Adi Parva sections on Devayani, Sharmishtha and Yayati.

title.en: Savitri Follows Death and Wins Back Her Husband
title.zh: 薩維特里隨死神而奪回夫君

region.en: Forest hermitage of Salva (symbolic pin at Chitrakoot)
region.zh: 薩羅訶王流放之林居（象徵性定位於質多羅俱吒）

period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Pativrata Upaparva), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, the story of Savitri and Satyavan

summary.en: Princess Savitri chooses as husband the exiled, doomed Satyavan, despite the seer Narada's prophecy that he will die within a year. On the fated day she follows her husband into the forest and trails Yama himself as he takes Satyavan's soul; her unanswerable courtesy and argument win three boons - and the third is worded so that the fourth, unasked, is his life.
summary.zh: 薩維特里公主不顧那羅陀仙人「夫將於一年內死」之預言，選流放而命定之薩蒂凡為夫。劫日當天，她隨夫入林，並尾隨親自取走薩蒂凡魂魄的閻摩；她以無可辯駁的禮數與言辭赢得三項恩諾——而第三項措辭巧妙，使未出口的第四項成為丈夫之命。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: the story is ritually recited at Vat-Savitri Vrata (married women's fast). Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: King Ashvapati, childless, worshiped Savitri the sun-goddess with offerings; the goddess granted him a daughter, Savitri, radiant as the sun. When she was of marriageable age, her father sent her to choose - and she returned from the forests having fixed her heart on Satyavan, blind Dyumatsena's son, living in exile at a hermitage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Savitri episode (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 國王阿濕波提膝下無子，以祭品供奉太陽女神娑維德麗；女神賜他一女，名為娑維德麗，光輝如太陽。待她到了婚配之年，父親遣她自行擇婿——她從森林歸來時，已將心許給了薩提亞梵，即盲眼的鳩摩提舍那之子，正流放隱居於淨修林。

passages.text: Narada the seer was present, and he pronounced the doom: Satyavan is virtuous beyond all men, but he has one defect - he shall die within a year. The king begged his daughter to choose another; Savitri answered that she had chosen once, for once only, whether he lives one year or more - she has made her choice. The marriage was performed, and she went to the forest, serving her husband's blind parents in homespun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Savitri episode (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 仙人那羅陀在場，道出了那厄運：薩提亞梵德行超越眾人，卻有一項缺陷——他將在一年之內死去。國王懇求女兒另擇他人；娑維德麗答道，她既已選定一次，便只此一次，無論他活一年或更久——她已作出選擇。婚禮舉行之後，她前往森林，身著粗布，侍奉丈夫盲眼的雙親。

passages.text: She counted the days. Four days before the term, she began a vigil, standing without food; on the fated day she obtained leave and went with Satyavan to the forest to cut firewood. He felled a tree, grew faint, and lay with his head in her lap; then came a dark-crowned figure with a rope - Yama, Death himself - who drew Satyavan's soul, small as a thumb, and turned south, binding it for the city of the dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Savitri episode (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她數著日子。期限前四日，她開始守夜，不食而立；到了命定之日，她求得許可，與薩提亞梵同往森林砍柴。他伐倒一樹，漸覺昏眩，便躺下將頭枕在她膝上；隨後出現一個戴著黑冠、手持繩索的身影——正是死神閻摩——他抽出薩提亞梵如拇指般大小的靈魂，轉身向南，將其縛住，押往亡者之城。

passages.text: Savitri followed. Yama told her to go back; she kept walking, speaking of duty and of the merit of following. Moved by her discourse, he offered boons: eyes and kingdom for her blind father-in-law; a hundred sons for her father; a hundred sons for herself. He had granted too much: a hundred sons require a living husband. Yama, bound by his own word and outmatched in argument, cut the rope, gave back the soul, and said: your husband shall live. Satyavan woke as from sleep, and the family's fortunes reversed from that day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Savitri episode (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 薩維特里跟隨著他。閻摩叫她回去；她仍繼續走著，談論職責與跟隨的功德。他被她的言論所感動，便賜予恩惠：為她失明的公公賜予雙眼與王國；為她的父親賜予百子；為她自己賜予百子。他賜予得太多了：百子需要一個活著的丈夫。閻摩受自己話語的約束，又在辯論中落敗，便割斷繩索，歸還靈魂，說道：你的丈夫將活下去。薩提亞萬如從睡眠中醒來，一家人的命運從那天起便逆轉了。

canonical_translation: Kisari Mohan Ganguli, The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, 1883-96 (public domain); modern: S. K. Belvalkar studies; also Julia Leslie's work on the Savitri vrata

narrative.en:
The Savitri episode (Vana Parva, told by Markandeya to Yudhishthira as the story of the perfect wife, pativrata) is the Mahabharata's great love-against-death narrative, and one of the most ritually alive stories in Hinduism: it is recited every year at the Vat-Savitri vrata, the fast married women keep for their husbands' longevity.

The choice: Ashvapati, king of Madra, is childless; he worships the sun-goddess Savitri with disciplined offerings, and she grants him a daughter as radiant as her namesake. When the girl is grown, the king - following custom - sends her on a pilgrimage of self-choice (svayamvara) in a chariot with aged counselors. She travels sanctuaries and hermitages and returns with her heart fixed: on Satyavan, son of the blind exiled king Dyumatsena, living in forest poverty. He is beautiful, dutiful - and doomed.

The oracle: Narada, the celestial seer, happens to be present and delivers the prophecy that gives the story its clock: Satyavan is virtuous beyond all men, but he has one defect - he shall die within a year. The father begs; the daughter's answer is the pivot of the story and the ethic it teaches: 'I have chosen once, whether he lives long or briefly; having chosen, I choose no more.' Death in a year is a defect of fate, not of the man. The marriage is performed with the doom standing, and Savitri goes to the hermitage in homespun, serving her blind parents-in-law.

The vigil: Savitri counts the days inward. Four before the term she begins a standing fast; her father-in-law tries to dissuade her; she answers with theology - the vow is kept, and what will be is known to the wise. On the fated day she obtains leave to go with her husband into the forest. He cuts firewood, faints, and lies with his head in her lap. Then she sees him: a dark-crowned figure carrying a rope, standing as if he owns the wood. It is Yama, and he draws Satyavan's soul - small as a thumb-length - binds it, and turns south toward his city.

The duel: Savitri follows. Yama three times commands her back; three times she stays, and her speeches - on dharma, on the company of the righteous, on the merit of following a husband - are so accomplished that Death himself concedes the conversation. He offers boons to get her to leave: for her father-in-law, eyes and his kingdom restored; for her father, a hundred sons; for herself, a hundred sons. The third boon is the trap she has been building: a hundred sons require a living husband. Yama, bound by his own granted word, laughs and releases the rope. 'Your husband shall live.' Satyavan wakes as from sleep; the exiled family's fortunes reverse; and the seers' prophecy is beaten not by force but by a wife's constancy, timed and worded.

Function: the story is the charter of the pativrata ideal - the devoted wife whose virtue has real cosmological purchase - and the ritual text of Vat-Savitri vrata, in which women fast, tie threads around a banyan, and retell Savitri's argument for their husbands' lives. Sri Aurobindo built his epic Savitri on it; comparative readers place it beside Orpheus (the descent for a wife, failed) and Psyche's tasks - here the descent is refused, and the argument wins where song could not.
narrative.zh: 薩維特里之章（大森林篇，由摩根德耶向堅戰講述，作為貞婦 pativrata 之典範故事）是摩訶婆羅多最偉大的抗死之愛敘事，也是印度教中儀式生命力最強的故事之一：每年 Vat-Savitri 齋戒——已婚婦女為夫壽而持之齋——都誦讀此篇。選擇：摩德羅王苑鏡婆底無子；他以嚴謹的供養禮拜太陽女神薩維特里，女神賜一女，光輝如其名。女長，王依俗遣其自擇夫婿（svayamvara）。她歷聖地與仙居，心有所定：薩蒂凡，盲眼流放王達優摩陀申之子，居林中貧困。彼俊美、孝謹——而命定將死。神諭：天界仙人那羅陀適在座，宣示預言，故事之鐘由此撥動：薩蒂凡德行冠世，然有一缺陷——他將於一年內死去。父懇求；女之回答是故事的樞紐與其教義：『我已擇定，無論其壽長壽促；既擇，不再擇。』一年之死乃命運之缺陷，非其人之缺陷。婚禮在預言成立之下舉行，薩維特里著粗衣至仙居，侍奉盲眼翁姑。守夜：薩維特里向內數日。期前四日始立齋；翁欲勸阻；她以神學作答——誓願已持，智者知其所將至。劫日，她求得許可與夫同入林中。伐木、昏厥，枕於她膝。隨即她見到他：頭戴暗冠、手持繩索之人，立於林間如主。是閻摩。他抽出薩蒂凡之魂——如拇指般小——繫之，轉向南往亡者之城。決鬥：薩維特里隨行。閻摩三令其返；三留，其言辭——論正法、論與義者同行、論隨夫之功——令死神自認辯不過。他為使其離去而賜恩諾：翁之眼與王國復得；父得百子；己得百子。第三項恩諾正是她步步築成的陷阱：百子需活著的丈夫。閻摩受己諾所縛，一笑斷繩：『汝夫將活。』薩蒂凡如從睡中醒來；流放之家時運逆轉；仙人之預言非為武力所破，而為一位妻子的堅貞——以恰當的時機與措辭——所破。功能：此篇為貞婦理想之憲章——貞婦之德具有真實的宇宙效力——亦為 Vat-Savitri 齋戒的儀式文本：婦女齋戒、於榕樹繫線、重述薩維特里的辯論以為夫爭命。室利阿羅頻多以此構築其史詩《薩維特里》；比較讀者置之於俄耳甫斯（為妻下行而失敗）之旁——此處下行被拒絕，歌所不能者，言辭得之。

functions: Charter of the pativrata ideal - wifely constancy with cosmological efficacy
Ritual text of Vat-Savitri vrata (annual fast for husbands' longevity)
Model of argumentative devotion: boons won by speech, not force
Narrative refutation of fatalism - prophecy beaten by timing and wording

title.en: The Birth of Skanda, the Six-Headed War God
title.zh: 六首戰神塞建陀之誕生

region.en: Saravana reed-beds of the Ganges (symbolic pin in the Himalayan foothills)
region.zh: 恆河薩羅伐那葦叢（象徵性定位於喜馬拉雅山麓）

period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Skanda's birth sections), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, the birth and consecration of Skanda

summary.en: The gods are losing to Taraka's demon armies - only a son of Shiva can kill him, but Shiva has withdrawn into yoga. Agni, sent to kindle Shiva's seed, carries it away glowing like molten gold; the Ganga receives it, six reed-nurturing mothers nurse the child, and Skanda rises with six faces to drink from all six at once. On the day he is born, he becomes general of the gods.
summary.zh: 諸神屢敗於達羅迦魔軍——唯濕婆之子能誅之，而濕婆已退入瑜伽。阿耆尼受命燃起濕婆之種，攜之而去，光如熔金；恆河承之，六位哺乳的母親撫育此子，塞建陀生而六首，得同時吮六乳。誕生之日，即被立為諸神之統帥。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: Skanda-Kartikeya-Murugan worship is major in South India (Murugan temples, Skanda Shashthi festival). Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The demon Taraka's boon made him nearly immortal: only a son of Shiva could kill him, and Shiva, in grief for Sati, had renounced the world for yogic seclusion. The gods, pressed hard in battle, went to Agni the fire-god, who entered Shiva's presence and received the god's seed, blazing like a second sun; unable to bear it, Agni carried it away to the Ganga, who bore it in her waters.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Skanda sections (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 惡魔塔拉卡的恩惠使他幾乎不死：唯有濕婆之子才能殺他，而濕婆因哀悼薩蒂，已棄絕塵世，隱居修行瑜伽。眾神在戰鬥中備受壓迫，便前往火神阿耆尼處，阿耆尼進入濕婆的所在，領受了這位神祇的精種，其光焰如第二個太陽；阿耆尼無法承受，便將它帶走，交給恆河，恆河便在她的水中孕育了它。

passages.text: The seed blazed in the river until the water grew hot; the reed-beds of the Saravana gleamed as if on fire. A child was born there among the reeds, beautiful, golden, with six faces; the six Krittika mothers, star-wives who had come to wash, each claimed him, each offered her breast - and the child grew six faces and drank from all six at once, so no mother was refused. He was therefore Kartikeya, of the Krittikas, and Skanda, of the reeds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Skanda sections (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那精種在河中熾燃，直到河水變熱；薩拉瓦納的蘆葦叢閃耀得彷彿著了火。一個孩子就在那裡誕生於蘆葦之間，美麗、金色、生有六面；六位克里蒂卡母親——前來沐浴的星宿之妻——各自認他為子，各自獻上乳房——那孩子便生出六面，同時從六處吮吸，因此沒有哪位母親被拒絕。他因此是克里蒂卡諸女之子迦絺吉夜，也是蘆葦之子室建陀。

passages.text: On the day of his birth the boy grew to youth; on that day the gods consecrated him general of their armies. He was armed, anointed, and seated on the assembled gods' lap in turn; he marshaled the hosts, took the cock standard and the peacock that had fought at his side, and led the army against Taraka's demons - the war the boon had reserved for him, won on the day he learned to walk.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Skanda sections (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在他誕生之日，這男孩便長成青年；就在那一天，眾神祝聖他為他們軍隊的統帥。他被授予武器、塗上聖油，並依次坐在聚集的眾神膝上；他整編軍隊，取來公雞旗幡和曾在他身旁作戰的孔雀，率軍對抗塔拉卡的惡魔——那場恩惠為他保留的戰爭，在他學會走路的那一天便贏得了。

canonical_translation: Kisari Mohan Ganguli, The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, 1883-96 (public domain); modern: J. A. B. van Buitenen, The Mahabharata, vol. 3, University of Chicago Press, 1975

narrative.en:
The birth of Skanda (Kartikeya, in the Tamil south Murugan) in the Vana Parva is one of the great miraculous-birth narratives of world mythology - a war god born full-armed and six-headed, made general of the gods on the day of his birth.

The problem the story solves is a theological knot. The demon Taraka's boon (from Brahma) makes him effectively unconquerable: only the son of Shiva may kill him. But Shiva - grief-mad since the death of Sati, his first wife - has renounced the world and sits in yogic seclusion, generating no lineage and answering no petitions. The gods' dilemma is Shiva's own withdrawal: the weapon exists, but the smith will not strike.

The delivery system is Agni. Sent (in some versions by the other gods, in some by Shiva's own consent) to receive the god's seed, Agni enters Shiva's presence at the moment the seed falls - blazing, the text says, like molten gold, like a second sun - and cannot hold it. He carries it to the Ganga, who bears it in her waters; the river grows hot; the reed-beds (saravana, 'the reeds') shine as though on fire. A child is born among the reeds: golden, beautiful, with six faces.

The six mothers: the Krittikas - star-wives of the seven seers in one telling, the Pleiades in another - had come to the river to bathe; each lays claim to the marvelous child and each offers her breast. The child's answer is the birth of his iconography: he sprouts six faces and drinks from all six mothers at once, so that no one is refused and every claim is honored. He is thus Kartikeya ('of the Krittikas') and Skanda ('of the reeds'), and in later iconography rides a peacock, carries a lance, and bears the cock-banner.

Consecration and war: the epic compresses childhood to a single day - on the day of his birth he grows to youth; the gods assemble and consecrate him senapati, general of the divine armies; Indra's jealousy flares and is pacified by an embrace (in the epic's comic aside, Indra strikes the newborn with his thunderbolt and the boy simply grows another body - and Indra, terrified, becomes his devotee). Skanda marshals the hosts, and the war that only he could win is won - Taraka's armies broken, the boon fulfilled, the cosmos re-ordered by an infant-day-old commander.

Function: the myth is a ritual charter of great consequence. It grounds Skanda's cult (huge in the Tamil south, where Murugan is lord of the hills and of youth and war), the Skanda Shashthi festival re-enacting his victory, and the iconic 'six mothers' theology that makes the Pleiades a nursing constellation. It also exemplifies the tradition's birth-miracle pattern: the seed travels (fire to river to reeds), the child is nursed by many mothers, and maturity arrives with cosmic speed. Compared with other miraculous-birth cluster members - Horus in the reeds of the Nile, Sargon in the reeds of a river - the shared grammar (dangerous child, water-birth, reed-cradle, immediate destiny) is unmistakable, but here the child's destiny is martial command rather than royal survival.
narrative.zh: 大森林篇中塞建陀（迦爾底克耶；南印度稱穆盧甘）之誕生是世界神話中最偉大的奇蹟誕生敘事之一——一位滿懷武備、六首而在誕生日即被立為諸神統帥的戰神。故事所解的神學結：魔王達羅迦之恩諭（得自梵天）使其近乎不可征服：唯濕婆之子可誅之。而濕婆——自其首妻薩提死後哀慟——已棄世入瑜伽深定，不生後嗣，不應請求。諸神的困境正是濕婆自身的隱退：武器存在，而鑄者不擊。遞送系統是阿耆尼。受命（或由諸神、或由濕婆許可）承接收神之種，阿耆尼入於濕婆之前，於種子落下之刻——其熾然如熔金、如第二太陽——不能持之。他攜之至恆河，恆河以其水承之；河水轉熱；葦叢（saravana，『葦』）熠然如焚。葦叢中生一子：金色、俊美、六首。六母：克里蒂迦（一說七仙人之星妻，一說昴星團）來河中沐浴；各欲認領此奇童，各奉其乳。孩童的回答即是其圖像學之誕生：他生出六面，同時吮六母之乳，無一被拒，每一主張皆得成全。故其名迦爾底克耶（『克里蒂迦之子』）與塞建陀（『葦中所生』）；後世圖像中騎孔雀、持長矛、立雞旗。授職與戰爭：史詩將童年壓縮為一日——誕生之日即長成青年；諸神集會，立其為元帥（senapati）；因陀羅之妒爆發而後平息（史詩的滑稽旁注：因陀羅以雷杵擊新生之嬰，孩童僅另生一身——因陀羅大懼，轉為其信徒）。塞建陀整頓神軍，唯他能贏的戰爭遂被贏得——達羅迦之軍潰，恩諭應驗，宇宙由一位出生未滿一日的統帥重整。功能：此神話是影響深遠的儀式憲章。它奠定塞建陀崇拜（南泰米爾尤盛，穆盧甘為山嶽、青春與戰爭之主）、重演其勝利的塞建陀六日節（Skanda Shashthi），以及『六母』神學——昴星團由此成為哺乳星座。它亦示範該傳統的誕生奇蹟模式：種子旅行（火至河至葦）、多母哺乳、成熟以宇宙速度降臨。與其他奇蹟誕生母題群成員相比——尼羅河葦中的荷魯斯、河中葦籃裡的薩爾貢——共享語法（危險之童、水生、葖搖籃、即刻命運）顯而易見，但此處孩童的命運是統軍而非王儲之存續。

functions: Miraculous-birth charter: seed travels by fire, river and reeds; six mothers nurse one child
Cultic foundation of Skanda-Kartikeya-Murugan worship and the Skanda Shashthi festival
Theology of the Pleiades as nursing constellation (the Krittikas)
Resolution myth: a boon-proof demon killed by the one son the boon excluded

title.en: Yudhishthira's Last Journey: The Dog at Heaven's Gate
title.zh: 堅戰的末程：天門前的犬

region.en: Mount Meru, path of ascent (symbolic pin at Kailash)
region.zh: 彌樓山登天之路（象徵性定位於凱拉什）

period: Mahabharata, Mahaprasthanika and Svargarohana Parvas, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Svargarohana Parva, Yudhishthira's ascent with the dog

summary.en: After the war and Krishna's passing, the five Pandavas and Draupadi walk west and north toward Mount Meru, dropping one by one as their particular sins are paid. Only Yudhishthira, the just, reaches heaven's gate in his body - with a stray dog that has followed him. Indra offers heaven without the dog; Yudhishthira refuses; the dog turns out to be Dharma, his father, testing him - and the gate opens.
summary.zh: 大戰之後、克里希那離世之際，般度五子與黑公主向西向北朝彌樓山而行，各因其私罪逐一倒下。唯堅戰——行義者——肉身抵達天門，伴有一路跟隨的流浪犬。因陀羅許其入天而棄犬；堅戰拒之；犬化為正法——其父——考驗而成，天門乃開。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (epic recitation, bhakti readings). Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: When word came of Krishna's death and the drowning of his clan, Yudhishthira resolved that the time of departure had come. The five brothers and Draupadi, adorned and fasting, turned from the city and walked toward the great mountain, the road of renunciation; a stray dog joined them and walked behind Yudhishthira, and the age's princes went as beggars toward Meru.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Mahaprasthanika Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當黑天逝世及其宗族溺亡的消息傳來，堅戰決意離去的時刻已到。五兄弟與黑公主盛裝齋戒，轉身離開城市，走向大山，即棄絕之路；一隻流浪狗加入了他們，走在堅戰身後，那個時代的王子們如乞丐般走向彌盧山。

passages.text: One by one they fell. Draupadi fell first, and Yudhishthira, without turning aside, named her fault - she leaned toward Arjuna. Sahadeva fell for vanity of wisdom, Nakula for pride in beauty, Arjuna for his boast, Bhima for his gluttony; each fell, and Yudhishthira walked on, grief and fault acknowledged, until only he and the dog climbed the peak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Mahaprasthanika Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們一個接一個倒下。黑公主最先倒下，堅戰沒有回頭，說出了她的過失——她偏愛阿周那。偕天因智慧之虛榮而倒下，無種因美貌之驕傲而倒下，阿周那因他的誇口而倒下，怖軍因他的貪食而倒下；各人皆倒下，堅戰繼續前行，承認悲傷與過失，直到只剩他與那隻狗登上峰頂。

passages.text: At the gate Indra came down to meet him and offered heaven in his chariot - but without the dog. Yudhishthira asked: what of my brothers and Draupadi? They are already there, said Indra - they went before you. Then, refusing heaven that excludes a creature that trusted him, Yudhishthira answered: the dog has followed me through the wilds; I will not abandon one who seeks my protection, not for the worlds themselves. A rescue of the helpless, he said, outcounts even heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Svargarohana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 因陀羅來到城門迎接他，在自己的戰車上邀他入天界——但不許帶狗。堅戰問道：我的兄弟們和黑公主呢？因陀羅說，他們已在那裡——他們先你而去。於是，堅戰拒絕了這將一個信賴他的生靈排除在外的天界，答道：這狗隨我穿越荒野；我絕不拋棄一個尋求我庇護者，縱為諸世界本身亦不。他說，拯救無助者，其功甚至勝過天界。

passages.text: At that the dog took the form of Dharma, god of justice, Yudhishthira's own divine father, and blessed him: thou hast renounced the carriage of heaven for a dog's companionship; no man on earth was ever thy equal in righteousness. Then Yudhishthira was carried up in glory - but the epic is not done: shown the heaven of his enemies, and his brothers in a hell being purified of a last sin, he refuses heaven that his loved ones cannot share, until hell and heaven are both remitted and the truth of the age's violence is paid in full.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Svargarohana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 言畢，那狗現出正法之神、即堅戰生身天父的形貌，祝福他道：你為與一狗為伴而捨棄天界之車輦；世上從無人在正義上與你匹敵。於是堅戰在榮光中被接升天——但史詩尚未終結：他被示以仇敵所在的天界，又見自己的兄弟們身處地獄，正為最後一樁罪愆受淨化，他拒絕了親愛之人無法共享的天界，直到地獄與天界皆得寬免，而此世暴行之真相得以徹底償清。

canonical_translation: Kisari Mohan Ganguli, The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, 1883-96 (public domain); modern: J. A. B. van Buitenen, The Mahabharata, vols. 6-7 (Chicago, incomplete)

narrative.en:
The Mahaprasthanika ('great departure') and Svargarohana ('ascent to heaven') Parvas are the Mahabharata's coda: after the war's desolation, Krishna's death, and the drowning of the Yadavas, the epic's heroes leave the world on foot - and the tradition's theology is tested at heaven's gate.

The departure: word arrives of Krishna's passing. Yudhishthira judges the age's work complete: 'the time has come for us to depart'. The five brothers and Draupadi, adorned like sacrificial victors and fasting, walk out of Hastinapura toward the west and north, the road of renunciation toward Mount Meru. A stray dog joins them - unbidden, unprompted - and attaches itself to Yudhishthira.

The falls: one by one they drop on the road, each fall explained by Yudhishthira in a single unturned sentence - the epic's harshest audit. Draupadi falls because she favored Arjuna in her heart; Sahadeva for vanity of wisdom; Nakula for pride in beauty; Arjuna for his boast (that he could consume his enemies in a day); Bhima for his gluttony. The just king alone keeps walking - his own flaw (the gambling, the lie that felled Drona) paid long before - until only he and the dog stand on the peak, and the gate of heaven shines before them.

The gate: Indra descends in his chariot and offers Yudhishthira heaven in his body. Yudhishthira asks for his brothers and Draupadi - told they are already there. Then the offer's condition: not the dog. A dog may not enter heaven, Indra says; cast it off and ascend. Yudhishthira's refusal is the epic's last teaching: the dog followed him through the wilds for its own reasons and now seeks his protection; to abandon a creature that has sought shelter is a sin no heaven could outweigh - 'I would not do such a thing for the sake of the three worlds, let alone heaven'. (The scene's genealogy is visible: it is a Vedic-test echo - in the Rigveda's Yama hymns the two four-eyed dogs guard the path of the dead; here the dog becomes the gate's own examiner.)

The theophany: at the refusal, the dog assumes the form of Dharma - the god of justice, Yudhishthira's own divine father - and reveals that the whole ascent was his test: 'thou hast renounced the carriage of heaven for a dog's companionship; no man on earth was ever thy equal in righteousness.' Yudhishthira is borne up in splendor.

But the epic's real brilliance is the twist that follows: shown around heaven, Yudhishthira finds his enemies honored (Duryodhana, radiant, among the gods) and his own brothers and Draupadi undergoing a brief hell, purifying the last sin - the lie and the war's guilt. Yudhishthira refuses to stay in a heaven built on such arrangements, demands to share their hell, and his renunciation of heaven itself completes the purification: hell and heaven both are remitted, and the age's violence is paid in full. The poem ends where its ethics began - with a king who will not accept a reward that costs others their share.

Function: the closing parvas are the epic's theodicy and its ethics' final exam; the dog-test became proverbial (dharma outcounts heaven), and the scene is retold in bhakti sermons as the model of compassion that outranks reward.
narrative.zh: 『大去篇』（Mahaprasthanika）與『登天篇』（Svargarohana）是摩訶婆羅多的尾聲：大戰之後、克里希那之死、雅度族之溺，史詩的英雄們徒步離世——傳統的神學在天門前受試。離去：克里希那逝去的消息傳到。堅戰斷定時機已至：『我們該啟程了。』五兄弟與黑公主如祭祀勝利者般飾身、持齋，步出象城向西向北，往彌樓山而行出離之路。一隻流浪犬不請自來，附於堅戰身後。倒下：他們一個個在路上倒下，每一次跌倒皆由堅戰以一句不回頭的話解釋——史詩最嚴厲的審計。黑公主因心偏阿周那而倒；無種因智慧之傲；偕天因美貌之驕；阿周那因誇言（一日盡殲敵軍）；怖軍因饕餮。唯義王繼續前行——他自身的過失（賭局、誅德羅納之謊）早已償清——直到唯他與犬立於峰頂，天門在眼前生輝。天門：因陀羅乘車而降，許堅戰肉身升天。堅戰求其兄弟與黑公主——被告知他們已先至。隨後是條件：犬不可入。因陀羅言：犬不得進天；棄之而升。堅戰的拒絕是史詩的最後一課：犬循其自身之由隨我穿過荒野，此刻尋我庇護；拋棄尋求庇護之生靈是任何天國都抵不過的罪——『為三界我亦不為此，何况天國』。（此景的譜系清晰可見：吠陀閻摩頌中守亡者之路的是雙四眼犬；此處犬成為門的考官本身。）神顯：拒絕之際，犬化為正法之神——堅戰的神性之父——揭示整段上升皆是其試：『汝為犬伴而棄天車；地上無人於義行汝之比。』堅戰於光榮中被舉起。然史詩真正的妙筆在其後的轉折：參觀天國時，堅戰發現其仇敵受尊（難敵光燦燦地立於諸神之中），而自己的兄弟與黑公主正於短暫的地獄中受煉，以淨最後之罪——謊言與戰爭之責。堅戰拒絕居於如此安排的天國，求與他們同下地獄；他對天國自身的棄絕完成了淨化：地獄與天國皆得釋免，時代的暴力償清。詩在其倫理開始處收尾——以一位不肯接受以他人之份為代價的賞賜的王。功能：末二篇是史詩的神義論與其倫理的終考；犬試成為諺語（正法勝於天國），此景在奉愛佈道中被重述為慈悲高於賞賜的典範。

functions: Final ethics of the epic: compassion outranks heaven's reward (the dog test)
Theodicy of the war - sin paid on the road, in hell, and by refusing heaven
Death-walk rite of renunciation (pravrajya) enacted by the heroes
Model for bhakti preaching on protection of the helpless

title.en: Sita's Trial by Fire (Agni-pariksha)
title.zh: 悉多的火證

region.en: Lanka (symbolic pin, Sri Lanka highlands)
region.zh: 楞伽（象徵性定位，斯里蘭卡高地）

period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Yuddha Kanda (Book VI), the fire trial of Sita

summary.en: Ravana is dead; Rama is reunited with Sita before the armies - and coldly tells her to go where she will, for honor dwells not with a woman who has lived in another's house. Sita bids Lakshmana build a pyre and enters the fire, praying to be proof of her faithfulness. Agni, the fire god himself, rises from the flames holding her unharmed - and gives her back, declaring her purity before the assembled hosts.
summary.zh: 羅波那已死；羅摩與悉多於兩軍之前重聚——卻冷言令其自去，言貞操不居於曾居他人之宅的女子。悉多命羅什曼那築火堆，投身入火，祈以火為其貞信之證。火神阿耆尼親自自焰中持不傷之悉多而起，於會眾之前宣告其貞潔，將她交還。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition and politically contested narrative (the agni-pariksha is debated in contemporary India; Uttara Kanda variants exist). Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Rama, having slain Ravana and received back his wife, stood before the hosts and spoke words colder than the battlefield: I have fought for honor, not desire; Sita has lived in another's house; let her go where she will - I take her back only as a man takes back his name, cleansed of suspicion.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, the fire trial (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 羅摩誅殺羅波那、迎回妻子之後，立於眾軍之前，說出比戰場更冷的話語：我征戰是為榮譽，非為情慾；悉多曾居他人之宅；任她去她想去之處——我接回她，只如一個人接回自己被洗清嫌疑的名聲。

passages.text: Sita, wounded, answered that she had not strayed in thought; and to the assembled army she made her vow: if my heart has never left my lord, then let the fire, witness of all, protect me. She ordered Lakshmana: build the pyre. Lakshmana, anguished, looked to Rama, who nodded - and the pyre was raised, and Sita, circling her lord three times, mounted it before the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, the fire trial (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 受傷的悉多回答說，她連念頭都不曾偏離；她向聚集的軍隊立誓：若我的心從未離開我的夫君，就讓那見證一切的火保護我。她吩咐羅什曼那：築起火堆。羅什曼那痛苦萬分，望向羅摩，羅摩點頭——火堆築起，悉多繞夫君三匝，在世人面前登上火堆。

passages.text: She entered the flames as into the presence of the gods; the fire burned bright around her, and the armies groaned - mothers of the monkeys wept, Rakshasa women lamented. Then the earth seemed to open: from the blazing pyre rose Agni himself, the fire-god in human form, red-lit, bearing Sita unharmed upon his hands, her garments white, her body cool as if she walked in moonlight - and with a voice like a conch he proclaimed her purity before gods and men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, the fire trial (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她走入火焰，如入諸神之臨在；火在她四周熾烈燃燒，眾軍悲嘆——猴族的母親們哭泣，羅剎女們哀號。接著大地彷彿裂開：從熊熊火堆中升起火神阿耆尼本人，以人形現身，通體紅光，雙手托著毫髮無傷的悉多，她衣白如雪，身體清涼，彷彿行走於月光之中——他以如螺號般的聲音，在諸神與眾人面前宣告她的貞潔。

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, The Ramayan of Valmiki, Benares, 1870-74 (public domain); modern critical: Robert P. Goldman et al., The Ramayana of Valmiki, vol. VI, Princeton University Press, 2017

narrative.en:
The agni-pariksha - Sita's trial by fire at the close of the Lanka war - is the Ramayana's most theologically charged scene and, in modern India, its most politically debated one.

The situation: Ravana is slain. Vibhishana brings Sita from the Ashoka grove to her husband, veiled and dishevelled after months of captivity, surrounded by the victorious armies of monkeys, bears and rakshasa defectors. The reunion the whole war has aimed at begins - and Rama stops it with a speech of public humiliation: he fought for honor and the family's name, not for desire; a woman who has dwelt in another man's house cannot be received by him without suspicion; let her go wherever she pleases - to Lakshmana, to Bharata, to Shatrughna, to the forest, or to Ravana's kin. The victory speech is a rejection.

Sita's response defines her. She has endured abduction, captivity, threats, the surveillance of demonesses - and now this. She answers first with the record of her faithfulness (in thought she never left him), then does the unthinkable: she orders Lakshmana to build a pyre. Her logic is stated as a vow to the assembled world: 'if my heart has never strayed from Rama, let the fire, witness of all deeds, protect me.' Lakshmana - the brother who never questioned Rama - hesitates, looks to Rama for instruction, and Rama's silent assent seals the horror. Sita circles her lord three times with folded hands, prays to Agni, and mounts the pyre as the two armies watch in tears.

The fire answers. From the blazing pyre the fire-god Agni himself rises in person - the text makes him a visible being, red-lit, human-formed - carrying Sita unharmed, her body cool, her garments unsinged, and proclaims to gods and men that she is pure: no sin touches her, in thought, word or deed; she was preserved through captivity as a pearl is kept in a shell. Rama receives her back - the text notes pointedly that he then claims he acted only to demonstrate her purity to the world, a claim the poem leaves sitting awkwardly beside the cruelty of the speech that began it.

Function and afterlife: in the epic's own theology, the trial authenticates Sita as the earth-daughter whose purity is cosmically guaranteed; fire is the Vedic witness of oaths, and here the witness speaks. But the scene's authority has always been contested inside the tradition: the Ramcharitmanas softens it; regional folk tellings often refuse it outright (Sita refuses the test, or Rama refuses to ask it); the Jain Paumacariya and some Tamil tellings remove the trial entirely; and modern India has turned the episode into a public argument about the treatment of women and the reading of scripture (Supreme Court hearings in the 1980s-90s turned on Sita's and Draupadi's trials as cultural arguments). The Uttara Kanda's later exile of Sita - despite the trial's verdict - makes the poem's own conclusion a second, crueler trial; the tradition has never fully reconciled the two.

Comparatively, the scene belongs to the ordeal-by-fire cluster (like the medieval ordeals of Europe, and the suttee rhetoric it would later be contaminated by) - but here the ordeal is divine theater: the god of fire himself is the judge, and the accused is vindicated. The record keeps both the vindication and the cruelty in view.
narrative.zh: 火證（agni-pariksha）——楞伽之戰尾聲悉多的火中試煉——是《羅摩衍那》神學上最沉重的一幕，在現代印度也是政治上爭論最烈的一幕。情境：羅波那已誅。維毗沙那自無憂樹林帶出歷經數月囚禁、蒙塵披髮的悉多，交給其夫，四周環繞著猴、熊與投誠羅剎的勝利大軍。整場戰爭所指向的重聚開始——而羅摩以一場公開羞辱的言辭止住它：我為榮譽與家族之名而戰，非為欲；曾居他人之宅的女子，我不能無疑地接納；隨其所欲而去——去羅什曼那處、婆羅多處、沙陀魯那處、去森林、去羅波那親族處。勝利之辭成為拒絕。悉多的回應定義了她。她受過擄掠、囚禁、威脅、羅剎女的監視——如今又是這個。她先陳述其貞信之記錄（心未曾離），繼而做出不可思議之事：命羅什曼那築火堆。其邏輯以向天下之誓表述：『若我心未曾離羅摩，願火——萬行之見證——護我。』羅什曼那——那位從不質疑兄長的弟弟——遲疑，望向羅摩求示；羅摩的默許封存了這場恐怖。悉多合掌繞夫三匝，祈於阿耆尼，於兩軍垂淚注視之下登上火堆。火作出回答。自熊熊火堆中火神阿耆尼親自升起——經文使其成為可見之存在，紅光人形——手持不傷之悉多，其身涼爽，衣無燎痕，並向諸神與世人宣告其純潔：思、言、行皆無罪；她於囚禁中被保全，如貝中之珠。羅摩復接納她——經文刻意記下他隨即宣稱此舉只為向世界昭示其貞潔——此說與開場那場殘酷言辭並置時顯得突兀，而詩篇並未解決這一張力。功能與後續：在史詩自身的神學中，此試驗認證悉多為大地之女、其貞潔具宇宙保證；火是吠陀誓言的見證者，而在此見證者開口。然而此景的權威在傳統內部始終有爭議：《羅摩功行錄》予以柔化；各地民間講述常直接拒絕（悉多拒試，或羅摩拒問）；耆那教《缽摩迦哩耶》與若干泰米爾講述整體移除此試；現代印度更將此幕轉為關於婦女處境與經典詮釋的公共論辯（1980-90年代最高法院聽證曾以悉多與黑公主之試為文化論據）。後篇（Uttara Kanda）中悉多縱經火證仍遭放逐——使詩篇自身的結論成為第二場、更殘酷的試煉；傳統從未完全調和二者。比較地看，此景屬於火審母題群（如歐洲中世紀火審，及其後被寡婦殉葬論述所污染的語境）——但此處神判是神聖劇場：火神親自為法官，被告獲平反。本錄同時保留平反與殘酷兩面。

functions: Ordeal theology: fire as Vedic witness of oaths, speaking its verdict
Authentication of Sita's purity as earth-daughter before the world
Most debated scene of the epic - charter of contested gender norms
Ritual resonance in Sita-related vows and folk retellings that refuse or soften the trial

variants.name: Ramcharitmanas of Tulsidas (Awadhi, 1574)
variants.summary: Softens the trial: Rama's speech is read as lila (divine play), the fire-trial staged as a spectacle of devotion rather than suspicion, and Sita's divinity foregrounded.

variants.name: Paumacariya of Vimalasuri (Jain, c. 3rd-5th c. CE)
variants.summary: Removes the trial entirely; Ravana is noble and Sita untested - the ideology reworked through Jain vows and karma, with Lakshmana as the slayer of Ravana.

variants.name: Folk refusals of the trial
variants.text_tradition: Regional oral tellings (e.g. Telugu, Bengali traditions)
variants.summary: In many village tellings Sita refuses to enter the fire, or Rama withdraws the demand; the trial is the most locally variable scene of the whole poem.

sensitivity_guidance: The agni-pariksha is ritually recited and politically contested (courts, public debate). Quote public-domain translations; attribute kanda and sarga; present the trial as the tradition's own contested scene, noting folk and Jain refusals; do not present the ordeal as normative or as historical fact.

title.en: Loki's Lesser Mischiefs: The Small Tricks Cataloged
title.zh: 洛基的小惡作劇：小型詭計目錄

region.en: The halls and roads of Asgard (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 阿斯加德的大廳與道路（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Skaldskaparmal and Eddic c. 1000-1230; the small-trick register

source.work: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal (the small-trick episodes); Reginsmal; Lokasenna; the trick-catalog

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916; Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Loki's small-trick catalog: the shape-tricks (the salmon's slip, the fly at the forge, the mare's lure, the seal's swim, the flea's bite), the theft-tricks (Sif's hair, Brisingamen, the? - 'the? - 'knife? - 'at? - the? - feast? - - the servant's killing), the tongue-tricks (the flyting's licenses, the insults' inventions, the false oaths), and the blame-tricks (the charges laid on others: 'the? - 'lies? - 'that? - 'stick? -). The record is the trick-catalog: the corpus's mischief-taxonomy.
summary.zh: 洛基小詭計目錄：化身詭計（化鮭魚溜走、鍛爐旁的蒼蠅、誘馬的母馬、泅水的海豹、叮咬的跳蚤）、竊取詭計（西芙之髮、布里辛嘉門、宴席上的殺僕）、舌頭詭計（吵罵特權、辱罵的發明、虛偽誓言），以及歸罪詭計（將罪名栽給他人——「黏著不放的謊言」）。此記錄是詭計目錄：語料的惡作劇分類學。

canonical_translation: Brodeur 1916 (public domain); Bellows 1923 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The trick-catalog holds Loki's small register beside the great episodes (the records norse-loki-genealogy, norse-lokasenna-flyting, norse-loki-bound-serpent). The shape-tricks: the corpus's most complete transformation-register (the salmon's slip through the net; the fly stinging the smith; the mare luring the stallion; the seal's surf-duel; the flea's bite-and-turn) - the trickster's body as the catalog's inventory.

The theft-tricks: the small larcenies (Sif's midnight shearing; Brisingamen's unclasping; the knife at the feast that kills the servant - the flyting's opening crime) - each theft a door to a larger story (the treasures-cycle, the duel, the binding). The tongue-tricks: the verbal register (the flyting's licenses; the invented insults; the false oaths sworn smoothly - the corpus's best-documented liar). And the blame-tricks: the charges laid on others ('the? - 'lies? - 'that? - 'stick? - - the mischief's transference: the corpus's portrait of scapegoating as craft).

The record's cultural functions are the trick-taxonomy doctrine (the mischief's kinds classified: shape, theft, tongue, blame - the trickster's method-file) and the small-trick engine doctrine (each small trick opening a cycle: the catalog as the myth-world's ignition-system). In the atlas, the record anchors the trick-catalog family: each a tradition's mischief-taxonomy; the Norse one is distinctive in the shape-inventory.

For the database, this node indexes the trick-records: here the small register.

The catalog's comparative frame completes the taxonomy: the trickster's register across traditions (the Greek Hermes' thefts, the Chinese Monkey's havoc, the Native American trickster-cycles) - each a mischief-taxonomy; the Norse one is distinctive in the villain-trajectory: Loki's small tricks escalate by rule into the corpus's catastrophe, the catalog documented as a career with a schedule. And the trick's victims completes it: the mischief aimed at the pantheon's own property (the gods' hair, necklace, wife, feast) - the trickster's economy documented as inside-theft rather than outside-attack.

The catalog's escalation-rule completes the taxonomy: the tricks' gradient documented (the small larcenies opening the treasure-cycle; the tongue-tricks ending in the flyting; the blame-tricks seeding the deaths - each trick's consequence tracked), so the catalog's order is causal: the mischief-chronology built from the trick-records' sequence - the corpus's own argument that the apocalypse is an aggregate of small thefts. And the trick-teller's license completes it: the catalog's delight (the sources relishing the tricks' ingenuity even as they condemn) - the myth-world's ambivalence documented in its own narration.

 The file's Sigurd-echo completes it: the trick's inheritance documented (Loki)s otter-deceit seeding the Sigurd-cycle’s curse - the record norse-reginsmal’s charter), the catalog’s small register shown to drive the corpus’s largest tragedy.

title.en: Odin's Ambiguous Deeds: Theft, Deceit and Oath-Evasion
title.zh: 奧丁的曖昧之舉：偷竊、欺騙與避誓

region.en: The halls of gods and giants (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 諸神與巨人的廳堂（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

period: Havamal st. 104-110; Skaldskaparmal; Lokasenna; Gesta Danorum's Odin

source.work: Havamal st. 104-110 (the mead-theft's self-account); Lokasenna (the charges); Saxo's Othinus (the deceitful god); Brodeur 1916

license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Elton 1894); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Odin's moral-shadow file: the thefts (the mead from Gunnlod - told by the thief in the first person: 'the? - 'rath? - 'I? - paid? - her? - - the seduction's self-accounting), the deceits (the broken betrothal of Billing's daughter; the name-masks; the shape-shifts), the oath-evasions (the flyting's charges: the oaths sworn and unsworn), and the ambiguity's doctrine (the god whose crimes are virtues: wisdom's price-list paid in fraud - the corpus's morally maximal deity). The record is the god's shadow-file.
summary.zh: 奧丁道德陰影檔案：偷竊（自貢恩洛德處竊取蜜酒——由竊賊本人第一人稱自述：「我為她的忠誠付了『恥價』」）、欺騙（背棄與比林之女的婚約；層層化名；種種化身）、避誓（吵罵中的指控：誓言立了又毀），以及曖昧教義（其罪即其德：智慧的價目以欺詐支付——語料中道德上最極端的神性)。此記錄是神的陰影檔案。

canonical_translation: Bellows 1923 (public domain); Elton 1894 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The god's shadow-file holds Odin's moral register. The thefts: the mead told by the thief ('Gunnlod? - gave? - me? - drink? - of? - the? - precious? - mead? - 'and? - 'I? - 'paid? - her? - rath? - 'well? - 'for? - her? - 'true? - faith? - - the Hávamál's self-accounting: the seduction priced, the theft confessed with a boast), and the thefts' economic frame (the record norse-kvasir-mead's exchange-chain). The deceits: the betrothal broken (Billing's daughter promised by night and mocking at dawn - the god's own lesson in oath-keeping's asymmetry), the name-masks (the record norse-odin-wanderer-tales' index), and the shape-shifts (the bird-forms, the serpent-forms).

The oath-evasions: the flyting's charges (the oaths sworn and broken 'to? - 'the? - 'eye? - 'of? - the? - spear-din? - - the corpus's charge-sheet against its chief-god; the record norse-lokasenna-flyting's audit), and Saxo's Latin Odin (the deceitful god of the Danish history: the prophet-god's frauds documented by the outsider - the corpus's harshest portrait). And the ambiguity's doctrine completes the file: the god whose crimes are virtues (wisdom's price-list paid in fraud - the corpus's morally maximal deity: the records norse-havamal-runes' hanging and norse-mimir-well-eye's eye as the counter-ledger: the thefts and sacrifices in one economy).

The record's cultural functions are the shadow-deity doctrine (the chief-god documented as trickster - the corpus's refusal of a clean god) and the price-list doctrine (each wisdom's purchase itemized: the frauds and wounds as receipts). In the atlas, the record anchors the ambiguous-deity family: each a tradition's morally mixed high-god; Odin is distinctive in keeping his own books.

For the database, this node complements the wanderer-record and the mead-record: here the shadow-register.

The file's self-defense clause completes the shadow-register: the god's own justifications recorded (the Hávamál's boast-frames, the flyting's counter-charges - the trickster-audit answered by the trickster-auditor), so the shadow-file documents a god arguing his own case: the corpus's most self-aware deity, keeping receipts and replies. And the cult's echo completes it: the wanderer-worship's form (the offerings to Odin at the crossroads and the gallows - the shadow-god's cult-sites matching his deeds) - the ambiguity documented in ritual geography.

The file's cult-of-the-hanged completes the register: the shadow-god's worship documented (the hanged offerings, the gallows-sacrifices of the saga-record - the god's cult-sites matching his deeds: the corpus's cult-archaeology of ambiguity), so the shadow-file's crimes are not editorial: the mythology's own cult practiced the god's methods. And the law's echo completes it: the oath-evasion's legal twin (the loophole-craft the sagas' lawyers practiced - the record norse-ulf-outlaw-boundary's courts) - the god's methods documented as the society's professional skill.

title.en: Þjálfi and Röskva: The Servant-Tricksters of Thor's Household

source.work: Snorri, Gylfaginning chs. 44-46 (Thjalfi's laming of the goat; the races); Hymiskvida; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916; Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The servant-tricksters' file: the origin-trick (Þjálfi laming one of Thor's goats by accident - 'the? - 'lame? - goat? - 'the? - transgression? - 'that? - 'bought? - their? - service: the children taken as bond-servants for the bone), the racing-trick (Þjálfi racing Hugi, who is Thought - the unbeatable), the digging-feat (Þjálfi digging under Hrungnir's feet - the footwork that beats the stone-giant), and Röskva's register (the sister's quiet service). The record is the camp-follower file: the mortals inside the god's adventures.
summary.zh: 僕役詭計者檔案：起源之詭（希亞爾菲失誤弄跛索爾山羊之一——「跛羊」：孩童因斷骨而被收為債役僕）、賽跑詭計（希亞爾菲對決「休吉」——對手竟是「思想」，無人能勝）、挖掘壯舉（希亞爾菲在赫朗格尼爾腳下掘坑——以腳步戰勝石巨人），以及羅斯克瓦名冊（妹妹的靜默服務）。此記錄是隨營者檔案：神之歷險中的凡人。

canonical_translation: Brodeur 1916 (public domain); Bellows 1923 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The camp-follower file holds the mortals inside Thor's adventures. The origin-trick: Þjálfi's laming of the goat ('the? - 'bone? - 'cracked? - 'while? - sucking? - the? - marrow? - - the boy's snack costing the god's beast its leg: the transgression that bought the children's service - Thor taking son and daughter as his bond-servants for the bone, the corpus's clearest servant-contract).

The racing-trick: Þjálfi against Hugi (the three races lost 'by? - 'a? - 'breadth? - - and the reveal: Hugi is Thought, whom nothing outpaces - the boy racing an abstraction, the trick-king's lesson in the mind's speed). The digging-feat: Þjálfi's footwork at the duel ('dug? - 'under? - Hrungnir's? - feet? - - the trick that beats the stone-giant: the servant's shovel-work winning the god's fight - the corpus's most practical heroism). And Röskva's register: the sister's service (the quiet half of the pair - the household's other worker, the corpus's least-sung servant).

The record's cultural functions are the servant-contract doctrine (mortals inside the gods' adventures: service as the price of a broken bone - the myth-world's labor-grammar) and the practical-heroism doctrine (the servant's footwork as the duel's engine: the corpus's heroism credited to its laborers). In the atlas, the record anchors the camp-follower family: each a tradition's mortals-in-the-divine-register; the Norse pair is distinctive in the goat-contract.

For the database, this node complements the Utgard-record and the Hrungnir-record: here the servants' file.

The file's labor-theology completes the register: the servants' contract documented as the myth-world's labor-law (the bone-debt serviced in kind: speed for speed, digging for digging - the corpus's clearest doctrine of mortal labor inside the divine economy), and the pair's folk-afterlife completes it: the servant-names' persistence in Scandinavian idiom ('to? - 'run? - like? - Thjalfi? - - the boy's speed surviving as proverb) - the camp-followers documented in speech as well as story.

The file's inheritance-note completes the register: the servants' descendants documented (Þjálfi's line claimed in the Icelandic genealogies - the camp-follower's family in the settlement-books), so the camp-follower file reaches the colonists' own pedigrees: the mortals inside the god's adventures claimed as ancestors - the myth-world's labor-contract continuing into the settlement's identity. And the goat-restitution completes it: the lamed beast's repair (the god's craft mending the bone - the servant's debt serviced even in flesh) - the contract's terms documented as healing as well as service.

 The file's Utgardr-racing-coda completes it: the three races’ reveal documented (Hugi as Thought - the breadth-margins’ meaning explained), the servant’s lesson delivered by the trick-king as the corpus’s own parable of the mind.

The record is the stone-lore file: the runic corpus's reception-register.

narrative.en:
The stone-lore file holds the runic corpus's reception-register. The moving-taboo: the curse-clauses' folk-afterlife (the farmers' stories of shifted stones and lost luck - 'the? - 'stone? - 'put? - back? - 'and? - 'the? - luck? - 'returned? - - the record norse-bjorketorp-curse's doctrine documented in rural memory: the inscription's threat still enforced in folk-belief).

The sight-lore and the singing-stones: the hidden treasures (the stones' buried hoards and the guardians' visions - the antiquarians' reports of the stones' secrets), and the animated runes ('the? - 'stones? - 'that? - 'speak? - 'at? - night? - - the inscription-lore's voices: the runes as living speech, the alphabet's magic-doctrine (the record norse-havamal-runes) persisting in village-lore).

The name-legends complete the file: each stone's christening (the local stories naming the stones: the Rok-stone's riddle-lord, the stones' heroes) - the monuments' biographies written by their neighborhoods. The record's cultural functions are the stone-lore doctrine (the runic monuments as living local documents: the inscription's afterlife in community-memory) and the taboo-persistence doctrine (the curse-law's clauses still enforced in folk-practice centuries after the runemasters died). In the atlas, the record anchors the stone-lore family: each a tradition's monument-legends; the runic one is distinctive in the moving-taboo.

For the database, this node complements the runic-records: here the stones' own reception-file.

The file's archival method completes the register: the stone-legends collected by the antiquarians beside their surveys (the 17th-20th-century runologists recording the local tales with the readings), so the lore is documented as scholarship's by-product: each stone's file holding inscription and neighborhood-memory together - the database's own method (inscription plus reception) modeled on the antiquarians' notebooks. And the folklore's variants completes it: the tales' regional differences (the singing-stones in one district, the moving-taboo in another) - the stone-lore's geography mapped.

The file's legend-genre completes the register: the stones' legend-types catalogued (the treasure-guardian, the sighted runemaster, the buried king, the stone's journey-walk) - the local-lore's own taxonomy documented, each stone's biography built from a shared story-kit. And the tourism-era completes it: the stones' modern reception (the runestone-tourism and the local societies' care of the monuments) - the stone-lore file's living continuation documented, the neighborhood-memory still maintaining the stones.

 The file's Rok-junction completes it: the Rok-stone’s local riddle-lord lore (the stone’s neighborhood naming its mystery) - the legend-file’s most famous entry documented beside the inscription-record.

 The file's antiquarian-notebook completes it: the scholars’ habit of recording the tales beside the readings (the surveys’ local-lore columns) - the stone-lore documented as scholarship’s by-product, each stone's file holding inscription and neighborhood-memory together.

summary.en: The hof-places' file: Ingimundr's Freyr-image (the god's image carried from Norway by the Finns' magic-tracking - 'the? - 'image? - 'found? - 'where? - 'the? - Sami? - 'sorcerers? - 'sent? - him? - - the temple-site chosen by divination), the Hof place-name map (the dozens of Hof- and Thor-s-names of Iceland: the temple-geography as the settlement's register), the saga hofs' courts and feasts (the temple as district-institution), and the archaeology (the Hofstadir excavation's hall-and-bowls). narrative.en:
The sacred-site file holds the hof-places' stories. Ingimundr's Freyr-image: the god's image tracking its own site (the chieftain's amulet-image lost from his purse? - 'found? - by? - the? - Sami? - sorcerers? - 'who? - 'saw? - 'its? - place? - in? - the? - far? - west? - - the divination-voyage: the Finns' magic locating the god's chosen ground in Iceland, the temple-site chosen by the image itself), and the founding at Hof (the image set up at the Vatnsdalur's hof: the god's residence establishing the district's cult-center).

The iconographic Sigurd-file holds the dragon-slayer's carved register. The Ramsund carving: the rock-cut frieze (Sigurd roasting the heart, sucking the thumb; Grani loaded with the hoard; the birds in the tree; Regin's headless body; the? - 'the? - 'whole? - cycle? - 'in? - 'one? - stone? - 'framing? - 'a? - rune-band? - 'for? - 'a? - memorial? - - the legend carved as the frame of a family's monument: the myth as memorial-decoration).

The Drävle and Gök stones: the dragon-scene in rune-stone form (the slayer, the horse, the? - 'the? - - the stones' carved panels naming the story beside the memorial-text), and the Hylestad portals: the stave-church's wood-carved cycle (the story told across a church-door: the dragon-slaying entering the church's own architecture - the conversion-era's favorite myth documented in the religion's building).

The record's cultural functions are the iconographic-Sigurd doctrine (the legend as the conversion-era's favorite: the dragon-slayer carved on Christian stone - the myth's reception-datum: which stories the Christian north kept) and the memorial-context doctrine (the myths carved as memorial-frames: the runestones' dead honored with dragon-slaying imagery - the heroic-myth as grief-technology). The file's metatextual layer completes the register: the stones' self-reference documented (the rune-bands speaking about the pictures: 'the? - 'carver? - 'and? - 'the? - 'commissioner? - 'named? - 'beside? - 'the? - scenes) - the myth-pictures and the memorials' own texts in one frame, the picture-file's documents speaking twice. And the cross-media consistency completes it: the carved scenes' agreement with the poems (the Ramsund frieze matching Fáfnismál's beats) - the iconography's fidelity documented, the picture-register certified against the verse.

narrative.en:
The migration-memory file holds the Gothic-material's northern afterlife. The Theodoric-material: the emperor's northern fame (the Rök stone's 'chief? - of? - sea-warriors? - seated? - armed? - on? - his? - Frankish? - steed? - - the record norse-rok-stone's earliest attestation; and the German Dietrich-songs' continuation), the memory's reach (the dead emperor remembered in Sweden a generation after his fall - the migration-age's news traveling north as heroic-legend).

The Ermanaric-material: the Gothic king's Scandinavian biography (the Latin history's Ermanaric - the king who died of the Rosomoni? - Sunilda's? - - the Hamic? - Hamdir-Sorli cycle's Jormunrek: the record norse-hamdir-sorli's plot documented in the Latin history's own clauses: the Sunilda-episode, the brother-avengers - the Gothic history and the Norse lay telling one event twice). The Amal-genealogies complete the file: the Gothic royal line claimed in Scandinavian descent-lore (the dynasties' Gothic-grandfather claims - the corpus's genealogical transfer), and the Danube-geography: the frontiers mapped into the saga-world (Reidgotaland, the Danpar-steads - the Goths' homeland named in the north's own saga-geography, the record norse-angantyr-huns' theater).

The record's cultural functions are the migration-memory doctrine (the continent's fall converted into northern heroic-legend: the great migrations' memory as the corpus's historical layer) and the transfer-method doctrine (the Gothic-history's characters renamed and relocated: the emperors and kings becoming the saga-world's kings). In the atlas, the record anchors the migration-memory family: each a tradition's continental afterlife; the Norse one is distinctive in the carved stones.

For the database, this node complements the Hervarar and Sigurd-records: here the Gothic file.

The file's transfer-mechanics completes the register: the names' transformations documented (Ermanaric to Jormunrek, Theodoric to Thjodrekr, the Amals to the northern lines - the phonology and genealogy of the transfer traced), so the migration-memory file documents not just the borrowings but the method: how continental history was naturalized into northern form - the names worn down by generations of retelling, the geography relocated to the saga-world's own frontiers.

The file's dynastic-use completes the register: the Gothic-grandfather claims' function documented (the Scandinavian dynasties' genealogies reaching to the migration-kings - the charter-value of a Gothic ancestor), so the transfer-file's borrowings are political: the continental past imported as legitimacy, the migration-memory serving the northern courts' titles. And the Ermanaric-cycle's spread completes it: the same tragedy told from Jordanes' Latin to the Norse lay to the German epics - the migration-memory's three-language circulation documented, the file's reach beyond Scandinavia.

 The file's Reidgotaland-gazetteer completes it: the saga-world's Gothic geography catalogued (the Danpar-steads, the Harvaða-fells, the Dnieper-names preserved in the Norse texts) - the migration-memory)s map documented as the tradition's own gazetteer.

title.en: The Death of Cuchulainn: the Hound at Bay
title.zh: 庫丘林之死：瀕死之犬

region.en: Murthemne Plain near Dun Delgan (Dundalk), Co. Louth, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭勞斯郡敦·德爾岡（鄧多克）附近穆爾西姆尼平原

period: Aided Con Culainn traditions, medieval Irish MSS; Eleanor Hull retelling 1910

source.work: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster (1910), Chapters XXVIII-XXIX, eBook #52963

summary.en: Three venomous spears from the otherworld — 'Wind', 'Good-luck' and 'Cast' — must each kill a king; friends hide the dying hero in the Glen of the Deaf until the Children of the Blast conjure him a phantom sea, and he goes out to die: three spears kill horse, charioteer and king of heroes in turn, and Cuchulainn binds himself standing to a pillar-stone to die upright before his enemies.
summary.zh: 彼岸三毒矛——『風』、『好運』、『擲』——各須殺一王；摯友將垂死英雄藏於失聰谷，直至「疾風之子」幻化海象誘其出戰；三矛依次殺馬、御者、英雄之王，庫丘林立身縛於石柱，直立而死於敵前。

sensitivity.note: The death by three geasa spears is a classic Irish doom-weapon narrative; the standing death is the icon of the cycle, carved on the Standing Stone of the Hero's Sigh.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910: Medb sent a brood of monstrous sprites, half-women, half-goblins, one-eyed in their foreheads, right legs and left arms lopped at the stump, to learn throughout the world the arts that bring men to death; five years they wandered and reached the realm where Vulcan forged his weapons, and from his hand took three spears named Wind, Good-luck and Cast, and three swords, the Wounder, the Hacker and the Hewer. 'By these three spears the splendid Hound shall die; each one of them shall kill a king of Erin, and among those kings the mighty king of Erin's hero-chiefs, whom men call Ulster's Hound.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, chs. XXVIII-XXIX; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 赫爾1910年版本的濃縮改寫：梅芙派遣了一群怪異的妖精，半是女人、半是哥布林，額頭正中只生一隻眼，右腿與左臂皆齊根斬斷，命牠們遍歷世界去學習那些致人於死的技藝；牠們遊蕩了五年，抵達武爾坎鍛造兵器之境，從他手中取走三支名為「風」、「好運」與「投擲」的長矛，以及三把劍，名為「創傷者」、「砍伐者」與「劈削者」。「這三支長矛將使那光榮的獵犬喪命；其中每一支都將殺死一位愛琳之王，而在那些君王之中，便有愛琳英雄之首的強大王，世人稱之為阿爾斯特的獵犬。」非逐字照錄。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Emer and his friends hid the hero in the Glen of the Deaf with music and chess, his weapons taken away. A raven croaked war into his ear; a phantom army of puff-balls and thistle-stalks was raised round the house; on the last day a magic sea rose wave on wave to the door, and Cuchulainn rose with madness upon him — 'I see the horses of Manannan riding on the waves; I hear Manannan's fairy harp; Manannan's ancient face I see beckoning me over the main' — and Emer knew the hour of his fate was come, and armed him herself. The horses wept tears of dusky blood and dropped his weapons at his feet; a maiden of the war-goddess washed his own garments crimson in the stream; he went on, the hero's light brighter than the sun on his forehead. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XXIX; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改寫：艾梅爾與他的友人以音樂和棋戲將這位英雄藏於聾谷之中，並取走了他的兵器。一隻渡鴉在他耳邊啼鳴戰爭；一座由馬勃菌與薊莖構成的幽靈軍隊在屋舍四周升起；到了最後一日，一片魔法之海一浪接一浪地漲至門前，庫胡林起身，狂亂臨於其身——「我看見馬納南的駿馬在浪上奔馳；我聽見馬納南的仙琴；我看見馬納南古老的容顏，正招手喚我渡過大海」——艾梅爾知道他的命數之刻已至，便親自為他披掛。馬匹流下暗色血淚，將他的兵器落在腳前；一位戰女神的少女在溪中將他自己的衣裳染成深紅；他繼續前行，額上英雄之光比太陽更為明亮。非逐字照錄。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Through the day he was alone against a host, and no sword would pierce his skin; then the Wild Women gave the three spears: Curoi's spear pinned the Grey of Macha to the ground; Erc's second spear wounded Cuchulainn and killed Laeg, and he sent his charioteer home with his blessing; Luga's third spear pierced Cuchulainn to the earth. The host stood in a silent ring while he drank at the loch and washed; then he leaned his back against a tall pillar-stone beside the water, bound himself to it with the girdle about his breast, sword in hand — 'I will not die before the men of Erin lying down nor sitting on the ground, but I will die before them standing up.' The Grey of Macha came and laid its head on his breast, weeping; the carrion birds gathered, but the host dared not come near for the hero's light that shone from his forehead; Luga came near, the great sword fell from the dying hand and struck his hand off — and with one deep sigh Cuchulainn's soul parted, and the pillar-stone split, as may be seen to this day. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XXIX; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改寫：整日之間他獨自面對千軍，沒有劍能刺穿他的皮膚；隨後狂野之女給了他三支長矛：庫羅伊之矛將馬哈的灰馬釘在地上；埃爾克之矛第二支傷了庫胡林並殺死萊格，他便祝福之後遣車夫歸家；盧加之矛第三支將庫胡林刺穿於地。眾人圍成沉默的一圈，他則在湖邊飲水洗滌；隨後他背靠水邊一根高聳的石柱，以腰帶繞胸將自己縛於柱上，手持劍——「我不會在愛琳眾男面前倒下而死，也不會坐在地上而死，我要在他們面前站立而死。」馬哈的灰馬前來，將頭枕在他胸前哭泣；食腐之鳥聚集，但眾人因他額上閃耀的英雄之光而不敢靠近；盧加走近，巨劍自垂死的手中落下，斬斷了他的手——庫胡林深深一嘆，靈魂就此離去，石柱亦裂開，至今仍可見到。非逐字照錄。

canonical_translation: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster, London 1910 (public domain); underlying: Aided Con Culainn (Book of Leinster version, ed. and trans. Whitley Stokes, 1902, public domain)

narrative.en:
The death-tale of the Hound of Ulster is built like a judicial execution that the whole otherworld has signed — and the hero, knowing every clause, walks into it upright.

The doom begins in an inventory. Medb, nursing her humiliation at the ford, stirred every enemy Cuchulainn had made and sent a brood of monstrous sprites — half-women, half-goblins, one-eyed in their foreheads, one leg and one arm lopped at the stump — to travel the world for five years and learn all the magic arts that bring men to death. In the realm of Vulcan they took three spears named Wind, Good-luck and Cast, and three swords, the Wounder, the Hacker and the Hewer; and the word of the forge was law: 'By these three spears the splendid Hound shall die; each one of them shall kill a king of Erin, and among those kings the mighty king of Erin's hero-chiefs, the triumphant, heavy-smiting noble youth, whom men call Ulster's Hound.'

The first weapon was concealment. Emer and his friends carried the exhausted hero — still sick from his wounds and his fairy sickness — to the Glen of the Deaf, where no sound of war could reach, took his chariot and weapons away, and set the women to music and chess to hold him. The Children of the Blast worked their lures in order: a raven croaking that Dun Dalgan burned; an army of puff-balls and thistle-stalks shouting round the house; and on the last day a phantom sea, wave on wave rolling to the door — 'I see the horses of Manannan riding on the waves; I hear Manannan's fairy harp play gently over the billows; Manannan's ancient face I see beckoning me over the main.' The seer's word had been: when he saw the horses of the ancient Ocean god, his hour was come. Emer herself armed him then, that he might die a chariot-chief and not a deceived man.

The omens fell in order: the horses wept tears of dusky blood and dropped his weapons at his feet; on the road a maiden of the war-goddess wrung his own garments crimson in a red-running stream — Laeg turned to flee, and the hero said, 'whether I stay I am devoted to death, or whether I go, the span of my life is run out... let me but once more avenge my country's wrongs, and gladly, with joy, I give my life.'

Then the battle, and the law of the three spears. Alone against a host from dewy morn to fall of night, no sword piercing his skin, twice he had the victory and was dragged back; the third time the Wild Women placed the spears in the hands of Curoi's son Luga, of young Erc king of Tara, and of dark Curoi. Curoi's spear missed Cuchulainn and pinned the Grey of Macha to the earth — the horse's death counted as a king's. Erc's spear wounded Cuchulainn's hip and went through to kill Laeg, who took his master's blessing and rode home to Emer to say her husband loved her yet. Luga's spear, thrown at last, rose over all the heads of the host and pierced Cuchulainn to the earth; and the whole army fell silent, standing in a ring, none daring to touch him.

He asked leave to drink at the loch — 'if I come not to you again, I bid you come for me' — drank, washed, and cast himself against a tall pillar-stone beside the water, bound his breast to it with his girdle, took sword in one hand and shield at the other, and said: 'I will not die before the men of Erin lying down nor sitting on the ground, but I will die before them standing up.' The Grey of Macha dragged its spear to him and laid its head, weeping bloody tears, on his breast; carrion birds gathered; the host stood off in awe of the hero's light. When Luga crept near to see whether he lived, the dying hand dropped the sword and struck Luga's hand off — a dead man's last blow — and with a deep sigh Cuchulainn's soul parted from his body, and the sigh split the pillar-stone, as may be seen to this day: the Pillar of the Hero's Dying Sigh.
narrative.zh: 阿爾斯特獵犬之死的故事，其構造如一場全彼岸簽署之處決——而英雄知曉每一條款，仍直立赴死。厄運始於一份清單。梅芙懷渡口受辱之恨，煽動庫丘林所有仇敵，並遣一隊半女半妖、額中獨目之妖物，環遊世界五年、學盡致人於死之魔法。在火神鍛造之地，她們取得三矛：名為『風』、『好運』、『擲』；爐邊之話即法：『此三矛將殺壯麗之獵犬；每矛各殺愛爾蘭一王，而諸王之中，將是人稱阿爾斯特獵犬者。』第一件武器是隱匿。艾默與眾友將力竭之英雄送往失聰谷——該谷不聞戰聲——收走其戰車兵器，令女子以音樂棋局留他。疾風之子依次施誘：烏鴉嘶叫敦·德爾岡已焚；絨球與薊莖組成幻軍繞屋吶喊；末日之時幻海生波、浪浪逼門——『我見瑪南南之馬騎於浪上；我聞瑪南南之仙琴於波間輕奏；我見瑪南南古老之面於海上向我招手。』先知之言曾是：見太古海神之馬之日，即其時辰至之日。艾默遂親自為其披甲，使其以戰車首領而非受欺者之身而死。凶兆依次落下：雙馬泣血淚、兵器落於其足；途中戰神之侍女於紅流之溪中絞洗他自己的衣裳——萊格欲逃，英雄曰：『留亦死，去亦死……讓我再一次復國之仇，欣喜奉上吾命。』繼而戰鬥與三矛之法。自露晨至夜幕孤身敵一軍；第三次，疾風之女將三矛分予庫洛伊之子盧加、塔拉幼王埃爾克、與黑暗之庫洛伊。庫洛伊之矛落空而釘灰駒灰之瑪哈於地——馬之死算作一王。埃爾克之矛傷庫丘林之髖、貫而殺萊格；萊格領主人之祝福騎歸艾默處。盧加之矛越全軍之頂、將庫丘林釘於大地；全軍肅立成環、無人敢近。他求往湖邊解渴——『若我不復返，請你們來找我』——飲水洗身，而後倚水邊高聳之石柱、以胸帶縛身於柱、一手持劍一手持盾：『我不願於阿爾斯特人前臥死或坐死，我願立於他們面前而死。』灰之瑪哈拖矛而來、以泣血之頭伏於其胸；食腐之鳥群集；全軍畏英雄之光而卻步。盧加潛近視其生死，垂死之手鬆劍、斬落盧加一手——死者最後一擊——隨一聲長嘆，庫丘林之魂離其身，嘆聲裂石柱，至今可見：英雄臨終之嘆之柱。

functions: Doom-weapon theology: the three named spears as geasa that must kill kings — fate administered as law
Icon of the standing death: sovereignty retained through the posture of dying, splitting the pillar-stone
The hero's light (loechra) as battle-aura: the visible sign that keeps armies at bay
Etiology of the standing stone at the loch in Murthemne and of the horse's loyalty at death
