title.en: The Death of Conor mac Nessa: the Brain-Ball Bursts
title.zh: 科恩·麥克·內薩之死：腦丸爆裂

region.en: Athnurchar (the Ford of the Sling-cast), Co. Westmeath, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭西米斯郡阿斯努查（彈射渡口）

period: Aided Conchobuir tradition, medieval Irish MSS; Rolleston retelling 1911

source.work: T. W. Rolleston, Myths & Legends of the Celtic Race (1911), Chapter VI, eBook #34081

summary.en: Conall of the Victories kills the king of Leinster unjustly and mixes the dead king's brains with lime into a sling-stone; the Connacht champion Ket finds it in Emain's treasury and years later slings it into Conor's forehead; the ball is sewn up with golden thread under a taboo of passion and horse-riding — until the king hears of a hill far away where a man hangs between two criminals, and the brain-ball bursts with his fury.
summary.zh: 勝利者科納爾不義地殺死萊因斯特王，取其腦髓混石灰製彈石；康諾特勇士康特於埃馬因寶庫尋得之，數年後彈射入科恩前額；腦丸以金線縫合、王受戒不得激憤騎馬——直至他聞知遠方山丘上有男子懸於二罪犯之間，激憤之下腦丸爆裂。

sensitivity.note: The Christianizing ending (Conor's death at the news of the Crucifixion) is a famous interpolation that welds the pagan Ulster cycle onto Christian chronology; retold from public-domain print.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911: An unjust and cruel attack had been made by Conor on Mesgedra, king of Leinster, in which that monarch met his death at the hand of Conall of the Victories. Conall took out the brains of the dead king and mingled them with lime to make a sling-stone — such 'brain balls' being accounted the most deadly of missiles — and the ball was laid up in the king's treasure-house at Emain Macha, where the Connacht champion Ket son of Maga found it one day when prowling in disguise through Ulster, and kept it always by him. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 羅爾斯頓1911年版本的濃縮改寫：康納曾對倫斯特王梅斯格拉發動一場不義而殘酷的攻擊，那位君主便死於「勝利者」康納爾之手。康納爾取出死王的腦髓，與石灰混合製成一顆投石——此類「腦丸」被視為最致命的投擲物——這顆腦丸被存放在埃曼瑪哈的王室寶庫中，康納特的勇士、瑪加之子凱特某日喬裝潛行於阿爾斯特時發現了它，此後便一直帶在身邊。非逐字照錄。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: The Connacht men took a spoil of cattle from Ulster, and the Ulstermen under Conor overtook them at a river-ford still called Athnurchar, the Ford of the Sling-cast, in Westmeath. Many of the ladies of Connacht came to their side of the river to view the famous Ulster warriors, and Conor drew near to show himself; Ket, lurking in ambush, rose and slung the brain-ball at Conor, striking him full in the forehead. His physician Fingen pronounced that if the ball were extracted he must die; it was sewn up with golden thread, and the king was bidden to keep himself from horse-riding and from all vehement passion and exertion, and he would do well. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改寫：康納特人擄掠了阿爾斯特的牛群，康納率領的阿爾斯特人在一處河灘追上他們，該地至今仍名為阿斯努爾哈，意即「投石之灘」，位於西米斯。康納特的許多貴婦來到河對岸，觀看那些著名的阿爾斯特戰士，康納便走近以展示自己；凱特潛伏於暗處，起身將腦丸擲向康納，正中他的額頭。他的醫師芬根斷言，若取出腦丸，他必死無疑；於是腦丸以金線縫合於內，並囑咐國王遠離騎馬，避免一切激烈的情緒與勞累，便可安然無恙。非逐字照錄。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Seven years afterwards Conor saw the sun darken at noonday and summoned his druid, who in a magic trance saw a hill in a distant land with three crosses on it, and a human form nailed to each, and one of them like the Immortals. 'Is he a malefactor?' asked Conor. 'Nay, but the Son of the living God,' said the druid, and told the king the story of the death of Christ. Conor broke out in fury, and drawing his sword hacked at the oak-trees in the sacred grove crying 'Thus would I deal with his enemies!' — and with the excitement and exertion the brain-ball burst from his head, and he fell dead. And thus was the vengeance of Mesgedra fulfilled. With Conor and with Cuchulainn the glory of the Red Branch and the dominance of Ulster passed away. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改寫：七年之後，康納見正午時分太陽昏暗，便召來他的德魯伊，德魯伊在魔法恍惚中看見遠方一座山丘，上面立著三個十字架，每個十字架上都釘著一個人形，其中一個宛如不朽之神。「他是罪犯嗎？」康納問道。「不，他是永生神的兒子。」德魯伊說道，並向國王講述了基督之死的故事。康納勃然大怒，拔出劍來砍向聖林中的橡樹，喊道：「我願如此對待他的仇敵！」——隨著這番激動與用力，腦丸從他頭中迸出，他倒地而死。梅斯格拉的復仇便如此得償。隨著康納與庫胡林的逝去，赤枝的榮耀與阿爾斯特的霸權也一同消逝了。非逐字照錄。

canonical_translation: T. W. Rolleston, Myths & Legends of the Celtic Race, London 1911 (public domain); underlying: Aided Conchobuir (Book of the Dun Cow version, ed. and trans. Kuno Meyer, 1894, public domain)

narrative.en:
The death of Conor mac Nessa is the Ulster cycle's most curious ending: a pagan king killed by an unhealed wound reopened at the news of a foreign execution — myth stitching itself onto history.

The wound begins as an atrocity. An unjust and cruel attack was made by Conor on Mesgedra, king of Leinster, in which that monarch met his death at the hand of Conall of the Victories. Conall took out the brains of the dead king and mingled them with lime to make a sling-stone — such 'brain balls' being accounted the most deadly of missiles in Irish warfare — and the ball was laid up in the king's treasure-house at Emain Macha. There the Connacht champion Ket son of Maga, prowling through Ulster in disguise, found it one day and kept it always by him: a king's death carried as a pocket weapon.

Its hour came at a cattle-spoil. The Connacht men drove a spoil from Ulster, and the Ulstermen under Conor overtook them at a river-ford in Westmeath still called Athnurchar, the Ford of the Sling-cast. The ladies of Connacht crowded to their bank to see the famous Ulster warriors, and Conor — the stateliest man of his time — drew near the water to show himself to the women; and Ket, lurking in ambush, rose and slung the brain-ball into the king's forehead. Conor fell and was carried living to Emain, where his physician Fingen pronounced that if the ball were extracted he must die; it was sewn up with golden thread, and the king was bidden to keep himself from horse-riding and from all vehement passion and exertion — a geis on emotion itself, and one of the strangest medical prescriptions in medieval literature.

Seven years he lived so. Then, one noon, Conor saw the sun darken, and summoned his druid, who in a magic trance traveled in vision to a hill in a distant land on which stand three crosses, with a human form nailed to each, and one of them like the Immortals. 'Is he a malefactor?' asked Conor. 'Nay,' says the druid, 'but the Son of the living God,' and he told the king the story of the death of Christ. Conor broke out in fury — the only recorded act of the King of Ulster's wrath being incurred on behalf of a foreign god — and drawing his sword hacked at the oak-trees in the sacred grove, crying, 'Thus would I deal with his enemies!' And with the excitement and exertion the brain-ball burst from his head, and he fell dead. Thus was the vengeance of Mesgedra fulfilled: the murdered king of Leinster reached through seven years and one darkened noon to kill his killer's killer's king. With Conor and with Cuchulainn the glory of the Red Branch and the dominance of Ulster passed away, and the next cycle — the Ossianic — brought different characters, different forests, and different ideals of life.
narrative.zh: 科恩·麥克·內薩之死乃阿爾斯特故事圈最奇特之結局：異國處決的消息使一處未癒之傷復裂，殺死異教之王——神話自行縫入歷史。創傷始於暴行。科恩不義地攻擊萊因斯特王梅斯蓋德拉，該王死於勝利者科納爾之手。科納爾取出死者腦髓、混以石灰製成彈石——此類『腦丸』被視為愛爾蘭戰爭中最致命之投射武器——而彈石被藏於埃馬因·瑪哈王之寶庫。康諾特勇士康特·馬加之子偽裝潛行阿爾斯特時一日尋得之，隨身攜帶：以一位國王之死為口袋兵器。其時機於一場牛群劫掠中到來。康諾特人自阿爾斯特驅走牛群，科恩率阿爾斯特人於西米斯郡至今仍稱阿斯努查（彈射渡口）之河渡追上。康諾特貴婦擁至河岸觀看阿爾斯特名將，科恩近水展示己身；埋伏之康特起身、以腦丸彈射入王之前額。科恩倒地、活著被抬回埃馬因，醫師芬根判定：若取出彈丸必死；彈丸以金線縫合，王受戒：不得騎馬、不得有任何激烈情緒與勞累——對情緒本身之geis。如此七年。一日正午，科恩見日頭變暗，召其德魯伊；德魯伊於魔法出神中神遊至遠方一山丘，丘上有三具十字架、各釘一人形，其一似不朽者。『他是罪犯嗎？』科恩問。『非也，』德魯伊答，『乃永生上帝之子。』並向王講述基督之死。科恩勃然大怒——阿爾斯特之王之憤怒惟一一次為異國之神而發——拔劍砍伐聖林橡樹，呼曰：『我將如此對待他的敵人！』激憤與勞累之間，腦丸自其頭顱迸出，王倒地而死。梅斯蓋德拉之復仇就此完成。科恩與庫丘林既亡，紅枝之榮光與阿爾斯特之霸權隨之而去；下一個故事圈——奧西恩系——帶來不同人物、不同森林與不同的生活理想。

functions: Theology of the unhealed wound: vengeance delayed through an object (the brain-ball) rather than a person
Christian chronology hinge: the pagan king dies at the news of the Crucifixion, dating the heroic age to the life of Christ
Geis on passion: a kingship of regulated emotion — the medical taboo as constitutional restraint
Etiology of Athnurchar (the Ford of the Sling-cast) in Westmeath

title.en: Bricriu of the Poison-Tongue: Incitement and Death Under the Bulls
title.zh: 毒舌布里克魯：挑撥與公牛之下的死亡

region.en: Tarbga in Mag Ai (Rathcroghan), Connacht, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭康諾特馬格艾之塔爾布加（拉思克羅根）

period: Tain Bo Cuailnge Recension I (Book of the Dun Cow, c. 1100); Faraday translation 1904

source.work: Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (1904), eBook #14391

summary.en: Bricriu Poison-tongue, the Ulster cycle's professional inciter, heckles Cuchulainn into breaking the Morrígan's shapes in the ford — then, years later, after Fergus has broken his head at chess, he crawls west in sadness to watch the two god-bulls fight at Tarbga, and the bulls go fighting over him and he dies; that is the Death of Bricriu.
summary.zh: 阿爾斯特故事圈之職業挑撥者——毒舌布里克魯——於渡口以譏言激庫丘林擊破摩里岡之百形；多年後，弗格斯弈棋擊破其頭，他悲傷西行觀二神牛於塔爾布加相鬥，二牛竟越其身而鬥，遂死——是為布里克魯之死。

sensitivity.note: Bricriu's death beneath the fighting bulls closes both the trickster and the bull-war theodicy of the Táin; the incitement scene includes the eel/wolf/heifer shapes owed to Táin Bó Regamna.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904: Bricriu Poison-tongue Mac Carbatha rose and began inciting Cuchulainn: 'Your strength is gone, when it is a little salmon that overthrows you when the Ulstermen are at hand coming to you out of their sickness yonder. Grievous for you to undertake a hero's deed in the presence of the men of Ireland and to ward off a formidable warrior in arms thus!' Therewith Cuchulainn arose and struck the eel so that its ribs broke in it, and the cattle were driven over the hosts eastwards; the she-wolf attacked him, and he threw a stone from his sling so that her eye broke in her head; and she came in the form of a hornless red heifer before the cows upon the pools and fords, and he threw a stone at the hornless red heifer so that her leg broke under her. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 法雷1904年著作的濃縮改寫：布里克里烏·毒舌·麥克·卡爾巴薩起身，開始煽動庫胡林：「你的力量已失，因為當烏爾斯特人從那邊的病榻中前來尋你時，竟是一條小鮭魚將你擊倒。你竟要在愛爾蘭眾男兒面前行英雄之舉，如此抵擋一名全副武裝的可怕戰士，於你實為可悲！」於是庫胡林起身擊打那條鰻魚，使牠體內的肋骨斷裂，牛群被驅趕著越過眾人向東而去；那母狼攻擊他，他便從投石索擲出一塊石頭，擊破了她頭上的眼睛；她又化為一頭無角紅母牛，出現在池沼與淺灘上牛群之前，他便向那無角紅母牛擲石，打斷了她身下的腿。非逐字照錄。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Then Cuchulainn did to the Morrígan the three things that he had promised her in the Táin Bó Regamna, and fought Loch in the ford with the gae bolga. At the end of the Táin the Bull of Cooley met the White-horned at Tarbga in Mag Ai, and every one who escaped the fight was intent on nothing but beholding the two bulls fighting. Bricriu Poison-tongue was in the west in his sadness after Fergus had broken his head with his draughtmen; he came with the rest to see the combat of the bulls. The two bulls went in fighting over Bricriu, so that he died therefrom. That is the Death of Bricriu. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改寫：隨後庫胡林對莫莉根做了他在《雷加姆納牛掠》中曾向她許諾的三件事，並在淺灘以蓋博爾加矛與洛赫交戰。在《牛掠》的末尾，庫利之牛與白角牛在馬格艾的塔爾布加相遇，凡從戰鬥中逃脫的人無不一心只想觀看兩牛相鬥。布里克里烏·毒舌因費格斯用其飲酒之角擊破他的頭，正滿懷悲傷地待在西方；他也隨眾人前來觀看兩牛之鬥。兩牛邊鬥邊從布里克里烏身上踏過，他因此而死。這便是布里克里烏之死。非逐字照錄。

canonical_translation: Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge, London 1904 (public domain); underlying: Táin Bó Cúailnge Recension I (Leabhar na hUidre, RIA MS 23 E 25, c. 1100)

narrative.en:
Bricriu of the Poison-tongue is the Ulster cycle's engine of plot — the satirist whose profession is to make heroes do stupid things — and the Táin grants him the strangest death in the cycle: crushed by the gods' own bulls.

His trade is incitement. In the middle of the Táin, when Cuchulainn is struggling at the ford with the Morrígan's shapes, Fergus can only tell his men to taunt the hero so that 'he may not fall for nothing' — and Bricriu rises to the work with relish: 'Your strength is gone, when it is a little salmon that overthrows you when the Ulstermen are at hand coming to you out of their sickness yonder. Grievous for you to undertake a hero's deed in the presence of the men of Ireland and to ward off a formidable warrior in arms thus!' Stung, Cuchulainn rises and does to the Morrígan the three things he had promised her in the Táin Bó Regamna: he strikes the eel so that its ribs break in it; when she comes as a she-wolf he breaks her eye with a sling-stone; when she comes as a hornless red heifer walking before the cows through the fords, he breaks her leg. The goddess retreats — three shapes, three wounds, the debt of the earlier tale paid — and the god-loans of the hero's anger are banked at Bricriu's word.

The great comic ending waits for the end of the war. After the Táin's battle, the two bulls of the gods met at Tarbga in Mag Ai, and every man who had escaped the war stood about only to watch them fight. Bricriu, in his sadness in the west — after Fergus had broken his head with the draughtmen at a game of chess, an insult recorded in the Echtra Nerai — came with the rest to see the combat. And the two bulls went in fighting over Bricriu, so that he died therefrom: the professional auditor of other men's duels is audited by the duel itself. 'That is the Death of Bricriu,' says the Táin, with the dry economy of a law-report — the only death in the cycle administered by cattle, and the exact penalty of a life spent whetting other men's violence.
narrative.zh: 毒舌布里克魯乃阿爾斯特故事圈之情節引擎——其職業即誘使英雄做蠢事之諷刺家——《奪牛記》賜他全圈最奇之死：被神之公牛碾斃。其業為挑撥。《奪牛記》中段，庫丘林在渡口與摩里岡之形搏鬥，弗格斯只能命部下嘲諷英雄『使其不至徒勞而死』——布里克魯欣然起身應工：『你的力量完了！區區一條鮭魚竟能擊倒你——阿爾斯特的人正從病中向你走來！在愛爾蘭眾人面前行英雄之舉、持械迎擊強敵——何等可悲！』庫丘林被刺而起身，行他在雷甘那牛劫記中許諾摩里岡的三事：擊鰻至肋骨斷於其中；她化母狼襲來，他以彈石碎其目；她化無角赤牝牛、牛群之前行於渡池，他擲石斷其腿。女神退卻——三形三傷，前篇之債已償——英雄之怒的信用記於布里克魯的話上。偉大的滑稽結局等著戰爭之末。戰後，二神牛於馬格艾之塔爾布加相會，凡自戰火逃脫之人皆只為觀牛鬥而立。布里克魯西行而悲——因弗格斯弈棋時以棋子擊破其頭，此辱記於奈拉的歷險——隨眾而來觀鬥。二牛竟於布里克魯之上相鬥而行，他因此而死。『是為布里克魯之死，』《奪牛記》以法律報告之乾燥筆法記之——全圈唯一由牛執行的死刑，亦是一生磨利他人暴力者之精確刑罰。

functions: Charter of the satirist's power: one insult redirects a hero's wrath against the divine
Comic theodicy of the Táin: the bull-duel as instrument of justice on the professional inciter
Interlace mechanism: Bricriu's taunt fuses two pre-tales (Regamna and the ford combats) into one action
Etiology of Tarbga (Bull-sorrow/Bull-fight) in Mag Ai

title.en: The Apparition of the Great Queen: the Driving of the Morrígan's Cow
title.zh: 偉大女王之顯形：驅趕摩里岡之牛

region.en: Dun Imrid (near Dundalk), Co. Louth, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭勞斯郡敦·伊姆里德（鄧多克附近）

period: Táin Bó Regamna, Yellow Book of Lecan (14th c.) and Egerton 1782; Leahy translation 1905

source.work: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, Volume II (1905), 'The Apparition of the Great Queen to Cuchulain', eBook #5679

summary.en: A cry from the north wakes Cuchulainn at Dun Imrid; a one-legged chestnut horse hauls a chariot with the pole passed through its body, a red woman drives a cow before her, and her name is unpronounceable; when he spears her she names herself the Morrígan, guardian of his death, and prophesies the Raid of Cúailnge — and the three shapes she will take against him: eel, wolf, white red-eared heifer.
summary.zh: 北方呼聲驚醒敦·伊姆里德的庫丘林；一條獨腿栗色馬拉車、轅貫其身，紅衣女子驅牛於前，名不可讀；他以矛相脅，她自名摩里岡、其死之守護者，預言庫利牛劫——並預言她將化之三形：鰻、狼、白身紅耳牝牛。

sensitivity.note: The Morrígan offers Cuchulainn her love in the fuller tradition ('I will come to you and take the semblance of a woman'); her shape-shifts here are exactly those paid back in the Táin's ford combats.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905: At Dun Imrid lay Cuchulainn and slept, when a cry rang out from the north; he fell as he woke from his slumber with the thud of a weight to the ground, and sought the chariot. At the ford of the Double Wonder a chariot rattled toward them from the clay-soiled Coolgarry land: a one-legged chestnut charger was harnessed to draw it, and right through the horse's body the pole of the car had passed, made fast to a halter across his forehead with a wedge. A red woman sat in the chariot, bright red were her eyebrows, a crimson cloak about her whose folds touched the plain, and close by her side a mighty giant strode, on his back a two-forked hazel staff, goading a cow that shambled on before. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 利希1905年著作的濃縮改寫：庫胡林在伊姆里德堡躺下入睡，忽有一聲呼喊自北方響起；他從睡夢中驚醒，如重物般砰然落地，隨即尋覓戰車。在雙奇之灘，一輛戰車自沾滿泥土的庫爾加里地方轆轆駛向他們：拉車的是一匹單腿栗色駿馬，車轅直穿過馬身，以楔子牢牢繫在牠額前的一條韁繩上。車中坐著一名紅衣女子，她的雙眉鮮紅，一襲深紅斗篷的褶邊垂及地面，緊隨她身側有一名魁梧巨人闊步而行，背上扛著一根雙叉榛木杖，驅趕著一頭蹣跚前行的母牛。非逐字照錄。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: 'Ye who drive that cow do wrong, for against her will do ye drive her!' cried Cuchulainn. 'Not to thee doth that cow belong.' The woman's name was unpronounceable — Coom-diewr-folt-skayv-garry-skye-ooa; the giant was Darry I mac Feena, and she was driving a cow home in fee for a poem. Cuchulainn leaped at the chariot, set his spear-point on her head, and bade her cease her sharp weapon-play and tell her name; her song was a song of insult, and when he sprang again the woman, the horse, the chariot, the cow and the man disappeared — she passed into the shape of a black bird on a bough. 'As a woman of danger I know you,' he cried. 'Evil in sooth can I send; of thy Bringer of Death I am guardian, shall guard it till cometh thine end. From the Under-world Country of Croghan this cow have I driven... So long as her calf be a yearling, for that time thy life shall endure; but then shall the dread Raid of Cualgne have beginning.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改寫：「你們這些驅趕那頭母牛的人做錯了，因為你們是違背她的意願驅趕她！」庫胡林喊道。「那頭母牛並不屬於你。」那女子的名字難以發音——庫姆迪厄爾福爾特斯凱夫加里斯基烏阿；那巨人是達里·伊·麥克·菲納，而她正驅趕一頭母牛回家，作為一首詩的酬勞。庫胡林躍向戰車，將矛尖抵在她頭上，命她停止那凌厲的兵器之戲並報上名來；她的歌是一首侮辱之歌，當他再次躍起時，那女子、馬、戰車、母牛與那男子全都消失了——她化作一隻黑鳥棲於枝頭。「我認得你，你是個危險的女子，」他喊道。「我確實能降下災禍；我是你那帶來死亡者的守護者，將守護它直到你的終結來臨。這頭母牛是我從克羅漢的冥界之國驅趕而來……只要她的牛犢尚是一歲之齡，你的性命便在此期間得以存續；但此後，庫爾格涅的可怕牛掠便將開始。」非逐字照錄。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: 'Thou shalt see me return alive from the Táin!' vowed Cuchulainn. 'How canst thou that strife be surviving?' sang the woman: when he contends with a hero as fearful and as strong as himself, 'then, in shape of an eel round thee coiling, thy feet at the Ford I will bind'; he swore he would break her on a green stone; then 'as a wolf myself shaping, I will spring on thee eager to slay, I will tear the flesh from thy chest from arm to arm'; he vowed spear-blows would force her to fly; then she would come 'as a heifer, white-skinned, but with ears that are red,' and a hundred white red-eared cows trampling him would take his head from him. The Morrígan, the great Battle Queen, departed with her cow to Rath Croghan and was seen no more by Cuchulainn — and the region took the name of the Clay-land of Evil from her deeds. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改寫：「你將見我從《牛掠》中生還！」庫胡林立誓道。「你怎能在那場爭鬥中倖存？」那女子唱道：當他與一名和他同樣可怖、同樣強悍的英雄相搏時，「那時，我將化作鰻魚纏繞你身，在淺灘縛住你的雙腳」；他發誓要將她砸碎在青石上；接著「我將化作狼形，急切地撲向你欲將你殺死，我將從你的胸膛上、從一臂到另一臂撕下皮肉」；他發誓矛擊必將逼她逃遁；接著她將化作「一頭母牛，白皮而紅耳」，一百頭白皮紅耳的母牛將把他踏於蹄下，取走他的頭顱。莫莉根，偉大的戰鬥女王，帶著她的母牛離去，前往拉斯克羅漢，庫胡林再也沒有見到她——而該地區因她的所作所為而得名「邪惡之泥地」。非逐字照錄。

canonical_translation: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, Vol. II, London 1905 (public domain); underlying: Táin Bó Regamna, ed. and trans. Ernst Windisch, Irische Texte II (1887), public domain

narrative.en:
Before the Táin begins, the war-goddess comes to audit the hero — the Táin Bó Regamna is the auditors' story that prices Cuchulainn's fate in cattle, prophecy and unpronounceable names.

At Dun Imrid lay Cuchulainn and slept, when a cry rang out from the north; he woke and fell with the thud of a weight to the ground. At the ford of the Double Wonder a chariot rattled toward them from the clay-soiled Coolgarry land, and it was harnessed wrongly on purpose: a one-legged chestnut charger drew it, the chariot-pole passing right through the horse's body, made fast to a halter across the forehead with a wedge — a vehicle from nightmare, driven by physics that deny the animal. In it sat a red woman, her eyebrows bright red, her crimson cloak's folds touching the plain, with two poles behind her and her mantle streaming between; and a mighty giant strode by her side with a two-forked hazel staff on his back, goading a shuffling cow ahead.

'Ye who drive that cow do wrong, for against her will do ye drive her!' cried Cuchulainn, claiming the cattle of Ulster as his to guard — and got only insoluble names for answer: the man was Uar-gaeth-sceo-luachair-sceo, then Faebor-begbeoil-cuimdiuir-folt-seenb-gairit-sceo-uath; the woman Coom-diewr-folt-skayv-garry-skye-ooa. Then he admitted the man's name was plain Darry I mac Feena, owner of the Dun of Cúailnge itself, and the cow was the fee for a poem. Cuchulainn sprang at the chariot, set his spear-point on her head and demanded her true name; her song was a song of insult; and when he sprang again, woman, horse, chariot, cow and man vanished together — she into the shape of a black bird on a bough. 'As a woman of danger I know you, and as powerful in spell!' 'Evil in sooth can I send. Of thy Bringer of Death I am guardian, and shall guard it till cometh thine end: from the Under-world Country of Croghan this cow have I driven, to breed by the Dun Bull of Darry mac Feena; so long as her calf be a yearling, for that time thy life shall endure; but then shall the dread Raid of Cúailnge have beginning.'

Then the duel of futures. He vowed to return alive from the Táin with bards singing of it; she sang the terms of his death with the three shapes she would wear against him — an eel coiling round his feet at the ford ('on a green stone by me shall be broken that eel,' he swore), a wolf springing on him to tear the flesh from his chest ('I will force thee to fly with blows of my spear-shaft'), and a white-skinned, red-eared heifer among a hundred red-eared cows, trampling him at a lake by the ford so that his head is smitten from him ('a stone for a cast will I take... thy right or thy left leg will break'). He promised her the wounds; she promised him the shapes; and the great Battle Queen went with her cow to Rath Croghan and was seen no more by Cuchulainn — and the ground took the name of the Clay-land of Evil from her deeds. Every promise in this tale is paid in full in the Táin's ford combats: a prophecy written in the grammar of livestock.
narrative.zh: 《奪牛記》開始之前，戰神即來查帳——雷甘那牛劫記即以牛群、預言與不可讀之名為庫丘林之命定價之查帳故事。庫丘林臥於敦·伊姆里德而眠，北方呼聲驚起；醒時如負重物砰然倒地。於「雙奇渡口」，一輛戰車自泥地庫爾加里嘎然而來，其轅故意錯配：一匹獨腿栗色馬拉之、車轅貫穿馬體、以楔固於額前之籠頭——噩夢之車、否定動物之物理。車中坐一紅衣女子，眉如赤霞、深紅披風之褶觸地；身側一偉岸巨人，背負兩叉榛杖，驅一頭蹣跚之牛於前。『驅牛者行不義，此牛非自願而行！』庫丘林喊道，稱阿爾斯特牛群盡屬他護——得到的只是不可解之名：其人先名烏爾-蓋特-斯凱歐-盧阿希爾-斯凱歐，又名法博爾-貝格貝奧爾-庫姆迪維爾-福爾特-塞恩布-加里特-斯凱歐-烏阿特；其女名庫姆-迪埃爾-福爾特-斯凱夫-加里-斯凱歐-烏阿。然後他承認其人名為達里·麥克·菲納——庫利環堡之主本身——而牛乃一首詩之酬金。庫丘林撲向戰車、矛尖置其首、索其真名；她的歌是一首侮辱之詩；他再度撲去時，女子、馬、戰車、牛與人一同消失——她化為枝上一黑鳥。『我識得你，危險之女，咒術強大！』『我能降禍於你。我是你死亡使者之守護者，必守至你終結之時：我自克魯亨冥世之地驅牛而來、與達里之棕牛相伴；其犢未滿歲，你命尚存；犢一歲，可怖的庫利牛劫便將開始。』繼而是未來之決鬥。他誓將自奪牛記生還、得吟遊詩人之歌；她則唱出他死亡之條款與她將化之三形——渡口纏繞其足之鰻（他誓將她於綠石上擊碎）、撕裂其胸膛之狼（他誓以矛桿之擊迫使她逃）、與百頭紅耳牛群中踐踏他的白身紅耳牝牛（他誓以彈石斷其右腿或左腿）。他許以傷，她許以形；偉大的戰后攜牛往拉思克羅根而去，庫丘林再未見她——該地因她之事而得「惡土」之名。此篇中每句諾言皆於《奪牛記》渡口之戰中全數兌現：以牲畜之文法寫成之預言。

functions: Prophecy of the hero's death in cattle grammar: fate priced as livestock and calf-years
Inventory of the Morrígan's three shapes: the eel, wolf and heifer paid back in the Táin's combats
The unpronounceable-name riddling: power withheld through names that cannot be spoken
Etiology of the Clay-land of Evil (Grellach Dolluid) and of the cow that breeds the Táin's bull-war

narrative.en:
The skaldic-reception file holds the court-poetry's mythic citations. The shield-poems: the myth-panels (Bragi's Ragnarsdrapa and Thjodolfr's Haustlong - the records norse-thor-fishing-serpent and norse-haustlong-skaldic: the corpus's oldest narrative-myth witnesses), the poets' ekphrasis as the courts' myth-books.

The genealogy-lays: the god-descent sung for jarls (Eyvindr's Háleygjatal - the record norse-jarls-foundation-stories' title-deeds; the mythic genealogy as court-commission), the cult-verses: the halls' images described (Úlfr Uggason's Húsdrápa: Baldr's funeral, Thor's fishing and Heimdall's? - the hall's painted walls skaldically narrated - the skald as the interior's guide-book), and the temple-verses: the exploits sung (Eysteinn's fishing-stanzas; Eilifr's Geirrod-lay - the records' skaldic witnesses).

The kenning-census completes the catalog: the myths as working vocabulary ('the? - mead? - 'of? - Odin? - 'for? - poetry; 'Ymir's? - 'blood? - 'for? - the? - sea; 'Freya's? - tears? - 'for? - gold? - - each kenning a myth-citation, the record norse-kenning-origin's grammar evidenced across the whole corpus). The record's cultural functions are the reception-catalog doctrine (the myth corpus's oldest continuous witness: the skaldic corpus documenting the myths' circulation century by century) and the citation-economy doctrine (each poem a myth-citation's receipt: the myths' court-currency documented). In the atlas, the record anchors the skaldic-reception family: each a tradition's court-poetry citation-file; the Norse one is distinctive in the kenning-economy.

For the database, this node indexes the skaldic-records already in the corpus: here the citation-census.

The catalog's chronology completes the register: the citations dated century by century (the 9th-century shield-poems' myths, the 10th-century genealogy-lays, the 11th-century cult-verses, the 12th-century lausavisur) - the skaldic-reception file as a timeline of the myth corpus's court-currency: which myths the courts still knew, and when, documented poem by poem. And the meter's discipline completes it: the dróttkvætt constraints guaranteeing the citations' antiquity (the myths embedded in verse-forms that could not be casually invented) - the reception-file's dating-method documented.

The file's lost-layer problem completes the register: the skaldic corpus's losses documented (the poems known only through quotations - Snorri's Edda preserving verses whose long poems are gone), so the reception-file's witnesses are fragments of a destroyed library: the citation-census compiled from survivals, the myth-corpus's court-currency known only where the quotations kept it. And the database's own use completes it: the skaldic citations as the corpus's dating-instrument (the myths' antiquity argued from the verse's attestation) - the reception-file working as the myth database's chronometer.

 The file’s Havamal-citation completes it: the wisdom-lay’s own verses cited in the court-tradition (the guest-craft maxims quoted in the sagas’ halls) - the reception-file’s reach documented from the shield-poems to the proverb-book.

title.en: Iconographic Episodes: The Myths Carved on Stones, Portals and Manuscripts

summary.en: The myth-corpus's picture-file: the Altuna stone (Thor's fishing carved with the hammer raised: 'the? - 'one? - 'stone? - 'with? - 'the? - 'whole? - scene), the Gotland picture-stones (Tjängvide's rider on the eight-legged horse - Odin's Sleipnir-ride carved; Ardre's hall-scenes), the runestone panels (the Sigurd-scenes of the record norse-sigurd-rune-stones; the Gosforth cross - the record norse-gosforth-cross), the stave-church portals (the Hylestad cycle), and the manuscript-drawings (the 17th-century Edda-paper MSS' illustrated myth-sheets: the myths drawn for learned readers). The record is the picture-register file.

language: Old Norse iconography (carved stone, wood, parchment)
canonical_translation: Identifications per standard iconographic scholarship; labeled

narrative.en:
The picture-register file holds the myth corpus's carved and drawn register. The Altuna stone: the fishing carved (the god, the ox-head bait, the hammer raised - the record norse-thor-fishing-serpent's scene in stone: 'the? - 'whole? - 'fishing? - 'on? - 'one? - face? - - the iconographic case-study). The Gotland picture-stones: the rider on the eight-legged horse (Tjängvide's mounted figure above the hall-scene - Odin's Sleipnir-ride carved for the dead: the ride-to-Valhalla as picture), and Ardre's scenes (the hall-images and the smith-scene - the Ardre VIII stone's Völundr-panels: the record norse-volund-smith's iconographic twin).

The runestone panels and portals: the Sigurd-scenes and the Ragnarök-cross (the records' carved material - the dragon-slayer and the doom on Christian stone), and the manuscript-drawings: the 17th-century myth-sheets (the Edda-paper MSS' illustrated pages: the myths drawn for the learned collectors - the corpus's picture-reception's late register). The record's cultural functions are the picture-register doctrine (the myths documented in image independent of the manuscripts: the iconography as a parallel witness-stream) and the image-context doctrine (each carving in its context: the memorial, the church-door, the collector's page - the pictures' functions dated by their settings). In the atlas, the record anchors the picture-register family: each a tradition's myth-image file; the Norse one spans stone to parchment.

For the database, this node complements the carved-records: here the pictures' file.

The file's identifications-method completes the register: the picture-record's evidentiary care documented (each carving's reading argued from the attributes: the eight legs, the ox-head, the heart - the iconography's grammar reconstructed attribute by attribute), so the picture-file's method is the database's own: inference from documented detail, with uncertainties labeled. And the manuscript-drawings' provenance completes it: the 17th-century myth-sheets' collectors (the learned Icelanders drawing the gods for the antiquarian market) - the picture-register's late layer documented as scholarship's first illustrated mythology.

The file's geographic-spread completes the register: the images' distribution documented (the Gotlandic picture-stones, the Swedish runestones, the English crosses, the Norwegian portals - one iconography across the Norse world's coasts), so the picture-file's reach is the diaspora's: the myths carved wherever the Norse settled, the image-register mapping the tradition's territory. And the dating-method completes it: the carvings' styles sequenced (the ornament-chronology used to date the myth-scenes) - the picture-register's chronology documented by style, the images' order argued from their borders.

 The file’s Gosforth-junction completes it: the English cross’s panels joining the Swedish stones in one register - the picture-file’s geography spanning the whole Norse world, the images dated and compared across the sea.

summary.en: The late-medieval compendia's file: Trójumanna saga (the Trojan War's Norse retelling: the classical epic translated into saga-prose), Breta sögur (Geoffrey's Historia regum Britanniae in Norse: the British kings' book), and Merlínússpá (Gunnlaugr Leifsson's verse translation of Merlin's prophecies in eddic metre - 'the? - 'prophecies? - 'sung? - 'in? - 'the? - old? - measure? - - the French prophecy translated into the North's prophetic form). The record is the learned-reception file: the imported prophecies read in the native genre.
summary.zh: 晚期中世紀彙編檔案：《特洛伊薩迦》（以薩迦散文轉述特洛伊戰爭——古典史詩的北歐化）、《布列塔尼人之書》（傑弗里的《不列顛諸王史》之諾斯譯本），以及《梅林預言詩》（貢勞格·萊夫松以埃達韻律譯寫的梅林預言——「以古體韻律吟唱的預言」：法蘭西預言被譯入北方的預言文體）。此記錄是博學接受檔案：外來預言以本土文體閱讀。

canonical_translation: Older editions (Hauksbok; learned-saga editions); paraphrase

narrative.en:
The learned-reception file holds the imported-myth register. Trójumanna saga: the classical epic in saga-prose (the Trojan War translated for the Norse courts - the Dares-Phrygius tradition's saga-form: the classical heroes made saga-kings), and Breta sögur: the British book in Norse (Geoffrey's Historia translated - the British kings' and Arthur's material entering the north's bookshelf).

Merlínússpá completes the file: the prophecies translated into the native genre (Gunnlaugr Leifsson's verse rendering of the Prophetiae Merlini - 'the? - 'prophecies? - 'sung? - 'in? - 'the? - old? - measure? - - the imported prophecy wearing the eddic form: the sibyl-tradition (the record norse-voluspa-sibyl) meeting Merlin - the reception's mirror: the North's prophecy-genre used to carry the imported doom). The record's cultural functions are the learned-translation doctrine (the romances translated into saga-prose: the North's bookshelf internationalized) and the genre-mirror doctrine (the imported prophecy carried in the native prophetic metre - the corpus's reception-datum: how the North read foreign dooms through its own). In the atlas, the record anchors the learned-romance family: each a tradition's imported-myth register; the Norse one is distinctive in the metre.

For the database, this node documents the late-medieval compendia: the reception-file's learned layer.

The file's translation-method completes the register: the romances' Norse renderings documented (the saga-prose's domestication of the classical and British materials: the heroes renamed, the geography relocated, the Christian frame added), so the learned-reception file documents the import's adaptation: how the North's translators naturalized the foreign dooms and dynasties. And the corpus's afterlife completes it: the rímur-tradition's continuation (the later verse-cycles reworking the imported material) - the learned layer's reception documented through the post-medieval centuries.

The file's verse-craft completes the register: Merlínússpá's metre documented (the eddic fornyrðislag carrying the French prophecies - the translation's formal choices itemized), so the learned-reception file documents the import at the level of metre: the foreign doom fitted to the native form, stanza by stanza. And the Hauksbok-context completes it: the compilation's program (Haukr Erlendsson's law-book and the learned texts bound together - the imports shelved beside the native law) - the learned layer's library documented as one household's canon.

 The file’s prophecy-genre junction completes it: the Voluspa-sibyl and Merlin read as the North’s two prophet-voices - the imported seer naturalized beside the native one, the learned-reception file’s genre-mirror closed.

 The file's Haukr-Erlendsson signature completes it: the compilation)s compiler documented (the law-man)s hand in the learned layer - the imports) patron named), the learned-reception file)s library traced to its owner.

title.en: The Ritual of Cursing: Runes, Poles and the Law
title.zh: 詛咒的儀式：如尼、木樁與法律

region.en: The courts and shore-lands of Iceland and Scandinavia (symbolic pin at Pingvellir)
region.zh: 冰島與斯堪的納維亞的法庭與海岸（象徵性定位於辛格維利爾）

period: Sagas and law-codes 13th-14th c. (older practice); the Grágás and Gulathing clauses on scolding and sorcery

source.work: Egils saga ch. 57 (the pole-curse); the law-codes' clauses (níð, scolding, sorcery as offences); Landnamabok's pole-clauses

license: Public domain (older editions); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The cursing-ritual's legal file: the pole-curse's procedure (the record norse-egill-nithing-pole: hazel, horse-head, formula, landward turn - the full technology), the law's clauses (níð and scolding as offences: the curse-word's legal weight - 'the? - 'word? - 'of? - shame? - 'that? - 'unmans? - - the chargeable insult), the rune-curse formulas (the runestones' threat-clauses - the record norse-bjorketorp-curse's descent-line), and the taboo's persistence (the curse's folk-afterlife in the post-conversion countryside). The record is the curse-law file.
summary.zh: 詛咒儀式法律檔案：木樁詛咒的完整程序（榛木、馬頭、套語、轉向內陸——見埃吉爾記錄）、法律條款（níð與辱罵為罪行——「使人失格的羞辱之言」可被控告）、如尼詛咒套語（如尼石的威脅條款——布約克托普石之後裔），以及禁忌延續（皈依後鄉野中詛咒的民俗後續）。此記錄是詛咒法律檔案。

canonical_translation: Islenzk Fornrit editions; Grágás ed. Finsen 1852; paraphrase

narrative.en:
The curse-law file holds the cursing-ritual's full procedure and its legal frame. The pole-curse's technology (norse-egill-nithing-pole holds the scene): the procedure's parts documented (the hazel-pole, the horse-head, the juridical formula, the landward turn - the curse filed as a lawsuit with the land itself). The law's clauses: the curse-word's legal weight ('níð? - 'and? - scolding? - 'chargeable? - offences? - 'the? - 'insult? - 'that? - 'unmans? - - the Grágás and Gulathing clauses: the spoken curse prosecuted as violence, the corpus's speech-law), and the rune-curse formulas: the runestones' threat-clauses (the records' descent-line from the Blekinge stones' doctrine to the Glavendrup outlaw-curse).

The taboo's persistence completes the file: the curse's folk-afterlife (the post-conversion countryside's cursing-stones and nith-poles documented in the later folklore - the record norse-rune-stone-legends-local's register), the ritual surviving its law. The record's cultural functions are the curse-as-law doctrine (the curse prosecuted: the north's speech-crimes documented - the corpus's clearest speech-jurisprudence) and the ritual-procedure doctrine (the curse's technology itemized: the corpus's most complete magic-instruction). In the atlas, the record anchors the curse-law family: each a tradition's formalized cursing; the Norse one is distinctive in the pole's procedure.

For the database, this node complements the pole-record and the rune-curse-records: here the legal frame.

The file's evidence-grammar completes the register: the curse's prosecution documented in the cases (the insult-lawsuits of the sagas: the níð charged, defended and compensated - the speech-crimes' court-procedure itemized), so the curse-law file documents not just the rules but their operation: the curse-word's price in the courts, the insult's compensation paid like a wound. And the runic-law's junction completes it: the carved curses' legal standing debated (the runestones' threats as law or as magic - the file's open question, the carved word's jurisdiction ambiguous by design).

The file's gendered-register completes the law: the curse's social reach documented (the women's cursing documented beside the men's poles - the saga-women's insult-craft as the household's weapon), so the curse-law file's subjects are both sexes: the formal pole-curse for the landowner, the spoken curse for the kitchen - the corpus's speech-crimes documented across the household. narrative.en:
The outlaw's dream-file holds Gísla saga's register. The oath-broken world: the blood-oath sworn and broken (the vengeance-oath at the feast - the record norse-ulf-outlaw-boundary's oath-grammar: 'the? - 'oath? - 'on? - 'the? - spear? - 'that? - 'the? - kin? - 'broke? - - the sisters' loyalty divided: Aude following her husband into exile, Thórdís loving her brother's killer's kin - the household split by the feud).

The secret killing: the brother-in-law killed at night (the sacrificial verses composed at the deed - 'the? - 'verse? - 'that? - 'betrayed? - the? - deed? - - the skaldic boast as the deed's witness: the corpus's poet-outlaw documenting his own crime in meter). The dream-vigil completes the file: the two dream-women ('the? - 'bright? - dream-wife? - 'who? - 'came? - 'every? - night? - 'counseling? - stanzas? - 'and? - 'the? - blood-handed? - one? - 'who? - 'promised? - death? - - the outlaw's fate in two dreams: comfort and sentence alternately, the corpus's most sustained dream-sequence).

And the last stand: the hero's death-register (the leaps between the boulders, the spear set in the hillside for the final jump - the death-position the verse preserves; and the sister's hand in it: the record's oath-breach completed). The record's cultural functions are the dream-vigil doctrine (the outlaw's fate foretold nightly in two dreams - the corpus's dream-fate at its fullest) and the oath-breach doctrine (the family's loyalty split by the feud: the oath's social cost documented inside one household). In the atlas, the record anchors the dream-vigil family: each a tradition's haunted fugitive; the Gísli one is distinctive in the two women.

For the database, this node extends the outlaw-register: here the dream-file.

The saga's verse-integration completes the dream-file: the outlaw's stanzas embedded in the prose (the lausavisur composed at each crisis - the lausavísa-form as the fugitive's diary), so the dream-vigil is documented in two media: the prose-night and the verse-morning - the corpus's most integrated outlaw-text. And the saga's Christianity-frame completes it: the conversion-era's pious touches on the old material (the dream-women re-read in the saga's final chapters) - the fate-doctrine's persistence under the new faith documented in the text's own revisions.

The saga's law-craft completes the dream-file: the oath-breach's legal aftermath documented (the kin's compensation-cases run after the killing - the feud's paper-trail in the courts), so the dream-vigil's tragedy is grounded in procedure: the fate running through settlements as well as dreams. And the saga's two-transmission completes it: the longer and shorter versions documented (the saga's manuscripts preserving two redactions with variant dream-sequences) - the dream-vigil's variants documented, the fate-doctrine's transmission visible in its copies.

title.en: Varaha Lifts the Drowned Earth
title.zh: 筏羅訶（野豬化身）救起沉没的大地

region.en: Varaha temple, Pushkar (symbolic pin at the ancient Varaha shrine)
region.zh: 布施伽爾野豬神廟（象徵性定位於古筏羅訶聖地）

period: Vishnu Purana, Book I, ch. 4, c. 300-800 CE (Wilson translation, 1840); epic sources older

source.work: The Vishnu Purana: A System of Hindu Mythology and Tradition, trans. H. H. Wilson (1840), Book I, ch. 4 (the Varaha avatar)

summary.en: At the end of the last kalpa, the earth sinks into the waters and the demon Hiranyaksha drags it deeper. Vishnu becomes a boar - the size of an elephant, tusked like a mountain - plunges into the cosmic sea, slays the demon in a battle lasting a thousand years, and raises the earth on his tusk from the abyss, setting it again upon its foundations.
summary.zh: 前一劫之末，大地沉入眾水，惡魔金座（希任耶克沙）將其拖得更深。毘濕奴化身野豬——大如巨象、獠牙如山——躍入宇宙之海，與惡魔搏殺千年，誅之，並以獠牙將大地自深淵托起，重立於其基座之上。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (Varaha temples and iconography across India). Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: When the world lay dissolved, the earth, deprived of her place, sank into the waters of the abyss; and the mighty demon Hiranyaksha, seeing her drifting in the deep, seized her and drew her down to his own realm below. The rishis and the gods, helpless, sought the Lord, and praised him, and he heard them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, ch. 4 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當世界歸於消融，大地失去了她的位置，沉入深淵之水；強大的阿修羅訶利耶迦舍見她漂流於深處，便抓住她，將她拖入他下方自己的領域。仙人與眾神無能為力，尋求至尊主，讚美他，他聽見了他們。

passages.text: Vishnu took the form of a boar, vast as the largest elephant, dark like the tualsi leaf, with tusks white and shining, eyes like the autumn moon; he plunged into the ocean and roared like thunder, and the waters trembled. Hiranyaksha, wrathful, came up from the abyss to meet him, and the two fought - hurling trees, darts, mountains - a battle that the sages measure in a thousand years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, ch. 4 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 毗濕奴化為野豬之形，巨大如最大的象，膚色深如圖爾西葉，獠牙潔白閃亮，眼如秋月；他潛入海洋，吼聲如雷，眾水震顫。訶利耶迦舍滿懷憤怒，從深淵上來迎他，二者交戰——投擲樹木、標槍、山嶽——一場智者以千年計量的戰鬥。

passages.text: At last the boar caught the demon on his tusk and slew him, as Indra slew the foe; then he sought out the earth where she lay in the lower regions, lifted her upon his tusk, glowing like a crescent moon, and rose from the waters. He set the earth upon her own foundations, level and firm as in the beginning, and the seas and rivers returned to their beds; the Brahma-fathers then shaped the world's inhabitants anew.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, ch. 4 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最後，野豬以獠牙擒住那阿修羅並殺了他，如因陀羅誅殺敵手；隨後他尋出躺於下界的大地，將她舉上自己的獠牙，光輝如新月，從水中升起。他將大地安置於她自己的根基之上，平坦而穩固如起初一般，海洋與河流各歸其床；梵天諸父於是重新塑造世間的眾生。

canonical_translation: Horace Hayman Wilson, The Vishnu Purana, London, 1840 (public domain); modern: Ludo Rocher, The Puranas, Wiesbaden, 1986

narrative.en:
The Varaha ('boar') avatar story is the Puranas' principal earth-rescue myth: a cosmogony in which creation is interrupted and restored - the world re-founded by an animal-bodied god.

The setup belongs to the end of time: when the previous kalpa closes, the earth (personified as Bhu-devi) is stripped of her place and sinks into the primordial waters. The demon Hiranyaksha - the golden-eyed Asura whose brother Hiranyakashipu stars in the Narasimha story - finds her drifting in the abyss and drags her down to the demon-realms below, a kidnapping of the planet itself. The gods and seers, unable to cope, praise Vishnu; and Vishnu answers by becoming the most ancient of his forms: a boar.

The transformation is described with relish: vast as the largest elephant, dark, with white shining tusks and eyes like the autumn moon, he roars into the cosmic sea 'like thunder' and dives. The battle with Hiranyaksha is full-scale cosmic combat - trees, darts, mountains hurled; the fight measured by the sages in a thousand years - and the demon's boast (that no god can withstand him) is answered by the boar's tusk. Hiranyaksha is killed, 'as Indra slew the foe', and the boar then descends into the lower regions, finds the earth lying faint on the abyss floor, lifts her upon his tusk - 'glowing like a crescent moon' - and rises from the waters, setting her back upon her foundations 'level and firm as in the beginning'. The rivers and seas return to their beds, and the re-creation of inhabitants proceeds under the Brahma-fathers.

Function: the myth does the work of a second creation story - the world's foundation is not single but cyclical, re-established whenever it sinks; the rescue is agricultural and cosmic at once (the earth as a field lifted from flood-waters is a vividly peasant image; Indra-Vritra's freed rivers are its Vedic cousin). In temple art the scene is rendered monumental - most famously at Mamandur, Eran, and Khajuraho - Vishnu-boar colossal, anthropomorphic, bearing the earth goddess on his arm: one of the largest stone figures in Indian art (the Eran Varaha). Theologically, Varaha is the avatar that shows Vishnu's body as the world's support - the link between the Purusha's cosmic body and the specific rescue of a living landscape. In the cross-tradition matrix, this is the Hindu member of the earth-diver/earth-raiser family (compare the birds of the Yoruba and Woodlands diving for soil, or the Chinese Pangu's corpse becoming the landscape): here the diver is the god himself, and the soil is the goddess.
narrative.zh: 筏羅訶（『野豬』）化身故事是往世書主要的大地救援神話：一部創世被中斷而復原的宇宙志——世界由獸身之神重新奠定。設定屬於時間之末：前一劫閉合之時，大地（人格化為地神 Bhu-devi）被剝離其所居，沉入原初之水。惡魔金座——其弟金輪即是獅面人故事的主角——發現她漂於深淵，將其拖入下方魔域，是對行星本身的綁架。諸神與仙人無力應對，頌讚毘濕奴；毘濕奴以最古老的形態回應：野豬。變身被津津有味地描述：大如巨象、體黑、白獠牙閃亮、目如秋月，他『如雷』般吼入宇宙之海而潛。與金座之戰是全面宇宙戰——擲樹、擲鏢、擲山；仙人以其千年計量——而惡魔的傲語（無神能當其鋒）由野豬之獠牙作答。金座被誅，『如因陀羅誅敵』；野豬繼而下行至下方之境，見大地昏厥於深淵之底，以獠牙托起她——『燦如新月』——自水中升起，將她重置於基座之上，『平坦而堅固，如太初』。諸河諸海歸於河床海床，居民族群的再創造由梵天之父們續行。功能：此神話行使第二創世故事之職——世界的奠基非一次性而是循環的，每逢沉没即被重立；救援既是農事的也是宇宙的（大地如被自洪水中托起的田畝，是鮮明的農人意象；因陀羅釋河是其在吠陀中的表親）。廟宇藝術將此景鑄為巨構——最有名者於馬曼杜、埃蘭與卡朱拉霍——毘濕奴-野豬巨大、擬人、臂承地母：印度藝術中最大的石像之一（埃蘭筏羅訶）。神學上，筏羅訶是顯示毘濕奴之身即世界之基的化身——連接原人的宇宙之身與對活的景觀之特定救援。在跨傳統矩陣中，此為『潛水取土/舉地』家族的印度成員（比較約魯巴與林地傳統中潛水取泥的鳥，或中國盤古屍身化為地貌）：此處潛者即神本身，而泥土即女神。

Iconic charter of Varaha worship and colossal temple sculpture
Earth-as-goddess (Bhu-devi) theology: the land as a being to be saved

title.en: The Man-Lion Kills the Unkillable King
title.zh: 獅面人誅不可殺之王

region.en: Ahobilam, Andhra Pradesh (principal Narasimha pilgrimage site)
region.zh: 安得拉邦阿霍比拉姆（獅面人首要朝聖地）

period: Vishnu Purana, Book I, chs. 15-19, c. 300-800 CE (Wilson translation, 1840)

source.work: The Vishnu Purana: A System of Hindu Mythology and Tradition, trans. H. H. Wilson (1840), Book I, Prahlada and the Narasimha avatar

summary.en: The demon king Hiranyakashipu wins a lawyer's boon - he cannot be killed by man or beast, indoors or out, by day or night, on ground or in air, by any weapon. His son Prahlada worships Vishnu anyway. At dusk, on a threshold, the king challenges a pillar; it splits, and Vishnu steps out as Narasimha - neither man nor beast - and kills him with claws on his lap, neither ground nor sky, at neither day nor night, with no weapon.
summary.zh: 魔王金輪贏得律師式恩諭——人獸皆不能殺之、屋內外皆不能、晝夜皆不能、地上空中皆不能、任何兵器皆不能。其子布羅赫拉達偏偏崇拜毘濕奴。黃昏，於門檻上，王挑釁廊柱；柱裂，毘濕奴化身獅面人那羅辛哈步出——非人非獸——以爪於膝上殺之，非地非天，非晝非夜，不用兵器。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition with major temples (Ahobilam, Simhachalam) and Narasimha Jayanti observances. Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Hiranyakashipu, brother of the slain Hiranyaksha, performed savage austerities until Brahma, shaken, granted his boon: let me not be slain by any being created by thee - man or beast, god or demon; let me not die inside a dwelling nor outside it, neither by day nor by night, neither on the ground nor in the air; no weapon shall reach me. Armed with impossibility, he conquered the three worlds and demanded worship.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, chs. 15-16 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 被殺的訶蘭耶迦尸普（Hiranyaksha）之兄訶蘭耶迦尸布（Hiranyakashipu）修習猛烈的苦行，直到梵天為之震動，賜予他恩典：願我不被你所造的任何眾生所殺——無論人還是獸，天神還是魔；願我不死於屋內，亦不死於屋外，不死於白晝，亦不死於黑夜，不死於地上，亦不死於空中；任何武器都傷不到我。他憑著這不可能之事，征服了三界，並要求眾生禮拜他。

passages.text: His son Prahlada, from the womb, knew the Lord; taught by sages, taught by Narada, the boy answered every tutor and every torture with the name of Vishnu. His father tried poison, fire, elephants, serpents; the boy was unharmed. Asked where this Vishnu was whom he worshiped, Prahlada said: He is in the pillar, as He is in me; the king, in fury, struck the pillar with his fist.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, chs. 16-18 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的兒子缽羅訶羅陀（Prahlada）自母胎中便認識了世尊；經由仙人教導，經由那羅陀（Narada）教導，這孩子對每一位師長、每一次折磨，都以毗濕奴之名作答。他的父親試過毒藥、烈火、大象、毒蛇；這孩子毫髮無傷。當被問及他所禮拜的這位毗濕奴在何處時，缽羅訶羅陀說：祂在柱中，正如祂在我心中；國王大怒，以拳擊柱。

passages.text: The pillar split with a sound like the world cracking, and out stepped a being never before seen: to the waist a man, below a lion, eyes like flame, a mane like midnight. Narasimha - neither man nor beast - seized the demon king at the threshold (neither inside nor out), at dusk (neither day nor night), laid him on his lap (neither ground nor sky), and opened him with his claws (no weapon), at the hour of neither day nor night. The boon survived; the king did not.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, chs. 18-19 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 柱子裂開，其聲如世界崩裂，從中走出一個前所未見的眾生：腰部以上是人，以下為獅，雙眼如火焰，鬃毛如午夜。那羅僧訶（Narasimha）——既非人亦非獸——在門檻處（既非內亦非外），於黃昏（既非晝亦非夜），將這魔王擒住，置於自己的膝上（既非地亦非天），以利爪將他剖開（不用武器），正是在既非白晝亦非黑夜的時辰。恩典依然成立；國王卻已不在。

canonical_translation: Horace Hayman Wilson, The Vishnu Purana, London, 1840 (public domain); modern: Ludo Rocher, The Puranas, Wiesbaden, 1986

narrative.en:
The Prahlada-Narasimha cycle is the Puranas' masterpiece of the boon-and-loophole plot - the tradition's most legally literate myth, in which omnipotence is demonstrated not by raw force but by reading a contract against its grantor.

The boon: Hiranyakashipu, brother of Hiranyaksha (the earth-stealing demon killed by the boar), performs ferocious austerities on the Mandara ridge until Brahma, scorching, grants his carefully drafted immunity: he shall not be slain by any being created by Brahma; not by man or beast, god or demon; not indoors or outdoors; not by day or night; not on ground or in air; not by any weapon; not by anything living or unliving that the creator made. With invulnerability drafted into every clause, he reconquers the three worlds and replaces worship of the gods with worship of himself.

The son: Prahlada - 'delight' - is the wrong kind of child for a demon-king. Instructed in the womb by Narada (the Purana's devotional theology: the name heard before birth takes root), he returns from every schooling with one curriculum: Vishnu is everywhere, in the pillar as in me. The father's countermeasures escalate through the Purana's catalogue of horrors - poison, fire, elephants, serpent-darts - and every attempt fails because the boy's protection is the very god his father excludes. The debates between father and son are the myth's real battleground: theology argued across a throne room.

The pillar: asked by his raging father whether his Vishnu is present in this pillar, Prahlada says yes - and the king strikes the column. It splits 'with a sound like the world cracking', and out steps a being the boon's author never created: Narasimha, to the waist a man, below a lion - outside every drafted category (neither man nor beast; not created by Brahma in any named kind). The kill is staged in the remaining loopholes: at the threshold (neither inside nor outside), at dusk (neither day nor night), on the god's own lap (neither ground nor sky), torn open by claws (no weapon). Each condition of the boon is honored; the king is dead; the contract is fulfilled and destroyed at once.

Aftermath: the gods fear the new form will not calm; Prahlada is asked to pacify him, and the boy's praise (the Prahlada-charita) does so - Narasimha crowns the child king of the demons. The imagery becomes one of the great iconographies of India: Narasimha bursting from the pillar carved on temple walls everywhere, the god's fury and the child's serenity paired.

Function: the story is the charter of bhakti's absolute claim (a child's faith defeats a demon's law) and of Vishnu's preserving justice - the lord answers prayers by arriving precisely where the rules say no one can. It is also the tradition's own satire of magical thinking: the boon that banishes every named possibility is beaten by a possibility the banisher forgot to name. In the boon-curse motif cluster, Narasimha is the perfect case: the boon is honored to the letter and inverted in spirit; the law is kept, and the lawbreaker's world ends.
narrative.zh: 布羅赫拉達-獅面人循環是往世書『恩諭-漏洞』情節的傑作——傳統中最具法律素養的神話：全能不以蠻力示人，而以按合同反治授予者示人。恩諭：金輪——被野豬所誅的竊地魔金座之弟——在曼陀羅山脊行兇暴苦行，直至梵天不堪炙烤而授予其精心起草的不死性：不被梵天所造之任何存在所殺；非人非獸、非神非魔；不在屋內屋外；非晝非夜；不在地上空中；不被任何兵器所及；不被造物主所造之任何有生或無生之物所殺。每一條款皆被豁免之後，他重新征服三界，並以對自身的崇拜取代對諸神的崇拜。其子：布羅赫拉達——意為『喜悅』——是魔王最不想要的兒子。經那羅陀於胎中教授（往世書奉愛神學：出生前聞名，其名生根），他自每一次求學歸來只帶一門課程：毘濕奴無所不在，在柱中亦在我中。父親的對策在往世書的恐怖目錄中升級——毒、火、巨象、蛇鏢——每一計皆敗，因孩童的護佑正是父親所排除的那位神。父子之辯是神話真正的戰場：神學在王座廳中交鋒。廊柱：被狂怒的父親問其毘濕奴是否在此柱中，布羅赫拉達答是——王以拳擊柱。柱『如世界碎裂之聲』裂開，走出一個恩諭作者未曾創造的存在：那羅辛哈，腰以上為人、以下為獅——在每一既定範疇之外（非人非獸；非梵天以任何命名之種所造）。誅殺在剩餘的漏洞中上演：在門檻（非內非外）、在黃昏（非晝非夜）、於神之膝上（非地非天）、以爪撕裂（無兵器）。恩諭的每一條件皆被遵守；王死；合同同時被履行與摧毀。後續：諸神懼新形態不能平息；布羅赫拉達被請去安撫，孩童的讚美（布羅赫拉達頌）奏效——獅面人立孩童為魔王之王。圖像成為印度最偉大的圖像學之一：獅面人自柱中迸出，雕於處處廟牆，神之怒與孩童之靜並列。功能：此故事是奉愛絕對主張的憲章（孩童之信勝魔王之法），也是毘濕奴護持之義——主應祈禱，恰在規則說無人能至之處降臨。它亦是傳統自身的魔法思維諷刺：排除一切已命名可能性的恩諭，被遺忘者未命名的一種可能性擊敗。在恩諭-詛咒母題群中，獅面人是完美案例：恩諭被逐字遵守而在精神上被反轉；法律被遵守，而違法者的世界終結。

functions: Charter of bhakti: a child's devotion defeats a demon's contract with fate
Theology of preserving justice - the god arrives inside the rules' loopholes
Boon-and-loophole plot: the tradition's most legally literate myth
Iconographic charter: the pillar-burst Narasimha in temples across India

title.en: The Dwarf's Three Steps: Vamana and King Bali
title.zh: 侏儒的三步：筏摩那與婆利王

region.en: Thrikkakara, Kerala (Vamana temple of the Onam festival)
region.zh: 喀拉拉邦特里卡卡拉（歐南節之筏摩那神廟）

period: Vishnu Purana, Book I-II (Bali's sacrifice), c. 300-800 CE (Wilson translation, 1840)

source.work: The Vishnu Purana: A System of Hindu Mythology and Tradition, trans. H. H. Wilson (1840), Book I, chs. 18-19 and Book II (Bali and the Dwarf avatar)

summary.en: The Asura king Bali, grandson of Prahlada, has conquered the three worlds by sacrifice and virtue, and the gods are homeless. Vishnu is born as a dwarf Brahmin and comes to Bali's great sacrifice asking for three paces of ground. Laughing at the tiny gift, Bali grants it - and the dwarf grows through sky and earth, taking heaven in one stride, earth in the second, and for the third steps on Bali's head, sending him to rule the netherworld. Each year, Bali is allowed home: the Onam festival.
summary.zh: 阿修羅王婆利——布羅赫拉達之孫——以祭祀與德行征服三界，諸神遂無家可歸。毘濕奴化身侏儒婆羅門，來到婆利的大祭上求三步之地。婆利笑許這份微小禮物——侏儒遂長貫天與地，一步取天，二步取地，第三步踏於婆利之首，遣其下治冥界。每年婆利獲准回家：此即歐南節。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: Onam is Kerala's principal festival (celebrated across communities, with its own political readings of Bali). Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Bali, grandson of the devotee Prahlada, ruled the three worlds by the power of sacrifice; he was just, generous, and invincible. The gods, stripped of their domains, went to Vishnu; and Vishnu, to restore them without breaking the law of the gift, was born as a dwarf Brahmin, Vamana, and came, staff in hand, to the vast sacrifice Bali was performing on the banks of the Narmada.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, chs. 18-19 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 缽利（Bali），信士缽羅訶羅陀之孫，憑藉祭祀之力統治三界；他公正、慷慨，且不可戰勝。眾天神被奪去領地，前去謁見毗濕奴；毗濕奴為了在不違背布施之法的情況下恢復他們的領地，便化生為婆羅門侏儒筏摩那（Vamana），手持木杖，來到缽利正在訥爾默達（Narmada）河畔舉行的盛大祭祀。

passages.text: The dwarf asked for a gift: three paces of ground. Bali's preceptor, Shukra, saw the trap and warned him; Bali answered that a Brahmin asking was a gift that could not be measured by size - and made the grant, water poured from his own hand. The dwarf then grew: his head rose through the worlds, the gods assembled in his body; one stride covered heaven, the second the earth and underworlds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, chs. 18-19 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這侏儒請求一份布施：三步之地。缽利的師尊輸迦羅（Shukra）看穿了這陷阱並警告他；缽利回答說，婆羅門有所求，乃是無法以大小衡量的布施——於是應允了這份布施，水從他自己手中傾注而出。這侏儒隨即增長：他的頭顱升越諸界，眾天神齊集於他的身中；一步覆蓋了天，第二步覆蓋了大地與地下諸界。

passages.text: For the third step there was nowhere left. Bali bowed his head; Vamana placed his foot upon it and pushed the king down to Patala, the netherworld, of which he was made the lord - honored, not humiliated. Because Bali's virtue was real, Vishnu granted him the annual return: each year, on the day kept as Onam, Bali comes up to see his people, and his kingdom for a day is the world again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Books 1-2 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了第三步，已無處可留。缽利俯首；筏摩那將腳踏在其上，把國王推下至缽多羅（Patala），即地下世界，並使他成為那裏的主宰——受尊崇，而非受屈辱。因為缽利的美德真實不虛，毗濕奴賜予他每年歸返之權：每年，在作為歐南節（Onam）奉守的那一日，缽利上來探望他的子民，他的王國便有一日重歸於這世界。

canonical_translation: Horace Hayman Wilson, The Vishnu Purana, London, 1840 (public domain); modern: Ludo Rocher, The Puranas, Wiesbaden, 1986

narrative.en:
The Vamana-Bali story is the Puranas' most elegant trickster myth - a conquest undone by a gift measured in steps - and it carries the one major Hindu festival whose hero is a demon.

The setup inverts the usual order: Bali, grandson of the great devotee Prahlada, is not a villain but an exemplary king - just, learned, generous, and undefeated because his power is sacrificial merit itself. Under his rule the three worlds are governed well; the problem is bookkeeping: if the Asuras hold everything, the gods have nothing to preside over. The gods complain to Vishnu, who refuses simple conquest - Bali's merit is real and the law of the gift protects it. Vishnu's solution is to be born as a dwarf Brahmin, Vamana ('the dwarf'), and to win back the worlds through the ritual economy: by asking.

The asking is staged at Bali's own great sacrifice on the Narmada's banks. A tiny Brahmin with an umbrella and a water-pot arrives; Bali receives him with full honor and asks his wish. The request - three paces of ground - is comically small, and Bali laughs as he grants it. But Shukra, the Asuras' preceptor, recognizes the shape of the trap (in the fuller tellings, Shukra shrinks himself into the spout of the water-vessel to block the gift, and Vamana blinds him with a blade of grass to clear the spout - the trickster answering the trickster). Bali, knowing the warning and granting anyway, chooses the law of the gift over prudence: a Brahmin's request cannot be refused, and a gift's worth is not its size. The water is poured; the grant is sealed.

Then the growth: Vamana's dwarf body expands through every world - gods assembled in his limbs - and he measures. One stride takes heaven; the second takes earth and the underworlds. For the third, there is nothing left but the giver. Bali bows and offers his own head; Vamana's foot sets upon it, and the king descends to Patala - not as a punished rebel but as the honored lord of the netherworld, a king of sorts still. The worlds return to the gods without a battle and without a broken promise.

The coda is what keeps the story alive: because Bali's virtue was real, Vishnu grants him a yearly return - each year Bali comes up to visit his kingdom and his people. In Kerala this day is Onam: the harvest festival at which households lay flower carpets and a feast (onasadya) to welcome the banished king's homecoming - a demon-king, exiled by the god, celebrated as the best of rulers. The festival's politics are part of the myth's afterlife: in Kerala, Mahabali's golden age is recalled as an era of equality (the proverb: all were equal when Maveli ruled), and modern movements have read Onam as the memory of a just order displaced. The record keeps both readings.

Function: the story teaches the ritual law of the gift (a promise made is a world transferred), the dwarf-as-god theology (smallness that contains all worlds), and the ambivalence of righteous conquest. Comparative readers place it beside the trickster-wager cluster and the three-strides motif known also in Indo-European poetry (the 'three paces' of Vishnu in the Rigveda are already cosmic - the myth is an epic expansion of a Vedic image).
narrative.zh: 筏摩那-婆利故事是往世書最優雅的詭計神話——一場以步為量度的贈禮所瓦解的征服——並且承載著印度教唯一一個以惡魔為主角的重大節日。設定反轉常規：婆利，大信徒布羅赫拉達之孫，並非惡棍而是模範之王——公正、博學、慷慨，因其力量即祭祀功德本身而不可戰勝。其治下三界井然；問題在於記帳：若阿修羅擁有一切，諸神便無所司掌。諸神向毘濕奴陳情，毘濕奴拒絕簡單的征服——婆利的功德真實，贈禮之法護佑之。毘濕奴之解為化身侏儒婆羅門筏摩那（『侏儒』），透過儀式經濟以『求』奪回世界。求取在婆利於納爾默達河畔舉行的大祭上上演。持傘與水罐的小婆羅門到來；婆利以全禮接待，問其所欲。所求——三步之地——小得可笑，婆利笑而允之。但阿修羅國師尸訶認出陷阱的形狀（較全的講述中，尸訶將自己縮入水器壺嘴以阻贈禮，筏摩那以草葉蔽其目以清壺嘴——詭計者對付詭計者）。婆利明知警告而仍允，以贈禮之法取勝於謹慎：婆羅門之求不可拒，禮之價不在其量。水已傾注；許諾封印。隨後是生長：筏摩那的侏儒之身擴張貫穿諸世界——諸神聚於其肢——而後丈量。一步取天；二步取地與冥界。第三步，唯餘施與者。婆利低首獻其頭；筏摩那之足踏其上，王下至缽陀羅（Patala）冥界——非為受罰之叛逆，而為受尊的冥界之主，仍是一種之王。世界未經一戰、未破一諾而歸於諸神。尾聲使故事長存：因婆利之德真實，毘濕奴准其年年歸返——每年婆利上來探望其王國與人民。在喀拉拉，此日即歐南節（Onam）：家家鋪花毯、設盛宴（onasadya）迎接被逐之王的歸來——一位被神放逐的魔王，被尊為最優的統治者。節日的政治是神話後續的一部分：在喀拉拉，摩訶婆利的黃金時代被追憶為平等之世（諺語：瑪韋利在位時人人平等），現代運動亦將歐南讀作被取代的公正秩序之記憶。本錄並存兩種讀法。功能：故事教授贈禮的儀式法（諾成則世界易主）、侏儒即神的神學（含納一切世界之小），以及義戰的曖昧。比較讀者置之於詭計者-賭注母題群與印歐詩歌已知的『三步』意象（梨俱吠陀中毘濕奴的三步已是宇宙性的——此神話是吠陀意象的史詩擴展）。

functions: Ritual law of the gift: a granted promise transfers worlds
Dwarf-theology: smallness containing all worlds (Vedic three strides expanded)
Festival charter of Onam - the annual return of the exiled demon-king
Ambivalence of righteous conquest: merit honored even as it is displaced

title.en: Krishna Born in Prison: The Midnight Child of Mathura
title.zh: 牢中誕生的克里希那：馬圖拉的午夜之子

region.en: Mathura, Krishna Janmabhoomi (birthplace temple)
region.zh: 馬圖拉（克里希那誕生地神廟）

period: Vishnu Purana, Book V, chs. 1-4, c. 300-800 CE (Wilson translation, 1840)

source.work: The Vishnu Purana: A System of Hindu Mythology and Tradition, trans. H. H. Wilson (1840), Book V, the birth of Krishna

summary.en: The tyrant Kamsa hears a prophecy - the eighth child of his cousin Devaki will kill him - and imprisons the couple, killing each infant at birth. The eighth child is born at midnight: Vishnu himself, who shows the parents his four-armed form, instructs the father to carry him across the Yamuna to Gokula, and vanishes into the herd-boys' world while a newborn girl is surrendered to Kamsa in his place.
summary.zh: 暴君甘薩聞預言——其表妹德瓦吉之第八子將殺之——遂囚禁夫婦，於每個嬰兒誕生時親手誅之。第八子於午夜誕生：即毘濕奴本人，向父母顯示四臂之形，囑父攜其渡亞穆納河至戈庫拉，隨即隱入牧童世界；甘薩則得一名代死的新生女嬰。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition of the highest intensity (Janmashtami, Mathura-Vraja pilgrimage). Classified 'myth' (Puranic narrative rather than scripture's legal sections).

passages.text: A voice from the sky told Kamsa at the wedding of Devaki: the eighth child of this union will slay thee. Kamsa drew his sword at once; Vasudeva pleaded, offering all his children; Kamsa spared the couple but imprisoned them, and destroyed each child as it was born.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 5, chs. 1-2 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在提婆吉的婚禮上，空中傳來一個聲音對康薩說：這對結合所生的第八個孩子將殺死你。康薩立刻拔出劍；婆蘇提婆苦苦哀求，願獻出自己所有的孩子；康薩饒了這對夫婦，卻將他們囚禁起來，並在每個孩子出生時將其殺死。

passages.text: At midnight on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, in the month of Bhadra, the eighth child was born - and the prison filled with light. The parents saw the newborn as Vishnu himself, four-armed, with the conch, discus, mace and lotus; the babe spoke: take me to Nanda's house in Gokula and put the girl-child just born there in my place. Vasudeva carried him through the barred doors, the guards slept, the Yamuna parted, and the exchange was made.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 5, chs. 3-4 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在黑暗半月第八天的午夜，於婆陀羅月，第八個孩子誕生了——牢房裡充滿了光明。父母看見這新生兒就是毗濕奴本人，四臂，手持螺貝、輪寶、權杖與蓮花；嬰兒開口說道：把我帶到牛增伽的難陀家中，並把那裡剛出生的女嬰放在我的位置上。婆蘇提婆抱著他穿過上了閂的門，守衛們都睡著了，閻牟那河分開，交換便完成了。

passages.text: Kamsa came for the child, seizing the girl to dash her against stone; she slipped from his hands into the sky as the goddess, prophesying: thy destroyer lives, thy death is certain. Kamsa thereupon ordered the massacre of all infants in his realm; but the child grew up in Gokula among herdsmen as Krishna, son of Nanda and Yashoda - known in the village only as a darling, dark, and fond of butter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 5, chs. 4-6 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 康薩來取這孩子，抓住女嬰要將她摔在石頭上；她從他手中滑脫，升入天空，化為女神，預言道：你的毀滅者活著，你的死是必然的。康薩於是下令屠殺他境內所有的嬰兒；但這孩子卻在牛增伽的牧牛人之間長大，成為黑天，難陀與耶輸陀之子——在村中只以一個可愛、黝黑、喜愛奶油的孩子為人所知。

canonical_translation: Horace Hayman Wilson, The Vishnu Purana, London, 1840 (public domain); modern sourcebook: Edwin F. Bryant, Krishna: A Sourcebook, Oxford, 2007

narrative.en:
The birth of Krishna in the Vishnu Purana is the tradition's fullest miracle-birth narrative - the infant god born under a death sentence, smuggled across a river, and raised in disguise as a cowherd's child.

The prophecy: at the wedding of his cousin Devaki to Vasudeva, a voice from the sky stops Kamsa's chariot: the eighth child of this marriage will kill you. Kamsa's response is immediate tyrant-logic: he seizes the couple, and - persuaded by Vasudeva to spare them - confines them in a guarded chamber and destroys each child at birth, one by one. The Purana is unsparing: six children die at their father-uncle's hands.

The eighth child: on the eighth day of the dark fortnight (the night kept today as Janmashtami), in the rain-month Bhadra, Devaki bears the eighth child at midnight - and the dungeon fills with light. The newborn is Vishnu himself: the parents see him four-armed, bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus - and the babe speaks, instructing them in the escape he has arranged. The theology is exact: this is not a god's avatara arriving later, but the lord born knowingly, giving orders as an infant.

The escape: Vasudeva carries the child out through the locked doors - the guards sunk in sleep by divine power, the chains unfastened, the Yamuna river (in flood, in the later tellings) parting or subsiding as he crosses to the herdsman's village of Gokula. There he exchanges the infant for the girl-child just born to Yashoda, Nanda's wife, and returns to his cell with the substitute. When Kamsa comes to kill the eighth child, the girl slips from his grip, rises into the air as the goddess, and prophesies his death - the tyrant is left with a massacre decree and no victim.

The disguise: the child grows in Gokula and Vraja as Krishna - 'the dark one' - darling of the cowherds, stealing butter, laughing, suckled by Yashoda who has no idea whose son she is raising. The Purana lets the disguise run for years before the prophecy closes: Kamsa's massacre (the slaughter of infants in his realm - a detail the Christian birth narrative mirrors, as scholars from Weber onward have noted), the demon attempts (Putana the poison-nurse among them in later books), and at last the wrestling-arena confrontation where the grown Krishna kills the tyrant who ordered his death at birth.

Function: this is the master narrative of Janmashtami, kept by fast and midnight vigil across India - the devotees imitate the vigil of the prison night. Theologically it fuses the avatara doctrine with the bhakti child-god: the same lord who is the cosmic sleeper on the waters is a baby that must be smuggled and hidden - omnipotence choosing helplessness, the adult god's disguise as a vulnerable child being the religion's central emotional engine. The birth scene's comparisons are direct: across the biblical mass-slaughter birth (Ramayana's and Christian telling both), the child smuggled past a tyrant is one of the world's oldest rescue plots; the Purana's version is distinctive in making the child the author of his own escape.
narrative.zh: 毘濕奴往世書中克里希那的誕生是該傳統最完整的奇蹟誕生敘事——嬰神在死刑之下誕生、被偷渡過河、偽裝為牧童之子養大。預言：表妹德瓦吉與婆藪提婆成婚之時，天外之聲止住甘薩的車：此婚之第八子將殺你。甘薩的反應是即刻的暴君邏輯：他抓住夫婦，經婆藪提婆求情饒其性命，將其囚於守衛之室，並在每個孩子誕生時逐一誅之。往世書毫不留情：六個孩子死於這位伯父之手。第八子：於黑半月初八之夜（今日守為建摩斯陀密節之夜）、雨月巴陀羅月，德瓦吉於午夜誕下第八子——牢獄充滿光芒。新生兒即毘濕奴本人：父母見其四臂，持法螺、輪、杵、蓮——而嬰兒開口，指示他已安排好的逃亡。神學精確：非神的化身後至，而是主自知而生，以嬰兒之身下達命令。逃亡：婆藪提婆抱子穿過緊鎖之門——守衛因神力沉睡，鎖鏈自解，泛濫的亞穆納河（後世講述中）在他渡往牧村戈庫拉時分開或退落。在那裡他以嬰兒換取耶雪陀（南陀之妻）剛生的女嬰，攜替身回獄。甘薩前來誅殺第八子時，女嬰自其掌中滑出，升空化為女神，預言其死——暴君落得一道屠殺令而無受害者。偽裝：孩子以克里希那——『黑者』——之名在戈庫拉與牧區長大，牛倌的寵兒，偷酪、嬉笑，由耶雪陀哺乳，而她並不知自己養的是誰的兒子。往世書讓偽裝持續多年，直至預言閉合：甘薩的屠殺（境內嬰兒盡誅——學者自韋伯以降皆注意到此細節與基督教誕生敘事的呼應）、妖魔的試探（後卷中的毒乳女普塔那等），最終在摔角場上，長成的克里希那誅殺那位在其誕生時即下令殺他的暴君。功能：此為建摩斯陀密節（Janmashtami）的主敘事，全印以齋戒與午夜守夜守持——信徒模仿牢獄之夜的守候。神學上它熔化身 doctrine 與奉愛的兒童神：臥於水上宇宙之眠的同一主，也是必須被偷渡與藏匿的嬰孩——全能選擇無助，成年神偽裝為易受傷的孩童，是此宗教情感的核心引擎。誕生場景的比較是直接的：跨越聖經的屠嬰誕生（羅摩衍那與基督教講述皆有），被偷渡越過暴君的孩子是世界上最古老的救援情節之一；往世書版本的獨特處在於讓孩子成為自己逃亡的作者。

functions: Master narrative of Janmashtami (midnight fast and vigil across India)
Avatara doctrine fused with the bhakti child-god: omnipotence choosing helplessness
Rescue plot of the doomed child smuggled past a tyrant
Pilgrimage charter of Mathura-Vraja (Janmabhoomi and Gokula sites)

title.en: Jimutavahana Gives His Body to the Garudas
title.zh: 吉穆多伐訶那以身餵金翅鳥

region.en: Malaya mountain, Vidyadhara realm (symbolic pin in the Vindhya uplands)
region.zh: 摩羅耶山，飛天國境（象徵性定位於溫迪亞高地）

period: Kathasaritsagara of Somadeva, c. 1070 CE, Kathapitha-lambaka, tarangas 22-24 (Tawney translation, 1880)

source.work: The Katha Sarit Sagara; or, Ocean of the Streams of Story, trans. C. H. Tawney (1880), vol. 1, the story of Jimutavahana

summary.en: Jimutavahana, prince of the Vidyadharas, renounces his throne for the life of a wandering ascetic and comes to a mountain where Garudas yearly carry off a Naga to eat. Finding a weeping serpent-child bound for the feast, he takes his place in the stone trough, offers his own body, and endures the voracious bird's first bite - whereupon the Garuda stops, transformed: the age of eating Nagas ends, and the prince, restored, is married to the princess he rescued on the way.
summary.zh: 飛天國王子吉穆多伐訶那放棄王位，過雲遊苦行生活，來到一座金翅鳥每年攫食一蛇的山。見一為盛宴被縛而泣的蛇童，他代之臥於石槽，獻出自己的身體，忍受貪饞之鳥的第一啄——金翅鳥遂止，轉化：食蛇之世終結；王子復原，娶途中相救的公主。

sensitivity.note: Secular-legendary katha literature read within living Sanskrit-katha traditions; the story also exists as the Buddhist-inflected Nagananda play tradition. Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Jimutavahana, eldest of the Vidyadhara princes, felt no joy in a throne: he gave the kingdom to his brother and set out to wander, having freed the prisoners of his father's realm and taken nothing. On his way he restored to life the son of a merchant slain by a snake, and won the love of Malayavati; then, still seeking nothing, he came with his retinue to the slopes of Malaya mountain, where he heard weeping.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara, tarangas 22-24 (Tawney 1880); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 持明仙王子中的長子吉穆陀婆訶那對王位毫無喜悅：他將王國讓給弟弟，釋放了他父親境內的囚犯，一無所取，便動身漫遊。途中，他使一個被蛇咬死的商人之子復活，並贏得了摩羅耶婆提的愛；隨後，他依然別無所求，帶著隨從來到摩羅耶山的山坡，在那裡聽見了哭泣聲。

passages.text: The weeper was a young Naga, bound and laid in a stone trough: once in every while, he said, the Garudas carry off one of our race and eat him, and this day the lot is mine. Jimutavahana, holding compassion dearer than his own body, bound the child, carried him home to his family, and laid himself in the trough in his place, oiling his own body to make it a proper meal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara, tarangas 22-24 (Tawney 1880); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 哭泣者是一個被捆綁著、躺在石槽裡的年輕那伽：他說，每隔一段時間，金翅鳥就會抓走我們族中的一個並吃掉他，而今天輪到了我。吉穆陀婆訶那視慈悲比自己的身體更為珍貴，便將這孩子綁好，送他回家與家人團聚，然後自己躺進石槽中代替他，並給自己的身體塗上油，使之成為一頓像樣的餐食。

passages.text: The Garuda came, great as the clouds at the world's end, and fixed his beak in the prince's shoulder; the flesh gave way, and Jimutavahana, bleeding, did not move or cry out - only prayed that his sacrifice be accepted. The bird, tasting him, stopped: this flesh is not a serpent's, he said, and learned from the dying prince who he was. The Garuda wept, restored the body with heavenly charms, and vowed before fire that no Naga should ever be seized again; the age of eating serpents ended that day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara, tarangas 22-24 (Tawney 1880); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 金翅鳥來了，大如世界末日時的雲層，將喙扎進王子的肩膀；血肉裂開，吉穆陀婆訶那流著血，卻不動也不叫喊——只祈求他的犧牲被接受。這鳥嚐了他之後停了下來：這肉不是蛇的，牠說，並從這垂死的王子口中得知他是誰。金翅鳥哭了，用天界的咒語恢復了他的身體，並在火前發誓，此後絕不再抓走任何那伽；吃蛇的時代在那一天結束了。

passages.text: The Nagas, led by the rescued child's father, arrived to honor the sacrifice and found their intended victim alive; the prince was healed, married Malayavati, and returned to rule - a king whose throne had been refused and whose body had been spent, and who thereby ended a whole species' predator-prey war with one act of lying still.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara, tarangas 22-24 (Tawney 1880); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 以获救孩童之父為首的那伽們前來向這犧牲致敬，卻發現他們原定的犧牲者仍活著；王子傷癒，娶了摩羅耶婆底，並回國執政——一位王位曾遭推辭、身軀曾遭捨棄的國王，就此以一動不動之舉，終結了整整一個族類的掠食者與獵物之戰。

canonical_translation: C. H. Tawney, The Katha Sarit Sagara; or, Ocean of the Streams of Story, Calcutta, 1880-84 (public domain); annotated: N. M. Penzer, The Ocean of Story, 10 vols., 1924-28

narrative.en:
Somadeva's Kathasaritsagara ('Ocean of the Streams of Story', c. 1070) is Sanskrit literature's great story-collection - a Kashmiri recasting of the Brihatkatha cycle - and among its most celebrated episodes is the self-sacrifice of Jimutavahana, a story so beloved that the playwright Harsha made it the plot of the Nagananda, and Buddhist storytellers adopted it as a Jataka-style exemplar.

The prince who refuses: Jimutavahana ('whose chariot is the clouds'), eldest son of a Vidyadhara king, is the anti-hero of inheritance: he frees all prisoners in his father's realm, hands the throne to his brother, and walks out to be a wandering ascetic 'taking nothing'. On the road the story layers its ethics: he restores to life a merchant's son dead of snakebite (compassion already outranking death), and wins - almost involuntarily - the love of the princess Malayavati, whose father offers her; the prince, pledged to renunciation, is gently maneuvered by the narrative into accepting a marriage he did not seek.

The mountain: arriving at Malaya with his retinue, he hears weeping and follows it. A young Naga - serpent-being of the underworld race - is bound in a stone trough: by covenant of long standing, the Garudas (the great golden raptor-birds, enemies of the Nagas) periodically seize one of the serpent race and eat him; this day the lot has fallen to this child. Jimutavahana's decision is made without drama: he binds the child, carries him home to his parents, and lies down in the trough himself, anointing his own body with oil 'to make it a proper meal' - the story's black-comic realism in one gesture.

The feeding: the Garuda descends, 'great as the clouds at the world's end', and drives its beak into the prince's shoulder. Flesh tears; the prince does not cry out, does not move - he prays only that his gift be accepted. The bird, mid-bite, stops: this flesh is not a serpent's. From the dying man it learns who he is, and the predator's transformation is the story's climax: the Garuda weeps, restores the torn body with celestial charms (the resurrection beat), and vows before fire that no Naga shall ever again be seized. The Nagas arrive with garlands to mourn their savior and find him alive; the covenant of predation ends in a single act of stillness.

Function: the tale is the katha literature's ethics of ahimsa dramatized - the prince's self-gift does what no battle could, ending a war between species by feeding it. It is the Hindu-courts' answer to the Buddhist Jataka of the Bodhisattva feeding himself to a tigress (the mother-tigress story): shared grammar of compassionate self-donation, resurrection, and conversion of the predator. In Penzer's annotated Ocean of Story the episode's afterlives are traced: Harsha's Nagananda play (7th c.) built a full drama on it, stage traditions in Kerala (Nagananda-based performance) and modern retellings keep it current. Within the motif clusters, the story pairs with resurrection and parable-teaching: the body given is restored, and the restored body becomes a teaching that reforms an entire race of eaters.
narrative.zh: 索摩提婆的《故事海》（kathasaritsagara，約 1070 年）是梵語文學偉大的故事集——對《大故事》循環的克什米爾重鑄——其中最受讚頌的情節之一即吉穆多伐訶那的捨身，故事如此受愛戴，以致戲劇家曷沙王以其情節作《龍喜記》（Nagananda），佛教說書人亦採之為 Jataka 式典範。拒絕王位的王子：吉穆多伐訶那（『雲為其車』），飛天國王之長子，是繼承權的反英雄：他釋放父國的所有囚犯，將王位讓與其弟，徒步出走為雲遊苦行者『一無所取』。途中故事層疊其倫理：他復活一位死於蛇咬的商人之子（慈悲已勝過死亡），並幾乎不自願地贏得公主摩羅耶伐蒂之愛；誓願出離的王子被敘事溫和地推入一場他未曾求取的婚姻。山：攜隨從至摩羅耶山，聞泣聲而循之。一位年幼的龍族（Naga）——地下蛇族——被縛於石槽：依古老盟約，金翅鳥（Garuda，蛇族之大敵）定期攫取蛇族一人食之；此日籤落此童。吉穆多伐訶那的決定毫無戲劇性：他縛起孩童，送回其父母家中，自己臥入石槽，以油塗身『使其為一頓像樣的餐食』——故事黑色喜劇式的寫實盡在一舉。餵食：金翅鳥降臨，『大如世界之末的雲』，喙入王子之肩。血肉撕裂；王子不出聲、不動——只祈他的贈禮被接受。鳥於啄食中停頓：此肉非蛇肉。自垂死者處得知其為誰，捕食者的轉化即故事的高潮：金翅鳥泣，以天界咒法復其撕裂之軀（復活節拍），並於火前立誓：蛇族永不再被攫。龍族攜花環而來哀悼其救主，卻見其生還；捕食的盟約在一次次靜止的行動中終結。功能：此篇是 katha 文學中不害（ahimsa）倫理的戲劇化——王子的捨身做了任何戰爭都做不到的事，以餵食結束兩族的戰爭。它是梵廷宮廷文學對佛教本生經中菩薩捨身餵虎母故事的回應：共享的語法是慈悲捨身、復活、捕食者的皈依。彭澤爾註釋版《故事之洋》追溯了此篇的後續：曷沙的《龍喜記》（七世紀）據此構築全劇，喀拉拉的舞台傳統（基於《龍喜記》的演出）與現代重述使其至今流傳。在母題群中，此篇與復活及譬喻說法相配：被給出的身體被復原，而復原的身體成為改革整個食者之族的教導。

functions: Ethics of ahimsa dramatized: self-gift ends a war between species
Resurrection motif in katha literature - the torn body restored and the predator converted
Hindu-court counterpart of the Buddhist self-donation Jatakas
Charter of Harsha's Nagananda play and Kerala performance tradition

variants.summary: The story staged as a five-act play with the Bodhisattva-flavored Jimutavahana and the goddess Gauri's intervention; the play's popularity fixed the tale in court and temple performance.

variants.name: Buddhist Jataka parallels (the tigress and the hare)
variants.summary: The Bodhisattva's self-feeding to a starving animal: shared grammar of compassionate self-donation and the predator's transformation; the katha version is its Sanskrit-court cousin.

variants.name: Garuda-Naga covenant endings elsewhere
variants.summary: In most Purana tellings the Garuda-Naga enmity ends by contract (elbow-shells of amrita, the wager of the stakes); the katha version ends it by sacrifice instead - law versus love.
