title.en: Lludd and Llefelys: the Three Plagues of Britain
title.zh: 盧德與勒弗利斯：不列顛三災

region.en: Dinas Emrys (Dinas Ffaraon), Snowdonia, Gwynedd, Wales
region.zh: 威爾斯格溫內斯斯諾登尼亞迪納斯·埃姆里斯（古名迪納斯·法拉翁）

period: Recorded in the Red Book of Hergest, c. 1382-1410 (earlier in Welsh chronicle tradition); Lady Charlotte Guest translation 1849

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1849), 'The Story of Lludd and Llevelys', eBook #5160

summary.en: Three plagues fall on Britain: the Coranians who hear every whisper on the wind, a shriek on May-eve that empties hearths and wombs, and a mighty magician who steals a year's provisions in a night; Lludd sails in secret to his brother Llefelys king of France, and they talk through a brass horn washed clean of its demon with wine — the healing of each plague prescribed, down to the two dragons that must be drunk, sleeping, into a mead-cauldron and buried in Snowdon.
summary.zh: 三災臨不列顛：能於風中聞一切低語之科拉尼人、五月夜使爐火空虛母腹落空的尖嘯、與一夜竊取一年存糧之強大術士；盧德秘密航行至其弟——法蘭西王勒弗利斯——二人以銅角對話、以酒洗去角中之魔；每一災皆有藥方——至於須使其沉睡飲盡蜜酒、葬於斯諾登之雙龍。

sensitivity.note: The buried dragons of Dinas Emrys are the origin-tale behind the red and white dragons of the Welsh flag; the center-of-Britain pit is dug at Oxford in this tale.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849: After a space of time three plagues fell on the Island of Britain. The first was a race called the Coranians, whose knowledge was so great that 'there was no discourse upon the face of the Island, however low it might be spoken, but what, if the wind met it, it was known to them. And through this they could not be injured.' The second was a shriek which came on every May-eve over every hearth in the Island of Britain, which went through people's hearts, 'so that the men lost their hue and their strength, and the women their children, and the young men and the maidens lost their senses, and all the animals and trees and the earth and the waters, were left barren.' The third was that however much of provisions and food might be prepared in the king's courts — even a year's provision — none of it could ever be found except what was consumed in the first night. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.
passages.zh: Guest 1849 年版本的濃縮意譯：過了一段時日，不列顛島上降臨了三場災禍。第一場是一個名為科拉尼亞人的族類，他們的知識極為淵博，「島上無論何處有人交談，縱使聲音再低，只要風將話語吹送過去，他們便無不知曉。因此，無人能傷害他們。」第二場是每逢五朔節前夕，全不列顛島每一戶人家的爐灶上都會響起一聲尖叫，那聲音穿透人心，「以致男人失去血色與氣力，女人失去孩子，青年與少女失去理智，而一切牲畜、樹木、大地與水流，皆歸於荒蕪。」第三場則是：無論國王的宮廷中備辦了多少糧食與食物——即使是一整年的儲備——除了第一夜所消耗的之外，其餘一概遍尋不著。非逐字照錄。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Lludd went to Llefelys king of France, and each came to meet the other with a single ship; they talked through a long horn of brass — 'but whatsoever words they spoke through this horn, one to the other, neither of them could hear any other but harsh and hostile words' — for a demon thwarted them, and Llefelys washed the horn with wine and drove the demon out. The cures: insects bruised in water to destroy the Coranians alone; and for the second plague, 'it is a dragon. And another dragon of a foreign race is fighting with it' — measure the island, dig at its exact central point, set a cauldron of the best mead covered with satin, and the dragons will fall fighting in the form of pigs, drink the mead and sleep. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮意譯：盧德前往法蘭西，去見法蘭西國王勒費利斯，二人各乘一船前來相會；他們隔著一支長長的黃銅號角交談——「然而他們透過這號角彼此所說的任何話語，雙方聽到的都只是刺耳而充滿敵意的言語」——因為有惡魔從中作梗，勒費利斯便以酒洗滌號角，將惡魔驅逐出去。解決之道如下：將蟲子搗碎於水中，可單單消滅科拉尼亞人；至於第二場災禍，「那是一條龍。另有另一條異族之龍正與牠爭鬥」——丈量全島，在其正中央之處挖掘，置一口盛滿最上等蜂蜜酒的大鍋，鍋上覆以緞布，兩龍便會化為豬的形貌相鬥而墜落，飲下蜂蜜酒後睡去。非逐字照錄。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Lludd buried the sleeping dragons in a kistvaen in the securest place in Snowdon — 'Now after that this spot was called Dinas Emreis, but before that, Dinas Ffaraon. And thus the fierce outcry ceased in his dominions.' For the third plague he armed himself and watched the banquet with a vessel of cold water at his side, plunging in when sleep oppressed him; a vast man in heavy armour came with a hamper and filled it with all the provisions, and Lludd fought him — 'the glittering fire flew out from their arms' — and threw the plague to the earth; the magician sought mercy and became his faithful vassal, and Lludd freed the Island of Britain from the three plagues. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮意譯：盧德將沉睡的兩龍埋葬於斯諾登山中最穩妥之處的一座石棺塚中——「此後這地方被稱為迪納斯·恩姆雷斯，但在此之前，則稱為迪納斯·法拉昂。於是那猛烈的尖叫聲便在他的領地內止息了。」至於第三場災禍，他披掛武裝，守候於宴席之旁，身邊備著一盆冷水，每當睡意襲來便將頭浸入水中；一個身披重甲的巨漢帶著一隻大籃前來，將所有糧食裝滿籃中，盧德與他搏鬥——「閃爍的火光自他們的兵器間迸射而出」——將那災禍摔倒在地；那術士求饒，成為他忠誠的臣屬，盧德遂使不列顛島脫離了三場災禍。非逐字照錄。

canonical_translation: Lady Charlotte Guest, The Mabinogion, 1849 (public domain); underlying: Cyfranc Lludd a Llefelys (Red Book of Hergest; earlier, 13th c. White Book tradition)

narrative.en:
Lludd and Llefelys is Britain's plague-diagnosis tale: a kingdom audited by three supernatural afflictions, and a king who cures each one with a different technology — poison, geology and a wrestling match.

Beli the Great had three sons, and Lludd the eldest inherited the Island of Britain; he rebuilt the walls of London and made them so beloved that the city was called Caer Lludd. His brother Llefelys, wisest of the family, had gone to France and won its crown with a daughter-heir. Then three plagues fell on Britain such as no island had ever seen. First, the Coranians: a race of such knowledge that no discourse on the face of the island, however low it was spoken, escaped them if the wind met it — a people whose hearing made them invulnerable. Second, a shriek on every May-eve over every hearth, that went through people's hearts so that men lost their color and strength, women their unborn children, youths and maidens their senses, and animals, trees, earth and waters were left barren — a scream with the force of a season's failed harvest. Third, the great theft: however much was prepared for the king's courts, even a year's provision, none could be found beyond the first night.

Two of the plagues had no known cause; so Lludd took the cure-seeking voyage of the era — in secret and in silence, lest the Coranians overhear the errand — to his brother in France. They met each other with a single ship each, embraced with brotherly love, and then had to invent a communications protocol: knowing the wind carried words to the Coranians, Llefelys had a long horn of brass made, and through it they spoke — and heard only harsh and hostile words, for a demon sat in the horn thwarting them. Wine washed the demon out; the horn becomes the tale's little parable of distorted counsel — every channel has its parasite, and the cure is a strong rinse.

Then the three prescriptions. Against the Coranians: certain insects, bruised in water, sprinkled over both races assembled as if for a peace-conference — the water poisons the Coranians alone, and the whole tribe was destroyed without hurt to any Briton. Against the shriek: diagnosis first — it is a dragon, and a foreign dragon fighting with it, and their battle is the outcry. Measure the island, find its exact central point (Oxford, in this telling), dig a pit, set in it a cauldron of the best mead covered with a satin cloth, and watch: the dragons will fight first as terrible animals, then as dragons in the air, and at the last fall as two pigs upon the covering, sink with it to the bottom of the cauldron, drink the mead, and sleep. Lludd folded the covering around the sleeping dragons and buried them in a kistvaen in the securest place in Snowdon: the spot was Dinas Ffaraon, and after that Dinas Emreis — the hill that Welsh legend keeps as the prison of the red and white dragons, whose contest Merlin would read for Vortigern in a later age. Against the third plague: a night-watch in arms at the great banquet, with a cauldron of cold water at hand — for the thief is a mighty man of magic whose charms put everyone to sleep. Lludd plunged himself into the cold water as often as drowsiness pressed, and when the vast armored man came in with his hamper — a hamper that could hold a year's provisions, a wonder in itself — Lludd followed, fought him until the glittering fire flew from their arms, and threw the plague to the earth. The magician begged mercy and paid with a vassal's oath: never again, and atonement for all the losses. Thus Lludd freed the Island of Britain from the three plagues, and ruled in prosperous peace to the end of his life.
narrative.zh: 《盧德與勒弗利斯》乃不列顛之災病診斷之篇：一個被三種超自然疾患查帳的王國，與一位以三種不同技術——毒物、地質與摔跤——逐一治癒災害的國王。貝利大王有三子，長子盧德繼承不列顛島；他重建倫敦城牆、深得民心、城遂名凱爾·盧德。其弟勒弗利斯最富智慧，赴法蘭西以婚約取得其冠。其後三災臨島，前所未見。其一為科拉尼人：其知識之強，島上任何言語無論多低、若遇風即為其所知——其聽力使其不可傷害。其二為五月夜臨於每一爐火之上之尖嘯，穿透人心——男子失色失力、女子失其腹中之子、少年少女失其神智、動物樹木土地水泉皆不育——一聲具有整季歉收之力之慘叫。其三為巨竊：王廷備糧縱多至一年之儲，除首夜所耗外盡皆無蹤。三災中二者原因不明；盧德遂行那個時代的求藥之旅——秘密而靜默，以免科拉尼人竊聽使命——赴法蘭西其弟處。二人各以單船相迎、兄弟相擁，繼而須發明通訊協議：知風可傳語於科拉尼人，勒弗利斯製長銅角一枚，經角對話——卻只聞粗暴敵意之言，因一惡魔居於角中擾之。以酒洗之、惡魔被逐；銅角遂成此篇關於扭曲諫言的小寓言——每一通道皆有其寄生者，解法是一次徹底的沖洗。繼而三張藥方。治科拉尼人：某種昆蟲搗於水中、於兩族如和會般集會時遍灑——此水獨毒科拉尼人、全族滅亡而布利頓人無一受損。治尖嘯：先診斷——那是一條龍，與一條異族之龍相鬥、其鬥即嘯聲。丈量全島、尋其正中點（此篇定為牛津）、掘坑、置最佳蜜酒之釜於坑中、以緞布覆之、守望：二龍先以可怖之獸形相鬥、繼以龍形鬥於空中，最後以二豬之形落於緞布之上、連布沉入釜底、飲盡蜜酒而眠。盧德以緞布裹住睡龍、葬於斯諾登最堅固處之石櫃中：該地先名迪納斯·法拉翁、後名迪納斯·埃姆里斯——威爾斯傳說保留此丘為紅白二龍之獄、其鬥後世將由梅林為沃蒂根釋讀。治第三災：盛裝持械夜守大宴、手邊置冷水一釜——因竊者為強大術士、其咒使人皆眠。睡意每至，盧德便投入冷水；待巨大披甲之漢攜大籃入內——一籃可容一年之糧、其本身就是奇觀——盧德隨之、戰之至兵器間火星飛迸、將災擲於地上。術士求恕、以封臣之誓償還：永不復犯、並賠償一切損失。盧德遂解不列顛島於三災，終身安治。

functions: Diagnosis-then-cure structure: each plague named as an agent (eavesdropping race, dueling dragons, sleeper-thief)
Etiology of Dinas Emrys and the red-white dragon contest behind the Welsh dragon emblem
Doctrine of the parasite in the channel: the demon in the brass horn as parable of distorted counsel
Charter of the vigilant king: sovereignty maintained by cold-water discipline against enchanted sleep

title.en: The Dream of Maxen Wledig
title.zh: 馬克森大帝之夢

region.en: Aber Sain (Caernarfon), Arfon, Gwynedd, Wales
region.zh: 威爾斯格溫內斯阿爾方阿伯·塞恩（卡那封）

period: Recorded in the Red Book of Hergest, c. 1382-1410 (earlier Welsh chronicle tradition); Lady Charlotte Guest translation 1849

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1849), 'The Dream of Maxen Wledig', eBook #5160

summary.en: The emperor Maxen sleeps beneath the shields of his thirty-two vassal kings and dreams his way up a river, over the highest mountain in the world, across the sea to the fairest island, into a castle at the mouth of a river in Snowdonia — where a maiden on a chair of ruddy gold is too bright to look at; he wastes away for a week until his page tells him the people revile him, and the dream is hunted down province by province until Rome itself is conquered for a Welsh bride.
summary.zh: 馬克森大帝於三十二藩王之盾蔭下入睡，夢中溯河而上、越世上最高之山、渡海至至美之島、入斯諾登尼亞河口城堡——其中金椅少女之美令人不能直視；他一週形銷骨立，侍童言百姓正譏其君，遂按夢逐省追索，直至羅馬本身為一位威爾斯新娘而被征服。

sensitivity.note: The tale historicizes Magnus Maximus (Macsen Wledig, emperor 383-388) and founds the origin-claims of Welsh dynasties and of the men of Armorica (Brittany).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849: Maxen Wledig was emperor of Rome, comelier and wiser than any emperor before him, and he went to hunt in the valley of the river that flowed toward Rome with two-and-thirty crowned kings his vassals. Sleep came upon him in the heat, his attendants set up their shields on spear-shafts about him and a gold enamelled shield under his head; and he saw a dream: journeying up the river to its source, over the highest mountain in the world, through the fairest level regions, down mighty rivers to the mouth of the largest river ever seen — a great city, a vast castle with high towers of various colours, the largest fleet ever seen, and one ship gilded one plank and silvered the next, with a bridge of whale-bone from the ship to the land. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.
passages.zh: Guest 1849 年版本的濃縮意譯：馬克森·弗萊迪格是羅馬的皇帝，比之前任何一位皇帝都更俊美、更睿智，他帶著三十二位加冕的國王作為臣屬，前往那條流向羅馬的河流之谷中狩獵。炎熱之中睡意降臨於他，隨從們將盾牌架在矛桿上圍繞著他，並在他頭下墊了一面鑲嵌琺瑯的金盾；於是他做了一個夢：他溯河而上直至源頭，越過世上最高的山，穿過最秀美的平原，順著浩蕩的河流而下，來到前所未見的最大河流的河口——一座偉大的城市，一座有著各色高塔的宏偉城堡，一支前所未見的龐大艦隊，以及一艘船，一塊船板鍍金、下一塊鍍銀，還有一道由鯨骨製成的橋，從船上通往陸地。非逐字照錄。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: He crossed to the fairest island in the world, traversed it from sea to sea to rugged land, saw another island facing it, and a castle at the mouth of a river — the fairest that man ever saw, its hall with a golden roof and walls of glittering gems, two auburn-haired youths playing chess, a hoary-headed man in an ivory chair carving chessmen, and a maiden in a chair of ruddy gold: 'Not more easy than to gaze upon the sun when brightest, was it to look upon her by reason of her beauty.' He threw his arms about her neck — and woke at the clashing of the shields and the neighing of the horses. For a week he could neither eat nor be with his household, till his page told him the people reviled him, and the wise men prescribed the hunt: seek the dream by the road it seemed to go. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮意譯：他渡海來到世上最美的島嶼，從一海橫越至另一海，直至崎嶇之地，望見對面另有島嶼，以及河口處的一座城堡——那是人所見過最美的城堡，其廳堂有著金色的屋頂與閃耀寶石的牆壁，兩名赤褐色頭髮的青年在下棋，一位白髮老翁坐在象牙椅上雕刻棋子，還有一位少女坐在赤金打造的椅子上：「要凝視她，比凝視最明亮的太陽還要困難，皆因她的美貌。」他張臂環抱她的頸項——卻在盾牌的撞擊聲與馬匹的嘶鳴聲中醒來。整整一週，他既不能進食，也無法與家人相處，直到他的侍童告訴他百姓都在辱罵他，而智者們則指示他再去狩獵：循著夢境似乎所經之路去尋找那夢。非逐字照錄。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Thirteen messengers wearing one sleeve of their caps in front followed the dream's route — up the river, over the mountain, down the great rivers, over the sea to the Island of Britain, to Snowdon, Arfon, and Aber Sain — and found the castle, the hall, the chess-playing youths, the carver, and the maiden exactly as in the dream. 'Empress of Rome, all hail!' — and she answered that if the emperor loved her, let him come to seek her himself. Maxen came with his army, conquered the island from Beli son of Manogan, saw that every place was as he had seen it in sleep, and married her — Helen, daughter of Eudav son of Caradawc. Her bride-price was the island for her father and three castles, earth from Rome beneath the highest; and she made the roads of Helen Luyddawc from castle to castle. When Rome made a new emperor, Maxen besieged the city a year until Helen's brothers came with a small host and took it in a day by ladders; and Kynan's host, cutting out the tongues of their captured women, gave the men of Armorica their name of Britons. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮意譯：十三名使者將帽子的同一側衣袖朝前戴著，循著夢境的路線前行——溯河而上，越過高山，順著大河而下，渡海來到不列顛島，抵達斯諾登、阿爾豐與阿伯賽恩——果然找到了那座城堡、那座廳堂、下棋的青年、雕刻者與那位少女，一切都與夢中無異。「羅馬的女皇，萬安！」——她回答說，倘若皇帝愛她，便讓他親自前來尋她。馬克森率軍前來，從馬諾甘之子貝利手中征服了這座島，見每一處地方都與他夢中所見相同，遂娶了她——海倫，歐達夫之子卡拉道克之女。她的聘禮是為她父親取得這座島以及三座城堡，並從羅馬最高處取來泥土；她又修築了海倫·盧伊道克的道路，連接城堡與城堡。當羅馬另立新帝時，馬克森圍攻該城一年，直到海倫的兄弟率領一支小軍前來，以雲梯於一日之內攻下該城；而基南的軍隊割下所俘婦女的舌頭，使阿莫里卡的男人得到了「不列顛人」之名。非逐字照錄。

canonical_translation: Lady Charlotte Guest, The Mabinogion, 1849 (public domain); underlying: Breuddwyd Macsen Wledig (Red Book of Hergest; earlier, White Book tradition)

narrative.en:
The Dream of Maxen Wledig is the founding dream of Welsh political mythology — the tale that makes the Roman Empire fall in love with a castle in Snowdonia, and a dream the size of geography.

Maxen Wledig was emperor of Rome, comelier and better and wiser than any emperor that had been before him. One day he went to hunt in the valley of the river that flowed toward Rome, with two-and-thirty crowned kings, his vassals — not for the delight of hunting, the tale notes, but to put himself on equal terms with those kings. The sun was high and the heat was great, and sleep came upon Maxen; his attendants stood their shields on the shafts of their spears about him, set a gold-enamelled shield under his head, and the emperor slept.

And the dream is told as a journey of natural scale. He went up the valley to the river's source, and over the highest mountain in the world, and through the fairest and most level regions man ever beheld on the other side; down large and mighty rivers to the sea, to the mouth of the largest river ever seen — a great city, a vast castle with many high towers of various colours, the largest fleet ever seen, and one ship among the fleet larger by far than all others, one plank gilded and the next silvered, with a bridge of the bone of a whale from ship to land. He crossed to the fairest island in the world and traversed it sea to sea to its rugged far shore; saw another island facing it across a plain as large as the sea; and at a river's mouth a castle, the fairest that man ever saw — a hall with a golden roof and walls of glittering gems, two auburn-haired youths playing chess on a silver board with golden pieces, a hoary-headed man in an ivory chair with golden eagles carving chessmen with a steel file — and a maiden in a chair of ruddy gold: 'Not more easy than to gaze upon the sun when brightest, was it to look upon her by reason of her beauty.' She arose and he threw his arms about her neck, and they sat in the chair of gold together — until the chafing of the dogs and the clashing of the shields and the neighing of the horses woke him.

Nor spirit nor existence was left him. For a week the emperor who owned the world could neither eat nor drink with his household, nor hear songs and tales, but slept as often as he could, to see in dreams the maiden he loved best. His page — a king of the Romans, though a page of the chamber — told him the people reviled him; and the wise men of Rome prescribed the cure as a research project: send messengers for three years to the three parts of the world to seek the dream. A year they wandered and learned nothing; then the king of the Romans spoke the tale's key sentence: 'Go forth to hunt by the way thou didst seem to go.' The dream, in other words, has a road.

Thirteen messengers, each wearing one sleeve of his cap in front as the badge of envoys, followed it: up the river, over the mountain that seemed to touch the sky, down the great rivers, over the sea to the Island of Britain, to Snowdon, to Arfon, to Aber Sain — and the castle stood with its portal open, the hall, the chess-playing youths, the carver, the maiden exactly as in the dream. 'Empress of Rome, all hail!' 'What mockery is this ye do to me?' — and then the condition every dreamer must meet: 'If the emperor love me, let him come here to seek me.' Maxen came with his army, conquered the island from Beli son of Manogan, saw that every field and ford was as he had seen it in sleep, and married Helen, daughter of Eudav. Her bride-price founded Welsh geography: the island for her father, three castles — the highest at Arfon with earth brought from Rome for the emperor's health, then Caerlleon and Caermarthen — and the roads of Helen Luyddawc running from castle to castle, made by the men of Britain for no one but her. When Rome made a new emperor and wrote a letter of one sentence — 'If thou comest, and if thou ever comest to Rome' — Maxen answered in kind, besieged the city for a year, and took it in a single day when Helen's brothers came with a small host and their ladders. And the tale ends with an etymology of a nation: Kynan's host, settled in Armorica, cut out the tongues of their captured women lest they corrupt their speech — 'and because of the silence of the women from their own speech, the men of Armorica are called Britons.' A dream, a marriage, an empire — and the demographic charter of Brittany, all in one sleep.
narrative.zh: 《馬克森大帝之夢》乃威爾斯政治神話之奠基之夢——此篇使羅馬帝國愛上斯諾登尼亞一座城堡，而夢境之大一如地理。馬克森·烏萊迪格乃羅馬皇帝，其俊美、賢明、智慧勝於先前任何皇帝。一日他赴河穀狩獵——該河流向羅馬——偕三十二位加冕藩王；狩獵非為其樂，故事註明，而是為與諸王處於同等。日高而熱，睡意臨於馬克森；侍衛以矛桿立盾環繞、以金琺瑯盾為枕，皇帝遂眠。夢被敘述為一段自然尺度之旅。他溯河穀至河源、越世上最高之山、經人類前所未見之至美平原；沿大川巨河而下至海、至所見最大河流之口——偉大之城、高塔各色之城堡、前所未見之最大艦隊、其中一艦遠大於眾艦、板木一金一銀、以鯨骨之橋連舟與岸。他渡至世上至美之島、自海至海行至其崎嶇之遠岸；見隔海平原如海之大之另一島；於河口見人類前所未見至美之城堡——金頂寶石牆之廳、兩名紅髮青年以銀板金子弈棋、白髮老者坐象牙椅以鋼銼雕棋子、以及金椅上之少女：『其美令人不能直視，較仰望正午烈日尤難。』她起身、他擁其頸、二人同坐金椅——直至犬吠盾擊馬嘶將他驚醒。精氣全失。擁有全世界之皇帝一週不能與家人同食共樂、不聞歌與故事，只能盡量睡眠、於夢中見其最愛之少女。其侍童——雖為侍童、實為羅馬人之王——告以百姓正譏其君；羅馬智者遂開出藥方：遣使三年、遍三洲尋夢。使者漫遊一年一無所知；羅馬人之王說出全篇關鍵之句：『循夢中似行之路前往狩獵。』換言之：夢有一條路。十三名使者——各以帽前之一袖為信節——循之而行：溯河、越似觸天之山、下大川、渡海至不列顛島、至斯諾登、至阿爾方、至阿伯·塞恩——城堡門戶洞開、廳堂、弈棋青年、雕工、少女與夢中毫無二致。『羅馬皇后，萬福！』『爾等如此戲弄於我何為？』——繼而是每位夢者必須應付之條件：『若皇帝愛我，令其親自前來尋我。』馬克森率軍而至、自馬諾根之子貝利手中征服其島、見每一田野渡口皆如夢中所見，遂娶埃達夫之女海倫。其聘禮奠定威爾斯地理：以島賜其父、三座城堡——最高者建於阿爾方、其下鋪自羅馬運來之土以利皇帝健康；繼而凱爾利昂與凱爾馬森——以及自城堡至城堡之海倫之路，不列顛男子除她之外不為任何人修此大路。當羅馬另立新帝、寄來僅一句之信——『若你來，若你居然敢來羅馬』——馬克森以同式回覆、圍城一年、直至海倫二兄率小股部隊與梯子一日之內取城。故事以一個民族之詞源結束：定居阿莫利卡之基南部隊、割去所俘婦女之舌以防其敗壞語言——『因婦女緘默於其本族之語，阿莫利卡之人遂被稱為布利頓人。』一夢、一婚、一帝國——及布列塔尼之人口憲章，皆在一睡之中。

functions: Founding charter of Welsh dynasty claims: descent from the emperor's marriage into the line of Eudav
Etiology of the roads of Helen Luyddawc and of Caernarfon's Roman earth
Dream as map: the empire conquered by following a dream's itinerary — geography as revelation
Etiology of the Britons of Armorica: the tongue-cut origin of Brittany's name and speech

title.en: The Hare, the Salmon and the Grain: Taliesin's Birth from Ceridwen
title.zh: 野兔、鮭魚與麥粒：塔利埃辛生於凱里德溫

region.en: Llyn Tegid (Bala Lake), Gwynedd, Wales
region.zh: 威爾斯格溫內斯巴拉湖（萊恩·泰吉德）

period: Recorded in Hanes Taliesin tradition, 16th c. MSS (earlier forms); Lady Charlotte Guest translation 1849

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1849), 'Taliesin', eBook #5160

summary.en: Ceridwen boils a cauldron of inspiration a year and a day for her ugly son; three drops leap onto the thumb of the boy Gwion Bach, who licks them and knows everything, flees through the shapes of hare, fish, bird and grain of wheat — and is swallowed as a grain by the black hen Ceridwen, reborn nine months later, set adrift in a leather bag, and drawn up in Gwyddno's weir by the luckless Elphin, who names him Taliesin, the radiant brow.
summary.zh: 凱里德溫為其醜子熬煮啟示之釜一年又一日；三滴神液躍上男孩格維恩·巴赫之拇指、舐之而知萬事；他化野兔、魚、鳥、麥粒而逃——被化為黑母雞的凱里德溫如麥粒般吞下，九月後重生、以皮袋漂於海、被厄運青年埃爾芬自格維德諾魚梁拉起、命名塔利埃辛——光輝之眉。

sensitivity.note: The Taliesin birth-tale is the Welsh charter of bardic initiation: inspiration gained by accident, sovereignty of speech won through a shapeshift chase and a second womb.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849: Caridwen, wife of Tegid Voel whose dwelling was in the midst of the lake Tegid, thought her ugliest son Avagddu unlikely to be admitted among men of noble birth unless he had some exalted knowledge; so she resolved 'according to the arts of the books of the Fferyllt, to boil a cauldron of Inspiration and Science for her son,' and it might not cease to boil for a year and a day until three blessed drops were obtained of the grace of Inspiration. Gwion Bach stirred the cauldron and the blind Morda kindled the fire. One day toward the end of the year three drops of the charmed liquor flew out of the cauldron and fell upon the finger of Gwion Bach; he put his finger to his mouth, and the instant he tasted the drops 'he foresaw everything that was to come, and perceived that his chief care must be to guard against the wiles of Caridwen.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.
passages.zh: Guest 1849 年譯本的濃縮改寫：Caridwen 是 Tegid Voel 之妻，居於 Tegid 湖中央。她認為自己最醜的兒子 Avagddu 若無某種超凡的知識，便不可能被接納於貴族出身者之列；於是，她決意「依照 Fferyllt 之書的技藝，為她的兒子熬煮一鍋靈感與知識之釜」，此釜須持續沸騰一年零一日，直到取得三滴蒙受靈感恩澤的福滴為止。Gwion Bach 攪動此釜，盲眼的 Morda 則燃起火來。臨近歲末的某一天，三滴受咒的液體自釜中飛濺而出，落在 Gwion Bach 的手指上；他將手指湊到嘴邊，一嚐到那幾滴，便「預見了一切將要發生之事，並察覺到自己首要之務，必是提防 Caridwen 的詭計」。非逐字照錄。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: The cauldron burst in two, and all the liquor except the three drops was poisonous — the horses of Gwyddno poisoned by the stream, and the confluence called the Poison of the Horses of Gwyddno from that time. Caridwen ran after Gwion: 'he changed himself into a hare and fled. But she changed herself into a greyhound and turned him. And he ran towards a river, and became a fish. And she in the form of an otter-bitch chased him under the water, until he was fain to turn himself into a bird of the air. She, as a hawk, followed him and gave him no rest in the sky.' He dropped among a heap of winnowed wheat as a grain; 'then she transformed herself into a high-crested black hen, and went to the wheat and scratched it with her feet, and found him out and swallowed him.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改寫：此釜裂為兩半，除那三滴之外，所有液體皆有毒——Gwyddno 的馬匹因那溪流而中毒，自那時起，那匯流之處便被稱為「Gwyddno 馬匹之毒」。Caridwen 追趕 Gwion：「他變成一隻野兔逃走。但她變成一只灰狗，使他轉向。他奔往一條河，變成一條魚。她則化為母水獺的形貌，在水下追逐他，直到他不得不將自己變成一隻空中的鳥。她化為一隻鷹跟隨他，在天空中不給他片刻安寧。」他化為一粒麥子，落在一堆揚淨的小麥之中；「於是她將自己變成一只高冠的黑母雞，走到那堆小麥前，用腳爪扒抓，把他找了出來，並將他吞下。」非逐字照錄。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: 'And, as the story says, she bore him nine months, and when she was delivered of him, she could not find it in her heart to kill him, by reason of his beauty. So she wrapped him in a leathern bag, and cast him into the sea to the mercy of God.' Elphin, the most hapless of youths, had been granted the drawing of his father Gwyddno's weir that May eve; he found nothing in the weir but a leathern bag on a pole, opened it and saw the forehead of the boy: 'Behold a radiant brow!' 'Taliesin be he called,' said Elphin — and the infant comforted him in verse: 'Although I am but little, I am highly gifted...
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改寫：「而正如故事所說，她懷了他九個月，當她將他生下時，因他容貌俊美，她實在不忍心殺他。於是她把他裹在一只皮袋裡，投入海中，聽憑上帝憐憫。」Elphin 是眾少年中最為不幸者，那年五朔節前夕，他獲准去拉開父親 Gwyddno 魚堰的閘門；他在魚堰中什麼也沒找到，只找到一根竿子上掛著的一只皮袋，打開一看，見到了那男孩的額頭：「瞧，一道光輝的額頭！」「就叫他 Taliesin 吧，」Elphin 說道——而那嬰兒以詩句安慰他：「雖然我形體微小，我卻天賦極高……」

passages.text: There lies a virtue in my tongue.' Later at Maelgwn's court, when Elphin was imprisoned for boasting of his bard, Taliesin silenced the twenty-four bards with the game of 'Blerwm, blerwm' and sang the great 'I have been' poem — 'Primary chief bard am I to Elphin... I have obtained the muse from the cauldron of Caridwen... Then I was for nine months in the womb of the hag Caridwen; I was originally little Gwion, and at length I am Taliesin.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest 1849; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「我的舌上自有其德能。」後來在 Maelgwn 的宮廷中，當 Elphin 因誇耀自己的吟遊詩人而下獄時，Taliesin 以「Blerwm, blerwm」之戲使那二十四位吟遊詩人啞口無言，並唱出那首偉大的「我曾是」之詩——「我是 Elphin 的首席吟遊詩人……我從 Caridwen 之釜中獲得了繆思的靈感……其後我在那老嫗 Caridwen 的腹中待了九個月；我原本是小小的 Gwion，最終我成了 Taliesin。」非逐字照錄。

canonical_translation: Lady Charlotte Guest, The Mabinogion, 1849 (public domain); underlying: Hanes Taliesin (16th c. MSS; earlier bardic tradition; ed. Williams, 1968, copyright)

narrative.en:
The tale of Taliesin is the Welsh initiation myth of poetry itself: inspiration brewed, stolen by accident, chased through the whole ladder of being, and born again as a baby who can out-talk kings.

In times past there lived in Penllyn a man of gentle lineage named Tegid Voel, whose dwelling was in the midst of the lake Tegid; his wife was Ceridwen, and their children were Morvran, Creirwy — the fairest maiden in the world — and a brother, the most ill-favoured man in the world, Avagddu. Ceridwen thought he was not likely to be admitted among men of noble birth by reason of his ugliness, unless he had some exalted merits or knowledge; so she resolved, according to the arts of the books of the Fferyllt, to boil a cauldron of Inspiration and Science for her son, that his reception might be honorable because of his knowledge of the mysteries of the future state of the world. The cauldron might not cease to boil for a year and a day, until three blessed drops were obtained of the grace of Inspiration; Gwion Bach the son of Gwreang stirred it, and the blind Morda kindled the fire beneath it, while Ceridwen gathered every day, in planetary hours, all the charm-bearing herbs.

Then the accident that is the tale's whole engine. One day, toward the end of the year, as Ceridwen was culling plants and making incantations, three drops of the charmed liquor flew out of the cauldron and fell upon the finger of Gwion Bach; and by reason of their great heat he put his finger to his mouth, and the instant he tasted the drops he foresaw everything that was to come, and perceived that his chief care must be to guard against the wiles of Ceridwen, for vast was her skill. The cauldron burst in two, and all the liquor except the three drops was poisonous: the horses of Gwyddno Garanhir died of the stream it ran into, and the confluence was called the Poison of the Horses of Gwyddno from that time. Ceridwen struck the innocent blind Morda on the head till one of his eyes fell out on his cheek — 'Wrongfully hast thou disfigured me, for I am innocent' — and then ran for the thief.

The chase is the ladder of being, in six shapes. He became a hare and fled; she became a greyhound and turned him. He ran to a river and became a fish; she became an otter-bitch and chased him under water. He turned himself into a bird of the air; she, as a hawk, followed him and gave him no rest in the sky. And at the last, in fear of death, he espied a heap of winnowed wheat on the floor of a barn, dropped among the wheat and turned himself into one of the grains. Then she transformed herself into a high-crested black hen, went to the wheat, scratched it with her feet, found him out and swallowed him. The magical duel ends not in an escape but in a conception: the grain of wisdom swallowed, the goddess pregnant.

As the story says, she bore him nine months, and when she was delivered of him she could not find it in her heart to kill him, by reason of his beauty; so she wrapped him in a leathern bag and cast him into the sea to the mercy of God, on the twenty-ninth day of April. Now Gwyddno's weir on the strand between Dyvi and Aberystwyth was worth a hundred pounds every May-eve, and that year its drawing was granted to Elphin, the most hapless and needy of youths. Nothing in the weir — and the weir-ward taunted that Elphin had destroyed the weir's virtue — 'there may be therein the value of a hundred pounds,' said Elphin. On the pole of the weir hung a leathern bag; they took it up, and he who opened it saw the forehead of the boy and said: 'Behold a radiant brow!' 'Taliesin be he called,' said Elphin — radiant brow, the name that would outlive kingdoms. The infant made a Consolation to his weeping finder in verse — 'Although I am but little, I am highly gifted... weak and small as I am... there lies a virtue in my tongue' — and years later, at the court of Maelgwn Gwynedd, when Elphin was chained in prison for boasting of his wife and his bard, Taliesin played 'Blerwm, blerwm' with his finger on his lips until all four-and-twenty royal bards could do nothing else, and then sang the great autobiography of the initiated: 'Primary chief bard am I to Elphin, and my original country is the region of the summer stars... I have been three periods in the prison of Arianrod... I have obtained the muse from the cauldron of Caridwen... Then I was for nine months in the womb of the hag Caridwen; I was originally little Gwion, and at length I am Taliesin.' Elphin was freed; and the boy who had been a grain of wheat became the chief of bards.
narrative.zh: 塔利埃辛之篇乃威爾斯詩歌啟蒙之入門神話：啟示被熬煮、因意外被竊、沿存在之全階梯被追逐、而以一個能勝過國王言辭之嬰兒重生。往昔彭利林地區有一位名為泰吉德·沃埃爾之紳士、居於泰吉德湖心；其妻名凱里德溫；其子女為莫爾夫蘭、世上至美少女克雷爾維、與世上最醜之人阿瓦格杜。凱里德溫思其子因醜陋恐不得入貴族之列，除非具備超凡之知識；遂決意依費里爾特之書之術、為其子熬煮啟示與學問之釜，使其以未來世界奧秘之知識得受尊榮。此釜一年又一日不得停止沸騰，直至取得三滴啟示恩典之福滴；格萊昂之子格維恩·巴赫攪拌、盲者莫爾達生火，而凱里德溫每日依行星時辰採集一切帶咒之草。然後是推動全篇之意外。歲末將近之一日，正當凱里德溫採草誦咒之際，三滴神液自釜中躍出、落於格維恩·巴赫之指；因液極熱，他將手指放入口中——一嚐之下便預知一切將來之事，並明白頭等大事乃是防範凱里德溫之詭計，因其法力廣大。釜裂為二，除三滴外之液皆有劇毒：格維德諾之馬死於其所入之溪，該溪匯流處自此稱格維德諾之馬之毒。凱里德溫擊無辜之盲者莫爾達至一眼落於頰——『你冤枉毀我，我乃無辜』——繼而追趕竊者。追逐即存在之階梯，共六形。他化野兔而逃；她化靈緹而逐。他奔向河流化為魚；她化水獺追之入水。他化飛鳥；她化鷹逐之於天、不給其喘息。最後，於死亡恐懼中，他瞥見穀倉地上篩淨之麥堆、落入麥中化作一粒麥。她化高冠黑母雞、走向麥堆、以足扒之、尋出他並吞下。魔法決鬥不以逃脫而以受孕終結：智慧之粒被吞、女神懷孕。如故事所言，她懷他九月，產下之時因其俊美而不忍殺之；遂以皮袋裹之、投於海中託付上帝之仁慈、時為四月二十九日。格維德諾位於迪維與阿伯里斯特威斯間海灘之魚梁每年五月夜產值百鎊之漁獲；是年其經營被賜予最不幸、最貧窮之青年埃爾芬。魚梁空空——梁守望者譏其毀梁之德——『其中或有百鎊之值，』埃爾芬曰。魚梁之桿上懸一皮袋；他們取下、開袋者見男孩之額曰：『看，光輝之眉！』『塔利埃辛就叫他這個名字，』埃爾芬曰——光輝之眉，此名將比王國長存。嬰兒以詩安慰哭泣的拾得者——『我雖微小，卻極有天賦……我雖弱小……我的舌頭中藏有一種美德』——多年後在格溫內斯馬爾格恩宮廷，埃爾芬因誇口其妻與其樂師而入獄，塔利埃辛以手指抵唇奏『布勒姆、布勒姆』直至二十四位宮廷樂師無一能作他事，繼而唱出受啟蒙者之偉大自傳：『我是埃爾芬之首席樂師，我原本之鄉乃夏日星辰之域……我曾三次居阿麗安蘿德之獄……我自凱里德溫之釜取得繆斯……繼而我在老嫗凱里德溫腹中九月；我原是小小的格維恩，而最終我是塔利埃辛。』埃爾芬獲釋；曾為一粒麥的男孩成為樂師之首。

functions: Charter of bardic initiation: poetic inspiration as potion, accident and second birth
Ladder-of-beings chase: the six-shape metamorphosis as the poet's curriculum of all forms
Etiology of the weir of Gwyddno and the naming of Taliesin (radiant brow)
Sovereignty of speech: the silenced court as demonstration that inspiration outranks institutional learning

title.en: The Birth of Agni
title.zh: 阿耆尼之誕生

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Books 1, 3, 10 (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), hymns to Agni (e.g. 10.21, 3.1, 1.143)

summary.en: Agni, youngest of the gods, was born three times: hidden in the waters, in the sky, and among men at the friction of two sticks. He fled his birthplace from fear, the gods hunted him, and his finding became the model of every sacrifice - the priestly fire-drama in which man grants the god his seat.
summary.zh: 阿耆尼為諸神最幼者，三次誕生：藏於水中、藏於天、以及於人間兩木相磨之中。彼懼而遁離誕生之處，諸神逐之；尋獲之儀遂成為一切祭祀之範式——人授予神座席的祭司劇。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn still recited; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Agni was born three times over: once in the highest heaven, once among the waters, once at the rubbing of two woods. Of the three births the men of old sang that the god's might was one; the same burning one is present in the kindled hearth and in the lightning's fall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Agni (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: Agni 曾三度降生：一次在最高的天上，一次在眾水之間，一次在兩木相摩擦之際。關於這三次誕生，古人歌頌說，此神之力乃是一體；同一個熾燃者既存在於點燃的爐灶之中，也存在於閃電的落下之際。

passages.text: But Agni fled and hid. He concealed himself in the waters and in the plants, afraid of the office set upon him - to carry the offerings to the gods. The gods searched, and found him by his track of smoke; they anointed him and set the priesthood on him as on a king, saying: carry up our oblations, be the messenger between worlds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Agni (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而 Agni 逃走了，並躲藏起來。他因畏懼被賦予的職司——將供品運送給眾神——便將自己藏匿於眾水與草木之中。眾神四處搜尋，循著他留下的煙跡找到了他；他們為他塗抹聖油，並如加冕君王一般，將祭司之職授予他，說道：將我們的祭品向上運送吧，做諸世界之間的信使。

passages.text: From that finding the sacrificial order came: the fire is kindled in a new place for each rite, the god is invited as a guest to the prepared seat, and he, the youngest, becomes the eldest of the gods by office - for through him every prayer travels, and whoever invites him becomes a sharer of heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Agni (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從那次的尋獲中，祭祀的秩序得以確立：火在每一次儀式中於新的地方被點燃，神被作為賓客邀請至備好的座席，而他，最年幼者，因職司而成為眾神中最年長者——因為一切祈禱都經由他而通行，凡邀請他者便成為天界的共享者。

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: Matarishvan Brings the Hidden Fire
title.zh: 摩達利濕梵取回隱藏之火

region.en: Rasa, the far stream (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 羅娑，遠方之流（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Books 1, 3, 10 (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), hymns naming Matarishvan (1.93, 3.29, 10.181)

summary.en: In the age before worship, the sacrificial fire lay hidden far away, kept among the waters by Ahi, the greedy watcher. The seer Matarishvan went, found the hidden flame where the great snake guarded it, and bore it to Bhrigu and Angiras, who first set it among men - the Vedic fire-theft that made worship possible.
summary.zh: 祭祀之火太古時遠藏他方，由貪守者阿希護於水中。仙人摩達利濕梵尋得藏於巨蛇守衛之處的隱焰，攜歸交予弗利伊與盎耆羅，二人首置火於人間——吠陀之盜火，使祭祀成為可能。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'. Fire-theft motif tag is a Euro-American index category - noted.

passages.text: In the earlier ages the god's flame lay hidden, withheld: it shone far off in the water, and the snake Ahi, the greedy one, kept guard over it where no worshipper could reach. Then the seer Matarishvan went where the fire lay hidden, passed the watcher, laid hold of the flame, and bore it back to the race of Bhrigu and Angiras, the first priests.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Matarishvan (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在更早的時代，這位神的火焰隱藏不顯，被扣留著：它在水中遠遠照耀，而貪婪的蛇阿希則在無人能及之處看守著它。後來，先知摩多利首凡前往火焰隱藏之處，越過看守者，抓住那火焰，將它帶回給婆利古與安吉羅族的首批祭司。

passages.text: Bhrigu and Angiras set the fire among men and made from it the first offerings; by that flame the gods came to eat the sacrifice, and men came to speak with heaven. Every hearth lit since is a descendant of that stolen, carried light.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Matarishvan (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 婆利古與安吉羅將火安置於人間，並以之製成最初的祭品；藉著那火焰，眾神前來享用祭祀，人也得以與天界交談。此後點燃的每一座火壇，都是那被竊取、被攜來的火光之後裔。

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: The Miraculous Birth of Indra
title.zh: 因陀羅的奇蹟誕生

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Books 2, 8 (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), hymns on Indra's birth (2.12, 8.45, 10.73)

summary.en: Indra is born sidewise from his mother's flank so as not to be born normally - for he is already drunk with strength. He drinks the Soma his mothers offer, fills both worlds with his body, and before his first day is out has seized the thunderbolt and declared heaven and earth to be his.
summary.zh: 因陀羅自母體側腹斜出而生，非循常道——因其力已醉滿。他飲母親們獻上的蘇摩，軀體撐滿兩界，未滿一日已握雷霆杵，宣稱天地皆屬於他。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: No ordinary womb could hold Indra; he turned himself as he was born and came out by his mother's side, and the mothers of the god stood about him offering the pressed Soma before he could even stand. He drank the Soma and grew - a body that filled two worlds; he overshadowed the sky and trod the earth, and the gods fled before their own newborn king until they set him at the head of all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns on Indra's birth (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 尋常的母胎無法容納因陀羅；他誕生時自行轉身，從母親的側腹而出，眾神之母環立於他身旁，在他尚且無法站立之前便獻上壓榨的蘇摩。他飲下蘇摩而增長——其身軀充滿了兩個世界；他遮蔽天空、踏遍大地，眾神在他們自己新生的君王面前逃遁，直到他們將他立於萬有之首。

passages.text: On the day of his birth he took the thunderbolt, made the sister-rivers flow, and slew the serpent - so the hymn compresses his whole career into his birthday: the king who does everything at once, before his first morning is over.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns on Indra's birth (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在他誕生之日，他取來雷霆，使眾姊妹河川奔流，誅殺巨蛇——頌詩如此將他整個功業壓縮於他的誕辰：那位一舉成就萬事的君王，在他第一個清晨尚未結束之前便已如此。

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: The Maruts, the Howling Storm-Boys
title.zh: 摩魯多：呼嘯的風暴兄弟

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Books 1, 5, 8 (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), hymns to the Maruts (e.g. 1.85, 5.54, 8.20)

summary.en: The Maruts are the storm-brigade of young gods - spearmen with lightning in their fists, deer-clad, who tear up trees, split mountains, and can barely be distinguished from their own thunder. They follow Indra to his fights and howl like newborn lions; Rudra their father disowns their manners but not their worship.
summary.zh: 摩魯多為風暴青年兵團——持雷於拳、披鹿皮而鬧，拔樹裂山，其咆哮幾乎與雷聲難分。他們隨因陀羅赴戰，吼如新生的獅群；其父樓陀羅斥其行徑而未拒其崇拜。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: They come as a cohort, not as a king: spears of light in their hands, golden breastplates, deerskins on their backs, and voices that break the frame of the sky. Where they go the trees are torn up by the roots and the mountains are carved like soft wood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to the Maruts (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們成群而來，而非如君王般獨行：手中持著光之矛，身披金色胸甲，背上覆著鹿皮，其聲響震裂天穹的框架。他們所到之處，樹木被連根拔起，山岳如軟木般被雕鑿。

passages.text: They are the youths of Rudra the howler, and they take after their father; yet even Rudra is said to have disowned the manner of their birth - the hymn-writers joke that a god so disciplined has sons so unruly. With Indra they are invincible: the storm-king and his storm-brigade clear the sky of serpents and open the rains. Their favor is asked like the favor of weather itself, for they are the monsoon's own retinue.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to the Maruts (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們是咆哮者樓陀羅的眾少年，且肖似其父；然而據說連樓陀羅也否認了他們出生的方式——頌詩作者們戲言，如此自律的神竟有如此不羈的兒子。與因陀羅同在，他們所向無敵：風暴之王與其風暴之眾掃清天際的巨蛇，開啟降雨。人們祈求他們的恩澤，如同祈求天氣本身的恩澤，因為他們正是季風的親隨。

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: Varuna's Thousand Ropes
title.zh: 伐樓那的千索

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Books 1, 7 (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), hymns to Varuna (e.g. 1.25, 7.86, 7.88)

summary.en: Varuna, king of the order of things, watches with spies the thousand witnesses he has set in heaven, and binds liars with a thousand ropes. The sinner Varuna's own poet sings his debt - 'not wilfully, but wine and dice and anger undid me' - and begs the god who fetters the guilty to loose the fetter.
summary.zh: 伐樓那，萬物秩序之王，以天中所置的千名見證者與密探監視，以千索縛謊者。詩人自詠其罪——『非有心，乃酒與骰與怒毀我』——乞那位縛罪者的神親手解索。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Varuna has numbered the breaths and winkings of men, set a thousand watchers over the lie, and placed his spies in heaven; his cords are said to be a hundred in his seat, a thousand as they go down the roads - whoever they seize shall not slip free.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Varuna (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伐樓拿已數算過人的呼吸與眨眼，為謊言設下千名守望者，並將他的密探安置於天；據說他的繩索在他的座處有百條，沿路而下時有千條——凡被它們擒住者，皆不得脫身。

passages.text: The confession-hymns give Varuna a sinner's own voice: I told the lie, not wilfully - wine and dice and anger undid me; my elders erred, and I erred after them. O god, let not the stone break me, as a man breaks a dish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Varuna (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 懺悔頌詩賦予伐樓拿罪人自己的聲音：我說了謊，並非有意——酒、骰子與憤怒使我失守；我的長輩有過，我也隨他們有過。哦，神啊，莫讓石頭擊碎我，如同人擊碎一隻碟。

passages.text: The answer sought is not battle but release: loosen the bond that holds me, and my sin shall not again be found; and the poet dreams of going to Varuna's house to see the wise king whose order keeps the rivers running and the stars from straying.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Varuna (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 所求的答覆並非戰鬥，而是解脫：鬆開束縛我的繩索，我的罪便不再被尋見；詩人夢想著前往伐樓拿的居所，去見那位智慧之王，其秩序使河流奔流、星辰不迷。

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: Ushas, the Awakener of Mankind
title.zh: 烏莎斯，人類的喚醒者

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Books 1, 7, 10 (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), hymns to Ushas (e.g. 1.113, 7.77, 10.73)

summary.en: Every dawn the goddess Ushas drives the same red-heifer chariot over the same road, and every dawn she is praised as if brand new - the hymns admit the joke: she is the 'old one' worshipped young, sister of Night, rival of the Sun, awakened by the priests' songs before the birds.
summary.zh: 每逢黎明，女神烏莎斯駕同一輛紅牛之車行同一條路，而每個黎明都被讚為嶄新——頌詩自承這一玩笑：她是『古老者』以青春受拜，夜之姊妹，日之勁敵，先於群鳥被祭司的歌聲喚醒。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Dawn comes to wake the world: she drives her bright heifer-car over the dark road, shakes open the closed eye of the sky, and the sleepers wake and the birds rise from their nests to sing before her. The hymns dare a human honesty: she is the old goddess come back with a new face - the same one we praised at every yesterday, and she goes before the Sun like a bride before a lord, or dances out of the east like a dancer out of the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Ushas (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 黎明前來喚醒世界：她駕著明亮的小母牛之車行於黑暗之路，搖開天際緊閉的眼，沉睡者醒來，鳥兒自巢中飛起，在她面前歌唱。頌詩敢於道出人的誠實：她是舊神以新顏歸來——正是我們在每一個昨日所讚頌的同一位，她行於太陽之前，如新娘行於夫君之前，或如舞者自屋中舞出東方。

passages.text: Her power is mortal time itself: she extends the life of men, sets the many days upon their way, and casts down darkness as a matron casts out a drunkard; one dawn, the singers say, is worth all the nights of hoarded gold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Ushas (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她的力量正是有死的時間本身：她延展人的壽命，將眾多日子安置於他們的途程，並傾覆黑暗，如主婦逐出醉漢；歌者們說，一個黎明，勝過所有囤積黃金的夜晚。

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: Sarasvati, the Great River and the Word
title.zh: 薩拉斯瓦蒂：大河與言語

region.en: Sarasvati river course (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩拉斯瓦蒂河道（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Books 2, 6, 10 (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), hymns to Sarasvati (e.g. 2.41, 6.61, 10.75 river hymn)

summary.en: Sarasvati is addressed as a real river - roaring from the mountains' ice, breaking ridges 'like a verdant elephant-horn', mightier than all other waters - and at the same time as the goddess of the Word that flows from the speaker's mouth. The river that later dried is the goddess that never did.
summary.zh: 薩拉斯瓦蒂被稱呼為真實的河流——自群山冰隙咆哮而下，『如青翠象牙』裂開山脊，壯於眾水——同時亦是自說者之口流出的言語女神。後來枯竭的河，成了永不枯竭的女神。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Sarasvati, mightiest of rivers, flows roaring from the mountains with the flood of her ice, breaking the ridges of the hills like a pierced elephant's tusk, a very army of waters going down to the sea. She is asked to enrich the sacrifice: come with thy floods, dear one, that our singers may be like rain-fed corn; she grants wealth, offspring and fame, and she is the mother of the Word itself. The same name runs through the tradition: the goddess of speech who later carries the veena, and the river whose dry bed stretches across the northwest plains - the geography the hymns loved and the language remembers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Sarasvati (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 薩拉斯瓦蒂，眾河之中最為強大者，自群山之間挾其冰雪之洪流咆哮而下，衝破山嶺之脊，如刺穿象鼻一般，宛如一整支水之大軍奔赴大海。人們祈求她使祭祀豐盛：親愛者啊，請帶著妳的洪流前來，願我們的歌者如受雨水滋養的穀物；她賜予財富、子嗣與聲名，而她本身即是言語之母。同一個名號貫穿整個傳統：那是後來手持維納琴的言語女神，也是那乾涸河床橫貫西北平原的河流——那是頌詩所鍾愛、而語言仍銘記於心的地理。

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: Rudra, the Howler of the Mountains
title.zh: 樓陀羅：山間的呼嘯者

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Books 1, 2, 7 (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), hymns to Rudra (e.g. 1.43, 1.114, 2.33)

summary.en: Rudra is the dangerous god: strong bow, hundred-faced darts, dogs with frightening mouths, dwelling in the mountains. The hymns are half praise, half bargaining - 'spare us, smite not us or our cattle; pass by us with thy felicity' - the first shape of the god who becomes Shiva.
summary.zh: 樓陀羅是危險之神：強弓、百面之鏢、嘴可畏的犬、居於群山。頌詩半為讚美，半為討價——『饒恕我們，勿擊我與我畜；攜吉慶繞過我們』——這就是後來成為濕婆之神的最初形態。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Rudra of the mountains, the strong one with the fair-limbed bow, has arrows that are sickness and darts that are fevers; his messengers are dogs with terrifying mouths, and his company walks the wild passes with him. The hymn prays like a neighbor soothing a temper: oh, divinity, be kind; spare us, injure not our strong steed nor our ram nor our offspring; put far from us thy bolt of heaven and thy stone of earth. But the danger is also medicine: he is the healer whose hand both strikes and cures, lord of herbs in the hill-forests, and the fierce god praised most sweetly becomes in the later tradition Shiva, the gracious one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda hymns to Rudra (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 山中的樓陀羅，那位手持美飾之弓的強健者，其箭矢即是疾病，其鏢矛即是熱病；他的使者是張著可怖之口的群犬，他的隨從與他一同行走於荒野的隘口。頌詩祈禱的語氣，如同鄰人安撫怒氣：噢，神聖者啊，請仁慈；饒過我們，勿傷害我們強壯的駿馬，勿傷害我們的公羊，勿傷害我們的子嗣；請將你的天之雷霆與地之石塊遠遠移開。然而危險亦是良藥：他是醫者，其手既能打擊亦能治癒，是山林間草藥之主；而這位被最甜美地讚頌的凶猛之神，在後來的傳統中成為濕婆，那位仁慈者。

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: Soma, the God That Is a Drink
title.zh: 蘇摩：即是飲料的神

region.en: Mujuvant mountains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 木周萬特山（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Book 9 (Soma Mandala) and others (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 9, hymns to Soma Pavamana

summary.en: The Soma hymns praise the plant as it is pressed: the god filtered through sheep's wool, roaring as he runs, cleaning himself like a horse washed in a river. He is the drink that makes gods immortal and poets invincible - Indra's ammunition - and the whole ninth book is a single day's brewing turned into liturgy.
summary.zh: 蘇摩頌讚那正在榨汁的植物：神經羊毛衣而濾清，奔流時如雷而吼，如河浴之馬自淨。他是使諸神不死、使詩人無敵的飲料——因陀羅的彈藥——第九冊整卷即把一日的榨釀化作禮儀。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The Soma is brought down from the mountains in carts; it is pressed between stones, filtered through the sheep's wool, and as it streams it is called Pavamana, the flowing clear one - the god washing himself as he runs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda Book 9 hymns (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蘇摩以車自山中運下；它在石塊之間被壓榨，透過羊毛濾淨，而當它流淌之時，被稱為「帕瓦瑪那」，即流動而澄澈者——那位在奔流之際沐浴自身的神。

passages.text: He mounts the sky as he flows: he begets light, sets the dawns in motion, drives the Sun upon his way, and puts strength into Indra's arms for the next serpent-slaying. The theology is intoxication made cosmic: whoever drinks of the pressed god becomes a seer; Indra himself grew so great on Soma that he filled two worlds - the hymns are the liturgy of a sacrament that means what it does.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda Book 9 hymns (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他流淌之時，他登上天空：他生出光明，推動黎明，驅策太陽踏上其途，並為因陀羅的雙臂注入力量，以備下一次誅殺巨蛇。其神學是將沉醉化為宇宙之理：凡飲下這被壓榨之神者，皆成為先知；因陀羅本人亦因蘇摩而壯大，乃至充滿兩個世界——這些頌詩乃是一項聖事的禮儀，而這聖事所言即其所行。

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: Mitra and Varuna: The Twin Upholders
title.zh: 密多羅與伐樓那：雙位撐持者

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Books 3, 5, 7 (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), dual hymns to Mitra-Varuna (e.g. 3.59, 5.62, 7.64)

summary.en: The twin sovereigns of the Vedic heaven: Mitra the friendship, Varuna the bond - together they prop the sky, direct the rivers, and sit as judges over oath and truth. Their shared hymns describe two kings of one law, one of them sovereign of the waters' deep and the other of the compact between men.
summary.zh: 吠陀天界的雙位君主：密多羅為友誼，伐樓那為盟約——同撐天穹、導引河流，並為誓言與真理之判官。其合頌描繪同一法律下的二王：一位為深水之主，一位為人際契約之王。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Mitra, when he speaks, stirs men to labor and to friendship; Varuna, when he decrees, holds the bound by their bonds. Together the two uphold the sky and the earth, and the hymns address them as one kingship with two names.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda dual hymns (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 密多羅開口之時，激勵人們勞作與結交；伐樓那頒定之時，以其束縛繫住被縛者。二者共同支撐天與地，而頌詩以一個王權、兩個名號來稱呼他們。

passages.text: They made the streams run to the sea, set the Sun upon his high road, and look down upon the dealings of men: the oath-breaker and the promise-keeper alike arrive at their seat, and the pair are invoked over every covenant. In the later spread of the god-language Mitra travels west - the Persian contract-god, the Roman Mithras - but in the Vedic home the two are the law's own face: order as friendship, order as fetter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda dual hymns (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們使眾流奔向大海，安置太陽於其高道之上，並俯視人間的種種作為：背誓者與守信者同樣來到他們的座前，而這對神祇在每一項盟約中皆被祈請。在後來神祇語言的傳播中，密多羅西行——成為波斯的契約之神、羅馬的密特拉——但在吠陀的家園裡，二者即是法律自身的面容：秩序即友誼，秩序即束縛。

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: The Two Dogs of the Dead
title.zh: 亡者的雙犬

region.en: Yama's pasture road (symbolic pin at Gaya)
region.zh: 閻摩牧野之路（象徵性定位於伽耶）

period: Rigveda, Book 10 (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, hymns 14, 135-136 (the dogs of Yama)

summary.en: On the path to Yama's pasture two four-eyed, broad-nosed dogs guard the road of the departed, dark of hue, with Sarama the divine bitch for their mother. The funeral hymns ask them to be lenient - to let the father through to the company of the old ones - while the dead man is sent ahead with gifts for the gate-keepers.
summary.zh: 通往閻摩牧野之路上，兩隻四眼闊鼻的犬守衛亡者之路，色暗，母親為神犬薩羅摩。葬歌求它們寬待——放父親入古者之群——死者則被先行差遣，攜禮物賄賂守門者。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funeral hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Run forward along the ancient paths, the hymn tells the dead man, where our forefathers have gone: there the two kings Yama and Varuna keep their seat, and the two dogs, the four-eyed ones, watch the path. The dogs are described by their mouths: broad-nosed, dark of body, drawn from the divine Sarama - one takes the black, one the parti-colored; they sit at Yama's city and lick at the lot of the dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 10.14 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 頌詩對死者說：沿著我們祖先走過的古老道路向前奔跑吧；在那裡，閻摩與伐樓那兩位君王守著他們的座位，而那兩隻四眼狗看守著道路。這些狗依其口部而被描述：寬鼻、體色深暗，出自神聖的娑羅摩——一隻帶走黑色者，一隻帶走雜色者；牠們坐在閻摩的城邑旁，舔舐死者的命運。

passages.text: The offering is practical theology: give these two dogs of thine, O father, thy rice and thy cake - they watch the road of the fathers - and then enter, with the old ones and their flocks, to the pasture of delight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 10.14 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這獻祭是務實的神學：哦，父親，把祢的米與糕餅給這兩隻屬於祢的狗——牠們看守著祖先的道路——然後與那些長者及其牲畜一同進入歡愉的牧場。

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: The Coming of Finn: the Boy in the Wood and the Burning of Teamhair
title.zh: 芬恩之來臨：林中之童與塔拉大火

region.en: Slieve Bladhma (Slieve Bloom), Offaly/Laois, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭奧法利/萊斯郡斯利夫·布拉德瑪山（布盧姆山）

period: Fenian cycle (Fianaigecht), medieval Irish MSS; Gregory retelling 1904

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book One: Finn, Chapter I, eBook #14465

summary.en: Born after his father Cumhal is killed by the sons of Morna, the boy Demne is nursed in secret in the woods of Slieve Bladhma, trained by two women druids in running, leaping and swimming, given the name Finn — the Fair — at a swimming match, finds the crane-skin treasure-bag of Manannan, eats the salmon of knowledge at the Boinn, and keeps Teamhair safe for a night from Aillen of the Sídhe by holding a spear against his forehead until sleep cannot come — winning the headship of the Fianna from Goll's own hand.
summary.zh: 其父庫哈爾死於莫爾納諸子之手後出生的男孩德姆內，被秘密撫養於斯利夫·布拉德瑪山中；兩位女德魯伊訓練其跑、跳、泳；因游泳比賽得『芬恩』（俊美）之名；尋得瑪南南之鶴皮寶袋；於博因河食智慧之鮭；以矛抵額不眠、守塔拉整夜不被西德之艾倫焚毀——自戈爾之手贏得費恩納之首。

sensitivity.note: The salmon of knowledge episode overlaps the existing base record salmon-knowledge; this record cuts the whole coming-of-age arc, with the Aillen fire-fight as its climax. Finn's thumb of knowledge is the Fenian cycle's signature.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904: At the time Finn was born his father Cumhal of the sons of Baiscne, Head of the Fianna of Ireland, had been killed in battle by the sons of Morna that were fighting with him for the leadership; and his mother, beautiful long-haired Muirne, daughter of Tadg, son of Nuada of the Tuatha Dé Danann, did not dare to keep him with her; and two women, Bodhmall the woman Druid and Liath Luachra, came and brought him away to the woods of Slieve Bladhma and nursed him secretly. They gave him good training: one would run round a tree with a thorn switch, Finn after her with another switch; they left him in a field with hares and bid him not let the hares quit the field; to teach him swimming they threw him into the water and let him make his way out. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book One ch. 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 格雷戈里1904年著作的濃縮意譯：芬恩出生之時，他的父親、巴伊斯克內諸子中的庫馬爾——愛爾蘭費尼亞的首領——已在與他爭奪領導權的莫爾納諸子的戰鬥中被殺；他的母親、美麗長髮的繆爾內——圖阿薩·德·達南的努阿達之子塔德格的女兒——不敢將他留在身邊；兩位女子，女德魯伊博德瓦爾與利亞赫·盧阿赫拉，前來將他帶往斯利夫·布拉德瑪的森林，秘密撫養他。她們給予他良好的訓練：一人拿著荊棘枝繞樹奔跑，芬恩拿著另一枝在後追趕；她們把他留在有野兔的田野裡，吩咐他不要讓野兔離開田野；為了教他游泳，她們把他扔進水中，讓他自己游出來。非逐字照錄。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Swimming against the lads of Magh Life, 'Fair he is and well shaped,' they said, and it was from that time he got the name of Finn, that is, Fair. He won seven games of chess from the king his mother had married, who guessed his blood and warned him away; he avenged a woman whose son had been killed, killing the champion who had given Cumhal his first wound, and took back the treasure-bag of crane-skin that had been Manannan's — Manannan's shirt and knife, Goibniu's belt and smith's hook, the shears of the King of Alban, the helmet of the King of Lochlann, the bones of Asal's pig — full at high tide and empty at ebb. Then for seven years he watched the salmon of the Boinn for the poet Finegas, and when it came and Finn roasted it, the blister on the skin burned his thumb and he put his thumb in his mouth: 'It is not Deimne but Finn your name is, and it is to you and not to myself the salmon was given in the prophecy.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book One ch. 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮意譯：他與馬格·利夫的少年們比賽游泳，「他俊美而體態勻稱，」他們說，正是從那時起他得了芬恩之名，意即「俊美」。他從他母親所嫁的國王那裡贏了七局棋，那國王猜出了他的血統並警告他離去；他為一名兒子被殺的女子復仇，殺死了曾給庫馬爾第一處創傷的那位勇士，並取回了曾屬於馬納南的鶴皮寶袋——馬納南的襯衫與刀、戈伊布紐的腰帶與鐵匠鉤、阿爾班國王的剪刀、洛赫蘭國王的頭盔、阿薩爾之豬的骨頭——漲潮時滿、退潮時空。此後七年，他為詩人菲內加斯看守博因河的鮭魚，當鮭魚出現、芬恩將其烤炙時，魚皮上的水泡燙傷了他的拇指，他把拇指放進口中：「你的名字不是德姆內而是芬恩，那鮭魚是依預言賜給你而非賜給我。」非逐字照錄。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: At Samhain Finn went up to the gathering of the High King at Teamhair and declared himself: 'I am Finn, son of Cumhal.' For nine years Aillen son of Midhna of Sidhe Finnachaidh had come every Samhain playing music of the Sídhe that put all who heard it to sleep, then breathing a flame out of his mouth and burning Teamhair. Finn pledged to keep it safe till morning: when the sorrowful music came he stripped the covering from the head of a deadly spear and held it to his forehead, so that sleep could not come on him; Aillen let his flame out, and Finn held up his fringed crimson cloak against it till the flame fell through the air into the ground; then Finn followed Aillen back to the Sídhe and cast the spear through his heart as he entered, and struck off his head. 'Well, Goll, is it your choice to quit Ireland or to put your hand in Finn's hand?' — and Goll, son of Morna, was the first to strike his hand in Finn's hand, the way there would be less shame on the rest. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book One ch. 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮意譯：在薩溫節，芬恩前往塔拉的高王集會並自陳身分：「我是芬恩，庫馬爾之子。」九年來，西德·芬納海德的米德納之子艾倫每逢薩溫節便來演奏精靈的音樂，使所有聽者入睡，然後從口中吐出火焰焚燒塔拉。芬恩立誓守護它至天明：當那哀傷的音樂傳來，他從一柄致命長矛的矛頭上剝下遮蓋物，將其抵在自己額前，使睡意無法降臨於他；艾倫吐出火焰，芬恩舉起他那鑲流蘇的深紅斗篷抵擋，直到火焰穿過空中落入地面；隨後芬恩尾隨艾倫回到精靈丘，在他進入時將長矛擲穿他的心臟，並砍下他的頭。「那麼，戈爾，你是選擇離開愛爾蘭，還是把手放進芬恩的手中？」——而莫爾納之子戈爾是第一個把手擊入芬恩手中的人，如此其餘眾人便少些羞恥。非逐字照錄。

narrative.en:
Every hero-cycle needs a foundling, and the Fenian cycle's foundling grows up in a wood with two druid-women for schoolmistresses — and becomes the most just, most generous king of a company of wild men.

At the time Finn was born his father Cumhal of the sons of Baiscne, Head of the Fianna of Ireland, had been killed in battle by the sons of Morna that were fighting with him for the leadership; and his mother, beautiful long-haired Muirne, daughter of Tadg — son of Nuada of the Tuatha Dé Danann and of Ethlinn, mother of Lugh of the Long Hand — did not dare to keep him with her. Two women, Bodhmall the woman Druid and Liath Luachra, came and brought him away to care for, to the woods of Slieve Bladhma, and nursed him secretly because of his father's enemies. His mother came once in six years, through every lonely place, to find the little hunting cabin and kiss him and sing him a sleepy song, and go away again.

His education was a chase. One woman would run round a tree with a thorn switch, Finn after her with another switch, each trying to hit the other; they would leave him in a field with hares and bid him not let the hares quit the field, but keep before them whichever way they went; to teach him swimming they threw him into the water and let him make his way out. He killed his first wild duck by a cast that cut the wings from her. A herd of mountain deer went past the cabin once, and Finn caught two stags and brought them home: 'I will get one for you.'

The name came at a swimming match in Magh Life: beating the lads of the plain at their own sport, 'Fair he is and well shaped,' they said — and it was from that time he got the name of Finn, the Fair, put on him like a crown for swimming. Jealousy drove him on: seven games of chess won from the king who had married Muirne — and that king knew his blood at once, 'you are the son that Muirne my wife bore to Cumhal. And do not stop here any longer, that you may not be killed under my protection.'

Then the spoils of ancestry. He avenged a woman whose only son had been killed, fighting and killing the great champion that had given Cumhal his first wound in his last battle — and took back from him the treasure-bag of crane-skin, whose pedigree runs through the whole mythological cycle: once the skin of Aoife, sweetheart of Ilbrec son of Manannan, changed to a crane through jealousy; kept in Manannan's house, holding Manannan's shirt and knife, Goibniu's belt and smith's hook, the shears of the King of Alban, the helmet of the King of Lochlann, and the bones of Asal's pig that the sons of Tuireann brought to Ireland — full at high tide and empty at ebb. It went from Manannan to Lugh son of Ethlinn, and after that to Cumhal, husband of Ethlinn's daughter: the Fenian cycle handing back to the Mythological cycle its own luggage.

Then poetry, and the salmon. Finn went to learn from Finegas the poet living at the Boinn, for the poets thought it was always on the brink of water poetry was revealed; and he gave no name of his own but took the name of Demne. Seven years Finegas had watched the salmon of the Boinn, for it was in the prophecy that he would eat it and have all knowledge after. At last it came; he bade Finn roast it and not taste it; and when Finn brought it back, 'Did you eat any of it at all, boy?' 'I did not; but I burned my thumb putting down a blister that rose on the skin, and after doing that I put my thumb in my mouth.' 'It is not Deimne, but Finn your name is, and it is to you and not to myself the salmon was given in the prophecy' — and Finegas gave him the whole of the salmon, and from that time Finn had the knowledge that came from the nuts of the nine hazels of wisdom that grow beside the well that is below the sea. A second draught followed by accident: hunting by the well of the moon of Beag son of Buan, whose three daughter-guardians would not part with a vessel of it for less than red gold, one of them threw the vessel's water at him to stop him, and a share went into his mouth — all the knowledge that well could give.

And then the master-feat of the cycle's beginning. At Samhain Finn went up to the High King's gathering at Teamhair and named himself before the horn of meetings: 'I am Finn, son of Cumhal... I am come now to get your friendship, and to give you my service.' For nine years, every Samhain, Aillen son of Midhna had come out of Sidhe Finnachaidh playing music of the Sídhe that put all who heard it to sleep — 'even women in their pains and men that were wounded would fall asleep' — and then breathed a flame out of his mouth and burned Teamhair. Finn pledged to keep it till morning, taking pledges of the king; and a fighting man, Fiacha son of Conga, who had loved Cumhal, sold him for a third of his winnings a deadly spear with a charm in its head: 'when you will hear the music of the Sídhe, let you strip the covering off the head of the spear and put it to your forehead, and the power of the spear will not let sleep come upon you.' The music came, the covering came off, the forehead took the spearhead's power; Aillen breathed his flame, and Finn held up his fringed crimson cloak against it until the flame fell down through the air and went into the ground. Then Finn followed Aillen back to the Sídhe and made the cast through his heart at the door, struck off his head and fixed it on a crooked pole at Teamhair till sunrise, while Aillen's mother keened: 'Nine times he burned Teamhair.'

The reward was the thing itself: 'Well, Goll, son of Morna, is it your choice to quit Ireland or to put your hand in Finn's hand?' 'By my word, I will give Finn my hand' — and when the charms of good luck had done their work, the chief men of the Fianna struck their hands in Finn's, Goll first, the way there would be less shame on the rest for doing it. The headship of the Fianna was Finn's until the end, at Almhuin of Leinster, in the white dun of Nuada of the Tuatha Dé Danann; and of him the sayings ran: a king and a seer and a poet; a Druid and a knowledgeable man; if his enemy and his own son had come before him to be judged, a fair judgment he would have given between them.
narrative.zh: 每個英雄故事圈都需要一個棄兒，而費恩納故事圈的棄兒在林中由兩位女德魯伊撫育成人——成為一隊野性男子的最公正、最慷慨之王。芬恩出生之時，其父——愛爾蘭費恩納之首、拜斯克尼之子庫哈爾——已在爭奪首領之位的戰鬥中被莫爾納諸子殺死；其母、美麗長髮的穆爾妮——塔德格之女、塔拉哈·迪·丹安之努阿達與魯格之母艾斯琳的後裔——不敢將他留在身邊。兩位婦女——女德魯伊波德馬爾與利亞·盧阿赫拉——將他帶往斯利夫·布拉德瑪山中秘密撫育。其母每六年穿過所有僻地來一次，尋到小獵屋、抱起他親吻、為他唱一支催眠短歌，而後離去。其教育即追逐：一名女子持棘枝繞樹奔跑、芬恩持另一枝追之互擊；他們把他與野兔留在田野、命他不許兔群離開田野、無論兔往何方都要趕在其前；教游泳之法是將他拋入水中、任其自行出水。他以一擊削去其翼殺死第一隻野鴨。一次一群山鹿經過小屋，芬恩追而捕得兩隻牡鹿帶回家：『我為你們弄一隻來。』其名得於馬格·利夫之游泳賽：他勝過平原上所有少年，眾人曰『他真俊美、身形真好』——自此他得名芬恩（俊美），如游泳之冠加於其身。嫉妒驅其前行：他從母親改嫁之王手中連勝七局棋——王即刻識出血統：『你便是穆爾妮為庫哈爾所生之子。別再停留於此，以免在我的庇護之下被殺。』繼而是祖先之戰利品。他為獨子被殺的婦人復仇，殺死曾在其父最後一戰中給予庫哈爾第一傷的巨漢——並取回鶴皮寶袋：其譜系貫穿整個神話故事圈——原為瑪南南之子伊爾布雷克之戀人艾奧菲因妒被化為鶴之皮；存於瑪南南家中，內藏瑪南南之衫與刀、戈伊布尼烏之帶與鍛鉤、阿爾巴王之剪、洛赫蘭王之盔、以及圖雷恩諾子攜來之阿薩爾豬骨——滿潮時滿、退潮時空。其袋由瑪南南傳至艾斯琳之子魯格、再至艾斯琳之女之夫庫哈爾：費恩納故事圈將神話故事圈自己的行李送還。繼而是詩與鮭。芬恩往博因河畔從詩人菲內加斯學詩——因詩人相信詩總在水邊顯現——隱名德姆內。菲內加斯守候博因智慧之鮭七年，因預言其食之而後得全知。鮭終至；他命芬恩烤之而不許嚐；芬恩捧鮭而回——『你究竟嚐過沒有，孩子？』『沒有；但皮上起了水泡、我按下去燙了拇指、隨後把拇指放進了嘴裡。』『你不叫德姆內，你的名字是芬恩，預言中的鮭是給你的、不是給我的』——菲內加斯將整條鮭給了他；自此芬恩擁有海底智慧泉旁九株榛樹堅果之知識。第二瓢知識又因意外而至：他在布安之子貝格的月亮井旁狩獵、三名持井之女不許他以少於赤金之價取水、其中一名擲水阻他、一口水入其口——該井所能給的知識盡歸於他。繼而是故事圈開篇之絕技。薩溫之夜芬恩上塔拉至至高王集會、於會議之角前自報家門：『我是芬恩、庫哈爾之子……我來求你的誼、獻我的忠。』九年來每逢薩溫，菲德納之子艾倫自北方菲納凱西德出來、奏西德之樂使聞者入睡——『連產中之婦與帶傷之男也會睡去』——繼而自口中吐火焚燒塔拉。芬恩立誓守至天明；曾敬庫哈爾的戰士菲亞赫以戰利品三分之一之價售他一支頭部藏咒的致命之矛：『聞西德之樂時，剝去矛頭之覆、以之抵額，矛之力便不容睡眠臨身。』樂聲至、覆布起、額頭承矛力；艾倫吐焰、芬恩舉紅穗斗篷相拒直至火焰穿空落地入土。隨後芬恩追艾倫至西德門前、乘其入門一矛穿心、斬首攜回塔拉、懸於彎杆至日昇，而艾倫之母哀哭：『他曾九次焚燒塔拉。』其賞即事物本身：『戈爾、莫爾納之子，你擇離開愛爾蘭、還是把手放進芬恩手中？』『我願把手交給芬恩』——吉兆咒行畢，費恩納首領們將手擊入芬恩手中、戈爾最先出手、好讓其餘之人少些羞恥。費恩納之首自始至終歸芬恩，於萊因斯特之阿爾文、塔拉哈·迪·丹安之努阿達所建白色雪堡之中；關於他的諺語如此流傳：王者、先知、詩人；德魯伊與博學之士；縱使仇敵與親子同至其前受審，他亦能公判。

region.en: Teamhair (Hill of Tara), Co. Meath, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭米斯郡塔拉王丘

summary.en: Grania, daughter of the High King, is betrothed to grey-haired Finn, Head of the Fianna, and regrets it at the wedding feast: a druid names each hero to her, the cap slips from Diarmuid's love-spot, an enchanted cup puts every man asleep, and she puts Diarmuid under geasa to carry her out — over the walls on the shafts of his spears, leaving unbroken bread behind him as proof he keeps his faith to Finn.
summary.zh: 至高王之女格蘭妮被許給灰髮的費恩納之首芬恩，婚宴之上心生悔意：德魯伊為她逐一唱名英雄、迪爾木德的愛痣帽落、施咒之杯使滿座入睡；她以geasa束縛迪爾木德攜她出走——踏矛桿越牆而過、身後留下未掰開之麵包以證他對芬恩守其忠信。

sensitivity.note: The elopement tale is Ireland's Helen-and-Paris story; the love-spot (ball seirce) granted to Diarmuid by the woman of the Sídhe makes consent literal and irresistible. Retold from public-domain print.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904: Finn sat out alone on the green lawn of Almhuin, without a wife or companion since Maighneis daughter of Black Garraidh died from him, and Diorraing the Druid named for him Grania, daughter of the High King of Ireland, 'the woman of the best make and shape and the best speech of the women of the whole world.' Oisin and Diorraing went to Teamhair to woo her; the king sent them to her own answer: 'If he is a fitting son-in-law for you, why would he not be a fitting husband for me?' But when Grania saw grey-haired Finn at the wedding, 'It is a great wonder it was not for Oisin Finn asked me, for he would be more fitting for me than a man that is older than my father.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book Seven chs. 1-2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 格雷戈里1904年著作的濃縮意譯：芬恩獨自坐在阿爾溫的綠色草坪上，自從黑加賴德之女邁格內斯離他而死後，便沒有妻子或伴侶；德魯伊迪奧蘭因向他提起愛爾蘭高王之女格拉尼婭，稱她為「全世界的女子中體態與容貌最佳、言語最佳的 woman」。奧辛與迪奧蘭前往塔拉為她求婚；國王讓他們去聽她自己的答覆：「若他是配得上你們的女婿，為何他不會是配得上我的丈夫？」但當格拉尼婭在婚禮上見到灰髮的芬恩時，「真是大奇事，芬恩為我求的不是奧辛，因為他會比一個比我父親還年長的男人更配得上我。」非逐字照錄。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Finn set her riddles and she answered better — 'What is sharper than a sword?' 'The wit of a woman between two men.' 'What is quicker than the wind?' 'A woman's mind.' At the feast a druid named to her each man of the Fianna, and of Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne, said 'that is the best lover of women in the whole world.' Diarmuid kept his cap always over the love-spot the woman had left on his forehead, for no woman could see that spot but she would give him her love; parting the fighting dogs, the cap fell from him, Grania saw it, and great love came on her there and then. She filled the great golden cup with wine that had enchantment in it, and all drank of it but Oisin, Osgar, Caoilte, Diarmuid and Diorraing — and all that drank fell into a deep sleep. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book Seven ch. 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 精簡改寫：芬恩向她提出謎題，她答得更好——「什麼比劍更鋒利？」「一個女人夾在兩個男人之間的心機。」「什麼比風更迅疾？」「女人的心思。」宴席上，一名德魯伊向她逐一指認費尼亞的每個男子，指到杜布涅之孫迪爾穆德時說：「那是全天下最善於贏得女人愛情的男子。」迪爾穆德始終把帽子蓋在那女人留在他額上的愛痣上，因為沒有哪個女人見了那顆痣而不把愛給他；當他分開爭鬥的狗時，帽子從他頭上掉落，格拉尼亞看見了，巨大的愛意當場湧上她心頭。她斟滿那隻施了魔法的大金杯，眾人都喝了，唯有奧辛、奧斯加、科伊爾特、迪爾穆德與迪奧蘭未飲——而所有飲者都陷入沉睡。非逐字照錄。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: 'Will you take my love, Diarmuid, son of Duibhne, and will you bring me away out of this house to-night?' 'I will not; I will not meddle with the woman that is promised to Finn.' 'Then I put you under Druid bonds, to bring me out of this house to-night before the awaking of Finn.' He asked the advice of each companion in turn — Oisin ('you are not guilty if the bonds were laid on you; follow Grania'), Osgar ('it is a pitiful man that would break his bonds'), Caoilte, Diorraing — and all said follow. He rose with tears of the size of mountain berries, passed over the wall of the dun on the shafts of his two spears — for 'every fighting man has leave to pass over the walls of any dun by the shafts of his spears' — and Grania met him on the grass. Wherever they went, Diarmuid left unbroken bread after him, as a sign to Finn he had kept his faith with him. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book Seven chs. 1-2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 精簡改寫：「迪爾穆德，杜布涅之子，你可願接受我的愛，今夜帶我離開這座宅邸？」「我不願；我不會去碰許配給芬恩的女人。」「那麼我以德魯伊的束縛加於你，要你在芬恩醒來之前帶我離開這座宅邸。」他依次向每位同伴求教——奧辛（「束縛加於你，你並無罪過；跟格拉尼亞走吧」）、奧斯加（「會破除自己束縛的，是可悲之人」）、科伊爾特、迪奧蘭——眾人都說跟隨。他起身，淚珠大如山莓，踏著兩支長矛的矛桿越過堡壘的牆——因為「每個戰士都有權踏著自己的矛桿越過任何堡壘的牆」——格拉尼亞在草地上迎他。無論他們去到何處，迪爾穆德都在身後留下未掰開的麵包，作為向芬恩表明他仍對他守信的信號。非逐字照錄。

narrative.en:
The Pursuit of Diarmuid and Gráinne is Ireland's great romance of the elopement — a bride who chooses for herself at her own wedding, and a hero who obeys the law of geasa into the tragedy it foretells.

Finn sat out alone on the green lawn of Almhuin of Leinster, without a wife or companion since Maighneis daughter of Black Garraidh had died from him, 'for quiet sleep is not used to come to a man that is without a fitting wife.' Oisin his son and Diorraing the Druid came to him, and Diorraing named the bride: Grania, daughter of the High King of Ireland, 'the woman of the best make and shape and the best speech of the women of the whole world.' Finn warned of the strife between himself and the High King; the two went to Teamhair to take the refusal for him. The king put them off to Grania's own answer — 'there is not a son of a king or of a great prince, there is not a champion in Ireland my daughter has not given a refusal to, and it is on me they all lay the blame' — and Grania answered with the wilful neatness of her whole character: 'If he is a fitting son-in-law for you, why would he not be a fitting husband for me?'

The wedding was set for a fortnight hence, and Finn gathered the seven battalions of the Fianna to Teamhair. But when Grania saw grey-haired Finn, she said it aloud: 'It is a great wonder it was not for Oisin Finn asked me, for he would be more fitting for me than a man that is older than my father.' Finn, who had the name of being quick with answers himself, set her riddles — what is whiter than snow (the truth), what is hotter than fire (the face of a hospitable man when he sees a stranger coming and the house empty), what is best for a champion (his doings to be high and his pride to be low), what is sharper than a sword ('the wit of a woman between two men'), what is quicker than the wind ('a woman's mind') — 'And indeed she was telling no lie when she said that.'

At the wedding feast, in the king's house of the Middle Court, the heroes were named to her one by one by a druid of Finn's people — Goll the ready fighter, Osgar son of Oisin, thin-legged Caoilte — and of the dark-haired man with cheeks like the rowan-berry, 'that is Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne... the best lover of women in the whole world.' 'That is a good company,' said Grania. Diarmuid kept his cap always over the love-spot the woman of the Sídhe had left on his forehead — for no woman could see that spot but she would give him her love — and while he drove apart the fighting dogs, the cap fell; Grania saw it, and the blood rose in her heart. She sent for the great golden cup that held drink for nine times nine men, filled it with wine that had enchantment in it, and gave it first to Finn and then through the hall: all that drank fell into a heavy sleep, none waking but Oisin, Osgar, Caoilte, Diarmuid and Diorraing.

'Will you take my love, Diarmuid, son of Duibhne, and will you bring me away out of this house to-night?' 'I will not. I will not meddle with the woman that is promised to Finn.' 'If that is so, I put you under Druid bonds, to bring me out of this house to-night before the awaking of Finn and of the King of Ireland from their sleep.' It is under bad bonds you are putting me, Grania — and he polled his friends like a judge: Oisin ('you are not guilty if the bonds were laid on you'), Osgar ('it is a pitiful man that would break his bonds'), Caoilte ('it would be better to me than all the riches of the world Grania to have given me that love'), Diorraing ('follow Grania, although you will get your death by it'). All said follow. He stood up and stretched out his hand for his weapons, and every tear he shed was of the size of a mountain berry; then he went out to the wall of the dun, put the shafts of his two spears under him — for 'every fighting man has leave to pass over the walls of any dun and of any strong place at all by the shafts of his spears' — rose with a light leap and came down on the grass outside, where Grania met him.

He tried once more to be honorable — turn back, and Finn will never get news of what you are after doing — and she refused: 'I will never part with you till death parts us.' He carried her to horses, and from there on foot, and wherever they went 'Diarmuid left unbroken bread after him, as a sign to Finn he had kept his faith with him.' At Doire-da-Bhoth, the Wood of the Two Huts, he cut down the wood around them and built a fence with seven doors of woven twigs, and set out a bed of soft rushes and birch tops for Grania in the very middle of the wood. The trackers found the trail the next morning; Finn's jealousy rose like weather; Bran the hound and Caoilte's shouting servant were sent as warnings by Oisin and Osgar; and Finn surrounded the wood. 'O Diarmuid, which of us is the truth with, myself or Oisin?' 'You never failed from your good judgment, Finn, and indeed I myself and Grania are here' — and Angus Og came on the cold wind and lifted the eloping pair over the hosts on his own cloak, and the pursuit of a lifetime began.
narrative.zh: 《迪爾木德與格蘭妮之追尋》乃愛爾蘭私奔愛情之大篇——在自己的婚禮上為自己做選擇的新娘，與服從geasa之法走入其預言之悲劇的英雄。芬恩獨坐萊因斯特阿爾文草場，自黑加雷之女梅西斯死後無妻無伴，『蓋無賢妻者夜間少得安眠』。其子奧辛與德魯伊迪奧林至其處；迪奧林報出新娘之名：愛爾蘭至高王之女格蘭妮——『全世婦女中身形最好、言談最佳之女』。芬恩自陳與至高王素有嫌隙；二人赴塔拉代其受拒。王把問題交還格蘭妮本人——『王族貴胄、全國勇士，我女無一不拒，責任全在我』——格蘭妮以其全篇性格之果斷俏答：『若他配作你之佳婿，為何不配作我之夫？』婚期定於兩週後，芬恩集費恩納七營至塔拉。而格蘭妮一見灰髮之芬恩便出聲：『奇哉，芬恩所求何不是我為奧辛所求，他比我父更年長之人更配於我。』芬恩自誇機敏、以謎語相試——什麼比雪更白（真理）、什麼比火更熱（屋空客至時好客者之面）、什麼於武士最佳（功高而傲低）、什麼比劍更利（『兩男之間一女之機智』）、什麼比風更快（『一女之心』）——『她說此話確無虛言』。婚宴於中廷王屋舉行，芬恩族中一德魯伊為她逐一唱名眾英雄——善戰者戈爾、奧辛之子奧斯加、瘦腿的卡爾特——而對那位黑髮、頰如花楸果之男子曰：『此即迪布內之孫迪爾木德……舉世最得女子歡心者。』『好一群人物，』格蘭妮曰。迪爾木德常年以帽覆西德女子留在其額上之愛痣——因無女子見痣而不以身相許——他驅散相鬥之犬時帽落；格蘭妮見之、心血上湧。她遣人取九九八十一人量之大金杯、盛以咒酒、先奉芬恩、再傳全廳：飲者皆入沉睡、不醒者惟奧辛、奧斯加、卡爾特、迪爾木德與迪奧林五人。『迪爾木德、迪布內之子，你願受我之愛、今夜攜我出此屋否？』『不願。我不染指許給芬恩之女。』『既如此，我以德魯伊之束縛加於你：今夜、在芬恩與愛爾蘭王醒來之前，攜我出此屋。』『格蘭妮，你加於我的是惡縛』——他如法官逐一問計於同伴：奧辛（『縛非你自取，則你無罪；追隨格蘭妮』）、奧斯加（『毀縛者可鄙』）、卡爾特（『格蘭妮若以那愛予我，勝過世上一切財富』）、迪奧林（『追隨格蘭妮，縱因此得死，亦令我痛』）。皆曰追隨。他起身伸手取兵器、每滴淚大如山莓；出至堡牆、以雙矛之桿撐身——『凡戰士皆有權踏矛桿越任何堡壘之牆』——輕躍而下、落於牆外草上、格蘭妮在彼相迎。他再試一次求其正——回去吧，芬恩永不知道你所行之事——她拒絕：『至死我與你不分離。』他攜她至馬、繼而步行；所到之處『迪爾木德身後皆留未掰開之麵包，作為對芬恩守其忠信之證』。於兩茅屋之林（Doire-da-Bhoth）他伐林四周、築七門編枝之籬、為格蘭妮於林之正中鋪設柔薦與樺梢之床。翌晨追蹤者循跡而至；芬恩之妒如天氣驟起；奧辛與奧斯加遣忠犬布蘭與卡爾特之呼聲僕人預警；芬恩圍林。『迪爾木德，你我之間誰說真話——我還是奧辛？』『芬恩，你的判斷從無差錯——我和格蘭妮確實在此』——安古斯·歐格乘冷風而來、以自己的斗篷將私奔二人送過大軍之頂，一生的追捕自此開始。

functions: Charter of the geasa bond: the elopement compelled by debt-language as the cycle's central legal event
The love-spot doctrine: beauty as compulsion — consent engineered by the otherworld
The unbroken bread: loyalty display within betrayal — faith kept in the very act of its breach
Riddle-courtship of Finn and Grania: wisdom dialogue as character diagnosis before tragedy
