summary.zh: 《故事海》的大框架：一個生來即被告知將戴飛天王冠——空中巫王之冠——的王子，終其青春在群山間探索：巫師、飛城、奪妻、魔戰與情愛，每一段皆為一個包含另一個的故事。王冠與其說是物，不如說是故事自身永不終結的方式。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The prophecy was read at the prince's naming: this child shall wear the crown of the Vidyadharas - and the prophecy became the book's spine, every episode a step up the mountain. The quest's inventory reads like a carnival of the imagination: flying palaces, wives won in dream and war, sorcerer-duels, feasts where the guests are not human - the crown at the top and the story content to climb. Somadeva's point is structural: a tale that promises an ending can afford to delay it forever - the crown is the ocean's horizon, and the waves are the tales.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara (Tawney 1880-84); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 預言在王子的命名禮上被宣讀：此子當戴持明者（Vidyadharas）之冠——而這預言成了全書的脊骨，每一段情節都是登山的一級。這趟追尋的行囊清單讀來宛如想像力的嘉年華：飛行的宮殿、於夢中與戰中贏得的妻子、巫師的決鬥、賓客並非人類的盛宴——冠冕在頂，而故事甘於攀登。蘇摩提婆（Somadeva）的用意是結構性的：一個許諾結局的故事，負擔得起永遠延宕結局——冠冕是海洋的地平線，而波浪便是那些故事。

canonical_translation: C. H. Tawney, 1880-84 (public domain)

title.en: Gunadhya Burns His Book and the God Laughs
title.zh: 貢那陀耶焚其書而神笑

region.en: Forest of Vindhya (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 溫迪亞林中（象徵性定位）

period: Kathasaritsagara, Kathamukha (frame), c. 1070 CE (Tawney translation, 1880-84)

source.work: The Katha Sarit Sagara, trans. C. H. Tawney (1880-84), Kathamukha, Gunadhya's burning

summary.en: Cursed into a demon's body, the sage Gunadhya wrote his great story-book in the language of beasts - Paiśachi - and no court would read it. Despairing, he began to burn his manuscript leaf by leaf; a king's men rescued seven chapters from the fire, read one aloud at a feast, and Shiva - who had given the world stories as a gift and seen them refused - laughed, and restored the sage. The Ocean of Story claims descent from those seven salvaged chapters.
summary.zh: 被詛咒入惡魔之身的仙人貢那陀耶以獸語（畢沙奇語）寫成其巨著，而宮廷無人肯讀。絕望中他開始逐葉焚毀手稿；一位王的臣僕自火中搶救出七章，於宴會上誦讀其一，濕婆——曾以故事為贈而見其被拒的神——大笑，復原了仙人。《故事海》自承源於那七章。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (literary lineage claim); classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The demon's book was written in the market language of goblins - brilliant, and unreadable to the Sanskrit courts it was offered to; rejection was the demon's second curse. He fed the manuscript to the fire leaf by leaf, a funeral for his own life's work - and the men who rescued seven chapters from the smoke rescued the tradition's ancestry with them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara, Kathamukha (Tawney 1880-84); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那魔的書是以鬼怪（goblins）的市井語言寫成的——才華橫溢，卻對它被呈獻的梵語宮廷而言不可讀；被拒是那魔所受的第二道詛咒。他一頁一頁地將手稿餵入火中，為自己畢生的作品舉行葬禮——而從煙中救出七章的人，也一併救出了這傳統的祖源。

passages.text: One chapter read at a feast fetched the king who read, and the god who had made stories out of his own smile laughed in approval: the sage was restored, the language forgiven, and the Ocean of Story began as a salvage-operation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara, Kathamukha (Tawney 1880-84); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在宴席上朗讀的一章，換來了那位閱讀的國王，而以自身微笑造出故事的這位神祇，讚許地笑了：仙人得以復原，語言獲得寬宥，而《故事之海》便始於一場打撈行動。

canonical_translation: C. H. Tawney, 1880-84 (public domain)

title.en: The Prince Who Trusted a Serpent and a Parrot
title.zh: 信任蛇與鸚鵡的王子

region.en: Southern city (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南方之城（象徵性定位）

period: Kathasaritsagara, Vetala-Panchavimshati, c. 1070 CE (Tawney translation, 1880-84)

source.work: The Katha Sarit Sagara, trans. C. H. Tawney (1880-84), Vetala tale of the prince and the serpent

summary.en: Exiled by astrologers' warnings, a prince took shelter with a serpent and a parrot - the two creatures nobody trusts - and was betrayed by the humans he did trust. His serpent friend gave its fang-gift, his parrot flew reconnaissance, and the betrayal was paid back with interest; the vetala's riddle: which adviser was the true one? Answer: the ones without hands to take bribes.
summary.zh: 被占星師的警告所放逐的一位王子，寄身於蛇與鸚鵡之間——兩種最不被信任的生靈——卻被他信任的人類背叛。蛇友贈其毒牙之禮，鸚鵡為其偵察，背叛以利息償還；毘舍遮的謎題：誰是真正的謀士？答：沒有手可以受賄的那些。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The astrologers' verdict cost the prince his kingdom; the creatures who sheltered him in the wild had no reason to flatter and no hands to pay - a serpent and a parrot. The humans who did shelter him sold him for gold; the serpent's venom and the parrot's wings undid the sale, and the thief paid what the astrologers had feared. The vetala's question - which counsel was true? - gets the king's answer and the tale's moral: advice without interest is the only kind worth taking; the rest is commerce with fangs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara, Vetala tales (Tawney 1880-84); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 占星家的判詞使王子失去了王國；在荒野中庇護他的生靈，既無理由奉承，也無手可付——一條蛇與一隻鸚鵡。真正庇護他的人類卻為黃金將他賣了；蛇的毒液與鸚鵡的翅膀撤銷了這樁買賣，而竊賊付出了占星家所畏懼的代價。毘陀羅的問題——哪一方的忠告才是真的？——得到了國王的回答，也得了此故事的寓意：無私的忠告，才是唯一值得聽取的；其餘的，皆是長著毒牙的交易。

canonical_translation: C. H. Tawney, 1880-84 (public domain)

title.en: Ratnaprabha, the Bride of the Flying City
title.zh: 羅陀那普羅婆：飛城之新娘

region.en: Vidyadhara city in the air (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 空中飛天之城（象徵性定位）

period: Kathasaritsagara of Somadeva, c. 1070 CE (Tawney translation, 1880-84)

source.work: The Katha Sarit Sagara, trans. C. H. Tawney (1880-84), Ratnaprabha episode

summary.en: The Naravahanadatta cycle's love-stories are the Ocean of Story's romances of the air: a prince carried to a flying city, a bride who tests him with three tasks, a sorcerer-antagonist turned ally by courtesy. Ratnaprabha's marriage is the cycle's model: the Vidyadhara worlds marry mortals when courage and wit outweigh the wings - and the crown at the story's end is worn by a couple, not a king.
summary.zh: 那羅婆訶那達陀循環的愛情故事是《故事海》的空中羅曼史：王子被攜至飛城，新娘以三重任務試探他，術士對手因禮數而化為盟友。羅陀那普羅婆之婚是循環的典範：當勇氣與機智勝過羽翼時，飛天世界便與凡人聯姻——而故事末端的王冠由一對夫婦所戴，非一位君王。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The flying city was a real address in the cycle's cosmology: reached by chariot, cloud or courage - and its princesses chose mortals by task rather than by gift. Ratnaprabha's three tests were a syllabus in loyalty: keep a secret in a treasury of wonders, hold a trust through a war of wizards, and ask for nothing - the marriage followed the exam. The crown of the Vidyadharas, promised at his birth, is won in these episodes as a shared thing: the epic of the air keeps insisting that its thrones are two-seated.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara (Tawney 1880-84); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在這部循環神話的宇宙觀中，飛行城是真實存在的地址：可乘戰車、駕雲或憑勇氣抵達——而其中的公主們是以任務而非禮物來挑選凡人。寶光（Ratnaprabha）的三項考驗是一份忠誠的課程大綱：在奇珍異寶的寶庫中守住一個秘密，在巫師的戰爭中堅守一份信託，並且一無所求——婚事隨考試而來。持明仙（Vidyadharas）的王冠，在他出生時便已許下，卻在這些篇章中作為共有之物被贏得：這部空中史詩一再堅持，它的王座是雙人共坐的。

canonical_translation: C. H. Tawney, 1880-84 (public domain)

title.en: Pururavas and Urvashi: The Mortal Who Lost His Heaven-Wife
title.zh: 補魯羅婆與優爾婆希：失去天妻的凡人

region.en: Kuru plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俱盧平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Book 10, Hymn 95, c. 1200-1000 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 95 (Pururavas and Urvashi)

summary.en: The apsara Urvashi lived with the mortal king Pururavas on three conditions: her two rams must never be exposed, and she must never see him unclothed. The gods stole the rams at midnight; he leapt naked after them, she saw him as he was - and the pact was over. Their farewell dialogue is the oldest love-poem of Indian literature: 'a hundred seasons we lay together', and the law stands: heaven's women return to heaven.
summary.zh: 飛天優爾婆希與凡人國王補魯羅婆同居，立有三條件：她的兩隻公羊永不可示人，她也永不可見他裸身。諸神於午夜盜走公羊；他裸身躍起追趕，她見其本色——盟約遂終。二人的告別對話是印度文學最古老的情詩：『我們同寢百季』，而法律如一：天之女歸天。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The marriage had conditions like a lease: two rams never unguarded, a body never seen bare - the gods' own sister living on a mortal's terms, and both parties watching for the breach. The breach came as a theft: the rams were taken at midnight, the king leapt after them without his robe, and the lightning of the gods showed him as he was - the pact ended in one flash.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 10.95 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這樁婚姻附有條件，如同一紙租約：兩隻公羊永不可無人看守，身體永不可被看見赤裸——眾神自己的姊妹以凡人的條件生活，而雙方都在提防違約。違約以盜竊的形式到來：公羊在午夜被奪走，國王未著長袍便躍身追趕，眾神的閃電照出了他的本相——盟約在一閃之間終結。

passages.text: The farewell is the hymn's greatness: she says the days are counted, he offers everything; she teaches him the truth that no rite can hold a heaven-woman - 'thy sons shall call thee father' - and the dialogue founded a thousand later romances of mortal and nymph.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 10.95 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 離別是這首頌詩的偉大之處：她說日子已屈指可數，他願獻出一切；她教給他一個真理——任何儀式都留不住一位天女——「你的兒子們將稱你為父親」——而這場對話奠定了後世千百部凡人與仙女之間的愛情故事。

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: The Goddess Speech Speaks of Herself
title.zh: 言語女神自述

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Book 10, Hymn 125, c. 1200-1000 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 125 (Vagambhrini)

summary.en: One of the world's oldest poems in a woman's voice: Vak, Speech herself, declares her own reign - 'I move in the rivers, I breathe in the winds, I am queen of the earth and the gathered waters, and whoever eats, drinks and breathes does it through me.' The god who does not know her, she says, is diminished; the hymn is theology done as a sovereign's self-portrait.
summary.zh: 世上最古老以女性之聲口出的詩之一：言語之神瓦格自陳其治——『我行於諸河，我息於諸風，我為大地與聚水之后；凡飲食呼吸者，皆經由我』。她言：不識她的神便被削弱；此頌即以君主自畫像所作的神學。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: I move with the Rudras, Vasus and Adityas, with the gods that surround me; I carry both Mitra and Varuna, both Indra and Agni, both the Ashvins - I am Speech, and the strong is supported on me. I am the queen, the gatherer of treasures, wise in all the sciences: on my shoulders the gods divided the dwellings; I am she who breathes in the word, who tastes what is mixed. The warning is the portrait's frame: whom I love I make mighty; whom I love not, he dwindles - the hymn's theology of speech is a politics of patronage, and it speaks in the first person female.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 10.125 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 我與樓陀羅（Rudras）、婆藪（Vasus）及阿底提耶（Adityas）同行，與環繞我的眾神同行；我承載密多羅（Mitra）與婆樓那（Varuna），承載因陀羅（Indra）與阿耆尼（Agni），承載雙馬童（Ashvins）——我是語言，強者依託於我。我是女王，是寶藏的聚集者，通曉一切學問：眾神在我的肩上劃分了居所；我是在言詞中呼吸者，是品嚐那調和之味者。警告是這幅畫像的框架：我所愛者，我使他強大；我所不愛者，他便衰微——這首頌詩的語言神學是一種恩寵的政治，並以女性的第一人稱說話。

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: The Long-Haired Ascetic (Muni)
title.zh: 長髮仙人（牟尼）

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Book 10, Hymn 136, c. 1200-1000 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 136 (Kesin hymn)

summary.en: The Rigveda's portrait of the wild ascetic: long-haired, wind-girt, drunk not on Soma but on the god's own madness, riding the wind with the Rudras' troop, visiting the whole world in thought. The hymn is half-amused, half-awed - the first literary description of the yogi, written by the settled priests about the terrifying men at the edge of their fire.
summary.zh: 梨俱吠陀對狂野苦行者的肖像：長髮、以風為衣，所飲非蘇摩而是神之狂，與樓陀羅隊伍同乘風而行，以思慮周遊全世界。頌詩半含笑意半含敬畏——這是文學中對瑜伽士的第一份描述，由定居的祭司寫下，寫他們祭火邊緣那些可畏之人。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The long-haired one holds fire, holds poison, holds heaven and earth: he is seen by all and is not the wind's shape - girt with the wind, the muni goes on the road of the whirlwind. The muni's drink is not Soma: drunk on a wilder intoxication, he rides with the troop of Rudra, moves with the gods' own coursers, and receives the ocean's sweetness - the gods do not bind him with the ropes they bind men with.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 10.136 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 長髮者執掌火，執掌毒，執掌天與地：他為眾人所見，卻不是風的形狀——束著風，牟尼（muni）行走在旋風之路上。牟尼的飲料不是蘇摩（Soma）：沉醉於更狂野的醉意，他與樓陀羅的部眾同行，與眾神自己的駿馬同奔，並領受海洋的甘美——眾神不用束縛凡人的繩索束縛他。

passages.text: The horses of the wind, the friend of Vayu, urged on by the gods, dwell in both seas: the hymn sees the yogi as weather - moving between the sea of air and the sea of water, terrifying and holy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 10.136 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 風的馬匹，伐由（Vayu）之友，受眾神驅策，棲居於兩片海洋之中：這首頌詩將瑜伽行者視為天候——在空氣之海與水之海之間移動，既可怖又神聖。

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: The Four Quarters of Speech
title.zh: 言語的四分

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Book 10, Hymn 71, c. 1200-1000 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 71 (Jnanam)

summary.en: The Rigveda's meditation on language: Speech was measured out in four quarters - three hidden, unspoken, known to the gods alone; the fourth, the spoken word, is what men use, and they use it badly: 'wise men who do not know it sit like a blind man's beasts'. The hymn is the tradition's first philosophy of language, delivered as a complaint.
summary.zh: 梨俱吠陀關於語言的冥想：言語被分為四分——三分隱藏、未言、唯諸神所知；第四分即被說出的詞，是人所用者，而人用之不善：『不識它的智者如盲人之畜般靜坐』。此頌是傳統最早的語言哲學，以抱怨的方式傳授。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Speech was measured into four quarters, three hidden and not spoken - the gods know them as the fourth alone; men speak the quarter they have and know not the rest. The complaint is gentle and exact: they who are called wise see not, sit deaf like a blind man's cattle; the word spoken without knowing is a corpse of sound. And the first sacrifice: where the seers yoked speech as craftsmen yoke a chariot, there the hymn ends - language as the tradition's first artifact, and using it as its first craft.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 10.71 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 語言被劃分為四部分，其中三部分隱藏而未說出——唯有第四部分為眾神所知；人們只說出他們所擁有的那一部分，而不知其餘。這抱怨溫和而精確：那些被稱為智者的人看不見，像盲人的牛群般呆坐如聾；不知其意而說出的話語，是聲音的屍體。而最初的獻祭：當先知們如工匠套上馬車般套上語言，頌詩便在此結束——語言作為傳統的第一件人造物，而使用它則是其第一門手藝。

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: The Hymn of Order: Rta and the Turning Days
title.zh: 秩序頌：梨多與流轉之日

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Book 10, Hymn 190, c. 1200-1000 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 190 (Rta hymn)

summary.en: Four verses on how the world runs: rta, the order, was born of heat (tapas); from it were born darkness and the waters; from them the year and the days, the sun's journey, and the heavens - 'the mighty ones set the sun's light in the sky'. The oldest statement of cosmic law in any literature, four verses long.
summary.zh: 四節詩寫世界如何運轉：秩序（梨多 rta）生於熱（tapas）；由之而生黑暗與諸水；由之而生年與日、日之行、以及諸天——『強者將日之光明安置於天』。任何文獻中最古老的宇宙法則之敘述，僅四節。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: From blazing tapas, rta, the order, was born - truth its engine: from it the night was born, and from it the ocean and the waters of the world. From the waters and the night came the year's first dawn; the universe's clock started with a birth - order, darkness, flood, then light on schedule. The close is legislation: the Earth's sovereigns set the sun's light in the sky; rta is the constitution the hymn writes - four verses, one government.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 10.190 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從熾熱的苦行中，秩序（梨多）誕生了——真理是其引擎：從它誕生了夜，從它誕生了海洋與世間之水。從水與夜中，誕生了年的第一道曙光；宇宙的時鐘隨著一次誕生而啟動——秩序、黑暗、洪水，然後是準時到來的光。結尾是立法：大地的主權者將太陽之光置於天空；梨多是頌詩所書寫的憲法——四節詩，一個政府。

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: Indra and Varuna: The Two Kings Talk
title.zh: 因陀羅與伐樓那：二王對話

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Book 4, Hymn 42, c. 1500-1200 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 4, Hymn 42 (Indra-Varuna dialogue)

summary.en: A rare Vedic dialogue of two kings dividing the world: Varuna claims the waters, the law and the deep; Indra claims the battle, the bolt and the hero's portion - 'I and Varuna, we two, hold the world between us'. The hymn is a constitutional document in verse: two sovereignties, one heaven, and an explicit statement that the poet knows exactly who he is flattering.
summary.zh: 一場罕見的吠陀雙王對話，劃分世界：伐樓那主張諸水、法律與深淵；因陀羅主張戰事、雷杵與英雄之分——『我與伐樓那，我倆共持此世界』。此頌是一份詩體憲法文件：兩種主權、一個天空，並且明言詩人清楚自己正在諂媚誰。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Varuna's claims are the claims of order: the hundred waters, the ropes of the lie, the deep where the dead are counted; the king of the law speaks like a court. Indra's claims are battle's: the bolt in hand, the serpent slain, the wealth of the enemy counted in cows - and the young king speaks like a field commander. The shared line is the constitution: I and Varuna, we two, hold the world - two thrones in one heaven, and the poet's riddle to the listener: which king are you praying to today?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 4.42 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伐樓拿的主張是秩序的主張：百水、謊言之繩、死者被清點的深淵；法之王說話如法庭。因陀羅的主張是戰鬥的主張：手握雷霆、誅殺巨蛇、以牛計數敵人的財富——而年輕的王說話如戰地指揮官。共有的詩行是憲法：我與伐樓拿，我們二人，執掌世界——一個天國中的兩座王座，而詩人向聽者提出的謎題是：你今天向哪位王祈禱？

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: Agni's Three Births and the Fire-Kindling Rite
title.zh: 阿耆尼的三次誕生與取火之禮

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Book 10, Hymn 21 and ritual hymns (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10 hymns on Agni's births (e.g. 10.21, 10.45)

summary.en: The birth-rite of fire as the Vedas tell it: the two aranis (sticks) are a marriage - the upper stick the bridegroom, the lower the bride - the churning is the union, the smoke the child's cry, and the kindled flame a birth in the household's presence. The hymns build a theology of fire as the god born of human hands every time a hearth is lit.
summary.zh: 吠陀所敘火的誕生禮：兩片取火木（阿羅尼）是一場婚配——上木為新郎，下木為新娘——旋鑽為其結合，煙為嬰啼，點燃的火焰為家人面前的一次誕生。頌詩構成一套火的神學：凡燃爐之處，神皆由人手所生。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The sticks are addressed as bride and groom: the upper one moves, the lower receives, and the hymn watches the marriage of wood the way it watches weddings - with blessings for the offspring. The churning is labor and liturgy: sweat, smoke, the first spark caught on straw like a newborn on a lap - the household present at the god's delivery. The theology follows the technology: Agni is the one god who is born every day of human skill, therefore the one whose favor is most certain - a hearth-god with a warranty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda fire-kindling hymns (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 木棍被稱作新娘與新郎：上方的一根移動，下方的一根承接，而頌詩注視著木頭的婚禮，一如它注視婚禮——以對後代的祝福。鑽木是勞作也是禮儀：汗水、煙霧，第一點火花落在稻草上如新生兒落在膝上——全家在場見證神的誕生。神學追隨技術：阿耆尼是唯一由人類技藝每日誕生的神，因此是恩寵最為確定的那一位——一位帶有保證的火爐之神。

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: Indra Breaks the Dawn's Chariots
title.zh: 因陀羅擊碎黎明的戰車

region.en: Punjab plains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

period: Rigveda, Book 4, Hymn 30, c. 1500-1200 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 4, Hymn 30 (Indra and Ushas)

summary.en: One of the Vedas' strangest scenes: the young king Indra, drunk on his first victories, chased the goddess Ushas from the sky and smashed her chariots - the dawn herself fleeing before the hero of the gods. The hymn records it without embarrassment: power polices even beauty's timetable, and the poet keeps the image of the dawn running away.
summary.zh: 吠陀最奇異的場景之一：初勝而醉的年輕國王因陀羅追逐黎明女神烏莎斯，擊碎其戰車——黎明本身在諸神的英雄面前奔逃。頌詩毫不尷尬地記載此事：權力甚至管轄美的時間表，而詩人保留了黎明逃走的意象。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Indra, fierce in his new strength, ran down the dawn-goddess as she drove her bright car across the heaven - the age's hero punishing the sky's oldest servant. Her chariots were broken where she fled; the hymn keeps the image without apology - the dawn arrives late or arrives broken, and the king of the storm is the reason. The theology of the scene is schedule: daybreak must come on time; a goddess who lingers is a rival to the sun's order - and the storm-god is heaven's clockmaker with a hammer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda 4.30 (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 因陀羅以其新生的力量兇猛無比，當黎明女神駕著她明亮的車輦駛過天際時，他追上了她——那個時代的英雄懲罰天空最古老的僕人。她的車輦在她逃離之處被擊碎；頌詩毫不諱言地保留了這一意象——黎明遲到或破碎而至，而風暴之王正是原因。這一場景的神學是時刻表：破曉必須準時到來；一位逗留的女神是對太陽秩序的競爭者——而風暴之神是手持錘子的天國鐘錶匠。

canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1896 (public domain)

title.en: The Music That Turns Wolves to Women
title.zh: 使狼化為女子的樂音

region.en: Cave of Cruachan, Co. Roscommon, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭羅斯康芒郡克魯阿坎洞

period: Fenian-Sidhe interface tradition, medieval Irish; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. VIII, eBook #14465

summary.en: On Samhain night Cascorach the musician spears the fairy woman who comes out of the Cave of Cruachan to take the best of the herds. The deeper affliction is three she-wolves that yearly destroy the sheep — daughters of Airetach of the last people of oppression, robbing in wolf-shape. Only they will come near to men having harps: so Cascorach plays till they stretch themselves to listen, speaks them into their own shapes, and Caoilte's one spear pierces all three — the Valley of the Shapes of the Wolves keeps the name.
summary.zh: 薩溫之夜，樂師卡斯卡拉赫擊殺自克魯阿坎洞出來奪取牛群最佳者之仙女。更深的禍患是每年噬羊的三隻母狼——她們是「最後壓迫者之民」艾雷塔克的三個女兒，以狼形行劫。唯有持豎琴者可近其身：卡斯卡拉赫奏樂使狼俯首傾聽，勸其現出人形，卡爾特一矛貫穿三人——「狼形谷」之名由此而來。

sensitivity.note: The Cave of Cruachan (Oweynagat, 'cave of the cats') is the documented Samhain gate of Connacht, the Irish entrance of the otherworld; the harp-lure-and-shape-reveal is a reverse of the usual enchantment — music unmasking, not bewitching. Coordinates are the real cave.

passages.text: Caoilte was one time at Cruachan of Connacht, and Cascorach was with him, and there he saw sitting on a heap of stones a man with very rough grey hair, steward to the King of Ireland, having a herd of cattle before him in a fenced field. "We have great troubles on us in this district.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次，科爾特在康諾特的克魯阿漢，卡斯克拉赫與他在一起，在那裡他看見一個人坐在一堆石頭上，那人頭髮灰白而十分粗亂，是愛爾蘭王的管家，面前有一群牛在圍欄田地裡。「我們這個地區有大麻煩在我們身上。」

passages.text: I have many herds of cattle, and every year at Samhain time, a woman comes out of the hill of the Sidhe of Cruachan and brings away nine of the best out of every herd." "It seems to me that to-night is Samhain night," said Caoilte, and Cascorach went to the door of the hill of the Sidhe, and it was not long till he saw the girl going past him out of the hill of Cruachan, having a beautiful cloak of one colour about her, a gown of yellow silk tied up with a knot between her thighs, two spears in her hands, and she not in dread of anything before her or after her. Then Cascorach blew a blast against her, and put his finger into the thong of his spear, and made a cast at the girl that went through her, and that is the way she was made an end of by Cascorach of the Music.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「我有許多群牛，每年在薩溫節時，便有一個女子從克魯阿汗的仙丘中出來，從每一群牛裡帶走最好的九頭。」「在我看來，今夜正是薩溫之夜。」考爾特說。卡斯科拉赫便走到仙丘的門口，不久便看見那女子從他身旁走過，出了克魯阿汗的丘，身上披著一件單色的美麗斗篷，一條黃色絲質長袍在兩腿之間繫了個結，手中握著兩支矛，而她對身前身後的一切都毫不畏懼。於是卡斯科拉赫朝她吹了一聲號角，把手指伸進矛上的皮帶，向那女子擲出一矛，矛穿透了她的身體，她便是這樣被「樂師」卡斯科拉赫結果了性命。

passages.text: The steward had a second oppression on him: three she-wolves that come out of the Cave of Cruachan every year and destroy the sheep and the wethers, and go back into the cave again. "They are the three daughters of Airetach, of the last of the people of oppression of the Cave of Cruachan," said Cascorach, "and it is easier for them to do their robbery as wolves than as women. They will only come near to one sort: if they see the world's men having harps for music, they will come near to them." So in the morning he rose up and went to the cairn and stopped on it, playing his harp till the coming of the mists of the evening, and the three wolves came towards him and lay down before him, listening to the music.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那管家又受了第二重壓迫：每年有三隻母狼從克魯阿汗的洞穴中出來，殘害羊群與閹羊，然後又回到洞中。「她們是艾雷塔赫的三個女兒，屬於克魯阿汗洞穴中最後一批壓迫之民，」卡斯科拉赫說，「她們以狼的形貌行劫，比以女子的形貌更為容易。她們只會接近某一類人：若看見世間之人帶著豎琴奏樂，她們便會靠近他們。」於是到了早晨，他起身走到那石堆上，停在上面彈奏豎琴，直到傍晚的霧氣降臨，那三隻狼便朝他走來，伏在他面前，聆聽音樂。

passages.text: And Caoilte bade him go to the same place again and say to them it would be better for them to be in the shape of women for listening to music than in the shape of wolves. And they heard that, and they threw off the dark trailing coverings that were about them, for they liked well the sweet music of the Sidhe; and when Caoilte saw them there side by side, elbow by elbow, he made a cast of his spear, and it went through the three women, that they were like a skein of thread drawn together on the spear. And that place got the name of the Valley of the Shapes of the Wolves.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 考爾特吩咐他再到同一處地方，對她們說，她們若化為女子的形貌來聽音樂，總比化為狼的形貌好些。她們聽見了這話，便脫去身上那層黑暗拖曳的覆蓋之物，因為她們十分喜愛仙族的甜美音樂；考爾特見她們並肩而立、肘挨著肘，便擲出一矛，矛穿透了那三個女子，使她們像一絞纏繞在矛上的線團一般。那地方便得了「狼形之谷」之名。

title.en: The Wedding at Ceann Slieve and the Battle with the Men of Dea
title.zh: 克恩斯利夫婚禮與神族之戰

region.en: Ceann Slieve (Slieve Felim), Co. Limerick, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭利默里克郡克恩斯利夫（象徵定位）

period: Fenian-Sidhe interface tradition, medieval Irish; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. IX, eBook #14465

summary.en: Finn asks the daughter of Conan of Ceann Slieve in marriage and, bound to answer everything, shows his knowledge — of the Dord Fiann sounded by nine men, and of the music that pleased him best: spear-shafts whining in cold wind, cups given out at Almhuin, the gull and the heron, the three sons of Meardha. The Men of Dea take offence that the woman promised to the third best of their champions is taken by a mortal; at the feast Ethne entices Finn out under his hero-bonds, fiery-beaked blackbirds burn the company, and Goll breaks through sixteen battalions to strike down Fionnbhar their king.
summary.zh: 芬恩向克恩斯利夫的科南之女求婚，立誓有問必答，展現其識見——九人合奏的菲亞納號角，以及最悅耳之音：寒風中矛桿的尖嘯、艾倫山宴上遞杯之聲、鷗與鷺的啼鳴。神族震怒：許配給其第三勇者的女子竟被凡人娶走。宴上艾妮以英雄之誓誘芬恩出戶，火喙烏鴉焚燒滿座賓客；戈爾衝破十六營，擊斃其王芬巴爾。

sensitivity.note: The catalogue of Finn's best-loved music is a jewel of Fenian nature-lyric embedded in a wedding-negotiation scene; the hero-bonds (geasa) being used to entrap the hero is the classic geis-trap device. Pin symbolic.

passages.text: Finn and the Fianna made a great hunting on the hill of Torc, and it happened that day no one stopped with Finn but only Diorraing. They came to the door of a well-lighted house of the Sidhe on the edge of the wood, belonging to Conan of Ceann Slieve, and got good attendance, and a grand feast was made ready. Finn saw Conan's daughter, Finndealbh, of the Fair Shape, the colour of gold on her curled hair and her eyes as blue as flowers, and he asked her of Conan for his wife. "Leave asking that, Finn, for your own courage is not greater than the courage of the man she is promised to — Fatha, son of the King of Ess Ruadh." "I will get her whether the Men of Dea think good or bad of it," said Finn.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. IX; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 芬恩與費尼亞人在托爾克山上舉行了一場盛大的狩獵，那天恰好只有迪奧蘭與芬恩同行，別無他人。他們來到林邊一座燈火通明的仙族屋舍門前，那屋舍屬於凱恩·斯利夫的科南，受到了殷勤的招待，並備下了盛大的宴席。芬恩看見了科南的女兒、容貌秀美的芬德爾芙，她捲曲的頭髮上泛著金色，雙眼藍如花朵，他便向科南求娶她為妻。「別再求這件事了，芬恩，因為你自己的勇氣並不比那與她訂了婚的人的勇氣更大——那人便是埃斯·魯阿王的兒子法薩。」「無論眾神之民認為此事是好是壞，我都要得到她。」芬恩說。

passages.text: Conan put him under bonds as a true hero to answer everything he asked, and Finn gave full answers to them all: who made the Dord Fiann, the Mutterer of the Fianna, made in Ireland by the three sons of Cearmait Honey-Mouth; and what was the music that pleased him best — "the time the seven battalions of the Fianna are gathered in the one place and raise their spear-shafts over their heads, and the sharp whining of the clear cold wind goes through them, that is very sweet to me; and when the drinking-hall is set out in Almhuin and the cup-bearers give out the bright cups, that is very sweet to me; and it is sweet to me to be listening to the voice of the sea-gull and the heron, and the noise of the waves of Traig Liath, the whistle of Lugaidh's Son, and the voice of the cuckoo in the beginning of summer."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. IX; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 科南要他以真正英雄的身分立誓，凡他所問皆須作答，芬恩便對所有問題一一作了完整的回答：費尼亞人的「低語者」多爾德·費恩是何人所造——乃是由「蜜口」凱爾邁特的三個兒子在愛爾蘭所造；以及什麼樣的音樂最令他歡喜——「當費尼亞人的七個營隊聚集於一處，將矛桿舉過頭頂，那清冷尖銳的風聲穿過他們之間，這對我來說非常甜美；當阿爾溫的飲酒廳擺設齊整，執杯者分發明亮的酒杯，這對我來說非常甜美；聆聽海鷗與蒼鷺的鳴聲，特拉格利亞斯海浪的喧響，盧蓋德之子的哨聲，以及初夏時節杜鵑的啼聲，這些對我來說都很甜美。」

passages.text: But when Finn had answered all the questions so well, Conan said he would give him his daughter, and have a wedding-feast ready at the end of a month. It happened that in the half of the drinking-hall at Almhuin given up to the King of Ireland's son there were sitting two of the Men of Dea, Failbhe Mor and Failbhe Beag, and it is what they said, that it is because they were in that side of the hall it was given up — and Finn going to bring away the woman promised to the third best man of the Tuatha de Danaan, against the will of her father and mother.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. IX; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而當芬恩如此出色地回答了所有問題之後，科南說他願把女兒許配給他，並在一個月後備好婚宴。恰巧在阿爾溫飲酒廳中劃歸愛爾蘭王之子的那一半裡，坐著兩位眾神之民，即大法爾韋與小法爾韋，他們所說的是：正因為他們坐在廳的那一邊，那一邊才被劃歸出去——而芬恩竟要去帶走那許配給達努神族第三勇士的女子，違背她父母的心意。

passages.text: Fionnbhar, that was king over the Tuatha de Danaan, gathered six good battalions, and later sixteen battalions hidden in a Druid mist came to the lawn before Conan's house; and Ethne, the woman-Druid, said: "Goll will not protect him this time, for I will entice Finn out of the house, however well he is watched." She stood before Finn and put him under the bonds a true hero never broke, to come out to her and run a race; and as they ran, Caoilte, shamed into swiftness, passed the witch and turned and made two equal halves of her. Then the Tuatha de Danaan let out a flock of blackbirds having fiery beaks that burned the people in the house, and Goll rushed out, looking like a tall mountain under his grey shield, and broke through till he reached Fionnbhar their leader, and at the last Fionnbhar of Magh Feabhail fell by the strokes of Goll. There never was a harder battle fought in Ireland, for there was no man on one side or the other had a mind to go back one step before whoever he was fighting against.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. IX; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 芬恩巴爾，那位曾統治圖哈德達南族的君王，召集了六個精良的營隊，隨後又有十六個營隊隱藏於德魯伊的迷霧之中，來到科南屋前的草地上；而女德魯伊埃特涅說道：「這次戈爾保護不了他，因為無論他被看守得多麼嚴密，我都要把芬恩從屋裡引出來。」她站到芬恩面前，將他置於一位真正英雄從未打破的束縛之下，要他出來與她賽跑；當他們奔跑時，凱爾特因羞愧而奮起疾奔，超越了那女巫，轉身將她劈成相等的兩半。接著圖哈德達南族放出一群黑鳥，牠們有著燃燒的喙，灼傷了屋裡的人們，戈爾衝了出去，在他灰色的盾牌下宛如一座高聳的山，一路突破直到抵達他們的首領芬恩巴爾面前，最終，瑪格費瓦爾的芬恩巴爾倒在了戈爾的擊打之下。愛爾蘭從未發生過比這更艱苦的戰鬥，因為雙方都沒有任何人在與對手交戰之前，有退後一步的念頭。

title.en: The Shadowy One and the Harp of Three Strings
title.zh: 暗影夫人與三弦之豎琴

region.en: Bearnas Mor (Gap of Dunloe), Co. Kerry, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡大山口（象徵定位）

period: Fenian-Sidhe interface tradition, medieval Irish; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. X, eBook #14465

summary.en: A wild pig kills the hounds of the Fianna until Bran masters it, and its screams bring a tall man from the hill who asks its freedom. Inside the Sidhe-house at Glandeirgdeis he strikes the pig with his Druid rod and it becomes a beautiful young woman, Scathach the Shadowy One; Finn asks her in marriage, and her father promises her that very night. But Scathach borrows a harp of iron, bronze and silver — one string sets the hosts of the world crying, one laughing, and the silver string puts them all to sleep — and Finn wakes on Bearnas Mor with no bride.
summary.zh: 一頭野豬殺死菲亞納群犬，直到布蘭將其制服；其尖嘯引出山上高人，求芬恩放生。入仙宅後他以德魯伊杖擊豬，豬化為美貌少女——暗影夫人斯卡薩赫。芬恩求娶，其父允以當夜成婚。然斯卡薩赫借得鐵、銅、銀三弦之豎琴——一弦令舉世痛哭、一弦令舉世大笑、銀弦令舉世沉睡——芬恩醒來時身在山口，新娘無蹤。

sensitivity.note: Scathach here is a Sidhe-bride of the Fenian cycle, distinct from the martial Scathach of Skye who trained Cuchulain — the name-complex is shared between training-island lore and fairy-bride lore; the three-string harp parallels Cormac's branch in its emotional dominion. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: It was on the mountain of Bearnas Mor Finn was hunting, and a great wild pig turned on the hounds of the Fianna and killed the most of them, but Bran made an attack on it then and got the best of it. And the pig began to scream, and with that a very tall man came out of the hill and he asked Finn to let the pig go free. And when he agreed to that, the man brought them into the hill of the Sidhe at Glandeirgdeis; and when they came to the door of the house he struck the pig with his Druid rod, and on the moment it changed into a beautiful young woman, and the name he called her by was Scathach, the Shadowy One.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那時芬恩正在貝爾納斯莫爾山上狩獵，一頭巨大的野豬轉而攻擊芬尼亞的獵犬，殺死了其中大多數，但布蘭隨即向牠發動攻擊，並佔了上風。那頭豬開始尖叫，隨著這叫聲，一個非常高大的男人從山中走出，他請求芬恩放那頭豬自由離去。當他同意之後，那人便將他們帶入格蘭代爾格代斯的希德丘陵之中；當他們來到屋門前時，他用他的德魯伊法杖擊打那頭豬，牠當即變成了一位美麗的年輕女子，他呼喚她的名字是斯卡塔赫，意即「幽影者」。

passages.text: He made a great feast for the Fianna, and Finn asked the young girl in marriage, and the tall man, her father, said he would give her to him on that very night. But when night came on, Scathach asked the loan of a harp, and it was brought to her. One string it had of iron, and one of bronze, and one of silver. And when the iron string would be played, it would set all the hosts of the world crying and ever crying; and when the bright bronze string would be played, it would set them all laughing from the one day to the same hour on the morrow; and when the silver string would be played, all the men of the whole world would fall into a long sleep. And it is the sleepy silver string the Shadowy One played upon, till Finn and Bran and all his people were in their heavy sleep. And when they awoke at the rising of the sun on the morrow, it is outside on the mountain of Bearnas they were, where they first saw the wild pig.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他為芬尼亞舉辦了一場盛大的宴會，芬恩請求娶那年輕女子為妻，那高大男子，即她的父親，說他願意就在當晚將她許配給他。但當夜幕降臨時，斯卡塔赫請求借一把豎琴，豎琴便被送到她面前。它有一根鐵弦、一根青銅弦和一根銀弦。當彈奏鐵弦時，它會讓世上所有的軍隊哭泣不止；當彈奏明亮的青銅弦時，它會讓他們從今日一直笑到明日同一時刻；而當彈奏銀弦時，全世界的所有男人都會陷入漫長的沉睡。幽影者所彈奏的正是那令人昏睡的銀弦，直到芬恩、布蘭以及他所有的族人都陷入了沉重的睡眠之中。而當他們在次日太陽升起時醒來，他們已身處貝爾納斯山外，正是他們最初見到那頭野豬的地方。

title.en: Daireann's Mead and Finn's Madness
title.zh: 戴倫的蜜酒與芬恩的狂亂

region.en: Ford of the Slaine, Co. Leix, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭萊斯郡斯拉因淺灘

period: Fenian-Sidhe interface tradition, medieval Irish; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. XI, eBook #14465

summary.en: Daireann, daughter of Bodb Dearg, asks Finn for one year as his only wife and half his time after, and when he refuses, offers him a cup of mead — and Finn, under bonds never to refuse anything belonging to a feast, drinks and goes mad, turning on his own people and springing on them every fault he knew. The Fianna walk away in sorrow; thirteen times Caoilte runs after them and brings them back, and by nightfall the bitterness is gone from Finn's tongue and he would sooner have died than lived to remember it.
summary.zh: 波德·迪爾格之女戴倫向芬恩求娶——為其獨妻一年、其後共度半生；被拒後獻上一杯蜜酒。芬恩身負「宴席之物不可拒」之誓，飲之而狂，反目向自己的族人，歷數其所知的一切過失。菲亞納眾人黯然離去；卡爾特十三度追回眾人；夜幕降臨，芬恩恢復神智，寧願自刎也不願活在這段記憶中。

sensitivity.note: The geis-trap again: Finn's taboo of never refusing a feast-gift is weaponised by a Sidhe suitor refused. The madness episode parallels the Ulster war-ríastrad — involuntary transformation under enchantment. Coordinates symbolic at the ford.

passages.text: One time Finn and the Fianna were come to a ford of the Slaine, and they saw on the round rock up over the ford a young woman, having a dress of silk and a green cloak about her, and the golden crown that is the sign of a queen on her head. "I am Daireann, daughter of Bodb Dearg, son of the Dagda, and I am come to be your wife if you will give me the bride-gift I ask — your promise, I to be your only wife through the length of a year, and to have the half of your time after that." "I will not give that promise to any woman of the world, and I will not give it to you."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XI; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次，芬恩與芬尼亞來到斯萊恩河的一處淺灘，他們看見淺灘上方那圓石上有一位年輕女子，她身穿絲綢衣裳，披著綠色斗篷，頭上戴著象徵王后的金冠。「我是達蕾安，達格達之子博德布·德爾格的女兒，我來此是為了成為你的妻子，只要你肯給我我所求的聘禮——你的承諾，讓我在整整一年之中成為你唯一的妻子，此後再分得你一半的時間。」「我不會向世上任何女子許下這個承諾，也不會向你許下。」

passages.text: On that the young woman took a cup of white silver from under a covering, and filled it with strong drink, and gave it to Finn. "It is very strong mead," she said. Now there were bonds on Finn not to refuse anything belonging to a feast, so he took the cup and drank what was in it, and on the moment he was like one gone mad. He turned his face towards the Fianna, and every harm and every fault and every misfortune in battle that he knew against any one of them, he sprang it on them, through the mad drunkenness the young woman had put on him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XI; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 聽罷，那年輕女子從一塊遮蓋物下取出一隻潔白的銀杯，斟滿烈酒，遞給芬恩。「這是極烈的蜂蜜酒，」她說。此時芬恩受有束縛，不得拒絕任何屬於宴會之物，於是他接過杯子，飲盡其中之物，剎那間他便如同發了瘋一般。他轉臉朝向芬尼亞，凡是他在戰鬥中所知的關於他們之中任何一人的每一種傷害、每一個過失、每一場不幸，他都藉著那年輕女子加諸於他的瘋狂醉意，向他們猛然拋出。

passages.text: Then the chief men of the Fianna rose up and left the place, every one setting out for his own country; and Caoilte followed after them: "Fianna of Ireland, do not leave your lord and your leader through the arts and the tricks of a woman of the Sidhe." Thirteen times he went after them, bringing them back to the hill in that way. And with the end of the day and the fall of night the bitterness went from Finn's tongue; and by the time Caoilte had brought back the whole of the Fianna, his sense and his memory were come back to him, and he would sooner have fallen on his sword and got his death, than have stayed living. And that was the hardest day's work Caoilte ever did, unless the day he brought the flock of beasts and birds to Teamhair to ransom Finn from the High King of Ireland.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XI; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是芬尼亞的首領們起身離開了那個地方，各人動身前往自己的家鄉；凱爾特跟隨在他們之後：「愛爾蘭的芬尼亞啊，不要因一個希德女子的法術與詭計而離開你們的君主和首領。」他十三次追趕他們，就這樣把他們帶回山丘。隨著白日的結束與夜晚的降臨，苦澀從芬恩的舌上消退；待到凱爾特將整個芬尼亞都帶回時，他的理智與記憶也已恢復，他寧願撲向自己的劍而死，也不願繼續活著。那是凱爾特做過的最艱難的一日之功，除非是他將成群的走獸與飛鳥帶到塔拉，以從愛爾蘭至高王手中贖回芬恩的那一日。

title.en: The Red Woman and the Beast with Two Moons
title.zh: 紅衣女子與雙月之獸

region.en: Cnoc-na-righ, Co. Kerry, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡王者丘（象徵定位）

period: Fenian-Sidhe interface tradition, medieval Irish; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. XII, eBook #14465

summary.en: A beast like a deer with a boar's head, long horns, and a shining moon on each side runs ahead of a Red Woman who has followed it a month and must follow it till it falls — her life and her three sons' depend on it. Finn defies her, is attacked in the shape of a water-worm and saved by Bran, and all night the hunt follows the bleeding beast into Cnoc-na-righ. Inside the opened hill sits a king of the rainbow-clad musicians; the beast, wooed forth at sunset, dies as Bran masters it — a tall man, says the Red Woman: the King of the Firbolgs, whose people will put great troubles on Ireland after Finn is under the sod.
summary.zh: 野獸如鹿而具豬首長角，兩側各映一輪明月；紅衣女子已追逐它一月，須追至它倒下方能免死——她與三個兒子的性命皆繫於此。芬恩不畏其威，被化為水蟲的她襲擊而賴布蘭得救；整夜追獵血獸至王者丘。開啟的山丘內坐著彩虹衣樂師簇擁的君王；日落時野獸應聲而出，為布蘭所制倒斃——竟是一名高大的男子。紅衣女子道破：此乃弗博爾格之王，其族將於芬恩入土後為害愛爾蘭。

sensitivity.note: The two-mooned beast is a Fenian marvel-beast (marvel-hunt opening a Sidhe-mound is the standard entry device); the dying Firbolg king's prophecy is an eschatological annex linking the Fenian cycle to later history. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: One time the Fianna were in Almhuin, and there came a very misty morning, and Finn said: "Make yourselves ready, and we will go hunting to Gleann-na-Smol." They were not gone far when the mist lifted, and they saw a strange beast coming towards them with the quickness of the wind, and a Red Woman on its track. Narrow feet the beast had, and a head like the head of a boar, and long horns on it; but the rest of it was like a deer, and there was a shining moon on each of its sides. "I do not know its name," said the Red Woman, "though I am on its track since I left the borders of Loch Dearg a month ago, and I never lost sight of it since then; and the two moons that are on its two sides shine through the country all around in the night time. And I must follow it till it falls, or I will lose my own life and the lives of my three sons that are the best fighting men in the whole world."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次，芬尼亞戰士團在阿爾溫，來了一個霧氣瀰漫的早晨，芬恩說：「你們都準備好，我們要到格倫納斯莫爾去打獵。」他們還沒走多遠，霧就散了，只見一頭奇怪的野獸朝他們奔來，其快如風，一個紅衣女子緊隨其後。那野獸腳爪細窄，頭像野豬的頭，還長著長長的角；但牠其餘的部分卻像鹿，而且兩側各有一輪閃耀的月亮。「我不知道牠叫什麼名字，」紅衣女子說，「雖然我從一個月前離開洛赫德爾格的邊界起就一直追蹤牠，從那時起我從未讓牠離開過我的視線；而牠兩側的那兩輪月亮在夜裡照亮周圍整個地方。我必須追牠直到牠倒下，否則我就會丟掉自己的性命，還有我那三個兒子的性命，他們是全世界最善戰的勇士。」

passages.text: "It is little heed I give to yourself or your share of men," said the Red Woman; "and if my three sons were here, they would stand up against you." With that he sounded his horn, and she made a great water-worm of herself and made an attack on Finn, and she would have killed him then and there but for Bran being with him: Bran took a grip of the worm and shook it, and it wound itself round Bran's body, and would have crushed the life out of her, but Finn thrust his sharp sword into its throat. The hunt followed the beast all night, the two moons giving light, and about midnight it began to scatter blood after it, and it never stopped till it went in at the foot of Cnoc-na-righ at the breaking of day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「我對你本人和你那份人手毫不在意，」紅衣女子說，「要是我那三個兒子在這裡，他們會站出來對抗你們。」說著他吹響號角，她便化身為一條巨大的水蟲，向芬恩發起攻擊，若不是布蘭與他同在，她當時當地就會殺了他：布蘭抓住那蟲子一甩，牠便纏繞在布蘭身上，幾乎要把她的性命擠出來，但芬恩將利劍刺入牠的喉嚨。狩獵整夜追著那野獸，兩輪月亮照著路，大約午夜時牠開始沿途灑血，一直不停，直到破曉時分鑽進了克諾克納里格山腳。

passages.text: The Red Woman struck the side of the hill with a Druid rod, and a great door opened with sweet music coming from within, and inside there was a king sitting in a golden chair, and his musicians were playing, and no one could know what colour were the dresses of the musicians, for every colour of the rainbow was in them. At sunset Bran made the beast turn and forced it, and its strength flagged and it fell dead — but in place of a beast it was a tall man lying before them. "High King of the Fianna, that is the King of the Firbolgs you have killed; and his people will put great troubles on this country in the time to come, when you yourself, Finn, and your people will be under the sod." And she offered to bring them to the Country of the Young, but Finn answered: "We would not give up our own country if we were to get the whole world as an estate, and the Country of the Young along with it."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 紅衣女子用德魯伊法杖擊打山側，一扇大門應聲打開，裡面傳出美妙的音樂，門內有一位國王坐在金椅上，他的樂師們正在演奏，誰也分辨不出樂師們衣服是什麼顏色，因為其中包含了彩虹的每一種顏色。日落時分，布蘭使那野獸轉身並逼迫牠，牠的力氣漸衰，倒地而死——但躺倒在他們面前的不是野獸，而是一個高大的男子。「芬尼亞戰士團的至高王，你殺死的是弗爾博格人的國王；他的族人將來會給這片土地帶來巨大的災禍，那時你自己，芬恩，還有你的族人，都將長眠於草皮之下。」她提出要帶他們去青春之國，但芬恩回答：「即使把整個世界連同青春之國都作為產業給我們，我們也不會放棄自己的國土。」

title.en: Finn and the Phantoms of the Elder-Wood House
title.zh: 芬恩與接骨木屋中的幻影

region.en: Berramain strand, Co. Kerry, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡貝拉曼海灘

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. XIII, eBook #14465

summary.en: Winning a black horse at the races, Finn outruns Caoilte and Oisin over the Plain of Health to the hill of Bairnech, where night forces them into a house none knew was there: a headless man with one eye in his breast, a three-headed hag, nine harsh singers, and a grey host who flays the horses and serves raw meat — refusal of which brings battle in the dark until sunrise. The three Shapes out of the Valley of the Yew Tree, avenging their sister Cuillen whose son died of the Fianna's envy, vanish at the light.
summary.zh: 賽馬得勝的芬恩縱黑馬疾馳，將卡爾特與歐辛甩在身後，夜宿於一處無名之屋：胸中生眼的無首者、三首巫嫗、九個尖嘯之影、剝馬皮奉生肉的灰衣主人——拒食即招致徹夜黑暗中的血戰。直到日出才知真相：他們是「紫杉谷三形」，為其妹「闊口之庫倫」復仇——她的兒子因菲亞納的嫉恨而亡。

sensitivity.note: The bruiden-hostel horror sequence is the fixed Fenian-hostel genre (compare Da Derga's hostel); 'envy-killing' via the evil eye is an attested Irish belief-motif. Raw-meat refusal is a geis of Finn's. Pin symbolic on the strand.

passages.text: Finn went to a gathering one time at Aonach Clochair, and the horses of the Fianna ran races against the horses of the men of Munster; Fiachu, son of Eoghan, gave him a lasting black horse that won the three prizes of the gathering, and a chariot, and a spear having a deadly spell. Finn went trying his black horse on the strand at Berramain, and it was only folly for Caoilte and Oisin to race against him, for he gave a blow to his horse and away with him to Traigh Liath and over the Plain of Health, till he came to the hill of Bairnech, and Caoilte and Oisin after him. "Night is coming on us, and go look for some place where we can sleep." He looked round at the rocks on his left hand and saw a house with a fire shining out from it in the valley below: "I never knew of a house in this valley." "It is best for us to go see it, for there are many things we have no knowledge of."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次芬恩去參加艾納赫克洛海爾的集會，芬尼亞戰士團的馬與芒斯特人的馬賽跑；埃奧甘之子菲亞胡給了他一匹持久的黑馬，這匹馬贏得了集會的三項獎品，還有一輛戰車，以及一支帶有致命咒術的長矛。芬恩在貝拉曼的海灘上試他的黑馬，考爾特和奧辛要與他賽馬只是徒勞，因為他給馬一擊，便一路飛馳到特拉伊利亞斯，越過健康平原，直到來到拜爾內克山，考爾特和奧辛緊隨其後。「夜色降臨我們身上了，去找個能睡覺的地方吧。」他環顧左手邊的岩石，看見下方山谷中有一所房子，裡面透出火光：「我從不知道這山谷裡有房子。」「我們最好去看看，因為有許多事我們一無所知。」

passages.text: The people of the house were very fierce and rough, and a big grey man took hold of their horses and shut the door with iron hooks: "My welcome to you, Finn of the great name; it is a long time you were in coming here." They saw a hag in the house having three heads on her lean neck, and on the other side a man without a head, having one eye, and it in his breast. Nine bodies rose up out of the corner nearest the Fianna, and nine heads rose up on the other side of the bed, and they raised nine harsh screeches together, and the music that was sung went near to breaking the bones of their heads. Then the big grey man began striking at the horses, flaying and destroying them, and put pieces of the flesh on fifty pointed spits of rowan — but when he set them before Finn, it is raw the flesh was on them yet.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那房子裡的人非常兇猛粗野，一個高大的灰衣人抓住他們的馬，用鐵鉤關上門：「歡迎你，大名鼎鼎的芬恩；你來這裡可花了很長時間。」他們看見屋裡有一個老巫婆，瘦削的脖子上長著三個頭，另一邊是一個沒有頭的人，只有一隻眼睛，長在胸口上。離芬尼亞戰士團最近的角落裡升起九具軀體，床的另一邊升起九個頭，它們一起發出九聲刺耳的尖叫，所唱的音樂幾乎要震碎他們頭骨的骨頭。接著那高大的灰衣人開始抽打那些馬，剝皮毀壞牠們，把肉塊穿在五十根尖銳的花楸木籤上——但當他把這些擺在芬恩面前時，上面的肉還是生的。

passages.text: "I have never eaten meat that was raw, and I never will eat it because of being without food for one day." "If you are come into our house to refuse our food, we will surely go against yourselves." All in the house made an attack on the three, and the fight went on through the whole night in the darkness; and when the sun rose and lighted up the house, there was nothing to be seen of the house or of the people of it, but they had all vanished. And those three that fought against them were the three Shapes out of the Valley of the Yew Tree that came to avenge their sister, Cuillen of the Wide Mouth — for her son Fear Og, that was hardly in Ireland a man so good as himself in shape and in courage, died of a heavy sickness that fell on him through the eyes and the envy of the Fianna, after he had done better than them all in their games.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「我從沒吃過生肉，也不會因為一天沒吃東西就去吃它。」「如果你是到我們屋裡來拒絕我們的食物，那我們肯定要對你們動手了。」屋裡所有人一齊向這三人發起攻擊，戰鬥在黑暗中持續了整夜；當太陽升起照亮屋子時，那房子和屋裡的人都不見了踪影，全都消失了。而與他們搏鬥的那三個，正是從紫杉谷來的三個幻影，來為他們的姊妹、寬嘴的庫伊倫報仇——因為她的兒子菲爾奧格，論身形和勇氣，在愛爾蘭幾乎找不出比他更好的人，卻因芬尼亞戰士團的嫉妒和目光而染上重病死去，此前他在他們的各種競技中都勝過所有人。

title.en: The Pigs of Angus and the Curse on Bran
title.zh: 安古斯之豬與對布蘭的詛咒

region.en: Brugh na Boinne (Newgrange), Co. Meath, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭米斯郡博因墓丘

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. XIV, eBook #14465

summary.en: At Angus Og's feast in Brugh na Boinne, Finn boasts that Bran and Sceolan would kill any pig the Men of Dea own; Angus sends a herd of deer-high pigs led by a black one — his own son in pig-shape. The hounds slaughter the herd, but Bran, hearing it is her foster-brother she holds, grips him like an enemy and keeps him for the Fianna; the unburnable pigs must be burned with three logs of unknown wood from Bran's foraging, and Angus curses her never to see with her eyes any deer she may kill. The breach is healed by fostering children between the houses.
summary.zh: 在博因墓丘的宴席上，芬恩誇言布蘭與斯克奧蘭能殺神族任何一頭豬；安古斯遂遣出高如鹿群的野豬——領頭黑豬竟是其子所化。群犬屠戮豬群；布蘭聞知所擒正是乳弟，緊咬不放如同仇敵。豬身火不能燃，賴布蘭尋來三段無名之木方得焚化；安古斯詛咒布蘭：所殺之鹿永不可目見。兩族以互換撫養子而和解。

sensitivity.note: The cursing of Bran (never to see the deer she kills) is a dindsenchas-style etiology retold in the cycle; the fosterage exchange that settles god-mortal blood-debt reflects real Irish fosterage law. Pin is Newgrange.

passages.text: Angus Og, son of the Dagda, made a feast one time at Brugh na Boinne for Finn and the Fianna of the Gael. "It is a better life this is than to be hunting," said Angus out in a loud voice. There was anger on Finn: "It is a worse life than hunting to be here, without hounds, without horses, without battalions, without the shouting of armies." "As to the hounds you have, they would not kill so much as one pig." "You have not yourself, and the whole host of the Tuatha de Danaan have not a pig that ever went on dry land that Bran and Sceolan would not kill." "I will send you a pig that will go from you and your hounds, and that will kill them in the end."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XIV; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 达格达之子安格斯·奥格有一次在博因河畔的布鲁为芬恩和盖尔人的芬尼亚勇士团设宴。「这样的生活比打猎好得多，」安格斯高声说道。芬恩动了怒：「待在这里，没有猎犬，没有马匹，没有队伍，没有军队的呐喊，这样的生活比打猎糟得多。」「至于你那些猎犬，它们连一头猪也杀不死。」「你自己没有，整个达南神族的全部人马也没有一头踏上过干地的猪，是布兰和斯凯奥兰杀不死的。」「我要送你一头猪，它会从你和你的猎犬手中逃走，最终还会杀死它们。」

passages.text: At the end of a year Angus sent messengers asking Finn if he was ready to keep his word, and on the plain to the east they saw a terrible herd of great pigs, every one the height of a deer, and one pig out in front blacker than a smith's coal, with bristles like a thicket of thorn-trees. Caoilte let out Adhnuall, and she was the first to kill a pig; and then Bran made away from the leash, and came up with the pigs, and took hold of a pig of them. "O Bran, fosterling of fair-haired Fergus, it is not a right thing you are doing, to kill my own son," said Angus; but when Bran heard that, her ways changed and it was like an enemy she took hold of the pig, and did not let it go, and kept it for the Fianna.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XIV; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一年将尽时，安格斯派使者去问芬恩是否准备践诺；在东边的平原上，他们看见一群可怕的巨猪，每一头都有鹿那么高，最前头有一头猪比铁匠的煤还黑，鬃毛像一片荆棘丛。凯尔泰放出了阿德努尔，她第一个杀死了一头猪；接着布兰挣脱了皮带，追上猪群，咬住了其中一头猪。「哦，布兰，金发弗格斯的养子啊，你杀死我自己的儿子，可不是该做的事，」安格斯说；但布兰听到这话，态度就变了，她像对待仇敌一样咬住那头猪，不肯松口，把它留给了芬尼亚勇士团。

passages.text: At evening there was not one pig of the whole herd without a hurt, but the hunt brought losses on the Fianna as well, for there were ten hundred of their men missing besides serving-lads and dogs. And they could not set fire to one pig till Bran went away and came back bringing three logs, and no one knows what wood it was they came from; and it is with them the pigs were burned, and their ashes thrown into the sea. And Angus said: "It is a pity for you, sweet daring Bran, that you did not do something worth praise before killing your own foster-brother. And I will put a curse on you, Bran, beyond every hound in Ireland, that you will never see with your eyes any deer you may ever kill." There was anger on Finn, and Oisin said it was best for them to agree between themselves; so they made peace, and gave children to be fostered by one another — a son of Finn's to Angus, and a son of Angus Og to the Fianna.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XIV; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了傍晚，整群猪没有一头不带伤，但这场狩猎也给芬尼亚勇士团带来了损失，因为他们失踪了一千人，还不算仆役和猎犬。他们也无法点燃任何一头猪，直到布兰离开又回来，带回三根木柴，没人知道那是什么木头；就是用这些木柴把猪烧了，骨灰被扔进了海里。安格斯说：「可惜啊，甜美勇敢的布兰，你在杀死自己的养兄弟之前，没能做一件值得称赞的事。我要给你布兰下一个咒，胜过爱尔兰所有的猎犬，叫你今后无论杀死什么鹿，都永远无法亲眼看见。」芬恩动了怒，奥辛说他们最好彼此和解；于是他们讲和，互相把儿子交给对方抚养——芬恩的一个儿子交给安格斯，安格斯·奥格的一个儿子交给芬尼亚勇士团。

title.en: Finn's Grey Hair and the Lake of Sorrow
title.zh: 芬恩的白髮與悲傷之湖

region.en: Loch Doghra, Slieve Cuilinn, Co. Down, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭唐郡庫林山悲傷湖

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. XV, eBook #14465

summary.en: A grey fawn leads Finn and his two hounds to Slieve Cuilinn and vanishes; a sorrowful girl on the lake-side puts Finn under bonds to dive for a red-gold ring, leaps away as soon as he hands it up, and the head and leader of the Fianna comes out of the water a weak old man. The lake would have turned all the men of the world grey; only Cuilinn of Cuailgne — some say Manannan himself — can undo it, and after the Fianna have rooted up his hill for three days and nights he gives the restoring draught. Finn's shape comes back but his hair stays grey, and from the vessel that slipped into the earth grows a tree whose morning gaze, fasting, shows the day's events.
summary.zh: 灰色母鹿引芬恩至庫林山後消失；湖畔愁容少女以誓約迫芬恩潛水尋回金環，接環即躍入水中。水中而出的菲亞納之首已成孱弱老人——此湖若照全人類，皆將白首。唯有庫伊爾涅的庫林——或謂即瑪那南——能解咒；菲亞納掘丘三日三夜，方得回春之飲。芬恩形貌復原而白髮不返；金杯遁入地處生出一樹，晨起齋戒觀其枝者可預知當日之事。

sensitivity.note: Fionn's white hair (fionn = fair) is here re-lexicologised as aged grey through the jealousy-plot of Miluchradh, sister of Aine — a famous etiological myth of the cycle. The prophetic tree is a dindsenchas-style object. Pin symbolic at Slieve Cuilinn / Lough Shannagh area.

passages.text: Finn was one time out on the green of Almhuin, and he saw what had the appearance of a grey fawn running across the plain. Neither hound nor man heard him but only Bran and Sceolan, and near as they kept to her, he himself kept nearer to them, till they reached to Slieve Cuilinn; but they were no sooner at the hill than the fawn vanished from them. Finn came to a lake, and there was sitting on the brink of it a young girl, the most beautiful he had ever seen, having hair of the colour of gold, and eyes like the stars in time of frost, but she seemed to be sorrowful. "It is what I am fretting after, a ring of red gold I lost off my finger in the lake.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XV; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次芬恩在阿尔穆因的草地上，看见一个像是灰色小鹿的东西跑过平原。除了布兰和斯凯奥兰，没有猎犬也没有人听见他，它们跟得她多近，他自己就跟得它们更近，直到他们到了库利恩山；可他们刚到山边，那小鹿就从他们眼前消失了。芬恩来到一个湖边，湖边坐着一个年轻姑娘，是他见过最美的，头发如金，眼睛像霜降时的星辰，但她似乎很忧伤。「我正为这个发愁，一枚赤金戒指，我从手指上掉进了湖里。

passages.text: And I put you under bonds, Finn of the Fianna, to bring it back to me out of the lake." Finn stripped off his clothes and went into the lake at the bidding of the woman, and went three times round the whole lake, till he brought back the ring; and no sooner had he handed it up out of the water than she gave a leap into the water and vanished. And when Finn came up on the bank of the lake, he, the head and the leader of the Fianna of Ireland, was but a grey old man, weak and withered, and Bran and Sceolan went on round the lake searching after their master, for they did not know him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XV; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 我以誓约束缚你，芬尼亚勇士团的芬恩，要你从湖里把它取回来给我。」芬恩脱下衣服，依那女人的吩咐走进湖里，绕着整个湖转了三圈，终于把戒指取了回来；他刚把戒指递出水面，她就一跃跳进水里消失了。而当芬恩回到湖岸上时，他，爱尔兰芬尼亚勇士团的首领和领袖，已成了一个衰弱枯槁的灰发老人，布兰和斯凯奥兰绕着湖寻找它们的主人，因为它们认不出他了。

passages.text: When he was missed in Almhuin, Caoilte began asking after him, and Conan said: "I never heard music pleased me better than to hear the son of Cumhal is missing. And that he may be so through the whole year, and I myself will be king over you all." At last they came to Slieve Cuilinn and saw a withered old man sitting beside the lake, and he had not the courage to say that he himself was Finn their leader, until Caoilte took out his sword: "It is short till you will have knowledge of death unless you will tell us what happened those three." To the lake they gave the name of Loch Doghra, the Lake of Sorrow. "I know well the enchantment was put on me by a woman of the Sidhe, Miluchradh, daughter of Cuilinn, through jealousy of her sister Aine.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XV; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿尔穆因那边发现他不见了，凯尔泰便开始打听他，科南说：「我从未听过比这更让我高兴的音乐，就是听说库哈尔之子不见了。但愿他整年都这样，我自己来做你们全体的王。」最后他们来到库利恩山，看见一个枯槁的老人坐在湖边，他没有勇气说他自己就是他们的领袖芬恩，直到凯尔泰拔出剑来：「你若不说出你们三个遭遇了什么，你离认识死亡就不远了。」他们给那湖取名为洛赫·多格拉，即悲伤之湖。「我很清楚，这魔法是西德族的女人、库利恩之女米卢赫拉德因嫉妒她妹妹艾妮而加在我身上的。」

passages.text: And bring me to the hill that belongs to Cuilinn of Cuailgne, for he is the only one can give me my shape again." The seven battalions began digging and rooting up the whole hill through the length of three nights and three days, and at the end of that time Cuilinn of Cuailgne, that some say was Manannan, son of Lir, came out of the hill holding a vessel of red gold, and no sooner did Finn drink what was in the vessel than his own shape came back to him. But only his hair never got its own colour again, for the lake that Cuilinn's daughter had made for Finn would have turned all the men of the whole world grey if they had gone into it. And in the place where the vessel slipped from his hand into the earth, a tree grew up, and any one that would look at the branches of that tree in the morning, fasting, would have knowledge of all that was to happen on that day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XV; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 並帶我到屬於庫艾爾格內的庫林的那座山丘去，因為只有他能讓我恢復原形。」七個營隊開始挖掘、翻遍整座山丘，歷經三夜三日；到那時，庫艾爾格內的庫林——有人說他就是里爾之子馬納南——從山丘中出來，手裡拿著一只赤金器皿，芬恩一喝下器皿裡的東西，自己的原形便立刻回到他身上。但唯有他的頭髮再也沒能恢復本來的顏色，因為庫林的女兒為芬恩造的那座湖，若有人走進去，會把全世界的男人都變成灰白。而在器皿從他手中滑落、掉進土裡的地方，長出了一棵樹；任何人若在清晨空腹時觀看那棵樹的枝條，便能知曉當天將要發生的一切。

title.en: Beara's Salmon Shirt for Eoghan the Bright
title.zh: 貝亞拉的鮭魚襯衫與「光明者」歐文

region.en: River Eibhear, Co. Kerry, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡艾巴河（象徵定位）

period: Fenian cycle genealogy, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book V, eBook #14465

summary.en: Eoghan, driven out of Ireland, lands in Spain the very night the Druid foretold: the King's daughter Beara goes east to the river Eibhear, finds a crimson-spotted salmon shining from head to tail, strips him of his clothing and makes a shining shirt for the husband the Druid promised her. The exile will not ask for her till he has treasures for poets and learned men; the king calls it the answer of a king, gives her that very night, and the shirt's shining is seen in every place — hence Eoghan the Bright.
summary.zh: 被逐出愛爾蘭的歐文抵達西班牙之夜，恰如德魯伊所預言：國王之女貝亞拉東行至艾巴河，尋得一條通體閃耀紅斑的鮭魚，剝下其衣為德魯伊許諾的夫婿縫製光衫。流亡者自言無以饋贈詩人學者而不敢求婚；國王稱此乃王者之答，當夜許婚。襯衫光芒四射——「光明者歐文」由此得名。

sensitivity.note: A genealogical marriage-tale linking the Fenian cycle to Munster dynasty (Beara gives her name to Beara peninsula); salmon-hides clothing mortals parallels the seal-skin and swan-skin motif family. Symbolic pin on the river.

passages.text: Oisin had a daughter that married the son of Oiliol, son of Eoghan, and of Beara, daughter of the King of Spain. It was that Eoghan was driven out of Ireland one time, and it is to Spain he went for safety. Beara, that was daughter of the King of Spain, was very shining and beautiful, and her father sent for his Druid and asked who would be her husband. "I can tell you that, for the man that is to be her husband will come to land in Spain this very night. And let your daughter go eastward to the river Eibhear, and she will find a crimson-spotted salmon in that river, having shining clothing on him from head to tail. And let her strip that clothing off him, and make with it a shining shirt for her husband."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧辛有一個女兒，嫁給了奧伊利奧爾之子、與西班牙國王的女兒貝拉所生之子。那位埃奧甘曾有一次被逐出愛爾蘭，他為求安全便去了西班牙。貝拉是西班牙國王的女兒，非常光彩照人、美麗動人，她父親召來他的德魯伊，問誰會做她的丈夫。「這我可以告訴您，因為將要做她丈夫的人，今夜就會在西班牙登陸。讓您的女兒往東到埃伯河去，她會在那條河裡找到一條帶深紅斑點的鮭魚，從頭到尾穿著閃亮的衣裳。讓她把那衣裳從他身上剝下來，用它為她的丈夫做一件閃亮的襯衫。」

passages.text: So Beara went to the river Eibhear, and found the golden salmon as the Druid had said, and she stripped him of his crimson clothing and made a shining shirt of it. As to Eoghan, the waves of the shore put a welcome before him, and he came the same night to the king's house, and it is what all the people said, that there was never seen a comelier man than Eoghan, or a woman more beautiful than Beara. But after a while the king sent his Druid to ask Eoghan why he did not ask for Beara. "It would not be fitting for me to be refused a wife, and I am but an exile in this country, and I have brought no treasures or goods with me out of Ireland for giving to learned men and to poets. But for all that the king's daughter is dear to me."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是貝拉去了埃伯河，果然如德魯伊所說，找到了那條金色的鮭魚；她剝下他深紅的衣裳，用它做了一件閃亮的襯衫。至於埃奧甘，岸邊的波浪為他獻上歡迎，他當夜便來到國王的宅邸；眾人都說，從未見過比埃奧甘更俊美的男子，也從未見過比貝拉更美麗的女子。但過了一陣，國王派他的德魯伊去問埃奧甘，為何不向貝拉求婚。「我若求娶而被拒絕，那是不合適的；我不過是這國中的一個流亡者，從愛爾蘭出來時並未帶任何財寶貨物，可以送給博學之士和詩人。儘管如此，國王的女兒於我仍是珍貴的。」

passages.text: "That is the answer of a king," said the King of Spain; "and bid my daughter to sit at Eoghan's right hand, and I will give her to him this very night." And when Beara heard that, she sent out her serving-maid to bring the shirt she had made for Eoghan, and he put it on him over his armour, and its shining was seen in every place; and it was from wearing that shirt he got the name of Eoghan the Bright. And Oiliol was the first son they had; it was he that had his ear bitten off by Aine of the Sidhe in revenge for her brother, and it was his son married Oisin's daughter afterwards.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「這才是國王的回答，」西班牙國王說；「叫我女兒坐在埃奧甘的右手邊，我今夜就把她許配給他。」貝拉聽見這話，便派她的侍女去取她為埃奧甘做的那件襯衫；他把它穿在鎧甲外面，它的光輝處處可見；正因穿著那件襯衫，他得了「明亮的埃奧甘」這個名字。他們所生的第一個兒子是奧伊利奧爾；正是他，被希德族的艾妮為了替她兄弟報仇而咬掉了耳朵；後來正是他的兒子娶了奧辛的女兒。

title.en: Etain of the Fair Hair Races the Fianna
title.zh: 金髮艾汀與菲亞納賽跑

region.en: Slieve Crot, Co. Sligo, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭斯利戈郡克羅特山（象徵定位）

period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book V, eBook #14465

summary.en: A crimson-cloaked woman on Slieve Crot asks a man of the Fianna to race her, and all run from Badhamair to the Sidhe of Beinn Edair — beaten, it turns out, by Be-mannair the shapeshifting messenger who takes every shape and gathers every secret. The racer was Etain of the Fair Hair, whose lover among the Fianna is Osgar, son of Oisin: he pledges never to leave her but for her own fault, with Goll and Finn as sureties. But when Osgar lies wounded at Beinn Edair, greyness comes on her and her heart breaks in her like a nut.
summary.zh: 克羅特山上的紅衣女子邀菲亞納賽跑，眾人自巴德馬爾一路狂奔至埃達山的仙丘——孰料勝過他們的，是能化萬形、窮盡秘密的信使貝·曼奈爾。賽跑者實為金髮艾汀，其菲亞納情郎乃歐辛之子奧斯加：他立誓除她自過，永不離棄，以戈爾與芬恩為保。然奧斯加重傷臥於埃達山時，她容顏灰敗，心如堅果碎裂而亡。

sensitivity.note: Etain name-complex recurs across the corpus (Midir's Etain, Etain mother of Conaire); this Fenian Etain is a distinct figure — the race-to-the-otherworld courtship is a fixed Fenian pattern (cf. Niamh and Oisin). Dying of grief at the husband's wound is the same motif as Credhe. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: One time Finn and his men came to Slieve Crot, and they saw a woman waiting there before them, having a crimson fringed cloak, and a band of yellow gold on her forehead. "Etain of the Fair Hair is my name, daughter of Aedh of the White Breast, of the hill of the Sidhe at Beinn Edair, son of Angus Og. To ask a man of the Fianna of Ireland to run a race with me I am come." All of the Fianna that were there set out to run with her, and they ran to the height over Badhamair and on to Ath Cliath, and from that on to the hill of the Sidhe at Beinn Edair.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次，芬恩和他的部下來到克羅特山，他們看見一個女子在那裡等候在他們面前，披著一件深紅流蘇斗篷，額上束著一條黃金帶。「我是金髮埃坦，白胸埃德的女儿，來自貝恩埃達爾的希德山丘，安格斯·奧格之子。我來此，是要向愛爾蘭芬尼亞的一個男子挑戰，與我賽跑。」在場的所有芬尼亞人都出發與她同跑，他們跑到巴德哈邁爾上方的高地，再跑到阿斯克利亞斯，又從那裡跑到貝恩埃達爾的希德山丘。

passages.text: There they saw a nice fair-haired girl in front of the vats, giving out drink to every one: "It seems to me that is the girl came asking the Fianna to race against her at Slieve Crot," said Finn. "It is not, for that is the slowest woman there is among us. It was Be-mannair, daughter of Ainceol, woman-messenger of the Tuatha de Danaan, and it is she that changes herself into all shapes; and she will take the shape of a fly, and of a true lover, and every one leaves their secret with her. And it was she outran you coming from the east."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在那裡，他們看見一個秀麗的金髮姑娘站在大桶前，給每個人斟酒：「在我看來，那就是到克羅特山來向芬尼亞人挑戰賽跑的那個姑娘，」芬恩說。「不是她，因為那是我們當中最慢的女子。那是艾恩科爾的女兒貝曼奈爾，達南神族的女性信使，正是她把自己變成各種形狀；她會變成蒼蠅的形狀，也會變成真正戀人的形狀，人人都把秘密託付給她。正是她從東邊跑來，跑贏了你們。」

passages.text: "Etain of the Fair Hair, a daughter of my own, and a darling of the Tuatha de Danaan, and it is the way with her, she has a lover of the men of the Fianna — Osgar, son of Oisin." The son of the High King of Ireland had offered a great bride-price for her, three hundreds of the land and his own weight of gold; but they did not take it, since she had no mind for it herself. "Never to leave me for anything at all but my own fault," said the girl, and Osgar made the agreement, giving the sureties of Goll for the sons of Morna and of Finn for the Fianna of Ireland; and the wedding-feast was made, and they stopped there for twenty nights.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「美髮的伊坦，是我親生的女兒，也是圖阿薩·德·達南的寵兒，而她的性情便是如此，她在費尼亞人中有一位情人——奧斯卡，奧伊辛之子。」愛爾蘭至高王的兒子曾為她獻上豐厚的聘禮，三百份土地以及與他自身等重的黃金；但他們並未接受，因為她本人無意於此。「除非是我自己的過錯，否則絕不為任何事離開我。」那少女說道，奧斯卡便立下了約定，以戈爾為莫爾納眾子作保，以芬恩為愛爾蘭的費尼亞人作保；於是辦起了婚宴，他們在那裡停留了二十夜。

passages.text: But a while after that, in a great battle at Beinn Edair, Osgar got so heavy a wound that Finn and the Fianna were as if they had lost their wits; and when Etain of the Fair Hair came to the bed where Osgar was lying and saw the great kinglike shape was gone from him, greyness and darkness came on her, and she went to her bed and her heart broke in her like a nut; and she died of grief for her husband and her first love.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而此後不久，在貝恩·埃達爾的一場大戰中，奧斯卡受了極重的傷，芬恩與費尼亞人彷彿都失了神智；當美髮的伊坦來到奧斯卡躺臥的床前，見他那王者般的偉岸身形已從他身上消逝，灰暗與陰翳便籠罩了她，她回到自己的床上，心如同堅果般碎裂；她因哀悼丈夫與初戀而死。

title.en: Yavakrida's War Against the Sun
title.zh: 耶伐克里陀與太陽的戰爭

region.en: Kurukshetra wastes (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俱盧之野荒地（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, Yavakrida episode

summary.en: The boy Yavakrida, watching a seer's son humiliate his father, vowed to outdo the sun: he stood in the river's stream with arms up, reciting the Vedas against the sunrise, determined to learn by power what discipline teaches by time. The Sun came down as an old brahmin and explained the fraud in one speech - knowledge is not a siege - and warned him twice. His warnings unheeded, the age collected: the boy died by another man's wife, in the way his own violence had chosen.
summary.zh: 目睹仙人之子羞辱其父的少年耶伐克里陀，誓要勝過太陽：立於河流之中高舉雙臂，向日出誦讀吠陀，要以力量奪取只有紀律才能教授之物。太陽化作老婆羅門降下，一席話說破其欺騙——知識非圍城可得——並警告他兩次。警告未被理會，因果到場：少年死於他人之妻，以他自己所選的暴力方式。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The vow was a child's siege: he stood waist-deep in the river at dawn, arms raised, reciting scripture against the sun itself - learn by force what the fathers learned by patience. The Sun came down in an old man's shape and gave the lesson the boy would not buy: knowledge is a path, not a wall; water does not flow by being bullied - nor does wisdom. The warning's fine print was about women: treat another's wife as fire's edge. The boy forgot it; the debt was called, and the epic's water-story ended in a well - the siege broken from inside.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那誓願是一場孩童式的圍攻：黎明時他立於河中，水深及腰，雙臂高舉，對著太陽本身誦讀經文——以強力求取父輩們以耐心所得之物。太陽化作一位老人的形貌降下，給了那男孩不肯領受的教誨：知識是一條道路，而非一堵牆；水不會因被脅迫而流動——智慧亦然。那警告的細則關乎女人：待他人之妻，當如火焰之邊緣。那男孩忘卻了它；債被索還，而史詩的水中故事終結於一口井——圍攻自內部被攻破。

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Shalya's Treacherous Hospitality
title.zh: 沙利耶的致命款待

region.en: Road to Hastinapura (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 赴象城之路（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Udyoga/Adi Parva traditions, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Shalya episode

summary.en: The Madra king Shalya, marching to join the Pandavas, was met on the road by a host whose hospitality he could not refuse - food, shelter, gifts beyond measure. Only at the end was the host named: Duryodhana's agents had bought the uncle of Nakula and Sahadeva into the Kaurava army - and honor-bound by the feast, Shalya went to war against his own sister's sons, serving as Karna's charioteer and complaining the whole way.
summary.zh: 馬德羅王沙利耶率軍來投般度族，途中受一位主人無法拒絕的款待——食物、屋舍、無法計量的贈禮。直到最後主人才被指名：難敵的代理者用盛宴把無種與偕天的舅舅買進了俱盧軍——受恩諾所縛，沙利耶對妹妹的兒子們作戰，充當迦爾納的御者，且一路上抱怨不休。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The road-host's welcome was engineered: a stranger's table beyond refusal, a night of comfort, gifts that weighed more than armies - and a guest does not ask his host's name before the feast is done. The host's name, when it came, was the war itself: the uncle of the youngest Pandavas had eaten his way into the enemy's roster, courtesy as conscription.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那路邊主人的款待是精心設計的：陌生人的餐桌令人無法推辭，一夜的安逸，比軍隊更沉重的禮物——而賓客在宴席結束之前不會詢問主人的名姓。主人的名姓，當它揭曉時，便是戰爭本身：最年幼的般度族兄弟們的舅父已一路吃進了敵方的名冊，禮數即是徵召。

passages.text: He kept the bargain and cursed it daily: as Karna's charioteer he praised the enemy's aim to the man holding the bow - the epic's comedy of honor, a general going to war against his own blood at a dinner's invitation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他守住了那約定，卻日日詛咒它：身為迦爾納的御者，他對著持弓之人讚美敵方的箭術——這是史詩中關於榮譽的喜劇，一位將軍應一頓晚餐之邀，與自己的血親作戰。

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Muchukunda's Sleep and Kalayavana's Ash
title.zh: 穆周昆陀的沉睡與迦羅耶梵之灰

region.en: Cave in the western hills (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西山之洞（象徵性定位）

period: Harivamsha / Mahabharata traditions, 19th-c. English prose translation (public domain)

source.work: A Prose English Translation of Harivamsha, 19th c. (public domain), the story of Muchukunda

summary.en: The human king Muchukunda had fought the gods' wars and been promised a sleep no age could break - a nap worth an eternity. Ages later Krishna, pursued by the barbarian Kalayavana, led the pursuer into a dark cave where a shape lay sleeping; Kalayavana kicked it awake, and the sleep-warmed gaze of the old warrior burned him to ash at one look. Krishna was forgiven the trick with a king's blessing.
summary.zh: 凡人國王穆周昆陀曾為諸神作戰，被允諾一場無齡可破的沉睡——一場等值永恆的午睡。無數劫後，被蠻王迦羅耶梵追擊的克里希那將追兵引入一處黑暗洞窟，其中躺著一個沉睡的身影；迦羅耶梵踢醒它，老戰士睡暖的目光一眼將他燒為灰燼。克里希那以王者的祝福被饒恕此計。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The pension of a soldier-king: after the gods' wars were won, Muchukunda asked only for rest - and was granted a sleep that would not end until he chose to wake. Kalayavana, the age's other tyrant, chased Krishna into the hills and into the cave; the dark shape on the stone floor was kicked - and the first thing it saw burned. The king's sleep-glare, hoarded through the ages, had become a weapon he did not know he owned; he blessed the god who had used it and went to the forest to think about what he had seen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harivamsha traditions (19th-c. prose translation); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位戰士之王的養老之賜：眾神之戰得勝之後，穆楚昆達只求安歇——而他被賜予一場不會終止的睡眠，直到他選擇醒來。迦羅耶瓦那，那個時代的另一位暴君，將黑天追入群山、追入洞穴；石地上那黑暗的形影被踢了一腳——而它第一眼所見之物便焚毀了。那國王積存了數個世紀的睡中怒視，已成了他不知自己擁有的武器；他祝福了那位曾使用它的神，而後前往森林，思索他所見之事。

canonical_translation: 19th-c. English prose translation (public domain)

title.en: Sahadeva Who Knew Everything and Said Nothing
title.zh: 知一切而不言的偕天

region.en: Hastinapura (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 象城（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, epic traditions, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), epic traditions on Sahadeva

summary.en: The epic's tradition of the youngest Pandava: having eaten his father Pandu's brain (in the folk-telling of the twins), Sahadeva could see everything that would happen - the dice, the exile, the war, the deaths - on one condition: he must never tell anyone, or the knowledge would kill him. He spent the whole epic as the family's silent oracle, smiling at disasters he was forbidden to name.
summary.zh: 史詩對般度幼子的傳說：據民間講述，雙生子中偕天曾食其父般度之腦，因而能預見一切將至之事——骰局、流放、戰爭、死亡——但有一條件：永不可告訴任何人，否則此知將殺死他。他終其史詩生涯作為家族沉默的神諭，對自己被禁止言說的災難報以微笑。

sensitivity.note: Folk-epic tradition rather than critical-edition text; recorded as tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The folk-telling gives the knowledge a price: the father's essence eaten, the sight of all futures granted - on the single condition of total silence. The silence is the tragedy's engine: he watched the dice game as an oracle watches a wreck he is forbidden to announce - his smile at catastrophe is the tradition's blackest joke. The epic uses him as its own narrator's shadow: the story that knows its ending and cannot say so - which is, of course, what a written epic is.
passages.note: Paraphrase of epic/folk traditions on Sahadeva (Ganguli 1883-96 and vernacular tradition); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 民間傳說為這份知識標了價：父親的精華被吞食，一切未來的景象被賜予——唯一的條件是完全的沉默。這沉默是悲劇的引擎：他觀看擲骰賭局，如同先知觀看一場他被禁止宣告的災難——他對災禍的微笑是傳統最陰暗的笑話。史詩將他用作自身敘述者的影子：那個知道自己的結局卻無法說出的故事——而這當然正是一部書寫史詩的本質。

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: Draupadi's Laughter and the Thigh
title.zh: 黑公主的笑與那條腿

region.en: Hall of illusions, Hastinapura (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 象城幻宮（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Sabha Parva, the maya-sabha

summary.en: In the Pandavas' hall of illusions, Duryodhana - touring his cousins' splendor in envy - stepped on water that looked like floor and fell into water that looked like floor. Draupadi laughed. The tradition treats that one laugh as the war's true fuse: the shame-burned prince demanded a rematch of pride, got it at the dice, and the thigh he later showed her in the assembly was the insult's revenge.
summary.zh: 在般度族的幻宮中，懷妒參觀表親華貴宮殿的難敵，踏上看似地板的水而跌入看似水的地板。黑公主笑了。傳統視那一笑為戰爭真正的導火索：恥辱燒灼的王子要求一場傲慢的重賽，得之於骰局，而他後來在廷上向她亮出的那條腿，正是羞辱的報復。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The hall was Maya's masterpiece: floors that were water, water that was floor - a prince of the real world taking the tour like an audit, and losing the audit to architecture. Draupadi's laugh was a queen's laughter at a rival's clumsiness - and the epic marks the sound as the point of no return: pride is the war's currency, and she had just devalued his. The rematch was the dice; the revenge was the thigh in the assembly; and the tradition's ledger shows a kingdom traded for one second of laughter - the price, the epic insists, was always known to both sides.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那座殿堂是摩耶的傑作：地板如水，水如地板——一位現實世界的王子像查帳般巡視，卻在建築面前輸掉了這場查帳。黑公主的笑是一位王后對對手笨拙的嘲笑——而史詩將這聲音標記為不歸點：傲慢是戰爭的貨幣，而她剛剛讓他的貶了值。再賽的是骰子；報復的是會堂上那大腿；而傳統的帳冊顯示，一個王國被換來一秒的笑聲——史詩堅稱，這代價雙方始終心知肚明。

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: The Mace Duel: Bhima and Duryodhana
title.zh: 鐵杵之鬥：怖軍與難敵

region.en: Kurukshetra (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俱盧之野（象徵性定位）

period: Mahabharata, Shalya Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Shalya Parva, the mace duel

summary.en: The war's last duel was two mace-men on empty ground: Bhima, the appetite, against Duryodhana, the grudge - fighting for hours on even terms while the whole war watched. Krishna touched his own thigh; Bhima understood, and below the waist - where the vow had been sworn in the dice-hall - the mace came down. The code was broken by a vow, and the winner was jeered by the loser to the end.
summary.zh: 戰爭的最後決鬥是空地上兩位杵士：怖軍，以食量為徽；難敵，以積怨為徽——在兩軍注視下於均勢中激戰數小時。克里希那拍了拍自己的大腿；怖軍會意，在腰以下——誓言於骰廳所立之處——鐵杵落下。規矩被一個誓言打破，而勝者至終仍被敗者譏笑。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The duel was even: mace on mace, hour after hour, the war's two appetites - food and grudge - deciding the age's account in single combat. Krishna's hand on his own thigh was the hint the vow required: the dice-hall's oath - thy thigh - answered below the waist, where the code forbade and the promise demanded. The dying king's last speech refused the verdict: my brothers are dead, I broke no promise I kept - and the epic leaves the winner standing on a broken rule while the loser keeps his argument.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Shalya Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那場決鬥勢均力敵：杵對杵，一小時又一小時，戰爭的兩種慾望——食慾與怨恨——在單打獨鬥中決定這個時代的帳目。黑天把手放在自己大腿上，正是誓言所需的暗示：擲骰廳中的誓——「你的大腿」——在腰下得到了回應，那是法典所禁止、而承諾所要求之處。垂死國王的最後演說拒絕了這判決：我的兄弟都死了，我沒有違背我所守的承諾——而史詩讓勝者站在一條被打破的規則上，敗者則保留著他的論辯。

canonical_translation: K. M. Ganguli, 1883-96 (public domain)

title.en: The Muster at Upaplavya
title.zh: 鄔婆普拉婆耶的點兵

region.en: Upaplavya, Matsya capital (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 鄔婆普拉婆耶，摩蹉都城（象徵性定位）
