summary.en: The last of the Fianna wear away: Caoilte's winter lament of the stag and the wolves, his shining rescue of a king lost in a dark wood — "I am your candlestick; I was with Finn one time" — and three times nine of the rest who come to Tara, find themselves unheeded in their lost strength, lie down and put their lips to the earth and die; Loch Dearg lies under mists for three days and a month and a year. But a smith finds a cave of the great men sleeping, blows the Dord Fiann twice, and flees — "You left us worse than you found us" — and some say the day will come when it is sounded three times and the Fianna rise as strong as ever.
summary.zh: 最後的菲亞納相繼凋零：卡爾特於冬雪中詠雄鹿與狼嗥之嘆；化為火焰般的巨人為迷路的國王引路——「我是你的燭台，我曾追隨芬恩」；三九殘部至塔拉，見無人理會衰朽的自己，伏地而亡；德爾格湖籠罩霧靄三日又一月又一年。然而一名鐵匠誤入沉睡巨人的洞窟，兩次吹響菲亞納號角——「你使我們比你發現我們時更糟」——傳說三次號角響起之日，菲亞納將如往昔般甦醒。

sensitivity.note: The sleeping-warrior expectation (Rot und die Fianna under hill until the horn sounds) is the Celtic sleeping-army eschaton — tagged 'resurrection' + 'world-renewal' for the promised rising; Caoilte as candlestick-guider parallels the later Finn-as-hero-reborn belief. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: And indeed that was the last time Finn and Oisin and the rest of the Fianna of Ireland were gathered together; for they all wore away after that, one after another. As to Caoilte, that was old and had lost his sons, he used to be fretting and lonesome after the old times, and one day that there was very heavy snow on the ground he made this complaint: "It is cold the winter is; the wind is risen; the fierce high-couraged stag rises up; it is cold the whole mountain is to-night, yet the fierce stag is calling. I, Caoilte, and brown-haired Diarmuid and pleasant light-footed Osgar, we used to be listening to the music of the wolves through the end of the cold night. To-day I am in my age, and I know but a few men; I used to shake my spear bravely in the ice-cold morning."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book X, ch. III; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 而那確實是芬恩、奧辛以及愛爾蘭其餘費尼亞戰士最後一次聚在一起；因為在那之後，他們便一個接一個地消逝了。至於凱爾特，他年事已高，又失去了兒子們，常為往昔的時光而憂傷孤寂；有一天，地上積著極厚的雪，他作了這般哀嘆：「冬天寒冷；風已颳起；凶猛而意氣高昂的雄鹿昂然起身；今夜整座山都寒冷，然而凶猛的雄鹿仍在呼號。我，凱爾特，與褐髮的迪爾穆德，以及性情溫和、步履輕捷的奧斯加，我們曾整夜在寒夜盡頭聆聽狼群的樂音。如今我已年老，認識的人寥寥無幾；我曾在冰冷刺骨的清晨勇敢地揮舞長矛。」

passages.text: But a long time after that again, there was a king of Ireland making a journey, and he and his people missed their way in a dark wood; and there came to them a very tall man, that was shining like a burning flame, and he took hold of the bridle of the king's horse and led him through the wood till they came to the right road. "I am your candlestick; and I was with Finn one time." And three times nine of the rest of the Fianna came out of the west one time to Teamhair, and they took notice that now they were wanting their full strength and their great name, no one took notice of them or came to speak with them at all; and when they saw that, they lay down on the side of the hill at Teamhair, and put their lips to the earth and died. And for three days and a month and a year from the time of the destruction of the Fianna of Ireland, Loch Dearg was under mists.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book X, ch. III; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但此後又過了很久，有一位愛爾蘭國王出行，他與他的臣民在一片幽暗的樹林中迷了路；這時有一名非常高大的男子來到他們面前，他閃耀如燃燒的火焰，他抓住國王坐騎的韁繩，領他穿過樹林，直到他們來到正確的道路上。「我是你的燭台；我曾一度與芬恩同在。」其餘費尼亞戰士中有三個九人曾一度從西方來到塔拉，他們察覺到如今自己已失去了全盛的氣力與偉大的名聲，無人理會他們，也無人前來與他們交談；他們見此情景，便躺倒在塔拉的山坡旁，將嘴唇貼向大地而死。而自愛爾蘭費尼亞戰士覆滅之時起，三天、一個月又一年之久，德爾格湖都籠罩在霧中。

passages.text: One time a smith made his way into a cave he saw, that had a door to it, and he made a key that opened it; and when he went in he saw a very wide place, and very big men lying on the floor, and one that was bigger than the rest lying in the middle, and the Dord Fiann beside him, and he knew it was Finn and the Fianna were in it. He took hold of the Dord Fiann, and it is hardly he could lift it to his mouth, and he blew a very strong blast on it, and the big men lying on the ground shook from head to foot; he gave another blast, and they all turned on their elbows.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book X, ch. III; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次，一名鐵匠闖進了他所見到的一個洞穴，那洞穴有一道門，他打造了一把鑰匙將它打開；當他走進去時，他看見一個非常寬闊的地方，地上躺著非常巨大的男子，其中有一個比其餘的都更巨大，躺在中央，他身旁放著費尼亞號角，他明白那是芬恩與費尼亞戰士在裡面。他抓住費尼亞號角，幾乎無法將它舉到嘴邊，他用力吹了一聲極響亮的號音，躺在地上的巨大男子們從頭到腳都震動起來；他又吹了一聲，他們全都以肘撐起了身子。

passages.text: And great dread came on him, and he threw down the Dord Fiann and ran from the cave and locked the door after him and threw the key into the lake, and he heard them crying after him, "You left us worse than you found us." And some say the day will come when the Dord Fiann will be sounded three times, and that at the sound of it the Fianna will rise up as strong and as well as ever they were.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book X, ch. III; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巨大的恐懼臨到他身上，他扔下費尼亞號角，逃出洞穴，隨手鎖上了門，將鑰匙丟進湖裡，他聽見他們在他身後呼喊：「你讓我們離開時比發現我們時更糟。」有人說，終有一日費尼亞號角將被吹響三次，而一聽到它的聲音，費尼亞戰士便會起身，如同昔日一般強壯、一般安好。

title.en: Bran Og and the Giant Bird That Proved Oisin's Word
title.zh: 布蘭·奧格與印證歐辛之言的巨鳥

region.en: Gleann-na-Smol (Glen of Smol), Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭斯莫爾谷

period: Fenian-Christian interface, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book XI, ch. II, eBook #14465

summary.en: Patrick calls Oisin's boast a lie — a blackbird quarter bigger than beef, a rowan berry bigger than a churn. Oisin rears the one pup that grips a raw hide, keeps it a year without blood or daylight, digs up the Fianna's horn, iron ball and sword, and blows three blasts that bring down three clouds of birds; Bran Og kills the biggest, goes mad with its blood, and dies by Oisin's iron ball — and inside the bird lie the rowan berry and the ivy leaf. "Truth that was in our hearts, and strength in our arms, and fulfilment in our tongues."
summary.zh: 帕特里克斥歐辛之言為謊——「黑鳥腿大過牛肉、花楸果大過牛油攪桶」。歐辛育成唯一咬住生皮不放的幼犬，養其一年不見血不見光；掘出菲亞納號角、鐵球與寶劍，三吹角聲引下三雲群鳥；布蘭·奧格誅最大之鳥、飲血而狂，死於歐辛鐵球之下——鳥腹中竟有花楸果與大過烤盤的常春藤葉。「心懷真理，臂有強力，言出必行。」

sensitivity.note: The tale-type is the truth-proof (aim-demonstration) between saint and pagan hero; the pre-Christian world's enormity vouched by physical relics is the cycle's central comparative device. The madness-and-death of Bran Og repeats the hound-death pattern of the corpus. Pin at Gleann-na-Smol, named in the tale.

passages.text: There was great anger on Oisin, and he went where there was a litter of pups, and he bade a serving-boy to nail up the hide of a freshly killed bullock to the wall, and to throw the pups against it one by one; and every one that he threw fell down from the hide till it came to the last, and he held on to it with his teeth and his nails. "Rear that one, and drown all the rest." Then he bade the boy to keep the pup in a dark place, and to care it well, and never to let it taste blood or see the daylight; and at the end of a year Oisin gave it the name of Bran Og, young Bran.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book XI, ch. II; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧辛大為震怒，他走到一窩幼犬所在之處，吩咐一名僕童將一頭剛宰殺的公牛之皮釘在牆上，再將幼犬一隻一隻地朝那張皮扔去；他每扔一隻，牠都從皮上跌落下來，直到最後一隻，牠用牙齒與爪子緊緊攀住不放。「就養那一隻，其餘的全溺死。」然後他吩咐那男孩把這隻幼犬養在暗處，好好照料，絕不讓牠嘗到血，也不讓牠見到日光；一年之後，奧辛給牠取名為布朗·奧格，意即小布朗。

passages.text: And one day he called to the serving-boy to come on a journey with him, and to bring the pup in a chain; and they passed by Slieve-nam-ban, where the witches of the Sidhe do be spinning with their spinning-wheels, and then turned eastward into Gleann-na-Smol. And Oisin raised a rock that was there, and he bade the lad take from under it three things, a great sounding horn of the Fianna, and a ball of iron they had for throwing, and a very sharp sword. "My thousand farewells to the day when you were put here!"
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book XI, ch. II; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，他喚那侍童與他同行，並用鏈子牽著那隻小狗；他們經過女妖山（Slieve-nam-ban），那裡常有希德（Sidhe）的女巫們轉動紡車紡線，隨後轉向東行，進入煙霧谷（Gleann-na-Smol）。奧辛（Oisin）掀起那兒的一塊岩石，命少年從石下取出三樣東西：一支費尼亞（Fianna）的洪亮號角、一顆他們用來投擲的鐵球，以及一把極其鋒利的劍。「我向你被放置於此的那一日致上千聲告別！」

passages.text: Oisin took the horn himself, and blew three great blasts on it, and the boy saw three great clouds coming and settling down in the valley: the first cloud a flight of very big birds, and the second a flight of birds bigger again, and the third flight of the biggest and the blackest birds the world ever saw. "What is the dog doing?" "The eyes are starting from his head, and there is not a rib of hair on him but is standing up." "Let him loose now." Bran Og rushed down and made an attack on one of the birds, the biggest of all, that had a shadow like a cloud, and at last made an end of it, and lapped its blood; but madness came on him, and he came rushing back towards Oisin, his jaws open and his eyes like fire, and Oisin made a cast of the iron ball that went into the mouth and the throat of the dog, and choked him, and he fell down the slope, twisting and foaming.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book XI, ch. II; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧辛親自拿起號角，吹了三聲巨響，少年便見三團巨大的雲降下，落在山谷之中：第一團雲是一群極大的鳥，第二團雲是一群更大的鳥，第三團雲則是世人所見最大、最黑的鳥群。「那狗在做什麼？」「牠的雙眼正從頭裡迸出，身上沒有一根毛不豎立起來。」「現在放開牠。」小布蘭（Bran Og）衝下去，向其中一隻鳥發動攻擊，那是眾鳥中最大的一隻，其影子宛如一片雲；牠終於結果了那鳥，舔飲其血；然而瘋狂襲上了牠，牠便朝奧辛猛衝回來，張著大口，雙眼如火；奧辛擲出鐵球，鐵球射入狗的嘴裡與喉嚨，將牠噎住，牠便倒下山坡，翻滾扭動，口吐白沫。

passages.text: And Oisin bade the lad cut open the body of the bird, and in it he found a rowan berry, the biggest he had ever seen, and an ivy leaf that was bigger than the biggest griddle. So Oisin went to where S. Patrick was, and showed him the quarter of the bird that was bigger than any quarter of a bullock, and the rowan berry that was bigger than a churning of butter, and the leaf: "And you know now, Patrick of the Bells, that I told no lie; and it is what kept us all through our lifetime, truth that was in our hearts, and strength in our arms, and fulfilment in our tongues."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book XI, ch. II; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧辛命少年剖開那鳥的身軀，在裡頭發現一顆花楸果，是他所見過最大的，還有一片常春藤葉，比最大的烤餅鐵板還要大。於是奧辛去到聖派翠克（S. Patrick）所在之處，給他看那鳥的四分之一，比任何一頭公牛的的四分之一還要大；又給他看那顆花楸果，比一桶攪製的奶油還要大；還有那片葉子：「你如今知道了，鳴鐘的派翠克，我並沒有說謊；正是這一切支撐我們度過一生：心中的真誠、臂膀的力量，以及舌上的踐諾。」

title.en: The Arguments of Oisin and Patrick
title.zh: 歐辛與帕特里克之辯

region.en: House of S. Patrick, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭聖帕特里克居所（象徵定位）

period: Fenian-Christian dialogue poems (Acallam-derived), medieval Irish; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book XI, ch. III, eBook #14465

summary.en: The poets of Ireland put down afterwards the two voices of the great quarrel: Patrick, that the Fianna are condemned to hell for their unbelief, and Oisin, that Finn the open-handed could not be held in any house made by God or devils — "if Osgar my own son is there, there is not in hell or in the Heaven of God a troop so great that he could not destroy it." Between the rounds run the catalogues of Finn's music and the hounds of the first hunt, and Oisin's word at the last: "I will cry my fill, but not for God, but because Finn and the Fianna are not living."
summary.zh: 愛爾蘭詩人後世記下了這場大爭論的兩種聲音：帕特里克稱菲亞納因不信而入地獄；歐辛則言——「慷慨的芬恩絕不會被神或魔所造的任何屋宇困住；若吾子奧斯加在彼處，地獄與天國中再無一支軍隊能抵擋他的毀滅」。爭論間穿插芬恩樂音的清單與初獵之犬的名冊；歐辛臨終之言：「我要哭盡我的淚——不是為了神，而是因為芬恩與菲亞納已不在人間。」

sensitivity.note: This is the pagan-Christian dialogue literature (Agallamh tradition) — a contested religious boundary treated here as documentary comparative material; the claim that the Fianna are in hell is Patrick's in-story position, not the corpus's. The catalogue of Finn's music recurs as the cycle's aesthetic witness. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: S. Patrick took in hand to convert Oisin, and to bring him to baptism, but it was no easy work he had to do, and everything he would say, Oisin would have an answer for it. PATRICK: "Oisin, it is long your sleep is. Rise up and listen to the Psalm." OISIN: "My readiness and my strength are gone from me since Finn has no armies living; I have no liking for clerks, their music is not sweet to me after his. I have heard music was sweeter than your music: the song of the blackbird in Leiter Laoi, and the sound of the Dord Fiann; the cry of the hounds was better to me than the noise of your schools, Patrick. Little Nut, little Nut of my heart, the little dwarf that was with Finn, when he would make tunes and songs he would put us all into deep sleep."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book XI, ch. III; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 聖派翠克著手要使奧辛皈依，領他受洗，但這樁差事並不容易，凡他所說的，奧辛總有話可答。派翠克：「奧辛，你這一睡已太久了。起來，聽那聖詠。」奧辛：「自從芬恩（Finn）麾下再無活著的軍隊，我的敏捷與力量便離我而去；我不喜歡那些教士，他們的樂音在我聽來，比不上他的樂音甜美。我聽過比你的音樂更甜美的音樂：萊特勞伊（Leiter Laoi）黑鳥的歌唱，以及費尼亞之笛（Dord Fiann）的聲音；派翠克，獵犬的吠聲在我聽來，勝過你那些學堂的喧鬧。小堅果，我心中的小堅果，那曾與芬恩同在的小矮人，當他奏起曲調、唱起歌來，便會使我們全都陷入沉睡。」

passages.text: PATRICK: "All the gold you and Finn used to be giving out, it is little it does for you now; he is in Hell in bonds because he did treachery and oppression." OISIN: "It is little I believe of your truth, man from Rome with the white books, Finn the open-handed head of the Fianna to be in the hands of devils or demons. If the sons of Morna were within it, or the strong men of the sons of Baiscne, they would take Finn out of it, or they would have the house for themselves." PATRICK: "If the five provinces of Ireland were within it, or the strong seven battalions of the Fianna, they could not bring Finn out of it." OISIN: "If Faolan and Goll were living, and brown-haired Diarmuid and brave Osgar, Finn of the Fianna could not be held in any house that was made by God or devils... If there was a place above or below better than the Heaven of God, it is there Finn would go, and all that are with him of his people."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book XI, ch. III; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 派翠克：「你與芬恩昔日所施捨的一切黃金，如今於你毫無益處；他因行背信與壓迫，正帶著鎖鏈身陷地獄。」奧辛：「手捧白書的羅馬人，我對你的真理所信甚少；費尼亞慷慨的首領芬恩，竟落入魔鬼或惡魔之手。倘若莫爾納（Morna）之子們在其中，或拜斯克涅（Baiscne）之子們的強壯男子在其中，他們必會把芬恩救出來，否則便會把那座宅子據為己有。」派翠克：「縱使愛爾蘭五省都在其中，或費尼亞強悍的七個營隊都在其中，他們也無法把芬恩從中帶出來。」奧辛：「倘若法奧蘭（Faolan）與戈爾（Goll）尚在人世，還有褐髮的迪爾穆德（Diarmuid）與勇敢的奧斯加（Osgar），那麼費尼亞的芬恩便不可能被拘禁於任何由上帝或魔鬼所造的宅子裡……倘若在上帝的天堂之上或之下，有比它更好的地方，芬恩便會去那裡，連同他所有與他同在的族人。」

passages.text: OISIN: "O Patrick, where was your God when the two came over the sea that brought away the queen of Lochlann of the Ships? Where was He when Dearg came, the son of the King of Lochlann of the golden shields? Why did not the King of Heaven protect them from the blows of the big man? Or when Tailc, son of Treon, came, the man that did great slaughter on the Fianna; it was not by God that champion fell, but by Osgar, in the sight of all. Many a battle and many a victory was gained by the Fianna of Ireland; I never heard any great deed was done by the King of Saints, or that He ever reddened His hand." And at the last Oisin said: "My story is sorrowful. The sound of your voice is not pleasant to me. I will cry my fill, but not for God, but because Finn and the Fianna are not living."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book XI, ch. III; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧辛：「噢，派翠克，當那兩人渡海而來、擄走船隻之洛克蘭（Lochlann）的女王時，你的上帝在哪裡？當金盾之洛克蘭國王之子德爾格（Dearg）來時，祂在哪裡？為何那天上之王不保護他們免於那巨人的打擊？又或者當特雷翁（Treon）之子泰爾克（Tailc）來時，那人曾對費尼亞大肆屠殺；那勇士並非因上帝而倒下，而是因奧斯加，在眾人眼前倒下。愛爾蘭的費尼亞贏得過多少戰役、多少勝利；我從未聽聞眾聖之王成就過任何偉業，也未曾聽聞祂曾染紅自己的手。」最後奧辛說道：「我的故事滿是悲傷。你的聲音在我聽來並不悅耳。我要痛哭一場，但不是為上帝，而是因為芬恩與費尼亞已不在人世。」

title.en: Oisin's Laments for the Household of Finn
title.zh: 歐辛悼芬恩家室之歌

region.en: House of S. Patrick, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭聖帕特里克居所（象徵定位）

period: Fenian-Christian interface, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book XI, ch. IV, eBook #14465

summary.en: Blind among Patrick's household, Oisin makes the laments that are remembered yet — "I saw the household of Finn; it was not the household of a soft race" — and, one night when the servants would not go out with him on his shoulders to mind the cattle, they lie to him of storms; a serving-girl truer than the rest sends him out, and the boy on his back dashes water in his face with a birch broom until Oisin finds the night quiet and asks no more news of the weather from the servants.
summary.zh: 失明的歐辛居於帕特里克家中，詠出流傳至今的哀歌——「我見過芬恩的家室；那絕非柔弱之族的家室」。一夜僕人拒絕讓他如常背負自己去看牛群，便謊報風雨；一名侍女較其餘人誠實，請他起身外出；背上的僕人以樺皮帚撩水入他面上冒充雨滴——直到歐辛發覺夜空無恙，此後再不向僕人打聽天氣。

sensitivity.note: The lying-weather-servants episode is a set-piece of the Oisin-in-Patrick's-house cycle (the blind hero cheated by Christian household — the corpus's comment on the new order); the laments are verse-transmitted memoria. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: And Oisin used to be making laments, and sometimes he would be making praises of the old times and of Finn: "I saw the household of Finn; it was not the household of a soft race; I had a vision of that man yesterday. I saw the household of the High King, he with the brown, sweet-voiced son; I never saw a better man. I saw the household of Finn; no one saw it as I saw it."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book XI, ch. IV; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 而奧辛慣常作哀歌，有時他也會頌讚往昔與芬恩：「我見過芬恩的家眷；那可不是柔弱之族的家眷；我昨日曾得見那人的異象。我見過那位至高王的家眷，他帶著那褐色頭髮、聲音甜美的兒子；我從未見過比他更好的人。我見過芬恩的家眷；沒有人像我這般見過它。」

passages.text: And when Oisin had no sight left at all, he used every night to put up one of the serving-men on his shoulders, and to bring him out to see how were the cattle doing. And one night the servants had no mind to go, and they agreed together to tell him it was a very bad night. And it is what the first of them said: "It is outside there is a heavy sound with the heavy water dropping from the tops of trees; the sound of the waves is not to be heard for the loud splashing of the rain." And then the next one said: "The trees of the wood are shivering, and the birch is turning black; the snow is killing the birds; that is the story outside." And the third said: "It is to the east they have turned their face, the white snow and the dark rain."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book XI, ch. IV; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 而當奧辛全然失明之後，他慣常每夜把一名僕役扛在肩上，帶他出去看看牛群情況如何。有一夜，僕役們都不願去，便一同商議，要告訴他那是個極壞的夜晚。頭一個人是這樣說的：「外頭有沉重的聲響，沉重的水從樹梢滴落；雨聲嘩啦作響，蓋過了浪濤之聲。」接著第二個人說：「林中的樹木在顫抖，樺樹正轉為烏黑；雪正凍殺鳥兒；外頭的情形便是如此。」第三個人說：「它們已把臉轉向東方，那白雪與黑雨。」

passages.text: But there was a serving-girl in the house, and she said: "Rise up, Oisin, and go out to the white-headed cows, since the cold wind is plucking the trees from the hills." Oisin went out then, and the serving-man on his shoulders; but it is what the serving-man did, he brought a vessel of water and a birch broom with him, and he was dashing water in Oisin's face, the way he would think it was rain. But when they came to the pen where the cattle were, Oisin found the night was quiet, and after that he asked no more news of the weather from the servants.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book XI, ch. IV; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但屋裡有一名侍女，她說：「起來吧，奧辛，出去看看那些白頭的母牛，因為寒風正把樹木從山丘上扯落。」奧辛於是出去了，肩上扛著那名僕役；但那僕役做的事是這樣：他帶了一盆水和一把樺樹掃帚，把水潑在奧辛臉上，好讓他以為那是雨。但當他們來到圈牛的圍欄時，奧辛發現那夜十分平靜，此後他就不再向僕役們打聽天氣的消息了。

title.en: Fedelm the Prophetess Sees the Host Red
title.zh: 菲德爾姆預言「我見赤色」

region.en: Road to Cualnge, Co. Louth, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭勞斯郡通往庫爾涅之路（象徵定位）

period: Tain Bo Cuailnge (Book of the Dun Cow recension), trans. L. Winifred Faraday (1904)

source.work: L. Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (1904), eBook #21557

summary.en: Medb asks Fedelm, prophetess of Connaught, fresh from Scotland, to read her hosting with the imbas forosnai. Three times the maiden answers, 'I see very red, I see red,' and against Medb's objections reads the boy she sees: a fair man with a hero's flame over his head, carrying two Gae-bolga in each hand, the Riastartha the distorted one — Cuchulainn Mac Sualtaim, who will make dense slaughters of the host and leave it many thousands of heads.
summary.zh: 梅芙請剛從蘇格蘭學成歸來的康諾特女先知菲德爾姆，以「智慧之視」占看大軍。少女三次答曰：「我見赤色，我見赤色。」無視梅芙的反駁，她讀出所見少年：頭頂英雄之火的俊美者，雙手各持雙重蛙矛——「扭曲者」里亞斯塔爾塔——庫丘林。他將使大軍血染成赤，留下千萬首級。

sensitivity.note: The imbas forosnai divination is an attested Irish legal-poetic practice; the frame (prophetess who sees only blood) is the epic's doom-device. Pin symbolic at the marching route.

passages.text: 'Fedelm, the prophetess of Connaught, is my name,' said the maiden. 'Whence do you come?' 'From Scotland, after learning the art of prophecy.' 'Have you the inspiration which illumines?' 'Yes, indeed.' 'Look for me how it will be with my hosting.' Then the maiden looked for it; and Medb said: 'O Fedelm the prophetess, how seest thou the host?' Fedelm answered and said: 'I see very red, I see red.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「康諾特的預言女費德爾姆，便是我的名字，」那少女說。「你從何處來？」「從蘇格蘭來，學得了預言之術。」「你可有那照亮人心的靈感？」「有的，確實有。」「替我看看我的大軍將會如何。」於是那少女為此察看；梅芙便說：「哦，預言女費德爾姆，你如何看待這支大軍？」費德爾姆回答說：「我見一片通紅，我見紅色。」

passages.text: 'That is not true,' said Medb; 'for Conchobar is in his sickness at Emain and the Ulstermen with him.' 'Fedelm the prophetess, how seest thou our host?' 'I see red.' 'That matters not; for there are mutual angers and quarrels in every host. Look again for us then, and tell us the truth.' 'I see very red, I see red... I see a fair man who will make play with a number of wounds on his girdle; a hero's flame over his head, his forehead a meeting-place of victory... Like is the nature of his valour to Cuchulainn of Murthemne. I do not know whose is the Hound of Culann, whose fame is the fairest. But I know that it is thus that the host is very red from him... He will strike on whole hosts, he will make dense slaughters of you, ye will leave with him many thousands of heads.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「那不對，」梅芙說；「因為康科巴正患病在埃明，阿爾斯特人也都隨他在那裡。」「預言女費德爾姆，你如何看待我們的大軍？」「我見紅色。」「那無關緊要；因為每一支大軍中都有彼此的忿怒與爭吵。那麼再替我們察看一次，把實情告訴我們。」「我見一片通紅，我見紅色……我見一位俊美之人，他將在腰帶上留下許多傷痕；他頭頂有英雄的火焰，他的額頭是勝利的會合之地……他勇武的本性與穆爾特姆內的庫胡林相似。我不知道庫蘭之犬是誰，他的名聲最為美好。但我知道，正因他，大軍才如此通紅……他將衝擊整支大軍，他將使你們死傷稠密，你們將在他那裡留下成千上萬的頭顱。」

title.en: The Ogam Withe on the Pillar
title.zh: 石柱上的歐甘柳環

region.en: Iraird Cuillend, Co. Meath, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭米斯郡伊拉爾德·庫倫（象徵定位）

period: Tain Bo Cuailnge (LU recension), trans. L. Winifred Faraday (1904)

source.work: L. Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (1904), eBook #21557

summary.en: Going to a tryst, Cuchulainn twists a spancel-withe of a single twig, writes an ogam on it, and throws it on a pillar-stone: let no one pass till a man throws a like withe with one hand, Fergus excepted. The four sons of the vanguard find it, Fergus reads the ogam, and warns: outrage this withe, and the hand of him who wrote will slay a goodly slaughter of you before morning. Ailill's host turns aside by the neck of the great wood rather than meet the geis.
summary.zh: 赴約之前，庫丘林以單枝柳條扭成繫獸環，刻歐甘文於其上，擲於石柱之頂：除非有人單手擲出同樣的環，無人可過——費爾古斯除外。前鋒四人發現此環，費爾古斯誦出歐甘之義並警告：若辱此環，刻文者的手將在黎明前屠戮你們。大軍遂繞大林而行，不敢觸犯此誓。

sensitivity.note: The withe-and-ogam geis is the Tain's master-token of single combat (compare the withe of the sons of Nechta Scene, whose removal is called a breach of geis in the Leinster gloss); ogam-writing on withe and oak recurs as Cuchulainn's road-magic. Pin symbolic.

passages.text: He made a spancel-withe then before he went — a twig twisted in the form of two rings, joined by one straight piece, as used for hobbling horses and cattle — and wrote an ogam on it, and threw it on the top of the pillar. The leadership of the way before the army was given to Fergus. Then Fergus went far astray to the south, till Ulster should have completed the collection of an army; he did this for friendship. 'O Fergus, this is strange, what kind of way do we go?... It is to avoid the great man who protects Mag Murthemne... But if perchance I may avoid even afterwards Cuchulainn Mac Sualtaim.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他臨行前便做了一根絆繩柳枝——一根扭成兩個環、以一段直枝相連的細枝，正如用來絆馬和牛的——並在上面刻了歐甘文字，然後把它扔在石柱頂上。大軍前頭領路之職交給了弗格斯。於是弗格斯向南遠遠地迷了路，好讓阿爾斯特得以完成軍隊的集結；他這樣做是出於情誼。「哦，弗格斯，這真奇怪，我們走的是什麼樣的路？……這是為了避開那位守護穆爾特姆內平原的大人物……但願我或許連此後也能避開蘇阿爾泰之子庫胡林。」

passages.text: They found the withe that Cuchulainn threw, and perceived the grazing that the horses had grazed, and gave the withe into the hands of Fergus Mac Roich; he read the ogam that was on it. 'We wait because of the withe yonder. There is an ogam on it, and this is what is in it: Let no one go past till a man is found to throw a like withe with his one hand, and let it be one twig of which it is made; and I except my friend Fergus.' Then Fergus said to them: 'If you outrage this withe, or if you go past it, though he be in the custody of a man, or in a house under a lock, the hand of the man who wrote the ogam on it will reach him, and will slay a goodly slaughter of you before morning, unless one of you throw a like withe.' 'It does not please us, indeed, that one of us should be slain at once,' said Ailill. 'We will go by the neck of the great wood yonder, south of us, and we will not go over it at all.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們找到了庫胡林所投的那根柳條，也察覺到馬匹所啃食過的草痕，便把那根柳條交到費格斯·麥克·羅伊赫手中；他讀出了柳條上的歐甘文字。「我們之所以在此等候，正是因為那邊那根柳條。上面刻有歐甘文字，其內容是這樣：任何人不得從此經過，除非找到一個能用單手投出同樣柳條的人，而且那柳條須由一根枝條做成；我唯獨把我的朋友費格斯除外。」於是費格斯對他們說：「你們若毀壞這根柳條，或從它旁邊經過，那麼即使他正受某人看管，或身處上了鎖的屋中，寫下這歐甘文字之人的手也會伸到他身上，並在明晨之前使你們遭受一場慘重的殺戮，除非你們之中有人投出同樣的柳條。」「我們實在不願我們之中有人當即被殺，」艾利爾說。「我們就從我們南邊那片大樹林的邊緣繞過去吧，我們絕不從它上面經過。」

title.en: The Sons of Nechta Scene
title.zh: 涅克塔·塞恩之子

region.en: Fort of the sons of Nechta Scene, Co. Louth, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭勞斯郡涅克塔之子堡壘（象徵定位）

period: Tain Bo Cuailnge (LU recension), trans. L. Winifred Faraday (1904)

source.work: L. Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (1904), eBook #21557

summary.en: Cuchulainn reaches the fort of Foill, Fandall and Tuachell, who say there are not more of the Ulstermen alive than they have slain, and breaks their withe into the stream — a breach of their geis. Sleeping by the pillar he bids the charioteer wake him not for few but for many; Foill's back is broken by the first spear, Fandall the Swallow is taken in the ford, and the javelin makes a red-sieve of Tuachell the Cunning. With three heads and a live deer and a flock of swans in the chariot he rides for Emain, where the naked women of the court must meet him before the heroes can seize him.
summary.zh: 庫丘林抵達福伊爾、凡達爾、圖阿凱爾三兄弟之堡——他們自誇所殺的阿爾斯特人不比餘下的少。他擲其柳環入溪流，破了兄弟們的誓約。倚柱而眠前囑咐車伕：「非多人勿醒我。」福伊爾首矛即斃；「燕」凡達爾殞於淺灘；一矛使「狡者」圖阿凱爾化為紅篩。攜三首級、活鹿與天鵝群馳向埃馬因——唯有裸身的宮中女子現身，英雄們方能將他制服。

sensitivity.note: The withe removed is explicitly a breach of geis in the Leinster gloss; the naked-women cooling is the standard riastrad (warp-spasm) control device — the boy-hero's heat quenched in vessels of water. Pin symbolic.

passages.text: They reached the fort of the three sons of Nechta Scene; Foill, Fandall, and Tuachell were their names. 'Is it they who say that there are not more of the Ulstermen alive than they have slain of them?' 'It is they indeed.' 'Let us go till we reach them.' 'Truly it is not to avoid it that we go.' Then they go forth, and he threw the withe that was on the pillar as far as he could throw into the river, for this was a breach of geis to the sons of Nechta Scene. They perceive it then, and come to them. Cuchulainn goes to sleep by the pillar after throwing the withe at the stream; and he said to the charioteer: 'Do not waken me for few; but waken me for many.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們抵達了內赫塔·斯凱內三子之子的堡壘；他們的名字是福伊爾、凡達爾與圖阿赫爾。「說烏爾斯特人活著的數目不多於他們所殺之數的，就是他們嗎？」「正是他們。」「我們走吧，直到我們抵達他們那裡。」「說真的，我們前去並非為了避開它。」於是他們向前行進，他把立於石柱上的那根柳條盡其所能地投進河裡，因為這對內赫塔·斯凱內諸子而言是違犯禁忌之舉。他們察覺到了，便向他們走來。庫胡林把柳條投向溪流之後，便在石柱旁睡去；他對馭者說：「不要為少數人叫醒我；要為許多人叫醒我。」

passages.text: 'Take heed of the man who comes against you. Foill is his name, for unless you reach him in the first thrust, you will not reach him till evening.' Then he cast the spear at him, so that his back broke. 'Take heed of another man, Fandall is his name. Not more heavily does he traverse the water than swan or swallow.' They meet then in the ford; Cuchulainn kills that man, and took his head and his arms. 'Take heed of another man who comes towards you. Tuachell is his name. It is no misname for him, for he does not fall by arms at all.' 'Here is the javelin for him to confuse him, so that it may make a red-sieve of him.' He cast the spear at him, and cut off his head. He heard then the cry of their mother, Nechta Scene, behind them, and put their spoils and the three heads in his chariot.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「當心向你迎來的那個人。他的名字叫福伊爾，因為除非你在第一擊就擊中他，否則你直到傍晚都擊不中他。」於是他把矛擲向他，使他的脊背折斷。「當心另一個人，他的名字叫凡達爾。他渡水之輕盈，不亞於天鵝或燕子。」他們於是在淺灘相遇；庫胡林殺死了那人，取下了他的頭顱與兵器。「當心向你走來的另一個人。他的名字叫圖阿赫爾。這對他而言並非誤稱，因為他根本不會被兵器擊倒。」「這裡有一支標槍給他，用以使他慌亂，好讓它把他打成一面紅色的篩子。」他把矛擲向他，砍下了他的頭顱。隨後他聽見他們母親內赫塔·斯凱內在他們身後發出的哭號，便把他們的戰利品與三顆頭顱放進他的戰車。

passages.text: They go on to Sliab Fuait, and Cuchulainn seized the deer that was nearest and finest of the herd and bound it between the two poles of the chariot, and struck eight swans with a small stone and twelve with a large, all by his return stroke, and bound the birds from the strings and thongs of the chariot; so that it was thus he went to Emain Macha: the wild deer behind his chariot, and the flock of swans flying over it, and the three heads in his chariot.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們繼續前往斯利亞布·富艾特，庫胡林捉住了鹿群中最近、最精壯的一頭雄鹿，把它綁在戰車的兩根轅桿之間，又用一塊小石子擊中八隻天鵝，用一塊大石子擊中十二隻，全憑他回手的一擊，並把這些鳥兒用戰車的繩索與皮帶綁住；於是他就這樣前往埃曼·瑪哈：野鹿跟在他的戰車之後，一群天鵝在戰車上方飛翔，三顆頭顱則在他的戰車之中。

passages.text: 'A man in a chariot is coming to you; he will shed the blood of every man who is in the court, unless naked women go to him.' Then the women of Emain go to meet him with Mugain, the wife of Conchobar Mac Nessa, and bare their breasts before him: 'These are the warriors who will meet you to-day.' He covers his face; then the heroes of Emain seize him and throw him into a vessel of cold water. That vessel bursts round him. The second vessel boiled with bubbles as big as the fist therefrom. The third vessel into which he went he warmed so that its heat and its cold were rightly tempered; and he sits at Conchobar's knee, and that was his couch always after that. 'The man who did this in his seventh year, it were not wonderful though he should rout an overwhelming force when his seventeen years are complete to-day.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「有一個乘戰車的人正向你們而來；他將使庭院中每一個人的血濺流，除非裸身的婦女前去迎他。」於是埃曼的婦女們帶著康霍巴爾·麥克·內薩的妻子穆蓋恩前去迎他，在他面前袒露胸脯：「這些就是今日要來迎你的戰士。」他遮住了臉；於是埃曼的英雄們抓住他，把他投入一桶冷水之中。那桶水在他周圍爆裂。第二桶水沸騰起來，冒出的氣泡有拳頭那麼大。他進入的第三桶水被他暖得冷熱恰好調和；於是他坐在康霍巴爾的膝旁，此後那便始終是他的坐處。「一個在七歲之年便做出這等事的人，今日他滿十七歲之時，縱然擊潰一支壓倒性的軍隊，也不足為奇。」

title.en: The Drowning of Fraech at the Ford
title.zh: 弗蕾赫溺亡於淺灘

region.en: Ath Fraich (Fraech's Ford), Co. Louth, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭勞斯郡弗蕾赫渡口（象徵定位）

period: Tain Bo Cuailnge (LU recension), trans. L. Winifred Faraday (1904)

source.work: L. Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (1904), eBook #21557

summary.en: Medb begs Fraech to remove the strait from the host, and he goes to Ath Fuait with nine men and finds Cuchulainn bathing. 'Do not come to me; you will die from it, and I should be sorry to kill you.' 'I shall come indeed, that we may meet in the water; and let your play with me be fair.' They wrestle long on the water; twice Cuchulainn lifts him up and twice Fraech refuses to yield, and the third time he is held under until he is killed. A troop of women in green tunics — his kin of the Sid, Bebind's sister being Boinn herself — draw his body away into a mound called after him, Sid Fraich.
summary.zh: 梅芙懇求弗蕾赫為大軍解圍；他攜九人至阿特·福伊特，見庫丘林正在河中沐浴。「別過來——你會送命，殺你我也痛心。」「我偏要來，讓我們在水中相會；且望你對我手下留情。」二人在水中長久角力；庫丘林兩度將他托起，弗蕾赫兩度拒絕認輸，第三次被按入水中至死。一隊綠衣女子——其仙族血親（貝賓德之妹即博因河本身）——將他的屍身引入以他命名的仙丘。

sensitivity.note: Fraech (Fráech mac Idaid) is the demi-divine Fenian-linked hero of the Ulster cycle (his raiment of Alban treasure, Findabair episode); the water-wrestling death with yield-refusal is the fixed ford-combat pattern that Fer Diad's episode repeats at scale. The fairy women bearing the body to a sid is the mortality-undoing motif. Pin symbolic.

passages.text: They are there till next morning; then Fraech is summoned to them. 'Help us, O Fraech,' said Medb. 'Remove from us the strait that is on us. Go before Cuchulainn for us, if perchance you shall fight with him.' He set out early in the morning with nine men, till he reached Ath Fuait. He saw the warrior bathing in the river. 'Wait here, till I come to the man yonder; not good is the water,' said he. He took off his clothes, and goes into the water to him. 'Do not come to me,' said Cuchulainn. 'You will die from it, and I should be sorry to kill you.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們在那裡待到次日清晨；隨後弗雷赫被召到他們面前。「幫助我們吧，弗雷赫，」梅芙說。「為我們解除壓在我們身上的困境。替我們到庫胡林面前去，或許你會與他交戰。」他清晨便帶著九個人出發，直到抵達阿特·富艾特。他看見那名戰士正在河中沐浴。「在這裡等著，直到我走到那邊那人跟前；這水可不妙，」他說。他脫下衣服，下水向他走去。「不要到我這裡來，」庫胡林說。「你會因此喪命，而我若殺了你會感到難過。」

passages.text: 'I shall come indeed, that we may meet in the water; and let your play with me be fair.' 'Settle it as you like.' 'The hand of each of us round the other,' said Fraech. They set to wrestling for a long time on the water, and Fraech was submerged. Cuchulainn lifted him up again. 'This time, will you yield and accept your life?' 'I will not suffer it,' said Fraech. Cuchulainn put him under it again, until Fraech was killed. He comes to land; his retinue carry his body to the camp. Ath Fraich, that was the name of that ford for ever. All the host lamented Fraech. They saw a troop of women in green tunics on the body of Fraech Mac Idaid — for Fraech was descended from the people of the Sid, his mother Bebind being a fairy woman, and her sister was Boinn, the river Boyne — they drew him from them into the mound; Sid Fraich was the name of that mound afterwards.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「我確實會來，好讓我們在水中相會；讓你的較量對我公平些。」「隨你怎麼定。」「我們彼此各以手臂環抱對方。」弗雷赫說道。他們在水上開始角力，持續了許久，弗雷赫被沒入水中。庫胡林又把他舉了起來。「這回，你可願意認輸、保住性命？」「我不願忍受。」弗雷赫說道。庫胡林又把他按入水中，直到弗雷赫被殺死。他上了岸；他的隨從把他的屍體抬回營地。Ath Fraich，那處淺灘自此便以此為名。全軍都為弗雷赫哀悼。他們看見一隊身穿綠色束腰外衣的女子圍在弗雷赫·麥克·伊代德的屍身上——因為弗雷赫出身於西德之民，他的母親貝賓德是一位仙女，而她的姊妹便是波因，即博因河——她們把他從他們身邊引進了土丘；此後那座土丘便名為西德·弗雷赫。

title.en: The Morrigan Offers Love and Threatens Shapes
title.zh: 摩里岡示愛與化身威脅

region.en: Ath Grencha (Ath Darteisc), Co. Louth, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭勞斯郡格倫哈渡口（象徵定位）

period: Tain Bo Cuailnge (LU recension), trans. L. Winifred Faraday (1904)

source.work: L. Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (1904), eBook #21557

summary.en: A young woman in a dress of every colour comes to Cuchulainn — daughter of Buan the king, she says — with her treasures and her cattle: 'I have loved you for your reputation.' 'The time at which you have come to us is not good; our condition is evil through hunger.' Then she names her threats: an eel about his feet in the ford; a grey she-wolf driving the cattle on him; a hornless red heifer rushing on him at the pools. He answers each: broken ribs between his toes, an eye broken with a sling-stone, a leg broken — till a doom of blessing comes on her.
summary.zh: 一位身披百色衣裙的少女向庫丘林走來——自稱王者布安之女，攜財富牛群：「我因你的名聲而愛你。」「此時非相見之時；我軍困於飢餓。」她一一陳其威脅：化作鰻魚纏足使其跌倒；化為灰母狼驅牛群衝撞；化為無角赤牝犢於水潭前突襲。他一一作答：趾間斷其肋骨、彈石碎其一目、斷其一腿——直到「吉運之命降於她」。

sensitivity.note: The Morrigan's courtship-refusal is the Tain's great theomachy hinge (she then fights him as a bird at the ford and is wounded); her eel-wolf-heifer shape-threats are a fixed triple-transformation set-piece. The 'doom of blessing' clause licenses her later healing. Pin symbolic.

passages.text: Cuchulainn saw a young woman coming towards him, with a dress of every colour on, and her form very excellent. 'Who are you?' 'Daughter of Buan the king. I have come to you; I have loved you for your reputation, and I have brought my treasures and my cattle with me.' 'The time at which you have come to us is not good. For our condition is evil, through hunger. It is not easy to me to meet a woman, while I am in this strife.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 庫胡林看見一個年輕女子朝他走來，身穿五彩斑斕的衣裳，身形極為出眾。「你是誰？」「布安王之女。我來找你；我因你的名聲而愛慕你，並且帶來了我的財寶和我的牛群。」「你來找我們的時機不好。因為我們的處境艱難，正受饑餓所困。在我身陷這場爭鬥之時，與女子相會於我並非易事。」

passages.text: 'I will be a help to you... I shall be more troublesome to you when I come against you when you are in combat against the men. I will come in the form of an eel about your feet in the ford, so that you shall fall.' 'I will take you between my toes, till your ribs are broken, and you will be in this condition till a doom of blessing comes on you.' 'I will drive the cattle on the ford to you, in the form of a grey she-wolf.' 'I will throw a stone at you from my sling, so that it shall break your eye in your head.' 'I will come to you in the form of a hornless red heifer before the cattle. They will rush on you on the plains and on the fords, and you will not see me before you.' 'I will throw a stone at you, so that your leg shall break under you, and you will be in this state till a doom of blessing comes on you.' Therewith she goes from him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「我會助你一臂之力……當你與眾人交戰之時，我若來與你為敵，便會給你添更多麻煩。我會化作一條鰻魚，纏在你於淺灘中的腳邊，使你跌倒。」「我會把你夾在我的腳趾之間，直到你的肋骨斷裂，你將一直處於這般境地，直到祝福的命運降臨於你。」「我會化作一頭灰色的母狼，把牛群趕到淺灘上向你衝來。」「我會用投石索向你擲出一塊石頭，讓它擊碎你頭中的眼睛。」「我會化作一頭無角的紅色小母牛，趕在牛群之前來到你面前。它們會在平原上和淺灘上向你衝來，而你將看不見我在你前方。」「我會向你擲出一塊石頭，讓你的腿在你身下折斷，你將一直處於這般境地，直到祝福的命運降臨於你。」說罷，她便離他而去。

title.en: The Healing of the Morrigan from the Three-Teat Cow
title.zh: 以三乳牛之奶醫治摩里岡

region.en: Tarthesc, Mag Murthemne, Co. Louth, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭勞斯郡穆瑟姆尼平原（象徵定位）

period: Tain Bo Cuailnge (LU recension), trans. L. Winifred Faraday (1904)

source.work: L. Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (1904), eBook #21557

summary.en: Worn out with battle, Cuchulainn meets an old hag, blind and lame, milking a cow with three teats, and asks a drink. 'He will be whole who has brought it; the blessings of gods and non-gods on you' — the gods with them the Mighty Folk of the Sid, the non-gods the people of husbandry. Milk of the first teat heals her head, of the second her eye, of the third her leg: 'You told me I should not have healing from you for ever.' 'If I had known it was you, I would not have healed you ever.'
summary.zh: 戰疲力竭之際，庫丘林遇見一位盲且跛的老嫗，正擠一頭有三乳的牛，他索水解渴。「帶來者必得痊愈；願神與非神賜福於你。」——彼所謂神即仙丘的「偉大之民」，非神即務農之民。第一乳之奶愈其頭，第二乳愈其目，第三乳愈其腿。「你曾說我永不得你的醫治。」「早知是你，我永遠不會治你。」

sensitivity.note: The milk-healing that undoes the healing-words is the inverse of the usual blessing-cure — the drinker's 'whole' pronouncement becomes the goddess's cure; gods and non-gods is the redactor's gloss on pre-Christian cult vocabulary. Tagged 'resurrection' for the wound-to-whole function as elsewhere in the corpus.

passages.text: When Cuchulainn was in this great weariness, the Morrigan met him in the form of an old hag, and she blind and lame, milking a cow with three teats, and he asked her for a drink. She gave him milk from a teat. 'He will be whole who has brought it,' said Cuchulainn; 'the blessings of gods and non-gods on you.' The gods with them were the Mighty Folk, the dwellers in the Sid; non-gods the people of husbandry. Then her head was healed so that it was whole.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當庫胡林陷入這極度的疲憊之時，摩莉甘化作一個老嫗來見他，她雙目失明、腿腳殘疾，正擠一頭有三個乳頭的母牛的奶，他向她要一口喝的。她從一個乳頭擠出奶給他。「帶來這奶的人將會痊癒。」庫胡林說道；「願眾神與非神之民的祝福降於你。」與他們同在的眾神便是那強力之民，即居住於西德者；非神之民則是農耕之民。於是她的頭便痊癒了，完好如初。

passages.text: She gave the milk of the second teat, and her eye was whole; and gave the milk of the third teat, and her leg was whole; and this was what he said about each thing of them, 'A doom of blessing on you.' 'You told me,' said the Morrigan, 'I should not have healing from you for ever.' 'If I had known it was you,' said Cuchulainn, 'I would not have healed you ever.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她從第二個乳頭擠出奶給他，她的眼睛便痊癒了；又從第三個乳頭擠出奶給他，她的腿便痊癒了；而對於其中每一樣，他都是這樣說的：「願祝福的命運降於你。」「你曾對我說過，」摩莉甘說道，「我永遠不會從你這裡得到治癒。」「倘若我早知是你，」庫胡林說道，「我永遠也不會治癒你。」

title.en: Lug of the Sid Heals His Son in Sleep
title.zh: 仙丘的魯格為其子催眠療傷

region.en: Mound in Lerga, Mag Murthemne, Co. Louth, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭勞斯郡勒爾加丘（象徵定位）

period: Tain Bo Cuailnge (LU recension), trans. L. Winifred Faraday (1904)

source.work: L. Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (1904), eBook #21557

summary.en: Alone against the four provinces of Ireland, Cuchulainn sees a fair tall warrior crossing the hostile camp unattacked and attacking no one: 'Which of my friends from the Sid is that who comes to have pity on me?' 'It is I, your father from the Sid, Lug Mac Ethlend. Sleep a little, O Cuchulainn, till the end of three days and three nights, and I will fight against the hosts for that space.' He sings the ferdord and casts herbs of curing into the wounds; and in those three days the boys of Emain give three battles and fall but Folloman Mac Conchobair, who dies boasting he would take Ailill's crowned head.
summary.zh: 獨對愛爾蘭四省大軍的庫丘林，見一名俊美高挑的戰士穿行敵營而無人察覺：「是仙丘中哪位故友前來憐憫我？」「我是你仙丘的父親，埃斯倫之子魯格。睡吧，三日三夜，我代你迎戰大軍。」他以費爾多德咒文催眠，將療傷草藥投入傷口；三日間，埃馬因的少年軍三戰三敗，唯福洛曼戰亡——他至死誇言要取埃利爾的金冠首級。

sensitivity.note: Lug Mac Ethlend's paternity of Cuchulainn (the god as absent father from the Sid) is the mythic core of the Ulster hero; the three-day sleep with god-guarded healing is the cycle's great restorative hinge — the Sleeping Beauty shape in heroic form. The boys' battle is the pathos-counterpoint. Pin symbolic.

passages.text: Then the four provinces of Ireland took camp in the Breslech Mor in Mag Murthemne, and Cuchulainn took his post at the mound in Lerga near them, and his charioteer Loeg Mac Riangabra kindled a fire for him. He saw the fiery sheen of the bright golden arms over the heads of the four provinces of Ireland at the setting of the clouds of evening, and fury and great rage came over him; he uttered his hero's shout from his throat, so that goblins and sprites and spectres of the glen and demons of the air answered, and the Nemain produced confusion on the host, so that a hundred warriors of them died of terror and of heart-burst in the middle of the camp.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是愛爾蘭的四個省份在穆爾泰姆內平原的布雷斯萊赫莫爾紮營，庫胡林則在他們附近萊爾加的土丘上守位，他的馭者洛伊格·麥克·里安格拉布拉為他生起了一堆火。在傍晚雲層沉降之時，他看見愛爾蘭四省人頭頂上那明亮金色武器的火焰般的光輝，狂怒與極度的暴怒便湧上他的心頭；他從喉嚨裡發出英雄的呼喊，以致幽谷中的妖精、鬼怪與幽靈以及空中的惡魔都應聲而起，涅曼也在軍中製造了混亂，使他們當中的一百名戰士在營地中央因驚恐與心臟迸裂而死。

passages.text: When Loeg was there, he saw something: a single man who came straight across the camp of the men of Ireland from the north-east, a man fair and tall, with waving yellow hair, a green mantle folded round him, and a five-pointed spear in his hand. 'Which of my friends from the Sid is that who comes to have pity on me, because they know the sore distress in which I am, alone against the four great provinces of Ireland?'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當利格在那裡時，他看見了一件事：一個孤身男子從東北方筆直穿過愛爾蘭人的營地而來，那人白皙而高大，一頭飄揚的黃髮，身上裹著一件綠色斗篷，手中持著一柄五尖的矛。「那前來憐憫我的，是我哪位來自西德的朋友？因為他們知道我正身陷何等痛苦的困境，獨自對抗愛爾蘭的四大行省。」

passages.text: 'It is I, your father from the Sid, Lug Mac Ethlend.' 'My wounds are heavy, it were high time that I should be healed.' 'Sleep a little, O Cuchulainn, your heavy swoon of sleep at the mound of Lerga till the end of three days and three nights, and I will fight against the hosts for that space.' Then he sings the ferdord to him, and he sleeps from it; and for three days and three nights Cuchulainn was asleep — for from the Monday after the end of summer to the Wednesday after Candlemas, for that space he had not slept, except a little while against his spear after midday, with his head on his clenched fist, and his clenched fist on his spear, and his spear on his knee; but he was striking and cutting and attacking and slaying the four great provinces of Ireland for that space. It is then that the warrior of the Sid cast herbs and grasses of curing and charms of healing into the hurts and wounds and injuries of Cuchulainn, so that Cuchulainn recovered in his sleep without his perceiving it at all.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「是我，你來自西德的父親，盧格·麥克·埃斯倫德。」「我的傷勢沉重，早該是我被治癒的時候了。」「睡一會兒吧，庫呼蘭，在萊爾加土丘上沉沉昏睡，直到三天三夜結束，而我將在這段期間替你與大軍作戰。」隨後他向他唱起費爾多爾，他便由此入睡；庫呼蘭睡了三天三夜——因為從夏末之後的星期一，到聖燭節之後的星期三，這段期間他一直未曾入睡，唯有正午之後靠在他的矛上小憩片刻，頭枕在他緊握的拳上，緊握的拳抵在矛上，矛抵在膝上；但在這段期間裡，他一直揮擊、砍殺、進攻並誅戮愛爾蘭的四大行省。就在那時，西德的戰士將療傷的藥草與治癒的咒語投入庫呼蘭的創傷、傷口與損傷之中，於是庫呼蘭在睡夢中痊癒，而他自己全然不覺。

passages.text: Now it was at this time that the boys came south from Emain Macha: Folloman Mac Conchobair with three fifties of kings' sons of Ulster, and they gave battle thrice to the hosts, so that three times their own number fell, and all the boys fell except Folloman Mac Conchobair. Folloman boasted that he would not go back to Emain for ever and ever until he should take the head of Ailill with him, with the golden crown that was above it; but the two sons of Bethe Mac Bain came on him and wounded him so that he fell by them. So that that is the death of the boys of Ulster and of Folloman Mac Conchobair. Cuchulainn arose then from his sleep, and put his hand over his face, and made a purple wheelbeam from head to foot: 'Pity for that, that I was not in my strength! For if I had been in my strength, the boys would not have fallen as they have fallen.' 'Strive further, O Little Hound, it is no reproach to thy honour and no disgrace to thy valour.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此時，那些少年從埃曼·瑪哈南下來：福洛曼·麥克·康科拜爾率領烏拉德的王族之子三個五十人，他們向大軍交戰三次，以致敵方三倍於他們的人數陣亡，而所有少年都戰死了，唯有福洛曼·麥克·康科拜爾倖存。福洛曼誇口說，他永永遠遠都不會回到埃曼，直到他帶著艾利爾的首級，連同其上的金冠一同歸來；但貝瑟·麥克·班恩的兩個兒子向他襲來，將他重創，使他死在他們手下。這就是烏拉德少年們與福洛曼·麥克·康科拜爾之死。庫呼蘭於是從睡夢中起身，以手覆面，從頭到腳泛起一陣紫色的輪輻般的怒光：「可嘆啊，我竟不在我的力量之中！因為倘若我在我的力量之中，那些少年便不會如他們這般陣亡了。」「再奮力吧，小獵犬，這於你的榮譽無損，於你的勇武無恥。」

title.en: Fraech's Fairy Raiment and the Host to Cruachan
title.zh: 弗蕾赫的仙衣與克魯阿坎之軍

region.en: Cruachan (Rathcroghan), Co. Roscommon, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭羅斯康芒郡克魯阿坎王陵

period: Tain Bo Fraich (remscela to the Tain), Heroic Romances of Ireland vol. II, trans. A. H. Leahy (1905)

source.work: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, vol. II (1905), eBook #5679

summary.en: To win Findabair, Fraech sends to his fairy kin, and from Boand his mother's sister at Mag Breg he receives the fairy splendour: black-blue mantles like a beetle's back, gold-looped tunics, fifty silver-rimmed shields, fifty grey mares with golden curbs and silver bells at every throat, seven chase-hounds linked in pairs by gold fetters holding bronze sheaths to their feet, and trumpeters with fairy-thread hair — so the host rides to Croghan, and the watchman swears no army so fair has come since Ailill first took the throne.
summary.zh: 為求娶芬娜芭爾，弗蕾赫遣使仙族求助；其姨母——女神博因——於瑪格·布雷格賜他仙家盛裝：甲蟲背般的黑藍斗篷、金環鑲邊的束衣、五十面銀緣盾、五十匹配金轡銀鈴的灰馬、以金鎖相連的七對獵犬與仙髮號手——大軍如此華美地馳向克羅漢堡，望樓哨兵斷言：自埃利爾登基以來，未見如此軍容。

sensitivity.note: The fairy-gift host is the classic entry set-piece of the Fraech tale (his Sid kindred on both sides — Bebind's sister is Boinn); cross-ref parallels: the marvellous a quoit-dropping of the Morrigan-Regamna woman and the Tuatha tribute-hosts. Pin is the real Rathcroghan royal site.

passages.text: Now the news of the love of that maid to Fraech, at his home where he dwelt, was brought, and they counselled him thus: "Let a message from thee be sent to thy fairy kin, to entreat their aid when we seek that maid; for the wondrous robes of the fairy land, and for gifts from the fairies plead." To Mag Breg, where his mother's sister dwelt, to Boand he away hath gone, and she gave to him mantles of dark black-blue, like a beetle's back they shone; four dark-grey rings in each cloak she gave were sewn, and a brooch shone bright with the good red gold in each mantle's fold; she gave tunics pale and white, and the tunics were bordered with golden loops, that forms as of beasts displayed; and a fifty she added of well-rimmed shields, that of silver white were made.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Fraich; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那少女愛慕弗拉赫的消息，傳到了他所居住的家園，於是他們這樣勸他：「且從你那裡送個訊息給你仙界的親族，求他們在我們去尋求那少女時相助；因為那仙界奇妙的袍服，以及仙界的贈禮，都去懇求吧。」他前往他母親的姊妹所居的瑪格·布雷格，去尋波安德，她給了他深黑藍色的斗篷，光澤如甲蟲之背；每件斗篷上縫著四枚深灰色的環，每件斗篷的褶層裡都有一枚以純赤金製成、閃閃發亮的胸針；她給了他淡白色的長衣，長衣鑲著金環的邊，顯出種種走獸的形貌；她又添了五十面鑲邊精良的盾牌，皆以銀白色製成。

passages.text: By each of the fifty heroes' side was a sword with a hilt of gold, and a soft-grey mare was for each to ride, with a golden curb controlled; at each horse's throat was a silver plate, and a bell with a golden tongue swinging with a tinkling sound to the horse's tread. By their sides, seven chase-hounds were springing at leashes of silver they strained, and each couple a gold apple, swinging on the fetter that linked them, sustained; and their feet with bronze sheaths had been guarded. Seven trumpeters strode on the road before, and their hair, soft and yellow, like fairy threads, shone golden their shoulders round.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Fraich; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 五十位英雄各自身旁，都有一柄金柄的劍，各人皆有一匹柔灰色的母馬可騎，配著金製的馬勒加以控馭；每匹馬的喉部都有一塊銀牌，還有一隻金舌的鈴鐺，隨著馬蹄的踏動發出叮噹的聲響。他們身旁，七隻獵犬躍躍欲試，拉扯著銀製的牽索，每一對都銜著一隻金蘋果，懸在連結牠們的鎖鏈上；牠們的腳都護著青銅的套。七名號手走在前面開道，他們柔黃的頭髮如仙絲一般，金燦燦地映照在肩頭四周。

passages.text: All these were the gifts that the fairy gave, and gaily they made their start, and to Croghan's hold, in that guise so brave, away did the host depart. On the fort stands a watchman to view them, and thus news down to Croghan he calls: "Never army so fair nor so splendid yet hath come, nor its like shall be seen." And the youth before them, for his spear a full shot's length he flingeth, yet the spear never reacheth to ground, for his silver-chained hounds follow after, in their jaws is the spear ever found!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Fraich; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這些全是那仙子所贈的禮物，他們歡歡喜喜地啟程，就以這般英武的裝束，隊伍前往克羅漢的堡壘而去。堡壘上有一名守望者觀望他們，於是向克羅漢傳下這樣的消息：「從來不曾有過如此俊美、如此壯麗的軍隊到來，其後也再不會見到與之相類的。」而他們前頭的那青年，將他的矛擲出足足一箭之程，然而那矛從未觸及地面，因為他那以銀鏈牽著的獵犬緊隨其後，矛總是在牠們的顎間被尋見！

title.en: Eocho Bec and the Horses of the Sid
title.zh: 埃歐霍·貝克與仙族之馬

region.en: Sid Cuillne (fairy mound of Cuillne), Co. Limerick, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭利默里克郡庫爾涅仙丘（象徵定位）

period: Tain Bo Dartada (remscela to the Tain), Heroic Romances of Ireland vol. II, trans. A. H. Leahy (1905)

source.work: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, vol. II (1905), eBook #5679

summary.en: Eocho Bec son of Corpre, king of Cliu, keeper of forty fosterlings of Munster's kings, is visited in sleep by a woman of the mound of Cuillne: 'A stately troop shall be round thee, and goodly foreign horses under thee.' At dawn fifty black horses with gold and silver bridles stand tied to his gate, with fifty sets of Sid equipment, fifty white horses with red ears and purple manes, whips of white bronze with golden ends — the fairy debt owed him for defending their country and their soil.
summary.zh: 克利烏王科爾普雷之子埃歐霍·貝克，收養四十位芒斯特王子為養子；某夜庫爾涅仙丘的女子入夢相訪：「榮耀的隊伍將環繞你，異邦的駿馬將載你。」黎明時分，五十匹繫金銀轡的黑馬拴在他的堡門上，還有五十套仙家馬具、五十匹紅耳紫鬃的白馬、金端的白銅馬鞭——這是仙族對他守土之功的酬答。

sensitivity.note: The Sid-gift horses (white with red ears) are the fixed otherworld-horse motif of Irish legend, recurring from Land-under-Wave to the later fairy-steed tradition; the dream-counsel sets the remscela frame. Pin symbolic at the mound.

passages.text: EOCHO BEC, the son of Corpre, king of Cliu, dwelt in the Dun of Cuillne, and with him were forty fosterlings, all sons of the kings of Munster; he had also forty milch-cows for their sustenance. By Ailill and Medb messengers were sent, asking him to come to a conference. One night Eocho lay there in his sleep, when he saw something approach him; a woman, and a young man in her attendance. "Ye are welcome!" said Eocho. "It seems to me as if I had been near to you." "I think that we have been very near to one another, though we have not seen each other face to face!" "In what place do ye dwell?" "Yonder in Sid Cuillne, the fairy mound of Cuillne. In order to give thee counsel we are come: something that will bring thee honour and renown on thy journey at home and abroad. A stately troop shall be round thee, and goodly foreign horses shall be under thee."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Dartada; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 科爾普雷（Corpre）之子、克利烏（Cliu）之王埃奧霍·貝克（Eocho Bec）居於庫伊爾內（Cuillne）之堡壘，與他同住的有四十名養子，皆為芒斯特（Munster）諸王之子；他另有四十頭乳牛以供養育他們。艾利爾（Ailill）與梅芙（Medb）遣使前來，請他赴會商議。一夜，埃奧霍臥於彼處睡眠之中，忽見有物向他靠近；乃一女子，並有一青年隨侍於側。「歡迎你們！」埃奧霍說道。「我彷彿覺得自己曾靠近過你們。」「我以為我們彼此曾十分靠近，雖然我們未曾面對面相見！」「你們居於何處？」「就在那邊的庫伊爾內仙丘（Sid Cuillne），庫伊爾內的精靈土丘。我們前來是為給你忠告：此事將在你在家與在外的旅程中為你帶來榮耀與名聲。一隊威儀堂堂的隊伍將環繞你左右，良種的異邦駿馬將在你胯下。」

passages.text: To-morrow in the morning fifty black horses, furnished with bridles of gold and silver, shall come to thee from me; and all of thy foster-children shall go with thee; well it becomes us to help thee, because thou art valiant in the defence of our country and our soil." Early in the morning they arise, there they see something: the fifty black horses, furnished with bridles of gold and silver tied fast to the gate of the castle, also fifty breeches of silver with embellishment of gold; and fifty youths' garments with their edges of spun gold, and fifty white horses with red ears and long tails, purple-red were all their tails and their manes, with foot-chains of brass upon each horse; there were also fifty whips of white bronze (findruine), with end pieces of gold.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Dartada; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 明日清晨，將有五十匹黑馬自吾處來到你處，皆配以金銀轡頭；你的所有養子都將隨你同行；我們理當助你，因為你在保衛我們的國土與土地時英勇無畏。」清晨他們起身，便見有物在彼：五十匹黑馬，配著金銀轡頭，緊繫於城堡大門之上；另有五十條飾金的銀色馬褲；五十件邊緣綴以金絲的青年衣裳；以及五十匹白馬，紅耳長尾，其尾與鬃皆為紫紅色，每匹馬皆佩有黃銅腳鏈；此外尚有五十條白青銅（findruine）製的鞭子，末端鑲金。

title.en: The Seven Maine and the Cattle of Regamon
title.zh: 七梅恩與雷加蒙牛群

region.en: Burg of Regamon, Corcomroe, Co. Clare, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克萊爾郡科爾科姆羅伊雷加蒙堡

period: Tain Bo Regamon (remscela to the Tain), Heroic Romances of Ireland vol. II, trans. A. H. Leahy (1905)

source.work: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, vol. II (1905), eBook #5679

summary.en: Regamon of Connaught has seven fair daughters, and the seven Maine — sons of Ailill and Medb, named for their mixtures of their parents' natures — love them. Medb sends her sons for cattle, telling them to go for filial love; but at the water-springs Mani Mingar draws his sword on three of the maidens, and 'Give life for life!' wins three full words that cannot be cows — the pretence of courtship turned cattle-raid, and the tale that schools the Tain's logic of ransom and bride-price.
summary.zh: 康諾特的雷加蒙有七位美女兒；埃利爾與梅芙的七子——「七梅恩」，其名各自熔鑄父母之性——皆愛慕她們。梅芙遣子求牛，囑以「親愛之名」出行；然在水泉邊，明加爾竟向三位少女拔劍，「以命換命！」逼得三個誓言——卻偏偏不得是牛。求愛之名成為劫牛之實，此篇遂為《奪牛記》贖金與聘禮邏輯的序章。

sensitivity.note: The life-for-life exchange (a réir for a réir) is an Irish legal formula here dramatised as courtship; the seven sons' mixed-nature bynames (like his father, like his mother, mouth of honey) are genealogical byname practice. Pin at the traditional Corcomroe location.

passages.text: In the time of Ailill and Medb, a glorious warrior and holder of land dwelt in the land of Connaught, and his name was Regamon. He had many herds of cattle, all of them fair and well-shaped: he had also seven daughters with him. Now the seven sons of Ailill and Medb loved these daughters: namely the seven Maine — Maine Morgor (Maine with great filial love), Maine Mingar (Maine with less filial love), Maine Aithremail (Maine like his father), Maine Mathremail (Maine like his mother), Maine Milbel (Maine with the mouth of honey), Maine Moepert (Maine too great to be described), Maine Condageb-uile (Maine who combined all qualities): now this one had the form both of father and mother. The seven daughters of Regamon were the three Dunann, and the four Dunlaith; from the names of these is the estuary of Dunann in western Connaught.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Regamon; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在艾利爾與梅芙的時代，有一位光榮的戰士兼地主居於康諾特（Connaught）之地，其名為雷加蒙（Regamon）。他擁有許多牛群，皆俊美而體態優良；他身邊另有七個女兒。艾利爾與梅芙的七個兒子愛慕這些女兒：即七位梅恩（Maine）——梅恩·莫爾戈爾（Maine Morgor，意為「懷有極大孝愛之梅恩」）、梅恩·明加爾（Maine Mingar，意為「孝愛較少之梅恩」）、梅恩·艾斯雷馬爾（Maine Aithremail，意為「似其父之梅恩」）、梅恩·馬斯雷馬爾（Maine Mathremail，意為「似其母之梅恩」）、梅恩·米爾貝爾（Maine Milbel，意為「蜜口之梅恩」）、梅恩·莫埃佩爾特（Maine Moepert，意為「偉大得難以描述之梅恩」）、梅恩·孔達格布·烏伊勒（Maine Condageb-uile，意為「兼具一切品質之梅恩」）：這一位兼具父母二人的形貌。雷加蒙的七個女兒是三位杜南（Dunann）與四位杜恩萊斯（Dunlaith）；康諾特西部的杜南河口即得名於這些名字。

passages.text: Now at a certain time, Ailill and Medb and Fergus held counsel together: "Some one from us should go to Regamon, that a present of cattle may be brought to us from him, to meet the need that there is on us for feeding the men of Ireland, when the kine are raided from Cualgne." "I know who would be good to go thither, if we ask it of them; even the Maine; on account of their love for the daughters." "Grateful is he, and a better journey does he go, who goes for the sake of his filial love." They set out, seven times twenty heroes was the number, till they were in the south of Connaught, near to the burg. Mani Mingar, with two others, went until he came upon three of the maidens at the water-springs, and at once he and his comrades drew their swords against them. "Give life for life!" said the maiden. "Grant to me then my three full words!" "Whatever thy tongue sets forth shall be done, only let it not be cows, for these have we no power to give thee." "For these indeed is all that now we do."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Regamon; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某時，艾利爾、梅芙與弗格斯（Fergus）共同商議：「我們之中應有人前往雷加蒙處，好讓他送一份牛畜之禮給我們，以應我們在從庫利（Cualgne）劫掠牛群之後、供養愛爾蘭眾人之所需。」「我知道誰去那裡最合適，若我們向他們提出請求；正是那幾位梅恩；因為他們對那些女兒的愛慕。」「他是知恩的，而為孝愛之故前往的人，會走得更好。」他們出發了，人數為七倍二十名英雄，直到抵達康諾特南部，靠近那座城堡。梅恩·明加爾帶著另外兩人前行，直到他在水泉邊遇上三位少女，他與同伴立刻拔劍相向。「以命換命！」那少女說道。「那麼就允我三句完整的話！」「你口中所說的一切都將照辦，只是不可提牛，因為這些我們無權給你。」「我們此刻所為，正是為了這些。」

title.en: Flidais and Her Cow That Milked Three Hundred Men
title.zh: 弗蕾丹與供三百人飲奶的神牛

region.en: Dun of Ailill the Fair, Co. Mayo, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭梅奧郡「俊美埃利爾」之堡（象徵定位）

period: Tain Bo Flidais (remscela to the Tain; oldest recension LU), Heroic Romances of Ireland vol. II, trans. A. H. Leahy (1905)

source.work: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, vol. II (1905), eBook #5679

summary.en: Flidais, wife of Ailill the Fair, loves Fergus mac Roich for the great deeds told of him, and keeps a marvellous cow that gives milk to more than three hundred men at one night's milking. Bricriu carries her message, and Fergus rides as ambassador — all the Ulster exiles with him — to carry off Flidais and her cow; the tale has two quite different endings in its manuscripts, and the Glenn Masain version makes Bricriu, the buffoon, a chief ollave whose satire on Fergus's broken promises is bitter and dignified.
summary.zh: 「俊美埃利爾」之妻弗蕾丹因聞芬恩·羅赫的英雄事跡而心生愛慕；她飼有一頭神牛，一夜之奶可供三百餘人。布里克留為信使傳話，芬恩以使者之名出行——阿爾斯特流亡者全數隨行——劫走弗蕾丹與神牛。此篇在手稿中有截然不同的兩種結局；而在格倫·馬辛本中，丑角布里克留化身首席詩人，諷刺芬恩背棄諾言之詩莊嚴而刻毒。

sensitivity.note: The wonder-cow (supplying a host) parallels Goibniu's ale and Manannan's self-renewing pigs — the otherworld-foodstuff family; the two-ending MS tradition is unique in Irish romance and is documented in the source's own introduction. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: The Tain bo Flidais, the Driving of the Cows of Flidais, occurs in both the two oldest collections of Old Irish romance, the Leabhar na h-Uidhri, and the Book of Leinster, besides the fifteenth century Egerton MS. After the dialogue with Fergus, Bricriu, with the poets that attend him, undertakes a journey to Ailill the Fair, to obtain from him the bounty that Fergus had promised but was unable to grant; he is received hospitably, and gets all he had asked for. He then asks about Ailill's wife Flidais, and is told about her marvellous cow, which was able to supply milk to more than three hundred men at one night's milking. Flidais returns from a journey, is welcomed by Bricriu, who produces a poem in honour of her and her cow.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Flidais; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《弗利戴斯之牛驅趕記》（Tain bo Flidais，即「驅趕弗利戴斯之牛」）見於兩部最古老的古愛爾蘭傳奇集——《牛皮書》（Leabhar na h-Uidhri）與《倫斯特書》（Book of Leinster）——此外亦見於十五世紀的埃格頓手稿（Egerton MS）。在與弗格斯對話之後，布里克里烏（Bricriu）偕同隨侍他的詩人們啟程前往「俊美的艾利爾」（Ailill the Fair）處，欲從他那裡取得弗格斯曾許諾卻無力給予的賞賜；他受到殷勤款待，並得到他所求的一切。隨後他問起艾利爾的妻子弗利戴斯（Flidais），並聽聞她那頭神奇的牛，此牛一夜之擠奶便能供給三百餘人飲用。弗利戴斯遠行歸來，受到布里克里烏的歡迎，他獻上一首詩以頌揚她與她的牛。

passages.text: A long conversation is then recorded between Flidais and Bricriu, in which Bricriu extols the great deeds of Fergus, supplying thereby a commentary on the short statement at the beginning of the older version, that Flidais' love to Fergus was on account of the great deeds which had been told her that he had done. Flidais declares to Bricriu her love for Fergus, and Bricriu consents to bring a message to Fergus that Flidais and her cow will come to him if he comes to her husband's castle to seek her. Bricriu induces him to go in the guise of an ambassador to Ailill the Fair, with the secret intention of carrying off Flidais; Fergus receives the sanction of Maev and her husband for his errand, and departs with all the Ulster exiles with him. And the Glenn Masain version makes Bricriu, who is a subordinate character in the older version, one of the principal actors: "Fergus, hear thy friend lamenting! Blunted is thy lofty mind; Thou, for hire, to Maev consenting, Hast thy valour's pride resigned."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Flidais; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隨後記載了弗利戴斯與布里克里烏之間的一段長談，布里克里烏在談中頌揚弗格斯的偉大事蹟，藉此為較古老版本開頭那句簡短的話作註解——即弗利戴斯對弗格斯之愛，乃是因為有人向她講述了他所行的偉大事蹟。弗利戴斯向布里克里烏宣告她對弗格斯的愛，布里克里烏遂同意帶信給弗格斯，說若他前來她丈夫的城堡尋她，弗利戴斯與她的牛便會隨他而去。布里克里烏誘使他以使者身分前往俊美的艾利爾處，暗中卻意圖劫走弗利戴斯；弗格斯獲得梅芙及其丈夫的許可前往辦事，並帶著所有阿爾斯特（Ulster）流亡者一同離去。而《格倫·馬薩因》（Glenn Masain）版本則使布里克里烏——他在較古老版本中只是次要人物——成為主要角色之一：「弗格斯，聽你的友人哀嘆！你那高遠的心志已鈍；你為酬賞而順從梅芙，已捨棄了你英勇的驕傲。」

title.en: The Red Woman of Regamna and the Cow of Cualnge
title.zh: 雷加姆納的紅衣女子與庫爾涅母牛

region.en: Ath da Ferta (Ford of the Two Marvels), Co. Louth, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭勞斯郡「雙異渡口」（象徵定位）

period: Tain Bo Regamna (also Tain bo Morrigna; LU-YBL recension), Heroic Romances of Ireland vol. II, trans. A. H. Leahy (1905)

source.work: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, vol. II (1905), eBook #5679

summary.en: A cry out of the north-west wakes Cuchulain at Dun Imrid, and he follows it to the Ford of the Double Wonder, where a chariot drawn by a one-legged chestnut horse with the pole driven through its body draws near: a red woman with crimson eyebrows, and a giant goading a cow before them. Their names are riddles of the Morrigan's satirical spells — she drives home as fee a marvellous poem — and when Cuchulain springs at her with spear and threats, the woman, the horse, the chariot, the cow and the man vanish, leaving the doom of the Brown Bull foretold.
summary.zh: 西北傳來的怪叫驚醒杜恩·伊姆里德的庫丘林；他循聲至「雙異渡口」，見一輛由三足獨腿栗色馬拖曳的戰車——車轅竟貫穿馬身——紅衣赤眉的女子與趕牛的巨人行於其前。二人名諱皆為摩里岡諷咒之謎——她以一首奇詩為酬，趕牛回家。庫丘林持矛躍起威嚇，女子、馬、車、牛與人霎時俱隱，庫爾涅褐牛的厄運已被預言。

sensitivity.note: Windisch conjectures the true title is Tain bo Morrigna, 'the driving of the Morrigan' — the red woman is the war-goddess herself in one of her forms; the one-legged horse and pole-through-body are the fixed marvel-chariot of her epiphanies, and the fee-for-a-poem is a reversal of the poet-fee custom. Pin symbolic.

passages.text: AT Dun Imrid lay Cuchulain, and slept, when a cry rang out; and in fear he heard from the north-land come ringing that terrible shout: He fell, as he woke from his slumber, with the thud of a weight, to the ground... Then he saw his harnessed chariot, and Laeg, his charioteer, from the north the car drew near: "And whence was the cry thou hast heard?" "From the north-west quarter it travelled, it crossed the great Cayll Cooen road!" "Follow on, on that track, till we know what that clamour may bode!"
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Regamna; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 庫胡林躺在頓伊姆里德，正睡著，忽然一聲呼喊響起；他驚恐地聽見那可怕的號叫從北方傳來，響徹耳際：他從睡夢中驚醒，像重物墜地般砰然倒在地上……隨後他看見他那備好馬具的戰車，以及他的馭者萊格，戰車從北方駛近：「你方才聽見的呼喊是從何而來？」「它從西北方傳來，越過了那條寬闊的凱爾庫恩大道！」「循著那條路追下去，直到我們弄清那喧嚷究竟預示著什麼！」

passages.text: At the ford of the Double Wonder, at Ath Fayrta, the car made stand, for a chariot rattled toward them from the clay-soiled Coolgarry land; and strange was the sight they saw: for a one-legged chestnut charger was harnessed the car to draw, and right through the horse's body the pole of the car had passed. A red woman sat in the chariot, bright red were her eyebrows twain, a crimson cloak was round her; and close by the side of that woman a mighty giant strode, on his back a staff of hazel, two-forked, and a cow he goaded, that shambled on before. "Ye who drive that cow do wrong, for against her will do ye drive her!" "Not to thee doth that cow belong. The kine of the land of Ulster are mine to guard!" "Dost thou sit on the seat of judgment? Too great is that task for thee!" "I of late made a marvellous poem; and as fee for the poem this cow do I drive to my home."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Regamna; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在雙奇之渡口，即阿特法爾塔，戰車停了下來，因為有一輛戰車從那沾滿泥土的庫爾加里地方嘎嘎作響地朝他們駛來；他們所見的景象十分怪異：因為拉車的是一匹獨腿的栗色馬，而戰車的轅桿竟直穿過馬的身軀。戰車裡坐著一個紅衣女子，她的雙眉鮮紅，身披一件深紅色的斗篷；緊挨在那女子身旁，一個魁梧的巨人邁步而行，背上扛著一根分叉的榛木杖，還驅趕著一頭在他前頭蹣跚而行的母牛。「你們這些驅趕那頭母牛的人做錯了，因為你們是違背她的意願驅趕她的！」「那頭母牛不屬於你。阿爾斯特之地的牛群歸我守護！」「你可是坐在審判之位上？那任務對你來說太重了！」「我近來作了一首奇妙的詩；作為這首詩的報酬，我便把這頭母牛趕回我家。」

passages.text: Then Cuchulain sprang at the chariot: "Would ye make me a fool with your jest?" He cried, as he leapt at the woman; his feet on her shoulders he pressed, and he set on her head his spear-point: "Now cease from thy sharp weapon-play!" "Then remove thyself from me! I am skilled in satirical spells." And the woman her song then sang, and the song was a song of insult. Again at the car he sprang, but nothing he found before him: as soon as the car he had neared, the woman, the horse, and the chariot, the cow, and the man disappeared.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Regamna; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是庫胡林朝戰車撲去：「你們想用你們的戲弄把我當傻瓜嗎？」他一面喊，一面朝那女子躍去；他把雙腳踩在她的肩上，又將矛尖抵在她的頭上：「現在停止你那銳利的武器把戲吧！」「那你從我身上下來！我精通諷刺的咒術。」於是那女子唱起她的歌，那歌是一首侮辱之歌。他又一次朝戰車撲去，卻發現面前空無一物：他剛一靠近戰車，那女子、那馬、那戰車、那母牛和那男子便全都消失了。

title.en: Kynon's Adventure at the Fountain
title.zh: 凱農在泉水旁的歷險

region.en: The fountain in the green valley (symbolic pin, Britain)
region.zh: 不列顛翠谷泉邊（象徵定位）

period: The Lady of the Fountain (Owain cycle), Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: After the feast of Arthur's court, Kynon tells his shameful adventure: a black man greater than any two men, one-eyed and one-footed on a mound, whose iron club would burden four warriors and whose bray of a stag called animals as numerous as stars to do him homage; a fountain under a greener-than-pine tree with a marble slab and silver bowl; a bowlful of water on the slab bringing thunder, a hail shower that reached to the bone, birds sweeter than any strain — and a black knight who unseated him and rode off with his horse.
summary.zh: 亞瑟王盛宴之後，凱農講述自己的恥辱歷險：一位獨眼獨足、比常人高出兩倍的黑巨漢立於丘頂，其鐵棒四人難舉；擊鹿一聲，召來繁星般眾多的野獸臣服如諸侯。松樹更綠的大樹下有泉，泉邊白石板上繫銀碗；碗中水潑於石上即聞雷鳴、雹如鑿骨；其後飛鳥之歌前所未聞——最後黑衣騎士將他擊落馬下，奪馬而去。

sensitivity.note: The fountain-slab-bowl adventure is the opening of Owain ou le chevalier au lion's Celtic core (Chretien's La Court de? actually the fountain scheme derives from an Irish/Welsh fountain-quest); the black man of the mound parallels the morrigan-adjacent guardian-keepers of the Fenian wells. Symbolic pin in Wales.

passages.text: "A little way within the wood thou wilt meet with a road branching off to the right, by which thou must proceed, until thou comest to a large sheltered glade with a mound in the centre. And thou wilt see a black man of great stature on the top of the mound. He is not smaller in size than two of the men of this world. He has but one foot; and one eye in the middle of his forehead. And he has a club of iron, and it is certain that there are no two men in the world who would not find their burden in that club...
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Lady of the Fountain; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「進入林中不遠，你會遇到一條向右分岔的路，你須沿著它前行，直到來到一片寬闊的、有遮蔽的林間空地，中央有一座土丘。你會看見一個身材高大的黑人站在土丘頂上。他的身量不小於這世上的兩個人。他只有一隻腳；額頭正中只有一隻眼。他有一根鐵棒，世上必定沒有兩個人合起來不會覺得那根鐵棒沉重……」

passages.text: And there was I three times more astonished at the number of wild animals that I beheld, than the man had said I should be... I asked him what power he held over those animals. 'I will show thee, little man.' And he took his club in his hand, and with it he struck a stag a great blow so that he brayed vehemently, and at his braying the animals came together, as numerous as the stars in the sky... There were serpents, and dragons, and divers sorts of animals. And he looked at them, and bade them go and feed; and they bowed their heads, and did him homage as vassals to their lord."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Lady of the Fountain; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 而我見到的野獸數目之多，令我驚訝的程度，比那人所說我會見到的還要超過三倍……我問他對那些野獸擁有什麼法力。「我會讓你看看的，小個子。」他手持鐵棒，用它在牡鹿身上重重一擊，牡鹿便高聲嘶叫，隨著牠的嘶叫，野獸們聚攏而來，多得如同天上的星辰……其中有蛇、有龍，還有各種各樣的野獸。他看著牠們，吩咐牠們去覓食；牠們便低下頭，向他致敬，如同臣屬向他們的主君致敬一般。」

passages.text: "There thou wilt find an open space like to a large valley, and in the midst of it a tall tree, whose branches are greener than the greenest pine-trees. Under this tree is a fountain, and by the side of the fountain a marble slab, and on the marble slab a silver bowl, attached by a chain of silver. Take the bowl and throw a bowlful of water upon the slab, and thou wilt hear a mighty peal of thunder, so that thou wilt think that heaven and earth are trembling with its fury. With the thunder there will come a shower so severe that it will be scarce possible for thee to endure it and live...
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Lady of the Fountain; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「你將在那裡見到一片開闊之地，宛如一座巨大的山谷，谷中央有一棵高樹，其枝葉比最翠綠的松樹還要翠綠。這樹下有一眼泉水，泉旁有一塊大理石板，大理石板之上有一隻銀碗，以一條銀鏈繫著。拿起那隻碗，把滿滿一碗水潑在大理石板上，你便會聽見一聲巨大的雷鳴，使你以為天地都因那雷霆之怒而震顫。伴隨雷鳴將降下一場猛烈的驟雨，你幾乎不可能承受得住而活下來……」

passages.text: I took the bowl, and cast a bowlful of water upon the slab; and thereupon, behold, the thunder came; and after the thunder came the shower... When I looked on the tree there was not a single leaf upon it, and then the sky became clear, and with that, behold the birds lighted upon the tree, and sang. And truly, Kai, I never heard any melody equal to that... and thereupon, behold, a Knight on a black horse appeared... and we charged each other, and, as the onset was furious, it was not long before I was overthrown. Then the Knight passed the shaft of his lance through the bridle rein of my horse, and rode off with the two horses."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Lady of the Fountain; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 我取了那碗，將滿碗的水潑在石板上；於是，看哪，雷聲來了；雷聲之後，驟雨隨之而來……當我望向那棵樹，樹上竟無一片葉子，隨後天空轉為晴朗，就在那時，看哪，鳥兒棲落樹上，歌唱起來。說真的，凱，我從未聽過任何旋律能與之相比……接著，看哪，一位騎著黑馬的騎士出現了……我們彼此衝鋒，由於攻勢猛烈，不久我便被擊落馬下。隨後那騎士將長矛的矛柄穿過我坐騎的韁繩，帶著兩匹馬揚長而去。」

title.en: Owain Slays the Black Knight and Wins the Countess
title.zh: 歐文誅黑騎士並贏得伯爵夫人

region.en: Castle of the Countess of the Broad Lands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 廣土伯爵夫人城堡（象徵定位）

period: The Lady of the Fountain (Owain cycle), Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: Shamed into the adventure, Owain follows Kynon's road, takes the bowl, and endures the thunder and the shower; the black knight rides out with an army at his back, and Owain slays him and pursues his host to the gate of their castle, where the portcullis falls on his horse's crupper and traps him. Inside, lunatic and wounded, he is found by a golden-haired maiden and healed with a flask of red ointment; the countess of the Broad Lands, whose husband the black knight was, takes him for lord of her Broad Lands and for her husband.
summary.zh: 受辱激起的歐文循凱農之路而行，取碗潑水，忍受雷霆冰雹；黑騎士率軍而出，歐文將其斬殺，追殺其軍至城堡門下，鐵閘落下夾住其馬臀，將他困在城內。發狂而重傷的他被金髮少女所救，以紅膏油醫愈。廣土伯爵夫人——黑騎士的遺孀——立他為廣土之主，並嫁之為夫。

sensitivity.note: The fountain-quest of Owain is the Welsh analogue of Yvain (Chretien) and of the Irish legend underlying both; the healing ointment and the trapped knight repeat the maiden-rescuer pattern of the corpus (cf. the maiden of the fountain in Culhwch's world). Symbolic pin.

passages.text: Owain followed the cross-road which the man had pointed out, till at length he arrived at the glade; and there was he three times more astonished at the number of wild animals that he beheld, than the man had said he should be... Then he went up to the tree, and beneath it saw the fountain, and by its side the marble slab, and the silver bowl fastened by the chain. Then he took the bowl, and cast a bowlful of water upon the slab; and thereupon, behold, the thunder came... When he looked on the tree there was not a single leaf upon it, and then the sky became clear, and with that, behold the birds lighted upon the tree, and sang.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Lady of the Fountain; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 歐文循著那人所指的岔路前行，終於抵達那片林間空地；他在那裡所見的野獸數目，令他比那人所說的還要驚詫三倍……接著他走向那棵樹，在樹下看見了泉水，泉水旁有大理石板，以及以鎖鏈繫住的銀碗。於是他取了那碗，將滿碗的水潑在石板上；於是，看哪，雷聲來了……當他望向那棵樹，樹上竟無一片葉子，隨後天空轉為晴朗，就在那時，看哪，鳥兒棲落樹上，歌唱起來。

passages.text: And Owain encountered the black knight and overthrew him and slew him; and he took possession of his horse and his arms and went to the castle where the knight's army was... And the people of the castle came out to meet him, and Owain charged the troops that guarded the gate, and slew them with his sword... And the portcullis descended to the floor, and the edge of it impinged upon the nose of Owain's horse, and the horse upon the crupper; and the portcullis descended to the floor. And the rowel of the spur of Owain's horse was caught, so that the horse could not move forward; and therefore did it enter the archway of the gate.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Lady of the Fountain; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 歐文與那黑騎士交鋒，將他擊落馬下並殺了他；他奪取了騎士的馬匹與武器，前往那騎士的軍隊所駐的城堡……城堡的居民出來迎接他，歐文向守門的部隊衝鋒，以劍將他們誅殺……鐵閘落至地面，閘緣撞上歐文坐騎的鼻端，馬則撞上後鞦；鐵閘落至地面。歐文坐騎馬刺的齒輪被卡住，以致馬無法前進；因此牠才得以進入城門的拱道。

passages.text: And the gates closed, and Owain was caught as in a trap, so that he was neither able to go forward nor backward... And the maiden who came first found him and saw him, and looked upon him, and he was sojourning in the court, wounded and diseased... And the maiden went into the hall, and there was a flask of precious ointment there, red like blood, and she bore the flask on her back and poured the ointment on Owain, and he became all whole, and the countess of the Broad Lands took him for her lord and her husband.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Lady of the Fountain; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 城門關閉，歐文如陷陷阱，既不能前進，也不能後退……最先到來的少女發現了他，看見了他，並端詳著他，而他正寄居於宮廷之中，負傷且患病……少女走進大廳，那裡有一瓶珍貴的藥膏，紅如鮮血，她背著那瓶藥膏，將藥膏塗抹在歐文身上，他便全然痊癒了，而廣土的女伯爵收他為她的領主與丈夫。

title.en: Owain and the Lioness That Was His Companion
title.zh: 歐文與相伴的母獅

region.en: Wastes between the Broad Lands and Arthur's court (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 廣土與亞瑟王廷之間的荒野（象徵定位）

period: The Lady of the Fountain (Owain cycle), Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: Gone three years from the countess without her leave, Owain is stripped of his arms and raiment by her maidens in a remote valley and wanders half-naked until he falls senseless; a courteous earl's son restores him, and he kills a black serpent with a stone to save a lioness from it — and the lioness, with her whelps gone to another land, cleaves to him from that day forward: he beats off the hunger of wild men with her help, and the lion is with him in every fight.
summary.zh: 歐文未經伯爵夫人允許，三年不歸；其侍女在荒谷中剝去他的甲胄衣衫，使他半裸流浪，終至昏厥。一位恭謹伯爵之子救起他；他擲石擊斃黑蛇，救出一頭母獅——母獅失去幼崽，自此與他形影不離：野蠻人圍困時她助他破陣，此後每一場戰鬥都有獅相伴。

sensitivity.note: The lion companion is the tale's title-device (the knight of the lion); serpent-slaying to win the beast's gratitude is a fixed beast-buddy origin (compare Oisín's hounds, the corpus's hound-kinship pattern). The stripping by the lady's maidens for a broken troth parallels Rhiannon's penalty in this corpus. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: And the countess said unto her maidens, "Since I have been deprived of my husband, Owain hath been away from me for three years; go, some of you, to the land of the countess, and take with you my horse and my arms, and find where he is, and when ye have found him, strip him of his arms and his raiment and take away with you the horse and the arms." And Owain had been three years without speaking to any one...
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Lady of the Fountain; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 女伯爵對她的侍女們說：「既然我已失去我的丈夫，歐文已離開我三年之久；你們之中去幾個人，前往那位女伯爵的領地，帶上我的馬匹與我的武器，找到他在何處，當你們找到他時，剝去他的武器與衣裳，並將那馬匹與武器帶回來。」而歐文已有三年未與任何人交談……

passages.text: And when Owain had finished his meal and was preparing to depart, the countess said unto him, "Stay with me until I have provided for thee a retinue." And the next day when Owain beheld the countess and her handmaidens arrayed in their finest apparel, and the great banquet prepared, there came over Owain an avid longing for his country and his kin, so that his sadness and his grief overcame him... And he fell into a deep slumber. And the countess came to wake him, but when she saw that he slept, and that his slumber was deep, she came not to wake him... And the maiden saw that the knight was without arms and without raiment, and that he was one who had been a knight of great renown.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Lady of the Fountain; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當歐文用畢餐食，正準備離去時，女伯爵對他說：「留在我身邊，直到我為你備妥一隊隨從。」翌日，當歐文看見女伯爵與她的侍女們身著最華美的衣裳，盛大的宴席也已備妥，一股對故鄉與親族的強烈渴望湧上歐文心頭，使他的悲傷與哀愁壓倒了他……他陷入了沉睡。女伯爵前來喚醒他，但當她見他睡著，且睡得深沉，她便沒有來喚醒他……少女見那騎士既無武器也無衣裳，且他曾是一位聲名顯赫的騎士。

passages.text: And when Owain beheld the lioness coming towards him, he drew his sword, for he thought that she would attack him... And the lioness came up to him, and her whelps had been gone to another land. And she caressed him with her paws like a dog, and she gambolled round him... And he saw a great black serpent, and the serpent had seized upon the lioness, and was striving with her, and dragging her along with him. And the serpent was a serpent of full monstrous size, and of great power...
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Lady of the Fountain; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當歐文看見那母獅朝他走來，便拔出劍來，因為他以為她要攻擊他……那母獅走到他跟前，而她的幼獅已去了別的地方。她像狗一樣用爪子撫弄他，又在他身邊蹦跳嬉戲……他看見一條巨大的黑蛇，那蛇已攫住了母獅，正與她搏鬥，並把她拖著走。那蛇是一條碩大無比的蛇，力大無窮……

passages.text: And when Owain saw that the serpent was gaining, and the lioness losing, he took his sword in his hand, and he saw that he could not prevail against the serpent without a stone; and he took a stone and threw it at the serpent, and struck him with it in the midst of his body, and the serpent was stunned and weakened. And the lioness sprang upon the serpent and rent it asunder.
