And the lioness was in great joy... and from that day forward she was with Owain as long as he lived, and she shared his food and his drink; and she was as true and faithful to him as any creature could be to its friend.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Lady of the Fountain; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 歐文見那蛇漸佔上風，母獅漸落下風，便握劍在手，又看出若無石頭便不能勝過那蛇；於是他取了一塊石頭，朝那蛇擲去，擊中牠身體的中段，那蛇便昏亂衰弱了。母獅撲向那蛇，把牠撕成碎片。母獅大喜……自那日起，她終其一生都與歐文相伴，與他同食同飲；她對他忠誠信實，勝過任何生靈對其友所能有的忠誠。

title.en: Peredur, His Mother's Hut, and the Angel Riders
title.zh: 佩雷杜爾、母親的木屋與天使般的騎士

region.en: Peredur's mother's glen, North Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 北不列顛佩雷杜爾母親的山谷（象徵定位）

period: Peredur the Son of Evrawc, Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: Peredur, last son of Evrawc, is hidden by his mother in a hut with dumb women and taught nothing of arms or horses, lest he take the road that killed his six brothers; he goes out to the hillside and sees three knights riding on the hill, with armour shining like pure white crystal and blood-red falls of gold on their horses, and thinks them angels. "I will go and become an angel with them," says the boy, and nothing his mother can say will stop him; he takes the bony nag, the rusty tools, and goes off for Arthur's court.
summary.zh: 埃夫拉克幼子佩雷杜爾被母親藏於木屋，與啞女們同住，不習兵馬，唯恐重蹈六位兄長的覆轍。他登上山丘，看見三位騎士——甲胄如純白水晶閃耀，鞍上金飾如血色瀑布——以為是天使。「我要與他們一同做天使。」任母親如何勸阻，他執意騎上瘦骨嶙峋的老馬，帶著生銹的農具，向亞瑟王的宮廷出發。

sensitivity.note: The Peredur boyhood is the Welsh Perceval: the isolated upbringing in the wilds is the fool-of-the-woods pattern the Grail romances transmit; the knights-as-angels misreading is the tale's famous comic pivot. Symbolic pin in the North.

passages.text: And Owain's mother said, "My son, if thou goest from me, I cannot hide from thee what will befall; for there were six sons of mine, and all have gone the way that thou wouldst go, and none of them have returned." And the youth said, "Mother, I will go notwithstanding." And they made for him a hut of sedge and rushes in a remote part of the country, and there he was taught to keep the herds and to till the ground; and there were with him the ladies of his mother's household, and they were dumb women, that no word of what he did might go forth from them; and there was not taught to him any of the deeds of arms or of the arts of the horse.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Peredur the Son of Evrawc; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 歐文的母親說：「我兒，你若離我而去，我無法向你隱瞞將要發生的事；因為我曾有六個兒子，他們都走上了你將要走的路，卻無一人歸來。」那少年說：「母親，我仍要去。」他們在鄉間僻遠之處為他搭了一間莎草與燈心草編成的茅屋，他在那裡學著放牧牲畜、耕種田地；與他同在的是他母親家中的侍女，而她們都是啞女，好叫他所行之事無一字從她們口中傳出；也沒有教他任何武藝或馬術。

passages.text: And Peredur went out to the hillside, and there he beheld three knights riding on the hill, and they were of so great a beauty, that he thought they were angels, and they were shining in their arms; for their arms were so bright, that it was like unto white crystal; and there was with them a blood-red fall of gold upon the horses... "Mother, what are those yonder?" "They are angels, my son." "By my faith," said Peredur, "I will go and become an angel with them." And Peredur went to the place where they were... And he went to the place where the horses were, and he took a bony piebald horse, that had, I ween, been grazing in the field no less than seven years... and he took the tools of his mother's household, that were of iron, rusty and old, and he went into the house, and the lady said, "Whither goest thou, my son?" "I am going to the Court of Arthur, where the knights are."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Peredur the Son of Evrawc; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 佩雷杜爾走到山坡上，在那裡他看見三位騎士騎馬行於山上，他們俊美非凡，他以為他們是天使，他們的甲胄閃閃發光；因為他們的甲胄如此明亮，宛如白水晶一般；他們與馬匹身上還帶著血紅色的金飾……「母親，那邊那些是什麼？」「他們是天使，我兒。」「我憑我的信德起誓，」佩雷杜爾說，「我要去與他們一同做天使。」佩雷杜爾走到他們所在之處……他又走到馬匹所在之處，牽了一匹瘦骨嶙峋的花斑馬，我料想那馬在田野裡吃草已不下七年……他取了他母親家中那些生鏽陳舊的鐵器，走進屋裡，那貴婦說：「我兒，你往何處去？」「我要去亞瑟的宮廷，那裡有騎士。」

title.en: The Witch's Serpents and the Ring of Invisibility
title.zh: 巫嫗之蛇與隱形之戒

region.en: Crag of the witch, Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 不列顛巫嫗之岩（象徵定位）

period: Peredur the Son of Evrawc, Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: Alone in a wild place, Peredur finds a ring in the eagles' nest that makes him invisible; then in the crag a sleeping witch, and in the manner of a serpent of monstrous size twisting itself about a bowl of gold — and in the manner of serpents round the stone; he slays them and wins the stone of invisibility. His companion for the Empress's tournament, the miller's son in rags, shares his triumph, and Peredur bares the truth that the knight beneath the rags is himself.
summary.zh: 荒野中的佩雷杜爾在鷹巢中拾得一枚隱形戒指；岩壁間見沉睡的巫嫗，以及怪蛇盤繞金碗、群蛇纏繞巨石之奇觀；他擊斃群蛇，贏得隱形之石。為君士坦丁堡女皇參加比武時，他與衣衫襤褸的磨坊主之子同行，比武大勝後揭示：錦衣騎士原是赤貧少年。

sensitivity.note: The ring of invisibility and the serpent-guarded stone repeat the Welsh treasure-guardian pattern (the witches of Caer Loyw own the stones); the miller's-son disguise is the fixed disguise-wealth inversion. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: And Peredur came to a wild place, and he beheld a crag, and he saw a nest of eagles, and there was in it a ring of red gold. And Peredur took the ring, and put it on his finger, and he knew that he was invisible... And he came to the place where the witch was, and there was a witch sleeping in the crag, and there was a serpent of a monstrous size twisting itself about a bowl of gold in the middle of the crag; and Peredur drew his sword, and struck the serpent upon the head, and slew it, and took the bowl with the ring... And he went into the place where the serpents were, and there were serpents in the manner of a serpent of monstrous size coiling itself about the stone of the witch.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Peredur the Son of Evrawc; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 佩雷杜爾來到一處荒野，看見一座峭壁，又看見一個鷹巢，巢中有一枚赤金戒指。佩雷杜爾取了那戒指，戴在指上，便知道自己隱了形……他來到那女巫所在之處，峭壁中有一個女巫正在睡覺，還有一條碩大無比的蛇盤繞在峭壁中央一隻金碗之上；佩雷杜爾拔出劍，擊中那蛇的頭，將牠殺死，取了那碗與戒指……他又走進群蛇所在之處，那裡有蛇如一條碩大無比的蛇一般，盤繞在女巫的石上。

passages.text: And then he went to the tournament of the Empress; and all the people went to look at the knight that was clothed in satin... And the miller's son said, "Lord, if thou wilt let me have one of thy horses and thy arms, I will go and fight in the tournament in thy place." "By my faith," said Peredur, "I will give thee my horse and my arms, and thou shalt go to the tournament in my place." And the miller's son went to the tournament, and he did feats of arms, and overthrew all that opposed him; and the Empress asked of him, "Whence art thou, bold knight?" "I am the son of the miller of yonder town," said he... And Peredur returned to the Empress, and told her all the truth of the miller's son, and she gave him rich gifts; and he took his horse and his arms and rode away with the Empress's blessing.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Peredur the Son of Evrawc; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隨後他去了女皇的比武大會；眾人都去觀看那位身穿綢緞的騎士……磨坊主的兒子說：「主上，若你肯把你的馬和甲胄給我一副，我便代你去比武大會上廝殺。」「我憑我的信德起誓，」佩雷杜爾說，「我把我的馬和甲胄給你，你便代我去比武大會。」磨坊主的兒子去了比武大會，施展武藝，擊倒了所有與他對陣的人；女皇問他：「勇武的騎士，你從何而來？」「我是那邊鎮上磨坊主的兒子，」他說……佩雷杜爾回到女皇那裡，把磨坊主之子的實情一一告訴了她，她便賜他豐厚的禮物；他帶上他的馬和甲胄，領受女皇的祝福，策馬而去。

title.en: The Castle of Wonders: the Head on the Salver
title.zh: 奇觀城堡：銀盤上的人首

region.en: Castle of Wonders, Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 不列顛奇觀城堡（象徵定位）

period: Peredur the Son of Evrawc, Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: Peredur comes to a castle where two youths play gwyddbwyll of gold, where a lance with three streams of blood runs from its point to the ground, and where a salver is carried round the hall with a man's head upon it, all swimming in blood. He is told nothing of the marvels and keeps silence as his uncle the emperor taught him — and the blood on the lance, and the head in the salver, are kinsmen of his own: it is the tale the Grail romances absorbed.
summary.zh: 佩雷杜爾來到一座城堡：兩名少年以金子玩「格威德布威爾」棋；牆上懸一柄長矛，矛尖三股血流直至地面；僕人捧著銀盤環行大廳，盤上放著一顆人首，盤中血液滿溢。叔父教他遇奇不問，他默守不言——而矛上之血與盤中之人首，竟皆他的親族。此即聖盃傳說所吸收的威爾士之源。

sensitivity.note: The lance-and-bleeding-head sequence of Peredur is the strongest Celtic claim on the Grail-romance complex (the head is his cousin's, slain by the witches of Caer Loyw); the enjoined silence is the Grail-question taboo in Welsh dress. Comparative-tagging deliberately: descent-underworld is used here for the quest-through-the-castle-of-death structure, noted as interpretive.

passages.text: And Peredur went into the castle, and there he saw a hall, and the hall was hung with shields and with spears. And he went into the hall, and there were two tables in it, and at one of them there were men playing at chess; and the chessboard was of gold, and the chessmen of silver... And Peredur saw a lance by the side of the chamber, and three streams of blood were flowing from the socket of it, and running down along the lance to the ground. And when Peredur beheld this, he stood amazed... And thereupon behold, two youths entered the hall, and they bore a large salver, and in the salver there was a man's head, and there was a great quantity of blood upon the salver.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Peredur the Son of Evrawc; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 佩雷杜爾走進城堡，在那裡看見一座廳堂，廳堂裡懸掛著盾牌與長矛。他走進廳堂，裡面有兩張桌子，其中一張桌旁有人在下棋；棋盤是金的，棋子是銀的……佩雷杜爾看見廳堂一側有一支長矛，矛的插孔中流出三道血流，沿著長矛淌到地上。佩雷杜爾見此，驚愕地站住……接著，看哪，兩名少年走進廳堂，他們抬著一個大托盤，托盤上有一顆人頭，托盤上沾著大量鮮血。

passages.text: And the youth said, "My uncle, I saw a lance, and from the socket of the lance there came three streams of blood, and they ran down along the lance to the ground; and I saw a salver that was borne by two youths, and a man's head was upon the salver, and there was a great quantity of blood about the head." "I marvel that thou didst not ask concerning it," said the uncle, "for then wouldst thou have known the meaning of it." "It was my purpose so to do, but I was afraid..." And the head that was upon the salver, it was thy cousin's, and the lance was the lance of thy cousin; and the witches of Caer Loyw slew him... And thy duty is to go and avenge him upon the witches of Caer Loyw, and to make war upon them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Peredur the Son of Evrawc; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 少年說：「叔父，我看見一支長矛，矛的插孔中流出三道血流，沿著長矛淌到地上；我又看見一個托盤，由兩名少年抬著，托盤上有一顆人頭，人頭周圍沾著大量鮮血。」叔父說：「你竟沒有問起此事，我很詫異，因為那樣你便會知道它的含義了。」「我本有意如此，但我害怕……」而那托盤上的人頭，是你表兄弟的頭，那長矛是你表兄弟的長矛；卡爾洛伊夫的巫婆們殺了他……你的職責便是前去向卡爾洛伊夫的巫婆們為他復仇，並向她們開戰。

title.en: Geraint at the Sparrow-Hawk Tournament
title.zh: 傑倫特與「燕隼」比武大會

region.en: Town of the sparrow-hawk tournament, South Wales (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南威爾士燕隼比武之城（象徵定位）

period: Geraint the Son of Erbin, Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: Riding with Gwenhwyvar after the hunt, Geraint follows a knight, a lady and a dwarf who abuses the queen's maiden and beats the men who defend her; at the town he learns the lady's knight holds the sparrow-hawk by right of victory, and that the dwarf will throw off any man who claims the honour for a poor knight's wife. Geraint undertakes the honour for Enid, whom he finds fitting to it, overthrows the knight, and wins both the sparrow-hawk and the hand of Enid the golden.
summary.zh: 獵後隨格溫赫薇爾出遊的傑倫特，遇見騎士、淑女與矮人一行；矮人辱打王后的侍女及其護衛。至城中，他得知那位騎士憑連勝保有「燕隼」殊榮，而矮人專門羞辱為貧窮騎士之妻爭榮者。傑倫特為埃妮德出戰——他認定她當得起此榮——擊敗對手，贏得燕隼與金髮埃妮德之手。

sensitivity.note: Geraint (Erec in Chretien) is the Welsh Arthurian romance; the sparrow-hawk custom (the victor's right at the tournament) is a chivalric institution grafted onto native tale-stock; the insult to the queen's maiden drives the plot as transgression. Symbolic pin in South Wales.

passages.text: And when they came near to the knight and the lady, and the dwarf, the dwarf was a jester that laughed at the queen; and he came near the maiden that was behind the queen, and he smote her a blow with his whip, so that she was wounded by it... And the maiden cried out, and cried for help: "Hast thou seen, lord," said she, "the treatment that the dwarf gave me?" And the men that were near her said to her, "Go after the dwarf." And she went, and Geraint, and she caught the dwarf by the collar of his dress... and the dwarf drew his sword, and he dealt her a blow with it; and the maiden stood aside, and the blow reached the ear of her hood; and Geraint drew his sword... and they fought, and Geraint overthrew the dwarf, and took his horse from him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Geraint the Son of Erbin; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他們走近那騎士、那貴婦與那侏儒時，那侏儒是個逗笑王后的弄臣；他走近王后身後的少女，用鞭子抽了她一下，使她受了傷……少女喊叫起來，呼喊求救：「主上，」她說，「你可看見那侏儒怎樣對待我？」她身旁的人對她說：「去追那侏儒。」她便去了，傑蘭特也去了，她抓住侏儒衣服的領口……侏儒拔出劍，用劍砍了她一下；少女閃身避開，那一擊打中了她兜帽的邊緣；傑蘭特拔出劍……他們打了起來，傑蘭特擊倒了侏儒，奪走了他的馬。

passages.text: And Geraint went to the town, and he asked a hoary-headed man, that was by the gate, what was the custom of the town: "The knight that is yonder," said he, "the lady that is with him, is his wife; and he keepeth the sparrow-hawk; and if any one will contend with him for it, he can win it by overcoming him in fair fight... And the dwarf will take the honour from him, because his wife is not of his rank." "Then will I contend for the sparrow-hawk for my wife," said Geraint... And Geraint overthrew the knight, and took his horse and his arms, and gave them to the hoary-headed man; and he took the sparrow-hawk, and bore it in his hand, and rode through the town to the place where Enid was, and he gave it to her, and he said, "This honour I have won for thee." And Enid rejoiced, and her father rejoiced with her, and Geraint took her to wife at Arthur's court.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Geraint the Son of Erbin; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傑蘭特進了城，向城門邊一位白髮老人詢問這城的習俗：「那邊那位騎士，」他說，「與他同行的貴婦是他的妻子；他守著那隻雀鷹；若有人願與他爭奪，便可在公平決鬥中勝過他而贏得它……而那侏儒會從他手中奪去這份榮譽，因為他的妻子與他身分不相稱。」「那麼我要為我的妻子爭奪那隻雀鷹，」傑蘭特說……傑蘭特擊倒了那騎士，奪了他的馬與甲胄，交給那白髮老人；他取了那隻雀鷹，持在手中，騎馬穿過城，來到伊妮德所在之處，把它交給她，說道：「這份榮譽是我為你贏得的。」伊妮德歡喜，她的父親也與她一同歡喜，傑蘭特在亞瑟的宮廷娶她為妻。

title.en: Enid's Whisper and the Robbers of the Road
title.zh: 埃妮德的低語與路上的強盜

region.en: Roads of the March, Wales (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 威爾士邊境之路（象徵定位）

period: Geraint the Son of Erbin, Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: Grown idle in love, Geraint neglects the affairs of the kingdom until Arthur restores him to his own; Enid's whisper that his arms are rusted for lack of use he takes for faithlessness, and rides out commanding silence on pain of death. Yet on the road three bands of robbers come upon them one after another, and Enid's three warnings save him each time; her silence kept and broken, the journey of the rusted arms becomes the trial that restores the marriage.
summary.zh: 溺於愛情的傑倫特荒廢國政，直至亞瑟王令他復位；埃妮德低語「他的甲胄已因閒置而生鏽」，他誤以為妻子變心，遂令她保持緘默——違者死。然路上一連三夥強盜襲來，埃妮德三次示警救他；緘默的禁令與破除，使這趟「生鏽甲胄」之旅成為修復婚姻的試煉。

sensitivity.note: The silence-on-pain-of-death taboo of Geraint is the fixed jealous-husband device of the Erec story-type; the three robbers' bands are the staged trial-rhythm of romance roads. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: And Geraint loved Enid, and loved her so entirely that he was glad to be alone with her in the chamber, and to make delight and conversation with her, and to leave the business of his kingdom and his subjects... And Enid was one morning in bed, and Geraint by her side, and she wept... "Alas, that I ever was born, that I have caused my lord's arms to rust for want of use!" And Geraint heard her words, and there came over him great wrath; and he rose up, and he took his arms and his horse, and he said, "Lady, I will go forth, and thou shalt go with me; and if thou speakest to me on the road, thy head shall be cut off."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Geraint the Son of Erbin; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傑蘭特愛伊妮德，愛得如此深切，以致樂於與她獨處房中，與她歡談取樂，而擱置王國與臣民的事務……一天早晨，伊妮德躺在床上，傑蘭特在她身旁，她哭了……「唉，我竟生於世間，竟使我的夫君的兵器因無用而生了鏽！」傑蘭特聽見她的話，心中湧起大怒；他起身，取了他的兵器與馬，說道：「夫人，我要外出，你須與我同行；若你在路上對我說話，你的頭便要被砍下。」

passages.text: And as they went thus, they beheld three horsemen coming towards them, and Enid knew that they were three robbers, and she was afraid for Geraint, and she sighed... and Geraint turned his head, and saw that Enid was opening her lips to speak; and he threatened her, and she was silent... And the three robbers made upon him with their weapons; and Geraint slew them, every one of them. And they went on, and there came against them three more, and after them three again; and every time Enid could not forbear to give warning, and every time Geraint overcame them; and at last he saw that the warnings had saved him. And at the supper in the Earl's court, when the Earl would have her by force, Enid cried aloud for Geraint, and he rose from the table, and smote off the Earl's head, and laid his sword by her side, and said, "Thou art free; and none shall harm thee."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Geraint the Son of Erbin; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們這樣走著，看見三名騎馬的人迎面而來，伊妮德知道他們是三個強盜，她為傑蘭特擔憂，嘆了口氣……傑蘭特轉過頭，看見伊妮德正張口欲言；他威脅她，她便不作聲了……那三個強盜持兵器向他撲來；傑蘭特把他們個個殺死。他們繼續前行，又有三人迎面而來，之後又是三人；每一次伊妮德都忍不住出言警告，每一次傑蘭特都擊敗了他們；最後他看出這些警告救了他。在伯爵宮廷的晚宴上，伯爵欲強奪她，伊妮德高聲呼喊傑蘭特，他從桌旁起身，砍下伯爵的頭，把劍放在她身旁，說道：「你自由了；無人能傷害你。」

title.en: Kilhwch Seeks Olwen at Arthur's Gate
title.zh: 基爾赫在亞瑟門前求娶奧爾文

region.en: Arthur's palace at Kelliwic, Cornwall (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 康沃爾凱利維克的亞瑟王宮（象徵定位）

period: Kilhwch and Olwen, Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: Culhwch — Kilhwch, son of Kilydd — is doomed by his stepmother to win no wife but Olwen, daughter of the giant Yspaddaden Penkawr, and blushing at a love he has never seen, he rides to Arthur to cut his hair: two silver-headed spears, gold-hilted sword, ivory horn, two white-breasted greyhounds with ruby collars bounding like sea-swallows, and an apple of gold at every corner of the purple cloth about him. The porter's laws and Arthur's renunciation of his own boons frame the greatest quest-catalogue of the corpus.
summary.zh: 庫爾赫（基利德之子基爾赫）被繼母施咒：除非娶巨人格雅斯帕達丹·彭考爾之女奧爾文，否則終身無妻。未曾謀面卻已然面紅心跳的他騎向亞瑟王求助：雙銀矛、金柄劍、象牙號角、紅寶石項圈的白胸靈緹如海燕般跳躍，紫袍四角各綴一枚百牛價值的金蘋果。守門者之法與亞瑟自縛的誓言，開啟了本語料庫最宏偉的探求清單。

sensitivity.note: The stepmother's love-spell doom (a destiny-wish said in anger) is the Welsh framing of the hostile-wish motif; the hair-cutting boon (Arthur as his cousin-godfather) parallels the haircut rite of Gaelic inauguration; the gate-laws catalogue is the fixed Arthurian-porter set-piece. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: Then said she unto him, "I declare to thee, that it is thy destiny not to be suited with a wife until thou obtain Olwen, the daughter of Yspaddaden Penkawr." And the youth blushed, and the love of the maiden diffused itself through all his frame, although he had never seen her... And the youth pricked forth upon a steed with head dappled grey, of four winters old, firm of limb, with shell-formed hoofs, having a bridle of linked gold on his head... And in the youth's hand were two spears of silver, sharp, well-tempered, headed with steel, three ells in length, of an edge to wound the wind, and cause blood to flow, and swifter than the fall of the dewdrop from the blade of reed-grass upon the earth when the dew of June is at the heaviest. A gold-hilted sword was upon his thigh... his war-horn was of ivory. Before him were two brindled white-breasted greyhounds, having strong collars of rubies about their necks... and like two sea-swallows sported around him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Kilhwch and Olwen; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是她對他說：「我向你宣告，你的命數便是：除非你得到伊斯帕達登·彭卡沃爾之女奧爾溫，否則你不得娶妻。」那少年臉紅了，那少女的愛意漫遍他全身，儘管他從未見過她……那少年策馬前行，胯下是一匹頭部斑灰的駿馬，四歲口齒，四肢矯健，蹄如貝殼，頭上戴著一副金環相扣的轡頭……少年手中握著兩支銀矛，鋒利、淬煉精良，矛尖為鋼，長三厄爾，其刃足以割傷風，使血流出，比六月露水最重之時，露珠從蘆葦葉尖墜落於地還要迅疾。他股上佩著一柄金柄劍……他的號角是象牙所製。他身前有兩隻白胸的斑紋獵犬，頸上戴著堅固的紅寶石項圈……牠們像兩隻海燕一般在他身旁嬉戲。

passages.text: Said the youth, "I came not here to consume meat and drink; but if I obtain the boon that I seek, I will requite it thee, and extol thee; and if I have it not, I will bear forth thy dispraise to the four quarters of the world, as far as thy renown has extended." Then said Arthur, "Since thou wilt not remain here, chieftain, thou shalt receive the boon whatsoever thy tongue may name, as far as the wind dries, and the rain moistens, and the sun revolves, and the sea encircles, and the earth extends; save only my ship; and my mantle; and Caledvwlch, my sword; and Rhongomyant, my lance; and Wynebgwrthucher, my shield; and Carnwenhau, my dagger; and Gwenhwyvar, my wife. By the truth of Heaven, thou shalt have it cheerfully, name what thou wilt." "I would that thou bless my hair." "That shall be granted thee."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Kilhwch and Olwen; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那少年說：「我來此並非為吃喝；但若我得到我所求的恩賜，我必報答你，並頌揚你；若我得不到，我便要將對你的貶斥傳遍世界四方，直至你的名聲所及之處。」於是亞瑟說：「首領啊，既然你不願留在此地，凡你口中所能道出者，你必得那恩賜，其範圍之廣，如風所吹乾、雨所潤濕、日所旋轉、海所環繞、地所延展之處；惟獨我的船、我的斗篷、我的劍卡萊德夫爾赫、我的矛榮戈米安特、我的盾溫內布格爾圖赫爾、我的匕首卡恩溫豪，以及我的妻子格溫娜維爾除外。以蒼天之真，你必欣然得之，凡你所願，儘管說出。」「我願你為我理髮祝福。」「此事必賜予你。」

title.en: Olwen's Flowers and Yspaddaden's Gate
title.zh: 奧爾文的花朵與彭考爾的巨堡

region.en: Yspaddaden Penkawr's fort (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 彭考爾巨人城堡（象徵定位）

period: Kilhwch and Olwen, Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: Where Olwen walked, four white trefoils sprang up behind her — wherefore she was called Olwen, she of the white track — and the maiden opened the gate and came forth, more glorious than any maiden in the world, with a robe of flame-coloured silk, a ruby torc, and hair yellower than the flower of the broom, whiter than the foam of the wave, redder than the red heather. Her father's fort has nine gates; each is guarded, and every gate Kilhwch's men break in turn until the giant's long contest of impossible tasks begins.
summary.zh: 奧爾文行走之處，身後便生出四葉白花——故名「白足者奧爾文」。少女推開堡門而出：火焰色絲袍、紅寶石頸環；秀髮比金雀花更黃、比浪花更白、比赤石楠更紅，世間無雙。其父城堡有九重門，門門有守衛；基爾赫的部下一一破門而入，巨人那場「不可能任務」的漫長角力由此展開。

sensitivity.note: Olwen's flower-footsteps are the fixed eponym-aetiology of the tale (white track) and one of the great nature-images of Welsh myth; the nine-gate fort with a warder at each is the tower-of-tests pattern. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: And they knew that it was Olwen that had opened the gate, and that she was coming forth; for where she walked, four white trefoils sprang up behind her; wherefore she was called Olwen, from the trefoils that sprang up in her track. And the maiden came forth, and she was arrayed in a robe of flame-coloured silk, and about her neck was a collar of rubies, with emeralds and pearls. And her hair was yellower than the flower of the broom, and whiter than the foam of the wave, and fairer than any sight that men had ever seen; and her skin was whiter than the snow, and her cheeks redder than the red heather.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Kilhwch and Olwen; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們便知道是奧爾溫開了門，正走出來；因為她走過之處，身後便生出四株白色的三葉草；因此她被稱為奧爾溫，正是因她足跡所生之三葉草。那少女走了出來，身穿一襲火焰色絲袍，頸上戴著一條紅寶石項圈，綴以祖母綠與珍珠。她的頭髮比金雀花更黃，比浪花之沫更白，比人們所曾見過的任何景象都更美；她的肌膚比雪更白，雙頰比紅石楠更紅。

passages.text: And Kilhwch saluted her: "Maiden, I love thee, nor can I live without thee." "I know thee not," said Olwen, "neither do I know thy name." "Kilhwch, son of Kilydd, am I; and my mother Goleuddydd, daughter of the prince Anlawdd..." "I will go and ask my father," said Olwen... And the fort had nine gates, and each of them had a warder; and every one of the gates was broken by Kilhwch's men; and the hall was broken through, and the huge warrior Yspaddaden was brought forth... "I will consult the virgin Olwen, and if she will have thee, thou shalt have her; but come hither again with the troop and see what I shall say." And Kilhwch's men broke the gates a second time, and a third time, until at the last the giant's wedding-feast and the hunts of the impossible boar were promised for the bride.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Kilhwch and Olwen; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 基爾赫奇向她致意：「少女啊，我愛你，沒有你我便不能活。」「我不認識你，」奧爾溫說，「也不知你的名字。」「我是基利德之子基爾赫奇；我的母親是安勞德王子之女戈萊迪德……」 「我去問我父親，」奧爾溫說……那堡壘有九道門，每道門皆有守衛；而每一道門都被基爾赫奇的人攻破；大廳被衝破，那巨大的戰士伊斯帕達登被帶了出來……「我要去問問處女奧爾溫，若她願意要你，你便可得她；但你須帶著這隊人馬再來此地，看我怎麼說。」基爾赫奇的人第二次、第三次攻破那些門，直到最後，巨人的婚宴與那不可能之野豬的狩獵，都被許諾為新娘之聘。

title.en: The Hunt of Twrch Trwyth
title.zh: 追獵特爾赫·特魯伊斯的野豬

region.en: From Dyfed to Cornwall, Wales
region.zh: 自德費德至康沃爾，威爾士

period: Kilhwch and Olwen, Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: Between the ears of the monstrous boar Twrch Trwyth lie the comb and the scissors Yspaddaden demands for his daughter's hair — a king transformed by God's curse into a swine with seven pigs at his back, who has slain many of Arthur's men. The hunt runs through all Wales: the boar lands at Amruth, crosses Severn, ravages Dyfed and Gower, is harried by Arthur himself, and at the last Grugyn and his boars are driven to the sea; the comb and shears are taken and the son of the king loses seven of his men for every gate of the fortress.
summary.zh: 巨野豬特爾赫·特魯伊斯雙耳之間藏著彭考爾為女兒梳髮所需的梳與剪——他本是受神詛化為豬形的國王，身後跟著七隻小豬，已殺亞瑟部眾多人。獵事縱貫全威爾士：登陸阿姆魯斯，橫渡塞文河，肆虐德費德與高爾，亞瑟王親自追擊，最終格魯金與豬群被逐入海。梳剪既得，城堡每道門的代價都是七條人命。

sensitivity.note: The transformed-king boar (Twrch Trwyth was a king turned to swine for sin, with seven pigs — the seven sons) is one of the finest Celtic shape-curse narratives; the comb-and-scissors prize parallels the Fenian comb-and-shears (Diarmuid's) — noted for cross-tradition echo. Pin follows the hunt's route.

passages.text: "It will not be easy for thee to obtain that which thou seekest," said Yspaddaden, "until thou get the comb and the scissors that are between the two ears of Twrch Trwyth... He is a king, and for his wickedness God transformed him into a swine, and he has seven pigs with him, and he will slay many of thy men." And Arthur made for him the muster of the whole island of Britain, and they set forth, and went as far as Dyfed... And Twrch Trwyth came and went to Severn, and the host came after him, and he crossed the Severn... and there was a great struggle between the host and the boar, and many men were slain of the one and of the other; and the boar went into Gower, and there the chase came upon him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Kilhwch and Olwen; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「你要得到你所求之物並不容易，」伊斯帕達登說，「除非你取得特爾赫·特爾維斯兩耳之間的那把梳子與剪刀……他本是一位君王，因他的邪惡，上帝將他化為一頭豬，他身邊有七頭豬，他必殺死你許多人。」亞瑟為他召集了不列顛全島的兵馬，他們出發，一路行至迪費德……特爾赫·特爾維斯來去，到了塞文河，大軍隨後追趕，他渡過了塞文河……大軍與那野豬之間展開大戰，雙方皆有許多人被殺；那野豬進入戈爾，追獵便在那裡追上他。

passages.text: And the hunt went on through the length of the land: Grugyn Silver-bristles, that was like a wing of wild birds, made his way through Din Tywi with his boars, and from Din Tywi to Din Emrys; and the men of Dyfed and the men of Gower could not prevail against him... And there was a great struggle between the host and the boar, and many men were slain of the one and of the other; and the boar went into Gower, and there the chase came upon him; and at the last Grugyn and his boars were driven into the sea, and the comb and the shears were taken from between the ears of Twrch Trwyth, and borne to Yspaddaden for the hair of Olwen.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Kilhwch and Olwen; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 追獵遍及全境：銀鬃格魯金，其狀如野鳥之翼，率其群豬穿過丁·特維，又從丁·特維至丁·埃姆里斯；迪費德之人與戈爾之人皆不能勝他……大軍與那野豬之間展開大戰，雙方皆有許多人被殺；那野豬進入戈爾，追獵便在那裡追上他；最後格魯金與其群豬被驅入海中，梳子與剪刀從特爾赫·特爾維斯兩耳之間取出，帶去給伊斯帕達登，以配奧爾溫的頭髮。

title.en: Mabon son of Modron Freed from the Walls of Gloucester
title.zh: 莫德隆之子馬邦自格洛斯特獄中獲釋

region.en: Caer Loyw (Gloucester), Britain
region.zh: 不列顛格洛斯特（卡厄爾·洛伊）

period: Kilhwch and Olwen, Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: One of Yspaddaden's boons is Mabon son of Modron, taken from his mother at three nights old and held where no man ever set him free. The oldest animals are asked in turn — the Blackbird of Cilgwri, the Stag of Rhedynfre, the Owl of Cwm Cawlwyd, the Eagle of Gwernabwy, and last the Salmon of Llyn Llyw — and the salmon carries Cai and Gwrhyr under the walls of Gloucester to the captive, who breaks the prison with his own strength, aided by the fighting of Arthur's host and the beasts of the hunt.
summary.zh: 彭考爾的條件之一是釋放「莫德隆之子馬邦」——出生三夜即被擄走，囚於無人曾令囚徒脫身之地。諸獸依次被問——基爾格里之黑鶇、雷丁弗雷之雄鹿、庫姆考爾維德之貓頭鷹、格威納布威之鷹——最終林利湖的鮭魚載著凱與格爾希爾潛入格洛斯特牆下；馬邦以自身神力破獄而出，亞瑟王的軍隊與獵獸協力相助。

sensitivity.note: The divine captive Mabon (maponos, the youth-god, son of Matrona/Modron) is attested in Romano-British cult; the chain of oldest animals (blackbird-stag-owl-eagle-salmon) is the classic cumulative-wisdom device, and the salmon-taxi under a prison wall parallels Finn's salmon of knowledge. Pin is the historical Gloucester.

passages.text: And they asked the Blackbird of Cilgwri, and he said, "When I first came here, there was a smith's anvil here, and I was then a young bird; and no work has been done on it save by my beak, and nothing is left of it but a nutmeg. And the oak has grown from a withered stub." And they asked the Stag of Rhedynfre... And they asked the Owl of Cwm Cawlwyd... And they asked the Eagle of Gwernabwy... "And I went to the rock of Llech Wen, and there I heard of Mabon son of Modron; and it was the Salmon of Llyn Llyw that told me, for he has been longer than I."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Kilhwch and Olwen; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們又去問奇爾古里的黑鳥，牠說：「我初來此地時，這裡有一座鐵匠的鐵砧，我當時還是隻幼鳥；除了我的喙之外，從未有過任何工夫施於其上，如今那鐵砧只剩下一顆肉豆蔻般大小。而那橡樹，是從一截枯樁長成的。」他們又去問雷丁弗雷的雄鹿……他們又去問庫姆考爾維德的貓頭鷹……他們又去問格韋爾納布維的鷹……「我又去到萊赫溫的岩石，在那裡我聽說了莫德隆之子馬本；是林利夫的鮭魚告訴我的，因為牠比我活得更久。」

passages.text: And Cai and Gwrhyr went upon the shoulders of the fishes, and they came to the wall of the prison of Mabon; and they heard one lamenting and crying out: "And what lamentation is that?" "It is Mabon, son of Modron, that is here imprisoned; and no imprisonment was ever so grievous as mine." And Cai and Gwrhyr came before Mabon, and told him that Kilhwch sought him for the bride of Olwen. And Mabon was released by the strength of his own hand and of Arthur's men; and he was brought before Kilhwch, and the giant's task was paid.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Kilhwch and Olwen; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 凱與古爾希爾踏上魚的肩背，來到馬本囚牢的牆邊；他們聽見有人在哀嘆呼喊：「那是什麼哀聲？」「是莫德隆之子馬本，被囚於此；從來沒有哪樁囚禁像我這般慘苦。」凱與古爾希爾來到馬本面前，告訴他基爾赫奇尋他，是為了歐文為新娘之事。馬本憑自己手的力量與亞瑟眾人的力量獲得釋放；他被帶到基爾赫奇面前，巨人的任務就此償清。

title.en: Rhonabwy's Dream and the Game of Gwyddbwyll
title.zh: 羅納布威之夢與格威德布威爾棋局

region.en: Rhiw Helwg (symbolic pin, Powys)
region.zh: 波伊斯里夫·赫爾維格（象徵定位）

period: The Dream of Rhonabwy, Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: Rhonabwy, a retainer of Madog ap Maredudd, sleeps three days and three nights on the yellow calf-skin of a wizard's house and dreams he is on the plain of Argyll: Arthur's vast host comes and goes, the Emperor wears a cape of purple and gold that shines like fire, Osla GylmaW plays gwyddbwyll with him while the battle is lost and won, and the dream's chronology — two days and a night — mocks the hour of a dreamer's sleep. The tale is the Mabinogion's most self-conscious satire of Arthurian memory.
summary.zh: 馬多格·阿普·馬雷杜德的侍從羅納布威在巫師屋中的黃牛皮上沉睡三日三夜，夢見自己身處阿蓋爾平原：亞瑟的大軍來去如潮，皇帝披著火光般輝耀的紫金披風；戰事成敗之際，奧斯拉正與他對弈格威德布威爾。夢中的時間——兩日一夜——嘲弄著做夢者片刻的沉睡。此篇是《馬比諾吉安》中最自覺的亞瑟記憶諷刺。

sensitivity.note: The Dream of Rhonabwy is a late (c. 13th c.) literary dream-vision satirising the inflated Arthurian host and its heraldry; the game of gwyddbwyll during battle is the Welsh analogue of the Irish fidchell-with-battle motif (Midir's fidchell, Cuchulainn's). Pin symbolic in Powys.

passages.text: And Rhonabwy went into the house, and there was the calf's skin of a red yellow spread on the floor, and he lay down on it... And he slept three days and three nights. And in his sleep he beheld a vision: he was going over the plain of Argyll, and he saw before him a shoal of horses, and riders, and companies... And he beheld a knight coming towards him, sitting upon a horse of pure white, with a red-yellow cape about him, fringed with gold... And Rhonabwy asked who he was: "I am Iddawg, son of Mynyo, and I was the messenger between Arthur and Medrawd, at the battle of Camlan."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, The Dream of Rhonabwy; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 羅納布伊走進屋裡，地上鋪著一張紅黃色的小牛皮，他便躺臥其上……他睡了三天三夜。睡夢中他看見一個幻象：他正走過阿蓋爾平原，看見前方有一群馬、騎者與隊伍……他看見一名騎士朝他而來，騎著一匹純白的馬，身上披著鑲金流蘇的紅黃色斗篷……羅納布伊問他是誰：「我是明約之子伊道格，在卡姆蘭之戰中，我曾是亞瑟與梅德勞德之間的使者。」

passages.text: And they came towards the place where Arthur was, playing at gwyddbwyll with Osla GylmaW; and the board was of gold, and the men of silver... And Arthur said, "Rhonabwy, hast thou news?" And he beheld the men of the host going and coming, and knights and arms, and yellow capes of gold upon the horses... And the Emperor Arthur wore a cape of purple and of gold, and it shone like fire, and he had a sceptre in his hand, and a circle of gold about his head. And Arthur said to Iddawg, "Call thou to me all the men of my host, that they may see Rhonabwy." And when the game of gwyddbwyll was lost and won, the battle that was fought between the host of Arthur and the host of Medrawd was seen coming to the spot where the game was ended; and he who won the game had won the battle.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, The Dream of Rhonabwy; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們朝亞瑟所在之處而去，亞瑟正與奧斯拉·吉爾馬夫對弈格威德布維爾；棋盤是金的，棋子是銀的……亞瑟說：「羅納布伊，你可有消息？」他看見大軍的人馬來來去去，騎士與兵甲，馬背上披著金黃色的斗篷……亞瑟皇帝身穿紫金斗篷，光耀如火，手中持著權杖，頭上環著金冠。亞瑟對伊道格說：「你替我召來我全軍的人，讓他們看看羅納布伊。」當那局格威德布維爾分出勝負之時，亞瑟大軍與梅德勞德大軍之間所進行的戰役，也被看見來到棋局終結之處；贏了棋局的人，也贏了那場戰役。

title.en: Math's Feet on a Maiden's Lap and Gilvaethwy's Punishment
title.zh: 數學王雙足倚於處女膝上與吉爾維斯威之懲罰

region.en: Caer Dathyl, Gwynedd, Wales
region.zh: 威爾士圭內斯卡厄爾·達斯爾

period: Math the Son of Mathonwy, Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: Math son of Mathonwy, lord of Gwynedd, cannot live but with his feet in the lap of a maiden, save when the land is at war; Goewin daughter of Pebin holds the office of foot-holder. Gwydion procures a war to draw Math out — a conjured fleet of pigs and shoes and shields, gifts that turn to toadstools by morning — and Gilvaethwy ravishes Goewin while the court is at Caer Dathyl. Math strikes with his wand: brother and brother become hind and stag, boar and sow, wolves for three years' terms, bearing young each year until the penance is paid.
summary.zh: 圭內斯之主馬松威之子馬，非戰時雙足必倚於處女膝上方能存活；佩賓之女格溫擔此職。吉威恩製造戰爭誘馬王離宮——以幻術變出豬群、鞋履與盾牌，晨光下盡成牛肝菌——而吉爾維斯威趁機玷污了格溫。馬以魔杖施刑：兄弟二人三年間輪為雌鹿與雄鹿、母豬與公豬、狼與狼，年年產幼，直到罪罰償清。

sensitivity.note: The foot-holder taboo (Math's feet in a maiden's lap) is the classic Welsh sacred-king infirmity motif, paralleled by Nuadu's arm in Irish tradition; the animal-transformation penance for rape is the fourth Branch's core justice-myth. The conjured war-gifts that become toadstools is Gwydion's signature magic. Pin is the named Caer Dathyl.

passages.text: Math the son of Mathonwy was lord over Gwynedd, and Pryderi the son of Pwyll was lord over the one-and-twenty Cantrevs of the South; and Math has this property, that if men whisper together, in a tone how small soever, so that the wind can catch it, no sooner had the wind borne it to him than his mind becomes confused, and he can have no delight in anything but to lie with his two feet in the lap of a maiden, unless the pressure of illness prevents him. Now the maiden who was with him was Goewin, the daughter of Pebin, of Dol Bebin, and she was the fairest maiden of her time who was known in all Britain. And Math lay with his feet in her lap, so long as there was peace in the land.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Math the Son of Mathonwy; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬索努伊之子馬斯是圭內斯的君主，普伊爾之子普里德里則是南方二十一郡的君主；馬斯有這樣一種稟性：若有人聚在一起低聲耳語，無論聲音多麼細微，只要風能捕捉到，風一將它送到他耳中，他的心神便會紊亂，除了把雙腳放在少女的膝上之外，再也不能從任何事物中得到樂趣，除非疾病的壓迫使他無法如此。當時陪伴他的少女是佩賓之女戈溫，來自多爾貝賓，她是當時全不列顛所知最美的少女。只要境內太平，馬斯便將雙腳放在她的膝上。

passages.text: And Gwydion procured that a fleet should be seen coming over the sea, and thirty ships in it, and the ships full of piss-glass... And there was with them every kind of arms and of horses; and Math went to the war, and his feet left the lap of the maiden. And Gilvaethwy the son of Don, and they that were with him, made an attack upon the maiden, and ravished her. And when Math came back, Goewin told him, and Math took his wand and struck Gilvaethwy, and changed him into a hind, and Gwydion into a stag, and he put them out from among men... And at the end of the third year he changed them into boars and swine, and at the end of three years more into wolves; and each year they brought forth young; and the young ones he took and baptized. And at the end of three years more he released them from that punishment, and changed them into their own shape.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Math the Son of Mathonwy; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 格威迪恩設法讓人看見一支艦隊渡海而來，其中有三十艘船，船上滿載著尿玻璃……隨船而來的有各式各樣的兵器與馬匹；馬斯前去征戰，他的雙腳便離開了少女的膝上。唐之子吉爾法斯威與跟隨他的人，向那少女發動襲擊，將她強暴。馬斯回來後，戈溫告訴了他，馬斯便取起他的魔杖擊打吉爾法斯威，把他變成一頭雌鹿，把格威迪恩變成一頭雄鹿，並將他們逐出人群之外……到了第三年年底，他又把他們變成野豬與家豬，再過三年，變成狼；他們每年都生下幼崽；那些幼崽他取來施以洗禮。再過三年之後，他解除了他們那懲罰，使他們變回本來的形貌。

title.en: Gronw's Dart and Lleu Standing on One Foot
title.zh: 格羅努之飛鏢與單足而立的勒烏

region.en: Gronw's hill of Bryn Kyvergyr, North Wales (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 北威爾士布萊恩·基維吉爾山（象徵定位）

period: Math the Son of Mathonwy, Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest (1838-49)

source.work: The Mabinogion, trans. Lady Charlotte Guest, eBook #5160

summary.en: Blodeuwedd's treachery asks Lleu the manner of his death, and the forbidden manner is told: by a river under a roofed cauldron, one foot on a cauldron and the other on a buck-goat, no weapon but a spear a year in the making and forged only on the Sabbath — and Gronw Pebyr rests on one knee on a hill and flings the poisoned dart. The wounded Lleu becomes an eagle in an oak, rotted flesh falling from him, until Gwydion finds him by the swine and restores him; and Lleu's own spear, cast with wrath, goes through Gronw and the stone he held before him, the stone that lies at Ardudwy still.
summary.zh: 布洛德威斯的背叛探知了勒烏的死法禁忌：屋中釜上、一足踏釜一足踏雄山羊、僅能以歷一年鍛成且只可在安息日打造的矛擊殺。格羅努·佩比爾單膝跪於山丘擲出毒鏢。重傷的勒烏化為橡樹上的雄鷹，腐肉片片剝落，直到吉威恩循豬蹤尋得並令其復形。勒烏懷憤擲出的長矛穿透格羅努及其身前的巨石——那塊石頭至今仍留在阿杜德威。

sensitivity.note: The paradoxical death-conditions (the spear of a year's forging, Sabbath-only) and the wounded-god-in-the-tree (Lleu as eagle in the oak, flesh rotting) are the Welsh Lugus-myth core — the closest British analogue to Balor's eye and the mistletoe of the oak; the spear through the stone is the corpus's standing-stone death (cf. Gronw's kinsman motif). Symbolic pin.

passages.text: "What means of death hast thou?" said Blodeuwedd. "That I will tell thee," said Lleu; "it is only by a manner of death that I can be slain: it is not easy to accomplish... I can only be slain by a spear, and it were a year in the making, and it were made only during the time of religious service on Sundays; and I cannot be slain within a house, nor in a tent; and if I be slain while I am standing with one foot upon a cauldron, and the other upon a buck-goat, and if I be killed beneath the canopy of a cauldron..." And Gronw rose up from the bill which is called Bryn Kyvergyr, and he rested on one knee, and flung the poisoned dart and struck him on the side, so that the shaft started out, but the head of the dart remained in his body; and Lleu rose up in the shape of an eagle, and flew away, and gave a horrible scream.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Math the Son of Mathonwy; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「你有什麼致死之法？」布洛黛薇說。「我這就告訴你，」勒烏說；「唯有以某種特定的死法，我才能被殺死：而這並不容易辦到……我唯有被一支矛所殺，而那支矛須耗時一年打造，且只能在星期日舉行宗教儀式之時打造；而我不能在屋內被殺，也不能在帳篷裡被殺；倘若我正一腳踏在鍋上、另一腳踏在公山羊上之時被殺，又倘若我是在鍋的華蓋之下被殺……」於是格隆威從那座名為布林·基弗吉爾的山崗上起身，單膝跪地，擲出那支毒鏢，擊中了他的腰側，以致矛桿穿出，而鏢頭卻留在他體內；勒烏遂化作鷹的形貌騰起，飛遁而去，發出一聲可怖的尖叫。

passages.text: And they came to that part of the country where they saw the oak, and they looked what it might be that the swine was feeding on... And Gwydion came under the tree, and looked what it might be that the eagle was. And he saw that he was an eagle, and the eagle was very wretched... And he sang an englyn, and the eagle came down to the lowest branch of the tree, and he sang another englyn, and the eagle came down to the third branch... until he came to the ground. And Gwydion struck him with his wand, and changed him into his own form... And Lleu rose up where he had rested on one foot and flung the spear at Gronw, and it pierced him through the stone that he held before him, and Gronw fell dead. And the stone that was pierced is yet to be seen, and it is called Llech Gronw.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guest translation, Math the Son of Mathonwy; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們來到那地方，看見了那棵橡樹，便察看那豬群所食的究竟是什麼……於是圭迪昂來到樹下，察看那隻鷹究竟是什麼。他看出那是一隻鷹，而那鷹十分憔悴悲慘……他唱了一首 englyn，那鷹便降到樹的最低枝上；他又唱了一首 englyn，那鷹便降到第三枝上……直到牠落到地面。圭迪昂以杖擊之，將牠變回他自己的形貌……勒烏從他單足所立之處起身，將矛擲向格隆威，那矛穿透了他舉在身前的石頭，格隆威便倒地而死。那塊被穿透的石頭至今仍可見，名為萊赫·格隆威。

title.en: Ness Wins Conor the Throne of Ulster
title.zh: 內斯為科納奪得阿爾斯特王位

region.en: Emain Macha (Navan Fort), Co. Armagh, Northern Ireland
region.zh: 北愛爾蘭阿馬郡埃馬因·瑪哈堡

period: Ulster cycle, Eleanor Hull retelling, Cuchulain the Hound of Ulster (1910)

source.work: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster (1910), ch. I, eBook #52963

summary.en: Ness, ambitious for her son Conor, agrees to wed King Fergus mac Roy on one condition: the sovereignty shall pass to Conor for a single year. In that year she buys the hearts of Ulster with wealth and schooling, and when Fergus demands his kingdom back, the chiefs refuse him — he has resigned it, they say, for a wife. Fergus forsakes her and goes into exile to Queen Meave in Connaught with the Black Exile at his side, swearing revenge.
summary.zh: 內斯為兒子科納謀劃王位，答應嫁給費爾古斯王——條件是王權移交科納一年。一年間她以財富收買人心、教導權術；年期既滿，費爾古斯索還王位，眾酋長卻拒絕：「為娶妻而棄國者，實已遜位。」費爾古斯拋妻出走，攜「黑色流亡者」投奔康諾特女王梅芙，立誓復仇。

sensitivity.note: The one-year regency trick is the fixed usurpation device of the Ulster cycle's opening; it frames the whole Tain (Fergus the exiled king guiding Meave's host). Fergus's rainbow-weaver's-beam sword is the cycle's great weapon lore. Coordinates are the documented Emain Macha.

passages.text: When Conor was but a lad, his mother was a widow, and there was no thought that Conor would be king. For the King of Ulster at that time was Fergus mac Roy, a powerful and noble king, whom his people loved; and though Conor was of high rank and dignity, he stood not near the throne. But his mother, Ness, was ambitious for him, and she used all her arts to bring it about that he should be called to the throne of Ulster. Ness was a handsome woman, and a woman of spirit, and in her youth she had been a warrior; and Fergus admired her, and she wrought upon him so that in the end he asked her to be his wife. She made it a condition that for one year Fergus would leave the sovereignty, and that Conor should take his place; "for," said she, "I should like to have it said that my son had been a king."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. I; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 康納還只是個少年時，他的母親是個寡婦，沒有人想過康納會成為國王。因為當時阿爾斯特的國王是弗格斯·麥克·羅伊，一位強大而高貴的國王，深受其人民愛戴；康納雖出身高貴、地位尊榮，卻與王位無緣。但他的母親內斯對他懷有野心，她用盡一切手段，務求使他被擁上阿爾斯特的王位。內斯是個美貌的女子，也是個有氣性的女子，年輕時曾是一名戰士；弗格斯愛慕她，她對他施加影響，終於使他向她求婚。她提出一個條件：弗格斯須讓出王位一年，由康納取而代之；「因為，」她說，「我希望能有人說我的兒子曾做過國王。」

passages.text: But, as soon as Conor was king, Ness set about to win away the hearts of the people of Ulster from Fergus, and to transfer them in their allegiance to Conor. She supplied her son with wealth, which he distributed secretly among the people, buying them over to his side; and when, the year being out, Fergus demanded back the sovereignty, he found that the league formed against him was so strong that he could do nothing. They agreed that Fergus should keep his wife, if he wished, but that the kingdom should pass to Conor. And Fergus was so wrath at this, that he forsook his wife, and went with a great host of his own followers into Connaught, to take refuge with Queen Meave and with Ailill, her spouse. Now Fergus mac Roy was of great stature, a mighty man and a famous warrior, and his strength was that of a hundred heroes; and all men spoke of the sword of Fergus, which was so great and long that men said that it stretched like a rainbow or like a weaver's beam.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. I; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而，康納一登王位，內斯便著手從弗格斯那裡贏取阿爾斯特人民的心，使他們轉而效忠康納。她供給兒子財富，他則暗中將這些財富分發給人民，收買他們歸附自己；及至一年期滿，弗格斯索還王位時，發現反對他的聯盟如此強大，以致他無能為力。他們議定：弗格斯若願意，可保留他的妻子，但王國須歸於康納。弗格斯為此大怒，竟捨棄了他的妻子，帶著一大群自己的追隨者前往康諾特，投奔梅芙女王及其配偶艾利爾以求庇護。話說弗格斯·麥克·羅伊身材魁梧，是個力大無窮的漢子，也是著名的戰士，其力量抵得上一百位英雄；人人都談論弗格斯的那把劍，那劍如此巨大而修長，人們說它伸展起來宛如彩虹，又似織布機的橫樑。

title.en: Cuchulain in Shadow-Land: the Training of Scathe
title.zh: 暗影之國：斯凱瑟的訓練

region.en: Shadow-land (Isle of Skye, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 暗影之國（象徵定位於斯凱島）

period: Ulster cycle, Eleanor Hull retelling, Cuchulain the Hound of Ulster (1910)

source.work: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster (1910), ch. VII, eBook #52963

summary.en: A boy yet, Cuchulain goes out to perfect every soldierly art, first with the grim Donnell and Big-fist for a year and a day, then alone across a scorched trackless desert to the Eastern world, riding a friendly lion four days and nights over the lightless land, to find the woman-champion Scathe, daughter of Ages, King of Shadow-land, from whom alone true knightly skill can be learned — Scathach of Skye, the teacher whose feats and weapons he will carry to the fords of the Tain.
summary.zh: 尚是少年的庫丘林立志習盡武藝：先隨陰森的多涅爾與「巨拳」學藝一年一日；再獨自穿越焦黑無路的荒漠，騎友善雄獅四日四夜橫越無光之境，抵達東方世界——唯「艾格斯之女斯凱瑟」所在的暗影之國，方能傳授真正的騎士技藝。此即斯凱島的女武師斯卡薩赫，其武藝與兵器日後將伴庫丘林征戰《奪牛記》的每一處渡口。

sensitivity.note: Scathach's Shadow-land is traditionally identified with the Isle of Skye (the Cuillin hills bear her name); the friendly lion carrying the boy across the desert is a fixed marvel-guide of the tale, and the year-and-a-day term is the Irish fosterage term. Pin symbolic on Skye.

passages.text: While Cuchulain was still a little lad, but strong and brave and full of spirit, it came into his mind that he would like to go out into the world to perfect himself in every kind of soldierly art, so that he might not be behind any warrior in feats of strength and skill. He went first to the Glen of Solitude in Munster, but he did not long remain there, but returned to Ulster, to invite his companions to go with him to visit the woman-warrior Scathe who dwelt in "Shadow-land." They came at last to a dark gloomy shore where dwelt a fierce woman-warrior, Donnell the Soldierly, and her daughter, Big-fist; they knew many feats of arms, so that the three warriors stayed with them a year and a day, learning all they knew. But Cuchulain was fain to go away from them, for the darkness and the gloom of the place and the ugly deeds of Big-fist troubled him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. VII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 庫胡林還是個少年時，卻已強壯勇敢、充滿氣概，他心中生念，想要外出闖蕩世界，精通各種軍事技藝，好使自己在力量與技巧的種種本領上不落於任何戰士之後。他首先前往芒斯特的孤寂之谷，但沒有久留，便返回阿爾斯特，邀請同伴與他一同去拜訪住在「影之國」的女戰士斯卡哈。他們終於來到一處幽暗陰沉的海岸，那裡住著一位兇猛的女戰士，名為戰士般的唐奈爾，以及她的女兒巨拳；她們精通許多武藝，於是這三位戰士與她們同住了一年零一日，學盡了她們所知的一切。但庫胡林卻想離開她們，因為那地方的黑暗與陰沉，以及巨拳的醜惡行徑，令他心中不安。

passages.text: Cuchulain was walking by the brink of the sea, when he saw close beside him, sitting on the shore, a man of enormous size, every inch of him from top to toe as black as coal: "If you want to learn true knightly skill and feats of valour, it is not here that you will learn them. Far better than she is Scathe, daughter of Ages, King of Shadow-land, who dwells in the Eastern world." And when his companions' homesick visions separated them from him, Cuchulain set out alone along the unknown road; for he was determined to reach Shadow-land, or to die in the attempt.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. VII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 庫胡林正沿著海邊行走，忽見緊挨著他、坐在岸上的一個身形巨大的男子，從頭到腳每一寸都黑如煤炭：「你若想學真正的騎士技藝與英勇本領，在這裡是學不到的。比她要高明得多的是斯卡哈，她是影之國王阿吉斯的女兒，住在東方世界。」及至同伴們思鄉的幻象使他們與他分離，庫胡林便獨自踏上那未知的道路；因為他決心要抵達影之國，否則便死於途中。

passages.text: He went on for many days over great mountains and through deep impenetrable forests, and dark, lonely glens, until he came to a wide-spreading desert and a lightless land, black and scorched and bare. Just then he saw a great beast like a lion coming out of the forest, and it made no attempt to injure him, but kept turning its side to Cuchulain, inviting him to mount; and for four days and nights they travelled thus through the dim, lightless land, until they saw a small loch and a boat on it, and boys rowing the boat backward and forward amongst the reeds of the shore, and the boys laughed at the sight of the hurtful beast doing service to a human being.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. VII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他越過巍峨的群山，穿過幽深難入的森林與陰暗孤寂的幽谷，行了許多日子，直到來到一片廣袤的荒漠與一片無光之地，那地漆黑、焦枯而荒蕪。就在此時，他看見一頭狀如雄獅的巨獸從林中走出，那獸並無傷害他之意，只是不斷側身向庫胡林，邀他騎乘；他們便如此在昏暗無光之地行走了四天四夜，直到看見一個小湖，湖上有一艘船，幾個少年在岸邊蘆葦間來回划著船，那些少年見這凶猛的巨獸竟為人效力，都笑了起來。

title.en: Fergus Misleads the Host and the Four-Pronged Pole
title.zh: 費爾古斯誤導大軍與四叉木柱

region.en: Ford on the Shannon borders, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭香農河畔渡口（象徵定位）

period: Ulster cycle, Eleanor Hull retelling, Cuchulain the Hound of Ulster (1910)

source.work: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster (1910), ch. X, eBook #52963

summary.en: Snow falls to the chariot-wheels, and Fergus — guiding Meave's host — leads it in circles out of love for his own province, warning: the standing of Cuchulain will be as the crouching of the Hounds of War upon your path. Cuchulain cuts a four-pronged oak pole with one sweep, throws it into the stream with one hand, and impales four heads on its points; the ring on it reads that the men of Erin may not pass till it is plucked up in the same manner — and chariot after chariot of Fergus's goes to splinters.
summary.zh: 大雪沒輪，費爾古斯領軍卻因故鄉之情率軍繞圈，並警告：「庫丘林之立，猶如戰犬伏於你們的必經之途。」庫丘林一揮劍削出四叉橡木柱，單手擲入溪流中央，柱尖各插一顆人頭；柱環刻文曰：除非有人以同樣單手之力拔起此柱，愛爾蘭之軍不得過河——費爾古斯的戰車一輛輛撞得粉碎。

sensitivity.note: This is Hull's retelling of the LU withe-and-pillar passage (existing record celtic-withe-ogam-geis-host covers Faraday's recension); Hull's version has the four-pronged pole with four heads — a variant form of the geis-token, kept as a distinct recension record. Pin symbolic.

passages.text: It was in the beginning of winter that they set out, and already snow lay heavy on the ground; on the very first night it fell so thickly, that it reached to the chariot-wheels. Meave called Fergus: "Go on before the hosts, O Fergus, and find us out the shortest road into Ulster." So with a few companions Fergus went on ahead; but as he drove along, the memory of old friends and of his home and country came upon him, and an overwhelming affection for Ulster took hold on him, and in his mind there arose shame and bitter self-reproach that he, the former King of Ulster, should be leading Ulster's foes against her. So to the North and the South he misled the host, while in the meantime he sent swift messengers to Conor and the Ulster chiefs, but especially to his own foster-son Cuchulain. "Beware and look out well for your troops to-night and every night from this; for it may be that Cuchulain will stand between you and Ulster, and the standing of Cuchulain will be as the crouching of the Hounds of War upon your path."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們出發時正值初冬，地上已積著厚雪；就在第一夜，雪下得極大，竟深及戰車之輪。梅芙喚來弗格斯：「弗格斯啊，你走在隊伍前頭，替我們找出通往阿爾斯特最短的路。」於是弗格斯帶著幾名同伴先行；然而他一路驅車前行，舊日友人的記憶、故鄉與家國之思湧上心頭，一股對阿爾斯特的強烈眷戀攫住了他，心中又生羞慚與苦澀的自責——他，昔日的阿爾斯特之王，竟領著阿爾斯特的敵人來攻打她。於是他領著大軍時而向北、時而向南，使他們迷失方向，同時又派遣迅捷的信使去見康納與阿爾斯特的眾首領，尤其是他自己的養子庫胡林。「今夜以及此後每一夜，都要小心提防、好好守望你們的軍隊；因為庫胡林或許會擋在你們與阿爾斯特之間，而庫胡林一旦站定，便如戰爭之犬伏踞於你們的路上。」

passages.text: No sooner had Sualtach gone his way than Cuchulain entered a forest close at hand and out of an oak sapling cut a four-pronged pole, which with one sweep of his swift sword he cleared of all its twigs and leaves and small branches. With the finger-tips of his right hand he hurled it out behind his chariot, going at full pace, so that it sank into the ground in the middle of the stream, and stood up just above the water. Upon the pole he flung a ring or twisted collar of young birch, and on the ring he carved his name and a message in secret runes; and two young men of the host of Meave, gone out before the troops to scout, he slew, and their heads and the heads of their charioteers were impaled on the four points of the forked pole.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蘇阿爾塔赫剛一走，庫胡林便進入近旁的一片森林，從一株小橡樹上砍下一根四叉的木樁，揮動他那迅捷的劍一掃，便削去了所有的細枝、葉子與小枝條。他以右手指尖將木樁從戰車後方全力擲出，木樁便插入溪流中央的河床，恰好立在水面之上。他在木樁上套了一只以嫩樺木編成的環或絞成的圈，並在環上以祕密符文刻下自己的名字與一段訊息；他又殺死梅芙軍中先行出營偵察的兩名青年，將他們與其馭者的頭顱分別插在叉樁的四個尖端上。

passages.text: "It is written on the ring that with one hand this pole was thrown, and fixed firmly in its bed; it is written here, moreover, that the men of Erin are forbidden to pass this ford, until in exactly the same manner it is plucked up again." A chariot was brought and Fergus mounted into it, and though he tugged and strained, so that the chariot flew into little bits and fragments, he could not stir or move the pole an inch; one chariot after another he essayed, and all of them went into splinters.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「環上寫著：此樁以單手擲出，並牢牢固定於河床；此處還寫著：愛琳之人不得通過此渡口，除非以完全相同的方式再將它拔出。」有人牽來一輛戰車，弗格斯登上車中，儘管他用力拉扯使勁，以致戰車碎成片片殘塊，卻仍不能使那木樁移動分毫；他一輛戰車接著一輛戰車地嘗試，結果全都裂成了碎片。

title.en: Nacrantal and the Nine Spits of Holly-Wood
title.zh: 納克蘭塔爾與九支冬青肉叉

region.en: Ford of challenge, Mag Murthemne, Co. Louth (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭勞斯郡穆瑟姆尼挑戰渡口（象徵定位）

period: Ulster cycle, Eleanor Hull retelling, Cuchulain the Hound of Ulster (1910)

source.work: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster (1910), ch. XIII, eBook #52963

summary.en: Nacrantal, promised land and Finnabar, takes no arms but nine spits of holly-wood hardened in fire; Cuchulain, hawking, leaps over each spit as it falls. Taunted with flight, he answers that he fights only men-at-arms fully equipped — and Fergus, ashamed, sends the rebuke that turns the trick: Laeg smears a false beard with blackberry juice and sheep's wool, the battle-fury transforms the boy's face, and he carries off a pillar-stone in his mantle without knowing its weight. Nacrantal's sword breaks on the stone and one blow lays him on his own shield.
summary.zh: 受諾土地與芬娜芭爾的納克蘭塔爾僅持九支火烤冬青尖叉出戰；庫丘林正在放鷹逐鳥，逐一躍過落下的尖叉。被誣臨陣脫逃後，他答曰只與全副武裝的戰士交手——費爾古斯羞愧傳話；萊格以黑莓汁與羊毛為他做假鬚，戰怒改易其容，斗篷間竟不自覺夾起一根石柱。納克蘭塔爾之劍斷於石上，一擊斃命，倒在自己的盾上。

sensitivity.note: The false-beard trick is Hull's version of the beard-magic of the Loch episode (Faraday's record covers the Long/Loch variant); the pillar-stone caught in the mantle unnoticed is the riastrad strength-sign. The holly-spits challenge repeats the spits-of-hollywood chapter title of the Tain. Pin symbolic.

passages.text: Among the chiefs was a rough burly man and a good fighter, whose name was Nacrantal, whom Meave used all her arts to force to challenge Cuchulain. And in the end, when she had promised him large gifts of land and even Finnabar, her daughter, to be his wife, he was induced to go. But even so he went not out as though to fight an equal. No arms or armour would he take, but for his sole protection nine spits of holly-wood, sharp at the points and hardened in the fire. He found the hero busied in pursuing wild-fowl that were flying overhead; for from the birds of the air and fish of the streams, and from the berries of the hedge and cresses of the brook, long had he been obliged to get his daily meal. Closer the warrior drew and with good aim he flung his spits of wood to pierce Cuchulain. But still the youth, not stopping for a moment in his task, leaped lightly over each spit as it fell, so that they struck the ground quite harmlessly.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 首領之中有一名粗壯魁梧、善戰的男子，名叫納克蘭塔爾，梅芙用盡種種手段逼他去向庫胡林挑戰。最後，當她許諾給他大片土地，甚至以她的女兒芬納巴爾許配他為妻時，他才被說動前往。然而即便如此，他出戰時也不像是去與旗鼓相當的對手交鋒。他不帶任何兵器甲冑，只以九根尖端銳利、經火淬硬的冬青木尖刺作為唯一的防護。他發現這位英雄正忙著追逐頭上飛過的野禽；因為長久以來，他只能靠天上的飛鳥、溪中的魚、樹籬上的漿果與溪邊的水芹來充飢度日。那戰士越走越近，瞄準妥當，擲出他的木刺，欲刺穿庫胡林。但那少年一刻也不停下手中的事，只是輕巧地躍過每一根落下的尖刺，使它們全然無害地扎在地上。

passages.text: "Do you and Fergus not yet understand that I, Cuchulain, fight no men unarmed, or messengers, or charioteers, but only men-at-arms, fully equipped?" Laeg took the juice of blackberries, and sheep's wool, and with it made a long two-pointed beard, such as prime warriors wore, and twined the ends and caught them in his belt, dyeing it black with juice. Then on the hero came anger and his battle-fury; a subtle change came over all his face; his stature seemed to grow, his form to enlarge, and terrible in its strength and fierceness was his aspect.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「你和弗格斯還不明白嗎？我庫胡林不與手無寸鐵的人、信使或馭者交手，只與全副武裝的甲士交戰。」萊格取來黑莓汁與羊毛，用它做成一副長長的雙尖鬍鬚，正是精銳戰士所蓄的樣式，又將兩端纏繞並扣在腰帶上，以汁液染成黑色。隨後，怒火與戰鬥的狂怒臨到這位英雄身上；他的整張臉起了微妙的變化；他的身量似乎增長，形體似乎膨大，其氣勢之強悍凶猛，著實可怖。

passages.text: So great his wrath and eagerness for combat, that as he passed a standing pillar-stone no smaller than himself, in flinging his mantle round him as he went he caught the stone up in his mantle's folds and carried it along with him, but never was he conscious of its weight. Then Nacrantal made a furious onset at Cuchulain with his sword, but it struck on the pillar-stone that he carried beneath his cloak, and broke off short, close to his hand; and lifting his sword on high with both hands, Cuchulain brought it down on his adversary's head, and there on his own shield he fell dead, smitten with one blow.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的憤怒與求戰之心如此強烈，當他經過一根與他一般高的立石柱時，他一邊前行一邊將斗篷往身上一甩，竟把石柱兜進斗篷的褶皺裡，一路帶著走，卻始終不覺其重。接著，納克蘭塔爾揮劍向庫呼蘭猛撲而去，但劍砍在他斗篷下所帶的那根石柱上，應聲折斷，斷口緊貼他的手邊；庫呼蘭雙手高舉寶劍，朝敵人的頭頂劈下，那人便在自己的盾牌上倒地而死，一擊斃命。

title.en: The Fairy Swan-Maidens of the Plain of Delight
title.zh: 極樂平原的仙鵝少女

region.en: Lake on the Plain of Murthemne, Co. Louth, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭勞斯郡穆瑟姆尼湖畔

period: Ulster cycle, Eleanor Hull retelling, Cuchulain the Hound of Ulster (1910)

source.work: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster (1910), ch. XX, eBook #52963

summary.en: At the autumn feast Cuchulain brings down birds for the women but gives none to Emer; two noble swans linked with a golden chain, chanting a mystic sleep-song, come sailing — and for the first time in his life his sling misses, his spear glances, and the wounded swan vanishes under water with Laeg asleep behind him. Two fairy women with osier switches strike his strength away: Liban, wife of Labra the Swift of Moy Mell, come to bid him welcome — the beginning of his trip to Fairy-Land.
summary.zh: 秋日盛宴，庫丘林為眾女獵鳥，卻未給埃妮德一隻；兩隻金鏈相連、吟唱催眠仙歌的貴天鵝緩緩而來——他一生中第一次失手：彈石掠過、矛刺落空、受傷的天鵝沒入水中，萊格在他身後酣睡。兩位執柳條的仙姝以杖輕點，吸走他的力氣：利巴恩——極樂平原「迅捷者」拉布拉之妻——前來相邀，仙遊之地由此開啟。

sensitivity.note: The swan-maidens are Hull's retelling of the Serglige (Sick-bed) prelude — the fairy-hostage pattern behind the Fand episode (existing record celtic-sickbed-fand covers the Fand core); the first-time-ever missed sling-shot is the tale's enchanted-capture device. Pin at Murthemne lake tradition.

passages.text: One day during an autumn feast, Cuchulain and Emer his wife were amusing themselves beside a lake, when they saw coming from a distance a flock of white, very beautiful swans, which settled down upon the lake, and began to swim out two and two. "How I wish that I could have two of those birds, one on each of my shoulders," said Emer. Cuchulain brought down a number of them with his sword and with stones, and threw them down before the women, but to Emer he gave not any birds at all. Then slowly sailing out of the far distance they saw two noble swans, larger and more splendid than any of those that had been on the lake before: the birds were chanting a gentle, mystic song, that soothed all who listened to it to sleep; and they were linked together with a golden chain.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XX; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某年秋日宴慶期間，庫呼蘭與他的妻子艾梅爾在湖邊嬉戲，忽見遠處飛來一群潔白而極其美麗的天鵝，落在湖面上，開始兩兩成對地游動。「我多希望能得到其中兩隻鳥，一邊肩上停一隻。」艾梅爾說道。庫呼蘭用劍和石塊擊落了不少天鵝，扔在眾女子面前，卻一隻也沒有給艾梅爾。隨後，他們望見兩隻高貴的天鵝從遠方緩緩游來，比先前湖上的任何一隻都更大、更華美：這兩隻鳥唱著一支柔和而神秘的歌，凡聽者皆被撫慰入眠；牠們彼此以一條金鏈相連。

passages.text: "There are your birds, O Emer," said Cuchulain, and he rose up to pursue them. But Emer was afraid: "Go not against those birds; there is some magic power in those birds, and you may come to harm." He took the sling and made a very careful aim, but for the first time in his life he missed his aim; and again the stone went past them; and he flung his spear, and it seemed as though the spear went through the swans, but the wing of one of them was broken, and they flew away unhurt, and disappeared beneath the water.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XX; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「你的鳥兒在那裡，艾梅爾啊。」庫呼蘭說道，隨即起身去追。但艾梅爾心生恐懼：「不要與那些鳥兒為敵；那些鳥兒身上有某種魔力，你恐怕會受到傷害。」他拿起投石索，極其仔細地瞄準，卻生平第一次失了準頭；石塊又一次從牠們身旁飛過；他又擲出長矛，那長矛看似穿過了天鵝，然而其中一隻的翅膀折斷了，牠們卻毫髮無傷地飛走，消失在水面之下。

passages.text: A strange weariness overtook him, and he leaned his back against a pillar stone, and drowsiness fell upon him. Then in a vision Cuchulain saw two graceful women approach him, clad in fairy mantles of green and purple, and they had little switches of osier in their hands, and they began to strike him gently with the rods, and it seemed to Cuchulain that all his strength departed from him while they touched him with their rods. "We are come," said the first, "out of Moy Mell, the Land of all Delight, the radiant Honey-Plain beyond the waves, to seek thy friendship. Liban am I, wife of Labra the Swift, the Wielder of the Sword, the monarch of that land."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XX; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一陣奇異的倦意襲上他身，他背靠一根石柱，睡意便降臨於他。接著，庫呼蘭在幻象中看見兩位優雅的女子向他走來，身穿綠與紫的仙家斗篷，手中各執一根細小的柳枝，開始用柳條輕輕抽打他；庫呼蘭只覺她們以柳條觸及他時，他全身的氣力盡皆離去。「我們來自莫伊梅爾，那萬般歡愉之地，浪濤彼岸那光輝的蜜原，前來尋求你的友誼。我乃莉班，迅捷者拉布拉之妻，他是執劍者，是那片土地的君主。」第一位女子說道。

title.en: Deirdre's Walled Garden and the Ball of Dreams
title.zh: 迪爾德麗的高牆花園與夢中之球

region.en: Lonely dell far from Emain Macha, Co. Armagh (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿馬郡遠離埃馬因的僻谷（象徵定位）

period: Ulster cycle, Eleanor Hull retelling, Cuchulain the Hound of Ulster (1910)

source.work: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster (1910), ch. XXIII, eBook #52963

summary.en: Conor's jealousy of the boy-corps takes Deirdre at seven years old from the playing fields and walls her in a lonely dell behind man-hounds, where nurse Levarcam teaches her every bird and herb and star. But the memory of Naisi's mis-thrown ball — caught by the child, returned with a smile and a promise — works in her dreams: every night Conor comes between and throws it back, till one night the ball strikes Naisi red and bleeding like the sacrificed calf, and the captive bride pines for a man she may not name.
summary.zh: 科納因妒忌少年軍，將七歲的迪爾德麗帶離球場，圈入深谷高牆之內，四猛犬日夜把守；智慧乳母教她百鳥、百草與星辰。然而奈西失手拋來、她撿回並得他微笑一諾的那顆球，夜夜入夢：科納總在中途奪球擲回，直到某夜球擊中奈西——紅染如祭壇上的牛犢——被囚的新娘為一個不能說出名字的男人憔悴。

sensitivity.note: Hull's version adds the walled garden and the captive-education topos to the Deirdre birth-prophecy (existing record celtic-deirdre-exile covers the exile and death); the dream-ball sequence is Hull's omen-psychology — the future killing foreseen as a child's game. Pin symbolic near Emain.

passages.text: Then Conor called his Druid Caffa to him, and he said, "Too long we leave this child at liberty among the chieftain's sons. She must henceforth be kept apart... She shall come to me of her own free will, because she knows no other man but me. She shall not even know what kind of thing a man may be, for I will shut her up apart from men, and, save yourself and me, she shall not ever see a manly face." So for the girl he built a place apart, far off from Emain in a lonely dell, surrounded by a wood; and all seemed fair enough, but round the place he built a mighty wall, so high that none could climb it, and a moat ran round within. Four savage man-hounds sent by Conor were on constant guard, watching on every side by night and day, so that no living thing could enter or pass out, save with the knowledge of Levarcam.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XXIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是康納爾召來他的德魯伊卡法，說道：「我們讓這孩子自由地與首領們的兒子們相處，實在太久了。從今以後，必須將她隔離起來……她必將出於自己的意願來找我，因為除了我，她不認識別的男人。她甚至不會知道男人是何等樣的存在，因為我要將她與男人們隔絕關閉起來，除了你自己和我，她將永遠見不到一張男人的臉。」於是，他為這女孩在遠離埃曼的一處僻靜山谷中、四周環繞著樹林的地方，建了一座居所；一切看似足夠美好，但他卻在居所四周築起一道巨牆，高得無人能攀，牆內還環繞著一道壕溝。康納爾派來的四隻兇猛獵犬日夜在各面守衛，因此除了經由萊瓦爾坎知情之外，任何活物都無法進入或出去。

passages.text: And for a time the child was happy, for Levarcam, the wise woman, taught her all she knew: how each bird sings to its mate, each different note of thrush or cuckoo or the soaring lark; the plants that spring towards heaven, and of their names and uses; and in the solemn night, they went abroad and watched the motion of the stars. But the maiden drooped and pined: "Seven bitter years since I beheld the joyous playing field, and saw the sports, and marked the manly face of Naisi, noblest and bravest of the corps of boys." "He told me so, when he threw the ball, by a mis-cast, backward, across the heads of the group of maidens who were standing on the edge of the green, and I rose up among them all, picked up the ball, and gave it back to him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XXIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一段時日，這孩子過得很快樂，因為那位智慧女子萊瓦爾坎將她所知的一切都教給了她：每一隻鳥如何向牠的伴侶歌唱，畫眉、杜鵑或高飛的雲雀各自不同的音調；那些向天而生的植物，以及它們的名稱與用途；在莊嚴的夜裡，她們外出觀測星辰的運行。但這少女卻日漸憔悴、憂鬱：「自我見到那歡樂的嬉戲場地、看見那些競技、並望見奈西那高貴而勇敢的男子面容以來，已過了七個苦澀的年頭——他是少年隊中最為高貴勇敢的人。」「他這樣對我說過，當他拋球時，一失手，球向後飛過那群站在綠地邊緣的少女們的頭頂，我便在她們眾人之中站起身來，拾起球，交還給他。」

passages.text: He pressed my hand and smiled, and promised he would see me oft again... But in my dreams I see him every night playing at ball with me; and when he flings the ball for me to catch, 'tis ever the same thing: King Conor comes between and seizes it, and throws it back at Naisi. But last night, King Conor flung the ball craftily at his head, and Naisi fell all red and stained with blood, like that poor calf that Caffa slew."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XXIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他握住我的手，微微一笑，答应会常来看我……但在我梦中，我每夜都见他与我一同玩球；当他抛球让我接时，情形总是如此：康纳王插身其间，把球夺去，又掷回给奈西。可昨夜，康纳王狡诈地把球掷向他的头，奈西便倒下了，浑身血红，血迹斑斑，就像卡法杀死的那头可怜的小牛。

title.en: The Hound at Bay against the Pillar-Stone
title.zh: 困守石柱的獵犬

region.en: Ford of Cuchulain's last battle, Mag Murthemne, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭穆瑟姆尼庫丘林最後戰場（象徵定位）

period: Ulster cycle, Eleanor Hull retelling, Cuchulain the Hound of Ulster (1910)

source.work: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster (1910), ch. XXVIII, eBook #52963

summary.en: Fighting his last fight against Meave's geas-breaking host, Cuchulain is mortally stricken; he will not fall but goes to the pillar-stone, straps his body upright with his belt, and dies on his feet facing his foes, his hand on his weapons, so that even his enemies dare not approach until a raven — the bird of the Morrigan — comes to settle on his shoulder. The Hound at bay is the Ulster cycle's dying-standing image.
summary.zh: 與梅芙背誓之軍作最後一戰的庫丘林身負致命傷；他不肯倒下，走向石柱，以腰帶縛身直立，面向敵人手握兵器而亡——直到摩里岡的烏鴉落上他的肩頭，敵軍才敢靠近。「困守之犬」是阿爾斯特史詩「戰死者挺立」的不朽意象。

sensitivity.note: The dying-upright at the pillar-stone (the Tain's ending image, and the standing-stone tradition of Cuchulain's memorial) parallels the corpus's standing-deaths (Balor buried standing; the Fianna's foot-to-foot falls); the Morrigan's raven landing on the shoulder closes her feud with the hero. Symbolic pin at the traditional site.

passages.text: And as the day wore on the tide of battle set thicker against Cuchulain; his foes closed in from every side, and though he slew them as they came, his wounds were many, and the death-sickness was upon him. Yet Cuchulain would not fall, for it was not the manner of a hero of the Fianna to fall before his foes while strength was left him; and he made his way to a great pillar-stone that stood hard by, and he set his back against it, and with his belt he bound himself upright to the stone, that he might die as a warrior should, facing his foes, with his weapons in his hand.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XXVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 随着白昼渐逝，战局对库胡林愈发不利；敌人从四面八方逼近，他虽来一个杀一个，却已伤痕累累，死疾临身。然而库胡林不肯倒下，因为费奥纳的英雄从不曾在尚有余力时倒在敌人面前；他挣扎着来到近旁一块巨大的立石前，背靠着它，用腰带把自己直立绑在石上，好让他能像一个战士应有的样子死去——面朝敌人，手持兵器。

passages.text: And there he died, standing up against the pillar-stone, and so terrible was his aspect even in death, that none of his enemies dared to come near him, until at last a raven came and settled upon his shoulder; and then they knew that the Hound of Ulster was no more. And his friends came, and Loeg his charioteer, and they loosed the belt from the stone and bore the body away; and the deeds of Cuchulain were told in Ulster from that day to this, and fame outlived life, and the Red Branch mourned its chief, and the standing-stone at the ford kept the memory of the Hound at Bay.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XXVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他就这样死在那里，直立靠着立石；即便死后，他的形貌仍如此可怖，以致没有一个敌人敢靠近他，直到最后一只渡鸦飞来，落在他的肩上；这时他们才知道，阿尔斯特的猎犬已经不在人世。他的友人、他的御者洛伊格来了，他们解开石上的腰带，把遗体抬走；自那日起直至今日，库胡林的事迹仍在阿尔斯特传颂，声名长存于生命之后，红枝团哀悼其首领，渡口的立石则铭记着这位困守待毙的猎犬。

title.en: Maeldun's Birth and the Boat of the Druid's Rule
title.zh: 梅爾敦的誕生與德魯伊法則之舟

region.en: Aran Islands, Co. Galway, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭戈爾韋郡阿倫群島

period: Voyage of Maeldun (Imram Maelduin, Book of the Dun Cow recension), retold in T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911)

source.work: T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911), ch. VII, eBook #34630

summary.en: Ailill of the Edge-of-Battle of the Owenacht of Aran is slain by reavers who burn the church of Doocloone over him, and a son is born who is reared as the queen's own — beautiful beyond flesh, out-throwing every boy at ball and stone. Taunted with not knowing his kindred, Maeldun fasts till his mother is found, learns his father's ashes lie under the scorched flagstone where he was casting the stone, and builds a coracle of skins threefold at a Druid's word: seventeen men only, on the days the wizard names — and the three foster-brothers who swim after the boat bring on them all the punishment of a transgressed rule.
summary.zh: 阿倫群島「戰刃埃利爾」遭萊克斯海寇焚教堂殺害；其遺腹子梅爾敦由王后撫養，俊美非凡、擲石賽跑冠絕同儕。因人嘲其不知親族，他絕食探母；最終得知父親骨灰正埋於他擲石而立的焦黑石板之下。他依德魯伊之言製三層皮革小舟：僅限十七人同行——而三名跳海追舟的乳兄弟，卻為全體招來觸犯法則的懲罰。

sensitivity.note: The voyage of Maeldun is the oldest Irish wonder-voyage (model for St Brendan's); the Druid's fixed rule (seventeen men, named days) and the transgression by the foster-brothers set the penance-frame of the whole immram — the tale teaches 'the oracular injunctions of wizards should be obeyed', as Rolleston notes, but it is Christian-era mythology built on pagan sea-quest stock. Pin is the real Aran Islands.

passages.text: One day a proud young warrior who had been defeated by him taunted him with his lack of knowledge of his kindred and descent. Maeldun went to his foster-mother, the queen, and said: "I will not eat nor drink till thou tell me who are my mother and my father." The queen at last took him to his own mother, the nun, who told him: "Thy father was Ailill of the Owens of Aran." Then Maeldun went to his own kindred, and was well received by them. After a time Maeldun happened to be among a company of young warriors who were contending at putting the stone in the graveyard of the ruined church of Doocloone; Maeldun's foot was planted, as he heaved the stone, on a scorched and blackened flagstone; and one who was by, a monk named Briccne, said to him: "It were better for thee to avenge the man who was burnt there than to cast stones over his burnt bones." "Who was that?" "Ailill, thy father." "Who slew him?" "Reavers from Leix."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一天，一个曾被他击败的骄傲的年轻武士讥讽他不知自己的亲族与出身。梅尔敦便去见他的养母——王后，说道：“你不告诉我谁是我的母亲、谁是我的父亲，我便不吃也不喝。”王后最终带他去见他的生母——那位修女，她告诉他：“你的父亲是阿兰的欧文家族的艾利尔。”于是梅尔敦去投奔自己的亲族，受到他们的善待。过了一些时候，梅尔敦偶然与一伙年轻武士为伍，他们在杜克卢恩废弃教堂的墓地里比赛掷石；梅尔敦在举起石头时，脚正踩在一块焦黑了的石板上；旁边一个名叫布里克内的修士对他说：“你与其往那人的焦骨上掷石，不如为他复仇。”——“那人是谁？”——“你的父亲艾利尔。”——“谁杀了他？”——“来自莱克斯的劫掠者。”

passages.text: Then Maeldun threw down the stone he was about to cast, and put his mantle round him and went home. At the advice of a Druid he then built him a boat, or coracle, of skins lapped threefold one over the other; and the wizard also told him that seventeen men only must accompany him, and on what day he must begin the boat and on what day he must put out to sea. So when his company was ready he put out and hoisted the sail, but had gone only a little way when his three foster-brothers came down to the beach and entreated him to take them. "Get you home, for none but the number I have may go with me." But the three youths would not be separated from Maeldun, and they flung themselves into the sea. He turned back, lest they should be drowned, and brought them into his boat; and all were punished for this transgression, and Maeldun condemned to wandering until expiation had been made.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 于是梅尔敦扔下正要掷出的石头，裹上斗篷回家去了。他听从一位德鲁伊的建议，为自己造了一只船，即用兽皮层层叠叠三重包覆而成的皮舟；那巫师还告诉他，只可有十七人随他同行，并告诉他何日动工造船、何日出海。于是当他的同伴齐备后，他便出海扬帆，但才走了不远，他的三个结义兄弟便来到海滩，恳求他带上他们。“你们回家去吧，因为除我规定的人数之外，谁也不能与我同去。”但那三个年轻人不肯与梅尔敦分离，纵身跳入海中。他怕他们淹死，便掉转船头，把他们接上船来；众人皆因这一违命而受罚，梅尔敦更被判四处漂泊，直至赎罪完毕。

title.en: The Island of the Slaves and the Wind of Punishment
title.zh: 奴隸島與懲罰之風

region.en: Two bare islands of the western ocean (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西海兩座荒島（象徵定位）

period: Voyage of Maeldun (Imram Maelduin), retold in T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911)

source.work: T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911), ch. VII, eBook #34630

summary.en: Rowing all day and half the night, the voyagers come to two small bare islands with two forts, and hear armed men quarrelling: 'Twas I slew Ailill of the Edge-of-Battle and burned the church of Doocloone over him, and no kinsman has avenged his death on me.' Maeldun is about to land for vengeance, but a great wind arises suddenly and blows them off into the boundless ocean — 'Ye have caused this to be, casting yourselves on board in spite of the words of the Druid' — and vengeance itself is postponed by the penalty of the broken rule.
summary.zh: 晝夜划行後，他們抵達兩座荒島，聽見武裝者的爭吵：「正是我殺了戰刃埃利爾、焚其教堂，至今無族人復仇。」梅爾敦欲登岸復仇，狂風驟起，將小舟吹入無垠大洋——「是你們違德魯伊之言擅自登舟，招此懲罰。」復仇因破誓之罰而延宕。

sensitivity.note: The wind that blows the avenger away from his vengeance is the immram's fixed moral device — the quest is penance, not reprisal; the two fort islands parallel the twin-fort openings of voyage literature (cf. the Coire Brecain twin isles). Symbolic pin.

passages.text: Maeldun and his crew had rowed all day and half the night when they came to two small bare islands with two forts in them, and a noise was heard from them of armed men quarrelling. "Stand off from me, for I am a better man than thou. 'Twas I slew Ailill of the Edge-of-Battle and burned the church of Doocloone over him, and no kinsman has avenged his death on me. And thou hast never done the like of that."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 梅尔敦与他的船员划了一整天又半夜，来到两座光秃的小岛，岛上有两座堡垒，从中传出武装之人争吵的声音。“离我远些，因为我比你强。是我杀了战阵边缘的艾利尔，并把杜克卢恩的教堂烧在他身上，至今没有哪个亲族为他向我复仇。而你从未做过这样的事。”

passages.text: Then Maeldun was about to land, and German and Diuran the Rhymer cried that God had guided them to the spot where they would be. But a great wind arose suddenly and blew them off into the boundless ocean, and Maeldun said to his foster-brothers: "Ye have caused this to be, casting yourselves on board in spite of the words of the Druid." And they had no answer, save only to be silent for a little space.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隨後梅爾敦正欲登岸，格爾曼與吟遊詩人迪烏蘭高呼，說天主已引領他們來到他們將要抵達之地。但一陣大風驟然颳起，把他們吹離，捲入無邊無際的大洋之中。梅爾敦便對他的義兄弟們說：「這是你們造成的，你們不顧德魯伊的話，硬是上了船。」他們無言以對，只得沉默片刻。

title.en: The Little Cat and the Necklace of Ashes
title.zh: 小貓與化灰的項鍊

region.en: Tower island of the white houses (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 白屋高塔之島（象徵定位）

period: Voyage of Maeldun (Imram Maelduin), retold in T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911)

source.work: T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911), ch. VII, eBook #34630

summary.en: Hungry and thirsting, they reach a tall white tower of chalk reaching up to the clouds, and enter the great house where no man is — only a little cat playing on four stone pillars, leaping from one to the other; on the walls hang three rows of brooches, neck-torques as big as cask-hoops, and great swords with gold and silver hilts, and a roasted ox with abundance of liquor lies ready. They eat and sleep; and next morning the youngest foster-brother takes a necklace from the wall — and the cat leaps through him like a fiery arrow, and he falls a heap of ashes.
summary.zh: 飢渴交加之際，他們登上一座直插雲霄的白堊高塔之島；大屋中無人，唯有一隻小貓在四根石柱間跳躍嬉戲；牆上掛著三排金銀胸針、桶箍般大的金銀項圈與金柄寶劍，烤牛與美酒已備。他們飽食安睡；翌晨最年輕的乳兄弟竟從牆上取走項鍊——小貓如烈焰之箭穿身而過，他倒地化為一堆灰燼。

sensitivity.note: The cat that leaps 'like a fiery arrow' is the fixed guardian-sprite of the immram's wonder-houses (the Island of the Little Cat is the voyage's most famous theft-punishment); hospitality taken freely but a jewel stolen = death — a clean moral of otherworld property. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: This was, as it were, a tall white tower of chalk reaching up to the clouds, and on the rampart about it were great houses white as snow. They entered the largest of them, and found no man in it, but a small cat playing on four stone pillars which were in the midst of the house, leaping from one to the other. It looked a little on the Irish warriors, but did not cease from its play. On the walls of the houses there were three rows of objects hanging up, one row of brooches of gold and silver, and one of neck-torques of gold and silver, each as big as the hoop of a cask, and one of great swords with gold and silver hilts. Quilts and shining garments lay in the room, and there, also, were a roasted ox and a flitch of bacon and abundance of liquor.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那彷彿是一座高聳的白堊白塔，直插雲霄，塔周圍的城牆上矗立著許多白如雪的巨屋。他們走進其中最大的一座，裡面不見一人，只有一隻小貓在屋中央的四根石柱上嬉戲，從一根跳到另一根。牠朝這些愛爾蘭武士稍稍看了一眼，卻並未停止玩耍。屋牆上掛著三排物件：一排是金銀胸針，一排是金銀項圈，每一個都大如木桶的箍環，還有一排是金銀劍柄的巨劍。屋內鋪著被褥和閃亮的衣裳，那裡還有一頭烤牛、一整條鹹肉，以及豐盛的美酒。

passages.text: "Hath this been left for us?" said Maeldun to the cat. It looked at him a moment, and then continued its play. So there they ate and drank and slept, and stored up what remained of the food. Next day, as they made to leave the house, the youngest of Maeldun's foster-brothers took a necklace from the wall, and was bearing it out when the cat suddenly "leaped through him like a fiery arrow," and he fell, a heap of ashes, on the floor. Thereupon Maeldun, who had forbidden the theft of the jewel, soothed the cat and replaced the necklace, and they strewed the ashes of the dead youth on the sea-shore, and put to sea again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.
