region.en: Bukidnon highlands, northern Mindanao, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Bukidnon tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨北部布基農高地（布基農故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Bukidnon oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Bukidnon: 'Magbangal', eBook #12814

summary.en: The powerful hunter Magbangal goes alone to clear land for planting, and his ten bolos and hatchets sharpen themselves on the stone and cut the forest with no hands to guide them. His wife, spying on him, breaks the magic: Magbangal wakes, seizes a bolo, and cuts off one of his own arms. He ascends to become the constellation Magbangal — appearing when it is time to plant rice — while his wife goes into the water and becomes a fish.
summary.zh: 獵人馬格邦加獨自前往墾地，其十柄波洛刀與斧頭自行就石磨利、無人操縱而砍伐林木。妻子窺探之舉破了法術：馬格邦加驚醒，抓起一刀自斷一臂。他升天化為馬格邦加星宿——稻作播種之季由此星昭示——妻子則入水化魚。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bukidnon narrators; presented as an archival record. The constellation is an agricultural sign-calendar; oracle-divination tag is used for the celestial sign that regulates the planting season.

passages.text: Magbangal was a good hunter who often went to a certain hill and killed wild pigs for food. One night, as the planting season neared, he told his wife he would go to the hill alone the next day to clear the land, and she was not to come. She begged to accompany him, but he refused, and in the morning she cooked rice and fish for him to eat on his return. He gathered up his ten hatchets and bolos, a sharpening stone, and a bamboo tube for water, and set out for the hill, where he cut small trees to make a bench and sat down upon it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Magbangal'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 马格班加尔是个好猎手，常到某座山上猎杀野猪为食。一天夜里，播种的季节将近，他告诉妻子，第二天他要独自上山开地，她不可跟来。她恳求同去，他却不肯；次日清晨，她煮了米饭和鱼，供他回来时吃。他收拾好十把斧头和砍刀、一块磨刀石，以及一节装水的竹筒，便出发上山，在那里砍下小树做了一条长凳，坐了上去。

passages.text: Then Magbangal spoke to his weapons: "You bolos must sharpen yourselves on the stone," and the bolos went to the stone and were sharpened. "You hatchets must be sharpened," and they also sharpened themselves. "Now you bolos cut all the small brush under the trees, and you hatchets must cut the large trees." The weapons went to work, and from his bench Magbangal watched the land being cleared while he slept. His wife, weaving a skirt at home, heard the trees continually falling and thought her husband must have found many helpers; walking toward the field, she stopped behind a tree and saw him asleep, while bolos and hatchets cut the trees with no hands to guide them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Magbangal'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 于是马格班加尔对他的武器说：“你们这些砍刀，必须在石上磨利自己。”砍刀便走到石边，磨利了。“你们这些斧头，必须磨利。”它们也磨利了自己。“现在，你们砍刀去砍光树下所有的小灌木，你们斧头去砍倒大树。”武器便动手干活，马格班加尔坐在长凳上，一边睡，一边看着土地被开垦出来。他的妻子在家织着裙子，听见树木不断倒下，心想丈夫必定找了许多帮手；她朝田地走去，停在一棵树后，只见他睡着了，而砍刀和斧头没有手引导，却在砍伐树木。

passages.text: She marveled that Magbangal had never told her of his power. Suddenly he jumped up, seized a bolo, and cut off one of his own arms; waking, he sat up and said, "Someone must be looking at me, for one of my arms is cut off." Knowing his wife was the cause, he went home with her, saying, "Now I am going away. It is better for me to go to the sky where I can give the sign to the people when it is time to plant; and you must go to the water and become a fish." Soon after he went to the sky and became the constellation Magbangal, and ever since, when the people see these stars appear, they know it is time to plant their rice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Magbangal'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她惊异于马格班加尔从未向她提起过自己的法力。忽然，他跳起身来，抓起一把砍刀，砍断了自己的一条手臂；他醒来坐起，说道：“一定有人在看我，因为我的一条手臂被砍断了。”他知道是妻子所致，便与她一同回家，说道：“现在我要走了。我去天上更好，到了播种的时候，我可以给人们示意；而你须到水里去，变成一条鱼。”不久之后，他上了天，化为马格班加尔星座；从此以后，人们一见这些星星出现，便知道该种稻了。

title.en: How Children Became Monkeys
title.zh: 孩童化猿猴

region.en: Bukidnon highlands, northern Mindanao, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Bukidnon tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨北部布基農高地（布基農故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Bukidnon oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Bukidnon: 'How Children Became Monkeys', eBook #12814

summary.en: A mother takes her two children along to color cloth in a carabao mud hole. As she stirs the dye pot, scalding water splashes her hand and she jumps and cries out; the children's laughter changes them into monkeys, and the shell spoons they hold become their tails. Their nails are still black from the days when, as children, they helped their mother dye cloth.
summary.zh: 母親攜二孩至水牛打滾的泥塘染布。攪動染鍋時滾水濺起燙手，她跳起驚叫；孩童大笑之際化作猿猴，手中貝殼湯匙化為其尾。猿猴的指甲至今仍黑——因為他們做孩子時曾幫母親染布。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bukidnon narrators; presented as an archival record. Etiological tale of monkey tails and black nails.

passages.text: One day a mother took her two children with her when she went to color cloth. Not far from her home was a mud hole where the carabao liked to wallow, and to this hole she carried her cloth, some dye pots, and two shell spoons. After she had put the cloth into the mud to let it take up the dark color, she built a fire and set over it a pot containing water and the leaves used for dyeing, and sat down to wait for the water to boil while the children played near by.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'How Children Became Monkeys'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一天，一位母亲带着她的两个孩子去染布。离家不远有一个泥坑，水牛喜欢在那里打滚；她把布、几只染锅和两把贝壳匙带到这个坑边。她把布放进泥里，让它染上深色，随后生起火，架上锅，锅里盛着水和染布用的叶子，然后坐下等水烧开，孩子们就在近旁玩耍。

passages.text: By and by, when she went to stir the leaves with a shell spoon, some of the water splashed up and burned her hand, so that she jumped and cried out. This amused the children, and their laughter changed them into monkeys, and the spoons became their tails. The nails of the monkeys are still black, because while they were children they had helped their mother dye the cloth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'How Children Became Monkeys'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 过了一会儿，她用贝壳匙去搅动叶子，一些水溅了起来，烫伤了她的手，她跳起来大叫。孩子们觉得好笑，他们的笑声把他们变成了猴子，那两把匙子成了他们的尾巴。猴子的指甲至今仍是黑的，因为他们还是孩子的时候，曾帮母亲染过布。

title.en: Bulanawan and Aguio: The Twin Brothers' Battle
title.zh: 布拉納萬與阿圭歐：雙生兄弟之戰

region.en: Bukidnon highlands, northern Mindanao, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Bukidnon tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨北部布基農高地（布基農故事圈之象徵定位）

period: Bukidnon oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Bukidnon: 'Bulanawan and Aguio', eBook #12814

summary.en: Twins Bulanawan and Aguio are separated in infancy when a whirlwind carries Bulanawan away to a far land, where he grows into a great warrior. Years later Aguio arrives in that land and, not knowing his brother, tries to steal his brother's wife; the duel shakes the earth. Rival second brothers sense the tremor and join the battle, and the quaking grows until Langgona's father, the twins' grandfather, arrives and makes peace — revealing that the combatants were brothers and grandsons.
summary.zh: 雙生子布拉納萬與阿圭歐幼時被旋風拆散，布拉納萬被吹至遠方，長成大勇士。多年後阿圭歐遠遊至此，不知彼此為兄弟，欲奪其嫂；二人決鬥撼動大地。各自的結拜兄弟感得地動，趕來助戰，震動加劇，大地幾乎崩裂。最後朗戈納之父——雙生子祖父——前來止戈，眾人方知交戰者竟是兄弟與孫輩。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bukidnon narrators; presented as an archival record. Twins/duality cluster: twin brothers whose battle shakes the cosmos, resolved by an elder peacemaker.

passages.text: Langgona and his wife had twin boys named Bulanawan and Aguio. When they were about two years old the mother took Bulanawan with her to the field to pick cotton, and while she was gathering more a great wind suddenly arose which wound the cotton around the baby and carried him away. Far away to a distant land the wind took Bulanawan, and in that place he grew up; when he was a man he became a great warrior. Aguio, too, grew into a great warrior, and one day he journeyed to this distant land, not knowing that his brother was there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Bulanawan and Aguio'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 朗戈納（Langgona）與妻子有一對雙胞胎男孩，名叫布拉納萬（Bulanawan）與阿吉奧（Aguio）。他們大約兩歲時，母親帶著布拉納萬到田裡採棉花，正當她採得更多時，忽然颳起一陣大風，把棉花纏繞在嬰兒身上，將他捲走了。風把布拉納萬帶到遠方一片遙遠的土地，他在那裡長大；長大成人後，他成了一名偉大的戰士。阿吉奧也長成一名偉大的戰士，有一天他遠行來到這片遙遠的土地，卻不知自己的兄弟就在那裡。

passages.text: That same day Bulanawan and his wife sat resting on a large flat rock by the seashore, and Bulanawan fell asleep. Aguio, walking along the shore in his war-dress, thought the woman very beautiful and determined to steal her. He asked for some of her husband's betel-nut to chew; when she refused, he went forward to fight her husband, not knowing they were brothers. When his wife awakened him, Bulanawan sprang up, seized her, and put her in the cuff of his sleeve before coming forth to fight. They fought until their weapons were broken and the earth trembled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Bulanawan and Aguio'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 就在同一天，布拉納萬與妻子坐在海邊一塊大而平坦的岩石上歇息，布拉納萬睡著了。阿吉奧穿著戰服沿著海岸走來，覺得那女人十分美麗，便決意要把她奪走。他向她要一些她丈夫的檳榔來嚼；她拒絕後，他便上前要與她丈夫搏鬥，卻不知彼此是兄弟。妻子喚醒布拉納萬後，他猛然躍起，一把抓住她，將她塞進自己的袖口，然後出來迎戰。他們一直打到兵器盡折、大地震顫。

passages.text: Far away, the rival brothers of the two combatants felt the earth tremble, and each, fearing his brother was in trouble, hastened to the scene — one from the mountains, one by boat across the sea. They arrived at the same time and joined the battle. The trembling increased so much that Langgona, father of the twins, sought out the spot and tried to make peace, but he only made matters worse, and they all began fighting him, until the earth was in danger of falling to pieces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Bulanawan and Aguio'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在遠方，這兩名交戰者的敵對兄弟感受到了大地的震顫，各自擔心自己的兄弟遭遇危難，便急忙趕往現場——一人從山中而來，一人乘船渡海而來。他們同時抵達，加入了戰鬥。震動越發劇烈，以致雙胞胎的父親朗戈納尋到該處，試圖調停，卻只是把事情弄得更糟，眾人竟全都開始與他打了起來，直到大地幾乎要崩裂成碎片。

passages.text: Then the father of Langgona came and settled the trouble, and when all were at peace again they discovered that Aguio and Bulanawan were brothers and the grandsons of the peacemaker. Thus the tale binds the great quake-makers of the Bukidnon past into one family, and the shaking earth becomes the sign of kindred turned against kindred without knowing it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Bulanawan and Aguio'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 後來朗戈納的父親前來平息了這場紛爭，當一切重歸安寧之後，他們才發現阿吉奧與布拉納萬原是兄弟，也是這位調停者的孫子。於是這個故事把布基農（Bukidnon）往昔那些偉大的地震製造者結為一家人，而震動的大地便成了親族在不知情之下彼此相爭的徵兆。

title.en: Origin: Toglai and Toglibon and the First Tribes
title.zh: 起源：托格萊與托格利邦及諸族之始

region.en: Cibolan, Mt. Apo, Davao, Mindanao, Philippines
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨達沃阿波火山錫博蘭

period: Bagobo oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Bagobo: 'Origin', eBook #12814

summary.en: The first couple Toglai and Toglibon live at Cibolan on Mt. Apo. After their eldest children depart across the waters — returning only as the Spaniards and Americans — a three-year drought dries every river, and the surviving children leave in pairs, each pair carrying some household thing from which a tribe takes its name: stones for the Magindanau, women's baskets for the Bilaan. Only a boy and girl too weak to travel remain; finding a single stalk of sugar-cane, they drink its water and survive, and their children are called Bagobo.
summary.zh: 初民夫婦托格萊與托格利邦居於阿波火山之錫博蘭。長子女渡水遠去，後裔即所謂西班牙人與美國人。其後三年大旱，河川盡涸；倖存子女兩兩離散，各攜一物——攜石者成馬京達瑙族，攜婦籃者成比拉蘭族，諸族之名皆源於所攜之物或所居之地。唯餘一對因飢渴過甚而無力遠行者，尋得一莖甘蔗飲汁度日；其子孫遂名巴戈博。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bagobo narrators; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Bagobo communities. Ethnogenesis legend naming Bagobo, Bilaan, and Magindanau; the late-colonial framing (Spaniards and Americans) is retained as recorded, noting the tale's living tradition of adaptation.

passages.text: In the beginning there lived one man and one woman, Toglai and Toglibon. Their first children were a boy and a girl, and when they were old enough they went far away across the waters seeking a good place to live. Nothing more was heard of them until their children, the Spaniards and Americans, came back. After the first boy and girl left, other children were born to the couple, but they all remained at Cibolan on Mt. Apo with their parents, until Toglai and Toglibon died and became spirits.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bagobo 'Origin'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 起初，世上住著一男一女，托格萊（Toglai）與托格利邦（Toglibon）。他們最初的孩子是一男一女，當他們長到足夠大時，便遠渡重洋，去尋找適宜居住的好地方。此後再無他們的消息，直到他們的子孫——西班牙人與美國人——歸來。最初那男孩與女孩離去之後，這對夫妻又生下了其他孩子，但他們都與父母一同留在阿波山（Mt. Apo）上的西博蘭（Cibolan），直到托格萊與托格利邦死去，化為神靈。

passages.text: Soon after, a great drought came which lasted three years. All the waters dried up, so that there were no rivers and no plants could live. "Surely," said the people, "Manama is punishing us, and we must go elsewhere to find food and a place to dwell in." So they started out. Two went toward the sunset carrying stones from Cibolan River, and after a long journey they reached broad fields of cogon grass and abundance of water; their children still live there and are called Magindanau, because of the stones the couple carried when they left Cibolan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bagobo 'Origin'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久之後，來了一場持續三年的大旱。所有水源都乾涸了，以致河川全無，草木也無法存活。「定然是，」人們說，「馬納馬（Manama）在懲罰我們，我們必須到別處去尋找食物和棲身之地。」於是他們出發了。有兩人帶著西博蘭河的石头朝日落的方向而去，經過長途跋涉，他們來到廣闊的茅草（cogon）原野與豐沛的水源之地；他們的子孫至今仍住在那裡，被稱為馬金達瑙人（Magindanau），因為這對夫妻離開西博蘭時帶著那些石頭。

passages.text: Two children went to the south carrying women's baskets (baraan), and settled where they found a good spot; their descendants are called Baraan or Bilaan, because of the women's baskets. So two by two the children of the first couple left the land of their birth, and in each place a new people developed — thus all the tribes in the world received their names from things the people carried out of Cibolan, or from the places where they settled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bagobo 'Origin'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兩個孩子帶著女人的籃子（baraan）往南走，找到一處好地方便定居下來；他們的後代因為那些女人的籃子，被稱為 Baraan 或 Bilaan。於是，第一對夫妻的孩子們兩個兩個地離開他們出生的土地，在每一個地方都發展出新的民族——因此，世上所有的部族，其名稱都來自人們從 Cibolan 帶出來的東西，或來自他們定居的地方。

passages.text: All the children left Mt. Apo save a boy and a girl whom hunger and thirst had made too weak to travel. One day, when they were about to die, the boy crawled out to the field to see if there was one living thing, and to his surprise he found a stalk of sugar-cane growing lustily. He eagerly cut it, and enough water came out to refresh him and his sister until the rains came. Because of this, their children are called Bagobo.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bagobo 'Origin'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 所有的孩子都離開了阿波山，只剩一個男孩和一個女孩，他們因飢渴而虛弱得無法趕路。有一天，他們快要死去時，男孩爬到田裡，看看是否還有活著的東西，令他驚訝的是，他發現一株甘蔗正茂盛地生長著。他急切地把它砍下，流出的汁水足夠讓他和妹妹恢復精神，直到雨季來臨。因為這件事，他們的後代被稱為 Bagobo。

title.en: Lumabet and the White Deer: The Ascent to the Sky
title.zh: 盧馬貝特與白鹿：升天

region.en: Cibolan, Mt. Apo, Davao, Mindanao, Philippines
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨達沃阿波火山錫博蘭

period: Bagobo oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Bagobo: 'Lumabet', eBook #12814

summary.en: Lumabet, who could talk at one day old and worked wonders, chases a white deer around the world nine times, feeding himself by planting the skins of one banana and one camote each night. He has the people kill and revive his father eight times to prove his god-given power, then leads all who believe him through the moving, jaw-like sky to the world above — the sky keeping the last man as its agreed prize. His son follows on an arrow and a golden gun carried by white bees, while one homesick follower is lowered on a chain of karan leaves and becomes an owl.
summary.zh: 盧馬貝特生而一日能言，行諸奇事。他追白鹿環繞世界九匝，夜夜植蕉皮與薯皮為食。為證其神授之力，他八度命眾人殺其父並以頭帶復活之。其後他引信眾穿過開闔如口之天界，天得最後一人為酬；其子乘箭與金槍，由白蜂引路升天。而一名思鄉者被以卡蘭草鏈垂降，落地化為貓頭鷹。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bagobo narrators; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Bagobo communities. Ascension cluster: a people-led migration to the sky at the horizon; resurrection tag covers the thrice-killed and revived father, an interpretive mapping.

passages.text: Soon after people were created on the earth there was born a child named Lumabet, who lived to be a very, very old man. He could talk when he was but one day old, and all his life he did wonderful things, until the people came to believe that he had been sent by Manama, the Great Spirit. As a young man he had a fine dog, and one day the dog scented a white deer. Lumabet and his companions pursued the swift deer but could not catch it; on and on they went until they had gone around the world, and one by one his companions dropped out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Lumabet'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 世上的人被創造出來後不久，便誕生了一個名叫 Lumabet 的孩子，他活到非常非常老。他才出生一天就會說話，一生中做了許多奇妙的事，直到人們開始相信他是偉大的神靈 Manama 所派來的。他年輕時有一隻好狗，有一天，那隻狗嗅到了一頭白鹿的氣味。Lumabet 和他的同伴們追趕那頭迅捷的鹿，卻抓不到牠；他們一路追下去，直到繞行了世界一圈，他的同伴們也一個接一個地掉了隊。

passages.text: All the time Lumabet had but one banana and one camote for food, but each night he planted the skins of these, and in the morning he found a banana tree with ripe fruit and a sweet potato large enough to eat. So he kept on until he had been around the world nine times, an old man with gray hair. At last he caught the deer, and he called all the people to a great feast. While they made merry, Lumabet told them to take a knife and kill his father. They were greatly surprised, but did as he commanded; when the old man was dead, Lumabet waved his headband over him and he came to life again. Eight times they killed the old man at Lumabet's command, and the eighth time he was small like a little boy, for each time they had cut off some of his flesh. They were certain Lumabet was a god.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Lumabet'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這段期間，Lumabet 只有一根香蕉和一顆甘藷（camote）作為食物，但每晚他都把這些的皮種下，到了早晨，他便發現長出了一棵結著熟果的香蕉樹，以及一顆大到足以充飢的甘藷。他就這樣繼續下去，直到繞行世界九圈，成了一個頭髮灰白的老人。最後他終於抓到了那頭鹿，便召集所有人來參加一場盛大的宴會。正當他們歡慶時，Lumabet 叫他們拿刀殺死他的父親。他們大為驚訝，但仍照他的命令做了；老人死後，Lumabet 在他身上揮動頭帶，他便又活了過來。他們照 Lumabet 的命令殺死老人八次，第八次時，老人變得像個小男孩一樣小，因為每一次他們都切掉了他的一些肉。他們確信 Lumabet 是一位神。

passages.text: One morning some spirits came to talk with Lumabet, and after they had gone he called the people into his house. Though the house was small and the people many, all went in and it did not seem crowded. Then he told them he was going on a long journey: all who believed in his power could go with him, while those who remained behind would be changed into animals and buso. He started out with many following, and those who refused were immediately changed into animals and buso. He led the people across the ocean to the place where the earth and sky meet, and there the sky moved up and down like a man opening and closing his jaws. "Sky, you must go up," commanded Lumabet, but the sky would not obey until Lumabet promised it the last man who tried to pass. The sky opened, the people entered, and near the last it shut down so suddenly that it caught not only the last man but also the long knife of the man before him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Lumabet'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天早晨，一些神靈來與 Lumabet 交談，他們離去後，他便把人們叫進他的屋裡。雖然屋子小、人又多，所有人卻都進去了，而且並不顯得擁擠。接著他告訴他們，他即將踏上漫長的旅程：所有相信他力量的人都可以跟他走，而留下來的人則會變成動物和 buso。他帶著許多人出發，那些拒絕的人立刻變成了動物和 buso。他帶領人們渡過海洋，來到大地與天空相接之處，那裡的天空像人開合下巴一樣上下移動。「天空，你必須升起，」Lumabet 命令道，但天空不肯服從，直到 Lumabet 承諾把最後一個試圖通過的人給它。天空打開了，人們走了進去，快到最後時，天空突然闔上，不僅夾住了最後一個人，還夾住了他前面那個人的長刀。

passages.text: On that same day Lumabet's son, out hunting, did not know his father had gone to the sky. Tired of the chase, he leaned an arrow against a baliti tree and sat on it; slowly it began to go down and carried him to his father's place, but he could find no people there — only a gun made of gold. White bees in the house said, "You must not weep, for we can take you to the sky where your father is," and they flew him up on the gun, reaching the sky in three days. Most of the followers were content in the sky, but one was unhappy, always looking down at the land below. The spirits made fun of him and wished to take out his intestines so he would be like them and never die, but he begged to go home. Finally Manama told them to allow it; they made a chain of the leaves of the karan grass, tied it to his legs, and let him down slowly head first — and when he reached the ground he was no longer a man but an owl.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Lumabet'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 就在同一天，Lumabet 的兒子外出打獵，並不知道父親已去了天空。他追獵疲倦了，便把一支箭靠在榕樹（baliti）上，坐了上去；箭緩緩下沉，載著他到了父親所在之處，但他在那裡找不到任何人——只有一把黃金打造的槍。屋裡的白蜂說：「你不必哭泣，因為我們能帶你到天空你父親那裡。」牠們便載著他乘著那把槍飛上去，三天後抵達天空。大多數跟隨者在天空中都過得安適，但有一個人卻不快樂，總是俯視下方的大地。神靈們取笑他，想要取出他的腸子，好讓他像他們一樣永遠不死，但他懇求回家。最後 Manama 吩咐他們准許他回去；他們用 karan 草的葉子編成一條鏈子，綁在他的腿上，讓他頭朝下緩緩降下——當他到達地面時，他已不再是個人，而是一隻貓頭鷹。

title.en: In the Beginning: The Four Beings on the Hat-Sized Island
title.zh: 太初：斗笠之島上的四神

region.en: Lake Sebu region, South Cotabato, Mindanao, Philippines (Bilaan homeland)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨南哥達巴托省賽布湖（比拉蘭人故地）

period: Bilaan oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Bilaan: 'In the Beginning', eBook #12814

summary.en: Four beings live on an island no larger than a hat with a single bird; the bird flies across the waters and returns with earth, rattan, and fruit. Melu, the greatest, shapes and beats the soil like a woman molding pots, making the earth, and plants the fruit seeds. The beings first try to make people out of wax, which melts; then out of dirt — but Melu's companion sets the noses upside down. While his back is turned, Melu seizes each nose and turns it right, hurrying so that his finger-press at the root of the nose remains on every human face.
summary.zh: 四神居於僅如斗笠大小之島，島上唯彼等與一鳥。鳥飛越水域銜回泥土、藤與果實。至大者梅盧如婦人製陶般捶塑泥土而成大地，並植果核，藤蔓果樹滋長。四神先以蠟造人，置火即融；改以泥土塑形——同伴卻把鼻子捏反。趁其轉身，梅盧逐個扳正鼻樑，倉促之間以指壓鼻根，人臉上那道指痕至今猶在。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Bilaan narrators; presented as an archival record. Clay-humans cluster (wax fails, earth succeeds, noses reversed).

passages.text: In the beginning there were four beings, and they lived on an island no larger than a hat. On this island there were no trees or grass or any other living thing besides these four people and one bird. One day they sent the bird out across the waters to see what it could find, and when it returned it brought some earth, a piece of rattan, and some fruit. Melu, the greatest of the four, took the soil and shaped it and beat it with a paddle in the same manner in which a woman shapes pots of clay, and when he finished he had made the earth. Then he planted the seeds from the fruit, and they grew until there was much rattan and many trees bearing fruit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bilaan 'In the Beginning'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 起初有四個生靈，他們住在一座不比一頂帽子更大的島上。這座島上沒有樹木、沒有青草，除了這四個人和一只鳥之外，也沒有任何其他生物。有一天，他們派那只鳥飛越水面，去看看能發現什麼；鳥回來時，帶回了一些泥土、一截藤蔓和一些果實。四人之中最偉大的梅魯（Melu）取來泥土，把它塑成形，又用槳拍打，就像女人塑造陶罐那樣；等他做完，便造出了大地。接著他種下果實裡的種子，種子生長起來，直到長出許多藤蔓和許多結著果實的樹木。

passages.text: The four beings watched the growth for a long time and were well pleased, but finally Melu said, "Of what use is this earth and all the rattan and fruit if there are no people?" The others replied, "Let us make some people out of wax." So they took wax and worked long, fashioning it into forms; but when they brought the figures to the fire the wax melted, and they saw that men could not be made in that way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bilaan 'In the Beginning'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這四個生靈久久地看著萬物生長，十分滿意，但最後梅魯說：「這大地和這一切藤蔓與果實，若沒有人，又有什麼用呢？」其他幾個回答：「讓我們用蠟來造一些人吧。」於是他們取來蠟，工作了許久，把它捏成人的形狀；但當他們把這些形體拿到火邊時，蠟便融化了，他們看出人是不能用這種方法造出來的。

passages.text: Next they decided to try dirt, and Melu and one of his companions began working. All went well until they were ready to make the noses: the companion, working on that part, put them on upside down. Melu told him the people would drown if he left them that way, but he refused to change them. When his back was turned, however, Melu seized the noses one by one and turned them as they now are — but he was in such a hurry that he pressed his finger at the root, and it left a mark in the soft clay which you can still see on the faces of people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Bilaan 'In the Beginning'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著他們決定試用泥土，梅魯和他的一個同伴便開始動手。一切都很順利，直到他們準備做鼻子：那個同伴在做這一部分時，把鼻子裝反了。梅魯告訴他，若照這樣留著，人會淹死，但他不肯改。然而，趁他轉過身去的時候，梅魯把鼻子一個一個抓住，轉成如今這副模樣——但他動作太急，手指在鼻根處按了一下，於是在柔軟的泥土上留下了印記，這印記至今仍能在人的臉上看到。

title.en: The Children of the Limokon
title.zh: 利莫康鳥之子

region.en: Mayo River, Davao Oriental, Mindanao, Philippines (Mandaya homeland)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨東達沃省馬耀河（曼達雅人故地）

period: Mandaya oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Mandaya: 'The Children of the Limokon', eBook #12814

summary.en: In the very early days, the limokon doves were powerful and could talk like men. One limokon laid two eggs, one at the mouth of the Mayo River and one farther up its course; the first hatched a man, the second a woman. The man lived alone on the riverbank until a hair swept against his legs as he crossed the river; following the current upstream, he found the woman, and they married — their many children are the Mandaya still living along the Mayo River.
summary.zh: 太初之世，利莫康鳥神力無邊，形雖似鳥而言如人。一利莫康產二卵，一於馬耀河口，一於上游；前者孵化為男，後者為女。男子獨居河岸甚久，一日渡河時有髮絲強力沖撞其腿；溯流而上，終尋得女子，二人成婚——其眾多子孫即今居馬耀河畔之曼達雅人。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Mandaya narrators; presented as an archival record. Ethnogenesis legend: humanity born of bird eggs on the river, with the first couple united by a hair in the current.

passages.text: In the very early days, before there were any people on the earth, the limokon, a kind of dove, were very powerful and could talk like men though they looked like birds. One limokon laid two eggs, one at the mouth of the Mayo River and one farther up its course. After some time these eggs hatched, and the one at the mouth of the river became a man, while the other became a woman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Children of the Limokon'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在很久很久以前，大地上還沒有人類的時候，limokon（一種鴿子）非常強大，雖然外形像鳥，卻能像人一樣說話。有一只 limokon 下了兩個蛋，一個下在馬約河（Mayo River）的河口，另一個下在河的上游較遠處。過了些時候，這些蛋孵化了，河口的那個變成了一個男人，另一個則變成了一個女人。

passages.text: The man lived alone on the bank of the river for a long time, very lonely, and wished many times for a companion. One day when he was crossing the river something was swept against his legs with such force that it nearly caused him to drown. Examining it, he found it was a hair, and he determined to go up the river to find where it came from. He traveled up the stream, looking on both banks, until finally he found the woman, and he was very happy to think that at last he could have a companion. They were married and had many children, who are the Mandaya still living along the Mayo River.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Children of the Limokon'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那個男人獨自住在河岸上很久，非常孤單，許多次盼望能有個伴。有一天，他過河時，有東西猛烈地撞上他的雙腿，幾乎使他淹死。他察看那東西，發現是一根頭髮，便決心沿河而上，找出它來自何處。他溯流而上，察看兩岸，終於找到了那個女人，想到自己終於能有個伴，他非常高興。他們結了婚，生了許多孩子，這些孩子就是至今仍住在馬約河沿岸的曼達亞人（Mandaya）。

title.en: The Sun, the Moon, and the Lightning Crab (Mandaya)
title.zh: 日月與雷光巨蟹（曼達雅）

region.en: Mayo River, Davao Oriental, Mindanao, Philippines (Mandaya homeland)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨東達沃省馬耀河（曼達雅人故地）

period: Mandaya oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Mandaya: 'The Sun and the Moon', eBook #12814

summary.en: The Sun and Moon are married, but the Sun is ugly and quarrelsome and chases the Moon eternally, sometimes almost catching her. Their first child, a great star like a man, is cut into small pieces by the angry Sun and scattered over the sky like a woman scatters rice — hence the many stars. Another child, a gigantic crab, causes lightning with each blink of his eyes, makes the tides from his hole in the sea's bottom, and when angry at his mother the Moon tries to swallow her — the people beat gongs and shout until he is frightened away.
summary.zh: 日月成婚，然太陽醜陋易怒，追逐月亮至今，時近時遠。長子為巨大星辰，形如人；被盛怒之太陽剁成小塊，如婦人撒米般散布天空——星辰由是繁多。另一子為巨蟹，一眨眼便生閃電，居海底巨穴而司潮汐；忤怒母親月亮時，竟欲吞之——世人愛月，見巨蟹近月便鳴鑼高呼，將其嚇退，月亮乃得保全。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Mandaya narrators; presented as an archival record. The giant crab is a cosmic sea-beast controlling tides and lightning; world-serpent tag is an interpretive mapping (vast creature underlying/threatening the cosmos). Gongs-against-the-eclipse custom is preserved.

passages.text: The Sun and the Moon were married, but the Sun was very ugly and quarrelsome. One day he became angry at the Moon and started to chase her. She ran very fast until she was some distance ahead of him, when she grew tired and he almost caught her. Ever since he has been chasing her, at times almost reaching her, and again falling far behind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Mandaya 'The Sun and the Moon'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 太陽和月亮結了婚，但太陽非常醜陋，又愛爭吵。有一天，他對月亮發了怒，便開始追她。她跑得很快，直到把他甩開了一段距離，這時她累了，而他幾乎追上了她。從那以後，他就一直在追她，有時幾乎追上，有時又遠遠落在後面。

passages.text: The first child of the Sun and Moon was a large star, and he was like a man. One time the Sun, becoming angry at the star, cut him up into small pieces and scattered him over the whole sky just as a woman scatters rice, and ever since there have been many stars. Another child of the Sun and Moon was a gigantic crab. He still lives and is so powerful that every time he opens and closes his eyes there is a flash of lightning. Most of the time the crab lives in a large hole in the bottom of the sea, and when he is there we have high tide; but when he leaves the hole, the waters rush in and there is low tide. His moving about also causes great waves on the surface of the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Mandaya 'The Sun and the Moon'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 太陽與月亮的第一個孩子是一顆巨大的星星，他長得像人。有一次，太陽對他發怒，把他切成小塊，撒遍整個天空，就像女人撒米一樣，從那時起就有了許多星星。太陽與月亮的另一個孩子是一隻巨大的螃蟹。他至今仍活著，而且力量強大，每當他睜眼閉眼，就會閃出一道閃電。大部分時間，螃蟹住在海底的一個大洞裡，當他在洞裡時，我們就有漲潮；但當他離開那個洞時，海水湧入，就有退潮。他的移動也會在海上引起巨浪。

passages.text: The crab is quarrelsome like his father, and he sometimes becomes so angry with his mother, the Moon, that he tries to swallow her. When the people on earth, who are fond of the Moon, see the crab near her, they run out of doors and shout and beat on gongs until he is frightened away, and thus the Moon is saved. This is the tale of the eclipse and of the custom of driving the devourer off with gongs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Mandaya 'The Sun and the Moon'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這隻螃蟹像他父親一樣好爭吵，他有時對母親月亮非常生氣，氣到想要吞下她。當地上的人們——他們喜愛月亮——看見螃蟹靠近她時，就會跑出門外大喊並敲鑼，直到把他嚇走，月亮因此得救。這就是月食的故事，以及用鑼驅趕吞噬者的習俗。

title.en: The Widow's Son: The Seven Warriors, the Giant, and the Spirit of the Stone
title.zh: 寡婦之子：七武士、巨人與石神

region.en: Zamboanga peninsula, western Mindanao, Philippines (Subanun homeland)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨三寶顏半島（蘇巴農人故地）

period: Subanun oral tradition; recorded 1916 (Cole)

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Subanun: 'The Widow's Son', eBook #12814

summary.en: A widow's son kills a white-legged pig that runs seven times up the mountain before dying on a great flat rock; a door opens in the stone and he spends seven days feasting with its master, who makes a brother of him. On the way home seven color-robed warriors with matching eyes attack him, and a spirit calls his weapons from home to defend him; he slays all seven in three days' fighting, then a giant, before the spirit reveals that the stone spirit sent the seven to kill him because it saw he would marry the orphan girl it wished to wed. Wine restored the slain to life, and at the great feast the widow's son married the orphan while the stone spirit wedded another.
summary.zh: 寡婦之子獵得一頭四足皆白之豬；豬七度奔上山巔，終斃於巨岩。岩中忽開一門，主人以七彩之衣盛宴款待，結為兄弟。歸途中七位衣色各異、眼色相配之武士截殺他；家中的矛盾劍受神靈召喚而來，他血戰三日連斃七人，再戰巨人三日，殺之而焚其宅。神靈揭示：石神見他命中將娶孤女（石神所願者），遂遣七武士殺他。眾人以酒復活死者，大宴上寡婦之子娶孤女，石神另娶美人。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Subanun narrators; presented as an archival record. Heroic quest tale with fate seen in the hand, slain enemies restored by wine, and a spirit-fated marriage.

passages.text: In a little house at the edge of a village lived a widow with her only son, and they made their living growing rice in clearings on the mountainside and hunting wild pig in the forest. One evening, with their meat low, the boy asked his mother to prepare rice before daylight so he could hunt. At dawn he set out with his spear and dog, walked far into the thick forest, and rested on a rock under the hot sun, chewing betel-nut, when his dog began barking sharply. He ran toward it and saw a fine large pig, all black save its four legs which were white.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Widow's Son'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在村莊邊緣的一間小屋裡，住著一位寡婦和她唯一的兒子，他們靠在山坡上的開墾地種稻、在森林裡獵野豬為生。有一天傍晚，肉快吃完了，男孩請母親在天亮前準備好米飯，好讓他去打獵。黎明時分，他帶著長矛和狗出發，走進茂密的森林深處，在烈日下的一塊岩石上休息，嚼著檳榔，這時他的狗開始尖聲吠叫。他朝狗跑去，看見一頭肥美的大豬，全身烏黑，只有四條腿是白色的。

passages.text: Six times the pig stopped just long enough for the boy to take aim, and then started on before he could throw, running straight up the mountain; the seventh time it halted on top of a large flat rock, and the boy succeeded in killing it. As he tied its legs, a door in the great stone swung open and a man stepped out asking why he had killed his master's pig. The boy followed him inside to a large room whose ceiling and floor were covered with cloth of seven wide red stripes alternating with seven yellow, and whose master wore trousers, jacket, and head-kerchief of seven colors. They chewed betel-nut and drank seven cups of wine from a jar so large a seat had to be brought for the boy to drink from its reed. The master did not blame him for the pig, declared he wished to make a brother of him, and the boy remained seven days in the stone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Widow's Son'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那頭豬停了六次，每次都只停到男孩來得及瞄準，隨即在他投擲之前又跑開，筆直往山上跑；第七次，牠停在一塊大扁石上，男孩終於把牠殺死了。當他綁住豬腿時，大石上的一扇門打開了，一個男人走出來，問他為什麼殺了他主人的豬。男孩跟著他進去，來到一間大房間，天花板和地板都鋪著布，布上是七道寬闊的紅條紋與七道黃條紋相間，而主人穿著七色的褲子、上衣和頭巾。他們嚼檳榔，從一個大得必須搬來一張凳子讓男孩墊腳才能就著蘆葦管喝的酒甕裡喝了七杯酒。主人沒有責怪他殺豬，還說想與他結為兄弟，男孩便在石中待了七天。

passages.text: On the journey home he was met by seven men, each armed with spear, shield, and sword, dressed in different colors, each man's eyes the color of his clothes. The leader in red said they were warriors who went up and down the world killing whatever they saw that had life, and now they must kill him also. A voice near him cried, "Fight, for they will try to kill you," and looking up he saw his spear, shield, and sword which he had left at home, sent by a spirit. For three days and nights they contended, and never before had the seven seen one man so brave; on the fourth day the leader fell dead, then one by one the other six. Crazed with fighting, the widow's son thought no more of home but started out to find more to slay.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Widow's Son'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在回家的路上，他遇到七個男人，每人各持長矛、盾牌和劍，穿著不同顏色的衣服，每個人的眼睛都與衣服同色。穿紅衣的首領說，他們是戰士，走遍世界，見到有生命的就殺，現在他們也必須殺他。他身旁有個聲音喊道：「戰鬥吧，因為他們會試圖殺你。」他抬頭一看，看見了他留在家裡的長矛、盾牌和劍，是精靈送來的。他們激戰了三天三夜，那七人從未見過一個人如此勇敢；第四天，首領倒地而死，接著其餘六人一個接一個倒下。寡婦的兒子殺得發狂，不再想家，而是出發去尋找更多可殺的對象。

passages.text: He came to the home of a great giant whose house was already full of the men he had conquered, and challenged him; the giant, whose spear-shaft was the trunk of a tree, called him only a fly, but for three days and nights they struggled until the giant fell wounded at the waist. The boy burned the giant's house, and the spirit spoke again: "The seven men whom you killed were sent to kill you by the spirit of the great stone, for he looked in your hand and saw that you were to marry the orphan girl whom he himself wished to wed. But you have conquered. Go home now and prepare a great quantity of wine, for I shall bring your enemies to life again, and you will all live in peace." His mother welcomed him home as one returned from the dead; jars of wine filled the widow's house, and that night at the great feast the spirit of the great stone, his seven warriors, the friendly spirit, and the giant all came. The widow's son married the orphan girl, while another beautiful woman became the wife of the spirit of the stone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Widow's Son'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他來到一個巨人的家，巨人的屋裡已滿是他所征服的人，他向巨人挑戰；那巨人以樹幹為矛桿，只稱他是隻蒼蠅，但他們搏鬥了三天三夜，直到巨人腰部受傷倒下。男孩燒了巨人的房子，精靈又說話了：「你殺的那七個人，是大石的精靈派去殺你的，因為他看你的手相，看出你將娶那個孤女，而他自己也想娶她。但你已經戰勝了。現在回家去，準備大量的酒，因為我要讓你的敵人復活，你們都將平安地生活。」他的母親迎接他回家，如同迎接死而復生的人；寡婦的屋裡裝滿了一甕甕的酒，那天夜裡在大宴會上，大石的精靈、他的七名戰士、友善的精靈和巨人都來了。寡婦的兒子娶了那個孤女，而另一位美麗的女子則成了石之精靈的妻子。

title.en: Jingwei, the Bird That Carries Stones to Fill the Sea
title.zh: 精衛填海

region.en: The East Sea of the myth, off China's east coast (symbolic pin: Fa Mountain lies in the Taihang range; the bird commutes between the western mountains and the sea)
region.zh: 神話東海（象徵性定位：發鳩山在太行，鳥往返西山與東海之間）

period: Shanhaijing, Bei Shan Jing chapter, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing (Classic of Mountains and Seas), Bei Shan Jing: the Fa Mountain and the Jingwei bird (Guo Pu recension)

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Nüwa, youngest daughter of the Flame Emperor, drowned while playing in the East Sea; her spirit became the bird Jingwei, who carries twigs and pebbles from the western mountains to fill the sea that took her — an endless, unavailing war between the small and the vast.
summary.zh: 炎帝幼女女娃遊於東海溺死，魂化為精衛鳥，常銜西山木石以填東海——小者與浩瀚之間無盡的 抗爭。

sensitivity.note: Mythic corpus from a Classical Chinese source without a public-domain English translation; passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the original text. Living cultural heritage of China. The Thompson-index motif 'culture-hero' is an interpretive stretch for a drowned girl-bird, noted here as a tagging caveat.

passages.text: On Fa Mountain, north of the mountains, grows mulberry of the kind that silkworms eat, and there lives a bird shaped like a crow, with a patterned head, a white beak and red feet. Its name is Jingwei, and its cry calls its own name — for the bird once was a girl, the youngest daughter of the Flame Emperor, called Nüwa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Bei Shan Jing, Fa Mountain passage (compiler's rendering from the public-domain Classical Chinese); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在北方的發鳩山上，長著蠶所吃的桑樹，那裡住著一種鳥，形狀像烏鴉，頭上有花紋，白色的嘴，紅色的腳。牠的名字叫精衛，牠的叫聲就是呼喚自己的名字——因為這鳥原本是一個女孩，是炎帝的小女兒，名叫女娃。

passages.text: The girl went swimming in the East Sea and drowned, and never came home. So she became the bird Jingwei, and ever after she carried twigs and small stones from the western mountains in her beak and dropped them into the East Sea, to fill up the water that had drowned her. The sea does not notice the stones; the bird does not stop.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Bei Shan Jing, Fa Mountain passage; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這女孩到東海去游泳，溺水而死，再也沒有回家。於是她就變成了精衛鳥，從此以後，她總是用嘴銜著西山上的樹枝和小石子，投到東海裡去，要填平那淹死她的海水。大海並不在意這些石子；這鳥卻不肯停歇。

title.en: Zhulong, the Torch Dragon Whose Eyes Are Day and Night
title.zh: 燭龍視為晝瞑為夜

region.en: Zhongshan, the far north where sun never reaches (symbolic pin: northern mountains, Inner Mongolia–Ningxia latitude)
region.zh: 北方鍾山，日所不及之地（象徵性定位）

period: Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Bei Jing and Da Huang Bei Jing chapters, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing (Classic of Mountains and Seas), Hai Wai Bei Jing / Da Huang Bei Jing: Zhongshan and the Torch Dragon (Guo Pu recension)

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: North of the sea, where the sun's light cannot reach, the Torch Dragon holds a torch of light: when he opens his eyes it is day on Zhongshan, when he closes them night; when he breathes out it is summer, when he breathes in winter; he neither eats nor sleeps nor rests, and for him the world runs on breath and eyelid.
summary.zh: 北方鍾山之神燭龍，身長千里，人面蛇身而赤；視為晝，瞑為夜，吹為冬，呼為夏——不飲不食不息，天地之明暗寒暑繫於其目息。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original (no public-domain English translation). Tagging caveat: 'sun-capture' is used for a being that replaces the sun in the lightless north, not a sun-theft; the comparative tag is interpretive.

passages.text: The god of Zhongshan is called Zhulong, the Torch Dragon. He is a thousand li long, with a human face and the body of a serpent, red as cinnabar, and he holds the light of a great torch even in the darkness north of the sea-gate, where the sunlight never arrives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Bei Jing, Zhongshan passage (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 鍾山的神叫燭龍。牠身長千里，長著人的臉、蛇的身子，紅得像硃砂，即使在海水門戶以北、陽光永遠照不到的黑暗之中，牠也擎著一支大火炬的光。

passages.text: When the Torch Dragon opens his eyes, it is day; when he closes them, it is night. When he blows, it is winter; when he breathes gently, it is summer. He does not drink, does not eat, does not sleep, and does not rest — and by his eyelids and his breath the weather of that land is made.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Bei Jing, Zhulong passage; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 燭龍睜開眼睛，就是白天；閉上眼睛，就是黑夜。牠吹氣，就是冬天；牠輕輕呼氣，就是夏天。牠不喝水，不吃東西，不睡覺，也不休息——那地方的氣候，就是由牠的眼皮和呼吸造成的。

title.en: Yinglong, the Winged Dragon Who Could Not Return to Heaven
title.zh: 應龍殺蚩尤復處南方

region.en: The south of the mythic world, where Yinglong settled after the war (symbolic pin: mid-south China)
region.zh: 神話南方，應龍戰後所居（象徵性定位）

period: Shanhaijing, Da Huang Dong Jing / Da Huang Bei Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing (Classic of Mountains and Seas), Da Huang Jing chapters: Yinglong's war service and the origin of rain-dragons (Guo Pu recension)

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Yinglong, the only dragon with wings, hoarded water for the Yellow Emperor and slew both Chiyou and Kua Fu; but he could not climb back to heaven, so he took up residence in the south — and that, says the Shanhaijing, is why the south has so much rain: whenever drought comes, people dress as Yinglong to call him, and he sends rain.
summary.zh: 應龍為黃帝畜水誅蚩尤、殺夸父，不得復上，故居南方——南方多雨之由；旱而作龍以請之，則應龍降雨。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original; the Guo Pu commentary on the rain-making rite is paraphrased from the traditional commentary.

passages.text: Yinglong, the answering dragon, was the only dragon that had wings. In the great war in the field of Jizhou he held back water in store for the Yellow Emperor, and he it was who slew Chiyou, and afterwards Kua Fu the sun-chaser also. But after the killing he was too spent to climb again to heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Dong Jing and Da Huang Bei Jing, Yinglong passages (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 應龍是唯一長著翅膀的龍。在冀州之野的大戰中，牠為黃帝蓄水，正是牠殺死了蚩尤，後來又殺死了追日的夸父。但經過這場殺戮之後，牠耗盡了力氣，再也無力升回天上。

passages.text: So Yinglong went to dwell in the south of the world, and because the rain-maker dragon lives in the south, the south gets much rain. When drought comes, the people make an image of Yinglong and call upon him — and the answering dragon sends the rain down again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Dong Jing passage with Guo Pu's traditional commentary; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是應龍就住到世界的南方去了，因為這興雨的龍住在南方，所以南方多雨。每逢乾旱來臨，人們就做成應龍的形像來呼求牠——應龍便又降下雨來。

title.en: The War of the Yellow Emperor and Chiyou at Zhuolu
title.zh: 黃帝戰蚩尤於涿鹿

region.en: Zhuolu, field of Jizhou (modern Hebei) — traditional battlefield site
region.zh: 冀州涿鹿之野（今河北）

period: Shanhaijing, Da Huang Bei Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE (parallel in Shiji, Wu Di Ben Ji)

source.work: Shanhaijing (Classic of Mountains and Seas), Da Huang Bei Jing: Chiyou attacks the Yellow Emperor (Guo Pu recension)

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Chiyou takes up arms against the Yellow Emperor, who orders the winged dragon Yinglong to flood the field of Jizhou; Chiyou calls the Wind Lord and Rain Master to unleash storms, and the Emperor brings down the heaven-maiden Ba to stop the rain — and so the rebel god falls, the first great war of the mythic dynasties.
summary.zh: 蚩尤作兵伐黃帝，黃帝令應龍攻冀州之野，應龍畜水；蚩尤請風伯雨師縱大風雨，黃帝乃下天女魃止雨，遂殺蚩尤——神話王朝第一場大戰。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original; Shiji (Burton Watson's modern translation is copyright, only consulted as summary) records the same war as history. Chiyou remains a culture-hero and war-god among the Miao/Hmong — the victors' chronicle framing is noted.

passages.text: Chiyou took up weapons and attacked the Yellow Emperor. The Emperor commanded Yinglong to meet him in the open country of Jizhou; the dragon gathered the waters and held them in store. Chiyou, in answer, called the Lord of the Winds and the Master of Rains to let loose great wind and rain upon the field.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Bei Jing, Chiyou passage (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蚩尤舉起兵器攻打黃帝。黃帝命令應龍在冀州的曠野迎戰他；應龍蓄積水，將水儲存起來。蚩尤回應，召來風伯與雨師，在戰場上放出狂風暴雨。

passages.text: Then the Yellow Emperor sent down from heaven the maiden Ba, the drought-spirit, and the rain stopped. The waters were broken, and in the field of Jizhou Yinglong killed Chiyou. But the drought-maiden could not return to heaven, and the land she stayed on never saw rain — a war won, and a curse set loose on the fields.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Bei Jing; see the separate Nüba record for her aftermath; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是黃帝從天上降下女魃——旱神，雨便止住了。水被破除，應龍在冀州的戰場上殺死了蚩尤。但旱魃無法返回天上，她所停留之地再也見不到雨——一場戰爭勝利了，卻也將詛咒釋放到了田野之上。

title.en: Nüba, the Drought Maiden the People Drive Out
title.zh: 天女魃不得復上

region.en: Red Water of the north, after the war of Jizhou (symbolic pin: northern plain)
region.zh: 北方赤水，戰後所居（象徵性定位）

period: Shanhaijing, Da Huang Bei Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing (Classic of Mountains and Seas), Da Huang Bei Jing: the drought maiden Ba after the fall of Chiyou (Guo Pu recension)

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The heaven-maiden Ba, the drought-bringer, stopped the rain and won the war — but could not go home. She wanders, and wherever she settles no rain falls; the Yellow Emperor's remedy is a ritual of clearing waterways and ditches, and the people drive her south, crying that she must go — the exorcism of the drought demon.
summary.zh: 天女魃止雨有功而不得復上，所居不雨；叔均言之帝，帝置之赤水之北；民逐之曰『神北行』——先除水道、決通溝瀆以逐旱魃之儀。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original. Tagging caveat: 'taboo-transgression' here marks the boundary-breaking of a heaven-being stranded among humans, not a moral crime.

passages.text: The maiden Ba, sent down from heaven, had stopped the rain and made the Emperor's victory possible; but the divine fire in her was spent, and she could not climb back to heaven. The Yellow Emperor set her in the north, by the Red Water — yet wherever she dwelt the rain never came, and the lands she passed over parched and cracked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Bei Jing, Nüba passage (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 女魃從天上被降下，止住了雨，使黃帝的勝利得以實現；但她體內的神火耗盡，無法再攀回天上。黃帝將她安置在北方赤水之畔——然而她所居之處從不下雨，她所經過的土地乾枯龜裂。

passages.text: Shu jun, the seed-sower, told the Emperor where she was wandering, and she was moved again and again. At last the people learned the remedy: clear the water-channels first, open the ditches and dikes, then drive her out, crying 'Spirit, go north!' — and so the drought demon is exorcised to this day in the ritual of the fields.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Bei Jing, end of the Nüba passage with the ritual prescription; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 后稷（ Shu jun，播種者）告訴黃帝她遊蕩何處，她便一次又一次被遷移。最後人們學會了解救之法：先疏通水道，開挖溝渠、修築堤防，然後驅逐她，喊道「神啊，往北去！」——因此至今在田野的儀式中，旱魃仍被驅除。

title.en: Yu Slays Xiangliu, the Nine-Headed Minister of Gonggong
title.zh: 禹殺相柳

region.en: Kunlun's northern marches, where the slain god's blood became marsh (symbolic pin: far northwest)
region.zh: 共工之臺北，血沼之地（象徵性定位）

period: Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Bei Jing / Da Huang Bei Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing (Classic of Mountains and Seas), Hai Wai Bei Jing: Xiangliu, minister of Gonggong, slain by Yu (Guo Pu recension)

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Xiangliu, Gonggong's minister, has nine heads that feed on nine mountains at once; wherever he touches becomes a swamp of snakes. Yu the flood-tamer kills him, but his blood is so foul that no grain will grow there; Yu fills the pit three times and three times it collapses — so he makes it a pool, and the gods build their terraces upon it.
summary.zh: 共工之臣相柳氏九首，自環食於九山，所抵處為澤谿；禹殺相柳，其血腥不可樹穀；禹三仞三沮，乃以為池，群帝因是以為臺。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original. Tagging caveat: 'world-serpent' marks the nine-headed aquatic monster type; the Chinese figure is a minister-god rather than a cosmic encircler.

passages.text: Xiangliu was the minister of Gonggong the water-power, a god with nine heads, who fed himself from nine mountains at once in a ring, and wherever his body or his heads came down, the ground became a bog of snakes and could not be lived in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Bei Jing, Xiangliu passage (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 相柳是水神共工的臣子，一個有九顆頭的神，能同時從環繞的九座山上進食，凡他的身體或頭顱所落之處，地面便成為蛇群聚集的沼澤，無法居住。

passages.text: Yu, in his work of taming the floods, killed Xiangliu — but the god's blood was so sharp and foul that where it soaked, the five grains would not sprout. Yu filled the pit with earth three times, and three times it sank down again; so he gave up and made the place a pool, and the many gods used the raised ground to build their terraces upon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Bei Jing, Yu's filling of the pit; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 禹在治理洪水的工程中殺死了相柳——但這神的血極為腥臭刺人，凡血所浸之處，五穀都無法生長。禹用土填塞那坑洞三次，三次都又陷落下去；於是他放棄填塞，將該處闢為水池，眾神便利用那隆起的地面建造他們的台榭。

title.en: Dijiang, the Faceless God of Chaos on Tianshan
title.zh: 天山帝江渾敦無面目

region.en: Tianshan, the Mountain of Heaven in the far west (symbolic pin: Tianshan range)
region.zh: 天山（遠西之天山）

period: Shanhaijing, Xi Ci San Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing (Classic of Mountains and Seas), Xi Ci San Jing: the god of Tianshan (Guo Pu recension)

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: On the Mountain of Heaven lives a god shaped like a yellow sack, red as cinnabar, with six feet and four wings, having no face and no eyes — hundun, the undifferentiated one — who nevertheless knows how to sing and dance: the primal chaos itself, preserved in a gazetteer of mountains.
summary.zh: 天山有神，狀如黃囊，赤如丹火，六足四翼，渾敦無面目，是識歌舞，實為帝江——混沌之神，寓於山經。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original. Commentators read Dijiang/Hundun as the primal chaos embodied; Zhuangzi's seven-orifices parable (chinese-zhuangzi-hundun) gives the same figure a death.

passages.text: The waters of the English River rise on the Mountain of Heaven, which is rich in gold and jade; and there lives a god whose shape is like a yellow sack, glowing red as cinnabar-fire, with six feet and four wings.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Xi Ci San Jing, Tianshan passage (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 英水發源於天山，山上盛產黃金與美玉；那裡住著一位神，形狀像黃色的袋子，赤紅如火丹，有六隻腳和四隻翅膀。

passages.text: He has no face and no eyes, no mouth and no features at all — hundun, the undivided — and yet this faceless one understands song and dance. He is Dijiang, the Lord-Emporor of the River of the lump of chaos; the name is read by commentators as 'Huang', the yellow sack of the primal whole.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Xi Ci San Jing, with Guo Pu's traditional reading; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他沒有臉，沒有眼睛，沒有嘴，也沒有任何面貌——混沌，渾然未分——然而這無面者卻懂得歌唱與舞蹈。他就是帝江，混沌之河的君王；注家將此名讀作「黃」，即原初渾全的黃色袋子。

title.en: Jianmu, the Ladder Tree at the Center of Heaven and Earth
title.zh: 建木眾帝所自上下

region.en: Duguang, the Wild Center where suns pass without shadow (symbolic pin: Chengdu plain)
region.zh: 都廣之野，天地之中（象徵性定位：成都平原）

period: Shanhaijing, Hai Nei Jing / Da Huang Xi Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE (parallel in Huainanzi, Xinglong Xun?)

source.work: Shanhaijing (Classic of Mountains and Seas), Hai Nei Jing: the tree Jianmu (Guo Pu recension)

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: In the Wild Center, where the suns cross without casting shadow and sounds carry without echo, stands the tree Jianmu: a hundred ren tall with no branches, nine hooked coils below, nine clustered crowns above, bearing its fruit like hemp seeds — the very ladder by which the gods ascend and descend between heaven and earth.
summary.zh: 都廣之野，天地之中，日月中無景、呼而無響；建木百仞無枝，下有九欘，上有九欘，實如麻——眾帝所自上下之天梯。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original (Hai Nei Jing passage, with the Duguang center from the Da Huang Xi Jing commentary tradition).

passages.text: In the Wild of Duguang, south of the twin rivers, lies the meeting place of heaven and earth: the suns and moons cross there and cast no shadow, and a shout there has no echo — because it is the very center of the world. Rice and grain grow of themselves, the phoenix sings, and nothing is planted yet nothing is lacking.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Hai Nei Jing, Duguang passage (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在都廣之野，雙江之南，是天與地交會之處：日月在此交錯而不投下影子，在此呼喊而沒有回聲——因為這裡正是世界的中心。稻穀自生自長，鳳凰歌唱，無所種植卻無所匱乏。

passages.text: There stands the tree called Jianmu, a hundred ren tall with no side branches, nine hooked coils below and nine clustered crowns above, its fruits like hemp seeds and its leaves like spears. Tai Hao passed across it — for Jianmu is the ladder by which the gods go up and come down between the sky and the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Hai Nei Jing, Jianmu passage; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那裡矗立著一棵名為建木的樹，高百仞而無側枝，樹下有九道盤曲的根，樹上有九簇叢聚的枝冠，果實如麻子，葉子如矛。太昊曾從它上面經過——因為建木是眾神在天與地之間上下往來的梯子。

title.en: The Fusang Tree and the Ten Suns Who Bathe in Tang Valley
title.zh: 扶桑十日所浴

region.en: Tang Valley (Tanggu), the hot spring of the rising sun in the far east (symbolic pin: East China Sea horizon)
region.zh: 東方湯谷，十日所浴（象徵性定位：東海日出處）

period: Shanhaijing, Da Huang Dong Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing (Classic of Mountains and Seas), Da Huang Dong Jing: Tanggu, Fusang, and the ten suns bathed by Xihe (Guo Pu recension)

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: In the southeast beyond the Great Waste lies Tang Valley, the boiling valley where the ten suns bathe; nine of them rest on the lower branches of the great mulberry Fusang and one sits on the top, and all are bathed by Xihe, mother of the suns — one sun arrives as one departs, so the sky never has two suns at once.
summary.zh: 東南大荒湯谷上有扶桑，十日所浴；九日居下枝，一日居上枝；皆浴於湯谷——一日方至，一日方出，皆載於烏。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original. This is the cosmic-rotation version of the suns; the broken-rotation version (all ten rising at once) is cut separately under Hou Yi (Huainanzi Benjing Xun).

passages.text: Southeast of the sea, past the Yellow Water, lies the Great Valley of Tang — the boiling valley — where the ten suns bathe. Above the valley grows the tree Fusang, the great support-mulberry, on which the suns rest after their bath; nine of them sit on the lower branches, and one takes the top of the tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Dong Jing, Tanggu-Fusang passage (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 海的東南，越過黃水，是湯谷——沸騰之谷——十個太陽在此沐浴。谷上生長著名為扶桑的樹，即巨大的支撐之桑，太陽們沐浴後便在其上歇息；其中九個坐在下面的枝條上，一個占據樹的頂端。

passages.text: Xihe, the mother of the ten suns, bathes them in the hot valley of the far east — and the order of the sky is kept by rotation: one sun arrives as one goes out. The suns travel riding on crows, says the text, and the watchers in Qi saw great crows carrying the disc of fire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Dong Jing, Xihe passage; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 羲和，十個太陽的母親，在極東的炎熱之谷為他們沐浴——天空的秩序靠輪替維持：一個太陽到來，另一個便離去。文中說，太陽們乘著烏鴉而行，而齊地的觀測者曾見到大烏鴉載著火輪。

title.en: Changxi Bathes the Twelve Moons
title.zh: 常羲浴月

region.en: The Great West, land of the turning suns (symbolic pin: far-west highland)
region.zh: 大荒西經，日月所入之山（象徵性定位）

period: Shanhaijing, Da Huang Xi Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing (Classic of Mountains and Seas), Da Huang Xi Jing: Changxi, wife of Di Jun, mother of twelve moons (Guo Pu recension)

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Di Jun's wife Changxi bears twelve moon-children in one birth — the twelve months of the year — and she washes them each in their turn; the Shanhaijing marks the passage of the moons into the western peaks as twelve points where the months go down.
summary.zh: 帝俊妻常羲，生月十有二，此始浴之——十二月之誕與浴；大荒西經列日月所入之山十二。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original.

passages.text: The Great West has mountains upon mountains where the suns and moons go down; the text counts the peaks of the sun's setting and the turning of the moons among the holy places of the far west, each one named and stationed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Xi Jing, entry on the sun-moon mountains (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大荒之西，群山層疊，日月於此西沉；書中歷數日落之峰與月轉之處，皆屬極西聖地，一一具名而列位。

passages.text: Di Jun took Changxi to wife, and she bore in one birth twelve moons — the twelve months. This, says the book, is where the bathing of the moons began: each month she washes her child in the waters of the west before it climbs the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Xi Jing, Changxi passage; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 帝俊娶常羲為妻，她一胎生下十二個月，是為十二月。書上說，月之沐浴自此始：每月她先在西方的水中為孩子洗浴，然後才讓它升上天空。

title.en: Xiwangmu, the Tiger-Toothed Queen Mother of the West
title.zh: 西王母豹尾虎齒

region.en: Yu Mountain (Jade Mountain) west of Kunlun (symbolic pin: Kunlun range)
region.zh: 崑崙之西玉山（象徵性定位：崑崙）

period: Shanhaijing, Xi Shan Jing / Hai Wai Bei Jing / Da Huang Xi Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing (Classic of Mountains and Seas), Xi Shan Jing and Hai Wai Bei Jing: Xiwangmu on Yu Mountain (Guo Pu recension)

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: West of the flowing sands, on Jade Mountain, dwells Xiwangmu: human in shape but with a leopard's tail and tiger's fangs, skilled in whistling-shout, shaggy-haired and wearing the sheng headdress — she who governs the calamities of heaven and the five punishments, fed by three green birds who fetch her food from the eastern mountain.
summary.zh: 玉山西王母，其狀如人，豹尾虎齒而善嘯，蓬髮戴勝，司天之厲及五殘；有三青鳥為取食——後世昇仙之主，其古形猙獰。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original; the later, gentle daoist-immortal form of Xiwangmu (Han onward, e.g. the Mu Tianzi Zhuan banquet) is cut as a separate record.

passages.text: Three hundred and fifty li past the flowing sands stands Yu Mountain, the Jade Mountain, the only place where the Queen Mother of the West may be found. She has the shape of a human being, yet with a leopard's tail and the fangs of a tiger, and she is a master of the long whistling-cry; her hair is wild and she wears the sheng, the jade comb-scepter, upon her head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Xi Shan Jing, Xiwangmu passage (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 流沙之後三百五十里，有玉山，即群玉之山，唯此處可尋得西王母。她形貌如人，卻有豹尾虎齒，善於長嘯；頭髮蓬亂，頭上戴著勝，即玉製的梳形髮飾。

passages.text: She is the governor of the calamities of heaven and of the five punishments of heaven — plague and destruction are in her keeping. In the far north, three green birds, strong of beak, serve her as messengers, and she sends them to the foot of the Great North Mountain to fetch her food; below Kunlun she is the one who holds the power of life and death of her quarter of the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Bei Jing and Da Huang Xi Jing passages; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她掌管上天的災禍與上天的五刑——瘟疫與毀滅皆由她執掌。在極北之地，有三隻青鳥，喙部強健，為她充當使者；她遣牠們飛往大北山麓為她取食；在崑崙之下，她執掌其所屬一方世界的生死之權。

title.en: The Nine-Tailed Fox of Qingqiu and the Omen of Tushan
title.zh: 青丘九尾狐與塗山瑞

region.en: Qingqiu, the Green Mounds, south of the mythic lands (symbolic pin: southeast hills)
region.zh: 青丘之山（象徵性定位）

period: Shanhaijing, Nan Shan Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE; Tushan omen in Wu Yue Chunqiu (Eastern Han)

source.work: Shanhaijing (Classic of Mountains and Seas), Nan Shan Jing: the nine-tailed beast of Qingqiu (Guo Pu recension); Wu Yue Chunqiu, Yue Wang Wai Zhuan: Yu's marriage omen at Tushan

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: On the Green Mounds lives a beast like a fox with nine tails, crying like a human baby, which eats men — yet whoever eats it is proof against guile and poison. Four centuries later the sign is turned: Yu, unwed at thirty, meets a white nine-tailed fox at Tushan, reads it as the marriage omen, and weds the girl of Tushan — the fox from man-eater to blessing of kings.
summary.zh: 青丘之山有獸如狐而九尾，其音如嬰兒，能食人；食者不蠱。塗山之歌曰：綏綏白狐，九尾龐龐——禹遇之而娶塗山氏，狐遂為王者之瑞。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing and Wu Yue Chunqiu originals. The nine-tailed fox later becomes the seductive fox-spirit of the Investiture of the Gods (Daji) — a radical inversion cut as a separate record.

passages.text: On Qingqiu, the Mountain of the Green Mounds, there is a beast shaped like a fox but with nine tails, and its voice is like the cry of a baby. It devours people; yet whoever manages to eat of it cannot be beguiled by poison or spells — the eater takes the fox's cunning into himself and is safe from guile.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Nan Shan Jing, Qingqiu passage (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 青丘之山有一獸，形狀如狐而有九條尾巴，叫聲如同嬰兒啼哭。牠吃人；然而凡能吃到牠的人，便不會被毒物或邪術所惑——食者將狐的狡黠納於己身，得以免於欺詐。

passages.text: Yu, thirty years old and unwed, passed Tushan and met a white fox with nine tails. The song of Tushan ran: 'The trailing white fox, nine tails all vast' — nine tails meaning nine generations of wives and heirs, and white meaning a shared lot. Yu read it as the omen of his marriage and took the girl of Tushan to wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wu Yue Chunqiu, Yue Wang Wai Zhuan, Tushan marriage omen (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 禹年三十而未娶，行經塗山，遇見一隻九尾白狐。塗山之歌唱道：『綏綏白狐，九尾龐龐』——九尾意指九代妻室與子嗣，白則意指共同的命運。禹以此解讀為自己婚姻的徵兆，遂娶塗山之女為妻。

title.en: The Book of Knowing the Evolutions of Ra: Neb-er-tcher Creates the World
title.zh: 《知拉演化之書》：內伯-特切爾創世

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (temple library of Amen-Ra; the Book of Overthrowing Apep was recited to secure the sunrise)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（阿蒙-拉神廟藏書；《滅阿波菲斯之書》誦讀處）

period: Papyrus copied c. 305 BCE (BM Papyrus 10188, reign of Alexander II), containing mythic material of far greater antiquity (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods: The Egyptian Texts, ed. and trans. E. A. Wallis Budge (London, 1912), ch. I, 'The Legend of the God Neb-er-tcher and the History of Creation'

summary.en: In the only connected Egyptian creation account, the infinite god Neb-er-tcher takes the form of Khepera and speaks the cosmos into being over the primeval ocean Nu: naming each thing lays its foundation, Shu and Tefnut are self-begotten, Geb and Nut form earth and sky, the sun and moon are the two Eyes, and humankind springs from the god's own tears.
summary.zh: 埃及唯一連貫的創世敘事：無限之神內伯-特切爾化為凱佩拉，於原初大洋努之上以言語創世——呼名即奠基，舒與泰芙努特自生，蓋布與努特成天地，日月為神之二眼，人類則自神之淚滴而出。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary-funerary corpus with no living community restrictions. Tagging note: 'clay-humans' is used here in the sense of humans formed directly from the creator's body-fluid (tears), the closest motif match in the Thompson-style index; this is an interpretive stretch recorded deliberately.

passages.text: Nebertcher says: 'I am the creator of what hath come into being. I myself came into being under the form of the god Khepera. I came into being under the form of Pautti (or, in primeval time), I formed myself out of the primeval matter, I made myself out of the substance that was in primeval time.' Nothing existed at that time except the great primeval watery mass called NU, but in this there were the germs of everything that came into being subsequently. There was no heaven, and no earth, and the god found no place on which to stand; nothing, in fact, existed except the god. He says, 'I was alone.' He first created himself by uttering his own name as a word of power, and when this was uttered his visible form appeared. He then uttered another kind of word of power, and as a result of this his soul came into being, and it worked in connection with his heart or mind.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. VI, summarizing BM Papyrus 10188.
passages.zh: 內貝切爾說：「我是已生成之物的創造者。我以凱佩拉神的形式自行生成。我以帕烏提（或說，在太初之時）的形式自行生成，我從太初的物質中塑造了自己，我從太初之時即已存在的實質中造出了自己。」當時除了名為努（NU）的偉大太初水體之外，別無一物存在，但其中已含有此後一切生成之物的胚芽。那時沒有天，也沒有地，神找不到可立足之處；事實上，除了神以外，別無一物存在。他說：「我孤身一人。」他首先以說出自己之名作為一句有力之言而創造了自己，當此言說出時，他可見的形體便出現了。接著他又說出另一種有力之言，由於此言，他的靈魂便生成了，並且與他的心或心智一同運作。

passages.text: Before every act of creation Nebertcher, or his visible form Khepera, thought out what form the thing to be created was to take, and when he had uttered its name the thing itself appeared in heaven or earth. To fill the heaven, or place where he lived, the god next produced from his body and its shadow the two gods Shu and Tefnut. These with Nebertcher, or Khepera, formed the first triad of gods, and the 'one god became three.' The tradition of the begetting of Shu and Tefnut is as old as the time of the pyramids, for it is mentioned in the text of Pepi I. The next act of creation resulted in the emerging of the Eye of Nebertcher (later identified with Ra) from the watery mass (NU), and light shone upon its waters. Shu and Tefnut then united and they produced Keb, the Earth-god, and Nut, the Sky-goddess.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. VI; not verbatim of the ancient text itself, which Budge renders from two parallel versions.
passages.zh: 在每一次創造行動之前，內貝切爾，或他可見的形體凱佩拉，都會先想好將造之物應採取何種形式，而當他說出其名時，該物本身便出現在天上或地上。為了充實天空，也就是他所居住之處，神接著從自己的身體及其影子中造出了舒與泰芙努特兩位神。這兩位與內貝切爾，或凱佩拉，構成了第一組三神，於是「一神成了三神」。舒與泰芙努特受生之說，其古老可追溯至金字塔時代，因為佩皮一世（Pepi I）的銘文中已提及此事。下一次創造行動的結果，是內貝切爾之眼（後世等同於拉）自太初水體（努）中浮現，於是光照耀在其水面上。舒與泰芙努特隨後結合，生出了蓋布，即大地之神，以及努特，即天空女神。

passages.text: The text then refers to some calamity which befell the Eye of Nebertcher or of Khepera, but what it was is not clear; at all events the Eye became obscured, and it ceased to give light. This period of darkness is, of course, the night, and to obviate the inconvenience caused by this recurring period of darkness, the god made a second Eye, i.e. the Moon, and set it in the heavens. The greater Eye ruled the day, and the lesser Eye the night. One of the results of the daily darkness was the descent of the Sky-goddess Nut to the Earth-god Keb each evening.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. VI.
passages.zh: 銘文接著提到內貝切爾之眼或凱佩拉之眼所遭遇的某種災禍，但究竟為何並不清楚；無論如何，那隻眼變得昏暗，不再發出光來。這段黑暗時期自然就是夜晚，為了避免這反覆出現的黑暗時期所造成的不便，神又造了第二隻眼，即月亮，並將其安置於天上。較大的眼掌管白晝，較小的眼掌管夜晚。每日黑暗的結果之一，便是天空女神努特每晚降臨於大地之神蓋布之處。

passages.text: Men and women were first formed from the tears that fell from the Eye of Khepera, or the Sun-god, upon his body; the old Egyptian word for 'men' very closely resembles in form and sound the word for 'tears.' Plants, vegetables, herbs, and trees owe their origin to the light of the moon falling upon the earth. Our text contains no mention of a special creation of the 'beasts of the field,' but the god states distinctly that he created the children of the earth, or creeping things of all kinds, and among this class quadrupeds are probably included. The men and women, and all the other living creatures that were made at that time by Nebertcher, or Khepera, reproduced their species, each in his own way, and thus the earth became filled with their descendants as we see at the present time.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. VI.
passages.zh: 男人與女人最初是由凱佩拉之眼，即太陽神之眼，落於其身上的淚水形成的；古埃及語中「人」一詞，在字形與讀音上都與「淚」一詞極為相近。植物、蔬果、草本與樹木，其起源則歸因於月光落於大地之上。我們的銘文並未提及對「田野之獸」的特別創造，但神明明確表示，他造了大地之子，即各式各樣的爬行之物，而四足動物大概也包含在這一類之中。當時由內貝切爾，或凱佩拉，所造的男人、女人以及所有其他生物，各依其方式繁衍其種類，於是大地便充滿了它們的後裔，正如我們今日所見。

language: Egyptian (hieratic, late New Kingdom/Ptolemaic copy of far older mythic material)
canonical_translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, Legends of the Gods: The Egyptian Texts (London, 1912), and Budge, Egyptian Hieratic Papyri in the British Museum (London, 1910)

narrative.en:
Egyptian religion never produced a single canonical cosmogony; instead each great cult center proclaimed its own god the creator. The one connected narrative of creation that has survived comes, fittingly, from a magical working: it is embedded in the Book of Overthrowing Apep, a liturgy recited in the temple of Amen-Ra at Thebes to keep the monstrous serpent Apep from blocking the sunrise. The scribe Nes-Menu copied it about 305 BCE onto BM Papyrus 10188, inserting two versions of the creation story amid the anti-Apep spells — apparently because the mere recital of the world's first words was held to be a spell of the most potent kind, deadly to every fiend of darkness.

BEGINNING: THE LORD OF THE LIMIT. The narrator calls himself Neb-er-tcher, 'the Lord to the uttermost limit' — a title that later Egyptian Christians (the Copts) used for God Almighty. Before heaven, before earth, before any place to stand, he exists as pure boundless being over the primeval ocean Nu, a vast inert mass of water holding the germs of every future thing, 'helpless and inert.' The god desires to create, and takes the form of Khepera, the self-created scarab-god, the creator par excellence. Khepera raises himself out of Nu into empty space and finds nothing beneath him. So he turns inward: he thinks out in his heart — the Egyptian word means literally 'laying the foundation in the heart' — the standing-place he needs, and when he speaks its name, it comes into being. Speech is not description here but manufacture: to name a thing is to make it exist.

MIDDLE: THE GOD BECOMES THREE, THE ENNEAD MULTIPLIES. Khepera next unites with his own shadow, and from this self-fecundation Shu (air, dryness) and Tefnut (liquids, moisture) are born — the Pyramid Texts of Pepi I preserve the older, franker form of this doctrine. From the union of Shu and Tefnut come Geb the Earth and Nut the Sky, the fundamental division of the cosmos. The god's Eye emerges from Nu and light first shines on the waters. But the Eye suffers a calamity — night, eclipse, or storm — and goes dark; the creator responds by making a second, lesser Eye, the Moon, ruling the night while the greater Eye, the Sun, rules the day. The legend then folds the Heliopolitan Ennead into the account: Nut's embraces with Geb bring forth five gods at one birth — Osiris, Horus, Set, Isis, and Nephthys — with Osiris singled out as the essence of the primeval matter itself, a reincarnation of the great-grandfather god, the ancestor and savior of souls. The moon, made to supply the sun's stolen splendor, governs the growth of trees, plants, and herbs — an etiology of lunar fertility.

END: TEARS OF HUMANKIND. Humans do not arise from the earth's clay as in Mesopotamia or China; they spring directly from the creator's own body. Khepera places his members together and weeps upon them, and men and women come into being from the tears that fall from his eyes — an etymology the Egyptians themselves read in the near-identity of the words for 'men' (remut) and 'tears' (remut). The god adds creeping things of every kind, presumably including the larger quadrupeds, and lets every species reproduce after its kind until the earth is filled. The account closes with theology rather than story: the Deity is too exalted to meddle in mortal affairs, while the subordinate 'gods' remain amenable to spells, flattery, and gifts — which is why the creation narrative itself functions as a weapon against Apep.

FUNCTION IN THE CORPUS. This record anchors the Egyptian creation cluster: it supplies the cosmogonic frame (chaos-waters, self-created god, generation of the Ennead) that the separate Memphite and Hermopolitan traditions reinterpret, and it links the birth of the world to the Osiris myth via the five children of Nut.

functions: Liturgical weapon: recited within the Book of Overthrowing Apep to guarantee the sun's rise against the chaos-serpent
Synthesizes the Heliopolitan theology (self-created god, Ennead) into narrative form for a late temple liturgy
Explains daily and nightly cosmic order (sun/moon as the two Eyes; Nut's nightly descent) and lunar plant-growth
Etiology of humanity: humans born of the creator's tears, linking human mortality to divine sorrow

variants.name: Two parallel versions in the same papyrus
variants.text_tradition: BM Papyrus 10188, cols. XXVI 21–XXVII 6 (short version) and XXVIII 20–XXIX 6 (longer version)
variants.summary: The papyrus contains two copies of the creation legend; the longer adds the heart-soul as co-creator and expands the Eye-of-the-sun material. Whether the scribe copied two sources or expanded the short version as he wrote is unknown.

variants.name: Heliopolitan Ennead cosmogony (Pyramid Texts)
variants.text_tradition: Pyramid Texts of the 5th–6th Dynasty pyramids (Unas, Teta, Pepi I), c. 2350–2175 BCE
variants.summary: The older doctrine: Atum-Tem self-arises on the benben stone at Heliopolis and generates the Ennead; fragments preserved in Budge's Literature of the Ancient Egyptians ch. II (Hymn to Tem-Kheprer) and in the king-in-heaven spells.

variants.name: Memphite theology (Ptah creates by heart and tongue)
variants.text_tradition: Shabaka Stone, 25th Dynasty copy of Memphite doctrine
variants.summary: Ptah creates all things by conceiving them in his heart and commanding them with his tongue — a philosophical restatement of the same 'foundation in the heart' doctrine that this legend makes narrative. Recorded as a pending record in the Egyptian ledger.

XXVI 21–XXVII 6 and XXVIII 20–XXIX 6. Ed. and trans. E. A. W. Budge, Archaeologia vol. 52 (1891) and Egyptian Hieratic Papyri in the British Museum (London, 1910); reprinted in Legends of the Gods (London, 1912).
