passages.text: Yao said: 'I will try him.' He gave Shun both his daughters in marriage, to watch how he governed a household; he sent his nine sons to live with him, to watch how he governed men. Shun made the two women humble among the humble, kept his farm, his jars and his coops in perfect order, and wherever he dwelt for a year a hamlet formed, for two years a town, for three a city.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shiji, Wu Di Ben Ji, the testing of Shun; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 堯說：「我來試試他。」他把自己的兩個女兒都嫁給舜，以觀察他如何治家；又派自己的九個兒子去與他同住，以觀察他如何治人。舜使二女在卑微之人中謙卑自處，他的田地、陶器與雞舍都井然有序；他居住之處，一年便成村落，兩年成鄉鎮，三年成城邑。

passages.text: Yao tried him further as minister of the five teachings, as chief officer, as master of guests and forests, and Shun succeeded at every post. At last Yao, grown old, yielded the throne to Shun, and died after twenty-eight years of watching him reign; the world received a new Son of Heaven not by birth but by worth — the abdication of Yao became for all later China the pattern of legitimate rule.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shiji, Wu Di Ben Ji, the abdication; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 堯又進一步試他，任他為掌五教的司徒、為總理百官的首領、為主掌賓客與山林之官，舜在每一職位上都勝任。最後，堯年老，將帝位禪讓給舜，並在觀察舜治國二十八年後去世；天下由此得到一位不以出身、而以德行而立的天子——堯的禪讓成為此後中國歷代合法統治的典範。

title.en: Shun's Family Tries to Kill Him
title.zh: 瞽叟焚廩掩井

region.en: Lishan and the farm country of Jizhou (symbolic pin: southern Shanxi)
region.zh: 歷山之田（象徵性定位：晉南）

period: Shiji by Sima Qian, c. 94 BCE, Wu Di Ben Ji chapter

source.work: Shiji, Wu Di Ben Ji: the blind father's plot — the granary fire and the filled well — and Shun's escape

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Even after Yao gave Shun his daughters, Shun's blind father still hated him: he sent Shun up to roof the granary and set fire below — Shun flew down on two bamboo hats; he sent him to dig a well and packed earth over him — Shun emerged from a hidden side-tunnel. Each time, Shun served him as a son, and the court of heaven heard of a filial son whom the family could not kill.
summary.zh: 瞽叟尚復欲殺之；使舜上塗廩，瞽叟從下縱火焚廩，舜乃以兩笠自扞而下，去，得不死；後瞽叟又使舜穿井，舜穿井為匿空旁出——舜猶復事瞽叟愛弟彌謹。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shiji original. The escape-tricks parallel world folktale types (murderous-parent tests); tagged as boundary transgression against filial order by the family, not by the hero.

passages.text: Yao's gifts had changed nothing at home. Shun's father, a blind man, still hated him, and with Shun's stepmother and his half-brother Xiang plotted to kill him. He sent Shun to the top of the granary to plaster its roof, then set fire to it from below.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shiji, Wu Di Ben Ji, the granary fire (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 堯的賞賜並未改變家中的情況。舜的父親是個盲人，仍然憎恨他，並與舜的繼母及異母弟象合謀要殺他。他派舜登上糧倉頂去塗抹屋頂，然後從下面放火焚燒。

passages.text: Shun seized two bamboo hats and, holding them like wings, floated down from the roof and ran — alive. His father sent him then to dig a well; when the well was deep, father and brother dropped earth and stones to fill it. But Shun had dug a hidden side-tunnel while he dug the well, and he came out alive through the earth beside it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shiji, Wu Di Ben Ji, the filled well; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 舜抓起兩頂斗笠，像翅膀一樣張開持著，從倉頂飄落而下，逃脫——活了下來。他的父親又派他去挖井；井挖深後，父親與弟弟投下泥土石塊將井填塞。但舜在挖井時已暗中挖了一條側道，於是從井旁的地中活著出來。

passages.text: Xiang rejoiced, went in to claim the house, and found Shun sitting on the bed playing his lute. Shun, alive, served his father and loved his brother more carefully than before — and when the court of Yao heard it, they knew the man whom the family could not destroy and who would not revenge himself was the man to be trusted with the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shiji, Wu Di Ben Ji, the lute scene; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 象大喜，進屋要佔取房屋，卻見舜坐在床上彈琴。舜活著，仍事奉父親，並比從前更用心地友愛弟弟——堯的朝廷聽聞此事，便知道這個家人無法害死、又不肯報復自己的人，正是可以託付天下的人。

title.en: The Two Consorts of the Xiang and the Speckled Bamboo
title.zh: 湘妃斑竹

region.en: Cangwu and the Xiang River, Hunan
region.zh: 蒼梧九嶷、湘江

period: Shiji, Wu Di Ben Ji, c. 94 BCE; consorts' lament in Liu Xiang's Lienü Zhuan (c. 18 BCE) and Bowu Zhi

source.work: Shiji, Wu Di Ben Ji: Shun dies in the wild of Cangwu; Lienü Zhuan: Ehuang and Nüying's weeping and the speckled bamboo

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Shun, in his hundredth year, went south to inspect and died in the wild of Cangwu, buried in the Nine Doubts. His two consorts — Yao's daughters Ehuang and Nüying — raced south after him, wept by the Xiang River until their tears speckled the bamboo stems, and drowned in the river; they became the goddesses of the Xiang, forever answering the calls of poets.
summary.zh: 舜南巡狩，崩於蒼梧之野，葬於江南九疑；二妃娥皇女英追之不及，淚下沾竹，竹為之斑；遂溺於湘江，為湘水之神——斑竹一枝千滴淚。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shiji and Lienü Zhuan originals. The river-goddess transformation anchors the Chu Ci Xiang-hymns (chinese-chuci-xiang-lords); 'sibling-creators' tags the pair as a double goddess — interpretive.

passages.text: In the hundredth year of his age, Shun went south on a circuit of inspection, and died in the wilderness of Cangwu. He was buried in the Nine Doubts of the south of the Yangzi, far from the capital he had ruled so long.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shiji, Wu Di Ben Ji, Shun's death (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 舜年屆百歲之時，南巡視察，崩於蒼梧之野。葬於江南九疑，遠離他長久所治之都城。

passages.text: His two consorts, Ehuang and Nüying, the daughters Yao had given him in test and marriage, hurried south after him and came too late to see him. They wept by the banks of the Xiang River, and their tears fell on the bamboo and stained it — and the speckled bamboo of Hunan carries their tear-marks to this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lienü Zhuan, the two consorts' lament; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的兩位妃子娥皇與女英，即堯為考驗並許配給他之人，急忙南追，卻來得太遲，未能見他一面。她們在湘江岸邊哭泣，淚水灑落竹上，染之成斑——湖南的斑竹至今仍帶著她們的淚痕。

passages.text: The consorts cast themselves into the river and were lost; the people of the Xiang called them its goddesses. The songs of Chu honor them as the lords of the Xiang — powers of love and loss that the poets summon when they sail the river in autumn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Xiang-goddess tradition, linking to Chu Ci; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 二妃投身江中而沒；湘地之人奉她們為湘水之神。楚辭之歌尊她們為湘君——愛與失落的權能，詩人於秋日泛舟江上時呼喚之。

title.en: King Mu of Zhou Banquets with the Queen Mother of the West at the Jade Pool
title.zh: 穆王西見西王母

region.en: The Jade Pool in the Kunlun highlands (symbolic pin: Kunlun range)
region.zh: 崑崙瑤池（象徵性定位）

period: Mu Tianzi Zhuan (Biography of the Son of Heaven Mu), excavated text from a Wei tomb, dated c. 4th c. BCE (buried 296 CE?; attested 3rd-4th c. CE discovery)

source.work: Mu Tianzi Zhuan, juan 3: King Mu's westward journey, the banquet at the Jade Pool, and the parting poems of Xiwangmu

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: King Mu of Zhou drives eight steeds a thousand li a day to the far west, crosses the flows of the sand, and at the Jade Pool of Kunlun is met by the Queen Mother of the West; she offers him wine and jade, they exchange songs of return and promise, and the Son of Heaven goes home — the banquet that made Xiwangmu the guest of emperors and the mother of immortality feasts.
summary.zh: 天子西征，驅八駿，馳千里至崑崙瑤池；西王母為天子謠：『白雲在天，山陵自出。道里悠遠，山川間之。』天子答歌；遂宴瑤池之上——賓主相酬而別。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Mu Tianzi Zhuan original. The polite exchange of poems is a courtly rendering of a mythic encounter; the marriage tag marks the courtship-song convention, interpretive.

passages.text: King Mu of Zhou, the Son of Heaven, drove his eight steeds of noble blood, a thousand li to the day, westward beyond the flowing sands, to the Black Waters, to the mountain where all jade is gathered — into the highlands where no road of men ran.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mu Tianzi Zhuan, juan 3, the western journey (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 周天子穆王駕其八匹駿馬，日行千里，西行越流沙，至黑水，抵聚玉之山——深入人跡不至的高原。

passages.text: At the Jade Pool of Kunlun he was met by the Queen Mother of the West. She brought white jade and dark jade for the Son of Heaven, and they feasted by the pool; and the Queen Mother sang to him: 'White clouds are in the sky, and the hills come forth from themselves; the road is long and far, and the mountains and rivers lie between — may you not die, and come again.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mu Tianzi Zhuan, juan 3, the banquet and song; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在崑崙之瑤池，西王母迎接了他。她為天子帶來白玉與玄玉，二人於池邊宴飲；西王母為他歌唱：『白雲在天，山陵自出；道里悠遠，山川間之——願君不死，再來相見。』

passages.text: The Son of Heaven answered in song that he would return and govern his people well, then come back to her in three years. They went up to the high mountain, set her words in the stone, and planted a locust tree to mark it — and the King of Zhou drove home eastward, a mythic envoy between the world of kings and the world of the immortals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mu Tianzi Zhuan, juan 3, the answer-song and the return; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天子以歌作答，言將歸去善治其民，三年之後再來見她。二人登上高山，將她的話刻於石上，並植槐樹為記——周王東歸而去，成為往來於君王之世與神仙之世間的神話使者。

title.en: Chong and Li Cut the Road Between Heaven and Earth
title.zh: 絕地天通

region.en: The courts of Shaohao and Zhuanxu (symbolic pin: eastern China)
region.zh: 少皞顓頊之世（象徵性定位：東方）

period: Guoyu (Discourses of the States), Chu Yu Xia, c. 4th c. BCE; parallel Shanhaijing, Da Huang Xi Jing

source.work: Guoyu, Chu Yu Xia: Guan Shefu's account of the severing of heaven-and-earth communication by Chong and Li under Zhuanxu

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: In the age of Shaohao, people and gods mingled freely: every household kept its medium, everyone could sacrifice and climb to heaven. Zhuanxu the emperor ordered his minister Chong to pull down the ladder and hold the sky, and Li to press down the earth — Chong and Li cut the road between heaven and earth, so that no one could ascend or descend at will: the mythic charter of the monopoly of sacrifice by priest and king.
summary.zh: 少皞之衰，九黎亂德，民神雜糅，家為巫史，民神同位；顓頊受之，乃命南正重司天以屬神，命火正黎司地以屬民——使復舊常，無相侵瀆，是謂絕地天通。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Guoyu original. This is the charter of religious monopoly in China — myth read as political theology; the Shanhaijing parallel places Chong and Li's separation among the cosmogonic acts.

passages.text: In the decline of Shaohao's age the Nine Li threw heaven's order into confusion: people and gods mingled their dwellings, every family kept its own medium and diviner, and everyone could sacrifice without measure — men ascended to heaven, and the gods descended wherever men called.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Guoyu, Chu Yu Xia, Guan Shefu's speech (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 少昊之世衰微，九黎擾亂天常：民與神雜處同居，家家自有巫覡，人人皆可任意祭祀——男子登天，神祇隨人所召而降。

passages.text: Zhuanxu received the age and set it right: he ordered Chong, master of the south, to keep the sky and gather the gods to heaven, and Li, master of fire, to keep the earth and gather the people below — Chong and Li cut the road between heaven and earth, so that none could pass between them at will again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Guoyu, Chu Yu Xia, the severing; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 顓頊承此世而正之：命南正重司天，以聚神於上；命火正黎司地，以聚民於下——重與黎斷絕天地之路，自此無人能任意往來其間。

passages.text: From that severing, sacrifice came to belong to the sanctified few: the priest-officers who alone spoke for heaven and the king who alone was its offspring. The myth is China's charter of religious monopoly — explaining why the multitude cannot climb to heaven and why altars need consecrated keepers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Guoyu, Chu Yu Xia, concluding argument; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 自此次斷絕，祭祀乃歸於受命之少數：唯祭司之官能代天而言，唯君王為天之所出。此神話乃中國宗教壟斷之典章——說明何以眾人不得登天，何以祭壇須有受命之守者。

title.en: Pan Hu, the Dog Who Married a Princess and Begat the Man Peoples
title.zh: 盤瓠犬祖

region.en: Wu Mountains of the south, homeland of the Man peoples (symbolic pin: Hunan–Guizhou border)
region.zh: 南方武陵蠻地（象徵性定位）

period: Hou Han Shu (Book of the Later Han) by Fan Ye, 5th c. CE, Nanman Liezhuan; older versions in Soushen Ji

source.work: Hou Han Shu, Nanman Liezhuan: the dog Pan Hu, the princess, and the origin of the Wu-ling Man peoples

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: In the time of Emperor Ku, an old woman heard an earwig crawl from her ear and raised it in a gourd-cover; the dog that grew from it, Pan Hu, slew the enemy general Wufan and carried his head to the king. Bound by the king's own promise of his daughter, the princess went to the dog on the southern mountains; their twelve children intermarried and became the twelve clans of the Man peoples of Wu-ling — to whom the empire forever granted tax-free lands in payment of the dog's service.
summary.zh: 高辛氏之老婦得疾，取物如繭置瓠籬，化為犬，其文五色，名曰盤瓠；時犬戎之寇，募天下能得吳將軍首者妻以少女；盤瓠銜人頭造闕下——帝不得已，以女配之；生十二人，自相夫妻，織績木皮，染以草實，好五色衣服——是為武陵蠻。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Hou Han Shu original. Ethnogenesis legend of the Yao/Miao/She peoples, recorded by the imperial Han court in the vocabulary of the time — the 'barbarian' frame of the source is noted critically; living descendant communities regard Pan Hu as honored ancestor.

passages.text: An old woman of the court of Emperor Gaoxin suffered in her ear, and drew from it a creeping thing the size of a silkworm cocoon; she set it in a gourd-cover, and it turned into a dog of five colors, and was named Pan Hu — Gourd-Cover.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hou Han Shu, Nanman Liezhuan, Pan Hu's birth (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 帝嚳宮中一老婦耳中患疾，自耳中取出一蟲，大如蠶繭；置之瓠籬中，化為五色之犬，名曰槃瓠——瓠籬之意。

passages.text: When the dog-rong tribes raided the border and no man could withstand their general Wufan, the king proclaimed that whoever brought the general's head should have his youngest daughter in marriage. Pan Hu slipped into the enemy camp and returned with the general's head in his mouth, laying it before the king's steps.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hou Han Shu, Nanman Liezhuan, the beheading of Wufan; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 時犬戎之族寇邊，無人能敵其將吳將軍，王乃下令：有能得吳將軍首級者，以少女妻之。槃瓠潛入敵營，銜將軍首而歸，置於王階之前。

passages.text: The king shrank from giving a princess to a dog, but the daughter would not have him break his word. Pan Hu bore her to the southern mountains, into a stone chamber no man could climb; the dog became a man for her, and their twelve children married one another, weaving bark-cloth and dyeing it bright — the twelve clans of the Man peoples, whose lands the empire ever after left untaxed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hou Han Shu, Nanman Liezhuan, the marriage and the ethnogenesis; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 王不忍以公主妻犬，而女不願其父背約。槃瓠負女入南山，至人跡不可登之石室；犬為女化為人，所生十二子女自相婚配，織樹皮為布而染之鮮明——是為蠻夷十二族，其後朝廷永不加賦其地。

title.en: Horus of Behutet and the Winged Disk
title.zh: 貝胡特特荷魯斯與雙翼日盤

region.en: Edfu (Behutet), Upper Egypt (temple of Horus, where the legend is inscribed)
region.zh: 埃及上埃及埃德富（貝胡特特，荷魯斯神廟刻壁處）

period: Inscribed at Edfu in the Ptolemaic temple; text purports to date from the 363rd year of Ra-Heru-Khuti (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), ch. IV, 'The Legend of Horus of Behutet and the Winged Disk'

summary.en: The founding myth of Egypt's most famous temple sign: Horus of Behutet flies into the horizon as the great Winged Disk and annihilates the rebels of Ra — followers turned crocodiles and hippopotami, slain by the hundreds before Edfu — until Set himself is captured, beheaded, and dragged through his own district; Thoth orders the Winged Disk placed above every temple in the land.
summary.zh: 埃及最著名神廟紋章之緣起：貝胡特特荷魯斯化為雙翼日盤翱翔天際，誅殺謀逆之眾——敵者化鱷與河馬，於埃德富城前被逐一誅戮——直至塞特被縛、斬首、以其矛貫首拖行己土；托特遂命日盤置於全國諸神廟之上。

sensitivity.note: Ancient temple foundation legend; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: And Heru-Behutet flew up into the horizon in the form of the great Winged Disk, for which reason he is called 'Great god, lord of heaven,' unto this day. And when he saw the enemies in the heights of heaven he set out to follow after them in the form of the great Winged Disk, and he attacked with such terrific force those who opposed him, that they could neither see with their eyes nor hear with their ears, and each of them slew his fellow. In a moment of time there was not a single creature left alive. Then Heru Behutet, shining with very many colours, came in the form of the great Winged Disk to the Boat of Ra-Harmachis, and Thoth said unto Ra, 'O Lord of the gods, Behutet hath returned in the form of the great Winged Disk, shining [with many colours] . . . . . . children;' for this reason he is called Heru-Behutet unto this day.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), the Winged Disk legend, section XIII.
passages.zh: 而荷魯—貝胡特化作巨大的有翼日輪飛升入地平線，因此至今他被稱為「偉大的神，天之主宰」。當他看見天上的高處有敵人時，便化作巨大的有翼日輪出發追趕他們；他以如此可怖的力量攻擊那些與他為敵者，使他們既不能以眼視物，也不能以耳聽聲，於是他們彼此相殺。頃刻之間，無一生物存活。隨後，荷魯—貝胡特閃耀著萬千色彩，化作巨大的有翼日輪來到拉—哈爾馬奇斯的船前，托特對拉說：「眾神之主啊，貝胡特已化作巨大的有翼日輪歸來，閃耀著〔萬千色彩〕……孩童；」因此至今他被稱為荷魯—貝胡特。

passages.text: And behold the enemies [of Ra] rushed into the water, and they took the forms of [crocodiles and] hippopotami, but nevertheless Ra-Heru-Khuti sailed over the waters in his boat, and when the crocodiles and the hippopotami had come nigh unto him, they opened wide their jaws in order to destroy Ra-Heru-Khuti. And when Heru-Behutet arrived and his followers who were behind him in the forms of workers in metal, each having in his hands an iron spear and a chain, according to his name, they smote the crocodiles and the hippopotami; and there were brought in there straightway six hundred and fifty-one crocodiles, which had been slain before the city of Edfu.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), section XIII.
passages.zh: 看哪，〔拉的〕敵人衝入水中，化作〔鱷魚與〕河馬之形，然而拉—荷魯—胡提仍乘其船航行於水上；當鱷魚與河馬逼近他時，牠們張大下顎，欲毀滅拉—荷魯—胡提。荷魯—貝胡特與跟隨其後、化作金屬工匠之形的隨從們抵達時，各人手中持一鐵矛與一鎖鏈，正如其名所示，他們擊打鱷魚與河馬；當下便有六百五十一條鱷魚被帶來，牠們是在埃德夫城前被殺的。

passages.text: Then Set rose up and came forth, and raged loudly with words of cursing and abuse because of the things which Heru-behutet had done in respect of the slaughter of the enemies. And Ra said unto Thoth, 'This fiend Nehaha-hra uttereth words at the top of his voice because of the things which Heru-Behutet hath done unto him;' and Thoth said unto Ra, 'Cries of this kind shall be called Nehaha-hra unto this day.' And Heru-Behutet did battle with the Enemy for a period of time, and he hurled his iron lance at him, and he threw him down on the ground in this region, which is called Pa-Rerehtu unto this day. Then Heru-Behutet came and brought the Enemy with him, and his spear was in his neck, and his chain was round his hands and arms, and the weapon of Horus had fallen on his mouth and had closed it; and he went with him before his father Ra, who said, 'O Horus, thou Winged Disk, twice great (Urui-Tenten) is the deed of valour which thou hast done, and thou hast cleansed the district.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), section XV.
passages.zh: 於是塞特起身而出，因荷魯—貝胡特屠殺敵人之事，高聲狂怒，口出咒罵與辱罵之言。拉對托特說：「這惡魔涅哈哈—拉因荷魯—貝胡特對他所作之事，正以最高聲量發出言語；」托特對拉說：「此類呼喊至今將被稱為涅哈哈—拉。」荷魯—貝胡特與那敵人交戰了一段時間，他將鐵矛擲向他，把他擊倒在此地地上，此地至今稱為帕—雷雷赫圖。隨後荷魯—貝胡特前來，帶著那敵人同來，他的矛刺在他的頸上，他的鎖鏈纏在他的雙手與臂上，荷魯斯的武器落在他口上並將其封閉；他帶著他來到父親拉面前，拉說：「荷魯斯啊，有翼日輪啊，你所行的英勇事蹟偉大無比（烏魯伊—滕滕），你已潔淨了此區。」

passages.text: Then Horus the son of Isis cut off the head of the Enemy [Set], and the heads of his fiends in the presence of father Ra and of the great company of the gods, and he dragged him by his feet through his district with his spear driven through his head and back. And Ra said unto Thoth, 'Let the son of Osiris drag the being of disaster through his territory;' and Thoth said, 'It shall be called Ateh,' and this hath been the name of the region from that day to this. And Isis, the divine lady, spake before Ra, saying, 'Let the exalted Winged Disk become the amulet of my son Horus, who hath cut off the head of the Enemy and the heads of his fiends.' — Then Thoth made the image of the Winged Disk to be in every sanctuary and in every temple, where they now are, wherein are all the gods and all the goddesses from this day onwards.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), sections XV and XIX.
passages.zh: 隨後，伊西斯之子荷魯斯在父親拉與眾神的大集會面前，砍下那敵人〔塞特〕的頭，以及他眾嘍囉的頭，並以矛刺穿他的頭與背，拖著他的腳穿過他的轄區。拉對托特說：「讓奧西里斯之子拖著那災禍之身穿過他的領地；」托特說：「此地將稱為阿特赫，」自此日至今，此區之名便是如此。神聖的女士伊西斯在拉面前說道：「願那崇高的有翼日輪成為我子荷魯斯的護身符，他已砍下那敵人的頭與他眾嘍囉的頭。」——於是托特製作有翼日輪之像，置於每一聖所與每一神廟之中，即如今它們所在之處，自今日以後，其中住著所有的神與所有的女神。

title.en: Isis the Kite: The Origin of Horus in the Marshes
title.zh: 鳶形伊西斯：荷魯斯之誕生

region.en: Chemmis marshes, Delta, Egypt (the hidden nest of Horus)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲克米斯沼澤（荷魯斯隱巢）

period: Hymn of the New Kingdom or later (Budge translation 1912); the doctrine goes back to the Pyramid Texts

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), 'A Hymn to Osiris and a Legend of the Origin of Horus'

summary.en: From the great Hymn to Osiris: Isis flies as a kite across the land crying her death-wails until she finds her murdered brother; with feathered light and the air of her wings she revives him, draws out his essence, and makes from it an heir — Horus — whom she suckles in solitude where none knows his place, until the gods gather to bestow on him the rank that is his by right.
summary.zh: 《奧西里斯頌》所載：伊西斯化為鳶鳥環飛大地、哀哭尋兄；以羽光與雙翼之氣使兄復甦，取其精而生嗣子荷魯斯；獨居荒沼哺育幼神，無人知其所在——至諸神齊集，方以固有之尊位歸還於他。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn material; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Thou settest [thy] son upon the great throne of his father Keb. Thou art the beloved one of thy mother Nut, whose valour is most mighty [when] thou overthrowest the Seba Fiend. Thou hast slaughtered thy enemy, and hast put the fear of thee into thy Adversary. Thou art the bringer in of the remotest boundaries, and art stable of heart, and thy two feet are lifted up; thou art the heir of Keb and of the sovereignty of the Two Lands, and he (i.e. Keb) hath seen thy splendid qualities, and hath commanded thee to guide the lands (i.e., the world) by thy hand so long as times [and seasons] endure.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), the Hymn to Osiris — the inheritance of Geb's throne.
passages.zh: 你將〔你的〕兒子安置在他父親凱布的大王座上。你是你母親努特所愛者，當你推翻塞巴惡魔時，你的英勇最為強大。你已屠殺你的敵人，並將對你的畏懼注入你的對手心中。你是引進最遙遠疆界者，你心志堅定，你的雙足高舉；你是凱布的繼承者，是兩地統治權的繼承者，他（即凱布）已見你的卓越品質，並命你以你的手引導諸地（即世界），只要時日〔與季節〕尚存。

passages.text: Thy sister [Isis] acted as a protectress to thee. She drove [thy] enemies away, she averted seasons [of calamity from thee], she recited the word (or, formula) with the magical power of her mouth, [being] skilled of tongue and never halting for a word, being perfect in command and word. Isis the magician avenged her brother. She went about seeking for him untiringly. She flew round and round over this earth uttering wailing cries of grief, and she did not alight on the ground until she had found him. She made light [to come forth] from her feathers, she made air to come into being by means of her two wings, and she cried out the death cries for her brother.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Hymn to Osiris — Isis the kite.
passages.zh: 你的姊妹〔伊西斯〕作了你的保護者。她驅逐〔你的〕敵人，她為你擋開〔災難的〕時節，她以口中魔力誦念咒語（或公式），〔她〕舌巧而從不滯於一言，於號令與言語皆臻完美。女魔法師伊西斯為她的兄弟復仇。她四處尋覓他，不知疲倦。她繞著這大地飛翔盤旋，發出悲痛的哀號，直到尋見他，她才降落於地。她從羽毛中放出光〔來〕，她以雙翼使空氣生成，她為她的兄弟喊出死亡的哀號。

passages.text: She made to rise up the helpless members of him whose heart was at rest, she drew from him his essence, and she made therefrom an heir. She suckled the child in solitariness and none knew where his place was, and he grew in strength. His hand is mighty (or, victorious) within the house of Keb, and the Company of the Gods rejoice greatly at the coming of Horus, the son of Osiris, whose heart is firmly stablished, the triumphant one, the son of Isis, the flesh and bone of Osiris.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Hymn to Osiris — the conception and hiding of Horus.
passages.zh: 她使那位心已安息者的无力肢体重新站起，从他身上取出他的精髓，并由此造出一位继承人。她独自哺育这孩子，无人知晓他身在何处，他便日渐强壮。他的手在凯布之家中大有能力（或曰得胜），众神会因荷鲁斯——奥西里斯之子、其心坚定稳固者、得胜者、伊西斯之子、奥西里斯的血肉与骨骼——的到来而大大欢喜。

passages.text: The Tchatcha of Truth, and the Company of the Gods, and Neb-er-tcher himself, and the Lords of Truth, gather together to him, and assemble therein. Verily those who defeat iniquity rejoice in the House of Keb to bestow the divine rank and dignity upon him to whom it belongeth, and the sovereignty upon him whose it is by right.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Hymn to Osiris — the vindication of Horus.
passages.zh: 真理的查查（Tchatcha）、众神会、涅布-埃尔-切尔本人，以及真理之诸主，都聚集到他那里，并在其中集会。诚然，那些战胜不义者，在凯布之家中欢喜，将神性的品级与尊荣赐予那本当拥有它者，并将主权赐予那按理本当拥有它者。

title.en: The Great Hymn to Osiris, Lord of Eternity
title.zh: 奧西里斯大頌，永恆之主

region.en: Abydos, Upper Egypt (Osiris' principal cult center, named throughout the hymn)
region.zh: 埃及上埃及阿拜多斯（頌中反覆稱名之主祭中心）

period: New Kingdom hymn (Budge translation 1912); recited in the Osiris temples of the Two Lands

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), 'A Hymn to Osiris and a Legend of the Origin of Horus' (opening sections)

summary.en: The great liturgical hymn of the Osiris cult: the god is addressed by his names at every city — Busiris, Heliopolis, Memphis, Herakleopolis, Abydos — as Lord of eternity whose transformations are sublime, whose gates of heaven open at his word, and whose son Horus sits established on his throne.
summary.zh: 奧西里斯祭團大頌：神以各城之名受拜——布西里斯、赫利奧波利斯、孟菲斯、赫拉克利奧波利斯、阿拜多斯——尊號連綿，變化無方；天門聞其言而啟，其子荷魯斯已定於其座。

sensitivity.note: Ancient temple hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Homage to thee, Osiris, Lord of eternity, King of the gods, whose names are manifold, whose transformations are sublime, whose form is hidden in the temples, whose Ka is holy, the Governor of Tetut, the mighty one of possessions in the shrine, the Lord of praises in the nome of Anetch, President of the tchefa food in Anu, Lord who art commemorated in [the town of] Maati, the mysterious (or, hidden) Soul, the Lord of Qerret, the sublime one in White Wall, the Soul of Ra [and] his very body, who hast thy dwelling in Henensu, the beneficent one, who art praised in Nart, [who inspirest] great terror in Shas-hetep, Lord of eternity, Governor of Abtu (Abydos).
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), the Hymn to Osiris, opening address.
passages.zh: 向你致敬，奥西里斯，永恒之主，众神之王，其名号繁多，其变形崇高，其形貌隐于诸神庙之中，其卡（Ka）神圣，特图特之总督，神龛中财富的强者，阿内奇诺姆中颂赞之主，阿努中特切法食物的主管，在[马阿提城]中被纪念之主，神秘（或曰隐藏）的灵魂，凯雷特之主，白墙中的崇高者，拉之灵魂[及]其本体，你居于赫嫩苏，仁慈者，你在纳尔特受颂赞，[你]在沙斯-赫特普激起极大的敬畏，永恒之主，阿布图（阿拜多斯）之总督。

passages.text: Thy seat (or, domain) reacheth far into Ta-tchesert, and thy name is firmly stablished in the mouth[s] of men. Thou art the two-fold substance of the Two Lands everywhere, and the divine food (tchef) of the Kau, the Governor of the Companies of the Gods, and the beneficent (or, perfect) Spirit-soul among Spirit-souls. The god Nu draweth his waters from thee, and thou bringest forth the north wind at eventide, and wind from thy nostrils to the satisfaction of thy heart. Thy heart flourisheth, and thou bringest forth the splendour of tchef food.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Hymn to Osiris.
passages.zh: 你的座位（或曰领域）远伸入塔-特切塞特，你的名在众人口中坚定稳固。你处处是两地的双重实体，是诸卡的 divine food（特切夫），众神会的主管，是诸灵-魂中仁慈（或曰完美）的灵-魂。努神从你那里汲取他的水，你在黄昏引出北风，从你鼻孔吹出的风使你心满意足。你的心繁盛，你引出特切夫食物的光辉。

passages.text: The height of heaven and the stars [thereof] are obedient unto thee, and thou makest to be opened the great gates [of the sky]. Thou art the lord to whom praises are sung in the southern heaven, thou art he to whom thanks are given in the northern heaven. The stars which never diminish are under the place of thy face, and thy seats are the stars which never rest. Offerings appear before thee by the command of Keb. The Companies of the Gods ascribe praise unto thee, the Star-gods of the Tuat smell the earth before thee, the domains [make] bowings [before thee], and the ends of the earth make supplication to thee [when] they see thee.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Hymn to Osiris.
passages.zh: 天之高处[及其]星辰都顺从于你，你使[天空的]大门开启。你是南天中受颂赞之主，你是北天中受感谢者。永不消减的星辰在你面容所在之处之下，你的座位是永不停息的星辰。祭品因凯布的命令而出现在你面前。众神会向你献上颂赞，图阿特的星辰之神在你面前嗅地，诸领域[向你]俯身，大地四极见你时向你祈求。

passages.text: Thou rollest up into the horizon, thou settest the light above the darkness, thou illuminest [the Two Lands] with the light from thy two plumes, thou floodest the Two Lands like the Disk at the beginning of the dawn. Thy White Crown pierceth the height of heaven saluting the stars, thou art the guide of every god. Thou art perfect in command and word. Thou art the favoured one of the Great Company of the Gods, and thou art the beloved one of the Little Company of the Gods.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Hymn to Osiris.
passages.zh: 你升入地平线，你将光置于黑暗之上，你以双羽之光照明[两地]，你如黎明之初的日轮般淹没两地。你的白冠刺入天之高处，向星辰致意，你是每位神的引导者。你在命令与言语上完美。你是众神大会的宠儿，你是众神小会的所爱者。

title.en: The Death and Resurrection of Horus: Isis and the Seven Scorpions
title.zh: 荷魯斯之死與復活：伊西斯與七蠍

region.en: Chemmis marshes and Pa-Sui, Delta, Egypt (Isis' flight with the child Horus)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲克米斯沼澤與帕-蘇伊（伊西斯攜子逃亡地）

period: Metternich Stele cycle, 30th Dynasty-Saite (c. 380-570 BCE); the cippus spells are older (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), ch. VIII, 'The Legend of the Death of Horus through the Sting of a Scorpion' and the Narrative of Isis

summary.en: Fleeing Set with the child Horus, Isis is escorted by seven scorpions; a rich woman who shuts her door against the goddess pays when her own son is stung, while Horus too is struck down and lies dead in the marshes. Isis' cry stops the Boat of Ra itself, and Thoth descends with the spells of maa-kheru to drive out the poison — the mythic warrant of Egypt's healing cippi, 'for him that is under the knife.'
summary.zh: 伊西斯攜幼荷魯斯避塞特之追，七蠍相隨；拒她入門的富家婦人其子遭螫，而小荷魯斯亦中蠍毒倒斃沼澤。伊西斯之哭喊令拉之舟停駛，托特攜『真言之威』降臨驅毒——此即埃及療病石碑之神話依據，『為刀下之人』而誦。

sensitivity.note: Ancient healing-stele cycle; no living community restrictions. The myth legitimized magical medicine (cippi of Horus), quoted here for comparative scholarship only.

passages.text: I came forth [from the dwelling] at the time of evening, and there came forth the Seven Scorpions which were to accompany me and to strike for me with [their] stings. Two scorpions, Tefen and Befen, were behind me, two scorpions, Mestet and Mestetef, were by my side, and three scorpions, Petet, Thetet, and Maatet (or, Martet), were for preparing the road for me. I charged them very strictly, and my words penetrated into their ears: 'Have no knowledge of [any], make no cry to the Tesheru beings, and pay no attention to the son of a man who belongeth to a man of no account.' So the guardian of the company brought me to the boundaries of the city of Pa-Sui.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), the Narrative of Isis, section I.
passages.zh: 我在傍晚時分[從居所]出來，那七隻蠍子也隨之而出，牠們要伴隨我，並以[牠們的]螫針為我擊刺。兩隻蠍子，特芬與貝芬，在我身後；兩隻蠍子，梅斯特特與梅斯特特夫，在我身旁；三隻蠍子，佩特特、泰特特與瑪阿泰特（或作瑪爾泰特），則為我預備道路。我嚴厲地囑咐牠們，我的話語傳入牠們耳中：『不可認識[任何人]，不可向泰舍魯眾靈呼喊，也不可理會那屬於無足輕重之人的凡人之子。』於是，這隊蠍子的守護者領我到了帕蘇伊城的邊界。

passages.text: When I had arrived at the place where the people lived I came to the houses wherein dwelt the wives [and] husbands. And a certain woman of quality spied me as I was journeying along the road, and she shut her doors on me. Now she was sick at heart by reason of those [scorpions] which were with me. Then [the Seven Scorpions] took counsel concerning her, and they all at one time shot out their venom on the tail of the scorpion Tefen; as for me, the woman Taha opened her door, and I entered into the house of the miserable lady. Then the scorpion Tefen entered in under the leaves of the door and smote (i.e., stung) the son of Usert, and a fire broke out in the house of Usert, and there was no water there to extinguish it; [but] the sky rained upon the house of Usert, though it was not the season for rain.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Narrative of Isis.
passages.zh: 當我到達人們居住之地，我來到那些住著妻子[與]丈夫的房屋。有一個貴婦在路旁窺見我正沿路而行，她便向我關上門戶。原來她因那些與我同在的[蠍子]而心中憂懼。於是[那七隻蠍子]為她商議，牠們一同將毒液射在蠍子特芬的尾上；至於我，那婦人塔哈打開了她的門，我便進入了那可憐婦人的屋中。隨後，蠍子特芬從門葉下進入，擊打了烏塞特之子，烏塞特家中便起了火，那裡卻沒有水可以撲滅；[然而]天空降雨在烏塞特家上，雖然那時並非降雨的季節。

passages.text: I went away to the city of Am, [where] the people gave thanks [for me] through [their] fear of my making trouble [for them]. I passed the day in seeking to provide food for the child, [and] on returning to take Horus into my arms I found him, Horus, the beautiful one of gold, the boy, the child, without [life]. He had bedewed the ground with the water of his eye, and with foam from his lips. His body was motionless, his heart was powerless to move, and the sinews (or, muscles) of his members were [helpless]. I sent forth a cry, [saying]: 'I, even I, lack a son to make answer [for me]. [My] two breasts are full to overflowing, [but] my body is empty. My father is in the Tuat, my mother is in Aqert, and my elder brother is in the sarcophagus.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Narrative of Isis, section 101 — the dead child Horus.
passages.zh: 我離去，前往阿姆城，[那裡]的人們因懼怕我為[他們]製造麻煩而[為我]稱謝。我終日尋求為那孩子預備食物，[但]當我回來要把荷魯斯抱入懷中時，我發現他——荷魯斯，那黃金之美者，那男孩，那孩子——已無[生命]。他眼中的水與唇邊的泡沫已沾濕了地面。他的身體一動不動，他的心無力跳動，他肢體的筋腱（或作肌肉）[皆軟弱無力]。我發出呼喊，[說]：『我，正是我，缺少一個兒子來為[我]應答。[我的]雙乳滿溢，[但]我的身體卻空虛。我的父親在圖阿特，我的母親在阿凱特，我的兄長在石棺之中。』

passages.text: And Isis sent forth her voice into heaven, and made supplication to the Boat of Millions of Years, and the Disk stopped in its journeying, and moved not from the place whereon it rested. Then came forth Thoth, who is equipped with his spells (or, words of power), and possesseth the great word of command of maa-kheru, [and said:] 'Fear not, fear not, O goddess Isis, fear not, fear not, O Nephthys, and let not anxiety [be to you]. I have come from heaven having life to heal(?) the child for his mother. Horus is protected as the Dweller in his Disk, who lighteth up the Two Lands by the splendour of his two Eyes; and he who is under the knife is likewise protected.' — [And Thoth said:] 'Wake up, Horus! Thy protection is established. Make thou happy the heart of thy mother Isis.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Narrative of Isis — the resurrection of Horus by Thoth.
passages.zh: 伊西斯向天發出她的聲音，向那百萬年之舟祈求，日輪便在其行程中停住，不再從其歇息之處移動。隨後，托特出來了，他配備著他的咒語（或作有力之言），並擁有瑪阿-凱魯的偉大號令之語，[說道]：『不要害怕，不要害怕，伊西斯女神；不要害怕，不要害怕，奈芙蒂斯；也不要讓憂慮[臨到你們]。我從天而來，帶著生命，為那孩子的母親醫治(?)那孩子。荷魯斯受保護，如同他圓盤中的居住者，以其雙眼的輝光照明兩地；那在刀下之人也同樣受保護。』——[托特又說：]『醒來吧，荷魯斯！你的保護已確立。你要使你母親伊西斯的心歡喜。』

title.en: Khnum and the Seven Years' Famine
title.zh: 庫努姆與七年饑荒

region.en: Elephantine (Abu), First Cataract, Egypt (temple and quarries of Khnum)
region.zh: 埃及第一瀑布象島（庫努姆神廟與採石場）

period: Stele text set in reign of Djoser (3rd Dynasty, c. 2670 BCE), carved in Ptolemaic times at Philae/Sahal (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), ch. VII, 'The Legend of Khnemu and a Seven Years' Famine'

summary.en: For seven years the Nile has failed and Egypt starves; King Tcheser (Djoser) sends his governor to the House of Life to find the river's birthplace, and learns that all waters come from the two caverns at Elephantine where Khnum dwells. In a dream the potter-god reminds the king who fashioned his body, then promises an eternal flood — and the king, waking, decrees the temple's tithe-endowment carved in stone forever.
summary.zh: 尼羅七年不漲，埃及大饑；王捷塞爾遣官往生命之屋查河源，得知諸水皆出象島雙穴，庫努姆居焉。陶匠之神夢中告王：『我造爾身』，許以永不匱乏之洪——王醒後刻石頒詔，永賦神廟什一之稅。

sensitivity.note: Late-period stele legend set in Old Kingdom; no living community restrictions. Coordinates at Elephantine (modern Aswan area) since the myth is anchored to the island's temple and quarries.

passages.text: Misery hath laid hold upon me [as I sit] upon the great throne by reason of those who dwell in the Great House. My heart is grievously afflicted by reason of the exceedingly great evil [which hath happened] because Hapi (i.e., the Nile) hath not come forth in my time to the [proper] height for seven years. Grain is very scarce, vegetables are lacking altogether, every kind of thing which men eat for their food hath ceased, and every man [now] plundereth his neighbour. Men wish to walk, but are unable to move, the child waileth, the young man draggeth his limbs along, and the hearts of the aged folk are crushed with despair.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), the Famine Stele, the king's despatch.
passages.zh: 我[坐在]大殿之上，因那些住在大屋中的人，困苦已臨到我身。因哈皮（即尼羅河）在我的時代未曾漲至[應有的]高度，至今已七年，那極大的災禍[臨到]，我的心因此極其憂傷。穀物極為稀少，蔬菜全然缺乏，人們作為食物所吃的一切都已斷絕，人人[如今]搶奪鄰舍。人們想要行走，卻不能移動；孩童哀哭，少年拖著肢體而行，老人的心因絕望而破碎。

passages.text: He said unto me: 'There is a city in the middle of the stream wherefrom Hapi maketh his appearance; Abu was its name in the beginning; it is the City of the Beginning, and it is the Nome of the City of the Beginning. [It reacheth] to Uaua, which is the beginning of the land. There is too a flight of steps, which reareth itself to a great height, and is the support of Ra, when he maketh his calculation to prolong life to everyone; Netchemtchem Ankh is the name of its abode. The two Qerti is the name of the water, and they are the two breasts from which every good thing cometh forth.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Famine Stele — the revelation of the Nile's birthplace.
passages.zh: 他對我說：『在河流中央有一座城，哈皮從那裡出現；起初它的名字是阿布；它是起始之城，也是起始之城的州。[它延伸]至烏阿烏阿，那是土地的起點。那裡還有一道階梯，高聳至極，是拉的支柱，當他計算以延長每人的壽命之時；奈切姆切姆·安赫是它居所的名字。兩座凱爾提是那水的名字，它們是雙乳，一切美善之物皆從其中而出。』

passages.text: He openeth his eyes, and his heart was inclined [to hear] me, and his words were strong [when he said], 'I am Khnemu, who fashioned thee. My two hands were about thee and knitted together thy body, and made healthy thy members; and it is I who gave thee thy heart. Yet the minerals (or, precious stones) [lie] under each other, [and they have done so] from olden time, and no man hath worked them in order to build the houses of the god, or to restore those which have fallen into ruin, or to hew out shrines for the gods of the South and of the North, or to do what he ought to do for his lord, notwithstanding that I am the Lord and the Creator.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Famine Stele — Khnum's rebuke.
passages.zh: 他睜開雙眼，他的心便傾向[聽]我，他的話語堅定[當他說]：『我是赫努姆，造你者。我的雙手環抱你，將你的身體編織結合，使你的肢體康健；正是我賜給你你的心。然而礦物（或作寶石）[彼此]層疊而臥，[自古以來]便是如此，無人開採它們以建造神的居所，或修復那些已傾頹荒廢的，或為南北之神鑿造神龕，或為其主盡應盡之責，儘管我乃是主與造物者。』

passages.text: I am [he] who created himself, Nu, the Great [God], who came into being at the beginning, [and] Hapi, who riseth according to his will, in order to give health to him that laboureth for me. I am the Director and Guide of all men at their seasons, the Most Great, the Father of the Gods, Shu, the Great One, the Chief of the Earth. A lake of water hath been poured out for me, [namely,] Hap (i.e., the Nile), which embraceth the field-land, and his embrace provideth the [means of] life for every one. I will make Hap (i.e., the Nile) rise for thee, and [in] no year shall [he] fail, and he shall spread himself out in rest upon every land. Green plants and herbs and trees shall bow beneath [the weight of] their produce. Misery shall pass away, and the emptiness of their store-houses of grain shall come to an end.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Famine Stele — Khnum's promise.
passages.zh: 我乃是[那]自造者努，偉大[之神]，太初即已存在者，[以及]哈皮，他隨己意漲起，為要使為我勞作之人得康健。我是眾人在其時節的引領者與嚮導，至大者，眾神之父，舒，偉大者，大地之首。一湖之水已為我傾注，[即]哈普（即尼羅河），它環抱田地，其環抱為每一人提供[生命之]資。我必為你使哈普（即尼羅河）漲起，[他]決不於任何一年失約，他必安然漫布於每一片土地。青綠的植物、草木與樹木必因它們的果實[之重]而低垂。苦難必將消逝，他們糧倉空匱之事必將終結。

title.en: Khonsu and the Princess of Bekhten
title.zh: 孔蘇與貝克滕公主

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (temple of Khonsu at Karnak, where the Bentresh stele stood)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（卡納克孔蘇神廟，本特雷什碑立處）

period: Bentresh Stele, 3rd Intermediate or early Late Period, set in year 33 of Ramesses II (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), ch. VI, 'A Legend of Khensu Nefer-hetep and the Princess of Bekhten'

summary.en: The Pharaoh marries the daughter of the Prince of Bekhten, but her sister falls possessed by a spirit no scribe can cure. Twice the god Khonsu is petitioned; his statue, given the elder god's protective power 'in a fourfold measure,' sails a year and five months to Bekhten, defeats the spirit in open conversation, and stays three years and nine months — until the god flies home as a golden hawk in the prince's dream.
summary.zh: 法老娶貝克滕王之女，其妹卻為邪靈所附，書吏莫能治。神孔蘇兩度受請；其像承長神護力『四倍』，舟行一年五月抵貝克滕，當眾折服邪靈，留三年九月——至王夢中化金鷹飛歸埃及。

sensitivity.note: Ancient healing-provenance stele; no living community restrictions. 'miraculous-birth' tag used here for the marvel-hagiography genre (healing miracle), the closest index category; recorded as an interpretive choice.

passages.text: And the Prince of Bekhten [also] caused his gifts to be brought, and he set his eldest daughter at the head of them all, and he addressed words of praise to His Majesty, and prayed to him for his life. And the maiden was beautiful, and His Majesty considered her to be the most lovely [woman] in the world, and he wrote down as her title, 'Great Royal Wife, Ra-neferu'; and when His Majesty arrived in Egypt, he did for her whatsoever was done for the Royal Wife.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), the Bekhten legend.
passages.zh: 貝克坦的王子[也]命人帶來他的禮物，並將其長女置於眾人之前，他向陛下致頌讚之辭，並為其性命向他祈求。那少女容貌美麗，陛下視她為世間最可愛的[女子]，便寫下她的稱號為『大王妻，拉-涅費魯』；當陛下抵達埃及時，他為她所行的一切，皆如為王妻所行的一般。

passages.text: He spake words of adoration to His Majesty, saying, 'I have come unto thee, my King and Lord, on behalf of Bent-Resht, the younger sister of the Royal Wife Ra-neferu. [Some] disease hath penetrated into her members, and I beseech Thy Majesty to send a man of learning to see her.' And when the man of learning had arrived in Bekhten, he found Bent-Resht in the condition of a woman who is possessed by a spirit, and he found this spirit to be an evil one, and to be hostile in his disposition towards him. And the Prince of Bekhten sent a messenger a second time into the presence of His Majesty, saying, 'O King, my Lord, I pray His (i.e., Thy) Majesty to command that a god be brought hither to contend against the spirit.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Bekhten legend.
passages.zh: 他對陛下說出崇敬之辭，說道：『我來到你面前，我的國王與主，是為王妻拉-涅費魯之妹本特-雷什特而來。[某種]疾病已侵入她的肢體，我懇求陛下派遣一位博學之人前去察看。』當那博學之人抵達貝克坦時，他發現本特-雷什特處於被神靈附身之女子的狀況，他發現這神靈乃是惡靈，且其性情對他懷有敵意。貝克坦的王子第二次遣使到陛下面前，說道：『國王，我的主啊，我祈求陛下（即你的陛下）下令帶來一位神祇，與這神靈相爭。』

passages.text: And Khensu in Thebes, [called] 'Nefer-Hetep,' inclined his head with a deep inclination twice. And he made [his] protective power to pass into Khensu, [called] 'Pa-ari-sekher-em-Uast,' in a fourfold measure. Then His Majesty commanded that Khensu, [called] 'Pa-ari-sekher-em-Uast,' should set out on his journey in a great boat, [accompanied by] five smaller boats, and chariots, and a large number of horses. And when this god had passed over to the place where Bent-Resht was, he worked upon the daughter of the Prince of Bekhten with his magical power, and she became better (i.e., was healed) straightway. And this spirit which had been with her said, in the presence of Khensu, [called] 'Pa-ari-sekher-em-Uast,' 'Come in peace, O great god, who dost drive away the spirits which attack! Bekhten is thy city, the people thereof, both men and women, are thy servants, and I myself am thy servant.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Bekhten legend.
passages.zh: 底比斯的孔蘇，[稱為]『涅費爾-赫特普』，深深俯首兩次。他將其護佑之力以四倍之量注入孔蘇，[稱為]『帕-阿里-塞赫爾-恩-烏阿斯特』。於是陛下下令孔蘇，[稱為]『帕-阿里-塞赫爾-恩-烏阿斯特』，乘大船啟程，[隨行]五艘小船、戰車與大量馬匹。當此神渡至本特-雷什特所在之處，他以法力作用於貝克坦王子之女，她立刻好轉（即得痊癒）。那曾附於她身上的神靈在孔蘇，[稱為]『帕-阿里-塞赫爾-恩-烏阿斯特』面前說道：『平安而來吧，偉大的神啊，你驅逐來犯的神靈！貝克坦是你的城，其中的人民，男女皆是你的僕人，我自己也是你的僕人。』

passages.text: And [when] this god had tarried for three years and nine months in Bekhten, the Prince of Bekhten, who was lying down asleep on his bed, saw this god come forth outside his shrine (now he was in the form of a golden hawk), and he flew up into the heavens and departed to Egypt; and when the Prince woke up he was trembling. And he said unto the prophet of Khensu, [called] 'Pa-ari-sekher-em-Uast,' 'This god who tarried with us hath departed to Egypt; let his chariot also depart to Egypt.' And the Prince of Bekhten permitted [the image of] the god to set out for Egypt, and he gave him many great gifts of beautiful things of all kinds.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), the Bekhten legend, closing.
passages.zh: 當此神在貝克坦逗留三年九月之後，貝克坦的王子正躺臥床上沉睡，見此神走出其神龕之外（當時他呈金色隼之形），飛升入天，離往埃及；王子醒來時渾身顫抖。他對孔蘇，[稱為]『帕-阿里-塞赫爾-恩-烏阿斯特』的先知說道：『這與我們同住的神已離往埃及；讓他的戰車也離往埃及吧。』貝克坦的王子允許[此神的]像啟程前往埃及，並贈他許多各式美物的厚禮。

title.en: The Lamentations of Isis and Nephthys
title.zh: 伊西斯與奈芙蒂斯哀歌

region.en: Abydos, Upper Egypt (recited at the Osiris festival in the temple)
region.zh: 埃及上埃及阿拜多斯（奧西里斯祭期間於神廟誦唱）

period: Recited on the 25th day of the 4th month of Akhet; Graeco-Roman copies of far older liturgy (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. V, 'The Lamentations of Isis and Nephthys' (Berlin papyrus)

summary.en: Two 'fair women' with the gods' names on their shoulders sang this alternately at the Osiris mysteries: Isis calls her murdered husband home — 'Come to thy house, come to thy house, O An... I am thy sister who loved thee upon earth; none other loved thee more' — and Nephthys joins her weeping, each verse a spell for the resurrection of Osiris and of the dead who hear it.
summary.zh: 肩佩神名的兩位『貞女』於奧西里斯祭中輪唱此歌：伊西斯召亡夫歸家——『歸家，歸家，安神……我乃世上愛你之姊，愛你者莫過於姊』；奈芙蒂斯泣而應和——每節皆為奧西里斯與聞者亡靈復活之咒。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ritual lament; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: ISIS SAITH: 'Come to thy house, come to thy house, O An, come to thy house. Thine enemy [Set] hath perished. O beautiful youth, come to thy house. Look thou upon me. I am the sister who loveth thee, go not far from me. O Beautiful Boy, come to thy house, straightway, straightway. I cannot see thee, and my heart weepeth for thee; my eyes follow thee about. I am following thee about so that I may see thee. Lo, I wait to see thee, I wait to see thee; behold, Prince, I wait to see thee. It is good to see thee, it is good to see thee; O An, it is good to see thee. Come to thy beloved one, come to thy beloved one, O Un-Nefer, whose word is truth.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. V, the Lamentations of Isis and Nephthys.
passages.zh: 伊西斯說：『到你的屋裡來，到你的屋裡來，哦，安，到你的屋裡來。你的仇敵〔塞特〕已經滅亡了。哦，俊美的少年，到你的屋裡來。請你看著我。我是愛你的姊妹，不要遠離我。哦，俊美的男孩，立刻到你的屋裡來，立刻，立刻。我見不到你，我的心為你哭泣；我的眼睛追隨著你。我跟隨著你，好讓我見到你。看哪，我等待著見你，我等待著見你；看哪，王子，我等待著見你。見到你是好的，見到你是好的；哦，安，見到你是好的。到你心愛的人這裡來，到你心愛的人這裡來，哦，烏恩-涅菲爾，他的話語即是真理。』

passages.text: Isis saith: 'Come to thy wife, O thou whose heart is still. Come to the lady of thy house; I am thy sister from thy mother's [womb]. Go not thou far from me. The faces of gods and men are turned towards thee, they all weep for thee together. As soon as I saw thee I cried out to thee, weeping with a loud voice which pierced the heavens, and thou didst not hear my voice. I am thy sister who loved thee upon earth; none other loved thee more than [thy] sister, thy sister.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Lamentations of Isis.
passages.zh: 伊西斯說：『到你的妻子這裡來，哦，你的心仍舊平靜。到你的屋子的女主人這裡來；我是你母親〔腹中〕的姊妹。你不要遠離我。眾神與眾人的臉都轉向你，他們一同為你哭泣。我一見到你便向你呼喊，以響徹雲霄的大聲哭泣，而你卻沒有聽見我的聲音。我是你的姊妹，在世上愛過你；沒有人比〔你的〕姊妹更愛你，你的姊妹。』

passages.text: NEPHTHYS SAITH: 'O Beautiful Prince, come to thy house. Let thy heart rejoice and be glad, for thine enemies have ceased to be. Thy two Sisters are nigh unto thee; they guard thy bier, they address thee with words [full of] tears as thou liest prone on thy bier. Look thou at the young women; speak to us, O our Sovereign Lord. Destroy thou all the misery that is in our hearts; the chiefs among gods and men look upon thee. Turn thou towards us thy face, O our Sovereign Lord. At the sight of thy face life cometh to our faces; turn not thou thy face from us. The joy of our heart is in the sight of thee. O Beautiful Sovereign, our hearts would see thee. I am thy sister Nephthys who loveth thee. The fiend Seba hath fallen, he hath not being. I am with thee, and I act as the protectress of thy members for ever and ever.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Lamentations of Nephthys.
passages.zh: 涅弗提斯說：『哦，俊美的王子，到你的屋裡來。讓你的心歡喜快樂吧，因為你的仇敵已不復存在。你的兩位姊妹在你身旁；她們守護你的靈柩，當你俯臥在靈柩上時，她們以〔充滿〕淚水的話語對你說話。請你看看這些年輕女子；對我們說話吧，哦，我們的主權之主。請你毀滅我們心中所有的悲苦；眾神與眾人中的首領都看著你。請你向我們轉過你的臉，哦，我們的主權之主。一見到你的臉，生命便臨到我們的臉上；請你不要把臉轉離我們。我們心中的喜樂在於見到你。哦，俊美的主權者，我們的心想見你。我是你的姊妹涅弗提斯，愛著你。惡魔塞巴已經倒下，他已不存在。我與你同在，我永遠保護你的肢體，直到永遠。』

passages.text: The rubric directs that the book were recited on behalf of any deceased person it would make his spirit to be glorious, and stablish his body, and cause his Ka to rejoice, and give breath to his nostrils and air to his throat. The two 'fair women' sang the sections alternately in the presence of the Kher-heb and Setem priests. One of these had the name of Isis on her shoulder, and the other the name of Nephthys, and each held a vessel of water in her right hand, and a 'Memphis cake of bread' in her left.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Budge (1910), ch. V rubric and performance directions; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 題記指示，此書若為任何亡者誦讀，便會使他的靈魂得榮耀，使他的身體堅立，使他的卡（Ka）歡喜，並賜氣息給他的鼻孔，賜空氣給他的喉嚨。兩位「美麗的女子」在赫爾-赫布祭司與塞特姆祭司面前輪流唱誦這些段落。其中一人的肩上寫著伊西斯的名字，另一人的肩上寫著涅弗提斯的名字，各人右手持一水器，左手持一塊「孟菲斯麵餅」。

title.en: How Suan Became Rich
title.zh: 蘇安如何致富

region.en: Pasig, Rizal province, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋黎薩省帕西格（敘述者居地）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 5a 'How Suan became Rich', eBook #8299

summary.en: Poor Suan borrows a building post from his rich friend Pedro, whose envy drives him to accuse Suan before the king. On the road Suan accidentally drowns a bather and tears off a carabao's tail, gathering three accusers. The king's literal decisions — post for rice-and-fish, bath for the bather's son, carabao until its tail regrows — are all exploited by Suan, who collects payments from every frightened accuser and finally, razor in hand at Pedro's house, extorts all of Pedro's riches.
summary.zh: 窮漢蘇安向富友佩德羅借屋柱；佩德羅眼紅，竟控告於王前。途中蘇安失手溺死沐浴老人、拉斷水牛尾，招致三路原告。國王照字面判決：柱換飯、以浴償溺、牛尾長全才還牛——蘇安遂逐個向怕事的原告索錢，最後持剃刀上門『取回飯魚』，佩德羅驚恐之下獻出全部家財。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog droll recorded by Fansler from a Pasig narrator; archival record. Part of the 'Wonderful Decisions' cycle; Fansler derives it from the Jataka 'Gamani-canda' No. 257.

passages.text: Pedro inherited a great fortune from his parents, but his friend Suan was as poor as the poorest of beggars. Suan borrowed one building post to construct a house that surpassed Pedro's own, and the envious Pedro demanded it back though its removal would destroy the house; refusing to be paid or replaced, he threatened to accuse Suan before the king. On the Monday journey Pedro carried silver, Suan only cooked rice and fish, which he generously shared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 5 'How Suan became Rich'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 佩德羅從父母那裡繼承了一大筆財產，但他的朋友蘇安卻窮得像最窮的乞丐。蘇安借了一根屋柱來建造一座勝過佩德羅自家的房子，心懷嫉妒的佩德羅便要討回那根柱子，儘管拆下它會毀了那房子；他拒絕接受賠償或替換，還威脅要在國王面前控告蘇安。星期一上路時，佩德羅帶著銀子，蘇安只帶了煮熟的米飯和魚，他慷慨地與人分享。

passages.text: At the broken bridge Suan fell from his jump onto an old man bathing in the river, knocking him silly so that he drowned; Isidro, the son, joined the party to accuse him. Then Suan, helping Barbekin rescue a carabao from the mire, pulled so hard that the tail broke off short, and Barbekin resolved to accuse him too. At the palace the king gave literal decisions: Suan must return the post and Pedro give him his rice and fish; Suan must bathe in the river and Isidro may jump on him; Barbekin must give Suan the carabao until its tail grows to full length.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 5 'How Suan became Rich'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在斷橋處，蘇安從跳躍中跌落，砸在河裡洗澡的老人身上，把他撞得昏頭轉向，以致溺死；老人的兒子伊西德羅便加入眾人一同控告他。接著，蘇安幫巴爾貝金把一頭水牛從泥沼裡救出來，拉得太用力，把尾巴拉斷了一截，巴爾貝金也決心控告他。在宮殿裡，國王作出了字面意義上的判決：蘇安必須歸還那根柱子，而佩德羅必須把自己的米飯和魚給他；蘇安必須在河裡洗澡，伊西德羅可以跳到他身上；巴爾貝金必須把水牛交給蘇安，直到牠的尾巴長回全長為止。

passages.text: Suan then milked every judgment: Barbekin paid ninety pesos to be quit of the carabao; Isidro, afraid to jump from the high bridge and unable to swim, bought pardon for five hundred pesos; and Pedro, facing Suan's razor as he announced he had come for his 'rice and fish,' cried out that he need not return the post and then, cut at the abdomen's edge, offered all his riches. Thus Suan became the richest man in town by using his tact and knowledge in outwitting his enemies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 5 'How Suan became Rich'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蘇安於是逐一榨取了每一筆判決：巴爾貝金付了九十披索，以擺脫那頭水牛；伊西德羅害怕從高橋上跳下，又不會游泳，便以五百披索換取寬恕；而佩德羅面對蘇安的剃刀，聽他宣稱自己是來取他的「米飯和魚」，便大喊說他不必歸還那職位，隨後在腹部邊緣被劃了一刀，獻出了他所有的財富。蘇安就這樣憑著他的機敏與見識智勝了他的敵人，成了鎮上最富有的人。

title.en: The King's Decisions: Juan and the Smell of Money
title.zh: 國王的判決：胡安與金錢之香

region.en: Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home province)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 5b 'The King's Decisions', eBook #8299

summary.en: Starving Juan's hunger is satisfied by the fragrance of a rich man's cooking, and the rich man demands payment — for a smell. On the road Juan breaks a horse's tail and frightens a pregnant woman into miscarriage, adding two accusers. The king rules that the smell of food be paid with the smell of silver coins, that the horse-tail regrow before return, and that the wife bear another child before restitution — literal justice that leaves every accuser empty-handed.
summary.zh: 飢餓的胡安被富戶飯香所飽，富人竟索香氣之錢。途中胡安拉斷馬尾、驚致孕婦流產，又添二告。國王判曰：飯香者以銀幣之香償之；馬尾長全方可還馬；妻再生一子方可抵命——照字面執行的判決，令所有原告空手而歸。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog droll recorded by Fansler from a Batangas narrator; archival record. Second variant of the 'Wonderful Decisions' cycle derived from Jataka No. 257.

passages.text: Poor Juan, weakened with hunger and fatigue, passed a rich man's house where food was cooking, and the fragrance satisfied his hunger. When the rich man learned that the smell of his food had satisfied Juan, he demanded money; Juan refused, having none, and having neither tasted nor touched the food. They set out for the king's palace to have the matter settled, and on the way gathered more accusers: Juan, helping a man free his horse from a mud-hole, pulled the animal's tail off; and at midnight, lodging downstairs, his sudden frightened shriek so startled the pregnant wife above that she miscarried, and her husband joined the party.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 5 'The King's Decisions'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 可憐的胡安因飢餓與疲憊而虛弱不堪，經過一戶富人的房子，那裡正在煮食，食物的香氣滿足了她的飢餓。當那富人得知自己的食物氣味滿足了胡安，便向他索討金錢；胡安拒絕了，因為他身無分文，也既未嘗過、也未碰過那食物。他們動身前往國王的宮殿，要把此事了結，途中又聚集了更多告狀的人：胡安幫一個人把馬從泥坑裡拉出來時，扯掉了那牲口的尾巴；而半夜裡，他住在樓下，突然發出一聲驚恐的尖叫，把樓上懷孕的妻子嚇得流了產，她的丈夫也加入了這一行人。

passages.text: Before the king, the rich man Pedro demanded pay for the smell of his food. The king commanded a servant to fetch two silver coins and place them on the table: 'Now, Pedro, come here and smell the coins. As Juan became satisfied with the smell of your food, so now satisfy yourself with the smell of the money.' Pedro could not say a word. The next decisions followed the same logic: Manuel must give his horse to Juan until another tail grows, and the married man must let Juan have his wife until she gives birth to another child. All three went home discontented — Pedro without pay, Manuel without his horse, and the other without his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 5 'The King's Decisions'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在國王面前，富人佩德羅要求為他食物的氣味付錢。國王命一名僕人取來兩枚銀幣，放在桌上：「現在，佩德羅，過來聞一聞這些錢幣。正如胡安因你食物的氣味而滿足，現在你也因這錢的氣味而滿足吧。」佩德羅一句話也說不出來。接下來的判決也依同樣的道理：曼努埃爾必須把他的馬交給胡安，直到長出另一條尾巴為止；而那已婚的男子必須讓胡安得到他的妻子，直到她生下另一個孩子為止。三人都滿心不悅地回了家——佩德羅沒拿到錢，曼努埃爾沒了馬，另一個則沒了妻子。

title.en: The Four Blind Brothers and the Pagui Tail
title.zh: 四盲兄弟與魟尾

region.en: Misamis, Mindanao, Philippines (origin of the narrator's tale)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨米薩米斯（故事原鄉）

period: Pampangan-retold Mindanao tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6a 'The Four Blind Brothers', eBook #8299

summary.en: Sent away to seek their fortunes, four blind brothers feel for cocoanuts in a grove and climb, one after another, a tree whose top had been broken — each fall counted as a 'Bung!' of dropped fruit by the brothers below, until the last one finds his three brothers dead. Weeping, he disturbs the patianac, who give him food, shelter, and the tail of a pagui (sting-ray) to find his fortune. Joined by a lame man, the two frighten a two-headed giant from his own house by dropping the sting-ray tail as a 'hair' — the prediction comes true and they live in the giant's house happily ever after.
summary.zh: 四盲兄弟外出謀生，在椰林中依次攀爬已被颱風折頂的椰樹，逐一墜亡；樹下者只當『咚』的一聲是椰子落地，數到第四聲才知真相。末弟哭聲驚動帕蒂亞納克幽靈，他們憐之，賜食、賜宿，並贈魟魚尾一枚以助其轉運。盲者與跛者同行，將魟尾當作『頭髮』拋下，嚇退雙頭巨人，奪其宅邸——預言應驗，二人從此安居樂業。

sensitivity.note: Tale collected by Fansler from a Pampangan narrator who heard it from a Misamis (Mindanao) boy; archival record. The patianac are Philippine night spirits; the sting-ray tail is a traditional demon-charm.

passages.text: There was once a man who had eight sons, four of them blind, and unable to keep them he sent all away to seek their fortunes. The blind brothers groped along the road, each holding the hand of the other, until in the evening they came to a cocoanut-grove. The eldest took off his camisa china and climbed a tree to gather a bunch of cocoanuts — but the tree broke, and down came the poor fellow. 'One!' cried the youngest brother. 'Three more!' shouted the rest, and 'Don't come down until you have dropped four!' they all cried at once. Who would answer them? Their brother lay dead on the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'The Four Blind Brothers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個人，他有八個兒子，其中四個是盲人，他養不起他們，便把他們全都打發出去自謀生路。那幾個盲兄弟沿著路摸索前行，彼此手牽著手，直到傍晚來到一片椰子林。老大脫下他的中國衫，爬上一棵樹去摘一串椰子——可是樹斷了，那可憐的傢伙就摔了下來。「一個！」最小的弟弟喊道。「再三個！」其餘的嚷道，接著他們異口同聲地一齊大喊：「不丟下四個就別下來！」誰來回答他們呢？他們的兄弟已躺在地上死了。

passages.text: While they waited for the second 'Bung!' the second brother climbed the same tree, and what had happened to the first happened to him, and so to the third in turn. When the youngest heard the third fall, he crept about to find the cocoanuts, and discovered instead that his three brothers lay dead on the ground. He went away crying very loud — and his crying disturbed the patianac, who were trying to sleep. Moved by the poor helpless blind man, they gave him food and shelter for the night, and the tail of a pagui which would help him find his fortune; at daybreak they showed him the way out of the grove.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'The Four Blind Brothers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他們等待第二聲「砰！」時，老二爬上了同一棵樹，發生在老大身上的事也發生在他身上，接著輪到老三也是如此。當最小的弟弟聽到第三次摔落，便摸索著四處尋找椰子，卻發現他的三個兄弟都躺在地上死了。他放聲大哭著離去——他的哭聲驚擾了正想睡覺的帕蒂亞納克。牠們被這個可憐無助的盲人所感動，便給他食物，供他過夜，又給了他一條帕吉的尾巴，這尾巴能幫他找到他的財富；天亮時，牠們為他指點了走出椰林的路。

passages.text: The blind man was hailed by a lame man resting under a shady tree, who asked to be carried on his shoulders; so they traveled together to a big, lonely house. When its owner, a two-headed giant, returned, he was afraid to enter but called in a voice of thunder, 'Who's there?' — 'We are big men... so big that the foundation of the house shakes when we walk.' 'Give me a proof!' cried the giant, and the two dropped from the window the tail of the pagui as 'one of our hairs.' The giant looked at it in wonder, convinced that they were more powerful than he, and picking up the 'hair' went away, afraid to face such antagonists in single combat. So the prediction of the patianac came true: the house and all the property of the giant fell into the hands of the blind man and the lame man, and they lived there happily all the rest of their lives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'The Four Blind Brothers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那盲人受到一個在樹蔭下休息的跛子招呼，跛子請求被扛在他的肩上；於是他們一同前往一棟孤零零的大房子。當房子的主人——一個雙頭巨人——回來時，他不敢進去，卻用雷鳴般的聲音喊道：「誰在那裡？」——「我們是巨人……大得我們一走動，房子的地基就震動。」「給我一個證明！」巨人喊道，於是兩人從窗口丟下那條帕吉的尾巴，說是「我們的一根頭髮」。巨人驚奇地看著它，確信他們比他更強大，便撿起那根「頭髮」離去，不敢與這樣的對手單打獨鬥。於是帕蒂亞納克的預言應驗了：巨人的房子和全部財產都落入了盲人和跛子手中，他們在那裡幸福地度過了餘生。

title.en: Juan the Blind Man and the Outlaws' House
title.zh: 盲人胡安與強盜之宅

region.en: Virac, Catanduanes, Philippines (where the story is common)
region.zh: 菲律賓卡坦端內斯維拉克（故事流行之地）

period: Bicol oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6b 'Juan the Blind Man', eBook #8299

summary.en: Eight blind friends who gather nightly in a cocoanut-grove lose seven of their number to broken typhoon-stumps, counting the falls as dropped fruit. The last, Juan, meets the lame Justo and they travel together, collecting a horn, a rusted axe, a rope, and an old drum. Hiding in a robbers' house, Juan answers the outlaws' challenge with the axe as his 'tooth,' the rope as his 'hair,' the horn as his whistle, and the drum as his stomach — terrifying them into flight. When the quarrel over the money comes, Justo's blow opens Juan's blind eyes and Juan's kick cures Justo's lameness; they divide the money fairly and live as close friends.
summary.zh: 八名盲友夜聚椰林，颱風折頂之樹令七人墜亡，盲者僅聞墜聲誤作椰子。倖存的胡安遇跛者胡斯托同行，沿途拾得號角、鏽斧、麻繩與舊鼓。二人躲進強盜之家，以斧為『牙』、繩為『髮』、號角為哨、鼓聲為肚——嚇得強盜跳窗而逃。分贓起爭執時，胡斯托一掌打開胡安的盲眼，胡安一腳踢癒胡斯托的跛腿；二人平分財富，結為莫逆。

sensitivity.note: Bicol folktale recorded by Fansler from a Virac, Catanduanes narrator; archival record. Fansler traces this tale-family to southern India (Frere's 'The Blind Man, the Deaf Man, and the Donkey').

passages.text: Many years ago there lived near a thick forest eight blind men who were close friends; at night they would go secretly to a neighboring cocoanut-grove, drinking tuba and eating young cocoanuts. One evening a severe typhoon struck the village and broke most of the cocoanut-trees off at the top. The next afternoon the joyous party went to steal fruit, and seven of them climbed the stump-trees while Juan, the youngest, remained below to count the cocoanuts his friends threw down. He had repeated his verse three times when he heard a fall — 'One' — then another and three in close succession: 'Good! five in all. Three more, friends.' A few minutes later he heard two more falls: 'Six, seven — well, only seven... One more for me, friends.' But it was his friends who had fallen, for the trees were only stumps.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'Juan the Blind Man'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 許多年前，在一座茂密的森林附近住著八個瞎眼的人，他們是親密的朋友；到了夜裡，他們便偷偷前往鄰近的一座椰子園，喝椰花酒、吃嫩椰子。一天傍晚，一場猛烈的颱風襲擊了村莊，把大部分的椰子樹從頂端折斷。第二天下午，這群興高采烈的人前去偷果子，其中七個人爬上了那些殘株似的樹，而年紀最小的胡安則留在下面，數著朋友們扔下來的椰子。他把自己的韻文念了三遍，忽然聽見一聲墜落——「一個」——接著又一聲，然後接連三聲：「好！一共五個。再來三個，朋友們。」幾分鐘後，他又聽見兩聲墜落：「六個、七個——好吧，只有七個……再給我一個，朋友們。」但掉下來的其實是他的朋友們，因為那些樹只不過是殘株罷了。

passages.text: When Juan found one of the dead bodies he ran away as fast as he could, until he struck Justo, a lame man, who advised him not to return lest the relatives of the others accuse him of murder. They agreed to travel together — 'Blind man, strong legs; Lame man, good eyes... But we'll walk on two, and we'll see with two' — gathering as they went a horn, a rusted axe, a piece of rope, and an old drum. Then Justo saw a very big house whose door stood open, its walls hung with bolos, spears, and shields; they hid in the ceiling, and when outlaws returned with bloody bolos and a big sack of money, the terrified Justo could not help crying out, 'Ay, here?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'Juan the Blind Man'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 胡安發現其中一具屍體後，便拼命奔逃，直到撞上了跛腳的胡斯托。胡斯托勸他不要回去，免得其他人 的親屬指控他殺人。他們商定一同上路——「瞎眼的人，腿腳強健；跛腳的人，眼睛明亮……但我們要用兩條腿走路，也要用兩隻眼睛看」——沿途收集了一隻號角、一把生鏽的斧頭、一段繩子和一面舊鼓。接著，胡斯托看見一棟非常大的房子，門敞開著，牆上掛滿了砍刀、長矛和盾牌；他們躲在天花板上，當強盜們帶著血跡斑斑的砍刀和一大袋錢回來時，驚恐的胡斯托忍不住喊出聲來：「哎呀，在這裡？」

passages.text: 'Ho, you mosquitoes! what are you doing there?' asked the chief of the outlaws. 'Aha, you rascals! we are going to eat you all,' answered the blind man in the loudest voice he could muster. 'To show you what kind of animals we are, here is one of my teeth' — and Juan threw down the rusted axe. 'Look at one of my hairs!' — and he threw down the rope. 'Now listen, you ants, to my whistle!' — and he blew the horn. 'And to show you how big our stomachs are, hear us beat them!' — and he beat the drum. The outlaws were so frightened that they ran away, some even jumping out of the windows. Dividing the money, Justo tried to cheat Juan; in the quarrel Justo struck him in the eyes with the palm of his hand, and the blind man's eyes were opened; Juan kicked Justo so hard that he rolled against a post and his lameness was cured. Seeing that each had done the other a great service, they divided the money fairly and lived ever after together as close friends.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'Juan the Blind Man'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「嘿，你們這些蚊子！在那裡做什麼？」強盜首領問道。「啊哈，你們這些惡棍！我們要把你們全都吃掉，」瞎眼的人用他能發出的最大聲音回答。「讓你們看看我們是什麼樣的動物，這是我的 一顆牙齒」——胡安扔下了那把生鏽的斧頭。「看看我的一根頭髮！」——他扔下了繩子。「現在，你們這些螞蟻，聽聽我的口哨！」——他吹響了號角。「再讓你們看看我們的肚子有多大，聽我們拍肚子！」——他敲起了鼓。強盜們嚇得落荒而逃，有些甚至從窗戶跳了出去。分錢的時候，胡斯托想欺騙胡安；爭吵中，胡斯托用手掌打了他的眼睛，瞎眼人的眼睛便睜開了；胡安一腳把胡斯托踢得滾到柱子上，他的跛腳也治好了。他們看出彼此都為對方做了極大的好事，便公平地分了錢，此後一直作為親密的朋友住在一起。

title.en: Teofilo the Hunchback and the Giant
title.zh: 駝背特奧菲洛與巨人

region.en: Bicol region, southeastern Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home region)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋東南比科爾地區（敘述者故鄉）

period: Bicol oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6c 'Teofilo the Hunchback, and the Giant', eBook #8299

summary.en: The wandering hunchback Teofilo, one-eyed and crooked, gathers a rope, a gun, and a duck, and sleeps in what turns out to be a giant's house. Challenged through the wall — 'If you are really a strong man and braver than I, let me see your hair!' — he throws out the rope; for his louse, the duck; for his voice, the gunshot the giant takes for spitting burning coals. The giant flees forever, and Teofilo lives happily in his house.
summary.zh: 流浪的獨眼駝背者特奧菲洛拾得麻繩、獵槍與鴨子，夜宿巨人宅中。巨人隔牆喝令『讓我看看你的頭髮！』——他拋出麻繩；『讓我看看你的蝨子！』——他拋出鴨子；『讓我聽聽你的聲音！』——他開槍，巨人誤以為他吐出的是燒紅的煤，倉皇而逃，永不復返。特奧菲洛從此安居其宅。

sensitivity.note: Bicol folktale recorded by Fansler from a student narrator; archival record. Token-deception variant of the blind-brothers tale-family.

passages.text: Once there lived a hunchback whose name was Teofilo. He was an orphan who got his food by wandering through the woods, sometimes sleeping under large trees; his one blind eye and crooked body would make almost any one pity his miserable condition. One day, wandering for something to eat, he found a piece of large rope, then a gun left against a fence, then caught a duck at a brook — sure of a good meal. Night coming on, he found a house with all its windows open, knocked, and entering, prepared his bed and slept, not knowing he was in a giant's house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'Teofilo the Hunchback'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個駝背，名叫特奧菲洛。他是個孤兒，靠著在樹林裡遊蕩覓食，有時睡在大樹下；他那隻瞎眼和彎曲的身軀，幾乎會讓任何人同情他悲慘的境況。一天，他四處遊蕩找吃的，發現了一段粗繩，接著又發現一支靠在籬笆上的槍，然後在小溪邊抓到一隻鴨子——這下可有把握吃上一頓好飯了。夜幕降臨，他找到一棟窗戶全都敞開的房子，敲了敲門，進去鋪好床便睡了，渾然不知自己身處巨人的家中。

passages.text: At midnight Teofilo was awakened by a loud voice. Through a hole in the wall he saw a very tall man, taller even than the house itself. 'I smell some one here,' said the giant, trying the locked door. 'If you are really a strong man and braver than I, let me see your hair!' — Teofilo threw out the piece of rope, and the giant was surprised at its size. 'Let me see your louse!' — and Teofilo threw out the duck, and the giant was terrified, for he had never seen such a large louse. 'Well, you seem to be larger than I. Let me hear your voice!' — Teofilo fired his gun, and when the giant heard it and saw it spitting fire, he trembled, thinking the man's saliva was burning coals. Afraid to challenge his strange guest any more, the giant ran away and disappeared forever — and so Teofilo the hunchback lived happily all the rest of his days in the giant's house without being troubled by any one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'Teofilo the Hunchback'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 半夜裡，特奧菲洛被一個響亮的聲音驚醒。他透過牆上的一個洞，看見一個非常高大的人，甚至比房子本身還高。「我聞到這裡有人，」巨人說著，試了試那扇鎖著的門。「如果你真是個強壯的人，而且比我還勇敢，讓我看看你的頭髮！」——特奧菲洛把那截繩子扔了出去，巨人對它的粗大感到驚訝。「讓我看看你的蝨子！」——特奧菲洛把鴨子扔了出去，巨人嚇壞了，因為他從未見過這麼大的蝨子。「好吧，你似乎比我還大。讓我聽聽你的聲音！」——特奧菲洛開了一槍，巨人聽到槍聲、看見它噴出火來，便渾身發抖，以為那人的口水是燃燒的炭火。巨人不敢再向這位奇怪的客人挑戰，便逃走了，從此消失無蹤——於是駝背的特奧菲洛在巨人的房子裡快樂地度過了餘生，再也沒有人來打擾他。

title.en: Juan and the Buringcantada
title.zh: 胡安與布林坎塔達

region.en: Albay, Bicol region, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home province)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋阿爾拜省（比科爾，敘述者故鄉）

period: Bicol oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6d 'Juan and the Buringcantada', eBook #8299

summary.en: Lazy Juan, gored between two fighting carabaos while trying to help, recovers and travels with his mother, collecting an axe, a rope, and a large drum. In the mansion of the Buringcantada — a one-eyed giant with tusks — mother and son hide in the ceiling; challenged to show a hair, a tooth, and the sound of his stomach, Juan produces the rope, the axe, and the drum. The terrified giant and his guests flee forever, and Juan and his mother live in the house like a rich family.
summary.zh: 懶惰的胡安為救被鬥牛所傷的水牛，反被雙牛角傷背；痊癒後與母親遠行，沿途拾得斧、繩與大鼓。他們藏身於獨眼長牙巨人布林坎塔達的府邸天花板中；應巨人之令展示『頭髮』（麻繩）、『牙齒』（斧頭）與『肚腹之聲』（鼓聲），巨人與賓客嚇得落荒而逃。母子從此在豪宅中過著富人般的生活。

sensitivity.note: Bicol folktale recorded by Fansler from a narrator who heard it from his grandmother; archival record. Token-deception variant; the Buringcantada is a Bicol one-eyed tusked giant.

passages.text: A long time ago, when the Bicols had not yet been welded into one tribe, a couple in the mountains of Albay had one son, Juan, whose father died before the boy was five. Growing up lazy, Juan was dearly loved and indulged by his mother, who told him to help anybody he met that needed help. One afternoon he saw two carabaos fighting and, mindful of her words, went between the animals to help the wounded one — and the two gored him in the back. Recovered, he persuaded his mother to go with him to look for money, gathering on the way an axe, a long rope stretching across the road, and a large drum on a river bank.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'Juan and the Buringcantada'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 很久以前，比科爾人尚未融合成一個部族的時候，阿爾拜山區有一對夫婦，他們有一個兒子叫胡安，父親在男孩不滿五歲時就去世了。胡安長得懶惰，卻深受母親疼愛與縱容，母親教他遇見任何需要幫助的人都要伸出援手。一天下午，他看見兩頭水牛在爭鬥，想起母親的話，便走到兩頭牲口中間去幫助那頭受傷的——結果兩頭水牛都用角頂傷了他的背。傷癒之後，他說服母親與他一同去尋找錢財，沿途收集了一把斧頭、一條橫跨道路的長繩，以及河岸上的一面大鼓。

passages.text: After about a week's travel they came upon a big house, well decorated with flowers and leaves, with a large hole in the dining-room ceiling. Juan proposed hiding there until they found out who the owner was, and mother and son went up into the ceiling with the axe, the rope, and the drum. Before many minutes the Buringcantada, a giant with one eye in the middle of his forehead and two long tusks projecting from the sides of his mouth, came in with his friends and servants to dine. Juan said in a loud voice that the viands were the best for them — and the giant thundered, 'If you are a big man like me, let me see one of your hairs!' Juan showed the rope; 'Let me see one of your teeth!' — Juan showed the axe; 'Beat your stomach, and let me hear the sound of it!' — and when Juan beat the drum, the Buringcantada and all the guests and servants ran away in fright, never having heard such a sound before.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'Juan and the Buringcantada'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大約經過一星期的旅程，他們來到一棟大房子，屋上裝飾著花與葉，餐廳的天花板上有一個大洞。胡安提議躲在那裡，直到他們查明屋主是誰；於是母子倆帶著斧頭、繩子和鼓，爬上天花板。不到幾分鐘，布林坎塔達——一個額頭正中長著一隻眼睛、嘴邊兩側各伸出一根長獠牙的巨人——便與他的朋友和僕人進來用餐。胡安大聲說，這些菜餚對他們來說是最好的——巨人雷鳴般吼道：「如果你是個像我一樣的大人物，就讓我看看你的一根頭髮！」胡安亮出繩子；「讓我看看你的一顆牙齒！」——胡安亮出斧頭；「拍拍你的肚子，讓我聽聽那聲音！」——而當胡安敲起鼓時，布林坎塔達和所有賓客與僕人都驚恐地逃走了，因為他們從未聽過這樣的聲音。

passages.text: Then Juan and his mother came down from the ceiling. In this house they lived like a rich family, for they found much money in one of the rooms; as for the Buringcantada, he never came back to his house after he left it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'Juan and the Buringcantada'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是胡安和他的母親從天花板上上下來。他們在這棟房子裡過得像富裕人家，因為他們在其中一個房間裡發現了許多錢；至於布林坎塔達，他離開之後就再也沒有回到他的房子。

title.en: The Manglalabas: The Ghost Who Guarded a Treasure
title.zh: 曼格拉巴斯：守財之靈

region.en: Balubad, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋巴盧巴德（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6e 'The Manglalabas', eBook #8299

summary.en: A haunted house in Balubad is emptied by the manglalabas, a spirit that throws stones, pinches the widow, and scatters the furniture. The blind Bulag and hunchback Cuba take shelter in its ceiling with a hatchet and an old gun they found on the road; the ghost's challenge is answered with a gunshot and the hatchet-head as a 'tooth.' The spirit, convinced it faces a powerful being, confesses it haunts the house nightly only to see its buried treasure dug up; the gold is found, the quarrel over division cures both men of their deformities, and they own the house together.
summary.zh: 巴盧巴德一鬧鬼之宅屢遭曼格拉巴斯作祟，家人棄宅而逃。盲者布拉格與駝背古巴借宿閣樓，以路拾的短斧與舊槍應對鬼魂：一聲槍響、一枚『牙齒』（斧頭）令幽靈信服——它坦白夜夜現身只為盼人掘出其藏金。二人掘得金銀，分贓爭執中布拉格眼睛復明、古巴駝背拉直，從此同住大宅。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a narrator who heard it from his father; archival record. The manglalabas is a house-haunting spirit; spirit-possession tag marks the living-with-ghosts situation, interpretively.

passages.text: In the small town of Balubad stood a big house inhabited by a rich family; when the head of the family died, the house grew gloomy and dark. Three days after the death the family began to be troubled at night by a manglalabas, who threw stones at the house, broke the water-jars, moved the beds, pinched the widow while she slept, and emptied all the jars. A band of brave men assembled to fight the spirit, but when they saw that it was a ghost they fled away, and from that time on nobody was willing to pass a night in that house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'The Manglalabas'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在巴盧巴德這個小鎮上，矗立著一棟大房子，住著一戶富裕人家；當這家的家長去世後，房子便變得陰鬱昏暗。死後三天，這家人開始在夜裡受到一個曼拉拉巴斯（manglalabas）的騷擾，它朝房子扔石頭、打破水罐、移動床鋪、在寡婦睡覺時捏她，還把所有的罐子都倒空。一群勇敢的人聚集起來要與這鬼魂搏鬥，但當他們看出那是個鬼時便逃走了，從那時起，再也沒有人願意在那棟房子裡過夜。

passages.text: In a certain barrio of Balubad lived two queer men — Bulag the blind and Cuba the hunchback — who agreed to go begging together, the blind man carrying the hunchback on his shoulder. On the way Cuba picked up a hatchet and an old gun, and in town they begged until they came to the large abandoned house, where they hid in the ceiling for the night. At midnight the manglalabas came again, shouting that he believed there were new persons in his house; Cuba, frightened, fired the gun, and the ghost, thinking the noise was someone crying, said, 'If you are truly a big man, give me some proofs.' Cuba took the handle out of the hatchet and threw the head down, which the spirit took for one of the teeth of his visitor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'The Manglalabas'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在巴盧巴德的某個村莊裡住著兩個古怪的人——瞎眼的布拉格和駝背的庫巴——他們約好一起去乞討，由瞎子把駝背扛在肩上。路上庫巴撿到一把斧頭和一支舊槍，他們在鎮上乞討，直到來到那棟廢棄的大房子，便躲在天花板上過夜。午夜時分，曼拉拉巴斯又來了，嚷著說他相信他的房子裡有新來的人；庫巴嚇壞了，開了一槍，那鬼魂以為那聲音是有人在哭，便說：「如果你真是個大人物，就給我一些憑證。」庫巴把斧柄從斧頭上取下來，把斧頭扔了下去，那鬼魂便把它當成了他訪客的一顆牙齒。

passages.text: Convinced that the intruder was a powerful person, the manglalabas said, 'I have a buried treasure near the barn. I wish you to dig it up. The reason I come here every night is on account of this treasure. If you will only dig it up, I will not come here any more.' The next night the two dug near the barn and found many gold and silver pieces. When Cuba kept three-fourths of the treasure for himself, Bulag felt the piles and discovered the cheating; angry, Cuba struck Bulag in the eyes, and they were opened; Bulag kicked Cuba in the back, and his deformity disappeared. They became friends again, divided the money equally, and owned the big house between them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 6 'The Manglalabas'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 曼拉拉巴斯確信這闖入者是位強大的人物，便說：「我在穀倉附近有一批埋藏的寶藏。我希望你去把它挖出來。我每晚來這裡，就是為了這批寶藏。只要你把它挖出來，我就不會再來這裡了。」第二天夜裡，兩人在穀倉附近挖掘，發現了許多金幣和銀幣。當庫巴為自己留下四分之三的寶藏時，布拉格摸著那些錢堆，發現了這樁欺騙；庫巴一怒之下打了布拉格的眼睛，他的眼睛便睜開了；布拉格踢了庫巴的背，他的畸形便消失了。他們又成了朋友，把錢平分，並共同擁有那棟大房子。

title.en: Sagacious Marcela and the Impossible Tasks
title.zh: 慧女瑪塞拉與難題

region.en: Pampanga, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home province)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦板牙省（敘述者故鄉）

period: Pampangan oral tale, set before the Spanish era; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 7a 'Sagacious Marcela', eBook #8299

summary.en: The king tests Marcela, his clever servant's daughter, with impossible tasks: make twelve dishes of one bird (she sends back a pin — twelve spoons from it first); sell a sheep for six reales and return it alive (she sells only the wool); fetch bull's milk for his physician's prescription. To the last she answers by washing birth-stained bedding at the river the king has forbidden to all others — 'my father gave birth to a child last night' — and the king, conceding that a bull's milk is as absurd, gives her his son in marriage.
summary.zh: 國王連出難題考驗僕人之女瑪塞拉：一鳥做十二道菜——她回敬一枚別針『先做出十二把湯匙』；六里亞爾賣羊且羊須生還——她只賣羊毛；為御醫取公牛之奶——她故意在王獨佔浴河之日洗滌產婦血污衣物，稱『家父昨夜生產』。國王啞口無言，認可公牛產奶同樣荒謬，遂以王子妻之。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan folktale recorded by Fansler from a Licup narrator; archival record. The Clever Lass cycle; Fansler notes a Bicol variant ('Marcela outwits the King') and two Tagalog corrido versions (Cay Calabasa, Rodolfo).

passages.text: Long before the Spaniards came there lived a man, a servant of the king, whose daughter Marcela was beautiful, virtuous, and above all clever. From childhood she had manifested a keen wit and undaunted spirit, refusing even to obey unjust orders from the king, and no question was too hard for her to answer. One day the king conceived a plan to test her: he had his servants carry a tiny bird to her house and tell her to make twelve dishes out of that one bird. After thinking five minutes, Marcela took one of her pins: 'If the king can make twelve spoons out of this pin, I can also make twelve dishes out of that bird.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 7 'Sagacious Marcela'; not verbatim.
