passages.zh: 早在西班牙人到來之前，住著一個人，是國王的僕人，他的女兒瑪塞拉美麗、賢淑，而且最重要的是聰明。她從小就表現出敏銳的機智和不屈的精神，甚至拒絕服從國王不公正的命令，也沒有任何問題難得倒她。有一天，國王想出一個計畫來考驗她：他讓僕人帶一隻小鳥到她家，告訴她用那一隻鳥做出十二道菜。瑪塞拉想了五分鐘，取出一根她的別針：「如果國王能用這根別針做出十二把湯匙，我也能用那隻鳥做出十二道菜。」

passages.text: Next the king sent a sheep with orders to sell it for six reales and bring back the money with the very same sheep alive. Marcela cut off the wool, sold it for six reales, and sent the money back with the live sheep. Then the king ordered her to get him a cup of bull's milk for his physician's prescription, or her father would lose his place in the palace — and issued an order that no one was to bathe or wash anything in the river, for he was going to take a bath the next morning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 7 'Sagacious Marcela'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著，國王送來一頭羊，下令將牠賣得六個雷亞爾，並要帶著這同一頭活羊把錢帶回來。瑪塞拉剪下羊毛，賣得六個雷亞爾，便讓活羊帶著錢回去。隨後，國王命令她為御醫的處方弄來一杯公牛的奶，否則她父親就要失去在宮中的職位——同時頒下命令：任何人都不准在河裡洗澡或洗任何東西，因為他次日早晨要沐浴。

passages.text: That night Marcela and her father killed a pig and smeared its blood over the sleeping-mat, blanket, and pillows; in the morning she took the stained bed-clothing to the source of the river where the king was bathing. In a voice of thunder he demanded why she washed her stuff in the river when nobody but he was to use it that day. 'It is the custom, my lord, in our country, to wash the mat, pillows, and other things stained with blood, immediately after a person has given birth to a child. As my father gave birth to a child last night, custom forces me to disobey your order.' — 'Nonsense! The idea of a man giving birth to a child! Absurd! Ridiculous!' — 'My lord, it would be just as absurd to think of getting milk from a bull.' Then the king, recollecting his order, said, 'Marcela, as you are so witty, clever, and virtuous, I will give you my son for your husband.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 7 'Sagacious Marcela'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當夜，瑪塞拉和父親殺了一頭豬，把豬血塗抹在睡席、毯子和枕頭上；清晨，她帶著染血的寢具來到國王沐浴的河源頭。國王以雷鳴般的聲音質問她，為何在當天只許他一人使用的河裡洗她的東西。『主公，在我們家鄉，習俗是產下孩子之後，要立刻清洗染血的席子、枕頭和其他物件。我父親昨夜產下了一個孩子，習俗迫使我違抗您的命令。』——『胡說！男人生孩子這種念頭！荒謬！可笑！』——『主公，想從公牛身上取奶，也同樣荒謬。』於是國王想起自己的命令，說道：『瑪塞拉，既然你如此機智、聰慧又賢德，我就把我的兒子許配給你為夫。』

title.en: King Tasio and the Squash in the Jar
title.zh: 塔西奧王與瓶中南瓜

region.en: La Laguna province, Luzon, Philippines (where the story is popular)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省（故事流行之地）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 7b 'King Tasio', eBook #8299

summary.en: Boasting kitchen-servant Juan is set impossible tasks by King Tasio: catch the rolling waves (a rope of seashore sand first), make fifty foods from one bird (stove, pan, and knife of this needle first). Expelled from the palace grounds, Juan rides in on a paragos loaded with earth from his own orchard; commanded to put a big squash into a narrow-necked jar unbroken, he grows a small squash inside the jar on its vine until it fills it — and the king faints before his court.
summary.zh: 自誇的御廚胡安被塔西奧王連出難題：先以海沙搓繩方可捕浪；先以縫衣針造灶、鍋、刀方可一鳥做五十道菜。被逐出宮後，胡安駕著載有自家果園泥土的耙子入宮——『我沒踩您的地』。最後國王令他把大南瓜完封放入小頸瓶；胡安讓幼瓜在瓶中藤上生長，數週後瓜漲滿瓶。國王當著滿朝賓客昏倒在地。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Faustino narrator; archival record. Clever-servant cycle, companion to Sagacious Marcela.

passages.text: Juan was a servant in the palace of King Tasio, and one day was heard in the kitchen saying he knew more than anybody else in the palace. The king called him and told him to go down to the seashore and catch the rolling waves: 'You said that you are the wisest man in the palace. Go and catch the waves of the sea for me.' 'That's very easy, O king! if you will only provide me with a rope made of sand taken from the seashore.' The king, not knowing what to answer, next commanded him to make fifty kinds of food out of a small bird — 'if you will only provide me with a stove, a pan, and a knife made out of this needle.' Again the king did not know what to do, and angrily expelled Juan: 'Don't you let me see you walking on my ground around this palace without my consent!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 7 'King Tasio'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 胡安是塔西奧國王宮中的僕人。有一天，有人在廚房裡聽見他說，他比宮中任何人都懂得多。國王召他來，吩咐他到海邊去捉住翻滾的波浪：『你說你是宮中最有智慧的人。去把海裡的波浪捉來給我。』『這太容易了，哦，國王！只要您給我一根用海邊沙子搓成的繩子就行。』國王不知如何作答，接著又命令他用一隻小鳥做出五十種食物——『只要您給我用這根針做成的爐子、鍋和刀就行。』國王又一次不知該怎麼辦，怒氣沖沖地把胡安趕走：『沒有我的允許，你別讓我看見你在我這宮殿周圍的地上行走！』

passages.text: The next day King Tasio saw Juan in front of the palace, riding on his paragos drawn by a carabao. 'Did I not tell you not to stand or walk on my ground around this palace? Do you mean to mock me?' — 'Will your Majesty's eyes please see whether I am standing on your ground or not? This is my ground,' and he pointed to the earth he had on his paragos, taken from his own orchard. Furious, the king handed Juan a squash and a jar whose neck was small: 'Put this squash into this jar. See that you do not break either the squash or the jar.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 7 'King Tasio'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天，塔西奧國王看見胡安在宮殿前，坐在由水牛拉著的帕拉戈斯雪橇上。『我不是告訴過你，不准在我這宮殿周圍的地上站立或行走嗎？你是存心要嘲弄我嗎？』——『請陛下親眼看看，我究竟是不是站在您的地上？這是我的地。』他指著放在雪橇上、取自自家果園的泥土。國王大怒，交給胡安一個南瓜和一個瓶頸細小的罈子：『把這個南瓜放進這個罈子裡。注意別弄破南瓜，也別弄破罈子。』

passages.text: Juan went home and put a very small squash, growing in his garden, inside the jar — but did not cut it from the vine. After a few weeks the squash had grown big enough to fill the jar; he then picked off the squash enclosed in the jar and presented it to the king before all the servants, courtiers, and visitors. As soon as the king saw the jar with the squash in it, he fainted, and it was many hours before he recovered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 7 'King Tasio'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 胡安回家，把園中長著的一顆很小的南瓜放進罈子裡——但沒有把它從藤上割下。幾週之後，南瓜長得夠大，填滿了罈子；他這才摘下封在罈中的南瓜，當著所有僕人、朝臣和賓客的面呈給國王。國王一看見裝著南瓜的罈子，便昏了過去，過了好幾個時辰才甦醒。

title.en: The Stone Monkey Is Born on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit
title.zh: 花果山石猴出世

region.en: Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, Eastern Purvavideha (symbolic pin: eastern islands of the mythic sea)
region.zh: 東勝神洲花果山（象徵性定位）

period: Journey to the West (Xiyou Ji), 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 1-2)

source.work: Journey to the West, ch. 1: the stone egg on Huaguo Mountain and the Water-Curtain Cave

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: On the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit a stone egg split, and a stone monkey came out with golden light that reached the Jade Emperor's throne. Bold enough to leap through a waterfall into a cave behind it, he was hailed Monkey King by the troop of apes he led inside — a king who would next set out to learn how not to die.
summary.zh: 花果山頂石卵迸裂，產一石猴，目運金光射斗牛；石猴跳入水簾洞，領群猿入居，眾猴拜為美猴王——王者不老之憂自此而生。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel (public-domain Ming text); no public-domain English translation is relied on — passages are the compiler's own renderings.

passages.text: On the topmost rock of the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit lay a stone egg, weathered by heaven and earth since creation. One day the egg split, and out came a stone monkey that knelt to the four quarters; his eyes flashed two beams of golden light that shot up to the Palace of the Pole Star, and the Jade Emperor himself was moved to look down and say: the thing below was born of heaven and earth — let it be.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 1 (compiler's rendering from the public-domain original); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 花果山最高處的岩石上，有一顆石卵，自開天闢地以來受天地風化。一日，石卵迸裂，產出一隻石猴，向四方跪拜；牠的眼中閃出兩道金光，直射至斗宿宮，連玉皇大帝也為之動容，俯視說道：下方那物乃天地所生——隨它去吧。

passages.text: One hot day the monkeys bathed in a stream and followed its source to a great waterfall. 'Whoever can enter and leave unhurt shall be our king!' cried the troop. The stone monkey shut his eyes, crouched, and leapt through the water — and found behind the fall a broad cave of iron bridges, stone seats and stone vessels, with a tablet reading 'Blessed Land of the Water-Curtain.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 1, waterfall episode; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一日炎熱，眾猴於溪中沐浴，又順流尋其源頭，直至一道大瀑布前。「誰能入內而毫髮無傷地出來，我們便奉他為王！」猴群高聲喊道。石猴閉上雙眼，蹲下身子，縱身躍過水簾——竟見瀑布之後別有洞天，乃一座寬闊的石洞，內有鐵橋、石座、石器，還有一方石碑，上書「福地水簾洞」。

passages.text: He led the whole troop through the falling water into the cave, and each claimed a stone apartment by age and rank. The monkeys fell on their knees: 'Thousand-year Sovereign!' So the stone monkey became the Handsome Monkey King, king of a hidden paradise — until one day at a feast he wept, for the kings of birds and beasts must still grow old and die, and that grief sent him out into the world to seek the way of deathlessness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 1-2 transition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他領著整群猴子穿過飛瀑，進入洞中，眾猴各依年齡與尊卑，分佔石室。群猴紛紛跪倒：「千年大王！」於是石猴成了美猴王，一方隱祕樂土之主——直到某日宴席之上，他忽然落淚，只因飛禽走獸之王終究仍會衰老而死；這份悲傷遂驅使他走出世外，去尋那長生不死之道。

title.en: The Monkey's Apprenticeship to the Patriarch Subodhi
title.zh: 美猴王拜師菩提祖師

region.en: Spirit-Platform Mountain, Western Niu-he-zhou (symbolic pin: far-west mountains)
region.zh: 西牛賀洲靈臺方寸山（象徵性定位）

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 1-2)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 1-2: the raft journey, the name Sun Wukong, the secret of the Formless Scripture, the seventy-two transformations

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The Monkey King crossed two oceans to the mountain of Patriarch Subodhi, who named him Sun Wukong, 'Awake-to-Emptiness.' Flogged for impatience, he caught the master's three raps — a secret lesson at the third watch — and received in silence the key of the Formless Scripture; he learned the cloud-somersault of one hundred and eight thousand li and the seventy-two transformations, until his old monkey vanity of showing off sent him away for good.
summary.zh: 猴王浮海求仙，拜菩提祖師，得名孫悟空；祖師打三下暗號，三更傳道，授以水簾洞口訣；學得筋斗雲十萬八千里、七十二般變化——因賣弄變松樹，被逐下山。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: He made himself a raft and crossed two oceans, wandering nine years until he came to Spirit-Platform Mountain and the cave of the Slanted Moon and Three Stars, where the Patriarch Subodhi taught. Asked his name and surname, the monkey could answer neither; the master laughed at his gait and gave him a surname, Sun, and a religious name, Wukong — Awake to Emptiness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 1-2 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他自造一筏，渡過兩重大海，漂泊九年，終於來到靈臺方寸山，斜月三星洞，那是須菩提祖師傳道之所。祖師問他姓名，那猴子卻答不上來；祖師笑他走路姿態，便賜他姓「孫」，又取法名「悟空」——覺悟於空。

passages.text: Seven years on, Wukong pestered the master for the art of long life. The master struck him three times on the head, closed the doors, and went in — and the monkey understood: three raps at the third watch, the back door open, a private lesson. That night he crept in at the third watch, and the master, delighted at his cunning, whispered to him the verse of the Formless Scripture, the secret of eternity within the body.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 2, the three-raps secret; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 七年之後，悟空纏著祖師求那長生之術。祖師在他頭上敲了三下，關上門，便進去了——那猴子心領神會：三更時分，三下敲擊，後門洞開，乃是私下傳授。當夜三更，他悄悄潛入，祖師見他這般機靈，心中歡喜，便低聲向他傳授那無形無相之經的偈語，乃是身中永恆之祕。

passages.text: Three years later the master taught him escape from the three calamities: the somersault cloud that covers one hundred and eight thousand li in a leap, and the seventy-two transformations of form. But when the young monkeys begged to see them, Wukong transformed into a pine tree in the courtyard — and the master, furious at the showing-off that would bring ruin, drove him out forever, forbidding him ever to name his teacher.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 2, transformations and expulsion; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 三年之後，祖師又教他躲避三災之法：一躍可翻十萬八千里的觔斗雲，以及七十二般變化之術。然而當那些小猴央求他顯露本領時，悟空竟在院中變作一棵松樹——祖師見他這般賣弄，必招禍患，勃然大怒，將他永遠逐出師門，並禁止他日後再提師父之名。

title.en: The Monkey King Borrows a Weapon from the Dragon King
title.zh: 龍宮索定海神針

region.en: Crystal Palace of Ao Guang, Dragon King of the Eastern Sea (symbolic pin: East China Sea floor)
region.zh: 東海龍宮（象徵性定位）

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, ch. 3)

source.work: Journey to the West, ch. 3: the Crystal Palace, the sea-needle Ruyi Jingu Bang, and the hoard of magic armors

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Needing a weapon worthy of himself, the Monkey King barged into the Eastern Sea's Crystal Palace; every blade was too light for him, until he laid hands on the pillar of the sea — the Ruyi Golden-Hooped Rod, the treasure Yu the Great used to fix the depths — which shrank to a needle he stowed behind his ear. Drunk on the visit, he also extorted a full suit of magic armor from the neighboring dragon-kings.
summary.zh: 悟空至東海水晶宮索兵器，諸般刀斧皆嫌輕；得定海神針如意金箍棒，重一萬三千五百斤，能大能小，化作繡花針藏於耳內；又索得鳳翅紫金冠、鎖子黃金甲、藕絲步雲履。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. The staff is Da Yu's flood-taming sea-needle — a link to the Gun-Yu flood cycle in the novel's cosmology.

passages.text: The Monkey King turned his somersault into the sea and dived to the Crystal Palace of Ao Guang, the old Dragon King of the East, who had no choice but to feast him. Asked for a weapon, he was offered swords, halberds and axes of thirty-six thousand pounds — and threw them all aside as light as sewing needles.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 3 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 猴王一個觔斗翻入海中，潛至東海老龍王敖廣的水晶宮，龍王無可推辭，只得設宴款待。猴王索要兵器，龍王先後奉上三萬六千斤的刀、戟、斧——他卻一一擲於一旁，只覺輕如繡花針。

passages.text: The dragon's wife whispered of the treasure in the palace's back hall: the Great Sea-Fixing Needle, the black iron pillar Yu the Great set in the depths when he tamed the floods, which grows and shrinks at its holder's will. It had lately been shooting sparks of light. Wukong lifted it, bade it be small, and it shrank to a rod of thirteen thousand five hundred pounds — golden hoops at both ends — then to the size of an embroidery needle, which he tucked behind his ear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 3, sea-needle episode; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 龍妻悄聲說出後殿中的寶物：那根定海神針，是大禹治水時插入深處的黑鐵柱，能隨持有者心意變大變小。近來它頻頻迸射光芒。悟空將它舉起，命它變小，它便縮成一根重一萬三千五百斤的鐵棒——兩端各有金箍——再縮成繡花針大小，他把它塞在耳後。

passages.text: Pleased with his prize but without armor, he hammered on the doors of the South, North and West Sea palaces and squeezed from their kings a phoenix-wing cap of purple gold, a coat of golden chain mail, and cloud-walking boots of lotus silk — then went home roistering, leaving four furious dragon-kings to send a memorial of complaint to heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 3, armor extortion; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他得了寶貝滿心歡喜，卻沒有披掛，便去捶打南海、北海、西海龍宮的大門，從三位龍王那裡強索來一頂紫金鳳翅冠、一件鎖子黃金甲和一雙藕絲步雲履——然後一路喧鬧著回家，留下四位怒不可遏的龍王向天庭遞上奏章告狀。

title.en: The Monkey Crosses Out His Name in the Book of Death
title.zh: 勾銷生死簿

region.en: The netherworld city of Fengdu, Tenth Court region (symbolic pin: Sichuan Fengdu)
region.zh: 幽冥界酆都（象徵性定位：四川豐都）

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, ch. 3)

source.work: Journey to the West, ch. 3: wine-sleep, soul seizure, and the Book of Life and Death

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Drunk asleep in his cave, the Monkey King was seized by two soul-catchers of the underworld with a summons to death; he broke their chains, beat his way into the Hall of Darkness, and demanded the Register of Life and Death — where he found his own allotted span of three hundred forty-two years, crossed it out, and every monkey name with it: the bureaucracy of death, rewritten by a drunk king with a pen.
summary.zh: 悟空醉臥，被勾魂使者索命；悟空掣棒打入森羅殿，索生死簿查閱，親註『孫悟空』該壽三百四十二歲——一筆勾銷，並凡猴屬之名盡勾之；大鬧幽冥界。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. Comic descent — contrast the solemn descent records; noted for the underworld cluster.

passages.text: After a night of celestial wine the Monkey King slept in his cave, and his soul was carried off by two men with black caps and iron chains, down to the city of the dead, where a court official ordered him to the Hall of Darkness as a soul whose time had come.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 3 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 飲了一夜天酒之後，猴王在洞中睡去，他的魂魄被兩個戴黑帽、持鐵鏈的人拘走，帶到幽冥城，那裡一位判官命人把他這個陽壽已盡的魂靈押往幽冥殿。

passages.text: The Monkey King pulled out his staff and knocked their chains to pieces. 'I am beyond old and young, beyond life and death, beyond king and subject,' he cried, and beat his way into the hall, where the Ten Kings of the netherworld sat trembling. He demanded the Register of Life and Death — soul-types one thousand three hundred and fifty, the ledger of every mortal fate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 3, Hall of Darkness; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 猴王掏出金箍棒，把他們的鐵鏈打得粉碎。「我超出老幼，超出生死，超出君臣，」他喊道，一路打進殿中，十殿閻王坐在那裡瑟瑟發抖。他索要生死簿——上面載著魂類一千三百五十種，記錄著每一個凡人的命數。

passages.text: He found his own page: Stone Monkey, span of years three hundred and forty-two, good death. He crossed it out with a pen, and every monkey name on the register with it, and flung the book back. Then, striding out of the underworld with his staff on his shoulder, he went home and told his troop: no one need die of old age again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 3, crossing-out; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他找到了自己那一頁：石猴，壽三百四十二歲，善終。他用筆把它劃掉，連同簿上所有猴類的名字一併劃去，又把簿子扔了回去。然後，他扛著金箍棒大步走出幽冥，回家告訴他的猴群：再沒有人需要因年老而死了。

title.en: Wukong Appointed Groom of the Heavenly Stables
title.zh: 悟空封弼馬溫

region.en: Heavenly Court, Southern Gate of Heaven (symbolic pin: mythic heaven)
region.zh: 天庭南天門（象徵性定位）

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 4-5)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 4-5: the Bimawen post, the return and the Great Sage banner, the Peach Garden theft

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Heaven, hoping to tame the monkey by employment, gave him the post of Bimawen, groom of the celestial stables — which he ran superbly until he learned it was the lowest rank in heaven; he smashed the office and went home, raising a banner that read 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven.' Heaven sent armies, and a second offer — true Great Sage, but still no place in the Peach Banquet — ended with him eating the elixir pills and drinking the feast dry.
summary.zh: 悟空上天受封弼馬溫，掌天馬甚勤；聞此乃未入流之小官，大怒打出南天門，回花果山自封齊天大聖；天兵討伐不勝，太白金星再招安——許大聖之名而無蟠桃會之份，悟空怒而攪亂蟠桃會，盜仙丹。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The Tai-Bai star brought the monkey up to heaven on a cloud, and the Jade Emperor, warned that this stone-born thing was fierce, gave him a post in the stables: Bimawen, keeper of the celestial horses. Wukong served brilliantly, feeding and training the thousand heavenly steeds to perfection — until at a banquet he learned that Bimawen was the meanest office in heaven, unworthy even to be ranked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, chs. 4 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 太白星君駕雲把猴子帶上天庭，玉帝得知這石生之物凶猛，便給了他一個馬廄裡的職位：弼馬溫，掌管天馬。悟空幹得極為出色，把千匹天馬餵養訓練得完美無缺——直到在一次宴會上，他得知弼馬溫是天庭裡最卑微的官職，甚至不配入品。

passages.text: Furious, he smashed the stables, beat his way out through the Southern Gate, and returned to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, where he set up a banner reading 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven.' Two armies of one hundred thousand heavenly soldiers came down and could not take him; so Heaven offered the empty title of Great Sage — and a new post: keeper of the Peach Garden, an orchard he was born to plunder.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, chs. 4-5; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他勃然大怒，搗毀了馬廄，一路打出南天門，回到花果山，立起一面旗幟，上書「齊天大聖」。十萬天兵分兩路殺來，卻奈何他不得；於是天庭給了他一個「齊天大聖」的空銜——外加一個新職：看管蟠桃園，而那果園本就是他生來便要劫掠的。

passages.text: When he learned that the great Peach Banquet had invited everyone but him, he cast sleeping charms on the servants, ate the garden's three-thousand-year peaches and its nine-thousand-year ones, drank the jade liquid and the dragon-liver delicacies dry, and topped it off by swallowing the entire jar of Laozi's golden elixir pills — then sobered in the wilderness, knowing he had made heaven his enemy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 5, the Peach Banquet ruin; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他得知盛大的蟠桃宴遍請諸仙，唯獨將他排除在外，便對僕役施了瞌睡咒，吃盡園中三千年一熟的桃與九千年一熟的桃，喝乾玉液，吃光龍肝珍饈，末了更把太上老君整葫蘆的金丹吞下肚去——隨後在荒野中酒醒，心知自己已與天庭為敵。

title.en: Wukong and Erlang Shen: The Duel of Transformations
title.zh: 悟空大戰二郎神

region.en: Guankou and the fields before the Southern Gate (symbolic pin: northern Sichuan, Erlang's cult seat)
region.zh: 灌口（象徵性定位）

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, ch. 6)

source.work: Journey to the West, ch. 6: the third transformation-duel between Sun Wukong and Erlang Shen, watched by heaven

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: No heavenly general could touch the Great Sage, so Guanyin recommended Erlang Shen, the three-eyed nephew of the Jade Emperor with his howling hound and seven companions. Monkey and god fought three hundred rounds, then dueled in transformations — sparrow against hungry hawk, fish against osprey, snake against gray crane, earth temple against hound — until Laozi's steel ring, thrown from the southern gate, felled the monkey and Erlang's hound took him by the leg.
summary.zh: 觀音薦二郎神；悟空與二郎神鬥三百餘合，又各顯神通：麻雀、餓鷹、魚鷹、大鷂、水蛇、灰鶴、土地廟——變化相制；太上老君金剛琢自南天門打下，哮天犬咬住腿，終被擒。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. The transformation-chase is a classic cumulative folktale sequence within a novel.

passages.text: Erlang Shen came with his six Meishan companions and his howling hound. The Great Sage and the three-eyed god met at the gate of the monkey's camp and fought three hundred rounds without result; then both rose into the sky and fought again amid the clouds, and neither could prevail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 6 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 二郎神帶著梅山六兄弟與他那哮天犬前來。大聖與這三眼之神在猴營門前相遇，大戰三百回合不分勝負；隨後二人皆騰空而起，在雲端再戰，誰也佔不了上風。

passages.text: So began the transformation-duel. Monkey became a sparrow on the bough; Erlang became a hungry hawk. Monkey plunged into the water as a fish; Erlang became an osprey. Monkey became a water-snake; Erlang a gray crane that pecked at his scales. Monkey became a flower-flies-fleeing-earth temple, his tail the flagpole rearing behind the shrine — but Erlang saw through it, and his hound stood ready.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 6, the transformation-chase; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是變化的較量開始了。猴王化作枝頭麻雀；二郎化作餓鷹。猴王潛入水中化為魚；二郎化作魚鷹。猴王化作水蛇；二郎化作灰鶴，啄其鱗甲。猴王化作一座花飛土走的廟宇，尾巴變作旗杆豎在廟後——但二郎識破了，他的哮天犬也蓄勢待發。

passages.text: At the height of it, Laozi flung his diamond bracelet from the Southern Gate and it struck the Great Sage's skull, felling him; Erlang's hound leapt and seized his leg, and the six Meishan brothers pinned him with hooks. Thus was the Great Sage Equal to Heaven brought to heaven in irons — to be cooked in Laozi's furnace and to fall out of it twice as dangerous.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 6, capture; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 正鬥到緊要處，太上老君自南天門擲下金剛琢，打中大聖天靈，將他擊倒；二郎的哮天犬躍上咬住他的腿，梅山六兄弟又以鉤索將他按住。齊天大聖就這樣被鐵鏈鎖著押上天庭——送進老君的爐中烹煉，又從爐中逃出，變得比先前更加凶險。

title.en: The Eight-Trigram Furnace and the Palm of the Buddha
title.zh: 八卦爐與佛掌

region.en: Laozi's furnace and Five-Elements Mountain (symbolic pin: mythic west of heaven)
region.zh: 兜率宮八卦爐、靈山兩界山（象徵性定位）

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, ch. 7)

source.work: Journey to the West, ch. 7: forty-nine days in the furnace, the golden fiery eyes, and the bet with the Buddha's palm

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The capture could not kill the Great Sage: he was thrown into Laozi's Eight-Trigram Furnace for forty-nine days, where the fire, kept from his feet by the position of the wind-trigram, only tempered him — and burned his eyes into golden fiery eyes that see through every disguise. Freed, he wrecked heaven again, until the Buddha wagered him: escape my palm and heaven is yours. One somersault of a hundred thousand li, and he wrote 'The Great Sage was here' on five flesh-pink pillars — urine at the middle pillar — for they were the Buddha's five fingers. The palm closed, pressed him under Five-Elements Mountain, and sealed him five hundred years.
summary.zh: 悟空被投入八卦爐煉四十九日，火不能傷，反煉成火眼金睛；出爐大鬧天宮，與如來賭賽：翻出手掌即讓天宮——筋斗雲至五肉柱處書『齊天大聖到此一遊』並遺尿；如來五指翻轉，將其壓於五行山下五百年。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: Blades and lightning could not harm the Great Sage, so Laozi offered him to the Eight-Trigram Furnace for forty-nine days of slow fire. But the monkey had sheltered in the wind-trigram corner, where there was smoke but no flame; the smoke seared his eyes into golden fiery eyes, that could see through every transformation and every illusion ever cast.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 7 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 刀斧與雷電都傷不了大聖，於是太上老君將他送入八卦爐中，以文火慢煉四十九日。但那猴子藏身於巽位，那裡有煙無火；煙燻壞了他的雙眼，煉成一雙火眼金睛，能看破一切變化與一切曾施的幻術。

passages.text: When the furnace was opened on the appointed day, the Great Sage sprang out, kicked over the crucibles, and with his staff wrought havoc from the halls of the thirty-three heavens down to the nine prisons of the stars — until the Jade Emperor called across the Western Heaven for the Buddha.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 7, the havoc renewed; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了行刑之日，爐門一開，大聖便跳將出來，踢翻丹爐，手持金箍棒，從三十三層天宮一路打到九幽星獄，直鬧得玉帝向西天呼喚佛祖。

passages.text: The Buddha bet him a wager: if the monkey could leap out of the Buddha's right palm, heaven would be his. Wukong tucked his staff small, leapt, somersaulted his hundred thousand li, and found five flesh-pink pillars — where he wrote 'The Great Sage was here' and, for a signature, relieved himself at the middle pillar. He leapt back in triumph; the Buddha showed him the words still inked on his middle finger. The palm turned over, pressed the monkey beneath the five peaks that became Five-Elements Mountain, and sealed him for five hundred years, to wait for a pilgrim.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 7, the palm-wager; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 佛祖與他打賭：若這猴兒能跳出佛祖右掌，便把天宮讓與他。悟空將金箍棒縮小藏起，縱身一躍，翻個筋斗十萬八千里，見五根肉紅色的柱子——便在上面寫下「齊天大聖到此一遊」，又在中柱撒尿為記。他得意洋洋跳了回來；佛祖卻讓他看，那字跡仍留在中指之上。手掌一翻，將猴兒壓在五座山峰之下，化作五行山，封了他五百年，等候一位取經人。

title.en: The Tang Monk's Parents: A Murder on the Yangzi
title.zh: 陳光蕊江流兒

region.en: The Yangzi at Hai Prefecture and Jiangzhou (pin: Yangzi river towns)
region.zh: 海州至江州（長江）

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, ch. 9)

source.work: Journey to the West, ch. 9: the scholar Chen Guangrui, the ferryman's murder, and the river-raised infant

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The top graduate Chen Guangrui, wed the same week to the prime minister's daughter Wenjiao and posted to Jiangzhou, was murdered mid-journey by the ferryman Liu Hong, who took his wife and his office. The pregnant widow bore a son by the river; fearing the usurper, she bound the baby on a plank with a blood-written plea and cast it on the current — the monk of Golden Mountain temple raised him as River-Float, and eighteen years later the son brought the murderer to justice and joined the Sangha, to become the pilgrim Xuanzang.
summary.zh: 狀元陳光蕊攜妻溫嬌赴江州，渡口被劉洪殺害霸妻；殷氏產子懼害，以血書縛兒於木板拋江；金山寺長老收養，法名江流兒；十八年後復仇雪冤，遂剃度為玄奘——取經人之由來。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. The floating-infant motif parallels Moses/Jumong-type riverbirths; noted for the birth cluster.

passages.text: Chen Guangrui of Hai Prefecture took first place in the palace examination, was married on the spot to the prime minister's daughter Yin Wenjiao, and set out for his post at Jiangzhou. At the flood-water crossing the ferryman Liu Hong murdered him in the night, threw the body into the river, took his papers, his post and his wife, and arrived at Jiangzhou as governor in the dead man's name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 9 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 海州陳光蕊殿試高中狀元，當即被招為丞相之女殷溫嬌的夫婿，隨即赴江州上任。行至洪江渡口，艄公劉洪夜裡將他殺害，把屍首拋入江中，奪了他的文書、官職與妻子，冒著死者的名號到江州做了州主。

passages.text: Wenjiao, pregnant, bore a son by the river. Terrified that Liu Hong would destroy him, she bit her finger, wrote a plea in blood telling who the child was, bound it to the baby's chest, tied the infant to a plank of wood, and set it on the current — and the river carried it to the gate of Golden Mountain temple, where the old abbot took it in and named it River-Float.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 9, the plank and the temple; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 溫嬌身懷有孕，在江邊產下一子。她生怕劉洪加害，便咬破手指，寫下血書訴明孩兒來歷，繫在嬰兒胸前，又將嬰兒綁在一塊木板上，放進江流——江水將他漂到金山寺門前，老方丈收留了他，取名江流。

passages.text: At eighteen the boy learned his story, found his mother by the water, and brought the case to justice: the usurper was executed, and the father's body, preserved in the sea, was revived by a dragon-king's favor. The son then shaved his head as a Buddhist monk and took the name Xuanzang — the pilgrim who would carry the scriptures from the west.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 9, justice and tonsure; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 孩兒十八歲時得知自己的身世，在江邊尋見母親，並將此案告到官府：那篡位之人伏法被誅，父親的屍身因海中龍王施恩得以保全，終得還魂復生。兒子隨後削髮為僧，法名玄奘——正是日後西天取經的取經人。

title.en: The Golden Fillet and the Six Robbers of the Senses
title.zh: 緊箍咒與六賊

region.en: Double-Fork Ridge on the road west of Five-Elements Mountain (pin: Gansu corridor route)
region.zh: 兩界山雙叉嶺以西（絲路）

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, ch. 14)

source.work: Journey to the West, ch. 14: the freed monkey kills six robbers, runs off, and is bound by Guanyin's golden fillet

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Freed after five centuries, the monkey killed six bandits whose names were the six senses — Eyes See Delight, Ears Hear Wrath, Nose Sniffs Love, Tongue Tastes Thoughts, Body Wishes Envy, Mind Seeks Sorrow — and the horrified monk rebuked him; the monkey stormed off, and Guanyin, disguised, gave the monk a cap that, when worn, became a golden fillet tightening with a spell. The monkey returned, tried the cap, and learned what obedience feels like on the skull.
summary.zh: 悟空出山，路殺六賊——眼看喜、耳聽怒、鼻嗅愛、舌嘗思、身本憂、意見欲（六根之喻）；三藏斥之，悟空負氣而去；觀音授緊箍兒，悟空戴之，咒起箍緊，遂受制於師。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. The six robbers are an allegory of the senses; the fillet episode is the novel's parable of discipline.

passages.text: The Tang monk climbed Five-Elements Mountain, lifted the seal, and the monkey burst free after five hundred years. On the road they met six bandits who demanded toll — bandits named Eyes See Delight, Ears Hear Wrath, Nose Sniffs Love, Tongue Tastes Thoughts, Body Wishes Envy, and Mind Seeks Sorrow. The monkey told them cheerfully they had met their ancestors, and clubbed every one of them dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 14 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 唐僧登上五行山，揭去封條，那猴兒便在被壓五百年後破山而出。行路途中，他們遇上六個攔路索要買路錢的強盜——這六賊名叫眼看喜、耳聽怒、鼻嗅愛、舌嘗思、身本憂、意見欲。猴兒笑嘻嘻地告訴他們，算是遇著祖宗了，便將他們一個個盡數打死。

passages.text: The monk, sickened that his disciple had killed men, rebuked him until the monkey stormed off in a huff of cloud. As the monk sat alone, an old woman came — Guanyin in disguise — and gave him a silk cap and a tight-tight spell: the cap was a golden fillet of heaven-forged rings, and the spell was the true-name chant of the Tightening Spell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 14, Guanyin's gift; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那僧人因徒弟杀了人而心生厭惡，責備他，直到那猴子怒氣沖沖地騰雲而去。僧人獨自坐著時，一位老婦人前來——那是觀音化身——給了他一頂絲帽和一道緊箍咒：那帽子是上天鍛造的黃金箍圈，那咒語則是緊箍咒的真言。

passages.text: The monkey returned, saw the cap, tried it on — and it shrank to his skull. The monk began the spell, and the golden hoop ground tighter and tighter until the Great Sage lay rolling and screaming on the ground. 'I will obey you forever,' he vowed — and from that day, the mightiest being in three realms carried a band that only mercy and obedience could loosen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 14, the fillet; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那猴子回來，看見帽子，試著戴上——它便縮緊到他的頭骨上。僧人開始念咒，金箍越勒越緊，直到那大聖躺在地上翻滾尖叫。「我願永遠聽從你，」他發誓道——從那天起，三界中最強大的存在便戴上了一道唯有慈悲與順從才能鬆開的箍。

title.en: Zhu Bajie, the Pig Groom of Gao Village
title.zh: 高老莊收八戒

region.en: Gao Village, Western Niu-he-zhou route (pin: mythic westward route)
region.zh: 烏斯藏高老莊（取經路）

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 18-19)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 18-19: the pig son-in-law, the battle at the cloud-crossing cave, and Bajie's confession

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: At Gao Old Village a son-in-law who arrived a stout honest fellow had turned into a pig-faced monster, working marvels by day and carrying off the daughter by night; the monk's new disciple fought him at the cave of the cloud-crossing, until the pig, pinned down, confessed: he had been Marshal of the Heavenly Canopy, banished for drunken importunity toward Chang'e, reborn in a sow's womb. Given the name Zhu Bajie, Pig of the Eight Prohibitions, he took the fillet of obedience and joined the journey.
summary.zh: 高老莊招贅之婿乃豬妖；悟空戰之於雲棧洞，豬妖自述本是天河元帥天蓬，酒戲嫦娥被貶，錯投豬胎；受戒取名豬悟能，法名八戒——遂拜三藏為師，擔行李隨行。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The Gao family had taken in a brawny, gluttonous laborer three years before, given him their third daughter in marriage — and discovered too late that by day he worked like an ox and by night showed the face of a long-snouted pig. He wallowed, he ate whole banquets, and he kept the bride locked away from her parents.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, chs. 18 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 高家三年前收留了一個身強力壯、貪吃無度的長工，把第三個女兒嫁給了他——卻發現得太晚：他白天幹活像頭牛，夜裡卻露出長嘴豬臉。他打滾泥中，能吃掉整桌宴席，還把新娘鎖起來不讓她見父母。

passages.text: The Monkey King fought him from the village to the Cloud-Road Cave and cornered him. Battered into honesty, the pig confessed: once he was Marshal Tianpeng, commander of the eighty thousand river-troops of the Milky Way, banished to earth for drunkenly laying hold of the moon-goddess Chang'e, reborn by mistake in a sow's body. The name of Wuneng — Awakened-to-Ability — was given him, and the eight prohibitions of the disciple's discipline.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 19, confession and tonsure; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 猴王從村裡一路與他打到雲棧洞，將他逼入絕境。那豬被打得服了軟，說出實情：他原是天蓬元帥，統領天河八萬水軍，因醉酒調戲月神嫦娥而被貶下凡，又錯投豬胎。他得了「悟能」之名——意為「覺悟能力」——以及徒弟戒律的八項禁戒。

passages.text: So Zhu Bajie, Pig of the Eight Prohibitions, shouldered the pilgrim's luggage and joined the journey west — lazy, gluttonous, lecherous and loyal, the great comic engine of the novel, and the only disciple who always wanted to turn back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 19, joining the pilgrimage; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是豬八戒——八項禁戒之豬——挑起取經人的行李，加入了西行之旅——懶惰、貪吃、好色卻忠誠，是這部小說偉大的喜劇引擎，也是唯一總想回頭的徒弟。

title.en: The White Dragon Horse Swallows the Pilgrim's Saddle
title.zh: 白龍馬

region.en: Eagle-Sorrow Stream (Yingchoujian), on the western road (pin: Gansu corridor)
region.zh: 鷹愁澗（絲路）

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, ch. 15)

source.work: Journey to the West, ch. 15: the third prince of the West Sea, the eaten horse, and Guanyin's conversion

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: A white dragon burst from Eagle-Sorrow Stream and swallowed the pilgrim's horse whole. Wukong fought it in the air; Guanyin came at the monk's plea, and the dragon — third son of the West Sea king, under sentence for burning his father's pearl in defiance — was given instead the pilgrimage: shorn of scales, it became a white horse to carry the Tang monk to the west, the last of the five to join.
summary.zh: 鷹愁澗白龍吞了三藏白馬；悟空戰之不下，觀音至，龍乃西海龍王三太子，因縱火燒殿上明珠而獲罪；觀音救之，鋸角退鱗，化白龍馬馱經西行。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: Passing the Eagle-Sorrow Stream, the pilgrims' white horse was swallowed whole by a white dragon that shot up out of the water; the monkey dove after it, and dragon and monkey fought in the air, cloud and water, without victory on either side.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 15 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 行經鷹愁澗時，取經人的白馬被一條從水中騰起的白龍整個吞下；那猴子潛入水中追去，龍與猴在空中、雲中、水中大戰，雙方皆未取勝。

passages.text: The monk wept over his lost horse, and the monkey fetched Guanyin. She rebuked the dragon, who confessed: he was the third prince of the West Sea, who had defied his father by burning the pearl of the palace gate, and had been sentenced to death — but she had stayed the sentence and set him waiting at the stream for the pilgrim he was fated to serve.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 15, the dragon's confession; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那僧人因失了馬而哭泣，猴王便去請來觀音。觀音責備那條龍，龍便招認：他本是西海龍王的三太子，因違逆父命，燒了殿上明珠，被判死罪——但觀音止住了刑罰，命他在溪邊等候那位他命中註定要服侍的取經人。

passages.text: Guanyin sawed off his horns, removed his scales, and changed him into a white horse of the purest breed, saddled and bridled. The Tang monk mounted, and the five pilgrims were complete in all but one — the gentle brother still waiting in the Flowing Sands River.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 15, transformation into the horse; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 觀音鋸去他的角，揭下他的鱗，把他變成一匹最純良種的白馬，備好了鞍轡。唐僧騎了上去，五個取經人便齊全了，只差一個——那位溫和的師弟還在流沙河裡等著。

title.en: The Ginseng Fruit Tree of Wuzhuang Abbey
title.zh: 五莊觀人參果

region.en: Wuzhuang Abbey on Longevity Mountain (pin: mythic westward route)
region.zh: 萬壽山五莊觀

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 24-26)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 24-26: the ginseng fruit, the fallen tree, and Guanyin's dew of revival

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The Great Immortal Zhenyuan kept a tree that flowered once in three thousand years and bore a fruit every nine thousand — each fruit like a baby, worth a man's whole life of years. His servants fed two to the pilgrims by error; Wukong stole more, and when the theft was found out his anger felled the tree. The immortal trapped the pilgrims, and only Guanyin's sweet dew, poured on the roots, could raise the tree — sealing a friendship and a lesson in hospitality.
summary.zh: 五莊觀人參果樹三千年一花，九千年結果，狀如嬰兒；清風明月奉果誤時，悟空偷果；被發覺，怒推樹倒。鎮元大仙以袖裡乾坤收四眾，悟空遍求醫樹之方——觀音以甘露活樹，結為兄弟。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: On Longevity Mountain stood the abbey of Zhenyuan the Great Immortal, and in its garden a tree older than the sea-roads: three thousand years to flower, nine thousand to fruit, a fruit that hung like a baby with limbs that moved — eat one, and a man gained four hundred and seventy years of life. Only thirty ripened at a time, and the tree feared the blow of any common hand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 24 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 長壽山上有一座鎮元大仙的道觀，觀中園裡有一棵比海路還要古老的樹：三千年開花，九千年結果，那果子掛著像一個四肢會動的嬰兒——吃一個，人便能增四百七十年的壽命。每次只熟三十個，而那棵樹最怕凡俗之手的敲打。

passages.text: The abbey's two boy-servants brought two fruits to the guests — who shrank from eating what looked like a child. Wukong, hearing of the fruit, stole a hammer, knocked three down, and they vanished into the earth; a fourth he caught in his robe, and he and his brothers shared it. The theft was found out, and the monkey — his monkey pride pricked by the servants' taunts — struck the tree with his staff and felled it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 24-25, theft and felling; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 觀裡的兩個童子端了兩個果子給客人——客人見那果子像個孩子，便不敢吃。悟空聽說有這果子，偷來一把錘子，敲下三個，果子卻鑽進土裡不見了；第四個他用衣襟接住，與師兄弟分吃了。偷果之事被發覺，猴王的自尊被童子的譏諷刺痛，便舉起金箍棒打去，把那棵樹打倒。

passages.text: Zhenyuan caught the pilgrims in his sleeve as they fled. Wukong promised to cure the tree, searched three continents for the way, and brought Guanyin, who dipped her willow branch in the sweet dew of her vase and sprinkled the roots — and the tree stood again, its fruits restored. The Great Immortal, overjoyed, swore brotherhood with the Tang monk: the tree's death had become a friendship's birth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 26, the revival; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 鎮元大仙在眾僧逃走時，用袖子把他們一併籠住。悟空答應醫活那棵樹，遍訪三洲尋求醫樹之法，請來了觀音；觀音將楊柳枝蘸了瓶中甘露，灑在樹根上——那樹便重新立起，果子也復原了。大仙大喜，與唐僧結為兄弟：樹之死竟成了友誼之生。

title.en: The White Bone Demon Thrice Disguised
title.zh: 三打白骨精

region.en: Snake- coiling ridge on the road west (pin: mythic westward route)
region.zh: 蛇盤山（取經路）

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, ch. 27)

source.work: Journey to the West, ch. 27: the White Bone Demon's three disguises, the golden fiery eyes, and the banishment of Wukong

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The White Bone Demon, one skeleton given life, wanted to eat the Tang monk for his deathless flesh: she came as a village girl with rice, then as an old woman seeking her daughter, then as an old man seeking them both — and each time Wukong's fiery eyes saw through her and struck her down; the third blow shattered her true form, a heap of white bone with the characters 'White Bone Lady' on the spine. But the monk, believing his disciple had murdered three innocents, recited the tightening spell and banished him — and the demon's purpose was half won.
summary.zh: 白骨夫人三戲唐僧：村姑、老嫗、老翁；悟空火眼金睛三打之，第三打現出白骨原形——然三藏肉眼不辨，念緊箍咒，逐悟空回花果山。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The White Bone Demon had one aim: a mouthful of the Tang monk's flesh, one bite of which gave immortality. Her first shape was a beautiful village girl, basket of rice and pot of soup, walking alone in the wilderness; she came up to the pilgrims with soft words — and the monkey, returning from peach-picking, saw at a glance the skull beneath the skin and brought his staff down on her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 27 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 白骨精只有一個目的：吃一口唐僧肉，吃一口便能長生不老。她第一次變作一個美貌的村姑，提著一籃米、一罐湯，獨自在荒野中行走；她走近眾僧，柔聲細語——而那摘桃歸來的猴王一眼看穿皮囊下的骷髏，舉棒便打。

passages.text: She let her false body fall and escaped in her spirit; then, an old woman bent on a staff, she came wailing for her daughter. Again the fiery eyes saw through her; again the staff fell, and again the demon fled from the false corpse. The third time she came as an old father seeking wife and child, and this time the monkey struck before she could breathe a spell — the blow shattered her true body, a heap of white bone with 'White Bone Lady' graven on the spine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 27, the three strokes; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她拋下假身，以神識逃去；隨後化作一個拄杖的老婦，哭喊著來尋女兒。火眼金睛又一次看穿了她；金箍棒又一次落下，那妖怪又一次棄下假屍而逃。第三次，她化作一個老翁，來尋妻兒，這一回猴子不等她念咒吸氣便一棒打去——這一棒打碎了她真正的身軀，只見一堆白骨，脊梁上刻著「白骨夫人」四字。

passages.text: But the monk's eyes were mortal ones. To him his disciple had killed a girl, a mother and a father, three innocents in the wilderness; the tightening spell brought the Great Sage to the ground, and his own words of banishment drove him from the pilgrimage — back over the eastern sea to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, weeping to his brothers of the troop as he left the man he could not stop defending.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 27, banishment; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而長老所具的是凡人之眼。在他看來，自己的徒弟打殺了一個女子、一個母親、一個父親，荒野之中三個無辜之人；緊箍咒使大聖跌倒在地，而他親口說出的貶逐之語，將他逐出了取經之路——渡過東海，回到花果山，臨行時他向眾猴兄弟哭訴，說自己離開了他無法不加以護衛的那個人。

title.en: The Yellow-Robed Demon and the Princess of Baohsiang
title.zh: 黃袍怪與百花羞

region.en: Wave-Moon Cave, Baohsiang Kingdom (pin: mythic westward route)
region.zh: 寶象國波月洞

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 28-31)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 28-31: the Yellow-Robed Demon, the princess's secret letter, and Wukong's return from exile

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: With Wukong banished, the Yellow-Robed Demon of Wave-Moon Cave — a star of heaven fallen into demonhood — seized the monk; the princess Bailongxiu, a mortal stolen from Baohsiang thirteen years before, bought his release with a lie and smuggled a letter home. The princes begged Wukong's pardon and help; the monkey, in the tiger's own borrowed shape, exposed the demon's true nature before the court, and the Tang monk — needing his first disciple's fire — took him back with open arms.
summary.zh: 黃袍怪乃二十八宿奎木狼下界；攝寶象國公主百花羞十三年；公主得唐僧託信還國；國王苦留，黃袍怪變虎攝三藏；八戒智激美猴王——悟空歸隊降妖，師徒重聚。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The demon of the Yellow Robe had carried off from Baohsiang, thirteen years before, a king's daughter, and kept her in the Wave-Moon Cave as his wife with two children by her. Coming upon the monkless pilgrims, he seized the Tang monk in his claws and bore him to the cave for his evening meal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, chs. 28-29 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那黃袍怪早在十三年前便從寶象國擄走了一位國王的女兒，將她留在波月洞中為妻，與她生了兩個孩子。他遇上了沒有師父的取經眾，便以爪抓住唐僧，將他擄回洞中，以備晚膳。

passages.text: The princess, homesick for a father's court she could not remember except in dreams, bargained for the stranger's life: she told the demon the monk was a saintly guest and begged his release, then secretly gave the monk a letter for her father. The king of Baohsiang read his daughter's blood-written plea and begged the passing pilgrims to rescue her — and the pig and the sand-monk failed in the attempt.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 29-30, the letter; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那公主思念父王的宮廷，卻除了在夢中再也記不起它的模樣，便為這陌生人的性命討價還價：她告訴妖怪這僧人是位聖僧貴客，懇求放他，隨後又暗中交給僧人一封給父親的信。寶象國王讀了女兒血書中的哀求，便懇求路過的取經眾救她——而豬八戒與沙僧的營救卻失敗了。

passages.text: Wukong, banished and far away, was found by the shamed Bajie, who — on a courtier's word — provoked him with a lie that the demon had cursed his name. The Great Sage bounded back with a roar, took the place of the transformed prince before the king, flayed the demon's disguise before the whole court, and rescued the princess; and the Tang monk, seeing what his own trust had cost, knelt and took his disciple back with tears.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, chs. 30-31, the rescue and reconciliation; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 被貶遠去的悟空，被羞愧的八戒尋到，八戒——聽了一位朝臣的話——用一句謊言激他，說那妖怪咒罵他的名字。大聖怒吼一聲躍回，在國王面前頂替了變化的王子，當著滿朝文武揭穿了妖怪的偽裝，救出了公主；而唐僧見自己的輕信付出了何等代價，便跪下含淚重新收回了徒弟。

title.en: The Wax Crocodile of Ubaaner
title.zh: 烏巴安奈爾的蠟鱷

region.en: Memphis, Egypt (temple of Ptah, court of King Nebka)
region.zh: 埃及孟菲斯（卜塔神廟，內布卡王廷）

period: Westcar Papyrus, copied 12th-18th Dynasty, tale set in reign of Nebka (3rd Dynasty); Petrie translation 1895

source.work: Egyptian Tales, First Series, ed. W. M. Flinders Petrie (London, 1895), 'Khafra's Tale'

summary.en: Prince Khafra entertains King Khufu with the tale of Ubaaner, whose wife takes a lover from among the royal pages. The chief reciter fashions a wax crocodile seven fingers long, enchants it, and when the page goes to bathe it becomes a seven-cubit crocodile and seizes him; the king commands, 'Take to thee thy prey', and the wife is burned.
summary.zh: 卡夫拉王子向胡夫王述烏巴安奈爾之事：其妻與王室侍從私通。大祭司捏蠟鱷七指長而咒之；侍從入湖沐浴時，蠟鱷化為七肘巨鱷，一口吞之。王命：『帶走爾之獵物』——其妻遂被焚於火。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary tale; no living community restrictions. Petrie's 1895 rendering is the cited public-domain source.

passages.text: Now when the wife of Uba-aner saw a page, among those who stood behind the king, her heart longed after him; and she sent her servant unto him, with a present of a box full of garments. And he came then with the servant. Now there was a lodge in the garden of Uba-aner; and one day the page said to the wife of Uba-aner, 'In the garden of Uba-aner there is now a lodge; behold, let us therein take our pleasure.' So the wife of Uba-aner sent to the steward who had charge over the garden, saying, 'Let the lodge which is in the garden be made ready.' And she remained there, and rested and drank with the page until the sun went down.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie, Egyptian Tales First Series (1895), Khafra's Tale.
passages.zh: 話說烏巴阿奈爾之妻見了侍立於國王身後眾人中的一名侍童，心中便戀慕他；她派自己的僕人前去，帶著一箱衣物為禮。那侍童便隨僕人而來。烏巴阿奈爾的園中有一座涼亭；一日，那侍童對烏巴阿奈爾之妻說：『烏巴阿奈爾的園中如今有一座涼亭；看哪，我們且到那裡去尋歡作樂。』於是烏巴阿奈爾之妻遣人告知掌管園子的管家，說：『把園中的那座涼亭預備妥當。』她便留在那裡，與那侍童一同歇息飲樂，直到日落。

passages.text: Then said Uba-aner, 'Bring me my casket of ebony and electrum.' And they brought it; and he fashioned a crocodile of wax, seven fingers long: and he enchanted it, and said, 'When the page comes and bathes in my lake, seize on him.' And he gave it to the steward, and said to him, 'When the page shall go down into the lake to bathe, as he is daily wont to do, then throw in this crocodile behind him.' And the steward went forth bearing the crocodile. — And the steward cast in the wax crocodile after him into the water; and, behold! it became a great crocodile seven cubits in length, and it seized on the page.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), Khafra's Tale.
passages.zh: 烏巴阿奈爾於是說：「把我那烏木與琥珀金的匣子拿來。」他們便拿來了；他用蠟做成一條鱷魚，長七指：他對它施了咒，說道：「等那侍童前來，在我湖中沐浴時，就抓住他。」他把它交給管家，對他說：「等那侍童下到湖裡沐浴，正如他每日慣常所做的那樣，你就把這條鱷魚扔到他身後。」管家便帶著鱷魚出去了。——管家把那蠟鱷魚扔到他身後的水中；看哪！它變成了一條長七肘的大鱷魚，抓住了那侍童。

passages.text: And Uba-aner called unto the crocodile and said, 'Bring forth the page.' And the crocodile came forth from the lake with the page. Uba-aner said unto the king, 'Behold, whatever I command this crocodile he will do it.' And his majesty said, 'I pray you send back this crocodile.' And Uba-aner stooped and took up the crocodile, and it became in his hand a crocodile of wax. And then Uba-aner told the king that which had passed in his house with the page and his wife. And his majesty said unto the crocodile, 'Take to thee thy prey.' And the crocodile plunged into the lake with his prey, and no man knew whither he went.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), Khafra's Tale.
passages.zh: 烏巴阿奈爾呼喚鱷魚說：「把那侍童帶上來。」鱷魚便帶著侍童從湖中出來。烏巴阿奈爾對國王說：「看哪，凡我吩咐這鱷魚的，它都會照做。」陛下說：「我請你把這鱷魚送回去。」烏巴阿奈爾便俯身把鱷魚拿起來，它在他手中又變成了一條蠟鱷魚。隨後，烏巴阿奈爾把家中那侍童與他妻子之間所發生的事稟告了國王。陛下對鱷魚說：「帶著你的獵物去吧。」鱷魚便帶著它的獵物潛入湖中，無人知道它去了何處。

passages.text: And his majesty the king of Upper and Lower Egypt, Nebka, the blessed, commanded, and they brought forth the wife of Uba-aner to the north side of the harem, and burnt her with fire, and cast her ashes in the river. This is a wonder that came to pass in the days of thy forefather the king of Upper and Lower Egypt, Nebka, of the acts of the chief reciter Uba-aner. His majesty the king of Upper and Lower Egypt, Khufu, then said, 'Let there be presented to the king Nebka, the blessed, a thousand loaves, a hundred draughts of beer, an ox, two jars of incense.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), Khafra's Tale, closing.
passages.zh: 上下埃及之王、蒙福的內布卡陛下下令，他們便把烏巴阿奈爾的妻子帶到后宮北側，用火燒了她，並把她的骨灰撒入河中。這是發生在你先祖、上下埃及之王、蒙福的內布卡時代的一件奇事，乃首席誦經祭司烏巴阿奈爾的作為。上下埃及之王、胡夫陛下於是說：「當向蒙福的內布卡王獻上麵包一千個、啤酒一百酌、牛一頭、香二罐。」

title.en: Zazamankh Splits the Lake
title.zh: 匝匝曼赫分湖取玉

region.en: Memphis, Egypt (palace lake of King Seneferu)
region.zh: 埃及孟菲斯（斯尼夫魯王宮之湖）

period: Westcar Papyrus, copied 12th-18th Dynasty, tale set in reign of Seneferu (4th Dynasty); Petrie translation 1895

source.work: Egyptian Tales, First Series, ed. W. M. Flinders Petrie (1895), 'Baufra's Tale'

summary.en: Weary King Seneferu is rowed about his lake by twenty harem maidens in net dresses; a steering girl's malachite jewel falls into twelve cubits of water and the rowing stops. The reciter Zazamankh speaks his magic speech, piles one half of the lake upon the other, takes up the jewel from a potsherd, and pours the water back — a wonder the bored king rewards.
summary.zh: 厭倦的斯尼夫魯王由二十名著網衣的嬪女划船遊湖；操舵少女之孔雀石墜落十二肘深水，歌止槳停。祭司匝匝曼赫誦咒，將半湖水疊於另一半之上，自碎瓦上拾回寶玉，復傾水還湖——厭王大悅而重賞。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary tale; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The royal son Bau-f-ra then stood forth and spake. He said, 'I will tell thy majesty of a wonder which came to pass in the days of thy father Seneferu, the blessed, of the deeds of the chief reciter Zazamankh. One day King Seneferu, being weary, went throughout his palace seeking for a pleasure to lighten his heart, but he found none. And he said, 'Haste, and bring before me the chief reciter and scribe of the rolls Zazamankh'; and they straightway brought him. And the king said, 'I have sought in my palace for some delight, but I have found none.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie, Egyptian Tales First Series (1895), Baufra's Tale.
passages.zh: 王子包弗拉於是起身說道。他說：「我要向陛下講述一件發生在你父親、蒙福的斯尼弗魯時代的奇事，乃首席誦經祭司扎扎曼赫的作為。有一天，斯尼弗魯王心中煩悶，走遍他的宮殿，想尋些消遣來舒緩心情，卻一無所獲。他說：『快去把首席誦經祭司兼卷冊書吏扎扎曼赫帶到我面前來』；他們立刻把他帶來了。國王說：『我在宮中尋些樂趣，卻一無所獲。』」

passages.text: Then said Zazamankh to him, 'Let thy majesty go upon the lake of the palace, and let there be made ready a boat, with all the fair maidens of the harem of thy palace; and the heart of thy majesty shall be refreshed with the sight, in seeing their rowing up and down the water, and seeing the goodly pools of the birds upon the lake, and beholding its sweet fields and grassy shores; thus will thy heart be lightened. And I also will go with thee. Bring me twenty oars of ebony, inlayed with gold, with blades of light wood, inlayed with electrum; and bring me twenty maidens, fair in their limbs, their bosoms and their hair, all virgins; and bring me twenty nets, and give these nets unto the maidens for their garments.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), Baufra's Tale.
passages.zh: 扎扎曼赫於是對他說：「請陛下到宮中的湖上去，備好一艘船，載上你宮中后宮所有美麗的少女；陛下見她們在湖上往來划槳，見湖上鳥兒棲息的美好水塘，又見那宜人的田野與青草離離的湖岸，心中必因這景象而舒暢；如此你的心便會輕鬆起來。我也將與你同去。給我拿二十支烏木槳來，鑲以黃金，槳葉用輕木，鑲以琥珀金；再給我帶來二十名少女，四肢、胸脯與頭髮皆秀美，盡是處女；再給我拿二十張網來，把這些網給少女們作衣裳。」

passages.text: And they rowed down the stream and up the stream, and the heart of his majesty was glad with the sight of their rowing. But one of them at the steering struck her hair, and her jewel of new malachite fell into the water. And she ceased her song, and rowed not; and her companions ceased, and rowed not. And his majesty said, 'Row you not further?' And they replied, 'Our little steerer here stays and rows not.' His majesty then said to her, 'Wherefore rowest thou not?' She replied, 'It is for my jewel of new malachite which is fallen in the water.' And he said to her, 'Row on, for behold I will replace it.' And she answered, 'But I want my own piece back in its setting.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), Baufra's Tale.
passages.zh: 她們順流而下，又逆流而上，陛下見她們划槳，心中歡喜。但她們中掌舵的一人碰落了頭髮，她那新孔雀石的首飾掉進了水裡。她便停止了歌唱，不再划槳；她的同伴們也停了下來，不再划槳。陛下說：「你們為何不再划了？」她們回答：「我們這小小的掌舵女停下來不划了。」陛下於是對她說：「你為何不划？」她回答：「是因為我那掉進水裡的新孔雀石首飾。」他對她說：「繼續划吧，看哪，我會補給你一件。」她卻回答：「我只要我自己那一件，連著它的鑲座還回來。」

passages.text: Then the chief reciter Zazamankh spake his magic speech. And he placed one part of the waters of the lake upon the other, and discovered the jewel lying upon a shard; and he took it up and gave it unto its mistress. And the water, which was twelve cubits deep in the middle, reached now to twenty-four cubits after he turned it. And he spake, and used his magic speech; and he brought again the water of the lake to its place. And his majesty spent a joyful day with the whole of the royal house. Then rewarded he the chief reciter Zazamankh with all good things.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), Baufra's Tale, closing.
passages.zh: 於是首席誦讀者扎扎曼赫念誦他的咒語。他將湖水的一部分置於另一部分之上，發現那寶石躺在一塊碎片上；他將它拾起，交給它的女主人。那湖中央本深十二肘，經他翻轉之後，如今竟達二十四肘。他開口念誦，施展他的咒語；又將湖水復歸原處。陛下與整個王室共度歡樂的一日。隨後，他以一切美物賞賜首席誦讀者扎扎曼赫。

title.en: Dedi before Khufu: Heads Rejoined
title.zh: 傑迪覲胡夫：斷首復接

region.en: Memphis, Egypt (hall of columns of Pharaoh)
region.zh: 埃及孟菲斯（法老柱廳）

period: Westcar Papyrus, copied 12th-18th Dynasty, tale set in reign of Khufu (4th Dynasty); Petrie translation 1895

source.work: Egyptian Tales, First Series, ed. W. M. Flinders Petrie (1895), 'Hordefef's Tale'

summary.en: Prince Hordedef fetches the 110-year-old sage Dedi, who restores severed heads before King Khufu — but refuses a living prisoner: 'We do not even thus to our cattle.' A duck, a goose, and an ox are beheaded and live again; Dedi knows where the designs of Thoth's dwelling lie, and prophesies that three sons of Ra will be born to rule the land.
summary.zh: 霍爾德代夫王子迎來百一十歲的聖者傑迪，於胡夫王前復接斷首——然拒殺活人囚犯：『吾儕待牛亦不出此。』鴨、鵝、牛斬首而復活；傑迪知托特居所圖樣所在，且預言拉之三子將生而王天下。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary tale; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The royal son Hordedef then stood forth and spake. He said, 'Hitherto hast thou only heard tokens of those who have gone before, and of which no man knoweth their truth. But I will show thy majesty a man of thine own days.' And his majesty said, 'Who is he, Hordedef?' And the royal son Hordedef answered, 'It is a certain man named Dedi, who dwells at Dedsneferu. He is a man of one hundred and ten years old; and he eats five hundred loaves of bread, and a side of beef, and drinks one hundred draughts of beer, unto this day. He knows how to restore the head that is smitten off; he knows how to cause the lion to follow him trailing his halter on the ground; he knows the designs of the dwelling of Tahuti. The majesty of the king of Upper and Lower Egypt, Khufu, the blessed, has long sought for the designs of the dwelling of Tahuti, that he may make the like of them in his pyramid.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie, Egyptian Tales First Series (1895), Hordefef's Tale.
passages.zh: 王子霍爾德德夫於是起身說道。他說：『迄今你只聽聞前人的奇蹟，而無人知其真偽。但我將向陛下顯示一位與你同時代的人。』陛下說：『他是誰，霍爾德德夫？』王子霍爾德德夫答道：『是一個名叫德迪的人，住在德德斯涅費魯。他年已一百一十歲；至今每日食五百個麵包、一側牛肉，飲一百口啤酒。他懂得如何接回被砍下的頭；他懂得如何使獅子拖著地上的韁繩跟隨他；他懂得塔胡提居所的圖樣。上下埃及之王、蒙福的胡夫陛下，長久以來尋求塔胡提居所的圖樣，欲在其金字塔中仿造。』

passages.text: And his majesty said, 'Is it true, that which men say, that thou canst restore the head which is smitten off?' And Dedi replied, 'Truly, I know that, O king (life, wealth, and health), my lord.' And his majesty said, 'Let one bring me a prisoner who is in prison, that his punishment may be fulfilled.' And Dedi said, 'Let it not be a man, O king, my lord; behold we do not even thus to our cattle.' And a duck was brought unto him, and its head was cut off. And the duck was laid on the west side of the hall, and its head on the east side of the hall. And Dedi spake his magic speech. And the duck fluttered along the ground, and its head came likewise; and when it had come part to part the duck stood and quacked. And they brought likewise a goose before him, and he did even so unto it. His majesty caused an ox to be brought, and its head cast on the ground. And Dedi spake his magic speech. And the ox stood upright behind him, and followed him with his halter trailing on the ground.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), Hordefef's Tale.
passages.zh: 陛下說：『人所言你能接回被砍下的頭，是真的嗎？』德迪答道：『確實，我懂得此事，國王（願他生命、財富與健康），我的主人。』陛下說：『讓人給我帶一名獄中的囚犯來，好使他的刑罰得以執行。』德迪說：『不要用人，國王，我的主人；看哪，我們對牲畜尚且不如此行。』於是有人帶一隻鴨子到他面前，砍下牠的頭。鴨子被放在廳堂西側，牠的頭放在廳堂東側。德迪念誦他的咒語。鴨子便沿地面撲動，牠的頭也同樣而來；當頭與身相接，鴨子便站起來嘎嘎叫。他們又帶一隻鵝到他面前，他對牠也照樣而行。陛下命人牽一頭牛來，將牠的頭擲在地上。德迪念誦他的咒語。牛便在他身後直立起來，拖著地上的韁繩跟隨他。

passages.text: And King Khufu said, 'And is it true what is said, that thou knowest the number of the designs of the dwelling of Tahuti?' And Dedi replied, 'Pardon me, I know not their number, O king, but I know where they are.' And his majesty said, 'Where is that?' And Dedi replied, 'There is a chest of whetstone in a chamber named the plan-room, in Heliopolis; they are in this chest.' And Dedi said further unto him, 'O king, my lord, it is not I that is to bring them to thee.' And his majesty said, 'Who, then, is it that shall bring them to me?' And Dedi answered to him, 'It is the eldest of the three children who are in the body of Rud-didet who shall bring them to thee.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), Hordefef's Tale.
passages.zh: 胡夫王說：『人所言你知曉塔胡提居所圖樣的數目，是真的嗎？』德迪答道：『恕我，我不知其數目，國王，但我知道它們在何處。』陛下說：『在何處？』德迪答道：『在赫利奧波利斯一間名為圖樣室的 chamber 中，有一隻磨石之匣；它們就在這匣中。』德迪又對他說：『國王，我的主人，並非由我將它們帶來給你。』陛下說：『那麼，是誰要將它們帶來給我？』德迪回答他說：『是魯德迪德特體內三子中的長子，他將把它們帶來給你。』

passages.text: And Dedi replied, 'She is the wife of a priest of Ra, lord of Sakhebu. And she has conceived these three sons by Ra, lord of Sakhebu, and the god has promised her that they shall fulfil this noble office (of reigning) over all this land, and that the eldest of them shall be high priest in Heliopolis.' And his majesty's heart became troubled for this; but Dedi spake unto him, 'What is this that thou thinkest, O king, my lord? Is it because of these three children? I tell thee thy son shall reign, and thy son's son, and then one of them.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), Hordefef's Tale.
passages.zh: 德迪答道：『她是薩赫布之主拉的一位祭司之妻。她因薩赫布之主拉而懷了這三個兒子，神已應許她，他們將在這全地之上履行這高貴的職分（即統治），而他們中的長子將為赫利奧波利斯的大祭司。』陛下心中為此不安；但德迪對他說：『國王，我的主人，你心中所想的是什麼？是因為這三個孩子嗎？我告訴你，你的兒子將統治，你兒子的兒子也將統治，然後他們中的一位。』

title.en: Rud-didet and the Three Sons of Ra
title.zh: 魯德代德與拉之三子

region.en: Sakhebu, Letopolite nome, Egypt (house of the priest Ra-user)
region.zh: 埃及萊托波利斯州薩赫布（拉-烏塞爾祭司之家）

period: Westcar Papyrus, copied 12th-18th Dynasty, tale set at the close of Khufu's reign; Petrie translation 1895

source.work: Egyptian Tales, First Series, ed. W. M. Flinders Petrie (1895), conclusion of 'Hordefef's Tale'

summary.en: Ra sends Isis, Nephthys, Meskhent, Hekt and Khnumu, disguised as dancing-girls, to the house of the priest Ra-user to deliver his wife Rud-didet of three kings; each child of a cubit with bones strong and hair of lapis lazuli is named and crowned king by the goddess, and the royal diadems, hidden in a bushel of barley, sing in a sealed chamber — until a jealous maid is carried off by a crocodile.
summary.zh: 拉遣伊西斯、奈芙蒂斯、美斯肯特、海卡特與庫努姆化妝為舞女，至祭司拉-烏塞爾家中，為其妻魯德代德接生三王；每子一肘高，骨骼強健，髮如青金石，神為之命名加冕。王冠藏於大麥斗中，封閉之室內歌聲與樂舞大作——直至妒婢為鱷魚所噬。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary tale; no living community restrictions. Petrie notes the tale likely reflects the 5th Dynasty's priestly usurpation and the title 'Son of Ra'.

passages.text: And one day it came to pass that Rud-didet felt the pains of birth. And the majesty of Ra, lord of Sakhebu, said unto Isis, to Nebhat, to Meskhent, to Hakt, and to Khnumu, 'Go ye, and deliver Rud-didet of these three children that she shall bear, who are to fulfil this noble office over all this land; that they may build up your temples, furnish your altars with offerings, supply your tables of libation, and increase your endowments.' Then went these deities; their fashion they made as that of dancing-girls, and Khnumu was with them as a porter.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie, Egyptian Tales First Series (1895), conclusion of Hordefef's Tale.
passages.zh: 有一天，魯德迪德特感到分娩的陣痛。薩赫布之主拉的威嚴對伊西斯、對涅巴特、對梅斯肯特、對哈克特、對克努穆說：『你們去，為魯德迪德特接生這三個她將生下的孩子，他們要在這全地之上履行這高貴的職分；好使他們建造你們的廟宇，以祭品充實你們的祭壇，供給你們的奠酒之桌，並增添你們的捐贈。』於是這些神祇前去；他們將自己的形貌化作舞女之狀，克努穆與他們同行，作腳夫。

passages.text: And Isis said, 'O child, by thy name of User-ref, do not do violence.' And the child came upon her hands, as a child of a cubit; its bones were strong, the beauty of its limbs was like gold, and its hair was like true lapis lazuli. They washed him, and prepared him, and placed him on a carpet on the brickwork. Then Meskhent approached him and said, 'This is a king who shall reign over all the land.' And Khnumu gave strength to his limbs. — And Isis said, 'O child, by thy name of Sah-ra, stay not in her.' Then the child came upon her hands, a child of a cubit... And Meskhent approached him and said, 'This is a king who shall reign over all the land.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), births of the three children (elisions marked).
passages.zh: 伊西斯說：『孩子啊，憑你烏塞爾-瑞夫之名，切勿施暴。』那孩子便落到她手中，是個一肘長的嬰孩；他的骨骼強健，四肢之美有如黃金，頭髮有如真正的青金石。他們為他洗浴，為他整備，把他放在磚台上的毯子上。於是梅斯赫奈特走近他，說：『這是一位將統治全地的國王。』克努穆賜力量給他的四肢。——伊西斯說：『孩子啊，憑你薩赫-拉之名，不要留在她那裡。』於是那孩子落到她手中，是個一肘長的嬰孩……梅斯赫奈特走近他，說：『這是一位將統治全地的國王。』

passages.text: And Isis spake unto these goddesses, and said, 'Wherefore have we come without doing a marvel for these children, that we may tell it to their father who has sent us?' Then made they the divine diadems of the king, and laid them in the bushel of barley. And they caused the clouds to come with wind and rain; and they turned back again unto the house. And they said, 'Let us put this barley in a closed chamber, sealed up, until we return northward, dancing.' — And the handmaid went, and opened the chamber. And she heard talking and singing, music and dancing, quavering, and all things which are performed for a king in his chamber.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895).
passages.zh: 伊西斯對這些女神說：『我們為何來了卻不為這些孩子行一件奇事，好讓我們告訴那差遣我們來的他們的父親呢？』於是她们為國王製作了神聖的王冠，放在大麥的斗裡。她们使雲帶著風和雨而來；她们又轉身回到那屋裡。她们說：『讓我們把這大麥放進一間封閉的密室，封存起來，直到我們向北歸去、一路舞蹈之時。』——那女僕前去，打開了密室。她聽見說話聲和歌唱聲、樂聲和舞蹈聲、顫動之聲，以及一切在國王密室中為他所行之事。

passages.text: And after these days it came to pass that Rud-didet was wroth with her servant, and beat her with stripes. And the servant said unto those that were in the house, 'Shall it be done thus unto me? She has borne three kings, and I will go and tell this to his majesty King Khufu the blessed.' And she went, and found the eldest brother of her mother, who was binding his flax on the floor. And he said to her, 'Whither goest thou, my little maid?' And he took a bunch of the flax to her, and laid on her a violent blow. And the servant went to fetch a handful of water, and a crocodile carried her away.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), closing of the tale (the remainder is lost).
passages.zh: 這些日子之後，魯德-迪德特對她的女僕發怒，用鞭子打她。那女僕對屋裡的人說：『豈可這樣待我？她生了三位國王，我要去把這事告訴蒙福的胡夫王陛下。』她去了，找到她母親的長兄，他正在地上捆綁他的亞麻。他對她說：『你往哪裡去，我的小丫頭？』他拿了一束亞麻給她，又重重打了她一下。那女僕去取一捧水，一隻鱷魚把她叼走了。

title.en: The Peasant and the Workman: Justice for the Sekhti
title.zh: 農夫與工人：塞克蒂之訟

region.en: Herakleopolis (Henenseten), Egypt, capital of the 9th-10th Dynasties
region.zh: 埃及赫拉克利奧波利斯（第九至第十王朝都城）

period: Tale of the 9th-10th Dynasties (c. 2160-2025 BCE); Petrie translation 1895

source.work: Egyptian Tales, First Series, ed. W. M. Flinders Petrie (1895), 'The Peasant and the Workman'

summary.en: A workman of a great steward blocks the tow-path with his cloak, steals a peasant's ass over a mouthful of corn, and warns him: 'Lift not up your voice, Sekhti, or you shall go to the Demon of Silence.' The wronged peasant petitions the steward nine times in famous rhetoric until the king, delighted, orders the speeches written down — and the whole property of the workman is given to the Sekhti.
summary.zh: 豪僕工人以斗篷阻道，藉口驢食其麥而奪農夫之驢，並威嚇：『塞克蒂，勿聲張，否則你將去見沉默之魔。』受屈農夫九次上訴，辭章之美感動君王，命書吏錄之——最後工人全部家產盡歸塞克蒂。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary tale; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: There dwelt in the Sekhet Hemat — or salt country — a peasant called the Sekhti, with his wife and children, his asses and his dogs; and he trafficked in all good things of the Sekhet Hemat to Henenseten. Behold now he went with rushes, natron, and salt, with wood and pods, with stones and seeds, and all good products of the Sekhet Hemat. And this Sekhti journeyed to the south unto Henenseten; and when he came to the lands of the house of Fefa, north of Denat, he found a man there standing on the bank, a man called Hemti — the workman — son of a man called Asri, who was a serf of the High Steward Meruitensa.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie, Egyptian Tales First Series (1895), The Peasant and the Workman.
passages.zh: 在塞赫特·赫馬特——即鹽鄉——住著一個名叫塞赫提的農夫，帶著他的妻子兒女、他的驢子和狗；他把塞赫特·赫馬特的一切好物販運到赫嫩塞騰。看哪，他帶著燈心草、泡鹼和鹽，帶著木柴和豆莢，帶著石頭和種子，以及塞赫特·赫馬特的一切好產物。這塞赫提往南行至赫嫩塞騰；當他來到德納特以北、費法家之地時，他發現那裡有一人站在岸上，此人名叫赫姆提——那工匠——是一個名叫阿斯里之人的兒子，阿斯里是大管家梅魯伊滕薩的農奴。

passages.text: Said Sekhti, 'I am going carefully; the one way is stopped, therefore took I my ass by the enclosed ground, and do you seize it for filling its mouth with a cluster of corn? Moreover, I know unto whom this domain belongs, even unto the Lord Steward Meruitensa. He it is who smites every robber in this whole land; and shall I then be robbed in his domain?' Said Hemti, 'This is the proverb which men speak: A poor man's name is only his own matter. I am he of whom you spake, even the Lord Steward of whom you think.' Thereon he took to him branches of green tamarisk and scourged all his limbs, took his asses, and drave them into the pasture. And Sekhti wept very greatly, by reason of the pain of what he had suffered. Said Hemti, 'Lift not up your voice, Sekhti, or you shall go to the Demon of Silence.' Sekhti answered, 'You beat me, you steal my goods, and now would take away even my voice, O demon of silence!'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895).
passages.zh: 塞赫提說：『我正小心行走；一條路被堵住了，因此我牽著我的驢從圍起的地旁經過，你卻抓住它，用一簇穀物塞它的嘴嗎？再者，我知道這片田地屬於誰，乃是屬於大管家梅魯伊滕薩。正是他擊打這全地每一個強盜；難道我竟要在他的田地裡遭搶嗎？』赫姆提說：『這就是人們所說的諺語：窮人的名聲只是他自己的事。我就是你所說的那人，正是你所想的大管家。』於是他就拿起青檉柳的枝條，抽打他的全身，牽走他的驢子，趕進牧場。塞赫提因所受的痛苦而大哭。赫姆提說：『不要提高你的聲音，塞赫提，否則你就要去見沉默之神了。』塞赫提回答說：『你打我，你偷我的財物，如今還要奪去我的聲音嗎，哦沉默之神！』

passages.text: Sekhti said, 'Ho! turn, that I may please thy heart with this discourse.' — 'O my Lord Steward, greatest of the great, guide of the needy: When thou embarkest on the lake of truth, Mayest thou sail upon it with a fair wind; May thy mainsail not fly loose. May there not be lamentation in thy cabin; May not misfortune come after thee. May not thy mainstays be snapped; Mayest thou not run aground. May not the wave seize thee; Mayest thou not taste the impurities of the river; Mayest thou not see the face of fear. For thou art the orphan's father, the widow's husband, The desolate woman's brother, the garment of the motherless. Let me celebrate thy name in this land for every virtue. Destroying deceit, encouraging justice; Coming to the cry, and allowing utterance. Abolish oppression, behold me, I am overladen, Reckon with me, behold me defrauded.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), the first petition.
passages.zh: 塞赫提說：『喂！轉過來吧，好讓我用這番話討你歡心。』——『哦我的大管家，偉大者中最偉大者，困乏者的引導者：當你登上真理之湖，願你順風航行其上；願你的主帆不致鬆脫飛揚。願你的船艙中沒有哀哭；願不幸不追隨你。願你的主桅索不致斷裂；願你不致擱淺。願波浪不攫住你；願你不嘗河水的污濁；願你不見恐懼的面容。因為你是孤兒的父親，寡婦的丈夫，孤苦女子的兄弟，無母者的衣裳。讓我在這地上因每一種美德頌揚你的名。消滅欺詐，鼓勵公正；應答呼求，允許申訴。廢除壓迫，看哪，我負重過甚，為我評理，看哪，我受了冤屈。』

passages.text: His majesty said, 'As thou wishest that I may see health! lengthen out his complaint, without replying to any of his speeches. He who desireth him to continue speaking should be silent; behold, bring us his words in writing, that we may listen to them. But provide for his wife and his children, and let the Sekhti himself also have a living. Thou must cause one to give him his portion without letting him know that thou art he who is giving it to him.' — But yet Meruitensa would not hearken unto his complaint; and the Sekhti came yet, and yet again, even unto the ninth time. Then the Lord Steward Meruitensa then said unto him, 'Fear not, Sekhti, for what thou hast done. The Sekhti has made many speeches, delightful to the heart of his majesty, and I take an oath — as I eat bread, and as I drink water — that thou shalt be remembered to eternity.' And moreover he gave all that which belonged unto the Hemti to the Sekhti, even all his property and his offices, and the Sekhti was beloved of the king more than all his overseers.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), closing (condensed by elision between the king's order and the ninth petition).
passages.zh: 陛下說：「既然你希望我得以安康！那就延長他的訴說，不要回應他的任何言辭。凡希望他繼續說下去的人，就當保持沉默；看哪，把他的話記錄下來呈給我們，好讓我們聆聽。但要供養他的妻子和兒女，也讓這塞克提本人得以維生。你須命人給他應得的那一份，卻不可讓他知道是你給他的。」——然而梅魯伊滕薩仍不聽從他的訴說；那塞克提一次又一次地前來，直到第九次。於是總管梅魯伊滕薩對他說：「塞克提，不要為你所做的事害怕。這塞克提說了許多話，令陛下心中喜悅，我起誓——正如我吃麵包、正如我喝水——你必被永遠記念。」此外，他把屬於赫姆提的一切都給了這塞克提，甚至他所有的財產和職位，而這塞克提比國王所有的監工都更受國王喜愛。

title.en: The Shipwrecked Sailor and the Serpent of Punt
title.zh: 遇難水手與彭特巨蛇

region.en: The Red Sea, on the route to the mines of Pharaoh (the serpent's island of Punt, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 紅海（前往法老礦山途中；巨蛇之彭特島，象徵定位）

period: Tale of the 12th Dynasty (c. 1985-1773 BCE); sole copy in the Hermitage papyrus; Petrie translation 1895

source.work: Egyptian Tales, First Series, ed. W. M. Flinders Petrie (1895), 'The Shipwrecked Sailor'

summary.en: The one survivor of a wreck spends three days alone on an island where nothing is lacking, until the earth shakes and a serpent thirty cubits long, gilded and lapis-covered, demands his story. The serpent of Punt comforts him, prophesies four months' wait and rescue, scoffs at the sailor's promised gifts — 'I am prince of Punt, and I have perfumes' — and the island sinks back into waves behind him.
summary.zh: 海難唯一倖存者獨處富足之島三日，直至大地震動——三十肘金鱗青金石紋之巨蛇現身，責其陳述來歷。彭特巨蛇慰其心，預言四月後獲救還鄉；水手許以香料而神笑之——『我乃彭特之君，我自有香料』——離島之後，其島沒於波濤。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary tale; no living community restrictions. Coordinates are symbolic over the Red Sea mining route, since the enchanted island cannot be located.

passages.text: Now I shall tell that which has happened to me, to my very self. I was going to the mines of Pharaoh, and I went down on the sea on a ship of 150 cubits long and 40 cubits wide, with 150 sailors of the best of Egypt, who had seen heaven and earth, and whose hearts were stronger than lions. They had said that the wind would not be contrary, or that there would be none. But as we approached the land the wind arose, and threw up waves eight cubits high. As for me, I seized a piece of wood; but those who were in the vessel perished, without one remaining. A wave threw me on an island, after that I had been three days alone, without a companion beside my own heart. I laid me in a thicket, and the shadow covered me.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie, Egyptian Tales First Series (1895), The Shipwrecked Sailor.
passages.zh: 現在我要講述臨到我自身的事。我正前往法老的礦場，我乘一艘長一百五十肘、寬四十肘的船下海，船上有埃及最精良的一百五十名水手，他們見過天地，其心比獅子更堅強。他們曾說風不會逆，或者根本不會有風。但當我們接近陸地時，風起了，掀起八肘高的浪。至於我，我抓住了一塊木頭；但船中的人都喪命了，一個也沒有留下。我獨自一人、除我自己的心以外別無伴侶地過了三天之後，一個浪把我拋到一座島上。我躺在一處灌木叢中，樹蔭遮蓋了我。

passages.text: Suddenly I heard a noise as of thunder, which I thought to be that of a wave of the sea. The trees shook, and the earth was moved. I uncovered my face, and I saw that a serpent drew near. He was thirty cubits long, and his beard greater than two cubits; his body was as overlayed with gold, and his colour as that of true lazuli. He coiled himself before me. Then he opened his mouth, while that I lay on my face before him, and he said to me, 'What has brought thee, what has brought thee, little one, what has brought thee? If thou sayest not speedily what has brought thee to this isle, I will make thee know thyself; as a flame thou shalt vanish, if thou tellest me not something I have not heard, or which I knew not, before thee.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895).
passages.zh: 忽然我聽見一陣如雷的聲響，我以為那是海中的浪。樹木搖動，大地震顫。我揭開臉上的遮蓋，看見一條蛇正靠近。他長三十肘，鬍鬚超過兩肘；他的身體彷彿覆著黃金，他的顏色如同真正的青金石。他在我面前盤繞起來。當時我伏在他面前，他便張開口，對我說：「是什麼把你帶來的，是什麼把你帶來的，小東西，是什麼把你帶來的？你若不快快說出是什麼把你帶到這島上，我就要叫你知道你自己；你若不對我說些我未曾聽過、或我先前所不知道的事，你就要像火焰一樣消失。」

passages.text: Then said he to me, 'Fear not, fear not, little one, and make not thy face sad. If thou hast come to me, it is God who has let thee live. For it is He who has brought thee to this isle of the blest, where nothing is lacking, and which is filled with all good after another, until thou shalt be four months in this isle. Then a ship shall come from thy land with sailors, and thou shalt leave with them and go to thy country, and thou shalt die in thy town. I will therefore tell thee of that which is in this isle. I am here with my brethren and my children around me; we are seventy-five serpents, children, and kindred; without naming a young girl who was brought unto me by chance, and on whom the fire of heaven fell, and burnt her to ashes.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895).
passages.zh: 於是他對我說：「不要怕，不要怕，小東西，不要讓你的臉憂愁。你既然來到我這裡，是神讓你活著的。因為正是祂把你帶到這座蒙福之島，這裡一無所缺，充滿各樣美好的事物，一件接著一件，直到你在这島上住滿四個月。那時必有一艘船從你的國土帶著水手而來，你便與他們一同離去，回到你的國家，並在你的城中死去。因此我要告訴你這島上的事。我在此與我的兄弟和兒女圍繞在我身邊；我們共有七十五條蛇，包括子女和親族；還不算一個偶然被帶到我這裡的年輕女子，天上的火落在她身上，把她燒成了灰燼。」

passages.text: Then he smiled at my speech, because of that which was in his heart, for he said to me, 'Thou art not rich in perfumes, for all that thou hast is but common incense. As for me I am prince of the land of Punt, and I have perfumes. Only the oil which thou sayedst thou wouldest bring is not common in this isle. But, when thou shalt depart from this place, thou shalt never more see this isle; it shall be changed into waves.' — And, behold, when the ship drew near, according to all that he had told me before, I got me up into an high tree, to strive to see those who were within it. Then he said to me, 'Farewell, farewell, go to thy house, little one, see again thy children, and let thy name be good in thy town; these are my wishes for thee.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Petrie (1895), closing (the serpent's farewell and gifts).
passages.zh: 於是他因我這番話而微笑，因為他心中所想的，因為他對我說：「你並不富於香料，因為你所有的不過是普通的香。至於我，我是朋特之地的君王，我有香料。只是你說你要帶來的那油，在這島上並不常見。但當你離開這地方以後，你將永遠不再見到這島；它將化為波浪。」——看哪，當那船靠近時，正如他先前所告訴我的一切，我爬上高樹，竭力想看看船中的人。於是他對我說：「別了，別了，回你的家去吧，小東西，再見你的兒女，願你的名在你的城中美好；這是我對你的祝願。」

canonical_translation: W. M. Flinders Petrie, Egyptian Tales, First Series (London, 1895), from the Golenischeff translation

narrative.en:
The Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor is the oldest surviving 'enchanted island' story, framed like a persuasive speech: a returnee from a failed expedition addresses his superior, who has begun to doubt him. 'Wash thee, and turn the water over thy fingers; then go and tell the tale to the majesty' — and when the master mocks his wandering words, the sailor answers that although a man's mouth may save him, words may also cover his face with confusion. Then he swears his story is of himself, and tells it.

BEGINNING: THE WRECK. Bound for the mines of Pharaoh with 150 sailors 'who had seen heaven and earth, and whose hearts were stronger than lions', the ship is struck by a wind that raises waves eight cubits high. All drown but the narrator, who clings to a plank and is thrown by a wave onto an island. Three days alone, he lies in a thicket and finds the island 'where nothing is lacking': figs and grapes, herbs, berries and grain, melons, fish and birds. He digs a pit, lights a fire, and makes a burnt-offering to the gods — the first act of a man who knows his survival depends on ritual correctness.

MIDDLE: THE SERPENT'S AUDIENCE. Thunder without a storm: trees shake, the earth moves, and a serpent thirty cubits long appears, its beard over two cubits, its body gilded and its scales true lapis. Coiling before the prostrate sailor, it threatens him: 'As a flame thou shalt vanish, if thou tellest me not something I have not heard.' It takes the man in its mouth — gently, unharmed — carries him to its resting-place, and demands his story a second time. The sailor's reply is a full formal speech of his voyage; the serpent relents: 'Fear not, little one... it is God who has let thee live. He has brought thee to this isle of the blest.'

END: THE PROPHECY AND THE VANISHING ISLAND. The serpent foretells his rescue: four months on the island, then a ship from Egypt, and home to 'die in thy town.'
