So, ever since that time, sparrow-hawks are often seen carrying off young chickens, while the cocks have been busy scratching the ground to find the lost bracelet; hens also scratch the soil, for they hate to lose their chicks and want to find the bracelet as soon as possible — they look up into the sky to see if the sparrow-hawk is near; then they scratch the soil vigorously and cry, 'Tac-ta-laoc!' which means, 'Come and help me!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 74 'The Cock and the Sparrow-Hawk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 公雞戴著借來的臂環去參加慶典；然而，當他在跳舞時，卻弄丟了那顆寶石，怎麼也找不到。「既然那臂環是傳家之寶，我當然格外珍視它，」雀鷹回答說。「你必須回到你認為弄丟它的地方，在那裡尋找，直到找到為止。在此期間，我保留隨時從你的雞群中取走一隻雞的權利。」於是，從那時起，人們常見到雀鷹叼走小雞，而公雞則一直忙著刨地尋找那丟失的臂環；母雞也刨土，因為牠們不願失去小雞，想盡快找到那臂環——牠們仰望天空，看看雀鷹是否在附近；然後牠們用力刨土，叫著：「Tac-ta-laoc！」意思是：「快來幫我！」

title.en: The Story of Our Fingers
title.zh: 五指的故事

region.en: Calamba, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省卡蘭巴（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 75 'The Story of our Fingers', eBook #8299

summary.en: In the days of the ancestors all five fingers stood together; hunger struck, and the Thumb proposed stealing. The four virtuous brothers refused — 'we would rather starve and die than steal' — and drove the Thumb out of their community in shame; so the thumb stands separate from the other four, and the little finger, who had nothing to eat, remains lean and weak.
summary.zh: 祖先的時代五指相連。飢餓降臨，拇指提議偷竊；四位正直的兄弟寧願餓死也不偷，羞逐拇指出族。故今日拇指與四指分離；小指因當年無食，至今瘦弱。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from an Uichanco narrator (Calamba); archival record. Told as grandfather's answer to a child's question about the thumb.

passages.text: 'Why does our thumb stand separate from the other fingers?' asked little Antonio; and old Julian answered that in the days of long ago the fingers of our ancestors stood together in the same position. One day one of these fingers, the one we call the little finger, became very hungry, and he asked the finger next to him to give him some food. 'O brother! I am hungry also; but where shall we get food?' said the Ring-Finger. 'Heaven is merciful,' put in the Middle-Finger; 'Heaven will give us some.' 'But what if Heaven gives us no food?' protested the Forefinger. 'Well, then,' interposed the Thumb, 'let us steal!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 75 'The Story of our Fingers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「為什麼我們的拇指和其他手指分開呢？」小安東尼奧問道；老朱利安回答說，在很久以前，我們祖先的手指都是並排連在一起的。有一天，其中一根手指，就是我們稱為小指的那根，變得非常飢餓，他便請旁邊的手指給他一些食物。「哦，兄弟！我也餓了；可是我們要到哪裡去弄食物呢？」無名指說。「上天是慈悲的，」中指插嘴道；「上天會給我們一些的。」「可是萬一上天不給我們食物呢？」食指反駁道。「那麼，」拇指插話說，「我們就去偷吧！」

passages.text: 'Steal!' echoed the Forefinger. 'Your idea is against morality, against God, against yourself, against everybody. Our conscience will not permit us to steal,' concluded the other three unanimously. 'Oh, no, no! You are greatly mistaken, my friends!' returned Thumb angrily. 'Ay, if that be your plan, you can go your own way,' said the other four fingers. 'As for us, we would rather starve and die than steal.' Then the four virtuous brothers drove Thumb in shame out of their community, and would have nothing more to do with him. 'So that is why we see our thumbs separated from the other four fingers,' concluded old Julian. 'He was a thief; and the other four, who were honest, did not care to live with him. And it is because Little-Finger did not have enough to eat that we see him lean and weak these days.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 75 'The Story of our Fingers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「偷！」食指附和道。「你的主意違背道德，違背上帝，違背你自己，也違背所有人。我們的良心不允許我們去偷，」其餘三根手指一致結論道。「哦，不不！朋友們，你們大錯特錯了！」拇指生氣地回答。「唉，如果那就是你們的打算，你們盡可各行其是，」其餘四根手指說。「至於我們，寧可挨餓而死，也不願去偷。」於是，這四位有德行的兄弟羞愧地把拇指趕出了他們的群體，再也不願與他有任何往來。「所以我們才會看到拇指和其他四根手指分開，」老朱利安結論道。「他是個賊；而其他四根手指為人誠實，不願與他同住。也正因為小指沒有吃飽，我們如今才見他瘦弱無力。」

title.en: Why Snails Climb Up Grass
title.zh: 螺為何攀草

region.en: Binalonan, Pangasinan, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦阿西楠省比納隆安（敘述者故鄉）

period: Pangasinan oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 76 'Why Snails climb up Grass', eBook #8299

summary.en: The mud-fish Dalag (head and provider), the dragon-fly (messenger), the wasp (guard), and the snail (cook) share a common house — until Dalag seizes a hook-laden frog and is caught; the vain dragon-fly tightens his neck-tie against a laughing fish until he cuts off his own head; the starving wasp draws in his belt until he breaks in two. Only the snail remains, wandering and weeping, climbing every grass-stalk to look for his friends — as snails still do.
summary.zh: 泥鰍達拉格（家長兼伙伕）、蜻蜓（信使）、黃蜂（衛士）、螺螄（廚子）同居一屋。達拉格抓鉤上之蛙而被捕；虛榮的蜻蜓誤把嘲笑的魚當譏其領帶，越繫越緊直至斷頭；飢餓的黃蜂勒緊『腰帶』直至斷為兩截。只剩螺螄，一路哭泣，攀上每一根草莖張望——至今依然。

sensitivity.note: Pangasinan etiological tale recorded by Fansler from a Tomeldan narrator (Binalonan); archival record. Explains snails climbing grass-stalks and weeping.

passages.text: Long ago, when the various kinds of animals dwelt together in a kind of community, a dalag (a kind of mud-fish), a dragonfly, a wasp, and a snail agreed to live together in a common house, dividing the household duties according to their power and skill. Dalag, the biggest and strongest, was made the head of the house and to provide food; Dragon-Fly, the swiftest, was made the messenger; Wasp, because of his poisonous sting, was made house-guard and repairer; Snail, too slow for any other duty, was made the cook. Early one day Dalag went out to look for food, saw a big frog swimming helplessly among the duck-weeds, seized it, and started home — but a sharp hook was inside the frog, and poor Dalag was caught fast; a fisherman came, put him in his basket, took him home and ate him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 76 'Why Snails climb up Grass'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 很久以前，當各種動物聚居在一起、形成某種社群時，一條dalag（一種泥魚）、一隻蜻蜓、一隻黃蜂和一隻蝸牛同意同住在一間屋子裡，並依各自的能力和本領分擔家務。dalag體型最大、最強壯，被立為一家之主，負責覓食；蜻蜓最敏捷，被派為信差；黃蜂因有毒刺，被派為守衛和修繕者；蝸牛動作太慢，做不了別的事，便被派為廚師。有一天清早，dalag外出覓食，看見一隻大青蛙在浮萍間無力地游著，便抓住牠，動身回家——可是青蛙體內藏著一枚尖鉤，可憐的dalag被牢牢鉤住；一個漁夫走來，把他放進籃子，帶回家吃掉了。

passages.text: Dragon-Fly was sent out to look for him, and before he went he spent a long time arranging his neck-tie; turning his head in all directions, he met Bolasi, a fish whose lips always move in and out on the surface of the water, and became very angry because he thought Bolasi was laughing at his neck-tie. He tightened it; still Bolasi laughed every time he saw him; Dragon-Fly kept drawing his tie tighter and tighter, until at last he cut his own head off, and that was the end of him. Two days later, Wasp and Snail were very hungry — Snail could eat mud, but Wasp could only draw in his belt a little tighter; at last, oppressed by hunger, he flew forth in search of his friends, tightening his belt again and again until he finally broke in two, and that was the end of Wasp.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 76 'Why Snails climb up Grass'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蜻蜓被派出去找他，出發前他花了很長時間整理自己的領帶；他轉頭四處張望，遇見了Bolasi——一條嘴唇總在水面上不停開合的魚，便大為光火，因為他以為Bolasi在嘲笑他的領帶。他把領帶勒緊；可是Bolasi每次見到他仍舊發笑；蜻蜓便把領帶越勒越緊，最後竟把自己的頭勒斷了，他就這樣送了命。兩天後，黃蜂和蝸牛都非常飢餓——蝸牛可以吃泥，黃蜂卻只能把腰帶稍微勒緊一點；最後，他被飢餓折磨得受不了，便飛出去尋找同伴，一次又一次勒緊腰帶，終於把自己勒成了兩截，黃蜂就這樣送了命。

passages.text: Now only Snail was left. He set out from his home and wandered everywhere in search of his three companions, weeping as he went; his food consisted mostly of mud. Whenever he could find a stalk of grass or the stem of a water-plant, Snail would climb up to look around and see if any of his old friends were in sight. Even to-day the snails still weep; and whenever they see a stalk of grass projecting above the surface of the water, they climb up and look around, trying to discover their old friends.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 76 'Why Snails climb up Grass'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 如今只剩下蝸牛了。他離家出發，四處遊蕩尋找他的三個同伴，邊走邊哭；他的食物大多是泥。每當能找到一根草莖或水草的梗，蝸牛便爬上去四下張望，看看有沒有哪位舊友的蹤影。直到今天，蝸牛仍在哭泣；每當牠們看見一根草莖伸出水面，便爬上去四下張望，想找到牠們的舊友。

title.en: Why the Cuttlefish and Squids Produce a Black Liquid
title.zh: 墨魚與魷魚為何吐墨

region.en: Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home province)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 77 'Why the Cuttlefish and Squids produce a Black Liquid', eBook #8299

summary.en: Bathala convenes all the fishes in the Dark Sea to appoint officers: the sting-ray sergeant-at-arms, the crocodile cadaver-carrier, the crab a soldier. The late cuttle-fish and squid interrupt, ask for work, are scolded again, and in fury throw mud over all the drawn-up appointments — so Bathala condemns them to carry pouches of mud forever, to move slowly under their heavy loads, and the squid to remain its present size.
summary.zh: 巴哈拉於黑暗之海召集群魚授職：魟為侍衛官（故有其鞭狀尾），鱷為抬棺者（故有其棺形背甲），蟹為士兵（故有其巨螯）。姍姍來遲的墨魚與魷魚屢遭斥責，憤而以泥塗汙所有已繕就之任命狀——巴哈拉震怒，罰其永世身負泥囊、行動遲緩，魷魚更不得再長大。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from a Ciudadano narrator (Batangas); archival record. Known by both Tagalogs and Visayans, she says.

passages.text: A long time ago, after Bathala had created the fishes, he assigned a certain day for all of them to meet in the Dark Sea, the object of this convention being to appoint some officers. When they reached the assembly hall they found Bathala sitting on a beautiful stone waiting for them; the roll was called, and the cuttle-fish and squid were found absent. After waiting half an hour, Bathala called the meeting to order and appointed the sting-ray sergeant-at-arms (hence all sting-rays now have whip-like tails), the crocodile cadaver-carrier (so now all its children have a coffin-like skin on their backs), and the crab a soldier (so to-day all its descendants have large and strong fore-legs). Bathala had not finished giving out his appointments when the two missing members came, and at once interrupted the meeting by asking what it was all about.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 77 'Why the Cuttlefish and Squids produce a Black Liquid'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 很久以前，巴塔拉創造了魚類之後，便指定了某一天讓所有魚類在黑暗之海集合，這場聚會的目的是要任命一些官員。當牠們抵達會場時，發現巴塔拉坐在一塊美麗的石頭上等著牠們；點名之後，發現烏賊和魷魚缺席。等了半個小時之後，巴塔拉宣布會議開始，並任命魟魚為糾察長（因此今日所有的魟魚都有像鞭子一樣的尾巴）、鱷魚為抬棺者（所以現在牠所有的孩子背上都有一層像棺材般的皮），以及螃蟹為士兵（所以今日牠所有的後代都有又大又強壯的前腳）。巴塔拉還沒宣布完任命，那兩名缺席的成員就來了，立刻打斷會議，詢問這究竟是怎麼一回事。

passages.text: Bathala became very angry at the interruption and scolded the cuttle-fish and the squid severely. The rebuke humiliated them so that they agreed between themselves to go get mud and throw it on the official appointments; when they had gotten the mud they came back and asked Bathala to give them something to do, but instead of appointing them to some work he only scolded them for being late. Angered, they now threw mud on all the appointments that had already been drawn up. This insulting act so enraged Bathala that he stood up and said in thundering tones, 'Now I shall punish you. From this time on, you and your descendants shall carry pouches of mud with you all the time. Besides, you shall be very slow in moving because of your heavy loads.' The squid tried to make excuses, but Bathala became angrier than ever: 'You are the naughtiest creature I ever had. As a punishment, you and your children shall remain the same size as you are now.' And all of Bathala's words have turned out to be true.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 77 'Why the Cuttlefish and Squids produce a Black Liquid'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴塔拉對這番打斷大為震怒，嚴厲地斥責了烏賊和魷魚。這番責罵令牠們深感羞辱，於是牠們彼此商定去取泥巴來，扔在那些官職任命上；取來泥巴之後，牠們回來請求巴塔拉派給牠們一些差事，但巴塔拉非但沒有任命牠們任何工作，反而只責罵牠們遲到。牠們一氣之下，便把泥巴扔在已經擬好的所有任命上。這侮辱性的舉動令巴塔拉勃然大怒，他站起身來，以雷鳴般的聲調說道：「現在我要懲罰你們。從今以後，你們和你們的子孫都要時時刻刻帶著泥囊。此外，由於你們負擔沉重，行動將會非常遲緩。」魷魚試圖辯解，但巴塔拉比先前更加憤怒：「你是我有過最頑劣的生物。作為懲罰，你和你的子孫將永遠保持現在這般大小。」而巴塔拉所說的一切都應驗了。

title.en: Why Cocks Have Combs on Their Heads
title.zh: 公雞為何有冠

region.en: Boac, Marinduque, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓馬林杜克島博阿克（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 78 'Why Cocks have Combs on their Heads', eBook #8299

summary.en: The magician Pablo finds his idle son Juan combing his hair before a mirror instead of working; he snatches the comb, strikes the boy's head so hard the comb sticks deep into the skull, and curses, 'Since you always want to use the comb, let it be on your head forever!' — transforming Juan into a cock, the comb into flesh, visible to this day on the heads of all his descendants.
summary.zh: 魔術師帕布洛撞見懶兒胡安對鏡梳頭而不做事；他奪梳怒擊其首，梳齒深陷顱骨，並咒曰：『你既愛梳，就永遠梳在頭上吧！』胡安化為公雞，梳齒化為肉冠——今之雄雞頂冠皆是胡安之後裔。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from a Nieva narrator (Boac, Marinduque); archival record.

passages.text: Once upon a time there was a magician named Pablo, who had a son called Juan. Pablo was very industrious, but Juan was lazy and disobedient: he cared for nothing but fine clothes and his own appearance, and would not help his father. One day Pablo went into his son's room to find out what he was doing; there he was, standing before a mirror and combing his hair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 78 'Why Cocks have Combs on their Heads'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個名叫巴布羅的魔法師，他有一個兒子叫胡安。巴布羅非常勤勞，但胡安卻懶惰又不聽話：他除了華服和自己的外表之外什麼都不在意，也不肯幫父親的忙。有一天，巴布羅走進兒子的房間，想看看他在做什麼；只見他站在鏡子前梳著頭髮。

passages.text: Pablo was so angry at his son that he immediately snatched the comb from his hand; then he angrily struck the boy's head with the comb, and spoke these harsh words: 'Since you always want to use the comb, let it be on your head forever! I prefer to have no son at all. I would rather see you changed into a bird than to remain such a disobedient, worthless boy.' The father struck his son's head so hard that the comb stuck deep into the skull; by Pablo's magic power, Juan was immediately changed into a cock, and the comb on his head was changed into flesh. We can see it to-day on the heads of all the descendants of Juan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 78 'Why Cocks have Combs on their Heads'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴布羅對兒子大為光火，立刻從他手中奪過梳子；接著他憤怒地用梳子敲打男孩的頭，並說出這番嚴厲的話：「既然你總是想用梳子，那就讓它永遠留在你頭上吧！我寧可根本沒有兒子。我寧願看到你變成一隻鳥，也不願你繼續做這樣一個不聽話、沒出息的男孩。」父親敲打兒子的頭敲得太用力，梳子深深嵌進了頭骨；憑著巴布羅的魔法，胡安立刻變成了一隻公雞，他頭上的梳子也化成了肉。我們今日可以在胡安所有後代的頭上看到它。

title.en: How the Crow Became Black: Bathala's Inkstand
title.zh: 烏鴉變黑：巴哈拉的墨水瓶

region.en: Cagayan de Oro, Misamis, Mindanao, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨米薩米斯卡加延德奧羅（敘述者故鄉）

period: Visayan oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79a 'How the Crow became Black', eBook #8299

summary.en: When Bathala's subjects steal Dumagat's fish, the sea-god opens the great pipe of the world's waters and floods the land, drowning nearly all the people. Bathala sends the crow, his pretty-plumaged favorite, to learn whether his subjects survived; the crow lands on the floating corpses and eats. The dove sent after him reports his disobedience, and Bathala seizes his big inkstand and hurls it — the crow covered black forever, condemned to be a scavenger hated by all, while the faithful dove becomes the beloved pet.
summary.zh: 巴哈拉子民偷食海神杜馬加特之魚；海神開啟世水巨管，洪水沒陸，生民幾絕。巴哈拉遣羽色絢麗的寵鳥烏鴉探查；烏鴉卻落於浮屍啄食。奉命尋找的鴿子告發其悖命；巴哈拉怒擲墨水瓶——烏鴉被潑成永黑，貶為人人憎惡的食腐者；忠實的鴿子則成眾人所愛。

sensitivity.note: Visayan etiological tale recorded by Fansler from a Neri narrator (Cagayan, Misamis); archival record. Flood cluster: the deluge here issues from a quarrel between two pagan deities, which Fansler reads as preserved old native tradition.

passages.text: A long time ago, when Bathala, the god of the land, was peacefully ruling his dominions, he had many pets, and among these his two favorites were the dove and the crow; the crow was noted for its bright, pretty plumage. One day Bathala had a quarrel with Dumagat, the god of the sea: Bathala's subjects had been stealing fish, which were the subjects of Dumagat. When Dumagat learned of this, and could get no satisfaction from Bathala, he retaliated: he opened the big pipe through which the water of the world passes, and flooded the dominions of Bathala, until nearly all the people were drowned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79 'How the Crow became Black'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 很久以前，當陸地之神巴塔拉和平地統治著他的領地時，他養了許多寵物，其中他最喜愛的兩隻便是鴿子和烏鴉；烏鴉以其明亮美麗的羽毛著稱。有一天，巴塔拉與海神杜馬加特起了爭執：巴塔拉的子民一直偷竊屬於杜馬加特子民的魚。杜馬加特得知此事後，又無法從巴塔拉那裡得到滿意的答覆，於是展開報復：他打開了世界之水所流經的大管道，淹沒了巴塔拉的領地，直到幾乎所有的人都溺死了。

passages.text: When the water had abated somewhat, Bathala sent the crow, his favorite messenger, to find out whether all his subjects had been killed. The crow flew out and soon saw the corpses of many persons floating about; he descended, alighted on one, and began to eat the decaying cadaver. When Bathala saw that it was late and the crow had not returned, he sent the dove on the same errand; the dove, looking for any signs of life, at last saw the crow eating the decaying bodies, told him the king had sent for him, and together they flew back to Bathala's palace, where the dove reported that the crow had been eating dead bodies and had not done what he was sent to do.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79 'How the Crow became Black'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當水稍微退去之後，巴塔拉派他最喜愛的使者烏鴉去查看他的子民是否全都死了。烏鴉飛了出去，很快就看到許多人的屍體漂浮著；牠降下身子，停在其中一具屍體上，開始吃起腐爛的屍骸。巴塔拉見天色已晚，烏鴉卻還沒回來，便派鴿子去辦同一件事；鴿子尋找著任何生命的跡象，最後看見烏鴉正在吃腐爛的屍體，便告訴牠國王召牠回去，於是牠們一同飛回巴塔拉的宮殿，鴿子在那裡稟報說，烏鴉一直在吃死屍，並沒有去做派給牠的事。

passages.text: Bathala was very angry at this disobedience. Without saying a word, he seized his big inkstand filled with black ink and threw it at the crow, which was immediately covered. Then he turned to the dove: 'You, my dove, because of your faithfulness, shall be my favorite pet, and no longer shall you be a messenger.' And to the crow: 'You, foul bird, shall forever remain black; you shall forever be a scavenger, and every one shall hate you.' So that is why to-day the dove is loved by the people and the crow hated; the crows to-day are all black, because they are descendants of the bird punished by Bathala.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79 'How the Crow became Black'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴塔拉對這般違抗極為震怒。他一言不發，抓起裝滿黑墨的大硯台，朝烏鴉擲去，烏鴉當即被墨汁覆滿全身。接著他轉向鴿子說：「你，我的鴿子，因你的忠信，將成為我最鍾愛的寵物，不再做傳信的使者。」又對烏鴉說：「你這污穢的鳥，將永遠保持黑色；你將永遠以腐肉為食，人人都要憎惡你。」所以今日鴿子受人喜愛，烏鴉遭人憎恨；今日的烏鴉全是黑的，因為牠們正是被巴塔拉懲罰的那隻鳥的後代。

title.en: Why the Crow Is Black: The Crows of Sinukuan
title.zh: 烏鴉變黑：蘇努庫安的雙鴉

region.en: Tarlac province, Luzon, Philippines (Pampangan tale, Ilocano narrator's home)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋丹轆省（邦板牙故事，伊洛卡諾敘述者居地）

period: Pampangan oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79b 'Why the Crow is Black', eBook #8299

summary.en: Two golden-plumaged crows sing in the gardens of Sinukuan's palace while a pestilence kills his animals. Returning from three days of relief among his dying subjects, he calls for his birds to sing away his anguish — and finds them feasting on decaying carcasses a mile away. Restraining himself from killing them, he curses them to be ugly black birds with only a harsh cry: the crows of today.
summary.zh: 瘟疫肆虐，蘇努庫安的金羽雙鴉卻在金園中歌唱。神行三日救疫歸來，喚鴉歌以解憂——竟見牠們在屍堆中饗腐肉。祂強忍殺意，咒其化為醜黑之鳥、聲啞而厲——今日之烏鴉即其後裔。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan etiological tale recorded by Fansler from an Ortega narrator (an Ilocano living in Tarlac); archival record. Sinukuan is the great Pampangan mountain-deity; no flood in this version, the occasion being a pestilence.

passages.text: The first crow that lived on the earth was a beautiful bird with a sweet voice. The universe was ruled over by the god Sinukuan, and all his subjects were either plants or animals, no human beings yet being in existence. Sinukuan lived in a beautiful palace surrounded with gardens of gold, and in these gardens lived two crows who sang sweet songs and did nothing but fly about among the flowers and trees; their golden plumage was beautiful to see, and Sinukuan took great delight in them. Once a terrible pestilence visited the earth, and a great many of Sinukuan's animals began to die.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79 'Why the Crow is Black'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 世上最初的一隻烏鴉，是一隻歌聲甜美、形貌美麗的鳥。宇宙由神明西努庫安統治，他的臣民盡是草木鳥獸，當時尚無人類存在。西努庫安住在一個花園環繞、以黃金築成的美麗宮殿裡，園中住著兩隻烏鴉，牠們唱著甜美的歌，終日只在花木之間飛翔；牠們金色的羽衣賞心悅目，西努庫安十分喜愛牠們。有一次，一場可怕的瘟疫降臨大地，西努庫安許許多多的動物開始死去。

passages.text: In his distress and sorrow Sinukuan at once set out and made a tour of his kingdom to give what relief he could to his suffering subjects; after being away three days he returned to his palace, his mind weighted down by all the death and sickness he had seen, and called to his two birds to come sing for him and relieve his mental anguish — but neither of the birds came. He went through his gardens and called in vain; thinking they had flown away and been attacked by the pestilence, he made another trip through his kingdom to look for them. He had not walked a mile when, approaching a number of dead animals, he saw the pair feasting on the decaying flesh; when they saw their master, they bowed their heads in shame.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79 'Why the Crow is Black'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 西努庫安憂傷苦惱，立刻動身巡行他的國度，盡其所能救助受苦的臣民；離去三日之後，他回到宮殿，心中因目睹種種死亡與病痛而沉重不堪，便喚他那兩隻鳥前來為他歌唱，以紓解心中的苦悶——但兩隻鳥都沒有來。他走遍花園呼喚，卻徒勞無功；他心想牠們或許已飛走，遭了瘟疫侵襲，於是又巡行國度尋找牠們。他走了不到一英里，走近一群死去的動物時，竟看見那對鳥正啄食腐爛的屍肉；牠們一看見主人，便羞愧地低下頭。

passages.text: Had not Sinukuan restrained himself, he might have killed them that very moment; but he thought of a better way to punish them. 'Now,' he said, as he cursed them, 'from this time on, you shall be very ugly black birds; you shall lose your beautiful voice, and shall be able to make only a harsh cry.' From that time on those birds were black, and their offspring are the crows of to-day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79 'Why the Crow is Black'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 若不是西努庫安克制住自己，他當時就可能把牠們殺了；但他想到了一個更好的懲罰辦法。「如今，」他一面詛咒牠們，一面說道，「從此刻起，你們將變成極其醜陋的黑鳥；你們將失去美妙的嗓音，只能發出刺耳的叫聲。」從那時起，那些鳥便是黑色的，牠們的後代就是今日的烏鴉。

title.en: The Dove and the Crow (Zambal): The Flood's Red Water
title.zh: 鴿與鴉（三描）：洪水赤水

region.en: Cabangan, Zambales, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋三描禮士省卡邦安（敘述者故鄉）

period: Zambal oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79c 'The Dove and the Crow', eBook #8299

summary.en: After the inundation of the world, God sends a crow to measure the water; finding dead animals everywhere, he forgets his command and stays to eat. The faithful dove, sent three days later, stands in the water reddened by the blood of the slain, finds it only an inch deep, and returns with crimson feet as evidence. The crow, returning without excuse, is punished with a chain on his legs — so crows can only hop from place to place, while the dove remains God's favorite with red feet to this day.
summary.zh: 洪水之後，上帝遣鴉探水深；鴉見遍地死獸，忘命飽食。三日後遣鴿——忠實的鴿子立於血染之水，量得水深僅一吋，紅足為證而歸。無辭以對的鴉被罰以鎖鏈繫足——至今只能跳不能走；忠鴿則為上帝至愛，紅足猶存。

sensitivity.note: Zambal etiological tale recorded by Fansler from a Carpio narrator (Cabangan); archival record. Flood-cluster variant: the raven-and-dove post-diluvian measuring episode in Philippine dress; Fansler traces the ultimate source to Arabian tradition (Tabari) via the Moros, noting uniquely Philippine details (the deity, the chained legs).

passages.text: A few days after the inundation of the world, God sent a crow down to earth to see how deep the water was on the land. When the crow flew down to earth, he was surprised to see so many dead animals everywhere; it came to his mind that perhaps they would taste good, so he alighted on one of them and began to eat. He was so very much pleased with the abundance of food about him that he forgot all about the command God had given him, and he remained on the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79 'The Dove and the Crow'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大洪水淹沒世界之後過了幾天，神派一隻烏鴉下到人間，察看地上的水有多深。烏鴉飛到地上，看見遍地都是死去的動物，大為驚訝；牠心想這些或許滋味不錯，便落在一具屍體上吃了起來。牠見四周食物如此豐盛，十分歡喜，竟把神給牠的命令忘得一乾二淨，就留在了地上。

passages.text: On the third day, since the crow had not returned, God sent a dove down to earth to find out the depth of the water and to make other observations of the things that had taken place on the earth. As the dove was a faithful creature, she did not forget what God told her: she did not alight on any dead animal, but alighted directly in the water — now red from the blood of so many creatures that had been slain — and found that it was only an inch deep. She at once flew back to heaven, where, in the presence of God, she related what she had seen on earth, while the crimson color on her feet was evidence of the depth of the water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79 'The Dove and the Crow'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了第三天，烏鴉仍未回來，神便派一隻鴿子下到人間，查明水的深淺，並察看地上所發生的其他種種情形。鴿子是個忠信的造物，沒有忘記神囑咐牠的話：牠不落在任何死去的動物身上，而是直接落在水中——那水已被眾多被殺生靈的血染成紅色——發現水只有一吋深。牠立刻飛回天上，在神面前述說自己在人間所見的一切，而牠腳上那深紅的顏色，正是水深的明證。

passages.text: After a short time the crow returned, and came before God, who spoke to him thus: 'What made you so long? Why did you not return sooner from the earth?' As the crow had no good reason to give for his delay, he said nothing; he simply bent his head. God punished the crow by putting a chain on his legs — so that to-day the crow cannot walk: all he can do is to hop from place to place. The dove, which was faithful to God, is now the favorite pet bird the world over, and the red color on her feet may be seen to-day as evidence that she performed her duty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79 'The Dove and the Crow'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 過了不久，烏鴉回來了，來到神面前，神這樣對牠說：「是什麼讓你去了這麼久？你為何不早些從地上回來？」烏鴉既然提不出延誤的好理由，便什麼也沒說，只是低下了頭。神懲罰烏鴉，把鎖鏈套在牠的腳上——所以直到今日，烏鴉都無法行走，只能從一處跳到另一處。那忠於神的鴿子，如今成了全世界最受寵愛的鳥兒，而牠腳上的紅色，至今仍可看見，作為牠盡了職責的證據。

title.en: Why the Ocean Is Salty: Ang-ngalo's Salt Bricks
title.zh: 海為何是鹹的：安恩加洛的鹽磚

region.en: Bangued, Ilocos Sur, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋南伊洛克斯省邦基（敘述者故鄉）

period: Ilocano oral etiological myth; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 80 'Why the Ocean is Salty', eBook #8299

summary.en: Ang-ngalo, only son of the god of building and Adam of the Ilocanos, digs caves in the mountains and wades the ocean — whose deep caverns are his footprints — to reach Sipnget, goddess of the dark, who demands a mansion of bricks as white as snow. Only salt is white enough; Asin, ruler of the kingdom of Salt, supplies pure salt bricks, and millions of men carry them across hundreds of bamboo bridges until Ocean, her slumber disturbed, sends big waves that bury bridge, carriers, and burden in her deep bosom — and in time the salt dissolved, and today the ocean is salty.
summary.zh: 建築神之獨子、伊洛卡諾人之亞當——巨人安恩加洛，鑿山為洞，蹚海赴約——海底深穴即其足跡。黑暗女神希普內特求建『白如雪之磚』的宮殿；世上唯鹽最白，鹽國之主阿辛獻純鹽磚。百萬人晝夜經竹橋運磚，直至海洋女神不堪其擾，掀起巨浪將橋樑、運夫與磚石盡沒其懷——鹽既溶，海水至今是鹹的。

sensitivity.note: Ilocano etiological myth recorded by Fansler from a Paredes narrator (Bangued); archival record. Ang-ngalo (Aolo) is the giant Adam of the Ilocanos per Blumentritt; the primordial ocean is 'the accumulated tears of disappointed goddesses.'

passages.text: A few years after the creation of the world there lived a tall giant by the name of Ang-ngalo, the only son of the god of building. Ang-ngalo was a wanderer and a lover of work; he lived in the mountains, where he dug many caves, protecting them from the continual anger of Angin, the goddess of the wind, by precipices and sturdy trees. One bright morning, while Ang-ngalo was climbing to his loftiest cave, he spied across the ocean — the ocean at the time was pure, its water being the accumulated tears of disappointed goddesses — a beautiful maid, who beckoned to him and waved her black handkerchief; so Ang-ngalo waded across to her through the water, and the deep caverns in the ocean are his footprints.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 80 'Why the Ocean is Salty'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 世界被創造之後過了幾年，住著一個名叫昂加洛（Ang-ngalo）的高大巨人，他是建築之神唯一的兒子。昂加洛是個漂泊者，也是個熱愛勞作的人；他住在山裡，在那裡挖了許多洞穴，並以懸崖和堅固的樹木保護它們，免受風之女神安金（Angin）不斷的怒氣侵擾。一個晴朗的早晨，昂加洛正攀向他最高的洞穴時，隔著海洋——當時的海洋是純淨的，其海水是失望的女神們所積聚的淚水——瞥見一位美麗的少女，她向他招手，揮動著她的黑色手帕；於是昂加洛涉水穿過海水走向她，而海洋中那些深邃的洞穴便是他的腳印。

passages.text: This beautiful maid was Sipnget, the goddess of the dark. 'I am tired of my dark palace in heaven. You are a great builder. What I want you to do for me is to erect a great mansion on this spot. This mansion must be built of bricks as white as snow.' Ang-ngalo could not find any bricks as white as snow — the only white thing there was then was salt; so he went for help to Asin, the ruler of the kingdom of Salt, who gave him pure bricks of salt as white as snow. Then Ang-ngalo built hundreds of bamboo bridges across the ocean, and millions of men were employed day and night transporting the white bricks from one side of the ocean to the other.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 80 'Why the Ocean is Salty'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這位美麗的少女是西普恩格特（Sipnget），黑暗女神。「我厭倦了我在天上的黑暗宮殿。你是個偉大的建築者。我要你為我做的，是在這個地方建起一座宏偉的宅邸。這座宅邸必須用白如雪的磚塊建成。」昂加洛找不到白如雪的磚塊——當時那裡唯一的白色之物便是鹽；於是他去向鹽之國度的統治者阿辛（Asin）求助，阿辛給了他白如雪的純鹽磚。於是昂加洛在海洋上架起數百座竹橋，並雇用了數百萬人日夜不停地將白色磚塊從海洋的一邊運到另一邊。

passages.text: At last the patience of Ocean came to an end: she could not bear to have her deep and quiet slumber disturbed. One day, while the men were busy carrying the salt bricks across the bridges, she sent forth big waves and destroyed them; the brick-carriers and their burden were buried in her deep bosom. In time the salt dissolved, and today the ocean is salty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 80 'Why the Ocean is Salty'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 終於，海洋的耐性到了盡頭：她無法忍受自己深沉而寧靜的沉睡受到打擾。有一天，當人們正忙著把鹽磚運過橋時，她送出巨浪將他們摧毀；運磚的人和他們所負的重擔都被埋葬在她深邃的懷抱中。時日一久，鹽便溶解了，於是今日的海洋是鹹的。

title.en: Why the Sky Is Curved
title.zh: 天穹為何彎曲

region.en: Santo Tomas, Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省聖托馬斯（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 81a 'Why the Sky is Curved', eBook #8299

summary.en: When souls went directly to heaven, heaven grew crowded until the sky began to fall on God's throne; he summoned five angels to hold up the sky with their heads while his carpenters repaired the heavens — and because the tallest angel stood in the centre of the group, the sky has been curved ever since.
summary.zh: 人死即昇天的年代，天堂人滿為患，天穹壓向神座。上帝召五天使以頭頂天，命木匠搶修天宮——因最高者立於中央，天穹從此呈弧形。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from a Malvar narrator (Santo Tomas, Batangas); archival record. Fansler knows no variants.

passages.text: Many, many years ago, when people were innocent, as soon as they died, their souls went directly to heaven. In a short time heaven was crowded with souls, because nearly every one went there. One day, while God was sitting on his throne, he felt it moved by some one; on looking up, he saw that the souls were pushing towards him, because the sky was about to fall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 81 'Why the Sky is Curved'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 許多年、許多年以前，當人們還天真無邪的時候，他們一死，靈魂便直接升往天堂。沒過多久，天堂便擠滿了靈魂，因為幾乎人人都去了那裡。有一天，神正坐在祂的寶座上，感覺寶座被什麼人推動了；祂抬頭一看，只見靈魂們正朝祂推擠過來，因為天空快要塌下來了。

passages.text: At once he summoned five angels, and said to them, 'Go at once to the earth, and hold up the sky with your heads until I can have it repaired.' Then God called together all his carpenters and said, 'Repair the heavens as soon as possible.' The work was done; but it happened that the tallest angel was standing in the centre of the group — and so, ever since, the sky has been curved.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 81 'Why the Sky is Curved'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 祂立刻召來五位天使，對他們說：「立刻到地上去，用你們的頭頂住天空，直到我把它修好。」接著，神召集了祂所有的木匠，說：「盡快修好天。」工作完成了；但恰好最高的那位天使站在眾人的中央——於是，從那時起，天空便一直是彎曲的。

title.en: Why the Sky Is High
title.zh: 天為何高

region.en: Janiuay, Iloilo, central Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓怡朗省哈紐艾（敘述者故鄉）

period: Visayan oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 81b 'Why the Sky is High', eBook #8299

summary.en: In olden days the sky was low enough to touch with a stick, so God could hear his people and send blessings — until a drunken sayao dancer at chief Abing's feast darted his spear and pierced the sky, wounding one of the gods; the angered Father raised the sky far from the earth as we have it today.
summary.zh: 昔天天低，竹竿可及——神諦聽民呼、隨時降福。酋長阿賓設宴，酒醉的戰舞者擲矛刺破天穹、傷及神明；盛怒的天父將天升高至今日的遙遠之處。

sensitivity.note: Visayan etiological tale recorded by Fansler from a Lutero narrator (Janiuay, Iloilo); archival record. A Malayan tradition: Fansler parallels the Bagobo 'Why the Sky Went Up' myths (Benedict) and Borneo versions (Hose-McDougall; Evans' Horned Owl and the Moon), plus Mabel Cook Cole's Bukidnon pestle-and-sky tale already in the corpus.

passages.text: In olden days the sky was low — so low that it could be reached by a stick of ordinary length. The people in those days said that God had created the sky in such a way that he could hear his people when they called to him, and in turn God could send his blessings to earth as soon as men needed them. Because of this close connection between God and his subjects, the people were well-provided for and did not need to work: whenever they wanted to eat, they would simply call God, and almost before their request was made the food would be on the table. But after the expulsion of Adam and Eve, God made men work for their own living; and with this change in their condition came the custom of holding feasts, when the men would rest from their labors.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 81 'Why the Sky is High'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古時天空很低——低到用一根普通長度的棍子就能觸及。那時的人們說，神創造天空的方式，使他能聽見子民呼喚他，而神也能在人們需要時立刻將祝福送到地上。由於神與其子民之間如此緊密的連結，人們生活富足，無須勞作：每當他們想吃飯，只要呼喚神，幾乎在請求提出之前，食物就已擺在桌上。但自從亞當與夏娃被逐之後，神便讓人類為自己的生計而勞作；隨著他們境況的這一改變，也興起了設宴的習俗，屆時人們便從勞作中歇息。

passages.text: One day one of the chiefs, Abing by name, held a feast, and many people came to enjoy it. A sayao, or native war-dance, was given in honor of the men belonging to the chief, acted by men brandishing spears. While acting, one of the dancers, who was drunk, tried to show his skill, but he forgot that the sky was so low: when he darted his spear, he happened to pierce the sky, and one of the gods was wounded. This angered God the Father: so he raised the sky as we have it to-day, far from the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 81 'Why the Sky is High'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，一位名叫阿賓的首領設宴，許多人前來享用。為了向屬於這位首領的勇士們致敬，舉行了一場薩亞奧，即土著的戰舞，由揮舞長矛的男子們表演。表演時，其中一名舞者喝醉了，想要展示自己的本領，卻忘了天空如此之低：當他擲出長矛時，恰好刺穿了天空，傷到了其中一位神。這激怒了天父：於是祂將天空升高到我們今日所見的模樣，遠離大地。

title.en: An Unequal Match: Why the Carabao's Hoof Is Split
title.zh: 不對等的較量：水牛蹄為何開裂

region.en: Pagsanjan, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省帕桑漢（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 82 'An Unequal Match; or, Why the Carabao's Hoof is split', eBook #8299

summary.en: Mocked as a slow thing unfit to hunt with him, the turtle challenges the carabao to a seven-hill race under threat of being called a coward; he stations a turtle-friend atop each hill, so the carabao finds his rival always ahead crying 'Here I am!' Convinced of defeat at the seventh hill, the carabao kicks the turtle — whose shell is unharmed, but whose hoof-splitting blow the carabao's own hoof bears to this day.
summary.zh: 水牛譏龜遲緩、不配同行；龜以『懦夫』相激，訂下七丘之賽——每丘頂伏一龜友，水牛每到一丘，總見對手在前大喊『我在這裡！』。第七丘認輸的憤怒水牛一腳踢去——龜殼無恙，龜蹄卻從此開裂。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from a Rivera narrator (Pagsanjan); archival record. The trickster-race cycle; Fansler parallels the Pampangan 'Deer and Snail' (deer's gall sucked out, snails bitter) and Visayan and Tinguian variants, and the Borneo plandok-and-crab race.

passages.text: Once a carabao and a turtle met on a road and walked in the woods, having a fine talk together. The turtle was a sort of humorist, constantly giving exhibitions of his dexterity in getting food by trickery; but he was especially anxious to win the friendship of the carabao, thinking that the big fellow would help him whenever he got into trouble. 'Let us live together and hunt out food together! thus we shall break the monotony of our solitary lives.' But the carabao snorted: 'You slow thing! you ought to live with the drones, not with a swift and powerful person like me.' Offended, the turtle challenged the carabao to a race; and when the carabao refused, thinking it a disgrace to run against a turtle, the turtle threatened to go to all the forests, woods, and mountains and tell all his friends and the whole animal kingdom that the carabao was a coward.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 82 'An Unequal Match'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次，一頭水牛和一隻烏龜在路上相遇，一同走進林中，愉快地交談。烏龜算是個滑稽的角色，不斷展示他靠詭計取得食物的靈巧本領；但他尤其渴望贏得水牛的友誼，心想這大塊頭在他遇到麻煩時會幫助他。「讓我們住在一起，一同覓食吧！這樣我們就能打破孤獨生活的單調。」但水牛哼了一聲：「你這慢吞吞的東西！你該和懶蟲住在一起，而不是和我這樣迅捷有力的人。」烏龜被冒犯了，便向水牛挑戰賽跑；水牛認為與烏龜賽跑是種恥辱而拒絕，烏龜於是威脅要走遍所有的森林、樹林和山嶺，告訴他所有的朋友以及整個動物王國，說水牛是個懦夫。

passages.text: Now the carabao was persuaded, and asked three days to get ready; the agreement was that the race should extend over seven hills. The turtle at once set out to visit seven of his friends, and by telling them that winning would be to the glory of the turtle kingdom got them to help — so the next day he stationed a turtle on the top of each hill, after giving them all instructions. On the third day the race began, and when the carabao reached the second hill he was astonished to see the turtle ahead of him shouting, 'Here I am!' — the turtle at once disappearing; and at every hill the carabao found his enemy ahead of him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 82 'An Unequal Match'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 水牛於是被說服了，要求三天時間準備；雙方約定賽跑要跨越七座山丘。烏龜立刻出發去拜訪他的七位朋友，告訴他們勝利將是烏龜王國的榮耀，從而讓他們幫忙——於是第二天，他在給他們所有人指示之後，在每座山丘的頂上各安置了一隻烏龜。第三天賽跑開始了，當水牛到達第二座山丘時，他驚訝地看到烏龜在他前面喊著：「我在這裡！」——那隻烏龜隨即消失；而在每一座山丘，水牛都發現他的對手在他前面。

passages.text: When the carabao was convinced at the seventh hill that he had been defeated, he became so angry that he kicked the turtle; on account of the hardness of its shell the turtle was uninjured, but the hoof of the carabao was split in two because of the force of the blow. And even to-day the carabaos still bear the mark which an unjust action on the part of their ancestor against one whom he knew was far inferior to him in strength produced on himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 82 'An Unequal Match'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當水牛在第七座山丘確信自己已被擊敗時，他氣得踢了烏龜一腳；由於龜殼堅硬，烏龜毫髮無傷，但水牛的蹄子卻因這一擊之力而裂成兩半。甚至到今天，水牛身上仍帶著這個印記——那是牠的祖先對一個明知在力氣上遠遜於自己的人所行不義之舉，在牠自己身上造成的。

title.en: The Heaven Questions: A Catalog of Cosmic Riddles
title.zh: 天問

region.en: The exiled poet's river country, south of the Yangzi (Chu, modern Hubei–Hunan)
region.zh: 楚地江湘（湖北湖南）

period: Chu Ci, Tianwen, attributed Qu Yuan, 3rd c. BCE

source.work: Chu Ci (Songs of Chu), Tianwen: the question-catalog of origins, gods and dynastic history

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: An exile, blackened by slander, wrote on the walls of a temple the questions no one could answer: before heaven and earth divided, what could be examined? Who paced the unstrolling darkness? Who made the suns and set the stars? Why did Gun die by the knife and Yu live? Where did the black bird carry its egg? — one hundred and seventy questions hurled at heaven, preserving for the mythic corpus the oldest catalog of Chinese cosmogonic, divine and heroic lore.
summary.zh: 屈原放逐，彷徨山澤，仰天歎息——見楚先王廟及公卿祠堂圖畫，呵而問之，遂作天問：遂古之初，誰傳道之？上下未形，何由考之？——一百七十餘問，貫穿開闢、神話、天象與興亡。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Chu Ci original. The Tianwen is the mythic corpus's master-index: nearly every pre-Han myth (Gun, Yi, the ten suns, Gun's transformation) is preserved here in question-form.

passages.text: At the very first of things, who told of it, who could measure it? Before the upper and the lower had taken shape, how could any examine them? Darkness and light went dark and bright, and who paced out their order? The spheres of heaven were wound and woven — who marked their crossing? What joined the cords of the nine heavens, and where are the steep-places of their borders?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Tianwen, opening questions (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 曰遂古之初，誰傳道之？上下未形，何由考之？冥昭瞢闇，誰能極之？馮翼惟像，何以識之？明明闇闇，惟時何為？陰陽三合，何本何化？圜則九重，孰營度之？惟茲何功，孰初作之？斡維焉繫？天極焉加？八柱何當？東南何虧？九天之際，安放安屬？隅隈多有，誰知其數？

passages.text: Who has numbered the hours of day and night? The brightness of the moon — what is it that dies in it and is born in it? The woman-queen and the she-goat, where do they gain their flavor? Where did Gun steal the living soil and try the dam? Why was he shut in the crag and cut open to the west? How, changed to a yellow bear, could he live on in the abyss?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Tianwen, Gun questions; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 誰數過晝夜的時刻？月亮的光明——其中何物死去，又何物誕生？女后與母羊，從何處得來牠們的滋味？鯀從何處偷來息壤，試圖堵塞洪水？他為何被囚於山崖，又被剖開於西方？他如何化為黃熊，竟能在深淵中存活？

passages.text: Yi the archer, how did he shoot the suns, and why did the crows' plumage fall? Where did he win the elixir, and why could he not keep it? The dark bird that brought the mandate of Shang — why did it favor that house? And the emperors of the five rises and falls — where did their ten thousand years of mandate go? Heaven does not answer the poet, says the tradition; but the questions themselves are the inventory of the myth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Tianwen, Yi and dynastic questions; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 射日的后羿，如何射落太陽，烏鴉的羽毛又為何墜落？他從何處贏得不死之藥，又為何不能保住它？帶來商朝天命的那隻玄鳥——為何偏愛那一族？而那五度興衰的帝王——他們萬年的天命又歸於何處？傳統說，上天不回答詩人；但這些問題本身，便是神話的清冊。

canonical_translation: Compiler's English rendering from the public-domain original; consulted (copyright, summary only): David Hawkes, The Songs of the South, 1985

narrative.en:
The Tianwen is not a narrative but a machine for generating one: one hundred and seventy questions strung in verse, asked of heaven about the origin of the cosmos, the acts of gods and heroes, and the rises and falls of dynasties. Tradition says the exiled Qu Yuan, wandering past the temples of Chu with their painted walls of gods and kings, interrogated the paintings question by question; the modern reader finds instead a survey of the mythic corpus in its most archaic stratigraphy.

STRUCTURE. The poem moves from cosmogony (what was before heaven and earth? who measured the darkness?) through cosmology (the suns, the moon's death and rebirth, the rain and the wind) into divine history (Gun and Yu, the flood and the living soil, Gun's transformation into the yellow bear; Yi and his sun-shooting and elixir; the black bird's gift to Shang) and ends in dynastic chronicle (the violent successions of Shang and Zhou, framed as questions about mandate and justice).

SIGNIFICANCE FOR THE CORPUS. Because the Tianwen asks rather than tells, it preserves myth-fragments no prose source records: the yellow-bear transformation of Gun, the sun-birds dropping their plumage, the marriage customs of the gods, the perverse fates of dynastic founders. The Han commentators (Wang Yi onward) built the tradition's mythology largely by answering the Tianwen — so this question-catalog stands at the root of Chinese mythography.

FUNCTION. As a ritual-poetic act, the Tianwen is itself a kind of oracle: the poet's questions, hurled at a silent heaven, dramatize the exile's quarrel with the mandate — if heaven orders all, why does the worthy perish? In cross-tradition terms it belongs with the catechism-forms of other cosmologies: the Zoroastrian questions, the Popol Vuh's dialogic divination, the Chinese tradition's own Book of Changes. Its uniqueness is the temper: irreverent, learned, and grieving at once. The poem's final movement turns from gods to kings: the violent successions of Shang and Zhou, the crowing of the white chicken, the oath at Meng Ford — history itself interrogated with the same breathless meter as the origin of the stars. For the mythic corpus this is invaluable: the Tianwen preserves myth-fragments in their most archaic stratigraphy — Gun's transformation into the yellow bear, the sun-birds dropping their plumage under Yi's arrows, the black bird's egg, the marriages of the gods — that no prose source records. The Han commentators, beginning with Wang Yi, built the tradition's mythology largely by answering the Tianwen, so this question-catalog stands at the root of Chinese mythography. As a ritual-poetic act it is itself a kind of oracle: the poet's questions, hurled at a silent heaven, dramatize the exile's quarrel with the mandate — if heaven orders all things, why does the worthy perish and the tyrant reign? In cross-tradition terms it belongs with the interrogative catechisms of other cosmologies, the dialogic divination of the Popol Vuh, and the Chinese tradition's own Book of Changes; its uniqueness is the temper — irreverent, learned, and grieving at once.
narrative.zh: 《天問》非敘事而為生成敘事之機器：百七十問貫穿宇宙起源、神話英雄與王朝興替。舊說屈原呵壁問天；實則為神話母體最古老之地層——鯀化黃熊、羿射日、玄鳥貽喜皆賴此篇而存。漢儒注疏多由答天問而建構神話學。功能：以問代占，流放者與天命之爭執；與瑣羅亞斯德問句、《波波爾烏》對話式占問同型，而其獨特處在憤懣與博學兼備。

functions: Master-index of pre-Han myth in question-form (preserving otherwise-lost fragments)
Ritual-poetic interrogation of heaven: oracle as accusation
Charter of the exile's theology: worthiness against mandate
Foundation text of Chinese mythography (Han commentators answered it)

variants.name: Han commentary tradition (Wang Yi)
variants.text_tradition: Chu Ci zhangju commentary, 2nd c. CE
variants.summary: Wang Yi's answers systematize the mythology behind the questions — the Tianwen as the key by which the mythic corpus was reconstructed.

variants.name: Temple-wall pictures tradition
variants.summary: The poem as written commentary on the painted walls of the Chu ancestral temples — myth as gallery walk.

primary_sources.citation: Attributed Qu Yuan, 3rd c. BCE; Han recension in Wang Yi's Chu Ci zhangju. Classical Chinese via Wikisource.

secondary_sources.work: David Hawkes, The Songs of the South
secondary_sources.citation: Hawkes 1985, Harmondsworth: Penguin — annotated translation of the Chu Ci.

secondary_sources.work: Sarah Allan, The Shape of the Turtle
secondary_sources.citation: Allan 1991, Albany: SUNY Press — the Tianwen's mythic stratigraphy.

title.en: The Lords of the Xiang: Hymns of the River Gods
title.zh: 九歌湘君湘夫人

region.en: The Xiang River, Dongting (Hunan)
region.zh: 湘水洞庭

period: Chu Ci, Jiu Ge (Nine Songs), 4th-3rd c. BCE (ritual hymns of Chu)

source.work: Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Xiang Jun and Xiang Furen, the paired hymns of waiting and the river gods

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Two hymns of the Chu river-rites: in one, the shaman-king awaits the Lord of the Xiang at the north ford — lavishly rides, breaks the ice of the river, and at dusk leaves the jade trinkets by the water; in the other, the consort waits on the isle of the north, gathers lotus for a gift that will never be received, and throws her girdle and sash into the river in token of a love the gods answer in their own season.
summary.zh: 湘君：君不行兮夷猶……捐玦遺佩兮遺浦；湘夫人：帝子降兮北渚，目眇眇兮愁予……捐餘袂兮江中，遺餘褋兮澧浦——迎神不至，待之彌篤。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Chu Ci original. Ritual hymns of the Chu shamanic cult, sung by priestesses for the river-gods; the two consorts are linked by later lore to Yao's daughters (chinese-shun-cangwu-xiangfei).

passages.text: The Lord of the Xiang does not come, and still he does not delay: the priestess on the north ford, her eyes misted with longing, chants of the beautiful one under the leaves of the autumn waves. She has washed the cups in the orchid water and paved the hall with pepper-herbs for the god's arrival.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Xiang Jun (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 湘君不來，卻仍不遲延：北渚上的女巫，雙眼因思念而迷濛，吟唱著秋波葉下那位美人。她已在蘭水中洗淨杯盞，又以椒草鋪設廳堂，等候神明降臨。

passages.text: She flies the river in a boat of sandalwood with flags of orchid; she plucks the lotus of the far bank, sees her tears on the bamboo of the isle, and at dusk — the god not come — throws her jade ring into the river and her girdle into the far shore-bank, tokens of a meeting set for another season.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Xiang Jun (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她乘著檀木之舟、掛著蘭旗飛渡江上；她採擷對岸的荷花，見自己的淚落在洲上的竹間，到了黃昏——神明仍未到來——便將玉環投入江中，把腰帶拋向遠岸，作為另擇一季相會的信物。

passages.text: In the answering hymn, the consort on the isle of the north waits with the same ritual of longing, gathers the duckweed for a gift, builds her dream-chamber of lotus and orchid and stone — and throws her sleeve into the river in token, for the Lord of the Xiang will come, says the hymn, though not when the priestess calls.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Xiang Furen (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在應答的頌歌中，北渚上的配偶懷著同樣的思念之禮等候，採集浮萍以為贈禮，以荷、蘭與石築起她的夢室——並將衣袖投入江中為信物，因為頌歌說，湘君終會到來，只是不在女巫呼喚之時。

title.en: The Great and Lesser Masters of Fate
title.zh: 九歌大司命少司命

region.en: The altars of Chu, south of the Yangzi
region.zh: 楚地祭壇

period: Chu Ci, Jiu Ge, 4th-3rd c. BCE

source.work: Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Da Siming and Shao Siming, the hymns to the masters of destiny

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The Great Master of Fate descends through the nine heavens on the whirling wind and rain, master of mortal lifespans, whom no ritual can sway; the Lesser Master, god of birth and child-life, comes with the orchid of the autumn orchard, greets the assembled shamanesses, and leaves — and the singers ask of both the same question: why does the god of fate never let go what he has grasped, and why must the one he favors depart?
summary.zh: 大司命：乘清氣兮御陰陽，君迴翔兮以下……固人命兮有當，孰離合兮可為；少司命：秋蘭兮麋蕪，羅生兮堂下……滿堂兮美人，忽獨與余兮目成——悲莫悲兮生別離。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Chu Ci original.

passages.text: The Great Master of Fate comes down from the nine heavens riding the clear breath, commanding the yin and the yang; his coming is the whirl of wind and the wash of rain, and the priestess who awaits him knows that in his hands are the spans of all mortal lives — and that no rite can lengthen them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Da Siming (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大司命乘著清氣自九天下臨，號令陰陽；他的到來是風的迴旋與雨的洗灑，而等候他的女巫知道，凡人的壽數皆在他手中——也知道任何儀式都不能使之延長。

passages.text: The Lesser Master of Fate comes down through the orchid-thick autumn air, attended by the green plants of birth; the hall of beautiful shamanesses greets him, and for one singer alone his glance kindles — and the hymn's lament is the farewell of that glance: 'Sorrow beyond all sorrow is the parting of the living.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Shao Siming (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 少司命穿過蘭草濃密的秋氣而降臨，由初生的綠植隨侍；眾美巫齊聚的殿堂迎接他，而他只對其中一位歌者目光灼然——頌歌中的哀嘆，正是那一眼的訣別：「悲莫悲兮生別離。」

passages.text: Of both masters the singers ask the same hard question: who can alter the fate a god has gripped? The hymns end in submission — the god of lifespans is worshipped, not bargained with — and in the Chu ritual year the two masters are honored as the bounds of birth and death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge, conclusion of the two Siming hymns; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 眾歌者對兩位司命之神提出同一個艱難的疑問：誰能改變神明所執掌的命數？頌歌終歸於順服——壽命之神受敬奉，而非可與之討價還價——在楚地的祭祀歲時中，兩位司命之神被尊為生與死的界限。

title.en: The Mountain Spirit: A Wildcat Cart and Red Leopard Team
title.zh: 九歌山鬼

region.en: The deep mountains of Chu (Hubei–Hunan highlands)
region.zh: 楚地深山

period: Chu Ci, Jiu Ge, 4th-3rd c. BCE

source.work: Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Shan Gui, the mountain spirit's vigil with wine and herbs

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: A mountain spirit — girt with ivy, girdled with fragrant herb, riding a wildcat cart drawn by red leopards — waits in the bamboo darkness for the one she loves, mixing cassia wine and roasting herbs. She comes to the high places of the mountain; clouds gather below her, the rain darkens, the wind sighs and the trees rustle — and the one she waits for does not come: 'You thought of me, and did not come,' she sings into the storm.
summary.zh: 若有人兮山之阿，被薜荔兮帶女蘿……乘赤豹兮從文狸，辛夷車兮結桂旗；留靈修兮憺忘歸——風颯颯兮木蕭蕭，思公子兮徒離憂。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Chu Ci original.

passages.text: There is someone in the fold of the mountain, girt with ivy and girdled with the fragrant herb, whose smile, when she smiles, is lovely — and who waits, they say, for one she loves. She rides a cart of the magnolia flower hung with banners of cassia, drawn by a red leopard and followed by the striped wildcat; she gathers the flower of the mountain and the vine of the rocks, and says she will meet her beloved in the deep of the trees where no one goes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Shan Gui (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 山坳之中有那麼一個人，身披薜荔、腰繫香草，她笑起來時笑靨動人——據說她正等待著她所愛的人。她乘著木蘭花做的車，掛著桂樹的旗幟，由赤豹拉車、文狸跟隨；她採集山中的花與岩石上的藤蔓，說她要在林木深處、無人前往之地與心上人相會。

passages.text: She stays and stays, forgetting to go home, mixing wine of cassia and herb-broths for the guest who does not come; the clouds rise beneath her from the valley, the rain darkens the mountain, the wind sighs in the trees and the monkeys cry — and the mountain spirit's song ends in the storm: you thought of me, and did not come.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Shan Gui (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她留了又留，忘了回家，為那不至的客人調和桂酒與香草湯；雲從她腳下的山谷升起，雨使山色昏暗，風在林中嘆息，猿猴哀鳴——山鬼之歌終於風雨之中：你思念我，卻不來相見。

title.en: The East Lord: Hymn to the Sun God
title.zh: 九歌東君

region.en: The dawn gates of the east, Chu rite (symbolic pin: eastern Chu)
region.zh: 東方日出之門（楚祭）

period: Chu Ci, Jiu Ge, 4th-3rd c. BCE

source.work: Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Dong Jun, the hymn of the rising and setting sun

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The East Lord, the sun, comes out warm from the hedge of the eastern gate; he bathes his horses at the pool of the dawn and lashes his chariot up the evening sky, and in between he feasts with the priestesses: they strike the drums, ring the bells, play the reed-pipes and sing, until the sun's rank fills the hall — and the god, in his own voice, says he will take the long bow to shoot the wolf of the sky and take the northern star for his cup, and go home to help the wine.
summary.zh: 東君：暾將出兮東方，照吾檻兮扶桑；撫余馬兮安驅，夜皎皎兮既明；羌聲色兮娛人，觀者憺兮忘歸；青雲衣兮白霓裳，舉長矢兮射天狼——操余弧兮反淪降，援北斗兮酌桂漿。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Chu Ci original. Tagging caveat: 'sun-capture' marks the archer's shooting of the sky-wolf star; the East Lord is a sun-god, not a sun-thief.

passages.text: Warmth comes from the east: the East Lord rises out of the eastern gate and lights the rail of the hall; he strokes his horses to a gentle pace and the night, clear and bright, turns to day. In the hall of the rite the drummers drum, the bell-chimes ring and the reed-pipes answer; the singers sing of the god's countenance, and the watching crowd, delighted, forget to go home — for the sun has come to his feast.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Dong Jun (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 溫暖自東方而來：東君從東門升起，照亮殿堂的欄杆；他輕撫馬匹，使牠們緩步而行，清朗明亮的夜色化為白晝。祭堂之中，鼓者擊鼓，鐘磬齊鳴，葦管相和；歌者歌頌神明的容顏，觀禮的人群歡喜得忘了回家——因為太陽已親臨他的盛宴。

passages.text: The god speaks: clothed in the blue clouds and the white rainbows, he draws the long bow to shoot the wolf-star of the sky, and takes the Northern Dipper for a ladle to pour the cassia wine — then loosens his reins and sinks westward, helping the rite's last cup as he goes down.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Dong Jun (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 神明開口：他身披青雲與白虹，挽起長弓射向天上的天狼星，取北斗為勺斟上桂酒——隨後鬆開韁繩向西沉落，一邊離去，一邊為祭禮飲下最後一杯。

title.en: Hymn to the Fallen of the War: Guo Shang
title.zh: 九歌國殤

region.en: The battlefields of the Chu wars (Hubei frontier)
region.zh: 楚疆戰場

period: Chu Ci, Jiu Ge, 4th-3rd c. BCE

source.work: Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Guo Shang, the hymn for the war dead of Chu

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The one hymn of the Nine Songs for human dead: chariots crosswise, drums of cloud, the swords of Wu and the hides of rhinoceros, the armies of Chu mingling with the enemy until the sun is darkened — the officers dead, the line broken, yet the men did not yield. 'Truly valiant and the strongest of all,' sings the ritual, 'strong beyond the strength of any land; the body dead, the spirit deathless — spirits of the fallen, you are the lords of ghosts.'
summary.zh: 旌蔽日兮敵若雲，矢交墜兮士爭先；誠既勇兮又以武，終剛強兮不可凌；身既死兮神以靈，子魂魄兮為鬼雄——國殤之祭。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Chu Ci original. The war dead are apotheosized as ghost-lords (gui xiong) — the hymn is the ritual charter of ancestor-military cult.

passages.text: Gripping the spear of rhinoceros-hide and clasping the drum of the chariots, the men of Chu went up in the dust of battle; the sky was darkened by their banners, the enemy dense as cloud, arrows falling crossing and crossing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Guo Shang (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 楚人手持犀牛皮製的盾牌與長矛，緊握戰車上的鼓，在戰塵中奮勇前進；旗幟遮蔽了天空，敵人密集如雲，箭矢交錯落下。

passages.text: The enemy pressed in, trampling the line; the left chariot died, the right was wounded; the two wheels buried in mud, four horses entangled, the general still struck the drum. Heaven was dark and the might of the gods angry — and the men were killed, all of them, and the field was abandoned to the fallen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Guo Shang (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 敵軍逼近，踐踏我軍陣線；左邊的戰車被毀，右邊的戰車受創；兩個車輪陷入泥中，四匹馬糾纏在一起，將領仍擊鼓不止。天色昏暗，神靈震怒——將士們全數陣亡，戰場上只留下倒下的屍體。

passages.text: The hymn that remains is not of defeat: 'Truly brave and truly strong, unbending to the end; the body dead, the spirit deathless — your souls are lords among ghosts.' The ritual gave the war dead of Chu a standing in the unseen world: not wanderers, but powers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Guo Shang (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 流傳下來的頌歌並非吟詠失敗：「真是勇敢，真是剛強，至死不屈；身體雖死，精神不死——你們的魂魄是鬼中的雄長。」這儀式賦予楚國陣亡將士在幽冥世界中的地位：他們不是漂泊的遊魂，而是有力量的神靈。

title.en: The Summons of the Soul: A Tour of the Four Quarters and the Underworld
title.zh: 招魂

region.en: The Chu court and the four quarters (ritual geography)
region.zh: 楚廷與四方

period: Chu Ci, Zhaohun, attributed Qu Yuan or Song Yu, 3rd c. BCE

source.work: Chu Ci, Zhaohun: the soul's four-quarters tour, the offerings of the summoning rite, and the return to the halls of Ying

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: A soul has left the body and wanders; the summoner — the shaman in the rite — calls it home by naming the perils of every direction: east has giants who feed on souls, south has men-eating snakes and nine-headed serpents, west has the quicksands of the red ants and the land of one-eyed things, north has the frozen mountains and the sky that swallows, and below is the underworld where the tiger's head steers the bull — 'your soul, come back!' — and only the halls of home are safe, with their foods, their music and their beds.
summary.zh: 魂兮歸來！東方不可以託兮……南方不可以止兮，蝮蛇蓁蓁、封狐千里；西方之害，流沙千里；北方不可以止兮，增冰峨峨；魂兮歸來！君無下此幽都些——土伯九約，其角觜觜些——入修門些，歸來歸來！

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Chu Ci original. The underworld tour of the summoning rite is the earliest full geography of the Chinese otherworld; the Tubo earth-master (tiger-horned warden of the dark capital) is the earliest Chinese hell-warden.

passages.text: The summoner cries to the wandering soul: do not go east, where giants ten-thousand-feet tall seek souls to devour, with ten suns blazing in company; do not go south, where the vipers mass and the great foxes run for a thousand li, and the nine-headed serpent swallows men whole; do not go west, where the moving sands swallow, and the one-eyed folk, and the red ants as big as elephants.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Zhaohun, the four-quarters tour (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 招魂者向遊魂呼喚：不要往東去，那裡有身高萬丈的巨人尋覓魂魄吞食，還有十個太陽一同灼燒；不要往南去，那裡蝮蛇成群，大狐奔走千里，九頭蛇將人整個吞下；不要往西去，那裡有流沙吞沒一切，還有獨眼之人，以及大如象的紅螞蟻。

passages.text: Do not go north, where the piled ice gleams over snow and a hundred li of it; do not go up to heaven, where the tiger-leopards guard the gates and the nine-headed men shake the nine-fringed trees; and do not go down, for below is the dark capital, where Tubo, the earth-master, sits coiled with nine joints, his horns like a tiger's claws, his back bloody, chasing men with swift hands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Zhaohun, the underworld passage; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不要往北去，那裡堆積的冰在積雪上閃著寒光，綿延百里；不要上天去，那裡虎豹守著門戶，九頭之人搖撼著九枝的樹；也不要下去，因為下方是幽暗的都城，土伯盤曲著九節的身軀，他的角像虎爪，背上血淋淋，用迅捷的手追逐著人。

passages.text: The soul is called home through all four quarters and the three worlds: to the gates of Ying, the halls and the antechambers, the winter-courtyard and the summer-hall, the foods of the feast and the wine of the court — 'return, return, for the old places are what they were.' The rite ends with the feast of the living offered for the return of the dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Zhaohun, the homeward summons; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 魂魄被從四方與三界招喚回家：回到郢都的城門，回到廳堂與廂房，回到冬日的庭院與夏日的廳堂，回到宴席上的食物與宮廷中的美酒——「歸來吧，歸來吧，舊日的地方依然如故。」儀式以生者為亡者歸來而設的宴饗作結。

title.en: Li Sao: The Poet's Flight Through the Gate of Heaven
title.zh: 離騷

region.en: The river-lands of Chu and the gates of heaven (symbolic pin: the mythic route of the flight)
region.zh: 楚地至天門（象徵性定位）

period: Chu Ci, Li Sao, attributed Qu Yuan, 3rd c. BCE

source.work: Chu Ci, Li Sao: the celestial flight of the poet, the matchmaking of the gods, and the fall back to the horse's tears

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The poet, slandered and rejected, turns his chariot through the gates of heaven in a flight of ascension: the dragons of yu and egrets draw his carriage, Fenglong the thunder-god acts as matchmaker to Fu Fei of the Ji river, the court of heaven is sought and found closed; he passes the gates of spring, the gardens of the deva, and the gardens of Kunlun — and at the last, mounted into the sky with his dragon-team, he looks down at his old home and sees his groom and his horse weeping for him, and will go no farther.
summary.zh: 吾令豐隆乘雲兮，求宓妃之所在；吾令帝閽開關兮，倚閶闔而望予；朝發軔於蒼梧兮，夕余至乎縣圃；陟升皇之赫戲兮，忽臨睨夫舊鄉——僕夫悲余馬懷兮，蜷局顧而不行。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Chu Ci original.

passages.text: The poet, rejected by the court and slandered by the crowd, dresses himself in orchid and solomon's-seal and mounts the whirlwind on a team of jade-dragons and phoenix-birds: he starts at dawn from the park of Cangwu and by evening reaches the hanging gardens of the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Li Sao, the flight (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 詩人為朝廷所棄、為眾人所讒，乃身披蘭草與甘松香，駕乘玉龍與鳳鳥，凌駕旋風：他清晨自蒼梧之苑啟程，至傍晚便抵達天上的懸圃。

passages.text: He bids the thunder-lord Fenglong ride the clouds to seek Fu Fei of the Ji river as a bride, and the match fails of the goddess's temper; he comes to the gate of heaven and calls the gate-keeper, who leans on the Door of the Vast Sky and looks at him but does not open — and the poet, shut out of heaven as out of court, turns to the gardens below.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Li Sao, matchmaking and gates; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他命雷神豐隆駕雲去尋求濟水之神宓妃為妻，然而因女神性情乖戾，這樁婚事終告不成；他來到天門，呼喚守門之人，那人倚著閶闔之門望他，卻不為他開啟——詩人被拒於天門之外，正如被拒於朝廷之外，於是轉向下界的園圃。

passages.text: At last, mounted high into the blaze of the rising sun, he looks down and sees the old country — and the groom grieves and the horse bends its head and refuses to move. The flight of Li Sao ends not in heaven but in the tears of a horse at the edge of home: the poet cannot ascend, because the land he served still pulls his heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Li Sao, the close; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最後，他高踞於初升朝陽的光焰之中，俯身下望，看見了故國——於是御者悲傷，馬亦低頭而不肯前行。《離騷》的飛升並非終於天庭，而是終於故鄉邊際一匹馬的眼淚：詩人無法升舉，因為他所事奉的土地仍牽繫著他的心。

title.en: Aponibolinayen and the Sun: Marriage in the House of Ini-init
title.zh: 阿波妮波莉納衍與太陽：伊尼伊尼特家中的姻緣

region.en: Abra Province, northwestern Luzon, Philippines (Tinguian homeland, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋西北阿布拉省（丁桂安故地，象徵定位）

period: Tinguian oral epic-cycle tale; collected 1903-1908, published 1915 (Fay-Cooper Cole)

source.work: Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian: A Study in Philippine Folk-Lore (Field Museum, 1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun', pp. 33-40

summary.en: The siksiklat vine carries Aponibolinayen to the sky, where she hides in the betel-nut trees of Ini-init, the Sun, who goes up each morning to make the sun. With her magic she cooks a fish-stick into fish; he spies on the beautiful woman whose presence makes the house seem ablaze, chews betel with her — the quids of both turning to holeless agate beads, a sign they are kin — and they marry. When she insists on riding up with him, the heat melts her to oil; he bottles her and drops her by the well at Kaodanan, and she arrives home at last.
summary.zh: 西克西克拉藤將阿波妮波莉納衍捲上天界；她藏於太陽神伊尼伊尼特的檳榔樹間，每日以其神力把魚簽變成魚。太陽歸家見屋內如燃，原是美人容光；二人嚼檳榔定親——兩枚檳榔渣皆化無孔瑪瑙珠，證明同族，遂成婚。她堅持隨他昇空，炎熱將她熔為油；太陽把她封入瓶中，拋回卡奧達南泉邊——她終於歸家。

sensitivity.note: Tinguian epic-cycle narrative recorded 1903-1908 by Fay-Cooper Cole among the Tinguian and published 1915; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Tinguian communities. The betel-quid divination that proves kinship is a Tinguian marriage custom.

passages.text: Aponibolinayen and her sister-in-law Dinay went to gather siksiklat greens; as soon as she began to break off the siksiklat she saw, it encircled and carried her up, and when they reached the sky the vine placed her below the alosip tree by a spring whose sands were oday beads and whose betel-nut tree was gold. The owner of the little house near the well was Ini-init, the Sun — but he was not there, because he had gone up to make the sun, which was his work in the daytime. The next morning Aponibolinayen followed him into his house and quickly cooked, using her magic power: she took the stick used for roasting fish and cooked it, and the fish-stick became cut-up fish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿波尼博利奈延與她的嫂嫂迪奈一同去採集西克西克拉特菜；她剛開始折斷眼前所見的西克西克拉特菜，那菜便纏繞住她、將她帶了上去，當她們到達天上時，那藤蔓將她安置在阿洛西普樹下、一眼泉水旁，那泉水的沙是奧代珠，檳榔樹則是金的。井邊小屋的主人是伊尼伊尼特，即太陽——但他不在那裡，因為他已上去造太陽，那是他白天的工作。翌日清晨，阿波尼博利奈延跟隨他進入他的屋子，迅速施展法力煮食：她取來烤魚用的木棍將它烹煮，那魚棍便化成了切好的魚肉。

passages.text: When afternoon came Ini-init went home after fishing, and saw that his house appeared as if it was burning — but it was not burning: what looked like flame at the place of his bed was a very pretty lady. He cooked, and she awoke to see the handsome man cutting fish; the pot she had cooked in looked like a rooster's egg, and the rice she had cooked was one grain of broken rice, and because of all this Ini-init was surprised — and the woman vanished into the leaves of the betel-nut where she hid. Next morning he went up again to make the sun; when afternoon came, his food was cooked though no one was in the house, and he resolved to hide and watch.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 午後時分，伊尼伊尼特釣魚歸來回家，看見他的屋子彷彿正在燃燒——但其實並非燃燒：在他床鋪之處看似火焰的，是一位極美的女子。他煮食，她醒來，看見那俊美的男子正在切魚；她煮食所用的鍋看起來像公雞蛋，她所煮的米只是一粒碎米，正因這一切，伊尼伊尼特感到驚異——而那女子便隱入她所藏身的檳榔葉中消失了。翌日清晨他又上去造太陽；午後時分，他的食物已煮好，儘管屋中並無他人，於是他決意躲藏起來窺看。

passages.text: At sunset he sent the big star to follow him in the sky, and went home to spy on the woman; he slammed shut the door and reached the woman cooking, who cried, 'You cut me only once, so that I only cure one time, if you are the old enemy.' 'If I were the old enemy, I should have cut before,' said Ini-init, and he sat near her. He arranged the betel-nut covered with gold for them to chew, since it is bad to talk who do not know each other's names; when she laid down her quid it looked like an agate bead with no hole for the thread, and the quid of Ini-init looked like a square bead — and when both quids had this form they knew they were relatives. 'My name is Ini-init, who often goes to travel over the world. I always stop in the afternoon. What can I do, it is my business,' he said; 'My name is Aponibolinayen, who lives in Kaodanan, who am the sister of Awig,' she said. 'We are relatives, and it is good for us to be married. Do not be afraid even though you did not come here of your own accord.' Then they married.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 日落時，他遣那顆大星在天上跟隨他，自己則回家窺探那女子；他砰然關上門，走到正在煮食的女子身旁，那女子喊道：『你只砍了我一次，所以我只療治一次，倘若你是那舊日的仇敵。』『倘若我是那舊日的仇敵，我早該先砍了，』伊尼伊尼特說，並在她身旁坐下。他備好覆著金的檳榔供二人共嚼，因為彼此不知姓名的人交談是不好的；當她放下口中的檳榔渣時，那渣看起來像一顆無孔可穿線的瑪瑙珠，而伊尼伊尼特的檳榔渣則看起來像一顆方珠——當兩人的檳榔渣都呈此形，他們便知道彼此是親戚。『我名叫伊尼伊尼特，常去遊歷世界。我總在午後停留。我能怎麼辦呢，這是我的職分，』他說；『我名叫阿波尼博利奈延，住在考達南，是阿維格的姊妹，』她說。『我們是親戚，我們結為夫妻是好的。即使你並非自願來到此地，也不要害怕。』於是他們結了婚。

passages.text: When it became the middle of the night, Aponibolinayen woke and said she would go up with him in the early morning; 'Do not come, for it is very hot up above... you will repent when we are there,' said Ini-init, but she answered and answered until he agreed, and they arranged many blankets and pillows to go under. They went east, and when they arrived there the sun shone, and Aponibolinayen became oil because it was so hot; Ini-init put her in a bottle, corked it, covered it with blankets and pillows, and dropped it down. She fell by the well in Kaodanan, and Indiapan, who was dipping water, unwrapped the bundle and found a pretty lady — none equal to her — and ran to the town crying that Aponibolinayen, whom they had long sought at the cost of many cows, had fallen by the spring; and her father and mother went quickly down to the well and found the daughter they had sought.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了半夜，阿波尼博利奈恩醒來，說她要在清晨隨他上去；「別來，因為上面非常炎熱……我們到了那裡妳會後悔的，」伊尼伊尼特說，但她一再回答，直到他同意為止，他們便備了許多毯子和枕頭，好墊在下面。他們往東去，到了那裡，太陽照耀著，阿波尼博利奈恩因為太熱而化成了油；伊尼伊尼特把她裝進一個瓶子，塞上瓶塞，用毯子和枕頭裹住，然後把她丟了下去。她落在考達南的水井旁，正在打水的印迪亞潘解開包裹，發現了一位美麗的女士——無人能與她相比——便跑回鎮上哭喊著說，他們長久以來花了許多牛隻尋找的阿波尼博利奈恩，已經落在泉邊了；她的父母急忙下到井邊，找到了他們所尋找的女兒。

title.en: The Baby from the Itching Finger and the Betel-Nuts That Grow on Knees
title.zh: 癢指生嬰與長膝檳榔

region.en: Kaodanan and Nagbotobotan (Tinguian mythic towns), Abra Province, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋阿布拉省卡奧達南與納格博托博坦（丁桂安神話城鎮，象徵定位）

period: Tinguian oral epic-cycle tale; collected 1903-1908, published 1915 (Fay-Cooper Cole)

source.work: Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian: A Study in Philippine Folk-Lore (Field Museum, 1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun' (conclusion), pp. 38-41

summary.en: Back home, Aponibolinayen feels her little finger itch; her mother pricks it and a pretty baby pops out. At the balaua ceremony the gold-covered betel-nuts are oiled and sent to invite the whole world — any who refuse will have the nut grow on their knee — and old Alokotan guesses the father: 'You invited all the people except Ini-init, who is above. Perhaps he made Aponibolinayen pregnant, because the siksiklat took her up.' The summoned Sun first lets the betel-nut grow on his head, then on his pig, before he comes; at the gate the baby springs to him, and the round stone that carries it turns into a man — the Sun — who builds the balaua and pays the marriage price.
summary.zh: 歸家後阿波妮波莉納衍小指發癢，母親一刺，俏嬰跳出。巴勞瓦大宴上，裹金檳榔受油後奉命邀請全世界——不來者，檳榔便在其膝上生根。老嫗阿洛科坦一語道破：『你們誰都請了，就是沒請天上的伊尼伊尼特——西克西克拉藤捲她上天時，許是他使她有孕。』太陽先任檳榔長在頭上、再長在豬頭上，方才應召；嬰兒在他近門時歡喜撲去，而抱嬰的圓石滾動間化作人形——正是太陽。他建巴勞瓦、付聘禮。

sensitivity.note: Tinguian epic-cycle narrative recorded 1903-1908 by Fay-Cooper Cole; archival record. The betel-nut compulsion and quid omens are Tinguian ritual conventions; the balaua and Sayang ceremonies are named, not described operationally.

passages.text: Back in Kaodanan, Aponibolinayen commanded them to prick her little finger, which itched; and when her mother pricked it, out popped a pretty baby. Her mother asked where she got the baby, but Aponibolinayen only said, 'I do not know where I got it, and I did not feel.' 'Ala, we make balaua to-morrow,' said the father and mother. They built the balaua, and Ebang used magic so that many people went to pound rice for them; then they went to get the betel-nut which is covered with gold for chewing, and when these arrived Ebang oiled them in the dark: 'You betel-nuts go to all the people in the whole world and invite them. If any of them do not come, you grow on their knees.' And those betel-nuts went to invite all the people in the whole world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun' (conclusion); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 回到考達南，阿波尼博利奈恩吩咐他們刺她發癢的小指；她母親一刺，便蹦出一個漂亮的嬰兒。她母親問她從哪裡得到這嬰兒，但阿波尼博利奈恩只說：「我不知道從哪裡得到的，我也沒有感覺。」「哎呀，我們明天要舉行巴勞阿，」父母說。他們建起了巴勞阿，艾邦施了法術，使許多人來為他們舂米；然後他們去取那覆著金箔、供咀嚼用的檳榔，這些檳榔送到時，艾邦在黑暗中給它們塗上油：「你們這些檳榔，去全世界所有的人那裡邀請他們。若有誰不來，你們就長在他的膝蓋上。」那些檳榔便去邀請全世界所有的人。

passages.text: The betel-nut that went to Nagbotobotan, the place where the old woman Alokotan lived, told her of the invitation — 'I wait for you, for if you do not come, I shall grow on your knee' — and it took her up. At the festival no one wanted the baby to go to them, for none wished it to approach; then the old woman Alokotan summoned the spirits and said, 'You invited all the people except Ini-init, who is above. You did not send the prepared betel-nut covered with gold to summon him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun' (conclusion); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那顆前往納格博托博坦——老婦阿洛科坦所居之地——的檳榔，向她傳達了邀請——「我等著妳，因為妳若不來，我就要長在妳的膝蓋上」——並把她帶了上去。在慶典上，沒有人願意讓那嬰兒到他們那裡去，因為沒有人希望它靠近；於是老婦阿洛科坦召來神靈，說道：「你們邀請了所有的人，卻唯獨沒有邀請在上面的伊尼伊尼特。你們沒有送去那覆著金箔、備好的檳榔去召喚他。」

passages.text: Perhaps he made Aponibolinayen pregnant, because the siksiklat took her up when they went to gather greens.' So they oiled and sent betel-nuts, and the one that arrived above said, 'Good morning, Sun, I do not tarry. If you do not wish to come, I will grow on your head.' 'Grow on my head, I do not wish to go,' said the Sun — and the betel-nut jumped up and grew, until it became so tall the Sun could not carry it and was in pain; 'You go to my pig, that is what you grow on,' he said, and the pig began to squeal under the weight. 'Ala! get off my big pig and I come,' said Ini-init, and the betel-nut got off the pig.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun' (conclusion); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 也許是他讓阿波尼博利奈恩懷了孕，因為他們去採集青菜時，那隻西克西克拉特鳥把她帶了上去。」於是他們給檳榔塗油並送了出去，那顆到達上面的檳榔說道：「太陽，早安，我不久留。你若不肯來，我就要長在你的頭上。」「長在我頭上吧，我不想去，」太陽說——那檳榔便跳上去長了起來，直到長得那麼高，太陽扛不動它，痛苦不堪；「你去我的豬那裡，長在牠身上吧，」他說，那豬便在重壓下開始尖叫。「哎呀！離開我的大豬吧，我來就是了，」伊尼伊尼特說，那檳榔便從豬身上下來了。

passages.text: When they came, Pagatipanan carried the baby near the gate, and as Ini-init and the betel-nut approached, the baby was happy and went to be carried by Ini-init. At the festival place the people saw that he who carried the baby rolled, because he was round, and that he was not a man but a stone; Ebang and Pagatipanan told Aponibolinayen to take off her arm beads and dress in rags, wrapping her wrists with strings, so that she could go with the stone when he took her to his home. She obeyed, and after the balaua was finished they went away to the town of the stone — and there the sun became a man, he who had been a stone before. 'When next month comes we shall build balaua, Aponibolinayen, so that we can invite our relatives, and I will pay the marriage price, because I marry you,' said Ini-init. They summoned the old woman Alokotan to start the balaua, and sang da-eng; the gold-covered betel-nuts went out again to invite the relatives, growing on the knee of anyone who refused, until all had come to the Sayang with the stone and Aponibolinayen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun' (conclusion); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們來時，帕加蒂帕南把嬰兒抱到門邊，當伊尼伊尼特和檳榔走近時，嬰兒很高興，便要去讓伊尼伊尼特抱。在慶典場上，人們看見抱嬰兒的那位在滾動，因為他是圓的，而且他不是人，而是一塊石頭；艾邦和帕加蒂帕南叫阿波尼博利奈恩取下臂環，換上破爛的衣裳，用繩子纏住手腕，好讓她在石頭帶她回他家時能隨他同去。她照做了，巴勞阿結束之後，他們便前往石頭的城鎮——在那裡，太陽變成了一個男人，就是先前那塊石頭。「下個月到了，我們要舉行巴勞阿，阿波尼博利奈恩，這樣我們就能邀請我們的親戚，我也要付聘禮，因為我要娶妳，」伊尼伊尼特說。他們召來老婦阿洛科坦來主持巴勞阿，唱起了達恩歌；覆著金箔的檳榔又出去邀請親戚，凡是拒絕的，檳榔就長在他的膝蓋上，直到所有的人都來到了薩揚，與石頭和阿波尼博利奈恩相聚。

title.en: Aponibolinayen and Algaba: The Mango and the Reviving Perfumes
title.zh: 阿波妮波莉納衍與阿爾加巴：芒果與復魂香

region.en: Dagala (Tinguian mythic town), Abra Province, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋阿布拉省達加拉（丁桂安神話城鎮，象徵定位）

period: Tinguian oral epic-cycle tale, told by Magwati of Lagangilang; collected 1903-1908, published 1915 (Fay-Cooper Cole)

source.work: Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian: A Study in Philippine Folk-Lore (Field Museum, 1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun' (Magwati's version), pp. 42-47

summary.en: Dying for a taste of Algaba's mangoes, Aponibolinayen sends Dalonagan with an egg that hatches into a crowing rooster by the time they reach the snake-fenced town of Dagala; Algaba's weapons weep tears of oil and blood when he moves to strike — a sign they are kin. He uses his power so she will die as he arrives, then revives her with three whips of perfume, marries her when the betel-quids turn to rows of holeless agates, and is renamed Aponitolau when he goes home to Kadalayapan.
summary.zh: 阿波妮波莉納衍渴望阿爾加巴的芒果而病危；信使達洛納甘攜蛋上路，抵達蟒蛇護城的達加拉時雛雞已長成啼鳴雄雞。阿爾加巴欲戰，其兵刃卻滴油淚血淚——這是親族之兆。他運神力使她恰在抵家時死去，再以三道香霧喚她復生；檳榔渣化為成排無孔瑪瑙珠，二人成婚；回卡達拉雅潘後，他獲賜新名阿波尼托勞。
