sensitivity.note: Tinguian epic-cycle narrative told by Magwati, a man of Lagangilang, Abra; collected 1903-1908 by Fay-Cooper Cole; archival record. The weeping weapons are a kinship omen; perfumes are used as reviving magic, named not described operationally.

passages.text: 'I am anxious to eat the mango fruit which belongs to Algaba of Dagala,' said Aponibolinayen, and when she said this she was almost dying, and she repeated it. 'Does she not know that anyone who goes there cannot return?' asked Dalonagan; but Aponibalagen sent Dalonagan and Dina-ogan with a belt and earrings to trade for the fruit, and Dalonagan took an egg which he held all the time they walked — and when they had almost arrived in Dagala the chicken had become a rooster which could crow. At the spring the women told them to follow the sagang (head poles) to the house of Algaba, and when they passed the defensive fence, which was made of boa constrictors, the snakes did not notice them, for the snakes slept.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), Magwati's version of 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「我很想吃達加拉那阿爾加巴所有的芒果，」阿波尼博利奈恩說，她說這話時幾乎要死了，還一再重複。「她難道不知道，去那裡的人沒有一個能回來嗎？」達洛納甘問道；但阿波尼巴拉根派達洛納甘和迪納奧甘帶著腰帶和耳環去換那果子，達洛納甘帶了一顆蛋，在他們行走的整個過程中一直拿著它——當他們快要到達達加拉時，那小雞已經變成了一隻會啼叫的公雞。在泉邊，婦人們叫他們順著薩岡（頭柱）走到阿爾加巴的家，當他們經過那道用蟒蛇築成的防禦柵欄時，那些蛇沒有察覺他們，因為蛇在睡覺。

passages.text: Algaba ran home very angry when he heard enemies had come inside the town, and went to get his headaxe and spear — but when he took them down the weapons shed tears which were of oil. 'What is the matter with my weapons that they weep oil? Perhaps these men are my relatives,' said the angry man; he dropped them, and when he took another set they shed bloody tears. The two men had come to buy the mango fruit for Aponibolinayen, who was nearly dead; Algaba showed them his yard where all the stones were gold, and smiled at the belt they offered: 'How pretty it is! I think the lady who owns this is much prettier.' He picked two mangoes himself and came along, saying to his alan mother, 'Do not feel anxious concerning me while I am gone... watch for enemies who come inside the town.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), Magwati's version of 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿爾加巴聽說有敵人進到鎮裡來，非常生氣地跑回家，去取他的頭斧和長矛——但當他把武器取下來時，武器竟流下油一般的眼淚。「我的武器怎麼了，竟流出油來？也許這些人是我的親戚吧，」這憤怒的人說道；他把武器放下，又取了另一副，那副卻流下血淚。那兩個人是來為阿波尼博利納延買芒果的，她已奄奄一息；阿爾加巴讓他們看他的院子，那裡的石頭全是金子，又對他們獻上的腰帶微微一笑：「多麼漂亮啊！我想擁有這條腰帶的女士要漂亮得多。」他親自摘了兩顆芒果，便隨他們同行，並對他的艾蘭母親說：「我離去期間，不要為我擔心……要提防進到鎮裡來的敵人。」

passages.text: On the way Algaba used his power so that the sick woman would feel very ill and nearly die; reaching the well that belonged to Aponibolinayen, he used his power so that she would die — and she truly died. But when he looked at her she was a lady without an equal for beauty, and he took the body in his arms: 'I use my power so that when I whip my perfume kaladakad she will move directly,' and the body moved; 'I use my power so that when I whip my perfume banawes she will say Wes,' and she at once said Wes; 'I use my power so that when I whip my perfume she will wake up,' and she woke up — 'Wes, how long my sleep was!' 'You have been dead,' said Algaba. Their rings exchanged themselves while he held her, and when she had regained her breath he divided the mango fruit and gave it to her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), Magwati's version of 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在路上，阿爾加巴施法，使那生病的女人感到極度不適、幾乎死去；到了屬於阿波尼博利納延的水井邊，他施法使她死去——而她果真死了。但當他看她時，她是一位美貌無與倫比的女士，他便把遺體抱在懷裡：「我施法，當我揮動我那支香水卡達拉卡德時，她就會立刻動起來，」遺體果然動了；「我施法，當我揮動我那支香水巴納威斯時，她就會說『威斯』，」她立刻說了「威斯」；「我施法，當我揮動我那支香水時，她就會醒過來，」她果然醒了——「威斯，我這一覺睡得多麼久啊！」「你已經死了，」阿爾加巴說。他抱著她時，他們的戒指自行交換了；等她恢復了氣息，他便把芒果分開，給了她。

passages.text: He made her chew betel-nut, for it is bad for them to talk when they do not know each other's names: 'My name is Algaba of Dagala. I have looked in all parts of the world for a wife, but I did not find anyone like you, and now I have found you, and I want you to be married to me.' 'My name is Aponibolinayen of Kaodanan, sister of Aponibalagen,' she said; and when they laid down their quids they were rows of agate beads which have no holes, so it was good for them to be married. They went to Dagala, where the alan mother gave them all her valuable things and flew away; at the Sayang they learned through the betel quids that Algaba was the brother of Aponigawani, and when all had been paid — the balaua filled nine times with jars — they took him to Kadalayapan, where he was renamed Aponitolau.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), Magwati's version of 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他讓她嚼檳榔，因為彼此還不知道對方名字時交談是不好的：「我的名字是達加拉的阿爾加巴。我走遍世界各地尋找妻子，卻沒有找到像你這樣的人，如今我找到了你，我希望你嫁給我。」「我的名字是考達南的阿波尼博利納延，阿波尼巴拉根之妹，」她說；當他們把嚼過的檳榔渣放下時，那竟成了一排排沒有孔的瑪瑙珠，所以他們結為夫妻是好的。他們前往達加拉，艾蘭母親把她的所有貴重物品都給了他們，然後飛走了；在薩揚，他們透過檳榔渣得知阿爾加巴是阿波尼加瓦尼的兄弟，而當一切聘禮都付清之後——巴勞屋九次裝滿了陶罐——他們便帶他前往卡達拉亞潘，在那裡他改名為阿波尼托勞。

title.en: Asibowan of Gegawan and the Hidden Bride at the Spring of Lisnayan
title.zh: 格加萬的阿西博萬與莉斯納揚泉畔的隱藏新娘

region.en: Gegawan and Lisnayan springs (Tinguian mythic places), Abra Province, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋阿布拉省格加萬與莉斯納揚泉（丁桂安神話之地，象徵定位）

period: Tinguian oral epic-cycle tale; collected 1903-1908, published 1915 (Fay-Cooper Cole)

source.work: Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian: A Study in Philippine Folk-Lore (Field Museum, 1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun' (Asibowan episodes), pp. 52-57

summary.en: A bird guides Aponitolau to Gegawan, where Asibowan cooks her fish-stick into a fish and lives alone; he stays nine months, siring Binaklingan, whose golden house his parents wake to find beside their own. Urged home by the pile of searchers' bones nine times the size of a balaua, Aponitolau later uses magic to draw all the sheltered girls to the spring of Lisnayan, where Aponibolinayen bathes like half a rainbow and vanishes into the betel-nut leaves. Found, she is carried off to Kadalayapan; her brother learns of the marriage when Langa-an, drunk on basi, lets it slip; Asibowan herself is compelled to attend the Sayang by the gold betel-nut that grows on her pig's head.
summary.zh: 飛鳥引路，阿波尼托勞至格加萬；阿西博萬以魚簽變魚、獨居一室。他留居九月，育女碧納克林安——其金屋一夜飛至祖屋旁。搜尋者的獸骨堆成九座巴勞瓦大小，他終被催歸。後他以神力使避光深閨的姑娘們燥熱出浴；莉斯納揚泉邊，阿波妮波莉納衍浴姿如半道彩虹，旋即隱入檳榔葉間。尋獲之後，她被接往卡達拉雅潘；兄長在朗嘉安酒後失言中方知婚事；阿西博萬亦被長在她豬頭上的金檳榔逼赴塞揚宴。

sensitivity.note: Tinguian epic-cycle narrative recorded 1903-1908 by Fay-Cooper Cole; archival record. The lala-am ('those within') — sheltered girls who never go outdoors — are a Tinguian custom the storytellers explain as protecting the prettiest girls' skin; Kaboniyan is a powerful spirit to whom Asibowan claims kinship.

passages.text: 'Sinogyaman, come and oil my hair so that I can go to war,' said Aponitolau — and, telling his wives Sinogyaman and Sinagayan he was going to fight, he set out for Gegawan, where Asibowan lived, whom every one said was a pretty girl. A bird met him and showed him the way. At the ladder of her house Asibowan claimed her guest had lost his way to Nagsingkawan and invited him in, cooking for him; while they talked he saw her break the fish-stick and put it in the pot and watched it become a fish — and she confessed she had no husband, and told him her name: 'Asibowan of Gegawan, who lives alone in the field, who has no neighbors, for this is my fortune.' So Aponitolau stayed with her nine months, while his father and mother searched for him with many people, killing many animals to feed the searchers until all their animals were gone; the bones which they threw away made a pile nine times as large as the balaua.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun' (Asibowan episodes); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「西諾吉亞曼，來替我抹油梳頭，好讓我去打仗，」阿波尼托勞說道——他告訴他的妻子們西諾吉亞曼和西納加揚他要去打仗，便動身前往格加萬，那是阿西博萬居住的地方，人人都說她是個漂亮的姑娘。一隻鳥遇見他，為他指路。在她屋子的梯子旁，阿西博萬聲稱她的客人是迷了路要去納格辛卡萬，並邀他進屋，為他煮食；他們交談時，他看見她折斷魚籤放進鍋裡，又看著它變成一條魚——她坦承自己沒有丈夫，並告訴他她的名字：「格加萬的阿西博萬，獨自住在田野裡，沒有鄰居，因為這就是我的命運。」於是阿波尼托勞與她同住了九個月，而他的父母帶著許多人尋找他，殺了許多牲畜來餵養搜尋的人，直到他們的牲畜全都用盡；他們丟棄的骨頭堆成了比巴勞屋大九倍的一堆。

passages.text: Asibowan became pregnant and gave birth to a girl they called Binaklingan; when she bathed the baby it grew one span, for she used magical power, until the child could walk. Aponitolau saw the pile of bones the searchers had thrown away, nine times larger than the balaua, and said the best thing was to go home to Kadalayapan — but Asibowan said it was not good for them to be married, because she had less magical power than he: 'The best thing for you to do is to go home and find a woman whom you should marry, and then when you are married you make Sayang, and I will come to Kadalayapan.' She commanded that a house be made for Binaklingan, and it was all of gold, finished in the middle of the night — and she used magic so that the golden house went to Kadalayapan, where Aponitolau woke to many roosters crowing and many people talking, and Langa-an saw the different house beside their own.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun' (Asibowan episodes); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿西博萬懷了孕，生下一個女孩，他們叫她比納克林安；她給嬰兒洗澡時，嬰兒長了一拃，因為她施了法術，直到孩子能走路。阿波尼托勞看見搜尋的人丟棄的骨頭堆，比巴勞屋大九倍，便說最好的辦法是回卡達拉亞潘的家去——但阿西博萬說他們結為夫妻並不好，因為她的法術比他的弱：「你最好回家去找一個你該娶的女人，然後等你成了婚，你辦薩揚，我就會到卡達拉亞潘來。」她吩咐為比納克林安造一座房子，那房子全是金子做的，在半夜裡完工——她又施法使那金屋前往卡達拉亞潘，阿波尼托勞在那裡醒來，聽見許多公雞啼叫、許多人說話，而蘭加安看見了他們自己屋子旁邊那座不同的房子。

passages.text: Five days after coming home, Aponitolau went at evening to the spring of Lisnayan, and used magic so that all the pretty girls who never go outdoors felt hot and went to the spring to bathe; Aponibolinayen felt very hot and went to bathe, and she looked like the half of a rainbow. 'Do not wound me in more than one place so I will not have so much to cure,' she said as he came; 'If I was an enemy I would have killed you at once,' said Aponitolau, cutting a betel-nut into two pieces, since it is bad to talk when they do not know each other's names. She told him her brother had put her at the place close to the spring of Lisnayan so that no one would see her, 'but you have found me' — and while they were talking she used magic so that she vanished and went among the betel-nuts on the branch of the tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun' (Asibowan episodes); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 回家五天之後，阿波尼托勞在傍晚前往利斯納延的泉水邊，施法使所有從不走出家門的漂亮姑娘都感到燥熱，紛紛到泉水邊沐浴；阿波尼博利納延感到非常燥熱，便去沐浴，她看起來就像半道彩虹。「不要在我身上多處弄傷，免得我要治的傷太多，」當他走近時她說道；「如果我是敵人，我早就把你殺了，」阿波尼托勞說道，一邊把一顆檳榔切成兩半，因為彼此還不知道對方名字時交談是不好的。她告訴他，她的哥哥把她安置在靠近利斯納延泉水的地方，好讓沒有人看見她，「但你卻找到了我」——他們交談時，她施法使自己消失，隱入樹枝上的檳榔之間。

passages.text: On the second night he went again, and when he looked up where there were many betel-nuts he saw Aponibolinayen taking a bath: 'Now I am going to take you home.' She feared her brother would hate her, but he took her to Kadalayapan and sent his mother to tell Aponibalagen. Langa-an crossed on her belt spread upon the water, and when the drops of water from her body became agate beads with no holes, the women dipping water said, 'How strange are the people of Kadalayapan.' Drinking basi with Aponibalagen and Ebang, who denied having any daughter, the old woman became drunk and let out that Aponibolinayen was in Kadalayapan — and Aponibalagen's heart jumped, for he had hidden his sister at Lisnayan so no one would see her. Langa-an paid the marriage price, the balaua filled nine times; and at the Sayang that followed, Asibowan herself was compelled to come by the oiled betel-nut covered with gold, which grew on her big pig's head until she promised; there Iwaginan danced with her while Gimbagonan, whose necklaces were of big jars that clattered so she could not hear the gansas, was jealous.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen and the Sun' (Asibowan episodes); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二夜他又去了，當他抬頭望向那許多檳榔樹之處，看見阿波尼博利納延正在沐浴：「如今我要帶你回家。」她擔心兄長會恨她，但他帶她到卡達拉雅潘，並派母親去告知阿波尼巴拉根。朗加安踏著鋪在水面上的腰帶渡過，當她身上的水滴化作無孔的瑪瑙珠時，汲水的婦人們說：「卡達拉雅潘的人真是奇特。」老婦與阿波尼巴拉根和埃邦同飲巴西酒，二人否認有女兒，老婦卻喝醉了，脫口說出阿波尼博利納延在卡達拉雅潘——阿波尼巴拉根的心猛然一跳，因為他原將妹妹藏在利斯納延，不讓任何人看見。朗加安付了聘禮，巴勞屋九次裝滿；而在隨後的薩揚宴上，阿西博萬本人也被那塗了油、覆著黃金的檳榔所迫而來，那檳榔在她那大豬的頭上生長，直到她應允為止；在那裡，伊瓦吉南與她共舞，而金巴戈南——她的項鍊是大陶罐，鏗鏘作響使她聽不見甘薩琴——則心生嫉妒。

title.en: The Five Days over the Year: Birthdays of the Gods
title.zh: 一年外之五日：諸神誕辰

region.en: Heliopolis and Thebes, Egypt (the divine birthdays fixed at the year's end)
region.zh: 埃及赫利奧波利斯與底比斯（歲末諸神誕辰）

period: Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride 12, 1st-2nd century CE (Budge translation 1912); doctrine as old as the calendars

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, sec. XII

summary.en: Rhea (Nut) is cursed by Helios never to be delivered in any month; Hermes wins from Selene, at dice, a seventieth part of every day and makes five new days, on which the five gods are born — Osiris with the herald's cry 'The Lord of All is born', Horus the Elder, Set born violently through his mother's wound, Isis, and Nephthys; the day of Set's birth is unlucky to this day's calendars.
summary.zh: 瑞亞（努特）受赫利俄斯詛咒，任何月日均不得分娩；赫耳墨斯與塞勒涅擲骰，贏得每日七十分之一，合成五日——五神遂誕：奧西里斯誕時聞呼『萬物之主生矣』，長荷魯斯、塞特自母身創口而出、伊西斯、奈芙蒂斯——塞特誕日至今不吉。

sensitivity.note: Ancient mythological-astrological doctrine via Plutarch; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The goddess Rhea, they say, having accompanied with Kronos by stealth, was discovered by Helios who straightway cursed her, and declared that she should not be delivered in any month or year. Hermes, however, being also in love with the same goddess, in return for the favours which he had received from her, went and played at dice with Selene, and won from her the seventieth part of each day. These parts he joined together and made from them five complete days, and he added them to the three hundred and sixty days of which the year formerly consisted. These five days are to this day called the 'Epagomenae,' that is, the superadded, and they are observed by them as the birthdays of their gods.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch, De Iside, sec. XII (Rhea=Nut, Kronos=Geb, Helios=Ra, Selene=the Moon-god Aah).
passages.zh: 他們說，女神瑞亞暗中與克羅諾斯結合，被赫利俄斯發現，他當即詛咒她，宣稱她不得在任何月份或年份中分娩。然而赫爾墨斯也愛上了同一位女神，為了報答她所給予的恩惠，他去與塞勒涅擲骰子，從她那裡贏得了每一天的七十分之一。他將這些部分合在一起，湊成完整的五天，並把它們加到從前一年所包含的三百六十天之上。這五天至今仍被稱為「厄帕戈墨奈」，即「附加之日」，他們將之作為諸神的生日來遵守。

passages.text: On the first of these, they say, Osiris was born, and as he came into the world a voice was heard saying, 'The Lord of All is born.' Some relate the matter in a different way, and say that a certain person named Pamyles, as he was fetching water from the temple of Dios at Thebes, heard a voice commanding him to proclaim aloud that the good and great king Osiris was then born, and that for this reason Kronos committed the education of the child to him, and that in memory of this event the Pamylia were afterwards instituted.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XII.
passages.zh: 他們說，在這五天中的第一天，俄西里斯誕生了，當他來到世上時，有人聽見一個聲音說：「萬物之主誕生了。」有些人則以另一種方式敘述此事，說有一個名叫帕米勒斯的人，在底比斯的狄俄斯神廟取水時，聽見一個聲音命令他大聲宣告：善良而偉大的國王俄西里斯此時已經誕生；正因如此，克羅諾斯將這孩子的教育託付給他，而為了紀念此事，後來便創立了帕米利亞節。

passages.text: Upon the second of these days was born Aroueris, whom some call Apollo, and others the Elder Horus. Upon the third day Typhon was born, who came into the world neither at the proper time nor by the right way, but he forced a passage through a wound which he made in his mother's side. Upon the fourth day Isis was born, in the marshes of Egypt, and upon the fifth day Nephthys, whom some call Teleute, or Aphrodite, or Nike, was born. Therefore, since the third of the superadded days was the birthday of Typhon, the kings considered it to be unlucky, and in consequence they neither transacted any business in it, nor even suffered themselves to take any refreshment until the evening.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XII.
passages.zh: 在這五天的第二天，阿魯埃里斯誕生了，有人稱他為阿波羅，另一些人則稱他為長者荷魯斯。第三天，堤豐誕生了，他既非在適當的時辰、也非經由正當的途徑來到世上，而是從他在母親肋旁所造成的傷口中強行鑽出。第四天，伊西斯在埃及的沼澤中誕生；第五天，奈芙蒂斯誕生了，有人稱她為忒勒忒，或阿佛洛狄忒，或尼刻。因此，由於附加之日的第三天是堤豐的生日，國王們認為它不吉利，因而在這一天既不處理任何事務，甚至也不容許自己進食，直到傍晚。

passages.text: They further add that Typhon married Nephthys, and that Isis and Osiris, having a mutual affection, enjoyed each other in their mother's womb before they were born, and that from this commerce sprang Aroueris, whom the Egyptians likewise call Horus the Elder, and the Greeks Apollo.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XII.
passages.zh: 他們又補充說，堤豐娶了奈芙蒂斯；伊西斯與俄西里斯彼此相愛，在出生之前便於母親的腹中相結合，而由這結合生出了阿魯埃里斯，埃及人同樣稱他為長者荷魯斯，希臘人則稱他為阿波羅。

title.en: Osiris the Civilizer: King and Teacher of the World
title.zh: 教化者奧西里斯：王與世界之師

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (from which Osiris set out to civilize the nations)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（奧西里斯由此啟程教化萬邦）

period: Plutarch, De Iside 13 (Budge translation 1912); the doctrine underlies Old Kingdom royal ideology

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, sec. XIII

summary.en: Osiris becomes king of Egypt and turns his people from indigent and barbarous life: he teaches them agriculture, gives them laws, and instructs them in the worship of the gods; then he travels over the world persuading all nations not by arms but by hymns and songs with instruments of music — the reason the Greeks identify him with Dionysos.
summary.zh: 奧西里斯為埃及之王，教民棄貧野之生——授以農耕、賜以律法、導以敬神；復周遊列國，不以兵刃而以頌歌與樂器說服萬民——希臘人遂以他同於狄俄倪索斯。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth via Plutarch; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Osiris having become king of Egypt, applied himself to civilizing his countrymen by turning them from their former indigent and barbarous course of life. He taught them how to cultivate and improve the fruits of the earth, and he gave them a body of laws whereby to regulate their conduct, and instructed them in the reverence and worship which they were to pay to the gods.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. XIII.
passages.zh: 俄西里斯成為埃及國王之後，致力於教化他的同胞，使他們脫離從前貧困而野蠻的生活方式。他教導他們如何耕作並改良大地的果實，又賜予他們一套法律以規範其行為，並教導他們對諸神應有的敬畏與崇拜。

passages.text: With the same good disposition he afterwards travelled over the rest of the world, inducing the people everywhere to submit to his discipline, not indeed compelling them by force of arms, but persuading them to yield to the strength of his reasons, which were conveyed to them in the most agreeable manner, in hymns and songs, accompanied with instruments of music. From this last circumstance the Greeks identified him with their Dionysos, or Bacchus.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XIII.
passages.zh: 他後來以同樣善良的心性遊歷世界其餘各地，勸導各地人民順從他的教化，並非以武力強迫他們，而是以道理的力量說服他們，這些道理以最令人愉悅的方式傳達給他們，配以音樂器伴奏的頌歌與歌曲。正因這最後一點，希臘人將他與他們的狄俄尼索斯，即巴克科斯，視為同一。

passages.text: During the absence of Osiris from his kingdom, Typhon had no opportunity of making any innovations in the state, Isis being extremely vigilant in the government, and always upon her guard. After his return, however, having first persuaded seventy-two other people to join with him in the conspiracy, together with a certain queen of Ethiopia called Aso, who chanced to be in Egypt at that time, he formed a crafty plot against him.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XIII.
passages.zh: 在俄西里斯離開他的王國期間，堤豐沒有機會在國中製造任何變亂，因為伊西斯在治理上極為警覺，時刻防備。然而在他歸來之後，堤豐先說服了另外七十二人與他共謀，又聯合了一位名叫阿索的衣索比亞女王——她當時恰好身在埃及——一同設下狡詐的計謀陷害他。

title.en: The Chest of Typhon: The Banquet and the Murder of Osiris
title.zh: 提豐之箱：宴席與奧西里斯遇害

region.en: Tanitic mouth of the Nile, Delta, Egypt (henceforth the accursed river-mouth)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲塔尼提克河口（自此為人憎惡之河口）

period: Plutarch, De Iside 13 (Budge translation 1912); dated in the myth to the 17th of Hathor, sun in Scorpio

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, sec. XIII

summary.en: Set, with seventy-two conspirators and the Ethiopian queen Aso, measures Osiris' body in secret and makes a beautifully decorated chest; at a banquet he promises it to whoever fits inside; when Osiris lies down the lid is clapped on, nailed, and sealed with molten lead, and the chest is carried to the sea through the Tanitic mouth of the Nile — a river-mouth the Egyptians ever after abominated.
summary.zh: 塞特聯七十二同謀與埃塞俄比亞王后阿索，密量奧西里斯身形製華箱；宴中戲言：『入箱而合者得之』；王臥箱中，眾徒蓋釘封鉛，由塔尼提克河口送箱入海——此河口遂為埃及人永世所憎。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth via Plutarch; no living community restrictions. This is the Plutarch register of the murder cut in the native tradition in the osiris-cycle record.

passages.text: Having privily taken the measure of the body of Osiris, he caused a chest to be made of exactly the same size, and it was very beautiful and highly decorated. This chest he brought into a certain banqueting room, where it was greatly admired by all who were present, and Typhon, as if in jest, promised to give it to that man whose body when tried would be found to fit it. Thereupon the whole company, one after the other, went into it, but it did not fit any of them; last of all Osiris himself lay down in it.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. XIII.
passages.zh: 他暗中量了俄西里斯身體的尺寸，命人打造了一只大小完全相同的箱子，做工精美、裝飾華麗。他把這只箱子帶到某間宴會廳中，在場眾人無不讚嘆，堤豐便彷彿開玩笑似地許諾，要把它送給身體試放進去恰好合適的人。於是全體賓客一個接一個地躺進去，卻沒有一人合適；最後俄西里斯本人躺了進去。

passages.text: Thereupon all the conspirators ran to the chest, and clapped the cover upon it, and then they fastened it down with nails on the outside, and poured melted lead over it. They next took the chest to the river, which carried it to the sea through the Tanaitic mouth of the Nile; and for this reason this mouth of the Nile is still held in the utmost abomination by the Egyptians, and is never mentioned by them except with marks of detestation.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XIII.
passages.zh: 於是所有同謀者一齊奔向箱子，蓋上箱蓋，然後在外面用釘子釘牢，並澆上熔化的鉛。接著他們把箱子抬到河邊，河水經由尼羅河的塔奈提克河口把它帶入海中；正因如此，尼羅河的這個河口至今仍為埃及人所深惡痛絕，他們提起它時無不帶著憎惡的表示。

passages.text: These things, some say, took place on the seventeenth day of the month of Hathor, when the sun was in Scorpio, in the twenty-eighth year of the reign of Osiris, though others tell us that this was the year of his life and not of his reign.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XIII.
passages.zh: 有人說這些事發生於哈托爾月的第十七日，當時太陽位於天蠍座，正值俄西里斯在位第二十八年；不過也有人告訴我們，這是他在世的年數，而非在位的年數。

title.en: The Panic of the Pans: Koptos, the Children's Omens, and Anubis
title.zh: 潘神之驚：科普托斯、童言之兆與安努畢斯

region.en: Chemmis and Koptos, Egypt (the news of the murder broke here first)
region.zh: 埃及克米斯與科普托斯（凶信首傳之地）

period: Plutarch, De Iside 14 (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, sec. XIV

summary.en: The Pans and Satyrs of Chemmis are the first to learn of the murder — giving the world its word for 'panic terror'; Isis cuts off a lock of her hair at Koptos, the city of mourning; children who saw the deed tell her which mouth of the Nile — and the Egyptians ever after read omens in children's play; searching too for the child her sister bore to Osiris, she is led by dogs, and raises him as Anubis, the dog that guards the gods.
summary.zh: 克米斯的潘與薩提爾最先聞凶信——『恐慌』一詞由此而生；伊西斯於科普托斯剪髮服喪；孩童告知河口——埃及人自此觀童戲以占卜；她又尋姊所生之子，由群犬引路，撫育為安努畢斯——守護諸神之犬。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth via Plutarch; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The first who had knowledge of the accident which had befallen their king were the Pans and Satyrs, who inhabited the country round about Chemmis, and they having informed the people about it, gave the first occasion to the name of Panic Terrors, which has ever since been made use of to signify any sudden fright or amazement of a multitude. As soon as the report reached Isis, she immediately cut off one of the locks of her hair, and put on mourning apparel in that very place where she happened to be; for this reason the place has ever since been called 'Koptos,' or the 'city of mourning.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. XIV.
passages.zh: 最先得知降臨於他們國王身上的這樁變故的，是居住在凱米斯一帶鄉間的潘神與薩堤爾，他們把此事告知民眾，遂首開「潘神式驚恐」這一名稱的先例，此後該詞一直用來指稱人群突發的驚嚇或驚愕。消息一傳到伊西斯耳中，她當即剪下自己的一綹頭髮，就在她當時恰好所在之處換上喪服；因此這地方此後一直被稱為「科普托斯」，即「哀悼之城」。

passages.text: She inquired of every person she met, including some children whom she saw, whether they knew what was become of it. Now, it so happened that these children had seen what Typhon's accomplices had done with the body, and they accordingly told her by what mouth of the Nile it had been conveyed to the sea. For this reason the Egyptians look upon children as endued with a kind of faculty of divining, and in consequence of this notion are very curious in observing the accidental prattle which they have with one another whilst they are at play, especially if it be in a sacred place, forming omens and presages from it.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XIV.
passages.zh: 她向所遇见的每一个人打听，包括她所见到的几个孩子，问他们是否知道它的下落。恰好这些孩子曾看见堤丰的党羽对那尸体所做的事，于是便告诉她，那尸体是从尼罗河的哪一个河口被运到海里去的。因此之故，埃及人认为孩子天生具有某种占卜的能力，并由于这种观念，他们非常留心观察孩子们在嬉戏时彼此之间偶然说出的话语，尤其是在神圣之地所说的话，并从中构成征兆与预兆。

passages.text: Isis meanwhile having been informed that Osiris, deceived by her sister Nephthys, who was in love with him, had unwittingly enjoyed her instead of herself, as she concluded from the melilot-garland which he had left with her, made it her business likewise to search out the child, the fruit of this unlawful commerce. Accordingly, after much pains and difficulty, by means of some dogs that conducted her to the place where it was, she found it and bred it up; and in process of time it became her constant guard and attendant, and obtained the name of Anubis, and it is thought that it watches and guards the gods as dogs do men.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XIV.
passages.zh: 与此同时，伊西斯得知奥西里斯被她的妹妹奈芙蒂斯所骗——奈芙蒂斯爱恋着他——竟在不知情的情况下与她而非自己同寝，这是她从他所遗留给她的那顶蜜草花冠上推断出来的；于是她也设法去寻找这段不正当结合所生的孩子。经过许多辛苦与困难，靠着几只狗把她引到那孩子所在之处，她找到了他并将他抚养长大；随着时光流逝，他成了她忠实的守卫与随从，并获得了阿努比斯之名，人们认为他看守护卫众神，正如狗看守护卫人一样。

title.en: Isis at Byblos: The Tamarisk Pillar and the Child in the Fire
title.zh: 伊西斯在比布魯斯：檉木柱與火中之子

region.en: Byblos, Phoenician coast (the king's palace built around the coffin)
region.zh: 腓尼基海岸比布魯斯（棺木成王宮之柱）

period: Plutarch, De Iside 15-16 (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, secs. XV-XVI

summary.en: The chest drifts to Byblos and is swallowed by a tamarisk that becomes the palace's roof-pillar; Isis comes as a stranger, breathes her fragrance into the queen's maids, is made nurse to the royal child — whom she flames each night to burn away his mortality while she, as a swallow, laments around the pillar — until the queen's cry robs the boy of immortality; the goddess takes the pillar, and its wood is worshipped at Byblos to this day.
summary.zh: 棺漂至比布魯斯，為檉樹所裹，竟成王宮之柱；伊西斯以異鄉人身至，以體香渡入侍女髮膚，受聘為王子乳母——夜夜置子於火中焚其凡軀，己化燕繞柱哀鳴——王后驚呼，王子失其不死；女神遂取柱，其木至今為比布魯斯人所拜。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth via Plutarch; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The chest had been carried by the waves of the sea to the coast of Byblos, and there gently lodged in the branches of a bush of tamarisk, which in a short time had grown up into a large and beautiful tree, and had grown round the chest and enclosed it on every side so completely that it was not to be seen. Moreover, the king of the country, amazed at its unusual size, had cut the tree down, and made that part of the trunk wherein the chest was concealed into a pillar to support the roof of his house.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. XV.
passages.zh: 那箱子被海浪冲到比布罗斯的海岸，在那里轻轻地搁置在一丛柽柳的枝条之间；这丛柽柳在短时间内长成了一棵又大又美的树，长得环绕住那箱子，将它四面完全包住，以致看不见它。此外，那地方的国王惊异于它异乎寻常的巨大，便命人把树砍倒，并将树干中藏有箱子的那一部分做成一根柱子，用来支撑他房屋的屋顶。

passages.text: Setting herself down by the side of a fountain, she refused to speak to anybody except the queen's women who chanced to be there. These, however, she saluted and caressed in the kindest manner possible, plaiting their hair for them, and transmitting into them part of that wonderful odour which issued from her own body. This raised a great desire in the queen their mistress to see the stranger... She therefore sent for her to court, and, after a further acquaintance with her, made her nurse to one of her sons. Now, the name of the king who reigned at this time at Byblos was Melkander, and that of his wife was Astarte.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XV.
passages.zh: 她在泉边坐下，除偶然在场的王后侍女外，不肯与任何人说话。然而，她以最亲切的方式向她们致意、抚慰她们，为她们编结头发，并将从她自己身上散发出的那种奇妙香气的一部分传给了她们。这使她们的女主人王后产生了极大的愿望，想见见这位陌生人……于是她派人召她进宫，在与她进一步相识之后，便让她做自己一个儿子的乳母。此时在比布罗斯统治的国王名叫墨尔坎德，他的妻子名叫阿斯塔耳忒。

passages.text: Isis nursed the child by giving it her finger to suck instead of the breast. She likewise put him each night into the fire in order to consume his mortal part, whilst, having transformed herself into a swallow, she circled round the pillar and bemoaned her sad fate. This she continued to do for some time, till the queen, who stood watching her, observing the child to be all of a flame, cried out, and thereby deprived him of some of that immortality which would otherwise have been conferred upon him. The goddess then made herself known, and asked that the pillar which supported the roof might be given to her.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XVI.
passages.zh: 伊西斯哺育那孩子，是把自己的手指给他吮吸，而非用乳房。她同样每夜把他放进火中，以烧去他有死的部分，同时把自己变成一只燕子，绕着那柱子盘旋，哀叹自己悲惨的命运。她这样持续了一段时间，直到站在一旁守望她的王后，看见那孩子浑身是火，便叫喊起来，因而使他失去了一部分本会赐予他的不朽。女神于是显露了自己的身份，并要求把那根支撑屋顶的柱子给她。

passages.text: Having taken the pillar down, she cut it open easily, and having taken out what she wanted, she wrapped up the remainder of the trunk in fine linen, and having poured perfumed oil over it, she delivered it again into the hands of the king and queen. Now, this piece of wood is to this day preserved in the temple, and worshipped by the people of Byblos.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XVI.
passages.zh: 她把柱子取下，轻易地将它剖开，取出她所要的东西之后，用细麻布把树干的剩余部分包裹起来，又在上面浇了香油，然后重新交到国王和王后手中。如今，这块木头至今仍保存在神庙中，受比布罗斯人民的崇拜。

title.en: Maneros and the Skeleton at the Banquet
title.zh: 馬奈羅斯與宴席之骷髏

region.en: Phaedrus river-mouth and Egyptian banquet halls (symbolic pin, Nile Delta coast)
region.zh: 法埃德魯斯河口與埃及宴廳（象徵定位，尼羅三角洲海岸）

period: Plutarch, De Iside 17 (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, sec. XVII

summary.en: Isis opens the chest to weep over her husband, and the little prince who stole up behind dies of her terrible look — he is Maneros, called on at every Egyptian banquet; Plutarch collects the rival explanations — that Maneros means 'may this be fortunate', and that the skeleton carried round at feasts is a memento mori, not the story of Osiris.
summary.zh: 伊西斯啟箱泣夫，偷窺的小王子被她一瞪而亡——他即馬奈羅斯，埃及宴席上所呼之神；普魯塔克並錄異說：『馬奈羅斯』意為『願此順遂』，宴中展示之骷髏乃提醒必死之諫，非述奧西里斯之事。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth via Plutarch; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: At the first place where she stopped, and when she believed that she was alone, she opened the chest, and laying her face upon that of her dead husband, she embraced him and wept bitterly. Then, seeing that the little boy had silently stolen up behind her, and had found out the reason of her grief, she turned upon him suddenly, and, in her anger, gave him so fierce and terrible a look that he died of fright immediately.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. XVII.
passages.zh: 在她最初停下的地方，当她以为自己独处无人时，便打开了箱子，将脸贴在她亡夫的面上，拥抱他并痛哭失声。随后，她看见那小男孩已悄悄溜到她身后，并已发现她悲伤的缘由，便猛然转向他，在盛怒之下，向他投以如此凶狠可怖的目光，以致他当场惊骇而死。

passages.text: Afterwards he received the greatest honour on account of the goddess, for this Maneros, whom the Egyptians so frequently call upon at their banquets, is none other than he. This story is contradicted by those who tell us that the true name of this child was Palaestinus, or Pelusius, and that the city of this name was built by the goddess in memory of him. And they further add that this Maneros is thus honoured by the Egyptians at their feasts because he was the first who invented music.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XVII.
passages.zh: 后来，他因这位女神而获得了最大的尊荣，因为埃及人在宴会上如此频繁呼唤的这位曼涅罗斯，正是他。这个故事遭到另一些人的反驳，他们告诉我们，这个孩子的真名是帕莱斯提努斯，或佩卢西乌斯，而以此命名的城市是女神为纪念他而建造的。他们进一步补充说，这位曼涅罗斯之所以在宴席上受到埃及人如此尊崇，是因为他是最早发明音乐的人。

passages.text: In like manner they say that the human skeleton which is carried about in a box on festal occasions, and shown to the guests, is not designed, as some imagine, to represent the particular misfortunes of Osiris, but rather to remind them of their mortality, and thereby to excite them freely to make use of and to enjoy the good things which are set before them, seeing that they must quickly become such as they there saw.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XVII.
passages.zh: 同样地，他们说，在节庆场合被装在箱中抬着游行、并向宾客展示的人体骨架，并非如某些人所想象的那样，意在象征俄西里斯个人的不幸遭遇，而是为了提醒他们自身的必死性，从而激励他们坦然享用并享受摆在他们面前的美好事物，因为他们很快也将变成他们在此所见的模样。

title.en: The Fourteen Pieces: Dismemberment, the Papyrus Boat, and the Fish
title.zh: 十四塊遺體：分屍、紙莎草舟與魚

region.en: Buto and the Delta marshes, Egypt (where Isis hid the chest, and where Set found it)
region.zh: 埃及布托與三角洲沼澤（藏箱與遇害之地）

period: Plutarch, De Iside 18 (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, sec. XVIII

summary.en: Set hunting by moonlight finds the chest at Buto and tears Osiris into fourteen pieces; Isis searches by papyrus boat — why the crocodile spares papyrus vessels to this day — and buries each piece where she finds it, seeding Egypt with rival tombs of Osiris; the phallus, thrown to the Nile, is eaten by the Lepidotus, Phagrus and Oxyrhynchus fish, and a model phallus is consecrated in its place at a festival that still exists.
summary.zh: 塞特月下獵獸偶遇布托之箱，碎奧西里斯為十四塊；伊西斯乘紙莎草舟遍尋——故鱷不傷紙莎草舟至今——每得一塊即葬一處，埃及遂多奧西里斯之墓；陽具拋於尼羅，為三魚所食，伊西斯乃塑代具、立祭典以補其失。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth via Plutarch; no living community restrictions. Pairs with the native-register osiris-cycle record; the fish-eaten phallus explains the fish taboos of several towns.

passages.text: One night, however, when Typhon was hunting by the light of the moon, he came upon it by chance, and recognizing the body which was enclosed in it, he tore it into several pieces, fourteen in all, and scattered them in different places up and down the country. When Isis knew what had been done, she set out in search of the scattered portions of her husband's body; and in order to pass more easily through the lower, marshy parts of the country, she made use of a boat made of the papyrus plant. For this reason, they say, either fearing the anger of the goddess, or else venerating the papyrus, the crocodile never injures anyone who travels in this sort of vessel.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. XVIII.
passages.zh: 然而，有一天夜里，堤丰借着月光打猎时，偶然遇见了它，认出封在其中的躯体，便将它撕成数块，共十四块，散布于全国各地不同的地方。伊西斯得知所发生之事后，便出发寻找她丈夫躯体的散落部分；为了更容易穿过该国低洼沼泽的地带，她使用了一艘用纸莎草制成的船。因此，他们说，鳄鱼或是畏惧女神的愤怒，或是崇敬纸莎草，从不伤害乘坐这种船只旅行的人。

passages.text: And this, they say, hath given rise to the report that there are very many different sepulchres of Osiris in Egypt, for wherever Isis found one of the scattered portions of her husband's body, there she buried it. Others, however, contradict this story, and tell us that the variety of sepulchres of Osiris was due rather to the policy of the queen, who, instead of the real body, as she pretended, presented to these cities only an image of her husband... to defeat Typhon, who, if he were victorious in his fight against Horus in which he was about to engage, would search for the body of Osiris, and being distracted by the number of sepulchres would despair of ever being able to find the true one.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XVIII.
passages.zh: 他们说，此事便引出了埃及有许多座不同的俄西里斯陵墓的传闻，因为伊西斯每找到她丈夫躯体的一处散落部分，便在那里将其埋葬。然而，另一些人反驳这个故事，告诉我们俄西里斯陵墓的多样，毋宁说是出于这位王后的策略，她并非献上真正的遗体，而是如她所佯称的那样，只向这些城市呈献她丈夫的一尊像……以挫败堤丰，因为堤丰若在与荷鲁斯即将展开的战斗中获胜，便会搜寻俄西里斯的遗体，而因陵墓数目众多而困惑，终将绝望于永远无法找到真正的那一座。

passages.text: We are told, moreover, that notwithstanding all her efforts, Isis was never able to discover the phallus of Osiris, which, having been thrown into the Nile immediately upon its separation from the rest of the body, had been devoured by the Lepidotus, the Phagrus, and the Oxyrhynchus, fish which above all others, for this reason, the Egyptians have in more especial avoidance. In order, however, to make some amends for the loss, Isis consecrated the phallus made in imitation of it, and instituted a solemn festival to its memory, which is even to this day observed by the Egyptians.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XVIII.
passages.zh: 此外，我们还被告知，尽管伊西斯竭尽全力，却始终未能找到俄西里斯的阳物，因为它一从躯体其余部分分离，便被投入尼罗河，随即被 Lepidotus（狐鲤）、Phagrus（鲷鱼）和 Oxyrhynchus（尖吻鱼）吞食，正因如此，埃及人尤其避忌这几种鱼，胜过其他一切。然而，为了对这份损失略作弥补，伊西斯将仿制其形的阳物奉为圣物，并为纪念它设立了一个庄严的节日，这个节日至今仍为埃及人所遵守。

title.en: Osiris' Return and the Horse Dialogue: Battles of Horus
title.zh: 奧西里斯歸來與馬之問答：荷魯斯之戰

region.en: Egypt between the Two Lands (the battles of Horus and Typhon)
region.zh: 埃及兩地之間（荷魯斯與提豐交戰之地）

period: Plutarch, De Iside 19 (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, sec. XIX

summary.en: Osiris returns from the other world to train Horus for war; asked what is most glorious, the boy answers 'To avenge his father', and chooses the horse over the lion because it cuts off a flying enemy. Horus wins his first battle and takes Typhon, whom Isis frees; enraged, Horus tears the crown from her head until Hermes replaces it with a cow's head; two further battles make Typhon's defeat final, and Harpokrates is born prematurely to Isis after Osiris' death.
summary.zh: 奧西里斯自冥界歸返，教子練武；問何為至榮，答『復父之仇』，又擇馬而捨獅——因其能追截逃敵。荷魯斯首戰勝而縛提豐，伊西斯竟釋之；子怒奪母冠，赫耳墨斯代以牛首；再戰兩合，提豐終敗；奧西里斯亡後，伊西斯早產生哈波克拉特斯。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth via Plutarch; no living community restrictions. Budge's footnote records the native Sallier version of the Isis-beheading that Plutarch omitted.

passages.text: Osiris returned from the other world, and appeared to his son Horus, and encouraged him to fight, and at the same time instructed him in the exercise of arms. He then asked him what he thought was the most glorious action a man could perform, to which Horus replied, 'To revenge the injuries offered to his father and mother.' Osiris then asked him what animal he thought most serviceable to a soldier, and Horus replied, 'A horse.' On this Osiris wondered, and he questioned him further, asking him why he preferred a horse to a lion, and Horus replied, 'Though the lion is the more serviceable creature to one who stands in need of help, yet is the horse more useful in overtaking and cutting off a flying enemy.' These replies caused Osiris to rejoice greatly, for they showed him that his son was sufficiently prepared for his enemy.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. XIX.
passages.zh: 歐西里斯從彼世歸來，向他的兒子荷魯斯顯現，鼓勵他奮戰，同時教導他操練兵器。他接著問他，認為一個人所能做出的最光榮之舉是什麼，荷魯斯答道：「為父母所受的傷害復仇。」歐西里斯又問他，認為什麼動物對士兵最有用，荷魯斯答道：「馬。」歐西里斯聽了大為驚異，便進一步追問他，為何寧取馬而不取獅，荷魯斯答道：「獅子對需要援助之人固然是更有用的生物，但馬在追擊並截斷逃竄之敵上更為有用。」這些回答令歐西里斯大為欣喜，因為它們向他表明，他的兒子已充分準備好面對他的敵人。

passages.text: Afterwards a battle took place between Horus and Typhon, which lasted many days, but Horus was at length victorious, and Typhon was taken prisoner. He was delivered over into the custody of Isis, who, instead of putting him to death, loosed his fetters and set him free. This action of his mother incensed Horus to such a degree that he seized her, and pulled the royal crown off her head; but Hermes came forward, and set upon her head the head of an ox instead of a helmet.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XIX.
passages.zh: 後來，荷魯斯與堤豐之間發生了一場戰鬥，持續多日，但荷魯斯終於獲勝，堤豐被俘。他被交到伊西斯手中看管，伊西斯並未將他處死，反而解開他的鎖鏈，將他釋放。他母親此舉令荷魯斯大為震怒，以致他抓住她，扯下她頭上的王冠；但赫爾墨斯上前，將一個牛頭戴在她頭上，代替頭盔。

passages.text: After this Typhon accused Horus of illegitimacy, but, by the assistance of Hermes, his legitimacy was fully established by a decree of the gods themselves. After this two other battles were fought between Horus and Typhon, and in both Typhon was defeated. Moreover, Isis is said to have had union with Osiris after his death, and she brought forth Harpokrates, who came into the world before his time, and was lame in his lower limbs.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XIX.
passages.zh: 此後，堤豐指控荷魯斯為私生，但藉著赫爾墨斯的協助，他的合法身分由眾神自身的裁決完全確立。此後，荷魯斯與堤豐之間又打了兩場仗，兩場皆以堤豐敗北告終。此外，據說伊西斯在歐西里斯死後與他結合，生下了哈波克拉底，他未足月便來到世間，且下肢殘疾。

title.en: The Many Tombs of Osiris: Abydos, Memphis, and Philae
title.zh: 奧西里斯眾墓：阿拜多斯、孟菲斯與菲萊

region.en: Abydos, Upper Egypt (the most coveted burial place in Egypt)
region.zh: 埃及上埃及阿拜多斯（全埃及最令人嚮往之葬地）

period: Plutarch, De Iside 20-21 (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, secs. XX-XXI

summary.en: Why Egypt is full of claimed graves of one god: Abydos holds his body — the rich buy burial beside him 'to lie in the grave with Osiris'; Memphis holds the Apis bull as the image of his soul kept near his body; and at Philae a tiny inaccessible island carries the true tomb, where no bird alights nor fish swims except when the priests come to crown it with flowers beneath a giant tamarisk.
summary.zh: 埃及何處皆稱葬有一神：阿拜多斯藏其身——富人競相購墓『與奧西里斯同眠』；孟菲斯養阿匹斯牛以近其體，牛乃其魂之像；而菲萊小島不可接近，非祭司至期登島獻花之時，鳥不落、魚不游，其墓為巨型檉樹所蔭。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth via Plutarch; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: That the history has a substantial foundation is proved by the opinion which obtains generally concerning the sepulchres of Osiris. There are many places wherein his body is said to have been deposited, and among these are Abydos and Memphis, both of which are said to contain his body. It is for this reason, they say, that the richer and more prosperous citizens wish to be buried in the former of these cities, being ambitious of lying, as it were, in the grave with Osiris.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. XX.
passages.zh: 關於歐西里斯陵墓的普遍看法，證明這段歷史有其堅實的基礎。據說他的遺體被安放於許多地方，其中包括阿拜多斯與孟菲斯，兩地皆被稱為存有他的遺體。據說正因如此，較富有、較昌盛的公民希望葬於前一座城市，因為他們渴望能彷彿與歐西里斯同葬一墓。

passages.text: The title of Memphis to be regarded as the grave of Osiris seems to rest upon the fact that the Apis Bull, who is considered to be the image of the soul of Osiris, is kept in that city for the express purpose that it may be as near his body as possible.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XX.
passages.zh: 孟菲斯被視為歐西里斯之墓，其依據似乎在於：被認為是歐西里斯靈魂之形象的阿匹斯公牛，正是為了盡可能靠近他的遺體而飼養於該城。

passages.text: The true sepulchre of Osiris lies in that little island which the Nile makes at Philae. This island is, they say, inaccessible, and neither bird can alight on it, nor fish swim near it, except at the times when the priests go over to it from the mainland to solemnize their customary rites to the dead, and to crown his tomb with flowers, which, they say, is overshadowed by the branches of a tamarisk-tree, the size of which exceeds that of an olive-tree.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XX.
passages.zh: 歐西里斯的真正陵墓位於尼羅河在菲萊所形成的那座小島上。據說這座島無法接近，既無鳥能棲落其上，也無魚能游近其旁，唯有祭司從大陸渡海前往，舉行他們對死者慣常的儀式，並以鮮花裝飾他的陵墓之時例外；據說那座陵墓為一棵檉柳的枝葉所覆蓋，其樹身之大超過橄欖樹。

title.en: The Veil of Isis at Sais: I Am All That Has Been
title.zh: 薩伊斯的伊西斯面紗：我乃萬有

region.en: Sais, Western Delta, Egypt (temple of Neit/Isis)
region.zh: 埃及西三角洲薩伊斯（奈特/伊西斯神廟）

period: Plutarch, De Iside 9, recording a 26th-Dynasty temple inscription (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, sec. IX

summary.en: The most famous sentence of Egyptian religion, recorded on the statue-base of the goddess of Sais: 'I am everything that has been, that is, and that shall be: and my veil no man hath raised' — joined in Plutarch to the etymology of Ammon as 'the hidden', the god whose name conceals the Supreme Being who is 'concealed in the universal nature.'
summary.zh: 埃及宗教最著名一語，刻於薩伊斯女神像座：『我乃曾存在、正存在、將存在之萬有；我之面紗無人掀起』——普魯塔克併以『阿蒙』之詞源『隱』：至尊之神『隱於萬物本性之中』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient inscription quoted via Plutarch; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: This the priesthood hints to us in many instances, particularly by the sphinxes, which they seem to have placed designedly before their temples as types of the enigmatical nature of their theology. To this purpose, likewise, is that inscription which they have engraved upon the base of the statue of Athene at Sais, whom they identify with Isis: 'I am everything that has been, that is, and that shall be: and my veil no man hath raised.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. IX (Athene of Sais = the goddess Net).
passages.zh: 祭司們在許多場合向我們暗示這一點，尤其是藉由那些斯芬克斯像；他們似乎刻意將這些雕像安置在神廟之前，作為其神學之謎樣本性的象徵。同樣，他們刻在賽斯城雅典娜雕像基座上的那段銘文也表達了此意——他們將雅典娜與伊西斯視為同一：『我是一切曾經存在、現在存在、以及將要存在之物：而我的面紗，無人曾揭起。』

passages.text: In like manner the word 'Amoun,' or as it is expressed in the Greek language, 'Ammon,' which is generally looked upon as the proper name of the Egyptian Zeus, is interpreted by Manetho the Sebennite to signify 'concealment' or 'something which is hidden.' Hecataeus of Abdera indeed tells us that the Egyptians make use of this term when they call out to one another. If this be so, then their invoking Amoun is the same thing as calling upon the supreme being, whom they believe to be 'hidden' and 'concealed' in the universal nature, to appear and manifest itself to them.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. IX.
passages.zh: 同樣地，『阿蒙』一詞——或如希臘語所表述的『阿蒙』——通常被視為埃及宙斯的專名，塞本尼托斯的曼涅托將其解釋為『隱藏』或『某種被隱匿之物』。阿布德拉的赫卡泰烏斯確實告訴我們，埃及人彼此呼喚時便使用此詞。若果真如此，那麼他們呼求阿蒙，便等同於呼求那位至高存在——他們相信祂『隱藏』且『隱匿』於宇宙本性之中——求祂向他們顯現並彰顯自身。

title.en: Why Wine Is Abhorred: The Blood of Fallen Enemies
title.zh: 酒之憎：敵血成藤

region.en: Heliopolis, Egypt (temple of the Sun; no wine within)
region.zh: 埃及赫利奧波利斯（日神廟內無酒）

period: Plutarch, De Iside 6, recording Eudoxus' Travels (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, sec. VI

summary.en: A ritual-origin myth explaining the wine taboo: when wine was poured on the altars it was treated not as a gift but as the blood of Egypt's enemies — for the vine first sprang from earth fattened with the bodies of those who fell in the wars against the gods, which is why drunkenness fills men 'with the blood of their own ancestors.'
summary.zh: 酒禁之緣起神話：祭壇奠酒非為敬獻，實為仇敵之血——因葡萄藤最初乃自『與諸神交戰陣亡者之屍所肥沃之土』生出，故狂飲者如飲『己祖之血』而癲狂。

sensitivity.note: Ancient aition via Plutarch/Eudoxus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The priests of the Sun at Heliopolis never carry wine into their temples, for they regard it as indecent for those who are devoted to the service of any god to indulge in the drinking of wine whilst they are under the immediate inspection of their Lord and King. The priests of the other deities are not so scrupulous in this respect, for they use it, though sparingly. During their more solemn purifications they abstain from wine wholly, and they give themselves up entirely to study and meditation, and to the hearing and teaching of those divine truths which treat of the divine nature.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. VI.
passages.zh: 赫利奧波利斯的太陽祭司從不將酒帶入他們的神廟，因為他們認為，那些奉獻於任何神明之侍奉的人，在其主與王的直接監視之下沉溺於飲酒，乃是不合宜的。其他神明的祭司在這方面則不那麼嚴謹，因為他們也飲用，儘管節制。在他們更為莊嚴的潔淨儀式中，他們完全戒絕酒，並將自身全然投入研習與冥想，以及聆聽與傳授那些論及神性本質的神聖真理。

passages.text: If they used it at any time in pouring out libations to the gods, it was not because they looked upon it as being acceptable to them for its own sake, but they poured it out over their altars as the blood of their enemies who had in times past fought against them. For they believe the vine to have first sprung out of the earth after it was fattened by the bodies of those who fell in the wars against the gods. And this, they say, is the reason why drinking its juice in great quantities makes men mad and beside themselves, filling them, as it were, with the blood of their own ancestors.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. VI.
passages.zh: 若他們有時以酒向神明奠酒，那並非因為他們認為酒本身為神明所悅納，而是他們將酒傾倒於祭壇之上，視之為昔日與他們為敵者之血。因為他們相信，葡萄藤最初是從大地中長出，而大地乃因那些在與神明之戰爭中陣亡者的屍體而肥沃。他們說，這便是為何大量飲用其汁液會使人瘋狂、失去理智，彷彿以他們自己祖先的血充滿了他們。

title.en: Ochus Slays the Apis: The Sword-King in the King-List
title.zh: 奧庫斯屠阿匹斯：王表中的『劍』

region.en: Memphis, Egypt (palace of the Apis bull)
region.zh: 埃及孟菲斯（阿匹斯聖牛之宮）

period: Historical memory of Artaxerxes III Ochus (c. 341 BCE), recorded in Plutarch, De Iside 11 (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, sec. XI

summary.en: The Persian king Ochus killed the Apis bull and served it at a banquet; the Egyptian priests entered him in their king-list not under his name but under a picture of a sword — teaching that sacred writing records character, not person, and that the slayer of the god of Memphis became, in their records, an instrument of destruction.
summary.zh: 波斯王奧庫斯殺阿匹斯聖牛以宴客；埃及祭司於王表不以名記之，而以一柄『劍』之圖像記其人——神聖文字記其品性而非其人，屠神者遂成毀滅之器。

sensitivity.note: Historical memory preserved mythically via Plutarch; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The cruel and bloody king of Persia, Ochus, who not only put to death great numbers of the people, but even slew the Apis Bull himself, and afterwards served him up in a banquet to his friends, is represented by them by a sword, and by this name he is still to be found in the catalogue of their kings. This name, therefore, does not represent his person, but indicates his base and cruel qualities, which were best suggested by the picture of an instrument of destruction.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. XI.
passages.zh: 那位殘酷而血腥的波斯國王奧庫斯，不僅處死大批人民，甚至殺害了阿匹斯公牛本身，隨後更將其做成宴席款待友人；他們以一把劍來代表他，而此名至今仍可見於他們的君王名錄之中。因此，此名所代表的並非其本人，而是標示其卑劣殘酷的品性，而以毀滅之器具的圖像來暗示此點最為恰當。

passages.text: If, therefore, O Clea, you will hear and entertain the story of these gods from those who know how to explain it consistently with religion and philosophy, if you will steadily persist in the observance of all these holy rites which the laws require of you, and are moreover fully persuaded that to form true notions of the divine nature is more acceptable to them than any sacrifice or mere external act of worship can be, you will by this means be entirely exempt from any danger of falling into superstition, an evil no less to be avoided than atheism itself.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XI, closing.
passages.zh: 因此，克萊亞啊，倘若你願意從那些懂得如何以合乎宗教與哲學的方式闡釋此事的人那裡聆聽並領受這些神明的故事，倘若你願意堅定不移地遵守法律要求你履行的一切神聖儀式，並且 furthermore 完全確信：對神性本質形成真確的觀念，比任何獻祭或僅只外在的崇拜行為更為神明所悅納，那麼你將藉此完全免於陷入迷信的任何危險——迷信之惡，與無神論本身同樣當避。

title.en: Osiris Is the Nile: Born on the Right, Perished on the Left
title.zh: 奧西里斯即尼羅：生於右、歿於左

region.en: The Nile from Elephantine to the sea (the allegorical reading of the god)
region.zh: 自象島至海口之尼羅（神之寓言讀法）

period: Plutarch, De Iside 32-39 (Budge translation 1912), philosophical allegoresis

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, sec. XXXII

summary.en: Plutarch's allegorists make Osiris the Nile, Isis the earth it fertilizes, and Typhon the sea that tears the river to pieces; the sacred dirge says he 'was born on the right side of the world and perished on the left' — south and north; the sacred chest means the river's withdrawal to its bed at Hathor, and at the sea festival the priests cry over the golden boat: 'Osiris is found.'
summary.zh: 普魯塔克之寓言派謂：奧西里斯即尼羅、伊西斯為其所沃之土、提豐為碎河之海；聖哀歌謂其『生於世界之右、歿於世界之左』（南與北）；藏箱之說即河水退回河床；至海祭之日，祭司捧金舟齊呼：『奧西里斯尋得了！』

sensitivity.note: Ancient philosophical allegoresis via Plutarch; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: So these philosophers say that by Osiris the Egyptians mean the Nile, by Isis that part of the country which Osiris, or the Nile, overflows, and by Typhon the sea, which, by receiving the Nile as it runs into it, does, as it were, tear it into many pieces, and indeed entirely destroys it, excepting only so much of it as is admitted into the bosom of the earth in its passage over it, which is thereby rendered fertile. The truth of this explanation is confirmed, they say, by that sacred dirge which they make over Osiris when they bewail 'him who was born on the right side of the world and who perished on the left.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. XXXII.
passages.zh: 這些哲學家說，埃及人所謂的俄西里斯，指的是尼羅河；所謂的伊西斯，指的是俄西里斯、亦即尼羅河所淹沒的那部分國土；所謂的堤豐，指的是大海，因為大海接納奔流入海的尼羅河，便彷彿把它撕成許多碎片，甚至將其全然毀滅，唯有尼羅河流經大地時滲入大地胸懷的那一部分得以留存，而大地也因此變得肥沃。他們說，他們在哀悼俄西里斯時所唱的聖歌——「那位生於世界右側、卻死於左側者」——正印證了這一解釋的真實性。

passages.text: As to what they relate of the shutting up of Osiris in a box, this appears to mean the withdrawal of the Nile to its own bed. This is the more probable as this misfortune is said to have happened to Osiris in the month of Hathor, precisely at that season of the year when, upon the cessation of the Etesian or north winds the Nile returns to its own bed, and leaves the country everywhere bare and naked. At this time the priests celebrate doleful rites, and they exhibit as a suitable representation of the grief of Isis a gilded ox covered with a fine black linen cloth.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XXXIX.
passages.zh: 至於他們所說俄西里斯被關進箱中的事，這似乎意指尼羅河退回到它自己的河床。此說更為可信，因為據說這一不幸發生在哈托爾月，恰是每年季風、即北風停息、尼羅河退回自身河床、使國土處處裸露光禿的時節。此時祭司們舉行哀悼儀式，並以一頭覆著精美黑色亞麻布的金牛，作為伊西斯之悲傷的恰當象徵。

passages.text: On the nineteenth of the month Pachons they march in procession to the sea, whither the priests and other officials carry the sacred chest, wherein is enclosed a small boat of gold; into this they first pour some water, and then all present cry out with a loud voice, 'Osiris is found.' This done, they throw some earth, scent, and spices into the water, and mix it well together, and work it up into the image of a crescent, which they afterwards dress in clothes. This shows that they regard the gods as the essence and power of water and earth.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XXXIX.
passages.zh: 在帕孔月十九日，他們列隊行進至海邊，祭司及其他官員抬著聖箱，箱中封存著一隻小金船；他們先往船中注入一些水，隨後在場眾人高聲呼喊：「俄西里斯被找到了。」此事既畢，他們將一些泥土、香料與香辛料投入水中，攪拌均勻，捏成新月之形，隨後為之穿上衣服。這表明他們視諸神為水與土的本質與力量。

title.en: The Column of Curses against Menes: The King Who Learned Poverty
title.zh: 詛咒美尼斯之柱：嘗貧之王

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (temple column inscribed with curses)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（神廟刻咒之柱）

period: Story set in the reign of Tafnekht (24th Dynasty, c. 730 BCE), recorded in Plutarch, De Iside 8 (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, sec. VIII

summary.en: King Technatis, eating mean soldier's food on the Arabian campaign and sleeping on the bare ground, conceived such love of poverty that with the priests' permission he raised in the temple of Thebes a column full of curses against Menes, the first king who had drawn the Egyptians from their frugal course of life.
summary.zh: 塔夫奈赫特王遠征時食兵卒之粗食、臥於赤地，遂生出對儉樸之深情，得祭司之許，於底比斯神廟立柱，刻滿詛咒——咒那第一位使埃及人離儉樸生活之王美尼斯。

sensitivity.note: Ancient anecdote-myth via Plutarch; no living community restrictions. Budge's footnote doubts Tafnekht's authority at Thebes.

passages.text: All agree, however, in saying that so great was the abhorrence which the ancient Egyptians expressed for whatever tended to promote luxury, expense, and voluptuousness, that in order to expose it as much as possible they erected a column in one of the temples of Thebes, full of curses against their king Meinis, who first drew them off from their former frugal and parsimonious course of life. The immediate cause for the erection of the pillar is thus given: Technatis, the father of Bocchoris, leading an army against the Arabians, and his baggage and provisions not coming up to him as soon as he expected, was therefore obliged to eat some of the very poor food which was obtainable, and having eaten, he lay down on the bare ground and slept very soundly. This gave him a great affection for a mean and frugal diet, and induced him to curse the memory of Meinis, and with the permission of the priests he made these curses public by cutting them upon a pillar.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. VIII. / Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. VIII.
passages.zh: 然而眾人都一致說道，古代埃及人對一切助長奢靡、耗費與淫逸之事所表現出的憎惡如此強烈，以至於為了盡可能揭露這種風氣，他們在底比斯的一座神廟中豎立了一根石柱，柱上滿是對其國王梅尼斯的詛咒，因為正是梅尼斯首先使他們背離了昔日節儉樸素的生活方式。豎立此柱的直接緣由是這樣的：波科里斯之父特克納提斯率軍征討阿拉伯人，其輜重與糧食未能如他所期望的那般及時送達，因此他不得不吃些所能得到的極粗劣的食物，食畢便躺在光地上，睡得十分酣沉。這使他對粗陋節儉的飲食大為喜愛，並促使他詛咒梅尼斯之名，經祭司許可，他將這些詛咒刻於石柱之上，公之於眾。

title.en: Ares Comes to His Mother: The Battle of Staves at Papremis
title.zh: 阿瑞斯探母：帕普雷米斯的棍戰

region.en: Papremis, Nile Delta, Egypt (festival of the war-god)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲帕普雷米斯（戰神祭日）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.63 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 62-63

summary.en: At the festival of the war-god (Ares) at Papremis, the image is drawn in its shrine toward the temple while a thousand men with clubs block the gate — for the god, once grown away from his mother, had to fight his way past her temple attendants to visit her; hence, say the priests, the ritual combat in his honor, in which heads are broken and (Egyptians insist) no one dies.
summary.zh: 帕普雷米斯戰神祭日，神像乘車欲入神廟，千名持棍者封門相拒——蓋因神自幼離母，長成後欲探母而不獲准入，遂引外人破門而入。祭司稱：此棍戰之禮即由此而立，且謂傷者眾而死者無。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ethnographic myth via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. 'ritual-origin' is the intended topic tag; see ledger note.

passages.text: At Papremis they do sacrifice and worship as elsewhere, and besides that, when the sun begins to go down, while some few of the priests are occupied with the image of the god, the greater number of them stand in the entrance of the temple with wooden clubs, and other persons to the number of more than a thousand men with purpose to perform a vow, these also having all of them staves of wood, stand in a body opposite to those: and the image, which is in a small shrine of wood covered over with gold, they take out on the day before to another sacred building.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.63.
passages.zh: 在帕普雷米斯，他們也如別處一樣獻祭禮拜；除此之外，當太陽開始西沉時，少數祭司忙於照料神像，而大多數祭司則手持木棒站在神廟入口處，另有一千多人為還願而來，他們也全都手持木杖，結成一隊與那些人相對而立；那尊神像供在一座覆以金箔的小木龕中，他們在前一日便將其抬出，送往另一座聖殿。

passages.text: The few then who have been left about the image, draw a wain with four wheels, which bears the shrine and the image that is within the shrine, and the other priests standing in the gateway try to prevent it from entering, and the men who are under a vow come to the assistance of the god and strike them, while the others defend themselves. Then there comes to be a hard fight with staves, and they break one another's heads, and I am of opinion that many even die of the wounds they receive; the Egyptians however told me that no one died.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.63.
passages.zh: 於是，留守在神像旁的少數幾人拉動一輛四輪車，車上載著神龕以及龕中的神像，而站在門口的其他祭司則設法阻止它進入，那些還願之人前來相助神明，毆打他們，另一方則自衛還擊。於是便發生了一場以木杖相搏的激烈打鬥，彼此打破頭顱，我認為甚至有許多人因所受的傷而死；然而埃及人卻告訴我，並無一人死亡。

passages.text: This solemn assembly the people of the place say that they established for the following reason: — the mother of Ares, they say, used to dwell in this temple, and Ares, having been brought up away from her, when he grew up came thither desiring to visit his mother, and the attendants of his mother's temple, not having seen him before, did not permit him to pass in, but kept him away; and he brought men to help him from another city and handled roughly the attendants of the temple, and entered to visit his mother. Hence, they say, this exchange of blows has become the custom in honour of Ares upon his festival.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.63.
passages.zh: 當地人說，他們之所以設立這莊嚴的集會，是為了以下緣故：——他們說，阿瑞斯的母親曾住在這座神廟裡，而阿瑞斯自幼被帶離她身邊撫養，長大後便來到此地，想探望母親；他母親神廟的侍從們先前未曾見過他，不許他進去，把他擋在外面；於是他從別的城市帶來人手相助，粗暴地對待神廟的侍從，並進去探望了母親。他們說，因此之故，在阿瑞斯的節慶上互相毆打便成了習俗。

title.en: The Voyage to Bubastis: Egypt's Wildest Festival
title.zh: 赴布巴斯提斯之舟：埃及最狂歡的節日

region.en: Nile from the Delta towns to Bubastis (temple of Bastet, Greek Artemis)
region.zh: 尼羅河自三角洲諸城至布巴斯提斯（貝斯特/阿爾忒彌斯神廟）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.59-60 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 59-60

summary.en: The greatest of Egypt's pilgrim feasts: men and women sail to Bubastis together in one boat, women rattling sistra, men piping; at every riverside town the women jeer at the shore-women and dance, some pulling up their garments; at Bubastis more wine is drunk in the festival than in the rest of the year, and, the natives say, seven hundred myriads of people gather yearly.
summary.zh: 埃及最盛大的朝節：男女同舟赴布巴斯提斯，婦人搖鈴，男子吹笛；沿途每城，船上的女人向岸上的女人叫喊戲謔，且舞且起衣；至布巴斯提斯，一節所耗之酒多於全年其餘時日——當地人稱歲歲聚者達七十萬眾。

sensitivity.note: Ancient festival description via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The Egyptians hold their solemn assemblies not once in the year but often, especially and with the greatest zeal and devotion at the city of Bubastis for Artemis, and next at Busiris for Isis; for in this last-named city there is a very great temple of Isis, and this city stands in the middle of the Delta of Egypt; now Isis is in the tongue of the Hellenes Demeter: thirdly, they have a solemn assembly at the city of Sais for Athene, fourthly at Heliopolis for the Sun (Helios), fifthly at the city of Buto in honour of Leto, and sixthly at the city of Papremis for Ares.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.59.
passages.zh: 埃及人舉行莊嚴集會並非一年一次，而是屢屢舉行，尤其以最大的熱忱與虔誠在布巴斯提斯城為阿耳忒彌斯舉行，其次在布西里斯為伊西斯舉行；因為在這後者之城有一座極大的伊西斯神廟，而此城位於埃及三角洲的中央；伊西斯在希臘人的語言中即得墨忒耳：第三，他們在賽斯城為雅典娜舉行莊嚴集會，第四在赫利奧波利斯為太陽（赫利俄斯），第五在布托城為勒托，第六在帕普雷米斯城為阿瑞斯。

passages.text: Now, when they are coming to the city of Bubastis they do as follows: — they sail men and women together, and a great multitude of each sex in every boat; and some of the women have rattles and rattle with them, while some of the men play the flute during the whole time of the voyage, and the rest, both women and men, sing and clap their hands; and when as they sail they come opposite to any city on the way they bring the boat to land, and some of the women continue to do as I have said, others cry aloud and jeer at the women in that city, some dance, and some stand up and pull up their garments. This they do by every city along the river-bank; and when they come to Bubastis they hold festival celebrating great sacrifices, and more wine of grapes is consumed upon that festival than during the whole of the rest of the year. To this place (so say the natives) they come together year by year even to the number of seventy myriads of men and women, besides children.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.60.
passages.zh: 如今，當他們前往布巴斯提斯城時，他們如此行事：——他們男女一同乘船，每艘船上男女皆為數眾多；有些婦女帶著響器，一路搖響，有些男子則在整個航程中吹奏笛子，其餘的人，無論男女，都唱歌拍手；當他們航行途中迎面經過任何城市時，便把船靠岸，有些婦女繼續如我所說的那樣做，另一些則高聲呼喊，嘲笑那城中的婦女，有些跳舞，有些站起來掀起衣裳。他們沿河岸每到一城都這樣做；當他們到達布巴斯提斯時，便舉行節慶，獻上盛大的祭品，而在此節慶上消耗的葡萄酒比一年其餘全部時間所消耗的還要多。據當地人說，每年聚集到這地方的人，男女合計竟達七十萬之眾，尚不計兒童。

title.en: The Black Doves of Thebes: The Origin of the Oracles
title.zh: 底比斯黑鴿：神諭之源

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (temple of Zeus/Amon; whence the oracle-priestesses were carried)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（宙斯/阿蒙神廟；神諭女祭司自此被擄）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.54-57 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 54-57

summary.en: The priests of Theban Zeus/Amon claim two consecrated women were carried off by Phoenicians, one sold to Libya, one to Greece — founding the oracles of Ammon and of Dodona; the Dodona priestesses themselves say two black doves flew from Thebes, one to an oak at Dodona speaking with human voice, one bidding the Libyans make an oracle; Herodotus half-believes: the 'doves' were Egyptian women, whose foreign speech sounded like birds.
summary.zh: 底比斯阿蒙祭司稱：兩名侍神女子被腓尼基人擄走，一售利比亞、一售希臘——分別創立阿蒙與多多納神諭；多多納女祭司則言：兩隻黑鴿自底比斯飛出，一落橡樹作人言，一令利比亞人立神諭。希羅多德半信半疑：『鴿』實為埃及女子，其異語聽來如鳥啼。

sensitivity.note: Ancient origin myth via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The priests of the Theban Zeus told me that two women in the service of the temple had been carried away from Thebes by Phenicians, and that they had heard that one of them had been sold to go into Libya and the other to the Hellenes; and these women, they said, were they who first founded the prophetic seats among the nations which have been named: and when I inquired whence they knew so perfectly of this tale which they told, they said in reply that a great search had been made by the priests after these women, and that they had not been able to find them, but they had heard afterwards this tale about them which they were telling.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.54.
passages.zh: 底比斯的宙斯神的祭司告訴我，有兩名在神廟中服役的婦女被腓尼基人從底比斯擄走，他們聽說其中一人被賣往利比亞，另一人被賣往希臘人那裡；他們說，正是這兩名婦女最先在方才所提及的那些民族中建立了預言的神諭之所：當我問他們何以如此確知他們所講的這個故事時，他們回答說，祭司們曾對這兩名婦女大加搜尋，卻未能找到她們，但後來聽到了他們正在講述的關於她們的這個故事。

passages.text: They say that two black doves flew from Thebes to Egypt, and came one of them to Libya and the other to their land. And this latter settled upon an oak-tree and spoke with human voice, saying that it was necessary that a prophetic seat of Zeus should be established in that place; and they supposed that that was of the gods which was announced to them, and made one accordingly: and the dove which went away to the Libyans, they say, bade the Libyans to make an Oracle of Ammon; and this also is of Zeus.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.55.
passages.zh: 他們說，有兩隻黑鴿從底比斯飛往埃及，其中一隻到了利比亞，另一隻到了他們的國土。這後一隻棲息在一棵橡樹上，發出人的聲音說話，說必須在那地方建立一座宙斯的神諭之所；他們便以為向他們宣告的乃是出於神意，於是照此建立了一座：而飛往利比亞人那裡的那隻鴿子，他們說，吩咐利比亞人建立阿蒙的神諭；這也同樣是出於宙斯。

passages.text: Moreover, I think that the women were called doves by the people of Dodona for the reason that they were Barbarians and because it seemed to them that they uttered voice like birds; but after a time (they say) the dove spoke with human voice, that is when the woman began to speak so that they could understand; but so long as she spoke a Barbarian tongue she seemed to them to be uttering voice like a bird: for had it been really a dove, how could it speak with human voice? And in saying that the dove was black, they indicate that the woman was Egyptian.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.57.
passages.zh: 此外，我認為多 Dodona 的人之所以稱這些婦女為鴿子，是因為她們是蠻族，且在他們看來她們發出的聲音像鳥鳴；但過了些時候（他們說），那鴿子便發出人的聲音說話了，也就是當那婦女開始說話、使他們能夠聽懂的時候；然而只要她說的是蠻族的語言，在他們看來她就像在發出鳥鳴：因為若真是隻鴿子，又怎能發出人的聲音說話呢？而他們說那鴿子是黑色的，則表明那婦女是埃及人。

title.en: Melampus Learns the Phallos Procession in Egypt
title.zh: 墨蘭普斯在埃及習得陽具遊行

region.en: Egyptian villages and Boeotia (transmission of the Dionysos rites)
region.zh: 埃及村莊與玻俄提亞（狄俄倪索斯祭祀之傳播）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.48-49 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 48-49

summary.en: Egyptian women carry cubit-high dancing figures of Dionysos with movable phallos through the villages behind a flute, singing his praises — the rites, says Herodotus, that Melampus son of Amytheon learned in Egypt and taught to the Greeks, who thereafter carried the phallos in procession for Dionysos.
summary.zh: 埃及婦女攜一肘高之狄俄倪索斯舞像巡行村落，像之陽具以線操動，笛聲前導，頌歌隨行——希羅多德謂：墨蘭普斯習此於埃及，而後傳授希臘人，故希臘有陽具遊行之祭。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ritual-origin account via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Then for Dionysos on the eve of the festival each one kills a pig by cutting its throat before his own doors, and after that he gives the pig to the swineherd who sold it to him, to carry away again; and the rest of the feast of Dionysos is celebrated by the Egyptians in the same way as by the Hellenes in almost all things except choral dances, but instead of the phallos they have invented another contrivance, namely figures of about a cubit in height worked by strings, which women carry about the villages, with the privy member made to move and not much less in size than the rest of the body: and a flute goes before and they follow singing the praises of Dionysos.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.48.
passages.zh: 於是，在狄俄尼索斯節的前夕，每個人都在自家門前割斷一頭豬的喉嚨將其宰殺，之後便把這頭豬交給賣豬給他的牧豬人，讓他再帶走；狄俄尼索斯節其餘的慶典，埃及人幾乎在一切事情上都與希臘人同樣慶祝，唯有歌舞合唱除外，而他們不用陽具，卻發明了另一種裝置，即約有一肘高、以繩索操縱的人偶，由婦女們帶著在村落間遊行，其人偶的私處被做得能活動，大小與身體其餘部分相差無幾：並有笛聲在前引路，她們隨後而行，歌唱頌揚狄俄尼索斯。

passages.text: Now I think that Melampus the son of Amytheon was not without knowledge of these rites of sacrifice, but was acquainted with them: for Melampus is he who first set forth to the Hellenes the name of Dionysos and the manner of sacrifice and the procession of the phallos. Strictly speaking indeed, he when he made it known did not take in the whole, but those wise men who came after him made it known more at large. I say then that Melampus being a man of ability contrived for himself an art of divination, and having learnt from Egypt he taught the Hellenes many things, and among them those that concern Dionysos, making changes in some few points of them.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.49.
passages.zh: 我認為，阿密忒翁之子墨蘭波斯並非不通曉這些獻祭的儀節，而是熟知它們：因為正是墨蘭波斯首先向希臘人闡明了狄俄尼索斯之名、獻祭的方式以及陽具的遊行。嚴格說來，他宣示之時並未囊括全部，而是那些追隨他的智者們更為詳盡地加以闡明。因此我說，墨蘭波斯身為能幹之人，為自己創製了一門占卜之術，並從埃及學得之後教給了希臘人許多事物，其中也包括與狄俄尼索斯有關的那些，並在其中少數幾點上作了更改。

title.en: The Phoenix Carries Its Father to the Temple of the Sun
title.zh: 不死鳥負父赴日廟

region.en: Heliopolis, Egypt (temple of the Sun, where the phoenix appears)
region.zh: 埃及赫利奧波利斯（不死鳥顯現之日神廟）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.73 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 73

summary.en: The people of Heliopolis say the phoenix comes at intervals of five hundred years, when its father dies: partly gold-feathered and partly red, like an eagle in outline, it flies from Arabia bearing its father — plastered up in myrrh — to the temple of the Sun, and buries him there. Herodotus saw the bird only in painting, and says he cannot believe the story.
summary.zh: 赫利奧波利斯人言：不死鳥每五百年一至，值其父死時而來；羽半金半赤，形若鷹，自阿拉伯攜其父——以沒藥封裹——負至日神廟而葬之。希羅多德僅於畫中見之，自言未敢盡信。

sensitivity.note: Ancient wonder-tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. The Egyptian Bennu bird underlies the Greek phoenix.

passages.text: There is also another sacred bird called the phoenix which I did not myself see except in painting, for in truth he comes to them very rarely, at intervals, as the people of Heliopolis say, of five hundred years; and these say that he comes regularly when his father dies; and if he be like the painting, he is of this size and nature, that is to say, some of his feathers are of gold colour and others red, and in outline and size he is as nearly as possible like an eagle. This bird they say (but I cannot believe the story) contrives as follows: — setting forth from Arabia he conveys his father, they say, to the temple of the Sun plastered up in myrrh, and buries him in the temple of the Sun.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.73.
passages.zh: 還有一種聖鳥名叫鳳凰，我本人除在圖畫中之外未曾見過，因為說實話它極少來到他們那裡，據赫利奧波利斯的人說，每隔五百年才來一次；他們說，它總是在其父死去時按時前來；倘若它與圖畫相符，其大小與性質便是如此，也就是說，它的一些羽毛呈金色，另一些呈紅色，而在輪廓與大小上，它盡可能地像一隻鷹。他們說這鳥（但我無法相信這故事）是這樣做的：——它從阿拉伯出發，他們說，將其父裹在沒藥中封好，運到太陽神廟，並葬於太陽神廟之中。

passages.text: And he conveys him thus: — he forms first an egg of myrrh as large as he is able to carry, and then he makes trial of carrying it, and when he has made trial sufficiently, then he hollows out the egg and places his father within it and plasters over with other myrrh that part of the egg where he hollowed it out to put his father in, and when his father is laid in it, it proves (they say) to be of the same weight as it was; and after he has plastered it up, he conveys the whole to Egypt to the temple of the Sun.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.73.
passages.zh: 它這樣搬運其父：——它先做成一個它力所能搬運的那麼大的沒藥蛋，然後試著搬運它，待試得足夠之後，便把蛋掏空，將其父置於其中，再用別的沒藥把蛋上為放入其父而掏空的那部分封塗起來，當其父被安置其中後，據說這蛋的重量與原先一樣；待它封塗完畢，便把整個蛋運到埃及的太陽神廟。

title.en: The Ibis and the Winged Serpents of Arabia
title.zh: 朱鷺與阿拉伯飛蛇

region.en: Mountain pass opposite Buto, edge of Egypt (where the ibis meets the flying serpents)
region.zh: 埃及邊境布托對面之山口（朱鷺迎擊飛蛇之地）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.75-76 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 75-76

summary.en: Each spring winged serpents fly from Arabia toward Egypt, and the ibises meet them at the narrow pass and kill them; heaps of their bones and spines cover the ground — the aition, Herodotus reports, of the ibis' great honour in Egypt, who saw the heaps himself and learned the tale from both Arabians and Egyptians.
summary.zh: 每歲春分，飛蛇自阿拉伯撲向埃及，朱鷺守狹口而擊殺之——蛇骨蛇棘遍堆於地，為埃及尊崇朱鷺之由。希羅多德自稱親見其堆，且此事得自阿拉伯人與埃及人兩方之口。

sensitivity.note: Ancient aition via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: There is a region moreover in Arabia, situated nearly over against the city of Buto, to which place I came to inquire about the winged serpents: and when I came thither I saw bones of serpents and spines in quantity so great that it is impossible to make report of the number, and there were heaps of spines, some heaps large and others less large and others smaller still than these, and these heaps were many in number. This region in which the spines are scattered upon the ground is of the nature of an entrance from a narrow mountain pass to a great plain, which plain adjoins the plain of Egypt; and the story goes that at the beginning of spring winged serpents from Arabia fly towards Egypt, and the birds called ibises meet them at the entrance to this country and do not suffer the serpents to go by but kill them. On account of this deed it is (say the Arabians) that the ibis has come to be greatly honoured by the Egyptians, and the Egyptians also agree that it is for this reason that they honour these birds.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.75. / Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.75.
passages.zh: 此外，在阿拉伯還有一個地區，幾乎正對著布托城，我曾到那裡去探問有關翼蛇之事：當我到達那裡時，我看見蛇骨與脊骨數量之多，多得無法報告其數目，而且脊骨堆積成堆，有些堆大，有些堆稍小，有些比這些還更小，而這些堆為數眾多。這些脊骨散落於地的地區，其地勢如同從一處狹窄的山隘通向一片大平原的入口，這片平原與埃及的平原相接；傳說在初春時節，翼蛇從阿拉伯飛向埃及，而名叫朱鷺的鳥在這地方的入口處迎擊它們，不許蛇通過，而是將它們殺死。正因這一功績（阿拉伯人說），朱鷺才受到埃及人的極大尊崇，埃及人也同意，正是為了這個緣故他們才尊崇這些鳥。

title.en: Sesostris the Conqueror: Pillars, Scythians, and the Fire of Daphnai
title.zh: 征服者塞索斯特里斯：石柱、斯基泰與達夫奈之火

region.en: From the Erythraian Sea to the Phasis (Sesostris' march; symbolic pin at Daphnai, Pelusium)
region.zh: 自紅海至法西斯河（塞索斯特里斯之遠征；象徵定位於達夫奈/佩魯西翁）

period: Priests' account of an Old or New Kingdom conqueror, recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.102-110 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 102-110

summary.en: Sesostris sails the Erythraian Sea, marches over the continent setting up pillars — brave nations get his name, cowards get the emblem of a woman — until he crosses to Europe and subdues the Scythians; returning through Daphnai, his brother invites him to a feast and piles the house with brushwood; his wife counsels laying two of his six sons upon the pyre as a bridge, and the king escapes over their bodies while the brothers burn.
summary.zh: 塞索斯特里斯先航紅海，後率大軍征陸，凡遇勇敢死戰之國則立柱刻名，懦弱者則刻女陰以辱之；及至歐洲，降斯基泰而返。歸途達夫奈，其弟邀宴，積薪焚宅；其妻獻策：以二子伏火為橋，王履之而過，二子焚死，餘者得生。

sensitivity.note: Ancient heroic legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. Egyptologists identify Sesostris with Senusret I/III or Ramesses II.

passages.text: Passing these by I shall make mention of the king who came after these, whose name was Sesostris. He (the priests said) first of all set out with ships of war from the Arabian gulf and subdued those who dwelt by the shores of the Erythraian Sea, until as he sailed he came to a sea which could no further be navigated by reason of shoals: then secondly, after he had returned to Egypt, according to the report of the priests he took a great army and marched over the continent, subduing every nation which stood in his way: and those of them whom he found valiant and fighting desperately for their freedom, in their lands he set up pillars ...; but as to those of whose cities he obtained possession without fighting or with ease, on their pillars he inscribed words after the same tenor as he did for the nations which had shown themselves courageous, and in addition he drew upon them the hidden parts of a woman, desiring to signify by this that the people were cowards and effeminate.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.102, condensed with ellipsis; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 略過這些，我將提及繼他們之後到來的那位國王，其名為塞索斯特里斯。他（祭司們說）首先率戰船從阿拉伯灣出發，征服了居住在厄律特剌海沿岸的人們，直到他航行至一片因淺灘而無法再通航的海為止：然後其次，在他返回埃及之後，據祭司們所述，他率領一支大軍在陸地上行進，征服了每一個擋在他路上的民族：對於其中他發現勇敢並為自由拼死作戰的那些人，他在他們的土地上立起石柱……；至於那些他未經戰鬥或輕易便佔有其城池的人，他在他們的石柱上刻下與對那些表現出勇氣的民族同樣意旨的文字，此外還在上面畫出女子的隱秘部位，想以此表示這些人是懦夫和柔弱之輩。

passages.text: Thus doing he traversed the continent, until at last he passed over to Europe from Asia and subdued the Scythians and also the Thracians. These, I am of opinion, were the furthest people to which the Egyptian army came, for in their country the pillars are found to have been set up, but in the land beyond this they are no longer found.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.103.
passages.zh: 他如此行事，走遍了這片大陸，最後從亞洲渡海到了歐洲，征服了斯基泰人，也征服了色雷斯人。我認為，這些人是埃及軍隊所到達的最遠的民族，因為在他們的國度裡可以發現那些石柱已被立起，而在這之外的更遠地方，就再也找不到石柱了。

passages.text: As this Egyptian Sesostris was returning and bringing back many men of the nations whose lands he had subdued, when he came (said the priests) to Daphnai in the district of Pelusion on his journey home, his brother to whom Sesostris had entrusted the charge of Egypt invited him and with him his sons to a feast; and then he piled the house round with brushwood and set it on fire: and Sesostris when he discovered this forthwith took counsel with his wife, for he was bringing with him (they said) his wife also; and she counselled him to lay out upon the pyre two of his sons, which were six in number, and so to make a bridge over the burning mass, and that they passing over their bodies should thus escape. This, they said, Sesostris did, and two of his sons were burnt to death in this manner, but the rest got away safe with their father.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.107.
