passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Xi Jing, the binding; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Guo Pu's commentary and the Yi-cycle cross-reference; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天帝命人將凶手擒獲，捆縛於疏屬山，右腳以石為桎，雙臂被刺穿並反鎖於山岩之後。二人便立於此處，直至刑期屆滿。然而被殺之神並未真正死去：他甦醒過來，化為一頭食人的龍首之獸，成為焚燒大地上的六怪之一——郭璞如此記載——直到射手羿的弓終結了這場復生。

title.en: Wang Hai, the Ox-Trader Murdered Among the Yi People
title.zh: 王亥僕牛

region.en: Youyi, the land of the Yi people, north of the Yellow River (symbolic pin: northern Hebei)
region.zh: 有易之邦（象徵性定位）

period: Shanhaijing, Da Huang Dong Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE (parallel in Guo Pu's quoted Bamboo Annals)

source.work: Shanhaijing, Da Huang Dong Jing: Wang Hai and the oxen of Youyi; the revenge of Shang Jia

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Wang Hai, forefather of the Shang royal house, sojourned among the Yi people with his herds of oxen, and the lord of the Yi murdered him and took the cattle. His son Shang Jia raised a host and appealed to the River God, who armed his soldiers; the Yi lord was killed and his people scattered — the oldest narrative episode in the Shanhaijing, and the founding crime-and-vengeance tale of the Shang dynasty.
summary.zh: 王亥託於有易、河伯僕牛，有易殺王亥，取僕牛；上甲微假師於河伯以伐有易，滅之——殷王子亥賓於有易，有易之君殺而放之（郭璞引竹書）。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original and Guo Pu's quoted Bamboo Annals note. The oldest continuous narrative in the Shanhaijing; foundational to Shang genealogy (cf. chinese-shijing-jian-di-blackbird).

passages.text: Wang Hai, a prince of the Shang royal line, took his droves of oxen and sojourned among the people of Youyi, trusting them with his herds and his household — the book says he traded with them through the River God's keeping.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Dong Jing, Wang Hai entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 商室王族之子王亥，帶著成群的牛隻寄居於有易之民中，將牲畜與家眾託付給他們——書上說，他透過河神的看顧與他們交易。

passages.text: The lord of the Yi coveted the herds, murdered Wang Hai, and seized the oxen — the hospitality broken, the trader killed in the country that had received him. Wang Hai's son Shang Jia raised an army and asked the River God for soldiers; the River God lent his host, and the army of Shang Jia destroyed the lord of Youyi and scattered his people. Thus the house of Shang began its power in the vengeance of a murdered son — with a river-god as ally.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Dong Jing, with Guo Pu's Bamboo Annals note; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Dong Jing, the revenge; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有易之君覬覦那群牲畜，殺了王亥，奪走牛隻——待客之義既已敗壞，行商者便死於曾接納他的國度。王亥之子上甲微興兵，向河神求取兵眾；河神借出他的部眾，上甲微的軍隊便滅了有易之君，驅散其民。商室之興，便始於為子者復仇之力——以河神為盟友。

title.en: The Flying Chariots of Qigong, the One-Armed Country
title.zh: 奇肱飛車

region.en: Qigong, the one-armed country of the far west (symbolic pin: western deserts)
region.zh: 奇肱之國（象徵性定位）

period: Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Xi Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE; flying-chariot note in Guo Pu (quoting Bowuzhi)

source.work: Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Xi Jing: the country of Qigong; Guo Pu's note on the wind-chariots of the westerners

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Far west lives the country of Qigong, whose people have one arm, three eyes, yin and yang both in their bodies, and mastery of machines: they make chariots that ride the wind. Guo Pu's note preserves the tale of one such chariot that flew a visitor clear to Yu Province by night, and was grounded ten years, waiting for a west wind to carry its maker home.
summary.zh: 奇肱之國，其人一臂三目，有陰有陽；郭璞注引博物志：奇肱人善為機巧，作飛車，乘風遠行——湯時飛車至豫州，十年西風乃歸。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing text and Guo Pu's quoted Bowuzhi note.

passages.text: In the far west is the country of Qigong, whose people have a single arm and three eyes, yin and yang both in one body — and hands skilled beyond all other peoples in the making of machines. Their machines are wind-chariots, says the old note: carriages that ride the moving air for ten thousand li. One such chariot, in the age of Tang, came down by night into the province of Yu with a maker of Qigong in it; the Emperor kept the machine grounded, and for ten years it waited until a west wind rose to carry its maker home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Xi Jing, Qigong entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Guo Pu's note quoting the Bowuzhi; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 極西之地有奇肱之國，其民一臂三眼，陰陽同具於一身——而其手之巧，製器之能，冠絕萬民。舊注云，其器為風車：乘風而行萬里之車。唐堯之世，曾有一車夜降於豫州，車中載一奇肱之匠；帝命留其器於地，十年之間，待西風起，方送其匠歸鄉。

title.en: Nüchou, Burned to Death by the Ten Suns
title.zh: 女丑之屍

region.en: North of the land of Husbands (symbolic pin: eastern waste)
region.zh: 丈夫之北（象徵性定位）

period: Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Xi Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Xi Jing: the corpse of Nüchou, roasted alive by the ten suns

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The corpse of Nüchou was born and roasted to death by the ten suns while she stood on a mountain north of the land of Husbands, shielding her face with her right hand — the ritual memory of the drought-ordeal in which a designated 'drought woman' is exposed to the sun's heat to break a dry spell, its victim fixed forever in the gazetteer.
summary.zh: 女丑之屍，生而十日炙殺之，在丈夫北，以右手鄣其面；十日居上，女丑居山之上——旱曬巫儀之記憶。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original. Commentators read the entry as the mythic record of drought-exorcism rites using exposed women (the 'ba' ritual); sensitive for its treatment of a female ritual victim — noted.

passages.text: The corpse called Nüchou — Woman Chou — was born, and the ten suns came out and roasted her to death; she stood on a mountain north of the land of Husbands, holding her right hand over her face as the heat came down.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Xi Jing, Nüchou entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 名曰女丑之尸——女丑生而十日並出，炙之而死；她立於丈夫國北之山上，熱氣降下之時，以右手遮面。

passages.text: The entry is read by commentators as the memory of a rite: in drought, a woman set apart as the 'drought-phantom' was exposed on a height to the sun's fire, to draw the sky's anger down on herself and release the rain. The Shanhaijing keeps the rite's victim where the suns left her — on the mountain, hand at her face, under ten burning skies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing entry with traditional commentary; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 注家讀此條，以為乃一祭儀之遺憶：遇旱，擇一女子為「旱魃」，曝於高處以受日火，欲引天之怒降於己身，而後釋雨。山海經將此祭儀之犧牲者留於十日所棄之處——山上，手掩其面，居於十輪烈日之下。

title.en: Xiage, the Headless General Who Still Stands
title.zh: 夏耕之屍

region.en: Wushan, the Shamans' Mountain (pin: Three Gorges region)
region.zh: 巫山

period: Shanhaijing, Da Huang Xi Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing, Da Huang Xi Jing: the headless corpse of Xiaiage, general of Jie

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: A figure stands in the Great Waste with no head, gripping his halberd and shield — Xiaiage, the corpse of the general whom Cheng-tang beheaded before him when he overthrew the last king of Xia. The headless general ran from his disgrace and descended on Wushan, the Shamans' Mountain, where he keeps his post to this day: defeat survived as standing.
summary.zh: 有人無首，操戈盾立，名曰夏耕之屍；故成湯伐夏桀於章山，克之，斬耕厥前——耕既立，無首，走厥咎，乃降於巫山。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original. Pairs with Xingtian (existing combined record shanhaijing-kua-fu): two headless standing figures of the corpus.

passages.text: There stands in the Great Waste a man with no head, gripping his halberd and his shield — the corpse of Xiaiage, general in the host of the last king of Xia. When Cheng-tang overthrew Jie and cut the general down before the king's own face, the beheaded Xiaiage rose and ran from his disgrace — headless still — and came down upon Wushan, the mountain of the shamans, where he keeps his stand in the wind with his weapons up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Xi Jing, Xiaiage entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Xi Jing; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大荒之中立一無頭之人，手持戈與盾——此乃夏后氏末王之軍中將領夏耕之尸。當成湯推翻桀，於王之面前斬殺此將，斷首之夏耕起身而逃，以避其辱——仍無首——下至巫山，群巫之山，持兵器而立於風中，守其位不去。

title.en: The Ten Gods of Nüwa's Bowels
title.zh: 女媧之腸

region.en: Liguang, the Wide Chestnut Wild (symbolic pin: western waste)
region.zh: 栗廣之野（象徵性定位）

period: Shanhaijing, Da Huang Xi Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing, Da Huang Xi Jing: the ten gods born of Nüwa's entrails

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: In the Wide Chestnut Wild there stand ten gods, called 'the bowels of Nüwa,' who became gods and lie athwart the road — the oldest Shanhaijing witness of the creator goddess: even her discarded innards turn divine, ten powers laid across the travellers' way like a living gate.
summary.zh: 有神十人，名曰女媧之腸，化為神，處栗廣之野，橫道而處——創世女神之腸亦化神。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original. The oldest textual witness of Nüwa in the corpus; links to the dismembered-creator pattern (Pangu pre-existing record).

passages.text: In the Wide Chestnut Wild of the Great Waste there are ten gods, and their name is the Bowels of Nüwa: the inner parts of the creator goddess, which changed into powers of themselves and took their place in the wild. They lie athwart the road, ten across the way — a gate of the goddess's own body, through which every traveller in the mythic west must pass; the entry is the oldest mention of Nüwa in the whole Shanhaijing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Xi Jing, Nüwa bowels entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Shanhaijing entry with traditional commentary; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在大荒的廣栗之野有十位神，名為女媧之腸：那是創世女神的內臟，化為自身的神力，佔據了荒野之地。他們橫臥於道路之上，十位並列擋住去路——那是女神自身軀體所化之門，神話西方每一位行旅者都必經此處；此段記載是全本《山海經》中關於女媧最早的一則。

title.en: Shu Hai Measures the World on Foot
title.zh: 豎亥步測天地

region.en: From the east limit to the west limit of the world (symbolic pin: whole-earth survey)
region.zh: 自東極至於西極（象徵性定位）

period: Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Dong Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Dong Jing: Shu Hai's world-measurement on the Emperor's command

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The Emperor commanded Shu Hai to pace out the world: from the east limit to the west limit, five hundred million and a hundred thousand and nine thousand and eight hundred paces. Shu Hai walked with the reckoning-rods in his right hand, pointing north of the Green Mounds with his left — the surveying myth that founds China's map of the world.
summary.zh: 帝命豎亥步，自東極至於西極，五億十萬九千八百步；豎亥右手把算，左手指青丘北——測地之神話。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original.

passages.text: The Emperor commanded Shu Hai to pace out the world, and Shu Hai walked from the limit of the east to the limit of the west, reckoning as he went: five hundred million, ten myriad, and nine thousand and eight hundred paces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Dong Jing, Shu Hai entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天帝命豎亥步量大地，豎亥便從東極走到西極，一路計算：五億十萬九千八百步。

passages.text: He walked with the reckoning-rods in his right hand and his left hand pointed at the north of the Green Mounds — a surveyor's posture fixed forever in the gazetteer. The measured world is the Emperor's world: the numbers walked out are the ground of all the maps that follow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Hai Wai Dong Jing; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他右手持算籌而行，左手指向青丘之北——這測量者的姿態，永遠定格於這部地志之中。所測量的大地即是天帝的大地：一步步走出的數字，便是其後所有地圖的根基。

title.en: The Lineage of Di Jun: Suns, Moons, and the Peoples of the Waste
title.zh: 帝俊世系

region.en: The Great Waste in every direction (mythic geography)
region.zh: 大荒諸野

period: Shanhaijing, Da Huang Jing chapters, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing, Da Huang Dong/Nan/Xi/Bei Jing: the children of Di Jun — the suns of Xihe, the moons of Changxi, and the ancestors of the waste peoples

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Di Jun, the supreme god of the Shanhaijing's genealogies, fathers the ten suns by Xihe and the twelve moons by Changxi — and by mortal wives the ancestors of the waste peoples: the Grain-growing country, the Black Teeth, the Middle-Rong, the Three-Body country, the Yan-long music-givers, and Houji himself, who in this version is Di Jun's son, not the footprint-child of the Shijing.
summary.zh: 帝俊妻羲和生十日，妻常羲生月十有二；又生中容、晏龍、黑齒、三身之國；大荒西經言帝俊生后稷，稷降以百穀——帝俊為大荒譜系之樞。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing genealogies. Variant-ancestry conflict with the Shijing's footprint-birth of Houji is deliberate comparative material, not error.

passages.text: Di Jun is the great father of the waste-world: by Xihe the sun-mother he begot the ten suns, by Changxi the moon-mother the twelve moons — the sky's whole order hangs on his two celestial marriages. By his mortal consorts he begot the founders of the waste peoples: the Grain-country, the Black Teeth who paint their teeth, the Middle-Rong, the Three-Body country of triple shadows, and Yan-long who first made music and invented the zither. The gazetteer turns blood into map: every people has a divine father to name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Dong Jing and Da Huang Xi Jing genealogies (compiler's rendering); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Jing genealogies; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 帝俊是荒外世界的大父：他與日母羲和生下十個太陽，與月母常羲生下十二個月亮——天空的整個秩序，都繫於他的兩樁天界婚姻。他與凡間配偶生下荒外諸族的始祖：穀國、染齒的黑齒國、中容國、三身三影的三身國，以及最先製作音樂、發明琴瑟的晏龍。這部地志將血脈化為地圖：每一族都有一位神聖的父親可供指名。

passages.text: One list even says Di Jun begot Houji, the Lord of Millet, who lowered the hundred grains from heaven for men — so in the Shanhaijing's version agriculture is a god's gift through a god's son, where the Shijing gives it through a footprint-born child. The genealogies disagree; the myth is richer for it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Xi Jing, Houji entry; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一份名錄甚至說，帝俊生后稷，即穀神，他從天上為人類降下百穀——因此在《山海經》的版本裡，農業是神藉其子所賜的禮物，而《詩經》則說它來自一個因足跡而生的孩子。諸家譜系說法不一；神話卻因此更加豐富。

title.en: The Lineage of the Flame Emperor: Zhurong, Gonggong, and the Earth God
title.zh: 炎帝世系

region.en: The rivers and wilds of the mythic south (symbolic pin: Yangzi basin)
region.zh: 江水之野（象徵性定位）

period: Shanhaijing, Hai Nei Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing, Hai Nei Jing: the genealogy of the Flame Emperor — Yandi, Yanshi?, Zhurong, Gonggong, Houtu

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The Hai Nei Jing strings the fire-line of the gods: the Flame Emperor's wife bore Yanshi, and the line ran through Jie-bing and Xi-qi, then Zhurong the fire-god, who went down to dwell on the Yangzi and fathered Gonggong — the pillar-striking water-power — and Gonggong fathered Houtu, the god of earth. Four elements in one dynasty: fire begets water begets earth.
summary.zh: 炎帝之妻，赤水之子聽訞，生炎居，炎居生節並，節並生戲器，戲器生祝融；祝融降處於江水，生共工；共工生術器……及后土——火生水、水生土之譜。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing genealogy. The Gonggong of this line links to the pillar-striking myth (chinese-gonggong-buzhou).

passages.text: The Flame Emperor married a daughter of the Red Water, and their line ran: Yanshi, then Jie-bing, then Xi-qi, then Zhurong the lord of fire — the book keeps each generation named, a dynasty of flame in four steps. Zhurong came down to dwell on the Yangzi and fathered Gonggong, the water-power who would one day strike the sky-pillar; and Gonggong fathered Houtu, the god of earth, who gives the ground its name. Fire begets water, water begets earth — the elements arranged as a family tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Hai Nei Jing, Yandi genealogy (compiler's rendering); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Hai Nei Jing; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 炎帝娶赤水之女，其世系依次為：炎居，然後節並，然後戲器，然後火神祝融——此書將每一代都記下名字，四步便成一個火焰的王朝。祝融下居於江水，生共工，即那位日後撞擊天柱的水神；共工生后土，即大地之神，大地之名即由他而來。火生水，水生土——諸元素被排列成一株家族樹。

title.en: The Lineage of the Yellow Emperor: Changyi, Hanliu, and Zhuanxu
title.zh: 黃帝世系

region.en: Ruoshui, the river of Changyi's descent (symbolic pin: Sichuan rivers)
region.zh: 若水（象徵性定位）

period: Shanhaijing, Hai Nei Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing, Hai Nei Jing: Huangdi, Lei-zu, Changyi, and the birth of Zhuanxu

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The Yellow Emperor's wife Lei-zu bore Changyi, who was sent down to live on the Ruoshui river and fathered Hanliu — a strange being with a long neck, small eyes, pig snout, and scaled body — who married a daughter of the Zhuo clan and fathered Zhuanxu, the emperor who would order the separation of heaven and earth: divinity passing through a pig-snouted river-lord to make the great regulator.
summary.zh: 黃帝妻雷祖，生昌意；昌意降處若水，生韓流；韓流擢首、謹耳、人面、豕喙、渠股、豚止，取淖子曰阿女，生帝顓頊——五帝之一由此降生。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing genealogy. The odd, animal-bodied ancestor (Hanliu) is a striking non-idealized genealogy entry — noted.

passages.text: The Yellow Emperor's wife was Lei-zu, and she bore Changyi; Changyi was sent down to dwell on the waters of the Ruo, and there fathered a son named Hanliu. Hanliu was shaped strangely: a long head and small ears, a man's face and a pig's snout, the legs of a heron and the hooves of a pig. He married a daughter of the Zhuo clan, and she bore Zhuanxu — the High Lord who would one day cut the road between heaven and earth. The greatest of the emperors descends through the strangest of bodies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Hai Nei Jing, Huangdi genealogy (compiler's rendering); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Hai Nei Jing; see chinese-guoyu-chongli for Zhuanxu's act; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 黃帝之妻為嫘祖，生昌意；昌意被貶謫，居於若水之濱，於彼處生一子，名曰韓流。韓流形貌怪異：長頭小耳，人面豬吻，鶴足豬蹄。他娶了淖氏之女，生下顓頊——那位日後將斷絕天地之間通路的至高君主。最偉大的帝王，竟由最奇異的形體傳承而下。

title.en: The Ten Shamans of Lingshan, Who Climb to Gather the Hundred Drugs
title.zh: 靈山十巫

region.en: Lingshan, the Shamans' Mountain (pin: Three Gorges region, Wushan)
region.zh: 靈山（巫山）

period: Shanhaijing, Da Huang Xi Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing, Da Huang Xi Jing: the ten shamans of Lingshan ascending and descending for the hundred medicines

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: There is a mountain called Lingshan, and on it live ten shamans named in the text — Wu Xian first among them — who go up and down between heaven and earth, gathering the hundred medicines: the ladder-climbing healers whose mountain, in later lore, is identified with the Wushan of the Three Gorges.
summary.zh: 有靈山，巫咸、巫即、巫盼、巫彭、巫姑、巫真、巫禮、巫抵、巫謝、巫羅十巫，從此升降，百藥爰在——群巫升降之天梯。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original.

passages.text: There is a mountain called Lingshan, the mountain of the spirit, and on it the book names ten shamans: Wu Xian, Wu Ji, Wu Pan, Wu Peng, Wu Gu, Wu Zhen, Wu Li, Wu Di, Wu Xie, Wu Luo. The ten go up and down by the mountain as by a ladder — between heaven and earth at will — and the hundred medicines grow there for their gathering: healers whose road to the sky is a mountain whose slopes are a pharmacopoeia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Xi Jing, Lingshan entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Xi Jing; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一座山名曰靈山，即神靈之山，書中記載山上共有十位巫者：巫咸、巫即、巫盼、巫彭、巫姑、巫真、巫禮、巫抵、巫謝、巫羅。這十位巫者上下於此山，如攀梯一般——隨心往來於天地之間——而百種藥草生長於此，供其採集：這些醫者通往天空的道路，是一座山坡即藥典的山。

title.en: The People of Wo, Who Eat the Phoenix's Eggs and Drink the Sweet Dew
title.zh: 沃民食卵

region.en: Wo, the fertile wild of the west (symbolic pin: western paradise)
region.zh: 沃之野（象徵性定位）

period: Shanhaijing, Da Huang Xi Jing, compiled c. 4th-2nd c. BCE

source.work: Shanhaijing, Da Huang Xi Jing: the wild of Wo and its people

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: There is a wild country called Wo — Fertile Ease — where people live on the eggs of the phoenix and drink the sweet dew, and whatever they desire is theirs at the wish: grain grows unasked, no plowing, no weeding, no toil, no theft and no grief — the Chinese Book of Earthly Delight, in one sentence of gazetteer.
summary.zh: 有沃之國，沃民是食鳳卵，是飲甘露；凡其所欲，其味盡存；爰有甘華、甘柤……百獸相群爰處——不耕不穫，食之以和。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shanhaijing original. The land-of-plenty archetype in the Chinese corpus.

passages.text: In the Great Waste of the west there is a wild called Wo, where the people live on phoenix eggs and drink sweet dew that falls from the sky; whatever taste they wish for is present there in its fullness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Xi Jing, Wo entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 西方大荒之中有一處荒野，名曰沃，其民以鳳凰之卵為食，飲天上降下的甘露；凡他們想嚐的滋味，那裡都完備地具足。

passages.text: Nothing is sown and nothing is reaped; the hundred plants grow to the hand, the beasts live in their herds without fear, and there is no labor, no theft and no grief in that country — the mythic west keeps a paradise on its far margin, and the gazetteer files it between mountains like any other place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shanhaijing, Da Huang Xi Jing; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不耕不穫；百草隨手可採而生長，野獸成群而居，無所畏懼；那國之中沒有勞作，沒有盜竊，也沒有憂愁——神話中的西方在其遙遠的邊際保留著一方樂土，而地志便如記載其他任何地方一般，把它夾記於群山之間。

title.en: Su Hu Writes 'Never Shall She Enter' on the Palace Wall
title.zh: 蘇護題詩反商

region.en: Jizhou and Zhaoge (pin: Henan–Hebei border)
region.zh: 冀州朝歌

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), 16th c. novel, chs. 1-3

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 1-3: the demand for Su Daji, Su Hu's defiant verse, the siege of Jizhou, and the mediation of Ji Chang

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Summoned to court, the border-lord Su Hu refused King Zhou's demand for his daughter — and wrote on the palace wall: 'Never shall I offer my daughter to the wine-soaked king.' The king declared war on Jizhou; the siege broke the town, and the sage King Wen's mediation saved the girl's life — by sending her to the capital after all, where the fox waited on the road.
summary.zh: 紂王索妲己，蘇護題反詩於午門：『冀州蘇護，永不朝商』；崇侯虎征討不克，姬昌修書勸和——護乃獻女入朝，而狐狸候於恩州道上。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The order came that Su Hu's daughter should join King Zhou's palace. The border-lord went to court, heard the demand, and answered with a verse cut on the palace wall: 'Jizhou's Su Hu shall never come to court' — an open declaration of war against the Shang, written in the king's own corridor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 1-2 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 命令傳來，要蘇護之女入紂王後宮。這位邊疆諸侯入朝，聽聞此要求，便以刻於宮牆上的一首詩作答：「冀州蘇護，永不入朝」——這是對商朝的公開宣戰，寫在君王自己的廊道之上。

passages.text: The armies of the north beat at Jizhou's walls until the town starved; then the sage of the west, Ji Chang, sent his letter of mediation, and Su Hu — reading in it the fate of his people — put down the defiance and set his daughter on the road to the capital.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 2-3; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 北方軍隊攻打冀州城牆，直至城中糧盡；隨後西方的聖人姬昌送來調解書信，蘇護——從信中讀出了自己族人的命運——遂放下抗拒，送女兒踏上前往都城之路。

passages.text: The escort reached the post-house of Enzhou at dusk — and there, in the black wind of that night, the fox of Xuanyuan tomb took the girl's body. The rebellion's compromise delivered the kingdom to the fox-queen: a peace that was the beginning of the fall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 4 transition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 護送隊伍於黃昏抵達恩州的驛館——就在那裡，那一夜的黑風之中，軒轅墳的狐狸奪走了那女子的身軀。叛亂的妥協將王國交到了狐后手中：這份和平，正是覆亡的開端。

title.en: Yunzhongzi's Wooden Sword Against the Fox
title.zh: 雲中子進劍除妖

region.en: Zhaoge, the Shang capital (pin: Henan)
region.zh: 朝歌

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 5-6

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 5-6: the immortal's wooden sword hung in the Hall of Divinity, the fox's sickness, and the burning of the sword

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The immortal Yunzhongzi, coming down from Mount End-Cloud, saw the demon-qi black over Zhaoge and carved a sword of peachwood for the king to hang in the Hall of Divinity. The fox in Daji's body sickened under it; but the king, told by the 'suffering' consort that the sword was a curse, had the peachwood burned — and the fox-queen, recovered, had Yunzhongzi driven from the city. One sword, burned; six hundred years, ended.
summary.zh: 雲中子見朝歌妖氣，削松木劍懸於分宮樓；妲己（狐）畏劍而病；紂王聽讒焚劍，妖氣復熾——一劍之失，江山傾頹之機。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: Yunzhongzi, riding down from the Cloud-End cave, saw a black column of demon-breath standing over the Shang capital, and judged the fall of the dynasty was one fox-deep. He carved a sword of peachwood in a single night and presented it, saying: hang it in the Hall of Divinity, and the evil will burn itself out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 5 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 雲中子自雲端洞府騎行而下，望見商都之上矗立著一道妖氣的黑柱，斷定此朝的覆滅，其深不過一狐。他連夜刻成一把桃木劍，獻上並說道：將它懸於神殿之中，邪祟便會自焚而盡。

passages.text: The sword was hung, and the fox in the consort's body lay as if dying, its borrowed skin smoking. The king, weeping at her sickbed, heard her whisper that the wooden blade was a curse meant for the palace — and had it burned in the courtyard.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 5-6, the burning; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 劍懸掛起來，附於妃子身上的狐狸便如將死一般躺著，牠借來的那層皮囊冒出煙來。君王在她病榻前哭泣，聽她低語說那木刃是衝著宮廷而來的詛咒——便命人在庭院中將它燒了。

passages.text: The fox rose whole, and the immortal was shown the gate. Yunzhongzi went back up the mountain saying one line that the whole novel proves: the mandate of the Shang is over — for when the remedy is burned by the patient, the disease is already the ruler.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 6, the immortal's departure; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 狐狸完好無損地起身，仙人則被逐出門外。雲中子返回山中，留下一句整部小說都為之印證的話：商之天命已盡——因為當解藥被病人燒毀時，這病本身早已成了主宰。

title.en: Shen Gongbao, the Recruiter of Every Mountain's Demons
title.zh: 申公豹

region.en: The roads between Kunlun and the Shang camps (symbolic pin: passes of the west)
region.zh: 崑崙至商營諸路

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), ch. 37 (and throughout)

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 37: Shen Gongbao's defection and his cry of 'Stay, fellow Daoist!'

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Jiang Ziya's own fellow-disciple Shen Gongbao, jealous of the marshal's commission, defected to the Shang with one irresistible skill: wherever he met an immortal, he cried 'Stay, fellow Daoist!' — and talked him into the war. Every beast, god and hermit of the islands came down to die on the Register; the war's whole second act is one man's gift of persuasion, and his head, cut off and thrown to the north wind, still laughs as it flies.
summary.zh: 申公豹妒子牙封神之任，叛而歸商；其所長者一句『道友請留步』——聞者無不反目投商；請來三山五嶽之仙，皆死於封神榜。其頭被砍，拋於北海，猶能飛。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: Shen Gongbao had sat forty years on Kunlun beside Jiang Ziya, and when the marshal's commission was given to the other, his jealousy found its weapon: he rode to the Shang camp and offered the fox-queen his services. His art was a single sentence, spoken wherever an immortal walked the roads: 'Stay, fellow Daoist!' — and with the stay began the talk, and with the talk the debt, and with the debt the camp of the Shang. Hermit after hermit came down the mountains to die on the Register of the Investiture, all recruited by one smiling man and one sentence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 37 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 37, the recruiting; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 申公豹在崑崙與姜子牙同坐四十年，當元帥之職授予了另一人，他的嫉妒便找到了武器：他騎往商營，向狐后獻上自己的效力。他的法術只有一句話，凡有仙人行走於道路之處便說：『道友請留步！』——有了這留步，便有了攀談；有了攀談，便有了人情債；有了人情債，便有了商營。一位又一位隱士下山，死於封神榜上，全由一個含笑之人、一句話招攬而來。

passages.text: The penalty of his treason was written into his own magic: his head, once cut from his shoulders, was flung to the north wind and flew away laughing — a head that could not die, a recruiter who could not stop, a curse on both armies to the last chapter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, the flying head; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他叛國之罪的懲罰，被寫進了他自己的法術之中：他的頭一旦從肩上被斬下，便被擲向北風，笑著飛走——一顆不死之頭，一個停不下來的招攬者，一道直到最後一章都纏著兩軍的詛咒。

title.en: Wen Zhong Dies at Absolute-Dragon Ridge
title.zh: 絕龍嶺聞太師歸天

region.en: Juelong Ridge, on the road home from Xiqi (symbolic pin: Shaanxi passes)
region.zh: 絕龍嶺

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), ch. 43

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 43: the Grand Preceptor's defeat, the prophecy of the character 'Jue', and the fire-pillars of Yunzhongzi

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Wen Zhong, the Grand Preceptor with the golden whip and the ink-black unicorn, had held the Shang together for a lifetime — and his master had warned him long ago of one character: 'Jue,' to cut off. Pursued home from his defeat at Xiqi, he came to a ridge signed with that very name, where the immortal Yunzhongzi waited with eight pillars of spirit-fire; the unicorn fell, the preceptor burned, and the most loyal of the Shang was the first great name carried to the Register.
summary.zh: 聞仲師從金靈聖母，師曾囑『逢絕而止』；兵敗西岐退至絕龍嶺，雲中子以通天神火柱焚之——太師魂歸封神臺，後為雷部之首。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: Wen Zhong, Grand Preceptor of the Shang, rode the ink-black unicorn with the golden pair of whips; his master had warned him once with a single word: wherever the character 'Jue' — to cut off, to end — meets you, turn back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 43 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 商朝太師聞仲騎著墨麒麟，手持雌雄雙鞭；他的師父曾以一語告誡他：凡遇「絕」字之處，便當回頭。

passages.text: Defeated at Xiqi, he fled home through the passes and came to a ridge whose stone was signed Absolute-Dragon. Yunzhongzi stood waiting with eight pillars of spirit-fire set around the valley; the pillars rose, the fire closed, and the unicorn and its rider burned where the prophecy had promised.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 43, the pillars; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他在西岐戰敗，逃出關隘返鄉，來到一道山嶺，嶺上石碣題著「絕龍嶺」三字。雲中子在谷中布下八根神火柱等候；柱起而火合，麒麟與騎者便在預言所指之處一同焚毀。

passages.text: The soul of the most loyal servant of a doomed house went first to the altar of the Investiture, to be made head of the Thunder Department — the Shang's last pillar turned heaven's own storm-lord, still riding the black clouds that had carried him into every battle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 43 and the investiture cross-reference; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這亡國之朝最忠之臣的魂魄，首先前往封神臺，受封為雷部之首——商朝最後的柱石化為天庭的司雷之主，仍舊駕著那曾載他奔赴每一場戰役的黑雲。

title.en: The Ten Absolute Formations and Their Ten Sacrifices
title.zh: 十絕陣

region.en: The field before Xiqi (pin: Shaanxi)
region.zh: 西岐城外

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 42-44

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 42-44: the ten formation-masters of the islands and the breaking of each array

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Ten hermit-masters of the islands, recruited by Shen Gongbao, raised ten formations around Xiqi — Heaven-Cutoff, Earth-Fire, Wind-Roar, Ice, Golden Light, Blood-Turn, Flame, Soul-Losing, Red Water, Red Sand — each demanding one mortal sacrifice before its virtue could be matched. The lamp-lighting Patriarch read each formation and fed it a volunteer; ten men went in, ten formations broke — and the broken masters went to the Register, the war's first industrial accounting of souls.
summary.zh: 十位島上散仙擺十絕陣（天絕、地烈、風吼、寒冰、金光、化血、烈焰、落魂、紅水、紅砂）；燃燈道人先以凡人祭陣，破之——十陣十破，陣主皆上榜。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. The volunteer-sacrifice mechanic (feeding each formation a mortal) is the novel's most morally stark war-ritual — noted.

passages.text: Ten formation-masters of the islands raised ten arrays before Xiqi, each a pocket of cosmology turned to siegecraft — arrays of cutting heaven, of burning earth, of howling wind, of ice, of golden light, of turning blood, of flame, of losing souls, of red water, of red sand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 42 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 海島十位陣主在西岐之前布下十座大陣，每一陣皆是天地造化之學化為攻城之術——天絕陣、地烈陣、風吼陣、寒冰陣、金光陣、化血陣、烈焰陣、落魂陣、紅水陣、紅砂陣。

passages.text: Each formation had its law: it could not be broken by force alone until one mortal had fed it — a volunteer walked in and was consumed, and only then could the immortal's counterspell enter. The Patriarch of the Lighting Lamp read each array like an account book, and paid each debt with a man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 42-44, the sacrifices; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 每一陣皆有其法：單憑蠻力不能破陣，須先有一名凡人填入陣中——一名自願者走入陣內被吞噬，仙人的破陣之法方能入陣。燃燈道人將每一陣如帳簿般細讀，並以一條人命償還每一筆債。

passages.text: Ten volunteers, ten formations broken, ten masters dead and on the Register: the war's mathematics made explicit. The arrays taught the Xiqi camp its cost, and taught the reader that in the economy of the Investiture, both sides feed the same ledger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 44, aftermath; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 十名自願者，十陣被破，十位陣主身死而入封神榜：此戰的算數於此明明白白。諸陣教會了西岐營中之人其代價，也教會了讀者：在封神的算計之中，敵我雙方所填的是同一本帳。

title.en: Zhao Gongming, the Black-Tiger God of Wealth, Struck by the Straw Doll
title.zh: 趙公明中箭

region.en: Emei's Luofu cave and the field before Xiqi (pin: Sichuan–Shaanxi)
region.zh: 峨眉羅浮洞至西岐

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 46-48

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 46-48: Zhao Gongming's descent on the black tiger, his iron whip, and the twenty-one days of the Nailhead Seven Arrows

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Zhao Gongming, the island-god who would become China's God of Wealth, rode down on a black tiger with an iron whip and no bow could touch him — until Lu Ya taught Jiang Ziya the Nailhead Seven Arrows: a straw doll of the god's own shape, shot with an arrow a day for twenty-one days, the last through the heart. The god of riches died of a doll, and his three sisters came to avenge him.
summary.zh: 趙公明騎黑虎執鐵鞭下山助商，鞭傷諸神；陸壓獻釘頭七箭書：草人書名，日射一箭，二十一日而命絕——財神之死，三霄起兵復仇。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. The straw-effigy rite is sympathetic magic turned assassination — the novel's most ritual warfare.

passages.text: Zhao Gongming came down from his cave on the back of a black tiger, iron whip in hand, and no weapon of the Xiqi host could touch him; the cloud of his fortune held. So Lu Ya the immortal came to the camp with a book called the Nailhead Seven Arrows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 46-47 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 趙公明騎著黑虎自洞中下山，手持鐵鞭，西岐眾將的兵器皆傷他不得；他頭上的雲氣護住了他。於是仙人陸壓帶著一部名為《釘頭七箭》的書來到營中。

passages.text: The rite took twenty-one days: a straw doll cut to the god's own shape, his name written on its chest, an altar raised north of the camp, and one arrow shot into the doll each day at dawn — the first through one eye, the second through the other, and the god on his tiger felt his own body darken with each wound.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 47-48, the straw-doll rite; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此術需行二十一日：依此神本相紮一草人，於其胸前寫上他的姓名，在營北築起法壇，每日黎明向草人射一箭——第一箭射穿一目，第二箭射穿另一目，此神騎在虎上，只覺自身隨每一處傷而漸漸昏黑。

passages.text: On the last morning the arrow went through the doll's heart, and Zhao Gongming fell from the black tiger dead. The god of wealth had been killed by a bundle of straw and a book of arrows — and his three sisters, the Ladies of the Three Islands, took up the golden scissors of the flood-dragon to avenge him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 48, the death and the vengeance; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最後一日清晨，那箭射穿了草人的心，趙公明便從黑虎上跌落而死。財神竟被一束稻草與一部箭書所殺——而他的三位姊妹，即三島娘娘，執起斬蛟金蛟剪，為他報仇。

title.en: The Nine-Bends Yellow River Formation: The Sisters Who Scooped Out the Twelve
title.zh: 九曲黃河陣

region.en: The field before Xiqi (pin: Shaanxi)
region.zh: 西岐城外

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 49-50

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 49-50: the three Ladies of the islands, the golden scissors, and the formation that unmade the twelve golden immortals

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The three sisters of Zhao Gongming raised their Nine-Bends Yellow River Formation over the field, with its gates of confusion and its scissors that cut dragons: twelve golden immortals of the Chan sect walked in and walked out stripped of their flower of three openings and their power of nine turns — emperors of the spirit turned to common men. Only the Patriarchs themselves could unmake the formation, and the sisters died on the Register for it.
summary.zh: 三霄娘娘（雲霄、瓊霄、碧霄）為兄報仇擺九曲黃河陣；金蛟剪落十二金仙，削其三花聚頂、閉其胸中五氣；老子、元始親破之——三霄皆上榜。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The three sisters of the islands — Yunxiao, Qiongxiao, Bixiao — raised the Nine-Bends Yellow River Formation for their murdered brother: a maze of nine turns whose gates turned men around, hung with the golden scissors that cut the flood-dragon in two.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 49 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 三島的三位姊妹——雲霄、瓊霄、碧霄——為被殺的兄長擺下九曲黃河陣：一座九轉迷陣，陣門令人迷失方向，陣上懸著能將蛟龍剪為兩段的金蛟剪。

passages.text: Twelve golden immortals of the Chan teaching walked in to break it, and walked out shorn: the formation scooped from each the flower of three openings and the breath of five powers, leaving them men of no magic — emperors of the spirit, unmade by two women with scissors and a maze.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 50, the unmaking; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 闡教十二金仙入陣破陣，出來時卻已被削去：此陣削去各人三花聚頂、五氣朝元，使他們成了無法術之人——這些神仙之尊，竟被兩個執剪與迷陣的女子所廢。

passages.text: Only Laozi and the Patriarch Yuanshi could enter it in safety; they broke the maze, took the scissors, and sent the three sisters to the Register — where the ladies of the Yellow River Formation received posts of their own, vengeance and punishment settled in one bookkeeping.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 50, the breaking; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 唯有老子與元始天尊能安然入陣；他們破了迷陣，取了金蛟剪，將三位姊妹送入封神榜——黃河陣的三位娘娘各得神職，報仇與懲罰，同在一部賬冊中結清。

title.en: The Slaying-Immortals Formation of Tongtian Jiaozhu
title.zh: 誅仙陣

region.en: The field before the final passes (pin: Shaanxi–Henan)
region.zh: 汜水關前

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 78-79

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 78-79: the Master of the Intercepts' four swords and the four patriarchs who entered the array

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The Master of the Intercepts, humiliated by his sect's losses, hung his four swords of the four gates — Slaying-Immortals, Slaying-Gods, Trapping-Immortals, Ending-Immortals — in a formation that no one being could enter and live. So four came: Laozi, Yuanshi, and the two Buddhas of the west; each took one gate, the swords were pulled, and the formation-master's last argument ended in his own sect's ruin.
summary.zh: 通天教主設誅仙陣，懸誅仙、陷仙、戮仙、絕仙四劍於四門，非四聖不能破；老子、元始、接引、準提各破一門——截教大劫由此而定。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The Master of the Intercepts raised the Slaying-Immortals Formation, one sword hanging at each of the four gates — Slaying-Immortals, Slaying-Gods, Trapping-Immortals, Ending-Immortals — and the law of the array was simple: no single being, however great, could pass any gate alive.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 78 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 通天教主布下誅仙陣，四門各懸一劍——誅仙、戮仙、陷仙、絕仙——陣法之律甚簡：任憑何等大能之輩，亦無一能生過此門。

passages.text: So four came to the four gates: Laozi of the cart, Yuanshi of the seal, and the two Buddhas of the western heaven. Each took one gate and one sword — and where the law required four, four arrived; the swords came down, the gates opened, and the formation that could not be beaten by one was unmade by four.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 79, the four patriarchs; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是四人分至四門：乘車之老子、執印之元始，以及西方天之二佛。各據一門、各當一劍——律法需四人者，四人果至；劍落門開，一夫不可破之陣，遂為四人所解。

passages.text: The Master of the Intercepts left the field swearing the final formation — the Ten Thousand Immortals — and the war moved to its last act: a teacher who had lost his array now losing his sect, one sword-debt at a time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 79, aftermath; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 通天教主離陣而去，誓立終陣——萬仙陣——戰事遂入末幕：失其陣之師，今復失其教，一劍一債，次第償之。

title.en: Bo Yikao's Qin and the Patties Fed to His Father
title.zh: 伯邑考肉餅

region.en: Zhaoge, the Youli prison (pin: Henan–Shaanxi)
region.zh: 羑里

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 22-23; rabbit variant in later folk layer

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 22-23: the eldest son's embassy, the fox-queen's snare, and the patty of the faithful son

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Bo Yikao, eldest son of the imprisoned King Wen, came to Zhaoge with treasures and a qin to ransom his father; the fox-queen lusted, he refused her, and she had him flayed alive and cooked into patties — which the king was fed, to prove his supposed ignorance. King Wen, who had divined the truth, ate the patties of his own son with a steady face; released, he vomited them on the road, and the three vomited lumps became three white rabbits that bounded into the hills — the folk layer's answer to unbearable grief.
summary.zh: 伯邑考進貢贖父，撫琴而妲己欲私之；邑考不從，被醢為肉餅，以賜文王食之；文王明知而啖之，出羑里吐於地，化為三兔奔入林——兔兒爺之由來（民俗層）。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. Cannibalism-by-trick and the rabbit transformation are the folk layer; handled as recorded narrative, not endorsement.

passages.text: Bo Yikao came down the mountain of his studies to ransom his father from the prison of Youli, bringing the treasures of the west and his own gift: the qin, whose playing drew the birds from the trees and the fox-queen from her chamber.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 22 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伯邑考下山就學歸來，欲贖其父於羑里之囚，攜西方之寶，並獻己之所長：琴。其操琴也，能使鳥下於樹，狐后出於室。

passages.text: She summoned him to teach her the instrument; he refused her with the same courtesy as before, and the refusal was death. The fox had him flayed alive and cooked into three patties, served to the imprisoned king with the words: eat, and prove you know nothing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 22, the snare and the patties; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 狐后召之授琴；彼以昔日之禮辭之，而辭即死。狐乃生剝其皮，烹為三餅，進於囚中之王，曰：食之，以證爾一無所知。

passages.text: King Wen, who had divined the whole of it, ate the patties of his own son without a tremor — knowledge swallowed whole — and won his release. On the road home he stopped the carriage, wept, and vomited the three lumps into the grass; the folk layer finishes it: the lumps sprang up as three white rabbits and bounded into the hills, and the moon remembers them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 23, with the folk rabbit variant; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 文王早已卜知其事，食其子之餅而面無悸色——所知者，吞而納之——遂得釋。歸途之中，停車而泣，嘔出三塊於草間；民俗之說終之曰：三塊化為三白兔，躍入山丘，而月猶記之。

title.en: The Two Princes Sworn to Two Masters
title.zh: 殷郊殷洪背誓

region.en: Zhaoge to Xiqi, the princes' roads (pin: Henan–Shaanxi)
region.zh: 朝歌至西岐

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 11-12 and 60-66

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 11-12 and 60-66: the two sons of King Zhou saved by two immortals, sworn to aid Zhou — and broken by one sentence

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The two princes of the Shang, sentenced to death by their own father, were snatched from the scaffold by two immortals, trained in the mountains, and sworn to aid Zhou's rise. Shen Gongbao found them with one sentence — 'Your father's throne, and you serve his killers?' — and both broke their oaths: Yin Hong burned in the Taiji diagram, and Yin Jiao, who had sworn to be ground under the plough-heads if he broke faith, was crushed under his own plough of fate — the novel's two cautionary tales of oaths made by the desperate and kept by no one.
summary.zh: 殷郊殷洪臨刑被救，各拜廣成子、赤精子為師，下山時立誓助周伐紂；申公豹一言（『爾父之天下，豈可伐之』）破其誓——殷洪死太極圖中，殷郊遭犁鋤而死，應其誓。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The two princes of the Shang, sons of the king who wanted them dead, were taken from the executioner's ground by two immortals of the western teaching and carried up into the mountains — Yin Jiao to the Peak of Jade-void, Yin Hong to the cave of the Red Master.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 11-12 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 商朝的兩位王子，是那位欲置其於死地的君王之子，被西方教門的兩位仙人從刑場帶走，攜往山中——殷郊往玉虛峰，殷洪往赤精子之洞府。

passages.text: Each swore at the mountain-gate the oath that released him: to aid the Zhou, to bring down his own father's house. Shen Gongbao met each on the road with one sentence — your father's throne, and you pull it down — and the oath broke: Yin Hong turned his master's teaching into siegecraft and burned in the Taiji diagram for it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 60-66, the broken oaths; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 二人各在山門前立下解脫自身之誓：助周滅商，傾覆親父之家國。申公豹於途中各以一言相迎——那是你父之王位，而你卻要將其傾覆——誓言遂破：殷洪將其師之教誨化為攻城之術，因此於太極圖中焚身。

passages.text: Yin Jiao swore the harder oath — that if he broke faith, his body should be ground between the plough-shares — and his oath was kept for him: the prince who died fighting for his father's house was crushed as he had promised, the novel's two mirror-cautionaries of oaths sworn by the desperate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 66, the plough-death; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 殷郊所立之誓更重——若背信棄義，其身當於犁鏵之間碾碎——而他的誓言竟為他應驗：那位為父之家國而戰死的王子，正如其所誓般被碾碎，此乃小說中兩面映照之鑑，皆為走投無路者所立之誓。

title.en: Tu Xingsun, the Dwarf Who Dug Through Walls and Was Married by Force
title.zh: 土行孫遁地成親

region.en: Jiulong Island and the camps of Xiqi (pin: Shaanxi)
region.zh: 九龍島至西岐

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 53-58

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 53-58: the earth-tunneling of Tu Xingsun, his master's collar, and the forced marriage to Deng Chanyu

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Tu Xingsun, four feet tall and master of the earth-tunnel art, could sink through walls and floors to steal weapons, princesses and battles; he fought for the enemy camp until his own master summoned him by the collar-art and shamed him back to the right side. His dowry was arranged by Jiang Ziya: he was married to Deng Chanyu, the warrior-girl who had beaten him in open field, and died at last in the tunnel-earth under a rival tunneler's rake.
summary.zh: 土行孫身高四尺，擅地行之術，穿牆遁地竊寶劫營；懼留孫以指訣喚之歸周；姜子牙主婚，配鄧嬋玉——最終死於張奎地遁之下。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. The forced-marriage arrangement is a novel convention of its period — recorded, not endorsed.

passages.text: Tu Xingsun stood four feet tall and could walk through the earth as through a door: he sank under walls to steal the war-chariots' banners, rose inside tents to cut sentries' throats, and tunneled into the women's towers of the enemy — a soldier whose battlefield was the ground itself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 53-54 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 土行孫身長四尺，能穿地而行如過門戶：他潛入城牆之下盜取戰車之旗，自營帳之內升起割斷哨兵之喉，並掘地道潛入敵方之女眷樓閣——一位以大地本身為戰場的士兵。

passages.text: His master, the immortal Juliuxun, called him home by the finger-sign and shamed him into the Zhou camp — where Jiang Ziya, needing the defector bound by more than loyalty, arranged his marriage to Deng Chanyu, the girl-general whose mace had once knocked him from his mount.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 55-56, the collar and the marriage; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 其師懼留孫仙人以指訣召他歸來，令他羞愧而投周營——姜子牙為使這名叛降者受縛於忠誠之外的羈絆，安排他娶鄧嬋玉為妻，這位女將曾以鐵錘將他擊落馬下。

passages.text: He fought the rest of the war from the right side, tunneling for the Zhou — until a rival tunnel-master, Zhang Kui, met him under the earth and killed him in his own element: the digger buried by a deeper digger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 86-87 cross-reference; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此後之戰，他皆從正義一方作戰，為周軍掘地道——直至敵方一位擅長地行之術的對手張奎，於地下與他相遇，在自己的擅長之地將他殺死：掘地者為更深之掘地者所埋葬。

title.en: Yang Jian and the Seven Monsters of Meishan
title.zh: 楊戩收梅山七怪

region.en: Meishan, the seven-peak mountain (pin: Sichuan)
region.zh: 梅山

period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 91-92

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 91-92: the seven beast-brothers of Meishan and Yang Jian's transformation-duels

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Seven beast-spirits of Meishan — a white ape first among them, with bull, boar, goat, dog, snake and centipede brothers — held the last mountain-pass for the Shang. Yang Jian, the three-eyed god, met them in kind: transformation against transformation, hound against hound, until the white ape Yuan Hong, match of the monkey-kind, was lured into the Mountain-Rivers Painting and roasted in the demon-refining cauldron. The last defenders fell, and the road to Zhaoge lay open.
summary.zh: 梅山七怪（白猿袁洪、豬精朱子真、牛精金大升等）守最後之關；楊戩以七十二變與哮天犬逐之；袁洪入山河社稷圖，斬於陸壓斬仙飛刀——梅山平，兵臨朝歌。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. The white ape Yuan Hong is a striking pre-echo of the Monkey King archetype — noted for the trickster cluster.

passages.text: Seven brothers of Meishan held the last mountain for the dying Shang: a white ape, a white ox, a pig, a goat, a dog, a serpent and a centipede, each a spirit of a thousand years in man's shape, each a general in the last army.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 91 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 梅山七兄弟為將亡的商朝堅守最後一座山：白猿、白牛、豬、羊、狗、蛇與蜈蚣，各是千年精怪化為人形，各是末代軍中的一員將軍。

passages.text: Yang Jian met them in their own coin — transformation against transformation, his hound against their beasts — until only the white ape Yuan Hong stood, a fighter of the monkey-kind whose changes matched the god's own and whose head, once cut, regrew.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 92, the duels; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 楊戩以彼之道還施彼身——以變化對變化，以他的細犬對他們的妖獸——直到只剩白猿袁洪立於陣前；他是猴類中的戰士，變化之術與這位神祇不相上下，頭顱被砍下後還能重新長出。

passages.text: The ape was lured into the Mountain-Rivers Painting of the goddess, and there, painted in, was burned in the demon-refining cauldron; the last of the seven fell, the pass opened, and the armies of Zhou came down upon Zhaoge with the war of the gods a chapter from its end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 92, the painting and the cauldron; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那猿猴被誘入女神的山河社稷圖中，在那裡被畫入圖內，於煉妖壺中燒盡；七者中的最後一個倒下了，關隘敞開，周軍降臨朝歌，封神之戰已近尾聲。

title.en: The Sand Monk of the Flowing Sands River
title.zh: 流沙河收沙僧

region.en: Flowing Sands River, eight hundred li of no-bottom water (pin: western deserts)
region.zh: 八百流沙界

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, ch. 22)

source.work: Journey to the West, ch. 22: the red-haired monster of the river, the nine skulls of the necklace, and Guanyin's conversion

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: In the Flowing Sands River, where even a goose feather sinks, lived a red-haired river-monster wearing a necklace of nine skulls — the nine previous pilgrims he had eaten, whose skulls alone could float on that water. The Monkey King could not fight him in his own element; Guanyin's disciple Muzha called him out, and the monster confessed: once the Curtain-Raising General of heaven, exiled for breaking a crystal cup at the Peach Banquet. Shorn and named, he became the third pilgrim, and his master's nine skulls made the raft that ferried the Tang monk west.
summary.zh: 流沙河水鵝毛飄不起；沙僧項掛九個骷髏——九世取經人之頭骨；本是捲簾大將，蟠桃會上失手打碎琉璃盞被貶；拜三藏為師，九骷髏結成法船渡師西行。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. The nine skulls of failed pilgrims are a dark recursion of the quest motif.

passages.text: The Flowing Sands River runs eight hundred li of water so foul and lightless that even a goose feather sinks; in its reeds lived a red-haired, blue-faced monster wearing a necklace strung with nine human skulls — the nine pilgrims who had tried to cross before, whose heads alone floated on that water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 22 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 流沙河綿延八百里，水質污濁晦暗，連鵝毛也會沉底；蘆葦叢中住著一個紅髮藍臉的妖怪，頸上掛著一串由九顆人頭骨穿成的項鍊——那是先前試圖渡河的九個取經人，唯有他們的頭顱漂浮在那水上。

passages.text: Guanyin's disciple called him out of the water, and the monster told his fall: he had been the Curtain-Raising General of heaven, and at the Peach Banquet his hand had slipped and broken a crystal cup; for the cup he was exiled to this river, seven knives of heaven striking him every seventh day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 22, the fall; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 觀音的弟子將他從水中喚出，妖怪訴說了自己的墮落：他本是天庭的捲簾大將，在蟠桃會上失手打碎了一隻琉璃盞；因這隻盞，他被貶到這條河，每七日便有七把天刀刺他。

passages.text: Named Wujing — Awakened to Purity — he took the fillet and joined the pilgrims; and when the Tang monk could not cross the sinking water, the nine skulls were strung into a raft-boat of the dead, and the ferry that bore the living monk west was made of the pilgrims who had failed before him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 22, the skull-raft; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他被賜名悟淨——覺悟清淨——戴上頭箍，加入了取經的行列；當唐僧無法渡過那沉陷之水時，九顆頭骨被串成一艘亡者之筏，載著活著的僧人西渡的渡船，正是由在他之前失敗的取經人所造。

title.en: The Yellow Wind Demon and the Wind That Blinded the Sky
title.zh: 黃風怪三昧神風

region.en: Yellow Wind Ridge, west of Double-Fork Pass (pin: Gansu corridor)
region.zh: 黃風嶺

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 20-21)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 20-21: the samadhi wind that stung the fiery eyes, and the marten of Lingshan taken home

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The Yellow Wind Demon breathed the true wind of samadhi — a wind that blackened the sky, whipped the rivers into the air, and struck the Monkey King's fiery eyes with a smart that no water could cool. Wukong fetched the Bodhisattva Lingji, whose wind-stopping pearl was the one thing the wind could not move; the demon's hole was blown open, and the demon proved to be a yellow marten stolen from under the Buddha's own lamp at Lingshan, led home by the collar.
summary.zh: 黃風怪三昧神風，迷悟空火眼金睛；靈吉菩薩以定風珠破之；黃毛貂鼠原是靈山腳下得道之妖，偷琉璃盞內清油——押回靈山見如來。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The Yellow Wind Demon breathed at his enemies the true wind of samadhi: a gale that rolled rocks and rivers into the sky, made the stars swim, and — worst of all — struck the Monkey King's fiery eyes with a stinging that neither stream nor salve could ease.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, chs. 20-21 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 黃風怪向敵人吹出三昧真風：那狂風捲起石塊與江河直上雲霄，吹得星辰搖晃，最糟的是，它刺中了孫悟空的火眼金睛，那刺痛既非溪水、也非藥膏所能緩解。

passages.text: Wukong sought the Bodhisattva Lingji, keeper of the wind-stopping pearl, the one thing in three realms the samadhi wind could not budge; with the pearl held against the gale, the demon's cave was broken open and the captor mastered. The demon proved to be a yellow marten that had lived at the foot of the Vulture Peak and drunk the oil of the Buddha's own lamp; for the theft and the harm it was led home by the collar to Lingshan, to be sentenced by the one whose lamp it had drunk dry.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 21, Lingji and the pearl; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 21, the marten's origin; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 悟空前去求助靈吉菩薩，菩薩持有定風珠，那是三界之中唯一能令三昧神風無可撼動之物；將定風珠迎向狂風，妖怪的洞府便被破開，擒人者亦被制伏。這妖怪原是一隻黃毛貂鼠，曾住在靈山腳下，飲過佛祖燈中之油；因偷油與傷人之罪，牠被牽著頸項帶回靈山，交由那盞被牠喝乾燈油的佛祖發落。

title.en: The Black River Demon and the Prince Called Handsome
title.zh: 黑水河妖

region.en: Black River, west of Cart-Slow Kingdom (pin: Qinghai–Gansu route)
region.zh: 黑水河

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, ch. 43)

source.work: Journey to the West, ch. 43: the alligator-demon of the Black River, the false ferryman, and the uncle who keeps his nephew's island

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: A ferry came for the Tang monk and sank with him in the middle of the Black River — the boatman was an alligator-demon who had seized a river-dragon prince's palace and wanted a taste of Tang monk for his table. His captive uncle, the dragon-prince Moto of the Western Sea, sent no rescue until Wukong confronted him: the prince fetched his own nephew out in chains, and the Black River returned to its rightful king.
summary.zh: 黑水河鼉龍怪（涇河龍王之子）扮艄公攝三藏；西海龍王太子摩昂率兵擒甥——河歸原主。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: A ferryman poled out to the pilgrims on the Black River; mid-stream the boat turned over, and the Tang monk was drawn down — the ferryman was an alligator-demon in man's shape, and his table wanted a taste of the flesh that grants long life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 43 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一名擺渡人撐船駛向黑河邊的取經人；船到中流翻了，唐僧被拖入水中——那擺渡人原是鱷魚精所化的人形，牠的餐桌正想嚐嚐那能令人長生不老的肉。

passages.text: The demon had a letter of kinship worth more than his stolen palace: he was a son of the slain Jinghe dragon, and the prince of the Western Sea — his mother's brother — held the nearest waters. Wukong carried the family's name up to the Dragon King of the West and put the choice plainly: your nephew eats the pilgrim, or your name pays for it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 43, the kinship; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這妖怪有一封比牠所奪宮殿更值錢的親緣書信：牠是被斬的涇河龍王之子，而西海龍王——牠母親的兄長——掌管著最近的水域。悟空帶著這份親族的名分上西海見龍王，把話挑明：要麼你的外甥吃了取經人，要麼你的名聲來抵這筆帳。

passages.text: Prince Moto came down the river with a squadron, arrested his own nephew in the demon's own hall, and handed over the monk unspoiled; the stolen palace was returned to its dragon, and the Black River ferried the pilgrims across like any honest water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 43, the arrest; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 摩昂太子率一隊水軍順河而下，在妖怪自己的廳堂裡擒住了牠的親外甥，並將毫髮無傷的唐僧交還；被奪的宮殿歸還了牠的龍王，黑河也像尋常清水一般，將取經人渡了過去。

title.en: The Green Ox of the Diamond Bracelet
title.zh: 金兜洞青牛精

region.en: Golden-Helmet Cave, Jindou Mountain (pin: western route)
region.zh: 金兜山金兜洞

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 50-52)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 50-52: the green bull that swallowed every weapon in heaven, and the bracelet that collected them all

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: A single white-clothed demon boy in the Golden-Helmet cave disarmed three realms: his ring — Laozi's own diamond bracelet, carried off by a green bull that had wandered from the Tushita stable — sucked up the Monkey King's staff, the fire-spear of the fire-gods, the swords of the water-gods, even the vajra of the thunder-host. Heaven's armories came down and went home empty-handed; only Laozi himself, came down with his own knowledge of the bracelet's law, closed the ring on the bull's nose and led it home.
summary.zh: 青牛精（兕大王）持金剛琢，套盡諸神兵器：金箍棒、火德星君火具、水德水具、雷公雷器皆被收；如來暗示，老君親至，以芭蕉扇喚出金剛琢套牛鼻——青牛歸兜率宮。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: In the cave of the Golden Helmet a demon styled himself the Great King Rhino, and his weapon was a plain ring of white diamond. Thrown in the air, it collected anything made of metal or magic: the staff was sucked off the Monkey King's shoulder in mid-battle, and the monkey fled home weaponless for the first time in his life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, chs. 50 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在金兜洞中，有個妖怪自稱獨角兕大王，牠的兵器是一隻樸素的白金鋼琢。那琢子拋向空中，便能收走一切金鐵或法寶所成之物：激戰之中，金箍棒竟從孫悟空肩上被吸走，猴子生平第一次空著手逃回家去。

passages.text: The fire-gods came down with spears of flame, the water-gods with torrents, the thunder-lords with their engines — and the ring drank them all; the hosts of heaven went home without their weapons, and the monkey went to the Buddha for a name rather than a spell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, chs. 51, the disarmed heavens; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 火神帶著火槍降下，水神帶著洪流降下，雷神帶著他們的器械降下——而那圈子把這一切都吞了進去；天兵天將丟了自己的兵器回天庭去了，猴子則去找佛陀求一個名號，而不是求一道咒法。

passages.text: The Buddha hinted without naming, and Laozi came down the mountain road on his green bull's own trail: the ring was his diamond bracelet, lost five days ago from his own sleeve when the stable-door stood open and the bull walked out. With a wave of his plantain fan the bracelet turned, the ring closed on the bull's nose, and the whole armory of heaven rained back from the cave-mouth into its owners' hands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 52, Laozi's retrieval; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 佛陀暗示而不明言，老子便循著青牛自己的蹄跡下山而來：那圈子是他的金剛琢，五天前從他自己的衣袖中失落，當時馬廄的門敞著，那牛便走了出去。他揮動芭蕉扇，金剛琢一轉，圈子便扣住了牛鼻，天庭的全副兵器從洞口如雨般落回各自主人的手中。

title.en: The Pagoda of Jisai and the Nine-Headed Son-in-Law
title.zh: 祭賽國掃塔辨冤

region.en: Jisai Kingdom and the pagoda of golden relics (pin: western route)
region.zh: 祭賽國金光寺

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 62-63)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 62-63: the dimmed relic, the night-thief of the pagoda, and the nine-headed insect of the lake

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: In Jisai a pagoda held a relic whose light had kept the four seas in tribute — until the light went out, and the kingdom fell from wealth to beggary, and the monks of the pagoda were chained for a theft they never made. The Monkey King swept the pagoda by night like a menial, caught the thieves at their work — the nine-headed insect-prince of the Emerald Wave Lake and his dragon-kin — and brought back the relic-bud that lit the tower again.
summary.zh: 祭賽國金光寺塔頂舍利放光，四夷朝貢；舍利被盜（亂石山碧波潭九頭蟲與萬聖龍王），國弱僧囚；悟空夜掃塔捉賊，二郎神助戰，舍利復明。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The pagoda of Jisai held a bone-relic whose light streamed so far that the kingdoms of four seas sent tribute unasked; one year the light went out, the tributes stopped, and the court, needing a criminal, chained the pagoda's monks in the courtyard.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 62 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 祭賽國的寶塔中供著一顆舍利，其光芒遠播，四海諸國不待索求便送來貢品；有一年那光熄了，貢品也斷了，朝廷需要一個罪犯，便把塔中的僧人鎖在庭院裡。

passages.text: The Monkey King took a broom and swept the pagoda's thirteen stories by night like a menial, and on the top floor caught the thieves at their second theft: the nine-headed insect-prince of the Emerald Wave Lake, with his dragon father-in-law's troopers, come back for another relic-stone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 62, the night sweep; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 猴王拿起掃帚，夜裡像個僕役一般掃遍寶塔的十三層，在頂層撞見了那夥賊第二次行竊：碧波潭的九頭蟲駙馬，帶著他龍岳父的兵卒，回來再取一顆舍利石。

passages.text: The Erlang god came at the monkey's summons, his hound took one of the nine heads, and the insect-prince fled minus a skull to live nine-headed no longer; the relic-bud was carried back and set in the pagoda, and the light of Jisai shone again to the four seas — with its monks freed and its king kneeling in the courtyard dust.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 63, the battle and the relic; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 二郎神應猴王之召而來，他的細犬咬下了九顆頭中的一顆，那蟲駙馬少了一個頭顱逃走了，再也不是九頭了；舍利芽被帶回，安放在塔中，祭賽國的光又照向四海——僧眾獲釋，國王跪在庭院的塵土中。

title.en: The Python of Tuoluo Village, Swallowed from the Inside
title.zh: 駝羅莊蟒蛇精

region.en: Tuoluo Village, seven hundred li of thorny road (pin: western route)
region.zh: 駝羅莊

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, ch. 67)

source.work: Journey to the West, ch. 67: the python that ate a village's road, and the monkey who let himself be eaten

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: A python the size of the village's water-tank had closed the seven-hundred-li thorn road: it ate an old man's grandson, then a wealthy man's herd, then the village's hired exorcists, one Buddhist and one Taoist. The Monkey King took the shape of a goatherd on the python's own road, let the snake swallow him whole, and turned inside its belly with his staff: the python died split open, its eyes like two palace lanterns, and the village hired its people to clear the thorns it had guarded.
summary.zh: 駝羅莊七百里蛇徑為大蟒所據；悟空變作牧童誘蛇吞之，入腹一棒自內穿破——蛇死橫路，目似燈籠；莊人復通其路。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The road west out of Tuoluo ran through seven hundred li of thorns, and in their heart a python as long as the village's water-tank had taken residence: it ate the village's hired exorcists — a Buddhist first, then a Taoist — and closed the road to every caravan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 67 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 出陀羅的西行之路穿過七百里荊棘，而在荊棘的中心，一條與村中水缸一般長的巨蟒住了下來：牠吃掉了村裡雇來的驅邪者——先是個和尚，然後是個道士——並斷絕了所有商隊的通路。

passages.text: The Monkey King went up the python's own road as a small goatherd with a flock of the village's sheep, and when the python came out with jaws like two palace gates, he let it swallow him whole — a volunteer, walking into the beast from the wrong end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 67, the swallow; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 猴王化身為一名小牧童，趕著村裡的一群羊，走上巨蟒自己開出的那條路；巨蟒張開如兩扇宮門般的巨口時，他便任其將自己整個吞下——一個自願者，從錯誤的一端走進了那頭巨獸的腹中。

passages.text: Inside the belly he straightened his staff to its full thirteen-thousand pounds and drove it outward; the python burst and died in the road, its lantern-eyes darkening on the thorn-bushes. The village, saved, hired its own people back to clear the seven hundred li of thorns — the road opened by the beast's death was finished by the village's own hands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 67, the death and the road; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在腹中，他將金箍棒伸直，漲到足足一萬三千斤，向外頂去；巨蟒爆裂而死於路上，牠那燈籠般的雙眼在荊棘叢上漸漸黯淡。村莊得救了，村民便雇回自己的鄉人來清除那七百里荊棘——巨蟒之死所開出的路，終究由村莊自己的雙手完成。

title.en: The Rhinoceros Thieves of the Oil-Vats
title.zh: 金平府犀牛精

region.en: Jinping Prefecture and the Green Dragon Mountain (pin: western route)
region.zh: 金平府慈雲寺青龍山

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, chs. 91-92)

source.work: Journey to the West, chs. 91-92: the three rhinoceros spirits who posed as the Buddha of the lamp-oil, and the four stars of the wood? — the four star-lords who took them

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: In Jinping the people burned a thousand catties of lamp-oil a year to a 'Buddha' whose light came down on the festival night — a Buddha that was three rhinoceros spirits in the Green Dragon Mountain, drinking the vats of oil and taxing the county for the favor. The Monkey King broke the sham Buddha's light with his staff, and the four star-lords of the wood-palace came down with saws: three rhinos, three heads boxed for the court of Jinping, and the oil-vat tax forever ended.
summary.zh: 金平府燈節供奉『佛爺』，實為青龍山三犀牛精冒佛食油；悟空戰之，四木禽星（角木蛟等）下界助戰，鋸角剝皮——犀角獻朝，油稅永免。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: Jinping burned a thousand catties of oil each festival year before a Buddha whose light descended on the altar — and the county called the tax fair, for the light was real. The pilgrims saw at once that the light was not the Buddha's: three rhinoceros spirits in the Green Dragon Mountain had worn the disguise for years, drinking the oil-vats and taxing the faithful.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 91 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 金平每逢節慶之年，都要在一尊佛前焚燒千斤香油，那佛的光輝會降臨祭壇——而郡縣都稱這稅賦公平，因為那光輝是真的。朝聖者一眼便看出那光並非佛光：青龍山中的三隻犀牛精多年來披著這層偽裝，飲盡油缸，還向信眾徵稅。

passages.text: The monkey broke the sham Buddha's night with one stroke of the staff; the rhinos fought, kidnapped the Tang monk for a second course, and fled to the sea-ice — where the four star-lords of the wood-palace, the rhino-kind's own celestial wardens, came down with ropes and saws.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 92, the pursuit; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 猴子一棒打破了假佛的夜色；犀牛精奮起迎戰，又擄走唐僧要作第二道菜，隨後逃往海冰之上——就在那裡，木星宮的四位星君，也就是犀牛一類本有的天界守護者，帶著繩索與鋸子降臨。

passages.text: Three rhinos were taken alive, three horns sawed, three hides boxed for the court of Jinping — presented as proof, with the oil-tax abolished forever and the vats of the festival given back to the lamps they were meant for.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 92, the sawing; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 三隻犀牛被生擒，三隻角被鋸下，三張皮被裝箱送往金平郡府——呈上作為憑證，油稅從此永遠廢除，節慶的油缸也歸還給它們本該供奉的燈火。

title.en: The Old Turtle Asks His Age, and the Monkey Forgets
title.zh: 通天河老黿沉師

region.en: Tongtian River, on the return road east (pin: western route)
region.zh: 通天河

period: Journey to the West, 16th c. (attrib. Wu Cheng'en, ch. 99)

source.work: Journey to the West, ch. 99: the turtle's ferry on the return, the forgotten question, and the wet scriptures

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Crossing the Tongtian River on the way west, the pilgrims rode the old white turtle who had ferried them before; he asked one fee — that the monkey ask the Buddha how many years a turtle of his merit might yet live. On the return crossing, loaded with scriptures, the monkey forgot the question, confessed it mid-stream — and the turtle, insulted, sank under them with the whole canon on his back: the scriptures saved from the water, but every page soaked, and the first sheets of the highest canon pasted to the rock to dry, torn where the drying tore them. The imperfection was kept: even the true books came home incomplete.
summary.zh: 老黿馱經東歸，問壽數於如來；悟空忘問，至河心方認——黿怒沉經；經本全濕，曬於石上，石留經痕，數卷殘破——『天地本不全，經文殘缺也應不全之理』。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. The torn pages are the novel's final theological statement: completeness belongs to heaven, not to books.

passages.text: The old white turtle of the Tongtian River carried the pilgrims west and named his fee: ask the Buddha how many years yet a turtle of my merit may live. The monkey promised; eight thousand li later, at the end of the quest, he forgot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 99 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 通天河的老白龜馱著朝聖者西行，並說出了他的報酬：問一問佛祖，我這有功德的龜還能活多少年。猴子答應了；八千里之後，取經將盡之時，他卻忘了。

passages.text: On the return crossing, mid-stream and laden with the whole canon, the monkey remembered — and confessed. The turtle, patient for fourteen years of pilgrim traffic, heard the forgetting and sank; the scriptures went into the river with the monks, and were fished out page by page in the shallows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 99, the sinking; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 回程渡河時，行至中流，滿載著整部經藏，那猴想起了此事——並且坦承了。那龜為朝聖者往來負載，已耐心等候十四年，聽聞這遺忘之事，便沉了下去；經卷隨眾僧一同落入河中，又在淺灘處一頁一頁地被撈了上來。

passages.text: The wet books were spread to dry on a sunlit rock, and the stone kept the characters' shadows; a few sheets of the highest canon stuck and tore away with the drying. The Buddha's own comment closed the novel's theology: the books of heaven are complete, but the world is not — the torn pages travel east because completeness is not for this shore.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Journey to the West, ch. 99, the drying and the comment; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濕透的書冊被攤開，晾在向陽的岩石上曬乾，石頭便留下了字跡的影子；最上乘經藏中有幾頁黏住了，隨著晾曬而撕裂脫落。佛陀親口所說的一番話，為這部小說的神學作了總結：天上的書是完整的，世間卻不是——那些撕破的書頁之所以東傳，正因為圓滿並不屬於此岸。

title.en: Pengzu, the Man Who Lived Eight Hundred Years
title.zh: 彭祖八百歲

region.en: Pengcheng, Peng's city (Xuzhou, Jiangsu)
region.zh: 彭城

period: Soushen Ji by Gan Bao, c. 350 CE, juan 1

source.work: Soushen Ji, juan 1: Pengzu, the wine-seller's mortality, and the eighty years that were nothing

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: At the end of the Yin dynasty Pengzu was eight hundred years old and did not look old. Asked how, he laughed: he had lost his parents in infancy, been sick a hundred illnesses in youth, buried forty-nine wives and fifty-four children — and the losses, he said, are what kept him; and when the King of Chu offered a thousand gold for the secret of his longevity, he told him plainly: an eight-hundred-year life is but one day to heaven, and even Pengzu himself is, by heaven's reckoning, a man who died young.
summary.zh: 彭祖殷末已八百歲而不衰老；自述少而多病，喪妻四十九、喪子五十四，憂患備嘗——壽八百為不足；天之視彭祖八百歲，猶人之夭也——長壽之寓言。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Soushen Ji original.

passages.text: At the end of the Yin, Pengzu was eight hundred years old, and his face did not show it. Asked how he managed, he counted his life instead of his secret: parents dead in his infancy, a hundred sicknesses in his youth, forty-nine wives buried and fifty-four children buried after them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 1, Pengzu entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 殷朝末年，彭祖已八百歲，面容卻不顯老態。有人問他如何做到，他不說祕訣，只細數自己的一生：幼年時父母雙亡，年少時百病纏身，先後安葬了四十九位妻子，之後又安葬了五十四個子女。

passages.text: The losses, he said, were the secret and the cost together: grief had kept him from the excesses that kill. And to the king who offered a thousand gold for the recipe he answered with the arithmetic of heaven: eight hundred years is to heaven's reckoning what a morning is to ours — by heaven's count, Pengzu himself is a man who died young.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 1, the answer; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他說，這些失去既是祕訣，也是代價：悲傷使他免於那些足以致命的縱欲。而對於那位願以千金換取祕方的君王，他以天界的算法作答：八百年在天界的計算中，不過相當於我們眼中的一個早晨——按天界來算，彭祖本人也不過是個早夭之人。

title.en: Chisongzi, the Rain Master Who Rode the Fire-Stone
title.zh: 赤松子雨師

region.en: The courts of the Flame Emperor (symbolic pin: south of the Yangzi)
region.zh: 炎帝之廷

period: Soushen Ji by Gan Bao, c. 350 CE, juan 1

source.work: Soushen Ji, juan 1: Chisongzi, the water-jade of self-combustion, and the rain-prayers of the Flame Emperor

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Chisongzi, the Red Pine Master, served the Flame Emperor as Rain Master: he took the drug of the water-jade, which burns without fuel, and floated with it in the fire; he went up to and down from the Jade Mountain by riding it, and taught the emperor's daughter the same — she followed him and was lost with him in the burning; in every drought the age called on him, and the rain came.
summary.zh: 赤松子者，神農時雨師也；服水玉以教神農，能入火不焚；往往至崑崙山上，炎帝少女追之，亦得仙俱去——至高辛時復為雨師。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Soushen Ji original.

passages.text: Chisongzi was the Rain Master in the days of the Flame Emperor: he took the drug of the water-jade, the stone that burns without burning up, and could walk in fire unscorched, riding its smoke up to the Jade Mountain of the gods and back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 1, Chisongzi entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 赤松子曾是炎帝時期的雨師：他服食水玉之藥，那石頭燃燒而不銷毀，因而能在火中行走而不被灼傷，乘著火的煙氣升上眾神的玉山，又再返回。

passages.text: He taught the art to the Flame Emperor's youngest daughter, who followed him into the fire and was gone with him — and ages later, in the reign of Gaoxin, the rain-prayers of the dry fields still called his name, and he served again as Rain Master.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他將這門法術傳授給炎帝的小女兒，她隨他走入火中，與他一同離去——而許久之後，在高辛氏的時代，乾旱田地的祈雨之祭仍呼喚著他的名字，他又再度出任雨師。

title.en: Ning Fengzi, the Fire-Drill Master Who Rode His Own Smoke
title.zh: 寧封子積火自焚

region.en: The kilns of the Yellow Emperor's court (symbolic pin: central plains)
region.zh: 黃帝陶正之官

period: Soushen Ji by Gan Bao, c. 350 CE, juan 1

source.work: Soushen Ji, juan 1: Ning Fengzi, the officer of pottery, and the fire of self-ascension

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Ning Fengzi was the Yellow Emperor's officer of pottery, and a stranger taught him the art of the fire's interior — the flame's own breathing. He gathered a great fire, walked into it, and rode the smoke upward: when the fire died, men found in the ashes the shape of his body, intact, and in time it too turned to smoke and rose — the master who ascended through his own kiln.
summary.zh: 寧封子，黃帝時為陶正；有異人過之，為其掌火，能出五色煙；久則以教封子，封子積火自焚而隨煙上下——火化而登仙。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Soushen Ji original.

passages.text: Ning Fengzi held the office of pottery in the Yellow Emperor's court, and a stranger came to his kilns who could handle fire from the inside, making it breathe out smoke of five colors; the stranger stayed long, and taught the officer the art of the flame's interior.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 1, Ning Fengzi entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 寧封子於黃帝之朝擔任陶正一職，有異人來到他的窯場，能從內部操控火焰，使窯中吐出五色煙氣；異人停留甚久，將火焰內在之術傳授給這位陶正。

passages.text: Ning Fengzi piled a great fire, walked into it, and rose with the smoke. When the fire cooled, the ashes held his body's shape unburned; in time that too dissolved into smoke and went up — the kiln-officer's ascension, filed in the gazetteer of immortals between the potters' marks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Soushen Ji, juan 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 寧封子堆起大火，走入火中，隨煙升騰而起。火熄之後，灰燼中留有他身形的輪廓，未曾燒毀；久而久之，那形骸也化為煙氣上升——陶正之飛昇，載於神仙傳記之中，列於陶工印記之間。

title.en: The Jade Maiden of Heaven and the Clerk Xian Chao
title.zh: 天上玉女弦超

region.en: Jibei, the county of the night visits (Shandong)
region.zh: 濟北郡

period: Soushen Ji by Gan Bao, c. 350 CE, juan 1

source.work: Soushen Ji, juan 1: the jade maiden of the sky, her coming to Xian Chao, and the affairs of the spirit-wife

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: A girl in radiant dress came by night to the clerk Xian Chao, saying she was a maiden of heaven, punished by exile to marry him; she came and went with the wind, brought wealth without work, foretold what would happen, and their children were seen by none. Twice she left in quarrels — once for seven years of an empty room — and each reconciliation came with an oracle: the tale is the oldest spirit-wife contract of the corpus, kept on its terms and broken at its price.
summary.zh: 濟北郡弦超，魏嘉平中，夜有美女來，自稱天上玉女，姓成公字知瓊，早失父母，天帝哀其孤苦，遣令下嫁；出入有光，預知未來；屢離屢合——神女婚約之原型。
