passages.text: Cui the young scholar loved a singing-girl kept in a locked tower of the great marshal's household; his servant Mole, a man of Kunlun with wrists of iron, said only: show me the wall — and carried the scholar over it at midnight, past the dogs of the garden, into the tower's chamber.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 194, Kunlun Nu entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 書生崔生愛上了一名歌女，那歌女被幽禁在大元帥府中一座上了鎖的高樓裡；他的僕人磨勒，是崑崙人，腕力如鐵，只說了一句：指給我看那牆——便於半夜背著書生越過牆去，避過園中的狗，進入那樓中的房間。

passages.text: The girl asked to be carried out of her gilded prison with him; Mole took her down the wall on his back and walked her home through the sleeping city, and did the same errand twice more before the marshal's men finally traced the escapes and came with halberds to the servants' quarters.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 194; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那女子請求與他一同逃出她那鍍金的牢籠；磨勒背著她下了牆，穿過沉睡的城池送她回家，又同樣跑了兩趟差事，直到元帥的人終於追查到這些逃亡的蹤跡，手持長戟來到僕役的住處。

passages.text: Mole scattered the halberdiers with his two hands, stepped over the compound wall unhurried, and was never seen in the city again — a slave who freed a scholar, a girl, and himself with the same skill, and paid for it with nothing but his own disappearance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 194, the ending; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 磨勒以雙手撥散持戟的衛兵，從容跨過院牆，此後城中再無人見到他——一個奴僕，以同樣的本領解放了一位書生、一名女子與他自己，而付出的代價不過是他自身的消失。

title.en: Hongxian, the Red Thread Across a Governor's Pillow
title.zh: 紅線盜盒

region.en: The camps of Luzhou and Weibo (Tang frontier, Hebei–Shanxi)
region.zh: 潞州至魏博

period: Taiping Guangji, juan 195, from the 'Hongxian' chuanqi (Tang, c. 830 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 195: the maidservant who flew three hundred li, took a gold box, and stopped a war with it

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The governor of Luzhou's household held a maidservant, Hongxian, who could fly three hundred li in a night with a red thread tied to her brow. When the warlord of Weibo massed an army to destroy the governor, she rode the night wind into his bedroom, stood at his sleeping head with her knife — and took, instead of his life, the gold box at his pillow, flying home by dawn. The box laid on the warlord's own breakfast-table stopped the war; the maidservant was, she said, a man of an earlier age reborn to pay a debt of one city's blood.
summary.zh: 紅線夜入魏博節度使田承嗣寢帳，取其枕前金盒而歸；承嗣懼而罷兵——紅線自言前生為男子，以誤傷人命，謫為女子償之。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text.

passages.text: When the warlord of Weibo massed his armies to destroy the governor of Luzhou, the governor's own maidservant Hongxian asked for one night and a red thread tied at her brow; she flew the three hundred li to the warlord's camp in the dark.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 195, Hongxian entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 魏博節度使聚兵欲滅潞州節度使，潞州節度使自家的婢女紅線，請以一宵為期，於額上繫一紅線；她於夜色中飛越三百里，直抵魏博節度使的軍營。

passages.text: In his bedroom she stood over the sleeping man with her knife at his head, and considered — the war to be paid in one life, or taught in one theft. She took the gold box from his pillow, left the knife, and flew home before dawn with the proof of how far a servant can reach.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 195, the theft; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在他的臥房中，她持刀立於熟睡之人頭側，思量著——這場戰事，是以一條性命償付，還是以一次竊取教訓。她自他枕邊取走金盒，留下刀，於天明前飛回家中，帶著一名僕婢能及多遠的憑證。

passages.text: The box was laid on the warlord's own breakfast-table by his own envoy, with a courteous letter; the warlord, understanding in one look that his bedroom had been visited by the household he meant to destroy, recalled his armies. The maidservant said farewell to her master and vanished — a man of an earlier age, she said, reborn as a woman to pay an old debt, and paid.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 195, the ending; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那金盒由魏博節度使自己派出的使者，連同一封措辭謙恭的書信，置於他自己的早餐桌上；魏博節度使一眼便明白，自己的臥房已被他打算毀滅的那戶人家造訪過，於是召回兵馬。那婢女辭別主人，就此消失——她說，自己乃前代之人，轉生為女身以償舊債，而今債已償清。

title.en: Laozi Born Old, and the Ox Through the Western Pass
title.zh: 老子出關

region.en: The Hangu Pass, west of Luoyang (Shaanxi–Henan)
region.zh: 函谷關

period: Shenxian Zhuan (Biographies of Divine Immortals) by Ge Hong, c. 300 CE, Laozi biography

source.work: Shenxian Zhuan, 'Laozi': the ancient mother's plum-? — the ancient origin, the keeper Yin Xi's request, and the five thousand characters

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The immortal biographies make Laozi the oldest of beings, born as an old man with white hair, and a keeper of archives in the declining Zhou. When the age decayed he rode a black ox toward the western passes; the gate-keeper Yin Xi saw the purple vapor riding the east wind and held the gate until the sage wrote down, in five thousand characters, the Way and its Power — then rode on west, leaving behind the smallest book and the largest theology.
summary.zh: 老子生而皓首，故稱老子；周室衰，乘青牛西出關；關令尹喜見紫氣東來，留之——為著五千言《道德經》，遂西去莫知所終。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shenxian Zhuan biography; the historical Laozi of the Shiji is a different genre — both are kept apart in the corpus.

passages.text: The immortal record says Laozi was older than heaven and earth, and was born with white hair — hence his name, the Old Child — and served the declining house of Zhou as keeper of the archives, watching the world's receipts pile up without its wisdom growing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shenxian Zhuan, Laozi biography (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 神仙傳記載，老子比天地更為年長，生來白髮——故其名為老聃——他事奉衰微的周室，擔任守藏室之史，眼看世間的帳目堆積如山，而世人的智慧卻不見增長。

passages.text: When the dynasty could no longer be helped, he mounted a black ox and rode west toward the passes. The gate-keeper Yin Xi, a student of the skies, saw a purple vapor riding the east wind and knew a sage was coming: he held the gate and asked for the teaching as toll.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shenxian Zhuan, Yin Xi episode; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當王朝已無可挽救，他騎上一頭青牛，西行往關隘而去。守關的尹喜，本是研習天象之人，望見一道紫氣乘東風而來，便知有聖人將至：他守住關口，以傳授道法為過關之資。

passages.text: Laozi stayed the night and wrote, in five thousand characters, the book of the Way and its Power; then he rode on through the pass and west beyond all records — the smallest book and the largest theology left at a customs gate, and the sage gone where no account of him follows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shenxian Zhuan, the departure; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 老子留宿一夜，寫下五千字的《道德經》；隨後他繼續前行，出關西去，不知所終——最小的一部書與最宏大的一部神學，被留在了一座關卡之前，而聖人已遠去，再無任何關於他的記載隨行。

title.en: The Yellow Emperor Casts the Tripod and Rides the Dragon From Dinghu
title.zh: 黃帝鼎湖騎龍

region.en: Mount Jing and the tripod-pool of Dinghu (Shaanxi)
region.zh: 荊山鼎湖

period: Shenxian Zhuan by Ge Hong, c. 300 CE, Huangdi biography; parallel in Shiji, Fengshan Shu

source.work: Shenxian Zhuan, 'Huangdi': the first tripod cast at Mount Jing, the dragon that came down, and the ministers clinging to the whiskers

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Having united the world, the Yellow Emperor mined the copper of Mount Jing and cast a tripod at the pool called Dinghu; when it was done a dragon came down with its whiskers hanging, and the emperor, his household and seventy ministers climbed aboard and rose. Those who could not climb seized the dragon's whiskers, which tore out and fell with the bows the crowd had clutched — and the village keeps the names to this day: Whisker Row, Bow-Grasping Hamlet, and the pool named Tripod-Lake.
summary.zh: 黃帝採首山銅，鑄鼎於荊山下；鼎既成，有龍垂胡髯下迎黃帝；黃帝上騎，群臣後宮從上者七十餘人；小臣不得上，持龍髯，髯拔墮，弓亦墮地；百姓抱弓而號，其弓曰烏號，其地曰鼎湖。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shenxian Zhuan biography and the Shiji parallel.

passages.text: The Yellow Emperor, having set the world in order, mined the copper of the first mountain and cast a great tripod at the pool of Dinghu — the cauldron of the state's completion, cast in the one metal worth the sky's attention.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shenxian Zhuan, Huangdi biography (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 黃帝既已平定天下，便開採首山之銅，在鼎湖之畔鑄造一尊大鼎——此乃國家功成之鼎，以唯一值得上天矚目的金屬鑄成。

passages.text: The tripod finished, a dragon came down with its whiskers trailing, and the emperor with his family and seventy of his ministers climbed upon it and rose from the pool into the clouds; the crowd below seized the whiskers and the bows of the departing — and the whiskers tore out and fell, and with them the bows. The villages of that mountain keep the names the fall earned: Whisker Row where the beard landed, Bow-Grasping Hamlet where the crowd held on, and the pool named Tripod-Lake — the founding emperor's exit from history filed as geography.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shenxian Zhuan, the ascension; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Shenxian Zhuan with the Shiji parallel; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 鼎成之後，一條巨龍垂著龍鬚降下，黃帝攜家眷與七十位臣子登上龍身，自湖中升入雲端；下方眾人抓住離去者的龍鬚與弓——龍鬚被扯斷落下，弓也隨之而落。那座山下的村落至今保留著因這場墜落而得的名稱：鬚落之處名為「鬚行」，眾人攀附之處名為「攀弓里」，而那湖泊則名為「鼎湖」——開國之君退出歷史的所在，竟被記載成了地名。

title.en: The Queen Mother of the West Feasts Emperor Wu, and the Peach Thieves Come
title.zh: 漢武帝內傳西王母降

region.en: The palace of Emperor Wu at Chang'an (Han court)
region.zh: 漢宮

period: Han Wudi Neizhuan (Inner Biography of Emperor Wu), c. 4th-5th c. CE; parallel in Han Wudi Zhuan

source.archive: Internet Archive (reference; the text via digitized collections)
source.work: Han Wudi Neizhuan: Xiwangmu's descent on the azure bird, the seven peaches of three-thousand-year ripening, and Dongfang Shuo caught at the window

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: On the seventh month's seventh day the Queen Mother of the West came down to Emperor Wu's palace on a chariot of purple clouds drawn by azure birds; she brought with her attendants and, wrapped in leaves, seven peaches of the garden where one ripening takes three thousand years. She gave two to the Emperor; the third vanished from the tray — and the Queen Mother laughed, for she knew who had taken it: Dongfang Shuo, her own thieving courtier, caught at the window with the peach in his mouth.
summary.zh: 漢武帝好仙道，西王母以七月七日降於宮中，命侍女索桃；桃盤盛七枚，大如鴨卵；王母以四枚與帝，自食其三，帝收其核欲種之——東方朔窺桃竊之，王母笑指之：『此桃三千年一生實。』

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Neizhuan text.

passages.text: The Emperor Wu of Han, hungry for the Way of the immortals, purified a palace tower, and on the night of the seventh month the Queen Mother of the West descended on a cloud-chariot of purple vapor, drawn by the azure birds that serve her and attended by a train of her singing-women.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Han Wudi Neizhuan (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 漢武帝渴慕仙道，潔淨了一座宮中高樓；七月七日夜裡，西王母乘紫氣雲車降臨，由為她服役的青鳥駕馭，隨行還有一眾侍女。

passages.text: She called for peaches, and a plate was brought from heaven's orchard: seven peaches of a size like a duck's egg, from the tree that ripens once in three thousand years. She gave two to the emperor, who ate and wanted the kernels to plant — and she laughed at the wish, for the tree of that garden does not grow in soil such as his.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Han Wudi Neizhuan, the peaches; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她命人取桃，一隻盤子便從天界果園送來：七枚桃子，大小如鴨蛋，出自那三千年一熟的樹。她賜了兩枚給皇帝，皇帝吃罷，想要留下桃核種植——她聽聞此願便笑了，因為那座園中的樹，並非生長在他這般的土壤裡。

passages.text: A third peach vanished from the plate while she spoke; the Queen Mother looked at the window and said, still laughing, the thief's name: Dongfang Shuo, her courtier, was already swallowing it behind the lattice — the peach-thief of heaven's garden employed, for the joke of it, in the emperor's own council hall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Han Wudi Neizhuan, Dongfang Shuo episode; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她說話之間，第三枚桃子從盤中消失了；西王母望向窗邊，仍笑著說出了竊賊的名字：東方朔，她的侍臣，早已在格柵之後把桃吞下——天界果園的偷桃賊，竟為博一笑，被安插在皇帝自己的議事廳中。

title.en: Du Zichun, the Man Who Could Not Stay Silent in Hell
title.zh: 杜子春

region.en: The tower of the ascetics on Mount Song (Henan)
region.zh: 嵩山煉丹院

period: Taiping Guangji, juan 16, from the 'Du Zichun' tale (Tang, c. 750 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 16: the squanderer made rich twice, the vow of silence, and the hell of every passion

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Du Zichun, a squanderer made rich twice by a strange old man, was given one trial for the third gift: keep silent in a tower for a day, whatever comes. All day hell came to him — lightning, demons, boiling cauldrons, the general's blade at his neck, his wife's head dropped in the fire, rebirth as a girl mute and scorned, marriage, a son — and his child, dashed against a stone, laughed in his face. At that his tongue unlocked with one cry of grief — and the tower's fire went out: the elixir needed a heart with no passions left, and his had one.
summary.zh: 杜子春兩受老人贈金；第三試：嵩山煉丹爐前終日緘口；歷雷電、刀山、油鼎、畜生道，為啞女生子；兒撲石而笑，子春失聲而呼——爐火遂熄，丹不成。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text.

passages.text: Du Zichun had squandered one fortune and been given a second by a strange old man in the market; squandered that too, and been given a third with a condition: a day's vigil of total silence in the old man's mountain tower, whatever came for him there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 16, Du Zichun entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 杜子春曾揮霍掉一份家財，市集上一位奇異的老人又給了他第二份；這份也花光了，老人再給他第三份，附帶一個條件：在老人的山間樓閣中靜默守候一整日，無論那裡有什麼來找他。

passages.text: The day brought hell in order: a storm that split the tower, generals and demons who beat and boiled and burned him, his wife's head dropped screaming into the fire — and he held. Then he was reborn in the vision as a mute girl, sold, married, given a son; and the son, at her silent mother's knee, laughed and stumbled toward the well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 16, the trials; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那一日，地獄依次降臨：一場風暴劈裂了樓閣，將軍與鬼怪將他毆打、烹煮、焚燒，他妻子的頭顱尖叫著落入火中——而他忍住了。接著，他在幻境中轉生為一名啞女，被賣出、嫁人、得了一子；而那孩子，在沉默母親的膝邊笑著，踉蹌著朝井邊走去。

passages.text: The child was dashed on the stones and laughed up at her, and Du Zichun's silence broke with one cry of love. The old man's voice came through the smoke: the elixir was ready but the heart was not — for the Way of the immortals wants no passions, and his had one, and it had cost them the furnace. He went home rich for the last time, having failed magnificently.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 16, the failure; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 孩子被摔在石上，卻仰頭朝她笑，杜子春的靜默隨著一聲出於愛的呼喊而破裂。老人的聲音穿過煙霧傳來：丹藥已備好，心卻未備——因為仙道不納情慾，而他尚存一情，這一情使他們失去了丹爐。他最後一次帶著財富回家，壯麗地失敗了。

title.en: The Old Man Under the Moon and the Red Thread Ledger
title.zh: 月下老人

region.en: The temple garden near Song city (Henan)
region.zh: 宋城龍興寺

period: Taiping Guangji, juan 159, from the 'Dinghun Dian' tale (Tang, c. 810 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 159: the moonlit ledger of marriages and the red thread that cannot be broken

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Wei Gu, walking in the moonlight at a temple near Song, found an old man reading a ledger against a bag of red threads; the ledger, the man said, was the book of all marriages, and one thread tied ankle to ankle joined two people wherever they ran. Wei Gu laughed at the entry that assigned him a greengrocer's baby daughter — and the old man, to settle it, took him by night to the vegetable market, where a woman with a scarred child of the vegetable stall sat selling greens. Wei Gu sent a servant to stab the child; she survived the knife with a scar over the brow. Years on, the magistrate gave him a daughter of beauty and brow-scarred: the greengrocer's baby, led by the red thread he had tried to cut.
summary.zh: 韋固遇月下老人於宋城，赤繩繫足以定婚姻；固怒遣僕刺菜市女孩，十四年後娶妻眉間有刀痕——月老祠由此立。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text. The child-stabbing episode is recorded as the tale's darker layer.

passages.text: Wei Gu walked in the moonlight outside a temple near Song and found an old man on the steps reading a ledger, with a bag of red threads at his feet; the ledger, the man said, was the book of all marriages, and a single red thread, tied ankle to ankle, joined every pair it named — however far they ran to escape it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 159, Dinghun Dian entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 韋固在宋城附近一座寺廟外的月光下行走，發現一位老人坐在台階上翻閱一本簿冊，腳邊放著一袋紅線；老人說，這簿冊記載著世間所有婚姻，而一根紅線，腳踝繫著腳踝，牽連著它所記載的每一對——無論他們逃得多遠。

passages.text: He showed Wei Gu his own entry: a daughter of the vegetable market, a baby in a cradle by the greens. Wei Gu, insulted, sent a servant that night to stab the child; the knife left a scar over the brow and the child lived.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 159, the stabbing; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他讓韋固看自己的條目：一個菜市人家的女兒，一個躺在菜蔬旁搖籃裡的嬰兒。韋固覺得受辱，當夜派僕人去刺那孩子；刀在孩子額上留下一道疤，孩子卻活了下來。

passages.text: Fourteen years on, the magistrate gave Wei Gu his daughter in marriage — a beauty, and brow-scarred; she told him at her mirror how she had been a grocer's baby stabbed in the cradle and adopted by an uncle. Wei Gu told her about the old man with the threads; both believed, and the temple of the Old Man Under the Moon has stood in the tale's honor ever since.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 159, the marriage; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 十四年後，縣令將女兒許配給韋固——一位美人，額上有疤；她在鏡前告訴他，自己原是雜貨商人的嬰兒，在搖籃中被人刺傷，後由叔父收養。韋固把那位持線老人的事告訴了她；兩人都信了，自此，月下老人的祠廟便為紀念這個故事而矗立。

title.en: Pei Hang and the Blue-Bridge of the Jade Mortar
title.zh: 裴航藍橋

region.en: The Blue-Bridge post-station on the Shang mountain road (Shaanxi)
region.zh: 藍橋驛

period: Taiping Guangji, juan 50, from Pei Xing's 'Pei Hang' tale (Tang, c. 860 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 50: the jade pestle and the hundred days of pounding herbs at the Blue Bridge

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Pei Hang, riding home in splendor, stopped at the Blue-Bridge station for water and heard the girl behind the curtain sing his own verse back at him — Yunying, the hostess's daughter, a girl of heaven's stock. An old woman demanded his jewels for the marriage; a master of the mountains told him the true price: a jade pestle, and a hundred days of pounding the herb of the immortals in the inn's own courtyard. He bought the pestle, pounded for a hundred days in the drizzle, and married Yunying — and the two were seen later riding a jade-lion into the clouds, inviters of the household of the immortals.
summary.zh: 裴航藍橋驛遇雲英；老嫗索玉杵臼為聘，航傾財購之，搗藥百日而娶雲英——夫婦俱仙去。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text.

passages.text: Pei Hang, richly dressed and riding home from a failed examination, stopped at the Blue-Bridge station for water; behind the partition a girl's voice sang three lines that matched his own heart's verse — Yunying, the innkeeper's daughter, who was not of the innkeeper's stock.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 50, Pei Hang entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 裴航衣著華美，落第後騎馬返家，在藍橋驛停下來討水喝；隔板之後，一名女子的歌聲唱出三句詩，正與他心中所吟之句相合——那女子便是驛站老婦之女雲英，而她並非老婦所生。

passages.text: The old hostess named a bride-price no man could pay: a jade pestle and mortar of the immortals, and a hundred days of pounding the herb that opens the Way. Pei Hang sold his estates, hunted the jade through the markets of the capital, found it, and came back to the Blue Bridge to work.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 50; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 老婦開出的聘禮，無人能付得起：仙人的玉杵與玉臼，以及百日搗煉那開啟大道的靈藥。裴航變賣家產，走遍京城市集尋訪玉器，終於尋得，便回到藍橋做工。

passages.text: A hundred days he pounded in the courtyard, hands in the drizzle, herbs to powder, powder to medicine; on the last night the doors of the inn opened on a hill of light, and the household came up the mountain as immortal guests. Years after, travelers saw two riders on a jade lion in the clouds and knew the pairing at the Blue Bridge had ended in heaven's register.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 50, the ascent; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他在院中搗了一百日，雙手沾著細雨，把藥草搗成粉末，再把粉末煉成藥；最後一夜，驛站的門扉敞開，現出一座光明之山，一家人便如仙客般登上山去。多年之後，行旅之人望見雲中有人騎著玉獅，便知藍橋之約已登仙籍。

title.en: The Passion Play of Osiris at Abydos
title.zh: 阿拜多斯奧西里斯受難劇

region.en: Abydos, Upper Egypt (temple, processional way, and the plain of Peqer)
region.zh: 埃及上埃及阿拜多斯（神廟、巡行道與佩克爾平原）

period: Annual play attested by the stele of I-kher-nefert, 12th Dynasty (c. 1900 BCE), reproducing Old Kingdom rites (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II, 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (London, 1911), ch. XIV, 'The Shrines, Miracle Play, and Mysteries of Osiris' (stele of I-kher-nefert, Berlin 1024)

summary.en: The earliest recorded drama in the world: at Abydos each year the death and resurrection of Osiris was acted — the god's boat attacked by the foes of Set, Ap-uat leading the defense, the Great Coming-forth of the dead god's body from the temple with wailing crowds and club-fights, the three-day search tracing the god by his footsteps, Thoth ferrying the body to the tomb at Peqer — with the official I-kher-nefert starring in every act.
summary.zh: 世上最古之戲劇：阿拜多斯歲歲搬演奧西里斯之死與復活——神舟遭塞特黨羽攻擊，阿普-烏阿特領眾禦敵；『大出遊』之日，亡神之體出廟，眾人號哭執杖相鬥；歷三日循神之足跡遍尋；托特以舟渡神體至佩克爾之墓——官員伊克赫爾-奈費爾特親歷每幕。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ritual drama; no living community restrictions. OCR text used with care; quotations cleaned of obvious OCR breaks.

passages.text: We know from the evidence of the inscriptions that such a play was performed at Abydos once a year under the Middle and New Empires, and it is only reasonable to assume that it reproduced all the essential features of the great annual festival of the god which was celebrated under the Ancient Empire. In religious matters at least the conservatism of the ancient Egyptians was absolute.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XIV.
passages.zh: 我們從碑銘的證據得知，在中王國與新王國時期，這樣的戲劇每年在阿拜多斯上演一次；而我們也有理由推斷，它重現了古王國時期所慶祝的該神年度大慶典的一切基本特徵。至少在宗教事務上，古埃及人的保守性是絕對的。

passages.text: The second portion of the inscription on the stele of I-kher-nefert is of very great importance, for it describes briefly the principal scenes in the Osiris play which was performed at Abydos annually. I-kher-nefert himself played a prominent part in this 'Mystery play', and he describes his own acts as follows: 'I performed the coming forth of Ap-uat when he set out to defend his father.' From this it is clear that in the XIIth dynasty Ap-uat was regarded as the son of Osiris, and that he acted the part of leader of Osiris's expedition, which was represented by a procession formed of priests and the ordinary people. Ap-uat walked in front, next came the boat containing the figure of the god and a company of priests or 'followers' of the god, and the rear was brought up by a crowd of people.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XIV.
passages.zh: 伊赫爾涅費爾特石碑銘文的第二部分極為重要，因為它簡要描述了每年在阿拜多斯上演的奧西里斯劇中的主要場景。伊赫爾涅費爾特本人在这齣「祕儀劇」中扮演了重要角色，他如此描述自己的行動：「我演出阿普瓦特的出場，當時他出發去保衛他的父親。」由此可見，在第十二王朝時期，阿普瓦特被視為奧西里斯之子，而他扮演的是奧西里斯遠征隊首領的角色，這支遠征隊由祭司與平民組成的遊行隊伍來表現。阿普瓦特走在最前面，接著是載著神像的船，以及一群祭司或神的「隨從」，最後則由一大群民眾殿後。

passages.text: 'I drove back the enemy from the Neshmet Boat, I overthrew the foes of Osiris.' The boat of the god was then attacked by a crowd of men who represented the foes of Osiris, and, as the god was defenceless, Ap-uat engaged them in combat, and beat them off, and the procession then continued on its way in the temple. 'I performed the Great Coming-forth, I followed the god in his footsteps.' This act was the greatest in the Osiris play, for it represented the 'coming forth' of Osiris from the temple after his death, and the departure of his body to his tomb. A solemn service was performed in the temple before the body was carried from it, and offerings were eaten sacramentally, and then the procession set out for the tomb.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XIV.
passages.zh: 「我從涅什梅特船上擊退了敵人，我打倒了奧西里斯的仇敵。」神的船隨後遭到一群代表奧西里斯仇敵之人的攻擊；由於神毫無防備，阿普瓦特便與他們交戰，將他們擊退，遊行隊伍於是繼續在神廟中前行。「我演出大出場，我跟隨神的足跡。」這一幕是奧西里斯劇中最偉大的一幕，因為它表現了奧西里斯死後從神廟中「出場」，以及他的遺體啟程前往陵墓。在遺體被抬出神廟之前，廟中舉行了莊嚴的儀式，供品被當作聖餐食用，隨後遊行隊伍便啟程前往陵墓。

passages.text: When it reached the door of the temple it was received by a mighty crowd of men and women who raised the death-wail, and uttered piercing shrieks and lamentations, and the women beat their breasts. Many of the men in the crowd were armed with sticks and staves, and some of them pressed forward towards the procession with the view of helping the god, whilst others strove to prevent them. Thus a sham fight took place, which, owing to the excitement of the combatants, often degenerated into a serious one. And, if Herodotus was correctly informed, this combat with clubs was waged with great obstinacy, and heads were broken... This fight was, of course, intended to represent the great battle which took place in prehistoric times between Set and Osiris, when Osiris was killed.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XIV.
passages.zh: 當它抵達神殿門口時，一大群男女迎接它，他們發出哀悼的哭號，發出刺耳的尖叫與悲嘆，婦女們捶打自己的胸膛。人群中有許多男子手持棍棒與杖，其中一些人向隊伍擠去，意圖幫助這位神，而另一些人則竭力阻止他們。於是發生了一場模擬的戰鬥，由於參與者的激動，這場戰鬥往往演變成真正的打鬥。而若希羅多德的記述正確無誤，這場持棍的搏鬥進行得極為頑強，頭顱都被打破了……這場打鬥，當然是為了表現史前時代賽特與歐西里斯之間發生的大戰，歐西里斯便是在那場大戰中被殺的。

canonical_translation: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (London, 1911), ch. XIV; stele of I-kher-nefert ed. Schaefer, Untersuchungen IV (1904)

narrative.en:
The Passion Play of Osiris is the oldest documented drama on earth: an annual staged death, battle, search, funeral, and victory, performed in the temple and processional ways of Abydos and attested by the autobiography of a man who acted in it.

THE SETTING. Abydos was the earthly centre of Osiris' kingdom: every tradition asserted that the god's head was buried there, the city's very symbol was the coffer-basket that held his head, and the rich bought burial beside him or had their mummies shipped upriver for a season's blessing. Under the 12th Dynasty the official I-kher-nefert, sent by King Usertsen III, rebuilt the god's shrine of sweet-smelling woods inlaid with gold, silver and lapis-lazuli, provided a new Neshmet Boat — a copy of the boat in which Osiris had sailed to the fatal meeting with Set — and established the office of 'Sa-mer-f', the god's 'beloved son', a priest with clean fingers who alone might dress the statue and touch the shrine's furniture. In his great stele (Berlin 1024) he records his own parts in the play.

THE ACTS. First, 'I performed the coming forth of Ap-uat when he set out to defend his father': Ap-uat, son and herald of Osiris, led a procession of priests and people, walking before the boat that carried the god's figure, the crowd streaming behind. Second, the boat was attacked by men playing the foes of Osiris; the god himself was defenceless, and Ap-uat engaged them and beat them off before the procession could continue. Third came the 'Great Coming-forth', the play's supreme act: the dead god's body left the temple for the tomb. Offerings were eaten sacramentally in the temple first; then the procession was received at the temple door by a mighty crowd of men and women wailing death-cries, the women beating their breasts; men armed with sticks and staves pressed in to help or hinder the god, and the sham fight — the re-fought battle of Netit where Set killed Osiris — often degenerated into real injury, just as Herodotus was told when he described the club-fight of Papremis.

THE SEARCH AND THE BURIAL. 'I followed the god in his footsteps' — the search party, led by I-kher-nefert, traced the dead god by his literal footprints across the battlefield, three days of wandering interrupted by renewed sham fights and great lamentations, until the body was found (a passage in the Pyramid Text of Pepi I names Isis and Nephthys as the finders, their cries of grief summoning Thoth, who came by boat and saw Isis caressing and embracing the body of her husband). Then 'I made the boat of the god to move': I-kher-nefert acted ferryman for Thoth, bringing the body from Netit; 'I provided the Boat of the Lord of Abydos called Kha-em-Maat (appearing in truth) with a cabin shrine', dressed the god in his festal apparel, fastened the two feathers of Maati on the coffin, tied a bandlet on the god's head, and placed a model of Set at his feet — and 'directed the ways of the god to his tomb in Peqer.'

PEQER. Excavations by Amelineau identified Peqer as the part of the Abydos plain called Umm el-Qa'ab, 'mother of pots', where the tombs of the First Dynasty kings stand — among them the tomb of King Khent, which the Egyptians of the New Kingdom firmly identified as the tomb of Osiris himself, and beside which a famous cenotaph of Osiris was made under the 22nd Dynasty. The play thus ends where the religion begins: the murdered god laid in the royal tomb, his faithful son following the ways of the god to the grave — and the whole city acting out, once a year, the death and rising that promised every Egyptian his own resurrection.

functions: Annual communal re-enactment of the Osiris cycle: murder, battle, search, funeral — Egypt's oldest recorded theatre
Pilgrimage economy of Abydos: burial and blessing absorbed from the god's shrine, mummies shipped upriver for a season
Sacral role of the official elite: I-kher-nefert records acting Ap-uat, ferryman of Thoth, and director of the god's ways to the tomb
Theology of the royal tomb: the First-Dynasty tomb of Khent at Peqer venerated as the grave of Osiris

variants.name: The club-fight of Papremis (Herodotus II.63)
variants.summary: Herodotus' account of a priestly battle at Papremis, rationalized as the war-god's visit to his mother, matches the Passion Play's club-fight around the god's boat — the same ritual combat at a different shrine.

variants.summary: The PT passage names Isis and Nephthys as the discoverers of Osiris' body and Thoth as its ferryman — the mythic text underlying the play's search and boat scenes.

variants.text_tradition: Temple reliefs and inscriptions of Denderah (Mariette, Denderah IV)
variants.summary: A later, more liturgical form of the same festival: corn-paste figures of Osiris made, buried and raised at Denderah; cut as its own record.

title.en: The Mysteries of Osiris at Denderah: The Corn Mummy and the Sixteen Cakes
title.zh: 丹德拉奧西里斯秘祭：穀神像與十六塊祭餅

region.en: Denderah (Tentyris), Upper Egypt (temple reliefs of the Khoiak mysteries)
region.zh: 埃及上埃及丹德拉（坦提里斯，荷阿克秘祭浮雕神廟）

period: Inscribed in the Ptolemaic temple of Denderah, reproducing rites attested from the Middle Kingdom (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II, 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (1911), ch. XV, 'The Mysteries of Osiris at Denderah' (Mariette, Denderah IV, pls. 35-39)

summary.en: Egypt's agricultural resurrection rite in full: through the month of Khoiak, wheat and paste are kneaded in gold moulds into figures of Khenti-Amenti and Seker, watered daily, tied with four papyrus bands, dried in the sun; cakes are baked in the shapes of the sixteen members of Osiris; a sacred field is ploughed by black cows and sown with barley, dhura and flax; the Tet is raised on the last day, and for seven days the unburied god rests 'in the branches of the sycamores of Mendes' — the seven months in the womb of Nut.
summary.zh: 埃及農事復活祭全景：荷阿克月間，小麥與漿料於金模中揉成肯提-阿門提與塞克爾之像，日日灌水，以四條紙莎草帶束之，曬於日光；餅烤作奧西里斯十六肢體之形；聖田由黑牛犁耕，播大麥、高粱與亞麻；月末日舉起泰特柱——七日未葬之神『棲於門德斯之梧桐枝間』，象其七月在努特胎中。

sensitivity.note: Ancient temple liturgy; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: At Mendes, a town closely connected with Busiris and the cult of Osiris, one kin of wheat and three kin of paste were placed in a large stone trough resting on four legs, and each day, from the 12th to the 21st day of Khoiak, three parts of a kin of water were poured from a gold goblet into the trough. On the 21st day the contents of the trough were taken out, and a measure of incense having been added to it, the whole was kneaded into the two halves of a gold mould for making the figure of Khenti-Amenti wearing the White Crown. The contents of the moulds were then taken out and tied together with four papyrus bands, and dried in the sun. At the eighth hour of the 22nd day of the month, the figure, and figures of gods and many lamps, were placed in boats, and taken by water to the tomb of the god, and there the figure of Khenti-Amenti was covered with a cloth, and afterwards buried.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XV.
passages.zh: 在門德斯——一個與布西里斯及歐西里斯崇拜密切相關的城鎮——人們將一金（kin）的小麥與三金的麵糊放入一個架在四條腿上的大石槽中，並自科伊阿克月十二日至二十一日，每日從一隻金杯往槽中倒入三份一金的水。到了二十一日，將槽中的內容物取出，加入一量器的乳香，再將全部揉捏進一個金製模具的兩半之中，以製作頭戴白冠的肯提—阿門提像。隨後取出模具中的內容物，用四條紙莎草帶將其綁在一起，置於陽光下曬乾。到了該月二十二日的第八時辰，這尊像與諸神的像以及許多燈盞被放入船中，經水路運往這位神的陵墓，在那裡，肯提—阿門提的像被覆上一塊布，隨後被埋葬。

passages.text: The moulds for the 'divine bread' were made of the wood of a red tree, and cakes were made from them in the forms of the sixteen members of Osiris, viz., his head, feet, bones, arms, heart, intestines, tongue, eye, fist, fingers, body, back, ears, backbone, ram's head, and hair. These cakes were put in a box, which was placed in a silver chest, and then set under the head of the god for protection.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XV.
passages.zh: 製作「神聖麵包」的模具以一種紅樹的木材製成，並用它們製成麵餅，其形狀為歐西里斯的十六個部位，即他的頭、腳、骨、臂、心、腸、舌、眼、拳、指、身、背、耳、脊、羊頭與髮。這些麵餅被放入一個箱子，箱子置於一個銀櫃之中，然後安放在這位神的頭下以作護佑。

passages.text: The Field of Osiris in which the sacred grain was to be sown was from 210 to 223 feet long; one end of it was sown with barley, its centre with dhura, and the other end with flax. The plough frame was made of two kinds of wood, and the ploughshare of black bronze; the cows which pulled it were black. The barley which grew in the Field was cut on the 20th day of Tobe, and was made into sacred cakes, the dhura was also made into cakes, and the linen made from the flax was used at the festival.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XV.
passages.zh: 用以播種聖穀的歐西里斯之田長二百一十至二百二十三步尺；其一端播種大麥，中央播種高粱，另一端播種亞麻。犁架以兩種木材製成，犁頭以黑青銅製成；拉犁的母牛是黑色的。田中長出的大麥於托貝月二十日收割，並製成聖餅，高粱也製成餅，而由亞麻製成的亞麻布則用於節慶。

passages.text: On the 16th the festival of Osiris Khenti-Amenti was celebrated, and on that day the transformation of the god took place. On the 19th the figure of Seker was taken from its mould, and on that day Horus saw his father. On the 21st the figure of Osiris was taken from its mould; on the 24th Osiris was embalmed, and on the last day of the month the Tet was raised up, and Osiris was buried. For seven days, from the 24th to the last day of the month, Osiris remained unburied, and during these days he rested in the branches of the sycamores of Mendes. The seven days symbolize the seven months which he passed in the womb of his mother Nut, and the branches symbolize the goddess.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XV.
passages.zh: 十六日慶祝歐西里斯—肯提—阿門提的節日，就在那一天，這位神發生了變形。十九日，塞克爾的像從其模具中取出，就在那一天，荷魯斯見到了他的父親。二十一日，歐西里斯的像從其模具中取出；二十四日，歐西里斯被製成木乃伊，而在該月最後一日，泰特柱被豎起，歐西里斯被埋葬。自二十四日至該月最後一日，共七天，歐西里斯一直未被埋葬，在這幾天裡，他安息於門德斯無花果樹的枝葉之間。這七天象徵他在其母努特腹中所度過的七個月，而枝葉則象徵這位女神。

language: Egyptian (temple inscription, Ptolemaic copy of older rites)
canonical_translation: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (London, 1911), ch. XV, from Mariette, Denderah, vol. IV, plates 35-39

narrative.en:
The Denderah inscriptions preserve, in Ptolemaic dress, the fullest surviving liturgy of Egypt's central mystery: the annual making, burying and raising of Osiris in grain — the god as seed-corn.

BEGINNING: THE MONTH OF KHOIAK. On the 12th day of Khoiak, at Busiris, Mendes, Abydos, Memphis, and every sanctuary of Osiris, priests filled a stone trough with one kin of wheat and three or four kin of paste. Each day, from the 12th to the 21st, three parts of a kin of water were poured from a gold goblet into the trough — the god being watered like a field. On the 21st the swollen mass was kneaded into the two halves of a gold mould, one carrying the figure of Khenti-Amenti wearing the White Crown, and the halves, tied together with four papyrus bands, were set in the sun to dry: a corn-effigy of the god, the 'Osiris garden' in its most complete form. On the 22nd the figure, with figures of gods and many lamps, was placed in boats and taken by water to the god's tomb and buried.

MIDDLE: THE SIXTEEN MEMBERS AND THE SACRED FIELD. The same inscriptions regulate the 'divine bread': cakes baked in gold moulds of red-tree wood in the shapes of the sixteen members of Osiris — head, feet, bones, arms, heart, intestines, tongue, eye, fist, fingers, body, back, ears, backbone, ram's head, and hair — boxed, placed in a silver chest, and set under the head of the god. A second rite made the figure of Seker from an egg-shaped paste of earth from the town of Neter, dates, incense, fresh myrrh, spices and precious stones, pressed into a one-cubit gold mould and laid on a bed. And the Field of Osiris itself — 210 to 223 feet long — was ploughed by black cows drawing a plough of two woods with a black bronze share, one end sown with barley, the centre with dhura, the other with flax; the barley was cut on the 20th of Tobe and baked into the sacred cakes, and the flax became the linen of the festival.

END: HORUS SEES HIS FATHER, THE TET RAISED. The liturgy's final days stage the resurrection in ritual time: on the 16th, the 'transformation of the god' at the festival of Osiris Khenti-Amenti; on the 19th the figure of Seker left its mould — 'on that day Horus saw his father'; on the 21st the figure of Osiris itself was removed; on the 24th, embalmed; and on the last day of Khoiak the Tet, the backbone-pillar of Osiris, was raised up and the god was buried. For seven days the god remained unburied, resting 'in the branches of the sycamores of Mendes' — the seven days symbolizing the seven months he passed in the womb of his mother Nut, the branches symbolizing the goddess. The thirty-four festival boats with their 365 lamps, the peace chamber with its 'lord of silence' seated hand-on-mouth, and the funeral furniture drawn by yoked heifers — two obelisks, four coffers of the Four Sons of Horus with veils of blue, red, green and white, sixteen vulture plumes, and behind them a figure of the serpent Apep holding a knife to sever the cordage — completed a festival that enacted, in grain and gold, the whole theology of death-as-sowing.

functions: Agricultural resurrection liturgy: Osiris made in wheat and paste, watered, dried, buried and raised — death as sowing
Eucharistic cakes of the sixteen members eaten by the community of the god
Ritual calendar of Khoiak fixing the festival days of every Osiris sanctuary in Egypt
Theology of gestation: the god's seven unburied days equated with seven months in the womb of Nut

title.en: The Road to Abydos: Mummies Shipped for a Blessing
title.zh: 通往阿拜多斯之路：運棺受祝福

region.en: Abydos, Upper Egypt (the shrine of the god's head and its pilgrim plain)
region.zh: 埃及上埃及阿拜多斯（神首之祠與朝聖平原）

period: Pilgrimage attested from the 12th Dynasty through the New Kingdom (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II, 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (1911), ch. XIV, the pilgrimage customs of Abydos

summary.en: Every good Egyptian's aim was 'to become an Osiris': the bodies of the wealthy who died far away were taken upriver to Abydos, laid by the shrine to absorb its beneficent emanations, and then returned home for burial — a traffic Budge compares with the modern Muslim festival of Shekh Sayyid al-Badawi at Tanta, where the dead are carried round the saint's tomb for a blessing.
summary.zh: 每個善者皆求『成為奧西里斯』：遠方亡故之富者，遺體必運往阿拜多斯，置於神祠之側以吸其靈福，而後運回故里安葬——伯奇以此比於今日坦塔之賽義德巴達維聖節：亡者繞聖墓一周以承福澤。

sensitivity.note: Ancient practice described in Budge 1911; no living community restrictions. The comparison with a living Muslim festival is Budge's own observation and is quoted neutrally.

passages.text: It was believed that the dead who were buried at Abydos would be joined by the god to his company of followers in the Other World, that they would enjoy his protection, and that they would share in his offerings on festival days, and become partakers with him in immortality and everlasting happiness. The aim of every good man was to become an Osiris, and even in the Pyramid Texts we find it tacitly assumed that the kings for whom they were written had each become an Osiris, and the name of Osiris is actually prefixed to the names of some of them.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XIV.
passages.zh: 人們相信，葬於阿拜多斯的死者將被這位神接納，加入他在彼世的隨從之列，他們將享有他的庇護，在節慶之日分享他的供品，並與他一同分享不朽與永恆的幸福。每一個善良之人的目標都是成為一個歐西里斯，甚至在《金字塔文》中，我們也發現其中默認，這些經文所為之而寫的諸王各自都已成為一個歐西里斯，而歐西里斯之名實際上被冠於其中某些王的名字之前。

passages.text: Very few Egyptians who were not natives of the neighbourhood could afford to buy tombs there and be buried in them, and the transport of mummified bodies from a great distance was both difficult and costly. Nevertheless, many men were so eager that their dead bodies should rest on the sacred soil of Abydos, and be near Osiris, if only for a short time, that it became the custom among the well-to-do classes to transport the mummies of their kinsfolk to Abydos so that they might absorb the beneficent emanations from the shrine of the god and be blessed by the influence of the place and its holy associations. These mummies were then taken back by river to the places whence they came, and buried in the tombs which had been provided for them.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XIV.
passages.zh: 在非本地出身的埃及人中，很少有人負擔得起在那裡購買墳墓並葬身其中，而從遠方運送木乃伊既困難又所費不貲。儘管如此，仍有許多人殷切盼望自己的遺體能安息於阿拜多斯的聖土之上，並親近歐西里斯，哪怕只是短暫的一段時光；因此，在富裕階層中形成了一種習俗：將親屬的木乃伊運往阿拜多斯，好讓他們得以汲取神明聖所所散發的恩澤，並蒙受此地及其神聖淵源的庇佑。這些木乃伊隨後再由水路運回原處，安葬於為他們預備好的墳墓之中。

passages.text: At Tanta I have seen dead bodies brought in and laid for a few moments by the tomb of the saint, or simply carried round his tomb-chamber, in order to obtain his blessing, and men and women stand motionless and silent by the iron gates of the tomb, merely to be blessed by its presence, and to gain a share in the spiritual benefits which are believed to emanate from it.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XIV, Budge's own observation at the festival of Shekh Sayyid al-Badawi, offered as a living parallel.
passages.zh: 在坦塔，我曾見過有人將遺體送來，在聖徒的墓旁停放片刻，或僅僅繞著他的墓室抬行一圈，以求獲得他的祝福；男男女女一動不動、默然無聲地站在墓的鐵門旁，只為蒙受其臨在的祝福，並分得一份人們相信由此散發的靈性恩澤。

title.en: Peqer, Mother of Pots: The Tomb of a King Became the Tomb of a God
title.zh: 佩克爾，罐之母：王墓成神墓

region.en: Umm el-Qa'ab (Peqer), Abydos, Egypt (the First Dynasty royal necropolis)
region.zh: 埃及阿拜多斯烏姆卡阿布（佩克爾，第一王朝王陵）

period: Royal tombs of the 1st Dynasty (c. 3000 BCE); identified as Osiris' tomb by New Kingdom pilgrims (Budge 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (1911), ch. XIV, the tomb of Osiris at Peqer

summary.en: Where was the god actually buried? The stele of I-kher-nefert answers 'Peqer' — and Amelineau's excavations identified Peqer with Umm el-Qa'ab, 'mother of pots', the Abydos plain holding the tombs of the First Dynasty kings, among them the tomb of King Khent which New Kingdom Egyptians firmly venerated as the tomb of Osiris himself, complete with a great cenotaph made under the 22nd Dynasty.
summary.zh: 神究竟葬於何處？伊克赫爾-奈費爾特碑答曰『佩克爾』——阿梅利諾之發掘證其即烏姆卡阿布（『罐之母』），阿拜多斯平原上第一王朝諸王之陵所在，其中有王肯特之墓，新王國埃及人篤信即奧西里斯之墓，且於二十二王朝為之立大神饋碑。

sensitivity.note: Ancient archaeology-myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Here we have a definite statement that the body of Osiris was buried, and that his tomb was situated in Peqer. But where was Peqer? This question has been satisfactorily answered by the extensive excavations of M. Amelineau at Abydos, who proved that Peqer is a portion of the great plain of Abydos which lies about a mile and a half from the temple of Osiris, and which is known to-day by the Arabic name of Umm al-Ka'ab, i.e., 'mother of pots,' because of the large quantity of pottery which has been found there. In this portion of the plain are found the tombs of the kings of the First dynasty, and among them is one, that of King Khent, which the Egyptians identified as the tomb of Osiris.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XIV.
passages.zh: 這裡我們有一項明確的記載，說明歐西里斯的遺體已被埋葬，而其陵墓位於佩凱爾。但佩凱爾在何處？這個問題已由阿梅利諾先生在阿拜多斯的大規模發掘圓滿解答；他證明佩凱爾是阿拜多斯廣大平原的一部分，距歐西里斯神廟約一英里半，今日以阿拉伯語名稱烏姆·卡阿布（Umm al-Ka'ab）為人所知，意即「陶罐之母」，因當地出土了大量陶器。在這片平原的這一區域，發現了第一王朝諸王的陵墓，其中一座是肯特王的陵墓，埃及人認定它就是歐西里斯的陵墓。

passages.text: There is not the least doubt about the fact of the identification, for numerous proofs have been obtained from the excavations that the place was called Peqer, and that under the New Empire the Egyptians were firmly convinced that the tomb of Khent was the tomb of Osiris. Moreover, the famous cenotaph of Osiris, which was made probably under the XXInd dynasty and which is described elsewhere, was found here by M. Amelineau.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XIV.
passages.zh: 關於這一認定的事實，絲毫沒有疑問，因為發掘工作已取得大量證據，證明此地名為佩凱爾，且在新帝國時期，埃及人深信肯特的陵墓就是歐西里斯的陵墓。此外，著名的歐西里斯衣冠塚——大約建於第二十二王朝，另在他處有所記述——也由阿梅利諾先生在此地發現。

title.en: Isis of the Thousand Names: She Who Makes the Nile to Swell
title.zh: 千名之伊西斯：使尼羅漲溢者

region.en: Egypt under the New Empire (the pan-Egyptian cult of Isis)
region.zh: 新王國埃及（伊西斯全境崇拜）

period: New Kingdom epithet lists (Brugsch, Thesaurus, cited in Budge 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (1911), ch. XVI, 'The Goddess Isis'

summary.en: Under the New Empire Isis became the greatest goddess of Egypt, and her titles run from cosmic office — 'The female Ra. The Eye of Ra. The maker of the sunrise. She who vomiteth fire' — to nourishing intimacy — 'The Cow Heru-sekha, who bringeth forth all things. Who nourished the child Horus with her milk. Lady of bread. Lady of beer. Lady of Love' — down to the calendar: 'Consort of her father. Whose husband is the inundation of the Nile. Who maketh the Nile to swell in his season.'
summary.zh: 新王國之世，伊西斯為埃及至大女神，尊號自宇宙職司——『女拉也。拉之眼也。日出之創造者。吐火者也』——至哺育之親——『赫魯-塞哈母牛，生萬物者。以乳哺荷魯斯者。麵包之主。啤酒之主。愛之主』——直至曆法：『父之配偶。其夫乃尼羅之洪。於其季使尼羅漲溢者。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient epithet lists via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Under the New Empire Isis became, beyond all doubt, the greatest goddess in Egypt, and the following titles illustrate the estimation in which she was held throughout the land: 'She of many names. The Great One who is from the beginning. The divine one. The only one. The greatest of the gods and goddesses. The Queen of all the gods. The best beloved of all the gods. The prototype of all beings. Queen of goddesses and women. The female Ra. The female Horus. The Eye of Ra. The right eye of Ra (as Sothis). The star-crown of Ra-Horus. The Queen of the Dekan stars. Sothis, who openeth the New Year.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XVI (Brugsch, Thesaurus).
passages.zh: 在新帝國時期，伊西斯無疑已成為埃及最偉大的女神，以下稱號說明了她在全境所受的尊崇：「多名的她。自太初即有的偉大者。神聖者。唯一者。諸神與諸女神中最偉大者。眾神之后。眾神最鍾愛者。一切存在者的原型。諸女神與眾婦女之后。女身的拉。女身的荷魯斯。拉之眼。拉之右眼（作為索提斯）。拉—荷魯斯之星冠。德坎諸星之后。開啟新年的索提斯。」

passages.text: 'The lady of heaven. The holy one of heaven. Light-giver in heaven with Ra. She of the beams of gold. The golden one. The most brilliant goddess. Lady of the north wind. The Queen of earth. The mightiest of the mighty. The mighty one on the earth of Keb. The Queen of the South and North. Lady of the solid earth. She who vomiteth fire. Blazing flame. She who filleth the Tuat with good things. The mother of the god Horus, the Mighty Bull. The Cow Heru-sekha, who bringeth forth all things. Who nourished the child Horus with her milk. Bestower of life. Lady of life. Creatress of green things.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XVI.
passages.zh: 「天之女主。天之聖者。與拉同在於天之光賜予者。金色光芒的她。金色者。最為輝煌的女神。北風之女主。大地之后。強者中最強有力者。蓋布大地上的強有力者。南與北之后。堅實大地之女主。吐火者。熾烈之焰。以美物充滿圖阿特者。荷魯斯神——強壯公牛——之母。赫魯塞卡母牛，化生萬物者。以己乳哺育荷魯斯孩童者。生命之賜予者。生命之女主。綠色萬物之創造者。」

passages.text: 'Lady of bread. Lady of beer. Lady of abundance. Lady of joy and gladness. Lady of Love. Who delivereth to the king his rank, without whom no king can exist. Mistress of spells. Weaver and fuller. Daughter of Keb. Child of Nut. First royal wife of Ra. Consort of her father. Whose son is the lord of the earth. Whose husband is the lord of the deep. Whose husband is the inundation of the Nile. Who maketh the Nile to swell and overflow. Who maketh the Nile to swell in his season.' The last-mentioned titles of the goddess refer to Isis-Sothis, whose appearance in the sky indicated the immediate advent of the inundation of the Nile, and warned men to be ready to begin the agricultural labours of a new year.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XVI, with the closing explanation.
passages.zh: 「麵包之女主。啤酒之女主。豐饒之女主。歡欣與喜樂之女主。愛之女主。賜予國王其地位者，無她則無國王能存在。咒語之女主人。織者與漂布者。凱布之女。努特之子。拉之首任王室正妻。其父之配偶。其子為大地之主。其夫為深淵之主。其夫為尼羅河之泛濫。使尼羅河漲溢者。使其時令中尼羅河漲溢者。」女神最後提及的這些稱號指伊西斯—索提斯，她於天空中的出現預示尼羅河泛濫即將到來，並提醒人們準備開始新一年的農耕勞作。

title.en: The Circumcision Rite: The Oldest Operation in Sculpture
title.zh: 割禮之儀：浮雕中最古之手術

region.en: Sakkarah, Egypt (the 6th-Dynasty tomb relief of the circumcision)
region.zh: 埃及薩卡拉（第六王朝墓室割禮浮雕）

period: Relief in a 6th-Dynasty tomb at Sakkarah (c. 2300-2200 BCE); Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XXIV

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (1911), ch. XXIV, sec. 6, 'Circumcision'

summary.en: A ritual-origin record from the edge of the mythic: the mummified bodies prove circumcision general at all periods in Egypt; the oldest known representation of the operation is a 6th-Dynasty relief at Sakkarah where a priest performs it; a 'god of circumcision' appears in the Pyramid Text of Teta — and Budge argues the rite originated as an offering made to the gods of virility, as it still is among many African tribes.
summary.zh: 禮儀緣起記錄：木乃伊證割禮於埃及歷代通行；其最古圖像乃薩卡拉第六王朝墓中浮雕，由祭司執刀；泰塔金字塔文中已見『割禮之神』——伯奇論其本為獻予陽剛之神之祭品，如今日非洲諸族所行。

sensitivity.note: Ancient rite discussed in Budge 1911; no living community restrictions. Tagged 'ritual-origin' (topic 5); see ledger note on motif mapping.

passages.text: The mummified bodies of the ancient Egyptians which are available for examination prove that circumcision was general at all periods in Egypt. As, however, the texts say little or nothing about the ceremony itself, or its significance, we must assume that it had no religious importance, at least in Dynastic times, and that, if the earlier inhabitants of the Nile Valley ever regarded it as an act of worship, this view of it was ignored by their descendants or forgotten. Originally, circumcision must have had a religious significance, and there is little doubt that the portion cut from the body of the boy was regarded as an offering which was made to one or other of the gods of virility or generation, just as it is to-day among many of the tribes of Africa.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XXIV, sec. 6.
passages.zh: 可供檢驗的古埃及人木乃伊證明，割禮在埃及各個時期都普遍實行。然而，由於文獻對這一儀式本身或其意義幾乎沒有或完全沒有記載，我們必須假定它至少在王國時期並無宗教上的重要性；而且，即便尼羅河谷較早的居民曾將其視為一種崇拜行為，這一看法也被他們的後代所忽視或遺忘。割禮最初必定具有宗教意義，而且幾乎無疑，從男孩身上割下的部分被視為獻給某位陽剛或生殖之神的祭品，正如今日非洲許多部落中的情形一樣。

passages.text: A representation of the performance of circumcision, probably the oldest known, is found on a relief in a tomb at Sakkarah, and it dates from the period of the VIth dynasty. The act is performed by a priest, but whether this official was a member of the boy's family, or a professional priest, cannot be said. A god of circumcision appears to be mentioned in the text of Teta (VIth dynasty), but in exactly what connection is not clear.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XXIV, sec. 6.
passages.zh: 一幅施行割禮的圖像——很可能是已知最古老的一幅——見於薩卡拉一座陵墓的浮雕上，其年代屬第六王朝時期。這一動作由一名祭司施行，但無法斷定這位官員是男孩家族的成員，還是專職祭司。提塔（第六王朝）的銘文中似乎提到了一位割禮之神，但究竟是在何種關聯下提及，並不清楚。

title.en: How Salaksak Became Rich
title.zh: 薩拉克薩克致富記

region.en: Angeles, Pampanga, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦板牙省安赫勒斯（敘述者故鄉）

period: Pampangan oral droll; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20a 'How Salaksak became Rich', eBook #8299

summary.en: Jealous Salaksak baits his brother Cucunu: a cow killed for trespassing becomes a thousand-peso claim on innocent herdsmen; a sack of ashes from his burned house is swapped with an old man's money-bag on the road; when Cucunu cages him by the river, Salaksak cries that he is imprisoned for refusing the ruler's daughter, is freed by a suitor with a herd of cows, and finally drowns his envious brother with the tale that their dead parents keep cows under the sea.
summary.zh: 薩拉克薩克步步設局：越界的牛被兄長殺死，他反以牛皮向無辜牧人索賠千金；燒屋後的灰燼在路途上換取老人背著的銀錢袋；被兄長關進河邊籠中時，他哭喊『因拒娶官家之女而囚』，被求婚者以牛群贖出。最後他謊稱海底有亡父亡母養著牛群，妒火中燒的兄長縱身入河，一去不返。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan droll recorded by Fansler from a Licup narrator (Angeles); archival record. Master-Cheat cycle (episodes F4BE1HJ).

passages.text: Once upon a time there lived two brothers, the elder named Cucunu and the younger Salaksak, their parents dead; each received a cow and a piece of land, and Salaksak built a small house of his own. Jealous because his brother's rice grew faster than his own, Salaksak one night turned his cow loose in Cucunu's field; when it happened again the impatient brother killed the cow, and Salaksak, ashamed and afraid, took only the skin and put it into a basket. Not long afterward several hundred cows passed him along the road; while the herdsmen were eating their dinner he threw his skin among the cows, then asked the chief of the herdsmen to count them, since his cow had been lost a week and might have become mixed with the herd. As the chief counted, Salaksak picked up the skin and shook his head: 'Alas! Here is the mark of my cow... You must pay me a thousand pesos, or else you shall be imprisoned. My cow was easily worth a thousand pesos; for when she was alive, she used to drop money every day.' In their great fear the herdsmen paid him at once.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'How Salaksak became Rich'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前住著兩兄弟，哥哥名叫庫庫努，弟弟名叫薩拉克薩克，他們的父母已去世；每人分得一頭牛和一塊地，薩拉克薩克還為自己蓋了一間小屋。由於嫉妒哥哥的稻子長得比自己的快，薩拉克薩克有天夜裡把自己的牛放進庫庫努的田裡；當這事再次發生時，不耐煩的哥哥殺死了那頭牛，薩拉克薩克又羞愧又害怕，只取了牛皮放進籃子裡。不久之後，有幾百頭牛沿路從他身旁經過；趁牧人們吃午飯時，他把自己的牛皮扔進牛群中，然後請牧人的首領清點牛數，因為他的牛已丟失一週，可能混進了牛群。首領清點時，薩拉克薩克撿起牛皮搖了搖頭：「唉！這是我那頭牛的記號……你們必須賠我一千比索，否則就要坐牢。我那頭牛輕易就值一千比索；因為她活著的時候，每天都下錢。」牧人們大為恐懼，當即賠了他。

passages.text: Salaksak went home and told his brother of his good fortune; hoping to become as rich as his brother, Cucunu immediately killed his own cow — and was summoned by the ruler of the town, accused of having stolen the hide, and whipped so badly that he could hardly walk home. Maddened by the disgrace, Cucunu burned his brother's house while he was away; when Salaksak came home to find nothing but ashes, he put them into a sack and set out to seek his fortune again. On the way he overtook an old man carrying a bag of money to the ruler's house, and said, 'I am sorry for you, old man. What do you say to exchanging loads? Mine is very light in comparison with yours.' 'With all my heart, kind boy!' — and they exchanged sacks; at a safe hiding-place Salaksak deserted his companion and went to tell his brother he had gotten a sack of silver for a sack of ashes. 'Why, my house is bigger than yours! I ought to get two sacks of ashes if I burn it. I think that would be a good bargain.' So Cucunu burned his house too, and went through the town crying, 'Who wants to buy ashes?' — until the ruler, remembering him, summoned him and lashed him again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'How Salaksak became Rich'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 薩拉克薩克回家把這樁好運告訴了哥哥；庫庫努希望變得和弟弟一樣富有，立刻殺了自己的牛——結果被鎮上的統治者傳喚，被指控偷了牛皮，還被鞭打得幾乎走不回家。庫庫努因這恥辱而發狂，趁弟弟外出時燒了他的房子；薩拉克薩克回家只見一片灰燼，便把灰裝進袋子，又動身去碰運氣。路上他趕上一位老人，老人正帶著一袋錢去統治者家，薩拉克薩克說：「我為你難過，老人家。你看交換負擔如何？比起你的，我的可輕多了。」「我完全願意，好孩子！」——於是他們交換了袋子；在一個安全的藏身處，薩拉克薩克拋下同伴，跑去告訴哥哥他用一袋灰換來了一袋銀子。「哎呀，我的房子比你的大！我要是燒了它，應該能換兩袋灰。我看這是一筆好買賣。」於是庫庫努也燒了自己的房子，在鎮上到處喊著：「誰要買灰？」——直到統治者記起他，把他傳喚來又鞭打了一頓。

passages.text: Thoroughly enraged, Cucunu determined his brother should not deceive him a third time: he made a strong cage, caught Salaksak, and confined him in it by the bank of the river — 'I will give you three days to repent. Now you cannot deceive me any more.' As a young man was passing by, Salaksak began to cry out, 'They have put me into this cage because I do not want to marry the ruler's daughter.' The young man, who had vainly striven for the hand of the girl, immediately approached: 'If you will let me take your place, so that I may marry her, I will give you all the cows I have with me.' So by this trick Salaksak escaped, while Cucunu, thinking the man in the cage was his brother, unmercifully threw him into the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'How Salaksak became Rich'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 庫庫努怒不可遏，決心不讓弟弟第三次欺騙自己：他做了一個結實的籠子，抓住薩拉克薩克，把他關在河岸邊——「我給你三天時間悔過。現在你再也騙不了我了。」一個年輕人路過時，薩拉克薩克開始大喊：「他們把我關進這籠子，是因為我不肯娶統治者的女兒。」那個曾徒勞追求那姑娘的年輕人立刻走上前來：「如果你讓我代替你，好讓我能娶她，我就把我帶在身邊的牛全都給你。」薩拉克薩克便用這計謀逃脫了，而庫庫努以為籠中人是自己的弟弟，毫不留情地把他扔進了河裡。

passages.text: A few days later Salaksak went to his brother's house and told him it was quite beautiful under the water: 'There I saw our father and mother. They told me I was not old enough to stay with them, so they sent me back here with a large number of cows.' 'Well, well!' said Cucunu, 'I too must go see our parents.' He then hastened to the river, threw himself in, and was drowned. Thus Salaksak grew rich because of his craftiness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'How Salaksak became Rich'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 幾天後，薩拉克薩克到他兄弟家去，告訴他水底下十分美麗：「我在那裡見到了我們的父母。他們說我還不夠大，不能和他們同住，於是就把我連同一大群牛送回了這裡。」「好啊，好啊！」庫庫努說，「我也得去看看我們的父母。」他隨即趕往河邊，縱身跳了進去，就此溺死。薩拉克薩克便因他的狡詐而發了財。

title.en: Clever Juan and Envious Diego
title.zh: 聰明的胡安與嫉妒的迭戈

region.en: Santa Maria, Bulakan, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's tale-source)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋布拉克省聖瑪麗亞（故事原鄉）

period: Tagalog oral droll; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20b 'Clever Juan and Envious Diego', eBook #8299

summary.en: Juan stage-manages his own mother's 'death' and revival with a bamboo tube; the thieving Diego tries the trick at a child's funeral and is kicked away. Left the thin carabao, Juan sells the hide by dropping it on bandits from a tree and looting their treasure; boxed for the sea by Diego, he swaps places with a gold-ring peddler and later drowns his brother with the tale of a mother beneath the waves giving away gold rings.
summary.zh: 胡安導演母親『死而復生』；迭戈竊管到喪禮上故技重施，反被踢走。分得瘦水牛的胡安以牛皮自樹上砸退匪幫、席捲其財寶；被迭戈装箱投海前，他與賣金戒指的中國小販調包。歸來後他謊稱海底的母親正以金戒指相贈——愚兄欣然下海，再未浮起。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog droll recorded by Fansler from an Anzures narrator (story from Santa Maria, Bulakan); archival record. Master-Cheat cycle (episodes G1F5HJ).

passages.text: There were once two brothers named Diego and Juan whose father had died long before, so they lived only with their good mother; Diego, the older, was envious and foolish, Juan was clever. One morning Juan called his mother: 'Mother, help me fool Diego! Please lie down as if you were dead; and when he arrives, I will blow air through your nose through a bamboo tube. As soon as you feel me blowing, get up and try to look like a woman that has risen from the dead.' When Diego came in and saw his brother crying, 'Don't you see? Our mother is dead,' Juan opened his trunk, took out a short bamboo tube, and blew through it into his mother's nose — and she pretended to revive. Diego rejoiced, very much surprised at his brother's possession.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Clever Juan and Envious Diego'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有兩兄弟，名叫迪耶戈和胡安，他們的父親早已去世，因此他們只和善良的母親同住；哥哥迪耶戈嫉妒又愚蠢，胡安則很聰明。一天早晨，胡安喚來母親：「母親，幫我騙騙迪耶戈吧！請您躺下裝死；等他來了，我就用一根竹管往您鼻孔裡吹氣。您一感覺到我吹氣，就起來，盡量裝成一個死而復生的女人。」迪耶戈進來，看見弟弟在哭，「你沒看見嗎？我們的母親死了。」胡安打開他的箱子，取出一根短竹管，對著母親的鼻孔吹氣——她便裝作活了過來。迪耶戈大喜，對弟弟擁有這等寶物驚訝不已。

passages.text: The next day the envious Diego stole the bamboo tube and went to the churchyard, where he waited for a funeral. When the procession of a small boy came along he stopped it, and called to the mother of the boy, 'Don't cry! Your son is only sleeping. Lay him down here, and you will soon see that he is alive.' After opening the coffin he began to blow air into the boy's nose, blowing harder and harder — but the boy remained as stiff and lifeless as ever, and the angry mother kicked Diego, saying, 'You are only trying to fool us!' Diego was very much ashamed, so he threw away the bamboo tube and ran home. Some days later the mother of Diego and Juan became ill and died, leaving her sons two carabaos: Diego took the fat one, Juan the thin one — and Juan, angry, killed his carabao and set out to sell the hide.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Clever Juan and Envious Diego'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天，嫉妒的迪耶戈偷走了那根竹管，到教堂墓地裡去，等在那裡守候一場葬禮。當一個小男孩的送葬隊伍走過來時，他攔住了他們，對男孩的母親喊道：「別哭！您的兒子只是睡著了。把他放在這裡，您很快就會看見他活過來。」打開棺材後，他開始往男孩的鼻孔裡吹氣，越吹越用力——可那男孩依舊僵硬冰冷，毫無生氣，憤怒的母親踢了迪耶戈一腳，說：「你不過是想騙我們罷了！」迪耶戈羞愧萬分，便扔掉竹管，跑回家去。幾天後，迪耶戈和胡安的母親病逝，給兩個兒子留下兩頭水牛：迪耶戈牽走了肥的那頭，胡安只得瘦的那頭——胡安一氣之下殺了自己的水牛，動身去賣牛皮。

passages.text: Finding no buyer in the neighboring villages, Juan walked on until he came to a forest, and climbing a tree hid himself with his hide among the branches — for a band of Tulisanes on horseback with a large amount of treasure was coming toward him. They stopped to eat under that very tree; Juan unintentionally moved the hide on the branch beside him, and it fell crashing down on the Tulisanes, who, frightened by this most unexpected noise, ran away as fast as they could, not stopping to take anything with them. Juan descended quickly, mounted a horse, and made off with as much as he could carry. When Diego heard that the riches had been given by the neighboring villages in return for the carabao-hide, he went out and killed his fat carabao, dried its hide, and tried to sell it in the villages — but many days passed and still no one would buy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Clever Juan and Envious Diego'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 胡安在鄰近幾個村子裡找不到買主，便一路走下去，來到一片森林，爬上一棵樹，帶著他的牛皮躲在枝葉之間——因為一夥騎馬的強盜正帶著大量財寶朝他這邊過來。他們就在那棵樹下停下來吃東西；胡安無意間碰動了身旁樹枝上的牛皮，牛皮嘩啦一聲掉在強盜們身上，他們被這突如其來的聲響嚇得拔腿就逃，什麼也顧不上拿。胡安迅速下樹，騎上一匹馬，盡其所能地帶著財物逃走了。迪耶戈聽說那些財富是鄰近各村為了換牛皮而給的，便出去殺了自己那頭肥水牛，把皮曬乾，拿到各村去賣——可是許多天過去了，仍然沒有人肯買。

passages.text: Now Diego was very angry. He took a wooden box and put his brother inside, bound it, and carried it to the seashore — but remembering that it was not locked, he left it and went back to the house for the key. Meanwhile a Chinese peddler selling gold rings came along, and Juan shouted, 'Chino, Chino, come and see these beautiful and precious things inside!' The Chinaman approached and opened the box, and Juan came out, saying, 'I will put you inside, and you will see many beautiful things in the bottom'; the willing Chino was shut in, and Juan took the gold rings and ran away. Not many minutes later Diego came up, locked the box, and threw it into the ocean. That same day, while Diego was eating his dinner, Juan came along with some fine gold rings; asked how he had escaped and where the rings came from, Juan answered that he had sunk to the bottom of the ocean, where he saw his mother, and that she had given him all those rings. The foolish Diego believed everything, and asked his brother to put him into a box and throw him into the ocean; Juan lost no time in obeying, and after that lived happily for many years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Clever Juan and Envious Diego'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這下迪耶戈氣壞了。他拿來一個木箱，把弟弟裝了進去，捆綁好，扛到海邊——可是想起箱子還沒上鎖，便把它放下，回家去取鑰匙。這時一個賣金戒指的中國貨郎走了過來，胡安喊道：「中國人，中國人，快來看這裡面漂亮又值錢的東西！」那中國人走近打開箱子，胡安便鑽了出來，說：「我來把您裝進去，您就會在箱底看見許多漂亮的東西」；那樂意的中國人就被關了進去，胡安拿了金戒指便跑走了。沒過幾分鐘，迪耶戈回來，鎖上箱子，把它扔進了大海。就在那天，迪耶戈正吃著晚飯，胡安帶著幾枚精美的金戒指來了；問他怎麼逃出來的、戒指又是從哪裡來的，胡安回答說他沉到了海底，在那裡見到了母親，那些戒指全是她給的。愚蠢的迪耶戈全都信了，便求弟弟把他裝進箱子扔進大海；胡安立刻照辦，此後幸福地生活了許多年。

title.en: Ruined Because of Invidiousness
title.zh: 因妒敗家

region.en: Jaen, Nueva Ecija, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋新怡詩夏省哈恩（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral droll; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20c 'Ruined because of Invidiousness', eBook #8299

summary.en: Poor Juan plants his cow-hide in a butcher's piles and extorts five hundred pesos 'or else a lawsuit'; climbing a tree at a crossroads, he drops the hide on armed men who flee believing it a curse from heaven, leaving sacks of money. Returning his brother's borrowed salop with coins stuck in the cracks, he lets Pedro conclude that one hide is worth two sacks of money — and the envious brother slaughters his whole herd for hides no one will buy.
summary.zh: 窮漢胡安把牛皮混入肉鋪皮堆，訛得五百比索『否則告官』；又在十字路口樹上將牛皮砸落武裝匪徒頭頂——匪徒以為天罰，棄錢囊而逃。歸還兄長的量米斗時，他把銀幣嵌進斗縫，令佩德羅相信『一張皮值兩袋錢』——妒火中燒的兄長宰盡牛群，製成的皮卻無人問津。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog droll recorded by Fansler from an Esquivel narrator (Jaen, Nueva Ecija); archival record. Master-Cheat cycle (episodes F4F5F6).

passages.text: In time out of memory there lived two brothers, Pedro and Juan: Pedro was rich, for he had a large herd of cattle, and had not much use for his younger brother, who was very poor. Juan had nothing he could call his own but a cow; one day, disappointed over his life of poverty, he killed his cow and set out to find his fortune with nothing but the hide. When he reached the next town he saw large piles of cattle-hides in front of a butcher's shop, and late that night he stole out secretly and put the skin of his cow in one of the piles. The next morning he went to the shop: 'Mr.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Ruined because of Invidiousness'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在記憶所不能及的年代裡，住著兩兄弟，佩德羅和胡安：佩德羅很富有，因為他有一大群牛，對他那非常貧窮的弟弟不大理睬。胡安除了自己的一頭母牛之外一無所有；有一天，他對自己的貧困生活感到失望，便殺了那頭母牛，只帶著一張牛皮就動身去尋找他的運氣。他到了下一個鎮子，看見一家肉鋪門前堆著大堆的牛皮，那天深夜他偷偷溜出去，把他那頭母牛的皮放進了其中一堆裡。第二天早晨，他來到那家鋪子：「先生。

passages.text: Butcher, I have come here to look for my lost cow. Have you not killed a cow with a mark J on the right hip?' 'No, all the cows which were killed here came from my herd out there in the mountains,' answered the honest man — until, searching the piles, they found the hide Juan had put there, and Juan began to quarrel: 'You must pay me five hundred pesos for my cow, or else I shall bring a law-suit before the court against you. You stole my cow, and now you have to pay for it.' The man, very much afraid of being brought before the court, gave Juan the five hundred pesos.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Ruined because of Invidiousness'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 屠夫啊，我來這裡是為了找我走失的母牛。你難道沒有殺過一頭右臀上有個J字記號的母牛嗎？』『沒有，這裡殺的牛全都是從我在山裡那群牛中來的，』那誠實的人回答——直到他們翻查那一堆堆的牛皮，發現了胡安放在那裡的牛皮，胡安便開始爭吵起來：『你必須賠我五百披索作為我那頭牛的錢，否則我就要向法庭對你提出訴訟。你偷了我的牛，現在你得賠償。』那人非常害怕被帶上法庭，便給了胡安五百披索。

passages.text: On his way home he came to a tree standing at a cross-roads; very tired and thirsty, he climbed it to look for a house, but instead of a house he saw a company of armed men coming down the road, who stopped under the tree to rest. Juan was so terrified that he hardly knew what to do; as he was trembling with fright, the hide fell down from the tree and frightened the men away — they thought it was a curse from heaven because of their misdeeds. When Juan realized the men were gone he quickly descended, and there on the ground he saw a number of sacks full of money; loading a horse with two of the sacks, he started for his home town.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Ruined because of Invidiousness'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在回家的路上，他來到一棵立在十字路口旁的樹前；他又累又渴，便爬上樹去尋找人家，但看到的不是人家，而是一隊武裝的人馬沿路而來，他們停在樹下休息。胡安嚇得幾乎不知如何是好；他正因恐懼而發抖時，那張牛皮從樹上掉了下來，把那些人嚇跑了——他們以為這是上天因他們的惡行而降下的詛咒。胡安發覺那些人走了之後，便趕快下來，在地上他看見許多裝滿錢的袋子；他把兩袋裝上一匹馬，便動身回自己的家鄉去了。

passages.text: As soon as he reached his house he went to his brother's to borrow a salop, inserted several pesetas and ten-centavo pieces in the cracks of the measure, and returned it. 'What did you do with the salop?' asked Pedro, seeing the coins sticking in the cracks. 'I measured money,' said Juan. 'Where did you get the money?' 'Don't you know that I went to the neighboring town to sell my cowhide? Just think! One hide is worth two sacks of money.' Pedro, who was envious of his brother's good fortune, killed all his cattle, old and young, and threw the meat into the river; then he started with several carretons full of hides — but he was disappointed, for nobody would buy hides. Discouraged and tired out, he returned to find Juan living comfortably in a fine new home: thus Pedro lost all his property because of his invidiousness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Ruined because of Invidiousness'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他一到家便去他哥哥家借一個沙洛普（量器），在量器的縫隙裡塞進幾枚披索和一角硬幣，然後還了回去。『你拿沙洛普做什麼用了？』佩德羅看見硬幣卡在縫裡，便問道。『我量錢來著，』胡安說。『你從哪兒弄來的錢？』『你難道不知道我到鄰鎮去賣牛皮了嗎？你想想看！一張牛皮值兩袋錢呢。』佩德羅嫉妒弟弟的好運，便把他所有的牛，不論老小，全都殺了，把肉扔進河裡；然後他帶著好幾車滿載牛皮的卡雷頓（牛車）出發了——但他失望了，因為沒有人肯買牛皮。他又沮喪又疲憊地回來，卻發現胡安舒舒服服地住在一座漂亮的新房子裡：佩德羅就這樣因為他的嫉妒而失去了全部財產。

title.en: The Two Friends: The Enchanted Hide and the Mother's Corpse
title.zh: 兩位朋友：『魔皮』與母親的屔體

region.en: Iloilo, central Philippines (narrator's home province)
region.zh: 菲律賓怡朗省（敘述者故鄉）

period: Filipino oral droll; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20d 'The Two Friends', eBook #8299

summary.en: Small, poor Andres outwits his rich, strong friend Juan again and again: watching through the floor of an adulterous house, he sells the husband an 'enchanted hide' that reveals a man in the trunk and fish in the cupboard; he sells his dead mother's corpse to a terrified doctor; and when Juan sacks him for the sea, the cowboy who 'willingly marries the king's daughter' takes his place — until the envious Juan dives after 'cows from under the sea' himself.
summary.zh: 瘦弱的安德烈斯屢屢戲弄富有的強壯朋友胡安：隔著屋板目睹偷情場面後，他把『能召人召魚的魔皮』高價賣給丈夫；他又把亡母屔體賣給驚惶的醫生。被胡安裝袋投海時，牛倌自稱『願娶國王之女』而代其受溺。最後妒火中燒的胡安，聽說海底有牛群，也自己跳了下去。

sensitivity.note: Filipino droll recorded by Fansler from a Vargas narrator (possibly of Iloilo); archival record. Master-Cheat cycle (episodes F2G2HJ).

passages.text: Once there lived in a certain village two friends, Juan and Andres: Juan, a very rich man, was tall, big, and strong, while Andres, a very poor man, was small, weak, and short; Andres worked very hard to earn his living, while Juan spent most of his time on pleasure. One morning Andres borrowed one of Juan's mules, promising to tell the truth if anyone asked who owned it — but when two neighbors asked where he got it, he said he had bought it, and the news spreading, Juan angrily ordered the mule brought back. A week later two of Juan's mules, including the one Andres had borrowed, died; Juan threw the carcasses away, but Andres took the skins and dried them to sell in the next town.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'The Two Friends'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前在某個村子裡住著兩個朋友，胡安和安德烈斯：胡安是個非常有錢的人，高大、魁梧、強壯，而安德烈斯是個非常貧窮的人，矮小、瘦弱、個子矮；安德烈斯非常辛勤地工作以維持生計，而胡安則把大部分時間花在享樂上。一天早晨，安德烈斯借了胡安的一頭騾子，答應若有人問起這騾子是誰的，他便說實話——但當兩個鄰居問他從哪兒弄來這頭騾子時，他卻說是他買的，消息傳開後，胡安氣憤地命令把騾子牽回來。一週之後，胡安的兩頭騾子，包括安德烈斯借去的那頭，都死了；胡安把屍體丟掉，但安德烈斯取走了皮，曬乾後準備拿到鄰鎮去賣。

passages.text: Overtaken by night near a solitary house between his village and the town, Andres asked a woman for lodging, and had to wait until her husband came; from where he sat he could see that the woman was preparing a good supper for a stranger who meanwhile had entered — and when another man approached in the distance, the woman hastily opened a big empty trunk and hid the first man inside, putting all the cooked fish in the cupboard. When the husband arrived and received him kindly, Andres told him at the supperless table that he had an enchanted hide: 'I ordered the skin to bring a man into the trunk; and when the trunk was opened, there was the man. Next I ordered the skin to bring cooked fish to the cupboard; and when the cupboard was opened, there was the cooked fish.' The husband then offered Andres a very high price for the enchanted skin, and Andres willingly sold it — early the next morning leaving the house before the others were up, and returning to the village rich.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'The Two Friends'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 安德烈斯在他村子和鎮子之間的一戶孤零零的人家附近被夜色趕上，便向一個婦人請求借宿，不得不等到她丈夫回來；從他坐的地方，他看得出那婦人正在為一個陌生人準備一頓豐盛的晚餐，那陌生人此時已經進來了——而當遠處又有一個男人走近時，那婦人急忙打開一個大空箱子，把第一個男人藏了進去，又把所有煮好的魚放進櫥櫃裡。丈夫回來後親切地接待了他，安德烈斯在沒有晚餐的桌旁告訴他說，他有一張有魔力的牛皮：『我命令這張皮把一個男人帶進箱子裡；打開箱子一看，那男人就在裡面。接著我命令這張皮把煮好的魚帶進櫥櫃裡；打開櫥櫃一看，煮好的魚就在裡面。』丈夫於是出極高的價錢向安德烈斯買那張有魔力的皮，安德烈斯欣然賣了它——第二天一大早，趁別人還沒起床便離開了那戶人家，富富裕裕地回到了村裡。

passages.text: When Juan noticed the money in his friend's pocket, Andres told him it was the price of the skins of his dead mules, which he had sold in the neighboring town — and Juan went directly home, killed all his mules, and flayed them. Passing the solitary house crying that he had skins for sale, he was taken for the same man who had sold the enchanted skin, and the husband whipped him nearly to death. Determined to kill his friend, Juan finally caught Andres — but Andres was very cunning and avoided him — and in his anger killed the mother of Andres. When Andres found his mother dead, he dressed her very well and took her to town, explaining definitely her sickness to the town doctor; but just after she had been given the medicine the doctor noticed that the woman was dead, and Andres accused him of having poisoned his mother: the doctor, fearing the consequences if Andres should seek justice, agreed to pay him a large sum of money.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'The Two Friends'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當胡安注意到朋友口袋裡的錢時，安德烈斯告訴他，那是他那些死騾子的皮所賣的價錢，他是在鄰鎮賣掉的——胡安便直接回家，把他所有的騾子都殺了，並剝了皮。他經過那戶孤零零的人家時，喊著說他有皮要賣，卻被當成就是那個賣過有魔力牛皮的人，那丈夫把他打得半死。胡安決心要殺死他的朋友，終於抓住了安德烈斯——但安德烈斯非常狡猾，躲開了他——胡安一怒之下殺死了安德烈斯的母親。安德烈斯發現母親死了，便把她打扮得非常體面，帶到鎮上，向鎮上的醫生詳細說明她的病情；但就在她服了藥之後，醫生發覺那婦人已經死了，安德烈斯便控告醫生毒死了他的母親：醫生害怕若安德烈斯尋求司法追究會帶來的後果，便同意付給他一大筆錢。

passages.text: Andres returned to his village richer than ever, and Juan became friendly again, asking where he had gotten his money: 'It was the price of my mother's corpse, which I sold in the town.' Juan went home and killed his mother; but taking the corpse to town to sell it, he was abused by a crowd of men and narrowly escaped with his life. Now determined not to let Andres escape him, Juan one day caught him, put him inside a sack, and carried it down to the seashore — going to a house on the way to get a light for a smoke. Meanwhile Andres, bound in the sack, was crying out that he did not wish to marry the daughter of the king, and was being forced against his will; a cowboy with his herd of cows passed by, heard him, and said he was willing to marry the king's daughter — so Andres had him unbind the sack, put the cowherd in his stead, and hurried away with the cows. Juan came back, picked up the sack, and threw it into the sea; when he returned home he found Andres there with a fine herd of cows, which Andres said he had gotten from under the sea. So Juan, envious as ever, ordered Andres to put him in a sack and throw him into the sea — and Andres gladly did so.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'The Two Friends'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 安德烈斯回到自己的村莊，比以往任何時候都更富有，胡安又與他親近起來，問他這筆錢是從哪裡得來的：「那是我母親屍首的價錢，我在鎮上把她賣了。」胡安回家殺了自己的母親；可是當他把屍首帶到鎮上去賣時，卻被一群人辱罵毆打，幾乎喪命。如今胡安決心不讓安德烈斯逃出自己手中，有一天他抓住了安德烈斯，把他裝進一個麻袋裡，扛著往海邊走去——途中他到一戶人家去借火點菸。與此同時，被綁在麻袋裡的安德烈斯正大喊著說他不願娶國王的女兒，卻被迫違背自己的意願；一個趕著牛群的牛仔經過，聽見了他的話，便說自己願意娶國王的女兒——於是安德烈斯讓他解開麻袋，把牛仔裝了進去代替自己，然後趕著牛群匆匆離去。胡安回來，扛起麻袋，把它扔進海裡；當他回到家時，卻發現安德烈斯就在那裡，還帶著一群上好的牛，安德烈斯說這些牛是他從海底得來的。於是胡安一如往常地嫉妒，命令安德烈斯把他裝進麻袋扔進海裡——安德烈斯欣然照辦。

title.en: Juan the Orphan: The Sirena Awaits
title.zh: 孤兒胡安：人魚在等他

region.en: Calamba, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省卡蘭巴（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral droll; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20e 'Juan the Orphan', eBook #8299

summary.en: Envious Uncle Diego kills Juan's only horse; Juan trades the horse-meat to a starving old man for his sack of money, and Diego, slaughtering all fifteen of his own horses, finds buyers only laugh at his asking price of 'three hundred ninety-nine thousand pesos, ninety-nine pesetas, six and one half centavos a pound.' Sacking the orphan for the river, he finds him back next morning 'returning to my love the Sirena' — and pleads to go first, tied in the rice-sack himself.
summary.zh: 嫉妒的叔叔迭戈殺了孤兒胡安唯一的馬；胡安以馬肉換得老人的錢袋。迭戈宰盡自家十五匹馬叫賣，開價『三十九萬九千九百九十九比索零九十九仙六分半一磅』，只惹來哄笑。他把胡安縫入麻袋準備投河，翌日卻見胡安笑著回來——『我要回到河底，我的人魚愛人在等我』——叔叔苦求先去，親手讓自己被縛入米袋。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog droll recorded by Fansler from an Uichanco narrator (Calamba); archival record. Master-Cheat cycle (episodes F4H-modified J); the Sirena is the Philippine mermaid.

passages.text: There once lived a boy whose name was Juan; his parents had died, leaving him nothing but a horse, which he begged his Uncle Diego to let stay in his stable, feeding it from time to time and caring for it as a father would for a son. One day Uncle Diego noticed that Juan's horse was growing fatter and more beautiful than any of his own animals, and in his envy he killed the horse of his nephew, telling the innocent boy that the animal had been stricken by 'bad air.' Being thus deprived of his sole wealth, Juan cut off the best meat from the dead horse, and with this food for his only provision set out to seek his fortune in another country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Juan the Orphan'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個男孩，名叫胡安；他的父母都已去世，只留給他一匹馬。他懇求他的叔叔迪亞哥讓這匹馬留在他的馬廄裡，不時餵牠，像父親照顧兒子那樣照料牠。有一天，迪亞哥叔叔注意到胡安的馬長得比他自己的任何牲畜都更肥壯、更漂亮，出於嫉妒，他殺死了姪子的馬，卻對這無辜的男孩說那牲畜是染上了「惡氣」。胡安就這樣失去了他唯一的財產，便從死馬身上割下最好的肉，帶著這份僅有的口糧，動身前往異國尋求他的 fortune。

passages.text: On his way through a forest he came across an old man dying of starvation, but with a bag full of money. 'Pray, what have you in your sack, my son?' 'Some dried horse-meat,' said Juan. 'Will you exchange your sack of meat for my sack of money? I have money here, but I cannot eat it... Since you are stronger, my son, pray take this sack of money in exchange, and go to the town and buy meat with it for yourself. For God's sake, leave this meat to me! I am starving to death.' Juan accepted the money, put the heavy bag on his shoulder, and with difficulty carried it home — 'I sold the meat of my dead horse. This is what I got for it,' he told his uncle, who once more became jealous: 'If with only one horse he could gain so much money, how much should I get for my fifteen horses!'
