So he killed all the horses he had in his stable and cut the meat from them; then he placed the meat in bags, and crying as he went along the street, 'Meat, meat! Horse-meat! Who wishes to buy fresh horse-meat?' answered the gray-headed old woman who asked the price: 'Three hundred ninety-nine thousand pesos, ninety-nine pesetas, six and one half centavos a pound,' said Uncle Diego. The people who heard him only laughed, and thought something was the matter with his head; nobody would buy his meat, and all his meat decayed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Juan the Orphan'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他在穿過一片森林的途中，遇到一個快要餓死的老人，那人卻帶著滿滿一袋錢。「孩子，請問你袋子裡裝的是什麼？」「一些馬肉乾，」胡安說。「你願意用你那袋肉換我這袋錢嗎？我這裡有錢，可我吃不了錢……既然你比我強壯，孩子，求你拿這袋錢去換，到鎮上給自己買肉吃吧。看在上帝的份上，把這肉留給我吧！我快餓死了。」胡安收下了錢，把那沉甸甸的袋子扛在肩上，好不容易才把它搬回家——「我把我那匹死馬的肉賣了。這就是我換來的東西，」他對叔叔說。叔叔又一次嫉妒起來：「他只憑一匹馬就能賺到這麼多錢，那我這十五匹馬該能賺多少啊！」於是他殺死了馬廄裡所有的馬，割下牠們的肉；然後把肉裝進袋子裡，一邊沿街走一邊喊：「肉啊，肉啊！馬肉！誰要買新鮮馬肉？」那位滿頭灰髮的老婦人問價錢，他答道：「每磅三十九萬九千九百九十九比索、九十九比塞塔、六又二分之一分，」迪亞哥叔叔說。聽見他這話的人只是大笑，以為他腦子出了毛病；沒有人肯買他的肉，他所有的肉都腐爛了。

passages.text: He went home in despair and planned to take vengeance on his nephew: he cast the little orphan into a big sack and sewed the mouth of the little prison all up, saying that at night he would take the sack and throw it into the river. However, Juan managed to get out of the bag, and in his place put a muzzled dog; when night came the uncle shouldered the bag, took it to the river, and hurled it into the deep water. But when morning came, Uncle Diego saw Juan smilingly enter the door of his house: 'I haven't time; there is not a moment to lose. I have only come here to bid you good-by. Back to the bottom of the river. My love, the Sirena, is waiting for me.' 'O Juan! If I could only go with you!' — 'No, no, no!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Juan the Orphan'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他絕望地回到家，謀劃著要向姪子報仇：他把這小孤兒扔進一個大麻袋裡，把這小牢籠的口子縫得嚴嚴實實，說夜裡要把這麻袋拿去扔進河裡。然而，胡安设法從袋子裡出來了，並在原處放了一隻戴著口套的狗；到了夜裡，叔叔扛起袋子，帶到河邊，把它扔進深水裡。可是到了早晨，迪亞哥叔叔卻看見胡安笑吟吟地走進他家門：「我沒時間；一刻也不能耽擱。我只是來這裡向你道別的。回河底去。我的愛人，塞麗娜，正等著我呢。」「哦，胡安！要是我能跟你一起去就好了！」——「不行，不行，不行！」

passages.text: Only one can go at a time. The Sirena would be angry, and she would consequently refuse to admit to her glorious habitation any being from this outside world.' But the uncle pleaded so earnestly that finally the boy yielded with pretended reluctance; the uncle then covered himself with a rice-sack, and Juan tied the mouth of the bag securely. 'I will fool him,' Uncle Diego said to himself. 'I will fool him,' Juan said to himself. 'There is no such thing as the Sirena in the river. Thank God, my dreadful uncle will soon be disposed of!' At midnight Juan hurled his happy uncle into the river, saying, 'There is no one who owes that must not pay his debt. May my act be justified!' The heavy sack sank to the bottom of the river, and nothing more was heard of Uncle Diego.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 20 'Juan the Orphan'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一次只能去一個。塞麗娜會生氣的，那樣她就會拒絕讓這外面世界的任何生靈進入她那光榮的居所。可是叔叔懇求得那麼懇切，最後男孩才裝作勉強答應了；於是叔叔用一個米袋把自己罩住，胡安把袋口牢牢紮緊。「我要騙過他，」迪亞哥叔叔心裡說。「我要騙過他，」胡安心裡說。「河裡根本沒有什麼塞麗娜。感謝上帝，我那可怕的叔叔很快就要被解決掉了！」午夜時分，胡安把他那興高采烈的叔叔扔進河裡，說道：「欠債的人沒有不還債的。願我這一行為是正當的！」沉重的麻袋沉到河底，此後再也沒有人聽到迪亞哥叔叔的消息。

title.en: The Grand Unity of the East: The First Hymn of the Nine Songs
title.zh: 九歌東皇太一

region.en: The rite-ground of the Chu court (Hubei)
region.zh: 楚祭之場

period: Chu Ci, Jiu Ge, 4th-3rd c. BCE

source.work: Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Dong Huang Tai Yi, the opening hymn of the grand rite

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The first hymn of the Nine Songs names the highest: the Grand Unity of the East — the One beneath all the gods. The rite is all preparation and no narrative: a day set on an auspicious star, jade-stuffed bamboo, cinnamon wine, herbs of the altar laid in rows, the shamaness in her flowered robes singing softly, drums and strings rising — and the god, pleased, gives the blessing of harmony in return for the sincerity of the rite.
summary.zh: 吉日兮辰良，穆將愉兮上皇；撫長劍兮玉珥，璆鏘鳴兮琳瑯……五音紛兮繁會，君欣欣兮樂康——九歌之首，祭太一。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Chu Ci original. The Grand Unity became the supreme theological figure of Han state cult and, much later, the Jade Emperor's precursor.

passages.text: An auspicious day and a well-chosen hour: the rite makes ready to delight the Sovereign on High. The shamaness takes up the long sword with its jade pommel, the bells of her girdle ringing as she moves, and lays the altar with rows of herbs and meats in flower-strewn mats.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Dong Huang Tai Yi (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 吉日兮良辰，敬將以愉上皇。巫女執玉首長劍，行則腰間鈴鳴，陳草藥與牲肉於繁花鋪陳之席，以設祭壇。

passages.text: Cinnamon wine mixed with pepper-herbs is poured; the drum-sticks are raised, the slow beating begins, and the five notes mingle in their heap of sound. The god, well pleased, grants the blessing he keeps for the sincere — the Grand Unity honored, the year made whole.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Dong Huang Tai Yi; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 桂酒摻入椒香之料而斟出；鼓槌舉起，緩慢的擊鼓開始，五音交織成一片渾然的聲響。神靈欣然，賜下祂為虔誠者所保留的福佑——東皇太一受享尊崇，年歲得以圓滿。

title.en: The Lord Within the Clouds
title.zh: 九歌雲中君

region.en: The sky-roads over the Chu lands (symbolic pin: cloud reaches)
region.zh: 雲中路

period: Chu Ci, Jiu Ge, 4th-3rd c. BCE

source.work: Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Yunzhong Jun, the cloud-god's bath and passage

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The Lord Within the Clouds bathes in the orchid soup, washes his hair in the fragrant steam, and passes along the sky in rainbow colors and dragon robes — the shamaness sings of his staying and going as of a lover who grants no tenure: he abides over Ji province with more than a mortal's power, then is gone beyond the clouds, and the heart follows him into the far light.
summary.zh: 浴蘭湯兮沐芳，華采衣兮若英；靈連蜷兮既留，爛昭昭兮未央……龍駕兮帝服，聊翱遊兮周章——雲中君之降與去。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Chu Ci original.

passages.text: The god bathes in the soup of orchid and washes his hair in the fragrant steam, robed in the flower's own colors; he lingers, glowing, in the shrine of the rite, brighter than the ends of things. He rides a dragon's carriage in the dress of an emperor, wheels and circles through the nine provinces; his light abides there, and the singer's heart goes after him into the dark — for the cloud-lord, like all the lords of the Nine Songs, grants a visit and not a residence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Yunzhong Jun (compiler's rendering); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: Yunzhong Jun; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 神靈以蘭湯沐浴，在芬芳的蒸氣中洗髮，身著花朵本色的衣裳；祂在祭典的神祠中容光煥發地流連，比萬物的盡頭更為明亮。祂乘龍車、著帝服，盤旋周行於九州；祂的光輝留駐於彼，而歌者之心追隨祂沒入幽暗——因為雲中君如同《九歌》中所有的神祇，所賜的是一場造訪，而非長居。

title.en: The River Lord, in the Hall of Shellfish and the Palace of Fish
title.zh: 九歌河伯

region.en: The Nine-River ford and the River Lord's water-halls (Yellow River)
region.zh: 九河

period: Chu Ci, Jiu Ge, 4th-3rd c. BCE

source.work: Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: He Bo, the river-god's hall of shells and the white turtle's dance

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The River Lord's hymn is a tour of the water-world: he plays with the nine rivers, breaks the ice of the Kunlun ford, rides his white turtle to a hall of shells and a palace of fish, follows the girl into the far isles, and at the ford they part — his hall of glories lies westward, and the singer watches the wave-face of the water carry him away.
summary.zh: 與女遊兮九河，衝風起兮橫波；乘水車兮荷蓋，駕兩龍兮驂螭……魚鱗屋兮龍堂，紫貝闕兮朱宮——河伯之遊。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Chu Ci original.

passages.text: The River Lord and his guest go up the nine rivers together, wind rising athwart the waves; he drives a water-carriage roofed with lotus, drawn by two dragons harnessed with the sea-horse team. He climbs the Kunlun ford and watches the world's end, his heart flying like sunlight on the water; he lodges in a house walled with fish-scales, in a hall of dragon-beams, behind gates of purple shell and vermilion palaces — the water-world as the shamaness tours it, god-guided.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: He Bo (compiler's rendering); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: He Bo; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 河伯與他的賓客一同溯九河而上，風逆著波濤興起；他駕著以荷葉為蓋的水車，由兩條龍拉著，與海馬之隊共駕。他登上崑崙的渡口，眺望世界的盡頭，其心如陽光躍動於水面；他棲居於魚鱗為牆之室、龍梁之堂，紫貝為門、朱宮為殿——這便是巫女在神靈引導下所遊歷的水底世界。

passages.text: They wander to the isle of the far islets, where the waters wheel; and the hymn ends at the ford with the farewell: his hall of glories lies toward the sunset, and the fish-neighbor greets him as he goes — the river-god's day of hospitality, closed at the crossing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Jiu Ge: He Bo; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們漫遊至遠方洲渚之島，水流迴旋；頌歌在渡口以告別作結：他的榮光之堂朝向日落之處，魚鄰在他離去時相迎——河神的款待之日，於渡口閉幕。

title.en: The Great Summons: The Feast Laid for a Returning Soul
title.zh: 大招

region.en: The Chu mourning-grounds and the halls of Ying
region.zh: 楚廷郢都

period: Chu Ci, Dazhao (The Great Summons), 3rd c. BCE

source.work: Chu Ci, Dazhao (The Great Summons): the four quarters' perils named again, and the catalog of feasts for the soul's return

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The Great Summons, companion-piece to the Summons of the Soul, calls the dead home by naming the perils of the four quarters and the six directions — and then lays out the feast of the Chu court in verse: wines, roasts, soups, fruits, music and dancers, a catalog of everything a household was, set out as the reason to return.
summary.zh: 魂乎歸來！四方上下皆不可託；楚廷之宴——酒漿、炙雁、龜羹、蜜餌、鐘鼓樂舞——以宴致魂。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Chu Ci original. Companion to chinese-chuci-zhaohun.

passages.text: The Great Summons calls the soul home by the same four-quarters litany as its companion piece: do not go east, or south, or west, or north, or up, or down — each direction named with its devourers, its ice, its sand, its dark capital — and home named with its gate of bright walls.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Dazhao (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《大招》以與其姊妹篇相同的四方連禱召喚魂魄歸來：不要向東、向南、向西、向北，也不要向上、向下——每一方都道出其吞噬者、其冰雪、其流沙、其幽暗之都——而家鄉則以其明亮城牆的門戶道出。

passages.text: Then the feast: the wines of the frost and the spring, the roast swan and the fat goose, the turtle-soup and the lamb, the honey-baits and the spiced duck, the music of the bells and the pipes, the dancers of the court — a catalog in verse of everything a household was, laid out as the reason to return. The soul is argued with by luxury rather than by fear, and the rite works both arguments at once.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chu Ci, Dazhao, the feast catalog; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著是盛宴：霜與春之酒，烤天鵝與肥鵝，龜羹與羔羊，蜜餌與香鴨，鐘與管之樂，宮廷的舞者——以韻文鋪陳一個家所曾有的一切，列為歸返的理由。魂魄是被奢華而非恐懼所勸服，而儀式同時施展這兩種論辯。

title.en: The Cowherd and the Weaver Girl: Two Stars and One Bridge of Birds
title.zh: 牛郎織女

region.en: The Milky Way's two banks and the river of the sky (symbolic pin: the sky itself)
region.zh: 天河兩岸

period: Folk cycle; oldest layer in Shi Jing, Xiao Ya: Da Dong (c. 8th-6th c. BCE); festival charter in Jingchu Suishiji, 6th c. CE

source.work: The Cowherd-Weaver cycle: the Ox Star and the Weaver Star, the magpie bridge of the seventh night, and the river of stars between them

license: Public domain (folk tradition; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The Weaver Girl of the sky wove the clouds at her loom and loved the Cowherd across the river of stars; the marriage pleased no one in heaven — she stopped weaving, and the separation was decreed: one night a year, the seventh of the seventh month, when all the magpies of the world fly up to make a bridge of their own bodies across the star-river and the two meet on the birds' backs in the dark. The rest of the year the river runs between them, and rain on that night is said to be their tears.
summary.zh: 織女為天帝之女，年年機杼，織雲錦天衣；牛郎織女隔天河相望——七月初七，鵲橋相會，一年一度；「迢迢牽牛星，皎皎河漢女」——乞巧節由此而立。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the folk cycle. Tagging caveat: 'sun-capture' marks the sky-star pair motif, interpretive. The festival (Qixi) is living heritage; the record is archival.

passages.text: In the sky-river's two banks two stars keep their places: the Weaver on the east, the Cowherd with his ox on the west. She wove the cloud-robes of heaven, he herded the sky's cattle, and the two loved across the water of stars.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Cowherd-Weaver folk cycle (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天河兩岸各有一星守著自己的位置：織女在東，牽牛郎與他的牛在西。她織天上的雲衣，他牧天上的牛群，兩人隔著星河相愛。

passages.text: The marriage so pleased neither court nor loom — the clouds went unwoven while she was happy — that a decree set the river between them forever, with one night of reunion each year. On the seventh night of the seventh month the magpies of the whole world fly up and spread themselves wing to wing as a bridge, and the Weaver walks across the birds to the Cowherd's side of the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the folk cycle with the Qixi charter; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這樁婚事既不稱天庭之意，也誤了織機——她歡喜之時雲錦便無人織——於是降下旨意，令天河永遠隔在兩人之間，只許每年相會一夜。七月初七之夜，天下喜鵲齊飛上天，展翅相銜成橋，織女踏著群鳥走過天河，到牽牛郎那一邊的天際。

passages.text: The girls of China lay out needles in the water that night to beg a thread of her skill — the feast of Begging for Skill — and if rain falls on the bridge of birds it is called the tears the couple cannot shed at any other time of the sky's year.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Qixi festival customs; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那一夜，中國的女子在水上擺針，乞求分得一縷她的巧藝——是為乞巧節——若鵲橋上落下雨來，便說是這對夫妻在天上一年的其餘時光裡流不出的眼淚。

title.en: Meng Jiangnü Weeps Down the Great Wall
title.zh: 孟姜女哭長城

region.en: The Great Wall works at Shanhaiguan (pin: Hebei coast)
region.zh: 山海關長城

period: Folk cycle; earliest layer in Zuo Zhuan, Xiang 23 (c. 4th c. BCE text); Tang Dunhuang bianwen recension; Ming shrines

source.work: The Meng Jiangnü cycle: the girl of the gourd-vine, the conscripted husband, and the weeping that cracked the wall

license: Public domain (folk tradition; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Two neighboring households raised a girl born from a gourd-vine that grew across both their walls; she married the young man Fan Xiliang, who was seized three days after the wedding for the Great Wall's works. She sewed winter clothes through the autumn and walked the whole wall north to find him — and found that he was dead, built into the wall's fill. Her weeping went on for days until the wall cracked for three hundred li and showed the bones; her blood marked her husband's among the nameless, and the First Emperor, arriving to punish the weeper, offered her what no one had offered before — and she chose the sea.
summary.zh: 孟姜女為兩家共植瓜藤所生，嫁范喜良；婚後三日夫被抓修長城；千里送寒衣，哭崩長城三百里，滴血認夫骨；始皇欲納之，姜女投海——貞女祠由此而立。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the folk cycle. The tale is a protest-legend against corvée labor; its layers (Zuo Zhuan's chaste widow, Tang bianwen, Ming folk drama) show a millennium of retelling.

passages.text: A gourd-vine planted by one household climbed the wall and fruited in the yard of the other, and from the gourd came a girl both families claimed; they raised her together as Meng Jiangnü, the child of the shared vine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Meng Jiangnü folk cycle (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一戶人家種下的葫蘆藤爬過牆頭，在另一戶的院裡結了果，葫蘆裡生出一個女孩，兩家都爭說是自家的；他們一同將她撫養長大，喚作孟姜女，是那株共有的藤所生的孩子。

passages.text: She had been married three days when the conscription took her husband Fan to the Great Wall's works; through the autumn she sewed winter clothes and walked the whole northern line to bring them to him — and learned at the works that he had died in the wall's own fill, one body among thousands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the folk cycle; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她成親才三日，徵役便將她的丈夫范郎捉去修長城；整個秋天她縫製冬衣，走遍北邊全線要送去給他——卻在工地上得知他已死，被填進了城牆之中，是千萬具屍骨裡的一具。

passages.text: She sat against the wall and wept until it cracked open for three hundred li, and the bones lay bare; her blood, dropped on the nameless heap, found and marked her husband's. The First Emperor came himself to punish the weeper and offered instead to marry her; she asked for a state funeral for her husband, rode out to the sea at the rite's end, and stepped off the cliff into the water rather than be the emperor's bride.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the folk cycle, the emperor and the sea; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她倚著城牆痛哭，哭得城牆崩裂三百里，白骨盡露；她將血滴在無名的屍堆上，血尋到了她丈夫的骸骨，作了記認。秦始皇親自前來懲治這哭城之人，卻轉而提出要娶她；她只求為丈夫舉行國葬，葬禮畢時騎馬來到海邊，縱身躍下懸崖，投入水中，也不肯做皇帝的妻子。

title.en: Liang Shanbo and Zhu Yingtai: The Butterfly Tomb
title.zh: 梁山伯與祝英臺

region.en: Hangzhou and Ningbo, the school and the tomb (Zhejiang)
region.zh: 杭州至寧波

period: Folk cycle; earliest Tang citations; full flowering in Song-Ming drama and storyteller books

source.work: The Liang-Zhu cycle: the girl disguised as a boy, the school of Hangzhou, the tomb that opened for the coffin

license: Public domain (folk tradition; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Zhu Yingtai dressed as a boy to study at the Hangzhou academy, and three years as deskmate taught Liang Shanbo everything about her but the one thing; she went home betrothed to another, and he died of the discovery. Her wedding procession stopped at his grave on the way; she wept, the tomb cracked open, and she stepped in — the grave closed on the two of them, and out of it rose two butterflies that flew together and did not part: the folk corpus's great love-death, and the reason Chinese butterfly pairs mean marriage.
summary.zh: 祝英臺女扮男裝入杭州求學，與梁山伯同窗三年；英臺許配馬家，山伯鬱鬱而終；英臺出嫁路經墓前，哭而墓裂，入墓合葬——化為雙蝶雙飛。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the folk cycle.

passages.text: Zhu Yingtai cut her hair, bound her chest, and enrolled at the Hangzhou academy as a boy, with a servant carrying her books; three years at the same desk taught Liang Shanbo her mind, her humor, her hand at the lute — everything about her but that she was a girl.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Liang-Zhu folk cycle (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 祝英台剪去長髮，束起胸脯，扮作男子進入杭州的書院就讀，由僕人替她挑著書箱；三年同窗，讓梁山伯認識了她的心思、她的幽默、她彈琴的手藝——關於她的一切，唯獨不知她是女兒身。

passages.text: She went home and left him hints he was too honest to read — the duck-and-mandarin pair, the well's two reflections — and was betrothed in her absence to the son of a rich house. He came to visit too late, understood, and died of it within the season.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the folk cycle; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她返家時留下種種暗示，他卻忠厚老實，讀不出其中之意——那對鴛鴦、井中雙影——而她已於他不在時許配給富家之子。他來訪時已太遲，明白了一切，並在同季之內因此而死。

passages.text: Her wedding procession passed his grave on the road to the other bridegroom's house, and she stopped it, wept, and prayed at the stone; the tomb split, she stepped in, the earth closed on the two of them — and two butterflies rose from the mound and flew together, wing for wing, out of the mourning crowd's sight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the folk cycle, the butterfly ending; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她的送嫁隊伍在前往另一新郎家的路上經過他的墳墓，她令隊伍停下，哭泣，在墓石前祈禱；墳墓裂開，她步入其中，大地在二人身上合攏——而後一對蝴蝶自墳塚升起，比翼齊飛，飛出送葬人群的視野之外。

title.en: The Eight Immortals Cross the Sea, Each by His Own Art
title.zh: 八仙過海

region.en: The eastern sea, between Penglai and the mainland (Shandong coast)
region.zh: 東海

period: Dongyou Ji (Journey to the East) by Wu Yuantai, Ming, c. 1562; cult much older

source.work: Dongyou Ji, juan on the sea-crossing: the eight immortals' crossing of the eastern sea, each riding his own treasure

license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Feasting at the pebble-beach after the Peach Banquet, the Eight Immortals refused the cloud-road home and crossed the sea instead, each riding his own treasure thrown on the waves: Zhongli Quan his fan, Lü Dongbin his sword, the girl He Xiangu her lotus flower, Iron-Crutch Li his crutch, Lan Caihe his flower-basket, Zhang Guolao his paper mule, Han Xiangzi his flute, and Royal Uncle Cao his jade tablets. The Dragon King's son stole He Xiangu, and the war that followed set the sea boiling — the eight of them against the four seas' hosts, ending with the immortals on top and a new temple on Penglai.
summary.zh: 八仙過東海，各顯神通：鍾離權扇、呂洞賓劍、何仙姑蓮花、鐵拐李拐、藍采和花籃、張果老紙驢、韓湘子笛、曹國舅玉板；龍王太子劫何仙姑，八仙大鬧龍宮——各憑本事。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Ming novel.

passages.text: Returning from the Peach Banquet over the eastern sea, the Eight Immortals refused the cloud-road Lü Dongbin offered and crossed on the water instead — each setting his own treasure on the waves and riding it: the fan, the sword, the lotus, the crutch, the flower-basket, the paper mule, the flute, the jade tablets of office.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dongyou Ji, sea-crossing chapter (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 八仙自東海蟠桃宴歸來，拒絕了呂洞賓所提議的雲路，改為渡水而過——各將自己的寶物置於波濤之上，乘之而行：扇、劍、蓮花、拐杖、花籃、紙驢、笛、玉笏。

passages.text: The show drew the Dragon King's son, who dragged the girl-immortal He Xiangu down to the sea-palace; the seven came for her with fire and frost and mountain-moving, and the four seas' hosts could not hold them — the immortals left with their own, the dragon-court fined, and the crossing entered the saying-books as the Chinese standard for eight people, eight methods, one shore.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dongyou Ji; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這場展示引來了龍王之子，他將女仙何仙姑拖入海底宮殿；其餘七仙帶著火與霜、移山之術前來救她，四海之眾也抵擋不住他們——眾仙帶著自己人離去，龍宮受罰，而這次渡海被載入說書之冊，成為中國「八人八法，同登一岸」的典範。

title.en: Wu Gang Chops the Cassia That Heals Itself
title.zh: 吳剛伐桂

region.en: The moon's cassia tree (symbolic pin: the moon)
region.zh: 月桂

period: Youyang Zazu by Duan Chengshi, c. 860 CE, Tianchi section

source.work: Youyang Zazu, Tianchi: Wu Gang of Hexi, the cassia tree of the moon, and the blows that never finish

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: In the moon stands a cassia tree five hundred zhang tall, under which a man named Wu Gang, exiled from the Hexi country for his faults in seeking the Way, chops at the trunk forever: the tree closes every wound as the axe lifts, ten thousand blows and none of them the last. The moon's shadow on clear nights is the tree; the man under it, said the Tang book, is the reason the tree is always whole and always being cut.
summary.zh: 月桂高五百丈，下有一人常斫之，樹創隨合；人姓吳名剛，西河人，學仙有過，謫令伐樹——萬世之斧與一樹之癒。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Youyang Zazu text.

passages.text: In the moon stands a cassia tree five hundred zhang tall, and under it a man named Wu Gang, of the Hexi country, chops at the trunk with an axe; the wound in the wood closes before the axe can be lifted, so that every blow is the first and none of them the last.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Youyang Zazu, Tianchi section, Wu Gang entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 月中有桂樹，高五百丈，樹下有一人名叫吳剛，是河西人氏，以斧砍伐樹幹；木上的傷口在斧頭舉起之前便已癒合，因此每一斧都是第一斧，而沒有一斧是最後一斧。

passages.text: He was sent there, says the Tang book, for faults in his seeking of the Way — a student exiled to an unfinishable labor in the brightest place in the sky. The moon's shadowed face on a clear night is the tree; the reason it is always whole and always being cut stands below it, swinging.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Youyang Zazu; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據《唐書》所載，他之所以被貶逐至此，是因求道有過——一個被流放的學徒，被罰去從事一樁永無了期的勞役，地點就在天宇中最明亮之處。晴夜裡月面上的陰影便是那棵樹；它之所以始終完整、又始終在被砍伐，是因為樹下那人正揮斧不止。

title.en: Nitetis and the Child's Vow: The Above Made Below
title.zh: 奈提提斯與童誓言：以上為下

region.en: Persia and Egypt (the disputed princess whose double marriage brought the conquest)
region.zh: 波斯與埃及（雙重身世的公主招致征服）

period: Persian-Egyptian tale recorded by Herodotus, Histories III.1-3 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book III, secs. 1-3

summary.en: Amasis, fearing Cambyses would wed him to his own daughter, sent him the only daughter of Apries instead, dressed as his own — until Cambyses called her by the wrong father's name and she told the truth; the Persians say this began the invasion, while the Egyptians make the reverse claim; and the boy Cambyses, hearing his mother scorned, vowed: 'I will make that which is above in Egypt to be below, and that which is below above.'
summary.zh: 阿馬西斯恐岡比西斯索其女為妻，遂以阿普里埃斯之獨女盛裝冒充己女送之——及岡比西斯誤喚其父名，公主道破真相；波斯人謂此即侵略之因，埃及人則反稱其血緣；童年的岡比西斯聞母受辱，誓曰：『我必使埃及之上者為下、下者為上。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient historical-legendary tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: There was a daughter of Apries the former king, very tall and comely of form and the only person left of his house, and her name was Nitetis. This girl Amasis adorned with raiment and with gold, and sent her away to Persia as his own daughter: but after a time, when Cambyses saluted her calling her by the name of her father, the girl said to him: 'O king, thou dost not perceive how thou hast been deceived by Amasis; for he adorned me with ornaments and sent me away giving me to thee as his own daughter, whereas in truth I am the daughter of Apries against whom Amasis rose up with the Egyptians and murdered him, who was his lord and master.' These words uttered and this occasion having arisen, led Cambyses the son of Cyrus against Egypt, moved to very great anger.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book III.1.
passages.zh: 前王阿普里埃斯有一女，身形頎長、容貌秀美，且是他家族中僅存的一人，名叫尼泰提斯。阿瑪西斯將這女子以華服與黃金盛飾，當作自己的親生女兒送往波斯。然而過了些時日，岡比西斯以她父親之名呼她、向她致意，這女子便對他說：「大王啊，你並未察覺自己如何受了阿瑪西斯的欺瞞；因為他為我盛加裝飾，把我當作他的親生女兒送來給你，而實際上我是阿普里埃斯的女兒——阿瑪西斯曾率埃及人起而反抗他，將他殺害，而他本是阿瑪西斯的主上。」這番話既已說出，時機又已成熟，便驅使居魯士之子岡比西斯興兵討伐埃及，他為此勃然大怒。

passages.text: Cassandane, who was the wife of Cyrus, spoke as follows: 'Nevertheless, though I am the mother of such children of these, Cyrus treats me with dishonour and holds in honour her whom he has brought in from Egypt.' Thus she spoke, they say, being vexed by Nitetis, and upon that Cambyses the elder of her sons said: 'For this cause, mother, when I am grown to be a man, I will make that which is above in Egypt to be below, and that which is below above.' This he is reported to have said when he was perhaps about ten years old, and the women were astonished by it: and he, they say, kept it ever in mind, and so at last when he had become a man and had obtained the royal power, he made the expedition against Egypt.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book III.3.
passages.zh: 居魯士之妻卡珊達涅如此說道：「然而，儘管我是這些孩子的母親，居魯士卻待我以輕慢，反倒尊崇他從埃及帶回來的那個女子。」據說她因尼泰提斯而心懷怨忿，說了這番話；於是她的長子岡比西斯說道：「母親，正因如此，等我長大成人，我要把埃及在上的一切翻到在下，把在下的一切翻到在上。」據說他說這話時大約才十歲，婦人們聽了都大為驚異；而據說他始終把這話記在心裡，所以到了最後，當他長大成人、取得王權之後，便發兵征討埃及。

title.en: Psammenitos at the Water-carriers: The Wise King's Tears
title.zh: 普薩美尼托斯與汲水者：智者之淚

region.en: Memphis, suburb of the city (the captive king seated before Cambyses)
region.zh: 埃及孟菲斯城郊（被俘之王坐於岡比西斯之前）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories III.14-15 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book III, secs. 14-15

summary.en: Cambyses leads the daughter of Psammenitos in slave's dress to draw water, his son to execution — and the deposed king only bows to the earth; but when an aged beggar of his own company passes, begging from the soldiers, Psammenitos weeps aloud: 'My own troubles were too great for me to lament them aloud, but the trouble of my companion was such as called for tears' — and Croesus wept too.
summary.zh: 岡比西斯使普薩美尼托斯之女著奴衣汲水，其子縛索牽往就刑——亡王僅俯身向地；及一窮老同僚乞食而過，王乃放聲大哭：『我自身之苦，過於我所能哭；而吾友之苦，堪當一哭』——居魯士亦為之泣。

sensitivity.note: Ancient moral tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Cambyses sent his daughter with the other maidens, dressed as was the daughter of the king: and as the maidens were passing by their fathers with cries and lamentation, the other men all began to cry out and lament aloud, seeing that their children had been evilly entreated, but Psammenitos when he saw it before his eyes and perceived it bent himself down to the earth. Then when the water-bearers had passed by, next Cambyses sent his son with two thousand Egyptians besides who were of the same age, with ropes bound round their necks and bits placed in their mouths; and these were being led away to execution.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book III.14.
passages.zh: 岡比西斯把他的女兒與其他少女一同送出，裝扮得如同國王的女兒一般；當這些少女哭喊哀號著從她們的父親面前走過時，其餘的男子見自己的孩子遭受如此虐待，全都放聲哭喊、高聲哀號，但普薩美尼托斯親眼看見這一幕、明白過來之後，卻俯身伏向地面。待那些提水的人走過之後，岡比西斯接著又送出他的兒子，另有兩千名與他同齡的埃及人，頸上縛著繩索，口中塞著嚼子；這些人正被押去處死。

passages.text: When these also had passed by, it chanced that a man of his table companions, advanced in years, who had been deprived of all his possessions and had nothing except such things as a beggar possesses, and was asking alms from the soldiers, passed by Psammenitos the son of Amasis and the Egyptians who were sitting in the suburb of the city: and when Psammenitos saw him he uttered a great cry of lamentation, and he called his companion by name and beat himself upon the head. — Cambyses marvelled at that which he did, and he sent a messenger and asked him: 'Psammenitos, thy master Cambyses asks thee for what reason, when thou sawest thy daughter evilly entreated and thy son going to death, thou didst not cry aloud nor lament for them, whereas thou didst honour with these signs of grief the beggar who, as he hears from others, is not in any way related to thee?'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book III.14.
passages.zh: 待這些人也走過之後，恰好有一個與他同席共餐的人，年事已高，被剝奪了全部家產，除了一個乞丐所有的東西之外一無所有，正向士兵們乞討，從坐在城郊的普薩美尼托斯——阿瑪西斯之子——和那些埃及人面前經過；普薩美尼托斯看見他，便發出一聲極大的哀號，呼喚那同伴的名字，並以手捶打自己的頭。——岡比西斯對他此舉大為驚異，便派了一名使者去問他：「普薩美尼托斯，你的主上岡比西斯問你：當你看見你的女兒遭受虐待、你的兒子走向死亡時，你既不哭喊也不哀悼他們，卻以這些悲傷的表示去致敬一個乞丐——而據他從旁人口中聽聞，這人與你毫無親屬關係，這是為什麼？」

passages.text: The other answered as follows: 'O son of Cyrus, my own troubles were too great for me to lament them aloud, but the trouble of my companion was such as called for tears, seeing that he has been deprived of great wealth, and has come to beggary upon the threshold of old age.' When this saying was reported by the messenger, it seemed to them that it was well spoken; and, as is reported by the Egyptians, Croesus shed tears (for he also, as fortune would have it, had accompanied Cambyses to Egypt) and the Persians who were present shed tears also; and there entered some pity into Cambyses himself, and forthwith he bade them save the life of the son of Psammenitos.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book III.14.
passages.zh: 那人回答如下：「居魯士之子啊，我自身的苦難太過深重，我無法為它們放聲哀哭；但我這同伴的苦難卻是足以令人流淚的，因為他被剝奪了巨大的財富，到了老年卻淪為乞丐。」這番話經使者稟報之後，眾人皆覺得他說得極好；而據埃及人所記，克羅伊斯也流下淚來（因為命運使然，他也隨岡比西斯來到了埃及），當時在場的波斯人也一同落淚；連岡比西斯本人心中也生出了幾分憐憫，當即下令他們饒普薩美尼托斯之子一命。

title.en: The Body of Amasis: The Oracle and the Substitute Corpse
title.zh: 阿馬西斯之身：神諭與替身屍

region.en: Sais, Egypt (the burial-place in the temple, near the doors)
region.zh: 埃及薩伊斯（神廟內之葬室，近門處）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories III.16 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book III, sec. 16

summary.en: Cambyses enters the palace of Amasis, drags out the embalmed king, has him scourged, plucked and stabbed — but the Egyptians say it was not Amasis at all: the king had learned from an oracle what would befall his body after death, buried a double of his own stature near the doors, and enjoined his son to lay his own body in the innermost recess; Herodotus half doubts, as 'pride and no good ground.'
summary.zh: 岡比西斯入阿馬西斯王宮，拖出其木乃伊鞭笞拔毛穿刺——而埃及人言：彼非阿馬西斯！王生前自神諭得知死後之事，遂以一身材相同者代葬於門側，並囑其子將己身安置室中最深之處。希羅多德半信半疑，謂此乃『出於驕矜而無實據』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: From Memphis Cambyses came to the city of Sais with the purpose of doing that which in fact he did: for when he had entered into the palace of Amasis, he forthwith gave command to bring the corpse of Amasis forth out of his burial-place; and when this had been accomplished, he gave command to scourge it and pluck out the hair and stab it, and to do to it dishonour in every possible way besides: and when they had done this too until they were wearied out, for the corpse being embalmed held out against the violence and did not fall to pieces in any part, Cambyses gave command to consume it with fire, enjoining thereby a thing which was not permitted by religion.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book III.16.
passages.zh: 岡比西斯從孟斐斯來到賽斯城，目的是要做他後來果然做出的事：因為當他進入阿瑪西斯的宮殿之後，便立刻下令把阿瑪西斯的屍體從其墳墓中搬出來；此事辦成之後，他又下令鞭打它、拔去它的頭髮、刺戳它，並且除此之外還用一切可能的方式對它加以凌辱：而當他們把這些事也做到疲倦為止——因為那屍體既經防腐處理，便抵住了種種暴行，任何部位都沒有碎裂——岡比西斯便下令用火把它燒掉，如此便命人做了一件宗教所不允許的事。

passages.text: However, the Egyptians say that it was not Amasis who suffered this outrage, but another of the Egyptians who was of the same stature of body as Amasis; and that to him the Persians did outrage, thinking that they were doing it to Amasis: for they say that Amasis learnt from an Oracle that which was about to happen with regard to himself after his death; and accordingly, to avert the evil which threatened to come upon him, he buried the dead body of this man who was scourged within his own sepulchral chamber near the doors, and enjoined his son to lay his own body as much as possible in the inner recess of the chamber. These injunctions, said to have been given by Amasis with regard to his burial and with regard to the man mentioned, were not in my opinion really given at all, but I think that the Egyptians make pretence of it from pride and with no good ground.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book III.16.
passages.zh: 然而，埃及人說，遭受這番暴行的並不是阿瑪西斯，而是另一個身材與阿瑪西斯相同的埃及人；波斯人以為自己是在對阿瑪西斯施暴，其實是對這人施暴：因為他們說，阿瑪西斯從神諭得知了關於他自己死後將要發生的事；於是，為了避開那威脅要降到他身上的災禍，他便把這個被鞭打而死之人的屍體葬在自己墓室內靠近門的地方，並囑咐他的兒子盡可能把自己的遺體安放在墓室最深處的內室。據說阿瑪西斯關於自己葬事以及關於上述那人所下的這些囑咐，依我看其實根本不曾下過，我認為埃及人是出於自負而無端編造此說的。

title.en: Cambyses Stabs the Apis: The Mad King and the Dying God
title.zh: 岡比西斯刺阿匹斯：狂王與垂死之神

region.en: Memphis, Egypt (the temple where Apis lay dying of his wound)
region.zh: 埃及孟菲斯（阿匹斯負傷垂死之神廟）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories III.27-30 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book III, secs. 27-30

summary.en: Apis appears and Egypt wears its fairest garments; Cambyses, assuming mockery of his failures, kills the officers, summons the god — and finds a calf 'black, with a white square on the forehead, the likeness of an eagle on its back, double hairs in the tail, and a mark like a beetle on the tongue,' born of a cow that a flash of light from heaven has struck. Drawing his dagger he stabs the calf in the thigh and laughs: 'Are gods born such as this, with blood and flesh, and sensible of the stroke of iron weapons?' — and straightway, the Egyptians say, he went mad.
summary.zh: 阿匹斯顯現，埃及人皆著盛裝慶賀；岡比西斯以為譏己之敗，誅官吏，召神入前——所見乃一黑犢：額有白方、背如鷹形、尾毛雙生、舌上若有甲蟲之印，乃天光下注之母牛所生。王拔匕首刺其股而笑曰：『神而生而有血肉、能覺鐵器之傷者，如此而已乎？』——埃及人謂其自此而狂。

sensitivity.note: Ancient king-atrocity tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. Pairs with the Ochus-apis record cut from Plutarch.

passages.text: When Cambyses arrived at Memphis, Apis appeared to the Egyptians, whom the Hellenes call Epaphos: and when he had appeared, forthwith the Egyptians began to wear their fairest garments and to have festivities. Cambyses accordingly seeing the Egyptians doing thus, and supposing that they were certainly acting so by way of rejoicing because he had fared ill, called for the officers who had charge of Memphis... They said that a god had appeared to them, who was wont to appear at intervals of long time, and that whenever he appeared, then all the Egyptians rejoiced and kept festival. Hearing this Cambyses said that they were lying, and as liars he condemned them to death.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book III.27.
passages.zh: 當岡比西斯抵達孟斐斯時，阿匹斯向埃及人顯現了，希臘人稱之為厄帕福斯：而當他顯現之後，埃及人便立刻穿上他們最華美的衣服，舉行歡慶。岡比西斯見埃及人如此行事，便以為他們這樣做必定是在為他遭遇不幸而歡欣鼓舞，於是召來負責孟斐斯的官員……他們說有一位神向他們顯現了，這神慣於隔很長的時間才顯現一次，而每當他顯現時，全體埃及人便歡欣鼓舞、舉行節慶。岡比西斯聽了這話，說他們在撒謊，並把他們當作撒謊者處死。

passages.text: This Apis-Epaphos is a calf born of a cow who after this is not permitted to conceive any other offspring; and the Egyptians say that a flash of light comes down from heaven upon this cow, and of this she produces Apis. This calf which is called Apis is black and has the following signs, namely a white square upon the forehead, and on the back the likeness of an eagle, and in the tail the hairs are double, and on the tongue there is a mark like a beetle.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book III.28.
passages.zh: 這阿匹斯—厄帕福斯是一頭由母牛所生的小牛，那母牛在此之後便不許再懷任何其他犢子；埃及人說有一道光芒從天而降，落在這母牛身上，她便由此生出阿匹斯。這頭稱為阿匹斯的小牛是黑色的，並有如下標記：額上有一塊白色的方形斑，背上有一個形似鷹的圖案，尾巴上的毛是雙重的，舌上有一個形似甲蟲的印記。

passages.text: When the priests had brought Apis, Cambyses being somewhat affected with madness drew his dagger, and aiming at the belly of Apis, struck his thigh: then he laughed and said to the priests: 'O ye wretched creatures, are gods born such as this, with blood and flesh, and sensible of the stroke of iron weapons? Worthy indeed of Egyptians is such a god as this. Ye however at least shall not escape without punishment for making a mock of me.'... Apis wounded by the stroke in his thigh lay dying in the temple. Him, when he had brought his life to an end by reason of the wound, the priests buried without the knowledge of Cambyses: but Cambyses, as the Egyptians say, immediately after this evil deed became absolutely mad, not having been really in his right senses even before that time.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book III.29-30.
passages.zh: 當祭司們把阿匹斯牽來時，岡比西斯有些發狂，便拔出短劍，對準阿匹斯的腹部刺去，卻刺中了他的大腿：於是他笑著對祭司們說：『啊，你們這些可憐的東西，神是這樣生出來的嗎？有血有肉，還會感受到鐵器的打擊嗎？這樣的神倒也真配得上埃及人。然而你們至少逃不掉因嘲弄我而受的懲罰。』……阿匹斯大腿上受了這一擊，便躺在廟裡奄奄一息。當他因這傷而斷了氣之後，祭司們瞞著岡比西斯把他埋葬了：但據埃及人說，岡比西斯在這件惡行之後便立刻徹底發瘋了，其實他在此之前也早已神志不清。

title.en: The Fifty Thousand Who Vanished in the Sand
title.zh: 消失於黃沙的五萬大軍

region.en: The desert between the Oasis (the Isle of the Blessed) and the Oracle of Ammon (symbolic pin over the Libyan sand sea)
region.zh: 祝福之島與阿蒙神諭之間的利比亞沙海（象徵定位）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories III.25-26 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book III, secs. 25-26

summary.en: Cambyses sent fifty thousand men from Thebes to enslave the Ammonians and burn the oracle of Zeus; they reached the Oasis — the Greeks' Isle of the Blessed — and from there, says the whole world, nothing: the Ammonians themselves tell that at their morning meal, mid-way through the sand, a violent south wind arose and buried the army under heaps of desert sand, 'and so they disappeared and were seen no more.'
summary.zh: 岡比西斯自底比斯遣五萬眾，欲奴役阿蒙人、焚宙斯神諭之座；軍至綠洲——即希臘人所謂『祝福之島』——此後天下無人能言其蹤：阿蒙人自述，正午餐之際，南風驟起，挾沙如山，盡埋其軍，『自此不復得見』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient marvel-tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. Tagged 'otherworld-voyage' for the vanishing-into-the-otherworld reading; recorded as an interpretive choice.

passages.text: When in the course of his march he had arrived at Thebes, he divided off about fifty thousand of his army, and these he enjoined to make slaves of the Ammonians and to set fire to the seat of the Oracle of Zeus, but he himself with the remainder of his army went on against the Ethiopians.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book III.25.
passages.zh: 當他在行軍途中抵達底比斯時，他從軍隊中分出約五萬人，命令這些人把阿蒙人變為奴隸，並放火燒毀宙斯神諭的所在地，而他自己則率領其餘的軍隊繼續向衣索比亞人進發。

passages.text: Those of the Persians who had been sent to march against the Ammonians set forth from Thebes and went on their way with guides; and it is known that they arrived at the city of Oasis, which is inhabited by Samians said to be of the Aischrionian tribe, and is distant seven days' journey from Thebes over sandy desert: now this place is called in the speech of the Hellenes the 'Isle of the Blessed.' It is said that the army reached this place, but from that point onwards, except the Ammonians themselves and those who have heard the account from them, no man is able to say anything about them; for they neither reached the Ammonians nor returned back.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book III.26.
passages.zh: 那些被派去征討阿蒙人的波斯人，從底比斯出發，由嚮導帶領前行；據說他們抵達了綠洲之城，該城由據稱屬於艾斯克里翁尼亞部落的薩摩斯人居住，距底比斯有七日穿越沙質沙漠的行程：此地用希臘人的話說，叫做「福島」。據說這支軍隊到達了此地，但從那裡以後，除了阿蒙人自己以及從他們那裡聽聞此事的人之外，沒有人能對他們說出任何消息；因為他們既沒有到達阿蒙人那裡，也沒有返回。

passages.text: This however is added to the story by the Ammonians themselves: — they say that as the army was going from this Oasis through the sandy desert to attack them, and had got to a point about mid-way between them and the Oasis, while they were taking their morning meal a violent South Wind blew upon them, and bearing with it heaps of the desert sand it buried them under it, and so they disappeared and were seen no more. Thus the Ammonians say that it came to pass with regard to this army.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book III.26.
passages.zh: 然而，阿蒙人自己對這故事補充了以下內容：——他們說，當軍隊從這綠洲穿越沙質沙漠前去攻擊他們，行至他們與綠洲之間大約中途的地方時，正當他們用早餐，一陣猛烈的南風吹向他們，隨風挾帶著成堆的沙漠沙土，把他們掩埋於其下，於是他們就此消失，再也沒有人見到。阿蒙人說，這支軍隊的遭遇便是如此。

title.en: Suguid and the Hidden Princess: The Musical Purlon
title.zh: 蘇吉德與隱居公主：奏樂的寶匣

region.en: Angeles, Pampanga, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦板牙省安赫勒斯（敘述者故鄉）

period: Pampangan oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 21 'Is he the Crafty Ulysses?', eBook #8299

summary.en: Abandoned by his parents for eating the house, the foundling Suguid outgrows his school in five months and, by mysterious combinations of characters on paper, discovers that the king has a hidden daughter — posting the fact on the palace door at the price of his head. Twelve goldsmiths build him the purlon, a five-foot jewel-box that plays the sweetest music mortal ears had ever heard; the charmed king borrows it for a night, Suguid steps out poniard in hand, wins the princess's ring by passionate speech, and is married to her when the wager is paid.
summary.zh: 因食量驚人而被父母遺棄的孤兒蘇吉德，五個月便學盡書堂；他以紙上神算推知國王藏有公主，竟在王宮門上貼出此事，以頭顱為注。十二名金匠為他打造『寶匣』——奏出凡人未曾聽過的仙樂。著迷的國王借匣一晚；蘇吉德持匕首現身，以深情言辭贏得公主戒指；賭約到期，二人成婚。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan folktale recorded by Fansler from a Licup narrator (Angeles); archival record. Bride-wager type (golden musical carriage); Fansler compares the Tagalog corrido 'Juan Bachiller' and southern-European variants.

passages.text: Balbino and Alaga had only one child, a son named Suguid, who was at first greatly beloved by them; the couple was very rich. But the son was a voracious eater: while still a baby he used to pull up the nails from the floor and eat them when his mother had no more milk to give him, and when all the nails were exhausted he ate the cotton with which the pillows were stuffed — his parents compared him to a mill which consumes sugarcane incessantly. Before many years the wealth of the couple had been greatly diminished by the lavish expenditure they had to make for Suguid's food; at last they decided to cast him away into a place from which he might not be able to find his way home again, and led him one day to a dense forest and abandoned him there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 21 'Is he the Crafty Ulysses?'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴爾比諾和阿拉加只有一個孩子，是個名叫蘇吉德的兒子，起初他們非常疼愛他；這對夫婦非常富有。但這兒子食量驚人：當他還是嬰兒時，母親沒有奶水可餵他，他便常把地板上的釘子拔起來吃，等釘子都吃光了，他又吃填充枕頭的棉花——他的父母把他比作一座不停消耗甘蔗的磨坊。不出幾年，這對夫婦的財富因供養蘇吉德食物而不得不花費的巨額開銷而大為減少；最後他們決定把他丟棄到一個他可能再也找不到回家路的地方，於是有一天把他帶到一片茂密的森林，將他遺棄在那裡。

passages.text: Luckily a merchant passed by, found the crying boy, took him home, and put him in school; in a few weeks the boy showed his superiority over his classmates, in time beat even the master in points of learning, and after only five months of studying he left the school because he found it too small for his expanding intellect. By some mathematical calculation, so the tradition says, or by certain mysterious combinations of characters that he wrote on paper, Suguid discovered one day that a certain princess was hidden somewhere, concealed so that her existence might not be known other than by her parents and the courtiers. He went to the palace of the king and posted a paper on the palace-door: 'Your Majesty cannot deny me the fact that he has a daughter secluded somewhere. Your humble servant, Suguid Bociu.' The king, now unable to keep the secret of his daughter's existence, summoned him: 'Very well — if you can prove what you have stated, I will give you my daughter for your bride. If within three days you fail to produce her before me, however, you shall be unconditionally executed.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 21 'Is he the Crafty Ulysses?'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 幸運的是，一位商人路過，發現了哭泣的男孩，把他帶回家，送他上學；幾週之內，這男孩便顯出勝過同班同學的優越，後來甚至在學識上勝過了老師，而僅僅學習五個月後，他便離開了學校，因為他覺得學校對他那不斷擴展的才智而言太小了。據傳說，蘇吉德某天藉由某種數學計算，或藉由他在紙上寫下的某些神祕字符組合，發現某位公主被藏在某處，被隱匿起來，以致除了她的父母和朝臣之外，無人知道她的存在。他前往國王的宮殿，在宮門上貼了一張紙：「陛下不能否認您在某處藏有一位女兒。您的卑僕，蘇吉德·博丘。」國王如今無法再保守女兒存在的祕密，便召見他：「很好——如果你能證明你所說的話，我就把女兒許配給你為妻。然而，若你在三日之內不能把她帶到我面前，你將被無條件處死。」

passages.text: 'Oh, do not be afraid, father! If you will but provide me with twelve of the best goldsmiths that can be found in the whole city, I have no doubt of finding and captivating the fair princess.' The merchant summoned all the good goldsmiths, and Suguid ordered them to make a purlon of gold, silver, and precious stones — oblong in shape, hollow inside, five feet high, three feet deep, and four feet long, with a chair and a lamp inside, and by a certain device a person inside could breathe; altogether its construction was so beautiful that it seemed as if it were intended for the sight of the gods alone. Suguid entered it with provisions, fine clothes, a poniard, and a guitar, and ordered five men to carry it toward the king's palace while he played the sweetest piece of music mortal ears had ever heard.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 21 'Is he the Crafty Ulysses?'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「哦，別害怕，父親！只要您為我提供全城所能找到的十二位最優秀的金匠，我毫不懷疑能找到並贏得那位美麗的公主。」商人召集了所有優秀的金匠，蘇吉德命他們用金、銀和寶石製作一座普隆——長方形，內部中空，高五英尺、深三英尺、長四英尺，內有一張椅子和一盞燈，並藉某種裝置使裡面的人能夠呼吸；整體構造如此精美，彷彿只供神明觀賞一般。蘇吉德帶著食物、華服、匕首和一把吉他進入其中，並命五個人抬著它朝國王的宮殿而去，同時他彈奏著凡人耳朵從未聽過的最甜美的樂曲。

passages.text: Near the palace the king, charmed by the melodious music, asked that the purlon be lent him: 'Oh, how happy our daughter would be if she should hear this enchanting piece of music! If you will lend me this purlon, you may ask of me as a compensation any favor that you may want.' The princess was so bewitched by the music that she told her father never to take it away from her; and when the king and queen had gone, Suguid listened carefully to their retreating footsteps, came out poniard in hand, and knelt: 'Fair princess, let not my presence cause any fear!... Your ring, my adored princess, will give me life or death — life, because I shall be spared from being beheaded; death, for I have promised your father to present your ring to him within three days as a token of your acceptance of my suit. Therefore, Queen of Beauty, choose: your ring, or my death. I have my poniard ready, and I prefer a hundred times to die — nay, die smiling — at your hands.' Moved by this passionate speech, after a difficult struggle within herself she gave him the ring; Suguid entered the purlon again, was returned to the agent in the morning, and on the appointed day appeared at the palace carrying the emblem of his victory. The king knew that he was lost, and he swooned; on recovering he reluctantly caused the princess to be summoned, and she and Suguid were married — and by Suguid's wise policy the kingdom prospered, and for the first time learned what peace really meant.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 21 'Is he the Crafty Ulysses?'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在宮殿附近，國王被那悠揚的音樂所吸引，要求把那座普隆借給他：「哦，要是我們的女兒聽到這迷人的樂曲，她會多麼快樂啊！如果你肯把這座普隆借給我，你可以向我要求任何你想要的恩惠作為補償。」公主被音樂迷得神魂顛倒，告訴父親永遠不要把它從她身邊拿走；當國王和王后離去後，蘇吉德仔細聆聽他們遠去的腳步聲，手持匕首出來，跪下說道：「美麗的公主，請不要因我的出現而恐懼！……您的戒指，我愛慕的公主，將賜我生或死——生，因為我將免於被斬首；死，因為我已向您父親承諾，三日之內把您的戒指呈給他，作為您接受我求婚的信物。因此，美的女王，請選擇：您的戒指，或我的死。我的匕首已備好，我寧願一百次死去——不，笑著死去——死在您手中。」被她這番熱烈的言辭所感動，經過內心一番艱難的掙扎，她把戒指給了他；蘇吉德再次進入普隆，早晨被送回代理人那裡，並在約定之日帶著他勝利的信物出現在宮殿。國王知道自己大勢已去，便昏了過去；醒來後，他勉強命人召來公主，於是她和蘇吉德成了婚——而在蘇吉德的明智治理下，王國繁榮昌盛，並第一次懂得了和平的真正意義。

title.en: The Reward of Kindness: The Devil's Seven-Year Wager
title.zh: 善行的報償：魔鬼的七年之賭

region.en: Pagsanjan, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省帕桑漢（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 22 'The Reward of Kindness', eBook #8299

summary.en: Childless Clara vows 'I would even let my son serve the Devil'; nine years later a bear-like visitor claims her Idó. The Devil exchanges clothes with the youth, gives him a bag of money, and frees him if he spends seven years' wandering doing good — or hell if he squanders it. In bear-skin he ransoms a poor old woman from prison, marries her youngest daughter who alone will have him, and returns at the seven years' end to swap suits with the Devil; the two sisters who mocked the bear nearly die of vexation when the knight arrives with the half-ring token.
summary.zh: 無子的克拉拉曾許願『寧讓兒子侍奉魔鬼』；九年後熊形惡魔登門索子。魔鬼與少年換衣、給其一袋金錢，訂約：七載行善則釋，揮霍則墮地獄。熊皮少年替老嫗還債免獄，老嫗以三女許婚，唯幼女應允。七年期滿，他與魔鬼換回騎士裝束，持半枚戒指登門——譏笑過熊的兩位姊姊幾乎氣死。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Cordero narrator (Pagsanjan); archival record. Fansler notes it as a Bear-Skin (Grimm No. 101) import, the only Orient-recorded version, with a native promised-child opening and a broken-ring recognition unique in Filipino tales.

passages.text: In a certain town there once lived a couple who had never had a child, though married nearly five years and very anxious for a son — Clara the wife, Philip the man. One cloudy night in December, while they were talking by the window of their house, Clara said to her husband that she was going to pray the novena so that Heaven would give them a child: 'I would even let my son serve the Devil, if he would but give us a son!' Her husband was willing that she should pray the novena, and Clara began the next day her fervent devotions to the Virgin Mary, going to church every afternoon for nine days. At last she finished her novenario — but no child was born to them, and the couple was disappointed. A month had passed when, to their great happiness, Clara gave birth to a son, whom they nicknamed Idó.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 22 'The Reward of Kindness'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在某個城鎮裡，曾住著一對從未有過孩子的夫妻，雖然他們結婚已將近五年，卻非常渴望能有個兒子——妻子名叫克拉拉，丈夫名叫菲利普。十二月一個多雲的夜晚，當他們在自家窗邊交談時，克拉拉對丈夫說，她要去祈禱九日敬禮，好讓上天賜給他們一個孩子：「只要能給我們一個兒子，我甚至願意讓我的兒子去服侍魔鬼！」丈夫也願意讓她去祈禱九日敬禮，於是克拉拉第二天便開始了她對聖母瑪利亞的虔誠祈禱，每天下午都上教堂，一連九天。她終於完成了她的九日敬禮——但他們並沒有生下孩子，這對夫妻十分失望。一個月過去了，令他們大喜過望的是，克拉拉生下了一個兒子，他們給他取了個小名叫伊多。

passages.text: Idó was greatly cherished by his parents, but did not care much to stay at home: he early began to show a fondness for travelling abroad, and was always to be found in the dense woods on the outskirts of the town. One afternoon, when the family was gathered around a small table, a knock was heard at the door, and Clara, trembling, opened it to see standing there a man who looked like a bear. 'A devil, a devil!' she exclaimed; but the Devil pacified her: 'Clara, I have come here to get your son you promised me a long time ago. Now that the day has come when your son can be of some service to me, will you deny your promise?' Clara called her son: 'Here is my son. Take him, since he is yours.' Idó, about seventeen years old, was not frightened by the Devil, and finally consented to go, because of his mother's promise.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 22 'The Reward of Kindness'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊多深受父母疼愛，卻不太喜歡待在家裡：他很早就顯露出喜愛遠遊的性情，總能在城郊茂密的樹林裡找到他。某天下午，一家人圍著一張小桌子坐著時，忽然聽見有人敲門，克拉拉顫抖著去開門，只見門外站著一個模樣像熊的男人。「魔鬼，魔鬼！」她驚叫道；但那魔鬼卻安撫她說：「克拉拉，我來這裡是要帶走你的兒子，你很久以前就把他許給我了。如今你兒子能為我效勞的日子已經到了，你還要否認你的承諾嗎？」克拉拉喚來她的兒子：「這就是我的兒子。既然他是你的，就把他帶走吧。」伊多大約十七歲，並不怕那魔鬼，最後因為母親的承諾，便答應跟他走。

passages.text: The Devil took Idó to his cave far away outside the town, and tried in many ways to tempt him but was unable, because Idó was a youth of strong character; finally the Devil decided to exchange clothes with him. Idó was obliged to put on the bear-like clothes of the Devil and to give him his own soldier-suit; then the Devil produced a large bag full of money: 'Take this money and go travelling about the world for seven years. If you live to the end of that time, and spend this money only in doing good, I will set you free. If, however, you spend the money extravagantly, you will have to go to hell with me.' And he disappeared. Idó began his wanderings from town to town; whenever people saw him they were afraid of him and would refuse him shelter, but Idó would give them money from his bag, and then they would gather about him and be kind to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 22 'The Reward of Kindness'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 魔鬼把伊多帶到城外遠處他的洞穴裡，用盡各種方法誘惑他，卻都無法得逞，因為伊多是性格堅強的青年；最後魔鬼決定與他交換衣服。伊多不得不穿上魔鬼那身像熊一樣的衣服，並把自己的士兵裝束給他；接著魔鬼拿出一隻裝滿錢的大袋子：「拿著這些錢，到世界各地去遊歷七年。如果你能活到那時，而且只把這些錢用在行善上，我就放你自由。但如果你揮霍這些錢，你就得跟我一起下地獄。」說完他便消失了。伊多開始從一個城鎮流浪到另一個城鎮；人們一看見他就害怕，不肯收留他，但伊多會從袋子裡拿出錢給他們，於是他們便圍攏過來，善待他。

passages.text: After many years he came to a town where he saw an old woman summoned before a court of justice, accused of owing a sum of money she was unable to pay; when Idó paid her fine for her and thus released her from prison, she could hardly express her gratitude, and as most of the other people were afraid of Idó, this woman decided to take him home with her. She had three daughters, and called her eldest: 'Here is a man who delivered me from prison. As I can do nothing to reward him for his great kindness, I want you to take him for your husband.' 'Mother, why have you brought this ugly man here? No, I cannot marry him'; the second daughter refused just as her sister had, and made fun of the man. Finally the youngest daughter said, 'Mother, if to have me marry this man is the only way by which you can repay him for his kindness, I'll gladly marry him.' A contract was signed between them, but before they were married the bear-like man asked permission to be absent one more year to finish his duty; she consented, and gave him half her ring as a memento.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 22 'The Reward of Kindness'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 許多年後，他來到一個城鎮，看見一個老婦人被傳喚到法庭上，被控欠了一筆她無力償還的錢；伊多替她付了罰金，使她免於牢獄之災，她幾乎無法表達自己的感激之情，而由於其他大多數人都害怕伊多，這婦人便決定帶他回自己家。她有三個女兒，她喚來長女說：「這個人把我從牢裡救了出來。我無以為報他的大恩，我要你嫁給他為妻。」「母親，您為什麼把這個醜陋的男人帶到這裡來？不，我不能嫁給他。」次女也像她姐姐一樣拒絕了，還嘲笑這個男人。最後小女兒說：「母親，如果讓我嫁給這個人是您報答他恩情的唯一辦法，我願意嫁給他。」他們之間簽了婚約，但在他們成婚之前，那個像熊一樣的男人請求允許再離開一年，以完成他的任務；她同意了，並把自己戒指的一半給他作為信物。

passages.text: At the end of the year, which was the last of his seven years' wandering, the bear-like man went to the Devil and told him that he had finished his duty. 'You have beaten me. Now that you have performed your seven years' wandering, and have spent the money honestly, let us exchange clothes again!' So the man received back his soldierlike suit, which made him look like a knight, and the Devil took back his bear-skin. Then the man returned to Clara's house; when his arrival was announced, the two older daughters dressed themselves in their best, thinking he was a suitor come to see them — but when the man showed the ring and asked for the hand of Clara's youngest daughter, the two nearly died with vexation, while the youngest daughter was very happy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 22 'The Reward of Kindness'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一年期滿，也就是他七年流浪的最後一年結束時，那個像熊一樣的男人去見魔鬼，告訴他自己已完成了任務。「你贏了我。既然你已完成了七年的流浪，又誠實地花掉了那些錢，我們再交換一次衣服吧！」於是那人取回了自己那身士兵裝束，使他看起來像個騎士，魔鬼則收回了他那張熊皮。然後那人回到克拉拉的家；他到來的消息傳開後，兩個年長的女兒都穿上自己最好的衣裳，以為他是上門來看她們的求婚者——但當那人拿出戒指，向克拉拉的小女兒求婚時，那兩個女兒幾乎氣得要死，而小女兒卻非常快樂。

title.en: Pedro and Satan: The Cross-Embroidered Gowns
title.zh: 佩德羅與撒旦：繡十字的長袍

region.en: Catanduanes, Philippines (narrator's home island)
region.zh: 菲律賓卡坦端內斯島（敘述者故鄉）

period: Bicol oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 23 'Pedro and Satan', eBook #8299

summary.en: A childless rich man sells himself and his wife to Satan for a son; born full-grown in five days, Pedro learns his fate and refuses to marry until he has wrested the golden document from hell. Armed with gowns hung with little crosses, he frightens hauling demons into flight by lifting his robe at each 'One, two, three!', ties the napping Satan to his own rocking-chair, and burns the bond before freeing the terrified fiend — saving his parents and his future child from a terrible fate.
summary.zh: 無子的富翁以己及妻獻給撒旦換取子嗣；五日即成的佩德羅得知契約，誓不婚娶，定要從地獄奪回金契。他身披綴滿小十字架的長袍下獄：每喊『一、二、三』便掀袍示十字，拖木的群魔抱頭鼠竄；他再把打盹的撒旦綁在搖椅上，火燒金契，方才鬆手——嚇破膽的魔王一逃了之。

sensitivity.note: Bicol folktale recorded by Fansler from a Sorreta narrator (Catanduanes); archival record. Promised-Child cycle; Fansler compares Lorraine, Wallachian, and Lithuanian variants.

passages.text: Once upon a time there lived a very rich man whose wife had never given birth to a child; the couple had made several pilgrimages and spent great sums of money for religious services in the hope that God might give them a child, even though a sickly one, to inherit their money — but all their efforts were in vain. Disappointed, the man resolved to rely upon Satan for the performance of his wish. One dark night, when he was thinking hard about the matter, he heard a voice say, 'Your wish will be quickly fulfilled if you but ask me for it.' Filled with joy, he turned towards the voice and knelt before the invisible speaker: 'I will give you my life, and even my wife's, in return for a son who will be the heir to my riches.' A figure in front of him assumed in an instant the form of Satan, and they made a golden document which provided that the first child of the heir was to be given to the Devil at the age of ten, and that the man and his wife were no longer God's subjects, but Satan's.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 23 'Pedro and Satan'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個非常有錢的人，他的妻子從未生過孩子；這對夫妻做過好幾次朝聖，又花了大筆錢財舉行了許多宗教儀式，希望上帝能賜給他們一個孩子，哪怕體弱多病也好，好繼承他們的財產——但一切努力都徒勞無功。那人失望之餘，決心倚靠撒旦來實現自己的願望。一個漆黑的夜晚，當他正苦苦思索這件事時，他聽見一個聲音說：「只要你向我求，你的願望很快就會實現。」他滿心歡喜，轉向那聲音，跪在那看不見的說話者面前：「我願把我的性命，甚至我妻子的性命，都給你，只求換一個兒子，好繼承我的財富。」他面前的一個身影剎那間化作撒旦的模樣，他們訂立了一份金色的文書，規定繼承人的第一個孩子要在十歲時交給魔鬼，而這人和他的妻子也不再是上帝的子民，而是撒旦的子民。

passages.text: The child was born at the appointed time and grew wonderfully fast, for in five days he was a full-grown youth; but the parents could not but blame themselves for their impious act. They intended to keep the secret from their son, but could not do so, for the boy was always asking about the nature of his existence. So when Pedro knew of his pitiful lot, he decided not to marry until he had succeeded in wresting the golden document from the hands of Satan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 23 'Pedro and Satan'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 孩子到了預定的時辰出生，長得異常迅速，因為才五天他就長成了一個成年青年；但父母不禁為自己不虔敬的行為自責。他們本打算對兒子隱瞞這個秘密，卻無法做到，因為這男孩總是追問自己存在的由來。於是當佩德羅得知自己可憐的命運後，他決定在成功從撒旦手中奪回那紙金色文書之前絕不成婚。

passages.text: Pedro knew that devils do not like crosses, and cannot even stay where they have to look at them; so one day he asked his mother to make for him two gowns, one having little crosses hanging from it. When these had been finished, Pedro asked his father to give him over to Satan, so that he might work with the demons in hell; no sooner had he expressed his desire than the Devil appeared and took the young man off to his kingdom, where Pedro was assigned the task of directing the demons in hauling the logs that were to be used for fuel. Pedro ordered the demons to tie a strong piece of rope to one end of a log and pull it while he stood on the other end; every time he counted 'One, two, three!' he would hold up his outer gown, and the demons, seeing the crosses, would run away in confusion.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 23 'Pedro and Satan'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 佩德羅知道魔鬼不喜歡十字架，甚至無法待在必須看著十字架的地方；於是有天他請母親為他做兩件外袍，其中一件上頭垂掛著小十字架。這些做好之後，佩德羅請父親把他交給撒旦，好讓他能在地獄裡與群魔一同勞作；他剛表達這個願望，魔鬼便現身，把這年輕人帶往自己的國度，佩德羅在那裡被分派指揮群魔拖運用作燃料的原木。佩德羅命群魔把一條結實的繩索綁在原木的一端拉動，自己則站在另一端；每當他數「一、二、三！」時，他便掀起外袍，群魔一見十字架便慌亂逃散。

passages.text: As the devils could not endure Pedro's conduct they ran to their master Satan, asking him to send the young man away, for he could not do any work — yet the demons could not say anything about Pedro's trick, for they did not dare even speak the word 'cross.' Satan then summoned Pedro to his office and had him work there. The young man had put a strong piece of rope under his gown: one day, when Satan was taking his siesta in a rocking-chair, Pedro tied him fast to the chair, removed his outer gown, and woke Satan. The Devil with closed eyes struggled hard to escape, but could not get loose; so he humbly requested Pedro to go away and leave him alone — but Pedro would neither leave him nor let him go. He demanded the document, and Satan would not give it up; so Pedro kept on frightening the Devil until at last Satan said he would give up the document if Pedro would release him. Pedro put on his outer robe, and the Devil called his secretary and told him to give the golden document to the young man; Pedro threw the bond into the fire, and when he saw that it was completely melted he took off his outer robe again and turned Satan loose. The Devil ran away exceedingly terrified. Then Pedro went home, where his parents received him with great joy: thus by his cleverness he saved his parents and his future child from a terrible fate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 23 'Pedro and Satan'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 由於群魔受不了佩德羅的行徑，便跑去向他們的主人撒旦求助，請他把這年輕人打發走，因為他什麼活也幹不了——然而群魔對佩德羅的把戲卻隻字不能提，因為他們連「十字架」這個詞都不敢說。撒旦於是召佩德羅到他的辦公處，讓他在那裡幹活。這年輕人已在袍下藏了一條結實的繩索：有一天，撒旦正躺在搖椅上睡午覺，佩德羅把他牢牢綁在椅子上，脫下外袍，喚醒了撒旦。魔鬼閉著眼睛拼命掙扎想逃脫，卻無法鬆綁；於是他低聲下氣地請求佩德羅離去、放他一馬——但佩德羅既不肯離開，也不肯放他走。他索要那紙文書，撒旦不肯交出；於是佩德羅不斷嚇唬魔鬼，直到最後撒旦說，只要佩德羅放開他，他便交出文書。佩德羅穿上外袍，魔鬼喚來他的秘書，吩咐他把金色文書交給這年輕人；佩德羅把契約扔進火裡，見它完全熔化後，便再次脫下外袍，放開撒旦。魔鬼驚恐萬分地逃走了。隨後佩德羅回到家中，父母滿心歡喜地迎接他：他就這樣憑著自己的機智，使父母和他未來的孩子免於可怕的命運。

title.en: Zhuanxu the High Lord Sets the Seasons and the Spirits
title.zh: 顓頊高陽氏

region.en: Diqiu, Zhuanxu's capital in the east (pin: Henan–Shandong)
region.zh: 帝丘

period: Shiji by Sima Qian, c. 94 BCE, Wu Di Ben Ji

source.work: Shiji, Wu Di Ben Ji: Zhuanxu, grandson of the Yellow Emperor, and his ordering of sky and spirits

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Zhuanxu the High Lord, the Yellow Emperor's grandson, was born by the Ruo river, quiet and deep, versed in earth's riches and heaven's laws: he appointed the officers of sky and earth, led the spirits' calendar, rode the clouds to the four quarters' shadowed sides, and tamed the lands from Yu province to the sea — his reign is the corpus's image of a world run like a well-kept temple schedule.
summary.zh: 黃帝之孫，昌意之子；靜淵以有謀，疏通而知事；養材以任地，載時以象天，依鬼神以制義，治氣以教化，絜誠以祭祀——乘龍而至四海。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shiji original. The same emperor severs heaven-earth communication in the Guoyu (chinese-guoyu-chongli) — reign and cosmology linked.

passages.text: The High Lord Zhuanxu, grandson of the Yellow Emperor, was quiet and deep, versed in earth's riches and heaven's measures: he raised the officers of sky and earth, led the calendar of the spirits, and taught the people by the winds of the seasons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shiji, Wu Di Ben Ji, Zhuanxu section (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 高陽氏顓頊，是黃帝之孫，沉靜而深沉，通曉大地之富與上天之度：他設置了司天與司地之官，統領神靈的曆法，並以四時之風教化百姓。

passages.text: He rode the clouds to the four quarters' shadowed sides, going by the sun's south to the sea-horizons; beasts, insects and plants alike were ordered under his hand, and the lands from Yu province to the far sea held to his regulation — the corpus's picture of a reign that runs the world like a temple schedule.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shiji, Wu Di Ben Ji; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他乘雲駕霧，巡行四方幽暗之處，循著太陽的南方行至海角天涯；飛禽走獸、昆蟲草木皆在他的掌管下井然有序，從豫州直到遠海的土地都遵從他的法度——這便是典籍所描繪的治世，如同按神廟的時程運轉整個世界。

title.en: Di Ku's Four Consorts and the Four Founders
title.zh: 帝嚳四妃

region.en: Bo, Di Ku's capital (pin: Henan)
region.zh: 亳

period: Shiji by Sima Qian, c. 94 BCE, Wu Di Ben Ji (with with the Da Dai Li Ji genealogies)

source.work: Shiji, Wu Di Ben Ji and the Da Dai genealogies: the four consorts of Di Ku — Jiang Yuan, Jian Di, Qingdu, Changyi — and the four sons who founded dynasties

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Di Ku the Deep Lord, Zhuanxu's kinsman, had four consorts and one from each: Jiang Yuan bore Houji, ancestor of the Zhou; Jian Di bore Xie, ancestor of the Shang; Qingdu bore Yao, the sage-king; Changyi bore Zhi, the first successor. Four mothers, four dynasties in one house — the Shiji's most efficient piece of genealogical engineering, making every ruling house of China's first three dynasties one family.
summary.zh: 帝嚳娶四妃：姜嫄生后稷（周祖），簡狄生契（商祖），慶都生堯，常儀生摯——四母四系，三代同宗。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shiji original.

passages.text: Di Ku the Deep Lord brought the sun and moon into their courses, and his house held the future in four marriages: Jiang Yuan of the great marsh, Jian Di of the dark bird's egg, Qingdu of the burning star, Changyi of the music-court.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shiji, Wu Di Ben Ji, with the Da Dai genealogies (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 帝嚳深君使日月各循其道，他的家室透過四樁婚姻承載了未來：大澤的姜嫄、玄鳥之卵的簡狄、燃燒之星的慶都、樂庭的常儀。

passages.text: Jiang Yuan's son was Houji, the Lord of Millet and ancestor of the Zhou; Jian Di's was Xie, ancestor of the Shang; Qingdu's was Yao, the sage-king of the flood age; Changyi's was Zhi, the eldest, who first wore the crown. Four founders under one father: the corpus's neat answer to the question of who may rule — everyone worth ruling, as cousins.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shiji, Wu Di Ben Ji; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 姜嫄之子為后稷，即穀神，周之始祖；簡狄之子為契，商之始祖；慶都之子為堯，洪水時代之聖王；常儀之子為摯，為長子，最先戴冠即位。一父之下四祖：此乃典籍對「誰可為君」之整齊答覆——凡值得統治者，皆為表兄弟。

title.en: Yu Cuts the Mountains, and the Nine Tripods Are Cast
title.zh: 禹劃九州鑄九鼎

region.en: The Nine Provinces from Jizhou to the Yangzi (mythic geography)
region.zh: 九州

period: Shiji by Sima Qian, c. 94 BCE, Xia Ben Ji (parallel in Zuozhuan, Xuan 3, on the tripods)

source.work: Shiji, Xia Ben Ji: Yu's thirteen years of dredging and the mountain-cutting; Zuozhuan on the nine tripods and their beast-pictures

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Yu mourned his father's failure thirteen years and never once looked back at his own door: he cut the dragon-gates in the mountains, dredged the Nine Rivers, drew the Nine Provinces' soil in tribute-colors, and — in the Zhou-era tale — cast the bronze of the nine provinces into nine tripods, each engraved with the beasts that harmed the people, so that the people might know them. The tripods became the regalia of every dynasty that could carry them.
summary.zh: 禹傷父鯀功之不成，勞身焦思，居外十三年，過家門不敢入；通九道、刊九山、滌九川——鑄九鼎，象百物，使民知神姦（左傳宣公三年：在德不在鼎）。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shiji and Zuozhuan originals. The tripods are the corpus's charter of political legitimacy.

passages.text: Yu mourned his father's death by finishing the work his father died for: he dredged the nine rivers, cut passages through the mountains that dammed the waters, and walked the land thirteen years without once passing his own gate at home — the famous shame of the labor, kept as the measure of a public man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shiji, Xia Ben Ji (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 禹哀悼其父之死，以完成其父為之而死之事業：他疏濬九河，鑿通阻水之山，行遍大地十三年，未嘗一次經過自家門口——此即著名之勞身之恥，被奉為衡量公眾人物之尺度。

passages.text: He measured the soil of each region by its color and its tribute, and divided the world into the Nine Provinces; and in the Zhou-era telling, the bronze of those provinces was cast into nine great tripods, each engraved with the beasts that harmed the people, so that a traveler might know them and not be taken.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Zuozhuan, Xuan 3, tripod passage; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他按各州土壤之色與其貢賦加以丈量，將天下劃為九州；而在周代之說中，諸州之銅被鑄為九大鼎，每鼎刻上害人之異獸，使行旅之人得以識之而不致受害。

passages.text: The tripods passed from Xia to Shang to Zhou as the regalia of heaven's own bookkeeping — and when a duke of Chu asked about their weight, the answer he got was the corpus's whole political theology: the concern of a ruler is virtue, not cauldrons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Zuozhuan answer; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 九鼎由夏傳於商，再傳於周，作為上天親自記帳之王權象徵——當楚子問其輕重時，所得之答覆正是典籍全部之政治神學：君主所當關心者為德，而非鼎。

title.en: Yu's Assembly at Kuaiji and the Giant of Fengshan
title.zh: 禹會諸侯殺防風氏

region.en: Mount Kuaiji, south of the Yangzi delta (Zhejiang)
region.zh: 會稽山

period: Guoyu (Discourses of the States), Lu Yu Xia, c. 4th c. BCE

source.work: Guoyu, Lu Yu Xia: Confucius questioned on the giant bones of Kuaiji, and the tale of Fengfengshi

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: A cart-hub of bone, too big for a house-beam, was dug up in Kuaiji and carried to the court of Lu, where Confucius was asked what it was. He answered like a catalog: when Yu summoned the lords at Kuaiji after the flood was tamed, the chief of Fengshan came late, and Yu had him killed on the spot: his bones were one joint of which this hub is a piece — and the giant of the tale, three zhang tall, is the earliest recorded execution for tardiness, and the reason the hill still bears the name of the executed chief's field.
summary.zh: 吳伐越，墮會稽，得骨節專車，使問仲尼；仲尼曰：禹致群神於會稽山，防風氏後至，禹殺而戮之，其骨節專車——汪芒氏之君，身長三丈，守封嵎之山。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Guoyu original.

passages.text: The men of Wu, breaking ground on Kuaiji, unearthed a single bone-joint that filled a whole cart, and sent it to the court of Lu for identification; Confucius, on leave at the gate, named its owner without inspecting it. When Yu had tamed the flood he summoned the lords and spirits to Kuaiji to settle the account of the land; the chief of Fengshan came late, and Yu had him executed on the assembly-ground before all the summoned — the giant's joint was that man's thighbone, and the hill's old name still marks the field of the killing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Guoyu, Lu Yu Xia, Fengfengshi entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Guoyu, Lu Yu Xia; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 吳人於會稽開地，掘出一節骨關節，竟裝滿一車，遂送至魯國朝廷以求辨識；孔子正休假於城門，未加察看便道出其主。禹治洪水既成，乃召諸侯與鬼神於會稽，以結算土地之帳；防風氏之君遲到，禹便於眾所召者之前，在集會之場將其處死——巨人之骨節即此人之股骨，而山丘之舊名至今仍標記著行刑之地。

passages.text: Confucius added the census: the executed chief had ruled the hill-men of the Wang-mang line, three zhang tall — a race, he said, whose like was shrinking age by age into the common stature: the giant's bone as the last receipt of an older, taller world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Guoyu, Lu Yu Xia, the census; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 孔子又補以戶口之說：被誅之君曾統治汪芒氏之山民，身高三丈——他說，此一族類，其形體隨世代遞減，漸成常人之身高：巨人之骨，乃更古老、更高大之世界所留之最後憑據。

title.en: Nüwa Mends the Broken Sky with Five-Colored Stones
title.zh: 煉五色石補天

region.en: The broken northwest sky and the flooded southeast (mythic geography)
region.zh: 天傾西北、水潦東南

period: Huainanzi, Lanming Xun, c. 139 BCE

source.work: Huainanzi, Lanming Xun: the ruined world after Gonggong's stroke, and Nüwa's five-colored stones, the turtle's legs, and the reed-ash

license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: When the four poles had collapsed and the Nine Provinces split, when heaven did not cover all nor earth bear all — fire blazed unquenchable, water surged without end, beasts devoured the people, and the black bird carried off the old and weak. Nüwa smelted five-colored stones to mend the sky, cut the great turtle's legs to stand for the four poles, slew the black dragon to save the lands of Ji, piled reed-ash to dam the floods — and lay down in peace under a mended sky, the corpus's great repair-myth.
summary.zh: 往古之時，四極廢，九州裂，天不兼覆，地不周載；火爁炎而不滅，水浩洋而不息……於是女媧煉五色石以補蒼天，斷鰲足以立四極，殺黑龍以濟冀州，積蘆灰以止淫水——蒼天補，四極正。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Huainanzi original. The great repair-myth; cross-refers to Gonggong's pillar-stroke (chinese-gonggong-buzhou) and to the pre-existing Werner-based 'nuwa-mending' record.

passages.text: In the age of ruins the four poles had collapsed and the Nine Provinces split: heaven did not cover all, earth did not bear all; fire raged and could not be quenched, water surged and could not be stayed; fierce beasts ate the gentle people, and the black bird carried off the old and the young.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Huainanzi, Lanming Xun, Nüwa passage (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在崩壞的時代，四極已塌，九州分裂：天不能覆蓋萬物，地不能承載萬物；烈火熊熊而無法撲滅，洪水滔滔而無法遏止；猛獸吞噬善良的百姓，黑鳥攫走老弱。

passages.text: Nüwa smelted stones of five colors and mended the sky with them; she cut off the great turtle's four legs to stand for the ruined poles; she killed the black dragon to save the land of Ji; she piled the ashes of reeds to stay the flood-waters — and the sky was whole, the poles upright, the beasts driven off, the waters calmed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Huainanzi, Lanming Xun; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 女媧冶煉五色石以補天；她斬斷大龜的四足，用來豎立崩塌的天柱；她殺死黑龍，以拯救冀州之地；她堆積蘆葦的灰燼，以遏止洪水——於是天補全了，天柱立正了，猛獸被驅逐了，洪水平息了。

passages.text: She laid the people on the ground of her own mending — and the world she left was peaceful under a blue sky; her name is the first repair in the Chinese record, and the reason the sky leans only slightly, and the reason there is a heaven worth living under at all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Huainanzi, Lanming Xun, the aftermath; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她讓百姓安臥在她親手修補的大地之上——她所留下的世界，在藍天之下安寧祥和；她的名字是中國記載中最早的修補者，也是天空僅微微傾斜的原因，更是蒼天之所以值得棲居的原因。

title.en: Zeus Behind the Ram's Fleece: Why Amun Has a Ram's Face
title.zh: 拉姆皮毛後的宙斯：阿蒙何以有羊首

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (temple of the Theban Zeus, Amun)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（底比斯宙斯/阿蒙神廟）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.42 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 42

summary.en: Heracles begged to see Zeus, and Zeus did not desire to be seen: at last, flaying a ram, he held the head before his own and threw the fleece over himself, and so showed himself — hence the image of the Theban Zeus (Amun) wears a ram's face, and once a year the Thebans flay a single ram, drape its skin over the god's image, and beat themselves in lamentation over the beast.
summary.zh: 海拉克勒斯懇求一見宙斯，而宙斯不欲被見——終乃剝一公羊，執其首於己面之前，以羊毛皮覆身而現形——故底比斯宙斯（阿蒙）之像作羊面；底比斯人歲一剝羊，以其皮披於神像，眾皆擊胸哀悼此羊。

sensitivity.note: Ancient aition via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Now all who have a temple set up to the Theban Zeus or who are of the district of Thebes, these, I say, all sacrifice goats and abstain from sheep: for not all the Egyptians equally reverence the same gods, except only Isis and Osiris (who they say is Dionysos), these they all reverence alike... Now the men of Thebes and those who after their example abstain from sheep, say that this custom was established among them for the cause which follows: — Heracles (they say) had an earnest desire to see Zeus, and Zeus did not desire to be seen of him; and at last when Heracles was urgent in entreaty Zeus contrived this device, that is to say, he flayed a ram and held in front of him the head of the ram which he had cut off, and he put on over him the fleece and then showed himself to him.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.42.
passages.zh: 如今，凡為底比斯的宙斯設立神廟的人，或屬於底比斯地區的人，我說，這些人都獻祭山羊而不食羊肉：因為並非所有埃及人都同等敬奉相同的神祇，唯有伊西斯與奧西里斯（他們說即狄俄尼索斯）除外，這兩位是所有人都同樣敬奉的……如今，底比斯人以及效法他們而不食羊肉的人說，這一習俗在他們中間的建立，原因如下：——據說赫拉克勒斯熱切渴望見到宙斯，而宙斯卻不願被他看見；最後，當赫拉克勒斯懇求不已時，宙斯想出了這樣一個計策，也就是說，他剝下一隻公羊的皮，把他砍下的羊頭舉在自己面前，又將羊毛披在身上，然後向他顯現。

passages.text: Hence the Egyptians make the image of Zeus into the face of a ram; and the Ammonians do so also after their example, being settlers both from the Egyptians and from the Ethiopians, and using a language which is a medley of both tongues: and in my opinion it is from this god that the Ammonians took the name which they have, for the Egyptians call Zeus Amun. The Thebans then do not sacrifice rams but hold them sacred for this reason; on one day however in the year, on the feast of Zeus, they cut up in the same manner and flay one single ram and cover with its skin the image of Zeus, and then they bring up to it another image of Heracles. This done, all who are in the temple beat themselves in lamentation for the ram, and then they bury it in a sacred tomb.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.42.
passages.zh: 因此，埃及人把宙斯的形象造成公羊的面貌；阿蒙人也效法他們這樣做，因為他們既是埃及人的移民，也是埃塞俄比亞人的移民，所說的語言是兩種語言的混合：而在我看來，阿蒙人正是從這位神那裡得到了他們現在的名稱，因為埃及人稱宙斯為阿蒙。因此，底比斯人不獻祭公羊，而是因這個緣故把公羊視為神聖；然而在一年中的某一天，即宙斯的節日，他們以同樣的方式宰殺並剝下一隻公羊的皮，用它的皮覆蓋宙斯的形象，然後再向它獻上赫拉克勒斯的另一尊形象。此事做完之後，所有在神廟中的人都為公羊捶胸哀悼，然後把它埋葬在一座神聖的墳墓中。

title.en: The Greek Lie of Busiris: Heracles Was Not Sacrificed in Egypt
title.zh: 布西里斯謊言辨：海拉克勒斯未嘗於埃及被祭

region.en: Egypt as imagined by Greek story (the sacrifice that never happened)
region.zh: 希臘故事想象中的埃及（未嘗發生之祭）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.45 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 45

summary.en: Against the Greek tale that the Egyptians crowned Heracles and led him out to sacrifice him to Zeus, Herodotus answers with law: the Egyptians, to whom it is not lawful to sacrifice even most beasts — swine, clean oxen and geese excepted — could never sacrifice human beings; 'Having said so much of these matters, we pray that we may have grace from both the gods and the heroes for our speech.'
summary.zh: 希臘人言埃及人曾加冠於海拉克勒斯、牽之就祭壇欲獻祭於宙斯——希羅多德以律法駁之：彼邦連多數畜類尚不可祭（豬與潔淨牛犢、鵝除外），豈能祭人？——『言及於此，惟願神與英雄宥我此言。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient ethnographic polemic via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Moreover, besides many other stories which the Hellenes tell without due consideration, this tale is especially foolish which they tell about Heracles, namely that when he came to Egypt, the Egyptians put on him wreaths and led him forth in procession to sacrifice him to Zeus; and he for some time kept quiet, but when they were beginning the sacrifice of him at the altar, he betook himself to prowess and slew them all. I for my part am of opinion that the Hellenes when they tell this tale are altogether without knowledge of the nature and customs of the Egyptians.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.45.
