passages.zh: 此外，除了希臘人不加審慎地講述的許多其他故事之外，他們關於赫拉克勒斯所講的這個故事尤其愚蠢，即當他來到埃及時，埃及人給他戴上花冠，列隊將他引出，要把他獻祭給宙斯；他起初沉默了一陣，但當他們在祭壇上開始獻祭他時，他奮起勇力，把他們全都殺了。就我而言，我認為希臘人在講述這個故事時，完全不了解埃及人的天性與習俗。

passages.text: For how should they for whom it is not lawful to sacrifice even beasts, except swine and the males of oxen and calves (such of them as are clean) and geese, how should these sacrifice human beings? Besides this, how is it in nature possible that Heracles, being one person only and moreover a man (as they assert), should slay many myriads? Having said so much of these matters, we pray that we may have grace from both the gods and the heroes for our speech.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.45.
passages.zh: 因為對於那些連牲畜都不許獻祭的人——除了豬、公牛與小牛的雄性（凡潔淨的）以及鵝之外——他們怎麼可能獻祭活人呢？除此之外，赫拉克勒斯既然只是單獨一人，而且如他們所主張的，還是一個人，又怎麼可能在自然上誅殺成千上萬的人呢？關於這些事既已說了這麼多，我們祈求能從眾神與眾英雄那裡為我們的言論求得恩惠。

title.en: The Brick Pyramid Speaks: 'Despise Not Me in Comparison with Stone'
title.zh: 磚金字塔自銘：勿以我比石塔

region.en: Memphis, Egypt (the brick pyramid of Asychis by the lake)
region.zh: 埃及孟菲斯（湖畔阿西基斯磚塔）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.136 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 136

summary.en: In the reign of Asychis money moved so slowly that a man might borrow against the mummified body of his father, losing his own burial and his family tomb if he defaulted; and the king, to surpass all before him, built a pyramid of bricks dug from the lake mud — with an inscription in stone on it: 'Despise not me in comparison with the pyramids of stone, seeing that I excel them as much as Zeus excels the other gods.'
summary.zh: 阿西基斯之世貨幣滯澀，乃立借貸之法：可以亡父之木乃伊作抵押；欠債者自身與族墓皆不得葬——王欲凌駕前王，乃以湖泥所取之磚築塔，塔上刻石銘曰：『勿以我比石塔而輕我：我之勝彼，如宙斯之勝諸神。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient king-legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In this king's reign they told me that, as the circulation of money was very slow, a law was made for the Egyptians that a man might have that money lent to him which he needed, by offering as security the dead body of his father; and there was added moreover to this law another, namely that he who lent the money should have a claim also to the whole sepulchral chamber belonging to him who received it, and that the man who offered that security should be subject to this penalty, if he refused to pay back the debt, namely that neither the man himself should be allowed to have burial when he died, either in that family burial-place or in any other, nor should he be allowed to bury any one of his kinsmen whom he lost by death.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.136.
passages.zh: 據他們告訴我，在這位國王統治期間，由於貨幣流通極為緩慢，便為埃及人制定了一條法律：一個人可以借得他所需要的錢，方法是拿他父親的遺體作為抵押；此外，這條法律還附加了另一條，即放貸者對借款者所屬的整個墓室也應享有權利，而提供該抵押的人若拒絕償還債務，便應受此懲罰，即他本人死後不得葬於該家族墓地或任何其他墓地，也不得安葬任何一位他所失去的親屬。

passages.text: This king desiring to surpass the kings of Egypt who had arisen before him left as a memorial of himself a pyramid which he made of bricks, and on it there is an inscription carved in stone and saying thus: 'Despise not me in comparison with the pyramids of stone, seeing that I excel them as much as Zeus excels the other gods; for with a pole they struck into the lake, and whatever of the mud attached itself to the pole, this they gathered up and made bricks, and in such manner they finished me.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.136.
passages.zh: 這位國王渴望超越在他之前興起的埃及諸王，便為自己留下了一座他以磚砌成的金字塔作為紀念物，其上刻有石製銘文，如此寫道：『不要因石造金字塔而輕視我，因為我勝過它們，正如宙斯勝過其他眾神；因為他們用竿插入湖中，凡黏附於竿上的泥土，他們便收集起來製成磚，就這樣完成了我。』

title.en: The Twelve Kings and the Labyrinth: One Cup, One King
title.zh: 十二王與迷宮：一盃一王

region.en: Above the lake of Moiris, Middle Egypt (the labyrinth opposite the City of Crocodiles)
region.zh: 埃及中埃及莫伊里斯湖畔（鱷城對面之迷宮）

period: Priests' account of the 12 kings (26th Dynasty prelude), recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.147-149 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 147-149

summary.en: Twelve kings divide Egypt and swear friendship on one oracle: he who pours a libation from a bronze cup in the temple of Hephaistos shall be king of all; they leave as a common memorial the labyrinth — twelve roofed courts, three thousand chambers, and under ground the sepulchres of the kings and of the sacred crocodiles, which Herodotus was not permitted to see; and it surpassed, he swears, all the works of the Greeks together, pyramids included.
summary.zh: 十二王分治埃及，共誓不相侵，蓋因一神諭：於赫菲斯托斯神廟以銅盂奠酒者必王全埃及；彼等共築迷宮以為紀念——十二座有頂庭院、三千間房室，地下則為諸王與聖鱷之墓，希羅多德不得入觀；彼自誓：此迷宮勝希臘一切建築之總和，金字塔亦不及。

sensitivity.note: Ancient foundation-legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Being set free after the reign of the priest of Hephaistos, the Egyptians, since they could not live any time without a king, set up over them twelve kings, having divided all Egypt into twelve parts. These made intermarriages with one another and reigned, making agreement that they would not put down one another by force, nor seek to get an advantage over one another, but would live in perfect friendship: and the reason why they made these agreements... was this, namely that an oracle had been given to them at first when they began to exercise their rule, that he of them who should pour a libation from a bronze cup in the temple of Hephaistos should be king of all Egypt (for they used to assemble together in all the temples).
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.147.
passages.zh: 在赫菲斯托斯祭司的統治結束之後，埃及人獲得自由，但由於他們無法長時間沒有國王而生活，便推舉十二位國王統治他們，將整個埃及分為十二部分。這些人彼此通婚並共同統治，約定他們不以武力推翻彼此，也不圖謀勝過彼此，而要生活在完美的友誼之中；而他們立下這些約定的原因……乃是如此：當他們開始行使統治時，起初便有一道神諭賜予他們，說他們之中誰若在赫菲斯托斯神廟中從青銅杯裡奠酒，誰就應為全埃及的國王（因為他們慣於在所有的神廟中聚會）。

passages.text: It has twelve courts covered in, with gates facing one another, six upon the North side and six upon the South, joining on one to another, and the same wall surrounds them all outside; and there are in it two kinds of chambers, the one kind below the ground and the other above upon these, three thousand in number, of each kind fifteen hundred... For the passages through the chambers, and the goings this way and that way through the courts, which are admirably adorned, afforded endless matter for marvel... Over the whole of these is a roof made of stone like the walls; and the walls are covered with figures carved upon them, each court being surrounded with pillars of white stone fitted together most perfectly.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.148.
passages.zh: 它有十二座有頂的庭院，門戶彼此相對，北側六座，南側六座，彼此相連，同一道牆從外面環繞它們全部；其中有兩種房間，一種在地下，另一種在其上，各有三千間，每種一千五百間……因為穿過房間的通道，以及穿過庭院四通八達的路徑，裝飾得極為精美，提供了無盡的奇觀……在這些之上，有一道如牆一般以石製成的屋頂；牆上覆滿雕刻的圖像，每座庭院都被以最完美方式拼合的白石柱環繞。

passages.text: The upper set of chambers we ourselves saw, going through them, and we tell of them having looked upon them with our own eyes; but the chambers under ground we heard about only; for the Egyptians who had charge of them were not willing on any account to show them, saying that here were the sepulchres of the kings who had first built this labyrinth and of the sacred crocodiles. Accordingly we speak of the chambers below by what we received from hearsay, while those above we saw ourselves and found them to be works of more than human greatness. The pyramids also were greater than words can say... but the labyrinth surpasses even the pyramids.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.148.
passages.zh: 上面那一組房間我們親自走過並看見了，我們是憑自己的眼睛看過之後才講述它們的；但地下的房間我們只是聽說而已；因為負責看管它們的埃及人不論如何都不願展示，說這裡是首先建造這座迷宮的諸王以及神聖鱷魚的陵墓。因此，關於下面的房間，我們是憑聽聞所得而講述，至於上面的房間，我們則親眼看見，並發現它們是超乎人力偉大的作品。金字塔也大得非言語所能形容……但迷宮甚至勝過金字塔。

title.en: The Devil and the Guachinango
title.zh: 魔鬼與闖蕩漢

region.en: Guagua, Pampanga, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦板牙省瓜瓜（敘述者故鄉）

period: Pampangan oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 24 'The Devil and the Guachinango', eBook #8299

summary.en: A devil wins the hand of Piriang, who 'would rather have a devil for a husband'; the priest arms her mother with a Virgin image, cintas, and a sting-ray tail, and the devil is whipped into a jar sealed with holy-water cloth and handed to a guachinango to bury. Ransomed three times with money he always loses at casino, the devil wins his freedom by promising to possess the princess — and the guachinango, terrified at the third day by the cry 'Here she comes!' and the tolling bells, is married to the princess.
summary.zh: 魔鬼娶得『寧嫁魔鬼』的琵莉安；神父授其母聖母像、聖帶與魟尾鞭，將魔鬼鞭入大甕、以聖水布封口，交由闖蕩漢埋葬。闖蕩漢三次受賄埋得更淺，又三番賭輸；魔鬼終以『入公主之身』換得自由。第三日期至，鐘聲齊鳴、高呼『她來了！』——魔鬼魂飛魄散而出，闖蕩漢娶得公主。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan tale recorded by Fansler from a Laki narrator (Guagua); archival record. Fansler traces the main outlines to Spain (Caballero's 'The Demon's Mother-in-Law'), with the Cukasaptati/Tuti-nameh family behind it; the sting-ray tail is the traditional anti-aswang charm.

passages.text: There once lived in a suburb of a town a very religious old widow who had a beautiful daughter, Piriang by name. Young men from different parts of the town came to court Piriang, and the mother always preferred the rich to the poor; whenever Piriang's friends told her that the man whom she rejected would have been a good match for her, she always answered that she would rather have a devil for a husband than such a man. One day a devil heard Piriang giving this answer to one of her friends; thus encouraged, he disguised himself as a young man of noble blood and went to Piriang's house to offer her his love, and in the richness of his dress he was unexcelled by his rivals. After a few weeks the old widow told him to come prepared to be married on the following Tuesday — but on the Sunday before the wedding-day he calmly asked Piriang to take off the cross that she had about her neck, for it made her look ugly, he said; she refused, because she had worn this cross ever since she was a child.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 24 'The Devil and the Guachinango'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前，在某鎮的郊區住著一位非常虔誠的老寡婦，她有個美麗的女兒，名叫皮里昂。鎮上各處的年輕男子都來向皮里昂求愛，而母親總是偏愛富人、輕視窮人；每當皮里昂的朋友告訴她，被她拒絕的那個男子本會是她的良配時，她總是回答說，她寧願嫁給一個魔鬼，也不願嫁給那樣的男人。有一天，一個魔鬼聽見皮里昂對她的一位朋友作出這樣的回答；他因此受到鼓舞，便把自己裝扮成一位貴族血統的年輕人，到皮里昂家向她求愛，而他衣著的華麗，連他的情敵們也望塵莫及。幾週之後，老寡婦叫他準備好，在下一個星期二來成婚——但在婚禮前的星期日，他卻平靜地要求皮里昂取下她脖子上戴著的十字架，他說，因為那使她顯得難看；她拒絕了，因為她從小就一直戴著這個十字架。

passages.text: The next day the mother went to the church and told the priest that Piriang's bridegroom had ordered her to take off her cross; the priest said that that man was a devil, for no man, as a son of God, would say that a cross made the one who wore it look ugly. He gave the mother a small image of the Virgin Mary, instructing her: if when the bridegroom beheld it he turned his back on her, she was to tie him around the neck with her cintas, put him in a large jar, and bury him at least twenty-one feet under the ground. That night he came with his friend dressed like him; when the old woman held up the image of the Virgin Mary, the two men turned their backs on her. She immediately wound her cintas around the neck of her daughter's bridegroom, and Piriang came in with the dried tail of a sting-ray in her right hand and whipped him as hard as she could; then the two together forced him into a large jar, and after warning him not to come back to earth again, the old woman covered the jar with a piece of cloth wet with holy water. The other devil suddenly disappeared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 24 'The Devil and the Guachinango'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天，母親去了教堂，告訴神父說，皮里昂的新郎命令她取下她的十字架；神父說那個男人是個魔鬼，因為沒有人，作為上帝的兒子，會說十字架使佩戴它的人顯得難看。他給了母親一幅聖母瑪利亞的小聖像，吩咐她說：如果新郎一見到它就背過身去，她就要用她的腰帶纏住他的脖子，把他裝進一個大罈子裡，並把他埋在地下至少二十一英尺深的地方。那天晚上，他帶著一個打扮得和他一樣的朋友來了；當老婦人舉起聖母瑪利亞的聖像時，那兩個男人都背過身去。她立刻用腰帶纏住她女兒的新郎的脖子，而皮里昂右手拿著一根乾燥的魟魚尾走了進來，用盡全力鞭打他；然後兩人合力把他塞進一個大罈子裡，在警告他不要再回到人間之後，老婦人用一塊沾了聖水的布蓋住了罈子。另一個魔鬼突然消失了。

passages.text: The next morning a guachinango happened to pass by the house of the old woman; she called him in, showed him the jar, and told him to bury it at least twenty-one feet deep, promising him ten pesos. At a quiet place he discovered that the whispers were coming from inside the jar: 'I am a devil, my friend. The old woman forced me to go into this jar. Be kind to me, my friend, and liberate me!' 'I shall obey the old woman in order to get my pay. I will bury you even deeper than twenty-one feet.' 'If you will bury me just three feet deep, I will give you a large sum of money' — 'I will bury you just one and a half feet deep, if you can give me much money' — 'I will give you five hundred pesos. Dig the ground near the stump of that mabolo-tree. There you will find the money in a dirty black purse.' After burying the devil, the guachinango went to the village and played casino, and as soon as he lost all his money he returned: 'I will now bury you twenty-one feet deep.' Twice more the devil bought himself shallower graves — and twice more the money was lost at gambling.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 24 'The Devil and the Guachinango'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天早上，一個瓜奇南戈人恰好路過老婦人的家；她把他叫了進來，給他看那個罈子，叫他把它埋到至少二十一英尺深，並許諾給他十個比索。在一個僻靜的地方，他發現那些低語聲是從罈子裡面傳出來的：『我是個魔鬼，我的朋友。那老婦人強迫我進了這個罈子。行行好，我的朋友，放我出來吧！』『我要聽從老婦人的話，好拿到我的報酬。我要把你埋得比二十一英尺還要深。』『如果你只把我埋三英尺深，我就給你一大筆錢』——『如果你能給我很多錢，我就只把你埋一英尺半深』——『我給你五百個比索。在那棵馬波羅樹的樹樁附近挖地。你會在一個骯髒的黑色錢包裡找到那筆錢。』埋了魔鬼之後，瓜奇南戈人去了村裡玩卡西諾賭博，他一輸光了所有的錢就回來了：『我現在要把你埋二十一英尺深。』魔鬼又兩次為自己買了更淺的墳墓——而那筆錢又兩次在賭博中輸光了。

passages.text: 'Aha! I won't let you go,' said the guachinango. 'I will bury you thirty-nine feet now.' 'I have a plan in mind which will benefit you extremely,' said the devil. 'Let me ask you if you would like to marry the daughter of the king. As soon as you set me free, I will enter the mouth of the princess and go into her brains. Then I will give her a very painful headache which no physician can cure. The king will make an announcement saying that he who can cure his daughter of her disease shall marry her. When you hear this announcement, go to the palace at once, and offer your services to the king. As soon as you reach the princess, tell me that you have come, and I will leave her immediately... Do not fail to go to the palace, for I am determined to reward you for your kindness to me.' The guachinango liberated the devil and set out for the city; there he met a group of soldiers crying that he who could cure the princess should have her to wife, and a written agreement was made: failure in three days meant death, success meant marriage. But when he approached the princess and told the devil he had come, the devil refused to leave, because he wanted to get revenge: 'He further told the guachinango that he wanted him to die, for then his soul would go to hell.' More and more hopeless, on the morning of the third day the guachinango thought of a good plan: he asked the king to order all the bells of the neighboring churches to be tolled, while every one in the palace was to cry out loud, 'Here she comes!' While all this noise was going on, the guachinango approached the princess and told the devil that the old woman was coming with her cintas; when the devil heard this he was terribly frightened, and left the princess and disappeared. The next day the guachinango was married to the princess.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 24 'The Devil and the Guachinango'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 『啊哈！我不會放你走的，』瓜奇南戈人說。『我現在要把你埋三十九英尺深。』『我心裡有個計畫，會給你帶來極大的好處，』魔鬼說。『讓我問問你，你想不想娶國王的女兒。你一放我出來，我就會進入公主的嘴裡，鑽進她的腦子。然後我會讓她頭痛得非常厲害，任何醫生都治不好。國王會發布公告說，誰能治好他女兒的病，誰就能娶她。你聽到這個公告，就立刻去王宮，向國王自薦。你一到公主那裡，就告訴我你來了，我馬上就離開她……千萬別忘了去王宮，因為我決心報答你對我的好意。』瓜奇南戈人放了魔鬼，動身前往那座城市；在那裡他遇到一群士兵，他們喊著說，誰能治好公主，誰就能娶她為妻，並且立下了書面約定：三天之內失敗就要處死，成功就能成婚。但當他走近公主，告訴魔鬼他來了時，魔鬼卻拒絕離開，因為他想報仇：『他還告訴瓜奇南戈人說，他想讓他死，因為那樣他的靈魂就會下地獄。』越來越絕望的瓜奇南戈人，在第三天的早晨想到了一個好辦法：他請求國王下令敲響鄰近所有教堂的鐘，同時王宮裡的每個人都要大喊：『她來了！』當這一切喧鬧進行的時候，瓜奇南戈人走近公主，告訴魔鬼說老婦人正帶著她的腰帶來了；魔鬼一聽這話，嚇得要命，便離開公主消失了。第二天，瓜奇南戈人就和公主成了婚。

title.en: Mabait and the Duende
title.zh: 馬巴伊特與都恩德

region.en: Manila and Cebu, Philippines (narrator's home cities)
region.zh: 菲律賓馬尼拉與宿霧（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog fairy-tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), notes to Tale 24, 'Mabait and the Duende', eBook #8299

summary.en: The duende — one of the angels dropped to earth when Lucifer fell, becoming tigbalang in the forests, mermaids in the seas, and duendes in the cities — befriends the honest slave Mabait and pays him daily isabels. The envious Masama betrays him, traps the spirit under a saint's dress in a jar, and is cheated of it twice; freed on his promise to possess the king's daughter, the duende tells Masama 'Give your head to the king' when he comes, and leaves the princess's abdomen only for Mabait, who is crowned.
summary.zh: 路西法墮落時被拋下大地的天使化為林中虎靈、海中人魚、城中都恩德。都恩德與誠實的奴隸馬巴伊特結交，日日贈伊莎貝爾幣。妒忌的馬薩馬告密，以聖袍鎮住甕中精靈，兩番騙錢不開甕；都恩德以『入公主之腹』換得自由——馬薩馬趨前索婚時，只聽得一句『把你的頭獻給國王吧』；唯有馬巴伊特一到，精靈念舊情而出，他加冕為王。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog fairy-tale collected and written down by Manuel Reyes (a native of Manila, tale from Cebu), printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 24; archival record. Duende/duwende is the Philippine little-people spirit; Fansler considered this fairy-tale possibly older in the Islands than the imported Devil-and-Guachinango Märchen.

passages.text: Menguita, a king of Cebu, had two slaves, Mabait and Masama; Mabait was honest and industrious and did nearly all the hard work in the palace, so he was admired very much by the king, while Masama, who was addicted to gambling, envied Mabait. One night, while Mabait was asleep, a duende awakened him and said, 'I have seen how you labor here patiently and honestly. I want to be your friend.' Mabait looked at the duende carefully, and saw that it resembled a very small man with long hair and a white beard, about a foot high, with a red shirt, a pair of green trousers, a golden cap, and a pair of black shoes. 'Listen! When Lucifer was an angel, a contest in creating animals arose between him and God. He and his followers were defeated and thrown into hell. Many angels in that contest belonged neither to God's side nor to Lucifer's. They were dropped on the earth. Those that fell in the forests became tigbalangs, ikis, and mananangals; those in the seas became mermaids and mermen; and those in the cities became duendes.' From that time on Mabait and the duende were good friends, and the duende gave Mabait two or three isabels every day, so that by the end of the month he had saved much money and bought a fine hat and a pair of wooden shoes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the fairy-tale printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 24, 'Mabait and the Duende'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 宿霧的一位國王有兩個奴隸，馬拜特和馬薩馬；馬拜特誠實勤勞，幾乎包攬了王宮裡所有的苦活，因此深受國王賞識，而沉迷賭博的馬薩馬則嫉妒馬拜特。一天夜裡，馬拜特正在睡覺，一個杜恩德叫醒了他，說：『我看到了你在這裡多麼耐心而誠實地幹活。我想做你的朋友。』馬拜特仔細打量那個杜恩德，見它像一個很小的人，長髮白鬚，約一英尺高，穿著紅襯衫、綠褲子，戴著金帽子，穿著一雙黑鞋。『聽著！當路西法還是天使的時候，他和上帝之間發生了一場創造動物的競賽。他和他的追隨者被打敗，扔進了地獄。那場競賽中有許多天使既不屬於上帝一方，也不屬於路西法一方。他們被拋到了地上。落在森林裡的成了蒂格巴朗、伊基和馬納南加爾；落在海裡的成了美人魚和男人魚；落在城市裡的則成了杜恩德。』從那時起，馬拜特和那個杜恩德就成了好朋友，杜恩德每天給馬拜特兩三個伊薩貝爾，因此到了月底，他已經攢下了不少錢，買了一頂好帽子和一雙木鞋。

passages.text: Masama wondered how Mabait, who was very poor, could buy so many things, and in great envy went to the king: 'Master, Mabait, your favorite slave, has a friend. This friend is a duende, which will be injurious to us if you let it live here. It will be the means of his acquiring all of your wealth and taking your daughter for his wife.' The king, in great rage, summoned Mabait and punished him severely by beating his palms with a piece of leather, then ordered his servants to find the duende and kill it. The duende hid in a small jar, and Masama covered the mouth of the jar with a saint's dress; the duende was afraid of the dress and dared not come out. 'Open the jar, and I will give you ten isabels,' said the little man. 'Give me the money first.' After Masama received the money he went away to the cockpit without opening the jar; on his way there he lost his money. He went back to the duende: 'Friend, give me ten isabels more, and I will open the jar.' 'I know that you will cheat me. Just let me come out of the jar, and I promise that you shall have the princess here for your wife.' 'How can you make her love me?' 'I will enter the princess's abdomen. I will talk, laugh, and do everything to make her afraid. I will not leave her for anybody but you.' 'Good, good!' Masama opened the jar, and the duende flew away to the princess's tower.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the fairy-tale printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 24, 'Mabait and the Duende'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬薩馬很納悶，馬拜特那麼窮，怎麼能買這麼多東西，於是滿懷嫉妒地去見國王：『主人，您最寵愛的奴隸馬拜特有個朋友。這個朋友是個杜恩德，如果您讓它住在這裡，它會對我們有害。它會成為他奪取您全部財富、娶您女兒為妻的手段。』國王大怒，召來馬拜特，用一塊皮革狠狠地打他的手掌懲罰他，然後命令僕人們找到那個杜恩德並把它殺死。杜恩德躲進一個小罈子裡，馬薩馬用一件聖人的衣服蓋住罈口；杜恩德害怕那件衣服，不敢出來。『打開罈子，我就給你十個伊薩貝爾，』那小矮人說。『先把錢給我。』馬薩馬拿到錢後，沒有打開罈子就去鬥雞場了；在路上他把錢輸光了。他回到杜恩德那裡：『朋友，再給我十個伊薩貝爾，我就打開罈子。』『我知道你會騙我。你就讓我從罈子裡出來吧，我保證你會娶到公主為妻。』『你怎麼能讓她愛上我？』『我會進入公主的肚子裡。我會說話、大笑，想盡辦法嚇唬她。除了你，我不會為任何人離開她。』『好，好！』馬薩馬打開了罈子，杜恩德便飛往公主的塔樓去了。

passages.text: Only a few weeks after that time a proclamation of the king was read in public: 'The princess, my daughter, has something in her abdomen. It speaks and laughs. No one knows what it is, and no one can force it to come out. Whoever can cure my daughter shall be my heir and son-in-law; but he who tries and fails shall lose his head.' When Masama heard this, he said to Mabait, 'Why don't you cure the princess? You are the only one who can cure her. It is the duende, your friend, who is in her abdomen, and no one can persuade it to come out but you. Go now, for fortune is waiting for you.' Mabait was at last persuaded, and before going to the king first went to a church, where he prayed Bathala that he might be successful.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the fairy-tale printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 24, 'Mabait and the Duende'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此後不過數週，國王的詔令便當眾宣讀：「我女兒——公主——腹中有物，會說話、會發笑。無人知曉那是什麼，也無人能逼它出來。誰能治好我女兒，誰就將成為我的繼承人與女婿；但凡嘗試而失敗者，將被斬首。」馬薩馬（Masama）聞之，便對馬拜特（Mabait）說：「你何不去治好公主？唯有你能治好她。那正是你的朋友杜恩德（duende）在她腹中，除你之外無人能勸它出來。去吧，命運正等著你。」馬拜特終於被說服，動身前往國王處之前，先到教堂向巴塔拉（Bathala）祈禱，願自己能成功。

passages.text: But Masama reached the palace first, telling the king he could cure his daughter; conducted into the princess's room, he touched her abdomen and asked who was there. 'I am the duende.' 'Why are you there?' 'Because I want to be here.' 'Go away!' 'No, I won't.' 'Don't you know me?' 'Yes, I know you. You are Masama, who cheated me once. Give your head to the king' — and the executioner cut Masama's head off. Then Mabait came, and told the king that he could cure the princess; after he was given permission to try, he said to the duende, 'Will you please come out of the princess's abdomen?' 'Yes, I will, for the sake of our friendship.' Mabait was married to the princess, was crowned king, and lived happily with his friend the duende.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the fairy-tale printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 24, 'Mabait and the Duende'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而馬薩馬先到了王宮，向國王聲稱自己能治好公主；他被領進公主的房間，摸了摸她的腹部，問道：「誰在裡面？」「我是杜恩德。」「你為何在此？」「因為我想在此。」「走開！」「不，我不走。」「你不認得我嗎？」「認得，我認得你。你是馬薩馬，曾欺騙過我一次。把你的頭交給國王吧。」——劊子手便砍下了馬薩馬的頭。隨後馬拜特來了，告訴國王自己能治好公主；獲准一試之後，他對杜恩德說：「可否請你從公主腹中出來？」「好，我願意，看在你我情誼的份上。」馬拜特娶了公主，加冕為王，與他的朋友杜恩德一同過著幸福的生活。

title.en: Juan Sadut: The Snake-King's Ring
title.zh: 胡安·薩杜特：蛇王的戒指

region.en: San Fernando, La Union, Luzon, Philippines (story very popular there)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋聯合省聖費爾南多（故事甚為流行）

period: Ilocano oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 25 'Juan Sadut', eBook #8299

summary.en: His father lays the sleeping idler Juan Sadut beside a snake-hole to be stung dead — but the snake is the king of the snakes, who gives him a gold signet that advises its wearer how to obtain anything. Advised by the ring, he blinds the king's tiger with sand and red pepper, commands the cave-serpents with the sacred ring to fetch the dragon's burning stone, and answers the king's treacherous question — 'What am I thinking about now?' — in the ring's precise words, winning the princess and finally the crown.
summary.zh: 父親把酣睡的懶漢胡安放在蛇穴旁，欲借蛇吻除之——那蛇卻是蛇王，贈他一枚金印戒指，凡有所求皆能指點。依戒指之策，他以沙混紅椒迷瞎猛虎；以神聖戒指號令洞中群蛇取來龍的火石；又以戒指的原話答中國王刁鑽的『我在想什麼』——贏得公主，終承王位。

sensitivity.note: Ilocano folktale recorded by Fansler from a Zafra narrator (San Fernando, La Union); archival record. Bride-wager group with the snake-jewel; Fansler notes the tiger is not native to the Islands, suggesting Indian or Malayan tradition for the first task.

passages.text: Many years ago there lived a certain old couple who had an only son. Juan was known throughout the village as an idler, and for this reason he was called Juan Sadut; his contempt for all work was so great that he never even helped his father or mother. One day his father took him to the fields to help harvest their crops, but instead of going to work Juan betook himself to a shady spot on the edge of the field and fell asleep. His father, very much enraged, determined then and there to dispose of him: he carried the sleeping boy to another part of the field and laid him down just beside a large snake-hole, expecting that the snake, when it came out of its hole, would sting the sleeping idler, who would thus be disposed of quietly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 25 'Juan Sadut'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 許多年前，住著一對老夫婦，他們只有一個獨子。胡安（Juan）在村中素以懶惰聞名，因此被人稱作「懶漢胡安」（Juan Sadut）；他對一切勞作都極為鄙夷，甚至從不曾幫過父母。有一天，父親帶他到田裡幫忙收割莊稼，但胡安非但不去幹活，反而走到田邊一處陰涼的地方睡著了。父親勃然大怒，當下便決定要把他除掉：他把熟睡的男孩抱到田的另一處，放在一個大蛇洞旁，指望那蛇出洞時會咬死這個沉睡的懶漢，如此便可悄無聲息地將他解決。

passages.text: When Juan awoke he found a large snake coiled near him; in his fright he sprang to his feet to run away, but the snake looked up at him sympathetically and began to speak: 'Why do you fear me? Don't you know that I am the king of the snakes? I am going to give you a wonderful gift that will make you happy forever.' Having said this, it dropped a gold ring on the ground, and bade Juan pick it up and wear it on his finger; the ring was of pure gold, with initials that Juan could not understand. 'Keep that ring carefully, for it will be of great use to you. Consult it for anything you want, and it will advise you how to proceed to obtain the object of your desire.' After thanking the snake, Juan set out on his travels, never worrying about his food from day to day, for from his magic ring he could get anything he needed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 25 'Juan Sadut'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 胡安醒來時，發現一條大蛇盤踞在他身旁；他驚恐地跳起身來要逃，那蛇卻同情地抬頭望著他，開口說道：「你為何怕我？你難道不知我是蛇中之王嗎？我要賜你一件奇妙的禮物，使你永遠幸福。」說罷，它把一枚金戒指丟在地上，叫胡安撿起來戴在指上；那戒指是純金所製，上面刻著胡安看不懂的字母。「好好保管這枚戒指，它對你大有用處。凡有所求，便向它請教，它會指點你如何行事，以獲得你心中所求之物。」胡安謝過那蛇，便啟程遠行，從此不必為每日的吃食憂心，因為他從那魔戒中可得一切所需。

passages.text: In his wanderings word reached Juan's ears that the king of that country would give his beautiful daughter to anyone who could fulfil three conditions. His slovenly appearance and awkward movements only excited laughter among the nobles — 'What chance have you of winning the prize?' — but 'Let me know the conditions, and time will show,' said Juan. 'First, you must fight with my tiger, and kill it if you can; second, you must go get and bring back to me the burning stone that the dragon in the mountains has in its possession; third, you must answer correctly a question that I shall ask you.' Many a young man had risked his life for the princess's hand, but no one had yet succeeded in winning even the first contest: the king's tiger was ferocious and strong, as agile as a mouse, and the formidable dragon's breath alone was deadly poisonous, its cave guarded by poisonous serpents; every morning the dragon would come out to play with its wonderful stone, tossing it into the air and catching it in its mouth when it fell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 25 'Juan Sadut'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在遊歷途中，胡安聽聞該國國王要將美麗的女兒許配給能完成三項條件的人。他邋遢的外表與笨拙的舉止只引得貴族們發笑——「你哪有機會贏得這獎賞？」——但胡安說：「且讓我知道那些條件，時候到了自有分曉。」「第一，你須與我的老虎搏鬥，若能便殺死牠；第二，你須去取回山中巨龍所擁有的那塊燃燒之石，帶回來給我；第三，你須正確回答我將問你的一個問題。」許多青年都曾為公主的芳心冒死一試，卻無人能贏得哪怕第一項比試：國王的老虎兇猛強壯，靈活如鼠；而那可怕的巨龍單是吐息便足以致命，其洞穴由毒蛇守衛；每天早晨，巨龍都會出來把玩牠那塊奇石，將它拋向空中，待其落下時再以口接住。

passages.text: When Juan arrived home he took up his little ring: 'Advise me as to how I may overcome the king's tiger.' 'Get a handful of sand, and mix with it an equal quantity of red pepper. Take the mixture with you into the arena, and when the tiger comes near you, fling the sand into its eyes.' The next day, as the tiger advanced rapidly toward him, Juan flung the mixture of sand and pepper into its eyes; the tiger was blinded, and Juan drew his dagger and buried it deep in the animal's heart. The ring advised him for the second task: 'Go to the cave, and, in order to gain admittance, show me to the serpents. I am sacred to them, and they will fulfil whatever commands my possessor gives them.' The hissing serpents came toward him in threatening attitudes — but at the sight of the signet ring they at once became tame and showed they were glad to obey; 'Go and get the dragon's stone,' he ordered, and soon they came back with the much-coveted treasure. When the king saw that Juan had fulfilled two of the hardest conditions he became alarmed because the new bridegroom was to be a person of very low birth, and devised the most difficult question possible: 'What am I thinking about now?' Juan appeared to hesitate a moment, but he was really consulting his ring, which said, 'The king has in mind the assurance that you will not be able to answer his question.' Looking up, Juan answered in the precise words of the ring, and thus answered it correctly. Astonished at the wonderful power of Juan, the king gave his daughter to him; and when he died, the young couple inherited the crown of the kingdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 25 'Juan Sadut'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 胡安回到家中，拿起他的小戒指：「指點我如何戰勝國王的老虎。」「取一把沙，摻入等量的紅辣椒。帶著這混合物進入競技場，待老虎靠近你時，把沙撒進牠的眼睛。」次日，老虎迅猛地朝他撲來，胡安便將沙與辣椒的混合物撒進牠眼中；老虎瞎了，胡安拔出匕首，深深刺入牠的心臟。戒指又為第二項任務指點他：「到洞穴去，為了獲准進入，把我出示給那些蛇看。我對牠們而言是神聖的，凡持有我者所下的命令，牠們都會遵行。」嘶嘶作響的蛇群以威脅的姿態朝他而來——但一見那枚印章戒指，便立刻馴服，表示樂於聽命；「去取巨龍的石頭來。」他命令道，不久牠們便帶著那眾人覬覦的寶物回來了。國王見胡安已完成兩項最艱難的條件，心中驚慌，因為這位新女婿將是個出身極低微的人，於是他想出了最難的問題：「我此刻在想什麼？」胡安似乎遲疑了片刻，其實是在請教他的戒指，戒指說：「國王心中正篤定你答不出他的問題。」胡安抬起頭來，一字不差地照戒指的話回答，因而答對了。國王驚嘆於胡安的神奇本領，便將女兒許配給他；國王死後，這對年輕夫婦繼承了王國的冠冕。

title.en: The Ladder of the God: Ascending to Heaven by the Bull's Sinews
title.zh: 神之天梯：以天牛之筋登天

region.en: Sakkarah, Egypt (Pyramid Texts of Unas, Teta, Pepi I-II)
region.zh: 埃及薩卡拉（烏納斯、泰塔、佩皮金字塔文）

period: Pyramid Texts, 5th-6th Dynasties, c. 2350-2175 BCE (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I, 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. III, the Ladder of the god (Pepi II 975 ff., Unas 579, Pepi I 192 ff.)

summary.en: The machinery of ascension: the ladder's wooden sides are shaped by the adze of the god Sashsa, its rungs made of the strong sinews of Kasut, the Bull of the Sky, fastened with knotted thongs from the hide of the god Utes, son of Hesat; Horus and Set, or Horus and Ra, set it up from earth to heaven, and as the dead god climbs, Isis is in front of him, Nephthys behind, Ap-uat opens the way, Shu bears him up, and Nut gives him her hands.
summary.zh: 登天之機器：天梯木欄由神沙沙之錛削成，橫檔乃天牛卡蘇特之強筋，以神烏特斯（赫薩特之子）之皮所結皮索縛定；荷魯斯與塞特（或荷魯斯與拉）置梯於天地之間；亡神攀之時，伊西斯在前，奈芙蒂斯在後，阿普-烏阿特開路，舒承之，努特伸手相迎。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal funerary texts via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions. OCR text cleaned of obvious scanning breaks.

passages.text: From the text of Pepi II (1. 975 ff.) we learn the tradition that the wooden sides of the ladder were shaped by an adze wielded by the god Sashsa, that the rungs were made of the strong sinews of Kasut, the Bull of the Sky, and that they were fastened in their places on the sides of the ladder with knotted thongs made from the hide of the god Utes, the son of Hesat. This divine ladder was set up from earth to heaven by Horus and Ra according to one legend, and according to another by Horus and Set.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. III.
passages.zh: 從佩皮二世（Pepi II）的文本（第975行及以下）中，我們得知一項傳統：梯子的木製兩側是由神薩什薩（Sashsa）所揮動的錛子削成的，橫檔則由天之公牛卡蘇特（Kasut）的強韌筋腱製成，並以神烏特斯（Utes，赫薩特〔Hesat〕之子）之皮所製的結繩，將它們固定於梯子兩側的各自位置上。根據一則傳說，這座神聖的梯子是由荷魯斯（Horus）與拉（Ra）自地面架設至天上；根據另一則傳說，則是由荷魯斯與塞特（Set）架設。

passages.text: The text of Unas says: 'Ra setteth up the ladder before Osiris, Horus setteth up the ladder before his father Osiris in his going to his spirit. One of them [standeth] on this side, and one of them on that side. Unas is between them.' In the text of Pepi I we find: 'Homage to thee, Ladder of the god! Homage to thee, Ladder of Set! Stand up, Ladder of the god, stand up, Ladder of Set, stand up, Ladder of Horus, whereby Osiris made his way into heaven.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III, quoting the Pyramid Texts of Unas and Pepi I.
passages.zh: 烏納斯（Unas）的文本說道：「拉在歐西里斯（Osiris）面前架起梯子，荷魯斯在他父親歐西里斯前往其靈的路上，在他面前架起梯子。他們之中一個〔立〕在此側，另一個立在彼側。烏納斯在他們之間。」在佩皮一世（Pepi I）的文本中，我們見到：「向您致敬，神的梯子！向您致敬，塞特的梯子！立起來吧，神的梯子，立起來吧，塞特的梯子，立起來吧，荷魯斯的梯子，歐西里斯藉以登上天界之路。」

passages.text: Lo, Khensu, lo, Aahes, Chief of the South-Land, lo, Tetun the Great, Chief of Ta-sti (Nubia), lo, Sept under his trees. They carry the ladder for this Pepi, they set up the ladder for this Pepi, they make firm the ladder for this Pepi. With the assistance of Horus and Set, Osiris stood on the ladder, and with their help he ascended and entered heaven. 'Every spirit and every god opened his hand to Pepi when he was on the ladder.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.
passages.zh: 看哪，肯蘇（Khensu），看哪，阿阿赫斯（Aahes），南地之首，看哪，特圖恩（Tetun）大帝，塔斯提（Ta-sti，努比亞）之首，看哪，塞普特（Sept）在其樹下。他們為這位佩皮搬來梯子，他們為這位佩皮架起梯子，他們為這位佩皮穩固梯子。在荷魯斯與塞特的協助下，歐西里斯立於梯上，並在他們的幫助下登上並進入天界。「當佩皮在梯上時，每一個靈與每一位神都向他伸出手來。」

passages.text: When Osiris ascended the ladder, he 'was covered with the covering of Horus, he wore the apparel of Thoth, Isis was in front of him, Nephthys was behind him, Ap-uat opened the way for him, Shu bore him up, the Souls of An drew him up the steps of the ladder, and Nut gave him her hands.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III, quoting Pepi I l. 308.
passages.zh: 當歐西里斯登上梯子時，他「披著荷魯斯的覆蓋，穿著托特（Thoth）的衣裳，伊西斯（Isis）在他前方，奈芙蒂斯（Nephthys）在他後方，阿普烏阿特（Ap-uat）為他開路，舒（Shu）將他托起，安（An）的眾靈將他拉上梯子的階級，努特（Nut）向他伸出她的雙手。」

title.en: Osiris the Word: 'The God Cometh, the God Cometh'
title.zh: 話語之奧西里斯：『神來了，神來了』

region.en: Heaven of the Egyptian Other World (symbolic pin, Abydos region)
region.zh: 埃及冥界天堂（象徵定位，阿拜多斯一帶）

period: Pyramid Texts, 5th-6th Dynasties (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I, 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. III, Osiris in heaven

summary.en: The risen Osiris as creator-king in heaven: 'Osiris was the great word, and he gave orders to the Spirits, and he was the word of what cometh into being and what is not' — the Word through which all things in heaven came into being from non-existence; he transmits his odour to those he loves, his chosen sit on his shoulder, and at the proper moment his bodyguard cries out, 'The god Cometh, the god cometh, the god Cometh.'
summary.zh: 復起之奧西里斯為天上創制之王：『奧西里斯乃偉大之言語，彼向諸靈下令，彼乃『將有之物與未有之物』之言』——天堂萬有皆由此語自無而有；彼以己馨香授其所愛，所選者坐於其肩；其護衛依時齊呼：『神來了，神來了，神來了。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal funerary texts via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: He was 'Chief of the Powers,' he was 'master of heaven,' and he had the power to bestow 'life and well-being' upon those in heaven who went to him. He transmitted his own odour to those whom he loved, and his chosen ones sat on his shoulder. He sat upon a throne, holding sceptres emblematic of his various powers in his hands, and he was surrounded by his bodyguard, and nobles, and trusted servants, after the manner of an African king; at the proper moment these cried out, 'the god Cometh, the god cometh, the god cometh.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. III.
passages.zh: 他是「眾力之首」，他是「天界之主」，他有權力將「生命與福祉」賜予那些前往他那裡的天界之人。他將自己的氣息傳遞給他鍾愛的人，他的選民坐在他的肩上。他坐在寶座上，手中握著象徵他各種權力的權杖，並依非洲國王的樣式，被他的衛隊、貴族與親信僕從所環繞；在適當的時刻，這些人高呼：「神來了，神來了，神來了。」

passages.text: 'Heaven speaketh, and the earth trembleth, the Earth-god Keb quaketh, and the two regions of the god utter a noise,' and as a result the food whereon the gods and the blessed live is created. Osiris was the 'great word,' and he gave orders to the Spirits, and he was the 'word of what cometh into being and what is not.' In other words, Osiris the Word spake the words through which all things in heaven came into being from non-existence.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.
passages.zh: 「天說話，地顫抖，地神凱布（Keb）震動，神的兩域發出聲響」，其結果便是眾神與蒙福者所賴以維生的食物被創造出來。歐西里斯是「偉大的言語」，他向眾靈下達命令，他是「存在之物與不存在之物的言語」。換言之，言語之神歐西里斯說出了那些話語，天界萬物便藉此從不存在中生成。

title.en: Osiris-Nepra, the Grain-god: To Plough Corn and Reap Barley
title.zh: 穀神奧西里斯-奈普拉：犁麥刈大麥

region.en: The Fields of Reeds (Sekhet-Aaru), Egyptian Other World
region.zh: 埃及冥界蘆葦之田

period: Pyramid Texts (Unas 141, Pepi II 1316), 5th-6th Dynasties (Budge 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. III, the Domains of Osiris

summary.en: Osiris in the Pyramid Texts is already the Grain-god: the deceased commands the Domains of Horus, of Set, and of Osiris — the Fields of Reeds — where Osiris makes the king 'to plough corn and to reap barley'; the blessed drinks the emissions of Osiris and eats what comes forth from him, living on the moisture and meal that are the body of the Grain-god.
summary.zh: 《金字塔文》中奧西里斯已是穀神：亡者向荷魯斯之領、塞特之領、奧西里斯之領下令——即蘆葦之田——彼使王『犁麥刈大麥』；蒙福者飲奧西里斯之分泌、食其所出，以穀神之濕與粉為食。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal funerary texts via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In the text of Unas the deceased is said to give the word of command to the Domains of Horus, the Domains of Set, and the Domains of Osiris, and from another passage the Domains of Osiris appear to have been also called 'Sekhet-Aaru,' i.e., 'The Fields of Reeds.' Among these 'fields of reeds' there must have been many fair fields wherein grain of various kinds was grown, for in the text of Pepi II, 1. 1316, it is said that Osiris makes Pepi 'to plough corn and to reap barley.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. III.
passages.zh: 在《乌纳斯》的文本中，据说亡者向荷鲁斯之域、塞特之域与奥西里斯之域发出号令；而由另一段文字看来，奥西里斯之域似乎也被称为「塞赫特-阿鲁」，即「芦苇之野」。在这些「芦苇之野」之中，必定有许多肥沃的田地，其中种植着各种谷物，因为在《佩皮二世》第1316行中，据说奥西里斯使佩皮「耕麦并收割大麦」。

passages.text: From this passage we are probably right in assuming that Osiris was, even at this early period, identified with the Grain-god Nepra. This view is, moreover, supported by the statement that the deceased drinks the emissions of Osiris and eats what comes forth from him, i.e., he lived on the moisture and meal which formed the Grain-god.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.
passages.zh: 由这段文字，我们或许可以正确地推断：即便在此早期，奥西里斯也已被等同于谷物之神涅普拉。此一观点 furthermore 得到如下陈述的支持：亡者饮用奥西里斯所流出的液体，并吃下从他身上生出之物，也就是说，他靠构成谷物之神的湿气与谷粉而活。

title.en: The Eye of Horus: Snatched from Set and Given to His Father
title.zh: 荷魯斯之眼：奪自塞特而獻於父

region.en: Egypt, the contest between Horus and Set (symbolic pin, Edfu-Abydos corridor)
region.zh: 埃及荷魯斯與塞特爭戰之地（象徵定位，埃德富-阿拜多斯走廊）

period: Pyramid Texts (Pepi I 107 ff., Teta 70 ff.), 6th Dynasty (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I, 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. III, the Eye of Horus passages in full

summary.en: The theology of the eye in full: Set carried away the Eye of Horus, and while it was in his hands Horus was a dead god; Horus wrests it back, Thoth drives back the followers of Set, Keb sets his sandal on the head of the enemy, and the Eye is given to Osiris — 'thou obtainest a soul through it, thou gainest the mastery through it at the head of the Spirits' — 'Thou hast eaten the eye, thy body is fortified through it, thou livest thereby.'
summary.zh: 眼之神學全篇：塞特奪荷魯斯之眼，眼在其手則荷魯斯如死神；荷魯斯奪回，托特逐塞特之黨，蓋布以履踏敵首——眼乃獻於奧西里斯：『爾因之得魂，因之居諸靈之首而得權柄』——『爾食其眼，賴之身強，賴之得生。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal funerary texts via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Reference has been made above to the religious tradition in Egypt which asserted that the Eye of Horus had been carried away from him by Set, and that Horus only succeeded in wresting it from him after a fierce fight in which Set suffered serious injury. Now the Eye of Horus contained his soul, that is to say, his life, and during the period when his Eye was in the hands of Set he was a dead god.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. III.
passages.zh: 上文已提及埃及的一项宗教传统，该传统宣称荷鲁斯之眼曾被塞特夺走，而荷鲁斯唯有在一场激烈的争斗中、使塞特遭受重创之后，才成功将其夺回。如今荷鲁斯之眼蕴含着他的灵魂，也就是说，他的生命；而在他的眼睛落入塞特之手的期间，他是一位死去的神。

passages.text: 'Hail, thou Osiris Teta, Horus cometh, he embraceth thee. He causeth Thoth to drive back for thee the followers of Set, he bringeth them unto thee [as] prisoners. He hath turned backwards the heart of Set, [for] behold, he is stronger than he. — Keb looketh upon thy form, he setteth thee on thy throne. Keb bringeth thy two sisters to thy side, that is, Isis and Nephthys.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III, quoting the Pyramid Text of Teta (ll. 70 ff.).
passages.zh: 「致敬啊，奥西里斯·泰塔，荷鲁斯来了，他拥抱你。他使托特为你击退塞特的追随者，他将他们作为俘虏带给你。他已使塞特的心转向后退，因为看哪，他比他更强。——凯布注视你的形貌，他使你登上你的王座。凯布将你的两位姊妹带到你身旁，即伊西斯与奈芙蒂斯。」

passages.text: 'Keb hath set his sandal on the head of thine enemy [saying], Get thee back. Thy son Horus hath smitten him. He hath delivered (or, snatched away) his eye from him, he hath given it to thee, thou obtainest a soul through it, thou gainest the mastery through it at the head of the Spirits... Thy mother Nut hath stretched herself over thee in her name of Shet-pet. Horus hath seized Set, he hath set him under thee, he lifteth thee up, he is helpless under thee as Nurta. Thou art more majestic than he in thy name of Ta-tchesert.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.
passages.zh: 「凯布已将他的凉鞋踏在你敌人的头上〔说道〕：退去吧。你的儿子荷鲁斯已击打了他。他已从他那里夺下（或夺走）他的眼睛，他已将它赐给你，你借此获得一个灵魂，你借此在众灵之首获得主宰之权……你的母亲努特已以她「舍特-佩特」之名伸展于你之上。荷鲁斯已擒住塞特，他已将他置于你之下，他扶起你，他在你之下如努尔塔般无能为力。你以「塔-切塞特」之名比他更为威严。」

passages.text: 'Thou hast eaten the eye, thy body is fortified through it, thy son Horus seized it for thee, thou livest thereby.' — Thus in the above extracts we have a definite statement about the means employed by Horus to bring his father Osiris to life.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.
passages.zh: 「你已吃下那只眼睛，你的身体借此得以强固，你的儿子荷鲁斯为你夺得了它，你借此而活。」——因此，在上述摘录中，我们对于荷鲁斯用以使他的父亲奥西里斯复活的手段，有了明确的陈述。

title.en: Set the Brother Who Gives Life: The Conditional Spell
title.zh: 賜生之弟塞特：條件式咒文

region.en: Sakkarah, Egypt (Pyramid Texts of Unas and Pepi II)
region.zh: 埃及薩卡拉（烏納斯與佩皮二世金字塔文）

period: Pyramid Texts (Unas 236, 246 = Pepi II 710-711), 5th-6th Dynasties (Budge 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. III, Set as the friend and foe of Osiris

summary.en: The strangest theological knot in the Pyramid Texts: in one place Set and Thoth are called the two brothers of the dead man, with Isis and Nephthys weeping for him; in another Set is called upon to give life to Osiris — 'if he liveth, this Unas liveth; if he dieth not, this Unas dieth not; if he begetteth, this Unas begetteth' — before other texts make him the arch-enemy whose defeat by Horus is described with satisfaction.
summary.zh: 《金字塔文》中最奇的神學紐結：一處稱塞特與托特為亡者之二兄，與伊西斯、奈芙蒂斯同哭；一處則呼塞特賜奧西里斯以生——『彼活則烏納斯活；彼不死則烏納斯不死；彼生則烏納斯生』——而其他文本復以其為死敵，樂述荷魯斯之勝。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal funerary texts via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions. The ambivalence of Set is a famous crux of Egyptian theology.

passages.text: The dismemberment of the body was the work of a god called Set, who, curiously enough, appears at one time to be a friend of the dead man, and at another to be his bitter foe. Thus, in one place, Set and Thoth are called his two brothers, and they are mentioned in connection with Isis and Nephthys who weep for him.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. III.
passages.zh: 身體遭肢解，乃是名為賽特之神所為；說來奇怪，他有時似乎是死者的朋友，有時卻又是他的死敵。因此，在一處記載中，賽特與托特被稱為死者的兩位兄弟，並與為他哭泣的伊西斯和奈芙蒂斯一同被提及。

passages.text: In another, Set is called upon to give life to Osiris and to make him live, for, continues the text, 'if he liveth, this Unas liveth; if he dieth not, this Unas dieth not; if he is not destroyed, this Unas is not destroyed; if he begetteth not, this Unas begetteth not; if he begetteth, this Unas begetteth.' On the other hand, we have in the text of Teta (1. 170 ff.) definite statements that Set is the arch-enemy of Osiris, as he was of Horus, and the defeat of Set and his followers by Horus is described with great satisfaction.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.
passages.zh: 在另一處，賽特被祈求賜予歐西里斯生命，使他存活，因為經文接著說：「他若活著，這烏納斯就活著；他若不死，這烏納斯就不死；他若不被毀滅，這烏納斯就不被毀滅；他若不生育，這烏納斯就不生育；他若生育，這烏納斯就生育。」另一方面，在泰塔經文（1. 170 及以下）中，有明確的陳述說賽特是歐西里斯的頭號大敵，正如他也是荷魯斯的頭號大敵；而荷魯斯擊敗賽特及其追隨者一事，則以極大的欣慰之情加以描述。

title.en: The Embrace That Gives Life: The Souls of Osiris and Ra at Busiris
title.zh: 賦生之擁抱：奧西里斯與拉之魂相擁於布西里斯

region.en: Busiris (Tattu), Nile Delta, Egypt (where the souls of Osiris and Ra meet)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲布西里斯（塔圖，二魂相擁之地）

period: Pyramid Texts (Pepi II 568, Teta 268) and Papyrus of Nesi-Amsu; depicted in the Papyrus of Ani (Budge 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. III, the embrace of Horus and Osiris

summary.en: How life is transferred in Egyptian theology — by embrace: Horus embraces his dead father and so passes to him his own Ka; Isis gathers the flesh, binds the hands and embraces Osiris; Nephthys builds the body in her character of Seshat the architect-goddess; Khepera takes Shu and Tefnut in his arms to give them life; and when Osiris usurped the power of Ra, the souls of the two became one after each had embraced the other at Busiris.
summary.zh: 埃及神學中生命之傳遞——以擁抱：荷魯斯擁亡父，以己卡授之；伊西斯聚肉縛手而擁之；奈芙蒂斯化身為建築女神莎沙特而造其身；凱佩拉亦擁舒與泰芙努特以賜生；及奧西里斯代拉秉權，二魂於布西里斯相擁而為一。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal funerary texts via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Horus first came to Osiris, who was in the state of a dead man, and embraced him. By this embrace he transferred to him either his own Ka (double), or a portion of the power which dwelt in it; the embrace was, in fact, an act whereby something of the vital energy of the embracer was transferred to the embraced. When Isis wished to revivify Osiris she gathered together his flesh, and bound up his hands, and embraced him, and Nephthys took in her arms his flesh when she had gathered it together, and was about to build it into a body in her character of the goddess Seshat, who presided over the planning of buildings.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. III.
passages.zh: 荷魯斯首先來到處於死者狀態的歐西里斯面前，擁抱了他。藉著這一擁抱，他將自己的卡（Ka，即「雙重身」），或棲居於其中的一部分力量，轉移給了他；事實上，這擁抱乃是一種行為，藉此將擁抱者的一部分生命活力轉移給被擁抱者。當伊西斯希望使歐西里斯復活時，她將他的肉體聚攏起來，綁好他的雙手，並擁抱了他；而奈芙蒂斯則以她作為塞莎特女神——掌管建築規劃之神——的身分，將他的肉體聚攏之後抱入懷中，準備將其築成一個身體。

passages.text: Similarly, when Khepera, the primeval Sun-god, had created Shu and Tefnut, and wished to give them life, he took their forms in his arms, and they became living gods. The life of a god could be absorbed by the king's embracing the statue of the god, and in later times, when Osiris had been made to usurp the power of Ra, the souls of Osiris and Ra became one after each god had embraced the other.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III, citing the Papyrus of Nesi-Amsu and Moret's Ritual.
passages.zh: 同樣地，當原初的太陽神凱布利創造了舒與泰芙努特，並希望賜予他們生命時，他將他們的身形抱入懷中，他們便成了活著的神。國王擁抱神的雕像，便能吸收神的生命；而在後世，當歐西里斯被安排篡奪拉的力量之後，歐西里斯與拉的靈魂便在彼此擁抱之後合而為一。

title.en: The Weighing of Words: Thoth Makes True the Voice of Osiris
title.zh: 言辭之秤：托特使奧西里斯之言成真

region.en: An (Heliopolis), Egypt (the hall of the Aged God, where Set accused Osiris)
region.zh: 埃及赫利奧波利斯（長者神之廳，塞特訟奧西里斯處）

period: Pyramid Texts (Teta 271) and Book of the Dead ch. 18 (Budge 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. III, the trial of Osiris at An

summary.en: The murder was only Set's first move: he stirred the gods of heaven to bar Osiris from their company and laid formal charges against him; Thoth tried the matter in the hall of the Aged God at An — 'on the night of the battle, on the night of the shackling of the Sebau fiends, and on the day of the destruction of Neb-er-tcher' — a weighing of words in which Thoth 'made true the voice' of Osiris and declared Set the liar; henceforth maa kheru, 'true of voice,' is written after the name of every dead follower of Osiris.
summary.zh: 弒君僅為塞特之始：彼煽惑天神拒奧西里斯於神列之外，並具狀訟之；托特乃於長者神之廳審之——『於戰鬥之夜、於縛塞寶惡靈之夜、於內伯-特切爾滅亡之日』——此乃『言辭之秤』，托特『使其言成真』，而判塞特為謊者；自此凡奧西里斯門下亡者之名後皆書『言真實』（maa kheru）。

sensitivity.note: Ancient theology via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Under the VIth dynasty it was commonly believed that this trial of Osiris took place in the city of An (the On of the Bible), as is clear from the passage in the text of Teta (1. 271), in which the deceased is exhorted to go and 'sit at the head of the gods, and to do what Osiris did in the House of the Prince which is in An.' The same view is taken in the XVIIIth Chapter of the Theban Recension of the Book of the Dead wherein Thoth is thus addressed: 'Hail, Thoth, who didst make Osiris to be victorious over his enemies, make thou... to be victorious over his enemies, as thou didst make Osiris to be victorious over his enemies in the presence of the Tchatcha who are with Ra and Osiris in An, on the night of things of the night, on the night of the battle, on the night of the shackling of the Sebau fiends, and on the day of the destruction of Neb-er-tcher.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. III.
passages.zh: 在第六王朝之下，人們普遍相信對歐西里斯的這場審判發生在安城（即聖經中的翁城），這一點從泰塔經文（1. 271）中的一段話可以清楚看出；該段勸勉死者前去「坐在眾神之首，並在安城中的王子之殿裡做歐西里斯所做之事」。《死者之書》底比斯修訂本第十八章亦持同樣看法，其中如此向托特致辭：「致敬，托特，你曾使歐西里斯戰勝他的敵人，願你使……戰勝他的敵人，正如你曾在安城中、在與拉和歐西里斯同在的查查（Tchatcha）面前，在夜間之事的那一夜、戰鬥的那一夜、鎖縛塞鮑（Sebau）惡魔的那一夜，以及毀滅涅貝爾-切爾（Neb-er-tcher）的那一日，使歐西里斯戰勝他的敵人一樣。」

passages.text: To these [accusations] Osiris replied, and when Thoth had heard the evidence he summed up the case, and then declared that Osiris had spoken the truth, in fact that it was not he who was a liar, but Set. Thoth held the word of Osiris to be true, or 'made the word true,' as the Egyptian text has it. The trial in the hall at An was, in reality, a 'weighing of words,' the words being the accusations of Set and the defence of Osiris; it was no trial of strength like the fight between Horus and Set, and Ra and Apep. The matter which Thoth had to decide was, Which witness is true, Set or Osiris?
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.
passages.zh: 歐西里斯對這些〔指控〕作了答辯；托特聽取證據之後，總結了案情，隨即宣布歐西里斯所言屬實，事實上說謊的不是他，而是賽特。托特認定歐西里斯之言為真，或如埃及經文所說，「使此言成真」。安城廳中的這場審判，實際上是一場「稱量言語」，所稱量的言語便是賽特的指控與歐西里斯的辯護；這並非如荷魯斯與賽特之戰、拉與阿佩普之戰那樣的力量較量。托特所要裁決的事乃是：哪一個證人說的是真話，是賽特還是歐西里斯？

passages.text: When a god, or a man, or a woman, is said to be maa kheru we are to understand that when he or she has spoken, or 'uttered words,' the words are followed immediately by the effect desired, that is to say, he who is maa kheru possessed unlimited power, and there is nothing which he cannot do or obtain. Moreover, Osiris, having been declared true of word, or true of voice, by Thoth, went up into heaven, and reigned there as king. He also became judge of the dead, for all men knew that he had proved Set to be a liar when he was tried by the gods.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.
passages.zh: 當一位神、一個男人或一個女人被稱為「maa kheru」時，我們應理解為：當他或她說話，或「發出言語」之後，言語隨即產生所期望的效果；也就是說，被稱為 maa kheru 的人擁有無限的力量，沒有什麼是他做不到或得不到的。此外，歐西里斯經托特宣告為「言辭真實」或「聲音真實」之後，便升入天界，在那裡以君王的身分統治。他也成為亡者的審判者，因為眾人都知道他受諸神審判時，已證明塞特是個說謊者。

title.en: The Title-Deed of Horus: The Iron Tablet in the House of Books
title.zh: 荷魯斯之地契：書屋中的鐵版

region.en: The House of Books, Egyptian Other World (symbolic pin, Memphis)
region.zh: 埃及冥界書屋（象徵定位，孟菲斯）

period: Book of the Dead ch. 183, Hymn to Osiris of Hunefer (Budge 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. III, the succession of Horus

summary.en: The legal machinery of the succession myth: 'The throne of Keb hath been adjudged unto him, along with the rank which hath been established by the god Temu, and also by the title-deed (or, will), in the House of Books, which hath been cut upon an iron tablet according to the command of thy father Ptah-Tanen, when he sat upon the great throne' — Set is set over what Shu bears up, the waters stretched over the high lands, grain made to grow, and 'gods celestial and gods terrestrial transfer themselves to the service of thy son Horus.'
summary.zh: 繼承神話之法律機器：『蓋布之座已判歸於他，連同阿圖姆所立之位，以及書屋中所存之地契（遺囑）——依其父卜塔-坦能於大座之上所命，鐫於鐵版』——塞特受命於舒所舉者之上，水漫高地，五穀生長——『天上地下諸神皆轉而事爾子荷魯斯。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary hymn via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: 'Thy son Horus is triumphant in the presence of the whole company of the gods, the sovereignty of the whole world hath been given unto him, and his dominion is in the uttermost parts of the earth. The throne of Keb (the earth-god) hath been adjudged unto him, along with the rank which hath been established by the god Temu, and also by the title-deed (or, will), in the House of Books, which hath been cut upon an iron tablet according to the command of thy father Ptah-Tanen, [when he sat upon] the great throne.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. III, quoting the hymn to Osiris of Hunefer (Book of the Dead ch. 183).
passages.zh: 「你的兒子荷魯斯在諸神全體會眾面前得勝，整個世界的統治權已賜予他，他的權柄直到地極。凱布（大地之神）的寶座已判歸他，連同由特穆神所確立、並藉著藏書之家中那塊依你父親普塔-塔嫩之命刻於鐵板上的契據（或遺囑）所確立的地位，[當他坐在]那大寶座上時。」

passages.text: 'He hath set his brother over that which the god Shu beareth up [i.e., heaven], and hath made him to stretch out the waters over the high lands, and to cause to grow that which springeth up on the hills, and the grain which groweth up from the earth, and to give increase by water and by land. Gods celestial and gods terrestrial transfer themselves to the service of thy son Horus, and they follow him into the hall, where a decree is passed which declareth that he is their lord, and the gods accept the same straightway.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.
passages.zh: 「他已立他的兄弟掌管舒神所承載之物[即天]，並使他將水鋪展於高地之上，使山丘上生長之物、從地裡長出的穀物得以生長，並藉水與藉地賜下增益。天上的諸神與地上的諸神都轉而事奉你的兒子荷魯斯，跟隨他進入那廳堂，在那裡頒下詔令，宣告他是他們的主，諸神也立刻接受了這詔令。」

title.en: Isis Great with Child Like the Star Sept
title.zh: 如天狼星而懷孕之伊西斯

region.en: Saut, Egypt (where Isis and Nephthys work the knotted cords)
region.zh: 埃及紹特（伊西斯與奈芙蒂斯行結織法術之地）

period: Pyramid Texts (Teta 275 ff. = Pepi I 28 ff.), 6th Dynasty (Budge 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. III, the begetting of Horus

summary.en: The oldest text of the miraculous conception: 'Isis and Nephthys work magic on thee with knotted cords in the city of Saut... Thy sister Isis cometh unto thee rejoicing in her love for thee. Thou settest her upon thee, thy issue entereth into her, and she becometh great with child like the star Sept (the Dog-star). Horus-Sept cometh forth from thee in the form of Horus, dweller in Sept. He avengeth thee in his name of Heru-sa-netch-atef' — Horus the avenger of his father.
summary.zh: 神蹟懷孕之最古文本：『伊西斯與奈芙蒂斯於紹特城以結繩行法於爾……爾姊伊西斯欣然懷愛而來。爾置之於上，爾之後嗣入之，彼遂如天狼星塞普特而懷孕。荷魯斯-塞普特自爾而出，形如棲於塞普特之荷魯斯。彼以『復父仇者』之名為爾復仇。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal funerary texts via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In the text of Teta it is said: 'Isis and Nephthys work magic on thee with knotted cords in the city of Saut, for their lord is in thee in thy name of Neb-Saut (i.e., Lord of Saut), for their god is in thee in thy name of god (Neter). They adore thee; do not depart from them in thy name of Tua-neter (i.e., Morning Star). They present [themselves] before thee; be not wroth in thy name of Tchenteru.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. III.
passages.zh: 在特塔的文本中說：「伊西斯與奈芙蒂斯在紹特城以打了結的繩索對你施行法術，因為他們的主在你裡面，以你『涅布-紹特』（即紹特之主）之名；因為他們的神在你裡面，以你『神』（涅特爾）之名。他們敬拜你；不要以你『圖阿-涅特爾』（即晨星）之名離開他們。他們[現身]在你面前；不要以你『欽特魯』之名發怒。」

passages.text: 'Thy sister Isis cometh unto thee rejoicing in her love for thee. Thou settest her upon thee, thy issue entereth into her, and she becometh great with child like the star Sept (the Dog-star). Horus-Sept cometh forth from thee in the form of Horus, dweller in Sept. Thou makest him to have a spirit in his name of Spirit, dweller in Tchenteru. He avengeth thee in his name of Heru-sa-netch-atef.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.
passages.zh: 「你的姊妹伊西斯滿懷對你的愛，歡喜地來到你這裡。你使她伏於你身上，你的種子進入她裡面，她便如塞普特星（天狼星）一般懷了孕。荷魯斯-塞普特以荷魯斯——居於塞普特者——的形象從你而出。你使他以『神靈——居於欽特魯者』之名而有神靈。他以『赫魯-薩-涅奇-阿特夫』之名為你復仇。」

title.en: An Act of Kindness: The Red Cloth, the Stones, and the Canes
title.zh: 一樁善行：紅布、飛石與魔杖

region.en: Pagsanjan, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省帕桑漢（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 26 'An Act of Kindness', eBook #8299

summary.en: Andres ransoms a small snake with his five cents for rice; at the snake-cave the chief gives him a red cloth that supplies whatever he wants. He trades it to a hut-woman for two fighting stones, then sends the stones back to seize it again, dining at a witch's hut and accepting two canes that kill on command. When a selfish rich neighbor sends robbers to his cottage, the stones and canes leave every thief dead.
summary.zh: 安德烈斯以買米的五仙贖下一條小蛇；蛇王贈他『要什麼有什麼』的紅布。他以紅布換得兩枚會打人的飛石，又遣石索回紅布；在巫婆小屋飽餐後再得兩根能誅敵的魔杖。當自私的富鄰遣盜夜襲時，飛石與魔杖盡誅群盜。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Cordero narrator (Pagsanjan); archival record. Knapsack-Hat-and-Horn cycle with a unique pair of fighting stones, which Fansler calls 'very primitive.'

passages.text: Early one morning Andres went out to buy five cents' worth of rice. On his way he came across a man who was about to kill a small snake. 'Please don't kill the poor creature! Did it harm you?' 'No, but it may bite us or some other passer-by,' answered the man, again drawing out his bolo; but Andres restrained him: 'Leave it alone, for pity's sake! Here are five cents! Don't injure the harmless creature!' The man, very glad to get the money, went away; and the snake said to Andres, 'Kind friend, come home with me. There you will find our huge chief snake, and many others like myself... When we reach our dwelling, I will recommend you to our chief. He will be harsh to you at first, since you are a stranger; but never mind that! When he asks you what you want, ask him to give you his red cloth. This enchanted cloth can supply you with whatever you want.' So the two friends started for the horrible snake-cave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 26 'An Act of Kindness'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一天清晨，安德烈斯出去買五分錢的米。途中他遇見一個人正要殺死一條小蛇。「請別殺這可憐的小東西！牠傷害你了嗎？」「沒有，但牠可能會咬我們或別的路人，」那人回答，又抽出他的波洛刀；但安德烈斯攔住他：「看在老天份上，放過牠吧！這裡有五分錢！別傷害這無害的小東西！」那人得了錢非常高興，便走開了；那條蛇對安德烈斯說：「善良的朋友，跟我回家吧。在那裡你會見到我們那條巨大的首領蛇，還有許多像我一樣的……等我們到了住處，我會把你引薦給我們的首領。起初他會對你很嚴厲，因為你是陌生人；但別在意！當他問你想要什麼時，就求他把他的紅布給你。這塊施了法的布能供給你所想要的一切。」於是這兩個朋友便動身前往那可怕的蛇洞。

passages.text: 'Who is that stranger with you — a murderer, or a robber?' hissed the chief as soon as the snake and Andres entered. 'He is neither of the two. Had it not been for him, my life would have been lost.' 'Well, what reward do you want me to give you?' 'Only your red cloth, and nothing else,' answered Andres. The chief went into a very dark cell and got out the red cloth: 'Since you have saved the life of one of our number, I give you this cloth as a reward. You can ask of it anything you want.' It was now ten o'clock, and Andres had not yet bought rice for breakfast: 'Poor mother! she must be very hungry' — and he asked the red cloth to bring him food; soon a breakfast richer than the ordinary ones he was accustomed to was spread before him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 26 'An Act of Kindness'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「跟你一起的那個陌生人是誰——是殺人犯，還是強盜？」蛇和安德烈斯一進門，首領便低聲喝道。「他兩者都不是。若不是他，我早就沒命了。」「那麼，你要我給你什麼獎賞？」「只要你的紅布，別的都不要，」安德烈斯回答。首領走進一間非常昏暗的牢房，取出那塊紅布：「既然你救了我們一員的性命，我就把這塊布給你作為獎賞。你可以向它求任何你想要的東西。」這時已是十點鐘，安德烈斯還沒買早飯的米：「可憐的母親！她一定餓極了」——他便向紅布求取食物；不久，一頓比他平日所吃的更豐盛的早飯便擺在他面前。

passages.text: After a few hours' walk he again became hungry, and went to a hut asking the old woman there if he might eat in her house, bringing his own food; Andres invited the old woman to eat with him, and she liked the food so very much that she asked to have his wonderful red cloth: 'Give me this cloth, and I will let you have my two stones in exchange. When you want to get rid of persons who annoy you, just tell these two stones where to go, and they will inflict heavy blows on the evil-doers.' Andres agreed to the exchange — but tired and exhausted, and hungry again with his red cloth gone, he sent his two stones back to their former mistress: 'Tell her that I take back my red cloth. If she refuses to give it to you, do what you think it best to do.' The stones struck the old woman with heavy blows until she fell down senseless on the floor, then rolled themselves in the red cloth and hastened back to their master with it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 26 'An Act of Kindness'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 走了幾個鐘頭後，他又餓了，便走到一間茅屋，問裡面的老婦人可否在她家吃飯，食物他自己帶來；安德烈斯邀老婦人與他同吃，她非常喜歡那食物，便要求得到他那塊神奇的紅布：「把這塊布給我，我就把我的兩塊石頭跟你交換。當你想擺脫那些煩擾你的人時，只要告訴這兩塊石頭該去哪裡，它們就會重重地打那些惡人。」安德烈斯同意交換——但他又累又乏，紅布沒了又餓起來，便把兩塊石頭送回它們從前的主人那裡：「告訴她，我要收回我的紅布。如果她不肯給你們，你們就看著辦吧。」石頭重重地打那老婦人，直到她昏倒在地，然後裹起紅布，急忙帶著它回到主人身邊。

passages.text: Resuming his journey, hungry again, Andres easily gained admittance to another hut by the roadside where the witch, its only person, had just finished her dinner and had nothing left to give the starving boy. Andres spread his red cloth and ate, then asked for an extraordinary breakfast besides — and said to the witch, 'You need not prepare anything for your breakfast to-morrow. Here is a good meal that I have asked my red cloth to give to you, you have been so kind in letting me come to your hut.' The witch was very glad, and thanked the boy: 'Boy, I have here two magic canes which I want to dispose of. They can kill your enemies, or any bad persons whom you want to be put to death. Just give them directions, and they will obey you.' Andres now had three enchanted possessions. When he reached home late, his hungry and angry mother met him at the foot of the stairs with a loud scolding; but Andres just laughed, asked his red cloth to bring her a good dinner, and related the occurrences of the day while she ate. Andres and his mother were not rich, and their wealthy neighbors were greatly surprised to see them become rich so soon; one particularly selfish neighbor, eager to deprive them of their wealth, sent a band of robbers to the cottage one night. At midnight Andres heard his dogs barking; when he saw the robbers coming, he took out his magic stones and canes, and commanded them to get rid of the thieves — in a few minutes all the robbers lay dead. Andres and his mother remained rich.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 26 'An Act of Kindness'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 安德烈斯繼續上路，又餓了，輕易地獲准進入路邊另一間茅屋，屋裡唯一的巫婆剛吃完晚飯，沒有東西可給這飢餓的男孩。安德烈斯鋪開紅布吃了起來，接著又求了一頓特別的早飯——並對巫婆說：「你明天不必為早飯準備什麼了。這是一頓好飯，我請我的紅布給你，你讓我進你的茅屋，真是太好了。」巫婆非常高興，向男孩道謝：「孩子，我這裡有兩根魔杖，想把它們處理掉。它們能殺死你的敵人，或任何你想置於死地的壞人。只要給它們指示，它們就會服從你。」安德烈斯現在有了三件施了魔法的東西。他很晚才到家，飢餓又惱怒的母親在樓梯腳下大聲責罵他；安德烈斯只是笑笑，請紅布給她送來一頓好晚飯，並在她吃時講述當天發生的事。安德烈斯和母親並不富有，他們有錢的鄰居見他們這麼快就富起來，大為驚訝；有一個特別自私的鄰居，急於奪走他們的財富，一天夜裡派了一幫強盜到他們的小屋。午夜時分，安德烈斯聽見狗叫；他見強盜來了，便取出魔石和魔杖，命令它們除掉那些賊——幾分鐘內，所有強盜都倒地而死。安德烈斯和母親從此一直富有。

title.en: The Indolent Husband: Purse, Goat, Table, and Cane
title.zh: 懶漢丈夫：錢袋、山羊、神桌與魔杖

region.en: Tigaon, Camarines, Bicol region, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋比科爾地區蒂高安（敘述者故鄉）

period: Bicol oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 27 'The Indolent Husband', eBook #8299

summary.en: Whipped and kicked by his shrewish wife Barbara, the idle Alejo meets an old humpback who gives him a money-crying purse, then a gold-giving goat, then a self-serving table — each demonstrated to his drinking friends and each swapped for a common one while he sleeps. The fourth gift, a cane that lashes 'no princes, kings, or emperors' excepted, is used at home with the doors shut: the treacherous compadre and comadre buy back all three treasures, and Barbara learns her husband's wanderings were profitable.
summary.zh: 被悍妻芭芭拉拳腳相加的懶漢阿萊霍遇見老駝背：錢袋喊錢、山羊產金、神桌自陳佳餚——每次都在酒友面前顯靈，每次醉睡之後都被那對奸詐的乾親夫婦調包。第四件禮物是根連王侯也照打不誤的魔杖；他閉門宴客，魔杖飛舞——奸夫婦慌忙奉還三寶。芭芭拉終於明白：丈夫的遊歷其實有賺。

sensitivity.note: Bicol folktale recorded by Fansler from a Frondoso narrator (Tigaon, Camarines); archival record. Ass-Table-Stick cycle (Grimm No. 36 family); Fansler compares Caballero's 'Tio Curro el de la porra.'

passages.text: Many hundreds of years ago there lived in the isolated village of Hignaroy a poor couple who had many children to care for: Barbara, the wife, was an industrious but shrewish woman who worked all day in a factory to support her many children, while the husband, Alejo, idled away his time, either eating, or drinking, or sleeping all the time his wife was away at work. Barbara's anger grew so strong that she no longer used words to reform her husband: she would kick him as he lay lazily on his bed and would even whip him like a child. Finally the thought of leaving home came into his head, partly to get away from his wife, who was always interfering with his ease, and partly to seek his fortune.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 27 'The Indolent Husband'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 幾百年前，在偏僻的希格納羅伊村住著一對貧窮的夫妻，他們有許多孩子要照料：妻子芭芭拉勤勞卻凶悍，整天在工廠做工養活眾多孩子，而丈夫阿萊霍則虛度光陰，妻子外出做工時，他不是吃，就是喝，要不就是睡。芭芭拉的怒氣越積越盛，她不再用言語來管教丈夫：他懶洋洋地躺在床上時，她就踢他，甚至像對孩子一樣鞭打他。最後，離家的念頭進了他的腦海，一半是為了躲開那總是妨礙他安逸的妻子，一半是為了去尋自己的運氣。

passages.text: Roaming through woods, over hills, and along river-banks where no human creature could be seen, he lay down to rest in the shade of a tree, meditating on his wretched condition, when an old humpback came upon him: 'Don't be worried, my son! Here, take this purse! It has nothing in it; but, if you need money at any time, just say these words — Sopot, ua-ua sopot! — and it will give you money.' Alejo went home in lively spirits, stopping at the house of his compadre and comadre, who entertained him well; when he took out his magic purse and pronounced the words, showers of silver coins dropped on the floor, and the covetous couple gave him glass after glass of wine until he was dead-drunk — then the wife stealthily untied the purse from Alejo's waist and put in its place one of their own. Before his own children, the purse gave nothing, and Barbara stormed at him with all the bitter words that can be imagined and drove him from the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 27 'The Indolent Husband'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他漫遊穿過樹林、翻過山丘、沿著河岸行走，那裡見不到半個人影，他在樹蔭下躺下休息，思量自己悲慘的處境，這時一個駝背老人來到他面前：「別發愁，孩子！來，拿著這個錢袋！裡面什麼也沒有；但如果你什麼時候需要錢，只要說這些話——索波特，烏阿烏阿索波特！——它就會給你錢。」阿萊霍興高采烈地回家，途中在他孩子的教父教母家停留，他們好好款待了他；當他取出魔袋念出那些話時，成陣的銀幣落在地板上，那對貪心的夫妻一杯接一杯地給他斟酒，直到他爛醉如泥——然後妻子悄悄從阿萊霍腰間解下錢袋，換上他們自己的一個。在他自己的孩子面前，那錢袋什麼也給不出，芭芭拉用盡能想像的惡語痛罵他，把他趕出了家門。

passages.text: He wandered away again and found the old man, who gave him a goat: 'It will give you money if you ask for it. Whenever you want any money, just say these words: Canding, pag coroquinanding!' Again he passed by his friends' house and was entertained; when he fell asleep they exchanged his beast for one of their own, and again the magic failed before Barbara, who railed at her husband more than ever. A third gift followed — a table which, at the words 'Tende la mesa!', provides all kinds of delicious food and drink — and again the deceitful couple plied him with wine, exchanged his magic table for a common one, and Alejo went home to receive from his wife's hands 'what blows, what pinches, what whips' when not even a single grain of rice appeared on the table.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 27 'The Indolent Husband'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他又流浪出去，找到了那老人，老人給了他一隻山羊：「你向它要，它就會給你錢。每當你想要錢，只要說這些話：坎丁，帕格科基南丁！」他又路過朋友家，受到款待；當他睡著時，他們把他的牲口換成他們自己的一隻，於是那魔法在芭芭拉面前又失效了，她比以往更厲害地責罵丈夫。接著又來了第三件禮物——一張桌子，只要說「滕德，拉梅薩！」，它便供應各種美味的食物和飲料——那對騙人的夫妻又灌他喝酒，把他的魔桌換成一張普通的桌子，阿萊霍回家後，當桌上連一粒米也沒出現時，便從妻子手中領受了「多少拳打、多少掐擰、多少鞭抽」。

passages.text: 'I pity you, indeed,' said the old man. 'Take this cane as my last gift. Be very careful in using it, for I have no other object to give you. The secret of this cane is this: if somebody has done you wrong, say to the cane, Baston, pamordon! and then it will lash that person. There are no princes, kings, or emperors that it will not punish.' This time, when he reached the village, Alejo did not pass by his friends' house but went directly home, telling his wife to call in all their friends, relatives, and neighbors for a sort of banquet; when all were gathered, he shut all the doors and even the windows, and shouted to his magic cane, 'Baston, pamordon!' — and it at once began to lash all the people in the house, throwing them into great confusion. At last Alejo's two friends, the deceitful couple, exclaimed almost in one voice, 'Compadre, please stop, and we will give you back your magic purse, goat, and table.' When Alejo heard them say this he was filled with joy, and commanded the cane to cease. That very day the magic purse, goat, and table were returned to him by his compadre and comadre, and now Barbara realized that her husband's wanderings had been profitable; the husband and wife became rich, and they lived many happy years together.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 27 'The Indolent Husband'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「我實在可憐你，」老人說。「把這根手杖當作我最後的禮物收下吧。使用它時務必非常小心，因為我沒有別的東西可以給你了。這根手杖的祕密是這樣的：若有人虧待了你，就對這手杖說：『手杖，pamordon！』它便會抽打那人。沒有哪個王子、國王或皇帝是它不會懲罰的。」這一次，阿雷霍回到村裡時，並沒有經過朋友的家，而是直接回家，吩咐妻子把所有的朋友、親戚和鄰居都請來，辦一場宴會；等眾人都到齊了，他關上所有的門，甚至連窗戶也關上，然後對他的魔法手杖喊道：「手杖，pamordon！」——它立刻開始抽打屋裡所有的人，使他們陷入極大的混亂。最後，阿雷霍的兩個朋友，也就是那對狡詐的夫妻，幾乎異口同聲地喊道：「教父，請停下來吧，我們會把你的魔法錢包、山羊和桌子還給你。」阿雷霍聽見他們這麼說，滿心歡喜，便命令手杖停下。就在那一天，他的教父和教母把魔法錢包、山羊和桌子還給了他，芭芭拉這才明白丈夫的流浪是有收穫的；夫妻二人變得富有，一同幸福地生活了許多年。

title.en: Cecilio, the Servant of Emilio: The Guitar That Makes All Dance
title.zh: 塞西利奧與埃米利奧：令眾人起舞的吉他

region.en: Santa Cruz, Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省聖克魯斯（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 28 'Cecilio, the Servant of Emilio', eBook #8299

summary.en: Cheated of his wages, Cecilio is twice robbed — the first robbers kill each other over the division — before an old woman lends him a beating cane and sells him a magic guitar. Playing it innocently as his master climbs through thorned bamboo, he makes Emilio dance among the spines; bought off with the hacienda money, accused, and condemned to be shot, Cecilio plays again at the scaffold until the whole firing party dances and Emilio, begging him to stop, bestows on the boy all his wealth.
summary.zh: 被剋扣工錢的塞西利奧兩度遭劫——第一對強盜為分贓自相殘殺而死——老嫗借他神杖、賣他魔吉他。他在竹刺叢邊無意撥弦，主人埃米利奧便在刺叢中跳個不停；他以莊園款項贖身，又被誣告判死刑。刑場之上，他再度撥弦，行刑隊跳作一團——埃米利奧哀求停止，並把全部家產贈予少年。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a de Leon narrator (Santa Cruz, Laguna); archival record. Fansler traces the dance-compelling fiddle family to the Middle-English 'Frere and the Boye' via Albrecht's 1599 German form.

passages.text: Once upon a time there lived a witty orphan whose name was Cecilio; his parents had died when he was six years old, and after that time he became a servant of Emilio, a man of wealth living in a very lonely and desolate barrio. The boy was faithful and kind-hearted, but his master was cruel: Cecilio had no wages at all, and served Emilio for four years, at the end of that time being given five hundred centavos as payment for his services. He thought he had been given too much — he was so simple-minded that he did not know he had been cheated by his master, who should have given him ten times five hundred centavos.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 28 'Cecilio, the Servant of Emilio'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個機靈的孤兒，名叫塞西利奧；他的父母在他六歲時便去世了，此後他就成了埃米利奧的僕人，那人是個富翁，住在一個非常偏僻荒涼的村落裡。這男孩忠厚善良，但他的主人卻很殘酷：塞西利奧完全沒有工錢，替埃米利奧做了四年工，到頭來只得到五百仙塔沃作為他服務的報酬。他以為自己得到的太多了——他頭腦太單純，竟不知道自己被主人騙了，主人本該給他十倍於五百仙塔沃的錢。

passages.text: Cecilio put his money in a new purse and rushed out into the main road to find his companions; so very happy that before he knew it he had reached another barrio. Suddenly on his way he met two men with drawn bolos: 'Boy, your money, or your life!' Frightened, he gave up the money at once, and sat under a tree lamenting his fortune — but the two robbers were in trouble, because one of them wanted a greater share than the other; at this they began to fight, and soon both fell so severely wounded that they died before Cecilio, who had heard the noise of the struggle, could reach the place where they were disputing. Now the boy was very happy again, for he had gotten his money back — until he met another man who said roughly, 'Give me your money, or else you will die!' Cecilio gave his purse to the man and went away and wept.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 28 'Cecilio, the Servant of Emilio'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 塞西利奧把錢放進一個新錢包，衝到大路上去找他的同伴；他高興得不知不覺就到了另一個村落。忽然，他在路上遇到兩個拔出波洛刀的人：「小子，把錢交出來，不然就要你的命！」他嚇壞了，立刻交出錢，坐在一棵樹下哀嘆自己的命運——但那兩個強盜卻出了麻煩，因為其中一人想分得比另一人多；於是他們打了起來，不久兩人都受了重傷倒下，還沒等塞西利奧（他聽到了爭鬥的聲響）趕到他們爭執的地方，兩人就已經死了。這男孩又高興起來，因為他拿回了自己的錢——直到他遇到另一個人，那人粗暴地說：「把錢給我，不然你就得死！」塞西利奧把錢包交給那人，走開去哭了。

passages.text: While he was crying over his bad luck, a very old woman came near him: 'Take this cane with you, and whenever you see him, let it loose and pronounce these words — Sigue garrote, sigue garrote, strike that fellow over there! When you want the cane to stop, all you need to say is — Stop, stop, for that is enough!' Cecilio ran to overtake the man who had robbed him: 'Give me back my money, or else you now shall die, and not I!' The man laughed at him — and the cane at once began to rain blows on the stranger's head and body; when he could no longer endure the blows he promised to return the purse, and Cecilio pardoned him: 'If you had treated me as you should have treated me and others, you would not have been harmed.' On his way back toward the old woman, Cecilio met another man who wanted to rob him — and the cane rained blows again until the man asked his pardon, and as the youth was kind-hearted he forgave him. When he reached the old woman's house, Cecilio told her that the cane had been very useful to him, for it had saved both his life and his money; then he returned the stick and thanked her very much. She now offered to sell him a guitar she had, the price of which was five hundred centavos, and Cecilio at once agreed to the exchange.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 28 'Cecilio, the Servant of Emilio'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 正當他為自己的壞運氣哭泣時，一個很老的老婦人走近他：「把這根手杖帶上，每當你看見他，就放開它，念出這些話——Sigue garrote, sigue garrote，打那邊那個傢伙！當你想讓手杖停下來時，你只需說——停，停，這樣就夠了！」塞西利奧跑去追上那個搶他錢的人：「把我的錢還給我，不然現在該死的是你，不是我！」那人嘲笑他——手杖立刻開始雨點般打在那陌生人的頭上和身上；當他再也受不了這些打擊時，便答應歸還錢包，塞西利奧饒恕了他：「如果你當初照該有的方式對待我和別人，你就不會受到傷害了。」在回去找老婦人的路上，塞西利奧又遇到一個想搶他的人——手杖又雨點般打了下去，直到那人求他原諒，而這青年心地善良，便饒恕了他。到了老婦人的家，塞西利奧告訴她那手杖對他非常有用，因為它救了他的命也保住了他的錢；然後他歸還了手杖，萬分感謝她。她這時提出要把自己擁有的一把吉他賣給他，價錢是五百仙塔沃，塞西利奧立刻同意交換。

passages.text: When he came near his old home, Cecilio saw his master Emilio shooting at a very handsome bird on the top of a bamboo-tree; the bird fell down, and the man ran to pick it up. As Emilio was making his way through the thorny bamboo undergrowth, Cecilio sat down to wait for him and, having nothing else to do, began to play his guitar — and the master at once began to dance among the bamboo-trees, receiving many wounds because of the sharp spines. In reality the boy was playing his guitar unintentionally and did not know of its magic power, but Emilio thought that Cecilio had discovered the deceit that had been practised on him and was playing for revenge; it happened that Emilio had a purse of money with him to give to the laborers working in his hacienda, so he promised to give all this money to Cecilio if he would only stop playing — and the boy, who had by this time learned of the magic power of his guitar, stopped his music and received the money. The crafty Emilio at once hastened to the town and asked the magistrate to apprehend Cecilio, a young robber; arrested and sentenced to death the next morning, Cecilio asked permission to play his guitar once more when he was about to be shot, and was not refused it. As soon as he began to play, all began to dance, even his master, who was still sore from the previous day's exercise; finally Emilio could endure no more: he begged Cecilio to stop playing and promised to give him all his wealth, then told the soldiers to set the boy free, for it was all his own fault. Emilio kept his word, and bestowed on the boy all his wealth; when the old man died, Cecilio was the richest man in the town — he became a capitan, and was greatly honored by the inhabitants of his barrio.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 28 'Cecilio, the Servant of Emilio'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他走近舊日的家時，塞西利奧看見他的主人埃米利奧正在射一隻停在竹樹頂上的非常漂亮的鳥；鳥掉了下來，那人跑去撿。正當埃米利奧在荊棘叢生的竹林下穿行時，塞西利奧坐下來等他，因為無事可做，便開始彈他的吉他——主人立刻在竹林間跳起舞來，由於尖銳的竹刺而受了許多傷。其實這男孩是無意中彈著吉他，並不知道它的魔力，但埃米利奧卻以為塞西利奧發現了對他所施的欺騙，正彈琴報復；恰好埃米利奧身上帶著一袋錢，是要發給在他莊園裡做工的工人的，於是他答應只要塞西利奧停止彈奏，就把這些錢全給他——而這男孩此時已得知吉他的魔力，便停止彈奏，收下了錢。狡猾的埃米利奧立刻趕到鎮上，請治安官逮捕塞西利奧這個年輕強盜；塞西利奧被捕，並被判處次日早晨處死，他在即將被槍決時請求再彈一次吉他，得到了允許。他一开始彈奏，所有人便都跳起舞來，連他的主人也不例外，那人還因前一天的折騰而渾身痠痛；最後埃米利奧再也受不了了：他求塞西利奧停止彈奏，答應把自己所有的財富都給他，然後吩咐士兵釋放這男孩，因為這全是他自己的過錯。埃米利奧信守諾言，把全部財富都贈給了這男孩；老人死後，塞西利奧成了鎮上最富有的人——他當上了首長，深受他那個村落居民的敬重。

title.en: The King Smites the Captive: Sacrifice Before the God's Standard
title.zh: 王擊戰俘：於神旗之前獻祭

region.en: Abydos and Thebes, Egypt (the royal sacrifice reliefs)
region.zh: 埃及阿拜多斯與底比斯（王祭浮雕刻壁處）

period: 1st Dynasty ivory plaque of King Den (c. 3000 BCE) through reliefs of all periods (Budge 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. VI, 'Osiris and Human Sacrifice, and Funeral Murders'
