summary.en: The iconography of royal sacrifice: on an ivory plaque from Abydos King Den (Semti) grasps a captive's hair and lifts the mace, behind him the jackal standard of Anubis or Ap-uat — the sacrifice is made to a god by the king; Amenhetep II 'slew seven chiefs with his own club... and hung their bodies, head downwards, at the bows of his boat', and the Palermo Stele records an annual festival called 'the smashing of the Antiu.'
summary.zh: 王祭之圖像：阿拜多斯出土象牙牌上，第一王朝王丹（塞姆提）執俘之髮、舉杖欲擊，身後為阿努畢斯/阿普-烏阿特之豺旗——王於神前獻祭；阿蒙霍特普二世『親杖誅七酋……以其屍倒懸於舟首』；巴勒摩石銘且記一年一度『擊碎安提烏人之祭』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient iconography discussed in Budge 1911; no living community restrictions. Sensitive subject matter handled descriptively, as historical record.

passages.text: The cult of Osiris set a curb on the cannibalistic tendencies of the Egyptians, but it did not eradicate them, any more than it put a stop to human sacrifice and funeral murders. As far as the evidence goes it seems to show that, although the Egyptians ceased to eat each other generally, they ate their enemies on occasions, and that they certainly slew their enemies, especially those whom they regarded as belonging to inferior races, and offered them up as sacrifices to their gods.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. VI.
passages.zh: 對歐西里斯的崇拜約束了埃及人食人的傾向，但並沒有根除它，正如它也沒有制止人祭和殉葬殺人一樣。就現有的證據來看，似乎表明：儘管埃及人一般不再互相吞食，他們有時仍會吃自己的敵人，而且他們確實會殺死敵人，尤其是那些他們視為屬於劣等種族的敵人，並把他們作為祭品獻給自己的神。

passages.text: Here Ten, a king of the 1st dynasty, better known as Hesepti, or Semti, in whose reign certain Chapters of the Book of the Dead were 'found', is seen in the act of sacrificing a conquered enemy. He grasps the hair of the enemy's head with his left hand, in which he also holds a bow, and is about to smash the skull with the mace which he holds uplifted in his right hand. Immediately behind the captive is a standard surmounted by a figure of a jackal, which represents a god, either Anubis or Apuat, and thus it is clear that the sacrifice is being made to a god by the king. This scene occurs over and over again in reliefs of all periods of Egyptian history.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. VI.
passages.zh: 此處所見者為第一王朝國王特恩（Ten），其更為人熟知之名為赫塞普提（Hesepti）或塞姆提（Semti），據稱《死者之書》的若干篇章即在其治下「被發現」；圖中他正將一名被征服的敵人獻祭。他以左手抓住敵人頭上的頭髮，手中同時握著一張弓，並正要舉起右手所持的權杖擊碎其頭骨。俘虜的緊後方立有一根旗杆，杆頂飾有一尊胡狼形象，代表一位神祇，或為阿努比斯（Anubis），或為阿普阿特（Apuat）；由此可見，這場獻祭乃由國王獻予一位神祇。此一情景在埃及各時期歷史的浮雕中反覆出現。

passages.text: We read on a stele of Amen-hetep II at Amada that the king 'slew seven chiefs with his own club when they were living in the country of Thekhsi, and that he hung their bodies, head downwards, at the bows of his boat.' When he returned to Thebes he hung six of these opposite the pylon of the temple of Amen, and the seventh he sent to Napata, in Nubia, to be hung on the wall of the city to terrify rebels.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. VI.
passages.zh: 我們在阿瑪達（Amada）所立阿蒙霍特普二世（Amen-hetep II）的一方石碑上讀到：國王「當七名首領居於特赫西（Thekhsi）之地時，以親手持棍將其擊殺，並將他們的屍體頭朝下懸掛於其船首。」當他返回底比斯後，將其中六具懸掛於阿蒙神廟塔門對面，第七具則送往努比亞的納帕塔（Napata），懸於城牆之上，以威懾叛亂者。

passages.text: This only can be the meaning of the festival which is mentioned on the Palermo Stele under the name of 'smashing of the Antiu.' The Antiu were the dwellers in the Eastern Desert and Sinai, with whom the early kings of Egypt waged war continually. It seems that one of them must have won some decisive battle, which was held to be of such importance that an annual festival was established to commemorate it.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. VI.
passages.zh: 這只能是巴勒莫石碑（Palermo Stele）上以「擊碎安提烏人（Antiu）」之名所提及之節慶的含義。安提烏人乃居於東部沙漠與西奈之地者，埃及早期的諸王與之連年征戰。看來他們之中必有人贏得了一場決定性的戰役，此役被視為如此重要，以至於為紀念它而設立了一年一度的節慶。

title.en: The King Dances Before His God: The Tablet of Semti
title.zh: 王舞於神前：塞姆提木牌

region.en: Abydos, Egypt (the wooden tablet of King Semti/Hesepti)
region.zh: 埃及阿拜多斯（塞姆提/赫塞普提木牌）

period: Wooden tablet of the 1st Dynasty (c. 3000 BCE); Budge 1911, chs. II and VII

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. VII, 'Osiris and Dancing' and ch. II

summary.en: The earliest picture of Egyptian worship is a king dancing: on the tablet of Semti the god sits in his shrine on the top of a flight of steps under a canopy, and before him stands the king with paddle and flail, his back turned to the god — 'Dancing was, and still is, an act of worship in Africa, and Osiris, according to Diodorus, was a patron of dancers and musicians of all classes.'
summary.zh: 埃及崇拜之最古圖像為王之舞蹈：塞姆提木牌上，神坐於階頂棚下之龕中，王持槳與枷立於前，背向神而舞——『舞於非洲素為崇拜之儀；據狄奧多羅斯，奧西里斯乃舞者與樂師——男女皆然——之庇護者。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient iconography via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The top of a flight of steps, and above it is a canopy, supported in front by poles, similar in every respect to the canopy under which Osiris is invariably seen seated in later monuments. Before the canopy is a figure of a king wearing the double crown of the South and North, and holding in one hand a paddle, and in the other a flail. On each side of him are three signs, which represent objects that were associated with dancing. The king, I believe, is dancing, though his back is turned to the god, and this representation appears to be the prototype of all the scenes, down to the Ptolemaic Period, in which the king dances before his god.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. II.
passages.zh: 一段階梯的頂端，其上方有一頂華蓋，前方由立柱支撐，各方面皆與後世紀念碑中奧西里斯（Osiris）恆常端坐其下的華蓋相似。華蓋之前是一位國王的形象，頭戴南北雙冠，一手持槳，另一手持連枷。他的兩側各有三個符號，代表與舞蹈相關聯的物件。我認為國王正在舞蹈，儘管他背對著神祇；而此一圖像似乎正是直至托勒密時期所有國王於其神祇之前舞蹈之場景的原型。

passages.text: Dancing was, and still is, an act of worship in Africa, and Osiris, according to Diodorus, was a patron of dancers and musicians of all classes, both male and female. The tablet on which the above scene is cut appears to be one of several on which the principal events of the reign of King Semti (Hesepti) were recorded, and to contain a list of the chief events of a particular year... The first event noted of the year was the performance by the king of some ceremony which was connected with the god who sat in a shrine placed on the top of a short flight of steps. The ceremony must have been a very important one, or it would not have been noted in this manner.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. II, citing Diodorus. / Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. VII.
passages.zh: 舞蹈在非洲過去是、如今依然是崇拜的一種行為；據狄奧多羅斯（Diodorus）所言，奧西里斯乃各階層男女舞者與樂師的庇護者。刻有上述場景的這塊石板，似乎屬於記載塞姆提國王（赫塞普提）治下主要事件的數塊石板之一，且載有某一特定年份主要事件的一覽……該年所記的第一件事，是國王舉行了某種與端坐於置於一段短階梯頂端之神龕中的神祇有關的儀式。此儀式必定極為重要，否則不會以此種方式被記載下來。

title.en: Osiris in the Moon: Twenty-Eight Years and Fourteen Pieces
title.zh: 月宮之奧西里斯：廿八年與十四塊

region.en: The moon of Egypt (the Utchau, where Osiris unites himself to heaven like Ra)
region.zh: 埃及之月（烏特紹，奧西里斯如拉而合於天者）

period: Lunar theology of the late period; Plutarch De Iside 42-43; Book of Making the Spirit of Osiris (Budge 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. XII, 'Osiris as a Moon-god'

summary.en: Osiris is the power of the moon: on the new moon of Phamenoth the Egyptians celebrated 'the Entrance of Osiris into the Moon'; the liturgy hails the moon as 'bull, that groweth young in the heaven each day' and cries that when Osiris enters the Utchau 'the beings on earth flourish' — the Nile appears at his utterance; and Plutarch's learned circles explained his 28 years of reign as the moon's days and his fourteen torn members as the days of the waning moon.
summary.zh: 奧西里斯即月之力：法梅諾斯新月之節名『奧西里斯入月』；禮文呼月為『日日在天而復壯之牛』，且謂奧西里斯入烏特紹之時『地上萬物遂得繁育』——尼羅應其言而出；普魯塔克時代之學者則釋其廿八年為月之週日、十四塊殘軀為下弦月之日數。

sensitivity.note: Ancient lunar theology via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: It is certain, however, that just as at one time the star Orion was regarded as his abode in the sky, and Sothis that of Isis, so at one period Osiris was identified with the moon. This fact was well known to Plutarch, who says that on the new moon of the month of Phamenoth, which falls in the beginning of the spring, the Egyptians celebrate a festival which is expressly called by them 'the Entrance of Osiris into the Moon.' He goes on to say that by Osiris are meant the power and influence of the moon, just as by Isis they understand the generative faculty which resides in it.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. XII, citing Plutarch, De Iside 43.
passages.zh: 然而可以肯定的是，正如獵戶座星辰曾一度被視為他在天空中的居所、而索提斯（Sothis）為伊西斯（Isis）的居所，同樣地，奧西里斯在某個時期也曾被等同於月亮。此事實為普魯塔克（Plutarch）所熟知，他說在法墨諾斯月（Phamenoth）的新月之日——該月落在春季之初——埃及人慶祝一個他們明確稱之為「奧西里斯進入月亮」的節慶。他接著說，所謂奧西里斯，意指月亮的力量與影響，正如所謂伊西斯，他們理解為寓於月亮之中的生殖之力。

passages.text: 'Thou risest into the sky, Thou art united [thereto] like Ra. The sailors in [thy] boat give thee acclamations. The mouths of the gods of the horizon rejoice, Their throats follow thee. The love of thee is in hearts, awe of thee is in breasts. As soon as thou enterest the Utchau, And unitest thyself thereto, The beings on earth flourish (or, become fertile).'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XII, from the Book of Making the Spirit of Osiris.
passages.zh: 「你升入天空，你與之合一，如同拉。你船上〔的〕水手向你歡呼。地平線諸神之口歡欣，他們的喉嚨跟隨你。對你的愛在諸心中，對你的敬畏在諸胸中。你一進入烏特喬（Utchau），並與之合一，地上眾生便興旺（或，變得肥沃）。」

passages.text: The lines which follow add: 'The Nile appeareth at thy utterance, making men to live through the effluxes which come forth from thy members, making all cultivated lands to be green by thy coming, great source of things which bloom, sap of crops and herbs. Lord of millions of years, sustainer of wild animals, lord of cattle; the support of whatsoever is is in thee, what is in earth is thine, what is in the heavens is thine, what is in the waters is thine.' Thus it is quite clear that Osiris was regarded as the Power of the moon, which produced the Nile-flood and therefore all the fertility in Egypt.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XII.
passages.zh: 其後數行補充道：「你一開口，尼羅河便出現，使人因從你肢體流出的溢流而活，使一切耕地因你的到來而翠綠，你是綻放之物的偉大源泉，是穀物與草木的汁液。萬年之主，野獸的維持者，牲畜之主；萬有之支撐皆在你內，地上之物屬於你，天上之物屬於你，水中之物屬於你。」由此可見，奧西里斯顯然被視為月亮之力，此力產生尼羅河洪水，因而產生埃及的一切豐饒。

passages.text: Plutarch says that Osiris lived or reigned twenty-eight years, and thinks that the number twenty-eight manifestly alludes to the number of days in which the moon runs her course round the earth. He also refers to the ceremony which is performed at the funeral of Osiris, when a tree trunk is made into the shape of a crescent, and assumes that this symbolizes the waning moon. And he records the views of certain investigators who stated that the death of Osiris took place at full moon, and that the number of pieces into which his body was torn — fourteen — marks the number of days of the waning moon.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XII, citing Plutarch, De Iside 42.
passages.zh: 普魯塔克說奧西里斯活了或統治了二十八年，並認為二十八這個數目顯然暗指月亮繞地球運行一圈的天數。他又提及奧西里斯葬禮上所行的儀式，即把一根樹幹做成新月之形，並假定這象徵虧缺之月。他還記載某些研究者的看法，他們稱奧西里斯死於滿月之時，而其身體被撕成的塊數——十四——標誌著虧缺之月的天數。

title.en: Osiris the Bull: Apis Begotten by a Ray of Moonlight
title.zh: 牛神奧西里斯：月光之射所生之阿匹斯

region.en: Memphis, Egypt (seat of the cult of Apis; Heliopolis for Mnevis)
region.zh: 埃及孟菲斯（阿匹斯祭之中心；赫利奧波利斯奉姆內維斯）

period: Bull cult from the 2nd Dynasty (Manetho on Ka-kau) into the Ptolemaic period (Budge 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. XIII, 'Osiris as a Bull-god'

summary.en: The theology of the bull: kings are 'Mighty Bulls rising like the sun'; Apis is the black bull with the white blaze, the eagle on his back, double hairs in his tail, the beetle-mark on his tongue — 'begotten by a ray of light falling from the moon upon his dam'; at his death his soul joins Osiris to form the dual-god Asar-Hep, Graecized as Serapis; and in heaven the dead are promised a bull and seven cows of Sekhet-hetepet whose names the deceased must know (BD ch. 148).
summary.zh: 牛之神學：王皆自號『如日出於底比斯之公牛』；阿匹斯為黑牛白斑、背負鷹形、尾生雙毛、舌具蟲印——『月光之射落於其母而生』；其死則魂升而合於奧西里斯，成雙神阿薩爾-赫普，希臘化為塞拉庇斯；天堂中更有蘇赫特-赫特普特之牛與七牛，亡者須識其名（亡靈書一四八章）。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cult history via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The kings of Egypt delighted to call themselves 'Bulls,' and one of the highest compliments the Court scribe could pay the king was to liken him to a 'young bull,' or a 'mighty bull.' Thothmes III describes himself as the 'Mighty Bull, rising like the sun in Thebes,' and the composer of the Hymn of Praise of him which is put into the mouth of the god Amen-Ra, says: 'I have made the people of Syria and Cyprus to see thee as a young bull, of determined courage, with horns ready to gore, indomitable.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. XIII.
passages.zh: 埃及諸王樂於自稱「公牛」，而宮廷書吏所能獻給國王的最高讚辭之一，便是將他比作「小公牛」或「強壯的公牛」。圖特摩斯三世自稱為「強壯的公牛，如太陽般升起於底比斯」，而為他所作的、置於阿蒙-拉神口中的頌讚詩的撰者說：「我已使敘利亞和賽普勒斯之民見你如小公牛，意志堅定，雙角準備牴觸，不屈不撓。」

passages.text: Apis was a black bull, with a white blaze on his forehead; on his back was the figure of an eagle, in his tail were double hairs, and on his tongue a beetle... The Egyptians connected Apis, both living and dead, with Osiris. He was the son of Osiris, as well as of Ptah, and was the 'living image of Osiris'; he was said to have been begotten by a ray of light falling from the moon upon his dam. After the death of his body, his soul was thought to go to heaven, where it joined itself to Osiris, and formed with him the dual-god Asar-Hepi, or Osiris-Apis. Early in the Ptolemaic Period the Greeks ascribed to this dual god the attributes of Pluto or Hades, and Graecized the Egyptian names under the form 'Serapis.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XIII.
passages.zh: 阿匹斯是一頭黑公牛，額上有一道白色斑紋；背上有一隻鷹的形象，尾中有雙重毛髮，舌上有一隻甲蟲……埃及人將阿匹斯，無論生前死後，都與奧西里斯聯繫起來。他既是奧西里斯的兒子，也是普塔的兒子，並且是「奧西里斯的活像」；據說他是因一道月光從月亮落在他母親身上而受孕所生。其肉身死後，人們認為他的靈魂升天，在那裡與奧西里斯結合，並與他構成雙神阿薩爾-赫皮（Asar-Hepi），即奧西里斯-阿匹斯。托勒密時期初期，希臘人將普路托或哈得斯的屬性歸於這位雙神，並將埃及名稱希臘化為「塞拉匹斯」（Serapis）之形。

passages.text: In the Theban Recension of the Book of the Dead we find such passages as these: 'Homage to thee, Bull of Amentet,' 'Hail, Bull of Amentet,' 'Osiris, Bull of Amentet,' 'Thou art raised up, O Bull of Amentet.' As, according to one view, the Egyptians hoped to eat bull's flesh and to drink milk in the Other World, they assumed the existence in Sekhet-hetepet of a bull and seven cows, but to obtain the gifts of these creatures it was necessary for the deceased to know their names, which were supplied by the CXLVIIIth Chapter of the Book of the Dead.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XIII.
passages.zh: 在《死者之書》的底比斯校訂本中，我們見到諸如以下的段落：「向你致敬，阿門特之公牛」，「萬歲，阿門特之公牛」，「奧西里斯，阿門特之公牛」，「你被扶起，哦，阿門特之公牛」。由於按照一種看法，埃及人希望在另一個世界吃牛肉、喝牛奶，他們便假定塞赫特-赫特佩特（Sekhet-hetepet）中存在一頭公牛和七頭母牛，但要獲得這些生靈的贈禮，死者必須知道牠們的名字，而這些名字由《死者之書》第一百四十八章提供。

title.en: The Ka, the Double: The Statue in the Niche
title.zh: 卡，兩重者：壁龕中之像

region.en: Egyptian tombs (the Ka statue behind the stone partition)
region.zh: 埃及陵墓（石壁之後的卡像）

period: Doctrine attested from the Pyramid Texts onward (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II, 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (1911), ch. XIX, 'The Ka or Double'

summary.en: Egypt's soul-anatomy begins with the Ka: born with every healthy child, an abstract individuality whose abode is the body — the 'DOUBLE'; when the body dies the Ka lives on, and a statue is made for it in the tomb, sometimes behind a stone partition with an opening, so the Ka may see and hear all that goes on when visitors come; it consumes not the bread and beer but 'only the spirits, or doubles, of the bread, beer, vegetables, meat, oil.'
summary.zh: 埃及靈魂解剖自『卡』始：凡健全之嬰皆伴生一抽象個體，居於身而導其行——即『兩重者』；身死而卡不滅，陵中為之造像，或置於有孔石壁之後，使卡得以視聽祭者之來；彼所食非餅與酒之實體，乃『餅酒菜肉油之靈，即其兩重者』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient doctrinal synthesis via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: When the body was born there came into existence with it an abstract individuality or spiritual being, which was wholly independent and distinct from the physical body, but its abode was the body, whose actions it was supposed to direct, and guide, and keep watch over, and it lived in the body until the body died. No healthy child was ever born without this spiritual being, and when the Egyptians drew pictures of it they always made it resemble the body to which it belonged; in other words, they regarded it as its 'DOUBLE.' Its name in Egyptian was KA, and the hieroglyph which represents it is two human arms extended at right angles to the breast as if ready to embrace someone.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XIX.
passages.zh: 當身體誕生之時，與之同時也產生了一種抽象的人格或靈性存在，它完全獨立於肉體之外，與肉體截然有別，但它的居所乃是身體；據說它負責指揮、引導並看守身體的種種行為，它住在身體之中，直到身體死去。沒有哪個健康的孩子出生時不帶著這靈性存在；當埃及人描繪它時，總使它肖似它所屬的那具身體；換言之，他們視之為身體的「雙重身」。它在埃及語中的名稱是KA，用以表示它的象形文字是兩條與胸膛成直角伸展的人類手臂，彷彿準備擁抱某人。

passages.text: When the body died the Ka did not die with it, but continued its existence... The Egyptians prepared a figure or statue of the dead person to whom the Ka belonged, taking great pains to give it all the characteristics of the deceased, so that the Ka might recognize it as an image of its body and be pleased to enter into the figure and take up its abode there. The Egyptians placed the figure or statue so prepared in the tomb with the body, sometimes in a niche, and sometimes in a very small chamber behind a stone partition with an opening in it, so that the Ka might see and hear all that was going on in the tomb when visitors came there to pay visits in its honour.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XIX.
passages.zh: 當身體死去時，Ka並不隨之而死，而是繼續存在……埃及人為死者（即Ka所屬之人）製作一具人像或雕像，費盡心力賦予它死者的一切特徵，好讓Ka能認出這是自己身體的形象，並樂於進入這具人像、在其中安住。埃及人將如此備妥的人像或雕像與遺體一同安置於墓中，有時置於壁龕之內，有時置於石製隔牆後的一間極小的墓室中，隔牆上開有一孔，好讓Ka在訪客前來致意時，能看見並聽見墓中所發生的一切。

passages.text: Not only was it necessary to provide a figure for the Ka to dwell in, but if it was not to perish of cold, hunger, and thirst, offerings of meat, drink, clothing, etc., must be placed in the tomb by the friends and relatives of the dead, so that the Ka might eat and drink, anoint and dress itself, even as its body had done when upon earth. The Ka did not, of course, consume the actual offerings of food which were given to it, but only the spirits, or 'doubles,' of the bread, beer, vegetables, meat, oil, etc., and similarly it arrayed itself in the spirits of the suits of linen.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XIX.
passages.zh: 不僅必須為Ka預備一具可供棲身的人像，而且，若要不使它因寒冷、飢餓與口渴而消亡，死者的親友還必須在墓中放置肉、飲料、衣物等供品，好讓Ka能如它的身體在世時那般飲食、塗油與穿衣。Ka當然並不消耗實際供上的食物，而只吸取麵包、啤酒、蔬菜、肉、油等的靈或「雙重身」，同樣地，它也以亞麻衣物的靈來裝扮自己。

title.en: Four Million Six Hundred Thousand Spirit-Souls
title.zh: 四百六十萬零一千二百之靈

region.en: The Tuat, Egyptian Other World (population of the spirit-land)
region.zh: 埃及冥界圖阿特（靈界之人口）

period: Book of the Dead ch. 64, cited in Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (1911), ch. XX, 'Spirits and the Spirit-World'

summary.en: A census of the otherworld: an obscure passage in the Book of the Dead mentions 4,601,200 (or 4,301,200) spirit-souls (khu); the spirits who reap the wheat and barley in the Domain of Osiris are nine cubits tall against five-cubit corn, and in the Fifth Division the spirits who live on the helpless shadows of the dead have thighs seven cubits long — 'Though naturally of a gay and light-hearted disposition, the Egyptian must have lived in a perpetual state of fear of spirits of all kinds.'
summary.zh: 冥界之戶籍：亡靈書一 obscure 段落載有『四百六十萬零一千二百（或四百三十萬零一千二百）之靈』；於奧西里斯之領刈麥者高九肘而麥高五肘；第五區以亡者之無助之影為食者，其股長七肘——『埃及人天性樂天，然必恆居於對諸靈之恐懼之中。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary cosmology via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: An obscure passage in the Book of the Dead mentions 4,601,200, or 4,301,200, Spirit-souls (Khu), but whether these represented all the inhabitants of the spirit-world of Egypt cannot be said. In the Short Version of the Chapter '12 cubits' are mentioned, and this may be the height of the spirits. If so, spirits must have been of varying heights, for the spirits who reaped the wheat and barley in the Second Division of the Domain of Osiris were nine cubits in height, the wheat and barley being five cubits high. In the Fifth Division the spirits who lived on the helpless shadows of the dead had thighs (?) seven cubits long.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XX, citing Book of the Dead ch. 64 and ch. 149.
passages.zh: 《死者之書》中有一段晦澀的文字提到4,601,200個或4,301,200個靈魂（Khu），但這些是否代表埃及靈界的全體居民，則無從斷言。在該章的短版本中提到了「十二肘」，這或許是靈的身高。若果真如此，則靈的身高必定各不相同，因為在奧西里斯領域第二區收割小麥與大麥的靈，身高九肘，而小麥與大麥則高五肘。在第五區，以死者無助的陰影為食的靈，其大腿（？）長七肘。

passages.text: Now, we read in many funerary texts of the 'Gods of the Tuat,' so we must assume that after death entered the world, and souls began to go to the Tuat, they found there these gods, who had been created by the unknown God... As time went on these gods became more and more independent, and the unknown God appears to have allowed them to do as they pleased, and in the end they became the arbiters of the destinies of the souls of men. Though naturally of a gay and light-hearted disposition, the Egyptian must have lived in a perpetual state of fear of spirits of all kinds.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XX.
passages.zh: 如今，我們在許多葬儀文本中讀到「圖阿特之神」，因此我們必須假定：當死亡進入世界、靈魂開始前往圖阿特之後，它們在那裡遇見了這些由那位未知之神所創造的神祇……隨著時間推移，這些神祇愈來愈獨立，那位未知之神似乎任憑它們為所欲為，最終它們成了人類靈魂命運的裁決者。埃及人雖天性歡快而輕鬆，卻必定終日生活在對各種靈的恐懼之中。

title.en: Chonguita the Monkey-Wife
title.zh: 猴妻瓊桂塔

region.en: Pagsanjan, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省帕桑漢（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 29 'Chonguita', eBook #8299

summary.en: Directed by an old man to a palace guarded by monkeys — whom he must feed his bread before entering — Don Juan is married on the spot to Chonguita, the big monkey's daughter. Hauled home in shame, she outdoes her human sisters-in-law at every task set by the king hoping to destroy her: the embroidered coat, the cap, the prettiest picture. When Don Juan, furious that she insists he dance with her, hurls her against the wall, the hall darkens and Chonguita is transformed into a beautiful woman.
summary.zh: 老人指路，令唐·胡安以麵包餵過守宮猴群方可入內——他當場與大猴之女瓊桂塔成婚。羞愧還鄉，國王屢設難題欲除猴媳；繡衣、繡帽、繪畫，猴妻樣樣奪魁。慶典之上，唐·胡安被妻子逼舞，怒將她擲向牆壁——大廳驟暗復明，瓊桂塔化為絕色佳人。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from an Ejercito narrator (Pagsanjan); archival record. Monkey-bride cycle; Fansler compares the Greek monkey-wife of Von Hahn No. 67 and Grimm's Three Feathers family, and notes the wall-hurling disenchantment matches Grimm's frog-prince.

passages.text: There was a king who had three sons, named Pedro, Diego, and Juan. One day the king ordered these three gentlemen to set out from the kingdom and seek their fortunes; they took different directions, but before they separated they agreed to meet in a certain place in the forest. After walking for many days, Don Juan met an old man on the road, who gave him bread and told him to go to a palace a mile away: 'But as you enter the gate, you must divide the bread which I have given you among the monkeys which are guarding the gate to the palace; otherwise you will not be able to enter.' Don Juan took the bread, and when he reached the palace he did as the old man had advised him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 29 'Chonguita'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一位國王，他有三個兒子，名叫佩德羅、迭戈和胡安。有一天，國王命這三位公子離開王國，去開創自己的前程；他們分道而行，但在分別之前約定在森林中某個地方會合。走了許多天之後，唐胡安在路上遇見一位老人，老人給了他麵包，並叫他前往一英里外的一座宮殿：「但你進門時，必須把我給你的麵包分給那些守著宮殿大門的猴子；否則你就進不去。」唐胡安接過麵包，到了宮殿時，便照老人的建議做了。

passages.text: After entering the gate he saw a big monkey, and frightened at the sight of the animal he was about to run away — when the animal called to him and said, 'Don Juan, I know that your purpose in coming here was to find your fortune; and at this very moment my daughter Chonguita will marry you.' The archbishop of the monkeys was called, and Don Juan and Chonguita were married without delay. A few days afterwards Don Juan asked permission from his wife to go to the place where he and his brothers had agreed to meet; when Chonguita's mother heard that he was going away she said, 'If you are going away, take Chonguita with you.' Although Don Juan was ashamed to go with Chonguita because she was a monkey, he was forced to take her, and they set out together. When Don Juan met his two brothers and their beautiful wives at the appointed place, he could not say a word — 'Here she is... Behind me,' he sadly replied to their questions, and at Don Pedro's exclamation, 'What happened to you? Did you lose your head?' he could say nothing but 'Let us go home! Our father must be waiting for us.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 29 'Chonguita'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 進門之後，他看見一隻大猴子，一見這動物便嚇得正要逃走——那動物卻喚住他說道：「唐璜，我知道你來此是為了尋找你的財富；就在此刻，我的女兒瓊吉塔將嫁給你。」猴子的總主教被召了來，唐璜與瓊吉塔便即刻成婚。數日之後，唐璜向妻子請求允許他前往他與兄弟們約定相會之處；瓊吉塔的母親聽說他要離去，便說：「你若要走，就把瓊吉塔一同帶去。」唐璜雖因瓊吉塔是隻猴子而羞於與她同行，卻不得不帶上她，於是二人一同出發。當唐璜在約定之地見到他的兩個兄弟和他們美麗的妻子時，他一句話也說不出來——「她在這裡……在我身後，」他悲傷地回答他們的詢問；而當唐佩德羅驚呼「你怎麼了？你瘋了嗎？」時，他也只能說：「我們回家吧！父親一定在等著我們。」

passages.text: Upon learning that one of his sons had married a monkey, the king fainted; after recovering his senses he said to himself, 'This misfortune is God's will. I must therefore bear it with patience,' and assigned a house to each couple. But the more he thought of it, the greater appeared the disgrace his youngest son had brought on the family, and one day he called his three sons together: 'Tell your wives that I want each one of them to make me an embroidered coat. The one who falls to do this within three days will be put to death.' He issued this order in the hope that Chonguita would be put to death, because he thought she would not be able to make the coat — but on the third day his daughters-in-law presented the coats, and the one embroidered by Chonguita was the prettiest of all. Still anxious to get rid of the monkey-wife, the king next ordered his daughters-in-law to embroider a cap for him in two days, under penalty of death; the caps were all done on time. At last, thinking of no other way, the king summoned his three daughters-in-law: 'The husband of the one who shall be able to draw the prettiest picture on the walls of my chamber within three days shall succeed me on the throne.' At the end of the three days, when the king went to inspect the pictures, he found that Chonguita's was by far the prettiest, and so Don Juan was crowned king.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 29 'Chonguita'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 國王得知自己的一個兒子娶了一隻猴子，當場昏了過去；恢復神智之後，他自言自語道：「這不幸是上帝的旨意。因此我必須耐心承受。」於是為每一對夫妻各分配了一所房子。可是他越想越覺得，小兒子給家族帶來的恥辱越大，於是一天他把三個兒子召到一起：「告訴你們的妻子，我要她們每人為我縫一件繡花外衣。三天之內做不到的人將被處死。」他下這道命令，是希望瓊吉塔會被處死，因為他以為她做不出外衣——然而到了第三天，媳婦們都呈上了外衣，而瓊吉塔所繡的那一件是其中最漂亮的。國王仍急於除掉這猴妻，接著又命令媳婦們在兩天之內為他繡一頂帽子，違者處死；帽子全都按時完成。最後，國王再也想不出別的辦法，便召來三個媳婦：「誰能在三天之內在我寢室的牆上畫出最漂亮的圖畫，她的丈夫就將繼承我的王位。」三天期滿，國王前去察看圖畫，發現瓊吉塔所畫的遠比其他的漂亮，於是唐璜被加冕為王。

passages.text: A great feast was held in the palace in honor of the new king. In the midst of the festivities Don Juan became very angry with his wife for insisting that he dance with her, and he hurled her against the wall. At this brutal action the hall suddenly became dark; but after a while it became bright again, and Chonguita had been transformed into a beautiful woman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 29 'Chonguita'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 宮中為新國王舉行了盛大的宴會。歡慶之中，唐璜因妻子堅持要他與她跳舞而大為惱怒，便把她猛力摔向牆壁。由於這殘暴的舉動，大廳忽然變得一片黑暗；但過了一會兒又明亮起來，瓊吉塔已變成了一位美麗的女子。

title.en: The Golden Lock
title.zh: 金髮之謎

region.en: Balayan, Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's tale-source)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省巴蘭彥（故事原鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 30 'The Golden Lock', eBook #8299

summary.en: Proud Pio wagers his life against Ludovico's that he can learn the secrets of the recluse Clotilde in fifteen days; a bribed chaperon sells him one of the three golden locks under his wife's left armpit. Condemning her as faithless, Ludovico awaits the scaffold — until Clotilde arrives in her jeweled golden slipper, accuses Pio before the king of stealing 'my other slipper which looks like this one,' and his denial — 'I don't even know her. This is the first time I have ever seen her' — convicts him of the lie about her secrets. Pio is hanged in Ludovico's place, and the treacherous old woman ends her days in a dungeon.
summary.zh: 狂徒皮奧以性命打賭：十五日內必探得隱居的克洛蒂爾德的秘密。受賄的老侍婢賣給他一縷『左腋下三縷金髮』。盧多維科見金髮，信妻不貞，靜待極刑。刑前片刻，克洛蒂爾德穿著鑲寶金鞋趕到，當眾指控皮奧『偷了我另一隻一模一樣的金鞋』；皮奧矢口『從未見過她』——恰恰證明他所謂的秘密純屬謊言。皮奧代盧多維科受絞，賣主的老婆子終老地牢。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Hilario narrator (tale from Balayan); archival record. Chastity-wager cycle; Fansler traces the family from the Roman de Guillaume de Dole through Boccaccio Decameron 2:9 and Shakespeare's Cymbeline, and parallels the Tagalog corridos Duke Almanzor and Rodolfo.

passages.text: Long ago there lived in a distant kingdom an influential noble named Ludovico, who vastly increased his wealth by his marriage to a rich heiress called Clotilde. During the first ten years of their union she had never peeped out of her window or stirred out of her room: she only walked to the door of her chamber to bid farewell to her husband, and to meet him with a tender embrace when he returned. Nobody else but Ludovico and her chaperon could see or talk with her; she spent her time in voluntary seclusion, not in the luxuries of the court or the gaieties of society, but in embroidery, knitting, and in the unnecessary embellishment of her extremely lovely person.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 30 'The Golden Lock'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 很久以前，在一個遙遠的王國裡住著一位名叫盧多維科的權貴，他娶了一位名叫克洛蒂爾德的富有女繼承人，財富因而大增。在他們結合的頭十年裡，她從未向窗外張望過一眼，也從未走出過自己的房間：她只走到房門口與丈夫道別，並在他歸來時以溫柔的擁抱迎接他。除了盧多維科和她的女伴之外，沒有人能見到她或與她交談；她自願幽居度日，不追求宮廷的奢華，也不涉足社交的歡樂，而是從事刺繡、編織，以及為她那極其動人的容貌作多餘的裝飾。

passages.text: At the king's banquet in one of the principal frontier cities, the garrulous Pio, a bold, sharp-tongued rich youth, ridiculed the noble constancy of the fair Clotilde. 'I will bet you anything you want to bet, that you cannot learn the secrets of my wife in fifteen days,' said Ludovico, his face flushed with wrath. 'All right,' said Pio, exasperated by Ludovico's boast. 'The loser shall be hanged. I will bet my life that I'll know the secrets of your wife within fifteen days.' The terms of the contract were carefully written down, solemnly ratified by the king, and signed by the two contestants and by the other high-born gentlemen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 30 'The Golden Lock'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在邊境一座主要城市舉行的國王宴會上，多嘴的皮奧——一個大膽、口舌鋒利的富家青年——嘲笑美麗的克洛蒂爾德的貞潔堅定。「我敢跟你賭任何你想賭的東西，你在十五天之內也探不出我妻子的秘密，」盧多維科漲紅了臉怒道。「好啊，」皮奧被盧多維科的誇口激怒，說道，「輸的人要被絞死。我拿性命打賭，我能在十五天之內得知你妻子的秘密。」賭約的條款被仔細寫下，由國王莊嚴批准，並由兩名當事人及其他出身高貴的紳士簽字。

passages.text: Pio set out the next day for Ludovico's home town, and by his persuasive language and the magnetic touch of his hands he easily insinuated himself into the confidence of the gray-haired chaperon, then dropping a piece of gold on her palm: 'Will you tell me the secrets of your mistress?' The brilliant coin proved too great a temptation for her. 'Clotilde has three golden locks of hair under her left armpit. I know this fact, because I bathe her every day.' A second gold-piece bought her promise of the lock itself, and early the next morning, while bathing Clotilde as usual, she pulled out one of the golden locks — 'Aray! What's the matter with you?' — 'Never mind, never mind! This is the only reward I want for my many faithful services to you.' Ignorant of the treasonable intrigues of her chaperon, Clotilde said nothing more, and the old woman was amply rewarded with a purse of gold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 30 'The Golden Lock'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 皮奧第二天便動身前往盧多維科的家鄉，憑著他那能言善道的口才和雙手富於魅力的觸碰，輕易地博得了那位白髮女伴的信任，然後把一枚金幣丟在她掌心：「你願意告訴我你女主人的秘密嗎？」那枚燦爛的金幣對她而言誘惑太大了。「克洛蒂爾德的左腋下有三綹金色的頭髮。我知道這件事，因為我每天為她沐浴。」第二枚金幣換來了她交出那綹金髮的承諾；次日清晨，她照常為克洛蒂爾德沐浴時，拔下了其中一綹金髮——「哎喲！你怎麼了？」——「別在意，別在意！這就是我多年忠心服侍你所想要的唯一報酬。」克洛蒂爾德對女伴的背叛陰謀毫不知情，便沒有再多說什麼，而那老婦人則得到了一袋金幣作為豐厚的報酬。

passages.text: Ludovico was struck aghast at the sight of the golden lock, and at once wrote to his wife: 'I have spent ten years of my life in perfect happiness with you... But now everything is hopeless. My life shall be ended by violence, because of your faithlessness. We shall see each other no more. Receive the sad farewell of your Ludovico.' When Clotilde read this letter she swooned; coming to her senses, she read again the opprobrious word 'faithlessness' in her husband's handwriting, not knowing what act of disloyalty she had committed. At last a thought came to her mind: she sent for the best goldsmith in town and told him to make her a gold slipper adorned with precious stones; then she put on her best clothes and the precious slipper and with all possible expedition set out for Ludovico, arriving in the city just a few minutes before the execution. The turbulent persons gathered in the public square were awed by the loveliness and magnificent attire of Clotilde; when she reached the king and had heard all the details of Ludovico's case, she turned and pointed toward Pio: 'That man has stolen my other slipper which looks like this one I am wearing.' 'I have not committed any crime against her,' said Pio angrily. 'I don't even know her. This is the first time I have ever seen her.' 'Sir, why, then, did you tell his Majesty and other persons that you have discovered my secrets? I am the wife of Ludovico, whose life you have threatened to end by your deceit. I know now by what means you got possession of my golden lock.' Clotilde's statement sealed Pio's fate: he was hanged in place of Ludovico, who deeply regretted having doubted his faithful wife — and the old woman who preferred the gold of an impostor to the kindness of a virtuous woman was sentenced to spend the remainder of her life in a damp, dreary dungeon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 30 'The Golden Lock'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 魯多維科見到那縷金髮，驚愕不已，當即寫信給妻子：「我與你共度了十年圓滿幸福的生活……但如今一切都已無望。因你的不忠，我的性命將以暴力告終。我們再不能相見了。請接受你魯多維科悲傷的告別。」克洛蒂爾德讀罷此信，昏厥過去；醒來後，她又讀了一遍丈夫親筆寫下的那刺人的「不忠」二字，卻不知自己究竟犯下了何等不忠之舉。終於，她心中生出一念：她召來城裡最好的金匠，命他為她打造一隻綴滿寶石的黃金拖鞋；隨後她換上最好的衣裳，穿上那隻珍貴的拖鞋，以最快的速度動身前往魯多維科處，抵達城中時，距行刑僅有幾分鐘。聚集在公共廣場上的騷動人群，皆為克洛蒂爾德的美貌與華服所震懾；當她來到國王面前，聽罷魯多維科一案的全部細節後，她轉身指向皮奧：「那人偷走了我的另一隻拖鞋，與我腳上這隻一模一樣。」「我未曾對她犯下任何罪行，」皮奧怒道，「我根本不認識她。這是我頭一回見到她。」「先生，那麼你為何告訴陛下和其他人，說你發現了我的秘密？我正是魯多維科的妻子，而你曾揚言要以你的欺詐終結他的性命。如今我明白你是用何種手段得到了我的金髮。」克洛蒂爾德的一番話注定了皮奧的命運：他被處以絞刑，代替了魯多維科——魯多維科深悔自己曾懷疑忠貞的妻子——而那個寧取騙子之黃金、不取貞婦之善意的老婦，則被判處在陰濕陰暗的地牢中度過餘生。

title.en: The Pygmy of the Dances: Pepi II Sends for a Dwarf of the God
title.zh: 舞神之侏儒：佩皮二世迎矮人

region.en: Aswan, Egypt (tomb of Herkhuf, the caravan-governor) and the Land of the Spirits far south
region.zh: 埃及阿斯旺（赫爾庫夫之墓）與極南『神靈之地』

period: Royal despatch of Pepi II, year 2, 6th Dynasty (c. 2278 BCE); cut on the facade of Herkhuf's tomb (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IX, the Autobiography of Herkhuf and the letter of Pepi II

summary.en: The oldest piece of royal correspondence on earth: Herkhuf writes from the far south that he has brought back a pygmy 'who can dance the dance of the god, from the Land of the Spirits, like the pygmy whom the seal-bearer of the god Baurtet brought back from Punt in the time of Assa' — and the child-king Pepi II replies that he longs to see the pygmy 'more than any offering of the countries of Ba and Punt', with orders that trustworthy men sleep beside him ten times a night lest he fall into the water.
summary.zh: 世上最古之王家書信：赫爾庫夫自極南奏報，已自『神靈之地』攜回『能舞神舞』之侏儒，如阿薩王時神之印吏自彭特攜回者；幼王佩皮二世覆書：朕欲見此侏儒之心，勝於巴與彭特一切貢品——並敕可靠者守於其側，夜察十次，恐其墜水。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal letter via Budge 1910; no living community restrictions. 'Land of the Spirits' (Ta-Neter) is the Egyptian name for the far-southern divine lands; the pygmy was regarded as a being of the god's own country.

passages.text: Thou sayest in this thy letter that there hath been brought back by thee [also] a pygmy (or dwarf) who can dance the dance of the god, from the Land of the Spirits, like the pygmy whom the seal-bearer of the god Baurtet brought back from Punt in the time of Assa. Thou sayest to [my] Majesty, 'The like of him hath never been brought back by any other person who hath visited Amam.' Behold, every year thou performest what thy Lord wisheth and praiseth.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IX, the letter of Pepi II.
passages.zh: 你在這封信中說，你從神靈之地帶回了一個能跳神之舞的侏儒（或矮人），就像阿薩時代神之印璽持有者包爾泰特從蓬特帶回的那個侏儒一樣。你對[我的]陛下說：『凡到訪阿瑪姆的人，從未有人帶回過與他相類者。』看哪，你年年都在履行你主上所願、所讚許之事。

passages.text: Come down the river at once to the Capital. Bring with thee this pygmy whom thou hast brought from the Land of the Spirits, alive, strong, and healthy, to dance the dance of the god, and to cheer and gratify the heart of the King of the South and North, Neferkara, the everliving. When he cometh down with thee in the boat, cause trustworthy men to be about him on both sides of the boat, to prevent him from falling into the water. When he is asleep at night cause trustworthy men to sleep by his side on his bedding. See [that he is there] ten times [each] night. [My] Majesty wisheth to see this pygmy more than any offering of the countries of Ba and Punt.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. IX.
passages.zh: 即刻順流而下，前往都城。將你從神靈之地帶回的這個侏儒活著、健壯、安康地帶來，讓他跳神之舞，以歡娛、取悅上下埃及之王、永生的涅斐爾卡拉之心。當他隨你乘船而下時，命可靠之人守在他兩側，以防他落入水中。夜間他入睡時，命可靠之人睡在他身旁的臥具邊。每夜察看[他在那裡]十次。[我的]陛下想見這個侏儒，勝過巴與蓬特諸國的一切貢品。

passages.text: If when thou arrivest at the Capital, this pygmy who is with thee is alive, and strong, and in good health, [My] Majesty will confer upon thee a greater honour than that which was conferred upon the bearer of the seal Baurtet in the time of Assa, and as great is the wish of [My] Majesty to see this pygmy orders have been brought to the smer, the overseer of the priests, the governor of the town ... to arrange that rations for him shall be drawn from every station of supply, and from every temple.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. IX.
passages.zh: 若你抵達都城時，隨你而來的這個侏儒還活著、健壯、安康，[我的]陛下將賜予你比阿薩時代賜予印璽持有者包爾泰特更大的榮耀；而[我的]陛下想見這個侏儒的心願如此之大，已下令給司庫、祭司長、城尹……安排從各供給站、各神廟為他支取口糧。

title.en: Una Alone in the Hall: The Secret Inquiry into the Chief Wife
title.zh: 烏納獨任推事：王后密案之審

region.en: Abydos, Egypt (tomb stele of Una, judge belonging to Nekhen)
region.zh: 埃及阿拜多斯（烏納墓碑，奈肯之判官）

period: 6th Dynasty (reigns of Teta, Pepi I, Merenra); stele now in Cairo (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IX, the Autobiography of Una

summary.en: A harem drama of the 6th Dynasty, told in stone: when a secret inquiry was opened in the royal household concerning the Chief Wife Amtes, King Pepi made the estate-overseer Una hear the case by himself — no Chief Justice, no town governor, no nobleman, only a man of middle rank 'because the heart of His Majesty was filled with me' — and Una wrote the judgment alone, a thing never before done for a man of his rank.
summary.zh: 第六王朝宮闈劇，刻於石上：王后阿姆特斯之密案起，王命田莊督烏納獨任聽審——無大法官、無城守、無貴族在座——僅以中級官員一人，『因王心為我所充滿』；烏納獨自錄其判詞——同僚位者未嘗有此。

sensitivity.note: Ancient autobiographical inscription via Budge 1910; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: His Majesty made me a 'judge belonging to Nekhen.' His heart was more satisfied with me than with any other of his servants. Alone I heard every kind of private case, there being with me only the Chief Justice and the Governor of the town ... in the name of the king, of the royal household, and of the Six Great Houses.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IX, the Autobiography of Una.
passages.zh: 陛下任命我為『涅肯的法官』。他對我的滿意，勝過對他的任何其他僕人。我獨自審理各類私案，身旁僅有首席法官與城尹……以國王、王室與六大宅之名。

passages.text: During the secret inquiry which was made in the king's household concerning the Chief Wife Amtes, His Majesty made me enter to hear the case by myself. There was no Chief Justice there, and no Town Governor, and no nobleman, only myself, and this was because I was able and acceptable to the heart of His Majesty, and because the heart of His Majesty was filled with me. I did the case into writing, I alone, with only one judge belonging to Nekhen, and yet my rank was only that of overseer of the estates of Pharaoh. Never before did a man of my rank hear the case of a secret of the royal household.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. IX.
passages.zh: 在國王家中就正妻阿姆特斯所進行的秘密審查期間，陛下讓我獨自入內聽審此案。那裡沒有首席法官，沒有城尹，也沒有貴族，只有我一人；這是因為我有能力、且蒙陛下之心喜悅，也因為陛下之心充滿了我。我獨自將此案錄寫成文，身旁僅有一名涅肯的法官，而我的官階不過是法老田產的總管。在我這個官階的人，從未有誰審理過王室秘密之案。

passages.text: This army returned in peace, having raided the Land of the dwellers on sand. This army returned in peace, having thrown down the fortresses thereof. This army returned in peace, having cut down its fig-trees and vines. This army returned in peace, having set fire [to the temples] of all its gods. This army returned in peace, having slain the soldiers there in many tens of thousands. This army returned in peace, bringing back with it vast numbers of the fighting men thereof as living prisoners. His Majesty praised me for this exceedingly.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. IX, Una's five campaigns at the head of the army.
passages.zh: 這支軍隊平安歸來，劫掠了沙居者之地。這支軍隊平安歸來，推倒了當地的堡壘。這支軍隊平安歸來，砍倒了當地的無花果樹與葡萄藤。這支軍隊平安歸來，放火焚燒了當地眾神的［神廟］。這支軍隊平安歸來，在當地殺死了數以萬計的士兵。這支軍隊平安歸來，帶回了當地為數眾多的戰士作為活俘。陛下為此大大讚賞我。

title.en: Who Is the Nearest Relative?
title.zh: 誰是最親的親人？

region.en: Calamba, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省卡蘭巴（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral riddle-tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 31 'Who is the Nearest Relative?', eBook #8299

summary.en: Grandfather Julian tells his grandson the tale of Josefa, whose husband, son, and brother are all caught with the Banahaw bandits and condemned to die at sunrise without trial; the capitan general, moved by her pleading, will release one only. Held a week for the answer, Antonio sneaks it from his uncle — the brother — because 'what to a woman is a husband? She can marry again... but is it possible for her to bring into the world another brother?' The old man is satisfied.
summary.zh: 祖父講述約瑟法的故事：丈夫、兒子、兄長同為班納豪山賊被捕，無審即決；上尉將軍憐其哀求，允釋一人。孫兒苦思一週，偷偷從叔叔處得答案——選兄長：『丈夫可以再嫁，兒子可以再生，可再有一個同母兄弟嗎？』老祖父滿意點頭。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog riddle-tale recorded by Fansler from an Uichanco narrator (Calamba); archival record. The choosing-the-brother situation is ancient: Fansler cites Herodotus III, 119 (Intaphernes' wife), Sophocles' Antigone 909-912, the Ucchanga-jataka (No. 67), Ramayana 6.24, and a Persian tale of Dahak's serpent.

passages.text: 'On my life! You will soon become insane with stories,' exclaimed old Julian one day to his grandson Antonio, who was clinging fast to his elbows and bothering him as usual. 'Now, I will tell you a story on this condition: you must answer the question I shall put at the end of the narrative. If you give the correct answer, then I will tell you some more tales.' Then the old man began: 'There was once a young man who had completed his course of study and was to be ordained a priest. Whenever a man was about to be entrusted with the duty of being a minister of God, it was the custom to trace his ancestry back as far as possible, to see that there was no bad member on any branch of his family tree. Unfortunately his mother's brother was an insurrecto. The boy wanted very much to become a priest, so he set out for Mount Banahaw to look for his uncle.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 31 'Who is the Nearest Relative?'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「以我的性命發誓！你很快就會被故事弄得發瘋的。」老胡利安有一天對他的孫子安東尼奧喊道，這孩子正緊緊抓住他的胳膊肘，像往常一樣纏著他。「這樣吧，我講一個故事給你聽，但有個條件：你必須回答我在故事末尾提出的問題。如果你答對了，那我就再講幾個故事給你聽。」於是老人開始說道：「從前有個年輕人，他完成了學業，即將被授予神父之職。每當一個人即將被託付擔任天主之僕的職責時，按照慣例，總要盡可能追溯他的祖先，看看他的家族樹上任何一枝有沒有不肖的成員。不幸的是，他母親的兄弟是個叛亂分子。這男孩非常想成為神父，於是便動身前往巴納豪山去找他的舅舅。」

passages.text: As he was walking along the mountain road, he came across his uncle, but neither knew the other; the uncle had a long bolo in his hand. 'Hold! Hands up!' shouted the old man as the boy came in sight. 'Mercy! I am a friend, not an enemy... I have come in search of my uncle named Paulino, general of the Patriots of Banahaw.' 'If that is so, I am the man you are looking for. I am your uncle.' Federico was very glad to have found his uncle so easily, and the old man took his nephew to the cave where he dwelt with his soldiers. Weeks passed by, months elapsed, but Federico never thought of going back to his mother; so one day Federico's father went out to seek for his son, found him and his uncle, and also remained there with the soldiers, never thinking of going back home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 31 'Who is the Nearest Relative?'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他沿著山路行走時，他碰巧遇到了他的舅舅，但兩人互不相識；舅舅手裡握著一把長砍刀。「站住！舉起手來！」那男孩一出現，老人便喊道。「饒命！我是朋友，不是敵人……我是來找我那名叫保利諾的舅舅的，他是巴納豪愛國者的將軍。」「既然如此，我就是你要找的人。我是你的舅舅。」費德里科很高興這麼容易就找到了舅舅，老人便帶著外甥到他與士兵們居住的山洞去。一週週過去，一月月過去，但費德里科從未想過要回到母親那裡；於是有一天，費德里科的父親出門尋找兒子，找到了他和他的舅舅，也就和士兵們一起留在了那裡，從未想過要回家。

passages.text: One day Josefa received news that the bandits of Banahaw had been caught by the government authorities; among the prisoners were her brother Paulino, her son Federico, and her husband, and the captives were to be executed at sunrise without any trial. Josefa hurried to the capitan general, and pleaded with him to release her husband, her son, and her brother, presenting the officer with some gifts besides; she pleaded so hard that finally the capitan general was moved with pity, and consented to release one of the prisoners — but one only. Josefa did not know what to do. Whom should she select of the three: her husband, the other half of her life; her son, the fruit of her love; or her brother, that brother who came from the same womb and sucked the same milk from the same mother? To take one would mean to condemn the other two to death; she wished to save them all, but she was allowed to select only one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 31 'Who is the Nearest Relative?'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，何塞法接到消息說，巴納豪的土匪已被政府當局抓獲；俘虜之中有她的兄弟保利諾、她的兒子費德里科和她的丈夫，而這些俘虜將在日出時未經審判便被處決。何塞法急忙趕到總督那裡，懇求他釋放她的丈夫、兒子和兄弟，還送了些禮物給那位軍官；她苦苦哀求，最後總督動了憐憫之心，同意釋放其中一名俘虜——但只能一個。何塞法不知該怎麼辦。三人之中她該選誰：她的丈夫，她生命的另一半；她的兒子，她愛情的果實；還是她的兄弟，那個與她同出一母之腹、同吮一母之乳的兄弟？選一個就意味著判另外兩個死刑；她希望把他們全都救下，但她只被允許選一個。

passages.text: 'If you, Antonio, were in her place, whom would you select?' Antonio did not speak for some moments, but with knitted eyebrows looked up to the ceiling; 'Nonsense! You cannot find the answer in the ceiling! You really do not know, do you? Very well. I will give you until next Tuesday to get your answer.' When Tuesday came, Antonio had gotten the answer to his grandfather's puzzle-tale — but the rascally little boy deceived the old man: he had sought the information from his uncle. Timidly he said he would select the brother, and gave his reason: 'What to a woman is a husband? She can marry again; she can find another. And what to a woman is her son? Is it not possible to bear another one after she marries again? But is it possible for her to bring into the world another brother? Is it possible? The woman's parents were dead. Therefore she would be right in selecting her brother instead of her husband or her son.' 'Exactly so, my boy,' returned the satisfied old man, nodding his gray head. 'Since you have answered correctly, to-morrow I will tell you another story.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 31 'Who is the Nearest Relative?'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「安東尼奧，如果你處在她的位置，你會選誰？」安東尼奧沉默了片刻，皺著眉頭望向天花板；「胡說！你不可能在天花板上找到答案！你其實不知道，對吧？好吧。我給你到下星期二為止的時間來想出答案。」星期二到了，安東尼奧已經得到了祖父那道謎題故事的答案——但這個狡猾的小男孩騙了老人：他是從他舅舅那裡打聽到的。他怯生生地說他會選兄弟，並說出了理由：「對一個女人來說，丈夫算什麼？她可以再嫁；她可以另找一個。對一個女人來說，兒子又算什麼？她再嫁之後難道不能再懷一個嗎？但她有可能再生出另一個兄弟嗎？有可能嗎？這女人的父母已經死了。因此，她選擇兄弟而不選丈夫或兒子，是對的。」「正是如此，我的孩子，」心滿意足的老人點著他那灰白的頭答道。「既然你答對了，明天我再講一個故事給你聽。」

title.en: With One Centavo Juan Marries a Princess
title.zh: 一文錢娶公主

region.en: Bicol region, southeastern Luzon, Philippines (traditional among the Bicols)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋東南比科爾地區（比科爾人傳統故事）

period: Bicol oral droll; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 32 'With One Centavo Juan marries a Princess', eBook #8299

summary.en: A gambler finds one centavo and builds a fortune by sophistry: the chicken that ate his cake is his; the dog that ate his chicken is his; the iron bar whose gate killed his dog is his; the river that swallowed his bar is his — and the princess who bathes in his river belongs to him. Unable to refute the reasoning, her father marries her to Juan.
summary.zh: 賭徒拾得一文錢，以詭辯步步起家：吃了他的糕的雞是他的；吃了他的雞的狗是他的；壓死他的狗的鐵門之欄是他的；吞了他鐵欄的河是他的——在他河裡沐浴的公主自然也是他的。國王無法反駁這番推理，欣然將女兒嫁給胡安。

sensitivity.note: Bicol droll recorded by Fansler from a Frondoso narrator (traditional among the Bicols); archival record. Profitable-exchange cycle; Fansler compares the Cullaka-setthi-jataka (No. 4) and Grimm's Hans in Luck family, and judges the Filipino version old and likely native.

passages.text: In ancient times, in the age of foolishness and nonsense, there lived a poor gambler, all alone in the world: he had no parents, relatives, wife, or children. What little money he had he spent on cards or cock-fighting; every time he played he lost, so he would often pass whole days without eating, going around the town begging like a tramp. At last he determined to leave the village to find his fortune. One day, without a single cent in his pockets, he set out on his journey, and as he was lazily wandering along the road he found a centavo and picked it up. When he came to the next village he bought with his coin a small native cake, ate only a part of it, wrapped the rest in a piece of paper, and put it in his pocket; then he sat down by a little shop to rest and fell asleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 32 'With One Centavo Juan marries a Princess'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古時候，在愚昧荒唐的時代，住著一個貧窮的賭徒，他在世上孤身一人：沒有父母、親戚、妻子或兒女。他僅有的一點錢都花在紙牌或鬥雞上；每次賭博他都輸，因此常常整日不吃東西，像流浪漢一樣在鎮上四處乞討。最後他決心離開村子去尋找自己的運氣。有一天，他口袋裡一文錢也沒有，便踏上了旅程，當他懶洋洋地在路上閒逛時，發現了一枚一分錢硬幣，便撿了起來。他來到下一個村子，用那枚硬幣買了一塊當地的小糕餅，只吃了一部分，把剩下的用紙包好放進口袋；然後他在一家小店旁坐下來休息，睡著了。

passages.text: As he was lying on the bench asleep, a chicken came along, and, seeing the cake projecting from his pocket, pecked at it and ate it up; tickled by the bird's beak, the tramp woke up and immediately seized the poor creature. The owner claimed the chicken, but Juan would not give it up, on the ground that it had eaten his cake; indeed, he argued so well that he was allowed to walk away, taking the chicken with him. Scarcely had he gone a mile when he came to another village; there he took a rest in a barber-shop and fell asleep again, and soon a dog came in and began to devour his chicken. Awakened by the poor bird's squawking, Juan jumped up and caught the dog still munching its prey; in spite of the barber's protest and his refusal to give up his dog, Juan seized it and carried it away with him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 32 'With One Centavo Juan marries a Princess'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他正躺在長凳上睡覺，一隻雞走了過來，看見從他口袋裡露出來的糕餅，便啄了啄，把它吃光了；流浪漢被鳥喙啄得發癢，醒了過來，立刻抓住那可憐的畜生。雞的主人前來認領那隻雞，但胡安不肯交出，理由是牠吃了他的糕餅；他爭辯得如此有理，最後獲准帶著那隻雞離開。他走了還不到一英里，便來到另一個村莊；他在那裡的一間理髮店歇息，又睡著了，不久一隻狗走了進來，開始吞食他的雞。胡安被那可憐的雞的尖叫聲驚醒，跳起身來，抓住了那隻還在咀嚼獵物的狗；儘管理髮師抗議，並拒絕交出他的狗，胡安仍舊抓住牠，帶著牠走了。

passages.text: He proceeded on his journey until he came to another village; passing by a small house he felt thirsty, so he decided to go in and ask for a drink, tying his dog to the gate. When he came out again he found his dog lying dead, the iron gate on top of him — evidently, in its struggles to get loose, the animal had pulled the gate over. Without a word Juan pulled off one of the iron bars from the gate and took it away with him; when the owner shouted after him, Juan said, 'The bar belongs to me, for your gate killed my dog.' When Juan came to a wide river he sat down on the bank to rest, and while he was sitting there he began to play with his iron bar, tossing it up into the air and catching it as it fell; once he missed, and the bar fell into the river and was lost. 'Now, river,' said Juan, 'since you have taken my iron bar, you belong to me. You will have to pay for it.' So he sat there all day, watching for people to come along and bathe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 32 'With One Centavo Juan marries a Princess'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他繼續趕路，直到來到另一個村莊；經過一間小屋時他感到口渴，便決定進去討水喝，把狗拴在門上。當他再出來時，發現他的狗躺在地上死了，鐵門壓在牠身上——顯然，那畜生為了掙脫，把門拉倒了。胡安一言不發，從門上扯下一根鐵條，帶著它走了；當主人從後面喊他時，胡安說：『這根鐵條是我的，因為你的門殺死了我的狗。』胡安來到一條寬闊的河邊，坐在岸上休息，坐著的時候便玩起他的鐵條，把它拋向空中，落下時再接住；有一次他沒接住，鐵條掉進河裡，丟了。『那麼，河啊，』胡安說，『既然你拿走了我的鐵條，你就是屬於我的了。你得賠償它。』於是他整天坐在那裡，等著有人過來洗澡。

passages.text: It happened by chance that not long after, the princess came to take her bath. When she came out of the water, Juan approached her and said, 'Princess, don't you know that this river is mine? And, since you have touched the water, I have the right to claim you.' 'How does it happen that you own this river?' said the astonished princess. 'Well, princess, it would tire you out to hear the story of how I acquired this river; but I insist that you are mine.' Juan persisted so strongly that at last the princess said she was willing to leave the matter to her father's decision; on hearing Juan's story, and after having asked him question after question, the king was greatly impressed with his wonderful reasoning and wit, and, as he was unable to offer any refutation for Juan's argument, he willingly married his daughter to Juan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 32 'With One Centavo Juan marries a Princess'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 碰巧不久之後，公主前來沐浴。當她從水中出來時，胡安走近她說：『公主，你難道不知道這條河是我的嗎？既然你碰過這水，我就有權認領你。』『你怎麼會擁有這條河呢？』驚訝的公主說。『唉，公主，聽我講我如何得到這條河的經過，會讓您厭煩的；但我堅持說你是屬於我的。』胡安堅持得如此強烈，最後公主說她願意把這件事交給她父親裁決；國王聽了胡安的故事，又問了他一個又一個問題之後，對他那奇妙的推理與機智大為折服，而且既然他無法對胡安的論證提出任何反駁，便欣然把女兒嫁給了胡安。

title.en: The Three Humpbacks
title.zh: 三個駝背

region.en: Pagsanjan, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省帕桑漢（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 33a 'The Three Humpbacks', eBook #8299

summary.en: Badly treated Pablo marries out and prospers; his gambler brothers, ruined, beg at his wife's door and are hidden in two trunks when Pablo returns. Forgotten, they suffocate; the wife pays a neighbor five pesos to bury 'one brother-in-law,' then shows him another each time he returns for his pay — until, digging a grave under water for the last, he meets a live humpback carrying fish from the fishery and kills the 'corpse that will not stay buried': her own husband.
summary.zh: 受盡苛待的帕布洛成婚自立、生活安穩；敗光的兄長上門乞食，被藏進兩口衣箱，竟窒息而死。主婦以五比索僱鄰人埋『一位內兄』，此人每回討錢都見『屍體復活』，埋了又埋——最後在水下掘墓埋葬，歸途卻遇見一個挑魚回家的活駝背，一刀結果這『屢埋不起的屍身』——正是她的丈夫。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Cordero narrator (heard from her washerwoman); archival record. Fansler finds the nearest parallel in Straparola 5:3 and the Seven Wise Masters family; 'Thus Marta tried to deceive, but she was the one who was deceived.'

passages.text: Pablo was badly treated by his older brothers Pedro and Juan: the coarsest food was given to him, his clothes were ragged, he slept on the floor while his two brothers had very comfortable beds — in fact, he was deprived of every comfort and pleasure. In the course of time this unfortunate youth fell in love with a well-to-do girl, and after a four-years engagement they were married; thus Pablo was separated from his brothers, to their great joy. Pedro and Juan now began spending their money lavishly on trifles and learned how to gamble, while Pablo was living happily and out of want with his wife Marta, going every morning to fish, for his wife owned a large fishery.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 33 'The Three Humpbacks'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴勃羅受到哥哥佩德羅和胡安的虐待：最粗劣的食物給他吃，他的衣服破破爛爛，他睡在地板上，而兩個哥哥卻有非常舒適的床——事實上，他被剝奪了一切舒適與歡樂。隨著時間流逝，這個不幸的青年愛上了一位富裕人家的姑娘，訂婚四年之後他們結了婚；於是巴勃羅與他的哥哥們分開了，這讓他們大為高興。佩德羅和胡安如今開始把錢揮霍在瑣碎之物上，還學會了賭博，而巴勃羅則與妻子瑪爾塔過著幸福而無匱乏的生活，每天早晨都去捕魚，因為他妻子擁有一大片漁場。

passages.text: One day, as Pablo was just leaving the house at the usual hour to go fishing, he said to his wife, 'Wife, if two humpbacks like myself ever come here, do not admit them. As you know, they are my brothers, and they used to treat me very badly.' That very afternoon Pedro and Juan came to pay their brother a visit and begged Marta to give them some food, for they were starving: they had squandered all their money. Marta was so impressed by the wretched appearance of her brothers-in-law that she admitted them despite her husband's prohibition, and gave them a dinner. When they had finished eating she said, 'It is now time for my husband to come home. He may take vengeance on you for your past unkindness to him, if he finds you here, so I'll hide you in two separate trunks. You stay there till to-morrow morning, and I'll let you out when my husband is gone again.' She had scarcely locked the trunks when Pablo entered; he did not find out that his brothers had been there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 33 'The Three Humpbacks'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，巴勃羅正要在往常的時刻離家去捕魚，他對妻子說：『妻子，如果有兩個像我一樣的駝背來到這裡，千萬不要放他們進來。你知道，他們是我的哥哥，他們以前待我非常壞。』就在那天下午，佩德羅和胡安前來探望他們的弟弟，並懇求瑪爾塔給他們一些食物，因為他們快餓死了：他們把錢全揮霍光了。瑪爾塔被她兩位大伯子那副可憐相打動，不顧丈夫的禁令，把他們放了進來，並給他們一頓飯吃。他們吃完之後，她說：『現在是我丈夫回家的時候了。要是他發現你們在這裡，可能會為你們過去對他的不仁而報復你們，所以我把你們藏在兩個分開的箱子裡。你們待在那裡直到明天早上，等我丈夫再出門時，我就放你們出來。』她剛把箱子鎖好，巴勃羅就進來了；他並沒有發現他的哥哥們來過。

passages.text: The next morning Pablo went to his work as usual; Marta had so much to do about the house that day that she forgot all about Pedro and Juan, and the poor boys, deprived of air and food, died inside the trunks. Not until two days later did Marta think of the two humpbacks; she ran and opened the trunks and found their dead bodies inside. Her next thought was how to dispose of them. She called her neighbor and asked him to come bury one of her brothers-in-law who had just died in her house, promising to pay him five pesos when he came back from his work. The neighbor lifted the heavy body of Pedro, carried it away to a far place, dug a hole waist deep, put the corpse into it, and covered it up; then he hastened back to Marta: 'Madam, I have buried the dead man in a very deep grave.' 'No, you have not,' said Marta. 'What is that lying over there?' — and she pointed to the corpse of Juan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 33 'The Three Humpbacks'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天早晨，巴勃羅照常去上工；那天瑪爾塔家裡有那麼多事要做，竟把佩德羅和胡安忘得一乾二淨，那可憐的兩個小夥子因缺氧又無食物，死在箱子裡了。直到兩天之後，瑪爾塔才想起那兩個駝背；她跑去打開箱子，發現裡面是他們的屍體。她接著想到的是如何處置他們。她叫來鄰居，請他來埋葬她的一位剛在她家裡死去的大伯子，並答應等他上工回來就付他五比索。鄰居抬起佩德羅沉重的屍體，把它搬到很遠的地方，挖了一個齊腰深的坑，把屍體放進去，蓋上土；然後他急忙回到瑪爾塔那裡：『太太，我已經把死人埋進一個很深的墳墓裡了。』『不，你沒有，』瑪爾塔說。『那邊躺著的是什麼？』——她指著胡安的屍體。

passages.text: 'That's very strange!' exclaimed the neighbor, scratching his head. 'You are very artful,' he said to the dead body of Juan; angry now, for he had not yet received his pay, he bore the corpse of Juan to the seashore, got a banca, and dug a very deep grave beneath the water: 'If you can come out of this place, you are the wisest person in the world.' Then he returned to Marta's house — and on his way back he happened to look behind him, when he saw, to his great surprise, the humpback following him, carrying some fish. He gazed at him; and when he saw that he resembled exactly the corpse that he had just buried, he said, 'So you have come out of the grave again, have you, you naughty humpback!' And with these words he killed the humpback that very instant. This humpback was Marta's husband returning home from the fishery. Thus Marta tried to deceive, but she was the one who was deceived.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 33 'The Three Humpbacks'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「這真是太奇怪了！」鄰居搔著頭驚呼道。「你可真是狡猾啊。」他對著胡安的屍體說；此時他已怒火中燒，因為他還沒拿到工錢，於是他把胡安的屍體扛到海邊，找來一艘小船，在水底下挖了一個極深的墳墓：「你要是能從這地方出來，你就是世上最聰明的人了。」然後他回到瑪爾塔的家——回程途中他偶然回頭一看，竟大為驚訝地看見那駝背跟在他身後，還帶著一些魚。他盯著他瞧；當他看出這人與他方才埋葬的屍體長得一模一樣時，便說：「這麼說你又從墳墓裡出來了，是嗎，你這調皮的駝背！」話一說完，他當場就把那駝背殺了。這駝背正是瑪爾塔的丈夫，捕魚歸來正要回家。瑪爾塔本想騙人，結果被騙的卻是她自己。

title.en: The Seven Humpbacks
title.zh: 七個駝背

region.en: Manila, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home city)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋馬尼拉（敘述者居地）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 33b 'The Seven Humpbacks', eBook #8299

summary.en: Seven look-alike humpback brothers; one marries and supports the other six, until his stingy wife, hating the burden, murders all six while her husband is away and cheats the grave-digger into burying corpse after 'resurrected' corpse — until, meeting the married humpback riding home, he strikes down 'the same man he had buried so many times before,' and the wicked woman dies of a broken heart when she learns it was her very husband.
summary.zh: 七個相貌酷似的駝背兄弟；一人娶妻供養其餘六人。慳吝的妻子厭其負擔，趁丈夫外出殺害六位內兄，又哄騙掘墓人：『埋不牢便不付錢』——一具又一具『死而復生』的屍體。埋到第六具時，騎馬歸家的丈夫迎面而來；掘墓人一鋤下去——『原來你就是那個總能爬出墳墓的傢伙！』惡婦得知殺的是親夫，心碎而亡。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Reyes narrator (Manila); archival record. Companion to The Three Humpbacks; the Pampango variant 'The Seven Hunchbacked Brothers' (Vitug) is nearly identical.

passages.text: Once there lived seven brothers who were all humpbacks and who looked very much alike. Ugly as these humpbacks were, still there was a lady who fell in love with one of them and married him; this lady, however, though she loved her husband well, was a very stingy woman. Finally the time came when the unmarried humpbacks had to depend on the other one for food; naturally this arrangement was very displeasing to the wife, and in time her hate grew so intense that she planned to kill all her brothers-in-law.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 33 'The Seven Humpbacks'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前住著七個兄弟，他們全都是駝背，而且長得十分相像。這些駝背雖然醜陋，卻仍有一位女士愛上了其中一個並嫁給了他；然而這位女士雖深愛丈夫，卻是個非常吝嗇的女人。終於，時候到了，那些未婚的駝背不得不仰賴另一個兄弟供養食物；這樣的安排自然令妻子十分不悅，久而久之，她的憎恨變得如此強烈，以致她謀劃要殺光所有的小叔。

passages.text: One day, when her husband was away on business, she murdered the six brothers. Next she hired a man to come and bury a corpse, telling him of only one corpse because she wanted to deceive the man. When he had buried one of the bodies he came back to get paid for his work; the woman, before he had time to speak, began to reproach him for not burying the man in the right place: 'See here! You did not do your work well. Go and bury the body again. Remember that I will not pay you until you have buried the man so that he stays under the earth.' The man took the second corpse and buried it; but when he returned, there it was again. And so on: he repeated the operation until he thought that he had buried the same corpse six times.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 33 'The Seven Humpbacks'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，趁丈夫外出辦事，她殺害了六個兄弟。接著她雇了一個男人來埋葬屍體，卻只告訴他有一具屍體，因為她想欺騙那人。那人埋好其中一具屍體後，便回來領取工錢；那女人不等他開口，就開始責罵他沒把人埋對地方：「你看看！你活兒沒幹好。去把屍體再埋一次。記住，除非你把那人埋得穩穩待在地下，否則我是不會付你錢的。」那人搬來第二具屍體埋了；可是等他回來，那屍體又出現了。就這樣一再重複：他反覆做著同樣的事，直到他自以為已經把同一具屍體埋了六次。

passages.text: But after the sixth, the last humpback, had been buried, the married humpback came home from his work. When the grave-digger saw this other humpback, he immediately seized and killed him, thinking he was the same man he had buried so many times before. When the wicked woman knew that her very husband had been killed, she died of a broken heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 33 'The Seven Humpbacks'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 可是在第六個、也就是最後一個駝背被埋好之後，那已婚的駝背幹完活回家了。掘墓人一看見這另一個駝背，立刻抓住他把他殺了，以為他就是自己先前埋了那麼多次的同一個人。那惡毒的女人得知被殺的竟是自己丈夫時，便心碎而死。

title.en: Respect Old Age: The Half-Blanket and the Wooden Plate
title.zh: 敬老：半條毯與木盤

region.en: Malabon, Rizal, and Mangaldan, Pangasinan, Luzon, Philippines (two tellings)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋黎薩省馬拉翁與邦阿西楠省曼加爾丹（兩則講述）

period: Tagalog and Pangasinan oral exempla; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 34a 'Respect Old Age' and 34b 'The Golden Rule', eBook #8299

summary.en: Two Filipino tellings of the old-age exemplum: forced on a rainy morning to send his eighty-year-old father to a farm hut, the boy cuts the carrying-blanket in two — 'When you grow old, I will leave you in a hut, and give you this half' — and the father recalls the order; and in Pangasinan, the son who must eat from a wooden plate because his trembling hands break the china begins carving boards 'for you and my mother when you are old,' and the father weeps and seats the old man at the table again.
summary.zh: 兩則菲律賓孝道故事：雨晨被迫送八十歲老父去農舍的父親，見兒子把毯子剪成兩半——『您老了，我就用這半條送您去小屋』——連忙召回祖父；另一則裡，因老人手抖摔盤而被罰用木盤吃飯的孩子，竟在屋下雕起木板：『給您和媽媽老了用』——父親流淚，從此老人重上飯桌。

sensitivity.note: Two related exempla recorded by Fansler from an Ignacio narrator (Malabon, Rizal) and a Serafica narrator (Mangaldan, Pangasinan); archival record. A Pampango variant ('The Old Man, his Son, and his Grandson' with the rope 'to have it ready when your turn comes') was printed by H. E. Fansler. Known in many countries.

passages.text: Once there lived a poor man who had to support his family: a hot-headed wife who predominated over the will of her husband, a small boy of ten, and an old man of eighty, the boy's grandfather. The old man could no longer work because of his feebleness, and was the cause of many quarrels between the husband and wife, though he was loved by their son. One rainy morning the husband was forced by his wife to send his father away; he called his son and ordered him to carry a basket full of food and also a blanket, telling the boy they were to leave the old man in a hut on their farm some distance away. The boy wept and protested against this harsh treatment of his grandfather, but in vain; he then cut the blanket into two parts, and when he was asked to explain his action, he said to his father, 'When you grow old, I will leave you in a hut, and give you this half of the blanket.' The man was astonished, hurriedly recalled his order concerning his father, and thereafter took good care of him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 34 'Respect Old Age'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前住著一個窮人，他得養活一家人：一個脾氣火爆、處處壓過丈夫意志的妻子，一個十歲的小男孩，還有一位八十歲的老人，也就是男孩的祖父。老人因身體衰弱再也無法工作，成了夫妻倆許多爭吵的起因，儘管他們的兒子很愛他。一個下雨的早晨，丈夫被妻子逼著要把父親送走；他叫來兒子，吩咐他提一籃食物，再帶上一條毯子，告訴男孩他們要把老人留在離家一段距離的農場上一間小屋裡。男孩哭了，抗議這樣苛待祖父，卻毫無用處；於是他把毯子剪成兩半，當被問起為何這麼做時，他對父親說：「等您老了，我也會把您留在小屋裡，把這半條毯子給您。」那人大為震驚，急忙收回關於父親的命令，此後便好好照料他。

passages.text: A long time ago there lived in a town a couple who had a son, and the father of the husband lived with his son and daughter-in-law happily for many years; but when he grew very old he became very feeble, and every time he ate at the table he always broke a plate, because his hands trembled so. The old man's awkwardness soon made his son angry, and one day he made a wooden plate for his father to eat out of; the poor old man had to eat all his food from this wooden plate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 34 'The Golden Rule'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 很久以前，鎮上住著一對夫妻，他們有個兒子，而丈夫的父親與兒子、媳婦一同幸福地生活了許多年；但當他變得非常年老時，身體也變得十分衰弱，每次在餐桌上吃飯，他總會打破盤子，因為他的手抖得太厲害。老人的笨拙不久便惹得兒子生氣，有一天他做了一個木盤給父親吃飯用；那可憐的老人只得用這個木盤吃下所有的飯菜。

passages.text: When the grandson noticed what his father had done, he took some tools and went down under the house, and there took a piece of board and began to carve it. When his father saw him and said, 'What are you doing, son?' the boy replied, 'Father, I am making wooden plates for you and my mother when you are old.' As the son uttered these words, tears gushed from the father's eyes; from that time on, the old man was always allowed to eat at the table with the rest of the family, nor was he made to eat from a wooden plate. Moral: Do unto others as you want them to do unto you.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 34 'The Golden Rule'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 孫子察覺到父親所做的事之後，便拿了些工具，走到屋子底下，取了一塊木板，開始雕刻起來。父親看見他，便問：「孩子，你在做什麼？」男孩回答：「父親，我在為您和母親做木盤，等你們年老的時候用。」兒子說出這番話時，父親眼中淚水奪眶而出；從那時起，老人總是被允許與家中其他人一同在桌旁吃飯，也不再被迫用木盤進食。寓意：你希望別人怎樣待你，你就要怎樣待人。

title.en: The Trial of Osiris Before the Great Gods: Thoth the Advocate
title.zh: 諸神前之奧西里斯審判：辯護者托特

region.en: Celestial Anu (Heliopolis), Egypt (the Hall of Judgment of the Great Gods)
region.zh: 埃及天界赫利奧波利斯（諸神審判之廳）

period: Ancient tradition retold from Pyramid Text hints (Budge, The Book of the Dead, 1901, ch. V)

source.work: The Book of the Dead, by E. A. Wallis Budge (1901), ch. V, 'Thoth and Osiris'

summary.en: Set's case against his murdered brother is tried before the Greater and Lesser Companies assembled in celestial Anu: Isis and Nephthys bring Osiris in, Horus 'the avenger of his father' comes to watch, Thoth appears as scribe — and as advocate, proving Set's charges unfounded and Set himself a liar; the gods order Osiris a Great God with rule of the Under World, throw Set down, make Osiris mount upon his back, bind him 'with cords like a beast for sacrifice,' and hack him in pieces before Thoth.
summary.zh: 塞特訟其被害之兄，案審於天界赫利奧波利斯之大小二神團前：伊西斯與奈芙蒂斯引奧西里斯至，荷魯斯『復父仇者』臨庭監審，托特以書記之職而兼辯護——證塞特之訟皆虛、其人乃謊者；諸神遂判奧西里斯為大神、王冥界；塞特被擊倒於地，奧西里斯登其背以示勝，復縛之『如祭祀之獸』，於托特之前碎其身。

sensitivity.note: Ancient theological narrative via Budge 1901; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The Egyptians were not satisfied with the mere possession of the texts of Thoth, when their souls were being weighed in the Great Scales in the Judgment Hall of Osiris, but they also wished Thoth to act as their Advocate on this dread occasion and to prove their innocence as he had proved that of Osiris before the great gods in prehistoric times.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, The Book of the Dead (1901), ch. V.
passages.zh: 埃及人並不滿足於僅僅擁有托特的經文，當他們的靈魂在奧西里斯審判廳的大天平上被稱量時，他們還希望托特在這可怕的場合充當他們的辯護者，並證明他們的無罪，正如他在史前時代曾在眾大神面前證明奧西里斯無罪一樣。

passages.text: The Greater and the Lesser Companies of the Gods assembled in the celestial Anu, or Heliopolis, and ordered Osiris to stand up and defend himself against the charges brought against him by Set. Isis and Nephthys brought him before the gods, and Horus, 'the avenger of his father,' came to watch the case on behalf of his father, Osiris. Thoth appeared in the Hall of Judgment in his official capacity as 'scribe,' i.e., secretary to the gods, and the hearing of the evidence began. Set seems to have pleaded his own cause, and to have repeated the charges which he had made against Osiris.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. V.
passages.zh: 諸神的大會與小會聚集在天上的阿努，即赫利奧波利斯，命令奧西里斯站起來，為自己辯護，以應對塞特對他的指控。伊西斯與奈芙蒂斯將他帶到諸神面前，而「為父報仇者」荷魯斯則前來代表他的父親奧西里斯旁聽此案。托特以「書記」的官方身分，即諸神的秘書，出現在審判廳中，證據的聽審便開始了。塞特似乎為自己的案子自行辯護，並重複了他對奧西里斯提出的指控。

passages.text: The defence of Osiris was undertaken by Thoth, who proved to the gods that the charges brought against Osiris by Set were unfounded, that the statements of Set were lies, and that therefore Set was a liar. The gods accepted Thoth's proof of the innocence of Osiris and the guilt of Set, and ordered that Osiris was to be considered a Great God and to have rule over the Kingdom of the Under World, and that Set was to be punished. Thoth convinced them that Osiris was 'MAA KHERU,' 'true of word,' i.e., that he had spoken the truth when he gave his evidence, and in texts of all periods Thoth is frequently described as S-MAA KHERU ASAR, i.e., he who proved Osiris to be 'true of word.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. V.
passages.zh: 奧西里斯的辯護由托特承擔，他向諸神證明塞特對奧西里斯提出的指控毫無根據，塞特的陳述是謊言，因此塞特是個說謊者。諸神接受了托特關於奧西里斯無罪、塞特有罪的證明，並命令應將奧西里斯視為一位偉大的神，統治冥界王國，而塞特應受懲罰。托特使他們確信奧西里斯是「MAA KHERU」，即「言辭真實」，也就是說他在作證時說了真話；而在各個時期的經文中，托特常被描述為 S-MAA KHERU ASAR，即證明奧西里斯「言辭真實」的那一位。

passages.text: As for Set the Liar, he was seized by the ministers of the Great Gods, who threw him down on his hands and face and made Osiris mount upon his back as a mark of his victory and superiority. After this Set was bound with cords like a beast for sacrifice, and in the presence of Thoth was hacked in pieces.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. V.
passages.zh: 至於說謊者塞特，他被眾大神的僕役抓住，他們將他推倒，使他手臉朝下趴著，並讓奧西里斯騎上他的背，作為奧西里斯勝利與優越的標誌。此後，塞特像獻祭的牲畜一樣被繩索捆綁，並在托特面前被剁成碎塊。

title.en: The Crocodile and the Trochilus: The Bird That Enters the Mouth
title.zh: 鱷與鶺鴒：入其口之鳥

region.en: The Nile and the lake of Moiris, Egypt (where the tamed crocodiles wear golden earrings)
region.zh: 埃及尼羅與莫伊里斯湖（馴鱷戴金耳環之處）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.68-70 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 68-70

summary.en: The sacred-crocodile rite: around Thebes and the lake of Moiris each people keeps one crocodile trained to tameness, hung with ornaments of molten stone and gold in its ears and anklets on its front feet, fed on appointed food and sacrificial victims — while at Elephantine they eat them, 'not holding them to be sacred'; and the trochilus, the one bird at peace with the crocodile, enters its open mouth to swallow the leeches.
summary.zh: 聖鱷之禮：底比斯與莫伊里斯湖畔各奉一馴鱷，耳懸熔石與金飾、前足戴環，以定制之食與祭牲飼之——而象島之民竟食之，『不以為聖』；獨有鶺鴈與鱷相安，入其啟口而吞其螞蟥。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ethnography via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Now for some of the Egyptians the crocodiles are sacred animals, and for others not so, but they treat them on the contrary as enemies: those however who dwell about Thebes and about the lake of Moiris hold them to be most sacred, and each of these two peoples keeps one crocodile selected from the whole number, which has been trained to tameness, and they put hanging ornaments of molten stone and of gold into the ears of these and anklets round the front feet, and they give them food appointed and victims of sacrifices and treat them as well as possible while they live, and after they are dead they bury them in sacred tombs, embalming them: but those who dwell about the city of Elephantine even eat them, not holding them to be sacred.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.69.
passages.zh: 如今，對某些埃及人而言，鱷魚是神聖的動物，對另一些人則不然，他們反而把鱷魚當作敵人對待；然而那些居住在底比斯附近以及莫伊里斯湖附近的人，卻視鱷魚為最神聖之物，這兩地的人各自從全部鱷魚中挑選一條，馴養得溫順，並在牠們的耳中掛上熔石與黃金的飾物，在前腳上戴上腳環，給牠們規定的食物與獻祭的犧牲，生前盡可能善待牠們，死後則將牠們防腐處理，葬於神聖的墓中；但那些居住在象島城附近的人甚至吃鱷魚，並不視牠們為神聖。

passages.text: Whereas all other birds and beasts fly from him, the trochilus is a creature which is at peace with him, seeing that from her he receives benefit; for the crocodile having come out of the water to the land and then having opened his mouth (this he is wont to do generally towards the West Wind), the trochilus upon that enters into his mouth and swallows down the leeches, and he being benefited is pleased and does no harm to the trochilus.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.68.
passages.zh: 然而所有其他鳥獸都避開牠，而鱷鳥卻是一種與牠和平共處的生物，因為牠從鱷魚那裡得到好處；鱷魚從水中上岸後張開嘴（牠通常朝向西風這樣做），鱷鳥便進入牠的口中，吞下螞蟥，鱷魚因此受益而心滿意足，並不傷害鱷鳥。

title.en: Cats to Bubastis, Hawks to Buto: The Burial Map of Sacred Animals
title.zh: 貓葬布巴斯提斯、鷹葬布托：聖獸葬地圖

region.en: Egypt, the sacred animal cemeteries (Bubastis, Buto, Hermopolis)
region.zh: 埃及聖獸墓群（布巴斯提斯、布托、赫爾莫波利斯）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.65-67 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 65-67

summary.en: A geography of grief: whoever kills one of the sacred animals willingly dies, and the killer of an ibis or hawk dies whatever his intent; when fire breaks out the cats leap into the flames 'divinely possessed' and great mourning comes upon Egypt; the dead cats are carried to Bubastis and embalmed, dogs buried in city tombs, shrew-mice and hawks to Buto, ibises to Hermopolis.
summary.zh: 哀悼之地理：擅殺聖獸者死，殺朱鷺或鷹者不問有心無心皆死；火起之時，貓『如神所憑』躍入火中，全埃及為之舉哀——貓死運至布巴斯提斯製為木乃伊；犬葬城中聖墓；鶹鶹與鷹運至布托；朱鷺運至赫爾莫波利斯。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ethnography via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: If any one kill any of these animals, the penalty, if he do it with his own will, is death, and if against his will, such penalty as the priests may appoint: but whosoever shall kill an ibis or a hawk, whether it be with his will or against his will, must die.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.65.
passages.zh: 若有人殺害這些動物中的任何一種，若是出於自願，刑罰便是死刑；若非出於自願，則由祭司們裁定刑罰：但凡是殺死朱鷺或鷹的人，無論是出於自願還是非自願，都必須處死。

passages.text: Moreover when a fire occurs, the cats seem to be divinely possessed; for while the Egyptians stand at intervals and look after the cats, not taking any care to extinguish the fire, the cats slipping through or leaping over the men, jump into the fire; and when this happens, great mourning comes upon the Egyptians. And in whatever houses a cat has died by a natural death, all those who dwell in this house shave their eyebrows only, but those in whose houses a dog has died shave their whole body and also their head.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.66.
passages.zh: 此外，當火災發生時，貓似乎受到神靈的附體；因為當埃及人隔著一段距離站著照看貓，毫不設法撲滅火焰時，貓卻從人群中溜過或跳過，躍入火中；此事發生時，埃及人便陷入極大的哀悼。而在任何有貓自然死亡的家中，住在這屋裡的所有人只剃去眉毛；但那些家中有狗死亡的人，則剃去全身的毛髮，連頭部也一併剃去。

passages.text: The cats when they are dead are carried away to sacred buildings in the city of Bubastis, where after being embalmed they are buried; but the dogs they bury each people in their own city in sacred tombs; and the ichneumons are buried just in the same way as the dogs. The shrew-mice however and the hawks they carry away to the city of Buto, and the ibises to Hermopolis; the bears (which are not commonly seen) and the wolves, not much larger in size than foxes, they bury on the spot where they are found lying.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.67.
passages.zh: 貓死後被送往布巴斯提斯城的聖所，在那裡經過防腐處理後埋葬；狗則由各族人埋葬在自己城中的聖墓裡；獴的埋葬方式與狗完全相同。至於鼩鼱和鷹，他們送往布托城，朱鷺則送往赫爾摩波利斯；熊（不常見到的）和狼（體型不比狐狸大多少），則就地埋葬在發現牠們倒臥之處。

title.en: Three Ways of Embalming: Cedar Oil, Natron, and Seventy Days
title.zh: 三種防腐之法：雪松油、泡鹼與七十日

region.en: The embalmers' workshops of Egypt (symbolic pin, Memphis)
region.zh: 埃及防腐師作坊（象徵定位，孟菲斯）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.86-88 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 86-88
