Come and help me, for I am in great need of assistance'; the king of the fishes appeared, and, as the fish could not refuse the request of the queen of the birds, he said to Carlos, 'Carlos, lie on my back and close your eyes: within five minutes you'll be in the home of the goddess.' When he opened his eyes, he found himself in a very beautiful house, lying on a golden bed, and beside him was standing a beautiful woman with a star on her forehead and a moon on her throat. Carlos related his story, and the goddess could not refuse help to one who had spoken so well of her beauty: she took her diamond ring off her finger and gave it to Carlos, saying, 'Take this ring with you. Whenever you want or need my help, touch the ring thrice, and say, O God, help me! If the king wants my presence, touch the ring six times, and I'll appear before you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 44 'The Magic Ring'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡洛斯眼含淚水，心思專注於上帝，沿著黃金河的岸邊走去，在一棵帕加特帕特樹下坐下來休息；一隻在樹頂築巢的鷹看見他在哭泣，非常同情他：『來吧，卡洛斯，來吧！我會引你走上正路。』在河口處她喊道：『哦，魚之王！來幫幫我，因為我急需援助』；魚之王出現了，由於魚無法拒絕鳥之女王的請求，他對卡洛斯說：『卡洛斯，躺到我的背上，閉上眼睛：五分鐘之內你就會到達女神的家。』當他睜開眼睛時，發現自己身處一座非常美麗的房子裡，躺在一張金床上，身旁站著一位美麗的女子，額上有星，喉上有月。卡洛斯講述了自己的經歷，女神無法拒絕幫助一個如此讚美她美貌的人：她從手指上取下鑽石戒指，交給卡洛斯，說道：『帶著這枚戒指。每當你想要或需要我的幫助時，就觸摸戒指三次，並說：哦，上帝，幫助我！如果國王想要我出現，就觸摸戒指六次，我便會出現在你面前。』

passages.text: When morning came the next day, Carlos was ordered into the king's presence, all the lords and nobles of the kingdom being in the palace, anxious to see the Goddess of the Sea. It was already eight o'clock, and the goddess had not yet appeared. 'Where is she, Carlos?' 'She cannot come; but, if your Highness wants me to, I'll give you a trunk filled with gold in exchange for my life.' 'No. What we want is the Goddess of the Sea. If you cannot show her to us, prepare to be hanged.' Carlos touched the ring six times, and the beautiful Goddess of the Sea appeared; all were amazed to see a woman with curly hair, a star on her forehead, a moon on her throat, and wearing a white dress glistening with diamonds. 'Carlos is an enchanter!' cried the king, and he ran to embrace the goddess; in five minutes she disappeared, and Carlos's life was saved. Don Fernando now proposed to marry his daughter Florentina to Carlos; at first the princess hesitated to say yes, but at last she consented, and Carlos was glad to marry the beautiful princess — but before the marriage took place, he went to get his poor mother, who was anxiously awaiting his return home. Carlos with his diamond ring could now have everything he needed; in fact, he made the chapel in which he was married all of gold, and the wedding-dress of the princess was adorned with diamonds. Immediately after the wedding, poor Carmen died of happiness. Carlos continued to live in the palace with his wife Florentina, but he never came to know the meaning of his name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 44 'The Magic Ring'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 翌日清晨，卡洛斯奉命入宮覲見國王，王國所有的領主與貴族都齊聚宮中，急切地想見識那位海之女神。時辰已至八點，女神卻仍未現身。「她在何處，卡洛斯？」「她無法前來；但若殿下要我這麼做，我願獻上一只裝滿黃金的箱子，換取我的性命。」「不。我們要的是海之女神。你若無法讓我們見到她，就準備受絞刑吧。」卡洛斯觸碰戒指六次，美麗的海之女神便現身了；眾人見一名女子滿頭鬈髮，額上有一顆星，喉間有一輪月，身穿一襲閃爍著鑽石的白色長裙，無不驚嘆。國王高喊：「卡洛斯是個巫師！」隨即奔上前去擁抱女神；五分鐘後，她便消失了，卡洛斯的性命也因此得救。唐·費爾南多此時提議將女兒弗洛倫蒂娜許配給卡洛斯；起初公主猶豫不肯應允，最後終於同意了，卡洛斯也很樂意娶這位美麗的公主——但在婚禮舉行之前，他先去接來了他那可憐的母親，她正焦急地盼著他回家。如今有了鑽石戒指，卡洛斯想要什麼便有什麼；事實上，他將舉行婚禮的那座禮拜堂都變成了純金，公主的婚服也綴滿了鑽石。婚禮之後不久，可憐的卡門便因過於欣喜而死去。卡洛斯與妻子弗洛倫蒂娜繼續住在宮中，但他始終不曾明白自己名字的含義。

title.en: Maria and the Golden Slipper
title.zh: 瑪利亞與金鞋

region.en: Pagsanjan, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省帕桑漢（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 45a 'Maria and the Golden Slipper', eBook #8299

summary.en: Servant-girl Maria is told by a crab — her dead mother — to bury its shell, from which grows a wish-tree that clothes her for Prince Malecadel's balls in a coach of fine horses and golden slippers. Fleeing at midnight she loses one slipper; the prince's order — 'The lady whom this slipper fits is to be my wife' — finds her foot exactly, the other slipper beneath her dress, and her sisters faint with astonishment as she becomes the prince's wife, dear to them from that day on.
summary.zh: 侍女瑪利亞聽從螃蟹——她亡母所化——之囑，將蟹殼埋於園中；長出的神樹為她變出華服、駿馬之車與一雙金鞋，赴王子馬里克阿德爾的舞會。午夜逃歸失落一鞋；王子懸令『鞋合腳者為妻』——瑪利亞穿上正合，裙下另鞋一出，兩位姊姊驚得幾近昏厥。她成為王子之妻，從此亦得家人珍愛。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog Cinderella tale recorded by Fansler from a Zafra narrator (Pagsanjan); archival record. Fansler notes Crab-as-mother and the shell-tree; cf. the Visayan Abadeja variant and Rusk's 'The Wonderful Tree' (mother drowned, fins planted).

passages.text: Once there lived a couple who had an only daughter, Maria. When Maria was a little girl her mother died; a few years later Maria's father fell in love with a widow named Juana, who had two daughters, the elder Rosa and the younger Damiana, and when Maria was grown to be a young woman her father married the woman Juana. Maria continued to live with her father and step-mother, but Juana and her two daughters treated Maria as a servant: she had to do all the work in the house — cook the food, wash the clothes, clean the floors — and the only clothes she herself had to wear were ragged and dirty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 45 'Maria and the Golden Slipper'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一對夫妻，只有一個獨生女，名叫瑪麗亞。瑪麗亞還小的時候，母親便去世了；幾年之後，瑪麗亞的父親愛上了一位名叫胡安娜的寡婦，她帶著兩個女兒，長女羅莎與次女達米安娜，待瑪麗亞長成少女，父親便娶了胡安娜。瑪麗亞繼續與父親和繼母同住，但胡安娜和她的兩個女兒都把瑪麗亞當作僕人使喚：家中所有的活兒都得由她來做——煮飯、洗衣、擦地——而她自己僅有的衣裳，盡是破爛骯髒的。

passages.text: One day Prince Malecadel wanted to get married, so he gave a ball to which he invited all the ladies in his kingdom, saying that the most beautiful of all was to be his wife. When Damiana and Rosa knew that all the ladies were invited, they began to discuss what clothes they would wear to the ball; but poor Maria was in the river, washing the clothes, very sad and weeping, for she had no clothes at all in which she could appear at the prince's fête. While she was washing, a crab approached her, and said, 'Why are you crying, Maria? Tell me the reason, for I am your mother.' While she was talking to the crab, Juana came up, very angry, and ordered her to catch the crab and cook it for their dinner; Maria seized the crab and carried it to the house, at first refusing to cook it, for she knew that it was her mother — but Juana whipped her so hard that at last she was forced to obey. Before it was put in the earthen pot to be cooked, the crab said to Maria, 'Maria, don't eat my flesh, but collect all my shell after I am eaten, and bury the pieces in the garden near the house. They will grow into a tree, and you can have what you want if you will only ask the tree for it.' After her parents had eaten the flesh of the crab, Maria collected all its shell and buried it in the garden; at twilight she saw a tree standing on the very spot where she had buried the shell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 45 'Maria and the Golden Slipper'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，馬勒卡德爾王子想要成婚，便舉辦了一場舞會，邀請王國中所有的女士，並宣稱其中最為美麗者將成為他的妻子。達米安娜與羅莎得知所有女士都受邀之後，便開始商議該穿什麼衣裳赴會；可憐的瑪麗亞卻在河邊洗衣，滿心悲傷，哭泣不已，因為她根本沒有衣裳可以出席王子的盛宴。她正洗著衣裳，一隻螃蟹來到她身旁，說道：「瑪麗亞，你為何哭泣？告訴我緣由吧，因為我就是你的母親。」她正與螃蟹說話時，胡安娜走了過來，怒氣沖沖，命她把螃蟹捉來煮了當晚餐；瑪麗亞抓住螃蟹，帶回家中，起初不肯煮牠，因為她知道那是她的母親——但胡安娜狠狠地鞭打她，最後她只得順從。在螃蟹被放進陶鍋烹煮之前，牠對瑪麗亞說：「瑪麗亞，不要吃我的肉，等我被吃完之後，把我所有的殼收集起來，將這些碎片埋在屋旁的花園裡。它們會長成一棵樹，你只要向那棵樹求取，便能得到你想要的東西。」她的父母吃完螃蟹的肉之後，瑪麗亞收集了牠所有的殼，埋在花園裡；黃昏時分，她看見一棵樹立在她埋殼的那個地方。

passages.text: When night came, Rosa and Damiana went to the ball, and Juana retired for the night as soon as her daughters were gone; when Maria saw that her aunt was sleeping, she went into the garden and asked the tree for what she wanted. The tree changed her clothes into very beautiful ones, and furnished her with a fine coach drawn by four fine horses, and a pair of golden slippers. 'You must be in your house before twelve o'clock. If you are not, your clothes will be changed into ragged, dirty ones again, and your coach will disappear.' At the ball she was received by the prince very graciously: she was the most beautiful of all, and sat between her two sisters, neither of whom recognized her; the prince danced with her all the time. When Maria saw that it was half-past eleven, she bade farewell to the prince and went home, where the tree changed her beautiful clothes back into her old ones and the coach disappeared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 45 'Maria and the Golden Slipper'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 夜幕降臨，羅莎與達米安娜前去赴舞會，胡安娜等女兒們一走便回房就寢；瑪麗亞見姑母睡著了，便走進花園，向那棵樹求取她想要的東西。那棵樹將她的衣裳變成十分美麗的華服，又為她備好一輛由四匹駿馬拉著的華美馬車，以及一雙金鞋。「你必須在十二點之前回到家中。若不然，你的衣裳會再度變成破爛骯髒的，你的馬車也會消失。」舞會上，王子殷勤地接待她：她是全場最美麗的人，坐在兩個姊妹之間，而她們誰也沒認出她來；王子整晚都與她共舞。瑪麗亞見時已十一點半，便向王子告辭回家，那棵樹又將她的華服變回舊衣，馬車也消失了。

passages.text: The next night the prince gave another ball; Maria again went to the garden to ask for beautiful clothes, and this time was given a coach drawn by five horses, the tree again warning her to return before twelve. The prince was delighted to see her, and danced with her the whole evening — but Maria was so enchanted that she forgot to notice the time; while she was dancing she heard the clock striking twelve, and ran as fast as she could down stairs and out the palace-door, in her haste dropping one of her golden slippers. One of her golden slippers she had with her; but the other, which she had dropped at the door, was found by one of the guards, who gave it to the prince, saying that the slipper had been lost by the beautiful lady who ran out of the palace when the clock was striking twelve. 'The lady whom this slipper fits is to be my wife,' said the prince to all the people present. The first house visited was the one in which Maria lived: Rosa tried to put the slipper on her foot, but her foot was much too big; then Damiana put it on her foot, but her foot was too small — the two sisters tried and tried again to make the slipper fit, but in vain. Then Maria told them she would try; but her sisters said, 'Your feet are very dirty. This golden slipper will not go on your foot, for your feet are larger than ours,' and laughed at her — but the guard who had brought the slipper said, 'Let her try. It is the prince's order that all shall try.' Then Maria put it on, and it fitted her foot exactly; she then drew the other slipper from underneath her dress and put it on her other foot, and when the two sisters saw the two slippers on Maria's feet, they almost fainted with astonishment. So Maria became the wife of the prince, and from that time on she was very dear to her sisters and aunt.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 45 'Maria and the Golden Slipper'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二夜，王子又舉辦了一場舞會；瑪麗亞再次走進花園求取美麗的衣裳，這回得到一輛由五匹馬拉著的馬車，那棵樹又警告她須在十二點前回去。王子見到她欣喜萬分，整晚都與她共舞——但瑪麗亞沉醉其中，竟忘了留意時辰；她正跳舞時，聽見鐘敲十二下，便盡可能快地奔下樓梯、衝出宮門，匆忙之間掉落了一隻金鞋。她身邊還帶著一隻金鞋；另一隻掉在門口的，被一名衛兵拾得，交給王子，說這隻鞋是那位在鐘敲十二下時奔出宮殿的美麗女士所遺落的。「這隻鞋合腳的女士，將成為我的妻子。」王子對在場所有人說道。他們造訪的第一戶人家便是瑪麗亞所住的那一戶：羅莎試著把鞋穿上腳，但她的腳太大了；接著達米安娜把鞋穿上腳，但她的腳太小了——兩姊妹試了又試，想讓鞋合腳，卻徒勞無功。於是瑪麗亞告訴她們，她願意一試；但她的姊妹們說：「你的腳很髒。這隻金鞋穿不上你的腳，因為你的腳比我們的大。」並嘲笑她——但帶來那隻鞋的衛兵說：「讓她試試。王子有令，所有人都得試。」於是瑪麗亞把鞋穿上，恰好合腳；她隨即從裙下取出另一隻鞋，穿在另一隻腳上，兩姊妹見瑪麗亞腳上穿著兩隻鞋，驚愕得幾乎昏厥。於是瑪麗亞成了王子的妻子，從那時起，她便深受姊妹們與姑母的喜愛。

title.en: Abadeja: The Black Handkerchief Made White
title.zh: 阿巴德婭：白帕染黑、黑帕洗白

region.en: Baybay, Leyte, central Philippines (Visayan tale)
region.zh: 菲律賓萊特省拜拜（米沙鄢故事）

period: Visayan oral tale from Leyte; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 45b 'Abadeja', eBook #8299

summary.en: Orphaned Abadeja, abused by her step-mother, is set impossible tasks — a white handkerchief black, a black one white; a torn mat made new — each solved by a beautiful woman of the high trees. A gift chicken killed and cooked leaves only its feet, which the woman tells her to plant east and west in a forest garden, where they grow into air, bearing pearls, diamonds, gold dresses, rings, bracelets, shoes, necklaces, and ear-rings. The rich man's son who steals a ring can only be cured by the girl whose hand removes it — Abadeja in a gold dress — and she becomes his wife, the beautiful woman attending the wedding unseen.
summary.zh: 繼母苛待孤女阿巴德婭，屢出難題——白帕染黑、黑帕洗白、破蓆復新——皆由高樹間的美婦化解。受贈的雞被殺烹，只餘雙足；美婦教她把左右足分植東西，森林小園中竟長出珠寶、金衣、戒指、手鐲與項鍊。富家公子摘戒指中毒腫，唯有取戒者可為其妻——金衣加身的阿巴德婭一觸即解。二人成婚，美婦隱身觀禮。

sensitivity.note: Visayan Cinderella variant from Leyte (narrator unrecorded), printed by Fansler; archival record. Fansler notes its distinctive items: the black-white handkerchief task, the tree from chicken-feet, and the ring-cure marriage device.

passages.text: Once upon a time there lived in the town of Baybay a man whose name was Abac; the name of his wife was Abadesa, and they had a beautiful daughter named Abadeja. The mother died when her daughter was about thirteen years old, and in a year her father married again, a widow who had three daughters. The second wife envied her step-daughter because Abadeja was much more beautiful than her own children: consequently she treated the poor girl very badly, made her do all the hard work, and punished her severely when she could not do the work.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 45 'Abadeja'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前，在拜拜鎮上住著一個名叫阿巴克的男人；他的妻子名叫阿巴德薩，他們有一個美麗的女兒，名叫阿巴德哈。母親在女兒大約十三歲時去世，一年之後，父親續了弦，娶了一位帶著三個女兒的寡婦。繼母嫉妒這個繼女，因為阿巴德哈比她自己親生的孩子們漂亮得多：因此她待這可憐的女孩十分苛刻，要她做所有的粗活，做不完便嚴加責罰。

passages.text: One evening the step-mother said to Abadeja, 'Take these two handkerchiefs to the river and wash them. The white one must be black, and the black one white, when you bring them back to me. If they are not, I shall beat you.' Abadeja went to the river, where she sat down on a rock and began to cry — until a beautiful woman stood before her, took the handkerchiefs, and in an instant they were transformed; then she gave them back to Abadeja and invited the girl to come see her any time she needed help. The next morning Abadeja was ordered to put some rice on a mat in the sun to dry; while she was in the house doing other work, a pig came, ate up the rice, and tore the mat to pieces — and her step-mother whipped her severely for having lost the rice and told her she would have to repair the mat so that it was as good as new. Abadeja took the mat and went across the river, crying; the beautiful woman met her again, and, taking her by the hand, led her to her home among the high trees, where she took the mat from the girl and waved it in the air — immediately it became a whole mat again. Then she gave Abadeja a beautifully-colored chicken.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 45 'Abadeja'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天傍晚，繼母對阿巴德哈說：「把這兩條手帕拿到河邊去洗。你把它們帶回來給我的時候，白的那條必須變成黑的，黑的那條必須變成白的。要是沒變成這樣，我就打你。」阿巴德哈來到河邊，坐在一塊石頭上哭了起來——直到一位美麗的女子站在她面前，接過手帕，轉眼之間手帕就變了樣；然後她把帕子還給阿巴德哈，並邀請這女孩隨時需要幫助就來找她。第二天早上，阿巴德哈奉命把一些米鋪在蓆子上曬太陽；她正在屋裡做別的事時，一頭豬來了，把米吃了個精光，還把蓆子撕成碎片——繼母因為她弄丟了米，狠狠地抽了她一頓，還說她得把蓆子修補得跟新的一樣。阿巴德哈拿著蓆子，哭著過河去了；那位美麗的女子又遇見了她，牽著她的手，領她到高樹之間的家中，在那裡從女孩手中接過蓆子，在空中一揮——蓆子立刻又變回一整張。然後她給了阿巴德哈一隻色彩美麗的雞。

passages.text: The next day, when Abadeja was away from the house, her cruel step-mother took the chicken, killed it, and cooked it; when the girl returned, only the feet of her chicken were left. She cried over her loss, and ran to the river to ask the beautiful woman what she should do — and the beautiful woman told the girl to take the chicken's feet and plant them in the forest. Abadeja went home, took the feet, and carried them with her to the forest; there she made a little garden, in which she planted the right foot toward the east, and the left foot toward the west. A month later she visited her garden in the woods, and was astonished to see that the feet had grown up into the air, and that they bore pearls, diamonds, gold dresses, rings, bracelets, shoes, necklaces, and ear-rings. She was delighted, but she did not tell her step-mother about her garden.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 45 'Abadeja'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天，阿巴德哈不在家的時候，她那狠心的繼母抓起那隻雞，殺了煮熟；女孩回來時，只剩下她那隻雞的腳。她為失去的雞痛哭，跑到河邊去問那位美麗的女子該怎麼辦——美麗的女子告訴女孩，把雞腳拿去種在森林裡。阿巴德哈回到家，拿了雞腳，帶到森林裡去；她在那裡開了一個小園子，把右腳種朝東，左腳種朝西。一個月後，她到林中園子去看，驚訝地發現那兩隻腳已經長到半空中，上面結滿了珍珠、鑽石、金衣裳、戒指、手鐲、鞋子、項鍊和耳環。她滿心歡喜，卻沒有把園子的事告訴繼母。

passages.text: One day the son of the richest man in Baybay came across this little garden in the forest, picked off a ring, and put it on his finger; when he reached home, his finger began to swell. His father called in all the best physicians, but they could not remove the ring; then he called in all the girls of the town, and said that the one who could take the ring from the finger of his son should be his son's wife. All the girls of the town tried except Abadeja, who did not try because her mother would not allow her to go — at last someone told the rich man that there was still a girl who had not tried, and that it was Abadeja, so he sent for her. Now her step-mother did not dare refuse to let her go; Abadeja ran to her little garden, put on one of the gold dresses, and went to the rich man's house — and as soon as she touched the ring, it slid off. The next day Abadeja was married to the son of the rich man; the beautiful woman attended the wedding unseen by everyone except Abadeja, and the young couple lived happily for many years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 45 'Abadeja'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，拜拜城最富有的人的兒子偶然發現了森林裡的這個小園子，摘下一枚戒指戴在手指上；他回到家時，手指開始腫脹。他父親請來所有最好的醫生，卻都取不下那枚戒指；於是他把城裡所有的姑娘都叫來，說誰能從他兒子手指上取下戒指，誰就做他兒子的妻子。城裡所有的姑娘都試過了，只有阿巴德哈沒試，因為她母親不許她去——最後有人告訴那富人，還有一個姑娘沒試過，就是阿巴德哈，於是富人派人去叫她。這回繼母不敢不讓她去；阿巴德哈跑到她的小園子，穿上一件金衣裳，來到富人家中——她一碰那戒指，戒指就滑落了。第二天，阿巴德哈嫁給了那富人的兒子；那位美麗的女子出席了婚禮，除了阿巴德哈，誰也看不見她，這對年輕夫妻幸福地生活了許多年。

title.en: Juan the Poor: Doña Maria on Her Mountain
title.zh: 窮漢胡安與山上的瑪利亞

region.en: Pagsanjan, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省帕桑漢（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog folk-tale form of the romance 'King Asuero'; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 46 'Juan the Poor', eBook #8299

summary.en: A sad king proclaims half his kingdom to whoever fetches Doña Maria from her distant mountain. Beggar Juan shares his alms with an old woman who equips him: a handkerchief that produces whatever is asked, the lean last horse that can endure hardships, an ant's leg and eagle's feathers whose ashes summon armies of helpers. The saddled horse lures Doña Maria from her garden; the king, in love with her, sets Juan a death-task — separate a hundred cavans of mixed rice and transport her palace in one night — and the ants and birds of Juan's kindness perform both by morning.
summary.zh: 鬱鬱的國王懸賞半國，求人自遠山請來瑪利亞。行乞的胡安與老嫗分享所得，得手帕、瘦馬、蟻足與鷹羽。備鞍的駿馬誘瑪利亞出園；垂涎的國王刁難胡安：一夜之內分揀百石糙米、並將山中宮殿搬來——胡安焚蟻足與鷹羽，萬蟻分米、群鳥搬殿，拂曉功成，遂與瑪利亞成婚。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog tale recorded by Fansler from a Zafra narrator (Pagsanjan); archival record. Clearly derived from the Tagalog metrical romance 'The Life of King Asuero, Doña Maria, and Juan the Poor in the City of Jerusalem,' but told as a folk-tale; Fansler includes it for completeness of Philippine popular literature.

passages.text: Many years ago there lived a king who was always sad; he used to go to a mountain and climb the highest tree that was growing there. One day, when he was in the top of the tree, he saw on another high mountain a beautiful princess, Doña Maria; when he returned home to his palace, he sent a proclamation all over his kingdom, saying that the one who could take Doña Maria from her mountain and bring her before him should have one-half of his kingdom. Juan was a beggar; and it was his custom, whenever he saw a beggar like himself, to share with that beggar the alms which had been given him. One day he saw a wretched old woman, and out of pity for her he gave her all the food he had begged that day; then the old woman, who knew of the proclamation of the king, said to Juan, 'You must tell the king, my boy, that you will fetch Doña Maria for him' — and at last she persuaded Juan to go by telling him that she would accompany him, and promising her help.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 46 'Juan the Poor'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 許多年前，有一位國王總是愁眉不展；他常到一座山上去，爬上那裡長得最高的一棵樹。有一天，他正在樹頂上，望見另一座高山上有一位美麗的公主，瑪麗亞小姐；他回到宮中後，向全國頒布詔令，說誰能把瑪麗亞小姐從她的山上帶到他面前，誰就能得到他王國的一半。胡安是個乞丐；他有一個習慣，每當看見像自己一樣的乞丐，就把別人施捨給他的東西分給那乞丐。有一天，他看見一個可憐的老婦人，出於憐憫，把那天討來的食物全給了她；那老婦人知道國王的詔令，便對胡安說：「孩子，你得去告訴國王，說你能替他把瑪麗亞小姐帶來」——最後她說服了胡安，說她會陪他一起去，並答應幫助他。

passages.text: After Juan had visited the palace and told the king that he would bring the princess Doña Maria to him, the poor boy and the old woman set out on their journey to the distant mountain; when they reached the gates of the city, the old woman said to Juan, 'Juan, I am very tired, and I cannot go any farther, but I will give you this handkerchief. When you come to the first mountain, you must spread the handkerchief on the ground, and many fat horses will approach you; but I advise you not to choose any of them. You must choose the very last one, which will be lean and weak-looking. That is the horse which can endure hardships, and which will be able to carry you to the princess's palace.' Juan followed the advice of the old woman, and mounted the thin horse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 46 'Juan the Poor'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 胡安到宮裡見過國王，說他會把瑪麗亞小姐帶來之後，這可憐的男孩和老婦人便動身前往那座遠方的山；他們來到城門口時，老婦人對胡安說：「胡安，我累得很，再也走不動了，不過我把這條手帕給你。你到了第一座山，要把手帕鋪在地上，會有許多肥壯的馬朝你走來；但我勸你哪一匹都別挑。你一定要挑最後那一匹，那匹看起來又瘦又弱。那才是能吃苦耐勞的馬，能把你載到公主的宮殿去。」胡安聽從了老婦人的話，騎上了那匹瘦馬。

passages.text: When he had ridden very far, he saw before him a hill full of ants, and was afraid to pass over lest the ants should devour him and his animal. 'You must ask the handkerchief for food, and we will feed the ants,' said the horse. Juan spread out the handkerchief and asked it to bring him much food; after he had scattered it on the ground for the ants, the leader of the ants approached Juan and said, 'Since you have been very kind to us, I will give you one of my legs; and at any time you want aid from us, you must burn the leg, and let the ashes be carried by the wind. Then we will come to help you.' Again, when the sky was full of birds flying around and looking for food, Juan fed them all they wanted to eat, and the king of the birds, the eagle, flew up to him: 'To repay you for your kindness, I will give you some feathers from my wings. Any time you want aid from us, just burn some of the feathers, and let the ashes be carried by the wind. Then we will come to you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 46 'Juan the Poor'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他騎了很遠很遠，看見前面有一座滿是螞蟻的小山，不敢過去，怕螞蟻把他和他的坐騎吃掉。「你得向手帕要食物，我們來餵螞蟻，」那匹馬說。胡安鋪開手帕，求它送來許多食物；他把食物撒在地上給螞蟻吃過之後，螞蟻的首領來到胡安面前說：「既然你對我們這麼好，我就把我的一條腿給你；以後你什麼時候需要我們幫忙，就把這條腿燒了，讓灰隨風飄去。那時我們就會來幫你。」後來，天上滿是飛來飛去找食的鳥兒，胡安又餵飽了牠們，鳥中之王老鷹飛到他跟前：「為了報答你的好意，我把我翅膀上的幾根羽毛給你。以後你什麼時候需要我們幫忙，只要燒幾根羽毛，讓灰隨風飄去。那時我們就會來找你。」

passages.text: When they came near the palace of Doña Maria, the horse told Juan to hide, and said that he alone would enter her garden; but before he should hide, Juan should ask his handkerchief for a complete equipment of saddle and bridle, so that the horse could be mounted by a lady. When the princess saw the horse she became very angry, 'Who is the one who is so bold as to let his horse enter my garden?' — but she could see no one, so she said to herself, 'I will mount this horse and find out who its owner is'; she mounted the horse, which immediately ran to the place where Juan was hiding and told him to get up on its back, carrying them swiftly back to the small house of Juan. The king, accompanied by all his retinue, went in great state to Juan's house, made over to him one-half of his dominion, and took Doña Maria back to his palace — but Doña Maria was very beautiful, and the king fell deeply in love with her. 'Only the one who can do what I wish him to do shall be my husband. I will mix one hundred cavans of husked rice with one hundred cavans of unhusked rice. He who in one night can separate the two kinds of rice, and also bring my palace here to your kingdom, shall be married to me,' she said — and told the king there was one who could accomplish the tasks, and that was Juan. 'To-night you must separate the grain into two piles, and also transport the palace of Doña Maria to my kingdom. If you have not done both by to-morrow morning, you shall lose your head.' Juan went away very sad toward the mountain; as he was walking along, he met the thin horse which had helped him before: 'Don't be sad, Juan! You can accomplish both those difficult tasks. Don't you remember the leg of the ant and the feathers of the eagle which were given to you, and the promise of the ant and eagle?' So Juan took the ant's leg and the feathers from his pocket, burned them, and threw the ashes into the air; in a short time thousands of birds and ants came to him and asked him what he wanted — 'I want the palace of Doña Maria brought here before daybreak, and the two hundred cavans of mixed rice separated.' The birds flew to the mountain to get the palace, and the ants hastened to the king's grounds to separate the unhusked from the husked rice; by morning both tasks were completed, so Juan was married to Doña Maria, for she would have no other husband.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 46 'Juan the Poor'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他們走近瑪麗亞小姐的宮殿時，馬兒叫胡安躲起來，並說牠自己會進入她的花園；但在胡安躲起來之前，他應該向他的手帕求取一整套馬鞍和韁繩，好讓一位女士能夠騎上這匹馬。當公主看見那匹馬時，她非常生氣：「是誰這麼大膽，竟讓他的馬進入我的花園？」——但她誰也看不見，於是自言自語道：「我要騎上這匹馬，查出牠的主人是誰。」她騎上了馬，那馬立刻跑到胡安躲藏的地方，叫他爬上馬背，迅速把他們載回胡安的小屋。國王帶著全體隨從，浩浩蕩蕩地來到胡安的家，把一半的領地移交給他，並把瑪麗亞小姐帶回自己的宮殿——但瑪麗亞小姐非常美麗，國王深深地愛上了她。「只有能完成我所要求之事的人，才能做我的丈夫。我要把一百卡邦的糙米和一百卡邦的稻穀混在一起。誰能在一夜之間把這兩種米分開，並且把我的宮殿搬到你們的王國來，誰就能娶我。」她說道——並告訴國王有一個人能完成這些任務，那就是胡安。「今晚你必須把穀物分成兩堆，並且把瑪麗亞小姐的宮殿搬到我的王國來。如果到明天早上你還沒把兩件事都辦好，你就要人頭落地。」胡安悲傷地往山裡走去；走著走著，他遇見了先前幫助過他的那匹瘦馬：「別難過，胡安！你能完成這兩件艱難的任務。你不記得螞蟻的腿和鷹的羽毛曾交給你，還有螞蟻和鷹的承諾嗎？」於是胡安從口袋裡取出螞蟻的腿和鷹的羽毛，把它們燒了，並把灰燼撒向空中；不久，成千上萬的鳥和螞蟻來到他面前，問他想要什麼——「我要瑪麗亞小姐的宮殿在天亮前被搬到這裡來，還要把兩百卡邦混在一起的米分開。」鳥兒飛到山上去取宮殿，螞蟻急忙趕到國王的場院去把稻穀和糙米分開；到了早晨，兩件任務都完成了，於是胡安娶了瑪麗亞小姐，因為她不肯嫁給別人。

title.en: The Fate of an Envious Woman
title.zh: 嫉妒者的下場

region.en: Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home province)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 47 'The Fate of an Envious Woman', eBook #8299

summary.en: Pockmarked Maria, forsaken by her husband Juan for the beautiful Flora, prays before the image of St. Vicente Ferrer, whose animated hand touches her face into extraordinary beauty; Juan returns to the wife he had despised. Envious Flora kneels at the same image — and becomes as black and ugly as the mistress of a Kaffir household, her lips thick and coarse, her nose as long as a monkey's tail; she pines away and dies, while Juan confesses his sins and the two live in peace and happiness.
summary.zh: 麻面的瑪利亞被丈夫胡安拋棄；她在聖維森特·費雷爾像前祈禱，聖像之手撫面，醜女化為絕色，浪子重歸髮妻。妒火中燒的弗洛拉同往聖像前祈求——竟變得如卡菲爾家的黑婦，唇厚鼻長如猿尾。她羞慚而歸，憔悴而死；胡安懺悔贖罪，夫妻自此安樂終老。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog tale recorded by Fansler from a Hilario narrator (Batangas); archival record. Toads-and-Diamonds group with two wives instead of two sisters; Fansler compares the Visayan 'The Two Wives and the Witch' and Lal Behari Day's Bengal tale No. 22. The period's colonial comparisons are retained as recorded and noted.

passages.text: There lived once upon a time a young couple of the middle class: the man was a reckless scapegrace and spendthrift, but the woman was a pious, faithful, and virtuous housewife — Juan the husband, Maria the wife. One of the worst things about Juan was that he spent on another woman the greater part of the money which Maria could with difficulty scrape together; this other woman's name was Flora, who surpassed Maria in personal charm but in real worth was greatly Maria's inferior. Hence Maria soon grew distasteful to her husband, and after a year of married life he sought to be entertained by a more beautiful woman, spending most of his time in listless indolence by the side of Flora, returning home only to get his meals, which Maria prepared with the greatest care. But her efforts were all to no purpose: in vain did Maria array herself in her best clothes, and scent herself with the most delicate perfumes — her face remained pitted with small-pox scars, as before.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 47 'The Fate of an Envious Woman'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一對中產階級的年輕夫妻：丈夫是個魯莽的浪蕩子、揮霍無度，妻子卻是個虔誠、忠貞、賢淑的主婦——丈夫叫胡安，妻子叫瑪麗亞。胡安最糟糕的一點，是他把瑪麗亞好不容易才攢起來的大部分錢財，花在另一個女人身上；這另一個女人名叫弗洛拉，她在容貌上勝過瑪麗亞，但在真正的品德上卻遠不如瑪麗亞。因此，瑪麗亞很快就令丈夫生厭，婚後一年，他便想找個更漂亮的女人尋歡作樂，大部分時間都無精打采地懶散在弗洛拉身邊，只回家吃飯，而瑪麗亞總是極其用心地為他準備飯菜。但她的努力全都白費：瑪麗亞徒然穿上最好的衣服，給自己灑上最細緻的香水——她的臉上依然像從前一樣滿是天花留下的麻點。

passages.text: Years came and passed, and Juan became more and more harsh to his wife. At last Maria sought the aid of St. Vicente Ferrer: she knelt before the image, and asked the saint to rescue her husband from the pit into which he had fallen. Her prayers were soon answered: the image became animated; it touched her face several times, and in a few seconds Maria was converted into an extraordinary beauty — her once rough skin was now smooth and velvety. She then went to the window to await her husband's return; when he arrived an hour later, he was at first unwilling to come up into the house, for he did not believe that the beautiful woman was his wife, but at last she disclosed her true self to him. A great change now came over Juan: the once despised wife now began to enjoy the caresses of her husband, who pressed her close to his heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 47 'The Fate of an Envious Woman'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 歲月流逝，胡安對妻子越來越嚴厲。最後，瑪麗亞尋求聖文森特·費雷爾的幫助：她跪在聖像前，祈求聖人把丈夫從他所陷入的深淵中拯救出來。她的祈禱很快就得到了回應：聖像有了生命；它在她臉上觸碰了幾次，幾秒鐘之內，瑪麗亞就變成了一個非凡的美人——她曾經粗糙的皮膚如今光滑如絨。然後她走到窗邊等候丈夫歸來；一小時後他到了，起初他不願上樓進屋，因為他不相信那個美麗的女人就是他的妻子，但最後她向他顯露了真實的自己。胡安身上從此發生了巨大的變化：曾經被鄙視的妻子如今開始享受丈夫的愛撫，他把她緊緊摟在胸前。

passages.text: Days elapsed, and Flora began to get uneasy at her home, wondering why Juan did not come to see her; at length she went to his house, and after asking Maria how she had acquired her beauty decided to try her fortune also. She too knelt before the image of St. Vicente Ferrer — but, alas! instead of becoming as white and as beautiful as she hoped, she became black and ugly; her once delicate lips became thick and coarse, and her nose became as long as a monkey's tail. Filled with shame at her appearance, and with a consciousness of her own guilt, she went home, where she pined away and died. The once homely Maria, whose home had rung with the taunt and ridicule of those who made fun of her ugliness, now graced her house with sweet smiles and engaging features, which drew scores of visitors to her home; Juan confessed his sins and underwent penance for his wickedness, and the two lived together in peace and happiness the rest of their lives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 47 'The Fate of an Envious Woman'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 日子一天天過去，弗洛拉在家裡開始感到不安，納悶胡安為什麼不來看她；最後她去了他家，問過瑪麗亞是如何得到這般美貌之後，便決定也去試試自己的運氣。她也跪在聖文森特·費雷爾的聖像前——可是，唉！她非但沒有如她所願變得那麼白皙美麗，反而變得又黑又醜；她曾經嬌嫩的嘴唇變得又厚又粗，鼻子長得像猴子的尾巴。她對自己的容貌滿懷羞恥，又意識到自己的罪過，便回家去了，在那裡日漸憔悴而死。曾經相貌平庸的瑪麗亞，她的家曾迴盪著那些嘲笑她醜陋之人的譏諷與戲弄，如今卻以甜美的微笑和迷人的容貌為家增光，引來數十位訪客登門；胡安懺悔了自己的罪過，並為自己的惡行苦修贖罪，兩人此後一生和睦幸福地生活在一起。

title.en: The Monkey and Juan Pusong Tambi-tambi
title.zh: 猴子與條紋胡安

region.en: Tiring-tirang, La Campana hill, Ilocos region, Luzon, Philippines (tale's home barrio)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋伊洛克斯地區蒂陵蒂蘭與『鐘』山（故事原鄉）

period: Ilocano oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48a 'The Monkey and Juan Pusong Tambi-tambi', eBook #8299

summary.en: The waxen Juan image traps the thieving monkey, who buys his life with a promise of service. The monkey steals money, returns the king's borrowed ganta with coins in the cracks, and builds the tale of Don Juan Pusong Tambi-tambi, richest man in the world; he frightens the Burincantadas into the well, frees their prisoners, claims their herds, and leads the crooked farmer, striped-clothed, to marry Doña Elena — the king dying of joy at his new palace, the queen broken-hearted at her ugly husband, and Juan sole ruler of two kingdoms with the monkey as chief minister.
summary.zh: 蠟像胡安黏住偷玉米的猴子；猴子以『終身效力』換得性命。牠偷錢、以藏幣的量斗抬主成名，嚇得布林坎塔達三妖跳井，釋放囚徒、接收獸群，最後把衣衫襤褸的農夫打扮成『條紋胡安』迎娶埃蓮娜公主——國王見新宮樂極而亡，王后嫌夫醜陋抑鬱而終；胡安兼併兩國，猴子拜相。

sensitivity.note: Ilocano Puss-in-Boots variant recorded by Fansler from a Gonzaga narrator (Jaro, Iloilo; tale popular among 'the inhabitants of yesterday'); archival record. Fansler derives the cycle ultimately from Buddhistic lore (the helpful monkey as Bodhisatta; Tar-Baby via the Pancavudha-jataka).

passages.text: Tiring-tirang was a barrio in the town of Tang-tang, situated at the foot of a hill called 'La Campana' because of its shape; around the hill, about a mile from the barrio, flowed the Malogo River, in which the people of the town used to bathe. It so happened that one time an epidemic broke out in the community, killing off all the inhabitants except one couple, who had an only son named Juan Pusong Tambi-tambi. When Juan had reached his twelfth year his father died, and the boy had to go to work to earn money for the support of himself and his mother; at first he followed the occupation of his father, that of fisherman, but seeing that he made little money from this, he decided to become a farmer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48 'The Monkey and Juan Pusong Tambi-tambi'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蒂林蒂朗是唐唐鎮的一個小村莊，位於一座因形狀而被稱為「拉坎帕納」的山丘腳下；環繞這座山丘、距村莊約一英里處，流淌著馬洛戈河，鎮上的人常在那裡洗澡。有一次，社區裡恰好爆發了一場瘟疫，除了一對夫妻之外，所有居民都死光了，這對夫妻有一個獨生子，名叫胡安·普松·坦比坦比。胡安長到十二歲時，父親去世了，這男孩只得去工作賺錢，養活自己和母親；起初他繼承父業當漁夫，但眼看靠此賺不了多少錢，便決定去當農夫。

passages.text: One day Juan went to Pit-pit to buy medicine for his mother, and on his way back, seeing a flock of crows still eating his corn, he became angry: he picked up a stone about the size of his fist, crept into a bush near by, and hurled his stone with such accuracy and force that one of the crows fell dead to the ground; he tied the dead crow to a bamboo pole and planted it in the middle of his cornfield, and no sooner was he out of sight than the crows flew back to the field again — but when they saw their dead companion they flew off, and never troubled Juan again. For six months Juan had no trouble from birds; he did not know, however, that not far from his field there was a monkey (chongo) living in a large tree, which used to come to his field every day and steal two or three ears of corn. He made an image of a crooked old man like himself, covered it with sticky wax, and placed it in the middle of the field — and when the hungry monkey found it and asked courteous permission for three or four ears of corn, receiving no answer from the waxen statue, he slapped it with his right paw and stuck fast, then his left paw, then first one foot and then the other, until at last he could no longer move. Juan, who had been hiding in a bush near by, presented himself: 'Now I have caught you, you thief!' — but the monkey begged for mercy and promised that he would at some future time repay him for his kindness if he would only spare his life, so Juan set the monkey free.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48 'The Monkey and Juan Pusong Tambi-tambi'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，胡安去皮特皮特為母親買藥，回來的路上，看見一群烏鴉還在吃他的玉米，他很生氣：他撿起一塊約有拳頭大小的石頭，悄悄鑽進附近的灌木叢，又準又狠地把石頭擲了出去，一隻烏鴉當場落地而死；他把死烏鴉綁在一根竹竿上，插在玉米田中央，他剛一離開視線，烏鴉就又飛回田裡——但當牠們看見死去的同伴時，便飛走了，此後再沒來騷擾胡安。有六個月，胡安都沒有鳥患；然而他不知道，離他的田不遠處的一棵大樹上住著一隻猴子（chongo），牠每天都會到他的田裡偷兩三穗玉米。他照自己的模樣做了一個彎腰老人的雕像，塗上黏蠟，放在田中央——那隻飢餓的猴子發現了它，客客氣氣地請求給三四穗玉米，卻得不到蠟像的回答，便用右爪打了它一下，結果被牢牢黏住，接著是左爪，然後一隻腳、再另一隻腳，直到最後再也動彈不得。一直躲在附近灌木叢裡的胡安現身了：「這下我可逮住你了，你這個賊！」——但猴子求饒，並承諾只要胡安饒牠一命，日後一定會報答他的恩情，於是胡安把猴子放了。

passages.text: 'Master Juan, do you want to marry the king's daughter? If you do, I'll arrange everything for you,' said the monkey in April, and Juan, little thinking that what the monkey promised could be true, replied yes. The monkey stole a boy's money in the market, then went to the king's palace: 'Sir, my master, Juan, wants to borrow your ganta, for he desires to measure his money.' In three days the monkey returned the measure with three centavos stuck in the bottom — 'My master cares not for three cents. He has too much money. He is very, very rich' — and the king, much surprised to hear there was a man richer than himself, stuck four pieces of gold on the four corners of the ganta when the monkey next borrowed it, to find out who was the richer, Juan or he. Two weeks later the monkey returned the measure with a gold dollar on each corner: 'My master, Juan, returns you your ganta with a thousand thanks. He is the richest man in the world... He goes to church every morning wearing his striped (tambi-tambi) clothes. This is why he is known among his people as Juan Pusong Tambi-tambi. If you will just look out of your window to-morrow morning, you will see him pass by your garden.' The king's anger was appeased; and when the monkey added, 'My master, Juan, sends me to tell you frankly that he loves your daughter, and that, if it pleases you, he will marry her,' the king, being very desirous to get more money, at last consented without even asking his daughter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48 'The Monkey and Juan Pusong Tambi-tambi'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「胡安少爺，您想娶國王的女兒嗎？如果您想，我會替您安排一切。」猴子在四月說道。胡安幾乎沒想到猴子所承諾的事會成真，便回答說想。猴子在市場上偷了一個男孩的錢，然後前往國王的宮殿：「大人，我的主人胡安想借用您的量斗，因為他想量一量他的錢。」三天後，猴子歸還了量斗，斗底黏著三枚分幣——「我的主人不在乎三分錢。他的錢太多了。他非常、非常有錢。」——國王聽說有人比他還富有，大為驚訝，於是當猴子下次來借量斗時，國王在量斗的四角各黏上一枚金幣，想弄清楚究竟是胡安還是他自己更富有。兩週後，猴子歸還了量斗，四角各有一枚金元：「我的主人胡安歸還您的量斗，並致上千次的謝意。他是世上最富有的人……他每天早晨都穿著他的條紋（tambi-tambi）衣裳上教堂。這就是為什麼在他的子民當中，他被稱為胡安·普松·坦比坦比。您只要明天早晨往窗外一看，就會看見他經過您的花園。」國王的怒氣平息了；而當猴子又補上一句：「我的主人胡安派我來坦率地告訴您，他愛您的女兒，若您願意，他就要娶她。」國王因為極想得到更多錢財，最後連女兒都沒問一聲就答應了。

passages.text: Frightening an old man out of his bundle of clothes by shaking a tree, the monkey dressed his master for the wedding; then he ran to the home of the Burincantadas on the summit of the hill, where he began to scoop up the ground as fast as he could: 'Our king has been defeated in the war... The princess is dead, and it is said that everybody will be killed before tomorrow noon. I am resolved to hide myself under the ground to save my life.' 'For mercy's sake, have pity on us! Tell us where we can hide!' cried the three Burincantadas, already trembling with fear — 'If you will not let me scoop out a hole here, I'll jump into the well' — and as soon as they heard the word 'well,' they all ran as fast as they could, following the monkey, shouting 'Let us jump first!' — and so they did. The monkey made a motion as if he were going to follow, but instead lifted up the biggest stone he could find and threw it down the well: 'They are dead. Ah, I have caught you!' The Burincantadas now being dead, the monkey entered their palace, found many prisoners waiting to be eaten, set them all free, and told them to clean up the palace at once: 'My brothers and sisters, if any one comes and asks you who your master is, tell him that he is Don Juan Pusong Tambi-tambi.' Then he claimed for his master the thousands of horses, cows, and sheep on the farm, and hastened to Juan: 'Throw away your plough. Let's go to the king's palace, for to-night you will be married to the princess Doña Elena.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48 'The Monkey and Juan Pusong Tambi-tambi'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 猴子搖晃一棵樹，嚇得一個老人丟下他的衣物包袱，然後替主人打扮好去參加婚禮；接著牠跑到山頂上布林坎塔達斯人的家，開始盡快地刨挖地面：「我們的國王在戰爭中被打敗了……公主死了，據說明天正午之前所有人都會被殺。我決心躲到地底下保命。」「求您發發慈悲，可憐可憐我們吧！告訴我們可以躲在哪裡！」三個布林坎塔達斯人喊道，他們早已嚇得發抖——「你們若不讓我在這裡挖個洞，我就跳進井裡去。」——他們一聽到「井」這個字，便全都盡快地跟著猴子跑，喊著：「讓我們先跳！」——他們果真跳了。猴子裝出要跟著跳的樣子，卻反而舉起所能找到的最大的一塊石頭，往井裡扔下去：「他們死了。啊，我逮住你們了！」布林坎塔達斯人既已死去，猴子便進了他們的宮殿，發現許多俘虜正等著被吃掉，於是將他們全部釋放，並吩咐他們立刻把宮殿打掃乾淨：「我的兄弟姊妹們，若有人來問你們的主人是誰，就告訴他，是唐·胡安·普松·坦比坦比。」然後牠替主人認領了農場上成千的馬、牛和羊，又趕到胡安那裡：「扔掉你的犁吧。我們到國王的宮殿去，因為今晚你就要娶公主唐娜·艾蓮娜了。」

passages.text: Night came, and the palace was splendidly adorned; the princess was sitting by her father when Don Juan, dressed in his striped clothes and accompanied by the monkey, entered the gate. Soon the priest came, and the princess was called to the reception-hall — but when she saw her bridegroom she ran away in despair, crying to her father, 'Father, how dare you accept as my husband such a base, dirty, crooked man! Look at him! Why, he is the meanest of the mean.' But the king replied, 'He is rich. If you don't marry him, I'll punish you very severely,' and the princess had to obey her father; but before giving her hand to Juan Pusong she said, 'O God! Let me die.' When the marriage ceremony was over, they set out by carriage for Don Juan's palace; four hours passed, and still no palace was to be seen — 'Monkey, if what you have said to me is not true, your head shall answer for your lie' — but then the shepherds answered that the herds were all owned by Don Juan Pusong, and the palace came in sight, so magnificent that the king said, 'Why, it is not a palace; it is heaven itself.' Upstairs the king confessed, 'I am not the richest man on earth' — and soon he died of joy, his body being placed in a golden coffin and buried in the church. The couple inherited his dominion; but Queen Elena could not endure her ugly husband, and two weeks later she died broken-hearted — so Juan was left as sole ruler of two kingdoms, and the monkey became his chief minister.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48 'The Monkey and Juan Pusong Tambi-tambi'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 夜晚來臨，宮殿裝飾得富麗堂皇；公主正坐在父親身旁，這時唐·胡安穿著他的條紋衣裳，由猴子陪同，走進了大門。不久神父來了，公主被叫到接待廳——但她一看見新郎，便絕望地跑開，向父親哭喊：「父親，您怎麼敢接受這樣一個卑賤、骯髒、歪斜的人做我的丈夫！您看看他！哎呀，他是最卑賤者中最卑賤的。」但國王回答：「他有錢。你若不嫁給他，我要嚴厲地懲罰你。」公主只得服從父親；但在把手交給胡安·普松之前，她說：「噢，上帝！讓我死吧。」婚禮儀式結束後，他們乘馬車出發前往唐·胡安的宮殿；四個時辰過去了，仍不見宮殿的蹤影——「猴子，你若對我說的話不是真的，你的頭就要為你的謊言負責。」——但接著牧人們回答說，那些牲畜全都屬於胡安·普松，宮殿也映入眼簾，宏偉得讓國王說：「哎呀，這不是宮殿；這簡直就是天堂。」上樓之後，國王坦承：「我不是世上最富有的人。」——不久他便因歡喜而死，遺體被放入金棺，葬於教堂。這對夫妻繼承了他的領地；但艾蓮娜王后受不了她那醜陋的丈夫，兩週後便心碎而死——於是胡安成了兩個王國唯一的統治者，而猴子則成了他的首席大臣。

title.en: Andres the Trapper
title.zh: 捕鳥人安德烈斯

region.en: San Carlos, Pangasinan, Luzon, Philippines (story popular among the Pangasinanes)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦阿西楠省聖卡洛斯（邦阿西楠人流行故事）

period: Pangasinan oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48b 'Andres the Trapper', eBook #8299

summary.en: Andres, an orphan trapper, spares a monkey caught in his snare; the grateful animal sells his wild chickens, borrows the rich Don Toribio's measures with coins stuck in the cracks to prove his master counts his money, dresses Andres in shoes and ready-made clothes, teaches him elegance, and marries him to the most beautiful girl in the province — Aning — whose inheritance he commands when Don Toribio dies.
summary.zh: 孤兒捕鳥人安德烈斯放了陷在網中的猴子；知恩的猴子替他賣野雞、向富紳東·托里比奧借斗量錢——斗縫裡嵌滿銀幣，謠言遂起。猴子為他添置鞋帽新衣、教他舉止談吐，終促成他與全省最美的姑娘阿寧的婚事；東·托里比奧死後，安德烈斯繼承全部家產。

sensitivity.note: Pangasinan Puss-in-Boots variant recorded by Fansler from a Perez narrator (San Carlos); archival record. Fansler notes the monkey takes the place of the cat, fox, or jackal of other traditions, and connects the animal's gratitude to Buddhistic lore.

passages.text: Once upon a time there lived in a village a poor widow who had an only son named Andres; they lived in a small hut situated near the Patacbo forest. When Andres was between twelve and thirteen years old his mother died, and from then on he lived alone in his mean little hut, where he had to cook his own food and wash his own clothes. One morning some boys invited Andres to go to the woods with them to trap; his companions set their traps in the places where the wild chickens used to feed, and when they returned in the afternoon each trap had caught a wild cock. Andres became envious of his companions, took his knife and made two traps of his own, and found two wild cocks snared the next morning; he sold one and ate the other for his dinner, made many more traps, and from then on made his living by trapping, often catching as many as fifteen birds in a day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48 'Andres the Trapper'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前，有個村子裡住著一位貧窮的寡婦，她有個獨生子名叫安德烈斯；他們住在帕塔克博森林附近的一間小屋裡。安德烈斯十二三歲時，母親去世了，從此他便獨自住在簡陋的小屋裡，得自己煮飯、自己洗衣。一天早晨，幾個男孩邀安德烈斯和他們一起去樹林裡設陷阱捕獵；同伴們把陷阱設在野雞常來覓食的地方，下午他們回來時，每個陷阱都捕到了一隻野公雞。安德烈斯對同伴們心生羨慕，便拿起刀，自己做了兩個陷阱，第二天早晨發現捕到了兩隻野公雞；他賣掉一隻，另一隻當晚餐吃了，又做了更多陷阱，從此便以設陷阱捕獵為生，常常一天捕到多達十五隻鳥。

passages.text: One day, after Andres had been a trapper for many years, he went to the forest as usual to see what he had caught, and found that his traps had been moved and that in one of them was a big monkey caught by the leg. As Andres was about to kill the monkey with a big stick, the animal said to him, 'My dear Andres, don't harm me! And I will be your helper by and by.' Andres was much astonished to hear the monkey talk; he was moved to pity and set the animal free, and when he started toward his home the monkey followed him — from then on they lived together, and soon the monkey learned how to sell wild chickens in the market.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48 'Andres the Trapper'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，安德烈斯當了多年捕獵者之後，照常到森林裡去看自己捕到了什麼，卻發現他的陷阱被人移動過，其中一個陷阱裡有一隻大猴子被夾住了腿。正當安德烈斯要拿大棍子打死那猴子時，那動物對他說：「親愛的安德烈斯，別傷害我！日後我會做你的幫手。」安德烈斯聽到猴子說話，大為驚訝；他心生憐憫，便把牠放了，而當他動身回家時，猴子跟在他後面——從此他們便住在一起，不久猴子就學會了在市場上賣野雞。

passages.text: In that town there lived a very rich man by the name of Toribio, who had a daughter named Aning; the people considered Aning the most beautiful lady in the province, but none of the young men of the town courted Aning, for they felt unworthy and ashamed to woo the richest and most beautiful girl. One fine day the monkey went to town and sold wild chickens as usual; on his way home he stopped at Don Toribio's house and said that his master had sent him to borrow their money-measure — 'Don't you know? Don Andres, a very rich, handsome young gentleman who lives in the valley of Obong.' Don Toribio at once lent the ganta-measure to the monkey, who, before returning it to the owner the next morning, put a peso, a fifty-centavo piece, a peseta, and a media-peseta in the cracks of the measure. 'Has your master finished measuring his money?' — 'No, sir! We have not finished; but this box is too small, and it takes us too long to measure with it' — and Don Toribio brought a cavan, which equals about twenty-five gantas, for the monkey to keep till the next day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48 'Andres the Trapper'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那個鎮上住著一位非常富有的人，名叫托里比奧，他有個女兒名叫阿寧；人們都認為阿寧是全省最美麗的姑娘，但鎮上年輕男子沒有一個去追求阿寧，因為他們覺得自己不配，也羞於向最有錢、最美麗的姑娘求愛。一個晴朗的日子，猴子照常進城賣野雞；回家途中，牠在唐·托里比奧家門前停下，說牠的主人派牠來借他們的量錢斗——「您不知道嗎？唐·安德烈斯，一位非常富有、英俊的年輕紳士，住在奧邦谷地。」唐·托里比奧立刻把量斗借給了猴子；猴子在第二天早晨歸還之前，在量斗的縫隙裡塞了一枚比索、一枚五十分幣、一枚皮塞塔和一枚半皮塞塔。「你的主人量完他的錢了嗎？」——「還沒有，先生！我們還沒量完；但這個盒子太小了，用它量太費時間。」——於是唐·托里比奧拿來一個卡班（約等於二十五個量斗），讓猴子留到第二天。

passages.text: 'Ah, me! What money are you going to count? Don't you know that we are very poor?' said Andres when he saw the large measure. 'Let me manage things, Andres, and I promise you that you shall marry the beautiful daughter of the rich man,' said the monkey. The following day Andres caught many wild chickens, and when the monkey had sold them all in the market he went back to their hut and took the cavan he had borrowed, sticking money in the cracks before returning it to Don Toribio, as he had done to the first measure. 'I am the richest man in town, yet I cannot throw money away like the master of this fellow,' said Don Toribio to himself; 'perhaps he is even richer than I am.' When the monkey was about to take his leave, the rich man told him to tell his master to come there on the third day; the monkey stopped at the market on his way home to buy a pair of shoes, some ready-made clothes, and a hat for Andres, and in three days had taught Andres how to walk easily with shoes on, how to speak elegantly, how to eat with a spoon and fork and knife, and how to tell Don Toribio that he wanted to marry his daughter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48 'Andres the Trapper'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「哎呀！你要數什麼錢？你難道不知道我們很窮嗎？」安德烈斯看見那個大斗時說道。「讓我來處理事情吧，安德烈斯，我向你保證，你會娶到那富人的美麗女兒。」猴子說。第二天，安德烈斯捉了許多野雞，猴子把牠們全賣到市場後，回到他們的小屋，取出他借來的斗，在還給唐·托里比奧之前把錢塞進斗的縫隙裡，就像他對第一個量器所做的那樣。「我是鎮上最有錢的人，卻不能像這傢伙的主人那樣把錢亂扔，」唐·托里比奧自言自語道；「也許他比我還富有。」猴子正要告辭時，富人叫牠轉告牠的主人第三天到那裡來；猴子在回家途中停在市場，為安德烈斯買了一雙鞋、一些現成的衣服和一頂帽子，並在三天內教會安德烈斯如何穿著鞋子輕鬆走路、如何優雅地說話、如何用湯匙、叉子和刀子吃飯，以及如何告訴唐·托里比奧他想娶他的女兒。

passages.text: When the time came, Andres and the monkey set out for the town; they were welcomed by Don Toribio and his daughter Aning, and after a short talk Andres spoke of his purpose in coming there — he wanted to marry Don Toribio's daughter. Don Toribio gladly accepted the offer and said that the wedding would be held the next morning; hasty preparations were made for the ceremony, and in the morning a priest came, and Andres and Aning were married. Many guests were present, and everybody had a good time. A few years later Don Toribio died, and Andres inherited all his wealth; he then became a very rich man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48 'Andres the Trapper'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 時候到了，安德烈斯和猴子動身前往鎮上；他們受到唐·托里比奧和他的女兒阿寧的歡迎，簡短交談之後，安德烈斯說出了他來此的目的——他想娶唐·托里比奧的女兒。唐·托里比奧欣然接受了這門親事，並說婚禮將於第二天早上舉行；人們匆忙為典禮做準備，到了早上，一位神父來了，安德烈斯和阿寧結了婚。許多賓客到場，大家都玩得很盡興。幾年後，唐·托里比奧去世，安德烈斯繼承了他所有的財富；他於是成了非常富有的人。

title.en: Juan the Fool: The Dead Wife, the Crabs, and the Lizard
title.zh: 糊塗胡安：死妻、螃蟹與蜥蜴

region.en: Bocawe, Bulakan, Luzon, Philippines (where the story was told at a barrio gathering)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋布拉克省博卡維（ barrio 聚會所講的故事）

period: Tagalog noodle-tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 49 'Juan the Fool', eBook #8299

summary.en: Told to take a quiet, tongue-tied wife, Juan finds a corpse in bed; told that 'those who stink are dead,' he buries his napping mother and floats downstream on a banana raft as a dead man himself. Housekeeper to robbers, he kills a murmuring pot that mocks him, sends two dozen crabs swimming across the river 'straight home,' falls on a lizard and cries 'Tao, tao!' in terror — until, living in a mango-tree, he drops his bamboo table on two money-bearers and makes off with the bag, buying a house, a carabao, and a cart.
summary.zh: 奉母命娶『安靜寡言』之妻的胡安，抱回一具女屍；學得『發臭者必死』的教訓後，他埋葬了午睡的母親，又自認已死，乘香蕉筏順流漂去。為強盜當家：他打死『嘲笑他』的沸鍋、讓廿四隻螃蟹『自行游回家』、被蜥蜴落背嚇得喊『有人！有人！』——直到棲身芒果樹上，他把竹桌砸向兩個帶錢人，席捲錢袋，置屋置牛置車而去。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog noodle-tale recorded by Fansler from a Mendoza narrator (story from Bulakan, told at an informal barrio gathering); archival record.

passages.text: Juan is twenty years old, and at this age begins to become famous in his little barrio: short in stature, with very black eyes that slowly roll in their sockets, a narrow mouth, a double chin, a short flat nose, a broad forehead, thick lips, black straight hair, a body round like a pumpkin, and short legs — he seems to be always tired, yet he is invited to every bayluhan and katapusan because he is sure to bring with him laughter and merriment. Juan lives in a poor barrio which consists of a few poor nipa huts, with a small chapel of stone with a turret and bells, a cross erected in the courtyard, and a rivulet just outside the village hidden in a thick forest extending to the foot of a mountain. At the time the story opens Juan is eating his breakfast with his mother, an old widow whose sole ambition is to establish Juan in a good social position; she is constantly advising her son that a good wife is always quiet and tongue-tied, and does not go noisily about the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 49 'Juan the Fool'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 胡安二十歲了，在這個年紀，他開始在他那個小小的街區裡出名：身材矮小，眼睛非常黑，在眼窩裡緩緩轉動，嘴巴窄小，有雙下巴，鼻子短而扁，額頭寬闊，嘴唇厚，頭髮黑而直，身體圓得像南瓜，腿很短——他似乎總是疲倦，卻被邀請參加每一場舞會和聚會，因為他必定會帶來歡笑與熱鬧。胡安住在一個貧窮的街區，那裡只有幾間破舊的尼帕小屋，一座帶有小塔和鐘的石造小教堂，庭院裡立著一座十字架，村外不遠處有一條小溪，隱沒在茂密的森林中，森林一直延伸到山腳下。故事開始時，胡安正和母親一起吃早餐，他母親是個老寡婦，唯一的願望就是讓胡安建立良好的社會地位；她不斷告誡兒子，好妻子總是安靜而沉默寡言，不會在家裡吵吵鬧鬧地走來走去。

passages.text: As Juan is an obedient son, he soon determines to get him a good wife; after a short time he comes home to his mother and says, 'Mother, I have found the girl you will like — the one who shall be my wife. She is speechless and motionless. Her eyes are staring in just one place. Though I have watched her closely for about twelve hours, I have not observed the slightest motion in her lips and eyelids. She remained quiet in her bed, although there were many noisy people in the house.' 'And is that all?' says his mother. 'No, mother... Her hands were very cold. She was deaf, and she did not answer me. This fact makes her all the lovelier... There is only one thing you did not tell me, however. The girl had a stinking waxy-like odor.' 'O Juan! I already suspected from your long description that you followed my instructions too literally. The girl you found is a dead one. Now, remember: those who stink are dead.' 'Thanks, mother. I will never forget that.' A few days later, when Juan and his mother are eating their breakfast, Juan smells a stinking odor; as he does not see anyone else in the little room, he thinks that his mother is dead. Then, when his mother is taking her siesta, Juan says to himself, 'Surely mother is dead'; he goes out quietly and digs a grave for her, buries her in it, and mourns for her nine days — now Juan is alone in the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 49 'Juan the Fool'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 胡安是個孝順的兒子，他很快就決定要給自己找個好妻子；不久之後，他回家對母親說：「母親，我找到了一個您會喜歡的姑娘——就是將要成為我妻子的那一個。她不說話，也不動。她的眼睛直盯著一個地方。雖然我仔細觀察了她大約十二個小時，卻沒有察覺她的嘴唇和眼皮有絲毫動靜。她安靜地躺在床上，儘管屋裡有許多吵鬧的人。」「就這些嗎？」他母親說。「不，母親……她的手非常冰冷。她耳聾，也沒有回答我。這一點使她更加可愛……不過，只有一件事您沒有告訴我。那姑娘身上有一股像蠟一樣的臭味。」「噢，胡安！從你冗長的描述中，我就已經懷疑你把我的話照字面理解得太過了。你找到的那個姑娘是個死人。現在，記住：發臭的人都是死的。」「謝謝您，母親。我永遠不會忘記這一點。」幾天後，胡安和母親正在吃早餐時，胡安聞到一股臭味；由於他在小房間裡沒看到其他人，便以為母親死了。後來，當母親在午睡時，胡安自言自語道：「母親肯定死了」；他悄悄走出去，為她挖了一個墳墓，把她埋了進去，並為她哀悼了九天——如今胡安在這世上孤身一人。

passages.text: One morning, when Juan is eating his breakfast by himself, he smells again a stinking odor; he looks around, and, as he does not see anyone, he thinks that he himself is dead. There is nobody to bury him, so he goes to the river, takes five or six banana-trunks, and makes a raft of them; he lies down on the raft and lets the current of the river carry him away. In three hours the current has carried him into the woods, where all of a sudden he is called in a fierce voice by the captain of a band of robbers; Juan does not stir in his place, but sadly tells the robbers that he is a dead man — until the captain frightens him, saying he will shoot if he does not get up. As Juan does not care for the taste of bullets, he goes to the bank of the river, still thinking that he is a walking dead body, and goes with the robbers into the woods, where the captain appoints Juan their housekeeper, ordering him to cook rice but to keep very still and quiet, for they may be caught by the Spanish soldiers (cazadores).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 49 'Juan the Fool'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一天早上，胡安獨自吃早餐時，又聞到一股臭味；他環顧四周，由於沒看到任何人，便以為自己死了。沒有人來埋葬他，於是他走到河邊，取了五六根香蕉樹幹，用它們做了一個木筏；他躺在木筏上，讓河水把他沖走。三個小時後，水流把他帶進了樹林，在那裡，一夥強盜的首領突然用兇惡的聲音叫他；胡安在原地一動不動，只是悲傷地告訴強盜們他是個死人——直到首領嚇唬他，說如果他不起來就開槍。由於胡安不喜歡子彈的滋味，他便走到河岸邊，仍然以為自己是個會走路的死屍，跟著強盜們進了樹林，首領在那裡指派胡安當他們的管家，命令他煮飯，但要保持非常安靜，因為他們可能會被西班牙士兵（獵兵）抓到。

passages.text: Juan shuts the windows, and everything is quiet and undisturbed; he even tries to control his breathing for fear of the noise it may make. Cautiously he takes an earthen pot and puts rice and water into it, places the pot on the fire, and sits down near it — everything is silent until suddenly a murmuring sound seems to come from the pot (the water is beginning to boil). Juan thinks that the pot is saying, 'Buluk ka' — 'You are decayed' — and gets very angry; he whispers to the pot to stop, but the sound becomes louder and louder, until at last, exasperated, he takes a piece of bamboo-bellows and gives the pot a fatal blow, putting an end to the pot, the rice, and the flames. At noon the hungry robbers come home to find Juan almost breathless in the darkest corner of the house, the pot broken and the rice scattered over the floor; Juan says that the naughty pot was making too much noise and mocking him, and the captain cannot help smiling at Juan's foolishness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 49 'Juan the Fool'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 胡安關上窗戶，一切安靜無擾；他甚至試著控制自己的呼吸，唯恐發出聲響。他小心翼翼地拿來一個陶罐，把米和水放進去，將罐子放在火上，然後在旁邊坐下——一切都很寂靜，直到突然似乎有喃喃的聲音從罐子裡傳出（水開始沸騰了）。胡安以為罐子在說「Buluk ka」——「你腐爛了」——便非常生氣；他低聲叫罐子停下來，但聲音卻越來越大，最後他忍無可忍，拿起一片竹製的風箱，給了罐子致命的一擊，結束了罐子、米飯和火焰。中午，飢餓的強盜們回家，發現胡安幾乎喘不過氣地躲在屋裡最暗的角落，罐子破了，米撒了一地；胡安說那個頑皮的罐子太吵，還嘲笑他，首領不禁對胡安的愚蠢笑了起來。

passages.text: The next day the captain gives Juan some money and tells him to go to the market to buy some earthen pots and some crabs; Juan buys all the crabs he can find and about two dozen large earthen pots, then threads them all on a long piece of sharpened rattan to carry them easily. Soon he comes to a large, wide river with a very strong current: he remembers that crabs are good swimmers, so he decides to untie them and let them swim to the other side. 'Now, crabs, we have to cross this broad river. I know that you are good swimmers... Please swim to the other side of the river as quickly as you can, for I cannot carry you. If you reach the other side before I do, you may go straight home, or wait for me' — and he is very glad to see them swim so fast. He looks around for the crabs, but, seeing none, he says to himself, 'Perhaps they have become tired of waiting for me and have gone straight home, as I ordered them to do. What a surprise for the captain!' — and when he finds out that not one of the naughty crabs obeyed him, he blames himself for his quiet nature and swears that he will never trust a crab again; when the robbers see the holes in the bottom of all the pots they cannot help laughing, and the captain addresses Juan with all the epithets found in a common slang dictionary. Several days later the captain calls Juan one night to rob a certain house, and says, 'Juan, go into the silong of the house, and see if the people are awake. Now, remember, if you feel something hot, it is a man; but if it is cold, it is a bolo.' After a while something hot falls on Juan's back; he quickly runs away crying, 'Tao, tao!' — 'Man, man!' — and all the robbers flee too. When the robbers light a match they see only a little lizard clinging to Juan's worn-out camisa; the captain tells Juan he may go away, for he is not worth anything.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 49 'Juan the Fool'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天，船長給胡安一些錢，叫他去市場買些陶罐和一些螃蟹；胡安把他能找到的螃蟹全買了下來，又買了大約兩打大陶罐，然後用一根削尖的長藤條把它們全串起來，好方便搬運。不久，他來到一條又寬又大、水流湍急的河邊：他想起螃蟹很會游泳，便決定把牠們解開，讓牠們游到對岸去。「好了，螃蟹，我們得渡過這條寬闊的河。我知道你們很會游泳……請你們盡快游到河的對岸去，因為我沒辦法帶你們過去。如果你們比我先到對岸，你們可以直接回家，或者等我。」——他看到牠們游得那麼快，非常高興。他四下張望找螃蟹，卻一隻也沒看見，便自言自語道：「也許牠們等得不耐煩了，就照我吩咐的直接回家了。船長準會大吃一驚！」——而當他發現那些頑皮的螃蟹一隻也沒聽他的話時，他怪自己性子太溫和，發誓再也不相信螃蟹了；強盜們看見所有陶罐底部都有洞，忍不住大笑起來，船長則用一本普通俚語詞典裡能找到的所有稱呼來罵胡安。幾天後的一個晚上，船長叫胡安去搶某戶人家，說道：「胡安，進到那戶人家的樓下（silong）去，看看那些人醒了沒有。記住，如果你摸到熱的東西，那是人；如果是冷的，那是波洛刀。」過了一會兒，有樣熱乎乎的東西落到胡安背上；他立刻跑開，大喊：「Tao, tao!」——「人，人！」——強盜們也都逃走了。強盜們點亮一根火柴，只看見一隻小蜥蜴黏在胡安破舊的襯衫上；船長叫胡安滾開，因為他一文不值。

passages.text: Juan leaves the band of robbers and decides to live up in a tree, because he is all alone: he takes a low bamboo table and goes up into a very large mango-tree, choosing a well-hidden place, and ties his table firmly to the branches; he spends the day in the neighboring towns looking for food, but at night he comes back to the tree and sleeps there. Early one morning Juan wakes up and hears faint whispers: he looks down and sees two men talking very earnestly together, one of them carrying a bag of money. Juan loosens his table and lets it fall on the men; it makes a loud crash, and they run away. Juan quickly climbs down the tree and makes off with the bag of money. He now decides to live in town: after he has found a barrio that suits him, he buys a house, a carabao, and a cart, and lives peacefully in his new house — sometimes he works, but he spends most of his time sleeping, for he is a very lazy fellow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 49 'Juan the Fool'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 胡安離開強盜團夥，決定住到樹上去，因為他孤身一人：他帶了一張矮竹桌，爬上一棵很大的芒果樹，挑了個隱蔽的好地方，把桌子牢牢綁在樹枝上；他白天到鄰近的鎮上找吃的，晚上就回到樹上睡覺。一天清晨，胡安醒來，聽見隱約的低語聲：他往下一看，看見兩個男人正非常認真地交談，其中一人帶著一袋錢。胡安鬆開桌子，讓它掉到那兩人身上；桌子發出很大的撞擊聲，他們便逃走了。胡安趕緊爬下樹，帶著那袋錢溜走。他現在決定住到鎮上：找到一個合意的村莊（barrio）後，他買了一棟房子、一頭水牛和一輛牛車，在新家裡平靜地過日子——他有時幹活，但大部分時間都在睡覺，因為他是個非常懶惰的傢伙。

title.en: Juan and His Painted Hat
title.zh: 胡安與彩繪帽

region.en: Manila, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home city)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋馬尼拉（敘述者居地）

period: Tagalog oral droll; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 50 'Juan and his Painted Hat', eBook #8299

summary.en: Down to seventy pesos, Juan deposits twenty in each of a town's three stores, contracting that a bow of his hat shall be payment. Publicly feasting at each, he sells the 'magic' hat to the highest bidder for five thousand pesos and sails away — while the buyer, bowing in a store he has not paid, is arrested, and faints with sickness on learning the simple trick.
summary.zh: 胡安僅剩七十比索，便向鎮上三家店鋪各存二十比索，約定『脫帽一躬即為付款』。他在各家當眾宴請、行禮離店，把『有魔法的帽子』以五千比索售予出價最高者，揚帆而去——而買主在他未存錢的店鋪行禮，遭店家喝令逮捕；聽聞這簡單的把戲後，當場昏厥。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog droll recorded by Fansler from a Scheerer narrator (Manila); archival record. The 'hat pays' episode, imported from Europe where it is part of the Master-Cheat cycle (Bolte-Polívka on Grimm No. 61).

passages.text: There once lived a man by the name of Juan, who did nothing but fool people all the time. Once, when he had only seventy pesos left in his pockets, he determined to resort to the following scheme: he bought a balangut hat (a very cheap straw), and painted it five different colors. In the town where Juan was to operate there were only three stores; he went to each one of them and deposited twenty pesos, saying to the owner of each, 'I will deposit twenty pesos in your store, and to-morrow afternoon I will bring some friends here with me. We will perhaps take some refreshments or buy some goods, but in any case I will see to it that the total amount of the things we take is not over the twenty pesos. Then, when we leave, do not ask me to pay you for the things. I will simply make you a bow with my hat, and your attendants should thank me with much courtesy. That mere bow with my hat is to be the payment. You may keep the twenty pesos, but you must also keep this little plan a secret.' The owners of the three stores promised.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 50 'Juan and his Painted Hat'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個人名叫胡安，他什麼都不做，整天只會愚弄別人。有一次，他口袋裡只剩下七十披索，便決定使出以下計謀：他買了一頂巴朗古特帽（balangut，一種非常便宜的草帽），把它漆成五種不同的顏色。胡安要行騙的那個鎮上只有三家店；他逐家走訪，每家存了二十披索，並對每一家的店主說：「我要在你的店裡存二十披索，明天下午我會帶幾個朋友來這裡。我們也許會吃些點心，或者買些貨物，但無論如何，我會確保我們拿的東西總價不超過這二十披索。然後，我們離開時，不要叫我付錢。我只要用帽子向你們鞠個躬，你們的夥計就該很有禮貌地向我道謝。單憑我用帽子鞠的那個躬，就是付款。那二十披索你可以留著，但你也必須對這個小計畫保密。」三家店的店主都答應了。

passages.text: The next day Juan was walking in the street with his painted hat on, when one of his friends met him: 'Halloo, Juan! Where did you get that funny hat?' Juan looked serious, and said, 'Don't be foolish! Don't you know that this hat is the only means I have of earning a living? Why, of course. I can go in any store, take anything I please, and pay for it with a mere bow of my hat.' By this time two other friends of Juan had come along, and they too were surprised to see what Juan had on his head; to convince them of the marvellous character of the hat, Juan took his friends to one of the stores, where they sat down and Juan ordered some refreshments; they ate much, and of the best that the store could furnish — then Juan stood up, made a bow to the proprietor with his hat, and they all left, the same thing taking place in another store.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 50 'Juan and his Painted Hat'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天，胡安戴著他那頂彩繪帽子走在街上，他的一個朋友遇見了他：「喂，胡安！你從哪兒弄來那頂滑稽的帽子？」胡安一本正經地說：「別傻了！你難道不知道這頂帽子是我謀生的唯一手段嗎？那當然啦。我可以走進任何一家店，想拿什麼就拿什麼，只要用帽子鞠個躬就能付帳。」這時，胡安另外兩個朋友也走了過來，他們看到胡安頭上戴的東西也很驚訝；為了讓他們相信這頂帽子的神奇之處，胡安帶朋友們去了一家店，他們坐下來，胡安點了幾樣點心；他們吃了很多，而且都是店裡能供應的最好的東西——然後胡安站起來，用帽子向店主鞠了一躬，他們便全都離開了，在另一家店裡也發生了同樣的事。

passages.text: The friends of Juan were very much astonished, and each wished to possess the hat: one offered him a thousand pesos for it; another, two thousand; and the third, one-half of all his property, which amounted to about five thousand pesos. Juan, of course, was willing to sell it to the highest bidder; but when the sale was about to be concluded, the buyer began to doubt the power of the hat, so he asked Juan to take him to another store to prove once more the qualities of the hat — and Juan took his friend to the third store, and the friend was now sure that the hat could really work wonders. So he paid Juan the five thousand pesos.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 50 'Juan and his Painted Hat'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 胡安的朋友們大為驚奇，每個人都想得到那頂帽子：一個出價一千披索買它；另一個出價兩千；第三個則願出他全部財產的一半，那大約值五千披索。胡安當然願意賣給出價最高的人；但就在買賣即將成交時，買主開始懷疑帽子的威力，於是請胡安帶他去另一家店，再證明一次帽子的功效——胡安便帶他的朋友去了第三家店，這下朋友確信這頂帽子真能創造奇蹟。於是他付給胡安五千披索。

passages.text: When he had received the money, Juan left his friends, went on board ship, and sailed away to a foreign country. One day the friend who had bought the hat desired to make a showing with it; so he invited several friends, among them some ladies, took them to one of the stores, and ordered some refreshments to be served — and when they had finished, the man bowed with his hat and started to leave. 'Thank you, sir! But where is my payment for the refreshments you have just eaten?' The owner of the hat was astonished, and, thinking that perhaps he held the hat in the wrong way, or else his fingers were not on the right color, he turned the hat around and made another bow; the owner of the shop now became angry and began to swear at the man, who, excited, twirled the hat around and held it in as many different ways as he could think of — finally the shop-keeper ordered the man arrested. When the owner of the hat heard how Juan had played his trick by paying twenty pesos in advance, he fainted and became very sick; in the meantime Juan was performing other tricks in some different country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 50 'Juan and his Painted Hat'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 胡安拿到錢後，便離開朋友們，上了船，揚帆前往外國。有一天，買下那頂帽子的朋友想拿它炫耀一番；於是他邀請了幾位朋友，其中還有幾位女士，帶他們去一家店，點了幾樣點心來吃——吃完後，那人用帽子鞠了一躬，正要離開。「謝謝您，先生！可是您剛才吃的點心錢呢？」帽子的主人大吃一驚，心想也許是自己拿帽子的方式不對，或者是手指沒按在正確的顏色上，於是他把帽子轉了一圈，又鞠了一躬；店主這下生氣了，開始咒罵那人，那人一急，便把帽子轉來轉去，盡可能想出各種不同的拿法——最後店主叫人把那個人抓了起來。當帽子的主人得知胡安是怎麼預付二十披索來耍這個把戲時，他昏了過去，病得很重；與此同時，胡安正在別的國家耍著其他的把戲。

title.en: Juan and Clotilde: The Ladder of Nails and the Matched Necklaces
title.zh: 胡安與克洛蒂爾德：釘梯與相配的項鍊

region.en: Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's tale-source)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省（故事原鄉）

period: Tagalog Märchen; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 51 'Juan and Clotilde', eBook #8299

summary.en: A dying magician locks Princess Clotilde and three winged horses in a tower 'inaccessible to any human being'; kings' sons fail, but the peasant Juan builds a ladder of nails and rope, receives one of her two matchless necklaces, and flees a winged horse to a strange land when his treacherous brother pulls out the nails. Years later, hired as a farmhand, he borrows the princess's necklace from his adopted father and hammers an exact match — 'By the aid of the Lord! My lover is here again' — and the festivities continue nine days and nine nights before Juan succeeds to the throne.
summary.zh: 垂死的魔法師把公主克洛蒂爾德與三匹有翼馬鎖進『凡人不可攀』的高塔；諸王子皆敗，農夫胡安卻以長釘與繩索搭成釘梯登頂，得公主一條無雙項鍊；惡兄拔釘斷路，他乘飛馬飄落異鄉。多年後，他藉義父之名借來公主的項鍊，徹夜鎚打出分毫不差的複製品——『上天保佑！我的愛人又來了』——婚宴連慶九日九夜，胡安終登王位。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog Märchen recorded by Fansler from a Hilario narrator (Batangas); archival record. Fansler relates it to the eighteenth-century Spanish ballad by Alonso de Morales ('Las Princesas Encantadas'), itself founded on Oriental material transmitted by the Arabs.

passages.text: In ages vastly remote there lived in a distant land a king of such prowess and renown that his name was known throughout the four regions of the compass; his name was Ludovico, and his power was increased twofold by his attachment to an aged magician, to whom he was tied by strong bonds of friendship. Ludovico had an extremely lovely daughter by the name of Clotilde; ever since his arrival at the palace the magician had been passionately in love with her, but his extreme old age and his somewhat haughty bearing were obstacles in his path to success, and whenever he made love to her she turned aside and listened instead to the thrilling tales told by some wandering minstrel. The magician finally succumbed to the infirmities of old age, his life made more burdensome by his repeated disappointments; he left to the king three enchanted winged horses, to the princess two magic necklaces of exactly the same appearance, of inimitable workmanship and of priceless worth — and before he expired he locked Clotilde and the three magic horses in a high tower inaccessible to any human being, where she was to remain in this enchanted prison until some man succeeded in setting her free.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 51 'Juan and Clotilde'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在極其遙遠的太古時代，遠方的一片土地上住著一位英勇與名聲如此顯赫的國王，以致他的名字傳遍四方八極；他的名字叫盧多維科，而他因與一位年邁魔法師的交情，力量倍增，他與那魔法師以牢固的友誼紐帶相繫。盧多維科有一個極其可愛的女兒，名叫克洛蒂爾德；自魔法師來到宮廷以來，他便熱烈地愛上了她，但他極高的年歲與略顯傲慢的舉止，成了他成功之路上的障礙，每當他向她求愛，她便轉過身去，轉而聆聽某位遊吟詩人所講的動人故事。魔法師最終不敵年邁體衰，屢次的失望使他的生命更加沉重；他留給國王三匹施了魔法的有翼馬，留給公主兩條外觀完全相同、工藝無與倫比、價值連城的魔法項鍊——而在嚥氣之前，他將克洛蒂爾德與那三匹魔法馬鎖在一座高塔之中，任何人類都無法進入，她將留在這座施了魔法的牢獄裡，直到有某個男子成功將她解救出來。

passages.text: Naturally, King Ludovico wanted to see his daughter before the hour of his death, which was fast approaching; he offered large sums of money, together with his crown and Clotilde's hand, to anybody who could set her free. Hundreds of princes tried, but in vain: the stone walls of the tower were of such a height that very few birds, even, could fly over them. But a deliverer now rose from obscurity: this man was an uneducated but persevering peasant named Juan, who possessed a graceful form, herculean frame, good heart, and unrivalled ingenuity. His two learned older brothers tried to scale the walls of the tower but fared no better than the others; at last Juan's turn came, and though his parents and his older brothers expostulated with him not to go — for what could a man unskilled in the fine arts do? — Juan, in the hope of setting the princess free, paid no attention to their advice, and took as many of the biggest nails as he could find, a very long rope, and a strong hammer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 51 'Juan and Clotilde'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 國王盧多維科自然想在死期來臨之前見女兒一面，而他的死期正迅速逼近；他向任何能解救她的人許下大筆金錢，外加他的王冠與克洛蒂爾德的手。數百位王子嘗試過，卻徒勞無功：塔的石牆高得連極少數鳥兒都飛不過去。但如今有一位解救者自微賤中崛起：此人是一個未受過教育卻堅忍不拔的農民，名叫胡安，他身姿優雅、體格魁梧、心地善良，且機智無人能及。他那兩位博學的兄長曾試圖攀上塔牆，卻並不比其他人順利；最後輪到胡安，儘管他的父母與兄長勸阻他不要去——因為一個不諳精妙技藝的人能做些什麼呢？——胡安懷著解救公主的希望，對他們的勸告毫不理會，並帶上他能找到的盡可能多的大釘子、一條極長的繩子與一把堅固的錘子。

passages.text: One day Juan set out with all his equipment; on the way he met his disappointed second brother returning after a vain attempt, who tried in every way he could to divert Juan from his purpose. Juan's parents, actuated partly by a sense of shame if he should fail and partly by a deep-seated hatred, had poisoned his food without his knowledge; when he felt hungry he suspected them of some evil intention, so before eating he gave his horse some of his provisions — the poor creature died on the road amidst terrible sufferings, and Juan was obliged to finish the journey on foot. When he arrived at the foot of the tower, he drove a nail into the wall, then tied one end of his rope to this spike; in this way he succeeded in making a complete ladder of nails and rope to the top of the tower, where Clotilde met him with her eyes flooded with tears, giving him one of the magic necklaces as a reward for his great services.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 51 'Juan and Clotilde'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，胡安帶著全部裝備出發；途中他遇見了徒勞嘗試後失望而歸的二哥，二哥千方百計想讓胡安放棄他的目的。胡安的父母，一部分出於他若失敗便覺羞恥的心理，一部分出於深藏的憎恨，在他不知情的情況下在他的食物裡下了毒；當他感到飢餓時，他懷疑他們懷有某種惡意，於是進食前先把他的一些口糧給了他的馬——那可憐的牲口在劇烈的痛苦中死在路上，胡安只得徒步走完旅程。當他抵達塔腳下時，他將一枚釘子釘入牆中，然後把繩子的一端繫在這枚釘子上；就這樣，他成功地用釘子與繩子做成了一道直達塔頂的完整梯子，克洛蒂爾德在那裡迎接他，淚水盈眶，並將其中一條魔法項鍊贈予他，作為對他那偉大功績的獎賞。

passages.text: While they were whispering words of love in each other's ears, they heard a deafening noise at the bottom of the tower: 'Rush for safety to your ladder!' cried Clotilde. 'One of the fiendish friends of the magician is going to kill you.' But, alas! Some wanton hand had pulled out the nails — and this person was none other than Juan's second brother. 'I am a lost man,' said Juan. 'Mount one of the winged horses in the chamber adjoining mine,' said Clotilde; so Juan got on one of the animals without knowing where to go, and the horse flew from the tower with such velocity that Juan had to close his eyes, his breath almost taken away — in a few seconds he was landed in a country entirely strange to his eyes. After long years of struggle with poverty and starvation, Juan was at last able to make his way back to his native country, and went to live in a town just outside the walls of the capital, where a rich old man named Telesforo hired him to work on his farm; Juan's excellent service and irreproachable conduct won the good will of his master, who adopted him as his son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 51 'Juan and Clotilde'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 正當他們在彼此耳邊低語情話時，他們聽見塔底傳來震耳欲聾的聲響：「快逃到你的梯子上去！」克洛蒂爾德喊道。「魔法師的一個惡魔般的朋友要來殺你了。」但是，唉！有隻肆意妄為的手拔掉了釘子——而這人不是別人，正是胡安的二哥。「我完了，」胡安說。「騎上與我房間相鄰的那間房裡的一匹有翼馬，」克洛蒂爾德說；於是胡安騎上其中一匹牲口，卻不知要往何處去，那馬以極快的速度飛離高塔，胡安不得不閉上眼睛，幾乎喘不過氣來——幾秒鐘之內，他便降落在一片他眼中全然陌生的國度。在與貧窮和飢餓抗爭了漫長歲月之後，胡安終於得以返回故國，並前往首都城牆外的一座城鎮居住，那裡有一位名叫特萊斯福羅的富有老人僱他在農場幹活；胡安出色的工作與無可指摘的品行贏得了主人的好感，主人便收他為養子。

passages.text: At about this time King Ludovico gave out proclamations stating that anyone who could exactly match his daughter's necklace should be his son-in-law; thousands tried, but they tried in vain — even the most dexterous and experienced smiths were baffled in their attempts to produce an exact counterfeit. When word of the royal proclamations was brought to Juan, he decided to try: one day he pretended to be sick and asked Telesforo to go to the palace to get Clotilde's necklace; the old man went that very afternoon and borrowed the necklace, so that he might try to copy it. After supper Juan went to his room and locked himself in, took from his pocket the necklace which Clotilde had given him in the tower, and compared it carefully with the borrowed one; when he saw that they did not differ in any respect, he took a piece of iron and hammered it until midnight. Early the next morning Juan wrapped the two magic necklaces in a silk handkerchief and told the old man to take them to the king. 'By the aid of the Lord!' exclaimed Clotilde when her father the king unwrapped the necklaces. 'My lover is here again. This necklace is not a counterfeit, for it is written in the magician's book of black art that no human being shall be able to imitate either of the magic necklaces. Where is the owner of this necklace, old man?' — 'He is at home,' said Telesforo with a bow. 'Go and bring him to the palace.' Within a quarter of an hour Juan arrived; after paying due respect to the king, Juan embraced Clotilde affectionately, and they were married in the afternoon, the festivities continuing for nine days and nine nights. Juan was made crown-prince, and on the death of King Ludovico he succeeded to the throne; King Juan and Queen Clotilde lived to extreme old age in peace and perfect happiness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 51 'Juan and Clotilde'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大約在這個時候，國王盧多維科頒布詔令，宣布凡能與他女兒的項鍊完全相配者，便將成為他的女婿；成千上萬的人嘗試過，卻徒勞無功——即便是最靈巧、最有經驗的工匠，在試圖製造出完全相同的仿製品時也束手無策。當王室詔令的消息傳到胡安耳中時，他決定一試：有一天他假裝生病，請特萊斯福羅去宮裡取來克洛蒂爾德的項鍊；老人當天下午便去了，並借來了那條項鍊，以便試著仿製。晚飯後，胡安回到自己的房間，把自己鎖在裡面，從口袋裡取出克洛蒂爾德在塔中給他的那條項鍊，仔細地與借來的那條相比較；當他看出它們在任何方面都毫無差異時，他取來一塊鐵，一直錘打到午夜。第二天一大早，胡安把兩條魔法項鍊包在一方絲帕裡，叫老人把它們帶去給國王。「蒙主相助！」克洛蒂爾德在父親國王打開項鍊時驚呼道。「我的愛人又回來了。這條項鍊不是仿製品，因為魔法師的黑魔法書中寫明，任何人類都無法仿製這兩條魔法項鍊中的任何一條。老人，這條項鍊的主人在哪裡？」——「他在家裡，」特萊斯福羅躬身說道。「去把他帶到宮裡來。」不到一刻鐘，胡安便到了；在向國王致以應有的敬意之後，胡安深情地擁抱了克洛蒂爾德，他們在下午成了婚，慶典持續了九天九夜。胡安被封為王儲，並在國王盧多維科駕崩後繼承了王位；國王胡安與王后克洛蒂爾德在和平與圓滿的幸福中活到極高的年歲。

title.en: The Poor Man and His Three Sons: The Scythe, the Rooster, and the Cat
title.zh: 貧父與三子：鐮刀、雄雞與貓

region.en: Pasig, Rizal, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋黎薩省帕西格（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog fable; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 52 'The Poor Man and his Three Sons', eBook #8299

summary.en: A dying father leaves each son one humble thing — a scythe, a rooster, a cat — 'which, if you will only be able to find a place in which it has no equal, will make you happy men.' The scythe is bought by rice-pullers amazed at its convenience; the time-crowing rooster by a town that has none; the rat-killing cat by a king whose palace it clears. All three return rich, having followed their father's wise advice: select the right place in which to trade.
summary.zh: 垂死的父親給三子各留一件平凡之物——鐮刀、雄雞、貓——『若能找到無可替代之地，便可致富。』拔稻而作的鄉民驚異於鐮刀之便；無雞的城鎮重金購下報時的雄雞；鼠患的王宮以鉅資買走捕鼠的貓。三兄弟皆富而歸——父親的遺訓是：貴在所售之地。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog fable recorded by Fansler from a Velasquez narrator (Pasig); archival record. Imported from the Occident (Grimm No. 70 family; oldest form in Nicholas de Troyes, 1535); Fansler suspects introduction through a French religious.

passages.text: Once there lived a poor man who had three sons. When the father was on his death-bed, he called his sons and said to them, 'My sons, I shall die very soon; and I shall not be able to leave you much wealth, for wealth I have not. But I will give each one of you something which, if you will only be able to find a place in which it has no equal, will make you happy men.' The father then gave to one a rooster, to another a cat, and to the third a scythe; then he died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 52 'The Poor Man and his Three Sons'; not verbatim.
