passages.zh: 從前有一個窮人，他有三個兒子。當父親臥病垂危時，他把兒子們叫來，對他們說：「我的兒子們，我很快就要死了；我無法給你們留下多少財富，因為財富我並沒有。但我要給你們每人一樣東西，只要你們能找到一個它無與倫比的地方，它就會使你們成為幸福的人。」父親隨後給了一個兒子一隻公雞，給了另一個兒子一隻貓，給了第三個兒子一把長柄鐮刀；然後他便死了。

passages.text: The owner of the scythe was the first to try his fortune and test his father's advice: he left his brothers and went on a journey until he came to a town where he saw the people harvesting rice by pulling the stalks out of the ground. He showed the people the convenience of the scythe; they were so delighted and astonished that they offered to give him a large sum of money in exchange for the tool — of course he was willing to sell it, and he went home a rich man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 52 'The Poor Man and his Three Sons'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 鐮刀的主人最先去試自己的運氣，驗證父親的忠告：他離開兄弟們上路，來到一座城鎮，看見人們收割稻子是把稻稈從土裡連根拔起。他把鐮刀的便利展示給眾人看；他們又驚又喜，便提出以一大筆錢換取這件工具——他自然樂意賣掉，於是成了富人回到家鄉。

passages.text: The owner of the rooster, seeing the good luck of his brother, next resolved to try his fortune with the bird; like his brother, he travelled until he came to a town where there was no rooster. The people were very much interested in the rooster's crowing, and asked the owner why the bird crowed; he said that the bird told the time of day by its crowing — 'The first crow in the night announces midnight; the second, three o'clock in the morning; and the third crow announces five o'clock.' The people were very anxious to get the rooster for their town and offered to buy it; the owner was willing, and he returned to his home as rich as his brother who had sold the scythe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 52 'The Poor Man and his Three Sons'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 公雞的主人見兄弟交了好運，接著也決定帶著這隻鳥去試自己的運氣；他像兄弟一樣一路前行，來到一座沒有公雞的城鎮。人們對公雞的啼叫極感興趣，便問主人這鳥為何啼叫；他說這鳥以啼聲報時——「夜裡第一聲啼叫報午夜；第二聲報凌晨三點；第三聲報五點。」人們極想為自己的城鎮得到這隻公雞，便提出要買；主人欣然同意，於是像賣掉鐮刀的兄弟一樣富有地回到家鄉。

passages.text: The last brother now set out to try his luck with his cat; at last he came to a town where the rats were vexing the people very much. He showed them the use of his cat; with wonder the people watched the cat kill the rats, and were astounded to see how the rats fled from this strange animal. The news of the cat reached the king, who summoned its owner to the palace; the king asked the brother to try his cat on the rats in the palace, and so the cat was turned loose — in a short time all the rats had either been killed or driven away. The king wanted the cat, and offered to pay a large sum of money for it; so the owner of the cat, after the king had paid him, went home as rich as his other two brothers. Thus the three brothers became rich, because they followed their father's wise advice: select the right place in which to trade.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 52 'The Poor Man and his Three Sons'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最後一個兄弟這回帶著他的貓出去碰運氣；他終於來到一座城鎮，那裡的老鼠把人們擾得苦不堪言。他把貓的用處展示給他們看；眾人驚奇地看著貓捕殺老鼠，又見老鼠如何逃離這隻奇怪的動物，無不目瞪口呆。貓的消息傳到國王耳中，國王便召喚貓的主人進宮；國王請這兄弟讓貓在宮中捉鼠，於是貓被放了出來——不一會兒，所有老鼠不是被殺死就是被趕走。國王想要這隻貓，提出以一大筆錢買下；於是貓的主人得了國王的錢，像另外兩個兄弟一樣富有地回到家鄉。三個兄弟就這樣致富，因為他們聽從了父親的明智忠告：要選對做買賣的地方。

title.en: The Denied Mother
title.zh: 被拒的母親

region.en: Calamba, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省卡蘭巴（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog verse tale sung by a beggar with a guitar; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 53 'The Denied Mother', eBook #8299

summary.en: The king's pet dog bears three human daughters — Feliza, Juana, Maria — each married to a prince of a different kingdom. After the king's death their dog-mother, cast out of the palace, travels to each in turn: Feliza kicks her down the ladder, Juana has her tied in a distant forest — only Maria, finding her crying and yelping, unties her with her own hands, wraps her veil around her, and brings her home: 'this dog that I am carrying is my mother.' Light floods the dining-room, the dog disappears, and in its place stands a beautiful woman in glorious attire: 'I am the dog your mother. God bless you, my good child!'
summary.zh: 國王的愛犬生下三個人形女兒——菲莉莎、胡安娜、瑪利亞——分嫁三國王子。國王死後，狗母被逐出宮，輾轉尋女：菲莉莎把她踢下扶梯；胡安娜命衛士將她縛於遠林；唯瑪利亞聞其哀鳴，親手解縛、以面紗裹之載回王宮——『我懷中的狗，是我的母親。』餐廳驟亮，狗影化為華服美人：『我是你那狗身的母親。上帝保佑你，我的好孩子！』

sensitivity.note: Tagalog tale sung in Tagalog verse by a beggar with a guitar, framed by Fansler as heard on the road to a bone-setter; archival record. Fansler offers no close parallels, though the roles are reversed in Frere's Indian 'A Funny Story' (No. 2).

passages.text: In a certain country there lived a king who had a pet dog; he loved the dog so much and treated it so kindly that, wherever he went, the dog followed him. In the course of time the dog gave birth to three puppies — the most striking thing about these new-born creatures was that they were real human beings in every particular; so the king ordered them to be baptized: the eldest sister was named Feliza, the second Juana, and the youngest Maria. When they grew up into beautiful young women, they married three princes, each of a different kingdom; after the marriage-festivities each went to live in the country of her husband.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 53 'The Denied Mother'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某個國家有一位國王，養著一隻寵犬；他極愛這隻狗，待牠十分慈愛，無論他走到哪裡，狗都跟著他。日子一久，這狗生下三隻小狗——這些新生的小東西最引人注目的是，牠們每一處都完完全全是真正的人；於是國王下令為牠們施洗：長女取名費莉莎，次女取名胡安娜，幼女取名瑪麗亞。她們長成美麗的年輕女子後，各自嫁給一位王子，三位王子分屬不同的王國；婚禮慶典之後，各人便到丈夫的國度居住。

passages.text: Feliza was very happy: she dressed elegantly, and had all that a woman of her rank could wish for. One day, when her husband was away from home, a lean, dirty, spectre-looking dog came to her — it was Feliza's mother, who, after the death of her master the king, had been cast out of the palace; the poor dog had had nothing to eat for many days, had been driven away from every house, and had been frightened by mischievous boys with sticks and stones. Although Feliza's kingdom was very far away, she had managed, in spite of difficulty, to reach it, hoping to gain her daughter's pity. 'My daughter, have compassion on me! I, your mother, am in a very wretched condition.' 'What care I? What business have you to come here? Don't you know that I will never sacrifice anything for your sake? Get out of here!' — and she kicked the poor dog until it fell tumbling to the ground, for Feliza did not want her husband to find out that her mother was a dog.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 53 'The Denied Mother'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 費莉莎非常幸福：她衣著華貴，凡是她這等身份的女子所能想望的，她樣樣都有。有一天，她丈夫離家外出，一隻瘦骨嶙峋、骯髒不堪、形如鬼魅的狗來到她面前——那是費莉莎的母親，牠的主人國王死後，牠便被逐出王宮；這可憐的狗多日來粒米未進，被家家戶戶趕走，還被頑童用棍棒和石頭嚇得驚惶。費莉莎的王國雖然十分遙遠，牠仍千方百計、歷盡艱難來到這裡，指望得到女兒的憐憫。「我的女兒，可憐可憐我吧！我，你的母親，境況非常悲慘。」「我管得著嗎？你有什麼事到這裡來？你難道不知道我絕不會為你犧牲什麼嗎？滾出去！」——她還踢那可憐的狗，直到牠翻倒在地，因為費莉莎不願讓丈夫發現她的母親是一隻狗。

passages.text: Sadly the dog went away, and decided to go to her daughter Juana's kingdom; the country was far away, but what else could she do? As Juana was coming out of the church with her husband, she saw the dog hurrying after her; like Feliza, she was ashamed of her mother, and whispered to one of the guards to catch the dog and tie it securely in a distant forest, so that it might no longer annoy her. Not long after this, Maria, the youngest daughter, was riding through the forest with her husband; there they found the poor dog crying and yelping in a pitiful manner. Maria recognized her mother: she got out of the carriage, and with her own hands untied the dog, wrapped her veil around it, and ordered the carriage to turn back to the palace. 'Husband, this dog that I am carrying is my mother, so please your Majesty.' The husband only said, 'Thank God!' and not another word.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 53 'The Denied Mother'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那狗傷心地離去，決定前往女兒胡安娜的王國；那地方很遠，但牠又能怎麼辦呢？胡安娜正與丈夫走出教堂時，看見那狗匆匆跟在她後面；她像費莉莎一樣以母親為恥，便低聲吩咐一名衛兵抓住那狗，牢牢綁在遠處的森林裡，免得牠再來煩她。不久之後，幼女瑪麗亞與丈夫騎馬穿過森林；他們在那裡發現那可憐的狗正悲慘地哭叫哀鳴。瑪麗亞認出了母親：她下了馬車，親手解開那狗，用自己的面紗裹住牠，並吩咐馬車掉頭回宮。「夫君，我抱著的這隻狗是我的母親，懇請陛下恩准。」丈夫只說了一句：「感謝上帝！」再無別話。

passages.text: Maria ordered the cook to prepare delicious food for the dog, and assigned the best chamber in the palace to the animal; while the dog was eating with Maria, the prince, and the courtiers, the dining-room was suddenly illuminated with a bright light — the dog disappeared, and in its place stood a beautiful woman in glorious attire. The woman kissed Maria, and said, 'I am the dog your mother. God bless you, my good child!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 53 'The Denied Mother'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 瑪麗亞吩咐廚師為那隻狗準備美味的食物，並把宮中最上等的房間分配給這隻動物；當那隻狗與瑪麗亞、王子及朝臣們一同進食時，餐廳忽然被一道明亮的光照亮——那隻狗消失了，取而代之的是一位身著華麗服飾的美麗女子。那女子親吻了瑪麗亞，說道：「我就是你的母親，那隻狗。願上帝保佑你，我的好孩子！」

title.en: Tomarind and the Wicked Datu
title.zh: 托馬林與惡達圖

region.en: Mexico, Pampanga, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town; pre-Spanish datu setting)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦板牙省墨西哥鎮（敘述者故鄉，西班牙時代前的達圖背景）

period: Pampangan oral tale (old Pampangan tradition); collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 54 'Tomarind and the Wicked Datu', eBook #8299

summary.en: Datu Nebucheba covets his warrior Tomarind's beautiful wife and sends him twice to die: for an enchanted marble ball guarded by village-burning monsters, and to carry a letter to the datu's parents 'living under ground, in the realm of the spirits' — down a well to be buried under piled stones. The witch of Tipuca arms him with a magic cane and digs him a secret passage between the two wells; the 'answer' letter Tomarind brings back invites Nebucheba to visit his parents below, and the crushed datu is never seen again — Tomarind ruling with justice and equity for many years.
summary.zh: 達圖尼布徹巴覬覦勇士托馬林的美妻，兩度設局害之：取怪獸看守的魔法石球；再命他『送信給住地底神域的雙親』——實是誘入井中、以堆石活埋。蒂普卡的女巫授他魔杖，並挖通兩井間的秘密地道。托馬林帶回的『回信』竟邀達圖下井探親——石落人亡，尼布徹巴永不復見；托馬林以公正之道統治多年。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan tale recorded by Fansler from a Garcia narrator (Mexico, Pampanga), who says it is an old Pampangan tale; archival record. Fansler knows no variants and judges it 'pretty evidently... old tribal Pampangan tradition'; the witch's rites are named, not described operationally.

passages.text: Before the Spanish occupation there were in the Philippines many petty kingdoms headed by native princes known as datus. Luzon, the scene of countless ravages and hard fightings of warlike tribes, was the home of Datu Nebucheba. His kingdom — at first only a few square miles — was greatly extended by the labor of his young brave warrior, Tomarind. Tomarind had a very beautiful wife, with whom Datu Nebucheba fell in love; but the ruler kept his vile desire secret in his heart for many years, and many times he thought of getting rid of his warrior Tomarind, and thus getting possession of his beautiful wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 54 'Tomarind and the Wicked Datu'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在西班牙人佔領之前，菲律賓有許多由稱為「達圖」的本地王子所統治的小王國。呂宋島是好戰部族無數劫掠與激戰的場所，也是達圖·涅布切巴的家園。他的王國——起初只有幾平方英里——因他年輕勇敢的戰士托馬林德的努力而大為擴張。托馬林德有一位非常美麗的妻子，達圖·涅布切巴愛上了她；但這位統治者多年來將這邪惡的慾望深藏於心，並多次想除掉他的戰士托馬林德，從而佔有他美麗的妻子。

passages.text: One day Tomarind was sent on a dangerous errand: he was ordered to get an enchanted marble ball from one of the caves in a certain mountain, where two monsters of terrible aspect, whose joy was the burning of villages and whose delight was the killing of human beings, guarded the entrance — many persons had entered the door of that death-chamber, but nobody had come from it alive. Suspicious of the coming danger, Tomarind did not go directly to the cave; he sought the famous witch of Tipuca and told her about his situation. Immediately the witch performed a sort of diabolical ceremony, gave Tomarind a magic cane, and sent him away — and when he reached the cave, those that guarded the cave received Tomarind very kindly, and delivered the enchanted marble ball to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 54 'Tomarind and the Wicked Datu'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，托馬林德被派去執行一項危險的任務：他被命令從某座山的一個洞穴中取回一顆施了魔法的石球，那裡有兩隻面目猙獰的怪物守衛著入口——牠們以焚燒村莊為樂，以殺人為快——許多人曾進入那死亡之室的門，卻無人活著出來。托馬林德察覺到即將來臨的危險，便沒有直接前往洞穴；他去找了提普卡著名的女巫，向她訴說自己的處境。女巫立刻舉行了一種魔鬼般的儀式，給了托馬林德一根魔杖，便打發他離去——而當他抵達洞穴時，守衛洞穴的那些怪物非常友善地接待了托馬林德，並將那顆施了魔法的石球交給了他。

passages.text: 'To-morrow, the wife of Tomarind will be mine,' said Nebucheba to himself — 'Alas for him! Very early the next morning Tomarind presented the marble ball to Datu Nebucheba. How quickly he executed my orders! What shall I do to destroy this brave man? The next time he will not escape the danger. I will ask him to take a letter to my parents, who are living under ground, in the realm of the spirits.' The datu caused a well to be dug, and big stones to be piled near the mouth of it; when everything was ready, he summoned the brave warrior, gave him the letter, and told him to start the next morning. Tomarind went again to the witch of Tipuca: 'This is a very great task; but never mind! You will get even with Datu Nebucheba.' That night the witch, with the help of unseen spirits, made a subterranean passage connecting the bottom of the datu's well with that of Tomarind's. 'Nebucheba will ask you to go down into his well; and as soon as you are at the bottom, he will order that the pile of stones be thrown on you. Lose no time, but go in to the subterranean passage that I have prepared for you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 54 'Tomarind and the Wicked Datu'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「明天，托馬林德的妻子就將屬於我了，」涅布切巴自言自語道——「他可要遭殃了！」翌日清晨，托馬林德便將石球呈獻給達圖·涅布切巴。他執行我的命令竟如此迅速！我該如何除掉這個勇敢的人呢？下一次他絕逃不過危險。我要派他送一封信給我的父母，他們住在地下，住在神靈的國度裡。達圖命人挖了一口井，並在井口附近堆起大石；一切準備就緒後，他召來那位勇敢的戰士，把信交給他，吩咐他次日清晨出發。托馬林德又去找提普卡的女巫：「這是一件非常艱鉅的任務；但無妨！你會與達圖·涅布切巴算清這筆帳的。」那天夜裡，女巫在無形神靈的幫助下，挖了一條連接達圖的井底與托馬林德的井底的地下通道。「涅布切巴會要你下到他的井裡去；你一到井底，他就會下令把那些石頭扔到你身上。不要耽擱，趕快進入我為你準備好的地下通道。」

passages.text: Now, Nebucheba firmly believed that Tomarind was dead, and there was great rejoicing in the datu's house; in the evening, while the revelry was going on, Tomarind appeared with the pretended answer from Nebucheba's parents. The letter read, 'We wish you to come and see us here. We have a very beautiful girl for you.' Nebucheba was greatly surprised, and made up his mind to go down into the well the next day; he gathered all his subjects together and said to them, 'I am going to see my parents. If the place there is better than the place here, I shall not come back. Tomarind will be my successor.' In the morning Nebucheba's subjects took him to the well and lowered him slowly into it; when he reached the bottom, Tomarind threw big stones down on him, and Nebucheba was crushed to death — the people never saw him again. Tomarind became datu, and he ruled his subjects with justice and equity for many years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 54 'Tomarind and the Wicked Datu'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此時，涅布切巴深信托馬林德已死，達圖家中一片歡騰；傍晚，正當狂歡進行之際，托馬林德帶著涅布切巴父母假託的回信出現了。信中寫道：「我們希望你來這裡看望我們。我們為你準備了一位非常美麗的姑娘。」涅布切巴大為驚訝，決心次日下到井裡去；他召集了所有臣民，對他們說：「我要去看望我的父母。如果那裡的地方比這裡好，我就不回來了。托馬林德將繼承我的位置。」早晨，涅布切巴的臣民把他帶到井邊，緩緩將他放下井去；當他到達井底時，托馬林德把大石頭扔向他，涅布切巴被壓死了——人們再也沒有見到他。托馬林德成為達圖，他以公正與公平統治他的臣民許多年。

title.en: Hatshepsut the Female Horus: Punt and the Garden for Amun
title.zh: 女荷魯斯哈特謝普蘇特：彭特與阿蒙之園

region.en: Deir el-Bahari, Thebes, Egypt (the queen's terraced temple and the Punt reliefs)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯代爾巴哈里（女王階台神廟與彭特浮雕）

period: Reign of Hatshepsut, 18th Dynasty (c. 1479-1458 BCE); retold in D. A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXV, 'Amenhotep the Magnificent and Queen Tiy' (Hatshepsut section)

summary.en: The queen who reigned alone as 'the female Horus': on the walls of her terraced temple the mythical scenes of her birth were carved so she might be recognized as 'a son of the sun', depicted with her male double and wearing a false beard on state occasions; her most famous undertaking was the eight ships sent to Punt for myrrh trees and sacred animals — 'It was her pious wish that Amun should have a garden to walk in.'
summary.zh: 獨掌國柄之『女荷魯斯』：其階台神廟壁上刻其誕生之神話場景，使世人認其為『日神之子』——像旁雕其男性雙身，國典則戴假鬚；其最著之事乃遣八舟赴彭特求沒藥樹與聖獸——『其虔誠之願：使阿蒙有園可遊。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient history-legend retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling. The 'male double' and false beard are the queen's own royal ideology.

passages.text: After a time the usurping prince had to recognize the co-regency of Hatshepsut. But, ere long, he was thrust aside, and the queen reigned alone as 'the female Horus'. She completed the great mortuary temple at Der-el-Bahari, which had been begun under Thothmes II. It was modelled on the smaller temple of Mentuhotep, and is still magnificent in ruin. Situated against the western cliffs at Thebes, it was constructed in three terraces with sublime colonnades finely proportioned and exquisitely wrought. An inner chamber was excavated from the rock. On the temple walls the mythical scenes in connection with the birth of the queen were sculptured in low relief, and to get over the difficulty of being recognized as a 'son of the sun', Hatshepsut was depicted in company of her male 'double'. On state occasions she wore a false beard.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXV. / Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXV.
passages.zh: 過了一段時間，篡位的王子不得不承認哈特謝普蘇特的共同攝政。但不久之後，他便被排擠到一旁，女王以「女荷魯斯」的身分獨自統治。她完成了在德爾巴赫里動工於圖特摩斯二世時期的那座宏大的葬祭神廟。它仿照門圖霍特普的較小神廟而建，至今雖成廢墟仍舊壯麗。它依傍底比斯西岸的懸崖而建，由三層平台構成，配有比例勻稱、雕工精美的壯麗柱廊。一間內室是從岩石中開鑿出來的。神廟牆上以淺浮雕雕刻著與女王誕生有關的神話場景；為了克服被承認為「太陽之子」的困難，哈特謝普蘇特被描繪成與她的男性「雙身」相伴。在正式場合，她戴著假鬍鬚。

passages.text: The queen's most famous undertaking was to send an expedition of eight ships to the land of Punt to obtain myrrh trees, incense, rare woods, and sacred animals for the temple. It was her pious wish that Amun should have a garden to walk in.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXV.
passages.zh: 這位女王最著名的壯舉，是派遣一支由八艘船組成的遠征隊前往朋特之地，為神廟取得沒藥樹、香料、珍稀木材與神聖動物。她虔誠地希望阿蒙能有一座可供漫步的花園。

passages.text: After her death no more is heard of her favourite Senmut, or her daughter, whom she had selected as her successor. Her name was ruthlessly erased from her monuments. All the indications point to a military revolt, supported by a section of the priesthood, at a time of national peril.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXV.
passages.zh: 她死後，她最寵愛的森穆特，以及她選為繼承人的女兒，便不再見於記載。她的名字被無情地從她的紀念碑上抹去。種種跡象都指向一場軍事叛亂，由一部分祭司支持，發生於國家危難之際。

title.en: Ramesses at Kadesh: 'My Hand Is More to Thee Than Hundreds of Thousands'
title.zh: 拉美西斯於卡迭石：『我手勝於爾之十萬大軍』

region.en: Kadesh on the Orontes, Syria (the trap of the Hittite chariots)
region.zh: 敘利亞奧龍特斯河畔卡迭石（赫梯戰車之陷阱）

period: Battle of year 5 of Ramesses II (c. 1275 BCE); retold in D. A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXVII, 'The Empire of Rameses and the Homeric Age'

summary.en: The army in four divisions named Amon, Ra, Ptah and Sutekh; the overconfident Pharaoh lured to Kadesh and surrounded with only a fragment of his force — until, as the court poet sang, he called upon Ra, and the sun god appeared before him: 'Alone thou art not, for I, thy father, am beside thee, and my hand is more to thee than hundreds of thousands. I who love the brave am the giver of victory.' The battle became the subject of temple reliefs in which Ramesses bends his bow like a giant — and the war ended in a treaty witnessed by a thousand Egyptian gods and a thousand Hittite gods.
summary.zh: 大軍分四團，即以阿蒙、拉、卜塔、蘇特克四神為名；王輕信俘言，中伏於卡迭石，幾全軍盡沒——宮廷詩人詠曰：王呼拉，日神即現其前：『爾非獨也，我父在側，我手勝於爾之十萬大軍；我愛勇者，乃勝利之賜者。』此戰遂鐫於神廟浮雕，王彎弓如巨人——戰終以和約：一千埃及神與一千赫梯神共為見證。

sensitivity.note: Ancient battle-poem retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling. The Kadesh 'poem' is the Ramesses II court-literature version of the battle.

passages.text: The Egyptian army was in four divisions, named Amon, Ra, Ptah, and Sutekh. Rameses was in haste to invest Kadesh, and pressed on with the Amon regiment, followed closely by the Ra regiment. The other two were, when he reached the city, at least a day's march in the rear. — The overconfident Pharaoh was being led into a trap.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXVII.
passages.zh: 埃及軍隊分為四個師團，分別以阿蒙、拉、普塔與蘇特克命名。拉美西斯急於圍攻卡疊什，率阿蒙軍團推進，拉軍團緊隨其後。當他抵達該城時，其餘兩支至少還落後一日行程。——這位過於自信的法老正被引入陷阱。

passages.text: Rameses had achieved a victory, but at a terrible cost. He returned to Egypt without accomplishing the capture of Kadesh, and created for himself a great military reputation by recording his feats of personal valour on temple walls and monuments. A poet who sang his praises declared that when the Pharaoh found himself surrounded, and, of course, 'alone', he called upon Ra, whereupon the sun god appeared before him and said: 'Alone thou art not, for I, thy father, am beside thee, and my hand is more to thee than hundreds of thousands. I who love the brave am the giver of victory.' The treaty, which was drawn up in 1271 B.C., made reference to previous agreements, but these, unfortunately, have perished; it was signed by the two monarchs, and witnessed by a thousand Egyptian gods and a thousand Hittite gods.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXVII.
passages.zh: 拉美西斯取得了勝利，但代價慘重。他未能攻下卡疊什便返回埃及，並將他個人的英勇事蹟記錄在神廟牆壁與紀念碑上，為自己締造了偉大的軍事聲名。一位歌頌他的詩人宣稱，當法老發現自己身陷重圍，而且理所當然地「孤身一人」時，他呼求拉，於是太陽神現身於他面前說道：「你並非孤身一人，因為我，你的父親，就在你身旁，我的手對你而言勝過千千萬萬。我愛勇者，我是勝利的賜予者。」這項條約訂立於公元前一二七一年，其中提及先前的協議，但不幸的是，這些協議已經失傳；條約由兩位君主簽署，並有千位埃及神祇與千位西臺神祇作證。

title.en: Bes the Dwarf God: Music, War, and Serpents Between His Teeth
title.zh: 矮神貝斯：樂神、戰神與碎蛇者

region.en: Deir el-Bahari, Thebes, Egypt (oldest Bes image, attending the birth of Hatshepsut)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯代爾巴哈里（最古之貝斯像，侍哈特謝普蘇特誕生）

period: Prominent from the 18th Dynasty, possibly 12th; oracle at Abydos into Roman times (Mackenzie 1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXVII, the imported and grotesque gods

summary.en: The grotesque household god from Africa: Bes the dwarf with long arms and crooked legs, cat-like ears, bushy hair and beard, wearing the skin of a wild animal with the tail trailing — a war god, a god of music playing a harp, and a love god, always drawn full face; he attends at the birth of Hatshepsut in the oldest surviving image, keeps an oracle at Abydos, and as nurse of Harpokrates guards the child god against serpents 'which he tore to pieces between his teeth.'
summary.zh: 非洲來之怪誕家宅神：貝斯矮而臂長腿曲，耳如貓、鬚髮蓬然，披獸皮曳尾——為戰神、抱琴之樂神、亦是愛神，恆以正像示人；代爾巴哈里最古之像中侍哈特謝普蘇特誕生，於阿拜多斯有神諭，又為哈波克拉特斯之乳保，護嬰神而碎蛇『於齒間』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cult retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling.

passages.text: The grotesque god Bes also came into prominence during the Eighteenth Dynasty; it is possible that he was introduced as early as the Twelfth. Although his worship spread into Syria he appears to have been of African origin and may have been imported from Somaliland. Like the Deng, he was a dwarf with long arms and crooked legs; his nose was broad and flat, his ears projected like those of a cat, he had bushy hair and eyebrows and a beard, his lips were thick and gross. Over his back he wore the skin of a wild animal, the tail trailing behind.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXVII.
passages.zh: 怪異的貝斯神也在第十八王朝期間嶄露頭角；他可能早在第十二王朝便已傳入。雖然他的崇拜傳播至敘利亞，他似乎源自非洲，可能是從索馬利蘭傳入。如同登神，他是個長臂曲腿的矮人；他的鼻子寬而扁，耳朵像貓耳般突出，頭髮與眉毛濃密，並蓄著鬍鬚，嘴唇厚而粗陋。他背上披著一張野獸皮，尾巴拖在身後。

passages.text: He was a war god, a god of music playing a harp, and a love god. The oldest surviving representation of Bes is found in the Der el Bahari temple of Amon, where he attends at the birth of Hatshepsut. As late as Roman times he was known by his oracle at Abydos. Absorbed by the sun worshippers, he became the nurse of Harpokrates (Horus) whom he nourished and amused. He also guarded the child god against the attacks of serpents, which he tore to pieces between his teeth.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXVII.
passages.zh: 他是戰神、彈奏豎琴的音樂之神，也是愛神。現存最古老的貝斯形象見於阿蒙的德爾巴赫里神廟，他在那裡出席哈特謝普蘇特的誕生。遲至羅馬時代，他仍以其在阿拜多斯的神諭為人所知。他被太陽崇拜者所吸收，成為哈波克拉底斯（荷魯斯）的保姆，撫育他並逗他開心。他也保護這位孩童神祇免受蛇的攻擊，用牙齒將蛇撕成碎片。

title.en: The Imported Goddesses: Astarte, Lady of Horses, and Kadesh the Holy One
title.zh: 外來女神：馭馬者阿斯塔特與『聖者』卡迭石

region.en: Memphis and Tanis, Egypt (temples of the imported love-and-war goddesses)
region.zh: 埃及孟菲斯與塔尼斯（外來愛與戰女神之廟）

period: Imported during the 18th Dynasty wars with Syria (c. 1450-1300 BCE); retold in Mackenzie 1913

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXVII, the foreign elements in the Egyptian religion

summary.en: The empire brought Asiatic goddesses up the Nile: Astarte, 'introduced into the Nile valley with the horse', a lunar deity and goddess of war with the head of a lioness — as the 'Lady of Horses' she stands in a chariot driving four horses over a fallen foe; Kadesh 'the holy one', another form of Astarte, the moon goddess nude on the back of a lioness carrying lotus flowers and two serpents — and Baal was worshipped at Tanis, where a temple of the 'strange Aphrodite' stood in Herodotus' day.
summary.zh: 帝國時代異邦女神沿尼羅而上：阿斯塔特『隨馬而入埃及』，為月神與戰神，獅首——稱『馭馬之主』，立於戰車驅四馬踏倒敵者；『聖者』卡迭石為其別形，裸身立於獅背，一手持蓮與鏡，一手持雙蛇；坦尼斯則奉巴阿爾——希羅多斯所見之『異邦阿佛洛狄忒』小廟即在孟菲斯。

sensitivity.note: Ancient syncretism retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling.

passages.text: Astarte was worshipped in Egypt early in the Eighteenth Dynasty, and was a lunar deity and goddess of war. She appears to have been introduced into the Nile valley with the horse. Like Tefnut, and other Egyptian feline goddesses, she was depicted with the head of a lioness. As the 'Lady of Horses' she stands in a chariot driving four horses over a fallen foe.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXVII.
passages.zh: 阿斯塔特（Astarte）早在第十八王朝時期便已在埃及受到崇拜，她是一位月神，也是戰爭女神。她似乎是隨著馬匹一同傳入尼羅河谷的。如同泰芙努特（Tefnut）及其他埃及貓科女神一般，她被描繪為長著母獅之首。作為「馬之女主」，她立於戰車之上，驅策四馬，輾過倒地的敵人。

passages.text: Kadesh (Quedesh) 'the holy one', was another form of Astarte. As the 'mistress of all the gods', and the patroness of the 'unmoral' women connected with her temples, she emphasized the licentious phase of the character of Ashtoreth... The Egyptians depicted her as a moon goddess, standing nude on the back of a lioness, which indicated that she was imported from the Hittites; in one hand she carries lotus flowers and what appears to be a mirror, and in the other two serpents. As 'the eye of Ra' she links with Hathor and Sekhet. At Memphis she was adored with the moon god Ah, and when Herodotus visited the city he found a small temple dedicated to 'the strange Aphrodite' (Venus). She was the goddess of the eastern part of Tanis (Zoan).
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXVII.
passages.zh: 卡迭石（Kadesh，Quedesh），意為「聖者」，是阿斯塔特的另一種形態。作為「眾神之女主」，以及與其神廟相關之「不守禮法」女子的守護神，她凸顯了阿什托蕾特（Ashtoreth）性格中放縱淫逸的一面……埃及人將她描繪為月神，赤身立於母獅背上，這表明她是從赫梯人那兒傳入的；她一手持蓮花及看似鏡子之物，另一手持兩條蛇。作為「拉之眼」，她與哈托爾（Hathor）及塞赫美特（Sekhet）相聯繫。在孟菲斯，她與月神阿赫（Ah）一同受崇拜；希羅多德造訪該城時，發現了一座供奉「奇異的阿佛洛狄忒」（維納斯）的小神廟。她是塔尼斯（Tanis，瑣安 Zoan）東部地區的女神。

title.en: Gawigawen of Adasin: The Three-Nosed Husband and the Bride Who Became Oil
title.zh: 阿達辛的加維加溫：三鼻夫與化油的婚娘

region.en: Natpangan and Adasin (Tinguian mythic towns), Abra Province, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋阿布拉省納特潘甘與阿達辛（丁桂安神話城鎮，象徵定位）

period: Tinguian oral epic-cycle tale; collected 1903-1908, published 1915 (Fay-Cooper Cole)

source.work: Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian: A Study in Philippine Folk-Lore (Field Museum, 1915), 'Gawigawen of Adasin' episode, pp. 58-61

summary.en: Gawigawen of Adasin asks his mother Dinawagan to arrange his marriage with the sister of Aponibalagen; the balaua is filled eighteen times with valuable things, the spring's sand is beads, and Aponibalagen beheads old Taodan to make a spring and a shade-tree for the bride. But Aponibolinayen, told by Indiapan that her husband has three noses, keeps her face covered, melts to oil every night — and on the fifth night drops herself away into the jungle, where a rooster and a monkey both tell her Indiapan lied because she wanted to marry Gawigawen herself.
summary.zh: 加維加溫託母親迪納瓦甘說親；聘禮十八次填滿巴勞瓦，泉邊金沙如珠。為討新娘歡心，阿波尼巴拉根斬老者陶丹之首化泉成蔭。但新娘被英迪亞潘告知『夫有三鼻』，始終以手遮面、夜夜化為油；第五夜她悄然棄身而遁，入密林——雄雞與巨猿皆言：英迪亞潘只因自己想嫁加維加溫，故出此謊。

sensitivity.note: Tinguian epic-cycle narrative recorded 1903-1908 by Fay-Cooper Cole; archival record. The head taken to make the spring is placed on the sagang; the balaua and pakdlon ceremonies are named, not described operationally.

passages.text: 'Mother Dinawagan, go and engage me to someone, for I want to be married. I like the sister of Aponibalagen of Natpangan,' said Gawigawen of Adasin. His mother took her hat which looked like the moonbeam and started; when she arrived in Natpangan, Ebang broke up the fish stick and put it in the pot and it became fish, and they drank from the basi jar which was nine times inherited before Dinawagan said, 'My son Gawigawen of Adasin wants to marry your sister.' Aponibalagen agreed, so she gave a golden cup which looked like the moon as an engagement present, and they agreed on a day for pakdlon. When all whom they had invited arrived they agreed how much Gawigawen should pay for his wife: Aponibalagen told them to fill the balaua eighteen times with valuable things — so the balaua was filled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Gawigawen of Adasin' episode; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「迪納瓦甘（Dinawagan）母親，去替我向人提親吧，因為我想成婚了。我喜歡納特潘甘（Natpangan）的阿波尼巴拉根（Aponibalagen）的妹妹。」阿達辛（Adasin）的加維加文（Gawigawen）說道。他的母親拿起她那頂狀如月光的帽子便出發了；當她抵達納特潘甘時，埃邦（Ebang）掰碎魚棒放入鍋中，它便化成了魚，他們又從那隻歷經九代傳承的巴西（basi）酒甕中飲酒，之後迪納瓦甘才開口道：「我兒子，阿達辛的加維加文，想娶你的妹妹。」阿波尼巴拉根應允了，於是她拿出一隻狀如明月的金杯作為聘禮，雙方並議定了舉行帕克德隆（pakdlon）的日子。當他們所邀請的人悉數到齊後，眾人便議定加維加文應為娶妻付出多少：阿波尼巴拉根要他們把巴拉瓦（balaua）屋裝滿貴重之物十八次——於是巴拉瓦屋便被裝滿了。

passages.text: At the spring of Gawigawen of Adasin they were surprised, for it was very beautiful and its sands were of beads, and the grass they used to clean pots with was also beads, and the place where the jars sat was a big dish. 'Go and tell Gawigawen that he must come here and bring an old man, for I am going to take his head and make a spring for Aponibolinayen,' said Aponibalagen. So someone went and told Gawigawen to bring the old man Taodan with him to the spring; Aponibalagen cut off his head and he made a spring, and the water from it bubbled up and the body became a big tree called Alangigan which used to shade Aponibolinayen when she went to the spring to dip water, and the blood of the old man was changed to valuable beads. The place where they walked, from the spring to the ladder of the house, was all big plates.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Gawigawen of Adasin' episode; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在阿達辛的加維加文的泉邊，他們大為驚奇，因為那兒極其美麗，其沙粒是串珠，他們用來刷鍋的草也是串珠，而擺放陶罐之處則是一隻大盤子。「去告訴加維加文，他必須到這兒來，並帶一個老人來，因為我要取他的首級，為阿波尼博利納延（Aponibolinayen）造一眼泉。」阿波尼巴拉根說道。於是有人前去告訴加維加文，要他把老人陶丹（Taodan）帶到泉邊；阿波尼巴拉根砍下他的頭，造出了一眼泉，泉水自其中汩汩湧出，而他的身體則化作一棵名為阿朗吉甘（Alangigan）的大樹，每當阿波尼博利納延到泉邊汲水時，這棵樹便為她遮蔭，而老人的血則化作了貴重的串珠。從泉邊到屋梯之間他們所行經之處，盡是大盤子。

passages.text: Aponibolinayen covered her face all of the time and sat down in the middle of the house, for Indiapan said that she must not uncover her face, for her husband Gawigawen had three noses, and she was afraid to look at him — but Gawigawen was a handsome man, and Aponibolinayen believed what Indiapan had told her. Not long after Dinawagan spread the string of agate beads along the floor where Aponibolinayen sat; when Gawigawen went to Aponibolinayen at night she changed to oil, and she did that every night, and they put the carabao hides under her mat so the oil would not drop to the ground. On the fifth night she used magic so that they could not see her go out: she dropped her beads under the house, then she became oil and dropped her body, and so she went away, always walking, while Gawigawen looked for her for a long time and went to Natpangan, for he could not find her in any of the towns.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Gawigawen of Adasin' episode; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿波尼博利納延終日遮著臉，坐在屋子中央，因為印迪亞潘（Indiapan）說她萬萬不可揭開臉，因為她的丈夫加維加文有三個鼻子，她害怕看他——然而加維加文是個俊美的男子，阿波尼博利納延卻相信了印迪亞潘對她所說的話。不久之後，迪納瓦甘把一串瑪瑙珠沿著阿波尼博利納延所坐的地板鋪開；夜裡加維加文走向阿波尼博利納延時，她便化作油，她每夜都如此，而他們把水牛皮下墊在她的席子底下，好讓油不致滴落地面。到了第五夜，她施了法術，使他們看不見她出去：她把串珠丟到屋下，隨即化作油，讓自己的身體滴落，就這樣離去了，一路不停地走，而加維加文尋了她許久，又前往納特潘甘，因為他在任何城鎮都找不到她。

passages.text: When Aponibolinayen was in the middle of the jungle she met a wild rooster which was crowing: 'Where are you going, Aponibolinayen? Why are you walking in the middle of the jungle?' — 'I came here, for I am running away from my husband, for I do not want to be married to him, for he has three noses.' 'No, Gawigawen is a handsome man. I often see him, for this is where he comes often to snare chickens. Do not believe what Indiapan said to you, for she is crazy,' said the rooster. Aponibolinayen walked on until she reached the place of many big trees, and the big monkey met her: 'Why don't you wish to marry Gawigawen?' — 'Because Indiapan told me he has three noses.' The monkey laughed and said, 'Do not believe that. Indiapan wants to marry Gawigawen herself. He is a handsome man.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Gawigawen of Adasin' episode; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當阿波尼博利納延身處叢林中央時，她遇見一隻正在啼叫的野公雞：「你要去哪兒，阿波尼博利納延？你為何走在叢林中央？」——「我來到這兒，是因為我在逃離我的丈夫，因為我不想嫁給他，因為他有三個鼻子。」「不，加維加文是個俊美的男子。我常見到他，因為這兒正是他常來張網捕雞之處。別相信印迪亞潘對你說的話，因為她瘋了。」公雞說道。阿波尼博利納延繼續前行，直到抵達那有許多大樹之處，一隻大猴子遇見了她：「你為何不願嫁給加維加文？」——「因為印迪亞潘告訴我他有三個鼻子。」猴子笑了，說道：「別相信那個。印迪亞潘自己想嫁給加維加文。他是個俊美的男子。」

title.en: Kadayadawan and the Carabao: The Bride Found Across the Ocean
title.zh: 卡達雅達萬與水牛：越洋尋得的新娘

region.en: Pintagayan and Natpangan (Tinguian mythic towns), Abra Province, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋阿布拉省平塔加揚與納特潘甘（丁桂安神話城鎮，象徵定位）

period: Tinguian oral epic-cycle tale, told by Magwati of Lagangilang; collected 1903-1908, published 1915 (Fay-Cooper Cole)

source.work: Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian: A Study in Philippine Folk-Lore (Field Museum, 1915), 'Kadayadawan and the Carabao' episode, pp. 61-64

summary.en: Aponibolinayen, fleeing her three-nosed husband, rides a carabao across the ocean to an orange tree; the carabao fetches Kadayadawan of Pintagayan — 'there is a good toy for you' — who wins her when their betel-quids become agate beads. At the balaua Gawigawen seizes her into his belt during the dance and Kadayadawan spears him down and revives him; the alan who raised Kadayadawan reveals he was picked up as blood that fell from Langa-an — so he is re-named Aponitolau, the marriage price repaid, and a golden house flies to Kadalayapan.
summary.zh: 逃離三鼻丈夫的阿波妮波莉納衍，騎水牛渡海至橘樹下；水牛喚來平塔加揚的卡達雅達萬——『給你尋了個好玩具』。兩人檳榔渣化為瑪瑙珠，遂成婚。塞揚宴上，加維加溫於舞中將她收進腰帶；卡達雅達萬擲矛擊倒他、復又救活。養育他的阿蘭揭示：他原是朗嘉安失血所化——遂得新名阿波尼托勞；金屋一夜飛抵卡達拉雅潘。

sensitivity.note: Tinguian epic-cycle narrative told by Magwati of Lagangilang; collected 1903-1908 by Fay-Cooper Cole; archival record. The belt-seizure incident 'is frequently found in these tales; it also occurs in Javanese literature' (Cole); the alan are lesser spirits.

passages.text: Not long after she reached a wide field, and she did not know where she was; she stopped in the middle of the field, and she thought she would go on to the other side. Not long after she reached the ocean and she sat down on a log, and a carabao came along; it passed often where she sat, and Aponibolinayen thought she would ride on the carabao, and she got on its back and it took her to the other side of the ocean. When they reached the other side Aponibolinayen saw a big orange tree with much fruit on it. The carabao said, 'Wait here while I eat grass and I will return soon' — but the carabao went to the place of the man who owned him and said, 'Come over here, for there is a good toy for you.' So he combed his hair and oiled it and put on his striped coat and his clout and belt, and he took his spear and rode on the carabao's back — and when they reached the orange tree, Aponibolinayen looked down and saw a handsome man. 'Good morning, lady,' he said.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Kadayadawan and the Carabao' episode; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久之後，她來到一片廣闊的原野，卻不知自己身在何處；她停在原野中央，心想自己該繼續走到另一邊去。不久之後，她來到海邊，坐在一根木頭上，一頭水牛走了過來；牠頻頻經過她坐著的地方，阿波尼博利納延心想自己不妨騎上那頭水牛，於是便爬上牠的背，水牛便載她到了海的另一邊。當他們抵達對岸時，阿波尼博利納延看見一棵結實纍纍的大橘子樹。水牛說：『在這裡等著，我去吃草，很快就回來。』——但水牛卻去了牠主人所在的地方，說道：『到這邊來吧，有個好玩的東西給你。』於是他梳了頭、抹了油，穿上他的條紋外衣、遮布和腰帶，拿起他的矛，騎上水牛的背——當他們來到橘子樹前，阿波尼博利納延往下一看，看見一個英俊的男子。『早安，姑娘。』他說。

passages.text: Not long after they chewed betel-nut and they told their names: 'My name is Kadayadawan of Pintagayan, who is the son of an alan.' 'My name is Aponibolinayen of Natpangan, who is the daughter of Pagbokasan and Ebang, who is the sister of Aponibalagen.' Their betel-nut quids became agate beads, and Kadayadawan said to her, 'Ala, it is good for us to marry. I am going to take you home.' So he took her to his home and he was good to his carabao, because it had found him a pretty woman. When they reached the house the Ati commanded the soldiers to call Kadayadawan — the king said, 'Why, Kadayadawan, have you a pretty girl in your house? Every night I notice that your house appears as if it were burning' — 'No, I have not,' answered Kadayadawan; 'I think you have, for I notice the flames every night.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Kadayadawan and the Carabao' episode; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久之後，他們一同嚼了檳榔，互通了姓名：『我叫卡達亞達萬，來自平塔加揚，是阿蘭之子。』『我叫阿波尼博利納延，來自納特帕岸，是帕格博卡桑與艾邦之女，艾邦是阿波尼巴拉根的姊妹。』他們嚼過的檳榔塊變成了瑪瑙珠，卡達亞達萬對她說：『哎呀，我們成親是件好事。我要帶你回家。』於是他帶她回自己的家，他善待他的水牛，因為牠替他找到了一個美麗的女子。當他們抵達屋子時，阿蒂吩咐士兵們去叫卡達亞達萬——國王說：『怎麼回事，卡達亞達萬，你家裡有個美麗的姑娘嗎？我每晚都注意到你的屋子好像著了火似的。』——『不，我沒有。』卡達亞達萬回答；『我想你有，因為我每晚都看見那火光。』

passages.text: When he reached home Aponibolinayen said to him, 'It is best for us to make Sayang' — and Kadayadawan asked how they could make Sayang by themselves, their neighbors being all soldiers; but Aponibolinayen used magic so that when she thrust the molave stick in the ground it became a balaua, and the betel-nuts they oiled went to the towns of their relatives to invite them. The betel-nut that arrived in Natpangan said to Aponibalagen, 'We came to call you, for Kadayadawan of Pintagayan is making balaua' — 'How can we attend the balaua when we are searching for my sister?' — 'If you do not wish to come I will grow on your knee' — 'Go on my pig' — and the betel-nut grew on the pig until it squealed; 'Ala, get off from the pig and we will come.' At the river Kadayadawan used his power so that their old clothes, which they wore in mourning for Aponibolinayen, were taken off from them, and they were surprised, for they did not know when their old clothes had been taken off; he brought clothes for them, and urged them until they accepted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Kadayadawan and the Carabao' episode; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他回到家時，阿波尼博利納延對他說：『我們最好來辦一場薩揚。』——卡達亞達萬問，他們的鄰居全是士兵，他們怎麼能自己辦薩揚；但阿波尼博利納延施了法術，當她把欖仁木棍插入土中，它便化成了一座巴勞屋，而他們抹了油的檳榔則前往他們親族所在的城鎮去邀請他們。抵達納特帕岸的那顆檳榔對阿波尼巴拉根說：『我們來請你，因為平塔加揚的卡達亞達萬正在辦巴勞。』——『我們正在尋找我的姊妹，怎麼能去參加巴勞呢？』——『你若不肯來，我就要長在你的膝蓋上。』——『去長在我的豬身上吧。』——於是檳榔長在那頭豬身上，直到牠尖叫起來；『哎呀，從豬身上下來吧，我們這就來。』在河邊，卡達亞達萬施展他的法力，使他們身上為阿波尼博利納延服喪而穿的舊衣被脫了下來，他們十分驚訝，因為他們不知道自己的舊衣是何時被脫下的；他為他們帶來衣裳，一再催促，直到他們接受為止。

passages.text: Soon they reached the town and they danced; Iwaginan made Gawigawen and Aponibolinayen dance, and while they were dancing Gawigawen watched Aponibolinayen, and when they had danced around nine times Gawigawen seized her and put her in his belt. 'Why do you do that, Gawigawen?' said Kadayadawan to him, and he threw his spear and Gawigawen fell down, and Aponibolinayen escaped, and Kadayadawan put her in a room; as soon as he put her in the room he went to bring Gawigawen back to life. 'Why did you do that, Gawigawen? I did not steal Aponibolinayen from you.' 'Even if you did steal Aponibolinayen from me, she was my wife and I could not find her until now. That is why I put her in my belt, and Aponibalagen knows that she is my wife.' 'She is my wife now.' Not long after, the alan who took care of Kadayadawan told Langa-an, 'Kadayadawan is your son. I picked him up when he was only blood which fell from you' — and they were very happy; they paid the marriage price, filled the balaua nine times with valuable things, repaid Gawigawen what he had paid when he married Aponibolinayen, and took Kadayadawan home as Aponitolau, the alan giving all her things and flying to the other part of the world while Langa-an used magic so that the golden house which the alan gave went to their town of Kadalayapan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Kadayadawan and the Carabao' episode; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久他們抵達城鎮，便跳起舞來；伊瓦吉南讓加維加溫與阿波尼博利納延共舞，當他們跳舞時，加維加溫一直注視著阿波尼博利納延，當他們繞了九圈之後，加維加溫抓住她，把她塞進自己的腰帶裡。『加維加溫，你為什麼這樣做？』卡達亞達萬對他說，並擲出他的矛，加維加溫倒了下去，阿波尼博利納延脫了身，卡達亞達萬把她安置在一間房裡；他一把她安置進房裡，便立刻去把加維加溫救活。『加維加溫，你為什麼這樣做？我並沒有從你那裡偷走阿波尼博利納延。』『就算你從我這裡偷走了阿波尼博利納延，她本來是我的妻子，而我直到如今才找到她。這就是我把她塞進腰帶裡的原因，阿波尼巴拉根也知道她是我的妻子。』『她現在是我的妻子了。』不久之後，那位照料卡達亞達萬的阿蘭對朗加安說：『卡達亞達萬是你的兒子。我撿到他時，他不過是從你身上落下的一灘血。』——他們非常歡喜；他們付了聘禮，用貴重的物品把巴勞屋裝滿了九次，償還了加維加溫娶阿波尼博利納延時所付出的一切，並把卡達亞達萬以阿波尼托勞的身分帶回家，那位阿蘭把她所有的東西都給了他們，然後飛往世界的另一端，而朗加安則施了法術，使阿蘭所贈的那座黃金屋遷到了他們位於卡達拉亞潘的城鎮。

title.en: Aponibolinayen Goes to War: Ginambo of Gonigonan
title.zh: 阿波妮波莉納衍出征：貢尼貢南的金南波

region.en: Kaodanan and Gonigonan (Tinguian mythic towns), Abra Province, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋阿布拉省卡奧達南與貢尼貢南（丁桂安神話城鎮，象徵定位）

period: Tinguian oral epic-cycle tale; collected 1903-1908, published 1915 (Fay-Cooper Cole)

source.work: Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian: A Study in Philippine Folk-Lore (Field Museum, 1915), 'Aponibolinayen as Warrior' episodes, pp. 64-69

summary.en: Ginambo of Gonlgonan comes to carry off Aponibolinayen 'whom we do not like'; her father would go in her place, but she refuses — 'you are weak.' On a high rock she glances off their spears like rain and charms her own: spear, kill six and seven at one time; headaxe, cut off their heads from the left and right, from in back and in front. She spares Ginambo alone, agreeing to fight in her town next month; meeting Aponigawani on the road — her quid covered with gold to the other's agate — they go to war together, their invisible helpers summon the brothers Lingiwan and Dangdangayan, who scoop the 'girls who never go out of the house' into their belts.
summary.zh: 金南波率眾來劫『不喜歡的女子』；父親欲代戰，阿波妮波莉納衍拒之——『你太弱了。』她立於高岩，以肘格開雨點般的飛矛，再施咒於己器：矛一擲殺六七人；斧左右前後皆能取首。她獨赦金南波，約下月再戰；途中遇同樣出戰的阿波妮加瓦妮——檳榔渣一金一瑪瑙——二人結伴出征，隱形靈使喚來其兄弟林基萬與當當加揚，將『足不出戶的姑娘』攬入腰帶。

sensitivity.note: Tinguian epic-cycle narrative recorded 1903-1908 by Fay-Cooper Cole; archival record. Head-taking and head poles (sagang) are part of the narrative world; the lala-am ('those within') are the sheltered girls. The betel-quid omen (gold vs agate) marks relative power.

passages.text: There was a woman whose name was Ginambo of Gomgonan, who went to fight Aponibolinayen of Kaodanan; when she reached the place where the spring was she said, 'You people who are dipping water from the spring, whose place is this where the spring is?' — 'It belongs to Aponibolinayen of Kaodanan.' When they went up to the town they raised a clamor: 'There are many women who have come to fight against you, at the place where the spring is.' Aponibolinayen hurried to take her spear. 'Do not go, Aponibolinayen, for I will go,' said her father Pagatipanan; 'No, for you are weak. What can you do now? Once you did kill people in the place where the spring is, and now perhaps it is my fortune.' She went to the spring, and looked down — and truly the enemies looked like many locusts about the spring.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen as Warrior' episodes; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一個女人名叫貢戈南的吉南博，她去攻打卡奧達南的阿波尼博利納延；當她來到泉水所在的地方時，她說：『你們這些從泉裡汲水的人，這泉水所在的地方是誰的？』——『是卡奧達南的阿波尼博利納延的。』當他們上到城鎮時，他們喧嚷起來：『有許多女人來到泉水所在的地方，要攻打你。』阿波尼博利納延急忙去拿她的矛。『別去，阿波尼博利納延，我去。』她的父親帕加蒂帕南說；『不，因為你已衰弱了。你如今還能做什麼？從前你確曾在泉水所在的地方殺過人，如今這或許是我的命運。』她來到泉邊，往下一看——敵人果然多得像是泉邊的一大群蝗蟲。

passages.text: Ginambo of Gonlgonan said, 'You people who live with me, you are anxious to carry away this woman whom we do not like' — 'Yes, but only our names will go back to the towns we came from,' they answered, i.e. they expected to be killed. Aponibolinayen said, 'You old enemy, take this betel-nut,' and she cut it in two and gave it to them. 'Ala, now do what you can,' shouted Aponibolinayen, who stood on a high rock; when they started toward her their spears looked like rain, they were so many, and she glanced off the spears with both elbows. 'Now I am the next to throw my spears,' said Aponibolinayen. She said, 'I will use my magic, and you, my spear, shall kill six and seven at one time, and you, my headaxe, cut off their heads from the left side and from the right side, and in back and in front.' 'Ala, you spare me so that I may tell the people in Gonigonan where I live,' said Ginambo; 'Yes, but next month I will come to your town Gonigonan to fight,' said Aponibolinayen — and Ginambo went home alone to her town, for all her companions were lost, because they did not throw their spears at Aponibolinayen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen as Warrior' episodes; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 貢戈南的吉南博說：『你們這些與我同住的人，你們急著要把這個我們不喜歡的女人帶走。』——『是的，但只有我們的名字會回到我們來自的城鎮。』他們回答，也就是說，他們預料自己會被殺。阿波尼博利納延說：『你這個老仇敵，拿著這顆檳榔。』她把檳榔切成兩半，交給他們。『哎呀，現在你們就盡力而為吧。』站在高岩上的阿波尼博利納延喊道；當他們朝她衝來時，他們的矛多得像雨一樣，她用兩肘把矛一一格開。『現在輪到我擲矛了。』阿波尼博利納延說。她說：『我要施展我的法術，你，我的矛，要一次殺死六個、七個，你，我的戰斧，要從左邊、從右邊、從背後、從前面砍下他們的頭。』『哎呀，你饒了我吧，好讓我去告訴貢戈南的人我住在哪裡。』吉南博說；『好，但下個月我要到你的城鎮貢戈南去攻打。』阿波尼博利納延說——於是吉南博獨自回到她的城鎮，因為她所有的同伴都喪失了，只因他們沒有向阿波尼博利納延擲矛。

passages.text: Soon after that Ginawan of Nagtinawan said, 'Let us go to fight Aponigawani of Kadalayapan' — 'No, we do not wish to go, because the people who live in Kadalayapan are powerful like Kaboniyan' — 'No, we go,' said Ginawan. When they reached the spring at Kadalayapan, the women who dipped water said, 'We do not know who is the bravest, whom we should tell, for Aponigawani has no brother.' Then Aponigawani was in a hurry to go: 'Do not go, you will kill somebody,' said her father; 'No, father, the spring will be lost and then what can we do? Father, I am a woman and since I have no brother, perhaps it is my fortune to fight, for you are weak.' She took her skirt, headaxe, and spear and went to the edge of the hill above the spring, where the enemies were thick like locusts about the well; she stood on a high stone with her hands on her hips while they threw their weapons — 'Now, I am next: You, my spear, when I throw you, kill at once seven and six; and you, my headaxe, cut off their heads from the left and right sides, from in back and in front' — until Ginawan begged, 'Please, my friend, let me live so that someone may go back to the town we came from.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen as Warrior' episodes; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久之後，納丁塔萬的吉納萬說道：『我們去攻打卡達拉亞潘的阿波尼加瓦尼吧。』——『不，我們不想去，因為住在卡達拉亞潘的人像卡波尼揚一樣強大。』——『不，我們去。』吉納萬說道。當他們抵達卡達拉亞潘的泉水處時，汲水的女人們說道：『我們不知道誰最勇敢，該向誰稟報，因為阿波尼加瓦尼沒有兄弟。』於是阿波尼加瓦尼急著要去：『別去，你會殺死人的。』她的父親說道；『不，父親，泉水會失去，那我們該怎麼辦？父親，我是女人，既然我沒有兄弟，或許戰鬥就是我的命運，因為你軟弱。』她拿起她的裙子、戰斧和長矛，走到泉水上方山丘的邊緣，敵人像蝗蟲般密集在井邊；她站在一塊高石上，雙手叉腰，而他們投擲武器——『現在，輪到我了：你，我的長矛，當我投出你時，立刻殺死七個和六個；還有你，我的戰斧，從左右兩側、從前後砍下他們的頭。』——直到吉納萬求饒：『求求你，我的朋友，讓我活著，好有人能回到我們來的城鎮。』

passages.text: Bye and bye Aponibolinayen, walking in the middle of the road, stopped because she was tired, and Aponigawani, also walking, looked up and saw a woman to whom none compared, and was startled: 'Here is a woman who looks like me.' They leaned their spears together between them and then talked; 'Ala, let us chew betel-nut' — and the quid which had been chewed by Aponigawani was covered with agate beads which are called pinogalan, and the quid of Aponibolinayen was covered with gold. 'You are more beautiful and have more power than I, because your betel-nut is covered with gold,' said Aponigawani. They told their names — both going to war for the agreed month — and went first to Gonigonan, then to Nagtinawan, their invisible helpers flying to summon Dangdangayan of Naglitnan and Lingiwan of Nagtangpan. When the two men arrived they looked into the town and saw the two women who looked like flames of fire, because of their beauty; the people whom they killed were so many that the pig troughs floated in their blood, and Dangdangayan went in front of the women and scooped them up with his headaxe and put them inside of his belt.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen as Warrior' episodes; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 過了一會兒，走在路中央的阿波尼波利納延因為疲倦而停了下來，同樣走著的阿波尼加瓦尼抬頭看見一個無人能比的女人，大吃一驚：『這裡有個長得像我的女人。』她們把長矛靠在一起，放在兩人之間，然後交談；『來吧，我們嚼檳榔。』——阿波尼加瓦尼嚼過的那口檳榔上覆滿了稱為皮諾加蘭的瑪瑙珠，而阿波尼波利納延的那口則覆滿了黃金。『你比我更美麗，也更有力量，因為你的檳榔覆著黃金。』阿波尼加瓦尼說道。她們互通姓名——兩人都為約定的月份出征——先去了戈尼戈南，然後去了納丁塔萬，她們的隱形助手飛去召喚納格利特南的當當加延和納唐潘的林吉萬。當那兩個男人到達時，他們往城鎮裡看，看見那兩個女人因美貌而宛如火焰；她們殺死的人如此之多，以致豬槽都漂浮在血中，當當加延走到女人們前面，用他的戰斧把她們舀起，放進他的腰帶裡。

passages.text: They went home and sent all the heads before them and also the plunder, and carried the women inside of a big jar. 'Why, Aponibolinayen is here and Lingiwan also,' they said at Kaodanan; Dingowan of Nagtangpan took Aponibolinayen and put her inside of a big jar. At the balaua that followed, old Pagbokasan took Aponibolinayen from the jar and put her inside of his belt; and when they chewed the betel-nut covered with gold to see if the two young men who took home Aponigawani were their relatives, the spittle of Lingiwan went to the spittle of Pagatipanan, and the spittle of Aponigawani went there also; the spittle of Dangdangayan went to the spittle of Pagbokasan and that of Aponibolinayen also, and thus they found out that they were relatives — Pagbokasan was surprised, for he did not know that he had a son, and Ebang took her son and carried him as if he was a baby, while Lingiwan was glad, because he had met his sister during the fight, and Langa-an carried him as if a baby. The heads were put on the sticks around the town; the alan mothers were compelled to attend by the betel-nut which grew on their heads, gave all their things to the sons they had raised, and flew somewhere; and Lingiwan asked his father to make pakdlon for Aponibolinayen, for he wanted to marry her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen as Warrior' episodes; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們回家，把所有頭顱和戰利品先送回去，並把女人們裝在一個大甕裡抬著。『哎呀，阿波尼波利納延在這裡，林吉萬也在。』他們在考達南說道；納唐潘的丁戈萬帶走阿波尼波利納延，把她放進一個大甕裡。在隨後舉行的巴拉瓦儀式中，老帕格博卡桑把阿波尼波利納延從甕裡取出，放進他的腰帶裡；當他們嚼覆著黃金的檳榔，以察看帶阿波尼加瓦尼回家的那兩個年輕人是否是他們的親戚時，林吉萬的唾液流向帕加蒂帕南的唾液，阿波尼加瓦尼的唾液也流向那裡；當當加延的唾液流向帕格博卡桑的唾液，阿波尼波利納延的唾液也一樣，於是他們發現彼此是親戚——帕格博卡桑大吃一驚，因為他不知道自己有兒子，而埃邦帶走她的兒子，像抱嬰兒般抱著他，林吉萬則很高興，因為他在戰鬥中遇見了他的姊妹，朗加安也像抱嬰兒般抱著他。頭顱被掛在城鎮四周的竿子上；阿蘭母親們因頭上長出的檳榔而被迫出席，把她們所有的東西都交給她們撫養的兒子們，然後飛往某處；林吉萬請求他的父親為阿波尼波利納延舉行帕克德隆儀式，因為他想娶她。

title.en: The Two Souls: Gimokud Takawanan and Gimokud Tebang
title.zh: 兩魂：右魂與左魂

region.en: Mt. Apo slopes, Davao, Mindanao, Philippines (Bagobo country)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨達沃阿波火山坡（巴戈博人之地）

period: Bagobo belief recorded 1910-1914, published 1916 (Laura W. Benedict)

source.work: Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences, 1916), 'The Souls of Man', pp. 49-60

summary.en: Every Bagobo has two souls: the right-hand gimokud takawanan, the good soul that shows itself as the shadow on the right of the path and never leaves the body until death — when it slips out through the pulsing crown and goes down to the Great Country below the earth; and the left-hand gimokud tebang, the bad soul, whose dream-flight into the world is nightmare, whose reflection in the water must never be laughed at, and who at death becomes a buso-ghost prowling graves and tall trees.
summary.zh: 巴戈博人各有二魂：右魂吉莫庫德·塔卡瓦南為善魂，顯為右側身影，終身不離肉體——死時自頭頂脈動處逸出，下入地下大邦；左魂吉莫庫德·特邦為惡魂，夜半飛離即成夢魘，水中倒影不可譏笑，死後化為布索幽靈，出沒墳場與孤樹之間。

sensitivity.note: Bagobo eschatology recorded by Benedict among the Bagobo of Davao (fieldwork 1910-1914); archival record, not permission to speak for Bagobo communities. The reflection-in-water taboo is described as a left-hand-soul belief.

passages.text: Inhabiting every individual, two souls called gimokud are recognized — shadowy, etherial personalities that dominate the body more or less completely. The right-hand soul, known in Bagobo terminology as the gimokud takawanan, is the so-called 'good soul' that manifests itself as the shadow on the right-hand side of one's path. The left-hand soul, called gimokud tebang, is said to be a 'bad soul' and shows itself as the shadow on the left side of the path; the name for either shadow is alung. The takawanan is associated, in native thinking, with those factors of existence that stand for life, health, activity, joy; while the tebang is associated with factors that tend toward death, sickness, sluggishness, pain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (1916), 'The Souls of Man'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 每個人都居住著兩個稱為吉莫庫德的靈魂——朦朧的、空靈的人格，或多或少完全支配著身體。右手邊的靈魂，在巴戈博語中稱為吉莫庫德·塔卡瓦南，是所謂的『善魂』，它顯現為一個人道路右側的影子。左手邊的靈魂，稱為吉莫庫德·特邦，據說是『惡魂』，顯現為道路左側的影子；任一種影子的名稱都是阿隆。在土著思想中，塔卡瓦南與代表生命、健康、活動、歡樂的生存因素相關聯；而特邦則與傾向死亡、疾病、遲鈍、痛苦的因素相關聯。

passages.text: The left-hand soul often departs from the human body and does unlooked-for things that have an unhappy influence on the body: it undertakes alarming exploits; it wanders about as a dream-spirit, thus producing nightmare, or, at least, horrible mental images during sleep. The right-hand soul, on the contrary, is associated with the normal continuity of existence, for it never leaves the body from birth until death, except to lie, at times, as the right-hand shadow, still attached clingingly to the physical frame. Death is the simple fact of the passing of the right-hand soul out from the body, and becoming permanently separated from it. But the stream of individual existence is not checked by death, for the takawanan goes at once to the Great Country below the earth, and there continues to live, in much the same manner as on earth, except for the non-corporeal and ghostly appearance that characterizes all of its activities.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (1916), 'The Souls of Man'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 左手邊的靈魂常離開人體，做出對身體有不幸影響的意想不到之事：它從事令人驚恐的冒險；它作為夢魂四處遊蕩，因而產生噩夢，或者至少在睡眠中產生可怕的心理意象。相反地，右手邊的靈魂與存在的正常延續相關聯，因為它從出生到死亡從不離開身體，除了有時作為右手邊的影子躺著，仍緊緊依附於肉體。死亡就是右手邊的靈魂離開身體並永久與之分離的簡單事實。但個體存在的洪流並不因死亡而中斷，因為塔卡瓦南立刻前往地下的偉大國度，並繼續在那裡生活，方式與在世上大致相同，只是其一切活動都具有非肉體和幽靈般的外貌。

passages.text: When a Bagobo is mortally sick and death is imminent, an attendant holds the wrist of the patient to note whether the gimokud is still there; when the pulse ceases to throb, the gimokud is ready to take leave of the body, but, since it cannot find an exit through the wrist or the finger-tips, it passes up to the head of the dying man and goes out through that point in the crown where a pulsation is apparent — somebody lays fingers or palm of the hand on top of the head to ascertain the exact moment when the gimokud takes its flight. Sometimes they make efforts to detain the takawanan in the body: they seize and shake the arms of the dying man; they grasp his head and make it wag to and fro, in the hope of checking the spirit's departure — but as the sure signs of death become apparent they cease all efforts to hold the gimokud.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (1916), 'The Souls of Man'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當一個巴戈博人病危、死亡迫近時，一名侍者握住病人的手腕，以察覺吉莫庫德是否還在；當脈搏停止跳動時，吉莫庫德就準備離開身體，但由於它無法從手腕或指尖找到出口，便上行到臨死之人的頭部，從頭頂上一個明顯搏動的地方出去——有人把手指或手掌放在頭頂上，以確定吉莫庫德飛離的確切時刻。有時他們努力把塔卡瓦南留在體內：他們抓住並搖晃臨死之人的手臂；他們抓住他的頭，讓它來回搖動，希望阻止靈魂離去——但當死亡的確切徵象顯現時，他們就停止一切留住吉莫庫德的努力。

passages.text: When a Bagobo catches sight of his reflection in a clear stream, he must look at it soberly; he must not betray any feeling of pleasure or of amusement: if he laughs at his image in the water, he will die — presumably because he has mocked his left-hand soul. As a Bagobo youth explained: 'When I dream at night, my gimokud tebang is flying and the buso is catching me, or I am falling from a cliff. I dream that I am riding on a boat and fishing in the sea. Many ships I see there that the buso are riding. They look like men with ugly faces and coarse black hair all over their bodies, and some have wings. Then I try to run away.' At the moment of death the tebang leaves the body for the last time, now to become a buso-ghost, and to join the innumerable company of buso that haunt graves and tall trees and lonely places.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (1916), 'The Souls of Man'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當巴戈博人瞥見自己在清澈溪流中的倒影時，他必須神情嚴肅地凝視；他絕不可流露出任何愉悅或覺得有趣的神情：倘若他對著水中的影像發笑，他便會死去——據推測，這是因為他嘲弄了自己的左手靈魂。正如一位巴戈博青年所解釋的：「當我夜裡做夢時，我的gimokud tebang正在飛翔，而buso正追捕著我，或者我正從懸崖上墜落。我夢見自己乘著船在海裡捕魚。我在那裡看見許多船，buso正乘坐在上頭。他們看起來像人，卻面容醜陋，全身長滿粗糙的黑髮，有些還長著翅膀。於是我便試圖逃走。」在死亡的時刻，tebang最後一次離開身體，此時它將化為buso鬼魂，加入那無數出沒於墳墓、高樹與荒僻之地的buso之列。

title.en: The Journey to Gimokudan: The Black River and the Leaf-Vessels
title.zh: 往吉莫庫丹之旅：黑河與葉舟

region.en: Gimokudan (the Great Country below the earth), Bagobo mythic geography, Mindanao, Philippines (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨地底大邦吉莫庫丹（巴戈博神話地理，象徵定位）

period: Bagobo belief recorded 1910-1914, published 1916 (Laura W. Benedict)

source.work: Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences, 1916), 'The One Country of the Dead', pp. 54-58

summary.en: The right-hand soul, warned of its last journey by the chirping ghost-bug that visits every house between death and burial, travels two days to a week to Gimokudan with its onong travel-outfit buried in the grave. It first passes through the City of the Black River, where under Mebuyan — whose whole body is supplied with milk glands for the nursing infants she keeps — the soul bathes head and joints in the dark water, lest it slip back and reanimate the body. Then all the dead work and dance all night, while our sun lights their world — each melting at sunrise into a leaf-vessel that fills with water, and reforming at our nightfall.
summary.zh: 善魂由夜間啼鳴的鬼蟲報喪，攜葬中隨行的『行囊』，行二日至一週抵吉莫庫丹。先過黑河之城——在滿身乳腺、哺育夭嬰的梅布揚治下，於黑水浴頭沐節，以免魂魄溜回人間復附其身。此後眾死者晝寢夜作：日出時各摺寬葉為舟，坐待烈日將己蒸融、舟中積水；待我方入夜，又復凝聚成形。

sensitivity.note: Bagobo eschatology recorded by Benedict; archival record, not permission to speak for Bagobo communities. The lustration term loamalugu is shared with the living Ginum festival rite; the ghost-bug summons and banishing formula are quoted in summary.

passages.text: Between the time of death and burial it is still possible for the right-hand soul to communicate with the living, and this it does on a vast scale. Immediately after leaving the body, it is customary for the spirit to give notice of its last journey, and at the same time try to secure a companion, by visiting in the form of an insect every house in the world — the entire series of visits supposed to be made during the short period that elapses between death and burial. The insect enters a house and sings in a small voice that is like the chirp of a cricket, or the soft tinkling of a little bell called korung-korung; nobody can see the gimokud, but at night when 'the bug with the sweet voice chirps on the wall' one knows that somebody is dead. Then the person listening must say: 'Who are you? my brother? my sister?' If the singing stops immediately, it is a sign that a near relative is dead, but if the sound keeps on it indicates that some other family has been bereaved.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (1916), 'The One Country of the Dead'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在死亡與埋葬之間的這段時間裡，右手靈魂仍有可能與生者溝通，而它確實大規模地這麼做。靈魂離開身體之後，慣例是立即通報它的最後旅程，同時試圖尋得一名同伴，其方式是化為昆蟲造訪世上的每一戶人家——據說這整系列的造訪，是在死亡與埋葬之間所流逝的短暫期間內完成的。這昆蟲進入一戶人家，以細小的聲音鳴唱，那聲音像蟋蟀的唧唧聲，或像一只名為korung-korung的小鈴所發出的輕柔叮噹聲；沒有人能看見gimokud，但夜裡當「那聲音甜美的蟲子在牆上唧唧鳴唱」時，人便知道有人死了。於是聆聽的人必須說：「你是誰？我的兄弟？我的姊妹？」倘若鳴唱立即停止，這便是近親已死的徵兆；但倘若聲音持續不斷，則表示是別戶人家遭逢了喪親之痛。

passages.text: Sometimes the chirping is interpreted as a summons to some friend or relative to follow the dead one, who asks for a fellow traveler to the lower world; fearful of sickness and death coming upon him, the listener quickly replies: 'You can come here no more because you are now going to the Great City. You have still a little love for me; do not bring me sickness.' This formula is usually potent to banish the importunate spirit. A rain lasting several days, or even a week, is a phenomenon very significant when it occurs immediately after the death of a Bagobo, for it is caused by the tears of the dead gimokud, who is lingering about, waiting for a friend to accompany him; a magical rite must then be performed to still the lamentations of the spirit — the father places a few areca-nuts and betel-leaves, with perhaps a little tobacco, on the ground as an offering, and cajoles the spirit: 'Do not cry any more, for you know you do not love your father; you would rather go to the Great City.' The spell is efficacious; the rain ceases; the gimokud stops its weeping and starts alone on the last journey.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (1916), 'The One Country of the Dead'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有時這唧唧聲被解讀為對某位朋友或親人的召喚，要他們追隨死者而去，因為死者正要求一名同行者一同前往下界；聆聽者因害怕疾病與死亡降臨己身，便連忙回答：「你不能再來這裡了，因為你如今正前往大城。你對我仍存有一點愛；別把疾病帶給我。」這套說辭通常足以驅退那糾纏不休的靈魂。若在巴戈博人死後立即降下持續數日、甚至一週的雨，這現象便極具意義，因為這雨是由死去gimokud的眼淚所致，它正徘徊不去，等待一名朋友伴它同行；此時必須舉行一場法術儀式以止息靈魂的哀泣——父親在地上放置幾顆檳榔子與檳榔葉，或許再加一點菸草，作為供品，並哄勸那靈魂：「別再哭了，因為你知道你並不愛你的父親；你寧可前往大城。」這咒語靈驗有效；雨停了；gimokud停止哭泣，獨自踏上最後的旅程。

passages.text: The time required for the journey from earth down to the land of the dead, called Kilut, is variously estimated at from two days to one week; a traveling outfit, technically known as onong, is prepared by the friends of the deceased so that he may lack for nothing on the road — betel-box and lime-case, areca-nuts, buyo-leaf, tobacco, boiled rice, and other necessaries — all of which are placed in carrying-bag or basket and buried with the body. It is the spiritual substratum or essence of the rice, the buyo or the tobacco, that the gimokud abstracts and enjoys, while the material element is left in the grave with the corpse: every manufactured thing has its own soul, and all these go down to Kilut with the human gimokud. On reaching Gimokudan, it is necessary to pass, first, through the City of the Black River, which has also the name of Alamiawan; here, under the direction of Mebuyan, chief priestess of the place, the soul undergoes a ceremonial lustration in the dark waters of the river, a bathing of head and joints. This process stands for naturalization in the world of spirits, and serves also to infuse a feeling of restfulness and content into the newly arrived gimokud and to dispel any lingering desire that it may have to return to earth — failing this rite, the spirit might slip away, go back to the world and reanimate the body.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (1916), 'The One Country of the Dead'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從人間下行至死者之地（稱為Kilut）所需的時間，說法不一，從兩天到一週不等；死者的親友會備妥一套行裝，術語稱為onong，好讓他在路上樣樣不缺——檳榔盒與石灰盒、檳榔子、buyo葉、菸草、煮熟的米飯，以及其他必需品——這些全都放入提袋或籃子裡，隨屍體一同埋葬。gimokud所抽取並享用的，是米飯、buyo或菸草的靈性基底或精華，而物質成分則隨屍體留在墳墓裡：每一件製成品都有它自己的靈魂，而所有這些靈魂都隨人的gimokud一同下到Kilut。抵達Gimokudan時，首先必須穿過黑河之城，此城又名Alamiawan；在這裡，在該地首席女祭司Mebuyan的指引下，靈魂要在河水的幽暗之中經歷一場儀式性的洗淨，洗濯頭部與各關節。這過程代表著在靈界中取得歸化，同時也有助於為新到的gimokud注入一種安歇與滿足之感，並驅散它可能殘存的任何重返人間的欲望——若缺了這儀式，靈魂或許會溜走，回到人間，使身體重新復活。

passages.text: The same sun that shines on us by day travels around under the earth, and illuminates the world of the dead while we are in darkness, so that our day is synchronous with night in Kilut, and our night, with their day. It is during their period of darkness that all the dead are in action: the gimokud — weak, attenuated, shadowy as they are conceived to be — work and dance and play and eat in the customary Bagobo manner; they sow and harvest rice; they dig camotes and cut sugar cane. The rice of Kilut is of immaculate whiteness, and each grain as big as a kernel of corn; the camotes are the size of a great round pot, and every stick of sugar cane is as large as the trunk of a cocoanut-palm. At the rising of the sun all these activities come to a halt: every gimokud plucks one of the broad leaves of a plant called maguian and twists it into a vessel suggesting the form of a boat, called by the same name as the ceremonial dishes of hemp-leaf in use at Bagobo festivals, kinudok; each one of the gimokud seats himself upon his individual leaf-vessel, and there sits, waiting, until the hot rays of the sun cause him to dissolve, leaving the leaf-vessel full of water — not until our day begins, and darkness spreads over the land of the dead, does the life of the ghosts swing back into action.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (1916), 'The One Country of the Dead'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那在白晝照耀我們的同一輪太陽，也在地底之下環行，當我們身處黑暗之時照亮死者的世界，因此我們的白天與Kilut的夜晚同時，而我們的夜晚則與他們的白天同時。所有死者都在他們的黑暗時段裡活動：gimokud——儘管如人們所設想的那般虛弱、稀薄、如影一般——仍以巴戈博人慣常的方式工作、跳舞、嬉戲與進食；他們播種並收割稻米；他們挖掘甘藷、砍伐甘蔗。Kilut的稻米純白無瑕，每一粒都大如玉米粒；甘藷大如一口巨大的圓鍋，每一根甘蔗都粗如椰子樹的樹幹。太陽升起時，所有這些活動便戛然而止：每一個gimokud都摘下一片名為maguian的植物的寬葉，將它扭折成一只形似小船的容器，其名稱與巴戈博節慶中所用的麻葉儀式餐盤相同，皆稱作kinudok；每一個gimokud都坐上自己專屬的葉製容器，就那樣坐著等待，直到太陽的灼熱光線使他消融，留下那盛滿水的葉製容器——直到我們的白天開始、黑暗籠罩死者之地，鬼魂的生命才又再度活躍起來。

title.en: Mebuyan, Nurse of the Dead Children
title.zh: 梅布揚：亡嬰的乳母

region.en: Banud Mebuyan, the infant section of Gimokudan, Bagobo mythic geography, Mindanao, Philippines (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨吉莫庫丹嬰靈之區梅布揚（巴戈博神話地理，象徵定位）

period: Bagobo belief recorded 1910-1914, published 1916 (Laura W. Benedict)

source.work: Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences, 1916), 'Topography of the one country', pp. 56-57

summary.en: A part of the country through which the Black River runs is set apart specially for nursing infants: as narrated in an ancient tale, one of Lumabat's sisters descended into the lower world, took the name of Mebuyan, and became chief of a special section of Gimokudan named for her. Little children who die while still nourished at their mothers' breasts go at once to Mebuyan, who welcomes them and gives milk to all — for not merely her breasts, but her arms and her whole body are plentifully supplied with milk glands; under her protection the babies remain until they cease to be parasites and can shift for themselves, when they are sent to join their own families in the main banua of Gimokudan.
summary.zh: 黑河流經之地，特闢一區以哺夭嬰。古傳魯瑪巴特之妹入冥界，取名梅布揚，成為以其名命之靈境之主。尚在母乳哺育中夭亡的幼兒，即刻歸於梅布揚——她不僅雙乳，連雙臂與周身都密布乳腺，歡迎眾嬰並賜奶哺之。嬰靈在她的護佑下成長至能自立，方被送往吉莫庫丹大邦與家人團聚。

sensitivity.note: Bagobo eschatology recorded by Benedict; archival record, not permission to speak for Bagobo communities. Benedict notes Mebuyan's position suggests the worship of the 'Great Mothers' of northern India; for the story of Mebuyan see Benedict's 'Bagobo myths' (JAFL 26:20-21).

passages.text: The topography of Gimokudan is correlated, first, with age, and second, with the manner of death: the primary grouping consists in a segregation of young children from adults. A part of the country through which the Black River runs is set apart specially for nursing infants; as narrated in an ancient tale, one of Lumabat's sisters descended into the lower world, took the name of Mebuyan, and became chief of a special section of Gimokudan, which is named for her, Banud Mebuyan. Little children who die when they are still being nourished at their mothers' breasts — a long period with Bagobo children — go at once to Mebuyan, who welcomes them and gives milk to all; for not merely her breasts, but her arms and her whole body, are plentifully supplied with milk glands. Under her protection, the babies remain until they cease to be parasites and can shift for themselves, when they are sent to join their own families in the main banua of Gimokudan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (1916), 'Topography of the one country'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: Gimokudan的地形分佈，首先與年齡相關，其次與死亡的方式相關：最基本的區分方式，是將幼童與成人隔離。黑河流經之地的一部分，特別劃分出來哺育嬰兒；正如一則古老傳說所述，Lumabat的一位姊妹下到陰間，取名為Mebuyan，成為Gimokudan一個特別區域的首領，該區便以她命名，稱為Banud Mebuyan。那些尚在母親懷中吃奶時便死去的幼童——對巴戈博孩童而言這是一段漫長的時期——會立刻前往Mebuyan那裡，她迎接他們，並餵奶給所有孩子；因為不僅她的雙乳，連她的手臂與整個身體，都豐盈地佈滿乳腺。在她的庇護下，嬰兒們留在此處，直到他們不再是寄生者、能夠自行照料自己為止，屆時他們便被送往Gimokudan主要banua中，與自己的家人團聚。

passages.text: A special region, called Kag-bunoan, is reserved for those who are slain by sword or spear, and it is said to be situated at some distance from the other divisions of the country of the dead; in Kag-bunoan there are everywhere suggestions of blood, or of death by violence — for example, all the plants are of a blood-red color, and the spiritual bodies of the inhabitants retain the scars of their wounds, yet all occupations go on just as in the other parts of Gimokudan. The Great Country, that is to say, Dakul Banua proper, forms the most extensive section of Gimokudan, since it is intended for all people, good and bad, who die from disease, or from sickness in any form; hither, too, come trooping all the children who are old enough to leave the fostering care of Mebuyan — pale in color, or pure white, are all the plants and trees here.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (1916), 'Topography of the one country'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個名為卡格布努安（Kag-bunoan）的特殊區域，是為那些被刀劍或長矛所殺者保留的，據說它位於死者之國其他分區的某段距離之外；在卡格布努安，處處都暗示著血，或暴力致死——例如，所有的植物都是血紅色的，居民的精神身體仍留有傷口的疤痕，然而一切勞作都如吉莫庫丹（Gimokudan）其他地方一樣照常進行。大國，也就是說，達庫爾·巴努阿（Dakul Banua）本部，構成吉莫庫丹最廣闊的部分，因為它是為所有因疾病或以任何形式之病痛而死的人——無論善惡——所預備的；所有年長到足以離開梅布揚（Mebuyan）撫育照料的孩童也都成群來到此地——這裡所有的植物和樹木都是蒼白的顏色，或純白色。

title.en: Kilat, the Thunder Horse
title.zh: 基拉特：雷霆之馬

region.en: The sky above Mt. Apo, Davao, Mindanao, Philippines (Bagobo mythic sky)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨阿波火山上空（巴戈博神話之天）

period: Bagobo belief recorded 1910-1914, published 1916 (Laura W. Benedict)

source.work: Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences, 1916), 'Thunder and lightning' (Kilat), pp. 48-49

summary.en: Thunder and lightning are referred to an enormous horse, Kilat by name, that belongs to one of the diwata: Kilat runs and fights, prances and gambols in the sky, making lightning flash when he shakes his bright mane, sending out thunderclaps when he neighs in a mighty, roaring voice. His power is feared like that of buso, for the heaviest peals mean he is about to drop down to earth; lemon-water thrown on the ground frightens him back. The bluish-black whetstones of meteoric origin are his dropped teeth — and it is the action of Kilat's teeth that splits open cocoanuts and dents the bananas lying on the ground.
summary.zh: 雷霆閃電乃屬於天神之巨馬基拉特：他馳騁天際、奮蹄嘶鳴——鬃毛一抖便電光乍現，昂首長嘶便雷聲隆隆。其威如布索，最沉的雷鳴意味他將墜地；潑灑檸檬水可將其嚇退。藍黑色隕石是他的落齒——椰子迸裂、香蕉帶齒痕，皆因基拉特的牙齒。

sensitivity.note: Bagobo meteorological myth recorded by Benedict; archival record, not permission to speak for Bagobo communities. The whetstone-teeth belief connects the myth to real objects.

passages.text: The phenomena of thunder and lightning are referred to an enormous horse, Kilat by name, that belongs to one of the diwata. Kilat runs and fights, prances and gambols in the sky, making lightning flash when he shakes his bright mane, sending out thunder-claps when he neighs in a mighty, roaring voice. The power of this mythical animal is feared like that of buso, since the heaviest peals of thunder indicate that Kilat is about to drop down to earth, bringing sickness and death to domestic animals and to the Bagobo; when Kilat's voice is heard at its loudest, they cut up a lemon in water and throw the water here and there on the ground, since this will frighten him back to his place in the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (1916), 'Thunder and lightning'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 雷電的現象被歸因於一匹名叫基拉特（Kilat）的巨馬，牠屬於某位迪瓦塔（diwata）。基拉特在天空中奔跑、爭鬥、騰躍、嬉戲，當牠搖動明亮的鬃毛時便使閃電閃爍，當牠以強而有力的咆哮之聲嘶鳴時便發出雷鳴。這隻神話動物的力量如布索（buso）一般令人畏懼，因為最沉重的雷聲表示基拉特即將降落到地上，給家畜和巴戈博人（Bagobo）帶來疾病與死亡；當基拉特的聲音聽起來最響亮時，他們把一顆檸檬切碎放入水中，並把水四處潑灑在地上，因為這會把牠嚇回天空中的原位。

passages.text: There is an interesting tradition connected with certain small, bluish-black stones, several inches long, that are, perhaps, of meteoric origin; the Bagobo use them for whetstones and for scouring-bricks, but they say that they are the teeth of Kilat, which dropped out of his mouth when it was wide open for emitting thunder-claps, or that he lost some teeth while eating. It is the action of Kilat's teeth that splits open cocoanuts and makes them fall to the ground — this is the reason that cocoanuts are so often heard to drop, when no man has climbed the tree to cut them off. Bananas, also, are found lying on the ground, spoiled evidently by the teeth of Kilat, for the dents may be seen in the skin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (1916), 'Thunder and lightning'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一種有趣的傳說與某些數英寸長、藍黑色的小石頭有關，這些石頭也許源自隕石；巴戈博人用它們作磨刀石和擦洗磚，但他們說這些是基拉特的牙齒，是牠張大嘴發出雷鳴時從口中掉落的，或是牠在進食時掉了幾顆牙。正是基拉特牙齒的作用使椰子裂開並使它們落到地上——這就是為什麼常常聽到椰子掉落，卻沒有人爬上樹去把它們砍下來。香蕉也同樣被發現躺在地上，顯然是被基拉特的牙齒弄壞的，因為果皮上可以看到齒痕。

title.en: The Transformations of the Dead: Hawk, Lotus, Benu, Swallow, and Crocodile
title.zh: 亡者之變形：鷹、蓮、貝努、燕與鱷

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (Book of the Dead, chapters of taking forms)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（亡靈書變形諸章）

period: Book of the Dead chs. 76-89, Theban recension c. 1550-1292 BCE (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IV, the summary of the transformation chapters

summary.en: The shapeshifter's catalogue of the Book of the Dead: chapters 76-89 enable the dead to transform into the Light-god, the primeval soul of God, Ptah, Osiris, a golden hawk, a divine hawk, a lotus, a benu bird, a heron, a swallow, a serpent, and a crocodile — 'and into any being or thing he pleased' — while ch. 89 lets the soul rejoin its body at pleasure.
summary.zh: 亡靈書之變形目錄：第七六至八九章使亡者能化為光神、太初神魂、卜塔、奧西里斯、金鷹、神鷹、蓮花、貝努鳥、蒼鷺、燕、蛇與鱷——『且能化為任何存在或之物』；第八九章更使魂可隨意歸返其身。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary chapters summarized in Budge 1910; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Chaps. 76-89 enabled a man to transform himself into the Light-god, the primeval soul of God, the gods Ptah and Osiris, a golden hawk, a divine hawk, a lotus, a benu bird, a heron, a swallow, a serpent, a crocodile, and into any being or thing he pleased. Chap. 89 enabled the soul of the deceased to rejoin its body at pleasure, and Chaps. 91 and 92 secured the egress of his soul and spirit from the tomb.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IV, summary of the Book of the Dead chapters.
passages.zh: 第七十六至八十九章使一個人能夠將自己變形為光之神、神最原初的靈魂、普塔（Ptah）與歐西里斯（Osiris）兩位神、一隻金鷹、一隻神鷹、一朵蓮花、一隻貝努鳥（benu bird）、一隻蒼鷺、一隻燕子、一條蛇、一條鱷魚，以及任何他喜歡的存在或事物。第八十九章使死者的靈魂能夠隨意重新結合其身體，第九十一與九十二章則確保他的靈魂與精神能從墳墓中出去。

title.en: The Souls of Pe and Nekhen: Knowing the Gods of the Cities
title.zh: 布托與奈肯之魂：識城之神

region.en: Pe (Buto) and Nekhen, Egypt (the pre-dynastic capitals and their souls)
region.zh: 埃及布托（佩）與奈肯（前王朝故都及其神魂）

period: Book of the Dead chs. 108-119, Theban recension (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IV, the chapters on the Souls of the towns

summary.en: Before the dead may sail the skies he must know the souls of the ancient cities: chapters 108-119 enable him 'to know the Souls of the East and West, and of the towns of Pe (Buto), Nekhen, Khemenu (Hermopolis), and Anu (Heliopolis)' — the divine inhabitants of Egypt's oldest shrines, the predynastic souls whose company admits the newcomer.
summary.zh: 亡者欲航於天，必先識古城之魂：第一〇八至一一九章使其『得知東西之魂，及布托、奈肯、赫爾莫波利斯與赫利奧波利斯諸城之魂』——埃及最古聖地之神居，知其名者方得同行。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary chapters summarized in Budge 1910; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Chaps. 108, 109, 112, and 116 enabled him to know the Souls (i.e. gods) of the East and West, and of the towns of Pe, Nekhen, Khemenu, and Anu. Chaps. 117-119 enabled him to find his way through Rastau, a part of the kingdom of Seker, the god of Death.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IV, summary.
passages.zh: 第一〇八、一〇九、一一二與一一六章使他能夠認識東方與西方的靈魂（即諸神），以及佩（Pe）、涅肯（Nekhen）、赫梅努（Khemenu）與阿努（Anu）諸城的靈魂。第一一七至一一九章使他能夠在拉斯塔烏（Rastau）中找到道路，那是死亡之神塞克爾（Seker）王國的一部分。

title.en: Herfhaf the Ferryman: None but the Righteous May Land
title.zh: 渡者赫爾哈夫：唯義者得登岸

region.en: The celestial river of the Egyptian Other World (symbolic pin, Abydos region)
region.zh: 埃及冥界天河（象徵定位，阿拜多斯一帶）

period: Book of the Dead chs. 98-99 and 125, Theban recension (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IV, the celestial ferryman

summary.en: The ferryman of the dead: chapters 98-99 secure the use of the magical boat and the services of the celestial ferryman, who ferries the justified across the river of the Tuat to the Island of Fire where Osiris lives — and none but the righteous may enter his boat, none but the righteous land on the island; at the Great Judgment the deceased declares 'I have testified before Herfhaf, and he hath approved me.'
summary.zh: 亡者之渡者：第九八至九九章使亡者得用魔法之舟，由天渡者載其渡冥界之河至奧西里斯所居之火島——唯義者得登其舟、得履其島；大審判時亡者自陳：『我已陳於赫爾哈夫之前，而彼許我。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary chapters via Budge 1910; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Chaps. 98 and 99 secured for him the use of the magical boat, and the services of the celestial ferryman, who would ferry him across the river in the Tuat to the Island of Fire, in which Osiris lived. Chaps. 101 and 102 provided access for him to the Boat of Ra.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IV, summary.
passages.zh: 第九十八與九十九章為他確保了魔法船的使用，以及天界擺渡人的服務，那人會載他渡過圖阿特（Tuat）中的河流，前往歐西里斯所居住的火之島。第一〇一與一〇二章為他提供了通往拉（Ra）之船的途徑。

passages.text: I have testified before Herfhaf, and he hath approved me. I have seen the things over which the Persea tree spreadeth [its branches] in Rastau. I offer up my prayers to the gods, and I know their persons. I have come and have advanced to declare the truth and to set up the Balance on its stand in Aukert.
