passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. IV, from Book of the Dead ch. 125 (Herfhaf = the celestial ferryman; footnote: 'None but the righteous could enter his boat, and none but the righteous was allowed to land on the Island of Osiris').
passages.zh: 我已在赫爾哈夫面前作證，他已認可我。我見過那棵在拉斯塔烏伸展枝幹的珀耳塞亞樹所覆蓋之物。我向眾神獻上祈禱，我認識祂們的形貌。我已前來，並上前宣揚真理，在奧克特將天平立於其座上。

title.en: The Ship of Osiris and the Argo: Canopus the Pilot
title.zh: 奧西里斯之舟與阿爾戈號：舵師卡諾普斯

region.en: The night sky between Orion and the Dog Star (constellation of the ship of Osiris)
region.zh: 獵戶座與天狼星之間的夜空（奧西里斯舟之星座）

period: Recorded by Plutarch, De Iside 22 (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, sec. XXII

summary.en: The euhemerist reading of the gods, from Plutarch's Egyptian priests: Hermes had one hand shorter than the other, Typhon was red-complexioned, Horus fair, Osiris black — men subject to human accidents; Osiris was a general, Canopus (the star) a pilot, 'and the ship which the Greeks call Argo, being made in imitation of the ship of Osiris, was, in honour of him, turned into a constellation and placed near Orion and the Dog-star, the former being sacred to Horus and the latter to Isis.'
summary.zh: 普魯塔克筆下埃及祭司之優赫莫魯斯說：托特一手較短、塞特赤面、荷魯斯晳白、奧西里斯玄黑——皆同於凡人；奧西里斯乃將軍，卡諾普斯（星名）乃舵師——『希臘所謂阿爾戈號，乃仿奧西里斯之舟而造，因尊其人，化為星座，置於獵戶與天狼之側：前者屬荷魯斯，後者屬伊西斯。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient allegoresis via Plutarch; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: For when the Egyptians themselves tell us that Hermes had one hand shorter than another, that Typhon was of red complexion, Horus fair, and Osiris black, does not this show that they were of the human species, and subject to the same accidents as all other men? Nay, they go farther, and even declare the particular work in which each was engaged whilst alive.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. XXII.
passages.zh: 因為當埃及人自己告訴我們，赫爾墨斯的一隻手比另一隻短，堤豐膚色赤紅，荷魯斯白皙，俄西里斯黝黑，這豈不表明他們屬於人類，並與所有其他人一樣會遭遇同樣的變故？不僅如此，他們還更進一步，甚至道出各人活著時所從事的具體工作。

passages.text: Thus they say that Osiris was a general, that Canopus, from whom the star took its name, was a pilot, and that the ship which the Greeks call Argo, being made in imitation of the ship of Osiris, was, in honour of him, turned into a constellation and placed near Orion and the Dog-star, the former being sacred to Horus and the latter to Isis.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XXII.
passages.zh: 因此他們說俄西里斯是一位統帥，卡諾普斯——那顆星即由他得名——是一名舵手，而希臘人稱為阿爾戈號的那艘船，乃是仿照俄西里斯的船所造，為了尊崇他而化為星座，置於獵戶座與天狼星附近，前者為荷魯斯所聖，後者為伊西斯所聖。

title.en: No Women in the Temples: The Egyptian Rule of Purity
title.zh: 殿中無男女之事：埃及潔淨之律

region.en: Egyptian temples of all the gods
region.zh: 埃及諸神廟

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.64 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 64

summary.en: The Egyptians, says Herodotus, were the first to make it a point of religion not to lie with women in temples, nor to enter a temple after going away from women without first bathing — while nearly all other men, 'since they hold that there is no difference in this respect between men and beasts', point to beasts coupling in the sacred enclosures as proof of divine consent; the Egyptians answer with Plato's dictum that none but the pure should approach the pure.
summary.zh: 希羅多德言：埃及人首立宗教之律——殿中不行男女之事，自婦人處來亦必先浴而後入廟——他邦之人則指聖域中獸之相配為神許之證，謂人獸無別；埃及人則守『唯淨者近於淨』之義。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ethnography via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The Egyptians were the first who made it a point of religion not to lie with women in temples, nor to enter into temples after going away from women without first bathing: for almost all other men except the Egyptians and the Hellenes lie with women in temples and enter into a temple after going away from women without bathing, since they hold that there is no difference in this respect between men and beasts: for they say that they see beasts and the various kinds of birds coupling together both in the temples and in the sacred enclosures of the gods; if then this were not pleasing to the god, the beasts would not do so. Thus do these defend that which they do, which by me is disallowed: but the Egyptians are excessively careful in their observances, both in other matters which concern the sacred rites and also in those which follow.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.64. / Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.65.
passages.zh: 埃及人是最先將此事定為宗教規條的人：不在神廟中與女子交合，且與女子分離後未先沐浴不得進入神廟；因為除埃及人和希臘人之外，幾乎所有其他人都在神廟中與女子交合，並在與女子分離後未沐浴便進入神廟，蓋他們認為在此事上人與獸並無分別：他們說自己看見野獸與各種鳥類在神廟中及眾神的神聖圍地內交配；倘若此事不為神所喜，野獸便不會如此行。這些人便如此為自己的行為辯護，而我對此不予認可；但埃及人在其儀軌上極為謹慎，無論是其他關乎聖禮之事，還是以下所述之事。

title.en: The Goat of Mendes: Pan with the Goat's Face
title.zh: 門德斯之羊：羊面之潘

region.en: Mendes, Nile Delta, Egypt (the sacred goat of the district)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲門德斯（其地聖羊）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.46 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 46

summary.en: The Mendesians count Pan among the eight elder gods, and the image-makers carve him with goat's face and legs 'not supposing him to be really like this but to resemble the other gods' — the reason for the form Herodotus declines to tell; they reverence all goats, the males above the females, goatherds above other herdsmen, and mourn greatly when their one sacred goat dies, for 'both the goat and Pan are called in the Egyptian tongue Mendes.'
summary.zh: 門德斯人列潘於八位先在之神；造像者刻其羊面羊足——『非謂其形實如此，乃擬他神之狀』——其形之故，希羅多德不欲言。彼等敬一切羊，雄踞雌上，牧羊人尊於他牧；其聖羊獨享尊榮，死則舉境大哀——蓋『羊與潘，埃及語皆名門德斯』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ethnographic myth via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. Herodotus' final clause about the public marvel is reported without detail and is not quoted here.

passages.text: Now the reason why those of the Egyptians whom I have mentioned do not sacrifice goats, female or male, is this: — the Mendesians count Pan to be one of the eight gods (now these eight gods they say came into being before the twelve gods), and the painters and image-makers represent in painting and in sculpture the figure of Pan, just as the Hellenes do, with goat's face and legs, not supposing him to be really like this but to resemble the other gods; the cause however why they represent him in this form I prefer not to say.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.46.
passages.zh: 我所提及的那些埃及人不獻祭山羊——無論雌雄——的原因如下：門德斯人將潘算作八神之一（他們說這八神先於十二神而存在），而畫師與造像者在繪畫與雕塑中表現潘的形象，一如希臘人所為，生著山羊的面孔與腿，並非認為他真是這般模樣，而是認為他與其他神相似；至於他們為何以此形貌表現他，我寧願不說。

passages.text: The Mendesians then reverence all goats and the males more than the females (and the goatherds too have greater honour than other herdsmen), but of the goats one especially is reverenced, and when he dies there is great mourning in all the Mendesian district: and both the goat and Pan are called in the Egyptian tongue Mendes.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.46.
passages.zh: 於是門德斯人崇敬所有山羊，且更崇敬公山羊甚於母山羊（牧羊人也比其他牧人更受尊崇），但在山羊之中，有一隻尤受崇敬，當牠死去時，整個門德斯地區都大為哀悼：而山羊與潘在埃及語中皆稱為門德斯。

title.en: Pigs of Dough: The Poor Man's Sacrifice to the Moon
title.zh: 麵團之豕：貧者祭月

region.en: Egypt, the full-moon sacrifice of the swine
region.zh: 埃及望月祭豕之地

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.47 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 47

summary.en: The pig is an abominable animal: whoever touches one dips in the river with his clothes on, swineherds may not enter temples or marry outside their caste — yet to the Moon and Dionysos alone, at the same full moon, swine are sacrificed and eaten; the priest burns the tail, spleen and caul in the fat, and 'the poor among them, by reason of the scantiness of their means, shape pigs of dough and having baked them they offer these as a sacrifice.'
summary.zh: 豕為可憎之獸：觸之者連衣入河自淨；牧豕者不得入廟、不得與他姓婚——然每月望日，唯月與狄俄倪索斯受豕祭而民得食之；祭司以脂裹尾、脾、網膜焚之——『其貧者因匱乏，乃摶麵為豕，炙而祭之。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient ritual description via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. Herodotus records that the mythic reason for the swine sacrifice is 'not a seemly one for me to tell'.

passages.text: The pig is accounted by the Egyptians an abominable animal; and first, if any of them in passing by touch a pig, he goes into the river and dips himself forthwith in the water together with his garments; and then too swineherds, though they be native Egyptians, unlike all others do not enter any of the temples in Egypt, nor is anyone willing to give his daughter in marriage to one of them or to take a wife from among them; but the swineherds both give in marriage to one another and take from one another.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.47.
passages.zh: 豬被埃及人視為可憎的動物；首先，他們之中若有人路過時碰觸到豬，便會下到河裡，連同衣物立刻浸入水中；此外，養豬人雖是土生土長的埃及人，卻與所有其他人不同，不得進入埃及的任何一座神廟，也沒有人願意把女兒嫁給他們中的一人，或從他們之中娶妻；養豬人只彼此通婚，互相嫁娶。

passages.text: Now to the other gods the Egyptians do not think it right to sacrifice swine; but to the Moon and to Dionysos alone at the same time and on the same full-moon they sacrifice swine, and then eat their flesh: and as to the reason why, when they abominate swine at all their other feasts, they sacrifice them at this, there is a story told by the Egyptians; and this story I know, but it is not a seemly one for me to tell. — The poor however among them by reason of the scantiness of their means shape pigs of dough and having baked them they offer these as a sacrifice.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.47.
passages.zh: 至於其他神明，埃及人認為不宜獻豬為祭；但唯獨對月亮與狄俄尼索斯，他們在同一時刻、同一個滿月之日獻豬為祭，然後食其肉；至於為何他們在所有其他節慶中都厭惡豬，卻在此時獻豬為祭，埃及人流傳著一個故事；這故事我知道，但由我講述並不妥當。——然而他們之中的窮人因財力微薄，便用麵團捏成豬的形狀，烤好之後以此作為祭品獻上。

title.en: The Sky Rose Up: The Mona and the First Couple
title.zh: 天初高：摩納人與始祖夫婦

region.en: Mountainous interior of Mindanao, Philippines (Bagobo homeland)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨內陸山地（巴戈博故地）

period: Bagobo tradition recorded 1910-1914, published 1916 (Laura W. Benedict)

source.work: Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences, 1916), 'Traditions of Mythical Ancestors', pp. 65-68

summary.en: Before man was made the universe was peopled by creatures now called monkeys, but then human in all respects. The aged mona, clothed in cocoanut-palm sheaths, lived stooping under a sky so low that none could stand upright, hiding from the blazing sun in a deep pit — until an old woman, chid while pounding her rice, made the sky rush up to a great height. Then houses were built, the mountains grew cocoanuts and bananas and cane, the first boy Malaki and first girl Bia were born, and the buso, now death-carriers, were then kindly spirits on intimate terms with the people.
summary.zh: 人未造之前，世界屬於今日所稱的猿猴——當時卻全然人形。披椰鞘為衣的長老摩納，在低垂的天穹下終日佝僂，烈日之下躲入深坑——直到一位舂米的老婆婆嗔怪天空礙事，天穹猛然升高。此後竹屋茅舍始建，山間椰蕉甘蔗叢生；首個男孩名瑪拉基、首個女孩名比亞；而今日司病的布索，當時竟是與人親善的善靈。

sensitivity.note: Bagobo tradition recorded by Benedict; archival record, not permission to speak for Bagobo communities. The chid-sky motif parallels Mabel Cook Cole's Bukidnon pestle tale (bukidnon-moon-stars) and the Bagobo 'Why the Sky Went Up' myths of Benedict's JAFL article.

passages.text: Bagobo tradition records that before time began to be reckoned, before man was made, the universe was peopled by creatures that are now called monkeys (liitung); but at that primeval period monkeys had the form of man and were in all respects human. After man appeared on the earth, the apes took on their present form. Although the line of separation between monkeys and human beings was then pretty well established, there still lingered a tendency toward metamorphosis, by which the simian groups gained an occasional recruit from the ranks of man. At the dawn of more authentic oral tradition, there were living in the world very aged people called mona, whose home, some say, was at the center of the earth, but others think that the ancestors of the Bagobo, even back to the mona, have always occupied the mountainous sites in Mindanao where their descendants live to-day. The old men were called tuglay, and the old women, tuglibung, names originally given to the first pair of ancestors, and afterward applied to all the mona; the god Pamulak Manobo, who created the earth and the mona, was assisted by the first tuglibung and tuglay in making the plants and stones and other objects that appeared on the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (1916), 'Traditions of Mythical Ancestors'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴戈博人的傳統記載，在時間開始被計算之前，在人類被造之前，宇宙中居住著如今被稱為猴子（liitung）的生物；但在那太初時期，猴子具有人的形體，在各個方面都是人。人類出現在世上之後，猿猴才變成如今的模樣。儘管當時猴子與人類之間的界線已相當分明，卻仍殘存著一種變形的傾向，使猿猴族群偶爾從人類的行列中增添成員。在更可信的口述傳統初現之時，世上生活著被稱為莫納（mona）的極其年邁之人，有人說他們的家在地心，但另有人認為巴戈博人的祖先，甚至上溯至莫納，一直佔據著民答那峨的山地，也就是其後裔今日所居之地。老年男子被稱為圖格萊（tuglay），老年女子被稱為圖格利邦（tuglibung），這些名號原先是給第一對祖先的，後來則用於所有莫納；創造大地與莫納的神帕穆拉克·馬諾博（Pamulak Manobo），在製造大地上出現的植物、石頭及其他物件時，得到了第一對圖格利邦與圖格萊的協助。

passages.text: There were no young people in those days, and no babies were born for a very long time. All the mona were extremely poor, for this was before the days of cultural inventions: they knew not the art of weaving hemp into garments, and were accustomed to clothe themselves in bunut, the soft, dry sheath that envelops the trunks of cocoanut palms and can be torn off in pieces of considerable size. The old people had rice and fruit to eat, but they lived under miserable conditions, for the low-hanging sky brooded so near the earth that nobody was able to stand upright; all were forced to keep continually a stooping posture.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (1916), 'Traditions of Mythical Ancestors'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那些日子裡沒有年輕人，很長一段時間也沒有嬰兒出生。所有莫納都極其貧窮，因為這是在文化發明之前的時代：他們不懂得將麻編織成衣物的技藝，習慣以布努特（bunut）裹身，那是包覆椰子樹幹的柔軟乾燥的葉鞘，可以撕成相當大的片狀。老人們有米和水果可吃，但生活條件惡劣，因為低垂的天空逼近大地，沒有人能夠直立；所有人都被迫時刻保持彎腰的姿勢。

passages.text: Worst of all, the sun blazed in the sky, and so close to the earth that the mona had to seek refuge in a deep hole from the terrible heat; during the hottest part of the day, they crawled into a great pit in the ground, just as those fabulous black men that live at the door of the sun are said to do this very day. Stung to exasperation at last, an old woman, while stooping to pound her rice, chid the sky for impeding her work, and straightway the sky rushed up to a great height from the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (1916), 'Traditions of Mythical Ancestors'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最糟的是，太陽在天空中熾烈照耀，且離大地如此之近，莫納不得不躲進深洞以避開酷熱；在一天中最熱的時候，他們爬進地上的一個大坑裡，正如據說那些住在太陽之門的傳說中的黑人至今仍所做的那樣。最後，一位老婦人在彎腰舂米時，終於被激得忍無可忍，責罵天空妨礙了她的工作，天空隨即從大地升到極高之處。

passages.text: After the sky went up, things were better: the people could then stand upright and walk at ease. They built houses of bamboo thatched with nipa palm, or with cogon grass; the air was cooler; plants grew in abundance, and the mountains were covered with cocoanut palms and banana plants and sugar cane. The mona had plenty to eat, except in seasons of drought, when the sun wilted the rice-plants and spoiled the bananas; yet they were still called poor, since they had no material wealth in fine textiles, or in ornaments, and they still continued to wrap themselves in pieces of bunut as clothing. By and by, the old people began to give birth to children: the first boy was called Malaki, and the first girl, Bia — famous names, retained in myth for brave heroes and for ladies of distinction. All the country came to be full of people, for nobody died in those days; the buso who now function as disease-bringers and death-carriers were then kindly spirits, on intimate terms with the people. It was at some later period that a quarrel is alleged to have broken out that resulted in the buso assuming a hostile attitude toward man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (1916), 'Traditions of Mythical Ancestors'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天空升起之後，情況好轉了：人們於是能夠直立，自在行走。他們用竹子建造房屋，以尼帕棕櫚葉或白茅草覆頂；空氣較為涼爽；植物繁茂生長，山巒覆滿椰子樹、香蕉樹與甘蔗。莫納有充足的食物，唯有在乾旱季節例外，那時太陽使稻株枯萎，毀壞香蕉；然而他們仍被稱為窮人，因為他們沒有精緻紡織品或飾品之類的物質財富，仍繼續以布努特片裹身作為衣物。漸漸地，老人們開始生育子女：第一個男孩名叫馬拉基（Malaki），第一個女孩名叫比亞（Bia）——這些著名的名字留存於神話中，用以稱呼勇敢的英雄與尊貴的女士。整個地方漸漸人煙稠密，因為那些日子裡沒有人死去；如今充當疾病帶來者與死亡攜帶者的布索（buso），當時是友善的精靈，與人們關係親密。據說是在後來某個時期，才爆發了一場爭執，致使布索對人類採取敵對的態度。

title.en: Lumabat and Mebuyan: The Quarrel That Sent Man Below the Earth
title.zh: 魯瑪巴特與梅布揚：定人歸下之爭

region.en: Mythic Mindanao (Mt. Apo to the lower world), Philippines (symbolic pin on Bagobo homeland)
region.zh: 菲律賓神話民答那峨（阿波火山至地下之邦，以巴戈博故地象徵定位）

period: Bagobo tradition recorded 1910-1914, published 1916 (Laura W. Benedict)

source.work: Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences, 1916), 'Lumabat and Mebuyan', pp. 67-68

summary.en: The renowned Lumabat tried to lead his relatives to heaven; his famous sister refused, fought with him, sat upon the rice mortar and made it sink into the earth, dropping handfuls of rice as a sign that many should go down below but none go up. She became Mebuyan, who guards the entrance to the One Country of the dead and shakes a lemon-tree there, the random fall of green or ripe fruit calling youth or age to the lower world. Lumabat's expedition perished on the road; he alone jumped between the flying edges of the horizon and became a great diwata.
summary.zh: 英名蓋世的魯瑪巴特欲率親族上天；其姊拒絕，與之爭鬥後坐於舂臼之上，令臼沉入地中，並撒落稻米為記：眾人將下而不上。她遂為梅布揚——守冥界之門，搖動冥界的檸檬樹，青果熟果之落，定人壽之修短。魯瑪巴特的族人盡歿途中；唯他躍過開合的地平線之間，登天為大神。

sensitivity.note: Bagobo tradition recorded by Benedict; archival record, not permission to speak for Bagobo communities. Benedict notes the lemon-tree element 'seems very suggestive of Aryan influence, since the tendency of pure Malay myth is to make demons and ghosts responsible for all sickness and death.'

passages.text: One of the most renowned individuals of this early period was Lumabat, and several important episodes turn upon the achievements of himself, and of his brothers and sisters. It was at this time that several people, following the lead of a brother of Lumabat's, turned into monkeys, just as their mythical predecessors had done. A quarrel between Lumabat and a famous sister of his fixed the destiny of man, consigning him at death, not to heaven, but to the country below the earth. It appears that Lumabat insisted upon his sister's accompanying him in an attempt that he was about to make to reach heaven; but the girl refused to go, and, after a fight with Lumabat, she sat down on the rice mortar and caused it to sink into the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (1916), 'Lumabat and Mebuyan'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這早期時代最著名的人物之一是盧馬巴特（Lumabat），若干重要的事件都圍繞著他本人以及他的兄弟姐妹的功業而展開。正是在此時，有幾個人追隨盧馬巴特一位兄弟的帶領，變成了猴子，正如他們神話中的先輩昔日所為一般。盧馬巴特與他一位著名的姊妹之間的爭吵，決定了人類的命運，使人在死後不是被送往天上，而是被送往地下的國度。據說，盧馬巴特堅持要他的姊妹陪同他進行一次他即將嘗試的登天之行；但那女子拒絕前往，並且在與盧馬巴特爭鬥之後，她坐到稻米臼上，使它沉入地下。

passages.text: As she disappeared, while sitting on the mortar, she dropped handfuls of rice upon the ground, for a sign that many should go down below the earth, but that none should go up into heaven. This woman came to be known as Mebuyan, a notable character in myth, for it is she who guards the entrance to the One Country of the dead, and it is she who determines the age at which each individual shall die. Down there in Gimokudan, she shakes a lemon-tree, and the random fall of green or ripe fruit, like the blind-snipping shears of the Greek fate Atropos, calls youth or age to the lower world. Shortly after the disappearance of Mebuyan, Lumabat conducted an expedition having for its object the gaining of an entrance to the country above the sky; a great number of his relatives went with him, but all save Lumabat himself perished in one way or another on the road. He alone succeeded in jumping between the sharp edges of the horizon, as they flew apart and locked together in rapid succession, and he alone reached heaven and became a great diwata.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (1916), 'Lumabat and Mebuyan'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當她坐在臼上消失之時，她把一把把的稻米撒落在地上，作為一個徵兆：許多人將要下到地下，但無人能夠升入天上。這女子後來被稱為梅布揚（Mebuyan），是神話中一位著名的人物，因為正是她守衛著亡者「一國」的入口，也正是她決定每個人將在什麼年歲死去。在那下面的吉莫庫丹（Gimokudan），她搖動一棵檸檬樹，而青澀或成熟果實的隨機墜落，猶如希臘命運女神阿特羅波斯（Atropos）盲目的剪刀，召喚青春或老年前往下界。梅布揚消失後不久，盧馬巴特率領了一支遠征隊，其目的是要取得進入天上方國度的入口；他的眾多親屬隨他同行，但除盧馬巴特本人之外，其餘的人都在途中以種種方式喪命。唯有他一人成功地在天際那銳利的邊緣之間跳過——那些邊緣飛速分開又接合，接連不斷——也唯有他一人抵達了天上，成為一位偉大的迪瓦塔（diwata）。

title.en: The Age of Transformation: Malaki, Bia, and the Changing Skins
title.zh: 變形之世：瑪拉基、比亞與易服之變

region.en: Mythic Mindanao (golden-age Bagobo villages), Philippines (symbolic pin on Bagobo homeland)
region.zh: 菲律賓神話民答那峨（巴戈博黃金時代之鄉，象徵定位）

period: Bagobo tradition recorded 1910-1914, published 1916 (Laura W. Benedict)

source.work: Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences, 1916), 'The Golden Age' and 'Metamorphosis' sections, pp. 69-72

summary.en: In the golden age the tuglay and tuglibung lived in houses of gold with ivory pillars and mirrored doors, beside lakes whose waves were pure white, wishing objects into existence. The invincible malaki could slay buso in countless numbers, hold up his spear and turn daylight to darkness, and fly through the air on his shield; malaki and bia beamed rays of light so brilliant the houses needed no torches. Metamorphosis was ordinary: Wari became a screech-owl, the tree-hornbill's man-skin proves it was once a man, the kingfisher once turned into a beautiful woman, and the poor tuglay of the ulit becomes a great malaki inside of one day — by a change of clothes.
summary.zh: 黃金時代，長老居金屋、象牙柱、鏡門；屋旁白浪之湖，心想事成。無敵的瑪拉基能誅無數布索、舉矛令白晝變黑、乘盾飛空；瑪拉基與比亞周身放光，室內不需火把。變形乃尋常事：瓦里化鴞；犀鳥皮下仍有人皮，故知其曾為人；翠鳥曾化美人； ulit 史詩中的貧寒 tuglay，一日之內三度易服，即成偉大的瑪拉基。

sensitivity.note: Bagobo tradition recorded by Benedict; archival record, not permission to speak for Bagobo communities. Benedict notes the radiant-light motif is common in ancient Indian tales (Katha Sarit Sagara).

passages.text: Be that as it may, a golden age was dawning for those prehistoric Bagobo: the tuglay and the tuglibung, the malaki and the bia, lived in houses of gold with pillars of ivory and doors of mirrored glass; on the eaves hung linked brass chains; the rattan bindings of the floor sent out flashes of forked lightning that played perpetually throughout the house. Beside their homes were mountain lakes whose waves were pure white; all around grew fragrant plants with flowers of gold, and the leaves on the trees were hung with little bells; textiles of gold covered the meadows like layers of dry leaves, and the blades of grass were points of rare embroidery. Cocoanuts and areca-nuts grew in clusters at the height of a man's waist, so that one had not the labor of climbing for them. In those days, many individuals had magic power, and of many a malaki it is sung that he was matolus: when the tuglay lacked anything, he had only to wish for it, and at once the wish was accomplished — if he wanted a tall behuka to grow in a certain place, it was there; at the summons of the bia there came, on the instant, a wealth of ivory and gold and fine garments.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (1916), 'The Golden Age'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不管怎樣，對那些史前的巴戈博人（Bagobo）而言，一個黃金時代正在來臨：圖格萊（tuglay）與圖格里邦（tuglibung）、馬拉基（malaki）與比亞（bia），住在黃金造的房屋裡，柱子是象牙的，門是鏡面玻璃的；屋簷上掛著相連的黃銅鏈；地板的藤條綁紮散發出叉狀閃電的光芒，在整座屋中不停地閃爍。他們的家宅旁是山中的湖泊，湖水純白；四周生長著芬芳的植物，開著金色的花，樹上的葉子掛著小鈴鐺；金色的織物像層層枯葉般覆蓋著草地，草葉則是稀有刺繡的針腳。椰子與檳榔成串地長在人腰的高度，因此人們不必費力攀爬去採摘。在那個時代，許多人擁有法力，許多馬拉基被歌頌為馬托盧斯（matolus）：當圖格萊缺少什麼時，他只需許願，願望便立刻實現——若他想讓一株高大的貝胡卡（behuka）在某處生長，它便長在那裡；在比亞的召喚下，象牙、黃金與華美的衣裳便會即刻湧現。

passages.text: The invincible malaki could slay buso in countless numbers, simply by holding the sword first in his right hand, then in his left; he was invulnerable to attack, since all the weapons of his foes dissolved at the first thrust; he held up his spear and caused daylight to turn to darkness; he flew through the air, riding on his shield or on the swift wind. There were malaki and there were bia from whose bodies beamed rays of light so brilliant that the houses which they entered needed no torch on the dark nights. In song and in romantic tale, even in the current talk of to-day, there is assumed to be a vital relation between beauty in personal adornment and a virtuous character: there is an ideal Bagobo, a true malaki, who is young and perfectly chaste, and who is clad in the finest of garments — one young Bagobo girl defined a malaki thus: 'Very good man who wears very good clothes — kerchief, jacket, trousers, all very good — young man who has no wife.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (1916), 'The Golden Age'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那無敵的馬拉基能殺死無數的布索（buso），只需先把劍握在右手，再握在左手；他對攻擊刀槍不入，因為他敵人的一切武器在第一次刺擊時便會消散；他舉起長矛，便能令白晝變為黑暗；他乘著盾牌或疾風在空中飛翔。有些馬拉基和比亞，身上散發出如此燦爛的光芒，以至於他們所進入的房屋在漆黑的夜晚也無需火炬。在歌謠與浪漫的故事中，甚至在今天日常的談話裡，人們都假定個人裝飾之美與品德之善之間存在著至關重要的關聯：有一位理想的巴戈博人，一位真正的馬拉基，他年輕且完全貞潔，身著最華美的衣裳——一位年輕的巴戈博女子如此定義馬拉基：「非常好的男人，穿著非常好的衣服——頭巾、上衣、褲子，全都非常好——沒有妻子的年輕人。」

passages.text: In those ancient days, metamorphosis was an ordinary event. Many persons were turned into trees and stones and rocks, sometimes as a swift judgment upon them for presumptuous undertakings: Wari, a brother of Lumabat's, was transformed into a screech-owl for his disregard of the commands of a god. That the tree-hornbill used to be a man is a well-known fact, and the proof is that if you look at the body of a hornbill, under the feathers, at some point between the neck and the wing, you will see that its skin is like the skin of man; on the other hand, the kingfisher, as we learn from a myth, once turned into a beautiful woman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (1916), 'Metamorphosis'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在那古老的時代，變形是尋常之事。許多人被變成樹木、石頭和岩石，有時是對他們僭妄之舉的迅速懲罰：盧馬巴特的一位兄弟瓦里（Wari），因無視一位神的命令而被變成了一隻角鴞。犀鳥從前是人，這是眾所周知的事實，其證據是：你若察看一隻犀鳥的身體，在羽毛之下、頸與翼之間的某處，你會看到牠的皮膚像人的皮膚；另一方面，我們從一則神話中得知，翠鳥曾一度變成一位美麗的女子。

passages.text: Transformations of monkeys to buso, of a squirrel to a malaki, even the metamorphosis of a cat's head into a cocoanut — all these changes are recorded by oral tradition. Over and over again does the poor tuglay of the ulit become a great malaki, while the ill-dressed man called basolo turns into a splendidly-dressed malaki and again returns to the state of a basolo, and passes through his final metamorphosis into a malaki — a series of transformations that is achieved inside of one day. In the last-named cases it is always by a change of clothes that the metamorphosis is effected; while the squirrel, too, takes off his little coat, and the kingfisher her feather dress, when the time is ripe for them each to take on human form.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Laura W. Benedict, A Study of Bagobo Ceremonial, Magic and Myth (1916), 'Metamorphosis'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 猴子變成布索、松鼠變成馬拉基，甚至貓頭變成椰子——所有這些變化都由口頭傳統記錄下來。烏利特（ulit）中那可憐的圖格萊一次又一次地變成偉大的馬拉基，而那個衣著襤褸、被稱為巴索洛（basolo）的人則變成衣著華麗的馬拉基，又再度回復到巴索洛的狀態，並經歷他最終的變形而成爲馬拉基——這一系列的變形都在一天之內完成。在最後提到的這些情形中，變形總是藉由換衣而實現；而松鼠也同樣脫下牠的小外套，翠鳥也脫下牠的羽衣，當牠們各自化身為人形的時機成熟之時。

title.en: Ricardo and His Adventures: The Frog School and the Seven-Headed Giant
title.zh: 里卡多歷險記：青蛙學堂與七首巨人

region.en: Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home province)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省（敘述者故鄉）

period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), notes to Tale 49, 'Ricardo and his Adventures', eBook #8299

summary.en: Sent to school, Ricardo studies at the frog-pond and learns to 'read' by croaking; told that 'whenever a body smells bad, you may be sure that it is dead,' he concludes he himself is dead and lies lamenting under a ripe guava he dares not eat. Learning his father was killed by a giant who carried off his sister, he is armed with two bottles of magic water — one making invulnerable, one draining all strength — and a flying saddle from a grateful leper, kills the seven-headed monster, frees the prisoners, and marries Lucia.
summary.zh: 里卡多上學卻在蛙塘『苦讀』，以蛙鳴為誦經；學得『凡發臭者必死』的教訓後，他自認已死，躺在熟番石榴下哀嘆不敢吃。得知父親為七首巨人所殺、妹妹被擄後，他得兩瓶神水（一瓶護體、一瓶奪力）與飛鞍，誅巨人、釋囚徒，娶露西亞為妻。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog tale given in abstract in Fansler's notes to Tale 49 ('If it smells bad, it's dead' droll joined to a giant-slaying tale); archival record.

passages.text: Once there was a widow who had a son named Ricardo. One day the mother said to the boy, 'Ricardo, I want you to go to school, so that you may learn something about our religion.' Ricardo was willing enough, so he took his Catechism and set out — but instead of going to the school, he went to a neighboring pond and listened to the merry croaking of the frogs. When eleven o'clock came, he went home and told his mother about the real school; the poor woman was very happy, thinking that her son was spending his time wisely. Ricardo took great delight in joining the chorus of the frogs, for his mother gave him food as a reward for his diligence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the tale given in Fansler's notes to Tale 49, 'Ricardo and his Adventures'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一位寡婦，她有個兒子名叫里卡多。有一天，母親對這男孩說：「里卡多，我要你去上學，好讓你學些關於我們宗教的事。」里卡多很樂意，於是帶著他的教理問答書出門了——但他沒有去學校，反而去了附近的池塘，聽青蛙歡快的鳴叫。到了十一點，他回到家，向母親講述那所真正的學校；那可憐的婦人非常高興，以為兒子把時間用得很有智慧。里卡多非常喜歡加入青蛙的合唱，因為母親因他的勤勉而給他食物作為獎賞。

passages.text: One morning the woman asked her son to read his lesson; the boy opened his Catechism and croaked very loudly, and his mother was glad when she heard that her son could croak so well, because she thought that was the way to read the book. As Ricardo was playing with his schoolmates one day, he saw a dead cat; it smelled very bad, so he left the pond and went home: 'Mother, I saw a cat lying near our school. It had a very bad odor.' The mother said, 'My son, remember this: whenever a body smells bad, you may be sure that it is dead' — and Ricardo repeated the words of his mother many times to himself, and learned them by heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the tale given in Fansler's notes to Tale 49, 'Ricardo and his Adventures'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天早晨，婦人叫兒子讀他的功課；男孩打開教理問答書，大聲地呱呱叫，母親聽到兒子能叫得這麼好很是高興，因為她以為那就是讀書的方法。有一天，里卡多正與同學玩耍時，看見一隻死貓；牠的氣味非常難聞，於是他離開池塘回家：「母親，我看見一隻貓躺在我們學校附近。牠有一股很難聞的氣味。」母親說：「我的兒子，你要記住：凡是身體散發難聞氣味的，你就可以確定它是死的」——里卡多把母親的話反覆對自己念了許多遍，並把它背了下來。

passages.text: One day, when he was on his way to the pond, Ricardo smelled something bad; he looked in every direction, but he could not find anybody: 'Since I cannot find any dead body here, I must be the one who is dead.' He lay down on the ground, and said, 'Ricardo is dead! I cannot eat any more. O how unhappy I am!' While he was lying there, he saw a ripe guava above his head: 'Delicious fruit, you are very fortunate! If I were alive, I would eat you.' He wished to get the fruit, but he dared not do so; after a while, when he could no longer smell the stink, he got up and went home, and told his mother his story.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the tale given in Fansler's notes to Tale 49, 'Ricardo and his Adventures'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，里卡多在前往池塘的路上聞到一股難聞的氣味；他朝四面八方張望，卻找不到任何人：「既然我在這裡找不到任何屍體，那我一定就是那個死人。」他躺在地上，說道：「里卡多死了！我再也吃不下東西了。唉，我多麼不幸啊！」他躺在那裡時，看見頭頂上方有一顆熟了的番石榴：「美味的果子，你真幸運！要是我還活著，我就會把你吃掉。」他想摘那果子，卻不敢這麼做；過了一會兒，當他再也聞不到那股臭味時，他起身回家，把事情的經過告訴了母親。

passages.text: One day Ricardo learned from his mother how his father had been killed by a giant who had afterwards carried away his sister; the boy set out in search of the giant. An old man along the way, whom he treated kindly, gave him two bottles of magic water — one that would make invulnerable the man who should drink it, another that would take away all the strength of him on whose head it should be poured; later a leprous old woman to whom he gave some food presented him with a magic saddle that would carry him through the air. So equipped, he soon arrived at the cave of the giant; he succeeded in killing that seven-headed monster and in freeing his sister and many other prisoners. Ten barrels of money were found in the cave; of these, Ricardo took two, the rest he gave to the prisoners he had freed. Later Ricardo married a beautiful woman named Lucia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the tale given in Fansler's notes to Tale 49, 'Ricardo and his Adventures'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，里卡多從母親那裡得知父親如何被一個巨人殺害，那巨人後來又擄走了他的妹妹；這男孩便出發去尋找那巨人。途中一位老人受他善待，給了他兩瓶魔法水——一瓶能使喝下它的人刀槍不入，另一瓶則能奪去被澆在頭上之人的全部力氣；後來，一位他給了食物的患痲瘋的老婦人送給他一具能載他飛越空中的魔法馬鞍。帶著這些裝備，他很快抵達了巨人的洞穴；他成功殺死了那七頭怪物，並解救了他的妹妹和許多其他囚徒。洞穴中發現了十桶錢；里卡多從中取了兩桶，其餘的都給了他所釋放的囚徒。後來，里卡多娶了一位名叫露西亞的美麗女子。

title.en: The Bronze Men from the Sea: The Oracle That Crowned Psammetichos
title.zh: 海上銅人：加冕普薩美提科斯之神諭

region.en: Buto, Nile Delta, Egypt (the most truthful oracle of Egypt, in the city of Leto)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲布托（雷托城中，全埃及最靈驗之神諭）

period: Oracle-fulfilment set in the 26th Dynasty (c. 664 BCE); recorded by Herodotus, Histories III.152 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book III, sec. 152

summary.en: Eleven kings strip Psammetichos of his power and drive him to the fen-country — because, having no golden cup, he poured his libation from a bronze helmet, fulfilling the oracle; from Buto, Egypt's most truthful oracle, comes the promise: 'vengeance would come when men of bronze appeared from the sea'; and when Ionians and Carians in bronze armour land from a plunder cruise, Psammetichos befriends them, overthrows the eleven, and makes himself king of all Egypt.
summary.zh: 十一王奪普薩美提科斯之權而逐之於沼澤——因其無金盂，乃以銅盔奠酒，適應神諭；布托（全埃及最靈之神諭）許之：『及海上銅人出，復仇必至』——既而衣銅甲之伊奧尼亞與卡里亞人因劫掠漂至，普薩美提科斯與之善，遂傾十一王而王全埃及。

sensitivity.note: Ancient oracle-tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Now the twelve kings continued to rule justly, but in course of time it happened thus: — After sacrifice in the temple of Hephaistos they were about to make libation on the last day of the feast, and the chief-priest, in bringing out for them the golden cups with which they had been wont to pour libations, missed his reckoning and brought eleven only for the twelve kings. Then that one of them who was standing last in order, namely Psammetichos, since he had no cup took off from his head his helmet, which was of bronze, and having held it out to receive the wine he proceeded to make libation: likewise all the other kings were wont to wear helmets and they happened to have them then.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.151.
passages.zh: 如今這十二位國王繼續公正地統治，但隨著時間推移，事情竟如此發生：——他們在赫菲斯托斯神廟獻祭之後，正要在節慶的最後一天行奠酒之禮，而大祭司在為他們取出他們慣常用來奠酒的黃金杯時，算錯了數目，只為十二位國王帶來了十一只。於是他們中排在最後的那一位，也就是普薩美提克，因為沒有杯子，便從頭上取下他那頂青銅頭盔，把它伸出去接酒，接著行奠酒之禮：同樣地，其他所有國王也慣常戴頭盔，而他們當時恰好都戴著。

passages.text: They taking note of that which had been done by Psammetichos and of the oracle, namely how it had been declared to them that whosoever of them should make libation with a bronze cup should be sole king of Egypt, recollecting, I say, the saying of the Oracle, they did not indeed deem it right to slay Psammetichos, since they found by examination that he had not done it with any forethought, but they determined to strip him of almost all his power and to drive him away into the fen-country.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.151.
passages.zh: 他們留意到普薩美提克所做的事，也留意到那神諭，就是曾向他們宣告：他們之中凡以青銅杯奠酒者，當為埃及唯一的國王；我說，他們回想起神諭之言，便確實不認為殺死普薩美提克是正當的，因為他們查究之後發現他並非出於任何預謀而為之，但他們決定剝奪他幾乎全部的權力，並把他驅逐到沼澤地區去。

passages.text: When he had sent to the Oracle of Leto in the city of Buto, where the Egyptians have their most truthful Oracle, there was given to him the reply that vengeance would come when men of bronze appeared from the sea. And he was strongly disposed not to believe that bronze men would come to help him; but after no long time had passed, certain Ionians and Carians who had sailed forth for plunder were compelled to come to shore in Egypt, and they having landed and being clad in bronze armour, one of the Egyptians, not having before seen men clad in bronze armour, came to the fen-land and brought a report to Psammetichos that bronze men had come from the sea and were plundering the plain. So he, perceiving that the saying of the Oracle was coming to pass, dealt in a friendly manner with the Ionians and Carians... and with the help of those Egyptians who favoured his cause and of these foreign mercenaries he overthrew the kings.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.152.
passages.zh: 當他派人前往布托城中勒托的神諭所——埃及人在那裡擁有最為靈驗的神諭——求問時，他得到的答覆是：當青銅之人自海上出現時，復仇便會到來。他極不願相信會有青銅之人前來相助；然而不久之後，一些為劫掠而出海的伊奧尼亞人與卡里亞人被迫在埃及登岸，他們登陸後身披青銅鎧甲，有一個埃及人此前從未見過身披青銅鎧甲之人，便來到沼澤地，向普薩美提科斯報告說，有青銅之人從海上而來，正在劫掠平原。於是他領悟到神諭之言正在應驗，便友善地對待伊奧尼亞人與卡里亞人……並藉助那些擁護他事業的埃及人以及這些外邦僱傭兵的幫助，推翻了諸王。

title.en: The Lake of Moiris: Two Pyramids Rising from the Water
title.zh: 莫伊里斯湖：水中雙塔

region.en: The Fayum, Egypt (the artificial lake beside the labyrinth)
region.zh: 埃及法尤姆（迷宮旁之人工湖）

period: Works of the kings of the 12th Dynasty; recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.149-150 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 149-150

summary.en: A greater marvel than the labyrinth itself: the lake of Moiris, 3,600 furlongs in circuit, fifty fathoms deep, formed by digging, 'for about in the middle of the lake stand two pyramids, each rising above the water to a height of fifty fathoms, the part which is built below the water being of just the same height; and upon each is placed a colossal statue of stone sitting upon a chair' — its water brought by canal from the Nile, flowing in six months and out six months.
summary.zh: 較迷宮更奇者乃莫伊里斯之湖：周三千六百弗隆，深五十噚，掘地而成——『湖心立二金字塔，各高出水面五十噚，其沒於水下者亦等高；塔頂各置坐於椅上之巨大石像』——湖水由運河引自尼羅，六月入湖、六月還河。

sensitivity.note: Ancient engineering-legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Such is this labyrinth; but a cause for marvel even greater than this is afforded by the lake, which is called the lake of Moiris, along the side of which this labyrinth is built. The measure of its circuit is three thousand six hundred furlongs (being sixty schoines), and this is the same number of furlongs as the extent of Egypt itself along the sea. The lake lies extended lengthwise from North to South, and in depth where it is deepest it is fifty fathoms. That this lake is artificial and formed by digging is self-evident, for about in the middle of the lake stand two pyramids, each rising above the water to a height of fifty fathoms, the part which is built below the water being of just the same height; and upon each is placed a colossal statue of stone sitting upon a chair.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.149.
passages.zh: 這座迷宮便是如此；然而比這更令人驚嘆的，是那座湖，它被稱為莫伊里斯湖，這座迷宮便沿著湖的一側而建。其周長的尺度為三千六百斯塔德（即六十斯亥諾伊），這與埃及本身沿海岸的長度所佔的斯塔德數目相同。此湖自北向南縱向延伸，其最深處深達五十英尋。此湖乃人工開鑿而成，這一點不言自明，因為在湖的中央附近矗立著兩座金字塔，各高出水面五十英尋，其建於水下的部分也恰好有同樣的高度；每座金字塔上都安置著一尊坐在座椅上的巨型石像。

passages.text: The water in the lake does not come from the place where it is, for the country there is very deficient in water, but it has been brought thither from the Nile by a canal: and for six months the water flows into the lake, and for six months out into the Nile again.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.149.
passages.zh: 湖中之水並非來自其所在地，因為該地極為缺水，而是經由一條運河從尼羅河引來的：在六個月裡，水流入湖中，而在另外六個月裡，水又流回尼羅河。

title.en: Bekos: The Experiment That Dated the Nations
title.zh: 『貝科斯』：為萬民定先後之試驗

region.en: The flock-pastures of King Psammetichos, Egypt
region.zh: 埃及普薩美提科斯王之牧場

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.2 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 2

summary.en: The first recorded experiment in history: the Egyptians held they were the first of all men, until Psammetichos, 'desiring to know what men had come into being first', gave two new-born children to a shepherd with orders that no word be uttered in their presence; after two years the children cried bekos — bread, in Phrygian — 'and in this manner... the Egyptians were brought to allow that the Phrygians were a more ancient people than themselves.'
summary.zh: 史上首載之實驗：埃及人自謂為萬民之首；普薩美提科斯『欲知何族最先』，乃以二新生嬰兒付牧者，囑其前不得有一言——二歲之後，二兒呼『貝科斯』（弗呂吉亞語『麵包』）——『埃及人遂承認弗呂吉亞人先於己。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient pseudo-experiment tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Now the Egyptians, before the time when Psammetichos became king over them, were wont to suppose that they had come into being first of all men; but since the time when Psammetichos having become king desired to know what men had come into being first, they suppose that the Phrygians came into being before themselves, but they themselves before all other men. Now Psammetichos, when he was not able by inquiry to find out any means of knowing who had come into being first of all men, contrived a device of the following kind: — Taking two new-born children belonging to persons of the common sort he gave them to a shepherd to bring up at the place where his flocks were, with a manner of bringing up such as I shall say, charging him namely that no man should utter any word in their presence.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.2.
passages.zh: 如今，在普薩美提科斯成為他們的國王之前，埃及人慣於認為自己是人類中最先產生的；但自從普薩美提科斯成為國王之後，他想要知道究竟哪一族人最先產生，於是他們便認為弗里吉亞人先於自己而產生，而自己則先於所有其他民族。普薩美提科斯既然無法透過探詢找到任何得知誰最先產生的辦法，便設計了如下一種計策：——他取了兩名屬於平民階層的新生嬰兒，交給一個牧人，讓他在自己羊群所在之地撫養他們，並以我將要述說的方式撫養，即吩咐他不得讓任何人在他們面前說出任何話語。

passages.text: And accordingly so it came to pass; for after a space of two years had gone by, during which the shepherd went on acting so, at length, when he opened the door and entered, both the children fell before him in entreaty and uttered the word bekos, stretching forth their hands. At first when he heard this the shepherd kept silence; but since this word was often repeated... at last he declared the matter to his master. Then Psammetichos having himself also heard it, began to inquire about what nation of men named anything bekos, and inquiring he found that the Phrygians had this name for bread. In this manner and guided by an indication such as this, the Egyptians were brought to allow that the Phrygians were a more ancient people than themselves.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.2.
passages.zh: 事情果然如此應驗；因為兩年過去之後，在這期間牧人一直如此行事，終於，當他開門進去時，兩個孩子都向他伏身懇求，伸出雙手，說出了「貝科斯」這個詞。起初牧人聽到這話時默不作聲；但由於這個詞時常被重複……最後他便將此事稟告了他的主人。普薩美提科斯自己也聽到了，便開始探詢哪一族人把什麼東西稱作「貝科斯」，經探詢他發現弗里吉亞人用這個名稱來指麵包。埃及人便以這種方式、並受這樣一種徵象的引導，不得不承認弗里吉亞人是比他們自己更古老的民族。

title.en: The Shepherd Kings: They Ruled 'Not Knowing Ra'
title.zh: 牧人之王：『不識拉』而治

region.en: Avaris, eastern Delta, Egypt (the Hyksos fortress with its garrison of 240,000)
region.zh: 埃及東三角洲阿瓦里斯（牧人王之堡，守軍二十四萬）

period: Hyksos rule of the 15th-16th Dynasties (c. 1650-1550 BCE); retold in D. A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XX, 'The Hyksos and Their Strange God'

summary.en: The age Egypt tried to forget: the invaders 'were a people of ignoble race who had confidence to invade our country, which they subdued easily without having to fight a battle. They set our towns on fire; they destroyed the temples of the gods' — called Hyksos, 'Shepherd Kings'; they fortified Avaris with a garrison of 240,000 men, and Hatshepsut could still declare: 'Since the Asiatics were in Avaris of the north land... they governed, not knowing Ra.'
summary.zh: 埃及欲忘之世：入侵者『乃卑賤之族，竟敢犯吾國，不戰而易取之；焚吾城，毀諸神之廟』——號曰希克索斯，『牧人之王』；築阿瓦里斯堡，屯軍二十四萬；至哈特謝普蘇特猶能誦曰：『亞細亞人居北國之阿瓦里斯……彼等治而不識拉。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient memory of foreign rule retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling.

passages.text: Josephus, the patriotic Jewish historian, who believed that the Hyksos were 'the children of Israel', quoted Manetho as saying that 'they were a people of ignoble race who had confidence to invade our country, which they subdued easily without having to fight a battle. They set our towns on fire; they destroyed the temples of the gods, and caused the people to suffer every kind of barbarity. During the entire period of their dynasty they waged war against the people of Egypt, desiring to exterminate the whole race. The foreigners were called Hyksos, which signifies Shepherd Kings.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XX, quoting Manetho via Josephus.
passages.zh: 約瑟夫斯，這位愛國的猶太歷史學家，相信喜克索斯人就是「以色列的子孫」，他引用曼涅托的話說：「他們是一個出身卑賤的民族，卻有膽量入侵我們的國家，未經一戰便輕易將其征服。他們放火焚燒我們的城鎮；他們毀壞神祇的廟宇，使人民遭受種種野蠻暴行。在他們整個王朝期間，他們一直對埃及人民作戰，意圖滅絕整個種族。這些外族人被稱為喜克索斯，意即牧羊人之王。」

passages.text: Manetho's reference to a carnival of destruction is confirmed by the inscription of Queen Hatshepsut of the Eighteenth Dynasty, who declared with characteristic piety: I have restored what was cast down, I have built up what was uncompleted, Since the Asiatics were in Avaris of the north land, And the barbarians were among them, destroying buildings, While they governed, not knowing Ra.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XX.
passages.zh: 曼涅托所提及的毀滅狂歡，由第十八王朝哈特謝普蘇特女王的銘文所證實；她以特有的虔敬宣稱：我已修復被傾覆之物，我已重建未竟之工，因亞洲人曾居於北地之阿瓦里斯，而蠻族亦在其中，毀壞建築，當他們統治之時，並不認識拉。

passages.text: The Hyksos overwhelmed the land at the close of the Fourteenth Dynasty. Then they chose for a king 'one of their own people'. According to Manetho his name was Salatis... He selected Memphis as his capital, and there 'he made Upper and Lower Egypt pay tribute', while he left garrisons at places which were 'considered to be proper for them'... the foreigners erected a strongly fortified town called Avaris — afterwards destroyed by the Egyptians — and there they kept a garrison of 240,000 men.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XX.
passages.zh: 喜克索斯人在第十四王朝末年蹂躪了這片土地。隨後他們從「自己人中」選出一人為王。據曼涅托所言，此人名為薩拉提斯……他選定孟斐斯為都城，並在那裡「使上下埃及繳納貢賦」，同時在「被認為適宜於他們」的地方留下駐軍……這些外邦人築起一座防禦堅固的城鎮，名為阿瓦里斯——後來被埃及人摧毀——並在那裡駐守二十四萬人。

title.en: Thoth, Heart and Tongue of the Creator: Author of the Book of the Dead
title.zh: 托特：造主之心與舌，《亡靈書》之作者

region.en: Egypt, all periods (Thoth as the Recording Angel of the gods)
region.zh: 埃及歷代（托特為諸神之錄天使）

period: Doctrine from the 1st Dynasty onward (Budge, The Book of the Dead, 1901, ch. IV)

source.work: The Book of the Dead, by E. A. Wallis Budge (1901), ch. IV, 'Thoth, the Author of the Book of the Dead'

summary.en: The theology of the scribe-god: Thoth was the heart and mind of the Creator, 'and he at all times voiced the will of the great god, and spoke the words which commanded every being and thing in heaven and in earth to come into existence' — his words almighty and once uttered never without effect; he framed the laws, ordered the courses of sun, moon and stars, invented writing and mathematics, kept the celestial register as the 'Recording Angel', and as weigher of words and deeds became 'more powerful in the Other World than Osiris himself'.
summary.zh: 書吏之神之神學：托特為造主之心與智，『恆述大神之意，發言而令天地萬有皆得生成』——其言無所不能，一出而不虛；彼立天之律法、序日月星辰之行，創繪畫文字與數學，掌天界登記而為『錄天使』；司權衡言行，其判不移，遂於冥界之力『凌駕奧西里斯本人之上』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient doctrine via Budge 1901; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Thoth was also the 'tongue' of the Creator, and he at all times voiced the will of the great god, and spoke the words which commanded every being and thing in heaven and in earth to come into existence. His words were almighty and once uttered never remained without effect. He framed the laws by which heaven, earth and all the heavenly bodies are maintained; he ordered the courses of the sun, moon, and stars; he invented drawing and design and the arts, the letters of the alphabet and the art of writing, and the science of mathematics.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, The Book of the Dead (1901), ch. IV.
passages.zh: 托特亦是造物主的「舌」，他時時傳達那位偉大神的旨意，說出那命令天上與地上一切生靈與萬物得以存在的言語。他的言語全能，一旦說出便從不落空。他制定了維繫天、地及一切天體的律法；他安排日、月與星辰的運行；他發明了繪畫、設計與種種技藝、字母以及書寫之術，還有數學。

passages.text: At a very early period he was called the 'scribe (or secretary) of the Great Company of the Gods,' and as he kept the celestial register of the words and deeds of men, he was regarded by many generations of Egyptians as the 'Recording Angel.' He was the inventor of physical and moral Law and became the personification of JUSTICE; and as the Companies of the Gods of Heaven, and Earth, and the Other World appointed him to 'weigh the words and deeds' of men, and his verdicts were unalterable, he became more powerful in the Other World than Osiris himself.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. IV.
passages.zh: 早在極古之時，他便被稱為「諸神大團體的書記（或秘書）」；由於他掌管著記錄世人言行之天冊，許多世代的埃及人都視他為「記錄天使」。他是自然律與道德律的發明者，並成為正義的化身；又因天上、地上與他界諸神團體委派他「衡量」世人的言行，而他的裁決不可更改，故他在他界比奧西里斯本人更有權勢。

passages.text: Osiris owed his triumph over Set in the Great Judgment Hall of the Gods entirely to the skill of Thoth of the 'wise mouth' as an Advocate, and to his influence with the gods in heaven. And every follower of Osiris relied upon the advocacy of Thoth to secure his acquittal on the Day of Judgment, and to procure for him an everlasting habitation in the Kingdom of Osiris.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. IV.
passages.zh: 奧西里斯在諸神的大審判廳中對塞特的勝利，完全歸功於「智口」托特作為辯護者的技巧，以及他在天上諸神中的影響力。而奧西里斯的每一位追隨者都仰賴托特的辯護，以確保自己在審判之日獲判無罪，並為自己求得在奧西里斯王國中的永恆居所。

title.en: Why the Body Must Be Kept Whole: Thoth's Protection of the Mummy
title.zh: 身何以必全：托特護木乃伊

region.en: Egyptian tombs, from predynastic graves to the rock chambers
region.zh: 埃及陵墓（自前王朝至巖窟墓室）

period: Funerary doctrine attested from the 1st Dynasty (Budge, The Book of the Dead, 1901, ch. II)

source.work: The Book of the Dead, by E. A. Wallis Budge (1901), ch. II, 'The Preservation of the Mummified Body in the Tomb by Thoth'

summary.en: The theology of embalming in one paragraph: dynastic Egyptians 'attached supreme importance to the preservation and integrity of the dead body... and then sealed it up in a coffin... in a chamber hewn in the bowels of the mountain' — but the enemies of the dead were not only worms and beetles: both mummy and the spiritual elements had to be protected 'from a multitude of devils and fiends, and from the powers of darkness generally', whose road lay along the way of the dead — so Thoth's spells were set around them, even as the sun god himself owed his continued existence to a secret name Thoth provided against Aapep.
summary.zh: 防腐神學一言以蔽之：王朝埃及人『以保全亡身之完整為至要』——以香料香脂防腐，裹以百碼亞麻，封於棺槨，藏於巖腹之室——然亡者之敵非止蛆蟲甲蟲：木乃伊與寓於其身之靈素，皆須防『群魔與暗界諸力』——其途正沿亡者之路——故以托特之咒護之，如日神賴托特所授秘名以抗阿波菲斯而得永存。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary doctrine via Budge 1901; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The dynastic Egyptians, either as the result of a difference in religious belief, or under the influence of invaders who had settled in their country, attached supreme importance to the preservation and integrity of the dead body, and they adopted every means known to them to prevent its dismemberment and decay. They cleansed it and embalmed it with drugs, spices and balsams; they anointed it with aromatic oils and preservative fluids; they swathed it in hundreds of yards of linen bandages; and then they sealed it up in a coffin or sarcophagus, which they laid in a chamber hewn in the bowels of the mountain.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, The Book of the Dead (1901), ch. II.
passages.zh: 王朝時期的埃及人，或由於宗教信仰上的差異，或受定居於其國土的入侵者影響，對死者遺體的保存與完整賦予至高的重要性，並採用他們所知的一切手段以防其肢解與腐壞。他們清洗遺體，以藥物、香料與香膏加以防腐；以芳香油與防腐液塗抹；用數百碼的亞麻繃帶層層包裹；然後將其封入棺槨或石棺之中，安置於山腹鑿出的墓室裡。

passages.text: But these were not the only enemies of the dead against which precautions had to be taken, for both the mummified body and the spiritual elements which had inhabited it upon earth had to be protected from a multitude of devils and fiends, and from the powers of darkness generally. These powers of evil had hideous and terrifying shapes and forms, and their haunts were well known, for they infested the region through which the road of the dead lay when passing from this world to the Kingdom of Osiris.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. II.
passages.zh: 但這些並非亡者唯一必須提防的敵人，因為無論是木乃伊化的遺體，還是曾寄居其內的種種精神要素，都必須受到保護，以免遭受眾多魔鬼與惡靈的侵擾，並抵禦一般所謂的黑暗勢力。這些邪惡勢力擁有猙獰可怖的形貌，其出沒之地亦為人所熟知，因為牠們盤踞在亡者之路所經之地——即亡者由此世前往奧西里斯王國途中所必經的區域。

passages.text: In fact it was believed in very early times in Egypt that Ra the Sun-god owed his continued existence to the possession of a secret name with which Thoth had provided him. And each morning the rising sun was menaced by a fearful monster called Aapep, which lay hidden under the place of sunrise waiting to swallow up the solar disk. It was impossible, even for the Sun-god, to destroy this 'Great Devil,' but by reciting each morning the powerful spell with which Thoth had provided him he was able to paralyse all Aapep's limbs and to rise upon this world.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. II.
passages.zh: 事實上，埃及極早的時代便相信，太陽神拉之所以能持續存在，是因為他擁有一個由托特所授予的祕密之名。而每天清晨，初升的太陽都受到一頭名為阿佩普的可怖怪物威脅，牠潛伏在日出之地底下，伺機吞沒日輪。即便是太陽神，也無法毀滅這「大惡魔」，但藉著每天早晨誦念托特所授予他的強力咒語，他得以令阿佩普四肢麻痺，從而升臨此世。

title.en: The Charge of Illegitimacy: How the Judgment Hall Got Its Name
title.zh: 非婚生之訟：審判廳得名之由

region.en: The Hall of the Two Truths, Egyptian Other World
region.zh: 埃及冥界雙真理之廳

period: Doctrine reconstructed from the Metternich Stele and Pyramid Texts (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I, 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. III, the charge of illegitimacy and the Hall of the Two Truths

summary.en: Why the Hall of Judgment is called the Hall of the Two Truths: Set had tried to seize his brother's widow and accused Isis of playing the harlot and Horus of illegitimacy; at the trial before the gods Thoth declared Osiris 'true of word', Isis by implication 'true of voice', and she and her sister were ever after present at the judgment of the dead bearing the title 'Ladies (i.e., possessors) of the Truth.'
summary.zh: 審判之廳何以稱『雙真理之廳』：塞特欲奪兄嫂不遂，遂訟伊西斯為娼、荷魯斯為非婚生；諸神庭前，托特既判奧西里斯『言真實』，伊西斯亦因之為『言真實』者——自此姊妹常侍亡者之審判，佩『真理之主』之榮號，而其廳遂名『雙真理之廳』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient theology reconstructed via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Set, it seems, had shut her up in some building, but she effected her escape, and fled to the city of Buto (Pe-Tep) in the Delta. There in the papyrus swamps she brought forth Horus, and there she reared him unknown to anyone.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. III, from the Metternich Stele narrative.
passages.zh: 看來是賽特將她囚禁於某座建築之中，但她設法逃脫，逃往三角洲的布托城（佩-泰普）。在那裡的紙莎草沼澤中，她生下了荷魯斯，並在無人知曉的情況下將他撫養長大。

passages.text: With the Egyptian accounts of the begetting of Horus before us, we are right in assuming that Set brought a charge of illegitimacy against Horus, and that his accusations were levelled as much against Isis as against her son. The text of the Metternich Stele suggests that Set had tried to seize his brother's widow for himself, and it states quite clearly that she escaped from the place wherein he had managed to confine her for a time.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.
passages.zh: 有了眼前這些關於荷魯斯受孕的埃及記載，我們便有理由推定：賽特曾對荷魯斯提出私生子的指控，而他的控訴既是針對她的兒子，也同樣針對伊西斯。梅特涅石碑的銘文暗示，賽特曾試圖將兄長的遺孀據為己有，並且明確記載她從他一度設法囚禁她的地方逃脫了出來。

passages.text: Isis and her sister Nephthys were present at the trial before the gods, the latter presumably as a witness, and Thoth having declared that Osiris had spoken the truth, Isis was by implication also declared 'true of word,' or 'true of voice,' and she and her sister were ever after present at the judgment of the dead, and they bore the honourable title of 'Ladies (i.e., possessors) of the Truth,' and the Hall of Judgment became known as the 'Hall of the two Truths.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.
passages.zh: 伊西斯與她的姊妹奈芙蒂斯皆出席了眾神面前的審判，後者想來是作為證人；由於托特宣告奧西里斯所言屬實，伊西斯也因而被隱含地宣告為「言辭真實」或「聲音真實」，她與姊妹此後便常伴於亡者的審判之側，並享有「真理之女主人（即擁有者）」的榮銜，而審判之廳也就被稱為「雙真理之廳」。

title.en: The Origins of the Resurrection: Graves of Predynastic Egypt
title.zh: 復活信仰之源：前王朝埃及墓葬

region.en: Nakadah and the prehistoric graves of Upper Egypt
region.zh: 埃及上埃及納卡達與史前墓群

period: Predynastic burials (c. 6000-3500 BCE); doctrine traced in Budge, Egyptian Ideas of the Future Life (1899), ch. V

source.work: Egyptian Ideas of the Future Life, by E. A. W. Budge (1899), ch. V, 'The Resurrection and Immortality'

summary.en: Where the whole Egyptian hope of rising began: the three kinds of predynastic graves — bodies laid on the left side in the ante-natal position wrapped in gazelle skin ('the symbol of a hope that as the child is born from this position into the world, so might the deceased be born into the life in the world beyond the grave'); bodies stripped and jointed; bodies burnt — each with offerings of food and flint weapons: 'The man who would hunt and fight in the next world must live again.'
summary.zh: 埃及復活之望所自始：前王朝三類墓葬——其一，屍左臥屈肢如胎兒，裹以羚羊皮（『如嬰兒自是位而生於世，願亡者亦如是生於彼界』）；其二，剝肉剔骨；其三，焚屍——然皆隨葬食物與燧石兵器：『欲於來世獵而戰者，必先得再生。』

sensitivity.note: Archaeological doctrine via Budge 1899; no living community restrictions. Budge's 'ante-natal position' reading is his own inference.

passages.text: In the oldest tombs we find the skeleton laid upon its left side, with the limbs bent: the knees are on a level with the breast, and the hands are placed in front of the face. Generally the head faces towards the south, but no invariable rule seems to have been observed as to its orientation. Before the body was laid in the ground it was either wrapped in gazelle skin or laid in loose grass... In burials of this class there are no traces of mummification, or of burning, or of stripping the flesh from the bones.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Egyptian Ideas of the Future Life (1899), ch. V.
passages.zh: 在最古老的墓葬中，我們發現骸骨側臥於左側，四肢彎曲：雙膝與胸部齊平，雙手置於面前。一般而言，頭部朝向南方，但關於其方位，似乎並未觀察到一成不變的規則。在遺體入土之前，或以瞪羚皮包裹，或置於鬆散的草叢之中……此類墓葬中，並無木乃伊化、火化或剔除骨上血肉的痕跡。

passages.text: Now in all classes of tombs belonging to the prehistoric period in Egypt we find offerings in vases and vessels of various kinds, a fact which proves beyond all doubt that the men who made these graves believed that their dead friends and relatives would live again in some place, of the whereabouts of which they probably had very vague ideas, in a life which was, presumably, not unlike that which they had lived upon earth. The flint tools, knives, scrapers and the like indicate that they thought they would hunt and slay their quarry when brought down, and fight their foes... The man who would hunt and fight in the next world must live again; and if he would live again it must be either in his old body or in a new one; if in the old body, it must be revivified.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1899), ch. V.
passages.zh: 如今，在埃及屬於史前時期各階層的墓葬中，我們都發現以各式瓶罐器皿盛裝的供品；此事確鑿無疑地證明，建造這些墳墓的人相信他們死去的親友將在某處再度復活——他們對那地方的所在，大概只有極為模糊的概念——所過的，想必是與他們在世上所過相差無幾的生活。燧石工具、刀子、刮削器等物，顯示他們認為自己將能獵捕並宰殺被追下的獵物，並與敵人搏鬥……凡要在來世狩獵與戰鬥的人，就必須再度復活；而若他要再度復活，就必須或在他舊有的軀體中，或在一具新的軀體中；若在舊軀體中，那軀體就必須重新獲得生命。

passages.text: The former are buried in the ante-natal position of a child, and we may perhaps be justified in seeing in this custom the symbol of a hope that as the child is born from this position into the world, so might the deceased be born into the life in the world beyond the grave; and the presence of amulets, the object of which was to protect the body, seems to indicate that they expected the actual body to rise again. The latter, by the mutilation of the bodies and the burning of the dead, seem to show that they had no hope of living again in their natural bodies.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1899), ch. V.
passages.zh: 前者以胎兒在出生前的姿勢埋葬，我們或許有理由認為，此一習俗象徵著一種希望：正如嬰孩以此姿勢誕生於世，死者也同樣能誕生於墳墓之外那個世界的生活之中；而護身符的存在——其目的在於保護軀體——似乎表明他們期待實際的軀體再度升起。後者則藉由毀損遺體與焚燒死者，似乎顯示他們並不懷有以自然軀體再度復活的希望。

language: Archaeological evidence (no text); Egyptian funerary doctrine
canonical_translation: E. A. W. Budge, Egyptian Ideas of the Future Life (London, 1899), ch. V

narrative.en:
Egypt's grandest idea — that the dead rise — did not begin with a text but with a grave. In the oldest burials of Upper Egypt, at Nakadah and other prehistoric sites, the skeleton is laid upon its left side with the knees at the breast and the hands before the face, wrapped in gazelle skin or loose grass: the ante-natal position of a child. There are no inscriptions (writing was unknown), but there are offerings in vases, flint knives for the hunt, and schist amulets against invisible enemies — everything a dead man would need to live, hunt, and fight again.

Budge's argument, from the evidence of three burial customs, is that the earliest Egyptians already held two distinct theologies of the corpse. The first kind of grave — the crouched, unmutilated body — belongs to people who expected the actual body to rise: born once from the foetal position, born again from the grave in the same body, revivified. The second kind — bodies stripped of flesh, bones cast in wild confusion or 'jointed' to save space, sometimes with the head separated, sometimes burnt — belongs to people who seemingly had no hope of living again in the natural body, and whose conception of a resurrection, if any, must have been of a spiritual body only. The third kind marks the transition: clay casings over folded bodies.

What the dynastic Egyptians then did was to reverse the second custom and universalize the first. By the 4th Dynasty every funerary text assumes the body will be buried whole — a reversal to which we owe the great anti-decay spells ('O flesh of Pepi, rot not, decay not, stink not') and, in time, the whole apparatus of embalming, the Ka statues, the Book of the Dead, and the promise of Osiris: that the god who had been a mortal and had risen from the dead would make his followers rise likewise. The belief in a future life, Budge concludes, is older than the belief in God as Egypt formulated it: its beginnings must be as old as the oldest human remains found in the valley — traces of bitumen on prehistoric bones showing that the attempt to preserve the dead, and the hope it embodied, was there at the very beginning.

THE DATING QUESTION. Budge is careful about chronology: the interval between these graves and the reign of Mena, the first historical king, 'must have been very considerable', representing thousands of years — yet the beliefs handed on through that interval were not wiped out and were scarcely modified, surviving 'in an almost unchanged state at the latest period of Egyptian history'. Even the College of Heliopolis, editing the ancient funeral texts, did not dare to delete the savage allusions their ancestors had written: objectionable passages were merely softened or left, out of 'their own reverence for the written word'. The theology of the resurrection was thus, in the strictest sense, prehistoric — older than the dynasty, older than writing, older than the gods as Egypt named them; and the later religions of Osiris and of Ra did not invent it but inherited it, clothing an immemorial grave-hope in ever more splendid garments.

functions: Documentary origin of the resurrection doctrine: burial customs as the pre-textual theology of rising
Etiology of embalming: the reversal of predynastic mutilation-customs explains the whole-body doctrine of the dynastic age
Social anthropology of the grave: offerings, weapons and amulets as the equipment of a life expected to continue

variants.name: The dynastic whole-body doctrine
variants.text_tradition: Pyramid Texts and early funerary inscriptions
variants.summary: By the 4th Dynasty all texts assume burial of the body whole, reversing the predynastic mutilation customs — the doctrinal basis of embalming and the Ka statue.

variants.name: The bitumen traces
variants.text_tradition: Predynastic human remains from Egypt (de Morgan, Ethnographie Prehistorique, 1897)
variants.summary: The oldest human remains found in Egypt bear traces of bitumen, showing that the attempt to preserve the dead was made at the very beginning of settlement in the valley.

primary_sources.work: Predynastic burials at Nakadah and other Upper Egyptian sites
primary_sources.citation: Excavations reported in J. de Morgan, Ethnographie Prehistorique (Paris, 1897), p. 189; synthesized in Budge, Egyptian Ideas of the Future Life (1899), ch. V.

secondary_sources.work: E. A. W. Budge, Egyptian Ideas of the Future Life
secondary_sources.citation: Budge 1899, London: Kegan Paul — the classic statement of the argument from grave-types to doctrine.

source_urls.description: Project Gutenberg eBook #11277 — Budge, Egyptian Ideas of the Future Life (1899), full text used at collection time

title.en: Euhemerus and His Letters of Gold: Plutarch Refuses to Humanize the Gods
title.zh: 優赫莫魯斯與其金書：普魯塔克拒神化為人

region.en: Alexandria and the Panchaean letter of gold (the debate over the gods' nature)
region.zh: 亞歷山大城與潘凱亞金書（神祇性質之辯）

period: Recorded by Plutarch, De Iside 23 (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, sec. XXIII

summary.en: Plutarch's warning against the historians who bring gods down to earth: 'It would be to shake and loosen a worship and faith which have been firmly settled in nearly all mankind from their infancy... and to give a clear sanction to the impostures of Euhemerus the Messenian, who from mere imagination... has invented a new mythology of his own, asserting that all those in general who are called and declared to be gods are none other than so many ancient generals and sea-captains and kings' — found, he claimed, written in letters of gold in a country that no one else has ever visited.
summary.zh: 普魯塔克警告將神拽落人間之史家：『此乃動搖並鬆弛自人類嬰年即深植之崇拜與信仰……且授偽造者以明據——優赫莫魯斯憑空捏造新神譜，斷言凡所謂神者，無非古之將軍、舵師與君王』——其所據者，乃一無人曾至之國中『以金字書成』之文。

sensitivity.note: Ancient polemic via Plutarch; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: But I am much afraid that to give in to this explanation of the story will be to move things which ought not to be moved; and not only, as Simonides says, 'to declare war against all antiquity,' but likewise against whole families and nations who are fully possessed with the belief in the divinity of these beings. And it would be no less than dispossessing those great names of their heaven, and bringing them down to the earth.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. XXIII.
passages.zh: 但我十分擔心，若接受對這個故事的這番解釋，就將是去搬動那些本不該搬動之物；而且不僅如西摩尼得斯所言，是「向整個古代宣戰」，同時也是向那些完全篤信這些存在者之神性的整個家族與民族宣戰。而這無異於剝奪這些偉大名字的天界地位，把他們貶落凡間。

passages.text: It would be to shake and loosen a worship and faith which have been firmly settled in nearly all mankind from their infancy. It would be to open a wide door for atheism to enter in at, and to encourage the attempts of those who would humanize the divine nature. More particularly it would give a clear sanction and authority to the impostures of Euhemerus the Messenian, who from mere imagination, and without the least appearance of truth to support it, has invented a new mythology of his own, asserting that 'all those in general who are called and declared to be gods are none other than so many ancient generals and sea-captains and kings.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XXIII.
passages.zh: 這將是動搖並鬆解一種幾乎全人類自幼便已牢固確立的崇拜與信仰。這將是為無神論敞開一扇大門，任其進入，並助長那些想把神性人性化之人的企圖。尤其，這將明確地認可並授權墨西尼的歐赫邁羅斯之欺詐；他純憑想像，毫無半點真理的依據，便杜撰出一套屬於他自己的新神話，斷言「凡被稱為並宣稱為神者，一概不過是若干古代的將帥、船長與國王。」

passages.text: Now, he says that he found this statement written in the Panchaean dialect in letters of gold, though in what part of the globe his Panchaeans dwell, any more than the Tryphillians, whom he mentions at the same time with them, he does not inform us. Nor can I learn that any other person, whether Greek or Barbarian, except himself, has ever yet been so fortunate as to meet with these imaginary countries.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XXIII.
passages.zh: 如今，他說他發現這段記載是以潘凱亞方言、用金字寫成的，然而他的潘凱亞人究竟居於地球上的哪一部分——正如他同時提及的特里菲利亞人一樣——他卻並未告知我們。我也無法得知，除他本人之外，還有任何其他人——無論希臘人或蠻族——曾如此幸運，得以遇見這些想像中的國度。

title.en: The Riddle of the Hall: 'Whose Heaven Is Fire, Whose Walls Are Serpents?'
title.zh: 廳中之謎：『孰有天如火、牆為蛇者？』

region.en: The Hall of Truth, Egyptian Other World (symbolic pin, Abydos region)
region.zh: 埃及冥界真理之廳（象徵定位，阿拜多斯一帶）

period: Book of the Dead ch. 125, final scene (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IV, the closing riddle of the Great Judgment

summary.en: The last obstacle in the Hall of Truth: even the justified soul must answer the gate-keeper's riddle before entering — Thoth asks him, 'Who is he whose heaven is fire, whose walls are serpents, and the floor of whose house is a stream of water?' — and the deceased replies 'Osiris', and is bidden to advance; the priest's magic, Budge notes, thrusts itself 'into the most sacred of texts' at this point.
summary.zh: 真理之廳最後一關：縱屬義者，入內之前亦須應門者之謎——托特問曰：『孰有天如火、牆為蛇、其屋之地基為流水者？』——亡者答曰『奧西里斯』，遂蒙召而進；伯奇按：祭司之魔法於此處亦『插入最神聖之文』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary scene via Budge 1910; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: One would think that the moral worth of the deceased was such that he might then pass without delay into the most holy part of the Hall of Truth where Osiris was enthroned. But this is not the case, for before he went further he was obliged to repeat the magical names of various parts of the Hall of Truth; thus we find that the priest thrust his magic into the most sacred of texts. At length Thoth, the great Recorder of Egypt, being satisfied as to the good faith and veracity of the deceased, came to him and asked why he had come to the Hall of Truth, and the deceased replied that he had come in order to be 'mentioned' to the god.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IV.
passages.zh: 人們或許會以為，死者的道德價值已足以使他隨即毫無延遲地進入真理之廳中最神聖的部分，即奧西里斯登臨寶座之處。但事實並非如此，因為在繼續前行之前，他必須複誦真理之廳各部分的魔法名號；由此可見，祭司竟將魔法置入了最神聖的經文之中。最後，埃及偉大的記錄者托特對死者的誠信與真實感到滿意，便來到他面前，問他為何來到真理之廳，而死者回答說，他來是為了被「引見」給那位神。

passages.text: Thoth then asked him, 'Who is he whose heaven is fire, whose walls are serpents, and the floor of whose house is a stream of water?' The deceased replied, 'Osiris'; and he was then bidden to advance so that he might be introduced to Osiris. As a reward for his righteous life sacred food, which proceeded from the Eye of Ra, was allotted to him, and, living on the food of the god, he became a counterpart of the god.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. IV.
passages.zh: 托特於是問他：「誰的天為火，誰的牆為蛇，誰的屋宇之地板為水流？」亡者答道：「歐西里斯」；隨後他被命上前，以便被引見給歐西里斯。作為他正直一生的獎賞，源自拉之眼的聖食被分派給他；他靠著神明的食物而活，遂成為神明之對應者。

title.en: Behold, I Am in Thy Presence: Ani Becomes a Spirit-Body
title.zh: 看哪，我立於爾前：阿尼化為靈體

region.en: The Kingdom of Osiris, Egyptian Other World
region.zh: 埃及冥界奧西里斯之國

period: Papyrus of Ani, 18th Dynasty (c. 1400-1300 BCE); trans. Budge, The Book of the Dead (1901), ch. VII

source.work: The Book of the Dead, by E. A. Wallis Budge (1901), ch. VII, the judgment scenes of the Papyrus of Ani

summary.en: The verdict of the scales, in the words of the vignette: 'I have come to thee, Un-Nefer, I have brought to thee the Osiris Ani. His heart is righteous and hath come forth from the Balance. It hath no sin before any god or any goddess. Thoth hath set down his judgment in writing, and the Company of the Gods have declared on his behalf that [his] evidence is very true' — and Ani answers: 'Behold, I am in thy presence, O Lord of Amentet. There is no sin in my body. I have not uttered a lie knowingly... Grant that I may be like the favoured (or rewarded) ones who are in thy train.' Under favour of Osiris Ani then became a sahu, or 'spirit-body.'
summary.zh: 天秤判詞之畫銘：『我來就爾，安-奈菲爾；我攜奧西里斯-阿尼以來。其心正直，自天秤而出；於諸神之前無罪。托特筆錄其判，諸神團為之證言其實。』——阿尼答曰：『看哪，我立於爾前，阿門特之主。我身無罪。我未明知故言謊……願我如爾行列中蒙恩之人。』——蒙奧西里斯之恩，阿尼遂化為『靈體』（sahu）。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary vignette text via Budge 1901; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: I have come to thee, Un-Nefer, I have brought to thee the Osiris Ani. His heart is righteous [and] hath come forth from the Balance. It hath no sin before any god or any goddess. Thoth hath set down his judgment in writing, and the Company of the Gods have declared on his behalf that [his] evidence is very true. Let there be given unto him of the bread and beer which appear before Osiris. Let him be like the Followers of Horus for ever!
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, The Book of the Dead (1901), ch. VII (the words of the gods over Ani).
passages.zh: 我已來到你面前，溫涅菲爾，我已將歐西里斯·阿尼帶到你面前。他的心是正直的，[並且]已從天平中出來。他在任何神或任何女神面前都無罪。托特已將他的判決記錄下來，諸神之會眾也已為他宣告，[他的]證詞極為真實。願將呈現在歐西里斯面前之麵包與啤酒賜予他。願他永遠如同荷魯斯的追隨者！

passages.text: Next we see Ani kneeling in adoration before Osiris, and he says, 'Behold, I am in thy presence, O Lord of Amentet. There is no sin in my body. I have not uttered a lie knowingly. [I have] no duplicity. Grant that I may be like the favoured (or rewarded) ones who are in thy train.' Under favour of Osiris Ani then became a sahu, or 'spirit-body,' and in this form passed into the Kingdom of Osiris.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. VII.
passages.zh: 接著我們看見阿尼跪在歐西里斯面前崇拜，他說：「看哪，我就在你面前，阿門特之主。我的身體裡沒有罪。我沒有明知而說謊。[我]沒有口是心非。請賜我得以如同在你行列中那些蒙恩（或受賞）者一樣。」在歐西里斯的恩寵下，阿尼於是成為薩胡，即「靈體」，並以此形態進入歐西里斯之國。

title.en: Burning Apep in Wax: The Daily Rites of Banishing the Serpent
title.zh: 焚蠟製阿波菲斯：日日驅蛇之儀

region.en: The temple of Amen-Ra at Thebes (where the Book of Overthrowing Apep was performed)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯阿蒙-拉神廟（行滅阿波菲斯之書處）

period: Ptolemaic copy of a far older liturgy, BM Papyrus 10188 (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. VI, the rites of the Book of Overthrowing Apep

summary.en: The daily war against the serpent, fought in wax and fire: when the sun-god arrived at the place of Apep he 'first of all cast a spell upon the monster, which rendered him helpless, and then he cast his fiery rays upon him, which shrivelled him up, and the fire of the god consumed him entirely'; in the temple the priests recited the spells that helped the god, 'burnt waxen figures of the monster in specially prepared fires, and, uttering curses, they trampled them under foot and defiled them' — rites believed also to break up rain clouds, scatter fog and mist, and dissipate thunder-storms.
summary.zh: 以蠟與火日日征蛇：日神至阿波菲斯處，『先以咒縛之使其無力，繼以火焰之射灼之，神火遂盡焚其身』；廟中祭司誦咒助神，『於特備之火中焚蠟製蛇像，口出咒詛，踐踏而污之』——此儀亦信能破雨雲、散霧靄、消雷暴。

sensitivity.note: Ancient execration liturgy via Budge 1910; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: This work is a liturgy, which was said at certain times of the day and night in the great temple of Amen-Ra at Thebes, with the view of preventing the monster Aapep from obstructing the sunrise. Aapep was supposed to lie in wait for the sun daily just before sunrise, with the view of doing battle with him and overthrowing him. When the Sun-god arrived at the place where Aapep was, he first of all cast a spell upon the monster, which rendered him helpless, and then he cast his fiery rays upon him, which shrivelled him up, and the fire of the god consumed him entirely.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. VI.
passages.zh: 此作品是一部禮儀文，於底比斯阿蒙-拉大神廟中在晝夜某些時刻誦讀，目的是阻止怪物阿佩普阻礙日出。人們認為阿佩普每日在日出前潛伏等候太陽，意圖與之交戰並將其推翻。當太陽神抵達阿佩普所在之處時，他首先對怪物施咒，使其無力，然後投下熾熱光芒，將其灼縮，神之火便將它徹底吞噬。

passages.text: In the temple of Amen-Ra the priests recited the spells that were supposed to help the Sun-god to burn up Aapep, and they burnt waxen figures of the monster in specially prepared fires, and, uttering curses, they trampled them under foot and defiled them. These spells and burnings were also believed to break up rain clouds, and to scatter fog and mist and to dissipate thunder-storms, and to help the sun to rise on this world in a cloudless sky. Aapep was a form of Set, the god of evil of every kind, and his allies were the 'Red Fiends' and the 'Black Fiends,' and every power of darkness.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. VI.
passages.zh: 在阿蒙-拉神廟中，祭司們誦讀據信能幫助太陽神燒毀阿佩普的咒語，並在特別準備的火中焚燒該怪物的蠟像，且口出詛咒，將其踩在腳下並加以污損。人們也相信這些咒語與焚燒能驅散雨雲、吹散霧氣與薄霧、消散雷暴，並幫助太陽在無雲的天空中升臨此世。阿佩普是塞特——一切邪惡之神——的一種形態，其盟友是「紅色惡魔」與「黑色惡魔」，以及一切黑暗之力。

title.en: The House of Leto Carved from a Single Stone
title.zh: 整石所鑿之雷托神室

region.en: Buto, Nile Delta, Egypt (the oracle enclosure of Leto)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲布托（雷托神諭聖域）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.155 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 155

summary.en: The marvel that made Herodotus marvel most at Buto: 'There is in this sacred enclosure a house of Leto made of one single stone as regards both height and length, and of which all the walls are in these two directions equal, each being forty cubits; and for the covering in of the roof there lies another stone upon the top, the cornice measuring four cubits.'
summary.zh: 希羅多德於布托最嘆為奇者：『聖域中有一雷托之室，高廣皆由整石鑿成，四面等長，各四十肘；其頂則以一石覆之，簷廣四肘。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient travel-wonder via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. The house sheltered the oracle and the floating island of Chemmis nearby.

passages.text: This Oracle which is in Egypt is sacred to Leto, and it is established in a great city near that mouth of the Nile which is called Sebennytic, as one sails up the river from the sea; and the name of this city where the Oracle is found is Buto... In this Buto there is a temple of Apollo and Artemis; and the temple-house of Leto, in which the Oracle is, is both great in itself and has a gateway of the height of ten fathoms: but that which caused me most to marvel of the things to be seen there, I will now tell.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.155.
passages.zh: 這座位於埃及的神諭所是獻給勒托的，它建立在尼羅河那個名為塞本尼托斯河口附近的一座大城中，該河口是從海上溯河而上時所經之處；而這座發現神諭所的城市名為布托……在這布托有一座阿波羅與阿耳忒彌斯的廟宇；而勒托的廟宇，即神諭所在之處，本身既宏大，又有一座高達十噚的門廊：但在此所見之物中最令我驚奇者，我現在就來說明。

passages.text: There is in this sacred enclosure a house of Leto made of one single stone as regards both height and length, and of which all the walls are in these two directions equal, each being forty cubits; and for the covering in of the roof there lies another stone upon the top, the cornice measuring four cubits.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.155.
passages.zh: 在這片聖域之中，有一座勒托之屋，其高度與長度皆由單一石塊構成，四面的牆在這兩個方向上皆相等，各為四十肘；而為了覆蓋屋頂，頂上另置一石，其簷口量度為四肘。

title.en: Kheti the Fire-Spitter: The Serpent That Burns the Damned
title.zh: 噴火之蛇克赫提：焚罪者之蛇

region.en: The Eighth Division of the Book of Gates, Egyptian Other World
region.zh: 埃及冥界《門之書》第八區

period: New Kingdom netherworld books (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II, 1911, ch. XXIV)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (1911), ch. XXIV, sec. 11, 'The Spitting Serpent'
