summary.en: In the Eighth Division of the Book of Gates stands the speckled serpent Kheti with seven undulations, in each of which a god stands; his mouth open, he belches a stream of fire into the faces of the enemies of Ra — 'Open thy mouth, distend thy jaws, belch forth thy fire against the enemies of my father, burn up their bodies, and consume their souls' — a monster, Budge shows, modelled on the real spitting cobras of Africa, whose venom Livingstone saw distil for hours from a severed head.
summary.zh: 《門之書》第八區立有斑蛇克赫提，身具七曲，每曲立一神；其口大張，向拉之仇敵噴火焰之流——『張爾口，展爾頜，向吾父之敵噴火，焚其身，以爾口所出之火與爾身之焰滅其魂』——伯奇證其型乃非洲實有之噴毒眼鏡蛇：利文斯頓曾見斷首之蛇歷時數小時仍滴清毒。

sensitivity.note: Ancient netherworld iconography via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In the Eighth Section of the Book of Gates a picture is given of a monster speckled serpent called 'Kheti,' with seven undulations, in each of which stands a god. The mouth of the serpent is open, and through it he belches a stream of fire into the faces of the enemies of Ra, whose arms are tied behind their backs in agonizing positions. Horus says to the serpent: 'Open thy mouth, distend thy jaws, belch forth thy fire against the enemies of my father, burn up their bodies, and consume their souls by the fire which issueth from thy mouth, and by the flames which are in thy body.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XXIV, sec. 11.
passages.zh: 在《門之書》第八部分中，繪有一隻名為「赫提」的斑紋怪物蛇，其身有七道蜿蜒起伏，每一道起伏之中皆立著一位神祇。此蛇張開其口，自口中向拉神的敵人們噴吐出一道火焰，那些敵人的雙臂被反綁於背後，姿態痛苦不堪。荷魯斯對那蛇說道：「張開你的口，撐開你的顎，向我父的敵人噴吐你的火焰，焚燒他們的身體，以你口中噴出的火與你體內的烈焰，吞噬他們的靈魂。」

passages.text: It was formerly thought spitting serpents did not exist, and that the Egyptian drawings were the result of the artist's imagination. Livingstone, however, killed a serpent of the species picakholu, which was 8 feet 3 inches long, and was so copiously supplied with venom that it continued to distil clear poison from the fangs for hours after its head was cut off. He says, 'This was probably that which passes by the name of spitting serpent, which is believed to be able to eject the poison into the eyes when the wind favours its forcible expiration.' In the Book Am-Tuat (IXth Division) we also have a group of twelve little serpents, the duty of which was to pour out fire from their bodies, which was to light the dead Sun-god on his way.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XXIV, citing Livingstone, Missionary Travels. / Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XXIV, sec. 11.
passages.zh: 從前人們認為噴毒之蛇並不存在，而埃及的圖畫不過是畫家想像的產物。然而，李文斯頓曾殺死一條屬於皮亞科盧（picakholu）種類的蛇，長八英尺三英寸，其毒液極為充沛，以致在其頭被砍下之後數小時，毒牙仍不斷滲出清澈的毒液。他說：「這大概便是那被稱為噴毒蛇的蛇，據信當風助其用力呼氣之時，牠能將毒液噴射入人的眼中。」在《阿姆圖阿特之書》（第九區）中，我們亦可見到一組十二條小蛇，其職責乃是從體內傾瀉出火焰，以照亮死去的太陽神前行之路。

title.en: Serpent Worship: The Snake as God and as Devil
title.zh: 蛇之崇拜：蛇為神亦為魔

region.en: Egypt and the Nile valley (the serpent revered and abhorred)
region.zh: 埃及與尼羅河谷（受敬與被憎之蛇）

period: From the Pyramid Texts of Unas onward (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II, 1911, ch. XXIV)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (1911), ch. XXIV, sec. 13, 'Snake-Worship'

summary.en: The double theology of the serpent: 'the serpent was either a power for good or the incarnation of diabolical cunning and wickedness' — the Book of the Dead names the serpent Ami-hemf that lived on the top of a mountain and was thirty cubits long, and the shipwrecked sailor's conversing serpent had a beard two cubits long; the Egyptians drew two-headed serpents and winged human-headed snakes, while Herodotus and Aristotle themselves believed in 'flying serpents' — and reverence still paid to pythons in Africa, where the Dinka call snakes 'brethren' and wash them with milk.
summary.zh: 蛇之雙重神學：『蛇或為善力，或為魔之狡惡化身』——《亡靈書》載居山頂、長三十肘之蛇阿米-赫姆夫，遇難水手所對談之蛇亦長三十肘、鬚長二肘；埃及人畫雙首蛇與有翼人首蛇，而希羅多德與亞里士多德亦信『飛蛇』——非洲至今敬蟒，丁卡人呼蛇為『兄弟』，以乳洗之、以酥膏之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient serpent-cult evidence via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The Egyptians regarded certain kinds of snakes with reverence, and their religious books contain many allusions to them; on the other hand, the mythological writings show that some snakes or serpents were regarded as incarnations of evil. Among these are the serpents the names of which are given in the text of Unas, and several others are mentioned in the Book Am-Tuat and the Book of Gates; but all of them appear to have been regarded as forms of the monster serpent Apep, which was the type of all physical and moral evil. In short, the serpent was either a power for good or the incarnation of diabolical cunning and wickedness.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XXIV, sec. 13.
passages.zh: 埃及人對某些種類的蛇懷有敬意，其宗教典籍中亦有許多提及牠們之處；另一方面，神話著作則顯示某些蛇被視為邪惡的化身。其中便有在烏納斯文獻中提及名字的那些蛇，另有數條見於《阿姆圖阿特之書》與《門之書》；然而牠們似乎全都被視為怪物蛇阿佩普的種種形態，而阿佩普乃是一切肉體與道德之邪惡的典型。簡言之，蛇要麼是為善的力量，要麼便是惡魔般狡詐與邪惡的化身。

passages.text: The Book of the Dead mentions (Chapter CVIII) the serpent Ami-hemf, which lived on the top of a mountain and was thirty cubits long, and the Papyrus Golenischeff also mentions a serpent thirty cubits long, which had a beard two cubits long, and which conversed with the shipwrecked mariner on the enchanted island.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XXIV, sec. 13.
passages.zh: 《死者之書》（第一〇八章）提及一條名為阿米-赫姆夫的蛇，牠居於山頂，長三十肘；而《戈列尼謝夫紙草》亦提及一條長三十肘的蛇，其鬚長二肘，曾在受魔法籠罩的島上與遇難的水手交談。

passages.text: The Egyptians represented certain snakes with a head at each end of the body, and Miss Kingsley mentions one serpent which the natives declared to have 'a head at each end.' The Egyptians drew figures of serpents with human heads and legs, and the wings of a bird, but this is not very remarkable when we remember that even Herodotus and Aristotle believed in 'flying serpents.' Reverence is still paid to the serpent in many parts of Africa. Thus the Dinkas revere pythons, and call snakes in general their 'brethren'; they wash them with milk and anoint them with butter.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XXIV, sec. 13.
passages.zh: 埃及人將某些蛇繪成身體兩端各有一頭，金斯利小姐曾提及一條蛇，當地人宣稱牠「兩端各有一頭」。埃及人還繪製過長著人頭人腿、並有鳥翼的蛇形圖像，但這並不十分稀奇，只要我們記得連希羅多德與亞里斯多德都相信「飛蛇」的存在。時至今日，非洲許多地方仍對蛇懷有敬意。例如丁卡人崇敬蟒蛇，並泛稱蛇為他們的「兄弟」；他們以乳汁為蛇洗身，並以奶油塗抹牠們。

title.en: Osiris Is Moisture: The Black Land and the Black God
title.zh: 奧西里斯即濕氣：黑土與黑神

region.en: Egypt, the black land (Chemia, the pupil of the eye)
region.zh: 埃及黑土之邦（『凱米亞』，目之瞳）

period: Plutarch, De Iside 33-38 (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, secs. XXXIII-XXXVIII

summary.en: The second allegorical reading of the myth: Osiris does not symbolize the Nile only but 'the principle and power of moisture in general', Typhon everything scorching, burning and fiery; hence Osiris is of a black colour, 'for water gives a black tinge to everything with which it is mixed' — the Mnevis Bull of Heliopolis is black like him, 'and even Egypt itself, by reason of the extreme blackness of the soil, is called by them Chemia, the very name which is given to the black part or pupil of the eye'; the sun and moon sail their courses in ships 'because they owe their motion, support, and nourishment to the power of humidity', and Homer and Thales both learned from Egypt 'that water was the first principle of all things.'
summary.zh: 神話之第二寓言讀法：奧西里斯非僅象尼羅，乃『濕氣之原理與權力』，而提豐則為一切灼熱焚燒之物；故奧西里斯色黑——『水使所染皆黑』——赫利奧波利斯之姆內維斯牛亦黑如其主；『埃及因土色至黑，遂名凱米亞（Chemia），即目瞳之黑之稱』；日月不駕車而乘舟行天——『以其行、支與養皆賴濕氣之力』；荷馬與泰勒斯之『水為萬物本原』，皆得自埃及。

sensitivity.note: Ancient philosophical allegoresis via Plutarch (Budge's summaries of secs. XXXIII-XXXVIII); no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Some of the more philosophical priests assert that Osiris does not symbolize the Nile only, nor Typhon the sea only, but that Osiris represents the principle and power of moisture in general, and that Typhon represents everything which is scorching, burning, and fiery, and whatever destroys moisture. Osiris they believe to have been of a black colour, because water gives a black tinge to everything with which it is mixed. The Mnevis Bull kept at Heliopolis is, like Osiris, black in colour, 'and even Egypt itself, by reason of the extreme blackness of the soil, is called by them Chemia, the very name which is given to the black part or pupil of the eye.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch secs. XXXIII-XXXIV (Budge's summary).
passages.zh: 有些較具哲思的祭司主張，奧西里斯並非僅象徵尼羅河，堤豐也並非僅象徵海洋，而是奧西里斯代表濕氣的一般原理與力量，堤豐則代表一切灼熱、燃燒、如火之物，以及一切毀壞濕氣之物。他們相信奧西里斯是黑色的，因為水會使與之混合的一切染上黑色。飼養於赫利奧波利斯的姆涅維斯公牛，與奧西里斯一樣是黑色的，「甚至埃及本身，也因其土壤極度黝黑，而被他們稱為凱米亞，這正是他們賦予眼睛黑色部分或瞳孔的名稱。」

passages.text: The Sun and Moon are not represented as being drawn about in chariots, but as sailing round the world in ships, which shows that they owe their motion, support, and nourishment to the power of humidity. Homer and Thales both learned from Egypt that 'water was the first principle of all things, and the cause of generation.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), secs. XXXIII-XXXIV (Budge's summary).
passages.zh: 太陽與月亮並非被描繪成乘戰車而行，而是乘船環繞世界航行，這表明它們的運動、支撐與滋養皆仰賴濕氣之力。荷馬與泰勒斯皆從埃及學得「水是萬物的第一原理，也是生成的原因」。

passages.text: The Nile and all kinds of moisture are called the 'efflux of Osiris.' Therefore a water-pitcher is always carried first in his processions, and the leaf of a fir-tree represents both Osiris and Egypt. Osiris is the great principle of fecundity, which is proved by the Pamylia festivals, in which a statue of the god with a triple phallus is carried about.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), sec. XXXVI (Budge's summary).
passages.zh: 尼羅河與各種濕氣皆被稱為「奧西里斯的流溢」。因此，在他的遊行隊伍中，總是最先抬著一只水罐；而冷杉之葉則同時代表奧西里斯與埃及。奧西里斯是豐饒的偉大原理，這由帕米利亞節慶可得證明——在該節慶中，人們抬著一尊具有三重陽具的神像遊行。

title.en: The Amulet Chapters: Tet, Vulture, Collar, Sceptre, and Pillow
title.zh: 護符諸章：泰特、禿鷲、項圈、權杖與枕

region.en: Egyptian funerary workshops (the amulet spells of the Book of the Dead)
region.zh: 埃及喪葬作坊（亡靈書護符諸咒）

period: Book of the Dead chs. 155-167, Theban recension (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IV, the amulet chapters of the Book of the Dead

summary.en: The dead man's jewellery was a spell-book in metal and stone: chapters 155-167 formed the spells engraved on the amulets — the Tet (male), the Tet (female), the Vulture, the Collar, the Sceptre, the Pillow, the Pectoral — which 'gave to the deceased the power of Osiris and Isis and other gods, and restored to him his heart, and lifted up his head'; ch. 162 kept heat in the body until the day of resurrection, and ch. 177 raised up the dead body, ch. 178 the spirit-soul.
summary.zh: 亡者之飾物乃金石器上的咒文之書：第一五五至一六七章為刻於護符之咒——男泰特、女泰特、禿鷲、項圈、權杖、枕、胸飾——『使亡者得奧西里斯與伊西斯及他神之力，復得其心，舉起其首』；第一六二章為其體保暖以待復活之日；第一七七章舉起屍身，一七八章舉起靈魂。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary chapters summarized in Budge 1910; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Chaps. 155-160, 166, and 167 formed the spells that were engraved on amulets, i.e. the Tet (male), the Tet (female), the Vulture, the Collar, the Sceptre, the Pillow, the Pectoral, &c., and gave to the deceased the power of Osiris and Isis and other gods, and restored to him his heart, and lifted up his head. Chap. 162 kept heat in the body until the day of the resurrection. Chaps. 175 and 176 gave the deceased everlasting life and enabled him to escape the second death. Chap. 177 raised up the dead body, and Chap. 178 raised up the spirit-soul.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IV, summary.
passages.zh: 第一五五至一六〇章、第一六六章與第一六七章構成刻於護身符上的咒語，即泰特（男）、泰特（女）、禿鷲、項圈、權杖、枕、胸飾等，並賦予死者奧西里斯、伊西斯及其他諸神的力量，使其心復歸於身，並抬起其頭。第一六二章使熱留存於體內，直到復活之日。第一七五章與第一七六章賦予死者永生，並使其得以逃脫第二次死亡。第一七七章使死者的身體升起，第一七八章使靈魂升起。

title.en: A Homestead in the Fields of Peace: Ani's Petition
title.zh: 安樂田中之家宅：阿尼之祈

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (Papyrus of Ani, the opening hymn to Osiris)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（阿尼紙草，奧西里斯開篇頌）

period: Book of the Dead, opening hymn, 18th Dynasty (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IV, the prayer of the scribe Ani

summary.en: The scribe Ani's wish-list for eternity: 'Grant that I may sail down to Tatu in the form of a living soul, and sail up to Abydos in the form of the Benu bird; that I may go in and come out without being stopped at the pylons of the Lords of the Other World. May there be given unto me bread-cakes in the house of coolness, and offerings of food in Anu (Heliopolis), and a homestead for ever in Sekhet Aru, with wheat and barley therefor.'
summary.zh: 書吏阿尼之永恆清單：『願我化為活魂下行至塔圖，化為貝努鳥上行至阿拜多斯；願我於冥界諸主之牌樓前出入無阻。願涼宅中賜我餅，赫利奧波利斯賜我食，而於蘆葦之田賜我永宅，並其大小麥之田。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary prayer via Budge 1910; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Grant thou to the Ka of the Osiris the scribe Ani splendour in heaven, power upon earth, and triumph in the Other World. Grant that I may sail down to Tatu in the form of a living soul, and sail up to Abydos in the form of the Benu bird; that I may go in and come out without being stopped at the pylons of the Lords of the Other World. May there be given unto me bread-cakes in the house of coolness, and offerings of food in Anu (Heliopolis), and a homestead for ever in Sekhet Aru, with wheat and barley therefor.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IV, the opening hymn to Osiris in the Papyrus of Ani.
passages.zh: 願你賜予奧西里斯、書記阿尼的卡以天上的光輝、地上的權能，以及彼世的勝利。願我得以以活魂之形航下至塔圖，並以貝努鳥之形航上至阿拜多斯；願我得以出入而不在彼世諸主的塔門前受阻。願在清涼之屋中賜我麵餅，在阿努（赫利奧波利斯）賜我食物供品，並在塞赫特阿魯永遠賜我家宅，附有小麥與大麥。

title.en: The Machines of the Pyramid: Finished from the Top Downwards
title.zh: 金字塔之機：自頂而下成之

region.en: Giza, Egypt (the great pyramid of Cheops)
region.zh: 埃及吉薩（胡夫大金字塔）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.125 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 125

summary.en: The oldest account of pyramid engineering: 'they raised the remaining stones with machines made of short pieces of timber, raising them first from the ground to the first stage of the steps... for as many as were the courses of the steps, so many machines there were also, or perhaps they transferred one and the same machine... to each stage successively' — and the pyramid, Herodotus insists, 'was made after the manner of steps' and finished from the top downwards, with sixteen hundred talents of silver spent on radishes, onions and leeks for the workmen.
summary.zh: 金字塔工程之最古記載：『彼等以短木所製之機起餘石，先自地面升至第一層階台……階級有幾，機即有幾；或以一機遞轉於各層』——希羅多德力言塔為『階台式』，自頂而下而成；工友所食蘿蔔洋蔥韭蒜，銘文記耗銀一千六百他蘭同。

sensitivity.note: Ancient engineering-legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. Herodotus' machines are a literary tradition, not archaeology.

passages.text: This pyramid was made after the manner of steps, which some call 'rows' and others 'bases': and when they had first made it thus, they raised the remaining stones with machines made of short pieces of timber, raising them first from the ground to the first stage of the steps, and when the stone got up to this it was placed upon another machine standing on the first stage, and so from this it was drawn to the second upon another machine; for as many as were the courses of the steps, so many machines there were also, or perhaps they transferred one and the same machine, made so as easily to be carried, to each stage successively, in order that they might take up the stones.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.125.
passages.zh: 這座金字塔是以階梯的方式建造的，有人稱之為「層」，有人稱之為「基座」：當他們先把它造成這樣之後，便用短木料製成的機械抬起其餘的石塊，先從地面抬到階梯的第一層，當石塊升到這裡時，便把它放在置於第一層上的另一具機械上，如此再從這裡由另一具機械拉至第二層；因為階梯有多少層，機械也就有多少具，或者他們也許把同一具機械——造得便於搬運——依次轉移到每一層，以便把石塊抬上去。

passages.text: However that may be, the highest parts of it were finished first, and afterwards they proceeded to finish that which came next to them, and lastly they finished the parts of it near the ground and the lowest ranges. On the pyramid it is declared in Egyptian writing how much was spent on radishes and onions and leeks for the workmen, and if I rightly remember that which the interpreter said in reading to me this inscription, a sum of one thousand six hundred talents of silver was spent.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.125.
passages.zh: 無論如何，其最高部分最先完成，之後他們接著完成緊鄰其下的部分，最後才完成靠近地面及最低層的部分。金字塔上以埃及文字記載著為工人花費在蘿蔔、洋蔥與韭蔥上的開銷；若我記得沒錯，據那位解讀者為我誦讀此銘文時所言，共花費了一千六百塔蘭特銀子。

title.en: The Book Found Under a Shrine: The Discovery of the Per-t Em Hru
title.zh: 神龕下得書：《來日之書》之發現

region.en: The shrine of Hennu, Egypt (where the Book of the Dead was 'found' in the 1st Dynasty)
region.zh: 埃及赫努神龕（第一王朝時『發現』亡靈書處）

period: Rubric of the Papyrus of Nu (BM 10477), tradition set in the 1st Dynasty (Budge, The Book of the Dead, 1901, ch. III)

source.work: The Book of the Dead, by E. A. Wallis Budge (1901), ch. III, 'The Book Per-t em hru'

summary.en: The Book of the Dead's own discovery legend: a rubric states the text 'was discovered by a high official in the foundations of a shrine of the god Hennu during the reign of Semti, or Hesepti, a king of the 1st dynasty'; another says it was cut on the alabaster plinth of a statue of Mycerinus with letters inlaid in lapis lazuli, found by Prince Herutataf and exhibited to Khufu as 'a most wonderful thing' — a text that 'would make a man victorious upon earth and in the Other World... and would prevent him from dying the [second] death.'
summary.zh: 《亡靈書》自述之發現傳說：一條眉批云其書『乃一高官於第一王朝塞姆提王世，自赫努神龕之基下發得』；另一條則云其文『刻於門卡烏拉像之雪花石膏座上，字嵌青金石』，為胡夫王子赫魯塔塔夫所得，呈王以為『至奇之物』——其書『能使人在世與冥界皆得勝……並免遭第二次死亡』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient rubric tradition via Budge 1901; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: One rubric in the Papyrus of Nu (Brit. Mus. No. 10477) states that the text of the work called 'PER-T EM HRU,' i.e., 'Coming Forth (or, into) the Day,' was discovered by a high official in the foundations of a shrine of the god Hennu during the reign of Semti, or Hesepti, a king of the 1st dynasty. Another rubric in the same papyrus says that the text was cut upon the alabaster plinth of a statue of Menkaura (Mycerinus), a king of the IVth dynasty, and that the letters were inlaid with lapis lazuli. The plinth was found by Prince Herutataf, a son of King Khufu (Cheops), who carried it off to his king and exhibited it as a 'most wonderful' thing.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, The Book of the Dead (1901), ch. III.
passages.zh: 努氏紙草卷（大英博物館編號10477）中有一則題記記載：名為「PER-T EM HRU」，即「出來（或，進入）白日」之著作的文本，乃是由一位高級官員於第一王朝國王塞姆提（或赫塞普提）在位期間，在一座赫努神神殿的地基中發現的。同一紙草卷中的另一則題記則稱，該文本刻於第四王朝國王孟卡拉（米刻林）一尊雕像的雪花石膏底座上，且文字以青金石鑲嵌。該底座為庫夫（奇奧普斯）之子赫魯塔塔夫王子所發現，他將其帶走獻給他的國王，並將其展示為一件「最為奇妙」之物。

passages.text: This composition was greatly reverenced, for it 'would make a man victorious upon earth and in the Other World; it would ensure him a safe and free passage through the Tuat (Under World); it would allow him to go in and to go out, and to take at any time any form he pleased; it would make his soul to flourish, and would prevent him from dying the [second] death.' For the deceased to receive the full benefit of this text it had to be recited by a man 'who was ceremonially pure, and who had not eaten fish or meat, and had not consorted with women.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. III.
passages.zh: 此作品備受尊崇，因為它「能使人在世上與彼世皆成為勝利者；能確保他安全而自由地通過圖阿特（冥界）；能使他出入自如，並隨時隨意化身為任何形貌；能使他的靈魂繁盛，並使他免於死亡（第二次死亡）。」亡者若要獲得此文本的全部裨益，須由一名「在儀式上潔淨、未曾食魚或肉、且未曾與女子交合」的男子誦讀。

title.en: A Seat in the Boat of Millions of Years
title.zh: 百萬年之舟中一席

region.en: The sky-river of Ra, Egyptian Other World
region.zh: 埃及冥界拉之天河水道

period: Book of the Dead chs. 101-102, Theban recension (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IV, the chapters of the Boat of Ra

summary.en: The great ambition of the blessed dead: chapters 101 and 102 of the Book of the Dead 'provided access for him to the Boat of Ra' — the Boat of Millions of Years in which the sun crosses the sky-river daily — the same boat that stopped its course when Horus lay dead (cut in the Horus record) and that the scribe Ani begged: 'Let there be prepared for me a seat in the Boat of Ra on the day when the god goeth forth.'
summary.zh: 蒙福亡者之大志：亡靈書第一〇一至一〇二章『使其得登拉之舟』——即日日渡天河之『百萬年之舟』——即荷魯斯死時為之停駛之舟（見荷魯斯之死條），亦書吏阿尼所求：『當神出行之日，願為我備拉舟中之一席。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary chapters via Budge 1910; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Chaps. 101 and 102 provided access for him to the Boat of Ra. Chaps. 108, 109, 112, and 116 enabled him to know the Souls (i.e. gods) of the East and West, and of the towns of Pe, Nekhen, Khemenu, and Anu. Let there be prepared for me a seat in the Boat of Ra on the day when the god goeth forth. Let me be received into the presence of Osiris, in the Land where Truth is spoken.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IV, summary. / Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. IV, the prayer of Ani (Book of the Dead ch. 15).
passages.zh: 第一〇一與第一〇二章使他得以接近拉之船。第一〇八、一〇九、一一二與一一六章使他得以認識東方與西方之靈魂（即諸神），以及佩、奈肯、赫梅努與阿努諸城之靈魂。願有人在拉之船中為我備好一個座位，就在神出行的那一日。願我能在真理被宣說之地，被接納進入奧西里斯面前。

title.en: Nephthys the Barren Shore: Anubis Born of the Overflow
title.zh: 荒岸奈芙蒂斯：因氾濫而生之安努畢斯

region.en: The sea-shore and desert edges of Egypt (the land Nephthys represents)
region.zh: 埃及海岸與大漠之緣（奈芙蒂斯所象之地）

period: Plutarch, De Iside 38 (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, sec. XXXVIII

summary.en: The allegory of the fourth sister: 'Horus, the offspring of Osiris, the Nile, and Isis, the Earth, was born in the marshes of Buto, because the vapour of damp land destroys drought. Nephthys, or Teleute, represents the extreme limits of the country and the sea-shore, that is, barren land. Osiris (i.e., the Nile) overflowed this barren land, and Anubis was the result.'
summary.zh: 四姊妹之寓言：『荷魯斯——尼羅（奧西里斯）與土（伊西斯）之子——生於布托之沼，蓋濕地之氣克旱。奈芙蒂斯（或名特琉忒）則象國之極限與海岸，即不毛之地。尼羅（奧西里斯）氾濫於此荒岸，遂生安努畢斯。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient allegoresis via Plutarch (Budge's summary of sec. XXXVIII); no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Horus, the offspring of Osiris, the Nile, and Isis, the Earth, was born in the marshes of Buto, because the vapour of damp land destroys drought. Nephthys, or Teleute, represents the extreme limits of the country and the sea-shore, that is, barren land. Osiris (i.e., the Nile) overflowed this barren land, and Anubis was the result.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. XXXVIII (Budge's summary).
passages.zh: 奧西里斯之子、尼羅河與大地女神伊西斯之子荷魯斯，誕生於布托的沼澤之中，因為濕地的水氣能消解乾旱。奈芙蒂斯，或稱忒勒烏忒，代表國土的極遠邊界與海岸，即貧瘠之地。奧西里斯（即尼羅河）淹沒了這片貧瘠之地，而阿努比斯便是其結果。

title.en: Seventeen Thousand Years of Heracles: The Seniority of the Egyptian Gods
title.zh: 一萬七千年之海拉克勒斯：埃及諸神之年資

region.en: Egypt and Tyre (Herodotus' inquiry into the age of the gods)
region.zh: 埃及與推羅（希羅多德究神祇之年壽）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.43-44 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 43-44

summary.en: Herodotus' pilgrimage of antiquity: in Egypt Heracles is one of the twelve gods, seventeen thousand years old by the priests' reckoning; sailing to Tyre he found the temple of Heracles 'set up at the same time when Tyre was founded... a period of two thousand three hundred years', and at Thasos a Heracles-temple five generations before the son of Amphitryon was born — 'So then my inquiries show clearly that Heracles is an ancient god.'
summary.zh: 希羅多德考神祇年壽之旅：於埃及，海拉克勒斯列十二神之數，祭司推算距今一萬七千年；至推羅，見其廟『與推羅建城同時……二千三百年』；於塔索斯，其廟早於安菲特里翁之子誕生五代——『我之查究明證：海拉克勒斯乃古之神也。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient comparative inquiry via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: About Heracles I heard the account given that he was of the number of the twelve gods; but of the other Heracles whom the Hellenes know I was not able to hear in any part of Egypt... In fact however Heracles is a very ancient Egyptian god; and (as they say themselves) it is seventeen thousand years to the beginning of the reign of Amasis from the time when the twelve gods, of whom they count that Heracles is one, were begotten of the eight gods.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.43.
passages.zh: 關於赫拉克勒斯，我聽到的說法是：他屬於十二神之列；但對於希臘人所知的另一位赫拉克勒斯，我在埃及任何地方都無法聽到相關記載……然而事實上，赫拉克勒斯是一位極為古老的埃及神；而且（如他們自己所言），從八神生出十二神（他們認為赫拉克勒斯是其中之一）之時起，至阿瑪西斯統治開始，已有一萬七千年。

passages.text: I made a voyage also to Tyre of Phenicia, hearing that in that place there was a holy temple of Heracles; and I saw that it was richly furnished with many votive offerings besides, and especially there were in it two pillars, the one of pure gold and the other of an emerald stone of such size as to shine by night: and having come to speech with the priests of the god, I asked them how long time it was since their temple had been set up: and these also I found to be at variance with the Hellenes, for they said that at the same time when Tyre was founded, the temple of the god also had been set up, and that it was a period of two thousand three hundred years since their people began to dwell at Tyre.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.44.
passages.zh: 我也曾航行到腓尼基的推羅，因為聽說那裡有一座神聖的赫拉克勒斯神廟；我見到廟中陳設華麗，除其他許多還願祭品外，尤其有兩根柱子，一根是純金的，另一根是祖母綠寶石，其大如許，夜間能發光。我與該神的祭司交談，問他們這座神廟建立至今已有多久；我發現這些人也與希臘人說法不同，因為他們說，推羅建城之時，該神的神廟也同時建立，而自其族人開始定居推羅以來，已有兩千三百年之久。

passages.text: So then my inquiries show clearly that Heracles is an ancient god, and those of the Hellenes seem to me to act most rightly who have two temples of Heracles set up, and who sacrifice to the one as an immortal god and with the title Olympian, and make offerings of the dead to the other as a hero.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.44.
passages.zh: 因此，我的探究清楚表明赫拉克勒斯是一位古老的神；而在我看來，那些希臘人行事最為正確，他們建立了兩座赫拉克勒斯神廟，向其中一座以不朽之神的身分獻祭，並冠以奧林匹亞的稱號，向另一座則以英雄的身分獻上奠祭。

title.en: The Colchians of Sesostris: Circumcision, Linen, and Kinship Across the Sea
title.zh: 塞索斯特里斯之科爾基斯人：割禮、亞麻與跨海血緣

region.en: Colchis at the river Phasis, at the far end of Sesostris' march
region.zh: 法西斯河畔科爾基斯（塞索斯特里斯遠征之極處）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.104-105 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 104-105

summary.en: Herodotus' proof that an Egyptian army once reached the Black Sea: the Colchians 'are evidently Egyptian', dark-skinned and curly-haired — 'but also still more because the Colchians, Egyptians, and Ethiopians alone of all the races of men have practised circumcision from the first' — and 'they alone work flax in the same fashion as the Egyptians', weaving the linen called Sardonic in Hellas and Egyptian in Egypt.
summary.zh: 希羅多德證埃及大軍曾達黑海：科爾基斯人『顯為埃及人』——膚黑髮卷，『尤以科爾基斯、埃及與埃塞俄比亞三者為世上最初行割禮之族』——且『彼等織亞麻之法，與埃及人全同』，所織者在希臘稱薩爾多尼克、在埃及稱埃及麻布。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ethnographic argument via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. The Colchian claim became a set-piece of the Sesostris legend.

passages.text: For the people of Colchis are evidently Egyptian, and this I perceived for myself before I heard it from others. So when I had come to consider the matter I asked them both; and the Colchians had remembrance of the Egyptians more than the Egyptians of the Colchians; but the Egyptians said they believed that the Colchians were a portion of the army of Sesostris. That this was so I conjectured myself not only because they are dark-skinned and have curly hair (this of itself amounts to nothing, for there are other races which are so), but also still more because the Colchians, Egyptians, and Ethiopians alone of all the races of men have practised circumcision from the first.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.104.
passages.zh: 因為科爾基斯人顯然是埃及人，這是我在聽別人說之前自己就察覺到的。所以當我考慮此事時，便向雙方詢問；科爾基斯人對埃及人的記憶比埃及人對科爾基斯人的記憶更多；但埃及人說他們相信科爾基斯人是塞索斯特里斯軍隊的一部分。此事如此，我不僅因為他們膚色黝黑、頭髮捲曲（這一點本身不足為憑，因為還有其他種族也是如此）而自己推測，更因為在所有人類種族中，唯有科爾基斯人、埃及人和衣索比亞人自始便行割禮。

passages.text: Now let me tell another thing about the Colchians to show how they resemble the Egyptians: — they alone work flax in the same fashion as the Egyptians, and the two nations are like one another in their whole manner of living and also in their language: now the linen of Colchis is called by the Hellenes Sardonic, whereas that from Egypt is called Egyptian.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.105.
passages.zh: 現在讓我再講一件關於科爾基斯人的事，以顯示他們如何與埃及人相似：唯有他們像埃及人一樣加工亞麻，而且這兩個民族在整個生活方式上彼此相似，在語言上也如此；如今科爾基斯的亞麻被希臘人稱為薩多尼亞麻，而來自埃及的則稱為埃及亞麻。

title.en: No Text Has His History: Osiris Usurps the Powers of All Other Gods
title.zh: 無一書載其史：奧西里斯兼眾神之權

region.en: Egypt, all periods (the rise of the Osiris cult)
region.zh: 埃及歷代（奧西里斯祭之興）

period: Synthesis from texts of every period (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I, 1911, ch. I)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. I, 'The History of Osiris as told by Classical Writers' (preface)

summary.en: The missing biography of Egypt's greatest god: 'In no text do we find any connected history of the god, and nowhere are stated in detail the reasons why he assumed his exalted position as the judge of souls... No funerary inscription exists, however early, in which evidence cannot be found proving that the deceased had set his hope of immortality in Osiris' — and 'it is Osiris who is made to usurp the attributes and powers of other gods', his cult growing 'in proportion to the growth of the power and wealth' of Egypt itself.
summary.zh: 埃及至大神之『失傳列傳』：『無一文本載其連貫之史，亦無一處詳述其何以居亡魂判官之尊位……無論何古之葬銘，皆可證亡者以不朽之望寄於奧西里斯』——且『乃奧西里斯兼他神之性與權』，其祭之盛『與埃及國勢財力之盛並進』。

sensitivity.note: Egyptological synthesis via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The religious literature of all the great periods of Egyptian history is filled with allusions to incidents connected with the life, death, and resurrection of Osiris, the god and judge of the Egyptian dead; and from first to last the authors of religious texts took it for granted that their readers were well acquainted with such incidents in all their details. In no text do we find any connected history of the god, and nowhere are stated in detail the reasons why he assumed his exalted position as the judge of souls, or why, for about four thousand years, he remained the great type and symbol of the Resurrection.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. I.
passages.zh: 埃及歷史上所有偉大時期的宗教文獻，都充滿了對與奧西里斯——埃及亡者的神與審判者——的生、死與復活相關事蹟的暗示；而宗教文本的作者們自始至終都理所當然地認為，他們的讀者對這些事蹟的一切細節都耳熟能詳。我們在任何文本中都找不到關於這位神的連貫記載，也無處詳細說明他為何取得其作為靈魂審判者的崇高地位，或為何在大約四千年間始終是復活的重要典型與象徵。

passages.text: No funerary inscription exists, however early, in which evidence cannot be found proving that the deceased had set his hope of immortality in Osiris, and at no time in Egypt's long history do we find that the position of Osiris was usurped by any other god. On the contrary, it is Osiris who is made to usurp the attributes and powers of other gods, and in tracing his history in the following pages we shall find that the importance of the cult of this god grew in proportion to the growth of the power and wealth of the country.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. I.
passages.zh: 然而，無論多麼古老的葬儀銘文，其中無不含有證據，證明死者曾將永生的希望寄託於奧西里斯；而在埃及漫長的歷史中，任何時期我們都找不到奧西里斯的地位曾被任何其他神篡奪。相反，正是奧西里斯被說成篡奪了其他神的屬性和權力；在以下各頁追溯他的歷史時，我們將會發現，對這位神的崇拜之重要性，是隨著該國權力與財富的增長而增長的。

title.en: Apet the Great Mother: Life Came from Death, Light from Darkness
title.zh: 大母神阿佩特：死生於死，光生於暗

region.en: Thebes and Ombos, Egypt (the hippopotamus Mother of the gods)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯與翁博斯（河馬大母神）

period: Theban lunar theology, pre-Hyksos; retold in D. A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXII, the Apet theology

summary.en: The oldest Theban creation theology: Ah is the son of the great Mother deity Apet, identified with the female hippopotamus Taurt, goddess of maternity and mother of the gods; at Thebes and Ombos Osiris was regarded as the son of the sacred hippopotamus; at the beginning there was naught save darkness and water — the spirit of the night was the Great Mother, and her first-born was the moon child: life came from death and light from darkness.
summary.zh: 底比斯最古之創世神學：月神阿為大母神阿佩特之子——她被認同於雌河馬陶爾特，孕育之神、眾神之母；底比斯與翁博斯則以奧西里斯為聖河馬之子；太初唯有暗與水——夜之靈即大母，其長子為月之子：死生於死，光生於暗。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Theban theology retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling. The Apet-Taurt identification is Mackenzie's synthesis.

passages.text: It is highly probable that Ah was the son of the great Mother deity Apet, who was identified with the female hippopotamus Taurt, the mighty one, goddess of maternity, and mother of the gods. At Thebes and Ombos, Osiris was regarded as the son of the sacred hippopotamus. As we have seen in the Introduction, he was, like Ah, identified with the moon spirit, which symbolized the male principle. The Apet hippopotamus was the animal incarnation of the Great Mother; as a water goddess, therefore, Apet links with Nut, who rose from the primordial deep and was the waters above the firmament.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXII, with the retelling's quoted epithets rendered as plain text.
passages.zh: 阿赫極可能是偉大母神阿佩特的兒子，阿佩特與雌河馬陶爾特被視為同一神，陶爾特是強而有力者、母性女神、諸神之母。在底比斯與翁布斯，奧西里斯被視為聖河馬之子。正如我們在導論中所見，他與阿赫一樣，被視為月神的同一體，月神象徵男性本原。阿佩特河馬是偉大母親的動物化身；因此，作為水神，阿佩特與努特相連，努特自太初深淵升起，是蒼穹之上的諸水。

passages.text: At the beginning there was naught save darkness and water. The spirit of the night was the Great Mother, and her first-born was the moon child. Life came from death and light from darkness. Such appears to have been the conception of the worshippers of the sky-and-water goddess and the lunar god.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXII.
passages.zh: 太初之時，除了黑暗與水，別無他物。夜之精靈是偉大母親，她的長子便是月之子。生命來自死亡，光明來自黑暗。崇拜天空與水之女神以及月神的人，其觀念似乎便是如此。

passages.text: As moon worship was of greater antiquity in Egypt than sun worship, and was associated with agricultural rites, the Theban cult must have made popular appeal, and helped to rally the mass of the people to throw off the yoke of the Hyksos Ra and Sutekh worshippers. The political significance of Apepa's order to slay the hippopotami is therefore apparent.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXII, referring to the Hyksos king's order in the Apophis-Seqenenre tale tradition.
passages.zh: 由於在埃及，月神崇拜比日神崇拜更為古老，且與農業儀式相關聯，底比斯崇拜必定深得民心，並有助於凝聚民眾，使他們擺脫崇拜拉與蘇特克的喜克索斯人的枷鎖。因此，阿佩帕下令屠殺河馬的政治意義便顯而易見。

title.en: Amon the Husband of His Mother: The Hidden God Becomes King
title.zh: 母之夫阿蒙：隱者成王

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (the rise of the Amon cult)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（阿蒙祭之興）

period: Theban theology of the 18th-20th Dynasties; retold in D. A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXII, Amon the God of Empire

summary.en: How the lunar god of Thebes became Egypt's great father: Amon was originally the son of Mut-Apet, a moon-spirit traverser of space like Khonsu-Thoth who kept his lunar crescent even in hawk-headed form; as a Great Father deity, Amon, husband of his mother, became king of the gods and lost his original lunar character; his fusion with Ra was accomplished for political purposes — yet a Theban hymn still hails him in Memphis: Memphis receives thee in the form of Ptah, he who is the first-born of all gods.
summary.zh: 底比斯月神如何成為埃及偉父：阿蒙本為穆特-阿佩特之子，如孔蘇-托特般遍行之月靈，縱為鷹首仍戴月弦；大父神阿蒙既為母之夫，遂為諸神之王而失其月性；其與拉之融合乃為政治而成——然底比斯頌猶云：孟菲斯以卜塔之形迎爾——眾神之首生者。

sensitivity.note: Ancient theology retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling.

passages.text: As we have already suggested, it is possible that Amon was originally the son of Mut-Apet. He may have developed as a symbolized attribute of Ah. Fragments of old hymns make reference to him as a lunar deity, and as a traverser of space like Khonsu-Thoth. Indeed, even in his hawk-headed form, he retains his early association with the moon, for he wears the solar disk with the lunar crescent.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXII.
passages.zh: 正如我們已經提出的，阿蒙最初可能是穆特—阿佩特之子。他可能是作為阿赫的一種象徵化屬性而發展起來的。古老讚歌的殘篇提到他是月神，並像孔蘇—托特一樣穿越太空。事實上，即使在他呈鷹首之形時，他仍保留著與月亮的早期聯繫，因為他頭戴日盤與月牙。

passages.text: As a Great Father deity, Amon, husband of his mother, became king of the gods, and lost his original lunar character. His fusion with the sun god of Heliopolis, which was accomplished for political purposes, made the change complete, for he became Amon-Ra, the great representative deity of Egypt, who combines the attributes of all other gods.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXII.
passages.zh: 作為偉大父神，阿蒙娶其母為妻，成為諸神之王，並失去了他原本的月神特性。他出於政治目的而與赫利奧波利斯的日神融合，這使這一轉變徹底完成，因為他成了阿蒙—拉，埃及偉大的代表性神祇，兼具所有其他神祇的屬性。

passages.text: As a god of war he rose into great prominence during the Eighteenth Dynasty. The victorious kings, who became owners of all the land in Egypt, and returned with great spoils from many battlefields, were lavish in their gifts to his temple, and his priests became exceedingly wealthy and powerful. There never was in Egypt a more influential cult than that of Amon-Ra.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXII.
passages.zh: 作為戰神，他在第十八王朝期間聲名大振。得勝的諸王成為埃及全境土地的所有者，並從許多戰場帶回大量戰利品，他們對他的神廟慷慨捐贈，他的祭司們變得極為富有且權勢顯赫。在埃及，從未有過比阿蒙—拉崇拜更具影響力的崇拜。

passages.text: At Memphis Amon-Ra was worshipped as Ptah. In a hymn addressed to the great Theban deity it was declared: Memphis receives thee in the form of Ptah, He who is the first-born of all gods, He who was at the beginning.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXII, quoting the hymn to the Theban god.
passages.zh: 在孟菲斯，阿蒙-拉被当作普塔来崇拜。在一首献给这位底比斯伟大神祇的颂诗中，有这样的宣告：孟菲斯以普塔的形象接纳你，他是众神的长子，他自太初便已存在。

title.en: The Deified Royal Couple: Ahmes-Nefertari and Amenhotep I
title.zh: 封神之王室伉儷：阿赫梅西-奈菲爾塔莉與阿蒙霍特普一世

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (the royal cult of the founders of the 18th Dynasty)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（第十八王朝開國者之王室祭）

period: Cult from the 18th Dynasty onward (c. 1500-1100 BCE); retold in D. A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXII, the deified royal founders

summary.en: Kings who became protecting gods: the great Pharaohs were the religious Pharaohs — if a monarch was assiduous in venerating the gods, and especially in erecting and endowing temples, his fame was assured, for the grateful priests kept his memory green; Amenhotep I and his wife Aahmes-Nefertari were, after their death, revered as deities, protectors and punishers of men in the next world.
summary.zh: 成神之王：埃及所頌者乃虔敬之法老——王者若勤於敬神、建廟賜產，其名必不朽，感恩之祭司使其記憶常青；阿蒙霍特普一世及其妻阿赫梅西-奈菲爾塔莉死後受拜為神，為冥界之護者與罰者。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal cult retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling.

passages.text: Although Ahmes I was the liberator of Egypt, his memory was not revered so greatly as that of his son and successor Amenhotep I (Amenophis). The great Pharaohs of the records were the religious Pharaohs; if a monarch was assiduous in venerating the gods, and especially in erecting and endowing temples, his fame was assured; the grateful priests kept his memory green. Amenhotep I and his wife Aahmes-Nefertari were, after their death, revered as deities; references are made to them as protectors and punishers of men in the next world.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXII, with the retelling's quoted phrase rendered as plain text.
passages.zh: 尽管阿赫摩斯一世是埃及的解放者，但人们对他的追念却远不如对其子兼继位者阿蒙霍特普一世（阿蒙诺菲斯）那般尊崇。史册所载的伟大法老皆为虔敬的法老；倘若一位君主勤于敬奉诸神，尤其致力于兴建并捐赐神庙，其声名便得以确保；心怀感激的祭司们使他的记忆长存不衰。阿蒙霍特普一世及其妻阿赫摩斯-奈费尔塔里在死后被尊为神祇；人们提及他们，视之为来世中人类的保护者与惩罚者。

title.en: Osiris the Ancestor-god: From the Family Table to All Egypt
title.zh: 祖神奧西里斯：自家祭之席至全國之神

region.en: Egyptian tombs and stelae, from the Old Kingdom false doors onward
region.zh: 埃及陵墓與石碑（自古王國假門以降）

period: Stele development Old Kingdom to 19th Dynasty (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I, 1911, ch. IX)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. IX, Osiris the Ancestral Spirit and God

summary.en: Why the dead man's stele stopped showing the dead man: the Old Kingdom false door shows the deceased seated at his offering-table, venerated as an ancestor who has attained to the life of the gods, a divine patron of his family; but under the 12th Dynasty the gods take the upper part of the stone, and by the 18th Osiris occupies the place of honour while the deceased is relegated to a corner — because, Budge argues, Osiris began as the ancestor-god of a small community and was adopted, town by town, until he became the ancestor-god of the whole country, exactly as African peoples elevate a chosen hero to be tribal ancestor.
summary.zh: 亡者之碑何以不再現亡者：古王國假門上，亡者坐於供案之側，如得神壽之祖宗受拜，乃家族之神護；至十二王朝，神像漸據碑首；至十八王朝奧西里斯居尊位而亡者退於一隅——伯奇論曰：奧西里斯本一小社群之祖神，城鎮逐一奉之，終為全國之祖神——恰如非洲諸族擇一英雄立為部落之祖。

sensitivity.note: Ancient iconographic argument via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions. The African parallels (Barotse, Shilluk) are Budge's comparative evidence.

passages.text: The deceased sits in state, and we see him venerated as an ancestor who has attained to the life of the gods; he is, in fact, a divine patron of his family to whom petitions for help can be addressed in time of need.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. IX.
passages.zh: 亡者端坐如仪，我们见他被尊为一位已臻于诸神之生命的祖先；事实上，他是其家族的守护神，人们在困厄之时可向他祈求救助。

passages.text: On a great many stelae of this period Osiris occupies the place of honour, and the figure of the deceased is relegated to a corner. From the above facts it is clear that the figure of Osiris, or Osiris Khenti-Amenti, usurped the place occupied in stelae of the Ancient Empire by the deceased. Up to the time when the cult of Osiris spread throughout Egypt, the Egyptians, I believe, worshipped their ancestors, according to the custom of the African in most parts of the Sudan, then and now.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. IX.
passages.zh: 在这一时期的大量石碑上，奥西里斯占据着尊荣之位，而亡者的形象则被贬置于一隅。由上述事实可见，奥西里斯、即奥西里斯-肯提-阿门提的形象，篡夺了古王国时期石碑上本由亡者所占的位置。我确信，直至奥西里斯崇拜传遍全埃及之时，埃及人仍依照苏丹大部分地区非洲人的习俗——无论当时还是如今——崇拜他们的祖先。

passages.text: Everything about the figure of Osiris suggests that in one aspect at least he was an ancestor-god, probably at first of a comparatively small community. As the cult of the god spread, town and village communities all over Egypt adopted him as their ancestor-god, par excellence, and little by little he became the ancestor-god of the whole country.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. IX.
passages.zh: 关于奥西里斯形象的一切都表明，至少在其某一面向中，他是一位祖先神，起初很可能只是一个相对狭小群体的祖先神。随着这位神祇的崇拜传播开来，全埃及的城镇与村落群体都将他奉为最卓越的祖先神，他也就逐渐成为整个国家的祖先神。

passages.text: The Shilluks were in the habit of selecting a particular hero from among the dead, and they constituted him the ancestor of their tribe; when they needed rain or a good harvest they called upon him by name to provide it.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. IX, the comparative African evidence.
passages.zh: 希卢克人惯于从亡者中挑选一位特定的英雄，立其为部族的祖先；当他们需要雨水或好收成时，便呼唤他的名字，求他赐予。

canonical_translation: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (London, 1911), ch. IX

narrative.en:
Every Egyptian tomb of the Old Kingdom confronts the visitor with a false door, and carved or painted on the stone a man seated at his meal: the deceased on a four-legged African stool, a table of bread, beer, oil, wine, geese and legs of beef before him, his wife sometimes beside him, and around the walls reliefs of family and servants carrying offerings for the funerary commemorative service held daily or at intervals. The dead man sits in state, venerated as an ancestor who has attained to the life of the gods — a divine patron of his family to whom petitions for help can be addressed in time of need. This is the everyday theology of African ancestor worship, cut in limestone.

Budge's chapter tracks what happened to that man on his own stone. Under the Middle Kingdom, gods begin to share the stele: on one 12th-Dynasty stone the king's cartouche stands at the top with Khenti-Amenti and Ap-uat beside it; on another, Isis and Horus set up the pole bearing the head-box of Osiris, the cow-headed Hathor behind them, and the kneeling owner of the tomb is pushed to the margin. Under the 18th Dynasty the figure of Osiris is usually sculptured on the upper part of the stone, the deceased below him in a subordinate position; on many stones Osiris occupies the place of honour and the figure of the deceased is relegated to a corner. Under the 19th Dynasty the upper field fills with Amen-Ra Ka-mut-f in ithyphallic form, with the foreign goddesses Anthat and Kent, Mut and Khensu, and groups of solar boats.

Budge's reading is that the stone records a social revolution in theology. Before the Osiris cult spread, Egyptians worshipped their ancestors, according to the custom of the African in most parts of the Sudan, then and now; everything about the figure of Osiris suggests that in one aspect at least he was an ancestor-god, probably at first of a comparatively small community. As the cult spread, town and village communities all over Egypt adopted him as their ancestor-god, par excellence, and little by little he became the ancestor-god of the whole country — which explains why at Abydos, the central city of his cult, the stelae of strangers are crowded with his figure. The mechanism is not Egyptian alone: the Barotse divine with knuckle-bones whether an ancestor is displeased and sacrifice grain and honey at the grave; the Shilluk select a particular hero from among the dead and constitute him the ancestor of their tribe, calling on him by name for rain and harvest. Osiris is Egypt's selected hero — the dead king who rose — promoted from one family's table to the national table of offerings.

functions: Documentary evolution of ancestor worship into state god: the stele sequence as theology in stone
Family religion: the deceased as divine patron to whom petitions are addressed in time of need
Comparative ethnology: Osiris' rise explained through African hero-elevation customs (Barotse, Shilluk)

title.zh: 沙伯提俑：天界勞役之僕

region.en: Egyptian tombs, 6th Dynasty to the Roman Period
region.zh: 埃及陵墓（第六王朝至羅馬時期）

period: Shabti figures from the 6th Dynasty onward, inscribed from the 12th (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I, 1911, ch. VI)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. VI, the Shabtiu figures

summary.en: The worker-figures buried with the dead: the Shabti is a figure of stone, alabaster, wood or faience found in tombs from the 6th Dynasty to the Roman Period, mummy-shaped at first, later with hands crossed, then each hand holding an ankh, later a hoe, and last of all a basket thrown over the shoulder; the inscribed text is identical with the 6th Chapter of the Book of the Dead and calls the figure, in the dead man's name, to perform his labours in the Other World — tilling, planting, watering the fields, bringing sand from the East to the West; and Maspero's explanation, Budge argues, is the right one: the earliest uninscribed figures represent the slaves who were buried with their masters.
summary.zh: 與死者同葬之工人俑：沙伯提俑以石、雪花石膏、木、彩陶等製成，自第六王朝至羅馬時期見於墓葬——初為無手木乃伊形，繼而交手於胸，再各執安卡、後持鋤，末則肩荷筐籃；其銘文即《亡靈書》第六章，以亡者之名呼其俑代行冥界之勞——耕種灌田、自東運沙至西；馬斯佩羅之解最確：古之無銘者，乃代殉葬之僕。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary practice via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions. Maspero's retainer-sacrifice reading links the shabti to the funeral-murders evidence.

passages.text: The Shabti, or Shauabti, is a figure made of stone, alabaster, wood, faience, etc., and is found in tombs from the VIth dynasty to the Roman Period. In the VIth dynasty the Shabti appears to have been uninscribed; in the XIIth it frequently bears the name and titles of the person for whom it was made, and with whom it was buried; and in the XVIIIth and following dynasties, in addition to the name and titles of the deceased, it bears a text which is identical with the VIth Chapter of the Book of the Dead. Its earliest form is that of a mummy with no hands showing, later it has its hands crossed over the breast, later each hand holds the emblem of life, still later each hand holds a hoe, and last of all a basket is thrown over the shoulder.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. VI.
passages.zh: 舍卜提（Shabti，或作 Shauabti）是以石、雪花石膏、木、彩陶等材質製成的人像，見於第六王朝至羅馬時期的墓葬中。在第六王朝，舍卜提似無銘文；至第十二王朝，其上常載有為之製作並與之同葬者的姓名與頭銜；至第十八王朝及其後諸王朝，除亡者姓名與頭銜外，尚載有一段與《死者之書》第六章完全相同之文字。其最早之形制為不露雙手的木乃伊形，其後雙手交疊於胸前，再其後每手各持生命之符號，又其後每手各持鋤，最後則於肩上斜掛一籃。

passages.text: The text, which is cut or written on figures from the XIIth dynasty onwards, explains quite clearly the purpose which the figures were intended to serve, for in it the figure is called upon, in the name of the deceased person written upon it, to perform whatsoever labours he might be adjudged to do in the Other World. These labours consisted in tilling and planting and watering the fields, and in bringing sand from the East to the West, and in doing whatsoever had to be done in connection with agriculture in the Other World.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. VI.
passages.zh: 自第十二王朝以降刻寫或書寫於人像上之文字，清楚說明了此類人像所欲達成之目的，因其文中以書於其上之亡者名義，召喚該人像代行亡者在彼世可能被判處從事之一切勞役。此類勞役包括耕田、種植與灌溉田地，以及自東方運沙至西方，並從事彼世中與農事相關之一切必要工作。

passages.text: The custom of burying mummy-figures of this kind with the dead seems to be senseless unless we accept the view which we owe first of all to Professor Maspero, viz., that they represent the slaves who were buried, alive or dead, with their masters, in order that their spirits might serve the spirits of their masters in the Other World, just as their bodies had ministered to their masters' bodies in this world.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. VI, citing Maspero's reading of the retainer burials.
passages.zh: 此種以木乃伊形人像與死者同葬之習俗，若非接受我們首先歸功於馬斯佩羅（Maspero）教授之觀點，似屬毫無意義；該觀點即：此類人像代表隨其主人一同埋葬（或生或死）的奴隸，為使其靈魂能在彼世服侍其主人之靈魂，正如其肉體曾於此世服侍其主人之肉體一般。

title.en: The Monolith That Refused to Move: The Artificer's Groan
title.zh: 不欲行之巨石：匠人之嘆

region.en: Sais, Egypt (the temple of Athene/Neit, before whose door the colossus lies)
region.zh: 埃及薩伊斯（雅典娜/奈特神廟，巨構臥於門前）

period: Reign of Amasis (26th Dynasty, 570-526 BCE); recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.175 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 175

summary.en: The stopped colossus of Sais: Amasis dedicated a chamber of one single stone, hauled from Elephantine by river, twenty days' journey, by two thousand chosen men of the boatmen class, three years in the work — but while the house was being drawn along the chief artificer groaned aloud, seeing that much time had been spent and he was wearied by the work, and Amasis took it to heart as a warning and did not allow them to draw it further onwards; so it stands outside the temple gate, and some say a man was crushed under it.
summary.zh: 薩伊斯之停運巨構：阿馬西斯以整石鑿室，自象島由水路運來、程二十日，用二千選自舟子階層者、工歷三年——然室行之際，主匠大聲而嘆，嘆工程之久、其身之疲，王以為警，遂止而不令再運——故其室立於廟門之外；一說有槓夫壓死於石下，故亦不復內運。

sensitivity.note: Ancient prodigy-tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Amasis also dedicated in Sais the chamber of the temple of Athene, which is over against the entrance; it is of the length of one-and-twenty cubits, and the breadth fourteen cubits, made of one single stone... the stone was brought from the town of Elephantine by the river, a distance of twenty days' journey: and the matter of the transport was the work of two thousand chosen men allotted to the class of boatmen, and this class of men had this business in charge for three years.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.175.
passages.zh: 阿瑪西斯（Amasis）亦於賽斯（Sais）奉獻雅典娜神廟正對入口之廳堂；其長二十一腕尺，寬十四腕尺，以單一巨石製成……此石由象島（Elephantine）城經河運送，路程二十日；運輸之事由撥歸船夫階級之兩千名精選男子擔任，而此階級之人掌理此事達三年之久。

passages.text: This lies by the side of the entrance to the temple; for within the temple they did not draw it, because, as it said, while the house was being drawn along, the chief artificer of it groaned aloud, seeing that much time had been spent and he was wearied by the work; and Amasis took it to heart as a warning and did not allow them to draw it further onwards. Some say on the other hand that a man was killed by it, of those who were heaving it with levers, and that it was not drawn in for that reason.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.175.
passages.zh: 此石置於神廟入口之側；因其並未運入廟內，據云，當此石屋被拖曳前行時，其首席工匠高聲呻吟，因見耗費時日甚多而自身已為此工所疲；阿瑪西斯以此為警戒而銘記於心，不許他們再將其向前拖曳。另一方面，有人說，在那些以槓桿撬動此石的人中，有一人被此石壓死，因此之故，此石未被運入。

title.en: Declare Your Livelihood: The Law Solon Took from Egypt
title.zh: 申爾生計：梭倫自埃及取回之法

region.en: Egypt under Amasis and Naucratis, the Greek trading city
region.zh: 阿馬西斯治下之埃及與希臘商城諾克拉提斯

period: Reign of Amasis (570-526 BCE); recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.177-178 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 177-178

summary.en: The lawgiver's debt to Egypt: in Amasis' reign Egypt flourished as never before, and it was Amasis who established the law that every year each Egyptian should declare to the ruler of his district from what source he got his livelihood, on pain of death — and Solon the Athenian received from Egypt this law and had it enacted for the Athenians.
summary.zh: 立法者之埃及師承：阿馬西斯之世，埃及之盛冠絕往昔——王立法定制：凡埃及人歲告其州長以何術謀生，違者處死——雅典人梭倫自埃及得此法而頒行之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient legal-history tradition via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In the reign of Amasis it is said that Egypt became more prosperous than at any other time before, both in regard to that which comes to the land from the river and in regard to that which comes from the land to its inhabitants, and that at this time the inhabited towns in it numbered in all twenty thousand. It was Amasis too who established the law that every year each one of the Egyptians should declare to the ruler of his district, from what source he got his livelihood, and if any man did not do this or did not make declaration of an honest way of living, he should be punished with death. Now Solon the Athenian received from Egypt this law and had it enacted for the Athenians, and they have continued to observe it, since it is a law with which none can find fault.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.177. / Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.177.
passages.zh: 據說在阿瑪西斯統治期間，埃及比以往任何時候都更為繁榮，無論就河流所帶給土地之物，或就土地所帶給其居民之物而言皆然，且此時其境內有人居住之城鎮總計達兩萬座。亦為阿瑪西斯訂立法律，規定每年每位埃及人皆須向其所在區域之統治者申明其生計來源；若有人不如此行，或未申報誠實之謀生方式，即應處以死刑。雅典人梭倫（Solon）自埃及獲此法律，並為雅典人制定之，他們此後一直遵守，因這是一部無人能加以指摘的法律。

title.en: The God-man with Two Natures: Osiris Incarnate
title.zh: 雙性之神人：化身之奧西里斯

region.en: Egypt, the theology of divine kingship (the Pharaoh's ancestor)
region.zh: 埃及神王神學（法老之祖）

period: Classical sources assessed against 3000-year-old Egyptian texts (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I, 1911, ch. I)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. I, the god-man doctrine of Osiris

summary.en: Budge's central theological claim, drawn from Plutarch and Diodorus read against the oldest texts: both classical authors assign Osiris a divine origin and state that he reigned in the form of a man upon the earth, 'so it is clear that the Egyptians generally believed that a god made himself incarnate, and that an immediate ancestor of the first Pharaoh of Egypt was a being who possessed two natures, the one human and the other divine' — the mortal body alone suffered death, 'in the divinity and immortality of the god-man Osiris lay the strength of the power with which he appealed to the minds and hopes of the Egyptians for thousands of years.'
summary.zh: 伯奇之核心神學論，取普魯塔克與狄奧多羅斯對讀最古文本：二古典作家皆謂奧西里斯出身神聖、以人形王於地上——『故可斷言：埃及人一般信神曾自化其身，而埃及首位法老之直系祖先乃具雙性者，一屬人、一屬神』——死者僅其凡體；『神人奧西里斯之神聖與不朽，即其數千年感召埃及人心與希望之力之所在。』

sensitivity.note: Egyptological theology via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions. Budge's own comparison of the two-natures doctrine with Christian incarnational language is implicit in his framing.

passages.text: Both Plutarch and Diodorus agree in assigning a divine origin to Osiris, and both state that he reigned in the form of a man upon the earth. This being so it is clear that the Egyptians generally believed that a god made himself incarnate, and that an immediate ancestor of the first Pharaoh of Egypt was a being who possessed two natures, the one human and the other divine.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. I.
passages.zh: 普魯塔克與狄奧多羅斯皆同意賦予歐西里斯神聖的起源，兩人也皆述及他曾以人的形貌統治大地。既然如此，顯而易見，埃及人普遍相信有一位神使自己化身為人，而埃及第一位法老的直系祖先，乃是一個兼具兩種本性——一為人性、一為神性——的存在。

passages.text: As a man he performed the good works which his divine nature indicated to him, he abolished cannibalism, he improved the manners and morals of men, he taught them to live according to law, to worship the gods, and to practise the arts of agriculture. Filled with love for man he set out to travel over the whole world so that he might teach all non-Egyptians to embrace his beneficent doctrine, and enjoy the blessings which accrue to God-fearing and law-abiding peoples. This god-man was hated by his brother, who by a cunning device inveigled him into a box, which he closed and sealed with lead, and thus killed him.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. I.
passages.zh: 作為人，他行了其神性向他指示的善行：他廢除了食人之風，改善了人的習俗與道德，教導他們依律法而生活、敬拜諸神，並從事農耕之藝。他滿懷對人的愛，啟程遊歷整個世界，以便教導所有非埃及人接納他那造福世人的教義，並享有敬畏神明、遵守律法之民族所獲的種種福澤。這位神人為其兄弟所憎恨，其兄弟以狡詐之計誘他進入一隻箱子，將箱蓋闔上並以鉛封緘，就這樣殺了他。

passages.text: The divine part of Osiris did not die, it was only the mortal body, which he put on when he came from the abode of the gods to reign upon earth, that suffered death. In the divinity and immortality of the god-man Osiris lay the strength of the power with which he appealed to the minds and hopes of the Egyptians for thousands of years, and we shall see in the course of the following pages that both these conceptions of Osiris are of purely African origin, and that they were in existence long before the Dynastic Period in Egypt.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. I.
passages.zh: 歐西里斯的神性部分並未死去，死去的只是那具凡人之軀——那是他從諸神的居所前來統治大地時所披上的身體。歐西里斯這位神人的神性與不朽，正是其力量之所在，使他數千年來得以感召埃及人的心靈與希望；而在以下各頁中我們將會看到，關於歐西里斯的這兩種觀念皆純然源自非洲，且早在埃及王朝時期之前便已存在。

language: Egyptian texts read through classical sources
canonical_translation: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (London, 1911), ch. I

narrative.en:
What exactly did Egypt believe had happened to Osiris? Budge's first chapter frames the answer as a two-natures doctrine. Plutarch and Diodorus, whatever their confusions, agree on the essential points: Osiris was of divine origin and 'reigned in the form of a man upon the earth' — from which Budge draws the far-reaching conclusion that 'the Egyptians generally believed that a god made himself incarnate, and that an immediate ancestor of the first Pharaoh of Egypt was a being who possessed two natures, the one human and the other divine.'

As a man, this god-man 'performed the good works which his divine nature indicated to him' — abolished cannibalism, improved the manners and morals of men, taught law, worship and agriculture — and then, 'filled with love for man', set out to teach the whole world. His brother's cunning box killed only what was mortal in him. The body that went into the river and floated to the reed marshes was the mortal body 'which he put on when he came from the abode of the gods to reign upon earth'; the divine part did not die. Hence the possibility that Plutarch records and the Pyramid Texts confirm: that Osiris returned from the Other World, spoke, and appeared 'in a form which Horus could recognize' — a spirit, or his own body raised, Budge leaves open, but with 'the power of speech and thought'.

The payoff, for Budge, is historical: 'in the divinity and immortality of the god-man Osiris lay the strength of the power with which he appealed to the minds and hopes of the Egyptians for thousands of years' — and both conceptions, the divine man and the risen body, are, he argues, 'of purely African origin', older than the Dynastic Period. The narrative material Plutarch gathered can be substantiated, piece by piece, 'by texts written three thousand years before the Christian Era', though the classical writers 'are arranged in wrong order' and joined in ways their informants could no longer understand. The god-man of Egypt is thus the through-line from the predynastic grave to the Passion Play of Abydos: a god who wore a body, died in it, and rose to rule the dead — and whose royal successors on earth each put on, at their coronation, the same two natures.

THE PHARAONIC CONSEQUENCE. The doctrine has a political edge that Budge makes explicit only by implication: if an immediate ancestor of the first Pharaoh was a god incarnate, then every Pharaoh who sat on the throne renewed the incarnation — the living king as Horus, the dead king as Osiris, both wearing the two natures. This is why the Osiris funerary texts are royal texts at their oldest, and why the god's rise tracks the king's: the Passion Play at Abydos rehearses annually the passion of the first god-man, the corn-mummy of Denderah buries and raises him in grain, and the ancestor stele of every village eventually puts his figure where the family's dead used to sit. The classical testimony, checked clause by clause against texts three thousand years older, thus confirms rather than distorts the native theology — it is the native theology, seen through Greek eyes, 'arranged in wrong order' but substantiated in nearly every part. For Budge the two-natures Osiris is the master-key of Egyptian religion: a god who wore a body, died in it, rose from it, and left the risen body as the pattern for every mummy laid in the tombs of Egypt.

functions: Theology of incarnation: the Pharaoh as successor to a god who wore two natures, human and divine
Soteriology: the mortal body alone died; the divine part survived — the ground of every Egyptian hope of rising
Source-critical method: testing Plutarch and Diodorus clause by clause against 3000-year-old texts
