title.en: Byblos Is a Reed Marsh: A Philological Rescue of the Myth
title.zh: 比布魯斯本為蘆葦之沼：神話之語文校正

region.en: The papyrus marshes of the eastern Delta, Egypt (the true destination of the coffin)
region.zh: 埃及東三角洲紙莎草沼（棺槨真正漂至之地）

period: Budge's source-critique of Plutarch, De Iside 15-18 (1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. I, the Byblos question

summary.en: Did the coffin really sail to Phoenicia? Budge argues not: 'The events which are stated by Plutarch to have happened to the body in this place are, clearly, interpolations of a comparatively late period, and were, I believe, invented to explain the similarity of the popular worship of Byblos with that of Osiris. Where the box was carried seems beyond doubt to have been the papyrus swamps... Byblos is a well-known word for the papyrus plant, and some copyist, who knew nothing of the fact that the Delta was full of papyrus marshes, concluded that the word in his text referred to the town of Byblos.'
summary.zh: 棺果真遠航腓尼基耶？伯奇以為否：『普魯塔克所述之事，顯為較晚之增插，蓋為解釋比布魯斯民俗與奧西里斯祭之相似而設；箱之所漂，無疑為紙莎草沼……Byblos（比布魯斯）本為紙莎草之通名；有抄工不知三角洲遍地莎草，遂誤以文中之字指腓尼基之比布魯斯城，而大改其傳說。』

sensitivity.note: Egyptological philology via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions. Modern scholarship is divided; the record preserves Budge's argument.

passages.text: The events which are stated by Plutarch to have happened to the body in this place are, clearly, interpolations of a comparatively late period, and were, I believe, invented to explain the similarity of the popular worship of Byblos with that of Osiris. Where the box was carried seems beyond doubt to have been the papyrus swamps, or the reedy marshes in the east of the Delta. Byblos is a well-known word for the papyrus plant, and some copyist, who knew nothing of the fact that the Delta was full of papyrus marshes, concluded that the word in his text referred to the town of Byblos, and so modified the legend considerably.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. I.
passages.zh: 普魯塔克所述在此地發生於遺體上的種種事件，顯然是較晚時期插入的內容，而我認為，它們是為了說明比布魯斯與歐西里斯之間民間崇拜的相似性而被編造出來的。那隻箱子被帶往何處，似乎毫無疑問是紙莎草沼澤，即三角洲東部的蘆葦濕地。比布魯斯（Byblos）乃是紙莎草植物的著名詞語，而某位抄寫者不知三角洲遍地皆是紙莎草沼澤，遂斷定其文本中的該詞指的是比布魯斯城，因而大幅改動了此傳說。

passages.text: Now, the well-known legend cut on the Metternich Stele says that Isis brought forth her son Horus among the papyrus swamps, and that she reared him there herself, therefore there must be some confusion in the sources of Plutarch's information. At all events, Isis seems to have left the box for some reason, and during her absence Typhon found it, dragged out the body of Osiris, and tore it into fourteen pieces, which he scattered about the country.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. I.
passages.zh: 如今，刻於梅特涅石碑上那著名的傳說記載，伊西斯在紙莎草沼澤中生下其子荷魯斯，並親自在那裡撫養他，因此普魯塔克所據資料的來源中必定存在某種混淆。無論如何，伊西斯似乎因某種緣故而離開了那隻箱子，而在她離去期間，堤豐發現了它，拖出歐西里斯的遺體，將其撕成十四塊，散棄於各地。

title.en: The Sceptre with the Eye: Osiris as the Sun in Hieroglyph
title.zh: 嵌目之杖：象形文字中之日神奧西里斯

region.en: Egypt, the writing system of the gods (symbolic pin, Heliopolis)
region.zh: 埃及神聖文字（象徵定位，赫利奧波利斯）

period: Macrobius (5th century CE) and Diodorus, via Budge 1911

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. I, the hieroglyph of Osiris as the sun

summary.en: The solar reading of Osiris, from Macrobius: 'nor is it a secret that Osiris is nothing else than the sun, and Isis nothing else than the earth... whenever the Egyptians wish to express Osiris as the sun in their hieroglyphic letters they engrave a sceptre, and in it the form of an eye, and by this sign they show Osiris, signifying that this god is the sun, and that, with regal power raised on high, he looks down upon all things.'
summary.zh: 馬克羅比烏斯之日神讀法：『無可諱言：奧西里斯非他，即日也；伊西斯非他，即土也……埃及人欲於聖書中表日神奧西里斯，則刻一杖，杖中作目形——以此符號示彼神即日，以王者之權居高臨下、俯視萬有。』

sensitivity.note: Classical reading of hieroglyphs via Budge 1911 (quoting Macrobius, Saturnalia I); no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Macrobius, who flourished in the first half of the fifth century A.D., held the view that Osiris was the sun and Isis the earth. In proof of his assertion that Osiris is the sun he says that the Egyptians represent this god in their hieroglyphs under the form of a sceptre with an eye in it, and that they indicate by this the idea of the god surveying the universe from his exalted throne in the sky.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. I.
passages.zh: 馬克羅比烏斯活躍於公元五世紀上半葉，他主張歐西里斯是太陽，伊西斯是大地。為證明歐西里斯即太陽，他說埃及人在其象形文字中以一根嵌有眼睛的權杖來表現這位神，並藉此表示這位神自其天上高踞的寶座俯視宇宙之意。

passages.text: Nor is it a secret that Osiris is nothing else than the sun, and Isis nothing else than the earth... Whenever the Egyptians wish to express Osiris as the sun in their hieroglyphic letters they engrave a sceptre, and in it the form of an eye, and by this sign they show Osiris, signifying that this god is the sun, and that, with regal power raised on high, he looks down upon all things.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. I, translating Macrobius, Saturnalia I.
passages.zh: 奧西里斯不過是太陽，伊西斯不過是大地，這也並非秘密……每當埃及人想以象形文字表達奧西里斯即太陽時，他們便刻出一支權杖，並在其中刻上眼睛的形狀，以此符號顯示奧西里斯，表示這位神即是太陽，且他以高舉的王權俯視萬物。

title.en: The Spirit Burial: Isis' Formula for Making the Spirit of Osiris
title.zh: 靈之安葬：伊西斯塑奧西里斯之靈之咒

region.en: Abydos, Egypt (recited at every festival of Osiris, 22nd-26th of Khoiak)
region.zh: 埃及阿拜多斯（奧西里斯祭日誦之，荷阿克月22-26日）

period: Paris papyrus, Graeco-Roman copy of Osiris liturgy (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II, 1911, ch. XVI)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (1911), ch. XVI, the Spirit Burial of Osiris

summary.en: The rubric of the Osiris liturgy in full: the formula 'shall make glorious his soul, it shall stablish his body, it shall make his soul to shine in the sky, and shall make him to renew his youth each month, it shall stablish his son Horus upon his coffer' — recited by Isis and her sister Nephthys and also by her son Horus; 'it will benefit a man if he reciteth it, for he shall become a favoured one of Osiris upon earth among the living' — and in the litany Isis snares Set 'like a goose', kindling a lamp at the door of the urit chamber.
summary.zh: 奧西里斯禮文之眉批全篇：此咒『使其靈榮耀、堅其身、使其靈輝於天、使其月月復其青春、堅其子荷魯斯於其棺之上』——由伊西斯與其妹奈芙蒂斯及其子荷魯斯誦之；『人誦之則受益，必於世間為奧西里斯所眷』——禮文中伊西斯於烏瑞特室門前燃燈，『以網捕塞特如捕鵝』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient liturgical rubric via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The formula for making the spirit of Osiris in Akertet, which shall be made (i.e., recited) for this god, the Lord of Abydos, at every festival of Osiris, and at every appearance [of the god] in the temples. It shall make glorious his soul, it shall stablish his body, it shall make his soul to shine in the sky, and shall make him to renew his youth each month, it shall stablish his son Horus upon his coffer. This formula was recited by the sister [of the god]. It will benefit a man if he reciteth it, for he shall become a favoured one of Osiris upon earth among the living; his son shall be established in his house every day, and his children upon the earth.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XVI, the rubric of the Spirit Burial.
passages.zh: 在阿凱爾特為奧西里斯造魂的咒式，須為此神、阿拜多斯之主，於奧西里斯的每個節慶，以及[此神]在諸神殿中每次顯現時誦讀。它將使他的魂得榮耀，使他的身得堅立，使他的魂在天上發光，並使他每月更新其青春，它將使他的兒子荷魯斯穩立於他的櫃上。此咒式曾由[此神之]姊妹誦讀。人若誦讀它必蒙其益，因為他將在世上成為奧西里斯在生者中的寵愛者；他的兒子將每日穩立於其家，他的子孫亦將立於地上。

passages.text: This formula was recited by Isis and her sister Nephthys, and also by her son Horus. And if it be recited for Osiris, it will cause the soul of the deceased to live in Akertet every day, it will gladden his heart, and will overthrow all his enemies; and it shall be recited during the IVth month of the season Akhet, from the XXIInd day to the XXVIth day thereof.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XVI, the rubric continued.
passages.zh: 此咒式曾由伊西斯及其姊妹奈芙蒂斯誦讀，亦由其子荷魯斯誦讀。若為奧西里斯誦讀，它將使亡者之魂每日在阿凱爾特存活，使他的心歡喜，並推翻他的一切仇敵；且須於阿赫特季第四月，自該月第二十二日至第二十六日誦讀。

passages.text: Hail, Seker-Osiris! This calamity happened to thee in the primeval time. There have been made for thee mighty chambers in Tettu (Busiris). The god Utekh embalmed thee and made sweet the smell of thee. The god Anpu (Anubis) toiled for thee in the place of purification, and performed all the things which he had to perform. I and my sister Nephthys kindled a lamp at the door of the urit chamber, so that [we] might snare in a net Set like a goose. Anubis came forth from the place of purification and overthrew all thine enemies.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XVI, the litany of Isis.
passages.zh: 致敬，塞克爾—奧西里斯！此災禍於太初之時降於你身。在泰圖（布西里斯）已為你造了雄偉的廳堂。神烏泰赫為你施以香料防腐，使你芬芳。神安普（阿努比斯）在潔淨之地為你辛勞，並完成了他所須完成的一切。我與我的姊妹奈芙蒂斯在烏里特室的門口點燃了一盞燈，以便[我們]如捕鵝般以網羅擒住塞特。阿努比斯自潔淨之地而出，推翻了你的一切仇敵。

title.en: The Heart, the Weigher of All: Ab Before the Scales
title.zh: 心，萬行之衡：天秤前之阿布

region.en: The Hall of Maati, Egyptian Other World
region.zh: 埃及冥界瑪阿特之廳

period: Book of the Dead chs. 26-30B and 125 (Budge, The Book of the Dead, 1901, ch. VII)

source.work: The Book of the Dead, by E. A. Wallis Budge (1901), ch. VII, 'The Judgment of Osiris' (the heart ab)

summary.en: What is weighed at the Great Judgment: 'The heart, ab, was taken as the symbol of all the emotions, desires, and passions, both good and evil, and out of it proceeded the issues of life. It was intimately connected with the ka, i.e., the double or personality of a man, and several short spells in the Book of Coming Forth by Day were composed to ensure its preservation (Chapters XXVI-XXXB)' — the organ on which the whole verdict turned.
summary.zh: 大審判所秤者何：『心（ab）乃一切情感、欲念與激情——善惡皆然——之符號，生命之諸流皆出於其中；其與卡（人之兩重者）密切相連；故《來日之書》中若干短咒（第二六至三十B章）專為保其不失而作』——此器官繫全案之判。

sensitivity.note: Ancient doctrine via Budge 1901; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The heart, ab, was taken as the symbol of all the emotions, desires, and passions, both good and evil, and out of it proceeded the issues of life. It was intimately connected with the ka, i.e., the double or personality of a man, and several short spells in the Book Coming Forth by Day were composed to ensure its preservation (Chapters XXVI-XXXB). The great Chapter of the Judgment of Osiris, the CXXVth, is divided into three parts, which are sometimes (as in the Papyrus of Ani) prefaced by a Hymn to Osiris.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, The Book of the Dead (1901), ch. VII.
passages.zh: 心，即阿布，被視為一切情感、慾望與情慾的象徵，無論善惡，生命的種種結果皆由它而出。它與卡——即人的雙身或人格——密切相連，《白日出現之書》中有若干短咒，專為確保其保存而作（第二十六章至第三十章乙）。關於奧西里斯審判的偉大篇章，即第一百二十五章，分為三部分，其前有時（如阿尼紙草卷中）冠以一篇奧西里斯頌歌。

title.en: The Temple in the Water: Bubastis and Its Sacred Grove
title.zh: 水中之廟：布巴斯提斯與其聖林

region.en: Bubastis, Nile Delta, Egypt (the temple of Bastet, Artemis of the Greeks)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲布巴斯提斯（貝斯特神廟，希臘人之阿爾忒彌斯）

period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.138 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 138

summary.en: The temple everyone could look down upon: Bubastis stands raised on embankments thrown up by centuries of corvee labour — 'Except the entrance it is completely surrounded by water; for channels come in from the Nile... each a hundred feet broad and shaded over with trees; and the gateway has a height of ten fathoms, and it is adorned with figures six cubits high'; within runs a grove of very large trees planted round the temple-house where the image of the goddess stands, and a paved road of three furlongs leads east 'to the temple of Hermes.'
summary.zh: 人人可俯視之神廟：布巴斯提斯因數世勞役築堤而高——『除入口外，廟四面皆水；運河自尼羅引入……各寬百尺，兩岸有樹蔭蔽；門樓高十噚，飾以六肘之神像』；廟內繞大樹成林，環女神之室；更有一三弗隆石路向東『通赫耳墨斯之廟』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient travel description via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In this city there is a temple very well worthy of mention, for though there are other temples which are larger and built with more cost, none more than this is a pleasure to the eyes. Now Bubastis in the Hellenic tongue is Artemis, and her temple is ordered thus: — Except the entrance it is completely surrounded by water; for channels come in from the Nile, not joining one another, but each extending as far as the entrance of the temple, one flowing round on the one side and the other on the other side, each a hundred feet broad and shaded over with trees; and the gateway has a height of ten fathoms, and it is adorned with figures six cubits high, very noteworthy.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.138.
passages.zh: 此城中有一座極值得稱述的神廟，因為雖有其他神廟更為宏大、耗費更多，卻無一座比此廟更悅人眼目。布巴斯提斯在希臘語中即阿耳忒彌斯，其神廟的格局如下：——除入口外，它完全為水所環繞；因為有水道自尼羅河引入，彼此並不相通，而是各自延伸至神廟入口，一條繞行於一側，另一條繞行於另一側，各寬一百尺，並有樹木蔭蔽；門樓高達十噚，其上飾有六肘高的人像，極為可觀。

passages.text: This temple is in the middle of the city and is looked down upon from all sides as one goes round, for since the city has been banked up to a height, while the temple has not been moved from the place where it was at the first built, it is possible to look down into it: and round it runs a stone wall with figures carved upon it, while within it there is a grove of very large trees planted round a large temple-house, within which is the image of the goddess: and the breadth and length of the temple is a furlong every way. Opposite the entrance there is a road paved with stone for about three furlongs, which leads through the market-place towards the East, with a breadth of about four hundred feet; and on this side and on that grow trees of height reaching to heaven: and the road leads to the temple of Hermes.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.138.
passages.zh: 這座神廟位於城市中央，繞行四周時，從各面皆可俯瞰它；因為城市已被墊高至一定高度，而神廟並未從最初建造之處遷移，所以能夠俯視其內：神廟周圍環繞著一道刻有圖像的石牆，牆內有一片由極高大的樹木構成的樹林，環繞著一座大型神殿，神殿內供奉著女神的雕像；神廟的寬與長各為一斯塔德。入口對面有一條以石鋪成的道路，長約三斯塔德，穿過市集廣場通向東方，寬約四百英尺；道路兩側生長著高聳入雲的樹木：這條路通向赫爾墨斯神廟。

title.en: The Pine Trunk of Isis: A Roman-Egyptian Funeral Rite
title.zh: 伊西斯之松：羅馬-埃及葬儀

region.en: The Isis temples of the Roman Empire (the annual rite of the pine)
region.zh: 羅馬帝國之伊西斯神廟（松木歲儀）

period: Recorded by Firmicus Maternus (4th century CE), quoted in Budge 1911

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. I, the rite of the pine of Isis

summary.en: The Egyptian mystery rite as Rome practised it, in Firmicus Maternus' testimony: 'In the sacred rites of Isis a trunk is cut from a pine tree; the middle part of this trunk is hollowed out with skill; into it an image of Osiris made of reeds is buried' — the same trunk, and the other woods of the rite, 'a flame consumes; for even after a year the fire of the pyre feeds upon those very logs.'
summary.zh: 羅馬所行之埃及秘儀，菲爾米庫斯證之：『於伊西斯聖儀中，自松樹斬一幹；其幹之中段精巧鑿空；以葦製之奧西里斯小像葬於其中』——此幹與儀中諸木，『火焰盡焚之；歲餘，火仍食其薪』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient mystery-rite testimony via Budge 1911 (translating Firmicus, De errore profanarum religionum); no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In the sacred rites of Isis a trunk is cut from a pine tree. The middle part of this trunk is hollowed out with skill. Into it an image of Osiris made of reeds is buried. And the other woods also, which I have mentioned, a similar flame consumes; for even after a year the fire of the pyre feeds upon those very logs.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. I, translating Firmicus Maternus, De errore profanarum religionum (Latin quoted in Budge's footnote).
passages.zh: 在伊西斯的聖儀中，人們從一棵松樹上砍下一段樹幹。這段樹幹的中間部分被巧妙地挖空。其中埋入一尊以蘆葦製成的奧西里斯像。而我所提及的其他木材，也同樣被相似的火焰吞噬；因為即使過了一年，火葬堆的火焰仍以那些木柴為食。

title.en: Izanagi Slays the Fire God Kagutsuchi
title.zh: 伊耶那岐斬火神迦具土

region.en: Mount Hiba, Izumo-Hahaki boundary (symbolic pin, Izumo coordinates; grave of Izanami and scene of the fire god's slaying)
region.zh: 出雲與伯耆交界之比婆山（象徵性標記，採出雲座標；伊耶那美葬地與斬火神場景）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Izanami dies giving birth to the fire god Kagutsuchi, whose burning consumes her; grief-stricken Izanagi buries her on Mount Hiba, then draws his ten-grasp sabre and cuts off his child's head. Deities of rock, torrent and spring spring from the blood on the blade, and eight mountain deities are born from the slain god's head, chest, belly, hands and feet.
summary.zh: 伊耶那美因生火神迦具土而陰部被灼身亡；伊耶那岐悲慟葬妻於比婆山，隨即拔十握劍斬下其子之頭。劍刃濺血生出磐裂、根裂等神，迦具土屍身頭、胸、腹、手、足各生山神，化為日本群山之地貌。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki, Shinto sacred narrative still revered in Japan); passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Chamberlain translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: When the Fire-Burning-Swift-Male Deity, Kagutsuchi, was born, the burning of the child consumed his mother's private parts, and Izanami lay sick and dying. Even her sickness was generative: from her vomit were born the Metal-Mountain deities, from her faeces the Clay deities, and from her urine the Water deities, whose child was the Luxuriant-Food-Princess. Then the Female-Who-Invites divinely retired, and Izanagi, wrung with grief, cried that he had exchanged his beloved wife for this single child. As he crept round her pillow and her feet weeping, a weeping female deity was born from his tears, and he buried Izanami on Mount Hiba at the boundary of Izumo and Hahaki.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 115-117 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當火燃速男神迦具土誕生時，這孩子的灼燒焚毀了母親的私處，伊邪那美臥病垂危。甚至她的病也具生育之力：從她的嘔吐物中誕生了金山神，從她的糞便中誕生了土神，從她的尿中誕生了水神，而水神之子即為豐受姬。隨後，伊邪那美神退隱，伊邪那岐悲痛欲絕，哭訴自己以愛妻換來了這一個孩子。當他繞著她的枕邊與腳邊哭泣爬行時，從他的淚水中誕生了一位哭泣的女神，他將伊邪那美葬於出雲與伯耆交界處的比婆山。

passages.text: Then grief turned to rage. Izanagi drew the ten-grasp sabre girded at his side, the sword named Heavenly-Point-Blade-Extended, and cut off the head of his child the Fire-Shining-Elder. From the blood that stuck to the point of the august sword and bespattered the multitudinous rock-masses were born the Rock-Splitter, the Root-Splitter and the Rock-Possessing-Male Deity. From the blood on the upper blade came the Awfully-Swift Deity, the Fire-Swift Deity and the Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male Deity; and from the blood that collected on the hilt and leaked between Izanagi's fingers came Kura-okami and Kura-mitsuha.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 117-119 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隨後，悲痛化為憤怒。伊邪那岐拔出腰間所佩的十握之劍，即名為天之尾羽張之劍，砍下了他的孩子火神迦具土的首級。從附著於聖劍劍尖並濺灑於無數岩石上的血中，誕生了石析神、根析神與磐裂男神。從上刃之血中，誕生了速秋津日神、火速神與武勇威猛男神；而從積聚於劍柄、自伊邪那岐指縫間滲出的血中，誕生了闇御津羽神與闇罔象神。

passages.text: The slain fire god's own body proved no less fertile. From his head was born the Possessor-of-the-True-Pass-Mountains; from his chest, the Possessor-of-Descent-Mountains; from his belly, the Possessor-of-the-Innermost Mountains; from his private parts, the Possessor-of-the-Dark-Mountains; from his left and right hands, the Possessors of the Dense and Outlying Mountains; and from his left and right feet, the Possessors of the Moorland and Outer Mountains. Thus the dismembered fire deity, cut apart part by part from head to foot, peopled the mountains of Japan with their divine lords.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 119-120 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 被殺的火神之身軀同樣富於生育之力。從他的頭部誕生了正哉吾勝勝速日天之忍穗耳命之山神；從他的胸部誕生了降山神；從他的腹部誕生了奧山神；從他的私處誕生了闇山神；從他的左右手誕生了密山神與外山神；從他的左右腳誕生了野山神與外山神。於是，這被肢解的火神，從頭到腳逐部切開，以其神主使日本群山遍佈神靈。

narrative.en:
The fire god Kagutsuchi — the Fire-Burning-Swift-Male Deity, Fire-Shining-Prince, Fire-Shining-Elder — was the last-born child of the creator pair Izanagi and Izanami, and his birth destroyed his mother. As the child passed through her, his burning consumed her private parts, and Izanami lay down sick unto death. Even her sickness was generative: from her vomit were born the deities of the metal mountains; from her faeces, the deities of clay; from her urine, the water deities, whose child was the Luxuriant-Food-Princess. Then the Female-Who-Invites divinely retired — the Kojiki's phrase for the death of a deity — and Izanagi lost the partner with whom he had made the islands of Japan.

His grief was extravagant. He clung to the body, crept round her pillow and her feet, and wept, and from his tears was born a weeping female deity who dwells on Mount Kagu near Unewo. 'Oh, thine Augustness, my lovely younger sister! Oh, that I should have exchanged thee for this single child!' he cried — a child valued against a wife. Then he buried Izanami on Mount Hiba, on the boundary between the lands of Izumo and Hahaki, and her grave-mountain stands there in the mythic geography of Japan.

Grief curdled into rage against the child who had cost him his wife. Izanagi drew the ten-grasp sabre girded on him — its names recorded as Heavenly-Point-Blade-Extended and Majestic-Point-Blade-Extended — and cut off the head of the fire god.

But in this myth nothing dies without giving birth. From the blood that clung to the point of the sword and spattered the multitudinous rock-masses sprang three deities: the Rock-Splitter, the Root-Splitter and the Rock-Possessing-Male Deity, lords of bedrock and quarry. From the blood that clung to the upper blade and again bespattered the rocks came three more: the Awfully-Swift Deity, the Fire-Swift Deity and the Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male Deity, with his alternative names Brave-Snapping and Luxuriant-Snapping. From the blood that collected on the hilt and leaked out between Izanagi's fingers were born Kura-okami and Kura-mitsuha, dragons of the valleys and springs from whom old priestly houses traced their descent.

The slain god's own body was no less fertile. From his head was born the Possessor-of-the-True-Pass-Mountains; from his chest, the Possessor-of-Descent-Mountains; from his belly, the Possessor-of-the-Innermost Mountains; from his private parts, the Possessor-of-the-Dark-Mountains; from his left hand, the Possessor-of-the-Dense Mountains; from his right hand, the Possessor-of-the-Outlying-Mountains; from his left foot, the Possessor-of-the-Moorland-Mountains; and from his right foot, the Possessor-of-the-Outer-Mountains. Eight mountain deities, mapped onto the corpse part by part from head to foot, took lordship over Japan's mountain landscape — the passes, the inner depths, the dark defiles, the wooded slopes, the moorland heights.

Comparative mythologists have long set this episode beside the great dismemberment cosmogonies: Ymir, hacked apart by Odin and his brothers so that his flesh became the earth and his skull the sky; Tiamat, split by Marduk and halved into heaven and sea; Pangu, whose body became the world at his death; the Vedic Purusha, whose sacrificed limbs yielded the social classes and the beasts of sacrifice. The Kagutsuchi episode is the Japanese member of that cluster, with a characteristic twist: the dismembered being is not a primordial giant who already contained the world, but a young god of the element that most terrifies rice-farmers — fire. And the world created from his parts is not the cosmos itself but the specific, practical geography of mountains, rocks and water that a mountainous archipelago lives from. The blood spilled in the slaying generates not social orders but raw terrain: rock, cliff, torrent, spring, wooded height and moor.

The episode also does quieter work in the Kojiki's larger plot. It supplies the motive — Izanami's death — that sends Izanagi down to Yomi, where he will break the taboo of looking and bring death's permanence into the world. It supplies the first of the great divine swords: the blade that severed Kagutsuchi is the ancestor of the ten-grasp sabre Susanoo carries, the sword with which he slays the eight-headed serpent, and from whose tail the Herb-Quelling Great Sword of the imperial regalia is drawn. And it institutes the principle that violence toward the gods is cosmologically productive: Susanoo's own rampage and the slaying of the food goddess Ogetsuhime, which brings forth rice, millet and beans, repeat the same pattern in a later generation.

Ritually, the story underwrites the mountain cults of Japan — the mountain deities, lords of passes, forests and moors, who receive worship from foresters, hunters and mountain villages — and the dragon-deities of valley water from whom notable priestly clans claimed descent. It frames fire as both indispensable and murderous: Kagutsuchi must exist, for he is the origin of fire in the world, yet must be slain, for his uncontrolled force burns even the gods. In later Shinto fire-rituals the dangerous fire is ritually split and pacified, a pattern that readers have traced back to this mythic cutting-up of the fire god.

functions: Etiological charter for Japan's mountain cults: eight mountain lords from the slain god's body map the mythic geography of passes, forests, cliffs and moors, and underwrite worship of mountain deities by foresters, hunters and mountain communities.
Explains and tames the terror of fire: the indispensable but murderous fire element must be divided and pacified, a pattern echoed in later Shinto fire-calming rites.
Ancestral genealogy: the blood deities born from the sword were claimed as founders by old water-clan and priestly lineages, welding local cults into the imperial myth-cycle.
Narrative hinge of the Kojiki's first book: Izanami's death at Kagutsuchi's birth sends Izanagi to Yomi, bringing death into the world, and passes the ten-grasp sword on to Susanoo's later deeds.

variants.name: Nihongi version: Kagutsuchi cut into five pieces
variants.text_tradition: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Book I, 'One writing says...' (trans. Aston 1896)
variants.summary: The Nihongi variant has Izanagi cut the fire god into five pieces, which become deities, while the blood on the sword likewise begets gods and the blade itself is revered as a deity; the emphasis falls on the divinity of the sword rather than the geography of the corpse.

variants.name: Norse: Ymir slain by Odin, Vili and Ve
variants.text_tradition: Prose Edda and Voluspa (Icelandic, c. 1220s / c. 1270s manuscripts)
variants.summary: The primordial giant Ymir is killed and his flesh becomes the earth, his blood the sea, his bones the mountains, his skull the sky — the classic dismemberment cosmogony parallel to Kagutsuchi's limbs becoming mountains.

variants.name: Babylonian: Marduk splits Tiamat
variants.text_tradition: Enuma Elish (Babylonian, c. late 2nd millennium BCE)
variants.summary: Marduk slays the chaos-mother Tiamat and splits her like a shellfish into heaven and earth, her waters forming the world — a combat-dismemberment creation parallel.

variants.name: Chinese: Pangu's body becomes the world
variants.summary: The giant Pangu, who separated heaven and earth, dies and his body transforms into mountains, rivers, wind, clouds and stars — like Kagutsuchi, a dissolved body yields the landscape.

variants.name: Vedic: the sacrifice of Purusha
variants.summary: The primeval man Purusha is offered up and dismembered; from his parts come the social classes, animals and the worlds — the ritual-dissection parallel to the Kagutsuchi blood-and-limb births.

title.en: Izanagi Divides the Realm: Susanoo's Weeping and Expulsion
title.zh: 伊耶那岐命三子分治與須佐之男命哭泣被逐

region.en: Plain of High Heaven (Takachiho plateau, Miyazaki - symbolic pin)
region.zh: 高天原（宮崎高千穗高原，象徵性標記）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Washing after his return from the land of the dead, Izanagi begets three illustrious children and divides the cosmos among them: Amaterasu the sun rules Heaven, Tsukuyomi the night, Susanoo the sea. Susanoo refuses his charge and weeps until mountains wither and seas dry, and his father expels him with a divine expulsion.
summary.zh: 伊耶那岐自黃泉歸來後於日向洗滌己身，洗面而生三貴子：天照大神治高天原，月讀命治夜之國，須佐之男命治海原。須佐之男命不受命，哭嚎至鬚長八握，青山枯萎、河海乾涸，遂被父神以神逐驅逐。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki, Shinto sacred narrative); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: After fleeing the polluted land of Yomi, Izanagi purified himself in a river-mouth near Tachibana in Himuka. As he washed his face, three illustrious children were born: from his left eye the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity, Amaterasu; from his right eye the Moon-Night-Possessor, Tsukuyomi; and from his nose the Brave-Swift-Impetuous-Male-Augustness, Susanoo. Rejoicing that his final begetting had produced three illustrious children, Izanagi jingled off his necklace, named it the August-Storehouse-Shelf-Deity, hung it on Amaterasu and charged her to rule the Plain of High Heaven; to Tsukuyomi he gave the Dominion of the Night; and to Susanoo the Sea-Plain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 128-130 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 逃離污穢的黃泉國之後，伊邪那岐在日向橘小門附近的河口淨身。當他洗臉時，誕生了三位尊貴的孩子：從他的左眼誕生了天照大神；從他的右眼誕生了月夜見尊；從他的鼻子誕生了建速須佐之男命。伊邪那岐欣喜於自己最後的生育產下了三位尊貴的孩子，便搖響頸上的項鍊，將其命名為御倉板舉神，掛在天照大神身上，命她統治高天原；將夜之食國賜予月夜見尊；將海原賜予須佐之男命。

passages.text: Amaterasu and Tsukuyomi each assumed their rule, but Susanoo did not. He wept and howled until his eight-grasp beard reached the pit of his stomach, withering the green mountains and drying up all the rivers and seas, while the sound of bad deities swarmed like the flies of the fifth month and every portent of woe arose. Asked why he wept instead of ruling the land he had been charged with, he answered that he wished to depart to his deceased mother's land, the Nether Distant Land. Enraged, Izanagi declared that he should not dwell in this land, and expelled him with a divine expulsion; then Izanagi retired to dwell at Taga in Afumi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 130-131 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天照大神與月讀命各自承擔其統治之責，惟素戔嗚尊不然。彼哭泣號叫，直至其八握之鬚長及腹底，使青山枯萎、眾河海盡竭，而惡神之聲如五月之蠅群聚嗡鳴，種種凶兆並起。人問其既受命治國，何為哭泣而不治，彼答曰欲往其亡母之國，即根之堅洲國。伊邪那岐大怒，宣言彼不當居於此國，乃以神逐之法逐之；其後伊邪那岐退居近江之多賀。

title.en: Susanoo and Amaterasu's Oath Contest
title.zh: 須佐之男命與天照大神的誓約

region.en: Tranquil River of Heaven, Plain of High Heaven (Takachiho plateau, Miyazaki - symbolic pin)
region.zh: 天安川，高天原（宮崎高千穗高原，象徵性標記）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Expelled from his father's realm, Susanoo ascends to heaven to take leave of his sister; suspecting invasion, Amaterasu arms herself in war-gear and challenges him. To prove his sincerity they swear an oath on opposite banks of the Tranquil River of Heaven, crunching each other's jewels and sword and blowing the fragments away as deities — three females from his blade, five males from her jewels.
summary.zh: 須佐之男命被逐後上高天原辭別姊姊天照大神；天照疑其來意不善，束髮佩玉、執弓負箭嚴陣相待。二神乃立於天安川兩岸誓約，互取對方之劍玉咬嚼吹氣而生神：其劍生三女神（多紀理毘賣等），其玉生五男神。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki, Shinto sacred narrative); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Expelled from his father's realm, Susanoo resolved to take leave of his sister before departing, and his ascent shook all the mountains and rivers, so that every land quaked. Amaterasu, alarmed, declared his intent surely no good and readied for war: she unbound her hair, twisted it into bunches, threaded strings of curved jewels through hair, head-dress and both arms, slung a quiver of a thousand arrows and another of five hundred, brandished her bow, stamped her feet into the hard ground up to her thighs, kicking away the earth like rotten snow, and stood valiantly like a mighty man, demanding wherefore he had ascended. Susanoo swore he had no evil intent, only a wish to take leave, and proposed that each of them swear an oath and produce children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 131-133 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 素戔嗚尊既見逐於父之領域，決意於離去前向其姊辭別，其登天也，震動群山與眾河，使諸國皆動。天照大神驚懼，斷言其來意必無善意，乃備戰：解其髮而束之成結，以勾玉串貫於髮、頭飾及兩臂，背負千箭之筒及五百箭之筒，手執其弓，足踏堅地至股，踢土如踢腐雪，威武而立如壯士，詰問其何故登天。素戔嗚尊誓曰其無惡意，唯欲辭別，並請二人各立誓而生子。

passages.text: On opposite banks of the Tranquil River of Heaven they performed the ordeal. Amaterasu begged Susanoo's ten-grasp sabre, broke it into three fragments, washed and crunched the pieces with her jewels in the True-Pool-Well of Heaven, and blew the mist away, begetting three female deities: Torrent-Mist-Princess, Lovely-Island-Princess and Princess-of-the-Torrent — the three great deities of the Munakata shrines. Susanoo then begged her five strings of jewels from her hair, head-dress and arms, crunched them one by one and blew the mist away, begetting five male deities, among them the Truly-Conqueror-I-Conquer-Conquering-Swift-Heavenly-Great-Great-Ears and Ame-no-hohi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 133-136 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 二人於天之安河之兩岸行盟誓之儀。天照大神乞素戔嗚尊之十握劍，折之為三段，於天之真名井中洗之、嚼之，與其勾玉同嚼，吹散其霧，而生三女神：湍津姬、市杵島姬及田心姬——即宗像三社之三女神。素戔嗚尊乃乞其髮、頭飾及臂上之五串勾玉，逐一嚼之，吹散其霧，而生五男神，其中有正哉吾勝勝速日天忍穗耳尊及天穗日命。

passages.text: Amaterasu declared the division: the five male deities were born from things of hers, so they were undoubtedly her children; the three female deities were born from a thing of his, so they were doubtless his. But Susanoo, impetuous with what he took for victory — had he not, from his own sword, begotten delicate females? — grew reckless, and the oath that should have sealed his good faith instead opened the season of his outrages in heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 136-138 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天照大神宣告其分判：五男神生自其物，故無疑為其子；三女神生自彼物，故無疑為彼子。然素戔嗚尊以其所自認之勝利而躁動——彼豈非以己之劍而生柔弱之女子乎？——乃漸肆無忌憚，本應固其誠信之誓，反開啟其在天之暴行時期。

title.en: Susanoo Ravages Heaven and Is Punished
title.zh: 須佐之男命肆虐高天原被罰

region.en: Plain of High Heaven (Takachiho plateau, Miyazaki - symbolic pin; ends with expulsion toward Torikami, Izumo)
region.zh: 高天原（宮崎高千穗高原，象徵性標記；終於被逐往出雲鳥髮）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Convinced his oath contest proved victory, Susanoo wrecked his sister's heaven: breaking the rice-field ridges, filling ditches, fouling the food-palace, and dropping a backward-flayed heavenly horse into the weaving-hall, where a startled weaving woman was killed by her shuttle. For these crimes the eight hundred myriad deities fined him a thousand tables, cut his beard, pulled his nails, and expelled him.
summary.zh: 須佐之男命自以誓約得勝，於高天原大肆破壞：毀天照大神之田埂、填溝渠、於大嘗殿污穢，又於織殿頂破洞，倒剝天之斑駒投入，織女受驚為梭所擊而死。八百萬神乃議罰，令其設千座贖罪、剃鬚拔手足爪，以神逐驅逐之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki, Shinto sacred narrative); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Judging from the delicate females his oath had produced, Susanoo concluded he had gained the victory, and, impetuous with victory, wrecked his sister's realm. He broke down the divisions of the rice-fields Amaterasu had laid out, filled up the ditches, and strewed excrement in the palace where she partook of the great food. Amaterasu upbraided him not, excusing him: what looked like filth must be what her elder brother had vomited through drunkenness, and his wrecking of the fields must be his grudge for the land. But he only continued his evil acts, more and more violent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 138-139 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 素戔嗚尊由其誓所生之柔弱女子判斷，自以為已獲勝利，因勝利而躁動，乃毀其姊之領域。彼破壞天照大神所闢之田埂，填塞溝渠，並於其食大嘗之宮殿散佈穢物。天照大神不責之，反為之辯解：看似污穢者，必其兄因醉而吐之物；其毀田者，必其對土地之怨。然彼唯續行其惡，愈益暴烈。

passages.text: At last, while Amaterasu sat in her weaving-hall seeing to the weaving of the august garments of the deities, Susanoo broke a hole in the top of the hall and through it let fall a heavenly piebald horse which he had flayed backwards. The women weaving the heavenly garments were so much alarmed at the sight that one of them struck her private parts against the shuttle and died. This outrage drove the sun goddess to hide in the Heavenly Rock-Dwelling, and the whole plain of heaven and the Central Land of Reed-Plains went dark.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 139-140 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 終焉，當天照大神坐於其織殿，督織眾神之御衣時，素戔嗚尊破殿頂之洞，自其中投下一天斑駒，乃其剝皮而倒剝者。織天衣之女見狀大驚，其一以私處觸梭而死。此暴行迫使日神隱於天之岩戶，於是高天原盡暗，葦原中國亦皆晦冥。

passages.text: When she had been brought out of the rock-dwelling and light returned, the eight hundred myriad deities took counsel together and punished Susanoo: they imposed on him a fine of a thousand tables of offerings, cut off his beard, and caused the nails of his fingers and toes to be pulled out, expelling him with a divine expulsion. So the storm god, shorn of beard and nails, descended from the Plain of High Heaven to Torikami at the head-waters of the River Hi in the land of Izumo.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 145-146 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當她從岩屋中被請出、光明復返之後，八百萬神祇共同商議懲罰素戔嗚尊：他們判他繳納千座供品的贖罪之物，割去他的鬍鬚，並拔去他手指與腳趾的指甲，以神罰將他驅逐。於是這位風暴之神被剃去鬍鬚、拔去指甲，從高天原降臨到出雲國肥河上游的鳥髮之地。

title.en: The Slain Food Goddess Ogetsuhime
title.zh: 大宜都比賣之死與五穀起源

region.en: Plain of High Heaven (Takachiho plateau, Miyazaki - symbolic pin)
region.zh: 高天原（宮崎高千穗高原，象徵性標記）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Expelled from heaven, Susanoo begs food of the goddess Princess-of-Great-Food; seeing her draw dainties from her own nose, mouth and fundament, he judges it filth and kills her. From the slain goddess's body spring silkworms, rice, millet and beans, which the Deity-Producing-Wondrous-Ancestor causes to be used as seed — the origin of cultivated food.
summary.zh: 須佐之男命被逐後向大宜都比賣神乞食；女神自鼻、口乃至穢處取出珍饌調成諸餚奉上。須佐之男命窺其所為，疑其以穢物相饗，遂殺之。其屍身頭生蠶，目生稻種，耳生粟，鼻生小豆，陰生麥，穀生大豆；神產巢日御祖命皆取為種，是為五穀蠶桑之起源。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki, Shinto sacred narrative); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Expelled from heaven, Susanoo begged food of the Deity Princess-of-Great-Food, Ogetsuhime. She took out all sorts of dainty things from her nose, her mouth and even her fundament, and made them up into all sorts of dishes, which she offered to him. But Susanoo watched her proceedings, considered that she was offering up filth to him, and at once killed the goddess.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain page 145 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 素戔嗚尊被逐出天界後，向大氣津比賣神乞食。她從鼻中、口中乃至肛門取出種種珍饈，做成各式菜餚獻給他。但素戔嗚尊窺見她的舉動，認為她是在獻上穢物給他，便立刻殺死了這位女神。

passages.text: From the body of the slain goddess food sprang for the world: silkworms were born in her head, rice seeds in her two eyes, millet in her two ears, small beans in her nose, barley in her private parts and large beans in her fundament. The Deity-Producing-Wondrous-Ancestor had them all taken and used as seed, so that the killing of the food goddess became the origin of the crops and the silkworms that feed and clothe humankind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 145-146 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從被殺女神的遺體中，為世人誕生了食物：她的頭中生出了蠶，雙眼生出了稻種，雙耳生出了粟，鼻中生出了小豆，陰部生出了大麥，肛門生出了大豆。神產巢日神將這些全部取來用作種子，於是食物女神的死，便成了養育並衣被人類的穀物與蠶的起源。

title.en: Susanoo Builds the Palace of Suga
title.zh: 須佐之男命造須賀宮

region.en: Suga, Izumo
region.zh: 出雲須賀

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: After slaying the eight-forked serpent, Susanoo seeks a place to build his palace and arrives at Suga in Izumo, where his heart feels pure; clouds rise as he builds, and he sings the first waka of the Kojiki, the eight-fold fence song. He appoints the old man Foot-Stroking-Elder head of his palace and marries his daughter, the rescued Wondrous-Inada-Princess, begetting the Deity Eight-Island-Ruler.
summary.zh: 須佐之男命斬八岐大蛇後，於出雲覓地造宮，行至須賀，曰「吾心清淨」，遂建宮殿，雲氣騰起，乃詠「八雲立出雲八重垣」之歌。以足名椎為宮之長，娶其獲救之女櫛名田比賣為妻，於新婚之室生八島士奴美神。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki, Shinto sacred narrative); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: After cutting the eight-forked serpent to pieces, Susanoo sought in the land of Izumo for a place where he might build a palace. He arrived at a place called Suga and said: 'On coming to this place my august heart is pure.' There he built a palace to dwell in, and that place is called Suga to this day. When the Great Deity first built the palace of Suga, clouds rose up from it, and he made an august song: 'The eight-fold clouds of Izumo arise to make an eight-fold fence about my wife within the eight-fold fence — a wondrous eight-fold fence indeed.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 149-151 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 將八岐大蛇斬成數段之後，素戔嗚尊在出雲國尋覓可建造宮殿之地。他來到一處名為須賀的地方，說道：「我來到此地，我心清淨。」於是在那裡建造宮殿居住，那地方至今仍稱為須賀。當大神初次建造須賀宮殿時，雲氣自宮中升起，他作了一首御歌：「出雲的八重雲升起，為我妻築起八重籬牆——真乃奇妙的八重籬牆。」

passages.text: There Susanoo called the old man Foot-Stroking-Elder and appointed him head-man of his palace, and took as his wife the Wondrous-Inada-Princess, the daughter whom the serpent had been about to devour. In their bridal chamber they begot a child, the Deity Eight-Island-Ruler, from whom — so the record traces — the line of the Great-Name-Possessor, Master of the Great Land, was descended. Thus the serpent-slayer settled the land of Izumo, founding lord of its palace, song and shrines.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain pages 151-152 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 素戔嗚尊在那裡召來名為足名椎的老人，任命他為宮殿的長官，並娶了那條大蛇即將吞食的女兒——奇稻田姬為妻。二人在新房中誕下一子，即八島士奴美神；據記載所溯，大國主神——大名持——的世系便是由此而來。於是這位斬蛇者奠定了出雲之地，成為其宮殿、歌謠與神社的創建之主。

title.en: The White Hare of Inaba and the Deity Great-Name-Possessor
title.zh: 因幡之白兔與大己貴神

region.en: Inaba and Cape Keta (pin at Izumo; symbolic pin for the hare's crossing)
region.zh: 因幡與氣多岬（出雲象徵性定位）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: A hare deceives the crocodiles of the sea into forming a bridge, is flayed by the last of them, and is cruelly worsened by the eighty deities; the deity Great-Name-Possessor (Okuninushi) teaches him the true cure, and the healed hare prophesies that Okuninushi alone shall win the Princess of Yakami.
summary.zh: 白兔欺騙海中鱷魚列身為橋，被末尾鱷魚剝去皮毛；八十神教以海水曝風之法，傷勢愈重；大己貴神授以清水漱洗、蒲黃敷身之方，兔身復原，遂預言八十神必不得八上比賣，唯大己貴神可娶之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology. The trickster-hare reading is interpretive.

passages.text: The hare who had lost his own home island had no means of crossing over to Inaba. For this reason he deceived the crocodiles of the sea, saying: Let you and me compete, and compute the numbers of our respective tribes. Go and fetch every member of your tribe, and make them all lie in a row across from this island to Cape Keta; then I will tread on them and count them as I run across, and we shall know whether my tribe or yours is the larger. They were deceived and lay down in a row, and the hare trod on them, counting as he went. But just as he was about to step on land he shouted that they had been deceived by him, and the last crocodile in the line seized him and stripped off all his clothing, leaving his raw skin bare.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 154-155 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那隻失去了自己故鄉島嶼的兔子，無法渡海到稻羽。為此牠欺騙海中的鱷魚，說道：「你和我來比一比，數一數我們各自族類的數目。你去把你全族的成員都帶來，讓牠們從這座島一直排列到氣多岬；然後我踏在牠們身上，一邊跑一邊數，這樣我們就知道是我的族類多，還是你的族類多。」鱷魚們受了騙，排成一列趴下，兔子便踏在牠們身上，一邊走一邊數。但就在牠即將踏上陸地之時，牠高聲喊道自己騙了牠們，於是行列中最後一條鱷魚抓住了牠，剝去了牠所有的皮毛，讓牠赤裸的皮肉暴露在外。

passages.text: Weeping and lamenting in his flayed state, the hare was met by the eighty deities going on ahead, who commanded and exhorted him: Bathe in the salt water, and lie down exposed to the wind. He did as they said, and his whole body was only hurt the more. Then the deity Great-Name-Possessor, who was following behind carrying his brothers' luggage, saw him and taught him the remedy: Go quickly to the river-mouth, wash your body with the fresh water, then take the pollen of the sedges growing at the river-mouth, spread it about, and roll upon it. The hare did as he was instructed, and his body was restored to its original state. This was the White Hare of Inaba, now called the Hare Deity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, p. 155 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那隻被剝了皮的兔子正哭泣哀號，迎面遇上了先行的八十位神祇，他們命令並訓誡牠說：用鹽水沐浴，再躺臥在風中。牠照著做了，全身卻只是更加疼痛。這時，殿後替兄長們背負行囊的大穴牟遲神看見了牠，便教牠救治之法：快快前往河口，用清水洗淨身體，然後取來生長在河口的莎草花粉，撒布開來，在上頭翻滾。兔子照著指示做了，身體便恢復如初。這就是稻羽的白兔，如今被稱為兔神。

passages.text: The hare then spoke to the deity Great-Name-Possessor a prophecy: These eighty deities shall certainly not get the Princess of Yakami. Though you carry their bag, Your Highness shall obtain her. When the princess herself was asked, she answered the eighty deities: I will not listen to your words; I mean to marry the deity Great-Name-Possessor. So the eighty deities, enraged, took counsel together to slay him — the beginning of the persecutions that drove Okuninushi down to the Nether-Distant-Land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 155-156 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兔子於是向大穴牟遲神說出預言：這八十位神祇必定得不到八上比賣。雖然您替他們背著行囊，殿下卻將娶得她。當人們去問八上比賣本人時，她回答八十位神祇說：我不聽你們的話；我打算嫁給大穴牟遲神。八十位神祇因此大怒，共同商議要殺他——這便是迫害的開端，後來把大國主逼下了根之堅洲國。

title.en: Okuninushi's Journey to the Nether-Distant-Land: Persecution, Ordeals, and Flight with the Treasures
title.zh: 大己貴神遠訪根之堅洲國：迫害、考驗與攜寶而逃

region.en: Ne-no-katsu-kuni, the Nether-Distant-Land where Susanoo dwells (symbolic pin at an inland neutral spot)
region.zh: 根之堅洲國，須佐之男命所居之冥遠之國（象徵性定位）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Persecuted by his eighty brothers and twice killed and revived, the deity Great-Name-Possessor flees to the Nether-Distant-Land, marries Susanoo's daughter the Forward-Princess (Suseri-hime), survives the snake-house, wasp-house and burning-moor ordeals, and escapes with the life-sword, life-bow-and-arrows and speaking-lute; Susanoo, pursuing him to the Even Pass of Hades, blesses him to become Master of the Great Land and husband of Suseri-hime.
summary.zh: 大己貴神屢遭八十神殘害，兩度被害而兩度復生；母命其遠走根之堅洲國，謁須佐之男命。與其女須勢理毘賣一見成婚，歷蛇屋、蚰蜒蜂屋、火燒原諸難，得鼠之助；乘翁熟睡，縛其髮於椽，負妻攜生大刀、生弓矢與鳴琴而逃。須佐之男追至黃泉平坂，遙呼而祝之：持此劍弓驅逐八十神，成大國主神、活土神，以須勢理毘賣為妻。遂逐八十神於阪途河曲，始作國土。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki), central to the Izumo shrine tradition; passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: When the Princess of Yakami declared she would marry the deity Great-Name-Possessor and none of the eighty deities, they resolved to slay him. On Mount Tema in the land of Hahaki they told him: On this mountain there is a red boar; when we drive it down, catch it, or we will kill you. Then they took fire, burned a great stone into the likeness of a boar, and rolled it down; he caught it, was burned by it, and died. His mother went up to Heaven and entreated the Divine-Producing-Wondrous-Augustness, who sent Princess Cockle-Shell and Princess Clam to bring him to life: one scorched her shell, the other smeared him as with mother's milk, and he became a beautiful young man. The eighty deities again deceived him, led him into the mountains, drove a wedge into a large cut tree, made him stand in the gap, and pulled the wedge out, torturing him to death. His mother cleaved the tree, took him out and revived him a second time, and sent him swiftly to the Deity Great-House-Prince in the land of Ki; still pursued, he escaped by dipping under the fork of a tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 156-157 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當八上比賣宣告她要嫁給大穴牟遲神，而不嫁八十位神祇中的任何一位時，他們便決意殺他。在波波岐國的手間山上，他們對他說：這座山上有隻紅野豬；我們把牠趕下來時，你要接住牠，否則就殺了你。於是他們取來火，把一塊大石燒成野豬的模樣，再把它滾下山；他接住了它，被它灼傷而死。他的母親登上高天原，懇求神產巢日御祖神，神便派遣蛤貝比賣與蚶貝比賣前去救活他：一個燒灼自己的貝殼，另一個如以母乳般塗抹他，他便成了俊美的青年。八十位神祇又欺騙他，引他入山，在一株砍開的大樹上打入楔子，命他站在裂口之中，再拔出楔子，將他折磨至死。他的母親劈開樹木，把他取出，第二次使他復活，並急忙送他到紀伊國的大屋毘古神那裡；仍被追趕，他潛入樹杈之下才得以逃脫。

passages.text: The Deity Great-House-Prince counseled him: You must set off to the Nether-Distant-Land where dwells His Impetuous-Male-Augustness; that Great Deity will certainly counsel you. So Great-Name-Possessor obeyed and journeyed to the august place of the Impetuous-Male-Deity. At the gate he met the Impetuous-Male-Deity's daughter, the Forward-Princess; they exchanged glances and were married, and she went in and told her father that a very beautiful deity had come. The Great Deity went out, looked, and said: This is the Ugly-Male-Deity-of-the-Reed-Plains — and at once made him sleep in the snake-house. His wife gave her husband a snake-scarf: When the snakes are about to bite, drive them away by waving this scarf three times. He did so, the snakes grew quiet, and he came out after calm slumbers. On the next night his father-in-law shut him in the centipede-and-wasp house, but she gave him a centipede-and-wasp scarf, and again he came out unharmed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 157-159 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大屋毘古神勸告他說：你必須前往根之堅洲國，那裡住著速須佐之男命；那位大神必定會指點你。於是，大穴牟遲神聽從了，啟程前往速須佐之男神的神聖居所。在門前，他遇見了速須佐之男神的女兒，即前比賣；兩人交換目光，結為夫妻，她便進去告訴父親，說來了一位非常俊美的神祇。大神出來一看，說道：這是蘆原的醜男神——便立刻命他睡在蛇屋裡。他的妻子交給丈夫一條蛇巾：當蛇要咬人時，揮動這條巾三次，把牠們趕開。他照著做了，蛇便安靜下來，他在安穩的睡眠之後走了出來。第二天夜裡，岳父把他關進蜈蚣與蜂的屋子，但她給了他一條蜈蚣與蜂的巾，他又一次安然無恙地走了出來。

passages.text: The Impetuous-Male-Deity then shot a whizzing barb into the middle of a great moor and sent his son-in-law to fetch it; when the young deity had entered the moor, fire was set burning all around it, and he stood knowing no place of exit. A mouse came and said: The inside is hollow-hollow; the outside is narrow-narrow. He trod where it pointed, fell through, and hid while the fire burnt past; then the mouse brought the barb in its mouth, and all the mouse's children carried the feathers. His wife came out bearing mourning-implements and weeping, for she believed him dead; her father too went out upon the moor thinking him done for — and the young deity presented the arrow alive. Taking him into the house, the Great Deity seated him in an eight-foot spaced room and had him pick the lice from his head; but the head swarmed with centipedes. His wife gave him berries of the muku tree and red earth, and he chewed the berries and spat them out with the earth, so that his father-in-law believed him to be chewing up and spitting out the centipedes, grew fond of him, and fell asleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 159-160 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 速須佐之男神接著把一支響箭射入一片大草原的中央，派他的女婿去取回來；當這位年輕的神祇進入草原時，四周放起火來燃燒，他站著，卻不知何處可以逃出。一隻老鼠前來說道：裡面是空空洞洞，外面是窄窄狹狹。他踩著老鼠所指的地方，陷落下去，躲藏起來，等火燒過去；然後老鼠用嘴啣來那支響箭，老鼠的子女們全都搬運著箭羽。他的妻子帶著喪具出來哭泣，因為她相信他已死去；她的父親也走到草原上，以為他完了——而這位年輕的神祇卻活生生地呈上那支箭。大神把他帶進屋裡，讓他坐在一間八尋殿中，命他捉頭上的蝨子；但頭上爬滿了蜈蚣。他的妻子給了他櫟樹的果實和紅土，他嚼碎果實，連同紅土一起吐出，岳父便以為他是在嚼碎並吐出蜈蚣，於是喜愛他，並睡著了。

passages.text: Then Great-Name-Possessor grasped the Great Deity's hair and tied it fast to the rafters, blocked up the floor with a rock of five hundred men's draught, took his wife Suseri-hime on his back, and carried off the great life-sword, the life-bow-and-arrows, and the heavenly speaking-lute, and ran out. But the lute brushed against a tree and the earth resounded; the sleeping Great Deity pulled down the house, and while he disentangled his hair from the rafters the fugitive fled far away. Pursuing him to the Even Pass of Hades, he gazed from afar and called out: With the great life-sword and life-bow-and-arrows you carry, pursue your half-brethren till they crouch on the slopes of the passes and are swept into the rivers; and do you, wretch, become the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land and the Deity Spirit-of-the-Living-Land; make my daughter the Forward-Princess your consort, and dwell there, you villain. So, bearing the sword and bow, he scattered the eighty deities at every pass and river, and then he began to make the land. He brought home the Princess of Yakami as promised; but fearing Suseri-hime, she abandoned the child she had borne in a tree-fork and went back — the Tree-Fork-Deity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 160-161 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是，大穴牟遲神抓住大神的頭髮，牢牢地綁在椽子上，用一塊需五百人才能拉動的巨石堵住地面，把妻子須勢理比賣背在背上，奪走了生大刀、生弓矢和天詔琴，跑了出去。但琴擦到一棵樹，大地發出聲響；沉睡中的大神拉倒了屋子，當他從椽子上解開頭髮時，逃亡者已逃得很遠了。大神追他到黃泉的比良坂，從遠處凝望並喊道：帶著你所拿的生大刀和生弓矢，追趕你的庶兄們，直到他們蜷伏在坡道之上、被掃入河中；而你這惡徒，就成為大國主神與幽世大神吧；讓我的女兒前比賣做你的正妻，住在那裡吧，你這惡棍。於是，他帶著刀與弓，在每一處坡道和河川驅散了八十位神祇，然後開始經營國土。他如約迎回了八上比賣；但她畏懼須勢理比賣，便將自己所生的孩子遺棄在樹杈之間，獨自回去了——那便是木俁神。

language: Old Japanese (phonetic use of Chinese characters, kanbun-style)
canonical_translation: Basil Hall Chamberlain, A Translation of the Ko-ji-ki, Transactions of the Asiatic Society of Japan supplement, Kobe 1882 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The Kojiki's great Izumo cycle opens with a hero made by suffering. The deity called Great-Name-Possessor — Okuninushi, the future Master of the Great Land — is first known as the youngest and least of eighty brothers, all marching to Inaba to court the Princess of Yakami. On the road the flayed White Hare of Inaba, cruelly advised by the eighty to bathe in salt water and dry in the wind, is healed by the youngest brother's counsel of fresh water and sedge pollen, and prophesies that he alone shall win the princess. The princess confirms the prophecy, and the enraged brothers begin to murder him.

THE TWO DEATHS. On Mount Tema in Hahaki the brothers decoy him with a boar of burning stone: he clutches it and is burned to death. His weeping mother ascends to Heaven and entreats the Divine-Producing-Wondrous-Deity, who sends Princess Cockle-Shell and Princess Clam; shell-ground and shell-water revive him as a beautiful youth. The brothers then lead him into the mountains, drive a wedge into a great felled tree, set him inside the cut, and withdraw the wedge, crushing him to death; his mother finds him, cleaves the tree, and revives him a second time, warning that he will be destroyed if he stays. She sends him to the Deity Great-House-Prince in the land of Ki, and from there, still pursued, he is directed onward: You must set off to the Nether-Distant-Land where dwells His Impetuous-Male-Augustness — the storm-god Susanoo — for that Great Deity will certainly counsel you.

THE DESCENT AND THE BRIDE. Okuninushi's journey to the Nether-Distant-Land (Ne-no-katsu-kuni) is a marriage-ordeal quest. At the house of Susanoo he meets the Forward-Princess, Suseri-hime; they exchange glances and are married at once. Susanoo, contemptuously calling him the Ugly-Male-Deity-of-the-Reed-Plains, sets the tests that are the myth's set-piece: first a night in the snake-house — Suseri-hime's snake-scarf, waved three times, quiets the serpents; then the centipede-and-wasp-house — disarmed by the second scarf; then the whizzing barb shot into a great moor which is fired on all sides, until a mouse directs him: The inside is hollow-hollow, the outside is narrow-narrow; he slips into the hollow earth while the fire passes over, and the mouse and its children bring back the arrow. Suseri-hime arrives with mourning-implements, weeping; her father, believing the young man dead, walks out onto the moor — and the living bridegroom presents the barb. Turned from victim to guest, Okuninushi is set to delousing Susanoo's head, which swarms with centipedes; Suseri-hime gives him muku berries and red earth to chew and spit, deceiving her father into thinking the vermin are being eaten. Fond at last, Susanoo sleeps.

THE FLIGHT AND THE BLESSING. The escape is a descent myth's return in miniature: Okuninushi ties Susanoo's hair to the rafters, blocks the floor with a five-hundred-man rock, takes Suseri-hime on his back, and carries off the three treasures — the great life-sword, the life-bow-and-arrows, and the heavenly speaking-lute. The lute brushes a tree; the earth resounds; Susanoo pulls down the house, frees his hair, and pursues the pair to the Even Pass of Hades. There, unable to cross, he calls the renunciation-blessing across the boundary: with the sword and bow pursue your half-brethren till they crouch on the slopes of the passes and are swept into the rivers; become the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land and the Deity Spirit-of-the-Living-Land; take my daughter for your consort; build the temple-pillars on the nethermost rock-bottom and the cross-beams up to the Plain of High Heaven. Okuninushi returns with sword and bow, scatters the eighty deities at every pass and river, and begins to make the land. He marries the Princess of Yakami; fearing Suseri-hime, she abandons her child in a tree-fork — the Tree-Fork-Deity, the Deity-of-August-Wells — and goes home.

The story's cultural work is layered. It is a katabasis-and-return narrative in which sovereignty over the visible world is won in the world below and certified by a father-in-law's curse-blessing; the regalia carried up (sword, bow, lute) are the mythic forerunners of kingship emblems. The snake-house, wasp-house and burning-moor trials belong to the widespread son-in-law-trials genre (cf. the Aarne-Thompson bride-test tales), read by scholars as mythologized initiations. And the two deaths and revivals mark Okuninushi as a twice-born deity whose right to create and rule is earned through death, descent, and resurrection — the theological ground on which he will later yield the land to the heavenly descendants and retire to his nethermost-pillared palace at Izumo.
narrative.zh: 大己貴神為八十神之幼弟，因因幡白兔之預言與八上比賣之允婚，遭八十神兩度謀害：燒石如豬壓殺之，以貝神蛤神敷漿復活；又誘入山中，以巨木楔殺之，其母剖木復生，戒以出走。遂依大屋毘古神之勸，遠赴根之堅洲國謁須佐之男命。於門前遇其女須勢理毘賣，相視成婚。須佐之男呼之為葦原色許男醜男，先使宿蛇屋，妻授蛇比禮三振而蛇靜；次宿蚰蜒蜂屋，復以比禮免難；又射鳴鏑於大野而四面縱火，鼠教以內虛外狹，掘地而伏，火過乃出，銜鏑而歸。妻持喪具出哭，翁出視，己貴獻鏑得生。入室令拾頭蝨，髮滿蚰蜒；妻與構樹實與赤土，嚼而吐之，翁誤為食蝨，愛之而寢。己貴乃結翁髮於椽，以五百人引之石塞門，負妻背生大刀、生弓矢及天沼琴而逃。琴觸樹而地鳴，翁寤，拽髮拔椽，屋倒追之，至黃泉平坂不得過，遙祝曰：持劍弓追爾異母兄弟至阪途河曲，成大國主神、活土神，娶吾女為妻，於宇加山腳巖根堅柱，高天原架棟梁而居。遂驅八十神，始作國土，娶八上比賣；懼須勢理毘賣，棄子樹杈，是為木俁神，一名御井神。

functions: Establishes the descent-and-return template of Japanese sovereignty myth: the ruler's land-claim is won through trials in the otherworld and sealed by a rival deity's curse-blessing at the boundary of Hades.
Charter of the Izumo shrine tradition: the temple-pillars on the nethermost rock-bottom and cross-beams to High Heaven prefigure the great Izumo sanctuary and Okuninushi's cult there.
Encodes the son-in-law trial-ordeal genre (snake-house, wasp-house, burning moor), read as mythologized initiation of the young hero by the powerful father-in-law.
Marks Okuninushi as a twice-born resurrection figure whose creative power follows death and revival, preparing the theology of the dying-and-yielding land-god of the kuni-yuzuri.

variants.name: Izanagi's flight from Yomi (Kojiki, Book 1)
variants.summary: The same descent-flight-boundary pattern a generation earlier: a living deity enters the world of the dead, wins or loses a spouse there, is pursued to the pass, and a boulder seals the boundary while the fugitive returns transformed. Okuninushi's Even Pass of Hades pursuit deliberately echoes Izanagi's flight.

variants.name: Inanna's Descent to the Netherworld
variants.text_tradition: Sumerian cuneiform epic (trans. from the Sumerian; English in Spence 1916 and later editions)
variants.summary: A deity descends to the land of the dead, is stripped of powers gate by gate, dies, and is revived by clever helpers, returning with new authority — the Mesopotamian parallel to the stripped-and-revived land deity's otherworld journey.

variants.name: Nihongi versions of the Okuninushi cycle
variants.text_tradition: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Book I, one-writing variants (trans. Aston 1896)
variants.summary: The official chronicle preserves rival tellings in which Okuninushi (Ashinaduchi/Osobiko figures) undergoes persecution, receives the treasures from Susanoo, and cedes the land, with different name-forms and episode order.

primary_sources.work: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), compiled 712 CE
primary_sources.citation: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882), Wikisource djvu pages 155-161 (the White Hare, the two deaths, the Nether-Distant-Land journey, the trials, flight and blessing)

secondary_sources.work: Donald L. Philippi, Kojiki
secondary_sources.citation: Philippi 1968, Tokyo: University of Tokyo Press — standard modern translation and commentary on the Okuninushi cycle.

secondary_sources.work: Michael Ashkenazi, Handbook of Japanese Mythology
secondary_sources.citation: Ashkenazi 2003, Santa Barbara: ABC-CLIO — synthesis of Kojiki/Nihongi variants of the Okuninushi-Susanoo episodes.

source_urls.description: Wikisource edition of Chamberlain's 1882 English translation of the Kojiki (public domain)

sensitivity_guidance: Kojiki narrative is living Shinto material and imperial mythology: Izumo Taisha maintains the active cult of Okuninushi. Present the myth comparatively and critically; avoid devotional or nationalist framing; note that passages are paraphrases of the public-domain Chamberlain translation.

title.en: The Courtship Songs of Okuninushi and Nunakawa-hime, and the Pledge of Suseri-hime
title.zh: 大己貴神求沼河姬之歌與須勢理毘賣之盟

region.en: Nunakaha in the land of Koshi (symbolic pin at the Noto Peninsula, Sea of Japan coast)
region.zh: 越之國沼河姬之鄉（日本海能登半島象徵性定位）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: The Deity-of-Eight-Thousand-Spears (Okuninushi) travels to Koshi to woo the Princess of Nunakaha, and the two exchange courtship songs through her closed door; when his chief empress Suseri-hime grows jealous and he prepares to leave for Yamato, she offers him the great liquor-cup with a pledge-song, and the couple pledge each other by the cup and rest together to this day.
summary.zh: 八千矛神往越之國求沼河姬，隔門互歌求婚；正妻須勢理毘賣妒之，八千矛神欲往大和，臨行歌別。須勢理毘賣奉大酒杯而歌：君有如草之妻無數，而我女子唯有君一人。遂交杯為誓，至今安眠——是為神語。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); the courtship songs are among the oldest recorded Japanese poetry. Passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Deity-of-Eight-Thousand-Spears, having set his heart on wooing the Princess of Nunakaha in the land of Koshi, arrived at her house and sang a wooing-song at the door: he told how he had traversed night after night through the darkness of the pass, over the black hilly path, seeking her; how the little birds of the island had cried their ill-omened cries, and how he had wondered what devilish thing had guided him astray, while the star of the evening had dragged along and hung upon him. The song mixes longing, weariness of the road, and the fear of a malign power obstructing the lovers' meeting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 161-163 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 八千矛神傾心於求娶越國之沼河比賣，來到她家門前，於門外唱了一首求婚之歌：他訴說自己如何夜復一夜，穿越山路的黑暗，行過黝黑崎嶇的小徑，前來尋她；島上的小鳥如何啼出凶兆之聲，他又如何疑心是什麼邪魔之物引他迷途，而晚星一路拖曳，懸掛在他身上。這首歌交織著思慕、旅途的疲憊，以及對有惡力阻撓戀人相會的恐懼。

passages.text: The Princess of Nunakaha, without yet opening the door, sang in reply from inside: she likened their love to birds of the beach — the dotterel and the gentle bird — who, though they strike their wings, will not mate wrongly; she declared that her jewel-like arms would be pillowed on no one else, and sang that the man should be the dear jewel-arm of the woman and the woman the jewel-arm of the man. Then, as the song said, that night they did not yet come together; but on the following night they came together in due and stately union. Later tellers add that the refrain-lines of the song were carried down by the singing-women as a messenger running to future ages.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 163-165 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 沼河比賣尚未開門，便從屋內唱和作答：她將二人的情愛比作海濱之鳥——千鳥與柔順之鳥——牠們雖拍擊雙翼，卻不會錯配成偶；她宣告自己如玉的雙臂不會枕於他人，並唱道男子當為女子親愛之玉臂，女子當為男子之玉臂。於是，正如歌中所言，那一夜他們尚未同寢；但到了翌夜，他們便依禮而莊重地結合了。後世的傳述者補充說，這首歌的疊句由歌女們傳唱下來，如使者一般奔往未來的世代。

passages.text: Again this deity's chief empress, the Forward-Princess, was very jealous; the Deity-of-Eight-Thousand-Spears, distressed, was about to go up from Izumo to the land of Yamato. Standing attired at his horse's saddle, he sang his farewell: how he had changed his garments three times — black as the moor's true jewels, green as the kingfisher, madder-dyed from the mountain fields — and how, though his wife might not weep, when he departed like the flocking birds her head would hang like a single eulalia and her weeping would rise as the morning mist. Then his empress took a great liquor-cup, drew near, offered it, and sang: Oh, Deity-of-Eight-Thousand-Spears, my Master-of-the-Great-Land — being a man, you probably have wives like the young herbs everywhere; but I, being a woman, have no man but you; beneath the ornamented fence and the soft coverlet, your white arms patting my soft breast, let us interlace our jewel-arms and sleep. Lift up the luxuriant august liquor. Having thus sung, they pledged each other by the cup with their hands on each other's necks, and are at rest till the present time. These are called divine words.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 165-167 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此外，此神的正妻前比賣極為嫉妒；八千矛神為此苦惱，將要從出雲上往大和國。他立於馬鞍旁，整裝唱出離別之歌：訴說自己如何三度更換衣裳——黑如原野上真正的寶石，綠如翠鳥，以山田的茜草所染——又訴說縱然妻子不哭，當他如群鳥般離去時，她的頭也會如單株芒草般低垂，她的哭泣會如朝霧般升起。於是他的皇后取來一只大酒盃，走近前來，獻上酒，唱道：哦，八千矛神，我的大國之主——身為男子，你大概處處都有如嫩草般的妻室；但我身為女子，除你之外別無男子；在飾紋籬笆之下、柔軟衾被之中，你潔白的雙臂輕撫我柔軟的胸膛，讓我們交纏玉臂而眠吧。舉起這豐盛尊貴的美酒。唱罷，他們便以盃互誓，手搭在彼此頸上，至今安歇。這些被稱為神語。

title.en: The Tiny God Sukunabikona and the Making of the Land
title.zh: 少名毘古那神與共造國土

region.en: The august cape of Miho, Izumo (symbolic pin; Mount Mimoro named in Yamato)
region.zh: 出雲美保岬（象徵性定位；三輪山在大和）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: A tiny deity in flayed-goose skins rides the wave-crest to Miho cape in Izumo and answers no question until the toad sends Okuninushi to the Crumbling-Prince — the scarecrow who knows everything under heaven — who identifies him as Little-Prince-the-Renowned-Deity, child of the Divine-Producing-Wondrous-Deity; the two then consolidate the land together until the tiny god crosses to the Eternal Land, and Okuninushi, alone, is told by a deity of the sea to be worshipped on Mount Mimoro.
summary.zh: 有神著剝鵝皮之衣，乘鏡船踏波至出雲美保岬，問名不答；蛙神曰腐朽神（田間稻草人）必知之，遂請其指認：此神產巢日神之子少名毘古那神，自其指間漏出者。二神遂共造國土；後少名毘古那神渡常世國去。己貴神獨嘆：與何神共造此國？有神光照海而至，曰：若善祭我，則與汝共造之——當祭於大和青垣東山之上，即三輪山之神。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); the Mimoro passage is the charter of the Omiwa (Miwa) shrine cult. Passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: When the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land dwelt at the august cape of Miho in Izumo, there came riding on the crest of the waves a deity dressed in complete flayings of goose skins, in a boat of heavenly kagami. Asked his name, he replied not; the deities who accompanied him, though asked, all said they did not know him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 171-172 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大國主神居於出雲之美保岬時，有一位神祇身穿完整的鵝皮剝製之衣，乘著天之羅摩船，騎在波浪之巔而來。問其名，他不作答；隨從的眾神雖被詢問，也都說不認識他。

passages.text: Then a toad spoke: As for this, the Crumbling Prince will surely know it. The Master-of-the-Great-Land summoned the Crumbling-Prince — the figure who, though his legs do not walk, knows everything in the empire, and is now the scarecrow in the mountain fields — and he identified the stranger: This is Little-Prince-the-Renowned-Deity, the august child of the Deity-Producing-Wondrous-Deity, the child who dipped between the fork of that deity's hand. On respectfully informing the Divine-Producing-Wondrous-August-Ancestor, he replied: This is truly my child. Do he and you become brethren, and make and consolidate this land together.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 172-173 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是蟾蜍說道：此事，崩彥必定知曉。大國主神召來崩彥——此者雙腿雖不能行，卻通曉天下萬事，如今即山田中的稻草人——他辨明了這位陌生者：此乃少名毘古那神，是高皇產靈神之尊子，是曾潛入該神指縫之間的孩子。恭敬地稟告產靈日神祖之後，祂答道：這確實是我的孩子。你與他結為兄弟，一同造築並鞏固此國吧。

passages.text: From that time forward the two deities made and consolidated the land conjointly; but afterwards Little-Prince-the-Renowned-Deity crossed over to the Eternal Land, the world beyond the sea. Then the Master-of-the-Great-Land lamented: How shall I alone be able to make this land? With what deity can I make it? At that time a deity came, illuminating the sea, and said: If you will lay me to rest well, I can make it together with you; if not, the land cannot be made. Asked the manner of reverently laying him to rest, he replied: Reverently worship me on Yamato's green fence, on the top of the eastern mountain. This is the deity who dwells on the top of Mount Mimoro.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 173-174 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 自此以後，二神共同造築並鞏固此國；但後來少名毘古那神渡往常世國，即海彼之世界。於是大地主神哀嘆道：我一人如何能造此國？我能與哪位神一同造它？其時有一位神降臨，照亮了海面，說道：你若能好好地將我安奉，我便可與你一同造它；若不然，此國便無法造成。問其恭敬安奉之法，祂答道：請在大和之青垣、東山之頂，恭敬地祭祀我。此即居於三諸山頂之神。

title.en: The Failed Missions and the Death of Ame-waka-hiko
title.zh: 天若日子受命不返中鏑矢而亡

region.en: The Central Land of Reed-Plains and the Tranquil River of Heaven (symbolic pin at the Yamato/Nara court)
region.zh: 葦原中國與天上安河（大和宮廷象徵性定位）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Amaterasu deputizes the Central Land of Reed-Plains to her child, but her first envoys defect or tarry — Ame-no-hohi for three years, and the Heavenly-Young-Prince Ame-waka-hiko, who weds Okuninushi's daughter, for eight years. A pheasant messenger is shot dead by Ame-waka-hiko, and the returned arrow, tested by the High-Integrating-Deity, strikes him dead in his sleep; the funeral house built by his mourners is cut down in fury by the deity Ajishiki-takahikone, whom they had mistaken for the corpse.
summary.zh: 天照大御神命其子治葦原中國，先遣天穗日神，三年不報；再遣天若日子，娶大己貴神之女下光比賣，八年不返。天神遣鳴女雉問責，天若日子受其妻之慫恿射殺之，其箭逆貫而上至高天原。神產巢日神試其心，回擲此箭，貫其胸而死。哭喪造喪屋，味耜高彥根神來弔，眾誤認其為死者，其怒拔十握劍斬喪屋——是故俗諺云唯雉為使者。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity commanded that the Luxuriant-Reed-Plains, the Land of Fresh Rice-ears of a Thousand Autumns, should be governed by her august child, and sent him down from Heaven. Standing on the Floating Bridge of Heaven, he looked and announced that the land was painfully uproarious, and immediately re-ascended to inform her. So the High-August-Producing-Wondrous-Deity and the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity assembled the eight hundred myriad deities in the bed of the Tranquil River of Heaven, had the Deity Thought-Includer think of a plan, and sent the Deity Ame-no-hohi to subdue the violent and savage Earthly Deities. But he at once curried favour with the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land, and for three years brought back no report.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 179-180 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天照大御神命其御子治理豐葦原之千秋長五百秋水穗之國，並遣其自天而降。御子立於天之浮橋上，望見此國，奏言此國甚為喧擾，遂立即復升天，以奏於天照大御神。於是高御產巢日神與天照大御神乃於天之安河之河原，召集八百萬神，命思兼神思慮方策，遣天菩卑能命以平定暴惡之國津神。然天菩卑能命旋即諂事大國主神，三年之間不復奏報。

passages.text: A fresh mission was debated, and the Deity Thought-Includer replied: The Heavenly-Young-Prince, son of the Deity Heaven's-Earth-Spirit, should be sent. They bestowed on him the heavenly true deer-bow and the heavenly feathered arrows and sent him down. Descending to that land, the Heavenly-Young-Prince at once wedded Princess Under-Shining, daughter of the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land, and moreover planned how he might gain possession of the land — and for eight years brought back no report.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, p. 180 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 乃更議新使，思兼神奏曰：當遣天若日子，此乃天國玉神之子也。遂賜以天之真鹿兒弓及天之羽羽矢，遣之下凡。天若日子降至其國，旋即娶大國主神之女下照姬，更圖謀如何得此國，八年之間不復奏報。

passages.text: The Heavenly Deities then sent the pheasant called Name-Crying-Female to ask why he brought back no report. She descended, perched on the multitudinously-branching cassia-tree at his gate, and delivered the mandate; but the Heavenly-Spying-Woman who heard her said: The sound of this bird's cry is very bad; you should shoot it to death. Urged on, the Heavenly-Young-Prince took the heavenly bow and arrows and shot the pheasant dead; and the arrow, shot up upside down through the bird's breast, reached the place where the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity and the High-Integrating-Deity were sitting in the bed of the Tranquil River of Heaven. The High-Integrating-Deity saw blood on the feathers, recognized the arrow bestowed on the Heavenly-Young-Prince, and showed it to all the deities, saying: If this be an arrow shot at the evil deities in obedience to our command, let it not hit him; if he has a foul heart, let the Heavenly-Young-Prince perish by this arrow. He took the arrow and thrust it back down through the arrow's hole, so that it struck the sleeping prince in the breast and he died; and the pheasant returned not. This is the origin of the proverb about the pheasant as sole messenger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 181-183 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是天神遣雉名鳴女，問其何以不復奏報。鳴女下降，止於其門之多枝桂樹上，傳達天命；然聞其聲之天探女曰：此鳥鳴聲甚惡，宜射殺之。天若日子受其慫恿，取天之弓矢射殺雉；其箭自雉胸倒射而上，至於天照大御神與高木神坐於天之安河河原之處。高木神見箭羽染血，識為賜予天若日子之箭，乃示諸神曰：若此箭乃奉吾等之命射惡神者，則不當中天若日子；若其心懷穢惡，則天若日子當斃於此箭。遂取箭，自箭孔反刺而下，中臥寢之天若日子之胸，天若日子遂死；而雉亦不返。此即雉為唯一使者之諺所由起也。

passages.text: The wailing of the prince's wife, re-echoing in the wind, reached Heaven, and his father, wife and children came down with cries, built a mourning-house, and made the wild goose the head-hanging bearer, the heron the broom-bearer, the kingfisher the person of the august food, the sparrow the pounding-woman, and the pheasant the weeping woman, disporting themselves for eight days and eight nights. Then the Deity Ajishiki-takahikone came to condole; the mourners cried that their child, their lord was not dead, and clung to his hands and feet, for the two deities closely resembled each other in countenance. Then Ajishiki-takahikone was very angry: It was only because he was my dear friend that I came to condole. Why should I be likened to an unclean dead person? He drew the ten-grasp sabre girded on him, cut down the mourning-house, and kicked away the pieces, at what is called Mount Mourning in the land of Minu; the sword was named Great-Blade-Mower. He flew away in his anger, and his younger sister sang to reveal his august name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 183-185 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天若日子之妻哭聲，隨風迴響，上達於天，其父、妻及子乃哭泣而降，築喪屋，以野雁為持首者，以白鷺為持帚者，以翠鳥為御食之人，以雀為舂女，以雉為哭女，嬉遊八日八夜。於是夷毗志枳高日子神前來弔問；喪家哭曰吾子吾君未死，攀其手足，蓋二神容貌酷似故也。夷毗志枳高日子神大怒曰：吾唯因彼為吾摯友，故來弔問。何乃以吾比於穢死之人？遂拔所佩十握之劍，斫倒喪屋，踢散其片，於美濃國所謂喪山之處；其劍名曰大量刈。夷毗志枳高日子神忿而飛去，其妹作歌以顯其御名。

title.en: Takemikazuchi Takes the Land: The Surrender of Okuninushi
title.zh: 建御雷神平定葦原中國

region.en: The little shore of Inasa, Izumo (symbolic pin at Izumo; Lake Suwa named in Shinano)
region.zh: 出雲稻佐濱（象徵性定位；信濃諏訪湖在傳說中）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: After the failed missions, the Heavenly Deities send the Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male-Deity Takemikazuchi with the Deity Heavenly-Bird-Boat; the two descend to the little shore of Inasa, plant their ten-hand-breadth swords upside down on a wave-crest and sit cross-legged on the points to demand the land. Okuninushi's son Kotoshironushi consents and vanishes into the sea; the other son Takeminakata challenges the envoy to a trial of strength and is defeated and chased to the Sea of Suwa; and Okuninushi himself yields, exchanging the Central Land for a great palace at Tagishi in Izumo.
summary.zh: 天之逆手不果，高皇產靈神與天照大神再集八百萬神，思兼神薦天之石屋之經津主神之子建御雷神。建御雷神與經津主神降至出雲稻佐濱，拔十握劍倒立於浪頭，盤坐劍尖問大己貴神之志。其子事代主神允諾，踏船緣化青柴垣而隱；次子建御名方神負千引石而來欲較力，建御雷神之手化冰劍，反握其手如取葦，逐至諏訪湖，名方神誓不離此土。大己貴神遂依二子之言獻國，惟求以出雲多藝志之濱建天御巢宮，隱於八十路曲而侍之。事代主神為百八十神之後先而奉仕；天八士神化鸕鶿取海底赤土，鑽火設膳。建御雷神歸天復命。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki): the kuni-yuzuri (transfer of the land) legitimates imperial rule over Izumo; present comparatively and critically. Passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations.

passages.text: After the Heavenly-Young-Prince's death, the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity asked again which deity should be sent. The Deity Thought-Includer and all the deities named the Deity Majestic-Point-Blade-Extended, who dwells in the Heavenly Rock-Dwelling by the source of the Tranquil River of Heaven — or, if not he, his child the Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male-Deity. Since the father had blocked and turned back the waters of the Tranquil River and dwelt with the road blocked up, so that other deities could not go there, the Heavenly-Deer-Deity was sent specially to ask him. He replied: I will obey, and will respectfully serve you. Nevertheless, on this errand send my child, the Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male-Deity — and at once offered his son to the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity. So the Deity Heavenly-Bird-Boat was attached to the Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male-Deity, and the two were sent off.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 185-186 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天若日子死後，天照大御神復問當遣何神。思兼神及諸神乃舉居於天之安河水源天之石屋之建御雷之男神，或若非此神，則其子經津主神。因父神堵截天之安河之水而居，塞其道路，使他神不得往，故特遣天鹿兒神往問之。建御雷之男神答曰：吾當遵命，恭順奉事。然此行請遣吾子經津主神——遂即獻其子於天照大御神。於是天鳥船神附於經津主神，二神遂被遣發。

passages.text: The two deities descended to the little shore of Inasa in the land of Izumo, drew their swords ten hand-breadths long, stuck them upside down on the crest of a wave, seated themselves cross-legged on the points of the swords, and asked the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land: The Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity and the High-Integrating-Deity have charged us and sent us to ask: We have deigned to charge our august child with your dominion, the Central Land of Reed-Plains, as the land which he should govern. So how is your heart? He replied: I am unable to say. My child the Deity Eight-Fold-Thing-Sign-Master will be the one to tell you; but he is gone to Cape Miho to pursue birds and catch fish and has not yet returned. So the Deity Bird-Boat was sent to summon him; and being graciously asked, the Deity Eight-Fold-Thing-Sign-Master spoke to his father: I will obey. Respectfully present this land to the august child of the Heavenly Deity — and thereupon he trod on the edge of his boat so as to capsize it, clapped his heavenly departing hands against the fence of green branches, and disappeared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 186-188 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 二神降至出雲國伊那佐之小濱，拔十拳之劍，倒植於波濤之上，踞坐劍尖，問大國主神曰：天照大御神與高木神命吾等來問：吾等欲以汝所治之葦原中國，授吾御子為其所治之國。汝心如何？大國主神答曰：吾不能言。吾子八重事代主神當能告汝；然彼往三穗崎捕鳥獵魚，尚未歸。於是遣鳥船神召之；八重事代主神承蒙垂問，乃告其父曰：吾當遵命。謹以此國奉獻於天神之御子——遂踏其舟舷使舟覆，以天離手拍青枝之籬，隱沒而去。

passages.text: The envoys asked whether there was another son who should speak; and while the father spoke of his son the Deity Brave-August-Name-Firm, that deity came up bearing on the tips of his fingers a thousand-draught rock, saying: Who is this that has come to our land and thus secretly talks? I should like a trial of strength; let me begin by taking your hand. When the Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male-Deity let him take it, the grip turned it at once into an icicle, and then into a sword-blade, and the challenger drew back frightened.
