Then the envoy grasped the hand of Brave-August-Name-Firm, crushed it like a young reed, and cast it aside; the challenger fled, and the envoy pursued and came up with him at the Sea of Suha in the land of Shinanu and was about to slay him, when Brave-August-Name-Firm said: I will obey. Slay me not. I will go to no other place but this, neither will I go against the command of my father or the words of my brother. I will yield up this Central Land of Reed-Plains according to the command of the august child of the Heavenly Deities.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 188-189 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 使者問是否另有應由他發言的兒子；當父親談及其子「建御雷神」時，那位神祇捧著千引之磐石，以指尖托起，說道：「是何人來到我等的國土，如此私下交談？我願一試力氣；讓我先握你的手。」當「建御雷神」讓他握住時，那一握立刻將他的手變成冰柱，繼而變成劍刃，挑戰者驚懼退縮。於是使者握住「建御雷神」的手，如揉嫩葦般將其捏碎，並拋擲一旁；挑戰者逃遁，使者追趕，在信濃國須波海追上他，正要將他殺死，此時「建御雷神」說道：「我願服從。請勿殺我。我除此地之外不往他處，亦不違抗我父之命或我兄之言。我將依天神御子之命，讓出這葦原中國。」

passages.text: So they asked the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land how his heart was now that both his children had consented. He replied: As my two children have said, I too will not go against them; in accordance with the heavenly command I will at once yield up this Central Land of Reed-Plains. But if you will make stout the temple-pillars on the nethermost rock-bottom and make high the cross-beams to the Plain of High Heaven, and will establish me there, I will hide in the eighty road-windings and wait on him; and if the Deity Eight-Fold-Thing-Sign-Master will be the rear and van of my hundred and eighty children, there will be no disobedient deities. Having thus spoken he hid himself; and they built a heavenly august abode on the shore of Tagishi in the land of Izumo. There the Deity Wondrous-Eight-Spirits was made butler of the heavenly banquet: turning into a cormorant he dived to the sea-bottom for red earth, made eighty platters, cut sea-weed stalks for a fire-drill, drilled out fire, and offered the heavenly true fish-food. Then the Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male-Deity re-ascended to Heaven and reported that he had subdued and pacified the Central Land of Reed-Plains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 189-191 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他們問「大國主神」，如今兩個兒子都已同意，他心中作何打算。他答道：「正如我兩個兒子所言，我也不會違背他們；我將依天神的命令，立刻讓出這葦原中國。但若你們能將神殿的柱子堅固地立於最底層的磐石之上，並將橫樑高架至高天原，且在那裡安置我，我將隱居於八十道曲折之中侍奉他；若「八重事代主神」能為我一百八十個孩子的後衛與前鋒，便不會有不服從的神祇。」說罷，他便隱匿起來；他們在出雲國多岐志的海濱建造了一座天神的宮殿。在那裡，「奇八靈神」被任命為天神饗宴的司膳：他變作鸕鶿潛入海底取紅土，製作八十個盤子，切海藻莖作鑽火棒，鑽出火來，獻上天神真正的魚食。於是「建御雷神」重返高天原，稟報他已平定並綏靖了葦原中國。

title.en: The Drowning of Sarutahiko and the Slit Mouth of the Sea-Cucumber
title.zh: 猿田毗古神溺海與海參裂口

region.en: Azaka on the shore of Ise Bay (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 伊勢灣阿邪珂（象徵性定位）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: The Deity Prince of Saruta, fishing at Azaka, has his hand caught by a hirabu shell-fish and drowns in the brine, receiving three posthumous names as he sinks, gurgles and bubbles; the Heavenly-Alarming-Female Uzume, returned from escorting him, musters all finned things and asks whether they will serve the august son of the Heavenly Deities — all consent except the bêche-de-mer, whose silent mouth she slits with her stiletto, whence its slit mouth today and the first-fruits of Shima granted to the Duchesses of Saru.
summary.zh: 猿田毗古神於阿邪珂垂釣，手被海芹貝夾住，溺於鹹水。沉底時稱底觸之神，潮鳴時稱潮湧之神，泡沫起時稱泡開之神——故有三重御名。天鈿女命送之而歸，驅集諸海族問曰：汝等願奉仕天神之子乎？眾魚皆諾，唯海鼠不言。鈿女命曰：此乃無言之口也！遂以小針裂其口，故海鼠之口至今有裂。故歷代進獻志摩初穗之時，必以一分賜猿女之君。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); etiological episode for the sea-cucumber's mouth and the Sarume ritual guild. Passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations.

passages.text: Now when the Deity Prince of Saruta dwelt at Azaka, he went out fishing, and had his hand caught by a hirabu shell-fish, and was drowned in the brine of the sea. The name by which he was called when he sank to the bottom was the Bottom-Touching-August-Spirit; the name by which he was called when the sea-water gurgled up was the Gurgling-Up-August-Spirit; and the name by which he was called when the bubbles formed was the Bubble-Bursting-August-Spirit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, p. 200 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當時，「猿田彥神」住在阿坂，外出捕魚，手被比良夫貝夾住，溺斃於海水之中。他沉入海底時所稱之名為「底觸天津神」；海水咕嘟湧上時所稱之名為「咕嘟湧上天津神」；氣泡形成時所稱之名為「泡破天津神」。

passages.text: The Heavenly-Alarming-Female, having escorted the Deity Prince of Saruta back, returned, and at once drove together all the things broad of fin and the things narrow of fin, and asked them: Will you respectfully serve the august son of the Heavenly Deities? All the fishes declared that they would respectfully serve him; only the bêche-de-mer said nothing. Then the Heavenly-Alarming-Female spoke to it: Ah, this mouth is a mouth that gives no reply! — and with these words slit its mouth with her stiletto. So at the present day the bêche-de-mer has a slit mouth; and wherefore, from august reign to august reign, when the offerings of the first-fruits of Shima are presented, a portion of them is granted to the Duchesses of Saru.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 200-201 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「天鈿女命」護送「猿田彥神」回去後，隨即將所有寬鰭之物與窄鰭之物驅集一處，問牠們道：「你們可願恭敬侍奉天神御子？」所有魚類都聲明願恭敬侍奉他；唯有海參默不作聲。於是「天鈿女命」對牠說道：「啊，這張嘴是不作回答的嘴！」說罷，便以小刀割裂了牠的嘴。因此至今海參仍是裂嘴；故而，從一代御治世到一代御治世，當獻上志摩的初穗供品時，其中一部分便賜予猿女君。

title.en: Ninigi Rejects Iwanaga and Weds Konohanasakuya: The Origin of Mortal Lives
title.zh: 瓊瓊杵尊棄磐長娶木花咲耶姬：人壽不長之由

region.en: The august cape of Kasasa, Satsuma (symbolic pin for the mythic meeting)
region.zh: 薩摩笠狹岬（象徵性定位）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: At the cape of Kasasa, Ninigi meets Konohanasakuya, daughter of the Great-Mountain-Possessor, and asks for her; her father sends both daughters, but Ninigi, alarmed at the hideous elder Iwanaga (Long-as-the-Rocks), sends her back and keeps only the blossoming younger sister for one night. The shamed father explains that the rock-daughter would have given the heavenly offspring lives eternal as the rocks and the flower-daughter lives flourishing as tree-blossoms; because the rock-sister was rejected, the lives of the Heavenly Sovereigns are short as flowers to this day.
summary.zh: 瓊瓊杵尊於笠狹岬遇木花咲耶姬，遣使求婚。大山津見神大喜，以百機盤盛禮，並送長女磐長姬與次女咲耶姬。磐長姬貌醜，尊懼而遣還之，獨留咲耶姬，一宵成婚。大山津見神恥之，遣使曰：吾所以並獻二女者，欲使磐長姬致天神御子壽如磐石，咲耶姬致其榮如花開；今遣還磐長姬，故天神御子之御壽必如木花之脆弱矣。故至今天皇御壽不長。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); this is the mythic origin of imperial mortality and of the Konohan (Sakuya) shrine tradition. Passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations.

passages.text: Hereupon His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty met a beautiful person at the august cape of Kasasa, and asked her whose daughter she was. She replied: I am a daughter of the Deity Great-Mountain-Possessor, and my name is the Divine-Princess-of-Ata, another name by which I am called being Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees. Asked whether she had brethren, she said: There is my elder sister, Princess-Long-as-the-Rocks. So he asked for her hand, sending the request to her father, the Deity Great-Mountain-Possessor, who was greatly delighted, respectfully sent her off, joined to her her elder sister, and caused merchandise to be carried on tables holding a hundred.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 201-202 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是，「天津日高日子穗穗手見命」在笠狹御崎遇見一位美麗的女子，問她是誰的女兒。她答道：「我是大山津見神的女兒，名為阿多都姬，另一名為木花之開耶姬。」問她是否有兄弟姊妹，她說：「有我的姊姊，名為石長姬。」於是他向她求婚，將請求送達她的父親大山津見神，大山津見神大為欣喜，恭敬地將她送來，並將她的姊姊一同附上，又命人以百張几案載運財貨。

passages.text: But owing to the elder sister being very hideous, His Augustness was alarmed at the sight of her, and sent her back, keeping only the younger sister, whom he wedded for one night. The Deity Great-Mountain-Possessor was covered with shame, and sent a message: My reason for presenting both my daughters together was that, by sending Princess-Long-as-the-Rocks, the august offspring of the Heavenly Deity, though the snow fall and the wind blow, might live eternally immovable like the enduring rocks; and again that by sending Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees they might live flourishingly like the flowering of the blossoms of the trees: to insure this I offered them. But owing to your sending back Princess-Long-as-the-Rocks and keeping only her younger sister, the august offspring of the Heavenly Deity shall be but as frail as the flowers of the trees. So it is for this reason that down to the present day the august lives of the Heavenly Sovereigns are not long.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 202-203 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但因姊姊容貌極其醜陋，御子一見她便驚懼，將她送回，只留下妹妹，與她共度一宵。大山津見神深感羞恥，遣使傳話道：「我之所以將兩個女兒一同獻上，是因為獻上石長姬，可使天神御子縱然雪降風吹，也能如磐石般永恆不動地長存；又獻上木花之開耶姬，可使他們如樹木開花般繁榮昌盛：為確保此事，我才將她們獻上。但因你送回石長姬，只留下她的妹妹，天神御子的壽命將如樹木之花般脆弱。因此之故，直至今日，天皇們的御壽皆不長久。」

title.en: The Ordeal by Fire: Konohanasakuya Gives Birth in the Burning Hall
title.zh: 木花咲耶姬火中產子之誓

region.en: Himuka in Tsukushi (Kyushu)
region.zh: 筑紫日向

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Pregnant after a single night, Konohanasakuya announces her delivery; Ninigi doubts her, saying the child must be an Earthly Deity's. She vows that if the child be of an Earthly Deity her delivery will be unfortunate, builds a hall eight fathoms long without doors, plasters up the entrance, and, when her time comes, sets fire to the hall and is delivered in the flames — of Fire-Shine, Fire-Climax, and Fire-Subside, the ancestors of the imperial line.
summary.zh: 木花咲耶姬一宵而有身，臨產奏曰：妾今有孕，產期將至，天神御子不可私產，故以奉告。瓊瓊杵尊疑曰：一宵而孕，必非吾子，當是國神之子。姬誓曰：若所懷為國神之子，產必不吉；若為天神之子，則吉。遂造無戶八尋殿，入而以土堇其戶，臨產時縱火焚殿，於火中生三子：火照命、火須勢理命、火遠理命。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); the fire-birth validates the divine descent of the imperial line. Passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations.

passages.text: Later on Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees waited on His Augustness Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty and said: I am pregnant, and now the time for my delivery approaches. It is not fit for me to be delivered of the august offspring of Heaven privately, so I tell you. Then His Augustness said: Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly! What — pregnant after one night? It cannot be my child. It must surely be the child of an Earthly Deity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, p. 203 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 後來，木花開耶姬命侍奉火遠理命，說道：「我已懷孕，如今臨產之期將近。我不宜私下產下天神之御子，故稟告於您。」於是火遠理命說道：「木花開耶姬啊！什麼——一夜之後便懷孕了？這不可能是我的孩子。必定是地神的孩子的。」

passages.text: She replied: If the child with which I am pregnant be the child of an Earthly Deity, my delivery will not be fortunate; if it be the august child of the Heavenly Deity, it will be fortunate. Thereupon she built a hall eight fathoms long without doors, went inside and plastered up the entrance with earth; and when the time came for her delivery, she set fire to the hall and was delivered. The child born when the fire was burning most fiercely was His Augustness Fire-Shine; the child born next was His Augustness Fire-Climax; and the child born next was His Augustness Fire-Subside — whose other name is His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Great-Rice-ears-Lord-Ears.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 204-205 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她回答說：「我腹中所懷之子，若是地神之子，則我的生產將不順遂；若是天神之御子，則將順遂。」於是，她築起一座長八尋、無門的殿宇，進入其中，以土封塞入口；到了臨產之時，她放火燒殿，就在火中生產。火燒得最猛之際所生之子，是火照命；其次所生之子，是火須勢理命；再次所生之子，是火遠理命——其別名為天津日高日子穗穗手見命。

title.en: The Luck Exchange and the Lost Fish-Hook of Hoori
title.zh: 火照命與火遠理命換福失鉤

region.en: Himuka in Tsukushi (Kyushu); the brothers' fortunes of sea and mountain
region.zh: 筑紫日向；海幸山幸之福

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Fire-Shine (Hoderi) holds the luck of the sea and Fire-Subside (Hoori) the luck of the mountains; at Hoori's thrice-repeated request the brothers exchange fortunes, but Hoori, angling with the borrowed sea-luck, catches nothing and loses the fish-hook in the sea. His brother demands the original hook back; Hoori breaks his own ten-grasp sabre to forge five hundred and then a thousand compensating hooks, all refused, and he weeps and laments on the sea-shore.
summary.zh: 火照命得海之福，火遠理命得山之福。火遠理命三請相換其福，久乃得允。然其以兄之福釣魚，一魚不得，且失其鉤於海。兄索還原鉤，弟自斷其十握劍，作五百鉤以償，兄不受；復作千鉤以償，仍不受，曰：吾猶欲原鉤。弟遂泣於海濱。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki), the Umisachi-Yamasachi (sea-luck, mountain-luck) folktale core. Passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations.

passages.text: His Augustness Fire-Shine was a prince who got his luck on the sea, and caught things broad of fin and things narrow of fin. His Augustness Fire-Subside was a prince who got his luck on the mountains, and caught things rough of hair and things soft of hair. Then Fire-Subside said to his elder brother: Let us mutually exchange, and use each other's luck. Though he thrice made the request, his elder brother would not accede to it; but at last with difficulty the mutual exchange was obtained.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, p. 205 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 火照命是一位得海幸的王子，捕獲廣鰭之物與狹鰭之物。火遠理命是一位得山幸的王子，捕獲粗毛之物與柔毛之物。於是火遠理命對其兄說道：「讓我們彼此交換，互用對方的幸運吧。」他雖三次請求，其兄皆不肯應允；但最後終於勉強達成了互換。

passages.text: Fire-Subside, undertaking the sea-luck, angled for fish but never got a single one, and moreover lost the fish-hook in the sea. Thereupon his elder brother asked for the fish-hook, saying: A mountain-luck is a luck of its own, and a sea-luck is a luck of its own; let each of us now restore to the other his luck. The younger brother replied: As for your fish-hook, I did not get a single fish by angling with it, and at last I lost it in the sea. But the elder brother required it of him the more urgently. So the younger brother broke the ten-grasp sabre girded on him and made five hundred fish-hooks of the fragments as compensation; but his brother would not take them. Again he made a thousand fish-hooks as compensation; but he would not receive them, saying: I still want the real original fish-hook. So the younger brother wept and lamented by the sea-shore.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 205-206 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 火遠理命承擔海幸，垂釣卻一尾未得，而且還將魚鉤失落在海中。於是其兄索討魚鉤，說道：「山幸是山幸，海幸是海幸；如今讓我們各自將幸運歸還對方吧。」弟弟回答說：「至於您的魚鉤，我持之垂釣卻一尾未得，最後還失落在海中。」然而其兄更加急切地索討。於是弟弟折斷佩於身上的十握劍，以碎片造了五百個魚鉤作為賠償；但其兄不肯接受。他又造了一千個魚鉤作為賠償；其兄仍不肯接受，說道：「我還是要那真正的原鉤。」於是弟弟在海濱哭泣哀嘆。

title.en: Hoori in the Sea Palace: Marriage to Toyotama-hime and the Tide Jewels
title.zh: 火遠理命入海宮娶豐玉姬得潮滿潮涸之珠

region.en: The palace of the Deity-Ocean-Possessor beneath the sea (symbolic pin; undersea otherworld)
region.zh: 海神綿津見之宮（海底異界，象徵性定位）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: The Deity Salt-Possessor builds Hoori a stout little boat and directs him to the palace of the Sea-Deity, built like fishes' scales, where he sits on the cassia tree above the well, wins the hand of Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess (Toyotama-hime) and dwells three years. Sighing for home, he is given back the fish-hook — found in the throat of the tahi — with cursing words to speak over it, and the tide-flowing and tide-ebbing jewels with which to drown or spare his brother and impoverish him within three years; the Sea-Deity then summons the crocodiles to escort him back to the Upper-Land.
summary.zh: 鹽椎神為火遠理命造無隙小舟，教其循芳香之道至鱗如魚鱗之宮——海神綿津見之宮。其攀井上香木而坐，海神女豐玉姬之侍女汲水見光，奉水於尊，尊不飲而脫頸珠吐入器中，珠黏器不去。豐玉姬出視而喜，海神見之曰：此天照大神之子也。遂鋪八重海驢皮褥、八重絹褥，設百機盤之膳，以女妻之。尊居其國三年。一日深嘆，妻以告父。海神乃集大魚小魚，於鯛喉中取還魚鉤，授以咒鉤之語，並以潮滿珠、潮涸珠賜之：兄作高田汝作低田，兄作低田汝作高田，三年之內兄必貧；兄若怒而攻汝，出潮滿珠以溺之，兄若請命，出潮涸珠以活之。遂召鱷魚護送尊歸上國。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki), the sea-palace (Ryugu) episode of the Umisachi-Yamasachi cycle; the saga continues with the return and the birth in the burning hall beyond this batch's source range. Passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations.

passages.text: As the younger brother was weeping and lamenting by the sea-shore, the Deity Salt-Possessor came and asked him the cause of the Sky's-Sun-Height's weeping and lamentation. He told how he had exchanged a fish-hook with his elder brother, lost it in the sea, and offered many compensating hooks in vain, his brother insisting that he still wanted the original. Then the Deity Salt-Possessor said: I will give good counsel to Thine Augustness — and built a stout little boat without interstices, set him in it, and instructed him: When I push the boat off, go on for some time. There will be a savoury august road; go along that road and there will appear a palace built like fishes' scales, which is the palace of the Deity-Ocean-Possessor. When you reach the august gate of that deity's palace, there will be a multitudinously-branching cassia-tree above the well at its side; sit on the top of that tree, and the Sea-Deity's daughter will see you and counsel you.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 207-208 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當弟弟在海濱哭泣哀嘆時，鹽椎神前來，詢問天津日高日子穗穗手見命哭泣哀嘆的緣由。他訴說自己如何與兄長交換魚鉤、失落於海中，並獻上許多賠償之鉤而徒勞無功，兄長堅持仍要原鉤。於是鹽椎神說道：「我將為尊神獻上良策。」便造了一艘無縫隙的堅固小船，讓他坐入其中，並指示道：「當我推船離岸後，你便前行一段時日。將會有一條芬芳的御路；沿著那條路前行，便會出現一座如魚鱗般建造的宮殿，那便是海神綿津見神的宮殿。當你到達那位神宮殿的御門時，其旁井上會有一株枝葉繁茂的桂樹；坐在那樹頂上，海神的女兒看見你，便會給你指點。」

passages.text: Everything happened as the Salt-Possessor had said. When the handmaidens of the Sea-Deity's daughter Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess came to draw water with jewelled vessels, there was a light in the well; looking up, they saw a beautiful young man on the cassia-tree, more illustrious even than their king. He begged water of them, and, without drinking it, loosened the jewel at his neck, took it in his mouth, and spat it into the jewelled vessel; the jewel adhered to the vessel, and the handmaidens could not separate them, so they brought the vessel to their mistress. She went out to look, and was delighted at the sight. Having exchanged glances with the stranger, she told her father that a beautiful person was at their gate; and the Sea-Deity himself went out, saying: This person is the Sky's-Sun-Height, the august child of the Heaven's-Sun-Height. He led him into the interior of the palace, spread eight layers of rugs of sea-asses' skins and on the top eight more of silk rugs, set him on them, arranged merchandise on tables holding a hundred, made an august banquet, and forthwith gave him his daughter Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess in marriage; and he dwelt in that land for three years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 208-209 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一切皆如鹽椎神所言發生。當海神之女豐玉姬的侍女們持玉器前來汲水時，井中有光；她們抬頭一看，見桂樹上有一位美麗的青年，甚至比她們的君王更為出眾。他向她們乞水，卻不飲用，而是解下頸上的玉，含入口中，吐入玉器；那玉附著於器上，侍女們無法將之分開，便將玉器帶回給她們的女主人。她出來一看，見此情景大喜。她與那陌生人交換了眼波，便告訴父親說門前有一位美麗之人；海神親自出來，說道：「此人是天津日高日子穗穗手見命，是天照大神的御子。」他領他進入宮殿內部，鋪上八層海驢皮的褥子，其上再鋪八層絲綢的褥子，讓他坐於其上，在陳列百物的桌上擺設貨物，舉行御宴，隨即將女兒豐玉姬許配給他；他就在那國度住了三年。

passages.text: Then His Augustness thought of what had gone before, and heaved one deep sigh. His wife heard it and told her father, who asked his son-in-law the cause; and the prince told how his elder brother had pressed him for the lost fish-hook. The Sea-Deity summoned all the fishes of the sea and asked whether any had taken the hook; all replied that lately the tahi had complained of something sticking in its throat preventing it from eating. The hook was found in its throat, taken out, washed, and presented to Fire-Subside. The Great-Ocean-Possessor then instructed him: When you grant this fish-hook to your elder brother, say: This fish-hook is a big hook, an eager hook, a poor hook, a silly hook — and bestow it with your back hand. When your elder brother makes fields, make the opposite kind, and he will certainly be impoverished within three years, for I rule the water. If he attacks you, put forth the tide-flowing jewel to drown him; if he expresses grief, put forth the tide-ebbing jewel to let him live. He then gave him the two tide jewels and summoned the crocodiles to escort him back to the Upper-Land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 209-210 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是，尊想起先前發生的事，深深嘆了一口氣。他的妻子聽見了，便告訴她的父親；父親問女婿緣由，王子便訴說兄長如何逼他交出那枚失落的魚鉤。海神召來海中所有的魚，問有誰拿了那魚鉤；眾魚都說，近來鯛魚抱怨喉中卡了什麼東西，害牠無法進食。魚鉤在牠喉中尋獲，取出、洗淨，呈給火遠理命。大綿津見神於是囑咐他：當你把這魚鉤交還兄長時，要說：這魚鉤是大鉤、急鉤、貧鉤、愚鉤——並以反手遞給他。當你兄長闢田時，你就闢相反的田，他三年之內必定貧困，因為水由我掌管。若他來攻擊你，就取出漲潮珠淹他；若他顯出悲苦，就取出退潮珠讓他活命。他隨後把兩顆潮珠交給他，並召鱷魚護送他回葦原中國。

title.en: Oranyan's Iron, the Cock, and the Scrap of Soil
title.zh: 奧蘭揚的鐵器、雄雞與一撮泥土

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (symbolic pin: Oduduwa's homeland, whence Oranyan set out)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（象徵定位：奧杜杜瓦的祖地）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale I

summary.en: When old King Oduduwa died, his youngest grandson Oranyan was away hunting and inherited only twenty-one pieces of iron, a cock, and soil tied in a rag. Spreading these on a world covered with water, he watched the cock scratch the soil across the flood until islands and dry land appeared, and the iron became the minerals under the ground.
summary.zh: 老王奧杜杜瓦去世時，最幼的孫兒奧蘭揚遠行狩獵，只分得二十一塊鐵器、一隻雄雞和一束以布包裹的泥土。他將這些攤在覆水的大地上，雄雞以爪抓散泥土，島嶼與陸地逐一浮現，鐵器則化為地下的礦藏。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition. This is the folk version of the Oduduwa-Oranyan cosmogony; told as an archival record, not as an authoritative statement for Orisha worshippers. The earth-over-water creation is a flood/first-earth motif (Thompson A812).

passages.text: The ancient King Oduduwa had a great many grandchildren, and on his death he divided among them all his possessions. But his youngest grandson, Oranyan, was at that time away hunting, and when he returned home he learnt that his brothers and cousins had inherited the old King's money, cattle, beads, and native cloths, and had left him but twenty-one pieces of iron, a cock, and some soil tied up in a rag. At that time the whole earth was covered with water, on the surface of which the people lived.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale I (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古代的奧杜杜瓦國王有許許多多孫子，他死時把全部財產分給了他們。但他最小的孫子奧蘭揚當時外出打獵，回家後才得知兄弟與堂表兄弟們繼承了老王的金錢、牛隻、珠串與土布，只留給他二十一件鐵器、一隻公雞，以及用破布包起來的一些泥土。那時整個大地都被水覆蓋，人們就生活在水面上。

passages.text: The resourceful Oranyan spread upon the water his pieces of iron, and upon the iron he placed the scrap of cloth, and upon the cloth the soil, and on the soil the cock. The cock scratched with his feet and scattered the soil far and wide, so that the ocean was partly filled up and islands appeared everywhere. The pieces of iron became the mineral wealth hidden under the ground. Oranyan's brothers and cousins all desired to live on the land, and he allowed them to do so on payment of tribute; thus he became King of all the Yorubas, rich and prosperous through his grandfather's inheritance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale I (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 足智多謀的奧蘭揚把鐵器鋪在水面上，又把那塊布放在鐵器上，再把泥土放在布上，然後把公雞放在泥土上。公雞用腳扒抓，把泥土撒得又遠又廣，於是海洋有一部分被填平，到處都出現了島嶼。那些鐵器則成了藏在地下的礦藏。奧蘭揚的兄弟與堂表兄弟都想住在陸地上，他便允許他們居住，但要繳納貢賦；他因此成為全體約魯巴人的國王，因祖父的遺產而富有興旺。

title.en: How Tribal Marks Came to Be Used
title.zh: 臉紋身紋之由來

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (symbolic pin: Sango's royal court)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（象徵定位：尚戈王的宮廷）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale II

summary.en: King Sango punished a failed mission by ordering a slave cut with 122 razor marks; the healed scars so impressed the king's wives that Sango made cutting a mark of royalty instead of punishment. He could bear only two cuts, and those two cuts on the arm remain the sign of royalty.
summary.zh: 尚戈王以一百二十二道剃刀紋懲罰一位辦事不力的奴隸；傷痕癒合後竟令王妃傾慕，尚戈遂將刀紋由懲罰改為王室的標記。他自己只能忍受兩刀，自那日起臂上兩刀便成王族之記。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; etiological tale for facial/body scarification. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A certain King named Sango sent two slaves to a distant country on an important mission. In due course they returned, and he found that one slave had achieved successfully what he had been sent to do, while the other had accomplished nothing. The King therefore rewarded the first with high honours, and commanded the second to receive a hundred and twenty-two razor cuts all over his body.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale II (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一位名叫桑戈的國王，派兩名奴隸前往遠方執行一項重要任務。時候到了，他們回來，他發現其中一名奴隸成功完成了派他去辦的事，另一名卻一事無成。國王於是重重賞賜第一名，並下令在第二名全身割上一百二十二道刀痕。

passages.text: This was a severe punishment, but when the scars healed, they gave to the slave a very remarkable appearance, which greatly took the fancy of the King's wives. Sango therefore decided that cuts should in future be given, not as punishment, but as a sign of royalty, and he placed himself at once in the hands of the markers. However, he could only bear two cuts, and so from that day two cuts on the arm have been the sign of royalty, and various other cuts came to be the marks of different tribes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale II (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這是嚴厲的懲罰，但傷痕癒合後，卻使那名奴隸顯得格外奇特，大受國王妻妾們的喜愛。桑戈於是決定，今後割痕不再作為懲罰，而作為王族的標記，他立刻把自己交到割痕師手中。然而他只受得住兩道割痕，因此從那天起，手臂上的兩道割痕便成了王族的標記，而各種不同的割痕則成了不同部族的記號。

title.en: Akiti the Hunter and the Elephant
title.zh: 獵人阿基提與大象

region.en: Yoruba forest country (symbolic pin: forest edge near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴森林地帶（象徵定位：伊費城近郊林緣）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale III

summary.en: Akiti, who has beaten giant, leopard, lion, wolf and boa, calls himself King of the forest until the wise Elephant — protected by charms — challenges his claim. Spears, arrows and knives glance off; only when Akiti transforms himself into a fly, enters the Elephant's ear, and cuts its heart does he truly become the forest's king.
summary.zh: 獵人阿基提戰勝巨人、豹、獅、狼與蟒，自封「森林之王」，直到通曉符咒的大象前來挑戰。矛、箭、刀皆無法傷其身；阿基提只能化身蒼蠅，鑽入象耳直抵心臟，化回人形以獵刀剖其心，方才真正稱王。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; hero contest with charm-magic. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A famous hunter and wrestler named Akiti boasted that he was stronger than any other man or animal. He had easily overcome a giant, a leopard, a lion, a wolf, and a boa-constrictor, and as nobody else opposed his claim, he called himself the King of the forest. But he had forgotten the Elephant, who is a very wise animal and knows many charms. One day the Elephant challenged him, declaring that he had no right to call himself King, as the Elephant himself was the monarch of the forest and could not be defeated.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale III (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一位名叫阿基蒂的著名獵人兼摔跤手，誇口說自己比任何人或野獸都強壯。他輕易擊敗了一個巨人、一頭豹、一頭獅子、一隻狼和一條大蟒蛇，既然沒有別人反對他的說法，他便自稱森林之王。但他忘了大象，大象是極為聰慧的動物，懂得許多法術。有一天，大象向他挑戰，宣稱他無權自稱國王，因為大象自己才是森林的君主，且不可能被擊敗。

passages.text: Akiti flung his spear, but because of the Elephant's charm the weapon glanced off his hide and did him no harm; bow, poisoned arrows, and hunting-knife availed nothing. The hunter then used his own charm and changed himself into a lion and flew at the Elephant, but was flung off; next he became a serpent, but could not crush the Elephant to death. At last he changed himself into a fly, flew into the Elephant's large flapping ear, went right down inside until he came to the heart, changed into a man again, and cut up the heart with his hunting-knife. The Elephant fell dead, and Akiti stepped out of his body in triumph, now without question the King of the forest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale III (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿基蒂擲出長矛，但因大象的護符之力，武器從牠的皮上滑開，未能傷牠分毫；弓、毒箭與獵刀皆無濟於事。獵人於是施展自己的護符，化身為獅子撲向大象，卻被甩開；接著他變成一條蛇，卻無法將大象纏死。最後他變成一隻蒼蠅，飛進大象那拍動的大耳朵，一路鑽入其體內，直至心臟，再變回人形，以獵刀將心臟割碎。大象倒地而死，阿基蒂得意地從牠體內走出，此時他無疑已是森林之王。

title.en: Sons of Sticks
title.zh: 木棍之子

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: royal court at Oyo)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：奧約王廷）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale IV

summary.en: A young prince complains that his allotted territory is too small and its people too few; his father, displeased, turns a great bundle of sticks into human beings and gives them to him as subjects. The tribe thenceforth bears the nickname Omo Igi, Sons of Sticks.
summary.zh: 一位年輕王子抱怨父親分給他的封地太小、子民太少；國王不悅，便將一大捆木棍化為人形，賜給兒子作臣民。該族自此得名「奧莫伊吉」——木棍之子。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition. Tagged clay-humans as the nearest motif (humans manufactured from base matter); the material is wood, not clay — an interpretive substitution. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A great King sent his various sons to rule over different parts of his kingdom, and all were satisfied but one, the youngest and most ambitious, who returned to his father after some time with the complaint that his territory was much too small and his subjects too few. The King was displeased with his son, and sent for a large bundle of sticks, which he converted into human beings. "Here are some more subjects for you!" he said to the astonished Prince. From that time the tribe was famous for its strength and stupidity, and went by the nickname of Sons of Sticks, or Omo Igi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale IV (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位偉大的國王派遣他的諸位兒子分治王國各地，眾人都心滿意足，唯獨一人不然——那最年幼也最有野心的兒子，過了些時日回到父親面前抱怨，說他的領地太小、子民太少。國王對這兒子甚為不悅，便命人取來一大捆木棍，將其化為人形。「這裡還有一些子民給你！」他對驚愕的王子說道。自此以後，這個部族便以其強悍與愚鈍聞名，並得了「木棍之子」的綽號，即奧莫·伊吉。

title.en: Why Women Have Long Hair
title.zh: 女子長髮之由來

region.en: Yoruba village (symbolic pin: village path near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴村落（象徵定位：伊費近郊村徑）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale V

summary.en: A quarrelling woman digs a pit on the path to the well; when her rival falls in and is hauled out by the hair, the hair stretches long — a shameful oddity that becomes a coveted beauty, until every woman jumps into the pit to be pulled out by her hair.
summary.zh: 兩名婦人爭吵，其一在井邊路上掘深坑；宿敵墜坑後被眾人抓髮拉起，頭髮愈拉愈長。起初羞愧難當，後竟成艷羨之美，眾婦爭相跳坑任人拉髮，女子長髮自此而來。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; etiological folktale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Two women quarrelled, and one of them went out secretly at night and dug a deep pit in the middle of the path leading from her enemy's house to the village well. Early next morning, when all were going to the well for water with jars balanced on their heads, this woman fell into the pit and cried loudly for help. Her friends ran to her and, seizing her by the hair, began to pull her out; to their surprise, her hair stretched as they pulled, and by the time she was safely on the path, her hair was as long as a man's arm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale V (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兩個女人起了爭執，其中一人夜裡悄悄外出，在從她仇敵家通往村中水井的小路中央挖了一個深坑。翌日清晨，眾人頭頂水罐前往井邊取水時，這女人跌入坑中，大聲呼救。她的朋友們奔向她，抓住她的頭髮開始將她拉出；令她們驚訝的是，隨著拉扯，她的頭髮竟越拉越長，待她安然回到路上時，她的頭髮已長如一條男人的手臂。

passages.text: At first she hid herself in shame, but soon she saw that her long hair was beautiful and scorned the short-haired women. They, consumed with jealousy, began to be ashamed of their own hair. "We have men's hair. How beautiful it would be to have long hair!" So one by one they jumped into the pit, and their friends pulled them out by the hair — and in this way they, and all women after them, had long hair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale V (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 起初她羞愧地躲藏起來，但不久她便看出自己的長髮十分美麗，於是鄙視那些短髮的女人。她們滿心嫉妒，開始為自己的頭髮感到羞愧。「我們長的是男人的頭髮。若能有一頭長髮，該有多美啊！」於是她們一個接一個跳進坑裡，朋友們抓住她們的頭髮將她們拉出——就這樣，她們以及其後所有的女人，都擁有了長髮。

title.en: Sango Calls Down Lightning on His Own Palace
title.zh: 尚戈自召雷電焚宮

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (symbolic pin: palace below the hill)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（象徵定位：山腳王宮）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale VI

summary.en: Sango tries a lightning-attracting charm on his own palace, which burns with his whole family inside; in grief and rage he executes 160 courtiers, abandons his rule, and takes his own life when deserted. His people bury him honourably and worship him as god of thunder — and to this day Yorubas cry "Long live the King!" when thunder follows lightning.
summary.zh: 尚戈在自宮試驗引雷之咒，宮殿焚毀闔家罹難；他悲怒交加處死一百六十名近臣，棄國出走，眾叛親離後自盡。族人厚葬之，奉為雷神。至今約魯巴人見雷隨電至，必呼「國王萬歲！」。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the death-and-deification of Sango, the thunder orisha and third king of Oyo. Sensitively embedded in ongoing Shango devotion. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: King Sango was acquainted with many deadly charms, and he once happened to discover a preparation by which he could attract lightning. He foolishly decided to try the effect of the charm first of all on his own palace, which was at the foot of a hill. Ascending the hill with his courtiers, the King employed the charm; a storm suddenly arose, the palace was struck by lightning and burnt to the ground, together with Sango's whole family.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale VI (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 桑戈國王通曉許多致命的護符，有一次他偶然發現了一種能引來閃電的配方。他愚蠢地決定先在自己位於山腳下的宮殿上試驗這護符的效力。國王帶著廷臣登上山丘，施展護符；一時風暴驟起，宮殿遭閃電擊中，連同桑戈的全家一同燒成灰燼。

passages.text: Overcome with grief at the loss of his possessions and above all his sons, the impetuous King resolved to rule no more. In his rage he executed a hundred and sixty of his courtiers — eighty who had disagreed with his plan, and eighty who had agreed too eagerly. Then, accompanied by a few friends, he left the place; one by one they deserted him, and in despair he put an end to his own life. His people came to the spot and gave him an honourable funeral, and he was ever afterwards worshipped as the god of thunder and lightning. So, when the Yorubas see the flash of lightning followed by the sullen roar of thunder, they remember Sango's rage and exclaim: "Long live the King!"
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale VI (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這性情急躁的國王因失去財產、尤其是失去眾子而悲痛欲絕，決心不再統治。他在盛怒之下處死了一百六十名廷臣——八十名曾反對他的計畫，八十名則過於急切地贊同。隨後，他在少數友人的陪伴下離開此地；友人一個個棄他而去，他在絕望中結束了自己的性命。他的子民來到該地，為他舉行了隆重的葬禮，此後他永遠被奉為雷電之神。因此，當約魯巴人看見閃電閃過、繼而響起沉悶的雷鳴時，便會想起桑戈的怒火，驚呼道：「國王萬歲！」

title.en: The Olofin and the Mice
title.zh: 奧洛芬王與群鼠

region.en: Yoruba river country (symbolic pin: riverside near Oyo)
region.zh: 約魯巴河鄉（象徵定位：奧約近郊河畔）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale VII

summary.en: Imprisoned in a sealed hut to starve, an Olofin spares the mouse he was about to eat; the grateful mouse returns with a troop of mice bearing grain and fruit that keep the king alive for five days. His captors, convinced he must be a powerful charmer, free him and send him home in a war-canoe.
summary.zh: 奧洛芬王被囚於無門無窗的茅屋中等死，他舉刀欲食一鼠，旋即心生憐憫放下刀。知恩的鼠群連日送來穀物乾糧，五日後仇家開屋，見王安好如常，深信他有強大符咒，遂釋之，並以戰舟送其歸國。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; mercy-to-animals folktale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A famous Olofin, or Yoruba King, was once imprisoned by his enemies in a hut without any door or roof-opening, and left to die of starvation. As he sat gloomily on the ground, he saw a little mouse running across the hut and seized his knife, exclaiming: "Rather than die of hunger, I will eat this mouse!" But on second thoughts he put away his knife, saying: "Why should I kill the mouse? I shall starve later on, just the same."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale VII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一位著名的奧洛芬，即約魯巴國王，曾被敵人囚禁在一間既無門也無屋頂開口的小屋裡，任其餓死。他鬱鬱地坐在地上時，看見一隻小老鼠跑過小屋，便抓起刀來，喊道：「與其餓死，不如吃了這隻老鼠！」但轉念一想，他又收起刀，說道：「我何必殺這隻老鼠？反正我終究還是要餓死的。」

passages.text: To his surprise the mouse addressed him: "Noble King! Greetings to you on your generosity! You have spared my life, and in return I will spare yours." The mouse disappeared into a hole and returned followed by twenty or thirty other mice, all bearing grains of corn, gari, and small fruits. For five days they fed him in this manner, and on the sixth day the captors opened the hut, astonished to find him alive and in good health. "This Olofin must have a powerful charm!" they declared. "It appears that he can live without eating or drinking!" Thereupon they released him, gave him a war-canoe, and let him return in freedom to his own country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale VII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 令他驚訝的是，那老鼠竟開口對他說道：「尊貴的國王啊！因您的寬厚，向您致敬！您饒了我的性命，作為回報，我也要救您的性命。」老鼠鑽進一個洞裡，回來時身後跟著二三十隻老鼠，全都銜著穀粒、木薯粉和小果子。它們就這樣餵養了他五天，到了第六天，捉他的人打開小屋，驚愕地發現他竟還活著，而且身體健康。「這位奧洛芬必定有強大的護身符！」他們說道，「看來他不吃不喝也能活！」於是他們釋放了他，給了他一艘戰舟，讓他自由地返回自己的國度。

title.en: The Iroko Tree and Its Wandering Spirit
title.zh: 伊羅科樹與夜行樹靈

region.en: Yoruba forest (symbolic pin: grove near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴森林（象徵定位：伊費近郊樹叢）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale VIII

summary.en: In the great iroko tree lives an old man's spirit that prowls at night with a little torch; meeting it face to face brings madness and death, and cutting iroko wood brings misfortune on woodcutter and family. Even furniture of iroko groans at night — the imprisoned spirit longing for the forest.
summary.zh: 巨大的伊羅科樹中棲著一位老人的魂魄，夜裡提著小火把遊蕩，直視其面者瘋癲而亡；砍伐伊羅科木者全家招殃。凡以此木製傢俱之屋，夜半常聞呻吟吱呀之聲——那是被囚的樹靈，渴望重歸林間。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the iroko remains a feared and ritually significant tree. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: In the forest there is a giant tree called by the Yorubas the Iroko, which is shunned by all people, for in it lives the spirit of an old man who prowls about at night with a little torch and frightens travellers. Anyone who sees the Iroko-man face to face goes mad and speedily dies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale VIII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 森林中有一棵巨樹，約魯巴人稱之為伊羅科，人人皆避之唯恐不及，因為樹中住著一位老人的神靈，他夜間提著一盞小火把四處遊蕩，驚嚇旅人。任何面對面見到伊羅科老人的人都會發瘋，並很快死去。

passages.text: Seeing the thick branches and mighty trunk of the Iroko, woodcutters are often tempted to cut the tree down, but this is very unlucky, as it brings the displeasure of the Iroko-man and misfortune on the woodcutter and all his family. In any house which contains furniture made of Iroko-wood, strange groaning and creaking noises are heard at night: it is the spirit of the Iroko, imprisoned in the wood, who longs to wander about again through the forest with his little torch.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale VIII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 樵夫們見到伊羅科粗壯的枝幹和巨大的樹身，常忍不住想把它砍倒，但這非常不吉利，因為會招致伊羅科老人的不悅，並給樵夫及其全家帶來災禍。任何擺有用伊羅科木製成家具的屋子裡，夜間都會聽到奇怪的呻吟聲和吱嘎聲：那是伊羅科的神靈，被囚禁在木頭之中，渴望再次提著他的小火把在森林中遊蕩。

title.en: Orisa Oko and the Demon Polo
title.zh: 奧里莎奧科與惡魔波洛

region.en: Yoruba farmland (symbolic pin: cave country near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴農鄉（象徵定位：伊費附近岩洞地帶）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale IX

summary.en: A solitary old hunter with a fife and dog becomes a renowned soothsayer in a cave, where suspected witches are led and beheaded by the demon Polo he keeps. After his death, his followers hide a strongman as the "demon" — until a muscular accused kills the impostor, the fraud is exposed, and the cave is abandoned forever.
summary.zh: 一位孑然一身的獵人以笛聲喚犬引路，老來棲身岩洞，成了聲名遠播的占者。凡涉嫌巫術者被拖至洞前，無辜者由他親手引出，有罪者則由他所豢養的惡魔「波洛」斬首擲出。老人死後，信徒藏一壯漢假扮惡魔，直到某日一名魁梧嫌犯反將假惡魔殺死、毫髮無傷走出洞穴，騙局敗露，聖洞自此荒廢。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; orisha Oko is the agriculture deity — here the tale treats his cave-oracle cult satirically. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Orisa Oko was a poor hunter, solitary save for his fife and his dog. If ever he lost his way in the fields or the forest, he would play a plaintive melody on his fife, and the sounds would lead the faithful dog to his side to guide him home. As years went by he grew too old for hunting and took up residence in a cave; people thought him more mysterious than ever, came to him for advice about the future, and he won great renown as a soothsayer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale IX (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧里薩·奧科是個貧窮的獵人，除了他的笛子和他的狗之外，孤身一人。每當他在田野或森林中迷了路，他便用笛子吹奏一段哀婉的旋律，那聲音便會引來忠實的狗來到他身邊，領他回家。歲月流逝，他年事已高，不再適合打獵，便住進了一個洞穴；人們覺得他比以往更加神秘，紛紛前來向他請教未來之事，他作為占卜師贏得了極大的名聲。

passages.text: In those days witchcraft was punished by death, and anyone suspected of the evil art was dragged to Orisa Oko's cave. If the soothsayer found him innocent, he led him forth by the hand; if guilty, his head was cut off and thrown to the waiting crowd by the demon Polo, which Orisa Oko kept in the cave. After the old hunter's death his followers hid a very strong man in the cave to act as the demon. But one day a tall, muscular man was accused, and it was the head of the supposed "demon" that came rolling out instead — soon the strong man reappeared unharmed and triumphant. The people, indignant at the deception, deserted the cave of Orisa Oko from that day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale IX (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在那個年代，巫術會被處以死刑，任何被懷疑施行邪術的人都被拖到奧里薩·奧科的洞穴前。若占卜師判定他無罪，便牽著他的手領他出來；若判定有罪，他的頭便被砍下，由奧里薩·奧科養在洞中的惡魔波羅扔給等候的人群。老獵人死後，他的追隨者把一個非常強壯的人藏在洞中，讓他扮演那個惡魔。但有一天，一個高大健壯的人被指控，結果滾出來的卻是那個所謂「惡魔」的頭——不久那強壯的人竟安然無恙、得意洋洋地重新出現。人們對這騙局感到憤慨，從那天起便不再踏足奧里薩·奧科的洞穴。

title.en: Moremi and the Grass-Cloaked Igbos
title.zh: 莫雷米與草甲伊格博人

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (symbolic pin: Moremi's city and the stream of her vow)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（象徵定位：莫雷米之城與許願之溪）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale X

summary.en: The Ife noblewoman Moremi lets herself be captured by the terrifying Igbos, learns they are ordinary men in mantles of dry grass who fear fire, and escapes to tell her people. The Ifes defeat them with torches; but the stream-god she had promised a sacrifice demands her son Ela, who — only half dead on the altar — climbs a rope of grass to heaven, to return one day and reap his mother's sacrifice.
summary.zh: 伊費貴婦莫雷米自願落入可怕的伊格博人手中，探得他們不過是身披乾草戰甲、畏懼火焰的凡人，逃歸後獻計火攻，敵人大敗。然而她曾向溪神許下重願，神竟索其子埃拉為祭。埃拉臥於祭壇僅半死，甦醒後以草繩攀上天界，終有一日將歸來領受母親犧牲之果。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Moremi is one of Ile-Ife's most honoured heroines with an active cult and festival (Edi). Presented as an archival folktale record.

passages.text: A nobleman of Ile-Ife had a beautiful and virtuous wife named Moremi, and a handsome young son, Ela. The country of the Ifes was subject to fierce raids by a tribe called the Igbos, whose uncanny appearance in battle made the Ifes think them not human but a visitation sent by the gods in punishment for some evil. In vain did they offer sacrifices; the raids continued and the land was thrown into panic. The heroic Moremi resolved to let herself be captured during a raid, so that she might be carried to the land of the Igbos and learn their secrets. Bidding farewell to her husband and little son, she went to a certain stream and promised its god that, if her attempt succeeded, she would offer him the richest sacrifice she could afford.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale X (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊費城有一位貴族，娶了一位美麗賢德的妻子，名叫莫雷米，並育有一個俊秀年幼的兒子，名叫埃拉。伊費人的國度屢遭一個稱為伊格博人的部族兇猛侵襲；這些人在戰場上的怪異形貌，使伊費人以為他們並非人類，而是神明為懲罰某種罪惡而降下的災禍。他們徒然獻上祭品；侵襲仍持續不斷，舉國陷入恐慌。英勇的莫雷米決心讓自己在一次侵襲中被擄走，好讓她能被帶到伊格博人的國度，探知他們的祕密。她辭別丈夫與年幼的兒子，來到某條溪流旁，向那溪流之神許諾：倘若她的計謀成功，她必獻上自己力所能及最豐厚的祭品。

passages.text: Captured as she planned, she was given as a slave to the King of the Igbos and soon rose to a position of importance, learning that the raiders were not gods but ordinary men who wore strange mantles of grass and bamboo fibre and were much afraid of fire. She escaped home; her tidings were joyfully received at Ile-Ife, and the Igbos were utterly defeated by the trick she had suggested. But when Moremi made her great sacrifice of sheep, fowls, and bullocks, the god of the stream demanded the life of her son. Sorrowing, she consented and sacrificed the boy Ela — yet he was only half dead; when the people had departed he recovered, sprang up, made a rope of grass, climbed up to heaven, and it is certain that he will one day return to reap the benefits of his mother's noble sacrifice. The Ifes wept at the spectacle and promised to be her sons and daughters for ever.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale X (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她如計畫般被擄，被賜予伊格博人的國王為奴，不久便升居要位；她得知那些侵襲者並非神明，而是尋常男子，只是披著草與竹纖維製成的奇異披風，而且非常懼怕火。她逃回家鄉；她的消息在伊費城受到歡欣的迎接，而伊格博人則因她所獻的計策而徹底敗亡。然而，當莫雷米獻上羊、雞與公牛作為她的大祭時，溪流之神卻索求她兒子的性命。她悲痛地應允，獻出了男孩埃拉——但他只是半死；當眾人離去後，他甦醒過來，一躍而起，用草編成繩索，攀上天庭；可以確信，他總有一天會歸來，收穫他母親高貴犧牲所結的果實。伊費人見此情景無不哭泣，並承諾永遠做她的兒女。

title.en: Why the Bat Hides by Day
title.zh: 蝙蝠晝伏之由來

region.en: Yoruba village (symbolic pin: rafters near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴村落（象徵定位：伊費近郊屋簷）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XI

summary.en: Half bird and half rodent, the Bat fights among the rats until the birds seem likely to win, then flies up to change sides. Both disgusted hosts turn on him together, and ever since he hides in dark places by day and ventures out only in the evening.
summary.zh: 蝙蝠半鳥半鼠，原與鼠親並肩作戰，見鳥將勝便飛上半空倒戈。兩軍皆惡其背信，罷戰合攻蝙蝠。自那日起，牠白天躲藏於暗處，唯有暮色降臨方敢露面。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; animal folktale of treachery punished. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: The Bat is half a bird and half a rodent, and lives partly on the earth and partly in the air, but both rats and birds shun him, and this is why: the rats, his cousins, were once fighting a great battle with the birds, and Bat fought in their midst. But when he saw that the birds were likely to be victorious, he left the rats and flew up into the air to fight on the side of the birds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XI (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蝙蝠半是鳥、半是鼠，一部分時日住在地上，一部分時日住在空中，但鼠與鳥都避開牠，原因如下：鼠是牠的表親，曾與鳥展開一場大戰，蝙蝠在牠們當中作戰。但當牠看出鳥很可能得勝時，便離開鼠群，飛上空中，站在鳥的一方作戰。

passages.text: Both the rats and the birds were disgusted at this cowardly action, so they ceased from fighting one another and all combined to attack the Bat. Since that day he has been forced to hide in dark places all day, and only comes out in the evening when his enemies cannot see him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XI (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 鼠與鳥都對這怯懦的行徑感到厭惡，於是牠們停止互相爭鬥，全體聯合起來攻擊蝙蝠。自那天起，牠便被迫整日躲藏在幽暗之處，只在傍晚敵人看不見牠時才出來。

title.en: The Leopard-Man and the Forest Bride
title.zh: 豹郎與林中新娘

region.en: Yoruba forest (symbolic pin: river woods near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴森林（象徵定位：伊費近郊河林）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XII

summary.en: A silent, handsome stranger comes monthly to a village; a maiden follows him into the forest against repeated warnings. At a leopard-skin under a tree he sings that he is in truth a savage leopard, resumes that form, and pursues her. A tree falls across a river to save her, she reaches the village, and the leopard-man is never seen again.
summary.zh: 一位沉默俊美的陌生人每月造訪村中，少女不聽再三勸阻執意隨他入林。在樹下的豹皮旁，他歌道自己實為兇豹，隨即現出原形追逐少女。危急之際一棵樹倒臥河上助她渡河，她終於逃回村中，豹郎從此絕跡。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; were-animal marriage tale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A handsome Stranger once came into a certain village and strolled about among the people in mysterious silence. All the maidens admired him and wished that he would choose one of them for his bride; but he said nothing and at last walked away into the forest. A month later he came again, and this time one of the maidens fell so much in love with him that she resolved to follow him, for she could not bear to be separated from him. He stopped and begged her to return home; but she would not: "I will never leave you, and wherever you go, I will follow." "Beautiful maiden, you will regret it," replied the stranger sadly — and said so again at his second stop.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 曾有一位俊美的陌生人來到某個村莊，帶著神祕的沉默在人群中漫步。所有少女都愛慕他，希望他會選中自己為新娘；但他一言不發，最後走入森林離去。一個月後他又來了，這一次，其中一位少女愛他愛得如此之深，決心跟隨他，因為她無法忍受與他分離。他停下腳步，懇求她回家；但她不肯：「我永遠不會離開你，無論你到哪裡，我都要跟隨。」「美麗的少女，你會後悔的，」陌生人悲傷地回答——並在第二次停下時又這麼說。

passages.text: Deep in the forest they reached a tree at the foot of which lay a leopard-skin. Standing under it, the stranger sang a melancholy song telling her that though he was allowed once a month to wander like a man, he was in reality a savage leopard and would rend her in pieces as soon as he regained his natural form. He flung himself on the ground, became a snarling leopard, and pursued her. Fear gave speed to her feet; as he pursued, he sang that he would tear her in small pieces, and she replied in song that he would never overtake her. At a deep but narrow river a tree took pity on her and fell across it so she could cross. Nearly exhausted, she reached the village in safety; the leopard slunk back into the forest, and the handsome stranger was never seen again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們深入森林，來到一棵樹下，樹腳下攤著一張豹皮。陌生人站在樹下，唱起一首憂傷的歌，告訴她：雖然他被允許每月一次像人一樣漫遊，但他實際上是一頭兇猛的豹，一旦恢復本來的形貌，就會把她撕成碎片。他撲倒在地，變成一頭咆哮的豹，追趕她。恐懼使她腳下生風；他一面追趕，一面唱著要將她撕成小塊，而她以歌聲回應，說他永遠追不上她。在一條深而狹窄的河邊，一棵樹憐憫她，倒下橫跨河面，讓她得以渡過。她幾乎筋疲力盡，終於平安抵達村莊；豹悄然退回森林，而那俊美的陌生人此後再無人見過。

title.en: Why the Water-Bird Stands on One Leg
title.zh: 涉禽單足獨立之由來

region.en: Yoruba lagoon country (symbolic pin: coastal lagoon near Lagos)
region.zh: 約魯巴潟湖之鄉（象徵定位：拉哥斯近郊湖畔）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XIII

summary.en: A water-bird swallows the King of the crabs; the crab tribe vows to nip off the bird's bright pink legs in revenge. The water-rat warns the bird and advises a disguise: standing on one leg. The crabs, seeing a one-legged pink creature, pass by — and the bird stands on one leg to this day.
summary.zh: 一隻涉禽吞下了蟹王，蟹族憤而立誓報復，要夾斷牠那雙粉紅亮腿。水鼠聞訊報信，教牠收起一足裝作異鳥。蟹群見了獨腿高鳥，道「我們的仇敵有兩腿，此必非牠」，逕自離去。涉禽自此單足獨立至今。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; animal etiology. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A water-bird once, in search of food, swallowed the King of the crabs, and the whole tribe of crabs were so enraged that they swore they would have their revenge. "We will find this horrible bird and nip off its legs. We shall not fail to find it, for its legs are bright pink in colour and its feathers are pink and white."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XIII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一隻水鳥，在覓食時吞下了蟹王，整族的螃蟹都憤怒不已，發誓定要報仇。「我們要找到這隻可惡的鳥，把牠的腿鉗斷。我們絕不會找不到牠，因為牠的腿是鮮豔的粉紅色，羽毛是粉紅與白色相間的。」

passages.text: But the water-rat overheard the crabs plotting and hastened to tell the water-bird. "They will nip off my beautiful pink legs, and then what will become of me?" cried the bird. "It is very simple," replied the water-rat: "if you stand on one leg, they will think you are some other creature." The bird tucked up one leg; when the crabs came they saw, as they thought, a very tall pink bird with one leg and a large beak. "Our enemy has two legs. This cannot be he." And they passed by.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XIII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 可是水鼠偷聽到了螃蟹們的密謀，急忙去告訴水鳥。「牠們會把我美麗的粉紅腿鉗斷，那我該怎麼辦呢？」鳥兒叫道。「這很簡單，」水鼠回答說：「只要妳用一條腿站著，牠們就會以為妳是別的生物。」鳥兒收起了一條腿；螃蟹們來到時，牠們自以為看到的是一隻很高大、只有一條腿、長著大喙的粉紅色鳥。「我們的仇人有兩條腿。這不可能是牠。」於是牠們便走了過去。

title.en: The Ants and the Miser's Treasure
title.zh: 蟻群與守財奴的金子

region.en: Yoruba village (symbolic pin: compound near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴村落（象徵定位：伊費近郊院落）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XIV

summary.en: A poor man feeds ants and parrots; a cruel miser hoards gold and crushes their kindred. The ants dig a tunnel from the miser's hut to the poor man's house and carry the treasure over three nights — but when the tunnel's end is found, the poor man is condemned as a witch, until the ants devour his hut overnight so the villagers believe the gods have punished him in their stead.
summary.zh: 窮漢以碎穀飼蟻餵鳥；吝嗇鬼囤金虐生。蟻群掘地道，三夜之間將守財奴的金子搬入窮漢屋中。地道被發現後，窮漢被誣為施法竊金、翌日將焚身。蟻群連夜噬毀囚屋，村人誤以為天罰已代行其刑，蟻群卻獨知真相。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; animal-justice folktale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: There once was a poor man who was very kind to animals and birds; however little he had, he always spared a few grains for his parrot and spread titbits every morning for the industrious ants. In the same village lived a miser who had by crafty means collected a large store of gold, which he kept tied up in the corner of a hut, sitting outside all day and night. He threw stones at any bird and crushed any ant he found, for he detested every living creature and loved nothing but his gold. When he had killed a great many of their number, the ants began to think how they might punish his cruelty. "What a pity it is," said the King of the ants, "that our friend is a poor man, while our enemy is so rich!"
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XIV (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個窮人，對動物和鳥類都非常仁慈；無論自己擁有多少，他總會省下幾粒穀物給他的鸚鵡，每天早晨又撒些食物碎屑給勤勞的螞蟻。同一個村子裡住著一個守財奴，他用狡猾的手段聚斂了一大堆金子，把它捆好藏在茅屋的角落裡，自己則日夜坐在屋外守著。他見了鳥就扔石頭，見了螞蟻就踩死，因為他憎惡一切生靈，只愛他的金子。當他殺死了為數眾多的螞蟻之後，螞蟻們開始思索該如何懲罰他的殘忍。「多麼可惜啊，」螞蟻王說，「我們的朋友是個窮人，而我們的仇人卻如此富有！」

passages.text: So the ants dug a great tunnel, one end in the poor man's house and the other in the miser's hut, and over three nights carried the whole treasure into the poor man's house, who rejoiced, thinking the gods had rewarded his years of humble toil. The miser accused witchcraft; the tunnel was traced, the gold found under native cloths in the poor man's hut, and he was shut up to be burnt alive. The ants, sorely perplexed at what their plan had wrought, ate up the whole of the prison-hut overnight. In the morning the people said: "The gods have taken the punishment out of our hands! The ants have devoured both the hut and the prisoner!" And only the ants knew that this was not true.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XIV (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是螞蟻們挖了一條大隧道，一端通到窮人的屋裡，另一端通到守財奴的茅屋，花了三個夜晚把全部財寶搬進了窮人的家中，窮人歡喜不已，以為神明賞賜了他多年來的辛勤勞作。守財奴指控有人施巫術；隧道被追查出來，金子在窮人屋裡的土布下被找到，於是他被關起來，要活活燒死。螞蟻們對自己計謀所造成的結果深感困惑，便在一夜之間把整座囚屋吃個精光。到了早晨，人們說：「神明已經替我們執行了懲罰！螞蟻把茅屋和囚犯都吃掉了！」只有螞蟻知道這並非實情。

title.en: The Magician Who Bought the Birds' Voices
title.zh: 以羽易聲的巫師

region.en: Yoruba forest grove (symbolic pin: grove near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴林間樹叢（象徵定位：伊費近郊樹叢）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XV

summary.en: A jealous magician envies the songs of a grove's brown birds and tricks them into trading their voices — stored in a calabash he swallows — for brightly coloured feathers. His singing draws hearers from far and near, while the most beautiful birds remain quite unable to sing.
summary.zh: 巫師嫉妒林間褐鳥的歌聲，以「換得彩羽」為餌，誘使群鳥將聲音裝入葫蘆交出，他一口吞下，從此歌喉甜美，聽者雲集；而最豔麗的鳥兒卻自此啞然無聲。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; animal etiology. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A magician once passed through a grove where a great many brown birds filled the air with songs. He sat and listened, enraptured, but in the end became very jealous, for he himself could not sing. He felt he must by some means possess the voices of the singing birds, so he called them together and said it grieved him that the gods had given them such poor, ugly brown feathers — how happy they would be if they were brilliantly coloured with red, blue, orange, and green! The birds agreed that it was a great pity to be so ugly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XV (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個巫師經過一片樹林，那裡有許多褐色的小鳥，歌聲充滿了空中。他坐下來聆聽，聽得如痴如醉，但最後卻變得非常嫉妒，因為他自己不會唱歌。他覺得自己非得設法得到這些鳴鳥的歌聲不可，於是把牠們召集起來，說神明賜給牠們如此難看醜陋的褐色羽毛，令他十分難過——倘若牠們能披上鮮紅、藍、橙、綠的豔麗色彩，該有多麼幸福啊！鳥兒們也都同意，長得這般難看實在太可惜了。

passages.text: The magician suggested that by his charms he could give them beautiful feathers in exchange for their voices, which were of little use since nobody came into the grove to hear them. The birds desired the beauty he promised and foolishly agreed; their voices were placed in a large calabash, and their dull brown feathers were turned to orange, green, and red. The magician hurried away and swallowed the calabash's contents, and from that day he had an exceedingly sweet voice, so that people came from far and near to listen. But the birds were satisfied with their bright feathers — and this is why the most beautiful birds are quite unable to sing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XV (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巫師提議，他可以用法術給牠們美麗的羽毛，來換取牠們的歌聲，反正這歌聲也沒什麼用處，因為沒有人會走進樹林來聽。鳥兒們渴望他所許諾的美麗，便愚蠢地答應了；牠們的歌聲被裝進一個大葫蘆裡，牠們暗淡的褐色羽毛則變成了橙色、綠色和紅色。巫師匆匆離去，把葫蘆裡的東西吞了下去，從那天起，他便有了一副極其甜美的嗓子，人們從遠近各地趕來聆聽。可是鳥兒們對自己鮮豔的羽毛很滿意——這就是為什麼最美麗的鳥兒完全不會唱歌。

title.en: Elenre and the Three Magicians
title.zh: 三巫師與埃倫雷

region.en: Yoruba royal court (symbolic pin: Oyo palace)
region.zh: 約魯巴王廷（象徵定位：奧約王宮）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XVI

summary.en: When a war-king refuses to let his three magician retainers go home, two vanish by magic; the third, Elenre, cannot be harmed — sword breaks, arm withers, spear crumples, rock rolls away. Betrayed by his wife's hint (a blade of thatch will cut him), he is beheaded, but his head sticks to the king's hand and devours his food until a wiser magician greets it respectfully. The head falls, becomes Elenre's river, and the treacherous wife is changed into a stagnant pool.
summary.zh: 戰時為王造符的三位巫師戰後請歸，王不許。兩位各顯神通遁走；第三位埃倫雷刀不能傷、矛不能刺、石不能壓。其妻洩密——以茅草一片即可斷其首——巫師人頭落地，卻黏在王手上，吞盡王的飲食，群巫無策。唯有一位謙卑的巫師致敬於頭顱，頭顱方落，化為「埃倫雷河」；背妻則化為不流的死水潭。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; magic-contest tale with a place-name etiology (Odo Elenre). Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A certain King had engaged in a series of wars, during which he employed three magicians to make charms for him. At the war's end they humbly asked to be allowed to return home; the King foolishly refused, and the magicians replied: "We asked your permission out of courtesy, O King, but we can very easily depart without it." The first fell on the ground and disappeared; the second threw a ball of twine into the air, climbed up the thread, and vanished likewise. The third, Elenre, remained standing. "It is your turn to disappear," said the King, trembling with anger, "or I will slay you." "You cannot harm me," replied the magician.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XVI (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某位國王連年征戰，期間曾雇用三名術士為他製作護符。戰爭結束後，他們謙卑地請求准許返鄉；國王愚昧地拒絕了，術士們便答道：「大王啊，我們請求您的許可，只是出於禮貌，但我們要離去，即使沒有許可也輕而易舉。」第一個術士倒在地上便消失了；第二個把一團細繩拋向空中，攀著繩索而上，也同樣消失無蹤。第三個是埃倫雷，仍舊站立不動。「輪到你消失了，」國王氣得發抖地說，「否則我就殺了你。」「您傷不了我，」術士回答。

passages.text: Ordered beheaded, Elenre saw the sword break in two and the executioner's arm wither; the spear crumpled; the great rock rolled over his body like a child's ball. At last his wife confessed his secret: a blade of thatch grass could cut off his head. This was done — but the head stuck fast to the King's hand and consumed all his food and drink, so that the King seemed likely to die. Magicians summoned from all over the kingdom were laughed at by the head, until one prostrated himself: "Who am I to oppose you, great Elenre? I come only because the King commands me." "You are wiser than all the rest!" said Elenre, and the head fell to the ground and became a flowing river called to this day Odo Elenre, Elenre's river. His treacherous wife was likewise changed into a river, but Elenre commanded it not to flow, and it became a stagnant pool.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XVI (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 埃倫雷被下令斬首，卻見刀劍斷成兩截，劊子手的手臂枯萎；長矛折彎；巨石滾過他的身體，宛如孩童的球一般。最後，他的妻子吐露了他的秘密：一根茅草葉便能砍下他的頭。此事果然辦成——但那顆頭顱緊緊黏在國王手上，吃光了他所有的飲食，國王眼看就要喪命。從全國各地召來的術士都遭那顆頭顱嘲笑，直到其中一人俯伏在地：「我算什麼，豈敢與您作對，偉大的埃倫雷？我來只是因為國王命令我。」「你比其餘所有人都聰明！」埃倫雷說，那顆頭顱便落到地上，化作一條奔流的河，至今仍名為奧多·埃倫雷，即埃倫雷之河。他那背信的妻子也同樣被變成了一條河，但埃倫雷命令它不得流動，於是它成了一潭死水。

title.en: Isokun and the Stolen Baby
title.zh: 伊索昆偷嬰記

region.en: Yoruba royal town (symbolic pin: palace near Oyo)
region.zh: 約魯巴王城（象徵定位：奧約附近王宮）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XVII

summary.en: Barren queen Isokun wanders to every shrine of tree, stream and rock seeking a child, and is refused. Stealing a two-day-old baby by the wayside, she passes it off as the king's heir amid palace rejoicing — until the hungry baby's cries draw its true mother, who snatches it to her breast; the fraud is exposed and Isokun flees the palace for ever.
summary.zh: 無子的王妃伊索昆遍訪草木溪石之神的聖所求子，皆遭拒絕。歸途中她偷走路邊一名出生兩日的嬰兒，謊稱為王誕下麟兒，宮中慶宴大作。嬰兒啼飢，生母循聲而至，一把攬兒入懷即時止啼。真相大白，伊索昆羞愧出逃，永不回宮。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; shrine-circuit and stolen-child tale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A certain King Dekun had a wife named Isokun who bore him no children, on which account there was great unhappiness in the palace. One day Isokun disappeared and was absent for many weeks: she had set out to visit the shrines of all the gods, in the hope that one of them would promise her a child. But though she travelled far and wide, the gods of all the trees and streams and rocks refused her prayer. Nearing home, she came upon a poor woman asleep by the wayside with her baby two days old. Isokun stole the baby and hastened to the palace, where she informed the King that she had disappeared in order to give him the joyous surprise of his little son. There were great rejoicings; sacrifices were made and the drums beat loudly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XVII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某位名叫德昆的國王有位妻子名叫伊索昆，她未能為他生育子女，因此宮中十分愁苦。有一天，伊索昆失蹤了，一連數週不見人影：她動身去參拜所有神祇的聖所，希望其中一位能應許賜她一個孩子。然而她雖遠近遍歷，所有樹木、溪流與岩石之神都拒絕了她的祈求。快到家時，她遇見一個貧苦婦人在路旁睡著，身旁帶著出生才兩天的嬰兒。伊索昆偷走了嬰兒，急忙趕回宮中，告訴國王她之所以失蹤，是為了給他一個得子的驚喜。舉國歡慶；獻上祭品，鼓聲雷動。

passages.text: Meanwhile the real mother awoke and found her baby gone; she searched every house and at last insisted on entering the palace, where all were celebrating the arrival of the King's heir. All this time the baby cried with hunger, and Isokun, unable to feed him, invented other reasons for the crying. Drawn by the cries, the mother entered and snatched the baby to her breast, where it was at once contented. In a few moments the deception was made clear; the mother departed with her child, and Isokun, ashamed and fearing the King's anger, fled from the palace and never returned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XVII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 與此同時，真正的母親醒來，發現嬰兒不見了；她挨家挨戶尋找，最後堅持要進入宮中，那裡人人都在慶祝國王繼承人的降臨。這段時間裡，嬰兒一直因飢餓而啼哭，伊索昆無法餵養他，便編造了其他理由解釋哭聲。那母親被哭聲引來，進入宮中，一把將嬰兒抱到胸前，嬰兒立刻安靜下來。片刻之間，騙局便真相大白；母親帶著孩子離去，伊索昆羞愧難當，又懼怕國王發怒，便逃出宮中，此後再未回來。

title.en: The Twin Brothers of King Ajaka
title.zh: 阿賈卡王的孿生子

region.en: Yoruba river town (symbolic pin: riverside near Oyo)
region.zh: 約魯巴河城（象徵定位：奧約附近河畔）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XVIII

summary.en: Under the cruel custom that twins must be destroyed, King Ajaka secretly exiles his favourite wife and her twin sons. When the father dies heirless, the brothers cast stones for the throne; the winner reigns, sends for his twin — then, jealous, drowns him. A fish rises singing "Your brother lies here," and when the king kills it, the river itself sings the same words before the court, and the murderer takes poison in disgrace.
summary.zh: 按當時孿生子女須被處死的殘俗，阿賈卡王暗中將愛妃與雙生二子送至僻地。父王駕崩無嗣，兄弟以擲石決定王位；登基者迎回胞弟，卻因嫉妒將他推入河中溺斃。魚兒浮水唱「你兄弟在此」，王殺魚；河水又當廷高唱同一句歌。真相大白，惡弟遭民唾棄，服毒而亡。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition. Twins (Ibeji) hold a special honoured place in Yoruba religion; this tale is set in the old era when the twin-taboo operated, and echoes the twins motif cluster. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A certain Yoruba King, Ajaka, had a favourite wife; but she gave birth to twins. At that time it was the universal custom to destroy twins immediately at birth, and the mother with them. But the King had not the heart to put this cruel law into execution, and secretly charged one of his nobles to conduct the royal mother and her babes to a remote place where they might live in safety. There the twin brothers grew to manhood, loving one another greatly; when one began to speak, the other completed his phrase, so harmonious were their thoughts. Their mother, before she died, told them of their royal birth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XVIII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某位約魯巴國王阿賈卡有一位寵妃；但她生下了雙胞胎。當時普遍的習俗是將雙胞胎一出生便立即處死，連同母親一併處死。但國王不忍心執行這條殘酷的法律，便暗中吩咐一位貴族將王子的母親和她的嬰兒帶到偏遠之地，讓他們安然生活。雙胞胎兄弟在那裡長大成人，彼此十分友愛；一人開口說話，另一人便接著說完他的話，他們的心思如此契合。他們的母親在臨終前告訴了他們自己的王室出身。

passages.text: When news came that their father was dead leaving no heir, they decided to cast stones for the throne. The lot fell on the younger, who became King and sent for his brother to share his splendour. But jealousy overcame brotherly affection: walking by the river, he pushed his brother into the water, where he was drowned, and gave out that he had left the country in his favour. Some time later, passing the spot, he saw a fish rise and sing: "Your brother lies here." He killed it with a sharp stone. But another day, attended by his nobles under the royal umbrella, the river itself rose into waves and sang the same words; the courtiers looked into the water and found the body of the King. The secret disclosed, the wicked brother was rejected in horror by his people, and at this disgrace took poison and died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XVIII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當消息傳來，說他們的父親已死且未留下繼承人時，他們決定以擲石來決定王位。籤運落在弟弟身上，他成為國王，並召來兄長共享榮華。但嫉妒壓倒了手足之情：他在河邊散步時，將兄長推入水中，兄長溺斃，他則對外宣稱兄長已為成全他而離開國度。過了些時日，他經過該處，看見一條魚浮出水面唱道：「你的兄長躺在這裡。」他用一塊尖石將魚打死。但另一天，他在貴族隨侍、王傘之下經過時，河水本身湧起波濤，唱出同樣的話語；朝臣往水中一看，發現了國王的屍體。秘密揭穿後，邪惡的弟弟被人民厭惡地唾棄，他因這恥辱而服毒自盡。

title.en: How the Leopard Got His Spots
title.zh: 豹紋之由來

region.en: Yoruba forest (symbolic pin: undergrowth near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴森林（象徵定位：伊費近郊密林）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XIX

summary.en: Pursued by the hunter Akiti, the lion-coloured leopard eats the roots of a magic plant and becomes invulnerable — but at every poisoned arrow that strikes him a dark mark appears, until his body carries so many arrow-marks that among the trees he looks like the mingling of sun and shadow.
summary.zh: 被獵人阿基提追捕的豹原與獅同色、身無斑紋；牠服食仙草之根變得刀槍不入，但每中一箭便留一道黑痕。箭痕累積滿身，豹穿行林間時恰似日光與樹影交錯——豹紋由此而來。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; animal etiology. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: At one time the Leopard was coloured like a lion, and he had no dark markings; but he was pursued by Akiti, the renowned hunter, and feared that he might be slain. To avoid this he ate the roots of a certain magic plant, which had the effect of making him invulnerable to any of the hunter's weapons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XIX (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前，豹的毛色如同獅子，身上沒有任何深色斑紋；然而牠被著名的獵人阿基提（Akiti）追捕，擔心自己可能被殺。為了避免此事，牠吃下某種神奇植物的根，這具有使牠不受獵人任何武器所傷的效果。

passages.text: Soon afterwards Akiti saw him slipping through the dense undergrowth, and though he shot his poisoned arrows, the Leopard escaped — but where each arrow struck him, there appeared a dark mark. Now, though hunters still pursue him, he is rarely caught, and his body is covered with the marks of the arrows, so that as he goes among the trees he looks exactly like the mingling of the sun and shadow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XIX (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久之後，阿基提看見牠從茂密的灌木叢中悄悄溜過，儘管他射出毒箭，豹仍逃脫了——但每當一支箭射中牠，那裡便出現一道深色痕跡。如今，儘管獵人仍追捕牠，牠卻鮮少被捉住，而牠身上佈滿了箭的痕跡，因此當牠行走於樹林之間時，看起來恰似日光與陰影的交錯。

title.en: Another Story of the Leopard's Spots
title.zh: 豹紋的另一段故事

region.en: Yoruba village compound (symbolic pin: bathing-hut near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴村落院落（象徵定位：伊費近郊浴棚）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XX

summary.en: A dark-skinned leopard prowls round a hut where a woman is bathing; she flings her soap-filled loofah at him. He flees — but to this day the leopard is flecked with soap from foot to head.
summary.zh: 一頭黑豹繞著婦人沐浴的小屋打轉，欲撲食屋中人；婦人驚呼間將滿是皂沫的絲瓜絡擲去。豹負皂而逃——至今豹身自足至首仍斑斑點點，盡是皂漬。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; humorous animal etiology. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: According to another story, Leopard once had a very dark skin. He was prowling one day in a beautiful compound when he noticed a little hut in which a lady was taking her bath. Round and round the hut Leopard walked, waiting for an opportunity to spring in and seize his victim, for he was hungry.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XX (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 根據另一個故事，豹從前有一身非常深色的皮毛。有一天，牠在一個美麗的庭院裡徘徊，注意到一間小屋，裡面有位婦人正在沐浴。豹繞著小屋走了一圈又一圈，等待機會衝進去抓住獵物，因為牠餓了。

passages.text: But as he passed the opening of the hut, the lady saw him and, uttering a scream of terror, threw at him her loofah, which was full of soap. She flung it at him and he fled — but to this day the Leopard still is flecked with soap from foot to head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XX (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但當牠經過小屋的門口時，婦人看見了牠，發出一聲驚恐的尖叫，朝牠扔出她那沾滿肥皂的絲瓜絡。她朝牠扔去，牠便逃走了——但直到今日，豹從腳到頭仍帶著肥皂的斑點。

title.en: The Head That Borrowed a Body
title.zh: 借身的頭顱

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: roads between village and river, near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費與河岸之間的村路）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXI

summary.en: In a land of bodiless jumping Heads, one Head sets out to see the world, politely borrowing a slave's body, a sleeper's arms, and a fisherman's legs. Whole again, he wins a bride at the dancing-ground — then returns each borrowed part on the journey home, and his horrified wife runs away, leaving the Head alone for ever.
summary.zh: 在某國度，人人只有會跳躍的頭而無身軀。一顆頭偷偷出遊，依次向老婦借得奴隸的身體、向樹下沉睡的青年借得雙臂、向漁夫借得雙腿，拼成完人，在舞場贏得美眷。歸途中他一一奉還所借：腿還漁夫，臂還青年，身還老婦。新娘見丈夫只剩一顆頭，驚恐逃去，頭顱再也追不上，永失所愛。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; wonder tale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: There is a certain country where the inhabitants have heads but no bodies. The Heads move about by jumping along the ground, but they never go very far. One of the Heads desired to see the world, so he set out one morning secretly. He saw an old woman looking out of the door of a hut and asked her to lend him a body; she willingly lent him the body of her slave. Later he came upon a young man sleeping under a tree and asked to borrow a pair of arms, as he did not appear to be using them; the young man agreed. At the river-bank where fishermen sat mending their net, one of them lent him a pair of legs. Now he had legs, arms, and a body, and appeared like any other man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXI (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一個國家，那裡的居民有頭卻沒有身體。這些頭靠著在地上跳躍來移動，但牠們從不走得很遠。其中一個頭渴望見識世界，於是某天早晨悄悄出發了。牠看見一位老婦人從小屋的門口向外張望，便請她借牠一副身體；她欣然把她的奴隸的身體借給牠。後來牠遇到一個在樹下睡覺的年輕人，便請求借一雙手臂，因為他似乎並沒有在使用它們；年輕人同意了。在漁夫們坐著補網的河岸邊，其中一人借給牠一雙腿。現在牠有了腿、手臂和身體，看起來就像任何其他男人一樣。

passages.text: In the evening he reached a town and saw maidens dancing while onlookers threw coins to those they favoured. The Head threw all his coins to one dancer, who so admired his handsome form that she consented to marry him and live in his own country. Next day they set out, but at the river-bank the stranger took off his legs and gave them back to the fisherman; later he returned his arms to the young man sleeping under the tree; finally he gave up his body at the old woman's cottage. When the bride saw that her husband was merely a Head, she was filled with horror and ran away as fast as she could go — and now that he had neither body, arms, nor legs, the Head could not overtake her, and so lost her for ever.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXI (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傍晚時牠抵達一座城鎮，看見少女們在跳舞，旁觀者則把錢幣扔給他們所青睞的人。這個頭把牠所有的錢幣都扔給了一位舞者，她如此仰慕牠英俊的形貌，以至於同意嫁給牠，並住在牠自己的國家。翌日他們出發了，但在河岸邊，這個陌生人脫下牠的腿，還給了漁夫；後來牠把手臂還給了在樹下睡覺的年輕人；最後牠在老婦人的小屋前交還了身體。當新娘看見她的丈夫只不過是一個頭時，她滿懷恐懼，以最快的速度逃走了——而如今牠既沒有身體、手臂，也沒有腿，這個頭追不上她，於是永遠失去了她。

title.en: Ole and the Ant-Pillar
title.zh: 懶漢奧雷與蟻柱

region.en: Yoruba village (symbolic pin: compound near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴村落（象徵定位：伊費近郊院落）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXII

summary.en: Lazy, nosy Ole lets the ants build a pillar in his compound so he can perch on top and spy on his neighbours without moving. While he sits there crowing, the ants demolish his house and everything in it; he becomes the village laughing-stock — "Ku ijoko!" greetings on your sitting! — and dies of it.
summary.zh: 懶惰又多事的奧雷任由螞蟻在院中築起高柱，只為坐上柱頂窺探鄰居動靜。他終日高坐唱道「我如大酋長，萬事盡入眼」，螻蟻卻趁機啃光他的房屋糧食。村人見他皆喊「庫伊佐科——恭賀高坐！」，不久他便羞愧（或懶）而死。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; moral folktale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: There was a certain lazy and disagreeable man whom everyone called Ole, the Lazy one. He liked to profit by the work of others and was very inquisitive about other people's affairs. Once he saw that the ants had begun building a pillar in the compound of his house; though they destroyed all the plants and stripped the trees, Ole would not trouble to kill them or break down their pillar. Instead he thought: "When the ants have made this pillar very high, I will sit on the top of it, and then I shall be able to see all that my neighbours are doing without leaving my compound."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個懶惰又惹人厭的人，大家都叫他奧萊，也就是「懶惰鬼」。他喜歡靠別人的勞力佔便宜，而且非常愛打聽別人的閒事。有一次，他看見螞蟻開始在他家院子裡築起一根柱子；雖然螞蟻毀壞了所有植物、把樹木剝得精光，奧萊卻懶得去殺牠們，也懶得拆掉那根柱子。他反而心想：「等螞蟻把這根柱子築得很高，我就要坐在柱頂上，這樣我不用離開自家院子，就能看見鄰居們所做的一切。」

passages.text: This thought pleased him, and each day the pillar grew higher until the ants ceased building and began again elsewhere. Ole climbed up and spent the whole day observing his neighbours, singing: "Here sit I like a great Chief, and I see all things!" But while he sat on the pillar, the ants began to demolish his house and all that it contained, and soon nothing was left of his food and possessions. Ole thus became the laughing-stock of the village, and everyone who saw him cried: "Ku ijoko!" — Greetings to you on your sitting! Soon afterwards he died, and it is not known to this day whether he died of shame or of laziness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這個念頭令他十分得意，柱子一天比一天高，直到螞蟻停止築造，又到別處另起爐灶。奧萊爬上柱子，整天觀察鄰居，唱著：「我坐在這裡，像一位偉大的酋長，萬事萬物我都看得見！」可是當他坐在柱子上時，螞蟻開始拆毀他的房子和屋裡的一切，不久他的食物和財物就一無所剩。奧萊於是成了全村的笑柄，每個看見他的人都喊道：「Ku ijoko！」——願你安坐！不久之後他就死了，至今無人知道他是羞愧而死，還是懶惰而死。

title.en: The Old Hunter Who Became a Boa-Constrictor
title.zh: 化蟒的老獵人

region.en: Yoruba forest (symbolic pin: hunting paths near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴森林（象徵定位：伊費近郊獵徑）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXIII

summary.en: Too old to hunt, Ogunfunminire buys a pair of magic pots from a magician: dipping his head in the first turns him into a boa-constrictor to hunt the forest, the second restores him at nightfall. His family discovers the secret and, horrified, overturns both pots — and the serpent glide that was once their father disappears into the forest for ever.
summary.zh: 老獵人奧貢芬米尼雷不願捨棄狩獵之樂，向巫師求得兩只魔罐：晨將頭探入第一罐即化為蟒入林捕獵，夜以第二罐復形。家人窺破後驚駭不已，其子一怒踢翻雙罐。化蟒的他無法還原，繞宅數日尋覓咒液不果，終於沒入林中，家人再無所見。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; shapeshifting tale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Ogunfunminire, the famous hunter, lived to such a great age that he was no longer able to go into the forest and chase the deer and the leopard. Life had no other pleasure for him than hunting, so he went to a magician and asked for a charm which would enable him to continue his occupation. The magician gave him two pots, each containing a charm: every day Ogunfunminire dipped his head into the first pot and was at once transformed into a boa-constrictor, in which form he glided into the forest and hunted to his heart's content; at night he dipped his head into the second pot and became a man again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXIII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 著名的獵人奧貢芬米雷活到很大的年紀，再也無法進入森林追逐鹿和豹了。除了打獵，人生對他已沒有別的樂趣，於是他去找一位巫師，求一道能讓他繼續打獵的符咒。巫師給他兩個罐子，每個罐子裡各裝一道符咒：每天奧貢芬米雷把頭浸入第一個罐子，立刻變成一條蟒蛇，以這副形貌滑進森林，盡情打獵；到了夜裡，他把頭浸入第二個罐子，又變回人。

passages.text: This went on for a long time unknown to the old hunter's family; but when at last they chanced to discover the secret, they were filled with horror, and his son in a rage kicked at the pots and overturned them both. Ogunfunminire was hunting in the forest at that moment; returning, he found the magic pots empty and was filled with dismay, for he had no means of regaining his human form. For some days the boa-constrictor glided about near the house, seeking a few drops of the charm, but in vain, and at last he disappeared into the forest and was never seen by his family again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXIII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這樣過了很久，老獵人的家人都不知道；但當他們終於偶然發現這個秘密時，都驚恐萬分，他的兒子一怒之下踢向罐子，把兩個罐子都踢翻了。奧貢芬米雷當時正在森林裡打獵；他回來後發現魔法罐子空空如也，驚惶失措，因為他已無法再恢復人形。有好幾天，那條蟒蛇在房子附近滑來滑去，想找幾滴符咒，卻徒勞無功，最後他消失在森林裡，家人再也沒有見過他。

title.en: Oluronbi's Broken Vow to the Iroko
title.zh: 奧魯倫比違誓伊羅科

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (symbolic pin: the iroko grove outside the village)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（象徵定位：村外伊羅科樹叢）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXIV

summary.en: A childless village begs the Iroko-man for children, promising gifts; young Oluronbi promises her first child.
