Children come — but she and her husband cannot give up their beautiful daughter. Passing through the forest, she is seized and changed into a small brown bird singing of the broken promise, until her wood-carver husband carves a lifelike doll with a gold chain that the Iroko-man accepts in exchange.
summary.zh: 多年無孩的村莊齊赴伊羅科樹前求子，許諾獻上穀物山羊；木雕匠之妻奧魯倫比卻許諾「頭胎孩子」。孩子們降生了，夫妻卻捨不得交出最美的女兒。奧魯倫比路過樹叢，被樹靈捉住化為小褐鳥，終日唱著毀諾之歌。丈夫深思多日，雕出逼真木偶、繫上金鏈置於樹下；樹靈信以為真，將鳥還為人形，攜「孩兒」入林，奧魯倫比得以還家，自此再不敢入林。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; vow-to-spirit tale bound to iroko veneration. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: In a certain village no children had been born for many years, and the people were greatly distressed. At last all the women went together into the forest, to the magic tree, the Iroko, and implored the spirit of the tree to help them. The Iroko-man asked what gifts they would bring if he consented, and the women eagerly promised corn, yams, fruit, goats, and sheep; but Oluronbi, the young wife of a wood-carver, promised to bring her first child. In due course children came to the village, and the most beautiful of all was the one born to Oluronbi. She and her husband so greatly loved their child that they could not consent to give it up to the Iroko-man; the other women took their promised gifts, but Oluronbi took nothing to propitiate the tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXIV (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某個村子多年沒有孩子出生，村民為此十分苦惱。最後所有婦女一起進入森林，來到那棵魔法之樹伊羅科前，懇求樹靈幫助她們。伊羅科人問她們，若他應允，她們要獻上什麼禮物，婦女們急切地承諾玉米、山藥、水果、山羊和綿羊；但木雕匠的年輕妻子奧盧龍比，卻承諾獻上她的第一個孩子。後來村裡果然有了孩子，而其中最漂亮的，就是奧盧龍比所生的那一個。她和丈夫太愛這孩子，實在不願把他交給伊羅科人；其他婦女都獻上了承諾的禮物，奧盧龍比卻什麼也沒拿去討好那棵樹。

passages.text: Alas! one day as Oluronbi passed through the forest, the Iroko-man seized her and changed her into a small brown bird, which sat on the branches of the tree and plaintively sang: "One promised a sheep, one promised a goat, one promised fruit — but Oluronbi promised her child." When the wood-carver heard the song he realized what had happened. After thinking for many days he carved a large wooden doll, like a real child, with a small gold chain round its neck, covered it with a beautiful native cloth, and laid it at the foot of the tree. The Iroko-man thought this was Oluronbi's child, transformed the little bird once more into a woman, and snatched the doll up into the branches. Oluronbi joyfully returned home, and was careful never to stray into the forest again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXIV (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 唉！有一天奧盧龍比經過森林時，伊羅科人抓住她，把她變成一隻褐色小鳥，停在樹枝上哀怨地唱著：「有人許了一隻羊，有人許了一隻山羊，有人許了水果——但奧盧龍比許了她的孩子。」木雕匠聽見這歌聲，便明白發生了什麼事。他想了許多天之後，雕了一個大木娃娃，像真孩子一樣，脖子上圍著一條小金鏈，給它蓋上美麗的本地布料，放在樹腳下。伊羅科人以為這就是奧盧龍比的孩子，便把小小鳥變回女人，又把木娃娃一把抓上樹枝。奧盧龍比歡歡喜喜地回家，此後格外小心，再也不誤入森林。

title.en: The Staff of Oranyan
title.zh: 奧蘭揚之柱

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (symbolic pin: site of the obelisk outside Oyo)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（象徵定位：奧約城外的石柱遺址）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXV

summary.en: Oranyan, founder of Oyo, leaves his son in charge during a long expedition; believed dead, he returns to hear the Kakaki trumpet sounded for a new king — his own son. Preferring his son's happiness to his throne, he withdraws to obscure retirement, and only at his death is the truth known. The grieving young king raises the obelisk still called the Staff of Oranyan.
summary.zh: 奧約城的建立者奧蘭揚王遠征未歸，國人以為他已戰死，立其子為王。他歷盡艱辛返抵城外，卻聽見只為國王而鳴的卡卡基號角。田間農人答道：「奧蘭揚之子已為王，其父早歿於戰陣。」他甘願讓位，攜少數隨從退居僻野，至死方為其子所知。年輕的國王悲痛父親的犧牲，於其身故之地立碑，即今猶存的「奧蘭揚之柱」。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the Staff of Oranyan (Opa Oranyan) is a real monolith at Oyo-Ile associated with the Alaafin line. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Oranyan, a brave and warlike King, founded the city of Oyo. As it was necessary for him to lead an expedition to a distant part of his kingdom, he left his son in charge of the capital during his absence. But the King was away for so long a period that it was thought he and his soldiers must have perished, and at last the people made his son King, who for some time ruled them wisely and happily. However, Oranyan was not dead, and after many delays and hardships he again drew near to Oyo with his few surviving followers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXV (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧蘭揚是一位勇敢且好戰的國王，他建立了奧約城。由於他必須率領遠征隊前往王國偏遠之地，便在離去期間將首都交託給兒子掌管。然而國王離去太久，人們以為他與士兵們必定已經罹難，最後便擁立他的兒子為王，而這兒子有一段時日治理百姓既明智又安樂。然而奧蘭揚並未死去，在歷經諸多延誤與艱難之後，他帶著少數倖存的追隨者再度接近了奧約。

passages.text: As he approached the city he was startled to hear the notes of the Kakaki trumpet, which is sounded for the King alone. A man working in the fields told him: "Do you not know that the son of Oranyan is King, and rules over us wisely and well? His father was killed in battle many months ago." Desiring his son's happiness more than his own, the old King retraced his steps and settled down with his few friends in humble retirement in a remote part of the country; only at Oranyan's death was his presence made known to his son. The young King, grieving at his noble father's sacrifice, erected an obelisk over the spot where he died, and the monument, known as the Staff of Oranyan, is still to be seen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXV (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他接近城市時，聽見卡卡基號角的聲響而大吃一驚，因為這號角只為國王一人吹響。一名在田裡工作的人告訴他：「你難道不知道奧蘭揚的兒子是國王，治理我們既明智又妥善嗎？他的父親數月前已在戰中陣亡。」老國王盼兒子幸福更甚於自己，便折返原路，與少數友人在鄉間偏遠之地過著謙卑的隱居生活；直到奧蘭揚去世，他的存在才被兒子知曉。年輕的國王為高貴父親的犧牲而悲痛，在他去世之處立起一座方尖碑，這座名為「奧蘭揚之杖」的紀念碑至今仍可見。

title.en: How the Elephant Got His Trunk
title.zh: 象鼻之由來

region.en: Yoruba forest (symbolic pin: watering place near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴森林（象徵定位：伊費近郊獸徑）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXVI

summary.en: Inquisitive Elephant pokes his short snout into a dark hole and is seized by the great snake within; his wife and he himself pull so hard against the serpent that his nose is drawn out into the long trunk all elephants carry now. The monkey who tried to imitate him was simply swallowed.
summary.zh: 好奇的大象把短吻探入地洞，被洞中巨蛇咬住不放。象妻拉尾、大象前掙，一拉一扯之間，象鼻被拉長成今日的長鼻。起初大象羞於見同伴，如今眾獸反而豔羨。愛模仿的猴子也去探洞，卻被巨蛇一口吞下，從此再無獸敢學象。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; animal etiology. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Now it is a matter of common knowledge that Elephant has a long trunk, which he uses both as a nose and as a sort of hand. But he was once without it, and had a very ordinary short snout like other animals. Elephant was always inquisitive and went sniffing about the forest, prying into the secrets of the other animals. One day he came across a dark hole in the ground, and into this hole he poked his nose, to see what was there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXVI (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 如今眾所皆知，大象有一條長鼻，既當鼻子用，也當某種手來用。但牠曾經沒有長鼻，而像其他動物一樣只有非常普通的短吻。大象總是好奇，在森林裡四處嗅探，窺探其他動物的秘密。有一天牠遇到地上一個黑暗的洞，便把鼻子伸進洞裡，想看看裡面有什麼。

passages.text: He at once regretted his curiosity, for a large snake who lived in the hole seized him by the nose and tried to swallow him. Elephant made a great uproar, and his wife came rushing to his assistance; she seized his tail and pulled and pulled, and Elephant himself pulled and pulled, but the snake would not leave go. And as a result, Elephant's nose was drawn out into the long trunk which he still has. At first he was ashamed to appear in the forest, but now the other animals envy him. One day the monkey, which imitates everybody, looked down the same hole thinking a long trunk would let him swing from the trees by his nose — but the big snake swallowed him, and since then nobody else has tried to imitate Elephant.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXVI (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 牠立刻後悔自己的好奇，因為一條住在洞裡的大蛇咬住了牠的鼻子，試圖把牠吞下。大象大聲喧鬧，牠的妻子急忙趕來相助；她抓住牠的尾巴拉呀拉，大象自己也拉呀拉，但蛇就是不肯鬆口。結果，大象的鼻子被拉長成了牠至今仍有的長鼻。起初牠羞於在森林中露面，但如今其他動物都羨慕牠。有一天，什麼都愛模仿的猴子朝同一個洞裡望去，心想長鼻能讓牠用鼻子從樹上盪來盪去——但那條大蛇把牠吞了，自此再也沒有別人試圖模仿大象。

title.en: The Secret of the Fishing-Baskets
title.zh: 魚籠的秘密

region.en: Yoruba river country (symbolic pin: staked weir near a Yoruba river)
region.zh: 約魯巴河鄉（象徵定位：河中魚籠堤堰）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXVII

summary.en: An unlucky fisherman shares his supper with a silent stranger who vanishes; from that evening his baskets overflow with fish, until the last basket holds a monstrous fish that speaks: it is the King of the fishes, the stranger he had befriended, come to reward his kindness.
summary.zh: 運蹇的漁夫在河中下籠，日日空手。某日他遇一沉默的外鄉人臥於岸邊，非但未傷害他，還分與晚餐；外鄉人不語而食，倏忽隱去。當晚起魚籠滿溢，第三日末籠中竟有一尾會說話的巨魚：「你忘了那受你款待的旅人嗎？我正是魚王，特來報答你的善意。」言畢躍入河中，漁夫自此富足。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; gratitude-of-animals tale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Across a certain river a poor fisherman set a row of stakes, and on each stake was fastened a basket in which he hoped to trap the fishes as they swam down the river. But his luck was very bad, and every evening he went from basket to basket in his canoe to find no fishes, or only a few very small ones. This made him very sad, and he was forced to live frugally. One day he found a stranger lying asleep on the river-bank; instead of killing the stranger, the fisherman spoke kindly to him and invited him to share his evening meal. The stranger ate and drank but spoke no word at all, and quite suddenly vanished — only the remains of the meal convinced the fisherman he had not been dreaming.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXVII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在一條河對岸，一個貧窮的漁夫立了一排木樁，每根木樁上都綁著一個籃子，他盼著在魚兒順流而下時將牠們困住。但他的運氣極差，每天傍晚他划著獨木舟從一個籃子到另一個籃子，卻找不到魚，或只有幾條非常小的魚。這使他十分悲傷，被迫節儉度日。有一天，他發現一個陌生人睡在河岸上；漁夫沒有殺那陌生人，反而親切地對他說話，並邀他共進晚餐。陌生人又吃又喝，卻一句話也沒說，然後突然消失了——只有那頓飯的殘餘讓漁夫確信自己並非在做夢。

passages.text: The next evening the baskets were overflowing with fish, and the same thing occurred day after day. On the third day the last basket contained a single monstrous fish. "Do you not know me?" said the fish. "Have you forgotten the stranger whom you treated so courteously? It was I, and I am the King of the fishes. I am grateful for your kindness and intend to reward you." Then the fish jumped into the river with a great splash; but ever afterwards the fishing-baskets were full every evening, and the fisherman became rich and prosperous.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXVII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天傍晚，籃子裡滿是魚，同樣的事一天接一天發生。到了第三天，最後一個籃子裡裝著一條碩大無比的魚。「你不認識我嗎？」那魚說。「你忘了那個你如此殷勤款待的陌生人嗎？那就是我，我是魚中之王。我感激你的善心，打算報答你。」接著那魚嘩啦一聲大響跳進河裡；但自此以後，漁籃每天傍晚都滿載，漁夫也變得富有興旺。

title.en: The Ten Goldsmiths and the Ear of Golden Corn
title.zh: 十金匠與金粟穗

region.en: Yoruba craft village (symbolic pin: smithing quarter near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴工匠村（象徵定位：伊費近郊金匠坊）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXVIII

summary.en: A dying goldsmith sets his ten sons a contest: the most skilful shall keep the village trade. Nine present chains, knives, caskets and rings; the eldest, Ayo, seems to have made nothing — until the last hour, when the family sits round the fire parching corn and the father's full pipe of corn proves to be pure gold. Ayo keeps the bench.
summary.zh: 垂死的金匠命十子競技，技藝最高者可承父業。九人獻上金鏈、小刀、寶匣、蛇形戒環；長子阿約卻兩手空空，遭父嚴斥。阿約請全家最後一次圍火烘玉米講故事——父親拿起身邊滿滿一管玉米，竟發現是純金所鑄。技藝瞞過眾人，阿約當之無愧繼承父業。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; craft-competition tale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A goldsmith in a small village had ten sons, to all of whom he taught his trade. When the old man was dying he called the ten around him: in this small village there was not enough work for ten goldsmiths, so the most skilful should remain in his place while the rest went out into the world. He allowed them a month to make some article of gold, and at the end of that time would judge which had been most skilfully executed. When the articles were laid before him, he found there were only nine: the eldest son, Ayo, had produced nothing. After bitterly reproaching him, the father prepared to judge the work of the other brothers; but Ayo stepped forward and begged him to wait another hour. "Meanwhile, Father, let us sit round the fire all together for the last time, parching corn and telling stories."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXVIII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個小村莊裡有位金匠，育有十個兒子，他把手藝傳授給他們每一個人。老人臨終時把十個兒子喚到身邊：這座小村莊養不起十個金匠，因此手藝最精湛的應留下來繼承他的位置，其餘的則要外出闖蕩世界。他給他們一個月的時間，各自打造一件金器，期限一到，便由他評判誰的作品手藝最為精湛。當作品擺到他面前時，他發現只有九件：長子阿約什麼也沒做出來。父親狠狠地責備了他一番之後，正準備評判其他兄弟的作品；但阿約走上前來，懇求父親再等一個時辰。「趁這段時間，父親，讓我們大家最後一次圍著火堆坐在一起，烤玉米、講故事吧。」

passages.text: As they seated themselves on the ground, the father took up a full pipe of corn which lay near him. What was his astonishment when he tried to pick the grains to discover that it was made of gold! For this was what Ayo had made, and he had prepared the little trick to test the perfection of his work: so skilfully was it executed that all had been deceived, thinking it a real ear of corn. On this account the father and the nine brothers all agreed that Ayo's work was certainly the best. Thus Ayo took his father's place, and the rest set out in different directions to seek their fortune.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXVIII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他們席地而坐時，父親拿起放在身旁的一根飽滿的玉米穗。當他試著去剝玉米粒時，發現那竟是金子做的，不禁大吃一驚！原來這正是阿約所做的作品，他準備這個小把戲，是為了考驗自己作品的完美程度：它製作得如此精巧，以致所有人都受了騙，以為那是一根真正的玉米穗。因此，父親和九個兄弟一致認為阿約的作品無疑是最好的。於是阿約接替了父親的位置，其餘的人則分道揚鑣，各自去尋求自己的前程。

title.en: The Cooking-Pot That Turned Ashes to Gold
title.zh: 化灰為金的炊鍋

region.en: Yoruba village (symbolic pin: hearthside compound near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴村落（象徵定位：伊費近郊灶邊院落）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXIX

summary.en: A man makes his wife cook nightly in a battered old pot that turns the fire's ashes to gold; he gathers the golden ashes secretly each night. A young man who has spied on him trades a fine new pot for the old one — and is said to have spent his life cooking thereafter, earning the nickname Chop, or Food.
summary.zh: 丈夫命妻子夜夜用一口破舊炊鍋煮飯——此鍋能將灶灰化為黃金，他每夜趁人睡熟偷偷收取金灰。村中青年窺得蹊蹺，趁丈夫外出以新鍋換走舊鍋。相傳此人自此終生煮飯，得了「喬普」（食物）的綽號。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; magic-object tale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A man once brought home to his wife a very old cooking-pot and told her to use it every day when preparing the evening meal. The woman was not pleased at the idea of using such a battered vessel and feared her friends would ridicule her, but she dared not disobey and began to use the pot as he demanded. Little did she guess that the pot was a magic one, with the virtue of turning the ashes of the fire, on which it rested, into gold. Every night the husband crept out, when all were asleep in the huts around the compound, and gathered together these golden ashes, which he stored safely away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXIX (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有個男人帶回家一口非常破舊的鍋給妻子，吩咐她每天準備晚飯時都用它。那女人想到要用這麼一口破爛的鍋，心裡很不高興，又怕朋友們會笑話她，但她不敢違抗，便開始照他的要求使用這口鍋。她萬萬沒料到這是一口有魔力的鍋，具有把鍋下所燒之火的灰燼變成金子的效力。每天夜裡，當院子四周茅屋裡的人都睡著了，丈夫便悄悄溜出來，把這些金色的灰燼收集起來，穩妥地收藏好。

passages.text: One day a young man in the village came to the woman while her husband was absent and asked a favour of her: he had taken a fancy to her old cooking-pot and would give her a fine new one in exchange. The woman hesitated, but she was ashamed of the ugly old pot and was glad of an excuse to be rid of it. When her husband found what she had done he was very angry and beat her soundly; but it was too late to recover the pot, as the young man was already far away in the forest. Naturally he had not obtained the pot without knowing its secret, for he had observed the actions of the man who so mysteriously collected the ashes every night; and it is said that from that day the young man spent his life cooking, and so earned the name of Chop, or Food.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXIX (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，村裡一個年輕人在她丈夫外出時來到那女人跟前，向她求個人情：他看中了她那口舊鍋，願意拿一口漂亮的新鍋跟她交換。女人猶豫了一下，但她嫌那口舊鍋難看，覺得能有個藉口把它打發掉倒也高興。她丈夫發現她做的事後非常生氣，狠狠地打了她一頓；但要把鍋找回來已經太遲了，因為那年輕人早已遠去森林之中。他自然不會在不知其秘密的情況下得到這口鍋，因為他早已觀察到那個每晚神秘地收集灰燼的人的舉動；據說從那天起，那年輕人便以烹飪為生，因而得了個「煮食」之名，也就是「食物」。

title.en: The Parrot That Could Not Lie
title.zh: 不會說謊的鸚鵡

region.en: Yoruba village (symbolic pin: threshold near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴村落（象徵定位：伊費近郊門檻）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXX

summary.en: A grey parrot with the habit of correcting every untruth first exposes its lying owner, then its new one — and when the new owner is searched for stolen goods, the parrot's "He lies!" sends the searchers back until the buried hoard is found. In rage the thief wrings the bird's neck, but the truth is out.
summary.zh: 灰鸚鵡慣於當眾揭穿謊言，先拆穿原主人的虛言，再令新主人的謊話無所遁形。新主人竊得財物埋於深坑，搜查者無功將退之際，鸚鵡一聲「他撒謊！」引人重搜，終在小木樁標記的坑中起出贓物。盛怒的竊賊扭斷鳥頸，然而真相已大白。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; truth-telling animal tale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: There was a grey parrot which knew how to speak and had the habit of correcting anybody who did not tell the truth. The parrot was the pet of an untruthful woman, who found the habit so inconvenient that she at length decided to get rid of it. One day a neighbour was passing her house, and the woman called out to him from the threshold to come and see the beautiful tame parrot which she intended to give him as a present. Asked why she desired to part with so beautiful a bird, she replied: "Because it eats a great deal, and I am poor." The parrot cried out: "She lies!"
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXX (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一隻灰鸚鵡，懂得說話，還有個習慣，就是凡是有人不說真話，牠就要加以糾正。這隻鸚鵡是一個愛說謊的女人的寵物，她覺得這習慣實在太不方便，終於決定把牠打發掉。有一天，一位鄰居從她家門前經過，那女人從門檻上朝他喊，叫他過來看看這隻美麗的馴服鸚鵡，說她打算把牠送給他作禮物。鄰居問她為何捨得送走這麼美麗的一隻鳥，她回答說：「因為牠食量很大，而我很窮。」鸚鵡高聲叫道：「她撒謊！」

passages.text: The neighbour took the bird home, and when his wife asked where he had found it, he said it had flown down and perched on his shoulder as he came through the forest — but the parrot quickly cried: "He lies!" The man was dishonest and had stolen many articles which he buried in a deep hole unknown to anybody. When the thefts were discovered, the searchers found nothing in his house and were about to accept his denial, but the parrot cried: "He lies!" In rage he seized the bird and twisted its neck, but the suspicion of the searchers was aroused, and eventually they discovered the hole, which was marked with a little stake, and all the stolen articles were found. Had it not been for the truthful parrot, the secret would never have been revealed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXX (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 鄰居把鳥帶回家，當他妻子問他在哪裡找到牠時，他說牠是在他穿過森林時飛下來落在他肩上的——但鸚鵡立刻叫道：「他撒謊！」這人不誠實，偷了許多東西，把它們埋在一個無人知曉的深洞裡。盜竊事發後，搜查的人在他家裡一無所獲，正要接受他的否認，鸚鵡卻叫道：「他撒謊！」他勃然大怒，一把抓住那隻鳥，扭斷了牠的脖子，但搜查者的疑心已被勾起，最終他們發現了那個以一根小木樁作標記的洞，所有失竊之物都被找到了。若不是那隻說真話的鸚鵡，這個秘密永遠也不會被揭穿。

title.en: Abipa the Ghost-Catcher
title.zh: 捉鬼王阿比帕

region.en: Oyo-Ile (Old Oyo), Nigeria (symbolic pin: the hill chosen for the new capital)
region.zh: 奈及利亞舊奧約城（象徵定位：擬建新都的山丘）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXXI

summary.en: King Abipa resolves to move his court to a new capital on a hill; four nobles send slaves — a hunchback, an albino, a leper, and a dwarf — to haunt the site crying "No room!" His hunters capture the "ghosts," and at a banquet each rebel noble is served his beer by his own supposed spectre. The court removes without opposition, and Abipa is known ever after as the Ghost-Catcher.
summary.zh: 阿比帕王決定遷都於一座悅目的山丘；四位不願遷移的貴族遂派出各自的奴隸——駝背、白化者、痲瘋者、侏儒——裝鬼在山上高呼「無地可容！」。王遣獵人將「鬼」盡數捉回，宴席上又命各「鬼」為其主子上酒。四位貴族見奉酒者正是自家奴隸，嚇得不敢作聲。朝廷順利遷都，阿比帕自此被稱為「捉鬼王」。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the tale is attached to Abipa's historical refoundation of Oyo-Ile's capital. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: King Abipa took a fancy to remove his whole court to a new capital, and for this purpose decided to build a town on a certain hill which pleased him. His nobles did not at all desire the change, and some of them met together to make a plan which would turn the King away from his project: they agreed to send certain slaves of repulsive appearance to haunt the hill after the manner of ghosts. One noble sent a hunchback, another an albino, another a leper, and a fourth a dwarf. When the King's messengers arrived to survey the hill, they saw these strange apparitions leaping about with torches in their hands, shouting with one voice: "Ko si aye! Ko si aye!" (No room! No room!). They returned in terror and told him the hill was haunted by ghosts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXI (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿比帕國王突發奇想，想把整個宮廷遷往一座新都城，為此他決定在一座令他中意的山丘上建城。他的貴族們全然不願搬遷，其中幾人聚在一起商議對策，想讓國王放棄這項計畫：他們商定派幾個相貌醜陋的奴隸到那座山丘上裝神弄鬼。一位貴族派去一個駝背，另一位派去一個白化病人，第三位派去一個痲瘋病人，第四位則派去一個侏儒。國王的使者前來勘察山丘時，看見這些怪異的身影手持火把四處跳躍，齊聲高喊：「Ko si aye！Ko si aye！」（沒有地方！沒有地方！）。他們驚恐地回去，稟報國王說那座山丘有鬼魂作祟。

passages.text: However, one of the royal advisers suspected a plot and advised the King to send hunters to the hill to capture the "ghosts." The hunters returned with the supposed ghosts, who were in abject terror at being discovered; instead of killing them, the King kept them hidden and invited all his nobles to a banquet. When they had feasted merrily, he sent round to each noble a calabash of beer by the hands of a slave: what was the dismay of the four rebellious nobles to receive the calabash, one from his hunchback, another from his albino, and the others from the hands of the leper and the dwarf! Obviously the plot had been discovered, and all four expected death; but the wise Abipa said no word about the matter, and the banquet ended in silence. Soon afterwards the court removed to the new town without any opposition, and henceforth the King was known as the Ghost-Catcher.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXI (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而，國王的一位謀臣懷疑其中有詐，便建議國王派獵人到山丘上捉拿那些「鬼魂」。獵人們帶著那些所謂的鬼魂回來了，他們因被識破而驚恐萬狀；國王並未殺他們，而是把他們藏了起來，並邀請所有貴族赴宴。眾人歡宴正酣時，他派奴隸給每位貴族送去一葫蘆啤酒：那四位謀反的貴族接過葫蘆時何等驚惶——一人接過的是自己駝背奴隸送來的，一人接過的是自己白化病人送來的，其餘兩人接過的則分別出自痲瘋病人和侏儒之手！陰謀顯然已經敗露，四人都以為必死無疑；但睿智的阿比帕對此隻字未提，宴會在沉默中結束。不久之後，宮廷毫無阻礙地遷往新城，自此國王便被稱為「捉鬼者」。

title.en: Tortoise Traps the Elephant and Wins the Princess
title.zh: 龜智擒象得公主

region.en: Yoruba royal town (symbolic pin: pit outside the town walls, near Oyo)
region.zh: 約魯巴王城（象徵定位：奧約城外陷坑）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXXII

summary.en: An elephant ravages the country, escaping every trap by charms, and the King offers his daughter to whoever can destroy it. Tortoise flatters the beast that the people wish to crown him, leads him onto a velvet-draped platform over a pit, and the hunters slay him. Cheated of the promised bride, Tortoise turns the field-mice loose on the crops, then sells peace for the princess — and settles the mice with a promised feast before each harvest.
summary.zh: 大象肆虐田園，諸般陷阱因牠通曉符咒而無效；國王懸賞女兒為妻。龜君吹捧大象「舉國盼你登基」，引牠踏上蓋著天鵝絨與豹皮的高臺，臺下正是陷坑，獵手隨即誅之。國王卻嫌龜君卑小而悔婚，龜君便放縱田鼠毀莊稼；王被迫允婚，龜君再以「歲歲豐宴」與鼠輩立約，莊稼自此安寧。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Tortoise (Ijapa) trickster cycle. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: One year the Elephant had done a great deal of damage, breaking down the trees, drinking up the water in a time of scarcity, and eating the first tender crops from the fields. The King's hunters tried in vain to destroy him, for Elephant knew many charms and always escaped from their traps. At last the King offered the hand of his daughter in marriage to anyone who would rid the country of the pest. Tortoise went to the palace and offered to catch Elephant, and then made his preparations: outside the town a large pit was dug, and on the top of it was laid a thin platform covered with velvet cloths and leopard-skins, like a throne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一年，大象造成了極大的破壞，撞倒樹木，在缺水時節喝光水源，還吃掉田裡初生的嫩苗。國王的獵人屢次想除掉牠，卻徒勞無功，因為大象懂得許多法術，總能逃脫陷阱。最後，國王許諾：凡能為國除去此害者，便將女兒許配給他。烏龜前往王宮，自請捉拿大象，隨後著手準備：在城外挖了一個大坑，坑上鋪了一層薄薄的平台，覆以天鵝絨布與豹皮，宛如一座寶座。

passages.text: Tortoise set off into the forest, accompanied by slaves and drummers, and told the astonished Elephant that the old King was dead and the people all wished Elephant to rule over them, because he was the greatest of all animals. Flattered, Elephant agreed to accompany him to the town — but when he went up onto the platform to be crowned King, the wood gave way beneath him, he crashed down into the pit, and was speedily slain by the King's hunters. All the people praised the cunning of Tortoise, who went to the palace to receive his bride; but the King refused to give his daughter to such an insignificant creature. In revenge, Tortoise called together all the field-mice and elves to eat up and carry away the new crops, and when famine threatened he was ready to help again — but only after the Princess became his bride. The King was forced to consent, and Tortoise then made the pests a feast and promised the same twice every year before the harvests if they agreed never to touch the corn in the fields. They consented, and after that the mice and elves never troubled the country again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 烏龜帶著奴隸和鼓手動身進入森林，告訴大為吃驚的大象說，老王已經駕崩，百姓都希望由大象來統治他們，因為牠是萬獸之中最偉大者。大象受寵若驚，答應隨他前往城中——但當牠登上平台接受加冕時，木板在牠腳下塌陷，牠墜入坑中，隨即被國王的獵人迅速殺死。百姓無不稱讚烏龜的機智，烏龜也前往王宮迎娶新娘；但國王拒絕把女兒嫁給如此卑微的動物。烏龜為了報復，召集了所有田鼠與精靈，把新種的莊稼吃光搬盡；當饑荒逼近時，他又表示願意出手相助——但條件是公主必須嫁給他。國王被迫應允，烏龜於是為這些害蟲設宴，並承諾只要牠們同意永不碰田裡的穀物，每年收成前便會同樣設宴兩次。牠們同意了，此後田鼠與精靈再也沒有侵擾過這個地方。

title.en: Tortoise in Mr. Fly's Sack
title.zh: 龜躲蠅翁布袋

region.en: Yoruba market town (symbolic pin: dancing-ground near Oyo)
region.zh: 約魯巴市集（象徵定位：奧約近郊舞場）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXXIII

summary.en: Hungry Tortoise hides in the full sack his prosperous neighbour Mr. Fly carries to the dancing-ground each day and steals the thrown coins. Caught at last, the drummer beats the sack until Tortoise is black and blue — whence his bruised shell — and Mr. Fly drops him from the air before his own house; he and his wife Nyanribo flee the country in shame.
summary.zh: 龜家斷炊，鄰居蠅翁卻天天背袋赴舞場收錢。龜君藏入袋中連日偷錢，終被捉住。鼓師把袋口紮緊猛擂如鼓，打得龜背青一塊紫一塊——龜甲上的斑痕由此而來。蠅翁又高飛擲袋，正落在龜宅門前；妻子尼揚里博當眾開袋見夫，夫婦羞愧難當，遷往他鄉。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Tortoise (Ijapa) trickster cycle, with shell-pattern etiology. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Once Tortoise and his family fell on hard times and had nothing to eat, but their neighbour Mr. Fly seemed very prosperous and feasted every night. Watching him, Tortoise discovered that Mr. Fly flew away every morning early with a large empty sack on his back and returned in the evening with the sack full. One morning Tortoise hid in the sack. Mr. Fly descended in the market-place of a large town, where drummers beat the tones of the dance and maidens danced before a crowd; when the people threw money, Mr. Fly picked the coins up and hid them in his sack. Tortoise quickly got out and took most of the money with him, so that poor Mr. Fly was surprised to find the sack almost empty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXIII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次，烏龜一家陷入困境，無物可食，但他們的鄰居蒼蠅先生卻似乎十分富裕，每晚都大擺筵席。烏龜暗中觀察，發現蒼蠅先生每天一早便背著一個大空袋飛走，傍晚回來時袋子卻裝得滿滿的。一天早晨，烏龜藏進了那個袋子裡。蒼蠅先生降落在一座大城的市集上，那裡鼓手敲出舞曲的節奏，少女們在人群前起舞；人們拋出錢幣時，蒼蠅先生便將錢幣撿起，藏進自己的袋中。烏龜迅速鑽出來，帶走了大部分錢財，可憐的蒼蠅先生發現袋子幾乎空空如也，大為驚訝。

passages.text: This happened several times, until one day as he put money in the sack Mr. Fly caught sight of Tortoise hiding inside it. He told the drummer, who had been losing coins: "Look inside this sack and you will see the thief sitting among the money he has stolen." "How shall the thief be punished?" cried the drummer. "Just tie up the sack," said Mr. Fly, "and then beat upon it as if it were a drum." So the drummer tied up the sack and beat upon it until Tortoise was black and blue — and this is why his back is covered with bruises. Then Mr. Fly picked up the sack, flew high up in the air, and dropped it, by chance just outside Tortoise's house. When Nyanribo, his wife, opened the sack before a crowd, she found Tortoise inside, more dead than alive; Mr. Fly made a song narrating the whole story, and Tortoise and Nyanribo were so ashamed that they left the place and went to live in another country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXIII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這樣的事發生了好幾次，直到有一天，蒼蠅先生往袋裡放錢時，瞥見烏龜正藏在裡面。他告訴那個一直丟錢的鼓手：「看看這袋子裡面，你就會看見那賊正坐在他偷來的錢堆裡。」「這賊該怎麼懲罰？」鼓手喊道。「把袋子綁緊，」蒼蠅先生說，「然後就當它是面鼓，使勁敲打。」於是鼓手把袋子綁緊，猛敲不停，直到烏龜被打得遍體鱗傷——這就是為什麼他的背上滿是傷痕。隨後蒼蠅先生拎起袋子，高高飛上天空，又把它丟下，恰好落在烏龜家門外。他的妻子尼揚里博當著眾人的面打開袋子，發現烏龜就在裡面，半死不活；蒼蠅先生編了一首歌，把整件事從頭到尾唱了出來，烏龜和尼揚里博羞愧難當，便離開此地，遷往別國居住。

title.en: Erin and Erinomi: Tortoise's Great Tug-of-War
title.zh: 陸象與河馬拔河記

region.en: Yoruba river-bank (symbolic pin: river-bank meeting place, near Oyo)
region.zh: 約魯巴河岸（象徵定位：奧約近郊河岸）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXXIV

summary.en: Mischievous Tortoise tells each of the two great elephants of land and water that the other calls him a weakling, and ropes them together for a strength test. Elephant hauls on land, Hippo hauls in the river, neither yields — until, meeting to drink, they discover the rope binds them to each other, and the trickster is long gone.
summary.zh: 陸象與河馬本是同源兄弟。好事的龜君分別告訴兩位：「對方譏你無力。」遂以粗繩將二者相繫，教他們較勁。象在岸上拖、馬在水中拽，誰也不肯認輸；直到相會喝水，才發現繩索兩端繫的正是彼此。二獸怒尋龜君，早已逃之夭夭。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Tortoise (Ijapa) trickster cycle. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Tortoise was always fond of making mischief between harmless people. One day as he walked along the river-bank he came upon the Elephant and said to him: "The Hippo is boasting that you are only a weakling, and that you have not strength to pull a log out of the river." "That is false!" cried the Elephant, and to prove his strength he allowed Tortoise to tie a strong rope to his trunk and attach the other end to a log in the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXIV (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 陸龜一向喜歡在無害的人們之間搬弄是非。有一天，他沿著河岸走著，遇見了大象，便對他說：「河馬誇口說你只是個弱者，說你沒有力氣把一根木頭從河裡拉出來。」「胡說！」大象喊道，為了證明自己的力氣，他讓陸龜把一條粗繩綁在自己的鼻子上，並把另一端繫在河裡的一根木頭上。

passages.text: Tortoise went down to the water holding the rope and said to Hippo: "The Elephant is boasting of his strength, and he declares that you are a weakling and could not pull down a tree." "That is false!" cried the Hippo. "I can pull down any tree." Tortoise then said he had attached the rope to a tree, and fastened the other end to Hippo's horn. The two animals began to pull, one on each end of the rope; Elephant pulled and pulled, and the Hippo pulled and pulled, and neither gave way. After some time Hippo rested, and Elephant came down to the water to quench his thirst — and then they saw the trick that had been played on them. Snorting with anger, they began to look for the mischievous Tortoise, but by this time he was, you may be sure, very far away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXIV (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 陸龜拉著繩子下到水邊，對河馬說：「大象誇耀自己的力氣，還宣稱你是個弱者，連一棵樹都拉不倒。」「胡說！」河馬喊道，「我能拉倒任何一棵樹。」陸龜於是說他已把繩子綁在一棵樹上，並把另一端繫在河馬的角上。兩隻動物開始拉扯，各拉繩子的一端；大象拉呀拉，河馬也拉呀拉，誰也不肯退讓。過了一會兒，河馬歇了口氣，大象下到水邊解渴——這時他們才看清了被捉弄的把戲。他們氣得直噴氣，開始尋找那隻愛惡作劇的陸龜，但你可以確定，此時他早已逃得遠遠的了。

title.en: The Three Deaths of Tortoise
title.zh: 龜君三死不死

region.en: Yoruba village (symbolic pin: village outskirts near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴村落（象徵定位：伊費近郊村外）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXXV

summary.en: Tortoise's enemies try fire (he draws into his shell), drowning (the sun dries the pool), and burial (a treasure-digger unearths him at the bamboo stake). Three deaths escaped, he is left in peace — the charm is his shell.
summary.zh: 仇家三次謀害龜君：縱火燒屋——他縮入殼中安然無恙；拋入深池——烈日蒸乾池水；活埋土中——過路人誤以為竹樁下埋著寶藏，掘出的竟是熟睡的龜。三死不遂，仇家嘆服「他自有符咒」，自此不再相擾。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Tortoise (Ijapa) trickster cycle. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Tortoise had many enemies, and they plotted together to kill him. One night when Tortoise was asleep in his hut they set fire to it, and as they saw the flames leaping up they said: "He cannot escape. He will die." But Tortoise drew himself into his shell and was untouched by the fire, and in the morning his enemies were astonished to see him walking about as usual.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXV (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 陸龜有許多仇敵，他們合謀要殺死他。一天夜裡，趁陸龜在茅屋裡熟睡時，他們放火燒屋，看著火焰騰起，他們說：「他逃不掉了。他死定了。」但陸龜縮進自己的殼裡，火焰傷不到他；到了早晨，仇敵們驚奇地看見他像往常一樣走來走去。

passages.text: Soon they threw Tortoise into a pool of water: "The pool is deep. He will drown." But Tortoise had drawn himself into his shell and was secure, and at noon the sun shone fiercely and dried up the pool; that evening Tortoise walked about the village as if nothing had happened. The next day they buried him in a deep hole, marking the place with a bamboo stake. Meanwhile a passing man saw the stake and thought, "Someone has buried a treasure here!" He called his friends, and they began to dig — but all they found was Tortoise fast asleep inside his shell. He walked about the village again looking very happy, and his enemies were filled with astonishment: "He has a charm, and we shall never be able to kill him." And from that day they left him in peace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXV (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久，他們把陸龜扔進一池水裡：「這池子很深。他會淹死。」但陸龜早已縮進殼裡，安然無恙；到了正午，烈日當空，把池水曬乾了；那天傍晚，陸龜像什麼事也沒發生一樣在村裡走來走去。第二天，他們把他埋進一個深坑，並用一根竹樁標記那個地方。這時，一個路過的人看見那根竹樁，心想：「有人把寶貝埋在這裡了！」他叫來朋友，他們開始挖掘——卻只發現陸龜在殼裡睡得正香。他又在村裡走來走去，看起來非常快活，他的仇敵滿心驚詫：「他有護身符，我們永遠也殺不死他。」從那天起，他們就不再打擾他了。

title.en: Tortoise and the Silent Fowls
title.zh: 龜與噤聲的雞群

region.en: Yoruba farmstead (symbolic pin: fowl-yard near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴農家（象徵定位：伊費近郊雞舍）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXXVI

summary.en: Starving, Tortoise frightens the fowls with a lie: the farmer's wife will kill the first to crow or cluck. All keep silent while Tortoise steals every egg; the cheated wife, finding the nests empty, slaughters the whole flock — and while the farmers feast on chicken, Tortoise and Nyanribo feast on eggs.
summary.zh: 飢腸轆轆的龜君向雞群謊報：「主婦明日要宰最先啼叫的那隻。」雞群噤若寒蟬，龜君趁夜遍偷雞蛋。主婦清晨見蛋巢盡空，盛怒之下把雞群殺個精光。農家大啖雞肉之時，龜君與尼揚里博正邀友大啖蛋宴。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Tortoise (Ijapa) trickster cycle. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: One day Tortoise and Nyanribo felt very hungry, but they could not afford to buy food. Tortoise heard a cock crowing, and it gave him an idea. He went to the cock and said: "I have come to warn you. I heard the farmer asking his wife to prepare chicken for dinner to-morrow." At this all the fowls were in great distress and wondered which of them was to be killed. Tortoise replied: "I heard the farmer's wife say that she will kill the first of you which she hears crowing or clucking in the morning." Naturally the fowls decided to be absolutely silent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXVI (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，陸龜和尼揚里博覺得非常飢餓，卻買不起食物。陸龜聽見一隻公雞在啼叫，這讓他有了個主意。他走到公雞那裡說：「我來給你報信。我聽見農夫叫他妻子準備明天晚餐吃的雞肉。」聽了這話，所有的家禽都十分苦惱，猜想他們當中誰要被宰殺。陸龜回答說：「我聽見農夫的妻子說，明天早上她聽見誰先啼叫或咯咯叫，就先殺誰。」家禽們自然決定絕對保持沉默。

passages.text: Very early in the morning Tortoise went creeping among the fowls and stole all the eggs from the nests, taking them one by one to his house; but the cock was afraid to crow and the hens were afraid to cluck, and when the farmer's wife came to collect the eggs she found that they had all been stolen. At this she flew into a rage and killed all the fowls instead of one, and while the farmer and his wife had a feast of chicken, Tortoise and Nyanribo invited their friends to a feast of eggs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXVI (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一大早，陸龜便悄悄爬到雞群中，把巢裡的蛋全部偷走，一個一個地搬回自己家；但公雞不敢啼叫，母雞也不敢咯咯叫，等農夫的妻子來收蛋時，發現蛋全被偷光了。她因此勃然大怒，把所有的家禽都殺了，而不只殺一隻；當農夫和他的妻子享用雞肉大餐時，陸龜和尼揚里博則邀請朋友們享用蛋的盛宴。

title.en: Tortoise and Crab, the Two Boasters
title.zh: 龜與蟹誇口記

region.en: Yoruba seashore (symbolic pin: lagoon shore near Lagos)
region.zh: 約魯巴海濱（象徵定位：拉哥斯近郊湖岸）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXXVII

summary.en: Tortoise and Crab fight to a draw on the seashore, neither shell able to hurt the other, and agree they are the strongest creatures in the world — until a boy picks up both: Tortoise is boiled, Crab goes into the stew. Their descendants are ashamed to meet ever since.
summary.zh: 龜與蟹在海邊決鬥，彼此硬甲相抗、互不能傷，於是自誇為「天下最強」。話音未落，一個少年把他倆一併拾走：龜被入鍋水煮、甲殼做飾物，蟹成了少年的晚餐。自此兩家子孫羞於相見，至今仍互相迴避。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; pride-punished folktale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Everyone knows that Tortoise and Crab are enemies. One morning on the seashore they decided to fight to see which was the stronger, but, as both of them are protected by a hard shell, neither could succeed in injuring the other. Finally they came to an agreement that they were equal in strength.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXVII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 人人都知道烏龜與螃蟹是仇敵。某天早晨，他們在海邊決定打一場，看看誰更強壯，但由於雙方都有堅硬的甲殼保護，誰也無法傷到對方。最後他們達成協議，認為彼此力量相當。

passages.text: "We are so well protected by our armour," said Tortoise, "that no one can harm us." "And thus," said Crab, "we are the strongest creatures in the world." But at this moment a boy passed by and picked them both up. Tortoise was boiled in a pot and his shell was made into ornaments, while Crab was cooked in a stew for the boy's supper. Since that day the descendants of the two boasters have always been ashamed to meet, and that is why they always shun one another.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXVII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「我們的甲殼把我們保護得這麼好，」烏龜說，「沒有人能傷害我們。」「所以，」螃蟹說，「我們是世上最強壯的生物。」但就在此時，一個男孩路過，把他們兩個都撿了起來。烏龜被放進鍋裡煮，龜殼被做成裝飾品，螃蟹則被煮成燉菜，成了男孩的晚餐。從那天起，這兩個自誇者的後代總是羞於相見，這就是他們總是彼此迴避的原因。

title.en: Tortoise, Pigeon, and the Horses'-Head Tree
title.zh: 龜、鴿與馬頭樹

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: field with dead horse, near Oyo)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：奧約近郊荒田）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXXVIII

summary.en: Tortoise feeds greedily at his cousins' feast and lets Pigeon wait hungry outside. On the river Pigeon drops him — onto a crocodile's back. Avenging himself, Pigeon plants a horse's head in a field; Tortoise tells the King that horses' heads grow there, stakes his life on it, and is condemned to fire when the head has vanished — until the birds beat out the flames and he is pardoned.
summary.zh: 龜君在表親家中獨享盛宴，讓背他渡河的鴿子在門外捱餓。歸途鴿子半河將他拋下，恰好落在鱷魚背上得以逃生。鴿子再施報復：把馬頭插在田裡如樹。龜君向國王誇口馬頭能如草木生長，國王以性命為注——馬頭已失，龜被判火刑。鴿子悔恨召集群鳥撲火救主，國王赦之，兩友和好離去。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Tortoise (Ijapa) trickster cycle. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Tortoise and Pigeon were often seen walking together, but Tortoise treated his friend badly and often played tricks on him. Once Tortoise invited Pigeon to visit his cousins; at the river Pigeon was forced to take Tortoise upon his back and fly across with him. At the cousins' house Tortoise left his friend standing at the door while a feast was eaten, and when the cousins asked him to invite his friend, the greedy Tortoise replied: "My friend is a silly fellow, he will not eat in a stranger's house, and he is so shy that he refuses to come in."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXVIII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 人們常看見烏龜與鴿子一起走路，但烏龜對朋友很壞，經常捉弄他。有一次，烏龜邀請鴿子去拜訪他的表親；到了河邊，鴿子被迫把烏龜背在背上，帶著他飛過河。到了表親家，烏龜讓朋友站在門口，自己卻去吃宴席；當表親要他邀請朋友進來時，貪心的烏龜回答：「我的朋友是個傻瓜，他不會在陌生人家裡吃東西，而且他太害羞了，不肯進來。」

passages.text: At the river-bank Pigeon took Tortoise up again, flew half-way across, and allowed him to fall — but by chance Tortoise landed on the back of a floating crocodile and descended safely at the bank. Pigeon flew ahead to a field where a dead horse lay, cut off its head, and stuck it in the ground as if it grew there like a plant. When Tortoise reached the field he went to the King and told him he knew a place where horses' heads grew like plants. "If this is true, I will reward you with a great treasure; but if it is false, you must die." The King and a crowd accompanied him to the field, but Pigeon had removed the head; Tortoise was condemned and thrown on a large fire. Then Pigeon repented of his trick, called together all the birds of the air; they came like a wind, beating out the fire with their wings, and so rescued Tortoise. The King pardoned him, and the two friends departed in safety.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXVIII (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了河岸，鴿子又把烏龜馱起來，飛到半途，便讓他掉了下去——但烏龜碰巧落在一條浮在水面的鱷魚背上，安然無恙地到了岸邊。鴿子先飛到一片田野，那裡躺著一匹死馬；他砍下馬頭，把它插在地上，彷彿它像植物一樣長在那裡。烏龜到了田野後，便去見國王，告訴他自己知道一個地方，馬頭像植物一樣生長。「如果這是真的，我會賞你一大筆財寶；但如果是假的，你就得死。」國王帶著一群人陪他來到田野，但鴿子已經把馬頭移走了；烏龜被判有罪，扔進一大堆火裡。這時鴿子對自己的惡作劇感到後悔，便召集空中所有的鳥；他們像一陣風般飛來，用翅膀撲滅了火，就這樣救出了烏龜。國王赦免了他，兩個朋友便平安離去。

title.en: The Chop-Tree and the Whip-Tree
title.zh: 饗食樹與鞭笞樹

region.en: Yoruba forest grove (symbolic pin: twin trees in the grove, near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴樹叢（象徵定位：伊費近郊雙樹林）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXXIX

summary.en: In famine-time Tortoise finds two trees: the little Chop-tree rains food at the words "Tree, do your duty!", while the great Whip-tree only beats. Feasting daily in secret, he grows fat as his family starves; Nyanribo follows him, feasts her whole household at the Chop-tree — and Tortoise's spite sends them under the Whip-tree, where they are beaten to death. When the King demands an accounting, Tortoise leads the court to the trees; the crowd beats itself, Tortoise hides in his shell, and forever after he hides at the words "Chop" and "Whip."
summary.zh: 饑荒之年，龜君在林中遇見兩棵樹：矮的「饗食樹」一經呼喚便落雨般的美食；高大的「鞭笞樹」卻只會抽打。他瞞著家人日日赴宴、日漸肥碩，妻兒卻面黃肌瘦。尼揚里博跟蹤發現後，率全家兒孫赴饗食樹下大快朵頤；龜君懷恨毒言，教他們站到鞭笞樹下——眾人竟被活活打死。國王逼其交代，他領群臣至樹下重演，國王親呼口訣而眾人遭殃。憤怒的群眾遍尋不得，龜君早已縮殼藏身；至今他一聽「饗食」「鞭笞」二字便躲入殼中。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Tortoise (Ijapa) trickster cycle. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: There was a famine in the land, and each day Tortoise went into the forest to find food, returning with only a few herbs and dried-up nut-kernels for his family. One day in a grove he saw two trees close together, a small stunted tree and a big tree with thick foliage. The little tree told him it was the Chop-tree, and at his words its branches waved and a shower of food fell to the ground, on which Tortoise ate until nothing remained. The splendid tall tree was named Whip-tree, and at Tortoise's question of what it could produce it bent its branches and beat him until he cried for mercy. Being greedy, Tortoise said nothing of the two trees, showed his wife only a few poor nuts, and went every day to the Chop-tree and feasted to his heart's content while his family and all the people, even to the King, grew thin — and Nyanribo began to suspect.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXIX (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那地方鬧饑荒，烏龜每天進森林找食物，卻只帶回幾株草藥和乾癟的果仁給家人。有一天，他在一片小樹林裡看見兩棵樹緊挨著，一棵矮小發育不良，另一棵高大茂密。小樹告訴他，自己是「砍樹」，話音剛落，樹枝便搖動起來，一陣食物如雨般落在地上，烏龜吃了個精光。那棵高大華美的樹名叫「鞭樹」，當烏龜問它能產出什麼時，它彎下樹枝抽打他，直到他求饒。由於貪心，烏龜對這兩棵樹隻字不提，只給妻子看幾顆可憐的果仁，自己卻每天去砍樹那裡盡情大吃，而他的家人和所有人，甚至連國王，都日漸消瘦——尼揚里博開始起了疑心。

passages.text: Nyanribo followed him, saw him say "Tree, do your duty!", and hastened back for the whole family of children and cousins, who feasted under the Chop-tree. But spiteful Tortoise was displeased and exclaimed: "I wish you would stand under the other tree and receive your proper reward!" They all went to stand under the Whip-tree, Nyanribo cried "Tree, do your duty!", and the branches began to beat them all soundly until they died. Tortoise hastily returned home, but the King soon ordered him to account for his family's disappearance. He led the King and all the nobles into the forest, feasted them under the Chop-tree, then asked them to stand underneath the other tree — and the King himself cried out "Tree, do your duty!" to terrible effect. In a great rage the people hunted for Tortoise, but he hid inside his shell in a secret place until the King died and a new King was found. Yet whenever he hears the two words Chop and Whip, he hides in his shell, thinking himself in danger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXIX (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 尼揚里博跟蹤他，看見他說「樹啊，盡你的職責吧！」，便急忙回去，帶著全家大小孩子和表親們一起來，在砍樹下大吃一頓。但心懷惡意的烏龜很不高興，喊道：「我希望你們站到另一棵樹下去，領取你們應得的獎賞！」他們全都站到鞭樹下，尼揚里博喊道「樹啊，盡你的職責吧！」，樹枝便開始狠狠地抽打他們所有人，直到他們死去。烏龜急忙回家，但國王很快便命令他交代家人的下落。他帶著國王和所有貴族進入森林，在砍樹下宴請他們，然後請他們站到另一棵樹下——國王自己也喊出「樹啊，盡你的職責吧！」，結果慘不忍睹。人們勃然大怒，四處搜捕烏龜，但他躲進殼裡，藏在一個隱秘的地方，直到國王死去、新國王繼位。然而，每當他聽到「砍」和「鞭」這兩個字，他便縮進殼裡，以為自己有危險。

title.en: Tortoise and the Cloud
title.zh: 龜與雲的買賣

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: open sky-road above Tortoise's compound, near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費近郊龜宅上空）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XL

summary.en: Tortoise contracts with a Cloud: "Pass!" for sunshine, "Fall!" for rain, payment in cowries laid on the ground. He sells fine weather to a wedding-chief and rain to a fisherman, keeps every cowrie, and grows rich — until the cheated Cloud, after once more granting his "Pass!", rolls back and drowns Tortoise and all his family in the flood he asked to be spared.
summary.zh: 龜君與雲訂約：喊「散！」便天晴，喊「落！」便下雨，每次以貝幣為酬。他先替愁雨的酋長婚宴求晴，又替漁夫求雨，貝幣全入私囊，愈發富貴。雲終於動怒：龜君出行喊「散！」，雲應聲退開——待他上路，雲又捲回，暴雨傾盆，洪水中龜君闔家淹斃。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Tortoise (Ijapa) trickster cycle; ends in a local flood retribution, linking to the flood motif cluster. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Tortoise and a Cloud once made the following agreement: whenever Tortoise very much desired fine weather, he was to stand outside his house and call "Pass! Pass!", and then the Cloud would roll away and allow the sun to shine; and when he desired rain, he was to cry "Fall! Fall!" and the rain would pour down. In payment Tortoise was to place a certain number of cowries on the ground each time. At first he duly paid, but on the occasion of a Chief's wedding he sold the Chief fine weather for a sum of cowries and kept the whole amount for himself. The next day he likewise sold rain to a man whose fishing-stakes needed a swollen river — "I will throw a spear into the clouds, and the rain will fall" — and again kept every cowrie.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XL (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 烏龜與雲曾立下如下約定：每當烏龜極欲晴朗天氣，便須站在屋外呼喊「散去！散去！」，於是雲便會滾開，讓太陽照耀；而當他欲求雨水，便須呼喊「落下！落下！」，於是雨水便會傾盆而下。作為報酬，烏龜每次須在地上放置一定數量的貝幣。起初他依約支付，但適逢某位酋長舉行婚禮，他將晴朗天氣賣給酋長，換得若干貝幣，卻將全數據為己有。翌日，他又照樣將雨水賣給一名需要河水暴漲以立漁樁之人——「我將投矛入雲，雨水便會落下」——而再次將每一枚貝幣盡數私吞。

passages.text: Soon, in this way, he grew rich and famous, almost every day someone asking for fine or rainy weather; he stored many bags of cowries in his house and gave nothing to the Cloud, pretending, when two customers clashed, that he had grown tired of holding up the clouds on his back. But seeing how rich Tortoise became, the hard-working Cloud was angry and decided to punish him. One day Tortoise wished to set out on a journey with his family, so he stood outside his house and cried: "Pass! Pass! Let the sun shine on my journey!" But as soon as he had set out, the Cloud rolled back again and rain poured down in torrents, causing a great flood in which Tortoise and all his family were drowned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XL (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 如此不久，他便致富成名，幾乎每日都有人求晴或求雨；他在屋中囤積了許多袋貝幣，卻分文不給雲，每逢兩名顧客的需求相衝突時，便佯稱自己已厭倦將雲背負於背上。然而，雲見烏龜如此富有，辛勤勞作的祂心生憤怒，決意懲罰他。某日，烏龜欲攜家眷出遊，於是站在屋外呼喊：「散去！散去！讓陽光照耀我的旅程！」然而他甫一出發，雲便再度翻捲而回，雨水傾盆如注，釀成一場大洪水，烏龜及其全家皆溺斃其中。

title.en: Nihongi Book I: The Variant Cosmogonies of the Age of the Gods
title.zh: 日本書紀神代卷創世異傳

region.en: Plain of High Heaven (symbolic pin on the Takachiho plateau, Miyazaki — the celestial scenes of the myth have no earthly location)
region.zh: 高天原(象徵定位:宮崎高千穗高原)

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: The opening of the Nihongi preserves not one cosmogony but a dossier of them: an official account in which heaven and earth split from a chaotic mass like an egg, and a series of 'In one writing it is said' alternatives in which the first gods spring from a reed-shoot, from floating oil, or from a cloud over the sea, down through seven divine generations to Izanagi and Izanami.
summary.zh: 《日本書紀》開篇並存多種創世說:正文謂天地如雞卵混沌初開,其後又引'一書曰'諸說,謂神自葦芽、浮油或海上雲氣中化生,經神世七代而至伊耶那岐、伊耶那美二神。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book I), sacred to Shinto; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology. The Nihongi's variant-listing method reflects the eighth-century court's compilation of rival written sources.

passages.text: Of old, heaven and earth were not yet separated, and the Yin and Yang not yet divided; they formed a chaotic mass like an egg whose limits were ill defined but which contained the germs of all things. The purer and clearer part was thinly drawn out and formed heaven, while the heavier, grosser element settled down and became earth; heaven was therefore formed first and earth established afterwards. Divine beings were then produced between them. The soil of which the lands were composed floated about like a fish sporting on the surface of the water. At that time a thing was produced between heaven and earth in the shape of a reed-shoot, and it became a god, Kuni-toko-tachi no Mikoto. Next came Kuni no sa-tsuchi no Mikoto and Toyo-kumu-nu no Mikoto — three deities in all, pure males spontaneously developed by the operation of the principle of heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §1–2 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 上古之時，天地尚未分離，陰陽亦未剖判；二者混然一團，如卵之狀，其界限模糊難辨，卻蘊含萬物之胚種。其較純淨清明者，稀薄舒展而成天，其較沉重粗濁者，沉降凝結而為地；故天先成形，地後奠定。其後，神靈乃生於天地之間。構成大地之土壤，漂浮游動，宛如魚兒嬉戲於水面。其時，天地之間生出一物，其形如葦芽，是即神國常立尊。次有國狹槌尊，次有豐斟渟尊——凡三神，皆為純陽之男神，乃依天之原理自然化生而成。

passages.text: The Nihongi then lets rival traditions speak. In one writing it is said: when heaven and earth began, a thing existed in the midst of the void, its shape beyond description, and within it a deity was spontaneously produced, Kuni-toko-tachi, also called Kuni-soko-tachi; next Kuni no sa-tsuchi, next Toyo-kuni-nushi, who bears many alternate names. In another, when the land was young and floated about like floating oil, a thing shaped like a sprouting reed-shoot was produced within it, and from this was developed the deity Umashi-ashi-kabi-hiko-ji, next Kuni no toko-tachi and Kuni no sa-tsuchi. Another says that in the beginning there was first Umashi-ashi-kabi-hiko-ji and then Kuni-soko-tachi, no others.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §3–5 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《日本書紀》其後則載錄諸家異說。一書云：天地初闢之時，虛空之中有物存在，其形狀不可名狀，其中有神自然化生，是為國常立，亦稱國底立；次為國狹槌，次為豐國主，其別名甚多。又一書云：大地年幼，漂浮游動如浮油，其中生出一物，其形如萌發之葦芽，由此化育出神宇摩志阿斯訶備比古遲，次為國常立，次為國狹槌。又一書云：初始先有宇摩志阿斯訶備比古遲，其後為國底立，別無他神。

passages.text: A further writing says that when heaven and earth began, deities were produced together — first Kuni-no-toko-tachi and Kuni no sa-tsuchi — and that in the Plain of High Heaven there were born Ama no mi-naka-nushi, then Taka-mi-musubi, then Kami-mi-musubi. Still another compares the beginning to a cloud floating over the sea, with no place of attachment for its root; from its midst a thing arose resembling a reed-shoot first produced in the mud, which straightway took human shape as Kuni no toko-tachi. Another again has a reed-shoot in the void become the god Ama no toko-tachi, with Umashi-ashi-kabi-hiko-ji next, and floating oil in the void from which Kuni-toko-tachi developed. Paired deities followed — Uhiji-ni and Suhiji-ni, Oho-to-nochi and Oho-to-mahe, Omo-taru and Kashiko-ne — until Izanagi and Izanami closed the seven generations of the age of the gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §5–6 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 又一書云：天地初闢之時，諸神並生——首為國常立與國狹槌——又於高天原上，先後誕生天之御中主，次高御產巢日，次神產巢日。又一書將初始比作浮於海上之雲，其根無所附著；其中央生出一物，宛如初生於泥中之葦芽，旋即化為人形，是為國常立。又一書云：虛空之中有葦芽化為神天常立，次為宇摩志阿斯訶備比古遲，又有浮油存於虛空，由是化育出國常立。其後乃有對偶之神——蛭兒與須蛭兒、大戶之道與大戶之間、面足與惶根——直至伊邪那岐與伊邪那美，乃終結神代之七世。

narrative.en:
The first pages of the Nihongi, Japan's second-oldest written chronicle (720 CE), do something almost no other national myth-cycle does: they preserve a series of competing cosmogonies side by side, introduced by the formula 'In one writing it is said', and let the reader hear each tradition in turn before the narrative proceeds. The opening account, which shows clear Chinese rationalistic influence, describes the original state as a chaotic mass like an egg of obscurely defined limits, containing the germs of all things. The purer, clearer essence spread thinly upward to form heaven, while the heavier, grosser element settled below to become earth — heaven therefore formed first. Between the two, the soil of the future lands floated like a fish sporting on water, and from a thing shaped like a reed-shoot there became manifest the first god, Kuni-toko-tachi no Mikoto, 'Land-Eternal-Stand', followed by Kuni no sa-tsuchi and Toyo-kumu-nu: three nameless, sexless, spontaneously generated deities who represent the bare fact of existence before differentiation.

The 'one writing' alternatives then rework this frame. One says that a thing of indescribable shape existed in the void, and within it a deity spontaneously produced, Kuni-toko-tachi, also called Kuni-soko-tachi; the same text extends the list with Toyo-kuni-nushi, a rich-land-master deity who carries a string of alternate names. Another places the beginning in the land itself, young and drifting like floating oil, and makes the first emergence a thing shaped like a sprouting reed-shoot, from which developed Umashi-ashi-kabi-hiko-ji, 'Sweet-Reed-Shoot-Prince-Elder', with Kuni no toko-tachi and Kuni no sa-tsuchi after him — a different opening god and a different order. A third, terser, gives only two deities: Umashi-ashi-kabi-hiko-ji first, then Kuni-soko-tachi. A fourth locates the first birth not in the void but in the Plain of High Heaven, producing the celestial triad Ama no mi-naka-nushi (the August-Centre-Master of Heaven, whom one commentator identified with the pole star), then Taka-mi-musubi and Kami-mi-musubi, the two growth-gods who dominate later Japanese myth. A fifth imagines a cloud floating over the sea with no root or attachment, from whose midst a reed-shoot-like thing arose and 'straightway became transformed into human shape' as Kuni no toko-tachi — the only variant that stresses immediate anthropomorphism. A sixth gives Ama no toko-tachi, 'Heaven-Eternal-Stand', as the first god, with Umashi-ashi-kabi-hiko-ji following, and adds floating oil from which Kuni-toko-tachi developed.

After the variants, the text resumes a common thread: paired deities come into being — Uhiji-ni and Suhiji-ni (mud-earth and sand-earth), Oho-to-nochi and Oho-to-mahe, Omo-taru and Kashiko-ne — until the series culminates in the male and female pair Izanagi and Izanami. This line of seven generations, from Kuni no toko-tachi through the mating pairs to Izanagi and Izanami, is what the tradition calls the seven generations of the age of the gods. One appended writing even offers a chain in which Kuni no toko-tachi produced Ame-kagami, who produced Ame-yorodzu, who produced Aha-nagi, who produced Izanagi — eight deities formed by the mutual action of the heavenly and earthly principles.

The cultural function of this dossier is twofold. Politically, it anchors the imperial line in an unbroken divine genealogy: the eighth-century court needed the gods that precede the creation of Japan to be ordered, named, and countable, so that the descent of the imperial ancestors from them could be certified. Theologically and comparatively, it shows the compilers' honesty about the plurality of tradition: the same corpus that asserts one official cosmogony also archives five or six rivals. Some of the variants bear the stamp of imported Chinese philosophy (the Yin-Yang egg, the paired 'principles of heaven and earth'); others look like older native germination-myths, in which life sprouts like a reed in mud. The figure of the reed-shoot links this Japanese material to the wider cluster of creation-from-chaos myths — the dismembered primordial bodies of Ymir or Pangu, or the watery chaos of Babylonian Tiamat — though here nothing violent happens: the world differentiates by settling and sprouting, not by combat. The variant list was quarried for centuries by Shinto theologians, who used the abundance of names either to harmonize the sources or to defend the orthodox Kuni-toko-tachi-centered sequence of later state Shinto.

functions: Legitimates the imperial dynasty by anchoring it in a certified seven-generation divine genealogy.
Exposes the Nihongi's court-compilation method: Chinese-style cosmological framing set beside older native sprouting-myths.
Provides the deity-list (Kuni-toko-tachi, Umashi-ashi-kabi-hiko-ji, the Musubi gods) used by Shinto ritual and by later theologians to harmonize rival traditions.
Explains the origin of the land as spontaneous differentiation of a chaotic egg-like mass rather than through combat.

variants.name: Official Nihongi account: the egg of chaos and the reed-shoot
variants.summary: Heaven and earth split from a chaotic egg-like mass; a reed-shoot between them becomes Kuni-toko-tachi; three sexless deities precede the mating pairs.

variants.name: Writing A: the deity in the void
variants.text_tradition: 'In one writing it is said', Nihongi Book I
variants.summary: An indescribable thing in the void contains the spontaneously produced Kuni-toko-tachi (Kuni-soko-tachi); the list runs on to Toyo-kuni-nushi and his many names.

variants.name: Writing B: the floating-oil land and the first sprout
variants.text_tradition: 'In one writing it is said', Nihongi Book I
variants.summary: The young land floats like oil; a reed-shoot-like thing within it becomes Umashi-ashi-kabi-hiko-ji, the first deity, before Kuni-toko-tachi and Kuni no sa-tsuchi.

variants.name: Writing C: two deities only
variants.text_tradition: 'In one writing it is said', Nihongi Book I
variants.summary: In chaos, Umashi-ashi-kabi-hiko-ji comes first and Kuni-soko-tachi second — a two-god cosmogony with no further list.

variants.name: Writing D: the triad of the Plain of High Heaven
variants.text_tradition: 'In one writing it is said', Nihongi Book I
variants.summary: Kuni-no-toko-tachi and Kuni no sa-tsuchi begin, then the heavenly triad Ama no mi-naka-nushi, Taka-mi-musubi and Kami-mi-musubi is born in the Plain of High Heaven.

variants.name: Writing E: the cloud over the sea
variants.text_tradition: 'In one writing it is said', Nihongi Book I
variants.summary: Before heaven and earth, a cloud floats over the sea; a reed-shoot-like thing arises and immediately becomes human-shaped as Kuni no toko-tachi.

variants.name: Writing F: Ama no toko-tachi first
variants.text_tradition: 'In one writing it is said', Nihongi Book I
variants.summary: A reed-shoot in the void becomes the god Ama no toko-tachi, with Umashi-ashi-kabi-hiko-ji next; floating oil elsewhere yields Kuni-toko-tachi.

variants.name: Kojiki version: five single and paired deities before Izanagi and Izanami
variants.summary: The Kojiki's opening gives a different deity-list (including Ame no mi-naka-nushi, Taka-mi-musubi and Kami-mi-musubi in the Plain of High Heaven) with no 'one writing' apparatus and different orders and names.

language: Classical Chinese (kanbun) framing native Japanese mythic traditions
canonical_translation: W. G. Aston, Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, 1896

sensitivity_guidance: These cosmogonies remain part of official Shinto mythology and are ritually recited at Ise and other major shrines. Records paraphrase public-domain translations for comparative study and should not be presented as a single authoritative 'true' account; the Nihongi itself preserves the variants precisely because they are rival traditions.

title.en: Nihongi Variant: Izanagi and Izanami Create the Island of Onogoro
title.zh: 日本書紀異傳·伊耶那岐神與伊耶那美神造淤能碁呂島

region.en: Onogoro / Awaji (symbolic pin between Awaji Island and the Inland Sea)
region.zh: 淤能碁呂島/淡路島(象徵定位)

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Izanagi and Izanami stand on the floating bridge of heaven, stir the ocean with the jewel-spear of heaven, and the dripping brine congeals into the island of Onogoro. Circling the central pillar, the couple marries — but the woman speaks first, an omen of ill luck, and the Nihongi preserves several variant accounts of how the islands of Japan were produced and ordered.
summary.zh: 伊耶那岐、伊耶那美二神立於天上浮橋,以天沼矛攪動滄海,滴落之鹽凝成淤能碁呂島。二神繞國中之柱成婚,因女子先發言而遭不祥;書紀並存多種島嶼誕生順序的異傳。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book I); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Izanagi and Izanami stood on the floating bridge of heaven and held counsel: was there not a country beneath? They thrust down the jewel-spear of heaven and groped about therewith until they found the ocean; the brine dripping from the point coagulated and became the island Onogoro-jima. Descending, the two deities wished to become husband and wife and to produce countries, and made Onogoro the pillar of the centre of the land. The male deity, turning by the left, and the female deity by the right, went round the pillar separately; when they met, the female spoke first — 'How delightful! I have met with a lovely youth!' The male was displeased: by right he, a man, should have spoken first; this was unlucky. They went round again, and this time the male spoke first: 'How delightful! I have met a lovely maiden.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §5 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊邪那岐與伊邪那美立於天之浮橋之上，相議曰：其下豈無國乎？遂以天之瓊矛向下探刺，摸索尋覓，終得大海；矛尖滴落之鹽水凝結，遂成淤能碁呂島。二神降臨其上，欲結為夫婦，以生國土，遂以淤能碁呂島為國中之柱。男神自左繞行，女神自右繞行，各自分道繞柱而行；及至相遇，女神先開口曰：「何其可喜！我遇見一位俊美少年！」男神不悅：按理當由他這男子先開口；此為不祥。二人再繞行一周，此次由男神先開口曰：「何其可喜！我遇見一位美麗少女。」

passages.text: He asked the female deity whether in her body there was aught formed; she said there was a place which was the source of femineity. He answered that his body had a place which was the source of masculinity, and he wished to unite the two. So they became husband and wife. When the time of birth came, the island of Ahaji was first reckoned as the placenta, and their minds took no pleasure in it, so it was named the island which will not meet. Next they produced Oho-yamato-toyo-aki-tsu-shima, then Iyo and Tsukushi; Oki and Sado were born as twins, the prototype of twin-births among mankind; then Koshi, Oho-shima and Kibi no Ko — hence the name Great-Eight-Island country — while Tsushima, Iki and the small islands congealed from the foam of the salt water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §5–6 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他問女神，她的身體中是否有所生成之物；她說有一處，是女性之源。他回答說，他的身體有一處，是男性之源，他願將兩者結合。於是他們成為夫妻。當生產之時，淡路島首先被算作胎盤，他們心中不悅，因此將其命名為「不相遇之島」。接著他們生出大倭豐秋津島，然後是伊予與筑紫；隱岐與佐渡生為雙胞胎，成為人類雙生的原型；然後是越、大島與吉備子——因此有了「大八島國」之名——而對馬、壹岐以及由鹽水泡沫凝結而成的小島。

passages.text: In one writing it is said: the Gods of heaven addressed Izanagi and Izanami — there is the floating country Toyo-ashi-hara-chi-i-wo-aki no midzu-ho; do ye proceed and bring it into order — and gave them the jewel-spear of heaven. The two gods stood on the floating bridge, plunged the spear down and stirred the ocean; the dripping brine coagulated into Onogoro, where they descended, dwelt, erected an eight-fathom palace, and set up the pillar of heaven. Their first child was the leech, whom they placed in a reed-boat and sent adrift; next was Ahaji, also not counted among their children. They returned to heaven and made report; the Heavenly Gods divined and instructed them that the woman's having spoken first was the cause, so they went round the pillar again, the male this time from the left, and thereafter had children who were the islands of Japan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §6–7 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一書記載：天神對伊邪那岐與伊邪那美說——有那漂浮之國，豐葦原千五百秋之瑞穗國；你們前去，將其治理——並賜予他們天之瓊矛。二神立於浮橋之上，將矛刺下，攪動海洋；滴落的鹽水凝結成淤能碁呂島，他們降臨其上，居住下來，建造了八尋殿，並立起天之御柱。他們的第一個孩子是水蛭子，他們將其放入蘆舟之中，任其漂流；其次是淡路島，也不計入他們的孩子之數。他們返回天庭報告；天神占卜後指示他們，是女子先開口所致，於是他們再次繞柱而行，這次男子從左側開始，此後所生的孩子便是日本諸島。

passages.text: Still other writings vary the quest for land. The two deities stood in the midst of the mist of heaven, wished to find a country, thrust down the spear and found Onogoro, drawing it back with joy: 'Good! there is a country!' In another they sat in the Plain of High Heaven and scraped the island together with the spear; in another, seeing something resembling floating oil, they suspected a country in its midst and formed the island by groping with the spear. One curious writing relates that after the female deity spoke first and they went round again, the couple longed to unite but knew not the art, until a wagtail flew up, shook its head and its tail, and the two gods imitated the bird and so obtained the art of union. The order of the islands also varies from writing to writing, with Ahaji, Onogoro or Aha variously named as the placenta.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §7–8 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 還有其他書記載了尋求國土的不同說法。二神立於天之霧中，欲尋一國，將矛刺下，發現了淤能碁呂島，欣喜地將其拉起：「善哉！有國矣！」另一書記載，他們坐在高天原上，用矛刮聚成島；又一書記載，他們看見一物似浮油，疑其間有國，便用矛摸索而形成了島。有一奇特的記載說，女神先開口之後，他們再次繞柱而行，這對夫妻渴望結合卻不知其法，直到一隻鵲鳥飛來，搖動其頭與尾，二神模仿此鳥，於是得到了結合之法。諸島的順序也因書而異，淡路、淤能碁呂或阿波各有被稱為胎盤者。

title.en: Nihongi Variant: The Birth of the Sun, the Moon and the Leech Child
title.zh: 日本書紀異傳·日月誕生與水蛭子

region.en: Plain of High Heaven (symbolic pin on the Takachiho plateau, Miyazaki — celestial scenes)
region.zh: 高天原(象徵定位:高千穗高原)

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Having made the islands, mountains and trees, Izanagi and Izanami ask who shall be lord of the universe and produce the resplendent Sun-Goddess Oho-hiru-me, then the Moon-god, then the leech child who cannot stand, and finally the violent Susanoo, whom they expel to the Nether Land. Variant writings make the sun and moon born from Izanagi's copper mirrors, and reorder the leech child's place in the sequence.
summary.zh: 伊耶那岐、伊耶那美造國既畢,欲生治理天下之貴子,遂生大日孁貴(天照大神)、月神,復生不能站立之水蛭子,及性情暴戾之素戔嗚尊,其父母逐之往根國。一書另謂日月自伊耶那岐手中白銅鏡化生。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book I); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: After producing the sea, the rivers and the mountains, and the ancestors of trees and herbs, Izanagi and Izanami consulted together: they had produced the Great-Eight-Island country with its mountains, rivers, herbs and trees — why not now produce someone who should be lord of the universe? So they together produced the Sun-Goddess, Oho-hiru-me no muchi, whose resplendent lustre shone through all six quarters. Rejoicing, the parents said that though they had many children, none equalled this wondrous infant; she ought not to be kept long in this land, so they sent her up to heaven by the ladder of heaven to be entrusted with the affairs of heaven. Next they produced the Moon-god, Tsuki-yumi, whose radiance was next to the sun's; he was to be the Sun-Goddess's consort and share her government, and him also they sent up to heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §16 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在生出海洋、河流與山岳，以及樹木與草木之祖之後，伊邪那岐與伊邪那美商議：他們已生出大八島國及其山、河、草木——何不現在生出一個應為宇宙之主宰者？於是他們共同生出了太陽女神，大日孛女尊，其輝煌之光普照六合。父母歡喜地說，雖然他們有許多孩子，卻無一能與這奇異的嬰兒相比；她不應長久留於此國，於是他們將她送上天之階梯，升往天庭，託付她掌管天之事務。接著他們生出了月神，月弓，其光輝僅次於太陽；他將成為太陽女神的配偶，共享她的統治，他們也將他送上了天庭。

passages.text: Next they produced the leech child, which even at three years of age could not stand upright; they placed it in the rock-camphor-wood boat of heaven and abandoned it to the winds. Their next child was Sosa no wo (Susanoo), of fierce temper and given to cruel acts, continually weeping and wailing, bringing many people of the land to untimely death and withering the green mountains. His parents therefore addressed him: it was not meet that he should reign over the world; he must depart far away to the Nether Land — and at length they expelled him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §16–17 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著他們生出了水蛭子，此子即使到了三歲也不能站立；他們將其放入天之磐樟船中，棄於風中。他們的下一個孩子是素戔嗚（須佐之男），性情暴烈，好行殘酷之事，終日哭泣哀號，使國中許多人夭折，並使青山枯萎。因此他的父母對他說：他不宜統治世界；他必須遠去黃泉之國——最終他們將他驅逐。

passages.text: In one writing it is said: Izanagi declared that he wished to procreate the precious child who was to rule the world. He took a white-copper mirror in his left hand, and a deity was produced from it, Oho-hiru-me; a mirror in his right hand produced Tsuki-yumi; and while turning his head and looking askance, a god was produced who was Sosa no wo. The two mirror-born deities were bright and beautiful in nature and were made to shine down on heaven and earth, but Susanoo's nature was to love destruction, so he was sent down to rule the Nether Land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §17 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一書記載：伊邪那岐宣稱，他願生出那將統治世界的貴子。他左手持白銅鏡，從中生出一位神，即大日孛女；右手持鏡，生出了月弓；而當他轉頭斜視之時，又生出一位神，即素戔嗚。兩位由鏡所生之神，天性明亮美麗，被命照耀天地，但須佐之男的天性喜好毀滅，因此被遣往下界統治黃泉之國。

passages.text: Another writing places the leech child after the sun and moon, and explains his deformity: because, when the parents first went round the pillar, the female deity was the first to utter a cry of pleasure, the law of male and female was broken. This Susanoo was of a wicked nature, always fond of wailing and wrath, so that many of the people died and the green mountains withered; his parents told him he must govern the far-distant Nether Land. Their next child, in this version, was the bird-rock-camphor-wood boat of heaven, in which they placed the leech child and abandoned it to the current; their next child was Kagutsuchi, the fire god, by whom his mother Izanami was burnt.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §18–19 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 另一種寫本將蛭子置於日神與月神之後，並解釋其殘疾之由：因父母初次繞柱而行時，女神先發出歡愉之聲，遂破壞了男女之法則。此素戔嗚尊性情邪惡，素好號哭與忿怒，以致多人死亡、青山枯萎；其父母命其治理遠方的根之國。在此版本中，他們的下一個孩子是天鳥磐樟船，他們將蛭子置於船中，任其隨流而去；再下一個孩子是火神迦具土，其母伊弉冉命為其所焚。

title.en: Nihongi Variants: Kagutsuchi the Fire God and the Death of Izanami
title.zh: 日本書紀異傳·火之迦具土神與伊耶那美之死

region.en: Arima in Kumano, Kii province (burial place of Izanami in one variant; modern Kumano district, Kii Peninsula)
region.zh: 紀伊國熊野有馬村(異傳中伊耶那美葬地)

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: When the fire god Kagutsuchi is born, his mother Izanami is burnt and dies; on her deathbed she brings forth the water and earth goddesses, and in one startling variant from her vomit, urine and excrement. Izanagi in grief cuts Kagutsuchi into three or five pieces, which become thunder, mountains and rock-gods, while the blood on his sword becomes deities in the bed of the Milky Way; one variant tells of an annual flower festival still held at Izanami's grave in Kumano.
summary.zh: 火神迦具土誕生時燒傷其母伊耶那美,母臨終生水神、土神;一書更謂其吐物、尿、糞亦化為神。伊耶那岐悲痛,拔劍斬迦具土為三段或五段,化為雷神、山神等;血濺劍刃化為神,草木瓦石遂含火性。一書謂伊耶那美葬於熊野有馬村,其地民間以花祭祀。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book I); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: When Izanami gave birth to the fire god Kagutsuchi she was burnt by the child and died. As she lay dying she gave birth to the earth goddess Hani-yama-hime and the water goddess Midzu-ha-no-me. Kagutsuchi then took Hani-yama-hime to wife, and they had a child, Waka-musubi, on whose head were produced the silkworm and the mulberry tree, and in whose navel the five kinds of grain — a tradition which betrays a comparatively recent origin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §19–20 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊弉冉命生火神迦具土時，為此子所焚而死。她臨終之際，生下土神埴山姬與水神罔象女。迦具土遂娶埴山姬為妻，生子稚產靈，其頭上生出蠶與桑樹，其臍中生五穀——此傳說透露出其起源相對晚近。

passages.text: Other writings embroider the death. In one, when Izanami was about to die she brought forth, besides the water and earth goddesses, the gourd of heaven, to hold water for subduing the fire god when he grew violent. In another, at the birth Kagutsuchi made her feverish and ill: she vomited, and the vomit became the metal-mountain god Kana-yama-hiko; her urine became the water goddess Midzu-ha-no-me; her excrement became the clay goddess Hani-yama-hime. A third adds that Izanami was buried at the village of Arima in Kumano in Kii, where the inhabitants worship her spirit with offerings of flowers in the time of flowers, and with drums, flutes, flags, singing and dancing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §20–21 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 其他寫本則對其死加以鋪陳。其一云：伊弉冉命將死之時，除水神與土神外，又生出天之瓠，以盛水制火神之暴烈。另一本云：生產迦具土時，使她發熱患病：她嘔吐，嘔吐物化為金山神金山彥；其尿化為水神罔象女；其糞化為土神埴山姬。第三本又補充云：伊弉冉命葬於紀伊熊野有馬村，當地居民於花季以花為供，並以鼓、笛、旗幟、歌舞祭祀其靈。

passages.text: Izanagi was wroth, lamenting that he had given his beloved younger sister in exchange for a single child, and crawled at her head and feet weeping; the tears became the deity Naki-saha-me, weeping-abundant-female, who dwells at Unewo no Konomoto. At length he drew the ten-span sword at his girdle and cut Kagutsuchi into three pieces, each of which became a god. The blood dripping from the sword's edge became the multitudinous rocks in the bed of the Easy River of heaven — the Milky Way; the blood from the hilt-ring spurted out and became deities, among them the ancestor of Take-mika-dzuchi; the blood from the point became Iha-saku, Ne-saku and Iha-tsutsu-wo, the father of Futsu-nushi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §22–23 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊弉諾尊大怒，悲嘆自己以心愛的妹換來一子，遂伏於其頭足之間哭泣；淚水化為泣澤女神，居於畝傍之木本。終於，他拔出腰間十握劍，將迦具土斬為三段，每段各化為一神。劍刃滴下之血化為天之安河——即銀河——河床中眾多之岩石；劍柄環處之血噴出，化為諸神，其中有建御雷之祖；劍尖之血化為磐裂、根裂與磐筒男，即經津主之父。

passages.text: Another writing has him cut Kagutsuchi into five pieces, which became the five mountain gods: the head became Oho-yama-tsu-mi, the trunk Naka-yama-tsu-mi, the hands Ha-yama-tsu-mi, the loins Masa-katsu-yama-tsu-mi, and the feet Shiki-yama-tsu-mi. At that time the blood from the wounds spurted out and stained the rocks, trees and herbage: this is the reason that herbs, trees and pebbles naturally contain the element of fire — an etiology of how fire lies dormant in all growing and mineral things.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §24 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 另一寫本云他將迦具土斬為五段，化為五山神：頭化為大山津見，軀化為中山津見，手化為葉山津見，腰化為正勝山津見，足化為闇山津見。其時傷口之血噴出，染及岩石、樹木與草木：此即草木、樹木與石子天然含有火元素之緣由——此為火潛藏於一切生長之物與礦物之中這一觀念的成因解釋。

title.en: Nihongi Variant: Izanagi's Flight from Yomi, the Land of the Dead
title.zh: 日本書紀異傳·伊耶那岐神逃出黃泉國

region.en: Yomi, the Even Pass of Yomi (symbolic inland pin)
region.zh: 黃泉國、黃泉比良坂(象徵內陸定位)

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Izanagi follows his dead wife into Yomi, breaks the taboo against looking at her by torchlight, and flees as she swarms with maggots and thunder-gods. He flings down grapes, bamboo shoots and a peach, blocks the Even Pass with a great rock, and pronounces the formula of divorce; Izanami threatens to kill a thousand people a day and he answers he will cause fifteen hundred to be born. The Nihongi's telling adds details absent from the Kojiki: the spitting purification, the council of Kukuri-hime, and the superstitions about single lights and discarded combs.
summary.zh: 伊耶那岐入黃泉尋妻,違禁以火照視,見妻屍腐爛生蟲,倉皇逃歸。黃泉醜女追之,他投葡萄、筍與桃以阻之,以大石塞黃泉坂,並誦絕婚之辭;伊耶那美揚言日殺千人,他答日生千五百人。書紀此異傳增入吐唾祓除、菊理姬調停及夜間忌單燈、忌棄梳等俗信。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book I); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Thereafter Izanagi went after Izanami and entered the land of Yomi. She asked why his coming was so late: she had already eaten of the cooking-furnace of Yomi, yet she was about to lie down to rest — do not look on me. He did not give ear, but secretly took his many-toothed comb, broke off its end tooth for a torch, and looked at her: putrefying matter had gushed up and maggots swarmed. This, the text says, is why people still avoid using a single light at night, and avoid throwing away a comb at night. Shocked, Izanagi cried that he had come unawares to a hideous and polluted land, and ran away; Izanami, shamed and angry, sent the eight Ugly Females of Yomi to pursue and stay him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §24 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 其後，伊弉諾尊追尋伊弉冉命，進入黃泉之國。她問他為何來得如此之遲：她已食黃泉之竈所烹之食，然正欲臥而休息——勿視我。他不聽，暗中取其多齒之梳，折其末端一齒為炬，而窺視她：腐敗之物湧出，蛆蟲蠕動。經文云，此即今人夜間仍避用一燈、夜間避棄梳子之緣故。伊弉諾尊大驚，呼曰己乃不意而至醜穢之國，遂逃去；伊弉冉命羞憤，遣黃泉八醜女追而留之。

passages.text: Izanagi drew his sword, flourished it behind him, and flung down his black head-dress, which became grapes the Ugly Females ate before resuming the chase. He flung his comb, which became bamboo shoots, which they pulled up and ate — and still they pursued. Then Izanami herself came after him.
