passages.text: One of the visitors was Ko-hu, one was Ko-ch'ung, but the name of the third is lost. The king called the first Sung-ju, Lord of the Star; the second Wang-ja, King's Son; and the third Tona, The One who has Come. He named their country T'am from the name of the port where they landed, and na, which seems to have meant kingdom, for we find that the last syllable of Sil-la is this same na changed by euphonic laws to la. So the kingdom was called T'am-na.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 10 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 來客中一人為高厚，一人為高沖，第三人之名則失傳。國王稱第一人為星主，稱第二人為王子，稱第三人為徒內，意即「前來之人」。他以其登陸之港名，將他們的國度命名為「耽」，而「那」似指王國之意，因為我們發現新羅的末一音節正是同一個「那」，經音韻規律之變化而為「羅」。於是該王國便稱為耽羅。

title.en: Ichadon's Blood Runs White as Milk
title.zh: 異次頓血白如乳

region.en: Execution ground, Silla capital (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新羅刑場（象徵性定位）

period: Silla hagiographic legend from Korean annals, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated AD 527 (Hulbert dates the execution 524)

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 10, eBook #52127

summary.en: The courtiers of Silla, alarmed that the king has fallen wholly under the monks' influence, press him to execute the high priest Yi Cha-don (Ichadon). Tradition says that at the scaffold he exclaimed: when you slay me, my blood will flow not red like blood but white as milk, and then you will know that Buddhism is true. And so it proved: when his head was severed, his blood flowed white as milk. None could gainsay the evidence, and from that day Buddhism advanced with rapid steps; the following year the king made a law against the killing of animals.
summary.zh: 新羅群臣懼僧勢之盛，迫王誅高僧異次頓。刑前異次頓宣言：『若斬我頭，血當不赤而白如乳，爾曹可知佛法不虛。』及刑，血果白如乳。舉國無敢異言，自是佛法大行。翌年王遂下令禁殺生。

sensitivity.note: Buddhist martyr miracle central to Silla history; no living-community restriction on retelling.

passages.text: The king had come so completely under the influence of the monks that now in 524 the courtiers feared that their power would be seriously threatened. They therefore used every means to induce the king to moderate his views. The king gave his reluctant assent to the execution of the high priest, Yi Cha-don.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 10 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 國王受僧侶影響如此之深，以致到了五二四年，朝臣們憂慮自身權勢將受到嚴重威脅。因此他們千方百計促使國王緩和其立場。國王勉強同意處死大祭司異次頓。

passages.text: Tradition says that when he was brought to execution he exclaimed, 'When you slay me, my blood will flow not red like blood but white as milk, and then you will know that Buddhism is true.' And so it proved, for when his head was severed from the trunk his blood flowed white like milk. None could gainsay this evidence, and from that day Buddhism advanced with rapid steps. The following year the king made a law against the killing of animals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 10 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 相傳當他被押赴刑場時，他高呼：「你們殺我之時，我的血不會像血那樣紅，而會白如乳汁，那時你們便知佛法是真實的。」事情果然如此，當他的頭被斬離身軀時，血白如乳汁般流出。無人能否認此一明證，自那日起，佛教便迅速進展。翌年，國王制定法律，禁止殺生。

title.en: The Omens of Silla's Fall
title.zh: 新羅亡國妖異

region.en: Silla capital and provinces (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新羅都鄙（象徵性定位）

period: Silla decline omens from Korean annals, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); events scattered over the eighth and ninth centuries AD

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), ch. 13, eBook #52127

summary.en: As Silla declines, tradition preserves a catalogue of portents prophetic of the fall: a white rainbow pierces the sun, the sea turns to blood, hail falls like hens' eggs, a monastery is shaken sixteen times, a cow brings forth five calves at a birth, two suns rise together, three stars fall and fight in the palace, the land subsides fifty feet and fills with blue-black water, a tiger enters the palace, boulders rise and stand alone and move a hundred paces by themselves, pagodas fight each other, snow falls in September, and a whirlwind starts from the grave of Kim Yu-sin and stops at the grave of Hyokkose — all pointing toward the coming catastrophe.
summary.zh: 新羅之衰，史載妖異屢見以為亡徵：白虹貫日、海血如潮、雹大如雞卵、寺震十六、一產五犢、二日並出、三星隕而鬥於宮、地陷五十尺而水青黑、虎入宮闕、黑霧蔽野、巨石自立而獨行百步、雙塔相擊、九月降雪、杏再花，尤奇者，旋風自金庾信墓起而止於赫居世王陵。韓人皆以為覆亡之兆。

sensitivity.note: Annalistic omen catalogue; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The story of the next century and a half is the story of Sil-la's decline and fall. The following is the list of omens which tradition cites as being prophetic of that event: a white rainbow pierced the sun; the sea turned to blood; hail fell of the size of hens' eggs; a monastery was shaken sixteen times by an earthquake; a cow brought forth five calves at a time; two suns arose together; three stars fell and fought together in the palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 13 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此後一個半世紀的歷史，便是新羅衰亡的歷史。以下為傳統所稱預示此事之徵兆清單：白虹貫日；海水化為血；降下如雞蛋大小之冰雹；一座寺院遭地震震動十六次；一頭母牛一次產下五頭小牛；兩日並出；三星墜落，於宮中相鬥。

passages.text: A tract of land subsided fifty feet and the hollow filled with blue black water; a tiger came into the palace; a black fog covered the land; famines and plagues were common; a hurricane blew over two of the palace gates; a huge boulder rose on end and stood by itself; two pagodas at a monastery fought with each other; snow fell in September; at Han-yang a boulder moved a hundred paces all by itself; stones fought with each other; a shower of worms fell; apricot trees bloomed twice in a year. A whirlwind started from the grave of Kim Yu-sin and stopped at the grave of Hyuk-ku-se. These omens were scattered through a series of years, but to the Korean they all point toward the coming catastrophe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, ch. 13 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一片土地下陷五十尺，凹陷處注滿青黑色之水；一隻老虎闖入宮中；黑霧籠罩大地；饑荒與瘟疫頻仍；一陣颶風吹倒宮門中的兩座；一塊巨石自行豎立而起；一座寺院的兩座佛塔相互爭鬥；九月降雪；漢陽有一塊巨石自行移動百步；石頭相互爭鬥；一陣蟲雨降下；杏樹一年開花兩次。一陣旋風自金庾信之墓興起，止於赫居世之墓。這些徵兆分散於數年之間，然對韓國人而言，它們皆指向即將到來的大災難。

title.en: Kung-ye Thrown from the Window
title.zh: 弓裔嬰擲窗

region.en: Silla palace, Kyongju (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新羅王宮（象徵性定位）

period: Koryo-era annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated AD 878

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), medieval ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: Kung-ye, son of King Hon-gang by a concubine, is born on the least auspicious day of the year, the fifth of the fifth moon, and with teeth already in his mouth. The king orders the child destroyed, so he is thrown out of the window — but the nurse rescues him, and in carrying him to safety accidentally puts out one of his eyes. He grows to manhood, becomes a monk under the name Sun-jong, then joins bandit camps and rises to found his own kingdom.
summary.zh: 弓裔者，新羅憲康王庶子也。生於五月五日大凶之日，口已有齒，王命棄之，遂擲於窗下。乳母竊而育之，途中誤傷其一目。長為僧，號善宗，後投賊中，終自建國號泰封。

sensitivity.note: Annalistic biographical legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Kung-ye was the son of King Hon-gang by a concubine. He was born on the least auspicious day of the year, the fifth of the fifth moon. He had several teeth when he was born, which made his arrival the less welcome.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 弓裔為憲康王與一名妾室所生之子。他出生於一年中最不吉利的日子，即五月初五。他出生時便已長有數顆牙齒，這使他的降生更不受歡迎。

passages.text: The King ordered the child to be destroyed, so it was thrown out of the window. But the nurse rescued it and carried it to a place of safety where she nursed it and provided for its bringing up. As she was carrying the child she accidentally put out one of its eyes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 國王下令將此嬰兒處死，於是他被從窗戶扔了出去。但乳母救下了他，將他帶到一處安全之地，在那裡哺育他並供養他長大。在她抱持嬰兒的途中，不慎弄瞎了他的一隻眼睛。

passages.text: When he reached man's estate he became a monk under the name of Sun-jong. He was by nature ill fitted for the monastic life, and soon found himself in the camp of the bandit Ki-whun at Chuk-ju, where his talents were better appreciated.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他長大成人後，便以善宗之名出家為僧。他的天性實在不適合修道生活，不久便發現自己置身於竹州盜賊箕萱的營寨之中，在那裡他的才能得到了更好的賞識。

title.en: The Mock Buddha Who Read Minds
title.zh: 彌勒佛偽智

region.en: Ch'ul-wun, Taebong capital (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 鐵原松岳（象徵性定位）

period: Koryo-era annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated AD 911-918

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), medieval ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: Kung-ye proclaims himself a Buddha called Mi-ryuk-pul, dresses as a high priest and goes nowhere without censers. Heated to madness, he thrusts a white-hot iron bar into his wife's womb and kills his sons. When he suddenly orders the popular young general Wang-gon to the capital and accuses him of conspiracy — claiming to read men's minds through his sacred office — a clerk drops his pen beside the prostrate Wang-gon and whispers: confess that you have conspired. Wang-gon confesses; the mock Buddha is delighted at his own supposed power of reading minds, forgives him, and seals his own doom.
summary.zh: 弓裔僭號彌勒佛，衣袈裟，持香爐，自謂能讀人心。狂疾日深，烙妻殺子。一日忽召大將王建至京，誣以謀逆，曰『俟吾內證』。俯首良久，有書吏故墮筆於地，俯拾而竊語王建：『自承之！』王建悟，遂自認。偽佛大喜，自謂真有他心通，厚賜而縱之，實自速其亡。

sensitivity.note: Annalistic biographical legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In 911 Kung-ye changed the name of his kingdom to Taebong. It is probable that this was because of a strong Buddhistic tendency that had at this time quite absorbed him. He proclaimed himself a Buddha, called himself Mi-ryuk-pul, dressed as a high priest and went nowhere without censers. He pretended to teach the tenets of Buddhism.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 九一一年，弓裔將其國號改為泰封。這很可能是因為此時一種強烈的佛教傾向已完全將他吞沒。他自稱為佛，號稱彌勒佛，身著高僧之服，所到之處無不攜帶香爐。他假裝講授佛教教義。

passages.text: At last Kung-ye became so infatuated that he seemed little better than a madman. He heated an iron to a white heat and thrust it into his wife's womb because she continually tried to dissuade him from his Buddhistic notions. He followed this up by killing both his sons, and was hated as thoroughly as he was feared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最後弓裔變得如此痴迷，幾乎與瘋子無異。他將一塊鐵燒至白熱，刺入妻子的腹中，因為她不斷試圖勸他放棄佛教的念頭。此事之後，他又殺了自己的兩個兒子，人們對他的憎恨與對他的畏懼同樣深重。

passages.text: Suddenly Kung-ye ordered the young general Wang-gon up to the capital and exclaimed, 'You conspired against me yesterday.' The young man calmly asked how. Kung-ye pretended to know it through the power of his sacred office as Buddha, and said, 'Wait, I will again consult the inner consciousness.' Bowing his head he pretended to commune with his inner self.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 忽然，弓裔召年輕的將軍王建入京，並喝道：『你昨日圖謀反叛我。』那年輕人平靜地問何以見得。弓裔佯稱是憑藉他身為佛陀的神聖職位之力得知，並說：『且等著，我再問一問內在的意識。』他低下頭，假裝與自己的內心交談。

passages.text: At this moment one of the clerks purposely dropped his pen, letting it roll near the prostrate form of Wang-gon. As the clerk stooped to pick it up he whispered, 'Confess that you have conspired.' When the mock Buddha raised his head and repeated the accusation, Wang-gon confessed that it was true. The King was delighted, believing he had actually acquired the faculty of reading men's minds, readily forgave the offence and gave Wang-gon rich gifts — and in this blind confidence sealed his own fate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 就在此時，一名書吏故意讓筆掉落，使它滾到俯伏在地的王建身旁。那書吏彎腰拾筆時低聲說道：『招認吧，你確實圖謀反叛。』當那假佛陀抬起頭來重複這項指控時，王建便招認確有其事。國王大喜，相信自己真已獲得洞悉人心的能力，欣然赦免了這項罪過，並賜給王建豐厚的禮物——而正是這份盲目的自信，注定了自己的命運。

title.en: The Mirror with the Riddle of Two Kings
title.zh: 鏡中讖語

region.en: Ch'ul-wun, Taebong court (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 鐵原泰封宮（象徵性定位）

period: Koryo-era annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated c. AD 918

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), medieval ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: A Chinese merchant buys a mirror of a Silla man, and in the mirror these words can be seen: Between three waters — God sends his son to Chin and Ma — First seize a hen and then a duck — in the year Ki-ja two dragons will arise, one in a green forest and one east of black metal. The merchant presents it to Kung-ye, who prizes it and seeks everywhere for the solution, until the scholar Song Han-hong explains: Chin-han and Ma-han are the two Hans; the hen is Kye-rim (Silla); the duck is the duck-blue Amnok River; the green forest is pine, Song-do, the Pine Tree Capital; and black metal is Ch'ul-wun. So a king must arise in Song-do, Wang-gon, and a king must fall in Ch'ul-wun, Kung-ye.
summary.zh: 唐商買新羅人古鏡，背有讖曰：『三水之間，上帝遣子於辰韓馬韓；先取雞，後取鴨；甲子年二龍起，一在青林，一在玄金之東。』弓裔寶之，遍求解者。學士宋含弘解曰：雞者雞林（新羅），鴨者鴨綠江，青林者松岳松京（王建興處），玄金者鐵原（弓裔亡處）。故松京當出王，鐵原當出亡。

sensitivity.note: Annalistic prophecy legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Tradition says that the fall of Kung-ye was all in fulfillment of a prophecy given in the form of an enigma. A Chinese merchant bought a mirror of a Sil-la man, and in the mirror could be seen these words: 'Between three waters — God sends his son to Chin and Ma — First seize a hen and then a duck — in the year Ki-ja two dragons will arise, one in a green forest and one east of black metal.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傳說弓裔的覆滅，全然應驗了一則以謎語形式給出的預言。一名中國商人從一位新羅人手中買下一面鏡子，鏡中可見這樣的話語：『三水之間——神遣其子至辰與馬——先擒一雞，再擒一鴨——箕子之年，二龍將起，一在青林，一在黑金之東。』

passages.text: The merchant presented it to Kung-ye, who prized it highly and sought everywhere for the solution of the riddle. At last the scholar Song Han-hong solved it: the Chin and Ma mean Chin-han and Ma-han; the hen is Kye-rim, Silla; the duck is the Am-nok, the duck-blue River; the green forest is pine tree, or Song-do, the Pine Tree Capital; and black metal is Ch'ul-wun. So a king in Song-do must arise, Wang-gon, and a king in Ch'ul-wun must fall, Kung-ye.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那商人將此鏡獻給弓裔，弓裔極為珍視，四處尋求謎底。最後學者宋漢弘解開了它：辰與馬意指辰韓與馬韓；雞是鷄林，即新羅；鴨是鴨綠江，即鴨青之河；青林是松樹，即松都，松樹之都；黑金則是鐵原。因此，松都必將興起一位君王，即王建；鐵原必將傾覆一位君王，即弓裔。

title.en: The Monk Toson Foretells a Great Man
title.zh: 道詵預言

region.en: Wang-yong's house, Songak (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 松岳王龍家（象徵性定位）

period: Koryo-era annal tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated before AD 878

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), medieval ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: The birth of Wang-gon, founder of Koryo, had long been prophesied by the monk Toson, who told Wang-yong as he was building his house that a great man would be born within its walls, and left with him a letter to be given to the unborn child when he could read. When the boy was seventeen the same monk reappeared, became his tutor, instructed him in the art of war, and showed him how to obtain aid from the heavenly powers and to sacrifice to the spirits of mountain and stream so as to propitiate them. The night the boy was born, a luminous cloud stood above the house and made it as bright as day.
summary.zh: 高麗太祖王建之生，僧道詵早有預言。當王隆宅第將成，道詵語之曰：『此屋內當生大人物。』臨去，遺書一封，囑俟其子長成授之。建生之夜，家有光雲，燭室如晝。及年十七，道詵復至，為其師，授兵法，並教以祈天助、祭山川之神之法。

sensitivity.note: Koryo dynastic legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Sil-la, AD 878: the night the boy was born a luminous cloud stood above the house and made it as bright as day, so the story runs. The child had a very high forehead and a square chin, and he developed rapidly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 新羅，公元八七八年：據說那男孩出生的夜晚，一朵發光的雲停在屋舍上方，使屋內亮如白晝。這孩子額頭極高、下巴方正，而且發育迅速。

passages.text: His birth had long since been prophesied by a monk named To-sun, who told Wang-yung, as he was building his house, that within its walls a great man would be born. As the monk turned to go, Wang-yung called him back and received from him a letter which he was ordered to give to the yet unborn child when he should be old enough to read.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的出生早已由一位名為道詵的僧人預言。道詵曾對正在建造房屋的王隆說，在他的屋牆之內將誕生一位偉人。僧人轉身離去時，王隆將他喚回，從他手中接過一封信，並奉命在尚未出生的孩子長到能識字時，將這封信交給他。

passages.text: When the boy reached his seventeenth year the same monk reappeared and became his tutor, instructing him especially in the art of war. He showed him also how to obtain aid from the heavenly powers, and how to sacrifice to the spirits of mountain and stream so as to propitiate them. Such is the tradition that surrounds the origin of the youth who, in the troubled days of Sil-la, founded the kingdom of Koryo.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當這男孩年滿十七歲時，同一位僧人再度出現，成為他的老師，特別教導他兵法之術。僧人也教他如何求得天界神力的援助，以及如何祭祀山神與水神，以博取祂們的歡心。這便是圍繞著這位青年出身來歷的傳說；正是這位青年，在新羅的動盪歲月中創建了高麗王國。

title.en: The Priest of the Hand-Washing Water
title.zh: 洗手水活佛

region.en: Song-do, Koryo capital (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 松京（象徵性定位）

period: Koryo annal anecdote, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated AD 1182

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), medieval ch. 6, eBook #52127

summary.en: In the twelfth year of the reign, 1182, a priest claims to be able to cure any disease. Called before the king, he explains: if anyone drinks water in which I have washed my hands he will be immediately cured; after drinking, pray earnestly to Buddha, rise and say 'I am cured', and if you really believe you are cured, you will be so. Crowds of people apply for treatment — and he seduces many of the women who come to him.
summary.zh: 高麗明宗十二年（1182），有僧自言能治百病。王召問之，對曰：『凡飲我洗手之水，其病立愈。飲後當至誠念佛，起而自呼「我愈矣」，誠信則必效。』求療者雲集，僧乘機污其婦女。

sensitivity.note: Annalistic anecdote about fraudulent healing; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In the twelfth year of the reign, 1182, we find an interesting application of what goes in these days under the name of faith cure. A priest claimed to be able to cure any disease. Being called before the king he said, 'If anyone drinks water in which I have washed my hands he will be immediately cured.' He further explained, 'After drinking the water, pray earnestly to Buddha. Then rise and say I am cured; and if you really believe you are cured, you will be so.' Crowds of people applied to him for treatment, and he seduced many of the women who came to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在即位的第十二年，即一一八二年，我們見到一樁有趣的例子，正是今日所謂的「信心療法」。有位僧人自稱能治百病。他被召到國王面前，說道：「任何人若喝下我洗過手的水，便會立刻痊癒。」他又進一步解釋：「喝下這水之後，要懇切地向佛陀祈禱。然後起身說：我已痊癒了；你若真心相信自己已痊癒，便會真的痊癒。」成群的人前來求他醫治，而他還誘姦了許多前來求治的婦女。

title.en: The Tana Well Filled with Earth
title.zh: 太男井填土

region.en: Tana well, Song-do (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 太男井，松京（象徵性定位）

period: Koryo annal anecdote, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated c. AD 1196

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), medieval ch. 6, eBook #52127

summary.en: A saying current among the people shows how superstitious they were and how the eunuchs abused their power: if the King uses water from the Ta-na Wall, many eunuchs will arise and cause the government to be administered badly. So the well was filled up.
summary.zh: 松京有諺曰：『王飲太男井水，則閹宦必盛而政亂。』遂填其井以絕之。

sensitivity.note: Annalistic anecdote; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: There was a saying current among the people which shows at once how superstitious they were and to what an extent the eunuchs were wont to abuse their power. They said, 'If the King uses water from the Ta-na Wall, many eunuchs will arise and will cause the government to be administered badly'; so the well was filled up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, medieval ch. 6 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 民間流傳著一句話，既顯示出他們何等迷信，也顯示出宦官們慣於濫用權力到何種地步。他們說：「國王若飲用陀羅井的水，便會有許多宦官興起，致使政事治理敗壞」；於是那口井便被填塞了。

title.en: The Plum Trees Mutilated for the Yi
title.zh: 李樹被伐之讖

region.en: Kyeryong-san, Ch'ung-ch'ung (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 雞龍山，忠清道（象徵性定位）

period: Choson founding tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 1392-1394

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), modern ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: With the beginning of the new dynasty a new capital must be founded, and King Tae-jo first begins work at Kyeryong Mountain. But it is found that in Silla days the celebrated priest Toson prophesied that in days to come Yi would found a capital at Han-yang, and one of the Koryu kings, planting many plum trees there, had them mutilated as fast as they matured, hoping thus to harm the fortunes of the Yi family — for the Chinese character for Yi is the same as that for plum. The surveys move to Han-yang.
summary.zh: 新朝既建，必遷新都。太祖初欲都雞龍山，工程已啟。然考得新羅時道詵禪師預言：『後世李氏當都漢陽。』高麗某王曾遍植梅樹於其地，且隨長隨伐，欲絕李氏之運——蓋朝鮮語李、梅同字。都遂定於漢陽。

sensitivity.note: Choson founding geomancy legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: According to unwritten law, with the beginning of a new dynasty a new capital must be founded, and King Tae-jo began to look about for a new site. At first he determined to build his capital at Kyeryong Mountain, and went so far as to begin work on it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, modern ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 依照不成文的法則，新王朝肇建之時必須另立新都，於是太祖王開始尋覓新的地點。起初他決定在雞龍山建都，甚至已動工興建。

passages.text: But it was found that in the days of Sil-la a celebrated priest, To-sun, had prophesied that in the days to come Yi would found a capital at Han-yang; and one of the Koryu kings had planted many plum trees at that place and as fast as they matured had them mutilated, hoping thus to harm the fortunes of the Yi family, for the Chinese character for Yi is the same as that for plum. Two commissioners were thereupon sent to Han-yang to make surveys for a palace site, and the capital of the new dynasty was planted there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, modern ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但人們發現，新羅時代曾有一位著名的僧人，名為道詵，預言日後李氏將在漢陽建都；而高麗的一位國王曾在那地方種下許多李樹，並在樹木長成後隨即加以砍傷，希望藉此損害李氏家族的氣運，因為「李」字的漢字與「李樹」的「李」相同。於是便派了兩名官員前往漢陽勘察宮殿的選址，新王朝的都城便定於該地。

title.en: Monk Muhak and the Two-Hundred-Year Warning
title.zh: 無學二百年讖

region.en: Palace site, Han-yang (Seoul) (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢陽宮基（象徵性定位）

period: Choson founding tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 1394, fulfilled 1592

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), modern ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: Tradition says King Tae-jo had a dream in which a spirit told him that Kyeryong San was reserved for the capital of a future kingdom, so surveys moved to Han-yang. There the monk Mu-hak met the commissioners at Ha-yang and told them the palace should face toward Pagak Mountain and Mong-myuk Mountain; they persisted in facing it south. 'Very well,' the monk replied, 'if you do not listen to my advice you will have cause to remember it two hundred years from now.' His words were unheeded, but precisely two hundred years later, in 1592, the Japanese hordes of Hideyoshi landed on the shores of southern Korea.
summary.zh: 相傳太祖夢神人語曰：雞龍山乃留為他日之王都者，都遂遷漢陽。營宮室時，無學大師至，告使者曰：『宮當向爬開山、龍馬山。』使者不聽，定朝南。師曰：『不從吾言，二百年後必悔。』竟如其言，至萬曆二十年（1592）倭寇大舉登岸，是為報應之期。

sensitivity.note: Choson founding geomancy legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Tradition also says that the king had a dream in which a spirit came and told him that Kyeryung San was reserved for the capital of a future kingdom which should be founded by a member of the Chong family.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, modern ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傳說亦云，國王曾得一夢，夢中有神靈前來相告，言雞龍山乃留待未來王國建都之地，該王國當由鄭氏一族之人所開創。

passages.text: Two commissioners were thereupon sent to Han-yang to make surveys for a palace site. It is said that a monk, Mu-hak, met them at Ha-yang and told them that the palace should face toward Pagak Mountain and Mong-myuk Mountain, but they persisted in making it face the south.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, modern ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是派遣兩名委員前往漢陽，勘察宮址。據說有位僧人無學在漢陽與他們相遇，告訴他們宮殿應朝向婆岳山與夢默山，但他們堅持要讓宮殿朝南。

passages.text: 'Very well,' the monk replied, 'if you do not listen to my advice you will have cause to remember it two hundred years from now.' His words were unheeded, but precisely two hundred years later, in the year 1592, the Japanese hordes of Hideyoshi landed on the shores of southern Korea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, modern ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「好吧，」僧人答道，「你們若不聽我的勸告，兩百年後自有緣由記起此話。」他的話未受採納，但恰在兩百年後，即一五九二年，秀吉的日本大軍登陸朝鮮南岸。

title.en: The Spirit Who Reserved Kyeryong-san
title.zh: 神留雞龍山

region.en: Kyeryong-san, Ch'ung-ch'ung (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 雞龍山，忠清道（象徵性定位）

period: Choson founding tradition, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated 1392

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), modern ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: King Tae-jo dreams that a spirit comes and tells him Kyeryong San is reserved for the capital of a future kingdom, to be founded by a member of the Chong family — a dream that redirects the dynasty from its first chosen site and leaves the mountain waiting for a Chong king who never came.
summary.zh: 太祖夜夢神人來告：雞龍山乃留與鄭氏子孫他日建都者。遂捨其地而都漢陽。山至今空留，以待未至之王。

sensitivity.note: Choson founding dream legend; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Tradition says that the king had a dream in which a spirit came and told him that Kyeryung San was reserved for the capital of a future kingdom which should be founded by a member of the Chong family. Two commissioners were thereupon sent to Han-yang to make surveys for a palace site, and the site at Kyeryong was left to the future — a mountain kept waiting for a king of another name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, modern ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傳說云，國王曾得一夢，夢中有神靈前來相告，言雞龍山乃留待未來王國建都之地，該王國當由鄭氏一族之人所開創。於是派遣兩名委員前往漢陽勘察宮址，而雞龍之地則留待未來——一座靜候他姓之王的青山。

title.en: The Hen that Swallowed the Silkworm
title.zh: 雞吞蠶夢

region.en: Palace, Han-yang (Seoul) (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢陽王宮（象徵性定位）

period: Choson annal anecdote, recorded in Hulbert's History of Korea (1905); episode dated c. 1398

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, Vol. 1 (1905), modern ch. 1, eBook #52127

summary.en: An interesting prophecy is said to have been current at the time. The king dreamed that he saw a hen swallow a silkworm. No one could explain the dream until an official more imaginative than discreet averred that it meant Kyeryung would swallow Cham-du — kye means hen, and cham-du, silkworm's head, is the name of a spur of Nam-san. But Kyeryong was the site of the future capital of the next kingdom according to prophecy, so the interpretation was that the new dynasty would fall before another founded at Kyeryong. The poor fellow paid for this bright forecast with his life.
summary.zh: 相傳國初有讖。王夢見雞吞蠶，群臣莫解。有一臣強解曰：『雞吞蠶者，雞龍吞蠶頭也。』雞者雞龍，蠶頭乃南麓之山名。依舊讖雞龍乃後朝之都，是謂新朝將滅於雞龍之朝。此人以多言而遭誅。

sensitivity.note: Choson annal anecdote; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: An interesting prophecy is said to have been current at the time. The king dreamed that he saw a hen swallow a silk-worm. No one could explain the meaning of the dream until at last an official more imaginative than discreet averred that it meant that Kyeryung would swallow Cham-du. Kye means hen, and Cham-du, silkworm's head, is the name of one of the spurs of Nam-san in Seoul.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, modern ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說當時流傳著一則有趣的預言。國王夢見一隻母雞吞下一條蠶。無人能解此夢之意，直到最後有位富於想像而欠謹慎的官員斷言，此夢意指雞龍將吞蠶頭。雞即母雞，而蠶頭乃首爾南山之一支脈之名。

passages.text: But Kyeryong was the site of the future capital of the next kingdom according to prophecy, while silk-worm's head is the name of the spur; so the interpretation was that the new dynasty would fall before another founded at Kyeryong. The poor fellow paid for this bright forecast with his life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hulbert, History of Korea, Vol. 1, modern ch. 1 (1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而依預言，雞龍乃下一王國未來都城之所在地，而蠶頭則為該支脈之名；故其解為新王朝將敗於另一建都於雞龍之王朝之前。這可憐人為這番高明的預言付出了性命。

title.en: One Hunahpu and Seven Hunahpu Play Too Loudly
title.zh: 一烏納普與七烏納普球聲過響

region.en: Q'umarkaj (Utatlan), K'iche' highlands, Guatemala (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 2, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: The two brothers, sons of the daykeepers Xmucane and Xpiyacoc, are skilled in dice and the ballgame. Every day they play at the ballcourt above Xibalba, and their game resounds over the dark place, troubling its lords, who assemble to consider the noise that has come into their council.
summary.zh: 日守者徐穆坎與希皮亞科克之子二兄弟，精於擲骰與賽球。日日於希巴爾巴上方球場對弈，球聲震盪冥府，擾其諸主，諸主遂聚議此擾及其議事之聲。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: There are two sons, One Hunahpu and Seven Hunahpu, and their mother is the daykeeper Xmucane, their father Xpiyacoc. The two of them are wise and gentle in their hearts: they learn the count of days and the casting of the lot, and above all they delight in the ballgame, playing one against seven, face to face, each with the rubber ball bouncing between them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有兩個兒子，一胡納赫普與七胡納赫普，他們的母親是司日者什穆卡內，父親是什皮亞科克。二人心中聰慧而溫和：他們習得日子的計數與籤的投擲，而最令他們欣喜的莫過於球賽，一對七，面對面，各自隨著橡膠球在彼此之間彈跳。

passages.text: They play every day at the court of their grandmother, above the place of Xibalba, which is called the place of fear. Their playing is clear and loud, and it echoes down into the darkness, where the lords hear it: One Death and Seven Death, and the lords of Pus and Blood, of the Bone Scepter, of the Scrapings, of the Wing, of the Packstrap, of Blood Teeth, and of All Seizes You. What is this noise that rolls over our heads and mocks our stone? the lords say among themselves.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們每日在祖母的球場上打球，那球場位於希巴爾巴之上，希巴爾巴被稱為恐懼之地。他們的打球聲清晰而響亮，迴盪而下傳入黑暗之中，眾領主聽見了：一死與七死，以及膿與血、骨杖、刮屑、翼、背帶、血牙與「萬物擒汝」的眾領主。這在我們頭頂上滾動、嘲弄我們石頭的聲響究竟是什麼？眾領主彼此說道。

passages.text: So the lords of Xibalba hold council: let them come down here, they say, to play their game on our court, and we shall see what they are worth. And they send their messengers, the owls of the dark roads, to summon the players below. The brothers, hearing the summons, are glad — they think it is a game and nothing more.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是希巴爾巴的眾領主召開議會：讓他們下來這裡，他們說，在我們的球場上打球，我們便看看他們有何本事。他們派出使者，那些黑暗道路上的貓頭鷹，去召喚下方的球員。兄弟二人聽見召喚，心中歡喜——他們以為那不過是一場球賽，別無其他。

title.en: The Four Roads Down to the Council of Death
title.zh: 四條冥路直抵死亡議會

region.en: Xibalba (the place of fear), symbolic pin at the Candelaria caves, Guatemala highlands
region.zh: 希巴爾巴（懼地），以危地馬拉高地坎德拉里亞洞群為象徵定位

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 2, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: The brothers descend the dark roads of Xibalba, cross the river of blood and the river of pus, and enter the council chamber, where the lords mock them with the order to make their own darts. They pass the cold stone bench and the resinous fire, but at night they are burned to death on the sacrificial stone.
summary.zh: 兄弟二人下行冥府暗路，渡血河與膿河，入議事之堂；諸主以「自製飛鏢」譏之。他們越過冷石之凳與松脂之火，然當夜即死於祭石之上。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The road down is dark and crosses itself four times, black, white, red, and green. The brothers send a mosquito ahead of them to learn the names of the lords, and it stings the carved men on the benches one by one, so that each living lord answers, 'Who is biting me?', and thus their names and ranks are revealed from the darkness of the hall.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 下行的道路黑暗，且四度自我交叉，黑、白、紅、綠。兄弟二人派一隻蚊子先行，去打聽眾領主的名字，牠逐一叮咬坐在長凳上的雕刻人像，使每一位活著的領主都答道：「是誰在咬我？」於是他們的名字與階位便從廳堂的黑暗中顯露出來。

passages.text: But they have no answer for the trials. At the first crossing they fail to call their names; they walk past the rivers of blood and the river of pus without being able to drink of them or cross them dry, and they arrive finally in the hall where One Death and Seven Death sit at the head of the benches. There they are ordered to make their darts and to sit on the cold stone bench, and they are given torches of resin and sticks of pitch to keep burning through the night.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但他們對種種試煉毫無應對之策。在第一個交叉口，他們未能報出自己的名字；他們走過血河與膿河，既不能飲之，也不能乾著身子渡過，最終抵達一死與七死坐於長凳首位的廳堂。在那裡，他們被命令製作自己的飛鏢，並坐在冰冷的石凳上，又被給予樹脂火把與瀝青木棍，須徹夜燃燒不熄。

passages.text: The torch and the stick are failures: the torch is red at one end only, a trick, and both go out at once. The brothers despair, are consumed in the night, and are buried together at the ballcourt of the place of fear. Such is the death of the fathers of the Hero Twins, who must descend in their turn to avenge it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 火把與木棍皆告失敗：火把只有一端通紅，是個把戲，兩者同時熄滅。兄弟二人絕望，在夜中被吞噬，一同葬於恐懼之地的球場。英雄雙胞胎之父們的死便是如此，而他們終須輪到自己下降，為此復仇。

title.en: The Head in the Gourd Tree
title.zh: 葫蘆樹上的頭顱

region.en: Xibalba (the place of fear), symbolic pin at the Candelaria caves, Guatemala highlands
region.zh: 希巴爾巴（懼地），以危地馬拉高地坎德拉里亞洞群為象徵定位

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 2, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: The Lords of Xibalba bury One Hunahpu at the ballcourt but hang his severed head in a gourd tree at the road's edge, where it ripens like a fruit. The tree is forbidden fruit to the lords, and the head begins to speak — the seed of the Hero Twins' return is planted in a tree of gourds.
summary.zh: 冥府諸主將一烏納普葬於球場，卻將其首懸於路旁葫蘆樹上，任其如果實般成熟。此樹對諸主為禁果，而頭顱開始說話——英雄雙子歸返的種子，就此植入葫蘆之樹。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: After the brothers die on the sacrificial stone, the lords bury them at their ballcourt, but they cut off the head of One Hunahpu and plant it in a gourd tree at the crossing of the roads. The head takes root and ripens with the gourds until the whole tree is heavy with round faces, and no one dares to pick them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兄弟二人死在獻祭石上之後，諸位領主將他們葬在他們的球場，卻砍下一胡納赫普的頭，把它種在道路交會處的一棵葫蘆樹上。那顆頭生了根，隨著葫蘆一同成熟，直到整棵樹都沉甸甸地掛滿圓圓的臉孔，無人敢去摘取。

passages.text: The Lords of Xibalba cry out against it: do not come near this tree; do not eat its fruit, for it is ours. The head says nothing to the lords, but it is ripe with speech, waiting in the tree like a lantern on the road of the dead. This is the tree that a girl will approach with an outstretched arm, and the place where the story of the twins begins.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 希巴爾巴的諸位領主對此高聲喝止：不可靠近這棵樹；不可吃它的果子，因為它是我們的。那顆頭對諸位領主一言不發，卻滿是言語，像一盞燈籠般在亡者之路上等候在樹中。這就是一名少女將伸著手臂走近的樹，也是雙生子故事開始的地方。

title.en: Xquic and the Spitting of the Skull
title.zh: 血女希魁克與頭顱之唾

region.en: Xibalba (the place of fear), symbolic pin at the Candelaria caves, Guatemala highlands
region.zh: 希巴爾巴（懼地），以危地馬拉高地坎德拉里亞洞群為象徵定位

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 2, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: Xquic, daughter of the lord Cuchumaquic, hears a voice in the fruit tree and goes to pick a gourd. The skull speaks: 'You do not want fruit; you want my face.' It spits into her outstretched hand, and she conceives the Hero Twins — a birth by word and saliva, not by seed.
summary.zh: 冥主庫丘馬魁克之女希魁克，聞果樹中有聲，遂往摘葫蘆。頭顱言道：「妳要的不是果子，而是我的面容。」遂唾於其伸出的掌心，她因此懷了英雄雙子——由言語與唾沫所成之孕，不由種子。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Xquic is the daughter of Cuchumaquic, a lord of Xibalba, and she hears an account of the fruit tree: the gourds that ripen in the shape of heads, along the crossing of the roads. She goes there alone, and she stretches out her hand toward the round fruit she has chosen.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 斯琪克是希巴爾巴領主庫楚馬琪克的女兒，她聽人說起那棵果樹：在道路交會處，那些成熟時呈頭顱形狀的葫蘆。她獨自前往那裡，朝她選中的那顆圓果伸出了手。

passages.text: Then the head of One Hunahpu speaks from the tree: 'You are not coming for fruit. Is it not plain that you want my face?' And she answers that she does not, but the skull has already risen into her hand: it spits its saliva into her palm, and says, 'This saliva and this spittle have not failed. My face is in it.' So she goes home, her hand wet with the word of the dead.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是一胡納赫普的頭從樹上開口說道：『你不是來取果子的。你想要我的臉，這不是很明白嗎？』她回答說不是，但那顆頭顱已經升入她的手中：它把唾液吐進她的掌心，說道：『這唾液與這口水沒有落空。我的臉就在其中。』於是她回了家，手上濕著亡者的話語。

passages.text: In six months she carries the twins, without having known a man. Her father hears of it and questions her, but she answers only for herself: the child was put in her palm, not in her lap. She is condemned to be killed for the disgrace, and the owls who lead her out are given a substitute — they cut open a crocodile's belly and set its blood on the petals of a red bottle flower, faking the maiden's blood, and she is sent up the dark roads alive.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 六個月後，她懷著雙生子，卻未曾認識過男人。她的父親聽聞此事便盤問她，但她只為自己辯白：孩子是被放進她的掌心，而非她的懷中。她因這樁恥辱被判處死刑，帶她出去的貓頭鷹得到了一個替身——他們剖開一條鱷魚的肚子，把牠的血塗在紅瓶花的瓣上，偽作少女的血，而她則活著被送上黑暗的道路。

title.en: The Net and the Maize Ear: Xmucane Tests Xquic
title.zh: 網與玉米穗：徐穆坎試希魁克

region.en: Q'umarkaj (Utatlan), K'iche' highlands, Guatemala (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 2, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: Xquic presents herself to Xmucane as daughter-in-law; the grandmother refuses and tests her with impossible tasks, sending her for netfuls of corn where no corn grows. The maiden goes straight to One Hunahpu's former field, and the maize pours itself into the net. Xmucane is convinced: the twins' mother has arrived.
summary.zh: 希魁克向徐穆坎自稱媳婦；祖母不信，以不可能之事試之，遣其至無玉米之地取一網玉米。希魁克直往一烏納普昔日之田，玉米竟自行落入網中。徐穆坎信服：雙子之母已然到來。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Xquic comes up out of the dark roads to the house of Xmucane and Xpiyacoc and says, 'I have come, my mother-in-law.' But the grandmother is not pleased: she sees only a girl who has come to eat their food. 'Who are you, and where is your husband?', she asks, and will not allow her to sit at the hearth.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 斯琪克從黑暗的道路上來，到了斯穆卡內與斯皮亞科克的家中，說道：『我來了，我的婆婆。』但祖母並不歡喜：她只看到一個來吃他們食物的少女。『你是誰，你的丈夫在哪裡？』她問道，且不許她坐在爐邊。

passages.text: Then the grandmother sets a test: 'Go and bring me a netful of corn, and we shall see whether you are my daughter-in-law.' She sends her to a field where nothing has been planted. But Xquic goes to the field of One Hunahpu, where the boys played their ballgame, and speaks to the night: two ears of corn open themselves, one of red and one of white, and the husks pour their grain into her net until it is full.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著，祖母設下一個考驗：「去替我帶一整網的玉米回來，我們便看看你究竟是不是我的媳婦。」她把她派到一片什麼也沒種的田裡。但希基克去到「一胡納赫普」的田地，那是兄弟倆玩球戲的地方，她對黑夜說話：兩穗玉米自行綻開，一穗紅的、一穗白的，玉米苞把穀粒傾入她的網中，直到裝滿為止。

passages.text: She leaves the corn in the house and sets a red bottle flower in the corner, the flower she was given on the road. The grandmother, furious, goes out to the field, but the field tells her by the leaves that her son has been avenged in this maiden: the corn answers for Xquic. So Xmucane takes her in, and the twins she carries will avenge the deaths at the ballcourt.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她把玉米留在屋裡，並在角落放上一朵紅瓶花，那是她在路上被賜予的花。祖母勃然大怒，走到田裡去，但田地藉著葉子告訴她：她的兒子已在這名少女身上得到了報復；玉米替希基克作了回答。於是希穆卡內收留了她，而她自己所懷的雙胞胎，將為球場上的死難復仇。

title.en: The Monkey Brothers Envy the Twins
title.zh: 猴兄之妒

region.en: Q'umarkaj (Utatlan), K'iche' highlands, Guatemala (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 2, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: Xmucane bears the twins Hunahpu and Xbalanque, but the elder brothers Hun Batz and Hun Chouen — flute players, singers, and writers — despise them. The little ones are sent away to the fields with nothing, and the monkey brothers resolve in their jealousy to be rid of them.
summary.zh: 徐穆坎產下雙子烏納普與斯巴蘭克，而長兄洪·巴茲與洪·秋恩——笛手、歌者與書家——卻輕視二人。幼弟被遣往田間，一無所有；猴兄妒火中燒，決意除之。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In due time the twins are born, Hunahpu and Xbalanque, sons of Xquic. But there are already two older sons in the house, Hun Batz and Hun Chouen, sons of Xmucane, skilled in flute and drum, in song and in painting, and in the count of days. They resent the newcomers and treat them like slaves sent to clear ground and carry burdens.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 時候到了，雙胞胎誕生了，就是希基克所生的胡納赫普與希巴蘭克。但屋裡早已有兩個年長的兒子，胡恩巴茨與胡恩喬恩，是希穆卡內的兒子，擅長笛與鼓、歌唱與繪畫，以及計算日子。他們憎惡這兩個新來者，把他們當作被派去開墾土地、搬運重物的奴僕一般對待。

passages.text: The grandmother favors the elder pair and gives the twins nothing; they are given only the hard work of the cornfield, day after day, while their brothers play music. Yet the little ones are patient, and they say nothing of what they intend, for they already know the instruments their fathers used in the ballgame and the count of days kept in the house.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 祖母偏愛年長的那一對，什麼也不給雙胞胎；他們只分得玉米田裡的苦活，日復一日，而他們的兄長卻奏樂取樂。然而這兩個小的很有耐性，對自己的打算隻字不提，因為他們早已知道父親們在球戲中所用的器具，以及家中世代相傳的計算日子之法。

title.en: The Garden That Rewove Itself
title.zh: 自重生長的花園

region.en: Q'umarkaj (Utatlan), K'iche' highlands, Guatemala (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 2, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: Each night the twins clear the garden, and each night the cut brush stands up and re-weaves itself. The elder brothers come to mock, and the little boys explain they had been cutting their own bodies. A singing bird reveals the trick to Hun Batz and Hun Chouen, who set a snare — and are caught in it instead.
summary.zh: 雙子夜夜墾園，然被砍的枝蔓夜夜復立，自行交織重生。猴兄前來嘲弄，幼弟則答曰所砍乃己身。一鳴鳥向洪·巴茲與洪·秋恩洩露其術，二人遂設陷——卻自陷其中。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The twins go out to clear the garden, cutting vines and brush all day; but at night the plants straighten themselves and close the clearing as if nothing had been cut. When the elder brothers come to laugh at their uselessness, the twins answer: we cut the ground of our own bodies; the garden is only its shadow.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 雙胞胎出門去開墾園地，整日砍伐藤蔓與灌木；但到了夜裡，那些植物便自行挺直，把開墾出的空地重新合攏，彷彿什麼也沒被砍過。當兄長們前來嘲笑他們徒勞無功時，雙胞胎回答：我們砍的是自己身體的土地；園地不過是它的影子。

passages.text: A bird called the earth-keeper, or keeper of the singing, watches them work from a stump and sings about what it sees. The elder brothers offer it a cigar and a Chapopote, asking how the little ones manage. The bird tells them of the nightly re-weaving, and they set their snare in the garden to catch whatever restores the brush.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一隻名叫「大地守護者」、或「歌唱守護者」的鳥，從樹樁上看著他們工作，並唱出牠所見的一切。兄長們遞給牠一支雪茄與一份查波波特，問那兩個小的究竟是如何辦到的。那鳥便把夜夜重新編織的事告訴了他們，於是他們在園地裡設下陷阱，要捉住那使灌木復原的東西。

passages.text: The snare takes the elder brothers themselves: they walk into it, and the trap tightens as they step, catching them by the ankles. They cry out and cannot free themselves, and the little boys come upon them caught like animals. It is the moment when the garden has chosen its own keepers.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 陷阱捉住了兄长们自己：他们走入其中，随着他们迈步，机关便收紧，套住了他们的脚踝。他们呼喊，却无法挣脱，而那两个小男孩来到近前，见他们像野兽一样被擒住了。这正是园子已选定了自己的看守者的时刻。

title.en: The Tree of Game Birds: The Elder Brothers Become Monkeys
title.zh: 獵鳥之樹：猴兄化形

region.en: Q'umarkaj (Utatlan), K'iche' highlands, Guatemala (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 2, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: The twins send the humiliated elders up a tree for birds, then make the trunk grow; the brothers are stranded above, their breechclouts becoming tails and their faces muzzles. They descend as howler monkeys and remain monkeys, artists of the forest, while Xmucane sings of her sons' fate.
summary.zh: 雙子遣受辱的兄長上樹捉鳥，繼而令樹幹生長；二人被困樹頂，腰布化為尾，臉化為獸吻。落地時已為吼猴，永為林間藝者；徐穆坎則歌其子之命。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: After the snare, the twins tell their brothers: go up the tree and bring us the birds. Hun Batz and Hun Chouen climb, wishing for game, and the little boys stay below and enlarge the tree: the trunk thickens and rises, and the climbers cannot get down. They call out, but the tree keeps growing, and their breechclouts grow tight and hairy into tails.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 设下陷阱之后，双胞胎对兄长们说：上树去，把鸟给我们带下来。胡恩·巴茨与胡恩·乔恩爬上树去，一心盼着猎物，而那两个小男孩留在下面，把树变大：树干变粗、升高，攀爬的人再也下不来。他们呼喊，可树不停地生长，他们的缠腰布也绷紧了，长出毛来，变成了尾巴。

passages.text: Their faces change too: their mouths thrust out and their eyes go wild. They come down as howler monkeys, screeching in the branches, and they never become human again. But they do not forget their art: the monkeys still play the flute and the drum, paint, and keep the old songs, artists transformed by their own envy.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他们的面容也变了：嘴巴向前突出，眼睛变得狂野。他们下来时已是吼猴，在枝头尖声鸣叫，从此再未变回人形。但他们并未忘记自己的技艺：猴子们依旧吹笛击鼓、绘画，并保存着古老的歌谣，这些艺人被自己的嫉妒所改变。

passages.text: Xmucane is frightened and angry; she sings a spell to call them back, blowing a bone whistle and chanting their names, and the monkeys answer from the trees with their pipes. But the twins have done with them, and the grandmother must accept what the garden has decided: the singers are monkeys, and the ballplayers remain.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 什穆卡内又惊又怒；她唱起咒语召他们回来，吹响骨哨，念诵他们的名字，猴子们便用他们的排箫从树上应答。但双胞胎已与他们了结，祖母只得接受园子所决定的事：歌者成了猴子，而球手依旧留存。

title.en: The Rat and the Instruments of the Fathers
title.zh: 鼠與父親的器物

region.en: Q'umarkaj (Utatlan), K'iche' highlands, Guatemala (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 2, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: A rat lives in the rafters of Xmucane's house, gnawing and telling the twins about the ballgame gear of their dead fathers hidden above. The boys bribe it with dried chili, lower it in a jar, and recover the rubber ball, yoke, arm guards, and paint — and with these they begin to play at the same court where their fathers died.
summary.zh: 一鼠居於徐穆坎家屋椽上，啃咬並向雙子述及其亡父藏於其上的賽球器物。男孩以乾辣椒賄之，以瓦罐垂之而上，取回橡膠球、腰軛、護臂與顏料——從而在父親殞命之場開始賽球。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In the house of Xmucane a rat has made its home above the rafters, and it gnaws there and sings to itself. The twins hear it and ask what it knows, and the rat tells them: above your heads are the instruments of your fathers — the ball, the yoke, the arm guards, the headdresses, the paint and the paper of the ballgame, all hidden since they went down to Xibalba.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在什穆卡内的屋子里，一只老鼠在椽子上方安了家，在那里啃咬，自吟自唱。双胞胎听见了，便问它知道些什么，老鼠告诉他们：你们头顶之上是你们父辈的器具——球、轭、护臂、头饰、颜料以及球赛的纸，自他们下到西巴尔巴以来，全都藏在那里。

passages.text: The boys promise it a meal of dried chili and a gourd of corn gruel if it will bring them the gear, and they lower it by a rope in a jar. The rat chews through the hiding place and drops down the instruments, one by one, until the ball rolls on the floor of the house.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 男孩们许诺，若它肯把器具取来，便给它一顿干辣椒和一葫芦玉米粥，他们用绳子把它吊在一只罐子里放下去。老鼠咬穿藏物之处，把器具一件一件地丢下来，直到那只球滚落在屋子的地面上。

passages.text: Then the twins take the ball to the great court above the place of fear, where their fathers used to play, and they begin the game. The sound of it rolls down into the dark, and the Lords of Xibalba hear it again: someone is playing above us, and it is not the players who died.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 2 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著，雙生子帶著球前往恐懼之地之上的大球場，也就是他們的父親昔日打球之處，開始比賽。球的聲響滾落進黑暗之中，希巴爾巴的眾領主又聽見了：有人在我們上方打球，而且不是那些死去的球員。

title.en: The Lords Hear the Ball Again
title.zh: 冥主重聞球聲

region.en: Xibalba (the place of fear), symbolic pin at the Candelaria caves, Guatemala highlands
region.zh: 希巴爾巴（懼地），以危地馬拉高地坎德拉里亞洞群為象徵定位

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: The Lords of Xibalba hear the ballgame of the new players and are enraged that their court is being used without permission. They send messengers with the summons to descend, and Xmucane, remembering her sons' fathers, weeps — but the twins plant a substitute pair of brothers in the house and go down smiling.
summary.zh: 冥主聞得新球者之球聲，怒其球場未經許可而被用。遂遣使者下召，命其下行。徐穆坎念及其子之父，泣之——然雙子在屋中安置一對替身兄弟，含笑下行。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The game is heard again over the place of fear, and the lords rise up in their council: who is playing on our court without leave? They remember the brothers who were put to death for this very game, and they send messengers to the house of Xmucane to summon the new players down, by night, with the same courteous menace.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 球賽的聲響再度越過恐懼之地傳來，眾領主在議會中起身：是誰未經允許在我們的球場上打球？他們想起正是為了這場球賽而被處死的兄弟，於是派遣使者前往什穆卡內之家，以同樣彬彬有禮的威脅，趁夜召喚新的球員下來。

passages.text: The twins accept the invitation, but first they speak with their grandmother and plant in the house two substitutes — a pair of maize-stalk men shaped in their image — telling Xmucane that if she calls them and they do not answer, she will know they have gone below, and that these will take their place in the household.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 雙生子接受了邀請，但他們先與祖母商議，並在家中安置了兩名替身——一對依他們形貌塑成的玉米稈人——告訴什穆卡內：若她呼喚他們而他們不應，便知他們已下到地底，而這兩人將在家中取代他們的位置。

passages.text: Then they go down the roads of Xibalba, and this time they pass the crossings in order, naming themselves and their road as they go, and they arrive in the hall of the lords without delay, ready to play the game that killed their fathers.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著他們走上希巴爾巴的道路，這回他們依序通過各個交叉路口，一路報出自己的名字與所行之路，毫不延遲地抵達眾領主的殿堂，準備進行那場害死他們父親的球賽。

title.en: The House of Darkness and the Fireflies
title.zh: 黑暗之屋與螢火蟲

region.en: Xibalba (the place of fear), symbolic pin at the Candelaria caves, Guatemala highlands
region.zh: 希巴爾巴（懼地），以危地馬拉高地坎德拉里亞洞群為象徵定位

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: The twins are given the second trial their fathers failed: keep a red cigar and a pitch torch burning through the night in the House of Darkness. Instead of lighting them, they fix a red-feathered firefly to each — and at dawn, having burned nothing, they are alive and the game goes on.
summary.zh: 雙子遭遇其父失敗的同一試煉：須於黑暗之屋中，令紅雪茄與松脂火把徹夜不熄。他們不點燃真火，而以兩隻紅羽螢火蟲充之——黎明時火未燃而人未死，賽事繼續。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The lords of the place of fear are delighted: these are the players who will die as their fathers did. On the first night they are shut in the House of Darkness, and a red cigar and a stick of pitch are set before them with the order to keep them whole and burning until morning, without consuming them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 恐懼之地的眾領主大喜：這些就是將如他們父親一般死去的球員。第一夜，他們被關進黑暗之屋，一支紅雪茄與一根瀝青棒被放在他們面前，命令他們要讓這兩樣東西完好無損地燃燒到天明，且不得將其燒盡。

passages.text: The twins do nothing of the kind: they set a firefly on the tip of the cigar and another on the end of the torch, and the glow and motion of the red-flies deceive the watchers in the dark. All night the watchers see the lights moving and burning, and the twins lie down unburned.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 雙生子卻完全不這麼做：他們在雪茄尖端放了一隻螢火蟲，又在火炬末端放了另一隻，紅螢的光亮與動態騙過了黑暗中的看守者。整夜，看守者看著那些光點移動、燃燒，而雙生子安然躺下，毫髮無傷。

passages.text: At dawn the cigar and the stick are brought out whole, unlit, and the lords are furious and confused. 'Who brought these in? Where did they come from? They look like us.' The twins have passed the first house, and the lords begin to suspect they are not boys at all but something beyond their tricks.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 黎明時分，雪茄與木棍被完好無損、未曾點燃地送了出來，眾領主又怒又惑。「是誰把這些東西帶進來的？它們從哪兒來的？它們看起來和我們一模一樣。」雙胞胎已經通過了第一座屋子，眾領主開始懷疑他們根本不是男孩，而是某種超乎他們把戲之外的東西。

title.en: Razor, Cold, and Jaguar Houses
title.zh: 利刃、嚴寒與美洲豹之屋

region.en: Xibalba (the place of fear), symbolic pin at the Candelaria caves, Guatemala highlands
region.zh: 希巴爾巴（懼地），以危地馬拉高地坎德拉里亞洞群為象徵定位

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: Night after night the houses try them: the House of Razors, whose blades the twins talk into gathering up their edges; the House of Cold, kept off with old pine knots; the House of Jaguars, whose teeth they feed with the bones of other animals. Each morning they walk out whole and cheerful.
summary.zh: 夜復一夜，諸屋試煉他們：利刃之屋——雙子以言語令利刃自行收攏鋒芒；嚴寒之屋——以陳年松柴御寒；美洲豹之屋——以獸骨餵其利齒。每個清晨，他們完好而歡愉地走出。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Next is the House of Razors, full of blades that move on their own, the razors that belong to Xibalba. But the twins speak to them: 'Yours are the bones; ours is the flesh.' And the razors stand down and gather themselves up and keep quiet in the corners, so the boys sleep soundly among their edges.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著是剃刀之屋，滿是自行移動的刀刃，那是屬於希巴爾巴的剃刀。但雙胞胎對它們說話：「骨頭歸你們；血肉歸我們。」於是剃刀停了下來，收攏自身，在角落裡保持安靜，男孩們便在刀刃之間安然入睡。

passages.text: Then comes the House of Cold, where the frozen wind kills whoever lies in it; they warm themselves with pine knots saved from the woodpile, old ones, and pass the night. After it, the House of Jaguars, loud with cats that bite; but the twins scatter the bones of other animals for them and feed them what jaguars like, and the cats are content and do not touch the boys.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然後是寒冷之屋，凍結的風會殺死任何躺臥其中的人；他們用從柴堆裡留下的松節——陳舊的松節——取暖，度過這一夜。之後是美洲豹之屋，滿是咬人的猛獸喧鬧之聲；但雙胞胎為牠們撒下其他動物的骨頭，餵牠們美洲豹喜歡的東西，於是那些猛獸心滿意足，不去碰男孩們。

passages.text: Each morning the lords come to look, hoping for bones, and each morning the twins walk out undamaged, laughing among themselves. The houses are failing one by one, and the Lords of Xibalba begin to play for the end: the House of Bats, which no one has survived.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 每天早晨眾領主都來查看，盼著見到骨頭，而每天早晨雙胞胎都毫髮無傷地走出來，彼此說笑。屋子一座接一座地失敗了，希巴爾巴的眾領主開始為終局而謀劃：蝙蝠之屋，從沒有人能活著出來。

title.en: The House of Bats: Camazotz Snips Off a Head
title.zh: 蝙蝠之屋：卡馬佐茲剪首

region.en: Xibalba (the place of fear), symbolic pin at the Candelaria caves, Guatemala highlands
region.zh: 希巴爾巴（懼地），以危地馬拉高地坎德拉里亞洞群為象徵定位

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: In the House of Bats the twins hide inside their blowguns while the death bats cut the air. At noon Camazotz comes down looking for the dawn; Hunahpu peeks out, and his head is snipped off. Xbalanque calls the animals for help, and the tortoise and the daykeepers fashion a new head — the boy goes out with a squash for a face.
summary.zh: 蝙蝠之屋中，雙子藏身於吹箭筒內，死亡蝙蝠在空中剪掠。正午卡馬佐茲下來尋覓黎明；烏納普探頭而出，頭顱隨即被剪。斯巴蘭克召集獸眾求助，烏龜與日守者為其塑新首——男孩以葫蘆為面而出。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The House of Bats is a cave of knives on wings. The twins crawl inside their blowguns and wait while the bats slice the dark, and Xbalanque says: look after your head, brother, and keep still. The bats circle all night, cutting the air where the boys breathe.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蝙蝠之屋是一個滿是帶翅刀刃的洞穴。雙胞胎爬進他們的吹箭筒裡等待，蝙蝠切割著黑暗，而希巴蘭克說：當心你的頭，兄弟，別動。蝙蝠整夜盤旋，在男孩們呼吸之處劃破空氣。

passages.text: At noon Camazotz comes down to look for the light. Hunahpu lifts his head from the tube to see whether the dawn has come, and the great bat's snipping blades take it off like a ripe fruit. The head rolls away, and the body in the tube does not move again that day. Xbalanque calls the animals: coati, coyote, all of you come, and they gather and bring the head before the Lords of Xibalba, who are overjoyed at the loss.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 正午時分，卡馬索茨下來尋找光亮。胡納普從筒中抬起頭來，想看看黎明是否已經到來，那巨蝙蝠的剪狀刀刃便像摘取熟果一般把它切了下來。頭顱滾落而去，筒中的身體那一天再沒有動過。希巴蘭克呼喚眾動物：南美浣熊、郊狼，你們全都來吧，牠們聚集起來，把頭顱帶到希巴爾巴的眾領主面前，眾領主為這一損失欣喜若狂。

passages.text: But Xbalanque does not grieve: he sets a turtle on his brother's neck and the daykeepers shape the shell into a face, and then a round squash is brought in from the cornfield and painted like a head, and Hunahpu is given that to wear. He goes out at the next muster with his squash face among the lords, who laugh at the two poor boys and do not understand what has been rebuilt in the House of Bats.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但胥巴蘭克並不悲傷：他將一隻烏龜放在兄長的頸上，日守者們把龜殼塑成一張臉，接著從玉米田裡取來一顆圓南瓜，畫得像一顆頭顱，讓胡納普穿上它。下一次集會時，他頂著南瓜臉走在眾領主之間，眾領主嘲笑這兩個可憐的男孩，卻不明白蝙蝠之屋裡究竟重建了什麼。

canonical_translation: Brasseur de Bourbourg (French, 1861); Tedlock (1996); Christenson (2003)

narrative.en:
The House of Bats is the one trial in Xibalba that the Hero Twins cannot charm, and it nearly ends the cycle. Popol Wuj places it last among the terrible houses of the place of fear, after Darkness, Razors, Cold, and Jaguars — a descending sequence toward the house whose guardian, Camazotz (Snatch Bat, the Death Bat), is not a lord in the council but a killer animal waiting overhead.

The twins enter by order of the Lords of Xibalba, who are now desperate: every trap has failed. In the bat house the darkness is full of wings that cut. Hunahpu and Xbalanque take shelter inside their blowguns, which in Maya ballgame iconography are the emblem of the game and its players; hiding inside the instrument of their art, they wait out the night. Xbalanque warns his brother: do not lift your head until the light comes; watch over yourself. The advice matters because the bats here are hunting, and their targets are heads.

At noon — a chilling inversion, since noon is when the sun is highest and should be safest — Camazotz comes down from the roof, looking for the dawn. Hunahpu peeks out to see if the day has arrived, and the bat severs his head in one cut. In the K'iche' text the bat snips it 'from off his body', and the head rolls in the dark. Xbalanque calls the animals of the earth — the coati and the others — and they bring the head into the open, where the Lords of Xibalba, seeing it, rejoice: at last one of the two is dead.

What follows is the quiet countermove. Xbalanque does not mourn. He summons the daykeepers (the grandmother and grandfather figures of the tradition) and sets a tortoise against his brother's neck; the shell is shaped into a face, and over it goes a squash from the cornfield, painted like a head. When the lords next muster the brothers for the ballgame, Hunahpu stands among them with his squash face, and the Lords of Xibalba laugh at the poor boys, not realizing that the boy they killed has been put together again out of turtle shell and gourd. The episode's cultural function is double: it marks the absolute limit of trickery — there are powers (Camazotz, noon, the bat's blade) that cannot be talked into mercy — and it shows the method of the twins' whole victory, which is never to fight the underworld at strength but to treat each loss as material for reconstruction. The reassembled Hunahpu, his head a painted gourd, is one of the most recognizable images of Maya narrative: the hero whose face is provisional and who therefore cannot be finished off.

functions: Marks the limit of the twins' trickery: death itself is suffered, not avoided
Models resurrection through substitution (turtle shell, painted squash), a motif of Maya funerary art
Justifies noon as the hour when death-bats (and, by extension, household taboos on noon naps) are dangerous

variants.name: Xibalba as the Candelaria cave complex
variants.text_tradition: Archaeological identifications of Xibalba's road systems with the Candelaria caves (Guatemala lowland-highland border)
variants.summary: Some scholars read the rivers, crossings, and dark houses of Popol Wuj as a description of a real cave system; the bat house matches bat colonies in deep chambers.

variants.name: Classic-period ceramic bat imagery
variants.text_tradition: Late Classic polychrome vessels (e.g., the 'Cosmic Plate' and bat-headed lords)
variants.summary: Bat-headed figures and the 'flying' death-bat appear on Classic Maya vessels, suggesting the Camazotz episode's iconography predates the colonial text.

title.en: Ground to Powder, Cast in the River
title.zh: 碾為粉末，投入河中

region.en: Xibalba (the place of fear), symbolic pin at the Candelaria caves, Guatemala highlands
region.zh: 希巴爾巴（懼地），以危地馬拉高地坎德拉里亞洞群為象徵定位

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: At the lords' final request the twins stage their own deaths: they grind each other's bones in a mortar and pour them into the river. From the ground bones they reappear — first as catfish, then as boys again — and resume their dances in the council hall, apparently none the worse.
summary.zh: 應冥主最後所求，雙子自導死亡：於臼中互碾其骨，傾入河中。碎骨化形重現——初為鯰魚，復為男孩——回到議事堂中起舞，看似毫髮無損。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The lords send for the twins and ask for the miracle plainly: we want to see you die and come back. The brothers answer that it is easy. Then they arrange everything and stand together in the court, and they drop down dead at the same moment, in front of all the benches.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 眾領主召來這對雙胞胎，直截了當地要求那奇蹟：我們要親眼看見你們死去又復活。兄弟倆回答說這很容易。於是他們安排妥當，一同站在球場中央，就在所有座位之前，同時倒地而死。

passages.text: The lords are overjoyed; but they are also uneasy, and they take the bodies to a large mortar and grind them to powder, bones and all, and pour the ground bone and meal into the river. The river carries it off, and the lords think the matter finished — the players are nothing but water.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 眾領主大喜過望；但他們也感到不安，便將屍體帶到一個大臼裡，連骨帶肉磨成粉末，再把磨碎的骨與粉倒進河裡。河水將它沖走，眾領主以為事情就此了結——那些球員不過是水罷了。

passages.text: On the fifth day two boys appear in the river as young catfish, and the next day as boys again, and they walk back into the hall of Xibalba in the clothes of their dance, keeping their faces down. The lords do not know them. They ask for the dance, and the boys say: we are the little dancers; give us the fire.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第五天，兩個男孩以幼鯰之姿出現在河中，隔天又變回男孩，穿著他們舞蹈的衣裳走回希巴爾巴的殿堂，低垂著臉。眾領主認不出他們。他們要求看那支舞，男孩們說：我們是小舞者；把火給我們。

title.en: The Dance of the Poor Sufferer
title.zh: 受苦者之舞

region.en: Xibalba (the place of fear), symbolic pin at the Candelaria caves, Guatemala highlands
region.zh: 希巴爾巴（懼地），以危地馬拉高地坎德拉里亞洞群為象徵定位

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: As entertainers the twins burn the lords' house with themselves inside and step out unharmed; they sacrifice a dog and restore it; they cut each other apart and reassemble. The Lords of Xibalba, watching, are carried away — and ask to be shown the dance of death as well.
summary.zh: 雙子扮作藝者，與房屋同焚而毫髮無傷走出；獻祭犬隻又使其復原；互剖其身而復合。冥主觀之入迷——進而求觀死亡之舞。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The twins perform. They set fire to a house with themselves inside and dance out of the flames unhurt; they kill a dog and bring it back to life; they cut themselves open, take out their hearts, and put them back, and go on dancing. Each trick is announced by the one who is about to die, who tells the other, and then it is done.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 雙胞胎開始表演。他們點燃一棟房子，自己身在屋內，卻毫髮無傷地從火焰中舞了出來；他們殺死一隻狗，又讓牠復活；他們剖開自己，取出心臟，再放回去，繼續跳舞。每一項戲法都由即將死去的那人預先宣告，他告訴另一人，然後便付諸實行。

passages.text: The lords of the place of fear are beside themselves. They crowd the benches to watch, calling for more: kill each other, burn yourselves, do it again. The twins oblige with faces of sorrow and feats of laughter, until One Death and Seven Death themselves begin to boast: if the boys can die and return, so can the Lords of Death.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 恐懼之地的眾領主看得神魂顛倒。他們擠滿座位觀看，連聲要求再來：互相殺死對方，燒死你們自己，再來一次。雙胞胎帶著哀傷的面容、演出令人發笑的絕技，直到「一死」與「七死」自己也開始誇口：既然男孩們能死去又歸來，死亡領主們自然也能。

passages.text: And so they ask for their turn, which is exactly what the twins have danced toward. The boys tell them: it is right that it should be tried, and the lords prepare to die in front of everyone, certain of their resurrection, having watched two boys do it three times without harm.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他們請求輪到自己，而這正是雙胞胎一路舞向的結果。兩個男孩告訴他們：理當一試，於是眾領主準備在所有人面前死去，確信自己必將復活，因為他們已親眼看著兩個男孩做了三次而毫髮無傷。

title.en: Sacrifice Without Resurrection: One Death and Seven Death Die
title.zh: 有祭無復：一死神與七死神之死

region.en: Xibalba (the place of fear), symbolic pin at the Candelaria caves, Guatemala highlands
region.zh: 希巴爾巴（懼地），以危地馬拉高地坎德拉里亞洞群為象徵定位

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: The senior lords demand the twins' dance of death for themselves. The twins open their chests, take out their hearts, and revive — but when One Death and Seven Death are sacrificed the same way, the boys do not revive them. The two great lords die in front of their court, and the lesser lords confess and submit.
summary.zh: 兩位首主求觀雙子的死亡之舞，欲親身一試。雙子剖胸取心而復生——然當一死神與七死神以同法受祭時，男孩們卻不令其復原。兩大主死於其廷前，餘主俯首認罪。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The twins tell the two senior lords: dance your death; it is proper. One Death and Seven Death come forward to the middle of the court, and their hearts are taken out, and they are opened like the boys were — and this time the boys do not put anything back and do not say the word that restores.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 雙胞胎對兩位年長的領主說：舞出你們的死亡吧；這是合宜的。一死與七死走到球場中央，他們的心被取出，他們像男孩們那樣被剖開——而這一次男孩們沒有把任何東西放回去，也沒有說出那使人復原的話語。

passages.text: The two lords die before all their bench of underlords, and the court cries out for them to be brought back. The twins answer mildly: they were tricked by the dance, as they tricked others; they wanted what they saw. And the remaining lords, Pus, Blood, Bone Scepter, Wing, and the rest, come in a body to confess and to offer whatever the boys demand.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兩位領主在他們整排下級領主面前死去，球場上眾人高聲呼喊，要求把他們救回。雙胞胎溫和地回答：他們是被舞蹈所騙，正如他們曾欺騙他人；他們想要的就是他們所看見的。而其餘的領主——膿、血、骨杖、翼，以及其餘諸位——一同前來懺悔，並獻上男孩們所要求的一切。

passages.text: The twins spare the lesser lords but strip them of their emblems and their court: they will no longer be named in order of their cruelties, and their power over the ballgame and over men's hearts is taken. They confess their sins — the failures of hospitality, the deaths of players — and from then on they carry out only the small offices of the place of fear, no longer its judgments.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 雙胞胎饒過了較次的領主，卻剝奪了他們的徽記與他們的宮廷：他們將不再依其殘暴的次序被稱名，他們對球賽以及對人心靈的權力也被奪去。他們懺悔自己的罪過——待客之道的失職、球員的死亡——從此以後，他們只執行那恐懼之地的微小職務，不再掌有它的裁決。

canonical_translation: Brasseur de Bourbourg (French, 1861); Tedlock (1996); Christenson (2003)

narrative.en:
The defeat of One Death and Seven Death is the climax of the Hero Twins' cycle and the most juridical scene in the Popol Wuj: a trial that reverses itself. The two boys, having survived every house and risen twice from their own staged deaths, have by now converted the underworld's justice hall into a theater, and the theater into a trap. The Lords of Xibalba, who opened the cycle by summoning two ballplayers to a rigged game, now beg two ballplayers for one last spectacle — and the spectacle is their own execution, performed in the form they themselves designed: death on demand, resurrection on demand.

The sequence is deliberately simple. Hunahpu and Xbalanque, asked to repeat their wonders, kill themselves again — this time before the full court — and come back dancing. One Death and Seven Death, senior lords of the council of the dead, are so persuaded by repetition that they volunteer: if boys can die and return, surely the masters of death can. The twins consent with perfect courtesy and perfect honesty ('it is proper that it be tried') and then simply decline the last step. When the lords' hearts are out, the boys do not speak the word of restoration; they leave the two great lords dead on the floor of their own hall. There is no trick in the death itself — only in the promise of its reversal, which was never made.

The lesser lords then do what courts do when their heads are gone: they confess. In the K'iche' text they come in a body, admitting the deaths of the players, the abuse of guests, and the theft of the ballgame, and they offer submission. The twins respond not with massacre but with demotion: the remaining lords of Xibalba are kept as functionaries of death — they will still receive the dead, but without the emblems of judgment, without the power to summon the living, and stripped of the titles by which their cruelties were remembered. Death is not abolished; it is domesticated. From this point on, Xibalba is a place where people go, not a power that comes to fetch people by trick summons.

Ritually, the episode licenses the Maya practice of sacrifice as negotiation rather than submission: blood is given because a covenant can be made, not because the underworld's whims must be bought. Politically, it authorizes the K'iche' ballgame and its courts as places where disputes are settled by rules rather than ambush — the twins win by knowing the rules better than the house does. And theologically, it grounds the calendar: the twins' final transformation into sun and moon (elsewhere in the record) rests on this victory over the lords of the katun's dark days.

functions: Climax of the twins' cycle: the reversal of the underworld's court
Licenses sacrifice as covenant with the gods rather than tribute to death
Explains why the dead are received but no longer summoned: Xibalba's demotion
Authorizes the ballgame as a rule-bound settlement of contests

variants.name: Broad arc in the single-record tradition
variants.summary: The whole Xibalba defeat is often told as one story ('the Hero Twins in Xibalba'); this record cuts its final, juridical scene.
