summary.en: A dragon in a sea-cave devours the children of Koshigoe; in the sixth century Benten causes an earthquake, descends from the clouds, marries the dragon, and ends the slaughter - and from the sea rises the island of Enoshima, sacred to the Goddess of the Sea ever since.
summary.zh: 腰越村有龍居洞中，吞食童子。六世紀辯才天降大地震，乘雲而下，入洞與龍成婚，以善念化之，食童遂止。海中湧出江之島，自此為海神聖地。

sensitivity.note: A shrine-legend of Enoshima recorded 1912 in Davis; category myth since it is shrine lore rather than scripture; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Benten, the Goddess of the Sea, is also one of the Seven Divinities of Luck, romantically referred to as the Goddess of Love, Beauty, and Eloquence. She is represented riding on a dragon or serpent, which may account for the fact that in certain localities snakes are regarded as sacred; images depict her with eight arms, six hands holding bow, arrow, wheel, sword, key, and sacred jewel, and two hands reverently crossed in prayer. Her shrines are usually to be found on islands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XV 'Benten' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 辯天，海之女神，亦為七福神之一，被浪漫地稱為愛、美與辯才之女神。她被描繪為騎乘於龍或巨蛇之上，這或許可解釋為何在某些地方蛇被視為神聖；圖像中的她生有八臂，其中六手持弓、箭、輪、劍、鑰匙與神聖寶珠，另兩手則虔誠地交叉合十祈禱。她的神社通常建於島上。

passages.text: In a certain cave there lived a formidable dragon which devoured the children of the village of Koshigoe. In the sixth century Benten was determined to put a stop to this monster's unseemly behaviour: having caused a great earthquake, she hovered in the clouds over the cave, then descended, entered the cavern, married the dragon, and was thus able, through her good influence, to put an end to the slaughter of little children. With the coming of Benten there arose from the sea the famous Island of Enoshima, which has remained to this day sacred to the Goddess of the Sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XV 'Benten and the Dragon' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某處洞穴中住著一條可怕的龍，吞噬著腰越村的孩子們。六世紀時，辯天決心制止這怪物不端的行徑：她引發了一場大地震，在洞穴上方的雲端盤旋，繼而降下，進入洞中，與那龍結為夫妻，於是得以憑藉自身的善德影響，終結了對幼童的殺戮。隨著辯天的到來，著名的江之島自海中升起，至今仍為海之女神的神聖之地。

title.en: The Festival of the Dead
title.zh: 盂蘭盆

region.en: The Bon festival, houses, cemeteries and rivers of Japan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 盂蘭盆會（象徵定位）

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: At death the soul must cross the River of Three Roads, paying Old Woman Sodzu-Baba or losing its pilgrim's garments; the Festival of the Dead (July 13-15) welcomes the ghosts home with tiny meals, feeds the friendless dead of Gakido - as Mokenren's mother was freed when he fed the priests - and sends them away at midnight in little boats with lanterns at the prow.
summary.zh: 人死魂渡三途川，付六文錢於奪衣婆；不然白衣被奪掛樹。七月十三至十五日盂蘭盆，備小膳迎歸魂，施食於無主餓鬼——目連救母即其源。十五夜以載膳小舟送靈，燈浮川海。

sensitivity.note: The Bon festival complex recorded 1912 in Davis; category myth since the Sodzu-Baba and Mokenren elements are folk-Buddhist narrative rather than canonical scripture; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: At death the body is washed, shaven, and arrayed in the garment of a pilgrim, with a wallet containing three or six rin hung round the neck and buried with the deceased; for all who die, children alone excepted, must journey to the Sanzu-no-Kawa, the River of the Three Roads. On its dismal bank Sodzu-Baba, the Old Woman of the Three Roads, awaits the coming of souls together with her husband, Ten Datsu-Ba; if the three rin are not paid, she takes away the white garments of the dead and, regardless of entreaties, hangs them on trees. Add Emma-O, the Lord of the Dead, and the terrors of the Buddhist hells, and it is no surprise that the gentle Japanese founded a festival to afford a pleasant, if all too brief, respite from the horrors of Hades.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XVII 'The Festival of the Dead' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 人死之後，遺體會被洗淨、剃髮，並穿上朝聖者的衣裝，頸上掛著一只裝有三文或六文錢的錢袋，隨死者一同下葬；因為凡死去之人，除孩童以外，都必須前往三途川，即「三條路之河」。在其陰森淒涼的岸邊，三途婆——「三條路之老嫗」——與她的丈夫奪衣婆一同等候亡魂的到來；若未付那三文錢，她便奪去死者的白衣，且不顧哀求，將衣物掛在樹上。再加上閻魔大王——死者之主——以及佛教地獄的種種恐怖，難怪溫和的日本人要創立一個節慶，好從冥府的恐怖中獲得一段愉快卻又過於短暫的喘息。

passages.text: The festival takes place from July 13 to 15. New mats of rice straw are spread on the altars and household shrines, and every home is provided with a quaint, minute meal in readiness for the great company of ghosts; lanterns are lit, incense burned, and water poured in the cemeteries. On the evening of the 15th the ghosts of the Circle of Penance, Gakido, are fed, and those who have no friends among the living. There is a legend for this: Dai-Mokenren, a great disciple of Buddha, was permitted to see the soul of his mother in the Gakido, but every time she tried to eat the food he gave her it turned to fire and ashes; told to feed the ghosts of the great priests of all countries on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, he did so, and found his mother dancing for joy. In this happy dance after tribulation we trace the origin of the Bon-odori, which takes place on the third night of the festival.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XVII 'The Festival of the Dead' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此節慶於七月十三日至十五日舉行。祭壇與家中佛龕上鋪著新的稻草蓆，家家戶戶都備好一份古樸而微小的飯食，以迎接大批亡魂的到來；燈籠點亮，線香焚燒，墓地裡則澆上清水。十五日傍晚，要供養餓鬼道——即「餓鬼」——的亡魂，以及那些在陽間沒有親友的亡魂。為此有一則傳說：佛陀的大弟子目犍連（大目犍連）獲准在餓鬼道中見到母親的亡魂，但每當她試圖吃下他所給的食物，食物便化為火焰與灰燼；他被告知須在七月十五日供養各國大僧侶的亡魂，他照做了，於是見到母親歡喜起舞。從這苦難之後的歡舞中，我們可追溯盆踊的起源，而盆踊正是在節慶的第三夜舉行。

passages.text: On the evening of the third day preparations are made for the departure of the ghosts. Thousands of little boats are packed with food and loving messages of farewell; into these boats step the departing ghosts, and loving hands set the frail craft upon river, lake, or sea - a small lantern glowing at the prow, pale blue clouds of incense floating from the stern. Down all the creeks and rivers the phantom fleets go glimmering to the sea; all the sea sparkles to the horizon with the lights of the dead, and the sea wind is fragrant with incense.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XVII 'The Festival of the Dead' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第三日傍晚，人們為亡魂的離去做準備。數千隻小船裝滿食物與充滿情意的道別之語；離去的亡魂踏上這些小船，充滿情意的雙手將這脆弱的舟隻放上河、湖或海——船首亮著一盞小燈籠，船尾飄出淡藍色的裊裊香煙。幽靈船隊沿著所有的小溪與河流閃爍微光，駛向大海；整片海面直到地平線都閃耀著亡者的燈火，海風中瀰漫著線香的芬芳。

title.en: The Peony Lantern
title.zh: 牡丹燈籠

region.en: Yanaka-no-Sasaki and the cemetery of Shin-Banzui-In, Edo
region.zh: 江戶谷中與坂尺・新番所作

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: The samurai Shinzaburo, kept from visiting Tsuyu by a jealous old doctor, learns of her death too late; at the Festival of the Dead she and her maid Yone come each night behind a peony lantern, his servant spies a half-corpse in the mosquito-net, and when the servant sells back the sacred charms the dead woman's bones twine about his neck - love between the living and the dead ends in the destruction of the living.
summary.zh: 萩原新三郎與常陸女戀，為老醫所阻，女憂鬱而歿。盆節之夜，牡丹燈籠引女與侍女音來會；僕窺蚊帳見半身枯骨。後僕貪百兩，毀佛印，女骨纏郎頸而同寢。

sensitivity.note: The Botan Dorō ghost story, Japanese in local colour though inspired by a Chinese tale, retold 1912 by Davis after Hearn; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Tsuyu, Morning Dew, was the only daughter of Iijima. When her father married again she found she could not live happily with her stepmother, and a separate house was built for her, where she lived with her servant-maid Yone. One day the family physician Yamamoto Shijo brought a handsome young samurai, Hagiwara Shinzaburo, and the young people fell in love at sight; at parting Tsuyu whispered, 'Remember! if you do not come to see me again I shall certainly die!' Etiquette would not allow Shinzaburo to visit alone, and the old doctor, having seen more than the young people supposed, purposely refrained from keeping his promise. Believing her lover unfaithful, Tsuyu slowly pined away and died, and Yone soon followed her mistress; they were buried side by side in the cemetery of Shin-Banzui-In.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XVIII 'Morning-Dew' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 露（Tsuyu，意為「晨露」）是飯島家的獨生女。父親續弦之後，她發覺自己無法與繼母和睦相處，於是家中為她另建了一棟房子，她與侍女米（Yone）同住其中。某日，家庭醫師山本志丈帶來一位英俊的年輕武士萩原新三郎，這對年輕人一見鍾情；臨別時，露低聲說道：「記住！你若不再來看我，我一定會死的！」禮法不允許新三郎獨自登門拜訪，而那位老醫生所見的比年輕人所想的更多，便故意不履行承諾。露以為情人不忠，漸漸憔悴而死，米不久也追隨主人而去；兩人並肩葬於新番隨院的墓地。

passages.text: On the first day of the Festival of the Dead Shinzaburo set food on the Shelf of Souls and hung out lanterns, and waited in the warm moonlit night. Suddenly the stillness was broken by kara-kon, kara-kon, the soft patter of women's geta: over the hedge he saw two women, one carrying a long lantern with silk peonies stuck in at the upper end. It was Tsuyu and Yone - each, as it turned out, told by the same old doctor that the other was dead. They entered the house and remained that night, returning home a little before sunrise; night after night they came, always Yone carrying the shining peony-lantern, always departing at the same hour.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XVIII 'The Dead Return' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 盂蘭盆節首日，新三郎在靈位上供奉食物、掛起燈籠，並在溫暖的月夜中等待。忽然，寂靜被「喀啦——喀啦——」的聲音打破，那是女子木屐輕柔的聲響：他越過樹籬望去，看見兩名女子，其中一人提著一盞長燈籠，燈籠上端插著絲製的牡丹花。那正是露與米——後來才知，兩人都被同一位老醫生告知對方已死。她們進了屋，當夜留宿，於日出前不久返家；夜復一夜她們都來，總是米提著那盞發光的牡丹燈籠，總是在同一時刻離去。

passages.text: One night Tomozo, a servant living next door, peeped through a crack in the sliding door: within the mosquito-net his master talked with a woman whose face was that of one long dead, her fingers a bunch of jangling bones, and only her upper body of substance, below the waist a dim moving shadow. A second figure sprang up and made for Tomozo's eye at the chink, and he fled shrieking to Hakuodo Yusai, a man well versed in all manner of mysteries, who told him that his master was a doomed man if the woman proved a ghost, for love between the living and the dead ends in the destruction of the living. Shinzaburo sought the quarter where the women said they lived and found only the two tombs of Shin-Banzui-In, one adorned with the very peony-lantern - their 'very small house' in Yanaka-no-Sasaki was a grave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XVIII 'The Mystery is Revealed' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某夜，住在隔壁的僕人友藏從拉門的縫隙偷窺：蚊帳之內，主人正與一名女子交談，那女子的面容屬於死去已久之人，她的手指是一把叮噹作響的枯骨，只有上半身具有實體，腰以下則是一道朦朧移動的暗影。另一個身影猛然躍起，朝友藏偷窺的縫隙撲來，他尖叫著逃到博學多聞、通曉各種玄秘之事的白雲堂湯淺那裡；湯淺告訴他，若那女子證實是鬼魂，他的主人便是在劫難逃之人，因為生者與死者之間的愛情，終將以生者的毀滅收場。新三郎尋訪女子們所說居住的地方，卻只找到新番隨院的兩座墳墓，其中一座上頭正裝飾著那盞牡丹燈籠——她們在谷中佐佐木的「極小之屋」，其實是一座墳。

passages.text: The high-priest Ryoseki gave Shinzaburo a small gold image of Buddha to wear next his skin, the Treasure-Raining Sutra to recite every night, and a bundle of sacred texts to paste over every opening in the house. That night the ghostly geta pattered at the doors in vain - the sacred words held them back, and he heard Yone tell her mistress that his love had changed. Then Yone went night after night to Tomozo and threatened him till his wife counselled him to bargain: for a hundred ryo the wicked servant took the gold Buddha, took down one of the sacred texts, and buried the sutra. With their entry began again the horrible love of the dead, presided over by the power of Karma; next morning Tomozo found his master dead under the mosquito-net, beside him the white bones of a woman, and the bones of Morning Dew twined round the neck of one who had loved her too well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XVIII 'The Betrayal' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 高僧良石給新三郎一尊小金佛像，讓他貼身佩戴；又給他一部《雨寶經》，要他每晚誦念；還給他一束經文，要他貼在屋內每一處縫隙上。當夜，鬼魅的木屐聲在門外嗒嗒作響，卻徒勞無功——經文的神聖字句將它們擋了回去；他聽見米告訴她的女主人，說他的愛已經變了。此後，米夜復一夜地去找友三，威脅他，直到他的妻子勸他講和：那邪惡的僕人收下一百兩銀子，取走了金佛像，揭下其中一張經文，又將那部經埋了起來。隨著它們的進入，亡者那可怕的愛戀在業力的主宰下再度開始；翌日清晨，友三發現主人在蚊帳下死去，身旁是一具女子的白骨，而晨露的白骨則纏繞在一個曾愛她太深之人的頸上。

title.en: Dan Kun the Sandal Prince of the Ever-White Mountains
title.zh: 檀君白山傳說別本

region.en: Ever-White Mountains (Paektu) (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 長白山（象徵性定位）

period: Corean traditional history recorded by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882; rev. ed.); episode dated c. 2356 BC

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 34, eBook #67141

summary.en: In this variant of the founding, of old the land had neither prince nor chiefs. A Divine Being descended from heaven and took up his abode at the foot of a sandalwood tree on the Ever-White Mountains. The people of the land became his subjects, made him sovereign, and called him Dan Kun, the Sandal Prince, and his realm Cho-sen, Morning Calm. His descendants reigned more than a thousand years, until the occupation of the country by the Chinese noble Ki Tsze.
summary.zh: 古時朝鮮無君無長。有神人自天而降，止於白山檀樹之下。土人尊之為君，號曰檀君，其國曰朝鮮（晨靜之國）。子孫相承千餘年，至中國貴人箕子東來而代興。

sensitivity.note: Nineteenth-century Western compilation of the Dangun tradition; variant form of the same founding story as records 'dangun' and 'korean-dangun-wanggeom'.

passages.text: According to Corean tradition, of old the land had neither prince nor chiefs. A Divine Being descended from heaven and took up his abode at the foot of a sandalwood tree on the Ever-White Mountains. The people of the land became his subjects, made him their sovereign, and called him Dan Kun, the Sandal Prince, and his realm Cho-sen, Morning Calm. This took place in the time of Tang Ti Yao, in 2356 BC.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據朝鮮的傳統說法，古時這片土地既無君王，也無首領。一位神明自天而降，在長白山上的一棵檀香樹下定居。這片土地上的百姓成了他的子民，奉他為君，稱他為檀君，即檀香王子，並稱他的國度為朝鮮，意為「晨靜」。此事發生於唐堯之時，即公元前二三五六年。

passages.text: His first residence was at Ping-an; later he transferred it to Pe-yo, where his descendants remained till the eighth year of the emperor Wu Ting, when they were established in Mount Asstak. His descendants reigned in Cho-sen more than one thousand years, and then followed the occupation of the country by the Chinese noble Ki Tsze.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他最初的居所位於平壤；後來他遷至貝約，他的後裔一直留居該地，直到吳丁皇帝八年，他們才被安置於阿斯達山。他的後裔在朝鮮統治了一千多年，此後便是中國貴族箕子佔據該國。

title.en: Born of the Gourd-Egg: The Shinra Founding Variant
title.zh: 瓠卵新羅別傳

region.en: Mountain village, east coast (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 嶺東山村（象徵性定位）

period: Local legend recorded by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882); episode dated legendary Silla antiquity

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 34, eBook #67141

summary.en: In the local legends of Shinra, after the invasion of Cho-sen many of the original inhabitants fled and scattered over the east coast. The head man of a village, hearing the neighing of horses toward a mountain, finds not a horse but an egg of extraordinary size shaped like a gourd; breaking it open he discovers a beautiful rosy boy-baby, adopts him, and when the boy is thirteen the elders of the six principal towns choose him as their lord. The country is named Born of the Gourd-Egg, and the new king takes to wife a fair maiden reputed the offspring of a well-dragon; they reign sixty years, when their daughter succeeds to the throne.
summary.zh: 新羅別傳云：古朝鮮被侵，遺民散居嶺東。一村長聞山間馬嘶而往視，非馬也，乃大卵一枚，形如瓠。剖之，得赤色俊兒，養為己子。兒年十三，六部酋長共立為主。名其國曰瓠卵所生，王娶井龍之女為后，在位六十年，女繼其統。

sensitivity.note: Variant of the Hyokkose birth legend (cf. korean-hyeokgeose-luminous-egg); Western compilation of local tradition.

passages.text: The mythical origin and founding of Shinra is thus told in the local legends of the place. After the invasion of Cho-sen by the Chinese emperor, many of the original inhabitants fled and scattered over the east coast, making settlements on the mountains, in the valleys, and along the sea-shore, some of which grew to be cities and large towns.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 新羅的神話起源與建國，在當地的傳說中是這樣講述的。中國皇帝入侵朝鮮之後，許多原住民逃亡離散，散居於東海岸一帶，在山間、谷中與海濱建立聚落，其中有些後來發展成了城市與大鎮。

passages.text: One day the attention of the head man of one of the villages was attracted by the neighing of horses toward a mountain. He went in the direction of the sounds, but instead of a horse he found an egg of extraordinary size, shaped like a gourd. Carefully breaking it open, he discovered a beautiful rosy boy-baby inside. The old man's heart was touched, and he took the child home and adopted it as his own.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一天，其中一個村落的村長被朝山那邊傳來的馬嘶聲吸引了注意。他循聲而去，卻沒有見到馬，只發現一枚碩大無比的蛋，形狀像葫蘆。他小心翼翼地將蛋敲開，發現裡面是一個美麗的、面色紅潤的男嬰。老人心生憐愛，便將孩子帶回家，收養為己出。

passages.text: The boy grew up beloved of all. When but thirteen years old, the elders of the six principal towns gathered together and chose him as their lord and master. They gave him a name signifying Coming Out of the West, and to the country a name meaning Born of the Gourd-egg. The new king took to wife a fair maiden reputed to be the offspring of a well-dragon. They reigned for sixty years, when their daughter succeeded to the throne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這男孩長大後，深受眾人喜愛。他年僅十三歲時，六個主要城鎮的長老便聚集一堂，選他為他們的君主與主人。他們給他取了一個意為「出自西方」的名字，又給這個國家取了一個意為「生自葫蘆蛋」的名字。這位新國王娶了一位據說是井龍後裔的美麗少女為妻。他們統治了六十年，之後他們的女兒繼承了王位。

title.en: Opened in Presence of the Crows
title.zh: 烏前剖卵別傳

region.en: Shinra harbor (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新羅海港（象徵性定位）

period: Local legend recorded by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882); episode dated legendary Silla antiquity

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 34, eBook #67141

summary.en: In the fifth year of the daughter-queen's reign she marries a youth from afar whose origin is as wonderful as her parents'. His mother the queen had been delivered of an egg; her husband threw it away, but the queen wrapped it in a silk napkin with other treasures, set it adrift on the sea, and after many days it washed ashore. Fishermen netted it and threw it back into the sea; it drifted into a harbor of Shinra, where an old woman opened the lid and found a lovely boy with a smile on his face. Crows stood around the shore at his finding, and the crone named him Opened in Presence of the Crows. He grew nine feet high, excelled in geomancy, built himself a house on a lucky site, and the queen married him to her daughter.
summary.zh: 女主五年，嫁遠來奇男子。其母亦係產卵者：夫棄卵，后以繒裹之，雜寶物納櫝浮海。久之漂至新羅港，漁者網得復投海，旋為老嫗所拾，啟櫝見兒，笑靨嫣然。時羣鴉集岸，嫗因名之曰『烏前開者』。兒長九尺，精堪輿，自擇吉地而居。女王遂以女妻之。

sensitivity.note: Variant of the Seok Talhae drift-egg legend (cf. korean-seoktalhae-egg-across-sea); Western compilation.

passages.text: In the fifth year of her reign she married a youth who had come from afar, whose origin was as wonderful as that of her own parents. His mother the queen had been delivered of an egg. Her husband, not enjoying such a form of offspring, threw the egg away, but the queen recovering it, carefully wrapped it in a silk napkin, and with many other treasures put it in a box and set it adrift on the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在她統治的第五年，她嫁給了一位從遠方來的青年，他的來歷和她自己的父母一樣奇妙。他的母親，也就是王后，生下了一顆蛋。她的丈夫不喜歡這樣的子嗣形式，便把蛋丟棄了，但王后把它撿了回來，小心地用絲巾包裹，連同許多其他寶物一起放進一個箱子裡，任其漂流於海上。

passages.text: After many days the box was washed ashore on a distant coast. The fishermen who picked it up in their nets thought nothing of it, and threw it into the sea again. It drifted into one of the harbors of Shinra. An old woman finding it, opened the lid and found a lovely boy with a smile on his face.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 過了許多天，箱子被沖上了遠方海岸。用網把它撈起來的漁夫們並不以為意，又把它扔回海裡。它漂流到了新羅的一個港口。一位老婦人發現了它，打開蓋子，看見一個面帶微笑的可愛男孩。

passages.text: When the old woman first picked up the waif, there were a number of crows standing around the shore, and the crone gave him a name referring to the presence of these birds — Opened in Presence of the Crows. He grew up a man of strength, nine feet high, excelling all other youths in bodily vigor. Excelling in the knowledge of geomancy, he found a good place for a residence and built on it. Hearing of his renown, the queen of Shinra married him to her daughter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當老婦人最初撿起這個棄兒時，岸邊站著一群烏鴉，老婦人便依這些鳥兒在場的情形為他取了名字——「烏鴉在場時開啟」。他長大成人，身強力壯，身高九尺，體力勝過所有其他青年。他精通堪輿之術，找到了一處好地方作為居所，並在上面建造房屋。新羅的王后聽聞他的名聲，便把女兒嫁給了他。

title.en: The Golden Boy from the Grove where the Cock Crowed
title.zh: 金櫝雞鳴童

region.en: Western woods, Shinra (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新羅西林（象徵性定位）

period: Local legend recorded by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882); episode dated legendary Silla antiquity

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 34, eBook #67141

summary.en: One evening the newly made king hears a cock crow in the woods toward the west. His servants find a small golden casket suspended from a tree with a white cock crowing beneath it; opened, the casket contains a boy baby, named The Golden Boy from the Grove in which the Cock Crowed. The boy grows up and succeeds his father; in the reign of the twenty-second king the people change the name of their country, Shin-han, to Shinra.
summary.zh: 新王一夜聞西林雞鳴，遣僕往探，見樹懸金櫝，下有白雞而鳴。取櫝啟之，中得一兒，名曰『雞鳴林中金童』。兒長而嗣父位。傳至二十二王，國人改新韓之名為新羅。

sensitivity.note: Variant of the Kim Alji / hen-casket legend (cf. korean-keumyunji-hen-woods-renaming); Western compilation.

passages.text: One evening the newly made king heard a cock crow in the woods toward the west. He sent his servants after it, who found a small golden casket suspended from a tree. Under it a white cock was crowing. The servant reported the matter to his master. Another servant was despatched to the place. He returned with the box, which, being opened, was found to contain a boy baby, who was given the name signifying The Golden Boy from the Grove in which the Cock crowed. The baby boy grew up and succeeded his father. In the reign of the twenty-second king of the line, the people of the country, then called Shin-han, changed the name of their country to Shinra.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一天傍晚，新登基的國王聽見西邊樹林裡有公雞啼叫。他派僕人去查看，僕人發現樹上懸掛著一個小小的金匣。匣下有一隻白公雞正在啼叫。僕人把此事稟報主人。又一名僕人被派往該處。他帶著箱子回來，打開一看，裡面是一個男嬰，於是給他取了個名字，意為「公雞啼叫之林中來的金童」。這男嬰長大後繼承了父親。傳至該朝第二十二代國王時，當時國名為新韓的國中百姓，將國名改為新羅。

title.en: The Four Dragon-Kings of the Seas
title.zh: 四海龍王

region.en: Palaces under the four seas (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 四海龍宮（象徵性定位）

period: Mythical zoology recorded by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 33, eBook #67141

summary.en: The riong, or dragon, chief of scaly monsters, embodies all the forces of motion and change. It possesses the gift of transformation, rendering itself visible or invisible at will; in spring it ascends to the skies and in autumn buries itself in the watery depths; it can shrink to the size of a silkworm or swell till it fills the space of heaven and earth. Celestial dragons guard the mansions of the gods so they do not fall; spiritual dragons make wind and rain for mankind; terrestrial dragons mark the courses of rivers; and another watches over hidden treasures — the dragon of mines and gems whom mortals must propitiate to win the metals. There are four dragon-kings with palaces under the northern, eastern, southern and western seas, whose terrible minister-dragons, battling in air and deep, cause the commotion of the elements; and the dragon carries on its forehead a pear-shaped pearl of wondrous healing and power. So intense is this belief that the mines of Cho-sen are little worked.
summary.zh: 龍者鱗蟲之長，具變化之能：可隱可現，春升秋潛，小如蠶而大則充塞天地。天龍守神宮使不傾，神龍興雲雨以利民，地龍畫江河之流，復有守寶之龍司礦藏——故朝鮮礦山多不開採，懼觸龍怒也。四海有龍王各居其宮，其屬龍相鬥於空中深海，遂起風雷。龍額有珠，療疾增力，得之者勝。

sensitivity.note: Sino-Korean dragon cosmology compiled by a Western observer; shared East Asian heritage rather than uniquely Korean.

passages.text: The riong, or dragon, whose figure as depicted in Corean art is perhaps nothing more than a highly idealized form of an extinct geological species of saurian, is one of the four supernatural creatures. He is an embodiment of all the forces of motion, change, and power in animal life, with the mysterious attributes of the serpent. It possesses the gift of transformation and of rendering itself visible or invisible at will; in the spring it ascends to the skies and in the autumn buries itself in the watery depths.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 龍（riong），其在朝鮮藝術中所描繪的形象，或許不過是一種已滅絕的蜥蜴類地質物種的高度理想化形態，是四種超自然生物之一。牠體現了動物生命中一切運動、變化與力量，並具有蛇的神秘屬性。牠擁有變形之能，也能隨意使自己顯現或隱形；春天升上天空，秋天潛藏於深水之中。

passages.text: This omnipotent monster becomes at will reduced to the size of a silkworm or swollen till it fills the space of heaven and earth. It desires to mount, and it rises until it affronts the clouds; to sink, and it descends until hidden below the fountains of the deep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這無所不能的怪物能隨意縮小至蠶的大小，或膨脹至充滿天地之間。牠想升騰，便上升直到觸及雲端；想下沉，便下降直到隱沒於深淵的泉源之下。

passages.text: The functions of the celestial dragon are to guard the mansions of the gods in heaven so that they do not fall; of the spiritual, to cause the wind to blow and produce rain for the benefit of mankind; of the terrestrial, to mark out the courses of rivers and streams; while another watches over the hidden treasures concealed from mortals. This last is the dragon that presides over mines and gems, and which mortals must propitiate or overcome in order to gain the precious metals out of the earth. Intense belief in the dragon is one of the chief reasons why the mines in Cho-sen are so little worked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天龍的職責是守護天上的諸神宮殿，使其不致傾頹；神龍的職責是興風降雨，以造福人類；地龍的職責是標定河川溪流的路徑；另有一龍則看守著對凡人隱藏的寶藏。這最後一龍主管礦藏與寶石，凡人必須安撫牠或制服牠，方能從地中取得貴金屬。對龍的強烈信仰，正是朝鮮礦藏開採如此稀少的主要原因之一。

passages.text: There are four dragon-kings who have their palaces in the world under the sea, one ruling in the northern, one in the eastern, one in the southern, and one in the western sea. The ministers and messengers of these four monarchs are the terrible dragons whose battles in the air and in the deep are the causes of the commotion of the elements. In common belief the dragon carries on his forehead a pear-shaped pearl, supposed to possess wondrous virtues of healing and power.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有四位龍王，宮殿位於海底世界，一位統治北方之海，一位統治東方之海，一位統治南方之海，一位統治西方之海。這四位君主的臣屬與使者，便是那些可怕的龍；牠們在空中與深淵中的爭鬥，正是風雨雷電等天象騷動的成因。民間普遍相信，龍的額上負著一顆梨形珍珠，據說具有神奇的療癒與力量之德。

title.en: The Guardian Serpent of the Household
title.zh: 家宅守蛇

region.en: Rural household shrine (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 鄉村家宅（象徵性定位）

period: Ethnographic observation recorded by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 33, eBook #67141

summary.en: In the peninsula not only are trees reverenced as the abode of spirits, but the sa, or snakes, are rarely if ever harmed. The people feed, venerate and even worship them as the guardian genii of their households; the epkurong-gi is the name they call the serpent which presides over their family Edens. Instead of being looked on as the embodiment of evil as in Semitic lore, the serpent's presence is hailed as an omen of blessing. A serpent that lives a thousand years bears in its head a glistening gem called ya-kang-chiu; the guardian serpent is pictured as double-winged, with forked tongue, flying among the clouds and protecting its worshippers by pursuing their enemies — as on the war-flags the Corean mountaineers carried to the Han River forts in 1871.
summary.zh: 朝鮮人敬樹為神棲之所，而於蛇尤不敢害。飼之、敬之、甚至奉之為家宅守護之神，名曰埃闊龍基（家蛇）。蛇至千年，首生寶珠，名牙剛珠（如鑽石）。守蛇之神有雙翼、吐信，飛行雲間，逐敵護主——同治十年（1871）漢江要塞獵虎軍之戰旗，即繪此蛇神。

sensitivity.note: Household serpent cult recorded ethnographically; no living-community restriction on describing historical belief.

passages.text: In the peninsula not only are trees reverenced as the abode of spirits, but the sa, or snakes, are rarely, if ever, harmed. The people feed, venerate, and even worship them as the guardian genii of their households. The epkurong-gi is the name by which they call the serpent which presides over their family Edens.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在這半島上，不僅樹木因被視為神靈的居所而受到敬奉，蛇（sa）也極少受到傷害，甚至從未受害。人們餵養、敬奉，甚至崇拜牠們，視之為家宅的守護神。他們稱那守護家族樂園的蛇為「epkurong-gi」。

passages.text: Instead of being looked upon as the embodiment of the principle of evil, as in Semitic lore, their presence is hailed as an omen of blessing. They are treated like pets. In their heads they are believed to carry a precious jewel after they have lived long. A serpent often lives to be one thousand years old, and then bears in his front a glistening gem, called ya-kang-chiu, a name the people also apply to any glittering stone, especially the diamond.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 牠們並不像在閃米特傳說中那樣被視為邪惡本源的化身，反而其出現被歡呼為福佑的徵兆。牠們被當作寵物般對待。人們相信牠們活得長久之後，頭上會帶著一顆寶石。蛇往往能活到一千歲，屆時其額前便會長出一顆閃耀的寶石，稱為「ya-kang-chiu」；人們也用這個名稱來稱呼任何閃亮的石頭，尤其是鑽石。

passages.text: The guardian serpent is represented as double-winged, with forked tongue, flying among the clouds and protecting its worshippers by pursuing their enemies. The illustration here given is copied from one of the war-flags carried by the Corean mountaineers from their homes to the forts on the Han River in 1871.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 守護之蛇被描繪為生有雙翼、吐著分叉之舌，飛翔於雲間，並藉由追擊仇敵來保護其信奉者。此處所附的插圖，是摹自一八七一年朝鮮山民從家鄉帶往漢江堡壘的一面戰旗。

title.en: The Kirin and the Phoenix as Omens of Good Rule
title.zh: 麒麟鳳凰瑞應

region.en: Royal court, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城王宮（象徵性定位）

period: Mythical zoology recorded by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 33, eBook #67141

summary.en: The kirin, with the body of a deer and the tail of an ox and a single soft horn, never treads on or injures any living being. It is the emblem of perfect rectitude and the incarnate essence of the five primordial elements; its appearance on earth is ever a happy omen, the harbinger of good government and the birth of good rulers. The phoenix likewise appears at or near the birth of a good ruler; in its plumage the sheen of five colors typifies the five cardinal virtues, and it is the emblem not only of auspicious government but of inseparable fellowship and conjugal love.
summary.zh: 麒麟鹿身牛尾，額有軟角，不履生草，不傷生靈，為至德之瑞、五行之精。其現世則善政將興、明君將生。鳳凰亦然：五色文采應五常之德，見則天下太平，且象夫婦和鳴之義。

sensitivity.note: Shared East Asian auspicious-beast lore compiled by a Western observer.

passages.text: The kirin is another of the four supernatural creatures, depicted in Corean art especially as a symbol of peace and joy. This beast has the body of a deer and the tail of an ox, and on its forehead a single soft horn. It is said never to tread on or injure any living being. It is the emblem of perfect rectitude, and the incarnate essence of the five primordial elements of all things: water, fire, wood, metal, earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 麒麟是四種超自然生物之一，在朝鮮藝術中尤其被描繪為和平與喜樂的象徵。此獸有鹿的身軀、牛的尾巴，額上生有一隻柔軟的獨角。據說牠從不踩踏或傷害任何生靈。牠是完美正直的象徵，也是萬物五大本源元素——水、火、木、金、土——的具體精華。

passages.text: Its appearance on the earth is ever regarded as a happy omen, as the harbinger of good government and the birth of good rulers. The male beast is called ki and the female rin or lin; the two words combined form the general term kirin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 牠降臨於世，總被視為吉兆，是善政與賢君降生的先聲。雄獸稱為「麒」，雌獸稱為「麟」或「麐」；二字合而為「麒麟」這一通稱。

passages.text: The phoenix, like the kirin, appears on the earth at or near the birth of a good ruler, and hence is the emblem of peace and good government. In its marvellous plumage the sheen of the five colors may be descried, each of which is typical of the five cardinal virtues. It is not only a symbol of auspicious government, but of inseparable fellowship, and many stanzas of poetry refer to it as typical of courtship and conjugal love.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 鳳凰與麒麟一樣，會在賢君降生之時或其前後降臨於世，因此是太平與善政的象徵。在牠奇妙的羽色中，可以辨出五色的光澤，每一色各象徵五種基本德行之一。牠不僅是祥瑞之治的象徵，也是形影不離之情的象徵，許多詩句都以牠來比喻求偶與夫妻之愛。

title.en: The Divine Tortoise of the Yellow River
title.zh: 神龜負書

region.en: City gate, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城城門（象徵性定位）

period: Mythical zoology recorded by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 33, eBook #67141

summary.en: The tortoise is the center of a great circle of superstitions. In Chinese legend a divine tortoise emerged from the Yellow River, on the shell of which a sage discovered the system of numerals and thus the foundation of mathematics and the rudiments of philosophy. This tortoise was the embodiment of the star in Ursa Major and progenitor of the tortoise tribe; it can transform itself into other forms of life and lives to ten thousand years, the symbol of long life. Ten kinds of tortoises exist, one half dragon with a tail like a fringe of silver — attendant of the god of waters, and so used as the top of a well. Many Corean gateways are surmounted with huge stone tortoises; the great seal of state, the regalia of sovereignty in Cho-sen, has the form of a tortoise; and the huge tortoise that supports mountains on its back has a shell a thousand leagues in circumference.
summary.zh: 龜負河圖而出，聖人得數理之原，遂開數學與哲學之端。此龜乃北斗之星精所化，龜族之祖；能變形他類，壽萬歲，故為長壽之符。龜有十種，其一半龍半龜，尾如銀纓，為水神之侍，故井欄多飾龜形。城門石龜、御寶龍龜，皆以鎮固之意；至若馱山巨龜，甲周一千里，則天地之支柱也。

sensitivity.note: Sino-Korean tortoise symbolism compiled by a Western observer.

passages.text: The tortoise is the centre of a great circle of pleasing superstitions, and hence is one of the set of symbols oftenest employed in Corean art. The practice of divination is mostly associated with tortoise-shell, the figuring of a tortoise's back having a mystic signification.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 龜是一大圈令人愉悅的迷信之中心，因此是朝鮮藝術中最常使用的象徵之一。占卜之術多與龜甲相關，龜背上的紋樣具有神秘的意涵。

passages.text: In Chinese legend a divine tortoise emerged from the Yellow River, on the shell of which a sage discovered the system of numerals, and thus obtained the foundation of mathematics and the rudiments of philosophy. This tortoise was said to be the embodiment of the star in Ursa Major, and the progenitor of all the tortoise tribe. It can transform itself into other forms of life and lives to the age of ten thousand years. Hence it is the symbol of long life. It is said to conceive by thought alone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 中國傳說中，有一隻神龜從黃河浮出，一位聖人在牠的龜甲上發現了數字體系，因而得到數學的基礎與哲學的雛形。據說這隻龜是北斗七星的化身，也是所有龜類的始祖。牠能變形為其他生命形態，壽達萬年。因此牠是長壽的象徵。據說牠僅憑意念便能受孕。

passages.text: There are said to be ten kinds of tortoises, one of them being half dragon, half tortoise, with a tail like a fringe of silver. This is the attendant of the god of waters, and hence is often used as the top of a well. Many Corean gateways are surmounted with huge tortoises sculptured in stone. The great seal of state, the regalia of sovereignty in Cho-sen, has the form of a tortoise. A common idea in Cho-sen, as in China, is the huge tortoise which supports mountains on its back, and having a shell which is one thousand leagues in circumference.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說龜有十種，其中一種半龍半龜，尾巴如銀色流蘇。牠是水神的侍從，因此常被用作井欄的頂飾。朝鮮的許多門樓頂上都飾有石雕的巨龜。國之大璽，即朝鮮王權的御器，形制即為龜形。朝鮮與中國一樣，常見的觀念是一隻巨龜以背馱山，其龜甲周長達千里。

title.en: The Fish-Man of the Eastern Sea
title.zh: 東海人魚

region.en: Eastern Sea (Sea of Japan) (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 東海（象徵性定位）

period: Mythical zoology recorded by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 33, eBook #67141

summary.en: The in-e, fish-man or merman, is a sort of siren supposed to inhabit the Sea of Japan and the Eastern Sea. It is six or seven feet long, and in head and body resembles a human being, its nose, mouth, ears and arms or flippers covered with white skin without scales; it has a long slender tail like a horse's. It suckles its young and sheds tears when its offspring are captured — and perhaps this is the creature around Quelpart whose tears produce pearls.
summary.zh: 東海有人魚，長六七尺，首身似人，鼻口耳臂皆有白膚無鱗，尾細長如馬尾。能哺乳其子，子為人所獲則泣。或謂濟州海中亦有其類，其淚化為珠。

sensitivity.note: Folk-zoology record; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The in-e, fish-man or merman, is a sort of siren that is supposed to inhabit the Sea of Japan and the Eastern Sea, but whether partly fabulous or entirely real, we are unable to say. It is six or seven feet long, and in its head and body resembles a human being, as its nose, mouth, ears, and arms, or flippers, are covered with white skin without scales. It has a long and slender tail, like that of a horse. It suckles its young, and sheds tears when its offspring are captured. It is probable that this creature is the same as a reported dog-fish or shark living in the seas around Quelpart, whose tears produce pearls.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 人魚（in-e），即魚人或人魚，是一種據說棲息於日本海與東海的海妖，但牠究竟是部分出於虛構還是全然真實，我們無法斷言。牠長六七尺，頭與身體似人，其鼻、口、耳以及手臂或鰭肢皆覆有無鱗的白皮。牠有一條細長的尾巴，狀如馬尾。牠以乳汁哺育幼崽，幼崽被捕時會流淚。這種生物很可能就是據稱棲息於濟州島（Quelpart）周邊海域的一種角鮫或鯊魚，其淚能化為珍珠。

title.en: Dragons' Teeth: The Drought Riot of 1882
title.zh: 庚午釀亂龍牙

region.en: Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城（象徵性定位）

period: Contemporary event interpreted by folk belief, recorded by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882); episode dated July 1882

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 33, eBook #67141

summary.en: The people believe that all the forces of nature are under the control of spirits, who will give or withhold sunshine or rain, send blasting mildew and pestilence, or fertility, plenty and joy, according as they are pleased or displeased. On this soil a demagogue may sow dragons' teeth: in the long drought that ruined the rice crop of 1882, the leaders of the anti-foreign faction persuaded the common people that the spirits were annoyed at the introduction of foreigners and therefore withheld the rain. This belief was strengthened when it rained heavily for many hours after the Japanese had been driven out of Seoul in the frightful massacre of the ministers.
summary.zh: 朝鮮人信天地風雨皆聽於神，神喜怒則雨暘疫豐隨之。故煽惑者可播『龍牙』而亂起。光緒八年（1882）大旱米貴，排外黨魁乃倡言：神怒西人入境，故不降雨。及壬午兵變殺日本使館人後，大雨連時，眾信愈堅，以為神鑒其誅而降澤。

sensitivity.note: Historical riot interpreted through folk belief; mentions real violence (1882 Imo mutiny) in summary terms only.

passages.text: They believe that all these creatures and all the forces of nature are under the control of the spirits, who will give or withhold sunshine or rain, send blasting mildew and pestilence, or fertility, plenty and joy, according as they are pleased or displeased.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們相信，所有這些生靈以及一切自然之力，皆受神靈掌控；神靈依其喜怒，或賜予或扣留晴雨，或降下摧折的霉害與瘟疫，或賜予豐饒、富足與歡樂。

passages.text: It will be seen at once what a soil the demagogue has for sowing dragons' teeth, and what frightful popular commotion may be stirred up by playing upon the fears of the populace. The most recent illustration of this is seen in the frightful massacre of the ministers and the Japanese, in July 1882.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 由此立刻可見，煽動者有何等土壤可供播撒龍牙，而藉操弄民眾的恐懼，又能掀起何等可怕的民變。此事最近的例證，見於一八八二年七月對大臣與日本人的駭人屠殺。

passages.text: The long drought having ruined the rice crop, the leaders of the anti-foreign faction persuaded the common people that the spirits were annoyed at the introduction of foreigners, and therefore withheld the rain. In this belief they were strengthened from the fact that it rained heavily for many hours after the Japanese had been driven out of Seoul.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 長久乾旱毀了稻作，排外派的領袖們便使平民相信：神靈因外人引入而震怒，故而扣住雨水。日本人被逐出漢城之後，連降大雨達數時之久，此一事實更堅定了他們的這番信念。

title.en: The Three Wishes and the Pudding on the Nose
title.zh: 三願餅黏鼻

region.en: Poor cottage, winter night (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 寒夜陋室（象徵性定位）

period: Korean folk tale collected in the Grammaire Coreenne, retold by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 34, eBook #67141

summary.en: Two poor old married folk lament the winter, pray to Heaven, and an angel grants them three things and no more. They cannot decide between riches, health, long life and a child — until at bedtime the old woman wishes for three feet of pudding to toast on the brazier, which appears at once. The enraged husband wishes it to hang from her nose; it does. He laments losing a wish; she tries to hang herself; and finally she spends the last wish on getting the pudding off. A voice from heaven rebukes their vain desires; they eat the pudding, adopt an orphan, and from that night abstain from foolish wishes.
summary.zh: 貧夫婦寒夜相對歎貧，禱於天。天使忽降，賜三願。議之未決，嫗臨睡忽曰：『若有三尺餅炙於爐，豈不美哉！』言未畢，餅已置於側。翁怒罵：『願此餅黏於汝鼻！』餅即飛黏嫗鼻。嫗欲自縊，翁懼而止之，許以末願取下。嫗曰：『願餅落。』言訖餅墜地，天上有聲責其妄願。二人啖餅，養孤兒為嗣，自是不復妄求。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale from missionary-collected material; the ATU 'three wishes' type in a Korean telling.

passages.text: There were once two old married folks who had not a single child. Extremely poor, they lived a pitiable life. One cold winter evening, after supper, they gazed into the fire in the brazier and lamented that for the poor, winter is a rough time, with neither food for the mouth nor fuel; if they go out over the mountain through rain or snow to seek wood, they die of cold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一對老夫婦，一個孩子也沒有。他們極其貧窮，過著可憐的生活。一個寒冷的冬夜，晚飯之後，他們凝望著火盆裡的火，哀嘆窮人過冬真是艱難，既無食物入口，也無柴薪可用；若冒著雨雪翻山越嶺去尋柴，便會凍死。

passages.text: They prayed fervently to the Deity, when suddenly an angel appeared: 'In spite of your sin of murmuring, Heaven having pitied you, accords you three things, after which you can ask no more. Reflect well, choose, and ask.' They could not decide: riches, freedom from sickness, long life, or a child? At the moment of lying down to sleep, the old woman, stirring the fire with the tongs, reflected, 'If we could have three or four feet of pudding to set to toast on this brazier, that would be royally excellent.' She spoke, and there was three feet of food placed by her side.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們向神明殷切祈禱，忽然一位天使顯現：「你們雖有怨言的罪過，上天憐憫你們，賜你們三件事，此後便不可再求。好好思量，選定，然後求吧。」他們拿不定主意：財富、免於疾病、長壽，還是一個孩子？就在躺下就寢之際，老婦人用火鉗撥著火，心想：「若能有三四尺長的布丁放在這火盆上烤，那真是再好不過了。」她話一出口，便有三尺長的食物放在她身旁。

passages.text: The husband, beside himself with rage, screamed out, 'Oh, what a woman! To punish you I wish the pudding would hang itself on the point of your nose.' Immediately the pudding made a leap and attached itself to the old dame's nose. He cried that he too had lost a wish; the woman in tears took a cord to strangle herself; and the husband, touched with compassion, said, 'Stop, there remains one wish to us. Have your own way about it.' 'If that is so, I wish that what hangs to my nose comes loose.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 丈夫氣得發狂，尖聲叫道：「哎呀，這女人！為了懲罰妳，我願那布丁掛在妳鼻尖上。」布丁立刻一躍，黏上了老婦人的鼻子。他嚷道自己也失去了一個願望；婦人哭著拿來繩子要自縊；丈夫心生憐憫，說道：「住手，我們還剩一個願望。就隨妳的意思吧。」「既然如此，我願掛在我鼻子上的東西鬆脫下來。」

passages.text: She had hardly finished speaking when the sausage fell plump to the ground, and out of the midst of heaven an angry voice was heard: 'You have obtained the three things you wished for, and have you gained a great advantage? If you wish to enjoy true blessing, be content to live with what Heaven gives, and do not form vain desires.' The two old folks ate the pudding, and on the morrow, agreeably to their supreme ambition of having a baby, adopted a little fatherless and motherless orphan, and lived happily to extreme old age.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她話音剛落，那香腸便噗的一聲掉在地上，只聽得天際之間傳來一個憤怒的聲音：「你們已經得到了所願的三樣東西，難道還得了天大的好處嗎？你們若想享有真正的福分，就當安於上天所賜，與之共處，不可生出虛妄的念頭。」老夫婦二人吃了那布丁，到了次日，便順從他們那想要一個孩子的至高心願，收養了一個無父無母的孤兒，幸福地活到了極高的年歲。

title.en: The History of a Nose
title.zh: 一鼻之債

region.en: Cholla provincial city (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 全羅道邑城（象徵性定位）

period: Korean folk tale collected in the Grammaire Coreenne, retold by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 34, eBook #67141

summary.en: A politician in the chief city of Chulla owes the government ten thousand strings of cash and awaits execution. He cajoles the jailer into letting him out at night, then persuades the governor that a dead debtor is worth nothing alive, and secures a stay — visiting nightly. On his rounds he has a sketch of a human nose sealed by the governor, then travels the coast with three accomplices telling a rich doctor's son that the king is sick and can be cured only by a medicine concocted from a nose exactly like the sketch, which matches his father's. The son buys off the 'royal messengers' at vast cost, and dares tell no one until his father's death: 'I have bought my father's nose for ten thousand strings of cash.'
summary.zh: 全羅道邑有政客負官帑萬緡，論死。賂獄卒夜縱之，說太守曰：『殺我則帑無著，生我則帑可還。』得緩刑。又請太守於人鼻畫上用印，乃攜黨徒沿海行詐：詭言王疾，非得與畫同之鼻入藥不瘳，而某富翁之父之鼻恰合。其子懼，出巨金贖之。父死乃自言：『吾以萬緡買父之鼻也。』

sensitivity.note: Folk satire on officialdom; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In the chief city of Chulla there was a politician who was in debt to the government to the amount of ten thousand strings of cash. Unable to pay, he was condemned to death. Bethinking himself of a stratagem, he so besought the jailer that, struck with compassion, the man let him go free for a while.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在全羅的首府，有一個為官之人欠了官府一萬串錢。他無力償還，被判了死罪。他心中想出一條計策，便苦苦哀求獄卒，獄卒動了憐憫之心，便放他暫時自由。

passages.text: At midnight he presented himself before the door where the governor slept, and argued: 'If you put your servant to death this will be simply one man of means less in the world, and the money I owe will be lost to the government. If, on the contrary, you preserve my life, I shall repay the whole of my debt.' He visited again the next night, drew from his sleeve a sketch representing a human nose, and besought the governor to put his seal upon it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了半夜，他來到府使安睡的那扇門前，辯說道：「您若將小人處死，這不過是世上少了一個有錢的人，而我所欠的錢也就成了官府的一筆損失。反之，您若保全我的性命，我便會將全部欠債償還。」第二夜他又來訪，從袖中取出一幅畫著人鼻的圖樣，懇求府使在上面蓋印。

passages.text: He now associated three companions, and on the coast of the Eastern Sea they found the grand mansion of a rich noble. Taking the son aside, the officer declared: 'The king is very sick, and all the physicians have declared that the only means of healing is to find the nose of a man just like this and to concoct a remedy from it. We have been commanded, without distinction of place or person, to strike off such a nose and produce it at Court. Your honorable father's nose exactly resembles this.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他於是結交了三名同伴，在東海之濱，他們尋到一位富貴顯宦的宏偉宅第。那差役把兒子拉到一旁，說道：「國王病得很重，眾醫官都說，唯一的治法便是尋得一個與此圖一模一樣的人的鼻子，用它配成藥。我們奉命，不分地方、不問何人，都要割下這樣的鼻子送到朝廷。令尊的鼻子與此圖分毫不差。」

passages.text: The son cried out that cutting off his old father's nose was impossible, and the officer replied: 'As this is a matter of a son devoted to his father, we shall not cut off the nose; but if you will give us a certain sum we will go elsewhere to procure a nose which we shall present to the king.' He accepted a sum equal to many times ten thousand strings of cash, and warned the son to say nothing. Overjoyed at not having his parent's nose amputated, the son dared let no one know until the day of his father's death; then breaking the silence he said, 'I have bought my father's nose for ten thousand strings of cash.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那兒子大叫道，割下老父的鼻子是萬萬不行的，差役便回答說：「既然這是出於兒子孝順父親之事，我們便不割這鼻子了；但你若肯給我們一筆錢，我們就到別處去弄一個鼻子，獻給國王。」他收下了一筆相當於好幾萬串錢的銀錢，並叮囑那兒子不可聲張。兒子因父親的鼻子免於被割而大喜過望，直到父親去世之日，都不敢讓任何人知道；這時他才打破沉默說道：「我用一萬串錢買下了我父親的鼻子。」

title.en: King Cheng-chong and the Examination in the Night
title.zh: 正祖夜試錄賢

region.en: Streets and examination hall, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城市廛試院（象徵性定位）

period: Korean royal anecdote recorded by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882); King Chongjo reigned 1776-1800

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 34, eBook #67141

summary.en: King Cheng-chong, celebrated for goodness, goes out one night disguised as a countryman. Peeping through a hole in the paper door of a miserable house he sees an old man weeping, a man in mourning singing, and a nun dancing. Questioned, the man in mourning explains: his wife has cut and sold her last hair to buy bean-soup for his starving old father, becoming bareheaded like a nun; the old man weeps at degrading her; and to console him, wife and husband dance and sing. The king, moved, invents an examination for the morrow with the subject 'the song of a man in mourning, the dance of a nun, the tears of an old man'; no student can fathom it, but the poor householder alone knows it perfectly, wins the doctorate, and is loaded with office for his filial piety.
summary.zh: 正祖微行夜出，穴紙窺一貧家：見老翁泣、居喪者歌、尼而舞者三人。詰之，其人曰：『家貧無以養親，妻剪盡髮鬻之市豆羹以奉舅姑，遂如尼。舅愧而泣，妻舞以解之，我亦歌。』王大異之，翌日突設科試，題即『喪者之歌、尼之舞、老翁之淚』。諸生皆不解，惟此人切中，遂擢甲第，旌其孝。

sensitivity.note: Royal anecdote; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: There was in Cho-sen a king called His Majesty Cheng-chong, celebrated in all the kingdom for his goodness. One night, disguised as a countryman and accompanied only by a single companion, he started out to make a circuit to inform himself of the temper of his subjects. Arrived at a certain point he looked in the window of a miserable house, punched a peep-hole in the paper door and perceived an old man weeping, a man in mourning singing, and a nun or widow dancing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 朝鮮有一位國王，稱為成宗大王，舉國上下都因他的仁德而稱頌他。一天夜裡，他扮作鄉下人，只帶一名隨從，便出發巡行，以察知臣民的心意。行至某處，他往一間破屋的窗內張望，在紙門上戳了一個小孔，看見一個老人在哭泣，一個服喪的人在歌唱，還有一個尼姑或寡婦在跳舞。

passages.text: Questioned, the man in mourning explained: 'In my hut one could never find sufficient grain for a meal. I have no victuals for my old father. Morning and evening, in default of all other resource, my wife has often cut off a tress of her hair and sold it to buy a cup of bean-soup, which she offers to my father. This evening she clipped and sold all the hair that remained, and has become bare-headed like a nun. My old father, seeing that for his sake his young daughter-in-law has become a nun, broke out weeping: why have I lived to degrade my daughter-in-law? To console him my wife danced, and I, although in mourning, joined in with song.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那服喪之人被詰問後解釋道：「在我的茅屋裡，一頓飯的糧食從來都湊不齊。我沒有食物供養老父。早晚之間，別無他法，我的妻子常剪下一綹頭髮賣掉，換一杯豆羹來奉給我的父親。今晚她把剩下的頭髮全都剪下賣了，成了光頭，像個尼姑一般。我的老父見他的年輕媳婦為了他成了尼姑，便放聲大哭：我為何活著，竟使我的媳婦受此屈辱？為安慰他，我的妻子跳起舞來，而我雖在服喪，也跟著唱了起來。」

passages.text: The king was impressed with such marked devotion, and said, 'How will it do to present you at the examination to-morrow?' No examination was known; but no sooner did the great clock-bell vibrate than he ordered an examination published during the night, to the astonishment of the literary men. The subject was: 'The song of a man in mourning, the dance of a nun, the tears of an old man.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 國王深為這般顯著的孝心所感動，說道：「明日讓你赴試，如何？」並未聽聞有甚麼考試；然而那大鐘一響，他便下令連夜開科取士，令文人們大為驚訝。題目是：「服喪者之歌，尼姑之舞，老翁之淚。」

passages.text: Of all the students not one could derive the sense of such a subject; this man alone knew it perfectly well, because he had had experience of those very things in his own house. He treated the theme clearly, and the king, having examined the essay and found it without a mistake, gave the degree of doctor and loaded him with office, recompensing the filial piety of the son and daughter-in-law.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 所有學子之中，無一人能領會這般題目的意旨；唯有此人完全明白，因為這些事他自家裡親身經歷過。他將此題闡發得清清楚楚，國王閱其文章，見毫無差錯，便賜他進士及第，授以官職，以酬報那兒子與媳婦的孝行。

title.en: The Prodigious Effects of a Looking-Glass
title.zh: 寶鏡奇冤

region.en: Kyongsang province village (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 慶尚道村邑（象徵性定位）

period: Korean folk tale collected in the Grammaire Coreenne, retold by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 34, eBook #67141

summary.en: A young noble of Kiung-sang province journeys to Seoul, and his wife begs him to bring back the lovely glass-like thing of which she has heard: if you look in it you will see a very curious thing. He buys a mirror and packs it unexamined. At home the wife looks, sees a woman, and storms that he has brought home a concubine; he looks and sees a man, and cries that she keeps a libertine — the old mother looks and sees the widow Pak, the grandfather the fee-collecting teacher, and the whole village sees only itself. Finally the magistrate summons his men and horses to receive the new officer he supposes has displaced him — until a young policeman demonstrates how the glass reflects every face that gazes into it.
summary.zh: 慶尚士人將赴漢京，其妻囑購『照之則見奇物』之寶鏡。歸而妻照，見婦，怒詬夫攜妾；夫照，見男，斥妻藏漢；婆照，見白媼；翁照，見索脩之塾師；闔村競照，唯見己身，喧然告官。太守照之，見一官人，以為新官至而奪己位，亟備車馬。一少年捕快熟視，乃悟：鏡中所見，皆照者之面也。

sensitivity.note: Folk satire; city-folk tale about country bumpkins; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: A young noble of Kiung-sang province was going on a journey to Seoul. Just as he was about to depart, his wife called him: 'I have heard the mother of Mr. Kim speak of a very lovely thing which looks like glass and pretty metal. They say that if you look in it you will see a very curious thing. You must bring me one.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 慶尚道有一位年輕貴族要前往漢城。正要動身之際，他的妻子喚住他：「我聽金先生的母親說起一件極美的東西，看起來像玻璃，又像好看的銅器。他們說往裡一照，便會看見一件十分奇妙的東西。你一定要替我帶一個回來。」

passages.text: Having finished his business at Seoul he made the purchase of a mirror through one of his friends, and put his wife's commission in his wallet without even looking at it. When he arrived home, she hastened to take out the mirror. At once she perceived in it a woman, and began to weep and berate her husband for bringing along a concubine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他在漢城辦完事後，託一位朋友買了一面鏡子，連看也沒看一眼，就把妻子囑咐之物放進了他的行囊。回到家中，她急忙取出鏡子。她立刻在鏡中看見一個女人，便哭了起來，責罵丈夫竟帶回一個妾。

passages.text: The amazed husband looked in the mirror, and at the side of his wife perceived a man; he was about to murder his wife, when his old mother came in. Looking in the mirror she saw a woman and broke into a laugh: 'Is it because you see the old woman, your neighbor, that you dispute? The widow Pak has come to get some fire.' The venerable grandfather entered the children's room, perceived in the mirror an aged man, and grumbled that the puppy of the teacher Tsoi had come to collect his fees.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 驚愕的丈夫往鏡中一看，在妻子身旁看見一個男人；他正要殺妻，他的老母親走了進來。她往鏡中一看，看見一個女人，便笑出聲來：「你爭吵，莫非是因為看見了老婦人，你的鄰居？朴寡婦來討點火了。」老祖父走進孩子們的房間，在鏡中看見一個年邁的男人，便嘟囔著說崔先生的狗崽子來討他的學費了。

passages.text: The people of the village, one by one, two by two, all looked at the mirror and made a tumult. They carried it to the magistrate, who, more astonished than the others, ordered: 'A new officer has arrived, why have I lost my place? Get ready men and horses for him.' He believed he had been cashiered, until a young policeman, after careful examination of the mirror, pointed out the manner in which the visage of each individual was reflected.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 村中之人，或一人獨往，或兩人結伴，皆來觀鏡，因而喧嚷騷動。眾人將鏡呈於地方官，地方官較諸人更為驚異，遂下令曰：「新任官員已到，我何以失其職位？為其備好人馬。」他以為自己已被革職，直至一名年輕差役仔細察看此鏡之後，指出各人之面容映於鏡中之方式。

title.en: The Winged Tiger of the War-Flags
title.zh: 有翼神虎旗

region.en: Han River forts, 1871 campaign (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢江要塞（象徵性定位）

period: Ethnographic record by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882); the banner described from the 1871 campaign

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 36, eBook #67141

summary.en: Both actually and ideally the tiger is the symbol of power and fierceness in Corea; popular superstition attributes to him the powers of flying, of emitting fire and hurling lightning. The flag of the tiger-hunters from the northern provinces who faced the marines in 1871 was a winged tiger rampant, spitting fire and holding the lightnings in his lifted fore-claws, embodying the powers of earth, air and heaven — the tutelary genius of the descendants of the aboriginal worshippers of the tiger. From the most ancient times the tiger has been an object of religious reverence; the cry of the name tu-e', the fabulous enemy of the tiger, acts as a charm against the man-eater.
summary.zh: 虎者朝鮮威猛之象。俗信其能飛、口吐火、爪掣雷。同治十年獵虎軍戰旗，繪有翼猛虎，口噴火，爪擎電，蓋天地人三才之力萃焉——此虎圖騰遺民之守護神也。虎自古被尊為神。又有神獸曰土嵬者為虎所懼，夜呼『土嵬』可退虎患。

sensitivity.note: Tiger cult recorded ethnographically; the 1871 conflict is referenced only as provenance of the banner.

passages.text: Both actually and ideally the tiger is the symbol of power and fierceness. The flag of the tiger-hunters, from the northern provinces of Ping-an or Ham-kiung, who bravely faced the rifles of the United States marines and sailors in 1871, was a winged tiger rampant, spitting fire, holding the lightnings in his lifted fore-claws, and thus embodying the powers of earth, air, and heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 36 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 無論在實際上或理想上，虎皆為權力與兇猛之象徵。虎獵者之旗，出自平安道或咸鏡道等北方諸道，彼等曾於一八七一年勇敢面對美國海軍陸戰隊與水兵之步槍；其旗上繪一有翼之虎，作躍立之姿，口吐火焰，舉起之前爪中握有閃電，如此體現了地、空、天三界之力量。

passages.text: It is the tutelary genius of the descendants of the aboriginal worshippers of the tiger, who even yet cling to the religion of the soil. Popular superstition attributes to him the powers of flying, of emitting fire and hurling lightning. From the most ancient times it has been an object of religious reverence: 'They also worshipped the tiger, which they looked on as a god,' was written of the people living on the sea of Japan before the Christian era.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 36 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 虎乃最初崇拜虎之先民後裔之守護神，此等後裔至今仍堅守鄉土之宗教。民間迷信賦予虎飛翔、吐火與投擲閃電之能力。自最古老之時代起，虎即為宗教崇敬之對象：「彼等亦崇拜虎，視之為神」，此語乃用以記述基督教紀元以前居住於日本海沿岸之民族。

passages.text: To drive away the dreaded kal-pem, the people invoke the aid of the tu-e, a fabulous monster, which is the enemy of the tiger, and which the latter greatly fears. The cry of his name, tu-e, tu-e, is believed to act as a charm, and is often raised by villagers at night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 36 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 為驅逐可怖之 kal-pem，人們祈求 tu-e 之助；tu-e 乃一傳說中之怪物，為虎之敵，虎對之極為畏懼。據信呼其名 tu-e、tu-e 可作符咒之用，村民常於夜間高呼此名。

title.en: The Four Tulans and the Obsidian Stone's Creation
title.zh: 四圖蘭與黑曜石之造人

region.en: Tulan (mythic place of origin), symbolic pin on the Pacific slope of Chiapas-Guatemala
region.zh: 圖蘭（神話起源地），以恰帕斯-危地馬拉太平洋坡地為象徵定位

period: Cakchiquel annals compiled 1571-1604 by Xahila family; Brinton translation 1885

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels (Memorial de Tecpan Atitlan), trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 4-5

summary.en: Gagavitz and Zactecauh teach that there are four Tulans — at sunrise, at Xibalbay, at sunset, and where God is — and that man was first made in misery by the Maker and Creator, sustained by the Obsidian Stone, until the coyote, crow, and Tiuh Tiuh brought maize from Paxil and human flesh was kneaded into being.
summary.zh: 加加維茨與扎克特考教示：圖蘭有四——日出處、希巴爾巴、日落處與神之所在。人初受造於苦難，由塑造者所造、以黑曜石為支柱，直至郊狼、鴉與蒂烏·蒂烏自帕希爾帶來玉米，人之肉身方由玉米揉成。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase/summary of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: Four men came from Tulan: there is one Tulan at the sunrise, one at Xibalbay, one at the sunset — from this one at the sunset we came, from Tulan beyond the sea — and one is where God is. Therefore there are four Tulans, and it was at Tulan that, arriving, we were brought forth and begotten by our mothers and our fathers.
passages.note: Quoted and lightly condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 4; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 有四人自圖蘭而來：一圖蘭在日出之處，一在希巴爾拜，一在日落之處——我們即來自這日落之處之圖蘭，來自海外之圖蘭——另有一處乃神所在之地。故圖蘭共有四處，而正是在圖蘭，我們抵達之時，由我們的母親與父親孕育而生。

passages.text: Then the Obsidian Stone is brought forth by the precious Xibalbay, and man is made by the Maker, the Creator; the Obsidian Stone was his sustainer when man was made in misery. He was fed with wood and leaves; he wished only the earth; he could not speak, could not walk; he had no blood, he had no flesh.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 5; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 於是，珍貴之希巴爾拜取出黑曜石，而人由造物者、創造者所造；當人於困苦中被造之時，黑曜石乃其維生之物。他以木與葉為食；他只渴望土地；他不能言語，不能行走；他沒有血，沒有肉。

passages.text: Nothing was found to feed him, until two brutes knew there was food in the place called Paxil: the Coyote and the Crow. The Coyote, killed by the brute Tiuh Tiuh as he gathered maize, yielded the grain for kneading, and the blood of the serpent and the tapir was brought from within the sea to mix the maize. Of it the flesh of man was formed — thirteen men and fourteen women, who talked, walked, had blood, had flesh, and married.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 5; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 沒有人找到可以餵養他的東西，直到兩個粗野的傢伙得知，在一個名叫帕希爾的地方有食物：那便是郊狼與烏鴉。郊狼在採集玉米時被那粗野的傢伙蒂烏·蒂烏殺死，獻出了用以揉麵的穀粒，而蛇與貘的血則從海中取來，用以調和玉米。人的肉體便由之而成——十三個男人與十四個女人，他們能言語、能行走、有血、有肉，並且婚配。

title.en: Tribute at the Gate of Tulan and the Idols of Wood and Stone
title.zh: 圖蘭門口的貢賦與木石之像

region.en: Tulan (mythic place of origin), symbolic pin on the Pacific slope of Chiapas-Guatemala
region.zh: 圖蘭（神話起源地），以恰帕斯-危地馬拉太平洋坡地為象徵定位

period: Cakchiquel annals compiled 1571-1604; Brinton translation 1885

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 6-8

summary.en: Thirteen divisions and seven tribes gather at Tulan in darkness and pay tribute in jade, silver, featherwork, painted and sculpted wares, calendars, and songs. The Obsidian Stone assigns them their burdens, and as they descend they are given 'the wood and stone which deceive' — the idols that will travel with them.
summary.zh: 十三部與七族於黑暗中聚於圖蘭，奉納玉、銀、羽飾、雕繪之物、曆法與歌。黑曜石為其定下重負；下行之際，獲授「欺騙的木與石」——即將隨行的神像。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: We were ordered to come by our mothers and fathers, we the thirteen divisions and the seven tribes, and we came to Tulan in the darkness and the night. There we gave our tribute: jade and silver, green feathers worked and sewed, articles painted and sculptured, flutes, songs, astrological calendars and reckoning calendars, fine and common cacao — only such riches were paid in Tulan.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 6; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 我們的母親與父親吩咐我們前來，我們這十三支系與七個部族，在黑暗與夜色中來到了圖蘭。我們在那裡獻上我們的貢品：玉石與白銀、加工縫綴的綠羽、彩繪與雕刻的器物、笛子、歌曲、占星曆與推算曆、上等與普通的可可——在圖蘭所繳納的財富僅有這些。

passages.text: Then the Obsidian Stone spoke: 'You, my sons, my daughters, these are your burdens which you shall sustain. There are your hills and plains, beyond the ocean; there it is that you shall lift up your faces. These are the burdens I shall give you, your riches, your majesty.' And as they descended from Tulan and Xibalbay they were given the wood and stone which deceive — the idols that would stand in their houses.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 7; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 於是黑曜石開口說道：『你們，我的兒子們，我的女兒們，這些是你們將要承擔的重擔。那邊有你們的山丘與平原，在大洋彼岸；你們要在那裡抬起你們的臉。這些是我要賜給你們的重擔，你們的財富，你們的威嚴。』而當他們從圖蘭與希巴爾巴伊下來時，他們被賜予了那欺瞞人的木與石——那些將立於他們屋中的偶像。

title.en: The Portent Birds at the Gate
title.zh: 門口的兆鳥

region.en: Tulan (mythic place of origin), symbolic pin on the Pacific slope of Chiapas-Guatemala
region.zh: 圖蘭（神話起源地），以恰帕斯-危地馬拉太平洋坡地為象徵定位

period: Cakchiquel annals compiled 1571-1604; Brinton translation 1885

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 13-14

summary.en: As the tribes go forth from Tulan, three birds cry their omens: the 'guard of the ravine' predicts death, the owl claims to be their portent, and the parroquet wails from the sky. The migrants answer each bird in its turn, refusing fear and reading the parrot as merely the sign of spring.
summary.zh: 諸族自圖蘭啟程之際，三隻鳥相繼啼兆：「谷之守衛」預言死亡；鴞自稱其兆；鸚鵡於空中哀鳴。遷徙者逐鳥回應，拒斥恐懼，並謂鸚鵡僅是春天的信號。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: A bird called the guard of the ravine began to complain within the gate of Tulan as we went forth: 'You shall die, you shall be lost, I am your portent. Do you not believe me? Truly your state shall be a sad one,' said this brute to us.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 13; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 一隻名叫峽谷守衛的鳥，在我們出去時於圖蘭的門內開始哀鳴：『你們將死去，你們將毀滅，我是你們的凶兆。你們不信我嗎？你們的境況當真將是悲慘的，』這粗野的傢伙對我們說道。

passages.text: Then the owl, seated on a red tree, complained: 'I am your portent.' 'You are not our portent, although you would like to be,' we answered it. And the parroquet cried from the sky: 'I am your portent; you shall die.' But we said: 'Do not speak thus; you are but the sign of spring; you wail first when it is spring, and when the rain ceases you wail.'
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 14; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 接著那棲於紅樹上的貓頭鷹哀鳴道：『我是你們的凶兆。』『你不是我們的凶兆，儘管你倒想是，』我們回答牠。而那鸚鵡從天空中叫道：『我是你們的凶兆；你們將死去。』但我們說：『別這樣說；你不過是春天的徵兆；春天一到你便先哀鳴，雨停之時你也哀鳴。』

title.en: The Staff of the Red Tree: Crossing the Sea
title.zh: 紅樹之杖：渡海

region.en: The sea crossing from Tulan, symbolic pin on the Gulf of Tehuantepec coast
region.zh: 自圖蘭渡海，以特萬特佩克灣岸為象徵定位

period: Cakchiquel annals compiled 1571-1604; Brinton translation 1885

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 15-16

summary.en: At the sea all the warriors of the seven villages despair — no one has ever crossed. Gagavitz and Zactecauh plant the root of the red staff they carried from Tulan in the sand, and the sea parts from the sand, uncovering a road above and below the water. All pass over and rejoice: the staff, not a boat, is the vessel of the migration.
summary.zh: 抵海之際，七村戰士皆絕望——從無人渡此海。加加維茨與扎克特考將自圖蘭攜來的紅杖之根植入沙中，海水與沙分離，露出水上水下之道。眾人相繼渡海而喜：杖而非舟，是遷徙的舟楫。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: There were gathered together the warriors of all the seven villages at the sea, and a great number perished, devoured by sorrow. 'There is no means of passing, nor is it told of anyone who has passed the sea,' they said. 'In thee alone, my brother, in thee alone have we hope.'
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 15; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 七個村落的所有戰士都聚集在海邊，許多人死去，被悲傷所吞噬。『沒有辦法過去，也未曾聽說有誰渡過這片海，』他們說道。『唯有在你身上，我的兄弟，唯有在你身上，我們才有希望。』

passages.text: Then there was a red tree, our staff, which we had taken in passing from the gate of Tulan — and therefore we are called the Cakchiquel people. The root of this staff was pushed into the sand of the sea, and soon the sea was separated from the sand; the sand became as a line and grew wide above the sea and below the sea, and we passed out. Then all rejoiced when they saw sand in the sea.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 16; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 接著有一棵紅樹，那是我們的杖，是我們在經過時從圖蘭的城門取得的——因此我們被稱為卡克奇克爾人。這杖的根被推入海中的沙裡，不久海便與沙分開；沙成了一條線，在海之上與海之下都變寬了，我們便走了出去。然後眾人看見海中有沙，都歡喜了。

title.en: War with the Nonoualcats: Names Drawn from Salvation
title.zh: 與諾諾瓦爾卡特之戰：由救法取名

region.en: Zuyva (mythic eastern city), symbolic pin on the Pacific coastal plain of Guatemala
region.zh: 祖伊瓦（東方神話之城），以危地馬拉太平洋岸平原為象徵定位

period: Cakchiquel annals compiled 1571-1604; Brinton translation 1885

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 19-20

summary.en: The migrants meet the Nonoualcats in their boats on the ocean border, rout them, and seize the boats to cross; but entering the great town of Zuyva in the east, they meet sorcery — fighting in the houses, with dogs and wasps, attackers ascending into the air — and are driven back. Each nation then names itself by its salvation: Tohohil in the sky, Cakix in the ara's mouth, Gucumatz in the water, Akalahay in the honeycomb.
summary.zh: 遷徙者於海際遭逢乘舟的諾諾瓦爾卡特人，擊潰之並奪舟渡海；然而入東方大城祖伊瓦，遭遇妖術——屋內搏鬥、與犬蜂作戰、敵人升空——而被逐回。諸族遂各以其救法命名：托霍希爾在天、卡基希在鸚鵡之口、庫庫馬茲在水、阿卡拉哈伊在蜂巢。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: Soon we met face to face a party of warriors called those of Nonovalcat and those of Xulpit, on the border of the ocean, in their boats. The fighting was fearful; they were routed by us, half the fighting being in the boats, and we entered the boats of those of Nonovalcat to cross the sea while our battle was not yet known.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 20; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 不久，我們在海洋的邊界上，面對面遇見了一隊戰士，稱為諾諾瓦爾卡特的人與蘇爾皮特的人，他們乘著船。戰鬥十分可怕；他們被我們擊潰，有一半的戰鬥是在船上進行的，我們便進入諾諾瓦爾卡特人的船中渡海，而我們的戰事尚未為人所知。

passages.text: Truly it was fearful in the town and houses of those of Zuyva, there in the east: the noise was great, the dust oppressive; fighting went on in the houses, fighting with the dogs, the wasps — for they were in the air and in the earth, ascending and descending everywhere against us, and thus they showed their magic and sorcery. We were routed, and all the warriors returned each one by himself to Tapcu Oloman, gathering in sadness.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 20; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 在蘇伊瓦人的城鎮與房屋中，真可怕，就在那東方：喧聲甚大，塵土逼人；戰鬥在房屋中進行，與狗、與黃蜂戰鬥——因為牠們在空中，也在地下，各處上上下下地攻擊我們，牠們就這樣顯出牠們的魔法與巫術。我們被擊潰了，所有戰士各自一人回到塔普庫奧洛曼，在悲傷中聚集。

passages.text: When we asked each other where our salvation was, each nation named it and took its name: the Quiche men said their salvation was in the sky, and were called Tohohil; the Zotzil said it was in the mouth of an ara, and were called Cakix; we said it was in the middle of the valley, entering the earth, and were called Chitagah; another said it was in the water and was called Gucumatz; and the Akahals, who said they might be saved in a honeycomb, were called Akalahay. Do not believe that many were saved: the Evil One scattered us abroad.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 20; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 當我們彼此詢問我們的拯救在哪裡時，各族都說出它並取了它的名：基切人說他們的拯救在天上，便被稱為托霍希爾；索齊爾人說它在金剛鸚鵡的口中，便被稱為卡基什；我們說它在山谷之中，進入地裡，便被稱為奇塔加赫；另一個說它在水中，便被稱為古庫馬茨；而阿卡哈爾人說他們或可在蜂巢中得救，便被稱為阿卡拉哈伊。不要相信有許多人得救：那惡者把我們驅散到各處。

title.en: Zakiqoxol, the Heart of the Forest
title.zh: 扎基科紹爾，森林之心

region.en: Forests between Chiyol and Hunahpu, Guatemalan highlands
region.zh: 危地馬拉高地奇奧爾與烏納普之間的森林

period: Cakchiquel annals compiled 1571-1604; Brinton translation 1885

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 21-22

summary.en: Passing between the mountain ranges, the migrants meet a fire built on the road by Zakiqoxol, the spirit of the forest, who kills many men. Challenged as a hideous guardian, he begs for clothes, and they dress him in his blood-red cuirass and shoes; thus clothed and named, he spares them and sinks back into the woods.
summary.zh: 穿越山脊之間，遷徙者遇見扎基科紹爾——森林之靈、殺人甚多的凶神——在路旁所燃之火。眾人斥其為醜陋的守路者，他求衣蔽體；他們便為他穿上血紅胸甲與血紅鞋履；穿著命名之後，他放過他們，隱回林中。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: Twice they turned their steps and passed between the mountain ranges to the fire, to Hunahpu; and there they met face to face in the spirit of the forest the fire called Zakiqoxol. Truly, this Zakiqoxol kills many men; truly he is fearful, a robber, they say.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 21; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 他們兩次轉步，穿過山脈之間，往火那裡去，往胡納赫普那裡去；他們在那裡於森林的靈中，面對面遇見了那稱為薩基科肖爾的火。真的，這薩基科肖爾殺死許多人；真的，他可怕，人們說他是個強盜。

passages.text: Going on, they arrived in the middle of the woods at a fire built by one guarding the road. 'Who are these boys whom we see?' said he. And they sent forward the Qoxahil and the Qobakil with their mysterious vision, and they said: 'Who are you? We shall kill you. Why do you guard the road here?'
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 22; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 他們繼續前行，來到林中一處由一個守路者所生的火旁。「我們所見的這些少年是誰？」他說。他們便派科沙希爾與科巴基爾帶著他們神秘的異象前去，他們說：「你是誰？我們要殺你。你為何在此守路？」

passages.text: Then he said: 'Do not kill me; I, who am here, I am the heart of the forest.' And he asked that he might clothe himself, and they gave him wherewith to clothe himself: a change of garment, his blood-red cuirass, his blood-red shoes, the dying raiment of Zakiqoxol. By this means he saved himself, descending into the forest, and the trees and birds murmured where he had been — the place called Chitabal, the Place of Disquiet.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 22; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 接著他說：「不要殺我；我，在此的我，就是森林之心。」他請求讓他穿上衣物，他們便給了他用以蔽體之物：一套替換的衣裳、他血紅的胸甲、他血紅的鞋，扎基科索爾臨死之衣。藉此他保全了自己，遁入森林，而在他曾所在之處，樹木與鳥兒低鳴——那地方名叫奇塔巴爾，即不安之地。

title.en: The Mute People of Mem
title.zh: 梅姆的啞族

region.en: Mem and Tacna (mythic stations of the migration), Guatemalan highlands
region.zh: 梅姆與塔克納（遷徙途程），危地馬拉高地

period: Cakchiquel annals compiled 1571-1604; Brinton translation 1885

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, sec. 24

summary.en: Among the peoples of Mem and Tacna the migrants cannot make themselves understood — hence the name Mem, the mute. The people are kind and beg them to stay, wishing them to forget their own speech; but their heart is 'as a stone', and they hold to their tongue and move on.
summary.zh: 在梅姆與塔克納的人們中，遷徙者無法使己意被解——故名梅姆，即啞。其人雖善，懇請他們留下，望其忘卻己語；但其心如石，遂守其舌，前行而去。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: They went to the places, Meme and Tacna, for the second time. They could not speak well, hence the name Mem. Truly, they were good people. They spoke to mock us, and we remained to learn their language. They said to us: 'Thou our lord, remain with us; we are thy elder and younger brother; abide with us.' They wished us to forget our speech, but our heart was as a stone when we arrived with them, and we went on with our words and our days intact.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 24; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 他們第二次前往那些地方，梅梅與塔克納。他們無法好好說話，因而得名梅姆。誠然，他們是良善之人。他們說話是為了嘲弄我們，而我們留下來學習他們的語言。他們對我們說：「你，我們的主，與我們同住；我們是你的兄長與幼弟；與我們同住吧。」他們希望我們忘卻自己的言語，但當我們與他們同抵之時，我們的心堅如石，我們繼續說著我們的話語，我們的日子也完好無損。

title.en: The Threshold Stone of Nacxit
title.zh: 納克希特的門檻石

region.en: Carchah (mythic station of the migration), Guatemalan highlands
region.zh: 卡爾恰（遷徙途程），危地馬拉高地

period: Cakchiquel annals compiled 1571-1604; Brinton translation 1885

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, sec. 25

summary.en: At Carchah the migrants come before Nacxit, a great lord, whose vassals guard his sovereignty. They are told to bow beneath a carved stone threshold in his house to receive majesty and the Panther Seat; some obey and receive sovereignty, others refuse the stone and receive nothing.
summary.zh: 在卡爾恰，遷徙者來到偉大的君王納克希特面前，其封臣守衛其王權。眾被告知：須俯身於其屋中雕琢的石門檻之下，方可獲得威儀與豹座；有人從之而得王權，有人拒石而一無所獲。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: They passed over with the sons of Valil and the sons of Tzunun; they went forth from Merac and Nacxit. Truly this Nacxit was a great lord, and the vassals who aided him to seize the sovereignty were assembled there.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 25; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 他們與瓦利爾之子們和尊農之子們一同經過；他們從梅拉克與納克希特出發。誠然，這位納克希特是位偉大的領主，而那些助他奪取王權的封臣都聚集在那裡。

passages.text: It was beautiful to see all the warriors there, and Nacxit spoke to them: 'Bow beneath the carved stone threshold of my house, and I will give you your majesty, your canopy, your royal seat.' Then the warriors consulted among themselves; some bowed beneath the stone, and to them sovereignty was given, and they came forth crowned with the power of Nacxit.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 25; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 看見所有武士齊聚於此，真是美事，納克希特對他們說：「俯身於我屋中雕石門檻之下，我便賜予你們尊榮、你們的華蓋、你們的王座。」於是武士們彼此商議；有些人俯身於石下，王權便賜給了他們，他們便帶著納克希特的力量加冕而出。

title.en: Gagavitz Captures the Heart of the Mountain
title.zh: 加加維茨奪得山之心

region.en: Volcano Gagxanul (Fuego), Guatemalan highlands
region.zh: 加克紹爾火山（富埃戈火山），危地馬拉高地

period: Cakchiquel annals compiled 1571-1604; Brinton translation 1885

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 31-32

summary.en: The volcano Gagxanul burns for a whole year, and no one can pass. Gagavitz and Zakitzunun put aside bow and shield, dig a trench, set water and green grass against the fire, and Gagavitz descends head-first into the mountain. He reappears terrible with the fire subdued — 'he died, and yet he has come down' — and the dance of the Heart of the Mountain is founded.
summary.zh: 加克紹爾火山整整燃燒一年，無人能過。加加維茨與扎基特蘇放下弓盾，掘壕引水、以青草敵火，加加維茨頭先探入山體。他再現時面目可怖而火已馴服——「他死了，卻又走出來」——「山之心」之舞由此而立。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: They saw the fire of the mountain called Gagxanul; truly it was frightful, the fire shooting forth afar. The mountain was on fire for a whole year, and no one could say how it could be passed. When all the warriors had arrived at its foot, no one spoke; they grieved at heart, and could not say how the fire could be captured.
