passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 31; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 他們看見那座名叫加格沙努爾的山上的火；誠然，那火遠遠噴射而出，著實可怖。那山整整燃燒了一年，無人能說該如何通過。當所有武士都抵達山腳時，無人言語；他們心中悲傷，無法說出該如何制伏那火。

passages.text: Then Gagavitz spoke: 'Who of you wishes that I try my fortune? He has a heart of a hero that fears not. I will go first. You must not fear so soon.' Zakitzunun wished to go with him, and together they said: 'There is no use of bows or shields.' They laid them aside, dug a trench, and placed by the water the banana trees called raxah.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 31; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 接著加加維茨說道：「你們之中誰願讓我試試我的運氣？擁有英雄之心者無所畏懼。我願先行。你們不必這麼快就害怕。」扎基尊農願與他同去，他們一同說道：「弓與盾都無用處。」他們將之擱置一旁，挖了一條壕溝，並把名為拉沙赫的香蕉樹置於水邊。

passages.text: Then Gagavitz descended into the fire — head first, then neck, then arms, hands, and feet — while Zakitzunun conducted the water to the fire, and the green grass and maize mixed with water flowed upon it. All at the foot of the mountain fled. Gagavitz remained in the mountain, and the day drew to a close and their courage died — the fire was captured, but it was not captured for them.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 31; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 於是加加維茨（Gagavitz）降入火中——先是頭，接著是頸，然後是雙臂、雙手與雙腳——同時扎基祖努恩（Zakitzunun）將水引向火，青草與玉米和著水流淌於其上。山腳下的一切盡皆逃散。加加維茨留在山中，白晝將盡，他們的勇氣也隨之消逝——火被擒獲了，卻不是為他們而擒獲。

passages.text: Then he came from within the mountain, truly terrible to see, and all the warriors said: 'Truly his power, his knowledge, his glory and his majesty are terrible. He died, and yet he has come down.' They seated him on the throne and made much of him, and he answered: 'The heart of the mountain has come as my slave, my captive.' When the heart of the mountain is opened, the fire separates from the stone — hence comes the dance called the Heart of the Mountain, danced violently with many troops.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 32; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 接著他從山腹之中出來，模樣著實可怖，眾武士皆說：「他的力量、他的智慧、他的榮耀與他的威嚴著實可怖。他死了，卻又下來了。」他們讓他坐上寶座，極力尊崇他，他答道：「山之心已作為我的奴僕、我的俘虜而來。」當山之心被打開時，火便與石分離——由此便有了名為「山之心」的舞蹈，以眾多部眾猛烈地跳著。

title.en: The Sacrifice of Tolgom, Son of the Mud That Quivers
title.zh: 獻祭顫泥之子托爾戈姆

region.en: Qakbatzulu, on the shore of Lake Atitlan, Guatemala
region.zh: 危地馬拉阿蒂特蘭湖畔卡克巴祖魯

period: Cakchiquel annals compiled 1571-1604; Brinton translation 1885

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 35-38

summary.en: At trembling Qakbatzulu the migrants seize Tolgom, who calls himself 'son of the Mud that Quivers'. He is exhibited, honored as first among the warriors, then bound before a tree: as the dance begins and the arrows fly, none reach the mark until Gagavitz's own arrow leaps over Cheetzulu and pierces him. His body is divided among the seven towns, and the festival of Uchum — with children shot as his substitutes — is founded.
summary.zh: 在顫動的卡克巴祖魯，遷徙者擒獲自稱「顫泥之子」的托爾戈姆。先被展示、尊為戰士之首，後縛於樹前：舞起箭發，無一中的，直至加加維茨親自射出之箭躍過切祖魯而貫穿其身。其屍分予七鎮，烏楚姆月之祭典——以孩童中箭代之——由此而立。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: After this they arrived at the place Qakbatzulu, where they met the one named Tolgom. Truly, terror was there, and the place Qakbatzulu trembled. At first all the warriors feared lest they should meet death, and Gagavitz said: 'Who are you, oh warriors? Let us look at his face. Can we not fight?' And he sent the warriors to seize Tolgom.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 35; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 此後他們抵達卡克巴祖魯（Qakbatzulu）之地，在那裡遇見了名為托爾戈姆（Tolgom）的那一位。那裡著實充滿恐怖，卡克巴祖魯之地為之震顫。起初眾武士都害怕自己會遭遇死亡，加加維茨說：「你們是誰啊，眾武士？讓我們看看他的臉。我們難道不能一戰嗎？」於是他派武士們去擒拿托爾戈姆。

passages.text: Then Gagavitz went to see Tolgom and cried to him: 'Who are you? You are neither my brother nor my elder. This very day I shall slay you.' And Tolgom, filled with fear, replied: 'I am the son of the Mud that Quivers. This is my house where I dwell, oh my lord.' He submitted and was made prisoner, and Gagavitz said: 'Show forth the face of my prisoner. We will adorn and sacrifice my captive, and thus celebrate the name of this spot.'
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 35; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 於是加加維茨前去見托爾戈姆，向他喊道：「你是誰？你既非我的兄弟，也非我的兄長。就在今日，我要殺了你。」托爾戈姆滿心恐懼，答道：「我是顫動之泥的兒子。這是我居住的屋子，哦我的主。」他屈服了，被俘為囚，加加維茨說：「讓我俘虜的臉顯露出來。我們要裝飾並獻祭我的俘虜，藉此頌揚此地之名。」

passages.text: Then began the execution of Tolgom. He arrayed himself and entered suddenly; his arms were extended in front of a tree, to be shot with arrows. A dance was begun by all the warriors while Tolgom began his death song; but not one of the arrows reached the cord, until the arrow of Gagavitz was discharged: it passed over the place named Cheetzulu and pierced Tolgom, and then all the arrows found him from near and from afar.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 37; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 於是托爾戈姆的處決開始了。他整裝列陣，驟然進入；他的雙臂伸展在一棵樹前，以供箭射。眾武士開始跳起舞來，托爾戈姆則開始唱他的臨終之歌；但沒有一支箭射中那繩索，直到加加維茨的箭射出：它飛過名為切埃祖魯（Cheetzulu）之地，射中了托爾戈姆，隨後所有的箭無論遠近都射中了他。

passages.text: A great stream of blood came forth behind the tree, and his body was cut in pieces and divided among all the seven towns. This gift and this sacrifice of his death founded the festival of the month Uchum, at which all were equal, with eating and drinking — and little children were shot with arrows, their heads adorned with elder flowers as his substitute, as if they were Tolgom. When they were on the hill, they threw part of the body of Tolgom into the lake, and a noise was heard in the waters, and the festival of 'Throwing the Nose of Tolgom' began.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), secs. 37-38; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 樹後湧出一大股血流，他的身體被切成碎塊，分給全部七座城鎮。他死亡的這份贈禮與獻祭，奠定了烏丘姆月（Uchum）的節慶，屆時人人平等，一同吃喝——而幼童則被箭射，頭上飾以接骨木花作為他的替身，彷彿他們就是托爾戈姆。當他們在山丘上時，他們把托爾戈姆身體的一部分投入湖中，水中便傳來一陣聲響，於是「投擲托爾戈姆之鼻」的節慶便開始了。

title.en: Gagavitz Becomes a White Cloud: The Lake Is Divided
title.zh: 加加維茨化白雲：湖水乃分

region.en: Lake Atitlan, Guatemala
region.zh: 危地馬拉阿蒂特蘭湖

period: Cakchiquel annals compiled 1571-1604; Brinton translation 1885

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, sec. 38

summary.en: Gagavitz crosses Lake Atitlan transformed into Zutzu-Cumatz, the white crested serpent: the water darkens, a wind rises, and a white cloud circles the lake. The Tz'utujil's power must first be reduced; then the lake is halved between the two peoples, and Gagavitz remains with the Tz'utujil women while the tribes move on.
summary.zh: 加加維茨化為祖祖·庫馬茲——白冠之蛇——渡阿蒂特蘭湖：水色轉暗，風起，一朵白雲繞湖而行。先須削減祖圖希爾之力；然後湖水分半，兩族各得其一，加加維茨留於祖圖希爾的女子之中，諸族前行。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: A little while after the arrival of Gagavitz, truly a fearful thing took place when he entered the water, having changed himself into Zutzu-Cumatz. It suddenly darkened on the water, a wind rose, and a white cloud rested on the surface, making a circuit of the water in the lake.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 38; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 加加維茨到來之後不久，當他化身為蘇楚—庫馬茨入水之時，著實發生了一件可怖之事。水面上驟然昏暗，一陣風颳起，一朵白雲停駐於水面，繞著湖中之水環行一周。

passages.text: They desired to remain there, but it was first necessary to reduce the power of the Tz'utuhils. All the seven nations looked about and then descended to the water, and those who were there said to the children of the Ahtziquinahay: 'We have scarcely made the circuit of this lake of ours, this sea, oh my brother. But let one half of the lake be yours, and one half of the fruits, of the wild geese, of the crabs, of the fish.' And they answered: 'It is well, my brother; half of the lake be ours, and half of thy acorns and thy bananas, and of all living things you kill in or below the waters.'
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 38; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 他們想要留在那裡，但首先必須削弱楚圖希爾人的勢力。七個部族四下張望，隨後下到水邊，那些在那裡的人對阿齊基納哈伊的子孫說：「我的兄弟啊，我們才剛繞行過我們這座湖、這片海一圈。但讓這湖的一半歸你們，一半的果實、野雁、螃蟹與魚也歸你們。」他們回答說：「好，我的兄弟；湖的一半歸我們，你的一半橡實與香蕉，以及你們在水中或水下所殺的一切活物，也歸我們。」

passages.text: Then they separated, but soon returned, desiring to obtain wives, for none were married and no women had come with them. The Ahtziquinahay said: 'My lord, my brother, my elder, here indeed is thy maiden. You have divided with us the waters; half of the lake is thine, half is ours.' And Gagavitz said: 'I hear thy words; their victory is by the organs of their women. Remaining, I shall do this.' In this manner, say our elders, the lake was divided, and our brother and elder remained with the Tz'utuhils.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 38; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 於是他們分開了，但不久又回來，想要得到妻子，因為無人成婚，也沒有女人隨他們同來。阿齊基納哈伊人說：「我的主、我的兄弟、我的兄長，這裡確實有你的少女。你已與我們分水；湖的一半歸你，一半歸我們。」加加維茨說：「我聽見你的話；他們的勝利是靠他們女人的器官。我留下來，就這麼辦。」我們的長者說，湖便是這樣分開的，而我們的兄弟與兄長便與楚圖希爾人留在一起。

title.en: Baqahol Buys a Kingship and the Jaguars Tear It Down
title.zh: 巴克霍爾以寶石購王位，豹獸拆毀之

region.en: Pantzic and Paraxone (dawn stations of the Cakchiquel), Guatemalan highlands
region.zh: 潘茲與帕拉雄（卡克奇克爾的黎明之地），危地馬拉高地

period: Cakchiquel annals compiled 1571-1604; Brinton translation 1885

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 39-40

summary.en: At the first settlement — the tribe's 'day-breaking' — Baqahol arrives last and claims the kingship: 'I am king, I received you.' Refused, he offers a carved precious stone, is refused again, builds himself a stronghold, and has his works demolished by the Chuluc Balam beasts sent by Gagavitz, who resents the usurpation.
summary.zh: 在初次定居——族人的「黎明之時」——巴克霍爾最後抵達，卻宣稱王位：「我是王，我接納了你們。」遭拒後，他獻上一方雕琢寶石，再遭拒；遂自建要塞，但其工事被加加維茨所遣的「楚盧克豹」獸拆除——加加維茨不容其竊據。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: The first who went forth were Gekaquch, Baqahol, Cibakihay and Cavek, who came together — you were the first, oh my tribe, to bring about our day-breaking, some time before the dawn. There their dawn appeared, there they built houses, and there took place the marriage of their chief named Nimahay.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 39; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 最先出去的是格卡庫奇、巴卡霍爾、齊巴基哈伊與卡維克，他們一同前來——我的部族啊，你們是最先促成我們黎明的人，時在破曉之前若干時候。他們的黎明在那裡顯現，他們在那裡建造房屋，他們那位名叫尼馬哈伊的首領的婚禮也在那裡舉行。

passages.text: The last who arrived was Baqahol, and they had already begun to build when he came. He said to Gekaquch: 'I, I am king, I received you.' The others answered: 'Thou! no, thou art not our king; we do not wish you to be our king.' Then he showed them a precious stone and said: 'I will give you this precious stone carved with four feet, and hands and toes, if I am your chief.' But that suited them not.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 39; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 最後抵達的是巴卡霍爾，他來時他們已經開始建造了。他對格卡庫奇說：「我，我是王，是我接納了你們。」其他人回答說：「你！不，你不是我們的王；我們不希望你做我們的王。」於是他拿出一塊寶石說：「若我做你們的首領，我就把這塊雕有四足、雙手與腳趾的寶石給你們。」但這不合他們的心意。

passages.text: Then he began to build himself a stronghold, and soon the labor was completed, for he coveted the power. For this reason his constructions were destroyed by the Chuluc Balam sent by Gagavitz, because Gagavitz liked it not that Baqahol desired the leadership. After that the day-breaking took place on Pantzic and Paraxone, each clothed with changing green.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), secs. 39-40; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 於是他開始為自己建造一座堡壘，工程不久便完成了，因為他覬覦權力。正因如此，他的建築被加加維茨所派的楚盧克·巴拉姆摧毀，因為加加維茨不喜歡巴卡霍爾圖謀首領之位。此後，黎明便在潘齊克與帕拉雄內顯現，二者各自披著變幻的翠綠。

title.en: The Bathing and Anointing of a Chief
title.zh: 酋長的沐浴與塗聖

region.en: Iximche region, Guatemalan highlands
region.zh: 伊辛切地區，危地馬拉高地

period: Cakchiquel annals compiled 1571-1604; Brinton translation 1885

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, sec. 41

summary.en: The Annals preserve the ceremony by which a chief entered power: bathed by attendants in a large painted vessel, clad in flowing robes, girded with the sacred fillet, anointed with the holy colors, and adorned with jewels — the moment when a household head becomes a ruling chief.
summary.zh: 《紀年》保存了酋長就任之儀：由侍者在大彩盆中為其沐浴，披流衣，繫聖帶，以聖色塗身，佩以寶石——家戶之首由此成為執政酋長。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: Then the chief entered upon his royalty: he was seated on the seat of power, and then he was bathed in the bathing-vessel with its yellow water and its flowers. He was bathed by the attendants in a large painted vessel; he was clad in flowing robes; a sacred girdle or fillet was tied upon him; he was painted with the holy colors, was anointed, and jewels were placed upon his person.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 41; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 於是首領開始其王權：他坐於權力之座上，隨後在盛有黃水與花朵的沐浴器中受浴。侍從們在一只繪有圖案的大盆中為他沐浴；他身披飄逸的長袍；一條神聖的腰帶或頭帶被繫於他身上；他被塗以神聖的色彩，受膏抹，珠寶被置於其身上。

passages.text: Thus the chief of the clan was raised above his house, and all the warriors in the settlement were arrayed by their houses and clans in the same order. The whole people were numbered within the settlement, and the royalty was shared and judged by the households, so that power was measured, counted, and distributed like the days themselves.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 41; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 如此，氏族首領被舉於其家之上，聚落中所有戰士皆依其家與氏族以同樣的次序排列。全體人民在聚落之內被計數，王權由各戶共享並裁斷，於是權力如日子本身一般被衡量、計數與分配。

title.en: Cay Noh and Cay Batz Hide in the Cave Within a Cave
title.zh: 卡伊·諾與卡伊·巴茲匿於洞中之洞

region.en: Pecparupec cave, Guatemalan highlands
region.zh: 佩克帕魯佩克洞穴，危地馬拉高地

period: Cakchiquel annals compiled 1571-1604; Brinton translation 1885

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 51-55

summary.en: Sons of Gagavitz, the two brothers shine like fire by night and shake the earth like Cabrakan as they collect Tepeuh's tribute. Betrothed by the Ahtziquinahay's daughters who steal their treasure jar, they marry the chief's daughters and dare not face the king who sent them: they hide in Pecparupec, the cave within a cave, until Tepeuh's forgiveness brings them out to rule.
summary.zh: 加加維茨之子兄弟二人，夜行如火炬，行地如卡布拉坎撼地震動，代特佩烏收取貢賦。阿希基納哈伊之女偷走其寶罐，兄弟因而聯姻酋長之女，卻不敢面對遣其前來之王：遂匿於佩克帕魯佩克——洞中之洞——直至特佩烏赦免，方出而執政。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: Our ancestors Caynoh and Caybatz came to Tepeuh. 'Who are you?' was said to them. 'We are the sons of Gagavitz,' they replied, and Tepeuh marveled greatly, and strengthened them, for they were humble before him. They were then sent to collect the tribute from the tribes, and no one of the many people died while they were taking it.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 51; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 我們的祖先凱諾與凱巴茨來到特佩烏。有人對他們說：『你們是誰？』他們答道：『我們是加加維茨之子。』特佩烏大為驚異，並使他們強壯，因他們在他面前謙卑。隨後他們被派往各部落收取貢賦，在他們收取之時，眾多人民中無一人死亡。

passages.text: Truly all feared their magic power and wisdom: where they were at night it shone like fire, and there was trembling as of an earthquake. Quite to the far East they were paid what they demanded, precious metals and spun stuffs, by the tribes from whom they took tribute. Mighty were their words.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 52; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 誠然，所有人都畏懼他們的法力與智慧：他們夜間所在之處，光亮如火，並有如同地震般的顫動。遠至東方極處，他們向那些他們收取貢賦的部落索求貴金屬與紡織品，皆得償付。他們的言語大有威力。

passages.text: They came to collect tribute from the Ahtziquinahay, and the Ahtziquinahay said among themselves: 'Let us make these messengers of Tepeuh our sons-in-law; we will give them women and take back what they have designated.' Indeed the daughters of the chiefs came secretly and stole the jar of treasures while the brothers slept, and Caynoh and Caybatz took them as wives.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 53; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 他們前來向阿齊基納哈伊收取貢賦，阿齊基納哈伊人彼此商議：『讓我們使這些特佩烏的使者成為我們的女婿；我們將把女子給他們，並取回他們所指定的東西。』果然，首領們的女兒們暗中前來，趁兄弟二人熟睡時偷走了寶藏之罐，凱諾與凱巴茨便娶她們為妻。

passages.text: Then our ancestors, not seeing their treasure, were filled with fear: 'You have indeed ruined us, oh you Ahtziquinahay! Tepeuh will be angered against us.' They went to speak with Tepeuh, but did not reach him, for they feared to come before him; so they hid themselves in a cavern and retired into the cavern. The place where they hid was called by Caynoh Pecparupec — a cave within a cave — and the tribe sought them there until Tepeuh forgave them and they came out to rule.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), secs. 53-55; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 於是我們的祖先不見其寶藏，心中充滿恐懼：『你們著實毀了我們，啊，阿齊基納哈伊人！特佩烏必向我們發怒。』他們前去與特佩烏說話，卻未能見到他，因為他們害怕來到他面前；於是他們藏身於一洞穴之中，退入洞穴之內。他們藏身之處被凱諾稱為佩克帕魯佩克——洞中之洞——部落在那裡尋找他們，直到特佩烏寬恕了他們，他們才出來統治。

title.en: King Qikab Humbled by His Own Sons
title.zh: 基卡布王為其子所辱

region.en: Gumarcaah (Utatlan), K'iche' capital, Guatemala
region.zh: 古馬卡（烏塔特蘭），基切王都，危地馬拉

period: Cakchiquel annals compiled 1571-1604; Brinton translation 1885

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 79-82

summary.en: The Quiche revolt against their own king Qikab: his sons Tatayac and Ah Itza side with the people, refuse him tribute, and kill his chiefs of the royal service. Twice the old king humbles himself before the populace, giving up his jewels, his metals, and finally the royal power itself — 'since then the people acted, and the king is made such by the people.'
summary.zh: 基切人反叛其王基卡布：其子塔塔雅克與阿伊察站於民眾一邊，拒納貢賦，誅殺王室之臣。老王兩度向民眾俯首，交出寶石、金屬，終至交出王權本身——「自此而後，民眾行事，王由民眾所立」。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: Then began a revolt against the king Qikab by the Quiche men; the family of the king was the cause of the contest. The Quiches would not promise the homage as vassals which he asked of them; they wished that the roads should be free to the Quiche people, which the king would not grant.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 79; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 於是基切人開始反抗國王奇卡布；國王的家族正是這場爭鬥的起因。基切人不願應他所求，以臣屬之身許下效忠之諾；他們希望道路能對基切人開放通行，而國王不肯應允。

passages.text: Tatayac and Ah Itza, the two distinguished sons of the king, took the part of the Quiches, and the king was thus opposed to his own sons, who incited the people not to pay their dues; for they coveted the royal power, and desired the precious stones, the metals, the slaves and people of their father. A council of the Quiches was held against the warriors maintained by the king, and they began to put to death all those of the first rank in the royal service.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 80; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 國王兩位傑出的兒子塔塔亞克與阿伊察站在基切人一邊，國王因此與自己的兒子們對立，他們煽動人民不繳納應納的貢賦；因為他們覬覦王權，渴望得到父親的寶石、金屬、奴隸與人民。基切人召開議會，對抗國王所豢養的武士，並開始處死所有位居王室差役第一等的人。

passages.text: The king Qikab humbled himself before the people, trying to appease them with his precious stones and metals; he gave up the power of the rulers to the people and divided with them his royal rights. The heart of the king was bruised by his sons, by that which they had done. Then perished the ancient glory of the nation: since then the people acted, and the king is made such by the people.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 81; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 國王奇卡布在人民面前卑躬屈膝，試圖以他的寶石與金屬平息他們；他將統治者的權力讓與人民，並與他們分享自己的王權。國王的心被他的兒子們所傷，為他們所做之事而痛。於是這個民族古老的榮光就此消亡：自此以後，由人民行事，而國王也由人民所立。

title.en: Iximche on the Ratzamut Is Founded
title.zh: 伊辛切建城於拉察姆特

region.en: Iximche (Tecpan Guatemala), Chimaltenango, Guatemala
region.zh: 伊辛切（特克潘危地馬拉），奇馬爾特南戈，危地馬拉

period: Cakchiquel annals compiled 1571-1604 (city founded c. 1470s); Brinton translation 1885

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 82-85

summary.en: After another revolt, the four rulers — Huntoh, Vukubatz, Chuluc, and Xitamal Queh — quit Chiavar, burn the roads twice behind them, and establish Iximche on the Ratzamut, the almost inaccessible plain ringed by ravines. The warriors of the seven nations rejoice: 'You have done well to come here to Iximche' — and the glory of the Quiches disappears.
summary.zh: 另一次反叛之後，四王——洪托、武庫巴茲、楚盧克與希塔馬爾·克——離開奇亞瓦爾，兩度焚路於身後，建城伊辛切於拉察姆特——四周環以深谷、幾不可達的平地。七族戰士皆喜：「你們來到伊辛切，做得很好」——基切的榮光從此消逝。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: Then another revolt began against the four leaders, Huntoh, Vukubatz, Chuluc and Xitamal Queh, occasioned by a woman of the Zotzils Tukuches; and after twice burning the roads behind them, they established the town of Iximche on the Ratzamut and settled there, the four rulers, the sovereigns of the Cakchiquel people.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 82; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 於是又開始了一場反抗四位首領——溫托赫、武庫巴茨、丘盧克與希塔馬爾·凱赫——的叛亂，起因是一名索齊爾·圖庫切族的女子；他們兩度燒毀身後的通道之後，在拉察穆特建立了伊希姆切城並定居於此，這四位統治者，即卡克奇克爾人的君主。

passages.text: As soon as they were settled, they placed themselves in readiness for war with the Quiches, and our ancestors built a stronghold. All the people rejoiced at the establishment of the city by these illustrious heroes; for they had fought on the side of the king Qikab, and therefore all the warriors of the seven nations rejoiced.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 83; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 他們一經定居，便做好與基切人交戰的準備，我們的祖先築起了一座堡壘。全體人民都為這些顯赫英雄建立此城而歡欣；因為他們曾站在國王奇卡布一方作戰，因此七個民族的全体武士都歡欣鼓舞。

passages.text: The warriors of the seven nations gave their words when the city of Iximche was founded: 'You have done well to leave Chiavar, my brother; you have done well to come here to Iximche. There was but one brave man with Cavek and the Quiches; but hereafter he will not go to war with the Quiches.' And when war came, two strongholds of the Quiches were seized, Qizqab was killed at Xechituh, and thus disappeared the glory of the Quiches.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), secs. 83-85; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 伊希姆切城建立之時，七個民族的武士們立下誓言：『我的兄弟，你離開奇亞瓦爾做得對；你來到伊希姆切這裡做得對。與卡維克及基切人在一起的勇士只有一個；但從今以後，他不會再與基切人交戰了。』而當戰爭來臨，基切人的兩座堡壘被攻佔，奇斯喀布在謝奇圖赫被殺，基切人的榮光就此消逝。

title.en: The Four Heroines of the Eleventh Ah
title.zh: 十一阿赫之日的四位女傑

region.en: Iximche, Chimaltenango, Guatemala
region.zh: 伊辛切，奇馬爾特南戈，危地馬拉

period: Cakchiquel annals compiled 1571-1604 (revolt of 1496); Brinton translation 1885

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 101-103

summary.en: On the day 11 Ah the great insurrection breaks out at Iximche: the Tukuches are drawn out of the city and slaughtered at the bridgehead. Four women arm themselves with lances and bows, fight as four young men, and their arrows strike the very mat of the enemy captain Chucuybatzin; images of these heroines are later set up before the Zotzil and Xahil buildings.
summary.zh: 十一阿赫之日，伊辛切大暴動爆發：楚庫切人被逐出城，於橋頭遭屠戮。四位女子持矛張弓而戰，勇如四名少年，其箭直中敵將楚庫伊巴欽的坐席；此後，這些女傑的塑像被立於佐茲爾與薩希爾建築之前。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: The day of the revolt was appointed by the chief Cay Hunahpu, and on this day, 11th Ah, the revolt broke out. The Tukuches were drawn out of the city to the other side of the river, and all their warriors went there also, that they might enter the city; but the warriors of the kings Cablahuh Tihax and Oxlahuh tzy opposed them.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 101; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 起事之日由酋長卡伊·胡納赫普所定，就在這一日，即十一阿赫日，起事爆發。圖庫切人被引出城外，到河的對岸，他們所有的戰士也都前往該處，以便進入城中；但諸王卡布拉胡·蒂哈克斯與奧什拉胡·齊亞赫的戰士抵禦了他們。

passages.text: When the dawn appeared on the day 11th Ah, the Tukuches began on the opposite side from the city, and the drums and trumpets of the chief Cay Hunahpu were heard. Then the warriors armed and displayed their brilliant feathers, shining banners, gold and precious stones. Truly it was terrible for the number of the Tukuches, who could not be counted by eight thousands nor by sixteen thousands.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 102; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 當十一阿赫日黎明出現時，圖庫切人從城的對岸開始行動，酋長卡伊·胡納赫普的鼓聲與號角聲隨之可聞。於是戰士們披掛武裝，展示他們光輝的羽毛、閃耀的旗幟、黃金與寶石。誠然，圖庫切人為數之眾著實可怖，其數目既非八千亦非一萬六千所能計。

passages.text: There were four women who had armed themselves with lances and bows and taken part in the battle, fully equal to four young men. The arrows launched by these heroines struck the very mat of Chucuybatzin. The chiefs of the battle afterwards set up the images of these women before the buildings of the Zotzils and the Xahils, whence these women had gone forth.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 102; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 有四位婦女以長矛與弓武裝自己，參與了戰鬥，全然堪比四名青年。這些女英雄所射出的箭，直中楚庫伊巴欽的坐席。戰後，首領們將這些婦女的形象立於索齊爾人與沙希爾人的建築之前，這些婦女正是從該處出發的。

passages.text: Then began a general attack on the Tukuches; they were cut to pieces at once; no one resisted; the rout was complete; men, women and children were given up to slaughter. The chief Cay Hunahpu was slain, and those of Tibaqoy and Raxakan retired, partly to Quiche, partly among the Tzutuhils, and were thus dispersed. Such was the destruction of the Tukuches, in old times, oh my children.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 103; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 於是對圖庫切人的全面攻擊開始了；他們當即被砍成碎片；無人抵抗；潰敗徹底；男子、婦女與孩童皆遭屠殺。酋長卡伊·胡納赫普被殺，蒂巴科伊與拉沙坎之人則退去，一部分往基切，一部分往楚圖希爾人之中，就此四散。我的孩子們啊，圖庫切人古時的毀滅便是如此。

title.en: Tunatiuh Comes to Iximche and Burns the K'iche' Kings
title.zh: 圖納提烏至伊辛切，焚基切諸王

region.en: Iximche, Chimaltenango, Guatemala
region.zh: 伊辛切，奇馬爾特南戈，危地馬拉

period: Cakchiquel annals compiled 1571-1604 (events of 1524); Brinton translation 1885

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 144-149

summary.en: The Castilians arrive at Xetulul; Tunatiuh (Alvarado) destroys the Quiche nation before Xelahuh, burns three K'iche' chiefs alive, and demands Cakchiquel warriors for the slaughter. He enters Iximche without a fight, is feasted, and asks with terrible courtesy for more warriors: 'I want to make war with them.'
summary.zh: 卡斯蒂利亞人抵達希圖盧爾；圖納提烏（阿爾瓦拉多）在希拉胡之前摧毀基切族，將基切三王活活燒死，並索要卡克奇克爾戰士以行殺戮。他不戰而入伊辛切，受宴之後，以可怕而客氣的口吻再索戰士：「我要與他們作戰。」

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: It was during this year that the Castilians arrived. Forty-nine years have passed since the Castilians came to Xepit and Xetulul. On the day 1 Ganel the Quiches were destroyed by the Castilians. Tunatiuh Avilantaro, as he was called, conquered all the towns. Their countenances were previously unknown, and the people rendered homage to sticks and stones.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 144; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 正是在這一年，卡斯蒂利亞人抵達。自卡斯蒂利亞人來到謝皮特與謝圖盧爾以來，已過了四十九年。在一加內爾日，基切人被卡斯蒂利亞人所毀滅。被稱為圖納蒂烏·阿維蘭塔羅者，征服了所有的城鎮。他們的容貌先前不為人知，而人們向木杖與石頭獻上敬意。

passages.text: On their arrival at Xelahuh, the Quiche nation was routed and destroyed; all of them had hastened there to oppose the Castilians, and there the Quiche nation was destroyed in front of Xelahuh. He then went to the city Gumarcaah, and there came before him the chiefs, the king and the next in rank, and tribute was paid by the Quiches; and the chiefs suffered many torments from Tunatiuh.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), secs. 145-146; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 當他們抵達謝拉胡赫時，基切民族被擊潰並毀滅；他們全都趕到該處以抵抗卡斯蒂利亞人，就在那裡，基切民族在謝拉胡赫之前被毀滅。他隨後前往城鎮古馬爾卡阿赫，首領們、國王以及次於其位者都來到他面前，基切人繳納了貢賦；而首領們遭受了圖納蒂烏的諸多折磨。

passages.text: On the day 4 Qat three chiefs, the king and the next in rank, were burned alive by Tunatiuh, nor was the heart of Tunatiuh satisfied with war. Soon a messenger from Tunatiuh came to the chiefs: 'Let the warriors of the Ahpozotzils and Ahpoxahils come to the slaughter of the Quiches! I want to make war with them.'
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), secs. 147-148; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 在四卡特日，三位酋長——國王與次於其位者——被圖納提烏活活燒死，而圖納提烏之心亦不因戰爭而滿足。不久，圖納提烏的使者來到酋長們面前：「讓阿波索齊爾與阿波沙希爾的戰士們前來屠殺基切人！我要與他們開戰。」

title.en: Esu Finishes the Half-Made Human
title.zh: 艾舒補完半成之人

region.en: Benin-Oyo border country (symbolic pin: the east, whence the sun comes)
region.zh: 貝寧與奧約交界地帶（象徵定位：日出之東方）

period: Yoruba-Bini shared tradition; recorded 1906 (Dennett)

source.work: R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (London, 1906), ch. XIX

summary.en: While Osa'lubwa, the maker, was fashioning man he left the work unfinished; Esu came along and finished the figure according to his own ideas. When Osa'lubwa returned and saw what had been done he was much annoyed, and banished Esu to the east, whence the sun comes.
summary.zh: 造物者奧薩盧布瓦塑人之時，工程半輟；艾舒路過，按自己的心意把人補完。奧薩盧布瓦歸來見狀大怒，將艾舒放逐到日出之東方。

sensitivity.note: Recorded by Dennett among the Bini (Benin) as a shared Yoruba-Bini mythic stratum; Esu (Èṣù) is the Yoruba trickster deity. The 'unfinished and finished by another' motif is a strong cross-tradition parallel to trickster-spoiling-creation tales. Recorded 1906 in colonial-era ethnography.

passages.text: When OSALUBWA was making man he left him in an unfinished state: Esu came along and finished him according to his ideas. OSALUBWA returned, and was much annoyed, and banished Esu to the east, where the Sun comes from (Animinihia Mivi).
passages.zh: 當奧薩盧布瓦造人時，他將人留於未完成之狀態：埃舒前來，依其己意將人完成。奧薩盧布瓦歸來，大為惱怒，遂將埃舒放逐至東方，即太陽所出之處（阿尼米尼希亞·米維）。

title.en: The Old Lady Banished to the Moon
title.zh: 被逐上月宮的老婦

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the moon seen from the Ogun country)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：奧貢之鄉仰望的月亮）

period: Yoruba-Bini shared tradition; recorded 1906 (Dennett)

source.work: R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (London, 1906), ch. XIX

summary.en: On the first day of the week — the day of rest — an old woman would insist on cutting wood, though the axe is taboo on Ogun's day; she was banished to the moon, where her figure may still be traced. Ogun himself is the blacksmith who, by the help of fire, makes his implements.
summary.zh: 週首之日（安息之日）本不得動斧，一位老婦偏偏執意劈柴，違犯奧貢日之禁；她被放逐到月亮上去，月面上的身影至今猶見。奧貢正是那位借火之力鍛造工具的鐵匠之神。

sensitivity.note: Moon-banishment etiology tied to Ogun's rest-day taboo; recorded 1906 by Dennett in the Bini-Yoruba border country. Cross-tradition parallels (mark on the moon) are widespread; presented as archival record.

passages.text: The story says that an old lady who would cut wood on their first day (= Sunday) was banished to the moon. Ogun = blacksmith who by the help of fire makes his implements.
passages.zh: 故事說，一位老婦因在他們的第一日（即星期日）砍柴，而被放逐至月亮。奧貢＝鐵匠，藉火之力製造其器具。

title.en: The Chief Who Built a Ladder to the Home of Thunder
title.zh: 築梯直搗雷宮的酋長

region.en: Sapoba road, Benin (symbolic pin: the tree marking where the ladder fell)
region.zh: 奈及利亞貝寧薩波巴道（象徵定位：梯斷之處的紀念樹）

period: Yoruba-Bini shared tradition; recorded 1906 (Dennett)

source.work: R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (London, 1906), ch. XIX

summary.en: The great war chief Ezomo heard it thunder and, taking the storm for an enemy of the Oba who wished to fight him, built a ladder to reach the home of thunder. When he and all his people were on the ladder and just getting at the home of thunder, it gave way, and the top of it fell where a tree now grows — planted, with mound and cowries, to mark the place.
summary.zh: 大戰酋長埃佐莫聞雷聲大作，誤以為是奧巴王的仇敵前來挑戰，遂造長梯直上雷電之宮。正當他率領全部人馬登梯、將抵雷宮之際，長梯折斷，梯頂墜落之處如今長著一棵大樹——土丘貝幣環繞，正是紀念之地。

sensitivity.note: Bini legend about war with the thunder-power (read here as the Yoruba thunder-complex of Shango); the heaven-storming ladder is a world motif (cf. Tower of Babel). Recorded 1906.

passages.text: On the Sapoba road there is a tree with the usual mound of earth and cowries in front of it, planted they say to mark the place where the top of Ezomo's ladder fell. The story goes that this great war chief heard it thunder and wanted to know what enemy of the Oba's it was who evidently wished to fight him, so he built a ladder to reach up to the heavens. When he and all his people were on the ladder and just getting at the home of thunder, it gave way, and the top end of it fell where the tree is growing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind, ch. XIX (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在薩波巴路上有一棵樹，樹前有慣常的土堆與貝殼，據說種植此樹是為標記埃佐莫之梯頂端墜落之處。故事說，這位偉大的戰酋聽見雷鳴，想知道究竟是奧巴的哪個敵人顯然想與他交戰，於是建造了一座梯子以達天庭。當他與其所有人民都在梯上、正要抵達雷之家時，梯子斷裂，其頂端墜落於今樹生長之處。

title.en: Ovia, the Slandered Wife, Becomes a River
title.zh: 奧維亞——受誣的王妃化為河

region.en: Ovia river, Benin (the river named for the runaway wife)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧維亞河（以出走王妃為名的河流）

period: Yoruba-Bini shared tradition; recorded 1906 (Dennett)

source.work: R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (London, 1906), ch. XXI

summary.en: Ovia is said to have been one of the wives of Awlawyo, the Alafin of Oyo. A jealous rival slipped a rat and water into her cloth and told the Alafin that Ovia had fouled herself; in his anger he shamed her, and she cried and ran away. When the truth came out he killed the slanderer and begged Ovia to return, but she refused — nor would she come back when Okwo was sent to fetch her, fearing to return without her, and the two became river spirits in the Benin country, Ovia's sign being the dress of strips of palm leaves.
summary.zh: 相傳奧維亞曾是奧約阿勞芬王（奧拉沃約）的妃子。嫉妒者把老鼠和水塞進她的衣袍，向王告發她「失禁污衣」；王大怒羞辱於她，她泣而出走。真相大白後，王誅殺讒婦，求她回宮，她不肯；遣奧科沃前去接她，亦遭拒絕——奧科沃不敢空手而回，二人遂在貝寧之地化作河靈。奧維亞的聖徵是棕櫚葉編織之裙。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1906 among the Bini, but explicitly names the Alafin of Oyo — a Yoruba-Bini shared legend. Ovia remains one of the great living cults of Benin. Cross-ref with the Shango-Oya flight cycle.

passages.text: Ovia is said to have been one of the wives of Awlawyo, the Alafin of Awyaw (Oyo). A wife who was jealous of her put a rat and some water into her cloth, and then went and told the Alafin that Ovia had made water in her cloth. Awlawyo was very cross with her, so she cried and ran away. And when Awlawyo made inquiries, and found out that he had been deceived, he killed the jealous wife, and asked Ovia to come back to him, but she refused. Then he sent Okwo to bring her back, but she refused to go back, and Okwo feared to return without her; so they both became river spirits in the Benin country. The sign of the Ovia is the dress made of strips of palm leaves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind, ch. XXI (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說奧維亞是阿沃約（奧約）的阿阿拉芬阿瓦勞約的妻子之一。一位嫉妒她的妻子將一隻老鼠和一些水放入她的布中，然後前去告訴阿阿拉芬說奧維亞在布中撒了尿。阿瓦勞約對她大為惱怒，於是她哭著跑走了。而當阿瓦勞約查問之後，發現自己受了欺騙，便殺了那嫉妒的妻子，並請奧維亞回到他身邊，但她拒絕了。於是他派奧克沃去帶她回來，但她拒絕回去，而奧克沃害怕不帶她而歸；於是二人皆成為貝寧地方的河靈。奧維亞的標誌是以棕櫚葉條製成的衣裳。

title.en: Olukun and Oha: The Hiccough That Broke a Marriage
title.zh: 奧魯貢與奧哈——一聲打嗝拆散的水族婚

region.en: Benin river country (symbolic pin: the great Benin river of Olukun)
region.zh: 貝寧水鄉（象徵定位：奧魯貢大河）

period: Yoruba-Bini shared tradition; recorded 1906 (Dennett)

source.work: R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (London, 1906), ch. XXI

summary.en: Oha drank Ainyo and hiccoughed, which so vexed her husband Olukun that she ran away from him. Olukun wept — for in those days he was very poor. Then Olukun married Igbagon and grew rich; and when Oha wished to return and prayed his forgiveness, he, being rich now, forgave her — but only on condition that she come back as the wood-bearer to Igbagon.
summary.zh: 奧哈飲了阿伊尼約之水，打了個嗝，竟觸怒丈夫奧魯貢，她遂負氣出走。彼時奧魯貢尚且貧窮，唯有哭泣。後來他娶了伊格巴貢，日漸富足；奧哈悔悟歸來求恕，已富貴的奧魯貢原諒了她——但只准她回來做伊格巴貢的拾柴婢。

sensitivity.note: River-marriage myth of the Benin Olukun (identifiable with the Yoruba sea-god Olokun), recorded 1906. Names of rivers are marriage-linked in this water-pantheon tale.

passages.text: Oha drank Ainyo and hiccoughed, which vexed Olukun, so she ran away from him. Olukun cried. This was when Olukun was very poor. Then Olukun married Igbagon. Then Oha wished to return and prayed Olukun to forgive her. He was rich now, so he forgave her and said she might come back, but as the wood bearer to Igbagon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind, ch. XXI (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧哈喝了艾尼約而打嗝，這激怒了奧盧昆，於是她從他身邊跑走了。奧盧昆哭了。這是奧盧昆非常貧窮的時候。後來奧盧昆娶了伊格巴貢。於是奧哈希望回來，並祈求奧盧昆原諒她。他如今富有了，便原諒了她，說她可以回來，但只能作為伊格巴貢的搬柴者。

title.en: Tortoise Betrays the Parrot's Mother
title.zh: 龜君出賣鸚鵡之母

region.en: Yoruba-Bini animal country (symbolic pin: famine council ground near Benin)
region.zh: 貝寧獸國（象徵定位：饑年聚義場）

period: Yoruba-Bini shared tradition; recorded 1906 (Dennett)

source.work: R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (London, 1906), ch. XXI

summary.en: In famine the animals agree to eat their mothers one by one, the parrot secretly sparing his own in a hidden hole with a rope. Tortoise the deceiver spies out the hiding-place and betrays it; the elephant's song fails, but Tortoise's song deceives the mother parrot into lowering the rope — until her son returns singing the cut-rope song: let the elephant fall and crush the tortoise.
summary.zh: 饑年獸國盟約：輪流奉獻己母為食。鸚鵡暗藏其母於地穴，穴中藏繩。騙子龜君窺得密窟並告發眾獸；大象以歌誘母，未果；龜君一曲竟騙得母鸚鵡垂下繩索。危急之際，兒子鸚鵡歸來高唱斷繩之歌——「母親啊，砍斷繩子！讓大象摔落，壓碎那龜！」

sensitivity.note: Animal trickster tale of the Tortoise (Ijapa/Igwi) cycle, told Dennett 1906 among the Bini with the Yoruba trickster-tortoise; the tortoise's bad character ('a deceiver') is stated in the source.

passages.text: There is a story that says one day Igwi (the tortoise) was a person, and all animals spoke one language. There was a famine in the land. A meeting was called, and it was decided that all should bring in their mothers. The elephant brought in his mother. They killed and ate her. And each day an animal brought in its mother, and they always gave some of the meat to the parrot, most of which he preserved. And when each animal had killed its mother they told the parrot to go and fetch his; but he had hidden his mother away in a hole where she kept a rope. As he refused to bring in his mother all the animals set about to look for her, but they could not find her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind, ch. XXI (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有故事說，有一天伊格維（Igwi，即陸龜）還是人，而所有動物都說同一種語言。那地方鬧饑荒。大家召開會議，決定所有動物都應把自己的母親帶來。大象把他的母親帶來了。他們把她殺了吃掉。此後每天都有動物把自己的母親帶來，而他們總是把一些肉分給鸚鵡，其中大部分他都保存了下來。等到每隻動物都殺了自己的母親之後，他們便叫鸚鵡去把他的母親帶來；但他早已把母親藏進一個洞裡，她在洞中守著一根繩子。由於他拒絕把自己的母親帶來，所有動物便著手尋找她，卻找不到。

passages.text: Then the Igwi watched the parrot and found the mother's hiding-place, and told all the other animals. When they all knew where the mother parrot was to be found they asked the parrot to go on an errand for them to a distant part, and he went — but returned quickly to the court-house and found no one there, for, guided by the Igwi, they had gone to find his mother. When they were near the hole the elephant sang a song, thinking the mother would take his voice for her son's; but she was not taken in. Then the Igwi sang, and the mother parrot was deceived and put out the rope for him. All the animals seized hold of the rope. But just then the son parrot came along and sang to his mother, telling her to cut the rope: "O Mother, Mother, cut the rope! Let the elephant fall, Mother, and crush the tortoise, Mother!" — and so it was done.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind, ch. XXI (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是伊格維監視鸚鵡，發現了那母親的藏身之處，並告訴了所有其他動物。當他們全都知道鸚鵡的母親可以在何處找到之後，便派鸚鵡替他們到一個遙遠的地方辦事，他去了——但很快又回到議事堂，發現那裡一個人也沒有，因為他們在伊格維的帶領下，已經去找他的母親了。當他們走近那個洞時，大象唱起歌來，以為那母親會把他的聲音當成她兒子的聲音；但她沒有上當。接著伊格維唱了起來，鸚鵡的母親受了騙，便把繩子放給他。所有動物都抓住了繩子。但就在那時，鸚鵡兒子走了過來，對他的母親唱道，叫她割斷繩子：「哦母親，母親，割斷繩子！讓大象摔下去，母親，壓死陸龜，母親！」——事情就這樣成了。

title.en: Eware and the Two Hundred and One Powers
title.zh: 埃瓦雷與二〇一神力

region.en: Benin City, Nigeria (the temple where the powers were burnt)
region.zh: 奈及利亞貝寧城（神力被焚的廟宇）

period: Yoruba-Bini shared tradition; recorded 1906 (Dennett)

source.work: R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (London, 1906), ch. XXII

summary.en: Eware, a son of the sixth king of Benin, was refused the throne and driven into the bush; after 201 years he returned with 201 followers who, like men, were not really men but Ebami — powers dwelling in rivers and sacred groves. He taught the people the foundation of their religion; but the people, saying there were too many Ebami, built a fine temple, feasted the powers, fastened the doors, and burned the house down. Many escaped into the rivers and became river spirits.
summary.zh: 貝寧第六王之子埃瓦雷求位不遂，被逐入林。二〇一年後，他攜二〇一隨從歸城——他們形似人而非人，是棲於河川聖林的「埃巴米」神力。埃瓦雷傳授宗教之本；但民眾嫌神力太多，建美廟設宴灌醉，閉門縱火焚屋。倖存者紛紛遁入河川，化為河靈。

sensitivity.note: Founding legend of the Benin religion as told to Dennett by a babalawo (1906); the 201 Ebami parallel the Yoruba reckoning of 401/600 powers and the Bini bronze plates that recorded them in the Oba's palace.

passages.text: Eware, he said, was a son of the sixth king of Benin, and when his father died he wished to succeed to the throne. The people, however, would not have him, and drove him into the bush. After 201 years he returned to Benin city with 201 followers. He and his followers were like men but were not really men; they were Ebami (powers in rivers and sacred groves) — Eware then taught the Bini people the foundation of their present religion. But the people said that there were too many Ebami and set about thinking how their number could be diminished. They built a fine house or temple and invited them all to a feast; then gave them plenty to eat and drink, and when they were nearly drunk fastened the doors and burned the house down. Many of the Ebami escaped and entered the different rivers and became river spirits.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind, ch. XXII (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他說，埃瓦雷（Eware）是貝寧第六位國王的兒子，當他的父親去世時，他希望繼承王位。然而人民不願意接受他，把他趕進了叢林。二〇一年後，他帶著二〇一名追隨者回到貝寧城。他和他的追隨者像人卻並非真正的人；他們是埃巴米（Ebami，河川與聖林中的神靈）——埃瓦雷隨後教導比尼人（Bini）他們現今宗教的基礎。但人們說埃巴米太多了，便開始思索如何減少他們的數目。他們建造了一座精美的房屋或神廟，邀請他們全體赴宴；然後給他們大量吃喝，當他們快要醉倒時，便閂上門，把房子燒毀。許多埃巴米逃了出來，進入各條河流，成了河神。

title.en: God Comes Down to Talk About Death
title.zh: 神臨人間，議定死律

region.en: Benin City, Nigeria (symbolic pin: the road by which God walked in via Agbor, Oza and Ugo)
region.zh: 奈及利亞貝寧城（象徵定位：神經阿格博爾、奧扎與烏戈入城之路）

period: Yoruba-Bini shared tradition; recorded 1906 (Dennett)

source.work: R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (London, 1906), ch. XXII

summary.en: Eware, returned from exile, was much troubled that he had to die, and sent a messenger to Oyisa (God) asking him to come and talk the matter over. God came down, landed at Agbor east of Benin City, was told that was not the city, and was directed via Oza and Ugo until he arrived and met Eware — when it was finally decided that every man must die. Esu, the devil, is said to have accompanied Oyisa bearing a knife.
summary.zh: 流亡歸來的埃瓦雷煩惱於自己終有一死，遣使請奧伊薩（神）下凡相商。神降於貝寧城東的阿格博爾，被告知此非王城，遂經奧扎、烏戈一路問路而至，與埃瓦雷相見——最終議定：凡人皆須一死。相傳惡神艾舒持刀隨行。

sensitivity.note: Origin-of-death decision myth recorded 1906 (Bini setting, Yoruba names Oyisa/Esu). Strong member of the origin-of-death cluster (messenger of death accords). Cross-refs: san-kaggen-eland (origin of death), hindu-rigveda-yama-yami.

passages.text: Eware also was much troubled about the fact that he had to die, so he sent a messenger to Oyisa (= God) to ask him to come to Benin city and talk the matter over. God came down and landed at Agbor, a place to the east of Benin city, and asked if that were Benin city. They told him no, and directed him via Oza and Ugo to the city, so that at length he arrived and had a meeting with Eware, when it was finally decided that every man must die. Eshu (the devil) is said to have accompanied Oyisa bearing a knife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind, ch. XXII (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 埃瓦雷也為自己終究必須死去這件事深感苦惱，於是派了一名使者去見奧伊薩（Oyisa，即神），請他來貝寧城商議此事。神降臨，在貝寧城以東的阿格博爾（Agbor）著陸，問那裡是不是貝寧城。他們告訴他不是，並指引他經由奧扎（Oza）和烏戈（Ugo）前往該城，於是他終於抵達，與埃瓦雷會面，最後議定人人都必須死。據說埃舒（Eshu，即魔鬼）帶著一把刀陪同奧伊薩前來。

title.en: Why the Gods Are Called Orisha: The Quarrelled Potsherd
title.zh: 奧里莎之名的由來——陶片之爭

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the shrine where the potsherd is kept, near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費附近供陶片的小祠）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1906 (Johnson, in Dennett)

source.work: Bishop James Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (1906), Appendix

summary.en: Two friends, Anini and Ogbek, quarrelled over a potsherd (isha) that had been given as a present and then, out of envy, demanded back; elders interfered, the returned sherd was accounted sacred and worshipped — and from this, it is said, every object of worship was afterwards called an Orisha (Ori-isha). Bishop Johnson records another etymology: Orunmila sent beings out to search for and gather the wisdom he had strewn about, and those who succeeded — 'those who were successful in making their collection' — became objects of worship.
summary.zh: 友人阿尼尼與奧格貝克為一片陶器起爭執：一方贈出，另一方因嫉而索回；長老調停後，這片被退回的陶片竟被尊為聖物受人膜拜——自此一切崇拜之物皆名為「奧里莎」（ ori-isha，即「陶片之頭」）。約翰遜主教另記一說：奧倫米拉曾遣眾靈四出搜集他散落世間的智慧，凡搜集有成者（「得其所得者」）遂成受祭之神。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1906 from Bishop James Johnson (an African bishop of Yoruba origin) — an insider-adjacent Yoruba source. Etiology of the word orisha.

passages.text: Others have represented the term Orisha as derived from the circumstance of a serious difference on a particular occasion between two friends named Anini and Ogbek, a difference in which some elders interfered, over a potsherd (isha) which the one had made a present of to the other, but a return of which the giver afterwards from envy demanded, and which after its return was accounted sacred and became an object of worship; and they say that from this every other object of worship has been called an Orisha (Ori-isha), in allusion to the potsherd over which there had been a severe difference.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 另有人認為「奧里沙」（Orisha）一詞源於這樣一件事：某個場合，兩位名叫阿尼尼（Anini）和奧格貝克（Ogbek）的朋友之間發生了嚴重的爭執，一些長者出面干預，爭執的起因是一塊陶片（isha），這塊陶片原是一人贈予另一人的禮物，但贈予者後來出於嫉妒又要求歸還，歸還之後它被視為神聖之物，成了崇拜的對象；他們說，自此以後，每一個別的崇拜對象都被稱為奧里沙（Ori-isha），以影射那塊曾引起嚴重爭執的陶片。

passages.text: These deities are generally known among us as Orishas, a term which, after the religious tradition of the country, was originally applied to some beings whom Ifa, or Orunmila, the Son of God, had sent out with others to search about for and collect together the wisdom which he had strewn about, and who were successful in their search and collection whilst others failed, and who were then spoken of as Awon ti o ri sha — those who were successful in making their collection — and who after, and in consequence of this, became objects of worship.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這些神祇在我們中間通常被稱為奧里沙，依照本國的宗教傳統，這個詞最初是指某些存在者，伊法（Ifa），即奧倫米拉（Orunmila），神之子，曾派他們與其他一些存在者一同去搜尋並收集他散落各處的智慧，他們在搜尋與收集上成功了，而其他存在者則失敗了，於是他們被稱為「Awon ti o ri sha」——那些成功完成收集者——此後，正因如此，他們成了崇拜的對象。

title.en: The Six Hundred: Two Hundred on the Right, Four Hundred on the Left
title.zh: 六百神——右二百，左四百

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the pantheon at Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費萬神殿）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1906 (Johnson, in Dennett)

source.work: Bishop James Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (1906), Appendix

summary.en: The number of Yoruba gods commonly reckoned is 401, but it is strictly more correct, says Bishop Johnson, to say 600, arranged under two divisions: 200, as the babalawos would say, placed on the right-hand side, and 400 on the left-hand side — with Ifa, Oduduwa, Obanta and Obanla, Oshun, Ogun, Yemaja, Eshuriku, Obalufon, Orisha-oko, Shankpanna, Shango and Obatala among those most commonly worshipped; some of the divinities are borrowed from other tribes, and each deity has its day in the five-day week.
summary.zh: 約魯巴眾神俗稱四百零一；約翰遜主教指正確之數當為六百，分作兩班——如巴巴拉奧所言：右列二百，左列四百。最受崇奉者有伊法、奧杜杜瓦、奧班塔與奧班拉、奧舜、奧貢、耶莫雅、痘神、奧巴魯豐、農神、尚戈與奧巴塔拉等；亦有自他族引入之神，五日一週，各有其日。

sensitivity.note: Yoruba pantheon arithmetic recorded 1906 by Bishop Johnson; the 200/400 division matches the older Bini 201-Ebami reckoning. Cross-ref: yoruba-eware-201-spirits.

passages.text: The number of Yoruba gods commonly reckoned is 401, but it is strictly more correct to say that the number is 600, arranged generally under two divisions, 200, as the babalawos would say, placed on the right-hand side, and 400 on the left-hand side. But the gods more commonly worshipped are Ifa, Oduduwa, Obanta and Obanla his wife, Oshun, Ogun, Yemaja, Eshuriku, Obalufon, Orisha-oko, and Shankpanna, Shango and Obatala.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 約魯巴人所慣常計算的神明數目為四百零一，但更嚴格而言，說數目是六百更為正確，大致分為兩部：如巴巴拉沃們所說，二百置於右側，四百置於左側。然而更常受崇拜的神明是伊法、奧杜杜瓦、奧班塔及其妻奧班拉、奧雄、奧貢、耶瑪賈、埃舒里庫、奧巴盧豐、奧里沙-奧科，以及尚克潘納、尚戈與奧巴塔拉。

passages.text: Some of the Yoruba divinities have been borrowed from other tribes: Shango from the Niger territory; Eka-Ifa from the Akoko tribe; and Aje from the Egbin or Popo tribe. Yorubans, whose worship is a recurring festival at which a particular divinity is worshipped, have from this circumstance often denominated a day in every cycle of five days from the name of the deity to whose worship it is devoted — the day of Jakuta (Shango), the day of Obatala, the day of Ifa, when he sits on a throne like a king; the day of Abameta; and the day of Yemaja, which is the day of Oro as well, when both Yemaja and the spirits of deceased ancestors are worshipped.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 約魯巴的若干神明借自其他部族：尚戈來自尼日河地區；埃卡-伊法來自阿科科部族；阿傑來自埃格賓或波波部族。約魯巴人的崇拜是一種循環往復的節慶，於其中崇拜某位特定的神明，因此他們常以所敬奉之神明的名字，來稱呼每五日一循環中的某一天——賈庫塔（尚戈）之日、奧巴塔拉之日、伊法之日（屆時他如君王般端坐於寶座之上）、阿巴梅塔之日，以及耶瑪賈之日，此日亦為奧羅之日，屆時耶瑪賈與已故祖先的靈魂同受崇拜。

title.en: Opele, the Slave Oracle of Ifa
title.zh: 奧佩萊——伊法座下的奴僕神諭

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the diviner's bowl at Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費占卜師的占碗）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1906 (Johnson, in Dennett)

source.work: Bishop James Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (1906), Appendix

summary.en: Behind each of Ifa's sixteen representative palm-nuts stand sixteen subordinate divinities: 256 odu in all, each with 1,680 traditional stories — a corpus no babalawo has ever memorised whole. Opele, Ifa's constant attendant and slave, is the oracle of eight flat pieces strung in two rows of four: cheaper, easier, consulted every morning, but a servant's answer not always to be relied on.
summary.zh: 伊法十六枚聖果仁之後各立十六位小神，合二百五十六「奧杜」，每奧杜附一千六百八十則傳統故事——無人能全數背誦。奧佩萊是伊法的貼身侍從與奴僕神諭：八片扁平木牌分兩排各四，占之較易，晨晨必占；然其應答僅是僕人代主之言，未必句句可恃。

sensitivity.note: Living Ifa practice (UNESCO-listed 2008); recorded 1906 by Bishop Johnson. The 'Owe ni Ifa npa' — Ifa speaks in parables — saying anchors the oracular hermeneutic.

passages.text: The great Oracle of the Yoruba country is Ifa, represented chiefly by sixteen palm nuts, each having from four to ten or more eyelets. Behind each one of these representative nuts are sixteen subordinate divinities; each one of the whole lot is termed an Odu, which means a chief, a head — altogether 256. Besides these there are sixteen other odus connected with each of the 256. There is a series of traditional stories, each of which is called a road, a pathway, or a course, and is connected with some particular odu; each odu is supposed to have 1,680 of these stories connected with it, and these, together with those of the other odus, every one aspiring to the office of babalawo is expected to commit to memory, though scarcely has anyone been found to perform the feat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 約魯巴地方的大神諭是伊法，主要以十六顆棕櫚果代表，每顆有四至十個或更多的孔眼。在這每一顆作為代表之果的背後，有十六位從屬的神明；整批之中的每一個皆稱為一個奧杜，意為首領、頭——共計二百五十六個。除此以外，尚有十六個其他的奧杜與這二百五十六個中的每一個相連。有一系列傳統故事，每一個皆稱為一條路、一條途徑或一道歷程，並與某個特定的奧杜相連；據信每個奧杜有一千六百八十則這類故事與之相連，而這些故事，連同其他奧杜的故事，每一位有志於巴巴拉沃之職者都須熟記於心，儘管幾乎從未有人被發現能完成此一壯舉。

passages.text: Opele, or Opepere, is an oracle of inferior rank to Ifa, and is regarded as his constant attendant, commonly spoken of as his slave. He is always represented by eight flat pieces of wood, or metal, strung together in two rows of four; the disposition of one or other of these pieces when the whole ensign is thrown out upon the ground would represent a particular odu; and one of Opele's chief duties is to show to the babalawo what particular odu he should consult. Opele is often consulted because it carries less labour than consulting the master Ifa himself, but on matters of minor importance; its response would be that of a servant for his master, and is not always absolutely relied upon. Opele is expected to be consulted every morning; whilst a babalawo is expected to consult his Ifa every fifth day, the close of a week of oses or worshipping days. Hence the parable: "There is never a morning when a babalawo does not consult his Opele, as there is never a morning that a blacksmith is not called upon to sharpen a cutlass for a farmer."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧佩萊，或稱奧佩佩雷，是位階低於伊法的神諭，被視為伊法的常隨侍從，通常被稱為他的奴僕。他總是以八片扁平的木片或金屬片來代表，串成兩排、每排四片；當整個標記被拋擲於地上時，其中某一片的排列位置便代表某個特定的奧杜；而奧佩萊的主要職責之一，便是向巴巴拉沃顯示他該請教哪個特定的奧杜。人們常請教奧佩萊，因為這比請教主人伊法本人省力得多，但僅限於較次要的事務；其回應猶如僕人代主人作答，並不總是絕對可靠。奧佩萊理應每日早晨請教一次；而巴巴拉沃則理應每第五日請教其伊法一次，即一週奧塞（崇拜之日）之終。故有如此譬喻：「巴巴拉沃沒有一個早晨不請教其奧佩萊，正如鐵匠沒有一個早晨不被召去為農夫磨利砍刀。」

title.en: Ela Has Descended: We Shall Die No More
title.zh: 埃拉已降世——吾儕不再死

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the yam fields where the Ela songs are sung, near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費近郊唱埃拉之歌的薯田）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1906 (Johnson, in Dennett)

source.work: Bishop James Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (1906), Appendix

summary.en: Ela is Ifa's great name of salvation: the strong and mighty Deliverer unconquerable by Death itself, the offspring of the hard stone from the bed of a spring. His devotees identify with that stone — "we are ourselves become Oyigiyigi, and will no longer die" — and cry "Ela has descended to the earth, we shall die no more; and this is Ifa's name." At yam harvest they split the Ela yam and sing Ela's festival song: our friend of the past year has come again.
summary.zh: 「埃拉」是伊法的救贖尊名：剛強無匹的拯救者，連死亡也不能勝過——他是泉底磐石所生。信眾以此石自比：「吾儕已成奧伊吉伊吉之石，不再死亡！」並高呼：「埃拉已降世，吾儕不再死——此即伊法之名。」收穫季節，信眾剖開「埃拉之薯」，唱起節歌：「埃拉重現了！去歲故人今又來，赴此一年一度的祭典。」

sensitivity.note: Living Ifa/Orunmila devotion recorded 1906; the Ela-saviour theology is a distinctive Yoruba soteriology. Presented as archival record of hymnody and rite.

passages.text: Ela is one of the many attributive names by which Ifa is described, and a very principal one: a contraction of the term Orunmila, intended to represent the divinity to all its worshippers principally as a Saviour and Deliverer, one that is strong and mighty and unconquerable by Death itself, so that all who look to him for help in trouble and against any other evil, death not excluded, will find their confidence has not been misplaced.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 埃拉是描述伊法的眾多附加名號之一，且是極為主要的一個：它是「奧倫米拉」一詞的縮略，意在向其所有崇拜者主要呈現這位神明為救主與拯救者，一位強壯有力、連死亡本身也無法征服者，以致所有在患難中、在對抗任何其他邪惡（死亡亦不例外）時仰望他求助的人，都會發現自己的信心並未錯置。

passages.text: He is sometimes described in songs of praises as Ela Osin, Ela the child of Osin the Ruler; sometimes as Ela omo Oyigi Ota-omi, Ela the offspring of a stone, the hard stone from the bed of a spring of water, an emblem of great strength; a quality which, believed in, enables devotees to identify themselves with him and regard themselves as free from death, saying, "Awa di oyigiyigi, a ki o ku" — we are ourselves become Oyigiyigi, the stone which gave birth to Ela, and will no longer die — or at other times to say, "Ela ti a ki o ku mo; Okiribiti, Ela ni oruko Ifa" — Ela has descended to the earth, we shall die no more, and this is Ifa's name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他有時在讚美歌中被描述為埃拉·奧辛，即埃拉，統治者奧辛之子；有時被描述為埃拉·奧莫·奧伊吉·奧塔-奧米，即埃拉，石頭的子嗣，那堅硬的石頭出自泉水之床，是巨大力量的象徵；信徒們相信這一特質，便能與他認同為一，視自己免於死亡，說道：「阿瓦·迪·奧伊吉吉吉，阿·基·奧·庫」——我們自己已化為奧伊吉吉吉，那生出埃拉的石頭，將不再死亡——或有時說道：「埃拉·蒂·阿·基·奧·庫·莫；奧基里比蒂，埃拉·尼·奧魯科·伊法」——埃拉已降臨大地，我們將不再死亡，這便是伊法的名字。

passages.text: It is the divinity to which harvest offerings are always presented by worshippers, especially in the yam season before any portion of the harvest is partaken of, and when they are said to split the Ela yam — and when Orunmila is said to come and partake of the yam with them — singing lustily to Ela's praises: "Ela poko! Our friend of the past year has come again to observe the yearly festival; the anniversary has returned. I am come, O Iroko, lord of the cultivated field, to observe the yearly festival. O thou our worthy Father! the Son who hast descended from heaven to this earth, who hast placed us in the world."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 这是一位神明，崇拜者总是向祂献上收成的祭品，尤其是在山药季节，在尚未食用收成的任何部分之前，据说那时他们会剖分埃拉的山药——据说奥伦米拉会前来与他们一同食用山药——并放声高唱赞美埃拉之歌：「埃拉波科！我们去年的朋友又回来了，来守每年的节庆；周年又到了。我来了，伊罗科啊，耕地之主，来守每年的节庆。我们可敬的父亲啊！那位从天降到此世的儿子，那位将我们安置于世间者。」

title.en: Orun Apaadi: The Heaven of Potsherds
title.zh: 奧倫阿帕迪——碎陶天堂

region.en: The Yoruba upper world (symbolic pin: the sky-land above Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴上天之境（象徵定位：伊費上空的天界）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1906 (Johnson, in Dennett)

source.work: Bishop James Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (1906), Appendix

summary.en: The spirits of all the dead go after death to Orun, the heavens or world above, divided in two. One part is the heaven of sweet air and peace where the souls of the good are admitted; the other is Orun Apaadi, the world of potsherds, where the spirits of the wicked live after death as a heap of refuse, a mass of God-rejected souls, treated as potsherds flung to a dunghill — or as dry leaves covering an ear of corn, thrown into the fire. The soul is not liable to death, and the good return to be born again — hence the names Babatunde, our father has returned, and Iyabode, our mother has returned.
summary.zh: 人死之後，眾靈皆往「奧倫」——上天之界。天界分兩部：一為「甜風安寧之天」，善者之魂居之；一為「奧倫阿帕迪」——碎陶之界，惡者之靈如垃圾成堆、為神所棄，像擲向糞堆的破陶片，又如覆在穀穗上的枯葉，終歸火中。靈魂本無死；善靈重返人間再世——故名「巴巴通德」（父親歸來）、「伊亞博德」（母親歸來）。

sensitivity.note: Yoruba eschatology recorded 1906 by Bishop Johnson; reincarnation-within-lineage (Yiyi, the shooting forth of a branch) is a living Yoruba belief. The 'judgment after death' appears only in proverbial sayings.

passages.text: It teaches that the soul of man is not liable to death, and that after the death of the body, which results from its quitting it, it hovers about the earth for some time, and after this departs into the world of spirits above. The spirits of all the dead go after death to Orun, the heavens or the world above. It is divided into two parts. One part is commonly called Isalu Orun, or Orun Afejefere, the heaven of sweet air, or Orun Alafia, the heaven of peace and happiness, where the souls of all the good from this world are admitted and live after death; and another part is called Orun Apaadi, the world of potsherds, where the spirits of the wicked here pass to and live in after death as a heap of refuse and rubbish, a mass of God-rejected souls — treated there as potsherds are here, commonly flung to a dunghill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 它教导说，人的灵魂不会遭受死亡，而在身体因灵魂离去而死之后，灵魂会在地球周围徘徊一段时间，此后便离开，升入上方的灵界。所有死者的灵魂在死后都前往奥伦，即诸天或上方世界。它分为两部分。一部分通常称为伊萨卢奥伦，或奥伦阿费杰费雷，即和风之天，或奥伦阿拉菲亚，即和平与幸福之天，凡此世一切善人的灵魂死后都被接纳其中并在那里生活；另一部分称为奥伦阿帕阿迪，即陶片之世界，此世恶人的灵魂死后便前往那里，如一堆废物垃圾般生活，是一群被上帝弃绝的灵魂——在那里受到如同此世陶片般的对待，通常被抛到粪堆上。

passages.text: Sometimes this world is described as Orun Ihaririha, the heaven where both the sun and fire meet together, and where the roar of their united flames and heat is like the shout of a great multitude. The spirit of a good dead returns from the spirit world to be again born into this world, into the family of which it had before death been a visible part; hence, when a name would be given to a child, a babalawo is consulted to know whether the departed one who has returned has come through the father's or the mother's line — this accounts for names such as Babatunde, our father has returned, and Iyabode, our mother has returned. This transmigration is spoken of as Yiyi, the shooting forth of a branch.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有时这个世界被描述为奥伦伊哈里里哈，即太阳与火相聚之天，那里它们合而为一的火焰与炽热之轰鸣，如同大群人的呼喊。善死者的灵魂从灵界返回，再次降生于此世，降生于它死前曾是其可见一部分的家庭；因此，当要为孩子取名时，会请教一位巴巴拉沃，以知晓归来的亡者是通过父系还是母系而来——这便解释了诸如巴巴通德（我们的父亲回来了）和伊亚博德（我们的母亲回来了）这样的名字。这种转生被称为「伊伊」，即枝条的萌发。

title.en: Agberu, Who Carries the Sacrifices to Heaven
title.zh: 阿格貝魯——捎祭上天者

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the heaven-ward path above the shrine, near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費近郊祠壇上空的天路）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1906 (Johnson, in Dennett)

source.work: Bishop James Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (1906), Appendix

summary.en: Sacrifices offered to the orishas, who stand as subordinate deities and mediators, are believed to be taken to the Great One by a spirit called Agberu, the carrier — Agberu who carries people's sacrifices to heaven. The basket in which he carries them is lined with Ifa's sacred leaves, each leaf a spoken wish: the toto leaf, that the offerer may be equal to those above him; the eyinriju leaf, that he may surpass others; the igberese leaf that accompanies a sacrifice to heaven; and the yeye leaf that brings blessing into our houses.
summary.zh: 獻給奧里莎（居於次神與中保之位）的祭品，相傳由一位名為「阿格貝魯」的神靈送呈至至尊——「阿格貝魯，捎祭上天者」。其背籃以伊法聖葉襯底，葉葉皆是祝詞：多多之葉，盼與上位者比肩；埃因里朱之葉，盼超越他人；伊格貝雷塞之葉，伴祭品同登天界；耶耶之葉，為家中帶來福澤。

sensitivity.note: Living sacrificial theology recorded 1906; the leaf-wish code is part of Ifa-associated practice.

passages.text: These sacrifices which are offered by heathens to their orishas, who occupy the place both of subordinate deities and mediators, are believed to be taken to the Great One by a spirit whom they denominate Agberu, the carrier, whose special business it is to take them to him and wait upon him with them. He goes by the title Agberu ti igbe ebo re orun — Agberu who carries people's sacrifices to heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 异教徒向他们的奥里沙（既充当下级神明又充当中介者）所献的这些祭品，据信由一位他们称为阿格贝鲁（即搬运者）的灵送往那位伟大者，其专门职责便是将祭品送到祂那里，并带着祭品侍奉祂。他拥有「阿格贝鲁提伊格贝埃博雷奥伦」的称号——即把人们的祭品搬往天上的阿格贝鲁。

passages.text: The basket in which he is supposed to carry the sacrifices to heaven is lined with leaves sacred to Ifa: the toto leaf, symbolical of the wish and prayer of the offerer that he may be equal to those who are before and above him; the eyinriju leaf, symbolical of his wish that he may surpass others; the Igberese leaf, generally described as the leaf which accompanies a sacrifice to heaven; and the Yeye leaf, often described as the yeye leaf that brings blessing into our houses.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 据信他用来将祭品搬往天上的篮子，内衬着献予伊法的神圣树叶：托托叶，象征献祭者的愿望与祈祷，愿他能与在他之前和之上的人相等；埃因里朱叶，象征他希望超越他人；伊格贝雷塞叶，通常被描述为伴随祭品升天的叶子；以及耶耶叶，常被描述为将福佑带入我们家中的耶耶叶。

title.en: The Oluwo Who Carried the Town's Sins
title.zh: 負一城之罪的奧魯沃

region.en: Yoruba royal city (symbolic pin: the Igbodu grove's three partitions, near Oyo)
region.zh: 約魯巴王城（象徵定位：奧約附近伊格博杜聖林三重門）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1906 (Johnson, in Dennett)

source.work: Bishop James Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (1906), Appendix

summary.en: The human victim chosen for the king's great sacrifice, called an Oluwo, is well fed while confined; then led through the streets — ashes thrown over his head, face painted with chalk — while people rush out to lay hands on him, transferring their sin, guilt, trouble and death to him. Through the Igbodu's three partitions he goes, sings his last song, and the announcement of his last word or groan is the signal for joy, drumming and dancing: the sacrifice is accepted, the divine wrath appeased.
summary.zh: 為王舉行大祭所選的人牲稱「奧魯沃」，圈禁期間養尊處優。祭日他沿街遊行——灰撒其首、白堊塗面——家家戶戶衝出門來撫摸其身，將自己一家老小的罪咎、災禍與死亡盡數轉嫁其身。隨後經伊格博杜聖林三重門而入，唱起訣別之歌；歌聲或呻吟一斷，全城便鑼鼓齊鳴、歌舞相慶——祭已受納，神怒平息。

sensitivity.note: Historical record of pre-colonial royal human sacrifice as described in 1906 by an African bishop of Yoruba origin; violence is described non-graphically. This is archival ethnography of a practice that colonial-era abolition ended — not a description of living Yoruba religion.

passages.text: The human victim chosen for sacrifice, who may be either a free-born or a slave, a person of noble or wealthy parentage or one of humble birth, is, after he has been chosen and marked out for the purpose, called an Oluwo. He is always well fed and nourished and supplied with whatever he should desire during the period of his confinement. When the occasion arrives for him to be sacrificed, he is commonly led about and paraded through the streets of the town or city of the sovereign who would sacrifice him for the well-being of his government and of every family and individual under it, in order that he might carry off the sin, guilt, misfortune and death of all without exception; ashes and chalk would be employed to hide his identity, the one being freely thrown over his head and his face painted with the latter, whilst individuals would often rush out of their houses to lay their hands upon him, that they might thus transfer to him their sin, guilt, trouble and death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim. Historical ethnography of pre-colonial royal sacrifice; presented as record, not practice.
passages.zh: 被选作祭品的人牲，可以是自由民或奴隶，出身高贵或富有者或出身卑微者，在被选中并指定为此用途之后，便被称为奥卢沃。在他被囚禁期间，他总是被好好喂养、滋养，并供给他所欲求的一切。当献祭他的时机到来时，他通常会被带着游遍那位要为他治下之福祉以及其下每一家庭与个人而献祭他的君主的城镇或城市的街道，以便他能带走无一例外地所有人的罪、罪责、不幸与死亡；人们会用灰与白垩来掩盖他的身份，前者被随意撒在他的头上，他的脸则用后者涂白，同时人们常常会冲出家门把手按在他身上，以便借此将自己的罪、罪责、烦恼与死亡转移给他。

passages.text: This parading done, he is taken through a temporary sacred shed of palm and other tree branches — the Igbodu — and to its first division, where many persons might follow him, and through a second, where only the chiefs and other very important persons might escort and accompany him, and to a third, where only the babalawo and his official assistant, the Ajigbona, are permitted to enter with him. Here, after he himself has given out or started his last song, which is to be taken up by the large assembly of people who will have been waiting to hear his last word or his last groan, his head is taken off and his blood offered to the gods. The announcement of his last word or his last groan, heard and taken up by the people, would be a signal for joy, gladness and thanksgiving, and for drum-beating and dancing, as an expression of their gratification because their sacrifice has been accepted, the divine wrath is appeased, and the prospect of prosperity assured.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim. Historical ethnography; presented as record, not practice.
passages.zh: 這番遊行結束後，他被帶進一座以棕櫚葉及其他樹枝臨時搭成的神聖棚屋——伊格博杜（Igbodu）——並進入其第一區，許多人可以跟隨他入內；再穿過第二區，只有首領及其他極重要的人物可以護送並陪同他；最後到第三區，唯有巴巴拉沃（babalawo）及其正式助手阿吉博納（Ajigbona）獲准與他一同進入。在此，待他親自說出或領唱他最後一首歌之後——這首歌將由大批一直等待著聽他最後一句話或最後一聲呻吟的群眾接唱——他的頭便被砍下，其血獻給眾神。他最後一句話或最後一聲呻吟被眾人聽見並接唱，便是歡欣、喜樂與感恩的信號，也是擊鼓與舞蹈的信號，以表達他們的欣慰，因為他們的獻祭已被接受，神怒已得平息，昌盛的希望已然確保。

title.en: Hoori Drowns and Spares His Elder Brother with the Tide Jewels
title.zh: 火遠理命以潮滿潮涸珠懲戒兄長

region.en: Sea-crossing and shore of Himuka, Tsukushi (Kyushu) (symbolic pin for the sea-path between the Sea-Plain and the Upper Land)
region.zh: 日向筑紫海岸與海路（象徵性定位）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Returning to the Upper Land from the Sea-Deity's palace, Hoori rides home on a one-fathom crocodile in a single day and leaves his stiletto girded on its neck, whence the creature is called the Deity Blade-Possessor. He hands back the fish-hook exactly as instructed, and when his sea-luck elder brother attacks him he first drowns him with the tide-flowing jewel, then releases him with the tide-ebbing jewel, until the brother bows and becomes his guard by day and night. The origin of the Hayabito court jesters' drowning-antics is traced to this humiliation.
summary.zh: 火遠理命騎一尋鱷魚一日返家，留短劍於鱷頸，故稱劍持神。他依海神教導交還魚鉤，兄長海幸（火照）怒而攻之，火遠理命先以潮滿珠淹沒，再以潮涸珠救活，直至兄長臣服，日夜侍衛。隼人朝廷弄臣之舞即源於此辱。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Sea-Deity summoned all the crocodiles together and asked which of them would escort his son-in-law, the august child of the Heaven's-Sun-Height, back to the Upper Land, and in how many days. One crocodile just one fathom long promised to make the journey in a single day, and the Sea-Deity chose him: carry him respectfully, he said, and do not alarm him while you cross the middle of the sea. So the god seated Hoori on the crocodile's head and saw him off. The crocodile kept his word and delivered Hoori home in one day. As the creature turned to go back, Hoori untied the stiletto girded at his own waist, set it on the crocodile's neck, and sent him away with that mark of honour. Ever since, the one-fathom crocodile has been called the Deity Blade-Possessor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 210-211 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 海神將所有鱷魚召集在一起，問牠們之中誰願意護送他的女婿、即天照大神之子返回上界，又需多少時日。一條僅一尋長的鱷魚承諾一日之內便可走完這段路程，海神便選中了牠：他說，要恭敬地馱著他，渡過海中央時不可驚嚇他。於是海神讓火遠理命坐在鱷魚頭上，為他送行。鱷魚信守諾言，一日之內便將火遠理命送回家中。當這生物轉身返回時，火遠理命解下繫在自己腰間的短刀，置於鱷魚頸上，以這榮譽的標記送牠離去。自此以後，那條一尋長的鱷魚便被稱為「持刀之神」。

passages.text: Hoori now handed the fish-hook back to his elder brother exactly as the Sea-Deity had instructed. From that day the elder brother grew poorer and poorer, and in fresh savagery came to attack him. As the attack began, Hoori put forth the tide-flowing jewel and drowned him; when he cried out in grief, Hoori put forth the tide-ebbing jewel and let him live. Thus harrassed, the sea-luck brother bowed his head and promised: henceforward I will be your guard by day and by night, and respectfully serve you. Down to the present day, says the record, the drowning-brother's posturings are ceaselessly served up before the court - for the Hayabito, descendants of the Prince of Fire-Shine, still perform before the sovereign the dances that mimic the antics their divine ancestor went through while the waters rose about him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 211-212 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 火遠理命此時依照海神的指示，將魚鉤原樣交還給他的兄長。從那天起，兄長日益貧困，又以新的凶暴前來攻擊他。攻擊開始時，火遠理命取出漲潮珠，將他淹沒；當他悲號哀哭時，火遠理命又取出退潮珠，讓他活命。受此折磨，這位海幸之兄俯首承諾：從今以後，我願日夜為你守衛，恭敬地侍奉你。記載說，直到今日，那位被淹之兄的種種姿態仍不斷在宮廷前獻演——因為火照命子的後裔隼人，至今仍在天皇面前表演舞蹈，模仿他們的神祖在水勢漫上其身時所經歷的種種動作。

title.en: Toyotama-hime's Seaside Childbirth and the Crocodile Reveal
title.zh: 豐玉姬海濱產房化鱷之秘

region.en: Sea-shore at the wave-limit of Himuka, Tsukushi (Kyushu) (symbolic pin on the parturition-hall of cormorants' feathers)
region.zh: 日向筑紫海濱波限鵜葺草葺不合命誕生地（象徵性定位）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: The Sea-Deity's daughter Toyotama-hime, pregnant by Hoori, refuses to bear the heavenly child in the sea-plain and comes ashore, where a parturition-hall roofed with cormorants' feathers is hastily built. Unable to wait for the thatch, she enters it in travail and forbids her husband to watch, for a woman of another land takes her native shape in childbirth. Hoori peeps at the moment of delivery and sees a crocodile eight fathoms long writhing on the floor; he flees in terror, and the shamed sea-bride abandons her child, closes the sea-path, and returns to her father's realm - though love draws her back once more with a song.
summary.zh: 海神女豐玉姬懷火遠理命之子，不肯於海中原產，遂至陸上以鵜羽葺屋待產。未及葺成，陣痛難忍，遂入產房，囑夫勿窺：異國婦人生產必復本形。火遠理命偷窺，見八尋鱷魚爬行蠕動，驚逃。豐玉姬知之，羞慚棄子，閉海路而去；然情難自禁，託妹玉依姬獻歌一次。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Toyotama-hime herself came to wait upon Hoori and told him the time of delivery was near: I am already with child, she said, but the august child of a Heavenly Deity ought not to be born in the Sea-Plain, and so I have come to you. On the very limit of the waves she began a parturition-hall, thatching it with cormorants' feathers. Before the thatch was half finished the urgency of her womb could no longer be restrained, and she went in to be delivered. At the door of her labour she made her husband swear: whenever a foreign woman is delivered, she takes the shape of her native land; so I too shall now take my native shape. Pray, do not look upon me!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. p. 212 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 豐玉姬親自前來侍候火遠理命，告訴他臨產之期已近：她說，我已懷有身孕，但天神之子不應降生於海原，因此我來到你這裡。她在波浪的盡頭開始建造一座產房，以鸕鶿的羽毛覆蓋屋頂。屋頂尚未蓋好一半，她腹中的急迫已無法再忍，便進去分娩。在產房門口，她讓丈夫立誓：每當異鄉女子分娩時，她都會化為其故鄉的形貌；因此我現在也要化為我的原形。懇請你，不要看我！

passages.text: Hoori found the words strange, and at the very moment of delivery he could not help stealing a look. There, writhing and crawling on the floor of the hall, was a crocodile eight fathoms long. Terrified, he fled. Toyotama-hime knew at once that he had peeped; filled with shame she abandoned the child she had just borne and said: I had wished always to come and go across the sea-path between us; but your having looked upon my true shape leaves me very shame-faced. So she closed the sea-boundary and went down again to the sea. The son she left behind was named Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Wave-Limit-Brave-Cormorant-Thatch-Meeting-Incompletely, after the unfinished roof of his birth-hall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 212-213 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 火遠理命覺得這番話奇怪，在分娩的那一刻忍不住偷看了一眼。只見一條八尋長的鱷魚在產房的地板上翻滾爬行。他大為驚恐，連忙逃走。豐玉姬立刻知道他偷看了；她滿懷羞慚，拋下剛剛生下的孩子，說道：我本希望永遠往來於我們之間的海路；但你窺見了我的真形，令我羞愧難當。於是她封閉了海界，重又下到海中。她留下的兒子，因產房屋頂未及完工，被命名為「天津日高日子波限建鵜葺草葺不合命」。

passages.text: Though angry at her husband's wish to peep, the sea-bride could not restrain her loving heart. At the time her younger sister Jewel-Good-Princess came to nurse the abandoned child, Toyotama-hime entrusted to her a song to be presented to Hoori, and he answered with a song in return - the parting exchange of the sea and the land. The child, Hoori's heir, dwelt thereafter in the palace of Takachiho, and in time wedded his maternal aunt Jewel-Good-Princess: from that marriage the line of the future emperors of Yamato descends.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 213-215 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 海妻雖對丈夫窺視的意願感到惱怒，卻無法抑制她的愛心。當她的妹妹玉依姬前來哺育這被拋下的孩子時，豐玉姬託她帶一首歌獻給火遠理命，火遠理命也以一首歌作答——這是海與陸的離別對唱。這孩子是火遠理命的繼承人，此後居住在高千穗宮中，後來娶了他的姨母玉依姬為妻：未來的大和天皇世系便由此婚姻傳下。

title.en: Emperor Jimmu's Eastward Expedition
title.zh: 神武天皇東征

region.en: Yamato plain at Unebi-Kashibara (Nara); route of the expedition from Himuka in Kyushu through Tsukushi and Kibi to Yamato
region.zh: 畝傍橿原宮（奈良）；東征路線自日向經筑紫、吉備至大和

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: The two princes Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko (the future Emperor Jimmu) and Itsuse leave Himuka to seek a land from which to govern the empire peaceably. Itsuse dies of an arrow-wound from Nagasune-biko, declaring it wrong to fight facing the sun; Jimmu's whole army is struck down by a phantom bear in Kumano until a cross-sword drops through the roof of Takakurazhi's storehouse in answer to a dream of the gods. Guided by the crow of eight feet sent from heaven, Jimmu recruits earth-deities, traps the traitor Ukashi in his own pitfall, has eighty tailed earth-spiders slain at a banquet song, and receives the heavenly regalia from Nigi-hayabi before ruling the empire from Kashibara.
summary.zh: 神渟名川耳尊（神武天皇）與兄五瀨命自日向東征，欲擇善地治天下。五瀨命中長髓彥毒箭，言不可面日而戰，傷重而亡。熊野遇巨熊幻影，全軍昏倒；高倉下夢得建御雷神自屋頂落入之劍，軍乃復甦。天照大神與高皇產靈遣八咫烏引路，收服土神，誅兄狹兄磯城，設伏誅八十梟帥，邇藝速命獻天璽瑞寶，遂於畝傍橿原宮即位治天下。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki), foundational narrative of the imperial line; passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology, not as endorsement of any imperial or nationalist reading.

passages.text: In the palace of Takachiho the two deities Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko and his elder brother Itsuse took counsel: dwelling in what place shall we most quietly carry on the government of the empire? It were best, they decided, to go east. They left Himuka and progressed to Tsukushi, where at Usa in the land of Toyo the natives Usa-tsu-hiko and Usa-tsu-hime built a one-legged raised platform and served them a great banquet. They dwelt a year at Wokada in Tsukushi, seven years at Takeri in the land of Agi, and eight years at Takashima in Kibi. Setting out again, they met in the Hayasuhi Channel a man riding the carapace of a tortoise and raising his wings as he angled. Questioned, he answered: I am an Earthly Deity; I know the sea-path well, and I will respectfully serve you. They drew him into the vessel with a pole and named him Sawo-ne-tsu-hiko.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 216-218 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在高千穗之宮中，神倭伊波禮毘古與其兄五瀨命二人共議：當居何處，方能最安然地經營天下之政？他們決定，最好是東行。於是離開日向，行至筑紫，在豐國宇佐之地，當地人宇佐津彥與宇佐津姬築起一足之高臺，為他們設下盛大之宴。他們在筑紫之岡田住了一年，在阿岐國之多祁理住了七年，在吉備之高島住了八年。再度啟程，於速吸之門遇見一人，騎於龜甲之上，張翼垂釣。問之，答曰：我乃地祇，熟知海路，願恭敬侍奉。他們以竿將其引入舟中，名之曰佐尾根津彥。

passages.text: Passing the Namihaya Crossing they brought up at the haven of Shirakata, where Nagasune-biko of Tomi raised an army to meet them. The brothers disembarked behind shields taken from their vessel - the place was named Tadetsu for it - and in the fighting Itsuse was pierced in the hand by the Prince of Tomi's hurtful arrow. He cried out: it is not right for me, an august child of the Sun-Deity, to fight facing the sun; that is why this wretched villain's hand has stricken me. I will turn and smite him with my back to the sun. Making a circuit by the south, he reached the sea of Chinu and washed the blood from his hand; then at the river-mouth of Wo in the land of Ki he lamented - ah, that I should die stricken by a wretched villain's hand! - and expired as a valiant man. His mausoleum is on Mount Kama in Ki.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 218-219 (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 經過浪速之渡，泊於白肩之津，登美之長髓彥起兵相迎。兄弟二人自舟中取盾為蔽而下——其地因此名為盾津——戰中，五瀨命之手為登美皇子之毒箭所穿。他喊道：我乃日神之御子，向日而戰，實為不當；此所以此賤賊之手傷我也。我當背日而擊之。於是迂迴南方，至血沼之海，洗去手上之血；復於紀國男之水門哀嘆——嗚呼，我竟為賤賊之手所傷而死！——遂以勇武之姿而薨。其陵在紀之竈山。

passages.text: Progressing round to the village of Kumanu, Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko met a great bear that came out of the mountain and vanished into it again. At that instant the prince suddenly fainted away, and his whole army fell prostrate. Then Takakurazhi of Kumanu came bearing one cross-sword and presented it to the fallen prince, who rose at once saying: how long I have slept! - and the savage deities of the mountains of Kumanu fell cut down of themselves while the bewildered army awoke.
