period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. X

summary.en: Behind the whole Orisha system stands Ossenj — the power of wizardry — worked by the Ada-ushe, the shaman-physicians. Only a child of Ossenj may become a shaman; the art is inherited from a dying father, perfected by years of travel to famous masters, and stamped by the god's medicine. Every orisha priest is subordinate to the shaman, for from Ossenj alone comes the magic that animates gods and men: the Shango priest must fetch his fire-protection from a shaman before dancing with fire, and even the great god Shango, they say, could only win the height of his power through the witchcraft of a shaman.
summary.zh: 整個奧里莎體系的背後，矗立著「奧森傑」——巫術之力，由「阿達烏謝」（巫醫）執掌。唯奧森傑之子可為巫；其術承自垂死的父親，再歷經多年遊歷名師而後大成，並以神賜之「藥」為印。凡奧里莎祭司皆隸屬於巫——因為能賦神與人以靈力的，唯有奧森傑：尚戈祭司欲在祭典踏火，必先向巫師求取護身之力；傳說連大神尚戈本人的威權，也是從一位巫師的巫術中得來的。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the shaman (Ada-ushe, Onisegun) institution recorded 1910-12. Ossenj = Osun (the medicine power), distinct from the river goddess Oshun in Frobenius's usage.

passages.text: The Yorubans, in common with almost all other African nations, believe in malignant, unrealizable, supernatural powers at the beck and call of but a very few persons specially endowed by heredity to control them. Only one class of man can afford such defence and is able to do battle against these nocturnal beings, namely, the Shamans, whom the Yorubans call Ada-ushe. This Ada-ushe's ordinary calling is that of a medicine-man, or physician, who is a master of much pharmaceutical knowledge. But it is possible to possess this not so much by descent from Ossenj, but rather by being inspired because of this descent; and the art has to be regularly learnt and carefully studied.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. X (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 约鲁巴人与几乎所有其他非洲民族一样，相信存在着种种恶性的、不可捉摸的超自然力量，这些力量听命于极少数因遗传而天生具有驾驭之能的人。只有一类人能够提供这样的防护，并能够与这些夜间出没的存在交战，那就是萨满，约鲁巴人称之为阿达乌谢（Ada-ushe）。这位阿达乌谢的寻常职业是巫医，或称医师，精通诸多药理知识。然而，拥有这种本领，与其说靠的是奥森吉（Ossenj）的血统，不如说是因为这血统而受到灵感；而这门技艺必须按部就班地学习，并细心地钻研。

passages.text: When an aged Ada-ushe feels the pressure of years all too heavy upon him and is plagued by premonitions of death, he begins to indoctrinate his son, so that he may, in time, be his equal in knowledge and skill. After his own father's induction he has to take up his staff and go travelling for many a year, visiting famous exponents of his father's professional caste, paying for his lore and instruction, and wends his way onwards. Only an Om-Ossenj (child of the Ossenj) may become an Ada-ushe, and this Godhead gives him the medicine which stamps him as a Shaman of the first water. Every Orisha priest is also subordinate to the Ada-ushe, for from Ossenj alone is derived the source of the power of magic, which animates both Gods and men: before the ministrant to Shango dances with the fire at this deity's holy feast, he fetches the power to protect himself from an Ada-ushe. And even the God Shango, in the beginning of things, could only win the height of his power and might through the witchcraft of an Ada-ushe — thus, from Ossenj.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. X (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 当一位年迈的阿达乌谢感到岁月压身、沉重难当，又为死亡的预感所苦时，他便开始教导自己的儿子，好让他有朝一日在知识与技艺上与自己比肩。在受父亲启蒙之后，他还须拿起手杖，外出游历多年，遍访父亲那一行当里声名卓著的人物，为求学问与指教而付酬，一路前行。只有奥姆-奥森吉（Om-Ossenj，即奥森吉之子）才能成为阿达乌谢，而这位神祇赐予他药物，使他成为第一流的萨满。每一位奥里沙祭司也都隶属于阿达乌谢，因为法术之力唯独源自奥森吉，这力量既激励神明，也激励世人：在供奉香戈（Shango）的祭司于这位神祇的神圣节庆上持火起舞之前，他须先从一位阿达乌谢那里取得护身之力。甚至香戈神在太初之时，也唯有借助一位阿达乌谢的法术——亦即源自奥森吉的法术——才能达到其权力与威势的顶峰。

title.en: Edju Brings the Sixteen Palm-Nuts Down to Men
title.zh: 埃茹攜十六聖果下凡

region.en: Kukuruku border country (symbolic pin: the palm-plantation where the monkeys dropped the nuts)
region.zh: 庫庫魯庫邊地（象徵定位：群猴擲果的棕櫚園）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XII

summary.en: The Gods went hungry: men no longer offered them burnt sacrifice, and even pestilence and lightning-bolts could not bring them back to the altars. Yemaya counselled Edju that men do not fear death — give them something so good they will yearn to go on living. Orungan told him of a great thing made of sixteen palm-nuts; the monkeys gave him the nuts and counselled him to go round the world and ask their meaning everywhere, sixteen sayings in each of sixteen places. Edju went, returned to the sky, and told the Gods; knowledge passed to men, who could then read each day's fate and escape what was coming by offering sacrifice — and this was the way Edju brought the Ifa palm-nuts down to men.
summary.zh: 眾神斷糧：人間久無燔祭，瘟疫與雷擊也嚇不回信眾。耶莫雅教埃茹：人不怕死——須賜他們求之若渴之物，他們才想活下去。奧倫岡指點他：有一件由十六枚棕櫚仁織成的「大事」；群猴獻果，並教他環遊世界、十六處各聽十六訓，方能解其玄機。埃茹依言行遍天下，歸天轉授眾神；知識下及人間，人們從此能日日占知禍福、以祭品消災——這便是埃茹把伊法聖果帶到人間的經過。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the Edju version of the Ifa-origin myth (Frobenius 1910-12), the trickster-teacher variant complementing the Elegba bargain variant. Cross-ref: yoruba-ifa-elegba-bargain.

passages.text: Once upon a time the Gods were very hungry. They did not get enough to eat from their wandering sons on the face of the earth. They were discontented with each other and quarrelled. Some of them went forth to hunt; other Gods, and Olokun in particular, wanted to go fishing; yet, although one antelope and one fish were caught, these did not last long. Now their descendants had forgotten them, and they asked themselves how they were to get their sustenance from men again. Men no longer made them burnt offerings, and the Gods wanted meat. So Edju set out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 从前，众神非常饥饿。他们从在大地上漂泊的子孙那里得不到足够的食物。他们彼此不满，起了争执。其中一些神出去打猎；另一些神，尤其是奥洛昆（Olokun），想去捕鱼；然而，虽然捕到了一只羚羊和一条鱼，这些也维持不了多久。此时他们的后裔已将他们遗忘，他们便自问，如何才能再度从世人那里获得供养。世人不再向他们献燔祭，而众神想吃肉。于是埃朱（Edju）出发了。

passages.text: He asked Yemaya for something with which to regain man's goodwill. Yemaya said: "You will have no success. Shankpanna has scourged them with pestilence, but they do not come and make sacrifice to him. Shango struck them dead with the lightning which he sent upon them, but they do not trouble themselves about him. Men do not fear death. Give them something so good that they will yearn for it and, therefore, want to go on living." Edju went further on and said to himself: "What I cannot get from Yemaya, Orungan will give me." He went to him, and Orungan said: "I know why you are come. The sixteen Gods are a-hungered. They must now have something which shall be good. I know of such a thing. It is a big thing made of sixteen palm-nuts. If you get them and learn their meaning, you will once more gain the goodwill of mankind."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他向耶玛雅（Yemaya）求取能重新赢回世人善意的东西。耶玛雅说：“你不会成功的。尚克潘纳（Shankpanna）曾以瘟疫鞭笞他们，他们却不来向他献祭。香戈曾以他降下的闪电将他们击死，他们却对他毫不在意。世人不畏惧死亡。给他们一样极好的东西，好让他们渴慕它，因而愿意继续活下去。”埃朱继续前行，自言自语道：“我从耶玛雅那里得不到的，奥伦甘（Orungan）会给我。”他前去见他，奥伦甘说：“我知道你为何而来。十六位神祇正在挨饿。他们如今必须得到一样美好的东西。我知道有这样一样东西。它是一件由十六颗棕榈果做成的大事物。你若得到它们并领悟其含义，你便能再度赢回世人的善意。”

passages.text: Edju went to where the palm-trees were, and the monkeys gave him sixteen nuts. He looked at these but did not know what to do with them, and the monkeys counselled him: "You got the sixteen nuts by guile. Now go round the world and ask for their meaning everywhere. You will hear sixteen sayings in each of the sixteen places. Then go back to the Gods. Tell men what you yourself have learned, and then men will also learn once more to fear you." Edju did as he was told; he went to the sixteen places round the world, went back into the sky, and told the Gods what he had learned. The Gods imparted their knowledge to their descendants, and now men can know the will of the Gods every day and what will come to pass in the future; when men saw what evil things would happen and what they could escape by offering sacrifices, they began to slaughter animals again and burn them for the Gods. This was the way in which Edju brought the Ifa (palm-nuts) down to men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 埃朱走到棕櫚樹所在之處，猴子們給了他十六顆果實。他看著這些果實，卻不知該如何處置，猴子們便勸告他：「你以詭計得到了這十六顆果實。如今你走遍世界，到處詢問它們的意義。在十六個地方，每個地方你都會聽到十六句諺語。然後回到眾神那裡。把你親自學到的告訴世人，如此世人便會重新學會敬畏你。」埃朱照著吩咐做了；他走遍世上十六個地方，回到天上，把他所學到的告訴眾神。眾神將他們的知識傳授給後代，如今世人每日都能知曉眾神的旨意，以及未來將要發生之事；當世人看見將有何等災禍降臨，又看見藉由獻祭可以逃脫什麼，他們便重新開始宰殺牲畜，焚燒獻給眾神。埃朱便是以這種方式，將伊法（棕櫚果）帶下人間。

title.en: Edju Swaps the Houses of Sea, Sun and Moon
title.zh: 埃茹調換海、日、月之家

region.en: Yoruba sky-country (symbolic pin: the crossroad before Oshalla's house)
region.zh: 約魯巴天界（象徵定位：奧夏拉宅前十字路口）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XII

summary.en: In the beginning Olokun lived in the river, Oshu the Moon wandered out every evening, Orun the Sun rose high above his home and returned at eve. Edju told each in turn: "Thy house is not comfortable; come, I will show thee a better" — and lodged the Sea in the Moon's house, the Sun in the Sea's, the Moon in the Sun's. Oshalla, Lord of the Gods, watching from his house at the crossroad, set every wanderer back; Edju drove Olokun out of the water with threats, and Oshalla had Shankpanna hand him a blade of grass with the word: change yourself into a hill. Olokun's children who came looking for him were turned into monkeys; then Shankpanna thrashed Edju — the Sun opened his eyes and struck him blind — and Edju washed his welts in the river, decreeing that all who bathe there shall burn as with fire: hence the smallpox and its scars.
summary.zh: 太初之時，奧洛貢居河中，月神奧舒夜夜出遊，日神奧倫高升晚歸。埃茹挨個對三人說：「你家不舒適，我帶你去更好的。」——於是海住進月宮，日遷入海宅，月搬進日居。眾神之主奧夏拉從十字路口的宅中看穿一切，逐一令其歸位；埃茹持刀威脅奧洛貢出水，奧夏拉便令香潘納賜他一片草葉：「化為山丘！」奧洛貢的兒女們出水上岸尋父，被埃茹引路繞行，悉數化作猿猴。隨後香潘納以草帚痛擊埃茹，太陽一睜眼便刺盲他；埃茹負傷入河洗創，詛咒凡入此水者如遭火灼——天花與其疤痕由此而來。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the Edju cosmological prank (Frobenius 1910-12) — origin of the heavenly bodies' courses, the hill-Orisha and smallpox in one tale.

passages.text: Olokun (the Sea God), Orun (the Sun God), and Oshu (the Moon God), in the beginning of things, had each their own abode. Olokun lived in the river. Oshu left his own dwelling every evening and went out whither it listed him. But Orun rose high above his own home and returned there at eve. One day, Edju came to Olokun, saying: "Thy house is not comfortable; come, I will show thee a better." Olokun said: "It is well; show it me." Edju went to Oshu and said the same to him; Oshu replied in the same words as Olokun. Edju went to Oru, and Oru also said: "It is well." Then Edju took Olokun to Oshu's, Orun to Olokun's, and Oshu to Orun's house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧洛昆（海神）、奧倫（太陽神）與奧舒（月神），在太初之時各有自己的居所。奧洛昆住在河裡。奧舒每天傍晚離開自己的住處，隨心所欲地去往他處。但奧倫升到自己家屋的高處，傍晚又回到那裡。有一天，埃朱來到奧洛昆面前，說：「你的屋子不舒服；來吧，我指給你看一處更好的。」奧洛昆說：「好；指給我看吧。」埃朱又到奧舒那裡，對他說同樣的話；奧舒的回答與奧洛昆一字不差。埃朱又到奧倫那裡，奧倫也說：「好。」於是埃朱把奧洛昆帶到奧舒的家，把奧倫帶到奧洛昆的家，把奧舒帶到奧倫的家。

passages.text: Now, Oshalla was Lord of all the Gods. He dwelt in a house at a cross-road, from which he saw Orun go by every day, and Oshu every night. But once Oshalla saw Oshu pass by in the daytime, and asked why; Oshu answered that an old man made him do it. Oshalla bade each wanderer return and sent for the old man. Then Edju went to Oshu and said: "You, Oshu, if you don't do to-day what I tell you, I will kill you to-day. Go, then, to Orun's house, and, not to anger Oshalla, go round Oshalla's house in a circle." Oshu set out, and coming to Orun's house the two quarrelled violently, Edju stirring each against the other. Oshalla heard them, went there at once — and Edju, hearing him coming, went to meet him and said: "I have already made them agree with one another. Only go home again."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 話說奧沙拉住於十字路口的一所房屋，從那裡他每天看見奧倫經過，每夜看見奧舒經過。但有一次，奧沙拉住在大白天看見奧舒經過，便問其緣故；奧舒回答說是一個老人叫他這麼做的。奧沙拉住吩咐每個遊蕩者各自回去，並派人去召那老人。於是埃朱來到奧舒面前，說：「你，奧舒，倘若你今天不照我說的去做，我今天就要殺了你。那麼，到奧倫的家去，而且，為了不惹奧沙拉住生氣，繞著奧沙拉住的家轉一圈。」奧舒出發了，來到奧倫的家，兩人激烈地爭吵起來，埃朱從中挑撥，使彼此相鬥。奧沙拉住聽見了，立刻趕往那裡——埃朱聽見他來了，便上前迎接，說：「我已經使他們彼此和好了。你只管回家去吧。」

passages.text: Then Edju went into the water to Olokun and said: "Come out of it, or I will kill you." Olokun said: "You did not give me life." But he came out, and Edju showed him the road into the bush. Oshalla gave Shankpanna a blade of grass, saying: "Go to Olokun, who has gone into the bush against my will. Tell him he shall not go back again into the water, for he was not with me when he left the water which I gave him to dwell in." Shankpanna took the blade of grass to Olokun, saying: "Oshalla sends you this. You left the water without his permission. Change yourself into an Oke (hill)." Olokun did so. Then all the children of Olokun came out of the water to look for him on the hill; Edju met them and said: "Go through the bush to find your father. Do not pass by Oshalla's place." Oshalla saw that Olokun's children had gone round his own dwelling, and transformed them all into monkeys. Since that time Olokun's children gambol about like apes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著，埃朱下水去見奧洛昆，說：「出來，否則我就殺了你。」奧洛昆說：「我的性命不是你給的。」但他還是出來了，埃朱便指給他通往灌木叢的路。奧沙拉住給尚潘納一片草葉，說：「到奧洛昆那裡去，他違背我的意願進了灌木叢。告訴他，他不得再回到水中，因為他離開我賜給他居住的水時，並不在我身邊。」尚潘納帶著草葉到奧洛昆那裡，說：「奧沙拉住送來這個給你。你未經他許可便離開了水。把你自身變為一座奧凱（山丘）。」奧洛昆照做了。於是奧洛昆所有的孩子都從水中出來，到山上尋找他；埃朱遇見他們，說：「穿過灌木叢去找你們的父親。不要經過奧沙拉住的地方。」奧沙拉住看見奧洛昆的孩子們繞過了自己的住所，便把他們全都變成了猴子。自那時起，奧洛昆的孩子們便像猿猴一般蹦跳嬉戲。

passages.text: Now Oshalla called Shankpanna and said to him: "Bring Edju to me!" Shankpanna set out with his Auwo (ceremonial broom of sedge-grass), found Edju at the market-place, and began to belabour him; but Edju took up his Ogo, or shoulder-club, and beat Shankpanna in return. Orun heard the sound of blows and said: "Shankpanna is contending with Edju. I needs must help Shankpanna." He approached and opened his eyes; Edju was struck blind, and Shankpanna drove in with his broom against the now defenceless Edju. Oshalla let all the little children go and rejoice because Shankpanna had conquered Edju. Shankpanna went on beating him, till all his blows left wales on Edju's body, and Edju ran to the river to bathe his wounds. When Edju was in the water, he said: "Henceforth the blows Shankpanna gave me shall flow with the water upon all those who bathe in it, and they all shall burn as with fire." And whoso bathes in the water in which Edju washed the wounds Shankpanna gave him gets the smallpox and the scars it leaves behind it. So Edju's mischief has been handed down to mankind and with them remains a living thing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是奧沙拉住召來尚潘納，對他說：「把埃朱帶到我面前來！」尚潘納帶著他的奧沃（以莎草製成的儀式掃帚）出發，在市場上找到埃朱，便開始痛打他；但埃朱拿起他的奧戈，即肩棒，回擊尚潘納。奧倫聽見打鬥之聲，說：「尚潘納正與埃朱爭鬥。我必須幫助尚潘納。」他走近並睜開雙眼；埃朱被照得雙目失明，尚潘納便以掃帚猛擊此時已無力自衛的埃朱。奧沙拉住放所有的小孩出去歡慶，因為尚潘納戰勝了埃朱。尚潘納繼續打他，直到他所有的擊打都在埃朱身上留下鞭痕，埃朱便跑到河裡洗滌傷口。埃朱在水中時，說：「從今以後，尚潘納打在我身上的鞭打，將隨水流到所有在水中沐浴的人身上，他們都將如火燒般灼痛。」凡在以埃朱洗滌尚潘納所致傷口之水沐浴的人，都會染上天花以及它所留下的疤痕。如此，埃朱的禍害便傳給了人類，並與他們同在，成為活生生的存在。

title.en: The Four-Coloured Cap and the Two Friends
title.zh: 四色帽與反目二友

region.en: Yoruba town and outlying fields (symbolic pin: the footpath between two adjoining farms near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴城鎮與郊野（象徵定位：伊費近郊兩田相鄰的小徑）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XII

summary.en: Two inseparable friends farmed adjoining fields; Edju resolved to make them differ, "and that will be a fine beginning for a very big lawsuit." He made himself a cap green before, black behind, red and white at the sides, stuck his pipe in the nape of his neck and carried his staff upside down, greeting each from the path between their fields. Each friend saw the cap of a different colour and swore the other was lying; they drew knives, ran bleeding to the town, and were haled before the king — where Edju stepped forward: "I put on this cap... The two friends couldn't help quarrelling. I made them do it. Sowing dissension is my chiefest delight." When the king bade seize him, Edju fired the town, swapped the rescued goods between their owners, and ran off laughing, no one able to catch him.
summary.zh: 兩位形影不離的好友田疇相鄰；埃茹存心使其反目，「好開一場大訴訟」。他製了前綠後黑、左右紅白的四色帽，煙斗插在後頸、手杖倒扛，沿田間小徑向二人問好。一人看見黑帽，一人看見紅帽，互斥對方撒謊，拔刀相向，血濺而逃，被押到王前對質。埃茹站出來自首：「我戴上這頂帽子……二友不得不吵，是我叫他們吵的。播弄糾紛乃吾至樂。」王下令拿人，埃茹縱火焚城，趁亂把各家的搶救之物互相調包，再大笑遁去，無人能擒。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the classic Edju cap-trick tale (Frobenius 1910-12), among the most famous Yoruba trickster narratives. The four-coloured cap doubles as the four-quarters cosmogram in Frobenius's analysis.

passages.text: Once upon a time, Olorun first created Enja, or mortal man, and, after that, Edju, the God. Once there was a pair of friends. When they went out they were always dressed alike, and everyone said: "These two men are the best of friends." Edju saw them and said: "These men are very dear to each other. I will make them differ, and that will be a fine beginning for a very big Idja (lawsuit or palaver)." The fields of these friends adjoined; a path ran between and separated them, on which Edju used to walk of a morning wearing a black cap. Now, when Edju wanted to start this quarrel, he made himself a cap of green, black, red, and white cloth, which showed a different colour from whatever side it was looked at. He put it on one morning, took his tobacco pipe and put it not in his mouth but at the nape of his neck, and carried his staff upside down, so that it hung over his shoulder behind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前，奧洛倫首先創造了恩賈，即有死的人類，之後又創造了神埃朱。從前有一對朋友。他們出門時總是穿著相同的衣服，人人都說：「這兩個人是最好的朋友。」埃朱看見他們，說：「這兩個人彼此極為親愛。我要使他們產生分歧，這將是一場極大的伊賈（訴訟或爭執）的絕佳開端。」這兩位朋友的田地相鄰；一條小徑從中穿過，將兩塊田隔開，埃朱每天早晨都戴著一頂黑帽走在那條小徑上。話說當埃朱想要挑起這場爭吵時，他為自己縫了一頂以綠、黑、紅、白四色布料製成的帽子，無論從哪一面看去，都顯出不同的顏色。一天早晨，他戴上這頂帽子，拿起他的菸斗，卻不放在嘴裡，而是插在後頸上，又把他的手杖倒著拿，讓它從背後懸在肩上。

passages.text: Both the friends were at work in their fields; they looked up for a second as Edju called out "Good morning!" and went on with their toil. Then they went home together. One said to the other: "The old man went the opposite road through the fields to-day. I noticed that by his pipe and his stick." The other said: "You're wrong. He went the same way as usual." "It's a lie; I saw his pipe and staff much too plainly; and, besides, he had on a white instead of a black cap." "You must be blind or asleep; his cap was red." "Then you must already have had some palm-wine this morning." "I haven't even seen a drop, but you must be crazed." "You are making up lies to annoy me." "Liar yourself! And not for the first time by a good deal!" One of them drew his knife and went for the other, who got a wound; he also drew his, and cut his assailant over the sconce. They both ran away bleeding to the town.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兩個朋友都在各自的田裡幹活；艾朱喊了一聲「早安！」他們抬頭看了一眼，又繼續勞作。隨後他們一起回家。一個對另一個說：「那老頭今天穿過田地走的是另一條路。我是從他的菸斗和手杖看出來的。」另一個說：「你錯了。他走的是平常那條路。」「胡說；我看他的菸斗和手杖看得再清楚不過了；而且，他戴的是白帽子，不是黑帽子。」「你準是瞎了，要不就是睡著了；他的帽子是紅的。」「那你準是今早已經喝過棕櫚酒了。」「我一滴都沒見著，倒是你準是瘋了。」「你編瞎話來氣我。」「你自己才是撒謊的！而且這可不是頭一回了，差得遠呢！」其中一個拔出刀來撲向另一個，那人受了傷；他也拔出刀來，砍破了對方的頭皮。兩人流著血，一起跑回了鎮上。

passages.text: The King summoned the two friends and asked what made them fall out; they said they could not agree as to what it was that went through their fields that morning. "Who knows this old man?" asked the King. Edju said: "It was I. These two fellows quarrelled because I so willed it." He pulled out his cap: "I put on this cap, red on one side, white on the other, green in front and black behind. I stuck my pipe in my nape. So my steps went one way while I was looking another. The two friends couldn't help quarrelling. I made them do it. Sowing dissension is my chiefest delight." The King said: "Seize this fellow; bind him; he baits folks to fall out!" But he ran very swiftly to a neighbouring hill, struck stones together till the dry grass caught fire, and threw the burning hay down upon the town, where the thatch caught fire. Then Edju came back and, jumping about, took the loads the fleeing townsfolk carried — baskets, sacks, calabashes, jars — and carried the bundle of pots to the owner of the calabashes, the load of baskets to the owner of the sacks, and the parcel of sacks to the heap's owner of pots. After the fire everyone looked for his own goods, and each called the other thief; in their rage they took to their clubs and pestles and destroyed what the fire had spared, and several people were killed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 國王召來這兩個朋友，問他們為何反目；他們說，兩人對那天早晨從田裡經過的究竟是什麼東西爭執不下。「誰認識這個老頭？」國王問。艾朱說：「是我。這兩個傢伙爭吵，是因為我故意要他們如此。」他掏出自己的帽子：「我戴上這頂帽子，一邊紅，一邊白，前面綠，後面黑。我把菸斗插在後頸上。於是，我腳走一個方向，眼睛卻看著另一個方向。這兩個朋友不由得爭吵起來。是我叫他們這樣的。播撒不和是我最大的樂趣。」國王說：「拿下這傢伙；把他綁起來；他挑唆人們反目！」但他飛快地跑到鄰近的一座山上，把石頭相互敲擊，直到乾草著了火，又把燃燒的乾草扔到鎮上，那裡的茅草屋頂便燒了起來。隨後艾朱回來，蹦蹦跳跳地，把逃難的鎮民所背的擔子——籃子、麻袋、葫蘆、罈子——拿了過來，把一捆陶罐送到葫蘆的主人那裡，把一擔籃子送到麻袋的主人那裡，又把一包麻袋送到那堆陶罐的主人那裡。火災過後，人人都去找自己的東西，個個都罵別人是賊；他們怒氣沖沖，抄起棍棒和杵臼，把火災倖免的東西也砸了個稀爛，還有好幾個人被殺。

passages.text: The King had the maniacs sundered and asked what had been the matter; each shouted of the other that he had stolen his goods during the fire. All the people shouted at once. Then the King asked: "What, are all my people thieves?" Then Edju stepped forward, saying: "Nay, O King, thy people are not thieves, they are but fools. I had a game with them and they played it well. If ever I should want to laugh right heartily again, 'twill be to this place I shall come." Edju ran off. No one could catch him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 國王叫人把這些發狂的人分開，問究竟是怎麼回事；每個人都大喊大叫，說對方在火災中偷了自己的東西。所有的人都同時嚷了起來。於是國王問：「怎麼，我的子民全都是賊嗎？」這時艾朱走上前來，說道：「不，國王啊，你的子民不是賊，他們不過是傻瓜。我跟他們玩了一場遊戲，他們玩得挺好。倘若哪天我又想痛痛快快地大笑一場，我要來的就是這個地方。」艾朱跑掉了。誰也抓不住他。

title.en: Edju, Marshal of the Gods, at Every Crossroad
title.zh: 眾神儀仗長——十字路口的埃茹

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: a clay cone at an Orita crossroad near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費附近奧里塔路口的泥錐神壇）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XII

summary.en: Edju is no devil, whatever the missionaries taught, but a boon companion like the Polynesian Maui — the fomenter of strife and, at the same time, the giver of the Ifa oracle and of the sun. He ranks as leader or inspector of the group of sixteen Gods — their director and chief marshal, responsible for keeping law and order on the Yoruban Olympus: the other Orishas would be unable to do anything whatever without him. He dwells at all the crossroads, where small cones of clay are set up to him; his effigies are always in profile, with disproportionate broad feet, a pigtail, and a pipe in mouth or hand; his festival, the Odu-Edju, at the solstice, when the town's ruler raises the new carved image and last year's is given to a new-born child of an Edju family.
summary.zh: 埃茹絕非傳教士口中的魔鬼，而是如波利尼西亞毛伊般的搗蛋夥伴——既播弄紛爭，又賜下伊法神諭與太陽。他是十六神團的領班與督察——眾神的儀仗長，掌管約魯巴奧林帕斯上的秩序：沒有他，眾神一事無成。他棲身所有十字路口，路口供其泥錐；其像必為側面，闊足、辮尾、口銜或手持煙斗。歲至夏至，舉行奧杜埃茹祭：城主親抬新雕神像安座，舊像則交由埃茹氏族新生兒終身供奉。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Èṣù/Edju at the crossroads (Orita) recorded 1910-12 — the classic portrait of the misunderstood trickster, whom Frobenius explicitly refuses to call a devil. Cross-ref: afroatlantic-legba-crossroads (diaspora Legba/Exu).

passages.text: Edju! The Devil — as the missionaries coming from the Coast to preach the Saviour of Mankind to the Yorubans have taught them to believe. Yet go into the compounds, talk to them kindly and they will tell you: "Ah, yes! Edju played many tricks; Edju made kindred peoples go to war; Edju pawned the moon and carried off the sun; Edju made the Gods strive against themselves. But Edju is not evil. He brought us the best of all there is; he gave us the Ifa oracle; he brought the sun. But for Edju, the fields would be barren." He is a boon companion, up to all sorts of games, something like the Polynesian deity Maui; he showed himself above all measure friendly to men by giving them the Ifa oracle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 艾朱！就是魔鬼——那些從海岸來、向約魯巴人宣講人類救主的傳教士，就是這樣教他們相信的。然而走進那些院落，和他們親切地交談，他們會告訴你：「啊，是的！艾朱耍過許多花招；艾朱讓同族的人們打起仗來；艾朱把月亮當了，又把太陽帶走了；艾朱讓眾神彼此爭鬥。但艾朱並不邪惡。他給我們帶來了世上最好的一切；他把伊法神諭賜給了我們；他帶來了太陽。若沒有艾朱，田地就會荒蕪。」他是個好夥伴，什麼把戲都玩得來，有點像波利尼西亞的神祇毛伊；他把伊法神諭賜給人類，以此表明自己對人類無比友善。

passages.text: Everywhere Edju ranks as a sort of leader or inspector of the group of some sixteen Gods. He is only the God-inspector in the sense of being, so to say, their director and chief marshal, and responsible for keeping law and order on the Yoruban Olympus. Edju-worshippers declared that the other Orishas would be unable to do anything whatever without this deity, and as the descendants of the others held their peace, they practically admitted this divinity's supremacy. He is not, however, to be considered as the Ruler of the Gods, but rather as the marshal of their procession. Edju dwells at all the cross-roads, or Orita, where small cones of clay are set up to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在各地，艾朱都被列為大約十六位神祇這一群體的首領或督察。他之所以只是神祇的督察，是說他算是他們的導演和總元帥，負責維持約魯巴奧林匹斯山上的法紀與秩序。艾朱的崇拜者宣稱，其他奧里沙若沒有這位神祇，便什麼也做不成；而其他神祇的後裔都默不作聲，實際上也就承認了這位神明的至高地位。然而，他並不被視為眾神的統治者，而更像是他們行列中的元帥。艾朱住在所有的十字路口，即奧里塔，那裡為他立著小泥錐。

passages.text: There are many plastic effigies of Edju, either heads only or entire figures; whenever these are represented on doors or planks, it is always in profile, which never occurs on any other occasions of his portrayal. All his images are characterized by feet of disproportionate breadth. They all have a pigtail. They are all naked, though sexless. A tobacco pipe is found held in his hand or in his mouth with astonishing frequency. This great holiday in his honour, the Odu-Edju, takes place about the close of June or the beginning of July; the principal part consists in the erection of a new Edju-image carved in wood: the ruler of the town himself carries it to its place, raises it several times in a ritual rhythm, and places it on the spot previously occupied by its predecessor. Meanwhile the last year's image has been entrusted to a new-born child of some Edju family of repute, which remains its first sacred possession for the rest of its natural life. After the festival the days begin to decline; had it not been held, there would be no night whatever. It is clear, then, that it celebrates the solstice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 艾朱有許多塑像，或只有頭部，或為全身；每當這些形象被繪在門上或木板上時，總是側面像，而在他形象的其他任何場合都從不出現這種畫法。他所有的形象都有一個特徵：雙腳寬得不成比例。它們都梳著一條辮子。它們都赤身裸體，卻沒有性別。令人驚訝的是，他手中或嘴裡常常叼著一支菸斗。為他舉行的大節日「奧杜-艾朱」約在六月底或七月初；節日的主要內容是立起一尊新刻的木製艾朱像：鎮上的統治者親自把它搬到安放之處，以儀式的節奏把它舉起數次，然後放在前任所佔的位置上。與此同時，去年的舊像則被託付給某個有名望的艾朱家族的新生嬰兒，這像便成為他一生中第一件神聖的財物。節日過後，白晝便開始變短；倘若不舉行這個節日，就根本不會有黑夜。由此可見，這個節日慶祝的是冬至（至點）。

title.en: "This Is Thy Ifa": The Making of a Babalawo
title.zh: 「此乃汝之伊法」——巴巴拉奧的養成

region.en: Oshun river near Ibadan, Nigeria (the white-robed washing and the three holy spaces)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊巴丹近郊奧舜河（白衣洗禮與三重聖地）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XII

summary.en: Ifa is not a God with posterity but the oracle any man of means and patience may serve; those initiated into its mysteries are not sons of Ifa but Babalawo, Fathers of the Secret. The candidate brings five things — parrot tail-feathers, the fish Boli, an Ekete, an Eku mouse, and the washing-root Kanka — and, robed all in white with his Oluwo, is washed in the Oshun river. In the bush's three holy spaces (the third, the Holy of Holies, only the teacher may tread), the hierophant casts the palm-nuts on the flour-strewn tray; if the Odu is a yea-word, he rubs white medicine into the youth's hair, ties the parrot feathers round him, endues him with the Oquelle and gives him sixteen palm-kernels: "This is thy Ifa."
summary.zh: 伊法並非有後嗣的神，而是一切有錢、有悟性、有耐心者皆可侍奉的神諭；入其秘傳者不稱「伊法之子」，而稱「巴巴拉奧」——秘密之父。候選者備五物——鸚鵡尾羽、波利魚、埃克特、家鼠與洗禮之坎卡根——與師尊同著白衣，先在奧舜河中受洗。林中三重聖地，第三重唯師尊可入。長老在撒了白粉的占板上擲果問卜；若卦辭應允，便以白色聖藥抹其髮，繫鸚鵡羽、披奧克萊占繩，授予十六枚果仁：「此乃汝之伊法。」

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; babalawo initiation recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius). The 'Fathers of the Secret' opening rite is an established Ifa practice (UNESCO-listed 2008); presented as archival description.

passages.text: Ifa is nothing but the expression of the need of searching for a final cause, of the endeavour to find a concrete idea of a Universe which transcends native intellectual capacity; and this world of thought is incredibly full of wonders. Ifa is not to be found at the head of a totemistic clan; Ifa has no claim to a posterity like Shango, or Shankpanna, or Oja, or any other deity. Anybody can devote himself to the cult of Ifa; and, thus, those who are thoroughly initiated in its mysteries are not called Omo (son of) Ifa, but Baba-la-wo (Father of the Secret). Everyone may become a Baba-lawo, provided he have sufficient worldly means, brains and the necessary patience.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊法無非是表達一種尋求終極因的需要，一種力圖為一個超越土著智識能力的宇宙找到具體概念的嘗試；而這個思想世界充滿了令人難以置信的奇蹟。伊法並不見於某個圖騰氏族的首領之位；伊法不像尚戈、尚克潘納、奧賈或任何其他神祇那樣，有權要求子嗣後裔。任何人都可以獻身於伊法的崇拜；因此，那些徹底入其奧祕之門的人，不稱為伊法之奧莫（Omo，意即「子」），而稱為巴巴拉沃（Baba-la-wo，意即「奧祕之父」）。人人都可以成為巴巴拉沃，只要他有足夠的世俗財力、頭腦以及必要的耐心。

passages.text: First of all the novice or candidate has to furnish himself with the following five ingredients: Ikode, or parrot tail-feathers; the fish, Boli; an Ekete; an Eku (mouse); and the root Kanka, used in washing. He beseeches a Baba-lawo to instruct and induct him into the mysteries, addressing him as Oluwo. This Oluwo conducts him, carrying this bundle of the five articles on his head, to the nearest river, the Oshun, near Ibadan. They are both robed all in white; they lay their things down on the bank and the priest washes the pupil. Then they go into the bush, where there is a holy spot consisting of three consecutive broad spaces: anyone may stand upon the first, the introduction takes place on the second, and the Holy of Holies, which is the third, may only be trodden by the teacher in person.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 首先，新手或候選人必須為自己備齊以下五樣物品：伊科德（Ikode），即鸚鵡尾羽；名為博利（Boli）的魚；一個埃凱特（Ekete）；一隻埃庫（Eku，即老鼠）；以及用於洗滌的坎卡（Kanka）根。他懇求一位巴巴拉沃教導他並引領他進入奧祕，稱其為奧盧沃（Oluwo）。這位奧盧沃將這五樣物品捆成一束頂在頭上，引他前往最近的河流，即伊巴丹附近的奧順河（Oshun）。二人皆全身著白衣；他們把東西放在岸邊，祭司為弟子洗滌。然後他們進入灌木叢，那裡有一處聖地，由三個相連的開闊空間組成：任何人都可以站在第一處，入門儀式在第二處舉行，而第三處至聖之所，則唯有導師本人方可踏足。

passages.text: The hierophant opens his pouch, a wallet of leather mostly with cowrie-embroidered edges, takes out the palm-nuts, strews finely powdered wood upon the Oqua-Ifa, or tray, and the Ifa oracle is interpreted once in the novice's sight: the odd or even number of the nuts caught up in falling is recorded in a series of double or single lines, four of which make up an Odu, and the question is whether the marks announce the deity's consent to the youth's initiation. If the Odu is a yea-word, the main business of the day is settled. The priest then rubs a white mixture into the youth's hair, ties the parrot's feathers round him and endues him with the Oquelle, so that the middle portion of it falls over his shoulders with its ends hanging down in front like a stole. He then gives him sixteen palm-kernels with these words: "This is thy Ifa."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 聖祕導師打開他的袋子——一隻多為皮革製、邊緣繡有貝殼的錢袋——取出棕櫚果，將細磨的木粉撒在奧夸伊法（Oqua-Ifa，即托盤）上，並在新手眼前解讀一次伊法神諭：落下時被接住的果實數為奇或偶，以一系列雙線或單線記錄，四條線構成一個奧杜（Odu），而問題在於這些記號是否宣告神祇同意這名青年入門。若該奧杜為肯定之詞，當日的主要事務便算議定。接著，祭司將一種白色混合物揉進青年的頭髮，把鸚鵡羽毛繫在他身上，並為他披上奧奎勒（Oquelle），使其中段垂過雙肩，兩端在身前垂下，宛如一條聖帶。然後他給他十六顆棕櫚仁，說道：「這是你的伊法。」

title.en: The Ifa Tray: Edju's Face and the Four Quarters
title.zh: 伊法占板——埃茹之面與四方

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (symbolic pin: the diviner's tray turned to the East)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（象徵定位：朝東安放的占板）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XII

summary.en: Every Ifa tray bears a face on its rim, repeated on each of the four sides — and everywhere the answer is the same: "There is no picture of Ifa; those on the Ifa trays and caskets are images of Edju." The interpreter turns to the East, the tray's Edju face intervening between him and the sun. The tray is divided into the four quarters of the compass; beside it stand the Iroke tusk-clapper struck at dawn to salute Edju, the Adjelefa cups carved with riders and drummers and women at their looms, the Oduso ivory head with Edju's pigtail standing sentinel over the sixteen nuts, and the divided caskets holding sulphur (sun-dung), charcoal, chalk and redwood — one compartment for each presiding god.
summary.zh: 每塊伊法占板邊緣皆有一張面孔，四側重複——而舉國上下答案如一：「板上並非伊法之像；那些是埃茹之像。」占者面東而坐，板上埃茹之面恰好擋在他與太陽之間。占板分劃四方位；一旁立著清晨擊板致敬埃茹的象牙響板「伊羅克」、雕著騎手與織女的小托杯、以埃茹辮尾為記的奧杜索象牙首——為十六果仁站崗——以及分格的木匣：硫磺（日糞）、炭、白堊與紅木粉，各歸其主神。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Ifa material culture recorded 1910-12. The cosmological reading of the tray (Frobenius's analysis) is his interpretation, reported as such.

passages.text: I said there were no images of Ifa, the god. Every one looking at the Ifa trays will observe a face on the edge, which is often repeated on each of the four sides, and ask whether this is not, perhaps, the Ifa. The author inquired the meaning of this head in every corner of this land, and always got the same answer, namely: "There is no picture of Ifa; those on the Ifa trays and caskets are images of Edju."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 我說過，伊法這位神祇並沒有形象。每一個觀看伊法托盤的人都會注意到邊緣上有一張面孔，這面孔常常在四邊各重複一次，於是便問：這莫非就是伊法？作者在這片土地的每一個角落探問這頭像的含義，得到的答覆始終如一，即：「伊法沒有畫像；伊法托盤與匣子上那些，是埃朱（Edju）的形象。」

passages.text: The Oqua-Ifa, or tray, is rectangular towards the south, but, as a rule, circular towards the north. Even its mere arrangement proves its deep meaning: on the uppermost part there is always a dominant face, throned like a watchman over the bare inner surface. Opposite to this, or at equal spaces to the left and right, there are other divisions, separated by ornaments, so that the whole is, as it were, divided into the four quarters of the compass. They are the most beautiful products of ancient West African industrial art. When a Baba-lawo finally attained the dignity of an Oluwo, he generally received the finest tray from the ancient family possessions; and when the Baba-lawo died, this tray was of old put into his grave for him to rest upon. The interpreter always turns to the East, and places the tray on the ground with the Edju always pointing in that direction; there is at least one such face on every board, which is named Edju-Ogbe, so that it intervenes between him and the sun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧夸伊法，即托盤，朝南的一面為矩形，但通常朝北的一面為圓形。單是其排列方式便證明其深意：最上方總有一張居於主位的面孔，如守望者般端坐於光素的內面之上。與此相對，或在左右等距之處，另有其他分區，以裝飾相隔，使整體彷彿被劃分為羅盤的四個方位。它們是古代西非工藝藝術最美麗的產物。當一位巴巴拉沃最終獲得奧盧沃的尊位時，他通常會從家族古老的珍藏中獲得最精美的托盤；而當這位巴巴拉沃去世時，這托盤古時會被放入他的墓中，供他安息其上。解讀者總是轉向東方，將托盤置於地上，使埃朱始終指向那個方向；每塊板上至少有一張這樣的面孔，名為埃朱奧格貝（Edju-Ogbe），如此它便介於他與太陽之間。

passages.text: The Iroke is a clapper which was in the beginning probably an elephant tusk; at dawn the Baba-lawo strikes the tray with the Iroke and so salutes Edju, the deity presiding over the Ifa. Particularly wealthy people have an Okwong-Ifa, a box with many divisions: the middle compartment is meant for keeping the nuts, the surrounding space is mostly divided in four, and contains clay, charcoal, chalk and redwood pigment — sulphur, called Emi-Orun, or sun-dung, takes the place of clay with the extremely rich. And, lastly, there is the Oquelle, a string connecting eight halved palm-nuts: in fortune-telling by the Oquelle it is taken by the middle, so that four of the nuts hang down on either side, and when it falls an Odu or figure is formed by the number of convex or concave positions assumed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊羅凱（Iroke）是一種敲擊器，起初大概是一根象牙；黎明時分，巴巴拉沃以伊羅凱敲擊托盤，以此向主持伊法的神祇埃朱致敬。特別富有的人有一個奧克翁伊法（Okwong-Ifa），即一隻有許多分格的盒子：中間的格子用來存放果實，周圍的空間大多分為四格，分別盛放黏土、木炭、白堊與紅木顏料——硫磺，稱為埃米奧倫（Emi-Orun），即「太陽之糞」，在極富有者那裡則取代黏土。最後，還有奧奎勒，即一條串起八顆對半剖開的棕櫚果的繩子：以奧奎勒占卜時，它被從中段提起，使四顆果實垂在兩側，落下時，依其所呈凸面或凹面的數目，便形成一個奧杜或圖形。

title.en: Olodumare Commands the Four Quarters into Being
title.zh: 奧洛杜馬雷令四方成形

region.en: Yoruba sky-country (symbolic pin: the ordered horizon seen from Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴天界（象徵定位：伊費望見的整齊地平）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XII

summary.en: "When very, very long ago everything was in great confusion, and old and young things dead, Olodumare (God) called Edju-Ogbe to him and said: 'Order thou the region where the sun doth rise!' He said to Ojako-Medji: 'Order thou the region where the sun doth set!' Thereupon Edju-Ogbe put the region of the East in order in the morning and, in the evening, Ojako-Medji did so in the West." Evori-Medji and Odi-Medji between them arrange the course of things from dawn to sunset — the venerable babalawo's account of how the four principal Odus, the four faces on the Ifa tray, and the four winds of the world came to be.
summary.zh: 「遠古之時，萬物混亂，新舊皆亡。奧洛杜馬雷召埃茹-奧格貝曰：『你去整理日出之方！』又對奧賈科-梅吉說：『你去整理日落之方！』於是埃茹-奧格貝於晨整理東方，奧賈科-梅吉於暮整理西方。」埃沃里-梅吉與奧迪-梅吉則共理自晨至暮的萬事之序——這是老巴巴拉奧所述：占板四面的主奧杜、四張面孔與天下四方由此而生。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the cosmogonic word of a Lokojan elder recorded by Frobenius 1910-12 — the Ifa scheme's ordering of the four quarters.

passages.text: All that could be learned in addition with regard to the four faces was derived from a venerable Lokojan, viz., this: "When very, very long ago, indeed, everything was in great confusion, and old and young things dead, Olodu-mare (God) called Edju-Ogbe to him and said: 'Order thou the region where the sun doth rise!' He said to Ojako-Medji: 'Order thou the region where the sun doth set!' Thereupon Edju-Ogbe put the region of the East in order in the morning and, in the evening, Ojako-Medji did so in the West."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 關於這四張面孔，凡能額外得知的一切，皆得自一位可敬的洛科詹人，即如下所述：「當很久、很久以前，確實一切皆處於極大的混亂之中，老幼之物皆已死去，奧洛杜馬雷（神）召埃朱-奧格貝到他跟前，說道：『你去整頓太陽升起的那一區域！』他又對奧賈科-梅吉說：『你去整頓太陽落下的那一區域！』於是，埃朱-奧格貝在早晨將東方那一區域整頓就緒，而到了傍晚，奧賈科-梅吉則在西方如此而行。」

passages.text: When asked to tell something about the Evori-Medji's functions, the old babalawo said that one of them was to arrange the course of things from dawn to sunset, and that Odi-Medji helped him in it — an explanation given with great hesitation. In reality the matter is not as obscure as it first appears: once it has been seen that the tray represents the four quarters of the compass, that these correspond to the four principal Odus, and that the tray must always be held and read in the same way, various things can be brought into parallelism.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當被要求談談埃沃里-梅吉的職能時，那位年老的巴巴拉沃說，其中之一便是安排事物從黎明到日落的進程，而奧迪-梅吉則從旁協助他——這一解釋是帶著極大的猶豫說出的。實際上，此事並不像初看時那般晦澀：一旦看出托盤代表羅盤的四方，看出這四方對應於四個主要的奧杜，並看出托盤必須始終以同樣的方式持握與解讀，便可將種種事物並列比對。

title.en: Four Gods of the Four Quarters: East Edju, North Ogun, West Shango, South Oshalla
title.zh: 四方四神——東埃茹、北奧貢、西尚戈、南奧夏拉

region.en: Ilesha, Nigeria (the holy mount with four heads facing the cardinal points)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊萊沙（四首各朝方位的聖山）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XII

summary.en: Edju met Shango on the Chief Way that runs east and west, and Obatala visited Ogun on the Second Way that runs south and north: Edju rules the East, Ogun the North, Shango the West, Oshalla the South. The Ifa caskets confirm it — sulphur for Edju, charcoal for Shango, chalk for Obatala, redwood for Ogun — as does the five-day week (Ifa's day, Ogun's, Shango's, Oshalla's, and the holy day), and the ancient holy mount near Ilesha with a monument of four heads facing the cardinal points, to which sacrifices were offered four times a year, the processional route running East to North, to West, to South. Frobenius read in this the same scheme of the universe the Etruscans carved in their Templum — sixteen celestial divisions, a five-day week, and a world divided fourfold.
summary.zh: 貫通東西的「大路」上，埃茹與尚戈相會；貫通南北的「二路」上，奧巴塔拉訪奧貢——故埃茹主東、奧貢主北、尚戈主西、奧夏拉主南。伊法木匣為證：硫磺屬埃茹、炭屬尚戈、白堊屬奧巴塔拉、紅木屬奧貢；五日一週亦然——伊法日、奧貢日、尚戈日、奧夏拉日，外加潔廟的聖日。伊萊沙古聖山上有四首各朝一方之碑，歲祭四次，儀程由東而北而西而南。弗羅貝紐斯將此讀為與伊特魯里亞「聖界」（Templum）同構的宇宙圖式——十六天區、五日一週、四分天下。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the four-quarter cosmology (Frobenius 1910-12). His Etruscan/Korean/Pueblo comparisons are his own diffusionist thesis, reported as such and not endorsed here. Note: the sacrifice of children at the Ilesha mount is given as the recorded tradition; presented as archival.

passages.text: The Elder who explained the tray's quadruple partition drew a picture of it in the sand. He put East, West, North and South together as the limbs of a cross, in which Edju-Ogbe led to Ojako-Medji, and Evori-Medji to Odi-Medji. Then he called the line running East and West the Chief Way, that from South to North the Second Way. When asked the difference between the two, he said Edju met Shango on the first, and Obatalla visited Ogun on the second. Obviously, then, Edju rules the East, Shango the West, Obatalla the South and Ogun the North.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那位解釋托盤四重劃分的長老在沙地上畫了一幅它的圖。他將東、西、南、北合在一起，作為一個十字的四臂，其中埃朱-奧格貝通向奧賈科-梅吉，埃沃里-梅吉通向奧迪-梅吉。接著，他稱東西走向的那條線為「主道」，稱由南至北的那條為「第二道」。當被問及兩者有何差異時，他說埃朱在第一條道上遇見了尚戈，而奧巴塔拉在第二條道上拜訪了奧貢。那麼，顯而易見，埃朱統轄東方，尚戈統轄西方，奧巴塔拉統轄南方，奧貢統轄北方。

passages.text: An Oluwo said that the contents of the caskets were apportioned thus: the sulphur was for Edju, the charcoal for Shango, the chalk for Obatalla and the red-wood for Ogun. This corroborates the locality of these Godheads. And the four-coloured cap of Edju's cap-trick legend turns these colours to the presiding deities: yellow (green) to the East, black to the West, and the colours sacred to Obatalla and Ogun to the North and South. The Yoruban five-day week presents a parallel: the day of the secret (Ifa's day), the day of Ogun, the day of Yakuta (Shango, the slinger of stones), the day of Oshe-Oshalla (the Lord of Heaven), and the holy day on which all the Gods are honoured by the cleansing of their temples — and an Old-Ojo veteran said that in former times not one but four Gods were worshipped on each of these four days, sixteen Gods in all within the week.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位奧盧沃說，小匣中的物品是這樣分配的：硫磺歸埃朱，木炭歸尚戈，白堊歸奧巴塔拉，紅木歸奧貢。這印證了這幾位神祇的方位。而埃朱變帽戲法傳說中那頂四色帽，則將這些顏色歸於各自的主司神祇：黃色（綠色）歸東方，黑色歸西方，而歸於奧巴塔拉與奧貢的神聖顏色則分屬北方與南方。約魯巴的五日一週呈現出一個對應：祕密之日（伊法之日）、奧貢之日、雅庫塔之日（尚戈，擲石者）、奧謝-奧沙拉之日（上天之主），以及那藉潔淨其神廟來敬奉眾神的神聖之日——而一位老奧喬老兵說，從前在這四日中的每一日，所敬奉的並非一位神，而是四位神，一週之內共計十六位神。

passages.text: There was formerly a particularly holy mount near Ilesha, esteemed to be of such sanctity that a city was built round it. In the centre of this hill there was said to have been a monument, with four heads severally facing a cardinal point. Sacrifices were offered up to these at equi-distant periods, four times a year, and every time the victim was a little child. The days so appointed were one in June for the Eastward, one in September for the Northward, one in December for the Westward, and one in March for the head turned Southward; and the processional route is from East to North, to West, to South. Comparing this with the rest of the observations, the four heads on the Ileshan hill were the recipients of sacrifice four times annually, and the days of the week follow in the same order: Eastern Edju, Northern Ogun, Western Shango and Southern Oshalla.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前在伊萊沙附近有一座特別神聖的山，被推崇為如此聖潔，以致圍繞它建起了一座城。據說在這座山的中央曾有一座紀念碑，上有四個頭，各自朝向一個方位。人們以相等的間隔向這些頭獻祭，一年四次，而每次的祭品都是一個幼童。所定的日子是：六月的一日獻給朝東的那個頭，九月的一日獻給朝北的那個頭，十二月的一日獻給朝西的那個頭，三月的一日獻給轉向南方的那個頭；而巡行的路線是由東至北，至西，至南。將此與其餘的觀察相比較，伊萊沙山上的四個頭便是每年四次接受獻祭的對象，而一週中各日的順序也依同樣的次序而行：東方的埃朱、北方的奧貢、西方的尚戈與南方的奧沙拉。

title.en: The Drunken Sculptor and the Sand-Spreading Hen
title.zh: 醉酒的塑者與撒沙的母雞

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the spot where the hen spread the sand, the hole of Osha)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（母雞撒沙之地、奧沙聖泉之穴）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XIII

summary.en: At first there was no earth: only Okun (Olokun), the ocean, a water stretched over all things, with Olorun above it, coeval and all-containing. Olorun summoned his elder son Orishalla, gave him some earth and a hen with five fingers, and bade him go down and make the earth upon Okun. On the way Orishalla found palm-wine, drank, slumbered; and Olorun called the younger son Odudua, who descended, laid the sand on the sea, and set the five-fingered hen on it — she scratched and spread the sand, forcing the water aside. Ilife was the spot where this took place, round which at first the sea still flowed; Odudua ruled the land as its first king, and the sea ran away through a small hole — the Osha, whence to this day one fetches holy water, much water and it never fails. Then Orishalla, wrathful at losing the creation, made war on Odudua; they contended long, made peace, and went underground together, never to be seen again.
summary.zh: 太初無陸地，唯有奧貢（奧洛貢）——漫蓋萬物的汪洋，其上為奧洛倫，二者同生並包羅萬有。奧洛倫召長子奧里夏拉，授以泥土與一隻五趾母雞，命他下去在奧貢之上造陸。途中奧里夏拉拾得棕櫚酒，飲醉酣眠。奧洛倫改召次子奧杜杜瓦；他下凡將沙鋪於海面，放上五趾母雞——母雞抓散沙土，逼水退讓。伊費正是此事發生之地，四圍海水環流；奧杜杜瓦為此地首王，海水則從一處小孔退去——即「奧沙」，至今取之不竭的聖水之穴。奧里夏拉憤而與奧杜杜瓦開戰，久戰言和，二人一同入地，從此不見蹤影。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the first of Frobenius's three Ife creation versions (1910-12) — the Ife-Benin city version, distinct from the coastal (Ellis) Yemaja-cycle. Oduduwa is here a male God, as Frobenius notes for the interior. Cross-refs: yoruba-ife-creation, obatala-creation.

passages.text: At first there was no earth. There was only Okun (or Olokun), the ocean, a water stretched over all things. Above it was Olorun. Olorun, the Orisha of the sky, and Olokun, the Orisha of the sea, were coeval. They contained (or possessed) all that there was. Olorun had two sons. The first one's name was Orishalla (the same as Otaballa, who here is also simply called Orisha); the younger's, Odudua. Olorun summoned Orisha. He gave him some earth. He gave him a hen with five fingers. He said to him, "Climb down and make the earth upon Okun." Orisha went. On the way he found some palm-wine. He began to drink and got drunken. Then he slumbered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 起初沒有大地。只有奧昆（或奧洛昆），即海洋，一片覆蓋萬物的水。在它之上是奧洛倫。奧洛倫，天空的奧里沙，與奧洛昆，海洋的奧里沙，是同時代的。他們包含（或擁有）了存在的一切。奧洛倫有兩個兒子。長子的名字是奧里沙拉（與奧塔巴拉相同，在此也簡稱為奧里沙）；幼子的名字是奧杜杜瓦。奧洛倫召喚奧里沙。他給了他一些泥土。他給了他一隻五趾的母雞。他對他說：「下去，在奧昆之上造出大地。」奧里沙去了。在路上他發現了一些棕櫚酒。他開始喝，喝醉了。隨後他便沉沉睡去。

passages.text: Olorun saw this. Then Olorun summoned Odudua and said to him: "Thy (elder) brother has got drunken on his way down below. Go thou, take the sand and the hen with five fingers and make the earth upon Okun." Odudua went. He took the sand. He went down and laid it on the sea. He put the hen with five fingers on it. The hen began to scratch and spread the sand about and forced the water aside. Ilife was the spot where this took place, round which, at first, the sea still flowed. Odudua ruled the land of Ilife as its first king. The sea of Olokun grew less and less and ran away through a small hole from there, a hole from which to this day one can fetch the holy water — much water and it never fails. It is called Osha. Now, Orisha was very wrath that he had not created the earth; he began to wage war against Odudua. They contended for a long time, but then made peace. They both went underground and were never seen again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧羅倫見此情景。於是奧羅倫召來奧杜杜瓦，對他說：「你的（兄長）在下去下界途中喝醉了。你去吧，帶上沙子和那隻五爪母雞，在奧昆之上造出大地。」奧杜杜瓦去了。他取了沙子。他下去，把沙鋪在海面上。他把那隻五爪母雞放在沙上。母雞開始刨抓，把沙子四處扒開，並把水逼到一旁。伊費便是此事發生之地，起初海水仍環繞其四周流淌。奧杜杜瓦作為首位國王統治伊費之地。奧洛昆之海漸漸退去，從那裡的一個小孔流走，那孔至今仍可取到聖水——水多而不竭。它被稱為奧沙。此時，奧里沙因自己未曾造出大地而大為震怒；他開始向奧杜杜瓦開戰。他們爭鬥了許久，但後來講和。二人皆入地下，自此再未被人見到。

title.en: The Mirror of Awo-Aje, and the Stone Brothers of Ife
title.zh: 埃沃-阿傑之鏡與伊費石像兄弟

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the stones worshipped where the two workers finished their labours)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（二神完工化石受祭之地）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XIII

summary.en: In the second version, Olorun sent down Oshalla with a ball of sand: "Spread this out upon the face of the waters." Oshalla picked up a flask of palm-wine on the road and drank whenever he was athirst, until he grew weary, went to sleep and forgot his errand. Then the other Orishas took a mirror (Awo-aje), looked into it, and saw him drinking down below, asleep; whereupon Olorun sent Odudua, a strong man, who made the earth and pushed the water aside, and to him Olorun gave the five-fingered hen that pushed the water back so that it became the sea. When the two had finished their work they went into the earth at Ife where they had begun their labours, and were turned to stone; since then men have worshipped those stones — and Odudua is so greatly feared that before anyone in Ife may speak his name, a sheep must be slain and its blood drunk.
summary.zh: 第二版本中，奧洛倫遣奧夏拉攜一團沙下凡：「把沙鋪在水面上。」他在路上拾得一瓶棕櫚酒，渴即痛飲，倦極入睡，竟忘了神命。諸神取出「埃沃-阿傑」之鏡照看，見他在下界飲酒酣眠、有負所託。奧洛倫於是改派壯士奧杜杜瓦——他造陸退水，又獲五趾母雞把水推回成海。功成之後，二人走進伊費他們始工之地，化作石頭；世人自此拜石為神。奧杜杜瓦威嚴可畏——伊費人欲提其名，必先宰羊飲血。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; second Ife creation version (Frobenius 1910-12). The name-taboo (sheep sacrifice before speaking Odudua's name) is an etiological custom detail. Cross-ref: yoruba-oduduwa-sand-hen.

passages.text: In the beginning the earth was not. There was only water. Olorun sent down Oshalla. He gave him a ball of sand on his way. He said: "Spread this out upon the face of the waters." Oshalla went. On the road Oshalla picked up a flask of palm-wine. He tasted it and said: "This is good." He drank while going. Whenever he was a-thirst he drank a mouthful. Then he grew weary, went to sleep and forgot what Olorun had bidden him. Then the other Orishas took a mirror (Awo-aje), looked into it and saw that Oshalla had been drinking down below, gone to sleep and forgotten Olorun's behest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 起初並沒有大地。只有水。奧羅倫遣下奧沙拉。他在途中給了他一團沙子。他說：「把這鋪在水面上。」奧沙拉去了。路上奧沙拉撿到一瓶棕櫚酒。他嘗了嘗，說：「這很好。」他一邊走一邊喝。每逢口渴，他便喝上一口。後來他疲倦了，便睡著了，忘了奧羅倫吩咐他的事。於是其餘的奧里沙取來一面鏡子（阿沃-阿傑），往裡一看，便見奧沙拉在下界飲酒、睡著了，忘了奧羅倫的吩咐。

passages.text: Thereupon Olorun sent Odudua, saying: "Do thou what I told Oshalla to do." Odudua was a strong man. He took a ball of earth with him. He descended. He made the earth and pushed the water aside. Olorun then gave Odudua a hen, called Adje-alesse-mahun; it was a hen with five fingers; it pushed the water back so that it became the sea. When Odudua and Oshalla had finished their work, they went into the earth at Ilife where they had begun their labours, and were turned to stone. Since then men worshipped these stones. Odudua is greatly feared. So powerful is this Godhead that before the people in Ife can speak the name of Odudua, they must slay a sheep and drink its blood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是奧羅倫遣下奧杜杜瓦，說：「你去做我吩咐奧沙拉去做的事。」奧杜杜瓦是個強壯的人。他隨身帶了一團泥土。他降了下去。他造出大地，把水推到一旁。奧羅倫隨後給了奧杜杜瓦一隻母雞，名叫阿傑-阿萊塞-馬洪；那是一隻五爪母雞；它把水逼退，水便成了海。奧杜杜瓦與奧沙拉完成工作後，便進入伊費的地下——他們開始勞作之處——化為石頭。自那時起，人們便崇拜這些石頭。奧杜杜瓦極受畏懼。這位神祇如此強大，以致伊費的人們在說出奧杜杜瓦之名以前，必須宰殺一隻羊並飲其血。

title.en: The Island in the Waters: Olorun Founds Ife and Seats the Sixteen
title.zh: 水中之洲——奧洛倫奠伊費、安十六神

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the hill of the three palms, navel of the Yoruba universe)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（三棕之丘——約魯巴宇宙之臍）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XIII

summary.en: In the beginning all was water, but in the middle of it there was an island (Illa-odo), on which the first chieftains wandered, not knowing what they should do. After a long time Olorun came down from the sky and sat in the middle of the island, the other Gods with him: "Edju, sit thou behind me; thou, Shango, in front of me. Ogun, sit thou on my right hand; Obatalla, thou on my left. Ye other Gods, sit round me in a circle." He called the chieftains: "This city shall in future be called Ife. The hill on which I am seated shall bear three palm trees. Better than in any other place the babalawos will here read the Odus. Sixteen Gods have come with me; these will have children, and they shall live around you. Thus will Ife have a great people. But thou, Oni, thou shalt here hold sway and tell the Alafins what is the will of the Gods." Thus arose the city of Ife, wherein of old abode the sixteen Gods — its hill with the three palms the navel of the Yoruban idea of the universe.
summary.zh: 太初遍地是水，唯水中央有一小洲（伊拉-奧多），首批酋長在洲上茫然遊蕩。良久，奧洛倫自天而降，坐於洲心，眾神隨侍：「埃茹，坐我身後；尚戈，坐我身前；奧貢，坐我右手；奧巴塔拉，坐我左手；其餘眾神，環我而坐。」他召酋長們說：「此城今後名為伊費。我所坐之丘將生三株棕櫚。天下巴巴拉奧讀奧杜，無過於此地。隨我而來者十六神；他們將生兒育女，環居爾等四鄰。伊費因此將有偉大之民。而你，奧尼，你當在此掌權，向歷代阿勞芬轉達諸神之旨。」伊費古城由此而立，十六神舊居於此；城中三棕之丘，便是約魯巴宇宙觀的臍心。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; third Ife creation version, told by a priest from Offa (Frobenius 1910-12). The founding charter of Ife as spiritual capital and of the Oni's mediating role. Cross-ref: yoruba-ife-creation (deep record).

passages.text: In the beginning all was water. But in the middle of it there was an island (Illa-odo). The first chieftains wandered about on it, not knowing what they should do. After a long time Olorun came down from the sky. He sat down in the middle of the island. The other gods came with him. Olorun said: "Edju, sit thou behind me; thou, Shango, in front of me. Ogun, sit thou on my right hand; Obatalla, thou on my left. Ye other Gods, sit round me in a circle."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 起初一切都是水。但在水中央有一座島（伊拉-奧多）。最初的酋長們在島上遊蕩，不知該做什麼。過了很久，奧羅倫從天而降。他坐在島的中央。其他神祇隨他而來。奧羅倫說：「埃朱，你坐在我身後；你，尚戈，坐在我前面。奧貢，你坐在我右手邊；奧巴塔拉，你坐在我左手邊。你們其餘的神祇，圍著我坐成一圈。」

passages.text: Olorun called the chieftains and said to them: "Ye see what there is here. Now, mark ye this well. This city shall in future be called Ife. The hill on which I am seated shall bear three palm trees. Better than in any other place the Baba-lawos will here read the Odus. Sixteen Gods have come with me. These will have children and they shall live around you. Thus will Ife have a great people. But thou, Oni, thou shalt here hold sway and tell the Alafins what is the will of the Gods." Olorun departed. Thus arose the city of Ife wherein of old abode the sixteen Gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧羅倫召來酋長們，對他們說：「你們看見這裡有什麼了。現在，你們要好好記住這一點。這座城今後要稱為伊費。我所坐的這座山將長出三棵棕櫚樹。巴巴-拉沃們將在此讀出奧杜，勝過任何其他地方。有十六位神祇隨我而來。他們將有子嗣，這些子嗣將住在你們周圍。如此，伊費將有眾多的人民。但你，奧尼，你將在此掌權，並告訴阿拉芬們什麼是眾神的意旨。」奧羅倫離去了。伊費城便這樣興起，古時十六位神祇曾居於其中。

title.en: The Farm Stone That Made an Oni: Lajamisan the Usurper
title.zh: 田中一石造就奧尼——篡位者拉賈米散

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (Oke-Ado, the coronation hill)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（奧克-阿多加冕丘）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XIII

summary.en: The ancient shaman of Ife, whose statements Frobenius found reliable, said that the Oni stock itself was in the worst case of all: a forbear of the reigning Oni had been a man from the West who one day found a stone upon his farm, announced that it was the Orisha Lajamisan (an Orisha previously unheard of), and turned it into his own Orisha-father. Then the sly dog deposed the Oni one day and had the Oni-mitre put upon his own head on the Oke-Ado, the coronation hill. Tradition adds that this Lajamisan (Rojamisa) later made a clean sweep of his prelates and patriarchs — driving whole families into exile to Oyo, exterminating others to the tiniest babe — and chose the four highest clan offices from his own family, whose leaders were named Igaru, Agoru, Arrote and Djarra.
summary.zh: 伊費的老巫醫（其言最為可靠）說：奧尼一系本身就是篡奪而來——在位奧尼的某位先祖本是西來之人，一日於田中拾得一石，便宣告此乃「拉賈米散」奧里莎（此前從未有人聽過此名），奉為自家祖神。這滑頭傢伙遂於某日廢黜奧尼，在奧克-阿多加冕丘把奧尼法冠戴上自己頭頂。相傳這位拉賈米散（羅賈米散）事後清洗長老貴族——有的舉族放逐奧約，有的斬草除根——並把四大氏族要職盡數授予本族親信：伊加魯、阿戈魯、阿羅特與賈拉。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the dynastic-origins tradition of the Ife Oni line (Frobenius 1910-12), reporting the memory of an usurpation still alive in the province. Extreme violence reported as the recorded tradition states it, non-graphically.

passages.text: The old man said that many of the others made mutual accusations of having stolen their Orishas and were therefore not descendants of the Gods upon whom they alleged dependence; many were not entitled in any way to make a claim to such descent, for in the earlier warlike times everything got mixed. Both the clans of the Orishas Olokun and Odudua scarcely existed any longer, and they lied who called themselves after these Gods. But the Oni stock itself was in the worst case of all: a forbear of the reigning Oni had been a man from the West, who one day found a stone upon his farm, announced that it was the Orisha Lajamisan (an Orisha previously unheard of), and had turned it into his own Orisha-father. Then the sly dog had deposed the Oni one day and had the Oni-mitre put upon his own head on the Oke-Ado (or coronation hill).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那老人說，其餘許多人互相指控對方偷了自己的奧里沙，因此並非他們所聲稱依賴的那些神祇的後裔；許多人根本無權聲稱有這樣的血統，因為在早先好戰的時代，一切都混雜了。奧洛昆與奧杜杜瓦這兩個奧里沙的氏族幾乎已不復存在，而那些以這些神祇之名自稱的人是在說謊。但奧尼一族本身的處境最為糟糕：在位奧尼的一位祖先本是來自西方的人，他有一天在自己的田裡發現一塊石頭，宣稱那是奧里沙拉賈米桑（一個此前聞所未聞的奧里沙），並把它變成了自己的奧里沙之父。隨後這狡猾之徒有一天廢黜了奧尼，並在奧凱-阿多（即加冕山）上把奧尼的冠冕戴到了自己頭上。

passages.text: A former Oni is said, at some very remote period, to have made a pretty clean sweep of his prelates and patriarchs: he had driven entire families into exile — they fled mostly to Ojo — and exterminated others to the tiniest babe. More than that, this particular Oni, obviously desirous of throwing off the superiority of his princes, chose the representatives of the four highest offices out of his own family; the names of these four new clan leaders were given as Igaru, Agoru, Arrote and Djarra, and the same informant said that this Oni's name was Rojamisa. Thus the Ilifian Shaman's statement is verified: an usurper named Lajamisan had once cleared the ground, exterminated his most dangerous opponents and appointed adherents of his own clan. He not only killed the previous Oni, but handed over to the son of the deceased the administration of the central quarter of Ife, whose successor is the ninth Agbafe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說在某個極為久遠的時期，有一位前任奧尼（Oni）曾相當徹底地掃除了他的高級神職人員與宗長：他將整個家族驅逐流放——他們大多逃往奧喬（Ojo）——又將另一些人滅絕至最幼小的嬰兒。不僅如此，這位特定的奧尼顯然有意擺脫其諸侯的優越地位，便從自己的家族中選出四個最高職位的代表；這四位新氏族首領的名字據載為伊加魯（Igaru）、阿戈魯（Agoru）、阿羅特（Arrote）與賈拉（Djarra），而同一名提供消息者說，這位奧尼的名字是羅賈米薩（Rojamisa）。如此一來，伊利費（Ilife）巫師的說法便得到了證實：一位名叫拉賈米桑（Lajamisan）的篡位者曾一度肅清地面、滅絕他最危險的對手，並任命自己氏族的追隨者。他不僅殺害了前任奧尼，還將伊費（Ife）中央區域的行政權交給了死者的兒子，其繼承者即為第九代阿格巴費（Agbafe）。

title.en: The Oyo Folk Who Brought Shango Back to Ife
title.zh: 把尚戈請回伊費的奧約人

region.en: Ile-Ife and Modakeke, Nigeria (the twin-city that fought over Ebolokun)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費與莫達凱凱（爭奪埃博洛貢的雙子城）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XIII

summary.en: The Oyo clan who settled at Modakeke beside Ife — paying their taxes, significantly, not to the Oni who gave them hospitality but to the Alafin — brought Shango, who had been driven forth from Ife, back again, and many Ilifians resumed their ancient Shango-worship. When the Modekans asked leave to hold a great festival for Shango in Ife itself, the Oni refused; families migrated, war broke out, and after years of struggle the Modekans seized Ebolokun, source of Ife's wealth. Then a babalawo in Ife prophesied that the Ilifians would be freed from the evil spirits called Modekans by white people — thought at first to be the Fulbe — and the peace of 1886 restored the city to the Ilifians, who took back from the departing Modekans all the beads they had found in the sacred soil.
summary.zh: 定居伊費西郊莫達凱凱的奧約人——所納賦稅不交收留他們的奧尼，而交奧約的阿勞芬——把曾被驅離伊費的尚戈請了回來，許多伊費人重拾舊日尚戈之祭。莫達凱凱人請求在伊費城內舉行尚戈大典，奧尼不允；民戶出走，兵戎相見。連年爭戰之後，莫達凱凱人奪取伊費財源埃博洛貢。其時伊費有位巴巴拉奧預言：將有「白人」為伊費人驅逐名為莫達凱凱的惡靈——起初眾人以為是富爾貝人。1886年的和約把聖城還給伊費人；莫達凱凱人遷走時，伊費人收回了他們在聖土中掘得的所有珠子。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the Ife-Modakeke conflict tradition recorded 1910-12, before the town's destruction in the 1882 war and its 1886 restoration (also reported by Ellis 1894). Cross-ref: yoruba-ife-creation.

passages.text: A complete revolution took place in the condition of Ilifian affairs when the strange neighbours from Oyo put in an appearance. They paid their rates and taxes — and this is significant — not to the head of Ilife, who gave them hospitality, but to the chief magistrate of Ojo, whom they to the last looked upon as their head. My old Ada-ushe friend said: "The Ojo-folk brought Shango, who had been driven forth from Ilife, back again." They therefore brought their influence to bear on essentially internal religious affairs, and many Ilifians resumed their ancient Shango-worship.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當來自奧約（Oyo）的奇特鄰人現身時，伊利費的事務狀況發生了一場徹底的變革。他們繳納自己的稅款與規費——而這一點意義重大——並非繳給給予他們款待的伊利費首領，而是繳給奧喬的首席行政官，他們直到最後都視此人為自己的首領。我那位年邁的阿達烏謝（Ada-ushe）朋友說：「奧喬人把曾被逐出伊利費的尚戈（Shango）又帶了回來。」因此，他們將自己的影響力施加於本質上屬於內部的宗教事務，而許多伊利費人恢復了古老的尚戈崇拜。

passages.text: The Modekans one day asked for leave to solemnize a great festival in honour of Shango in Ilife itself. The Oni and his counsellors refused to grant it. In the result a great number of Ilife families migrated to Modeke. This started the quarrel: the prelates declared that the Modekans were to depart from the city precincts; the Ilifians wanted to bring back their escaping citizens by force of arms, and war broke out. The Modekans got the worst of it, but the Oni and his people entrenched themselves within the palace walls, preserved from extermination by a certain reverential awe felt by the victors for the Holy One and the sanctity of his fastness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 莫德坎人（Modekans）有一天請求准許在伊利費本地為尚戈舉行一場盛大的節慶。奧尼及其顧問拒絕批准。結果，大量伊利費家族遷往莫德凱（Modeke）。這引發了爭端：高級神職人員宣稱莫德坎人必須離開城邑範圍；伊利費人則想以武力帶回他們出逃的公民，於是戰爭爆發。莫德坎人吃了敗仗，但奧尼及其人民退守宮牆之內，因勝利者對聖者及其堡壘之神聖性所懷的某種敬畏之情而免於滅絕。

passages.text: A peace as unsound as possible was concluded; but now the Modekans cast an eye at the source of Ilife's wealth, Ebolokun, and in the second period of dissensions they seized it — it is they who are said to have driven most of the pits which have torn up its soil. The Ilifians never again dug there after that, but when they drove them away took from the Modekans all the beads they had found during their occupation of Ebolokun. At that time a Baba-lawo in Ilife is reported to have prophesied that the Ilifians would be freed from the evil spirits, called Modekans, by white people; it was then thought that these were the Fulbes. They now say, "We were wrong, they are the Europeans (English)." The good offices of the Governor of Lagos ended in the conclusion of peace in 1886; the protocol insisted especially on Ilife's restoration to the Ilifians.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIII (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 雙方締結了一項再不可靠不過的和平；但此時莫德坎人將目光投向了伊利費的財富之源埃博洛昆（Ebolokun），並在第二階段的紛爭中奪取了它——據說正是他們開鑿了那些撕裂其土壤的大多數坑洞。此後伊利費人再未在那裡挖掘，但當他們將莫德坎人趕走時，奪走了莫德坎人在佔據埃博洛昆期間所發現的全部貝珠。據報當時伊利費的一位巴巴拉沃（Baba-lawo）曾預言，伊利費人將由白人從被稱為莫德坎人的惡靈手中解救出來；當時人們以為這些白人就是富拉尼人（Fulbes）。他們如今說：「我們錯了，他們是歐洲人（英格蘭人）。」拉各斯總督的斡旋促成了1886年和平的締結；該議定書特別堅持將伊利費歸還給伊利費人。

title.en: Kobo Daishi, the Wonder-Working Saint
title.zh: 弘法大師的神蹟

region.en: Mount Koya, where the saint's miracles centre
region.zh: 高野山

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: The life-cycle of Japan's greatest Buddhist saint: a miraculous birth amid shining light, marvels of calligraphy and magic in China, a return home capped by miracles over water, dead and barren mountain, and a compact with the fox-god Inari; even after burial at Koya he rises from his grave to conduct a dead emperor's funeral rites.
summary.zh: 弘法大師（空海）傳說一生：降生放光、赴唐習法顯神通、歸國後令荒山開花、與稻荷神結盟，死後猶自墳中起而主持天皇葬儀。

sensitivity.note: Hagiographic saint legend of Kobu Daishi (Kukai), founder of Shingon Buddhism, still venerated in living Japanese Buddhism; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The most holy and famous of Japan's Buddhist saints was born in the Baron's Hall by the shore of Byobu in the year 774. At his birth a bright light shone, and the child came into the world with his hands folded as if in prayer. At five years old he sat among the lotuses and conversed with Buddhas, keeping secret the wisdom he gained. On Mount Shashin he tried to sacrifice his own life as an act of propitiation, but angels prevented him until he had fulfilled his destiny. Once, playing at building a clay pagoda, he was surrounded at once by the Four Heavenly Kings; the Imperial Messenger who passed by declared the boy 'a divine prodigy.' At Muroto in Tosa, while he performed his devotions, a bright star fell from heaven into his mouth, and at midnight an evil dragon came against him, but he spat upon it and killed it with his saliva.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 日本佛教諸聖中最神聖、最著名的一位，於774年誕生於屏風海濱的男爵廳。他出生時一道明亮的光芒照耀，這孩子降生於世時雙手合十，宛如祈禱。五歲時，他坐在蓮花之間與諸佛交談，並將所獲的智慧秘而不宣。在沙心山（Shashin）上，他試圖犧牲自己的生命作為贖罪之舉，但天使們阻止了他，直到他完成自己的天命。有一次，他玩耍著建造一座泥塔時，四天王立刻環繞在他四周；路過的敕使宣稱這男孩是「神童」。在土佐的室戶（Muroto），當他修行禮拜時，一顆明亮的星從天而降落入他口中，午夜時分一條惡龍前來攻擊他，但他向它吐唾沫，以唾液將其殺死。

passages.text: In his nineteenth year he took the black robes of a priest. Reading an abstruse book of Shingon doctrine he could not master, he asked and received the Emperor's leave to visit China, where he unravelled its mysteries and attained miraculous saintship. The Chinese Emperor, hearing his fame, bade him rewrite the faded name of a palace room; he did it with a brush in each hand, another in his mouth and two between his toes, earning the name Gohitsu-Osho, 'the Priest who writes with Five Brushes.' Once he flung his brush into the air above a palace gate and the brush made the missing dot and returned to his hand. Leaving China, he threw his thunder-bolt vajra across the ocean waves, and it was afterwards found hanging on a pine at Takano in Japan. On the Naked Mountain he offered incantations so powerful that the barren slopes broke into flowers and trees. He made brackish water pure, raised the dead, and on Mount Fushime the rice-god Inari appeared and accepted his sacrifice; 'Together, you and I,' said Kobo Daishi, 'we will protect this people.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 十九歲那年，他披上了僧侶的黑色法衣。他閱讀一部深奧的真言宗（Shingon）教義典籍而無法通曉，便請求並獲得了天皇的許可前往中國，在那裡他解開了其中的奧秘，並達到了奇蹟般的聖者境界。中國皇帝聽聞他的名聲，命他重寫宮殿一室中褪色的匾額名；他雙手各執一筆，口中銜一筆，腳趾間夾兩筆，一揮而就，因而贏得了「五筆和尚」（Gohitsu-Osho）之名，意即「以五筆書寫的僧人」。有一次，他將毛筆拋向宮門上空，毛筆補上了缺失的一點，然後回到他手中。離開中國時，他將自己的雷電金剛杵擲過海濤，後來人們發現它懸掛在日本高野（Takano）的一棵松樹上。在裸山（Naked Mountain）上，他獻上的咒語如此強大，以致荒蕪的山坡綻放出花木。他使鹹水變為潔淨，使死者復生，並在伏見山（Fushime）上，稻荷神（Inari）顯現並接受了他的獻祭；「你與我，」弘法大師（Kobo Daishi）說道，「將共同守護此民。」

passages.text: The saint died in 834 and was buried in the graveyard of Okunoin at Koya, and lay and priestly mourners wept there. But his miracles did not cease: when Emperor Saga died, his coffin was mysteriously borne through the air to Koya, and Kobo Daishi himself came forth from his grave to perform the funeral obsequies. Emperor Uda received the sacred baptism from him, and when the Imperial Messenger to his temple could not see the saint's face, Kobo guided the worshipper's hand until it touched the saint's knee — a touch the Messenger never forgot. At Kawasaki a temple stands over an image of the saint which he carved of himself while in China and committed to the waves; a fisherman's net caught it, and the trees in the temple grounds, trained like junks under sail, attest the devotion of seafaring folk.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這位聖人於八三四年圓寂，葬於高野山奧之院的墓園，僧俗弔喪者皆在此哭泣。然而他的奇蹟並未止息：嵯峨天皇駕崩時，其棺槨竟神秘地凌空運至高野山，而弘法大師親自自墓中現身，為之主持葬儀。宇多天皇曾從他受神聖灌頂；當朝廷派往其寺的敕使無法得見聖人之面時，弘法大師引導這位禮拜者的手，直到觸及聖人的膝蓋——這一觸，敕使終生難忘。川崎有一座寺院，供奉著聖人親手自刻的自身像，那是他在中國時所雕，並投入波濤之中；一張漁網將其撈起，而寺境內狀如揚帆船隻的樹木，見證了航海之人的虔誠。

title.en: Nichiren and the Sword that Broke
title.zh: 日蓮與斷劍奇蹟

region.en: Beach of Koshigoye, Kamakura
region.zh: 鎌倉小町濱處刑地

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: The iconoclast founder of the Nichiren sect, who foretold the Mongol invasion and attacked the other Buddhist sects, is sent to be beheaded at Kamakura; his executioner's sword shatters against his praying neck, lightning strikes the shogun's palace, and a rider with a pardon meets the reprieve-messenger at the ford still called the Place of Meeting.
summary.zh: 日蓮預言蒙古入侵、攻擊諸宗，被判斬首。臨刑念佛，劍觸頸即斷，閃電擊中鎌倉宮殿，天光護體；赦使與劊子手使者於今猶稱「相逢川」之渡口相遇。

sensitivity.note: Hagiographic legend of Nichiren (1222–1282), founder of a living Buddhist school; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Nichiren, whose name means Sun Lotus and who was so named because his mother dreamt the sun rested on a lotus when she conceived him, was an iconoclast. Seeing earthquake, hurricane, pestilence and famine ravage Japan, he read in them the hand of Fate rebelling against corrupt religion and politics. The priests had neglected Shaka Muni, the Buddha himself, to worship Amida and Kwannon instead; no one can serve two masters, he cried — no man has two fathers, no sky holds two suns, no country two kings. He sought to replace the mantra Namu Amida Butsu with Namu Myoho Renge Kyo, 'Oh, the Scripture of the Lotus of the Wonderful Law!', and in his Rissho An-Koku Ron he predicted the Mongol invasion and flung bitter attacks at the rival sects.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 日蓮，其名意為「日蓮」，因母親懷他時夢見太陽停駐於蓮花之上而得名，他是一位破除偶像者。目睹地震、颶風、瘟疫與饑荒肆虐日本，他從中讀出命運之手對腐敗宗教與政治的撻伐。僧侶們冷落了佛陀釋迦牟尼本身，轉而崇拜阿彌陀與觀音；他疾呼：無人能事二主——無人能有二父，無天能容二日，無國能容二王。他試圖以「南無妙法蓮華經」取代「南無阿彌陀佛」的咒語，意即「噢，妙法蓮華經！」，並在其《立正安國論》中預言蒙古入侵，且對敵對諸宗發起猛烈抨擊。

passages.text: Hojo Tokiyori exiled him to Ito; he escaped and renewed his attacks, and the Regent Tokimune condemned him to be beheaded on the beach of Koshigoye. As he waited for the stroke, Nichiren prayed to Buddha, and the sword broke as it touched his neck. Immediately a flash of lightning struck the palace at Kamakura and a heavenly light surrounded the saint. The awed executioner sent to the Regent for a reprieve, but Tokimune's own horseman bearing a pardon met him at a river now called Yukiai, the Place of Meeting. Nichiren's escape was followed by renewed attacks and a second exile; he took up his abode on Mount Minobu, where a beautiful woman came while he prayed. 'Resume your natural state,' he said; after drinking water she changed into a snake nearly twenty feet long, with iron teeth and golden scales.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 北條時賴將他流放至伊東；他逃脫後再度發起抨擊，而執權時宗判他在腰越海灘斬首。當他等待刀落之際，日蓮向佛祈禱，刀觸其頸即斷裂。霎時一道閃電擊中鎌倉的宮殿，天光環繞聖人。驚懼的劊子手向執權請求暫緩行刑，但時宗自派的赦免騎手卻在一條今名「行合」（相遇之地）的河邊與他相遇。日蓮逃脫之後，抨擊再起，並遭第二次流放；他定居於身延山，當他祈禱時，一位美麗女子前來。「恢復你的本來面目吧，」他說；飲水之後，她化作一條近二十英尺長、鐵牙金鱗的蛇。

title.en: The Crackling Mountain: Hare and Badger
title.zh: 喀啦山：白兔與狸

region.en: An old couple's cottage and a wood-cutting mountain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 老夫婦的山居與伐木山（象徵釘）

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: A badger freed from his rope kills an old woman, serves her boiled flesh as broth to her husband, and is hunted down by the faithful white hare — burnt on the Crackling Mountain, salted with cayenne, and drowned at last in his clay boat on the way to the moon.
summary.zh: 狸被釋後殺老嫗、煮其肉為湯騙老翁吃下；白兔為主復仇，於喀啦山燒其背、敷辣椒，終以泥舟沉溺之法處死惡狸，忠兔得主人厚待。

sensitivity.note: Japanese animal folktale of the hare-and-badger cycle, with grim anthropophagic imagery; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: An old man and his wife kept a white hare. One day a badger came and ate the pet's food; the old man caught him and tied him to a tree before leaving to cut wood. The badger wept until the old woman untied the rope, then proclaimed vengeance and ran away. When the white hare heard, he set out to warn his master; in his absence the badger returned, killed the old woman, assumed her form, and converted her corpse into broth. 'I have made such excellent broth,' he told the returning husband, 'sit down and make a good meal!' The old man ate and pronounced it excellent — 'Excellent?' sneered the badger. 'You have eaten your wife! Her bones lie in that corner,' and he disappeared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位老人與妻子養了一隻白兔。一天，一隻獾前來吃掉了這寵物的食物；老人捉住牠，將牠綁在樹上，便去砍柴了。獾哭泣不止，直到老婦解開繩索，牠隨即宣稱要報仇，然後逃走了。白兔聽聞後，便動身去警告主人；趁牠不在時，獾返回，殺死老婦，化作她的形貌，並將她的屍體煮成湯。「我煮了如此鮮美的湯，」牠對歸來的丈夫說，「坐下來好好吃一頓吧！」老人吃了，並讚其鮮美——「鮮美？」獾冷笑著說。「你吃的是你的妻子！她的骨頭就躺在那個角落裡，」說罷便消失了。

passages.text: The hare returned, grasped the situation, and scampered to the mountain resolved on vengeance. Creeping behind the badger, who carried a bundle of sticks, he set them alight so they crackled. 'What is this strange noise?' asked the badger. 'The Crackling Mountain,' replied the hare. The burning badger sprang into a river, but his scorched back was then treated by the delighted hare to a cayenne poultice. Later the hare invited the badger to sail to the moon in his boat; refusing, the badger built a boat of clay. Down the river went the wooden boat and the crumbling clay boat, and when the badger's vessel came to pieces the hare laughed derisively and killed his enemy with his oar. The loyal animal received much praise and loving care from his grateful master.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 白兔歸來，明白了一切，便奔上山去，決心報仇。牠悄悄跟在背著一捆柴的獾身後，點燃了柴火，使其劈啪作響。「這是什麼怪聲？」獾問道。「是劈啪山，」白兔答道。著火的獾跳入河中，但牠燒焦的背隨即被欣喜的白兔敷上辣椒糊。後來，白兔邀獾乘牠的船航向月亮；獾拒絕了，並造了一艘泥船。木船與崩解的泥船順流而下，當獾的船碎裂時，白兔嘲弄地大笑，並以槳殺死了牠的仇敵。這忠誠的動物受到感激的主人諸多讚賞與疼愛。

title.en: The Miraculous Tea-Kettle of Morinji
title.zh: 分福茶釜——茂林寺寶壺

region.en: Morinji temple and a tinker's house (symbolic pin: Tatebayashi)
region.zh: 茂林寺與補鍋匠之家（象徵釘：館林）

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: A priest's old tea-kettle grows the head, tail and legs of a badger and dances wildly until boxed; sold to a tinker, it becomes a tight-rope-dancing fortune that draws princes and princesses and amasses riches, and is finally restored to Morinji temple to be worshipped as a precious treasure.
summary.zh: 僧人舊茶壺入火即長出狸之首尾四肢，飛舞於室；賣與補鍋匠後能歌舞走索，王侯爭看，匠人大富，最後將壺奉還茂林寺，供為寶物。

sensitivity.note: Japanese folktale of the bunbuku-chagama badger-kettle cycle; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: A priest of Morinji temple set his old tea-kettle on the fire to make tea, and no sooner had it touched the fire than it changed into the head, tail and legs of a badger. The novices were called to see the sight: the badger with the body of a kettle rushed nimbly about the room, flew into the air and circled it again and again until the priests captured it and thrust it into a box. A tinker then called at the temple; the priest, thinking it a fine idea to sell his extraordinary kettle, bargained until the unsuspecting man bought it and took it away, assured he had done a good day's work.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 茂林寺的一位僧人將他的舊茶釜置於火上煮茶，茶釜一觸火，便化作獾的頭、尾與腿。見習僧們被喚來觀看這景象：這隻有著茶釜身軀的獾在室內敏捷地奔竄，飛入空中，一圈又一圈地盤旋，直到僧人們將牠捉住，塞進一隻箱子裡。隨後，一名補鍋匠來到寺中；僧人覺得賣掉這隻奇異的茶釜是個好主意，便討價還價，直到那毫不知情的男子買下並帶走，確信自己這一天收穫頗豐。

passages.text: That night the tinker was awakened by a sound close to his pillow: the kettle he had bought was not a kettle at all but a lively and clever badger. His friends advised him to take the animal on show, for it could dance and walk the tight-rope. The fame of the performing badger spread far and wide; princes and princesses came to see it, and from royal patronage and the delight of the people the tinker amassed a great fortune. When he had made his money he restored the kettle to Morinji temple, where it was worshipped as a precious treasure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那天夜裡，補鍋匠被枕邊一陣聲響驚醒：他買下的那隻茶釜根本不是茶釜，而是一隻活潑機靈的狸。朋友們勸他帶這隻動物去展演，因為牠會跳舞，還會走繩索。這隻會表演的狸名聲遠播四方；王子與公主都前來觀看，靠著王室的賞識與百姓的喜愛，補鍋匠積攢了偌大的財富。賺得錢財之後，他將茶釜歸還茂林寺，寺中把它當作珍貴的寶物供奉。

title.en: The Vampire Cat and the Lady O Toyo
title.zh: 貓妖與愛妾阿豐

region.en: The Prince of Hizen's palace, Hizen province
region.zh: 肥前國諸侯宮邸

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: A great cat strangles the favourite lady O Toyo, buries her, and takes her form; the Prince wastes nightly until the lowly soldier Ito Soda keeps a self-wounding vigil against the enchanted drowsiness, forces the cat to reveal itself, and the hunted beast is slain in the mountains.
summary.zh: 大貓扼死愛妾阿豐，埋屍於廊下，化其形貌。藩主夜夜衰弱，百名侍衛十時即睡。足輕伊藤守多忍痛以短刀刺股驅睡，兩夜逼退貓妖，並率八人搜殺；貓中箭遁走山中，終於狩獵中被誅。
