sensitivity.note: Japanese vampire-cat legend of the Nabeshima clan cycle; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Prince of Hizen lingered in the garden with O Toyo, the favourite among his ladies, unaware that a large cat followed them into the palace. At midnight O Toyo awoke to a dreadful presence: a gigantic cat crouched beside her, sprang upon her and strangled her. The animal made a hole under the verandah, buried the corpse, and assumed the form of the beautiful O Toyo. The Prince, unknowing, caressed a foul beast and grew dangerously ill, suffering most at night and troubled by horrible dreams; the hundred retainers set to watch him fell every night into a mysterious drowsiness at ten o'clock, and even three loyal councillors had the same experience.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 肥前藩主與他最寵愛的侍女阿豐在庭園中流連，渾然不知一隻大貓跟著他們進了宮殿。午夜時分，阿豐醒來，察覺到一股可怕的氣息：一隻巨大的貓蹲伏在她身旁，猛然撲上她，將她勒死。那畜生在看臺下挖了個洞，埋了屍體，然後化作美麗的阿豐的模樣。藩主毫不知情，撫愛著一頭邪惡的妖獸，身體日益病重，夜裡最為難受，還被可怕的夢境所擾；奉命看守他的一百名侍從，每晚十點都陷入一種莫名的昏睡，甚至連三位忠心的家老也有同樣的遭遇。

passages.text: A priest named Ruiten, appointed to pray for the Prince, noticed a young soldier washing himself before an image of Buddha and praying for his lord's recovery. 'I am Ito Soda of the infantry of Nabeshima,' the man said, 'the Prince is bewitched, and if I might remain with him I would find and crush the evil power.' Admitted to the watch, Soda spread oil-paper on the mats and stuck his dirk into his thigh, twisting the knife as drowsiness returned; blood dripped steadily while the sliding doors opened and the false O Toyo crept in, smiled at the sleepers, and was always frustrated by the dauntless eyes of the watcher until she retired. The Prince at last slept peacefully and began to recover.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位名叫龍天（Ruiten）的僧人奉命為藩主祈禱，他注意到一名年輕武士在佛像前淨身，祈求主君康復。「我是鍋島步兵隊的伊藤宗太（Ito Soda），」那人說道，「藩主中了妖術，若能讓我留在他身邊，我定要找出並粉碎那邪惡的力量。」獲准加入守夜之後，宗太在榻榻米上鋪了油紙，將短刀刺入自己的大腿，趁睡意再度襲來時轉動刀鋒；鮮血不斷滴落，拉門開啟，假阿豐悄悄潛入，對沉睡者微笑，卻總是被守夜者無畏的目光所阻，只得退去。藩主終於安然入睡，身體也開始好轉。

passages.text: Soda planned to kill the creature in her own room, with eight retainers waiting outside. Posing as a messenger with a letter, he drew his dirk; the false O Toyo seized a halberd and blow answered blow until, seeing flight was better than battle, she threw away her weapon and in a moment the lovely maiden turned into a cat and sprang to the roof. The eight men shot at it but it escaped, made for the mountains and troubled the neighbourhood until it was killed during a hunt ordered by the Prince of Hizen. The Prince became well again, and Ito Soda received the honour and reward he so richly deserved.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 宗太打算在那妖怪自己的房裡將她殺死，並讓八名侍從在外等候。他假扮成送信的使者，拔出短刀；假阿豐抓起一柄長戟，一擊還一擊，直到她發覺逃走勝過交戰，便丟下武器，轉眼間那美麗的少女化作一隻貓，躍上屋頂。八人朝牠射箭，牠卻逃脫了，奔向山中，擾害鄰里，直到肥前藩主下令狩獵，才將牠殺死。藩主恢復了健康，伊藤宗太也得到了他理應享有的榮譽與獎賞。

title.en: The Old Man Who Made the Trees to Blossom
title.zh: 花咲爺——讓枯樹開花的老人

region.en: An old couple's cottage and a buried pine (symbolic pin: Edo region)
region.zh: 老夫婦茅屋與埋犬之松（象徵釘：江戶地方）

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: A faithful dog leads a kind old couple to buried treasure; killed by greedy neighbours, it returns as a spirit to guide its master to a magic mortar and its ashes that blossom withered trees — while the wicked neighbours, burning the mortar and scattering ashes in a prince's court, are beaten and driven off in disgrace.
summary.zh: 善良老翁的犬掘得金銀，被貪心鄰人借去又殺害埋於松下。犬靈指點：松木做臼舂米成寶；臼被惡鄰焚毀後，犬靈再教其以灰撒枯樹即開花。善翁受賞，惡鄰仿效卻使灰瞎了王子眼，遭痛打而逃。

sensitivity.note: Japanese folktale of the Hanasaka-jiisan cycle; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: An old couple's dog became excited in the garden and sniffed one particular spot of ground; digging there, the old people unearthed gold and silver pieces and precious treasures, which they at once distributed in alms to the poor. The neighbours borrowed the dog and fed it delicacies, but the animal, previously ill-treated by them, refused to eat; where they dug at the sniffed spot they found only refuse. Angry and disappointed, they killed the dog and buried him under a pine-tree. The good old man, full of sorrow, laid food and flowers on the grave, weeping.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一對老夫婦的狗在庭園裡興奮起來，嗅著地上某一處；老夫婦在那裡挖掘，挖出了金銀與珍寶，他們立刻將這些施捨給窮人。鄰居借了那隻狗，餵牠美食，但這隻先前受過他們虐待的狗卻不肯吃；他們在狗嗅過的地方挖掘，只找到些廢棄之物。他們又氣又惱，便殺了那隻狗，埋在松樹下。善良的老人滿懷悲傷，在墳上擺放食物與鮮花，哭泣不已。

passages.text: That night the dog's spirit appeared and said: 'Cut down the tree where I am buried, and from the wood fashion a mortar, and think of me whenever you use it.' Rice ground in the pine mortar turned every grain to treasure. The wicked couple borrowed the mortar too, but for them the rice turned to filth, and in anger they broke and burnt the vessel. The dog's spirit came again: 'Sprinkle the ashes of the mortar over withered trees and they will immediately blossom.' Carrying a basket of ashes, the kind old man journeyed from village to town, and withered trees burst into flower; a prince commanded an exhibition and sent him home loaded with gifts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那天夜裡，狗的魂魄顯現，說道：「砍下埋葬我的那棵樹，用那木頭做一個臼，每次使用它時就想著我。」用那松木臼磨出的米，每一粒都化為珍寶。那對惡夫婦也借了臼去，但對他們而言，米卻化成了穢物，他們一怒之下砸毀並燒掉了那器具。狗的魂魄再度前來：「把臼的灰燼撒在枯樹上，它們便會立刻開花。」善良的老人提著一籃灰燼，從村莊一路走到城鎮，枯樹紛紛綻放花朵；一位親王下令舉辦展覽，並送他滿載禮物而歸。

passages.text: The neighbours gathered the remaining ashes and the greedy fellow went about claiming to revive dead trees. Summoned before the prince, he climbed into a tree and scattered the ashes, but the tree stayed withered and the flying ashes nearly blinded and suffocated the prince; the impostor was almost beaten to death and slunk away in misery. The kind old couple rebuked their neighbours for their wickedness, allowed them to share their wealth, and the once mean and crafty couple led good and virtuous lives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 鄰人收集了剩下的灰燼，那貪心的人便四處宣稱自己能讓枯死的樹木復活。他被召到王子面前，爬上樹去撒灰，但那棵樹依然枯萎，飛揚的灰燼幾乎使王子雙目失明、窒息；這騙子幾乎被打死，狼狽地溜走了。善良的老夫婦責備鄰人的惡行，卻仍允許他們分享自己的財富，那對原本刻薄狡詐的夫婦從此過著善良而有德的生活。

title.en: The Jellyfish and the Monkey
title.zh: 水母與猿——龍宮失肝記

region.en: Rin-Jin's palace beneath the sea; an island offshore (symbolic pin: Tango coast)
region.zh: 龍王海底宮殿與海上小島（象徵釘：丹後海岸）

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: The Dragon Queen will be cured only by a live monkey's liver; the jellyfish flatters a monkey into riding to the Dragon Palace, blunders out the true purpose, is outwitted by the tale of spare livers hanging on a pine, and returns empty — whereupon the enraged Sea King beats him until he loses his shell forever.
summary.zh: 龍后垂危，唯活猿之肝可救。水母奉命誘猿騎背入海，途中說漏真情；猿託詞松樹上掛著備用肝臟，騙水母載其回島，一躍而逃。龍王大怒，下令把水母打得骨頭不剩，水母從此失殼，子孫皆為軟體。

sensitivity.note: Japanese sea-king etiological folktale; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Rin-Jin, King of the Sea, had taken to wife a beautiful Dragon Princess, and when she fell ill no physician availed. 'If I eat the liver of a live monkey I shall recover,' sobbed the Queen. So Rin-Jin called the jellyfish and told him to swim to the land and return with a live monkey, telling him of the wonders of the deep — the palace with its floor of pearl and walls of coral. The jellyfish found a fine-looking monkey playing in a pine and sang the praises of the Kingdom of the Sea; the monkey accepted the invitation and seated himself comfortably on the thick shell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 海中之王龍神娶了一位美麗的龍公主為妻，當她病倒時，沒有醫生能治好她。「我若吃下活猴的肝，就會痊癒。」王后啜泣著說。於是龍神召來水母，吩咐他游到陸地，帶一頭活猴回來，並向他述說深海之奇——那以珍珠鋪地、珊瑚為牆的宮殿。水母找到一隻正在松樹上嬉戲的漂亮猴子，便歌頌海之國度的種種美妙；猴子接受了邀請，舒舒服服地坐在那厚厚的殼上。

passages.text: Halfway home the foolish jellyfish asked whether the monkey had brought his liver, and blurted out that a doctor would use it to save the sick Queen. The monkey lamented that he had forgotten it — 'I have several livers hanging up on a pine-tree; take me back to the island and I will fetch one.' The credulous jellyfish turned and swam back; the monkey sprang from his back and danced on the branches. 'Liver? You silly old jelly-fish, you'll certainly never get mine!' When the jellyfish told his dismal tale, the Sea King fell into a great passion: 'Beat him to a jelly! Beat this stupid fellow till he hasn't a bone left in his body!' So the jellyfish lost his shell from that hour, and all jellyfishes born after him remain nothing but jelly to this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 回家途中，愚蠢的水母問猴子有沒有帶肝來，還脫口說出醫生要用它來救生病的王后。猴子哀嘆說自己忘了帶——「我有好幾個肝掛在松樹上呢；帶我回島上去，我去取一個來。」輕信的水母便轉身游了回去；猴子從他背上跳下，在枝頭跳起舞來。「肝？你這愚蠢的老水母，你絕對得不到我的肝！」當水母講述了他那悲慘的經過，海王大發雷霆：「把他打成肉醬！把這蠢貨打到身上一根骨頭都不剩！」於是水母從那一刻起就失去了他的殼，而在他之後出生的所有水母，至今仍不過是一團膠質而已。

title.en: The Tongue-cut Sparrow
title.zh: 舌切雀

region.en: An old couple's cottage and the sparrow's home on a mountain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 老嫗洗衫處與雀居深山（象徵釘）

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: A cross neighbour cuts out a pet sparrow's tongue for eating her starch; the kindly owners find the bird feasting and dancing in his mountain home, and choose the light basket that proves an inexhaustible treasure — while the greedy tongue-cutter chooses the heavy basket and is torn to pieces by the devils inside.
summary.zh: 惡鄰老嫗誤雀食其漿糊，剪去雀舌。雀之主人翁媪入山尋雀，受雀家款待；臨別任選輕重二筐，老夫婦選輕筐，得金銀珠寶取之不竭；惡嫗貪選重筐，開之群鬼躍出將其撕碎。

sensitivity.note: Japanese folktale of the Shita-kiri Suzume cycle; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: A cross old woman at her wash-tub found her neighbour's pet sparrow had eaten all the starch, mistaking it for food; in her anger she cut out the sparrow's tongue, and the bird flew away to a mountain. The old couple who owned the sparrow journeyed far until they found their pet again. Delighted, the sparrow begged them into his house, feasted them with fish and sake, had them waited upon by his wife, children and grandchildren, and danced for them the Sparrow's Dance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個脾氣暴躁的老婦人在洗衣盆邊發現鄰居的寵物麻雀把漿糊全吃光了，誤以為那是食物；她一怒之下剪掉了麻雀的舌頭，那鳥兒便飛往山中去了。麻雀的主人老夫婦走了很遠的路，終於又找到了他們的寵物。麻雀歡喜地請他們進屋，以魚和清酒款待他們，讓妻子、兒女和孫輩侍奉他們，並為他們跳了麻雀之舞。

passages.text: When it was time to go home the sparrow brought out two wicker baskets, saying one was heavy and the other light, and asked which they would rather have. Choosing the light one for their age and the long journey, the old couple found on opening it gold, silver, jewels and silk — an inexhaustible supply that made them rich and prosperous. The cruel tongue-cutter hastened to the sparrow, chose the heavy basket hoping for more treasure, and when at last she opened it at home, devils sprang upon her and tore her to pieces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了該回家的時候，麻雀拿出兩個柳條籃子，說一個重、一個輕，問他們想要哪一個。老夫婦因年邁且路途遙遠，選了輕的那個，打開一看，裡面是金、銀、珠寶和絲綢——取之不盡，使他們富足興旺。那殘忍的剪舌婦人急忙趕到麻雀那裡，選了重的籃子，希望能得到更多財寶，而當她終於在家中打開它時，魔鬼撲向她，把她撕成了碎片。

title.en: Sanemori-San and the Cucumber Beetle
title.zh: 實盛蟲與瓜守蟲

region.en: Rice-fields of Izumo
region.zh: 出雲稻田

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: The warrior Sanemori, slain when his horse rolled in a rice-field, becomes the rice-devouring insect Sanemori-San, whom Izumo peasants summon each summer night with fires, flutes, gongs and a straw rider burnt or thrown into water; a guilty physician's angry ghost becomes the shiwan beetle that gnaws cucumbers.
summary.zh: 武者實盛因馬失蹄陷田而被殺，化為食稻之蟲「實盛蟲」。出雲農民夏夜於田中焚火、吹笛擊鑼，呼「實盛大人請來」，並焚或擲稻草騎者於水以驅蟲；又傳犯過的醫師被追殺，腳纏瓜藤而死，怨靈化為食瓜之蟲。

sensitivity.note: Japanese legends of humans transformed into insects, attached to living rites in Izumo; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Sanemori, a great warrior, was fighting on horseback when his horse slipped and rolled into a rice-field; his antagonist seized the chance to slay him, and from that hour Sanemori became a rice-devouring insect known to the peasantry of Izumo as Sanemori-San. On certain summer nights the peasants light fires in their rice-fields to attract the insect, play upon flutes and beat gongs, crying: 'O Sanemori, augustly deign to come hither!' A religious rite is performed, and a straw representation of a rider upon a horse is burnt or thrown into the water, which it is believed will free the fields from the rice-devouring insect.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 勇士實盛騎馬作戰時，他的馬滑倒滾進了稻田；對手趁機殺死了他，從那一刻起，實盛就變成了一種噬食稻穀的蟲子，出雲的農民稱之為「實盛先生」。在某些夏夜，農民會在稻田裡點起火來引誘這種蟲子，吹奏笛子、敲打鑼鼓，喊道：「哦，實盛，請大駕光臨此地！」人們會舉行宗教儀式，焚燒或投入水中一個騎馬者的稻草人像，據信這能使田地免於噬食稻穀的蟲害。

passages.text: The shiwan, a small yellow insect that feeds upon cucumbers, is said to have once been a physician. This physician, guilty of some intrigue, was forced to leave his home; in attempting to escape his foot caught in the sinuous coils of a cucumber vine, and he was killed by his pursuers. His angry ghost became a shiwan, and from that day to this the insect feeds upon cucumbers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: shiwan 是一種以黃瓜為食的黃色小昆蟲，據說牠從前曾是一名醫師。這名醫師因涉入某種陰謀而獲罪，被迫離開家園；他在試圖逃走時，腳被黃瓜藤蜿蜒的捲鬚纏住，因而被追捕者殺死。他滿懷怨怒的亡魂化為 shiwan，自此之後，這種昆蟲便以黃瓜為食。

title.en: Daruma and the Legend of the Tea-Plant
title.zh: 達摩與茶樹之起源

region.en: Lo Yang, China, as retold in Japan (symbolic pin: Kyoto)
region.zh: 中國洛陽（日本傳述；象徵釘：京都）

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: The Indian sage Daruma, son of a Hindu king, meditates nine years facing the temptations of St Anthony until he falls asleep; in penance he cuts off his offending eyelids and casts them to the ground, where they become the first tea-plant — a drink that repels slumber for monks' vigils — and three years after death he walks the western mountains carrying one shoe.
summary.zh: 印度聖者達摩（禪宗初祖）面壁九年，因誦經入夢受魔誘；醒後大愧，自割雙瞼擲地，瞬即化為第一株茶樹，其葉能驅睡魔，供僧侶守夜之用。傳其死後三年有人見其行於中國西山，開棺僅得一履。

sensitivity.note: Buddhist etiological legend of Bodhidharma and the origin of tea; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Daruma was an Indian sage, said to have been the son of a Hindu king and to have received instruction from Panyatara. When his studies were complete he retired to Lo Yang and remained seated in meditation for nine years. During that period he was tempted after the manner of St Anthony; he wrestled against the temptations by reciting sacred scriptures, but the word 'jewel' lost its spiritual meaning and suggested the precious stone in a lovely woman's ear, and even 'lotus' suggested the opening of a girl's fair mouth. The temptation transported him to an Indian city, among strange deities, rajahs and dancing-girls, to a temple covered with foul forms, where it seemed he met and kissed the woman who had changed the meaning of jewel and lotus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIV (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 達摩是一名印度聖者，據說是一位印度教國王的兒子，曾師從潘亞塔拉（Panyatara）受教。學業完成後，他隱居於洛陽，靜坐冥想達九年之久。在那段期間，他受到如聖安東尼那般的誘惑試探；他藉由誦讀神聖經典來對抗誘惑，但「珠寶」一詞卻失去了其靈性意涵，令他聯想到一位美麗女子耳上的寶石，甚至「蓮花」也令他聯想到一位少女美麗嘴唇的綻開。誘惑將他帶往一座印度城市，置身於奇異的神祇、王公與舞女之間，來到一座滿布醜惡形像的廟宇，在那裡他似乎遇見並親吻了那位使「珠寶」與「蓮花」改變意涵的女子。

passages.text: Suddenly the vision departed and Daruma awoke under the Chinese sky, truly penitent for his neglect of devotions. Taking a knife from his girdle he cut off his eyelids and cast them upon the ground, saying: 'O Thou Perfectly Awakened!' The eyelids were transformed into the tea-plant, from whose leaves was made the beverage that repels slumber and allows good Buddhist priests their vigils. Daruma is generally shown without legs, for one version says he lost his limbs through the nine-year meditation; netsuke-carvers depict him scowling, with lidless eyes. Three years after his death he was seen walking across the western mountains of China carrying one shoe in his right hand; when his tomb was opened by order of the Emperor it contained only a shoe, which the saint had forgotten to take with him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIV (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 忽然，幻象消散，達摩在中國的天空下醒來，對自己疏忽了修行而真心懺悔。他從腰帶上取出一把刀，割下自己的眼皮，擲於地上，說道：「噢，您這全然覺悟者！」那雙眼皮化作了茶樹，其葉製成的飲料能驅退睡意，讓虔誠的佛教僧侶得以守夜修行。達摩的塑像通常不現雙腿，因為有一種說法稱他因九年冥想而失去了四肢；根付雕刻家將他刻畫為蹙眉、無眼皮的模樣。他死後三年，有人見他行走於中國西部的山間，右手提著一隻鞋；當皇帝下令開啟他的墳墓時，墓中只有一隻鞋，是那位聖者忘了帶走的。

title.en: Hoichi-the-Earless
title.zh: 無耳芳一

region.en: Amidaji temple and the cemetery of Akamagaseki, Dan-no-ura
region.zh: 赤間關阿彌陀寺與壇之浦墓園

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: The blind biwa-player Hoichi is led nightly by a ghostly samurai to perform the Heike battles before a noble assembly — the Taira dead at their tombs — until his body is covered with sacred texts; the invisible visitor finds only two ears left uncovered and tears them off, and ever after he is called Hoichi-the-Earless.
summary.zh: 盲眼琵琶法師芳一每夜被幽靈武士引去，為平家亡靈誦唱壇之浦之戰。同伴以般若心經遍書其身，唯漏雙耳；夜來者遍尋不見其人，唯見雙耳，遂取以獻主。自此人稱「無耳芳一」。

sensitivity.note: Japanese ghost legend of the Taira dead, adapted from Lafcadio Hearn; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: After the sea-fight of Dan-no-ura, where the Taira perished with their infant Emperor Antoku, the coast was haunted for seven hundred years by their ghosts; mysterious fires shone on the waves and the air was filled with the noise of warfare until the temple of Amidaji was built at Akamagaseki and a cemetery laid out around it. There lived a blind priest named Hoichi, famous for his recitation and his marvellous biwa-playing, above all for the story of the war between the Taira and Minamoto clans.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXV (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在壇之浦海戰中，平氏與其幼帝安德天皇一同覆滅之後，其亡魂在此海岸作祟達七百年之久；海面上閃爍著神祕的火光，空氣中充滿了爭戰的喧囂，直到赤間關建起了阿彌陀寺，並在其周圍闢出一片墓地為止。那裡住著一位名叫芳一的盲眼法師，以誦唱及精湛的琵琶演奏聞名，尤其是關於平氏與源氏兩族之戰的故事。

passages.text: One warm evening a deep voice called 'Hoichi!' from the garden: his lord was staying at Akamagaseki with many noble followers and had heard how excellently the blind man recited the battle of Dan-no-ura. Led by a retainer with an iron grip, past a gate where 'Kaimon!' unbarred the doors, up steps and through rustling screens, Hoichi played to a vast assembly — the strings of his biwa imitating oars, ships, shouting men and whirring arrows — until, chanting of the women and children and of Niidono sinking a thousand fathoms with the infant Emperor in her arms, the company wept and wailed. Commanded to return nightly in secret, he did so; but his fellow priest grew suspicious, and the servants, following with lanterns, found him at the tomb of Antoku Tenno, playing and chanting loudly among mysterious fires like a gathering of lighted candles.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXV (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個溫暖的傍晚，庭園中傳來一個低沉的聲音呼喚：「芳一！」原來是他的主公正留宿於赤間關，隨行有許多高貴的侍從，聽聞這盲人誦唱壇之浦之戰何等精妙。芳一由一名手勁如鐵的家臣引領，經過一道喊聲「開門！」便應聲開啟的門，登上階梯，穿過窸窣作響的屏風，為一大群聽眾演奏——他的琵琶弦音模仿著槳聲、船隻、吶喊的人們與呼嘯的箭矢——直到他唱到婦孺，以及二位尼懷抱幼帝沉入千尋深海之時，滿座聽眾無不哭泣哀號。他被吩咐每夜祕密前來，他也照做了；然而與他同寺的法師起了疑心，僕人們提著燈籠跟隨其後，發現他竟在安德天皇的墓前，於宛如一簇點燃蠟燭般的神祕火光之中，大聲演奏誦唱。

passages.text: 'Your great skill has called forth the ghosts of the Taira,' said the priest; 'you are in great danger.' He had an acolyte inscribe the sutra Hannya-Shin-Kyo upon every part of the blind man's body — breast, head, back, face, neck, arms, legs, even the soles of his feet — and bade him sit silent and still. That night the deep voice called and called, and the invisible visitor at last sprang onto the verandah: 'In place of the player I see only two ears! Those ears I will take to my lord!' Hoichi's ears were torn off, though he remained mute in agony, and thus the priest found him when he returned, with the trickling of blood on the verandah. 'It is all my fault — the acolyte failed to write the sacred texts on your ears.' From that day the blind priest was known as Mimi-nashi-Hoichi, Hoichi-the-Earless.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXV (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「你的高超技藝召來了平氏的亡魂，」法師說道，「你身陷極大的危險。」他命一名侍僧在盲人全身各處——胸、頭、背、臉、頸、臂、腿，甚至腳底——寫下《般若心經》，並囑咐他靜坐不出聲、不動彈。當夜，那低沉的聲音一再呼喚，那看不見的訪客終於躍上緣廊：「代替那演奏者，我只見到兩隻耳朵！我就把這兩隻耳朵帶去獻給我的主公！」芳一的耳朵被扯了下來，他卻在劇痛中默不作聲，法師歸來時便見他這般模樣，緣廊上淌著血跡。「這全是我的過錯——那侍僧忘了把經文寫在你的耳朵上。」自那天起，這盲眼法師便被稱為耳無芳一，即「無耳芳一」。

title.en: The Corpse-Eater of Mino
title.zh: 食屍鬼——美濃僧窟

region.en: A hermitage and hamlet in the province of Mino
region.zh: 美濃國草庵與村落

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: Lost in Mino, the priest Muso Kokushi is refused shelter by a churlish recluse but welcomed by a village where the corpse must be left alone; at night a terrible Shape devours the body and the offerings, and the rude hermit is unmasked as a jikininki — a greedy priest reborn as a man-eating goblin — whose hermitage then vanishes beside a moss-covered tomb.
summary.zh: 雪巷國師夜宿美濃山中草庵被拒，投宿村中恰逢喪事，眾人依俗離去，唯留僧守屍。夜半怪形現身食屍兼吞祭品。翌日村民言山上並無庵堂；僧再訪，老僧自認為食屍鬼（生前貪法衣之利而墮此報），言畢連庵俱滅，唯餘青苔古墓。

sensitivity.note: Japanese goblin legend adapted from Lafcadio Hearn; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Muso Kokushi, a priest, lost his way in the province of Mino and despaired of finding shelter till he came upon a little hermitage called anjitsu. The aged priest there greeted him churlishly: 'I never give shelter to any one. In yonder valley you will find a hamlet; seek a night's repose there.' At the headman's dwelling Muso was hospitably received, only to learn that the father of the house had died and that, by the custom of the village, all must go away at night because strange and terrible things happen to corpses when they are left alone — perhaps a priest would not be afraid to remain. Muso answered he was in no way afraid and performed the funeral service, keeping his solitary vigil.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXV (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 夢窓国師是一位僧人，在美濃國迷了路，正絕望於找不到棲身之處時，來到一間名為庵室的小茅廬。那裡的老僧粗魯地招呼他：「我從不留宿任何人。你在那邊的山谷裡會找到一個小村落；去那裡求一夜安歇吧。」在村長家中，夢窓受到殷勤款待，卻得知這家的父親已經去世，而按照村中習俗，所有人夜裡都必須離開，因為屍體若被獨自留下，便會發生怪異而可怕的事——或許僧人不會害怕留下。夢窓回答說他一點也不怕，於是主持了葬儀，獨自守夜。

passages.text: When the night had far advanced a strange Shape advanced, so terrible that the priest could neither move nor speak. It raised the corpse and quickly devoured it; not content, it ate the offerings too, then vanished. In the morning the villagers returned and expressed no surprise that the corpse had disappeared; but when Muso mentioned the hermitage on the hill they were amazed — there was no priest and no anjitsu on yonder hill; he had been deluded by some evil spirit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXV (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 夜已深沉，一個奇異的身影走上前來，其形貌之可怖令僧人既不能動彈也不能出聲。它抬起屍體，迅速將其吞食；猶不滿足，又吃掉了供品，隨後消失無蹤。翌日清晨，村民們回來，對屍體消失一事並不感到驚訝；但當夢窓提起山上的那間茅廬時，他們卻大為驚異——那邊山上既沒有僧人，也沒有庵室；他是被某個邪靈所迷惑了。

passages.text: Muso found the hermitage again, and the old priest came out bowing and ashamed: 'You have seen my real shape. I am a jikininki, a man-eating goblin. Many years ago I was a priest in this district and performed many burial services, but I was not influenced by true religion and thought only of the fine clothes I could get from my calling; for that reason I was reborn a jikininki and have ever since devoured the corpses of all who died here. Have pity on my miserable plight, and repeat certain prayers on my behalf, that I may speedily find peace.' The moment the words were spoken the recluse and his hermitage vanished, and Muso found himself kneeling beside a moss-covered tomb, probably the tomb of the unfortunate priest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXV (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 夢窓又找到了那間茅廬，老僧出來行禮，滿面羞愧：「你已見到了我的真身。我是一個食人鬼，一個吃人的妖怪。許多年前，我是這一帶的僧人，主持過許多葬儀，但我並未受真正的信仰感化，只想著能從這份差事中得到華美的衣物；因此之故，我轉生為食人鬼，自此便一直吞食此地所有死者的屍體。請憐憫我悲慘的處境，為我誦讀某些經文，好讓我早日得到安息。」話音剛落，那隱者與他的茅廬便消失了，夢窓發現自己跪在一座覆滿青苔的墳墓旁，那大概就是那位不幸僧人的墳墓。

title.en: The Maiden with the Wooden Bowl
title.zh: 鉢被頭娘——木碗下藏珍

region.en: A rice-farming household (symbolic pin: Edo region)
region.zh: 稻作農家（象徵釘：江戶地方）

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: A dying mother fixes a lacquered bowl upon her beautiful daughter's head to hide her from temptation; hired as a servant, mocked by all, she refuses her master's son until her dead mother bids her in a dream — and at the wedding, as the bride raises the three-times-three cup, the bowl bursts with cries and groans and pours out gold, silver and jewels, revealing the most beautiful woman in all Japan.
summary.zh: 寡母恐女兒貌美招禍，臨終為她戴上木碗遮顏。姑娘入富農家為僕，受盡嘲弄；少主鍾情欲娶，她屢拒，直至亡母夢中囑婚。婚禮合巹之際，木碗呻吟碎裂，金銀珠寶傾瀉而出為嫁資，碗下竟是全日本最美的新娘。

sensitivity.note: Japanese folktale of the bowl-hidden bride cycle; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: An old couple had one child, a girl of remarkable charm and beauty. When the father died the widow grew concerned for her daughter's future: 'Your face is all too fair. It must be hidden from the eager eyes of men, lest it cause you to fall from your good and simple life to one of shame.' She placed a lacquered bowl upon the maiden's head and bade her always wear it. Shortly after, the old woman died, and the maiden earned her living in the rice-fields, known throughout the country as the Maiden with the Bowl on her Head; young men laughed and tried to pull off the wooden covering, but it could not be removed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXVI (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一對老夫婦有一個孩子，是個容貌出眾、美麗動人的女孩。父親去世後，寡母為女兒的未來憂心起來：「你的容貌實在太過姣好。必須把它從男人們熱切的目光中藏起來，免得它使你從善良純樸的生活墮入羞恥之境。」她將一隻漆碗放在少女頭上，吩咐她永遠戴著。不久之後，老婦人去世了，少女便在稻田裡謀生，全國上下都稱她為「頭頂木碗的少女」；年輕男子們嘲笑她，試圖扯下那木製的遮蓋物，卻怎麼也取不下來。

passages.text: A rich farmer, struck by her diligence, took her into his house to nurse his sick wife, and treated her as a child of their own. His eldest son, home from gay Kyoto, grew day by day more impressed by the girl's gentleness and nobility until he resolved to marry her; most of his relations opposed the union bitterly, and the maiden herself refused, believing marriage could only bring discord to the home that had sheltered her. That night her mother came to her in a dream: 'Marry the farmer's son and all will be well again.' She awoke full of joy and yielded with a gracious smile.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXVI (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位富農被她的勤勉所打動，將她帶進家中照料他生病的妻子，待她如同親生女兒。他從熱鬧的京都歸來的長子，日復一日愈發被這女孩的溫柔與高貴所打動，直到決心娶她為妻；他的大多數親戚都激烈反對這樁婚事，少女自己也拒絕了，她認為婚姻只會給這個曾庇護她的家庭帶來不和。那天夜裡，她的母親在夢中來到她面前：「嫁給那農夫的兒子吧，一切都會好起來的。」她醒來時滿心歡喜，帶著溫婉的微笑應允了。

passages.text: At the wedding none could remove the bowl, which uttered strange cries and groans when the relations pulled at it. The bridegroom commanded the ceremony to proceed, and as the bride put the wine-cup to her lips for the three-times-three, the bowl broke with a great noise and from it fell gold and silver and precious stones, so the maiden who had been a beggar now had her marriage portion; and the guests, looking up, saw that the bride was the most beautiful woman in all Japan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXVI (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 婚禮上，誰也取不下那隻碗，當親戚們拉扯它時，碗竟發出奇怪的叫聲與呻吟。新郎命令儀式繼續進行，當新娘將酒杯舉到唇邊行三三九度之禮時，那碗隨著一聲巨響破裂開來，從中落下金銀與寶石，於是這位曾是乞丐的少女如今有了自己的嫁妝；而賓客們抬頭望去，只見新娘是全日本最美麗的女子。

title.en: Prince Ousu Steals His Father's Brides
title.zh: 小碓命代娶美人

region.en: Yamato court (Nara), Japan
region.zh: 大和宮廷（奈良）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Emperor Keiko, hearing of the beauty of two sisters, sends his son Prince Oho-usu (the young Yamato-takeru) to summon them to court. The prince instead weds both sisters himself and sends up other women under their names.
summary.zh: 景行天皇聞二女之美，遣王子小碓命召之入宮。王子竟自娶二女，而以他人冒名送入。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Emperor Oho-tarashi-hiko (Keiko) had heard wondrous reports of the beauty of the sisters Ye-hime and Oto-hime, daughters of King Kamu-oho-ne, ancestor of the Rulers of the Land of Minu. To see them for himself he sent his own son, the fierce Prince Oho-usu, with the errand of summoning the two maidens up to the capital.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 290-291 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大足彥天皇（景行天皇）聽聞神大根王——即三野國造之祖——之女兄姬與弟姬姊妹二人容貌美麗的奇聞。為了親眼見證，他派遣自己的兒子，勇猛的皇子大碓，命他召喚兩位少女上京。

passages.text: The prince did not carry out the command. Instead of sending the sisters to his father, he took both maidens to wife himself. Then, so that his deceit should not be discovered, he sought out other women, falsely gave them the two sisters' names, and sent them up to the capital in their place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 290-291 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 皇子並未執行命令。他沒有將姊妹送往父親處，反而自己娶了兩位少女為妻。隨後，為了不讓自己的欺瞞被發覺，他另尋其他女子，假稱她們是那兩位姊妹的名字，將她們送往京城作為替代。

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign, knowing the women who arrived to be substitutes and not the beauties he had asked for, looked long upon them again and again with longing; yet he never wedded them, and so they were made to sorrow. From Ye-hime the prince begot King Oshi-kuro-no-ye-hiko, and from Oto-hime King Oshi-kuro-no-oto-hiko.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 290-291 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天皇得知前來的女子是替代者，而非他所求的美人，便一再戀戀不捨地凝視她們；然而他始終未曾娶她們為妻，因此她們為此悲傷。皇子與兄姬生下了忍熊大郎子王，與弟姬生下了忍熊二郎子王。

title.en: Prince Ousu Crushes His Elder Brother
title.zh: 小碓命折殺兄

region.en: Yamato court (Nara), Japan
region.zh: 大和宮廷（奈良）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Ordered by his father to make his lazy elder brother attend the royal meals, Prince Ousu instead seizes him in the privy, crushes and tears him apart, and flings the limbs away. Terrified by his son's ferocity, the emperor sends him against the Kumaso brigands.
summary.zh: 天皇命小碓命勸兄赴朝夕御膳。小碓竟於廁中捕兄，折裂其肢而棄之。天皇懼其凶猛，乃遣其西征熊襲。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign asked his younger son, Prince Wo-usu: 'Why does your elder brother not come forth to the morning and evening great august repasts? Take the trouble to teach him his duty.' Yet five days passed and the elder prince still did not appear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 291-292 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天皇問他的幼子小碓皇子：「為何你的兄長不來參加早晚的大御食？勞煩你去教導他應盡的本分。」然而五日過去，兄皇子仍未出現。

passages.text: Asked again how he had taken the trouble, the younger prince answered flatly: 'In the early morning, when he went into the privy, I grasped hold of him and crushed him, and, pulling off his limbs, wrapped them in matting and flung them away.' He had killed his own elder brother with his bare hands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 291-292 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當被再次問及他是如何教導的，幼皇子直截了當地回答：「清晨他進入廁所時，我抓住他並將他壓碎，扯下他的四肢，用草蓆包裹後丟棄。」他徒手殺死了自己的兄長。

passages.text: Alarmed at the valour and ferocity of his child's disposition, the emperor resolved to turn that violence outward. 'In the West there are two Kumaso bravoes, unsubmissive and disrespectful men. So take them,' he commanded, and thus he sent the prince off on the campaign that would make him Yamato-takeru.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 291-292 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天皇對這孩子性情中的勇猛與凶暴感到驚恐，決心將這股暴力轉向外邦。「西方有兩個熊襲的勇士，是不順從、不恭敬之人。去討伐他們。」他如此命令，於是派遣皇子出征，這場戰役將使他成為日本武尊。

title.en: Yamato-takeru Slays the Kumaso Bravoes in a Girl's Dress
title.zh: 日本武尊女裝誅熊襲

region.en: Kumaso land (Kyushu), Japan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 熊襲之地（九州，象徵座標）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Sent west against two unsubmissive Kumaso bravoes, Prince Wo-usu disguises himself as a girl in his aunt Yamato-hime's clothing, infiltrates their feast, and stabs them both. The dying elder bravo, acknowledging no one braver in the west, bestows on him the name Yamato-take.
summary.zh: 小碓命奉命西征熊襲二豪傑，借姨倭姬命之衣女装，混入宴席刺殺之。垂死之兄豪傑讚其勇，賜名日本武尊。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Sent west to destroy the two Kumaso bravoes, the young prince first prayed at the shrines. His aunt, Her Augustness Yamato-hime, priestess of Ise, granted him her own august upper garment and skirt, and he set out with a sabre hidden in his bosom. Reaching the bravoes' cave, ringed with a three-fold belt of warriors, he found a feast being prepared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 292-294 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 年輕的皇子被派往西方去討伐熊曾的兩位勇士，他先在神社祈禱。他的姑母倭姬尊，即伊勢的齋宮，將自己的上衣與裙賜予他，他便懷藏刀劍出發。抵達勇士們的洞穴時，那裡圍著三重武士的防線，他發現正準備著一場宴會。

passages.text: On the day of the rejoicing he combed down his bound hair after the manner of girls, put on his aunt's garment and skirt, and, looking quite like a young girl, stood amid the women inside the cave. The two brothers, delighted with the supposed maiden, set her between them and rejoiced exuberantly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 292-294 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在歡慶之日，他仿照女子的樣式梳下束起的頭髮，穿上姑母的上衣與裙，看起來宛如一位少女，站在洞穴內眾女子之間。兩兄弟見這所謂的少女，滿心歡喜，將她置於二人之間，盡情歡樂。

passages.text: When the feast was at its height the prince drew the hidden sabre, seized the elder bravo by the collar, and thrust the blade through his chest; the younger fled, but was caught at the foot of the steps and stabbed through the buttock. 'Do not move the sword; I have something to say,' the wounded bravo begged, and told him: no one in the west is so brave as we two, yet in Great Yamato there is a man braver still - take, then, the name Yamato-take.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 292-294 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 宴會正酣之際，皇子拔出暗藏的刀劍，抓住年長勇士的衣領，將刀刃刺穿他的胸膛；年幼者逃走了，卻在階梯下被抓住，臀部遭刺穿。「不要動劍；我有話要說，」受傷的勇士懇求道，並告訴他：西方沒有人比我們二人更勇敢，然而在大倭國中，還有一人更為勇敢——那麼，就取名叫倭建吧。

passages.text: The moment the bravo finished speaking, the prince ripped him up like a ripe melon. Thenceforward he was praised as His Augustness Yamato-take. Returning to the capital he subdued and pacified every deity of the mountains, rivers, and Anado on his way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 292-294 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 勇士話音剛落，皇子便將他像熟瓜一般剖開。自此以後，他被讚譽為倭建尊。返回都城途中，他平定並安撫了沿途山川與穴戶的每一位神祇。

title.en: The Wooden-Sword Trick at Izumo
title.zh: 出雲木劍計

region.en: Izumo (Shimane), Japan
region.zh: 出雲（島根）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Wishing to slay the Izumo bravo, Yamato-takeru pretends friendship, secretly girds a false sword of oak, and proposes an exchange of blades after bathing. When the bravo cannot draw the wooden sword, Yamato-takeru cuts him down.
summary.zh: 倭建命欲誅出雲豪傑，偽結盟好，密佩櫟木假劍。浴於斐伊川後，提議互換佩劍；出雲豪傑拔不出木劍，遂被斬殺。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Entering the Land of Izumo, Yamato-takeru wished to slay the Izumo bravo. On arriving he bound himself to the man in friendship, and secretly shaped an oak tree into a false sword, girded it on, and went with the bravo to bathe in the River Hi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 294-295 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 倭建進入出雲國，想要殺死出雲的勇士。抵達後，他與那人結為朋友，暗中將一棵橡樹削成假劍，佩在身上，與勇士一同前往肥河沐浴。

passages.text: He got out of the river first, took up the real sword the bravo had laid down and girded it on himself, saying 'Let us exchange swords!' The unsuspecting bravo, climbing out after him, drew on Yamato-takeru's wooden imitation without noticing the difference.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 294-295 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他先從河中出來，拿起勇士放下的真劍佩在自己身上，說道：「我們交換劍吧！」毫無戒心的勇士隨後爬出，拔出倭建的木製仿劍，卻未察覺其中的差異。

passages.text: 'Come on! Let us cross swords,' Yamato-takeru suggested. The Izumo bravo could not draw the false blade. Instantly Yamato-takeru drew his own sword and slew him, singing a triumphal song; so he extirpated the bravoes, made the land orderly, and went up to report to the Heavenly Sovereign.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 294-295 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「來吧！讓我們交劍。」日本武尊如此說道。出雲的勇士無法拔出那把假劍。日本武尊立刻拔出自己的劍將他殺死，並唱了一首凱歌；於是他誅滅了那些勇士，使國土井然有序，然後上奏天皇。

title.en: The Herb-Quelling Sabre and the Suruga Fire
title.zh: 草薙劍與駿河野火

region.en: Sagami/Suruga moor, Japan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 駿河野原（象徵座標）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Sent east against the twelve roads, Yamato-takeru visits Ise, where his aunt Yamato-hime gives him the Herb-Quelling Sabre and a bag with a fire-striker inside. In Sagamu a lying ruler sets fire to the moor around him; he mows the grass with the sword, strikes a counter-fire, escapes, and destroys the rulers, giving the place its name Yakidzu.
summary.zh: 倭建命東征，於伊勢受姨倭姬命賜草薙劍與火石囊。駿河國主縱火燒野，倭建命以劍刈草，擊石取火，燃逆火突圍，盡誅國主，其地遂名燒津。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Again the emperor commanded Yamato-takeru to subdue the savage deities and unsubmissive people of the twelve roads of the East, giving him no army. Going into the temple of the Great Deity of Ise, he wept to his aunt Yamato-hime that his father must surely think he would die quickly. She bestowed on him the Herb-Quelling Sabre and an august bag, saying: 'If there should be an emergency, open the mouth of the bag.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 295-297 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天皇再度命令日本武尊討伐東方十二道之凶神與不順服之人，卻不給他軍隊。他進入伊勢大神宮，向他的姑母倭姬哭泣訴說，父親必定認為他會很快死去。姑母賜予他草薙劍與一個御袋，說道：「若有急難，便打開袋口。」

passages.text: In the Land of Wohari he plighted his troth to Princess Miyadzu, promising to wed her on his return, then pushed into the eastern lands and pacified their savage deities. Reaching Sagamu, its ruler lied that a violent deity dwelt in the middle of a great moor; when Yamato-takeru entered the moor to see it, the ruler set the dry grass ablaze around him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 295-297 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在尾張國，他與宮簀媛互訂婚約，約定歸來時迎娶她，隨後深入東方諸國，平定當地的凶神。抵達相模時，當地的首長謊稱大澤中央住著一位暴虐之神；當日本武尊進入澤中察看時，首長便在他四周點燃乾草。

passages.text: Knowing he was deceived, he opened the bag: inside was a fire-striker. First he mowed away the surrounding herbage with his august sword, then struck fire and kindled a counter-fire that burnt the herbage and drove back the flames, and he returned forth alive.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 295-297 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他自知受騙，便打開袋子：裡面是一把火打石。他先用御劍割除四周的草叢，然後擊石取火，點起反向之火，燒盡草叢並逼退火勢，於是活著歸來。

passages.text: Then he took vengeance: he killed and destroyed all the Rulers of that land and set fire to them, so that the place is called Yakidzu, the burning. Thus the Herb-Quelling Sabre earned its name by mowing the grass that would have destroyed its bearer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 295-297 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著他展開報復：將該地所有的首長盡數殺戮毀滅，並放火焚燒他們，因此該地被稱為「燒津」，意即焚燒之地。草薙劍便因割除那本會毀滅其持有者的草叢而得名。

title.en: Oto-tachibana Enters the Sea; the Naming of Adzuma
title.zh: 弟橘媛投海與東國得名

region.en: Hashirimizu crossing, Tokyo Bay, Japan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 走水海峽（東京灣，象徵座標）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: At the Hashiri-midzu crossing a sea deity raises waves against Yamato-takeru's ship. His empress Oto-tachibana seats herself on eight thicknesses of rugs spread on the water and enters the sea in his stead, calming the waves. Seven days later her comb drifts ashore and is buried. At the Ashigara pass a white deer is struck down and the pass named Adzuma.
summary.zh: 走水渡海時，海神興浪阻船。弟橘媛於浪上鋪八重席而投海代君，浪立平。七日後其梳漂至海濱，葬為陵。足柄峠白鹿被擊斃，其地遂名阿豆摩（東）。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Penetrating eastward, Yamato-takeru crossed the sea of Hashiri-midzu. The deity of that crossing raised the waves, tossing the ship so that it could not proceed. Then his empress, Her Augustness Princess Oto-tachibana, spoke: 'I will enter the sea instead of the august child. The august child must complete the service on which he has been sent, and take back a report to the Heavenly Sovereign.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 297-299 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 日本武尊向東深入，渡過走水海。該渡口之神掀起波濤，使船隻顛簸無法前進。於是他的皇后弟橘媛命說道：「我願代替皇子入海。皇子必須完成所受之使命，並回奏天皇。」

passages.text: As she was about to enter the sea she spread eight thicknesses of sedge rugs, eight of skin rugs and eight of silk rugs on the top of the waves, and sat down upon them. At once the violent waves went down, and the august ship was able to proceed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 297-299 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她正要入海時，在波濤之上鋪了八重菅蓆、八重皮蓆與八重絹蓆，然後坐於其上。頃刻間，狂濤平息，御船得以繼續前行。

passages.text: Seven days afterwards the empress's august comb drifted onto the sea-beach; it was taken and placed in an august mausoleum built for her. Yamato-takeru pushed on, subdued all the savage Yemishi and the deities of the mountains and rivers, and turned homeward.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 297-299 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 七日之後，皇后之御櫛漂流至海濱；有人拾取，置於為她所建之御陵中。日本武尊繼續前進，平定所有凶悍之蝦夷及山川之神，然後踏上歸途。

passages.text: At the foot of the Ashigara pass he was eating his provisions when the deity of the pass, transformed into a white deer, stood before him; he struck it with a scrap of wild chive and it died, hit in the eye. Mounting the pass he sighed three times and cried 'Adzuma ha ya!' - oh my wife! - and so that land is called Adzuma, the East.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 297-299 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在足柄峠山麓，他正進食乾糧，峠之神化為白鹿立於其前；他以一片野韭擊之，中其目而死。登上峠時，他三度嘆息，喊道「阿豆麻波夜！」——吾妻啊！——因此那地方便稱為阿豆麻，即東方。

title.en: The Deity of Mount Ibuki and Yamato-takeru's Death
title.zh: 伊吹山神與倭建命之死

region.en: Moor of Nobo (Sanuki), Japan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 能褒野野原（象徵座標）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Honouring the old fire-lighter Sakawori and wedding Princess Miyazu, Yamato-takeru leaves his Grass-Quelling Sabre in her house and goes empty-handed to take the deity of Mount Ibuki. A white boar - the deity's messenger - is spared but his boastful insolence brings ice-rain that breaks him; his legs fail, he sings land-regretting songs and dies at the moor of Nobo.
summary.zh: 倭建命嘉獎老火夫佐川折，娶美夜務媛，留草薙劍於其家，空手征伊吹山神。見白豬而口出狂言，山神降雹雨擊之；腿如船舵不能行，沿途嘆歌，至能褒野而死。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Crossing into Kahi, Yamato-takeru dwelt in the palace of Sakawori, the old man who had been the lighter of the august fire; the prince praised him and bestowed on him the Rulership of the Eastern Lands. He then subdued the deity of the Shinanu pass, and in Wohari went to the house of Princess Miyazu, to whom he had plighted his troth; seeing her menstruation, he sang, cohabited with her, and left the Grass-Quelling Sabre in her house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 300-302 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 日本武尊進入甲斐，居於曾為御火焚者之老人酒折宮中；皇子讚賞他，並賜以東國之治。他隨後平定信濃峠之神，又在尾張前往與他訂立婚約之宮簀媛家中；見其月事，乃作歌，與之同寢，並將草薙劍留於其家。

passages.text: Then he went to take the deity of Mount Ibuki, declaring he would take him empty-handed. On the mountain-side a white boar the size of a bull met him. 'This creature transformed into a white boar must be a messenger from the deity. Though I slay it not now, I will slay it when I return,' he said, and ascended, insolently sparing it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 302-303 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著他前往討伐伊吹山之神，宣稱將空手取之。山腰處，一頭如牛般大小之白豬迎面而來。「此化為白豬之物，必是神之使者。我今雖不殺之，歸來時必殺之。」他說道，遂登山，傲慢地放過了牠。

passages.text: The deity punished his boast: heavy ice-rain fell, striking and perplexing him. Descending, he rested at the fresh spring of Tama-kura-be and his heart awoke somewhat; but at the moor of Tagi his legs had become rudder-shaped, unable to walk. He leaned on an august staff at the Tsuwe-tsuki pass, found his forgotten sword still at the single pine of Cape Wotsu, and sang at the village of Mihe that his legs were like three-fold crooks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 303-305 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 神懲其誇言：猛烈的冰雨降下，擊打他，使他惶惑。下山後，他在玉倉部之清泉歇息，心神稍復；但在多藝之原，他的雙腿已變得如船舵一般，無法行走。他在杖築峠倚著御杖，於尾津崎之孤松處尋回遺忘之劍，並在三位村作歌，說他的腿如三重之彎鉤。

passages.text: Reaching the moor of Nobo, he regretted his native land, singing that he longed for Yamato with its green layers of trees, for his wife and children. His sickness became very urgent; as soon as he finished singing his final song, he died. A courier was despatched to the Heavenly Sovereign to announce his death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 305-306 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 抵達能煩野時，他思念故鄉，詠歌表達對層層綠樹的倭國、對妻兒的思念。他的病勢轉為危急；一詠完最後一首歌，便死去。使者被派往天皇處稟報他的死訊。

title.en: The White Bird of Yamato-takeru's Tomb
title.zh: 倭建命白鳥陵

region.en: Shiki, Kawachi (Osaka), Japan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 河内志幾（象徵座標）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: At Yamato-takeru's funeral his empresses and children build a mausoleum and crawl through the rice-fields sobbing songs. The dead prince becomes a white dotterel eight fathoms long and soars to heaven; they pursue it through stubble and sea, singing the four songs still sung at imperial burials, and bury him at Shiki in Kawachi - yet the bird flies up to heaven again.
summary.zh: 倭建命葬禮上，后妃皇子筑陵而匍匐歌哭。死者化為八尋白鳥沖天，眾人踏芒入海追之而歌；其四歌至今天皇大葬時皆詠之。葬於河内志幾，白鳥再度沖天而去。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: When word of Yamato-takeru's death reached the capital, his empresses and august children dwelling in Yamato went down and built an august mausoleum, crawling hither and thither through the rice-fields surrounding it and sobbing out songs of grief over his grave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 306-308 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 倭建命死訊傳至京城後，居於倭國的皇后們與皇子們下至該地，建造了一座陵墓，在陵墓周圍的稻田間爬行往來，於其墓前哭泣詠唱哀歌。

passages.text: Then the dead prince turned into a white dotterel eight fathoms long and, soaring up to heaven, flew off towards the shore. The mourners tore their feet treading the bamboo-grass stubble yet forgot the pain, pursuing him with lamentations across the fields and out into the salt sea as the bird flew and perched on the seaside.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 306-308 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隨後，死去的皇子化為一隻長達八尋的白千鳥，飛昇上天，朝海濱飛去。送葬者踏著篠竹的殘株，雙腳磨破卻忘卻疼痛，一路悲嘆追隨他穿過田野，直至飛鳥飛去、停歇於海邊的鹽海之中。

passages.text: The four songs sung at that chase are sung to this day at the great august interment of a Heavenly Sovereign. The bird flew on to Shiki in the land of Kafuchi, where another mausoleum was made and Yamato-takeru laid to rest - the Mausoleum of the White-Bird. Nevertheless the bird soared up thence to heaven again and flew away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 306-308 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當時追趕時所唱的四百歌，至今仍在天皇盛大葬儀時詠唱。那鳥繼續飛往河內國志紀，該處另建了一座陵墓，將倭建命安葬於此——即白鳥陵。然而那鳥又從該處飛昇上天，飛走了。

title.en: Yamato-takeru: The Kuwagata Hero Cycle
title.zh: 日本武尊英雄紀：從熊襲到白鳥

region.en: Yamato (Nara) to eastern Japan, Kojiki hero cycle (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 大和至東國（倭建命巡歷，象徵座標）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Flagship deep record: the full Kojiki cycle of Yamato-takeru, from his fratricidal youth and the Kumaso trick that earned his name, through the Herb-Quelling Sabre and the Suruga fire, Oto-tachibana's sacrifice at sea, the naming of Adzuma, and the ice-rain punishment of Mount Ibuki, to his death songs at Nobo and apotheosis as the white bird.
summary.zh: 本紀全錄《古事記》倭建命一生：弑兄、熊襲女裝得號、草薙劍與駿河火、弟橘媛投海、東國得名、伊吹山雹雨懲罰、能褒野絕命之歌與白鳥升天。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); the hero is woven into imperial genealogy, so this record is handled as sacred-legendary material, presented as condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Ordered to make his negligent elder brother attend the royal meals, the young Prince Wo-usu crushed him in the privy and tore off his limbs. Alarmed at such ferocity, Emperor Keiko sent him west to take the two Kumaso bravoes. Dressing in his aunt Yamato-hime's garments as a girl, he infiltrated their feast, stabbed both brothers, and heard the dying elder name him Yamato-take - the one braver than any man of the west.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 291-294 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 小碓命奉命讓怠慢的兄長出席御膳，便將其兄長壓死於廁中，並扯斷其四肢。景行天皇對這般殘暴感到驚恐，便派他西征討伐熊襲的兩名勇者。他換上姑母倭姬的衣裳扮作女子，潛入他們的宴席，刺殺兩兄弟，並聽聞將死的兄長為他取名為倭建——即西方無人能及之勇者。

passages.text: With a false wooden sword he tricked and slew the Izumo bravo. Sent east without an army - and certain his father meant him to die - he received from Yamato-hime at Ise the Herb-Quelling Sabre and a bag. When the ruler of Sagamu fired the moor around him, the bag's fire-striker let him mow the grass, strike a counter-fire, and burn his deceivers in their own flames: the place is Yakidzu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 294-297 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他以假木刀欺騙並殺死了出雲的勇者。他被派往東方卻不給軍隊——他確信父親是要他死——於是在伊勢從倭姬處得到草薙劍與一個袋子。當相模的國造在他四周放火燒原時，袋中的火打石讓他割草、點起反擊之火，將欺騙他的人燒死於他們自己放的火中：該地即燒津。

passages.text: At the Hashiri-midzu crossing the sea deity raised deadly waves, and his empress Oto-tachibana, seated on eight thicknesses of rugs spread on the water, gave her life to the sea in his stead; her comb, drifting ashore seven days later, was buried as a mausoleum. Sighing 'Adzuma ha ya' - oh my wife - at the Ashigara pass, he gave the East its name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 297-299 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在「走水」渡口，海神掀起致命的巨浪，他的皇后弟橘媛坐在鋪於水面的八層席褥之上，代他投身入海，獻出了生命；她的梳子七日後漂抵岸邊，被埋葬為陵墓。他在足柄山口嘆道「吾妻はや」（啊，我的妻子），由此為東方賦予了「吾妻」之名。

passages.text: Homeward, he honoured the old fire-lighter Sakawori, wed Princess Miyazu and left the Grass-Quelling Sabre in her house - whence it came to rest at the shrine of Atsuta - then went empty-handed against the deity of Mount Ibuki. A white boar, the deity's messenger, he insolently promised to slay later; the deity answered with ice-rain that broke his legs to rudders. Dragging himself from pass to moor he sang his land-regretting songs, and died at Nobo as the last song ended.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 300-306 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 歸途中，他厚待了年老的點火人佐川織，娶了宮津姬，並將草薙劍留在她的家中——此劍後來安奉於熱田神宮——隨後便空手前往討伐伊吹山之神。一頭白豬乃該神的使者，他卻傲慢地揚言日後再將其誅殺；神以冰雨回應，將他的雙腿擊折如舵。他從山口拖著身子行至海濱，唱罷他的思鄉之歌，最後一曲終了時，死於能褒野。

narrative.en:
Yamato-takeru is the Kojiki's great tragic hero, and his cycle begins in blood. When Emperor Keiko asks why his eldest son never comes to the morning and evening meals, he orders the younger prince, Wo-usu, to teach him his duty. Wo-usu's answer is to seize his brother in the privy, crush him, tear off his limbs, and wrap them in matting. Horrified by his son's ferocity, the emperor redirects it outward: two unsubmissive Kumaso bravoes in the west must be taken.

For this errand the prince's aunt Yamato-hime, priestess of Ise, gives him her own upper garment and skirt. Binding his hair like a girl's, hiding a sabre in his bosom, he waits until the day of the bravoes' feast, slips into their cave among the women, and is set between the delighted brothers as if he were a beautiful girl. At the height of the feast he draws the blade, stabs the elder through the chest, runs down the younger and pierces his buttock. Dying, the bravo offers him a name: no men in the west are braver than they two, yet in Great Yamato there is one braver still - so let him be praised as Yamato-take. The prince rips him up like a ripe melon, and the name Yamato-takeru stays with him forever. A second trick follows at Izumo, where he girds a wooden imitation of a sword, exchanges blades with the unsuspecting bravo after a bath in the River Hi, and cuts down the man who cannot draw his own weapon.

The third command is the fatal one: pacify the twelve roads of the East, without an army. Yamato-takeru weeps at Ise that his father must think he will die quickly, and Yamato-hime grants him the Herb-Quelling Sabre and a bag he must open in emergency. After plighting troth with Princess Miyadzu of Wohari, he reaches Sagamu, whose ruler lies that a violent deity dwells in the middle of a moor; once the prince is inside, the ruler fires the dry grass. Out of the bag comes a fire-striker: he mows the herbage with the sacred sword, strikes fire, kindles a counter-fire that drives back the flames, escapes, and burns the deceivers alive - giving Yakidzu, the Burning, its name.

At the crossing of Hashiri-midzu the sea deity heaps up waves no ship can ride. His empress, Princess Oto-tachibana, resolves to enter the sea in her husband's place so that he may finish his service; she spreads eight thicknesses of sedge, skin and silk rugs upon the waves, sits down on them, and the storm subsides. Seven days later her comb drifts to the beach and is buried in a mausoleum of its own. On his return he slays a white deer that is the deity of the Ashigara pass, sighs three times - 'Adzuma ha ya!' oh my wife - and names the whole East Adzuma. In Kahi he honours the fire-lighter Sakawori with the rulership of the Eastern Lands; in Wohari he weds Princess Miyazu, and leaves the Grass-Quelling Sabre in her house, from which it passes into the keeping of the Atsuta shrine.

Then comes his undoing at Mount Ibuki. Boasting that he will take its deity empty-handed, he meets a white boar the size of a bull, recognizes it as the deity's messenger, and insolently says he will slay it on his way back. The deity replies with heavy ice-rain. His legs grow rudder-shaped and will not carry him; he names the places of his suffering - Tagi, Tsuwe-tsuki, Mihe - leaning on a staff, finding a forgotten sword whole at Cape Wotsu, and singing songs of regret for Yamato, its layered green trees, his wife and his children. At the moor of Nobo, as his final song ends, he dies.

His empresses and children build his mausoleum and crawl through the rice-fields about it, sobbing. Then the dead prince becomes a white dotterel eight fathoms long and soars toward heaven; they pursue it through stubble and sea, and the four songs of that chase are sung at every imperial burial to this day. He is laid to rest at Shiki in Kawachi, in the Mausoleum of the White-Bird - but the bird rises once more and flies to heaven, leaving the tomb empty. The cycle closes with genealogy: his sons carry the imperial line onward, and the hero who slew gods' messengers and enemies of the realm ends as a bird crossing the boundary between Yamato and the sky.
narrative.zh: 此為《古事記》所載日本武尊之完整英雄紀：弑兄而畏、女装誅熊襲而得尊號、木劍誅出雲豪傑、伊勢受草薙劍與火石囊、駿河野火中刈草逆燒、弟橘媛鋪八重席投海平浪、足柄峠嘆而名東、伊吹山白豬口出狂言遭雹雨、腿如船舵、能褒野絕命之歌、化八尋白鳥沖天，葬於河内志幾白鳥陵，其四歌至今用於天皇大葬。

functions: Explains the origin of the hero's name Yamato-takeru and of the place-name Adzuma for eastern Japan, binding geography to heroic narrative.
Etiologizes the Grass-Mowing (Herb-Quelling) Sword's cult at Atsuta shrine and the fire-escape rites associated with it.
Provides the canonical funeral songs sung at the burial of Japanese sovereigns, ritualizing imperial death as transformation into a bird.
Models the ideal of the unflinching sacrificial prince whose consort's self-offering calms the sea, a paradigm of loyalty in later Japanese literature.

variants.name: Nihongi version (Aston, Books VII and XIII, Yamato-takeru / Ousu no Mikoto)
variants.text_tradition: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), compiled 720 CE, trans. W. G. Aston 1896
variants.summary: The Nihongi retells the Kumaso deception, the Suruga fire, Oto-tachibana's sacrifice and the hero's death with different songs, expanded dialogues, and a more sinicized court frame, making the prince more openly a human emperor's son.

variants.name: Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912), ch. II 'Yamato Take' retelling
variants.text_tradition: Meiji-era popular digest of Kojiki/Nihongi material, trans./retold by F. Hadland Davis 1912
variants.summary: A late Victorian popular retelling that fuses the Kumaso trick, the wooden sword, the grass-cutting fire and the sea sacrifice into one continuous tale for general readers.

sensitivity_guidance: Yamato-takeru is part of the imperial genealogy still revered in Shinto practice (Atsuta shrine keeps the Grass-Mowing Sword). This record presents the 712 CE mythic material in public-domain paraphrase for comparative study, not as a claim about historical persons; avoid devotional or political use.

title.en: The Deity Rebukes Emperor Chuuai
title.zh: 神託斥仲哀天皇

region.en: Kashii palace, Tsukushi (Fukuoka), Japan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 香椎宮（筑紫，象徵座標）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: At Kashii in Tsukushi, preparing to attack the Kumaso, Chuuai plays his lute while Take-uchi asks the divine will. His empress Jingu, divinely possessed, announces a treasure-land to the west; the emperor disbelieves and falls silent, the deities declare the land is not his to rule, and he dies as the lute's sound dies. A great purification follows, and the oracle repeats: the child in her womb will rule this land and the westward one.
summary.zh: 仲哀天皇在筑紫香椎宮，欲討熊襲，命武內宿禰奏神意。神功皇后神靈憑依，宣示西方寶國；天皇不信，坐而沉默，諸神怒言其不堪治此國，天皇遂於琴音絕處崩殂。其後大祓，神諭重申：腹中皇子將治此國與西方之國。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: In this reign Heir Apparent Homuda-wake was born to Empress Okinaga-tarashi, named Oho-tomo-wake for the flesh like an elbow-pad on his newborn arm - a sign, known while he was still in the womb, that he would rule countries; and the granaries of Ahaji were established. Then the emperor, dwelling at the palace of Kashihi in Tsukushi, was about to smite the land of Kumaso: he played on his august lute while the Prime Minister, the Noble Take-uchi, stood in the pure court requesting the divine orders.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 313-316 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在此御世，皇后息長足姬生下了皇太子譽田別，因其新生手臂上的肉狀如臂韝，故得名大鞆別——這是他尚在母腹之中便已顯明的徵兆，預示他將統治諸國；此外，阿治的糧倉也在此時設立。其後，天皇居於筑紫橿日宮，正欲討伐熊襲之地：他彈奏御琴，而大臣武內宿禰立於清淨的庭中，請求神諭。

passages.text: The Empress, divinely possessed, charged him with this counsel: 'There is a land to the Westward, and in that land is abundance of various treasures dazzling to the eye, from gold and silver downwards. I will now bestow this land upon thee.' The Heavenly Sovereign replied that from a high place looking west one sees no country - only the great sea - and, saying the deities lie, pushed away his lute, sat silent, and would not play.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 315-316 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 皇后為神靈所附，向他傳達了這番教誨：「西方有一片土地，那土地上盛產種種令人目眩的寶物，自金銀以下，不勝枚舉。我如今將把這片土地賜予你。」天皇答道，從高處西望，不見任何國度——唯見茫茫大海——於是斥責神明說謊，推開御琴，默然端坐，不再彈奏。

passages.text: Then the deities were very angry: 'Altogether this empire is not a land over which thou oughtest to rule. Do thou go to the one road!' Take-uchi begged him to continue playing; he drew the lute slowly and languidly played - and almost immediately the sound became inaudible. Lifting a light, they found the Heavenly Sovereign dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 315-316 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是眾神大為震怒：「這帝國全然不是你應當統治的土地。你且往那條路去吧！」武內宿禰懇求他繼續彈奏；他緩緩取過御琴，慵懶地彈奏起來——幾乎就在頃刻之間，琴聲便聽不見了。眾人舉燈一照，發現天皇已然駕崩。

passages.text: Astonished and alarmed, they set him in a mortuary palace and made a great purification, seeking out all crimes - flaying alive and backwards, breaking rice-field divisions, filling ditches, fouling, and unions of superiors and inferiors, with horses, cattle, fowls and dogs. Take-uchi again requested the divine command, and the answer was the same: this land is to be ruled by the august child in the empress's womb, a male child, by the doing of the Great Heaven-Shining Deity and the three Possessing-Male deities.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 316-317 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 眾人驚愕惶恐，將他安置於殯宮之中，並舉行盛大的禊祓，遍查一切罪愆——活剝獸皮且倒剝、破壞田埂、填塞溝渠、污穢不潔，以及上下尊卑的苟合，並以馬、牛、雞、犬為祭。武內宿禰再次請求神諭，所得的答覆依然相同：這片土地當由皇后腹中的皇兒——一位男兒——來統治，此乃大日孁貴神與三位產靈神之所為。

title.en: Empress Jingu's Conquest of Shiragi
title.zh: 神功皇后征新羅

region.en: Shiragi/Silla (Gyeongju), Korea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新羅（慶州，象徵座標）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Following the deities' instructions, Empress Jingu scatters podocarpus ashes, chopsticks and chopped wands on the waves as sea-charms, and her fleet crosses on the backs of the fish of the sea-plain. The wave pushes up into the middle of Shiragi; its chieftain surrenders, promising horses and tribute forever, and Jingu plants her staff on his gate and installs the Rough August Spirits of Sumiye as guardians before returning.
summary.zh: 神功皇后依神敕，以竹木灰、箸、折枝散於海波為呪具，海中大小魚類負舟而渡，順風直入新羅國中。新羅王懼而降服，永為馬飼與貢船之國；皇后插御杖於其門，立住吉荒魂為鎮守神，而後歸國。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); this is a legendary conquest narrative with later nationalist readings, handled here as myth via public-domain paraphrase for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The deities instructed: present offerings to all the Heavenly, Earthly, mountain, river and sea deities, set the august spirits on the top of the vessel, put the ashes of the podocarpus tree into gourds, and make quantities of chopsticks and chopped material, scattering them all on the waves of the great sea so as to cross over. Jingu punctually fulfilled these instructions, equipped an army and marshalled her vessels.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 317-318 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 眾神指示：向所有天神、地祇、山神、河神與海神獻上供物，將御靈置於船首，把羅漢松樹的灰放入葫蘆中，並製作大量筷子與切碎的物料，將它們全數撒在大海的波浪上，以便渡海。神功皇后準時遵行了這些指示，裝備軍隊並整頓船隻。

passages.text: As she crossed, the fish of the sea-plain, both great and small, bore the august vessel across on their backs, a strong favourable wind arose, and the vessel followed the billows. The wave of the august vessel pushed up onto the land of Shiragi, reaching the middle of the country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 317-318 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當她渡海時，海原中的魚不分大小，皆以背負御船渡過，一陣強勁的順風興起，船隻隨波而行。御船的波浪推上了新羅的土地，直達國中。

passages.text: The chieftain of the country, alarmed and trembling, petitioned: 'From this time forward, obedient to the Heavenly Sovereign's commands, I will feed his august horses and will marshal vessels every year, never letting their keels or poles and oars dry, and will respectfully serve him without drawing back while heaven and earth shall last.' So Shiragi was made the feeder of the august horses and Kudara the crossing store.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 318-319 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 該國的首長驚惶顫抖，奏請道：『從今以後，我願順從天皇之命，餵養其御馬，並每年整備船隻，絕不讓船龍骨或篙槳乾燥，且在天長地久之間恭敬事奉，絕不退縮。』於是新羅成為御馬的餵養者，百濟則成為渡海的儲備。

passages.text: The Empress stuck her august staff on the gate of the chieftain of Shiragi, made the Rough August Spirits of the Great Deities of the Inlet of Sumiye the guardian deities of the land, laid them to rest, and crossed back to Tsukushi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 318-319 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 皇后將御杖插在新羅首長的門上，命住吉津大神們的荒御魂為該國的守護神，將其安頓下來，然後渡回筑紫。

title.en: Jingu Binds the Stone; the Birth at Umi
title.zh: 神功皇后束石生譽田別

region.en: Umi, Tsukushi (Fukuoka), Japan
region.zh: 宇美（筑紫）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: While the conquest of Shiragi is yet unfinished and the empress is heavy with child, she binds a stone about her skirt to restrain her womb, crosses back to Tsukushi, and gives birth at the place called Umi. At Tamashima she sits on a midstream shoal, picks threads from her skirt, and hooks trout with grains of rice - a custom still kept by women of the first decade of the fourth moon.
summary.zh: 征新羅事未竟而皇后有孕，乃取石繫於裙腰以束胎，渡歸筑紫，於宇美之地誕皇子。又於玉島里坐川中洲，抽裙線以米粒釣鱸，至今四月上旬婦女釣鱸之俗由此而來。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: While the business of Shiragi was yet unconcluded, the child with which the Empress Okinaga-tarashi was pregnant was about to be born. To restrain her august womb she took a stone and wound it round the waist of her august skirt, and so went on with the campaign; the stone is still to be seen at the village of Ito in the Land of Tsukushi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 319-320 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當新羅之事尚未了結時，息長足姬皇后所懷的孩子即將出生。為了抑制御胎，她取來一塊石頭，纏繞在御裙的腰間，如此繼續征戰；那塊石頭至今仍可在筑紫國伊都村見到。

passages.text: Only after she had crossed back to the Land of Tsukushi was the august child born, and the place was given the name Umi - the birth. The future emperor Homuda-wake had been carried through a foreign campaign in his mother's womb.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 319-320 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 直到她渡回筑紫國之後，御子才誕生，該地因而得名為「宇美」——即誕生之意。未來的應神天皇譽田別，是在母親腹中經歷了一場異國征戰。

passages.text: Later, reaching the village of Tamashima in the Department of Matsura in the first decade of the fourth moon, she partook of an august meal on the river bank, then sat on a shoal in the middle of the river, picked out threads from her august skirt, used grains of rice as bait, and hooked the trout. Down to the present time women in the first decade of the fourth moon pick threads from their skirts, use grains as bait, and hook trout after her example.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 320 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 其後，行至松浦縣玉島村，於四月上旬在河邊享用御膳，隨即坐於河中之洲，從御裳上抽出線縷，以米粒為餌，釣取鱒魚。直至今日，女子於四月上旬抽裳線、以米粒為餌、釣鱒魚，皆仿其例。

title.en: The Mourning-Vessel Ruse: Kagosaka and Oshikuma
title.zh: 喪船之計：香坂王與忍熊王之亂

region.en: Naniwa to Yamashiro, Japan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 難波至山城（象徵座標）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Returning to Yamato, Jingu spreads a rumour that her newborn prince is dead, setting her child in a mourning-vessel. The princes Kagosaka and Oshikuma rise in revolt; a boar devours Kagosaka during an omen hunt; Oshikuma's forces are broken by a false-surrender trick of snapping bowstrings, and the prince and his general plunge together into the sea singing.
summary.zh: 神功皇后歸大和，恐人心不服，設喪船載皇子而謠傳皇子已死。香坂王、忍熊王聞而叛；香坂王出獵占兆，遭大豬連根拔櫟樹吞之。忍熊王據兵相抗，武內宿禰之將折弦詐降，敵解弓而遭伏擊潰敗；忍熊王與將領伊佐比臣同赴海而歌，相抱投海而死。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Returning up to Yamato, Princess Okinaga-tarashi, doubting the disposition of the people, prepared a mourning-vessel, set the august child in it, and let a report ooze out that the child was already dead. King Kagosaka and King Oshikuma, sons of the late emperor, heard of it and thought to waylay her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 321-322 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 還上倭地，息長帶日女命疑人心之向背，乃備喪船，置御子於其中，並散佈御子已死之說。先帝之子香坂王與忍熊王聞之，思欲中途截擊。

passages.text: At the moor of Toga they hunted for an omen: King Kagosaka climbed an oak-tree, whereupon a large angry boar came forth, dug up the tree, and devoured him. His younger brother Oshikuma, undaunted, raised an army to close with the mourning-vessel as an empty vessel.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 321-322 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於門賀之泊卜求兆驗：香坂王攀上橡樹，忽有大怒之野豬出現，掘倒其樹而噬食之。其弟忍熊王不為所懼，興兵欲以喪船為空船而迫近之。

passages.text: An army was landed from the mourning-vessel and fought the rebels back to Yamashiro, where both sides stood without retreating. Then Take-furu-kuma planned: it was spread abroad that the Empress was already dead and there was no need for further fighting, and his men snapped their bowstrings, feigning submission. Believing the falsehood, Oshikuma's men unbent their bows and put away their arms - whereupon the empress's troops drew prepared bowstrings from their topknots, re-stretched their bows, and pursued and smote them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 321-322 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 自喪船登陸之軍與叛軍交戰，逐之至山背，兩軍相持，皆無退意。時武振熊設謀：揚言皇后已死，無須再戰，其眾乃斷弓弦，佯示歸順。忍熊王之眾信其虛言，遂解弓弛弦、收斂兵器——於是皇后之軍自髮髻中取出預藏之弓弦，重新張弓，追擊而破之。

passages.text: The rebels rallied at Afusaka and were defeated again at Sasanami. King Oshikuma and the Noble Isahi, pursued and pressed, got aboard a vessel, floated on the sea, sang a song of their fate, and together plunged into the water and died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 322-323 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 叛眾聚於阿夫坂，又於狹波遭敗。忍熊王與難波吉師被追逼，登船浮於海上，歌其命運之歌，遂共投水而死。

title.en: The Name-Exchange Deity and the Broken-Nosed Dolphins
title.zh: 伊紗自氣神換名與海豚獻食

region.en: Tsunuga beach, Echizen (Fukui), Japan
region.zh: 敦賀之浦（越前）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Taking the Heir Apparent Homuda-wake for purification through Afumi and Wakasa, Take-uchi halts at Tsunuga, where the local deity Izasa-wake appears in a dream asking to exchange names. The shore is found lined with broken-nosed dolphin-fishes as the deity's thank-offering, the child grants him the name Great Deity of August Food, and the blood-stinking strand is called Chiura.
summary.zh: 武內宿禰攜譽田別皇子經近江、若狹行祓，宿於敦賀。伊紗自氣神夜夢求與皇子換名，翌晨海濱盡是破鼻海豚，為神之謝禮。皇子賜神名「御食津神」，海豚鼻血腥臭之浦遂名血浦，今稱敦賀。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Noble Take-uchi, taking with him the Heir Apparent for the purpose of purification, passed through the lands of Afumi and Wakasa and built a temporary palace at Tsunuga at the mouth of the Road of Koshi for the child to dwell in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 323-324 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 武內宿禰攜皇太子以行祓禊，經近江、若狹之地，於越之道口角鹿建臨時宮殿，使御子居之。

passages.text: There the Great Deity Izasa-wake, who dwelt in that place, appeared at night in a dream: 'I wish to exchange my name for the august name of the august child.' The answer was reverently given that the name should be exchanged, and the deity charged: 'To-morrow morning the Heir Apparent must go out on the beach; I will present my thank-offering for the name given me in exchange.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 323-324 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當地所居之大神伊邪佐和氣，夜間現於夢中曰：「吾欲以吾名易皇太子之尊名。」答以當敬易其名，神乃囑曰：「明日晨，皇太子須出至海濱；吾將以易名之謝禮獻上。」

passages.text: When the child went out in the morning, the whole shore was lined with broken-nosed dolphin-fishes. He caused the deity to be addressed: 'Thou bestowest on me fish of thine august food' - and so again his august name was honoured by his being called the Great Deity of August Food, styled today the Food-Wondrous-Great-Deity. The blood from the dolphins' noses stank, so the strand was called Chiura, now Tsunuga.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 323-324 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 及晨，童子出，見濱岸盡列破鼻之海豚。乃使人告神曰：「汝以汝之御食之魚賜我。」於是其尊名復得尊崇，稱之為御食大神，今號食物奇偉大神。海豚鼻中之血臭甚，故其濱名曰血浦，今為敦賀。

title.en: Oho-sazaki's Answer and the Kohata Maiden
title.zh: 大雀命之對與木幡稚女

region.en: Uji moor, Afumi (Lake Biwa area), Japan
region.zh: 宇治野（近江）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: Emperor Homuda (Ojin) asks his sons which is dearer, elder or younger child. Oho-sazaki answers that the younger, still a child, is dearer, matching his father's thought; the succession is arranged accordingly. On a progress to Kohata the emperor meets the maiden Miya-nushi-ya-kaha-ye, is entertained in her decorated house, and weds her, singing.
summary.zh: 譽田天皇問二子：長子與次子孰親？大雀命答以年幼之次子為親，暗合天皇之意，遂定傳位之制。後天皇幸近江，於木幡里遇稚女三室屋娘，其父飾屋以待，天皇娶之而歌。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign Homuda asked his sons Oho-yama-mori and Oho-sazaki: 'Which think ye dearer, an elder child or a younger child?' Oho-yama-mori said the elder; Oho-sazaki, divining the feeling behind the question, answered that the elder, already a man, gives no trouble, but the younger, not yet a man, is the dearer. 'My lord Sazaki's words agree with my thoughts,' said the emperor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 330-331 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天津日嗣譽田天皇問其子大兄山守與大鷦鷯曰：「汝等以為長子與幼子，孰為可愛？」大兄山守曰長子；大鷦鷯則窺知問意所在，答曰：「長子既已成丁，無所煩憂；幼子尚未成丁，故為可愛。」天皇曰：「鷦鷯卿之言，合吾意也。」

passages.text: The inheritance was divided accordingly: Oho-yama-mori to administer the government of the mountains and sea, Oho-sazaki to take charge of the government of the realm, and Uji-no-waki-iratsuko to rule the succession of Heaven's sun - and Oho-sazaki was not disobedient to the commands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 330-331 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是分定繼承：大兄山守掌山海之政，大鷦鷯主國政，菟道稚郎子嗣天日之緒——而大鷦鷯不違命。

passages.text: One day, standing on the moor of Uji and gazing at the moor of Kadzu, the emperor sang of the lands spread before him. At the village of Kohata a beautiful maiden met him at a fork in the road: 'I am the daughter of the Grandee Wani-no-Hifure, and my name is Princess Miya-nushi-ya-kaha-ye.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 330-331 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一日，天皇立於菟道野，望葛野，歌其所臨之地。至木幡村，有美女迎於路歧：「吾乃和邇臣日觸之女，名曰宮主八河江媛。」

passages.text: Promising to enter her house on his return, he came the next day; her father, grandly decorating the house, served a great feast, and the maiden presented the great august liquor-cup. The emperor sang in her praise, cohabited with her, and begot the child Uji-no-waki-iratsuko.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 331-333 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天皇許以歸途入其家，翌日果至；其父盛飾其宅，設大宴，少女親奉大御酒盞。天皇歌以讚之，與之同居，而生菟道稚郎子。

title.en: The Grant of Princess Kami-naga
title.zh: 賜神長媛

region.en: Naniwa port (Osaka), Japan
region.zh: 難波（大阪）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: The emperor sends for the beautiful Princess Kami-naga of Himuka; his son the Heir Apparent Oho-sazaki sees her land at Naniwa, falls in love, and begs her through the Prime Minister. The emperor, feasting, sings of the maiden as a mid-tree orange, and bestows her on his son, who sings his joy.
summary.zh: 天皇徵日向縣主之神長媛；太子大雀命見其泊於難波之港，心動，託武內宿禰求之。天皇宴上歌詠少女如橘中實，遂以其女賜太子，太子亦歌以謝。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign, hearing of the beauty of Princess Kami-naga, daughter of the Duke of Muragata in the land of Himuka, thought to employ her at court and sent down for her. Word of the maiden's arrival ran through the palace, and before he could take her for himself, his eldest son saw her first.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 333-335 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天皇聽聞日向國村方郡守之女神長姬貌美，欲納之於宮中，遂遣使召之。少女入宮之事傳遍宮中，天皇尚未及納之，其長子已先見之。

passages.text: But the Heir Apparent Oho-sazaki, seeing the maiden land at the port of Naniha and charmed with her grace, directed the Prime Minister, the Noble Take-uchi, to intercede for him, and the Heavenly Sovereign forthwith granted Princess Kami-naga to his august child.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 333-335 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然皇太子大鷦鷯見少女自難波港登陸，悅其容儀，乃命大臣武內宿禰為之通意，天皇遂以神長姬賜其皇子。
