passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book V, §§8–9 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天皇頒詔天下，尋求大田田根子，於茅渟縣陶邑得之。問其為誰之子，答曰：「我父名曰大物主大神；我母名曰活玉依媛。」天皇曰：「今我等當得昌盛。」祭祀之器由八十物部之手製作，大田田根子被任命為大物主神之祭主，長尾市被任命為倭大國魂神之祭主。八十萬神各別祭祀，定天神地祇之社，並分置田地與屋舍以供神事。於是疾疫止息，國內安寧，五穀豐登，百姓富足。

passages.text: In the eighth year the brewer Ikuhi was appointed to the Great Deity, and when Oho-tata-neko worshipped the Great Deity, Ikuhi in person presented sacred sake to the Emperor with a song: 'This sacred sake is not my sacred sake: 'tis sacred sake brewed by Oho-mono-nushi of Yamato - how long ago! how long ago!' (a pun on the brewer's own name). Having sung, they feasted in the shrine of the God, and afterwards the high officials and the Emperor answered with songs about the morning-door of the Hall of Miwa, of sweet sake fame; so the door of the shrine was thrown open and the Emperor proceeded on his way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book V, §10 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 八年，釀酒者活日被任命侍奉大神，當大田田根子祭祀大神時，活日親自獻神酒於天皇，並歌曰：「此神酒非我之神酒：乃大和之大物主所釀之神酒——何其久遠！何其久遠！」（此乃以釀酒者己名為雙關之諧音）。歌畢，眾人在神宮中宴飲，其後群臣與天皇以三輪殿之朝門、美酒之名的和歌相答；於是神宮之門大開，天皇啟程前行。

title.en: The Four Generals of the Roads and the Maiden's Warning Song
title.zh: 崇神遣四道將軍與少女警世之歌

region.en: Wani acclivity, Yamashiro
region.zh: 山城和邇坂

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Sujin sends four generals with seals and ribbons to the four quarters - Oho-hiko to the north, Takenu-kaha-wake to the Eastern Sea, Kibi-tsu-hiko to the western road, Tamba-no-chi-nushi to Tamba. At the Wani acclivity Oho-hiko hears a roadside maiden sing a song warning that some are stealthily preparing to cut the thread of the Emperor's life; she vanishes, and the shrewd Yamato-toto-hi-momoso-hime reads the omen as Take-hani-yasu's coming treason and orders the generals recalled.
summary.zh: 崇神天皇十年，詔選群臣遣於四道，賜印綬為將軍：大彥命主北道，武渟川別主東海道，吉備津彥主西道，丹波道主命主丹波，誡曰「有不順者即擊之」。大彥命至和邇坂之上，見路旁少女歌曰「呀彌動高日!豈知竊防竊欲絕王命之緒，逍遙如少女者!」復詠而忽滅。跡跡日百襲姬命占之，知武埴安彥將謀反，其妻吾田媛已取香山土以咒國土，乃悉召四道將軍還。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi); passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Emperor proclaimed to his ministers that for the guidance of the people the chief thing is education: the distant savages did not yet receive the calendar, being unaccustomed to the civilizing influences of rule, so ministers would be sent to the four quarters to make the Imperial Will known. He sent Oho-hiko no Mikoto to the northern region, Takenu-kaha-wake to the Eastern Sea, Kibi-tsu-hiko to the western road, and Tamba-no-chi-nushi no Mikoto to Tamba, addressing them: 'If there be any who do not receive our instructions, prepare war and smite them.' He granted them all alike seals and ribbons and appointed them generals; later, in winter, the four generals set out on their journeys simultaneously.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book V, §§12–13 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天皇向群臣宣告：引導百姓的首要之事在於教化。遠方的蠻夷尚未接受曆法，不習慣統治的教化影響，因此應派遣大臣前往四方，以昭示天皇的旨意。他派遣大彥命前往北方，武渟川別前往東海，吉備津彥前往西路，丹波道主命前往丹波，並對他們說：「若有不肯接受我們教令者，便整備軍隊討伐他們。」他賜予他們所有人同樣的印璽與綬帶，任命他們為將軍；後來在冬天，四位將軍同時踏上各自的旅程。

passages.text: Oho-hiko no Mikoto arrived at the top of the Wani acclivity - another version has the Hira-zaka acclivity in Yamashiro. There was by the road-side a young woman who sang: 'Ah! Prince Mimaki-iri! Unaware that some are stealthily preparing to cut the thread of thine own life, thou amusest thyself like a lady!' Wondering at this, Oho-hiko inquired what words these were; she answered that she was only singing, sang the song over again, and suddenly disappeared. Oho-hiko returned and reported the circumstances to the Emperor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book V, §14 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大彥命抵達和邇山坡的頂端——另一版本作山城國的平坂。路旁有一位年輕女子唱道：「啊！御間城入彥皇子！殊不知有人正暗中準備剪斷你自身的性命之線，你卻像女子一般自得其樂！」大彥命對此感到奇怪，便問這是什麼話；她回答說她只是在唱歌，又把那首歌重唱了一遍，然後忽然消失了。大彥命返回，將此事稟報天皇。

passages.text: Yamato-toto-hi-momoso-hime no Mikoto, the Emperor's aunt, a shrewd and intelligent person who could foresee the future, understood what was portended by the song, and told the Emperor that it was a sign that Take-hani-yasu-hiko was about to plot treason. 'I have heard,' she said, 'that Ata-bime, Take-hani-yasu-hiko's wife, came secretly and took earth from Mount Kako in Yamato, which she wrapped in her neckerchief and prayed over, saying: This earth represents the Land of Yamato - and turned it upside down. By this I know that there will be troubles. If thou dost not speedily take measures, it will assuredly be too late.' Hereupon the Emperor recalled all the generals and consulted with them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book V, §14 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天皇的姑母倭迹迹日百襲姬命是一位精明聰慧、能預知未來的人，她明白那首歌所預示的是什麼，便告訴天皇，這是武埴安彥即將圖謀叛亂的徵兆。她說：「我聽說武埴安彥的妻子阿多姬暗中前來，取了大和香下山上的土，用她的領巾包裹起來祈禱，說道：這土代表大和國——然後把它倒轉過來。由此我得知將有禍亂。你若不速速採取措施，必定為時已晚。」於是天皇召回所有將軍，與他們商議。

title.en: Yamato-toto-hime and the Snake Husband of Mount Mimoro
title.zh: 倭跡跡姬婚大物主蛇神，簪刺而崩

region.en: Mount Mimoro (Miwa), Yamato
region.zh: 大和三輪山

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Yamato-toto-hi-momoso-hime becomes the wife of Oho-mono-nushi, who visits her only by night. Begging to behold his majesty, she is told he will enter her toilet-case at dawn - where she finds a beautiful little snake the length of a garment-cord. She cries out in fright; the shamed god puts her to shame in turn, treads the Great Void and ascends Mount Mimoro. She stabs herself in remorse with a chopstick, and her tomb is built by men in the daytime and by gods at night.
summary.zh: 倭跡跡日百襲姬命為大物主神之妻。神惟夜至，不見晝形。姬曰「願得仰覩尊之威容」，神許以朝入其櫛笥。姬旦視笥中，見小蛇，其色如錦續子，長大如衣緒，大驚而叫。神慚，忽化人形，語其妻曰「汝不慎忍，令我羞恥；我還令汝知恥」，遂踏大虛，登三輪山而止。姬仰而悔之，則於座上以箸撞陰而死，葬大市。時人號其墓曰箸墓。墓晝人作、夜神作，運大坂山石築之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi): the serpent-husband episode of the Miwa cult, a standard snake-suit motif in comparative mythology; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: After this Yamato-toto-hi-momoso-hime no Mikoto became the wife of Oho-mono-nushi no Kami. This God, however, was never seen in the daytime, but came at night. Yamato-toto-hime said to her husband: 'As my Lord is never seen in the daytime, I am unable to view his august countenance distinctly. I beseech him to delay a while, that in the morning I may look upon the majesty of his beauty.' The Great God answered: 'What thou sayest is clearly right. To-morrow morning I will enter thy toilet-case and stay there. I pray thee be not alarmed at my form.' She wondered secretly at this, and waiting until daybreak, looked into her toilet-case. There was there a beautiful little snake, of the length and thickness of the cord of a garment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book V, §17 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此後，倭迹迹日百襲姬命成為大物主神的妻子。然而這位神白天從不露面，只在夜間前來。倭迹迹日姬對她的丈夫說：「既然我的夫君白天從不露面，我便無法清楚地瞻仰他尊貴的容顏。我懇求他稍作停留，好讓我在早晨能一睹他美好的威儀。」大神回答說：「你所說的確實有理。明早我將進入你的梳妝盒中待在那裡。我祈求你不要對我的形貌感到驚慌。」她暗自對此感到奇怪，等到天亮，便往梳妝盒裡看。那裡有一條美麗的小蛇，長短粗細如同一條衣帶。

passages.text: Thereupon she was frightened and uttered an exclamation. The Great God was ashamed, and changing suddenly into human form, spoke to his wife: 'Thou didst not contain thyself, but hast caused me shame. I will in my turn put thee to shame.' So treading the Great Void, he ascended to Mount Mimoro. Yamato-toto-hime looked up and had remorse. She flopped down on a seat and with a chopstick stabbed herself in the pudenda so that she died. She was buried at Oho-chi, and the men of that time called her tomb the Hashi no haka, the Chopstick Tomb.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book V, §17 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是 she 驚嚇不已，發出了一聲驚叫。大神感到羞愧，忽然變成人形，對他的妻子說：「你未能克制自己，反而使我蒙羞。我也要反過來使你蒙羞。」於是他踏著大虛，升上了三諸山。倭迹迹日姬仰望而去，心生悔恨。她跌坐在座位上，用一根筷子刺入自己的下體而死。她被葬於大市，當時的人們稱她的墓為「箸墓」。

passages.text: This tomb was made by men in the daytime and by Gods at night. It was built of stones carried from Mount Oho-saka, the people standing close to each other and passing the stones from hand to hand from the mountain to the tomb. The men of that time made a song about this: 'If one passed from hand to hand the rocks built up on Oho-saka, how hard 'twould be to send them!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book V, §17 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這座墓白天由人建造，夜間由神建造。它由從大坂山運來的石頭砌成，人們緊挨著彼此站立，把石頭從山上逐手傳遞到墓前。當時的人們為此作了一首歌：「若能將堆砌在大坂上的岩石逐手傳遞，要送過去該有多難啊！」

title.en: The White Stone Becomes a Maiden: Arashito's Lost Divine Bride
title.zh: 白石化麗姬：阿羅斯等失神女

region.en: Kara (southern Korea) and Naniha (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 加耶與浪速（象徵錨點）

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: A variant account of Arashito: when villagers slaughter his lost ox, an old man advises him to demand not treasures but the god of the village - a white stone. Carried home, the stone becomes a beautiful maiden; while he is away she vanishes eastwards, and drifting far over the sea he arrives in Japan following her. The maiden becomes the Deity of the Himegoso shrines at Naniha and in the Land of Toyo.
summary.zh: 一說：都怒我阿羅斯等在本國以牛載田器而行，牛忽亡。跡入一村，村人宰牛欲食之，一老人教之曰「求償勿求珍寶，但求其村所祭之神」。其神乃白石化之。持歸寢室，忽化為美好少女。阿羅斯等欲婚之，暫離其間，女忽遁而東去。逐之，漂流泛海，遂至日本。女至浪速為比古佐之神，又至豐國許岐山，亦為比古佐之神，兩所祀之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi); passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: In the beginning, when Tsunoga-arashito was still in his own land, he went into the country with an ox loaded with implements of husbandry. The ox suddenly disappeared, and seeking for it by its tracks, he found that the foot-prints ceased in a certain village. An old man there told him that the village chiefs had slain and eaten the ox to use the implements, and instructed him: 'If thou art asked what thing thou desirest as the price of the ox, do not ask for treasures, but say that thou wishest to have the God worshipped by the village.' The God whom they worshipped was a white stone. So they gave the white stone to the owner of the ox, and he brought it away with him and placed it in his bed-chamber.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §6 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 起初，當津野賀荒人還在自己的國土時，他帶著一頭載著農具的牛進入鄉間。那頭牛忽然不見了，他循著足跡尋找，發現足跡在某個村落裡斷了。那裡的一位老人告訴他，村中的首長們已殺了那頭牛並吃了牠，好取用那些農具，又囑咐他道：「若有人問你想要什麼作為這頭牛的代價，切勿求取財寶，只說你希望能得到這村所祭祀的神。」他們所祭祀的神是一塊白石。於是他們把那塊白石給了牛的主人，他便帶著它離去，將它安置在自己的臥室之中。

passages.text: This divine stone became changed into a beautiful maiden, upon which Arashito was greatly rejoiced and wished to be united to her. But while he was away in another place the maiden suddenly disappeared. Arashito was greatly alarmed, and inquired of his wife where the maiden had gone; she replied that she had gone towards the East. So he went in search of her, and at length, drifting far over the sea, he thus arrived in Japan. The maiden whom he sought came to Naniha, where she became the Deity of the Himegoso shrine; then proceeding to the district of Kusaki in the Land of Toyo, she afterwards became the Deity of the Himegoso shrine there. She is worshipped in both these places.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §6 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這塊神石化作了一位美麗的少女，荒人見了大為歡喜，想要與她結合。但當他遠赴他處時，那少女忽然不見了。荒人大為驚慌，問他的妻子少女去了何處；她回答說少女已往東方去了。於是他就去尋找她，終於漂洋過海，遠遠地來到了日本。他所尋覓的那位少女來到了難波，在那裡成了姬社神社的神；隨後又前往豐國楠木郡，後來便成了當地姬社神社的神。這兩處地方都祭祀她。

title.en: Ama-no-hi-hoko Brings the Divine Treasures of Silla
title.zh: 天日槍獻新羅寶物

region.en: Harima and Tajima (Sea of Japan coast)
region.zh: 播磨與但馬

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Ama-no-hi-hoko, son of the King of Silla, gives his realm to his younger brother and sails to Japan with seven (or eight) treasures - gems, sun-mirror, Idzushi sword and spear, and a Kuma-himorogi. Allowed to seek his own dwelling, he tours by way of Lake Biwa and Wakasa and settles in Tajima; the potters of Kagami become his servants, and through his wife Matawo he becomes great-grandfather of Tajima-mori.
summary.zh: 垂仁天皇三年，新羅王子天日槍來。獻寶物七種（一說八種）：葉細珠、足高珠、鹿石赤石珠、出石短劍、出石槍、日鏡、熊神籬（及伊莎莎刀）。帝命擇播磨宍鹿或淡路出島而居，天日槍請自遊行諸國擇所愿之地，歷近江、若狹而定居但馬。近江鏡谷土師皆其奴。娶出石真緋女，四世而至田道間守。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi) on the Korean (Silla) transmission of cult objects to Japan; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Silla prince, Ama-no-hi-hoko, arrived, bringing seven objects in all: one Ha-buto gem, one Ashi-daka gem, one red-stone Ukaka gem, one Idzushi short sword, one Idzushi spear, one sun-mirror, and one Kuma-himorogi. These were stored in the Land of Tajima and made divine things for ever.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §7 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 新羅王子天日槍抵達，一共帶來七件物品：一枚羽太玉、一枚足高玉、一枚赤石起玉、一口出石小刀、一柄出石槍、一面日鏡，以及一具熊神籬。這些都被存放在但馬國，永遠作為神聖之物。

passages.text: One version says that in the beginning Ama-no-hi-hoko, riding in a ship, anchored at the land of Harima and dwelt in the village of Shisaha. Inquired who he was, he answered that he was the son of the King of Silla: hearing that in the Land of Japan there was a sage monarch, he had given his country to his younger brother Chiko and come to offer his allegiance with his treasures. The Emperor gave orders that he should dwell in Shisaha in Harima or Idesa in the island of Ahaji at his pleasure. Ama-no-hi-hoko asked that he might himself visit the various provinces to seek the place agreeable to his mind; ascending the river Uji he went north to the village of Ana in Ohomi, proceeded through Wakasa, and going westward arrived at the province of Tajima, where he fixed his dwelling. Therefore the potters of Kagami-no-hasama in Ohomi are the servants of Ama-no-hi-hoko. Ama-no-hi-hoko took to wife Matawo, daughter of Futomimi, a man of Idzushi in Tajima, who bore to him Tajima Morosuke - father of Tajima-no-Hinaraki, father of Kiyohiko, father of Tajima-mori.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §7 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一說法謂：起初天日槍乘船而來，停泊於播磨國，住在志佐波村。有人問他是何人，他回答說自己是新羅國王的兒子：聽說日本國有一位聖明的君主，便把自己的國家讓給弟弟知古，帶著財寶前來歸順。天皇下令讓他隨意住在播磨的志佐波，或淡路島的出淺。天日槍請求讓他親自巡訪各國，尋覓合他心意的地方；他溯宇治川而上，北行至近江的穴村，經過若狹，再向西行抵達但馬國，便在那裡定居下來。因此，近江鏡間村的陶工是天日槍的僕役。天日槍娶了但馬出石人太耳之女麻多烏為妻，她為他生下了但馬諸助——但馬日名杵之父，清彥之父，但馬守之父。

title.en: Sahohiko's Treason and the Rice-Castle of Fire
title.zh: 沙本毘古之叛與稻城之火

region.en: Makimuku, Yamato
region.zh: 大和纏向

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: The Empress's brother Sahohiko asks whom she loves best and entreats her to murder Suinin with a hidden dagger. As she bends over her sleeping husband her tears fall on his face; his dream of a brocade snake coiled round his neck and rain from Saho wrings the whole plot from her. Sahohiko resists a month in a castle of piled rice-stalks; the Empress enters with her child to plead for his life, leaves as it burns, and dies with her brother, recommending five ladies of Tamba to the Emperor.
summary.zh: 垂仁后沙本姬之兄沙本毘古欲弒帝，誘妹曰「汝愛兄與夫孰深」，予小刀使藏於衣，伺帝寢而刺其頸。姬泣於帝膝枕之側，帝覺而占夢曰「錦蛇繞頸，大雨自沙本潦面」，姬懼而盡吐其情。帝曰「非汝罪」，起兵遣筒田連田狹命誅沙本毘古。毘古積稻作稻城而拒，一月不拔。后抱皇子入稻城，帝圍之益急，趣送后與皇子出。后曰「臣妾罪當死，但願以妾所主之五后宮宅奉帝」，言訖，於烈火中與兄俱死。其后丹波有五女，皆賢，後召入後宮。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi); passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Empress's elder brother by the mother's side, Prince Sahohiko, plotted treason and tried to endanger the State. Watching an occasion when the Empress was at leisure, he asked her whom she loved best - her elder brother or her husband - and she innocently answered, her elder brother. Then he enticed her: 'If one serves a man by beauty, when the beauty fades his affection will cease... I wish to ascend to the immense felicity and rule over the Empire along with thee. So making high our pillows, we shall complete a long hundred years. I beg thee, therefore, to slay the Emperor for me.' He took a dagger and gave it to the Empress: 'Gird on this dagger among thy garments, and when the Emperor goes to sleep, do thou stab him in the neck and thus kill him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §§8–9 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 皇后的同母兄長佐保彥王圖謀叛逆，想要危害國家。他窺伺皇后閒暇之時，問她最愛的是誰——是兄長還是丈夫——她天真地回答說是兄長。於是他誘惑她道：「若有人以美貌侍奉男子，美貌一旦衰減，他的情意便會斷絕……我希望能登上無上的福運，與你一同統治天下。如此我們便可高枕無憂，共度百年長壽。因此，我求你為我殺了天皇。」他取出一把短刀交給皇后：「把這短刀佩在衣裳之內，等天皇入睡時，你就刺他的頸項，將他殺死。」

passages.text: The Emperor took his noonday sleep with the Empress's knees as his pillow. She thought vainly that this would be the time to accomplish her brother's plot, and her tears fell on the Emperor's face. He woke and said: 'To-day We have had a dream. A small brocade-coloured snake coiled itself round Our neck and a great rain arose from Saho, which coming hither wet Our face. What does this portend?' Knowing she could not conceal the plot, she bowed herself to the earth and told him all: the small brocade-coloured snake is nothing else than the dagger given her; the great rain is her own tears. The Emperor said, 'This is not thy crime', raised a force from the neighbouring districts, and commanded Yatsunada to slay Sahohiko.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §§9–10 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天皇午睡時，以皇后的膝為枕。她徒然地想著，這正是實現兄長計謀的時機，淚水便落在了天皇的臉上。他醒來說道：「今日我做了一個夢。一條錦色的小蛇盤繞在我的頸上，又從佐保降下大雨，落到這裡淋濕了我的臉。這預示著什麼？」皇后知道自己無法隱瞞這計謀，便伏地叩首，將一切告訴了他：那條錦色的小蛇不是別的，正是給她的那把短刀；那場大雨便是她自己的眼淚。天皇說：「這不是你的罪過。」便從鄰近各郡調集兵力，命令八綱田誅殺佐保彥。

passages.text: Sahohiko withstood him with an army, hastily piling up rice-stalks to make a castle so solid it could not be breached - a rice-castle. A month passed and it did not surrender. The Empress, grieving, said that though she was Empress she could not preside over the Empire after bringing ruin on her brother; she took the Imperial Prince Homutsu-wake in her arms and entered the rice-castle. The Emperor increased his army, surrounded the castle on all sides, and proclaimed to those within to send out the Empress and Prince quickly, but they would not. So the general Yatsunada set fire to the castle. The Empress, taking the child in her bosom, crossed over the castle and came out, beseeching the Emperor: her flight into the castle had been in hope of absolving her brother for her sake; that failing, there was nothing for her but to strangle herself - only she prayed that her palace be granted to fair mates for him, and that five virtuous ladies, daughters of Prince Michi-no-Ushi of Tamba, be placed in the side courts. To this the Emperor agreed; then the fire blazed up, the castle was destroyed, and Sahohiko and his younger sister died together inside it. Yatsunada was commended and granted the new name Yamato-hi-muke-take-hi-muke-hiko.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §10 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 狹穗彥以軍隊抵抗他，匆忙堆起稻稈築成一座堅固得無法攻破的城——稻城。過了一個月，城仍未投降。皇后悲傷地說，她雖身為皇后，卻使自己的兄長遭致毀滅，此後無法再統治帝國；她抱起皇太子譽津別，進入稻城。天皇增派軍隊，從四面圍住此城，並向城內宣告，要他們速速交出皇后與皇子，但他們不肯。於是將軍八綱田放火燒城。皇后將孩子抱在懷中，越過城牆出來，向天皇懇求：她進入城內，本是希望兄長能因她的緣故而獲赦免；此事既已不成，她除了自縊之外別無他法——只祈求將她的宮殿賜予兄長的美貌伴侶，並將丹波道主王之女五位賢淑女子安置於側宮。天皇應允了此事；隨後火勢大起，城被焚毀，狹穗彥與其妹一同死於其中。八綱田受到褒獎，並獲賜新名倭日向武日向彥。

passages.text: In the fifteenth year the five women of Tamba were sent for and placed in the side-court: Hibasu-hime, Nuba-tani-iri-hime, Matonu-hime, Azami-ni-iri-hime, and Takano-hime. Hibasu-hime was appointed Empress and her three younger sisters made concubines; Takano-hime, on account of the ugliness of her form, was sent back to her own country. In her shame at being sent back, when she came to Kadono she purposely tumbled from the carriage and was killed; therefore that place received the name of Ochi-kuni, Fall-country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §15 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 十五年，天皇遣人迎來丹波五位女子，安置於側宮：日葉酢媛、渟葉田瓊入媛、真砥野媛、薊瓊入媛與高野媛。日葉酢媛被立為皇后，其三位妹妹則為妃；高野媛因容貌醜陋，被遣返本國。她因被遣返而感到羞恥，來到葛野時，故意從車上跌落而死；因此該地得名為墮國，即「跌落之國」。

title.en: Nomi no Sukune and Kuyehaya: The First Wrestling-Match
title.zh: 野見宿禰與當麻蹶速相撲

region.en: Daini district (Taima), Yamato
region.zh: 大和當麻

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: The courtiers report a champion of the Empire, Kuyehaya of Taima, who can break horns and straighten hooks and challenges all comers. A minister recalls the valiant Nomi no Sukune of Idzumo; the two men stand opposite and kick at each other until Sukune breaks Kuyehaya's ribs and loins and kills him. Taima's land is seized and given to Sukune, and the field of the broken loins keeps its name - the origin of sumo.
summary.zh: 垂仁七年，人奏當麻蹶速力絕人，能折角勾曲，揚言四海之內莫己若者，欲得力者比試生死。帝問群臣，有奏「出雲國有野見宿禰，宜召而試之」。即遣使者召之。二人相對踢蹴，宿禰踢蹶速脅而折其肋，又踢而折其腰，遂殺之。取其地悉賜宿禰，故其地有腰折田之名。是為相撲之始。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi): the legendary origin of sumo wrestling; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The courtiers represented to the Emperor: 'In the village of Taima there is a valiant man called Kuyehaya of Taima. He is of great bodily strength, so that he can break horns and straighten out hooks. He is always saying to the people: You may search the four quarters, but where is there one to compare with me in strength? O that I could meet with a man of might, with whom to have a trial of strength, regardless of life or death.' Hearing this, the Emperor proclaimed to his ministers that Kuyehaya was the champion of the Empire and asked if there might be any to compare with him. One of the ministers came forward and said that in the Land of Idzumo there was a valiant man named Nomi no Sukune, whom it would be desirable to send for and match with Kuyehaya.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §12 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 朝臣們向天皇稟奏：「當麻村有一位勇士，名叫當麻蹶速。他體格強壯，力大無窮，能折斷獸角、扳直鐵鉤。他常對人說：你們儘管遍尋四方，何處有人能與我比力？但願我能遇到一位力士，與他較量力氣，生死不論。」天皇聽聞此事，便向群臣宣告蹶速乃天下無敵，並詢問是否有人能與他相比。一位大臣上前說道，出雲國有位勇士名叫野見宿禰，宜召他前來與蹶速較量。

passages.text: That same day the Emperor sent Nagaochi to summon Nomi no Sukune, who came from Idzumo, and straightway he and Taima no Kuyehaya were made to wrestle together. The two men stood opposite to one another; each raised his foot and kicked at the other, when Nomi no Sukune broke with a kick the ribs of Kuyehaya and also kicked and broke his loins, and thus killed him. Therefore the land of Taima no Kuyehaya was seized and was all given to Nomi no Sukune. This was the cause why there is in that village a place called Koshi-ore-da, the field of the broken loins. Nomi no Sukune remained and served the Emperor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §12 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同日，天皇派遣長生千召喚野見宿禰，宿禰自出雲前來，隨即命他與當麻蹶速相撲。二人相對而立，各自抬腳互踢，野見宿禰一腳踢斷蹶速的肋骨，又踢折其腰，因而致其於死。於是當麻蹶速的領地遭沒收，全數賜予野見宿禰。此即該村有地名「腰折田」之由來。野見宿禰留仕天皇。

title.en: The Living Burial of Yamato-hiko's Tomb
title.zh: 倭彥命陵活殉之慟

region.en: Tsukizaka in Musa, Yamato
region.zh: 大和身狹桃花鳥坂

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: When Yamato-hiko, the Emperor's brother, dies, his personal attendants are buried alive upright in the precinct of the tomb. For several days they do not die but weep and wail day and night until they rot, and dogs and crows eat them. Hearing the sound of their weeping, Suinin is grieved and decrees an end to the practice of following the dead - the story later generations attach to the age of Kōrei.
summary.zh: 垂仁二十八年，倭彥命崩，葬身狹桃花鳥坂。乃集其從僕數十人，悉生埋於陵域。數日不死，夜哭晝泣，遂腐而畢，犬烏聚而食之。帝聞哭聲，心甚哀慟，詔左右曰「生者殉死，甚可痛傷。古雖如此，何用追從？自今以後，議而止之」。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi) concerning junshi, the burial of attendants with their lord; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Yamato-hiko no Mikoto, the Emperor's younger brother by the mother's side, died, and was buried at Tsukizaka in Musa. Thereupon his personal attendants were assembled and were all buried alive upright in the precinct of the misasagi. For several days they died not, but wept and wailed day and night. At last they died and rotted. Dogs and crows gathered and ate them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §19 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天皇同母弟倭彥命去世，葬於牟狹的築坂。於是將其近侍召集起來，全數活埋於陵墓境內，直立而葬。他們數日未死，晝夜哭泣哀號。最後終於死去腐爛。犬與烏鴉聚集而來，啄食其屍。

passages.text: The Emperor, hearing the sound of their weeping and wailing, was grieved in heart, and commanded his high officers: 'It is a very painful thing to force those whom one has loved in life to follow him in death. Though it be an ancient custom, why follow it, if it is bad? From this time forward, take counsel so as to put a stop to the following of the dead.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §19 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天皇聽見他們的哭泣哀號之聲，心中悲傷，便命令其高官：「強迫生前所愛之人隨死者而去，實為極痛苦之事。雖為古來習俗，若屬惡俗，何必遵行？從今以後，宜商議辦法，廢止殉葬之風。」

title.en: Nomi no Sukune Substitutes Clay Figures for Living Men
title.zh: 野見宿禰造土偶代生人

region.en: Tomb of Hibasu-hime, Yamato
region.zh: 大和日葉酢媛命陵

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: When Empress Hibasu-hime dies, the abolished yet still-expected practice of following in death poses a problem. Nomi no Sukune proposes an expedient: he summons a hundred clay-workers' men from Idzumo and has them shape figures of men, horses and other objects. These haniwa are first set up at her tomb, and a decree orders clay figures, not harmed men, at all tumuli henceforth - and the Hashi no Muraji superintend imperial burials ever after.
summary.zh: 垂仁三十二年，日葉酢媛命崩。帝曰「從死之風不良已悟，今葬何宜？」野見宿禰進曰「於君之陵生埋人，非良，何傳後世？請進一事」。乃遣使自出雲召土師部工人百，自執作土牛馬等物以獻，曰「自今以後，以土物代生人，置於陵域，以為後世法」。帝大喜，命此土物曰埴輪。下詔「陵必置土物，無傷人」。宿禰獲賞，掌土師部，故土師連執掌帝葬至今。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi): the legendary origin of the haniwa clay figures; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Empress Hibasu-hime no Mikoto died. Some time before the burial, the Emperor commanded his Ministers: 'We have already recognized that the practice of following the dead is not good. What should now be done in performing this burial?' Thereupon Nomi no Sukune came forward and said: 'It is not good to bury living men upright at the tumulus of a prince. How can such a practice be handed down to posterity? I beg leave to propose an expedient which I will submit to Your Majesty.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §20 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 日葉酢媛命皇后崩逝。下葬之前若干時日，天皇詔諭群臣曰：「吾等已知殉死之習不善。今行此葬，當如何為之？」於是野見宿禰進言曰：「於皇子之陵墓生埋活人而立之，實為不善。如此之習，何以傳於後世？臣請獻一權宜之計，以奏於陛下。」

passages.text: He sent messengers to summon up from the Land of Idzumo a hundred men of the clay-workers' Be, and himself directed them to take clay and form therewith shapes of men, horses and various objects, which he presented to the Emperor: 'Henceforward let it be the law for future ages to substitute things of clay for living men, and to set them up at tumuli.' The Emperor was greatly rejoiced and commanded Nomi no Sukune: 'Thy expedient hath greatly pleased Our heart.' The things of clay were first set up at the tomb of Hibasu-hime, and a decree was issued: 'Henceforth these clay figures must be set up at tumuli: let not men be harmed.' Sukune was bountifully rewarded, received a kneading-place and the charge of the clay-workers' Be, and was thenceforth called Hashi no Omi; this was how it came to pass that the Hashi no Muraji superintend the burials of the Emperors.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §20 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 乃遣使者自出雲國徵召土師部百人，親自督率之，令取黏土，塑作人、馬及諸般器物之形，獻於天皇曰：「自今以後，當立為法，使後世以土物代活人，置於陵墓之上。」天皇大悅，詔野見宿禰曰：「卿之權宜之計，甚愜朕心。」土物初置於日葉酢媛之墓，乃下詔曰：「自今以後，此土偶當置於陵墓；不得傷害人命。」宿禰受賞優厚，獲賜埴場，並掌土師部之事，自此稱為土師臣；此即土師連掌理天皇葬儀之由來也。

title.en: Yamato-hime Carries Amaterasu to Ise of the Divine Wind
title.zh: 倭姬命奉天照大神祀伊勢

region.en: Ise (Isuzu river, Province of Ise)
region.zh: 伊勢國五十鈴川畔

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Amaterasu is taken from Toyo-suki-iri-hime and entrusted to the princess Yamato-hime, who wanders through Sasahata, Ohomi and Mino seeking a shrine, until the Great Goddess names the secluded and pleasant land of Ise of the divine wind as her dwelling. There an abstinence palace is built on the Isuzu. In a variant, the Emperor makes Yamato-hime his august staff offered to the Goddess. The Great God of Yamato also possesses a minister to rebuke Sujin's incomplete worship, and Nunaki-waka-hime is divined as priestess.
summary.zh: 垂仁二十五年三月，以天照大神自豐鍬入姬命傳於倭姬命。倭姬命求鎮坐之地，歷宇陀、近江、美濃而後至伊勢。大神託曰「神風伊勢者，常世之浪打寄之國，此地美哉，願居此」。乃奉齋於五十鈴川畔，建齋宮，是為伊勢齋宮之始。一說帝以倭姬為御杖，奉於天照大神。又大倭大國魂神託物部大磯城，諫帝祭祀不周，帝乃廣加奉祭。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi) on the founding of the Grand Shrine of Ise, sacred to living Shinto tradition; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Ama-terasu no Oho-kami was taken from Toyo-suki-iri-hime no Mikoto and entrusted to Yamato-hime no Mikoto. Yamato-hime sought for a place where she might enshrine the Great Goddess: she proceeded to Sasahata in Uda, then turning back entered the land of Ohomi, went round eastwards to Mino, and arrived in the province of Ise. Now Amaterasu instructed her: 'The province of Ise, of the divine wind, is the land whither repair the waves from the eternal world, the successive waves. It is a secluded and pleasant land. In this land I wish to dwell.' In compliance with this instruction a shrine was erected to her in the province of Ise, and an Abstinence Palace was built at Kaha-kami in Isuzu - the palace of Iso.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §17 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天照大神自豐鍬入姬命處取出，託付於倭姬命。倭姬命尋求可供奉祀大神之處：先至宇陀之佐佐波太，繼而折返入近江國，東行至美濃，終抵伊勢國。時天照大神誨之曰：「伊勢國者，神風之國，乃常世之浪、重浪歸來之國也。此地幽靜而可喜。吾願居於此國。」遵此誨命，乃於伊勢國為之建神社，並於五十鈴川上，即磯宮之處，營建齋宮。

passages.text: One story is that the Emperor made Yamato-hime no Mikoto his august staff, that is his assistant or deputy, and offered her to Amaterasu: she enshrined the Goddess at Idzu-kashi-no-Moto in Shiki and offered sacrifice, and thereafter, in compliance with the Goddess's instructions, removed in winter to the Palace of Watarahi in the province of Ise.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §17 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一說謂天皇以倭姬命為御杖，即其輔佐或代理，獻之於天照大神：倭姬命乃於磯城之出雲樫本奉祀大神並獻祭，其後遵大神之誨命，於冬遷至伊勢國度會宮。

passages.text: At this time the Great God of Yamato inspired Ohominakuchi no Sukune and admonished the Emperor by his mouth: 'At the time of the Great Beginning it was covenanted that Amaterasu should govern all the Plain of Heaven, and that her august Imperial descendants should hold absolute rule over the eighty spiritual beings of the Central Reed-plain Land. My personal tenure of the governance of the great land is already at an end. Although the late Emperor Mimaki maintained the worship of the Gods in Heaven and Earth, he failed to search out the root of the matter, wanting in thoroughness: therefore that Emperor was short-lived. Do thou show regret for his shortcomings and be watchful as to the ceremonies of worship; so thine august life will be long and the Empire will have peace.' By divination Nunaki-waka-hime was appointed to conduct the worship of the Great God of Yamato; her body being already emaciated and unfit to sacrifice, Nagaochi offered the sacrifices in her stead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VI, §17 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此時，大和之大神降諭於大物主櫛甕玉命，藉其口以誡天皇曰：「天地初闢之時，已有盟約：天照大神當治高天原，其皇孫當君臨葦原中國八十神靈。吾親掌大國之政，今已告終。先皇御間城雖奉祀天神地祇，然未能探其本源，有所疏漏：故彼天皇享壽不長。汝當追悔其闕失，慎於祭祀之禮；如是則汝之御壽長久，國家安寧。」乃以占卜任渟名城稚姬命主持大和之大神之祭祀；然其身體已羸弱，不堪獻祭，故長道彥代其獻祭。

title.en: The Ugly Boy Who Could Not Be Moved
title.zh: 撼不動之妖童

region.en: Nobleman's house, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢京貴族宅（象徵性定位）

period: Collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Awful Little Goblin', eBook #51002

summary.en: At a great feast in a nobleman's house an uncombed, ugly boy of fifteen appears in the women's quarters and will not go. Servants, then ten men with ropes, then giants with clubs try to move or crush him — he is like a rock fast in the earth, and the club-blows sound like reverberating thunder without turning a hair of him. The crowd, fearing this is not a man but a god, bow and supplicate until he gives a sarcastic smile, goes out of the gate and disappears. From that day the people of the house are taken ill; those who scolded him, tied him and pounded him all die within a few days. It was commonly held that the boy was the Too-uk Spirit.
summary.zh: 漢京貴族宴客，有垢面醜童忽然立於婦人房前，喝之不去。以繩縛、以巨木擊，皆如撼山擊卵，童子紋絲不動。眾懼，以為神，羅拜乞哀。童冷笑而出，旋杳。自是闔家及諸客相繼病歿。俗謂此即土尤之神云。

sensitivity.note: Goblin-visitor tale; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: There was an occasion for a celebration in the home of a nobleman of Seoul. In front of the women's quarters there suddenly appeared an uncombed, ugly-looking boy about fifteen years of age. One of the women guests sent a servant to reprimand him and put him out, but the boy stood stock-still with no word of reply.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Awful Little Goblin' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 漢城有一貴族之家，適逢喜慶之事。內院之前，忽現一蓬頭垢面、容貌醜陋之少年，年約十五。賓客中一婦人遣僕責之並逐之出，然少年兀立不動，未答一語。

passages.text: Several took hold of him to pull him, but he was like a fixed rock fast in the earth, absolutely immovable. They sent ten strong men with ropes to bind him, but like a giant mountain he remained fast; five or six giant fellows with clubs laid on with all their might, the sound of their pounding like reverberating thunder, yet not a hair did he turn, not a wink did he give. The crowd began to fear, saying, 'This is not a man, but a god,' so they entered the courtyard, one and all, and began to bow before him, joining their hands and supplicating earnestly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Awful Little Goblin' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有幾個人上前抓住他想把他拉走，他卻像牢牢嵌在地裡的磐石一般，紋絲不動。他們派了十個壯漢用繩索來捆他，他卻像一座大山般穩固不動；五六個巨漢拿著棍棒使盡全力打他，捶擊之聲如雷鳴迴盪，他卻連一根頭髮都沒轉動，連眼都不眨一下。眾人開始害怕，說道：「這不是人，是神。」於是他們一個接一個走進庭院，開始向他叩拜，拱手懇切地祈求。

passages.text: At last the boy gave a sarcastic smile, turned round, went out of the gate and disappeared. The company, frightened out of their wits, called off the feast. From that day on, the people of that house were taken ill, including host and guests; those who scolded him, those who tied him with ropes, those who pounded him, all died in a few days. It was commonly held that the boy was the Too-uk Spirit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Awful Little Goblin' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最後，那少年露出譏諷的一笑，轉過身，走出大門便消失了。眾人嚇得魂飛魄散，取消了宴席。從那天起，那戶人家的人接連染病，主人與賓客皆然；那些責罵他的人、那些用繩索捆他的人、那些捶打他的人，都在幾天內死去。人們普遍認為那少年就是禿翼神。

title.en: God's Way: The Lightning Strikes the Mother-Beater
title.zh: 天雷殛逆子

region.en: Buckwheat field outside a country town (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 郊野蕎麥田（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'God's Way', eBook #51002

summary.en: A man of fierce and ungovernable disposition beats his mother, who screams: 'Oh, God, why do you not strike dead this wicked man who beats his mother?' Thrusting his sickle through his belt he goes to reap buckwheat under a fine clear sky — until a dark fleck of cloud appears in mid-heaven and all the sky becomes black. Furious thunder follows; the villagers see in the field a man with lifted sickle trying to ward off the flashes, and when the storm clears they find the mother-beater struck dead and riven to pieces. God takes note of evil doers on this earth, and deals with them as they deserve.
summary.zh: 有悍夫常毆其母，母呼天曰：『天何不殛此逆子！』其人攜鐮往田刈蕎。晴空萬里，忽黑雲一點，頃刻天晦，雷雨大作。村人遙見田中一人舉鐮遮雷。雨霧往視，則逆子已遭雷殛，碎裂於地。天道報應，可不畏哉。

sensitivity.note: Moral exemplum of filial piety; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In a certain town there lived a man of fierce and ungovernable disposition, who in moments of anger used to beat his mother. One day, thus beaten, the parent screamed out, 'Oh, God, why do you not strike dead this wicked man who beats his mother?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'God's Way' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某鎮上住著一個性情凶暴、難以管束的人，他動怒時常毆打自己的母親。有一天，母親又遭毆打，便高聲喊道：「哦，神啊，你為何不劈死這個毆打母親的惡人呢？」

passages.text: The son thrust his sickle through his belt and went slowly off to the fields where he was engaged by a neighbour in reaping buckwheat. The day was fine and the sky beautifully clear, when suddenly a dark fleck of cloud appeared in mid-heaven, and a little later all the sky became black. Furious thunder followed, and rain came on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'God's Way' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兒子把鐮刀插在腰帶上，慢慢走向田間，在那裡受雇於鄰居收割蕎麥。天氣晴朗，天空一片澄澈，忽然天中央出現一小片烏雲，不久整個天空都黑了。接著雷聲大作，下起雨來。

passages.text: The village people looked out toward the field, where the flashes of lightning were specially noticeable; they seemed to see there a man with lifted sickle trying to ward them off. When the storm had cleared away, they went to see, and lo, they found the man who had beaten his mother struck dead and riven to pieces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'God's Way' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 村人朝田裡望去，那裡的閃電格外顯眼；他們似乎看見一個舉著鐮刀的人正試圖抵擋閃電。風暴過後，他們前去查看，只見那個毆打母親的人已被擊死，身體裂成碎片。

title.en: The Old Man in the Dream Beseeches for the Turtle
title.zh: 夢中老人乞龜

region.en: Lotus Lake near Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢京蓮池（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Old Man in the Dream', eBook #51002

summary.en: Kwon Jai, high in rank and given to sport, dreams that an old man bows low in tears: 'Sir, Minister Hong wishes to kill off me and all my posterity. Please save me — if you desist, Hong will give it up and I shall live and all mine.' A rap at the door wakes him: it is Hong, come to invite him to fish for turtles at Lotus Lake. Then Kwon knows the turtle appeared in the dream in the form of an old man, and declines, saying he is ill — and he learned later that Hong also did not go.
summary.zh: 權居士夢一老人泣拜曰：『洪公欲盡誅吾族，公救之。』覺而洪公適來邀，往蓮池釣龜。權悟夢中之老人即龜也，辭以疾。後聞洪公亦未往。

sensitivity.note: Animal-dream omen tale; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Kwon Jai was a man high in rank and well advanced in years, much given to sport and various kinds of pleasure. One night he had a dream, when an old man came to him, bowed low, and in tears said, 'Sir, Minister Hong wishes to kill off me and all my posterity. Please save me, won't you?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Old Man in the Dream' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 權宰是一位官高位顯、年事已高的人，十分喜好遊獵與各種享樂。一天夜裡，他做了一個夢，夢中一位老人來到他面前，深深鞠躬，流著淚說：「大人，洪大人想要殺死我和我所有的子孫。請您救救我，好嗎？」

passages.text: 'Hong will assuredly ask Your Excellency to help him. Desist from it, please, for if you do, Hong will give it up and I shall live and all mine,' said the old man. A little later there came a rap at the door, when Kwon awakened and asked, 'Who is there?' It was Hong, who that day had planned an excursion to Lotus Lake to fish for turtles, and now had come specially to invite Kwon to go with him. Then Kwon knew that the turtle had appeared to him in a dream in the form of an old man, so he declined, saying he was ill. It was learned later that Hong also did not go.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Old Man in the Dream' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 老人說：「洪必定會請大人幫他。請您千萬別答應，因為您若答應，洪就會放棄此事，如此我與我一家老小才能活命。」過了一會兒，門外傳來敲門聲，權醒來問道：「是誰？」來人正是洪；他當天計畫前往蓮花池捕龜，特地前來邀權同行。權這才明白，那隻龜曾化作老人出現在他夢中，於是推說自己有病而婉拒。後來得知，洪也沒有去。

title.en: Softy, the Priest Who Took the Floggings
title.zh: 軟和尚代刑

region.en: Pagoda Temple, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢京塔寺（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Perfect Priest', eBook #51002

summary.en: A priest called Namnu has perfected his ways in Buddhist doctrine: he undresses and gives his clothing to the cold, and everybody calls him Softy. Whenever he sees anyone sentenced to a flogging in the temple or official yamen, he invariably begs to take the culprit's place. At a great function at Pagoda Temple he tells Prince Hong of Yon-san, 'You are indeed a very great man,' takes a box on the ear, and laughs: 'Please, Hong, don't do that, it hurts! it hurts!' Before the Temple he looks at Prince Yi and says, 'I know your face, but I have forgotten your name. Oh, I remember now, you are Yi Sok-hyong' — to the scandal of the monastery priests, who hurry to apologize: 'Softy was born so, God made him so.'
summary.zh: 有僧曰南婁，戒行圓滿，遇寒者輒解衣衣之，人呼曰軟和尚。凡見受笞者必以身代。於塔寺大會中謂燕山君之子曰『公真偉人也』，被批頰，笑曰『勿爾，痛哉』。又於寺前直呼親王名諱，僧眾大驚謝罪，曰『此天生如此，惟乞恕之』。

sensitivity.note: Holy-fool (holy fool/palmun) figure in Buddhist context; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: There was once a priest called Namnu who had perfected his ways in the Buddhistic doctrine. Whenever he had clothing of his own he would willingly undress and give it to those who were cold. His spirit was gentle, with no creases or corners in it. Everybody, high and low, rich and poor, called him by the nickname of Softy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Perfect Priest' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有位名叫南無的僧人，於佛法中修行圓滿。他每逢自己有衣物，便甘願脫下，送給受寒之人。他的性情溫和，毫無稜角。無論尊卑貧富，人人都以「軟兒」這個綽號稱呼他。

passages.text: Whenever he saw any one sentenced to a flogging in the temple or official yamen, Namnu invariably begged that he might take the culprit's place. Once, when there was a great function in progress at Pagoda Temple and many high officials were assembled, Softy, too, was seen kneeling at the side. He suddenly remarked to Prince Hong of Yon-san, 'You are indeed a very great man.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Perfect Priest' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 每當他看見有人在寺院或官衙被判鞭笞，南無必定懇求讓自己代替受刑者受罰。有一次，寶塔寺正舉行盛大法會，許多高官齊聚，軟兒也被人看見跪在一旁。他忽然對蓮山洪王子說道：「您真是個了不起的大人物。」

passages.text: Hong replied, 'What do you mean by great man, you impudent brat? Take that,' and gave him a box with his fist on the ear. Softy laughed, and said, 'Please, Hong, don't do that, it hurts! it hurts!' Later, stopping before the Temple with Prince Yi and other high officials, Softy looked at Yi and said, 'I know your face, but I have forgotten your name. Afterwards he said, Oh, I remember now, you are Yi Sok-hyong.' The priests of the monastery who heard this familiarity were scandalized, and hurried to make no end of apology to the Prince: 'Softy was born so, God made him so. Please, Your Excellency, forgive him.' The Prince forgave him and so he was not disturbed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Perfect Priest' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 洪回答：「你這無禮的小子，說什麼大人物？吃這個！」說著便揮拳打了他一記耳光。軟兒笑著說：「洪啊，求您別這樣，好痛！好痛！」後來，軟兒與李王子及其他高官一同停在寺前，他看著李說道：「我認得您的臉，卻忘了您的名字。」隨後又說：「哦，我想起來了，您是李錫亨。」寺中僧人聽見這般不拘禮數的話，大為震驚，連忙向王子百般賠罪：「軟兒生來就是這樣，是上天把他造成這樣的。請大人恕罪。」王子原諒了他，因此他並未受到追究。

title.en: The Propitious Magpie and the Imitation Nest
title.zh: 鵲巢報喜

region.en: Outside the South Gate, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城南門外（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk (1439-1498), with personal testimony; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Propitious Magpie', eBook #51002

summary.en: People say that when the magpie builds its nest directly south of a home, the master of the house will be promoted. King T'ai-jong's poor friend, failing in all his projects, sends a servant to build an imitation magpie's nest in a propitious place before the royal procession; caught and questioned, the servant explains the belief, and the King takes pity and orders the appointment at once. Yi Ryuk testifies from his own life: as a boy he moved a fallen nest to a propitious tree south of his home, and that very winter his father was promoted three degrees; when a slave pulled down the nest at his Chong-pa summer-house the magpies built again the next year, and in that year Ye-jong came to the throne and Yi was promoted again; a third nest by his office brought a third promotion. 'There is a spiritual power in the magpie surely.'
summary.zh: 俗云鵲巢於宅南者，主人必遷官。太宗有貧友，遣僕於蹕路造偽鵲巢以邀福；事發，僕直陳其故，王憐而即予除目。柳夢寅自記：少時移鵲巢於宅南楮樹，其冬父連升三級；後館前鵲巢被婢拆作薪，次年復營，是年睿宗即位而柳復遷官。鵲之有靈，信矣。

sensitivity.note: Bird-omen belief; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: People say that when the magpie builds its nest directly south of a home, the master of the house will be promoted in office. King T'ai-jong had a friend once who was very poor and had failed in all his projects; he decided to wait till the King went out on procession and then send a servant to build an imitation magpie's nest in some propitious place before him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Propitious Magpie' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 人們說，喜鵲若在人家正南方築巢，那家的主人便會升官。太宗王有一位朋友，非常貧窮，凡事皆不順遂；他決定等國王出巡時，派一名僕人在國王面前某個吉利的地方，築一個假喜鵲巢。

passages.text: The King saw it and asked the man what he was doing. He said in reply that when a magpie builds its nest straight south of a home the master of the house instantly gets promotion; his master had waited so long and nothing had come, that he was building an imitation nest to bring it about. The King took pity on him and ordered his appointment at once.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Propitious Magpie' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 國王看見了，便問那人在做什麼。那人回答說，喜鵲若在人家正南方築巢，那家主人便會立刻升官；他的主人等了許久，卻什麼也沒等到，所以才築個假巢以求此事成真。國王憐憫他，當即下令任命他。

passages.text: When I was young myself a magpie built its nest before our home, but with other boys I cut off the branch so that the whole nest fell to the ground; feeling sorry and afraid, on a propitious site to the south I had the nest hung up on a tree, where the young all lived and flourished and flew away. In that very winter my father was promoted three degrees in rank. Afterwards, before my summer-house at Chong-pa, magpies built a nest in a date tree; a woman slave pulled it down for fuel, but they came again the next year and built once more, and that year Ye-jong came to the throne and I was promoted again. In the spring of 1471 magpies built their nest in a tree just south of my office: 'There is a spiritual power in the magpie surely, as men have said from olden times and as I myself have proven.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Propitious Magpie' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 我年少時，有喜鵲在我們家門前築巢，但我與其他男孩砍斷那樹枝，以致整個鳥巢墜落地面；我心感歉疚與恐懼，便在南邊一處吉地將鳥巢掛在樹上，雛鳥皆存活茁壯，終至飛去。就在那年冬天，我父親連升三級官階。後來，在我位於淙坡的避暑別墅前，喜鵲在棗樹上築巢；一名女婢將巢拆下當柴燒，但牠們翌年又來，再次築巢，而那年睿宗登基，我又獲升遷。一四七一年春，喜鵲在我官署正南的一棵樹上築巢：「喜鵲確有靈性，正如古人所言，亦如我親身所證。」

title.en: The Old Buddha Rides Past the Magistrates
title.zh: 老佛過橋

region.en: Kai-ryong county riverbank (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 鶏龍縣江干（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Old Buddha', eBook #51002

summary.en: Prime Minister Choi Yun-tok, mourning his mother, rides south with a single horse and one servant through the county of Kai-ryong, where district magistrates are drinking under a tent by the riverbank. Offended that the mourner does not dismount, they arrest his servant and demand his master's name. 'Choi, the Old Buddha.' 'But what's his real name?' 'The old Buddha.' Beaten over the head, the servant says slowly: he is called Choi the Buddha, but his real name is Yun-tok, on his way to his country home in Chang-won. The magistrates recognize the Prime Minister, strike their tent, clear away the eatables, and run to make their deepest salaam and ask pardon for their sin.
summary.zh: 崔有敦相公居喪南行，道經鶏龍縣。縣令宴於江亭，怒其不下馬，逮其僕問主人名。僕曰『老佛崔公』；再問，曰『老佛』。笞之，僕徐言曰『佛者字也，諱有敦，今往昌原私第』。令等大懼，撤席奔拜請罪。老佛者，相公之別號也。

sensitivity.note: Officialdom anecdote; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Prime Minister Choi Yun-tok was in mourning once for his mother. With a single horse and one servant he made a journey to the south where the road led through the county of Kai-ryong. At that very time two or three of the district magistrates had pitched a tent on the bank of the river and were having refreshments.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Old Buddha' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 崔允德丞相曾為母親守喪。他僅帶一匹馬和一名僕人南行，路途經過開龍縣。就在那時，兩三位地方縣令在河岸搭起帳篷，正在享用茶點。

passages.text: They said to one another, 'Who is that mourner that goes riding by without dismounting? It must be some country farmer who has never learned proper manners. We shall certainly have to teach him a lesson.' They sent an attendant to arrest and bring his servant, and asked who his master was. 'Choi, the Old Buddha.' 'But what's his real name?' 'The old Buddha.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Old Buddha' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們彼此說道：「那個騎馬經過卻不下馬的守喪者是誰？想必是個從未學過禮數的鄉下農夫。我們定要好好教訓他一番。」他們派一名隨從逮捕並帶來他的僕人，問他的主人是誰。「崔，老佛。」「但他真名叫什麼？」「老佛。」

passages.text: Then they grew very angry and beat him over the head. Then the servant said slowly, 'He is called Choi the Buddha, but his real name is Yun-tok, and he is now on his way to his country home in Chang-won.' At once they recognized that it was no other than the Prime Minister, and great fear overcame them. They struck their tent, cleared away the eatables, and ran to make their deepest salaam and to ask pardon for their sin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Old Buddha' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他們勃然大怒，打他的頭。那僕人這才緩緩說道：「他叫崔佛，但真名是允德，如今正前往長原的鄉間宅邸。」他們立刻認出此人正是丞相，大為驚恐。他們拆了帳篷，收拾食物，跑去深深行禮，為自己的罪過請求寬恕。

title.en: The Kill-Devil Pills of Prince Cheung
title.zh: 殺鬼丸

region.en: Minister's mansion, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢京相府（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'A Wonderful Medicine', eBook #51002

summary.en: Prince Cheung, First Minister for thirty years and now nearly ninety, has his home attacked by goblins and devils: in broad daylight they snatch the hat from a young official's head and crumple it, and keep throwing stones till the whole court is in confusion. The Prince escapes to another house, prepares a special medicine called sal-kwi-whan, kill-devil-pills, which he offers in prayer — and from that time the goblins depart. After five or six years no sign of them has reappeared, and Prince Cheung is well and strong and free from sickness.
summary.zh: 張相公府中為鬼所擾，白晝擲石，奪客之帽而揉之，闔宅大亂。相公避居別第，製藥曰殺鬼丸，持咒服之。自是群鬼遁去，五六載不復至，相公亦康強無恙。

sensitivity.note: Exorcism-medicine anecdote; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Prince Cheung had been First Minister of the land for thirty years, a man just and upright, now nearly ninety years of age. His home was suddenly attacked by goblins and devils: when a young official came to call on him, these mysterious beings in broad daylight snatched the hat from his head and crumpled it up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'A Wonderful Medicine' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 鄭親王擔任本國首相三十年，為人公正剛直，如今已年近九十。他的宅邸忽然遭到鬼怪侵擾：當一位年輕官員前來拜訪他時，這些神秘的東西竟在大白天搶走他頭上的帽子，並將其揉皺。

passages.text: They threw stones, too, and kept on throwing them so that all the court was reduced to confusion. Prince Cheung made his escape and went to live in another house, where he prepared a special medicine called sal-kwi-whan, kill-devil-pills, which he offered in prayer. From that time the goblins departed, and now after five or six years no sign of them has reappeared; Prince Cheung, too, is well and strong and free from sickness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'A Wonderful Medicine' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 它們還扔石頭，且扔個不停，使整個庭院陷入混亂。鄭親王逃出，遷居另一處宅邸，在那裡配製一種名為殺鬼丸的特效藥，用以祈禱供奉。自那時起，鬼怪便離去，至今五六年間未再出現任何蹤跡；鄭親王也身體康健，無病無恙。

title.en: Mo, the Slave Wife Who Died Rather than Part
title.zh: 無娘殉情

region.en: Camel Mountain ridge, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 駱山嶺（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk, told by kin of the scholar An Yun; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Faithful Mo', eBook #51002

summary.en: An Yun, a noted scholar, loves Mo, the beautiful daughter of Prince Ha's slave, and takes her for his wife. The furious Prince has her arrested to marry her to one of his bondsmen; she escapes over the wall back to An, and together they swear to die rather than be parted. Arrested again, she is found hanging by the neck dead. Months later, returning from the Confucian Temple over Camel Mountain ridge in the autumn moonlight, An is musing love verses to her memory when a soft footfall comes from among the pines — there is Mo. Knowing her long dead, he runs to catch her hand: 'How did you come here?' — and she disappears. He cries out, falls ill, cannot swallow, and dies of a broken heart. 'Faithful unto death was she. Even of the faithful among the ancients was there ever a better than Mo?'
summary.zh: 安允與婢女無娘私結為夫婦，主人家怒而執之。無娘踰牆歸安，誓死不離。再被捕，縊死。後安自廟還，月夜過駱山嶺，忽聞松間履聲，則無娘也。安知其鬼，然情不能自已，趨執其手，瞬息而滅。安慟而病，粒食不下，遂卒。或曰：『至死靡他，雖士族之婦有不及者。』

sensitivity.note: Love-tragedy ghost tale; depicts Joseon slave status; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Prince Ha had a slave who was a landed proprietor and lived in Yang-ju county; he had a daughter, fairest of the fair, whom he called Mo. An Yun was a noted scholar, a man of distinction in letters. He saw Mo, fell in love with her and took her for his wife. Prince Ha heard of this and was furiously angry: 'How is it that you, a slave, dare to marry with a man of the aristocracy?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Faithful Mo' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 河王子有一名奴僕，是擁有田產的業主，住在楊州郡；他有一個女兒，容貌絕美，無人能及，他喚她作慕。安允是位知名的學者，文才出眾、聲名顯赫。他見了慕，便愛上了她，娶她為妻。河王子聽聞此事，勃然大怒：「你這奴僕，怎敢與貴族之人成婚？」

passages.text: He had her arrested and brought home, intending to marry her to one of his bondsmen. Mo learned of this with tears and sorrow, made her escape over the wall and went back to An; together they took an oath to die rather than to be parted. Later Prince Ha sent his underlings to arrest her again and carry her off; after this all trace of her was lost till Mo was discovered one day in a room hanging by the neck dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Faithful Mo' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他派人將她逮捕、帶回家中，打算把她嫁給自己的一名家奴。慕得知此事，淚流滿面、悲傷不已，翻牆逃走，回到安允身邊；兩人一同立誓，寧死也不分離。後來，河王子又派手下將她捉走；此後她的蹤跡便全然消失，直到有一天，有人發現慕在房中懸樑自盡。

passages.text: Months of sorrow passed over An till once, under cover of the night, he was returning from the Confucian Temple to his house over the ridge of Camel Mountain. It was early autumn and the wooded tops were shimmering in the moonlight. Musing longingly of Mo, and repeating love verses to her memory, he suddenly heard a soft footfall as though coming from among the pines — there was Mo. An knew that she was long dead, but because he was so buried in thought of her, doubting nothing, he ran to her and caught her by the hand, saying, 'How did you come here?' — but she disappeared. An gave a great cry and broke into tears. He fell ill; a little later he died of a broken heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Faithful Mo' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 安允在悲傷中度過了數月，直到有一回，他趁夜色從孔廟回家，行經駱駝山的山脊。時值初秋，林木覆蓋的山頂在月光下閃爍。他思念慕，滿懷眷戀，對著她的記憶吟誦情詩，忽然聽見輕柔的腳步聲，彷彿從松林間傳來——是慕。安允明知她早已亡故，卻因思念太深，毫不懷疑，便奔向她，握住她的手，說道：「你怎麼會來到這裡？」——但她卻消失了。安允放聲大哭，淚流不止。他因而病倒；不久之後，便因心碎而死。

title.en: The Minister in Plain Clothes and the Proud Scholar
title.zh: 微行相公折傲士

region.en: Roadside pavilion, southern journey (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南行道旁亭（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Renowned Maing', eBook #51002

summary.en: Minister of State Maing Sa-song, dressed in plain clothes, is overtaken by rain and shelters in a side pavilion where the young scholar Whang Eui-hon, hands behind his back, reads the verse-boards. 'Well, grand-dad, do you know the flavour of verses like these?' The Minister pretends ignorance and asks the meaning; Whang lectures him on the great men of the past and living pictures in poetry. Then pack-horses, servants, tent poles and canvas packs come in a long procession, and Whang, to his amazement, learns the old man is Maing Sa-song, and drops unconsciously onto his knees in a deep and long obeisance. The Minister laughs: 'There is no difference in the value of mere men; they are high or low according to the thoughts that prompt them, but unfortunately all are born with a proud heart. You are not a common scholar; why, therefore, should you be so proud to begin with and so humble now?' — and comforts him and sends him away.
summary.zh: 蕭瑟松微服南行，避雨於亭。有書生黃義憲方負手讀壁上題詠，傲然問曰『老丈解此詩味否』。松佯為不知，請其講解。俄而行李駝馬續至，黃始知即蕭相公，不覺長跪。松笑曰：『人之貴賤在乎其心，而不在於貌。子始倨而後恭，何也？』乃慰而遣之。

sensitivity.note: Moral anecdote; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Minister of State Maing Sa-song once upon a time, dressed in plain clothes, started south on a long journey. On the way he was overtaken by rain, and turned into a side pavilion for rest and shelter. There was a young scholar already in the pavilion by the name of Whang Eui-hon, who with his two hands behind his back was reading the pavilion inscription board.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Renowned Maing' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 國相孟思誠有一次身著便服，啟程南下遠行。途中遇雨，便轉入一座路旁的亭子歇息避雨。亭中已有一位年輕書生，名叫黃義軒，正雙手背在身後，讀著亭中的匾額題字。

passages.text: At last he turned to the old man and said, 'Well, grand-dad, do you know the flavour of verses like these?' The famous Minister, pretending ignorance, arose and said, 'An old countryman like myself, could you expect him to know? Please tell me the meaning.' Whang said, 'These verses were written by the great men of the past. What they saw and experienced they wrote down to inspire the souls of those who were to come after them. They are like pictures of sea and land, for there are living pictures in poetry, you know.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Renowned Maing' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最後他轉向老人，說道：「老爺爺，您可懂得這類詩句的滋味嗎？」這位名相假裝不懂，起身說道：「像我這樣的鄉下老農，您怎能指望我懂呢？還請您告訴我其中的意思。」黃義軒說：「這些詩句是前代的大人物所寫。他們所見所歷，都寫了下來，以激勵後人之心。它們就像海陸的圖畫，因為詩中自有活的圖景，您知道的。」

passages.text: A little later came pack-horses loaded with all sorts of things, servants and retainers, tent poles, canvas packs and other equipment, a long procession. Whang, surprised, made inquiry, and to his amazement learned that the old man was none other than Maing Sa-song; unconsciously he dropped onto his knees in a deep and long obeisance. The Minister laughed and said, 'That will do; there is no difference in the value of mere men, they are high or low according to the thoughts that prompt them, but unfortunately all are born with a proud heart. You are not a common scholar; why, therefore, should you be so proud to begin with and so humble now?' The Minister took him by the hand, led him to his mat, made him sit down, comforted him and sent him away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Renowned Maing' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 過了一會兒，來了滿載各樣物件的馱馬，還有僕從與隨從、帳竿、帆布行囊及其他裝備，排成長長的一隊。黃義軒大為驚訝，連忙打聽，才驚愕地得知那老人正是孟思誠；他不覺雙膝跪地，深深長長地行了一禮。國相笑道：「行了；人本身的價值並無分別，或高或低，全看驅使他們的念頭如何，只可惜人生來都帶著一顆驕傲的心。你並非尋常書生，那麼，為何起初如此驕傲，如今又如此謙卑呢？」國相牽著他的手，引他到自己的坐席上，讓他坐下，安慰了他一番，便打發他離去。

title.en: Who Decides, God or the King?
title.zh: 富貴在天

region.en: Heung-yang Palace, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城慶熙宮（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; story of King Tae-jong (r. 1400-1418); English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Who Decides, God or the King?', eBook #51002

summary.en: Resting in Heung-yang Palace, King Tae-jong overhears two eunuchs arguing whether riches and honour are in the king's hand or ordered of God. To test it, he writes a secret despatch — 'Raise the bearer of this letter one degree in rank' — and commands A to deliver it. At the palace gate a furious pain takes A in the stomach, and he begs B to go in his place. The next day the record of promotions shows B advanced, and not one word about A. King Tae-jong makes inquiry, and when he knows the circumstances he gives a sudden start of wonder and remains long in deep thought.
summary.zh: 太宗休於宮中，聞二閹辯富貴由王抑由天。乃手書密札曰『持此札者進一階』，命甲賫送。甲至宮門腹痛如割，倩乙代往。明日甲名不與，而乙登籍。太宗驚愕，沉思良久。

sensitivity.note: Fate-vs-royal-power tale; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: King Tai-jong was having a rest in Heung-yang Palace, while outside two eunuchs were talking together over the law that governs the affairs of men, as to whether it is man or God. One said, 'Riches and honour are all in the king's hand.' The other said, 'Nothing of the kind; every atom of wealth and every degree of promotion are all ordered of God. Even the king himself has no part in it and no power.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Who Decides, God or the King?' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 太宗大王在興陽宮歇息，外頭有兩名宦官正談論著主宰人間萬事的法則，究竟是出於人還是出於天。一人說：「富貴全在君王手中。」另一人說：「並非如此；每一分財富、每一級升遷，皆由上天安排。即便是君王本人，也無從參與，亦無能為力。」

passages.text: The King, overhearing what was said, wrote a secret despatch, saying, 'Raise the Bearer of this letter one degree in rank.' He sealed it and commanded the first eunuch to take it. He made his bow and departed, but just when he was about to leave the palace enclosure a furious pain took him in the stomach, so that he begged his fellow to take his place and go into the city.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Who Decides, God or the King?' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 君王無意間聽見了這番話，便寫下一道密旨，寫道：「將持此書信者晉升一級。」他封好密旨，命第一名宦官送去。那宦官行禮後離去，但正當他將要走出宮牆之際，腹中忽然劇痛難忍，只得央求同伴代他前往，進城去送。

passages.text: The next day, when the record of promotions was placed before the King, he read how the second had been advanced, but not one word was there about the first. King Tai-jong made inquiry, and when he knew the circumstances he gave a sudden start of wonder and remained long in deep thought.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Who Decides, God or the King?' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 次日，升遷的名冊呈到君王面前，他讀到第二名宦官獲得晉升，卻隻字未提第一名宦官。太宗大王加以查問，得知箇中緣由後，猛然一驚，驚異不已，久久陷入沉思。

title.en: Im Sung-jong's Three Years on the Door-sill
title.zh: 任世宗三絕苦練

region.en: Outside the South Gate, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城南門外（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; story of the reign of King Se-jong; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Three Things Mastered', eBook #51002

summary.en: Im Sung-jong, a relative of the king and the first performer of his time on the harp, is seen every morning for three years kneeling on the sill of his front door beating his hands up and down on his knees — people think him mad, but thus he learns the motions required for the harp. Night and day he blows and practises with his fingers for three years to learn the motions for the flute; and being light of body and poor at riding and archery, he sighs that he must yet know how to make the bull's-eye, takes his bow into the hills every morning and shoots all day long for three years till he becomes a renowned archer.
summary.zh: 任世宗為王之懿親，善琴。日日跪於門限上以手擊膝，如是者三年，人皆以為狂，而琴法遂成。又畫夜吹簫習指，三年而簫法成。體弱不善騎射，乃日日擕弓矢入山射之，三年而為名射。精誠所至，金石為開。

sensitivity.note: Self-cultivation exemplum; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: There was a relative of the king, named Im Sung-jong, who was a gifted man in thought and purpose. He was the first performer of his time on the harp. King Se-jong said of him, 'Im's harp knows but one master, and follows no other man.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Three Things Mastered' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 君王有一位親族，名叫林成宗，是個心思與志向皆出眾的人。他是當世第一的琴手。世宗大王曾這樣評他：「林氏的琴只認一位主人，不追隨他人。」

passages.text: His home was outside the South Gate, and every morning he was seen kneeling on the sill of his front door beating his hands upwards and downwards on his knees, and this practice he carried on for three years. People could not imagine what he meant by it, but thought him mad. Thus he learned the motions required for the harp. Also he blew with his mouth and practised with his fingers day and night without stopping, and kept this up for three years and so learned the motions for the flute.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Three Things Mastered' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的家在城南門外，每天早晨都見他跪在自家大門的門檻上，雙手在膝上上下拍擊，如此練習持續了三年。人們猜不透他這般舉動是何用意，只當他瘋了。他就這樣學會了彈琴所需的動作。他又以口吹氣、以指練習，日夜不停，如此持續三年，因而學會了吹笛的動作。

passages.text: He was a lightly built man in body, and poor at riding and at archery. He often sighed over this defect, and said, 'Though I am weak and stupid and not able to shoot a long distance, I shall yet know how to hit the target and make the bull's-eye. This also must be acquired by practice.' So every morning he took his bow and arrows and went off into the hills, and there he shot all day long, keeping it up for three years, till he became a renowned archer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Three Things Mastered' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他體格輕瘦，不善騎馬，也不善射箭。他常為此缺陷嘆息，說道：「我雖孱弱愚鈍，射不了遠距離，卻仍要懂得如何中的、射中靶心。這也必須靠練習才能得來。」於是每天早晨他帶著弓箭走入山中，終日在那裡射箭，如此持續三年，終於成為一名聞名的射手。

title.en: The Dead General Who Came Back to Shoot a Thief
title.zh: 故將軍鬼射賊

region.en: General Kim's former home (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 金故宅（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; story of Kim Tok-saing, honored at the court of Tae-jong; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Strangely Stricken Dead', eBook #51002

summary.en: Kim Tok-saing, a soldier of fortune several times generalissimo, has been dead ten years and more when one night his intimate friend is twice awakened with a fright. He has just seen General Kim riding a white horse with bow and arrows at his belt: 'A thief has just entered my home, and I have come to shoot him dead' — and returning, drew an arrow with blood marks on it: 'I have just shot him, he is dead.' In the morning the friend goes to Kim's former home and learns that that very night Kim's young widow had decided to remarry, and as soon as the chosen fiancé entered her home a terrible pain shot him through; before morning he died in great agony.
summary.zh: 金德星歿已十年。一夕其故友連驚醒，言夢見將軍乘白馬佩弓矢來曰『有賊入吾家，吾射殺之矣』，且出矢示之，矢上血痕宛然。晨往其故宅問之，則是夜其寡婦方議改適，所聘者甫入門，暴痛而絕於床。鬼射之說，駭人聽聞。

sensitivity.note: Ancestor-ghost vigilante tale; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: There was once a man called Kim Tok-saing, a soldier of fortune who had been specially honoured at the Court of Tai-jong, and had several times been generalissimo of the army. Kim had been dead now for some ten years and more, when one night this friend of his was awakened with a start and gave a great outcry.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Strangely Stricken Dead' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個人名叫金德生，是個浪跡天涯的武人，曾在太宗朝廷上受到特別的恩寵，還屢次擔任軍隊的統帥。金氏死去至今已有十多年了，某夜，他的一位朋友猛然驚醒，大聲叫喊起來。

passages.text: 'I have just seen General Kim riding on a white horse, with bow and arrows at his belt. He called to me and said, A thief has just entered my home, and I have come to shoot him dead. He went and again returned, and as he drew an arrow from his quiver, I saw that there were blood marks on it. He said, I have just shot him, he is dead.' The husband and wife in fear and wonder talked over it together.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Strangely Stricken Dead' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「我剛剛看見金將軍騎著白馬，腰間佩著弓箭。他呼喚我說道：『有個賊剛闖進我家，我這就來把他射死。』他去而復返，當他從箭囊裡抽出一支箭時，我看見箭上有血跡。他說：『我剛射中了他，他死了。』夫妻二人又驚又異，一同議論此事。

passages.text: When morning came the friend went to General Kim's former home to make inquiry. He learned that that very night Kim's young widow had decided to remarry, but as soon as the chosen fiancé had entered her home, a terrible pain shot him through, and before morning came he died in great agony.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Strangely Stricken Dead' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天亮之後，那位朋友前往金將軍舊日的宅邸打聽。他得知就在那一夜，金氏年輕的寡妻決定改嫁，可是那選定的未婚夫剛一踏進她家門，便感到一陣劇痛貫穿全身，未及天明，就在極大的痛苦中死去了。

title.en: The Archers under the Hoi Tree
title.zh: 海樹下之射者

region.en: Inside the Great East Gate, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城東大門內（象徵性定位）

period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Mysterious Hoi Tree', eBook #51002

summary.en: Before Prince Pa-song's house inside the great East Gate stands a large Hoi tree. One night the Prince's son-in-law, passing the archers' pavilion, sees a great company of bowmen shooting at the target, practising riding, throwing spears and hurling bowls till the road is blocked. 'Look at that impudent rascal! He attempts to ride by without dismounting.' They catch and beat him till a tall fellow comes out of the ranks: 'He is my master; why do you treat him so?' — undoes his bonds and leads him home. At the gate the son-in-law looks back and sees the man walk under the Hoi tree and disappear: all the crowd of archers were spirits, and the tall one had come forth from their particular Hoi tree.
summary.zh: 怕松公宅在東大門內，門前有海樹一本。其婿夜過射亭，見無數射手習射馳馬擲矛，喧然塞路。眾怒其不下馬，執而笞之。忽有一偉者出曰『此吾主也，何得如此』，為解其縛而送之歸。至門回顧，其人已行入海樹下而滅。蓋群射者皆鬼，偉者即樹中之神也。

sensitivity.note: Tree-spirit lore; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Prince Pa-song's house was situated just inside of the great East Gate, and before it was a large Hoi tree. On a certain night the Prince's son-in-law was passing by the roadway that led in front of the archers' pavilion. There he saw a great company of bowmen, more than he could number, all shooting together at the target; a moment later he saw them practising riding, some throwing spears, some hurling bowls, some shooting from horseback, so that the road in front of the pavilion was blocked against all comers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Mysterious Hoi Tree' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴松王子的宅邸就坐落在東大門內側，門前有一棵高大的槐樹。某夜，王子的女婿正走過通往弓手亭前的那條路。他在那裡看見一大群弓手，多得數不清，全都朝著靶子一齊射箭；片刻之後，他又看見他們練習騎射，有的投擲長矛，有的拋擲碗器，有的在馬背上放箭，以致亭前的道路被堵得水洩不通，誰也過不去。

passages.text: Some shouted as he came by, 'Look at that impudent rascal! He attempts to ride by without dismounting.' They caught him and beat him, paying no attention to his cries for mercy, till one tall fellow came out of their serried ranks and said in an angry voice, 'He is my master; why do you treat him so?' He undid his bonds, took him by the arm and led him home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Mysterious Hoi Tree' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他經過時，有人喊道：「瞧那個放肆的傢伙！他竟想不下馬就騎過去。」他們抓住他，打他，全然不顧他的求饒，直到一個高個子從密密的行列中走出來，怒聲說道：「他是我的主人，你們為什麼這樣對待他？」他解開他的綁縛，挽著他的手臂，領他回家。

passages.text: When the son-in-law reached the gate he looked back and saw the man walk under the Hoi tree and disappear. He then learned, too, that all the crowd of archers were spirits and not men, and that the tall one who had befriended him was a spirit too, and that he had come forth from their particular Hoi tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Mysterious Hoi Tree' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 女婿到了門口，回頭一看，只見那人走到槐樹下便消失了。他這才明白，那一群弓手全是鬼魂而非活人，那個幫他的高個子也是鬼魂，而且是從他們那棵槐樹裡出來的。

title.en: Ta-hong, Who Hid Herself until the Honours Came
title.zh: 桃花潛身待郎君

region.en: Chang-eui ward, Seoul; Keumsan county (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢京彰義坊（象徵性定位）

period: Story of Minister Sim Heui-su (1535-1622), told before his death; collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Ta-hong', eBook #51002

summary.en: At sixteen, the beautiful boy Sim Heui-su sees the kisaeng Ta-hong, Flower-bud, at a banquet and cannot forget her. Days later she alights before him in the street, reveals she asked his name that night, and plights her troth: he must first win first place at the examination and his three days of public rejoicing, and until then she will hide herself in safety. He studies day and night for her sake, marries at his parents' word without joy, and five years after their farewell wins his honours — and on the third evening, called in to an old Minister's house by the Sillai whistle, finds her. For a year she has been a voluntary slave in that house, 'called my concubine in name lest my nephews should steal her away,' confident to the end. She becomes his only wife, forbids their too-frequent happiness as interfereing with duty, and in Keumsan county announces her own death four or five days beforehand: 'Our life is ordered, God decides it all; bury me by my master, that we may meet again.' After her death she still comes to warn him of things to come, never with a mistake, until the dream in which she says 'Master, the time of your departure has come' — and Sim dies the day following, as was foretold.
summary.zh: 沈羲壽十六歲遇名妓桃花（花苞），一見傾心。數日後桃花馬上相認，與之盟曰：『君登科之日乃我歸期，我自匿身以全其節。』沈乃發憤苦讀五年而魁天下。第三日夜誤入某老相公家，桃花果在。原來伊自願為婢於其家，託名側室以避匪人。後為沈正室，賢而克勤。任金山縣令時，桃花預言己死期，至日果卒。遺言葬於夫塋之側。死後猶託夢預告家事，末乃告夫死期，翌日果卒。

sensitivity.note: Love-and-fidelity tale with prophecy; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Minister Sim Heui-su was, when young, handsome as polished marble and white as the snow. At about sixteen years of age he went with a half-dozen comrades to see a banquet with dancing-girls, where among them was a young woman whose face was very beautiful, not like an earthly person, but like some angelic being: her name was Ta-hong, Flower-bud.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Ta-hong' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 沈希壽（Sim Heui-su）年少時，容貌俊美如琢磨過的大理石，潔白如雪。約莫十六歲時，他與五六名同伴一同去觀賞有舞妓助興的宴會，席間有一名年輕女子，容貌極美，不似凡間之人，倒像天上的仙子：她名叫泰紅（Ta-hong），意為花苞。

passages.text: Ten days later, carrying his books along the main street, he suddenly met a pretty girl beautifully dressed, riding a handsome horse, who alighted just in front of him and taking his hand said, 'Are you not Sim Heui-su?' It was Ta-hong. 'I saw you at the gathering, and to me your face was like a god's. From that day on I longed to meet you. Our meeting thus is surely of God's appointment.' They plighted their troth in her aunt's house. 'You have your parents to think of. As I reflect upon your ability and chances for promotion, I see you already a Minister of State. Let us separate just now, and I'll keep myself for you till the time when you win the first place at the Examination and have your three days of public rejoicing. I have a plan by which to hide myself away in safety.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Ta-hong' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 十日之後，他帶著書本行經大街，忽然遇見一名打扮豔麗的漂亮女子，騎著駿馬，正好在他面前下馬，牽起他的手說道：「你不就是沈希壽嗎？」那正是泰紅。「我在聚會上見過你，在我眼中，你的面容宛如神明。自那日起，我便渴望與你相見。我們這樣相遇，定是上天的安排。」兩人在她姑母家中私訂終身。「你還有父母要顧念。我思量你的才幹與晉升的機會，看得出你必將成為宰相。我們此刻暫且分別，我會為你守身，直到你科舉奪魁、享有三日公開慶賀之時。我自有辦法安然藏身。」

passages.text: From that time forth, with all his might, he went at his lessons, day and night, not for the sake of the Examination, but for the sake of once more meeting her. It was five years after his farewell to Ta-hong that he won his honours, but on the first day and the second he did not meet her, and the third day was passing with no word. Evening was falling, when his father sent him to call on an old friend in Chang-eui ward; as he was returning, just as he was passing a high gateway, he heard the Sillai call and was obliged to dismount and enter the house of an old Minister, who entertained him and then lifted his glass and inquired, 'Would you like to meet a very beautiful person?' When she came, it was his lost Ta-hong: 'Is this not within the three days of your public celebration, and according to the agreement by which we parted?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Ta-hong' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 自此以後，他日夜竭盡全力用功讀書，並非為了科舉，而是為了能再見她一面。與泰紅訣別五年之後，他終於金榜題名，然而第一日、第二日都未能見到她，第三日也音訊全無。暮色漸沉，他父親派他去長義坊拜訪一位故友；歸途中，正經過一座高門，忽聞「失禮」之聲，只得下馬，進入一位老宰相的宅邸，老宰相款待了他，隨後舉杯問道：「你可想見一位極美的女子？」待她出來，竟是他失散的泰紅：「這不正是在你公開慶賀的三日之內嗎？也正合我們分別時的約定？」

passages.text: The old man told her history: 'On a certain day this young girl came to us saying, May I have the place of slave with you? I am not running away from any master. She called herself my concubine so as to be safe, lest my nephews or some younger members of the clan should steal her away. We watched the Examination reports, and this time on looking over the list I found your name. She is first of all a faithful woman: I have not known her like before.' His parents gave consent that he should have her, and she was made a member of his family, really his only wife. A little later, as magistrate of Keumsan county, he heard her say one day, 'I am going to die, for my span of life is finished.' In four or five days she fell ill, and a day or two later died, saying, 'Our life is ordered, God decides it all. As I die I ask only that my body be buried where it may rest by the side of my master when he passes away, so that when we meet in the regions beyond I shall be with you once again.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Ta-hong' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 老人道出她的來歷：「某日這名年輕女子來到我們這裡，說道：『可否讓我在您府上做奴婢？我並非從哪個主人那裡逃出來的。』她自稱是我的妾，以求安全，免得我的姪兒或族中晚輩將她奪走。我們留意科舉放榜的消息，這次查看名單，我見到了你的名字。她首先是個忠貞的女子：我從未見過像她這樣的人。」他的父母應允他納她為妻，她便成了他家的一員，實際上是他唯一的妻子。不久之後，他出任錦山郡守，有一天聽她說道：「我快要死了，因為我的壽數已盡。」四五日後她便病倒，再過一兩日便去世了，臨終時說道：「我們的生命自有安排，一切皆由上天決定。我死之際只求將我的遺體葬在能與主人相伴之處，待他日後辭世，好讓我們在彼方重逢時，我能再與你相守。」

passages.text: After her death, whenever anything serious was to happen in his home, she always came to tell him beforehand, and never was there a mistake in her announcements. For several years it has continued thus, till a few days ago she appeared in a dream saying, 'Master, the time of your departure has come, and we are to meet again. I am now making ready for your glad reception.' Last night she came once more and said, 'To-morrow is your day.' In the morning, when he awoke, marks of tears were still upon his cheeks: 'This is not because I fear to die, but because I have seen my Ta-hong.' So Sim died, as was foretold, on the day following.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Ta-hong' (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她死之後，每逢他家中將有大事發生，她總會事先前來告知，她的預告從未有過差錯。如此持續了好幾年，直到幾日前，她於夢中現身說道：「主人，你離去的時候到了，我們將再相見。我如今正為迎接你而作準備。」昨夜她又來說道：「明日便是你的日子。」清晨醒來時，他臉頰上仍留著淚痕：「這並非因為我怕死，而是因為我見到了我的泰紅。」於是沈希壽正如所預言，於次日辭世。

title.en: The Oriole That Sings for Kim
title.zh: 黃鳥呼金

region.en: Royal palace, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城王宮（象徵性定位）
