summary.en: When the time comes for her departure, a large and beautiful flower is brought into her chamber, so arranged that Sim Chung can conceal herself inside, nourished by its perfume and juice; floated to the surface, it is secured by her friend the merchant and presented to the King, who keeps it in a glass house and never tires of watching. One restless night the King sees her walking in the moonlight before she can hide; the flower vanishes, leaving her standing alone, and she calms his fear: she is but a human being. An officer versed in astronomy reports a brilliant star descended from heaven and alighted upon the palace; the queen being deceased, the King takes the remarkable maiden for his wife in the royal wedding hall. Loneliness for her father moves the Queen to summon all the blind men of the country to a feast of clothing, food and cash; on the third day a feeble old man in rags comes tottering up, and at her pavilion she screams, 'My father! my father!' and falls at his feet senseless. 'Oh! my child, can the dead come back to us? I hear your voice; I feel your form; but how can I know it is you, for I have no eyes? Away with these sightless orbs!' — and tearing at his eyes with his nails, the scales fall away, and he stands rejoicing in his sight once more. The King makes the old man an officer of high rank, appoints him a fine house, and marries him to the accomplished daughter of an officer of suitable rank, fulfilling the last of the prophecy of both the aged priest and the King of the Sea.
summary.zh: 龍王以神花浮送沉清還陽，商得之獻於王，王置之琉璃亭，旦夕玩賞。一夕王見花中步出美人，遂冊立為后。后思父，乃下詔集天下盲人賜宴三日。第三日有一襤褸老人扶杖至，后一見呼曰『父也』，暈於其前。翁曰『吾目已盲，安知汝為吾女』，以手自抉其目，瞖膜忽落，目光頓復。王授翁以高官，聘名門之女妻之，果如老僧與龍王所預言。

sensitivity.note: Pansori classic; restoration-of-sight miracle; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: When the proper time arrived for her departure for the world she had left, a large and beautiful flower was brought into her chamber, so arranged that Sim Chung could conceal herself inside of it, while the delicious perfume and the juice of the plant were ample nourishment. The flower was conveyed to the surface of the sea, at the place where she had plunged in; the merchant steering close managed to secure the flower and place it safely in his boat, deciding at once to present it at the palace if he could get it there. The plan succeeded, and His Majesty, delighted with the gift, spent his time gazing upon it to the exclusion of state business.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 8 (1889); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當她返回原先離開的那個世界的適當時機到來時，一朵又大又美的花被送進她的房中，安排得讓沈清能藏身其中，而花朵芬芳的香氣與汁液便是充足的養分。這朵花被送到海面，正是她當初投身入海之處；那商人將船駛近，設法取得了這朵花，穩妥地安置在船中，當即決定若能將它帶到，便要呈獻給宮廷。計畫果然成功，國王對這份禮物十分欣喜，終日凝視著它，連國事都擱下了。

passages.text: At night, when all was quiet, Sim Chung was wont to come forth and rest herself by walking in the moonlight; the King, being indisposed, went to breathe the rich perfume and chanced to see her before she could conceal herself. She took refuge in her flower, when, to the amazement of both, the flower vanished, leaving her standing alone; she called to him not to fear, that she was but a human being, and no spirit. An officer versed in astronomy stated that on the previous night they had observed a brilliant star descend from heaven and alight upon the palace, boding good to the royal family; the queen being deceased, it was soon decided that the King should take this remarkable maiden for his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 8 (1889); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 夜裡萬籟俱寂之時，沈清慣常出來，在月光下散步舒展身心；國王因身體不適，前去呼吸那濃郁的花香，竟在她還來不及藏身之前瞥見了她。她躲回花中，不料那朵花竟消失了，令兩人同感驚愕，只留下她獨自站立；她喚他不要害怕，說自己只是凡人，並非鬼魂。一位精通天象的官員稟報說，前一夜他們觀察到一顆明亮的星自天而降，落於宮殿之上，預示王室將有吉兆；由於王后已然去世，眾人很快便決定國王應娶這位非凡的女子為妻。

passages.text: Sim Chung became lonely and mourned for her poor father; she was oppressed by a strange dream concerning a poor blind man, and was desirous of alleviating in some way the sufferings of the many blind men in the country. Together they agreed to summon all the blind men of the country to a great feast, at which they should be properly clothed, amply fed, and treated each to a present of cash. The Queen secreted herself in a pavilion; she watched the first day and the second in vain, when, as the feast was closing on the third day, a feeble old man in rags came tottering up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 8 (1889); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 沈清漸感孤寂，思念她可憐的父親；一個關於一位貧苦盲人的奇異夢境困擾著她，她渴望能設法減輕國內眾多盲人的苦難。兩人商定召集全國的盲人前來參加一場盛大的宴會，會上要讓他們衣著得體、飽食充足，並各贈一份錢財。王后暗自藏身於一座亭閣之中；她第一天、第二天都徒然守候，直到第三天宴會將近結束時，一位衣衫襤褸的衰弱老人踉踉蹌蹌地走了過來。

passages.text: Her Majesty scrutinized him closely, and then screamed, 'My father! my father!' and fell at his feet senseless. As the full truth began to dawn upon the poor old blind man, he cried: 'Oh! my child, can the dead come back to us? I hear your voice; I feel your form; but how can I know it is you, for I have no eyes? Away with these sightless orbs!' And he tore at his eyes with his nails, when to his utter amazement and joy the scales fell away, and he stood rejoicing in his sight once more. His Majesty made the old man an officer of high rank, appointed him a fine house, and had him married to the accomplished daughter of an officer of suitable rank, thereby fulfilling the last of the prophecy of both the aged priest and the King of the Sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 8 (1889); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 娘娘仔細端詳他，隨即尖叫：「我的父親！我的父親！」便昏倒在他腳邊。那可憐的老盲人漸漸明白全部真相，哭喊道：「哦！我的孩子，死人怎能回到我們身邊？我聽見妳的聲音，我觸到妳的身形；但我怎能知道那就是妳，因為我沒有眼睛？把這對無珠的眼眶拿走吧！」他用指甲抓自己的眼睛，令他萬分驚異又歡喜的是，鱗片般的障蔽脫落了，他重又站立，為復得的視力而歡欣。國王封老人為高官，賜他一所華宅，並讓他娶了一位品級相當的官員的才德兼備之女為妻，從而應驗了老祭司與海王之預言的最後一項。

title.en: Hong Kil Tong and the Dragon in the Dream
title.zh: 洪吉童夢龍

region.en: Hong mansion (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 洪府（象徵性定位）

period: Novel tale (c. 1600s) collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 9 'Hong Kil Tong', eBook #55539

summary.en: Hong Pansa, a noble of high rank, dreams he hears the noise of thunder and sees a huge dragon entering his apartment, too small to contain the enormous body; he takes it as a good omen of a blessing, hoping another son. Within the year a son of marvellous beauty is born to a concubine from the dancing girls — much to the annoyance of his wife — and is named Hong Kil Tong. The boy learns rapidly and surprises every one by his remarkable ability; he rebels at being placed with the slaves and at not being allowed to call his parent father. 'Heaven has made all things for the use of men,' he tells his father in the moonlit courtyard, 'and the laws of men are only made to assist a few; but I am not inclined to submit to any such tyranny, but will become a great man in spite of my evil surroundings.' 'What a pity that he is not my proper and legitimate son,' muses the father. 'As it is, I fear he will cause me serious trouble.'
summary.zh: 洪參判夢雷聲大作，巨龍入室，身大而室小不能容。以為吉兆，果妾生子，貌極美，名洪吉童。吉童穎悟絕倫，而以庶出不得稱父，憤曰：『天生萬物以養人，人法乃護少數人者；吾終不受此縛，必為人上人。』父歎曰：『此兒非常人，惜非嫡子，恐為吾家之禍。』

sensitivity.note: Robin-Hood hero of the first Korean vernacular novel; class discrimination theme.

passages.text: During the reign of the third king in Korea there lived a noble of high rank and noted family, by name Hong. When Hong Pansa was the father of but two sons, he dreamed by night on one occasion that he heard the noise of thunder, and looking up he saw a huge dragon entering his apartment, which seemed too small to contain the whole of his enormous body. The dream was so startling as to awaken the sleeper, who at once saw that it was a good omen, a token of a blessing about to be conferred.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 朝鮮第三代國王在位期間，住著一位出身名門的高官，姓洪。洪判事只有兩個兒子時，有一夜夢見雷聲大作，抬頭一看，只見一條巨龍進入他的房間，那房間似乎太小，容不下牠龐大的身軀。這夢如此驚人，以致驚醒了睡者，他立刻看出這是吉兆，是即將降下福澤的徵象。

passages.text: Within the year, however, a son of marvellous beauty was born to one concubine, much to the annoyance of his wife, for he would have been glad to have the beautiful boy a full son, and eligible to office. The child was named Kil Tong. He grew fast, and became more and more beautiful; he learned rapidly, and surprised every one by his remarkable ability. As he grew up he rebelled at being placed with the slaves, and at not being allowed to call his parent, father.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而不出一年，一名妾室便生下一個容貌俊美的兒子，這令他的妻子十分惱怒，因為他本希望這俊美的男孩是嫡子，有資格做官。這孩子取名吉童。他長得很快，越發俊美；他學東西極快，以非凡的才能令眾人驚異。長大後，他對被安排與奴僕為伍、不被允許稱生父為父親一事深感憤慨。

passages.text: One bright moonlight night Hong Pansa saw his son in the court-yard practising the arts of the soldier, and asked him what it meant. Kil Tong answered that he was fitting himself to become a man that people should respect and fear. 'I know that heaven has made all things for the use of men, if they found themselves capable of using them, and that the laws of men were only made to assist a few that could not otherwise do as they would; but I am not inclined to submit to any such tyranny, but will become a great man in spite of my evil surroundings.' 'This is a most remarkable boy,' mused Hong Pansa. 'What a pity that he is not my proper and legitimate son, that he might be an honor to my name. As it is, I fear he will cause me serious trouble.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個明亮的月夜，洪判事看見兒子在庭院中練習武藝，便問他這是什麼意思。吉童回答說，他正在把自己鍛鍊成一個受人敬畏的人。「我知道上天造萬物是供人使用的，只要人們覺得自己有能力使用它們；而人間的法律只是為了幫助少數無法隨心所欲的人；但我不願屈服於這樣的暴政，儘管身處惡劣的環境，我也要成為一個偉大的人。」「這是個極不尋常的孩子，」洪判事暗自思忖。「可惜他不是我名正言順的嫡子，不能為我的家名增光。照這樣下去，我怕他會給我惹來大麻煩。」

title.en: The Fortune-Teller's Prophecy and the Escape from the Assassins
title.zh: 術士讖語劍下逃生

region.en: Hong mansion and mountain storm (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 洪府與荒山（象徵性定位）

period: Novel tale (c. 1600s) collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 9, eBook #55539

summary.en: The jealous wife and concubine hire sorceresses, who send an old woman from the east gate to 'foretell' the boy's future: 'This will be a very great man; if not a king, he will be greater than the king, and will avenge his early wrongs by killing all his family.' The father locks Kil Tong in a strong room; the concubine finally persuades him to send assassins, while a spirit fills the father with disease and the mootang drum and dance in vain. Musing in the dark on the unjust laws that allow sons to be born of concubines but deny them rights, Kil Tong hears a crow caw three times — 'This means something ill to me' — and the window opens on the assassins, who find the room empty and wound each other, killing the old woman their guide; the room has disappeared, they are surrounded by high mountains in a mighty storm with rocks flying through the air, until music sounds and a boy comes riding by on a donkey playing a flute: Kil Tong, who takes their weapons and spares them on condition they never try to kill another man. He cures his father with medicine in a night visit, bades his mother good-by, and starts for an unknown country.
summary.zh: 嫡母與妖妾賄巫嫗，誣吉童他日必弒全家。父乃禁之密室，尋命刺客殺之。吉童夜聞烏鴉三噪，自知有變；刺客入室，空無一人，反自相殘殺，並斃其導者嫗。忽大風起，飛沙走石，四山合圍。忽聞笛聲，見一童騎驢吹笛而至，即吉童也，奪其兵刃，誓不許再殺人乃貸其死。吉童以藥起父疾，別母而遁。

sensitivity.note: Assassination attempt depicted at summary level.

passages.text: The wife of Hong Pansa and his other concubine, seeing how much their lord and master thought of Kil Tong, grew to hate the latter intensely, and called some mootang, or sorceresses, who sent the old woman who lives by the east gate. Kil Tong came as called, and on seeing him the hag bowed and said: 'Send out all of the people. This will be a very great man; if not a king, he will be greater than the king, and will avenge his early wrongs by killing all his family.' At this the father called to her to stop, and enjoined strict secrecy upon her; he sent Kil Tong at once to a strong room and had him locked in for safe keeping.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 洪判事的妻子和另一名妾室，見主人如此看重吉童，便越發痛恨他，於是召來幾名巫女，又派了住在東門的老婦人前去。吉童應召而來，老婦一見他便行禮說道：「把所有人都打發出去。這將是個極了不起的人；即使不是君王，也會比君王更偉大，並且會殺盡全家，以報早年的冤屈。」父親聽罷，喝令她住口，並嚴囑她絕對保密；他立刻把吉童送到一間堅固的房間，將他鎖在裡面嚴加看管。

passages.text: The unnatural father was kept in continual excitement by his wicked concubine, and was finally persuaded to send for the assassins. But a spirit filled the father with disease, and he told the men to stay their work; the mootang women were called in, and they beat their drums and danced about the room conjuring the spirit to leave, but it would not obey — till they said, at the suggestion of the concubine, that Kil Tong was the cause of the disorder.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這狠心的父親被他邪惡的妾室弄得終日心神不寧，最後被說服去召刺客。但有一個鬼魂使父親染上疾病，他便吩咐那些人暫緩動手；巫女們被召來，她們敲鼓繞室起舞，召請那鬼魂離去，但它不肯聽從——直到她們依那妾室的建議說，吉童才是這病亂的根源。

passages.text: While thus musing in the darkness of the night, he heard a crow caw three times and fly away. 'This means something ill to me,' thought he; and just then his window was thrown open, and in stepped the assassins. They made at the boy, but he was not there; in their rage they wounded each other and killed the old woman who was their guide. To their amazement the room had disappeared, and they were surrounded by high mountains; a mighty storm arose, and rocks flew through the air. Music was heard, and a boy came riding by on a donkey, playing a flute: he took away their weapons, showed himself to be Kil Tong, and promised not to kill them on condition that they should never try to kill another man — for he would know if the promise was broken.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他正這樣在夜色中沉思，忽然聽見一隻烏鴉叫了三聲便飛走了。「這對我是不祥之兆。」他心想；就在此時，窗戶猛然被推開，刺客們走了進來。他們撲向那少年，他卻已不在那裡；他們一怒之下互相砍傷，還殺死了替他們帶路的老婦。令他們驚愕的是，房間竟消失了，他們被高山環繞；一場猛烈的風暴驟起，石塊在空中飛舞。只聽得樂聲響起，一名少年騎著驢子吹著笛子經過：他奪走了他們的兵器，表明自己就是吉童，並允諾不殺他們，條件是他們永遠不得再企圖殺害任何人——因為若違背此約，他必會知曉。

passages.text: Kil Tong went by night to see his father, who thought him a spirit and was very much afraid. He gave his father medicine, which instantly cured him; and sending for his mother, bade her good-by, and started for an unknown country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 吉童夜裡去見父親，父親以為他是鬼魂，十分害怕。他給父親服下藥，父親立刻痊癒；他又派人請來母親，向她辭別，然後動身前往一個陌生的國度。

title.en: The Stone Door of the Robber Stronghold
title.zh: 石門盜窟

region.en: Barren peak in the southern mountains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南方高山絕頂（象徵性定位）

period: Novel tale (c. 1600s) collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 9, eBook #55539

summary.en: Free at last, Kil Tong journeys south, ascends the lonely mountains where tigers abound yet molest him not, and finds high on a barren peak a huge stone door in the bare wall of rock. Opening it he steps into an open plain surrounded by inaccessible mountains, with over two hundred good houses and many men. 'We are called thieves; but we only despoil the hated official class of some of their ill-gotten gains. No man can enter our stronghold and depart alive, unless he has become one of us; and he must prove himself strong in body and mind.' Kil Tong chooses his own trial: going up to a huge rock on which several men are seated, he lays hold of it and hurls it to some distance. He is installed a member, the contract sealed by mingling blood from the lips of all the members, and made chief. For their first great raid he disguises himself in the red gown of a betrothed youth, presents a forged letter and a promised train of one hundred ponies loaded with rice to the rich, licentious temple priests — and when the ponies arrive, the 'grooms' hiding robbers seize the servants while the priests are bent in humiliation over a pebble produced from the guest's mouth. The band loads the ponies with jewels, rice and cash, and escapes by the main road while Kil Tong, disguised as a priest, leads the belated soldiers down a by-path in the wrong direction.
summary.zh: 吉童遁入深山，見石壁上有巨門一扇，啟之則別有天地，屋舍二百餘，盜眾聚焉。眾曰：『吾儕所劫者贓官耳。入吾山者非入夥即死，且須力試。』吉童舉巨石而擲之，眾驚服，歃血為盟，推為首領。吉童乃扮紅衣新郎，偽稱洪參判之子，齎父書並百匹載米之駝隊往巨刹布施；寺僧大喜，設宴。吉童忽自口中吐石一粒，曰『以此待客耶』，僧慚俯首。伏兵齊起，盡縛僧眾，載其金寶而去；吉童又扮僧引官兵於歧路。眾益神之。

sensitivity.note: Social-bandit romance; anti-elite satire; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Kil Tong, free at last, journeyed to the south, and began to ascend the lonely mountains. Tigers were abundant, but he feared them not, and they seemed to avoid molesting him. After many days he found himself high up on a barren peak enveloped by the clouds. Through the clouds at some distance he espied a huge stone door in the bare wall of rock; opening it, he stepped inside, when, to his amazement, he found himself in an open plain, surrounded by high and inaccessible mountains, with over two hundred good houses, and many men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 吉童終於脫身，一路南行，開始攀登荒僻的山嶺。山中老虎眾多，他卻毫不畏懼，而老虎似乎也避開他，不來侵擾。過了許多天，他發現自己身處雲霧繚繞的高聳荒峰之上。透過雲霧，他望見不遠處光禿的岩壁上有一扇巨大的石門；他推開門走進去，竟驚異地發現自己置身於一片開闊的平原，四周環繞著高峻難攀的山巒，平原上有兩百多間完好的房屋，還有許多人。

passages.text: 'We are called thieves,' was answered; 'but we only despoil the hated official class of some of their ill-gotten gains. No man can enter our stronghold and depart alive, unless he has become one of us; and to do so he must prove himself to be strong in body and mind.' Kil Tong consented to the conditions. Going up to a huge rock on which several men were seated, he laid hold of it and hurled it to some distance, to the dismay of the men, who fell from their seat, and to the surprised delight of all. He was at once installed a member, the contract sealed by mingling blood from the lips of all the members, and later made their chief.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「我們被稱為盜賊，」對方答道，「但我們只掠奪那可憎的官吏階級一些不義之財。沒有人能進入我們的寨壘後活著離去，除非他成為我們的一員；而要成為我們的一員，他必須證明自己身心皆強健。」吉童應允了這些條件。他走向一塊坐著數人的巨石，一把抓住它，將它拋到遠處，座上的人驚慌跌落，眾人則又驚又喜。他當即被接納為一員，眾人以各自唇上之血相混，立下盟約，後來他又被推為首領。

passages.text: On a given day Kil Tong, dressed in the red gown of a youth just betrothed, covered himself with the dust of travel and mounted on a donkey made his way to a large and strong Buddhist temple, well patronized by officials who made it a place of retirement for pleasure and debauch. He presented a letter to the head priest, stating that a train of one hundred ponies loaded with rice had been sent as a present from his father; the priests were delighted, and a great feast was ordered. Suddenly Kil Tong clapped his hand over his cheek with a cry of pain, and produced from his mouth a pebble, previously introduced on the sly: 'Is it to feed on stones that my father sent me to this place?' The priests bowed their shaven heads to the floor in humiliation, and at a sign from Kil Tong the robbers who had entered as grooms and in the rice bags seized servants and priests alike, loading the ponies with jewels, rice, cash and whatever of value they could lay hands upon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了約定之日，吉童換上剛訂親的少年所穿的紅袍，滿身風塵，騎上驢子，前往一座宏大堅固的佛寺。這座佛寺深受官吏們的供養，他們把它當作尋歡作樂、縱情聲色的退隱之所。他呈上一封信給住持，信中說他父親送來一百匹載滿稻米的馬隊作為禮物；僧侶們大喜，隨即吩咐備下盛大的宴席。忽然，吉童捂著臉頰痛呼一聲，從口中吐出一顆事先偷偷含入的小石子：「難道我父親送我到這裡來，是要我吃石子的嗎？」僧侶們羞愧得把剃光的頭伏在地上，吉童一聲示意，那些扮作馬伕、藏身於米袋中潛入的盜賊便一擁而上，把僕役和僧侶一併擒住，將珠寶、稻米、錢幣以及一切能拿到手的貴重財物裝上馬隊。

passages.text: An old priest made off quietly to the yamen and called for soldiers. Kil Tong, disguised as a priest, called to them to follow him down a by-path after the robbers; while he conveyed the soldiers over the rough path, the robbers made good their escape by the main road, leaving the soldiers groping helplessly in the dark among the rocks and trees in a direction opposite that taken by the robbers. Kil Tong's name was noised abroad, and the robber band made him their chief with the consent of all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一名老僧悄悄溜到衙門，召來兵丁。吉童扮作僧人，招呼他們跟著他沿一條小徑去追盜賊；當他把兵丁引過崎嶇小路時，盜賊們卻從大路安然逃脫，留下兵丁在黑暗中於岩石樹木間茫然摸索，所循方向與盜賊所走的方向恰恰相反。吉童的名聲於是傳揚開來，盜賊團夥在眾人的一致同意下推他為首領。

title.en: Eight Kil Tongs, the Palace Cloud, and the Stork of the Garden
title.zh: 八洪吉童跨鶴朝王

region.en: Royal palace, Seoul; islands off the west coast (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城王宮（象徵性定位）

period: Novel tale (c. 1600s) collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 9, eBook #55539

summary.en: The audacity multiplies: the Pochang who boasted he would capture the robber alone is drugged at the stronghold and carried in a bag to a high mountain overlooking the capital, where he casts himself down; reports come of great depredations in each of the eight provinces at the same time, and when the orders are obeyed, a guard comes from each province bringing Kil Tong — eight men alike in every respect, each with the scar on the left thigh, and all found to be figures in straw and wax. A letter on the Palace gate offers to stop the depredations if the government confers the rank of Pansa; when Kil Tong comes to make his bow before the King, the assassins waiting are confounded — he is caught up in a cloud and borne away amid strange music. Later, in the royal gardens under a full moon, a flute sounds and a man descends seated upon the back of a gracefully moving stork: 'Fear not, O King. I am simply Hong Pansa. I have come to make my obeisance before your august presence and be confirmed in my rank.' Asking only three thousand bags of rice, he sails to an island off the west coast, founds a settlement, and the story turns on the rescue of a stolen lady from savage mountain bandits, whom he slays with the aid of his old friends the spirits (quay sin).
summary.zh: 捕頭自誇能擒吉童，反被藥啞，囊載至御苑山上，慚而投崖。未幾八道同時報警，朝廷按名捕拿，八道各解一人至，形貌無異，皆曰腿有瘢，驗之，乃稻草蠟人所為。吉童乃投書闕下，乞除參判之職即罷掠。入朝之際，忽乘雲而去，眾皆愕然。後於御苑月夜，自騎鶴而降，再拜請罪，乞米三千石，浮海而西，據島為王。山中遇劫掠民女之野人，以毒箭誅其酋，復召神兵（鬼神）盡殲其黨，遂娶所救之女。

sensitivity.note: Bandit-hero fantasy; violence summarized.

passages.text: The Pochang, who had charge of the prisons and was a man of great courage, boasted he would capture the thief alone. Disguised as a traveller he fell in at a little inn with Kil Tong in disguise, was guided into the mountains and the stone-door stronghold, drugged with wine, and put into a bag and conveyed in a marvellous manner to a high mountain overlooking the capital; not daring to face his sovereign with such a fabulous tale, he cast himself down and was picked up dead in the morning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 負責管理監獄、膽識過人的捕盜將（Pochang）誇口說他能獨自擒住那盜賊。他喬裝成旅人，在一間小客棧裡與同樣喬裝的吉童（Kil Tong）巧遇，被引進山中那座石門寨壘，遭人以酒灌醉，裝進袋裡，又以奇妙的方式被送到俯瞰都城的一座高山上；他不敢帶著這般荒誕不經的故事去面見君王，便縱身跳下，翌晨被人發現時已氣絕身亡。

passages.text: Simultaneous reports of great depredations came in each of the eight provinces, all attributed to Kil Tong. Official orders were issued to each of the eight governors; the orders were so well obeyed that upon a certain day soon after, a guard came from each province bringing Kil Tong, and there in a line stood eight men alike in every respect. Asked to decide which was his true son, the father stated that his son had a scar on the left thigh — instantly each of the eight men pulled up the baggy trousers and displayed a scar. When the guard was commanded to kill all of them, the men were found to be only figures in straw and wax.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 八道同時傳來遭到大肆劫掠的稟報，全都歸咎於吉童。官府向八道觀察使下達命令；命令執行得極為徹底，不久之後的某一天，每一道都各有一名差役押著吉童前來，八個人並排而立，處處一模一樣。父親被要求指認哪一個才是他真正的兒子，便說他兒子左大腿上有一道疤——八個人立刻撩起寬鬆的褲子，個個都露出一道疤。當差役奉命將他們全部處死時，才發現這些人不過是稻草與蠟做成的假人。

passages.text: A letter posted on the Palace gate announced that if the government would confer upon Kil Tong the rank of Pansa, thus removing the stigma attaching to him as the son of a slave, he would stop his depredations. The decree was issued; but knowing the plans laid for him, as he passed through the gates and came near enough to be seen of the King, he was caught up in a cloud and borne away amid strange music, wholly discomfiting his enemies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 宮門上貼出一封信，聲明倘若朝廷賜予吉童判事（Pansa）之職，從而洗去他身為奴婢之子所蒙受的污名，他便停止劫掠。詔令頒下了；但他早已識破為他設下的計謀，當他穿過宮門、走近到足以讓國王看見時，便被一朵雲托起，在奇異的樂聲中飄然而去，令他的敵人全然狼狽失措。

passages.text: Some time after, the King was walking with eunuchs and attendants in the royal gardens, the leaves blood-red on the maples, when all were astonished by the sound of a flute played by some one up above them. Looking up among the tree-tops a man was seen descending toward them, seated upon the back of a gracefully moving stork. 'Fear not, O King. I am simply Hong Pansa. I have come to make my obeisance before your august presence and be confirmed in my rank.' 'I wish to go to a distant land, and settle down to the pursuit of peace and happiness. If I may be granted three thousand bags of rice I will gladly go and trouble you no longer.' In the early morning a fleet of junks appeared off the royal granaries, took on the rice, and made away before the people were well aware of their presence; Kil Tong sailed for an island off the west coast, and with his followers founded a settlement there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 過了些時日，國王與宦官及侍從在御苑中散步，楓葉血紅，忽然眾人聽見上方有人吹笛，無不驚詫。抬頭望向樹梢之間，只見一人坐在一隻姿態優雅地移動的鶴背上，正向他們降下。「大王不必驚慌。我不過是洪判事（Hong Pansa）。我特來御前叩拜，並請正式確認我的官職。」「我想到遠方去，安頓下來，追求安寧與幸福。若能賜我三千袋米，我便樂意離去，不再叨擾您。」清晨時分，一支帆船隊出現在御用糧倉外，裝上米糧，趁人們尚未察覺便揚帆而去；吉童航向西海岸外的一座島嶼，與他的追隨者在那裡建立了一處聚落。

title.en: Tokoyo and the Serpent God Yofune-Nushi
title.zh: 常世斬蛇——夜船主之神

region.en: Rocky bay of the Oki Islands, and the sea cave of the serpent
region.zh: 隱岐群島岩灣與蛇神海底洞窟

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: Banished to the Oki Islands, Oribe Shima's daughter Tokoyo rows alone across the sea to find him; she saves a girl from sacrifice to the serpent god Yofune-Nushi, offers herself instead, dives with a dagger between her teeth into the cave where the white serpent guards a cursed image of Hojo Takatoki, blinds its right eye, pierces its heart, and by carrying the image ashore unwittingly cures the tyrant's disease and frees her father.
summary.zh: 織部島被流放隱岐，其女常世渡海尋父。夜聞少女將被獻祭蛇神夜船主，遂以身相代，口銜短劍潛入海底洞窟；洞中供著北條高時之像，白蛇瞪目竄出。常世先刺其右眼，再刺其心，斬之；抱神像與蛇屍出水。高時之疾恰在此時痊癒，織部島被赦還鄉，父女團聚。

sensitivity.note: Japanese hero-maiden legend adapted from R. Gordon Smith; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Oribe Shima had offended the great ruler Hojo Takatoki and was banished to Kamishima, one of the Oki Islands, forced to leave his beautiful daughter Tokoyo, whom he deeply loved. Unable to bear the separation, Tokoyo set out on a long journey to Akasaki in the province of Hoki; the fisher-folk laughed at her plan to row to the islands, but at nightfall she got into the lightest vessel she could find and by dint of a fair wind and persistent rowing came to one of the rocky bays of the Oki Islands. A fisherman warned her that the search might cost them both their lives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXVII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 織部志摩（Oribe Shima）得罪了偉大的統治者北條高時（Hojo Takatoki），被流放到隱岐群島之一的上海島（Kamishima），被迫離開他深愛的美麗女兒常世（Tokoyo）。常世不堪別離之苦，便踏上長途旅程，前往伯耆國（Hoki）的赤崎（Akasaki）；漁民們嘲笑她打算划船前往群島的計畫，但入夜後她登上所能找到的最輕便的船，憑著順風與不懈的划槳，來到隱岐群島的一處岩灣。一名漁夫警告她，這番尋訪可能使他們兩人喪命。

passages.text: That night, sleeping beneath a shrine dedicated to Buddha, Tokoyo was wakened by clapping of hands: a weeping maiden in white stood beside a priest who was about to push her over the rocks into the roaring sea. On the thirteenth of June, the priest explained, the Serpent God Yofune-Nushi demanded the sacrifice of a young girl, else he caused terrible storms. 'I am glad to have saved this poor girl's life,' said Tokoyo; 'I gladly offer myself in her place.' Taking the maiden's white robe and praying to the image of Buddha, she placed a small dagger between her teeth and plunged into the tempestuous sea, down through the moonlit water till she came to a mighty cave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXVII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那一夜，常世睡在一座供奉佛陀的神社下，被拍手的聲音驚醒：一名身穿白衣、泣不成聲的少女站在一名祭司身旁，那祭司正要將她推下岩石，投入怒號的大海。祭司解釋說，每逢六月十三日，蛇神夜船主（Yofune-Nushi）便要求獻祭一名年輕少女，否則便掀起可怕的風暴。「我很高興救了這可憐女孩的性命，」常世說道，「我樂意代替她獻出自己。」她接過少女的白袍，向佛像祈禱，將一柄小匕首銜在齒間，縱身躍入狂暴的大海，穿過月光映照的海水向下潛去，直到來到一座巨大的洞穴。

passages.text: In the cave stood a statue of Hojo Takatoki, who had sent her father into exile; she was about to tie the image on her back when a great white serpent crept out with eyes gleaming angrily — Yofune-Nushi himself. Tokoyo drew her dagger and thrust it through the right eye; the serpent retired into the cave, she followed and struck at its heart, and with a shriek of pain it fell dead upon the cavern floor. The priest and the maiden on the rocks saw her rise to the surface carrying the image and a mighty fish-like creature. Reported to Hojo Takatoki, the story had a strange sequel: the ruler had long suffered from an incurable disease, and he regained his health precisely at the hour when his image — cursed and thrown into the sea by some exile — was restored. Hearing the brave girl was the daughter of the banished Oribe Shima, he sent her father home with all speed, where he and his daughter lived in peace and happiness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXVII (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 洞窟中矗立著一尊北條高時的雕像，正是他將她的父親流放；她正要把這尊像綁在背上時，一條巨大的白蛇爬了出來，雙眼閃爍著憤怒的光芒——那正是夜船主。常世拔出匕首，刺穿了牠的右眼；那蛇退回了洞窟之中，她跟了進去，刺向牠的心臟，牠發出一聲痛苦的尖叫，便倒地死在洞窟的地上。岩石上的祭司與少女看見她浮上水面，帶著那尊像和一隻巨大的魚形生物。此事稟報給北條高時之後，故事有了奇異的後續：這位統治者長年飽受不治之症之苦，而他恢復健康的時刻，恰恰就是他那尊被某位流放者詛咒並投入海中的雕像被尋回之時。他聽說這位勇敢的少女正是被流放的織部志摩之女，便火速送她的父親返鄉，父女二人自此過著平安幸福的生活。

title.en: The Kappa's Promise
title.zh: 河童的簽字——川子之約

region.en: The river Kawachi near Matsue, Izumo
region.zh: 出雲松江川內川

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: The river goblin of the Kawachi drowns villagers and cattle until it seizes a horse and is dragged ashore and bound; refusing to write, the creature presses its inky hand upon a document swearing never to harm the village again, and the mark is still preserved in the temple of Kawako-no-miya — for to defeat a kappa is as unlucky as to be beaten by one.
summary.zh: 河童居川內川，屢害村民牲畜。一日擒馬失手，被拖上岸縛住。村人不忍殺之，令其立誓不害村中一人一畜；河童不能寫字，蘸墨按手印為據，放歸川中。其印至今存於川子神社，蓋河童不可殺亦不可勝——勝之者必衰。

sensitivity.note: Japanese river-goblin (kappa) legend of Izumo; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Kappa is a river goblin with the body of a tortoise and scaly limbs, an ape-like head with a cavity containing a mysterious fluid that is the source of its power. Fierce yet extremely polite, it challenges wayfarers to single combat, but a profound bow makes it bow in reply, spilling the strength-giving liquid from its cranium and rendering it feeble. To defeat the Kappa, however, is as unfortunate as to be beaten by it, for momentary glory is followed by a wasting away; in some parts of Japan it claims two victims every year, striking bathers in lake or river and sucking their blood like a vampire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 河童是一種河中的妖怪，身軀如龜，四肢覆鱗，頭似猿猴，頭頂有一個凹窩，窩中盛著一種神秘的液體，那正是牠力量的來源。牠性情凶猛卻極為有禮，會向路人挑戰單打獨鬥，但只要有人深深一鞠躬，牠便會回禮鞠躬，頭頂那賦予力量的液體便會灑出來，使牠變得虛弱無力。然而，擊敗河童與被牠擊敗同樣不幸，因為短暫的榮耀之後便是日漸衰敗；在日本某些地方，牠每年要奪走兩條性命，襲擊在湖中或河中沐浴的人，像吸血鬼一樣吸食他們的鮮血。

passages.text: In ancient days a Kappa dwelt in the river Kawachi and seized and destroyed villagers and their domestic animals. One day a horse entered the river and the Kappa, trying to capture it, twisted its neck; the frightened horse sprang up the bank into a neighbouring field with the Kappa still holding on, and the owner and many villagers securely bound the Child of the River. 'Let us kill this horrible creature,' said the peasants; but the owner answered: 'We will make him swear never to destroy the inhabitants or the domestic animals of this village.' A document was prepared and the Kappa was asked to sign it. 'I cannot write,' it replied, 'but I will dip my hand in ink and press it upon the document.' When the inky mark was made the creature was released to its river, and from that day to this the Kappa has remained true to its promise — the mark preserved in the little temple of Kawako-no-miya near Matsue.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古時候，有一隻河童住在河內川中，擄掠並殘害村民和他們的家畜。有一天，一匹馬走進河裡，那河童想要捉住牠，便扭住了牠的脖子；受驚的馬躍上岸，衝進鄰近的田裡，河童仍緊緊抓著不放，於是馬主和許多村民便把這「河之子」牢牢綁住。「我們把這可怕的東西殺了吧，」農人們說；但馬主回答：「我們要逼牠發誓，絕不再傷害這個村子的居民和家畜。」於是擬好了一份文書，要河童簽字。「我不會寫字，」牠回答，「但我會把我的手蘸上墨，按在文書上。」墨印按下之後，這隻生物便被放回牠的河中，從那天直到今日，河童始終信守承諾——那墨印至今仍保存在松江附近河子宮的小神社裡。

title.en: Yosho, the First Sennin of Japan
title.zh: 日本仙人元祖陽成

region.en: The mountains of Noto
region.zh: 能登山地

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: Born at Noto in 870 after his mother dreamt she swallowed the sun, the recluse Yosho lives on a single grain of millet a day and departs the earth in 901, leaving his mantle on a tree-branch bequeathed to Emmei of Dogen-ji; his stricken father, praying to see his son again, hears the Lotus of the Law recited overhead and is promised a monthly descent drawn by flowers and incense.
summary.zh: 能登聖人陽成，母夢吞日而生。日食一粟，誦法華經；901年離世，留衣缽於樹枝，遺書「以衣傳法眼寺榮明」。其父病篤思子，忽聞空中誦經——陽成言：每月十八日設花焚香，我魂必隨香降臨相見。

sensitivity.note: Japanese legend of the mountain-recluse sennin (Taoist-immortal cycle); passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Sennin are mountain recluses who, though in human form, are immortal and adepts in the magical arts. The first great Japanese sennin was Yosho, born at Noto in A.D. 870; just before his birth his mother dreamt she had swallowed the sun, a dream that foretold the miraculous power of her child. Studious and devout, Yosho spent most of his time studying the 'Lotus of the Law', lived very simply, and at length reduced his diet to a single grain of millet a day. He departed from the earth in A.D. 901, having attained much supernatural power.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 仙人乃是山中的隱士，雖具人形，卻長生不死，且精通法術。日本第一位偉大的仙人是陽升，於西元八七〇年生於能登；就在他出生之前，他的母親夢見自己吞下了太陽，這夢預示了她孩子奇蹟般的力量。陽升好學而虔誠，大部分時間都用來研讀《法華經》，生活極為簡樸，最後更把飲食減至每日僅一粒粟米。他於西元九〇一年離開人世，此時已修得諸多神通。

passages.text: Yosho left his mantle hanging on the branch of a tree, together with a scroll bearing the words: 'I bequeath my mantle to Emmei of Dogen-ji.' In due time Emmei became a sennin and, like his master, performed many marvels. Shortly after Yosho's disappearance his father became seriously ill and prayed ardently to see his well-loved son again; in reply Yosho's voice was heard overhead reciting the 'Lotus of the Law', and when the recitation ended he said to his stricken father: 'If flowers are offered and incense burned on the 18th of every month, my spirit will descend and greet you, drawn by the perfume of the flowers and the blue smoke of incense.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 陽升把他的道袍留在樹枝上，並附上一卷寫著這些話的卷軸：「我將我的道袍遺贈給道元寺的惠命。」後來惠命果然成了仙人，並像他的師父一樣行了許多奇蹟。陽升消失後不久，他的父親病重，殷切祈禱能再見到他深愛的兒子；回應他的，是陽升的聲音從上方傳來，誦讀著《法華經》，誦經完畢後，他對病重的父親說：「若在每月十八日獻上鮮花、焚燒香火，我的神靈便會降臨問候您，被花香與香火的青煙所吸引而來。」

title.en: The Shojo's White Sake
title.zh: 猩猩的白酒

region.en: The seashore below the miraculous Mount Fuji (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 富士山麓海濱（象徵釘）

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: A dying father's wish for sake sends the boy Koyuri to the shore, where red-haired sea-monsters fill his gourd with their sacred white sake that restores youth to the good; a jealous neighbour who beats the boy tastes only filthy water and is poisoned until he repents — then Yurine and Mamikiko brew the Shojo's sake on Fuji's southern side and live three hundred years.
summary.zh: 油根病危思酒，其子小百合海濱遇紅髮海妖，以葫芦乞得白酒，父飲之病癒。貪鄰萬吉仗勢索酒，入口即吐，反而毒發；海妖自稱猩猩，白酒可使善者延年、貪者中毒。服藥悔過後得赦；後二人於富士南麓釀猩猩酒，活三百歲。

sensitivity.note: Japanese sea-monster (shojo) legend adapted from R. Gordon Smith; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: On the day following the miraculous appearance of Mount Fuji a poor man named Yurine, who lived near the mountain, became extremely ill and desired to drink a cup of sake before he died. But there was no rice wine in the hut, and his boy Koyuri wandered along the shore with a gourd in his hand. There he found two strange creatures with long red hair and skin the colour of pink cherry-blossom, wearing green seaweed girdles, drinking white sake from large flat cups replenished from a great stone jar. 'My father is dying and much desires a cup of sake,' said the boy; and one of the creatures filled his gourd. The old man drank eagerly: 'This is no common wine. It has given me strength, and already I feel new life flowing through my old veins.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 富士山奇蹟般出現的次日，住在山附近一個名叫百合的窮人病得極重，想在死前喝一杯酒。但小屋裡沒有米酒，他的兒子小百合便拿著一個葫蘆沿著海岸遊蕩。他在那裡發現了兩個奇怪的生物，長著長長的紅髮，皮膚呈粉紅櫻花之色，腰間圍著綠色的海藻，正從一只大石甕中斟出白色的酒，盛在大而扁的杯子裡飲用。「我父親快死了，非常想喝一杯酒，」男孩說；其中一個生物便斟滿了他的葫蘆。老人急切地喝下：「這不是普通的酒。它給了我力氣，我已經感覺到新的生命在我衰老的血脈中流動。」

passages.text: Yurine's neighbour Mamikiko, hearing of the supply, grew jealous, snatched the gourd, spat out the sake as filthy water and beat the boy, forcing him to lead the way to the red-haired people. Koyuri wept as he told how his honesty had been doubted; the red man refilled the gourd and chuckled over Mamikiko's experience, then filled his huge cup — and the greedy man felt sick at the first taste. 'You are not aware that I am a Shojo and live near the Sea Dragon's Palace. This sacred white sake restores youth and years to human beings, and to Shojo it vanquishes death; to the greedy and selfish it is poison.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 百合的鄰居真美子聽說有這樣的酒，心生嫉妒，搶過葫蘆，把酒吐出來說它是髒水，還打了那男孩，逼他帶路去找紅髮的人。小百合哭著訴說自己的誠實如何遭到懷疑；紅髮人重新裝滿葫蘆，對真美子的遭遇暗自好笑，接著斟滿他那巨大的杯子——那貪婪的人一嚐便覺得噁心。「你不知道我是個少女，住在海龍宮附近。這神聖的白酒能使人恢復青春與年歲，對少女而言能戰勝死亡；對貪婪自私的人來說，它卻是毒藥。」

passages.text: 'Poison?' groaned the contrite Mamikiko; 'good Shojo, have mercy and spare my life!' The Shojo gave him a powder, saying: 'Swallow this in sake and repent of your wickedness.' He did so, and this time the white sake was delicious. Mamikiko lost no time in making friends with Yurine, and some years later the two men took up their abode on the southern side of Mount Fuji, brewed the Shojo's white sake, and lived for three hundred years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「毒藥？」悔悟的真美子呻吟道；「善良的少女啊，請發發慈悲，饒我一命！」少女給了他一包藥粉，說：「用酒吞下這個，為你的惡行懺悔吧。」他照做了，這回白酒美味極了。真美子立刻與百合結為好友，幾年後兩人定居在富士山南麓，釀造少女的白酒，活了三百歲。

title.en: Issunboshi and the Magic Mallet
title.zh: 一寸法師與小槌

region.en: The Prince Sanjo's house and the Temple of Kwannon, Kyoto
region.zh: 三條殿與觀音堂（京都）

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: An old couple who pray to the deified Empress Jingo for a child 'even if no bigger than a finger' receive exactly that, and angrily send the One-Inch Priest away; sailing a soup-bowl with a chopstick to Kyoto, he becomes the Princess Sanjo's page, defeats two oni from inside the first one's stomach, and when the Princess taps the oni's dropped lucky mallet, his wish to be as big as other people is granted — ending as a great lord married to the Princess.
summary.zh: 老夫婦向神功皇后神社求子：「小如指頭也好。」果然得一寸法師，十三歲不長，遂辭親出遊。以湯碗為舟、筷子為槳，抵京都為三條公主侍童。參拜觀音堂時二鬼攔路，一鬼吞之，一寸法師於鬼腹中持針劍亂刺，鬼咳而吐出；再登另一鬼鼻孔刺其目，二鬼逃遁。公主拾鬼遺小槌擊地祝禱，一寸法師頃刻長成正常青年，終成大官，娶三條氏幼女。

sensitivity.note: Japanese folktale of the Issunboshi cycle; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: An old married couple went to the shrine of the deified Empress Jingo and prayed that they might be blessed with a child, even if it were no bigger than one of their fingers. A voice sounded from behind the bamboo curtain, and they were told their wish would be granted. In due time the old woman gave birth to a child no bigger than a little finger; the parents were extremely angry, though the Empress had fulfilled their prayer to the letter. The little fellow was called Issunboshi, the One-Inch Priest, and at thirteen he was still the same size as at birth, so exasperated were his parents at neighbours' jeers — 'Little Finger', 'Grain-of-Corn' — that they determined to send him away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一對老夫婦前往神化皇后神功的祠廟祈禱，希望能蒙恩得子，哪怕孩子只有他們一根手指那麼大也好。竹簾後傳來一個聲音，告訴他們心願將會實現。時候到了，老婦人生下一個只有小指那麼大的孩子；父母雖然如願以償，皇后也分毫不差地應了他們的禱告，他們卻極為惱怒。這小傢伙被叫作一寸法師，到了十三歲仍和出生時一樣大小，鄰居們的嘲笑——「小指頭」、「玉米粒」——令他的父母十分惱火，於是決定把他送走。

passages.text: He asked for a needle, a small soup-bowl and a chop-stick, and set off on his adventures, propelling the bowl like a boat with the chop-stick until he reached Kyoto. At the house of Prince Sanjo his minute voice won him a place, and he became the Princess Sanjo's page, accompanying his mistress everywhere. One day, leaving the Temple of Kwannon, two oni (evil spirits) sprang upon them. Issunboshi drew his needle-sword from its hollow straw; one oni laughed, 'I could swallow you as a cormorant swallows a trout, my funny little bean-seed, and I will!' — and opened its mouth, and the little hero found himself slipping down a huge dark throat. Nothing daunted, he bored away with his needle-sword until the spirit coughed him back into the sunny world; the second oni fared worse, for Issunboshi climbed its nostril and pierced its eyes, and both creatures fled yelling.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他要了一根針、一個小湯碗和一根筷子，便踏上冒險之路，用筷子像撐船一樣推動湯碗，直到抵達京都。在三條親王的宅邸，他細小的聲音為他贏得了一個位置，他成了三條公主的侍童，隨侍小姐到處去。有一天，他們離開觀音寺時，兩個鬼（惡靈）向他們撲來。一寸法師從空心的草鞘中抽出針劍；一個鬼笑道：「我能像鸕鶿吞鱒魚一樣把你吞下去，我滑稽的小豆子，我這就吞！」——牠張開嘴，這小英雄發現自己正滑進一個巨大漆黑的喉嚨。他毫不畏懼，用針劍不停地鑽，直到那鬼把他咳回陽光普照的世界；第二個鬼更慘，因為一寸法師爬上牠的鼻孔，刺穿了牠的眼睛，兩個鬼都尖叫著逃走了。

passages.text: On the way home the Princess picked up a small wooden mallet dropped by the wicked oni — a lucky mallet: 'You have only to wish and then tap it upon the ground, and your wish, no matter what, is always granted.' When Issunboshi wished to be as big as other people, the Princess tapped the mallet on the ground and in a moment he was transformed from a bijou creature to a lad just like other youths of his age. The curious Emperor summoned him, gave him many gifts and made him a high official; finally Issunboshi became a great lord and married Prince Sanjo's youngest daughter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 回家路上，公主撿起惡鬼掉落的一把小木槌——一把幸運槌：「你只要許願，然後把它往地上一敲，無論什麼願望都總會實現。」當一寸法師希望變得和別人一樣高大時，公主把木槌往地上一敲，轉眼間他就從一個玲瓏的小人兒變成了一個和他同齡少年一模一樣的男孩。好奇的天皇召見了他，賜給他許多禮物，封他為高官；最後一寸法師成了大領主，娶了三條親王最小的女兒。

title.en: Kintaro, the Golden Boy of Ashigara
title.zh: 金太郎——足柄山黃金童子

region.en: Ashigara Mountain
region.zh: 足柄山

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: Born to the disgraced courtier Sakata Kurando and the lady Yaegiri on lonely Ashigara Mountain, the Golden Boy fells trees like a woodcutter and speaks the language of bear, deer, hare and monkey; he uproots a tree to bridge a river before the astounded hero Yorimitsu, who takes the boy as retainer, names him Sakata Kintoki, and makes him a famous warrior whom children still carry in their bosoms.
summary.zh: 禁軍武士坂田藏人不名誉離京，與女嬖八重切逃亡成婚未果而自盡。八重切於足柄山生金太郎：孩提持斧伐木如樵，與熊鹿猿兔為友，通獸語。一日拔樹為橋渡溪，適為賴光所見，遣人問明來歷，收其為家臣，賜名坂田金時，後成名武將，孩童至今佩其像。

sensitivity.note: Japanese hero-legend of Kintaro/Sakata Kintoki; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Sakata Kurando, an officer of the Emperor's bodyguard, brave yet gentle, loved the beautiful lady Yaegiri; falling into disgrace, he left the Court to become a travelling tobacco merchant. Yaegiri escaped her home and wandered the country until she found him — but the unhappy man put an end to his humiliation by taking his own life. When she had buried her lover she went to Ashigara Mountain, where she gave birth to a child called Kintaro, the Golden Boy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 坂田藏人是天皇侍衛隊的一名軍官，勇敢而溫和，愛上了美麗的八重桐小姐；他失寵後離開宮廷，成了走街串巷的煙草商。八重桐逃出家門，在鄉間流浪，直到找到他——但這不幸的人為了結束自己的屈辱而自盡了。她埋葬了情人後，前往足柄山，在那裡生下了一個孩子，名叫金太郎，即黃金男孩。

passages.text: Kintaro was remarkable for extreme strength: when only a few years old his mother gave him an axe with which he felled trees as quickly as an experienced woodcutter. Lonely on the desolate mountain, he made companions of the bear, deer, hare and monkey and spoke their strange language. One day he arranged a wrestling match, a kindly old bear digging the daïs, a hare and a monkey grappling while a deer gave encouragement and kept the sport fair; Kintaro tactfully rewarded the equally strong pair with tempting rice-cakes. Coming to a river on the way home, he put his strong arms round a tree on the bank and pulled it across so that it formed a bridge — and the famous hero Yorimitsu and his retainers witnessed the extraordinary feat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 金太郎以力大無窮著稱：他不過幾歲時，母親便給了他一把斧頭，他砍起樹來竟和經驗豐富的樵夫一樣快。他在荒涼的山上感到孤單，便與熊、鹿、兔和猴子為伴，還會說牠們那些奇怪的話。有一天，他安排了一場角力比賽：一頭慈祥的老熊挖出比賽用的土臺，兔子和猴子扭打較量，鹿則在一旁加油打氣，並維持比賽的公平；金太郎則機巧地以誘人的米糕獎賞這對勢均力敵的對手。回家途中來到一條河邊，他伸出強壯的雙臂抱住岸上的一棵樹，把它拉倒橫跨河面，成了一座橋——而著名的英雄賴光和他的家臣親眼目睹了這樁非凡的壯舉。

passages.text: Watanabe Isuna followed Kintaro home and learned his story from Yaegiri. Yorimitsu came himself: 'If you will give me your child I will make him my retainer.' The woman gladly consented, and the Golden Boy went away with the great hero, who named him Sakata Kintoki. He became a famous warrior whose wonderful deeds are recited to this day, and children regard him as their favourite hero; little boys who would emulate his strength and bravery carry his portrait in their bosoms.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 渡邊綱跟著金太郎回家，從八重桐口中得知了他的來歷。賴光親自前來，說道：「你若肯把孩子交給我，我便收他為家臣。」那婦人欣然應允，金太郎便隨這位大英雄而去，賴光為他取名坂田金時。他成了著名的武士，其種種奇功偉績至今仍為人傳誦，孩子們更視他為最喜愛的英雄；那些想要效法他力氣與勇氣的小男孩，都把她的畫像揣在懷裡。

title.en: How the Old Man Lost His Wen
title.zh: 瘤取爺——鬼舞取瘤

region.en: A hollow tree in the mountains (symbolic pin: Edo region)
region.zh: 山中空心樹（象徵釘：江戶地方）

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: An old wood-cutter shelters from a storm in a hollow tree where demons dance; his unexpected good dancing delights them, and their chief removes the wen from his cheek as a pledge for tomorrow's performance — while the wicked neighbour who next hides in the tree dances so badly that the demons fling the wen back onto his right cheek, leaving him a wen on either side.
summary.zh: 老翁避雨躲進空心樹，窺見群鬼宴舞。鬼王嫌其舞伴笨拙，老翁不自覺失笑而現身獻舞；群鬼大喜，邀翌夜再舞，並以他右頰之瘤為質，無痛取下。惡鄰仿效前來，舞藝低劣惹鬼厭，臨走把昨夜質物——那顆瘤——擲回他右頰；從此惡鄰左右各一瘤。

sensitivity.note: Japanese folktale of the Kobu-tori Jii cycle; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text of Davis (1912), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: There was once an old man who had a wen on his right cheek that all medicines had made worse. One night, returning home laden with firewood, he was overtaken by a terrible thunderstorm and sheltered in a hollow tree. When the storm abated he heard sounds of merriment close at hand: a number of demons dancing, singing and drinking, one dancing clumsily by himself while the chief of the company was none too pleased. Forgetting caution, the old man left the tree, and when the leader cried, 'Enough! Is there no one who can dance better than this fellow?' it seemed that his youth returned; having once been an expert dancer, he offered to show his skill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXXI (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有個老人，右頰上長了一個瘤，什麼藥都試過，反而越治越糟。一天夜裡，他背著柴回家，途中遇上可怕的雷雨，便躲進一棵中空的樹裡避雨。風雨稍歇時，他聽見近處傳來歡鬧之聲：一群鬼正在跳舞、唱歌、飲酒，其中一個自顧自笨拙地跳著，首領卻顯得很不高興。老人忘了謹慎，從樹裡走了出來；首領喊道：「夠了！難道沒有人能比這傢伙跳得更好嗎？」這時老人彷彿回到了年輕時代；他從前本是跳舞的好手，便自告奮勇要顯一顯身手。

passages.text: The demons congratulated the old man on his performance, offered him a cup of sake and begged for more dances. When he agreed to dance again the following night, the chief said he must leave a pledge behind — and seeing the wen on the right cheek, judged it an excellent one, removing it without inflicting any pain before he and his companions vanished. The old man could scarcely realise that after many years of disfigurement he had at last lost his troublesome wen, and his old wife was none the less pleased.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXXI (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 群鬼稱讚老人的表演，遞給他一杯酒，又央求他再跳幾支。當他答應次夜再來跳舞時，首領說他必須留下一件抵押之物——看見他右頰上的瘤，便覺得這是極好的抵押品，於是毫不疼痛地把它取了下來，隨後便與同伴們一同消失了。老人幾乎不敢相信，多年來毀損他容貌的惱人瘤子竟終於去掉了，他的老妻也同樣歡喜。

passages.text: A wicked and cantankerous neighbour, afflicted for many years with a wen on his left cheek, heard the story and hid in the hollow tree at sunset. Before long one of the company said: 'The old man is a long time coming. I made sure he would keep his promise.' At these words the fellow crept out, flourished his fan and began to dance — but he knew nothing of dancing, and his extraordinary antics displeased the demons greatly. 'You dance extremely ill, and the sooner you stop the better we shall be pleased; but before you depart we will return the pledge you left with us last night.' The demon flung the wen at the right cheek of the old man, where it remained firmly fixed; so the deceiver went away with a wen on either side of his face.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXXI (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有個心術不正、脾氣乖戾的鄰居，左頰上長瘤已多年，聽說此事後，便趁日落時躲進那棵中空的樹裡。不久，群鬼中有一個說道：「那老頭兒來得可真久。我還以為他一定會守約呢。」聽了這話，那傢伙便爬了出來，揮舞扇子跳起舞來——可他根本不懂跳舞，他那古怪的動作令群鬼大為不悅。「你跳得極糟，你越早停下，我們越高興；不過在你離去之前，我們要把你昨夜留在我們這裡的抵押品還給你。」那鬼把瘤朝老人的右頰擲去，瘤便牢牢地黏在那裡；於是這騙子離去時，臉上兩邊各長了一個瘤。

title.en: The Fox-Bride and the Garden Shrine
title.zh: 狐新娘與庭園神社

region.en: The Inari shrines and fox-gardens of Kyoto: Mount Fushime and the miniature-mountain shrine garden
region.zh: 京都稻荷神社與庭園狐塚（伏見稻荷山）

period: Recorded 1912 (Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Japan (F. Hadland Davis, 1912)

summary.en: The bad fox's chief attribute is to delude human beings by taking the form of a beautiful woman — a shadow on water shows only the fox, a dog's glance strips the disguise — and the fullest fox-bride story in Davis is the Jewel Maiden, a fox who took bride-form at an emperor's court and was traced, life after life, back to the fox; at the garden shrine of the fox-god Inari the same creature-power is domesticated as stone foxes, and the household fox-ghost of the garden mountain watches over the people the god swore with Kobo Daishi to protect.
summary.zh: 惡狐最善化身美婦惑人：影落水中現狐形，遇犬則現原身。 Davis 書中最完整的「狐新娘」故事即「玉面夫人」——狐女入宮為妃，害主敗露，化狐而逃，歷劫受戒；而稻荷神社庭園中的石狐，則是同一神力的家宅化：與弘法大師立誓「你我一齊守護此民」的稻荷，以狐使的形式守在每一戶庭園的神龕旁。

sensitivity.note: Fox-woman (kitsune) legend cycle from Davis ch. V/XIX, central to living Japanese Inari worship; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Gutenberg text, presented for comparative mythology. The fox-bride episode-complex is conserved here with cross-references to the sibling base records rather than re-cut as duplicate episodes.

passages.text: All foxes possess supernatural powers to an almost limitless degree, and the chief attribute of the bad fox is the power to delude human beings by taking the form of a beautiful woman — the fox-bride — of whom many legends are told. Two tests reveal her: if the shadow of a fox-woman chance to fall upon water, only the fox, and not the fair woman, is revealed; and if a dog sees a fox-woman, the feminine form vanishes immediately and the fox alone remains. Demoniacal possession is frequently ascribed to foxes — kitsune-tsuki — the sufferer usually a sensitive woman of the poorer classes, into whose breast or finger-nails the fox enters, living a separate life of its own and speaking in a voice totally different from the human.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. V (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 所有狐狸都擁有幾乎無窮無盡的神通，而惡狐最主要的本領，便是化為美女——即狐妻——來迷惑世人，關於她的傳說不勝枚舉。有兩種方法可以揭穿她：若狐女的影子偶然映在水上，水中顯現的便只有狐狸，而非那美貌女子；又若狗看見狐女，女子的形貌便立刻消失，只留下狐狸。惡魔附體之事也常被歸咎於狐狸——即「狐憑」——受害者通常是窮苦人家中敏感的女子，狐狸從她的胸口或指甲鑽入，過著自己獨立的生活，並以與人截然不同的聲音說話。

passages.text: The fullest fox-bride story is that of the fox who became the Jewel Maiden, concubine to the Emperor at the court of the Rising Sun. At a great feast in the Summer Palace, black clouds raced across a starless sky and a mysterious wind blew out every lantern; from the Jewel Maiden's frame there darted a weirdly lustrous flame that filled the imperial halls, and from that hour the Mikado sickened until the Court Magician declared that she was a fiend who, with insidious art, ravaged the State by captivating the Emperor's heart. Spurned, the sorceress resumed her original shape, that of a fox, and ran away pursued by dogs and arrows until she sank exhausted into the Death-Stone on Nasu moor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. V (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最完整的狐妻故事，是關於那隻化為玉藻前、成為日出之國宮廷中天皇寵妃的狐狸。在夏宮的一場盛大宴會上，黑雲掠過無星的天空，一陣神秘之風吹熄了所有燈籠；從玉藻前的身上迸射出一道奇異而光澤閃爍的火焰，充滿了皇宮殿堂，自那一刻起，天皇便病倒了，直到宮廷法師宣告她是一個妖魔，以陰險的技藝迷惑天皇之心，從而摧殘國家。被唾棄之後，那女巫恢復了她原本的形貌，即一隻狐狸，並在狗與箭的追趕下奔逃，直到筋疲力盡地沉入那須原野上的殺生石之中。

passages.text: When the priest Genno offered flowers, incense and scripture before the Death-Stone, the spirit within confessed her former lives: a demon honoured by a prince in Ind, the consort of an emperor in Great Cathay, and at last the fox-bride of Japan; reborn to virtue by the priest's intercession, she swore an oath firm as the Death-Stone that from that hour she was virtue's child alone. On its beneficent side the same fox power stands at the garden shrines: Inari, the fox-god, appeared to Kobo Daishi on Mount Fushime, accepted his sacrifice, and heard the saint say, 'Together, you and I, we will protect this people'; stone foxes wag their tails at a woman's prayer for a child, and when the mean rich man Raiko struck at his nightly visitor with a dagger, the trail of blood-spots led through the garden to a miniature mountain where a great creature begged the servants to persuade their master not to attack the Gods nor to be mean again — Inari, who had taken beast-shape to teach the old man a lesson.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. V and ch. XIX (Davis 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當源翁禪師在殺生石前獻上鮮花、香與經文時，石中的亡靈懺悔了她前世的種種：曾是在印度受一位王子供奉的妖魔，曾是大契丹一位皇帝的妃嬪，最後又成了日本的狐妻；因禪師的祈願而重生向善，她立下如殺生石般堅定的誓言，說自那一刻起她只做美德之子。在其慈善的一面，這同樣的狐之力也立於庭園神社之中：狐神稻荷曾顯現於伏見山上，接受了空海大師的供奉，並聽聞這位聖者說道：「你我二人，當共同守護此民」；石狐會為婦人求子之禱而搖尾，而當吝嗇的富人賴光以匕首刺向他的夜訪者時，那斑斑血跡穿過庭園，直通向一座小丘，丘上有一隻巨大的生靈懇求僕人們勸阻主人，不要再攻擊神明，也不要再吝嗇——那正是稻荷，牠化為獸形，是為了給這老人一個教訓。

narrative.en:
In Japan the fox is the great shape-shifter of legend, and its power for good or evil stands under the fox-god Inari, originally the God of Rice, who in the eleventh century became identified with the Fox God. All foxes possess supernatural powers to an almost limitless degree: infinite vision, the hearing of every secret thought of humankind, and above all the power of transformation. The chief attribute of the bad fox is the power to delude human beings, and for this purpose it will take the form of a beautiful woman — the fox-bride — and many are the legends told in this connection. Two tests expose her. If the shadow of a fox-woman chance to fall upon water, only the fox, and not the fair woman, is revealed; and if a dog sees a fox-woman, the feminine form vanishes immediately and the fox alone remains. Demoniacal possession is frequently ascribed to the evil influence of foxes — kitsune-tsuki — the sufferer usually a sensitive woman of the poorer classes into whose breast or finger-nails the fox enters, living a separate life of its own and speaking in a voice totally different from the human.

The fullest fox-bride narrative Davis retells is the Death-Stone legend, whose heroine is the fox that became the Jewel Maiden, Flawless Jewel, concubine to the Emperor Toba at the court of the Rising Sun. At a great feast in the Summer Palace, while the wit, wisdom and beauty of the land ate and drank to music, black clouds raced across a starless sky and a mysterious wind blew out every lantern; and from the Jewel Maiden's frame there darted a weirdly lustrous flame that filled the imperial halls. From that hour the Mikado sickened, until the Court Magician declared that the Jewel Maiden was a fiend who, with insidious art, ravaged the State by captivating the Emperor's heart. Spurned, the sorceress resumed her original shape, that of a fox, and fled to the Death-Stone on Nasu moor — pursued by dogs and arrows, sinking exhausted into the stone, from time to time haunting the moor until the priest Genno, offering flowers, incense and scripture, conjured her to confess her former lives: a demon honoured by a prince in Ind, the consort of an emperor in Great Cathay, and at last the fox-bride of Japan. Reborn to virtue by the priest's intercession, she swore an oath firm as the Death-Stone that from that hour she was virtue's child alone. The fox-bride, in other words, is a coming and vanishing creature of alluring but destructive power — a Japanese version, Davis says, of Fata Morgana.

The fox-garden shrine shows the other face of the same animal power. When Kobo Daishi returned from China, holy and wonder-working, Inari appeared to him on Mount Fushime and accepted the sacrifice he offered, and the saint said: 'Together, you and I, we will protect this people.' From that compact the fox-god became the guardian of households: beneficent Inari cures coughs and colds, brings wealth to the needy, and answers a woman's prayer for a child — though only a part of the reward is real, for at least one tempting coin is bound to turn quickly into grass, and the little good done by Inari is weighed down by countless mischiefs of his fox-children. At the garden shrines the foxes stand in stone, and once, when the mean rich man Raiko was drained of life-blood by a nightly priest-visitor and struck out with his dagger in the dark, the trail of blood-spots led his servants through the garden to a miniature mountain at the extreme end, where from a large hole protruded the upper part of an enormous spider that begged them to persuade their master not to attack the Gods nor to be mean again — Inari, who had assumed the shape of priest and beast to teach the old man a lesson. The fox-bride of the court and the stone foxes of the garden are one continuous power: the deluding woman-form that enters human houses as bride and bedevils them, and the fox at the shrine that enters the same houses as protector, teacher and trickster, watching over the people Inari swore with Kobo Daishi to protect.
narrative.zh: 狐狸是日本傳說中最大的變形者，其善惡之力皆繫於稻荷神（原為米神，十一世紀起與狐神同體）。狐能無限視聽、知人心念，尤擅變化；惡狐最善化身美婦惑人——即「狐新娘」。影子落水現狐形、遇犬現原身，是識破二法。狐憑（kitsune-tsuki）多附敏感貧婦，自乳間或指縫入體，別有聲口。玉面夫人即狐新娘之最著者：宮中惑主，宴上現妖光，被魔師道破，化狐逃至那須野殺生石，被犬矢追逼，力竭入石；經Genno上人供花焚香誦經，方自陳前世——天竺王侯所敬之魔、震旦岩皇帝妃（Hoji）、日本帝妃玉面夫人——遂誓向善。狐園神社則見同一神力之善面：弘法大師歸國後，稻荷於伏見山受其供養，大師言「你我一齊守護此民」；自此稻荷以石狐守家宅，治病賜財、應婦人求子之禱（然所賜錢必有一枚化草）；慳吝的賴光被夜半「法師」吸血，拔刀亂揮，血點引家人至園中假山，石縫中巨蜘蛛（稻荷所化）勸其勿犯神明、勿再慳吝。狐新娘與園中石狐，一為入戶惑人的婦形，一為守戶教人的獸形，同是稻荷狐狸之力。

functions: Explains and polices the boundary between human marriage and animal otherworld: the fox-bride motif warns households against marriages and seductions whose origin cannot be traced.
Provides the diagnostic tests (shadow on water, dog's revelation) that structure fox-woman detection tales across Japanese folklore and into modern fiction.

Domesticates the same dangerous power at the Inari shrine: the fox as household guardian and rice-god's messenger, binding field fertility, prosperity and child-giving to the compact of Kobo Daishi and Inari.
Frames kitsune-tsuki (fox possession) as an interpretive category for trance, illness and spirit speech in folk healing.
