The king named the youthful archer and horseman East Light, Radiance of the Morning, and made him Master of the Royal Stables; the people called him Child of the Sun and Grandson of the Yellow River.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'East Light and the Bridge of Fishes' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 國王聽說了豬與馬這番奇妙的舉動後，便向天低下頭來；看來讓這男嬰存活、長大成人，乃是天上至尊者的旨意。於是國王允許她將孩子帶進宮中，他在那裡像國王的兒子一般接受教養長大，擅長騎馬與射箭，並且始終善待動物。國王為這年輕的弓箭手與騎手取名為「東光」，意即「晨之輝」，並任命他為御廄總管；百姓則稱他為「太陽之子」與「黃河之孫」。

passages.text: Fearing he might lose his life if he remained near the king, East Light with three trusty followers fled southward until he came to a great, deep river, wide and impassable, with his enemies swiftly pursuing. In a great strait he cried out, 'Alas, shall I, the Child of the Sun and the Grandson of the Yellow River, be stopped here powerless by this stream?' Then as if his father, the Sun, had whispered to him what to do, he drew his bow and shot many arrows here and there into the water. The waters appeared strangely agitated; the fish crowded together in so dense a mass that on their spines a bridge was soon formed, on which men could stand. Over the bridge of fish backs, scaly and full of spiny fins, the four young men fled; as soon as they gained the opposite shore the bridge of fishes dissolved, and scarcely had they swum away when the pursuers gained the water's edge — the shafts fell short and the river was too deep and wide to swim their horses over.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'East Light and the Bridge of Fishes' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 東光唯恐留在國王身邊會喪命，便帶著三名忠心的隨從向南逃亡，直到來到一條又寬又深、無法渡過的大河，而追兵正迅速逼近。身陷絕境之際，他高聲喊道：「唉，難道我這太陽之子、黃河之孫，竟要被這條河困在此處、束手無策嗎？」接著，彷彿他的父親太陽向他低語指示該怎麼做，他張弓搭箭，向水中各處射了許多箭。河水顯得異常翻騰；魚群密集地聚攏在一起，牠們的背脊上很快便形成了一座橋，足以讓人站立其上。四名年輕人便踏著這座由魚背——佈滿鱗片與多刺魚鰭——所成的橋逃了過去；他們一登上對岸，魚橋便消散無蹤，而他們才剛游離不久，追兵便已抵達水邊——箭矢射不到那麼遠，而河水又太深太寬，無法讓馬游渡過去。

passages.text: East Light met three strange persons who seemed to be awaiting his coming: the first dressed in seaweed, the second in hempen garments, and the third in embroidered robes — representing the three classes of society, fishermen and hunters, farmers and artisans, and rulers of the tribes. They welcomed him warmly and invited him to be their king. In the land named Fuyu, rich in the five grains, the new king ruled long and happily, teaching the proper relations of ruler and ruled, the laws of marriage, better methods of cooking and house-building, and the wearing of the topknot. Hundreds of years after East Light died, the tribes and states in the peninsula south of the Everlasting White Mountains, wanting to become one nation and one kingdom, called their country after East Light in a more poetical form — Cho-sen, Morning Radiance, the Land of the Morning Calm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'East Light and the Bridge of Fishes' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 東光遇見三個奇特的人，他們似乎正等著他的到來：第一個身穿海草，第二個身穿麻布衣裳，第三個身穿錦繡長袍——分別代表社會的三個階層：漁夫與獵人、農夫與工匠，以及各部落的統治者。他們熱情地歡迎他，並邀請他做他們的國王。在那個名為扶餘、盛產五穀的地方，這位新國王長久而幸福地統治著，教導君臣之間應有的倫常、婚姻的禮法、更好的烹飪與建房方法，以及束髮髻的習俗。東光死後數百年，長白山之南半島上的各部落與城邦，想要合為一個民族、一個王國，便以一種更具詩意的方式，用東光之名來稱呼他們的國家——朝鮮，意即「晨之輝」，也就是「晨曦之國」。

title.en: Prince Sandalwood and the First Topknot
title.zh: 檀君制髻

region.en: Sandalwood tree, Mt. Tabak, P'yongyang (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 平壤檀樹（象徵性定位）

period: Children's Dangun cycle from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'Prince Sandalwood, the Father of Korea', eBook #67180

summary.en: A bear and a tiger on the southern slope of Old Whitehead Mountain, not satisfied with the quality of human beings already on the earth, agree to go before Hananim, the Great One of Heaven and Earth, to ask that their form and nature be changed. A Voice speaks: 'Eat a bunch of garlic and stay in a cave for twenty-one days.' The tiger quits on the eleventh day; the bear waits out the twenty-one, her hairy hide and claws dropping off like an overcoat, and she stands upright a perfect woman beside a brook. Meanwhile Whanung, the Son of the Great One in the Heavens, asks for an earthly kingdom and is given the Land of the Dragon's Back — for our country rose on the first morning of creation out of the sea in the form of a dragon, whose spine is the mountain backbone and whose head is the Ever-White Mountain with the Dragon's Pool on its summit. He descends in a cloud of many colors, finds the bear-woman by the brookside, chooses her as his bride, and a baby boy is born, reared in a cradle of soft moss. The people under the sandalwood tree on Mt. Tabak see the cloud stand over the sacred tree, and a white-robed youth of grand and august appearance alights: 'I have come from my ancestors in Heaven to rule over you, my children.' They salute him the August and Venerable Sandalwood; he teaches why the bear is good and the tiger bad, ordains the topknot for married men and the braid for boys, the pagoda hairdo of women at marriage — 'Thus our Korean civilization was begun, and to this day the law of the hat and hair distinguishes us above all people.'
summary.zh: 熊與虎同詣天帝（漢拏）乞化人身。神諭曰『食蒜，居洞二十一日則化』。虎十一日而出；熊忍至二十一日，毛皮自脫，化為絕色女子，坐於溪畔。時天帝之子桓雄求下界治國，遂賜龍脊之地（朝鮮也——大地初闢之日自海湧出如龍，其脊為山脈，其首即白頭山龍淵）。桓雄降於彩雲之中，遇熊女而聘之，生子於苔蘚之搖籃。民見雲停檀樹之上，中有白衣神人，肅然曰『吾奉天命來治爾民』。眾拜曰檀聖。乃教民束髮為髻、婚嫁之禮，又授以熊善虎惡之訓。我國文明自此而始。

sensitivity.note: Dangun children's recension; parallel records dangun, korean-dangun-wanggeom, korean-dangun-sandal-prince-variant.

passages.text: Long, long ago, before there were any refined people in the Land of Dawn, a bear and a tiger met together on the southern slope of Old Whitehead Mountain in the forest. These wild animals were not satisfied with the kind of human beings already on the earth, and they wanted better ones: they agreed to go before Hananim, the Great One of Heaven and Earth, and ask him to change at once their form and nature. Then a Voice spoke out saying, 'Eat a bunch of garlic and stay in a cave for twenty-one days. If you do, you will become human.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Prince Sandalwood' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 很久很久以前，在晨曦之地還沒有任何文明之民的時候，一隻熊與一隻老虎在太白山南麓的森林裡相遇。這些野獸對世上現有的人類並不滿意，牠們想要更好的人類：牠們商定一同前去謁見天地至尊者哈納寧，求他立刻改變牠們的形貌與本性。接著有一個聲音說道：「吃下一束大蒜，在山洞裡待上二十一天。若你們做到，就會變成人。」

passages.text: It was cold and gloomy in the cave, and finally on the eleventh day the tiger, seeing no signs of losing his stripes, concluded to give up and bounded out of the cave to go hunting in the woods. But the bear, patiently sucking her paw, waited till the twenty-one days had passed. Then her hairy hide and claws dropped off, like an overcoat. Her nose and ears suddenly shortened and she stood upright — a perfect woman. Walking out of the cave the new creature sat beside a brook, and in the pure water beheld how lovely she was.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Prince Sandalwood' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 洞穴裡又冷又陰暗，到了第十一天，老虎見自己身上的條紋毫無消退的跡象，終於決定放棄，便躍出洞穴，到樹林裡去打獵。可是那頭熊卻耐心地吮著自己的腳掌，一直等到二十一天過去。這時，她那毛茸茸的皮和爪子像一件大衣般脫落下來。她的鼻子和耳朵忽然變短，她直立起來——成了一個完美的女人。這個新生的生靈走出洞穴，坐在一條小溪旁，在清澈的水中看見自己有多麼美麗。

passages.text: Whanung, the Son of the Great One in the Heavens, asked his father to give him an earthly kingdom to rule over, and the Lord of Heaven presented his son with the Land of the Dragon's Back, which men called Korea. This country rose up on the first morning of creation out of the sea in the form of a dragon; his spine, loins and tail form the great range of mountains that makes the backbone of our beautiful country, while his head rises skyward in the eternal White Mountain in the North, on whose summit lies the blue lake of pure water, the Dragon's Pool. Down out of his cloud of many colors Whanung descended first to the mountain top and then to the lower earth, where he found a beautiful woman sitting by the brookside — the bear that had been transformed into lovely human shape and nature. He chose her as his bride, and by and by a little baby boy was born, whom the mother made a cradle of soft moss and reared in the forest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Prince Sandalwood' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天上那位偉大者的兒子桓雄，請求父親賜給他一個人間的王國去統治，天帝便把「龍背之地」賜給了兒子，人們稱之為朝鮮。這片國土在創世的第一個早晨從海中升起，形如一頭龍；牠的脊背、腰腹與尾巴構成了那道巨大的山脈，成為我們這美麗國家的脊梁，而牠的頭則昂然朝天，化為北方那座永恆的白頭山，山頂上躺著一泓湛藍的清水，即龍潭。桓雄從他那五彩祥雲中降下，先落到山頂，再下到低處的大地，在那裡他發現一位美麗的女子坐在溪邊——正是那頭化為動人的人形與人性的熊。他選她為妻，不久便生下一個小男孩，母親用柔軟的苔蘚為他做了搖籃，在森林裡將他撫養長大。

passages.text: The people who dwelt at the foot of the mountain saw the cloud move southward until it stood over the sacred sandalwood tree on a small mountain named Tabak, when out stepped a white-robed being who alighted in the forest. There sat under the tree a youth of grand appearance, arrayed in princely dress; despite his youth, he was wise and venerable. 'I have come from my ancestors in Heaven to rule over you, my children.' At once the people fell on their knees: 'Thou art our king, we acknowledge thee.' Seeing that the people were rough and unkempt, Prince Sandalwood showed them how to tie up and dress their hair: men should wear their long locks in the form of a topknot, boys must braid their hair and let it hang down their backs, and women must plait their tresses plainly at the neck, except at marriage or on great occasions, when they might pile up their hair like a pagoda. Thus our Korean civilization was begun, and to this day the law of the hat and hair distinguishes us above all people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Prince Sandalwood' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 住在山腳下的人們看見那朵雲向南飄移，直到停在一座名叫太白的小山上那棵神聖的檀香樹上方，這時一位身穿白袍的存在走了出來，降落在森林中。樹下坐著一位氣度不凡的少年，身穿王子的服飾；儘管年輕，他卻睿智而令人敬重。「我從天上的祖先那裡來，要統治你們，我的孩子們。」人們立刻跪倒在地：「您就是我們的王，我們擁戴您。」檀君王見百姓粗野不整，便教他們如何束髮整裝：男子應把長髮挽成髻，男孩須把頭髮編成辮子垂在背後，女子須把長髮在頸後平實地編起，唯有在出嫁或重大場合時，方可把頭髮堆疊如塔。我朝鮮的文明便這樣開始了，時至今日，冠帽與髮式之法仍使我們超乎萬民之上。

title.en: The Rabbit's Crystal Eyes in the Sea-Palace
title.zh: 兔瞞龍宮

region.en: Palace of the fish-king under the waves (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 龍宮（象徵性定位）

period: Animal trickster tale from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'The Rabbit's Eyes', eBook #67180

summary.en: Every creature with fins and a tail is in distress, for the king of the fishes has a fishhook stuck fast in his gills, giving him fever and much pain. All the wise creatures are summoned, and Dr. Turtle, most learned of them all, decides that nothing less than a poultice made of rabbits' eyes will loosen the hook. Ordered to invite a rabbit down under the sea, the turtle dazzles Brother Bunny with tales of gems and jewels, golden trees and music in the world under the waves, and carries him down on his shell. While the rabbit enjoys the palace honors, he overhears the doctors and learns why he was brought there; told politely by the royal executioners that he must give up his eyes, he regrets 'that the eyes I have in my head now are not real eyes, but only crystal — I was afraid that sea water would hurt my sight, so I took out my ordinary eyes, buried them in the sand and put on these crystal ones.' If allowed to return to the beach he will dig them up. Getting on the turtle's back, Brother Bunny jumps off in a jiffy, scampers to the woods, and shows only his cotton tail; Dr. Turtle sheds tears and returns to tell how a rabbit had outwitted him.
summary.zh: 魚王喉中著鉤，百醫無策。龜大夫曰『非兔眼膏莫治』，乃上山以海底之富誘兔。兔欣然乘龜背入海，遊於龍宮。既而聞醫者議取其目，兔詭言『今所用者水晶目也，真目已埋於沙，懼海水傷之也；容吾返岸取之』。遂乘龜背出水上，一躥入林，惟見白尾。龜大夫垂淚而歸。

sensitivity.note: Variant of the Dragon-Palace rabbit tale (cf. korean-rabbit-turtle-eyes); no living-community restriction.

passages.text: There was trouble down in the fish world under the waves: the king of the fishes was suffering with a dreadful pain in his mouth, for while swimming around outside his palace he gulped down what looked good to eat and found he had barely escaped swallowing a fish hook, which stuck fast in his gills. All the wise creatures in the ocean were summoned to the palace, and the turtle, considered the most learned and expert of them all, finally decided that nothing less than a poultice made of rabbits' eyes would loosen the hook and end His Majesty's troubles.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Rabbit's Eyes' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 波濤之下的魚類世界裡出了亂子：魚王嘴裡疼痛難忍，因為他在宮外游弋時，一口吞下看似可口的東西，卻發現自己險些吞下一隻魚鉤，那鉤子牢牢卡在他的鰓裡。海中所有聰慧的生靈都被召到宮中，而被公認為其中最博學、最精通的烏龜，最後判定唯有以兔眼製成的敷藥，方能鬆動那魚鉤，解除陛下的痛苦。

passages.text: Dr. Turtle was ordered to go to the seashore and invite a rabbit to come down into the world under the sea. He dazzled Brother Bunny with tales of most wonderful mountains and valleys on the floor of the deep sea, with rare water plants, trees of gold and silver, flowers of every color, good things to eat and drink, music and dancing, handsome serving maids. 'Come along and be our guest. Our king has sent me to invite you.' Down, down below the blue waves they sank until they arrived at the king's palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Rabbit's Eyes' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 烏龜大夫奉命前往海濱，邀請一隻兔子下到海底世界來。他用深海海底那些最奇妙的山巒與峽谷、珍稀的水草、金樹銀樹、五顏六色的花朵、可口的美食與佳釀、音樂與舞蹈、俊美的侍女，把兔老弟說得眼花繚亂。「來吧，做我們的貴客。我們的王派我來邀請你。」他們一路下沉、下沉，沉到藍色波濤之下，直到抵達國王的宮殿。

passages.text: While Mr. Rabbit was enjoying himself he overheard them talking, and found out why they had brought him there and shown him such honors. Horrified at the idea of losing his eyes, he determined to save his sight and play the tortoise a smart trick. When politely informed by the royal executioners that he must give up his eyes to make the king well, Brother Bunny broke out with equally polite regrets: 'Really I am so sorry that His Majesty is ill, but the eyes I have in my head now are not real eyes, but only crystal. I was afraid that sea water would hurt my sight, so I took out my ordinary eyes, buried them in the sand and put on these crystal ones, which I usually wear in very dusty or wet weather. If you will allow me to return to the beach, I'll dig them up and return in time for the poultice-making.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Rabbit's Eyes' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兔先生正自得其樂時，卻聽到了他們的談話，弄清了他們為何把他帶到這裡、又為何如此禮遇他。一想到要失去自己的眼睛，他驚恐萬分，決心保住視力，並狠狠地捉弄烏龜一番。當王家劊子手客氣地告知他必須獻出眼睛來治好國王時，兔老弟同樣客氣地表示遺憾：「陛下染恙，我實在非常難過，可我如今腦中的這雙眼睛並非真眼，不過是水晶罷了。我怕海水傷了我的視力，便把平常的眼睛取了出來，埋在沙裡，換上這副水晶眼，我通常在塵土飛揚或潮濕的天氣裡戴它。若能准我回到海灘，我便把它們挖出來，趕在配藥之前回來。」

passages.text: So, getting on Dr. Turtle's back, Brother Bunny was soon out of the water and on land. In a jiffy he jumped off, scampered away, and reached the woods, showing only his cotton tail; soon he was out of sight. Dr. Turtle shed tears and returned to tell how a rabbit had outwitted him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Rabbit's Eyes' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是，兔兄弟爬上龜醫生的背，不久便離開水面，登上陸地。他一溜煙跳了下來，飛奔而去，抵達樹林，只露出他那棉花般的尾巴；轉眼間便不見了蹤影。龜醫生流下眼淚，回去訴說一隻兔子如何智勝了他。

title.en: Kija and the Crockery Hats
title.zh: 箕子陶冠

region.en: P'yongyang, Kija's capital (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 平壤（象徵性定位）

period: Kija legend retold in Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'Topknots and Crockery Hats', eBook #67180

summary.en: Long before Confucius was born, the wise Kija, chief counselor at court, refuses to serve the new dynasty, and emigrates eastward with five thousand of the best people to teach the savage people manners and refinement. Over the plains of Manchuria they march toward the rising sun, cross the Duck Green River (the Yalu) and come to the Great Eastern River, where the land is beautiful; from the tinted clouds at sunrise the new country has been named Cho-sen, Land of Morning Radiance. He builds the boat-shaped capital Ping Yang — within its walls no wells shall be dug lest the boat sink, and a rock pillar to the west to which the boat city shall be forever moored. With his wise men he publishes eight great laws, lays out roads and measures, and teaches the flue-warmed house. To stop the street fights of a rough people, he republishes the law of Dan Kun and establishes the topknot; and when the topknot becomes a handle for brawlers, he invents hats of baked clay four feet across and two feet high, weighing many pounds, so that quarrels become a silent battle of ugly faces — 'a noiseless duel, or a quarrel between deaf and dumb folks' — until a gentleness like a great calm settles over the land. The women get the clubs, changed from skull-crackers into starch polishers, and ruffians become gentlemen.
summary.zh: 箕子不忍事新朝，率五千良民東遷，渡鴨綠江，都平壤。城形如舟，城中不鑿井，恐舟沉也；城西立石柱，以為繫舟之樁。頒八條之律，教民掘地為炕以暖室。俗悍好鬥，乃復檀君束髮之令，定男子結髻、未婚者辮髮之制。鬥者揪髻，乃命陶工製陶冠，徑四尺、高逾二尺，戴者相鬥惟碎其冠，損則自償，費半歲之資。於是鬥毆化為瞪目切齒之啞戰，久而民風漸馴。碎顱之棒改為擣衣之杵，悍夫化為君子。

sensitivity.note: Kija founding legend retold; parallel korean-kija-colonization-choson (Hulbert version).

passages.text: Long, long ago in China, even centuries before the great Confucius was born, there lived a wise and learned man named Kija, the chief counselor at court. When a great war broke out and a new line of rulers came into power, Kija declined to serve the king of the country and resolved to emigrate to the far East, to teach the savage people manners and refinement. The new king allowed five thousand of the best people, most of them Kija's followers, to accompany their master.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Topknots and Crockery Hats' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 很久很久以前，在中國，甚至早在偉大的孔子誕生之前數百年，住著一位名叫箕子的智者與博學之士，他是朝廷的首席謀臣。當一場大戰爆發，新的統治者一系掌權之後，箕子拒絕為該國君王效力，並決心遷往遠東，去教導野蠻民族禮儀與文雅。新君允許五千名最優秀的人，其中大多是箕子的追隨者，隨他們的主人同行。

passages.text: They crossed the Duck Green River, which we call the Yalu, and came to the Great Eastern River, where the land was very beautiful; from the tinted clouds at sunrise the new country had been named Cho-sen, or Land of Morning Radiance. Having laid out a city for his colony, Kija began to build a wall, naming the city Ping Yang, Northern Castle. 'Now that we have safely arrived as after a voyage, the city shall be shaped like a boat. Within its walls no wells shall be dug, lest this, like boring holes, should make the boat sink; on the outside, to the west, shall stand the rock pillar to which the boat city shall be forever moored.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Topknots and Crockery Hats' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們渡過鴨綠江——我們稱之為鴨綠江——來到偉大的東方之河，那裡的土地非常美麗；由於日出時分雲霞的色彩，這片新土地被命名為朝鮮，意即「晨曦之國」。箕子為他的殖民地規劃了一座城市，開始築牆，將此城命名為平壤，意即「北方城堡」。「如今我們已如航行之後般平安抵達，這座城便應建成船的形狀。城牆之內不得掘井，以免這如同鑿孔一般，使船沉沒；城外西側應立一根石柱，船城將永遠繫泊於其上。」

passages.text: Kija was ably assisted by his wise men, who published eight great laws for the kingdom, laid out roads, established measures and distances, and taught the people how to build houses with a kang, warmed by flues running under the floors. The people were rough and savage and constantly given to hard fighting; so Kija republished the law of Dan Kun, the spirit of the mountain, and ordered that every married man should bind up his hair into a knot on top of his head, while the younger fellows must plait their hair in a braid down their backs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Topknots and Crockery Hats' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 箕子得到他那些智者的得力輔佐，他們為王國頒布了八條大法，開闢道路，訂立度量與距離，並教導人民如何建造帶有暖炕的房屋，炕由地板下通行的煙道加熱。人民粗野凶悍，時常好勇鬥狠；於是箕子重新頒布山神檀君的律法，並下令凡已婚男子都須將頭髮在頭頂挽成髮髻，而年輕小夥子則須將頭髮編成辮子垂在背後。

passages.text: Nevertheless the rough people used the topknot as a handle to catch hold of when fighting in the streets. To stop these quarrels, Kija caused big heavy hats to be moulded of clay, four feet across and two feet high, weighing many pounds, baked in ovens until hard as stone. Every fellow who was known to quarrel was compelled to wear one; when men fought they only cracked their crockery, and a good half year's wages was required to pay for a new hat. Before many months a street quarrel got to be a perfectly silent battle of ugly faces and terrible gestures; in time a gentleness like a great calm settled over the land. The clubs of the rough men were handed over to the wives and daughters for pounding and starching clothes, and thus by changing sticks that had been used as skull-crackers into starch polishers, Kija changed also ruffians into gentlemen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Topknots and Crockery Hats' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而，粗野的人們卻把髮髻當作把手，在街上打架時抓住它。為了制止這些爭鬥，箕子命人以黏土塑成又大又重的帽子，寬四尺、高兩尺，重達數磅，在窯中燒硬如石。凡已知好爭鬥者，都強制戴上這樣一頂帽子；人們打架時只會把陶帽打裂，而買一頂新帽要花掉足足半年的工錢。不出幾個月，街頭爭鬥便成了完全無聲的戰鬥，只有醜陋的鬼臉和可怕的手勢；久而久之，一種宛如巨大寧靜般的溫和之氣籠罩了這片土地。粗野漢子的棍棒被交給妻子和女兒們，用來捶打和漿洗衣服，於是箕子藉著把原本用來敲碎頭顱的棍子變成漿衣棒，也把惡棍變成了君子。

title.en: Fancha, the Heaven-Born and the Sacred Magpie
title.zh: 滿洲鵲佑

region.en: Lake of Heaven beyond the Ever-White Mountains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 白山天池（象徵性定位）

period: Ancestor-legend of the Manchus retold by Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'Fancha and the Magpie', eBook #67180

summary.en: When the Manchu conquerors sit on the thrones of China in satin and jeweled robes, they want to know who their ancestors were, and the Emperor summons the 117-year-old Mrs. Crinkles. On the other side of the Ever White Mountains is the Land of Lakes, whose crystal flood reflects the snow-covered mountains and is spangled with jewels at night; three lovely virgins of the Heavenly palaces descend with the Lord of Heaven's permission to bathe in it, choosing the magpie as their sacred bird. One day a magpie flies down bearing a blood-red fruit and drops it on the garment of the youngest sister; the gift is a happy omen, and from this divine token the youngest conceives and bears a son, Golden Family Stem, who will found a dynasty named Great Bright. Growing up under mountains that seem to touch the sky, he loses his mother, takes the name Fancha, Heaven-born, builds a boat and floats down the river to three tribes at war; his noble appearance and fearless arrival win the shout 'Our chief!' He builds a city, marries a princess — and when war kills him and all his sons but one, that son, pursued into a dark wood, is delivered by the sacred magpie that settles on his head: the pursuers take the still figure for a dried wood splinter and rush past. 'The rest of the story Your Majesty knows, for Fancha was your ancestor of seventeen generations ago.'
summary.zh: 滿洲既入主中國，欲知其祖之所自出。乃召百十七歲之嫗入宮述古。白山之外有鏡湖，三天女奉旨降浴於湖，以鵲為神鳥。一日鵲啣朱果置幼女衣上，女吞之而孕，生子曰『金族之幹』，將啟『大明』之基。孤兒長，自號『天生者』，乘舟而下，三族奉為酋長。傳至戰歿，惟一子逃於密林，神鵲集其首，追者以為枯木而過之。嫗曰：『此即陛下十七世之祖也。』帝厚賚之。

sensitivity.note: Manchu Three Fairies of Tianchi founding myth as told in a Korean children's book; cross-border origin narrative.

passages.text: On the other side of the Ever White Mountains, which divide Korea from Manchuria, is the Land of Lakes. On one of these, as in a mirror, the glorious blue sky and the snow-covered mountains are reflected, and at night when the stars come out the waveless mirror is spangled with jewels. There were three lovely virgins who dwelt in the Heavenly palaces and they wanted to come down and bathe in the water of this lake; permission was given them by the Lord of Heaven, and descending to the earth they were as happy as fairies could be, choosing the magpie as their sacred bird.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Fancha and the Magpie' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在分隔朝鮮與滿洲的長白山的另一側，是湖泊之地。其中一座湖如同一面鏡子，映照出絢麗的藍天與白雪覆蓋的群山，夜晚繁星出現時，這面無波的鏡子便點綴著珠寶。有三位可愛的處女住在天上的宮殿裡，她們想下凡到這座湖中沐浴；天帝准許了她們，於是她們降臨人間，快樂得如同仙女所能有的那般，並選擇喜鵲作為她們的神聖之鳥。

passages.text: One day they noticed a magpie flying far above them, which bore in its bill a blood-red fruit. Descending near where their clothes lay on the beach, it dropped the red fruit on the garment of the youngest of the sisters. They agreed that this gift of the bird, which was sacred in their eyes, was a happy omen; from this divine token brought by a magpie, the youngest of the virgins conceived and bore a son. They named the baby boy Golden Family Stem, for they felt sure that he would grow up and become the founder of a dynasty of kings, who should take the name of Great Bright from the shining water near which he was born.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Fancha and the Magpie' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，他們注意到一隻喜鵲在他們上方遠處飛翔，牠的喙裡啣著一顆血紅的果實。牠降落在他們擱在海灘上的衣物附近，把那顆紅果丟在姊妹中年紀最小者的衣裳上。他們一致認為，這隻在他們眼中神聖的鳥所帶來的贈禮是吉兆；因著喜鵲帶來的這神聖信物，眾處女中年紀最小的那一位懷了孕，生下一個兒子。他們為這男嬰取名為金族幹，因為他們確信他長大後必成為一個王朝的開創者，而那王朝將以他出生地附近那片閃耀的水域為名，號稱「大光明」。

passages.text: By and by his dear mother's breath ceased and she entered into the icy caves of the dead, and he found himself an orphan; he resolved to take the name of Fancha, or Heaven-born, and to go out into the world and lead men. He built a boat and floated down the outlet of the lake into a river, landing at a place where three tribes or clans were at war. When they saw this noble youth alone and unarmed step fearlessly over the gunwale of the boat, they were mightily impressed, and when he told the story of his birth they one and all shouted 'Our chief!' In time he built a city, and for his wife and queen married a princess of the principal tribe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Fancha and the Magpie' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久，他親愛的母親嚥下了最後一口氣，進入死者冰冷的洞窟，他發現自己成了孤兒；他決意取名為范察，意即「天降」，並要走向世間、領導眾人。他造了一艘船，順著湖的出口漂流而下，進入一條河，在一處有三個部落或氏族正在交戰的地方登岸。當他們看見這位高貴的青年獨自一人、手無寸鐵，卻無畏地跨過船舷上岸，都深受震撼；而當他講述自己出生的故事時，他們異口同聲高喊「我們的首領！」後來他築了一座城，並娶了主要部落的一位公主為妻，立她為后。

passages.text: In one of the battles he and all his sons except one were killed. This one, named Fancha, was chased by the enemy over the open plains; but when he reached a dense dark wood a deliverer came to him in the form of the sacred bird, the magpie, which settled on his head. He stood as still as a post, and the pursuers, seeing the bird, supposed the figure was a piece of dried wood or the splinter of a tree struck by lightning, and rushed on and past him. 'The rest of the story Your Majesty knows, for Fancha was your ancestor of seventeen generations ago' — and the great Emperor of all the Chinas loaded the aged woman with presents and honors, creating for her the office of Chief Story-Teller to the Imperial children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Fancha and the Magpie' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在其中一場戰役中，他與他所有的兒子都戰死了，只除了一個。這一個名叫范察，被敵人追趕，越過開闊的平原；但當他抵達一片濃密幽暗的樹林時，救星以神聖之鳥——喜鵲——的形貌來到他身邊，停在他的頭上。他像一根柱子般一動也不動地站著，追兵看見那隻鳥，以為那身影是一段枯木，或是被雷電擊中的樹枝碎片，便逕自衝了過去。『其餘的故事陛下都知道了，因為范察正是陛下十七代之前的祖先』——而統御全中國的偉大皇帝賞賜了這位老婦人無數禮物與榮耀，並為她創設了「御前說書長」一職，專為皇室的孩子們講故事。

title.en: The Sneezing Colossus and the Pear
title.zh: 石佛噴嚏

region.en: Mountain miryek, colossal stone Buddha (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 山中石佛（象徵性定位）

period: Fairy tale from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'The Sneezing Colossus', eBook #67180

summary.en: Lazy Mr. Kim, scolded by his wife to find something for the household, rambles over the rocks until noon, when he comes to one of the mighty mir-yeks, colossal stone Buddhas cut out of the solid mountain in the days when monasteries covered the land. Out of a crevice in the head grows a pear tree, and at the end of the outer branch a ripe pear nearly as big as a man's head. Seizing the vines he climbs to the chin, but the polished nose is slippery and the ears too smooth; so he crawls up into the right nostril — and suddenly a blast loud enough to rend the mountain: the colossus has sneezed, and got rid of the intruder. Mr. Kim flies through the air and lies unconscious till near sundown; in sneezing so hard the colossus has shaken its head, and the big pear has dropped off — Kim finds it lying by his side, and goes home rejoicing to a merry supper with his little dog.
summary.zh: 懶漢金氏奉妻命入山覓食，至山中石佛（彌勒）之前。佛首裂罅生梨樹，枝頭一梨大如人首。金攀藤至佛頷，鼻滑不可登，遂自鼻孔而入。忽聞巨響，石佛打嚏，噴之出，拋於荊棘之間，昏至日昃。梨亦因佛搖首而墜，適在其側。金攜歸，與犬共食，大快。

sensitivity.note: Comic legend of a Buddha image; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Mr. Kim went out to the mountains to find something. He came to one of the mighty mir-yeks, or colossal stone Buddhas, cut out of the solid mountain. Ages ago in the days of Buddhism, when monasteries covered the land, devout men, laboring many months, chiseled this towering colossus into human form: its nose stood out three feet, its mouth was four feet wide, and on its flat head was a cap of granite on which ten men could stand. But out of a crevice in the head of the figure grew a pear tree, and, oh joy! at the end of the outer branch was growing a ripe, luscious pear nearly as big as a man's head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Sneezing Colossus' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 金先生上山去找東西。他來到一尊雄偉的彌勒——也就是從整座山岩中鑿出的巨大石佛——跟前。很久很久以前，在佛教興盛的年代，當時寺院遍佈大地，虔誠的人們耗費數月，把這尊高聳的巨像鑿成人形：它的鼻子突出三呎，嘴巴寬達四呎，平坦的頭頂上戴著一頂花崗岩冠，上面可站十個人。但從這尊石像頭部的一道裂縫裡，長出了一棵梨樹，而且，喔，可喜可賀！在外側的枝條末端，正結著一顆熟透、甘美多汁的梨，幾乎有人的頭那麼大。

passages.text: Seizing hold of the bushes and wild grape-vines, Mr. Kim climbed upward and got as far as the chin of the great stone face. The nose, being polished, was slippery and the ears were too smooth to climb. A bright thought entered his head: he would crawl up into the right nostril and hope for an exit to the top, and soon the man Kim disappeared from sight as with hands and feet he climbed into the darkness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Sneezing Colossus' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 金先生抓住灌木和野葡萄藤，往上攀爬，爬到了那張巨大石臉的下巴處。那鼻子因為被打磨過而滑溜，兩耳又太光滑，難以攀附。他腦中閃過一個妙計：他要爬進右邊的鼻孔，指望能找到通往頂端的出口；不久，金先生便手腳並用地爬進黑暗中，從視線中消失了。

passages.text: Suddenly a blast loud enough to rend the mountain was heard. Hash-ho! No, the colossus had sneezed. Thus the stone man got rid of the intruder. The first thing Mr. Kim knew, he was flying through the air, and he tumbled upon the bushes. Mr. Kim lay asleep or unconscious till near sun-down; but in sneezing so hard, the colossus had shaken its head also and the big pear had dropped off. Kim found it lying by his side, and picking it up went on his way rejoicing; at home the little dog barked welcome, and a right merry supper they had over the big pear cut into slices.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Sneezing Colossus' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 突然，一聲足以震裂山岳的巨響傳來。哈啾！不，是那尊巨像打了噴嚏。石人就這樣擺脫了這個闖入者。金先生回過神來的第一件事，就是他正飛在空中，然後摔落在灌木叢上。金先生一直睡著，或者說昏迷著，直到接近日落時分；但巨像打噴嚏打得那麼用力，也同時晃動了它的頭，那顆大梨便掉了下來。金先生發現它躺在自己身旁，便撿了起來，歡歡喜喜地繼續上路；回到家時，小狗汪汪叫著歡迎他，他們把大梨切成一片片，吃了一頓著實愉快的晚餐。

title.en: A Bridegroom for Miss Mole
title.zh: 鼴女擇婿

region.en: Underground by the river Kingin's stone colossus (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 金因江畔石佛之下（象徵性定位）

period: Animal courtship tale from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'A Bridegroom for Miss Mole', eBook #67180

summary.en: By the river Kingin stands the great stone image cut out of solid rock; down under the earth near it lives a mole whose daughter is the most wonderful mole baby ever known, and Father Mole determines she shall marry only the grandest thing in the universe. The wise ones agree the Great Blue Sky is above everything; but the Sky refers him to the Sun, who controls it; the Sun confesses the Cloud is greater, able to cover him for days and weeks; the Cloud, inky black with storm, laughs and refers him to the Wind; the Wind confesses that before Miryek, the colossal stone image, his power is naught — smite him as he may, the stone stands unmoved and smiling. So the footsore Mole Father proceeds to Miryek, which grants that it fears not sky, sun, frost, clouds, lightning or thunder — 'Yes, I am great. But I am not the greatest: down under my feet is the Mole. His might I cannot resist; soon he shall undermine my base and I shall topple down. By universal confession, the Mole is the greatest thing in the universe, and to him I yield. Better marry your daughter to him.' The daughter's bridegroom is found at home, of the same family of creatures, and great is the joy at the wedding.
summary.zh: 鼴父欲以女嫁天下至尊者。問於智者，皆曰天也。天曰『日能主我』；日曰『雲能蔽我』；雲曰『風能驅我』；風曰『石佛之前，吾力為虛，吾吼之而彼不瞬』。遂謁石佛。佛曰：『誠然，吾不畏天，不畏日，不畏霜雪雷霆。然吾足之下有鼴焉，其力吾不能抗，日掘吾基，吾必傾覆。以天下之大，莫大於鼴。可以女妻鼴。』鼴父乃歸，嫁女於同族之美少年，閤家大喜。

sensitivity.note: Chain tale; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: By the river Kingin stands the great stone image, or Miryek, that was cut out of the solid rock ages ago. Down under the earth near this mighty colossus lived a soft-furred mole and his wife. One day a daughter was born to them, the most wonderful mole baby that ever was known. Father Mole determined to marry her only to the grandest thing in the whole universe, and the wise ones agreed that the Great Blue Sky was above everything else in glory and greatness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'A Bridegroom for Miss Mole' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在金仁河畔矗立著巨大的石像，或稱米勒克，那是很久以前從堅硬的岩石中雕鑿而成的。在這尊雄偉巨像附近的地底下，住著一隻軟毛鼴鼠和他的妻子。有一天，他們生下了一個女兒，是前所未見、最了不起的鼴鼠寶寶。鼴鼠爸爸決心只把她嫁給全宇宙最偉大的東西，而智者們也一致認為，偉大的藍天在榮耀與偉大上超越萬物。

passages.text: 'No, I am not the greatest,' said the Sky; 'I must refer you to the Sun. He controls me, for he can make it day or night as he pleases.' The mighty luminary seemed suddenly very modest: 'Alas! I am not master. The Cloud is greater than I, for he is able to cover me up and make me invisible for days and weeks.' The Cloud, its face inky black with the wrath of a storm, almost laughed: 'So far from being the greatest thing in the world, I am not even my own master. See already how the wind is driving me. Let me commend you to the Wind.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'A Bridegroom for Miss Mole' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「不，我並不是最偉大的，」天空說，「我必須請您去問太陽。他支配著我，因為他能隨心所欲地讓白天或黑夜降臨。」那偉大的發光體忽然顯得十分謙遜：「唉！我不是主宰。雲比我更偉大，因為他能把我遮蓋起來，讓我好幾天、好幾個星期都看不見。」雲的臉因暴風雨的怒氣而漆黑如墨，幾乎笑了出來：「我非但不是世上最偉大的東西，甚至連自己的主宰都不是。瞧，風已經在驅趕我了。讓我推薦您去找風吧。」

passages.text: The Wind was not half so proud as the Mole Father had expected, and confessed that before Miryek, the colossal stone image, his power was naught. 'I smite that Great Stone Face and its eyes do not even blink. I roar in his ears, but he minds it not. I try to make him sneeze, but he will not. Alas, no. I am not the grandest thing in the universe, while Miryek stands. Go to him.' Miryek granted with stony patience: 'I care not for the sky day or night. I fear not the sun, that cannot melt me, nor the frost that is not able to make me crumble. The clouds come and go, but they cannot move me. Yes, I am great.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'A Bridegroom for Miss Mole' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 風並不像鼴鼠爸爸所預期的那樣驕傲，他承認在米勒克那尊巨大的石像面前，自己的力量微不足道。「我擊打那張巨大的石臉，他的眼睛卻連眨都不眨。我在他耳邊咆哮，他卻毫不在意。我想讓他打噴嚏，他卻不肯。唉，不行。只要米勒克還站著，我就不是宇宙間最偉大的東西。去找他吧。」米勒克以石頭般的耐心准許道：「我不在乎白天或黑夜的天空。我不怕太陽，他無法融化我；也不怕霜，它無法使我崩裂。雲來了又去，卻動不了我。是的，我很偉大。」

passages.text: 'I would gladly do so, if I were greatest. But I am not,' said Miryek. 'Down under my feet is the Mole. He digs with his shovel-like hands and makes burrows day and night. His might I cannot resist. Soon he shall undermine my base and I shall topple down and lie like common stone along the earth. Yes! by universal confession, the Mole is the greatest thing in the universe and to him I yield. Better marry your daughter to him.' So after all his journeying the father sought no further; he found his daughter's bridegroom at home and of the same family of creatures, and great was the joy and rejoicing at the wedding.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'A Bridegroom for Miss Mole' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「如果我是最偉大的，我會樂意這麼做。但我不是，」米勒克說。「在我腳下的是鼴鼠。他用像鏟子般的手挖掘，日夜不停地打洞。他的力量我無法抵抗。不久他就會挖空我的根基，我就會倒塌下來，像普通的石頭一樣躺在地上。是的！舉世公認，鼴鼠是宇宙間最偉大的東西，我向他屈服。還是把你的女兒嫁給他吧。」於是，父親走遍了這一趟之後，不再往別處尋找；他在家中找到了女兒的新郎，而且是同一族的生物，婚禮上充滿了歡樂與喜慶。

title.en: Old White Whiskers and the Ring of Dry Grass
title.zh: 白鬚虎中計

region.en: Icy river crossing, Kang-wen mountains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 江原道冰河（象徵性定位）

period: Animal trickster tale from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'Old White Whiskers and Mr. Bunny', eBook #67180

summary.en: White Whiskers is the proudest tiger in the peninsula, retainer of the great genii of the mountains — the Mountain Spirit, when he wants to, can call together all the tigers in his domain and ride off on the clouds astride the biggest. White Whiskers' business is to visit the hill-pass shrines daily and see that offerings continue; the people offer sacrifice out of fear of the Mountain Spirit and his servants. Yet proud as he is, he is outwitted by a creature without strength or sting. Crossing the ice one cold winter's day, Mr. Rabbit meets him face to face, and offers a royal dinner: lie down on the ice, shut your eyes, and I will circle you with dry grass, driving the game to your very paws — 'don't open your eyes till I give you the word.' As quickly as one can blow out a candle the tiger is asleep; Mr. Bunny piles a thick ring of combustibles around him, sets it on fire, and watches. Awakened by the crackling, the tiger has to jump high to escape with his life, one paw scorched so that he limps and his fur singed so that all his long hair and fine looks are gone; the other tigers laugh at him, and the great Mountain Spirit no longer trusts such a stupid servant.
summary.zh: 白鬚虎者，山神之爪牙也，最驕。冬日冰上遇兔，兔曰『吾為王驅獸至爪下，王閉目臥於冰，吾以枯草環之』。虎喜而寢。兔積草成環，縱火焚之。虎跳而出，爪焦毛燼，威儀盡失。同類笑之，山神亦不復信用。

sensitivity.note: Trickster-outwits-tyrant tale; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: White Whiskers was the name of a huge, tawny tiger that lived in the mountains of Kang Wen, the proudest tiger in the whole peninsula of Korea. He was the retainer of the great genii of the mountains, that men feared and worshiped; the Mountain Spirit, when he wanted to, could call together all the tigers in his domain, and sitting astride the back of the biggest, ride off on the clouds or to victory over Korea's enemies. One particular matter of business confided to White Whiskers was to visit daily the shrines in the hill passes to see if offerings were continually made.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Old White Whiskers and Mr. Bunny' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 白鬚是一隻巨大的黃褐色老虎的名字，住在江原道的山裡，是整個朝鮮半島最驕傲的老虎。他是山裡偉大神仙的侍從，人們畏懼並崇拜那些神仙；山神只要願意，就能把他領地裡所有的老虎召集起來，然後騎在最大那隻的背上，乘雲而去，或去戰勝朝鮮的敵人。託付給白鬚的一項特別任務，就是每天巡視山隘中的神祠，看看是否持續有人供奉。

passages.text: Just as he was crossing a river on the ice, Mr. Bunny met Old White Whiskers face to face, and knew his last hour had come. 'Oh, why should you bother with me? I'm so little and skinny as hardly to make a mouthful for Your Majesty. Just listen to me and I'll get you a royal dinner. I'll go up the mountain and drive the game to your very paws. Only you must do exactly what I tell you: lie down on the ice here, shut your eyes and do not stir. If you hear a noise and even some crackling, don't open your eyes till I give you the word.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Old White Whiskers and Mr. Bunny' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 正當兔子先生踏著冰過河時，他與老白鬚面對面碰上了，知道自己大限已到。「噢，您何必跟我計較呢？我這麼瘦小，連給陛下塞牙縫都不夠。只要聽我說，我就能給您弄來一頓豐盛的晚餐。我會上山把獵物趕到您的爪下。只是您必須完全照我說的做：在這兒的冰上躺下，閉上眼睛，一動也不動。如果您聽到聲響，甚至有些噼啪聲，也別睜開眼睛，直到我給您信號為止。」

passages.text: Old White Whiskers, both hungry and tired, resolved while waiting to take a good nap; as quickly as one can blow out a candle, he was asleep. Mr. Bunny made himself busy pulling up all the dry grass he could find and piling it around and close up to Old White Whiskers, then set it on fire. Awakened by the crackling, the tiger had to jump high to escape from the flames with his life; one paw was scorched so that he limped, and his fur was singed so badly that all his long hair and fine looks were gone. When he got back home the other tigers laughed at him; henceforth he had to take second place, for the great Mountain Spirit no longer trusted such a stupid servant.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Old White Whiskers and Mr. Bunny' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 老白鬚又餓又累，決定趁等待時好好睡一覺；轉眼間，就像吹熄蠟燭那般迅速，他已沉沉睡去。兔先生忙著拔起所有找得到的乾草，堆在老白鬚四周並緊挨著他，然後點火燒了起來。老虎被劈啪聲驚醒，只得高高跳起，才僥倖逃離火燄保住性命；一隻爪子被燒傷，使他走起路來一瘸一拐，皮毛也被燒焦得厲害，長毛與俊美的模樣全都沒了。他回到家後，其他老虎都嘲笑他；從此他只能退居次位，因為偉大的山神再也不信任這樣愚蠢的僕人了。

title.en: King Peony and the Cinnamon Rose
title.zh: 牡丹王惑於薔薇

region.en: Royal gardens of Silla (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新羅御苑（象徵性定位）

period: Parable told by the scholar Sul Chong to King Sinmun of Silla; retold in Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'The King of the Flowers', eBook #67180

summary.en: Twelve centuries ago lived Sul Chong, the greatest of all the learned men of Korea, and when the King of Silla, Sin Mun, was living in luxury and filling his palace with too many pretty dancing girls, Sul Chong warned his master with a story: in spring the Peony, king of the flowers, blossomed so gorgeously that hundreds made long journeys to see him, and a single peony on one stem was saluted as king of the whole garden. All the flowers trooped to the floral court — Peach, Plum, Pear, Apple and Persimmon, then the virgin flowers, Tea-Rose, Azalea, Lily, Strawberry Blossom, and last of all the Cinnamon Rose, tripping along in a green skirt and red jacket with haughty air and breath of spice. King Peony lingers long with the spicy visitor, invites her to the palace, and leaves his ministers to carry on the government — Miss Cinnamon Rose seems the real ruler. But one day there comes the flower called Old Man, like an aged beggar in sackcloth: 'If you keep company with the wise and prudent, your reign will be long, powerful and glorious; but if you consort with the foolish your house will fall. Did not three dynasties of the emperors of Great China fall because of the beautiful women who tempted their Majesties to forget their duties?' The king blushes to a deep crimson, confesses his faults and reforms his life — and it is said the lesson was not lost on the real human king, who dismissed his harem and ruled wisely till the day of his death.
summary.zh: 新羅儒宗薛聰以花國之喻諫王：牡丹為百花之王，百卉來朝，末有薔薇，綠裙紅襖，妖冶善媚。王惑之，日與之處，而政事廢弛。後有『老翁花』者，襤褸如丐，入而諫曰：『近賢則國祚長；近佞則宗廟危。三代之亡，皆以女色。』王大悟，遂黜嬖倖，勵精圖治。此即薔薇所以配伎女、牡丹所以比賢君之故也。

sensitivity.note: Flower-court parable from Silla tradition; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Twelve centuries ago lived the renowned scholar Sul Chong, the greatest of all the learned men of Korea. When the King of Silla, Sin Mun, was living in luxury and filling his palace with too many pretty dancing girls, who distracted his mind from attending properly to the affairs of state, Sul Chong warned his master against the increasing influence of these women by telling him a story.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The King of the Flowers' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 十二個世紀以前，住著一位著名的學者薛聰，他是朝鮮所有博學之士中最偉大的一位。新羅國王神文王生活奢靡，宮中養了太多美貌的舞女，使他分心，無法妥善處理國事；薛聰便講了一個故事來警告君主，勸他提防這些女子日益增長的影響力。

passages.text: Once upon a time, in spring, the Peony, king of the flowers, blossomed so gorgeously that hundreds of people made long journeys to see the bright blossoms; the king of the whole garden was a single peony grown on one stem, so that all the strength and nourishment of the plant were concentrated in that unique royal bloom. All the other flowers came to pay their respects at the floral court: the Peach, Plum, Pear, Apple and Persimmon trooped in; then the Tea-Rose, the Azalea, the Lily, the Strawberry Blossom; last of all appeared the Cinnamon Rose, tripping nimbly along in a green skirt and red jacket, with haughty air and breath of spice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The King of the Flowers' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前，在春天，花中之王牡丹開得極為絢麗，數百人不辭長途跋涉前來觀賞這些明豔的花朵；整座花園之王是一株單獨長在一根莖上的牡丹，因此這株植物所有的力量與養分都集中在那朵獨一無二的王者之花上。所有其他的花都來到花卉朝廷致敬：桃、李、梨、蘋果與柿成群而來；接著是茶薔薇、杜鵑、百合、草莓花；最後出現的是肉桂薔薇，穿著綠裙紅衣、步履輕快地走來，神態高傲，氣息芬芳如香料。

passages.text: Of them all, the king seemed most to favor Miss Cinnamon Flower; he invited her to come and live in the palace, and leaving his ministers to carry on the government, spent all his time in her society, so that Miss Cinnamon Rose seemed to be the real ruler instead of the king himself. But one day there came to the palace the flower called Old Man, who looked exactly like an aged beggar dressed in sackcloth and leaning on a staff. 'Although you dress in Chinese silk and none are equal to you in the magnificence of your robes, yet you need a common knife string, as well as I. If you keep company with the wise and prudent, your reign will be long, powerful and glorious; but if you consort with the foolish your house will fall. Did not three dynasties of the emperors of Great China fall because of the beautiful women who tempted their Majesties to forget their duties?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The King of the Flowers' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在眾花之中，國王似乎最寵愛肉桂花小姐；他邀她住進宮中，並把政務交給大臣們處理，自己終日與她相伴，於是肉桂薔薇小姐彷彿成了真正的統治者，而非國王本人。但有一天，宮中來了一種名叫「老人」的花，他看起來活像一個年邁的乞丐，身穿粗麻布衣，拄著拐杖。「雖然你穿著中國絲綢，論華服的壯麗無人能與你相比，但你和我一樣，都需要一條普通的刀繩。你若與明智謹慎之人為伴，你的統治將長久、強大而光榮；但你若與愚昧之人廝混，你的家族必將衰敗。大中國的三個王朝，不正是因為那些美女誘惑君王忘卻職責而覆滅的嗎？」

passages.text: The king blushed, even to a deep crimson. He confessed his faults and reformed his life. It is said the lesson was not lost on the real human king: he dismissed his harem, sent away the dancing girls and ruled wisely till the day of his death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The King of the Flowers' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 國王臉紅了，甚至紅到深緋。他坦承自己的過錯，並改過自新。據說這番教訓並未白費在真正的人類君王身上：他遣散了后宮，送走了舞女，並明智地治國，直到去世之日。

title.en: Zamna and Kukulcan, Lords of the Dawn
title.zh: 扎姆納與庫庫爾坎：黎明之主

region.en: Izamal, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦伊扎馬爾

period: Compendium of sixteenth-century sources (Cogolludo, Lizana, Landa); Bancroft 1883

source.work: Hubert Howe Bancroft, The Native Races of the Pacific States, vol. III: Myths and Languages (1883), ch. XI

summary.en: Zamna came from the west after the fall of the Quinamean Empire and was received with respect wherever he stayed; he invented the alphabet and named every point and place in the country. Over his grave rose the city of Izamal, a chief center of pilgrimage, where the afflicted resorted to the temple of the working hand, Kab Ul, whose touch restored health.
summary.zh: 基納梅安帝國傾覆之後，扎姆納自西方而來，所至之處皆受尊禮；他發明文字，為國中每一處所命名。其墓上起城伊扎馬爾，遂為半島朝聖之中心；病者往其「工作之手」（卡布·烏爾）神廟，謂觸之可癒。

sensitivity.note: Compendium of sixteenth-century colonial sources; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: The tradition relates that some time after the fall of the Quinamean Empire, Zamna appeared in Yucatan, coming from the west, and was received with great respect wherever he stayed. Besides being the inventor of the alphabet, he is said to have named all points and places in the country. Over his grave rose a city called Izamal, which soon became one of the chief centres of pilgrimage in the peninsula, especially for the afflicted.
passages.note: Condensed from Bancroft (1883), ch. XI; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 傳說記載，基納梅安帝國滅亡後不久，薩姆納自西方出現在尤卡坦，無論他停留在何處，都受到極大的尊敬。據說他除了發明字母之外，還為全國所有的地點與地方命名。他的墳墓上興起了一座名為伊薩馬爾的城市，這座城市很快成為半島上主要的朝聖中心之一，尤其是對受苦之人而言。

passages.text: This class of devotees generally resorted to the temple where he was represented in the form of a hand, Kab Ul, or working hand, whose touch was sufficient to restore health. The most popular names were Zamna and Cukulcan, both culture-heroes, and considered by some to be identical; a very probable supposition when we consider that Quetzalcoatl, who is admitted to be the same as Cukulcan, had the attribute of the strong hand, as well as Zamna.
passages.note: Condensed from Bancroft (1883), ch. XI; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 這一類信徒通常前往以手——卡布·烏爾（Kab Ul），即工作之手——的形象代表他的神廟，據說其觸碰便足以恢復健康。最普遍的名字是薩姆納（Zamna）與庫庫爾坎（Cukulcan），二者皆為文化英雄，並被某些人視為同一人；若考慮到被公認為與庫庫爾坎相同的魁札爾科亞特爾（Quetzalcoatl）具有強手之屬性，薩姆納亦然，則此說極有可能。

title.en: Kinich Kakmo Draws the Fire of Noon
title.zh: 基尼奇·卡克莫引取正午之火

region.en: Izamal, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦伊扎馬爾

period: Compendium of sixteenth-century sources; Bancroft 1883

source.work: Hubert Howe Bancroft, The Native Races of the Pacific States, vol. III (1883), ch. XI

summary.en: In the same city was an image of Kinich Kakmo, 'face or eye of the sun', whom Landa represents as the offspring of the sun, but who subsequently became identified with that luminary. He is represented in the act of sacrifice, pointing the finger toward a ray from the midday sun, as if to draw a spark wherewith to kindle the sacred fire; to this idol the people resorted in times of calamity and sickness.
summary.zh: 同城有基尼奇·卡克莫之像——「日之面或目」——蘭達記其為太陽之子，後與太陽合一。像作獻祭之狀，指日中光芒，似欲引取火星以燃聖火；凡遭災病，民皆詣此求諭。

sensitivity.note: Compendium of sixteenth-century colonial sources; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: In the same city was an image of Kinich Kakmo, 'face or eye of the sun', whom Landa represents to be the offspring of the sun, but who subsequently became identified with that luminary and received divine honors in the very temple that he had erected to his father. He is represented in the act of sacrifice, pointing the finger toward a ray from the midday sun, as if to draw a spark wherewith to kindle the sacred fire. To this idol the people resorted in times of calamity and sickness, bringing offerings to induce oracular advice. Lizana translates the name as 'Sol con rostro' — the sun with a face whose rays are of fire.
passages.note: Condensed from Bancroft (1883), ch. XI; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 在同一座城市中有一尊基尼奇·卡克莫（Kinich Kakmo）的雕像，意為「太陽之面或太陽之眼」，蘭達（Landa）稱其為太陽之子，但後來他與那顆發光體合而為一，並在他為其父所建的那座神廟中受到神聖的崇敬。他被描繪為正在獻祭的姿態，手指指向正午太陽射出的一道光芒，彷彿要汲取一點火花以點燃聖火。人們在災難與疾病之時前往此偶像處，獻上供品以求神諭的指示。利薩納（Lizana）將此名譯為「Sol con rostro」——有面容的太陽，其光芒為火。

title.en: Yuncemil, Acat, and Baklum Chaam: The Deified Kings of Yucatan
title.zh: 尤恩塞米爾、阿卡特與巴克盧姆·查姆：猶加敦的神化君王

region.en: Merida (Tihoo), Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦梅里達（蒂霍）

period: Compendium of sixteenth-century sources; Bancroft 1883

source.work: Hubert Howe Bancroft, The Native Races of the Pacific States, vol. III (1883), ch. XI

summary.en: The gods of Yucatan were almost all kings placed among the divinities by gratitude or terror. Yuncemil was Lord of Death, propitiated with offerings of food; Acat was God of Life, who formed the infant in the womb; at Tihoo stood the temple of Yahau Kuna where Baklum Chaam, the Priapus of the Mayas, was worshipped; Chac, a former king of Izamal, was honored as god of fields and inventor of agriculture.
summary.zh: 猶加敦諸神幾乎皆為君王，因感恩或畏懼而位列神班。尤恩塞米爾為死亡之主，以食祭安撫；阿卡特為生命之神，於母腹中塑胎兒；蒂霍有雅豪·庫納神廟，供奉馬雅的普里阿普斯巴克盧姆·查姆；查克——伊扎馬爾昔日之王——尊為田疇之神、農耕之發明者。

sensitivity.note: Compendium of sixteenth-century colonial sources; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: Yuncemil was Lord of Death, or, perhaps, the personification of death itself; this dread deity was propitiated with offerings of food. Acat was God of Life; he it was that formed the infant in the womb. At Tihoo, the present Merida, stood the magnificent temple of Yahau Kuna in which Baklum Chaam, the Priapus of the Mayas and their most ancient god was worshipped.
passages.note: Condensed from Bancroft (1883), ch. XI; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 雲塞米爾（Yuncemil）是死亡之主，或者也許是死亡本身的化身；這令人畏懼的神祇以食物供品來撫慰。阿卡特（Acat）是生命之神；正是他在子宮中塑造了嬰兒。在蒂霍（Tihoo），即今日的梅里達（Merida），矗立著亞豪·庫納（Yahau Kuna）的宏偉神廟，其中供奉著巴克盧姆·查姆（Baklum Chaam），即瑪雅人的普里阿普斯（Priapus），也是他們最古老的神。

passages.text: Chac, or Chaac, a former king of Izamal, was honored as the god of fields, and fertility, and the inventor of agriculture. Some distance southwest of this city was the temple of Hunpictok, 'commander of eight thousand lances', a title given also to the general of the army. The most popular names were Zamna and Cukulcan, both culture-heroes.
passages.note: Condensed from Bancroft (1883), ch. XI; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 查克（Chac，或 Chaac），伊薩馬爾（Izamal）的前國王，被尊為田野與豐產之神，以及農業的發明者。在此城西南方不遠處是洪皮克托克（Hunpictok）的神廟，意為「八千矛之統帥」，此稱號亦授予軍隊的將軍。最普遍的名字是薩姆納與庫庫爾坎，二者皆為文化英雄。

title.en: The Cross of Cozumel and the Prophecy of the Strangers
title.zh: 科蘇梅爾之十字與異邦人預言

region.en: Cozumel, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦科蘇梅爾

period: Compendium of sixteenth-century sources; Bancroft 1883

source.work: Hubert Howe Bancroft, The Native Races of the Pacific States, vol. III (1883), ch. XI

summary.en: Among the prophets who arose before the Conquest was one who predicted the coming of a strange people from the direction of the rising sun, who would bring a monotheistic faith having the cross for its emblem; he admonished them to accept the new religion and erected a cross as a token of his prophecy. The first cross the Spaniards found stood in a temple on Cozumel, of lime and stone, and to it the natives prayed for rain, offering quails in times of drought.
summary.zh: 征服前夕，諸先知中有一位預言：將有奇異之族自日出之方而來，攜一神教，以十字為其表記；並勸民納新教，且立一十字為其預言之證。西班牙人所見的第一座十字立於科蘇梅爾島神廟之中，以石灰與石所造；土人向之祈雨，逢旱抬犧牲列隊而祭。

sensitivity.note: Compendium of colonial sources; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: The natives had a tradition, however, which placed the introduction of the cross a few years before the conquest. Among the many prophets who arose at that time was one who predicted the coming of a strange people from the direction of the rising sun, who would bring with them a monotheistic faith having the cross for its emblem. He admonished them to accept the new religion, and erected a cross as a token of his prophecy.
passages.note: Condensed from Bancroft (1883), ch. XI; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 然而，當地人有一種傳統，將十字架的傳入置於征服前數年。當時興起的眾多先知中，有一位預言將有一支奇異的民族從日出之方而來，他們將帶來一種以十字架為標誌的一神教信仰。他勸誡他們接受這新宗教，並立起一座十字架作為其預言的憑證。

passages.text: The first cross noticed by the Spaniards stood within the turreted courtyard of a temple on Cozumel Island; it was composed of lime and stone, and was ten spans in height. To this cross the natives prayed for rain, and in times of drought went in procession to offer vahomche, as they called the symbol, quails and other propitiatory gifts.
passages.note: Condensed from Bancroft (1883), ch. XI; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 西班牙人最先注意到的十字架矗立於科蘇梅爾島（Cozumel Island）上一座神廟的設有角樓的庭院內；它由石灰與石頭製成，高十拃。當地人向這十字架祈求雨水，並在乾旱之時列隊前往，獻上他們稱之為瓦霍姆切（vahomche）的此一象徵物、鵪鶉以及其他撫慰性的禮物。

title.en: Stones for Ekchuah: The Wayfarer's Heap
title.zh: 埃克丘瓦之石：行旅的石堆

region.en: Roads of Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦道路

period: Compendium of sixteenth-century sources; Bancroft 1883

source.work: Hubert Howe Bancroft, The Native Races of the Pacific States, vol. III (1883), ch. XI

summary.en: Ekchuah, the Holy Ghost of the traders, was the patron god of merchants and travelers. It was the custom of Yucatec wayfarers, when passing some prominent point on the road where an image of Ekchuah stood, to add a stone or two to the heap already accumulated there — an act of devotion similar to that performed by the Romans in honor of Mercury.
summary.zh: 埃克丘瓦——商旅的「聖靈」——為商賈與行旅的守護神。猶加敦旅人凡過路旁立有埃克丘瓦像之處，必投一石於既有石堆之上——一如羅馬人向墨丘利致敬之俗。

sensitivity.note: Compendium of sixteenth-century colonial sources; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: It was the custom of Yucatec wayfarers, when passing some prominent point on the road or spot where an image of Echuah stood, to add a stone or two to the heap already accumulated there, an act of devotion similar to that performed by the Romans in honor of Mercury. Echuah, or the Holy Ghost, was the patron god of merchants and travelers.
passages.note: Condensed from Bancroft (1883), ch. XI; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 尤卡坦的旅人有這樣的習俗：當他們經過路上某個顯眼的地點，或立有埃丘阿（Echuah）神像之處時，便會往那裡已堆積的石堆上添上一兩塊石頭；這是一種虔敬之舉，類似羅馬人為尊崇墨丘利（Mercury）所行的儀式。埃丘阿，或稱聖靈，是商人與旅人的守護神。

title.en: Votan, the Heart of the People: Founder of Palenque
title.zh: 沃坦——民族之心：帕倫克奠基者

region.en: Palenque (Nachan), Chiapas, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥恰帕斯帕倫克（納昌）

period: Tzendal tradition recorded by Nunez de la Vega and Ordonez y Aguiar; Bancroft 1883

source.work: Hubert Howe Bancroft, The Native Races of the Pacific States, vol. III (1883), ch. X

summary.en: Votan — 'heart', the most prominent deity of the Tzendals of Chiapas — proceeded by divine command to America and portioned out the land. Departing from Valum Chivim, passing the dwelling of the thirteen snakes, he arrived at Valum Votan, took several of his family, ascended the Usumacinta, and founded Nachan, or Palenque, the future metropolis of a mighty kingdom.
summary.zh: 沃坦——恰帕斯操特桑達爾語者最尊之神，其名意為「心」——奉神命而至美洲，分配其地。自瓦盧姆·奇維姆啟程，經「十三蛇之居」，抵瓦盧姆·沃坦；攜家族數人，上溯烏蘇馬辛塔河，建納昌——即帕倫克，日後強大帝國之都。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-recorded Tzendal tradition; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: From the confused tradition of the Tzendals, as rendered by Nunez de la Vega and Ordonez y Aguiar, it seems that Votan proceeded by divine command to America and there portioned out the land. He accordingly departed from Valum Chivim, passed by the dwelling of the thirteen snakes, and arrived in Valum Votan, where he took with him several of his family to form the nucleus of the settlement.
passages.note: Condensed from Bancroft (1883), ch. X; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 從策恩達爾人（Tzendals）混亂的傳統記載來看——這些記載由努涅斯·德·拉·維加（Nunez de la Vega）與奧爾多涅斯·伊·阿吉亞爾（Ordonez y Aguiar）所述——似乎沃坦（Votan）奉神聖的命令前往美洲，並在那裡劃分了土地。他於是從瓦盧姆·奇維姆（Valum Chivim）出發，經過十三條蛇的居所，抵達瓦盧姆·沃坦（Valum Votan），在那裡他帶上了家族中的若干人，作為定居地的核心。

passages.text: With them he passed through the island-strewn Laguna de Terminos, ascended the Usumacinta, and here, on one of its tributaries, founded Nachan, or Palenque, the future metropolis of a mighty kingdom. The Tzendal inhabitants bestowed upon the strange-looking new-comers the name Tzequiles, 'men with petticoats', on account of their long robes, but soon exchanged ideas and customs with them.
passages.note: Condensed from Bancroft (1883), ch. X; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 他與他們一同穿過島嶼星布的特爾米諾斯潟湖（Laguna de Terminos），溯烏蘇馬辛塔河（Usumacinta）而上，並在此處的一條支流上建立了納昌（Nachan），即帕倫克（Palenque），這座日後將成為一個強大王國的首府。策恩達爾人的居民因這些相貌奇特的新來者身著長袍，便賜予他們「策基萊斯」（Tzequiles）之名，意為「穿裙之人」，但不久便與他們交換了思想與習俗。

title.en: The House of Darkness and the Serpent Hole of Votan
title.zh: 沃坦的黑暗之屋與蛇穴

region.en: Huehuetan River, Chiapas, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥恰帕斯韋韋坦河

period: Tzendal tradition recorded by Nunez de la Vega and Ordonez y Aguiar; Bancroft 1883

source.work: Hubert Howe Bancroft, The Native Races of the Pacific States, vol. III (1883), ch. X

summary.en: Among the monuments left by the hero was a temple on the Huehuetan River called 'house of darkness', from its subterranean chambers, where the records of the nation were deposited under the charge of a fixed number of old men called tlapianes, or guardians, and an order of priestesses. A Tzendal legend relates that a subterranean passage leading from Palenque was constructed in commemoration of the celestial passage, the 'serpent hole', into which Votan, in his quality of snake, was admitted.
summary.zh: 英雄遺跡中，有韋韋坦河畔一廟，因地下密室而名「黑暗之屋」，國之典冊藏於其中，由定數的老者（特拉皮亞內斯，守護者）與一女祭司團看管。另傳帕倫克外有一地下甬道，為紀念那「蛇穴」而建——沃坦以其蛇身曾蒙允進入的天上通道。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-recorded Tzendal tradition; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: Among the monuments left by the hero was a temple on the Huehuetan River, called 'house of darkness', from its subterranean chambers, where the records of the nation were deposited under the charge of a fixed number of old men, termed tlapianes, or guardians, and an order of priestesses, whose superior was likewise the head of the male members. Here were also kept a number of tapirs, a sacred animal among the people.
passages.note: Condensed from Bancroft (1883), ch. X; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 這位英雄留下的遺跡中，有一座位於韋韋坦河（Huehuetan）畔的神廟，因其地下密室而被稱為「黑暗之屋」；國家的紀錄便存放於此，由固定人數的長者負責保管，這些長者稱為特拉皮亞內斯（tlapianes），即守護者，另有一階層的女祭司，其首領同時也是男性成員的首領。此地還飼養著若干貘，貘是當地人眼中的神聖動物。

passages.text: A Tzendal legend relates that a subterranean passage, leading from Palenque to Tulha, near Ococingo, was constructed in commemoration of the celestial passage, or 'serpent hole', into which Votan, in his quality of snake, was admitted. One of his titles was 'lord of the hollow tree', the teponaztli.
passages.note: Condensed from Bancroft (1883), ch. X; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 一則策恩達爾人的傳說講述，有一條地下通道從帕倫克通往奧科辛戈（Ococingo）附近的圖爾哈（Tulha），是為紀念那條天界通道，即「蛇洞」而建；沃坦以其蛇的身份得以進入其中。他的頭銜之一便是「空心樹之主」，即特波納斯特利（teponaztli）。

title.en: Comizahual, the Flying Tigress of Cerquin
title.zh: 塞爾欽的飛豹女科米薩瓦爾

region.en: Cerquin (Gracias), Honduras
region.zh: 宏都拉斯塞爾欽（格拉西亞斯）

period: Tradition recorded by Palacio and Torquemada; Bancroft 1883

source.work: Hubert Howe Bancroft, The Native Races of the Pacific States, vol. III (1883), ch. XI

summary.en: The culture-tradition of Cerquin speaks of a beautiful white woman, Comizahual, 'the flying tigress', a reputed sorceress, as the introducer of civilization. She descended from heaven, was carried by an invisible hand to the city of Cealcoquin, where she built a palace and set in the chief temple a stone bearing three hideous faces on each of its three sides, by whose aid she conquered her enemies. A virgin, yet three sons were born to her; grown old, she commanded her attendants to carry her bed to the highest part of the palace, and suddenly disappeared amid thunder and lightning — whereupon a beautiful bird flew upward and vanished.
summary.zh: 塞爾欽的文明起源傳說講到一位美麗的白人女子科米薩瓦爾——「飛豹」，傳為女巫，文明之引入者。她自天而降，被無形之手攜至西亞爾科欽城，建宮殿，於主廟立一石——三面各有三張猙獰面孔——憑此石降服諸敵。她守貞而誕三子；年老之際，命侍者抬其臥榻至宮殿最高處，遂於雷電之中消失——其時有一美鳥騰空而逝。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial-recorded tradition; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: Their culture-tradition speaks of a beautiful white woman, called Comizahual, or 'flying tigress', a reputed sorceress, as the introducer of civilization in Cerquin. She is said to have descended from heaven and to have been transported by an invisible hand to the city of Cealcoquin, where she built a palace adorned with monstrous figures of men and animals, and placed in the chief temple a stone having on each of its three sides three faces of strange and hideous aspect; by aid of this stone she conquered her enemies.
passages.note: Condensed from Bancroft (1883), ch. XI; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 他們的文化傳統提到一位美麗的白人女子，名叫科米薩瓦爾（Comizahual），意為「飛虎」，據傳是一位女巫，她是塞爾金（Cerquin）文明的引入者。據說她從天而降，並被一隻無形之手帶到塞阿爾科金城（Cealcoquin）；她在該城建造了一座宮殿，裝飾著怪異的人與動物形象，並在正殿中放置了一塊石頭，其三面各刻有三張怪異可怖的面孔；藉助這塊石頭，她征服了她的敵人。

passages.text: She remained a virgin, yet three sons were born to her, among whom she divided the kingdom when she grew old. After arranging her affairs, she commanded her attendants to carry her on her bed to the highest part of the palace, whence she suddenly disappeared amid thunder and lightning, doubtless to resume her place among the gods; directly afterwards a beautiful bird was seen to fly upwards and disappear. The people erected a temple in her honor, where the priest delivered her oracles.
passages.note: Condensed from Bancroft (1883), ch. XI; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 她終身保持童貞，卻生下了三個兒子，當她年老時，將王國分給了他們。安排好一切事務之後，她命令侍從將她的床抬到宮殿的最高處，她隨即在一陣雷電交加之中突然消失，無疑是回到了眾神之中；緊接著，有人看見一隻美麗的鳥兒向上飛去，消失不見。人們為她建了一座神廟，祭司在那裡傳達她的神諭。

title.en: The Itza Adore the Horse of Cortes
title.zh: 伊察人拜科爾特斯之馬

region.en: Tayasal, Lake Peten, Guatemala
region.zh: 危地馬拉佩滕湖塔亞薩爾

period: Events of 1525; recorded by Villagutierre (1701); Bancroft 1883

source.work: Hubert Howe Bancroft, The Native Races of the Pacific States, vol. III (1883), ch. XI, on the Itza worship

summary.en: When Cortes passed through the Itza country in 1525 he left a lame horse behind, which the Itza fed with flowers, flesh, and incense as a god; the offerings did not sustain it, and before long the bones of the apotheosized charger were all that remained to his worshippers. In another place was a stone-and-lime imitation of the horse, seated on the floor on its haunches, which the natives adored in the same manner — animal worship the more readily admitted since their gods were supposed to assume such forms.
summary.zh: 1525年科爾特斯過伊察之地，遺下一匹跛馬；伊察人奉之為神，以花、肉與香祭養；然供養不足，不久此「神馬」唯餘骸骨，徒留拜者。另處尚有一座以石灰石仿製的馬像，蹲坐於地，土人亦以同禮敬拜——因他們本信諸神可化獸形，故獸崇拜易被接受。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-recorded tradition; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: They brought it thunder, and brought it flowers, flesh, and incense; but such offerings did not sustain life, and it was not long before the bones of the apotheosized charger were all that remained to his worshippers. In another place was a stone and lime imitation of this horse, seated on the floor on its haunches, which the natives adored in the same manner. This animal-worship was the more readily admitted, since their gods were supposed to assume such forms.
passages.note: Condensed from Bancroft (1883), ch. XI, on the Itza worship (Villagutierre 1701); not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 他們向牠獻上雷電，並獻上鮮花、肉與香；但這樣的供品並不能維持生命，不久之後，那匹被奉為神明的駿馬留給崇拜者的，便只剩下骨骸了。在另一處，有一尊以石與石灰仿製的此馬像，以蹲踞之姿坐於地上，當地人以同樣的方式崇拜它。這種動物崇拜之所以更容易被接受，是因為人們認為他們的神明會化為這樣的形貌。

title.en: The Lacandones Adore the Sun Without Images
title.zh: 拉坎敦人不立像而拜日

region.en: Chiapas, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥恰帕斯

period: Compendium of sources; Bancroft 1883

source.work: Hubert Howe Bancroft, The Native Races of the Pacific States, vol. III (1883), ch. XI

summary.en: The purest form of sun-worship appears among the Lacandones, who adored the luminary without the intervention of an image, and sacrificed before it in the Mexican fashion. They had temples, the walls of which were decorated with hieroglyphs of the sun and moon, and with a figure in the act of praying to the sun.
summary.zh: 拉坎敦人保有最純粹的太陽崇拜：他們不假像設，直拜日輪，並仿墨西哥之式於日前獻祭。彼有神廟，牆上繪日月之象形文字，並繪一人向日祈禱之像。

sensitivity.note: Living Lacandón religion described in a compendium; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: The purest form of sun-worship appears among the Lacandones, who adored the luminary without the intervention of an image, and sacrificed before it in the Mexican fashion. They had temples, however, the walls of which were decorated with hieroglyphs of the sun and moon, and with a figure in the act of praying to the sun.
passages.note: Condensed from Bancroft (1883), ch. XI; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 最純粹的太陽崇拜形式出現在拉坎東人之中，他們崇拜這顆發光的天體，不借助任何偶像，並以墨西哥的方式在它面前獻祭。然而他們也有神廟，廟牆上裝飾著太陽與月亮的象形文字，以及一個正在向太陽祈禱的人物圖像。

title.en: Chamalcan: The Bat God of the Zotzil Royal House
title.zh: 查馬爾坎：佐茲爾王室的蝙蝠神

region.en: Guatemala highlands
region.zh: 危地馬拉高地

period: Compendium of sources (Brasseur 1861); Bancroft 1883

source.work: Hubert Howe Bancroft, The Native Races of the Pacific States, vol. III (1883), ch. XI

summary.en: The chief god of the Cakchiquels, Chamalcan, had many of the attributes of Tohil but took the form of a bat, the symbol of the royal house of the Zotzil. Every seventh and thirteenth day of the month the priests placed before him bloodstained thorns, fresh white resin, bark and branches of pine, and a cat, the emblem of night, which were burned in his honor.
summary.zh: 卡克奇克爾主神查馬爾坎具托希爾之諸德，卻以蝙蝠為形——此乃佐茲爾王室之徽。每月第七與第十三日，祭司置染血之刺、新潔白脂、松皮松枝，及象徵黑夜之貓於其前，焚之以為其榮。

sensitivity.note: Compendium of sources; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: The chief god of the Cakchiquels, Chamalcan, had many of the attributes of Tohil, but took the form of a bat, the symbol of the royal house of Zotzil. Every seventh and thirteenth day of the month the priests placed before him bloodstained thorns, fresh white resin, bark and branches of pine, and a cat, the emblem of night, which were burned in his honor.
passages.note: Condensed from Bancroft (1883), ch. XI; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 卡克奇奎爾人的主神查馬爾坎擁有托希爾的許多屬性，但化為蝙蝠之形，蝙蝠是索齊爾王室的象徵。每逢每月的第七日與第十三日，祭司便在他面前放置染血的荊棘、新鮮的白色樹脂、松樹的樹皮與枝條，以及一隻貓——夜的象徵，這些都在他的榮耀中焚燒。

title.en: Ori, the God of Fate in Every House
title.zh: 奧里——家家供奉的命運之神

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the household coffer near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費近郊家宅藏櫃）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part I ch. III

summary.en: The Ori (head) is the universal household deity, worshipped by both sexes as the god of fate: good or ill fortune attends one according to the will or decree of this god, and it is propitiated that good luck might be the votary's share. The representing image is forty-one cowries strung together in the shape of a crown, secreted in a large coffer, the lid of which is of the same form and material — called Ile Ori, Ori's house, and as large as the owner can afford to make it; some contain as much as six heads of cowries, and the leather-worker who makes it is paid the same number of cowries as he uses. As the Kori is the children's god, so the Ori is exclusively worshipped by adults; after the death of its owner the image with the coffer is destroyed, and the cowries spent.
summary.zh: 「奧里」（頭）是普受男女供奉的家宅之神——命運之神：禍福皆繫於祂的旨意，故人人奉祭以求好運。其神像為四十一枚貝幣串成王冠之形，藏於大木櫃中；櫃蓋同形同質，名「伊萊奧里」——奧里之宅，大小視主人財力而定，有的竟可容六「頭」（一萬二千枚）貝幣；製櫃的皮匠所得工錢，恰與用去的貝數相等。柯里是小兒之神，奧里則唯成人敬奉；主人亡故之後，神像與櫃同毀，貝幣隨之散盡。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921 by Johnson (an insider-adjacent Yoruba pastor-historian); the Ori (personal head-fate) cult. Cross-ref: yoruba-three-indwelling-spirits (Ellis's Olori head-spirit) and Dennett's odu readings.

passages.text: The Ori (head) is the universal household deity worshipped by both sexes as the god of fate. It is believed that good or ill fortune attends one, according to the will or decree of this god; and hence it is propitiated in order that good luck might be the share of its votary. The representing image is 41 cowries strung together in the shape of a crown. This is secreted in a large coffer, the lid of which is of the same form and material. It is called Ile Ori (Ori's house), and in size is as large as the owner can afford to make it; some usually contain as much as 6 heads (12,000) of cowries, and the manufacturer, who is generally a worker in leather, receives as his pay the same amount of cowries as is used in the article manufactured. As the Kori is the children's god, so the Ori is exclusively worshipped by the adults. After the death of its owner, the image of Ori with the coffer is destroyed, and the cowries spent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. III (1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧里（頭）是普世的家庭神祇，男女皆崇拜之，視之為命運之神。人們相信，一個人的吉凶禍福皆依此神的意願或旨意而定；因此人們向它祈求，好讓好運降臨於其信徒。代表它的形象是四十一枚串成王冠形狀的貝幣。這形象被藏於一個大箱子中，箱蓋亦為同樣的形狀與材質。它被稱為伊萊奧里（奧里之屋），其大小依主人所能負擔的程度而定；有些通常可容納多達六「頭」（即一萬二千枚）貝幣，而製作者——通常是皮革工匠——所獲得的報酬，與製成品中所用的貝幣數量相同。正如科里是孩童之神，奧里則專為成年人所崇拜。在其主人死後，奧里的形象連同箱子一併銷毀，貝幣也花費殆盡。

title.en: As the Aremo Reigned With His Father, He Must Die With Him
title.zh: 儲君與父同治，亦必與父同死

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (the Aremo's residence beside the palace)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（王宮旁的儲君官邸）

period: Yoruba constitutional tradition; recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part I ch. IV

summary.en: In the earliest days the eldest son succeeded his father, and to be educated in all the duties of the kingship he was associated with the father in important duties, practically reigning with him under the title of Aremo, the heir apparent, with his own official residence near the palace. But as the age grew corrupt, the Aremo often exercised sway quite as much as or more than the King himself, especially in the course of a long reign when age had rendered the monarch feeble; they had equal powers of life and death over the King's subjects, and there are cases on record of the Aremo being strongly suspected of terminating the father's life in order to attain full powers at once. It was therefore made a law and part of the constitution that as the Aremo reigned with his father, he must also die with him. This law had the effect, at any rate, of checking parricide; it continued to take effect up to last century, when (in 1858) it was repealed by Atiba, one of the later kings, in favour of his Aremo Adelu. The Aremo may now succeed if found worthy, but he must be elected in the usual way; and if passed over he must retire into private life in the provinces — unless he chooses of his own accord to die with the father.
summary.zh: 太古之制，長子承父業；為使他通曉為王之道，常使協理要務，事實上與父共治，稱「阿雷莫」——儲君，在王宮旁另設官邸。然而世風日壞，阿雷莫的權勢往往不遜於王，尤其老王年邁力衰、在位日久之時；二人生殺之權相等，史冊且載有儲君疑為早日攬權而弒父之案。於是憲制定規：儲君與父共治，亦必與父同死。此律至少遏制了弒父之行；施行至上世紀——1858年阿提巴王為其儲君阿德盧而廢之。今日儲君如經選立合格可繼位，但須循正途；若遭擯斥，便須退居外省——除非他自願隨父而死。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the companion-death constitutional law of the Oyo crown, reported with Johnson's own historical note on its 1858 repeal.

passages.text: In the earliest days, the eldest son naturally succeeded the father, and in order to be educated in all the duties of the kingship which must one day devolve upon him, he was often associated more or less with the father in performing important duties, and thereby he often performed royal functions, and thus gradually he practically reigned with his father under the title of Aremo (the heir apparent) having his own official residence near the palace. But as the age grew corrupt, the Aremo often exercised sway quite as much as or more than the King himself, especially in the course of a long reign, when age has rendered the monarch feeble. They had equal powers of life and death over the King's subjects, and there are some cases on record of the Aremo being strongly suspected of terminating the father's life, in order to attain full powers at once.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. IV (1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在最早的時代，長子自然繼承父親，而為了在終將落於其身的種種王權職責上受到教育，他常或多或少與父親一同處理重要事務，因而常行使王室職能，於是漸漸地，他以阿雷莫（法定繼承人）的稱號實際上與父親共同統治，並在宮殿附近擁有自己的官邸。但隨著時代日益敗壞，阿雷莫往往行使與國王相當甚至更大的權力，尤其是在漫長的統治期間，年歲已使君主衰弱之時。他們對國王的臣民擁有同等的生殺之權，而記載中亦有若干案例，阿雷莫被強烈懷疑為了一舉取得全權而終結了父親的性命。

passages.text: It was therefore made a law and part of the constitution that as the Aremo reigned with his father, he must also die with him. This law had the effect, at any rate, of checking parricide. It continued to take effect up to last century when (in 1858) it was repealed by Atiba, one of the later Kings, in favour of his Aremo Adelu. The Aremo may now succeed if found worthy, but he must be elected in the usual way; but if passed over or rejected by the king-makers he must leave the city and resort to a private retirement in the provinces. This, however, is not really obligatory, but as he must be superseded in his office, such a course is inevitable, unless he chooses of his own accord to die with the father.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. IV (1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 因此，這被訂立為一條法律，並成為憲制的一部分：既然阿雷莫（Aremo）與其父共同在位，他也必須與其父同死。這條法律無論如何都起到了遏制弒父的作用。它一直生效至上一世紀，直到（1858年）被較晚的諸王之一阿蒂巴（Atiba）為其阿雷莫阿德盧（Adelu）所廢除。如今，阿雷莫若被認為配得上，便可繼位，但必須按慣常方式被選出；倘若他被立王者們略過或拒絕，他就必須離開城市，退居外省隱居。然而，這其實並非強制性的，但既然他必須被免去其職位，這樣的做法便不可避免，除非他自願選擇與父親同死。

title.en: "You Have Eaten the King"
title.zh: 「你已食王」

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (the Otun-Iwefa's house where the king-elect is fed)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（王儲受饗的奧圖-伊韋法宅邸）

period: Yoruba constitutional tradition; recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part I ch. IV, note

summary.en: Tradition says that in the early times, while the King-elect is in the Otun-Iwefa's house, among other dishes brought to him to partake of is one prepared from the heart of the late King, which has been extracted and preserved. After partaking of this, he is told he has eaten the King: hence the origin of the word Je Oba — to become a King, literally to eat a King.
summary.zh: 相傳古時王儲居於奧圖-伊韋法宅邸期間，奉到他面前與諸餚並陳的，有一道取自已故先王心臟烹製的菜——那心臟已被取出保存。食畢，有人告訴他：「你已食王。」——「傑奧巴」（Je Oba，登基為王）一詞由此而來，字面義即「食王」。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921 as Johnson's footnote on the coronation sequence; the king-continuity rite reported as the recorded tradition states it, without graphic elaboration.

passages.text: Tradition says that in the early times while the King-elect is in the Otun-Iwefa's house, among other dishes brought to him to partake of is one prepared from the heart of the late King which has been extracted and preserved. After partaking of this he is told he has eaten the King. Hence the origin of the word Je Oba, to become a King (lit. to eat a King).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. IV, note (1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傳說在早期，當國王當選人還待在奧通-伊韋法（Otun-Iwefa）的家中時，端給他享用的諸多菜餚中，有一道是用已故國王的心臟製成的——那顆心被取出並保存下來。他吃過之後，便被告知他已吃下了國王。因此便有了「Je Oba」一詞的由來，意即成為國王（字面意思為「吃下一位國王」）。

title.en: The Bara: The Mausoleum a King Enters Once
title.zh: 巴拉陵——君王一生僅入一次

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (the royal mausoleum on the city's outskirts)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（城郊的王家陵廟）

period: Yoruba constitutional tradition; recorded 1921 (Johnson)

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part I ch. IV

summary.en: The coronation takes place at the end of three months, really at the third appearance of the new moon after the late King's death, and is attended with great public demonstration. This day is generally known as the King's visit to the Bara. The Bara or royal mausoleum is a consecrated building in the outskirts of the city, under the care of a high-priestess named Iyamode; there the Kings were formally crowned, and there buried. The King enters it but once in his lifetime, and that is on the day of his coronation.
summary.zh: 加冕禮於三個月之期滿時舉行——實即先王崩後第三次新月出現之時，全城盛裝慶賀，四方來賀者雲集。此日通稱「王臨巴拉」。巴拉即王家陵廟，是城郊一座奉為聖地的建築，由名為「伊亞莫德」的女大祭司執掌；歷代君王皆在此正式加冕，亦皆歸葬於此。而國王一生只入此門一次——就在他加冕的那一天。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the Bara rite binding coronation to the tomb. Cross-ref: yoruba-ida-oranyan-coronation (the Ife sword requirement).

passages.text: The coronation takes place at the end of three months, really at the third appearance of the new moon after the late King's death. The date is generally so fixed as to have it, if possible, before the next great festival. It is attended with a great public demonstration. It is a gala day in which the whole city appears in holiday dress. Visitors from the provinces and representatives of neighbouring states also flock into the city in numbers. This day is generally known as the King's visit to the Bara. The Bara or royal mausoleum is a consecrated building in the outskirts of the city, under the care of a high-priestess named Iyamode; there the Kings were formally crowned, and there buried. The King enters it but once in his lifetime, and that is on the day of his coronation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. IV (1921); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 加冕典禮在三個月期滿時舉行，實際上是在已故國王去世後新月第三次出現之時。日期通常如此選定，以便盡可能趕在下一場盛大節慶之前。典禮伴隨著盛大的公眾遊行。這是一個喜慶的日子，全城都身著節日盛裝露面。來自外省的訪客和鄰國的使節也成群結隊地湧入城中。這一天通常被稱為「國王蒞臨巴拉（Bara）之日」。巴拉，即王家陵墓，是城郊一座奉為神聖的建築，由一位名為伊亞莫德（Iyamode）的高級女祭司看管；歷代國王曾在那裡正式加冕，也在那裡安葬。國王一生只進入其中一次，那便是他加冕之日。

title.en: Ogun Turns the Smith's Tools to Stone: The Anvil of Lade
title.zh: 奧貢化鐵為石——鐵匠拉德的鐵砧

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the Oni's monument square, where the anvil stands)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（奧尼宮前聖物園中的鐵砧）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XIV

summary.en: In the Oni's palace at Ife, within a small space surrounded by a low wall, there is a ring of holy stones — and the strangest is an onion or drop-shaped block thirty inches in height and forty-one and a half inches round, which, though it is of iron, the people in general say is stone. The story of it is this: this stone was the anvil of Lade, the smith. Lade was the mightiest smith of the past; when he died, Ogun changed all his tools into stone. The stone in the Oni's palace is Lade's anvil, and its name is Ogun-Lade.
