It was washed out of the earth in a season of rains at the exact time when the Koran was brought into the land — so the legend. The material cracks off in cup-shaped scales, and a second like it, obviously sacrosanct, was found in the most secret parts of the Oni's palace, judged by its exterior to be cast and not wrought.
summary.zh: 伊費奧尼宮內，低牆環繞的小園中供著一圈聖石——最奇者是一塊洋蔥（或水滴）形巨物，高三十吋、周長四十一吋半；它雖是鐵鑄，人們卻堅稱是石。傳說如此：此石本是鐵匠拉德的鐵砧。拉德是古昔最偉大的鐵匠；他一死，奧貢便把他所有的工具都化成了石頭。奧尼宮中此石即拉德之砧，名為「奧貢-拉德」。相傳它是某個雨季從土中沖刷而出——恰在《可蘭經》傳入本地之時。其質地層層剝落如杯狀鱗片；在奧尼宮最深秘處另有一件同類聖物，觀其外表應為鑄造而非鍛打。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910-12; the petrified-tools legend of the smith Lade tied to Ogun's patronage of smiths. Johnson's Koran-contact tradition (yoruba-odudua-koran-peg) is echoed in the dating formula.

passages.text: Still stranger, however, is the monument placed between the two above-mentioned ones in the same place, namely, an onion or drop-shaped block thirty inches in height and forty-one and a half inches round, and thus a large and important specimen, when one remembers it is of iron! Although it is metal, the people in general say it is stone. The story of it is this: this stone was the anvil of Lade, the smith. Lade was the mightiest smith of the past. When he died, Ogun changed all his tools into stone. The stone in the Oni's palace is Lade's anvil, and its name is Ogun-Lade. It was washed out of the earth in a season of rains at the exact time when the Koran was brought into the land. So the legend.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIV (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而，更為奇特的是，在同一地點、上述兩座紀念物之間所立的那座紀念物，即一塊洋蔥形或水滴形的鐵塊，高三十英寸，周長四十一點五英寸，因而是一件巨大而重要的樣本——只要想到它是鐵製的！儘管它是金屬，一般人卻說它是石頭。關於它的故事是這樣的：這塊石頭是鐵匠拉德（Lade）的鐵砧。拉德是往昔最強悍的鐵匠。他死後，奧貢（Ogun）把他所有的工具都變成了石頭。奧尼（Oni）宮中的那塊石頭便是拉德的鐵砧，其名為奧貢-拉德（Ogun-Lade）。它是在一個雨季裡從土中被沖刷出來的，恰逢《古蘭經》傳入此地之時。傳說便是如此。

passages.text: The material of this lump cracks off in cup-shaped scales. The shape of the thing did not allow me to see whether this, considered from the point of view of African technical ability, was a gigantic piece of wrought iron or, as is less likely, a block of cast-iron. Later on, in the most secret parts of the Oni's palace, Martius came upon another like it, obviously sacrosanct, and his engineering knowledge led him to conclude that, judging by its exterior, it was cast and not wrought.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIV (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這塊鐵塊的材質會裂成杯狀的鱗片剝落。這東西的形狀使我無法看出，從非洲技術能力的角度來看，它究竟是一塊巨大的鍛鐵，還是——可能性較小——一塊鑄鐵。後來，在奧尼宮中最隱秘的地方，馬蒂烏斯（Martius）又遇到了另一塊與之相似的東西，顯然是神聖不可侵犯的；他的工程學知識使他得出結論：從其外觀判斷，它是鑄造的，而非鍛造的。

title.en: The Sixteen-Part Shadow Clock of Ife
title.zh: 伊費十六分影鐘

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the triangular monolith in the centre of the old town)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（古城中央的三角巨石）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XIV

summary.en: The real type of the tooth-stone monoliths is found frequently both in Ife and in ruined Modeke; they stand upright on slight elevations. One of these triangular monoliths, nearly eleven feet nine inches high, stands in the centre of the old town: the natives said it had formerly served as a kind of sundial. When the shadow of this stele reached a point on a circle drawn round it, it was time for certain sacred festivals — and this circle was divided into sixteen parts, which caused no surprise, for this number constantly recurs everywhere. These monoliths, then, were essentially time-measurers and sun-clocks.
summary.zh: 「齒石」類獨石柱在伊費與已毀的莫達凱凱屢見不鮮，皆立於微微隆起的高地。古城中央一座三角獨石柱高近十一呎九吋：土人相傳它古時用作日晷。當柱影觸及環繞柱基所畫圓周上的某點，便是舉行特定聖祭之期——而那圓周被分成十六等分，此數無處不現，不足為奇。這些獨石柱，本質上是量時之器、太陽之鐘。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910-12; the sixteen-part festival calendar stone, tying Ife's sacred geography to the Ifa sixteen (Frobenius's analysis). Cross-ref: yoruba-four-gods-four-quarters.

passages.text: The height of Oranja's obelisk above the ground was close upon eleven feet, nine inches. If, now, the Oranja tooth-stone takes on the monolith form, we find the real type of this frequently both in Ife and also in ruined Modeke. They stand upright on slight elevations. One of these triangular monoliths is illustrated on page 299. The natives said it had formerly served as a kind of sundial. When the shadow of this stele reached a point on a circle drawn round it, it was time for certain sacred festivals. This circle was divided into sixteen parts, which caused us no surprise, for this number constantly recurs everywhere. These monoliths, then, were essentially time-measurers and sun-clocks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIV (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧蘭賈（Oranja）方尖碑高出地面的高度將近十一英尺九英寸。那麼，如果奧蘭賈的牙石呈現出獨石柱的形態，我們便會在伊費（Ife）以及廢毀的莫德凱（Modeke）屢屢見到這種形態的真正類型。它們直立於略微隆起的高處。其中一座三角形獨石柱見於第299頁的插圖。當地人說它從前曾用作一種日晷。當這座石柱的影子到達圍繞它畫出的圓周上的某一點時，便是舉行某些神聖節慶的時候了。這個圓周被分為十六個部分，這並未使我們感到驚訝，因為這個數字在各處不斷出現。那麼，這些獨石柱本質上便是計時器和日鐘。

title.en: Illu-Olokun: The Town Where All Mankind Was Born
title.zh: 伊盧奧洛貢——全人類誕生之城

region.en: Igbo-Olokun forest, north of Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the drowned city's site)
region.zh: 伊費以北的伊格博-奧洛貢森林（沈沒古城之址）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XIV

summary.en: There once was an old town called Illu-Olokun, the Town of the Ruler of the Ocean, to the north of Ife. Our fathers before us have told us that in times long, long ago this city was surrounded by a lake to the south and a river on the north, by which one could get to the sea. Olokun, the Orisha, had founded this city before the creation of the earth; the Omo-Olokun, long since driven to the south, left behind them the tradition that it actually was Olokun who created the earth on which Ife stood. In former days he was the only god worshipped in Illu-Olokun and in Ife. The legendary name of the Sea God, Isindya's first priest, and of the first king, was Oba-Idyo. Illu-Olokun was believed to be the birthplace of all mankind, both fair and dark — the Europeans also came from there! The place where once it stood is to-day called Igbo-Olokun, because a great forest has overgrown it; but the name Ebolokun, sacrifice to the Sea God, is commoner, because offerings are still laid before the Poseidon of Atlantic Africa under the palms in the forest. In the depths of this vast forest there are large jars of glazed porcelain, and the discovery of Ebolokun furnishes proof that at some remote era glass was made and moulded in this very land — the beautiful long glass beads said to be found only in the temple of Olokun.
summary.zh: 伊費之北曾有古城，名「伊盧奧洛貢」——海王之城。祖輩相傳：太古之時，此城南湖北河環繞，循水道可通大海。海神奧洛貢在大地被造之前便建立了此城；早已南遷的奧莫-奧洛貢族人留下遺訓：伊費所立的大地，正是奧洛貢所造。古時伊盧奧洛貢與伊費所拜的唯一神祇便是祂。海神之號、伊斯因迪亞的首位祭司兼開國君王，傳說名為奧巴-伊迪約。伊盧奧洛貢被奉為全人類——膚白膚黑皆是——的誕生之地，連歐洲人也出自那裡！古城舊址今日稱「伊格博-奧洛貢」，因參天密林已將其吞沒；但更通行的名字是「埃博洛貢」——祭獻海神——因為人們至今仍在大西洋非洲的這位「波塞冬」面前的棕櫚林中擺放祭品。茫茫林海深處藏著大件釉瓷巨罐；埃博洛貢的發現證明：遠古之世，玻璃便在此地燒製成型——那種據說只在奧洛貢神廟中才見得到的美麗長形玻璃珠。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910-12; the drowned-city legend of Illu-Olokun and the Olokun-first-creation tradition, with the glassworking archaeology Frobenius connected to it. Cross-refs: yoruba-oduduwa-sand-hen, yoruba-olokun-flood-chained.

passages.text: There once was an old town called Illu-Olokun, that is, the Town of the Ruler of the Ocean, to the north of Ilife. Our fathers before us have told us that in times long, long ago this city was surrounded by a lake to the South and a river on the North, by which one could get to the sea. Olokun, the Orisha, had founded this city before the creation of the earth. The Omo-Olokun, who long since then had been driven to the South, left behind them the tradition that it actually was Olokun who created the earth on which Ilife stood. In former days he was the only god worshipped in Illu-Olokun and in Ilife. The legendary name of the Sea God, Isindya's first priest, and of the first king, was Oba-Idyo. Illu-Olokun was believed to be the birthplace of all mankind, both fair and dark; the Europeans also came from there!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIV (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一座古老的城鎮，名叫伊盧-奧洛昆（Illu-Olokun），意即「海洋統治者之城」，位於伊費（Ilife）以北。我們的祖先曾告訴我們，在很久很久以前，這座城市南面被一座湖環繞，北面有一條河，經由那條河可以通往大海。奧里沙（Orisha）奧洛昆（Olokun）在地球被創造之前便已建立了這座城市。奧莫-奧洛昆（Omo-Olokun）早已被驅逐到南方，他們留下了一項傳統，說實際上正是奧洛昆創造了伊費所坐落的那片大地。往昔，他是伊盧-奧洛昆和伊費唯一受到崇拜的神。這位海神、伊辛迪亞（Isindya）的第一位祭司以及第一位國王的傳說之名，是奧巴-伊迪奧（Oba-Idyo）。人們相信伊盧-奧洛昆是全人類的誕生地，無論膚色淺或深；歐洲人也是從那裡來的！

passages.text: As stated, the old city was known as Illu-Olokun. The place where once it stood is to-day called Igbo-Olokun, because a great Igbo, or forest, has overgrown it. But the name Ebolokun, or Ebo-olokun, i.e. sacrifice to the Sea God, is commoner, because offerings are still laid before the Poseidon of Atlantic Africa under the palms in the forest. In the depths of this vast forest there are large jars of glazed porcelain; and the discovery of Ebolokun and the Ebora furnishes proof that at some remote era glass was made and moulded in this very land, and that the nation which here of old held rule were brilliant exponents of apt dexterity in the production of terra-cotta images.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIV (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 如前所述，這座古城被稱為伊盧-奧洛昆。它昔日所在之地，今日被稱為伊格博-奧洛昆（Igbo-Olokun），因為一片廣大的伊格博（Igbo），即森林，已在其上蔓生。但埃博洛昆（Ebolokun），或埃博-奧洛昆（Ebo-olokun），即「獻給海神的祭品」這一名稱更為常見，因為人們至今仍在這片森林的棕櫚樹下，向大西洋非洲的波塞冬（Poseidon）獻上供品。在這片廣袤森林的深處，有大片上了釉的瓷甕；而埃博洛昆與埃博拉（Ebora）的發現，證明了在某個遙遠的時代，玻璃曾在这片土地上製造和模塑，且昔日在此地掌權的民族，在陶土塑像的製作上乃是靈巧精湛的能手。

title.en: Olokun's Holy Hill in Ilesha Country
title.zh: 伊萊沙之地的奧洛貢聖丘

region.en: Ilesha district, Nigeria (the secret tumulus of the sea god)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊萊沙近郊（海神的秘密古塚）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XIV

summary.en: The Ilifians believe that the Ocean deity lives not only in the sea, but dwells also in the beds of the streams, and the Niger itself is one of his favourite abodes. Nay, there was a myth current with the Ileshans according to which Olokun lived on a hill — and this fits in with the tale in which Shankpanna changed Olokun into a hill at Olorun's command. Frobenius declines to mention the site of Olokun's Holy Hill, about which the Ileshans fully informed him, limiting himself to saying that it is obviously an old tumulus which could be reached, within comparatively recent times, by a sacrificial path; he is told its interior is richly adorned — the natives declare that all its wall-coverings, headgear and body ornaments are of gold, though from what he could personally gather it must rather consist in the main of bronze with only small quantities of the precious metal.
summary.zh: 伊費人相信海神不只居於海中，也棲於河床——尼日河本身就是他鍾愛的居所之一。伊萊沙人中更流傳著一則神話：奧洛貢住在山上——這與香潘納奉奧洛倫之命把奧洛貢化為山丘的故事正相呼應。弗羅貝紐斯獲伊萊沙人詳告聖丘所在，卻不肯揭示其址，只說那顯然是一座古塚，直至晚近尚有一條祭祀小徑可達；據聞塚內陳設華美——土人堅稱壁飾、冠冕、佩飾盡為黃金；但據他親自考察所及，主體應為青銅，貴金屬僅佔少數。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910-12; the hill-tumulus cult of Olokun (site withheld by Frobenius and by this record). Cross-refs: yoruba-edju-four-houses-trick (Olokun changed to a hill), yoruba-oke-abeokuta-cavern.

passages.text: The Ilifians, however, believe that the Ocean deity lives not only in the sea, but rather dwells also in the beds of the streams, and the Niger itself is one of his favourite abodes. Nay, there was a myth current with the Ileshans according to which Olokun lived on a hill. But this also fits in with a tale told above, in which Shankpanna changed Olokun into a hill at Olorun's command. I do not consider it advisable here to mention the site of Olokun's Holy Hill, about which the Ileshans fully informed me. I will limit myself to saying that it is obviously an old tumulus, which could be reached within comparatively recent times by a sacrificial path. I am told its interior is richly adorned. The natives declare that all its wall-coverings, all the headgear and body ornaments, in fact, all its decorations, are of gold. But from what I was able personally to gather, I think this must be a mistake: it may even now, with almost positive certainty, be said that in the main it consists of bronze with only small quantities of the precious metal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIV (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而，伊利費人（Ilifians）相信，這位海洋神祇不僅住在海裡，更住在溪流的河床中，而尼日河（Niger）本身便是他最喜愛的居所之一。不僅如此，伊萊沙人（Ileshans）中流傳著一則神話，說奧洛昆住在一座山上。但這也與上文所述的一則故事相符，故事中尚克潘納（Shankpanna）奉奧洛倫（Olorun）之命將奧洛昆變成了一座山。我認為在此提及奧洛昆聖山的所在地並不合宜，關於此事伊萊沙人曾向我詳細說明。我只想說，它顯然是一座古老的墳塚，在較近的時代仍可經由一條祭祀之路抵達。有人告訴我，其內部裝飾華麗。當地人宣稱，它所有的壁飾、所有的頭飾與身體飾物，事實上，它所有的裝飾，都是黃金的。但根據我個人所能蒐集到的資料，我認為這必定是個誤解：即使現在，也幾乎可以肯定地說，它主要還是由青銅構成，只含有少量的貴金屬。

title.en: Three Spirits in Every Man: Head, Stomach and Great Toe
title.zh: 人人三靈——頭、胃與大足趾

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the household shrine near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費近郊家宅神龕）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. VII

summary.en: The Yorubas hold that each man has three spiritual inmates: Olori (lord of the head), sometimes called Ori, the protector, guardian and guide, who brings good fortune — offerings of fowls are made to him and the blood mixed with palm-oil rubbed on the forehead, his symbol being half a calabash studded with cowries; Ipin-ijeun, he who shares in the food, who shares in all the man eats and has no special sacrifice — hunger is personified as his agent, pinching the stomach to convey his principal's desire; and Ipori, the great toe, least important of the three, anointed with fowl's blood and palm-oil when a man is about to set out on a journey — a waterfowl, says the proverb, is not fit for the worship of Ipori. Curiously, Ipin-ijeun is connected with fire-worship: fire, which has no god of its own, is still spoken of as Abanigbele, the Inmate — for fire is necessary to prepare food, and food is necessary to Ipin-ijeun; therefore he takes fire under his protection and takes care that it is not extinguished.
summary.zh: 約魯巴人相信每個人身中住著三個靈：一是「奧洛里」（頭之主），或稱「奧里」——守護者、引導者，司掌好運；以雞祭之，血和棕櫚油抹額，其符為半邊嵌貝的葫蘆。二是「伊平-伊杰恩」——分食之靈，人吃什麼他分什麼，故無專祭；「饑餓」被擬人化為他的使者，掐胃以傳主人欲食之意。三是「伊波里」——大足趾之靈，三者中最卑微，唯臨行之際以雞血調油塗趾；諺云：水禽不配祭伊波里。奇妙的是，伊平-伊杰恩與拜火相連：約魯巴本無火神，火卻被稱為「阿巴尼格貝萊」——「同住者」——因為造食需火，而伊平-伊杰恩需食；他遂把火納入庇護之下，不許它熄滅。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1894; the triple-soul doctrine (compare the kra/luvo theories of the Tshi and Ewe). Cross-ref: yoruba-ori-head-fate (Johnson's Ori cult), yoruba-abiku-spirit-children.

passages.text: The Yorubas hold that each man has three spiritual inmates: Olori (owner, or lord, of the head), sometimes called Ori (head, faculty, talent), seems to be the spirit which answers to the kra or luvo. He is the protector, guardian, and guide. Offerings are made to him, chiefly fowls, and some of the blood, mixed with palm-oil, is rubbed upon the forehead. Olori brings good-fortune, whence the proverb: Olori causes the owner of the head to prosper, and not the crab on the bank of the river. The symbol of Olori is half a calabash studded over with cowries.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VII (1894); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 約魯巴人（Yorubas）認為，每個人都有三位內在的靈：奧洛里（Olori，意即頭的主人或主宰），有時也稱為奧里（Ori，意即頭、才能、天賦），似乎是相當於克拉（kra）或盧沃（luvo）的靈。他是保護者、守護者和引導者。人們向他獻祭，主要是獻上禽鳥，並將一些血與棕櫚油混合，塗抹在額頭上。奧洛里帶來好運，因此有諺語說：是奧洛里使頭的主人興旺，而非河岸上的螃蟹。奧洛里的象徵是半個綴滿貝幣的葫蘆。

passages.text: Ipin-ijeun, or ipin-ojeun (ipin, share, portion; ijeun, act of eating; hence he who shares in the food), is perhaps considered the most important of the three indwelling spirits, but as he shares in all that the man eats, he has no special sacrifice offered to him. A proverb says: There is no orisha like the stomach; it receives food every day. In some respects hunger (ebi) seems to be personified, and to be considered the agent of Ipin-ijeun; for he is said to communicate to the man, by pinching his stomach, the desire of his principal for food. Ipori, the great toe, is the least important of the three guardian spirits, and sacrifice is rarely offered to him except when a man is about to set out on a journey, in which case he anoints the great toe with a mixture of fowl's blood and palm-oil; a proverb says, a waterfowl is not fit for the worship of Ipori.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VII (1894); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊平-伊傑溫（Ipin-ijeun），或伊平-奧傑溫（ipin-ojeun）（ipin，意即份額、部分；ijeun，意即進食的行為；因此指分享食物者），或許被視為三位內在之靈中最重要的一位，但由於他分享人所吃的一切，因此沒有專門為他獻上的祭品。有諺語說：沒有哪位奧里沙比得上肚子；它每天都領受食物。在某些方面，飢餓（ebi）似乎被擬人化了，並被視為伊平-伊傑溫的代理人；因為據說他藉由掐人的肚子，向人傳達他的主上對食物的渴望。伊波里（Ipori），即大腳趾，是三位守護靈中最不重要的一位，人們很少向他獻祭，除非有人即將啟程遠行，在這種情況下，他會用禽鳥之血與棕櫚油的混合物塗抹大腳趾；有諺語說：水鳥不適合用來崇拜伊波里。

passages.text: Curiously enough, Ipin-ijeun is connected with fire-worship. There is among the Yorubas no god of fire, but fire (ina) was probably once personified, for it is still spoken of as Abanigbele, the Inmate. The natives explain the connection between the two by saying that fire is necessary for the preparation of food, and food is necessary to Ipin-ijeun; therefore he takes fire under his protection, and takes care that it is not extinguished. A proverbial saying runs: Ipin-ijeun does not allow fire to depart from the earth. When fire could only be produced by the tedious process of rubbing together two sticks, it was no doubt important to keep one or two embers of a fire always smouldering.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VII (1894); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 說來奇怪，伊平-伊傑溫與火崇拜有關。約魯巴人之中沒有火神，但火（ina）從前很可能曾被擬人化，因為它至今仍被稱為阿巴尼格貝萊（Abanigbele），即「內居者」。當地人解釋這兩者之間的關聯時說，火是準備食物所必需的，而食物是伊平-伊傑溫所必需的；因此他將火置於自己的保護之下，並留心使它不致熄滅。有一句諺語說：伊平-伊傑溫不許火離開大地。當火只能藉由將兩根木棍相互摩擦這種費時的過程來產生時，讓一兩塊火炭始終悶燒著，無疑是重要的。

title.en: Ipo-Oku, the Land of the Dead Beneath the Earth
title.zh: 伊波-奧庫——地下的亡者之國

region.en: Yoruba under-world (symbolic pin: beneath the burial floor of a compound near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴冥界（象徵定位：伊費近郊院落葬地之下）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1894 (Ellis)

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. VII

summary.en: The ghost-man, or soul, is called Iwun or Okan — the latter also means heart — or Ojiji, ghost, shade or shadow. After the death of the body the ghost-man goes to Ipo-Oku, the Land of the Dead, which is beneath the earth, and where each man does that which he has been accustomed to do and holds the same social position as he did in the world. To enable the ghost to reach this land it is essential that the prescribed funeral rites be performed over him; should they be omitted, the ghost wanders about the world, cold, hungry and homeless, and runs the risk of being seized by some of the evil spirits which roam about the earth in great numbers and cast by them into Orun-apadi, the unseen world of potsherds, an uncomfortable place like a pottery furnace, heaped up with charcoal and the debris of broken earthen pots. Funeral rites cannot be performed at the moment breath leaves the body, but as an earnest of their intention, and to prevent the evil spirits from seizing the ghost, the relations at once offer a sacrifice to propitiate them; and when the corpse is buried, a fowl called Adire-iranna, the fowl that buys the road — that is, that opens a right of way — is sacrificed.
summary.zh: 亡魂稱「伊烏恩」或「奧坎」——後者亦意為「心」——或稱「奧吉吉」，鬼影、陰影。身死之後，亡魂便往「伊波-奧庫」——地下之亡者國度；在那裡人人各行其平生所業，身位一如陽世。欲使亡魂抵達彼國，必得為他行足額的葬儀；若缺其禮，亡魂便在人間流浪，又冷又餓無家可歸，還可能被遍地的惡靈捉住，擲入「奧倫-阿帕迪」——碎陶的冥府，一處如陶窯般難受的地方，堆滿木炭與破陶碎瓦。斷氣之頃固不能行葬儀，但為表誠意、防惡靈攔魂，親屬隨即獻祭以慰之；下葬之際，必殺一隻名為「阿迪雷-伊蘭納」的雞——「買路之雞」，為亡魂開闢通行之路。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1894; the Yoruba Land-of-the-Dead geography, with the Orun-apadi potsherd hell paralleling Johnson's (yoruba-orun-apadi-potsherds). Ellis's grave-word etymology: iboji, place of the ghost.

passages.text: The ghost-man, or soul, the vehicle of individual personal existence, is called Iwun, or Okan, but the latter also means heart. Another word is Ojiji, which has the meanings of ghost, shade, or shadow. After the death of the body, the ghost-man goes to Ipo-Oku, the Land of the Dead (Ipo, place; Oku, dead), which is beneath the earth, and where each man does that which he has been accustomed to do, and holds the same social position as he did in the world. To enable the ghost to reach this land it is essential that he should have the prescribed funeral rites performed over him. Should they be omitted, the ghost wanders about the world, cold, hungry, and homeless, and he runs the risk of being seized by some of the evil spirits which roam about the earth in great numbers, and cast by them into Orun-apadi, the unseen world of potsherds, an uncomfortable place like a pottery furnace, heaped up with charcoal and the debris of broken earthen pots.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VII (1894); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 幽靈人，或稱靈魂，即個體人格存在之載體，名為Iwun，或Okan，然後者亦指心。另一詞為Ojiji，兼有幽靈、陰影或影子之意。肉身死後，幽靈人前往Ipo-Oku，即死者之地（Ipo，地方；Oku，死者），此地在地下，每人在彼處行其生前慣行之事，並保有其於世間之相同社會地位。為使幽靈得以抵達此地，必須為其舉行規定之喪葬儀式。若省略此等儀式，幽靈便於世間遊蕩，寒冷、飢餓且無家可歸，並有被大量漫遊於大地之惡靈攫取之險，且被彼等投入Orun-apadi，即不可見之陶片世界，一處如陶窯般不適之地，堆滿木炭與破碎陶罐之殘骸。

passages.text: Funeral rites cannot, of course, be performed at the moment that breath leaves the body, but as an earnest of their intention to perform them, and to prevent the evil spirits from seizing the ghost, the relations at once offer a sacrifice to propitiate them; and when the corpse is buried, a fowl, called Adire-iranna, the fowl that buys the road, that is, that opens a right of way, is sacrificed. The dead often return to earth, and are born again in the families to which they belonged in their former life; in fact, one might say that they always return, since every mother sends for a babalawo to tell her what ancestral ghost has animated her new-born child.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VII (1894); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 喪葬儀式自不能在氣息離體之剎那舉行，然為表明其舉行儀式之意願，並防止惡靈攫取幽靈，親屬立即獻祭以安撫彼等；及至屍體下葬，則獻祭一雞，名為Adire-iranna，即買路之雞，亦即開闢通行權之雞。死者常返回人間，並於其前生所屬之家族中重生；事實上，可謂彼等總是返回，因每位母親皆遣人請babalawo告知她，是何祖先幽靈賦靈於其新生之子。

title.en: The Four Days of the Week That Odudua Inspired
title.zh: 奧杜杜瓦啟示的四日之週

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the market-day round around Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費周邊的集市輪迴）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910 (Dennett)

source.work: R. E. Dennett, Nigerian Studies (London, 1910), ch. VI

summary.en: Upon asking people who first gave the days of the week their names, Dennett was always told that Odudua inspired them. The four days of the Yoruba week are: Jakuta's day, looked upon as a Sunday, on which they clean their houses and rub their floors and split kola for the Orishas Shango, Yemoja, Oshun and Buruku; Obatala's day, sometimes called Orishala, on which they rub the walls and floors, fill a pot of water on the altar and give part of their food to him — the white Orishas (Ijaiyi, Iluofun, Ogiyan and the rest) are worshipped on this day, appealed to by barren women, and must not be offered palm oil or pepper; Awo, Ifa's day, on which the Ifa priests renew the chalk marks on the ground in front of the altars, and Oshun and Odu are also consulted; and Odudua's or Ogun's day — when they build, clear a farm, cut a tree or hunt they split kola to Ogun, and Ija and Oshowsi are also worshipped. Odudua representing the creation, it is quite natural that they should consider her day as first in their week; the first, the fifth, the ninth and the seventeenth days, which they look upon as the beginning of a new month, are sacred to Odudua, and are all market days.
summary.zh: 問起誰首先為一週諸日命名，人們總答：是奧杜杜瓦啟示的。約魯巴一週四日：一為賈庫塔之日——視同主日，家家清屋擦地，為尚戈、耶莫雅、奧舜與布魯庫剖柯拉果；二為奧巴塔拉之日（或稱奧里夏拉）——擦牆抹地、壇上盛水、分食於神——白衣諸神（伊賈伊伊、伊盧奧芬、奧吉揚等）於此日受拜，不孕婦女特來祈求，祭之不得用棕櫚油與胡椒；三為「阿沃」——伊法之日，伊法祭司是日為諸壇前的地畫更新白堊符記，奧舜與奧杜亦於此日求問；四為奧杜杜瓦（即奧貢）之日——建屋、墾荒、伐木、狩獵之時皆向奧貢剖果，伊賈與奧肖西亦同日受拜。奧杜杜瓦代表創造，其日居一週之首自是理所當然；每月之第一、第五、第九、第十七日——他們視為新月的開端——皆為奧杜杜瓦聖日，也都是集市之日。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910; the four-day ritual week with Odudua's creative priority. Cross-ref: yoruba-four-gods-four-quarters (Frobenius's five-day and compass analysis).

passages.text: Upon asking people the question, who first gave the days of the week their names? I have always been told that Odudua inspired them. The four days of the Yoruba week, then, are: Jakuta's day, which is looked upon as a Sunday. On this day they clean their houses, and rub their floors. Then they split Kola for the Orishas Shango, Yemoja, Oshun and Buruku. Obatala's day, sometimes called Orishala. On this day they rub the walls and floor of the houses, and fill a pot of water on the altar; and when they eat they give part of their food to him. The following white Orishas are worshipped on this day: Ijaiyi, Iluofun, Ijemoiwi, Ogiyan, Alajugun, Owa Olufon. These white Orishas are appealed to by barren women, and they must not be offered palm oil or pepper.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. VI (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當向人們詢問，是誰最先為一週各日命名？我總是被告知是Odudua啟示了它們。那麼，約魯巴一週之四日為：Jakuta之日，被視為星期日。此日他們清潔房屋，擦拭地板。然後他們為Orishas Shango、Yemoja、Oshun與Buruku剖開可樂果。Obatala之日，有時稱為Orishala。此日他們擦拭房屋之牆壁與地板，並在祭壇上注滿一壺水；進食時，他們將部分食物分與他。此日受崇拜之白色Orishas如下：Ijaiyi、Iluofun、Ijemoiwi、Ogiyan、Alajugun、Owa Olufon。不孕之婦女向這些白色Orishas祈求，且不得向彼等獻上棕櫚油或胡椒。

passages.text: Awo, or Ifa's day. The people cannot consult Ifa except through a priest; in this way he is consulted about everything. On this day the Ifa priests renew the chalk marks on the ground in front of the altars; Oshun and Odu are also consulted on this day. Odudua's or Ogun's day: when they build, or clear a farm, or cut a tree, or hunt, they split kola to Ogun. Ija and Oshowsi are also worshipped on this day. Odudua representing the creation, it is quite natural that they should consider her day as first in their week. The first, the fifth, the ninth and seventeenth days, which they look upon as the beginning of a new month, are sacred to Odudua, and are all market days.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. VI (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: Awo，或Ifa之日。人們非經祭司不能請教Ifa；他們以此方式就一切事請教他。此日Ifa祭司更新祭壇前地上之粉筆記號；Oshun與Odu亦於此日受請教。Odudua或Ogun之日：當他們建造、開墾農地、砍樹或狩獵時，他們為Ogun剖開可樂果。Ija與Oshowsi亦於此日受崇拜。Odudua代表創世，故他們將其日視為一週之首，實屬自然。第一、第五、第九與第十七日，即他們視為新月之始者，為Odudua之聖日，且皆為市集日。

title.en: Idena's Staff and the Quartz Crocodiles
title.zh: 伊德納之杖與石英鱷像

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the Idena square and its enclosures)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（伊德納廣場及周邊聖區）

period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910-12 (Frobenius)

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XIV

summary.en: On the Idena square of Ife stand waist-high stone pillars, roughly hewn and absolutely bare of detail; nearby, amid the weeds and fallen thatch, rises a stone image thirty-two inches high with a chain round its neck and an apron skirt, and behind it the first of the stone-stools and a dish made out of quartz — a four-square block chiselled hollow above, standing on a raised ring, and ornamented at the side with lizards: these ancient stone saucers show indications of originally being basket-work developed in wood-carving and transferred finally to sculpture in stone. In the next enclosure stands the granite statue of the Idena himself, thirty-six inches high, thick-lipped and broad-nosed, with a tassel of hair hanging from its left ear — its hair represented by little iron pegs inserted in small holes, the first instance of this singular use of iron. Before the Idena's tooth-stone or obelisk lie the pieces of a long stone slab, broken in four, which the natives call the broken buckler of the Idena; and in the last enclosure a stone crocodile stands to right and left in front of drop-stones — crocodiles of quartz, one of them still worshipped in a private compound.
summary.zh: 伊費的伊德納廣場上立著齊腰高的粗石柱，鑿工粗糙、細節全無；近處雜草斷茅之間立著一尊三十二吋高的石像，頸掛鏈環、腰繫圍裙；其後是石凳與一件石英淺皿——方形石塊，上面鑿出凹槽，下有環足承托，側面飾以蜥蜴：這些古石皿尚存籃編工藝的痕跡——由草編而木刻、終至石雕的演變一目了然。隔區立著伊德納本人的花崗石像，高三十六吋，厚唇闊鼻，左耳垂著一縷髮束——頭髮竟以細小的鐵釘插入小孔表現，鐵的這種用法在此屬首次得見。伊德納的「齒石」（獨石柱）前橫臥一條斷成四截的長石板，土人稱之為「伊德納的破盾」；末區的聖物園中，兩尊石英鱷像左右分立於水滴形聖石之前——其中一尊至今仍在一戶私宅中受人祭拜。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910-12; the Idena complex of monoliths, quartz work and crocodile effigies, with Frobenius's craft-evolution reading reported as his interpretation.

passages.text: When, on leaving the main road, we arrive at the first small palm plantation, a group of quite coarse little pillars of stone about waist-high come into view; they are angular, roundish, and, at all events, roughly hewn or chipped off, absolutely bare of any detail. Going forward we come to another enclosure: here there is a wilderness of weeds, a mass of roof lattens and the straw of a collapsed thatch, amidst which rises a stone image about thirty-two inches high, roughly executed and defaced. It has one chain round its neck and another hangs over an apron skirt down to the hands folded over its stomach.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIV (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當我們離開大路，抵達第一片小棕櫚園時，一組相當粗糙、約及腰高之小石柱映入眼簾；它們有稜有角、略呈圓形，無論如何皆經粗略鑿削或敲落，全然不帶任何細節。繼續前行，我們來到另一處圍地：此處雜草叢生，一片屋頂板條與坍塌茅草屋頂之稻草，其中矗立一尊約三十二英寸高之石像，雕工粗糙且已磨損。其頸上繞有一鏈，另一鏈懸於圍裙之上，垂至交疊於腹部之雙手。

passages.text: Behind it I found the first of the stone-stools, and a dish made out of quartz: this, the first specimen of quartz work I had seen, was a four-square block whose upper surface had been chiselled to a depth of about one and a quarter inches, while the lower one had a raised ring on which it stood. All three stone-saucer specimens known to me were ornamented at the side with lizards. These ancient Ilifian stone saucers show indications of originally being basket work, developed in wood carving and transferred finally to sculpture in stone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIV (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在其後，我發現了第一個石凳，以及一隻以石英製成之盤：此乃我所見之第一件石英製品，為一方形石塊，其上表面被鑿至約一又四分之一英寸深，而下表面則有一凸起之環，供其立於其上。我所知悉之三件石碟標本，側面皆飾有蜥蜴。這些古老的Ilifian石碟顯示出最初為籃編工藝之跡象，後發展為木雕，最終轉移至石雕。

passages.text: In the next enclosure was a stone statue of the Idena, a granite figure about thirty-six inches high above ground-level, exactly like the other figure with folded hands over the belly, aproned and ornately tasselled on its left; it has armlets, and a ruff-like ornament round its neck. The interesting part of the Idena is most decidedly its head, which had been knocked off and only insecurely replaced: the thick-lipped, broad-nosed face is negroid in type. A long lock or tassel of hair, missing on the right, hangs down from its left ear. The treatment of the hair in this granite head is especially of the very greatest interest: the hair is represented by little iron pegs, inserted in small holes. We here for the first time come upon this singular use of iron.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIV (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在下一重圍欄中，有一尊伊德納（Idena）的石像，是一尊高出地面約三十六吋的花崗岩人像，與另一尊人像完全相同，雙手交疊於腹前，左側圍著圍裙，並飾有華麗的流蘇；它戴著臂環，頸上有一圈狀似皺領的飾物。伊德納最引人入勝之處，無疑是它的頭部，那頭部曾被擊落，只是不牢固地重新接上：厚唇、寬鼻的面容屬於尼格羅人種的類型。一綹長髮或髮纓自其左耳垂下，右側則已缺失。這顆花崗岩頭部對頭髮的處理方式尤其令人極感興趣：頭髮是以插入小孔中的小鐵釘來表現的。我們在此首次遇到這種奇特的鐵的用途。

passages.text: In front of the Idena's tooth-stone or obelisk are the pieces of a long, narrow stone slab, fairly thin and of rough workmanship; it lies prone, broken in four pieces, with evidence of six or perhaps more holes having been bored into it at equal distances in its longitudinal axis. The natives call these particular fragments the broken buckler of the Idena. In a carelessly constructed hut at the fourth and last Idena enclosure, symmetrically placed, there is a stone crocodile to right and left in front of a stone block artificially rounded, set on end — drop-stones, varying but little in shape between a drop, an egg or an onion. One of the crocodiles made of quartz we dug up in Modeke; one, still worshipped in a private compound, is somewhat smaller.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIV (1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在伊德納的齒石或方尖碑之前，有一塊狹長石板碎裂成的數塊殘片，石板相當薄，做工粗糙；它平臥於地，斷成四塊，其上可見沿縱軸等距鑽有六個、或許更多孔洞的痕跡。當地人稱這些特定的殘片為伊德納的破盾。在第四重、也是最後一重伊德納圍欄中一座搭建草率的小屋裡，對稱地安置著一條石鱷魚，位於一塊人工磨圓、豎立而置的石塊前方左右兩側——這些是墜石，形狀差異不大，或如水滴，或如蛋，或如洋蔥。其中一條以石英製成的鱷魚，是我們在莫德凱（Modeke）掘出的；另一條至今仍在一處私人宅院中受崇拜，體型略小一些。

title.en: The Witch Who Rose to the Moon
title.zh: 登月的女巫

region.en: Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦

period: Collected by Daniel G. Brinton from a native woman (recorded by Dr. Berendt); published 1894

source.work: Daniel G. Brinton, The Folk-Lore of Yucatan, in Maya Religion and Mythology (congress papers collection)

summary.en: A man marries a woman without knowing she is a witch. One night she slips out; he follows with his axe to a moonlit meadow and hides in the shade of a great ceiba. She strips off her garments, then strips off her skin, and remains mere bones; then she rises to the sky. Coming down again she asks: 'Wouldst thou reach to the sky?' But she cannot ascend again — because of the throwing of the salt he had ordered mixed.
summary.zh: 一男子娶妻而不知其為女巫。一夜她悄然外出；他持斧尾隨至月光皎潔的草地，匿於大木棉樹蔭之下。她褪去衣衫，繼而剝去其皮，僅餘骸骨；隨即昇天。重返之際她問：「你要上到天上嗎？」然而她再也上不去了——因為他先前命她調和的那把鹽。

sensitivity.note: Nineteenth-century Yucatec folk-lore collection; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: A man married with a woman; not did he know her as a witch. One day he said to her: 'Mix two measures of salt.' One night the man woke and he saw go out his wife. Then he took his axe and secretly followed behind her to the wood. When they arrived at a little meadow, there being a bright moon, then hid himself the man in the shade of a great ceiba tree.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan (from Berendt's manuscript); not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 一個男人娶了一個女人；他並不知道她是女巫。有一天他對她說：『量兩份鹽。』某夜男人醒來，看見妻子走了出去。於是他拿起斧頭，悄悄跟在她後面進了樹林。他們來到一片小草地，當時月光明亮，男人便藏身於一棵巨大的吉貝樹的陰影中。

passages.text: Then threw her garments the woman behind her, standing naked in the face of the moon: then she stripped off her skin, and remained mere bones. Then she rose to the sky. When she came down again, then she said to him: 'Wouldst thou reach to the sky?' But not could she ascend again, because of the throwing of salt.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 接著女人把衣裳往身後一拋，赤裸地站在月光下：然後她剝下自己的皮，只剩下骨頭。接著她升上天空。當她再下來時，便對他說：『你可想升到天上去？』但她再也無法升上去了，因為鹽被拋撒的緣故。

title.en: The Balams: Four Guardians of the Town
title.zh: 巴拉姆：鎮上的四方守護者

region.en: Tihosuco, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦蒂霍蘇科

period: Recorded from Licentiate Zetina of Tihosuco by Brinton, late 19th c.

source.work: Daniel G. Brinton, The Folk-Lore of Yucatan

summary.en: The Balams are very ancient men who take charge of and guard the towns: one stands north, a second south, a third east, a fourth west. Invisible by day, they are awake and vigilant at night, preventing violent rains, tornadoes, and pestilence. They summon each other by a loud shrill whistle and fly through the air with the swiftness of a bird; the signs of their nocturnal struggles with evil powers are seen next day in trees broken down and great stones split and thrown around.
summary.zh: 巴拉姆乃極古老的老人，司掌並守護鎮邑：一位立於北方，一位南方，一位東方，一位西方。晝間隱形，夜間警醒，防範暴雨、龍捲與瘟疫。他們以尖銳嘯聲相互召喚，飛行如鳥之疾；其與邪祟夜戰之跡，次日見於折斷之樹與迸裂四散的巨石。

sensitivity.note: Living Yucatec belief recorded by Brinton; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: These beings are supposed to be certain very ancient men who take charge of and guard the towns. One stands north of the town, a second south, a third east, and the fourth to the west. They are usually not visible during the day, and if one does see them it is a sign of approaching illness. At night the Balams are awake and vigilant, and prevent many an accident from befalling the village, such as violent rains, tornadoes, and pestilential diseases.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 這些存在被認為是某些非常古老的人，他們負責掌管並守護城鎮。一個立於城鎮之北，第二個在南，第三個在東，第四個在西。他們白天通常不可見，若有人見到了他們，便是疾病將至的徵兆。夜間巴蘭（Balams）清醒而警覺，防止許多意外降臨村莊，諸如猛烈的暴雨、龍捲風和瘟疫。

passages.text: They summon each other by a loud, shrill whistle; and, though without wings, they fly through the air with the swiftness of a bird. Occasionally they have desperate conflicts with the evil powers who would assail the town. The signs of these nocturnal struggles are seen the next day in trees broken down and uprooted, the ground torn up, and large stones split and thrown around.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 他們以響亮而尖銳的哨聲互相召喚；而且，雖然沒有翅膀，他們卻以鳥一般的迅捷在空中飛行。偶爾他們會與那些想要侵襲城鎮的邪惡力量展開殊死搏鬥。這些夜間搏鬥的痕跡，次日可見於被折斷、連根拔起的樹木，被掀翻的地面，以及被劈裂、四散拋擲的大石。

title.en: The Balam Who Struck Lightning from His Cigar
title.zh: 自雪茄擊出閃電的巴拉姆

region.en: Near Tihosuco, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦蒂霍蘇科附近

period: Recorded from Licentiate Zetina by Brinton, late 19th c.

source.work: Daniel G. Brinton, The Folk-Lore of Yucatan

summary.en: An Indian near Tihosuco neglected the usual offering to the Balam at corn-planting. As the ears ripened he found a tall man among the stalks with a great basket, gathering the ears: 'I am here gathering in that which I sent.' Resting, the stranger took out an immense cigar and struck a light with flint and steel — but the sparks were flashes of lightning, and the blows terrible thunderclaps that shook the earth. The Indian fell unconscious with terror; when he came to himself a hailstorm had destroyed his corn, and at home a fever seized him which nigh cost his life.
summary.zh: 蒂霍蘇科附近一位印第安人播種時忘了給巴拉姆奉上常祭。玉米將熟，他到田間查看，見一人立於稈間，肩負大籃，正疾速摘取玉米穗：「我來收我送出去的東西。」那人歇手，自袋中取出一支巨大雪茄，以火石取火——火星竟是閃電，擊聲竟是撼地的雷霆。印第安人嚇昏倒地；醒來時冰雹已毀其玉米，到家又染重病，幾乎喪命。

sensitivity.note: Living Yucatec belief recorded by Brinton; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: An Indian near Tihosuco had paid no attention to the usual offering, perhaps being infected with evil modern sceptical views. His crop grew fairly; and as the ears were about ripening he visited his field to examine them. As he approached he saw with some dismay a tall man among the stalks with a large basket over his shoulders, in which he threw the ripening ears as fast as he could pluck them. The Indian saluted him hesitatingly. The stranger replied, 'I am here gathering in that which I sent.'
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 提霍蘇科附近的一名印第安人沒有理會慣常的獻祭，或許是受了現代邪惡懷疑論觀點的感染。他的莊稼長得還算不錯；待到玉米穗快要成熟時，他到田裡去察看。走近時，他有些驚愕地看見禾稈之間站著一個高大的人，肩上背著一隻大籃子，正把成熟的玉米穗盡快地摘下扔進籃裡。那印第安人遲疑地向他一聲招呼。那陌生人答道：「我來這裡收取我所派出的東西。」

passages.text: Resting from his work, he drew from his pocket an immense cigar; and, taking out a flint and steel, began to strike a light. But the sparks he struck were flashes of lightning, and the sound of his blows was terrible thunderclaps which shook the very earth. The poor Indian fell to the ground unconscious with terror; and when he came to himself a hail-storm had destroyed his corn, and as soon as he reached home he himself was seized with a fever which nigh cost him his life.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 他歇了歇手，從口袋裡掏出一支巨大的雪茄；又取出火石與火鋼，開始打火。但他打出的火星是閃電，敲擊之聲是可怕的霹靂，震得大地都為之搖動。那可憐的印第安人驚恐之下昏倒在地；等他甦醒過來，一場冰雹已經毀了他的玉米，而他一回到家，自己便發起高燒，幾乎喪了性命。

title.en: Shooting Stars Are the Stumps of Cigars
title.zh: 流星乃神靈拋下的菸蒂

region.en: Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦

period: Recorded by Brinton, late 19th c.

source.work: Daniel G. Brinton, The Folk-Lore of Yucatan

summary.en: The Balams are great smokers, and it is a general belief among the Indians that the shooting stars are nothing else than the stumps of the huge cigars thrown down the sky by these giant beings.
summary.zh: 巴拉姆皆善抽菸；印第安人普遍相信：流星無他，正是這些巨靈拋向天空下方的巨大雪茄菸蒂。

sensitivity.note: Living Yucatec belief recorded by Brinton; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: The Balams are great smokers, and it is a general belief among the Indians that the shooting stars are nothing else than the stumps of the huge cigars thrown down the sky by these giant beings. For this reason the Indians look on falling stars with awe, as tokens that the balams are still keeping watch over the land by night.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 巴蘭們都是大煙鬼，印第安人普遍相信，流星不是別的，正是這些巨人從天上扔下來的巨大雪茄的煙蒂。因此，印第安人懷著敬畏之心看待隕星，視之為巴蘭們夜間仍在守望大地的徵兆。

title.en: The Balam Who Took the Boy of San Pedro
title.zh: 聖佩德羅島上擄走男孩的巴拉姆

region.en: Isla de San Pedro (Ambergris Cay), Belize
region.zh: 貝里斯安伯格里斯礁（聖佩德羅島）

period: Told to Dr. Berendt on the east coast of Yucatan; recorded by Brinton

source.work: Daniel G. Brinton, The Folk-Lore of Yucatan

summary.en: When Dr. Berendt was exploring the east coast of Yucatan he was told of such an occurrence on the Island of San Pedro, north of Belize. A little boy of four years wandered to some cacao bushes not more than fifty yards from the house, and there all trace of him was lost. There was no sign of wolf or tiger, no footprint of kidnapper. They sought him the whole day in vain, and then gave up the search, for they knew what had happened — the Balam had taken him.
summary.zh: 貝倫特醫生探勘猶加敦東岸時，聞於貝里斯以北之聖佩德羅島：一名四歲男孩走至離屋不足五十步的可可樹叢，從此無蹤。既無虎狼之跡，亦無擄者足印。眾人終日搜尋無果，遂罷——因他們知道發生了什麼：巴拉姆把他帶走了。

sensitivity.note: Living Yucatec belief recorded by Brinton; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: When Dr. Berendt was exploring the east coast of Yucatan he was told of such an occurrence on the Island of San Pedro, north of Belize. A little boy of four years wandered to some cacao bushes not more than fifty yards from the house, and there all trace of him was lost. There was no sign of wolf or tiger, no footprint of kidnapper. They sought him the whole day in vain, and then gave up the search, for they knew what had happened — the Balam had taken him!
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 貝倫特博士在探索尤卡坦東海岸時，聽人說起貝里斯以北的聖佩德羅島上發生過這樣一件事。一個四歲的小男孩走到離屋子不過五十碼遠的一些可可樹叢裡，就在那裡失去了他的一切蹤跡。既沒有狼或虎的痕跡，也沒有綁架者的腳印。他們找了他一整天，一無所獲，於是便放棄了搜尋，因為他們知道出了什麼事——巴蘭把他帶走了！

title.en: The Four Blows of Father Balam
title.zh: 巴拉姆之父的四記鞭撻

region.en: Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦

period: Recorded from Licentiate Zetina by Brinton, late 19th c.

source.work: Daniel G. Brinton, The Folk-Lore of Yucatan

summary.en: An Indian and his wife went to their corn-patch; the man left to fetch water, and the woman threw off her gown lest it be torn. Suddenly she heard a loud voice: 'Tapa ta culo, gran diablo!' and received two smart blows with a cane. She turned and beheld a tall man with a long beard and a gown reaching to his feet — the Balam. He gave her two more blows and disappeared; but the marks of the four blows remained as long as she lived.
summary.zh: 一對夫婦往玉米田收穗；丈夫取水去了，妻子恐撕破衣衫而脫之。忽聞大聲喝斥，並挨了藤杖兩下。回首見一高個男子，長髯曳袍——正是巴拉姆。他又加兩記鞭撻而消失；那四道鞭痕伴其終身。

sensitivity.note: Living Yucatec belief recorded by Brinton; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: One day an Indian and his wife went to their corn-patch to gather ears. The man left the field to get some water, and his wife threw off the gown she wore lest it should be torn, and was naked. Suddenly she heard some one call to her in a loud voice, and at the same time she received two smart blows with a cane. She turned and beheld a tall man with a long beard, and a gown which reached to his feet. This was the Balam.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 有一天，一個印第安人和他的妻子到他們的玉米地去收玉米穗。男人離開田地去找水，他的妻子怕衣服被扯破，便脫下身上穿的長袍，赤身裸體。忽然，她聽見有人高聲呼喚她，同時挨了兩下重重的杖打。她轉過身來，看見一個高大的人，蓄著長鬚，身穿一件垂到腳面的長袍。這就是巴蘭。

passages.text: He gave her two more smart blows, and then disappeared; but the marks of the four blows remained as long as she lived. The balam is esteemed a kindly and protective being, affectionately referred to as yum balam, Father Balam; he is said to have a human form, that of an old man with a long beard and ample flowing robes.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 他又重重地打了她兩下，然後便消失了；但那四下杖打的痕跡卻伴隨了她一生。巴蘭被視為一位仁慈而護佑的神靈，人們親切地稱他為「尤姆·巴蘭」，即巴蘭父；據說他具有人形，是一位蓄著長鬚、身披寬大飄逸長袍的老人。

title.en: Here Comes the Mighty Wind of the Great Father
title.zh: 大父之偉風將至

region.en: Forests of Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦森林

period: Told to Dr. Berendt in the forests; recorded by Brinton

source.work: Daniel G. Brinton, The Folk-Lore of Yucatan

summary.en: Dr. Berendt was travelling with some natives through the forests when the sound of a tropical tornado was heard approaching with its formidable roar through the trees. In awe-struck accents one of his guides said: 'He cutal nohoch yikal nohoch tat' — Here comes the mighty wind of the Great Father. The whistling of the wind is attributed to tat acmo, Father Strong-bird: the primeval bird, at once lord of the winds and father of the race.
summary.zh: 貝倫特醫生與土人穿行林中，忽聞龍捲之聲挾巨響自林間滾滾而來。其一嚮導驚惶低語：「大父的偉風來了。」風之嘯鳴被歸於「塔特·阿克莫」——強鳥之父：即既是風主又是族祖的原初之鳥。

sensitivity.note: Living Yucatec belief recorded by Brinton; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: One day Dr. Berendt was travelling with some natives through the forests when the sound of a tropical tornado was heard approaching with its formidable roar through the trees. In awe-struck accents one of his guides said: 'He cutal nohoch yikal nohoch tat' — Here comes the mighty wind of the Great Father.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 有一天，貝倫特博士與幾名原住民一同穿越森林，忽然聽見一陣熱帶旋風的聲響，伴隨著駭人的呼嘯聲穿林而來。他的一名嚮導以滿懷敬畏的語氣說道：「He cutal nohoch yikal nohoch tat」——大父的強風來了。

passages.text: It is only in an unguarded moment that in the presence of a white man the Indian betrays his beliefs. A hint is supplied by Senor Zetina: the whistling of the wind is called, or attributed to, tat acmo, words which mean Father Strong-bird — the notion of the primeval bird, at once lord of the winds and father of the race.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 印第安人只有在不經意的時刻，才會在白人面前流露自己的信仰。塞蒂納先生提供了一條線索：風的呼嘯聲被稱為，或被歸因於 tat acmo，這幾個字的意思是「強鳥之父」——即那原始之鳥的觀念，牠既是風之主，又是種族之父。

title.en: Giant Grab: The Terror of Night Walkers
title.zh: 巨抓：夜行者的恐怖

region.en: Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦

period: Recorded by Brinton, late 19th c.

source.work: Daniel G. Brinton, The Folk-Lore of Yucatan

summary.en: There are other gigantic spectres of terrible aspect and truculent humour. One is so tall that a man cannot reach his knees. He stalks into the towns at midnight, and planting his feet like a huge Colossus, one on each side of the roadway, seizes some incautious passer-by and breaks his legs with his teeth. The name of this terror of late walkers is Giant Grab, Ua ua pach.
summary.zh: 世間尚有形貌可怖、性情暴烈的巨型幽靈。其一高不可及人之膝。午夜潛入鎮中，如巨像般分立於道之兩側，擒住不慎的過客，以齒折其腿。此夜行者之恐怖，名為「烏阿·烏阿·帕奇」——巨抓。

sensitivity.note: Living Yucatec belief recorded by Brinton; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: But there are other gigantic spectres of terrible aspect and truculent humour. One of these is so tall that a man cannot reach his knees. He stalks into the towns at midnight, and planting his feet like a huge Colossus, one on each side of the roadway, he seizes some incautious passer-by and breaks his legs with his teeth. The name of this terror of late walkers is Giant Grab, Ua ua pach.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 但還有其他面目可怖、性情兇暴的巨型幽靈。其中之一高得連一個人也搆不到牠的膝蓋。牠在午夜潛入城鎮，像巨大的巨像般把雙腳分踏在道路兩側，抓住某個不慎的路人，用牙齒咬斷他的雙腿。這個令夜行者恐懼的怪物名叫「巨抓」，Ua ua pach。

title.en: The Man of the Woods and the Laughing Escape
title.zh: 林中人與一笑脫身

region.en: Forests of Yucatan, Peten, and Tabasco
region.zh: 猶加敦、佩滕與塔巴斯科的森林

period: Recorded by Brinton and Dr. Berendt, late 19th c.

source.work: Daniel G. Brinton, The Folk-Lore of Yucatan

summary.en: The Che Vinic, the Man of the Woods, called by the Spanish population the Salonge, is a huge fellow without bones or joints. His feet are reversed, the heels in front; he is larger and stronger than a bull, and his colour is red; in his long arms he carries a stick the size of a tree-trunk. He is on the watch for those who stray through the woods and will seize and devour them. But the ready-witted man plucks a green branch and, waving it before him, begins a lively dance: the Wood Man falls into convulsions of mirth and, having no joints, cannot rise once he has fallen to the ground.
summary.zh: 林中人——西班牙人稱為薩隆赫——是一個無骨無節的巨漢。其足反向，腳跟在前；比公牛更大更強，色紅；長臂之中握一根樹幹般的木棍。他伏候迷途於林中之人，擒而食之。然而機智者摘一青枝，在面前揮舞，歡快起舞：林中人笑得前仰後合，倒地不起——因為他無骨無節，跌倒便再也爬不起來。

sensitivity.note: Living Yucatec/Peten belief recorded by Brinton; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: Another is the Che Vinic, the Man of the Woods, called by the Spanish population the Salonge. He is a huge fellow without bones or joints. For that reason if he lies down he cannot rise without extreme difficulty; hence he sleeps leaning against a tree. His feet are reversed, the heels in front, the toes behind. He is larger and stronger than a bull, and his colour is red. In his long arms he carries a stick the size of a tree-trunk. He is on the watch for those who stray through the woods, and, if he can, will seize and devour them.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 另一個是 Che Vinic，即「林中之人」，西班牙居民稱之為 Salonge。牠是個沒有骨頭、沒有關節的龐然大物。正因如此，牠一旦躺下，便極難起身；所以牠總是靠著樹睡覺。牠的雙腳是反的，腳跟在前，腳趾在後。牠比公牛更大更強壯，顏色是紅的。牠在長臂中拿著一根樹幹般粗大的棍子。牠守候著那些在林中迷途的人，若能得手，便抓住他們並吞食。

passages.text: But a ready-witted man has always a means of escape. All he has to do is to pluck a green branch from a tree, and waving it before him begin a lively dance. This invariably throws the Wood Man into convulsions of mirth. He laughs and laughs until he falls to the ground, and once down, having no joints, he cannot rise, and the hunter can proceed leisurely on his journey. It is singular how widely distributed is the belief in this strange fancy: it recurs in precisely the same form in Yucatan, in Peten, in Tabasco, around Palenque.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 但機智的人總有脫身之法。他只需從樹上折下一根綠枝，在牠面前揮舞，並開始跳起活潑的舞蹈。這總會讓林中之人笑得前仰後合。牠笑個不停，直到倒在地上，而一旦倒下，由於沒有關節，牠便無法起身，獵人便可從容繼續上路。這種奇特想像的信仰流傳之廣，實在罕見：它在尤卡坦、佩滕、塔巴斯科以及帕倫克一帶，都以完全相同的形式出現。

title.en: The Aluxes: The Strong Clay Images
title.zh: 阿盧希：黏土小人之靈

region.en: Old temples and tombs of Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦古廟與古墓

period: Recorded by Brinton, late 19th c.

source.work: Daniel G. Brinton, The Folk-Lore of Yucatan

summary.en: The most common of the dwarfs and imps are the aluxes, the 'strong clay images': they are believed to be the actual idols and figures in clay found about the old temples and tombs, hence an Indian breaks these in pieces whenever he finds them. They only appear after sunset, in the shape of a child of three or four years, or sometimes not over a span in height, naked except for a large hat. They are swift of foot, and can run backwards as fast as forwards; their touch produces sickness, especially chills and fever.
summary.zh: 矮人與精怪之中，最常見者為阿盧希——「強力的黏土像」：人信其即古廟古墓旁的黏土神像本身，故印第安人凡見必碎之。它們日落后方現，形如三四歲孩童，或高不逾一拃，赤身而戴大帽。其足迅捷，倒行與正行同速；觸之則致病，尤生寒熱。

sensitivity.note: Living Yucatec belief recorded by Brinton; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: In contrast to the giants are the dwarfs and imps which are ready in their malicious ways to sour the pleasures of life. The most common of these are the aluxes, or more fully Kloxkatob, which means 'the strong clay images'. They are, indeed, believed to be the actual idols and figures in clay which are found about the old temples and tombs, and hence an Indian breaks these in pieces whenever he finds them.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 與巨人相對的是矮人和小鬼，牠們慣以惡意的手段破壞生活的樂趣。其中最常見的是 aluxes，更完整的稱法是 Kloxkatob，意為「堅固的泥像」。人們確實相信，牠們就是古廟與古墓附近所發現的泥製偶像與人像，因此印第安人一發現這些東西，便會把它們打碎。

passages.text: They only appear after sunset, and then in the shape of a child of three or four years, or sometimes not over a span in height, naked except wearing a large hat. They are swift of foot, and can run backwards as fast as forwards. Among other pranks, they throw stones at the dogs and cause them to howl. Their touch produces sickness, especially chills and fever. It is best, therefore, not to attempt to catch them.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 他們只在日落之後出現，且以三四歲孩童的形貌現身，有時身高不過一拃，赤裸著身子，只戴著一頂大帽子。他們腳程迅捷，倒退奔跑與向前奔跑一樣快。除了其他種種惡作劇，他們還向狗扔石頭，惹得狗兒嚎叫。凡被他們觸碰便會生病，尤其是發冷發熱。因此，最好不要試圖去捉他們。

title.en: X Tabai, the Deceiver of the Shady Bowers
title.zh: 希·塔拜：綠蔭深處的惑人女

region.en: Forests of Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦森林

period: Recorded by Brinton, late 19th c.

source.work: Daniel G. Brinton, The Folk-Lore of Yucatan

summary.en: The female sex is further represented in the Maya folk-lore by a personage who has a curious similarity to legendary ladies of the old world — sirens, mermaids, the Lorelei. She is called X Tabai, the (female) Deceiver. Her home is under shady bowers in the forests, and there the ardent hunter suddenly espies her, naked, combing her long and beautiful hair. As he approaches she turns and flees — not with discouraging haste, but with such backward glances as to invite pursuit. Just as he clasps her in his embrace, her body changes into a thorny bush, and her feet become claws like those of a wild fowl; torn and bleeding, he turns sadly homeward and soon succumbs to fever with delirium.
summary.zh: 馬雅民俗中另有一位與舊世界傳說女子——塞壬、美人魚、羅蕾萊——驚人相似的人物：希·塔拜，「惑人的女欺詐者」。她棲於林中綠蔭深處；熱切的獵人忽見其裸身梳理長髮。他走近，她轉身而逃——並非疾奔拒人，而是頻頻回眸引人追逐。正當他張臂擁她，其身化為荊棘之叢，其足化為野禽之爪；獵人遍體鱗傷，黯然歸家，不久即染熱病而譫妄。

sensitivity.note: Living Yucatec belief recorded by Brinton; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: The female sex is further represented in the Maya folk-lore by a personage who has a curious similarity to legendary ladies of the old world, sirens, mermaids, the Lorelei. She is called X Tabai, the (female) Deceiver. Her home is under shady bowers in the forests, and there the ardent hunter suddenly espies her, naked, and combing with a large comb her long and beautiful hair. As he approaches she turns and flees, but not with discouraging haste, rather in such a manner and with such backward glances as to invite pursuit.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 在馬雅民間傳說中，女性也由另一位人物來代表，她與舊世界的傳奇女子——塞壬、美人魚、羅蕾萊——有著奇特的相似之處。她名叫X Tabai，即（女）誘惑者。她的居所在森林中陰涼的樹蔭下，熱切的獵人會突然瞥見她赤裸著身子，正用一把大梳子梳理她那長而美麗的頭髮。當他走近時，她轉身逃走，但並非以令人氣餒的匆促，而是以那樣的方式、那樣頻頻回望，儼然是在邀請他追逐。

passages.text: He soon overtakes her, but just as he clasps her beauteous form in his strong embrace, her body changes into a thorny bush, and her feet become claws like those of a wild fowl. Torn and bleeding he turns sadly homeward, and soon succumbs to an attack of fever with delirium.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 他很快便追上她，但就在他以強壯的雙臂摟住她那美麗的身軀時，她的身體化作一叢荊棘，她的雙腳變成如野禽般的利爪。他遍體鱗傷、鮮血淋漓，悲傷地轉身回家，不久便因發燒並伴隨譫妄而倒下。

title.en: Miss Pound-the-Stones
title.zh: 擊石小姐

region.en: Villages of Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦村落

period: Recorded by Brinton, late 19th c.

source.work: Daniel G. Brinton, The Folk-Lore of Yucatan

summary.en: Another very similar creature is X Thoh Chaltun, Miss Pound-the-Stones. She slily waits around the villages, and when she sees some attractive youth she awakes his attention by tapping on the stones, or in default of these on an empty jar which she carries for the purpose. Does the foolish youth respond to the seductive invitation, she coyly moves to the woods, where the amorous pursuer meets like disappointment and a similar sad fate as the victim of the X tabai.
summary.zh: 另有一極相似之精怪：希·托赫·查爾頓——擊石小姐。她狡黠地伏於村落四周，見有俊俏青年，便以叩石——無石則叩其隨身攜帶的空罐——喚其注意。愚拙的青年若應其挑逗，她便婀娜移向林中；癡情追隨者在那裡得到的，與希·塔拜的犧牲者如出一轍的失望與悲慘結局。

sensitivity.note: Living Yucatec belief recorded by Brinton; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: Another very similar creature is X Thoh Chaltun, Miss Pound-the-Stones. She slily waits around the villages, and when she sees some attractive youth she awakes his attention by tapping on the stones, or in default of these on an empty jar which she carries for the purpose. Does the foolish youth respond to the seductive invitation, she coyly moves to the woods, where the amorous pursuer meets like disappointment and a similar sad fate as the victim of the X tabai.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 另一個極為相似的生物是X Thoh Chaltun，即「搗石小姐」。她狡黠地潛伏在村落四周，當她看見某個俊俏的青年，便敲擊石頭以引起他的注意；若無石頭，便敲擊她特意攜帶的空罐子。那愚笨的青年若回應了這誘人的邀約，她便故作羞澀地移向林中，而那滿懷愛意的追逐者在那裡遭遇同樣的失望，並落得與X tabai的受害者同樣悲慘的下場。

title.en: The Town of the Hares Under the Earth
title.zh: 地下的兔子之城

region.en: Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦

period: Told to Dr. Berendt; recorded by Brinton

source.work: Daniel G. Brinton, The Folk-Lore of Yucatan

summary.en: Each species of brute has its king, who rules and protects it; even the timid native hare may thus assert its rights. An Indian told Dr. Berendt that once upon a time a hunter with two dogs followed a hare into a cave. There he found a large hole leading under the earth; he descended, and came to the town of the hares. They seized him and his dogs and brought him before their king, and it was no easy matter for him to get off by dint of protests and promises.
summary.zh: 每一獸類皆有王者統攝其群；連怯懦的野兔也可自居其權。一印第安人告訴貝倫特醫生：昔有獵人攜二犬追兔入洞，見大穴通於地下；循之而下，竟抵兔子之城。兔眾擒其人與犬，押至兔王之前；他百般抗辯立誓，方得脫身。

sensitivity.note: Living Yucatec belief recorded by Brinton; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: Many superstitions cling around the animal world. Each species of brute has its king, who rules and protects it; even the timid native hare may thus assert its rights. An Indian told Dr. Berendt that once upon a time a hunter with two dogs followed a hare into a cave. There he found a large hole leading under the earth. He descended, and came to the town of the hares. They seized him and his dogs and brought him before their king, and it was no easy matter for him to get off by dint of protests and promises.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 動物世界周遭縈繞著許多迷信。每一種野獸都有自己的王，由它統治並保護同類；即便是膽小的本地野兔，也能如此主張自己的權利。一位印第安人曾告訴貝倫特博士，從前有個獵人帶著兩隻狗，追著一隻野兔進入一個洞穴。他在那裡發現一個通往地下的大洞。他往下走，來到了野兔之城。它們抓住他和他的狗，把他們帶到它們的王面前，而他費了好一番功夫，才憑著抗議和承諾脫身。

title.en: The Black Tail That Sucks the Milk
title.zh: 吸乳的黑尾蛇

region.en: Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦

period: Recorded by Brinton, late 19th c.

source.work: Daniel G. Brinton, The Folk-Lore of Yucatan

summary.en: An object of much dread is the Black Tail, Ekoneil, an imaginary snake with a black, broad, and forked tail. He glides into houses at night where a nursing mother is asleep; and, covering her nostrils with his tail, sucks the milk from her breasts.
summary.zh: 眾所畏懼者還有「黑尾」埃科內伊爾——一條尾闊而叉、通體漆黑的怪蛇。夜間滑入有哺乳母親酣睡之屋；以尾掩其鼻息，自其乳中吸吮乳汁。

sensitivity.note: Living Yucatec belief recorded by Brinton; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: An object of much dread is the Black Tail, Ekoneil, an imaginary snake with a black, broad, and forked tail. He glides into houses at night where a nursing mother is asleep; and, covering her nostrils with his tail, sucks the milk from her breasts.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 令人十分畏懼的是「黑尾」，即Ekoneil，一條想像中的蛇，尾巴黑色、寬闊而分叉。牠在夜間滑入屋內，那裡正有一位哺乳的母親熟睡；牠用尾巴蓋住她的鼻孔，從她的乳房吸吮乳汁。

title.en: The Phantom Bird That Falls as a Feather
title.zh: 落地化羽的幻鳥

region.en: Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦

period: Recorded by Brinton, late 19th c.

source.work: Daniel G. Brinton, The Folk-Lore of Yucatan

summary.en: There are also tales of the Straw Bird or Phantom Bird. The hunter unexpectedly sees a handsome bird on a branch before him. He fires and misses. He repeats his shot in vain. After a while it falls of itself, and proves to be nothing but a coloured feather. Then he knows that he has been fooled by the Zohol chich.
summary.zh: 關於「稻草鳥」或「幻鳥」亦有傳說。獵人忽見枝頭美鳥，舉銃而空；再射又空。稍頃，鳥自落，檢視竟只是一根染色的羽毛——他這才知道：自己被「佐霍爾·奇奇」捉弄了。

sensitivity.note: Living Yucatec belief recorded by Brinton; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: There are also tales of the Straw Bird or Phantom Bird. The hunter unexpectedly sees a handsome bird on a branch before him. He fires and misses. He repeats his shot in vain. After a while it falls of itself, and proves to be nothing but a coloured feather. Then he knows that he has been fooled by the Zohol chich.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton, Folk-Lore of Yucatan; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 也有關於稻草鳥或幻影鳥的傳說。獵人意外看見一隻美麗的鳥停在面前的樹枝上。他開槍，卻沒打中。他再試一次，仍是徒勞。過了一會兒，那鳥自己掉了下來，結果不過是一片彩色的羽毛。這時他才明白，自己是被佐霍爾奇奇（Zohol chich）愚弄了。

title.en: The White Hare of Inaba and the Deity Great-Name-Possessor
title.zh: 因幡之白兔與大己貴神

region.en: Inaba and Cape Keta (pin at Izumo; symbolic pin for the hare's crossing)
region.zh: 因幡與氣多岬（出雲象徵性定位）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: A hare deceives the crocodiles of the sea into forming a bridge, is flayed by the last of them, and is cruelly worsened by the eighty deities; the deity Great-Name-Possessor (Okuninushi) teaches him the true cure, and the healed hare prophesies that Okuninushi alone shall win the Princess of Yakami.
summary.zh: 白兔欺騙海中鱷魚列身為橋，被末尾鱷魚剝去皮毛；八十神教以海水曝風之法，傷勢愈重；大己貴神授以清水漱洗、蒲黃敷身之方，兔身復原，遂預言八十神必不得八上比賣，唯大己貴神可娶之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology. The trickster-hare reading is interpretive.

passages.text: The hare who had lost his own home island had no means of crossing over to Inaba. For this reason he deceived the crocodiles of the sea, saying: Let you and me compete, and compute the numbers of our respective tribes. Go and fetch every member of your tribe, and make them all lie in a row across from this island to Cape Keta; then I will tread on them and count them as I run across, and we shall know whether my tribe or yours is the larger. They were deceived and lay down in a row, and the hare trod on them, counting as he went. But just as he was about to step on land he shouted that they had been deceived by him, and the last crocodile in the line seized him and stripped off all his clothing, leaving his raw skin bare.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 154-155 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那隻失去了自己故鄉島嶼的兔子，沒有辦法渡海到稻羽。為此，牠欺騙海中的鱷魚說：你和我來比一比，算算我們各自族群的數目。你去把你族中所有的成員都帶來，讓牠們從這座島一直排到氣多岬；然後我踩在牠們身上，一邊跑過去一邊數，這樣我們就知道是我的族群多，還是你的族群多。鱷魚們受了騙，排成一列趴下，兔子便踩在牠們身上，一邊走一邊數。但就在牠即將踏上陸地的時候，牠高聲喊道自己騙了牠們，於是隊列中最後一條鱷魚抓住了牠，把牠身上的皮全部剝了下來，讓牠赤裸的皮肉暴露在外。

passages.text: Weeping and lamenting in his flayed state, the hare was met by the eighty deities going on ahead, who commanded and exhorted him: Bathe in the salt water, and lie down exposed to the wind. He did as they said, and his whole body was only hurt the more. Then the deity Great-Name-Possessor, who was following behind carrying his brothers' luggage, saw him and taught him the remedy: Go quickly to the river-mouth, wash your body with the fresh water, then take the pollen of the sedges growing at the river-mouth, spread it about, and roll upon it. The hare did as he was instructed, and his body was restored to its original state. This was the White Hare of Inaba, now called the Hare Deity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, p. 155 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兔子被剝了皮，正在哭泣哀嘆，遇上了走在前頭的八十位神。他們命令並勸告牠說：到鹽水裡浸泡，再躺下來吹風。牠照著他們的話做了，結果全身只是更加疼痛。這時，跟在後面替兄長們背行李的大穴牟遲神看見了牠，便教給牠救治的方法：快到河口去，用淡水洗淨身體，然後取河口生長的莎草的花粉，把它鋪散開來，在上頭打滾。兔子照著指示做了，身體便恢復了原樣。這就是稻羽的白兔，如今被稱為兔神。

passages.text: The hare then spoke to the deity Great-Name-Possessor a prophecy: These eighty deities shall certainly not get the Princess of Yakami. Though you carry their bag, Your Highness shall obtain her. When the princess herself was asked, she answered the eighty deities: I will not listen to your words; I mean to marry the deity Great-Name-Possessor. So the eighty deities, enraged, took counsel together to slay him — the beginning of the persecutions that drove Okuninushi down to the Nether-Distant-Land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 155-156 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兔子於是向大穴牟遲神說出一則預言：這八十位神必定得不到八上比賣。雖然您替他們背著袋子，您這位大人卻會得到她。後來有人去問那位公主本人，她回答八十位神說：我不會聽你們的話；我打算嫁給大穴牟遲神。八十位神因此大怒，聚在一起商議要殺他——這便是迫使大國主逃往根之堅洲國的種種迫害的開端。

title.en: The Descent of Ninigi: Amaterasu's Grandson Comes Down to Takachiho
title.zh: 瓊瓊杵尊天降高千穗

region.en: The peak of Kuzhifuru, Takachiho in Tsukushi (symbolic pin at the Takachiho plateau, Miyazaki)
region.zh: 筑紫日向高千穗峰狹梶山頂（宮崎高千穗高原象徵性定位）

period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (trans. Chamberlain 1882)

source.work: Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain (1882)

summary.en: With the Central Land subdued, the heir proposes that his child Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty (Ninigi) descend instead; at the eight-forking road of Heaven a deity of blinding radiance is confronted by the Heavenly-Alarming-Female Uzume, who learns he is the Deity Prince of Saruta come to serve as vanguard. The Heavenly Deities attach the mirror and curved jewels that once lured Amaterasu from the Rock-Dwelling, the Herb-Quelling-Great-Sword, and five chief companies, charge Ninigi to regard the mirror as their very spirit, and he descends, pushing asunder the eight-fold clouds, onto the peak of Takachiho.
summary.zh: 天之石屋既平葦原中國，皇孫命其子天邇岐志國邇岐志天津日高日子番能邇邇藝命降臨。於天上八衢遇輝光普照之神，命天鈿女命問之，乃猿田毗古神自薦為嚮導。遂以八尺瓊勾玉與八咫鏡、草薙大刀，並思兼神、手力男神、天石屋戶神等五部眾授之，敕曰：以此鏡視為我靈，當如視我而奉之。邇邇藝命遂離天之石座，排八重天雲，分道而下，降於筑紫日向高千穗之狹梶山頂。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki): Ninigi's descent and the mirror-charge are the charter myth of the imperial regalia and Ise shrine; present comparatively and critically. Passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations.

passages.text: Then the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity and the High-Integrating-Deity charged the Heir Apparent, His Augustness Truly-Conqueror-I-Conquer-Conquering-Swift-Heavenly-Great-Great-Ears: The Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male-Deity says he has now finished pacifying the Central Land of Reed-Plains; do you, in accordance with our gracious charge, descend to it, dwell in it, and rule over it. The Heir Apparent replied: While I have been getting ready to descend, there has been born to me a child whose name is His Augustness Heaven-Plenty-Earth-Plenty-Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty. This child should be sent down. So the Heavenly Deities laid their command on Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty: This Luxuriant Reed-Plain Land of Fresh Rice-ears is the land over which you shall rule; and he answered that he would descend from Heaven according to their commands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 192-193 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是，天照大御神與高御產巢日神吩咐皇太子天津彥彥火瓊瓊杵尊說：經津主神說他如今已平定葦原中國；你當遵照我們恩慈的吩咐，降臨那裡，居住其中，統治那地方。皇太子回答說：正當我準備降臨的時候，我生了一個孩子，名叫天葦原水穗國千五百秋瑞穗兒。這孩子應當被派遣下去。於是眾天神向瑞穗兒下達命令：這豐葦原瑞穗國是你應當統治的地方；他回答說，他會遵照他們的命令從天而降。

passages.text: When the prince was about to descend, at the eight-forking road of Heaven there stood a deity whose refulgence reached up to the Plain of High Heaven and down to the Central Land of Reed-Plains, so that his light made the way doubtful. The Heavenly Deities charged the Heavenly-Alarming-Female-Deity: Though you are but a delicate female, you are a deity who conquers in facing other deities; go and ask: This being the road by which our august child is about to descend from Heaven, who is it that stands there? To this gracious question he replied: I am an Earthly Deity named the Deity Prince of Saruta. Having heard of the intended descent of the august child of the Heavenly Deities, I have come humbly to meet him and respectfully offer myself as his vanguard.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 193-194 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當這位皇子即將降臨時，在天之八衢上站著一位神，祂的光輝上達高天原，下照葦原中國，使道路因祂的光芒而難以辨明。眾天神吩咐天鈿女命說：你雖只是柔弱的女子，卻是面對別的神時能取勝的神；去問一問：這條路是我等皇子即將從天降臨的路，站在那裡的是誰？對於這恩慈的詢問，祂回答說：我是名為猿田毘古神的地祇。聽說眾天神的皇子即將降臨，我便前來恭迎，並恭敬地自薦為他的先鋒。

passages.text: So they joined to him five chiefs of companies — the Heavenly-Beckoning-Ancestor-Lord, Grand-Jewel, the Heavenly-Alarming-Female, I-shi-ko-ri-do-me, and Jewel-Ancestor — and to the prince they joined the eight-feet curved jewels and the mirror that had allured the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity from the Rock-Dwelling, and the Herb-Quelling-Great-Sword, together with the Deity Thought-Includer, the Hand-Strength-Male-Deity, and the Deity Heavenly-Rock-Door-Opener of Eternal Night, charging him: Regard this mirror exactly as if it were our august spirit, and reverence it as if reverencing us; and let the Deity Thought-Includer take in hand our affairs and carry on the government.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 194-197 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他們為他配上了五位伴造之首——天忍日命、大久米命、天押雲命、伊斯許理度賣命與玉祖命；又為皇子配上了八尺瓊曲玉、曾將天照大御神從石室中誘出的鏡、草薙大劍，以及思兼神、手力男神與永夜之天石戶別神，並囑咐他道：「當視此鏡如視我等之神靈，敬之如敬我等；並令思兼神執掌我等之事，主持政務。」

passages.text: Then the prince, leaving the Heavenly Rock-Seat, pushing asunder the eight-fold heavenly spreading clouds, and dividing a road with a mighty road-dividing, set off floating shut up in the Floating Bridge of Heaven, and descended onto the peak of Kuzhifuru, which is Takachiho in Tsukushi. His attendant deities, taking the heavenly rock-quivers on their backs, the mallet-headed swords at their sides, the heavenly vegetable-wax-tree bows in their hands, and clasping the heavenly true deer-arrows under their arms, stood in his august van in respectful attendance. He looked about him and said: This place is opposite to the land of Kara; one comes straight across to the august Cape of Kasasa; it is a land whereon the morning sun shines straight and the evening sun's sunlight illumines — an exceedingly good place. Having thus spoken, he made stout the temple-pillars on the nethermost rock-bottom, made high the cross-beams to the Plain of High Heaven, and dwelt there. He then charged the Heavenly-Alarming-Female to escort the Deity Prince of Saruta back, to bear that deity's august name, and to serve him; wherefore the Duchesses of Saru bear the name of the Prince of Saruta to this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, pp. 197-199 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是皇子離開天石座，推開八重天雲，以大力闢路，乘天浮橋漂浮而行，降臨於筑紫高千穗之久士布流峰。其隨侍諸神背負天石鞆，腰佩槌頭劍，手持天菜摘弓，腋下挾天真鹿箭，恭敬侍立於皇子之御前。皇子環顧四周，說道：「此地與韓國相對，直渡可至笠沙御崎；此地晨日直照，夕日之光亦照臨——實為極佳之地。」言畢，遂將神殿之柱牢固地立於最下之磐石之上，將橫樑高架至高天原，而居於此地。他隨即命天押雲命護送猿田大神返回，承奉該神之御名，並侍奉之；因此，猿女君至今仍承猿田大神之名。

title.en: Jimmu's Eastward Expedition: The Ancient of the Sea and the Fair Land
title.zh: 神武東征：海神古老之言與筑紫出航

region.en: Tsukushi (Kyushu), starting point of the eastward expedition
region.zh: 筑紫國（九州），東征起點

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Emperor Jimmu, son of Hoori and the sea-goddess's daughter Tamayori-hime, resolves to leave the western land where every town has its own lord. He has heard from the Ancient of the Sea of a fair land encircled by blue mountains in the East, where a being descended in a Heavenly Rock-boat, and leads an expedition eastward, gaining a pilot, a banquet at Usa, and three years of provisioning in Kibi.
summary.zh: 神武天皇自言天祖授土而列邑各有君長、相侵相奪，聞海神古老言東方有青山四面環繞之美地，有人乘天磐船飛降。遂與兄弟子姪率舟師東征，得磯根津彥為舵工，宇佐氏築一柱之宮設宴，以宇佐津姬配天種子命，滯吉備三年治船積糧。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi) of Emperor Jimmu, first ancestor of the imperial line; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Emperor Kami-Yamato-Ihare-biko (Jimmu) addressed his elder brothers and his children. Of old, the Heavenly Deities Taka-mi-musubi and Oho-hiru-me had pointed to this land of fair rice-ears of the fertile reed-plain and given it to the Heavenly Grandchild Ninigi, who had thrown open the barrier of Heaven, cleared a cloud-path, and ruled the western border in an age of darkness and disorder. But remote regions still had no part in Imperial rule: every town had always been allowed its own lord and every village its own chief, who divided territory and practised mutual aggression and conflict. Now, he had heard from the Ancient of the Sea that in the East there was a fair land encircled on all sides by blue mountains, and that a being had flown down there riding in a Heavenly Rock-boat - one Nigi-haya-hi. This land, he judged, was suitable for extending the Heavenly task; it was doubtless the centre of the world. Why should they not proceed thither and make it the capital?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book III, §§1–2 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 神倭伊波禮毘古天皇（神武）對其兄長及子嗣說道：「昔日，高御產巢日神與大日孁神曾指此豐葦原之瑞穗國，賜予天孫邇邇藝命；天孫開啟天之屏障，闢出雲路，於幽暗紛亂之世統治西方邊境。然而偏遠之地仍未歸於皇化：每邑皆各立其主，每村皆各置其長，割據疆土，相互侵伐爭鬥。如今，他從海神老者處聽聞，東方有一美地，四面環繞青山，且有神靈乘天磐船飛降於彼——是為饒速日命。他認為此地適於拓展天業，必為世界之中心。何不前往彼處，建為都城？」

passages.text: In winter of that year the Emperor led the Imperial Princes and a naval force against the East. At the Haya-suhi gate they met a fisherman riding in a boat, who announced himself a Country-God named Utsu-hiko and offered to act as guide. The Emperor ordered the end of a shihi-wood pole given him, took him into the Imperial vessel as pilot, and named him Shihi-ne-tsu-hiko, first ancestor of the Yamato no Atahe. At Usa in Tsukushi the ancestors of the local lords, Usa-tsu-hiko and Usa-tsu-hime, built a palace raised on one pillar on the banks of the River Usa and offered a banquet; and by Imperial command Usa-tsu-hime was given in marriage to the Emperor's minister Ama-no-tane, remote ancestor of the Nakatomi house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book III, §§3–4 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 是年冬季，天皇率領皇子們及水軍東征。於速吸門遇一漁夫乘船而來，自稱為國神，名曰宇豆毘古，願為嚮導。天皇命人取椎木之杖末賜予他，納其入御船為水手，並命名為椎根津彥，是為倭直之始祖。在筑紫宇佐，當地豪族之祖宇佐津彥與宇佐津姬於宇佐川畔建一柱高聳之宮殿，設宴獻饗；天皇詔命將宇佐津姬嫁與天皇之臣天種，是為中臣氏之遠祖。

passages.text: The fleet went on to the harbour of Oka in Tsukushi and the province of Aki, and entering the land of Kibi built a temporary palace called the Palace of Takashima, where the Emperor dwelt three years, setting in order the helms of his ships and preparing a store of provisions, desiring by a single effort to subdue the Empire. Then the Imperial forces proceeded eastwards, the prow of one ship touching the stern of another. Just as they reached Cape Naniha they encountered a current of great swiftness, and the place was called Nami-haya, wave-swift, or Nami-hana, wave-flower - the origin of the name Naniha.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book III, §§4–5 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 船隊續航至筑紫岡港及安藝國，進入吉備之地，建臨時宮殿，名曰高島宮，天皇居此三年，整頓船舵，儲備糧食，欲一舉平定天下。其後皇軍東進，一船之首接一船之尾。方至難波崎，忽遇急流，其地遂名為浪速（浪速，意為浪之迅疾），或名浪花——此即難波之名所由來。

title.en: Oto-tachibana-hime Calms the Sea with Her Life
title.zh: 弟橘媛投海鎮神怒

region.en: Sea crossing from Sagami to Kadzusa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 相模上總海道（象徵錨點）

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: From Sagami Yamato-takeru wishes to cross to Kadzusa, boasting 'this is but a little sea: one might even jump over it.' In mid-channel a storm arises and tosses the ship. His consort Oto-tachibana-hime declares the winds and waves must be the wish of the God of the Sea, prays to be given to the sea to redeem his life, and plunges into the billows. The storm ceases, and the sea is ever after called Hashiri-midzu, running-water.
summary.zh: 尊自相模欲渡上總，望海大聲曰「此滄海咫尺，可躍而渡」。至中流忽起風暴，舟覆在即。尊妃弟橘媛曰「風浪驟起，舟將沒，必海神之意。願以身代王命，請入海」。言訖蹈波而沒，風波頓息，舟得抵岸。故時人名此海曰走水。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi); passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Next he marched on to Sagami, whence he desired to proceed to Kadzusa. Looking over the sea, he spoke with a loud voice and said: 'This is but a little sea: one might even jump over it.' But when he came to the middle of the sea a storm suddenly arose, and the Prince's ship was tossed about, so that he could not cross over.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VII, sec. 26 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 其次，他進軍至相模，欲由此前往上總。他眺望海面，高聲說道：『此不過小海，甚至可以一躍而過。』然而行至海中央，忽起暴風，皇子之船顛簸搖盪，無法渡過。

passages.text: At this time there was a concubine in the Prince's suite, named Oto-tachibana-hime, daughter of Oshiyama no Sukune of the Hodzumi house. She addressed the Prince, saying: 'This present uprising of the winds and rushing of the waves, so that the Prince's ship is like to sink, must be due to the wishes of the God of the Sea. I pray thee let me go into the sea, and so let the person of thy mean handmaiden be given to redeem the life of the Prince's Augustness.' Having finished speaking, she plunged into the billows. The storm forthwith ceased, and the ship was enabled to reach the shore. Therefore the people of that time called that sea Hashiri-midzu, running-water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book VII, sec. 26 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此時親王之側有一妾，名曰弟橘媛，乃穗積氏忍山宿禰之女也。她向親王進言曰：「今此風起浪湧，致親王之船將沉，必是海神之意欲也。妾願入於海中，以卑微侍女之身贖親王之尊命。」言畢，遂投身於波濤之中。風暴旋即止息，船乃得抵岸。故當時之人稱此海為「走水」。

title.en: The Seven-Night Divination: Jingu Names the Gods Who Spoke
title.zh: 神功皇后彈琴迎神，七日七夜知神名

region.en: Palace of worship at Wayamada, Tsukushi
region.zh: 筑紫山田宮

period: Nihongi compiled 720 CE (trans. Aston 1896)

source.work: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Grieved that Chūai died refusing the divine instructions, the Empress commissions purification and a Palace of worship at Wayamada, herself discharging the priest's office while Takechi no Sukune plays the lute. For seven days and nights the gods answer one by one: the deity of Ise representing herself as a Corean deity, the eulalia deity, the awful Koto-shiro-nushi, and the three water-gods of Hiuga. The Kumaso submit at once when Kamo no Wake is sent against them.
summary.zh: 神功皇后以帝不從神誨而早崩，欲知降禍之神，乃修祓築齋宮於山田，親為齋主，武內宿禰撫琴，中臣烏子為齋部。以千縈之幣置琴上祈曰前日誨帝者何神。七日七夜乃有答：伊勢五十鈴宮之神自稱，又有出於芻茅之耳之神，又有統理天地虛空之事代主神，又有日向橘小戶水底之三神。既得神名依誨奉祭，遣賀茂別命擊熊襲，不日而降。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi); passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: At this time the Empress was grieved that the Emperor would not follow the Divine instructions, and had consequently died a premature death. She thought she would find out what God had sent the curse, so that she might possess herself of the land of treasures. She therefore commanded her ministers and functionaries to purge offences and rectify transgressions, and to construct a Palace of worship in the village of Wayamada. The Empress, having selected a lucky day, entered the Palace of worship and discharged in person the office of priest. She commanded Takechi no Sukune to play on the lute, and the Nakatomi Ikatsu no Omi was designated as Saniha, the official who examines the utterances prompted by the Deity. Then placing one thousand pieces of cloth, high pieces of cloth, on the top and bottom of the lute, she prayed, saying: 'Who is the God who on a former day instructed the Emperor? I pray that I may know his name.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book IX, secs. 1-3 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
