An envious queen of the islands sends her priests to the seashore at low tide to call on the spirits of the deep; the Salt Water Giant, his head covered with clam and oyster shells, carries the request down to the Dragon King of the World Under the Sea, and at flood tide the sea opens and His Majesty presents the two sparkling tide-jewels that govern the ebb and the flood. Landing on the southern coast, the queen fights many battles and seizes not common prisoners but painters, artists, costumers, makers of pottery, men of books and priests, carrying them to the islands, where the smart men of skill teach the islanders how to build houses and temples and be like the Koreans. Great borrowers, the islanders ask what, in time of ceremony, they should put on their heads — and the offended Koreans, in contempt, give them their old shoes with strings; the islanders put them on their heads like skull caps, tie the white strings under their chins, and to this day, when making offerings to the fairies, wear this head-gear and think their shoe-caps are very fine.
summary.zh: 東海島國遣使乞冠於朝鮮。韓人惡其侵掠工匠，乃以敝履與之。島人不識，戴之於首，以白帶繫於頷下，自以為美冠。至今其祭神之冠，猶鞋形也。

sensitivity.note: Satirical national anecdote written from a Korean-children's viewpoint; represents Sino-Korean cultural-lending debates, not fact.

passages.text: Many centuries ago when Korea was named Chosen, or the Land of Morning Splendor, the island-kingdom out in the eastern sea was called The Land of the Dragon-Fly. The Koreans called these islanders dwarfs, because they were not tall of stature, though they were very warlike and brave. The isle men had no books or letters, and were very rude in their manners; therefore many kind teachers, filled with the spirit of Great Buddha, crossed the sea from Everlasting Great Korea, to teach these islanders politeness, and how to read and write, and to build pagodas, and temples and schools.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Shoes for Hats' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 許多世紀以前，當朝鮮名為「朝善」，即「晨曦之國」時，東方海上的島國被稱為「蜻蜓之國」。朝鮮人稱這些島民為矮人，因為他們身材不高，儘管他們非常好戰勇敢。島民沒有書籍或文字，舉止也十分粗魯；因此，許多懷著大佛精神的仁慈教師，從永恆的大朝鮮渡海而來，教導這些島民禮儀，以及如何讀書寫字，並建造佛塔、寺廟和學堂。

passages.text: The islanders had priests who went down by the seaside when the tide was low, and called on the spirits of the deep. The first living thing that poked its nose above the waters was the Salt Water Giant, his head all covered with clam and oyster shells, sea weed, shrimps and whatever grows in the bottom of the ocean; a grumpy sort of fellow, he carried the request down to his master, the Dragon King of the World Under the Sea. No sooner did the tide show flood than the sea opened, and His Majesty appeared in a great sea shell, holding the two sparkling tide-jewels which govern the ebb and the flood tides, which he presented to the Queen before quickly disappearing beneath the waves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Shoes for Hats' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 島上有祭司，趁退潮時下到海邊，呼喚深海中的神靈。第一個把鼻子探出水面的活物是鹹水巨人，他的頭上滿是蛤蜊殼、牡蠣殼、海草、蝦子，以及一切生長在海底的東西；他是個脾氣暴躁的傢伙，把這項請求帶下去給他的主人，也就是海底世界的龍王。潮水剛一顯出漲勢，海面便裂開了，陛下乘著一只巨大的海貝現身，手中握著兩顆閃閃發光、掌管退潮與漲潮的潮汐寶珠，他將寶珠獻給女王，隨即迅速消失在波濤之下。

passages.text: Immediately after receiving the tide jewels, the Queen landed on the southern coast of Korea; she cared nothing about common prisoners, but whenever she found a painter, an artist, a costumer, a maker of pottery, or a man of books, or a priest, she seized and took him along. In the islands these smart men of skill taught the islanders how to build houses, palaces, and temples, to make fine clothes, to paint pictures — so the islands became rich in fruit, rice, grain, pagodas and temples.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Shoes for Hats' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 女王一收到潮汐寶珠，便登陸朝鮮南岸；她對尋常的囚犯毫不在意，但每逢發現畫師、藝術家、裁縫、陶匠、讀書人或祭司，便將他們捉住帶走。在島上，這些聰慧的巧匠教導島民如何建造房屋、宮殿與廟宇，如何製作精美的衣裳，如何繪畫——於是島上果實、稻米、穀物豐饒，塔與廟宇林立。

passages.text: The Koreans were greatly offended at these savages from over the sea for invading their country and taking away their artists and craftsmen, and resolved to play a trick on the islanders. So when men from the isles sent a company of men to Korea and asked for caps to put on their heads, the Koreans in contempt gave them their old shoes, which had strings on them to tie over their feet. The islanders did not know what these shoes were, and put them on their heads like skull caps, tying them with the white strings down under their chins. So to this day the islanders, when making offerings to the fairies, wear this head-gear and think their shoe-caps are very fine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Shoes for Hats' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 朝鮮人對這些從海外來的野蠻人入侵他們的國家、擄走他們的藝術家與工匠大為憤怒，決心捉弄島民一番。於是，當島上的人派了一隊人馬到朝鮮，請求給他們戴在頭上的帽子時，朝鮮人輕蔑地給了他們自己的舊鞋，鞋上還繫著綁在腳上的帶子。島民不知這些鞋是什麼，便把它們像無邊帽一樣戴在頭上，用白色的帶子在下巴底下繫緊。因此直到今日，島民在向仙女獻祭時，仍戴著這種頭飾，並認為他們的鞋帽十分漂亮。

title.en: The Voice of the Bell: In-Jung of Seoul
title.zh: 人定鐘聲

region.en: Central square of Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城鐘樓（象徵性定位）

period: Bell legend from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913); bell cast under King Taejo (r. 1392-1398)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'The Voice of the Bell', eBook #67180

summary.en: When Tai Jo, first King of the new dynasty, built Han Yang, the workmen digging for the East Gate foundations came upon a bell — a lucky omen. But such a bell could only tinkle, and the king wanted one to boom loud and long, to excel even the famed bell of Silla: ten feet high, eight feet across, crowned by two terrible dragons, hung by whole tree-trunks, struck by a swinging log instead of a clapper, its guardian spirit of the city housed in the bell. Copper and tin came in by bullock-cart and donback from every province; the pit was dug, the crucibles fired — and the casting cracked. A second casting cracked; a third cracked, until the price of a palace had been paid and there was no bell. Out steps a workman who recalls a collector's story: in a certain village an old woman carrying a baby boy strapped to her back had no coin to give but offered the child herself. The baby is thrown into the half-filled mould — the casting is perfect, and the bell is named In Jung, 'Man Decides': every night at nine o'clock every man must decide to go to bed, and until midnight the women have the streets to themselves. When first sounded, the bell discovers it has a memory and a voice: 'Mu-u-u-ma-ma-ma-la-la-la' ending like a baby's cry — 'My mother's fault. My mother's fault.' To this day the mothers in Seoul, as they clasp their darlings to their bosoms, resolve it shall be no fault of theirs if these lack love or care.
summary.zh: 太祖築漢陽城，東門掘得古鐘，以為瑞。然其聲細，乃募銅鑄巨鐘，高丈、闊八尺，頂蟠雙龍。三鑄三裂。有司言某村嫗曾願以孺子獻銅，未收。至四鑄，銅半熔，擲嬰兒入之，鐘乃成，名曰『人定』——每夜九點，男子皆歸寢，婦人始得遊於街。初鳴之日，鐘聲如嬰啼，曰『母之過也，母之過也』。都中母氏聞之，益慈其子。

sensitivity.note: Child-sacrifice-in-casting legend attached to the Jongno bell (Bosingak); handled at summary level.

passages.text: When Tai Jo, the great general and first King of Korea, founded a new dynasty, he moved the capital near the great river Han and resolved to build a mighty city called Han Yang, the Castle on the Han. Happy was he when the workmen, in digging for the foundations of the East Gate, came upon a bell: it was a lucky omen. But such a bell could only tinkle, while King Tai Jo wanted one that would boom loud and long, that would excel even the famed striker of the hours in Silla, and flood miles of hill and valley with its melody. The guardian spirit of the city would have its home in the bell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Voice of the Bell' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當偉大的將軍、朝鮮開國君主太祖建立新王朝時，他將都城遷到大河漢江附近，決心建造一座名為漢陽的雄偉城市，意即「漢江上的城堡」。當工匠在挖掘東門地基時發現了一口鐘，他欣喜萬分：這是個吉兆。但這樣一口鐘只能發出叮噹之聲，而太祖王想要的是一口能響亮而長久轟鳴的鐘，甚至要勝過新羅那口著名的報時鐘，讓它的旋律漫過數里的山丘與山谷。這座城市的守護神將以鐘為家。

passages.text: Word was sent out to all the provinces to collect the copper and tin to make the bronze metal. When there was not yet enough, one of the collectors came to a certain village and called at a house where lived an old woman carrying a baby boy strapped to her back; she had no coin, cash, metal, or fuel to give, but was quite ready to offer either herself or the baby: 'May I give you this boy?' The collector paid no attention to her, but passed on; when in Seoul, however, he told the story, and thus it came to pass that many heard of the matter and remembered it later.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Voice of the Bell' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 命令傳達到各省，收集銅與錫以鑄造青銅。當收集到的金屬還不夠時，其中一名收集者來到某個村莊，拜訪了一戶人家，那裡住著一位老婦人，背上用帶子綁著一個男嬰；她沒有錢幣、現金、金屬或燃料可給，卻十分願意獻出自己或那嬰兒：「我可以把這個男孩給您嗎？」收集者沒有理會她，逕自離去；然而到了首爾，他卻把這件事講了出來，於是許多人聽說了此事，日後也記住了它。

passages.text: When the fire-clay crucibles were set on the white-hot coals and the hissing, molten stream ran out and filled the mould, alas! they found the bell cracked. A second casting was made, but again, when cool, it was found to be cracked. Three separate times this happened, until the price of a palace had been paid and yet there was no bell. King Tai Jo offered a large reward, whereupon out stepped a workman who told the story of the old woman, and said that the bell would crack after every cooling unless her proposal was accepted. So the baby boy was sent for and, when the liquid metal had half filled the pit, was thrown into the mass; when they hoisted the cooled bell up from the mould, lo, the casting was a perfect success. It was named In Jung, 'Man Decides': every night at nine o'clock let every man or boy decide to go to bed, and from that hour until midnight the women shall have the streets to themselves to walk in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Voice of the Bell' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當耐火泥坩堝架在白熱的炭火上，嘶嘶作響的熔流傾瀉而出、注滿模具時，唉呀！他們發現鐘裂了。於是進行第二次鑄造，但冷卻之後，又發現它裂了。這樣的事接連發生了三次，直到花費了一座宮殿的代價，卻仍沒有鐘。太祖王懸下重賞，於是有一名工匠站了出來，講述了那老婦人的事，並說除非接受她的提議，否則鐘每冷卻一次就會裂一次。於是那男嬰被送來，當液態金屬注滿坑洞一半時，他被投入其中；當他們把冷卻後的鐘從模具中吊起時，瞧，這次鑄造完美成功。它被命名為「仁鐘」，意即「人定」：每晚九點，讓每個男人或男孩決定上床睡覺，而從那個時辰到午夜，街道便歸女人們所有，任她們行走。

passages.text: As yet the bell was silent. When it did sound, the Seoul people discovered that it was the most wonderful bell ever cast: it had a memory and a voice, it could wail as well as sing. Its sounds actually made a sentence — 'Mu-u-u-ma-ma-ma-la-la-la-la' until it ended like a baby's cry: 'My mother's fault. My mother's fault.' And to this day the mothers in Seoul, as they clasp their darlings to their bosoms, resolve that it shall be no fault of theirs if these lack love or care.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Voice of the Bell' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這口鐘當時仍寂然無聲。待它真正鳴響時，首爾的百姓才發現，這是自古鑄造以來最奇妙的一口鐘：它有記憶，也有聲音，既能哀鳴，也能歌唱。它的聲響竟能拼成一句話——「Mu-u-u-ma-ma-ma-la-la-la-la」，直到最後像嬰兒的哭聲般收尾：「是我母親的錯。是我母親的錯。」直到今日，首爾的母親們把孩子緊摟在懷裡時，仍下定決心：倘若這些孩子缺少愛或照料，那絕不會是她們的過錯。

title.en: The King of the Sparrows and His Rewards
title.zh: 雀王酬恩

region.en: Sparrow Capital among the eaves (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 簷下雀國（象徵性定位）

period: Bird-reward tale from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'The King of the Sparrows', eBook #67180

summary.en: A young sparrow, caught in the split-bamboo curtain after escaping the roof-snake, has its leg put out of joint; the kind owner of the house sets the leg in place with moist clay and feeds it till it is strong. The sparrow flies to the King of Sparrow Land, and the court votes to reward the good man richly: by magic they pack gold, jade, brocade, cups and saucers, rice, horses and oxen, pretty maids, silk and cotton clothes and things to eat into a seed. Planted, it grows a luxuriant vine with one unusually fine gourd, which when opened in autumn yields a table of costly jade, a silver bottle of wine, gold tea-caddy, rolls of silk and satin, rice and cooked foods, horses and oxen, and last of all lovely girls who serve the feast — the old couple live as happy as king and queen. A wicked man who hated all sparrows hears of it, breaks a sparrow's leg and binds it with clay and a rag until it is dreadfully crooked; the Sparrow King hands him a seed, and the vine covers all three of his thatched roofs — but the gourds, opened one by one, yield the twelve curses of Korea: rope-dancers demanding pay, begging priests, hired mourners with a corpse, dancing girls, acrobats, loafers from the government offices, fortune-tellers, jugglers, blind folks with bells, and a giant threatening to eat the pair; the twelfth gourd holds all the smells of Korea, and as they run holding their noses a gale blows the house down, the thatch bursting into flame from the flue fires. Stripped of everything, the wicked fellow and his wife live the rest of their days on their neighbor's charity.
summary.zh: 雀為屋蛇所傷，善人為之接骨。雀王賜以一籽，種之生瓜，剖之則玉桌、金瓶、錦緞、僕婢皆出，夫婦遂富。惡鄰效之，故折雀足而偽為救之，雀王亦賜一籽。瓜成十二，剖之則雜技、游僧、喪班、歌伎、衙役、瞽者、巨人絡繹而出，皆索錢；末瓜臭不可近，烈風拔屋，火焚其廬。惡人夫婦遂賴善人之施以終老。

sensitivity.note: Same gourd-reward plot family as Hungbu-Nolbu (cf. korean-hungbu-gourd-treasures).

passages.text: One day a young sparrow that had hardly learned to fly was almost seized by the roof-snake, but was saved by a big, brave bird. Although escaped from the snake's jaws, the sparrow in falling caught its legs in the curtain made of split bamboo, and its limb was put out of joint. The owner of the house was a kind man, who loved the birds: taking pity on the poor sparrow, he set its leg in place, put moist clay around the broken part, kept it warm, and fed the birdie until it was strong again, letting it fly away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The King of the Sparrows' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，一隻還不太會飛的小麻雀差點被屋頂上的蛇抓住，幸虧一隻勇敢的大鳥救了牠。麻雀雖逃出了蛇口，卻在跌落時把腿卡進了竹片編成的簾子裡，腿骨因而脫了臼。這家的主人是個心地善良、喜愛鳥兒的人：他憐憫這隻可憐的麻雀，替牠把腿接回原位，在斷處敷上濕泥，讓牠保暖，又餵養這隻小鳥，直到牠恢復強健，才放牠飛走。

passages.text: It spread its wings to fly to the King of the Sparrows, and His Majesty and his counselors voted to reward richly so good a friend of all sparrows. By some magic process they packed gold, jade, brocade, cups and saucers, rice, horses, oxen, pretty maids, silk and cotton clothes and delicious things to eat and drink into a seed, and gave it to the sparrow to carry to the good man. The wife, who was a wise woman, begged her husband to keep it, and on a warm day in spring she planted it: it grew to be a luxuriant vine, and when the gourd, fully ripe, was sawed open, lo! a store of riches came out such as neither the man nor his wife had ever dreamed of — a table of costly jade, a silver bottle of delicious wine, rolls of silk and satin, rice and cooked food, strong horses and fat oxen, and last of all some lovely young girls, as fair as the moon, who served the feast, as if they had been used to waiting on ladies and gentlemen all their lives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The King of the Sparrows' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 牠展開雙翅飛去見麻雀之王，麻雀之王與眾臣商議後，決定重重獎賞這位所有麻雀的大恩人。他們以某種法術，把黃金、玉石、錦緞、杯碟、米糧、馬匹、牛隻、美貌的侍女、絲綢與棉布衣裳，以及種種美味飲食，全都封進一粒種子裡，交給麻雀帶去給那位善心人。他的妻子是個賢明的婦人，央求丈夫留下這粒種子；在一個溫暖的春日裡，她把它種下：它長成一株茂盛的藤蔓，待葫蘆完全成熟、鋸開之後，瞧！湧出了一大批那男人與妻子做夢也想不到的財寶——一張貴重的玉桌、一瓶醇美的銀瓶酒、一匹匹絲綢與緞子、米糧與熟食、健壯的馬匹與肥碩的牛隻，最後還有幾位如明月般姣好的年輕姑娘，她們在宴席上侍奉，彷彿一輩子都在服侍仕女紳士一般。

passages.text: But a wicked man that hated all sparrows heard of his neighbor's good fortune and was envious; he threw a stick at a bird and broke its leg, then bound up the limb with clay and a bit of rag, keeping the poor sparrow until its leg was well but dreadfully crooked. The Sparrow King handed out a seed to be given to the enemy of the sparrows; the naughty man planted it, and the vine covered the whole side of the house and all the thatched roofs of the three dwellings which made up his home. In the autumn he plucked the fruit and sawed them open.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The King of the Sparrows' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 可是有個憎恨所有麻雀的惡人，聽說了鄰居的好運，心生嫉妒；他朝一隻鳥扔棍子，打斷了牠的腿，然後用泥和一小塊破布把腿包紮起來，把這隻可憐的麻雀養到腿傷痊癒，卻歪得不成樣子。麻雀之王發下一粒種子，要交給這個與麻雀為敵的人；這壞心人把它種下，藤蔓爬滿了屋子的整面牆，也覆蓋了他那由三戶人家組成的住處所有茅草屋頂。到了秋天，他摘下果實，把它們鋸開。

passages.text: Instead of good things and treasures, there came out one after another the twelve curses of Korea: a party of rope dancers who demanded money; a line of Buddhist priests begging for the temples; a band of hired mourners carrying a corpse; a bevy of dancing girls; a pair of acrobats; loafers from the government offices, fortune-tellers, jugglers, and blind folks with sticks and bells; finally a giant that threatened to eat up both the man and his wife. By this time there was not a coin left. When the twelfth gourd was opened it seemed to have in it all the smells of Korea; holding their noses, the man and his wife ran out of their house — happily, for just then a gale of wind blew down the house, and the thatch and timbers burst into flames from the fire that had heated the flues. Thus stripped of all their possessions because of the man's cruelty to the birds, the wicked fellow and his wife would have starved, except for the kindness of the good man who treated the sparrows kindly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The King of the Sparrows' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 出來的不是好東西與財寶，而是一樣接一樣地湧出朝鮮的十二種災禍：一群索錢的走繩藝人；一隊為寺院募化的僧人；一幫抬著屍體的僱傭哭喪人；一群舞女；一對賣藝人；衙門裡的閒漢、算命先生、變戲法的人和拄杖搖鈴的盲人；最後還有一個巨人，揚言要把那男人和他的妻子一併吃掉。到這時，一個銅板也不剩了。第十二個葫蘆打開時，裡頭彷彿盛著朝鮮所有的氣味；那男人和妻子捏著鼻子跑出屋外——說來幸運，因為就在那時，一陣狂風吹倒了房子，而先前燒熱煙道的火，使茅草與樑木頓時燃燒起來。這惡人因虐待鳥兒而失去了一切家當，若不是那位善待麻雀的善心人相助，他和妻子早就餓死了。

title.en: Keel Wee and the Game with the Mountain Fairies
title.zh: 樵夫觀棋

region.en: Mountain clearing near P'yongyang (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 平壤山麓（象徵性定位）

period: Fairy-tale of Rip Van Winkle type from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'The Woodman and the Mountain Fairies', eBook #67180

summary.en: Over half a thousand years ago the wood-cutter Keel Wee of a northern village near P'yongyang climbs the mountain to cut wood and finds two fairy-like beings in the costume of the Chow dynasty of two thousand years before, seated on stones playing go-ban. They seem by eye-winks to invite him to look on; when he stretches forth his hand to move a piece, the fairy nearest gives him a crack on the fingers, then puts in the woodman's mouth something like a persimmon seed. Hour after hour he watches, forgetting that with mountain spirits there is no night or morning — in fairy-land there is no time. Suddenly the timber of his axe turns to dust, his chin falls, and he tumbles over the checker-board. The fairies are gone; the stones are warm to his touch; his iron axe-head is rusty and half buried in the ground. He has grown a long white beard, his hat has rotted away, his joints are stiff, his hair has burst its topknot string and hangs grayish-white down his back. Hobbling into the village he is knocked flat by a glass window, nearly run over by a house on wheels that hums like a squirrel — a trolley. When the stone drops from his mouth his tongue is loosed, and a dignified gentleman answers that a wood-cutter of that name went up into the mountains five hundred years ago and was eaten by a tiger; yonder in the graveyard are buried ten or more generations of his descendants. Next morning all that is seen of Keel Wee is a mass of dust, rags, some bones and much long white hair — and around his grave spring up strange flowers that bloom only on the high mountains.
summary.zh: 平壤樵夫奇遇：入山見二仙對弈，凝神觀之。仙投桃核一枚於其口，遂忘歲月。斧柄朽而墜，鬚髮皆白。歸村則電線、玻璃、鐵車遍佈，衣冠皆非。詢其家，則五百年前其人已為虎所食，墳中子孫十餘世矣。翌日樵夫化為塵土白髮一堆，墳頭生山中異花。

sensitivity.note: Rip Van Winkle / Urashima-type tale with a modern coda; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Over a half thousand years ago there lived in a northern village, near Ping Yang, a wood-cutter named Keel Wee. Arriving in the woods at a clearing, he spied at some distance off two fairy-like beings, dressed in the costume of the Chow dynasty of two thousand years ago; they sat on stones and played the game of go-ban. Coming near, the woodman took a respectful attitude, and the two fairies seemed by eye-winks to invite him to look on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Woodman and the Mountain Fairies' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 五百多年前，平壤附近的一個北方村落裡，住著一個名叫基爾威（Keel Wee）的樵夫。他來到林中一片空地，望見不遠處有兩個仙人般的人物，穿著兩千年前周朝的服飾；他們坐在石上，下著圍棋。樵夫走近，擺出恭敬的姿態，那兩位仙人似乎以眼色示意，邀他觀看。

passages.text: Forgetting himself and his manners, he stretched forth his right hand to move one of the pieces. At once the fairy nearest to him gave him a crack on the fingers for his impudence, and jerked his arm away; then, without saying a word, he took out from his wallet something that looked like a persimmon seed and put it in the woodman's mouth. Hour after hour the game proceeded; Keel Wee became more and more wrapped up in the game, for he had forgotten that with mountain spirits there is no night or morning, nor passing of the hours — in fairy-land there is no time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Woodman and the Mountain Fairies' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他忘乎所以，也顧不得禮數，伸出右手去移動其中一枚棋子。離他最近的那位仙人立刻因他這份冒失，在他指節上敲了一記，猛地把他的手臂拽開；接著，那仙人一言不發，從囊中取出某樣看似柿子核的東西，放進樵夫的嘴裡。棋局一小時又一小時地進行下去；吉威愈來愈沉醉於這盤棋，因為他已忘了：與山中的精靈同在，是沒有夜晚與清晨之分的，也沒有時辰的流逝——在仙境之中，是沒有時間的。

passages.text: Suddenly the timber of his axe seemed to turn to dust and his chin fell; he tumbled over, upsetting the checker-board. When he looked up, the fairies were gone, and the stones they had used as seats were warm to his touch. He put his hand to his breast and found that he had grown a long white beard; the iron axe-head was rusty and half buried in the ground, his hat rotted away, his joints stiff, his clothes a mass of rags, and his hair had burst its topknot string and hung down his back grayish-white.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Woodman and the Mountain Fairies' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 忽然，他斧頭的木材似乎化為塵土，他的下巴也垂落了下來；他一個踉蹌翻倒，撞翻了棋盤。等他抬頭一看，仙人們已不見蹤影，而他們曾當作座位的石頭，摸上去仍是溫熱的。他把手按向胸口，發現自己已長出長長的白鬍鬚；鐵斧頭生了鏽，半埋在地裡，他的帽子爛掉了，關節僵硬，衣裳成了一團破布，頭髮也撐斷了髮髻的繩子，灰白地垂在背後。

passages.text: Instead of the two grinning idol posts that had stood before every Korean hamlet since the days of Kija, there was a line of high thick poles with iron wire stretching for miles; his face was flattened against something hard which he could see through, and a young man shouted, 'Here, you mountain daddy, let that glass alone.' A house on wheels came right at him on two lines of shining iron, and the conductor called, 'Hello, old goblin, where did you get your pumpkin mouth? Look out or you'll swallow the moon. Get out of the way of the trolley.' Catching sight of a dignified gentleman in flowing white clothes, Keel Wee bowed his head low; as he did so the stone put in his mouth by the fairies dropped out, and his tongue was loosed. The gentleman cried, 'Heavens! man, are you a beggar-spirit of the mountains? Your speech sounds like the dialect spoken in these parts five hundred years ago; the head of such a family, a wood-cutter, is reported to have gone up into the mountains and was eaten up by a tiger. Yonder in the graveyard are buried ten or more generations of his descendants.' Next morning, all that was seen of Keel Wee was a mass of dust, rags, some bones, and much long white hair; when they buried him, there sprang up around his grave strange flowers that bloomed only on the high mountains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Woodman and the Mountain Fairies' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前自箕子時代起便立在每個朝鮮村落前的兩尊咧嘴而笑的木偶柱不見了，取而代之的是一排排又高又粗的柱子，鐵絲綿延數里；他的臉貼在某種堅硬而能看穿的東西上，一個年輕人喊道：「喂，你這個山裡老爹，別碰那玻璃。」一棟裝著輪子的房子順著兩道閃亮的鐵軌直朝他駛來，車掌喊道：「喂，老妖怪，你那南瓜嘴是打哪兒來的？當心點，不然你要把月亮吞下去了。快讓開，別擋著電車。」吉威瞥見一位身穿飄逸白衣、氣度莊重的紳士，便深深低頭行禮；就在他低頭之際，仙人放進他嘴裡的那顆石子掉了出來，他的舌頭也鬆開了。那紳士驚呼道：「天哪！漢子，你是山裡的乞丐鬼嗎？你說話的腔調，聽起來像是五百年前這一帶所講的方言；據說這樣一個家族的族長，一個樵夫，曾上山去，被老虎吃掉了。那邊的墓地裡，葬著他的子孫十幾代呢。」第二天早晨，吉威所剩下的，只有一堆塵土、破布、幾根骨頭，以及許多長長的白髮；人們埋葬他時，他的墳墓周圍長出了奇異的花朵，那花只在高山上綻放。

title.en: Gucumatz the Wonderful King: Seven Days of Transformation
title.zh: 奇王庫庫馬茲：七日化形

region.en: Q'umarkaj (Utatlan), K'iche' highlands, Guatemala (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 4, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861; quoted in Brinton, The Folk-Lore of Yucatan

license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: Truly this Gucumatz became a wonderful king: every seven days he ascended to the sky, and every seven days he followed the path to the abode of the dead; every seven days he put on the nature of a serpent and became truly a serpent; of an eagle, of a tiger, of coagulated blood — and became truly an eagle, a tiger, coagulated blood.
summary.zh: 誠然，這位庫庫馬茲成了奇妙的君王：每七日他昇天，每七日他行至亡者之居；每七日他披蛇性而成真蛇；披鷹性、豹性、凝血之性，而成真鷹、真豹、真凝血。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Truly this Gucumatz became a wonderful king. Every seven days he ascended to the sky, and every seven days he followed the path to the abode of the dead; every seven days he put on the nature of a serpent and he became truly a serpent; every seven days he put on the nature of an eagle and again of a tiger, and he became truly an eagle and a tiger; every seven days also he put on the nature of coagulated blood, and then he was nothing else but coagulated blood.
passages.note: Quoted from the Popol Wuj, Part 4, as reproduced in Brinton, The Folk-Lore of Yucatan (Brasseur 1861 base text); not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 這位古庫馬茨果真成了一位奇妙的君王。每隔七日，他便升上天空；每隔七日，他便循著通往亡者居所之路而去；每隔七日，他便披上蛇的本性，果真成了一條蛇；每隔七日，他便披上鷹的本性，又披上虎的本性，果真成了一隻鷹、一隻虎；每隔七日，他也披上凝結之血的本性，那時他便別無其他，只是凝結之血。

title.en: The K'iche' Prisoner of Rabinal
title.zh: 拉維納爾的基切俘虜

region.en: Rabinal (Rabinaleb'), Baja Verapaz, Guatemala
region.zh: 危地馬拉下維拉帕斯拉維納爾

period: K'iche' dance-drama, fifteenth-century (performed to this day); recorded mid-19th c.

source.work: Rabinal Achi, a fifteenth-century Maya dance-drama (K'iche' script; paraphrase after Tedlock 2003)

license: Script is a fifteenth-century K'iche' composition; paraphrase of modern scholarly translations only

summary.en: A K'iche' warrior is captured by the eagle and jaguar knights of Rabinal. Before the king, he refuses to kneel, names his deeds in war, and claims the right to speak before his death. He is feted, fed, and led through the town in the dance of the captive — then sacrificed to the gods of the town, dying on his feet with his own words as his monument.
summary.zh: 一名基切戰士為拉維納爾的鷹與豹騎士所擒。國王面前，他不肯下跪，歷數其戰功，並聲言死前有言語之權。他被設宴款待、餵養，並以俘虜之舞引行全城——終被獻祭於城中諸神，昂然而死，以其言語為碑。

sensitivity.note: Rabinal Achi is a living Maya ceremonial performed annually at Rabinal (January 25, feast of San Pablo); describe respectfully.

passages.text: The K'iche' Achi, captured in war by the warriors of Rabinal, is brought before the lord of the town. He will not kneel: 'I am a K'iche' lord; my heart stands within me.' He names the towns he has fought and the warriors he has faced, and demands that his speech be heard before he dies.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Rabinal Achi, scenes of the prisoner's defiance (Tedlock 2003); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那位在戰爭中被拉比納爾的戰士所俘的基切阿奇人，被帶到該城君主面前。他不肯下跪：「我是基切的領主；我的心志立於我身之內。」他一一說出自己曾與之交戰的城鎮、曾正面相抗的戰士，並要求在他死去之前，先聽他把話說完。

passages.text: The lord of Rabinal does not deny him: the prisoner is feted, given cacao and drink and the honored seat, and warned that his death is fixed. 'Then I shall die on my feet,' says the K'iche', 'with my words before me' — and the town prepares the dance of the captive.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Rabinal Achi (Tedlock 2003); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 拉比納爾的君主並未拒絕他：這名俘虜受到款待，獲賜可可與飲品，並坐上尊位，同時被告知他的死期已定。「那麼我便站著死去，」那基切人說道，「讓我的話語立於我身前」——於是全城著手準備俘虜之舞。

canonical_translation: Dennis Tedlock, Rabinal Achi: A Mayan Drama of War and Sacrifice (2003)

narrative.en:
The Rabinal Achi is the one complete pre-Columbian Maya drama to survive, preserved in a K'iche' script from the fifteenth century and performed every January 25 at Rabinal in Baja Verapaz. Its plot is a single action: a K'iche' warrior — the K'iche' Achi — has been captured in war by the eagle and jaguar knights of the town of Rabinal, and the drama is the working out of his death.

Brought before the king, the prisoner refuses to kneel and refuses the honors he is offered until his words are heard. He rehearses his own name and lineage, the battles of the great war between the K'iche' and Rabinal, and the places where he fought. The king of Rabinal answers with something between magnanimity and mockery: he grants the prisoner cacao, drink, a seat, even the companionship of his own daughters' household — but the sentence stands. The prisoner, for his part, asks that his death be honorable: he will die standing, his speech delivered, his name carried by the dance that follows it.

The second half of the drama is the sacrifice in performance. The eagle and jaguar knights — the two military orders of Rabinal — lead the captive through the dance-ground of the town in the dance of the prisoner, amid the sound of drums, trumpets, and whistles, while masked dancers take the parts of the king and his court. The K'iche' Achi is shown the instruments of his death, praises the beauty of his captors' town as a bridegroom praises, and at the climax asks to be tied to the sacrificial scaffold. His heart is given to the gods of Rabinal; the drama ends with the town justified and the prisoner immortal in speech.

As a corpus record, the Rabinal Achi supplies the Maya counterpart of the 'death before honor' cycle in other traditions — the tested hero whose speech is his victory — and preserves a ritual machinery (masked dance, the paired knight orders, the scaffold sacrifice) documented also in the Popol Wuj's ballcourt sacrifices. Its living performance under Catholic feast-day sponsorship makes it a textbook case of a colonial-era survival: the dance continued by being folded into the calendar of the conquering church.

The performance context matters as much as the text. The dance is danced every year on the feast of San Pablo, January 25, in the plaza of Rabinal, with masks, feathers, drums, and the two paired orders of eagle and jaguar knights; the roles are inherited by families, and the drama is taught as a whole, in K'iche', to each new generation of dancers. UNESCO lists it as a Masterpiece of the Intangible Heritage of Humanity precisely because the fifteenth-century script is still the performed script: the prisoner still refuses to kneel, still speaks his lineage, and still dies upright on the scaffold to the sound of the same drums. As a corpus record it anchors the Maya death-and-honor cycle and supplies the closest thing in the Maya corpus to a complete heroic drama.

functions: Charter of the Rabinal annual dance (January 25) still performed with masks and the eagle-jaguar knight pairs
Theology of the honorable captive death: speech, upright posture, sacrifice to town gods
Encodes the K'iche'-Rabinal war cycle as ritual memory

variants.name: Brasseur de Bourbourg's 1862 transcription
variants.text_tradition: K'iche' MS collected at Rabinal, mid-19th c.; French edition Brasseur 1862
variants.summary: The earliest transcription; differences in wording but the same five-part action.

primary_sources.citation: K'iche' dance-drama script, fifteenth century; Tedlock trans. 2003

secondary_sources.work: Dennis Tedlock, Rabinal Achi: A Mayan Drama of War and Sacrifice
secondary_sources.citation: Tedlock, 2003, Boulder: University Press of Colorado

source_urls.description: UNESCO entry on the living performance of the Rabinal Achi

sensitivity_guidance: The Rabinal Achi is performed by the Rabinal community as living ceremony. Do not reproduce restricted performance texts; use published scholarly translations, paraphrase, and credit the community's ownership of the dance.

title.en: The Eagle and Jaguar Knights of Rabinal
title.zh: 拉維納爾的鷹豹騎士

region.en: Rabinal, Baja Verapaz, Guatemala
region.zh: 危地馬拉下維拉帕斯拉維納爾

period: K'iche' dance-drama, fifteenth century

source.work: Rabinal Achi (paraphrase after Tedlock 2003)

license: Script is a fifteenth-century K'iche' composition; paraphrase only

summary.en: Two military orders serve the town of Rabinal: the eagle knights and the jaguar knights, masked dancers armed with bows, arrows, and bludgeons. It is they who capture the K'iche' prisoner in the field, they who lead him to the king, and they who execute him at the scaffold — the paired orders frame the entire drama as a single ritual machine of war.
summary.zh: 拉維納爾城有兩支武士團：鷹騎士與豹騎士，戴假面，持弓箭與棍棒。戰場上擒獲基切俘虜者，引其見王者，刑於架下者——皆此二團；一劇之首尾，盡由這對成對的武力圈成。

sensitivity.note: Living Maya ceremony; describe respectfully.

passages.text: The dance-drama is framed by two military orders of Rabinal, the eagle knights and the jaguar knights, who capture the K'iche' warrior in the field, march him before the king, and conduct the sacrifice at the scaffold — masked, armed with bows and bludgeons, and accompanied by drums, trumpets and whistles.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Rabinal Achi (Tedlock 2003); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這齣舞蹈劇由拉維納爾的兩個軍事教團——鷹武士與美洲豹武士——所框架，他們在田野中擒獲基切戰士，押解他至國王面前，並在刑臺上執行獻祭——他們戴著面具，手持弓與棍棒，並伴以鼓、號角與哨聲。

title.en: The Ball Court in the Sky
title.zh: 天上的球場

region.en: Chichen Itza (Great Ball Court), Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦奇琴伊察大球場

period: Studies published 1910-12 (Stansbury Hagar); codices medieval

source.work: Stansbury Hagar, The Celestial Bear and the Elements of the Maya and Mexican Zodiacs, in Maya Religion and Mythology collection

summary.en: The second asterism named by the chroniclers is Citlaltlachtli, the Ball Ground: a rectangular figure approximated by the stars of Leo's head, representing the ball courts found in Mexican and Yucatec ruins where the game of tlachtli — Maya, pok-ta-pok — was played. A pictograph in the Borgia Codex shows a deity sacrificed on a court on which the red and black Tezcatlipoca are at play; the ball represents the sun, and the court itself was primarily a temple consecrated by mystic rites.
summary.zh: 編年史所名第二星象即「球場」：一矩形星群，約合獅子座頭部諸星——即墨西哥與猶加敦遺址中所見賽球場之形，特拉斯克利——馬雅語波克塔波克——在此舉行。博爾吉亞抄本繪一神明受祭於球場之上，紅黑特茲卡特利波卡正在對局；球即太陽，而球場本身先是一座經秘儀祝聖的神廟。

sensitivity.note: Early twentieth-century scholarship; paraphrase only.

passages.text: The second asterism named by Tezozomoc is Citlaltlachtli, Ball ground Asterism. Sahagun shows this as a rectangular figure similar to the ball courts found in various Mexican and Yucatec ruins, in which the favorite game of Tlachtli, Maya Pok-ta-pok, was played. The outlines of the figure are closely approximated by the stars of the head of Leo.
passages.note: Condensed from Stansbury Hagar, Elements of the Maya and Mexican Zodiacs; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 特索索莫克所命名的第二個星群是 Citlaltlachtli，即球場星群。薩阿貢將其繪為一個矩形圖形，類似於在墨西哥與尤卡坦各地遺址中所見的球場，其中最受喜愛的球戲 Tlachtli（馬雅的 Pok-ta-pok）即在此進行。該圖形的輪廓與獅子座頭部的星辰十分相近。

passages.text: A number of representations of this ball court appear in the codices amongst other astronomical signs. One represents a deity sacrificed on a court upon which the red and black Tezcatlipoca are at play. Brinton and others have shown the probable association of the game with the solar journey, the ball representing the sun; the ball court itself was primarily a temple consecrated by mystic rites.
passages.note: Condensed from Hagar; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 此球場的若干圖像出現在抄本中，與其他天文徵象並列。其中一幅描繪一位神祇在球場上被獻祭，而紅與黑的特斯卡特利波卡正在該球場上嬉戲。布林頓等人已指出此球戲與太陽運行之間的可能關聯，球代表太陽；球場本身主要是一座經由神祕儀式所祝聖的神廟。

title.en: The Ara of Fire Descends at Noon
title.zh: 正午降臨的火鸚鵡

region.en: Izamal, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦伊扎馬爾

period: Studies published 1910-12 (Stansbury Hagar); codices medieval

source.work: Stansbury Hagar, The Elements of the Maya and Mexican Zodiacs, in Maya Religion and Mythology collection

summary.en: At Izamal Cancer is called Kinich Kakmo, the Sun-eye and the Ara of Fire, from the solar rays and a group of stars which were supposed to descend at noon upon an altar, as an ara with fiery plumage descends in its flight. In the codices the ara is often reproduced beside the water goddess. This supposed descent was a feature of the Mayan ritual of the supplementary days under Cancer.
summary.zh: 在伊扎馬爾，巨蟹座名為基尼奇·卡克莫——「日之目」與「火之鸚鵡」——得名於日光，以及相傳正午降於祭壇的星群，正如火羽鸚鵡飛降之姿。抄本中，鸚鵡常繪於水神之側。此「降臨」正是巨蟹座補充日馬雅儀式之一景。

sensitivity.note: Early twentieth-century scholarship; paraphrase only.

passages.text: At Izamal Cancer is called Kinich Kakmo the Sun-eye and the Ara of Fire, from the solar rays and a group of stars which were supposed to descend at noon upon an altar, as an ara with fiery plumage descends in its flight. In the codices the ara is often reproduced beside the water goddess. This supposed descent was a feature of the Mayan ritual of the supplementary days under Cancer; the Mexican festival in honor of the rain gods and the goddess of salt corresponds in time.
passages.note: Condensed from Stansbury Hagar, Elements of the Maya and Mexican Zodiacs; not verbatim throughout. / Condensed from Hagar; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 在伊薩馬爾，巨蟹座被稱為 Kinich Kakmo，即「太陽之眼」與「火之金剛鸚鵡」，此名源於太陽光線以及一組被認為會在正午降臨於祭壇上的星辰，正如一隻披著火焰羽毛的金剛鸚鵡在飛行中降落。在抄本中，金剛鸚鵡常被繪於水女神身旁。這種所謂的降臨是馬雅在巨蟹座之下補充日儀式的一項特徵；而墨西哥人為雨神與鹽女神舉行的節慶在時間上與之相應。

title.en: The Prophecy of the Bearded Strangers from the East
title.zh: 東方鬚客之預言

region.en: Tixcacayom (Mani), Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦蒂希卡科約姆（馬尼）

period: Prophecy current before 1517; recorded by Diego Lopez de Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688)

source.work: Diego Lopez de Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688), lib. II, on the prophecies of the Indian priests

summary.en: Chilam Balam, great priest of Tixcacayom, prophesied that in the end of the thirteenth age, at the city of Tancab, the sign of a God of the heights would come and the Cross would manifest itself to the world, shining from pole to pole. 'Your Father comes, you Ytzalanos; your brother comes, you Tantunites. Receive your bearded guests from the East, who come bringing the sign of God.' The priest had a stone cross made and set in the temple courts, calling it the true tree of the world.
summary.zh: 蒂希卡科約姆的大祭司奇拉姆·巴拉姆預言：第十三紀之末，於坦卡布之城，將有高處之神的記號來到，十字向全世界顯現，自極北至極南光芒大作。「你們的父親來了，伊察人啊；你們的兄弟來了，坦通人啊。迎接你們自東方而來、攜神之記號的鬚客。」祭司遂命人琢石十字，立於神廟庭院之中，稱之為世界的真樹。

sensitivity.note: Seventeenth-century colonial record of a Yucatec prophecy; paraphrase of the Spanish original.

passages.text: In the end of the thirteenth age, being in his puhanga of Ytza and the city named Tancab, there shall come the sign of a God who is in the heights, and the Cross shall manifest itself to the world, by which the orb was lighted. There will be a division among the wills when this sign is brought in the time to come. The priests, before they come within a league and a quarter, shall see the Cross which appears to them and dawns from pole to pole.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688), lib. II, prophecy of Chilam Balam; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在第十三個紀元的末期，當他身處伊察人的普漢加以及名為坦卡布的城市時，將有一位身居高處之神的神蹟降臨，而十字架將向世界顯現，世界即由此而被照亮。當這神蹟在未來被帶來時，眾意志之間將發生分裂。祭司們在進入一里又四分之一之前，將看見向他們顯現、從一極照耀至另一極的十字架。

passages.text: The cult of the vain gods shall cease. Your Father comes, you Ytzalanos; and your brother comes, you Tantunites. Receive your bearded guests from the East, who come bringing the sign of God. God is one, and merciful. The time of our life comes. Do not fear the world. Let us raise his sign on high, raise it to adore and to see it: the Cross we must raise. In opposition to the lie it appears today, against the first tree of the world. This is the sign of a God of the heights; this the Ytzalanas adore.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cogolludo (1688), prophecy of Chilam Balam; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 對虛妄神祇的崇拜將要止息。你們的父來了，你們這些伊察蘭人；你們的兄弟也來了，你們這些坦圖尼特人。迎接你們來自東方的蓄鬚賓客吧，他們帶著神的神蹟而來。神是獨一的，且是仁慈的。我們生命的時刻來臨了。不要懼怕這世界。讓我們將祂的神蹟高高舉起，舉起它來敬拜並瞻仰它：我們必須舉起十字架。為對抗謊言，它今日顯現，對抗世界的第一棵樹。這是一位身居高處之神的神蹟；這是伊察蘭人所敬拜的。

passages.text: Those who believe shall be lighted in the age to come. Behold if it imports you what I say, warns and charges your interpreter and master of credit, Balam by name; and with this I have finished saying what the true God commanded me, that the world may hear it. Soon after the coming of the Spaniards, the Indians, seeing how much reverence was paid to the Cross, held certain what their Prophet had told them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cogolludo (1688); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 信者將在來世得蒙光照。請看，我所說的話若對你有益，你的譯者兼可信賴之師，名叫巴蘭（Balam）者，便警告並囑咐你；至此，我已說完真神所吩咐我的一切，好讓世人得以聽見。不久之後，西班牙人來到，印第安人見十字架備受崇敬，便確信他們的先知所告訴他們的話。

language: Seventeenth-century Spanish record of a Yucatec prophecy
canonical_translation: Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688)

narrative.en:
Cogolludo preserves, in his 1688 history, the fullest colonial version of the prophecy cycle that Yucatec tradition attached to the coming of the Spaniards. The great priest of Tixcacayom, Chilam Balam (the 'jaguar priest'), is made to speak in the first person of the end of the thirteenth age: the sign of a God of the heights will appear, the Cross will dawn 'from pole to pole', the cult of the vain gods will cease, and bearded guests from the East — the Ytzalanos' father, the Tantunites' brother — must be received with good will because they carry the sign of God. The priest commands that his people raise the sign on high and adore it, in opposition 'to the lie' and 'against the first tree of the world' — a striking formulation in which the new cross displaces the old world-tree as the true axis of the world.

The historic kernel the chronicler gives is the episode of the woven mantle: before the strangers arrived, the prophet had a tribute-mantle woven in the pattern that the new tribute would take, and had it offered to the idols for safekeeping; he also had a cross made of stone and set in the courts of the temples, saying that this was the true tree of the world and that many peoples would come to venerate it. When Montejo entered Yucatán and the Indians saw the reverence paid to the Cross, they 'held certain what their Prophet had told them.'

Cogolludo reports several such prophecies from different priests (one from Ah Na Puc Tun about the last age purified by fire), and argues — with theological ingenuity — that the gift of true prophecy might have been given even to gentile priests, citing the example of Balaam: the prophetic word does not justify the prophet but serves the people who must hear it. As a corpus record this is the Maya 'return of the culture hero' motif transposed into colonial eschatology: the bearded god of the east whom the codices called Kukulcan reappears as the expected bearded strangers, and the prophecy becomes the ritual script with which the Maya of Yucatán narrated the catastrophe that overtook them.

The comparative value of the episode lies in its double framing. Read from within, it is a Maya prophecy: a priest foresees the foreigners, commands the reception of their sign, and orders a woven mantle as the pattern of the tribute to come. Read from without, it is a missionary construction: Cogolludo selects, translates, and theologically glosses the material to show that God announced the Gospel to the Indians through their own priests, citing Balaam as his warrant. Both readings are true, and the corpus record keeps both. For the Motif Atlas the record is the Maya contribution to the return-of-the-god cluster: the culture hero who promised to come from the east - Kukulcan, the bearded lord - is the figure whose return the bearded strangers are made to fulfill, in a colonial mirror image of the Popol Wuj expectation of the true dawn.

functions: Colonial-era eschatology: the conquest narrated as the fulfillment of a native prophecy
Explains the stone crosses found in Yucatec temple courts as pre-Christian tokens
Authorizes submission to the conquerors as obedience to the prophetic word

variants.name: Chilam Balam of Chumayel, katun prophecies
variants.text_tradition: Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel (Roys 1933)
variants.summary: The same expectation in katun form: '11 Ahau is the beginning of the count... the foreigners arrived from the east.'

primary_sources.work: Diego Lopez de Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan
primary_sources.citation: 1688, lib. II, cap. 10 (prophecies)

secondary_sources.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, Landa's Relacion
secondary_sources.citation: Tozzer, 1941, Cambridge: Peabody Museum (notes on the prophecies)

sensitivity_guidance: The prophecy text is mediated by a missionary author arguing for conversion; note the colonial frame rather than presenting it as unmediated Maya voice.

title.en: Ah Na Puc Tun: The World Purified by Fire
title.zh: 阿·納·普克·圖恩：以火淨世

region.en: Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦

period: Prophecy current before the Spanish arrival; recorded by Cogolludo 1688

source.work: Diego Lopez de Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688), lib. II

summary.en: Another gentile priest, called Ah Na Puc Tun, made the subjection to the Law of Grace notorious by his mouth, saying: In the last age, according to this reckoning, the cult of the vain gods will end, and the world will be purified with fire. He who sees it and weeps his sins with sorrow shall be called blessed.
summary.zh: 另有一位名阿·納·普克·圖恩的異教祭司，以其口使臣服於恩典之法一事昭然，他說：在最後的紀元，虛妄諸神的崇拜將終止，世界將以火淨化。凡見此事而含淚痛悔其罪者，有福了。

sensitivity.note: Seventeenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of the Spanish original.

passages.text: Notoria la hizo por la boca de otro Gentil Sacerdote, llamado Ah Na Puc Tun, que dijo: En la última edad, según esta determinación, habrá fin el culto de Dioses vanos, y el mundo será purificado con fuego. El que esto viere, y será llamado bienaventurado, si con dolor llorare sus pecados.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688), lib. II; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此事由另一位異教祭司，名叫阿納普克通（Ah Na Puc Tun）者之口而為人所知，他說：按此定論，在最後的時代，虛妄諸神的崇拜將告終結，世界將以火潔淨。凡見此者，若痛哭己罪，便將被稱為有福的。

passages.text: The antiquity of this priest has not been made out, but he appears to have flourished before the coming of the Spaniards, since he speaks of the last age; and by age they understood the space of time of twenty years. With the introduction of our Holy Catholic Faith the cult of the idols ceased, at least publicly, and this new world was purified with the fire of the Holy Spirit.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cogolludo (1688); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這位祭司的年代尚未考明，但他似乎興盛於西班牙人到來之前，因為他談及最後的時代；而他們所謂的一個時代，是指二十年的時間。隨著我們神聖天主教信仰的傳入，偶像崇拜至少公開地停止了，而這個新世界則以聖靈之火得以潔淨。

title.en: The Stone Cross: The True Tree of the World
title.zh: 石十字：世界的真樹

region.en: Mani, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦馬尼

period: Events before 1517; recorded by Cogolludo 1688

source.work: Diego Lopez de Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688), lib. II

summary.en: The prophet commanded that a cross be made of stone and set in the courts of the temples, saying that this was the true tree of the world, and that many peoples would come to see it and venerate it from that time — the reason why, when the Spaniards asked them, the Indians said they went toward where the sun was born.
summary.zh: 先知命人琢石為十字，立於諸神廟庭院之中，說此乃世界的真樹，自此而後將有許多人民來見它、敬它——這也是西班牙人問路時，土人答以「往日出之地去」的緣故。

sensitivity.note: Seventeenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of the Spanish original.

passages.text: He commanded the lord of Mani, who was called Mochan Xiu, to offer that mantle to the idols, that it might be kept; and the sign of the Cross he had made of stone, and set it in the courts of the temples, where it was usually seen, saying that this was the true tree of the world, and that for this many peoples would come to see it and venerate it from that time.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cogolludo (1688), lib. II; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他吩咐馬尼（Mani）的領主，名叫莫昌·修（Mochan Xiu）者，將那件斗篷獻給偶像，以便保存；他又用石頭做成十字架的記號，安置在神廟的庭院中，即通常可見之處，說這就是世界真正的樹，並說因此將有許多民族從那時起來觀看並敬奉它。

title.en: The Mantle of Tribute Woven as a Prophecy
title.zh: 織成預言的貢賦披毯

region.en: Mani, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦馬尼

period: Events before 1517; recorded by Cogolludo 1688

source.work: Diego Lopez de Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688), lib. II

summary.en: The prophet had a mantle of tribute woven, and said that in that manner the tribute was going to be paid to those people; and he commanded the lord of Mani to offer the mantle to the idols, that it might be kept — a woven prophecy deposited in the temple, to be read against the tribute lists of the conquerors.
summary.zh: 先知命人織一貢賦披毯，並說：這些人的貢賦，就要照這式樣繳納；又命馬尼之君將此毯獻於神像之前，妥為收藏——一張織入廟中的預言，將與征服者的貢冊相對而讀。

sensitivity.note: Seventeenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of the Spanish original.

passages.text: Hizo texer una manta de tributo, y dixo, que de aquella manera havia de ser el tributo que se avia de pagar a aquellas gentes: y mando al Señor de Mani, que se llamaba Mochan Xiu, que se la ofreciese a los Idolos, para que estuviese guardada.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cogolludo (1688), lib. II; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他命人織了一件貢賦用的斗篷，並說貢賦當以那種方式繳納給那些民族；他又吩咐馬尼的領主，名叫莫昌·修（Mochan Xiu）者，將它獻給偶像，以便保存。

title.en: Nacom Balam of Conil, the Old Man Who Received Montejo
title.zh: 科尼爾的納科姆·巴拉姆：接待蒙特霍的老人

region.en: Conil, coast of Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦海岸科尼爾

period: Events of 1527-28; recorded by Cogolludo 1688

source.work: Diego Lopez de Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688), lib. II

summary.en: They came to a place called Coni, where there was only a rancho, where an old man lived, called Nacom Balam, who afterwards was named Pedro, because this was the name of the principal Spaniard. The Indians did not determine at once to take up arms against the Spaniards, but provided themselves, waiting what would befall with them.
summary.zh: 他們行至一處名科尼之地，那裡只有一座棚屋，住著一位老人，名納科姆·巴拉姆，後來改名佩德羅，因這是那位西班牙首要人物的名字。印第安人並未即刻舉兵，而是各自治備，靜觀其變。

sensitivity.note: Seventeenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of the Spanish original.

passages.text: They were going from pueblo to pueblo until they reached one called Conil. It was not called Conil but Coni, because Conil is another seaport; and there was only a rancho, where an old man lived, called Nacom Balam, who afterwards was named Pedro, because this was the name of the principal Spaniard.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cogolludo (1688), lib. II; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們從一個村鎮走到另一個村鎮，直到抵達一個名叫科尼爾（Conil）的地方。它本不叫科尼爾，而叫科尼（Coni），因為科尼爾是另一處海港；那裡只有一間茅屋，住著一位老人，名叫納孔·巴蘭（Nacom Balam），他後來被取名為佩德羅（Pedro），因為這是一位主要西班牙人的名字。

title.en: The Eaters of Anonas: Indians Naming the Spaniards
title.zh: 食番荔枝者：土人為西班牙人命名

region.en: Coba, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦科巴

period: Events of 1527-28; recorded by Cogolludo 1688

source.work: Diego Lopez de Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688), lib. II

summary.en: They went to the pueblo of Coba, now depopulated, and there it was that the Spaniards were called by the Indians in their language Ah makal kopob, which means the eaters of anonas, a fruit of that land; the Indians, amazed, watched them eat the fruit without considering whether it was noxious or not.
summary.zh: 他們行至科巴村（今已荒蕪）；正是在那裡，西班牙人被土人以土語稱為「阿·馬卡爾·科波布」——食番荔枝者，番荔枝乃當地果物。土人驚異地看他們吃這果子，全然不問其是否有毒。

sensitivity.note: Seventeenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of the Spanish original.

passages.text: They passed to the pueblo of Coba, now depopulated, and there it was that the Spaniards were called by the Indians in their language Ah makal kopob, which means the eaters of anonas, which is a fruit of that land: the Indians were amazed to see them eat them without considering whether they were noxious or not.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cogolludo (1688), lib. II; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們前往如今已無人居住的科巴（Coba）村鎮，正是在那裡，印第安人以他們的語言稱西班牙人為「Ah makal kopob」，意即「吃番荔枝的人」，番荔枝是那片土地上的一種果實：印第安人見他們吃這些果子，卻毫不顧慮其是否有毒，因而大為驚異。

title.en: The Balche Vessels at the East of the God House
title.zh: 神屋東側的巴爾切酒槽

region.en: Lake Petha region, Chiapas
region.zh: 恰帕斯佩塔湖地區

period: Recorded 1901-03 (Tozzer fieldwork), published 1907

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part II: Religion of the Lacandones

summary.en: Owing to the necessity of fermentation, the balche must be made before the day of the rite. A large supply of the bark of the tree is collected and placed in one of the hollow logs situated at the east of the sacred hut; in a second hollow log a quantity of honey, or sugar cane and water, is placed. The syrup is strained and poured into the log containing the balche bark, and the contents allowed to ferment — sometimes for not more than a single day.
summary.zh: 因須發酵，巴爾切酒須於祭日之前釀成。取大量巴爾切樹皮，置於神屋東側的掏空木槽之一；另一槽盛蜂蜜——或蔗糖加水。糖漿濾淨，傾入盛樹皮之槽，令其發酵——有時僅一日即成。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); living ritual — describe respectfully.

passages.text: Owing to the necessity of fermentation, the balche must be made before the day set for the rite to come off. A large supply of the bark of the tree is collected and placed in one of the hollow logs made for the purpose and situated at the east of the sacred hut. In the second hollow log a quantity of honey or, if this is lacking, a large supply of sugar cane together with water is placed.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 由於發酵之必要，巴爾切（balche）必須在預定舉行儀式之日以前釀成。人們採集大量樹皮，放入為此目的而製作、位於聖屋東側的一根中空木幹之中。在第二根中空木幹裡，則放入一定量的蜂蜜，若無蜂蜜，則放入大量甘蔗連同水。

passages.text: The sirup is then strained and poured into the log containing the balche bark. The log is left uncovered and the contents allowed to ferment, sometimes for not more than a single day. The early accounts speak of this custom of drinking large quantities of balche as most healthful, and that after the common use of it was prohibited by the Spaniards, the natives suffered in consequence.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 隨後將糖漿濾出，倒入盛有巴爾切樹皮的那根木幹之中。木幹不加覆蓋，任其內容物發酵，有時不過一日而已。早期的記載稱，這種大量飲用巴爾切的習俗極為有益健康，並謂自從西班牙人禁止普遍飲用之後，原住民因而受苦。

title.en: Copal Before the Idols of the Encampment
title.zh: 營地諸神像前的柯巴脂

region.en: Lake Petha region, Chiapas
region.zh: 恰帕斯佩塔湖地區

period: Recorded 1901-03 (Tozzer fieldwork), published 1907

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part II

summary.en: In the prayers given before the idols, the other and lesser deities are invoked to come and carry the sacrifices offered and present them to 'the great lord.' The two Plumeria flowers, red and white, the father and mother of Nohochakyum, are placed one of each kind on the mouth of the brasero containing his idol, and the copal is burned before the stones brought home from the shrines.
summary.zh: 在神像前的禱詞中，另呼諸小神前來承載所獻犧牲，呈於「偉大之主」。紅白兩色雞蛋花——諾霍查庫姆之父與母——各一朵置於盛其神像的香爐口上；柯巴脂即焚於自聖地迎回的石像之前。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); living ritual — describe respectfully.

passages.text: In the prayers given before the idols, the other and lesser deities are invoked to come and carry the sacrifices offered and present them to 'the great lord.' Two flowers, the red Plumeria and the white Plumeria, are considered the father and mother respectively of Nohochakyum; one of each kind is placed on the mouth of the brasero containing the idol of Nohochakyum.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 在偶像前所誦的祈禱中，人們祈求其他較次級的神祇前來，攜走所獻的祭品，並將其呈獻給「偉大的主」。兩種花——紅雞蛋花與白雞蛋花——分別被視為諾霍奇阿克尤姆（Nohochakyum）的父親與母親；每種各取一朵，置於盛有諾霍奇阿克尤姆偶像的火盆口上。

title.en: Stones Carried Home from the Shrines of the Gods
title.zh: 自神聖地迎回的石像

region.en: Usumacinta River shrines, Chiapas
region.zh: 恰帕斯烏蘇馬辛塔河諸聖地

period: Recorded 1901-03 (Tozzer fieldwork), published 1907

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part II

summary.en: Only those gods are represented in an encampment to whose shrine a pilgrimage has been made and a stone either carved or otherwise brought back. These journeys cannot be made at will, but only after the god has shown himself as willing to receive such a pilgrimage; the home of Ioananohqu in a high cliff on the western shore of Lake Petha was visited in company with some Indians who went there to burn copal and offer sacrifices.
summary.zh: 營地中僅有那些曾往其聖地朝拜、並將雕成或取回之石迎回家的神明。此行不可任意為之，唯神自允之後方可；佩塔湖西岸高崖上的伊奧阿諾赫居所，即曾由印第安人相偕前往焚柯巴脂、行獻祭之地。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); living ritual — describe respectfully.

passages.text: All the gods named in the previous list are not usually represented in any one encampment. Only those are found to whose shrine a pilgrimage has been made and a stone either carved or otherwise brought back. These journeys cannot be made at will, but only after the god has shown himself as willing to receive such a pilgrimage.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 前文所列的一切神祇，通常並非都在任何一個營地中被供奉。只有那些曾有人前往其神龕朝聖、並帶回一塊雕刻或其他方式取得的石頭的神祇，才會被供奉。這些旅程不能任意而行，唯有在該神祇顯示願意接受此類朝聖之後方可成行。

passages.text: In a high cliff on the western shore of Lake Petha there lives the god Ioananohqu, and on the opposite side of the lake the deity called Kakoch. The home of the former is the only one that has been located precisely, the abode of the god having been visited in company with some Indians who went there to burn copal and offer sacrifices.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 在佩塔湖（Lake Petha）西岸的一處高崖上，住著神祇約阿納諾克（Ioananohqu）；而在湖的對岸，則住著名為卡科奇（Kakoch）的神祇。前者之居所是唯一被確切定位者，因為曾有人與一些前往該處焚燒柯巴脂並獻祭的印第安人同行，造訪了這位神祇的居所。

title.en: Suhuy Kaq: The Virgin Fire and Healing
title.zh: 蘇胡伊·卡克：聖潔之火與醫愈

region.en: Chiapas and Yucatan
region.zh: 恰帕斯與猶加敦

period: Recorded 1901-03 (Tozzer fieldwork), published 1907

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Parts II-III

summary.en: The god named Kaq (fire) lives near Tenosique; among the early Mayas there was a goddess called Suhuy Kaq (virgin fire), and this Lacandon god may be connected with her, as new fire has to be made at certain points in the various rites. Suhuyqaq is the spirit of the new fire, a god of healing: at every rite the old flame is put out and fire is drawn fresh for the gods.
summary.zh: 名為卡克（火）的神居於特諾西克附近；古馬雅人中有一位名蘇胡伊·卡克（貞潔之火）的女神，此拉坎敦神或與之相承——因各種祭儀中的特定環節都必須生新火。蘇胡伊·卡克即新火之靈、醫愈之神：每逢祭禮，舊火熄滅，為神另取新焰。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); living ritual — describe respectfully.

passages.text: The god named Kaq (fire) lives near Tenosique. Among the early Mayas there was a goddess called Suhuy Kaq (virgin fire). This god of the Lacandones may be connected with her, as new fire has to be made at certain points in the various rites. Suhuyqaq is the spirit of the new fire, a god of healing.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 名為卡克（Kaq，意為火）的神居住在特諾西克（Tenosique）附近。早期的瑪雅人之中有一位名為蘇胡伊·卡克（Suhuy Kaq，意為處女之火）的女神。這位拉坎敦人（Lacandones）的神可能與她有關，因為在各種儀式的某些特定時刻必須製造新火。蘇胡伊卡克（Suhuyqaq）是新火之靈，也是一位療癒之神。

title.en: Mensabak, the God Above the Rain Cloud
title.zh: 門薩巴克：雨雲之上的神

region.en: Near San Hipolito, Chiapas
region.zh: 恰帕斯聖伊波利托附近

period: Recorded 1901-03 (Tozzer fieldwork), published 1907

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part II

summary.en: Mensabak lives near San Hipolito; he is probably identified as the god of rain. He is also called Yumkanasabak — the god who is above the rain cloud — and this name is used when he is appealed to on behalf of a sick person. As Nohochakyum has the spirits of the east to aid him, so Mensabak has for his helpers the spirits of the west.
summary.zh: 門薩巴克居於聖伊波利托附近；或即雨神。他又名尤姆卡納薩巴克——「雨雲之上的神」——凡為病者祈禱時即以此名呼之。諾霍查庫姆有東方之靈為助，門薩巴克則以西方之靈為其僚屬。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); living ritual — describe respectfully.

passages.text: Mensabak lives near San Hipolito. He is probably identified as the god of rain. He is also called Yumkanasabak; the literal meaning would be the god, kana above, sabak the black powder — freely it is the god who is above the rain cloud. The latter name seems to be used when he is appealed to on behalf of a sick person. Just as Nohochakyum has the spirits of the east to aid him, so Mensabak has for his helpers the spirits of the west.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 門薩巴克（Mensabak）居住在聖伊波利托（San Hipolito）附近。他大概被認定為雨神。他也被稱為尤姆卡納薩巴克（Yumkanasabak）；字面意思會是「神，kana 在上，sabak 為黑色粉末」——意譯即為「位於雨雲之上的神」。後一個名字似乎是在為病人向他祈求時使用的。正如諾霍奇阿克尤姆（Nohochakyum）有東方之靈相助，門薩巴克也有西方之靈作為他的助手。

title.en: The Year-Bearer Pages of the Dresden Codex
title.zh: 德累斯頓抄本的歲首諸頁

region.en: Dresden Codex (Yucatec tradition), symbolic pin at Uxmal, Yucatan
region.zh: 德累斯頓抄本（猶加敦傳統），以墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾為象徵定位

period: Codex drawn c. 1200-1250; Forstemann facsimile 1880

source.work: Dresden Codex, pp. 25-28, Forstemann facsimile (1880); commentary in Schellhas (1904) and Tozzer (1941)

summary.en: Pages 25-28 of the Dresden Codex picture the four Uayeb rites that Landa describes: the year-bearer idols carried on litters, seated on the stone heaps at the four entrances of the town, each with its color, its Bacab, and its offerings. There are footprints on the idol, which Forstemann states represent the goal of a pilgrimage; the top and middle portions refer to the transportation of the idols, the bottom thirds to the feasts of the four Uayeb festivals.
summary.zh: 德累斯頓抄本25-28頁繪蘭達所述的四種瓦耶亞布祭儀：歲首神像被抬上擔架，安坐於鎮口四方的石堆之上，各具其色、其巴卡布與其祭品。神像上有足印，弗斯特曼謂其象徵朝聖之地；頁之上中二部繪神像的搬運，下三分之一繪四種瓦耶亞布祭的宴飲。

sensitivity.note: Published codex facsimile and public-domain commentary; paraphrase only.

passages.text: There is an extended discussion of the identification of idols, images, statues, and braziers in the four rituals inaugurating the years. The pages of the Dresden Codex (25-28) representing the Uayeb rites show the footprints on the idol or trunk which, Forstemann states, represent the goal of a pilgrimage; the top and middle portions refer to the transportation of the idols, whereas the bottom thirds refer to the feasts connected with the four Uayeb festivals.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1941), on Landa's New Year rituals and the Dresden pages; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 書中對四項開年儀式中偶像、圖像、雕像與火盆的辨識有詳盡的討論。德勒斯登抄本（Dresden Codex）中呈現烏阿耶布（Uayeb）儀式的書頁（第25至28頁）顯示了偶像或樹幹上的足跡，福斯特曼（Forstemann）指出這些足跡代表朝聖的目的地；頂部與中部部分涉及偶像的搬運，而下方三分之一則涉及與四個烏阿耶布節慶相關的宴會。

passages.text: In each of the four rituals Landa gives as 'the omen of the Bacab' four names, with the four colors, the four directions, and the four Pauah Tuns; the Chacs with them are rain gods comparable to the Tlalocs. It was in these very pages that Thomas showed the rites of the Uayeb days inaugurating the new years, the codical counterpart of the colonial description.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1941) and Schellhas (1904); not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 在蘭達（Landa）所述的四項儀式中，每一項都給出四個名字，作為「巴卡布（Bacab）的預兆」，並配以四種顏色、四個方位與四個帕烏阿赫通（Pauah Tun）；與之相伴的恰克（Chacs）是相當於特拉洛克（Tlalocs）的雨神。正是在這些書頁中，湯瑪斯（Thomas）展示了開創新年的烏阿耶布日儀式，即殖民時期記述在抄本中的對應內容。

title.en: Palm-Leaf Dogs for the Grave of the Dead
title.zh: 亡者墓上的棕櫚葉犬

region.en: Lake Petha region, Chiapas
region.zh: 恰帕斯佩塔湖地區

period: Recorded 1901-03 (Tozzer fieldwork), published 1907

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part II

summary.en: A mound about a foot high is made; ashes are sprinkled over it, and at each of the four corners there is placed a small figure made of palm leaves representing a dog — these are supposed to accompany the soul as guardians to its final resting place. Around the grave is a line of small sticks with bits of cloth dipped in beeswax, lit as rude candles, and a shelter of palm leaves is built over the grave with gourds of posol, water, and tortillas for the journey.
summary.zh: 墓上起一呎高的土冢，撒以灰；四隅各置棕櫚葉所製的小犬——人信其為靈之護衛，伴魂至其安息之地。墓環細枝一匝，枝頂置蘸蠟布片，家人點為粗燭；更以棕葉覆墓成棚，懸波索爾、水與玉米餅三瓢，以備魂之旅資。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); living funerary practice — describe respectfully.

passages.text: A mound about a foot high is made. Ashes are sprinkled over the mound, and at each of the four corners there is placed a small figure made of palm leaves and representing a dog. These are supposed to accompany the soul as guardians to its final resting place. Around the grave is a line of small sticks about four inches apart; on the top of each stick is a bit of cloth dipped in beeswax, lit by each member of the family as rude candles.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 築起一座約一英尺高的土丘。土丘上撒滿灰燼，並在四個角落各放置一個以棕櫚葉製成、代表狗的小人偶。據信這些狗會作為守護者陪伴靈魂前往其最終安息之地。墳墓周圍排著一圈小木棍，彼此相距約四英寸；每根木棍頂端都有一塊蘸了蜂蠟的布，由家中每位成員點燃，權作簡陋的蠟燭。

passages.text: A shelter of palm leaves is finally built over the grave. From the roof there is suspended a gourd filled with posol, another with water, and a third containing tortillas — this food, together with that placed directly on the grave, provisions the soul for its journey to the upper heavens.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 最後在墳墓上方搭建一座棕櫚葉的棚子。棚頂懸掛著一個裝滿波索爾（posol）的葫蘆、另一個裝水的葫蘆，以及第三個裝著玉米餅的葫蘆——這些食物連同直接放在墳上的食物，為靈魂前往上層天界的旅程提供補給。

title.en: They Ceased to Be Called Maya
title.zh: 他們不再被稱為馬雅人

region.en: Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦

period: Chumayel MS. written late 18th c.; Roys translation 1933

source.work: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, trans. Ralph L. Roys, 1933, ch. XX

license: Public domain (Roys 1933, not renewed at US Copyright Office)

summary.en: 8 Ahau was when their town was abandoned and they were scattered throughout the entire district. In the sixth katun after they were dispersed, then they ceased to be called Maya. 11 Ahau was the name of the katun when the Maya men ceased to be called Maya: they were called Christians, and their entire province became subject to St. Peter and the reigning King of Spain.
summary.zh: 八阿赫之年，其城被棄，族眾散於全境。離散後的第六卡特倫，他們便不再被稱為馬雅人。十一阿赫之卡特倫，馬雅人不再稱為馬雅：他們被稱為基督徒，全境臣服於聖伯多祿與西班牙在位之王。

sensitivity.note: Published colonial-era text; quote/paraphrase of Roys public-domain translation only.

passages.text: 8 Ahau was when their town was abandoned and they were scattered throughout the entire district. In the sixth katun after they were dispersed, then they ceased to be called Maya. 11 Ahau was the name of the katun when the Maya men ceased to be called Maya: they were called Christians; their entire province became subject to St. Peter and the reigning King of Spain.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. XX; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 8阿豪（Ahau）之時，他們的城鎮被棄，他們散居於整個地區。在他們離散之後的第六個卡盾（katun），他們便不再被稱為瑪雅。11阿豪是那個卡盾之名，其時瑪雅男子不再被稱為瑪雅：他們被稱為基督徒；他們整個省份歸屬於聖彼得與在位之西班牙國王。

title.en: The Third Chronicle: Katuns of the Itza
title.zh: 第三編年：伊察的卡特倫

region.en: Chichen Itza to Lake Peten, Yucatan-Guatemala
region.zh: 自奇琴伊察至佩滕湖（猶加敦-危地馬拉）

period: Chumayel MS. written late 18th c.; Roys translation 1933

source.work: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, trans. Ralph L. Roys, 1933, ch. XXI

license: Public domain (Roys 1933, not renewed at US Copyright Office)

summary.en: 5 Ahau was when the town of the ruler of Izamal, Kinich Kakmoo as well as Pop-hol Chan, was destroyed by Hunac Ceel. 1 Ahau was when the remainder of the Itza were driven out of Chichen, in the third tun of Katun 1 Ahau when Chichen was depopulated; 8 Ahau was the katun when the remainder of the Itza founded their town, coming forth from beneath the trees and bushes at Tan-Xuluc-Mul.
summary.zh: 五阿赫之年，伊扎馬爾王城——基尼奇·卡克穆與波普-霍爾·張——為胡納克·塞爾所毀。一阿赫之年，伊察餘部被逐出奇琴——奇琴於一阿赫卡特倫第三圖恩被遺空；八阿赫之卡特倫，伊察餘部自塔恩-許盧克-穆爾的樹叢之下出而建城。

sensitivity.note: Published colonial-era text; quote/paraphrase of Roys public-domain translation only.

passages.text: 5 Ahau was when the town of the ruler of Izamal, Kinich Kakmoo as well as Pop-hol Chan, was destroyed by Hunac Ceel. 1 Ahau was when the remainder of the Itza were driven out of Chichen. It was the third tun of Katun 1 Ahau when Chichen was depopulated.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. XXI; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 5阿豪之時，伊薩馬爾（Izamal）統治者基尼奇·卡克莫（Kinich Kakmoo）以及波普霍爾·陳（Pop-hol Chan）的城鎮被胡納克·塞爾（Hunac Ceel）所毀。1阿豪之時，伊察（Itza）的餘眾被逐出奇琴（Chichen）。奇琴荒廢，正當1阿豪卡盾的第三個盾（tun）。

passages.text: 8 Ahau was the katun when the remainder of the Itza founded their town, coming forth from beneath the trees and bushes at Tan-Xuluc-Mul, as it was called — the flight to the forest southward that ended only when the last Itza town on the Lake of Peten fell in 1697.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. XXI; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 8阿豪是那個卡盾，其時伊察的餘眾建立了他們的城鎮，從塔恩-舒盧克-穆爾（Tan-Xuluc-Mul）——其名如此——的樹木與灌木之下而出；那向南逃入森林之舉，直到1697年佩滕湖（Lake of Peten）上最後一座伊察城鎮陷落方告終結。

title.en: God K: The God with the Ornamented Nose
title.zh: 神K：飾鼻之神

region.en: Dresden Codex (Yucatec tradition), symbolic pin at Uxmal, Yucatan
region.zh: 德累斯頓抄本（猶加敦傳統），以墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾為象徵定位

period: Codex drawn c. 1200-1250; Schellhas 1904

source.work: Schellhas, Representation of Deities of the Maya Manuscripts, trans. Parker & Rau, 1904

summary.en: The god with the ornamented nose is not identical with God B, but is probably closely related to him. He is represented in Dresden 25 as perhaps conceived of as a priest wearing a mask with the face of the god; very frequently the well-known group 3 Oc is given with him — Forstemann sees in this the great period of the planet Venus, and the god as the storm-god of the sacrificial scenes.
summary.zh: 飾鼻之神與神B非同一，然關係密切。德累斯頓25頁中，他或被表現為戴神面假面的祭司；與其常伴者為著名的「三奧克」組合——弗斯特曼於此見金星大週期之數，而謝爾哈斯則於獻祭圖中視之為風暴之神。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain commentary; paraphrase only.

passages.text: This god, as already mentioned in connection with B, is not identical with the latter, but is probably closely related to him. He is represented in Dr. 25 (centre) where he is perhaps conceived of as a priest wearing a mask with the face of the god; also in Dr. 7a, 12a (with his own hieroglyph and that of E), 26 (bottom) with a variant of the sign.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on God K; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 此神，如已在論及B時所提及，與後者並非同一，但可能與之密切相關。他被表現於德勒斯登抄本（Dr.）25（中央），在那裡他也許被構想為一位戴著具有該神面容之面具的祭司；亦見於Dr. 7a、12a（帶有其自身之象形文字及E之象形文字）、26（底部），帶有該符號的一種變體。

passages.text: Very frequently the well-known group 3 Oc is given with him and in connection with his hieroglyph; Forstemann sees in this the great period of the planet Venus. In the sacrificial scenes of the Dresden Codex the figure at the right above is K, the storm-god, signifying with the rain deity at the left the productive season.
passages.note: Condensed from Schellhas (1904), on God K and the sacrificial scene; not verbatim throughout.
passages.zh: 非常頻繁地，著名的3奧克（Oc）組與他並列，並與他的象形文字相關聯；福斯特曼（Forstemann）在此看到金星的大週期。在德勒斯登抄本的獻祭場景中，右上方的形象是K，即風暴之神，與左側的雨神一同象徵豐產季節。

title.en: Sun-Yen and the Forged Letter
title.zh: 順緣誣書

region.en: Palace and highway, P'yongyang (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 平壤王城（象徵性定位）

period: Legend romance adapted and translated by Charles M. Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile (1919)

source.work: Charles M. Taylor (adapt.), Winning Buddha's Smile: A Korean Legend (1919), ch. 1, eBook #78208

summary.en: In the olden time when Hpyeng-Yang was the capital, the high dignitary Sun-Yen, beloved as a disinterested protector of the people, finds three of the King's subjects dead of starvation by the roadside while a grand banquet is being given. He goes straight to the King and reproaches him: 'Who pays the expenses of your amusements? Your people and no one else.' The King summons the Prime Minister Ja-Jo-Mi, the Unscrupulous, who has secretly conceived the scheme of usurping the throne, and Sun-Yen's frankness marks him out. The Prime Minister writes a letter full of bitter criticisms and threats against the King, signs it with Sun-Yen's name, and drops it in the path of a police agent in the darkness of the Korean night. 'Where there is smoke there is fire,' says the King; Sun-Yen is banished to the island of Kang-Sin and the scholar San-Houni, compromised in the plot, to Ko-Kum-To.
summary.zh: 平壤高官順緣，見餓殍三人於道，即入宮諫王曰：『王之宴樂，皆出於民；民飢而王不恤。』王召宰相子兆迷——其人陰懷篡位之心。子兆迷乃偽作逆書，署順緣之名，夜棄於巡捕之道。王曰『無風不起浪』，遂流順緣於江心島，其友山湖泥亦坐累徙於古金島。

sensitivity.note: Adapted Korean legend romance; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: While on his way Sun-Yen's attention was suddenly drawn to a great crowd of people by the roadside. His servant learned the reason: they were about to carry away several people who had died by the highway. 'Sire,' he said to the King, 'several of your subjects have just died of starvation by the roadside... Who pays the expenses of your amusements? Your people and no one else, and the Governors instead of doing their duty are also leading a frivolous and even vicious life.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 1 (1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 孫衍（Sun-Yen）在途中，注意力忽然被路旁一大群人吸引。他的僕人得知了原因：他們正要抬走幾個死在路旁的人。「陛下，」他對國王說，「您的幾名子民剛剛在路旁餓死了……誰來支付您娛樂的開銷？是您的百姓，別無他人；而總督們不但不盡職責，還過著輕浮甚至墮落的生活。」

passages.text: This official, Ja-Jo-Mi, was a man whose severity of character and conduct had earned for him a terrible reputation; no one knew of it, but he had conceived the scheme of usurping the throne. Feared that he might be removed by the revelations of Sun-Yen, he resolved to find a pretext for his exile: he wrote a letter full of bitter criticisms and threats against the King, signed it with the name of Sun-Yen, and, adopting a disguise, dropped the missive in the path of an agent of police in the darkness of the Korean night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 1 (1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這位官員子祖美，性情與行止嚴酷，因而惡名昭彰；無人知曉，他早已心懷篡奪王位之計。他唯恐自己會因順延的揭發而被除去，便決意尋個藉口將他流放：他寫了一封信，滿是對國王的嚴厲抨擊與威脅，署上順延之名，又喬裝改扮，趁著朝鮮夜色昏暗，將這封信丟在了一名差役行經的路上。

passages.text: 'Sire, it often happens that we are deceived by those whom we deem most faithful. As far as Sun is concerned, I consider him perfectly capable of this infamous business.' 'That's enough, my faithful Ja-Jo-Mi. Have Sun thrown into prison. He will be tried immediately.' The King withdrew, leaving Sun in despair, and ordered the Prime Minister to banish Sun at once to Kang-Sin; San-Houni, who was also compromised in the plot, was exiled to Ko-Kum-To.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 1 (1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「陛下，我們往往被自以為最忠誠的人所蒙蔽。至於順，我認為他完全幹得出這樁卑劣的勾當。」「夠了，我忠心的子祖美。把順投入大牢，立即審判他。」國王退去，留下順陷於絕望，並命宰相立刻將順流放至康信；同案受牽連的桑胡尼，則被流放至科昆島。

title.en: Cheng-Si Sells Herself for Three Hundred Bags of Rice
title.zh: 貞施賣身三百石

region.en: Island of Kang-Sin (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 江心島（象徵性定位）

period: Legend romance adapted by Charles M. Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile (1919)

source.work: Charles M. Taylor (adapt.), Winning Buddha's Smile: A Korean Legend (1919), ch. 2, eBook #78208

summary.en: Exiled to Kang-Sin, Sun-Yen's wife dreams of an angel from Heaven bending over her, and bears a daughter, Cheng-Si — but dies three days after the birth. From shedding so many tears Sun becomes blind, and his thirteenth-year daughter keeps him from starving by begging. When he falls into a pond, the disciple of an anchorite saves him and predicts: within three years you shall recover your sight and become Prime Minister — but he must be paid three hundred bags of rice. Cheng-Si hears of the merchants' ancient practice of purchasing a young girl in each village to throw into the sea, forestalling the perils of the Yellow Sea crossing. She offers herself for the rice, hands the debt-paper back to her father telling him she sold only her liberty, and then, at parting, confesses the truth: 'It was not my liberty but my life which I gave in exchange for the three hundred sacks of rice. I have to plunge to the bottom of the Yellow Sea to pray for a favorable passage for our sailors.' With another hundred bags given for his support and entrusted to the magistrate, she leaves her fainting father — 'Don't worry, we shall meet again in a better place where we shall be happy forever.'
summary.zh: 順緣妻夢天使而生貞施，三日後卒。順緣淚盡而盲。貞施行乞養父。某夜翁墮池，為苦行僧之弟子所救。弟子曰：『三年之內，爾目當復明，且為宰相；惟須施米三百石以代禱。』女聞海商歲以處女投海以祈安航之古俗，乃自請以身易米。父知之，慟絕。女以百石託於邑宰，含淚別父曰：『勿憂，他日吾儕當於極樂之地重逢。』

sensitivity.note: Human-sacrifice motif summarized; parallel to Sim Chung (cf. korean-simchung-indangsu-leap).

passages.text: Now it came to pass one night that Sun's wife had a dream: she saw an angel from Heaven bending over her. The truth was that this noble lady was soon to become a mother, and it was not long before she gave birth to a daughter to whom they gave the name of Cheng-Si; but scarcely three days had passed when her mother died. From having shed so many tears, Sun became blind. His greatest regret was in not being able to look upon the face of his little daughter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 2 (1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 且說有一夜，順的妻子做了一夢：她見一位天使自天而降，俯身於她。實情是，這位高貴的夫人不久便要為人母，果然沒過多久，她便生下一個女兒，取名澄詩；然而不過三日，她的母親便去世了。順因流了太多眼淚，雙目失明。他最為痛惜的，便是再也無法看見小女兒的面容。

passages.text: Happily Sun-Yen's cries were heard by the disciple of an anchorite who lived in a cave on the mountain slope. 'I predict, indeed I can read in your face, that your evil days will not last forever. Within three years you shall recover your sight and you shall become Prime Minister... you must pray diligently to Chen-Houang, the Emperor of Heaven. You must give me three hundred bags of rice and I will pray in your stead... It will be sufficient if you bind yourself in writing to pay me when you have the means to do so.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 2 (1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 所幸順延的哭聲被一位隱修者的弟子聽見，那隱修者住在山坡上的一處洞穴裡。「我預言，我確能從你的面容上看出，你的苦日子不會長久。三年之內，你將重見光明，並將成為宰相……你必須勤勉地向天皇陳皇祈禱。你須給我三百袋米，我便代你祈禱……只要你立下字據，待你有能力時償還於我，便足夠了。」

passages.text: In the days of our story, Korean merchants in search of business were accustomed to make one trip a year across the Yellow Sea. Thinking to avoid the danger, the merchants had recourse to a very ancient and very barbarous practice: in each village where they traded they purchased a young girl, and these victims were thrown into the sea, the perils of the voyage thought to be in this way forestalled. Cheng-Si met one of these traders in search of a human victim: 'You need not look any farther. If you want to take me, I will go, but what will you give me in exchange for my life?' 'Suppose I ask for three hundred bags of rice?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 2 (1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在我們這個故事所處的年代，朝鮮商人為求生意，慣於每年渡黃海一趟。商人們為求避險，便訴諸一種極為古老又極為野蠻的習俗：他們在經商的每個村落裡買下一名少女，將這些犧牲品投入海中，以為如此便可預先消解航途之險。澄詩遇見一名正尋覓活人祭品的商人：「你不必再往別處找了。你若要我，我便去，只是你拿什麼來換我的性命？」「倘若我索要三百袋米呢？」

passages.text: 'Father, I deceived you the other day. It was not my liberty but my life which I gave in exchange for the three hundred sacks of rice which you promised the disciple. I have to plunge to the bottom of the Yellow Sea to pray for a favorable passage for our sailors.' The blind man fell into a swoon. The merchant, a witness of the scene, said, 'I will give you another hundred bags of rice and we will not set sail for three days.' She sought an audience with the leading magistrate, who consented to take charge of the maintenance of the old gentleman; and 'Good-bye, father, don't worry, we shall meet again in a better place where we shall be happy forever.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 2 (1919); not verbatim.
