sensitivity.note: Missionary-era record (Codrington 1891); Aoba heritage.

passages.text: There is a man still living who one day followed his two wives down to the beach, and noticed there that some cocoa-nuts had been stolen from a tree he had made. Following footsteps he found two female vui, who said they were hungry. He promised them food and brought it to them — four baskets-full. One of the women was beautiful, the other full of sores. They asked him which he would have, and he answered that he would take them both.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 至今仍有一人活著，他有一天跟隨他的兩個妻子下到海灘，在那裡注意到有人從他栽種的一棵樹上偷走了些可可椰子。他循著腳印找到了兩個女vui，她們說自己餓了。他答應給她們食物，並把食物帶了來——滿滿四籃。其中一個女子貌美，另一個滿身瘡瘍。她們問他要哪一個，他回答說兩個他都要。

passages.text: Thereupon each gave him a stone full of mana, one to get him ten barrow-pigs, the other for ten sows; and they promised always to help him to get pigs, that he might mount to greatness in the Suqe. These women were vui, whose power lay in pigs; nevertheless, to this day, when the man's wives go down to the beach for their fishing, they find fish caught and lying ready for them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是每個女子都給了他一塊充滿mana的石頭，一塊使他得到十頭公豬，另一塊使他得到十頭母豬；她們還許諾永遠幫他得到豬，好讓他能在Suqe中登上高位。這些女子是vui，其力量在於豬；然而直到今日，當這人的妻子們下到海灘捕魚時，她們總會發現魚已被捕好，擺在那裡等著她們。

title.en: Tagaro Brings Night in a Shell
title.zh: 塔加羅以貝殼攜夜

region.en: Lepers Island (Aoba), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: It was Tagaro who went to Maewo and brought back night in a shell. When he let it out and darkness crept over the sky, men wept and beat their houses.
summary.zh: 正是塔加羅往馬埃沃去，用一枚貝殼把夜帶了回來。他放出夜來，黑暗爬滿天空，人們號哭起來，捶打自家的屋子。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era record (Codrington 1891); cross-ref qat-creation and melanesian-banks-night-released (Qat version).

passages.text: It was Tagaro also who went to Maewo and brought back night in a shell. When he let it out and darkness crept over the sky, men wept and beat their houses — the first nightfall of the Lepers' Islands, received with wailing rather than welcome.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 也是Tagaro前往Maewo，用一隻貝殼帶回了黑夜。當他把它放出來，黑暗便爬上了天空，人們哭泣著敲打自己的房屋——這是Lepers' Islands的第一個夜晚，人們以哀號而非歡迎來迎接它。

title.en: Tagaro's Little Son and the Garden of Crowns
title.zh: 塔加羅幼子與薯冠園

region.en: Lepers Island (Aoba), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: Tagaro was father of ten sons, the last, Tagaro-mbiti, exceedingly small. His nine brothers planted leaves and vines and called him idle, not knowing he was wise: he had planted the crown of the caladium, the suckers of the banana, the rind of the yam — and when the season came his garden was full of food.
summary.zh: 塔加羅有十子，最幼者塔加羅姆比提，身量極小。九位兄長出門耕作，只種芋葉、蕉芽、薯藤，見幼弟留家腿上生瘡，便罵他懶惰，不知他實則最能。幼弟所種者乃芋之頂冠、蕉之吸芽、薯之皮層——季節一到，兄長們無食可吃，幼弟的園中卻滿是收成。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era record (Codrington 1891); Aoba heritage.

passages.text: Tagaro is represented also as the father of ten sons, of whom Tagaro-mbiti, the Little, was the last, and exceedingly small. His brothers went out to work, but he stayed at home with a sore on his leg. They planted the leaves of the edible caladium, the top shoot of the banana, the vine of the yam; but when they were gone he took the crown of the caladium, the suckers of the banana, the rind of the yam, and planted them. His brothers scolded him for idleness, not knowing what he was about; but when the season came round and they had nothing to eat, he shewed them his garden full of food.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: Tagaro也被描述為十個兒子的父親，其中最小的是Tagaro-mbiti，即「小者」，他長得極其矮小。他的哥哥們出去幹活，他卻留在家裡，腿上生著一個瘡。他們種下可食用的芋頭的葉子、香蕉的頂芽、山藥的藤蔓；但等他們一走，他便拿來芋頭的冠部、香蕉的吸芽、山藥的外皮，把它們種了下去。他的哥哥們責罵他懶惰，卻不知他在做什麼；但當季節到來，他們一無可食之時，他便把長滿食物的園子指給他們看。

title.en: The Tavogivogi Changelings
title.zh: 塔沃基沃基易形靈

region.en: Lepers Island (Aoba), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: Beings called Tavogivogi — 'changelings' — appear as a youth or woman to entice one of the opposite sex; the one who yields dies. Their only test is to ask the name of a tree, for a wrong answer shows deceit; successful or not, the Tavogivogi vanishes suddenly, like a bird, and the seduced youth sickens at home and never recovers.
summary.zh: 有所謂塔沃基沃基之靈，意即『易形者』：或化青年、或化女子，專誘異性；一旦失身相從，其人必死。其唯一驗法是問附近樹木之名——答錯即見其騙。無論得手與否，塔沃基沃基會突然消失，『如鳥一般』化為鳥獸而去。受誘的青年回家便一病不起，自知遭了靈算，終無可救。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era record (Codrington 1891); Aoba heritage.

passages.text: Beings called Tavogivogi must be classed as spirits: they are certainly not human beings. A Tavogivogi is not thought ever to have the appearance of a snake; one of them appears in the form of a youth or woman, in order to entice one of the opposite sex, and the young man or woman who yields to the seduction dies. There is no outward sign of the real character of the Tavogivogi, but the test is to ask the name of a tree, and a wrong answer will shew that there is deceit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 被稱為Tavogivogi的存在必須歸類為精靈：它們肯定不是人類。人們認為Tavogivogi從不以蛇的形貌出現；其中一個會以青年或女子的形貌出現，以引誘異性，而屈服於這誘惑的青年或女子便會死去。Tavogivogi的真實本性沒有任何外在的標記，但考驗的方法是問一種樹的名字，答錯便會顯出其中有詐。

passages.text: Successful or not the Tavogivogi suddenly disappears, 'like a bird,' but in the form of a bird or other creature. The young man goes home and sickens; he remembers the sudden disappearance, knows what has befallen him, and never recovers. The name means 'changeling,' from the word, in the Banks' Islands, wog, to change the form.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 無論成功與否，Tavogivogi都會突然消失，「像一隻鳥」，但卻是以鳥或其他生物的形貌。那青年回家後便病倒；他記得那突然的消失，知道自己遭遇了什麼，便再也沒有康復。這個名字意為「換形者」，出自Banks' Islands中意為「改變形貌」的詞wog。

title.en: The Heron and the Turtle
title.zh: 蒼鷺與海龜

region.en: Florida (Ngela), Solomon Islands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 所羅門群島佛羅里達（恩格拉）島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Rev. A. Penny at Florida, printed in R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: A heron with his foot fast in the coral called every fish that passed — shark, bonito, garfish, rock-cod, crocodile — and every one said 'Wait a bit.' Only the turtle agreed to help, for pay: the sea-urchin beside the heron. Freed, the heron repaid his debt by dancing the children away from their prize and singing the turtle out of the net and into the sea.
summary.zh: 蒼鷺足陷珊瑚，潮水漸沒其頸。他向過路諸魚求救——鯊、鰹、長嘴魚、石斑、鱷——皆答『且等等』。唯海龜索酬而助之，蒼鷺身旁的海膽恰可為酬；龜食海膽大喜，碎石化石救出蒼鷺，並結生死之盟。後 Hagelonga 村捕得海龜，備宴待宰；蒼鷺翩然而至，向村童借得父母最貴之飾物，為其起舞，趁機歌咒解縛：『Kerembaembae！縛解矣……』一路舞咒，送龜潛入海中。村人追悔，見沙上龜跡，方知龜自行得脫。

sensitivity.note: Native-language text taken down by Rev. A. Penny at Florida; translated by Codrington (1891). Gela heritage.

passages.text: One day a Soo, a heron, caught his foot fast in the coral; the tide came in, but his neck was long. When the tide reached to the top of his neck there came along a Shark. 'Come and save me,' says the Soo. 'Wait a bit,' says the Shark. There comes a bonito: 'Come and save my life,' says the Soo; and the bonito says to him, 'Wait a bit.' There comes the great Garfish: 'Come and save me, brother,' says the Soo; the Garfish says, 'Wait a bit.' There comes a Rock-cod: 'Come and save my life,' says the Soo; 'Wait a bit,' says the Rock-cod. There comes a Crocodile: 'Come and save me,' says the Soo; 'Wait a bit,' says the Crocodile. In the end all the fish came, and nothing could be done.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), after Rev. A. Penny's Florida text; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，一隻蒼鷺（Soo）的腳緊緊卡在珊瑚裡；潮水漲了上來，但牠的脖子很長。當潮水漲到牠脖子的頂端時，來了一條鯊魚。「來救救我吧，」蒼鷺說。「等一等，」鯊魚說。來了一條鰹魚：「來救我一命吧，」蒼鷺說；鰹魚對牠說：「等一等。」來了一條大頜針魚：「來救救我吧，兄弟，」蒼鷺說；頜針魚說：「等一等。」來了一條石斑魚：「來救我一命吧，」蒼鷺說；「等一等，」石斑魚說。來了一條鱷魚：「來救救我吧，」蒼鷺說；「等一等，」鱷魚說。最後所有的魚都來了，卻什麼也辦不成。

passages.text: Then comes a Turtle. 'Brother! come here and save my life,' says the Soo. And the Turtle says, 'You will pay me of course.' And the Soo says, 'I have nothing with me to pay you with.' And there was a sea-urchin alongside the Soo, and he says, 'I will pay you with money,' says he. But the Turtle says, No. And the Soo says, 'Dog's teeth, and porpoise teeth'; but the Turtle says, 'No, I don't want it.' Then he offers him the sea-urchin, and the Turtle eats it up with great delight, and says joyfully, 'Now I will save you, you have given me my pay.' So he smashes to fragments the stone that held the bird's foot and the Soo is saved. And the Soo says, 'Now you have saved my life; if ever hereafter you are going to be killed and I should hear you call, I will come and save you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), after Rev. A. Penny's Florida text; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著來了一隻海龜。「兄弟！到這兒來救我一命吧，」蒼鷺說。海龜說：「你當然要報答我。」蒼鷺說：「我身上什麼也沒有，沒法報答你。」蒼鷺身旁有一隻海膽，牠說：「我用錢報答你，」牠說。但海龜說，不要。蒼鷺說：「狗牙和海豚牙」；但海龜說：「不要，我不要那個。」接著牠把海膽獻給牠，海龜大喜過望地把牠吃個精光，歡喜地說：「現在我來救你，你已經給了我報酬。」於是牠把那卡住鳥腳的石頭砸成碎片，蒼鷺得救了。蒼鷺說：「現在你救了我的命；今後你若有一天將要被殺，而我聽到了你的呼救，我一定會來救你。」

passages.text: After this the people of Hagelonga went to fish, and let down their net; every fish that passed they let go, but the turtle that came round they cried out over, 'Here he is! we will see what he is worth,' and took him, and tied him, and carried him ashore, and made a fence round him. The chief of Hagelonga says, 'To-morrow we will split wood for him, and get leaves, and dig yams for him, this turtle of ours.' So as soon as it was light they went off; and when they were far away the Soo comes along, and the boys watching say to him, 'Where have you come from?' and the Soo says, 'I am just idling about; should you like me to dance for you?' And he says, 'Bring me the porpoise teeth and dog's teeth ornaments of your fathers and mothers, that I may dress myself up in the best.' And he dressed himself out in them, and then he danced for them — dancing along to the fence in which the Turtle was. And the Turtle saw him coming, and cried out, 'Now I am to die, my brother.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), after Rev. A. Penny's Florida text; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此後，哈格隆加（Hagelonga）的人們去捕魚，撒下他們的網；凡是經過的魚他們都放走了，但對於繞過來的那隻海龜，他們卻大聲喊道：「牠在這兒！我們看看牠值多少錢，」於是捉住牠，把牠綁起來，抬上岸，並在牠周圍圍起一道籬笆。哈格隆加的首領說：「明天我們要為牠劈柴、採葉子、挖山藥，為我們這隻海龜。」所以天一亮他們就出發了；當他們走遠之後，蒼鷺走了過來，看守的男孩們對牠說：「你從哪兒來的？」蒼鷺說：「我只是閒逛罷了；你們要不要我跳舞給你們看？」牠又說：「把你們父母親的海豚牙和狗牙飾物拿來給我，好讓我打扮得漂漂亮亮。」牠穿戴好那些飾物，然後為他們跳舞——一路舞向圍著海龜的那道籬笆。海龜看見牠走來，大聲喊道：「這下我要死了，我的兄弟。」

passages.text: And the Soo says to him, 'And now I shall save your life, because you saved mine before.' And he came into the house where the boys were, and there he danced for them, singing 'Kerembaembae! Loosed is your leg that they have tied!' — and his leg is loosed. 'Kerembaembae! Slipped out is your head! Clear the forepart! Clear the hinder part! Clear the rest of you!' — and so it was. 'Kerembaembae! Follow the path! Reach the sand! Down with you into the sea! Dive out of sight! Go a fathom's length! Go two fathoms!' So he escaped with his life. And the people returned and looked at the fence, but the Soo was gone; and they said, 'Some one has stolen our turtle.' And the boys said, 'There was only a Soo came here and danced for us, and we gave him all your things, and he deceived us.' And they went and looked at the path, and there they saw the traces of the turtle, and they said, 'Yea, he has saved himself for certain, nobody has stolen him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), after Rev. A. Penny's Florida text; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蒼鷺對牠說：「現在我要救你的命，因為你先前救過我的命。」牠走進男孩們所在的屋子，在那裡為他們跳舞，唱道：「Kerembaembae！他們綁住你的腿，鬆開了！」——牠的腿便鬆開了。「Kerembaembae！你的頭滑脫出來了！前面清空！後面清空！你其餘的部分也清空！」——果然如此。「Kerembaembae！順著小路走！到達沙地！下去，下到海裡去！潛得不見蹤影！游出一噚遠！游出兩噚遠！」牠就這樣逃得了性命。人們回來看那道籬笆，但蒼鷺已經走了；他們說：「有人偷走了我們的海龜。」男孩們說：「只有一隻蒼鷺來過這裡為我們跳舞，我們把你們所有的東西都給了牠，牠騙了我們。」他們去查看那條小路，在那裡看到了海龜的痕跡，便說：「是啊，牠確實自己逃走了，沒有人偷走牠。」

title.en: The Three Fish
title.zh: 三魚鬥智

region.en: Ureparapara, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島烏雷帕拉帕拉島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: The box-fish Watwata and the sole scratched each other by turns, each leaving the other worse; then they played hide-and-seek. The sole buried himself in the sand where the Watwata could not find him — and the Song-fish, who stood laughing at the game, has grinned ever since.
summary.zh: 箱魚瓦瓦塔與比目魚互抓對方，一抓比一抓狠：比目魚抓得箱魚遍體，箱魚回敬竟把比目魚抓得極薄。二人於是玩捉迷藏：箱魚藏於石下被找到；比目魚埋身沙中，箱魚遍尋不著。一旁露齒的松魚看了大笑——牠至今還咧著嘴笑。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-anthropologist record (Codrington 1891); Ureparapara heritage.

passages.text: The story of the Watwata (an Ostracion) and the Sole. The two were scratching one another, and the Sole said to the Watwata, 'Scratch me.' But the Watwata said, 'No, you shall scratch me first.' And the Sole scratched the Watwata, scratched him well. And the Watwata said, 'Brother, you have scratched me badly,' but the Sole said, 'No, it is all right.' And the Watwata said, 'Well! now I shall scratch you in my turn.' After that he scratched him, scratched him extremely thin. And the Sole said, 'Well! you have scratched me badly, but we two will play hide and seek.' And the Sole said, 'You shall hide first.' After that the Watwata hid, and got out of sight under a stone. The Sole sought him and found him. After that the Sole hid in his turn, and buried himself in the sand; and the Watwata sought him in vain. But the Song (a fish which shews its teeth) stood and laughed at it; and he has grinned so ever since.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 瓦特瓦塔（Watwata，一種箱魨）與鰨魚的故事。兩者互相搔癢，鰨魚對瓦特瓦塔說：「搔搔我。」但瓦特瓦塔說：「不，你先搔我。」於是鰨魚搔瓦特瓦塔，搔得很好。瓦特瓦塔說：「兄弟，你把我搔得好痛，」但鰨魚說：「不，挺好的。」瓦特瓦塔說：「好吧！現在輪到我搔你了。」之後牠搔牠，把牠搔得極其瘦薄。鰨魚說：「好吧！你把我搔得好痛，但我們兩個來玩捉迷藏。」鰨魚說：「你先藏。」之後瓦特瓦塔藏了起來，躲到一塊石頭底下不見了。鰨魚找牠，找到了牠。之後輪到鰨魚藏，牠把自己埋進沙裡；瓦特瓦塔找牠卻找不著。但松魚（Song，一種露出牙齒的魚）站在一旁嘲笑此事；從那以後牠就一直咧嘴笑著。

title.en: The Birds' Voyage in the Arum-Leaf Canoe
title.zh: 群鳥泛舟芋葉舟

region.en: Mota, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島莫塔島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native Mota manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: The birds set out in a canoe of a giant arum leaf to eat the tawan fruit of Qakea, taking aboard every would-be passenger who sang 'I go and tell my daddy!' — even the hermit crab. But the crab's claw pierced the leafy hull; all leapt overboard and swam ashore while the crab sank and crawled along the bottom; the Weru dived till her body turned black and her eyes red in search of him — and the crab was already sitting quietly on the sand. Afterwards, in pairs, the birds tidied each other's feathers, and the Rat, combing the Owl's head with 'comb-comb-dung-dung,' defiled him; the betrayed Owl roasted a red-raia caladium to lure the Rat from his hole and killed him with his talons.
summary.zh: 群鳥以巨芋葉為舟，乘風往 Qakea 食塔萬果。綠鸚鵡、鸚嘴、鴿先後求搭船，皆唱『我要告訴爸爸去！風吹得你們夠嗆』而得上船；寄居蟹也想同行，眾鳥本以『你留下看島』拒之，被其『你們吃落果、我在地上撿』說動而載之。白鸛叮嘱：『莫亂動，別把舟抓破。』蟹爪終究把芋葉舟抓穿，海水灌入。眾鳥跳海游泳登岸，蟹沉底爬行；白鸛潛水尋蟹，尋到身黑眼紅——而蟹早已安坐沙灘。眾鳥成對互相理羽；鼠替貓頭鷹梳頭，口中念『梳梳—拉屎—拉屎』，竟在鷹頭上拉屎。鸚鵡告密，鷹怒而追鼠；鼠鑽洞不出。鷹烤紅薯達至香氣入洞，置其洞口，待鼠出而搏殺食之。

sensitivity.note: Native Mota manuscript translated by Codrington (1891).

passages.text: They lived in their place. The tattan was in fruit at Qakea; the wind began to blow; then said they, 'Well, now at last we will paddle over and eat tawan.' So they make a start and go. And the reitga, the Green Parrot, says, 'I go with you'; but they say, 'O-o-o! You just go back, lest your father should be angry with us about you.' And he sings, 'I go and tell my daddy! the wind has blown hard against you; beat, beat!' 'Ah, well! come along!' and he gets on board. Then the Mes and the Pigeon in turn ask to come, and sing the same song; and each gets on board. And when all were on board there was a Hermit Crab sitting there, and he said, 'You fellows, just let me come.' But they said, 'You just stay there to look after our island.' And he said, 'Nay, my brothers, you won't make me miserable. Take me over! I will sit under the tawan-trees, and you will eat making the fruit fall, and I will eat on the ground.' So they said, 'Very well! come along'; and he gets on board.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native Mota manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們住在自己的地方。卡克亞（Qakea）的塔坦樹（tattan）結果了；風開始吹起來；於是他們說：「好吧，現在我們終於可以划過去吃塔萬果（tawan）了。」於是他們動身出發。雷特加（reitga），那隻綠鸚鵡，說：「我跟你們一起去」；但他們說：「噢——噢！你還是回去吧，免得你父親為了你生我們的氣。」牠便唱道：「我去告訴我爹爹！風狠狠地吹向你們；打呀，打呀！」「啊，好吧！來吧！」牠便上了船。接著梅斯鳥（Mes）和鴿子輪流請求同去，唱著同樣的歌；各自都上了船。當大家都上了船，那裡還坐著一隻寄居蟹，牠說：「你們這些傢伙，就讓我一起去吧。」但他們說：「你就留在那兒照看我們的島吧。」牠說：「不，我的兄弟們，你們不會讓我難過的。帶我過去吧！我會坐在塔萬樹下，你們吃著讓果子掉下來，我就在地上吃。」於是他們說：「很好！來吧」；牠便上了船。

passages.text: Then the Weru says to the Crab, 'Friend, sit up this way near me; and while we two are sitting here, don't shuffle about, lest you make a hole in the canoe' — for the canoe was the leaf of a giant arum. And he says, 'Yes, I know all about that.' But the Weru keeps an eye upon him, and if he shuffles with his claws she says to him, 'Friend, I keep telling you, don't be shuffling about; eh! you will soon have made a hole in the canoe!' But he says, 'Eh! Friend, I know all about it.' The wind had come down into their sail, and they were already in the open sea; and the Crab shuffled about, and his claw pierced right through the canoe, and the water came pouring quickly in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native Mota manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是威魯對螃蟹說：「朋友，往這邊坐，靠近我；我們兩個坐在這裡的時候，你別亂挪動，免得你在獨木舟上弄出個洞來。」——因為那獨木舟是一片巨大的海芋葉。他又說：「是，這我都知道。」可是威魯一直盯著他，要是他用鉗子亂挪，她就對他說：「朋友，我一直跟你說，別亂挪動；唉！你馬上就要在獨木舟上弄出個洞來了！」可他說：「唉！朋友，這我都知道。」風已經灌進他們的帆裡，他們早已到了外海；那螃蟹亂挪亂動，鉗子正好戳穿了獨木舟，海水便迅速湧了進來。

passages.text: And they cried out, 'Be quick! our canoe has a hole in it, the Crab had trodden it through.' And they said, 'Well, let us leap overboard'; and they all of them leapt overboard, and the Crab leapt overboard, and sank right out of sight to the bottom of the sea; but they all of them swam, and he crawled along on the bottom. And they all swam and came out upon the shore, but not he you may be sure. Then they said, 'Fellows! are we all men alive or not?' And some one said, 'No, there is one poor fellow our friend missing.' And they spoke to one, and he refused, and to another, and he refused; then said the Weru, 'Here am I, I will go and look for him.' So she swims, and dives, and does not find him, and comes up to the surface; and dives again, and goes on diving, and her body turns black, and dives, and dives, and her eyes turn red. But the Crab had already crawled up ashore before them all; and there he was quietly sitting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native Mota manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們便喊道：「快！我們的獨木舟破了個洞，是螃蟹踩穿的。」他們又說：「好吧，我們跳下水去吧。」他們全都跳下了水，螃蟹也跳下了水，一直沉到海底，不見了蹤影；他們全都游著，他卻在海底爬行。他們都游著上了岸，可他當然沒有。於是他們說：「夥計們！我們是不是全都活著？」有人說：「不，我們可憐的朋友少了一個。」他們問了一個，那人不肯去；又問了一個，那人也不肯去；於是威魯說：「我在這兒，我去找他。」她便游著、潛下去，沒找著他，又浮上水面；再潛下去，一路潛著，她的身子變黑了，還潛著、潛著，她的眼睛變紅了。可那螃蟹早已在他們所有人之前爬上了岸；就那麼安安靜靜地坐在那裡。

passages.text: Then said the Tasis to the Tagere, 'Friend, come here and make me tidy'; and they all of them sat down in pairs. Then said the Rat to the Owl, 'Friend, come here, let me make you tidy'; and as he combs his head he keeps saying, 'Comb-comb-dung-dung'; and he dungs upon the head of the Owl. Then says the Rat, 'My paws are tired out.' The Mes parrot combs the Owl's head, and perceives that it smells, and cries out; and the Parrot says, 'Oh! your friend the Rat has played you a trick; he has made a pig of himself upon you.' Then the Owl flies off and chases the Rat; and the Rat saw a hole and ran into it, and the Owl sat by helpless. Then he roasts a red raia caladium, and as he scrapes that root the smell goes out and reaches the Rat in the hole; and when it was cooked he broke it and put it at the mouth of the hole. Then the Rat creeps out to eat, and the Owl swooped down upon him, and killed him with his talons, and ate him up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native Mota manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是塔西斯對塔格雷說：「朋友，過來，讓我給你梳理梳理。」他們便兩兩成對地坐了下來。於是老鼠對貓頭鷹說：「朋友，過來，讓我給你梳理梳理。」他一邊梳他的頭，一邊不停地說：「梳—梳—屎—屎」；他竟把屎拉在貓頭鷹頭上。老鼠便說：「我的爪子累壞了。」梅斯鸚鵡梳著貓頭鷹的頭，聞出有股臭味，便叫了起來；鸚鵡說：「哎呀！你的朋友老鼠捉弄了你；他在你身上像豬一樣胡來。」於是貓頭鷹飛起來追老鼠；老鼠看見一個洞便鑽了進去，貓頭鷹無可奈何地守在一旁。於是他烤了一個紅色的雷亞芋頭，刮那塊根的時候，氣味飄了出去，傳到洞裡的老鼠那裡；等烤熟了，他把它掰開，放在洞口。老鼠便爬出來吃，貓頭鷹猛撲下去，用爪子把他弄死，吃了下去。

title.en: The Shark and the Snake
title.zh: 鯊與蛇

region.en: Lepers Island (Aoba), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: The Shark quarrelled with the Snake and bade him come down into the sea to be eaten. The Snake answered, 'They will kill you, and I shall eat a bit of you.' And so it fell out: when the Shark was killed, the Snake went down into the sea and ate the Shark.
summary.zh: 鯊與蛇結怨，鯊令蛇下海，欲食之。蛇答曰：『人們會殺了你，而我要吃你一口。』後果然：人們殺鯊之時，蛇下海把鯊吃了。

sensitivity.note: Native manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); Aoba heritage.

passages.text: This is about the Shark and the Snake. They quarrelled, and the Shark told the Snake to come down into the sea, that the Shark might eat him. The Snake said to him, 'They will kill you, and I shall eat a bit of you.' Now when they killed the Shark, the Snake went down into the sea and ate the Shark — the small talker proved the surer prophet, and the boastful biter ended inside the belly he had threatened.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這是關於鯊魚和蛇的事。他們吵了起來，鯊魚叫蛇下到海裡去，好讓鯊魚吃了他。蛇對他說：「他們會殺了你，我還要吃你一塊肉呢。」後來他們殺了鯊魚，蛇便下到海裡吃了鯊魚——說小話的倒成了更準的預言家，誇口的咬人者最終落進了他所威脅的那個肚子裡。

title.en: Kamakajaku Swallowed by the King-Fish, Guest of the Sun
title.zh: 卡馬卡雅庫：鯖魚吞身、日宮作客

region.en: Gaji hill, Bugotu, Ysabel, Solomon Islands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 所羅門群島伊莎貝爾島布戈圖加吉山（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Kamakajaku of Gaji hill waded far out to dip salt-water as dark as the sea he had watched, and was swallowed by a great king-fish and carried east to the rising of the sun. He cut his way out with the obsidian in his ear, followed the Sun to his village, taught his fireless hosts cooked food, disobeyed their taboo and looked down the sky-hole at his own home — and was lowered back by canes, reaching the hill of Gaji to die there old.
summary.zh: 加吉山上的卡馬卡雅庫見海上奇黑，令孫兒取水來比，不似；親自下海，遠涉至能望見山處取水，水面轟鳴，一條巨鯖把他吞下，向日出之東游去。至淺灘，他取出耳中所藏之黑曜石割破魚肚躍出。旭日升起，滾滾而行，囑他『別擋路，站我右邊』。他隨日上天，至太陽兒孫之村作客；彼輩只食生冷，他教他們用火熟食。主人告誡一處禁地不可去；他忍不住，掀開蓋天石孔，俯見故里加吉，放聲大哭。主人乃以竹竿縛籃縋他下天，囑他『鳥獸齊鳴時莫抬頭，待地上蟬鳴再望』。竹竿接了一根又一根，直垂至加吉山。親友本以為他已死，見他自天而降，皆大歡喜。他活到高壽，終老於加吉山上。

sensitivity.note: Native Bugotu manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); Ysabel heritage.

passages.text: He dwelt upon the hill at Gaji; and he was mending his nets, and he looked down upon the ocean, and saw it dark exceedingly. And his grandchildren went down to the sea to fish upon the reef, and Kamakajaku said to them, 'Go and dip salt-water for me in the place I see the sea like that.' And his grandchildren went forth and dipped the salt-water, and came up and gave it to him. And he poured it down, and looked and did not find it like what he looked down upon from his place upon the hill. And it was morning, and he took the salt-water-vessel, and went forth down, and put in his ear a bit of obsidian, and waded far out from the shore till he saw the hill at Gaji, and then he dipped. And the surface of the sea sounded and bubbled, and he heard coming-to-him a Kombili, a king-fish, a very great fish; and it came and swallowed him, and went off with him eastwards to the lining up of the sun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他住在加吉的山上；他正在補網，往下一望，望見大洋，見它黑得厲害。他的孫兒們下到海邊，在礁上捕魚，卡馬卡雅庫對他們說：「去，到我望見海是那樣的地方，替我舀些海水來。」他的孫兒們便去了，舀了海水，上來交給他。他把它倒下去，看了看，覺得不像他從山上住處往下望見的那樣。到了早晨，他拿起盛海水的器皿，往下走去，往耳朵裡塞了一小片黑曜石，涉水走出岸邊很遠，直到望見加吉的山，這才舀水。海面發出聲響、冒起泡來，他聽見一個孔比利朝他而來，那是一條王魚，一條極大的魚；它過來把他吞了下去，帶著他往東去了，朝著太陽列隊的地方。

passages.text: And it went with him till it arrived with him at a shallow place, and it threw itself about so that Kamakajaku perceived that there was a beach probably. 'Here am I,' says he, and he thought of the obsidian in his ear, and felt for it and found it, and cut asunder the belly of the Kombili, and leapt out, and saw a brightness. So up rose the Sun with a tang, and rolling from side to side. And the Sun says, 'Don't stand in my way, you will die at once; stay on my right.' And he drew aside till the Sun rose away, and then he followed; and they two went up towards heaven, and went on and arrived at the village of the Sun's children. And he said, 'Here you stay'; so he stayed with them, with his children and grandchildren, and the Sun went off. And they asked him, 'Whence did you come hither?' And he said, 'From the earth; I dwelt in my place, and I dipped salt-water, and a big fish swallowed me, and so I arrived here at your good town.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 它帶著他走，一直帶他到一處淺灘，它在那裡翻騰起來，卡馬卡雅庫便覺察到，那大概是一片海灘。「我在這兒了，」他說，他想起耳朵裡的黑曜石，摸了摸，找到了，便割開孔比利的肚子，跳了出來，看見一片光亮。於是太陽帶著一股銳氣升了起來，左右搖晃著。太陽說：「別擋我的路，你會立刻死掉；待在我右邊。」他便讓到一旁，等太陽升遠了，然後跟了上去；他們兩個往天上走去，走著走著，到了太陽孩子們的村子。太陽說：「你就待在這裡吧」；他便和他們待在一起，和他的兒女、孫兒們待在一起，太陽則走開了。他們問他：「你是從哪裡到這兒來的？」他說：「從地上來；我住在我那地方，舀海水，一條大魚吞了我，我就這樣到了你們這座好城裡。」

passages.text: So they remained in company; and they ate only raw food, those people above; and he shewed them fire, so that they ate cooked food. And they said to him, 'Don't go to that place, it is taboo'; and they went their way. And he kept house, and thought what that was they had said, and went over, and opened up a stone which was the covering of a hole in the sky, and he looked down on his place at Gaji, and he cried. They brought him food, but it was not for him; so they asked him, 'Do you want to go down?' And he said, Yes. And they made a house, and gave him a banana, and gave him seed of pan to dye with, and they took a cane and tied it to the saddle-piece of the house, and he Kamakajaku sat in it. And they let it down, saying, 'When the birds cry, don't look out; when the cicalas cry, then you may look out.' And when one cane was too short, they tied another to it, and it reached down to the hill and rested.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他們便相伴而居；那些在上方的人只吃生食；而他向他們展示了火，於是他們便吃起熟食來。他們對他說：「別去那個地方，那是禁忌之地」；說完他們便各自離去。他留守屋中，思忖著他們所說的那究竟是什麼，便走了過去，打開一塊石頭——那石頭是天上一處洞穴的蓋子——他俯視下方自己在加吉的居處，便哭了。他們給他送來食物，但那並非為他而備；於是他們問他：「你想下去嗎？」他說：想。於是他們造了一座屋子，給了他一根香蕉，又給了他用以染色的檳榔種子，他們取來一根藤條，繫在屋子的鞍木上，他卡馬卡雅庫便坐了進去。他們將它放下去，說道：「鳥兒啼叫時，不要向外張望；蟬兒鳴叫時，你才可以向外張望。」當一根藤條太短時，他們便再接上一根，它一直垂到山丘上，停歇下來。

passages.text: And his friends had been seeking him, because they thought that he was dead already. And on the day that he came down again from heaven, they rejoiced because they saw him again, and good was their heart. And he lived a long while, till he died on his hill Gaji — the man who went up with the Sun, and came down again by a rope of canes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的朋友們一直在尋覓他，因為他們以為他早已死了。而在他從天上再次降下的那一天，他們因重見他而歡欣，心中甚好。他活了許久，直到死在他的山丘加吉上——那個隨太陽升上天、又順著藤索降下來的人。

title.en: Samuku Sent to the Ghosts' Mangroves
title.zh: 薩穆庫被逐往鬼沼

region.en: Tuhilagi, Bugotu, Ysabel, Solomon Islands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 所羅門群島伊莎貝爾島布戈圖圖希拉吉鬼沼（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Scolded by his wife — 'your father and mother are dead, who is to make you food? Go and see them in Tuhilagi' — Samuku paddled to the Ghosts' Mangroves and found the company of ghosts, who told him he was not dead yet. Their house vanished at dawn; he netted their fishing and saw their true forms; and when the ghost company left him at daybreak, the people of a certain place found him sleeping on the sand and took him in till he died.
summary.zh: 薩穆庫勤耕娶妻，家和食足。一日歸家索食，妻怒罵：『我厭倦為你備食；你父母已死，誰給你做飯？去圖希拉吉看他們去吧。』他負氣駕舟至鬼沼 Lelegia tarunga，登上鬼群之鄉。眾鬼問：『你還沒死，怎麼來了？』他答：『我妻罵我，把我趕來的。』夜宿鬼舍，天明屋竟消失。他設計織網與眾鬼下海捕魚，看清了鬼的真形；天亮鬼群散去，他睡在沙灘上，被附近村人拾回，供養至死。

sensitivity.note: Native Bugotu manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); Ysabel heritage.

passages.text: Samuku lived in his village, and built his house, and worked, and good and many were his affairs; so he took a wife and married, and they two lived well, and agreed perfectly well together, and worked, and much was their food. And Samuku came home and asked for food, because he was hungry, and his wife had not prepared any food, and Samuku was angry with his wife, and scolded her greatly. And his wife said to him, 'I am tired of making food for you, your father and mother are dead, who is to make you food? Go and see them in Tuhilagi.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 薩穆庫住在自己的村莊裡，造了他的屋子，辛勤勞作，他的事務又多又好；於是他娶了妻子成了婚，二人生活美滿，彼此十分和睦，一同勞作，食物豐足。薩穆庫回到家來討要食物，因為他餓了，而他的妻子沒有備下任何食物，薩穆庫便對妻子發怒，狠狠地責罵了她。他的妻子對他說：「我為你備食已備得厭倦了，你的父母都已死了，誰來給你備食呢？去圖希拉吉看他們吧。」

passages.text: And Samuku was angry, and he sat and thought; and he said, 'Good, I will go and see them.' So he hauled down a canoe and put out to sea to Tuhilagi, and landed at Lelegia tarunga, the Ghosts' Mangroves, and stepped up the beach and went in shore, and found the company of ghosts. And they asked him, 'Why have you come here? You are not dead yet.' And Samuku answered, 'My wife scolded me, and sent me here.' And at night he stayed in a house, and when it was morning the house disappeared. So he played them a trick and made a net, and they went to fish with it, and he saw the forms of the ghosts, and the net caught in the coral. And when it was light all the company of ghosts departed from him, and he went down and slept on the sand. And the people of a certain place found him and took hold of him, and took him to be with them till he died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 薩穆庫怒氣未消，坐下來思忖；他說：「好，我就去看他們。」於是他把一隻獨木舟拖下水，出海駛向圖希拉吉，在萊萊吉亞·塔倫加——鬼魂的紅樹林——登了岸，走上灘頭，往內陸走去，遇見了鬼魂的群眾。他們問他：「你為何到這裡來？你還沒死呢。」薩穆庫答道：「我的妻子責罵了我，把我打發到這裡來。」夜裡他宿在一座屋子裡，到了早晨那屋子便消失了。於是他對他們施了個計，織了一張網，他們便帶著網去捕魚，他看見了鬼魂的形貌，那網卻纏在了珊瑚上。天亮時，鬼魂的群眾全都離他而去，他便下去睡在沙上。某個地方的人發現了他，抓住他，把他帶在身邊，直到他死去。

title.en: The Mim People Drag the Yams Through the Islands
title.zh: 米姆人曳薯行島

region.en: Torres Islands (Hiw–Lo–Toga), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖托雷斯群島（希烏—洛—托加）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: The Mim people dragged yams ashore at Hiw and along to Tugua, slicing them in half for the men of each island; where the yams were dragged whole they are very large and long to this day. Only at Lo, where everyone was down on the reefs fishing, did the people hear nothing — and their yams are the small rinds the children later picked from the tree-roots along the path.
summary.zh: 米姆人把薯從希烏島曳至圖瓜，途經各島皆呼人來把薯切半分種；凡整薯拖過之地，其薯至今碩大修長。唯獨洛島之人盡下礁捕魚，無人聽見，事後只在沿路樹根上拾得黏著的薯皮，種而得薯——故洛島之薯不大，卻也足食。米姆人一路喊著『來切薯、替我們分擔』，把薯拖遍群島。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era record (Codrington 1891); Torres Islands heritage.

passages.text: They say that the Mim people dragged the yams from place to place, having brought them ashore at Hiw, and then dragged them to Tugua, for which reason the yams at Hiw and at Tugua are very large and long. But when they dragged them along here to Lo, all the people were down on the reefs fishing and heard nothing of it; nor did they know anything till they found the rind of the yams sticking to the roots of the trees along the path. These they picked up and planted; and on that account the Lo yams are not very large, but plentiful enough.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們說，米姆人把山藥從一處拖到另一處，先在希烏把它們拖上岸，然後拖到圖瓜，因此希烏和圖瓜的山藥又大又長。但當他們順著這裡一路拖到洛時，所有的人都在礁石上捕魚，什麼也沒聽見；他們也一無所知，直到發現山藥的皮黏在路旁樹木的根上。他們把這些撿起來種下；因此洛的山藥並不很大，但數量卻足夠多。

passages.text: Because the Mim people sliced their yams in half for the men of Hiw and of Tugua, and then passed on to Toga, and sliced again for them there, on which account the yams there are very large and long. Afterwards they crossed to Ureparapara, where the people sliced the yams in half and planted them. They did the same in all the islands that way; it was only at Lo that the people did not see and hear what was going on. The crowns of the yams remained and were planted somewhere. The Mim people went dragging the yams through all the islands, shouting and calling to the men of every place to come and slice the yams, and take their burden from them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 因為米姆人把山藥切成兩半，分給希烏和圖瓜的人，然後又繼續前往托加，在那裡又切了一半給他們，因此那裡的的山藥又大又長。後來他們渡海到了烏雷帕拉帕拉，那裡的人把山藥切成兩半種下。他們往那邊所有的島嶼都如法炮製；唯有在洛，人們沒有看見也沒有聽見正在發生的事。山藥的頂端留了下來，種在了某處。米姆人拖著山藥走遍所有的島嶼，高聲呼喊，召喚每一處地方的人前來切開山藥，從他們手中接過重擔。

title.en: Muesarava and the First Bone-Tipped Arrows
title.zh: 穆埃薩拉瓦與毒骨箭之始

region.en: Maewo (Aurora Island), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖馬埃沃島（奧羅拉島）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: In old times there was no fighting. But the blind old man Muesarava shot a pigeon he never saw, and two young men ate it from his oven while he sang. His revenge: he grubbed up a dead boy and ground his bones to arrow-points, which killed where wood and fish-bone could not. When his enemies begged the secret, he told them — and died of their first bone-tipped volley. That first dead man's bone still remains, a fofo arrow full of mana: point it towards a rumoured war, and the fighting comes to nothing.
summary.zh: 上古無戰事。盲叟穆埃薩拉瓦聞鴿啼，張弓亂射竟中鴿；與芋同烤，歌而待食。兩名少年偷開其爐，食盡鴿肉，另烤壞物塞回，遠處唱答。盲叟大怒，圖謀開戰：他以手刨出一座已埋之童屍，取骨磨利製箭；敵方仍以木、魚骨為鏃。開戰後，敵箭中他而不死，他的骨箭中人即斃。敵眾不解，求其法；他直言：『去刨我射死的人，刮其骨為鏃。』敵從其言，再戰，盲叟應聲而亡。那支親手所磨之人骨箭至今猶存，木柄屢換而骨鏃不朽，藏於其兄之弟家中，人以為滿蓄瑪那：若有戰訊，向那方向指之，戰事即消。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era record (Codrington 1891); Maewo heritage. Records a war-relic cult object.

passages.text: They say that in old times there was no fighting. But there was an old man whose name was Muesarava, who was blind and used to stay doing nothing in the house; and he heard a pigeon calling, and took a bow and broad-headed arrow and went under the tree; and the pigeon let drop a bit of the fruit it was eating, and that blind man shot at a venture into the tree, and hit the pigeon without seeing it. And he took it up, and went and put it into the oven together with the yams, and sat down and sang a song. But two young fellows came along and quietly opened that old man Muesarava's oven, and ate up his pigeon with some of his yams. Then they went to another place, and sang back a song to him; and he heard it, and went back to eat his pigeon, but found when he uncovered the oven that it was eaten up, and that something not good had been put in its place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說古時候沒有爭鬥。但有個老人名叫穆埃薩拉瓦，他雙目失明，終日在家中無所事事；他聽見一隻鴿子在叫，便取了弓和寬頭箭，走到樹下；那鴿子掉落了一點牠正在吃的水果，那盲人便朝著樹上胡亂射了一箭，竟在看不見的情況下射中了鴿子。他撿起鴿子，拿去和山藥一起放進烤爐裡，然後坐下唱起歌來。但有兩個年輕人走了過來，悄悄打開了那老人穆埃薩拉瓦的烤爐，把他的鴿子連同一些山藥一起吃了。接著他們走到另一個地方，回唱一首歌給他聽；他聽見了，便回去要吃他的鴿子，卻在揭開烤爐時發現鴿子已被吃光，而且裡面被放進了不好的東西。

passages.text: Then he was exceeding angry, and plotted a fight against the people of the place whence the two young men had come who had stolen and eaten Muesarava's food. And now Muesarava began to make fighting arrows of men's bones. Muesarava went and grubbed up with his hands a boy who had died, and took his bones, and beat them to splinters and rubbed them sharp. But his enemies on their side knew nothing of that; they only cut wood into shape, or bones of fish or birds, and fixed them in their arrows, while Muesarava on his side prepared men's bones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他勃然大怒，謀劃要與那兩個偷吃穆埃薩拉瓦食物的年輕人所來自的地方的人們爭鬥。這時穆埃薩拉瓦開始用人骨製作戰箭。穆埃薩拉瓦前去用雙手挖出一個死去的男孩，取了他的骨頭，把它們敲成碎片並磨尖。但他的敵人那一方對此一無所知；他們只是把木頭削成形，或用魚骨、鳥骨，把它們固定在箭上，而穆埃薩拉瓦這一方則準備的是人骨。

passages.text: And when they fought they shot at him and hit, but he did not die; and he shot them and they could not live, but died outright all of them. So it often happened, and they saw that they died in very great numbers; and they asked Muesarava why it was that they shot him and he did not die, while he shot them and they all of them died. Therefore he told them and said, 'Go and grub up one of the dead men I have shot, and scrape his bones, and point your arrows with that.' Upon this they listened to his counsel and did as he had said to them; and when they fought again they shot him, and he straightway died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 交戰時，他們朝他射箭並射中了，但他沒有死；他朝他們射箭，他們便活不成，全都當場死去。這樣的情形屢屢發生，他們見自己死傷極多；便問穆埃薩拉瓦，為何他們射他他卻不死，而他射他們，他們卻全都死去。於是穆埃薩拉瓦告訴他們說：『去把我射死的其中一個死人挖出來，刮下他的骨頭，用那骨頭來做你們箭的箭頭。』於是他們聽從了他的建議，照他所說的做了；再次交戰時，他們朝他射箭，他便立刻死了。

passages.text: And that thing, the dead man's bone that Muesarava ground to a point for himself with his own hand, still remains, and has not yet been spoilt; the reed-shaft has been spoilt and replaced over and over again, but that dead man's bone still remains; I have seen it myself in my brother's possession; it still remains. The people think a great deal of it, thinking that there is supernatural power, mana, in that fofo arrow. If there is heard a rumour of fighting, and that is pointed in the direction whence it comes, the fighting comes to nothing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 而那件東西，就是穆埃薩拉瓦親手為自己磨尖的那根死人骨頭，至今仍然留存，尚未損壞；蘆葦箭桿已一再損壞並更換，但那根死人骨頭仍然留存；我親眼在我兄弟那裡見過它；它仍然留存。人們非常看重它，認為那支福福箭中具有超自然的力量，即瑪納。若聽聞有爭鬥的風聲，而將它指向風聲傳來之處，那爭鬥便會化為烏有。

title.en: Tagaro the Little Feeds His Fish
title.zh: 小塔加羅飼魚記

region.en: Lepers Island (Aoba), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Tagaro-mbiti floated to a sea-rock, fed the rising fish, and sang them a promised meal of toko with coconut sauce. Merambuto overheard the song, stole the canoe, and called with a small copied voice — and the fish rose and were hooked, roasted and eaten. Tagaro followed the footprints, ate his host's 'bad food' claim to nothing, killed him in his house, burnt it, and set the half-eaten fish back in a salt-water pool, where they revived — one side gone, one side left: Tagaro's half-fish, the soles.
summary.zh: 小塔加羅划舟至海上岩畔，不槳自漂，見群魚自舟底湧起，便以手中之食飼之，並許諾：『後日我以椰漿拌托科來餵你們。』次日他唱著歌呼魚——『我的魚呀，無論你們是誰，好小魚，你們的飯來了，椰漿拌的飯來了。』默蘭布托在岸上偷聽，連夜備食，清早劃走小塔加羅之舟，學著喊那歌；只是嗓音太大，魚群不升。他壓低嗓子再唱，魚群盡浮，被他一一釣盡，回村烤食。天明，小塔加羅赴約撲空，循足跡至默蘭布托家，佯坐閒話，問『爐中是什麼？我餓了』；默蘭布托推說『那是我的飯，難吃得很，你吃不下』。小塔加羅道：『那分明是我的魚，叫你釣盡了。』遂擊殺之，焚其屋，把爐中魚取回，放進一小鹹水潭——魚竟復活，只是半邊已失。今人稱之為『塔加羅的半邊魚』——即比目魚。

sensitivity.note: Native manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); Aoba heritage.

passages.text: They say that he drew down his canoe and paddled out in search of fish; and he saw a great rock standing in the sea, and he floated gently without paddling to see whether he would find fish or not. And he saw many fish rising up to the surface from under his canoe, and he fed them with the food he had in his hand, and he perceived that these fish knew how to eat the food of the land. Then said he, 'I am going to leave you, but the day after to-morrow I shall grate some toko for you to eat, and shall pour cocoa-nut sauce over it, and bring it here to you.' So he left them and stayed, they say, one day at home. And when the second day came for him to go he took that toko which he had sauced with cocoa-nut juice, and launched his canoe, and paddled out to the place where those fish were. And he called them with a song: 'My fish, whatever you are, nice little fish, here is your food with sauce, your food done with cocoa-nut sauce.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說他拉下獨木舟，划槳出海尋找魚；他看見海中矗立著一塊巨岩，便不划槳，輕輕漂浮著，看看能否找到魚。他看見許多魚從獨木舟下方浮上水面，便用手裡的食餌餵牠們，他察覺這些魚懂得吃陸地上的食物。於是他說：『我要離開你們了，但後天我會磨些托科給你們吃，並澆上椰漿，帶到這裡給你們。』於是他就離開牠們，據說在家待了一天。到了第二天他該出發時，他帶上那拌了椰汁的托科，推下獨木舟，划槳出海到那些魚所在的地方。他用歌聲呼喚牠們：『我的魚，不論你們是什麼，可愛的小魚，這是你們拌了醬的食物，你們拌了椰漿的食物。』

passages.text: But there was another person, whose name was Merambuto, who stood on the beach, and heard Tagarombiti calling his fish with a song like that, and next day Merambuto, having made haste to prepare food in the night, drew down the canoe in the early morning, Tagarombiti's canoe, and paddled out till he came to the place where Tagarombiti had floated before. And he sang again that song. Then those fish heard his voice that it was loud, and did not rise, because they knew it was a different person by his loud voice. And Merambuto perceived that they did not rise, and he altered his voice so as to be small like Tagarombiti's. And he called them with a small voice singing that song. Then those fish heard that the voice was small, and they rose all of them to the surface, and he caught every one of them with a hook. And he made haste to paddle ashore, and went back into his village, and made up a fire, and put the fish in the oven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但另有一人，名叫梅蘭布托，站在海灘上，聽見塔加羅姆比提用這樣的歌聲呼喚他的魚，第二天梅蘭布托連夜趕忙備好食物，一大早就拉下獨木舟——塔加羅姆比提的獨木舟——划槳出海，直到塔加羅姆比提先前漂浮過的地方。他又唱起那首歌。那些魚聽見他的聲音響亮，便沒有浮上來，因為牠們從他響亮的聲音聽出這是另一個人。梅蘭布托察覺牠們沒有浮上來，便改變嗓音，使之像塔加羅姆比提那樣細小。他用細小的嗓音唱著那首歌呼喚牠們。那些魚聽見聲音細小，便全都浮上水面，他用魚鉤把牠們一一釣起。他趕忙划槳上岸，回到自己的村子，生起火，把魚放進烤爐裡。

passages.text: But when it was broad daylight Tagarombiti went himself, and they were all gone; and he understood that this thief Merambuto had caught all the fish, and paddled quickly back and hauled up his canoe. And he looked for footprints to know which way he had gone round; and he found footprints and followed them till he came to Merambuto's place; and there he went into the house to him, and sat down with him in a friendly way. Then said Tagaro, 'What is that in the oven? I am hungry.' And Merambuto said, 'That is my food, but it is very bad, you cannot eat it.' Then says Tagarombiti, 'Indeed is your food so very bad? But those are my fish, and you have caught them all.' And he struck him, and killed him in his house, and set fire to the house, and it was burnt and destroyed. And Tagarombiti took back the fish from the oven, and went back and put them into a little pool of salt-water, and the fish revived; one side of them was gone, one side still remained. And we call them, tavalui tge bulu Tagaro, Tagaro's half-fish — soles.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但到了大白天，塔加羅姆比提親自前去，魚卻全都不見了；他明白是那個賊梅蘭布托把魚全捉了去，便迅速划槳回來，把獨木舟拖上岸。他尋找腳印，想知道那人往哪個方向繞行；他找到了腳印，便一路跟隨，直到來到梅蘭布托的住處；他走進屋裡去找他，以友善的姿態與他同坐。於是塔加羅說：『爐裡那是什麼？我餓了。』梅蘭布托說：『那是我的食物，不過它很不好，你吃不得。』塔加羅姆比提便說：『你的食物真有那麼不好嗎？可那些是我的魚，而你把它們全捉了去。』他便打他，在屋裡把他殺了，又放火燒屋，屋子被燒毀了。塔加羅姆比提從爐裡取回那些魚，回去把它們放進一個小小的鹹水窪裡，魚便活了過來；牠們一邊沒有了，一邊還在。我們稱牠們為「塔瓦盧伊·特格·布盧·塔加羅」，即塔加羅的半邊魚——鰈魚。

title.en: The Old Woman Who Made the Sea
title.zh: 造海之嫗

region.en: Lepers Island (Aoba), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: An old woman kept her grandson-sons from the fenced ground behind her house, where she made water always into a giant via leaf. While she went to the garden they shot at a lizard sitting on the leaf and burst it — and the water burst forth too. She cried aloud her spell, 'Pour round about and meet! Round about the world!' — and so the sea for the first time stood full around the whole world, for before that they say there was no sea.
summary.zh: 無名老嫗與兩個外孫同居。屋後有一圈葦籬，籬內她獨自使用——那裡放著一片巨大芋葉，她素來就在葉上便溺，並嚴禁二童入內窺看。一日老嫗往園中耕作取食，二兄弟在家射蜥蜴取樂，終於商議：『去看看那禁地是什麼。』他們見到那片芋葉與水；恰有一蜥蜴停在葉上，一童彎弓射之，誤中葉身，葉破水湧。老嫗聞聲，知是二童射破了葉，便立起高聲念咒：『Marodafi bulu, korodafi bulu! Pour round about and meet! Round about the world!』念了三遍——於是海水初次環繞全世界漲滿；據說在此之前世上本無海。老嫗便這樣造出了海。

sensitivity.note: Native manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); Aoba heritage. Cross-ref melanesian-baining-tiny-sea (New Britain sea-origin).

passages.text: Nobody knows what her name was, but she was an old woman. And there were two children who lived with her in her house; the story about them is that the mother of these two was the daughter of this old woman. Her house was a good one, fenced about with reeds; there was a fence all round the house, and there was a fence also made against the back of the house, and those two children were forbidden to go into it, because she would be there by herself. And in that little fence at the back of the house she put carefully a leaf of the via, the gigantic caladium; and they say that in that leaf she always made water, and was always very strict in forbidding those two to go there, lest they should see it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 沒有人知道她叫什麼名字，只知道她是個老婦人。有兩個孩子和她一同住在她的屋裡；關於他們的傳說說，這兩個孩子的母親是這老婦人的女兒。她的屋子很好，四周用蘆葦圍著；屋子周圍有一道籬笆，屋後也另有一道籬笆，那兩個孩子被禁止進入那裡，因為她要獨自待在那兒。在屋後那道小籬笆裡，她小心地放了一片「維亞」葉，就是巨大的芋葉；他們說她總是在那片葉子裡解手，並且一向嚴厲地禁止那兩個孩子到那裡去，免得他們看見。

passages.text: And these two were both boys, and they were always shooting lizards. So one day when the old woman went into the garden to work and to bring back food for the three of them, she said to those two, 'Don't you go there!' and they answered, 'Very well, we shall not go.' And she went out of the house, and went into the gardens, and those two brothers played with their bows, shooting lizards. After a while one said to the other, 'It would be a good thing to go and see what it is where the old woman has forbidden us to go.' So they went, and they saw that via leaf and the water in it. Then they saw a lizard sitting on a part of that leaf, and one of them shot at it, but missed the lizard and hit the leaf, and the water that was in it burst quickly forth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這兩個都是男孩，他們總是在射蜥蜴。有一天，老婦人到園子裡去幹活，並為他們三人帶回食物，她對那兩個孩子說：『你們別到那裡去！』他們回答：『好的，我們不去。』她便出了屋子，走進園子，而那兩兄弟玩著弓箭，射蜥蜴。過了一會兒，一個對另一個說：『去看看老婦人禁止我們去的那地方究竟是什麼，倒是件好事。』於是他們去了，看見了那片維亞葉和葉裡的水。接著他們看見一隻蜥蜴停在那片葉子的一處，其中一人朝牠射去，卻沒射中蜥蜴，射中了葉子，葉裡的水便迅速迸湧而出。

passages.text: And the old woman heard it, and perceived that those two had probably shot the leaf. And she stood up and cried with a loud voice, 'Marodafi bulu, korodafi bulu! Pour round about and meet! Round about the world!' And thus the sea for the first time stood full around the whole world, for before that they say there was no sea. So the old woman you may say made the sea herself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 老婦人聽見了，察覺那兩個孩子多半是射了那片葉子。她便站起來，高聲喊道：『馬羅達菲·布盧，科羅達菲·布盧！湧向四方，匯合起來！環繞世界！』於是海水第一次漲滿，環繞了整個世界，因為他們說在那以前並沒有海。所以可以說，是這老婦人自己造出了海。

title.en: Dilingavuv and the Pit of Roasted Chestnuts
title.zh: 迪林加武武與烤栗陷阱

region.en: Torres Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖托雷斯群島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Dilingavuv ate his neighbours' bananas from the treetops; no one dared his bat-like stretched arms until Marawhihi shot off his ear. The thief cut himself a new ear from a Raw root, lured the celebrating dancers one by one onto a leaf-cloak over a pit, and rained hot stones in — but Marawhihi shot an arrow-chain up a banyan branch and led them all out alive.
summary.zh: 迪林加武武天天攀上香蕉樹偷食，村人畏其張臂如蝠，無人敢近；唯最機敏的馬拉威希希以卡薩林木箭射落其耳。迪林加武武回家瞞母索斧，自砍 Raw 樹根另造一耳，口中念『剁碎！剁開！』；村人偷聽而知。馬拉威希希率眾日日宴舞，迪林加武武欲報仇：他備下烤栗、火石與葉衣，在村旁掘深坑覆以葉衣，誘歇腳的舞者一一坐上而陷落，馬拉威希希最後也跌入。他把燒紅的石頭擲進坑裡；馬拉威希希卻叫眾人移到坑的另一邊避過。他抬頭見坑口懸著一根榕枝，便連環射箭成梯，眾人攀箭而出，皆得生還。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era record (Codrington 1891); Torres Islands heritage.

passages.text: They were living in their place, and his companions made a garden, and planted bananas in it. When the bananas bore fruit and ripened Dilingavuv went every day and ate bananas in their garden, not eating on the ground, but climbing into the trees and eating. After a while he was discovered; one of the party went into the garden and saw him up in a banana-tree eating; so he ran and told the others. Says he, 'You fellows, I have seen the one who steals and eats our bananas.' Then said Marawhihi, 'Hew out bows for us to go and shoot and kill him.' But they said, 'Marawhihi, no one will be able to shoot and kill him. It is wholly impossible.' However they hewed out bows, each for himself, and put points to their arrows; and when that was done Marawhihi said, 'Let us go after him one by one.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們住在自己的地方，他的同伴們開了一片園子，在裡面種了香蕉。香蕉結果成熟後，迪林加武武每天都到他們的園子裡吃香蕉，他不在上吃，而是爬上樹去吃。過了一陣子，他被人發現了；其中一人走進園子，看見他在香蕉樹上吃著；他便跑去告訴其他人。他說：『你們這些傢伙，我看見那個偷吃我們香蕉的傢伙了。』馬拉惠惠便說：『給我們削弓，我們去射死他。』但他們說：『馬拉惠惠，沒有人能射死他。這根本不可能。』然而他們還是各自削了弓，給箭裝上箭頭；做完之後，馬拉惠惠說：『我們一個一個地去追他。』

passages.text: So one went first, and came to the garden, and saw him sitting up in the banana-tree, and went on tiptoe towards him to shoot him. But Dilingavuv stretched out his arms like a bat, and the man was afraid, and ran back and told the others. Thus they all went in turn, and came back and disputed with Marawhihi, saying, 'It can't possibly be done.' Then said Marawhihi, 'I shall do it myself, I shall shoot him and kill him.' And this Marawhihi they say was more clever than them all; and he went last and saw Dilingavuv sitting in the banana-tree, and he stepped along on tiptoe under the banana, and when Dilingavuv stretched out his arms he was not frightened at him; but he shot him with a bird arrow of casuarina wood, and hit him on the ear, and shot it right off; and he fell headlong to the ground. So Marawhihi ran and told his friends; but Dilingavuv got up from under the banana and went home to his mother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是一人先去，來到園子裡，看見他坐在香蕉樹上，便踮著腳朝他走去，要射他。但迪林加武武像蝙蝠一樣張開雙臂，那人害怕了，跑回去告訴其他人。他們就這樣輪流前去，回來後都與馬拉惠惠爭辯，說：『這根本辦不到。』馬拉惠惠便說：『我自己來，我要射死他。』他們說這馬拉惠惠比他們所有人都機靈；他最後一個去，看見迪林加武武坐在香蕉樹上，便踮著腳走到香蕉樹下，當迪林加武武張開雙臂時，他並不害怕；他用木麻黃木的射鳥箭射他，射中他的耳朵，把它整個射掉了；他便一頭栽到地上。馬拉惠惠便跑去告訴他的朋友們；但迪林加武武從香蕉樹下爬起來，回家找他母親去了。

passages.text: When he reached his mother's house, he called to her within, and she answered him and said, 'What is it, my son?' And he said, 'Give me an axe.' But he deceived her, and did not tell her that Marawhihi had shot his ear off. Then he went and cut another ear for himself out of the root of a tree, and the name of that tree is the Raw, and as he was chopping the Raw root, he said, 'Chop in pieces! chop asunder!' But Marawhihi had sent one of his men who went and listened, and heard him saying this, and he ran back and told Marawhihi that Dilingavuv was chopping himself out an ear in place of the other. After this Marawhihi and his men made a feast and danced, and danced every day. And when Dilingavuv heard of it, he said, 'I will go and have my revenge.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他來到母親的屋子時，他向屋內的母親呼喚，母親應了他，說：「什麼事，我的兒子？」他說：「給我一把斧頭。」但他騙了她，沒有告訴她馬拉威希希把他的耳朵射掉了。於是他去從一棵樹的根上為自己砍下另一隻耳朵，那樹的名字叫拉烏（Raw），當他砍那拉烏根時，他說：「砍成碎片！砍成兩半！」但馬拉威希希派了他的一個手下前去偷聽，聽到了他說這些話，便跑回去告訴馬拉威希希，說迪林加武夫正為自己砍出一隻耳朵來代替另一隻。此後，馬拉威希希和他的手下設宴跳舞，天天跳舞。迪林加武夫聽說此事後，說：「我要去報仇。」

passages.text: So he gathered a great quantity of Tahitian chestnuts, and took fire, and collected stones, and took a dancing cloak of leaves, and went to them; but he did not go right up to them into the open, but stayed beside the village. Then he made up a fire and roasted his chestnuts, and heated the stones, and dug a very deep hole and covered over the mouth of it with the dress of leaves; and so he sat and watched them dancing. Before long one of them fell out to take breath; and when he saw Dilingavuv sitting and eating chestnuts, he called to him to give him one. 'Run over here,' says Dilingavuv; so he runs over to him, and sits down on this dancing dress; and as he throws himself down to sit he goes clean down into the hole. And Dilingavuv played the same trick to all the company at that dance, and let them all down into that one pit, and Marawhihi last of all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他採集了大量大溪地栗，帶了火，又收集了石頭，還拿了一件樹葉編成的舞衣，便往他們那裡去；但他沒有徑直走到他們中間的空地上，而是留在村子旁邊。然後他生起火來烤他的栗子，把石頭燒熱，挖了一個很深的坑，用那件樹葉舞衣蓋住坑口；他就這樣坐著看他們跳舞。不久，他們中有一個人出來透氣；他看見迪林加武夫坐著吃栗子，便叫他給自己一顆。「跑過來這裡，」迪林加武夫說；於是那人跑向他，坐在那件舞衣上；當他撲身坐下時，便直直地掉進了坑裡。迪林加武夫對那場舞會上的所有人如法炮製，把他們全都弄進了那一個坑裡，馬拉威希希是最後一個。

title.en: The Boy Who Made a Friend of an Eel
title.zh: 與鰻結交之童

region.en: Vanua Lava, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島瓦努阿瓦島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: A boy begged two yams of his parents, and the crumbs he dropped called up an eel that turned into a man. They anointed their heads and dug gardens together, till the jealous villagers fell on him; a flood carried the eel to the beach, where they cut him to pieces — but his brother's tears revived him, and he sent the family to another island before a great surf swept the persecutors' island wholly away.
summary.zh: 一童求父母留兩隻芋，烤食時碎屑落入水中，一條鰻來食，化為男子。二人抹油束髮，同去園中掘地；村人圍觀，婦女怠工，丈夫們怒而毆鰻；童以水澆之，鰻復原形，屢擒屢脫，躍入水中。村人言『放雨淹他』，遂作大雨，洪水把鰻沖上灘頭，眾人將鰻剁成數段。童之弟奔下灘，見而哭泣；淚落鰻身，鰻復化為人，起身對弟說：『你回去告訴父母，我們三人要遷往別島。』三人遷走後，某日一老嫗聽見鰻歌聲，村人初不信；聲音分明，歌罷忽有巨響，滔天巨浪席捲全村，無一倖存，全島盡沒。

sensitivity.note: Native manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); Vanua Lava heritage.

passages.text: They were living in their place, and they were planting their gardens; and one day when they went to plant, a boy said to his father and mother, 'To-morrow when you go again, you will put by a yam for me.' Next morning his father and mother went, and put by a yam for him; and he roasted it and ate it, and then went and asked some other boys for more. But they scolded him; and he cried and said, 'Very well!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們住在自己的地方，耕種著他們的園子；有一天他們去種地時，一個男孩對他的父親和母親說：「明天你們再去的時候，替我留一個山藥。」第二天早晨，他的父親和母親去了，替他留了一個山藥；他把它烤了吃掉，然後去向別的男孩再要一些。但他們責罵了他；他哭著說：「好吧！」

passages.text: Next morning they put two yams for the boy; and when he had roasted them he went and followed a stream, and found a nice place, and sat down to eat. As he was eating, crumbs of food fell into the water, and an Eel came out and ate, and turned into a man, and rose up and came to the boy. When they two had eaten all the yam, the Eel said to the boy, 'To-morrow you will roast two yams again, and bring them here, and we two will eat them.' And when they had finished eating the Eel said to the boy, 'Let us anoint our heads.' So they dressed their heads and adorned themselves, and went into the garden, and helped the people who were digging the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天早晨，他們替那男孩留了兩個山藥；他把它們烤好後，便沿著一條溪流走去，找到一個好地方，坐下來吃。他正吃著，食物的碎屑掉進了水裡，一條鰻魚出來吃了，變成了一個人，起身來到男孩面前。他們兩個把山藥都吃完後，鰻魚對男孩說：「明天你再烤兩個山藥，帶到這裡來，我們兩個一起吃。」他們吃完後，鰻魚對男孩說：「我們來塗抹我們的頭吧。」於是他們梳理頭髮、打扮自己，然後走進園子，幫那些挖地的人幹活。

passages.text: When they had finished eating the Eel said to the boy, 'Let us anoint our heads.' So they dressed their heads and adorned themselves, and went into the garden, and helped the people who were digging the ground. But when that Eel dug the ground all the people crowded to see him do it; some went back to their digging, but the women would not do their work, and their husbands were exceedingly angry with the Eel, and rushed upon him, and would have killed him; but the boy who came with him poured water on him, and he turned into an Eel again. And they caught hold of him, but he escaped; and they missed their hold upon him over and over again, and he jumped into the water. So they said, 'All right, we will make rain for him'; and they made a great rain, and the water swelled into a flood and carried the Eel to the beach. When the flood subsided they went down and found the Eel lying on the beach, and they cut him into short pieces, and left him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們吃完後，鰻魚對男孩說：「我們來塗抹我們的頭吧。」於是他們梳理頭髮、打扮自己，然後走進園子，幫那些挖地的人幹活。但當那鰻魚挖地時，所有的人都擠過來看他挖；有些人回去幹自己的活，但女人們不肯幹活，她們的丈夫對那鰻魚極為憤怒，衝向他，想要殺死他；但與他同來的男孩往他身上潑水，他又變回了鰻魚。他們抓住了他，但他逃脫了；他們一次又一次地抓不住他，他跳進了水裡。於是他們說：「好吧，我們來給他造雨」；他們造了一場大雨，水漲成了洪水，把鰻魚衝到了海灘上。洪水退去後，他們下去，發現鰻魚躺在海灘上，便把他切成短段，丟下他走了。

passages.text: But the boy, his brother, ran down and saw the Eel lying there, and wept; and his tears fell upon the Eel, and he turned into a man again, and stood up and said to his brother, 'You are to go up inland and tell your father and mother that you three are to go and take up your abode in another island.' The boy therefore said to his father and mother, 'We three are to move to another island.' After they had gone, one day an old woman was sitting, and she heard the Eel singing a song; and she said to the people, 'Listen to that singing a song like the Eel'; but some of them answered, 'It is not that, the Eel is dead'; but they heard plainly the Eel's voice, and said, 'It is true, it is the Eel's voice.' And when he had finished singing they heard a loud report; and as they were sitting a very great surf rose and swept them away, all of them; and they all died, and that island was entirely lost.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但他的兄弟那男孩跑下去，看見鰻魚躺在那裡，便哭了起來；他的眼淚落在鰻魚身上，鰻魚又變回了一個人，站起來對他的兄弟說：「你要往內陸去，告訴你的父親和母親，你們三個要搬到另一個島上去住。」於是那男孩對他的父親和母親說：「我們三個要搬到另一個島上去。」他們走後，有一天一個老婦人坐著，她聽見鰻魚在唱一首歌；她對人們說：「聽那唱歌的，唱得像鰻魚一樣」；但他們中有些人回答說：「不是的，鰻魚已經死了」；但他們清楚地聽見了鰻魚的聲音，便說：「是真的，是鰻魚的聲音。」當他唱完歌後，他們聽見一聲巨響；正當他們坐著時，一道極大的海浪湧起，把他們全都沖走了；他們全都死了，那個島也完全消失了。

title.en: Molgon and Molwor: The Brothers Whose Names Told Their Fate
title.zh: 莫爾貢與莫爾沃：名讖成真

region.en: Vanua Lava, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島瓦努阿瓦島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Orphaned Molgon was told to feed his little brother; but paddling up a stream after the galakv fruit that floated past, he left Molwor in the canoe and stayed with a woman named Rohehahal — who read out their names like a judgement: 'Your name is Molgon, Go-catch, and you have caught on to the goods of you and me; but he, his name is Molwor, Go-clear, and he has come here to be clear of all the goods of you and me.' Molwor lay dead in the sun; Molgon's tears revived him; and the brother's last song ended in the water, where blood rose up and both turned into stones in the water-course.
summary.zh: 父母臨終囑長兄莫爾貢照看幼弟莫爾沃。二人划舟溯流，見 galakv 果一枚枚漂來，數目漸增；至果源處，兄留弟守舟，獨自上岸採果。婦人 Rohehahal 自屋出，與他共炊共食；他吃不完便想帶給弟弟，婦人卻說『吃不完就丟給豬』。他哭。她問名，聞言道：『果然！你名莫爾貢（Go-catch），你已捉住了你我之家的財物；他那名莫爾沃（Go-clear），是來躲開你我全部家產的。』兄弟返舟見幼弟已被烈日曬死；莫爾貢淚滴弟胸，弟復活，責兄只顧自食。婦人屢催兄『跟我走』；弟唱罷離歌，雙足入水化鰻，一躍而沒，兄亦躍水；婦人立崖下望，只見水中泛起血光——二人化為溪中兩塊臥石。

sensitivity.note: Native manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); Vanua Lava heritage.

passages.text: The father and mother of these two brothers, who lived at Gaua, said to the elder of them, Molgon, 'You are to look well after him, the younger one, and feed him well.' 'All right,' he said; and then their father and mother died. They two lived on; and one day they drew down a canoe, and paddled up the course of a stream, and came upon galakv fruit floating down it. They broke it in two and ate it. They paddled on and there came floating down two, then three, then four, then five, then six, then seven, then eight, then nine, then ten, one for one and one for the other, and the odd one they broke in two; they paddled on and saw the source from which the fruits had floated down. Then the elder brother said to the younger, 'You sit here, and I will go and gather for us both to eat.' So he went and gathered fruit. But a woman, Rohehahal, came out of her house, and looked down to where he was standing, and called him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這兩兄弟的父親和母親住在加瓦，他們對年長的那個，即莫爾貢，說：『你要好好照看他，那年幼的，好好餵養他。』『好的，』他說；接著他們的父親和母親就死了。他們兩人繼續過活；有一天，他們把一艘獨木舟拖下水，沿著一條溪流划槳而上，遇到加拉克果實順流漂下。他們把它掰成兩半吃了。他們繼續划，接著漂下來兩個，然後三個，然後四個，然後五個，然後六個，然後七個，然後八個，然後九個，然後十個，一人一個，另一個他們掰成兩半；他們繼續划，看見了那些果實漂流下來的源頭。於是兄長對弟弟說：『你坐在這裡，我去採集我們兩人吃的。』於是他就去採集果實。但有一個女人，羅赫哈哈爾，從她的屋子裡出來，俯視他站著的地方，呼喚他。

passages.text: He went to her, and she said to him, 'We two will cook food in the oven'; and they two cooked food in the oven, and afterwards they ate. He could not eat all the qeta, and he said to her, 'I will go with this to my brother, that he may eat it'; but the woman said, 'If you can't eat it all, throw it outside for the pigs'; and he cried. Then she made a mush; he could not eat it all, and said, 'I shall take this for my brother to eat.' But she said, 'Throw it outside to the pigs'; and he cried. Then she asked their names, and said, 'Aia! true enough! your name is Molgon, Go-catch, and you have caught on to the pigs which belong to you and me, and the house, and the gamal, and the food, and the money; but he, his name is Molwor, Go-clear, and he has come here to be clear of all the goods of you and me.' And he cried and cried.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他走到她那裡，她對他說：『我們兩人在爐灶裡煮食物吧』；於是他們兩人在爐灶裡煮食物，之後他們吃了。他吃不完所有的凱塔，他對她說：『我把這個帶給我的弟弟，讓他吃』；但那女人說：『如果你吃不完，就把它扔到外面給豬吃』；於是他哭了。接著她做了一種糊狀食物；他吃不完，說：『我要把這個帶給我的弟弟吃。』但她說：『把它扔到外面給豬吃』；於是他哭了。接著她問了他們的名字，說：『哎呀！果然不錯！你的名字是莫爾貢，去抓，你已經抓上了屬於你我的豬，還有屋子、加馬爾、食物和錢財；但他，他的名字是莫爾沃爾，去清空，他來到這裡是要清空你和我的一切財物。』於是他哭啊哭。

passages.text: Then the woman said, 'Get up, let us go and see him'; and they went over and found him dead, lying in the canoe, for the sun had smitten him dead with its rays. And he cried and cried, and his tears dropped on his brother's breast, and he came to life again, and said, 'Brother, our father when he died told you to take care of me, but you have gone away to eat and have not thought of me.' But the woman urged Molgon, 'Come here! we two will go up away from him again.' Then Molwor sang a song to him, and got down from the canoe, and put his legs into the water, and began to turn into an eel; and when he had quite finished his song he plunged into the water, and his brother leapt down also into the water. And the woman stood and looked down, and blood came up from the water. And they two turned into stones lying in the water-course; and the woman stood and wept greatly, and went back again up the hill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著那女人說：『起來，我們去看看他』；他們走過去，發現他死了，躺在獨木舟裡，因為太陽用它的光芒將他擊死了。於是他哭啊哭，他的眼淚滴在他弟弟的胸膛上，他又活了過來，說：『哥哥，我們的父親死時囑咐你照看我，但你卻走開去吃東西，沒有想到我。』但那女人催促莫爾貢：『過來這裡！我們兩人再離開他上去吧。』於是莫爾沃爾對他唱了一首歌，從獨木舟上下來，把雙腿伸進水裡，開始變成一條鰻魚；當他完全唱完他的歌時，他縱身跳入水中，他的哥哥也跟著跳入水中。那女人站著俯視，血從水中冒了上來。他們兩人變成了躺在水道裡的石頭；那女人站著大哭，又回到山上去了。

title.en: The Ghost-Wife
title.zh: 鬼妻

region.en: Mota, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島莫塔島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: In famine, a son tracked his mother's secret gaviga-tree and met the ghost who owned it — his own uncle, who hid him from the whirring ghost-flock and fed him till daylight, then gave him a damsel for a wife. Her touch ripened every garden; her husband called her a sky-woman and beat her, and she burned banyan leaves and rose in the smoke to her own country, the child crying beside the fire — until Marawa the Spider spun a line to heaven, carried father and child up, and at the feast each pass of the dancing mother drew the cry 'Mother!' until she stopped, knew her own, and came home with them all.
summary.zh: 饑荒年，母子靠母親偷采的 gaviga 果度日；兒子發現果核追問，循母親折枝記號至果樹，夜攀樹而食。一個鬼落在他身旁，自認是他的舅舅，把他藏進樹洞，蓋住洞口；群鬼嗡嗡而至采果，舅舅摘果分他，直吃到天亮。臨散時，舅舅將一個少女許配給他。女子觸物皆熟：摸薯即得薯，摸香蕉即熟蕉，摸椰即得椰。丈夫見狀疑心，責打她，罵她屬天不屬地。她說『好，我就回天上去』，便燒起榕葉，火焰直上，她從煙中升天，孩子啼哭於火旁。丈夫求助於蜘蛛馬拉瓦；馬拉瓦吐絲成線直通天庭，背負父子而上。天庭正開盛宴，母子每相錯而過，孩子便哭喊一聲『媽媽！』；她終於停步，問『是誰在喊我媽媽？』認出孩子與丈夫，便隨蜘蛛攜全家平安回到地上。

sensitivity.note: Native manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); the ending comes from Codrington's summary of the continuation. Mota heritage.

passages.text: They were living and living in their place; a famine prevailed. And there was a woman and her son, and they both were hungry. After a time the mother went to dig qauro, wild yams, for them to eat, and as she went she found a gaviga (Malay apple) tree in fruit, in a deserted garden, and she put down her basket, and gathered with her hands and ate. And when she had finished eating she put some seeds into her basket; and as she went along she broke the tips of the branches to mark the path. And when she had arrived at the village she said to her son, 'Take the things out of our basket'; and he took them out one by one, and as he took them out he found the gaviga seeds in the basket which his mother had put there. Then says her son to her, 'What is this you have been eating, and have put the seeds in the basket for me to see?' But he says, 'No!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們在他們的地方住著住著；饑荒蔓延。有一個女人和她的兒子，他們兩人都餓了。過了一段時間，母親去挖考羅，即野山藥，給他們吃，她去的時候在一座荒廢的園子裡發現一棵結了果實的加維加樹（馬來蘋果樹），她放下籃子，用手採集來吃。她吃完後，把一些種子放進她的籃子裡；她一路走時折斷樹枝的尖端來標記路徑。當她到達村莊時，她對她的兒子說：『把東西從我們的籃子裡拿出來』；他把東西一件一件拿出來，當他拿出來時，他發現籃子裡有他母親放在那裡的加維加種子。於是她的兒子對她說：『這是什麼，你一直在吃，還把種子放在籃子裡讓我看見？』但他說：『沒有！』

passages.text: So he follows the word his mother gave him; and as he goes along the sun is setting, but he arrives at the gaviga-tree and climbs up. And when he had climbed up to eat it was dark. Then he sees something flying to him on the gaviga and settling. 'Where do you come from?' says the ghost. And the man tells him of his mother and her gaviga. Then said the ghost, 'She is my sister to be sure, and my own nephew are you; come here and let me hide you, for we are many of us now coming to eat gavigas.' So he makes him sit down in the hollow of the gaviga, and sits over the mouth of it. While he is in the hollow he hears a whirring sound like birds settling on the top of the tree. 'What is this?' says the man. 'Ghosts come to eat gavigas; don't be afraid, here am I with you,' says the uncle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他遵照他母親給他的話去做；他一路走時太陽正在下山，但他到達了那棵加維加樹並爬了上去。當他爬上去要吃時，天已經黑了。接著他看見有東西飛到加維加樹上向他而來並停落下來。『你從哪裡來？』那鬼魂說。那人告訴他關於他母親和她的加維加的事。接著那鬼魂說：『她確實是我的姊妹，而你是我的親外甥；過來這裡，讓我把你藏起來，因為我們現在有很多人要來吃加維加。』於是他讓他坐在加維加樹的空洞裡，自己坐在洞口上方。當他在空洞裡時，他聽見一種像鳥兒停落在樹頂上的呼呼聲。『這是什麼？』那人說。『鬼魂們來吃加維加；不要害怕，我在這裡陪著你，』那舅舅說。

passages.text: And when the day was dawning and some of the ghosts were taking flight he says to a damsel among them, 'Don't be in a hurry to fly off, you and I will fly together'; and she says, 'Very well.' But when they had all the lot of them taken flight, and it was clear daylight, the ghost says to the man, 'Well now, come out'; and he comes out from the hollow of the gaviga-tree. Then says the ghost his uncle to him, 'Well, here is a damsel for a qorolava [wife].'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當天剛破曉，有些鬼魂正要起飛時，他對其中一個少女說：『不要急著飛走，你和我一起飛』；她說：『好的。』但當他們全部一大群都起飛了，天已大亮時，那鬼魂對那人說：『好了，現在出來吧』；他從加維加樹的空洞裡出來。接著他的鬼魂舅舅對他說：『好了，這裡有一個少女做你的科羅拉瓦〔妻子〕。』

passages.text: So he married her. She takes her child up on her back, and goes with it to the yam garden; if she lays hold on the leaf of the yam, there is a tuber already in her hand; if she essays to pluck hibiscus leaves, they are in her hand already; and if she essays to take a cocoa-nut, there is a cocoa-nut already in her hand. But her husband will not believe her: 'You don't belong down here below, you belong above the sky. Get back into your own country.' And she says, 'Very well, I will soon go back into my own country.' So she gathers banyan leaves into a heap, and sets fire to them, and the smoke goes straight up into the clouds, and the child's mother goes up in it; and her child cries beside the fire, and she goes on up into the clouds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript and Codrington's summary of the continuation; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他就娶了她。她把孩子背在背上，帶著孩子到山藥園去；她若抓住山藥的葉子，手裡便已有一顆塊莖；她若試著去摘木槿葉，葉子便已在她手中；她若試著去取一顆椰子，椰子便已在她手中。但她的丈夫不肯相信她：「你不屬於這下面，你屬於天之上。回到你自己的地方去吧。」她便說：「好吧，我很快就回我自己的地方去。」於是她把榕樹葉聚成一堆，點火燒了起來，煙直直升入雲中，孩子的母親便隨著煙升了上去；她的孩子在火旁哭著，而她繼續升入雲中。

title.en: Ganviviris and Ro Som, the Woman Called Money
title.zh: 加維維里斯與『錢』女羅松

region.en: Uakea, Mota, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島莫塔島烏阿凱阿（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Ganviviris, an idle orphan kept poor by his uncle, shot at a rolling sauma at a voice's urging and was dragged by the fish into the cave of Ro Som — Money — who turned from fish to woman and promised him service. Ten plaited bags filled with coin in the night; he bought wives, taro-gardens, pigs, and rank after rank of the Suqe to the top. But at the height of his kolikole feast a woman with boar's tusks on her arms walked up the slope and into his house; his bags stood empty, his pigs were gone, and in five days he was dead.
summary.zh: 加維維里斯是孤兒，寄居舅家，舅母們譏他游手好閒、無產無份。一日他下灘射魚，正要放箭，忽聞身後有人催喝『放箭！放箭！』回頭無人；第三次放箭果中一條游動的 sauma 大魚；魚負他竄入乾洞——那正是羅松（意為『錢』）的住處。魚化為女子，說：『莫哭，是我在憐憫你。我天天看你，如今要幫你了。』她教他請舅母編十只袋子，掛滿屋中。夜裡屋梁被錢壓得吱呀作響——十袋皆滿。他以此娶妻、買園、養豬、一級級買進蘇蓋會社，直到最高之位。大宴 kolikole 之夕，見一女子拄矛拾級而上，臂戴鐲與野豬牙，髮插豬尾；她徑入加維維里斯屋中，轉眼不見。他上屋查看，十袋皆空，豬隻全無；分發出去的財物盡作廢。當夜他喊叫不安，自此病倒，第五日死去。

sensitivity.note: Native manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); records the Suqe rank-system economy in narrative form.

passages.text: The story about what Ro Som did for Ganviviris is not an old one; he was a man whom my father's grandfather and his friends had seen; an orphan, whose father and mother were both dead, he lived with his mother's brother. And his uncle did nothing for him in the suqe club; he still remained an arlava, because he was an idle fellow, and when they were all gone inland to the gardens he would go down to the beach to shoot fish, and do nothing else day after day. But one day he took his bow and went down to Ngerenow, and there he saw a sauma slowly swimming along and rolling from side to side quite close to him; and he took an arrow tipped with casuarina wood, and drew his bow to shoot. And just as he was releasing the string he heard a voice inciting him and saying, 'Let fly! Let fly!' And he turned his head again and again to look behind him, but there was no man. And the third time he drew his bow, and heard the voice, and loosed the string and hit the sauma.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 關於羅·索姆為甘維維里斯所做之事的故事，並不是一個古老的故事；他是我父親的祖父及其友人們親眼見過的一個人；他是個孤兒，父母雙亡，跟著舅舅過活。他的舅舅在蘇克社團中什麼也沒替他做；他仍是個阿拉瓦，因為他是個懶惰的傢伙，當大家都到內地去園子裡時，他卻下到海灘去射魚，日復一日什麼也不做。但有一天，他拿起弓下到恩格勒諾，在那裡他看見一條紹馬魚緩緩游著，左右翻滾，離他很近；他便取了一支木麻黃木作箭頭的箭，拉弓欲射。就在他正要放弦之際，他聽見一個聲音激勵他說：「放箭！放箭！」他一次又一次轉頭往後看，卻不見有人。第三次他拉開弓，又聽見那聲音，便放開弦，射中了那條紹馬魚。

passages.text: And he ran down and caught the fish by the tail, and threw his arms round it; but the fish struggled, and carried him off into a dry cave, which was, they say, the dwelling of Ro Som (Money). And Ganviviris cried aloud, but the sauma turned into a woman, and said, 'Don't cry, it is I who have had pity on you. I have seen you every day, and now I am going to do you a service. Tell your uncle to bid his wives plait bags for you, and let them be ten, and make a chamber for yourself parted off from the house, and hang up all the bags in the open; and don't eat anything to-day.' So Ganviviris dived out of the cave, and went back into the village, and got the three wives to plait the bags. And in the night Ro Som came and said, 'Make haste to hang up your bags.' And next day he hung up the bags; and in the night he heard the rafters creak because of the money which was filling the bags; and he felt one after another those ten bags, every one quite full.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他跑下去抓住魚尾，雙臂抱住牠；但那魚掙扎著，把他帶進一個乾燥的洞穴，據說那便是羅·索姆（金錢）的居所。甘維維里斯放聲大哭，但那條紹馬魚變成了一個女人，說道：「別哭，是我憐憫了你。我每天都看見你，如今我要替你出一份力。叫你的舅舅吩咐他的妻子們為你編袋子，要編十個，並在屋外另闢一間屬於你自己的房間，把所有的袋子掛在外面；今天什麼也別吃。」於是甘維維里斯從洞穴中潛出，回到村裡，讓三個妻子編袋子。夜裡羅·索姆來了，說道：「趕快把你的袋子掛起來。」第二天他把袋子掛了起來；夜裡他聽見椽子作響，因為金錢正裝滿那些袋子；他一個接一個摸那十個袋子，每一個都裝得滿滿的。

passages.text: And Ro Som said to him, 'Tell your uncle to give you his third wife'; and his uncle let him have one. And always he was buying food with large payments, and he paddled over to Vanua Lava and bought with large sums there, and to Mota and bought with large sums there: and he went on in the suqe till he reached the wemeleloa. Then he desired to make his suqe also at Mota, and he went and built his house at Tasmate; and he appointed the tenth day for a sawae, and at the sawae the tenth day for a kolekole.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 羅·索姆對他說：「叫你的舅舅把他的第三個妻子給你」；他的舅舅便讓他得到了一個。他總是以上千的厚禮購買食物，划船到瓦努阿·拉瓦，在那裡以重金購買，又到莫塔，在那裡以重金購買：他在蘇克社團中一路晉升，直到達到維梅萊洛阿。這時他又想在莫塔也辦他的蘇克，便去在塔斯馬特建了他的房子；他定下第十天舉行薩瓦埃，又在薩瓦埃上定下第十天舉行科萊科萊。

passages.text: And at the kolekole, when the noise of the sawae was sounding like thunder, and the feast was at its height, they saw a woman walking up the sloping ground below the cliff, using a spear for a walking stick, with bracelets on her arms reaching to the elbow, and on her right arm a boar's tusk, and her head smeared with red earth, and pigs' tails fastened to her hair; and they thought that some visitors had just landed from a canoe. And she went straight to the house of Ganviviris and passed out of sight within it. And they told Ganviviris, 'We have seen a woman go into your hole house, with bracelets and boars' tusks on her arms'; and he said, 'Don't mention it in the village.' And he went up there to bring out his money-bags on his back, and he saw that his ten bags had nothing in them; and he went outside and saw that all his pigs were gone; his distribution of property came to nothing at all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了科萊科萊那天，當薩瓦埃的喧鬧聲如雷鳴般作響、宴會正酣之際，他們看見一個女人走在崖下的斜坡上，用一支矛作手杖，臂上的臂環一直戴到肘部，右臂上有一隻野豬獠牙，頭上塗著紅土，髮上繫著豬尾；他們以為是某位訪客剛從獨木舟上岸。她徑直走向甘維維里斯的屋子，進去便不見了。他們告訴甘維維里斯：「我們看見一個女人走進你的洞屋，臂上戴著臂環和野豬獠牙」；他說：「別在村裡提起這事。」他上去要把他的錢袋背出來，卻看見他那十個袋子裡空無一物；他走到外面，看見他所有的豬都不見了；他分贈財物的盛舉全然落空。

title.en: The Little Orphan Whose Mother Was Money
title.zh: 小孤兒與錢母

region.en: Mota and Sanwawa landing, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島莫塔島三瓦瓦灘（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Scorned by the 'children of fathers' — 'you have no father, you have no mother, who will give you food to eat with your fish?' — the Little Orphan fished alone at Sanwawa, and out of the sea on his line came fish, a plaited hibiscus line, and at last a woman and her child: Ro Som, Money, and her child. She gave him house, gamal, endless cooked food, sprouting gardens, and pigs with curled tusks; he ate his way to the top of every rank of the Suqe, repaying his uncle's every payment. But when he scolded her without cause on his return from Gaua, Ro Som wept till sundown, then slipped away by night with her child, heavy with the money-bags — and the village was a deserted garden by morning.
