summary.zh: 『有父之子女』譏小孤兒：『你無父無母，誰給你備菜配魚？』他獨自到三瓦瓦灘垂釣，魚、編織的扶桑繩一一上鉤，最後竟從海裡上來一個女人帶著孩子——羅松（錢）母子。她說『我們三個一起走吧』，給他蓋了房與男子會所，備下吃不完的熟食，園中香蕉、芋頭自行抽芽，豬有卷牙的公豬與母豬成群。他一級級買進蘇蓋，直到頂級，舅父的每一次付出他都以錢與豬如數奉還。後隨船赴高阿島，無豬可送，只帶一枚未開的蛤；歸來見食物未動，疑母親另有野男人供養，出言羞辱。羅松與孩子哭到日落；待他睡熟，悄悄卸開錢袋負重而逃，一袋墜地，一頭卷牙豬仍縛在三瓦瓦灘。天明孤兒醒來，村中已是一片荒園。老嫗唱歌相告：『看那邊！兩個又從他釣起她們的海裡下去了。』

sensitivity.note: Native manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); Mota heritage.

passages.text: They were living in their place, the boys were growing up, and their father and mother said to them, 'Go down to the beach, and catch fish with hook and line for us, and we two will go inland and get vegetables for us all to eat with them.' And as they were going along the path the Little Orphan said, 'Let me go with you.' But they said, 'E-o-o! not you, a little orphan, we will go by ourselves alone, we who are children of fathers; if you were to go with us what would you eat? You have no father, you have no mother, who will give you food to eat with your fish?' And the children of fathers went down to the beach, and the Little Orphan went down a steep place eastwards to the landing-place at Sanwawa; and there he fishes for himself with a line and hook.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們住在自己的地方，男孩們漸漸長大，他們的父親和母親對他們說：「下到海灘去，用鉤和線為我們捕些魚，我們兩個到內地去採些菜，好讓我們大家配著魚吃。」他們正沿著小路走時，小孤兒說：「讓我跟你們一起去吧。」但他們說：「哎——喲！你不行，一個小孤兒，我們要自個兒去，我們這些有父親的孩子；你要是跟我們去，你吃什麼呢？你沒有父親，你沒有母親，誰會給你食物配你的魚呢？」有父親的孩子們下到海灘去了，小孤兒則往東走下陡坡，到了桑瓦瓦的登岸處；他在那裡獨自用線和鉤釣魚。

passages.text: And as he stood down there, a fish comes on his hook first; and then a nipanau; and a nongpitpit; and a gavaru; and then a plaited hibiscus line; and then a woman and her child come up out of the sea to him; and their name is Ro Som (Money), and he puts them down on the reef. Then Ro Som says to him, 'Let us three go together.' But he says, 'Not you two; I will go by myself, because I have no food to feed you with.' But she says, 'Never mind, string our fish together and we three will go.' So the three went along and arrived at the Little Orphan's dwelling-place; and he sees a house and a gamal; and he asks, 'Whose house is this?' And Ro Som says, 'It is the house of us three, and your gamal.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他站在那裡下方時，首先上鉤的是一條魚；接著是一條nipanau；接著是一條nongpitpit；接著是一條gavaru；接著是一條編織的芙蓉樹皮繩；接著，一個女人和她的孩子從海中上來，到他面前；他們的名字叫Ro Som（意為「錢」），他便把他們放在礁石上。於是Ro Som對他說：「讓我們三個一起走吧。」但他說：「你們兩個不行；我自己走，因為我沒有食物可以餵你們。」但她說：「沒關係，把我們的魚串起來，我們三個一起走。」於是三人一同前行，來到小孤兒的住處；他看見一間屋子和一座gamal；他問道：「這是誰的屋子？」Ro Som說：「這是我們三個的屋子，也是你的gamal。」

passages.text: Then Ro Som says to the Little Orphan, 'Come now, cook the fish for us three to eat.' But he says, 'What are we going to eat the fish with? I told you that you two must not come with me; I have no food.' But she says, 'Cook the fish, we three will eat them with some vegetable food presently.' So he makes up a fire for the fish, and they three sit down and wait. Then Ro Som says to him, 'Now then, take down our fish.' And she says, 'Look, there is a heap of cooked food there for us to eat the fish with.' So he goes over to the fish, and takes them off the fire, and they three ate. And when they had finished eating he goes out of the house into the village and sees gardens, a banana garden, and a tomago garden, and a yam garden, a wowosa garden, a reawea garden, a sugar-cane garden; and the bananas were beginning to rot, and the tomatoes were sprouting afresh, and the yams were sprouting. And Ro Som says to him, 'They belong to us three only.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是Ro Som對小孤兒說：「來吧，把魚煮了，讓我們三個吃。」但他說：「我們拿什麼來配魚吃呢？我告訴過你們兩個不要跟我來；我沒有食物。」但她說：「把魚煮了，我們三個待會兒配些菜蔬食物一起吃。」於是他為魚生起火，他們三個坐下來等候。接著Ro Som對他說：「那麼，現在把我們的魚拿下來吧。」她又說：「看，那裡有一堆煮熟的食物，讓我們配魚吃。」於是他走到魚那邊，把魚從火上取下，他們三個便吃了。吃完之後，他走出屋子來到村中，看見園圃，一片香蕉園，一片tomago園，一片山藥園，一片wowosa園，一片reawea園，一片甘蔗園；香蕉已開始腐爛，番茄正重新發芽，山藥也在發芽。Ro Som對他說：「這些只屬於我們三個。」

passages.text: And Ro Som says, 'To-morrow you will make up fires in the gamal in every oven, and we two will be here in the house, and we three will make mixture of cooked food and scraped cocoa-nut for food for pigs.' And as soon as they covered in the ovens the food was cooked; the pigs' food made by the two in the house was a hundred baskets-full, and that in the gamal a hundred. And Ro Som says, 'Well now, call the pigs, sumsum'; and he hears continued squealing, and he sees boars with tusks that curl and meet, and rawe, and sows; these all come rushing out to the three, and the three feed them and they eat. And while they are eating, Ro Som says to him, 'Have you got any uncle on your mother's side? Run and say to him, Tata, come and make the payments for my steps in the tuqe.' So his uncle paid rank after rank, and his nephew brought money out on his back, and gave pigs and rawes, and made return of his uncle's property.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: Ro Som說：「明天你要在gamal的每一個爐灶裡生起火，我們兩個會待在屋裡，我們三個要製作熟食拌刮碎的椰肉，作為豬的飼料。」他們一蓋上爐灶，食物就熟了；屋裡那兩個做的豬食有一百籃，gamal裡的那份也有一百籃。Ro Som說：「好了，現在叫豬吧，sumsum」；他聽見持續不斷的尖叫聲，看見長著彎曲相接獠牙的公豬，還有rawe，以及母豬；這些全都朝他們三個衝出來，他們三個餵牠們，牠們便吃。牠們吃著的時候，Ro Som對他說：「你母親那邊有沒有舅舅？跑去對他說：Tata，來為我在tuqe中的階位付款吧。」於是他的舅舅一級一級地付了款，他的外甥背著錢出來，給了豬和rawe，並回報了他舅舅的財物。

title.en: The Little Orphan's Voyage, and the Empty Village
title.zh: 小孤兒航海歸、村成荒園

region.en: Gaua and Mota, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島高阿島與莫塔島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: When the Motalava and Losalava people paddled over to Gaua, the Little Orphan went too — with no pig, only an unopened cockle-shell in his hand. On Gaua every man ran down crying 'This is my friend!' to every other; nobody wanted to be friends with the orphan. He came home and scolded Ro Som for the food they had not eaten, and she and her child wept till sundown; then while he slept they ran away with the money-bags, and the village became a deserted garden, one bag fallen by the path and a tusked pig still tied at Sanwawa.
summary.zh: 莫塔拉瓦與洛薩拉瓦人划舟赴高阿島，小孤兒也去；別人皆帶豬，他只帶一枚未開的蛤貝。抵岸時，村人一個個跑下灘喊『這是我的朋友！』與各自的友人攜手上岸；唯獨沒人要與孤兒結交。風起返航，他搶先跑回家中，見那堆食物原封未動，便疑心母親另有男人供野食給她們，出言相責。羅松母子哭到日落；孤兒靠近她們，躺在他們腿上哄勸不成，自己竟先睡去。她們輕輕抽腿放下他的頭，奔向錢袋，解開豬繩，背負而逃。她們一出村，村子立時變成荒蕪的園地。行至三瓦瓦灘，老嫗負袋吃力，一袋墜地；一頭插著卷牙的豬仍拴在那裡。孤兒醒來追尋，直至海邊，老嫗唱道：『看那邊！Iolo! Ialo! 兩個正從他釣起她們之處重新沉入海裡。』

sensitivity.note: Native manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); Mota heritage. Second half of the Little Orphan cycle.

passages.text: And the Little Orphan goes into the house, and makes a fire, and puts pig's flesh into the oven to make it keep. And when he has finished with his pig, then comes a report of a voyage, that the Motalava people with the Losalava people are going to paddle over to Gaua. Then says the Little Orphan to his mother, 'Oh, mother, those people are going to paddle over to Gaua to-morrow, and may I?' And his mother says, 'You must not: stay and look after your meat in the oven.' But he says, 'E-o-o! not so, mother, I shall go on the voyage with them; I am going to them, and you two will cook my pig for me.' So it was night and morning; and when morning was come he goes up inside the house and speaks to his mother and says, 'Well, mother, as I am going away from you two, and you two stay here, there is that heap of food you are to eat; but these you are not to touch.' And he goes off.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 小孤兒走進屋裡，生起火，把豬肉放進爐灶裡以便保存。他處理完他的豬之後，就傳來一個航行的消息，說Motalava人要和Losalava人一起划船到Gaua去。於是Little Orphan對他的母親說：「哦，母親，那些人明天要划船到Gaua去，我可以去嗎？」他的母親說：「你不可以去：留下來照看你爐灶裡的肉。」但他說：「E-o-o！不是這樣，母親，我要和他們一起去航行；我要到他們那裡去，你們兩個替我煮我的豬。」於是夜過去了，早晨來了；早晨一到，他走上屋裡，對他的母親說：「好了，母親，既然我要離開你們兩個，你們兩個留在這裡，那裡有一堆食物是給你們吃的；但這些你們不可以碰。」說完他就走了。

passages.text: And when he reaches the landing-place, he sees that those people have already dragged down the canoe and set it afloat on the edge of the sea; and he runs and jumps up and climbs right up on board the canoe, and they paddle off. But they all of them had taken pigs with them, but the Little Orphan had not taken one for himself, and he had brought nothing but a cockle-shell in his hand, and that shell-fish was not opened. And when they brought the canoes to shore at Gaua, the people there came down to meet them, and one of them runs over and cries, 'Friend!' and touches his friend's hand, and the two go up the beach together; and some other runs down and cries, 'This is my friend'; and some other runs down and cries, 'This is my friend,' and takes him; but that poor Little Orphan, they don't want to be friends with him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他到達登船處時，他看見那些人已經把獨木舟拖下水，讓它浮在海邊；他跑過去，跳起來，一直爬上獨木舟的船板，他們便划船出發了。他們所有人都帶了豬，但小孤兒自己一隻也沒帶，他手裡只帶了一個鳥蛤殼，而且那貝殼還沒打開。當他們把獨木舟靠岸到Gaua時，那裡的人下來迎接他們，其中一個跑過來喊道：「朋友！」並碰了碰他朋友的手，兩人一同走上海灘；另一個跑下來喊道：「這是我的朋友」；又一個跑下來喊道：「這是我的朋友」，並把他帶走；但那個可憐的小孤兒，他們都不想和他做朋友。

passages.text: And when those people drag up their canoe at Mota, he runs back, runs and runs, and reaches the house where they three lived, and sees the heap of yams still remaining as it was; and he says, 'What have you two been eating? this food still remains untouched.' But he says, 'No, there is some other man I think has been bringing you wild food of the forest.' Now he makes a fool of himself in this, supposing that it was as if his mother were living with a man. But that female Ro Som wept exceedingly because he had been angry with her, and she and her child wept till the sun went down; and they cried on, till they heard the nose of the Little Orphan whistling in sleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當那些人在Mota把獨木舟拖上岸時，他跑回去，跑啊跑，來到他們三個住過的屋子，看見那堆山藥仍舊原封不動地留著；他說：「你們兩個一直在吃什麼？這些食物還是原封未動。」但他又說：「不，我想是另有什麼男人一直給你們送來林中的野食吧。」他在這件事上把自己弄成了傻瓜，竟以為他的母親像是和一個男人同居。但那女的Ro Som因為他對她發了怒而痛哭不已，她和她的孩子一直哭到太陽下山；他們繼續哭著，直到聽見小孤兒睡夢中鼻子發出的呼哨聲。

passages.text: Then they removed softly their legs, and put down his head on the ground; and they run to the money-bags, and unloose the pig, and the two run off. And as they went out that village turned into a deserted garden. But as they ran away the old woman sat down, the bags of money were very heavy upon her, and one of the bags fell down. And a pig with tusks remained tied at that landing-place at Sanwawa, and that money-bag remained lying where it fell. And that Little Orphan woke and jumped up, and there he was in a deserted garden, and he ran looking for those two, and he came out upon the shore, and sees an old woman sitting there and asks, 'Oh! have you seen anybody at all here just now?' And she sings, 'Look, look over there! Iolo! Ialo! the two are plunging back into the sea at the place where the Little Orphan had fished them up.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他們輕輕地挪開自己的腿，把他的頭放到地上；接著他們奔向那些錢袋，解開那頭豬，兩人便跑走了。當他們離去時，那座村莊變成了一座荒廢的園子。然而就在他們逃跑之際，那老婦人坐了下來，那些錢袋對她而言十分沉重，其中一個袋子便掉了下來。而在桑瓦瓦的那處登岸處，一頭長著獠牙的豬仍被拴著，那個錢袋也仍躺在它掉落之處。那小孤兒醒來，一躍而起，發現自己身處一座荒廢的園子裡，他便跑去尋找那兩人，來到岸邊，看見一個老婦人坐在那裡，便問道：『哦！你剛才在這兒可曾看見什麼人嗎？』她唱道：『看哪，看那邊！伊奧洛！伊阿洛！那兩人正一頭扎回海裡，就在那小孤兒把他們撈上來的所在。』

title.en: Wowut-ta-Taragariga and the Orphan Who Fed the Dead Man's Feast
title.zh: 沃武特與送食孤兒

region.en: Mota, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島莫塔島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded (native MS, summarized) by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX note

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX, concluding note on two Mota stories

summary.en: Wowut-ta-Taragariga's parents kept him in the house till he was grown, then advanced him at once to the highest Suqe rank; no one dared approach his gamal but an orphan, who carried him a portion of another man's feast. Wowut took a liking to the orphan and paid him money; the boy came again and again with food till he had 'thousands of money, thousands of boars, thousands of pigs with curled tusks,' and rose himself to high rank. When Wowut died he directed that when his friend came to mourn over him he was to be given his wife in memory of him.
summary.zh: 沃武特·塔·塔拉加里加自幼被父母關在家中，直至成年，方一舉晉入蘇蓋最高之級；他的會所令人生畏，無人敢近，唯有一名孤兒受託替另一家把宴席的一份送進去。沃武特喜歡上這孤兒，以錢相酬。孤兒一次次送食，漸積『千錢、千頭卷牙公豬、千頭豬』，自己也一級級買進高位。沃武特死時留下遺命：待孤兒前來哭喪，須把自己的妻子贈予他，以為紀念。

sensitivity.note: Recorded only in Codrington's summary of a native Mota manuscript too long to print; flagged as condensed.

passages.text: One of two more Stories from Mota in native manuscript, too long for insertion in full: the Story of Wowut-ta-Taragariga, whom his parents kept in the house till he was grown up, and then advanced to the highest Suqe rank. Another man of the same island taking the same step sent a portion of his feast to Wowut-ta-Taragariga by an orphan, all others being afraid of approaching the gamal of so high a rank. Wowut takes a liking to the orphan, and pays him with money. He goes again and again with food till he has 'thousands of money, thousands of boars, thousands of pigs with curled tusks,' and with these advances himself to high Suqe rank. Then Wowut dies, and directs that when his friend comes to mourn over him he is to be given his wife in memory of him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX concluding note (1891); condensed summary, not verbatim.
passages.zh: 另有兩則來自莫塔島的土語手稿故事，篇幅過長，無法全文插入：其一為沃烏特－塔－塔拉加里加的故事，他的父母把他留在家中直到長大成人，然後將他晉升至最高的蘇克等級。同島的另一人也要踏上同樣的一步，便派一個孤兒把他宴席的一部分送去給沃烏特－塔－塔拉加里加，因為其他人都害怕接近地位如此之高的加馬爾。沃烏特對那孤兒心生喜愛，便以錢財酬謝他。那孤兒一次又一次地送來食物，直到他擁有『成千的錢財、成千的野豬、成千的捲牙之豬』，並藉著這些使自己晉升至高的蘇克等級。後來沃烏特死了，並吩咐說，當他的朋友前來為他哀悼時，要把他的妻子交給他，以紀念他。

title.en: Qat-wurunga, the Scurfy-Headed Boy, and Wetopunpun
title.zh: 結痂頭的卡特吳魯加與維托蓬蓬

region.en: Vanua Lava and Qakea, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島瓦努阿瓦島與烏阿凱阿（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded (native MS, summarized) by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX note

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX, concluding note on two Mota stories

summary.en: Qat-wurunga was born of a mother killed by a fall from a tree and grew up in the forest; his uncle found him, took him home, and his uncle's wives, neglecting and ill-using him, named him Scurfy-head. Carried back to the midst of Vanua Lava, he snared birds; fat dripping through the fire called up Wetopunpun from under the earth — his dead father's ghost. With the charm 'Soso-punpun' the boy made food, gardens, a village, a gamal, pigs, fowls, a drum — all native wealth — and ate his way up the Suqe. Beguiled aboard a canoe from Maewo, he was carried off to be killed and eaten; one of the party took pity and loosed him, and the two paddled back to find all disappeared. His father Wetopunpun sat grieving on the beach till the Qakea people took him to their famine-struck island, where his charm filled gardens with food. Envied, he left them, and sits by Ro Som with all his possessions; a stone there representing him is a place of sacrifice to this day.
summary.zh: 卡特吳魯加的母親從樹上跌落而死，他遂生於林間、長於林間。母舅尋得他帶回家；舅母們冷淡苛待，給他起名『結痂頭』。他求舅舅把他送回森林深處——瓦努阿瓦島腹地，遠離海面。他張網捕鳥；一日烤鳥的油脂滴落火中、滲入地下，喚出地下的維托蓬蓬——那是他亡父之魂。男孩以咒語『Soso-punpun』憑空造出食物、園圃、村莊、會所、豬、雞、鼓——一切土著財富。舅父代他買盡蘇蓋各級；舅母們起初不信，赴宴一見其盛況，竟要留下做他的妻子，甚至要他剖胸取肝來吃。一艘馬埃沃來的獨木舟見其豬頜成堆，驚羨之下誘他睡去，把他運回本島要殺而食之；同行一人憐而鬆綁放他，二人划舟返回瓦努阿瓦，一切已消失無蹤。他被擄時其父維托蓬蓬每日坐在灘頭悲悼；烏阿凱阿人見之，渡海接他回島——那裡正逢饑荒，他以咒語變出滿園食物。眾人嫉妒，他便離去，攜全部財產坐到羅松身旁；那裡有一塊代表他的石頭，至今為獻祭之所。

sensitivity.note: Recorded only in Codrington's summary of a native Mota manuscript too long to print; flagged as condensed.

passages.text: The other of the two Mota stories too long for insertion in full: the Story of Qat-wurunga, who was born of a mother who had been killed by a fall from a tree, and grew up in the forest like the children in the Story of Taso. His maternal uncle finds him and takes him home, where his uncle's wives neglect him and ill-use him, and give him his name of Scurfy-head. The boy begs his uncle to take him back to the forest, and he carries him out of the sight of the sea into the midst of the island, Vanua Lava. Then he settles himself, and after a while snares birds. One day the fat of a bird roasting over the fire fell through on to the head of Wetopunpun beneath the earth, and he comes up above ground. This is the boy's father, the ghost of his dead father.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX concluding note (1891); condensed summary, not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兩則莫塔故事中篇幅過長、無法全文插入的另一則：卡特效應－烏倫加的故事，他由一位因從樹上跌落而喪生的母親所生，並像塔索故事中的孩子們那樣在森林中長大。他的舅父找到了他，把他帶回家，在那裡舅父的妻子們忽視他、虐待他，並給他起了『頭皮屑頭』這個名字。那男孩懇求舅父把他帶回森林，舅父便把他帶離能望見大海之處，進入島嶼瓦努阿－拉瓦的中央。於是他安頓下來，過了一段時日便設網捕鳥。有一天，一隻鳥在火上烤著，牠的油脂滴落下來，落到地底下的韋托蓬蓬頭上，他便從地下升到地面上來。這男孩的父親，正是他死去父親的鬼魂。

passages.text: With the charm 'Soso-punpun, soso-punpun' — like the Kerembaembae of Story No. 1 — he makes food, gardens, a village, a gamal, pigs, fowls, a drum — all native wealth. Qat-wurunga's uncle comes to see him, and undertakes his advance to the highest ranks of the suqe, receiving his due payment of pigs. His wives, incredulous at first, go to a kolekole and see the youth they have despised in all his splendour. They desire to stay as his wives, and make him cut open his breast and give them some of his liver to eat. A canoe from Maewo comes over, and they find the fresh emblems of his rank; they challenge comparison with their own, and see open-mouthed with astonishment the number of jawbones of the pigs he has killed in his feasts. They beguile him to sleep, and carry him off to their own island to kill and eat him. While they are making preparations for their dance and feast, one of their party takes pity on him, unties and delivers him; the two paddle back to Vanua Lava. But when they reach Qat-wurunga's place all has disappeared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX concluding note (1891); condensed summary, not verbatim.
passages.zh: 憑著咒語『索索－蓬蓬，索索－蓬蓬』——就像第一則故事中的凱倫巴恩巴埃那樣——他變出了食物、園圃、一座村莊、一座加馬爾、豬、家禽、一面鼓——一切土人的財富。卡特效應－烏倫加的舅父前來看他，並著手將他晉升至蘇克最高的幾個等級，收取了他應得的豬作為報酬。舅父的妻子們起初不信，前去參加一場科萊科萊，看見她們曾鄙視的那青年如今何等榮耀。她們想要留下來做他的妻子，並要他剖開自己的胸膛，把她們一些肝給她們吃。一艘來自馬埃沃的獨木舟渡海而來，他們發現了他等級的新標誌；他們拿自己的與之相比，並目瞪口呆地驚嘆於他在宴席上所殺之豬的顎骨數量之多。她們哄他入睡，把他擄到她們自己的島上，要殺他來吃。正當她們為舞蹈和宴席作準備時，她們一行人中的一個憐憫他，解開他的束縛並救了他；兩人划槳回到瓦努阿－拉瓦。但當他們抵達卡特效應－烏倫加的地方時，一切都已消失了。

passages.text: When he was captured his father Wetopunpun had gone to the beach and sat there grieving. The Qakea people, seeing him there day after day, paddled over and took him to their place, where there was a famine. There with his charm 'Soso-punpun' he makes gardens full of food appear. They envy him and he leaves them, and seeks a solitary place, where he sits down by the side of Ro Som with all his possessions round him. A stone there representing him is a place of sacrifice to this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX concluding note (1891); condensed summary, not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他被擄走時，他的父親韋托蓬蓬曾到海灘上，坐在那裡悲傷。卡凱亞人見他日復一日地坐在那裡，便划槳過去，把他帶到他們的地方，那裡正鬧饑荒。在那裡，他憑著咒語『索索－蓬蓬』變出了滿是食物的園圃。他們嫉妒他，他便離開他們，去尋找一處僻靜之地，在那裡他坐在羅·索姆身旁，所有財物都環繞在他四周。那裡有一塊代表他的石頭，至今仍是獻祭之地。

title.en: The Deluge and the Box: Nations Raised from Clay at Tiahuanaco
title.zh: 洪水與箱子:蒂亞瓦納科以泥土造各族

region.en: Tiahuanaco, Collasuyu (Bolivia) (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科利亞蘇尤蒂亞瓦納科(今玻利維亞)(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In Molina's fable the deluge drowned all people and things, the water rising above the highest mountains; only a man and a woman in a box survived. When the waters sank the Creator raised each nation from clay at Tiahuanaco, gave it dress, language, song, seeds and food, gave each figure life, and sent the nations underground to emerge from caves, springs, hills and trees.
summary.zh: 莫利納的寓言中,洪水淹沒一切,水高過群山,僅一男一女藏於箱中倖存。水退後,造物主在蒂亞瓦納科以泥土塑造各族,賜予服飾、語言、歌謠、種子與食糧,賦予其生命,再命其入地,分別從洞穴、山泉、丘陵與樹幹中湧出。

sensitivity.note: Quechua creation lore recorded by a Cuzco parish priest c. 1575 from elderly Inca witnesses; a colonial compilation to be read critically. Flood parallels with other traditions are a comparative tagging choice.

passages.text: In the life of Manco Ccapac the painted boards of Poquen Cancha told of the deluge: all people and all created things perished, so that the water rose above all the highest mountains in the world. No living thing survived except a man and a woman who remained in a box, and when the waters subsided the wind carried them to Huanaco, more than seventy leagues from Cuzco.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, deluge fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在曼科·卡帕克的一生中，波肯·坎查的彩繪木板講述了那場大洪水：所有的人和所有受造之物都滅亡了，水漲過了世上所有最高的山。除了留在一隻箱子裡的一男一女之外，沒有任何活物倖存；當洪水退去，風把他們帶到了瓦納科，那裡距庫斯科有七十多里格之遙。

passages.text: There, in Tiahuanaco, the Creator of all things began to raise up the people and nations of that region, making one of each nation of clay, and painting the dresses that each one was to wear - those who were to wear their hair with hair, and those to be shorn shorn. To each nation he gave the language that was to be spoken, the songs to be sung, and the seeds and food to be sown.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, deluge fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在那裡，即蒂亞瓦納科，萬物的創造者開始興起該地區的人民與族群，以泥土為每一族群各造一個，並描繪各人當穿的服飾——該以髮覆首者繪以髮，該剃髮者繪以剃髮之狀。他賜給每一族群當說的語言、當唱的歌謠，以及當播種的種子與食物。

passages.text: When the Creator had finished painting and making the nations and figures of clay, he gave life and soul to each one, men and women alike, and ordered that they should pass under the earth. Thence each nation came up in the places to which he had ordered them: some from caves, others from hills, others from fountains, others from the trunks of trees. Because they came forth and multiplied from those places, they made them huacas and places of worship in memory of the origin of their lineages.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, deluge fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 創造者描繪並造畢各族群與泥偶之後，便賜予每一個生命與靈魂，男女皆然，並命他們從地下穿行而過。於是各族群便從他所指定之處冒出：有的出自洞穴，有的出自山丘，有的出自泉眼，有的出自樹幹。由於他們從那些地方湧出並繁衍，他們便將那些地方立為瓦卡與崇拜之所，以紀念其世系的起源。

passages.text: Other nations said that in the deluge a few escaped on hills, in caves, or in trees, and that these few began to multiply. In memory of the first of their race who had escaped in such places they made idols of stone, giving to each huaca the name of that first ancestor; and each nation worshipped and offered sacrifices of the things that they used.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, deluge fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 其他族群則說，在大洪水中，有少數人逃到山丘、洞穴或樹上，而這少數人開始繁衍。為了紀念其種族中最初逃到這類地方的人，他們以石造偶像，並以那位最初祖先之名為每一瓦卡命名；每一族群都崇拜並以他們所用之物獻祭。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Sun Speaks to Manco Capac: The Luminaries Fixed in Heaven
title.zh: 太陽對曼科·卡帕克說話:日月星辰升空

region.en: Island of Titicaca, Lake Titicaca (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 的的喀喀湖太陽島(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: It was dark when the Creator, at Tiahuanaco, made the sun, moon and stars and ordered them to the island of Titicaca to rise to heaven. As the sun, in the form of a man, ascended brilliant, it called to Manco Capac: he and his descendants would be lords and subjugate many nations; he was to look on the sun as father. It gave him the suntur-paucar and the champi as arms, and the luminaries took their places in the sky.
summary.zh: 天地尚暗,造物主在蒂亞瓦納科造日月星辰,命其前往的的喀喀島升天。太陽化人形,燦然升空,呼喚曼科·卡帕克:他和子孫將為眾主,征服萬國;當以太陽為父。太陽賜他「孫圖爾-保卡爾」權杖與「昌皮」戰斧等印信武器,日月星辰遂各安其位。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Quechua fable from Molina's compilation; the solar legitimation of Inca kingship is treated as sacred narrative.

passages.text: They say that it was dark, and that at Tiahuanaco the Creator made the sun, moon, and stars, and that he ordered the sun, moon, and stars to go to the island of Titicaca, which is near at hand, and thence to rise to heaven.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, solar fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們說，當時一片黑暗，創造者在蒂亞瓦納科造了太陽、月亮與星辰，並命太陽、月亮與星辰前往近在咫尺的的喀喀島，再從那裡升上天際。

passages.text: They also declare that when the sun, in the form of a man, was ascending into heaven, very brilliant, it called to the Yncas and to Manco Ccapac as their chief, and said: 'Thou and thy descendants are to be Lords, and are to subjugate many nations. Look upon me as thy father, and thou shalt be my children, and thou shalt worship me as thy father.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, solar fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們也宣稱，當太陽化為人形、光輝燦爛地升上天際時，它呼喚印卡人以及作為其首領的曼科·卡帕克，說道：『你與你的後裔將為領主，將征服諸多族群。當視我為你的父親，你們將為我的子女，並當以我為父而崇拜我。』

passages.text: With these words the sun gave to Manco Ccapac, for his insignia and arms, the suntur-paucar and the champi, and the other ensigns used by the Yncas like sceptres. At that point the sun, moon, and stars were commanded to ascend to heaven and fix themselves in their places, and they did so. At the same instant Manco Ccapac and his brothers and sisters, by command of the Creator, descended under the earth and came out again in the cave of Paccari-tambo, at the point where the sun rose on the first day after the Creator had divided night from day. Thus they were called children of the Sun.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, solar fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 說了這番話，太陽便賜給曼科·卡帕克作為其徽記與武器的孫圖爾-保卡爾與昌皮，以及印卡人所用如權杖般的其他旗幟。就在那時，太陽、月亮與星辰奉命升上天際，各就其位，它們便如此行了。同一瞬間，曼科·卡帕克與他的兄弟姊妹奉創造者之命，從地下穿行而下，又從帕卡里-坦博的洞穴中出來，正是在創造者分開晝夜之後第一日太陽升起之處。因此他們被稱為太陽之子。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Disobedient Turned to Stone: Fire from Heaven at Pucara
title.zh: 不從者化石:普卡拉的天火

region.en: Pucara on the Collao road, Collasuyu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科利亞道上的普卡拉(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: After peopling the nations the Creator walked the mountain road reviewing his work. Finding nations that had rebelled against his commands, he turned many of them into stones in the shape of men and women wearing their own dress - at Tiahuanaco, Pucara, Xauxa, Pachacamac and Cajamarca, where the huaca Huarivilca too was petrified. At Pucara fire came down from heaven and destroyed part of the people, and the fleeing were turned to stone.
summary.zh: 造物主造畫各族後,沿山路巡視所造之民。發現有族不服其命,便將許多石化為人形石塊,仍著其衣——蒂亞瓦納科、普卡拉、豪哈、帕查卡馬克、卡哈馬卡等處皆然,連瓦里維爾卡瓦卡也被石化。在普卡拉,天火降下,毀去部分人民,奔逃者亦化為石。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era fable explaining the standing monoliths of the Collao road; Molina rationalizes them as Roman work while preserving the native tale.

passages.text: The Creator, called Pachayachachi and Tecsiviracocha, the incomprehensible God, went by the road of the mountains from Tiahuanaco, visiting and beholding all the nations, and examining how they had begun to multiply and to comply with his commands. He found that some nations had rebelled and had not obeyed his commands, so he turned a large number of them into stones in the shape of men and women, with the same dress that they had worn. These conversions into stone were made at Tiahuanaco, at Pucara, at Xauxa - where they say he turned the huaca called Huarivilca into stone - and at Pachacamac and Cajamarca, and in other parts.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, stone fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 造物主被稱為帕查亞查奇（Pachayachachi）與特克西維拉科查（Tecsiviracocha），是不可思議的神；祂沿著山間的道路從蒂亞瓦納科（Tiahuanaco）出發，巡視並察看萬國萬族，查驗他們如何開始繁衍增多、如何遵行祂的命令。祂發現有些民族已經反叛，沒有聽從祂的命令，於是將其中一大批人變成石頭，形狀如男如女，身上穿著他們原先所穿的衣服。這些變成石頭的事，發生在蒂亞瓦納科、普卡拉（Pucara）、豪哈（Xauxa）——據說祂在那裡把名叫瓦里維爾卡（Huarivilca）的瓦卡（huaca，聖物）變成了石頭——以及帕查卡馬克（Pachacamac）與卡哈馬卡（Cajamarca）和其他地方。

passages.text: In truth there are great blocks of stone in those places, some nearly the size of giants, made by human hands in very ancient times; and by reason of the loss of memory and the absence of writing the people invented this fable, saying that people had been turned into stones for their disobedience by command of the Creator. They also relate that in Pucara, forty leagues from Cuzco on the Collao road, fire came down from heaven and destroyed a great part of the people, while those taking to flight were turned into stones.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, stone fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 事實上，那些地方確有巨大的石塊，有些幾乎有巨人那麼大，是極古時代由人手造成的；由於記憶失傳、又沒有文字，人們便編造了這個寓言，說人因不順從而奉造物主之命變成了石頭。他們還講述說，在普卡拉，即距庫斯科（Cuzco）四十里格、位於科利亞奧（Collao）大道上的地方，有火從天而降，毀滅了大半的人，而那些逃走的則變成了石頭。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Ymaymana and Tocapo: The Two Sons Name the World
title.zh: 伊馬伊馬納與托卡波:二子命名世界

region.en: Highland and lowland roads from Tiahuanaco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 自蒂亞瓦納科出的山路與平地之路(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The Creator had two sons, Ymaymana Viracocha, in whose power all things were placed, and Tocapo Viracocha, 'the maker'. The elder was sent by the mountain and forest roads to name every tree, flower and fruit, teaching which were food or medicine and which poison; the younger went by the plains, naming rivers and trees and teaching their fruits. Thus they went until they reached the sea, whence they ascended to heaven.
summary.zh: 造物主有二子:長子伊馬伊馬納·維拉科查,萬物皆在其掌中;次子托卡波·維拉科查,意為「造者」。長子奉命循山路林道而行,為大小樹木、花卉果實命名,教人何者可食可藥、何者有毒;次子循平地而行,為江河樹木命名,教導花果之性。二人行至海濱,遂自海中升天。

sensitivity.note: Naming-journey fable recorded by Molina; tagged as a culture-hero and sibling pair against the comparative clusters.

passages.text: They also have another fable, in which they say that the Creator had two sons, the one called Ymaymana Viracocha, and the other Tocapo Viracocha. Having completed the tribes and nations, and assigned dresses and languages to them, the Creator sent the sun up to heaven with the moon and stars, each one in its place.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, two-sons fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們還有另一個寓言，其中說造物主有兩個兒子，一個名叫伊邁馬納·維拉科查（Ymaymana Viracocha），另一個名叫托卡波·維拉科查（Tocapo Viracocha）。造物主造齊了各部族與各民族，並為他們指定了衣著與語言之後，便打發太陽上天，連同月亮與星辰，各歸其位。

passages.text: The Creator commanded that the elder, named Ymaymana Viracocha, in whose power all things were placed, should set out and go by the way of the mountains and forests through all the land, giving names to the large and small trees, and to the flowers and fruits that they bear, and teaching the people which were good for food or for medicine, and which should be avoided. He also gave names to all the herbs, and explained which had healing virtues and which were poisonous.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, two-sons fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 造物主命令長子，名叫伊邁馬納·維拉科查、萬物皆歸其掌管的那一位，出發沿著山嶺與森林的道路走遍全地，為大小樹木以及它們所結的花與果命名，並教導人們哪些宜於食用或作藥用，哪些應當避開。祂也為所有草本植物命名，並說明哪些具有療效，哪些有毒。

passages.text: The other son, named Tocapo Viracocha, which means 'the maker', was ordered to go by the way of the plains, visiting the people, and giving names to the rivers and trees, and instruction respecting the fruits and flowers. Thus they went until they reached the sea, whence they ascended to heaven, after having accomplished all they had to do in this world.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, two-sons fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 另一個兒子名叫托卡波·維拉科查，意即「造作者」，奉命沿著平原的道路前行，巡訪人們，為河流與樹木命名，並就果實與花卉加以教導。他們就這樣前行，直到抵達海邊，在完成了他們在這世上所當行的一切之後，便從那裡升上天去。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Birds Given Their Songs: Beasts and Reptiles Made at Tiahuanaco
title.zh: 賦鳥以歌:蒂亞瓦納科造鳥獸蟲蛇

region.en: Tiahuanaco, Collasuyu (Bolivia) (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科利亞蘇尤蒂亞瓦納科(今玻利維亞)(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: At Tiahuanaco, where all mankind was created, all the different kinds of birds were made, male and female, and each was given the songs it was to sing; those that were to live in the forest were sent there, and each kind to its place. In like manner all beasts, serpents and lizards were created, and the people were taught the names and qualities of every one.
summary.zh: 在造出全人類的蒂亞瓦納科,各類鳥也被造出,雌雄皆有,並各賜其當唱之歌;將棲於林中的被送往林間,各歸其所。野獸、蛇、蜥蜴亦如是造成,並教人民認識每一種的名字與習性。

sensitivity.note: Fragment of the Tiahuanaco creation cycle in Molina's compilation.

passages.text: They also relate, in this same fable, that at Tiahuanaco, where all mankind was created, all the different kinds of birds were made, male and female, and that each was given the songs they were to sing; those that were to live in the forest being sent there, and each kind to its respective place.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們在同一個寓言中還講述說，在蒂亞瓦納科，即全人類被創造之處，各種不同的鳥類都被造了出來，有雄有雌，並且各被賦予牠們所要唱的歌；那些要住在森林裡的便被送到那裡，每一種都送往各自的地方。

passages.text: In like manner all the different beasts were created, male and female, and all the serpents and lizards that are met with in the land; and the people were taught the names and qualities of each of these birds, beasts, and reptiles. These Indians believed for a certainty that neither the Creator nor his sons were born of woman, that they were unchangeable and eternal.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同樣地，所有各類走獸也都分雌雄被創造出來，還有此地所見的一切蛇與蜥蜴；人們也被教導了這些鳥、獸、爬蟲各自的名稱與特性。這些印第安人確信無疑：造物者及其諸子皆非婦人所生，他們不變而永恆。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Cañari Brothers and the Macaw Wives
title.zh: 卡尼亞里兄弟與金剛鸚鵡之妻

region.en: Cañaribamba (Cañar), province of Quito, Ecuador (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基多省卡尼亞里班巴(今厄瓜多卡尼亞爾)(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In the flood the Cañari brothers escaped to the mountain Huaca-yñan, which grew with the waters. Starving after the flood, they found their hut daily stocked with food and chicha they had not prepared. Watching from hiding, they saw two macaws come dressed as Cañari women, hair bound in front, and cook for them; seized in the hut, the smaller macaw became their wife and bore six sons and daughters, from whom all the Cañaris descend. They hold the hill Huaca-yñan as a huaca and revere macaws, valuing their feathers for festivals.
summary.zh: 洪水時,卡尼亞里二兄弟逃上山瓦卡伊尼亞,山隨水而高,洪水不至。水退後二人飢寒交迫,卻見屋中每日備有食物與奇恰酒。二人先後藏匿窺看,見兩隻金剛鸚鵡化作卡尼亞里女子,前束髮髻,為其炊食。二人閉門捕捉,小鸚鵡被擒,遂為其妻,生六子女——卡尼亞里人皆其後裔。故奉瓦卡伊尼亞山為瓦卡,尊崇金剛鸚鵡,節慶時珍用其羽。

sensitivity.note: Etiological ancestor tale of the Cañari nation; recorded within Molina's compilation.

passages.text: The Cañaris say that at the time of the deluge two brothers escaped to a very high mountain called Huaca-yñan. As the waters rose the hill also increased in height, so that the waters never reached them. After the flood had subsided their store of provisions being ended, they came forth and sought food in the hills and valleys. They built a very small house in which they dwelt, living on herbs and roots, and suffering much from hunger and fatigue.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Cañari fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡尼亞里人說，洪水之時有兩兄弟逃到一座名叫瓦卡伊尼安（Huaca-yñan）的極高山。水漲之時，山丘也隨之增高，因此水始終未及於他們。洪水退去之後，他們的存糧已盡，便出來在山岡與谷地間尋找食物。他們蓋了一間極小的屋子居住其中，以草根為食，飽受飢餓與疲憊之苦。

passages.text: One day, after going out in search of food, they returned and found food to eat and chicha to drink, without knowing who could have prepared it. This happened for ten days. They consulted how they should see the being who did them so much good, and the elder brother agreed to remain concealed. Presently he saw two birds of the kind called guacamayos, dressed as Cañaris, with their hair fastened in front as they now wear it. They began to prepare the food they had brought, the larger one taking off the lliclla or mantle worn by the Indians.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Cañari fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，他們外出尋食歸來，發現有食物可吃、有奇恰（chicha）可飲，卻不知是誰所備。如此持續了十天。他們商議該如何見那對他們如此行善之人，兄長遂同意留下藏身窺看。不久他看見兩隻名叫瓜卡馬約（guacamayo）的鳥，穿著如卡尼亞里人一般，頭髮束於前額，正如他們現今的樣式。牠們開始調理帶來的食物，其中較大的一隻脫下印第安人所披的利克利亞（lliclla）即斗篷。

passages.text: When the concealed man saw that they were beautiful, and had the faces of women, he came forth; but as soon as they saw him they were enraged and flew away without leaving anything to eat that day. On the next day the younger brother resolved to watch. At the end of three days the two guacamayos came back and began to prepare the food; the men watched for an opportune time, and, shutting the door, enclosed them inside. The birds showed great anger; but while they held the smaller one the larger went away.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Cañari fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 藏身之人見牠們容貌美麗、面如女子，便現身出來；然而牠們一看見他，便大怒，振翅飛去，當日未留下任何食物。次日，弟弟決心守望。三日之後，兩隻瓜卡馬約又回來，開始調理食物；兩兄弟伺機而動，關上門，將牠們困在屋內。那鳥兒大為震怒；但當他們抓住較小的一隻時，較大的一隻卻逃走了。

passages.text: Then they had carnal knowledge of the smaller one, and had by it six sons and daughters. It lived with them for a long time on that hill, and they subsisted on the seeds they sowed, which were brought by the guacamayo. From these brothers and sisters, children of the guacamayo, all the Cañaris proceed. Hence they look upon the hill Huaca-yñan as a huaca, and hold the guacamayos in great veneration, valuing their feathers for use at their festivals.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Cañari fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他們與較小的一隻交合，由她生了六個兒女。她與他們在那山丘上同住許久，他們靠所種的種子為生，種子乃由瓜卡馬約帶來。卡尼亞里人全族皆出自這對兄妹，即瓜卡馬約的子女。因此他們視瓦卡伊尼安山為瓦卡（huaca，聖物），並極度崇敬瓜卡馬約，珍視其羽毛以備節慶之用。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Sheep that Watched the Stars: Ancasmarca and the Flood
title.zh: 凝望星辰的羊群:安卡斯馬爾卡與洪水

region.en: Ancasmarca, Antisuyu, near Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科附近安蒂蘇尤安卡斯馬爾卡(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: A month before the flood the sheep of Ancasmarca grew sad, eating nothing by day and watching the stars by night. Asked what ailed them, they said the conjunction of stars showed the world would be destroyed by water. The shepherd consulted his six children, they gathered all the food and sheep they could, and climbed the very high mountain called Ancasmarca; the hill rose with the waters so the flood never covered them, and sank again when the waters sank. The six children returned and repeopled the province.
summary.zh: 洪水來前一個月,安卡斯馬爾卡的羊群終日不吃,夜夜望星。牧人問其故,羊答:星辰會合之象顯示世界將毀於水。牧人與六子商議,收集所有食物羊隻,登上一座極高的名為安卡斯馬爾卡之山。水漲山亦漲,洪水不得掩之;水退山亦減。六子下山,重造此省之民。

sensitivity.note: Animal-omen flood tale from Molina's compilation; the speaking sheep motif is compared across traditions.

passages.text: In the province of Ancasmarca, five leagues from Cuzco in the Anti-suyu division, they say that a month before the flood came their sheep displayed much sadness, eating no food in the day-time, and watching the stars at night. At last the shepherd who had charge of them asked what ailed them, and they said that the conjunction of stars showed that the world would be destroyed by water. When he heard this, the shepherd consulted with his six children, and they agreed to collect all the food and sheep they could, and to go to the top of a very high mountain called Ancasmarca. As the waters rose, the hill grew higher, so that it was never covered by the flood; and when the waters subsided, the hill also grew smaller. Thus the six children of that shepherd returned to people the province.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Ancasmarca fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在安卡斯馬爾卡（Ancasmarca）省，距庫斯科五里格，屬安蒂蘇尤（Anti-suyu）分區，據說洪水來臨前一個月，他們的羊群顯得十分悲傷，白日不進食，夜間則凝望星辰。最後，看管羊群的牧人問牠們有何不適，牠們說星辰的會合顯示世界將被水毀滅。牧人聞此言，便與他的六個子女商議，他們一致同意盡可能收集所有食物與羊隻，前往一座名叫安卡斯馬爾卡的極高山山頂。水漲之時，山丘也隨之增高，因此從未被洪水淹沒；水退之後，山丘也隨之縮小。於是那牧人的六個子女歸來，繁衍了這一省的人民。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Sun Cannot Be God: Inca Yupanqui Builds a Temple to the Creator
title.zh: 太陽不會是神:印加·尤潘琪建造物主神廟

region.en: Quisuar-cancha, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科基蘇瓦爾坎恰(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Inca Yupanqui, who first regulated the twelve months and their ceremonies, reasoned with his council that the Sun could not be the God who created all things: the sun never rests and journeys round the earth daily, and permits a small cloud to obscure his splendour. There must be someone who directs him - the Pachayachachi, the Creator. He therefore raised at Quisuar-cancha a golden statue of the Creator, a boy of ten years with right arm raised as if giving orders, ordered temples, flocks and estates throughout the empire, and sumptuously rebuilt the house of the Sun.
summary.zh: 印加·尤潘琪首定十二月之歲與其祭儀。他與眾臣論道:太陽不得為造萬物之神——太陽無一刻休息,日日繞地而行,還容許一小片雲遮其光輝。若太陽真是造物主,必當安坐一處,光照世界。故必有指揮太陽者,即造物主帕查亞查奇。他在基蘇瓦爾坎恰立一尊十歲孩童大小的造物主金像,右手高舉如發號施令;又令各行省建廟、置畜群莊園以供祭祀,並華美重建太陽神廟。

sensitivity.note: Theological-reflection fable attached to Inca Yupanqui (Pachacuti); a colonial-era compilation to be read critically.

passages.text: It was this Ynca who first began to conquer this land... He appears to have been the first to order and settle ceremonies and religions. He established the twelve months of the year, giving a name to each and ordaining the ceremonies to be observed in each; although his ancestors used months and years counted by the quipus, they were never before regulated in such order.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 正是這位印加王首先開始征服這片土地……他似乎是最先整頓並確立各種儀式與宗教的人。他確立了一年十二個月，為每個月命名，並規定各月應遵守的儀式；雖然他的祖先已用奇普（結繩）來計算月與年，但此前從未如此有秩序地加以規範。

passages.text: He was of such clear understanding that he reflected upon the reverence shown by his ancestors to the Sun, whom they worshipped as God. He observed that the Sun never had any rest, and daily journeyed round the earth; and he said to his council that it was not possible that the Sun could be the God who created all things, for if he were, he would not permit a small cloud to obscure his splendour; and if he were creator of all things he would sometimes rest, and light up the whole world from one spot.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他見識極為明澈，因而反思其祖先對太陽所表示的崇敬——他們將太陽當作神來崇拜。他觀察到太陽從不休息，每日繞行大地；於是對他的議會說，太陽不可能是創造萬物的神，因為若它是神，便不會容許一小片雲遮暗它的光輝；若它是萬物的創造者，它有時也該休息，並從一處照亮整個世界。

passages.text: Thus, it cannot be otherwise but that there is someone who directs him, and this is the Pacha-Yachachi or Creator. Influenced by this reasoning, he ordered the houses and temple of Quisuar-cancha to be made, where he raised a statue of gold to the Creator of the size of a boy of ten years - a man standing up, the right arm raised, the hand almost closed, the fingers and thumb raised as one who was giving an order. He gave orders to the heads of provinces that temples should be erected to him, with flocks, servants, farms and estates for sacrifices; and he sumptuously erected the house of the Sun at Cuzco, which before his time had been very small and poor.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 因此，必定另有一位在指揮它，那便是帕查-亞查奇（Pacha-Yachachi），即造物主。受此推理影響，他下令建造基蘇亞爾-坎查（Quisuar-cancha）的房屋與神廟，並在其中立起一尊金製的造物主雕像，大小如十歲男孩——一個站立的人，右臂舉起，手幾乎握攏，手指與拇指抬起，如同正在下令的人。他向各省首領下令，要為造物主興建神廟，並備牲畜、僕役、農田與地產以供獻祭；他又在庫斯科華麗地興建太陽之屋，而在他的時代之前，那屋非常簡陋。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Crystal in the Fountain: The Apparition at Susur-puquio
title.zh: 泉中水晶:蘇蘇爾普基奧的顯靈

region.en: Susur-puquio fountain, near Xaquixaguana (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 夏基夏瓜納附近蘇蘇爾普基奧泉(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Before his succession Inca Yupanqui, going to visit his father Viracocha Inca at Sacsahuana, saw a piece of crystal fall into the fountain of Susur-puquio, within which he beheld a figure: three brilliant sun-like rays from the back of the head, serpents twined round the arms, a llautu like an Inca's, ear-pieces, a lion's head between the legs and lions over the shoulders. He fled, but the apparition called him by name: 'Come hither, my son, and fear not, for I am the Sun thy father. Thou shalt conquer many nations.' It vanished, leaving the crystal, in which he afterwards saw everything he wanted; he then had a statue of the Sun made resembling the figure.
summary.zh: 印加·尤潘琪繼位前,赴薩克薩瓦納看望父親維拉科查·印加,途經蘇蘇爾普基奧泉,見一水晶落入泉中,內現神人:腦後射出三道如日光芒,雙臂纏蛇,額繫印加之「勞圖」,耳垂穿孔佩耳飾,裝束一如印加;兩腿間現獅首,肩上伏獅,肩後又有蛇纏。尤潘琪驚逃,神影自泉中喚其名:「來吧,吾子,勿懼——我是太陽,你的父親。你將征服許多國度;務必崇敬我,祭祀勿忘。」神影隨即消失,水晶留存。尤潘琪藏之,日後凡有所求,皆於水晶中得見。繼位後,他命工匠依泉中所見造太陽金像,並命各行省為太陽建廟,令民眾尊崇新神。

sensitivity.note: Vision fable attached to Inca Yupanqui; the crystal motif parallels scrying traditions elsewhere.

passages.text: They say that, before he succeeded, he went one day to visit his father Viracocha Ynca, who was in Sacsahuana, five leagues from Cuzco. As he came up to a fountain called Susur-puquio, he saw a piece of crystal fall into it, within which he beheld the figure of an Indian in the following shape: out of the back of his head there issued three very brilliant rays like those of the Sun; serpents were twined round his arms, and on his head there was a llautu like that of the Ynca. His ears were bored, and ear-pieces like those used by the Yncas were inserted; he was also dressed like the Ynca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Susur-puquio fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們說，在他繼位之前，有一天他去探望他的父親維拉科查·印加（Viracocha Ynca），當時父親在距庫斯科五里格的薩克薩瓦納（Sacsahuana）。當他走近一處名為蘇蘇爾-普基奧（Susur-puquio）的泉水時，他看見一塊水晶落入其中，在水晶裡他見到一個印第安人的形象，形貌如下：從他的後腦射出三道極明亮的光芒，如同太陽的光芒；蛇纏繞在他的雙臂上，頭上戴著與印加王相同的利亞烏圖（llautu）頭飾。他的耳朵穿了孔，並嵌入了印加王所用的耳飾；他的穿著也與印加王相同。

passages.text: The head of a lion came out from between his legs, and on his shoulders there was another lion whose legs appeared to join over the shoulders of the man, while a sort of serpent also twined over the shoulders. On seeing this figure the Ynca Yupanqui fled, but the figure called him by his name from within the fountain, saying: 'Come hither, my son, and fear not, for I am the Sun thy father. Thou shalt conquer many nations: therefore be careful to pay great reverence to me, and remember me in thy sacrifices.' The apparition then vanished, while the piece of crystal remained.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Susur-puquio fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一顆獅頭從他的兩腿之間伸出，他的肩上另有一頭獅子，那獅子的腿似乎交合在那人的肩上，還有一種類似蛇的東西也纏繞在肩上。印加王尤潘基（Yupanqui）見到這形象便逃走了，但那形象在泉中呼喚他的名字，說道：『到我這裡來，我的孩子，不要害怕，因為我是你的父親太陽。你將征服許多民族：因此務必對我大加崇敬，並在你的獻祭中記念我。』那顯現隨即消失，而水晶塊則留了下來。

passages.text: The Ynca took care of it, and they say that he afterwards saw everything he wanted in it. As soon as he was Lord, he ordered a statue of the Sun to be made as nearly as possible resembling the figure he had seen in the crystal, gave orders to the heads of the provinces in all the lands he had conquered that they should make grand temples richly endowed, and commanded all his subjects to adore and reverence the new Deity as they had heretofore worshipped the Creator. He also caused worship to be offered to the thunder, and had a statue of a man erected in gold in a temple in the city of Cuzco.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Susur-puquio fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 印加王小心保存了它，他們說他後來在其中看見了他所想看的一切。他一成為君主，便下令製作一尊太陽雕像，盡可能接近他在水晶中所見的形象；又向各省首領下令，凡他所征服之地，都要興建宏偉、捐贈豐厚的神廟；並命令所有臣民崇敬並敬畏這位新神，如同他們先前崇拜造物主一般。他又使人向雷電獻祭，並在庫斯科城的一座神廟中豎立了一尊金製的人像。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Five Orders of Diviners: Tubes, Flames, Maize and Thunder
title.zh: 五等占卜師:銅管、火焰、玉米與雷

region.en: Cuzco and the provinces (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科及各行省(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Molina lists the classes of wizards: Calparicu, who blew up the lungs of sacrificed birds and lambs to read signs of what was to come; Virapiricuc, who burned sheep's breasts and coca and divined from the burning - though those who consulted them said they always lied; Achicoc, who told fortunes by maize and sheep's dung, odd or even; Camascas, whose grace came from the thunder that struck them and revealed herb-curing; and Yacarcaes of Huaro, who blew charcoal fires through copper tubes until the devils delivered replies in the flames - asking whether a man was against the Sun his father, a thief, murderer or adulterer. By this invocation the Inca knew all that passed in his dominions.
summary.zh: 莫利納記各類巫師:一、卡爾帕里庫,剖祭鳥祭羊之肺吹脹視其徵兆;二、維拉皮里庫庫,焚羊乳與古柯,觀火焰占卜——求問者稱其「常常說謊」;三、阿奇科克,以玉米粒與羊糞占吉凶,視奇偶而定;四、卡馬斯卡,稱其法力得自雷霆——遭雷擊而復甦者,自言雷神授其草藥醫術;五、瓦羅地方的亞卡爾卡埃斯,以銅管吹旺炭火,魔鬼便在火中作答——所問者,某人是否違逆太陽之父、是否盜賊、兇手、姦夫。印加王借此召問,盡知帝國內所發生之事,故常攜其同行。

sensitivity.note: Ethnographic taxonomy of Quechua diviners; 'devil' is the missionary translation of native huaca-speaking.

passages.text: There were many kinds of wizards in the provinces, with names and attributes differing one from the other. Calparicu means those who bring luck and success, who were expected to obtain the things that were desired; they killed birds, lambs, and sheep, and, inflating the lungs through a certain vein, discerned signs of what was about to happen. Others, called Virapiricuc, burnt the breasts of sheep and coca in the fire and foretold from signs at the burning - though those who consulted them said they were the least to be relied on, because they always lied.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, wizards section (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 各省有許多種類的巫師，名稱與屬性各不相同。Calparicu 意指那些帶來好運與成功的人，人們期望他們能取得所渴望之物；他們殺鳥、羔羊與綿羊，並透過某條血管使肺臟膨脹，藉此辨識即將發生之事的徵兆。另有一些人稱為 Virapiricuc，他們在火中焚燒綿羊的胸肉與古柯葉，並從焚燒的徵兆中預言——不過請教他們的人說，他們是最不可靠的，因為他們總是說謊。

passages.text: Others were called Achicoc, sorcerers that told fortunes by maize and the dung of sheep, giving replies according as the things came out in odd or even numbers. Others were called Camascas, who declared their grace and virtue came from the thunder: when a thunderbolt fell and one of them was struck with terror, after he came to himself he proclaimed how the thunder had revealed to him the art of curing by herbs and how to give replies to those who consulted them; hence many Indians are great herbalists.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, wizards section (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 另有一些人稱為 Achicoc，是藉玉米與羊糞占卜的巫師，依事物出現的數目為奇或為偶來作答。另有一些人稱為 Camascas，他們宣稱自己的恩典與能力來自雷電：當雷電擊落，其中一人被驚嚇，待他回過神來，便宣稱雷電如何向他啟示以草藥治病之術，以及如何答覆前來請教的人；因此許多印第安人是偉大的草藥師。

passages.text: Others were called Yacarcaes, natives of Huaro, who had mighty pacts with the devil. They took tubes of copper mixed with silver, about the length of an arquebus, and brass vessels in which they lighted charcoal fires, which they blew and made to blaze up by means of the tubes. In these fires the devils delivered their replies, and the sorcerers said they were inquiring concerning the soul of such a man or woman, who might be in Quito or in any other part of the empire. The principal questions were whether such an one was against the Sun his father, or whether such others were thieves, murderers, or adulterers. By this invocation the Ynca knew all that passed in his dominions, and took the Yacarcaes with him wherever he went.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, wizards section (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 另有一些人稱為 Yacarcaes，是 Huaro 的本地人，與魔鬼訂有強大的盟約。他們取來攙銀的銅管，長約一支火繩槍，以及黃銅器皿，在器皿中點燃炭火，再藉銅管吹氣使之熊熊燃起。魔鬼就在這些火中作出答覆，而巫師們說他們是在探問某某男女的靈魂，那人可能在基多或帝國境內任何其他地方。主要的問題是：某人是否違逆其父太陽，或某些人是否為盜賊、殺人者或通姦者。藉此召喚，Ynca 得以知曉其領地內發生的一切，並且無論前往何處都帶著 Yacarcaes。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Confession to the Keepers of the Huacas
title.zh: 向瓦卡祭司懺悔

region.en: Huaro and Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦羅與庫斯科(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: All the people of the land confessed to the sorcerers who had charge of the huacas, and these confessions were made publicly; the priests tested them by signs and, with the aid of the speaking huaca, discovered who had confessed falsely and punished them severely. Grave crimes were confessed in secret. The Incas and people of Cuzco confessed in secret to the sorcerers of Huaro, accusing themselves of failing to reverence the sun, moon and huacas, of not celebrating the Raymi feasts with all their heart, of seducing a virgin not given by the Inca, of theft, murder, and of murmuring against the Inca or the Sun.
summary.zh: 全境人民皆向掌管瓦卡的祭司懺悔,懺悔公開舉行;祭司以徵兆驗其真偽,藉瓦卡之言查出謊供者,嚴加懲處。重罪者則私下密供。印加王室與庫斯科人皆向瓦羅祭司密懺,自陳不敬日月瓦卡、未全心慶祝雷米祭、姦污非印加所賜之處女、盜竊、殺人,以及對印加王或太陽之怨言。

sensitivity.note: Description of Andean confession practice from a priest-observer; his moral framing ('fornication against the law of the Ynca') is quoted critically.

passages.text: All the people of the land confessed to the sorcerers who had charge of the huacas, and these confessions were made publicly. In order to test the truth of the confessions, the sorcerers tried them by consulting signs, and in this way they discovered who had confessed falsely, and upon these they inflicted severe punishments. Those who had grave crimes to confess, which merited death, confessed them in secret to the sorcerer.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, confession section (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此地所有人民都向掌管 huacas 的巫師告解，而這些告解是公開進行的。為了檢驗告解的真偽，巫師藉請示徵兆來考驗他們，以此方式查出誰作了虛假的告解，並對這些人施以嚴厲的懲罰。那些有該告解的重罪、應處死刑的人，則私下向巫師告解。

passages.text: The Yncas and the people of Cuzco always made their confessions in secret, generally to the Indian sorcerers of Huaro. In their confessions they accused themselves of not having reverenced the sun, the moon, and the huacas; of not having celebrated the feasts of the Raymis with all their hearts; of having committed fornication against the law of the Ynca not to touch a strange woman or seduce a virgin unless given by the Ynca - and not because fornication was a sin, for they did not understand this. They also accused themselves of any murder or theft, and of murmurs, especially if against the Ynca or against the Sun.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, confession section (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: Yncas 與庫斯科的人民總是私下告解，通常是向 Huaro 的印第安巫師告解。他們在告解中自責未曾敬奉太陽、月亮與 huacas；未曾全心全意慶祝 Raymis 的節慶；犯了淫亂，違背 Ynca 的法律——不得觸碰他人之妻，不得誘惑處女，除非由 Ynca 賜予——而這並非因為淫亂是罪，因為他們並不理解這一點。他們也自責任何殺人或竊盜，以及怨言，尤其是針對 Ynca 或針對太陽的怨言。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Woman and the Eel at the Suqe Oven
title.zh: 婦人與鰻：蘇蓋爐中食鰻之禍

region.en: Maewo (Aurora Island), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖馬埃沃島（奧羅拉島）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: A woman's soaking pandanus leaves turned into an eel; the Suqe men dragged it up to roast. Only the lame man, warned by the eel's eye, refused to eat — and as the great men bit, their legs turned to eels, then their bodies, and the whole club glided away into the water after its chief.
summary.zh: 一婦人浸於水中備織席之露兜葉，晨起取葉，葉已化鰻。蘇蓋會社諸人聞訊，以繩縛鰻曳回村中；會所旁的跛子不能同去，目睹鰻尾捲住克羅頓樹。鰻低語跛子：『他們吃時你莫吃。』眾人烤鰻於蘇蓋爐中；大人物一聲令下，人人下箸——一口咬下，腿化鰻；再咬，身化鰻；三咬，人人皆鰻，隨大人物滑入水中而去。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era record (Codrington 1891); Maewo heritage.

passages.text: A woman went to lay pandanus leaves to weave mats with in the water, and she laid them there in the evening and went home. In the morning she went to take the leaves from the water; and when she went to take them out, behold, they were turned into an eel. Then she ran back and told it to some men who were engaged in the suqe, and they ran down and tied a cord to the eel and dragged it up to the village. But there was a lame man who could not go with them, and he lay in the gamal, the club-house; and by the side of the gamal there was a croton-tree; and as they dragged up that eel it curled its tail round the croton, and the croton was nearly broken, and the lame man saw it. But they dragged hard at the eel and it loosed its tail from the croton, and they brought it into the village, and laid it at the entrance of the gamal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有個女人到水裡去鋪放露兜樹葉，以備編織席子，她在傍晚把葉子鋪在那裡，然後回家。早晨她去從水中取回葉子；當她去取時，看哪，那些葉子竟變成了一條鰻魚。於是她跑回去，把事情告訴幾個正在參與 suqe 的男人，他們便跑下去，把一條繩子綁在鰻魚身上，將牠拖上村子。但有個跛腳的人無法與他們同去，他躺在 gamal，也就是會所裡；而在 gamal 旁邊有一棵巴豆樹；當他們把鰻魚往上拖時，牠把尾巴纏繞在巴豆樹上，巴豆樹幾乎被折斷，那跛腳的人看見了。但他們用力拖那鰻魚，牠便鬆開尾巴離開巴豆樹，他們把牠帶進村子，放在 gamal 的入口處。

passages.text: So when they ran off for fire-wood and banana leaves to cook it with, the eel said to the lame man, 'When they are eating don't you eat; they shall eat by themselves.' Consequently the lame man did not eat; but they put the eel to be cooked in the oven of the suqe, and covered in the oven. And when they opened the oven they all took up pieces of the eel, every one of them a piece, and when the great man said to them, 'Now put them ready,' then they all put them ready; and after that he said again, 'Now let us eat,' and they all took a bite at once. But as they bit once their legs turned into eels; and they bit a second time and the bodies of them all turned into eels; and they bit again, and they were all eels; and the great man glided away first, and they all followed him into the water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是，當他們跑去取柴火和香蕉葉來烹煮牠時，那鰻魚對那跛腳的人說：『他們吃的時候你不要吃；他們自己吃就好了。』因此那跛腳的人就沒有吃；但他們把鰻魚放進 suqe 的爐裡烹煮，並蓋在爐中。當他們打開爐子時，他們全都拿起鰻魚的碎塊，每一個人都拿了一塊；而當那大人物對他們說：『現在把它們擺好。』他們就全都把它們擺好；之後他又說：『現在我們吃吧。』他們就全都同時咬了一口。但當他們咬了一口，他們的腿就變成了鰻魚；他們咬了第二口，他們所有人的身體都變成了鰻魚；他們又咬了一口，他們就全都成了鰻魚；那大人物首先滑行離去，他們全都跟隨他進入水中。

title.en: The Little Owl Who Became a Husband
title.zh: 小鴞為夫

region.en: Maewo (Aurora Island), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖馬埃沃島（奧羅拉島）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Two women gathering firewood found a young owl with white feathers and very large eyes; one day it was a man, and they took him into the village and he became their husband. When he took to beating them they reminded him — 'you are a bird, and our property because we found you' — and when they blew up the fire against his ban, he turned back into a bird and flew away, throwing money down to them as he went.
summary.zh: 兩名拾柴女子拾得一隻白羽大眼之幼鴞，養於家中；一日去看，小鳥已化作男子。二女攜他回村，他便做了她們的丈夫。三人相安多年，蓋屋耕園；後來他動輒毆打她們，她們斥道：『你是鳥，是我們拾來的財物，憑什麼打我們？』他揚言離去；晚間他飲下卡瓦，嚴禁二女撥火；她們偏把火撥旺照他——他登時化回鳥身，展翅而去，一路把錢拋給她們。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era record (Codrington 1891); Maewo heritage.

passages.text: This is about two women who were getting fire-wood, and found a young owl, a bird with white feathers and very large eyes; it was a young bird of this kind that they found. And one day the two women went to look at their little bird, and found that he was turned into a man; so they took him into the village, and he became their husband. And the three lived always in perfect harmony together, and built their house, and worked in their garden, and so remained many years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這是關於兩個婦人的事，她們正在拾取柴火，發現了一隻小貓頭鷹，一種羽毛潔白、眼睛非常大的鳥；她們所發現的就是這樣一種幼鳥。有一天，這兩個婦人去看她們的小鳥，發現他已變成了一個男人；於是她们把他帶進村裡，他就成了她们的丈夫。這三人一直和睦相處地住在一起，建造了他们的房子，在园子里劳作，就这样过了许多年。

passages.text: But after that he took to beating them when they quarrelled, and they scolded him for it, saying, 'You there are a bird, and our property because we found you; why do you beat us like this?' So he said he would leave them; and in the evening he drank kava, and forbade them to blow the fire. But when he lay down to sleep the two women blew up the fire into a blaze, and looked at him, and he turned into a bird, and flew away. And the two women cried after him, and he threw down money to them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但此後，當她们争吵时，他就動手打她们，她们为此责骂他，说：『你不过是一只鸟，而且是我们发现你才成了我们的财产；你为什么要这样打我们？』于是他说他要离开她们；傍晚时他喝了卡瓦酒，并禁止她们吹火。但当他躺下睡觉时，那两个妇人把火吹旺，看着他，他就变成了一只鸟，飞走了。那两个妇人在他身后哭喊，他就扔下钱给她们。

title.en: Betawerai and Walolo: The Banyan of Snakes
title.zh: 貝塔維賴與瓦洛洛：蛇榕誅滅記

region.en: Maewo (Aurora Island), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖馬埃沃島（奧羅拉島）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: A boy kept a little red snake in a hollow yaqava trunk and fed it till it grew monstrous, ate him, and devoured the whole village — all but a pregnant woman who dug a pit and lived under a flat stone with her newborn twins. The serpent brood filled a banyan, chief among them Betawerai the branch-lord and Walolo the man-hunter; the twins grew, made bows, pelted the banyan, sang Walolo home end-over-end like a stick, and shot the snakes dead — burning the heap as a sign that the devouring snake was destroyed.
summary.zh: 一男孩執意收養一條小紅蛇，藏於空心亞瓜瓦樹幹中，以鼠、鳥、黑蜥、豬肉飼之；蛇漸成巨怪，一日搶食其豬，竟把男孩也吞了，出樹入村，把全村人吃盡。唯有一名孕婦掘地穴、以薄石板覆頂藏身，在穴中產下雙生子。巨蛇據榕而居，生下無數小蛇，為首者二：一為貝塔維賴，不能遠行，常駐榕枝（其名即取自大枝『貝塔』）；一為瓦洛洛，渡海獵人為食。雙子長成，求母製弓箭，往誅群蛇。二人以棒端翻擲擊榕，蛇紛紛墜地；貝塔維賴唱歌召瓦洛洛速歸殺敵——瓦洛洛聞歌，如木棍般一翻一翻地趕回；雙子輪番發箭，直至射斃瓦洛洛，再拉下貝塔維賴誅之。眾蛇堆於榕根，堆薪焚之，以為滅蛇之證；母子三人重返村中安居。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era record (Codrington 1891); Maewo heritage.

passages.text: The beginning was in this way; a woman and her child went to strip pandanus leaves for weaving mats, and the boy saw a young snake on the stalk of a leaf and begged his mother to let him have it, for he wanted it; his mother forbade him to take it. But he said that he wished for it, and so he laid hold on the little red snake, and took it and put it in the hollow trunk of a tree; and the name of that tree is the yaqava; he put it into the hollow of that, and he used to feed it with rats or birds or black lizards, or pig's flesh, and that snake became extremely large.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 开端是这样的；一个妇人和她的孩子去剥露兜树叶来编席子，那男孩看见一片叶子的茎上有一条小蛇，就求他母亲让他得到它，因为他想要它；他母亲不许他拿。但他说他想要它，于是他就抓住那条红色的小蛇，把它拿走，放进一棵树的空心树干里；那棵树的名字叫 yaqava；他把它放进那棵树的空心处，他常喂它老鼠、鸟、黑蜥蜴或猪肉，那条蛇就变得极其巨大。

passages.text: And one day when he killed a pig he went to give it some; but that snake snatched the pig from him, and ate him up also, and crawled out of the hollow tree, and came into the village and ate up all the people in the place. But there was one pregnant woman who survived; and she dug a pit, and took a thin flat stone and laid it over the pit, and she stayed within it. And she brought forth her children, twins, and they three remained in that pit in the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，他杀了一头猪，便去给它一些；但那蛇从他手中夺走了猪，也把他吞吃了，然后从空心树里爬出来，进了村子，把那地方所有的人都吃光了。但有一个怀孕的妇人活了下来；她挖了一个坑，拿了一块薄石板盖在坑上，自己待在里面。她生下了她的孩子，是一对双胞胎，她们三人就待在地里的那个坑中。

passages.text: And the snake ate up all the people, and then went and took up its abode on a banyan-tree, and brought forth exceedingly many young ones, and two the chief among them. The name of one of these was Betawerai, and this one was not able to go about, but stayed always on a branch of the banyan — the branch of a big tree like a banyan they call a betavrai, like the flat of the hand, and this was named after that, At the branch. And the other one used to go very far away seeking diligently men or pigs to eat, and his name was Walolo. But one day those two, the children of the woman who had lived in the ground, begged of their mother to make them bows and arrows; and after that they said they would go into the village and seek that snake to shoot it and kill it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那蛇吃光了所有的人，然后去住在一棵榕树上，生下了极多的幼蛇，其中两条是首领。其中一条的名字叫 Betawerai，这一条不能四处走动，总是待在榕树的一根树枝上——像榕树那样的大树的树枝，他们称为 betavrai，就像手掌的平面一样，这一条便因此得名，叫『在树枝上』。另一条则常到很远的地方去，勤勉地寻找人或猪来吃，他的名字叫 Walolo。但有一天，那两个曾住在地里的妇人的孩子，求他们的母亲为他们做弓和箭；之后他们说他们要进村去找那条蛇，射死它。

passages.text: And when they had gone and had seen from a distance that banyan where Betawerai and Walolo lived, they saw upon the branches, and on the little twigs, and on the leaves, nothing but snakes on that banyan. But Walolo was not on the tree, because he had gone across the sea and was still seeking for men to devour. And these two boys went up to the banyan-tree and began to pelt it with sticks thrown end over end; and while they were pelting so the snakes fell down in very great numbers. And Betawerai began to sing a song to make Walolo come quickly back and kill and eat them — 'Risuritu vano, Betawerai, a lang togalau, ti uvi goro nanagoiu, Walolo! Walolo! go vano mai! Turn and come to Betawerai, the wind is North-west, it blows against my face. Walolo, Walolo, come hither!' And they say that Walolo heard him singing, and came end over end like a stick; and as he came near, one of them shot him, and then the other shot, and both hit him; and they went on shooting like this, till they shot him to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他們離去，從遠處望見貝塔韋萊與瓦洛洛所居的那棵榕樹時，他們看見那棵榕樹的枝上、細枝上、葉上，盡是蛇，別無他物。但瓦洛洛不在樹上，因為他已渡海而去，仍在尋覓可供吞食之人。這兩個男孩走到榕樹前，開始用一端朝前擲出的棍棒擊打它；正當他們如此擊打時，蛇便大批大批地落了下來。貝塔韋萊於是開始唱起歌來，要使瓦洛洛快快回來把他們殺死吃掉——「Risuritu vano, Betawerai, a lang togalau, ti uvi goro nanagoiu, Walolo! Walolo! go vano mai! 轉身回來到貝塔韋萊這裏吧，風是西北風，它正吹打我的臉。瓦洛洛，瓦洛洛，到這裏來！」他們說瓦洛洛聽見了他的歌聲，便像一根棍棒般翻滾著趕來；當他靠近時，他們其中一人射了他，接著另一人又射，兩人都射中了；他們就這樣不停地射，直到把他射死。

title.en: Basi and the Snake Mother's Ten-Chambered House
title.zh: 巴希與蛇母十室之屋

region.en: Dama and Tanoriki, Maewo, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖馬埃沃島達馬與塔諾里基（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Basi, daughter of a snake that lived in a cave at Dama, married Dovaowari of Tanoriki and begged leave for her mother to move near them — a house of ten chambers. On her arrival by night the earth quaked and thundered, and her tail coiled chamber by chamber till the whole house was snake, only a woman's head at the door. When her husband plotted to burn the house behind a dance, the snake warned Basi: 'if you see sparks run quickly back to me' — and both were burnt to death together; their liver remains, full of mana.
summary.zh: 達馬有女子巴希，其母為穴居之蛇。她嫁與塔諾里基青年多瓦奧瓦里；婚後她常回遠處探母，夫心不悅，遂允其母遷來同住。蛇母自慮身軀巨大，命女婿建一座十室之屋。遷居之夜，地動雷鳴，如世界將盡；蛇尾先入第一室，盤曲而進，直至十室盡滿，僅一顆人首向門而臥。晨起村人來看，方見是條人首巨蛇。蛇母又吞食門前豬雞；夫深惡之，藉遠村赴舞之機，囑人縱火焚屋滅蛇。蛇母早知其謀，囑巴希：『宴舞時若見火星迸出，速跑回來與我同死。』巴希舞中見火星四散，奔回縱身火中——母女俱焚。其肝存留至今，滿蓄瑪那。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era record (Codrington 1891); Maewo heritage. Records a war/love-charm relic cult.

passages.text: She was a girl of Dama, and her mother, a snake, lived in a cave there. And there was a young man living at Tanoriki; and one day Basi and another girl went down to the beach to dip salt-water; and Dovaowari was the name of the youth, and he also went down to bathe in the sea, but on another part of the beach. These two girls stood looking over to the other part of the beach, and saw the fellow bathing, and washing his hair till it was exceedingly white; and they say, 'Let us two go and see who that is bathing.' And they went and saw that it was Dovaowari; and Basi said to the other girl, 'You go home to our mother, and tell her that I am going after Dovaowari.' But Dovaowari forbade her in vain to follow him, saying that he was poor, that he had no property and no garden; and she disputed with him, saying that she would certainly go with him. So they married.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她是達馬的一個姑娘，她的母親是一條蛇，住在那裏的一個洞穴中。有一個青年住在塔諾里基；有一天，巴西和另一個姑娘下到海灘去浸取海水；多瓦奧瓦里是那青年的名字，他也下到海裏洗澡，但卻在海灘的另一處。這兩個姑娘站著朝海灘的另一處望去，看見那青年在洗澡，洗著他的頭髮，直洗得極其潔白；她們說：「我們兩個去看看那是誰在洗澡吧。」她們去了，看見那是多瓦奧瓦里；巴西對另一個姑娘說：「你回家去見我們的母親，告訴她我要跟多瓦奧瓦里去了。」但多瓦奧瓦里徒然地禁止她跟隨他，說自己貧窮，沒有財產，也沒有園圃；她卻與他爭辯，說她一定要跟他去。於是他們結了婚。

passages.text: But Basi kept going to her mother at Dama a long way off, and Dovao was vexed at it, and he told Basi to go and say to her mother that she was to move to that place so that all might live together. But the chief thing she thought of was how she should manage, because she was a snake very long and large, and if a small house were built for her it would not be enough. She considered, therefore, and said to Basi, 'Go and tell my son-in-law to build me a house, and let there be ten chambers in it.' But Dovao did not yet know the truth, and when he heard about the house with ten chambers he was astonished at it. When the house was finished, Basi carried the news, saying, 'Your house is finished'; but she had said beforehand, 'I shall go in the night, and if my son-in-law should hear anything don't let him take notice of it.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但巴西不斷地到遠在達馬的母親那裏去，多瓦奧為此煩惱，便叫巴西去對她的母親說，要她搬到那個地方來，好讓大家住在一起。但她所思量的主要之事，是她該如何安排，因為她是一條極長極大的蛇，若為她造一所小房子，那是不夠的。因此她思量之後，對巴西說：「去告訴我的女婿，叫他為我造一所房子，裏面要有十間房。」但多瓦奧還不知道實情，當他聽說那所有十間房的房子時，大為驚訝。房子造好後，巴西帶了消息去，說：「你的房子造好了」；但她事先已說過：「我要在夜裏進去，倘若我的女婿聽見什麼聲響，別讓他理會。」

passages.text: So in the middle of the night they heard an earthquake, and thunder, and a very great rumbling as if all the world would come to an end; and when she reached that place, her tail entered first and coiled itself in the first chamber, and then in the second, until all those chambers were filled with the big snake; and her head, a woman's, lay opposite the door, though the whole house was full of the snake. In the morning the people came to see this person, and saw that it was a snake with a human head. And whenever Dovao and Basi went anywhere and returned, she would go to her mother, that snake, and rub her nose upon her; but her husband did not like that sort of thing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是半夜裏，他們聽見地震、雷鳴，以及極大的隆隆聲，彷彿整個世界都要終結了一般；當她到達那個地方時，她的尾巴先進去，在第一間房裏盤繞起來，接著在第二間，直到所有那些房間都被這條大蛇填滿；而她的頭，一個女人的頭，則對著門口臥著，儘管整所房子都充滿了蛇。早晨，人們來看這個人，看見那是一條長著人頭的蛇。而每當多瓦奧和巴西去到某處又回來時，她便到她的母親，那條蛇那裏去，用鼻子在她身上摩擦；但她的丈夫不喜歡這種事。

passages.text: But the snake knew this, and called Basi and told her that they were going to set fire upon her and burn her that night, and, 'When you are standing at the feast, if you see sparks run quickly back to me.' So it was done; while she was dancing she saw sparks flying and ran quickly back and leapt herself into the fire, and both were burnt to death. And after a long while the liver that was burnt was found, and still remains, the liver of Basi and of her mother; and I have seen a bone in possession of some wealthy people; there is mana, magic power, in it, they say, for pigs, and for wicked intercourse with women when they blacken their faces under the eyes with it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但那條蛇知道了這事，便叫來巴西，告訴她說他們要在那天夜裏放火燒她，又說：「當你站在宴會上時，若看見火星，就趕快跑回我這裏來。」事情就這樣做了；當她正在跳舞時，她看見火星飛濺，便趕快跑回去，自己跳進火裏，兩者都被燒死了。過了很久之後，那被燒過的肝被找到了，至今仍在，就是巴西和她母親的肝；而我曾見過一些富有之人所持有的一根骨頭；他們說，那裏面有 mana，即法力，可用於豬，也可用於當女人把眼睛下方塗黑時與她們行邪淫之交。

title.en: Deitari, the Boy Made of Tari's Blood
title.zh: 迪塔里：塔里血所生之子

region.en: Maewo (Aurora Island), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖馬埃沃島（奧羅拉島）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Tari cut himself in his garden, and set the blood by his fire-place in a bamboo vessel. Food began cooking itself; his wife spied out a boy, exceedingly fair, creeping from the bamboo — Deitari, Tari's blood. When the fish-man Taepupuliti changed himself into a fish and devoured the boy, Tari sent every fish and bird to search, until a little fish, extremely thin, found him hidden at the back of Taepupuliti's house — and a shared bowl of kava, which struck the eater of the child and not the father, let Tari carry his son home again.
summary.zh: 塔里在園中勞作時被劃傷，將血收入竹筒，置於灶邊。此後屢屢回家便有熟食等他，妻不知何人所備；她依夫言窺伺，見竹筒中爬出一個異常俊美的男孩——迪塔里，塔里之血所生。塔里夫婦大喜，視如己出。村童結伴浴於溪中唱歌，迪塔里亦往；有一名為 Taepupuliti 者，化身為魚，把這竹筒所出之童吞下，攜往他鄉。塔里遣盡百魚百鳥四出尋子，終由一條極瘦小魚尋得：孩子就藏在 Taepupuliti 屋後。塔里與其人共飲卡瓦，故意讓酒從口中漏出，使藥力不上身；而吞童者藥力大作，塔里遂把孩子又背了回去。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era record (Codrington 1891); Maewo heritage.

passages.text: They say that Tari went into his garden to work, and as he was working something cut him, and he put the blood into a bamboo vessel, and went into the village, and set it by his fire-place, and there it stayed. And after many days when he was going to work he told his wife to cook some food for him, and she went to get it. But when she came back into the house she found food already cooked, and she did not know who had prepared the food for her. Thus it happened very often, and the woman told her husband. And he when he heard it bade her sit and watch who it was that did it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們說塔里到他的園圃裏去幹活，正當他幹活時，有什麼東西割傷了他，他便把血裝進一個竹筒裏，走進村子，把它放在他的火爐旁，它便留在了那裏。過了許多天，當他要去幹活時，他叫妻子為他煮些食物，她便去取來。但當她回到屋裏時，卻發現食物已經煮好了，她不知道是誰為她準備了食物。這樣的事發生了許多次，那女人便告訴了她的丈夫。他聽了之後，便叫她坐著觀看，看究竟是誰做了這事。

passages.text: So she sat by the side wall of the house, and saw Deitari (Tari's Blood) creep out of the bamboo vessel which Tari had put aside; and she saw that he was exceedingly fair, and she hid him. Then when Tari came in from work he asked his wife, 'Haven't you seen him?' And she said, 'What was that you put by the fire-place?' Then he remembered about his blood, and he said to his wife, 'My blood was in that bamboo; and his wife said, 'I saw him come out of that bamboo that you had put there.' So she brought him forth, and Tari rejoiced very much to see him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是她就坐在屋子的側牆邊，看見德伊塔里（即塔里的血）從塔里擱在一旁的竹筒裡爬出來；她見他容貌極其俊美，便把他藏了起來。後來塔里做工回來，問他的妻子說：『你沒有見到他嗎？』她說：『你放在火爐旁的那是什麼東西？』於是他想起了自己的血，就對妻子說：『我的血就在那竹筒裡。』他的妻子說：『我看見他從你放在那裡的那個竹筒裡出來了。』於是她就把他帶了出來，塔里見了他，非常歡喜。

passages.text: And one day as they were living together the boys of the village, and Deitari with them, went to bathe in the stream, and sang songs. And there was a man called Taepupuliti, and they say that he changed himself into a fish, and went and devoured the boy who had come out of the bamboo, and went off with him into a different country. And Tari sent every kind of fish and bird to seek for Deitari; and he found a little fish, extremely thin, and this fish and Deitari's father found him hidden at the back end of Taepupuliti's house. And they two, Tari and Taepupuliti, sat down to drink kava; and the father of the one whom the other had devoured let the liquor fall from his mouth as he drank, so that the kava did not strike (affect) him: but as for the one who had eaten his child it struck him very much, and his father carried him off again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，他們同住在一起的時候，村裡的男孩們和德伊塔里一同到溪裡洗澡，唱著歌。有一個名叫塔埃普普利提的人，據說他把自己變成一條魚，前去把那從竹筒裡出來的男孩吞吃了，帶著他逃到別的地方去了。塔里派了各樣的魚和鳥去尋找德伊塔里；他找到一條極其瘦小的魚，這魚和德伊塔里的父親發現他被藏在塔埃普普利提屋子的後端。塔里和塔埃普普利提二人坐下來喝卡瓦酒；那被吞吃者的父親喝酒時讓酒液從嘴邊落下，所以卡瓦酒沒有觸及（影響）他；但那吃了人家孩子的人卻大受其影響，他的父親便又把他帶走了。

title.en: Tarkeke and the Woven Fish
title.zh: 塔爾克凱與藤編之魚

region.en: Maewo to Opa (Ambae), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖自馬埃沃至安巴埃（奧帕）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Tarkeke, a man-eater of all the islands, wove himself an image of a fish with vines and turned into it. His son, curious at his father's forbidden inner room, got into the image; a kingfisher's cry, a broken stick — and the fish with the boy inside crossed to Opa.
