The father followed in a rough netting on his breast, rescued the boy, then taught him his trade: 'Go, for you want to eat a man' — and the sea rose up the shore after his son, carrying him into the bread-fruit-tree and swallowing the man there. Laid at the back of the house, the boy saw the sea, the shark, the fishes with their mouths open, and died.
summary.zh: 塔爾克凱在各島間食人。他以藤蔓編成魚形，鑽入其中便化作魚，欲食人則游往奧帕或拉加。一日他外出去園中，其子擅入屋內禁地，鑽進那藤魚之中；翠鳥飛落屋頂為號，屋中老嫗聞聲折斷柴枝，藤魚便載著孩子下海，渡往奧帕。父親聞聲狂奔而回，已來不及，便取椰纖胡亂編物縛於胸前，下海尋子；至奧帕救回孩子——奧帕人幾乎把他射死。歸途見一人立於麵包樹上，父親對兒子說：『去，吃了他。』兒子答：『父親，他在陸上，我怎麼去？』父親斥責，他只得前去；海水竟隨他漲上沙灘，把他連人帶上樹，吞下那人。孩子被抬回屋後安置，他一動，便看見海、看見鯊、看見張口待食的群魚——就這樣在那裡死去了。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era record (Codrington 1891); Maewo/Ambae heritage.

passages.text: They say that he used to devour men in all the islands, and that he made the image of a fish with woven vines, and got into it and turned into a fish. And when he wanted to eat a man he entered into that fish and went to Opa or Raga. One day he went into his garden, and his son was in the village, and his father had forbidden the boy to go to the inner part of the house; but his father had gone away and he and his mother were in the village, and he was playing about alone, and he thought he would go and see what it was that his father had forbidden him to see. So he went into the further end of the house, and saw the image of the fish lying, and got into it. And a kingfisher flies down as a sign if any one gets into the figure of the fish; and the old woman lying in the house when she hears the kingfisher breaks a stick, and the image then goes into the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說他曾在各島上吞吃人，又說他用藤蔓編成魚的形像，鑽進去就變成一條魚。當他想吃人的時候，就進入那魚裡，前往奧帕或拉加。有一天他到自己的園子裡去，他的兒子在村中，他父親曾禁止這男孩到屋子裡頭去；但他父親已經走了，他和母親在村裡，他獨自玩耍，心想不如去看看父親禁止他看的究竟是什麼。於是他就走進屋子的裡端，看見那魚的形像躺在那裡，便鑽了進去。若有人鑽進那魚的形像裡，就有一隻翠鳥飛下來作為徵兆；躺在屋裡的老婦人聽見翠鳥的叫聲，就折斷一根木棍，那形像便下到海裡去了。

passages.text: And when the boy got into the figure of the fish, and the kingfisher flew down to the roof of the house, and the old woman heard it, she broke a piece of fire-wood, and the image of the fish with the boy inside it went down into the sea, and crossed to Opa. And the father was in his garden and he heard a noise, and he ran as fast as he could, but found that the fish was already gone. So he weaves together the stuff that is on a cocoa-nut, in no particular shape, and puts it on his breast, and goes into the sea to seek the boy. And he finds him at Opa; and the Opa people, they say, had very nearly shot him. And his father brought him home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當那男孩鑽進魚的形像裡，翠鳥飛落到屋頂上，老婦人聽見了，就折斷一根柴，那裡面載著男孩的魚的形像便下到海裡，渡到奧帕去了。父親正在園子裡，聽見一陣聲響，就盡力跑去，卻發現那魚已經走了。於是他把椰子樹上的東西編在一起，也不成什麼形狀，貼在胸前，下海去尋找那男孩。他在奧帕找到了他；據說奧帕的人幾乎把他射死了。他的父親就把他帶回家來。

passages.text: And as they were coming back they saw a man in a bread-fruit-tree, and the father said to his son, 'Go and eat him'; and the son said to his father, 'How shall I go, father, because he is on dry land?' And his father hit him hard, and said, 'Go, for you want to eat a man.' Then he went, and as he went up towards the shore the sea went up too upon the shore, and he was carried up into the bread-fruit-tree after that man and swallowed him. And they came back to the back part of the house, and put him there, for he was not yet dead. And when they put him there at the further end of the house, and he moved himself about, he saw the sea, and the shark, and the fishes with their mouths open to devour him. And so he stayed there and died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們回來的時候，看見一個人待在麵包樹上，父親對兒子說：『去把他吃了。』兒子對父親說：『父親，我怎麼去呢？他是在乾地上啊。』他父親重重地打了他一下，說：『去吧，因為你想吃人。』於是他就去了，當他朝著岸邊上去的時候，海水也跟著漲上岸來，他就被托上那棵麵包樹，追上那人，把他吞了下去。他們回到屋子的後部，把他放在那裡，因為他還沒有死。當他們把他放在屋子裡端，他動來動去的時候，他看見了大海、鯊魚，以及張著嘴要吞吃他的魚。於是他就待在那裡，死了。

title.en: The Widow and the Ghost Who Ate the Torch
title.zh: 寡婦與食火把之鬼

region.en: Maewo (Aurora Island), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖馬埃沃島（奧羅拉島）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: A widow with a child at her hip met a ghost she took for her husband. Torching for fish by the shore, she left the child with him — and the ghost ate a finger, then the whole child, then ran to eat the mother, eating the coconut branches she had planted instead of her; she fled up a pandanus-tree and pelted him with fruit till dawn, when she saw him turn into a hermit crab.
summary.zh: 一名寡婦攜幼兒尋夫，途中遇一鬼，誤認為夫。三人同往海邊持炬照魚；婦人燃炬，鬼抱孩子，先咬去其一小指；婦人問，鬼答『蚊蟲叮的』。孩子止哭——鬼已把孩子整個吃掉。婦人這才確知遇鬼：她早沿岸插下椰枝作記，鬼食畢孩子便撲向她，慌亂中竟把那些椰枝一一吃掉，以為那就是她。婦人奔逃，攀上露兜樹；鬼欲攀樹食她，她便用樹果砸他，如此直到天明——晨光中她看見那鬼化作一隻寄居蟹。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era record (Codrington 1891); Maewo heritage.

passages.text: This is about a woman who lost her husband, and went in search of him, and she had a child with her. And a ghost met the woman carrying the child on her hip, and the woman thought it was her husband. And the three went down to the beach to burn for fish. Then the ghost said to the woman, 'You go and burn for fish, and I will look after our child.' And when the woman went with the torch the ghost ate one finger of the child. And its mother asked him what hurt the child, and the ghost said, 'Nothing, a mosquito bit it.' After he had spoken the child ceased to cry, and the woman discovered that it was a ghost because it had eaten the child entirely up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這是關於一個失去了丈夫的女人，她去尋找他，身邊帶著一個孩子。一個鬼魂遇見了這抱著孩子（把孩子抱在腰側）的女人，女人以為那就是她的丈夫。他們三人下到海灘上去照火捕魚。那鬼魂對女人說：『你去照火捕魚吧，我來照看我們的孩子。』當女人拿著火把去了，那鬼魂就吃掉了孩子的一根手指。孩子的母親問他孩子怎麼受了傷，那鬼魂說：『沒什麼，是蚊子咬的。』他說了這話之後，孩子就不再哭了，女人這才發覺那是個鬼魂，因為它已把孩子整個吃光了。

passages.text: Then she knew for certain that it was a ghost, because she had set up cocoa-nut branches along the shore, and the ghost when it had eaten the child went to eat the mother, and as he ran along to eat her he ate the branches she had set up, thinking that the branches were the woman. And the woman ran away fast and climbed into a pandanus-tree, and when the ghost would have climbed up to eat her the woman pelted him down with the fruits. And so she did till dawn; and when it was light she saw that he turned into a hermit crab.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這時她才確信那確實是鬼，因為她曾在岸邊立起椰子樹枝，而那鬼吃了孩子之後又去吃母親，當他跑著要去吃她時，便把她立起的樹枝都吃掉了，以為那些樹枝就是那女人。那女人飛快逃走，爬上一棵露兜樹，當鬼要爬上樹去吃她時，女人便用果實把他打下去。她就這樣一直做到天亮；天亮之後，她看見他變成了一隻寄居蟹。

title.en: Tagaro the Little and the Conch-Shell Blast
title.zh: 小塔加羅與法螺之吼

region.en: Lepers Island (Aoba), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Night-caught on a lone gaviga-tree, Tagaro-mbiti listened as Merambuto and his brothers claimed branch after branch below him. Asked what was in his hand, he answered, 'The voice of you and me to be sure' — and promised to let them hear it from his cave. He slipped away, whistled his signal, and blew the conch with all his strength: the brothers fell from the tree and died, Merambuto leapt for joy till the rock of his cave stuck fast in his head and he died too; bushes grew where the brothers fell.
summary.zh: 小塔加羅訪 Vagimbangga 購豬，歸途天黑，遂攀一株孤零零的 gaviga 樹，食果而眠，手中握著法螺。夜半，默蘭布托與其兄弟們一路喧嚷而來，各自攀枝分佔，口稱『這是我的枝！』；默蘭布托攀至樹頂，撞見小塔加羅，問他手中何物。小塔加羅答：『正是你我二人的聲音。』並許諾：『先回去，你聽見我吹哨，便用這法螺說話給我聽。』他下樓騙過眾兄弟，回至洞府吹哨為號；小塔加羅聞哨，鼓足全力猛吹法螺——默蘭布托的兄弟們從樹上紛紛跌落而死；默蘭布托自己高興得在洞裡一次次跳起，頭撞洞頂岩石，岩石嵌進頭裡，也就死了。兄弟墜落之處，後來長出了灌木。小塔加羅天明回家。

sensitivity.note: Native manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); Aoba heritage.

passages.text: They say that he went to a part of the island called Vagimbangga to pay for a pig there, and that on his return the sun set while he was still in the forest. And he was hungry, for he had nothing whatever to eat. Now beside that path they say there was a single gaviga-tree, with many branches, and also ripe fruit on it; and he climbed up to eat, and to sleep awhile on that tree; and in his hand was his conch-shell trumpet to blow as he went along the path. And in the middle of the night, when he had finished eating, he climbed further up to the top of that gaviga-tree to sleep and rest there; and as he begins to fall asleep he hears the voices of a number of people coming along underneath the gaviga-tree. And he woke up thinking that it was probably his brothers looking for him; but it was not so — these were Merambuto and his brothers coming along, and they climbed up the gaviga-tree themselves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們說他去了島上一個叫瓦金班加的地方，到那裡去付一頭豬的錢，而當他回來時，太陽已經落下，他卻還在森林裡。他又餓，因為他什麼吃的都沒有。他們說，那條小路旁有一棵孤零零的加維加樹，枝葉繁多，樹上還結著熟果；他爬上去吃果子，並在那樹上睡一會兒；他手裡拿著他的海螺號角，預備一路走一路吹。到了半夜，他吃完了，便再往上爬到那棵加維加樹的頂上，在那裡睡覺歇息；他正要入睡時，聽見許多人聲從加維加樹下走過來。他醒來，以為大概是他的兄弟們來找他；卻不是這樣——這些是梅蘭布托和他的兄弟們走過來，他們自己也爬上了那棵加維加樹。

passages.text: And Tagaro-mbiti sits perfectly still lest they should see him, and he hears one of them say 'Ineu ranganggu ngaha' — This is my branch — and so say all of them. Then says Merambuto, 'Ineu ranganggu ngaha lo vuhungegi' — This is my branch at the top — and this he said with a loud voice. And Merambuto climbed straight up to the top of that gaviga-tree, and there he found Tagaro-mbiti. Then says Merambuto, 'Who are you?' And says he, 'I am Tagaro-mbiti.' And he asked Tagaro again, 'What is that in your hand?' And he says, 'The voice of you and me to be sure.' And he begged of him to speak in that conch that he might hear it; but he said also, 'Wait a bit till I go back to my dwelling-place, and when I get there you will hear me whistle; then you shall speak with the voice of us two that I may hear it for myself.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 塔加羅姆比提一動也不動地坐著，免得被他們看見，他聽見其中一個說「Ineu ranganggu ngaha」——這是我的樹枝——他們全都這樣說。接著梅蘭布托說：「Ineu ranganggu ngaha lo vuhungegi」——這是我在頂上的樹枝——他這話說得聲音很大。梅蘭布托一直爬到那棵加維加樹的頂上，就在那裡發現了塔加羅姆比提。於是梅蘭布托說：「你是誰？」他答道：「我是塔加羅姆比提。」他又問塔加羅：「你手裡拿的是什麼？」他答道：「自然是你我二人的聲音。」他求他吹那海螺，好讓他聽一聽；但他又說：「等一等，等我回到我的住處，我到了那裡你就會聽見我吹口哨；那時你再吹出我們二人的聲音，好讓我自己聽一聽。」

passages.text: And he made haste down from the tree, and his brothers said, 'Are we to come too?' 'No,' says he, 'I am only going to get rid of a mess and then I shall come back.' Thus he deceived them; and when he reached his dwelling, the cave, he whistled for Tagaro to hear, that he might blow the conch. And Tagaro heard Merambuto whistle, and he put forth all his strength to blow the conch hard, and he blew, and Merambuto's brothers fell every one of them from the tree; and he himself was delighted and jumped high again and again in his cave, and his head struck against the rock, and the rock stuck fast into his head, and there he died. And his brothers who had fallen down died every one; and on that account they say that bushes grew up in that place where Merambuto's brothers fell. And when it was light Tagaro-mbiti returned to his home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他急忙下樹，他的兄弟們說：「我們也一起來嗎？」「不，」他說，「我只是去解個手，然後就回來。」他就這樣騙了他們；當他到了他的住處，那山洞，他便吹口哨讓塔加羅聽見，好讓他吹海螺。塔加羅聽見梅蘭布托吹口哨，便使出全身力氣用力吹那海螺，他吹了，梅蘭布托的兄弟們便一個個從樹上掉了下來；他自己則歡喜得在山洞裡一次又一次高高跳起，他的頭撞在岩石上，岩石便牢牢嵌進他的頭裡，他就死在那裡。那些掉下來的兄弟們也一個個死了；因此他們說，梅蘭布托的兄弟們掉下來的那個地方長出了灌木叢。天亮之後，塔加羅姆比提就回自己的家去了。

title.en: Merambuto Cooks His Mother
title.zh: 默蘭布托煮母

region.en: Lepers Island (Aoba), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Merambuto fed Tagaro badly, so Tagaro wrapped and threw away the food; then fed him on grated barrow-pig — and Merambuto grated up his own barrow-pig; then on meat he claimed was his mother cooked in the oven — and Merambuto cooked his mother in the oven. Then came the fire: 'Light a fire over me,' said Tagaro, who had dug a hole and survived his own burning; Merambuto asked for his turn, and Tagaro burned him up.
summary.zh: 默蘭布托請塔加羅吃飯，飯卻極差；塔加羅把食物包起偷偷扔掉，回請時端出擦絲閹豬肉。默蘭布托追問吃的是什麼，塔加羅答『擦絲的閹豬』，他便回家把自己的閹豬擦成絲。再問時塔加羅答得厭煩，騙他道：『我母親；我把她煮在爐裡了。』默蘭布托便回家把母親煮進爐中。塔加羅又說：『在我屋上放火吧。』默蘭布托紮緊門縱火；塔加羅在火中哀哭，默蘭布托笑他：『莫哭，你從前騙我，如今就要死了。』他以為塔加羅已死——其實塔加羅早掘好地洞藏身。翌晨默蘭布托來看，塔加羅安坐如常。默蘭布托說：『該我了，今夜你燒我的屋。』塔加羅縱火，把他燒了個乾淨。

sensitivity.note: Native manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); Aoba heritage. Cross-ref melanesian-tagaro-burning-house (Dixon recension).

passages.text: Merambuto prepared food for himself, and then he invited Tagaro to come that they might eat together. So Tagaro came to him in his house; and the food of Merambuto was exceedingly bad, and as they ate Tagaro did not eat at all, but he wrapped the food up to deceive Merambuto, and went and threw it away, and then went back to his house. Afterwards Tagaro sent after him saying, 'Merambuto, come here to my house.' Merambuto came and they two ate. And the food was good; Merambuto liked Tagaro's food very much; he had made his own not at all good. So Merambuto considered silently, 'What sort of thing is this we two are eating?' So he asked Tagaro, and Tagaro said to him, 'I have grated up my barrow pig.' So Merambuto went and grated up his barrow-pig, and in due course they two ate it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 梅蘭布托為自己準備了食物，然後邀請塔加羅來一同吃。於是塔加羅來到他家裡；梅蘭布托的食物極其難吃，他們吃的時候，塔加羅一點也沒吃，只是把食物包起來騙梅蘭布托，然後拿去扔掉，接著就回自己家去了。後來塔加羅派人去對他說：「梅蘭布托，到我家來。」梅蘭布托來了，他們二人一同吃。那食物很好；梅蘭布托非常喜歡塔加羅的食物；他自己做的卻一點也不好。於是梅蘭布托暗自思量：「我們二人吃的這是什麼東西？」他便問塔加羅，塔加羅對他說：「我把我的公豬刨碎了。」於是梅蘭布托回去把他的公豬刨碎，時候到了，他們二人就把它吃了。

passages.text: After this Tagaro invited Merambuto to eat with him in return in his house. So he asked him again, 'What food is this we two are eating?' And Tagaro was tired of being asked, and deceived Merambuto, saying to him, 'My mother; I cooked her in the oven.' So Merambuto went home and cooked his mother in the oven. After this Tagaro said to him, 'Light a fire over me.' So Merambuto came, and tied up the door of Tagaro's house, bound it very tight, and set fire to Tagaro's house. Then Tagaro wept; Merambuto said to him, 'Don't cry, you deceived me formerly, now you are soon to die for it.' He thought that Tagaro was dead; but not at all, he had dug a hole, and stayed in it. In the morning thinking that he was dead he came, and Tagaro had been long sitting ready for him. So Merambuto asked him, 'Are you sitting like this?' Tagaro said, 'Yes.' So Merambuto said to him, 'My turn now, to-night you set fire to my house.' So Tagaro set fire to his house, and the fire burnt him up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此後，塔加羅回請梅蘭布托到他家裡一同吃。於是梅蘭布托又問他：「我們二人吃的這是什麼食物？」塔加羅被問得厭煩了，便騙梅蘭布托，對他說：「我的母親；我把她放在爐裡烤了。」於是梅蘭布托回家，把他的母親放在爐裡烤了。此後，塔加羅對他說：「在我身上點火吧。」於是梅蘭布托來了，把塔加羅家的門綁住，綁得緊緊的，然後放火燒塔加羅的房子。塔加羅便哭了；梅蘭布托對他說：「別哭，你先前騙了我，如今你就要因此而死。」他以為塔加羅死了；卻完全不是，他挖了一個洞，待在裡面。到了早晨，梅蘭布托以為他死了，便來了，而塔加羅早已坐著等他好久了。於是梅蘭布托問他：「你就這樣坐著嗎？」塔加羅說：「是的。」於是梅蘭布托對他說：「現在輪到我了，今晚你去放火燒我的房子。」於是塔加羅放火燒他的房子，火把他燒盡了。

title.en: Tane Presses Sky from Earth
title.zh: 塔內撐天：天空與大地裂離

region.en: Rotorua lakes district, Aotearoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 紐西蘭羅托魯瓦湖區（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 1 (London 1855)

summary.en: In the long dark the children of Rangi (Sky) and Papa (Earth) consult on whether to slay their parents or tear them apart. Four sons fail to force the embrace open; only Tane, father of forests, plants his head on the earth, raises his feet against the sky, and strains until heaven and earth are rent apart, revealing a multitude of beings hidden between them. Their parents' continuing love is seen in the mists that rise from Papa's bosom and the dew that falls as Rangi's tears.
summary.zh: 在長夜般的黑暗中，朗基（天）與帕帕（地）的眾子女商議：是殺死父母，還是將二人強行分開。羅果、坦加羅亞、豪米亞與屠諸兄相繼努力而失敗；唯有森林之父塔內以頭抵地、以足撐天，竭力舒展，終將天與地撕裂分開，露出藏於二者之間的無數生靈。父母之愛未絕：帕帕胸中所出暖霧即地氣，朗基夜夜垂淚即露水。

sensitivity.note: Living Maori tradition collected in the colonial era (Grey 1855) from named chiefly informants; nothing restricted reproduced. Tagging of Polynesian myth into Thompson-style motifs is interpretive.

passages.text: In the beginning all things came from Rangi, the vast heaven above, and Papa, the earth beneath, who still clave together in darkness. The children they had begotten multiplied without ever seeing light, and at last, worn out by the endless dark, they consulted among themselves what they should do with their parents: whether to slay them or to rend them apart. Tu-matauenga, the fiercest, said it was well to slay them. But Tane-mahuta, father of the forests, answered: not so - it is better to rend them apart, letting heaven stand far above and earth lie under our feet, so the sky becomes a stranger to us but the earth remains close, our nursing mother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 起初，萬物皆源自蘭吉——上方浩瀚的蒼天，以及帕帕——下方的大地；他們仍一同緊附於黑暗之中。他們所生的子女不斷繁衍，卻從未見過光明。最後，子女們被無盡的黑暗折磨得疲憊不堪，便彼此商議該如何處置父母：是將他們殺死，還是把他們分開。最兇猛的圖—馬陶恩加說，殺死他們為好。但森林之父塔內—馬胡塔答道：不可如此——把他們分開更好，讓蒼天高懸於遠方，讓大地躺在我們腳下，如此天空便與我們疏遠，而大地仍留在近旁，做我們哺育的母親。

passages.text: Only Tawhiri-ma-tea, father of winds and storms, refused to consent. Rongo-ma-tane, god of cultivated food, first rose to rend apart his parents and struggled in vain; then Tangaroa, father of fish and reptiles, and Haumia-tikitiki, father of wild foods, and Tu-matauenga himself each strove and failed. At last Tane slowly rose, paused, planted his head firmly on his mother the earth, lifted his feet to rest against his father the skies, and strained his back and limbs with mighty effort. Then Rangi and Papa were rent apart, shrieking aloud, 'Wherefore slay you your parents? Why rend them apart?' Tane heeded not their cries: he pressed the earth far below and thrust the sky far above, and darkness gave way to light.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 唯有風暴之父塔惠里—馬—特阿拒絕同意。栽培食物之神隆戈—馬—塔內首先起身要分開父母，卻徒勞掙扎；接著魚類與爬蟲之父坦加羅阿、野生食物之父豪米亞—蒂基蒂基，以及圖—馬陶恩加本人，也都各自奮力嘗試，卻都失敗了。最後，塔內緩緩起身，稍作停頓，把頭牢牢抵在母親大地上，抬起雙腳抵住父親蒼天，以巨大的力量繃緊背脊與四肢。於是蘭吉與帕帕被分開了，他們高聲尖叫：「你們為何要殺害父母？為何要把他們分開？」塔內不理會他們的呼喊：他把大地壓向極下方，把蒼天推往極上方，黑暗便讓位給了光明。

passages.text: The moment heaven was rent from earth, a multitude of human beings were discovered whom the primal pair had begotten and who had lain hidden between their bodies. The old saying ran that it was the fierce thrusting of Tane which tore heaven from earth, so that darkness was made manifest and so was the light. Yet the mutual love of the separated pair continues: the soft warm sighs of Papa's loving bosom rise from the wooded mountains and valleys as mists, and Rangi mourns his separation through the long nights, dropping tears upon her bosom which men call dew-drops.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蒼天與大地被分開的那一刻，人們發現了原始夫婦所生的一大群人類，他們一直藏匿在兩人的身體之間。古老的說法流傳著：正是塔內猛烈的推頂，把蒼天從大地上撕裂開來，於是黑暗顯露出來，光明也顯露出來。然而，被分開的夫婦彼此相愛之情仍延續不斷：帕帕慈愛胸懷中溫柔溫暖的嘆息，化作霧氣，從林木覆蓋的山巒與谷地升起；蘭吉則在漫漫長夜中哀悼自己的分離，把淚水滴落在她的胸懷上，人們稱之為露珠。

title.en: Tawhiri's War of Storms
title.zh: 塔維里馬泰亞的風暴之戰

region.en: Sky realms above Lake Taupo, Aotearoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 紐西蘭陶波湖上空之天界（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 1 (London 1855)

summary.en: Angry that his brothers had separated their parents, Tawhiri-ma-tea, father of winds and storms, flees to the hollows of the sky, begets a brood of winds on his father, and wages war on his siblings. He snaps Tane's giant forests, lashes Tangaroa's seas into cliff-high waves, and hunts Rongo and Haumia - whom Papa hides in the earth - but cannot shake Tu-matauenga, man, who alone stands erect and unshaken. The episode explains why storm is humanity's unconquered enemy.
summary.zh: 諸兄分開父母，風暴之神塔維里馬泰亞大怒，攜幼風入天父所居之避風凹所，於天界繁育風族，向諸弟宣戰。他吹折塔內的巨林，掀起高過斷崖的巨浪逼退坦加羅亞；羅果與豪米亞被地母藏於土中得免；唯屠馬陶恩加（人）挺立不搖，風暴不能勝他——此即人與風暴為世仇之緣由。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection of living oral tradition; interpretive motif tagging.

passages.text: In Tawhiri-ma-tea, father of winds and storms, a fierce desire rose to wage war on his brothers because they had rent apart their common parents. He alone had refused to consent to his mother being torn from her lord and children. So he rose, followed his father to the realms above, hurried to the sheltered hollows in the boundless skies, and there, nestling in the place of rest, consulted long with the vast Heaven; and between him and Heaven was begotten a numerous brood which rapidly increased. He despatched one child westward, one southward, one eastward, one northward, and named himself and his progeny, the mighty winds, accordingly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在風暴之父塔惠里—馬—特阿心中，升起了一股猛烈的渴望，要對兄弟們發動戰爭，因為他們把共同的父母分開了。唯有他拒絕同意讓母親從她的夫君與孩子們身邊被奪走。於是他起身，跟隨父親前往上方的領域，匆匆趕往無邊蒼天中受庇護的凹處，在那裡蜷伏於安歇之所，與浩瀚的蒼天長久商議；他與蒼天之間生出了一大群後代，迅速繁衍增多。他派一個孩子往西，一個往南，一個往東，一個往北，並據此為自己和自己的子嗣——強大的風——命名。

passages.text: He next sent forth fierce squalls, whirlwinds, dense and massy and dark and fiery clouds, clouds of thunder and clouds wildly bursting, and swept on in their midst. The blast of his mouth smote the gigantic forests of Tane-mahuta unawares; the trees snapped in the middle, were rent to atoms, and lay scattered for the insect, the grub, and rottenness. From the forests he swooped down upon the seas and lashed the ocean in his wrath, raising waves steep as cliffs whose summits made the beholder giddy; and Tangaroa, god of ocean, flew affrighted through his seas.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著，他放出猛烈的狂風、旋風、濃密厚重而黑暗熾熱的雲、雷鳴之雲與狂烈迸裂之雲，並在其間橫掃前進。他口中的疾風出其不意地襲擊了塔內—馬胡塔的巨大森林；樹木從中折斷，被撕成碎片，散落在地，供蟲子、幼蟲與腐爛享用。他從森林俯衝向大海，在憤怒中鞭打海洋，掀起陡如懸崖的巨浪，浪峰令觀者頭暈目眩；海洋之神坦加羅阿驚恐地逃竄於自己的海域之中。

passages.text: Tawhiri-ma-tea then rushed to attack Rongo-ma-tane and Haumia-tikitiki, gods of cultivated and wild food; but Papa caught them up and hid them so well in the earth that the storm-god sought them in vain. At last he flung all his force against Tu-matauenga; but what did Tu care for his brother's wrath? He was the one who had planned the parents' destruction and stood brave and fierce. All his brothers had yielded before the tremendous assaults, but Tu-matauenga, or man, still stood erect and unshaken upon the breast of his mother Earth; and the passions of Heaven and the storm-god were at last assuaged.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 塔惠里—馬—特阿隨即衝去攻擊栽培食物之神隆戈—馬—塔內與野生食物之神豪米亞—蒂基蒂基；但帕帕把他們抓起，穩妥地藏在大地之中，風暴之神徒然尋覓。最後，他把全部力量投向圖—馬陶恩加；但圖何曾在意兄弟的怒火？他正是謀劃毀滅父母的那一位，勇敢而兇猛。他所有的兄弟都在那可怕的攻擊前屈服了，但圖—馬陶恩加，也就是人，仍舊挺立於母親大地的胸膛之上，毫不動搖；蒼天與風暴之神的怒氣終於平息。

title.en: Fish and Reptiles Part Ways
title.zh: 魚族與爬蟲族分途

region.en: Tangaroa's seas, Aotearoa coast (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 紐西蘭海岸坦加羅亞之海（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 1 (London 1855)

summary.en: As Tawhiri's storm war breaks over the ocean, Tangaroa flees through his seas, and his grandchildren Ika-tere (father of fish) and Tu-te-wehiwehi (father of reptiles) dispute how to escape. One party cries 'fly to the sea', the other 'fly inland'; the fish rush to the water, the reptiles to the scrub, and each taunts the other with its doom: fish will be singed over fern fire as relish or cooked, reptiles will be laid atop baskets of vegetable food. Tangaroa ever after wages war on Tane for sheltering the deserters.
summary.zh: 風暴戰火燒及海洋，坦加羅亞倉皇逃入深海；其孫伊卡泰雷（魚祖）與圖泰維希維希（爬蟲祖）爭議避禍之道：一族喊『逃向海』，一族喊『逃往陸』。魚群奔入水中，爬蟲躲進林莽，彼此相譏對方的命運。坦加羅亞憤於部分子孫棄他而投奔森林之神塔內，自此與塔內永相征戰。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection of living oral tradition; interpretive motif tagging.

passages.text: When Tangaroa fled for safety to the ocean before Tawhiri's storms, his children consulted how they might escape, for he had begotten Punga, and Punga two children: Ika-tere, father of fish, and Tu-te-wehiwehi, father of reptiles. Tu-te-wehiwehi and his party cried aloud, 'Let us fly inland'; Ika-tere and his party cried aloud, 'Let us fly to the sea.' Some would not obey one order, some not the other, and they escaped in two parties: the reptiles hid themselves ashore, and the party of Punga rushed to the sea. In the ancient religious services this is called the separation of Tawhiri-ma-tea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當塔納羅阿在塔惠里里的暴風雨來臨前逃往海洋避難時，他的子女們商議如何逃脫，因為他生了蓬加，蓬加又生了兩個孩子：魚之父伊卡-特雷，以及爬蟲之父圖-特-韋希韋希。圖-特-韋希韋希及其一夥高聲喊道：『讓我們逃往內陸吧』；伊卡-特雷及其一夥高聲喊道：『讓我們逃往大海吧。』有些人不願服從這一道命令，有些人不願服從另一道，於是他們分成兩夥逃走了：爬蟲藏身於陸上，蓬加的一夥則奔向大海。在古老的宗教儀式中，這被稱為塔惠里里-馬-特阿的分離。

passages.text: Ika-tere taunted his rival: 'Fly inland, then; the fate of you and your race will be that when they catch you, before you are cooked, they will singe off your scales over a lighted wisp of dry fern.' Tu-te-wehiwehi answered: 'Seek safety in the sea, then; and the future fate of your race will be that when they serve out little baskets of cooked vegetable food to each person, you will be laid upon the top of the food to give a relish to it.' Then without delay the two races separated: the fish fled in confusion to the sea, and the reptiles sought safety in the forests and scrubs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊卡-特雷譏諷他的對手說：『那就逃往內陸吧；你和你族類的命運將是：當他們捉住你們時，在烹煮之前，他們會用一束點燃的乾蕨在火上燎去你們的鱗片。』圖-特-韋希韋希回答說：『那就到海裡尋求安全吧；你族類未來的命運將是：當他們把一小籃一小籃煮熟的植物性食物分給每個人時，你們會被擺在食物上面，用來增添滋味。』於是兩族毫不遲延地分開了：魚群慌亂地逃向大海，爬蟲則在森林與灌木叢中尋求安全。

passages.text: Tangaroa, enraged that some of his children deserted him and were sheltered on dry land by the god of the forests, has ever since waged war on his brother Tane, who wages war in return. Tane supplies the offspring of Tu-matauenga with canoes, spears, fish-hooks made from his trees, and nets woven from his fibrous plants, that they may destroy the offspring of Tangaroa; whilst Tangaroa in return swallows up the offspring of Tane, overwhelming canoes with surges and wasting away the shores with his lapping waves, that the giants of the forests may be swept out into his boundless ocean.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 塔納羅阿因他的一些子女背棄了他、並受森林之神的庇護而藏身於旱地，勃然大怒，自此便不斷向他的兄弟塔內開戰，塔內也回以征戰。塔內以他的樹木為圖-馬陶恩加的後裔提供獨木舟、長矛、魚鉤，以及用他的纖維植物編成的網，使他們得以消滅塔納羅阿的後裔；而塔納羅阿則反過來吞沒塔內的後裔，以巨浪淹沒獨木舟，以拍岸的波濤侵蝕海岸，使森林中的巨木被沖入他那無邊的海洋。

title.en: Tu-matauenga Avenges Himself on His Brothers
title.zh: 屠馬陶恩加向諸弟復仇

region.en: Breast of Papa, Aotearoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 紐西蘭地母胸膛（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 1 (London 1855)

summary.en: Left to fight the storm-god alone, Tu-matauenga resolves on revenge for his brothers' cowardice. Death as yet had no power over man, but Tu snares the birds of Tane's forest with whanake leaf nooses, drags Tangaroa's children ashore with nets of flax, and digs up Rongo's and Haumia's plants with a wooden hoe, consuming them all as food. Four brothers become food with fitting incantations; only Tawhiri, the storm, remains unconquered, forever attacking man by sea and land.
summary.zh: 諸弟怯戰棄他於風暴之中，屠馬陶恩加遂謀復仇。彼時死亡尚未轄制人。屠以瓦納基葉結成套索羅捕塔內之林鳥，以亞麻結網曳坦加羅亞之魚群上岸，又削木鋤掘起羅果與豪米亞之可食根莖，將諸弟盡數吞噬為食。四弟皆成『平常之食』並各有祭禱咒語；唯風暴塔維里未被降服，永為世仇，海陸之間攻人不息。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection; the 'eating the brothers' episode is a traditional explanatory myth, reproduced as paraphrase.

passages.text: Tu-matauenga, or fierce man, having successfully resisted the god of hurricanes, took thought how he could turn upon his brothers and slay them, because they had not assisted or fought bravely when Tawhiri-ma-tea attacked them, and had left him alone to show his prowess in the fight. As yet death had no power over man; it was not until the birth of the children of Taranga and Makea-tu-tara - of Maui-taha, Maui-roto, Maui-pae, Maui-waho, and Maui-tikitiki-o-Taranga, who tried to deceive Hine-nui-te-po - that death obtained power over mankind, for had that goddess not been deceived, men would have lived for ever.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 圖-馬陶恩加，即凶猛之人，在成功抵禦了颶風之神後，思量著如何轉而對付他的兄弟們並將他們殺死，因為當塔惠里里-馬-特阿攻擊他們時，他們未曾相助，也未曾英勇作戰，只留下他獨自在戰鬥中施展威猛。當時死亡對人尚無力量；直到塔蘭加與馬凱阿-圖-塔拉的孩子們——毛伊-塔哈、毛伊-羅托、毛伊-帕埃、毛伊-瓦霍，以及試圖欺騙希內-努伊-特-波的毛伊-蒂基蒂基-奧-塔蘭加——誕生之後，死亡才對人類有了力量，因為倘若那位女神未被欺騙，人類本可永生不死。

passages.text: He first sought means of injuring Tane-mahuta, who had a numerous progeny rapidly increasing and might prove hostile; so he collected leaves of the whanake tree and twisted them into nooses, went to the forest, hung his snares, and lo - the children of Tane fell before him, none could any longer fly or move in safety. Next he took revenge on Tangaroa, finding his offspring leaping and swimming in the water; he cut many leaves of the flax-plant, netted nets with the flax, and dragged and hauled the children of Tangaroa ashore.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他首先尋求傷害塔內-馬胡塔的辦法，因為塔內子嗣眾多、迅速繁衍，可能成為敵手；於是他採集了瓦納克樹的葉子，把它們搓成套索，前往森林，掛下他的陷阱，瞧——塔內的子女紛紛倒在他面前，再也無法安全地飛翔或行動。接著他向塔納羅阿報仇，發現他的後裔在水中跳躍游動；他割下許多亞麻葉，用亞麻編成網，把塔納羅阿的子女拖拽上岸。

passages.text: Then he determined also to be revenged upon Rongo-ma-tane and Haumia-tikitiki; he soon found them by their peculiar leaves, scraped into shape a wooden hoe, plaited a basket, dug in the earth, and pulled up all kinds of plants with edible roots, and the plants dug up withered in the sun. Thus Tu-matauenga devoured all his brothers, in revenge for their deserting him to fight alone against Tawhiri-ma-tea and Rangi. When his brothers were all overcome he assumed new names - Tu-ka-riri, Tu-ka-nguha, Tu-ka-taua, Tu-whaka-heke-tangata, Tu-mata-wha-iti, Tu-matauenga - one for each attribute displayed in his victories. Four brothers became his common food; but Tawhiri-ma-tea he could not vanquish or make common by eating, so he, the last-born child of Heaven and Earth, was left as an enemy for man, ever attacking him in storms and hurricanes by sea and land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然後他又決心向龍戈-馬-塔內與豪米亞-蒂基蒂基報仇；他憑藉它們特有的葉子很快找到了它們，削制了一把木鋤，編了一隻籃子，掘開泥土，拔出各種有可食根莖的植物，被拔出的植物在陽光下枯萎了。於是圖-馬陶恩加吞食了他所有的兄弟，以報復他們背棄他、讓他獨自對抗塔惠里里-馬-特阿與朗吉。當他的兄弟們全被制服後，他取了新的名字——圖-卡-里里、圖-卡-恩古哈、圖-卡-陶阿、圖-瓦卡-赫克-坦加塔、圖-馬塔-瓦-伊蒂、圖-馬陶恩加——每一個名字對應他在勝利中展現的一種特質。四個兄弟成了他的日常食物；但塔惠里里-馬-特阿他無法征服，也無法以吞食使之成為日常食物，因此他，這天與地最後出生的孩子，被留下作為人類的敵人，不斷在海上與陸上以暴風雨和颶風襲擊人類。

title.en: The Great Rain That Drowned the Land
title.zh: 大雨水沉陸：洪沒大地的雨族之怒

region.en: Aotearoa coastlands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 紐西蘭沿海陸地（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 1 (London 1855)

summary.en: In the aftermath of the storm-god's wrath, Grey's record tells how a great part of the dry land disappeared: the beings Terrible-rain, Long-continued-rain and Fierce-hail-storms, with their progeny Mist, Heavy-dew and Light-dew, submerged most of mother Earth, so that only a small portion of dry land projected above the sea. A Maori parallel to the world-deluge cluster, marking the world's first catastrophe after the separation.
summary.zh: 風暴之怒後，陸地大半消失：『可怖之雨』『久雨』『猛雹』諸靈及其後裔『霧』『重露』『輕露』共同淹沒大地母親的大部分，僅餘少許陸地露於海面。此為毛利口傳中與世界洪水母題相對應的篇章，記天裂地分之後世界的第一場浩劫。

sensitivity.note: Flood-cluster tagging follows the cross-tradition motif plan; the Maori text names rain-beings rather than a single flood hero.

passages.text: The bursting forth of the wrathful fury of Tawhiri-ma-tea against his brothers was the cause of the disappearance of a great part of the dry land; during that contest a great part of mother Earth was submerged. The names of those beings of ancient days who submerged so large a portion of the earth were Terrible-rain, Long-continued-rain, and Fierce-hail-storms; and their progeny were Mist, Heavy-dew, and Light-dew. These together submerged the greater part of the earth, so that only a small portion of dry land projected above the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 塔惠里-馬-特阿對其兄弟們洶湧爆發的憤怒狂怒，正是大片陸地消失的原因；在那場爭鬥中，大地母親的很大一部分被海水淹沒。使如此大一部分大地沉入水中的那些遠古時代之存在，其名為「可怖之雨」、「綿延之雨」與「猛烈冰雹風暴」；牠們的後裔則是「霧」、「重露」與「輕露」。這些一同淹沒了大地的大部分，以致僅有一小部分陸地高聳於海面之上。

passages.text: From that time clear light increased upon the earth, and all the beings which had lain hidden between Rangi and Papa before they were separated now multiplied upon the earth. The first beings begotten by the primal pair were not like human beings; but Tu-matauenga bore the likeness of a man, as did all his brothers, and so it continued through the generations of Ngainui, of Whiro-te-tupua, and of Tiki-tawhito-ariki, until it reaches at last the generation of Maui-taha and his brothers, down to Maui-tikitiki-o-Taranga, the demigod.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 自那時起，清明之光在大地上日益增長，而所有在朗吉與帕帕被分離之前隱藏於二者之間的存在，如今都在大地上繁衍增多。原初的一對所生育的最初諸存在，並不像人類；但圖-馬陶恩加具有人的形貌，他的所有兄弟亦然，如此延續於恩蓋努伊、惠羅-特-圖普阿與蒂基-陶希托-阿里基的世代，直至最後到達毛伊-塔哈及其兄弟們的世代，下至半神毛伊-蒂基蒂基-奧-塔蘭加。

title.en: The Zduhacz: Sleep-Souls Battling on the Mountain
title.zh: 茲杜哈茨：山頂之魂的征戰

region.en: Montenegro (symbolic pin at Mount Lovcen)
region.zh: 蒙特內哥羅（象徵性定位於洛夫琴山）

period: Belief recorded 19th-early 20th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1

summary.en: In Serbian and Montenegrin belief the soul leaves a sleeper's body as a Zduhacz, a winged guardian-genius; all the Zduhaczs of a region must fight on a mountain-top each spring, and whichever side wins brings its homeland rain, rich harvest, and healthy herds.
summary.zh: 塞爾維亞與蒙特內哥羅信仰中，靈魂於睡眠時化身茲杜哈茨守護精靈；各族之魂靈於山頂交戰，勝者一方賜其鄉土雨水、豐收與牛羊興旺。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief recorded by ethnographers; no living-community restrictions.

passages.text: In Serbian and Montenegrin belief a person's soul can leave the sleeping body and fly abroad as a Zduhacz, a guardian-genius; even the souls of cats, dogs, and oxen may become Zduhaczs. On mountain-tops the genii of every land assemble and battle with one another, man against man and troop against troop. The victors bring their countrymen rich harvest and success in breeding cattle; if a man's soul is slain in the fight, he never wakes again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在塞爾維亞與蒙特內哥羅的信仰中，人的靈魂能離開沉睡的軀體，化為茲杜哈奇——一位守護神靈——飛往他方；甚至貓、狗與牛的靈魂也可能成為茲杜哈奇。在群山之巔，各方的神靈聚集，彼此爭戰，人對人，隊伍對隊伍。勝者為其同胞帶來豐收與牲畜繁衍的興旺；若某人的靈魂在爭戰中被殺，他便再也不會醒來。

passages.text: In Montenegro the Zduhaczs of land and sea are distinguished: those of land cause drought, those of sea bring rain, and the weather of the year depends on which of the two prevails. A sudden storm betrays a battle among them. A man with such a soul is said to know all that passes at a distance, for he has seen it while flying abroad in sleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在蒙特內哥羅，陸上與海上的茲杜哈奇有所區別：陸上的帶來乾旱，海上的帶來雨水，而一年之天氣取決於二者之中何方佔上風。驟起的風暴洩露了牠們之間的一場爭戰。據說擁有此等靈魂的人知曉遠方發生的一切，因為他在睡眠中飛往他方時已親眼見過。

title.en: The Mora: Night-Demon of the Slavic Household
title.zh: 摩拉：斯拉夫家宅的夜魔

region.en: Slavic lands (symbolic pin at Kiev)
region.zh: 斯拉夫諸地（象徵性定位於基輔）

period: Belief recorded in 19th-c. ethnography (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1

summary.en: A Mora is a living person whose soul leaves the body at night to torment sleepers: sent as straw, shadow, cat, mouse, or snake, she first lulls her victims with sweet slumber, then chokes them in terrible dreams and drinks their blood.
summary.zh: 摩拉乃活人之靈夜間出竅作祟：化為稻草、陰影、貓鼠或蛇，先使人酣眠，繼而噩夢窒息、吮其血。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief; the Mora figure survives in modern Slavic fairy tales without community restrictions.

passages.text: The Slavs widely believe that certain living persons, man or woman, may be a Mora: the soul leaves the sleeping body at night and returns at dawn. Such a person may be known from birth by bushy black eyebrows that meet above the nose. The Mora takes many shapes — a piece of straw, a white shadow, a leather bag, a white mouse, a cat, a snake, or a white horse — and comes by night to the dwellings of men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 斯拉夫人普遍相信，某些活著的人，無論男女，可能是一名莫拉：其靈魂在夜間離開沉睡的軀體，於黎明時返回。這樣的人可從出生時便知其然，因其有在鼻樑上方相連的濃密黑眉。莫拉能化為多種形貌——一根麥稈、一道白色的影子、一只皮袋、一隻白鼠、一隻貓、一條蛇或一匹白馬——並於夜間來到人們的居所。

passages.text: She first sends refreshing slumber to those within, and then, when they sleep, torments them with terrible dreams, chokes them, and sucks their blood. Children are her chief victims, but she attacks horses and cattle too, and withers trees. In Russia the Mora becomes the Kikimora, a tiny household demon that lives behind the oven: at night it whines and whistles, spins endlessly, and tangles the tow of any spinner who fails to make the sign of the cross.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她先向屋內之人送去令人舒爽的睡眠，隨後，當他們入睡時，便以可怕的夢境折磨他們，扼住他們，並吸吮他們的鮮血。孩童是她主要的受害者，但她也會侵襲馬匹與牛隻，並使樹木枯萎。在俄羅斯，莫拉變為基基莫拉，一種住在爐灶後面的微小家宅惡魔：夜間它哀鳴、吹哨，無休止地紡線，並把任何未劃十字聖號的紡紗者所紡的麻絮纏結成一團。

title.en: The Vlkodlak: Werewolf and Eater of the Sun
title.zh: 維爾科拉克：狼人與吞日者

region.en: Southern Slavic lands (symbolic pin at Sarajevo)
region.zh: 南斯拉夫諸地（象徵性定位於薩拉熱窩）

period: Tradition of 13th-c. origin; recorded 19th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1

summary.en: The Vlkodlak is a man transformed into a wolf by magic, often a bride or bridegroom enchanted on the wedding road; a dark Southern-Slav tradition makes the werewolf chase the clouds and devour the sun or moon, so that drums, bells, and gunfire are raised to drive him from the light.
summary.zh: 維爾科拉克乃受魔術化狼之人，多為婚途上新娘新郎；南斯拉夫古傳其追雲吞日食月致蝕，故鳴鼓敲鐘放炮以驅之。

sensitivity.note: The eclipse-demon parallels the wolf that devours sun or moon in Norse, Chinese, and other traditions; tagging is interpretive.

passages.text: A child born feet first, or born with teeth, may become a Vlkodlak — a werewolf; more often a man is turned into one by the magic of another, and this happens most frequently to the bride and bridegroom as they go to the church to be married. The enchanted one runs about the village as a wolf, gazing plaintively at the people he once knew but harming no one, until the same enchanter destroys the charm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 腳先出生，或生來帶牙的孩子，可能成為沃爾科德拉克（Vlkodlak）——即狼人；更常見的情況是，一個人因他人的法術而變成狼人，而這最常發生在新郎新娘前往教堂成婚的途中。被施了法術的人會化作狼在村中奔走，哀怨地凝視著自己從前認識的人，卻不傷害任何人，直到同一個施術者破除咒語為止。

passages.text: Among the Southern Slavs a tradition dating from the thirteenth century tells of a Vukodlak who followed the clouds and devoured the sun or the moon, causing an eclipse. On such an occasion the people beat drums, ring bells, and fire guns to drive the demon from the light. By night the Vlkodlak also attacks cattle, sucks the milk of cows and mares, and strangles horses.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在南斯拉夫人之間，有一則可追溯至十三世紀的傳說，講述一隻武科德拉克（Vukodlak）追隨雲層，吞噬太陽或月亮，造成日食或月食。每逢此類情形，人們便擊鼓、鳴鐘、放槍，以驅逐那惡魔離開光明。夜間，沃爾科德拉克也會襲擊牲畜，吸食母牛與母馬的乳汁，並扼殺馬匹。

title.en: The Vampire: Unquiet Dead of the Slavs
title.zh: 吸血鬼：斯拉夫之不寧亡者

region.en: Balkans (symbolic pin at Belgrade)
region.zh: 巴爾幹（象徵性定位於貝爾格勒）

period: Belief attested from 11th c.; recorded 19th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1

summary.en: Sorcerers, suicides, and the violently dead cannot rest: their bodies are occupied by an unclean spirit, do not decay, and rise at night to wail on wayside crosses and drain the blood of the living until cock-crow; villages end the plague by digging up the corpse and staking and burning it.
summary.zh: 巫者、自盡者與橫死之人不得安息：屍身被穢靈所據，不腐不敗，夜起於十字架上哀哭、吸吮生人之血，雞鳴乃止；村人掘屍穿椿焚之，以絕其害。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief; keep in myth category (legendary) rather than folklore-verbatim testimony of real events.

passages.text: Among the Slavs the souls of sorcerers, great sinners, suicides, and the violently dead are loath to part with their bodies and return to trouble the living; such corpses were long denied churchyard burial and thrown into pits or swamps. From such graves rise the Vampires — the dead occupied by an unclean spirit, a belief traceable as far back as the eleventh century.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在斯拉夫人之間，巫師、大罪人、自殺者與橫死者的靈魂不願離開自己的軀體，會回來騷擾生者；這類屍體長久以來被拒絕葬於教堂墓地，而被拋入坑洞或沼澤。吸血鬼正是從這樣的墳墓中升起——即被不潔之靈佔據的死者，此一信仰可追溯至十一世紀之久。

passages.text: Any person over whom a dog or cat jumps, or upon whom an unclean shadow falls, may become a vampire after death; the corpse does not decay but keeps the colour of life. At night the vampire leaves the grave, rocks and wails upon wayside crosses, and sucks the blood of people and cattle until cock-crow ends his power. Villages defend themselves by exhuming the body, driving an ashen or hawthorn stake through its heart, and burning it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 任何被狗或貓跳過、或被不潔的陰影籠罩的人，死後都可能變成吸血鬼；其屍體不會腐爛，而保持著生前的顏色。夜間，吸血鬼離開墳墓，在路旁的十字架上搖晃哀號，吸食人與牲畜的血，直到雞鳴結束他的法力。村莊則以掘出屍體、將白蠟木或山楂木樁釘入其心臟、再將其焚燒來自衛。

title.en: The Ship-Pyre of a Rus Chieftain: Ibn Fadlan's Account
title.zh: 羅斯酋長的船葬火焚：伊本·法德蘭所記

region.en: Volga river, lands of the Volga Rus (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 伏爾加河羅斯人之地（象徵性定位）

period: Eyewitness account of 922 (Ibn Fadlan); retold by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 2, retelling Ahmad ibn Fadlan's risala of 922

summary.en: The Arab envoy Ibn Fadlan watched the funeral of a Rus chieftain on the Volga: the dead man's ship was hauled ashore, an old woman called the Angel of Death stabbed a slave girl who had volunteered to follow her lord, and all was burned in a ship-pyre crowned with days of feasting.
summary.zh: 阿拔斯使節伊本·法德蘭親見伏爾加河畔羅斯酋長葬禮：船屍上岸，老嫗名『死神天使』者刺殺自願殉葬之婢，船焚火起，宴飲連日。

sensitivity.note: Historical eyewitness account including ritual killing; treated soberly at ethnographic level as funerary religion, without graphic detail.

passages.text: When a nobleman of the Rus on the Volga died, his body lay in a provisional grave for ten days while a shroud was prepared. His property was divided three ways: a third to the family, a third for the funeral, and a third spent on the strong drink of the funeral banquet. On the appointed day a boat was drawn from the water, and the corpse, clad in costly garments, was seated in it upon a richly ornamented armchair, surrounded by his weapons, bread, fruit, and the flesh of sacrificed dogs, horses, cows, and fowls.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 2, from Ibn Fadlan (922); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當伏爾加河畔一位羅斯（Rus）貴族死去時，他的遺體會停放於臨時墓穴中十日，以待縫製裹屍布。他的財產分為三份：三分之一歸家族，三分之一用於葬禮，三分之一用於葬禮宴席上的烈酒。到了約定之日，一艘船從水中拖出，屍體身著華貴衣物，被安坐於一張裝飾華美的扶手椅上，四周環繞著他的武器、麵包、水果，以及獻祭的狗、馬、牛與家禽之肉。

passages.text: One of the dead man's wives had consented to die with him; an old woman called the Angel of Death conducted the rite at the boat's side, and after the sacrifice the wood piled beneath was fired. When ship, bodies, and offerings were consumed, the ashes were gathered and strewn over a cairn, and the ceremony closed with banqueting day and night without interruption.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 死者的一位妻子已同意與他同死；一位被稱為「死亡天使」的老婦在船旁主持儀式，獻祭之後，船下堆積的木柴被點燃。當船、屍體與祭品皆被燒盡，人們收集灰燼，撒於石塚之上，典禮最後以日夜不歇的宴飲作結。

title.en: The Dziady: Feeding the Ancestors of White Russia
title.zh: 吉亞迪：白俄羅斯的祭祖宴

region.en: White Russia / Belarus (symbolic pin at Minsk)
region.zh: 白俄羅斯（象徵性定位於明斯克）

period: Rite recorded 19th c.; pre-Christian in origin (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 2

summary.en: Four times a year the Belarusian Dziady bring the forefathers home: the house is scrubbed, a pail of water and a wisp of straw are set out for the dead to wash, the housefather invites the 'holy Dziadys' to the meal, and any rustle of leaves or drifting moth is greeted as their coming.
summary.zh: 白俄羅斯人一年四度行吉亞迪祭：灑掃家宅，置水與草束供亡魂盥洗，家主恭請『神聖祖靈』赴宴；風動葉響、蛾影飄至，皆視為先人臨門。

sensitivity.note: Living rite descended from ancestor cult; described at ethnographic level only.

passages.text: The autumnal Dziady fall on the eve of St. Demetrius, when the harvest is in. The courtyard is swept, tools stowed, and a beast set aside since spring is killed; the women cook from nine to fifteen dishes and scrub the room, giving special care to the corner behind the oven, the most important place in the house. A plentiful board and a clean house are thought to please the souls of the dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 秋季的「祖靈祭」（Dziady）落在聖德米特里節前夕，此時收穫已入倉。庭院打掃乾淨，工具收妥，春天以來養著的牲畜宰殺一隻；婦女們烹煮九至十五道菜餚，並擦洗房間，特別仔細照料爐灶後方的角落——那是屋中最要緊的地方。豐盛的餐桌與潔淨的屋舍，據信能取悅亡者的靈魂。

passages.text: In the evening the family bathes, sets out a pail of fresh water with a wisp of straw for the Dziadys to wash in, and assembles in Sunday best. The housefather lights a candle in a corner, prays, and solemnly invites the holy Dziadys to the meal. Before eating he sets a portion of every dish on a plate in the window; spoons are laid on the table for the ancestors to help themselves. A rustle of dry leaves, a stirring of air, even the appearance of an emperor-moth is taken for the coming of the forefathers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傍晚，全家人沐浴淨身，備好一桶清水，上頭擱一撮稻草，供祖靈洗滌，然後換上禮拜日的盛裝齊聚。一家之主在角落點燃蠟燭，祈禱，並莊重地邀請神聖的祖靈入席。進食之前，他從每道菜中取一份置於窗邊的盤中；桌上擺好湯匙，讓祖先自行取用。乾葉的沙沙聲、空氣的微動，甚至天蠶蛾的出現，都被視為先人來臨的徵兆。

passages.text: At the spring Dziady, called radunica, the family carries food to the churchyard on the Tuesday of Easter week: the women chant dirges, the men roll priest-blessed eggs, a cloth is spread on the grave, and the circle sits about it eating and talking of the dead, leaving the remains to beggars or the grave itself. The summer Dziady, on the Saturday before Whitsunday, sweep the graves with birch twigs — 'giving the Dziadys a steam-bath'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 春季的祖靈祭稱為「拉杜尼察」（radunica），家人在復活節週的星期二帶著食物前往墓園：婦女吟唱輓歌，男子滾動經神父祝聖的彩蛋，墳上鋪開布巾，眾人圍坐其旁，一面進食一面談論亡者，剩下的食物留給乞丐或歸於墳墓本身。夏季的祖靈祭在聖靈降臨節前的星期六舉行，以樺樹枝清掃墳墓——「給祖靈蒸個澡」。

title.en: The Stopan's Feast: A Bulgarian Ancestor Guards the House
title.zh: 斯托潘之宴：保加利亞家宅祖靈

region.en: Bulgaria (symbolic pin at Sofia)
region.zh: 保加利亞（象徵性定位於索菲亞）

period: Rite recorded 19th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 2

summary.en: In Bulgarian belief a Stopan — a valiant dead ancestor — guards the family home; at his yearly feast a black hen's blood is poured into the hearth hollow, cakes are cut and set in three corners of the loft with wine, and the family prays the Stopan for flocks, meadows, and vineyards.
summary.zh: 保加利亞人信家中斯托潘乃勇武先祖之靈；歲宴宰黑雞、血灑爐膛，切餅置酒於閣樓三角，闔家祈其佑羊群、草場與葡萄園。

sensitivity.note: Living ancestral rite described at ethnographic level.

passages.text: The Bulgarian Stopan is a deceased ancestor, distinguished for valour in his lifetime, who guards the house of the family: he secures health and long life, makes the sheep multiply, promotes harvests, and fills vineyards and orchards. His only price is honour and sufficient food; if the family neglects him, hail may ruin the fields and whole households come to ruin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 保加利亞的「斯托潘」（Stopan）是一位亡故的祖先，生前以英勇著稱，死後守護家族的家宅：他保祐家人健康長壽，使羊群繁衍，促進收成，並使葡萄園與果園豐盈。他唯一索取的代價是敬奉與充足的食物；若家人怠慢了他，冰雹可能毀壞田疇，整個家戶也將走向衰敗。

passages.text: At his feast the house is scrubbed, candles are lit by the hearth and door, and the oldest woman kills a black hen so that the blood flows into the hollow of the hearth, which is then smeared with clay. The head of the family pours half a cup of wine into the fire, cuts a cake into four parts while leaping about the room, and sets the gifts — buttered cake, the hen's left leg, three cups of wine — in three corners of the loft, praying the Stopan to guard the flocks, the meadows, and the vineyards.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在他的節慶上，屋舍刷洗潔淨，爐邊與門旁點燃蠟燭，最年長的婦人宰殺一隻黑母雞，讓雞血流入爐灶的凹處，再以黏土塗抹。一家之主將半杯酒倒入火中，一邊在屋內跳躍，一邊把糕餅切成四份，並將供品——塗了奶油的糕餅、母雞的左腿、三杯酒——分置於閣樓的三個角落，祈求斯托潘守護羊群、草場與葡萄園。

title.en: Dedushka Domovoy: The House-Lord Behind the Oven
title.zh: 多莫沃伊祖父：爐後家主

region.en: Russia (symbolic pin at a northern village)
region.zh: 俄羅斯（象徵性定位於北方村落）

period: Belief recorded 19th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 3

summary.en: Every Russian house has its Domovoy, a grizzled ancestral 'Grandfather' hairy as a beast, who lives behind the oven, tends the herds, weeps at night when death or calamity is coming — and must be carried to a new home in a pan of hot cinders when the family moves.
summary.zh: 俄家宅皆有其多莫沃伊：毛髮灰白之『祖父』居於爐後，照看牛馬；家有大故，夜半嗚咽預警；遷居時以炭火之盤恭迎其隨行。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief; the Domovoy is a beloved figure of Russian tales without restriction.

passages.text: Dedushka Domovoy, the House-Lord, is an old man with a grizzled bushy head, flashing eyes, and a body covered in thick soft hair, wearing a long cloak with a light red belt. He takes the shape of the master of the house, living or dead — or of a cat, dog, or bear whose coat matches the master's hair — and lives behind the oven, under the threshold, or in the stable, doing the master's work at night and guarding the herds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 3; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「家宅之主」多莫沃伊（Domovoy），人稱「老爺爺」，是一位滿頭灰白濃髮、目光炯炯的老人，身上覆著濃密柔軟的毛髮，披著一件繫有淡紅色腰帶的長斗篷。他會化為家主的模樣——無論家主在世或已故——或化為毛色與家主髮色相合的貓、狗或熊，住在爐灶後方、門檻之下或馬廄之中，夜裡替家主操持家務，並守護牲畜。

passages.text: The Domovoy shares the joy and sorrow of his home: if an inmate dies he howls at night, and bitter sobbing foretells the master's own death or a coming fire or plague. Angered by cursing or neglect, he may quit the house and let the cattle sicken and the family die. His favour is courted with the leftovers of supper, and an angry Domovoy is reconciled with the blood of a cock killed at midnight, or with bread and salt wrapped in white cloth while the household bows to the four quarters.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 3; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 家神與其家宅同享歡樂與悲傷：若家中有人死去，他會在夜裡嚎叫，而悲切的啜泣則預示著主人自身的死亡，或即將到來的火災、瘟疫。若因詛咒或疏於照料而動怒，他可能離家而去，任憑牲畜染病、家人死去。人們以晚餐的殘羹剩飯討好他；若家神發怒，則以午夜宰殺的公雞之血，或以白布包裹的麵包與鹽，同時閤家向四方鞠躬，來與他和解。

passages.text: When a family moves to a new house they never forget to take the Domovoy with them. An old woman heats the stove in the old house, puts the cinders in a clean pan covered with a napkin, and at the open window invites the spirit to come; at the gate of the new home the master and mistress wait with bread and salt, bowing low and asking him to enter. The coals are emptied into the new oven and the pan buried beneath the front corner of the room.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 3; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一家人遷入新居時，從不忘記把家神一同帶走。老婦人在舊宅中燒熱爐子，將餘燼放入覆著餐巾的乾淨平底鍋裡，在敞開的窗前邀請神靈前來；在新宅的大門口，男女主人帶著麵包與鹽等候，深深鞠躬，請他入內。煤燼被倒進新爐中，平底鍋則埋於房間前角的底下。

title.en: The Skritek: Hatching the Household Goblin
title.zh: 斯克里特克：孵出的小妖

region.en: Bohemia (symbolic pin at Prague)
region.zh: 波希米亞（象徵性定位於布拉格）

period: Belief recorded 19th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 3

summary.en: The Czech Skritek — a crowned wooden figure kept on the chiffonier — guards the house and brings grain and riches, but can also be hatched from an odd egg carried under the arm, and can be hired for a terrible price: one's own self, wife, and children, pledged in one's own blood.
summary.zh: 捷克斯克里特克——冠冕木像置於櫃上——守家賜穀致富；亦可由腋下孵化怪蛋而生；若欲其效力，須以己血簽契，獻上己身、妻、子。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief.

passages.text: The Czech Skritek, a hobgoblin like a small boy, lives behind the oven or in the stable, favours the household, weaves on the loom, sweeps the floor, and tends the flocks. He is represented by a wooden statue with crossed arms and a crown, set in the corner behind the table to guard the house in the family's absence. He may be bred from an egg of peculiar shape carried for a time beneath the armpit; in Poland his bird-form, a drenched chicken trailing wings and tail, flies by night scattering sparks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 3; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 捷克的斯克裡泰克（Skritek）是一種形似小男孩的家宅精怪，住在爐灶後方或馬廄裡，眷顧家宅，在織布機上織布、掃地、照料畜群。人們以一座雙臂交叉、頭戴王冠的木雕像來代表他，置於桌後的角落，以便在家人外出時守護家宅。他也可能由一枚形狀奇特的蛋孵育而來——此蛋須在腋下夾帶一段時日；在波蘭，他的鳥形是一隻濕淋淋、拖著翅膀與尾巴的雞，夜間飛翔，散落火星。

passages.text: He brings the householder grain and riches — when he carries money he flies down the chimney like a fiery broom — but his help has a price: one must promise him one's own self, wife, and children, signing the agreement in one's own blood. Millet gruel must always be left for him on the window-sill; three bits of every dish are his at the Christmas dinner, and if they are forgotten he storms and worries the household and wastes the flocks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 3; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他為戶主帶來穀物與財富——當他搬運錢財時，會像一把燃燒的掃帚般從煙囪飛下——但他的幫助是有代價的：人必須承諾將自己、妻子與兒女奉獻給他，並以自己的血簽下契約。窗台上必須時常為他留著小米粥；聖誕晚餐上每道菜的三小塊都歸他所有，若被遺忘，他便大發雷霆，擾亂家宅，糟蹋畜群。

title.en: The Sudice: Three Destinies at the Cradle
title.zh: 蘇迪采：搖籃邊的三命運女神

region.en: Bohemia and South Slavic lands (symbolic pin at Prague)
region.zh: 波希米亞與南斯拉夫（象徵性定位於布拉格）

period: Belief recorded 19th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 4

summary.en: On the night after a birth the Sudice come: white-robed, candle-bearing genii of fate who spin, measure, and cut the thread of the new-born's life; the last and oldest speaks decisively, and only gifts of bread, salt, and candles left on the table can soften the verdict.
summary.zh: 嬰兒誕生之夜，蘇迪采降臨：白衣持燭之命運精靈，紡線、量線、斷線以定一生；最末者最老，一言定讞；桌上麵包、鹽與燭乃軟化判語之禮。

sensitivity.note: Fate-spirits parallel the Greek Moirai and Norse Norns; interpretive tagging.

passages.text: The genii of fate — Sudice among the Czechs, Rodjenice among the Croats and Slovenes, Orisnici among the Bulgarians, Udelnicy in northern Russia — come to the bedside of a woman in childbed after casting her into deep sleep, set the new-born on the table, and decide its fate: how long it will live, whether it will be rich or poor, and what manner of death it will die. Usually they are three, the third and oldest the most powerful; what the last says is decisive and will be fulfilled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 4; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 命運的精靈——捷克人稱蘇迪采（Sudice），克羅埃西亞人與斯洛維尼亞人稱羅德耶尼采（Rodjenice），保加利亞人稱奧里斯尼齊（Orisnici），俄羅斯北部稱烏德爾尼齊（Udelnicy）——在使產婦陷入沉睡之後，來到她的床邊，將新生兒置於桌上，決定其命運：能活多久、將富或將貧，以及將以何種方式死去。她們通常有三位，第三位亦即最年長者最有權力；最後一位所說的話具有決定性，且必將應驗。

passages.text: They appear as beautiful lasses or kindly old women, white-robed, veiled, bearing burning candles. One spins, the second measures, and the third cuts off the thread whose length is the span of life. Their favour can be won: on the night after the birth the Slovenes and Croats set wax candles, wine, bread, and salt on the lying-in room's table; the Bulgarians prepare a supper for the Orisnici; in Bohemia a table was spread with white cloth, bread, salt, butter, cheese, and beer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 4; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她們以美麗的少女或慈祥老婦的形象出現，身著白袍，蒙著面紗，手持燃燒的蠟燭。一人紡線，第二人丈量，第三人則剪斷那長度即為壽數的線。她們的恩寵是可以贏得的：在生產後的夜裡，斯洛維尼亞人與克羅埃西亞人在產房的桌上擺放蠟燭、酒、麵包與鹽；保加利亞人為奧里斯尼齊備好一頓晚餐；在波希米亞，則鋪上白布，擺放麵包、鹽、奶油、乳酪與啤酒。

title.en: Dolya and Nedolya: The Woman Who Is One's Fate
title.zh: 多利亞與內多利亞：化身命運的女子

region.en: Russia (symbolic pin at Novgorod)
region.zh: 俄羅斯（象徵性定位於諾夫哥羅德）

period: Belief recorded 19th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 4

summary.en: Russian folk belief personifies each person's lot as Dolya, a poorly-dressed woman who lives behind the oven: a good Dolya labours invisibly for her man all his days, while an evil Nedolya sleeps, dresses, and laughs — and no horse can carry a man away from her.
summary.zh: 俄俗以『多利亞』喻人之一生命定：衣衫襤褸之婦居於爐後；善者日夜為其人勞作，惡者（內多利亞）唯睡、妝、嬉戲——諺云：駿馬亦載不走你的命。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief.

passages.text: Russian tradition makes the fate given a man at his birth a supernatural woman, Dolya, poorly dressed and able to change her shape, living behind the oven. A good Dolya protects her favourite day and night from birth to death: she waters his fields with dew, drives fish into his nets and swarms of bees into his hives, guards his flocks against wild beasts, finds buyers for his goods, and picks the full ears from other men's sheaves for him. Without her help no one succeeds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 4; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 俄羅斯傳統將人出生時所獲得的命運，設想為一位超自然的女子——多利亞（Dolya）。她衣衫襤褸，能變換形貌，住在爐灶後方。善良的多利亞從人出生到死亡，日夜守護她所眷顧之人：以露水澆灌他的田地，把魚趕入他的網中，把成群的蜜蜂趕入他的蜂箱，守護他的羊群免受野獸侵害，為他的貨物尋得買主，並從他人的禾束中為他摘下飽滿的麥穗。若無她的幫助，無人能夠成功。

passages.text: Woe to the man who draws an evil Dolya — Nedolya, or Licho. She does nothing but sleep, dress herself, and make merry, and all his labour is in vain; her power has no limits, and the proverb says 'not even your horse will get you away from your Dolya': selling her, losing her in the woods, drowning her in the sea — all fail. The Serbian counterpart, Sreca, is a beautiful girl spinning a golden thread for the man assigned to her; as Nesreca she is an old woman with bloodshot eyes, forever asleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 4; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 抽到邪惡多利亞——即涅多利亞（Nedolya），或稱利霍（Licho）——的人有禍了。她除了睡覺、打扮自己、尋歡作樂之外什麼也不做，而他的一切勞苦皆歸徒然；她的力量無邊無際，諺語說：「連你的馬也載你逃不開你的多利亞」：將她賣掉、把她遺失在森林裡、把她溺於海中——全都徒勞無功。塞爾維亞的對應者斯雷恰（Sreca），是一位美麗的少女，為分配給她的那名男子紡織金線；而作為涅斯雷恰（Nesreca），她則是個雙眼充血、永遠沉睡的老婦。

title.en: The Mavky Cry: 'Mother Bore Me and Left Me Unbaptized'
title.zh: 瑪芙卡哭聲：『母生我而不洗禮』

region.en: Ukraine (symbolic pin at Kyiv)
region.zh: 烏克蘭（象徵性定位於基輔）

period: Belief recorded 19th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 5

summary.en: Navky — souls of children unbaptized or drowned — rock on moonlit branches crying for baptism; whoever hears their wail and speaks the baptismal formula frees them, but after seven years unpitied they become dangerous water-nymphs.
summary.zh: 納芙基——未受洗或溺斃孩童之魂——月夜攀枝搖盪，哭求洗禮；聞其哀而誦洗禮經文者釋其靈；七年無人憐惜，遂化為索命水仙。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief entangling pagan water-spirits with Christian rite; tagged interpretively.

passages.text: The Little Russian Mavky is the soul of a child drowned by its mother or left unbaptized: a small baby, or a beautiful girl with curling hair, half-naked or in a white shirt. On moonlit nights she rocks on the branches of trees, imitating the crying of infants, laughing and clapping her hands to draw the young after her; whoever follows will be bewitched by her beauty, tickled to death, and drawn into deep water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 5; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 小俄羅斯的瑪芙基（Mavky）是被母親溺死或未受洗禮便被遺棄的孩童之魂：或為小小的嬰兒，或為一頭鬈髮的美麗少女，半裸著身子，或穿著白襯衫。在月明之夜，她們在樹枝上搖盪，模仿嬰兒的啼哭，又笑又拍手，以引誘年輕人跟隨其後；凡跟隨者，都會被她的美貌所蠱惑，被搔癢至死，並被拖入深水之中。

passages.text: In summer they swim in rivers beating the water merrily; in the fairy-week they run the fields and meadows wailing, 'Mother has borne me and left me unbaptized.' Whoever hears the cry and answers, 'I baptize thee in the name of God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit,' sets the soul free. But if for seven years no one pities them, they are turned into water-nymphs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 5; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 夏日裡，她們在河中游泳，歡快地拍打水面；在精靈週期間，她們奔馳於田野與草地，哀號著：「母親生了我，卻未為我施洗便遺棄了我。」凡聽見這哭聲並回答：「我以聖父、聖子、聖靈之名為你施洗」的人，便能令這靈魂獲得解脫。但若七年之內無人憐憫她們，她們便會化為水仙女。

title.en: Rusalka Week: The Water-Nymphs Walk the Rye
title.zh: 羅薩爾卡週：水仙行於麥浪

region.en: Russia (symbolic pin on the Dnieper banks)
region.zh: 俄羅斯（象徵性定位於第聶伯河岸）

period: Belief recorded 19th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 5

summary.en: Rusalky — drowned girls and unbaptized souls — rise at Whitsuntide to run the green corn, dance in moonlit fairy-rings, and tickle wanderers to death; for their week the villages bring no work into the fields and lay bread, cheese, and butter on the banks for them.
summary.zh: 羅薩爾卡——溺亡之女與未洗之魂——五旬節週起身，奔跑青麥、月下環舞、搔癢旅人致死；村人停田間之工，於河岸供麵包乳酪。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief; Rusalka imagery is a classic of Slavic art and music.

passages.text: The Rusalky are girls who died unnaturally or unbaptized children, appearing as maidens seven years old or in the full bloom of youth, dressed in green leaves or in a white shirt without a belt. They live in woods, meadows, and waters; when the corn begins to ripen they hide in it ready to punish whoever plucks the ears wantonly, and at Whitsuntide they rock among the high-standing grain, making it wave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 5; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 魯薩爾基（Rusalky）是非自然死亡的女子的魂魄，或是未受洗禮的孩童，以七歲的少女或正值青春年華的少女之姿出現，身著綠葉，或穿著不繫腰帶的白襯衫。她們住在森林、草地與水域之中；當穀物開始成熟時，她們便藏身其中，隨時準備懲罰那些肆意採摘麥穗的人；而在聖靈降臨節期間，她們在高立的穀物間搖盪，使穀物隨之起伏。

passages.text: On clear summer nights they rise from the streams to bathe and splash, sit on the mill-wheel crying 'Kuku', and dance on the banks, leaving fairy-rings of particularly deep green grass. They entangle fishermen's nets, break dikes to flood the fields, and lure wanderers to be tickled to death or drawn into the deep. During their week at Whitsuntide no one bathes, works the fields, or claps hands, and lads and lasses lay bread, cheese, and butter on the banks for them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 5; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在晴朗的夏夜，她們從溪流中升起，沐浴戲水，坐在磨坊水車上哭喊著「庫庫」（Kuku），並在岸邊跳舞，留下草色格外深綠的精靈環。她們纏繞漁夫的漁網，破壞堤壩以淹沒田地，引誘迷途者，將其搔癢至死或拖入深處。在她們於聖靈降臨節的那一週裡，無人沐浴、無人下田耕作、無人拍手，而少男少女們則在岸邊為她們擺上麵包、乳酪與奶油。

title.en: The Vily: Fairies Who Left When the Whips Were Cracked
title.zh: 維拉精靈：鞭聲響處，仙子離去

region.en: South Slavic mountains (symbolic pin in the Rhodopes)
region.zh: 南斯拉夫山地（象徵性定位於羅多彼山脈）

period: Belief recorded 19th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 6

summary.en: In the golden age the Vily helped mortals plough, sow, and bury their dead; when shepherds took to whips and cursing and the first guns were heard, the fairies left forever. Their life hangs in their golden hair — lose one hair and a Vila dies — and whoever steals her wings binds her to earth until she regains them.
summary.zh: 黃金時代維拉助人耕種葬亡；牧者一旦鞭撻咒詛、槍聲初響，仙子遂去不返。其命懸金髮——落一髮即亡；竊其羽者可繫之於世，羽還則逝。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief; Vila lore is central to South Slavic epic.

passages.text: In the happy days when fields bore wheat without man's labour, the Vily helped mortals garner harvests, mow grass, feed cattle, and build houses; they taught men to plough, to sow, to drain meadows, even to bury the dead. But when men departed from their old virtues — when shepherds threw away flutes and songs, took up whips, and cursed; when the first guns were heard and nations made war — the Vily left the country for foreign lands. Now only a few ever see them dancing in the fields or sitting on a bare rock, weeping and singing melancholy songs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 6; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在那些幸福的日子裡，田野不需人力耕作便長出小麥，維莉（Vily）幫助凡人收穫莊稼、割草、餵養牲畜、建造房屋；她們教人犁地、播種、疏乾草甸，甚至教人埋葬死者。但當人們背離了昔日的美德——當牧人丟棄笛子與歌聲，拿起鞭子，口出咒罵；當第一批槍聲響起，列國交戰——維莉便離開這片土地，前往異邦。如今只有極少數人曾見她們在田野中起舞，或坐在光禿的岩石上，哭泣著唱起憂傷的歌。

passages.text: The Vily are eternally young women, pale-cheeked, dressed in white, with long golden hair in which their life and strength reside: lose a single hair and she will die. Their eyes flash like lightning; their voices, once heard, are never forgotten. They ride horses and stags, live in clouds, on forest mountains, and in waters, and transform themselves into wolves, snakes, falcons, or swans. A man who robs a fairy of her pinions can bind her to himself; the moment she regains her wings she vanishes forever — though she still watches in secret over her children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 6; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 維莉是永遠年輕的女子，面頰蒼白，身著白衣，留著長長的金髮，她們的生命與力量就寄於髮中：失去一根頭髮，她便會死去。她們的雙眼如閃電般閃爍；她們的聲音一旦聽過，便永難忘懷。她們騎馬、騎鹿，住在雲中、林間山上與水中，並能化身為狼、蛇、隼或天鵝。奪走仙女羽翼的男子能將她束縛於己身；而她一旦重獲翅膀，便永遠消失——儘管她仍暗中看顧自己的孩子。

title.en: The Leshy: Lord of the Forest and His Echoes
title.zh: 雷希：林主與其回聲

region.en: Russian forest belt (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俄羅斯森林帶（象徵性定位）

period: Belief recorded 19th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 7

summary.en: The Leshy is an old man of the woods as tall as the trees he haunts, whose rustling walk and mocking echoes mislead travellers; his favourite is the bear, with whom he feasts, and he can be escaped only by putting the right shoe on the left foot and looking between one's legs.
summary.zh: 雷希乃林中老者，身高隨所棲之樹；行走時林木沙沙，慣以回聲戲弄迷途者；其寵為熊，與之宴樂；脫身之術乃右鞋穿左足、俯身跨腿回望。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief.

passages.text: The Russian Leshy shows himself as an old man with long hair and beard, flashing green eyes, a body covered with hair, and the stature of the trees he inhabits — tree-high in the forest, grass-high in the field. He takes the shapes of bears, wolves, and hares, or appears to travellers as an ordinary person, even as their own friend. One Leshy rules each wood; a silvan czar is lord where several dwell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 7; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 俄羅斯的列希（Leshy）現身為一位長髮長鬚的老人，雙眼閃著綠光，身上覆滿毛髮，身量與他所棲居的樹木相當——在林中如樹高，在田野中如草高。他化為熊、狼與兔的形貌，或以尋常人的模樣出現在旅人面前，甚至化作他們自己的朋友。每一片樹林由一位列希掌管；若有多位同住，則以一位林中之王為首。

passages.text: He guards the forest, forbidding whistling and shouting, frightening thieves with cries, and feasting with his favourite, the bear. When he walks, the trees rustle; he rocks on boughs, whistles, laughs, claps, cracks his whip, and neighs like a horse, lows like a cow, barks like a dog, mews like a cat — the echo is his work, and no man has ever found his footprints in sand or snow, for a strong wind always blows around him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 7; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他守護森林，禁止吹口哨與呼喊，以叫聲驚嚇盜賊，並與他的寵兒——熊——一同宴飲。他行走時，樹木沙沙作響；他在枝頭搖晃、吹哨、大笑、拍手、甩響鞭子，又像馬一樣嘶鳴，像牛一樣哞叫，像狗一樣吠叫，像貓一樣喵叫——回聲便是他的作為，而從無人在沙上或雪中發現過他的足跡，因為他周圍總有強風吹拂。

passages.text: Of a mocking temper, he removes boundary-stones and signposts, takes the shape of a wanderer's friend to lure him into thickets and morasses, and substitutes his own ugly, voracious children for human infants. Salted bread wrapped in linen laid in the woods is his due offering; huntsmen leave him the first game. To escape his bewitchment one turns one's garments inside out, puts the right shoe on the left foot, or bends down to look between one's own legs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 7; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他性情愛捉弄人，會移走界石與路標，化為旅人朋友的模樣引他進入灌木叢與沼澤，並以自己的醜陋貪食的孩子換走人類的嬰兒。以亞麻布包著的鹹麵包放在林中，便是獻給他的應有供品；獵人則把第一件獵物留給他。要逃脫他的蠱惑，可將衣物裡外翻穿，把右腳的鞋穿在左腳上，或彎下腰從自己兩腿之間望去。

title.en: The Wild Women of the Bohemian Woods
title.zh: 波希米亞林中的野婦

region.en: Bohemia / Lusatia (symbolic pin at Prague)
region.zh: 波希米亞／勞西茨（象徵性定位於布拉格）

period: Belief recorded 19th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 7

summary.en: The Divozenky — large-headed, long-haired Wild Women — lived in burrows under the Bohemian woods, baking bread from gleaned ears and weaving hemp; they kept the houses of those who left them food, raised never-failing crops, and vanished if anyone called them 'Wild Women'.
summary.zh: 迪沃真卡——方顱長髮之野婦——穴居波希米亞林下，拾穗磨石、烘麵織麻；凡供食者彼為之灑掃理家，賜永不枯竭之收成；一經喚作『野婦』，即刻消失。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief.

passages.text: In Bohemian and Lusatian belief the Wild Women (Divozenky, Dziwje Zony) were good-looking beings with large square heads, long ruddy or black hair, hairy bodies, and long fingers, living in underground burrows furnished like houses. They gleaned ears in the fields, ground grain between stones, and baked bread whose smell filled the whole wood; they combed and wove hemp into frocks and shirts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 7; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在波希米亞與盧薩蒂亞的信仰中，野女人（Divozenky、Dziwje Zony）是容貌姣好的存在，頭大而方，頭髮長而呈紅褐色或黑色，身上覆毛，手指細長，居住於布置如屋舍的地下洞穴中。她們在田間拾穗，用石磨磨穀，烤出的麵包香氣瀰漫整片樹林；她們梳理並編織大麻，做成連衣裙與襯衫。

passages.text: They knew the secret forces of nature and anointed themselves with unguents to become light and invisible; their wild frolicking was blamed for storms. They entered villages to borrow kneading-troughs, and repaid kindness richly: they kept houses in order, swept rooms and courtyards, cared for children, reaped corn, and gave the women crops that never diminished. But they vanished at once if anyone called them 'Wild Women', or left a fireside uncleared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 7; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她們知曉自然界的神秘力量，並以油膏塗抹自身，使自己變得輕盈而隱形；人們將暴風雨歸咎於她們狂野的嬉鬧。她們會進入村莊借用揉麵槽，並豐厚地回報恩情：她們替人整理家務、打掃房間與庭院、照料孩童、收割穀物，還賜予婦女永不減少的作物。但若有人稱她們為「野女人」，或有人未將爐火邊收拾乾淨，她們便會立刻消失。

title.en: Polednica: The Midday Spirit with the Sickle
title.zh: 波萊德尼察：持鐮的正午精靈

region.en: Bohemia / Poland (symbolic pin at Wroclaw)
region.zh: 波希米亞／波蘭（象徵性定位於弗羅茨瓦夫）

period: Belief recorded 19th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 8

summary.en: At the burning noon of harvest a tall white-robed woman with a sickle walks the fields: Polednica sets riddles to the reapers, twists the necks of those found working at midday, and carries off children left alone in the standing corn.
summary.zh: 收割烈日當空，白衣高挑持鐮之婦行於田間：波萊德尼察向割麥人出謎，扭折正午勞作者之頸，奪走獨留麥浪之孩童。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief; parallels the noon-demon of many traditions.

passages.text: In Bohemian belief the Poludnica is an airy white lady or an old woman who wanders the fields at noon, floating on violent gusts; whomsoever she touches will die a sudden death. Sometimes she is slight as a girl of twelve, whip in hand, striking anyone who crosses her path. She ambushes women lately become mothers who go out at midday, and carries off children left alone in the fields at harvest-time — hence mothers hush crying children with the threat that she is coming.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 8; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在波希米亞的信仰中，波盧德尼察是一位輕盈縹緲的白衣女子，或是一名老婦，於正午時分在田野間遊蕩，乘著猛烈的狂風飄浮；凡被她觸碰者，皆會猝然死去。有時她身形纖細如十二歲的少女，手持鞭子，抽打任何與她狹路相逢之人。她埋伏襲擊那些剛為人母、於正午外出之婦女，並擄走收穫時節被獨留於田野的孩童——因此母親們會以「她來了」的威脅來哄止啼哭的孩子。

passages.text: In Polish belief she is a tall woman in a white robe to her feet, carrying a sharp sickle; she chases the workers of the fields and woods through summer, propounding hard questions to them and sending grievous maladies on those who cannot answer. Among the Lusatian Serbs whoever meets her in the fields at noon must talk with her for a full hour on a single subject; those who fail forfeit their heads. She guards the corn from thieves and punishes children who tread upon the ears.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 8; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在波蘭的信仰中，她是一名身著及地白袍的高大女子，手持鋒利的鐮刀；整個夏季，她追逐田野與林間的工作者，向他們提出艱難的問題，並使那些無法作答者染上痛苦的疾病。在盧薩蒂亞塞爾維亞人之中，凡於正午在田野遇見她者，必須就單一話題與她交談整整一個時辰；未能做到者將喪失首級。她守護穀物以防盜賊，並懲罰踩踏麥穗的孩童。

title.en: Vodyanoy: The Water-Grandfather and His Hundred Daughters
title.zh: 沃吉亞諾伊：水祖父與百女

region.en: Russian rivers (symbolic pin on the Volga)
region.zh: 俄羅斯河川（象徵性定位於伏爾加河）

period: Belief recorded 19th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 9

summary.en: Vodyanoy, the bald water-grandfather with a reed crown and a coat that drips from the left side, keeps herds of horses and cattle in his underwater courtyards; when a river overflows its banks he is celebrating his wedding — drunk, and tearing down dikes and mills.
summary.zh: 沃吉亞諾伊——禿頂、戴蘆葦冠、左襟滴水之水祖父——於水底石院牧養馬牛豬群；江河氾濫之時，正是其婚宴酩酊、毀堤拆磨之日。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief; includes traditional foundation sacrifice motif described ethnographically.

passages.text: The Vodyanik, or Grandfather Vodyanoy, is a bald old man with fat belly, puffy cheeks, a high cap of reeds, and a belt of rushes; in the village he passes as a man, betrayed only by water oozing from the left side of his coat. He lives in the deep water near mills, where he keeps stone courtyards and herds of horses, cattle, sheep, and pigs driven out to graze at night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 9; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 沃佳尼克，或稱水爺爺沃佳諾伊，是一名禿頂的老人，大腹便便、雙頰浮腫，頭戴蘆葦編成的高帽，腰繫燈心草編成的腰帶；在村中他喬裝為常人，唯有從其外套左側滲出的水珠會洩露他的身分。他住在磨坊附近的深水之中，在那裡擁有石砌的庭院，以及成群的馬、牛、羊與豬，這些牲畜於夜間被趕出放牧。

passages.text: Master of the waters, terrible in his element and weak ashore, he drives fish into the nets of those he favours and wrecks the boats of those he does not; he tears spikes from mill-wheels and floods the mill, which is why a miller must bury a living being in the mill's foundations to make his dam endure. He has one hundred and eleven beautiful daughters who torment the drowned; when the waters rise over their banks he is celebrating his wedding, drunk, tearing down dikes and bridges.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 9; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 作為水域之主，他在自己的領域中令人生畏，上了岸卻虛弱無力；他將魚群趕入他所眷顧者的網中，並使他不眷顧者的船隻失事；他從磨輪上扯下輪齒，並淹沒磨坊，因此磨坊主必須將活物埋入磨坊的地基之中，方能使其水壩得以長存。他有一百一十一位美麗的女兒，她們折磨溺水者；當河水漫過堤岸，便是他在慶祝自己的婚禮，醉醺醺地拆毀堤壩與橋樑。

passages.text: In spring he wakes hungry and troublesome, breaking the ice and howling; a horse smeared with honey is sacrificed to him, and for three days he awaits the gift, betraying his greed by heaving waters and dismal howls. Fishermen pour butter into the water; millers kill a black, well-fed sow in his honour.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 9; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 春天時他醒來，飢餓而惹是生非，破開冰層並嚎叫；人們獻上一匹塗滿蜂蜜的馬作為祭品，而他會等候這份獻禮三日，以其翻騰的水浪與陰沉的嚎叫顯露他的貪婪。漁夫們將奶油倒入水中；磨坊主則為向他致敬而宰殺一頭肥壯的黑母豬。

title.en: Every Man a Star: The Falling Light of Death
title.zh: 人各有星：隕落之光即是死

region.en: Slavic lands (symbolic pin at Kiev)
region.zh: 斯拉夫諸地（象徵性定位於基輔）

period: Belief recorded 19th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 10

summary.en: Slavic folk astronomy binds every human life to a star: there are as many stars as men, each person receives one at birth, and when the star falls the man dies and his soul floats up among the clouds.
summary.zh: 斯拉夫星象俗信：天上有幾星，人間有幾人；人誕生則得一星，星落則人亡，魂魄化光升於雲間。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief.

passages.text: Arabian travellers report that the pagan Slavs adored the sun, and an old Bohemian homilist records that they worshipped not only sun, moon, and stars, but water, fire, mountains, and trees. The moon was held to be the abode of the souls of the departed, later of sinful souls transported there by way of punishment, and popular belief gave her power over the growth of plants and beasts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 10; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿拉伯旅行者記載，異教的斯拉夫人崇拜太陽；一位波希米亞的老佈道者則記述，他們不僅崇拜日、月與星辰，也崇拜水、火、山與樹木。人們認為月亮是亡者靈魂的居所，後來又認為那是罪人之靈魂被送往受罰之處；民間信仰賦予月亮掌管植物與牲畜生長的力量。

passages.text: All Slavs maintain a close relationship between stars and men: there are as many men on earth as stars in the sky. At his birth each man receives a star of his own; and when his end draws near, that star falls to earth, the man dies, and his soul floats upward to the clouds. The belief links the hearth-side deathbed to the whole machinery of heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 10; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 所有斯拉夫人都相信星辰與人之間有密切的關聯：地上有多少人，天上就有多少星。每個人出生時都得到屬於自己的一顆星；當他的死期臨近，那顆星便墜落地面，人便死去，他的靈魂則向上飄往雲端。這一信仰將爐邊的臨終之榻與整個天界的運行聯繫在一起。

title.en: The Badnjak: Bringing the Christmas Log Home
title.zh: 巴德尼亞克：迎聖誕原木入宅

region.en: Serbia and the South Slavs (symbolic pin at Belgrade)
region.zh: 塞爾維亞與南斯拉夫（象徵性定位於貝爾格勒）

period: Rite recorded 19th c.; pre-Christian in origin (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part IV ch. 2
