summary.en: Before sunrise on Christmas Eve the Serbian housefather fetches the badnjak log, clucking like a hen while the children cheep like chicks; the log is greeted, buttered with honey and wine, set on the new fire, and grain is scattered like a sowing for the children to peck — the hearth-genius welcomed home for the new year.
summary.zh: 聖誕前夕日出之前，塞爾維亞家主往林取聖誕原木，口作母雞聲、孩童學雛鳥；原木受迎、抹蜜澆酒，置於新火之上，撒穀如播種讓孩童啄拾——爐靈迎歸，歲歲更新。

sensitivity.note: Living rite; described at ethnographic level.

passages.text: Before sunrise on Christmas Eve the head of a Serbian household goes to the forest for the badnjak, a log of oak, beech, or ash. Doffing his cap he carries it into the room, clucking like a hen while the children stand in a row behind him, cheeping like chickens. With candles burning on either side of the door he walks the log into every corner, the household throwing corn upon him; then he lays the badnjak and a ploughshare by the fireside with honey, butter, and wine, and addresses the log: 'Welcome! Come and eat your supper!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part IV ch. 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 聖誕夜日出之前，塞爾維亞家庭的家長前往森林取回「巴德尼亞克」，即一段橡木、山毛櫸或白蠟木的圓木。他脫帽將它抱進屋內，一面像母雞般咯咯叫，孩子們則排成一列跟在他身後，像小雞般嘰嘰叫。門的兩側點著蠟燭，他抱著圓木走遍每個角落，家人則向他拋撒穀物；隨後他將巴德尼亞克與一具犁頭放在爐邊，並備上蜂蜜、奶油與酒，對圓木說道：「歡迎！來吃你的晚餐吧！」

passages.text: When the log burns well the farmer takes a festive bread modelled with animals of dough and a cup of wine to the corn-loft, leaving a portion on its window; then, filling a glove with wheat kernels and a silver coin, he strews the grain over the floor like a sowing, and the children throw themselves upon it picking it up like poultry — whoever finds the coin will have good luck. The hearth-fire, rekindled with the badnjak, renews the year; the log is the special symbol of the genius of the house in his capacity as protector of the hearth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part IV ch. 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當圓木燃燒旺盛時，農人便帶著以麵團捏成動物形狀的節慶麵包與一杯酒前往穀倉，在倉窗上留下一份；接著，他將麥粒與一枚銀幣裝滿一隻手套，像播種一般把穀粒撒在地板上，孩子們便撲上前去，像家禽般撿拾——誰找到那枚銀幣，誰就會有好運。以巴德尼亞克重新燃起的爐火更新了這一年；圓木是家宅守護神靈的特有象徵，因其職司在於守護爐灶。

title.en: Kupalo Night: Jumping the Fire to Read a Marriage
title.zh: 庫帕洛之夜：躍火以卜姻緣

region.en: Russia and the Slavic lands (symbolic pin at Vilnius)
region.zh: 俄羅斯與斯拉夫諸地（象徵性定位於維爾紐斯）

period: Rite recorded 19th c.; pre-Christian in origin (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part IV ch. 4

summary.en: On St. John's Eve the girls blindfold their prettiest companion — the kupaljo — who deals out garlands: fresh flowers mean a happy marriage, withered ones doom, and her touch means a year unwed; at nightfall couples jump the bonfire hand in hand, and a spark that follows them foretells a wedding.
summary.zh: 聖約翰之夜，少女們蒙住最美者之眼——是為『庫帕洛』——由其分發花環：新鮮者婚美，枯萎者不幸，觸之者一年不嫁；入夜情侶手挽手躍過火堆，火星隨後即兆成婚。

sensitivity.note: Living rite; described at ethnographic level.

passages.text: The Kupalo festival, now coinciding with St. John the Baptist's day, was in origin a domestic celebration of marriage and the admission of new members into the family, its erotic customs joined with funereal commemoration of the ancestors who once presided over such rites. On the morning the girls go to the woods and fields to pick flowers for wreaths.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part IV ch. 4; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 庫帕洛節如今與施洗者聖約翰紀念日重合，其起源本是慶祝婚姻、接納新成員進入家庭的家內慶典，其情慾習俗則與對祖先的喪葬追念相結合——這些祖先昔日曾主持此類儀式。當天早晨，少女們前往樹林與田野採花，用以編織花冠。

passages.text: Choosing the prettiest among them they lead her singing into the forest, blindfold and garland her, and dance about her while she, the kupaljo, picks up garland after garland and deals them out: a fresh wreath promises fortunate wedlock, withered flowers unhappiness. When all garlands are given the girls run away, for any maiden the kupaljo touches is fated to remain unwed for the year.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part IV ch. 4; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她們從中選出最美的一位，唱著歌領她進入森林，蒙住她的眼睛並為她戴上花冠，圍著她跳舞；而她——即庫帕洛——則一一拾起花冠分發出去：新鮮的花冠預示美滿的婚姻，枯萎的花朵則預示不幸。所有花冠分發完畢後，少女們便四散奔逃，因為凡被庫帕洛觸及的少女，註定整年都嫁不出去。

passages.text: At twilight a fire is kindled, and the lads and lasses, taking each other's hands, jump over the flame two by two: those who do not loosen hands in jumping will become husband and wife, and the same is predicted by a spark that comes out of the fire after them. Figures of Kupalo and Marena are made and drowned and burned like a Rusalka; in some places Jarilo and Kostroma are buried instead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part IV ch. 4; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 黃昏時分燃起一堆火，少男少女兩兩牽手，成雙成對地跳過火焰：跳躍時不鬆手的人將結為夫妻；從他們身後的火中迸出的火星，也預示著同樣的結果。人們製作庫帕洛與瑪雷娜的偶像，並像對待魯薩爾卡那樣將其溺死、焚燒；有些地方則改為埋葬雅里洛與科斯特羅馬。

title.en: The Rusalye: Dressing the Birch for the Drowned
title.zh: 羅薩利耶：為溺亡者妝點樺樹

region.en: Great Russia (symbolic pin at Vladimir)
region.zh: 大俄羅斯（象徵性定位於弗拉基米爾）

period: Rite recorded 19th c.; pre-Christian in origin (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part IV ch. 3

summary.en: On Semik the villages go singing into the woods, fell a young birch, dress it in woman's robes and ribbons, and carry it home in procession; a straw doll arrayed in holiday garments is finally thrown into the water or burned — a second funeral to content the Rusalky, the unburied dead of the waters.
summary.zh: 謝米克之日，村人歌行入林，伐幼樺，為之著女衣繫彩帶，列隊迎歸；草偶著節日盛裝，終則投入水中或焚之——此乃二次葬禮，以慰水中介埋之羅薩爾卡亡魂。

sensitivity.note: Living rite; described at ethnographic level.

passages.text: In Russia the Rusalye were celebrated at Whitsuntide. On Whitsun Monday a small shed adorned with garlands, flowers, and fragrant grasses was raised in the centre of an oak grove, a straw doll in holiday garments set inside, and people from all quarters brought food and drink, dancing round the shed in merriment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part IV ch. 3; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在俄羅斯，魯薩利耶節於聖靈降臨節期間慶祝。聖靈降臨節星期一，人們在橡樹林中央搭起一座飾有花環、鮮花與香草的小棚屋，裡面放置一個身穿節日盛裝的草紮人偶，四方之人帶來食物與飲料，歡快地繞著棚屋跳舞。

passages.text: On the Thursday before Whitsunday (Semik) the people leave town for the forests singing ancient songs, pick flowers for wreaths, and fell a nice young birch which the lasses dress in woman's robes trimmed with gaudy ribbons. Carrying the tree in procession with festive songs they bring it to a village house, where it stays till Sunday. The doll finally thrown into the water or burned is called a Rusalka, and the ceremony is probably a second funeral meant to secure the favour of the Rusalky — the spirits of those who died violently and were never buried with rites.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part IV ch. 3; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 聖靈降臨節前的星期四（謝米克節），人們唱著古老的歌謠出城前往森林，採花編製花環，並砍下一棵秀美的年輕白樺，少女們為它穿上飾有豔麗緞帶的女子長袍。人們唱著節慶歌曲，列隊抬著這棵樹來到村中一戶人家，它會留在此處直到星期日。最終被投入水中或焚燒的人偶被稱為魯薩爾卡；這一儀式很可能是第二次葬禮，意在博取魯薩爾基的歡心——魯薩爾基是那些橫死而從未按禮儀安葬者的亡靈。

title.en: Mantucalla and the Golden Sheep: The Yutip-Raymi Revels
title.zh: 曼圖卡利亞與金羊:太陽節歡宴

region.en: Mantucalla, royal resort near Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科附近王室別苑曼圖卡利亞(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: At the first month's festival of the Sun the Inca retired with all his lords to Mantucalla to drink and enjoy the taqui called Huallina, a dance with singing performed four times in the day by the Yncas alone, while the mama-cunas, women of the Sun, gave them drink. At this festival were brought out the two female figures Pallasillu and Ynca-uillu, clothed in rich dress and plates of gold, and great figures of sheep, two of gold and two of silver, carried on litters by principal lords - in memory, they say, of the sheep which came forth from the tambo with them.
summary.zh: 歲首太陽節,印加王與眾卿退居曼圖卡利亞,飲宴作樂,行「瓦利納」歌舞,一日四遍,唯印加貴族可舞,太陽貞女(瑪瑪庫納)奉酒。節慶中抬出帕拉西略與印加威略二女神像,遍飾金片;又抬兩尊金羊、兩尊銀羊,由貴族以轎抬行——據說是為紀念當年隨始祖一同走出坦波驛站的羊群。

sensitivity.note: Festival description from Molina's month calendar; the golden sheep commemorate the ancestral llama figures of the founding episode.

passages.text: The Ynca, with all his lords, went to Mantucalla, and there remained to drink and enjoy himself in revelry and taquis. They called this taqui Huallina, and it was a dance with singing which was performed four times in the day. The Yncas alone celebrated this feast; and the mama-cunas, women of the Sun, gave drink to those who performed it; their own wives did not enter the place where the Yncas were, but remained outside in a court. All the vases and utensils from which they ate and drank, and with which they cooked the food, were of gold.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of Hauca (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 印加王率領全體貴族前往曼圖卡拉，在那裡逗留，飲酒作樂，盡情歡宴歌舞。他們稱這種歌舞為「瓦利納」，是一種邊唱邊跳的舞蹈，一日表演四次。唯有印加人慶祝此節；太陽之女「媽媽庫納」為表演者奉上飲品；印加人自己的妻子不進入印加人所居之處，而是留在外面的庭院中。他們飲食所用的所有器皿，以及烹煮食物所用的器具，皆為黃金所製。

passages.text: At this festival they brought out the two female figures called Pallasillu and Ynca-uillu, covered with very rich clothes and small plates of gold. In front they bore the suntur-paucar and certain great figures of the size of sheep, two of gold and two of silver, with cloths placed over the loins in the fashion of horse cloths. They were carried on litters, and this was done in memory of the sheep which, they say, came forth from the tambo with them. The Indians who carried them were principal lords dressed in very rich clothes, and they call the figures of gold and silver sheep corinapa collque-napa.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of Hauca (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在此節慶中，他們請出兩尊名為「帕利亞西柳」與「印加維柳」的女性偶像，其上覆以極其華美的衣物與小金片。隊伍前方抬著「孫圖爾保卡爾」以及若干與羊一般大小的巨大偶像，兩尊為金、兩尊為銀，其腰間覆有布匹，形似馬衣。這些偶像以擔架抬行，此舉是為了紀念據說與他們一同從坦博出來的那些羊。抬運偶像的印第安人皆為身著極其華美衣物的顯貴領主，他們稱這些金銀羊偶像為「科里納帕·科爾克納帕」。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Yahuayra: The Sowing Fast and the Prayer for a Prosperous Year
title.zh: 亞瓦伊拉:播種齋戒與豐年祈禱

region.en: Limapampa, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科利馬潘帕(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In July, the sowing month, the people celebrated the festival called yahuayra, named from the song in which they besought the Creator for a full harvest. The Tarpuntaes fasted from the time the maize was sown until it stood a finger's length out of the ground, as did their wives and children, eating only boiled maize and herbs, drinking only the muddy concho, and chewing no coca. In red shirts to the feet, without mantles, they sang and danced at Limapampa, where the priests of the Creator sacrificed a white sheep, maize, coca, coloured plumes and mullu shells, praying that he who made all things out of nothing would grant a prosperous year; the priests of the Sun prayed for warmth and the Thunder, Chuqui Yllapa, for waters without hail.
summary.zh: 七月為播種之月,民眾慶祝「亞瓦伊拉」節,以所唱祈豐之歌為名。塔爾蓬泰祭司自播種之日起齋戒,直至玉米長出一指之高;其妻兒同齋,僅食煮玉米與野菜,不飲奇恰酒,只喝渾濁的孔喬,不嚼古柯。眾人身著及地紅衣、不披斗篷,在利馬潘帕唱歌起舞。造物主之祭司於清晨獻白羊、玉米、古柯、彩色羽飾與穆盧貝殼,祈求那位「從無中造出萬物」的主賜予豐年;太陽祭司祈日光暖育莊稼,雷神楚基伊亞帕降雨而不降雹。

sensitivity.note: Agricultural festival description; tagged with ritual-origin as a festival-calendar story.

passages.text: They called the month of July Moronpassa tarpuiquilla, and in it they celebrated the festivals called yahuayra, when they besought the Creator to grant them a full harvest in that year, for this was the month for sowing the seeds. The Tarpuntaes, who are a sort of priests, were careful to fast from the time the maize was sown until it was a finger's length out of the ground. Their wives and children also fasted, eating nothing during that time but boiled maize and herbs. They drank no chicha, but only muddy stuff called concho, and they chewed no coca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of July (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們稱七月為「莫龍帕薩·塔爾普伊基利亞」，並在此月慶祝名為「亞瓦伊拉」的節慶，屆時他們祈求造物主賜予當年豐收，因為此月正是播種之月。塔爾普恩塔伊——一種祭司——從玉米播下之時起，直到幼苗長出地面一指長為止，都謹守齋戒。他們的妻兒也一同齋戒，在此期間只吃煮熟的玉米與野菜。他們不喝奇恰酒，只喝一種名為「孔喬」的濁液，也不咀嚼古柯葉。

passages.text: All the common people celebrated a feast called yahuayra, from the name of the song they chaunted in which they besought the Creator to grant them a prosperous year. They sang it dressed in red shirts reaching to the feet, and no mantles. Then they came out to sing and dance in the place now called by the Spaniards Limapampa. Here the Priests of the Creator sacrificed a white sheep, maize, coca, plumes of coloured feathers, and sea shells called mullu, in the morning; beseeching the Creator to grant a prosperous year, and that, as He had made all things out of nothing and given them being, so He would be pleased to comply with their prayer.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of July (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 所有平民都慶祝一個名為「亞瓦伊拉」（yahuayra）的節慶，此名取自他們所吟唱之歌謠的名稱，歌中他們懇求造物主賜予豐收的一年。他們身著垂至腳踝的紅色襯衫、不披斗篷，唱著這首歌。隨後他們來到如今被西班牙人稱為「利馬潘帕」（Limapampa）的地方唱歌跳舞。造物主的祭司們在此於清晨獻祭一頭白羊、玉米、古柯、彩色羽毛以及名為「穆柳」（mullu）的海貝；他們懇求造物主賜予豐收的一年，並祈求祂既已從無中創造萬物、賦予其存在，便也樂意應允他們的祈禱。

passages.text: The Priests of the Sun, called Tarpuntaes, and the Priests of the Thunder also offered up sacrifices, praying the Sun to give warmth that so their food might be produced, and the Thunder, called Chuqui Yllapa, to send its waters to assist in the production, and not to bring down hail. As soon as the sacrifices were completed, the labourers went to their work, and the nobles to the house of the lord Ynca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of July (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 太陽的祭司，稱為「塔爾蓬泰」（Tarpuntaes），以及雷的祭司，也獻上祭品，祈求太陽賜予溫暖，使他們的糧食得以生長，並祈求名為「丘基·伊利亞帕」（Chuqui Yllapa）的雷降下雨水以助生長，而不降冰雹。祭品一經獻畢，勞動者便前去工作，貴族們則前往領主印加（Ynca）的宅邸。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Situa: Four Hundred Lances Drive the Evils to the Sea
title.zh: 淨疾節:四百長矛驅逐疫惡入海

region.en: Cuzco great square (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科大廣場(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In Coya-raymi, when the first rains brought sickness, the figures of the huacas were brought to Cuzco from Quito to Chile. Strangers, the broken-eared, the deformed and even the dogs were driven from the city, for their misfortune might drive away good fortune; then four hundred armed men, a hundred facing each of the four suyus, cried 'O sicknesses, disasters, misfortunes and dangers, go forth from the land', and relay-ran the shout along the four roads to the great rivers - the Apurimac, the river at Pisac, the river of Cusipampa - where the runners bathed themselves and their arms, so that the rivers of great volume would carry the evils away to the sea. All the people, great and small, shook their mantles at their doors crying 'Let the evils be gone', bathed at dawn, and played with burning straw torches called pancurcu.
summary.zh: 科亞雷米月(八月),初雨帶來疾病。各地瓦卡神像自基多至智利匯聚庫斯科。外人、耳裂者、畸形者乃至狗都被驅出城,因為厄運會趕走好運。四百名武裝男子在廣場集合,每百人面向一個蘇尤,高呼「疫病、災禍、不幸與危險,滾出此地!」隨後分四路接力奔跑傳喊,一路傳至阿普里馬克河等大河,傳喊者在河中沐浴並洗武器——大河終將把疫惡帶入大海。全城大小人民在門口抖動斗篷高呼「疫惡速去」,黎明赴河泉沐浴,再以點燃的草把(潘庫爾庫)互相拋擲嬉戲。

sensitivity.note: The great purification rite of Coya Raymi; its exclusion of the deformed is recorded here critically, as Molina preserves it.

passages.text: The month of August was called Coya-raymi, and in it they celebrated the Situa. To perform its ceremonies they brought the figures of their huacas from all parts of the land, from Quito to Chile, and placed them in the houses they had in Cuzco. The reason for celebrating the feast in this month was because the rains commenced, and with the first rains there was generally much sickness. They besought the Creator that during the year he would be pleased to shield them from sickness, as well in Cuzco as throughout the territory conquered by the Yncas.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Situa festival (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 八月被稱為「科亞·拉伊米」（Coya-raymi），他們在此月慶祝「西圖阿」（Situa）。為舉行其儀式，他們從全境各地，從基多（Quito）到智利（Chile），帶來其「瓦卡」（huacas）神像，並安置於他們在庫斯科（Cuzco）的屋舍中。之所以在此月慶祝此節，是因為雨季開始，而伴隨初雨通常多有疾病。他們懇求造物主在一年之中樂意庇佑他們免於疾病，無論在庫斯科抑或印加人所征服的全境皆然。

passages.text: First, all strangers, all whose ears were broken, and all deformed persons were sent out of the city, it being said that they should take no part in the ceremony, because they were in that state as a punishment for some fault; unfortunate people ought not to be present, because their ill-luck might drive away some piece of good fortune. They also drove out the dogs, that they might not howl. Then the people, armed as if for war, went to the square of Cuzco, crying out: 'O sicknesses, disasters, misfortunes, and dangers, go forth from the land.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Situa festival (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 首先，所有外來者、所有耳朵被穿孔者以及所有殘疾之人皆被逐出城外，據說他們不得參與典禮，因為他們處於此種狀態乃是對某種過錯的懲罰；不幸之人不應在場，因為他們的厄運可能驅走某些好運。他們也驅逐犬隻，以免其嚎叫。隨後，人們如臨戰般武裝起來，前往庫斯科的廣場，高喊：「噢，疾病、災禍、不幸與危難，離開這片土地吧。」

passages.text: Four hundred men of war assembled in the middle of the square where stood the urn of gold used at the sacrifice of chicha: one hundred faced towards Colla-suyu, one hundred to the westward towards Chincha-suyu, another hundred towards Anti-suyu, and the last hundred towards the south. They cried 'Go forth all evils', and each party set out at great speed along its appointed road, handing the cries on from lineage to mitimaes and from mitimaes to mitimaes, until at the great rivers - the Apurimac, the river at Pisac, the river at Quiquisana, the river of Cusipampa - they bathed themselves and washed their clothes and arms.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Situa festival (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 四百名戰士聚集於廣場中央，那兒立著獻祭「奇恰」（chicha）所用的金甕：一百人面向「科利亞蘇尤」（Colla-suyu），一百人向西面向「欽查蘇尤」（Chincha-suyu），另一百人面向「安蒂蘇尤」（Anti-suyu），最後一百人面向南方。他們高喊「一切邪惡皆離去」，各隊便沿其指定道路疾馳而出，將呼喊聲從一個世系傳至「米蒂馬埃斯」（mitimaes），再從米蒂馬埃斯傳至米蒂馬埃斯，直到在大河——阿普里馬克河（Apurimac）、皮薩克河（Pisac）、基基薩納河（Quiquisana）、庫西潘帕河（Cusipampa）——他們沐浴其身，洗滌其衣物與武器。

passages.text: Their reason for bathing in these rivers was because they were rivers of great volume, and were supposed to empty themselves into the sea, and to carry the evils with them. When the ceremony commenced in Cuzco, all the people, great and small, came to their doors, crying out, shaking their mantles and llicllas, and shouting, 'Let the evils be gone. How greatly desired has this festival been by us. O Creator of all things, permit us to reach another year, that we may see another feast like this.' They all danced, including the Ynca, and in the morning twilight they went to the rivers and fountains to bathe, saying that their maladies would come out of them. Having finished bathing, they took great torches of straw, bound round with cords, which they lighted and continued to play with, passing them from one to the other; they called these torches pancurcu.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Situa festival (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們在這些河中沐浴的原因，是因為這些河水量浩大，且被認為會流入大海，將邪惡一併帶走。當典禮在庫斯科開始時，所有人民，無論尊卑，皆來到自家門口，高聲呼喊，抖動其斗篷與「利克利亞」（llicllas），並喊道：「讓邪惡離去吧。這節慶是我們多麼殷切期盼的啊。噢，萬物的造物主，請允許我們活到來年，使我們得以再見一次這樣的慶典。」所有人皆起舞，包括印加在內；在晨光微曦之時，他們前往河流與泉源沐浴，說他們的病痛會從身上排出。沐浴完畢後，他們取來以繩索捆紮的大稻草火炬，點燃後繼續嬉戲，將其從一人傳至另一人；他們稱這些火炬為「潘庫爾庫」（pancurcu）。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Blood-Sprinkled Sancu and the Oath of the Four Suyus
title.zh: 血灑桑庫與四蘇尤之誓

region.en: Cuzco great square (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科大廣場(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: After the sacrifice of four unblemished unshorn sheep - one each to the Creator, the Thunder, the Sun and Huanacauri - the high priest sprinkled sancu pudding with their blood on plates of gold and warned the multitude: whoever eats the sancu in sin, with a double heart, is seen by the Sun their father, who will punish him with grievous troubles; but who eats with a single heart will be granted children and happy years. All rose, vowing never to murmur against the Creator, the Sun or the Thunder, and never to be traitors to the lord Inca; the priest took three fingers' worth, and all partook down to the little children, keeping no particle from falling to the ground - a great sin - and reserving portions for the absent and the sick. The lungs of the sacrificed sheep were inflated and read for the signs of the coming year.
summary.zh: 獻祭四隻無瑕未剪毛之羊(分別敬造物主、雷神、太陽、瓦納考里)後,大祭司以羊血灑金盤中的桑庫糊,向眾人宣告:凡心懷二意、帶罪而食者,太陽之父看得見,必降重災;凡誠心而食者,太陽與雷神必賜子嗣、豐年與所求之一切。全體起立立誓:絕不對造物主、太陽、雷神生怨,絕不背叛印加王,違者自領災殃。祭司取三指之量入口,眾人依次同食,直至孩童;為遠行者與病榻者留份,任何一粒落地都是大罪。祭畢,剖出羊肺吹脹,察其紋路以斷來年吉凶。

sensitivity.note: Oath rite preserved by Molina; demonstrates the fusion of kingship loyalty and solar cult.

passages.text: The Ynca and the people brought with them a very great quantity of flocks from all the four quarters... more than one hundred thousand, and it was necessary that all should be without spot or blemish, and with fleeces that had never been shorn. Presently the priest of the Sun selected four of the most perfect, and sacrificed them in the following order: one was offered to the Creator, another to the Thunder, another to the Sun, and another to Huanacauri. When this sacrifice was offered up, the priest had the sancu on great plates of gold, and he sprinkled it with the blood of the sheep.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Situa festival (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 印加王與人民從四方帶來數量極多的牲畜……超過十萬頭，且必須全無斑點或瑕疵，羊毛也須從未剪過。隨即，太陽的祭司挑選出四頭最完美的，並依下列順序獻祭：一頭獻給造物主，一頭獻給雷電，一頭獻給太陽，一頭獻給瓦納卡烏里。獻上這祭品後，祭司將桑庫放在大金盤上，並以羊血灑之。

passages.text: The high priest then said in a loud voice so that all might hear: 'Take heed how you eat this sancu; for he who eats it in sin, and with a double will and heart, is seen by our father the Sun, who will punish him with grievous troubles. But he who with a single heart partakes of it, to him the Sun and the Thunder will show favour, and will grant children and happy years, and abundance, and all that he requires.' Then they all rose up to partake, first making a solemn vow before eating the yahuar-sancu, in which they promised never to murmur against the Creator, the Sun, or the Thunder; never to be traitors to their lord the Ynca, on pain of receiving condemnation and trouble.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Situa festival (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大祭司隨即高聲說道，使眾人皆能聽見：「你們要當心如何吃這桑庫；因為凡在罪中、懷著二心二意而吃它的人，我們的父太陽都看得見，必以嚴重的災禍懲罰他。但凡以一心一意領受它的人，太陽與雷電必向他施恩，賜他子嗣與幸福的歲月、豐足，以及他所需的一切。」於是眾人皆起身領受，在吃亞瓦爾—桑庫之前先立下莊嚴的誓願，承諾永不抱怨造物主、太陽或雷電；永不背叛其君主印加王，違者甘受譴責與災禍。

passages.text: The priest of the Sun took what he could hold on three fingers, put it into his mouth, and returned to his seat; and in this order all the tribes rose up and partook, down to the little children. They kept some of the yahuar-sancu for those who were absent, and sent some to those who were confined to their beds by sickness; they took it with such care that no particle was allowed to fall to the ground, this being looked upon as a great sin. When they killed the sacrificial sheep, they took out the lungs and inflated them, and the priests judged, from certain signs on them, whether all things would turn out prosperously in the coming year or not.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Situa festival (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 太陽的祭司以三指撮起所能持取的份量，放入口中，然後回到座位；接著所有部族依此順序起身領受，直到幼童亦然。他們為缺席者保留了一些亞瓦爾—桑庫，並送一些給因病臥床者；他們取用時極為小心，不許有任何碎屑落在地上，因為這被視為大罪。當他們宰殺獻祭的羊時，取出肺臟並將其吹脹，祭司便依其上某些徵兆判斷來年諸事是否順遂。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Prayers of the Situa: Creator, Sun, Thunder, Huacas
title.zh: 淨疾節禱文:造物主、太陽、雷與瓦卡

region.en: Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Molina preserves the Quechua liturgy of the festival with Markham's translations: the prayer to the conquering, incomprehensible Creator who says 'let this be a man, let this be a woman' and dwells in the heights of heaven, in the thunder and the storm clouds; the prayer for fruitful flocks; the prayer to the huacas - Chanca-Uiracocha of Chuqui-chaca, Atun-Uiracocha of Urcos with its carved eagle and falcon, Apotin-Uiracocha of Amaybamba; the prayer that men be kept from hunger and the fruits from frost; the prayer to the Sun who said 'let there be day and night'; the prayer for the Inca that he may always be a conqueror, and for all the Incas that 'there may be Cuzcos and Tampus'; and the prayer to the sacred huacas, ancestors and grandsires, to bring their sons near to the Creator.
summary.zh: 莫利納保存了節慶的克丘亞禱文(馬卡姆英譯):向無可比擬、戰無不勝的造物主祈禱——祂說「使此人為男、使彼人為女」,居於高天、雷聲與風暴雲中;祈求羊群繁衍;向瓦卡祈禱——楚基查卡的昌卡-維拉科查、烏爾科斯的大維拉科查(廟門刻有鷹與隼)、阿馬伊班巴的阿波廷-維拉科查;祈求人民免於飢餓、五穀免於霜凍;向「說要有晝夜」的太陽祈禱;為印加王祈禱,願他常勝不敗;為歷代印加祈禱,「願庫斯科與坦波永存」;並向神聖瓦卡——祖先、先人們祈禱,求他們引子孫近於造物主。

sensitivity.note: Liturgical prayers are treated as religious records of the Quechua cult; marked 'religious' as canonical liturgy of the tradition.

passages.text: O Creator! [O conquering Uiracocha! Ever present Uiracocha!] Thou who art without equal unto the ends of the earth! Thou who givest life and strength to mankind, saying, let this be a man and let this be a woman: and as thou sayest, so thou givest life, and vouchsafest that men shall live in health and peace, and free from danger. Thou who dwellest in the heights of heaven, in the thunder, and in the storm clouds, hear us! and grant us eternal life. Have us in thy keeping, and receive this our offering, as it shall please thee, O Creator!
passages.note: Quechua prayer in Markham's 1873 translation (public domain), condensed; the liturgy is quoted as an archival religious text.
passages.zh: 造物主啊！〔征服者維拉科查啊！永在的維拉科查啊！〕祢無與倫比，直到地極！祢賜生命與力量給人類，說：願此為男，願此為女；正如祢所言，祢便賜下生命，並恩准人們在健康與平安中生活，免於危險。祢居於高天之上，在雷電中，在風暴的雲裡，求祢垂聽我們！賜我們永生。求祢保守我們，並收納我們這獻祭，隨祢喜悅，造物主啊！

passages.text: O Creator! who doest wonders and marvels. O most merciful and almighty Creator! multiply our flocks and cause them to bring forth young, let the land continue in peace and free from danger, and these whom thou hast made, hold them in thy hand. ... O Creator! Thou who gavest being to the Sun, and afterwards said let there be day and night. Raise it and cause it to shine, and preserve that which thou hast created, that it may give light to men. O Sun! Thou who art in peace and safety, shine upon us, keep us from sickness, and keep us in health and safety.
passages.note: Quechua prayers in Markham's 1873 translation (public domain), condensed.
passages.zh: 造物主啊！祢行奇事與神蹟。最慈悲、全能的造物主啊！求祢使我們的牲畜繁衍增多，使牠們生養幼崽，使大地持續平安、免於危險，並將祢所造這些人握在祢手中。……造物主啊！祢賜予太陽存在，隨後說：願有晝，願有夜。求祢使它升起、使它照耀，並保全祢所創造的，使其能光照世人。太陽啊！祢在平安與穩妥之中，求祢照耀我們，使我們免於疾病，保守我們在健康與安全之中。

passages.text: O pious Creator, who ordered and saw fit that there should be a Lord Ynca, grant to the Ynca that he may be kept in peace, with his servants and vassals, that he may obtain the victory over his enemies and always be a conqueror. Cut not short his days, nor the days of his children, and give them peace, O Creator! ... O Sun! Thou who hast said, let there be Cuzcos and Tampus, grant that these thy children may conquer all other people. We beseech thee that thy children the Yncas may be conquerors always, for this hast thou created them.
passages.note: Quechua prayers in Markham's 1873 translation (public domain), condensed.
passages.zh: 虔敬的造物主啊，祢命定並喜悅有一位印加王，求祢賜予印加王，使他與其僕從與臣民皆得保全於平安之中，使他能戰勝敵人，永遠為征服者。求祢不要縮短他的日子，也不要縮短他子嗣的日子，並賜他們平安，造物主啊！……太陽啊！祢曾說：願有庫斯科與坦普，求祢賜使這些祢的子女能征服所有其他民族。我們懇求祢，使祢的子女印加人永遠為征服者，因為祢正是為此創造了他們。

passages.text: O sacred Huacas, ancestors, grandsires, and parents! O Hatun-apu! O Apu Allastu! bring us near to the Creator, us thy sons, and our children, that they may be fortunate and near the Creator, as thou art. Chanca-Uiracocha was a huaca in Chuqui-chaca; Atun-Uiracocha is in the huaca of Urcos, where there was an eagle and a falcon carved in stone at the entrance of the huaca, and an image of a man with a white robe reaching to his feet; Apotin-Uiracocha is in Amaybamba, beyond Tampu.
passages.note: Quechua prayer and huaca notes in Markham's 1873 translation (public domain), condensed.
passages.zh: 噢，神聖的瓦卡、祖先、祖父與父母啊！噢，哈通阿普！噢，阿普阿亞斯圖！請引領我們這些您的子孫，以及我們的孩子，親近造物主，使他們能如您一般蒙福並親近造物主。昌卡維拉科查是丘基查卡的一處瓦卡；阿通維拉科查位於烏爾科斯的瓦卡之中，該瓦卡入口處曾有一隻鷹與一隻隼的石雕，以及一尊身穿垂至腳踝白袍的人像；阿波廷維拉科查位於坦普之外的阿邁班巴。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Lords of Gold Benches: Mummies in the Great Square
title.zh: 金座之主:大廣場上的王木乃伊

region.en: Cuzco great square (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科大廣場(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: During the Situa the embalmed bodies of dead lords and ladies were brought out, each by a person of the same lineage who had charge of it, washed in the baths which belonged to them when they were alive, warmed with the coarse sancu pudding, and set before them the food they had been most fond of when alive, which their keepers afterwards consumed. The image of the Sun called Apupunchau, the principal image of the temple, was set on a bench of gold in the square, with the images of the Creator and of the Thunder Chuqui-ylla each on its golden bench, the woman Coya-facssa dedicated to the Sun attending; the embalmed lords were deposited in the square on seats of gold in the order in which they had lived, Hanan-Cuzcos on one side and Hurin-Cuzcos on the other, and the whole city passed the day in eating and drinking.
summary.zh: 淨疾節中,先王王后的木乃伊由各世系專管之人抬出,放入其生前專用的浴池洗浴,以粗桑庫糊暖身,並在其前擺上生前最愛的食物,由看管者代食。太陽主像「阿普蓬喬」與造物主像、雷神楚基伊亞像各安金座於廣場,獻身太陽的科亞神女在旁侍立;歷代木乃伊按生前位次安放於金座,哈南庫斯科世系居一側,烏林庫斯科世系居另一側,全城飲宴終日。

sensitivity.note: Royal ancestor cult described by Molina; the mummies are treated as still-living lords, a central Andean belief.

passages.text: They also brought out the bodies of the dead lords and ladies which were embalmed, each one being brought out by the person of the same lineage who had charge of it. During the night these bodies were washed in the baths which belonged to them when they were alive. They were then brought back to their houses, and warmed with the same coarse pudding called sancu; and the food they had been most fond of when they were alive was placed before them, and afterwards the persons who were in charge of the bodies consumed the food.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Situa festival (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們也抬出經防腐處理的已故領主與貴婦的遺體，每一具皆由同宗族中負責保管該遺體的人抬出。夜間，這些遺體被清洗於其生前所屬的浴池中。隨後他們被送回各自的屋舍，並以名為桑庫的粗製布丁為之取暖；他們生前最喜愛的食物被擺放在其面前，之後由負責保管遺體的人員食用這些食物。

passages.text: There also came forth the woman called Coya-facssa, who was dedicated to the Sun; she was either the sister or the daughter of the ruler. The priests carried the image of the Sun and placed it on a bench prepared for it in the square; the priests of the Creator likewise brought forth his image, and so did the priests of the Thunder, called Chuqui-ylla. Each had its bench of gold, and before them were borne yauris, made like sceptres of gold. At this feast they brought out all the embalmed bodies of their lords and ladies, very richly adorned; the bodies were carried by the descendants of the respective lineages and were deposited in the square on seats of gold, according to the order in which they lived, the Hanan-Cuzcos on one side and the Hurin-Cuzcos on the other.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Situa festival (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 名為科亞法克薩的女子亦現身，她專奉太陽神；她或是統治者的姊妹，或是其女兒。祭司們抬著太陽神的偶像，將其安放於廣場上為之準備的長凳上；造物主的祭司們同樣抬出祂的偶像，雷神的祭司們亦然，雷神名為丘基伊利亞。各神皆有其所屬的金凳，其前方則抬著製成金權杖模樣的堯里。在此慶典中，他們抬出所有領主與貴婦經防腐處理的遺體，裝飾極為華麗；遺體由各自宗族的後裔抬運，並依其生前先後次序安放於廣場上的金座之上，哈南庫斯科諸王在一側，胡林庫斯科諸王在另一側。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Maui Formed in the Sea Foam
title.zh: 海沫所育的毛伊：五子相認

region.en: Bay of Plenty coast, Aotearoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 紐西蘭豐盛灣海岸（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 2, The Legend of Maui (London 1855)

summary.en: Taranga prematurely bore her fifth son, bound him in a tuft of her own hair, and threw him into the surf. Seaweed formed him; he was rescued from birds and flies by his ancestor Tama-nui-ki-te-Rangi, who hung him in the warm smoke of his house. Years later the boy crept into the dancing house, sat behind his brothers, and proved his birth by reciting the names Maui-taha, Maui-roto, Maui-pae and Maui-waho, winning his name Maui-tikitiki-o-Taranga, 'formed in the top-knot of Taranga'.
summary.zh: 塔朗加早產產下第五子，剪下自己的一束頭髮裹住嬰兒，拋入海浪泡沫之中。海草纏裹將其塑造成形；先祖大魯基基特朗基趕走啄食的飛鳥與蠅群，將其救起懸於屋內火煙取暖。多年後幼童潛入歌舞大廳，坐於諸兄身後，背誦毛伊塔哈、毛伊羅托、毛伊派、毛伊瓦霍四兄弟之名以證身世，得名副『塔朗加髮結所育之毛伊』。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection from named Te Arawa informants; Grey's footnote on discarded premature infants retained as cultural context only.

passages.text: One night, while the relations were dancing in the great House of Assembly, little Maui the infant crept into the house and sat behind one of his brothers. When their mother counted her children to stand up for the dance she said, 'One, that is Maui-taha; two, Maui-roto; three, Maui-pae; four, Maui-waho' - and then she saw another and cried out, 'Hollo, where did this fifth come from?' Little Maui answered, 'Ah, I am your child too.' She counted again, declared there could only be four, and told him to leave the house at once as no child of hers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 2 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某夜，親族們在大集會所中跳舞時，小嬰兒毛伊悄悄溜進屋內，坐在他一位兄長身後。當他們的母親清點孩子們以排隊起舞時，她說：「一，這是毛伊塔哈；二，毛伊羅托；三，毛伊帕埃；四，毛伊瓦霍」——接著她看見另一個，便喊道：「哎呀，這第五個是從哪兒來的？」小毛伊回答：「啊，我也是您的孩子呀。」她重新清點，宣稱只可能只有四個，並叫他立刻離開屋子，因為他根本不是她的孩子。

passages.text: Then the boy spoke boldly: he said he was born at the side of the sea, wrapped by her in a tuft of hair cut from her own head, and thrown into the foam of the surf. The seaweed formed and fashioned him as the surges rolled him from side to side; the breezes drifted him on shore; jelly-fish rolled round him to protect him; flies and flocks of birds collected to devour him, until his great ancestor Tama-nui-ki-te-Rangi ran up, stripped off the encircling jelly-fish, found a human being within, carried him to his house and hung him in the roof to feel the warm smoke and heat of the fire. In proof he recited his brothers' names one by one, and called himself Maui-the-baby, Maui-tikitiki-a-Taranga, formed in the top-knot of Taranga.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 2 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是那男孩大膽地開口：他說自己生於海邊，被她用從自己頭上剪下的一綹頭髮包裹，投入浪花的泡沫之中。海藻在波濤將他左右翻滾之際形成並塑造了他；微風將他吹送上岸；水母環繞他身旁以保護他；蒼蠅與成群的鳥兒聚集而來欲吞噬他，直到他的偉大祖先塔馬努伊基特蘭吉奔來，剝去環繞他的水母，發現其中竟是一個人，便將他帶回屋中，懸於屋頂之下，讓他感受溫暖的煙氣與爐火的熱度。為證明身世，他逐一背出兄長們的名字，並自稱毛伊寶寶、毛伊蒂基蒂基阿塔蘭加，成形於塔蘭加的髮髻之中。

passages.text: Taranga wept for joy: 'You dear little child, you are indeed my last-born, the son of my old age; your name shall be Maui-tikitiki-o-Taranga.' She bade him sleep with her; the elder brothers murmured jealously against the 'little abortion' thrown into the ocean who had come back a living human being, but the eldest reminded them of the children of Rangi-nui and Papa-tu-a-nuku, who fostered divisions until brother fought brother, and counselled peace: let him be their dear brother, and their murmuring ended there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 2 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 塔蘭加喜極而泣：「你這親愛的小孩子，你確實是我最後所生、我晚年的兒子；你的名字就叫毛伊蒂基蒂基奧塔蘭加。」她命他與自己同睡；兄長們嫉妒地低聲抱怨那個被投入大洋的「小流產兒」竟活著回來成了活人，但長兄提醒他們想起蘭吉努伊與帕帕圖阿努庫的孩子們，他們縱容紛爭，直至兄弟相殘，並勸以和睦：就讓他做他們親愛的弟弟吧，他們的抱怨也就此平息。

title.en: Maui Wins the Enchanted Jawbone
title.zh: 毛伊智取祖妣顎骨

region.en: Path to Muri-ranga-whenua's dwelling (symbolic pin, inland)
region.zh: 通往穆里朗加維努阿居所之路（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 2, The Legend of Maui (London 1855)

summary.en: Noticing that his parents' household sent daily food offerings to the ancestress Muri-ranga-whenua, Maui carries them himself and quietly lays them aside, never delivering them. At last the old chieftainess sniffs the breeze, detects the scent of a man from the west, and her distended stomach - ready to devour the cheat - shrinks when she learns he is her descendant. Challenged, Maui confesses he wanted the jawbone by which great enchantments are wrought; she gives it, for it had been reserved for him, and with it he fashions his magic fish-hook.
summary.zh: 毛伊發現父母家宅每日送食獻予祖妣穆里朗加維努阿，便自薦代送，卻把祭食私下擱置，從不交到她手中。老婦終起疑心，嗅風辨味，西風送來人氣；她膨脹欲吞詐欺者的胃腹一聽是孫裔便回縮原狀。被質問時，毛伊坦言欲得其顎骨——大法術所繫之骨；老嫗道此骨本為他而留，遂予之，毛伊以之製成神鉤。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection of living oral tradition.

passages.text: Whilst Maui stayed with his parents he remarked that some of their people daily carried away a present of food for some person, and at last asked them who it was for. They answered it was for his ancestress, Muri-ranga-whenua. He said that would do - leave the present with him and he would carry it himself. From that time the daily offerings were carried by Maui himself, but he never gave them to her to eat; he quietly laid them by on one side, and did this for many days.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 2 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 毛伊與父母同住期間，注意到他們的族人每天都會帶著一份食物送給某人，最後便問他們那是送給誰的。他們回答說是送給他的女祖先穆里-蘭加-韋努阿。他說那正好——把這份供品交給他，由他親自送去。從那時起，每日的供品都由毛伊親自送去，但他從不把供品交給她吃；他悄悄地把供品擱在一邊，如此過了許多天。

passages.text: At last Muri-ranga-whenua suspected something wrong. The next time he came along the path the old chieftainess sniffed and sniffed until she thought she smelt something coming, and was greatly exasperated, and her stomach began to distend itself, that she might be ready to devour Maui as soon as he arrived. She turned southward and sniffed - no scent; north, east - nothing; almost she thought she must have been mistaken. She tried once more, toward the westward: ah! the scent of a man came plainly to her, and she called aloud that she knew somebody was close by. Maui murmured assent, and knowing him her descendant, her swollen stomach at once shrank and contracted again. Had the western breeze not carried his scent, she would have eaten him up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 2 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最後，穆里-蘭加-韋努阿察覺到有些不對勁。下一次他沿著小徑走來時，這位年邁的女酋長一再嗅了又嗅，直到她自覺聞到有東西正走過來，勃然大怒，她的肚子開始鼓脹起來，好等她一到便將毛伊吞下肚去。她轉向南邊嗅了嗅——沒有氣味；向北、向東——什麼也沒有；她幾乎以為自己一定是弄錯了。她又試了一次，朝西邊：啊！人的氣味清清楚楚地傳到她這裡，於是她高聲呼喊，說她知道有人就在附近。毛伊低聲應了一聲，她認出他是自己的後裔，鼓脹的肚子立刻又縮了回去。若不是西風把他的氣味送來，她早就把他吞下肚了。

passages.text: Her voice asked, 'Art thou Maui?' - 'Even so.' 'Wherefore hast thou served thy old ancestress in this deceitful way?' Maui answered that he was anxious that her jawbone, by which the great enchantments can be wrought, should be given to him. She replied, 'Take it; it has been reserved for thee.' Maui took it and returned home, and with a barb pointed from that jawbone he soon after snooded his enchanted fish-hook, twisted a stout fishing-line to it, and set out for the open sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 2 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她的聲音問道：「你是毛伊嗎？」——「正是。」「你為何這般欺瞞你的老女祖先？」毛伊回答說，他急切希望她把那能施行偉大法術的下頜骨交給他。她答道：「拿去吧；它本就是為你留著的。」毛伊取了下來，返回家中，不久之後便用從那下頜骨削出的倒鉤繫上他那施了法術的魚鉤，又搓了一條結實的釣線綁在上面，動身前往外海。

title.en: Maui Fishes Up the Great Fish of Tonganui
title.zh: 毛伊釣起大地之魚

region.en: Open sea east of Hawke's Bay, Aotearoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 紐西蘭霍克灣以東遠海（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 2, The Legend of Maui (London 1855)

summary.en: Hid under the bottom boards of his brothers' canoe, Maui steers them far out of sight of land, baits his enchanted hook with his own blood, and hauls up the house of old Tonganui - a portion of Papa-tu-a-Nuku drowned by Rangi and Tawhiri. While he fetches a priest and offerings, the greedy brothers cut up the fish unlawfully; the land thrashes and contorts, and so New Zealand stands rough with mountains, valleys and cliffs instead of lying smooth as the model of the world.
summary.zh: 毛伊藏於兄船底板之下，隨船遠出海，以自身之血作餌，鉤住海底古屋，將被朗基與塔維里沉於海底的大地一隅——老湯加努伊之屋——緩緩釣起。他回村取祭品請祭司之際，貪嘴的兄長們違禁割切魚身；巨魚翻騰扭動，遂令此島山巒谷壑嶙峋，不能如大地典範般平坦光整。

sensitivity.note: Foundational legend of Aotearoa; 'dismembered-giant' motif tags the dismembered fish-land, an interpretive extension of the cluster list.

passages.text: When it was dark night, Maui went down to the shore, got into his brothers' canoe and hid himself under the bottom boards. Next forenoon they launched and paddled out to sea without seeing him; when they discovered him they wanted to turn back, but Maui by his enchantments stretched out the sea until the shore was far out of view. He persuaded them to paddle past every fishing ground, out of sight of land, quite into the open sea. There the brothers' lines had hardly touched bottom before each pulled up a fish; twice only they let down their lines, and behold, the canoe was filled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 2 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 夜色漆黑時，毛伊下到岸邊，鑽進他兄弟們的獨木舟，藏身在船底板下面。第二天上午，他們把船推下水，划向大海，並未見到他；當他們發現他時，本想掉頭回去，但毛伊施法術把海面伸展出去，直到海岸遠得看不見了。他說服他們划過每一處漁場，划到看不見陸地，一直划進外海。在那裡，兄弟們的釣線幾乎還沒觸到海底，每人便都釣起一條魚；他們只放下兩次釣線，瞧，獨木舟就裝滿了。

passages.text: Maui then drew out his own hook, carved and ornamented with tufts of dog-tail hair, the point of the jawbone of Muri-ranga-whenua. His brothers refused him bait, so he doubled his fist, struck his nose violently until the blood gushed out, smeared his hook with his own blood, and cast it into the sea. It sank down and down till it reached the carved figure on the roof of a house at the bottom of the sea, slid along the carved rafters, fell in at the doorway, and caught in the sill. Then he hauled in his line: the house of that old fellow Tonganui ascended; foam and bubbles gurgled up as from an island emerging, and Maui chanted the incantation Hiki, which makes heavy weights light, asking why Tonganui held so obstinately below.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 2 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著，毛伊取出自己的魚鉤，那鉤上雕刻著花紋，飾有狗尾毛的流蘇，鉤尖正是穆里-蘭加-韋努阿的下頜骨。他的兄弟們不肯給他魚餌，於是他握緊拳頭，猛擊自己的鼻子，直到鮮血直流，用自己的血塗抹魚鉤，然後把它拋入海中。魚鉤沉下去，沉下去，直到觸到海底一座房屋屋頂上的雕刻人像，沿著雕花的椽子滑下，從門口掉了進去，卡在門檻上。於是他收緊釣線：那老傢伙托恩加努伊的房屋升了起來；泡沫與氣泡咕嘟咕嘟地冒上來，彷彿一座島嶼浮出海面，毛伊吟誦起咒語「希基」，那咒語能使沉重的東西變輕，並質問托恩加努伊為何如此固執地待在下面。

passages.text: There floated up hanging to his line the fish of Maui, a portion of the earth of Papa-tu-a-Nuku, dry land fished up after it had been hidden under the ocean by Rangi and Tawhiri-ma-tea. Maui left his brothers, charging them to be patient, not to eat until his return and not to cut up the fish until offerings had been carried to the gods and fitting prayers made. Hardly had he gone than they trampled his words underfoot and began to eat and to cut up the fish. Then the gods turned with wrath upon them: the fish began to toss his head from side to side and lash his tail and fins, springing about on shore as briskly as if in the water. That is why this island is now so rough and uneven - here a mountain, there a plain, here a vale, there a cliff; had the brothers not acted deceitfully, the huge fish would have lain flat and smooth, a model for the rest of the earth. This was the second evil after the separation of Heaven from Earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 2 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 毛伊的魚便掛在他的釣線上浮了上來，那是帕帕-圖-阿-努庫大地的一部分，是被蘭吉與塔惠里-馬-特阿藏於海洋之下後釣起的乾燥陸地。毛伊離開他的兄弟們，囑咐他們要耐心，在他回來之前不要吃，在供品送到神那裡並做過適當的祈禱之前不要切割這條魚。他剛一走，他們就把他的話踩在腳下，開始吃起來，並切割這條魚。於是眾神滿懷憤怒地轉向他們：那魚開始把頭從一邊甩到另一邊，拍打著尾巴和鰭，在岸上活蹦亂跳，彷彿還在水中一般。這就是為什麼這座島如今如此崎嶇不平——這裡一座山，那裡一片平原，這裡一道谷，那裡一處崖；倘若兄弟們沒有做出這等欺詐之事，那條巨魚本會平平滑滑地躺著，成為其餘大地的典範。這是自天與地分離以來的第二樁禍事。

title.en: Maui and Mahuika, the Fire Mother
title.zh: 毛伊與火祖母瑪惠卡

region.en: Mahuika's dwelling inland, Aotearoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 紐西蘭內陸火神居所（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 2, The Legend of Maui (London 1855)

summary.en: After extinguishing every hearth in the village, Maui trickster-styles his way to Mahuika, goddess of fire, who pulls fire from her finger- and toe-nails one after another. He douses each gift and demands more until her last nail kindles the world: fire pursues him as eagle, boiling the very sea and burning land and forest, until he calls on Tawhiri-ma-tea for deluging rain that nearly kills Mahuika. Yet she saves a few sparks in the kaikomako tree - whence men kindle fire to this day.
summary.zh: 毛伊滅盡村中爐火，戲弄火祖母瑪惠卡：她一根根拔出指趾之甲，指甲生火贈他；他卻逐一弄熄，再索再討。最後一枚趾甲擲地即燃遍天地：火追毛伊化鷹而逃，海水近沸，陸林俱焚；他呼喚塔維里馬泰亞降下傾盆大雨滅火，反令瑪惠卡幾遭滅頂。然火神終將數粒火種擲入卡伊科馬科樹中珍藏——人們至今仍以此木取火。

sensitivity.note: Fire-theft cluster: Polynesian Maui parallel to Prometheus; note the variant motif of fire-giving ancestress rather than fire stolen from gods.

passages.text: The hero now thought he would extinguish and destroy the fires of his ancestress Mahuika. He got up in the night and put out the fires left in the cooking-houses of each family in the village; then quite early in the morning he called aloud that he hungered and food must be cooked, but every fire in the village was out and no light could be got. When Maui's mother heard this she told the servants to go to her great ancestress Mahuika and tell her that fire had been lost upon earth; but the slaves were alarmed and refused to obey, so Maui said he would fetch down fire for the world himself, and his parents directed him to the broad path leading to her dwelling.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 2 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這位英雄此時心想，他要熄滅並毀掉他的女性先祖瑪胡伊卡的火。他夜裡起身，把村中每一戶人家炊事房裡留下的火都弄熄了；接著，一大清早他便高聲呼喊，說自己餓了，必須煮食，但村裡所有的火都已熄滅，半點火光也取不到。毛伊的母親聽見這話，便吩咐僕人去見她的偉大女性先祖瑪胡伊卡，告訴她人間的火已經失傳；可是那些奴僕十分驚慌，不肯聽命，於是毛伊說他要親自為世人取回火來，他的父母便指點他走向通往她居所的那條寬闊道路。

passages.text: When he reached the abode of the goddess of fire he was filled with wonder, and begged fire from her. The aged woman pulled out one of her nails, and as she pulled it out fire flowed from it, and she gave it to him; but he went a short distance off and put the light out, then returned and asked for another. Thus he went on and on, until she had pulled out all the nails of one hand, then the other, then the nails of her feet - all but the nail of one big toe. Then she said to herself that this fellow was surely playing tricks with her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 2 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他來到火之女神的居所時，心中充滿驚奇，便向她求火。那老婦人拔下自己的一片指甲，一拔下來，火便從指甲中流出，她把火交給了他；可是他走到不遠處就把火弄熄了，然後回來再討一片。他就這樣一次又一次地討，直到她一隻手上的指甲全拔光了，接著是另一隻手，然後是她腳上的指甲——只除了一個大腳趾的指甲。這時她暗自思忖，這傢伙必定是在捉弄她。

passages.text: Out she pulled the one toe-nail she had left, and it too became fire; as she dashed it down on the ground the whole place caught fire, and she cried to Maui, 'There, you have it all now!' He ran off to escape, changing himself into a fleet-winged eagle, but the fire pursued and almost caught him as he flew; he dashed into a pool of water and found it almost boiling; the forests, the earth, the sea all caught fire, and Maui was very near perishing in the flames. Then he called on Tawhiri-ma-tea and Whatitiri-matakataka to send abundant water; squalls and gales appeared, heavy pelting rain fell and quenched the fire, and before Mahuika could reach shelter she almost perished, her shrieks as loud as Maui's had been.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 2 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她把僅剩的那片腳趾甲也拔了出來，那指甲也化成了火；她把它猛擲在地上，整個地方便都著了火，她對毛伊喊道：『喏，這下你全拿去吧！』他拔腿就逃，把自己變成一隻疾翅的鷹，可是火緊追不捨，在他飛翔時幾乎將他擒住；他衝進一潭水中，卻發現那水幾乎沸騰；森林、大地、海洋全都著了火，毛伊幾乎要在烈焰中喪命。於是他呼求塔惠里—馬—特阿與瓦提提里—馬塔卡塔卡降下豐沛的水；狂風驟雨頓時出現，傾盆大雨猛烈落下，澆熄了火，而瑪胡伊卡還沒來得及找到遮蔽之處，就幾乎喪命，她的尖叫聲與毛伊先前的叫聲一樣響亮。

passages.text: Thus was extinguished the fire of Mahuika, the goddess of fire; but before it was all lost she saved a few sparks, which she threw, to protect them, into the Kaikomako and a few other trees, where they are still cherished; hence men yet use portions of the wood of these trees for fire when they require a light. When Maui returned to the village his parents told him he had heard their warning and played tricks with his ancestress all the same, and it served him right; the young fellow answered that his perverse proceedings would not stop for this, and he intended to go on in the same way for ever.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 2 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 火之女神瑪胡伊卡的火就這樣被熄滅了；但在火全部失掉之前，她保全了幾點火星，為了護住它們，她把火星擲進凱科馬科樹和另外幾棵樹裡，火星至今仍在那裡被珍藏著；因此人們需要取火時，至今仍用這些樹木的木料來生火。毛伊回到村裡時，他的父母告訴他，他明明聽見了他們的警告，卻還是照樣捉弄他的女性先祖，他這是活該；這年輕人回答說，他這些乖張的行徑不會就此罷休，他打算永遠這樣幹下去。

title.en: Maui Turns Irawaru into the First Dog
title.zh: 毛伊將伊拉瓦魯化為第一犬

region.en: Fishing shore, east coast Aotearoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 紐西蘭東岸漁灘（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 2, The Legend of Maui (London 1855)

summary.en: Fishing with a barbless hook, Maui loses his temper when his brother-in-law Irawaru keeps hauling in fish. Feigning reconciliation, he crushes Irawaru under the capsized outrigger, tramples him, stretches his backbone into a tail, and by enchantment transforms him into a dog. Hinauri, told to call 'Mo-i, mo-i' for her husband, hears only the howling 'Ao! ao!' from the scrub; distracted with grief she casts herself with her enchanted girdle into the ocean. From Irawaru springs all dogs, and New Zealanders still call their dogs 'Mo-i'.
summary.zh: 毛伊無倒鉤釣魚屢屢落空，妹夫伊拉瓦魯卻連連獲魚，他怒火中燒。假意和好後，他令伊拉瓦魯以背撐起翻覆之舷外浮架，趁機壓下全身重量踩踏其身，拉長其脊椎成尾，以咒術將其化為犬。海娜烏里遵囑喚『毛伊、毛伊』，只聞灌木叢中『嗷、嗷』犬吠；她悲慟欲絕，攜魔法腰帶縱身入海。伊拉瓦魯遂為群犬之祖，至今毛利人喚犬仍呼『毛伊』。

sensitivity.note: Etiological origin of the dog; colonial-era collection. Grey records an alternative telling in a footnote (enchanted sleep while hair-dressing).

passages.text: Maui had a young sister named Hinauri, who was exceedingly beautiful; she married Irawaru. One day Maui and his brother-in-law went down to the sea to fish. Maui caught not a single fish with his hook, which had no barb to it, while Irawaru continued catching plenty. Then their lines entangled, each pulled for the fish; Maui hauled it in, and found, to his wrath, that it was on Irawaru's barbed hook, and that he had no chance with his barbless hook of catching as many fish as his brother-in-law.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 2 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 毛伊有一個年幼的妹妹名叫希瑙里，長得極其美麗；她嫁給了伊拉瓦魯。有一天，毛伊和他的妹夫下海捕魚。毛伊的魚鉤沒有倒刺，他一條魚也沒釣到，而伊拉瓦魯卻接連釣到許多。後來他們的釣線纏在一起，兩人各自爭著拉那條魚；毛伊把它拉了上來，卻憤怒地發現魚是掛在伊拉瓦魯那有倒刺的鉤上，而他拿著沒有倒刺的鉤，根本不可能像妹夫那樣釣到那麼多魚。

passages.text: When they reached the land and were going to haul the canoe up on the beach, Maui told his brother-in-law to get under the outrigger of the canoe and lift it up with his back. As soon as he had done so, Maui jumped on it and pressed the whole weight down upon him, almost killing Irawaru; then he trampled on his body, lengthened his back-bone, and by his enchantments drew it out into the form of a tail, transforming Irawaru into a dog, and fed him with dung. He went home as if nothing unusual had happened, and told Hinauri that if she did not see her husband on the beach she should call out 'Mo-i, mo-i, mo-i'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 2 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們回到陸地上，正要把獨木舟拖上灘時，毛伊叫他的妹夫鑽到獨木舟的舷外浮架下面，用背把它頂起來。他剛一照做，毛伊就跳到上面，把全身的重量都壓在他身上，幾乎把伊拉瓦魯壓死；接著他踐踏他的身體，拉長他的脊骨，又用咒術把它拉長成尾巴的形狀，把伊拉瓦魯變成了一隻狗，還拿糞便餵他。他回到家裡，裝作什麼不尋常的事都沒發生，並告訴希瑙里，如果她在海灘上沒看見她的丈夫，就該高聲呼喊『莫—伊，莫—伊，莫—伊』。

passages.text: Hinauri hurried down to the beach and called as she had been told; Irawaru, running about the bushes in the form of a dog, recognised her voice and answered, 'Ao! ao! ao!' howling like a dog, and followed her back to the village frisking along and wagging his tail. From him sprang all dogs, so that he is regarded as their progenitor, and New Zealanders still call their dogs by the words 'Mo-i, mo-i, mo-i'. When Hinauri saw that her husband had been changed into a dog she was distracted with grief; she caught up her enchanted girdle, ran to the rocks at the ocean's edge, lamented her cruel fate, repeated an incantation, and threw herself into the sea, and the tide swept her off from the shore.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 2 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 希瑙里急忙趕到海灘，照著先前吩咐她的話呼喚；伊拉瓦魯以狗的身形在灌木叢間奔跑，認出了她的聲音，便應道：「嗷！嗷！嗷！」像狗一樣嚎叫，隨後跟著她回到村裡，一路蹦跳著、搖著尾巴。所有的狗都從他而生，因此他被視為狗類的始祖，紐西蘭人至今仍以「莫伊，莫伊，莫伊」這幾個字呼喚他們的狗。希瑙里見丈夫已被變成了一隻狗，悲痛得心神錯亂；她抓起她那條施了魔法的腰帶，奔到海邊的岩石上，哀嘆自己殘酷的命運，念誦了一段咒語，便縱身投入海中，潮水將她從岸邊捲走了。

title.en: Procopius' Testimony: The One God Who Makes the Lightning
title.zh: 普羅科匹厄斯所證：造雷電之獨一神

region.en: Lower Danube, lands of the early Slavs (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 多瑙河下游早期斯拉夫人之地（象徵性定位）

period: Written c. 545 CE (Procopius, Gothic War III.14); recorded by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II intro, quoting Procopius, De Bello Gothico iii.14

summary.en: The oldest external witness to Slavic religion: Procopius reports that the Slavs and Antae believe in one single god, the creator of lightning and lord of all things, to whom they sacrifice cattle — while rivers, nymphs, and other beings receive offerings and oracles beside him.
summary.zh: 斯拉夫宗教最古之外證：普羅科匹厄斯記斯拉夫人與安特人信獨一神——雷電之造者、萬物之主，宰牲祭之；河流、仙靈等亦受祭並示神諭。

sensitivity.note: Byzantine literary source; no living community.

passages.text: Procopius, the Greek historian of the sixth century, writes of the Slavs and Antae: 'They believe that there is one single god who is the creator of the lightning and the sole lord of all things, and to him they sacrifice cattle and all sorts of animals.' Beside this supreme thunder-lord they worship rivers, nymphs, and other deities, sacrificing to all and divining the future from the offerings.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II intro, quoting Procopius; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 六世紀的希臘歷史學家普羅科匹厄斯如此記述斯拉夫人與安特人：「他們相信有一位唯一的神，是閃電的創造者，也是萬物的唯一主宰，他們向他獻祭牛隻與各種動物。」在這位至高的雷神之外，他們還崇拜河流、寧芙以及其他神祇，向所有這些神獻祭，並從祭品中占卜未來。

passages.text: Helmold, chronicling the Elbe Slavs six centuries later, preserves the same shape of belief: among the multiform divine powers who rule fields, forests, sorrows, and joys, one god rules over the others in heaven, pre-eminent in might and caring only for things celestial, while the rest obey the duties assigned them, sprung from his blood and honoured in proportion to their nearness to that god of gods. The name of the chief god has not come down to us, though belief identifies him with Svarog, the heavenly smith.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II intro, quoting Helmold; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 赫爾莫德在六個世紀之後記述易北河斯拉夫人的事蹟時，保存了同一種信仰形態：在掌管田野、森林、悲傷與歡樂的眾多神靈之中，有一位神在天上統轄其餘諸神，權能超群，只關切天上的事物；其餘諸神則各司其職，皆出自他的血脈，並依其與那位眾神之神的親近程度而受尊崇。這位主神的名字並未流傳下來，不過信仰將他與天界的鐵匠斯瓦羅格視為同一。

title.en: The Harvest Festival of Svantovit at Arkona
title.zh: 阿科納的斯萬托維特豐收祭

region.en: Arkona, isle of Rugen (symbolic pin at Cape Arkona)
region.zh: 呂根島阿科納（象徵性定位於阿科納角）

period: Recorded by Saxo Grammaticus c. 1200 (rite pre-1168); recorded by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 1, after Saxo Grammaticus

summary.en: After harvest all Rugen gathers at Arkona: the priest, holding his breath to keep from defiling the god's presence, reads the coming year in the mead sunk in the great horn; a man-sized honey cake is held up with the question 'Can you see me?' — and the wish not to see him next year promises a better harvest.
summary.zh: 豐收之後全島聚於阿科納：祭司屏息以免褻瀆神前，觀蜜酒之降以卜來歲；舉人形蜜糕問『可見我否』——祈來年不見，即兆豐年。

sensitivity.note: Historical rite; the 'see me' formula survives in Slavic Christmas and All-Souls customs.

passages.text: Shortly after harvest a great festival was held in honour of Svantovit, and people assembled from all quarters of the island of Rugen to sacrifice cattle and join the rites. The day before, the sanctuary was carefully swept by the priest, who alone had access to it; while he remained inside he was careful not to breathe, and when he could no longer hold his breath he hastened to the door, lest the presence of the deity be desecrated by the exhalation of a mortal man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 1, after Saxo; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 收穫之後不久，人們為尊崇斯萬托維特舉行了一場盛大的節慶，呂根島四面八方的人們聚集而來，獻祭牛隻並參與儀式。前一日，祭司將聖所仔細打掃乾淨，唯有他得以進入其中；他待在裡面時，小心翼翼地不呼吸，等到再也憋不住氣時，便急忙奔向門口，唯恐凡人的呼氣褻瀆了神明的臨在。

passages.text: On the following day, while the people waited before the entrance, the priest took the great horn from the god's hands: if the mead had sunk, a bad harvest was foretold and the hearers were advised to reserve grain against dearth. He poured the old wine at the divinity's feet, refilled the horn, and asked for victory and increase; then, at one draught, he emptied the cup himself and placed it again in the god's right hand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 翌日，當人們在入口前等候時，祭司從神像手中取下那隻大角杯：倘若其中的蜜酒減少了，便預示歉收，聽者也被勸告要儲糧以防饑荒。他將陳酒傾倒在神像腳前，重新斟滿角杯，祈求勝利與豐產；隨後，他自己一口氣飲盡杯中酒，再將角杯放回神像的右手。

passages.text: Then a festal cake as large as a man, flavoured with honey, was brought in. Placing it between himself and the people the priest asked whether he was visible to them, and on their answering yes, expressed the wish that they might not see him next year — a ceremony believed to ensure a better harvest. He admonished them to keep dutiful homage to the god, and the rest of the day was given to carousing, it being accounted a proof of piety to be drunk.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著，有人端來一個與人一般大、以蜂蜜調味的節慶糕餅。祭司將糕餅置於自己與眾人之間，問他們是否看得見他；眾人答說看得見，他便祝願他們明年見不著他——據信這一儀式能確保更好的收成。他告誡眾人要對神明恪盡崇敬之禮，當日餘下的時間則用於飲宴作樂，因為喝得酩酊大醉被視為虔誠的明證。

title.en: The White Horse of Svantovit: Divination by Spear-Fence
title.zh: 斯萬托維特之白馬：矛柵占卜

region.en: Arkona, isle of Rugen (symbolic pin at Cape Arkona)
region.zh: 呂根島阿科納（象徵性定位於阿科納角）

period: Recorded by Saxo Grammaticus c. 1200; recorded by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 1

summary.en: A sacred white horse is kept for Svantovit, groomed by the high priest, found sweating at dawn from the god's midnight rides; before any war the horse is led through a triple fence of crossed lances — right foot first means victory, and the wrong step forbids the expedition.
summary.zh: 斯萬托維特畜神聖白馬，由大祭司親飼，晨起見汗——神於夜間乘之征戰；凡有戰事，牽馬越三重交矛之柵：右足先跨則勝，錯步則罷兵。

sensitivity.note: Historical rite.

passages.text: A beautiful white horse was consecrated to Svantovit, fed and groomed by the head priest, whom the Rugians honoured as they would the king. The people believed that Svantovit, mounted on this steed, fought by night against those who opposed his worship; in the morning the horse was often found bathed in sweat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 1, after Saxo; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一匹美麗的白馬被奉獻給斯萬托維特，由首席祭司餵養並梳理，魯吉人敬奉他如同敬奉國王一般。人們相信斯萬托維特騎著這匹駿馬，在夜間與那些反對其崇拜的人作戰；到了早晨，這匹馬常被發現渾身是汗。

passages.text: Success or failure in weighty enterprises was divined by the animal. Before a warlike expedition the priests erected three rows of palings, each of two lances driven into the ground with a third laid across them; after solemn prayer the priest led the sacred horse to the palings. If it stepped over right foot first the omen was favourable; if the order was reversed, the expedition had to be abandoned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 重大事業的成敗皆由這動物占卜。在出征之前，祭司們立起三排柵欄，每排由兩支長矛插入地面、再以第三支橫架其上；經過莊嚴的祈禱後，祭司將神馬牽至柵欄前。若牠先邁出右腳跨越，便是吉兆；若順序相反，則須放棄出征。

title.en: The Fall of Arkona, 1168: The Demon Leaves the Broken God
title.zh: 一一六八年阿科納陷落：魔影自碎神而出

region.en: Arkona, isle of Rugen (symbolic pin at Cape Arkona)
region.zh: 呂根島阿科納（象徵性定位於阿科納角）

period: Event of 1168; recorded by Saxo Grammaticus c. 1200 (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 1, after Saxo Grammaticus

summary.en: When King Valdemar of Denmark took Arkona in 1168 the Rugians stood expecting Svantovit to annihilate the enemy to the last; instead the idol was roped and dragged down, a black animal was seen to flee from it, and the god of the western Slavs was smashed and burned.
summary.zh: 一一六八年丹麥王瓦爾德馬攻陷阿科納，呂根人直至最後猶信斯萬托維特將殲敵；神像終遭繩索拖倒，黑獸竄逸，西斯拉夫大神碎而焚之。

sensitivity.note: Historical conquest narrative from the conquerors' side; recorded as such.

passages.text: In 1168 Valdemar, king of the Danes, conquered Arkona after strong resistance. He first seized the treasure of the temple and then ordered the destruction of the sanctuary. A vast multitude of the inhabitants assembled, expecting every moment that Svantovit would annihilate their enemies; but the statue itself was finally torn down.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 1, after Saxo; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 1168年，丹麥國王瓦爾德馬在遭遇頑強抵抗後征服了阿爾科納。他先奪取神廟的財寶，隨後下令摧毀這座聖所。大批居民聚集起來，時時刻刻期待斯萬托維特將消滅他們的敵人；然而神像本身最終仍被推倒。

passages.text: The demon was said to have left the idol in the shape of a black animal which disappeared before the eyes of the spectators. The Danes cast ropes around the god and dragged him to the ground in sight of the Slavs; smashed in pieces, he was burned. The treasure — the offerings of tribute-paying nations, the tithes of war and freebooting gathered by three hundred horsemen devoted to the god — passed to the conquerors, and with it the independence of the western Slavs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說那惡魔化為一頭黑色動物離開了神像，並在旁觀者眼前消失。丹麥人將繩索套在神像上，在斯拉夫人眼前將其拖倒在地；神像被砸成碎片後焚毀。那些財寶——包括納貢諸民族的獻祭、由三百名專奉此神的騎兵所徵集的戰爭與劫掠什一稅——都歸於征服者，隨之而去的還有西斯拉夫人的獨立。

title.en: Triglav of Stettin: The Three-Headed God with the Veiled Face
title.zh: 斯德丁的三頭神：蒙面之特里格拉夫

region.en: Stettin (Szczecin), Pomerania
region.zh: 波美拉尼亞斯德丁（什切青）

period: Recorded by Ebbo/Otto of Bamberg's biographers, early 12th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 2

summary.en: On the central hill of Stettin stood the golden idol of Triglav, three-headed because he rules heaven, earth, and the underworld, veiled because he will not see the sins of men; his black horse, led thrice over nine lances, gave oracles for war — until Bishop Otto broke the statue and sent its head to the Pope.
summary.zh: 斯德丁中央山丘立特里格拉夫金像：三首以示其治天、地、冥三界，蒙面以示不視人罪；黑馬三越九矛以卜戰事——主教奧托碎其像，獻首於教皇。

sensitivity.note: Historical rite and mission narrative.

passages.text: In the town of Stettin were three hills, the central one dedicated to Triglav, the chief local deity. His idol was of gold with three heads, its eyes and lips covered with a golden veil. The pagan priests declared that Triglav — 'Three-Heads' — was tricephalous because he ruled over three realms, heaven, earth, and the underworld, and that he covered his face because he would not see the sins of men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 什切青城中有三座山丘，中央那座奉獻給特里格拉夫，即當地的主神。祂的神像以黃金製成，生有三頭，雙眼與雙唇覆以金色面紗。異教祭司宣稱，特里格拉夫——「三頭」——之所以有三個頭，是因為祂統轄三界：天、地與冥界；而祂遮住面容，是因為不願看見世人的罪惡。

passages.text: The chief of Stettin's four temples was built with wonderful skill, its inner and outer walls covered with embossed figures of men, birds, and animals that seemed to live and breathe. A tenth of all booty was stored in its treasury, with golden horns of wild bulls, gilded and jewelled, some for drinking, some for sounding. A black horse of noble stature was kept for the god: led thrice across nine lances planted before the temple, if he stepped over without touching any, the warlike expedition was decided upon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 什切青四座神廟中的主廟以精妙絕倫的技藝建成，其內外牆壁覆滿浮雕的人、鳥與獸的形象，栩栩如生，彷彿會呼吸一般。一切戰利品的十分之一貯藏於其寶庫中，另有野牛的金角，鍍金並鑲嵌寶石，有的用於飲酒，有的用於吹奏。一匹體態高貴的黑馬專為此神飼養：牽著牠三次跨越神廟前栽下的九支長矛，若牠跨越時未觸及任何一支，便決定出征。

passages.text: When Bishop Otto of Bamberg destroyed the heathen temples, the Slav priests of Wollin are said to have carried their Triglav secretly to a lonely woman, who hid it in the hollow of a large tree; a German, pretending to thank the god for saving him from shipwreck, betrayed her and stole the idol's old saddle. Otto himself broke the Stettin statue and sent its head to the Pope; churches of St. Ethelbert and St. Peter rose on the hill once sacred to Triglav.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當班貝格主教奧托摧毀異教神廟時，據說沃林的斯拉夫祭司將他們的三頭神祇祕密帶到一位孤獨的婦人那裡，她將它藏在一棵大樹的樹洞中；一名德國人假裝感謝神祇救他免於船難，卻背叛了她，偷走了這尊神像的舊馬鞍。奧托本人則砸毀了斯德丁的神像，並將其頭顱送往教宗；聖埃塞爾伯特與聖彼得教堂遂在曾屬三頭神聖地的山丘上興起。

title.en: Svarazic of Radgost: The Son of Svarog Armed in Bison and Bird
title.zh: 拉迪戈斯特的斯瓦拉日茨：佩野牛紋、戴鳥盔之神子

region.en: Radgost (Rethra), land of the Lutices between Elbe and Oder
region.zh: 盧蒂奇人之地拉迪戈斯特（雷特拉）

period: Recorded by Thietmar (c. 1012) and Adam of Bremen (c. 1075); recorded by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 3, after Thietmar and Adam of Bremen

summary.en: In the wooden temple of Radgost the Rhetarii kept Svarazic, 'Son of Svarog', in golden armour, his helmet shaped like a bird with outstretched wings and the black bison of the tribe on his breast; all the Slavic nations came to his oracles — and in 1066 the head of a captured bishop was offered at his altar.
summary.zh: 拉迪戈斯特木構神廟中，雷塔里人奉斯瓦拉日茨——『斯瓦羅格之子』——著金甲、戴展翅鳥盔、胸前飾部族黑野牛紋；斯拉夫諸族皆來求神諭——一〇六六年，被俘主教之首祭於其壇。

sensitivity.note: Historical chronicle material including a recorded human sacrifice; described critically, not endorsed.

passages.text: The Rhetarii, a division of the Lutices between the Elbe and the Oder, worshipped Svarazic — 'Son of Svarog'. The chronicler Thietmar testifies that their castle of Radigast contained a wooden temple full of statues of divinities, made by human hands, wearing armour and helmets that struck terror into beholders, each with his name carved on his image. St. Bruno, apostle of the Prussians, writing to Emperor Henry II, calls him 'Zuarasiz diabolus' — Svarazic the devil.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 3, after Thietmar and Adam of Bremen; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 雷特拉里人（Rhetarii）是易北河與奧得河之間盧蒂奇人的一支，他們崇拜斯瓦拉齊奇（Svarazic）——「斯瓦羅格之子」。編年史家提特馬爾見證，他們的拉迪加斯特城堡中有一座木造神廟，滿是凡人手所造的神祇雕像，身披鎧甲、頭戴頭盔，令觀者心生恐懼，每尊雕像上都刻有其名。普魯士人的使徒聖布魯諾在致皇帝亨利二世的書信中，稱他為「Zuarasiz diabolus」——魔鬼斯瓦拉齊奇。

passages.text: Adam of Bremen describes the god in a spacious sanctuary among other deities: made of gold, his base adorned with brocade, his helmet resembling a bird with outstretched wings, the head of a black bison — emblem of the Rhetarii — on his breast, his right hand resting on it and his left grasping a double-edged axe. The temple was visited by all the Slavic nations for prophecy and the annual festivities; and in 1066, in honour of a victory, the head of John, bishop of Mecklenburg, taken in battle, was offered up to this divinity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 3; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不來梅的亞當描述這位神祇立於其他神祇之間的一處寬敞聖所中：以黃金製成，其底座飾以錦緞，頭盔形似展翅之鳥，胸前有黑色野牛之首——雷特拉里人的標誌——右手按於其上，左手緊握一柄雙刃斧。所有斯拉夫民族皆為求神諭與年度慶典而造訪此廟；1066年，為慶祝一場勝利，於戰鬥中取得的梅克倫堡主教約翰的首級被獻給這位神祇。

title.en: Cernobog: The Toast to the Black God
title.zh: 切爾諾博格：敬黑神之酒

region.en: Elbe Slavic lands (symbolic pin at Lubeck)
region.zh: 易北斯拉夫人之地（象徵性定位於呂貝克）

period: Recorded by Helmold c. 1170 (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 4, after Helmold

summary.en: At their feasts the Elbe Slavs passed a cup around and uttered words in honour of the gods of good and evil alike, believing happiness from the good god but all misfortune from Cernobog, the Black God — and asking the Black God to be merciful.
summary.zh: 易北斯拉夫人宴席上傳杯致祭善惡二神：謂幸福出自善神，一切不幸皆由黑神切爾諾博格所降——故亦求黑神垂憐。

sensitivity.note: The dual-god formula parallels Zoroastrian dualism and Chernobog's modern pop-culture fame; interpretive tagging.

passages.text: Helmold records that at banquets the Slavs were wont to offer prayers to a divinity of good and one of evil: convinced that happiness comes from the god of good and misfortune from the deity of evil, they called the latter Cernobog, the 'Black God'. When the cup went round they uttered words — not only of praise, it seemed, but of appeasement toward the Black God as well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 4, after Helmold; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 赫爾莫德記載，斯拉夫人於宴會時慣於向一位善神與一位惡神祈禱：他們深信幸福來自善神，不幸來自惡神，遂稱後者為切爾諾博格（Cernobog），即「黑神」。當酒杯輪流傳遞時，他們所說的話語——看來不僅是讚美，也是對黑神的安撫。

passages.text: Machal reads the figure critically: the conception of Cernobog as the god of evil probably reflects Christian influence, the western Slavs having transferred to a devil-figure traits of the old deities. He was regarded as the cause of all calamities, and the prayers at banquets were in reality meant to avert misfortune. His bright counterpart, Byelobog the 'White God', appears only in late folk tradition.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 4; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬哈爾對此形象持批判態度：將切爾諾博格視為惡神的觀念，很可能反映了基督教的影響，西斯拉夫人將舊有神祇的特徵轉移到了魔鬼形象之上。他被視為一切災禍的起因，而宴會上的祈禱實際上意在避禍。其光明的對應者貝洛博格（Byelobog），即「白神」，僅見於晚近的民間傳統。

title.en: Ziva: The Goddess of the Living
title.zh: 日瓦：生者之女神

region.en: Polabian lands between Elbe and Baltic (symbolic pin at Lubeck)
region.zh: 易北河至波羅的海之間的波拉比亞（象徵性定位於呂貝克）

period: Recorded by Helmold c. 1170 (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 5

summary.en: The Elbe Slavs worshipped goddesses as well as gods; the only female divinity whose name survives is Ziva, 'the Living', goddess of the Polabians — while the Lutices once angrily avenged an affront done to a goddess whose name is lost.
summary.zh: 易北斯拉夫人既祀男神亦祀女神；女性神祇中唯其名傳世者為日瓦——『生者』，波拉比亞人之女神；盧蒂奇人曾為某失名女神受辱而憤然復仇。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary source; interpretive reconstruction flagged in note.

passages.text: Besides the great male deities the Elbe Slavs worshipped goddesses. Thietmar states that the walls of the temples of Radgost were adorned with figures of deities both male and female, and elsewhere tells how the Lutices angrily resented an affront done to a goddess. The only female divinity actually named, however, is Siva — Ziva, 'the Living' — whom Helmold calls goddess of the Polabians; her Polish counterpart is the Zywie of old tradition.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 5; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 除偉大的男性神祇外，易北河斯拉夫人亦崇拜女神。提特馬爾稱拉德戈斯特神廟的牆壁飾有男神與女神的形象，並在別處講述盧蒂奇人如何憤怒地對一位女神所受的侮辱表示不滿。然而，唯一實際被提及名字的女性神祇是西瓦（Siva）——即日瓦（Ziva），「活者」——赫爾莫德稱其為波拉比亞人的女神；她在波蘭的對應者為古老傳統中的日維（Zywie）。

passages.text: Other names drift through the sources without stories: Pripegala, likened by an astonished archbishop to Priapus; Podaga of Helmold's list; Turupid, Pisamar, and Tiernoglav from the Knytlingasaga. Whatever their rites, the memory of the Baltic-Slav pantheon died with the conversion of the twelfth century — only the bare names and this one goddess of life remain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 5; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 其他名字在史料中流傳，卻沒有故事：普里佩加拉（Pripegala），一位大為驚詫的大主教將其比作普里阿普斯；赫爾莫德名單中的波達加；以及出自《克努特林加傳奇》的圖魯皮德、皮薩馬爾與蒂爾諾格拉夫。無論其儀式如何，波羅的海—斯拉夫萬神殿的記憶都隨著十二世紀的改宗而消亡——只留下那些赤裸的名字，以及這一位生命女神。

title.en: The Gods of Korenice: Seven Faces, Five Heads, and the Forbidden Shield
title.zh: 科倫尼察諸神：七面五首與禁觸之盾

region.en: Isle of Rugen and Wolgast, Baltic coast
region.zh: 呂根島與沃爾加斯特，波羅的海沿岸

period: Recorded by Saxo Grammaticus c. 1200 (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 5

summary.en: Around Arkona stood the sister-shrines: Rugievit, an oak colossus with seven faces and eight swords; Porevit with five heads; Porenutius with four faces and a fifth in his breast; and at Wolgast, Gerovit, war-god of the golden shield that no mortal hand might touch in time of peace.
summary.zh: 阿科納周邊眾姊妹神廟：魯吉耶維特，橡木巨人七面八劍；波列維特五首；波列努提烏斯四面、胸前復一面；沃爾加斯特有戰神蓋羅維特，其金盾非戰時凡人之手不可觸。

sensitivity.note: Historical rite.

passages.text: In the sanctuary of Korenice (modern Garz) on Rugen stood a colossal oaken idol called Rugievit, so high that Bishop Absalon, though a very tall man, could scarcely reach its chin with his axe as he broke it. The image had a single head with seven faces, seven swords hung in its belt, and an eighth blade in its hand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 5, after Saxo; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在呂根島科雷尼采（今加爾茨）的聖所中，矗立著一尊名為魯吉耶維特的巨大橡木神像，其高聳之甚，縱使阿布薩隆主教身材極高，揮斧劈砍時也幾乎搆不到它的下巴。這尊神像只有一個頭，卻有七張面孔，腰帶上懸掛著七把劍，手中還握著第八把刀刃。

passages.text: Another sanctuary held Porevit, five-headed and unarmed, and Porenutius, whose idol had four faces with a fifth in its breast, the left hand raised to its forehead and the right touching its chin. The Pomeranians of Wolgast worshipped Gerovit, a war-god whose enormous shield, wrought with gold, hung in his shrine: carried before the army it ensured victory, but it could be taken down only in time of war, and mortal hands were forbidden to touch it. All these idols appear as local analogues of Svantovit himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 5; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 另一座聖所供奉著波雷維特，五頭而無兵器；還有波雷努提烏斯，其神像有四張面孔，第五張位於胸前，左手舉至額前，右手觸及下巴。沃爾加斯特的波美拉尼亞人崇拜格羅維特，這是一位戰神，其以黃金鑄成的巨盾懸掛於神龕之中：此盾隨軍前行便可確保勝利，但唯有戰時方可取下，且嚴禁凡人之手觸碰。所有這些神像都像是斯萬托維特本人的地方變體。

title.en: The Night on Huanacauri: Youths Ask Leave to Become Knights
title.zh: 瓦納考里之夜:少年求賜騎士之名

region.en: Huanacauri hill, south of Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科以南瓦納考里山(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In the month of Ccapac Raymi the youths about to receive their arms went to the huaca called Huanacauri, their principal huaca - the brother, as was said, of Manco Ccapac, whence they descend - to offer sacrifice and ask permission to receive knighthood. They passed the night on the hill where the huaca was kept, in memory of the journey which their ancestors commenced from that spot, and returned next day bearing loads of straw for their parents to sit on, having fasted on the road.
summary.zh: 卡帕克雷米月,受武之少年往瓦納考里瓦卡——此為其至聖瓦卡,乃曼科·卡帕克之「兄弟」,族人皆出其後——獻祭並求賜騎士之名。他們夜宿藏神像之山,以紀念祖先自該地啟程的旅程;次日攜草束而歸,供父母坐臥,一路齋戒。

sensitivity.note: Initiation vigil at the ancestral huaca-stone; Molina defers the stone-brother tradition to his history of the Incas (cut separately).

passages.text: The youths who were about to receive their arms went to the huaca called Huanacauri, to offer sacrifice, and to ask permission to receive knighthood. For this was their principal huaca, the brother, as was said, of Manco Ccapac, whence they descend.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of October (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 即將接受武器的青年們前往名為瓦納考里的瓦卡，獻上祭品，並請求獲准接受騎士封號。因為這是他們主要的瓦卡，據說是曼科·卡帕克的兄弟，他們即由此而來。

passages.text: The youths who were to be armed as knights passed that night on the hill of Huanacauri, where the huaca was kept, in memory of the journey which their ancestors commenced from that spot. On the next day they returned in the afternoon, bringing with them loads of straw, on which their parents and relations might sit. On this day the youths fasted; and the month was passed in preparing many kinds of chicha for the festival.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of October (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 即將被授予騎士之武器的青年們，當夜在瓦納考里山上度過，瓦卡即供奉於該處，以紀念他們的祖先從此地啟程的旅程。次日午後他們返回，帶回成捆的稻草，供其父母與親屬就坐。這一天青年們齋戒；整個月份都用來為慶典準備各種奇恰酒。

passages.text: At this time, and indeed throughout the year, the priests of the Creator, of the Sun, and of Thunder, and those who had charge of the huaca of Huanacauri, made three daily sacrifices; offering up three sheep, one in the morning, one at noon, and a third at night. The persons also who had charge of the embalmed bodies never came forth to offer up the food and pour out the chicha dedicated to them, such as they used when they were alive; these they consumed, because they held for very truth the doctrine of the immortality of the soul, and said that wherever the soul might be, it would receive the food and eat as when alive.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, month of October (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在此期間，乃至整年之中，造物主、太陽與雷電的祭司們，以及負責瓦納考里瓦卡的人們，每日獻祭三次；獻上三頭羊，一頭在清晨，一頭在正午，第三頭在夜間。負責保存遺體的人們也從不外出獻上食物、傾倒專為死者所備的奇恰酒，一如他們生前所用；這些他們自行享用，因為他們篤信靈魂不滅的教義，並說無論靈魂身在何處，都會領受食物，如同生前一般進食。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)
