passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在古俄羅斯史詩《伊戈爾遠征記》中，弗拉基米爾與羅斯人自稱為達日博格的子孫——古代斯拉夫人常把自己的起源追溯至神靈。達日博格在南斯拉夫人之中也為人所知，他的記憶保存在塞爾維亞童話《達博格》之中：「達博格，那位沙皇，曾在地上，而主神在天上」——這位古老的異教太陽王被重新塑造成一個邪惡的存在，因為早期的基督教把舊神視為魔鬼。

title.en: Svarog the Smith: Who Forged the First Marriage Law
title.zh: 斯瓦羅格鐵匠：鑄造第一婚姻法

region.en: Kiev (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基輔（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded in the Khronika of Malalas redaction, c. 1261; recorded by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 3

summary.en: Svarog, the heavenly smith identified with Hephaestus, forged the sun in his sky-forge and set it in heaven; the chronicle's scholia make him the founder of legal marriage — one man, one wife — ordaining that adulterers be cast into a fiery furnace.
summary.zh: 斯瓦羅格，天之鐵匠，被比為赫菲斯托斯；於天上火爐鑄太陽而置於蒼穹；編年史註疏謂其創婚姻之法——一男一妻，犯者投烈火之爐。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle scholia; the solar smith parallels Tvasty/Ilmarinen.

passages.text: Svarozic was worshipped by the Russians as the god of fire, his name a patronymic meaning 'Son of Svarog'. Svarog himself is mentioned in an old Russian chronicle — the Russian redaction of John Malalas — which identifies him with the Greek Hephaistos. In the Lithuanian redaction the celestial smith Telyaveli 'forged for Perkunas the sun as it shines on earth, and set the sun in heaven'; the same forge-craft belongs to the Slavic sky-smith.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 3; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 斯瓦羅日奇被羅斯人作為火神崇拜，他的名字是一個父稱，意為「斯瓦羅格之子」。斯瓦羅格本人見於一部古俄羅斯編年史——即約翰·馬拉拉斯編年史的俄羅斯修訂本——其中把他等同於希臘的赫菲斯托斯。在立陶宛修訂本中，天界的鐵匠特利亞韋利「為佩爾庫納斯鍛造了照耀於大地之上的太陽，並把太陽安置在天上」；同樣的鍛造技藝也屬於這位斯拉夫的天界鐵匠。

passages.text: The chronicle speaks of Svarog as the founder of legal marriage: under him it was made a law for every man to have only one wife, and for every woman to have only one husband; and whosoever trespassed against this command was to be cast into a fiery furnace. The tradition implies the centrality of fire — hearth and fire-side — for settled family life: the smith-god who forged the sun also forged the law that binds households.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 3; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 編年史稱斯瓦羅格為合法婚姻的創立者：在他治下，立下法律，每個男子只可有一個妻子，每個女子只可有一個丈夫；凡違背此命令者，都要被投入烈火熊熊的爐中。這一傳統意味著火——爐灶與爐火之畔——對於定居的家庭生活具有核心地位：那位鍛造太陽的鐵匠之神，也鍛造了維繫家戶的法律。

title.en: Veles: God of Cattle and Plaited Beard of the Harvest
title.zh: 韋萊斯：牛群之神與收割的『編辮』

region.en: Russia (symbolic pin at Rostov)
region.zh: 俄羅斯（象徵性定位於羅斯托夫）

period: Recorded in the Primary Chronicle (10th-11th c.); recorded by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 5

summary.en: Veles, god of flocks, shared the Russians' oaths with Perun and was cast into the river Pochayna at the baptism; to this day southern Russian reapers plait the last handful of ears and call it 'plaiting the beard of Veles', leaving a piece of bread among the ears.
summary.zh: 牛群之神韋萊斯與佩倫同受羅斯人之誓，受洗時其像被投入波恰伊納河；至今南俄收割者將最後一把麥穗打結，稱『為韋萊斯編鬚』，穗中猶置麵包一塊。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle and living custom.

passages.text: Veles, the god of flocks, was held in high honour by the Russians, who swore by him as well as by Perun when making a treaty. When Vladimir was baptized in 988 he caused the idols of Veles to be thrown into the river Pochayna; a stone statue of the same deity, worshipped by Slavic tribes in the neighbourhood of Finland, was destroyed by Abraham of Rostov, who preached Christianity on the banks of the Volga in the twelfth century. The Tale of Igor's Campaign calls the minstrel Boyan 'the grandson of Veles'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 5; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 韋萊斯是畜群之神，深受羅斯人尊崇，他們在締結條約時既向佩倫起誓，也向韋萊斯起誓。弗拉基米爾於988年受洗時，命人把韋萊斯的偶像投入波恰伊納河；同一神祇的一尊石像曾受芬蘭附近一帶斯拉夫部落的崇拜，於十二世紀被在伏爾加河畔傳播基督教的羅斯托夫的亞伯拉罕所毀。《伊戈爾遠征記》稱吟遊詩人博揚為「韋萊斯之孫」。

passages.text: The memory of Veles still lives among the Russian people: in southern Russia it is customary at harvest-time to tie the last handful of ears into a knot, 'plaiting the beard of Veles' or 'leaving a handful of ears for Veles's beard'; in some districts a piece of bread is put among such ears, probably a reminiscence of the sacrifices offered to the god. After the conversion his worship was transferred to St. Blasius, shepherd and martyr of Caesarea, guardian of flocks — while in Bohemia his very name came to mean simply 'the devil'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 5; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 韋萊斯的記憶至今仍活在俄羅斯人民之中：在俄羅斯南部，收穫時節有將最後一把麥穗打成結的習俗，稱為「編織韋萊斯的鬍鬚」或「留下一把麥穗作韋萊斯的鬍鬚」；有些地區會在這類麥穗中放一塊麵包，這大概是獻給此神的祭品之遺風。改宗之後，對他的崇拜轉移到了聖布拉修斯身上——他是凱撒利亞的牧者與殉道者、畜群的守護者——而在波希米亞，他的名字竟逕直意指「魔鬼」。

title.en: Stribog: Grandfather of the Winds
title.zh: 斯特里博格：眾風之祖父

region.en: Kiev hill (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基輔山丘（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded in the Primary Chronicle and the Tale of Igor's Campaign; recorded by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 5

summary.en: Stribog's idol stood on the Kiev hill beside Perun's; the Tale of Igor's Campaign calls the winds 'the grandsons of Stribog' — a god of cold and frost, from whose breath the winds themselves were thought to blow.
summary.zh: 斯特里博格之像立於基輔丘佩倫像之側；《伊戈爾遠征記》稱風為『斯特里博格之孫』——乃寒霜之神，風即自其呼息而生。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle source.

passages.text: Stribog, whose idol stood on the hill in Kiev beside that of Perun, was most probably the god of cold and frost. In the Tale of Igor's Campaign the winds are called 'the grandsons of Stribog' — a conception of the winds as the result of cold and frost, children and children's children of the frozen god.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 5; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 斯特里博格的偶像曾與佩倫的偶像並立於基輔的山丘上，他極可能是寒冷與霜凍之神。在《伊戈爾遠征記》中，諸風被稱為「斯特里博格的孫兒」——這是一種把風視為寒冷與霜凍之產物的觀念，即冰凍之神的子孫與曾孫。

passages.text: The chronicler Cosmas testifies that the Bohemians worshipped deities similar to Jupiter, Mars, Bellona, and Ceres, making idols of them; but their names are lost. Dlugosz records a crowd of Polish divinities, though his late and classicizing report is unreliable. Of the old Kiev pantheon, Stribog and Simargl stand as the barest names — the wind-god and the winged sentinel of the Persian imagination, both set one day on the same Dnieper hill as Perun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 5; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 編年史家科斯馬斯記載，波希米亞人崇拜類似朱庇特、瑪爾斯、貝羅娜與刻瑞斯的神祇，並為之造像；但他們的名字已失傳。德烏戈什記錄了一大群波蘭神祇，然而他這份晚出且帶古典化色彩的記述並不可靠。在舊基輔萬神殿中，斯特里博格與西馬爾格爾僅存其名——一為風神，一為波斯想像中的有翼守衛，二者有朝一日同被安置在與佩倫相同的第聶伯河山丘上。

title.en: The Sun in the Tower: Why the Iron Hammer Is Worshipped
title.zh: 塔中日頭：鐵錘受拜之故

region.en: Lithuania (symbolic pin at Vilnius)
region.zh: 立陶宛（象徵性定位於維爾紐斯）

period: Recorded by Aeneas Sylvius (Pius II, d. 1464) from missionary Jerome; recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V, after Aeneas Sylvius

summary.en: A mighty king once imprisoned the sun for months in a strongly fortified tower; the signs of the zodiac broke the tower with a huge hammer and set the sun free — which is why, the missionaries reported, the old Lithuanians worshipped an iron hammer of rare size.
summary.zh: 古有強王將太陽囚於堅塔數月；黃道諸宮以巨錘破塔救日——傳教士所記立陶宛人敬奉特大鐵錘之由即在此。

sensitivity.note: Early missionary report through Papal circles; tagged interpretively.

passages.text: Aeneas Sylvius (afterward Pope Pius II) reports, on the information of the Camaldolite hermit Jerome who had long served as missionary in Lithuania, that a Lithuanian people worshipped the sun and venerated with curious cult an iron hammer of rare size. When the priests were asked what the veneration meant, they answered that once upon a time the sun was not seen for several months, because a most mighty king had imprisoned it in the dungeon of a tower right strongly fortified.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V, after Aeneas Sylvius; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 埃涅阿斯·西爾維烏斯（後來的教宗庇護二世）根據曾在立陶宛長期擔任傳教士的卡馬爾多利會隱修士傑羅姆所提供的消息記載：有一個立陶宛民族崇拜太陽，並以奇特的儀式崇敬一把碩大罕見的鐵鎚。當祭司被問及這崇敬之意義時，他們回答說，從前有一次，太陽有好幾個月不見蹤影，因為一位極其強大的國王將它囚禁在一座防禦極為堅固的塔樓地牢之中。

passages.text: Then the signs of the zodiac bore aid to the sun, broke the tower with a huge hammer, and restored to men the liberated sun — so that the instrument by which mortals regained the light was held worthy of veneration. Mannhardt read the myth as the darkening of the sun in winter and its return in the storms of spring; the real destroyer of the tower was Perkunas, god of thunder and chief Baltic deity. Lithuanians call the prehistoric stone celt 'Perkunas's ball' or 'Perkunas's stone' — the parallel with Thor's hammer is immediate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是黃道十二宮的諸星座前來援助太陽，以一把巨鎚擊破塔樓，將獲釋的太陽還給了人們——因此，凡人藉以重獲光明的那件器具便值得崇敬。曼哈特將此神話解讀為太陽在冬季的晦暗及其在春日風暴中的回歸；真正摧毀塔樓的是佩爾庫納斯，即雷神與波羅的海諸神之首。立陶宛人稱史前石斧為「佩爾庫納斯之球」或「佩爾庫納斯之石」——與索爾之鎚的對應關係顯而易見。

title.en: Perkune Tete, Mother of Lightning: Who Bathes the Weary Sun
title.zh: 雷母佩爾庫內·泰特：為倦日沐浴

region.en: Lithuania (symbolic pin at Kaunas)
region.zh: 立陶宛（象徵性定位於考納斯）

period: Recorded from Lithuanian folk tradition; recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: Perkune Tete, mother of lightning and thunder, receives at night the weary, dusty sun; she washes her and sends her forth on the morrow bathed and shining — the nightly return of the day.
summary.zh: 雷電之母佩爾庫內·泰特，夜間迎回塵勞之倦日；為之沐浴，翌晨送其容光煥發而升——晝夜更替即如此夜夜重演。

sensitivity.note: Folk fragment.

passages.text: The second of the two old myths recorded of the Lithuanians is still briefer than the first: Perkune Tete, 'Mother of Lightning and Thunder', receives at night the weary, dusty sun, whom she sends forth on the morrow bathed and shining.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 立陶宛人所記載的兩則古老神話中的第二則，比第一則更為簡短：佩爾庫內·特特，即「閃電與雷霆之母」，在夜間迎接疲憊而滿身塵土的太陽，並於翌日將其沐浴潔淨、容光煥發地送出。

passages.text: In the dainas the same daily round is sung as an economy: Morning Star makes the Sun's fire and Evening Star prepares her couch; the golden cock on the edge of the Great Water rouses the sun's daughter to spin the silver thread of dawn. The Baltic sky is run like a great household, and the mother of lightning is the bath-keeper of the world's light.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在達伊納（dainas）中，同樣的日常輪轉被歌詠為一種生計：晨星為太陽生火，晚星為她鋪設床榻；大水邊緣的金色公雞喚醒太陽之女，讓她紡出黎明的銀線。波羅的海的天空如同一戶大家庭般運轉，而閃電之母則是世間之光的浴場看守。

title.en: Why the Moon Wanes: The Moon Who Forsook the Sun
title.zh: 月之所以虧：棄日而奔晨星之月

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Daina recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); material pre-Christian; recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V, after the dainas collected by Mannhardt

summary.en: In the primal spring the Moon wedded the Sun, but he forsook her and loved the Morning Star; Perkunas, filled with wrath, smote the Moon with his sword — 'Wherefore hast thou left thy Sun?' — and the god's grief-struck blow is the waning of the moon.
summary.zh: 原初之春，月娶日，旋棄之而愛晨星；佩爾庫納斯怒不可遏，拔劍擊月——『何故棄汝之日？』——那一擊之痛，即月之盈虧。

sensitivity.note: Celestial-marriage cluster parallel to Sumerian Nanna-Sarru? tagged as daina translation (Mannhardt's German rendering, PD).

passages.text: Home the Moon once led the Sun in the very primal spring; early did the Sun arise, but the Moon from her withdrew. Leaving her, he roamed afar, and the Morning Star he loved. Perkunas then was filled with wrath, and with his sword he smote the Moon: 'Wherefore hast thou left thy Sun? Wherefore roam'st thou alone by night? Wherefore lovest thou Morning Star?' Full of sorrow was his heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the daina as rendered by Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在最初的原初之春，月亮曾引領太陽回家；太陽早早升起，月亮卻從她身旁退去。他離開她，遠遊四方，並愛上了晨星。佩爾庫納斯（Perkunas）於是滿懷憤怒，以劍擊打月亮：「你為何離開你的太陽？你為何獨自夜遊？你為何愛上晨星？」他的心充滿悲傷。

passages.text: The daina holds the myth of the conjunction of sun and moon, their gradual divergence until the moon stands with the morning star, the wrath of Perkunas — who is not merely god of thunder but the great Baltic deity — and the explanation of the moon's changing form as he wanes. In the Baltic languages the sun is feminine and the moon masculine; the Lettish variant carries the tale further, for there the moon and sun have many children, the stars.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 達伊納承載著日月相合的神話、二者逐漸分離直至月亮與晨星並立、佩爾庫納斯的憤怒——他不僅是雷神，更是波羅的海的伟大神祇——以及月亮虧缺時形貌變化的解釋。在波羅的海諸語言中，太陽為陰性，月亮為陽性；拉脫維亞（Lettish）的異文將故事推得更遠，因為在那裡月亮與太陽育有許多子女，即群星。

title.en: The Broken Oak at the Wedding: The Sun's Daughter Washes Out the Blood
title.zh: 婚禮上斷裂的橡樹：日之女洗滌血漬

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Daina recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: When Morning Star wed the Sun's daughter, Perkunas rode through the doorway and shattered the green oak; its blood — the red rays of evening — spattered the bride's garments, and for three years she gathered the seared leaves, asking where to wash, where to dry, where to don her white — 'upon that day when nine suns shall be shining.'
summary.zh: 晨星娶日之女之日，佩爾庫納斯縱馬穿門、劈裂綠橡；橡之血——即暮空紅霞——濺遍新娘衣裙；三年間她拾枯葉，問何處可洗、何處可晾、何處可著素衣——『待九日同輝之時。』

sensitivity.note: Daina.

passages.text: When Morning Star was wedded, Perkunas rode through the doorway and the green oak he shattered; then forth the oak's blood spurted, besprinkling all the bride's garments and her crownlet. With streaming eyes the Sun's daughter for three years collected the leaves, all sear and withered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the daina as rendered by Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當晨星成婚之時，佩爾庫納斯騎馬穿過門道，擊碎了那棵綠橡樹；於是橡樹的血液噴湧而出，濺滿了新娘所有的衣裳與她的花冠。太陽之女淚眼汪汪，花了三年時間收集那些葉子，全都枯焦凋零。

passages.text: 'Oh where, oh where, my mother, shall I now wash my garments, and where wash out the blood-stains? — My daughterling, so youthful, swift haste unto the fountain wherein nine brooks are flowing. And where dry them in the breezes? — In the garden where roses nine are blooming. And where don my garments bright gleaming in their whiteness? — Upon that day, my daughter, when nine suns shall be shining.' The fountain of nine brooks, the nine roses, the nine suns, the apple-tree of nine branches — all are the rays of the sun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the daina as rendered by Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「哦，母親，我如今該到何處洗我的衣裳，又該到何處洗去血跡？——我的小女兒啊，如此年輕，快快趕往那有九條溪流流淌的泉邊。那又該在何處的微風中晾乾它們？——在九株玫瑰盛開的花園裡。那我該在何處穿上我潔白閃耀的衣裳？——我的女兒啊，就在九個太陽一同照耀的那一天。」九條溪流的泉、九株玫瑰、九個太陽、九枝的蘋果樹——全都是太陽的光芒。

title.en: The Devil Struck Down for Seven Years: Perkunas and the Unending Battle
title.zh: 魔墮七年：佩爾庫納斯與無盡之戰

region.en: Lithuania (symbolic pin at Vilnius)
region.zh: 立陶宛（象徵性定位於維爾紐斯）

period: Folk belief recorded 19th c.; recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: When Perkunas smites a devil with his bolt he does not kill him but casts him down to hell for seven years, after which the fiend is abroad again — the same unfinished victory as Indra's over the storm-dragon, so the battle between thunder-god and demon must be forever renewed.
summary.zh: 佩爾庫納斯以雷擊魔，不誅而逐之入冥七年；期满魔復出——與因陀羅之戰龍同一未竟之局，雷神與魔之戰遂永無終期。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief; Indo-European dragon-fight cluster.

passages.text: All sources for Baltic religion agree that Perkunas, god of thunder and lightning, was the chief deity: thunder was his voice, by which he revealed his will to men, and he sent the fertilizing rains — the Indra of the Prussians, Lithuanians, and Letts. He has, moreover, Indra's most telling resemblance: when he smites a devil with his bolt, he does not kill the fiend.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 所有關於波羅的海宗教的資料都一致認為，雷電之神佩爾庫納斯是主神：雷是他的聲音，藉此他向人揭示其意志，並送來滋養萬物的雨水——他是普魯士人、立陶宛人與拉脫維亞人的因陀羅（Indra）。此外，他還具有因陀羅最顯著的特徵：當他以雷霆擊打魔鬼時，他並不殺死那惡魔。

passages.text: He merely strikes the demon down to hell for seven years, after which time the fiend again appears on earth — exactly as Indra and his Iranian doublets do not slay the storm-dragon but only wound him or imprison him so insecurely that he escapes. The battle must therefore be constantly renewed; every bolt that splits an oak in the Lithuanian summer is another round of a fight that never ends.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他只把惡魔擊落地獄七年，七年之後那惡魔又出現在大地上——正如因陀羅及其伊朗的對應者並不殺死風暴之龍，而只是將它擊傷，或把它囚禁得如此不牢靠，以致它終能逃脫。因此這場戰鬥必須不斷重演；在立陶宛的夏日裡，每一道劈開橡樹的閃電，都是這場永無終止之戰的又一回合。

title.en: The Nine Sons of God: Three Shatter, Three Thunder, Three Lighten
title.zh: 神之九子：三碎三轟三閃

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Dainas recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: The dainas speak of God's sons — nine in number: three who shatter in pieces, three who thunder, three who lighten; they live in Germany, in the darkening west, where their father rides with smoke-grey horses to seek a bride.
summary.zh: 達伊納斯詠神之九子：三者碎物、三者鳴雷、三者閃電；皆居『德意志』——即西沉之暗方；其父乘灰雲之馬，往彼處覓偶。

sensitivity.note: Daina; 'God' here = Perkunas as all-god.

passages.text: In the dainas 'God' (Lettish Dievs) can mean in Baltic none other than Perkunas, the deity par excellence, just as in Greece the unqualified 'god' means Zeus. His sons are nine in number: three shatter in pieces, three thunder, and three lighten; in other poems he has only five; but in any case they all live in Germany — in other words, in the darkening west, whither their father himself goes, across the sea, to seek a bride.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在達伊納（daina）中，「神」（拉脫維亞語作 Dievs）在波羅的海地區所指的，不外乎就是佩爾庫納斯（Perkunas），那位至高無上的神祇，正如在希臘，不加限定語的「神」所指的就是宙斯。他的兒子共有九個：三個將萬物擊成碎片，三個打雷，三個閃電；在另一些詩歌中他只有五個兒子；但無論如何，他們全都住在德意志——換句話說，住在漸趨昏暗的西方，他們的父親本人也渡海前往那裡，去尋覓新娘。

passages.text: He smites the demonic Iohdi, the spirits that battle in the northern lights; he strikes the sea in which the sun is drowned at evening. But where he goes with his gentle smoke-grey horses — the clouds — the meadows flourish: the sun rises through the saddle of his steed and the moon through the bit, and at the end of the rein is the morning star. He gives the moon a hundred sons, the stars: a sky-god in process of elevation to all-god.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他擊打那惡魔般的約赫迪（Iohdi），那些在極光中爭戰的幽靈；他擊打那黃昏時分太陽沉溺其中的大海。但當他帶著他那溫順的煙灰色馬匹——即雲——所到之處，草甸便繁茂起來：太陽從他駿馬的鞍中升起，月亮從馬銜中升起，而韁繩的末端則是晨星。他賜予月亮一百個兒子，即群星：一位正被提升為萬有之神的天空之神。

title.en: The Sun in Silver Shoes: Dances on the Silver Mount
title.zh: 銀履之太陽：舞於銀山

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Dainas recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: In the dainas the Sun wears silver shoes and dances on the silver mount, sails a silver sea, is herself a silver apple; at evening she crowns the linden with gold, the oak with silver, each little willow with a ring — and weeps because the golden apple has fallen from the tree.
summary.zh: 達伊納斯中之太陽著銀履、舞銀山、泛銀海，其身亦如銀蘋果；日暮時以金冠贈菩提、銀冠贈橡樹、戒指贈柳枝——又因金蘋果離樹而泣。

sensitivity.note: Daina.

passages.text: We think of the sun as golden, and rightly; yet in the dainas she wears silver shoes and dances on the silver mount, sails over a silver sea, scatters gifts of silver, sows silver, or is herself a silver apple, a boat of silver, bronze, and gold, or half gold and half silver — all the shadings of her various stations in the sky. Her hundred brown horses are her rays; in the east, where she rises, lives a gold and diamond steed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 我們認為太陽是金色的，這想法不錯；然而在達伊納中，她穿著銀鞋，在銀山上起舞，航行於銀海之上，散播銀的禮物，播種銀子，或者她本身就是一顆銀蘋果，一艘由銀、青銅與黃金製成的船，或半金半銀——凡此種種，皆是她於天空中種種不同居處的色調變化。她那一百匹棕色馬匹便是她的光芒；在東方，即她升起之處，住著一匹金與鑽石的駿馬。

passages.text: When she sets she gives a golden crown to the linden, a silver coronet to the oak, and a golden ring to each little willow. She weeps bitterly because the golden apple has fallen from the tree — a myth of sunset — but 'God' will make her another of gold, brass, or silver. She herself is an apple sleeping in an apple-garden, decked with apple-blossoms: the fleecy clouds of dawn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當她落下時，她賜給椴樹一頂金冠，賜給橡樹一頂銀冠，並賜給每一株小柳樹一枚金戒指。她痛哭不已，因為那金蘋果已從樹上墜落——這是日落的祕儀——但「神」將為她另造一顆，或金、或黃銅、或銀。她本身就是一顆睡在蘋果園中的蘋果，綴滿蘋果花：那黎明的絮狀雲霞。

title.en: The Drowned Daughter: Fishing the Sun's Ring from the Sea
title.zh: 溺沒之女：自海中釣回太陽之戒

region.en: Latvia, river Daugava (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞道加瓦河（象徵性定位）

period: Dainas recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: The Sun's daughter's chief task is to wash her golden jug — the solar disk — at evening; she loses it and is herself drowned, falling into a golden boat left behind on the waves — until 'God's sons' row out and rescue her, that she may reappear at dawn.
summary.zh: 日之女之務為日暮洗其金壺——即日輪；壺失人溺，身墜金舟，舟尚留於浪間——直至『神之子』搖櫓而出，救其上岸，以待黎明重現。

sensitivity.note: Daina.

passages.text: The daughters of the sun and the sons of God are the Baltic counterparts of the Vedic Usas and Asvins, of the Greek Helen and Dioskouroi. The sun's daughter's chief task is to wash her golden jug — the solar disk — at evening. This she loses, and she herself is drowned; or else she falls into a golden boat which remains behind her on the waves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 太陽的女兒們與神之子們，是吠陀的烏莎斯（Usas）與阿濕波（Asvins）、希臘的海倫與狄俄斯庫里（Dioskouroi）在波羅的海地區的對應者。太陽之女的主要任務，是在傍晚洗滌她的金壺——即日輪。她失去了這金壺，自己也溺亡了；或者她跌入一艘金船，那金船留在她身後的波浪上。

passages.text: Sometimes 'God's sons' row the boat which rescues her as she wades in the sea, so that she can reappear at dawn. Occasionally the youth stands passively on the mountain while she sinks; or instead of wedding her he merely escorts her to Germany. Behind the mountain stands the oak beneath which the lovers dance: there 'God's son' hangs his girdle and the sun's daughter her crown. When, in other dainos, the solar jug is broken by 'little John', it is the waning strength of the sun's rays after Midsummer Eve.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有時「神的兒子們」划著船，在她涉水入海時將她救起，使她得以在黎明時重現。偶爾那青年只是被動地立於山上，看著她沉落；或者他不娶她為妻，只護送她前往德意志。山後立著那棵橡樹，戀人們在樹下起舞：在那裡，「神的兒子」掛上他的腰帶，太陽之女掛上她的冠冕。而在其他的達伊諾斯中，當太陽的陶罐被「小約翰」打破時，那所指的正是仲夏節前夕之後太陽光芒漸衰的力量。

title.en: Under the Maple: God's Son Courts the Sun's Daughter
title.zh: 楓樹泉畔：神之子求愛日之女

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Dainas recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: 'Neath a maple lies a fountain whither God's sons hasten to dance with God's daughters while the moon shines: the maiden washing her face loses her ring in the water, and the young hero on the brown charger comes asking her to speak of love where the stream is deepest — her mother chides, and the swans excuse was not believed.
summary.zh: 楓下有泉，神之子月明中疾趨與神之女共舞；少女濯面失戒於水，騎棕馬之少年來求她共語情長於最深处——母親嗔怪，天鵝攪水之託辭亦未獲信。

sensitivity.note: Daina.

passages.text: 'Neath a maple lies a fountain whither God's sons hastening go to dance with God's own daughters while the moon shines o'er them. In the fountain by the maple the maiden was laving her white face — and lo, her ring she washed off. 'Will the sons of God come hither with their nets all silken? Will they fish my ring so tiny from the depths of water?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the daina as rendered by Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一棵楓樹下有一泓泉水，神的兒子們匆匆趕往那裡，與神自己的女兒們共舞，月光照耀在她們身上。在楓樹旁的泉邊，那少女正洗濯她白皙的面龐——瞧，她把戒指洗落了。「神的兒子們會不會帶著全絲的網來到此地？他們會不會從水深之處把我那小小的戒指撈起？」

passages.text: Then there came a youthful hero, his brown charger riding, his shoes golden. 'Hither come, O maiden — with fair words let us be speaking, where the stream is deepest and love is sweetest.' 'Nay, I cannot, hero, for my mother dear will chide me if I tarry longer.' 'Speak thus to her: two swans came flying and troubled the water's depth; till it cleared I waited.' But the mother knew: 'Not true, my daughter — beneath the maple with a youth thou wast exchanging words of love's sweet language.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the daina as rendered by Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隨後來了位年輕的英雄，騎著他的褐色駿馬，腳穿金鞋。「來吧，哦少女——讓我們以美好的言語交談，就在那溪流最深、愛情最甜之處。」「不，我不能，英雄，因為我親愛的母親會責罵我，若我再多逗留。」「就這般對她說：兩隻天鵝飛來，攪渾了水深；我直等到水清。」但母親心裡明白：「不實，我的女兒——在楓樹下，你正與一個青年交換著愛情的甜言蜜語。」

title.en: The Orphan Girl of the Golden Hedge
title.zh: 金籬笆下的孤女

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Dainas recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: When the sun is drowned in the sea her daughter is an orphan; God makes a golden hedge — the sunset — and sets the orphan girl as its guardian, charging her not to break off the golden boughs; she disobeys and flees to Mary's bath-chamber, the darkness of night, where God and his sons refuse her forgiveness.
summary.zh: 日沉於海，其女成孤；神築金籬——即晚霞——立孤女為守，戒其勿折金枝；她抗命而逃至瑪利亞浴堂——夜之幽暗——神與其子至，拒予赦免。

sensitivity.note: Daina; 'Mary' read as Christianized evening star.

passages.text: When the sun is drowned in the sea, her daughter is naturally regarded as an orphan; and thus a daina tells how God makes a golden hedge — the sunset — to which his sons come riding on sweating horses. There they find the orphan girl, whom they make its guardian, charging her not to break off the golden boughs — the rays of the setting sun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當太陽沉沒於海中，她的女兒自然被視為孤兒；於是有一首達伊諾講述神如何造了一道金色的籬笆——即日落——他的兒子們騎著汗濕的馬來到籬前。他們在那裡發現了那孤女，便命她為籬笆的守護者，囑咐她不可折斷金色的枝條——即落日的光芒。

passages.text: She disobeys, and flees to the valley of Mary's bath-chamber — the darkness of night. Thither God and his sons come, but refuse forgiveness for her transgression of their commands. 'Mary' is perhaps a Christianized substitute for the planet Venus as the evening star: the orphan of the golden hedge is twilight itself, punished for outliving her parent light.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她違命了，逃往瑪利亞沐浴室的谷地——即夜的黑暗。神與他的兒子們來到那裡，卻拒絕寬恕她違背他們命令的過犯。「瑪利亞」或許是金星作為昏星的基督教化替代：金色籬笆的孤女正是暮光本身，因比她的母光存活得更久而受罰。

title.en: The Key to the House of Souls
title.zh: 亡魂之家的鑰匙

region.en: Latvia, river Daugava (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞道加瓦河（象徵性定位）

period: Dainas recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: The Great Water — the celestial Daugawa — flows black at evening because it is full of the souls of the departed; at midnight a star descends to the house of souls. The Sun's daughter keeps the key to the realm of the dead, and Mother Earth is besought to give it that a brother's grave may be unlocked.
summary.zh: 偉大之水——天上道加瓦——暮時流黑，因滿載逝者之魂；子夜一星降至亡魂之家。日之女掌冥界之鑰；欲啟亡兄之墓，須求大地之母賜鑰。

sensitivity.note: Daina.

passages.text: The sea of the dainas is the celestial ocean of Indo-Iranian mythology, and the 'Great Water' (Daugawa), though now identified by the Letts with the river Dvina, is to be read in the same way. This Daugawa flows black at evening because it is full of the souls of the departed, and at midnight a star descends to 'the house of souls'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 達伊諾斯中的海，即印伊神話中的天海；而「大水」（道加瓦），雖然如今被拉脫維亞人等同於德維納河，也應以同樣的方式解讀。這條道加瓦在傍晚時分流淌著黑色，因為它滿是亡者的靈魂；而在午夜，一顆星會降臨「靈魂之屋」。

passages.text: Very appropriately, therefore, the sun's daughter has the key to the realm of the dead; and at evening 'Mother Earth' (Zemes Mate), from whom one asks whatever may be lost or hidden, is besought to give this key. In the afternoon God's children shut the door of heaven, so that one should be buried in the morning; and the sun's daughter is entreated to give a key that an only brother's grave may be unlocked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 因此，太陽的女兒掌管亡者之域的鑰匙，實為再恰當不過；而到了傍晚，人們便向「大地之母」（Zemes Mate）祈求賜下這把鑰匙——凡有所失或有所隱匿者，皆向她求問。午後，神的孩子們關閉天門，故人應於清晨下葬；人們又懇求太陽的女兒賜下鑰匙，以便開啟獨生兄弟的墳墓。

title.en: Telyaveli: The Smith Who Forged the Sun for Perkunas
title.zh: 特利亞韋利：為佩爾庫納斯鑄日之鐵匠

region.en: Lithuania (symbolic pin at Vilnius)
region.zh: 立陶宛（象徵性定位於維爾紐斯）

period: Recorded in the Russian redaction (1261) of John Malalas; recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V, after the Malalas redaction of 1261

summary.en: In his sky-forge on the edge of the sea or of the Daugawa, the celestial smith Telyaveli makes spurs and a girdle for God's son and a crown and ring for the sun's daughter — the rays of the rising sun and the solar disk themselves; the old redaction says he 'forged for Perkunas the sun as it shines on earth, and set the sun in heaven.'
summary.zh: 天上鐵匠特利亞韋利於海畔或道加瓦畔之爐中，為神之子鑄馬刺與腰帶，為日之女鑄冠與環——即朝陽之芒與日輪本身；古抄本云其『為佩爾庫納斯鑄世上所照之太陽，置於天上』。

sensitivity.note: Smith-god parallels Tvasty, Ilmarinen, Wieland, Hephaistos.

passages.text: The celestial smith has his forge in the sky, on the edge either of the sea or of the Daugawa; there he makes spurs and a girdle for 'God's son', and a crown and ring for the sun's daughter — in other words, from his smithy come the rays of the rising sun and the solar disk itself. Mannhardt regards this smith as the glow of dawn or sunset, and compares him to the Finno-Ugric Ilmarinen, the Teutonic Wieland, and the Greek Hephaistos.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天上的鐵匠在天上有他的鍛爐，位於海邊或道加瓦河畔；他在那裡為「神之子」打造馬刺與腰帶，為太陽的女兒打造王冠與戒指——換言之，初升太陽的光芒乃至日輪本身，皆出自他的鐵匠鋪。曼哈特（Mannhardt）視此鐵匠為黎明或日暮的霞光，並將他比作芬諾—烏戈爾的伊爾瑪利寧（Ilmarinen）、條頓的維蘭德（Wieland）以及希臘的赫菲斯托斯（Hephaistos）。

passages.text: A still closer analogue is the Vedic Tvasty who wrought the cup that holds the gods' nectar; and it is even possible that he is ultimately the same as the Slavic deity Svarog, the heavenly smith. His name is given as Telyaveli or Telyavelik in the Russian redaction (dating from 1261) of the Byzantine historian John Malalas, which says that he 'forged for him (Perkunas) the sun as it shines on earth, and set the sun in heaven.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 更為相近的類比是吠陀的陀濕多（Tvasty），他鍛造了盛裝眾神瓊漿的杯盞；甚至有可能，他最終與斯拉夫神祇斯瓦羅格（Svarog）——天上的鐵匠——實為同一。他的名字在拜占庭史家約翰·馬拉拉斯（John Malalas）的俄文改編本（成書於1261年）中作 Telyaveli 或 Telyavelik，書中說他「為他（佩爾庫納斯）鍛造了照耀大地的太陽，並將太陽安置於天上」。

title.en: Up the Rose-Tree to Heaven: The Deserted Daughter's Climb
title.zh: 沿玫瑰樹攀天：被棄之女的攀登

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Daina recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: Zemina the flower-giver bids the deserted maiden plant her roses on the lofty mountain-summit; from the rose-trunk springs a mighty tree whose branches reach the heavens, and the girl climbs it to find a youthful hero riding God's charger — the evening star — who sends her down to the valley where her parents plan her sister's marriage.
summary.zh: 花之賜予者澤米娜命被棄少女將玫瑰植於高山之巔；玫瑰幹中長出參天巨樹，枝達天穹；少女攀樹上天，遇騎神駒之少年英雄——即晚星——被遣往山谷，父母正為其妹籌婚。

sensitivity.note: Daina; parallel to the Jack-and-the-Beanstalk cycle noted by Gray.

passages.text: 'O Zemina, flower-giver, where shall I now plant the roses?' — 'On the lofty mountain-summit, by the ocean, by the sea-side.' 'Where shall I find father, mother, I, deserted and a pauper?' — 'Haste thee to the lofty mountain.' Forth then from the rose-trunk springing grew a mighty tree and lofty till its branches reached the heavens: 'I will climb up to the heavens on the branches of the roses.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the daina as rendered by Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「哦，澤米娜（Zemina），賜花者啊，我如今該把玫瑰種在何處？」——「種在高聳的山巔，在大洋之畔，在海濱。」「我這孤苦無依之人，何處才能尋得父親、母親？」——「快快前往那高聳的山上。」於是，從玫瑰的莖幹中長出一株參天大樹，高聳入雲，枝條直抵天際：「我要順著玫瑰的枝條攀上天去。」

passages.text: There she found a youthful hero riding on God's charger. 'O fair youth, hast thou not seen father, mother?' — 'Seek the region of the valley; there thy father, there thy mother plan the marriage of thy sister.' So she hasted to the valley: 'Why did ye leave me, an infant, to the mercy of the stranger?' — 'Grown to be a sturdy maiden, I alone have found the cradle where in childhood I was happy.' Here sun and moon have departed from their daughter, the morning twilight; the hero on God's charger is the evening star, and the valley is the place of sunset in the darkening west.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the daina as rendered by Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她在那里遇见一位少年英雄，骑着神的骏马。「哦，俊美的少年啊，你可曾见过我的父亲、母亲？」——「去山谷之地寻找吧；你的父亲在那里，你的母亲在那里，正筹划着你姊妹的婚事。」于是她急忙赶往山谷：「你们为何将我——一个婴孩——弃于陌生人的怜悯之下？」——「我已长成健壮的少女，唯有我独自寻得了那摇篮，那是我幼年时曾快乐所在之处。」此处，太阳与月亮已离弃了他们的女儿——那晨光；骑着神之骏马的英雄是黄昏之星，而山谷则是日暮时分渐暗的西方落日之处。

title.en: The Battling Souls of the Northern Lights
title.zh: 極光中的亡魂之戰

region.en: Lithuania and Latvia, northern sky (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 立陶宛與拉脫維亞北方天空（象徵性定位）

period: Folk belief recorded 19th c.; recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: When the Aurora Borealis flames over the Baltic sky, the Murgi or Iohdi — spirits of the air and souls of the dead — are battling, or the souls of warriors are engaged in combat; Perkunas himself rides to smite the demonic Iohdi.
summary.zh: 極光燃於波羅的海夜空之時，乃穆爾吉／約赫迪——風中精靈與亡者之魂——正在交戰，或戰士之魂廝殺；佩爾庫納斯親往擊魔靈。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief.

passages.text: Baltic mythology survives chiefly as sun-myths, but other sky-phenomena had their readings too. When the Aurora Borealis appears, the Murgi or Iohdi — spirits of the air and souls of the dead — are battling, or the souls of warriors are engaged in combat; it is against the demonic Iohdi that Perkunas rides out to strike.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 波罗的海神话主要以太阳神话的形式流传下来，但其他天象亦有其解读。当北极光出现时，便是穆尔吉（Murgi）或约赫迪（Iohdi）——空中之灵与亡者之魂——在交战，或是战士的亡魂在搏斗；佩尔库纳斯正是策马出击，攻打那些恶魔般的约赫迪。

passages.text: The moon, in the dainas, wears a mantle of stars and, like the sun, is liable to be destroyed — eclipsed — by dragons, serpents, and witches; the celestial court is thus a world at war as well as a world at work, with souls, demons, and gods contending in the lights above the darkening sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在達伊納詩歌中，月亮披著星辰的斗篷，並且和太陽一樣，可能被龍、蛇與女巫毀滅——即被吞噬而蝕；因此這天界宮廷既是一個勞作的世界，也是一個征戰的世界，靈魂、惡魔與諸神在漸暗之海上方的那片光中相互爭鬥。

title.en: Cradle, Hair-Cutting and the Girl's Three-Day Fast
title.zh: 搖籃、剪髮與少女三日齋

region.en: Cuzco households (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科家戶(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The life-cycle rites of Molina's account: at conception (ayuscay) the baby was placed on the fourth day in a cradle called quirau before the assembled uncles; at one year came the rutuchico, when the eldest uncle cut the first hair and each relation followed, and the child received the name it was to bear until of age; and at puberty came the quicuchicu for girls, who fasted two days without food, were given a little raw maize on the third lest they die of hunger, were washed and dressed in ancalluasu clothes with white-wool shoes, set food before the principal relations, and received from the principal relation the name she was to bear until death, together with instruction how to behave and obey her parents. This custom was ordained by Inca Yupanqui.
summary.zh: 莫利納所記生命禮俗:懷孕時行「阿尤斯卡伊」,嬰兒於第四日入「基勞」搖籃,請叔伯親友相看;周歲行「魯圖奇科」,由最長的叔伯剪第一縷胎髮,親友依次剪之,並賜名至成年;及笄行「基庫奇庫」,少女前兩日絕食,第三日僅得少許生玉米以免餓斃,第四日沐浴,著白毛鞋與「安卡利亞蘇」衣,梳辮覆囊,向尊長奉食進酒,由至親賜予終身之名,並教以為人處世、孝順父母之道。此俗乃印加·尤潘琪所定。

sensitivity.note: Life-cycle rites from Molina; his remark that the gifts were given 'without any idolatrous practice whatever' is a missionary observation preserved.

passages.text: The ayuscay was when a woman conceived. On the fourth day they put the babies into a cradle called quirau, and they invited the uncles and other relations to see it; but no other ceremony of any kind was performed in consequence of this event.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, life-cycle rites (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿尤斯凱（ayuscay）是女子受孕之時。到了第四天，他們把嬰兒放進一種叫做基勞（quirau）的搖籃裡，並邀請叔伯及其他親屬前來觀看；但除此之外，並未因這一事件舉行任何其他儀式。

passages.text: The rutuchico is when the child attains the age of one year. Then, whether it be a boy or a girl, they give it the name that it is to have until it is of age. The child was then shorn, and to perform the ceremony the eldest uncle was called, who cut the first hair. Then the other relations did the same, and afterwards the friends of the parents. They all drank, and the principal uncle gave the child the name it was to bear until it came of age.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, life-cycle rites (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 魯圖奇科（rutuchico）是孩子滿一歲之時。屆時，無論是男孩還是女孩，他們都給孩子取一個名字，這名字將一直用到孩子成年。接著便給孩子剃髮，為舉行此儀式，他們請來最年長的叔伯，由他剪下第一撮頭髮。隨後其他親屬也照樣剪髮，之後是父母的友人。眾人一同飲酒，由主事的叔伯給孩子取一個名字，這名字將一直用到孩子成年。

passages.text: The quicuchica is when girls reach the age of puberty: they fasted during the two first days, without eating anything at all, and on the third day they were given a little raw maize, that they might not die of hunger. They were confined in a place within the house, and on the fourth day they were washed, and dressed in clothes called ancalluasu, with shoes of white wool. Their hair was plaited, and a sort of bag was placed on their heads. On this day the principal relations came, and the girl came forth to set food before them and to give them to drink. The principal relation gave her the name she was to bear from thenceforth, and taught her how she should behave and obey her parents; and this custom was ordained by Ynca Yupanqui.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, life-cycle rites (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 基庫奇卡（quicuchica）是女孩到達青春期之時：頭兩天她們要齋戒，什麼都不吃；到了第三天，才給她們一點生玉米，以免她們餓死。她們被關在屋內的一處地方；到了第四天，她們被洗淨，穿上叫做安卡利亞蘇（ancalluasu）的衣服，腳穿白羊毛製的鞋。她們的頭髮被編成辮子，頭上放了一種袋子。這一天，主要親屬前來，女孩出來在他們面前擺上食物，並給他們斟酒。主要親屬給她取一個從此以後要用的名字，並教導她應當如何為人處世、如何順從父母；這一習俗是由印加·尤潘基（Ynca Yupanqui）所規定的。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Marriage by the Inca's Gift: Serving in the Father-in-law's House
title.zh: 印加賜婚:婿入岳家服役

region.en: Cuzco and the provinces (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科及各行省(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: When the Inca gave women as wives they were received because it was the command of the Inca. The man went to the house of the girl's father, not to say that the Inca had given her, but that he desired to serve for her; the relations of the girl were assembled and their consent obtained. The youth remained in the house of his father- and mother-in-law for four or five days, carrying in fuel and straw for them. Thus the agreement was made, and he took the girl for his wife; and because the Inca had given her, it was considered that she was taken until death, and she was received on this understanding, and never deserted.
summary.zh: 印加賜婚之婦,因其為王命而受。男子往女子父親家中,不言印加已賜其女,只說欲為其服役;於是聚集女家親屬,取得同意。婿在岳父母家中留宿四五日,為其運薪搬草。婚約既成,遂娶其女;因是印加所賜,故視為終身之約,依此受之,永不離棄。

sensitivity.note: Marriage custom; tagged divine-marriage loosely as marriage-by-divine-right (the Inca as solar appointor) - interpretive.

passages.text: When the Ynca gave women as wives, they were received because it was the command of the Ynca. The man went to the house of the girl's father, not to say that the Ynca had given her, but that he desired to serve for her, and so the relations of the girl were assembled, and their consent was obtained.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, marriage custom (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當印加把女子賜予男子為妻時，她們之所以被接納，是因為這是印加的命令。男子前往女子父親的家，不是去說印加已將她賜下，而是說他願意為她服役；於是女子的親屬聚集起來，並取得了他們的同意。

passages.text: The youth remained in the house of his father and mother-in-law for a space of four or five days, and carried in fuel and straw for them. Thus the agreement was made, and he took the girl for his wife; and because the Ynca had given her, it was considered that she was taken until death, and she was received on this understanding, and never deserted.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, marriage custom (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這青年在岳父岳母家中住了四五天，為他們搬運柴薪和乾草。如此便達成了約定，他娶那女子為妻；又因為是印加將她賜下的，所以人們認為她是被娶來直到死的，她也是在此諒解下被接納的，從未被拋棄。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Ccapac-cocha: The Children Sent to Every Huaca of the Empire
title.zh: 卡帕克-科查:獻往全境瓦卡的孩童

region.en: Cuzco and the four suyus, to the empire's extremities (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科與四蘇尤至帝國極境(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The Ccapac-cocha, instituted by Pachacutec Ynca Yupanqui, was offered when a new Inca began to reign, that the huacas might give him health and preserve his dominions in peace. From every lineage or tribe of the four suyus one or two children of about ten years were brought to Cuzco with cloth, flocks, gold and silver. The children walked twice round the statues of the Creator, the Sun, the Thunder and the Moon; the sacrifices were divided in four for the four provinces; then the children were strangled - first given to eat and drink that they might not enter the presence of the Creator discontented and hungry - and buried with silver figures of sheep and gold and silver figures of men. Some hearts were torn out yet palpitating and offered to the huacas; the huaca was anointed with blood from ear to ear, which they called pirac. The offerings were relayed across the whole empire by quipu-keepers (the Vilca-camayocs, each charged with nearly five hundred leagues of huaca accounts); if a hill was too steep to climb, the sacrifices were hurled to its summit from slings; no huaca - tree, fountain, hill or lake - was left out, for it was feared the omitted would be enraged and punish the Inca. Bearers of the Ccapac-cocha passed villages in such veneration that the inhabitants stayed within their houses prostrate until they had passed.
summary.zh: 「卡帕克-科查」由帕查庫特克·尤潘琪所立,新王即位時獻祭,求瓦卡賜其安康、保其疆土太平。四蘇尤各族各送一二名約十歲孩童至庫斯科,隨行有布帛、畜群、金銀。孩童繞行造物主、太陽、雷、月神像兩匝;祭品分作四份,以應四省。孩童先予飲食,免其飢餓不滿而入造物主之前,隨後被勒斃,與銀羊、金銀人像一同下葬;有的活剖其心,獻於尚在搏動之際;以血自耳至耳塗抹瓦卡,謂之「皮拉克」。祭品由「維爾卡-卡馬約克」(每人掌管近五百萊格內瓦卡清單的結繩會計)接力送往全境;山勢過陡者,以吊索將祭品拋上峰頂。任何瓦卡——樹、泉、山、湖——皆不得遺漏,否則恐其震怒降罰於印加。抬祭者所過之村,村民深居俯首,待其過後方起。

sensitivity.note: The Capacocha rite is among the best-attested Inca ceremonies (mountain-pl burials corroborate it). Described soberly as an archival record; not romanticized.

passages.text: The Ccapac-cocha was instituted by Pachacutec Ynca Yupanqui. The provinces of Colla-suyu, Chincha-suyu, Anti-suyu, and Cunti-suyu brought to this city, from each lineage or tribe, one or two male and female children aged about ten years. They also brought cloth and flocks, gold and silver. Then the Ynca seated himself in the Huacay-pata, the great square of Cuzco. The children and the other sacrifices walked round the statues of the Creator, the Sun, the Thunder, and the Moon, which were placed in the square, taking two turns. The Ynca then commanded the Priests of the provinces to divide the sacrifices into four parts, in token of the four provinces.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Ccapac-cocha (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡帕科查（Ccapac-cocha）祭典由帕查庫特克·印卡·尤潘基（Pachacutec Ynca Yupanqui）所創立。科利亞蘇尤（Colla-suyu）、欽查蘇尤（Chincha-suyu）、安蒂蘇尤（Anti-suyu）與孔蒂蘇尤（Cunti-suyu）諸省，從每個世系或部族中，送來一至兩名約十歲的男童與女童至這座城市。他們也送來布匹與牲畜、金與銀。隨後，印卡親臨庫斯科的大廣場瓦凱帕塔（Huacay-pata）就座。那些孩童與其他祭品繞行安置於廣場上的造物主、太陽、雷與月亮的雕像，共繞行兩圈。接著，印卡命各省的祭司將祭品分為四份，以象徵四個省。

passages.text: The Lord Ynca offered these sacrifices when he began to reign, that the huacas might give him health and preserve his dominions in peace. No huaca or place of worship, how small soever, was left out in the distribution of the sacrifices. The reason why all the huacas - whether sacred trees, fountains, hills or lakes - received part of the sacrifice was because it was held to be an evil omen if any were left out, and because it was feared that if any were omitted they would be enraged, and would punish the Ynca. If any of the hills were very steep and could not be ascended, the sacrifices were hurled to the summits from slings.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Ccapac-cocha (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 印卡君主在開始統治時獻上這些祭品，以求瓦卡（huacas）賜他健康，並使他的領地保持和平。在分配祭品時，沒有任何瓦卡或祭祀場所，無論多麼微小，被遺漏。所有瓦卡——無論是神樹、泉源、山丘或湖泊——皆分得一份祭品，其緣由在於：若有所遺漏，便被視為凶兆；且人們擔心若有任何遺漏，它們便會發怒，並懲罰印卡。若有些山丘極為陡峭、無法攀登，祭品便以投石器拋擲至山頂。

passages.text: The first was offered to the Creator. After this prayer they strangled the children, first giving them to eat and drink, that they might not enter the presence of the Creator discontented and hungry. From others they took out the hearts while yet alive, and offered them to the huacas while yet palpitating. They anointed the huaca with the blood from ear to ear, and they called this pirac. For this service the Ynca had Indians in Cuzco who were natives of the four Suyus; each one had a knowledge of all the huacas in the province over which he was Quipucamayoc or Accountant. They were called Vilca-camayoc; each Indian had charge of nearly five hundred leagues of country, and had an account of the things to be sacrificed at every huaca within his district.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Ccapac-cocha (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第一份祭品獻給造物主。祈禱之後，他們將孩童勒死，事先給他們吃喝，以免他們心懷不滿、飢腸轆轆地進入造物主面前。對另一些孩童，他們則在其尚活著時取出心臟，趁其仍在跳動時獻給瓦卡。他們以鮮血從一耳塗抹至另一耳來塗抹瓦卡，並稱此為「皮拉克」（pirac）。為此職務，印卡在庫斯科有來自四個蘇尤（Suyus）原籍的印第安人；每人都通曉其所任職之省內所有瓦卡，他在那裡擔任基普卡馬約克（Quipucamayoc）或會計。他們被稱為維爾卡卡馬約克（Vilca-camayoc）；每個印第安人掌管近五百里格的疆域，並記錄其轄區內每一處瓦卡應獻的祭品。

passages.text: They held this sacrifice, called Ccapacocha or Cachahuaca, in such veneration that, when those who were making journeys over uninhabited tracts with the sacrifices met other travellers, they did not raise their eyes to look at them, and the travellers prostrated themselves on the ground until the sacrifice-bearers had passed. When those bearing sacrifices passed through a village, the inhabitants did not come out of their houses, but remained, with deep humility and reverence, until the said Ccapac-cocha had passed onwards. It was also their custom that, whenever they conquered and subjugated any nations, of selecting some of the handsomest of the conquered people and sending them to Cuzco, where they were sacrificed to the Sun who, as they said, had given them the victory.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Ccapac-cocha (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們對這項稱為卡帕科查（Ccapacocha）或卡查瓦卡（Cachahuaca）的祭典如此崇敬，以致當那些帶著祭品穿越無人煙地帶的人遇見其他旅人時，他們不抬眼觀看對方，而旅人則伏地叩拜，直到攜帶祭品者走過。當攜帶祭品者經過村莊時，居民不走出房屋，而是懷著極深的謙卑與敬意留在屋內，直到前述的卡帕科查隊伍繼續前行。他們的習俗還包括：每當他們征服並降服任何民族時，便從被征服者中挑選一些最俊美的人送往庫斯科，在那裡將他們獻給太陽，因為據他們說，太陽賜予了他們勝利。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Resurrection of the Huacas: The Seven-Year Apostasy
title.zh: 瓦卡復活:七年背教之亂

region.en: Parinacochas and the provinces of the Viceroyalty (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 帕里納科查斯及各省(象徵性標記)

period: Apostasy recorded from c. 1560, reported by Luis de Olivera; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: From about 1560 the Indians of Parinacochas, Cuzco, Guamanga, La Paz and even Lima and Arequipa fell into a great apostasy, believing that the huacas which the Christians had burnt and destroyed had been brought to life again, divided into two parts - one united with the huaca Pachacama, the other with the huaca Titicaca - and that they had formed in the air in order of battle against God and conquered Him, killing all the Spaniards and destroying their cities, while the sea would rise to drink them up that they might be remembered no more. The huacas, it was preached, had made the Indians and their land, while God had made only the Spaniards. Preachers declared that the huacas now wandered in the air, thirsty and starving because the Indians no longer sacrificed nor poured out chicha to them, and that fields were sown with worms to be planted in the hearts of Spaniards and of those Indians who remained Christians. The baptized were threatened with death unless they renounced the Christian faith, fasted from salt, aji, coloured maize and all Spanish things, and left their Christian names. Indians possessed by huacas trembled, fell to the ground, and were carried to straw lodgings to be worshipped; a possessed man raised a fragment of a burnt huaca crying 'You see here your support.' The apostasy lasted seven years before priests repressed it.
summary.zh: 約1560年起,帕里納科查斯、庫斯科、關曼加、拉巴斯乃至利馬、阿雷基帕的印第安人陷入大背教:他們相信被基督徒焚毀的瓦卡已經復活,分為兩部分——一合於帕查卡馬克瓦卡,一合於的的喀喀瓦卡——並在空中列陣與上帝作戰而勝之,盡殺西班牙人、毀其城,海水將上漲吞沒一切,使其無人記起。傳道者稱瓦卡造了印第安人與這片土地,上帝只造了西班牙人;瓦卡如今在空中游蕩,飢渴難忍,因為印第安人不再獻祭、不再傾灑奇恰酒;田間播下蠕蟲,將植入西班牙人與仍信基督的印第安人的心中。受洗者若不棄絕信仰、不戒鹽與辣椒與西班牙之物、不改回舊名,便遭殺戮。被瓦卡附體的印第安人顫慄倒地,被抬往草棚受拜;附體者高舉瓦卡殘石呼曰:「看啊,這就是你們的依靠。」背教持續七年,方由教士鎮壓平息。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-period syncretic revival movement, recorded by the persecuting side; tagged resurrection for the huacas-risen belief, a rare post-conquest myth in the making.

passages.text: In the province of Parinacochas, in the diocese of Cuzco, the priest Luis de Olivera learnt that not only in that province, but in all the other provinces and cities of Chuquisaca, La Paz, Cuzco, Guamanga, and even Lima and Arequipa, most of the Indians had fallen into the greatest apostasy, departing from the Catholic Faith and returning to the idolatries which they practised in the time of their infidelity.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, apostasy report (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在庫斯科教區的帕里納科查斯（Parinacochas）省，神父路易斯·德·奧利韋拉（Luis de Olivera）獲悉，不僅在該省，而且在丘基薩卡（Chuquisaca）、拉巴斯（La Paz）、庫斯科、瓜曼加（Guamanga），甚至利馬（Lima）與阿雷基帕（Arequipa）的所有其他省份與城市，大多數印第安人都陷入了最嚴重的背教，背離天主教信仰，重拾他們在未信教時期所奉行的偶像崇拜。

passages.text: The deception by which these poor people were deceived was the belief that all the huacas which the Christians had burnt and destroyed had been brought to life again; and that they had been divided into two parts, one of which was united with the huaca Pachacama, and the other with the huaca Titicaca. The story went on that they had formed in the air, in order of battle, against God, and that they had conquered Him. It was believed that God and the Spaniards were conquered, all the Spaniards killed, and their cities destroyed, and that the sea would rise to drink them up, that they might be remembered no more. In this apostasy they believed that God our Lord had made the Spaniards, and Castille, and the animals and provisions of Castille; but that the huacas had made the Indians, and this land, and all the things they possessed before the Spaniards came.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, apostasy report (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這些可憐人受騙的騙局，是相信所有被基督徒焚毀與摧毀的瓦卡都已復活；並且相信它們已被分為兩部分，一部分與瓦卡帕查卡馬（Pachacama）結合，另一部分與瓦卡蒂蒂卡卡（Titicaca）結合。傳說還稱，它們已於空中列陣對抗上帝，並且戰勝了祂。人們相信上帝與西班牙人已被擊敗，所有西班牙人被殺，其城市被毀，海水將上漲將他們吞沒，使他們不再被記念。在這場背教中，他們相信上帝我主創造了西班牙人、卡斯蒂利亞（Castille），以及卡斯蒂利亞的動物與糧食；但瓦卡則創造了印第安人、這片土地，以及他們在西班牙人到來之前所擁有的一切事物。

passages.text: Many preachers went forth from among the Indians, who preached as well in the desert places as in the villages, declaring the resurrection of the huacas, and saying that they now wandered in the air, thirsty and dying of hunger, because the Indians no longer sacrificed nor poured out chicha to them. They declared that many fields were sown with worms, to be planted in the hearts of the Spaniards, and of the Spanish sheep, and of the horses, and also in the hearts of those Indians who remained Christians. Those who would return to the love of the huacas and live were to fast for some days, not eating salt nor aji, nor coloured maize, nor any Spanish thing, nor entering churches, nor using their christian names.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, apostasy report (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有許多傳道者從印第安人當中出來，他們無論在荒野之地或在村落中都傳道，宣告瓦卡（huacas）的復活，並說瓦卡如今在空氣中遊蕩，又渴又餓，因為印第安人不再向它們獻祭，也不再為它們傾倒奇恰酒（chicha）。他們宣稱有許多田地種下了蟲子，要種在西班牙人的心裡，種在西班牙羊的心裡、馬的心裡，也種在那些仍然作基督徒的印第安人的心裡。凡願意回歸對瓦卡的愛而活著的人，要禁食數日，不吃鹽，不吃辣椒（aji），不吃有色玉米，不吃任何西班牙之物，不進教堂，也不用他們的教名。

passages.text: Many Indians trembled and fell to the ground, and others tore themselves as if they were possessed; and when they presently became quiet, they said that such and such a huaca had entered into their bodies. Then the people took such an one in their arms and carried him to a chosen spot, and there they made a lodging with straw and cloaks, and began to worship the huaca, offering sheep, colla-chicha, llipta, mollo, and other things. Then the possessed shouted and invoked the huaca, and rose up with the fragment of a burnt huaca in his hands, thus addressing the people: 'You see here your support. You see here that which can give you health, and children, and food. Put it in its place, where it was in the days of the Yncas.' At last the apostasy began to wane, but altogether it lasted for seven years.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, apostasy report (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 許多印第安人顫抖，仆倒在地，另一些人則像被附身一般撕扯自己；等他們隨即安靜下來，便說某某瓦卡已進入他們的身體。於是眾人將這樣的人抱在懷中，抬到一處選定的地方，在那裡用稻草和斗篷為他搭起住處，並開始敬拜那瓦卡，獻上羊、科利亞奇恰酒（colla-chicha）、利普塔（llipta）、莫略（mollo）及其他物品。隨後那被附身者呼喊並呼求瓦卡，手中拿著一塊燒過的瓦卡碎片起身，向眾人如此說道：『你們看，這就是你們的依靠。你們看，這就是能賜你們健康、子女和食物者。把它放回原處，放回印加（Yncas）時代它所在之處。』最後這背教之風開始減弱，但前後共持續了七年。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Cure at the Meeting of Two Rivers: Colli-sara and Hichoco
title.zh: 雙河匯流處的療疾:科利-薩拉與伊喬科

region.en: Confluence of two rivers, near Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科附近雙河匯流處(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: When an Indian fell sick the witches were called to cure him and say whether he would live or die. They ordered him to collect white maize called colli sara, red and yellow cuma-sara, yellow paro-sara, and sea shells of all colours called ymaymana mullu; the wizard ground the maize with the shell and the sick man, breathing on it, offered it to the huacas and vilcas with the words: 'O all the huacas and vilcas of the four provinces of the land, my grandfathers and ancestors, receive this sacrifice, wheresoever you may be, and give me health.' He breathed on coca and offered it to the Sun, Moon and Stars; with a little gold and silver he sacrificed to the Creator; he gave food to the dead on their tombs, pouring out chicha - for the wizard gave him to understand that he was visited with this sickness because the dead were starving. If he could walk to the junction of two rivers, the wizard made him go there and wash his body with water and flour of white maize, saying that he would there leave his illness; and at the end of the ceremony he must confess all his sins, without concealing any: this they called hichoco.
summary.zh: 印第安人患病,便請巫醫診視生死。巫醫命其備白色玉米「科利-薩拉」、紅黃玉米「庫馬-薩拉」、黃玉米「帕羅-薩拉」,以及各色海貝「伊馬伊馬納-穆盧」。巫醫以貝磨玉米,病者對之吹氣,獻於瓦卡與維爾卡,禱曰:「四省一切瓦卡與維爾卡,我的祖父們、先人們,無論你們身在何處,請領受此祭,賜我康健。」再對古柯吹氣,獻於日、月、星辰;以小金銀祭造物主;在墳墓上供食灑酒——因巫醫使他明白:此病乃因死者飢餓所致。若能步行至雙河匯流處,巫醫便命他前往,以水與白玉米粉洗身,說病將留在那裡。禮成之末,還須盡懺己罪、毫不隱瞞——此謂「伊喬科」。

sensitivity.note: Healing rite described from the missionary side; the ancestral invocation shows the huacas as lineage ancestors.

passages.text: When any Indian is sick, these witches are called in to cure him, and to say whether he will live or die. Having pronounced upon the case, they order the sick man to take white maize called colli sara, red and yellow maize called cuma-sara, yellow maize called paro-sara, sea shells called mullu mullu, of all the colours they can collect, which they call ymaymana mullu. When these things are collected, the wizard grinds the maize with the shell, and gives it ground to the sick man that, breathing on it, he may offer it to the huacas and vilcas, with these words: 'O all the huacas and vilcas of the four provinces of the land, my grandfathers and ancestors, receive this sacrifice, wheresoever you may be, and give me health.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, curing rite (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 每當有印第安人生病，這些巫師便被請來為他治病，並斷言他將活或將死。他們對病情作出判斷後，便吩咐病人取來稱為科利薩拉（colli sara）的白玉米、稱為庫馬薩拉（cuma-sara）的紅玉米和黃玉米、稱為帕羅薩拉（paro-sara）的黃玉米、稱為穆略穆略（mullu mullu）的海貝，凡能收集到的各種顏色都要，他們稱之為伊邁馬納穆略（ymaymana mullu）。這些東西收集齊後，巫師將玉米與貝殼一同磨碎，把磨好的東西交給病人，讓他對之吹氣，然後獻給瓦卡和維爾卡（vilcas），並說這些話：『哦，此地四省所有的瓦卡和維爾卡，我的祖父和祖先啊，無論你們身在何處，請接受這祭品，賜我健康。』

passages.text: They also make him breathe on a little coca, and offer it to the Sun, praying for health; and the same to the Moon and Stars. Then, with a little gold and silver of little value in his hand, the sick man offers sacrifice to the Creator. Then the wizard commands him to give food to the dead, placing it on their tombs, and pouring out chicha; for the wizard gives the patient to understand that he is visited with this sickness because the dead are starving.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, curing rite (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們也讓他對一點古柯（coca）吹氣，獻給太陽，祈求健康；對月亮和星辰也同樣而行。然後，病人手中拿著少許價值不高的金銀，向造物主獻祭。接著巫師吩咐他給死者供食，將食物放在他們的墳墓上，並傾倒奇恰酒；因為巫師讓病人明白，他之所以患此病，是因為死者正在挨餓。

passages.text: If he is able to go on foot to some junction of two rivers, the wizard makes him go there and wash his body with water and flour of white maize, saying that he will there leave his illness. At the end of this ceremony the wizard tells him that, if he would free himself from his sickness, he must confess all his sins, without concealing any. They call this hichoco.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, curing rite (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 倘若他能步行到某處兩河交匯之地，巫師便讓他到那裡去，用清水和白玉米粉洗淨身體，說他將在那裡留下他的病。這儀式結束時，巫師告訴他，若想擺脫疾病，就必須告明自己所有的罪，一點也不隱瞞。他們稱此為伊喬科（hichoco）。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Whatever Excels Is Huaca: Summits, Beauty and the Rest-Stop Gods
title.zh: 凡卓越者皆為瓦卡:峰頂、至美與歇腳之神

region.en: Mountain passes of the Andes (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 安第斯山口(象徵性標記)

period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: It was the custom that, whenever anything excelled all the rest of its kind in beauty, they worshipped it and made it huaca or sacred. They worshipped the summits of all peaks and mountain passes, and offered maize and other things; for they said that, when they ascended any pass and reached the top, they could there rest from the labour of the ascent. This they called chupasitas.
summary.zh: 凡某物在其類中至美超群,人們便崇拜之,奉為瓦卡或神物。一切峰頂與山口皆受崇拜,人們獻上玉米等物;因為他們說,攀登至口,得至其巔,便可歇息勞乏。此謂「丘帕西塔斯」。

sensitivity.note: A concise statement of the Andean logic of sacredness - excellence in kind marks the huaca.

passages.text: It was also their custom that, whenever anything excelled all the rest of its kind in beauty, they worshipped it, and made it huaca or sacred. They worshipped the summits of all peaks and mountain passes, and offered maize and other things; for they said that, when they ascended any pass and reached the top, they could there rest from the labour of the ascent. This they called chupasitas.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們的習俗還有：凡有某物在同類之中以美勝過其餘一切者，他們便敬拜它，使之成為瓦卡或聖物。他們敬拜所有山峰和山口的頂端，獻上玉米及其他物品；因為他們說，當他們攀登任何山口到達頂端時，便可在那里歇息，以解攀登之勞。他們稱此為丘帕西塔斯（chupasitas）。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Murder of Tuwhakararo
title.zh: 圖瓦卡拉羅遇害

region.en: Te Uru-o-Manono, house of the Ati-Hapai (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿蒂哈派部落大屋特烏魯奧馬諾諾（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 6, The Murder of Tuwhakararo (London 1855)

summary.en: Visiting his married sister Mairatea among the Ati-Hapai, the wrestler Tuwhakararo throws a young rival twice amid general laughter. While dressing, sand is thrown in his eyes and he is struck dead; the tribe devours his body and hangs his bones under the ridge-pole of their great house. There the bones rattle by night crying 'Tauparoro', and his sister mocks them - until the news reaches his brother Whakatau-potiki, who resolves on revenge.
summary.zh: 圖瓦卡拉羅前往探望嫁至阿蒂哈派的姐姐瑪伊拉泰亞，角力場上連勝年輕對手兩回，惹得全場哄笑。對手趁他穿衣以沙撒其眼，趁亂擊殺；部落分食其屍，將其骨懸於大屋脊樑之下。夜半骸骨自相碰擊，聲如『陶帕羅羅』；姐姐斥其白響——然凶信終傳至其弟瓦卡陶波蒂基耳中，復仇之志遂定。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection; cannibal-vengeance episode reproduced as paraphrase only.

passages.text: Tuhuruhuru, the son of Rupe's sister, married Apakura, and she bore a son named Tuwhakararo, and afterwards a daughter named Mairatea. When Mairatea grew up she was married to the son of a chief named Poporokewa, chief of the Ati-Hapai tribe, and went to his home; but Tuwhakararo remained at his own village, and after a time longed to see his sister and went to pay her a visit, arriving at a very large house belonging to the tribe Poporokewa, named Uru-o-Manono, where all the family of Poporokewa lived.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 6 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 圖胡魯胡魯（Tuhuruhuru）是魯佩（Rupe）之姊妹的兒子，他娶了阿帕庫拉（Apakura）為妻，她生下一子名為圖瓦卡拉羅（Tuwhakararo），之後又生一女名為邁拉特亞（Mairatea）。邁拉特亞長大後，嫁給了名為波波羅克瓦（Poporokewa）的酋長之子，此酋長乃阿蒂-哈派（Ati-Hapai）部落之首領，她便前往其家中；然而圖瓦卡拉羅仍留在自己的村落，過了些時日，他渴望見到姊妹，便前去探望她，抵達了波波羅克瓦一族所擁有的一棟極大的房屋，名為烏魯-歐-馬諾諾（Uru-o-Manono），波波羅克瓦全家皆居住於此。

passages.text: Some of the young men of the Ati-Hapai tribe asked him to wrestle, and the competitor who came forward was the sweetheart of his brother-in-law's young sister. Tuwhakararo laid hold of the young man and soon gave him a severe fall; they stood up again and he gave him another severe fall, and all the young people burst out laughing at the youth, who sat on the ground looking foolish and sulky. Tuwhakararo sat down too and began to put on his clothes again; while he was putting his head through his cloak, the young man he had thrown ran up and threw a handful of sand in his eyes. Wild with pain he could see nothing and began rubbing his eyes; the young man then struck him on the head and killed him. The people of the Ati-Hapai ran in upon him, cut his body up, devoured it, and hung his bones in the roof under the ridge-pole of their house Te Uru-o-Manono.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 6 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿蒂-哈派部落的一些年輕人邀他角力，而上前應戰的對手，正是他姊夫之幼妹的情人。圖瓦卡拉羅抓住那年輕人，不久便將他重重摔倒；他們再度站起，他又將他重重摔倒一次，所有年輕人都對那青年哄然大笑，那青年坐在地上，神情愚拙而慍怒。圖瓦卡拉羅也坐了下來，開始重新穿上衣服；當他正把頭套進斗篷時，被他摔倒的那年輕人跑上前來，朝他的眼睛扔了一把沙子。他疼痛難忍，什麼也看不見，便開始揉眼睛；那年輕人隨即擊打他的頭部，將他殺死。阿蒂-哈派的人湧上前來，將他的屍體切割，吞食殆盡，並把他的骨頭懸掛在他們房屋特烏魯-歐-馬諾諾（Te Uru-o-Manono）的屋脊之下、屋頂之內。

passages.text: Whilst they were hung up there the bones rattled together, and his sister heard them, and it seemed to her as if they made a sound like 'Tauparoro, Tauparoro'; and she listened again, and again heard the words. And the sister of Tuwhakararo, looking up to the bones, said, 'You rattle in vain, O bones of him who was devoured by the Ati-Hapai tribe, for who is there to lament over him or to avenge his death?' At last the news of the sad event reached the ears of his brother Whakatau-potiki and of his other brothers; they were grieved and pained, and Whakatau-potiki adopted a firm resolution to go and avenge Tuwhakararo's death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 6 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當骨頭懸掛於彼處時，它們相互碰撞作響，他的姊妹聽見了，在她聽來，那聲音彷彿是「陶帕羅羅，陶帕羅羅」（Tauparoro, Tauparoro）；她又傾聽，再次聽見這些話語。圖瓦卡拉羅的姊妹仰望那些骨頭，說道：「你們作響也是徒然，被阿蒂-哈派部落吞食之人的骨頭啊，因為有誰能為他哀悼，或為他的死復仇呢？」最後，這悲慘消息傳到了他的兄弟瓦卡陶-波蒂基（Whakatau-potiki）及其他兄弟的耳中；他們悲傷痛苦，瓦卡陶-波蒂基下定堅定的決心，要前去為圖瓦卡拉羅之死復仇。

title.en: Whakatau-potiki Burns Uru-o-Manono
title.zh: 瓦卡陶火焚烏魯奧馬諾諾

region.en: Thousand-canoe armada, Hawaiki seas (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哈瓦基海域千舟艦隊（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 6 (London 1855)

summary.en: In a thousand named canoes Whakatau-potiki sails to avenge his brother. At night his own band pulls the plugs from every other canoe so that a thousand crews sink and turn back, and his seven warriors alone reach Uru-o-Manono. Disguised with cropped hair and charcoal, he laughs with the crowd until Poporokewa laughs - revealing his broken tooth - then drops a noose over his head, hauls him out, and fires the house with all within it.
summary.zh: 瓦卡陶率千艘戰舟渡海復仇。夜色中他命親隨拔去其餘各舟之排水木塞，千舟盡沉、千隊敗退，唯其七勇士抵達烏魯奧馬諾諾。他剪短頭髮、以炭塗面混入屋中；待波波羅基瓦大笑露出缺齒，他趁機套索於其頸，將其拽出，隨即縱火焚屋，連人帶屋化為灰燼。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection.

passages.text: The rest of the tribe agreed in the purpose of revenge, and they began without delay to build canoes, naming some of them the Whiritoa, the Tapatapahukarere, the Toroa-i-taipakihi, the Haki-ere, and the Mahunu-awatea. When they had finished lashing on the top-boards, their mother Apakura with all her female attendants began to beat and prepare fern-root for the warriors as provisions, repeating a lament for the young man as they worked, to rouse the feelings of the war party. Lo, the army of Whakatau-potiki embarked in a thousand canoes and floated out into the open sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 6 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 部落其餘之人皆同意復仇之計，他們毫不遲延地開始建造獨木舟，將其中一些命名為維里托亞（Whiritoa）、塔帕塔帕胡卡雷雷（Tapatapahukarere）、托羅阿-伊-泰帕基希（Toroa-i-taipakihi）、哈基-埃雷（Haki-ere）與馬胡努-阿瓦特亞（Mahunu-awatea）。當他們完成上層船板的綁縛後，他們的母親阿帕庫拉率領所有女侍開始捶打並調製蕨根，作為戰士們的糧食，她們一面工作，一面反覆吟唱一首悼念那青年的哀歌，以激起征戰隊伍的鬥志。瞧，瓦卡陶-波蒂基的軍隊登上千艘獨木舟，駛向外海。

passages.text: At a landing on the route the army had a review, column after column charging with fierce shouts, and Whakatau's own chosen band leaping a creek in good order while others failed. Then Whakatau made a speech: they would not finish the voyage until dark night, lest they should be seen and fail in surprising the enemy. Just as it was dark he ordered his chosen band to go and pull the plugs out of all the canoes but their own, and they did so to the whole thousand. The canoes launched in the darkness one after another presently began to sink, one after the other, and the crews were compelled again to seek the shore; meanwhile the chosen band of Whakatau urged on their canoes, leaving the others behind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 6 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在途中一處登陸地，軍隊舉行了閱兵，一列又一列地衝鋒，發出猛烈的吶喊，而瓦卡陶親自挑選的隊伍則井然有序地躍過一條溪流，其餘人卻未能做到。接著瓦卡陶發表演說：他們要等到黑夜才完成航程，以免被發現而無法突襲敵人。正當天色昏暗時，他命令自己精選的隊伍前去拔掉除他們自己之外所有獨木舟的塞子，他們便對全部千艘獨木舟如此行。在黑暗中一艘接一艘下水的獨木舟，不久便開始一艘接一艘地下沉，船員們被迫再次尋岸；與此同時，瓦卡陶的精選隊伍催促他們的獨木舟前進，將其他人拋在後頭。

passages.text: Drawing near the great house called the Uru-o-Manono they landed; the warriors silently surrounded the house in ranks, guarding each of its eight doors with a band of men. Whakatau caught a man named Hioi outside the house and questioned him: where was his sister; where did Poporokewa sleep - at the foot of the large pillar that supports the ridge-pole; by what mark might he know him - one of his teeth was broken. Then Whakatau took the fellow and cut out his tongue, and made him talk; still he spoke quite distinctly, so he cut the tongue off quite close to the root and sent him in to call out Whakatau's sister.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 6 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們靠近那座名為烏魯-歐-馬諾諾的大屋，便登了岸；戰士們悄然成列包圍那房屋，以一小隊人馬守住它的八道門。瓦卡陶在屋外抓住一個名叫希歐伊（Hioi）的人，盤問他：他的姊妹在哪裡；波波羅克瓦睡在何處——在支撐屋脊的大柱腳下；憑什麼記號可以認出他——他有一顆牙齒斷了。於是瓦卡陶抓住那傢伙，割出他的舌頭，逼他說話；他仍吐字相當清晰，於是他將舌頭齊根割斷，並派他進去呼喊瓦卡陶的姊妹。

passages.text: The sister of Whakatau guessed in a moment this was some device of her brother's, went out to him, and they wept together. She warned him that many of the Ati-Hapai had seen him before and would know him, so she cut his hair quite close and rubbed his face all over with charcoal. When they entered, the people cried 'Here's a stranger, make up the fire', blew it up brightly, came to look at Whakatau-potiki, broke out laughing - 'What a black-looking fellow he is!' - and even Poporokewa burst out laughing at his appearance. Whakatau at once recognised him by his broken tooth. He had taken a stout rope with him, coiled in his hand with a noose at one end; as soon as he recognised Poporokewa he slily dropped the noose over his head and hauled it tight round his neck, then, lengthening the rope as he went, he and his sister rushed out, and he climbed up on the roof repeating a powerful incantation. Each warrior sprang up from concealment, set fire to the house in several places at once, and slaughtered all who tried to escape. Thus they burnt the Uru-o-Manono and all who were in it, and returned with joyful news to Apakura, the mother of Tuwhakararo.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 6 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: Whakatau 的姊妹立刻猜到這必是她兄弟的某種計謀，便出去見他，二人一同哭泣。她警告他說，Ati-Hapai 族中有許多人從前見過他，會認出他來，於是她把他的頭髮剪得很短，又用木炭把他的臉整個塗黑。他們進去時，眾人喊道：「來了個陌生人，把火燒旺些」，把火吹得通明，前來端詳 Whakatau-potiki，忽然大笑起來——「這傢伙長得真黑啊！」——甚至連 Poporokewa 也因他的模樣而放聲大笑。Whakatau 立刻憑他那顆斷牙認出了他。他隨身帶了一條粗繩，盤繞在手中，一端打了個活結；他一認出 Poporokewa，便悄悄把活結套在他頭上，緊緊勒住他的脖子，然後一邊走一邊把繩子放長，他與姊妹一同衝了出去，他爬上屋頂，念誦一道強力的咒語。眾武士各自從藏身之處躍起，同時在屋中數處放火，把所有試圖逃走的人盡數殺死。他們就這樣燒毀了 Uru-o-Manono 以及其中所有的人，帶著喜訊回到 Tuwhakararo 的母親 Apakura 那裡。

title.en: Whakatau, Formed from the Cast-off Apron
title.zh: 由棄裙所化的瓦卡陶

region.en: Sea-shore of Apakura, Hawaiki (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哈瓦基阿帕庫拉海濱（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 7, The Adventures of Rata (London 1855)

summary.en: Rata's son Tuwhakararo weds Apakura, who bears first Whakatau - not born as mortals are, but formed by the god Rongotakawiu from the little apron Apakura threw into the ocean, who then taught him every kind of enchantment. As a boy Whakatau flies kites while running about at the bottom of the waters; when watchers try to seize him he slips back under the sea, and only his mother Apakura can catch and hold him. He becomes a renowned hero, hiding nothing from his magic knowledge.
summary.zh: 圖瓦卡拉羅娶阿帕庫拉，生子瓦卡陶——他非同凡人而生：一日阿帕庫拉將所穿小圍裙擲入海中，神祇龍戈塔卡維烏拾起塑之賦形，瓦卡陶由此得生，並習得各種法術。幼年最愛放風箏，卻一邊執線一邊在海底奔跑；岸上之人屢屢捉拿，他都滑回水中，唯母親阿帕庫拉方能擒住。長大後他成了名震一方的英雄。

sensitivity.note: Object-born hero parallel to the 'humans molded' cluster; tagging interpretive.

passages.text: Rata took Tongarautawhiri as one of his wives, and she bore him a son whom he named Tuwhakararo; when this son came to man's estate he took Apakura as one of his wives, and from her sprang a son named Whakatau. He was not born in the manner that mortals are, but came into being in this way: one day Apakura went down upon the sea-coast and took off the little apron she wore in front as a covering and threw it into the ocean, and a god named Rongotakawiu took it and shaped it and gave it form and being, and Whakatau sprang into life, and his ancestor Rongotakawiu taught him magic and the use of enchantments of every kind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 7 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: Rata 娶 Tongarautawhiri 為妻之一，她為他生了一個兒子，他給他取名為 Tuwhakararo；這兒子長大成人後，娶 Apakura 為妻之一，由她生下一個兒子，名叫 Whakatau。他並非以凡人的方式出生，而是這樣來到世上的：有一天，Apakura 下到海邊，脫下她身前遮體的那條小圍裙，把它扔進海裡，一位名叫 Rongotakawiu 的神取過它，加以塑造，賦予它形體與生命，Whakatau 便由此而生，他的祖先 Rongotakawiu 教他法術以及種種咒語的運用。

passages.text: When Whakatau was a little lad, his favourite amusement was flying kites. Mortals then often observed kites flying in the air and could see nothing else, for Whakatau was running about at the bottom of the waters still holding the end of the string. One day he stole up out of the water by degrees and came upon the shore, when his whole body was plainly seen by some people near, and they ran as fast as they could to catch him; he slipped back again into the water and continued flying his kite as before. The watchers sat down upon the bank to wait, and when he came up out of the water again they all ran at full speed to seize him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 7 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: Whakatau 還是個小孩子時，最喜愛的消遣便是放風箏。那時凡人常常看見風箏在空中飛翔，卻什麼也看不見，因為 Whakatau 仍在水底跑來跑去，手裡還握著線的一端。有一天，他一點一點地從水中偷偷上來，來到岸上，附近有些人清清楚楚地看見了他的整個身體，便拼命跑去捉他；他又溜回水中，像先前一樣繼續放他的風箏。觀望的人坐在岸上等候，當他又從水中上來時，他們全都飛奔過去要抓住他。

passages.text: Whakatau cried out to them, 'You had better go and bring Apakura here; she is the only person who can catch me and hold me fast.' One of them ran to fetch her, and as soon as she saw little Whakatau she called out, 'Here I am, I am Apakura.' Whakatau stopped running, she caught hold of him with her hands and questioned him, 'Whom do you belong to?' And he answered, 'I am your child; you one day threw the little apron which covered you on the sands of the sea, and the god Rongotakawiu, my ancestor, formed me from it, and I grew up a human being, and he named me Whakatau.' From that time he left the water and lived on shore; nothing was concealed from him, and when he grew to be a man he became a renowned hero.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 7 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: Whakatau 向他們喊道：「你們最好去把 Apakura 帶到這裡來；只有她能捉住我、把我牢牢抓住。」其中一人跑去接她，她一見到小 Whakatau 便喊道：「我在這裡，我就是 Apakura。」Whakatau 停下不再跑，她用手抓住他，問他：「你是誰家的孩子？」他答道：「我是你的孩子；有一天你把遮著你的那條小圍裙扔在海邊的沙上，我的祖先 Rongotakawiu 神用它造出了我，我便長大成人，他給我取名為 Whakatau。」從那時起，他離開水中，住在岸上；沒有什麼能瞞得過他，當他長大成人，便成了一位聲名顯赫的英雄。

title.en: Rata Ambushes Matuku at the Fountains
title.zh: 拉塔泉邊伏殺馬圖庫

region.en: Two fountains of Matuku-takotako (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 馬圖庫塔科塔科之雙泉（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 7, The Adventures of Rata (London 1855)

summary.en: Rata, son of Wahieroa, sets out to avenge his father and finds a keeper who serves the man-eater Matuku-takotako - a being who rises from the earth at every new moon to devour men. The keeper warns that Matuku cannot be killed at the mirror-fountain (where a shadow would betray the ambusher), only at the fountain where he combs and washes his hair. At the next new moon Rata hides at the hair-washing fountain, and as Matuku lifts his streaming head from the water, seizes him by the hair and slays him.
summary.zh: 拉塔——瓦希耶羅亞之子——踏上為父復仇之途。守門人告知：吃人的馬圖庫每逢新月自地底鑽出；其不可在照影之泉旁殺之——影子會暴露埋伏者；唯有在其梳理洗滌亂髮之泉邊方可下手。新月初升之夜，拉塔藏於洗髮泉邊；馬圖庫跪地解開髮辮，將頭探入清泉，拉塔在其抬頭出水之際一手抓髮、一手揮擊，終於手刃仇敵。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Before Tawhaki ascended up into the heavens a son named Wahieroa had been born to him by his first wife. As soon as Wahieroa grew to man's estate he took Kura for a wife, and she bore him a son whom they called Rata. Wahieroa was slain treacherously by a chief named Matukutakotako, but his son Rata was born some time before his death. It therefore became his duty to revenge the death of his father, and having grown up, he gave his dependants orders and started on the journey, saying he was about to go in search of the man who slew his father.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 7 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在 Tawhaki 升上天界之前，他的第一個妻子已為他生下一個兒子，名叫 Wahieroa。Wahieroa 一長大成人，便娶 Kura 為妻，她為他生了一個兒子，他們給他取名為 Rata。Wahieroa 被一個名叫 Matukutakotako 的首領背信殺害，但他的兒子 Rata 在他死前一段時間便已出生。因此，為父報仇便成了他的責任；他長大後，便向他的部屬下令，動身啟程，說他要去尋找那個殺害他父親的人。

passages.text: At the entrance to the place of Matukutakotako he found a man left in charge sitting at the entrance to the court-yard, and asked where the man was who killed his father. The keeper answered that he lived beneath in the earth there, and that he himself was left to call to him and warn him when the new moon appeared; at that season Matuku rises and comes forth upon the earth and devours men as his food. Rata asked how he would know when the proper time came, and the keeper answered, 'I call aloud to him.' The new moon would be in two nights hence; Rata was to return to his village and come again on the morning of the second day.
