passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 7 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在 Matukutakotako 住所的入口處，他發現一個被留下看守的人坐在庭院的入口，便問那個殺害他父親的人在哪裡。看守回答說，那人住在那下面的地裡，而他自己被留下來，是為了在新月出現時呼喚他、警告他；到了那個時節，Matuku 便起身來到地面上，以人為食。Rata 問他怎樣才能知道適當的時機到了，看守答道：「我高聲呼喚他。」再過兩夜便是新月；Rata 須先回自己的村子，第二天早晨再來。

passages.text: The keeper showed him the two fountains of clear water. 'The spot we stand on is the place where Matuku rises up from the earth; yonder fountain is the one in which he combs and washes his dishevelled hair, but this fountain is the one he uses to reflect his face in whilst he dresses it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 7 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 看守者把兩處清澈的泉水指給他看。「我們所站的這個地方，正是馬圖庫從地裡升起之處；那邊那處泉水，是他梳理並洗滌他那蓬亂頭髮的地方，而這處泉水，則是他梳理頭髮時用來映照面容的。

passages.text: You cannot kill him whilst he is at the fountain he uses to reflect his face in, because your shadow would also be reflected in it and he would see it; but at the fountain in which he washes his hair, you may smite and slay him.' That evening the moon became visible; the keeper shouted aloud, 'Ho, the new moon is visible - a moon two days old!' Matuku heard him, seized his two-handed wooden sword, rose up from the earth and went straight to his two fountains; he laid the sword down at the mirror-fountain, knelt beside it, loosened the strings that bound his long locks, shook out his dishevelled hair and plunged his head into the cool clear waters. Rata crept from his hiding, rapidly moved up and stood behind him; and as Matuku-takotako raised his head from the water, Rata with one hand seized him by the hair, while with the other he smote and slew him - thus avenging the death of his father Wahieroa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 7 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他在那處用來映照面容的泉水邊時，你殺不了他，因為你的影子也會映在其中，他便會看見；但在那處他洗滌頭髮的泉水邊，你卻可以擊殺他。』那天傍晚，月亮顯現了；看守者高聲呼喊：『嗬，新月顯現了——是一輪兩天大的月亮！』馬圖庫聽見了，抓起他那把雙手握持的木劍，從地裡升起，徑直走向他那兩處泉水；他把劍放在那處映照面容的泉水邊，跪在旁邊，解開束縛他長髮的繩結，抖散他那蓬亂的頭髮，把頭浸入清涼澄澈的水中。拉塔從藏身之處爬出，迅速上前，站在他身後；正當馬圖庫-塔科塔科把頭從水中抬起時，拉塔一手抓住他的頭髮，另一手擊殺了他——以此為他父親瓦希埃羅阿之死復仇。

title.en: Rata and the Offspring of Hakuturi
title.zh: 拉塔與哈庫圖里的子嗣

region.en: Forest of Tane, Hawaiki (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哈瓦基塔內之林（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 7, The Adventures of Rata (London 1855)

summary.en: Seeking a canoe to fetch his father's bones, Rata fells a tall straight tree without first asking the forest's leave. Overnight the offspring of Hakuturi - the multitudes of insects, birds and spirits of the forest - replace every chip and shaving, singing their incantation: 'Fly together, chips and shavings; stand upright again, O tree!' Twice the tree rises; on the third day Rata hides and seizes them, is rebuked - 'Who gave you authority to fell the forest god?' - and, ashamed, returns home while the children of Tane complete his canoe for him in a moment.
summary.zh: 拉塔欲造獨木舟赴遠方取回父親遺骨，未經森林首肯便砍倒一棵高直大樹。夜裡，哈庫圖里的子嗣——林中無數蟲鳥與精靈——將每一片木屑木刨一一復位，齊聲誦咒：『木屑木刨，飛回原處，緊緊相連；大樹啊，重新挺立！』樹兩度復原；第三日拉塔藏身灌木窺伺、將其一舉擒獲，眾靈責問：『誰許你砍倒森林之神？』拉塔羞愧而歸；塔內的子嗣們霎時為他造好獨木舟，名為里瓦魯。

sensitivity.note: Etiological record: forest etiquette (permission from Tane's offspring before felling) explained by myth.

passages.text: Upon hearing that the bones of his father Wahieroa had been carried off by a strange people who live at a distance, Rata returned to his own village and reflected over many designs by which he might recover them. At length he thought of an excellent plan: he went into the forest, found a very tall tree, quite straight throughout its entire length, felled it, and cut off its noble branching top, intending to fashion the trunk into a canoe. All the insects which inhabit trees, and the spirits of the forests, were very angry at this.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 7 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一聽說他父親瓦希埃羅阿的骨骸被一個住在遠方的陌生民族帶走了，拉塔便回到自己的村莊，反覆思量了許多可以取回骨骸的計策。最後，他想出了一個極好的辦法：他走進森林，找到一棵非常高大的樹，整棵樹幹筆直，便把它砍倒，砍下它那雄偉多枝的樹冠，打算把樹幹做成獨木舟。所有棲居樹間的昆蟲以及森林的精靈，都為此大為憤怒。

passages.text: As soon as Rata had returned to the village at evening, when his day's work was ended, they all came and took the tree and raised it up again, and the innumerable multitude of insects, birds and spirits who are called 'The offspring of Hakuturi' worked away at replacing each little chip and shaving in its proper place, singing aloud their incantations as they worked: 'Fly together, chips and shavings; stick ye fast together; hold ye fast together; stand upright again, O tree!' Early the next morning back came Rata; if that fine tall straight tree which he saw standing whole and sound in the forest was the same he thought he had cut down, there it was now erect again. He stepped up to it and manfully hewing away felled it to the ground once more, and began to hollow out the hull and to slope off prow and stern; and in the evening, when it became too dark to work, returned to his village.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 7 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傍晚時分，拉塔一日的工作結束，剛一回到村莊，他們便全都前來，把那棵樹抬起，重新扶立起來；那數不清的昆蟲、鳥兒與精靈——被稱為「哈庫圖里之後裔」的——忙著把每一小片木屑與刨花放回原處，一邊勞作一邊高聲唱誦咒語：『木屑與刨花啊，一同飛聚吧；緊緊黏合吧；牢牢相連吧；再直立起來吧，哦，樹啊！』第二天清晨，拉塔又回來了；他所見那棵在森林中完好無損地矗立著的高大筆直的樹，若正是他以為已砍倒的那一棵，那麼它此刻又已重新立起。他走上前去，奮力砍伐，再一次把它砍倒在地，開始挖空船身、削出船首與船尾；到了傍晚，天色太暗無法工作時，他便回到村莊。

passages.text: As soon as he was gone, back came the innumerable multitudes and raised up the tree upon its stump once more, singing incantations as they worked, until the tree again stood sound as ever in its former place. The morning dawned and Rata returned once more; was not he amazed to see the tree standing up in the forest, untouched, just as he had at first found it? Nothing daunted, he hews away again and down it topples crashing to the earth; then he turned back and hid himself in the underwood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 7 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他剛一走，那數不清的眾多生靈便又回來，把樹重新扶立到樹樁上，一邊勞作一邊唱誦咒語，直到那棵樹又像從前一樣完好地立在原處。天明時分，拉塔又一次回來；他看見那棵樹立在森林中，毫髮無損，正如他最初發現它時那樣，怎能不驚詫萬分？他毫不氣餒，又砍了起來，樹轟然倒地；隨後他轉身躲進灌木叢中。

passages.text: He had not been hidden long when he heard the innumerable multitude of the children of Tane approaching, singing their incantations; he rushed upon them, seized some of them, and shouted, 'Ha, it is you, then, who have been exercising your magical arts upon my tree?' The children of Tane all cried aloud in reply, 'Who gave you authority to fell the forest god to the ground? You had no right to do so.' Rata was quite overcome with shame at what he had done. Then the offspring of Tane called out aloud to him, 'Return, O Rata, to thy village; we will make a canoe for you.' He obeyed without delay, and they were so numerous and understood each what to do so well, that they no sooner began to adze out a canoe than it was completed; the name they gave to that canoe was Riwaru.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 7 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他躲藏不久，便聽見塔內之子那數不清的眾多生靈走近，唱誦著咒語；他衝向他們，抓住其中幾個，喊道：『哈，原來是你們，一直在對我的樹施展法術？』塔內之子們齊聲高喊回答：『是誰給你權柄，把森林之神砍倒在地？你本無權這樣做。』拉塔對自己所做的事羞愧難當。於是塔內的後裔高聲對他說：『回去吧，哦，拉塔，回到你的村莊去；我們要為你造一隻獨木舟。』他立刻遵從；他們人數如此眾多，又個個深諳其職，剛一開始用錛子削鑿獨木舟，它便完工了；他們給那隻獨木舟取的名字是里瓦魯。

title.en: Rata Steals the Chant Titikura
title.zh: 拉塔竊得復生咒提提庫拉

region.en: Ponaturi sacred place (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波納圖里聖地（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 7, The Adventures of Rata (London 1855)

summary.en: Sailing to the Ponaturi, Rata finds their priests at the sacred fire beating his father's bones together as time-keepers for the powerful incantation Titikura, known to no one else. He listens until he knows it by heart, rushes the priests and slays them, and snatches the bones of Wahieroa. A thousand warriors pursue him and worst his tribe; but Rata repeats Titikura and his sixty slain warriors rise again to the combat, until the whole thousand pursuers are slain.
summary.zh: 拉塔率一百四十勇士航海至波納圖里。其祭司正在聖火旁，以瓦希耶羅亞之骨相互敲擊打拍，誦唸外人無從得知的強力咒語『提提庫拉』。拉塔潛聽至爛熟於心，驟然撲殺祭司，奪回父骨。千名敵兵追至，其族人戰死六十；拉塔默誦提提庫拉，死者悉數復起再戰，終將追兵千眾盡數殲滅。

sensitivity.note: Resurrection cluster: battlefield revival through a stolen chant; tagging interpretive.

passages.text: When the canoe was afloat upon the sea, 140 warriors embarked on board it, and without delay they paddled off to seek their foes. One night, just at nightfall, they reached the fortress of their enemies, who were named Ponaturi. Rata alone landed, leaving the canoe afloat and all his warriors on board; as he stole along the shore he saw that a fire was burning on the sacred place, where the Ponaturi consulted their gods and offered sacrifices to them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 7 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 独木舟浮于海面时，一百四十名战士登上了船，毫不迟疑地划桨出发，去寻找他们的仇敌。一天夜里，正当夜幕降临之际，他们抵达了敌人的堡垒，敌人名为波纳图里。唯有拉塔一人上岸，独木舟仍浮于水面，众战士皆留在船上；他沿着海岸悄悄前行，看见圣地之上燃着一堆火，波纳图里人正在那里向他们的神祇问卜，并献上祭品。

passages.text: Rata crept directly towards the fire and hid himself behind thick bushes of harakeke; on the other side of the same bushes were priests serving at the sacred place, who, to assist themselves in their magical arts, were making use of the bones of Wahieroa, knocking them together to beat time while repeating a powerful incantation, known only to themselves, the name of which was Titikura. Rata listened attentively to this incantation until he learnt it by heart; then he rushed suddenly upon the priests. Surprised and ignorant of the numbers of their enemy, they made little resistance and were in a moment smitten and slain. The bones of his father Wahieroa were eagerly snatched up; he hastened back to the canoe, embarked, and his warriors at once paddled away, striving to reach his fortified village.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 7 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 拉塔径直朝那火堆匍匐而去，藏身于茂密的哈拉凯凯灌木丛后；同一丛灌木的另一侧，是正在圣地侍奉的祭司们，他们为助成自己的法术，正使用着瓦希耶罗阿的骨骸，将骨头相互敲击以击打节拍，同时念诵一道只有他们自己才知晓的强力咒语，其名为蒂蒂库拉。拉塔凝神倾听这道咒语，直至将其熟记于心；随后他猛然扑向那些祭司。祭司们猝不及防，又不知敌人多寡，几乎未作抵抗，顷刻间便被击倒杀死。他父亲瓦希耶罗阿的骨骸被急切地夺了回来；他急忙返回独木舟，登船之后，众战士立刻划桨离去，奋力赶往他那设防的村落。

passages.text: In the morning some of the Ponaturi repaired to their sacred place and found their priests lying dead there just as they were slain by Rata; without delay a thousand warriors of their tribe pursued him. This army reached the fortress of Rata, and an engagement at once took place in which the tribe of Rata was worsted and sixty of its warriors slain. At this moment Rata bethought him of the spell he had learnt from the priests; immediately repeating the potent incantation Titikura, his slain warriors were by its power once more restored to life. Then they rushed again to the combat, and the Ponaturi were slaughtered by Rata and his tribe - the whole thousand were slain. Thus ended Rata's task of avenging his father's death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 7 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 清晨，一些波纳图里人前往他们的圣地，发现祭司们正如被拉塔杀死时那般倒毙在那里；他们毫不迟疑，一千名同族战士随即追赶他。这支军队抵达了拉塔的堡垒，战斗立刻爆发，拉塔的部族落败，六十名战士阵亡。就在此时，拉塔想起了他从祭司那里学来的咒语；他立刻念诵那道威力强大的咒语蒂蒂库拉，他阵亡的战士便凭其法力重获生命。于是他们再度冲入战斗，波纳图里人被拉塔及其部族屠杀殆尽——整整一千人尽数被杀。拉塔为父报仇的使命就此了结。

title.en: Whakatau Pulls Down Tihi-o-Manono
title.zh: 瓦卡陶拉倒提希奧馬諾諾

region.en: Great house Tihi-o-Manono (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 大屋提希奧馬諾諾（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, appendix variant)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 7 appendix: second legend of the destruction of Te Tihi-o-Manono (London 1855)

summary.en: In the often-quoted second recension, Tinirau sends Hine-i-te-iwaiwa to recruit Whakatau against the tribe that slew Tuwhakararo. Feasting the warriors with potted birds, Whakatau claims all the oil, crosses the sea by night with six men, and in single combat tricks ten champion warriors to their deaths - the diver Mango-huritapena transfixed through transparent oil, the leaper Pitakataka snared in mid-air. Disguised among firewood carriers, he ropes the great house Tihi-o-Manono post by post; when Mango-Pare finally names him as the strangler, he hauls the house down over the tribe and fires the ruin, its flames lighting the horizon as his sign to the watching widow.
summary.zh: 蒂尼勞遣希內特伊瓦伊瓦求賢，瓦卡陶受命復仇。他令大宴戰士、禽脂盡歸己用，夜渡大海。陣前連挫十位成名勇士：潛水冠軍被澄如明鏡的油水照見，一矛穿心；跳高冠軍凌空落網。他混入拾柴隊伍潛入大屋，用長繩逐柱纏繞整座提希奧馬諾諾；當被饒命的芒果帕雷認出『那個割舌者』時，他應聲承認，猛然拉繩——大屋轟然倒塌，全族葬身其中；烈焰映紅半邊天，正如他與守望寡婦約定的勝利信號。

sensitivity.note: Recorded as a variant appendix because it differs considerably from the main tale and is often alluded to in ancient poems.

passages.text: Tinirau determined to attempt to avenge the death of his descendant Tuwhakararo, and thought the best person to do this was Whakatau, whom he knew to be very skilful in war and in enchantments; so he directed his wife Hine-i-te-iwaiwa to find Whakatau. She found the kite-flying hero at last, and he told her: return at once and give a great feast to the warriors, abundance of potted birds from the forests, but let all the oil in which the birds were preserved be kept for me; do not go to the feast yourself, but, decking your head with a mourning dress of feathers, remain seated in the house of mourning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 7 appendix (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蒂尼劳决心设法为他的后裔图瓦卡卡罗之死报仇，他认为最适合担此重任的人是瓦卡陶，因为他知道瓦卡陶在战事与法术方面都极为娴熟；于是他吩咐妻子希内伊特伊瓦伊瓦去寻找瓦卡陶。她终于找到了那位放风筝的英雄，他对她说：立刻回去，为众战士备下一场盛大的宴席，要有大量林中腌制的鸟肉，但所有用来保存鸟肉的油都要留给我；你自己不要去赴宴，而要在头上戴起羽毛制成的丧服，坐在居丧之屋中。

passages.text: Whakatau and six warriors crossed to the anchorage before Tihi-o-Manono. Champions came forth one by one. Mango-huritapena declared himself a most skilful diver and plunged under the canoe; one of Whakatau's men poured Hine-i-te-iwaiwa's oil into the sea, the waters became quite transparent, and as the warrior came floating up beneath them Whakatau transfixed him with a wooden spade. Pitakataka boasted that he leapt so skilfully he seemed to fly in the air; Whakatau laid a noose upon the canoe, and as the warrior alighted in it he drew it tight and caught him as a bird in a springe. Thus one after the other he slew ten of the most famous warriors of his enemies; one he saved alive, but cut out his tongue, sending him back to tell them how he had overcome them all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 7 appendix (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 瓦卡陶与六名战士渡海来到蒂希奥马诺诺前的停泊处。勇士们一个接一个地出来挑战。曼戈胡里塔佩纳自称是极娴熟的潜水者，一头潜入独木舟之下；瓦卡陶的一名手下将希内伊特伊瓦伊瓦的油倒入海中，海水顿时变得清澈透明，当那名战士从他们下方浮起时，瓦卡陶用一把木铲将他刺穿。皮塔卡塔夸口说自己跳跃技艺高超，仿佛在空中飞翔；瓦卡陶在独木舟上布下套索，当那名战士落于其上时，他猛地收紧套索，如用陷阱捕鸟一般将他擒住。就这样，他一个接一个地杀死了敌人中最著名的十名勇士；他留下一个活口，却割去了他的舌头，放他回去告诉众人他是如何将他们全部制服的。

passages.text: He sent his men back with a sign: if heavy rain fell in large drops, he had been killed; but if a light misty rain fell and the whole horizon was lighted up with flames, he had conquered and burnt Tihi-o-Manono. Just before nightfall he dropped in amongst the people of the great chief Whitinakonako collecting firewood, pushed in front of them into the house with a long rope in his hand, pushed one end between each side-post and the plank walls until the rope had gone quite round the house, and made it fast to the last post, holding the other end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 7 appendix (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他派手下带着一个信号回去：若降下大颗雨点的骤雨，便是他被杀了；但若降下轻薄的蒙蒙细雨，且整个天际被火焰照亮，便是他已获胜，并烧毁了蒂希奥马诺诺。就在夜幕降临之前，他落入那位大酋长惠蒂纳科纳科的人群之中，他们正在拾取柴薪；他手持一条长绳，从他们前面挤进屋内，将绳子的一端穿入每一根侧柱与木板墙之间，直到绳子绕屋整整一周，并把它系在最后一根柱子上，另一端则握在手中。

passages.text: Ten fires were lit as the great house filled; when Mango-Pare, whose tongue he had cut out, was made to describe the strangler and finally declared, 'He looks very like this fellow - perhaps it is he himself', Whakatau shouted aloud, 'You are right, it was I.' As they sprang to their feet he laid hold of the rope-end, rushed out, pulled it with all his strength, and straightway the house fell down, crushing all within it. He set it on fire, and Hine-i-te-iwaiwa, watching from the roof of her house, saw one whole part of the heavens red with its flames and knew her enemies were destroyed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 7 appendix (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大屋渐渐坐满，十堆火被点燃；曼戈-帕雷（Mango-Pare）的舌头曾被他割去，此时被迫描述那个扼杀者，最后说道：『他看上去很像这家伙——也许就是他本人。』法卡陶（Whakatau）便大声喊道：『你说得对，就是我。』众人纷纷跳起身来，他一把抓住绳端，冲了出去，用尽全力拉绳，屋子随即倒塌，把里面的人全都压死。他放火烧屋，希内-伊-特-伊瓦伊瓦（Hine-i-te-iwaiwa）从自家屋顶上观望，看见半边天被火焰映得通红，便知道她的仇敌已被消灭。

title.en: Perkunas Chops the Moon in Two
title.zh: 佩爾庫納斯劈月為二

region.en: Lithuania (symbolic pin at Vilnius)
region.zh: 立陶宛（象徵性定位於維爾紐斯）

period: Daina recorded 19th c. (Rhesa); recorded by Grimm 1888

source.work: Jacob Grimm, Teutonic Mythology, vol. IV (Stallybrass trans., London 1888), addenda on sky and stars, citing L. Rhesa's dainas

summary.en: As the Edda calls the half-moon 'inn skarði máni', the ship-shaped moon, so the Lithuanian dainas tell that Perkunas chopped the moon in two with his sword — the waning moon is a god's blade-cut.
summary.zh: 如《埃達》稱半月為『船形之月』，立陶宛達伊納亦詠佩爾庫納斯以劍劈月為二——月虧即神劍之痕。

sensitivity.note: Variant of the moon-forsakes-sun myth; cross-tagged.

passages.text: In the Edda the half-moon is called 'inn skarði máni' — the notched, ship-shaped moon; and indeed Perkunas chops the moon in two, as the Lithuanian dainas collected by Rhesa tell. The thunder-god's blade explains the crescent: every waning night is another cut of the sword that avenged the Sun upon her faithless husband.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Grimm, Teutonic Mythology IV (Stallybrass 1888), addenda citing Rhesa's dainas; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在《埃达》中，半月被称为「inn skarði máni」——带缺口的、船形的月亮；而佩尔库纳斯（Perkunas）确实把月亮劈成两半，正如雷萨（Rhesa）所收集的立陶宛达伊纳（dainas）歌谣所述。雷神的刀刃解释了这弯新月：每一个渐亏的夜晚，都是那把为太阳向她不忠的丈夫复仇之剑的又一次挥砍。

passages.text: The comparison binds the Baltic sky-myths to the whole Indo-European family of waning-moon tales: moon-cows and moon-horns, new moons hailed as children, and a god whose stroke divides the light. In the dainas the stroke falls after the Moon forsook the Sun for the Morning Star — Perkunas's grief for the Sun's dishonour is written nightly across the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Grimm, Teutonic Mythology IV (Stallybrass 1888), addenda; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 这一比较把波罗的海的天空神话与整个印欧语系的亏月故事群联系起来：月牛与月角，被欢呼为孩童的新月，以及一位一击便将光明劈开的神。在达伊纳歌谣中，这一击落在月亮为晨星而背弃太阳之后——佩尔库纳斯为太阳所受的羞辱而悲伤，这悲伤每夜都写满天空。

title.en: The Stolen Sun Delivered by Perkun's Hammer
title.zh: 被竊之日：佩爾庫恩之錘解救

region.en: Baltic-Finnish borderlands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波羅的海-芬蘭邊地（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded in Neue Preussische Provinzial-Blätter; cited by Grimm 1888

source.work: Jacob Grimm, Teutonic Mythology, vol. IV (Stallybrass trans., 1888), addenda on sky and stars, citing Neue Preussische Provinzial-Blätter I

summary.en: In the far north of Pohjola the sun and moon were stolen and held captive — and it is Perkun's hammer that delivers the sun from captivity, the same blow that shattered the tower of the older Lithuanian myth.
summary.zh: 極北波赫尤拉之地，日月被竊遭囚——而救出太陽者乃佩爾庫恩之錘，即古立陶宛神話中擊破高塔之同一柄錘。

sensitivity.note: Variant mixing Finnish Kalevala imagery with the Lithuanian tower myth; cross_ref baltic-sun-tower-hammer.

passages.text: In Pohjola the sun and moon get stolen — the dark land of the Kalevala's north where light is carried away and hidden. In the version preserved in the Neue Preussische Provinzial-Blätter, the sun is delivered from captivity by Perkun's hammer: the thunder-god's weapon breaks the prison of the light, as it broke the tower in the old Lithuanian story told to Pope Pius II's informant.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Grimm, Teutonic Mythology IV (Stallybrass 1888), addenda; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在波赫尤拉（Pohjola），太阳和月亮被偷走了——那是《卡勒瓦拉》北方幽暗之地，光明在那里被带走并藏匿。在《新普鲁士省报》（Neue Preussische Provinzial-Blätter）所保存的版本中，太阳是靠佩尔昆（Perkun）的锤子从囚禁中获释的：雷神的武器击破了光明的牢狱，正如它在向教皇庇护二世的线人讲述的古老立陶宛故事中击破了那座塔。

passages.text: The motif joins the Baltic myth to the Finnish Sampo cycle and to the worldwide family of sun-theft tales — the dragon that swallows the moon, the demon Rahus that threatens both lights. Each tradition arms a rescuer with the thunder-weapon, and the release of the sun is counted as the first day of spring.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Grimm, Teutonic Mythology IV (Stallybrass 1888), addenda; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 这一母题把波罗的海神话与芬兰的桑波（Sampo）循环，以及世界范围的窃日故事群联系起来——吞月的巨龙，威胁两种光明的恶魔拉胡斯（Rahus）。每一种传统都为拯救者配备雷之武器，而太阳的获释被算作春天的第一天。

title.en: The Perkun Stone of Courland
title.zh: 庫爾蘭的佩爾庫恩石

region.en: Near Bauska (Battenhof), Courland, Latvia
region.zh: 庫爾蘭鮑斯卡附近（象徵性定位）

period: Stone legend recorded 19th c. (Kruse); cited by Grimm 1888

source.work: Jacob Grimm, Teutonic Mythology, vol. IV (Stallybrass trans., 1888), Thunar addenda, citing F. Kruse, Urgeschichte

summary.en: Near Battenhof in Courland stands the Perkunstein, a thunder-stone with its own legends, while a Livland rhymed chronicle of 1435 still names Perkune as the god 'who gave his abbot' — the old thunder-god remembered in stone and chronicle alike.
summary.zh: 庫爾蘭鮑斯卡附近矗立『佩爾庫恩石』，自有其傳說；一四三五年里夫蘭押韻編年史猶稱佩爾庫恩為彼等之神——雷神之記憶存於石與史。

sensitivity.note: Thunder-stone belief parallel to the Greek bidental and Vedic vajra.

passages.text: Near Battenhof in Courland stands a Perkunstein — Perkun's stone — a great boulder round which legends gathered, recorded by Kruse; and near Libau a place was still called Perkuhnen. The Livland rhymed chronicle of 1435, speaking of the old faith, says 'als ez Perkune ir abgot gap' — as Perkune, their idol-god, gave them — the thunder-god's name surviving a century into the era of chronicles.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Grimm, Teutonic Mythology IV (Stallybrass 1888), Thunar addenda, citing Kruse and the Livland rhymed chronicle; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在库尔兰（Courland）的巴滕霍夫（Battenhof）附近矗立着一块佩尔昆石（Perkunstein）——佩尔昆之石——一块巨大的漂砾，周围聚集了许多传说，由克鲁泽（Kruse）记录；而在利鲍（Libau）附近，有个地方仍被称为佩尔库嫩（Perkuhnen）。1435年的《利沃尼亚韵文编年史》在谈到古老信仰时说：「als ez Perkune ir abgot gap」——正如他们的偶像之神佩尔昆所赐予的——雷神之名在编年史时代又延续了一个世纪。

passages.text: Lithuanians call the prehistoric stone axe-head 'Perkuno kulka' — Perkunas's ball — and the belemnite 'Perkuno akmu' — Perkunas's stone: the god's bolts turned to stone lie in every ploughed field. In the older languages the same word served for thunder-stroke and for the god himself, as 'Perkuns twyksterejo' means the thunder has crashed and 'Perkuns uzdege' — the thunder has kindled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Grimm, Teutonic Mythology IV (Stallybrass 1888), Thunar addenda; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 立陶宛人稱史前的石斧為「Perkuno kulka」——佩爾庫納斯的球——又稱箭石為「Perkuno akmu」——佩爾庫納斯的石頭：神明的雷霆化為石頭，躺在每一片犁過的田裡。在較古老的語言中，同一個詞既指雷擊，也指神本身，例如「Perkuns twyksterejo」意為雷已轟然炸響，「Perkuns uzdege」則意為雷已燃起。

title.en: Ilyios Diena: The Day of Elias That Opens and Shuts the Rain
title.zh: 伊利亞之日：開雨閉雨之日

region.en: Lithuania (symbolic pin at Vilnius)
region.zh: 立陶宛（象徵性定位於維爾紐斯）

period: Custom recorded 19th c.; cited by Grimm 1888

source.work: Jacob Grimm, Teutonic Mythology, vol. IV (Stallybrass trans., 1888), Thunar addenda

summary.en: The Lithuanians call Lady-day 'Ilyios diena' — Elias's day — on which it begins or ceases to rain: the prophet who took over Perkunas's thunder still keeps the keys of the weather, holding back rain and letting it flow again at his pleasure.
summary.zh: 立陶宛人稱聖母領報日為『伊利亞之日』——是日雨水始降或止息；繼承佩爾庫納斯雷霆的先知仍掌天氣之鑰，欲蓄則蓄，欲放則放。

sensitivity.note: Pagan-into-Christian weather saint, as with St. Iliya in Russia.

passages.text: The Lithuanians call Lady-day 'Elyiõs diena' or 'Ilyios diena', on which day it begins or ceases to rain. Grimm asks whether the name comes from the Lithuanian verb for 'it sets in (to rain)' or rather from Elias's day — the prophet of the thunder-chariot who received the old rain-god's office.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Grimm, Teutonic Mythology IV (Stallybrass 1888), Thunar addenda; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 立陶宛人稱聖母節為「Elyiõs diena」或「Ilyios diena」，雨水在這一天開始降下或停止。格林姆問，這個名稱是來自立陶宛語中表示「（雨）開始下」的動詞，還是來自以利亞的日子——那位駕雷車的先知，承接了古老雨神的職司。

passages.text: The old German verses on Enoch and Elias say the two have the power to keep back the rain when they please, and again let it flow, their tongues able to shut up heaven and open it again — exactly the office Perkunas held in the Baltic, and St. Iliya in Russia and among the South Slavs, where no man works in the fields on the Thunderer's day lest the saint slay him with the bolt.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Grimm, Teutonic Mythology IV (Stallybrass 1888), Thunar addenda; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 關於以諾與以利亞的古德語詩句說，二人有能力隨意止住雨水，又能再讓它流下，他們的舌能閉合天，又能再開啟——這正是佩爾庫納斯在波羅的海地區所掌的職司，也是俄羅斯與南斯拉夫人中間聖伊利亞的職司；在雷神之日，無人下田勞作，唯恐聖者以雷霆將他擊殺。

title.en: Perkunas and Pikullos Travel the Earth Giving Gifts
title.zh: 佩爾庫納斯與皮庫洛斯行世贈禮

region.en: Old Prussia (symbolic pin at Konigsberg)
region.zh: 古普魯士（象徵性定位於柯尼斯堡）

period: Recorded by Tettau & Temme, Die Vor-Sagen und Volks-Sagen... (1837); cited by Grimm 1888

source.work: Jacob Grimm, Teutonic Mythology, vol. IV (Stallybrass trans., 1888), addenda on wandering gods, citing Tettau and Temme, Ostpreussische und Litthauische Sagen, p. 28

summary.en: The god and the devil, Perkunas and Pikullos, travel together through the Old Prussian land in borrowed shapes and give gifts to men: the old belief that the gods themselves came down to walk the roads, testing hosts and rewarding them — as Zeus and Hermes walked the earth.
summary.zh: 神與魔——佩爾庫納斯與皮庫洛斯——易形同行，行走普魯士大地，向世人贈禮：古信神明親自降世行於道路，試煉主人而賞罰之——如宙斯與赫爾墨斯之巡遊。

sensitivity.note: God-and-devil travel tale; parallel to Zeus-Hermes Baucis-Philemon and Odin wanderings.

passages.text: The Lithuanians tell of Perkunos — or, in later retellings, the Saviour — and his encounter with the horse and the ox; and in the Old Prussian tales collected by Tettau and Temme, Perkunos and Pikullos travel together through the country, and give gifts to men. The thunder-god and his dark companion walk the roads in disguise, coming themselves rather than sending messengers, as the old heathen gods were believed to do.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Grimm, Teutonic Mythology IV (Stallybrass 1888), addenda on wandering gods, after Tettau and Temme; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 立陶宛人講述佩爾庫諾斯——或在後來的轉述中作救主——與馬和牛的遭遇；而在泰陶與泰梅所搜集的古普魯士故事中，佩爾庫諾斯與皮庫洛斯一同遊歷鄉間，賜予人們禮物。雷神與他黑暗的同伴喬裝行走於道路之上，親自前來而非派遣使者，正如人們相信古代異教神明所做的那樣。

passages.text: The wandering keeps recurring to the antique incident of the divine visitor: gods and the Dioscuri travel unrecognised among men, a child is served up for Zeus, and three wishes are granted to the worthy host. In the Baltic telling the two travellers divide the offices — the god gives gifts, the devil his due — and the hospitality or churlishness of each house on the road fixes its fortune.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Grimm, Teutonic Mythology IV (Stallybrass 1888), addenda on wandering gods; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這種漫遊反覆回到神聖訪客的古老事蹟：神明與狄俄斯庫里兄弟不為人識地行走於人間，有人為宙斯端上一名孩童，三個願望被賜予那位配得的東道主。在波羅的海的講述中，兩位旅人分擔職司——神賜予禮物，魔鬼得其應得——而沿途每一戶人家的好客或慳吝，便決定了它的命運。

title.en: Auschteini: The Dawn Goddess of the Samogitians
title.zh: 奧施泰尼：薩莫吉提亞的黎明女神

region.en: Samogitia, western Lithuania (symbolic pin at Telsiai)
region.zh: 薩莫吉提亞，立陶宛西部（象徵性定位於特爾希艾）

period: Recorded by Lasicki, De diis Samagitarum (1582); recorded by Grimm 1888

source.work: Jacob Grimm, Teutonic Mythology, vol. IV (Stallybrass trans., 1888), goddess addenda, citing J. Lasicki, De diis Samagitarum (1582)

summary.en: In Lasicki's old list of Samogitian gods stands Auschteini — Aušra, 'dea occumbentis vel ascendentis solis', the goddess of the setting and rising sun, sister of the dainas' Aušrinė who tends the Sun's fire and couch.
summary.zh: 拉西茨基一五八二年薩莫吉提亞神譜中有奧施泰尼——奧什拉，『日落與日出之女神』，即達伊納斯中司日之火與榻的奧什林涅姊妹。

sensitivity.note: Dawn-goddess parallel to Vedic Usas and Greek Eos.

passages.text: Grimm traces the name from the Sanskrit Ushas, dawn, through the Lithuanian 'auszta' — it dawns — to 'auszrinne', the aurora. In Lasicki's old register of the Samogitian gods she stands as Auschteini, or Ausra, 'dea occumbentis vel ascendentis solis' — the goddess of the sun that sets and the sun that rises.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Grimm, Teutonic Mythology IV (Stallybrass 1888), goddess addenda, citing Lasicki; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 格林姆追溯這個名稱，從梵語的優沙斯（黎明），經立陶宛語的「auszta」——天亮了——到「auszrinne」，即極光。在拉西茨基那份古老的薩莫吉提亞神明名錄中，她以奧施泰尼（Auschteini）或奧斯拉（Ausra）之名出現，即「dea occumbentis vel ascendentis solis」——落日與升日之女神。

passages.text: She is the one the dainas call Aušrinė, the morning star and handmaid of Saule: Morning Star makes the Sun's fire, Evening Star prepares her couch. In the Lettish songs her masculine doublets are the 'sons of God', wooers of the Sun's daughter — the same being seen now as the shining maid who opens the day and now as the youth who rides to meet her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Grimm, Teutonic Mythology IV (Stallybrass 1888), goddess addenda; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 達伊納斯歌謠稱她為奧什里涅（Aušrinė），即晨星，亦是紹萊（Saule）的侍女：晨星燃起太陽之火，晚星為她鋪設臥榻。在拉脫維亞的歌謠中，她的男性對應者乃是「神之子」，即太陽之女的求婚者——同一個存在，時而被視為揭開白晝的閃耀少女，時而被視為策馬前來相迎的少年。

title.en: The Perpetual Fire of the Samogitians
title.zh: 薩莫吉提亞人的不滅之火

region.en: Samogitia / Prussia, shrine of Romowe (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩莫吉提亞／普魯士羅莫沃聖所（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded by Lasicki (1582); recorded by Grimm 1888

source.work: Jacob Grimm, Teutonic Mythology, vol. IV (Stallybrass trans., 1888), fire-worship addenda, citing Lasicki 56

summary.en: The Samogitians nourished a perpetual fire, as Lasicki records — one flame among the world's eternal fires, from Vesta's hearth to Parsee fire-temples: never allowed to die, because in that fire the god himself was thought to burn.
summary.zh: 如拉西茨基所記，薩莫吉提亞人養不滅之火——與維斯塔聖火、祆教火廟同列世界永燃之火：因其火中即神自身之燃，故不可使其熄。

sensitivity.note: Eternal-fire parallels: Vesta, Delphi, Delos, Parsee atash.

passages.text: The Samogitians nourished a perpetual fire, Lasicki records — the Baltic branch of the worldwide family of undying flames. A fire burned on the altar of Athena Polias at Athens, in the temple of Pan in Arcadia; the famous oracle of Delphi kept an ever-burning fire whose priests in war conveyed the sacred flame to Plataea; colonies took their sacred fire with them from the mother-city, and if it went out there alone could they light it again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Grimm, Teutonic Mythology IV (Stallybrass 1888), fire-worship addenda, citing Lasicki 56; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 拉西茨基記載，薩莫吉提亞人供奉著一團永不熄滅的火，這是遍佈世界的不滅之火家族中的波羅的海一支。雅典衛城上雅典娜·波利阿斯（Athena Polias）的祭壇上燃著火，阿卡迪亞的潘神廟中亦然；著名的德爾斐神諭守護著一團長明之火，其祭司在戰時將聖火傳送至普拉蒂亞；殖民地從母城帶走自己的聖火，而一旦那火熄滅，唯有在母城方能重新點燃。

passages.text: In the Baltic the eternal flame belongs to the shrine of Romowe, where the sacred oak stands green winter and summer, screened from profane gaze, and the piles of oak-wood for the sacred fire lie in the open spaces about it. The Vaidelots, the ordinary priests, keep the flame; on it every hearth of the land is lit anew — the fire that, once out, cannot be rekindled from anywhere but the god's own altar.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Romowe shrine description in Mythology of All Races III (1918) plate note and Grimm IV; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在波羅的海地區，永恆之火屬於羅莫韋（Romowe）的聖所，那裡的神聖橡樹冬夏常青，隔絕於凡俗的目光之外，而供聖火所用的成堆橡木則置於其周圍的空地上。瓦伊德洛特（Vaidelots），即普通的祭司，守護著這團火焰；全地每一處爐灶皆由此火重新點燃——這火一旦熄滅，便無處可以重燃，唯有從神自己的祭壇取火。

title.en: The Milk-Fed Snake: Household God Behind the Stove
title.zh: 飲乳之蛇：爐後家蛇神

region.en: Samogitia, Lithuania (symbolic pin at Kaunas)
region.zh: 薩莫吉提亞，立陶宛（象徵性定位於考納斯）

period: Recorded by Lasicki (1582); recorded by Grimm 1888

source.work: Jacob Grimm, Teutonic Mythology, vol. IV (Stallybrass trans., 1888), serpent addenda, citing Lasicki 51-56

summary.en: The Samogitians kept black snakes — the gluoitos, the žaltys — fed on milk and worshipped as household gods; whoever kills the house-snake kills the luck of the house, for the snake that drinks milk at the hearth is the family's own guardian genius.
summary.zh: 薩莫吉提亞人畜養黑蛇——格洛伊托斯（日之扎爾提斯）——以乳飼之，奉為家神；殺家蛇者即毀家宅之運，蓋爐邊飲乳之蛇乃一家守護之神。

sensitivity.note: House-snake cult parallels Greek oikouros ophis and Slavic Hospodaricek.

passages.text: The Greeks called the home-snake 'oikouros ophis', genius loci; the Albanian vittore is a homesprite imagined as a little snake; and the Samogitian gluoitos — black snakes — are fed and worshipped as household gods, Lasicki records. The snake drinks milk at the hearth, and the custom of milk-drinking is the mark of the family's own guardian.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Grimm, Teutonic Mythology IV (Stallybrass 1888), serpent addenda, citing Lasicki 51-56; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 希臘人稱家蛇為「oikouros ophis」，即地方守護神；阿爾巴尼亞的「vittore」是設想為小蛇的家宅精靈；而拉西茨基記載，薩莫吉提亞的「gluoitos」——黑蛇——被餵養並作為家神受到崇拜。蛇在爐邊飲奶，而飲奶的習俗正是這戶人家自有守護者的標誌。

passages.text: Serpents lick the ears of the sleeping Melampus, who wakes understanding the speech of birds; prophetic Cassandra and Helenus had their ears licked clean by snakes. In the Lithuanian household the same gift runs backward: feed the žaltys and it will hear what the house needs, foretell and prosper; slay it and the happiness and well-being of the family die with it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Grimm, Teutonic Mythology IV (Stallybrass 1888), serpent addenda; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蛇舔舐熟睡中墨蘭普斯（Melampus）的耳朵，他醒來便聽懂了鳥語；預言者卡珊德拉（Cassandra）與赫勒諾斯（Helenus）的耳朵也曾被蛇舔淨。在立陶宛人的家中，這同一種天賦卻反向而行：餵養扎爾蒂斯（žaltys），它便會聽見這戶人家的所需，預言並帶來興旺；殺死它，這家人的幸福與安樂便隨之而死。

title.en: The Gods Inside the Bark: Samogitian Tree Belief
title.zh: 樹皮中的神明：薩莫吉提亞樹木信仰

region.en: Samogitian groves (symbolic pin in western Lithuania)
region.zh: 薩莫吉提亞聖林（象徵性定位於立陶宛西部）

period: Recorded by Lasicki (1582); recorded by Grimm 1888

source.work: Jacob Grimm, Teutonic Mythology, vol. IV (Stallybrass trans., 1888), tree-worship addenda, citing Lasicki

summary.en: 'They believe the gods dwell in the groves... he believed the gods to hide within trees and bark', writes Lasicki of the Samogitians: not that a tree is dedicated to a god, but that the god is inside the wood — which is why the sacred oak of Romowe stays green winter and summer, screened from profane eyes.
summary.zh: 拉西茨基記薩莫吉提亞人云：『信神居於林中……信神藏於樹木樹皮之內』——非謂樹木屬神，乃神即在木中；故羅莫沃聖橡冬夏常青，隔絕俗目。

sensitivity.note: Tree-spirit belief.

passages.text: 'Deos nemora incolere persuasum habent,' Lasicki writes of the Samogitians — they are persuaded that the gods dwell in the groves; 'credebat deos intra arbores et cortices latere' — he believed the gods to hide within trees and bark. The god is not the tree's tenant but its inhabitant: fell the tree and you break the house of a god.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Grimm, Teutonic Mythology IV (Stallybrass 1888), tree-worship addenda, citing Lasicki; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「Deos nemora incolere persuasum habent」，拉西茨基如此記述薩莫吉提亞人——他們深信諸神居住在樹林中；「credebat deos intra arbores et cortices latere」——他相信諸神藏於樹木與樹皮之內。神並非樹的租客，而是樹的居民：砍倒那樹，你便毀了一位神的居所。

passages.text: With this compare the sacred oak of Romowe, which remained green summer and winter and was screened from profane gaze, the idols of Perkunas, Potrimpo, and Patollo within it, and the piles of sacred wood in the open spaces round about. In the Finnish north the oak is 'God's tree'; among the Greeks it was Zeus's oak, the robur Jovis — one belief from the Baltic to Dodona.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Grimm, Teutonic Mythology IV (Stallybrass 1888), tree-worship addenda; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 與此相比，羅莫韋（Romowe）的聖橡樹終年常綠，無論夏冬，且被遮蔽於凡俗目光之外，樹內有佩爾庫納斯（Perkunas）、波特林波（Potrimpo）與帕托洛（Patollo）的神像，四周空地上則堆積著聖木。在芬蘭北方，橡樹是「神之樹」；在希臘人之中，它是宙斯的橡樹，即 robur Jovis——從波羅的海到多多納，同為一種信仰。

title.en: Cocks for Kirnis: The Samogitian Offering
title.zh: 獻基爾尼斯之雞：薩莫吉提亞祭儀

region.en: Samogitia (symbolic pin at Telsiai)
region.zh: 薩莫吉提亞（象徵性定位於特爾希艾）

period: Recorded by Lasicki (1582); recorded by Grimm 1888

source.work: Jacob Grimm, Teutonic Mythology, vol. IV (Stallybrass trans., 1888), sacrifice addenda, citing Lasicki 47

summary.en: The Samogitians sacrificed cocks to their god Kirnis, as Lasicki records — one line of his old register that preserves the memory of a god whose altar received the bird of dawn.
summary.zh: 如拉西茨基所記，薩莫吉提亞人宰雞以祭其神基爾尼斯——其古老神譜一行，猶存此受晨雞之祭的神之記憶。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary deity; interpretive reconstruction flagged.

passages.text: Samogitians sacrificed cocks to Kirnos — Kirnis — as Lasicki's register records: a bare line, but enough to fix a god and his bird. Among the Estonians, when a cock is sacrificed, the blood spurts into the fire, the feathers, head, feet, and entrails are cast into the same, and the rest boiled and eaten; the offering is divided between god and household.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Grimm, Teutonic Mythology IV (Stallybrass 1888), sacrifice addenda, citing Lasicki 47; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 薩莫吉提亞人（Samogitians）向基爾諾斯（Kirnos）——即基爾尼斯（Kirnis）——獻祭公雞，正如拉西茨基（Lasicki）的紀錄所載：僅有一行簡略的文字，卻足以確定一位神祇及其鳥。在愛沙尼亞人之中，獻祭公雞時，鮮血噴入火中，羽毛、頭、腳與內臟一併投入同處，其餘則煮熟食用；祭品由神祇與家戶分食。

passages.text: The cock that crows at dawn belongs to the sky-gods of the whole Indo-European north; in the Prussian triad of Romowe the household snake is fed before Potrimpo, the goat is hallowed, and the cock cries to the thunderer. Kirnis's festival, whatever its month, was the householder's yearly gift upward and the god's blessing downward on flock and field.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Grimm, Teutonic Mythology IV (Stallybrass 1888), sacrifice addenda; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 黎明啼叫的公雞屬於整個印歐北方諸天空神祇；在羅莫韋的普魯士三神之中，家蛇先於波特林波（Potrimpo）受餵養，山羊被奉為神聖，公雞則向雷神鳴叫。基爾尼斯（Kirnis）的節慶，無論在何月，都是家戶每年向上的獻禮，以及神祇向下對畜群與田地的祝福。

title.en: Purun-pacha: Nations from Beyond Potosi and the Night Demons
title.zh: 普龍帕查:波托西之外的族群與夜間惡魔

region.en: Potosi region, from which the nations came (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 族群所來自的波托西地區(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua, native of Collasuyu, wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In the age called Purun-pacha all the nations of Ttahuantin-suyu came from beyond Potosi in four or five armies arrayed for war, settling district by district as they advanced. The period lasted a vast number of years. When the country was peopled there was a great want of space: wars and quarrels, fortresses on every side, daily encounters, and no peace. In the middle of the night the people heard the Hapi-ñuños - the demons who in ancient times walked visibly over the land and violently carried off men, women and children - disappearing with mournful complaints, crying out 'We are conquered, we are conquered, alas that we should lose our bands!' Salcamayhua, a Christian, reads this as the demons conquered by Christ on the cross of Calvary; in the native frame it records the silencing of the old night-spirits at the turning of the age.
summary.zh: 在名為「普龍帕查」的時代,大蘇尤(Ttahuantin-suyu)所有族群自波托西之外而來,分四五路列陣遷徙,且行且擇地而居。此期歷時極久。人滿之後,土地不足,戰爭四起,堡壘林立,日日交鋒,永無寧日。夜半之時,人們聽見「哈皮紐紐」——古時顯形於大地、夜裡擄走男女孩童的惡魔——哀號而去:「我們敗了,我們敗了,竟失了我們的隊伍!」基督徒薩爾卡馬瓦將此讀作惡魔在加爾瓦略山上被基督釘十字所敗;而在本源的神話語境中,這是舊夜靈隨時代更替而消音的記錄。

sensitivity.note: Salcamayhua (c. 1613) is the one major Andean-authored colonial narrative; his Christian overlay is quoted as part of the record, not as native belief.

passages.text: They say that, in the time of Purun-pacha, all the nations of Ttahuantin-suyu came from beyond Potosi in four or five armies arrayed for war. They settled in the different districts as they advanced. This period was called Ccallac-pacha or Tutayac-pacha. As each company selected suitable places for their homes and lands, they called this Purunpacharacyaptin. This period lasted for a vast number of years.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說，在普倫帕查（Purun-pacha）時代，塔萬廷蘇尤（Ttahuantin-suyu）的所有民族都從波托西（Potosi）之外而來，分成四五支列陣備戰的軍隊。他們隨著推進而分別定居於各區。這一時期被稱為卡利亞克帕查（Ccallac-pacha）或圖塔亞克帕查（Tutayac-pacha）。由於每一隊人馬都為自己的居所與土地選定了適宜之地，他們便稱此為普倫帕查拉查普廷（Purunpacharacyaptin）。這一時期持續了極其漫長的歲月。

passages.text: After the country was peopled, there was a great want of space, and, as the land was insufficient, there were wars and quarrels, and all the nations occupied themselves in making fortresses, and every day there were encounters and battles, and there was no rest from these tumults, insomuch that the people never enjoyed any peace. Then, in the middle of the night, they heard the Hapi-ñuños disappearing, with mournful complaints, and crying out: 'We are conquered, we are conquered, alas that we should lose our bands!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此地有人聚居之後，空間大為不足，且土地不敷使用，於是發生了戰爭與爭鬥，所有民族都忙於修築堡壘，每日都有交鋒與戰鬥，這些動亂從無止息，以致人們從未享有任何安寧。後來，在半夜時分，他們聽見哈皮紐紐斯（Hapi-ñuños）帶著悲傷的怨訴聲消失，並呼喊著：「我們被征服了，我們被征服了，唉，我們竟失去了我們的隊伍！」

passages.text: In ancient times, in the days of Purun-pacha, they say that the Hapi-ñuñus walked visibly over all the land, and it was unsafe to go out at night, for they violently carried off men, women, and children, like infernal tyrants and enemies of the human race. By the cry at midnight it must be understood, in Salcamayhua's reading, that the devils were conquered by Jesus Christ our Lord on the cross on Mount Calvary.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim; the Calvary gloss is the author's own.
passages.zh: 據說在遠古時代，即普倫帕查（Purun-pacha）的日子裡，哈皮紐紐斯（Hapi-ñuñus）曾可見地行走於整片大地之上，夜間外出並不安全，因為他們如地獄般的暴君與人類之敵，強行擄走男人、女人與孩童。依薩爾卡馬伊瓦（Salcamayhua）的解讀，半夜的呼喊必須理解為：眾魔鬼已於加爾瓦略山上，被我們的主耶穌基督在十字架上所征服。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Tonapa the Bearded Preacher: Staff, Stick of Commandments and Cursed Lakes
title.zh: 鬚髯傳道者托納帕:手杖、誡命之杖與受詛之湖

region.en: Village of Apo-tampu (Paccari-tampu), Collasuyu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科利亞蘇尤阿波坦波村(帕卡里坦波)(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Some years after the Hapi-ñuñus had been driven out, there arrived in Ttahuantin-suyu a bearded man of middle height, with long hair and a rather long shirt, somewhat past his prime, grey-haired and lean. He travelled with his staff, teaching the natives with much love, calling them all his sons and daughters, healing the sick by his touch, speaking all languages better than the natives. They called him Tonapa or Tarapaca (an eagle), the servant, the preacher. The people would not listen, thinking little of him. At the village of Apo-tampu - Paccari-tampu - he arrived very tired at a marriage feast; the chief listened kindly, and Tonapa gave him a stick from his own staff, on which each chapter of his precepts was marked and scored: the Caçi-caçi, the commandments of God. But in Yamquesupa he was treated with insolence and driven away, often sleeping in the fields with only his shirt, a mantle and a book; he cursed that village so that it was covered with water - the lake called Yamquisupaloiga. On the high hill Cacha-pucara he burned an idol in the form of a woman, destroying it with the hill; and where a wedding crowd would not hear him, he cursed them and they were turned into stones, seen to this day in Pucara and other places. Salcamayhua asks: was he not the glorious apostle St Thomas?
summary.zh: 哈皮紐紐被逐後數年,一位鬚髯、長髮、身著長衫的中年男子來到大蘇尤:他已過盛年,頭髮灰白,身形清瘦,拄杖而行,滿懷慈愛教導土人,稱眾人皆其兒女;他以手觸身治癒病者,操各種語言比土人還流利。人們稱他為托納帕或塔拉帕卡(意為鷹)、僕人、傳道者。但民眾不聽,輕視他。他疲憊地抵達阿波坦波村(即帕卡里坦波)時,正值婚宴;酋長善意聽道,托納帕便從自己手杖上折下一枝交給他,在杖上刻記誡命各章——即「卡西-卡西」,上帝的誡命。而在亞姆克蘇帕村,他遭辱罵驅逐,常只以長衫、斗篷與一本書露宿野外;他遂咒詛此村,大水將其淹沒,即今亞姆克蘇帕湖。在高山卡查-普卡拉,他焚毀一座女形神像,連山一併毀去。在另一處婚宴上,群眾不聽他講道,他咒詛眾人化為石頭——普卡拉等處至今猶見。薩爾卡馬瓦自問:這位托納帕,豈非榮耀的使徒聖多默?

sensitivity.note: The Tonapa cycle is the classic bearded-culture-hero tradition; Salcamayhua's apostle-Thomas identification is a colonial gloss to be reported, not endorsed. Tagged culture-hero against the cross-tradition cluster.

passages.text: Some years after the devils called Hapi-ñuñus Achacallas had been driven out of the land, there arrived, in these kingdoms of Ttahuantin-suyu, a bearded man, of middle height, with long hair, and in a rather long shirt. They say that he was somewhat past his prime, for he already had grey hairs, and he was lean. He travelled with his staff, teaching the natives with much love, and calling them all his sons and daughters. As he went through all the land, he performed many miracles. The sick were healed by his touch. He spoke all languages better than the natives. They called him Tonapa or Tarapaca (Tarapaca means an eagle) Uiracocharapacha yachipachan or Pachaccan - the servant, and Uicchaycamayoc, a preacher. Although he preached the people did not listen, for they thought little of him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那些被稱為哈皮－紐紐斯·阿查卡利亞斯的魔鬼被逐出此地若干年後，在這塔萬廷蘇尤的諸王國中，來了一個蓄鬚的男子，中等身材，長髮，身穿一件略長的襯衫。據說他已稍過壯年，因為他已有了白髮，且身形瘦削。他拄著手杖行走，滿懷慈愛地教導當地人，稱他們眾人為他的兒女。他走遍全地，行了許多奇蹟。病人經他一觸便得痊癒。他說各種語言都比當地人說得好。他們稱他為托納帕或塔拉帕卡（塔拉帕卡意為鷹）、烏伊拉科查拉帕查·亞奇帕昌或帕查坎——即僕人，以及烏伊奇查卡馬約克——即傳道者。雖然他傳道，人們卻不聽，因為他們輕視他。

passages.text: This man came to the village of a chief called Apo-tampu (this Apo-tampu is Paccari-tampu) very tired, at a time when they were celebrating a marriage feast. His doctrines were listened to by the chief with friendly feelings, but his vassals heard them unwillingly. From that day the wanderer was a guest of Apo-tampu, to whom it is said that he gave a stick from his own staff, and through this Apo-tampu the people listened with attention to the words of the stranger, receiving the stick from his hands. Thus they received what he preached in a stick, marking and scoring on it each chapter of his precepts. The old men used to say that Caçi-caçi were the commandments of God, and especially the seven precepts, with severe punishments for those who broke them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這人來到一位名叫阿波－坦普的首領的村莊（這阿波－坦普即帕卡里－坦普），疲憊不堪，當時他們正在慶祝婚宴。首領以友善之情聽他的教誨，但他的臣民卻不情願聽。從那天起，這漂泊者便成了阿波－坦普的客人；據說他把自己手杖上的一根杖送給了阿波－坦普，藉著這阿波－坦普，人們便專心聽這陌生人的話語，從他手中接過那根杖。他們就這樣在杖上領受他所傳的道，把他的每一章訓誡都刻記、劃線於其上。老人們常說，卡西－卡西就是上帝的誡命，尤其是那七條誡命，凡違背者必受嚴厲的懲罰。

passages.text: This worthy, named Thonapa, is said to have visited all the provinces of the Colla-suyu, preaching to the people without cessation, until one day he entered the town of Yamquesupa. There he was treated with great insolence and contempt, and driven away; they say that he often slept in the fields, without other covering than the long shirt he wore, a mantle, and a book. They say that Thonapa cursed that village, so that it was covered with water. The site is now called Yamquisupaloiga; it is a lake, and nearly all the Indians of that time knew that it was once a village and was then a lake.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這位名叫托納帕的賢者，據說曾走遍科利亞蘇尤的所有省份，不停地向人們傳道，直到有一天他進入揚克蘇帕鎮。在那裡他受到極大的無禮與輕蔑，並被趕走；據說他常在田野中睡覺，除了身上穿的長襯衫、一件斗篷和一本書之外，別無其他遮蓋。據說托納帕詛咒了那村莊，使它被水淹沒。該地如今名叫揚基蘇帕洛伊加；它是一個湖，而當時幾乎所有印第安人都知道那裡曾是一個村莊，後來變成了湖。

passages.text: They say that, on a very high hill called Cacha-pucara, there was an idol in the form of a woman, and that Tonapa was inspired with a great hatred against it, and afterwards burnt it, and destroyed it with the hill on which it stood; to this day there are signs of that awful miracle. On another occasion he began to preach with loving words in a town where they were holding a great festival and banquet to celebrate a wedding, and they would not listen: for this they were cursed and turned into stones, which may be seen to this day. The same thing happened in Pucara and other places. He is called Tonapa Uiracocha nipacachan; but was he not the glorious apostle St. Thomas?
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim; the St Thomas gloss is the author's own.
passages.zh: 據說在一座名叫卡查－普卡拉的高山上，有一尊女形的偶像，托納帕對它心懷極大的憎恨，後來焚燒了它，並連同它所立的那座山一併毀滅；至今仍有那可怕奇蹟的痕跡。另有一次，他在一個正舉行盛大節慶與宴會以慶祝婚禮的鎮上，開始以慈愛的話語傳道，他們卻不肯聽：因此他們被詛咒，變成了石頭，至今仍可看見。同樣的事也發生在普卡拉和其他地方。他被稱為托納帕·烏伊拉科查·尼帕卡昌；但他不就是那榮耀的使徒聖多馬嗎？

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Tonapa at Carapucu: The Cross, the Prison, and the Mantle that Sailed
title.zh: 托納帕在卡拉普庫:十字架、囚禁與浮水之氅

region.en: Carapucu, shore of Lake Titicaca (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 的的喀喀湖畔卡拉普庫(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In his wanderings Tonapa came to the mountains of Caravaya, where he erected a very large cross and carried it on his shoulders to the mountain of Carapucu, where he preached in a loud voice and shed tears. A chief's daughter was sprinkled on the head with water, and the Indians, seeing this, understood that he was washing his head; afterwards Tonapa was taken prisoner and shorn near the great lake of Carapucu, condemned to a cruel death. When day broke a very beautiful youth came to him: 'Do not fear; for I come to call you in the name of the matron, who alone watches over you, and who is about to go to the place of rest.' The youth touched the cords binding Tonapa hand and foot; at five in the morning Tonapa entered the lake with him, his mantle bearing him up on the water and serving in the place of a boat. The chiefs were disturbed, for their idol had been thrown down and destroyed: the huaca flew like the wind to a desert place never visited by men, mourning with its head down, until found by an Indian. Tonapa remained a long time on the rock called Titicaca, then passed Tiquina to Chacamarca and came to Tiyahuanacu (Tiahuanaco); the people, drinking and dancing, did not listen to his preaching, and out of pure anger he denounced them: all who were dancing were turned into stones, visible to this day. He followed the course of the river Chacamarca until he came to the sea.
summary.zh: 托納帕行至卡拉瓦亞山區,立起一座巨大十字架,肩負至卡拉普庫山,在那裡高聲講道,並流下淚水。一位酋長之女被他以水灑頭,印第安人見了,還以為他在洗頭;其後托納帕在卡拉普庫大湖附近被擒,剃去鬚髮,被判處極刑。天明時分,一位極俊美的少年前來對他說:「不要害怕;奉守護你的那位主母之名,我來召你——她即將歸於安息之地。」少年以手指觸開縛他手足的繩索。清晨五時,托納帕隨少年步入湖中,他的斗篷浮托其身,權作輕舟。酋長們惶惶不安:他們的神像已被推倒毀壞——那瓦卡如風般飛往荒無人跡之地,垂首哀哭,後為一印第安人尋見。托納帕獲釋後,長久留居名為提提卡卡的岩石上,繼而經提基納至查卡馬爾卡,來到蒂亞瓦納科。城中方在飲宴起舞,不聽他講道;他盛怒之下以當地語言咒詛之:正在起舞的人盡數化為石頭,至今可見。他沿查卡馬爾卡河而行,直至海濱。

sensitivity.note: The rescue-at-dawn and mantle-boat episode gives Tonapa a death-defeat pattern; tagged resurrection for the cluster, interpretively.

passages.text: They further say that this Tonapa, in his wanderings, came to the mountains of Caravaya, where he erected a very large cross, and he carried it on his shoulders to the mountain of Carapucu, where he preached in a loud voice, and shed tears. And they say that a daughter of a chief of that province was sprinkled on the head with water, and the Indians, seeing this, understood that he was washing his head. So, afterwards, Tonapa was taken prisoner and shorn, near the great lake of Carapucu.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們又說，這托納帕在漂泊途中來到卡拉瓦亞的山中，在那裡立了一個非常大的十字架，並把它扛在肩上帶到卡拉普庫山，在那裡大聲傳道，流下眼淚。他們還說，那省一位首領的女兒頭上被灑了水，印第安人見了，便明白他是在洗她的頭。因此，後來托納帕在卡拉普庫大湖附近被俘，並被剃去了頭髮。

passages.text: They say that, when day broke, when Tonapa was a prisoner, a very beautiful youth came to him, and said: 'Do not fear; for I come to call you in the name of the matron, who alone watches over you, and who is about to go to the place of rest.' So saying, he touched the cords, by which Tonapa was tied hand and foot, with his fingers. There were many guards, for Tonapa had been condemned to a cruel death. But at dawn, being five in the morning, he entered the lake with the youth, his mantle bearing him up on the water and serving in the place of a boat.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們說，當托納帕被囚之時，天亮之際，一個非常俊美的青年來到他面前，說：『不要害怕；因為我奉那位獨自看顧你、即將前往安息之地的夫人之名來召你。』說著，他用手指觸碰了綁住托納帕手腳的繩索。守衛眾多，因為托納帕已被判處殘酷的死刑。但黎明時分，約清晨五點，他與那青年一同進入湖中，他的斗篷托著他在水面上，代替了船的作用。

passages.text: On his arrival in the town and province of Carapucu, the chiefs and principal men were disturbed at having seen their idol thrown down and destroyed. They say that this idol flew like the wind to a desert place, which was never visited by men. Here the idol or huaca was mourning and lamenting with its head down; and in this plight it was found by an Indian. Tonapa, after he had been freed from the hands of those savages, remained for a long time on a rock called Titicaca, and afterwards he passed by Tiquina to Chacamarca, where he came to a town called Tiyahuanacu.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他抵達卡拉普庫（Carapucu）城及其省時，首領與顯貴們因見到自己的偶像被推倒摧毀而惶惶不安。他們說那偶像如風般飛往一處荒漠之地，那裡從未有人涉足。這偶像或瓦卡（huaca）在此垂首哀悼悲泣；一名印第安人便在此般境況中發現了它。托納帕（Tonapa）從那些野蠻人手中獲釋後，長久居於一塊名為的的喀喀（Titicaca）的岩石上，其後他經由蒂基納（Tiquina）前往查卡馬爾卡（Chacamarca），在那裡他來到一座名為蒂亞瓦納庫（Tiyahuanacu）的城鎮。

passages.text: They say that the people of that town were engaged in drinking and dancing when Tonapa came to preach to them, and they did not listen to him. Then, out of pure anger, he denounced them in the language of the land; and, when he departed from that place, all the people who were dancing were turned into stones, and they may be seen to this day. Tonapa then followed the course of the river Chacamarca until he came to the sea. This is reported by those most ancient Yncas.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們說，當托納帕前來向該城之人佈道時，他們正忙於飲酒跳舞，並不聽從他。於是，他純然出於憤怒，以當地語言斥責他們；當他離開那地時，所有正在跳舞的人都化為石頭，至今仍可見到。托納帕隨後沿查卡馬爾卡河而行，直至抵達海邊。此事由那些最古老的印加人（Yncas）所述。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Tupac-yauri, the Double Rainbow, and the Speaking Stone of Sañuc
title.zh: 圖帕克-亞烏里、雙虹與薩紐克的開口石

region.en: Sañuc, on the road from Paccari-tampu to Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 帕卡里坦波至庫斯科途中的薩紐克(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The staff Tonapa delivered into the hands of Apu-tampu was turned into fine gold on the birth of his son Manco Ccapac Ynca, who had seven brothers and sisters: Ayar-cachi, Ayar-uchu, Ayar-auca and others. Orphaned of Apu Tampu Pacha and Mama Achi, grown to man's estate, Manco Ccapac assembled his people and agreed with his brothers to seek new lands, taking his rich clothes and arms, the golden staff called Tupac-yauri, and two golden cups from which Tonapa had drunk, called Tupac-usi. Marching towards the hill over which the sun rose, he reached the highest point of that land: over Apu Manco Ccapac arose a very beautiful rainbow, and over the rainbow another, so that he seemed to stand in the midst of the rainbows. 'We have a good sign,' he exclaimed; 'we shall have great prosperity and gain many victories.' He descended to Collcapampa singing Chamay huarisca from delight. From Sañuc he saw afar off the form of a man; his youngest brother ran to it, thinking it some Indian, and when he approached the form raised its head: 'It is well that you have come in search of me; for you will find that I am looking for you, and now you are in my power.' The brother stayed; a sister sent to call him stayed too; both nearly died at the huaca of Sañuc. Manco Ccapac went in great wrath and struck the stone on the head with the tupac-yauri. Words came from the midst of the stone as if it was alive: if he had not got that staff, it would also do to him as it pleased. 'Go on,' it added, 'for you have attained to great honour. But these, your brother and sister, have sinned, and it is therefore right that they should be where I am' - meaning the infernal regions; this is called pitusiray sanasiray, one person fastened on the top of another. Manco Ccapac shed tears, returned to the place of the double rainbow, bemoaned his loss - 'the most unfortunate of orphans' - but the rainbow strengthened him and removed his sorrows; thence the place was called Huaynacaptiy.
summary.zh: 托納帕交到阿波坦波手中的那根手杖,在其子曼科·卡帕克出生時化為純金。曼科有兄弟姐妹七人:亞亞爾-卡奇、亞亞爾-烏丘、亞亞爾-奧卡等。父母(阿波坦波帕查與瑪瑪阿奇)亡故後,曼科長成,召集族人,與兄弟們商定另覓新土,帶上華服兵甲、名為「圖帕克-亞烏里」的金杖,以及托納帕飲過的兩只金杯「圖帕克-烏西」。他們朝太陽升起之山而行,登上此地最高之峰:一道彩虹現於曼科頭上,其上又現一道,曼科遂似置身雙虹之間。「此乃吉兆!」他歡呼,「我們必獲大運,多打勝仗。」他唱著《夏馬伊-瓦里斯卡》,欣然下到科爾卡潘帕。在薩紐克,他遠望見一個人影;最小的兄弟以為是個印第安人,跑上前去,那影子卻抬起頭來:「你來尋我,正合我意——我在此等你,如今你已落入我掌中。」兄弟一去不返;遣妹去喚,亦然;二人俱困於薩紐克瓦卡,瀕臨氣絕。曼科大怒親往,掄起金杖猛擊那石頭的頭部。石中竟傳出話語,彷彿活物:「若非你手持此杖,我亦能任意處置你。去吧——你已得大位。但你這兄妹二人有罪,理當與我同處」——意即幽冥之地。此謂「皮圖西拉伊-薩納西拉伊」,一人疊於另一人之頂。曼科見兄妹身陷險境,自然流淚,回到雙虹之地哀慟,自稱「最不幸的孤兒」;然而彩虹為他壯膽,掃盡其憂傷。自此那地方名為「瓦伊納卡普提伊」。

sensitivity.note: Salcamayhua's version of the founder's march, with the Tonapa staff linking the culture-hero to the dynasty; the petrified siblings parallel Sarmiento's Ayar-stone episodes.

passages.text: They say that the staff which Tonapa delivered into the hands of Apu-tampu was turned into fine gold on the birth of his son named Manco Ccapac Ynca, who had seven brothers and sisters. Their names were Ayar-cachi, Ayar-uchu, Ayar-auca, etc. The said Apu Manco Ccapac, after the death of his father and mother, named Apu Tampu Pacha and Mama Achi, being now an orphan, but grown to man's estate, assembled his people to see what power he had to prosecute the new conquests which he meditated. Finding some difficulties, he agreed with his brothers to seek new lands, taking his rich clothes and arms, and the staff which had been left by Tonapa. This staff was called Tupac-yauri. He also had two golden cups from which Tonapa had drunk, called Tupac-usi.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們說，托納帕交到阿普坦普（Apu-tampu）手中的那根杖，在他名為曼科·卡帕克·印加（Manco Ccapac Ynca）的兒子出生時化為純金，此子有七個兄弟姊妹。他們的名字是阿亞爾-卡奇（Ayar-cachi）、阿亞爾-烏丘（Ayar-uchu）、阿亞爾-奧卡（Ayar-auca）等。前述的阿普·曼科·卡帕克（Apu Manco Ccapac）在父母阿普·坦普·帕查（Apu Tampu Pacha）與媽媽·阿奇（Mama Achi）去世後，如今雖為孤兒，卻已長大成人，遂召集其民，以察看自己有何力量去進行他所謀劃的新征服。他發覺有些困難，便與兄弟們商定去尋覓新土地，帶上他華美的衣物與武器，以及托納帕所留下的那根杖。這根杖名為圖帕克-堯里（Tupac-yauri）。他還有兩隻托納帕曾用以飲水的金杯，名為圖帕克-烏西（Tupac-usi）。

passages.text: Thus he set out, with his brothers, towards the hill over which the sun rose. They say that, marching in this direction, he arrived at the hill which was the highest point in that land. Then, over Apu Manco Ccapac arose a very beautiful rainbow, and over the rainbow appeared another, so that Apu Manco Ccapac seemed to be in the midst of the rainbows. He exclaimed: 'We have a good sign. We shall have great prosperity and gain many victories, and we shall obtain all that we desire.' After saying this, he joyfully advanced, singing the song of Chamay huarisca from mere delight. Then he descended to Collcapampa with his brothers.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是，他與兄弟們動身前往太陽升起所越過的那座山丘。他們說，他朝此方向行進，抵達了那地方最高處的山丘。接著，在阿普·曼科·卡帕克上方升起一道極美的彩虹，而在彩虹之上又現出另一道，以致阿普·曼科·卡帕克彷彿置身於彩虹之中。他驚呼道：『我們有了好兆頭。我們將大為昌盛，贏得許多勝利，並將獲得我們所渴望的一切。』說完此話，他滿心歡喜地前行，純然出於喜悅而唱起查邁·瓦里斯卡（Chamay huarisca）之歌。隨後他與兄弟們下山前往科爾卡潘帕（Collcapampa）。

passages.text: From the town of Sañuc he saw, afar off, the form of a man. One of his brothers ran towards it, thinking that it was some Indian; but when he came up to it, he saw one like an Indian, looking most fierce and cruel with bloodshot eyes. When he approached, the form raised its head, and said: 'It is well that you have come in search of me; for you will find that I am looking for you, and now you are in my power.' Manco Ccapac, seeing that his brother was so long in returning, sent one of his sisters to call him. But she also remained away, and both were kept at the huaca of Sañuc. Manco Ccapac went himself in great wrath, and found them both nearly dead. He asked them why they stayed away so long, and they answered by complaining of a stone which was between the two.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他從薩紐克（Sañuc）城望見遠處有一人形。他的一個兄弟朝它奔去，以為那是某個印第安人；但當他走近時，卻見一個形似印第安人者，雙目充血，面目極為兇猛殘忍。當他靠近時，那形體抬起頭來，說道：『你來尋找我，這很好；因為你將發現我正在尋找你，如今你已落入我的掌中。』曼科·卡帕克見兄弟久久未歸，便派一個姊妹去喚他。但她也有去無回，兩人皆被留在薩紐克的瓦卡處。曼科·卡帕克大怒之下親自前往，發現兩人皆已奄奄一息。他問他們為何久留不歸，他們則抱怨說有塊石頭橫在兩人之間。

passages.text: Then Apu Manco Ccapac struck the stone or huaca with much fury, giving it blows with his tupac-yauri on the head. Then words came from the midst of the stone, as if it was alive, saying, that if he had not got that staff, it would also do to him as it pleased. 'Go on,' it added; 'for you have attained to great honour. But these, your brother and sister, have sinned, and it is therefore right that they should be where I am,' meaning the infernal regions. This is called pitusiray sanasiray, which means one person fastened on the top of another. Manco Ccapac shed tears of natural grief and sorrow, and went back to the place where he had first seen the rainbow. He bemoaned the loss of his brother and sister, and exclaimed that he was the most unfortunate of orphans. But the rainbow strengthened him, and removed all his sorrows and afflictions; from that time the place was called Huaynacaptiy.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是阿普·曼科·卡帕克滿懷怒火擊打那石頭或瓦卡，以他的圖帕克-堯里擊其頭部。接著，話語自石中傳出，彷彿它有了生命，說道：倘若他沒有那根杖，它也會隨心所欲地對付他。它又說：『繼續前行吧；因為你已獲得極大的榮耀。但你的這兄弟與姊妹犯了罪，因此他們理應留在我所在之處，』意指地獄。此處名為皮圖西賴·薩納西賴（pitusiray sanasiray），意即一人緊附於另一人之上。曼科·卡帕克流下出於天性之悲傷與哀痛的淚水，回到他初次見到彩虹之處。他哀悼兄弟與姊妹的喪失，驚呼自己是孤兒中最不幸者。但彩虹使他堅強，除去他一切悲傷與苦痛；自此那地方便名為瓦伊納卡普蒂（Huaynacaptiy）。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Hurin-cancha and Hanan-cancha: The Founding of Cuzco
title.zh: 下泉與上泉:庫斯科之奠基

region.en: Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: From Collcapampa Manco Ccapac went with the tupac-yauri in his hand, with a sister named Ypa Mama Huaco, and with another sister and a brother; they came to Huamantiana, where they remained some time, and thence marched to Coricancha, where they found a place suitable for a settlement. There was good water from Hurin-chacan and Hanan-chacan - whence the names of Hurin-Cuzco and Hanan-Cuzco - two springs. A rock was called by the natives by the name of Cuzco-cara-urumi, whence the place came to be called Cuzco-pampa and Cuzco-llacta, and the Yncas afterwards Cuzco-Ccapac and Cuzco-Ynca. This Ynca Apu Manco Ccapac married one of his own sisters named Mama Ocllo, and this marriage was celebrated that they might have no equal, and that they might not lose the caste. Then they began to enact good laws for the government of their people, conquering many provinces and nations of those that were disobedient; the tidings of a new Ynca spread widely: some were joyful, others afflicted, when they heard that the Ynca was the most powerful chief, the most valiant, and the most fortunate in arms.
summary.zh: 曼科·卡帕克手持圖帕克-亞烏里金杖,與妹妹伊帕·瑪瑪·瓦科及另一位兄妹,自科爾卡潘帕前往瓦曼蒂亞納,居留有時,再進至科里坎查,見一處宜於建城之地。此地有兩眼好泉,一為烏林-查坎,一為哈南-查坎——烏林庫斯科與哈南庫斯科之名即由此而來。當地人稱此地岩石為「庫斯科-卡拉-烏魯米」,故此地得名庫斯科潘帕、庫斯科利亞克塔;印加王族後亦稱庫斯科-卡帕克、庫斯科-印加。曼科·卡帕克娶其妹瑪瑪·奧克略為妻,此婚所以舉行者,為使二人無與匹敵、血統不致旁落。其後頒良法以治其民,征服諸多不從之邦。新印加之名傳遍四方:聞其為至強至勇、用兵常勝之主,有人歡喜,有人憂懼。

sensitivity.note: Founding with the sibling marriage justifying caste endogamy; tagged divine-marriage for the cluster.

passages.text: Thence he went to Collcapampa with the tupac-yauri in his hand, and with a sister named Ypa mama huaco, and with another sister and a brother. They arrived at Collcapampa, where they were for some days. Thence they went to Huamantiana, where they remained some time, and thence they marched to Coricancha, where they found a place suitable for a settlement. There was good water from Hurinchacan and Hananchacan (whence the names of Hurin-Cuzco and Hanan-Cuzco), which are two springs.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他手持圖帕克-堯里（tupac-yauri），帶著一位名叫伊帕·瑪瑪·瓦科（Ypa mama huaco）的姊妹，以及另一位姊妹和一位兄弟，從那裡前往科爾卡潘帕（Collcapampa）。他們抵達科爾卡潘帕，在那裡停留了數日。隨後他們前往瓦曼蒂亞納（Huamantiana），在那裡逗留了一段時日，接著又行進至科里坎查（Coricancha），發現該處適宜定居。那裡有來自烏林查坎（Hurinchacan）與哈南查坎（Hananchacan）的優良水源（烏林-庫斯科與哈南-庫斯科之名即由此而來），此二者為兩處泉水。

passages.text: A rock was called by the natives (who are the Allcayriesas, the Cullinchinas, and the Cayaucachis) by the name of Cuzco-cara-urumi, whence the place came to be called Cuzco-pampa and Cuzco-llacta; and the Yncas were afterwards called Cuzco-Ccapac and Cuzco-Ynca. This Ynca Apu Manco Ccapac married one of his own sisters named Mama Ocllo, and this marriage was celebrated that they might have no equal, and that they might not lose the caste.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當地原住民（即阿爾卡伊里薩斯人、庫林奇納斯人與卡堯卡奇斯人）稱一塊岩石為庫斯科-卡拉-烏魯米（Cuzco-cara-urumi），該地因而得名庫斯科-潘帕（Cuzco-pampa）與庫斯科-利亞克塔（Cuzco-llacta）；印卡人後來則被稱為庫斯科-卡帕克（Cuzco-Ccapac）與庫斯科-印卡（Cuzco-Ynca）。這位印卡·阿普·曼科·卡帕克娶了自己的一位姊妹，名叫瑪瑪·奧克略（Mama Ocllo），舉行這場婚姻是為了使他們無人能與之匹敵，也為了不致失去其種姓。

passages.text: Then they began to enact good laws for the government of their people, conquering many provinces and nations of those that were disobedient. The Ttahuantin-suyus came with a good grace and with rich presents. The tidings of a new Ynca had spread widely. Some were joyful, others were afflicted; when they heard that the Ynca was the most powerful chief, the most valiant, and the most fortunate in arms, that his captains and men of valour were better armed than other men, and that all his affairs were prosperous.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他們開始為治理其人民制定良法，征服了許多不服從的省份與民族。塔萬廷-蘇尤斯（Ttahuantin-suyus）欣然前來，並獻上豐厚的貢品。新印卡的消息廣為流傳。有人歡欣，有人憂愁；因為他們聽說這位印卡是最強大的首領、最為英勇、在征戰中最為幸運，他的將領與勇士比其他人裝備更精良，而他的一切事務皆興旺順遂。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Golden Plate, the Three Windows, and the Trees with Golden Fruit
title.zh: 金板、三窗與結金果之樹

region.en: Coricancha, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科科里坎查(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: This Ynca ordered the smiths to make a flat plate of fine gold, which signified that there was a Creator of heaven and earth, and caused it to be fixed in a great house called Ccuricancha pachayachachipac huasin - the house of the teacher of the world. Manco Ccapac was an enemy to the huacas, and as such he destroyed the Curaca Pinao Ccapac with all his idols, and conquered Tocay Ccapac, a great idolater. At the place of his birth he ordered works executed: a masonry wall with three windows, emblems of the house of his fathers whence he descended - the first window called Tampu-toco, the second Maras-toco, the third Sutic-toco, referring to his uncles and grandparents. Two trees typified his father and mother Apu-tampu and Apachamama-achi; he ordered them adorned with roots of gold and silver and with golden fruit; they were called Cceurichachac collquechachac tampu-yracan, for the two trees typified the parents, and the Yncas proceeded from them like fruit from the trees, the trees being as the roots and stems of the Yncas. Later, Huascar Ynca removed the plate of the Creator and substituted another round plate like the sun with rays; yet images of sun and moon stood on either side.
summary.zh: 曼科·卡帕克命金匠打製一塊純金薄板,以誌天地有一造物主,懸於大屋「科里坎查-帕查亞查奇帕克-瓦辛」(即「教世者之屋」)內。曼科敵視瓦卡,毀庫拉卡皮尼亞奧-卡帕克及其一切偶像,又征服大拜偶像者托卡伊-卡帕克。他還在其誕生之地營建工程:一道三窗石牆,象徵其祖居之屋——第一窗名「坦普-托科」,第二窗名「馬拉斯-托科」,第三窗名「蘇蒂克-托科」,分指其叔伯與祖父母。又有兩樹象徵其父母阿波坦波與瑪瑪阿奇;他命人飾以金銀之根、結以金果,稱之為「庫里查查克-科爾克查查克-坦普-伊拉坎」:兩樹喻雙親,印加出自二樹,如樹之結實;二樹即印加之根與幹。後來瓦伊納·卡帕克之後,瓦伊斯卡爾移去造物主金板,代之以日形放射之圓板,而日月之像仍列於兩側。

sensitivity.note: The famous Salcamayhua plate diagram: a Creator-emblem predating the solar cult substitution under Huascar - central to debates on Andean monotheism. Reported as the source has it.

passages.text: This Ynca ordered the smiths to make a flat plate of fine gold; which signified that there was a Creator of heaven and earth; and it was of this shape. He caused it to be fixed in a great house called Ccuricancha pachaya-chachipac huasin. This Ynca Manco Ccapac was an enemy to the huacas, and, as such, he destroyed the Curaca Pinao Ccapac with all his idols. He also conquered Tocay Ccapac, a great idolater.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這位印卡命工匠打造一塊精金的平板；此板象徵天地有一位造物主；其形狀如下。他命人將其安置於一座名為庫里坎查·帕查亞-查奇帕克·瓦辛（Ccuricancha pachaya-chachipac huasin）的大屋之中。這位印卡·曼科·卡帕克是瓦卡（huacas）的仇敵，因此他消滅了庫拉卡·皮瑙·卡帕克（Curaca Pinao Ccapac）及其所有偶像。他也征服了托凱·卡帕克（Tocay Ccapac），一位偉大的偶像崇拜者。

passages.text: Afterwards he ordered works to be executed at the place of his birth; consisting of a masonry wall with three windows, which were emblems of the house of his fathers whence he descended. The first window was called Tampu-toco, the second Maras-toco, and the third Sutic-toco: referring to his uncles and paternal and maternal grandparents. These two trees typified his father and mother Apu-tampu and Apachamama-achi, and he ordered that they should be adorned with roots of gold and silver, and with golden fruit. Hence they were called Cceurichachac collquechachac tampu-yracan, which means that the two trees typified the parents, and that the Yncas proceeded from them, like fruit from the trees, and that the two trees were as the roots and stems of the Yncas. All these things were executed to record their greatness.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 後來，他下令在其出生之地興建工程；包括一道砌石牆，上有三扇窗，象徵他出身所自的父祖之家。第一扇窗名為坦普-托科（Tampu-toco），第二扇名為馬拉斯-托科（Maras-toco），第三扇名為蘇蒂克-托科（Sutic-toco）：分別指他的叔伯以及父系與母系的祖父母。這兩棵樹象徵他的父親與母親阿普-坦普（Apu-tampu）與阿帕查瑪瑪-阿奇（Apachamama-achi），他並下令以金銀之根與金果裝飾它們。因此它們被稱為克烏里查查克·科爾克查查克·坦普-伊拉坎（Cceurichachac collquechachac tampu-yracan），意即這兩棵樹象徵其父母，印卡人由他們而出，如樹上之果實，而這兩棵樹猶如印卡人的根與幹。所有這些事物皆是為了記錄他們的偉大而建造。

passages.text: Although Huascar Ynca had placed an image of the sun in the place where that of the Creator had been, yet it shall not be omitted here; for there was an image of the sun and moon on either side of it. They say that a Spaniard gambled for this plate of gold in Cuzco, as Salcamayhua mentions in its place.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 雖然瓦斯卡爾印卡（Huascar Ynca）曾在造物主像所在之處安置了一尊太陽像，此事於此仍不應略去；因為在它兩側各有一尊太陽像與月亮像。據說一名西班牙人在庫斯科以這塊金板賭博，薩爾卡馬伊瓦（Salcamayhua）已在其相應之處提及此事。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Pacarisca: Every Tribe Chooses the Place of Its Origin
title.zh: 帕卡里斯卡:各族自擇發源之地

region.en: Ttahuantin-suyu (symbolic pin: Cuzco region)
region.zh: 大蘇尤(象徵性標記:庫斯科地區)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Manco Ccapac ordered that the dresses of each village should be different, that the people might be known, for down to this time there were no means of knowing to what village or tribe an Indian belonged. He also ordered, with a view to each tribe being clearly distinguished, that they should choose whence they were descended and from whence they came: as the Indians were very dull and stupid, some chose for their pacarisca or pacarimusca a lake, others a spring, others a rock, others the hills or ravines; but every lineage selected some object for its pacarisca. The hapi-ñuñus deceived those stupid people with little difficulty, entering into the false pacariscas and thence uttering deceitful promises. Every day these pacariscas continued to increase, the origin or pacarinim being the Pacari-tampu. The leading cause of the invention of the pacarinim was that the Ynca Manco Ccapac was often at a loss to know to what village an Indian belonged. He also ordered the heads of infants to be pressed, that they might grow up without audacity and disobedience.
summary.zh: 曼科·卡帕克命各村服飾各異,以便辨識——此前無從得知一印第安人屬何村何族。他又命各族自明其所自出、所從來:印第安人多愚魯,故或擇湖、或擇泉、或擇石、或擇丘陵溝壑為其「帕卡里斯卡」(發源之物),凡世系皆擇一物以奉之。哈皮紐紐惡魔極易欺哄愚民,潛入偽帕卡里斯卡,從中發出欺人之諾。帕卡里斯卡日漸增多,而其總源即「帕卡里坦波」。各州各族皆言:「帕卡里斯坎奇克,烏克斯坎奇克,烏馬昆,奇克帕-帕卡里斯坎。」立帕卡里尼姆(發源之制)之主因,乃印加王常難辨某印第安人屬於何村。曼科又命壓嬰兒之頭,使其長成後不致狂妄不遜。

sensitivity.note: The institutionalization of lineage origin-cults; Salcamayhua's contemptuous framing of commoners ('dull and stupid') is quoted critically.

passages.text: He ordered that the dresses of each village should be different, that the people might be known, for down to this time there were no means of knowing to what village or tribe an Indian belonged. He also ordered, with a view to each tribe being clearly distinguished, that they should choose whence they were descended and from whence they came, and, as the Indians generally were very dull and stupid, some chose, for their pacarisca or pacarimusca, a lake, others a spring, others a rock, others the hills or ravines; but every lineage selected some object for its pacarisca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他下令每個村莊的服飾都應各不相同，以便人們能夠辨識，因為直到那時為止，都沒有辦法知道一個印第安人屬於哪個村莊或部落。他又下令，為了使每個部落都清楚可辨，他們應當選擇自己源自何處、來自何方；而由於印第安人普遍十分遲鈍愚笨，有些人便為自己的 pacarisca 或 pacarimusca 選了一座湖，有些人選了一處泉，有些人選了一塊岩石，有些人選了山丘或峽谷；但每一個世系都為自己的 pacarisca 選了某個物件。

passages.text: The devils, or hapi-ñuñus, deceived those stupid people with little difficulty, entering into the false pacariscas, and thence uttering deceitful promises. Every day these pacariscas continued to increase, the origin or pacarinim being the Pacari-tampu. All the provinces and tribes said: Pacariscanchic huccsiscanchic umachun chicpa-pacariscan. The leading cause of the invention of the pacarinim was that the Ynca Manco Ccapac was often at a loss to know to what village an Indian belonged. This Ynca also ordered the heads of infants to be pressed, that they might grow up foolish and without energy; for he thought that Indians with large round heads, being audacious in any enterprise, might also be disobedient.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那些魔鬼，即 hapi-ñuñus，幾乎不費力氣就欺騙了那些愚笨的人，進入虛假的 pacariscas 之中，並從那裡發出虛假的承諾。這些 pacariscas 日益增多，其起源或 pacarinim 便是 Pacari-tampu。所有各省各部落都說：Pacariscanchic huccsiscanchic umachun chicpa-pacariscan。發明 pacarinim 的主要原因，是 Ynca Manco Ccapac 常常無法知道一個印第安人屬於哪個村莊。這位 Ynca 還下令按壓嬰兒的頭部，使他們長大後愚笨而無精力；因為他認為頭部又大又圓的印第安人，從事任何事業都膽大妄為，也可能不服從。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Apachitas: The Stone Heaps and the Thrower of Coca
title.zh: 阿帕奇塔斯:石堆與投古柯之俗

region.en: Ravines between Chacamarca and Angaraes (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 查卡馬爾卡至安加拉斯之間的溝壑(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Sinchi Ruca Ynca, who began to rule over all the territory of his father, was a great patron of agriculture, of weaving cloth and of mining, but seldom went abroad; when he desired to make conquests he sent his captains and their men. In each ravine they had to take stones to make usnus, certain stones arranged in heaps. They say that an Indian wizard appeared to one of the officers of war, and told him that the heaps must be called apachitas. A rite was established, that every passer by should bring a great stone; and the wizard also told the officer of the Ynca that all the soldiers must throw their coca pallets on the heap as they passed, saying: 'Saycoyñiycaypitac quipasiyon coyñiypashinatac.' From that time they began to bring stones and to throw coca, because the wizard had so ordered it.
summary.zh: 辛奇·羅卡·印加繼承父土,重農桑、織布、開礦,而少親征;欲征伐則遣將領兵。每逢溝壑,軍中須取石壘成「烏斯努」(成堆之石)。相傳一位印第安巫師顯現於某軍官之前,告知此堆當名為「阿帕奇塔斯」;並立一俗:凡過者皆須取一大石投之;巫師又囑軍官,眾兵過堆時須將古柯葉投於堆上,口誦:「賽科伊尼伊卡伊皮塔克,基帕西永,科伊尼亞希納塔克。」自此人人運石投古柯,皆因巫師之命。

sensitivity.note: Etiology of the apachita road-shrines still visible along Andean trails.

passages.text: Sinchi Ruca Ynca began to rule over all the territory of his father, and was a great patron of agriculture, of weaving cloth, and of mining. He was not much addicted to warlike affairs, for, being a very proud man, and of haughty disposition, he seldom went abroad. When he desired to make conquests he sent his captains and their men. In each ravine they had to take stones to make usnus, which are certain stones arranged in heaps.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: Sinchi Ruca Ynca 開始統治他父親的全部領土，是農業、織布與採礦的偉大庇護者。他並不十分熱衷於戰爭事務，因為他為人極為自負、性情傲慢，很少外出。當他想要征服時，便派遣他的將領及其部下。在每一道峽谷中，他們都必須搬運石頭來堆成 usnus，那是一些堆疊成堆的石頭。

passages.text: They say that an Indian wizard appeared to one of the officers of war, and told him that the heaps must be called apachitas. A rite was established, which was that every passer by should bring a great stone; and the wizard also told the officer of the Ynca that all the soldiers must throw their coca pallets on the heap as they passed, saying: Saycoyñiycaypitac quipasiyon coyñiypashinatac. From that time they began to bring stones and to throw coca, because the wizard had so ordered it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們說有一個印第安巫師向一位軍官顯現，告訴他這些石堆必須稱為 apachitas。於是訂立了一項儀式，即每個路過的人都應帶來一塊大石頭；那巫師還告訴 Ynca 的軍官，所有士兵經過時都必須把他們的古柯葉袋扔到石堆上，並說：Saycoyñiycaypitac quipasiyon coyñiypashinatac。從那時起，他們便開始搬來石頭並投擲古柯，因為巫師如此吩咐。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Silent Altar: Manco Capac's Last Prayer and the Head of His Son
title.zh: 沉默的祭壇:曼科·卡帕克末年祈禱與親子之血

region.en: Coricancha, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科科里坎查(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: When the Ynca Manco Ccapac was very old, he went down on his knees and prayed for the prosperity of his son in a long Quechua prayer, recalling the sun, moon and day, the silence of night and the light of dawn; after this he always remembered Tonapa in a second prayer. Having said this he watched to see if he might have a sign from the Creator. He offered a very white lamb upon an altar, a sacrifice called arpay.
