When no answer was given, he ordered the most beautiful of his sons, aged about eight years, to be offered up, cutting off his head, and sprinkling the blood over the fire, that the smoke might reach the Maker of heaven and earth. To all these offerings no answer was ever given in Coricancha.
summary.zh: 曼科·卡帕克年邁之際,跪而為其子祈福,以克丘亞語誦長禱,提及日月與晝、黑夜之靜與黎明之光;繼而常念托納帕,另誦一禱。禱畢,他守望求造物主賜一徵兆。他在祭壇上獻一極白之羔,此祭名為「阿爾帕伊」。無有應答,他便下令獻上自己最美的、年約八歲的兒子:斷其首,以血灑火,使煙上達天地之造主。然而在科里坎查,這一切祭獻始終未獲一答。

sensitivity.note: A stark episode of dynastic child sacrifice framed as unanswered prayer; Salcamayhua's religious melancholy is quoted as given.

passages.text: They say that when the Ynca Manco Ccapac was very old, he went down on his knees, and prayed for the prosperity of his son in these words: 'A Uiracochantic çicapac caycaricachun cay raimicachun ñeca apa hinamtima chiccha camac maypin canqui...' (a long Quechua petition recalling sun, moon, day, night and dawn). After this he always remembered Tonapa, saying: 'Runa rallcapacpalhacan yananssi cahuac...' - a second prayer, calling Tonapa by name.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim; Quechua prayers quoted in the translation's transcription.
passages.zh: 他們說，當 Ynca Manco Ccapac 年事已高時，他跪下來，為他兒子的昌盛祈禱，說道：『A Uiracochantic çicapac caycaricachun cay raimicachun ñeca apa hinamtima chiccha camac maypin canqui……』（一段冗長的克丘亞語祈願，提及太陽、月亮、白晝、黑夜與黎明）。此後他總是記念 Tonapa，說道：『Runa rallcapacpalhacan yananssi cahuac……』——這是第二段祈禱，以名字呼喚 Tonapa。

passages.text: Having said this he watched to see if he might have a sign from the Creator. He offered a very white lamb upon an altar, which sacrifice is called arpay. When no answer was given, he ordered the most beautiful of his sons, aged about eight years, to be offered up, cutting off his head, and sprinkling the blood over the fire, that the smoke might reach the Maker of heaven and earth. To all these offerings no answer was ever given in Coricancha.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 說完這些，他留心觀察是否能從造物主那裡得到徵兆。他在祭壇上獻上一隻極白的羔羊，這種獻祭稱為 arpay。當沒有得到任何回答時，他下令獻上他最俊美的兒子，年約八歲，砍下他的頭，並將血灑在火上，使煙能到達天地的創造者。對於所有這些獻祭，在 Coricancha 從未得到任何回答。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Whakaturia Dances His Way Out of the Smoke
title.zh: 瓦卡圖里亞煙中脫身

region.en: Hawaiki, village of Uenuku (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哈瓦基烏努庫之村（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 8, The Quarrels at Hawaiki (London 1855)

summary.en: The dog of Houmai-tawhiti eats the sloughed matter of Uenuku's ulcer and is killed, howling its death inside Toi-te-huatahi's belly - the origin of the proverb 'hush, hush, I thought I had hid you in the big belly of Toi'. In revenge Tama-te-kapua and Whakaturia steal Uenuku's poporo fruit nightly on stilts. Caught, Whakaturia is hung in the smoke of the meeting-house; coached through a hole in the thatch, he wins a stage to dance, secures Uenuku's red apron and carved sword, and leaps from the house while Tama bolts the door behind them. The cycle of feud that ends in the migration begins here.
summary.zh: 豪邁陶維提之犬吞食烏努庫潰瘍剝落之物，被殺後在圖伊特胡阿塔希腹中哀嚎——『噓、噓！我本以為把你藏進圖伊的大肚子，你這可恨的東西還在嚎』一諺由此而生。塔馬特卡普亞兄弟以高蹺夜偷烏努庫的波波羅果被擒；瓦卡圖里亞被吊在大屋炊煙之上。兄長從屋頂鑿孔傳授計策：先討油梳髮插羽，再討紅裙寶劍；舞蹈至門邊，一躍而出——塔馬自外閂門，兄弟雙雙逃脫，哈瓦基世代血仇由此而起。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection; foundational feud legend of the Arawa migration cycle.

passages.text: In the time of Houmai-tawhiti there had been a great war, and many battles were fought in Hawaiki; the troubles had arisen from the act of desecration committed by the dog of Houmai-tawhiti and of his sons in eating the matter that had sloughed from an ulcer of Uenuku's. When Toi-te-huatahi and Uenuku saw the dog, named Potaka-tawhiti, do this, they killed it; and the sons of Houmai-tawhiti, missing the dog, went searching from village to village. At last the dog howled in the belly of Toi', 'Ow!' - again and again, however tight the old man held his mouth shut - and Toi' said, and his words passed into a proverb: 'Oh, hush, hush! I thought I had hid you in the big belly of Toi', and there you are, you cursed thing, still howling away.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 8 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在Houmai-tawhiti的时代，曾发生过一场大战，在Hawaiki打过许多仗；这些纷争起于Houmai-tawhiti及其诸子的狗所犯下的亵渎之举——它吃掉了从Uenuku的溃疡上脱落下来的东西。当Toi-te-huatahi和Uenuku看见那条名叫Potaka-tawhiti的狗做出此事时，便将它杀死；Houmai-tawhiti的诸子不见了狗，便一个村庄一个村庄地搜寻。最后，那狗在Toi的腹中吠叫起来：『噢！』——一声又一声，任凭那老人把嘴闭得多紧——Toi便说道，他的话后来成了谚语：『哦，嘘，嘘！我本以为把你藏在了Toi的大肚子里，可你就在那儿，你这该死的东西，还在一个劲儿地吠叫。』

passages.text: As soon as the two brothers got home they began immediately to make stilts for Tama-te-kapua, and started that night for the village of Toi' and Uenuku, arriving at Uenuku's fine poporo tree; they remained eating its fruit a good long time, and continued this every night, until Uenuku and his people found the fruit nearly all gone, and traces of Tama's stilts. They kept watch; and whilst one party came to steal, the other lay in wait, and caught both of them - Whakaturia at the very foot of the tree, and Tama' on the sea-shore after a chase. Those holding Tama' cried that some should chop down his stilts with an axe so the fellow might fall into the water; but Tama' called down, 'If you fell me in the water I shall not be hurt, but if you cut me down on shore the fall will kill me' - so they cut him down on shore, and in a moment he was on his feet and off like a bird escaped from a snare.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 8 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 两兄弟一到家，便立刻开始为Tama-te-kapua制作高跷，当晚就动身前往Toi和Uenuku的村庄，来到Uenuku那棵上好的poporo树前；他们待在那里吃它的果子，吃了好长一段时间，此后每晚都如此，直到Uenuku和他的族人发现果子几乎全没了，还发现了Tama高跷的痕迹。他们设了埋伏；当一伙人来偷时，另一伙人便埋伏等候，把两人都捉住了——Whakaturia就在树脚下被捉，Tama则在经过一番追赶后在海边被捉。捉住Tama的人嚷着要有人用斧头砍断他的高跷，好让这家伙掉进水里；但Tama朝下喊道：『你们若把我弄到水里，我不会受伤；但你们若在岸上把我砍倒，这一摔就会要我的命』——于是他们在岸上把他砍倒，转眼间他便站起身来，像挣脱罗网的鸟儿一般飞跑而去。

passages.text: The village assembled to see Whakaturia put to death; instead of killing him at once they hung him up in the roof of Uenuku's house to be stifled by the smoke, kindling a fire and dancing and singing shockingly bad every night. A report reached his brother, who climbed by night upon the roof, made a little hole in the thatch over the spot where his brother hung, and whispered with him. He coached him: complain of their dancing, claim to dance better; ask for oil to dress the hair, feathers for the head, the red apron of Uenuku and his carved two-handed sword; then dance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 8 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 全村人聚在一起，要看Whakaturia被处死；他们没有立刻杀他，而是把他吊在Uenuku屋子的屋顶下，让他被烟熏得窒息，每晚还生起火来，跳舞唱歌，唱得难听至极。消息传到了他兄弟那里，他兄弟夜里爬上屋顶，在吊着他兄弟的地方上方的茅草上弄出一个小洞，与他低声交谈。他教他：抱怨他们的舞跳得不好，声称自己跳得更好；索要抹头发的油、插在头上的羽毛、Uenuku的红色围裙以及他那把雕花的双手剑；然后跳舞。

passages.text: When they were all given, Whakaturia stood up and danced, looking bright and beautiful as the morning star, his eyes flashing like the mother-of-pearl eyes in the sword's carved handle. At the door he said quietly he was dying with heat and the door should be slid back; then, as is the custom in the dance, he turned right and left making hideous faces, sprang about, and made a spring from the inside of the house - immediately he was beyond the door. Up sprang Tama-te-kapua and instantly bolted it; Whakaturia helped him bolt the window, and there they heard those inside cursing like a hole full of young parrots, whilst away ran Tama' and his brother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 8 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 东西全都给了之后，Whakaturia站起身来跳舞，容光焕发、俊美如晨星，双眼闪亮，如同剑柄雕花上的珍珠母眼睛。到了门口，他轻声说自己热得要死了，门应当滑开；随后，按照舞蹈的惯例，他左右转身，做出种种怪相，蹦跳腾挪，从屋内纵身一跃——转眼间他已到了门外。Tama-te-kapua一跃而起，立刻把门闩上；Whakaturia帮他闩上窗户，他们就在那里听见里面的人咒骂不休，活像一窝小鹦鹉，而Tama和他的兄弟早已跑远了。

title.en: Ngahue and the Fish of Greenstone
title.zh: 恩加胡埃與碧玉之魚

region.en: Arahura River, West Coast, Aotearoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 紐西蘭西岸阿拉胡拉河（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 9, The Legend of Poutini and Whaiapu / The Discovery of New Zealand (London 1855)

summary.en: Hine-tu-a-hoanga, whose stone is obsidian, drives out Ngahue and his greenstone Poutini; pursuing him island to island, she forces him to seek a place where his jasper may rest in peace - and he finds the island Aotearoa, making Arahura an everlasting resting-place for greenstone. Breaking off a portion, he returns to Hawaiki reporting a new country that produces the moa and jasper in abundance, and from his block - the 'fish of Ngahue' - the axes Tutauru and Hauhau-te-rangi are ground, with which the migration canoes are hewn.
summary.zh: 黑曜石之主希內圖阿洪阿驅逐碧玉主人恩加胡埃，一路追趕；恩加胡埃為其碧玉尋找安息之地，終在海上發現奧特亞羅亞島（紐西蘭北島），並以西岸阿拉胡拉為碧玉永恆之家。他掰下一塊帶回哈瓦基，報告新大陸盛產恐鳥與碧玉；後人以其石塊——『恩加胡埃之魚』——磨成圖陶魯與豪豪特朗吉雙斧，正是用它們砍鑿了移民大舟。

sensitivity.note: Poutini (greenstone) and Whaiapu (obsidian) are stone beings; the record explains both pounamu sources and the discovery chain of the migration.

passages.text: For a long time Poutini and Whaiapu both rested in the same place, and Hine-tu-a-hoanga, to whom the stone Whaiapu belonged, became excessively enraged with Ngahue and with his stone Poutini. At last she drove Ngahue out and forced him to leave the place, and he departed to a strange land taking his jasper. When she saw he was departing with his precious stone she followed after them; Ngahue arrived at Tuhua with his stone, and Hine-tu-a-hoanga landed there at the same time with him and began to drive him away again. Then Ngahue went to seek a place where his jasper stones might remain in peace, and he found in the sea this island Aotearoa, the northern island of New Zealand, and thought he would land there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 9 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 很长一段时间里，Poutini和Whaiapu都歇在同一个地方，而Whaiapu这块石头所属的Hine-tu-a-hoanga对Ngahue和他的石头Poutini极为恼怒。最后她把Ngahue赶走，迫使他离开那个地方，他便带着他的碧玉前往一片陌生的土地。她见他带着那块珍贵的石头离去，便跟在他们后面；Ngahue带着他的石头到达Tuhua，Hine-tu-a-hoanga也同时与他一同在那里登岸，又开始把他赶走。于是Ngahue去寻找一个能让他的碧玉石头安宁留存的地方，他在海中发现了这座岛Aotearoa，即新西兰的北岛，便想在那里登岸。

passages.text: He thought again, lest he and his enemy should be too close to one another and quarrel again, that it would be better for him to go further off with his jasper, a very long way off. So he carried it off with him, they coasted along, and at length arrived at Arahura on the west coast of the middle island, and he made that an everlasting resting-place for his jasper. Then he broke off a portion of his jasper and took it with him, returning by Wairere, Whangaparaoa and Tauranga, direct to Hawaiki, and reported that he had discovered a new country which produced the moa and jasper in abundance. He manufactured sharp axes from his jasper - two axes, Tutauru and Hauhau-te-rangi - and fashioned portions into neck and ear ornaments; the ear ornament Kaukau-matua was lost only in 1846 when Te Heuheu was killed with so many of his tribe by a landslip.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 9 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他又想，免得他和他的仇敌彼此离得太近、再度争吵，还是带着他的碧玉走得更远些为好，走到很远很远的地方去。于是他把碧玉带走了，他们沿着海岸航行，终于到达中岛西岸的Arahura，他便在那里为他的碧玉造了一个永久的安息之所。然后他敲下自己碧玉的一部分带在身边，经由Wairere、Whangaparaoa和Tauranga返回，径直回到Hawaiki，报告说他发现了一个新的国度，那里盛产恐鸟和碧玉。他用他的碧玉制成了锋利的斧头——两把斧头，Tutauru和Hauhau-te-rangi——又把其中一部分做成颈饰和耳饰；那件耳饰Kaukau-matua直到1846年Te Heuheu与他的许多族人一同死于一场山崩时才遗失。

passages.text: When Ngahue, returning, arrived again in Hawaiki, he found them all engaged in war; when they heard his description of the beauty of this country of Aotea, some of them determined to come here. All these axes were made from the block of green stone brought back by Ngahue to Hawaiki, which was called 'The fish of Ngahue'; he had previously come to these islands from Hawaiki when he was driven out from thence by Hine-tu-a-hoanga, whose fish or stone was obsidian, with which the natives grind down the jasper. The canoes which afterwards arrived here came in consequence of his discovery.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 9 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當恩加胡伊歸來，再次抵達哈瓦伊基時，他發現他們全都捲入了戰爭；當他們聽他描述這片奧特亞之地的美麗時，其中一些人便決心前來此地。所有這些石斧，都是用恩加胡伊帶回哈瓦伊基的那塊綠石製成的，那塊石頭被稱為「恩加胡伊之魚」；他先前曾從哈瓦伊基來到這些島嶼，當時他被希內圖阿霍安加從那裡驅逐出來，希內圖阿霍安加的魚或石頭是黑曜石，當地人用它來磨碧玉。後來抵達此地的獨木舟，都是因他的發現而來的。

title.en: The Canoes of the Great Migration Are Hewn
title.zh: 大移民之舟開鑿

region.en: Rarotonga, Hawaiki (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哈瓦基之拉羅湯加（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 10, Construction of Canoes to Emigrate to New Zealand (London 1855)

summary.en: In Rarotonga a totara is felled and the Arawa hewn by Rata, Wahie-roa, Ngahue and Paiata; Hotu-roa borrows the workmen and gains the Tainui. The fleet is named - Arawa, Tainui, Matatua, Taki-tumu, Kura-hau-po, Toko-maru, Matawhaorua - the canoes in which the forefathers crossed the ocean to Aotea-roa, all cut with Ngahue's greenstone axes, one of which, Tutauru, was the axe that cut off the head of Uenuku. But Rata slew the son of Manaia and hid his body in the chips and shavings of the canoes, planting a new curse in the exodus.
summary.zh: 眾人在拉羅湯加伐倒一棵羅漢松，由拉塔、瓦希耶羅亞、恩加胡埃、派亞塔等人鑿成阿拉瓦號；霍圖羅亞借得工匠，遂得泰努伊號。七艘大舟——阿拉瓦、泰努伊、馬塔圖亞、塔基圖穆、庫拉豪波、托科馬魯、馬塔瓦奧魯阿——載著先祖橫渡重洋。斧皆出自恩加胡埃碧玉，其中圖陶魯正是砍下烏努庫頭顱之斧。然拉塔殺死馬納亞之子、屍藏木屑之中，大遷徙中又埋下新的詛咒。

sensitivity.note: Founding-legend record for the Arawa/Tainui canoe traditions.

passages.text: They then felled a totara tree in Rarotonga, which lies on the other side of Hawaiki, that they might build the Arawa from it. The tree was felled, and thus the canoe was hewn out from it and finished. The names of the men who built this canoe were Rata, Wahie-roa, Ngahue, Paiata, and some other skilful men, who helped to hew out the Arawa and to finish it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 10 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他們在拉羅湯加砍倒了一棵托塔拉樹，拉羅湯加位於哈瓦伊基的另一側，以便用這棵樹建造阿拉瓦號。樹被砍倒，獨木舟便由此鑿成並完工。建造這艘獨木舟的人的名字是拉塔、瓦希耶羅阿、恩加胡伊、帕伊阿塔，以及其他一些協助鑿成並完成阿拉瓦號的巧匠。

passages.text: A chief of the name of Hotu-roa, hearing that the Arawa was built and wishing to accompany them, came to Tama-te-kapua and asked him to lend him his workmen to hew out some canoes for him too, and they went and built and finished the Tainui and some other canoes. These are the workmen who built the canoes in which the forefathers crossed the ocean to this island, to Aotea-roa. The names of the canoes were as follows: the Arawa was first completed, then Tainui, then Matatua, and Taki-tumu, and Kura-hau-po, and Toko-maru, and Matawhaorua. These are the names of the canoes in which the forefathers departed from Hawaiki and crossed to this island.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 10 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位名叫霍圖羅阿的酋長聽說阿拉瓦號已建成，想要與他們同行，便來到塔馬特卡普阿面前，請他借出自己的工匠，也為他鑿造幾艘獨木舟，於是他們前去建造並完成了泰努伊號及其他幾艘獨木舟。這些工匠建造了祖先們橫渡大洋來到這座島嶼——奧特亞羅阿——所乘的獨木舟。這些獨木舟的名字如下：阿拉瓦號最先完工，然後是泰努伊號，接著是馬塔圖阿號、塔基圖穆號、庫拉豪波號、托科馬魯號和馬塔瓦霍魯阿號。這些就是祖先們離開哈瓦伊基、橫渡來到這座島嶼時所乘獨木舟的名字。

passages.text: When they had lashed the topsides on to the Tainui, Rata slew the son of Manaia and hid his body in the chips and shavings of the canoes. The names of the axes with which they hewed out these canoes were Hauhau-te-Rangi and Tutauru; Tutauru was the axe with which they cut off the head of Uenuku. All these axes were made from the block of green stone brought back by Ngahue to Hawaiki, which was called 'The fish of Ngahue'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 10 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他們把船舷上緣綁到泰努伊號上之後，拉塔殺死了馬納亞的兒子，並把他的屍體藏在獨木舟的碎屑和刨花之中。他們鑿造這些獨木舟所用的石斧的名字是豪豪特蘭吉和圖陶魯；圖陶魯就是他們用來砍下烏埃努庫頭顱的那把石斧。所有這些石斧，都是用恩加胡伊帶回哈瓦伊基的那塊綠石製成的，那塊石頭被稱為「恩加胡伊之魚」。

title.en: Tama-te-kapua Steals the Priest Ngatoro
title.zh: 塔馬特卡普亞拐走祭司

region.en: Launching shore at Hawaiki (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哈瓦基啟航海灘（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 11, The Voyage to New Zealand (London 1855)

summary.en: Realizing the Arawa has no priest, Tama-te-kapua asks Ngatoro-i-rangi aboard 'to perform the necessary religious rites', lures his wife Kearoa too, and orders anchor raised the moment both are on deck. He tricks Ruaeo likewise: fetch my axe Tutauru from under the window-sill - and sails away with Ruaeo's wife as well. Two thefts, and the proverb: a descendant of Tama-te-kapua will steal anything he can.
summary.zh: 阿拉瓦號起航在即，塔馬特卡普亞發現船上無祭司，便以『行必要宗教儀式』為名，誘泰努伊號首領恩加托羅伊蘭基登舟，又以潔舟獻祭為由喚其妻基亞羅亞同來——二人才踏上甲板，他便喝令起錨張帆。他同樣戲耍魯亞奧：『替我取窗檻下的斧子吧』——待魯亞奧返回，舟已遠去，其妻也被擄走。兩樁偷竊，一諺流傳：塔馬特卡普亞的子孫，見物就偷。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection.

passages.text: When the canoes were built and ready for sea, they were dragged afloat, the separate lading of each canoe was collected and put on board, with all the crews. Tama-te-kapua then remembered that he had no skilful priest on board his canoe, and thought the best thing he could do was to outwit Ngatoro-i-rangi, the chief who had command of the Tainui. So just as his canoe shoved off, he called out to Ngatoro, 'I say, Ngatoro, just come on board my canoe, and perform the necessary religious rites for me.' Then the priest Ngatoro came on board, and Tama-te-kapua said he had better also call his wife Kearoa, that she might make the canoe clean or common with an offering of seaweed laid in the canoe instead of an offering of fish, for the second fish caught in a canoe, or seaweed, or some substitute, ought to be offered for the females, the first for the males.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當獨木舟建成、準備好出海時，它們被拖下水，每艘獨木舟各自的貨物都被收集起來裝上船，連同所有船員。這時塔馬特卡普阿想起自己的船上沒有能幹的祭司，便覺得最好的辦法是智取恩加托羅伊蘭吉——那位統領泰努伊號的酋長。於是就在他的獨木舟離岸之際，他對恩加托羅喊道：「喂，恩加托羅，快上我的獨木舟來，替我執行必要的宗教儀式。」於是祭司恩加托羅上了船，塔馬特卡普阿說他最好也把他的妻子凱羅阿叫來，好讓她用放在獨木舟裡的海藻作祭品，來使獨木舟潔淨或化為凡俗，以代替魚的祭品，因為在獨木舟裡捕到的第二條魚、或海藻、或某種替代物，應當為女性獻上，第一條則為男性獻上。

passages.text: Ngatoro assented to all this and called his wife, and they both got into Tama's canoe. The very moment they were on board, Tama' called out to the men, 'Heave up the anchors and make sail', and he carried off with him Ngatoro and his wife, that he might have a priest and wise man on board his canoe. Then they up with the fore-sail, the main-sail, and the mizen, and away shot the canoe. Up came Ngatoro and said, 'Shorten sail, that we may go more slowly, lest I miss my own canoe'; but Tama' replied, 'Oh no, wait a little, and your canoe will follow after us'; for a short time it kept near them, but soon dropped more and more astern, and each canoe proceeded on its own course.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 恩加托羅對這一切表示同意，並叫來了他的妻子，兩人便上了塔馬的獨木舟。他們一上船，塔馬就對眾人喊道：「起錨，揚帆！」他帶走了恩加托羅和他的妻子，好讓自己的船上有祭司和智者。於是他們升起前帆、主帆和後帆，獨木舟便飛馳而去。恩加托羅上前說道：「收帆吧，好讓我們走得慢些，免得我跟不上自己的獨木舟。」但塔馬回答說：「哦，不，稍等一會兒，你的獨木舟會跟在我們後面的。」有一小段時間它還跟他們靠得很近，但很快就越來越落在後面，於是每艘獨木舟各自沿著自己的航向前進。

passages.text: Two thefts were perpetrated by Tama-te-kapua: he carried off the wife of Ruaeo, and Ngatoro and his wife, on board the Arawa. He made a fool of Ruaeo too, saying, 'Oh, Rua', you, like a good fellow, just run back to the village and fetch me my axe Tutauru; I pushed it in under the sill of the window of my house.' Rua' was foolish enough to run back; then off went Tama' with the canoe, and when Rua' came back again, the canoe was so far off that its sails did not look much bigger than little flies. So he fell to weeping for all his goods on board the canoe, and for his wife Whakaoti-rangi, whom Tama-te-kapua had carried off as a wife for himself. Hence this proverb: 'A descendant of Tama-te-kapua will steal anything he can.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 塔馬特卡普阿犯了兩樁盜行：他擄走了魯阿埃奧的妻子，又將恩加托羅與其妻帶上了阿拉瓦號。他還戲弄了魯阿埃奧，說道：『喂，魯阿，你這個好人，快跑回村裡去，把我的斧頭圖陶魯拿來；我把它塞在我家窗檻底下了。』魯阿傻乎乎地跑了回去；於是塔馬帶著獨木舟走了，等魯阿再回來時，獨木舟已經遠得連船帆看上去也不比小蒼蠅大多少了。於是他為船上所有的財物、為他的妻子瓦卡奧蒂朗伊痛哭起來——塔馬特卡普阿把她擄去做了自己的妻子。因此有這句諺語：『塔馬特卡普阿的後裔，見什麼偷什麼。』

title.en: The Throat of Te Parata
title.zh: 特帕拉塔之喉：大漩渦

region.en: Mid-ocean whirlpool, Arawa voyage (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿拉瓦號航程大漩渦（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 11, The Voyage to New Zealand (London 1855)

summary.en: Insulted that Tama-te-kapua laid hands on his wife, the priest Ngatoro climbs the roof of the deckhouse and changes the stars of evening into the stars of morning, raising winds to drive the Arawa backwards until it dashes into the whirlpool called the Throat of Te Parata - 'the steep descent where the world ends'. Only when the crew's shrieks move him does he lift the canoe out by incantation; most of the lading is lost, whence the proverb of the half-filled basket of Whakaoti-rangi.
summary.zh: 祭司恩加托羅因妻受辱，登上艙房屋頂，將暮星化作晨星，呼起逆風逼使阿拉瓦號倒退，直衝入名為『特帕拉塔之喉』的大漩渦——即『世界盡頭之陡淵』。船頭沒頂，貨物滾落入海；他聽聞婦孺哭號、船員哀呼，方才動了惻隱之心，誦咒平息風浪，將獨木舟從漩渦中拔出。輜重盡失，僅存半籃口糧——『瓦卡奧蒂蘭基的半籃』一諺由此而來。

sensitivity.note: Deluge-adjacent peril episode within the migration cycle; the priest's star inversion is recorded as a magical feat.

passages.text: Before climbing upon the roof Ngatoro suspected treachery about his wife, for he had found out what a treacherous person Tama-te-kapua was; so he took a string and tied one end of it to his wife's hair and kept the other in his hand, then climbed to the top of the roof. He had hardly got there when Tama' laid hold of his wife, and cunningly untied the end of the string and made it fast to one of the beams of the canoe; Ngatoro, feeling it tight, thought his wife had not moved. Coming down, he found the string tied fast to the beam, and asked his wife, 'Has not some one disturbed you?' She answered, 'Cannot you tell that from the string being fastened to the beam of the canoe? Who was it, indeed? Could it be any one else but Tama-te-kapua?' Her husband said, 'You are a noble woman indeed thus to confess this; since he has dealt in this way, I will now have my revenge on him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在爬上屋頂之前，恩加托羅就疑心妻子那邊有詐，因為他已看穿了塔馬特卡普阿是個何等奸詐之人；於是他取來一根繩子，一頭繫在妻子的頭髮上，另一頭握在自己手裡，然後爬上屋頂。他剛到屋頂，塔馬就抓住了他的妻子，狡猾地解開繩頭，把它牢牢繫在獨木舟的一根橫樑上；恩加托羅覺得繩子繃緊，以為妻子沒有動。他下來後，發現繩子緊緊繫在橫樑上，便問妻子：『沒有人動過你嗎？』她答道：『繩子繫在獨木舟的橫樑上，這你還看不出來嗎？還能是誰呢？除了塔馬特卡普阿還能有別人嗎？』她丈夫說：『你真是個高尚的女子，竟這樣坦承此事；既然他這樣行事，我現在就要向他報復。』

passages.text: Then that priest went forth upon the roof of the house and stood there, and called aloud to the heavens in the same way that Rua' did, and he changed the stars of the evening into those of morning, and he raised the winds that they should blow upon the prow of the canoe and drive it astern, and the crew were at their wits' end and quite forgot their skill as seamen, and the canoe drew straight into the whirlpool called 'The throat of Te Parata' - which the people of New Zealand also call 'the steep descent where the world ends' - and dashed right into that whirlpool. The canoe became engulfed; the waters reached the first bailing place in the bows, then the second bailing place in the centre, and the canoe appeared to be going down head foremost.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是那位祭司走到屋頂上，站在那裡，像魯阿那樣向天空高聲呼喚，他把傍晚的星辰變成了清晨的星辰，又喚起風來，讓風吹向獨木舟的船首，把它往船尾方向吹，船員們束手無策，完全忘了自己的航海本領，獨木舟徑直駛入了那個名為『特帕拉塔之喉』的漩渦——紐西蘭人也稱之為『世界終結處的陡降』——一頭衝進了那個漩渦。獨木舟被吞沒了；海水漫到了船首的第一個舀水處，接著又漫到中央的第二個舀水處，獨木舟眼看就要船頭朝下沉沒。

passages.text: Up sprang Tama-te-kapua in despair, shouting, 'Oh, Ngatoro, the canoe is gone down so much by the bow that Kearoa's pillow has rolled from under her head.' The priest heard them, but neither moved nor answered until he heard the goods rolling from the decks and splashing into the water, the crew holding on with great difficulty, some having already fallen into the sea. When these things took place, the heart of Ngatoro was moved with pity, for he heard the shrieks of the men and the weeping of the women and children. Then up stood that mighty man again, and by his incantations changed the aspect of the heavens so that the storm ceased, and he repeated another incantation to draw the canoe back out of the whirlpool. Lo, the canoe rose up floating rightly; but a great part of its lading had been thrown out into the water, and a great part of their provisions lost. Thence comes the native proverb when they can give a stranger but little food: 'Oh, it is the half-filled basket of Whakaoti-rangi, for she only managed to save a very small part of her provisions.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 塔馬特卡普阿絕望地跳了起來，喊道：『喂，恩加托羅，獨木舟船首沉得太深了，凱阿羅阿的枕頭都從她頭下滾走了。』祭司聽見了他們，卻既不動也不答，直到他聽見貨物從甲板上滾落、濺入水中，船員們拼命抓住不放，有些人已經掉進了海裡。見此情形，恩加托羅的心被憐憫打動了，因為他聽到了男人們的尖叫和女人孩子們的哭聲。於是那位大力士又站起身來，用咒語改變了天象，使風暴平息，又念了另一道咒語，把獨木舟從漩渦中拉了出來。瞧，獨木舟浮了起來，端正地漂浮著；但它的大部分貨物已被拋入水中，大部分給養也丟失了。於是就有了這句土諺，用於他們只能給陌生人一點點食物的時候：『哦，這是瓦卡奧蒂朗伊的半籃子，因為她只設法保住了極小一部分給養。』

title.en: The Stranded Whale at Whangaparaoa
title.zh: 旺加帕羅亞擱淺鯨之爭

region.en: Whangaparaoa, East Cape, Aotearoa
region.zh: 紐西蘭東角旺加帕羅亞

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 11, The Voyage to New Zealand (London 1855)

summary.en: Landing at Whangaparaoa, the weary crews see pohutukawa trees in full red flower and take them for head-ornaments; Tauninihi throws his real red plumes into the sea, and the flowers crumble at a touch - the origin of the proverb of the red head-ornament found by Mahina. The crews then find a fresh stranded sperm whale and dispute the claim; the test of the thanksgiving altars - Tainui's posts dried over fire, Arawa's posts green - awards the whale to Tainui, who had already tied a rope to its jaw.
summary.zh: 兩舟先後抵達旺加帕羅亞：船員誤將盛開的紅花新西蘭聖誕樹當作頭飾，陶尼尼希遂將真紅羽飾拋入海中——上岸方知所謂紅飾不過落花，『馬希那撿到的紅頭飾，有借無還』一諺由此而來。海灘上橫著一頭新擱淺的抹香鯨，兩族人爭執誰先登陸誰先發現；遂以各自感恩祭壇之木檢驗——泰努伊的柱子經火烤乾，阿拉瓦的柱子猶帶青色——鯨歸泰努伊，其繩索早已拴上鯨顎。

sensitivity.note: First-landing dispute ritualized through altar-post inspection.

passages.text: Then they sailed on and landed at Whanga-Paraoa, in Aotea here. As they drew near to land they saw with surprise some pohutukawa trees of the sea-coast covered with beautiful red flowers, and the still water reflected back the redness of the trees. One of the chiefs of the canoe cried out to his messmates, 'See there, red ornaments for the head are much more plentiful in this country than in Hawaiki, so I'll throw my red head ornaments into the water'; and so saying he threw them into the sea. The name of that man was Tauninihi, and the name of the ornament was Taiwhakaea. The moment they got on shore they ran to gather the pohutukawa flowers, but no sooner did they touch them than the flowers fell to pieces; then they found out that these red head ornaments were nothing but flowers. Shortly afterwards the ornaments of Tauninihi were found by Mahina on the beach of Mahiti, who would not give them up - thence the proverb for anything lost and found by another: 'I will not give it up, 'tis the red head ornament which Mahina found.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他們繼續航行，在阿奧特阿這裡的旺阿帕拉奧阿登陸。當他們靠近陸地時，驚奇地看到海邊的一些波胡圖卡瓦樹開滿了美麗的紅花，靜止的水面映出了樹的紅色。獨木舟上的一位首領對同伴們喊道：『看哪，這地方的紅色頭飾比哈瓦伊基多得多，所以我要把我的紅色頭飾扔進水裡』；說著就把頭飾扔進了大海。那人的名字叫陶尼尼希，那頭飾的名字叫泰瓦卡埃阿。他們一上岸就跑去採波胡圖卡瓦花，可是剛一碰，花就碎了；他們這才明白這些紅色頭飾不過是花。不久之後，陶尼尼希的頭飾被馬希納在馬希蒂的海灘上發現，他不肯歸還——因此有了這句形容失物被他人拾得的諺語：『我不還，這是馬希納撿到的紅色頭飾。』

passages.text: As soon as the party landed at Whanga-Paraoa they planted sweet potatoes, that they might grow there; and they are still to be found growing on the cliffs at that place. Then the crew, wearied from the voyage, wandered idly along the shore, and found the fresh carcase of a sperm whale stranded upon the beach. The Tainui had already arrived in the same neighbourhood; when they met they began to dispute as to who had landed first and first found the dead whale, and as to which canoe it consequently belonged to.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這一行人一到旺阿帕拉奧阿登陸，就種下了甘薯，好讓它們在那裡生長；至今那地方的懸崖上仍能看到它們在生長。接著，因航行而疲憊的船員們沿著海岸閒逛，發現海灘上擱淺著一頭抹香鯨的新鮮屍體。泰努伊號早已到達同一帶；他們相遇後便爭論起來：究竟是誰先登陸、誰先發現這頭死鯨，因而這頭鯨該歸哪一艘獨木舟。

passages.text: To settle the question they agreed to examine the sacred place which each party had set up to return thanks to the gods for their safe arrival, that they might see which had been longest built; and doing so, they found that the posts of the sacred place put up by the Arawa were quite green, whilst the posts of the sacred place set up by the Tainui had evidently been carefully dried over the fire before they were fixed in the ground. The people who had come in the Tainui also showed part of a rope which they had made fast to its jaw-bone. When these things were seen, it was admitted that the whale belonged to the people who came in the Tainui, and it was surrendered to them. Whanga-Paraoa means the bay of the sperm whale, so called from the whale found there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 為了解決這個問題，他們同意去查看雙方各自為感謝神明保佑平安抵達而設立的神聖之地，以便看看哪一方的建造時間較久；他們照做之後，發現阿拉瓦人所立神聖之地的柱子還十分青綠，而泰努伊人所立神聖之地的柱子，顯然在插入地面之前曾仔細地用火烘乾過。搭乘泰努伊號而來的人也出示了他們曾繫在鯨魚下顎骨上的一段繩索。眾人見到這些事物之後，便承認那頭鯨魚屬於搭乘泰努伊號而來的人，並將鯨魚交還給他們。旺阿帕拉奧阿意為抹香鯨之灣，因在那裡發現的鯨魚而得名。

title.en: Marama Pins the Tainui at the Portage
title.zh: 瑪拉瑪咒釘泰努伊於搬運道

region.en: Otahuhu portage, Tamaki isthmus (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 奧塔胡胡搬運道，塔馬基地峽（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 11, The Voyage to New Zealand (London 1855)

summary.en: Surprised by sea-birds flying westward, the Tainui crews explore and find a vast sheet of salt water behind them, and resolve to drag their canoes over the Otahuhu portage. Toko-maru crosses easily; but Hoturoa's wife Marama-kiko-hura, unwilling that the tired crews should go further, fixes the Tainui to the earth by enchantment so that no human strength can stir it. At last Hoturoa's other wife, more learned in magic, chants a far more powerful incantation, and the canoe glides over the skids to float on the Manukau and settle at Kawhia.
summary.zh: 泰努伊眾人在塔馬基河口見海鷗蠣鷸自西飛來，探索之下發現身後竟有一大片鹹水，遂決定拖舟越過奧塔胡胡搬運道。托科馬魯號輕鬆過關；泰努伊號卻紋絲不動——霍圖羅亞之妻瑪拉瑪基科胡拉不願疲憊的船員再遠行，以咒術將其釘死於地，人力盡施亦不能撼動。直至霍圖羅亞另一位更精於法術之妻誦出更強咒語，大舟方滑過墊木，駛入馬努考港，最後安家卡菲亞。

sensitivity.note: Explains the Tainui waka's landfall at Kawhia and the naming of the portage.

passages.text: The Tainui left Whanga-Paraoa shortly after the Arawa, made the Gulf of Hauraki, coasted to Cape Brett, to the island with an arched passage through it called Motukokako, and on to Muriwhenua near the North Cape. Finding the land ended there, they returned along the coast until they reached the Tamaki, landed there, and proceeded up the creek to Tau-oma, the portage, where they were surprised to see flocks of sea-gulls and oyster-catchers passing over from the westward. They went off to explore in that direction and found, to their great surprise, a large sheet of water lying immediately behind them; so they determined to drag their canoes over the portage at a place they named Otahuhu and launch them again on the vast sheet of salt-water they had found.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 泰努伊號在阿拉瓦號之後不久便離開旺阿帕拉奧阿，抵達豪拉基灣，沿海岸航行至布雷特角，再到那座有拱形通道穿過、名為莫圖科卡科的島嶼，接著前往北角附近的穆里芬努阿。他們發現陸地到此為止，便沿著海岸折返，直到抵達塔馬基，在那裡登陸，並沿著小溪上行至搬運獨木舟的陸路通道陶奧馬，在那裡他們驚訝地看見成群的海鷗與蠣鴴從西邊飛越而過。他們便朝那個方向前去探察，大為驚訝地發現緊鄰其後方有一大片水域；於是他們決定在他們命名為奧塔胡胡的地方，把獨木舟拖過陸路通道，再將它們重新放入他們所發現的那片廣闊鹹水中。

passages.text: The first canoe which they hauled across was the Toko-maru - that they got across without difficulty. They next began to drag the Tainui over the isthmus; they hauled away at it in vain, they could not stir it; for one of the wives of Hoturoa, named Marama-kiko-hura, who was unwilling that the tired crews should proceed further on this new expedition, had by her enchantments fixed it so firmly to the earth that no human strength could stir it. They hauled, they hauled, they excited themselves with cries and cheers, but they hauled in vain, they cried aloud in vain, they could not move it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們拖過去的第一艘獨木舟是托科馬魯號——他們毫不費力地就把它拖了過去。接著他們開始把泰努伊號拖過地峽；他們使勁地拉，卻徒勞無功，根本無法使它移動分毫；因為霍圖羅阿的一位妻子，名叫馬拉馬基科胡拉，她不願疲憊的船員們繼續這趟新的遠征，便以她的法術把它牢牢地固定在大地上，任憑多少人力也無法使它移動。他們拉啊拉，他們以呼喊與歡呼激勵自己，但他們徒勞地拉，他們徒勞地大聲呼喊，他們就是無法移動它。

passages.text: When their strength was quite exhausted by these efforts, another of the wives of Hoturoa, more learned in magic and incantations than Marama-kiko-hura, grieved at seeing the exhaustion and distress of her people, rose up and chanted forth an incantation far more powerful; then at once the canoe glided easily over the carefully-laid skids, and it soon floated securely upon the harbour of Manuka. The willing crews urged on the canoes with their paddles, soon discovered the mouth of the harbour on the west coast, passed out into the open sea, coasted southwards, and discovering the small port of Kawhia, entered it and, hauling up their canoe, fixed themselves there for the time, whilst the Arawa was left at Maketu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他們的力氣因這些努力而完全耗盡時，霍圖羅阿的另一位妻子，比馬拉馬基科胡拉更精通法術與咒語，見到她的人民如此疲憊與痛苦而心生不忍，便起身吟誦了一段威力強大得多的咒語；於是獨木舟立刻輕易地滑過精心鋪設的滾木，很快便穩穩地浮在馬努卡港的水面上。樂意的船員們以槳推動獨木舟，很快便發現了西岸那處港口的入口，駛入開闊的大海，沿海岸向南航行，發現了卡菲亞這座小港，便進入其中，把獨木舟拖上岸，暫時在那裡安頓下來，而阿拉瓦號則被留在馬凱圖。

title.en: Ruaeo's Flute beneath the Arawa
title.zh: 魯亞奧笛聲羞辱塔馬

region.en: Maketu beach, Bay of Plenty, Aotearoa
region.zh: 紐西蘭豐盛灣馬凱圖海灘

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 11, The Voyage to New Zealand (London 1855)

summary.en: Ruaeo, following in his own canoe, reaches Maketu first, hooks the sleeping Arawa ashore with a fishing line, and plays his flute beneath her side until his stolen wife wakes and confesses. He coaches her to complain of a dream of his flute-playing, so that the jealous Tama-te-kapua strikes her; she flies to Ruaeo. At dawn his incantations keep the whole crew asleep; at noon he raps the hull, and 140 feather-clad warriors appear beneath the canoe. He challenges Tama-te-kapua to single combat, dashes him four times to the earth, and rubs a prepared heap of vermin into the giant's hair - 'keep the woman', he says, 'as payment for the insults I have heaped upon you' - and departs with his men.
summary.zh: 魯亞奧駕自己的普凱阿特瓦伊努伊號後發先至馬凱圖，用釣鉤將沉睡的阿拉瓦號拖上岸，在船舷下吹笛，喚醒被擄之妻並授以計策。清晨他以咒術令全船沉睡；正午以棒擊船，一百四十名羽飾勇士赫然現於船下。他向塔馬特卡普亞單獨挑戰，四次將其摔倒，最後把備好的寄生蟲抹進這位九尺巨人的頭髮：『女人留給你，算作我羞辱你的賠禮。』言畢率眾而去。

sensitivity.note: Grey notes the giants: Tama-te-kapua nine feet, Ruaeo eleven feet tall.

passages.text: Ruaeo, who had already arrived at Maketu, started up; he was the first to arrive there in his canoe, the Pukeatea-wai-nui, for he had been left behind by the Arawa, and his wife Whakaoti-rangi had been carried off by Tama-te-kapua. After the Arawa had left he sailed in his own canoe for these islands, landed at Maketu, and his canoe reached land the first. He started up, cast his line into the sea with the hooks attached to it, and they got fast in one of the beams of the Arawa, and it was pulled ashore by him whilst the crew were asleep; the hundred and forty men who accompanied him stood upon the beach with skids all ready laid, and the Arawa was dragged upon the shore in the night and left there. Ruaeo seated himself under the side of the Arawa and played upon his flute; the music woke his wife, who said, 'Dear me, that's Rua'!', and they passed the night together.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 早已抵達馬凱圖的魯阿埃奧一躍而起；他是最先乘獨木舟抵達那裡的人，他乘的是普凱阿特阿瓦伊努伊號，因為他曾被阿拉瓦號拋下，而他的妻子瓦卡奧蒂朗吉則被塔馬特卡普阿擄走。阿拉瓦號離開之後，他乘自己的獨木舟航向這些島嶼，在馬凱圖登陸，他的獨木舟最先靠岸。他一躍而起，把繫著魚鉤的釣線拋入海中，魚鉤牢牢鉤住了阿拉瓦號的一根橫樑，趁船員們熟睡之際，他把它拉上了岸；隨他同行的那一百四十人站在海灘上，滾木早已鋪設妥當，阿拉瓦號便在夜間被拖上岸，留在那裡。魯阿埃奧坐在阿拉瓦號的船舷下吹奏笛子；樂聲喚醒了他的妻子，她說：「哎呀，那是魯阿！」於是他們共度了一夜。

passages.text: At last Rua' said, 'O mother of my children, go back now to your new husband, and presently I'll play upon the flute and putorino, so that both you and Tama-te-kapua may hear. Then do you say to Tama-te-kapua, O! I had a dream in the night that I heard Rua playing a tune upon his flute' - and that will make him so jealous that he will give you a blow, and then you can run away from him as if you were in a rage and hurt, and come to me.' She did everything exactly as Rua' had told her; Tama' began to beat her and she ran away from him. Early in the morning Rua' performed incantations by which he kept all the people in the canoe in a profound sleep, and whilst they slept the sun rose and mounted high in the heavens. In the forenoon Rua' gave the canoe a heavy blow with his club; they all started up - it was almost noon, and when they looked down over the edge of their canoe, there were the hundred and forty men of Rua' sitting under them, all beautifully dressed with feathers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最後魯阿說道：「哦，我孩子的母親，現在回到你的新丈夫那裡去吧，待會兒我會吹奏笛子和普托里諾號，好讓你和塔馬特卡普阿都聽見。然後你就對塔馬特卡普阿說：哦！我夜裡做了個夢，夢見魯阿吹著笛子奏著曲調——這會讓他嫉妒得打你一拳，然後你就可以裝作又氣又受傷的樣子從他身邊跑開，到我這兒來。」她完全照魯阿所吩咐的做了；塔馬開始打她，她便從他身邊跑開。清晨，魯阿施行法術，使獨木舟上所有人都陷入沉睡，就在他們沉睡之際，太陽升起，高懸於天際。上午時分，魯阿用棍棒重重地敲了獨木舟一下；他們全都驚跳起來——時近正午，當他們從獨木舟邊緣往下望去，魯阿的那一百四十人正坐在他們下方，個個身披羽毛，裝扮得十分華美。

passages.text: Then Rua' shouted out as he stood, 'Come here, Tama-te-kapua; let us two fight the battle, you and I alone. If you are stronger than I am, well and good; if I am stronger than you are, I'll dash you to the earth.' Up sprang the hero Tama-te-kapua with a carved two-handed sword decked with red feathers; Rua' held a similar weapon. Tama' first struck a fierce blow; Rua' parried it, threw away his sword, seized both Tama's arms and dashed him to the earth. Tama' half rose and was again dashed down; once more he almost rose and was thrown again; still he fiercely struggled to rise.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是魯阿站起來大喊：「過來這裡，塔馬特卡普阿；讓我們兩人決一死戰，只有你和我。如果你比我強，那也好；如果我比你強，我就把你摔到地上。」英雄塔馬特卡普阿一躍而起，手持一把飾有紅羽的雕花雙手劍；魯阿也拿著類似的武器。塔馬先猛烈一擊；魯阿擋開，丟掉自己的劍，抓住塔馬的雙臂，把他摔到地上。塔馬半起身，又被摔倒；他再次幾乎站起，又被摔倒；他仍奮力掙扎著要起來。

passages.text: For the fourth time he almost rose up; then Rua', overcome with rage, took a heap of vermin he had prepared to cover Tama' with insult and shame, and rubbed them on Tama-te-kapua's head and ear, and they adhered so fast that Tama' tried in vain to get them out. Rua' said, 'There, I've beaten you; now keep the woman, as a payment for the insults I've heaped upon you and for having been beaten by me'; but Tama', driven almost mad with the pain and itching, could do nothing but stand scratching his head, whilst Rua' departed with his hundred and forty men to seek some other dwelling-place. These men were giants - Tama-te-kapua was nine feet high, Rua' was eleven feet high; there have been no men since that time so tall as those heroes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 11 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他第四次幾乎站起來；這時魯阿怒不可遏，取來一堆他準備好用來羞辱塔馬的害蟲，抹在塔馬特卡普阿的頭上和耳上，牠們黏得極牢，塔馬怎麼也弄不掉。魯阿說：「好了，我打敗你了；現在留著那女人吧，就當作我加諸你身上的羞辱、以及你被我打敗的補償」；但塔馬被疼痛和搔癢逼得幾乎發狂，只能站著抓頭，而魯阿則帶著他的一百四十名部眾離去，另尋住處。這些人是巨人——塔馬特卡普阿身高九英尺，魯阿身高十一英尺；自那時以來，再沒有像這些英雄那麼高的人了。

title.en: The Inca Interrogates a Huaca: Cana-chuap Yauirca Unmasked
title.zh: 印加王質問瓦卡:揭穿卡納-查普·亞烏爾卡

region.en: Capacuyo, village of the Andes, Antisuyu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 安蒂蘇尤安第斯村卡帕庫約(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Inca Ccapac Yupanqui wished to witness how the huacas conversed with their friends, and entered a village of the Andes called Capacuyo. The young Inca asked why they closed the doors and windows so as to leave them in the dark, and they all replied that in this way they could make the huaca come, who was the enemy of the name of God Almighty, and that there must be silence. When they had made an end of calling, it entered with a rush of wind that made them all in a cold sweat of horror. The Inca ordered doors and windows opened to see the shape of the thing they waited for with such veneration; but as soon as it was light the Devil hid its face and knew not how to answer. The dauntless Inca said: 'Tell me what you are called'; and, with much shame, it replied that its name was Cana-chuap yauirca. 'Why are you so frightened and ashamed? If you can grant children, long life, good fortune, coycollas and huacanquis, why do you stand there like a criminal without raising your eyes? I tell you that you are some false deceiver; for if you were powerful you would not be afraid nor hang down your head. I now feel that there is another Creator of all things, as my father Mayta Ccapac Ynca has told me.' The figure was ugly, with a foul smell and coarse matted hair; it fled out of the house raising shouts like thunder, and from that time all the huacas feared the Yncas, who also used the yacarcay, a rebuking formula in the name of the Creator.
summary.zh: 印加·卡帕克·尤潘琪欲親見瓦卡與其信眾對話,遂入安第斯村卡帕庫約。少年印加問眾人為何閉門塞窗、一片漆黑;眾答:如此方能召來瓦卡——它是全能上帝之名的仇敵,且須寂靜無聲。召喚完畢,那物挾一陣狂風而入,眾人嚇得冷汗直冒。印加命開門啟窗,要看清他們所虔敬恭候之物究竟何形;然而天光一亮,那魔鬼便遮住臉面,無言以對。無畏的印加喝道:「報上名來!」那物滿面羞慚,自承名為「卡納-查普·亞烏爾卡」。印加斥道:「你若真能賜子嗣、壽命、運氣、頭飾與愛情符物,為何像罪人一般垂首不敢仰視?你無非是個假騙子;你若有威能,何至於害怕?我如今確信,別有一位造物主——我父馬雅塔·卡帕克·印加早曾告我。」那形貌醜陋、氣味穢臭、毛髮蓬亂之物倉皇逃出屋外,呼叫如雷。自此諸瓦卡畏懼印加諸王;印加王亦以造物主之名誦「亞卡爾卡伊」斥逐之。

sensitivity.note: Royal huaca-interrogation episode; the Inca's monotheizing argument mirrors Salcamayhua's own Christian frame.

passages.text: It happened one day that the Ynca Ccapac Yupanqui wished to witness how the huacas conversed with their friends, so he entered the place selected, which was in a village of the Andes called Capacuyo. When the young Ynca entered among these idolaters, he asked why they closed the doors and windows so as to leave them in the dark, and they all replied that in this way they could make the huaca come, who was the enemy to the name of God Almighty, and that there must be silence. When they had made an end of calling the Devil, he entered with a rush of wind that made them all in a cold sweat of horror.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，印加卡帕克尤潘基想親眼看看瓦卡如何與牠們的朋友交談，於是進入選定的地方，那是在安地斯山一個名叫卡帕庫約的村莊。當年輕的印加人走進這些偶像崇拜者中間時，他問他們為何把門窗關上，讓裡面一片漆黑，他們都回答說，這樣才能把瓦卡請來，牠是全能上帝之名的仇敵，而且必須保持安靜。當他們召喚魔鬼完畢，牠隨著一陣疾風進來，使他們全都嚇出一身冷汗。

passages.text: Then the young Ynca ordered the doors and windows to be opened, that he might know the shape of that thing for which they had waited with such veneration. But as soon as it was light the Devil hid its face, and knew not how to answer. The dauntless Ynca Ccapac Yupanqui said: 'Tell me what you are called'; and, with much shame, it replied that its name was Cana-chuap yauirca. The Ynca then said: 'Why are you so frightened and ashamed? If you can grant children, long life, good fortune, coycollas and huacanquis, why do you stand there like a criminal without raising your eyes? I tell you that you are some false deceiver; for if you were powerful you would not be afraid nor hang down your head. I now feel that there is another Creator of all things, as my father Mayta Ccapac Ynca has told me.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是年輕的印加人下令打開門窗，好讓他看清他們如此虔敬等候的那東西是什麼模樣。但光一照進來，魔鬼就遮住臉，不知如何回答。無畏的印加卡帕克尤潘基說：「告訴我你叫什麼名字」；牠十分羞愧地回答說，牠的名字叫卡納丘阿普堯爾卡。印加人於是說：「你為何如此驚慌羞愧？如果你能賜予子女、長壽、好運、科伊科利亞和瓦坎基，為何還像個罪犯一樣站在那裡，不敢抬眼？我告訴你，你是個騙人的假貨；因為你若真有力量，就不會害怕，也不會垂頭喪氣。我現在覺得，萬物另有一位造物主，正如我父親邁塔卡帕克印加告訴我的那樣。」

passages.text: The figure of this devil was ugly, with a foul smell, and coarse matted hair. It fled out of the house, raising shouts like thunder; and they say that from that time all the huacas feared the Yncas; and the Yncas also used the yacarcay, in the name of the Creator, a rebuking formula beginning 'Hurinapachap hicrinpachap, cochamantarayocpa camaquimpa...'. With these words the Yncas made all the huacas tremble.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這魔鬼的形貌醜陋，氣味惡臭，頭髮粗亂糾結。牠逃出屋子，發出如雷的喊聲；據說從那時起，所有的瓦卡都懼怕印加人；印加人也以造物主之名使用亞卡爾卡伊，那是一段斥責的咒語，開頭是「胡里納帕查普·希克林帕查普，科查曼塔拉約克帕·卡馬金帕……」。印加人用這些話使所有的瓦卡顫抖。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Water Touched by Tonapa: Baptism of the Infant Inca Ruca
title.zh: 托納帕所觸之水:嬰兒印加·羅卡受洗

region.en: Titicaca spring and Cuzco great square (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 的的喀喀泉與庫斯科大廣場(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Inca Ccapac Yupanqui had a son by his wife Mama Corillpay-cahua, named Ynca Ruca, at whose birth there was much festivity. The Ynca sent men to search for the place called Titicaca, where the great Tonapa had arrived, and they brought water thence to pour over the infant Ynca Ruca while they celebrated the praises of Tonapa. In the spring on the top of the rocks, the water was in a basin called ccapacchama quispisutuc unu. Future Yncas caused this water to be brought in a bowl called curi-ccacca, and placed before them in the middle of the square of Cuzco, called Huacay-pata and Cusi-pata, where they did honour to the water that had been touched by Tonapa.
summary.zh: 印加·卡帕克·尤潘琪與王后瑪瑪·科里爾佩-卡瓦生子印加·羅卡,誕辰大宴。印加遣人尋訪偉大的托納帕曾到過的名為提提卡卡之地,從那裡取水,在頌揚托納帕之聲中,為嬰兒印加·羅卡灌頂。岩頂泉眼之水貯於石盆,名「卡帕克查馬-基斯皮蘇圖克-烏努」。後世印加皆命人以此水盛於「庫里-卡卡」碗中,陳於庫斯科大廣場(瓦卡伊帕塔、庫西帕塔)中央,向托納帕所觸之水致敬。

sensitivity.note: Royal baptism with Tonapa-water: the culture-hero's relic cult inside the dynasty.

passages.text: They say that this Ynca Ccapac Yupanqui had a son, by his wife Mama Corillpay-cahua, named Ynca Ruca, at whose birth there was much festivity. But the Ynca did not entirely separate himself from idolaters, as he allowed the huacas of each village to be worshipped. It is said that the Ynca sent men to search for the place called Titicaca, where the great Tonapa had arrived, and that they brought water thence to pour over the infant Ynca Ruca, while they celebrated the praises of Tonapa.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說這位印加卡帕克尤潘基與妻子瑪瑪科里爾帕伊卡瓦生有一子，名叫印加魯卡，他出生時舉行了盛大的慶典。但這位印加人並未完全脫離偶像崇拜者，因為他允許各村莊的瓦卡受崇拜。據說印加人派人去尋找一個名叫的的喀喀的地方，偉大的托納帕曾到過那裡，他們從那裡取水來澆在嬰兒印加魯卡身上，同時頌揚托納帕的功德。

passages.text: In the spring on the top of the rocks, the water was in a basin called ccapacchama quispisutuc unu. Future Yncas caused this water to be brought in a bowl called curi-ccacca, and placed before them in the middle of the square of Cuzco, called Huacay-pata and Cusi-pata: where they did honour to the water that had been touched by Tonapa.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 春天時，在岩石頂上，水積於一個名為 ccapacchama quispisutuc unu 的盆中。後世的印加人令人將這水盛於一個名為 curi-ccacca 的碗中帶來，並在庫斯科廣場中央、名為 Huacay-pata 與 Cusi-pata 之處，置於他們面前；他們就在那裡向那曾被 Tonapa 觸及的水致敬。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Tonapa Vihinquira Banishes the Idols to the Snowy Mountains
title.zh: 托納帕·維欣基拉逐偶像於雪山

region.en: Xauxa valley and the snowy Cordillera (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 豪哈谷與雪山脈(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In those days the Curacas of Asillu and Hucuru told the Ynca how, in ancient times, a poor thin old man, with a beard and long hair, had come to them in a long shirt, a wise councillor in affairs of state, whose name was Tonapa Vihinquira: he had banished all the idols and hapi-ñuñu demons to the snowy mountains - to Asancata, Quiyancatay, Sallcatay and Apitosiray. The Curacas of the Huancas said this Tonapa Varivillca had also been in their land, had made a house to live in, and had banished all the huacas and hapi-ñuñus of Hatun Sausa Huanca to the snowy mountains in Pariacaca and Vallollo; before their banishment these idols had done much harm, menacing the Curacas to make them offer human sacrifices. The Ynca ordered that the house of Tonapa should be preserved, at the foot of a small hill near the river as you enter Xauxa from the Cuzco road; before coming to it there are two stones where Tonapa had turned a female huaca into stone for having fornicated with a man of the Huancas: it was called Atapymapuranutapya, and afterwards, in the time of Huayna Ccapac Ynca, the two stones declared to the people that they were huacanqui coycoylla.
summary.zh: 當時,阿西盧與庫庫魯的庫拉卡們告訴印加王:古時有一位瘦弱老者,鬚髯皆白,長髮披肩,身著長衫而來,乃是國政的明智謀士,名為托納帕·維欣基拉;他將一切偶像與哈皮紐紐惡魔逐往雪山——阿桑卡塔、基揚卡塔伊、薩爾卡塔伊、阿皮托西拉伊。萬卡人的庫拉卡亦言:這位托納帕·瓦里維爾卡曾至其地,築屋而居,將瓦通-薩烏薩-萬卡全境的瓦卡與惡魔逐往帕里亞卡卡與瓦約略的雪山;被逐之前,那些偶像為害甚烈,威逼庫拉卡獻人祭。印加王命保存托納帕之屋——在自庫斯科道入豪哈城途中河畔小山之下;近屋有兩石,乃托納帕因一女瓦卡與萬卡男子私通而將其石化者,名「阿塔皮馬普魯努塔皮亞」;至瓦伊納·卡帕克時代,二石又自稱為「瓦坎基-科伊科伊利亞」。

sensitivity.note: Huarochiri-adjacent tradition (Xauxa/Pariacaca) preserved in an Inca-focused text; tagged culture-hero against the Tonapa cluster.

passages.text: In those days the Curacas of Asillu and Hucuru told the Ynca how, in ancient times, a poor thin old man, with a beard and long hair, had come to them in a long shirt, and that he was a wise councillor in affairs of state, and that his name was Tonapa Vihinquira. They said that he had banished all the idols and hapi-ñuñu demons to the snowy mountains. All the Curacas and chroniclers also said that this Tonapa had banished all the huacas and idols to the mountains of Asancata, Quiyancatay, Sallcatay, and Apitosiray.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那些日子裡，Asillu 與 Hucuru 的 Curacas 告訴印加人：古時曾有一個瘦弱貧窮的老人，蓄著鬍鬚、留著長髮，身穿長衫來到他們那裡；他是國事上的睿智顧問，名叫 Tonapa Vihinquira。他們說，他曾將所有的偶像與 hapi-ñuñu 惡魔放逐到雪山之上。所有的 Curacas 與編年史家也說，這位 Tonapa 曾將所有的 huacas 與偶像放逐到 Asancata、Quiyancatay、Sallcatay 與 Apitosiray 諸山。

passages.text: When all the Curacas of the provinces of Ttahuantin-suyu were assembled in the Huacay-pata, each in his place, those of the Huancas said that this Tonapa Varivillca had also been in their land, and that he had made a house to live in, and had banished all the huacas and hapi-ñuñus in the province of Hatun Sausa Huanca to the snowy mountains in Pariacaca and Vallollo. Before their banishment these idols had done much harm to the people, menacing the Curacas to make them offer human sacrifices.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當 Ttahuantin-suyu 各省的 Curacas 齊聚於 Huacay-pata、各就其位時，Huancas 人說，這位 Tonapa Varivillca 也曾到過他們的土地，曾造了一所房屋居住，並將 Hatun Sausa Huanca 省所有的 huacas 與 hapi-ñuñus 放逐到 Pariacaca 與 Vallollo 的雪山之上。在被放逐之前，這些偶像曾對人民造成許多傷害，脅迫 Curacas 使他們獻上人祭。

passages.text: The Ynca ordered that the house of Tonapa should be preserved. It was at the foot of a small hill near the river as you enter Xauxa from the Cuzco road, and before coming to it there are two stones where Tonapa had turned a female huaca into stone for having fornicated with a man of the Huancas. It was called Atapymapuranutapya, and afterwards, in the time of Huayna Ccapac Ynca, the two stones declared to the people that they were huacanqui coycoylla. In those days there were also huacanquis in the wilderness of Xauxa, and before coming to Pachacamac, and in a nest of the suyuntuy (turkey buzzard) and stones in Chincha-yunca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 印加人下令保存 Tonapa 的房屋。那房屋位於河邊一座小丘的腳下，正當你從庫斯科大道進入 Xauxa 之處；在到達那裡之前，有兩塊石頭，是 Tonapa 因一個女 huaca 與一名 Huancas 男子行淫而將她變成石頭的。那地方名叫 Atapymapuranutapya；後來在 Huayna Ccapac 印加時代，那兩塊石頭向人們宣稱它們是 huacanqui coycoylla。那些日子裡，Xauxa 的荒野中也有 huacanquis，在到達 Pachacamac 之前也有，還有在 Chincha-yunca 的 suyuntuy（火雞禿鷲）巢中與石頭之間。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Infant That Wept Blood: Yahuar-huaccac
title.zh: 泣血之嬰:亞瓦爾-瓦卡克

region.en: Cuzco great square (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科大廣場(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The eldest son of Inca Ruca was named Yahuar-huaccac Ynca Yupanqui; his mother was Mamicay-chimpu, and at his birth there was a grand feast. The square and all the streets were filled with arches of feathers, and the house of Curicancha was entirely covered with rich plumes, both within and without. They played on eight drums and sang the ayma, torca, cayo, huallma chamayuricssa, haylli and cachra, giving thanks to the Creator. While they were all singing in the Huacay-pata, the infant wept blood, an unheard-of miracle which caused much alarm - hence the name Yahuar-huaccac Ynca. His father diligently searched for someone to interpret the meaning of this incident. In those days the hualla-huisas, cunti-huisas and cana-huisas were great sorcerers, and there assembled such a vast number of canchus, carcas, umus, uscatus and huisas that there was not room for them all in Cuzco. The Ynca did not like to confide his secrets to so many, lest the people should lose their veneration for him; so he reprehended them publicly, saying that there were many wise men but little wisdom, and dismissed them - but they returned with more liberty than before, and their idolatrous practices increased.
summary.zh: 印加·羅卡之長子名亞瓦爾-瓦卡克·印加·尤潘琪,母為瑪米凱-欽普。誕辰大宴:廣場與街衢滿懸羽拱,科里坎查神屋內外遍覆華羽;鳴八鼓,唱阿伊瑪、托爾卡、卡約、瓦爾馬·夏馬尤里克薩、阿伊利、卡克拉諸曲,謝造物主。當眾人在瓦卡伊帕塔歌唱之際,嬰兒竟泣血——聞所未聞的神蹟,舉城震恐,故名「亞瓦爾-瓦卡克」(泣血者)。其父遍尋能解此兆之人。當時瓦利亞-瓜薩、昆蒂-瓜薩、卡納-瓜薩皆大巫師;坎楚、卡爾卡、烏穆、烏斯卡圖斯、瓜薩之流雲集,庫斯科竟無處容身。印加王恐密事外洩、失眾敬畏,乃公開訓斥:「智者雖多,智慧實少」,盡數遣散;然而巫覡去而復返,行巫更無忌憚。

sensitivity.note: Name-giving birth omen; the blood-weeping infant foreshadows the dynastic tragedies later tradition attached to Yahuar Huaccac.

passages.text: They say that the eldest son of this Ynca Ruca was named Yahuar-huaccac Ynca Yupanqui. His mother was Mamicay-chimpu; and at his birth there was a grand feast. The square and all the streets were filled with arches of feathers, and the house of Curicancha was entirely covered with rich plumes, both within and without. They played on eight drums, and sang the ayma, torca, cayo, and huallma chamayuricssa, and haylli, and cachra, giving thanks to the Creator.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們說，這位印加 Ruca 的長子名叫 Yahuar-huaccac Ynca Yupanqui。他的母親是 Mamicay-chimpu；他出生時舉行了盛大的慶典。廣場與所有街道都布滿了羽毛拱門，Curicancha 的房屋內外全都覆滿了華美的羽毛。他們敲擊八面鼓，唱著 ayma、torca、cayo 與 huallma chamayuricssa，以及 haylli 與 cachra，向造物主獻上感恩。

passages.text: While they were all singing in the Huacay-pata, they say that the infant wept blood, an unheard of miracle, which caused much alarm, and hence the name Yahuar-huaccac Ynca. His father the Ynca diligently searched for some one who could interpret the meaning of this incident.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他們全都在 Huacay-pata 歌唱時，他們說那嬰兒哭出了血，這是聞所未聞的奇蹟，引起了極大的驚恐，因此得名 Yahuar-huaccac Ynca。他的父親印加人勤加尋訪能解讀此事件含意的人。

passages.text: In those days the hualla-huisas, cunti-huisas, cana-huisas were great sorcerers; and there assembled such a vast number of canchus, carcas, umus, uscatus, huisas, that there was not room for them all in Cuzco. The Ynca did not like to confide his secrets to so many, lest the people should lose their veneration for him, so he reprehended them publicly, saying that there were many wise men but little wisdom, and he dismissed them; but these enchanters, necromancers, wizards, and witches returned with more liberty than they had had before, and their idolatrous practices increased.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在那個時候，瓦利亞維薩（hualla-huisas）、昆蒂維薩（cunti-huisas）、卡納維薩（cana-huisas）都是法力高強的巫師；而聚集了如此眾多的坎丘（canchus）、卡爾卡（carcas）、烏穆（umus）、烏斯卡圖（uscatus）、維薩（huisas），以致庫斯科（Cuzco）容納不下他們所有人。印加（Ynca）不願向這麼多人吐露自己的秘密，唯恐人民因此失去對他的敬畏，於是當眾斥責他們，說智者雖多，智慧卻少，並將他們遣散；然而這些巫師、通靈者、術士與女巫歸來之後，比從前更加肆無忌憚，他們的偶像崇拜之行也愈演愈烈。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Beautiful Youth on the Rock: Stones Become Soldiers Against the Chancas
title.zh: 巖上美少年:化石成兵抗昌卡

region.en: Cuzco, besieged by the Chancas (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 被昌卡圍困的庫斯科(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: When the Hanco-Allos and Chancas besieged the city of Cuzco, the Ynca Uira-ccocha Yupanqui knew not what course to pursue and went out to arrange a peace at Yuncay-pampa. His legitimate son, Ynca Yupanqui, whom his father detested, was afflicted at the sight of his capital encompassed by an enemy; his heart was emboldened and he took the road to Cuzco. Before he arrived at Callachaca, travelling alone, he saw a very fair and beautiful youth on the top of a rock, who said: 'O son, I promise, in the name of the Creator, on whom you have called in your troubles, that he has heard you, and will give you the victory over your enemies. Fight then without fear.' Then he disappeared, and the prince felt at once emboldened and capable of command. Entering the house of arms he took out all the weapons, armed men and women, took the tupac-yauri and ccapac unancha, and unfurled the standard of the Yncas; the city became a fortress. At the first encounter the prince was knocked down by a stone from a sling and lay half insensible; then he heard a voice from heaven saying that he had not got the sceptre of tupac-yauri; he returned to the temple, took the sceptre, and returned to the battle. Meanwhile an old Ynca, Tupac Ranchiri, a priest of the Ccuricancha, set some stones in a row and fastened shields and clubs to them, so that at a distance they looked like rows of soldiers sitting down. The prince cried out to the supposed soldiers to rise; and then he saw that the stones had become men, who rose up and fought with desperate courage, assaulting the Anco-Allos and Chancas: so the prince gained the victory and beheaded the hostile chiefs Tomay-huaraca, Asto-huaraca and Huasco-Tornay Rimac. A widow named Chanan Coricoca fought valiantly in the battle like a soldier.
summary.zh: 安科-阿約與昌卡人圍困庫斯科之際,老王維拉科查·尤潘琪不知所措,竟赴永卡潘帕議和。其正妻所生、為父所惡的王子印加·尤潘琪見都城受圍,心如火焚,獨自踏上歸途。未至卡利亞查卡,他在巖頂見一極俊美的少年,少年說:「兒啊,我奉造物主之名——你在患難中所呼求者——向你應許:祂已垂聽,必賜你戰勝仇敵。奮勇而戰,勿懼!」言畢隱去,王子頓覺膽氣自生,儼然可號令三軍。他入武庫取出兵器,武裝城中男女,持圖帕克-亞烏里權杖與卡帕克軍旗,展開印加大纛;全城化為堡壘。首戰之際,王子被飛石擊倒,昏沉半死;忽聞天上有聲,責其未攜圖帕克-亞烏里權杖。他返神廟取杖再戰。此時科里坎查老祭司圖帕克-蘭奇里沿路排列石塊,縛以盾與棍,遠望如伏兵數列。王子望之,大呼「伏兵起!」——石竟成人,奮勇死戰,衝擊安科-阿約與昌卡軍。王子大捷,斬敵酋托馬伊-瓦拉卡、阿斯托-瓦拉卡、瓜斯科-托爾奈·里馬克之頭。寡婦查南·科里科卡亦如戰士般奮勇力戰。

sensitivity.note: The Chanca siege miracle, the mythic core of Pachacuti's legitimation; variants differ between Sarmiento, Cieza and Salcamayhua.

passages.text: Then the Hanco-Allos and Chancas besieged the city of Cuzco, which roused the Ynca Uira-ccocha Yupanqui from his careless ease. He knew not what course to pursue, and applied to the Hanco-Allos and Chancas; eventually he came out to arrange a peace, to Yuncay-pampa. Then his legitimate son, named Ynca Yupanqui, whom his father detested, was afflicted at the sight of his capital encompassed by an enemy. His heart was emboldened and he took the road to Cuzco, but before he arrived at Callachaca, as he travelled along the road alone, he saw a very fair and beautiful youth on the top of a rock, who said: 'O son, I promise, in the name of the Creator, on whom you have called in your troubles, that he has heard you, and will give you the victory over your enemies. Fight then without fear.' He then disappeared, and the prince felt at once emboldened and capable of command.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是，漢科阿略（Hanco-Allos）與昌卡（Chancas）圍攻庫斯科城，這使印加·維拉科查·尤潘基（Ynca Uira-ccocha Yupanqui）從安逸中驚醒。他不知該如何應對，便向漢科阿略與昌卡求和；最終他出城前往雲凱潘帕（Yuncay-pampa）安排和議。此時，他那位被父親厭惡的嫡子，名叫印加·尤潘基（Ynca Yupanqui），見到自己的都城被敵人圍困，心中悲痛。他鼓起勇氣，踏上前往庫斯科的道路，但在他抵達卡拉查卡（Callachaca）之前，當他獨自沿路而行時，看見一位非常俊美出眾的少年立於岩石之上，少年說道：「哦，孩子，我以造物主之名向你許諾——你在患難中曾向祂呼求——祂已聽見你，並將賜你戰勝敵人的勝利。那麼，無所畏懼地戰鬥吧。」說罷，他便消失了，而王子頓時感到勇氣倍增，且有能力統帥。

passages.text: On reaching his palace, he cried out, saying: 'Cuzco Ccapac pac churacllay yana pahuay may pimcanqui.' Then he entered the house of arms, and took out all the offensive and defensive weapons. At that juncture twenty Orejones arrived, his relations, sent by his father. He armed all the men and women and, entering the temple, he took the tupac-yauri and ccapac unancha, and unfurled the standard of the Yncas. The city became a fortress, and the enemy commenced the attack; but the prince had forgotten the tupac-yauri. At the first encounter, the prince Ynca Yupanqui was knocked down by a stone from a sling, and remained half insensible. Then he heard a voice from heaven saying that he had not got the sceptre of tupac-yauri. So he went back to the temple and took the sceptre, and returned to the battle, encouraging the captains and soldiers to fight.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他一到自己的宮殿，便高聲喊道：「庫斯科·卡帕克·帕克·丘拉克萊·亞納·帕瓦伊·邁·皮姆坎基（Cuzco Ccapac pac churacllay yana pahuay may pimcanqui）。」隨後他進入兵器庫，取出所有進攻與防禦的武器。就在此時，他父親派來的二十名奧雷洪（Orejones，即「大耳人」）親族抵達。他將所有男女都武裝起來，並進入神廟，取出圖帕克·堯里（tupac-yauri）與卡帕克·烏南查（ccapac unancha），展開印加的旗幟。整座城變成了一座堡壘，敵人開始進攻；但王子卻忘了圖帕克·堯里。初次交鋒時，王子印加·尤潘基被投石索擲出的石頭擊倒，半昏半醒。這時他聽見從天上傳來一個聲音，說他尚未取得圖帕克·堯里的權杖。於是他回到神廟，取來權杖，重返戰場，激勵隊長與士兵奮勇作戰。

passages.text: Meanwhile an old Ynca, a near relation of the prince's father, named Tupac Ranchiri, who was a priest of the Ccuricancha, set some stones in a row, and fastened shields and clubs to them, so that they might look at a distance like rows of soldiers sitting down. The prince, looking out for succour from his father, saw these rows from a distance, and cried out to the supposed soldiers to rise, as his men were on the point of yielding. The Chancas continued the attack with increased fury, and then the prince saw that the stones had become men, and they rose up and fought with desperate courage and skill, assaulting the Anco-Allos and Chancas; so the prince gained a victory, and followed the enemy to Quizachilla, where he beheaded the chiefs of the hostile army, named Tomay-huaraca, Asto-huaraca, and Huasco-Tornay Rimac. They say that a widow named Chanan Coricoca fought valiantly in the battle like a soldier.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 與此同時，一位年老的印加人，是王子父親的近親，名叫圖帕克·蘭奇里（Tupac Ranchiri），他是庫里坎查（Ccuricancha）的祭司，將一些石頭排成一行，並在石頭上綁上盾牌與棍棒，使它們從遠處望去就像一排排坐著的士兵。王子正盼望著父親的援軍，遠遠望見這些行列，便向那些以為是士兵的對象高喊起身，因為他的人馬即將支撐不住。昌卡人愈加猛烈地進攻，這時王子看見那些石頭已化為人，他們起身以拼死的勇氣與嫻熟的戰技作戰，猛攻安科阿略（Anco-Allos）與昌卡人；於是王子贏得了勝利，並追擊敵人至基薩奇利亞（Quizachilla），在那裡將敵軍的首領斬首，他們名叫托邁瓦拉卡（Tomay-huaraca）、阿斯托瓦拉卡（Asto-huaraca）與瓦斯科普托爾奈里馬克（Huasco-Tornay Rimac）。據說有一位名叫查南·科里科卡（Chanan Coricoca）的寡婦，在戰鬥中如士兵一般英勇作戰。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: He Takes the Name of His Brother's Slayer: Pachacuti
title.zh: 他取了殺弟者之名:帕查庫提

region.en: Huayra-Cancha, Collasuyu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科利亞蘇尤瓦伊拉-坎恰(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Inca Urcu, the natural son to whom Viracocha Inca had renounced the kingdom in his lifetime, undertook the conquest of Colla-suyu; he passed through the country of the Caviñas taking with him the statue of Manco Ccapac to secure good fortune, but was defeated and killed at Huana-calla by the hand of Yamqui Pachacuti, the chief of Huayra-Cancha. After his victory over the Chancas, Inca Yupanqui followed the enemy to Andahuayllas, returned to Cuzco, and undertook the conquest of Colla-suyu; among the chiefs who submitted was the famous Yamqui-Pachacuti, whom the prince thanked for the death of Inca Urcu, his brother; and the prince took his name and added it to his own, which became Pachacuti Ynca Yupanqui. He conquered all the land of the Colla-suyu and invaded the provinces of the Chayas and Caravayas, where he destroyed a famous idol.
summary.zh: 維拉科查生前將王位讓與庶子印加·烏爾庫。烏爾庫率大軍征科利亞蘇尤,攜曼科·卡帕克神像以求勝運,然在瓦納-卡利亞為瓦伊拉-坎恰之酋雅姆基·帕查庫提所敗殺。王子印加·尤潘琪大破昌卡後,追敵至安達瓦伊利亞斯,返庫斯科,繼而征科利亞蘇尤;來降諸酋中,即有殺其兄烏爾庫的雅姆基-帕查庫提。王子謝其弒兄之功,並取其名加於己名之上,遂稱「帕查庫提·印加·尤潘琪」。他征服科利亞蘇尤全境,又侵查亞斯與卡拉瓦亞斯諸省,毀其著名神像。

sensitivity.note: Name-taking episode; Salcamayhua records the awkward fact that 'Pachacuti' was the name of the brother-slayer, against later idealized versions.

passages.text: He had a natural son named Ynca Urcu, to whom he renounced the kingdom during his life time. This Ynca Urcu undertook the conquest of Colla-suyu with a great army... He passed through the country of the Caviñas, taking with him the statue of Manco Ccapac, to secure good fortune for himself. But he was defeated and killed at Huana-calla, by the hand of Yamqui Pachacuti, the chief of Huayra-Cancha.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他有一個庶子，名叫印加·烏爾庫（Ynca Urcu），他在生前便將王國讓與此人。這位印加·烏爾庫率領大軍著手征服科利亞蘇尤（Colla-suyu）……他帶著曼科·卡帕克（Manco Ccapac）的雕像穿過卡維尼亞（Caviñas）人的地區，以求為自己帶來好運。但他在瓦納卡拉（Huana-calla）被擊敗並殺死，死於瓦伊拉坎查（Huayra-Cancha）首領亞姆基·帕查庫提（Yamqui Pachacuti）之手。

passages.text: The Ynca Yupanqui followed the enemy as far as Andahuayllas; and, on his return to Cuzco, he undertook the conquest of Colla-suyu; and other provinces submitted peaceably. Among them was that of the famous chief Yamqui-Pachacuti, whom the prince thanked for the death of Ynca Urcu, his brother. And the prince took his name and added it to his own, which became Pachacuti Ynca Yupanqui. He conquered all the land of the Colla-suyu, and invaded the provinces of the Chayas and Caravayas, where he destroyed a famous idol.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 印加·尤潘基（Ynca Yupanqui）追擊敵人直至安達瓦伊利亞斯（Andahuayllas）；返回庫斯科後，他著手征服科利亞蘇尤；其他省份也和平歸順。其中便包括那位著名的首領亞姆基·帕查庫提（Yamqui-Pachacuti）的省份，王子因他殺死了自己的兄弟印加·烏爾庫而向他致謝。王子取了他的名字，加在自己的名字之上，於是成為帕查庫提·印加·尤潘基（Pachacuti Ynca Yupanqui）。他征服了科利亞蘇尤全境，並入侵查亞斯（Chayas）與卡拉瓦亞斯（Caravayas）諸省，在那裡摧毀了一尊著名的偶像。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Amaru of Pachatusan: A Half-League Serpent and Comets of Fire
title.zh: 帕查圖桑之阿瑪魯:半萊格巨蛇與火焰彗星

region.en: Mountain of Pachatusan, above Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科上方帕查圖桑山(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: At Puma-cancha, where his eldest legitimate son Amaru Yupanqui was born, news arrived to Pachacuti of a miracle at Cuzco: a yauirca or amaru, a ferocious creature half a league long and two and a half brazas wide, with ears, eye-teeth, and a beard, had come forth from the mountain of Pachatusan and entered the lake of Quichuipay. Then two sacacas (comets) of fire came out of Ausancata, one going towards Arequipa and another towards snowy mountains near Huamanca: they were described as animals with wings, ears, a tail, and four legs, with many spikes on their backs, appearing from a distance to be made of fire. Pachacuti set out for Cuzco, where he found his father very old and infirm.
summary.zh: 帕查庫提留駐普馬-坎恰(長子阿瑪魯·尤潘琪誕生之地)時,得庫斯科神異之報:一條「亞烏爾卡」(阿瑪魯)——兇猛巨獸,長半萊格、寬兩布拉薩半,有耳、有獠牙、有鬚——自帕查圖桑山出,入基丘伊帕湖。又有兩顆火質「薩卡卡斯」(彗星)自奧桑卡塔出,一奔阿雷基帕,一奔瓦曼卡附近雪山;狀如有翼四足之獸,有耳有尾,背生尖刺,遠望如烈火所成。帕查庫提遂啟程回庫斯科,見其父維拉科查已衰老不堪。

sensitivity.note: Omen cycle around Pachacuti's return; the amaru serpent and fire-comets read as dynastic portents.

passages.text: In Puma-cancha his eldest legitimate son was born, named Amaru Yupanqui, and he rested there for some days. Here the news arrived of a miracle at Cuzco. A yauirca or amaru, a ferocious creature, half a league long and two brazas and a half wide, with ears, eye-teeth, and a beard, had come forth from the mountain of Pachatusan, and entered the lake of Quichuipay.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在普馬坎查，他的嫡長子出生了，取名為阿馬魯·尤潘基，他在那裡休養了數日。就在此地，庫斯科傳來一樁奇蹟的消息。一頭亞維爾卡，即阿馬魯，是一種兇猛的生物，長半里格、寬兩布拉薩半，生有耳朵、犬齒與鬍鬚，從帕查圖桑山中竄出，進入了基丘伊派湖。

passages.text: Then two sacacas (comets) of fire came out of Ausancata, and went towards Arequipa; and another went towards some snowy mountains near Huamanca. They were described as animals with wings, ears, a tail, and four legs, with many spikes on their backs; and from a distance they appeared to be made of fire. So Pachacuti Ynca Yupanqui set out for Cuzco, where he found that his father, Uira-ccocha Ynca Yupanqui, was now very old and infirm.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隨後，兩顆火之薩卡卡（彗星）從奧桑卡塔而出，朝阿雷基帕而去；另一顆則朝瓦曼卡附近的幾座雪山而去。牠們被描述為生有翅膀、耳朵、尾巴與四條腿的動物，背上長有許多尖刺；從遠處望去，彷彿是由火構成的。於是帕查庫蒂·印卡·尤潘基啟程前往庫斯科，在那裡發現他的父親維拉科查·印卡·尤潘基如今已年邁體衰。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: White Vicuña Wool and Shorn Women: The Mourning for Viracocha Inca
title.zh: 白駝馬毛與剪髮之婦:維拉科查·印加之喪

region.en: Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: When his father died, the mourning was vicuña wool of a white colour; and the soldiers were ordered to carry the body of the old man, with his arms and insignia, through the city, singing a war-song and bearing their shields and clubs, their llaca-chuquis, chasca-chuquis, suruc-chuquis. The women came forth in another procession, with their hair shorn, and dressed in black, and their faces blackened, flogging themselves with quichuas and coyas, secsec, sihuicas. They say that these women mourned for a whole week, and sought for the body of the dead Ynca.
summary.zh: 其父既歿,舉喪以白色駝馬毛為服;士兵奉命抬老王遺體,攜其兵甲印信,持盾執棍——拉卡-楚基、查斯卡-楚基、蘇魯克-楚基——唱戰歌巡行全城。婦人另成一隊,剪髮縞衣,面塗黑色,以基丘阿與科亞、塞克塞克、西瓜卡斯自笞其身。相傳婦人哀慟整整一週,遍尋先王遺體。

sensitivity.note: Royal mourning description from Salcamayhua's dynastic narrative.

passages.text: When his father died, the mourning was vicuña wool of a white colour; and the soldiers were ordered to carry the body of the old man, with his arms and insignia, through the city, singing a war-song and bearing their shields and clubs, their llaca-chuquis, chasca-chuquis, suruc-chuquis. The women came forth in another procession, with their hair shorn, and dressed in black, and their faces blackened, flogging themselves with quichuas and coyas, secsec, sihuicas. They say that these women mourned for a whole week, and sought for the body of the dead Ynca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的父親去世後，服喪所用的是白色的羊駝毛；士兵們奉命抬著老人的遺體，連同他的武器與徽記，穿行城中，唱著戰歌，手持盾牌與棍棒，以及他們的利亞卡丘基、查斯卡丘基、蘇魯丘基。婦女們則另成一列隊伍前來，剃去頭髮，身著黑衣，面容塗黑，以基丘阿與科亞、塞克塞克、西維卡鞭打自身。據說這些婦女哀悼了整整一週，並尋覓已故印卡的遺體。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Eagle and the Serpent of Canacuay
title.zh: 瓦納庫瓦的鷹蛇之鬥

region.en: Anca-pirca terrace, province of the Caviñas (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 卡維尼亞斯省安卡-皮爾卡階地(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The Capacuyos sent a poor man with hultis (clay pots for llipta), who gave Pachacuti a blow on the head with the intention of killing him. The man was tortured and confessed he was a Caviña of the Quiquijanas sent to kill the Ynca at the request of the Capacuyos, whose Curaca was Apu Calama Yanqui: nearly 20,000 of them, besides women and children, were put to death, for they had tried to murder the Ynca by advice of their huaca Canacuay. Then the Ynca's second son Tupac Ynca Yupanqui was born, and the Ynca undertook the conquest of the Antisuyus with 100,000 men. But the huaca of Canacuay sent forth fire, and stopped the passage with a fierce serpent which destroyed many people. The Ynca raised his eyes to heaven and prayed for help with great sorrow, and a furious eagle descended, and, seizing the head of the serpent, raised it on high and then hurled it to the ground. In memory of this miracle the Ynca ordered a snake to be carved in stone on the wall of a terrace in this province, which was called Anca-pirca.
summary.zh: 卡帕庫約人遣一貧漢,攜裝里普塔的陶罐,乘間重擊帕查庫提頭部,欲殺之。刑訊之下,其人自認乃基基哈納的卡維尼亞人,奉卡帕庫約人之請來刺印加王——其酋為阿普·卡拉馬·揚基。於是卡帕庫約男女老幼近二萬人盡遭處死,因其曾依其瓦卡「瓦納庫瓦」之謀試圖弒王。其後印加次子圖帕克·尤潘琪誕生;印加王率十萬大軍征安蒂蘇尤。然而瓦納庫瓦瓦卡噴出火焰,並遣一條兇蛇堵截隘道,噬殺甚眾。印加王悲慟仰望上天求援,一隻猛鷹撲下,攫住蛇頭,高舉而擲之於地。為誌此神蹟,印加王命人在該省一處階地牆上鑿石為蛇,其地名「安卡-皮爾卡」。

sensitivity.note: Serpent-guardian huaca and eagle miracle; the massacre of the Capacuyos is recorded as given, critically.

passages.text: At that time they say that the Capacuyos sent a poor man with hultis (clay pots in which they keep llipta), who gave Pachacuti Ynca a blow on the head with the intention of killing him. The man was tortured, and confessed that he was a Caviña of the Quiquijanas, and that he had come to kill the Ynca at the request of the Capacuyos. So the Ynca ordered the province of the Caviñas to be laid waste; but they said that the fault was not theirs, but the Capacuyos, whose Curaca was Apu Calama Yanqui, and who numbered near 20,000 men, besides women and children. They were all put to death. They say that they tried to murder the Ynca, by advice of their huaca, Canacuay.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說當時卡帕庫約人派了一個窮人，帶著烏爾蒂（用來盛放利普塔的陶罐），朝帕查庫蒂·印卡的頭部一擊，意圖將他殺死。那人遭到拷問，供認自己是基基哈納人的卡維尼亞，是應卡帕庫約人之請前來殺害印卡的。於是印卡下令將卡維尼亞人的省份夷為廢墟；但他們說錯不在己方，而在卡帕庫約人，其庫拉卡為阿普·卡拉馬·揚基，其男子近兩萬人，尚不包括婦孺。他們全都被處死。據說他們是聽從其瓦卡卡納夸伊的建議，才試圖謀害印卡的。

passages.text: Then the Ynca's second son was born, named Tupac Ynca Yupanqui; and the Ynca undertook the conquest of the Antisuyus with 100,000 men. But the huaca of Canacuay sent forth fire, and stopped the passage with a fierce serpent which destroyed many people. The Ynca raised his eyes to heaven and prayed for help with great sorrow, and a furious eagle descended, and, seizing the head of the serpent, raised it on high and then hurled it to the ground. In memory of this miracle the Ynca ordered a snake to be carved in stone on the wall of a terrace in this province, which was called Anca-pirca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隨後，印卡的次子出生了，取名為圖帕克·印卡·尤潘基；印卡率十萬大軍著手征服安蒂蘇尤人。但卡納夸伊的瓦卡噴出火焰，並以一頭兇猛的巨蛇阻斷了通道，巨蛇毀滅了許多人。印卡舉目望天，滿懷悲傷地祈求援助，於是一隻猛鷹降下，抓住巨蛇的頭，將其高高舉起，然後猛擲於地。為紀念這樁奇蹟，印卡下令在此省的某處梯田牆壁上以石雕出一條蛇，此地因而得名安卡皮爾卡。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Hatupatu Killed by His Brothers and Revived
title.zh: 被兄長所殺的哈圖帕圖

region.en: Bird-snaring camps between Rotorua and Taupo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 羅托魯瓦至陶波之間的獵鳥營地（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 13, Hatupatu and his Brothers (London 1855)

summary.en: Snaring birds in the hill country, Ha-nui, Ha-roa and Karika give their little brother Hatupatu only lean tough birds; he eats and weeps together. He gorges himself on the stored calabashes of preserved birds, fakes a war-party raid - trampled paths, self-inflicted spear-wounds - and is exposed at last, killed by his brothers and buried in the heap of plucked feathers. His parents send the spirit Tamumu-ki-te-rangi, 'He-that-buzzes-in-the-skies', shaped like a flag, who performs enchantments over the grave and brings Hatupatu to life again.
summary.zh: 哈努伊、哈羅亞、卡里卡三兄弟入山獵鳥，只把瘦硬的鳥分給幼弟哈圖帕圖；他含淚進食。他偷吃光窖中整罐整罐的油漬鳥肉，偽造敵襲現場——踩亂小路、自傷數處——終被識破；兄長將他殺死，埋進拔下鳥羽堆成的大堆。父母派形似旗幟的精靈『天際嗡嗡者』塔穆穆基特朗吉尋屍施咒，哈圖帕圖死而復生。

sensitivity.note: Resurrection cluster: revival through a dispatched familiar spirit; interpretive tagging.

passages.text: Ha-nui, Ha-roa, and Hatupatu went to Whakamaru, to Maroa, to Tuata, to Tutuka, to Tuaropaki, to Hauhungaroa, to Hurakia, and to Horohoro - the districts which lie between Lakes Taupo and Rotorua and between Rotorua and the head of the Waikato River - to snare birds, and followed their sport for many a day. But their little brother Hatupatu was all this time thinking that they never gave him any of the rare dainties, but at each meal he received nothing but the lean tough birds; so when the poor little fellow sat down by the fire to his food he kept on crying and eating, crying and eating, during his meals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 13 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 哈努伊、哈羅阿與哈圖帕圖前往瓦卡馬魯、馬羅阿、圖阿塔、圖圖卡、圖阿羅帕基、豪洪加羅阿、胡拉基亞與霍羅霍羅——即位於陶波湖與羅托魯瓦湖之間，以及羅托魯瓦與懷卡托河源頭之間的地區——去設陷阱捕鳥，如此行獵多日。然而他們的小弟哈圖帕圖一直心想，他們從不給他任何珍饈美味，每餐他只得到又瘦又韌的鳥；於是這可憐的小傢伙坐在火邊進食時，一邊哭一邊吃，一邊哭一邊吃，整頓飯皆是如此。
