passages.text: One day, whilst his brothers were out snaring birds and he was left to take care of the resting-place, the little rogue crept into the storehouse where the birds preserved in their own fat were kept in calabashes, and stole some and set resolutely to work to eat them with nicely beaten fern-root for a relish; so that to look at him you could not help thinking of the proverb, 'Bravo, that throat of yours can swallow anything.' He finished all the calabashes of preserved birds, attacked those kept in casks, then crept out and trampled over the pathway in all directions that his brothers might think a war party had come and eaten the food in their absence; then he ran a spear into himself in two or three places where he could not do himself much harm, gave himself a good bruise or two on the head, and lay down near the hut.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 13 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，他的兄弟們外出用套索捕鳥，留他一人看守住處；這個小無賴便悄悄溜進儲藏室，那裡存放著用葫蘆裝、浸在自身油脂中保存的鳥肉。他偷了一些，又拿搗得細碎的蕨根作配料，下定決心大吃起來；所以看著他那副模樣，你不由得想起那句諺語：『好哇，你那個喉嚨什麼都吞得下。』他吃光了所有裝著醃鳥的葫蘆，又向那些裝在木桶裡的醃鳥下手，然後悄悄爬出來，在小徑上四處亂踩，好讓兄弟們以為是一隊戰士來過，趁他們不在時吃掉了食物；接著他又把長矛往自己身上兩三處傷不著要害的地方刺去，在頭上撞出一兩塊瘀傷，然後躺在小屋旁邊。

passages.text: When his brothers came back they found him lying there in appearance very badly wounded, and the preserved birds all gone; he said a war party had done it, and they saw the footmarks and believed it. They melted fat and poured warm oil on his wounds, and he revived. Next day he stole again, every day, until at last his brothers laid in wait for him: 'Ha, ha, we've caught you now; your thievish tricks are found out, you little rogue?' His brothers killed him at once and buried him in the large heap of feathers pulled out from the snared birds. When they returned to Rotorua their parents insisted they must have killed him, for he went away with them and was missing on their return. At length Hatupatu's father and mother sent a spirit to search for him; its form was that of a flag, and its name was Tamumu-ki-te-rangi, He-that-buzzes-in-the-skies. It arrived at the place where Hatupatu was buried, found him, performed enchantments, and Hatupatu came to life again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 13 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兄弟們回來時，見他躺在那裡，看上去傷勢極重，而醃鳥全都不見了；他說是一隊戰士幹的，他們看到那些腳印，便信以為真。他們融化油脂，把溫熱的油澆在他的傷口上，他便甦醒過來。第二天他又偷，天天如此，直到最後兄弟們埋伏起來等他：『哈哈，這回可逮住你了；你那偷雞摸狗的勾當被識破了，你這個小無賴？』兄弟們當即把他殺死，埋進從套住的鳥身上拔下的一大堆羽毛裡。他們回到羅托魯瓦時，父母堅稱他們一定把他殺了，因為他是跟他們一起走的，回來時卻不見了。最後，哈圖帕圖的父母派了一個精靈去尋找他；那精靈的形貌是一面旗，名字叫塔穆穆-基-特-朗吉，意為「在天空中嗡嗡作響者」。它來到哈圖帕圖被埋葬的地方，找到了他，施行法術，哈圖帕圖便又活了過來。

title.en: Hatupatu and the Bird-Woman Kurangaituku
title.zh: 哈圖帕圖與鳥女庫蘭蓋圖庫

region.en: Whakarewarewa sulphur springs, Rotorua, Aotearoa
region.zh: 紐西蘭羅托魯瓦瓦卡雷瓦雷瓦硫磺泉

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 13, Hatupatu and his Brothers (London 1855)

summary.en: Revived, Hatupatu meets a woman spearing birds with her lips; she has wings on her arms and carries him to her cave, where she eats only raw food. When he tricks her into hunting a thousand mountain ranges away, he roasts birds, kills her tame lizards and pets, and escapes with her cloaks and carved sword. Guided by the one surviving bird, Kurangaituku strides home in three steps, calling 'There you are, O Hatupatu, not far from me'; the fleeing youth charms rocks open and shut behind him until, leaping the boiling sulphur springs of Whakarewarewa, he watches her wade in and sink through the crust, burnt to death.
summary.zh: 復活的哈圖帕圖遭遇以唇為矛、臂生雙翼的鳥女庫蘭蓋圖庫，被帶回石穴；她食生冷，他假意進食。他誆她遠赴千山之外獵鳥，趁機烤鳥飽食，殺其馴蜥寵鳥，攜紅羽披風、狗皮斗篷與雕柄寶劍而逃。唯一的倖存小鳥飛報主人；鳥女三步即回，一路喊著『哈圖帕圖，你就在前面不遠』追趕。他念咒令岩石開合相阻，直到跳過瓦卡雷瓦雷瓦滾燙的硫磺泉；鳥女誤以為泉水冰冷涉水而過，陷入泉底被活活燙死。

sensitivity.note: Sacred-landscape record: explains the boiling springs and place-names of the Rotorua geothermal field; bird-woman as ogre.

passages.text: Hatupatu came to life again, and went upon his way, and met a woman who was spearing birds for herself, and her spear was nothing but her own lips: Hatupatu had a real wooden spear. The woman speared at a bird with her lips, but Hatupatu at the same moment threw his spear at the same bird, and it stuck into her lips; when he saw this he ran off with all his speed, but he was soon caught by the woman, not being able to go so fast as she could, for her feet bore her along, and wings were upon her arms like those of a bird, and she brought him to her house, and they slept there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 13 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 哈圖帕圖又活了過來，繼續趕路，遇見一個正在為自己叉鳥的女人，她的矛不是別的，正是她自己的嘴唇；哈圖帕圖卻有一支真正的木矛。那女人用嘴唇向一隻鳥叉去，但哈圖帕圖同時也把自己的矛擲向同一隻鳥，矛扎進了她的嘴唇；他見狀便拼命飛奔而逃，但很快就被那女人追上，因為他跑不過她，她的雙腳載著她疾行，手臂上還長著像鳥一樣的翅膀。她把他帶回自己的住處，他們就在那裡睡了。

passages.text: Hatupatu found that this woman never ate anything but raw food, and she gave him birds to eat without their being dressed; but he only pretended to eat them, lifting them to his mouth and letting them fall slyly. He remained at home while she went out spearing, cooking food for himself and looking at all the things in the cave of rocks she lived in - her two-handed wooden sword, her beautiful cloak of red feathers torn from under the wing of the kaka, her red cloak of thick dog's fur, her ornamented cloak of flax, her tame lizards and tame little birds - and he kept thinking how he could run off with them all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 13 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 哈圖帕圖發現這女人只吃生食，她給他吃的鳥都不經烹調；但他只是假裝吃，把鳥舉到嘴邊又偷偷讓它掉下去。她外出叉鳥時，他就留在家裡，為自己煮食，並察看這座她所居住的岩洞裡的種種東西——她那把雙手握的木劍、她那件從卡卡鸚鵡翼下拔下的紅羽製成的美麗斗篷、她那件厚實狗皮製成的紅斗篷、她那件飾有花紋的亞麻斗篷、她那些馴養的蜥蜴和馴養的小鳥——他一直在盤算怎樣才能把這些東西全都席捲而逃。

passages.text: At last one day he told her to go a long distance to-day: to the first mountain range, to the second, the tenth, the hundredth, the thousandth range, and there begin to catch birds for them two. She consented and went; he remained roasting birds for himself, gathered up her cloaks and carved sword, brandished it and cut at the lizards and tame animals, killing them, and killed the perch of pet birds - all but one, which flew away to fetch back the woman, Kurangaituku, singing as it went, 'Oh, Kurangaituku, our home is ruined, our things are all destroyed.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 13 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 終於有一天，他叫她今天去很遠的地方：去第一道山脈，去第二道、第十道、第一百道、第一千道山脈，並在那裡開始為他們兩人捕鳥。她答應了便去了；他留下來為自己烤鳥，收拾起她的斗篷和雕花木劍，揮舞著它砍向那些蜥蜴和馴養的動物，把它們殺死，又殺死了那些當寵物養的棲鳥——只除了一隻，那隻鳥飛走去召回那女人庫朗蓋圖庫，一邊飛一邊唱：『哦，庫朗蓋圖庫，我們的家毀了，我們的東西全被毀了。』

passages.text: Kurangaituku made haste to get home, and as she went along kept calling out, 'Step out, stretch along; step out, stretch along. There you are, O Hatupatu, not far from me. Step out, stretch along. There you are, O Hatupatu, not far from me now.' She only made three strides before she had reached her cave, and could see nothing in it; but the little bird still guided her on, crying, 'I'll catch you there now, Hatupatu' - and she almost caught him, and he thought, I'm done for now. So he repeated his charm: 'O rock, open for me, open.' Then the rock opened and he hid himself in it, and the woman could not find him. Thus they went on the whole way, until they came to Rotorua; and when they arrived at the sulphur-springs called Te Whaka-rewa-rewa, Hatupatu jumped over these; but Kurangaituku, thinking they were cold, tried to wade through, sunk through the crust, and was burnt to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 13 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 庫朗蓋圖庫急忙趕回家，一路上不斷高喊：『邁步吧，伸展吧；邁步吧，伸展吧。你在那兒呢，哦哈圖帕圖，離我不遠了。邁步吧，伸展吧。你在那兒呢，哦哈圖帕圖，現在離我不遠了。』她只邁了三步就到了自己的岩洞，卻見洞裡空空如也；但那隻小鳥仍引著她往前，叫道：『這回我要在那兒抓住你，哈圖帕圖』——她幾乎抓住了他，他心想，這回我完了。於是他念起自己的咒語：『哦岩石，為我打開吧，打開吧。』岩石便裂開了，他藏身其中，那女人找不到他。他們就這樣一路追趕，直到來到羅托魯瓦；當他們到達那處名叫特·瓦卡-雷瓦-雷瓦的硫磺泉時，哈圖帕圖跳過了這些泉；而庫朗蓋圖庫以為泉水是涼的，想蹚水過去，卻陷穿了泉面的硬殼，被燒死了。

title.en: Hatupatu's Grass-Clump Army Takes Raumati's Head
title.zh: 草人疑陣取勞馬蒂首級

region.en: Maketu pa, Bay of Plenty, Aotearoa
region.zh: 紐西蘭豐盛灣馬凱圖寨堡

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 13, Hatupatu and his Brothers (London 1855)

summary.en: Denied a command because of his brothers' jealousy, Hatupatu ties creeping-plant roots into bundles, dresses them in cloaks, and marches at dawn against Raumati, who burned the ancestral canoe Arawa. The enemy dreads the 'multitude of chiefs' in superb feathered dresses; the brothers' three real divisions break and fly, the mock army charges, and Hatupatu fells the chief Karika, takes his head, and slips away with Raumati's. Returning to Rotorua he chants over a basket of heads, reveals the hidden head of Raumati, and his father promotes his last-born above his eldest sons.
summary.zh: 因兄弟妒忌而被剝奪兵權的哈圖帕圖，夜裡把蔓草根莖捆成束、裹上披風，裝扮成一支雄師。破曉出戰：敵人畏懼他那『眾酋雲集、羽飾華麗』的假軍團；兄長三個真實方陣卻接連潰敗，唯有草人大陣沉然不動。哈圖帕圖擊斃敵酋卡里卡，割其首級，又暗中取走燒毀祖先之舟阿拉瓦號的仇人勞馬蒂的首級。歸舟唱勝，父親岸上發問誰得勞馬蒂之頭——三兄皆稱有，父親長嘆；哈圖帕圖自筐中高舉其頭，舉族歡騰，幼子由此凌駕長兄之上。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection; revenge for the burning of Te Arawa closes the canoe-cycle feud.

passages.text: His three brothers sprang at him, three wooden swords levelled at Hatupatu to slay him; he held the blade of his sword pointed to the ground till the swords of his brothers almost touched him, then rapidly warded off the blows, and whirling round his wooden sword, two of the three were felled by the blade of it and one by a blow from the handle; they sprang up and rushed at him once more, and over they went again - it was enough, they gave in. Their father said, 'Oh my sons, I would that you were as strong in peace as you are in attacking one another; in seeking revenge for your ancestral canoe, Te Arawa, which was consumed in a fire by the chief Raumati. Long have you sought revenge upon him, but gained no advantage; perhaps you are only strong and bold when you attack your young brother, my last-born child.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 13 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的三個兄弟向他撲來，三把木劍平舉，直指哈圖帕圖，要將他殺死；他將自己劍的刃尖朝下指地，直到兄弟們的劍幾乎觸及他，這才迅速格開那些劈砍，並旋轉他的木劍，三人之中有兩人被劍刃擊倒，一人被劍柄擊倒；他們跳起身來，再次向他衝去，卻又再次倒下——這就夠了，他們認輸了。他們的父親說：『唉，我的兒子們，我但願你們在和平之時也如彼此攻擊時這般強壯；但願你們去為你們祖傳的獨木舟「特阿拉瓦」復仇，它曾被首領勞馬蒂燒毀於火中。你們尋求向他復仇已久，卻未得任何優勢；也許你們只有在攻擊你們年幼的弟弟、我最後所生的孩子時，才顯得強壯勇敢。』

passages.text: Three hundred and forty warriors were told off for each of the divisions under the command of each of Hatupatu's three brothers, but no division was placed under his command. He said, 'Oh my brothers, I did not refuse to hearken to you when you asked me to come with you; I came as you requested, just as I went readily with you upon that occasion when you killed me; I pray you, let some of the warriors be placed under my command, let there be fifty of them.' But they said, 'Pooh, pooh; come now, be off home again. What can you do? The only thing you are fit to destroy is food.' He said no more, but left his brothers, and on the same night sought out a rough thicket, turned to and began to tie together in bundles the roots of creeping plants and bushes, and dressed them up with the cloaks he had with him; the war band of these figures looked just like a band of real warriors.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 13 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 哈圖帕圖的三個兄弟各率一支隊伍，每支隊伍分派了三百四十名戰士，卻沒有任何一支隊伍歸他統領。他說：『唉，我的兄弟們，當你們要我隨你們同去時，我並未拒絕聽從你們；我如你們所請而來，正如那一次你們殺我時，我也曾欣然隨你們同去；我懇求你們，讓一些戰士歸我統領，讓其中有五十人吧。』但他們說：『呸，呸；來吧，現在回家去吧。你能做什麼？你唯一適合毀掉的東西就是食物。』他不再多言，離開了他的兄弟們，當夜便尋得一處雜亂的灌木叢，動手將蔓生植物與灌木的根綑綁成束，並用他隨身所帶的斗篷將它們裝扮起來；這些假人所組成的戰隊，看上去就與一隊真正的戰士一模一樣。

passages.text: The day had hardly dawned when the inhabitants sent off messengers that they should come and fight with them against the common enemy. All the warriors of the columns of Hatupatu's brothers were exhorting their men; when they had all ended, Hatupatu himself got up to encourage his mock party, and as he gracefully arose it was beautiful to see his plumes and ornaments fluttering in the breeze; he made speech after speech, each time changing his dress and the knots of his hair - now a cloak of red feathers, now a bordered flax cloak, now dog-skins with the long war-axe, now the whalebone mere - so that the enemy, seeing how numerous were the chiefs in his column and what clothes and weapons they had, dreaded his division much more than those of his brothers; yet it was only formed of clumps of grass dressed up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 13 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天幾乎還未破曉，居民們便派出使者，要他們前來與自己一同對抗共同的敵人。哈圖帕圖兄弟各縱隊的戰士都在激勵他們的部眾；當他們全都講完之後，哈圖帕圖本人起身鼓舞他那支假扮的隊伍，當他優雅地站起時，只見他的羽飾與飾物在微風中飄動，煞是好看；他一次又一次地發表演說，每次都更換他的衣著與髮髻——時而是一件紅羽斗篷，時而是一件鑲邊的亞麻斗篷，時而是配著長戰斧的狗皮衣，時而是鯨骨短棍——以致敵人見他縱隊中的首領如此眾多、衣著與武器如此精良，對他那支隊伍的畏懼遠勝於對他兄弟們的隊伍；然而那不過是由一叢叢裝扮起來的草束所組成。

passages.text: Now the people drew out to the battle, and pressed nearer, sending volleys of manuka spears at the column of Ha-nui; it is broken, they fly, they fall back on the division of Ha-roa, are rallied, but only poke forward their heads; the enemy is on them again; they run in upon the third line, that of Karika, and all the divisions of Hatupatu's brothers are broken and flying in confusion - what did it matter whether they were many or few, they were all cowards. All this time the division of Hatupatu appears sitting quietly upon the ground; when the men in full retreat came running in upon it, Hatupatu rose up crying 'Turn on them again, turn on them again!' At last they saw him; then rushes forward Hatupatu from one party and a chief of the enemy, named also Karika, from the other. The chief aims a fierce blow with a short spear; Hatupatu parries it, strikes him down with his two-handed sword, and motionless as food hidden in a bag, draws forth his whalebone mere, cuts off Karika's head, and grasps it by the hair. It is enough - the enemy break, fall back, fly; then his brothers and their warriors turn again on the foes and slay many thousands of them. Whilst his brothers are slaying the enemy, he eagerly seeks for Raumati; he is found; Hatupatu catches him, his head is cut off, and concealed. They return to Rotorua; his brothers in the canoe chant songs of triumph, and their father inquires from the shore which of them has the head of Raumati; one holding up the head he had taken said 'I have', and another 'I have', until their father calls out, 'Alas, alas! Raumati has escaped.' Then Hatupatu stands up in the canoe, chants a prayer to the god of war over a basket heaped with heads, grasps the head of Raumati which he had kept hid under his cloak, and cries, 'There, there; I have the head of Raumati.' All rejoice; their father strips off his cloak, rushes into the lake, and repeats a thanksgiving to the gods. When he had ended this, he promoted in honour his last-born child and debased in rank his eldest sons. Thus at last was revenge obtained for the burning of the Arawa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 13 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此時人們列隊出戰，越逼越近，向哈努伊的縱隊投擲一陣陣麥盧卡木矛；縱隊被擊潰了，他們逃竄，退回到哈羅阿的隊伍，重新集結，卻只是探頭探腦；敵人又撲了上來；他們又逃竄，衝向第三道防線，即卡里卡的隊伍，於是哈圖帕圖兄弟們的所有隊伍都被擊潰，混亂奔逃——他們是多是少又有何妨，他們全都是懦夫。這整段時間裡，哈圖帕圖的隊伍看似安靜地坐在地上；當全面撤退的人們奔逃到它跟前時，哈圖帕圖起身喊道：『再向他們反擊，再向他們反擊！』終於他們看見了他；於是哈圖帕圖從一方衝上前去，敵方一位同樣名叫卡里卡的首領從另一方衝上前來。那首領用短矛奮力一擊；哈圖帕圖格開它，用雙手劍將他擊倒，並如藏在袋中的食物般一動不動，抽出他的鯨骨短棍，砍下卡里卡的頭，抓住它的頭髮。這就夠了——敵人潰散、後退、奔逃；於是他的兄弟們與他們的戰士再度轉身攻擊敵人，殺死了他們數以千計的人。當他的兄弟們誅殺敵人時，他急切地尋找勞馬蒂；他被找到了；哈圖帕圖抓住他，砍下他的頭，並將其藏起。他們返回羅托魯瓦；他的兄弟們在獨木舟上唱著凱歌，他們的父親從岸上詢問他們之中誰拿到了勞馬蒂的頭；一人舉起他所取的頭說『我拿到了』，另一人也說『我拿到了』，直到他們的父親喊道：『唉，唉！勞馬蒂逃掉了。』於是哈圖帕圖在獨木舟中站起，對著一隻堆滿頭顱的籃子向戰神吟誦祈禱，抓住他一直藏在斗篷下的勞馬蒂的頭，喊道：『那兒，那兒；我拿到了勞馬蒂的頭。』眾人皆歡欣；他們的父親脫下斗篷，衝入湖中，向眾神重複一段感恩之辭。當他說完這些之後，他提升了他最後所生孩子的榮位，並貶抑了他長子們的位階。於是，為阿拉瓦被焚一事，復仇終於得償。

title.en: The Calling of the Varangians: 'Our Land Is Great and Rich, but There Is No Order'
title.zh: 瓦良格人之召請：『我土廣而富，獨無秩序』

region.en: Novgorod (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 諾夫哥羅德（象徵性定位）

period: Event dated 862; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text, trans. S. H. Cross and O. P. Sherbowitz-Wetzor (1930), s.a. 862

summary.en: The founding scene of Russian history: after expelling the Varangians who taxed them, the tribes fall to feuding; they send over the sea to the Rus, saying 'Our land is great and rich, but there is no order in it. Come to rule and reign over us' — and three brothers answer.
summary.zh: 俄羅斯史之開篇：驅走徵貢之瓦良格人後，諸部內亂不已；遂遣使渡海赴羅斯，曰『我土廣而富，獨無秩序。請來君臨而治之』——兄弟三人應召而至。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle founding legend; contested by modern historians (Normanist debate) — flagged in note.

passages.text: The tributaries of the Varangians drove them back beyond the sea and, refusing them further tribute, set out to govern themselves. There was no law among them, but tribe rose against tribe: quarrelling among themselves, they began to war one with another. They said to themselves, 'Let us seek a prince who may rule over us and judge according to the Law.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 862 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 瓦良格人的納貢者將他們趕回海的對岸，拒絕再向他們納貢，並著手自行治理。他們之中沒有法律，而是部族起來對抗部族：彼此爭吵，他們開始互相征戰。他們對自己說：『讓我們去尋一位王公，好讓他統治我們，並依照律法審判。』

passages.text: They accordingly went overseas to the Varangian Rus: these particular Varangians were known as Rus, as some are known as Swedes and others as Norwegians. The Chuds, the Slavs, the Krivichians, and the Ves then said to the people of Rus, 'Our land is great and rich, but there is no order in it. Come to rule and reign over us.' Thus three brothers, with their kinfolk, took with them all the Rus and came — and the eldest, Rurik, settled in Novgorod: the city that would name the dynasty of Russia for seven hundred years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 862 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他們渡海前往瓦良格羅斯人那裡：這些特定的瓦良格人被稱為羅斯，正如有些人被稱為瑞典人，另一些人被稱為挪威人。楚德人、斯拉夫人、克里維奇人和維斯人於是對羅斯人說：『我們的土地廣大而富饒，但其中沒有秩序。來統治我們、君臨我們吧。』於是三兄弟帶著他們的親族，攜同所有羅斯人前來——其中最年長的留里克定居於諾夫哥羅德：這座城市將為俄羅斯王朝命名達七百年之久。

title.en: Oleg and the Death of His Horse: The Skull of the Serpent
title.zh: 奧列格與愛馬之死：馬頭骨下之蛇

region.en: Kiev, mound by the Dnieper (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基輔第聶伯河畔古塚（象徵性定位）

period: Event dated 912; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 912

summary.en: Magi foretold Prince Oleg that the horse he rode would be his death; he had it kept and fed, never to be mounted, and five years later, the horse dead and its bones white, he laughed at the prophecy over the skull — and the serpent that glided from it stung his foot, fulfilling the word of the wise men.
summary.zh: 巫師預言奧列格王公：其坐騎將致其死；遂令人飼馬而不乘。五年後馬死骨白，王公臨馬頭骨笑其妄——骨中滑出之蛇嚙其足，巫言乃驗。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle legend; parallel to the death-foretelling horse of many traditions.

passages.text: Prince Oleg asked his wise men and magi what his death would be, and they answered that the horse he loved and rode would be the cause of his death. He took thought then, and commanded that the horse should not be brought before him again; he ordered it kept and fed apart, never to be mounted, and after some years had it led away. He wept for the beast he had ridden so long, and rebuked the magi, saying their words were false.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 912 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧列格親王問他的智者與術士，自己的死將從何而來，他們回答說，他所鍾愛、常騎的那匹馬將是他死的原因。他於是思量，下令那匹馬不得再帶到他面前；他命人將牠另行飼養，永不騎乘，數年之後又命人把牠牽走。他為這匹長久相伴的坐騎哭泣，並責備術士，說他們的話是虛假的。

passages.text: Five years after the death of his horse Oleg asked where its bones were, and learning they were still on the spot, he laughed at the prophecy: 'Are these my death?' He set his foot upon the skull; but a serpent glided out from it and stung him in the foot, so that he sickened and died — and all the people mourned him greatly. His tomb remains by legend to this day, and it is known as Oleg's Grave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 912 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的馬死後五年，奧列格問起牠的骨骸何在，得知仍留在原處，便譏笑那預言說：「這就是我的死嗎？」他將腳踏在頭骨上；卻有一條蛇從中滑出，咬了他的腳，於是他病倒而死——眾人皆為他哀悼甚深。據傳說，他的墳墓至今仍在，被稱為奧列格之墓。

title.en: The Death of Igor: A Prince Greedy for Tribute
title.zh: 伊戈爾之死：貢斂過甚之王公

region.en: Iskorosten, land of the Drevlians (symbolic pin at Korosten)
region.zh: 德列夫利安人之伊斯科羅斯堅（象徵性定位於科羅斯堅）

period: Event dated 945; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 945

summary.en: After collecting the tribute, Igor went back for more; the Drevlians said 'If a wolf comes among the sheep, he will carry off the whole flock' — and rising against the prince who returned with a small escort, they killed him and buried him beneath a felled tree.
summary.zh: 伊戈爾收貢之後復往求貢；德列夫利人云『狼入羊群，則盡驅其群』——遂起而殺此僅率少從復來之王公，斬樹覆其尸而葬之。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle narrative; the wolf-proverb became a Russian byword for predatory rule.

passages.text: After his campaign Igor had gone about the land of the Drevlians collecting tribute, and had added it to the former exactions. Returning to Kiev he sent to the people of Iskorosten, demanding a further tribute. On the advice of his retinue — Sweneld's men, who had gathered much wealth — Igor himself went back for more, with a small company, coveting the great sum.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 945 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊戈爾出征之後，曾巡行德列夫利安人的土地徵收貢賦，並將其加在原先的索求之上。他回到基輔後，又派人前往伊斯科羅斯堅的人那裏，要求再納貢賦。在親兵的建議下——那是斯韋內爾德的人，已聚斂了大量財富——伊戈爾親自帶著少數隨從折返索取更多，貪圖那筆巨款。

passages.text: The Drevlians, hearing of his approach, took counsel with their prince Mal: 'If a wolf comes among the sheep, he will carry off the whole flock, unless he be killed; so will it be with us, if we do not slay Igor — he will destroy us all.' Taking weapons they went forth against Igor and his few followers and killed him; the chronicle says they buried him beneath a felled tree. So died the prince whose oath on Perun's hill the year before had sworn his descendants into slavery if they broke faith.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 945 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 德列夫利安人聽聞他前來，便與他們的王公馬爾商議：「若有一隻狼進入羊群，牠必將整群羊叼走，除非牠被殺死；我們若不殺伊戈爾，也必如此——他會毀了我們所有人。」他們拿起武器，前去迎擊伊戈爾及其少數隨從，將他殺死；編年史記載，他們把他埋在一棵砍倒的樹下。這位親王就這樣死了——他前一年在佩倫的山丘上立誓，若他的後人背信，便將他們淪為奴隸。

title.en: Olga's First Revenge: The Envoy in the Boat-Pit
title.zh: 奧爾加的第一復仇：舟坑葬使

region.en: Kiev and the Drevlian land (symbolic pin at Korosten)
region.zh: 基輔與德列夫利安之地（象徵性定位於科羅斯堅）

period: Event dated 945-946; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 945

summary.en: When the Drevlians proposed that Olga marry their prince Mal, she had their first embassy carried in state — then tipped into a trench and buried alive; to their second she offered a bath of honour, and locked the door.
summary.zh: 德列夫利人提議奧爾加嫁其王公馬爾；她先禮遇第一批使節——隨即掀翻獨木舟、活埋於坑；再請第二批入浴室沐浴榮寵——而閉其門。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle legend; Olga's fourfold revenge became a classic of Russian storytelling and Orthodox sainthood.

passages.text: When the Drevlians heard that Igor was dead they sent twenty of their best men to Olga, proposing that she take their prince Mal for her husband. Olga answered graciously that her husband's death was a thing she could not forget, but that on the morrow she would do them honour before her people. She bade a great boat be brought, and the Drevlians sat in it, proudly, clad in their finest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 945 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 德列夫利安人聽聞伊戈爾已死，便派了二十名最傑出的人去見奧爾加，提議她嫁給他們的王公馬爾。奧爾加和顏悅色地回答說，丈夫之死是她無法忘懷的事，但明日她將在她的子民面前給予他們禮遇。她命人備好一艘大船，德列夫利安人便坐在船中，身著華服，神態傲然。

passages.text: Then Olga commanded a deep pit to be dug in the courtyard. The boat with the envoys was carried out, cast into the trench with the men still sitting in their splendour; and bending over them she asked: 'Is it to your taste?' — and ordered them buried alive. So the first embassy of the Drevlians went the way they had prepared for others.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 945 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著，奧爾加下令在庭院中挖一個深坑。載著使節的船被抬出，連同仍端坐其中、盛裝華麗的眾人一同拋入坑中；她俯身問他們：「這可合你們的意嗎？」——並下令將他們活埋。德列夫利安人的第一批使節，就這樣走上了他們為別人預備的道路。

title.en: Olga's Second Revenge: The Bath of Honour
title.zh: 奧爾加的第二復仇：榮寵之浴

region.en: Kiev (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基輔（象徵性定位）

period: Event dated 945-946; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 945

summary.en: The Drevlians sent their best men for a second wooing; Olga offered them the honour of a bath before an audience with the Princess — and the bathhouse door was barred behind them, the fire kindled beneath, so that all were steamed to death.
summary.zh: 德列夫利人再遣其最優之使求婚；奧爾加許以入浴之榮——浴堂之門閉而火起於下，眾使盡斃於蒸氣之中。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle legend.

passages.text: Olga then sent to the Drevlians: 'If you ask me in truth, send your best men to my city, that I may go to your prince with great honour.' The Drevlians chose their most distinguished men and sent them. On their arrival Olga offered water for the bath, saying: 'Wash yourselves and appear before me.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 945 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧莉加隨後派人去見德列夫利安人說：「你們若真心向我求問，就派你們最優秀的人到我的城裡來，好讓我帶著極大的榮耀去見你們的王子。」德列夫利安人挑選了他們最顯貴的人派去。他們到達後，奧莉加預備了沐浴用水，說：「你們洗淨身子，再來見我。」

passages.text: The bathhouse was heated, and the Drevlians entered in to wash; Olga ordered the door secured behind them and fire set to it from the windows, so that all were burned to death together. Then she sent a message to Iskorosten: 'I have received your first envoys, and now prepare a great feast for your best men, that I may mourn over the grave of my husband and hold a funeral feast for him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 945 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 浴堂燒熱了，德列夫利安人進去沐浴；奧莉加下令把門從外面閂上，並從窗戶點火，於是眾人一同被燒死。隨後她傳信到伊斯科羅斯堅說：「我已接納了你們的第一批使者，如今為你們最優秀的人預備一場盛大的宴席，好讓我在我丈夫的墳前哀悼，為他舉行喪宴。」

title.en: Olga's Third Revenge: The Funeral Feast of Iskorosten
title.zh: 奧爾加的第三復仇：伊斯科羅斯堅之喪宴

region.en: Grave of Igor at Iskorosten (symbolic pin at Korosten)
region.zh: 伊斯科羅斯堅伊戈爾之墓（象徵性定位於科羅斯堅）

period: Event dated 946; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 945

summary.en: At Igor's grave mound Olga bade the Drevlians drink to the stricken prince; when they were drunk she asked her followers to fall upon them — and five thousand died in the single night, so that she went home to raise an army against the rest.
summary.zh: 於伊戈爾塚前，奧爾加命德列夫利人為其『苦主』王公飲酒；眾醉之際，她命扈從掩殺——一夜之間五千人殞命；歸而點兵，以討其餘。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle legend.

passages.text: Olga went with a small retinue to the grave of Igor at Iskorosten and wept over her husband. Then she commanded her followers to pile a great mound, and when it was done ordered a funeral feast. When the Drevlians had drunk heavily she said to her followers, 'Now fall upon them' — and they cut down the Drevlians, and about five thousand of them perished.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 945 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧莉加帶著少數隨從前往伊斯科羅斯堅伊戈爾的墳前，為丈夫哭泣。隨後她命隨從堆起一座大墳丘，墳丘堆成後，便下令舉行喪宴。德列夫利安人痛飲之後，她對隨從說：「現在撲向他們」——他們便砍殺德列夫利安人，約有五千人喪命。

passages.text: Olga returned to Kiev and mustered an army against the remnant; the next year she marched with her son Svyatoslav into the Drevlian land. The city held against her the first summer; then, by her devices, the city was taken and burned — the fourth and greatest of her revenges, which the chronicle tells next with the pigeons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 945 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧莉加回到基輔，召集軍隊討伐殘餘之眾；次年她與兒子斯維亞托斯拉夫進軍德列夫利安人的土地。第一個夏天，城抵禦住了她；後來，憑她的計謀，城被攻下並焚毀——這是她第四次、也是最大的一次復仇，編年史接著以鴿子之事記述。

title.en: Olga's Fourth Revenge: Doves and Sparrows with Burning Tow
title.zh: 奧爾加的第四復仇：縛炬之鴿雀

region.en: Iskorosten, Drevlian land (symbolic pin at Korosten)
region.zh: 德列夫利安之伊斯科羅斯堅（象徵性定位於科羅斯堅）

period: Event dated 946; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 946

summary.en: The city offered three pigeons and three sparrows from every house as tribute; Olga bade each bird carry a burning match tied behind — and when they flew home to their nests, no house remained standing in the city that had killed her husband.
summary.zh: 城中按戶獻鴿雀各三隻為貢；奧爾加命每鳥縛燃火細芒於其後——鳥各飛歸其巢，殺其夫之城遂無一屋立於火後。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle legend; the trick is paralleled in Chinese, Norse, and Indian siege tales.

passages.text: Iskorosten stood firm behind its walls, and Olga encamped before the city the whole summer. Then she sent this message: 'What do you want of me? I have taken vengeance on your princes and your city — I do not desire tribute to levy it again; I asked it once. Pay me the tribute, and I will depart.' The Drevlians asked what she wanted, and Olga answered, 'Give me three pigeons and three sparrows from each house.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 946 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊斯科羅斯堅憑藉城牆堅守，奧莉加在城前紮營整整一夏。隨後她傳去這樣的話：「你們要我怎樣？我已向你們的諸王和你們的城復了仇——我不再想要徵收貢賦；我只索求過一次。把貢賦付給我，我便離去。」德列夫利安人問她要什麼，奧莉加回答：「每戶給我三隻鴿子和三隻麻雀。」

passages.text: The citizens rejoiced and gathered the birds. Olga gave her soldiers a command, saying to each: 'Tie a match to each pigeon and sparrow, with a small piece of cloth wrapped in sulphur and bound with thread.' When darkness fell she released the birds, and each flew to its own nest — to the pigeon-coops, the pigeon-perches, and the eaves — and so the dove-cotes, the roofs, the porches, and the hayricks caught fire, and there was not a house that was not consumed, so that all fled in flight from the city. The people who escaped were taken prisoner, the city burned, the first citizens slain, others made to pay tribute.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 946 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 居民歡喜，收集了鳥兒。奧莉加向士兵下令，對每人說：「給每隻鴿子和麻雀綁上一段火絨，用一小塊裹了硫磺的布，以線紮緊。」天黑之後，她放出鳥兒，每隻都飛回自己的巢——飛向鴿舍、鴿架和屋簷——於是鴿舍、屋頂、門廊和草堆都著了火，沒有一座房屋不被燒毀，眾人全都逃出城去。逃出的人被俘，城被焚毀，首要的居民被殺，其餘的被迫繳納貢賦。

title.en: Olga in Constantinople: Baptism and the Wily Emperor
title.zh: 奧爾加在君士坦丁堡：受洗與狡黠皇帝

region.en: Constantinople, Hagia Sophia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 君士坦丁堡聖索菲亞（象徵性定位）

period: Event dated 955 (or 957); recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 955

summary.en: Olga, regent of Russia, journeyed to Constantinople and was baptized Helena by the Patriarch; the Emperor Constantine, delighted by her beauty and wisdom, offered to make her his daughter — and she answered that she was his goddaughter and could not marry her own godfather, so he laughed and sent her home with gifts.
summary.zh: 俄羅斯攝政奧爾加赴君士坦丁堡，受洗名海倫娜；康斯坦丁帝慕其美貌才智，欲娶之為后——她答：我是您的教女，教父怎能娶教女？帝大笑而厚禮遣歸。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle-hagiographic account; historical details contested (baptism date, 'daughters' pun).

passages.text: Olga, regent for her son Svyatoslav, went to Constantinople with many gifts and arrived at the city of the Greek Emperor. The Emperor Constantine saw her and was struck by her beauty and her wisdom; he conversed with her and perceived that she was wise beyond all others. He said to her, 'You are worthy to reign in this city with me.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 955 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧爾嘉為其子斯維亞托斯拉夫的攝政，帶著許多禮物前往君士坦丁堡，抵達了希臘皇帝的城市。皇帝君士坦丁見了她，為她的美貌與智慧所打動；他與她交談，察覺她的智慧超越眾人。他對她說：「你配與我一同統治這座城市。」

passages.text: She was instructed in the faith and baptized by the Patriarch Polyeuktos, who named her Helena — after the mother of Constantine the Great. The Emperor said to her, 'I wish to take you as my wife.' She answered: 'How can you marry me, after yourself baptizing me and calling me your daughter? For among Christians that is not lawful. You know it yourself.' Then the Emperor said, 'You have outwitted me, Olga' — and gave her many gifts and dismissed her in peace, calling her his daughter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 955 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她接受了信仰的教導，由牧首波呂歐克托斯施洗，並為她取名海倫娜——取自君士坦丁大帝之母。皇帝對她說：「我願娶你為妻。」她答道：「你既親自為我施洗，又稱我為女兒，怎能娶我呢？因為在基督徒中，這是不合法的。你自己也知道。」於是皇帝說：「奧爾嘉，你智勝了我。」——便賜她許多禮物，平安地送她離去，稱她為女兒。

passages.text: She returned to Kiev with priests and Christian books, and tried to convert her son Svyatoslav, who laughed and would not follow; but the chronicle makes her the dawn of Russian Christianity — 'Olga was the forerunner of the Christian land, even as the day-spring precedes the sun, and as the moon precedes the day.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 955 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她帶著祭司與基督教書籍返回基輔，並試圖使她的兒子斯維亞托斯拉夫皈依，他卻大笑而不肯聽從；但編年史使她成為俄羅斯基督教的曙光——「奧爾嘉是基督教之地的先驅，正如晨光先於太陽，月亮先於白晝。」

title.en: The Faiths on Trial: Vladimir's Debate of 986
title.zh: 信仰的法庭：九八六年弗拉基米爾辯道

region.en: Kiev palace (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基輔王宮（象徵性定位）

period: Event dated 986; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 986

summary.en: Missionaries of four faiths came to Vladimir's hall — Volga Bulgars with one god and circumcision, Germans of the Pope, Khazar Jews of Abraham's wandering god, and a Greek philosopher with an icon of the Last Judgment; he dismissed the rest with 'Drinking is the joy of the Russes; we cannot exist without that pleasure' and kept only the Greek.
summary.zh: 四教使節至弗拉基米爾之殿——伏爾加保加利亞人（割禮一神）、教皇之德意志人、可薩猶太人（亞伯拉罕流離之神）、以及持末世審判像之希臘哲士；他遣走前者，言『飲酒乃羅斯人之樂，離之不能活』，獨留希臘哲士。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle polemic; the debate is a literary construction of Christian historiography, flagged in note.

passages.text: The Bulgars of Mohammedan faith came first, saying that though Vladimir was a wise and prudent prince, he had no religion: adopt theirs and believe in their god, who loved circumcision, eating no pork, no wine, and promising after death pleasures — every man seventy wives in paradise. Vladimir asked what their land's other delight was, and they answered no other delight; he found their law distasteful and answered that 'Drinking is the joy of the Russes. We cannot exist without that pleasure.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 986 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 信奉穆罕默德教的保加爾人先來，說弗拉基米爾雖是明智審慎的親王，卻沒有宗教：採納他們的宗教，信奉他們的神吧，那神喜愛割禮、不食豬肉、不飲酒，並許諾死後的享樂——每個人在天堂有七十個妻子。弗拉基米爾問他們國土還有何其他樂趣，他們答說別無樂趣；他覺得他們的律法令人厭惡，答道：「飲酒是羅斯人的歡樂。沒有這樂趣，我們無法生存。」

passages.text: Then came Germans from the Pope of Rome and Khazar Jews who told how their god Abraham had cast out the many nations of the land; Vladimir dismissed both — the Germans because their faith was but a Latin shadow of the Greek, the Jews asking 'Where is your land?' 'In Jerusalem.' 'God is angry with our fathers and scattered us for our sins; our land was given to the Christians.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 986 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著來了羅馬教皇派來的德意志人，以及可薩猶太人，他們講述他們的神亞伯拉罕如何驅逐了那地的眾多民族；弗拉基米爾把兩者都打發走了——德意志人，因為他們的信仰不過是希臘信仰的拉丁影子；猶太人則被問「你們的國土在哪裡？」「在耶路撒冷。」「神對我們的祖先發怒，因我們的罪將我們驅散；我們的國土已賜給了基督徒。」

passages.text: Last came a philosopher from the Greeks, who told Vladimir of the world from Adam to the Flood, and then spoke of the world to come. He showed him a curtain painted with the Last Judgment: the angels on the right and the sinners on the left, in torment. 'Glad are those on the right hand, but wretched those on the left.' Vladimir sighed and said, 'Good for them on the right; woe to those on the left.' He inclined his heart to Christianity, and having seen this vision, he delayed only until the wise men of his retinue could test the faith in the lands that kept it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 986-987 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最後來了一位希臘哲人，他向弗拉基米爾講述從亞當到大洪水的世界，然後談及來世。他給他看一幅繪有最後審判的帷幕：右邊是天使，左邊是受苦的罪人。「右邊的人有福了，左邊的人卻悲慘。」弗拉基米爾嘆息道：「右邊的人好；左邊的人有禍了。」他心中傾向基督教，既見此異象，便只延遲到隨從中的智者能在信奉此教的諸地檢驗這信仰為止。

title.en: Vladimir at Korsun: Blindness Healed in the Baptismal Font
title.zh: 弗拉基米爾在科爾松：洗禮池中復明

region.en: Korsun (Chersonesos), Crimea (symbolic pin at Sevastopol)
region.zh: 克里米亞科爾松（赫爾松涅斯）（象徵性定位於塞瓦斯托波爾）

period: Event dated 988; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 988

summary.en: Vladimir besieged Korsun and demanded the emperor's sister Anna; blind, he was baptized in the church of St. Basil at her urging — and opening his eyes, cried 'I have now beheld the true God!' He gave the city back to the Greeks, married Anna, and carried home the faith.
summary.zh: 弗拉基米爾圍科爾松，求帝妹安娜為妻；雙目失明，安娜勸其受洗——於聖巴西爾堂洗禮之際睜眼呼曰：『我今見真神矣！』歸城於希臘人，娶安娜，携信仰而返。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle legend of conversion; historical reality was more gradual.

passages.text: Vladimir marched on Korsun, the Greek city in the Crimea, and besieged it. From the ramparts a citizen named Anastasius shot arrows with messages, telling how the wells from which the city drank its water lay behind; Vladimir stopped the springs and the city thirsted into surrender. He sent word to Byzantium that he desired to marry the Emperor's sister Anna, threatening otherwise to do to Constantinople what he had done to Korsun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 988 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 弗拉基米爾向克里米亞的希臘城市科爾松進軍，將其圍困。城牆上一位名叫阿納斯塔修的市民射出縛有書信的箭，告知城內飲水所賴的水井位於何處；弗拉基米爾截斷了水源，城中人因乾渴而投降。他遣使前往拜占庭，說他欲娶皇帝的妹妹安娜為妻，否則便威脅要對君士坦丁堡施以他對科爾松所做的一切。

passages.text: Anna came weeping across the water, saying she was going as if to captivity; but when Vladimir, who had suffered an illness of the eyes and was quite blind, heard her say that if he were baptized he would regain his sight, he answered, 'If this alone be true, then truly is the God of the Christians great' — and was baptized in the church of St. Basil. When the priest laid his hand upon him, Vladimir opened his eyes and saw: 'I have now beheld the true God!' Astounded at the miracle, Anna and all who saw gave glory to God.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 988 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 安娜哭著渡水而來，說她此行如同前往囚虜之地；然而弗拉基米爾正患眼疾，幾乎全盲，當他聽她說若受洗便可復明時，他答道：「若單單此事為真，那麼基督徒的上帝確是偉大」——於是在聖巴西勒教堂受洗。當祭司將手按在他身上時，弗拉基米爾睜開雙眼，看見了：「我如今已得見真神！」安娜與所有目睹此奇蹟的人皆驚愕不已，一同將榮耀歸於上帝。

passages.text: He gave Korsun back to the Greeks as dowry for his bride, married Anna in the same church, and returned to Kiev with the princess, priests, and relics of St. Clement. There he baptized his twelve sons in the Dnieper, then ordered the idols overthrown and the whole city baptized in the river, princes and slaves alike standing in the water while the priests read the baptismal prayer — and heaven rejoiced over so many souls saved.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 988 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他將科爾松歸還希臘人，作為迎娶新娘的聘禮，並在同一座教堂中與安娜成婚，隨後帶著公主、祭司與聖克萊門特的聖髑返回基輔。他在那裡於第聶伯河為他的十二個兒子施洗，繼而下令推翻偶像，並為全城之人在河中施洗，王公與奴隸一同立於水中，祭司則誦讀洗禮禱文——上天為如此眾多靈魂得救而歡欣。

title.en: Boris and Gleb: The Princes Who Would Not Fight
title.zh: 鮑里斯與格列布：不肯相爭的兩位王公

region.en: River Alta and Smolensk (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿爾塔河與斯摩棱斯克（象徵性定位）

period: Events dated 1015; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 1015

summary.en: When Vladimir died, Svyatopolk seized Kiev and sent men to kill his half-brothers: Boris prayed on the riverbank as the assassins came and offered his throat; Gleb, still a boy in his boat on the river, was told his father wished to see him — and submitted, meek as a lamb, to the stroke.
summary.zh: 弗拉基米爾薨，斯維亞托波爾克據基輔遣人殺其異母弟：鮑里斯於河畔禱告，遇刺客至而引頸就戮；格列布尚在舟中，聞『父欲見汝』——如羔羊般順服受刃。

sensitivity.note: Hagiographic narrative; first native saints of Russia; political reading (Svyatopolk's guilt) is debated.

passages.text: Vladimir died at Berestovo, and Svyatopolk seized the throne at Kiev and killed his brother's men. Boris was marching home with his army when messengers told him of his father's death and offered him the throne — his men were many and Svyatopolk's were not. Boris answered that he could not lift his hand against his elder brother: 'It is not for me to rise against my elder brother; for if my father be dead, this man shall stand in my father's place.' His soldiers left him, and he stood alone on the river Alta with his household servants.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 1015 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 弗拉基米爾死於別列斯托沃，斯維亞托波爾克在基輔奪取王位，並殺害了他兄弟的親隨。鮑里斯正率軍返家，信使告知他父親的死訊，並向他獻上王位——他的人馬眾多，而斯維亞托波爾克的人馬寡少。鮑里斯回答說，他不能舉手反抗兄長：「我不該起來反抗我的兄長；因為即使我父親已死，這人也當代替我父親的位置。」他的士兵離他而去，他與家僕獨自站在阿爾塔河畔。

passages.text: Svyatopolk's assassins came at night; Boris sang the psalms and prayed, knowing that they were coming to kill him. He looked upon them and they came in — his servant George, a Hungarian, was slain defending him. Then they pierced Boris with lances and spears. Still breathing, he was carried to Svyatopolk's men, who ended him in his tent; so the prince died offering no resistance, and was mourned by all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 1015 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 斯維亞托波爾克的刺客夜間來到；鮑里斯誦唱詩篇並祈禱，知道他們是來殺他的。他望著他們，他們便進來了——他的僕人、匈牙利人喬治為護衛他而被殺。隨後他們以長矛與槍刺穿鮑里斯。他尚有一息，被抬到斯維亞托波爾克的人那裡，他們在他的帳幕中結果了他；這位王公就這樣毫不抵抗地死去，眾人皆為他哀悼。

passages.text: Gleb, sailing down the Dnieper, was met by Svyatopolk's messengers, who said his father wished to see him — for he was sick. Gleb landed and went along the bank; then they seized him, and their leader, like a second Cain, bade the cook kill the lamb of God. Gleb prayed aloud: 'Do not this deed, my brothers, do not this deed! What have I done to you? If my brother has done wickedness, am I also his brother? But do not take my life — a lamb in innocence stands amid the shearers.' He was killed in his boat, near Smolensk, and was mourned as one 'meek as a lamb'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 1015 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 格列布沿第聶伯河順流而下，途中遇到斯維亞托波爾克的信使，他們說他父親想見他——因為父親病了。格列布登岸，沿河岸而行；隨後他們捉住了他，為首者如同第二個該隱，命廚子殺死這上帝的羔羊。格列布高聲祈禱：「不要行此事，我的兄弟們，不要行此事！我對你們做了什麼？若我兄長行了惡，我難道也是他的兄弟嗎？但不要取我性命——一隻無辜的羔羊立在剪毛人中間。」他在船中被殺，地點近斯摩棱斯克，眾人哀悼他「溫順如羔羊」。

title.en: Yaroslav the Wise: Books like Rivers Watering the Earth
title.zh: 智者雅羅斯拉夫：書如江河潤澤大地

region.en: Kiev, church of St. Sophia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基輔聖索菲亞堂（象徵性定位）

period: Event dated 1037; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 1037

summary.en: Yaroslav loved books and assembled scribes to translate Greek volumes into Slavonic: 'Great is the benefit from book-learning; for books are like rivers that water the whole earth — they are the springs of wisdom, and have in themselves an immeasurable depth.'
summary.zh: 雅羅斯拉夫愛書，聚書手譯希臘典籍為斯拉夫文：『書學之益大矣；書如江河，潤澤大地——乃智慧之泉，其中蘊藏不可測之深。』

sensitivity.note: Chronicle encomium.

passages.text: Yaroslav loved books and religion, and was zealous for churches and for the Christian law. He gathered many scribes and set them to translate from Greek into Slavonic; and they wrote and collected many books by which true believers are instructed and enjoy religious education.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 1037 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 雅羅斯拉夫喜愛書籍與宗教，熱心於教堂與基督教律法。他召集了許多書吏，命他們將希臘文譯為斯拉夫文；他們便書寫並蒐集了許多書籍，真信徒藉此受到教誨，並得享宗教的教化。

passages.text: As one land is ploughed by many, so Yaroslav — in the chronicler's figure — sowed the written words of the law in the hearts of believers: 'Great is the benefit from book-learning; for by books we are taught and instructed in the way of repentance, and gain wisdom and continence. For books are like rivers that water the whole earth; they are the springs of wisdom, and books have in themselves an immeasurable depth.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 1037 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 正如一塊土地由許多人耕犁，雅羅斯拉夫——以編年史家的譬喻而言——也將律法的書寫之言播撒於信徒心中：「書籍之學的益處甚大；因為我們藉書籍受教，於悔改之道上得蒙指引，並獲得智慧與自制。因為書籍有如滋潤全地的河流；它們是智慧的泉源，而書籍本身蘊含著不可測度的深邃。」

title.en: Vladimir Monomakh's Testament: 'Do Not Let the Powerful Destroy the Weak'
title.zh: 莫諾馬赫遺訓：『勿令強者害弱者』

region.en: Kiev (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基輔（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1101-1117, appended to the Laurentian text; Cross trans. 1930

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), Appendix I: The Testament of Vladimir Monomakh

summary.en: The dying prince's letter to his children mixes psalm and proverb, battle and prayer: do not let the powerful destroy any — Christian or poor — nor the powerful eat the weak; give to the orphan, defend the widow, and never swerve from the oath sworn on the cross.
summary.zh: 垂死王公致其子之書，雜以詩篇、箴言、征戰與祈禱：勿令強者加害於人——無論基督徒或貧者——勿令強者吞弱者；撫孤兒、護寡婦，十字架前所立之誓，不可偏離。

sensitivity.note: Autobiographical testament, a classic of Old Russian literature.

passages.text: Vladimir Monomakh, prince of Kiev, wrote his children a testament seated in thought upon his sledge — an old man thinking on death. He tells them first what his father taught him, then sets down the lessons of his life: 'Have pride of soul in your hearts and minds, but think no pride of body, for all is mortal — the flower withers, the smoke disperses, the vapor scatters away.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Testament of Vladimir Monomakh in the Primary Chronicle, Appendix I (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 基輔王公弗拉基米爾·莫諾馬赫坐在雪橇上沉思，為子女寫下遺訓——一位老人思索著死亡。他先告訴他們父親對他的教誨，隨後記下自己一生的訓誨：「心中與意念裡當存靈魂的高傲，卻不可對身體存有驕矜，因為一切皆會消亡——花會枯萎，煙會消散，霧氣會四散而去。」

passages.text: 'Above all things, do not forget the poor, and support them and give to the orphan as far as you are able, and defend the widow yourselves, and do not let the powerful destroy any man. Kill neither right nor wrong, nor order any to be slain, even though he be unworthy of death. Do not let the powerful destroy any — Christian or otherwise.' His own account of his campaigns — hunting, riding, war, and councils from morning till night — stands as a prince's rule of work: never idle, never drunken, never prideful, and above all never forsworn of the oath made at the cross.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Testament of Vladimir Monomakh (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「最重要的是，不可忘記窮人，要扶助他們，並盡你所能施予孤兒，也要親自保護寡婦，不可讓有權勢者毀滅任何人。不可殺無辜，也不可殺有罪，亦不可命人殺害任何人，即使他罪不至死。不可讓有權勢者毀滅任何人——無論是基督徒與否。」他對自己征戰的記述——狩獵、騎行、戰爭，以及從早到晚的議事——樹立了王公勤勉的準則：從不閒惰，從不酗酒，從不驕矜，最重要的是從不背棄在十字架前所立的誓言。

title.en: Portents of 1065: The Eclipse and the Frankish Comets
title.zh: 一〇六五年之異象：日蝕與法蘭克彗星

region.en: Kievan Rus, sky over the Dnieper (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基輔羅斯第聶伯上空（象徵性定位）

period: Events dated 1065; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 1065

summary.en: In the year 1065 the sun was eclipsed — 'there was great sorrow over the Russian land, in consequence of the eclipse which God sent upon us'; a star of blood appeared over the church of the Holy Wisdom, and the chronicler links the sign to the princes' fatal quarrels.
summary.zh: 一〇六五年日有蝕——『俄羅斯大地因此神所降之蝕而大悲』；血色之星現於聖智堂上空，史家以此兆繫於王公們致命之內爭。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle portents.

passages.text: In the year 1065 the sun was eclipsed, and there was great sorrow over the Russian land in consequence of the eclipse which God sent upon us. A star in the west portended bloodshed; the sign was seen from the sky, like a dragon in the heavens, and the chronicler counts the calamities that followed — death among princes, battle, and famine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 1065 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一〇六五年，太陽被蝕，因這上帝降於我們的日蝕，俄羅斯之地上遂有大悲痛。西方的一顆星預示了流血；這徵兆自天空顯現，如同天上的巨龍，而編年史家歷數其後接踵而至的災禍——王公之死、戰事與饑荒。

passages.text: Portents in the chronicle are theology, not astronomy: God sends signs so that men may turn from evil deeds. The stars fall, the earth quakes, children speak words, and each marvel is set beside the sins that invited it. In the Old Russian cosmology the sky reads like scripture — and every eclipse is a parenthesis in a sentence about justice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 1065 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 編年史中的異象是神學，而非天文學：上帝降下徵兆，為使人們離棄惡行。星辰墜落，大地震動，孩童說出話語，每一奇蹟皆與招致它的罪愆並列。在古俄羅斯的宇宙觀中，天空讀來如同經文——而每一次日蝕，都是一句關於公義的話語中的括號。

title.en: A Ship on the Sea and a Book Given to the Old Inca
title.zh: 海上之船與獻給老王的書

region.en: Tococachi ward, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科托科卡奇坊(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The Ynca returned to Cuzco, and he was very old. News came that a ship had been seen on the sea; and after another year a youth entered the city with a great book which he gave to the old Ynca and then disappeared. The Ynca fasted for six months in Tococachi without ceasing.
summary.zh: 印加王返庫斯科,其時已屆暮年。傳來消息:海上有人見一艘船;又過一年,一少年入城,攜一部大書獻與老王,隨即隱去。老王遂在托科卡奇不輟齋戒六個月。

sensitivity.note: The mysterious ship-and-book omen (often read as a premonition of the Spanish arrival); left as Salcamayhua records it.

passages.text: The Ynca returned to Cuzco, and he was very old. News came that a ship had been seen on the sea; and after another year a youth entered the city with a great book which he gave to the old Ynca and then disappeared. The Ynca fasted for six months in Tococachi without ceasing.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 印加返回庫斯科，他已十分年邁。有消息傳來，說海上曾見一艘船；又過了一年，一名青年帶著一本大書進入城中，將書交給年老的印加，隨後便消失了。印加在托科卡奇不間斷地齋戒了六個月。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Seven Years of Hunger: Amaru Tupac's Farms That Frost Never Touched
title.zh: 七年饑饉:霜所不侵的阿瑪魯·圖帕克之田

region.en: Callachaca and Lucrioc-chullo farms, near Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科附近卡利亞查卡與盧克里奧克-丘略田莊(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In those days there was a great famine which lasted for seven years, and during that time the seed produced no fruit. Many died of hunger, and it is even said that some ate their own children; the Ynca was then living at Tumipampa. They say that Amaru Tupac Ynca, during those seven years of famine, obtained large harvests from his farms at Callachaca and Lucrioc-chullo: the dews always descended upon them at night, and frost never visited them, insomuch that the people would have worshipped him by reason of the miracle; but Amaru Tupac would not consent to this insult to the Creator. He rather humbled himself, feeding the poor during the seven years of famine, for his disposition was to be humble and meek to all; he had filled the collcas or granaries with food many months before. His descendants were the Ccapac-Ayllu.
summary.zh: 其時大饑七年,播種不實。餓死者眾,相傳竟有人食其子女;其時印加王駐圖米潘帕。相傳七年饑荒中,阿瑪魯·圖帕克·印加在卡利亞查卡與盧克里奧克-丘略的田莊卻大獲豐收:夜夜甘露自降,霜雪從不侵擾。民眾幾欲因此神蹟而拜他為神;但阿瑪魯·圖帕克不肯以此侮辱造物主,反而謙卑自處,七年間賑濟貧民——他天性謙沖,待眾以和;早在數月之前,他的糧倉便已貯滿食糧。其後裔即卡帕克-阿伊柳世系。

sensitivity.note: The refusing-worship motif attached to the prince who declined the throne; a humility exemplum inside the dynastic cycle.

passages.text: In those days there was a great famine which lasted for seven years, and during that time the seed produced no fruit. Many died of hunger, and it is even said that some ate their own children. The Ynca was then living at Tumipampa.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那些日子裡發生了一場持續七年的大饑荒，其間種子不結果實。許多人餓死，甚至據說有些人吃掉了自己的孩子。當時印加正住在圖米潘帕。

passages.text: They say that Amaru Tupac Ynca, during those seven years of famine, obtained large harvests from his farms at Callachaca and Lucrioc-chullo, that the dews always descended upon them at night, and that frost never visited them, insomuch that the people would have worshipped him by reason of the miracle; but Amaru Tupac would not consent to this insult to the Creator. He rather humbled himself, feeding the poor during the seven years of famine. For his disposition was to be humble and meek to all. He had filled the collcas or granaries with food many months before. His descendants were the Ccapac-Ayllu.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們說，阿馬魯·圖帕克·印加在那七年饑荒期間，從他在卡拉查卡和盧克里奧克丘略的農田獲得大豐收，夜裡總有露水降下，霜凍從不侵襲它們，以致人們因這奇蹟而要崇拜他；但阿馬魯·圖帕克不願同意這對造物主的冒犯。他反而謙卑自抑，在七年饑荒期間供養窮人。因為他的性情對所有人都是謙遜而溫和的。早在數月之前，他已將科利卡斯或糧倉裝滿了食物。他的後裔是卡帕-艾柳。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Chuchi-capac Dressed as a Woman: The Huacas Thrown into Lake Urcos
title.zh: 喬奇-卡帕克扮婦而逃:瓦卡沉入烏爾科斯湖

region.en: Llallahua-pucara and lake of Urcos, Vilcanota (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 利亞利亞瓦-普卡拉與烏爾科斯湖(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: On the death of Pachacuti the provinces of the Puquinas and Collas rebelled from Vilcañota to Chacamarca, making their fortress in Llallahua-pucara with two hundred thousand men. Tupac Ynca Yupanqui allowed the Hanan-Quichuas and Hurin-Quichuas, confident in their prowess, to march against them: twelve thousand marched from Cuzco full of confidence, taking with them a huaca or idol. They began to fight in Huarmi-Pucara with the women of the Quillacas, and the Quichuas were defeated and entirely cut to pieces at the fortress; one man escaped with the news, and Tupac Ynca Yupanqui mourned for the flower of his army. He set out himself with one hundred and twenty thousand men and besieged Llallahua-pucara for three years. Then the Collas offered up sacrifices to the sun, of children and cuis, and from the air there was an encouraging answer to their Tayta; then they waged war without any fear. But the Ynca attacked with renewed fury; at sunrise on the third day he drove back the Collas. Chuchi-Ccapac and his chiefs escaped to the province of the Lupacas dressed as women. They were brought before the Ynca in the town of Cac-yaviri with the huaca of Ynti and other huacas; Tupac Ynca Yupanqui ordered the chiefs and the huacas to be placed in the centre of their army of one hundred thousand men, where they were insulted - he sent for the huyachucos, suyuntus, llama-llamas and chuñires to trample upon them - and eventually they were thrown into the lake of Urcos, while the Collas were brought in triumph to Cuzco. In memory of these cruel wars the Ynca ordered two darts of gold and silver to be placed in Vilcañota.
summary.zh: 帕查庫提一死,普基納與科利亞諸省自維爾卡尼奧塔至查卡馬爾卡叛亂,以二十萬之眾據利亞利亞瓦-普卡拉為堡。圖帕克·尤潘琪拗不過自信滿滿的哈南與烏林基丘亞人,許其出征:一萬二千人攜一尊瓦卡自庫斯科昂然而行。他們在瓦爾米-普卡拉與基利亞卡之婦交戰,大敗;退至主堡又被科利亞人圍殲殆盡,僅一人逃歸報信。圖帕克·尤潘琪哀其精銳盡喪,親率十二萬人圍堡三年。科利亞人向太陽獻孩童與豚鼠為祭,空中竟有聲音鼓舞其祭司「塔伊塔」;他們遂無所畏懼而戰。然而印加王攻勢愈猛,第三日日出時大破科利亞軍。喬奇-卡帕克與諸酋扮作婦女逃往盧帕卡省,在卡克-亞維里鎮被押至印加王前,連同「因蒂」瓦卡及諸瓦卡。王命將酋長與瓦卡置於十萬大軍正中受辱——召來惠亞丘科、蘇雲圖斯、利亞馬-利亞馬斯、丘尼雷斯踏踐之——最後盡投烏爾科斯湖中,科利亞人則被凱旋押解庫斯科。為誌此慘烈戰事,印加王在維爾卡尼奧塔立金銀標槍各一。

sensitivity.note: Colla defeat cycle; the sun-oracle that answered the besieged is a notable case of an oracle answering the losing side.

passages.text: On his death the provinces of the Puquinas and Collas rebelled, from Vilcañota to Chacamarca, with all the Urco-suyus of Achacache, Huancane, Asillu, and Asancaru, and they made their fortress in Llallahua-pucara with two hundred thousand men. So Tupac Ynca Yupanqui assembled an army to attack them; and the Hanan-Quichuas and Hurin-Quichuas, confident in their prowess, petitioned to be allowed to march against the enemy. At last the Ynca yielded to their importunity, and a very powerful army of twelve thousand Quichuas marched from Cuzco, full of confidence, well armed, taking with them a huaca, or idol. They began to fight in Huarmi-Pucara with the women of the Quillacas, and the Quichuas were defeated. They retired to the principal fortress of Llallahua-pucara, where they were besieged by the Collas and entirely cut to pieces. One man escaped, and brought the news to Tupac Ynca Yupanqui, who mourned for the flower of his army.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他死後，普基納斯和科利亞斯諸省叛亂，從比爾卡尼奧塔到查卡馬爾卡，連同阿查卡切、萬卡內、阿西柳和阿桑卡魯的所有烏爾科-蘇尤斯，他們在利亞利亞瓦-普卡拉築起堡壘，聚眾二十萬人。於是圖帕克·印加·尤潘基集結軍隊進攻他們；哈南-基丘亞人和烏林-基丘亞人自恃勇武，請求准許他們前去迎敵。最後印加拗不過他們的再三請求，一支一萬二千名基丘亞人的強大軍隊從庫斯科出發，滿懷信心，裝備精良，隨身帶著一尊瓦卡，即偶像。他們在瓦爾米-普卡拉與基利亞卡斯人的婦女交戰，基丘亞人戰敗。他們退到利亞利亞瓦-普卡拉的主堡壘，在那裡被科利亞斯人圍困，全軍覆沒。只有一人逃脫，將消息帶給圖帕克·印加·尤潘基，他為軍隊的精銳之師哀悼。

passages.text: Then he set out himself from Cuzco with one hundred and twenty thousand men, and marched against the Collas, laying siege to the said fortress of Llallahua-pucara. This siege lasted for three years. Then the Collas offered up sacrifices to the sun, of children and cuis, and from the air there was an encouraging answer to their Tayta (Tayta means a minister of the huacas). Then they waged war upon the Ynca without any fear; but it fell out very differently from what they expected, for the Ynca attacked these Collas with renewed fury, and there was much bloodshed. On the third day the Ynca and his captains renewed the assault at sunrise and drove back the Collas.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隨後他親自從庫斯科出發，率十二萬人，向科利亞斯人進軍，圍攻上述的利亞利亞瓦-普卡拉堡壘。這場圍攻持續了三年。於是科利亞斯人向太陽獻祭孩童和豚鼠，空中傳來對他們的塔伊塔（塔伊塔意為瓦卡的祭司）的鼓舞性答覆。於是他們毫無畏懼地對印加開戰；但結果與他們所期望的大不相同，因為印加以更猛烈的怒火攻擊這些科利亞斯人，血流甚多。第三天日出時，印加和他的將領們重新發動進攻，擊退了科利亞斯人。

passages.text: Then Chuchi-Ccapac and his chiefs escaped to the province of the Lupacas dressed as women. They were brought before the Ynca in the town of Cac-yaviri, with the huaca of Ynti and other huacas. Tupac Ynca Yupanqui ordered the chiefs and the huacas to be placed in the centre of their army of one hundred thousand men, where they were insulted, and, to increase the affront, he sent for the huyachucos, suyuntus, llama-llamas, and chuñires to trample upon them, and eventually they were thrown into the lake of Urcos, while the Collas were brought in triumph to Cuzco. In memory of these cruel wars of the Collas, the Ynca ordered two darts of gold and silver to be placed in Vilcañota, and he left mitimaes and garrisons of loyal men for the security of the conquered provinces.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是丘奇-卡帕克和他的首領們裝扮成婦女，逃往盧帕卡斯省。他們在卡克-亞維里鎮被帶到印加面前，隨行的有因蒂的瓦卡和其他瓦卡。圖帕克·印加·尤潘基下令將首領們和瓦卡置於他們十萬大軍的中央，在那裡受盡侮辱，為加重羞辱，他又召來烏亞丘科斯、蘇雲圖斯、利亞馬-利亞馬斯和丘尼雷斯來踐踏他們，最終他們被投入烏爾科斯湖，而科利亞斯人則被凱旋帶回庫斯科。為紀念這些與科利亞斯人的殘酷戰爭，印加下令在比爾卡尼奧塔放置兩支金矛和銀矛，並留下忠誠之人的米蒂馬埃斯和駐軍，以確保被征服諸省的安全。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Huarmi-auca: The Province of Women Across the Great River
title.zh: 瓦爾米-奧卡:大河彼岸的女兒國

region.en: Huarmi-auca, eastern forests beyond the great river (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 大河以東森林中的女兒國(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The Ynca assembled 200,000 men to undertake a new conquest in the Andes, naming Uturuncu Achachi as general. These did good service in the conquest of the provinces of Manaresu and Upatari, as far as the confines of Huancavillca on one side and to Caravaya on the other, where they met with a province inhabited entirely by women, called Huarmi-auca. They then crossed a river of great volume; but at first, as no man could pass over, some audacious monkeys, belonging to a chief of the Manares, went across, and secured ropes and cables after overcoming great difficulties. This province is called the Golden, and in it they found a great and rich land called Escay-oya, with a very warlike race of people who were said to be cannibals; and they make such deadly poison, that it would seem they have a pact with the devil. They fought two desperate battles, and in the third they were defeated by the soldiers of the Ynca - not because they were less brave, but by superiority of arms and discipline. News then came that Tupac Ynca Yupanqui had banished a captain to a province of the Chirihuanas; Apu Quillacta proclaimed the news to his people, and they returned to their own land, leaving the Ynca army with the general - and Uturuncu Achachi returned to Cuzco, abandoning the conquests made by the labours of three armies.
summary.zh: 印加王集兵二十萬征安第斯之東,以烏圖倫庫·阿查奇為將。軍鋒經馬納雷蘇、烏帕塔里,東抵萬卡維利卡界,西至卡拉瓦亞,途中遇一省,居民全為女子,名「瓦爾米-奧卡」(女戰之地)。繼而欲渡一條極寬的大河;起初無人能渡,馬納雷斯酋長豢養的幾隻大膽猴子竟泅水而過,歷盡艱險,為大軍取回繩索纜索。此省名「金省」,其中有沃土名「埃斯卡伊-奧亞」,其民驍勇,相傳食人,又製劇毒,彷彿與魔鬼有約。兩場惡戰不分勝負,第三戰方為印加軍所敗——非其不勇,實因兵器與紀律之優。此時傳來圖帕克·尤潘琪放逐一將至奇里瓜納之地的消息;阿普·基利亞克塔向部眾宣告,眾人便棄軍歸鄉。烏圖倫庫·阿查奇只得班師回庫斯科,三軍將士浴血所拓之土,盡皆棄之。

sensitivity.note: Amazonian frontier legend inside an Inca chronicle; the land-of-women topos is compared across traditions.

passages.text: The Ynca then assembled 200,000 men to undertake a new conquest in the Andes, naming Uturuncu Achachi as general of the army. These did good service in the conquest of the provinces of Manaresu and Upatari, as far as the confines of Huancavillca on one side, and to Caravaya on the other, where they met with a province inhabited entirely by women, called Huarmi-auca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 印加王於是召集了二十萬人，準備在安地斯山脈展開新的征服，並任命烏圖倫庫·阿查奇為軍隊統帥。這些人在征服馬納雷蘇與烏帕塔里兩省時立下良好功績，其地一側遠及萬卡維爾卡邊界，另一側則至卡拉瓦亞；他們在那裡遇到一個全由女子居住的省份，名為瓦爾米-奧卡。

passages.text: They then crossed a river of great volume; but at first, as no man could pass over, some audacious monkeys, belonging to a chief of the Manares, went across, and secured ropes and cables after overcoming great difficulties. This province is called the Golden, and in it they found a great and rich land called Escay-oya, with a very warlike race of people who were said to be cannibals; and they make such deadly poison, that it would seem they have a pact with the devil. They fought two desperate battles, and in the third they were defeated by the soldiers of the Ynca, not because they were less brave, but by superiority of arms and discipline.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們隨後渡過一條水量浩大的河流；起初因為無人能夠渡過，一些屬於馬納雷斯某位酋長的膽大猴子便先渡了過去，並在克服重重困難之後固定了繩索與纜繩。這個省份被稱為「黃金省」，他們在其中發現一片廣大而富饒的土地，名為埃斯凱-奧亞，居民是一個非常好戰的族群，據說他們是食人族；他們還製造出如此致命的毒藥，彷彿與魔鬼訂有盟約。他們打了兩場殊死之戰，在第三場中被印加王的士兵擊敗，並非因為他們較不勇敢，而是因為對方在武器與紀律上佔有優勢。

passages.text: They say that while these new provinces were being numbered, news came that Tupac Ynca Yupanqui had banished a captain to a province of the Chirihuanas. The captain, Apu Quillacta, proclaimed this news to his people, and they returned to their own land, leaving the Ynca army with the general, Uturuncu Achachi. This was the reason that the Escay-oyas, and Upataxis, and Manares again took up arms, for the forces of Uturuncu Achachi were reduced; and he returned to Cuzco, abandoning the conquests made by the labours of three armies and at great cost of lives.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們說，正當這些新省份被清點登記之時，傳來消息說圖帕克·印加·尤潘基已將一名隊長流放到奇里瓦納人的一個省份。那名隊長阿普·基利亞克塔將這消息宣告給他的部眾，他們便返回了自己的土地，留下印加軍隊與統帥烏圖倫庫·阿查奇。這正是埃斯凱-奧亞人、烏帕塔希人與馬納雷斯人再度拿起武器的原因，因為烏圖倫庫·阿查奇的兵力已被削弱；於是他返回庫斯科，放棄了由三支軍隊的辛勞、並以重大生命代價所取得的征服成果。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Three Hundred Porters Buried with Their Gold at Pachatusan
title.zh: 三百腳夫與黃金同葬帕查圖桑

region.en: Hill of Pachatusan, above Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科上方帕查圖桑山(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: At this time there came from the Andes of Upatari three hundred Antis laden with gold in dust and tubes, and at the moment of their arrival it began to freeze, and all the crops were frozen to the roots. So, by advice of the old councillors, the Ynca ordered the three hundred men to carry their loads of gold to Pachatusun, a very high hill, and there to have them buried. So the unfortunates were killed and buried as a welcome.
summary.zh: 其時,自烏帕塔里安第斯來了三百名安蒂人,背負金沙與金管。他們抵達之際,天氣驟然結凍,莊稼連根凍斃。於是,依老臣之議,印加王命這三百人將黃金背負至極高的帕查圖桑山,就地埋藏。可憐的三百人遂被處死,與金同葬——作為對山神的「迎禮」。

sensitivity.note: A killing recorded with terrible economy ('as a welcome'); grouped with the Capacocha-like mountain offerings.

passages.text: At this time there came from the Andes of Upatari three hundred Antis laden with gold in dust and tubes, and at the moment of their arrival it began to freeze, and all the crops were frozen to the roots. So, by advice of the old councillors, the Ynca ordered the three hundred men to carry their loads of gold to Pachatusun, a very high hill, and there to have them buried. So the unfortunates were killed and buried as a welcome.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此時，從烏帕塔里的安地斯山區來了三百名安提人，滿載著金砂與金管；就在他們抵達的那一刻，天開始結霜，所有作物都被凍至根部。於是，印加王聽從年長顧問的建議，命令這三百人把他們所載的黃金運到帕查圖孫——一座極高的山丘——並在那裡將其埋藏。於是這些不幸的人被殺死並埋葬，作為獻上的迎賓之禮。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Governor's Plot and the Uncle's Dream: Saving the Child Huayna Capac
title.zh: 攝政之謀與叔父之夢:救下幼主瓦伊納·卡帕克

region.en: Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The Ynca died, being very old, as well as his brother Amaru Tupac Ynca: both died in the same year, leaving Huayna Ccapac Ynca as their heir, and Apu Hualpaya as governor, for the heir was of tender age. They buried many yanacunas, pachacas, women and servants beloved by the Ynca, whom the barbarous captains thought their Ynca would require to be served in the next world. This governor intended to raise himself to be ruler of Ttahuantin-suyu, ordering troops to be secretly assembled from all parts for a given day; he began to worship the sun and moon and thunder, assigning estates for these false gods, and some evil-disposed Curacas executed his orders with alacrity. One night a bastard uncle of Huayna Ccapac was lying half awake and half asleep, very early in the morning, when he saw troops headed by Hualpaya surrounding the city, and pointing their arrows at the child Huayna Ccapac. This was a dream; but the uncle jumped up as if it had been true, and went to the house of Cuys Manco.
summary.zh: 印加王年邁而終,其弟阿瑪魯·圖帕克·印加亦於同年去世;幼主瓦伊納·卡帕克年齒尚幼,由阿普·瓦爾帕亞攝政。眾人埋葬了先王生前鍾愛的雅納庫納、帕查卡斯、婦女與僕從——野蠻的將領們以為先王在來世仍需這些人侍奉。攝政王則欲自立為大蘇尤之主,密令各處調兵,定期舉事;他開始崇拜太陽、月亮與雷,為這些「偽神」撥賜田產,一些懷有異心的庫拉卡聞命而動。一夜拂曉,瓦伊納·卡帕克的庶叔半睡半醒之際,夢見瓦爾帕亞率兵圍城,箭簇盡指幼主瓦伊納·卡帕克。此雖一夢,叔父卻霍然而起,如夢成真一般,逕往庫伊斯·曼科家中而去。

sensitivity.note: Dream-warning episode; the human retinue burials are recorded as given.

passages.text: The Ynca died, being very old, as well as his brother Amaru Tupac Ynca, who had attained a great age. Both the brothers died in the same year, leaving Huayna Ccapac Ynca as their heir, and Apu Hualpaya as governor, for the heir was of tender age. They mourned for the Ynca as they had done for Pachacuti, forming two armies, one of men and the other of women, and they buried many yanacunas, pachacas, women, and servants, who were beloved by the Ynca. The barbarous captains thought that their Ynca would require to be served in the next world by these people.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 印加王以極高齡去世，他的兄弟阿馬魯·圖帕克·印加亦然，後者也已年邁。兩兄弟在同一年去世，留下瓦伊納·卡帕克·印加為繼承人，並以阿普·瓦爾帕亞為攝政，因為繼承人尚年幼。他們為印加王舉哀，一如當年為帕查庫提舉哀那樣，組成兩支隊伍，一支由男子組成，另一支由女子組成；他們還埋葬了許多印加王所喜愛的亞納庫納、帕查卡、婦女與僕役。這些野蠻的隊長認為，他們的印加王在來世需要這些人來服侍。

passages.text: They say that this governor and coadjutor intended to raise himself to be ruler of Ttahuantin-suyu, and that he ordered troops to be secretly assembled from all parts for a given day. They say that this governor began to worship the sun and moon and thunder; and Huayna Ccapac, being a young child, also adored them. And they say that the governor assigned estates for these false gods, and that some evil disposed Curacas executed his orders with alacrity.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們說，這位攝政兼輔臣意圖自立為塔萬廷-蘇尤的統治者，並下令各部隊在指定之日從各地秘密集結。他們說，這位攝政開始崇拜太陽、月亮與雷電；而瓦伊納·卡帕克當時還是個幼童，也一同崇拜它們。他們還說，這位攝政為這些假神分配了地產，而一些心術不正的庫拉卡則欣然執行了他的命令。

passages.text: This Hualpaya was now ready to rebel without the knowledge of the provinces; and one night a bastard uncle of Huayna Ccapac was lying half awake and half asleep, very early in the morning, when he saw troops headed by Hualpaya surrounding the city, and pointing their arrows at the child Huayna Ccapac. This was a dream; but the uncle jumped up as if it had been true, went to the house of Cuys Manco, and gave the alarm.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這位瓦爾帕亞此時已在各省不知情的情況下準備叛亂。一天拂曉，瓦伊納·卡帕克的一位庶出叔父正睡得朦朦朧朧，忽見瓦爾帕亞率領軍隊圍住城池，箭頭直指幼童瓦伊納·卡帕克。這原是一場夢，叔父卻一躍而起，彷彿夢境是真，奔到庫伊斯·曼科家中報了警。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Turi's Feast of Hearts and the Overheard Lament
title.zh: 圖里復仇與被竊聽的哀歌

region.en: Wharekura, Hawaiki (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哈瓦基瓦雷庫拉大屋（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 14, The Emigration of Turi (London 1855)

summary.en: When the boy Potikiroroa trips in the doorway of Uenuku's sacred house - a fatal omen - the high priest devours him uncooked. Turi revenges him by luring Uenuku's little son Hawepotiki into the summer river and killing him, then smuggles the baked heart into the food-basket sent up to Uenuku, who eats it lamenting his missing child. 'Let it be; he lies in the belly of Toi-te-huatahi', he says - a proverb of dreadful revenge. Rongo-rongo overhears the war chant in Wharekura summoning the tribes to destroy Turi, and the flight that becomes the Aotea migration begins.
summary.zh: 男孩波蒂基羅羅阿在烏努庫聖屋門口絆倒——凶兆！大祭司竟將其生吞。圖里為友報仇：誘烏努庫幼子哈維波蒂基下河戲水而殺之，又將其烤熟的心臟混入敬獻烏努庫的食籃；烏努庫食畢方知吃了愛子，卻只道『罷了；他躺在圖伊特胡阿塔希的肚腹裡』——此諺意為必報大仇。妻子龍戈龍戈竊得瓦雷庫拉中召喚諸部滅圖里的戰歌，遂啟逃亡——此即奧特亞號遷徙之始。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection; cannibal revenge episode reproduced as paraphrase.

passages.text: Hoiraatua, a near relation of Turi, had a little boy named Potikiroroa; this young fellow was sent one day with a message to Uenuku, who was an ariki, or chief high-priest, to let him know that a burnt-offering had been made to the gods, of which Uenuku, as ariki, was to eat part. The little fellow accidentally tripped and fell down in the very doorway of Wharekura, the house of Uenuku, and this being a most unlucky omen, Uenuku was dreadfully irritated, and he laid hold of the little fellow and ate him up without even having the body cooked, and so the poor boy perished.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 霍伊拉阿圖阿是圖里的近親，有個小兒子名叫波蒂基羅羅阿。一日這孩子被派去給烏埃努庫送信——烏埃努庫是一位阿里基（ariki），即大祭司酋長——通知他已向諸神獻過燔祭，身為阿里基的烏埃努庫該分食一部分。小孩在烏埃努庫的屋子瓦雷庫拉的正門口絆了一跤摔倒。這是極不祥的兆頭，烏埃努庫大怒，一把抓住那孩子，連身子都不曾烹煮就把他生吞了，可憐的孩子就這樣喪了命。

passages.text: Turi was determined to have revenge for this barbarous act, and saw that his best way was to seize Hawepotiki, the little son of Uenuku, and kill him. He ordered the children of his household to whip tops and whirl whizgigs where the boy could see them, but he could not be tempted. At last summer came with its heats; Turi, one very hot day, ordered all the little children to run and bathe in the river Waimatuhirangi, and when little Hawepotiki saw the other lads swimming and playing he was thrown off his guard and ran there too. Turi waylaid him and killed him in a moment, and thus revenged the death of Potikiroroa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 圖里決意為這野蠻的暴行復仇，認為最好的辦法是抓住烏埃努庫的幼子哈威波蒂基，把他殺死。他命家中孩子們在男孩看得見的地方抽陀螺、轉響哨，卻誘不動他。終於夏天帶著暑熱來了；一個酷熱的日子，圖里命所有小孩跑到懷馬圖希蘭吉河裏洗澡，小哈威波蒂基看見伙伴們戲水，再也把持不住，也跑了過去。圖里半路截住他，頃刻間便殺了他，就這樣為波蒂基羅羅阿報了仇。

passages.text: After killing the poor boy, Turi cut the heart out of his body, which was eaten by himself and his friends; but when a chieftainness named Hotukura sent up a present of baskets of food to the sacred prince Uenuku, some of Turi's friends pushed into the basket of baked sweet potatoes the heart of Te Hawepotiki, cut up and baked too, and so it was carried up and laid before him to eat. Uenuku, who had missed his little boy, sighed when he saw such an excellent feast: 'Poor little Hawepotiki, how he would have liked this, but he now no longer comes running to sit by my side at mealtime' - and he ate the food. Hardly had he ended when a friend came and told him, 'They have made you eat a part of Hawepotiki.' He answered, 'Very well, let it be; he lies in the belly of Toi-te-huatahi' - meaning by this proverb that he would have a fearful revenge - but showed no other sign of feeling.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 殺了那可憐的孩子後，圖里剖出他的心，與朋友們分食了。後來一位名叫霍圖庫拉的女酋長向神聖王子烏埃努庫獻上幾籃食物，圖里的朋友們把哈威波蒂基的心切塊烤熟，混進烤甜薯的籃子裏，就這樣端到烏埃努庫面前。思念幼子的烏埃努庫見了這豐盛的筵席嘆道：「可憐的小哈威波蒂基，他多麼喜歡這個啊，可他再也不會跑來坐在我的身邊陪我吃飯了。」說著便吃了。他剛吃完，一個朋友來告訴他：「他們讓你吃下了哈威波蒂基的一塊肉。」他答道：「好吧，就這樣吧；他躺在托伊-特-胡阿塔希的腹中了」——這句諺語的意思是他必將展開可怕的復仇——此外再無任何動容之色。

passages.text: One evening Rongo-rongo, Turi's wife, went out of their house Rangiatea to suckle her little girl and heard Uenuku in his house Wharekura chanting a poem: 'Oh! let the tribes be summoned from the south, oh! let the tribes be summoned from the north; let Ngati-Ruanui come in force, let Ngati-Rongotea's warriors too be there, that we may all our foes destroy and sweep them utterly away. Oh, they ate one far nobler than themselves.' She went back and told her husband, humming it gently over to him, and Turi at once divined the meaning: the poem was meant for him; because he had killed the child of Uenuku they meant to slay him as a payment for the boy, and the lament his wife had heard evinced that they were secretly laying their plans of revenge. He started off at once to his father-in-law Toto to get a canoe in which he might escape from his enemies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一天傍晚，圖里之妻朗戈朗戈走出他們的朗吉阿泰亞屋去給小女兒餵奶，聽見烏埃努庫在他的瓦雷庫拉屋裏吟誦一首詩：「哦，召南方各部前來吧，哦，召北方各部前來吧；讓納蒂-魯阿努伊大舉而至，讓納蒂-朗戈特亞的戰士同來，我們要把仇敵一網打盡，將他們徹底掃除。哦，他們竟吃掉了遠比自己高貴的人。」她回去把詩輕聲哼給丈夫聽，圖里立刻明白了寓意：這詩是衝著他來的；因為他殺了烏埃努庫的孩子，他們要殺他償命，妻子聽到的輓歌表明他們正暗中謀劃復仇。他即刻動身去找岳父托托，求一條獨木舟，好從仇敵手中逃脫。

title.en: Kupe Slays the Cuttlefish of Muturangi
title.zh: 庫佩斬穆圖蘭基巨魷

region.en: Kura-te-au, Tory Channel, Marlborough Sounds (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫拉特奧水道，馬爾堡峽灣（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 14, The Emigration of Turi (London 1855)

summary.en: Kupe covets his cousin Hoturapa's wife Kuramarotini: he pretends his line is foul, lets the good-natured cousin dive, cuts the anchor rope and strands him to drown, then flees in the stolen Matahorua and discovers the islands of New Zealand, coasting entirely round them without finding inhabitants - only the birds kokako and tiwaiwaka. At Castle Point a great cuttle-fish flees its cavern before him; in Tory Channel it rears its sucker-armed bulk to engulf the canoe, and Kupe throws over a huge water-calabash; the monster, taking it for the canoe, rears up to crush it, and Kupe severs it in two with his axe - the Wheke-a-Muturangi slain.
summary.zh: 庫佩覬覦表弟霍圖拉帕之妻庫拉馬羅蒂尼：他謊稱釣線被纏，誘好心的表弟潛水解線，趁機砍斷錨繩將其拋棄海中，帶著贓婦駕馬塔霍魯阿號遠遁，發現新西蘭群島並環航一周，未見人煙——只有科卡科與蒂瓦伊瓦卡兩鳥。至城堡角，巨魷自洞穴竄逃；在托里水道它張開吸盤巨臂欲吞獨木舟，庫佩擲下水葫蘆，巨魷誤以為舟，猛撲其上，庫佩趁勢一斧將其劈為兩半——穆圖蘭基之魷就此授首。

sensitivity.note: Monster-slaying episode tied to discovery of Aotearoa; world-serpent tagging is interpretive (octopus as sea-monster).

passages.text: One day Kupe and Hoturapa went out upon the sea to fish together, and when they had anchored the canoe at a convenient place, Kupe let down his line and said to his cousin, 'Hotu', my line is foul of something; do you, like a good young fellow, dive down and release it for me.' Hoturapa said, 'Just give me your line, and let me see if I cannot pull it up for you.' But Kupe answered, 'It's of no use, you cannot do it; you had better give a plunge in at once, and pull it up.' This was a mere stratagem on the part of Kupe, that he might obtain possession of Kuramarotini, who was Hoturapa's wife; however Hoturapa not suspecting this, good-naturedly dived down at once to bring up Kupe's line.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一天，庫佩與霍圖拉帕一同出海捕魚。獨木舟在一處合宜的地方下錨後，庫佩放下釣線，對他的表弟說：「霍圖，我的線鉤住了什麼東西；你是個好孩子，替我潛下去把它解開吧。」霍圖拉帕說：「把線給我，讓我看看能不能替你拉上來。」庫佩卻說：「沒用的，你辦不到；你不如一下子扎進水裏，把它拉上來。」這不過是庫佩的詭計，想藉此奪取霍圖拉帕之妻庫拉馬羅蒂尼。霍圖拉帕並未起疑，好心好意地立刻潛了下去，去替庫佩解線。

passages.text: As soon as he had made his plunge, Kupe at once cut the rope which was attached to the anchor and paddled off for the shore as fast as he could go, to carry off Hoturapa's wife Kuramarotini. When Hoturapa came up to the surface the canoe was already a long distance from him, and he cried out to Kupe to bring the canoe back to take him in; but Kupe would not listen, brought not back the canoe, and so Hoturapa perished. Kupe then made haste and carried off Kuramarotini, and to escape from the vengeance of the relations of Hoturapa he fled away with her on the ocean in her canoe Matahorua, and discovered the islands of New Zealand, and coasted entirely round them, without finding any inhabitants. He only found two inhabitants in the country, a bird which he named the Kokako, and another bird which he named the Tiwaiwaka; he did not ultimately remain in these islands, but returned to his own country, leaving the openings he had examined in the country as signs that he had been here.
