passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 庫佩一跳入水中，便立刻割斷繫在錨上的繩索，盡其所能地划槳向岸邊而去，好把霍圖拉帕的妻子庫拉馬羅蒂尼帶走。當霍圖拉帕浮上水面時，獨木舟已離他甚遠，他向庫佩呼喊，要他把獨木舟划回來載他上船；但庫佩不肯聽從，沒有把獨木舟划回來，霍圖拉帕於是喪命。庫佩隨即急忙帶走庫拉馬羅蒂尼，為了躲避霍圖拉帕親族的報復，他與她一同乘著她的獨木舟「馬塔霍魯阿」逃向大海，發現了紐西蘭的群島，並沿著群島繞行一周，未發現任何居民。他在這片土地上只找到兩個居民，一隻他命名為「科卡科」的鳥，以及另一隻他命名為「蒂瓦伊瓦卡」的鳥；他最終並未留在這些島嶼上，而是返回了自己的故鄉，只留下他在這片土地上探查過的各處開口，作為他曾來過此地的跡象。

passages.text: As Kupe was proceeding down the east coast of New Zealand and had reached Castle Point, a great cuttle-fish, alarmed at the sight of a canoe with men in it, fled away from a large cavern which exists in the south headland of the cove there; it fled before Kupe in the direction of Raukawa, Cook's Straits. When he arrived at those straits he crossed them to examine the middle islands; seeing the entrance of Awa-iti, now called Tory Channel, running deep up into the land, he turned his canoe in there to explore it; the entrance he named Kura-te-au. Strong as the current was, Kupe stemmed it until he was just surmounting the crown of the rapid. The great cuttle-fish or dragon that had fled from Castle Point, which Kupe named Te Wheke-a-Muturangi, the cuttle-fish of Muturangi, was lying hid in this part of the current; it heard the canoe approaching, and raised its arms above the waters to catch and devour the canoe, men and all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當庫佩沿著紐西蘭東岸前行，抵達城堡角時，一隻巨大的烏賊因見到載有人的獨木舟而驚慌，從當地小灣南岬中一個大洞穴裡逃了出來；牠在庫佩前方逃往勞卡瓦，即庫克海峽的方向。當他抵達那些海峽時，他橫渡海峽去探查中間的島嶼；他看見阿瓦伊蒂——今稱托里海峽——的入口深深伸入陸地，便把獨木舟轉向那裡去探察；他將那入口命名為「庫拉特奧」。儘管水流強勁，庫佩仍逆流而上，直到他正要越過急流之頂。那隻從城堡角逃出的大烏賊或巨龍——庫佩稱之為「特韋赫阿穆圖蘭吉」，即穆圖蘭吉的烏賊——正潛伏在這段水流之中；牠聽見獨木舟靠近，便將觸臂舉出水面，要抓住並吞食獨木舟，連人一併吞下。

passages.text: Kupe pondered how he might destroy the terrible monster. He had already found that, although he kept on chopping off portions of its gigantic arms furnished with suckers as it tried to fold them about the canoe to pull it down, the monster was too fierce to care for this; so Kupe seized an immense hollow calabash he had on board to carry his water in, and threw it overboard. Hardly had it touched the water ere the monster flew at it, thinking it was the canoe of Kupe; so it reared its whole body out of the water to press down the huge calabash under it, and Kupe, as he stood in his canoe, being in a most excellent position to cut it with his axe, seized the opportunity, and striking it a tremendous blow, severed it in two and killed it. Several spots upon the east coast are shown where Kupe touched with his canoes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 庫佩思量著如何才能消滅這可怕的怪物。他早已發現，儘管當那怪物試圖將長滿吸盤的巨臂纏繞獨木舟把它拖下水時，他不停地砍下牠巨臂的一部分，這怪物卻凶猛得毫不在乎；於是庫佩抓起船上用來裝水的一個巨大的空心葫蘆，把它扔到船外。那葫蘆幾乎才碰到水面，怪物便撲了上去，以為那是庫佩的獨木舟；於是牠把整個身體抬出水面，要把那巨大的葫蘆壓在身下，而庫佩站在獨木舟上，正處於極佳的方位，可以用斧頭砍牠，他抓住這個機會，猛力一擊，將牠劈成兩半，殺死了牠。東岸有幾處地點被指出是庫佩以獨木舟觸及之處。

title.en: Turi Plants Patea: Eight Potatoes, Eight Hundred Baskets
title.zh: 圖里墾帕蒂亞：八薯八百籃

region.en: Patea River, Taranaki coast, Aotearoa
region.zh: 紐西蘭塔拉納基海岸帕蒂亞河

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 14, The Emigration of Turi (London 1855)

summary.en: The Aotea sails east against Kupe's instructions: Potoru's Ririno is dashed on Taputapuatea reef - 'you are as obstinate as Potoru, who persisted in rushing on to his own destruction'. Turi's canoe refits at Rangitahua after dog sacrifices, a child Tutawa is born at sea and fed his first food from the last ninth potato, and at landfall the footprints of the crewman thrown overboard are found on the sand. Turi follows the coast naming harbours from Kawhia to Patea, plants karaka berries all along the route, builds the pa Rangitaawhi, and makes his eight remaining seed potatoes into eight hundred baskets - the harvest of the ancestor of the Whanganui tribes.
summary.zh: 圖里本應向東航向日出之方，卻聽任波托魯向西而行：里里諾號觸礁碎裂，成諺『你像波托魯一樣固執，偏要撞向自取滅亡之處』。奧特亞號在蘭吉塔胡亞島重整，以犬祭神；海上出生的幼子圖塔瓦以最後一枚甘薯行初食禮；登陸沙灘，先見被拋海船員的腳印。圖里沿海岸為各地命名，沿途播下卡卡樹果核，築蘭吉塔維要塞，將僅餘的八枚薯種分切栽種——收成八百籃，此即旺加努伊諸部之祖的功業。

sensitivity.note: Ethnogenesis legend of Whanganui tribes; extensive place-name etymology reproduced selectively.

passages.text: Amongst the chiefs who landed at the mid-ocean island Rangitahua with them was one named Porua, whose canoe was called Te Ririno. They were carrying dogs with them as these would be valuable in the islands for food and skins for warm cloaks; on this island they killed two, Whakapapa-tuakura and Tanga-kakariki; the first they cooked and shared, but the second they cut up raw as an offering for the gods, laid it open before them, built a sacred place and set up pillars for the spirits that they might entirely consume the sacrifice, and took the enchanted apron of the spirits and spread it open, calling on them for an omen and thus removing all ill-luck from the canoes by repeating over them the prayers called Keuenga, Takanga, Whakainuinumanga.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 與他們一同在汪洋中的島嶼朗吉塔瓦登陸的酋長之中，有一位名叫波魯阿，他的獨木舟名叫「特里里諾」。他們隨船帶著狗，因為這些狗在島上會很有價值，既可作食物，其皮又可製成保暖的斗篷；在這座島上他們殺了两隻狗，一隻叫「瓦卡帕帕圖阿庫拉」，一隻叫「坦加卡卡里基」；第一隻他們煮熟後分食，但第二隻他們生切成塊作為獻給神靈的祭品，將其剖開陳放在神靈面前，築起一處聖地，並為神靈立起柱子，好讓他們將祭品完全享用，又取來神靈的施法圍裙將其攤開，向神靈祈求徵兆，並藉著對獨木舟誦念稱為「凱烏恩加」、「塔坎加」、「瓦卡伊努伊努曼加」的祈禱，如此除去獨木舟上一切的不祥。

passages.text: When all these ceremonies were ended, a very angry discussion arose between Potoru and Turi as to the direction they should now sail in. Turi persisted in wishing to pursue an easterly course: 'Let us still sail towards the quarter where the sun first flares up'; but Potoru answered, 'I say nay, nay, let us proceed towards that quarter of the heavens in which the sun sets.' Turi reminded him that Kupe, who had visited these islands, had particularly told them to keep the prow ever towards the sunrise; but Potoru persisted, and Turi gave up the point. After they had pursued the westerly course for some time, the canoe Ririno, getting into the surf near some rocks, was lost on a reef they named Taputapuatea, swept by a strong current swiftly running on to the realms of death, and dashed to pieces - hence the proverb to the present day: 'You are as obstinate as Potoru, who persisted in rushing on to his own destruction.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當所有這些儀式結束後，波托魯與圖里之間就他們此後該朝哪個方向航行，爆發了極為激烈的爭論。圖里堅持希望取道向東：「讓我們仍舊朝太陽首先燃起的那一方航行」；但波托魯回答：「我說不然，不然，讓我們朝太陽落下的那一方天際前行。」圖里提醒他，曾到訪這些島嶼的庫佩特別囑咐他們要始終讓船首朝向日出之處；但波托魯仍固執己見，圖里便放棄了這個主張。在他們循著向西的航路行了一段時間之後，獨木舟「里里諾」駛入一些岩石附近的碎浪之中，在一處他們命名為「塔普塔普阿特阿」的暗礁上失事，被一股急速湧向死亡之域的強勁水流沖走，撞得粉碎——因此至今有這句諺語：「你固執得像波托魯，執意衝向自己的毀滅。」

passages.text: When the Ririno had been lost, Turi in the Aotea pursued his course towards the quarter of the rising sun; whilst they were yet in mid-ocean a child whom he named Tutawa was born to Turi. They had then but nine sweet potatoes left, and Turi took one, leaving now but eight, and offered it as a sacrifice to the spirits, touching with it the palate of little Tutawa, born in mid-ocean, at the same time repeating the fitting prayers. When they drew near the shore, one of the crew, named Tuanui-a-te-ra, was very disobedient and insolent, and Turi, getting exceedingly provoked, threw him overboard into the sea. They also foolishly threw their old red head-ornaments, named Pohutukawa, into the sea, thinking wrongly that the red things they saw in such abundance on the shore were similar ornaments. At length the Aotea is run up on the beach, the wearied voyagers spring out on the sands, and the first thing they remark are the footprints of a man; they run to examine them and find them to be those of Tuanui-a-te-ra, whom Turi had shortly before thrown overboard - there can be no doubt, for some of the footprints are crooked, exactly suiting the deformed foot he had.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當「里里諾」失事後，圖里乘著「奧特阿」繼續朝日出之處的方向前行；當他們還在汪洋之中時，圖里得了一個孩子，他為孩子取名為圖塔瓦。當時他們只剩下九個甘藷，圖里取了一個，如今只剩八個，他把它作為祭品獻給神靈，用它觸碰在汪洋之中誕生的小圖塔瓦的上顎，同時誦念相應的祈禱。當他們駛近岸邊時，一名名叫圖阿努伊阿特拉的船員非常不順從且傲慢無禮，圖里被激怒至極，便把他扔下船去，拋入海中。他們還愚蠢地把他們舊有的紅色頭飾——名叫「波胡圖卡瓦」——扔進海裡，誤以為他們在岸上看到的那麼多紅色之物是類似的頭飾。終於，「奧特阿」被拖上灘頭，疲憊的航海者們躍上沙灘，他們首先注意到的是地上有一個人的腳印；他們跑去察看，發現那是圖阿努伊阿特拉的腳印，也就是圖里不久前扔下船去的那個人——這毋庸置疑，因為有些腳印是歪斜的，恰好與他那隻畸形的腳相合。

passages.text: Turi, having rested after his voyage, determined to seek the river Patea which Kupe had described to him, leaving his canoe Aotea in the harbour he named after it. He travelled along the coast-line from Aotea to Patea, having sent one party before him under Pungarehu, ordering them to plant the stones of the karaka-tree berries which they had brought, all along their route, in order that so valuable an article of food might be introduced into these islands. He gave names to the places as he came: at Kawhia, the awhinga of Turi; Marokopa, where he wound round; Waitara, from his wide fording steps; Mokau, where he slept; Manga-ti, where the enchanted garment Hunokiko was spread out; Hongihongi, where he smelt the soil; Tapuwae, the footsteps of Turi; Oakura, from the bright redness of the cloak; Waingongoro, where Turi snored; Ohingahape, after the crooked foot of Tuanui-a-te-ra. At length he reached the river Kupe had described; there he built a pa which he named Rangitaawhi, erected a post Whakatopea, built a house Matangirie, laid down a threshold Paepaehakehake, a storehouse Paeahua, and dug a well Parara-ki-te-uru. The chant they sang as they dug: 'Break up our goddess mother, break up the ancient goddess earth; we speak of you, oh earth, but do not you disturb the plants we have brought hither from Hawaiki the noble; it was Maui who scraped the earth in heaps round the sides in Kuratau.' They had but eight seed potatoes, but divided these into small pieces put separately into the ground; when the shoots sprang up Turi made the place sacred with prayers and incantations, the name of which was Ahuaroa, lest any one should venture there and hurt the plants. Then harvest-time came: they gathered in the crop of sweet potatoes and found they had eight hundred baskets of them. Rongo-rongo was the name of his principal wife, and their children sprang the tribes of Ngati-Apa-nui and Ngati-Ruanui.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 圖里在航行之後稍事歇息，便決定去尋找庫佩曾向他描述過的帕泰亞河，將他的獨木舟「奧特亞」留在以它命名的港灣中。他沿著海岸線從奧特亞行至帕泰亞，並事先派出一隊人馬由蓬加雷胡率領，吩咐他們沿途將帶來的卡拉卡樹樹果實之核種下，好讓如此珍貴的食物能引入這些島嶼。他一路行來，為各處命名：在卡維亞，是圖里的「阿芬加」（纏繞之處）；馬羅科帕，是他迂迴繞行之地；懷塔拉，得名於他寬闊的涉水步伐；莫考，是他歇宿之處；曼加蒂，是那件施了魔法的衣裳「胡諾基科」鋪展之處；洪吉洪吉，是他嗅聞土壤之處；塔普瓦埃，意為圖里的足跡；奧阿庫拉，得名於斗篷鮮明的赤紅；懷恩貢戈羅，是圖里打鼾之處；奧欣加哈佩，則取自圖阿努伊阿特拉那彎曲的腳。他終於抵達庫佩所描述的那條河；他在那裡築了一座堡壘，命名為朗吉塔阿維，立起一根柱子「瓦卡托佩阿」，建了一間屋「馬坦吉里耶」，鋪下一道門檻「帕埃帕埃哈克哈克」，蓋了一座倉庫「帕埃阿胡阿」，又掘了一口井「帕拉拉基特烏魯」。他們掘井時所唱的歌謠是：「掘開我們的母神吧，掘開古老的大地女神；我們向您訴說，哦大地，但請您不要擾動我們從高貴的哈瓦伊基帶到此地的作物；是毛伊在庫拉陶將泥土堆刮成兩側的土堆。」他們只有八顆種薯，卻將其切成小塊，分別埋入土中；當嫩芽長出時，圖里以祈禱與咒語使該地成為聖地，其名為「阿胡阿羅阿」，以免有人膽敢前往而傷害了作物。接著收穫的時節到了：他們採收了甘藷的作物，發現竟有八百籃之多。朗戈朗戈是他正妻的名字，他們的子孫繁衍出恩加蒂阿帕努伊與恩加蒂魯阿努伊兩族。

title.en: The Three Kingdoms: Copper, Silver, and Gold
title.zh: 三國記：銅銀金

region.en: Russian fairyland (symbolic pin at Moscow)
region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境（象徵性定位於莫斯科）

period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'The Three Kingdoms'

summary.en: The youngest prince follows a golden falcon into three kingdoms of copper, silver, and gold, wins the prisoner princesses, and must descend into a well to rescue his brothers who have lowered him into the otherworld and abandoned him there.
summary.zh: 幼王子隨金獵鷹入銅銀金三國，救出被囚之三位公主；然其兄將他繫入冥井棄之，他須自尋歸路復救兄返。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale (ATU-type descent to the underground kingdom); standard collection.

passages.text: A tsar's three sons, hunting, rouse a golden falcon that carries off their father's horse; the youngest follows it through forests until he reaches the copper kingdom, where a princess taken by the falcon gives him a ball of thread that rolls ahead, showing the way. Kingdom by kingdom — copper, silver, gold — he finds a princess and a way onward, each telling him the falcon is to reach its father's house at last.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'The Three Kingdoms'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位沙皇的三個兒子在打獵時驚起了一隻金隼，那金隼叼走了他們父親的馬；最小的兒子一路追蹤它穿過森林，直到他抵達銅之國，那裡有一位被金隼擄來的公主，給了他一個線球，線球向前滾動，為他指路。他一個王國接著一個王國地走——銅之國、銀之國、金之國——在每一處都找到一位公主和繼續前行的路，每位公主都告訴他，那金隼終於要回到它父親的家了。

passages.text: He rescues all three princesses, and the brothers who waited above lower him into the well to the golden princess — then cut the rope and leave him below, taking the maidens home. In the underworld he is helped by a griffin (or eagle) that carries him up over the sea, fed by the carcasses he throws to it from his own flesh; the last bite he cuts from himself and heals at the golden princess's well. Returning, he exposes his brothers and marries the golden princess.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'The Three Kingdoms'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他救出了三位公主，而在上方等候的兄弟們將他縋入井中，送到金之國公主那裡——隨後割斷繩索，把他留在下面，帶著少女們回了家。在地下世界裡，一隻獅鷲（或鷹）幫助了他，載著他飛越海洋升上地面，牠以他從自己身上割下扔給牠的肉為食；最後一塊肉是他從自己身上割下的，並在金之國公主的井邊治癒了傷口。歸來之後，他揭發了兄弟們的罪行，並娶了金之國公主。

title.en: Ivan Tsarevich, the Fire-Bird, and the Gray Wolf
title.zh: 伊萬沙皇子、火鳥與灰狼

region.en: Russian fairyland, garden of the Fire-Bird (symbolic pin at Moscow)
region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境，火鳥之園（象徵性定位於莫斯科）

period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'Ivan Tsarevich, the Fire-Bird, and the Gray Wolf'

summary.en: Ivan Tsarevich is caught by the gray wolf for stealing the Fire-Bird, and must go on to steal the golden-maned horse of King Afron and the princess Yelena the Fair; his brothers murder him for the treasures — but the wolf brings back the water of death and water of life, and Ivan lives.
summary.zh: 伊萬沙皇子竊火鳥被灰狼擒，又受命去竊阿弗隆王之金鬃馬與美人葉連娜公主；其兄為奪寶而弒之——灰狼銜來死水與活水，伊萬復生。

sensitivity.note: Classic Russian fairy tale.

passages.text: The Fire-Bird came nightly to the tsar's garden and ate the golden apples; whoever caught it should win the kingdom. The eldest son watched and slept; the second watched and slept; the youngest, Ivan, caught one fiery feather — then, spurred by his brothers, sat up all the third night and seized the bird itself. But the brothers grew weary on the road, slept, and Ivan was caught by the gray wolf, who devoured the horse but, knowing who he was, spared the prince and promised to serve him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'Ivan Tsarevich, the Fire-Bird, and the Gray Wolf'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 火鳥每夜飛到沙皇的花園，啄食金蘋果；誰能捉住牠，誰就能得到這個王國。長子守望時睡著了；次子守望時也睡著了；最小的兒子伊凡捉住了一根火紅的羽毛——隨後，在兄弟們的慫恿下，他第三夜整夜守著，捉住了那隻鳥本身。然而兄弟們在途中睏倦睡去，伊凡卻被灰狼捉住，灰狼吞吃了他的馬，但因為知道他是誰，便饒了這位王子，並承諾為他效勞。

passages.text: The wolf changed itself into the horse of King Afron to trick that king into giving up the golden-maned steed, and again into a golden carriage to rescue Princess Yelena the Fair, who fell in love with Ivan on the road. At the end of the journey the brothers murdered Ivan, cut him to pieces, and rode home with the treasures.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 狼變作阿弗倫王的馬，騙得那位國王交出金鬃駿馬，又變作一輛金色馬車，救出了美麗的葉蓮娜公主，公主在途中愛上了伊凡。旅程將盡時，兄弟們謀害了伊凡，將他剁成碎塊，帶著財寶騎馬回家。

passages.text: The gray wolf gathered a raven's nest and forced the old raven to bring the water of death and the water of life; the dead water gathered the torn body together and the living water brought Ivan to life again. The wolf took the raven shape of the brothers' shame and Ivan came home ahead of them, to tell his father all — the treacherous brothers were punished, and Ivan married Yelena the Fair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 灰狼找來一個烏鴉巢，逼迫老烏鴉取來死水和活水；死水將被剁碎的身體聚攏在一起，活水使伊凡重獲生命。狼揭穿了兄弟們的恥辱，伊凡搶在他們之前回到家中，向父親稟明一切——那背信的兄弟們受到了懲罰，伊凡娶了美麗的葉蓮娜公主。

title.en: The Feather of Bright Finist the Falcon
title.zh: 明亮獵鷹菲尼斯特之羽

region.en: Russian fairyland (symbolic pin at Smolensk)
region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境（象徵性定位於斯摩棱斯克）

period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'The Feather of Bright Finist the Falcon'

summary.en: The youngest daughter buys a magic feather that becomes the falcon-hero Finist by night; her jealous sisters stab the falcon in his sleep, and the girl must wear out three pairs of iron shoes and beg at three women's doors before she can wake him with her tears.
summary.zh: 幼女購得神羽，夜間化為獵鷹英雄菲尼斯特；嫉妒的姐姐趁其睡時刺傷獵鷹；少女乃磨破三雙鐵鞋、三度叩三女之門，以淚水喚醒他。

sensitivity.note: Classic Russian fairy tale (Cinderella-type with bride quest in reverse).

passages.text: The youngest of three sisters bought at the market a feather of bright Finist the falcon. At night she opened the box, and out came a falcon that became a handsome young man; by day he flew away, by night he came again, and the girl loved him. Her jealous sisters learned of the youth, and while he slept they stuck needles and knives into his feathered coat, so that when the falcon flew up in the morning the iron had cut him, and he beat against the walls and vanished.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'The Feather of Bright Finist the Falcon'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 三姊妹中最年幼的那一個，在市場上買了一根光亮的雄鷹菲尼斯特的羽毛。到了夜裡，她打開匣子，一隻雄鷹從中飛出，化作一名英俊的青年；白天他飛走，夜裡他又歸來，少女便愛上了他。她那幾個心懷嫉妒的姊妹得知了這名青年的事，趁他熟睡時，把針與刀插進他的羽衣，於是當雄鷹在清晨飛起時，鐵器已割傷了他，他撞擊著牆壁，就此消失了。

passages.text: The girl set out to find him in three pairs of iron shoes and three iron staffs, which she wore out; she came to three old women in turn — one gave her a golden distaff, one a silver, one a golden spindle — and learned that Finist was bewitched into the Tsar's son and served by a false princess. She traded her gold and silver spinning gifts for three nights at his bedside, weeping until the third night, when her tears fell on the prince's shoulder and burned him, and he woke and knew her — for he had dreamed of her and never dreamed of the false bride.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 少女動身去尋他，帶了三雙鐵鞋與三根鐵杖，把它們都磨損耗盡了；她依次來到三位老婦人面前——一位給她一根金紡桿，一位給她一根銀紡桿，一位給她一根金紡錘——並得知菲尼斯特被施了魔法，化作沙皇之子，由一位假公主侍奉。她用自己的金銀紡織贈物，換來在他床邊守候三個夜晚，哭泣直到第三夜，她的淚水落在王子的肩上，灼燙了他，他便醒來，認出了她——因為他曾夢見她，卻從未夢見那假新娘。

title.en: The Water of Death and the Water of Life
title.zh: 死水與活水

region.en: Russian fairyland (symbolic pin at Ryazan)
region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境（象徵性定位於梁贊）

period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'Water of Youth, Water of Life, and Water of Death'

summary.en: Sent to fetch the waters of death and life for a blind or wounded tsar, the hero drinks the water of youth, is flung from a ship by treacherous brothers, is picked up by merchants, and returns — where the dead water and the living water sort the innocent from the guilty.
summary.zh: 為失明或重傷之沙皇取死水與活水，英雄途中飲青春之水，為奸兄拋入海中，為商船所救，終返——死水活水自會辨忠奸。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale.

passages.text: A tsar grown old and blind is told that only the waters of life, death, and youth can cure him; his sons set out after them. The youngest, misled and mocked by his brothers, finds the waters in the world beyond a mountain of glass — the dead water to gather a broken body, the living water to make it breathe, the water of youth to make it young.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'Water of Youth, Water of Life, and Water of Death'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位年老而失明的沙皇被告知，唯有生命之水、死亡之水與青春之水能治好他；他的兒子們便動身去尋這些水。最年幼的那一個被兄長們誤導與嘲弄，卻在玻璃山之外的世界裡找到了這些水——死亡之水用以聚攏破碎的軀體，活水使之呼吸，青春之水使之重返年輕。

passages.text: His brothers fling him into the sea with a stone to drown him and carry the false waters home; the youngest is picked up by merchants and comes back as a stranger to his own court. There the truth is proved by ordeal: the guilty are struck by the water of death and the innocent live. The blind tsar's eyes are washed with the true waters and he sees again; the traitors are punished and the youngest son inherits.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的兄長們把他綁上石頭扔進海裡，想淹死他，並把假的水帶回家；最年幼的那一個被商人救起，作為陌生人回到自己的宮廷。在那裡，真相藉由神判得以證實：有罪者被死亡之水擊中，無辜者則存活。盲眼沙皇的雙眼以真正的水洗滌，他重見光明；叛徒受到懲罰，最年幼的兒子繼承了王位。

title.en: Koshchei Without-Death: The Needle in the Egg
title.zh: 不死之科謝伊：蛋中針

region.en: Russian fairyland, island of Buyan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境，布揚島（象徵性定位）

period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'Koshchei Without-Death'

summary.en: Koshchei the Deathless carries his life hidden: in an egg, in a duck, in a hare, in a chest, on the island of Buyan — and only when the hunter breaks the egg and crushes the needle does the wizard's death arrive at last.
summary.zh: 不死之科謝伊藏其命於蛋中，蛋在鴨腹，鴨在兔腹，兔在箱中，箱在布揚島——唯獵手破蛋搗針，巫師之死方至。

sensitivity.note: Classic external-soul tale (parallel to Jack-and-the-Giant and Mwindo); cluster-tagged.

passages.text: Koshchei Without-Death cannot be killed, for his death is not in his body: it lies in an egg, the egg in a duck, the duck in a hare, the hare in a chest, and the chest stands on the island of Buyan under an oak — so the tales say. Whatever villainy he does, no sword can find him, for a man who holds his death elsewhere cannot be reached by weapons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'Koshchei Without-Death'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不死的科謝伊無法被殺死，因為他的死不在他的身體裡：它藏在一枚蛋中，蛋在鴨腹中，鴨在兔腹中，兔在寶箱中，而寶箱立於布揚島上的一棵橡樹之下——故事便是這樣說的。無論他犯下何等惡行，沒有哪把劍能尋到他，因為一個把死亡寄放於他處的人，是武器所觸及不到的。

passages.text: In Curtin's telling a princess — Vassilissa Golden Tress — is stolen by the wizard; the hero follows on horseback, is shattered and remade by friendly animals, and at last rides the hare down, opens the chest, and takes the egg in his hand. The wizard trembles, holds him by the hair, and begs — but the hunter breaks the egg, crushes the needle within, and Koshchei's death comes upon him at once; the stolen princesses are freed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在柯廷的敘述中，一位公主——金髮的瓦西麗莎——被巫師擄走；英雄騎馬追趕，被友好的動物擊碎又重塑，最終策馬追上了那隻兔子，打開寶箱，把蛋握在手中。巫師顫抖著，揪住他的頭髮，苦苦哀求——但獵人捏碎了蛋，碾碎了其中的針，科謝伊的死便立刻降臨於他；被擄的公主們得以獲釋。

title.en: Vassilissa Golden Tress, Bareheaded Beauty
title.zh: 金辮瓦西麗莎：不蒙頭之美

region.en: Russian fairyland (symbolic pin at Vladimir)
region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境（象徵性定位於弗拉基米爾）

period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'Vassilissa Golden Tress, Bareheaded Beauty'

summary.en: Bareheaded beauty — whose uncovered hair shames a whole court — is stolen by Koshchei, and won back by the youngest huntsman whom her golden hair has cured of blindness.
summary.zh: 不蒙頭之美——其散髮羞煞滿朝——為科謝伊所竊；被她金髮治癒眼盲之幼獵手終將她救回。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale.

passages.text: The tsar's general searches the land for the bareheaded beauty, Vassilissa Golden Tress, whose uncovered hair outshines every veiled head. Found and hidden, she is stolen by Koshchei the Deathless; her beauty is so strong that the tsar who would marry her is blinded by it, and only she herself can cure him — which is why the wizard carries her off.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'Vassilissa Golden Tress, Bareheaded Beauty'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 沙皇的將軍在全國各地搜尋那位不戴頭巾的美人瓦西麗莎·金髮，她未遮掩的頭髮勝過所有蒙著頭巾的頭。她被找到並藏匿起來後，又被不死者科謝伊擄走；她的美貌如此強烈，以致想娶她的沙皇為之目盲，唯有她本人能治好他——這正是巫師將她擄走的原因。

passages.text: The youngest huntsman of the blind tsar is cured when her hair touches his eyes, and he rides alone through the forest, sleeps in the dragon-lair, is remade by the animals he spared, and wins the egg of Koshchei's death; crushing the needle, he frees the princess, and Vassilissa opens her hair to the light and is bareheaded no more by any man's command.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 盲眼沙皇最年幼的獵人因她的頭髮觸及他的雙眼而復明，他獨自騎馬穿過森林，睡在龍穴之中，被他所饒恕的動物們重塑，並贏得了科謝伊之死的蛋；他碾碎那根針，釋放了公主，瓦西麗莎將頭髮敞向光明，從此不再因任何人的命令而不戴頭巾。

title.en: The Ring with Twelve Screws
title.zh: 十二道螺紋的戒指

region.en: Russian fairyland (symbolic pin at Nizhny Novgorod)
region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境（象徵性定位於下諾夫哥羅德）

period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'The Ring with Twelve Screws'

summary.en: A dying fisherman's son finds a ring shut with twelve screws; at midnight his dead father rises and tells him how to open it — and each screw released brings a wizard's servant and a fortune, until the twelfth brings the one the ring's true owner fears.
summary.zh: 瀕死漁夫之子得一枚十二道螺紋封閉的戒指；午夜亡父顯靈告其開法——每擰開一道，即召來一名精靈僕從與一份財富，直到第十二道引來戒指真正主人所懼者。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale.

passages.text: A fisherman's family is starving; the son nets a great fish and spares it, and is rewarded with a small ring shut with twelve screws. His dying father warns him: never open the ring by day. At midnight the father appears and teaches him to unloose the screws one by one, each releasing a spirit of the ring's service — gold, grain, ships, palaces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'The Ring with Twelve Screws'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個漁夫的家庭正在挨餓；兒子網住一條大魚並放生了牠，得到的回報是一枚由十二顆螺絲鎖住的小戒指。他垂死的父親警告他：白天絕不可打開戒指。午夜時分，父親現身，教他一顆一顆地鬆開螺絲，每鬆開一顆便釋放一個供戒指驅使的靈——黃金、穀物、船隻、宮殿。

passages.text: But the twelfth screw holds the master of the ring's first wife — a giant's widow with iron teeth — who seizes the youth and flies away with him to the world's end; the youth escapes by calling each released spirit back to serve him, and the twelve servants together pull the ring's fortunes back from the widow's iron grip, so that he comes home with the princess and the ring closed forever.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但第十二顆螺絲鎖著戒指主人的第一任妻子——一個長著鐵牙的巨人寡婦——她抓住少年，帶著他飛到世界的盡頭；少年藉由召回每一個被釋放的靈來服侍他而逃脫，十二名僕人合力將戒指的財富從寡婦的鐵爪中奪回，於是他帶著公主回家，戒指從此永遠關閉。

title.en: The Seven Simeons, Full Brothers
title.zh: 七兄弟西緬

region.en: Russian fairyland (symbolic pin at Tver)
region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境（象徵性定位於特維爾）

period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'The Seven Simeons, Full Brothers'

summary.en: Seven brothers each with one miraculous gift — a super-sighted eye, a stealer, a builder of a tower to heaven, a swift runner, a shooter, a fisher — use their gifts together to steal the tsar's famous beauty Helen, escape the fastest ship of the tsar by building an island of gold, and win pardon and riches.
summary.zh: 七兄弟各有一項神技——千里眼、妙手、造塔通天、疾行、神射、善漁——合力競技，偷取沙皇傾城美人海倫，以金島誘開追艦，得赦而富貴。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale.

passages.text: Seven brothers, full brothers, Simeons by name, each have one gift: the first sees a hundred versts with a single eye; the second can steal like a mouse; the third can build a tower to the sky; the fourth runs like the wind; the fifth shoots with unerring aim; the sixth catches fish with his bare hands. Each gift alone seems useless to the tsar, but together they are a kingdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'The Seven Simeons, Full Brothers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 七個兄弟，同父同母的親兄弟，皆名為西梅翁，各有一項天賦：第一個能以單眼看見一百俄里；第二個能像老鼠一樣偷竊；第三個能建造直達天際的高塔；第四個跑起來如風；第五個射擊百發百中；第六個能徒手捕魚。每一項天賦單獨看來對沙皇都毫無用處，但合在一起便是一個王國。

passages.text: They use them to steal the famous beauty Helen from the tsar himself: the watchful eye finds her ship, the thief takes her aboard unseen, the tower-builder raises the tower to carry them over the sea, the runner carries the boat, the shooter clears the way, the fisher finds the road under the water. Pursued by the tsar's fleet, they build an island of gold in the middle of the sea where the pursuers' ships founder, and the tsar, finding his Helen wedded and beyond reach, laughs instead of hanging them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們運用這些天賦從沙皇本人手中偷走了著名的美人海倫：警覺之眼找到了她的船，竊賊將她神不知鬼不覺地帶上船，建塔者築起高塔載他們越過大海，奔跑者扛著船，射手開闢道路，漁夫在水下找到路。被沙皇的艦隊追擊時，他們在海中央造出一座黃金島，追兵的船隻在那裡沉沒，而沙皇發現他的海倫已嫁為人婦、再也無法觸及，便一笑置之，而非將他們絞死。

title.en: The Enchanted Princess
title.zh: 被施魔法的公主

region.en: Russian fairyland (symbolic pin at Suzdal)
region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境（象徵性定位於蘇茲達爾）

period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'The Enchanted Princess'

summary.en: The hero must break an enchantment without a word spoken or a forbidden thing touched — and the smallest slip destroys everything, until a true silence of three days wins the princess and the castle.
summary.zh: 英雄須在不言一語、不犯一戒之下破除魔法——稍有失誤便前功盡棄；唯三日的真正靜默方能贏得公主與城堡。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale.

passages.text: A youth finds a palace of the enchanted princess where every servant is marble and everything lies under a spell. He is warned: he may take what he likes, but he must not speak a word nor touch what is forbidden; if he keeps the rule for three days the enchantment will break, but at the least slip everything turns to stone again and the princess is lost.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'The Enchanted Princess'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一名青年發現了一座受魔法公主所居的宮殿，宮中每一名僕役皆為大理石所造，萬物皆受咒語所困。他受到告誡：他可任意取用所欲之物，但不得說出一個字，亦不得觸碰禁忌之物；倘若他守此規矩三日，咒語便會解除，然而只要稍有閃失，萬物便會再度化為石頭，公主也將永遠失去。

passages.text: On the third night a fly torments him, a candle falls, and almost he speaks; but the true silence holds, the statues breathe, the princess wakes, and the whole court steps out of its spell. The youth marries the princess and rules the kingdom his silence bought.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第三夜，一隻蒼蠅折磨著他，一支蠟燭倒下，他幾乎開口說話；但真正的沉默守住了，雕像開始呼吸，公主甦醒，整座宮廷皆脫離了咒語。青年娶了公主，並統治了這片由他的沉默所換來的國度。

title.en: Vassilissa the Cunning and the Tsar of the Sea
title.zh: 機智的瓦西麗莎與海沙皇

region.en: Russian fairyland, sea kingdom (symbolic pin at Astrakhan)
region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境，海之王國（象徵性定位於阿斯特拉罕）

period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'Vassilissa the Cunning, and the Tsar of the Sea'

summary.en: When the Tsar of the Sea drags an old merchant down for a debt of magic, his daughter Vassilissa teaches her mortal lover to outwit the sea-court with a silver and a golden dove, a spinning wheel of invisibility, and the riddle that saves his life three times.
summary.zh: 海沙皇因魔法債拖走老商人；其女瓦西麗莎以銀鴿金鴿、隱形紡車與三度救命之謎，教會凡人戀人智鬥海宮。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale.

passages.text: An old merchant owes the Tsar of the Sea a debt of magic and is dragged down beneath the waters; his daughter Vassilissa is sent with him to learn what the sea-tsar wants. She meets the sea-tsar's daughter, the wise Vassilissa, who pities her and teaches her what the court demands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'Vassilissa the Cunning, and the Tsar of the Sea'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一名老商人欠了海沙皇一筆魔法之債，被拖入水底；他的女兒瓦西麗莎隨他同去，以探明海沙皇究竟想要什麼。她遇見了海沙皇的女兒——聰慧的瓦西麗莎，後者憐憫她，並教她宮廷所要求的一切。

passages.text: The mortal hero who comes to the rescue is told by the sea-tsar's daughter to answer the riddle, spin the invisible wheel, and change into the silver dove and the golden one, so that the sea-tsar's three tests are each met. The lover is saved three times — by the daughter's cunning, by his own patience, and by the waters themselves, which bear him home. He marries her, and the sea's debt is paid.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 前來搭救的凡人英雄聽從海沙皇之女的指示，解開謎題、轉動那看不見的輪子，並化身為銀鴿與金鴿，如此一來，海沙皇的三道考驗便一一得解。這名戀人三度獲救——憑著那女兒的機巧、憑著他自己的耐心，也憑著海水本身，將他送回家鄉。他娶了她，海之債就此償清。

title.en: The Footless and the Blind: Two Cripples Who Saved a Tsarevich
title.zh: 無足者與盲者：兩位殘者救回沙皇子

region.en: Russian fairyland (symbolic pin at Pskov)
region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境（象徵性定位於普斯科夫）

period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'The Footless and the Blind'

summary.en: A blind man and a man without feet are given to one another as if the tsar's joke — the blind one carries the footless one, who sees for them both; they find a cure for each other's disability at a witch's well, and together rescue the tsarevich.
summary.zh: 沙皇戲言令盲者與無足者相依——盲者背負無足者，無足者為其看路；他們在女巫之井找到互愈之水，合力救回沙皇子。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale.

passages.text: The tsar jests that the blind man shall carry the man without feet, and each shall be the other's legs and eyes; the pair set out to seek their fortunes. The footless one sees a fire in the forest, a witch's well, and the herbs that cure blindness and lameness, and the blind one carries him to it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'The Footless and the Blind'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 沙皇戲言道：盲人當背負那無腳之人，二人互為對方的腿與眼；這對搭檔便出發去尋覓各自的命運。無腳者望見林中有一團火、一口女巫之井，以及能治癒盲眼與跛足的药草，盲人便背著他前往該處。

passages.text: Each is cured at the well and hears, in the witch's garden, the fate of the stolen tsarevich; they free him, bear him home, and the tsar's joke has made the two cripples into the heroes of his kingdom — the blind man's legs and the lame man's eyes being worth more together than the tsar's whole court.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 二人在井邊各自痊癒，並在女巫的花園中聽聞了那被擄走的沙皇太子之命運；他們救出太子，將他揹回家中，而沙皇的戲言竟使這兩名殘疾之人成了他王國的英雄——盲人的腿與跛者的眼，合在一起，其價值勝過沙皇的整座宮廷。

title.en: The Pig with Gold Bristles, the Deer with Golden Horns
title.zh: 金鬃豬、金角鹿與金尾金鬃駿馬

region.en: Russian fairyland (symbolic pin at Voronezh)
region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境（象徵性定位於沃羅涅日）

period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'The Pig with Gold Bristles, the Deer with Golden Horns, and the Golden-Maned Steed'

summary.en: A father's dying command — to guard a garden of golden apples — is broken by the youngest son, who follows a golden pig, a golden-horned deer, and a golden-maned steed into the underworld garden of a many-headed dragon, and wins the girl there.
summary.zh: 父親臨終命幼子守護金蘋果園；幼子失職追尋金鬃豬、金角鹿、金尾金鬃駿馬，闖入多首龍之下界花園，贏得彼處少女。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale.

passages.text: On his deathbed a father warns his sons that thieves will come for the golden apples in the garden: the pig with gold bristles, the deer with golden horns, the golden-maned steed with golden tail. The eldest watches and sleeps; the second watches and sleeps; the youngest shoots at the thief and follows the blood into a hill, down into a garden where the dragon keeps its treasures.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'The Pig with Gold Bristles, the Deer with Golden Horns, and the Golden-Maned Steed'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位父親在臨終之際警告他的兒子們，盜賊會來偷園中的金蘋果：那頭長著金鬃毛的豬、那頭長著金角的鹿、那匹金鬃金尾的駿馬。長子看守卻睡著了；次子看守也睡著了；幼子朝盜賊射箭，並循著血跡追進一座山丘，深入一座園子，惡龍就在那裡守著牠的寶物。

passages.text: He takes the three wonders and the girl who tends the garden, and the dragon — a twelve-headed serpent riding its horse of fire — pursues; the girl's magic horse outstrips the serpent's, and the hero severs the serpent's heads and burns the body. The brothers take the treasures home; the youngest marries the garden's keeper, and the golden apples ripen again in the tsar's garden.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他取走了三件奇物與照料園子的姑娘，惡龍——一條騎著火馬的十二頭巨蛇——緊追不捨；姑娘的魔法馬勝過了巨蛇的馬，英雄斬下巨蛇的頭顱並焚燒了屍身。兄弟們把寶物帶回家；幼子娶了園子的看守人，金蘋果又在沙皇的園中成熟了。

title.en: Go to the Verge of Death and Split the Grain of Wood
title.zh: 行至死界，破木取紋

region.en: Russian fairyland (symbolic pin at Kaluga)
region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境（象徵性定位於卡盧加）

period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'Go to the Verge of Death and Split the Grain of Wood'

summary.en: Sent for a cure that lies at 'the verge of death', the hero learns to split the grain of living wood — inside which his sisters' stolen souls lie hidden — and finds the many-headed dragon that keeps them.
summary.zh: 為求『死界』之藥而行的英雄，學會劈開活木之紋——妹妹們被竊的魂靈即藏其中——並尋獲看守她們的多首龍。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale.

passages.text: A father lies dying and the cure is to be found 'at the verge of death, where the grain of wood must be split'; the youngest son goes alone, for the roads are deadly. He serves a witch who teaches him how to split wood — the grain of the forest — and finds in each split log a wonder his brothers laughed at.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'Go to the Verge of Death and Split the Grain of Wood'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位父親臥病垂危，而解藥須在「死亡之涯，於木紋必須劈開之處」尋得；幼子獨自前往，因為那些道路凶險致命。他服侍一位女巫，女巫教他如何劈木——劈開森林的木紋——並在每一塊劈開的木頭裡發現一件他的兄長們曾嗤笑的奇物。

passages.text: At the verge of death he comes to the dragon's garden and finds his stolen sisters there; he slays the dragon with the axe-split of living wood, gathers the sisters, and brings them home so that the dying father rises from his bed — the cure of the verge of death is the dragon's own blood, split out of the grain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在死亡之涯，他來到惡龍的園子，發現他被擄走的姊妹們就在那裡；他以劈開活木的一斧斬殺了惡龍，聚集了姊妹們，並把她們帶回家，使垂死的父親從床上起身——死亡之涯的解藥，正是從木紋中劈出的惡龍自身的血。

title.en: Streets Paved with Golden Pebbles: The Coronation Wedding of Huayna Capac
title.zh: 街道鋪滿金礫:瓦伊納·卡帕克的加冕婚禮

region.en: Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: After the fall of Hualpaya the councillors ruled three years, then prepared the coronation feast, assigning to Huayna Ccapac as wife his own sister Ccoya Mama Cusirimay, according to the custom of his ancestors. They were married on the day of the coronation: all the walls and roofs of the city were covered with rich plumes, and the streets were paved with golden pebbles. The Ynca came forth from the house of his grandfather Pachacuti followed by the Apu Curacas of Colla-suyu; Mama Cusirimay came from the palace of Tupac Ynca Yupanqui attended by the Curacas of the other suyus. The Ynca and his spouse entered the temple of the Creator Pachayachachi, each by a separate door, shod in llanques of gold. Raised to the platform, he said a prayer in a loud voice which concluded the day's proceedings and they were considered married. After three days the tupac-yauri and suntur-paucar were delivered, then the ccapac-llautu and unincha, the ccapac-unancha or royal standard, and the huaman-champi of two edges. The Ynca took an oath and touched the ground, promising to emulate the deeds of his forefathers, to attend to the things of Pachayachachi and his Ccuricancha, and to do no evil to the kingdom; then the Apu Challca Yupanqui said a prayer to the Creator, beseeching him to guard and protect the Ynca with his powerful hand.
summary.zh: 瓦爾帕亞伏誅後,眾臣執政三年,籌備加冕大典,依祖先舊俗,以王姊科亞·瑪瑪·庫西里瑪伊為瓦伊納·卡帕克之妻。加冕之日成婚:全城牆垣屋頂遍覆華羽,街道鋪以金礫。印加王自祖父帕查庫提之宅而出,科利亞蘇尤諸庫拉卡扈從;王后自圖帕克·尤潘琪之宮而出,餘三蘇尤庫拉卡侍從。王與后各由一門入造物主帕查亞查奇之神廟,足登金鞋。登台之後,王高聲誦禱,禱畢即視為成婚。三日後授圖帕克-亞烏里權杖與孫圖爾-保卡爾,再授卡帕克-勞圖頭帶、烏寧恰、卡帕克軍旗與雙刃瓦曼戰斧。王宣誓並以手觸地,誓效祖先功業、敬奉帕查亞查奇與其科里坎查、毋害大蘇尤之邦。大祭司阿普·查爾卡·尤潘琪隨之向造物主祈禱,求其以大能之手護佑印加王。

sensitivity.note: Coronation liturgy from the native-authored chronicle; sibling marriage recorded as dynastic custom.

passages.text: After three years they began to prepare for the feast of the coronation; and they assigned as the wife of Huayna Ccapac his own sister Ccoya Mama Cusirimay, according to the custom of his ancestors. They were married on the day of the coronation, when all the walls and roofs in the city were covered with rich plumes of feathers, and the streets were paved with golden pebbles. The people were gorgeously dressed in cumpis and plumes. They say that fifty thousand men guarded the city and the fortress of Sacsahuaman, and that the festival was a wonderful sight.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 三年之後，他們開始籌備加冕慶典；並依照祖先的習俗，指定瓦伊納·卡帕克自己的姊妹科亞·瑪瑪·庫西里邁為他的妻子。他們在加冕當日成婚，當時城中所有的牆垣與屋頂都覆滿了華美的羽飾，街道則以金色卵石鋪成。人們身著昆皮（cumpis）與羽飾，盛裝打扮。據說有五萬人守衛著城市與薩克薩瓦曼堡壘，而那場慶典是令人嘆為觀止的奇景。

passages.text: The Ynca and his spouse then entered the temple, each by a separate door, the temple being that of the Creator Pachayachachi; the High Priest was called Apu Challcu Yupanqui. The sovereign and his wife were shod in llanques of gold; and afterwards they gave him the chipana of gold and raised him to the platform whence he performed these ceremonies, where he said a prayer in a loud voice, which concluded the proceedings of that day, and they were considered to be married. Afterwards they delivered to him the tupac-yauri and the suntur-paucar, after three days, and the ccapac-llautu and the unincha in the same place where they were married.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隨後，印加與他的配偶各自從不同的門進入神廟，那神廟是造物主帕查亞查奇的神廟；大祭司名為阿普·查爾庫·尤潘基。君主與他的妻子腳穿金製的利安克鞋；之後他們授予他金製的奇帕納，並將他升上他舉行這些儀式的高台，他在那裡高聲誦念祈禱文，為當日的儀式畫下句點，他們便被視為成婚了。三日之後，他們在同一處他們成婚的地方，又將圖帕克-堯里與孫圖爾-保卡爾交付給他，以及卡帕克-堯圖與烏寧查。

passages.text: The Ynca took an oath and touched the ground, promising to emulate the deeds of his forefathers, and to attend to the things of Pachayachachi and his Ccuricancha, and to do no evil to the kingdom of Ttahuantin-suyu, keeping the laws of former Yncas, and favouring all loyal servants. Then the Apu Challca Yupanqui said a prayer to the Creator, beseeching him to guard and protect the Ynca with his powerful hand, and to defend him from his enemies. Those present then shouted out their acclamations, and all praised the Creator called Pachayachachi Uiracochan. Then the Ynca went to the Huacay-pata, where was his ccapac-usnu, and there each chief and captain, in his order, promised obedience to the new sovereign.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 印加王宣誓並觸地，承諾效法其祖先的功業，照料帕查亞查奇（Pachayachachi）及其科里坎查（Ccuricancha）之事，不危害塔萬廷蘇尤（Ttahuantin-suyu）王國，恪守歷代印加王的法律，並善待所有忠誠的僕從。隨後，阿普·查爾卡·尤潘基（Apu Challca Yupanqui）向造物主祈禱，懇求祂以強有力的手守護並庇佑印加王，護衛他免受敵人侵害。在場眾人隨即高聲歡呼，齊聲讚頌名為帕查亞查奇·維拉科昌（Pachayachachi Uiracochan）的造物主。之後，印加王前往瓦凱帕塔（Huacay-pata），即其卡帕克烏斯努（ccapac-usnu）所在之處，各首領與隊長依序向新君主宣誓效忠。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Sister Who Refused: Signs of Blood in the Heavens
title.zh: 拒婚之妹:天現血兆

region.en: Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Huayna Ccapac wished to marry his second sister, named Mama Cuca, who refused her consent; he then ill-treated her and began to use force, but her prayers and menaces made him desist. Then he went with presents and offerings to the body of his father, praying him to give her for his wife; but the dead body gave no answer, while fearful signs appeared in the heavens, portending blood. This was called Ccalla-sana. It made Huayna Ccapac give up his intention in regard to his sister, so he gave her to a very old and ugly Curaca who was a great chewer of coca - not for her good, but in order to bring shame upon her. She wept; and leaving the old man, whose name was Hacaroca, she entered the house of the Acllas as a princess, and became abbess, never having submitted to the old man. The Ynca was then married a second time, but not with such ceremonies, to Ccoya Chimpu Runtucay.
summary.zh: 瓦伊納·卡帕克欲娶次妹瑪瑪·庫卡,妹不允;王遂相逼,幾欲用強,然其妹哭求與怒斥並至,王乃罷手。王攜禮物祭品至先王遺體前,求亡父將此妹賜己為妻;亡父無言,而天際卻現可怖之兆,預示流血——此謂「卡利亞-薩納」。王遂打消娶妹之念,將她許給一位極老極醜、嗜嚼古柯的庫拉卡——非為其好,實欲羞辱之。妹泣;離開老翁哈卡羅卡,以公主之身入阿克亞貞女之屋,後為女院長,始終未屈身老翁。王乃第二次成婚,禮數較簡,娶科亞·欽普·倫圖卡伊。

sensitivity.note: The rejected-sister episode with its heaven omens; the mummy-consultation motif recurs in this cycle.

passages.text: Then Huayna Ccapac Ynca wished to marry his second sister, named Mama Cuca, who refused her consent, and he then ill-treated her and began to use force, but her prayers and menaces made him desist. Then he went with presents and offerings to the body of his father, praying him to give her for his wife, but the dead body gave no answer, while fearful signs appeared in the heavens, portending blood. This was called Ccalla-sana.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隨後，瓦伊納·卡帕克·印加（Huayna Ccapac Ynca）欲娶其名為瑪瑪·庫卡（Mama Cuca）的二妹，她拒絕應允，於是他便虐待她並開始動用武力，但她的祈禱與威脅使他作罷。之後，他帶著禮物與祭品前往其父的遺體前，祈求父親將她賜予他為妻，但遺體毫無回應，同時天空中出現預示流血的可怕徵兆。此事被稱為卡利亞薩納（Ccalla-sana）。

passages.text: This made Huayna Ccapac give up his intention in regard to his sister, so he gave her to a very old and ugly Curaca who was a great chewer of coca; and he did this, not for her good, but in order to bring shame upon her. She wept; and leaving the old man, whose name was Hacaroca, she entered the house of the Acllas as a princess, and became abbess, never having submitted to the old man.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此事使瓦伊納·卡帕克放棄了關於其妹的念頭，於是他將她許配給一位極其年老醜陋、酷愛嚼食古柯的庫拉卡（Curaca）；他這樣做並非為她著想，而是為了使她蒙羞。她哭泣著，離開那位名為哈卡羅卡（Hacaroca）的老人，以公主之身進入阿克利亞（Acllas）之屋，成為女院長，始終未曾順從那老人。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Oracle of Pachacamac Speaks Alone to the Inca
title.zh: 帕查卡馬克神諭獨對印加王

region.en: Ccuricancha of Pachacamac, coast of Lima (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 帕查卡馬克科里坎查(今利馬海岸)(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In those days messengers came from Rimac bringing word that, within the Ccuricancha of Pachacamac, the huaca had said that it desired to see the Ynca. So he went to visit Pachamac, and the huaca spoke to him alone, saying that he must take riches to Chimu, and honour it more than Uiracochan Pachayachachi. The Ynca consented, and the wizards rejoiced. But the Ynca was to blame, Salcamayhua says, for having confided in the promises of the huaca at Pachacamac and other idols: in the following war his Colla-suyu army was destroyed and his men left starved and in rags, while the war became more fierce than ever.
summary.zh: 彼時里馬克遣使來報:帕查卡馬克的科里坎查內,瓦卡有言,欲見印加王。王遂往訪帕查卡馬克,瓦卡獨對王而言:命他攜重寶至奇穆,並敬奉此瓦卡超越維拉科查·帕查亞查奇。王允之,眾巫歡騰。然而薩爾卡馬瓦說,王之過,在於輕信帕查卡馬克瓦卡與諸偶像的許諾:其後戰爭中,科利亞蘇尤大軍盡歿,部眾飢寒交迫,戰事反愈演愈烈。

sensitivity.note: The Pachacamac oracle episode linking coastal cult and highland kingship; the author's moralizing frame preserved.

passages.text: In those days messengers came from Rimac, bringing word that, within the Ccuricancha of Pachacamac (the Ccuricancha was a temple, and there were many in different parts, the largest being in Cuzco), the huaca had said that it desired to see the Ynca. So he went to visit Pachamac, and the huaca spoke to him alone, saying that he must take riches to Chimu, and honour him more than Uiracochan Pachayachachi. The Ynca consented, and the wizards rejoiced. But the Ynca was to blame for having confided in the promises of the huaca at Pachacamac and other idols. His men were now left starved and in rags, while the war became more fierce than ever.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那些日子裡，來自里馬克（Rimac）的使者帶來消息，說在帕查卡馬克（Pachacamac）的科里坎查（Ccuricancha）內（科里坎查乃是一座神廟，各地有許多座，最大者位於庫斯科），那瓦卡（huaca）曾言其渴望見到印加王。於是印加王前往拜訪帕查馬克，那瓦卡獨自對他說話，說他必須將財富帶往奇穆（Chimu），並比對維拉科昌·帕查亞查奇（Uiracochan Pachayachachi）更加尊崇他。印加王應允，巫師們歡欣鼓舞。但印加王錯在輕信帕查卡馬克那瓦卡及其他偶像的承諾。此時他的部下飢餓不堪、衣衫襤褸，而戰爭卻比以往更加激烈。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Yahuar-ccocha: The Lake Washed Red
title.zh: 亞瓦爾-科查:被血染紅的湖

region.en: Lake Yahuar-ccocha, near Otabalo, Ecuador (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 奧塔瓦洛附近亞瓦爾-科查湖(今厄瓜多)(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In the war against the Cayambis the Colla-suyu troops, ordered to take the enemy in the rear, marched very leisurely; the Cayambis fell upon them furiously and caused great slaughter, so that few escaped of the fine and powerful army of Colla-suyu. Reinforced at last, the Ynca attacked in three columns; the Colla-suyus climbed the fortresses of the Cayambis and attacked them fiercely, sparing neither age nor sex, the Ynca fighting in person. The Cayambis fled to the montañas of Otabala and assembled on the shores of a lake, where they were surrounded and there was great slaughter. The warriors washed their arms in the lake, and there was a mass of blood in the centre, so the lake was called Yahuar-ccocha - the lake of blood.
summary.zh: 征卡揚比之役,奉命迂迴敵後的科利亞蘇尤軍行動遲緩,被卡揚比人猛撲,屠戮殆盡。援軍既至,印加王分三路進攻:科利亞軍攀上卡揚比人的山寨,猛烈衝殺,老幼婦孺不留;印加王親自督戰。卡揚比人退往奧塔瓦洛山間,聚於一湖之濱,遭四面合圍,殺戮極慘。戰士們在湖中洗滌武器,湖心盡是血污,故名此湖為「亞瓦爾-科查」——血湖。

sensitivity.note: Battle-name etiology; the lake-name is still on the map near Otavalo.

passages.text: The Colla-suyu troops had been ordered to take the enemy in the rear, but meanwhile the Cayambis did great injury to the royal camp, and discovered that the Colla-suyus were marching very leisurely. So they fell upon them furiously, and caused great slaughter, so that few escaped in the fine and powerful army of Colla-suyu.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 科利亞蘇尤（Colla-suyu）的軍隊曾奉命從後方包抄敵人，但與此同時，卡揚比人（Cayambis）對王室營地造成重大損害，並發現科利亞蘇尤人正十分從容地行軍。於是他們猛烈撲向科利亞蘇尤人，造成大規模屠殺，以致科利亞蘇尤那支精銳強大的軍隊中鮮有人逃脫。

passages.text: The Cayambis fled to the montañas of Otabala, and assembled on the shores of a lake, where they were surrounded, and there was great slaughter. The warriors washed their arms in the lake, and there was a mass of blood in the centre, so the lake was called Yahuar-ccocha.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡揚比人逃往奧塔巴拉（Otabala）的山林，並聚集於一湖之畔，在那裡被團團圍住，遭到大規模屠殺。戰士們在湖中清洗武器，湖心積聚成一大片血泊，因此該湖被稱為亞瓦爾科查（Yahuar-ccocha）。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Box of Butterflies: The Message That Killed Huayna Capac
title.zh: 蝴蝶之盒:致瓦伊納·卡帕克於死的信使

region.en: Quito (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基多(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The Ynca advanced beyond Pasto but returned to Quito, where he solemnized the Ccapac-Raymi. At the hour for eating a messenger arrived in a black mantle, who reverently kissed the Ynca and gave him a pputi covered up. The Ynca told the messenger to open it, but he excused himself, saying that the command of the Creator was that the Ynca alone should do so. So the Ynca opened it, and there came flying out a quantity of things like butterflies or bits of paper, which spread abroad until they disappeared. This was the pestilence of sarampion, and in a few days the general Mihicnaca Mayta died, with many other captains, their faces being covered with scabs. When the Ynca saw this, he ordered a house to be built of stone, in which he hid himself, and there died. After eight days they took out the body quite dried up, and embalmed it, and took it to Cuzco on a litter, richly dressed and armed as if it had been alive. A son, named Tupac Atahualpa, was left in Quito with many chiefs and captains - Quis-quis, Challcuchima, Unacchuyllu, Rumi-ñaui, Ucumari, and many more.
summary.zh: 印加王遠征至帕斯托之外,折返基多,隆重舉行卡帕克-雷米祭。進餐時分,一名身披黑氅的信使來到,恭敬吻王之手,獻上一只覆蓋的「普普提」(小盒)。王命信使開盒;信使推辭,說造物主之命:唯印加王可開。王親啟之——盒中飛出無數似蝴蝶、似紙屑之物,四散飛揚,直至消失。此即「薩拉姆皮翁」(麻疹?)瘟疫。數日之間,大將米克納卡·馬伊塔與眾多隊長相繼死去,面上滿布痂痕。王見狀,命人以石築屋,自匿其中,竟死於斯。八日後啟視,遺體已乾,乃敷香裹殮,以轎抬回庫斯科,衣甲鮮明,一如生前。基多留有王子圖帕克·阿塔瓦爾帕,與基斯-基斯、查爾庫奇馬、烏納丘尤盧、魯米-尼亞維、烏庫馬里等大將。

sensitivity.note: The smallpox epidemic narrated as a boxed plague of butterflies sent by the Creator - one of the most striking omens in Andean literature.

passages.text: He then advanced beyond Pasto, but returned to Quito, where he solemnized the Ccapac-Raymi. At the hour for eating a messenger arrived in a black mantle, who reverently kissed the Ynca, and gave him a pputi covered up. The Ynca told the messenger to open it, but he excused himself, saying, that the command of the Creator was that the Ynca alone should do so.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他隨後越過帕斯托，但返回基多，在那裡舉行了卡帕-拉伊米慶典。到了進食的時刻，一名披著黑色斗篷的信使抵達，他恭敬地親吻了印加，並交給他一個蓋著的普蒂。印加吩咐信使打開它，但信使推辭了，說造物主的命令是只應由印加本人來打開。

passages.text: So the Ynca opened it, and there came flying out a quantity of things like butterflies or bits of paper, which spread abroad until they disappeared. This was the pestilence of Sarampion, and in a few days the general Mihicnaca Mayta died, with many other captains, their faces being covered with scabs.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是印加打開了它，從中飛出大量像蝴蝶或紙片般的東西，它們四散開來，直至消失。這便是薩拉姆皮翁的瘟疫，數日之內，將軍米希納卡·邁塔便死了，還有許多其他隊長也死了，他們的臉上佈滿了瘡痂。

passages.text: When the Ynca saw this, he ordered a house to be built of stone, in which he hid himself, and there died. After eight days they took out the body quite dried up, and embalmed it, and took it to Cuzco on a litter, richly dressed and armed as if it had been alive. A son, named Tupac Atahualpa, was left in Quito, and many chiefs and captains, called Quis-quis, Challcuchima, Unacchuyllu, Rumi-ñaui, Ucumari, and many more.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 印加見此，便下令用石頭建造一座房屋，他把自己藏於其中，並死在那裡。八天之後，他們取出已完全乾枯的屍體，將其防腐處理，並以華服盛裝、佩帶武器，彷彿生前一般，用擔架抬往庫斯科。基多留下了一個名叫圖帕克·阿塔瓦爾帕的兒子，以及許多首領和隊長，名叫基斯基斯、查爾庫奇馬、烏納克丘伊柳、魯米-尼亞維、烏庫馬里，還有許多其他人。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Married to the Dead: How Huascar Made His Mother Legitimate
title.zh: 與亡者成婚:瓦伊斯卡爾之「正名」

region.en: Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The body of Huayna Ccapac was conveyed to Cuzco with much ceremony and deposited with the other bodies of the Yncas; there was general mourning. Then Yuti Tupac Cusi Huallpa Huascar Ynca made his mother, Rava Ocllo, marry the dead body, in order that he might become legitimate, and the ministers of the temple performed the ceremony out of fear. Thus Tupac Cusi Huallpa took the title of legitimate son of Huayna Ccapac, and called upon all the chiefs of Ttahuantin-suyu to swear obedience to him, which was done. He induced the great Curacas to ask the ministers of Ccuricancha to deliver to him the ccapac-llautu, suntur-paucar, tupac-yauri and ccapac-uncu; at the end of a year he received the ccapac-llautu with the name of Yuti Cusi Huallpa Huascar Ynca. He married his sisters Chuqui-huy-pachuquipa and Ccoya Mama Chuqui huypa chuquipa.
summary.zh: 瓦伊納·卡帕克的遺體以大禮運回庫斯科,與歷代印加遺體同殿安放,全國舉哀。尤蒂·圖帕克·庫西·瓦爾帕(瓦伊斯卡爾)為使自己的嫡子身份成立,竟令其母拉瓦·奧克略與亡父遺體「成婚」;神廟執事懼其威,遂行婚儀。圖帕克·庫西·瓦爾帕自此稱瓦伊納·卡帕克之嫡子,召大蘇尤眾酋宣誓效忠,眾皆從之。他並促使眾庫拉卡請科里坎查執事授予卡帕克-勞圖、孫圖爾-保卡爾、圖帕克-亞烏里與卡帕克-溫庫。一年後,他受卡帕克-勞圖,稱「尤蒂·庫西·瓦爾帕·瓦伊斯卡爾·印加」,並娶其妹楚基-瓦伊-帕丘基帕與科亞·瑪瑪·楚基-瓦伊-帕丘基帕。

sensitivity.note: The mummy-marriage: legitimacy manufactured through the ancestor cult; a uniquely Andean political rite.

passages.text: The body of Huayna Ccapac was conveyed to Cuzco with much ceremony, and the people made obeisances to it. After it was deposited with the other bodies of the Yncas, there was general mourning for his death. Then Yuti Tupac Cusi Huallpa Huascar Ynca made his mother, Rava Ocllo, marry the dead body, in order that he might become legitimate, and the ministers of the temple performed the ceremony out of fear.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 瓦伊納·卡帕克的遺體以極大的排場被運往庫斯科，民眾向它行禮。當它與其他印加的遺體一同安放之後，人們為他的死舉行了普遍的哀悼。隨後，尤蒂·圖帕克·庫西·瓦爾帕·瓦斯卡爾印加讓他的母親拉瓦·奧克略與那具遺體成婚，以便使自己成為合法之子，而神廟的祭司們出於恐懼而主持了這一儀式。

passages.text: Thus Tupac Cusi Huallpa took the title of legitimate son of Huayna Ccapac, and called upon all the chiefs of Ttahuantin-suyu to swear obedience to him, which was done. He then prepared for his coronation, and induced the great Curacas to ask the ministers of Ccuricancha to deliver to him the ccapac-llautu, suntur-paucar, tupac-yauri, and ccapac-uncu. Great preparations were made for the coronation, and there was a distribution of rich dresses, plumes, and arms. At the end of a year he received the ccapac-llautu, with the name of Yuti Cusi Huallpa Huascar Ynca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是圖帕克·庫西·瓦爾帕取得了瓦伊納·卡帕克合法之子的稱號，並號召塔萬廷蘇尤的所有首領宣誓服從他，眾人皆照辦了。他隨後為自己的加冕做準備，並促使那些大庫拉卡們請求庫里坎查的祭司們將卡帕-勞圖、孫圖爾-保卡爾、圖帕克-堯里和卡帕-溫庫交給他。加冕的準備工作極為盛大，並分發了華貴的服飾、羽飾和武器。一年之後，他接受了卡帕-勞圖，並獲得尤蒂·庫西·瓦爾帕·瓦斯卡爾印加之名。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Damsels Cried to Heaven: Huascar's Outrage at Pocana-cancha
title.zh: 貞女仰天呼號:瓦伊斯卡爾在波卡納-坎恰的暴行

region.en: Pocana-cancha, Vilcas region (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 維爾卡斯地區波卡納-坎恰(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: On his return to Cuzco, passing through Titicaca where he set up a golden image of the sun, Huascar came to Pocana-cancha, where he found all the Apu Curacas coming in their litters according to the privilege granted by former Yncas. In this place he ordered the Acllas, of all four classes, to be brought into the open square, in the middle of all the Apu Curacas and the whole army. Then he told a hundred Indians of the Llama-llamas and Hayacuchos, while they were performing their dances, to seize the damsels and ravish them in public. The damsels, when they were thus treated, cried out and raised their eyes to heaven; and all the great men of the kingdom resented such conduct, and looked upon this Huascar Ynca as half a fool, and only treated him with reverence from fear.
summary.zh: 瓦伊斯卡爾回師庫斯科,途經的的喀喀,立太陽金像而拜,稱之為「維拉科查·因蒂」。行至波卡納-坎恰,見歷代印加特許乘轎的眾庫拉卡相繼而至。在此地,他命將四個等級的阿克亞貞女全部帶到大廣場中央——眾庫拉卡與全軍眼前——並命一百名利亞馬-利亞馬斯與哈亞庫科斯人趁起舞之際,當眾擄掠、姦污這些女子。貞女受辱,仰天哭號;王國的顯貴們無不憤恨,皆視瓦伊斯卡爾為「半個瘋子」,只因畏懼才表面恭敬。

sensitivity.note: The outrage on the Aclla houses' wards is recorded here as a dynastic indictment, part of the moral case against Huascar in the civil-war cycle.

passages.text: On his return to Cuzco he came to Pocana-cancha, where he found all the Apu Curacas coming in their litters according to the privilege granted by former Yncas, and Huascar Ynca laughed at this, although he did not take away the privilege. In this place he ordered the Acllas, of all four classes, to be brought into the open square, in the middle of all the Apu Curacas and the whole army. Then he told a hundred Indians of the Llama-llamas and Hayacuchos, while they were performing their dances, to seize the damsels and ravish them in public.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他返回庫斯科後，來到波卡納-坎查，在那裡他見到所有阿普庫拉卡按照歷代印加所授予的特權乘著他們的轎子前來，瓦斯卡爾印加見此大笑，儘管他並未取消這一特權。在此地，他下令將全部四個等級的阿克利亞帶到露天廣場上，置於所有阿普庫拉卡和全軍之中。然後他吩咐一百名利亞馬-利亞馬斯和哈亞庫喬的印第安人，在他們表演舞蹈時，抓住那些少女並當眾施暴。

passages.text: The damsels, when they were thus treated, cried out and raised their eyes to heaven; and all the great men of the kingdom resented such conduct, and looked upon this Huascar Ynca as half a fool, and only treated him with reverence from fear.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那些少女受到這般對待時，放聲哭喊，舉目望天；王國中所有的大人物都對這般行徑感到憤慨，視這位瓦斯卡尔·印卡為半個傻子，只是出於畏懼才對他保持敬意。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Drums of the Messengers' Skins: The Insult That Started the War
title.zh: 信使之皮製鼓:引爆內戰之辱

region.en: Quito and Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基多與庫斯科(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: At that time Tupac Atahuallpa sent to Huascar Ynca, beseeching him to give him the title and nomination of Governor of the Provinces of Quito, and the Ynca Huascar granted the request, and gave him the name of Ynca-ranti. Then the chief of the Cañaris, named Urco-calla, brought false news to Huascar Ynca, asking him why he consented that Tupac Atahuallpa should have the title of Ynca. This enraged the Ynca, and when Tupac Atahuallpa sent him rich presents he caused them to be burnt, and drums to be made of the skins of the messengers who brought them, except a few, whom he sent back to Quito dressed as women, and with very shameful messages to Auqui Atahuallpa. They were followed by a chief named Huaminca-atoc, whom the Ynca sent against Atahuallpa with 1200 men, and orders to take him and the other captains prisoners. The surviving messengers arrived at Quito and reported what had happened to Auqui Tupac Atahuallpa, who received the news in great sorrow, but in silence. The captain replied he would answer by his deeds; and Auqui Atahuallpa, with the consent of all his captains, determined to take up arms: the people of Quito swore to obey him, he assumed the title of Ynca, began to use a litter, and assembled 13,000 warriors.
summary.zh: 其時,圖帕克·阿塔瓦爾帕遣使求瓦伊斯卡爾封他為基多諸省總督;瓦伊斯卡爾允其所請,賜名「印加-蘭蒂」。然而卡尼亞里人酋長烏爾科-卡利亞向王進讒,問王為何容許阿塔瓦爾帕僭用印加之號。王大怒:阿塔瓦爾帕獻上的重禮被他付之一炬,並剝來使之人皮製鼓;僅留數人,男扮女裝,攜極盡羞辱之語送回基多。王又遣將瓦明卡-阿托克率一千二百人往執阿塔瓦爾帕及其諸將。生還的信使抵基多報信,阿塔瓦爾帕聞之,大慟而默然。他遣人問瓦明卡-阿托克興師何為,對方答曰「以行動作答」。阿塔瓦爾帕遂得眾將之諾,決意起兵:基多民眾宣誓效忠,他僭稱印加之號,乘坐轎輦,聚兵一萬三千。

sensitivity.note: The insult-cycle opening the civil war; the skin-drums motif is one of the war's signature atrocities.

passages.text: At that time Tupac Atahuallpa sent to Huascar Ynca, beseeching him to give him the title and nomination of Governor of the Provinces of Quito, and the Ynca Huascar granted the request, and gave him the name of Ynca-ranti. Then the chief of the Cañaris, named Urco-calla, brought false news to Huascar Ynca, asking him why he consented that Tupac Atahuallpa should have the title of Ynca. This enraged the Ynca, and when Tupac Atahuallpa sent him rich presents he caused them to be burnt, and drums to be made of the skins of the messengers who brought them, except a few, whom he sent back to Quito dressed as women, and with very shameful messages to Auqui Atahuallpa.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當時，圖帕克·阿塔瓦爾帕派人去見瓦斯卡尔·印卡，懇求他賜予自己基多諸省總督的頭銜與任命，印卡瓦斯卡尔應允了這一請求，並賜他「印卡-蘭蒂」之名。隨後，一位名叫烏爾科-卡利亞的卡尼亞里首領向瓦斯卡尔·印卡帶來假消息，問他為何竟同意讓圖帕克·阿塔瓦爾帕擁有印卡的頭銜。這激怒了印卡，當圖帕克·阿塔瓦爾帕送來豐厚禮物時，他命人將禮物燒毀，並用送禮使者的皮製成鼓，只留下少數幾人，把他們打扮成女人送回基多，並帶給奧基·阿塔瓦爾帕極為羞辱的口信。

passages.text: The surviving messengers arrived at Quito, and reported what had happened to Auqui Tupac Atahuallpa, who received the news in great sorrow, but in silence. Then he sent to the captain Huaminca-atoc, asking him to declare for what purpose he had come with an army; and the captain replied that he would answer by his deeds. Then Auqui Atahuallpa, with the consent of all his captains, determined to take up arms, and the people of Quito swore to obey him. He assumed the title of Ynca, and began to use a litter, and assembled 13,000 warriors.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 倖存的使者抵達基多，向奧基·圖帕克·阿塔瓦爾帕報告了所發生的一切，他聽聞這消息後悲痛萬分，卻默然不語。隨後他派人去見統帥瓦明卡-阿托克，問他率軍前來究竟意欲何為；那位統帥回答說，他將以行動作答。於是奧基·阿塔瓦爾帕在眾統帥的一致同意下，決意拿起武器，基多的人民也宣誓服從他。他自稱印卡，開始乘坐肩輿，並集結了一萬三千名戰士。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Two Lumps of Grease: The Oracle of the Burning Camps
title.zh: 兩塊油脂:燃燒營地的神諭

region.en: Hill of Cocha-cassa, near Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科附近科查-卡薩山(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: At midnight Challcuchima and Quisquis lighted a fire on their left hands with a piece of grease; putting one lump of grease to represent the camp of Huascar Ynca, and the other for the camp of Atahuallpa. And the one in the place of Huascar Ynca burnt much more than that in the place of Atahuallpa, so that the grease of Huascar, burning up so high, went out very quickly, while that of Atahuallpa went on burning. Then Challcuchima and Quisquis sang the haylli, and told their men that all would go well. They set out for Utcu-pampa in search of Huascar Ynca, and got there at sunset with six hundred and forty men, when the Ynca was asleep, and took him prisoner, routing the Rucanas who were his bearers, and so they carried him to Sallcantay. When the army found that Huascar Ynca was taken they were terrified, and each tribe went off to its own land.
summary.zh: 午夜,查爾庫奇馬與基斯-基斯以一塊油脂在左手邊生火:一塊脂代表瓦伊斯卡爾之營,一塊代表阿塔瓦爾帕之營。代表瓦伊斯卡爾的那塊油燒得猛烈異常,火苗高竄,轉瞬即熄;而代表阿塔瓦爾帕的那塊油卻持續燃燒不熄。二將遂唱「阿伊利」凱歌,告訴部眾:大事必成。他們率六百四十人於日落時抵烏特庫-潘帕,趁瓦伊斯卡爾酣睡之際將其生擒,擊潰其轎伕魯卡納斯人,押往薩爾坎泰。大軍聞王被擒,駭然四散,各族各歸故土。

sensitivity.note: Fire-grease divination before the decisive capture; a Quechua oracle rite recorded by a native author.

passages.text: At midnight Challcuchima and Quisquis lighted a fire on their left hands with a piece of grease; putting one lump of grease to represent the camp of Huascar Ynca, and the other for the camp of Atahuallpa. And the one in the place of Huascar Ynca burnt much more than that in the place of Atahuallpa, so that the grease of Huascar, burning up so high, went out very quickly, while that of Atahuallpa went on burning. Then Challcuchima and Quisquis sang the haylli, and told their men that all would go well.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 午夜時分，查爾庫奇馬與基斯基斯用一塊油脂在左手上點起火來；他們放一團油脂代表瓦斯卡尔·印卡的軍營，另一團代表阿塔瓦爾帕的軍營。代表瓦斯卡尔·印卡的那團燒得遠比代表阿塔瓦爾帕的那團猛烈，以致瓦斯卡尔的那團油脂燒得如此之高，很快就燃盡熄滅，而阿塔瓦爾帕的那團卻持續燃燒。於是查爾庫奇馬與基斯基斯唱起海利之歌，告訴手下的人一切都會順利。

passages.text: They set out for Utcu-pampa in search of Huascar Ynca, and got there at sunset with six hundred and forty men, when the Ynca was asleep, and took him prisoner, routing the Rucanas who were his bearers, and so they carried him to Sallcantay. When the army found that Huascar Ynca was taken they were terrified, and each tribe went off to its own land.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們出發前往烏特庫-潘帕尋找瓦斯卡尔·印卡，率六百四十人在日落時分抵達那裡，當時印卡正在睡覺，他們將他擒獲，擊潰了為他抬轎的盧卡納人，就這樣把他帶到了薩爾坎泰。當大軍得知瓦斯卡尔·印卡已被擒獲，驚恐萬分，各部族紛紛逃回自己的土地。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Chillca Leaves Instead of Coca: The Outraged Huascar Cries to the Creator
title.zh: 以奇爾卡葉代古柯:受辱的瓦伊斯卡爾哭訴造物主

region.en: Quepay-pampa, near Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科附近凱帕伊-潘帕(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: They insulted the Ynca by tying a rope round his neck, and Quisquis called him Cocahacho and Sulluya, which means bastard, eater of coca, and offered him many other affronts. Then Quisquis and Challcuchima abused the mother of the Ynca, saying: 'Come here, Mama Ocllo, you who were the concubine of Huayna Ccapac.' When Huascar heard this, he asked them who they were that they should pass judgment on his descent; upon which Quisquis struck him, and gave him chillca leaves instead of coca. When he was thus outraged, Huascar raised his eyes, and cried out: 'O Lord and Creator, how is it possible? Why hast thou sent me these burdens and troubles.' In those days Quisquis ordered all the children of Huascar Ynca to be slain, and all his servants, up to fifteen hundred persons, who were within the palace of Puca-marca.
summary.zh: 他們以繩套住印加王之頸以辱之;基斯-基斯喚他「科卡哈喬」與「蘇利亞」——意為私生子、嚼古柯者——並加以種種凌辱。二將又辱其母:「過來啊,瑪瑪·奧克略,你這瓦伊納·卡帕克的妾!」瓦伊斯卡爾聞言,反問對方何人,竟敢評斷他的血統;基斯-基斯當即掌摑之,並以奇爾卡葉充作古柯遞給他。受此奇恥,瓦伊斯卡爾舉目望天,呼曰:「主啊,造物主,怎麼可能如此?你為何將這些重負與苦難加於我身?」其後,基斯-基斯下令盡殺瓦伊斯卡爾諸子及其僕從——普卡-馬爾卡宮中的1500口皆死。

sensitivity.note: The humiliation cycle; the coca/chillca substitution is a specific ritual insult - coca is sacred, chillca is a weed.

passages.text: They insulted the Ynca by tying a rope round his neck, and Quisquis called him Cocahacho and Sulluya, which means bastard, eater of coca, and offered him many other affronts. Then Quisquis and Challcuchima abused the mother of the Ynca, saying: 'Come here, Mama Ocllo, you who were the concubine of Huayna Ccapac.' When Huascar heard this, he asked them who they were that they should pass judgment on his descent; upon which Quisquis struck him, and gave him chillca leaves instead of coca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們把繩索套在印卡的脖子上侮辱他，基斯基斯稱他為科卡哈喬和蘇利亞，意即雜種、嚼古柯者，還對他施加了許多其他侮辱。接著基斯基斯與查爾庫奇馬辱罵印卡的母親，說道：『過來，瑪瑪·奧克略，你這曾是瓦伊納·卡帕克情婦的女人。』瓦斯卡尔聽到這話，便問他們是何許人，竟敢評判他的血統；於是基斯基斯打了他，並給他奇爾卡葉子代替古柯。

passages.text: When he was thus outraged, Huascar raised his eyes, and cried out: 'O Lord and Creator, how is it possible? Why hast thou sent me these burdens and troubles.' In those days Quisquis ordered all the children of Huascar Ynca to be slain, and all his servants, up to fifteen hundred persons, who were within the palace of Puca-marca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 華斯卡爾遭受如此凌辱，便抬眼高呼：「啊，主與造物者，這怎麼可能？你為何將這些重擔與苦難加於我？」那些日子裡，基斯基斯下令將華斯卡爾·印卡的子女全數殺害，連同他的僕役，凡在普卡馬爾卡宮殿之內者，多達一千五百人。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Cock Knew His Name: Spaniards Taken for Uiracocha
title.zh: 雞鳴知名:西班牙人被誤作維拉科查

region.en: Caxamarca and Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 卡哈馬卡與庫斯科(象徵性標記)

period: Salcamayhua wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In a few days the news arrived that the Spaniards had landed, and there was great dismay; by the advice of Quisquis great riches were buried in the earth, and Huascar had previously ordered a chain of gold and three thousand loads of gold and silver concealed in Cunti-suyu. Francisco Pizarro captured Atahuallpa in the midst of a vast concourse of Indians, after he had spoken with the friar Vicente de Valverde, when twelve thousand men were killed: for the people thought that they were the messengers of Pachayachachic Uiracocha, and when they fired off their guns, it was supposed to be Uiracocha. When Atahuallpa was in prison the cock crowed, and he said that even the birds knew his name; from that time they called the Spaniards Uiracocha, because they declared they brought the law of God, and the cock Atahuallpa. Atahuallpa sent messages to Antamarca with orders that Huascar should be killed, and began to pretend to be sad to deceive Pizarro; Huascar Ynca was killed in Antamarca with his son, wife and mother, with great cruelty. Atahuallpa was baptized and called Don Francisco, and afterwards he was put to death as a traitor.
summary.zh: 數日之後,西班牙人登陸的消息傳來,舉國震恐。依基斯-基斯之議,大批財寶被埋入土中;瓦伊斯卡爾此前已命將金鏈與三千馱金銀藏於昆蒂蘇尤。弗朗西斯科·皮薩羅在萬民簇擁中擒獲阿塔瓦爾帕——此前他剛與瓦爾韋爾德修士對話——一萬二千人被殺:因為人民以為他們是帕查亞查奇·維拉科查的信使;他們放槍時,眾人以為那便是維拉科查。阿塔瓦爾帕在獄中,雄雞啼鳴,他說:連鳥兒都知道我的名字。自那時起,人們稱西班牙人為「維拉科查」——因為他們自稱帶來上帝的律法——而稱雄雞為「阿塔瓦爾帕」。阿塔瓦爾帕遣使至安塔馬爾卡,下令處死瓦伊斯卡爾,隨即假裝悲慟以欺騙皮薩羅;瓦伊斯卡爾與其子、妻、母在安塔馬爾卡慘遭殺害。阿塔瓦爾帕受洗名「堂·弗朗西斯科」,後以叛國之罪被處死。

sensitivity.note: The conquest told through native eyes: the theophanic misrecognition of the invaders; the ethnonym 'Viracocha' for Spaniards originates here.

passages.text: But in a few days the news arrived that the Spaniards had landed, and there was great dismay. By the advice of Quisquis great riches were buried in the earth; and it is also said that Huascar had previously ordered a chain of gold and three thousand loads of gold, with as many of silver, to be concealed in Cunti-suyu.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而數日之後，消息傳來，說西班牙人已經登陸，眾人驚惶不已。基斯基斯獻策，將大量財寶埋入地下；據說華斯卡爾先前也曾下令，將一條金鏈與三千擔黃金、同樣多的白銀，藏於孔蒂蘇尤。

passages.text: Francisco Pizarro captured Atahuallpa in the midst of a vast concourse of Indians, after he had spoken with the friar Vicente de Valverde, when twelve thousand men were killed. For the people thought that they were the messengers of Pachayachachic Uiracocha; and when they fired off their guns, it was supposed to be Uiracocha. When Atahuallpa was in prison the cock crowed, and he said that even the birds knew his name. From that time they called the Spaniards Uiracocha, because they declared to Atahuallpa that they brought the law of God. Hence they called the Spaniards Uiracocha, and the cock Atahuallpa.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 弗朗西斯科·皮薩羅在萬千印第安人聚集之中擒獲阿塔瓦爾帕，此前他已與修士維森特·德·巴爾韋德交談，當時有一萬二千人被殺。因為眾人以為他們是帕查亞查奇克·維拉科查的使者；而當他們鳴放火槍時，眾人便以為那是維拉科查。阿塔瓦爾帕在獄中時，公雞啼鳴，他說連鳥兒也知道他的名字。自那時起，人們便稱西班牙人為維拉科查，因為他們向阿塔瓦爾帕宣稱自己帶來了上帝的律法。因此他們稱西班牙人為維拉科查，稱公雞為阿塔瓦爾帕。

passages.text: This Atahuallpa sent messages to Antamarca with orders that Huascar should be killed; and after he had sent them he began to pretend to be sad, trying to deceive the captain, Francisco Pizarro. So, by orders of Atahuallpa, they killed Huascar Ynca in Antamarca, with his son, wife, and mother, with great cruelty. Atahuallpa was baptized and called Don Francisco, and afterwards he was put to death as a traitor.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這位阿塔瓦爾帕派人送信至安塔馬爾卡，下令殺死華斯卡爾；送出之後，他便開始裝作悲傷，企圖欺瞞隊長弗朗西斯科·皮薩羅。於是，奉阿塔瓦爾帕之命，他們在安塔馬爾卡以極其殘酷的手段殺害了華斯卡爾·印卡，連同他的兒子、妻子與母親。阿塔瓦爾帕受洗，取名唐·弗朗西斯科，之後以叛徒之罪被處死。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Kaiumars, the First King of Mankind
title.zh: 蓋尤馬爾斯：人類第一王

region.en: Mount Alburz heights (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿爾布茲山區（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Gaiumart, secs. 1-2

summary.en: The legendary record says Kaiumars first wore the crown among men, ruling from a mountain when the sun stood in Aries; his people wore leopard-skins and the arts of life began under him. Secretly Ahriman envied him and set his monstrous son against the king's beloved heir Siyamak, and the Black Div tore the young prince apart on the field of battle.
summary.zh: 傳說記載蓋尤馬爾斯首戴王冠，太陽在白羊座之時於山上稱王；其民披豹皮，生活技藝始於其朝。阿赫里曼暗中嫉妒，遣其怪異之子攻擊王之愛子西亞馬克，黑魔於陣前將王子撕裂，王國為之哀慟。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Zoroastrian figures rendered as medieval Persian legend. No living community restriction.

passages.text: The record of the first days has perished; yet the compiler of ancient legend says that Gaiumart first devised crown and throne and was a Shah. This order and grace and lustre came to earth when the sun was dominant in Aries and shone so brightly that the world grew young. Its lord dwelt at first upon a mountain, and thence his throne and fortune rose; he and all his troop wore leopard-skins, and under him the arts of life began, for food and dress were still in their infancy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Gaiumart sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最初時日的記載已經湮滅；然而古代傳說的編纂者說，蓋烏馬爾特首先創製了冠冕與寶座，成為沙赫。當太陽主宰白羊宮、光芒如此明亮，使世界重獲青春之時，這秩序、恩澤與光輝便降臨大地。其君主起初居於一座山上，他的寶座與命運由此而興；他與其全體部眾皆披豹皮，在他治下，生活技藝開始萌芽，因為飲食與衣著當時仍處於初始階段。

passages.text: He had a son named Siyamak, ambitious as his sire, his father's life and joy. Only in secret did the Shah have an enemy: wicked Ahriman, led by envy, who had a son like a fearless savage wolf and a host of warriors behind him. The son assembled that host and resolved to win the great Shah's throne, and he filled the world with clamour. Who told Gaiumart of the foe? The blessed Suriish appeared in fairy form, bedight in leopard-skin, and told the king what his enemies were plotting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Gaiumart sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他有一子名為西亞馬克，雄心勃勃如其父，是父親的生命與歡樂。沙赫只有一個暗中的敵人：邪惡的阿里曼，受嫉妒驅使，他有一子，如同無畏的野狼，身後還有一群戰士。其子召集那支軍隊，決心奪取偉大沙赫的寶座，使世界充滿喧囂。是誰將敵人告知蓋烏馬爾特？蒙福的蘇里什以仙女之形顯現，身披豹皮，告訴國王他的敵人們正在密謀何事。

passages.text: When host met host, Siyamak came unarmed to grapple with the son of Ahriman; that horrible Black Div clutched at him, bent down the prince of lofty stature, and rent him open. Gaiumart left his throne, wailed aloud, tore his face and body with his nails, and all the soldiers wept as birds and beasts flocked to the mountain with doleful cries. After a year the blessed Suriish came again: lament no more, said he, collect thy troops and turn thy foemen into dust. So the aged king girt himself for vengeance night and day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Gaiumart sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當兩軍相遇，西雅馬克赤手空拳上前與阿里曼之子搏鬥；那可怕的黑色迪夫一把抓住他，將這位身材高大的王子按倒，把他撕裂開來。蓋尤馬爾特離開王座，放聲痛哭，用指甲抓破自己的臉和身體，所有士兵都隨之哭泣，鳥獸也帶著悲鳴聚集到山上。一年之後，蒙福的蘇里什再度降臨：他說，不要再哀哭了，召集你的軍隊，把你的敵人化為塵土。於是這位年邁的國王日夜束裝，準備復仇。

title.en: Hushang Wins Iron, Canals, and Seed from the Rocks
title.zh: 胡尚格：鐵器、溝渠與五穀

region.en: Mount Alburz heights (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿爾布茲山區（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Hushang sec. 1

summary.en: Hushang, grandson of Kaiumars and son of the slain Siyamak, reigns forty years as a just Shah who civilises the world. He is the first to smelt iron from the rock and invent smithing, cutting axes, saws, and mattocks; he digs irrigation canals, and where men had lived on fruit and leaves they learn to sow, reap, and plant.
summary.zh: 胡尚格為西亞馬克之子、蓋尤馬爾斯之孫，公正治世四十年：首自岩石煉鐵，發明鍛造，造斧鋸鎬；鑿渠引水；昔日人類以果葉為生，自此學會播種收穫，安居其位。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.
