passages.text: The blessed Siyamak had left a son, his grandsire's minister, a prince named Hushang, a name implying sense and wisdom. Hushang, a just and prudent sovereign, assumed his grandsire's crown and for forty years heaven turned above him. I lord it over the seven climes, he said, victorious everywhere; my word is law, I practise bounteousness and equity; so hath God willed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Hushang sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蒙福的西雅馬克留下了一個兒子，是他祖父的臣相，一位名叫胡尚的王子，這名字含有見識與智慧之意。胡尚是一位公正而審慎的君主，繼承了祖父的王冠，上天在他頭頂運轉了四十年。他說，我統治七域，所向皆捷；我的話即是法律，我施行慷慨與公正；此乃上帝所願。

passages.text: He civilised the world and filled the surface of the earth with justice. He was the first to deal with minerals and win iron from the rock by craft; he gained more knowledge and, inventing smithing, made axes, saws, and mattocks. Next he turned to irrigation by canals and ducts, and grace made the labour short. As knowledge grew men sowed and reaped and planted, each produced the loaf whereof he ate, and kept his station. Till then men had lived on fruit in poor estate and clothed themselves in leaves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Hushang sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他教化世界，以正義充滿大地。他是第一個處理礦物、憑技藝從岩石中煉出鐵的人；他獲得了更多知識，發明了鍛鐵之術，製造出斧頭、鋸子和鋤頭。接著他轉向以運河與溝渠灌溉，天恩使這勞作變得短暫。隨著知識增長，人們播種、收割、栽植，各人生產自己所吃的麵包，並安守其位。在此之前，人們生活貧困，以果實為食，以樹葉蔽體。

title.en: How Hushang Found Fire and Founded the Feast of Sada
title.zh: 胡尚格取火與薩達節之起源

region.en: Mountains of Iran (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 伊朗山地（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Hushang sec. 2

summary.en: Hushang hurled a stone at a fire-breathing serpent on a mountain; it missed and struck a flint, and the sparks revealed fire hidden in stone. Hushang praised God for the radiant gift, taught men to worship it, made a great blaze with his people, and held the feast called Sada, which remains his memorial. He then domesticated ox, ass, and sheep for toil and produce.
summary.zh: 胡尚格於山中擲石擊蛇，石落燧石迸出火星，揭示石中藏火。他感謝神賜光焰，教人崇火，夜聚族人舉火設宴，是為薩達節，永為其紀念。其後馴服牛驢羊供役使，取其毛革而澤被萬民。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; etiological myth for the Sada festival and fire-cult. No living community restriction.

passages.text: One day Hushang reached a mountain with his men and saw afar a long swift dusky form with eyes like pools of blood and jaws whose smoke bedimmed the world. Hushang the wary seized a stone, advanced, and hurled it royally. The world-consuming worm escaped, the stone struck on a larger one, and both were shivered; sparks issued and the centres flashed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Hushang sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，胡尚帶著他的人馬來到一座山前，遠遠看見一個長而迅捷的暗色形體，雙眼如血池，下顎噴出的煙霧使世界昏暗。謹慎的胡尚抓起一塊石頭，上前，威風凜凜地擲了出去。那吞噬世界的巨蟲逃走了，石頭擊中了一塊更大的石頭，兩者都碎裂開來；火花迸出，中心閃耀。

passages.text: The fire came from its stony hiding-place, and the worldlord offered praise for such a radiant gift. He made of fire a cynosure: this lustre is divine, he said, and thou, if wise, must worship it. That night he made a mighty blaze and stood around it with his men and held the feast called Sada; that bright festival remaineth as his memorial.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Hushang sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 火從其石中藏身之處而來，世界之主為這般光輝的恩賜獻上讚美。他使火成為眾人矚目之物：他說，這光輝是神聖的，你若明智，就必須崇拜它。那一夜他燃起熊熊大火，與他的人馬環立四周，舉行了名為薩達的慶典；那光明的節日留存至今，作為他的紀念。

passages.text: By grace and kingly power he domesticated ox, ass, and sheep and turned them to good use: pair them, he said, use them for toil, enjoy their produce, and provide therewith your taxes. He slew the furry rovers for their skins, so that squirrel, ermine, fox, and sable clothed the talkers; he gave and spent freely, and when he passed he took naught with him but repute.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Hushang sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 憑藉天恩與王權，他馴化了牛、驢和羊，並善加利用：他說，讓它們配對，用它們勞作，享用它們的產物，並以此繳納你們的賦稅。他宰殺那些毛茸茸的遊走之獸以取其皮，於是松鼠、貂、狐與黑貂的皮毛穿在了會說話的人身上；他慷慨施予、盡情花費，當他離世時，除了聲名什麼也沒帶走。

title.en: Tahmuras, the Binder of the Div
title.zh: 塔胡穆拉斯縛魔

region.en: Mount Alburz heights (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿爾布茲山區（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Tahmuras

summary.en: Tahmuras son of Hushang invents spinning, drapery, and falconry, then binds the rebellious divs and their patron Ahriman with spells and rides him horsewise around the world. The captured demons beg their lives, promising a new and fruitful art in return, and teach him thirty scripts, among them Pahlavi, so that sounds may be delineated in writing.
summary.zh: 胡尚格之子塔胡穆拉斯（縛魔者）發明紡織與鷹獵；群魔叛亂，他以咒縛眾魔，又縛阿赫里曼如馬乘騎環行天下。被縛之魔求饒，許以新藝，遂授其三十種文字——帕拉維文在焉——聲音自此得以書寫。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source. The motif 'transformation' covers Ahriman turned horsewise for riding; interpretive tag. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Hushang possessed a wise and noble son hight Tahmuras, the Binder of the Div, who took the throne and girt his loins to rule. I will restrain the Div, he said, will reign supreme, and use the useful for the common good. He sheared the flocks and men began to spin; he thus invented clothes and draperies. He chose the swiftest quadrupeds and made them feed on barley and hay, lured the shyest beasts of prey from hill and plain to obey him, and began to tame the hawk and noble falcon while men looked on amazed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Tahmuras (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 胡尚有一子，名曰塔赫穆拉斯，聰慧而高貴，號稱「迪弗之縛者」。他繼承王位，束腰以治國。他說道：「我將制服迪弗，稱霸天下，並使有用之物造福眾人。」他剪下羊群的毛，人們於是開始紡線；他由此發明了衣服與布匹。他挑選最迅捷的四足獸，使之以麥與草為食；又將山間平原上最羞怯的猛獸誘出，使之聽命於他；並開始馴服鷹與高貴的隼，人們在一旁看得驚嘆不已。

passages.text: Glorious with the Grace, he bound Ahriman with spells and rode him horsewise at whiles around the world. Thereat the divs rebelled and held a conclave, for their throne of gold was void. When Tahmuras was ware he girt him with Grace, took his massive mace, and advanced against the huge magician host led by the Black Div; of the foe he bound the most by spells and quelled the others with his mace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Tahmuras (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他蒙受榮光而顯赫，以咒語縛住阿里曼，有時如馭馬般騎著他環遊世界。於是迪弗們起而反叛，召開會議，因為他們的金座已然空懸。塔赫穆拉斯察覺之後，以榮光束身，拿起巨大的狼牙棒，向由黑迪弗率領的龐大魔法師軍團進擊；他將敵人中的大多數以咒語縛住，其餘的則以狼牙棒擊平。

passages.text: The captives bound and stricken begged their lives: destroy us not, and we will teach thee a new and fruitful art. He gave them quarter, and they taught him how to write some thirty scripts, such as the Persian, Arabic, Sughdi, Chini, and Pahlavi, and thus delineate sounds. How many better arts he explored in a reign of thirty years, yet passed away, and all his toils became his monument.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Tahmuras (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 被縛受創的俘虜乞求活命：「不要毀滅我們，我們將教你一門新穎而豐產的技藝。」他饒恕了他們，他們便教他書寫約三十種文字，如波斯文、阿拉伯文、粟特文、秦文與巴列維文，並藉此描摹聲音。他在三十年的統治中探索了多少更為精妙的技藝，然而終究逝去，他的一切辛勞都成了他的紀念碑。

title.en: Jamshid's Crafts, Castes, and Aerial Throne
title.zh: 賈姆希德：百工、四階與凌空御座

region.en: Istakhr of Pars (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 帕爾斯伊斯塔赫爾（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Jamshid sec. 1

summary.en: Jamshid son of Tahmuras forges arms and silk, founds the four castes of priests, warriors, tillers, and artisans, teaches the divs to bake brick and raise baths and sanctuaries, unlocks gems and perfumes and leechcraft, and is first to cross the sea in ships. He builds a gem-inlaid throne that divs bear up to heaven, and the day is named New Year's Day — the first of Farwardin, memorial of that Shah.
summary.zh: 賈姆希德鑄兵甲、織絲綢，立祭司、戰士、農夫、工匠四階；教魔製磚築浴場聖所，發寶石香料醫道，首以舟渡海。更造鑲寶御座，魔抬升天，眾人撒寶石慶賀，是日定名歲首——法爾瓦爾丁月初一，永為其紀念。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Nowruz etiology included. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Jamshid, the mighty son of Tahmuras, succeeded to his glorious father's throne and wore in kingly wise the crown of gold. His girdle was the Grace of king of kings, and all the world obeyed him; contests ceased and the age had rest. Mine is the Grace, he said, I am both king and archimage; I will restrain ill-doers and make for souls a path toward the light. He first wrought arms and opened for warriors the door of fame, fashioning iron into helmets, hauberks, breastplates, and coats of armour for man and horse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Jamshid sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 賈姆希德，塔赫穆拉斯之子，強而有力，繼承了他榮耀父親的王位，以王者之姿戴上金冠。他的腰帶乃是萬王之王的榮光，全世界都服從他；爭鬥止息，時代安寧。他說道：「榮光屬於我，我既是君王又是大賢；我將約束作惡之人，為靈魂開闢一條通往光明之路。」他首先鍛造武器，為戰士們打開聲名之門，將鐵打造成頭盔、鎖子甲、胸甲，以及供人與馬穿戴的鎧甲。

passages.text: Then to the joy of all he founded castes for every craft: a sacerdotal caste to serve in quiet on the mountains, a military caste of lion-men to guard the royal throne, an agricultural caste of independent tillers — idleness maketh freemen slaves, quoth he — and the artizans who live by handiwork. He bade the foul divs temper earth with water and fashion moulds for bricks, laying foundations with stone and lime and raising hot baths, lofty halls, and sanctuaries. He searched the rocks for jewels — rubies, amber, silver, gold — and brought them forth by spells.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Jamshid sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隨後，為了眾人的喜悅，他為各種行業創立了種姓：祭司種姓，於山間靜默侍奉；武士種姓，如獅之人，守衛王座；農人種姓，為獨立自主的耕作者——他說，懶惰使自由人淪為奴隸；以及以手工為生的工匠。他命令污穢的迪弗以水調和泥土，製作磚模，以石與石灰奠基，並建造熱浴場、高聳的廳堂與聖所。他在岩石中尋覓寶石——紅寶石、琥珀、銀、金——並以咒語將它們取出。

passages.text: He introduced the scents men enjoy, as camphor, musk, sweet aloe, and bright rosewater; next leechcraft and the healing of the sick were secrets opened by Jamshid. He crossed the sea in ships. His wisdom achieved, he made himself a throne with what a wealth of gems inlaid, which when he willed the divs took up and bare from earth to heaven. There the Shah sat sunlike in mid air; the world assembled round his throne in wonder, and bestowed upon the day the name of New Year's Day, the first of Farwardin, which remaineth the memorial of that Shah.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Jamshid sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他引進了人們喜愛的種種香氣，如樟腦、麝香、沉香與清亮的玫瑰水；接著，醫術與治病之法也成了賈姆希德所揭開的祕密。他乘船渡海。他的智慧大成之後，為自己造了一座寶座，鑲嵌著何等豐富的寶石；當他有意時，迪弗們便將寶座抬起，從地面舉向天空。沙阿如太陽般端坐於半空之中；世人驚嘆地聚集在他的寶座周圍，並將那一日命名為新年之日，即法爾瓦丁月的第一日，此名至今仍是那位沙阿的紀念。

title.en: Jamshid Claims Godhead and Loses the Grace
title.zh: 賈姆希德僭稱神而失天恩

region.en: Sea of Chin shore (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 秦地海濱（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Jamshid secs. 2, 4

summary.en: Spoiled by three centuries of a deathless golden age, Jamshid summons the chiefs and claims to be the Maker of the world: who adores me not is an Ahriman. The Grace departs; the court empties; day darkens to him, and though he weeps tears of blood no pardon comes. Pretenders rise, and when Zahhak seizes the crown Jamshid flees, hides a century, and is at last caught beside the sea of Chin and sawn asunder.
summary.zh: 賈姆希德享三百年不死盛世，驕而僭稱造世主：「不拜我者即阿赫里曼。」天恩遂離，朝廷空寂，日為之暗；他泣血求恕而不可得。群雄並起，扎哈克奪位，賈姆希德遁藏百年，終於秦地海濱被擒，鋸為兩半。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; transgression-of-hubris narrative. No living community restriction.

passages.text: For three centuries all the while men never looked on death; they wotted not of travail or of ill, and divs like slaves were girt to do them service. One day contemplating the throne of power Jamshid deemed that he was peerless; he knew God, but acted frowardly and turned aside in his ingratitude. He summoned all the chiefs: the world is mine, I found its properties; leechcraft hath cured the world, disease and death are stayed; they who adore me not are Ahrimans; so now all hail me as the Maker of the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Jamshid secs. 1, 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 三百年間，世人從未見過死亡；他們不知勞苦，也不知災禍，眾迪弗如奴僕般束腰為他們服役。一日，賈姆希德凝視著權力之座，自覺舉世無雙；他認識神，卻行事乖張，因忘恩負義而背離正道。他召集所有首領：「世界歸我所有，我洞悉其性理；醫術已治癒世界，疾病與死亡皆已止息；凡不崇拜我者皆是阿赫里曼；因此如今眾人皆當稱我為世界的創造者。」

passages.text: Thereat the archmages hung their heads, perplexed to answer, and God's Grace departed from him. The world was filled with din, the Court deserted, and none who desired renown stayed in his presence. Day darkened to Jamshid; though with tears of blood he sought for pardon, Grace was not, and dread of coming evil was his lot. How saith the seer? King though thou art, serve God; great fears oppress the heart that is devoid of thankfulness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Jamshid sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 聞言，眾大祭司皆垂首，惶惑不知如何作答，而神的恩典便離他而去。世界充滿喧囂，宮廷空無一人，凡渴慕聲名者皆不留於其側。對賈姆希德而言，白晝化為昏暗；縱然他以血淚尋求寬恕，恩典已不復存，而對未來災禍的恐懼成了他的命運。先知怎麼說？縱然你身為君王，仍當事奉神；心中若無感恩，巨大的恐懼便壓迫著它。

passages.text: Pretenders started up and the disaffected nobles levied troops; hearing that there was an awe-inspiring king of dragon-visage in Arabia, they went to Zahhak and offered fealty. Zahhak came like wind and donned the Iranian crown, and thus fell Jamshid: he fled, surrendering crown, throne, and treasure. He was in hiding for a century, but in the hundredth year he appeared one day beside the sea of Chin; Zahhak clutched him forthwith and, sawing him asunder, freed the world from him and from the fear that he inspired.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Jamshid sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 覬覦者紛紛崛起，心懷不滿的貴族徵集兵馬；他們聽聞阿拉伯有一位龍面之相、令人敬畏的君王，便前往扎哈克處獻上忠誠。扎哈克如風而至，戴上伊朗王冠，賈姆希德就此傾覆：他逃亡而去，捨棄了王冠、王座與財寶。他藏匿了一個世紀，但在第一百年的某日，他出現在秦海之濱；扎哈克當即擒住他，將他鋸為兩半，使世界從他、從他所引起的恐懼中解脫。

title.en: Zahhak Swears His Father's Throne to Iblis
title.zh: 扎哈克向伊布利斯立誓弑父

region.en: Deserts of Arabia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿拉伯荒漠（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Zahhak secs. 2-3

summary.en: Iblis approaches Zahhak, the gallant but hasty son of the righteous Arab king Mardas, as a friendly monitor, wins his trust, and exacts an oath: first promise, then my story. The oath binds Zahhak to do Iblis' bidding, and the bidding is patricide — Iblis digs a masked pit in the garden-path where Mardas bathes at dawn, and the good king falls and breaks his back. Thus the abandoned son seizes the throne.
summary.zh: 伊布利斯偽作諍友接近阿拉伯賢王馬爾達斯之子扎哈克，誘其先誓後言。誓言縛其遵命行事，而命即弑父：伊布利斯於王黎明沐浴的花徑掘坑偽裝，賢王墜坑折背而亡。悖逆之子遂篡其位。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source. 'Iblis' is the Muslim fiend-name folded into the older Ahriman legend; interpretive. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Mardas was a virtuous king of the desert Bedouins, just, highborn, and generous, who kept a thousand head of milch cattle and Arab steeds and grudged the milk to none. He had a son whom much he loved: Zahhak, a gallant prince but hasty. One day Iblis approached him as a friend and led his wits astray; the youth gave ear with pleasure and, all unsuspectingly, gave to Iblis heart, reason, and pure soul.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak secs. 2-3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬爾達斯是沙漠貝都因人中一位有德的君王，公正、高貴而慷慨，養著千頭乳牛與阿拉伯駿馬，從不吝惜牛奶。他有一個深愛的兒子：扎哈克，一位英勇卻急躁的王子。一日，伊布利斯以朋友之姿接近他，引誘他的心智誤入歧途；這青年欣然聽從，毫無戒心地將心、理智與純潔的靈魂交給了伊布利斯。

passages.text: Tell me at once, my worthy monitor, said the youth. Iblis replied: first promise, then my story. The guileless youth swore as Iblis dictated: thy secret shall be kept, thy bidding done. Then said Iblis: shall any rule here but thyself? What profiteth a sire with such a son? The lifetime of this ancient potentate continueth; seize on his court and goods, thou shalt be king of the world if thou durst do my bidding.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「立刻告訴我吧，我可敬的勸告者。」青年說道。伊布利斯回答：「先立誓，然後我才說我的故事。」這天真的青年照伊布利斯所說立誓：你的秘密必被保守，你的命令必被遵行。於是伊布利斯說：「此地除了你，還有誰該統治？一個父親有這樣的兒子，又有何益？這年邁君王的壽命仍在延續；奪取他的宮廷與財物，只要你敢遵我之命，你便將成為世界之王。」

passages.text: Zahhak looked grave, for to shed his sire's blood grieved him, but Iblis told him to leave the scheming to himself; he only asked the prince's silence. In the palace was a jocund garth whither Mardas used to go at dawn to bathe him ere he prayed; the wicked Div dug in the garden-path a deep pit, masked and made it good with boughs. Ere dawn the Arab chieftain hied him thither, and as he reached the pit his fortunes fell: that good man tumbled, broke his back, and died. Thus vile and unjust Zahhak seized the throne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 扎哈克面色凝重，因為流父親的血令他悲傷，但伊布利斯叫他將謀劃之事交給自己；他只要求王子保持沉默。宮中有一座歡快的園圃，馬爾達斯慣於黎明時分前往那裡，在祈禱前沐浴；那邪惡的迪弗在園中小徑上挖了一個深坑，加以掩飾，並用樹枝鋪好。黎明之前，這阿拉伯首領便前往該處，當他走到坑邊，他的命運便傾覆了：那好人跌落其中，折斷脊背而死。邪惡不義的扎哈克便如此奪取了王座。

title.en: Two Cooks, Sheep's Brains, and the Birth of the Kurds
title.zh: 雙廚以羊腦代之：庫爾德人源流

region.en: Zahhak's palace, Babylon (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 扎哈克王宮（象徵巴比倫）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Zahhak sec. 1

summary.en: During Zahhak's thousand-year reign two youths a night are slaughtered to feed the serpents on their brains. The pious high-born Persians Irmail and Karmail learn cookery, enter the king's kitchen, and save one of every pair by mixing sheep's brains with the slain youth's; thirty a month, two hundred in all, are furnished with sheep and goats and sent desertward. Thus spring the Kurds, who dwell in woollen tents and know no settled home.
summary.zh: 扎哈克千年暴政期間，每夜殺二青年以腦飼蛇。虔誠貴族伊爾邁勒與卡爾邁勒學藝入庖，每對救一：以羊腦混入死者之腦。每月三十人，共二百人，賜羊遣往荒漠——庫爾德人由此而生，居氈帳而無定所。

sensitivity.note: Medieval etiology of the Kurds framed around human sacrifice; read as epic legend, not as ethnography. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Zahhak sat on the throne a thousand years, obeyed by all the world; through that long time the customs of the wise were out of vogue, the lusts of madmen flourished everywhere, and all virtue was despised while black art was esteemed. Each night two youths of high or lowly birth were taken to the palace by the cook, who having slaughtered them took out their brains to feed the snakes and ease the monarch's anguish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 扎哈克坐在王位上統治了一千年，全世界都服從他；在那漫長的歲月裡，智者的習俗不再流行，瘋子的慾望四處猖獗，一切美德都遭鄙視，而邪術卻備受尊崇。每晚，廚子都會把兩名出身高貴或低微的青年帶進宮中，將他們宰殺後取出腦髓，用來餵蛇，以緩解君王的痛苦。

passages.text: In the realm were two good high-born Persians, the pious Irmail and Karmail the prescient. Talking of the lawless Shah and his hideous meals, one said: by cookery we might approach the Shah, and by our wits devise a scheme to rescue one from each pair doomed to death. They went and learned that art, became the monarch's cooks, and rejoiced in secret.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 國中有兩位出身高貴的善良波斯人，虔誠的伊爾邁勒與有先見之明的卡爾邁勒。談起那位無法無天的沙阿和他那駭人的膳食，其中一人說道：我們可以藉烹飪之術接近沙阿，再憑我們的機智設計一計，從每一對注定赴死的青年中救出一人。他們前去學會了那門技藝，成了君王的廚子，並在暗中歡喜。

passages.text: When some murderous minions of the Shah dragged two youths to them, they slew one and mingled his precious brains with sheep's, sparing the other, to whom they said: make shift to hide thyself, approach not any dwelling-place of man, thine are the wastes and heights. A worthless head thus fed the serpents, and in every month the cooks preserved from slaughter thirty youths; when the number reached two hundred they provided them with sheep and goats and sent them desertward. Thus sprang the Kurds, who know no settled home but dwell in woollen tents and fear not God.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當沙阿的一些兇殘爪牙把兩名青年拖到他們面前時，他們殺死其中一人，把他珍貴的腦髓與羊腦混在一起，放過了另一人，並對他說：設法把自己藏起來，不要接近任何人的居所，荒野與高地都歸你。一個無價值的頭顱就這樣餵了蛇，而廚子們每個月都從屠殺中救下三十名青年；當人數達到兩百時，他們便給他們羊和山羊，把他們送往沙漠方向。庫爾德人便由此而生，他們沒有固定的家園，住在毛氈帳篷裡，也不敬畏神。

title.en: Zahhak's Dream of the Ox-Headed Mace
title.zh: 扎哈克夢見牛首狼牙棒

region.en: Zahhak's palace, Babylon (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 扎哈克王宮（象徵巴比倫）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Zahhak sec. 2

summary.en: Zahhak dreams that three warriors, boughs of the tree of kings, come against him; the youngest, a tall cypress of kingly face, smites him with an ox-head mace, flays him, binds his hands with his own skin, yokes his neck, and drags him in shame toward Mount Damawand. He wails from sleep; the wise archimage Zirak, forced to speak under threat of hanging, names the future destroyer: not yet born, his name is Faridun.
summary.zh: 扎哈克夢見三勇士——王族之枝——其中最幼者面如君王、身若翠柏，持牛首狼牙棒擊其首，剝其皮縛其手，加軛於頸，拖向達馬萬德山。他驚叫失色；術士齊拉克迫於王命道破天機：那尚未出生者名為法里東，將傾其王座。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; prophetic-dream motif. No living community restriction.

passages.text: One longsome night Zahhak slumbered in the arms of Arnawaz and saw a vision of three warriors, boughs of the tree of kings. The youngest, who held the middle place, was a tall cypress, in face, in armour, and in mien a king. He rushed with ox-head mace to fight Zahhak, smote him upon the head, stripped off his skin, used it as a rope to bind his hands firm as a rock, placed on his neck a yoke, and dragged him in shame and anguish toward Mount Damawand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個漫長的夜晚，扎哈克在阿爾納瓦茲的懷中沉睡，看見三位武士的幻象，他們是王者之樹的枝幹。最年輕的那位居於中間，是一株高大的柏樹，面容、鎧甲與神態都像一位君王。他手持牛頭錘衝上前去與扎哈克搏鬥，擊中他的頭部，剝下他的皮，把皮當作繩索將他的雙手牢牢縛住，堅如磐石，又在他頸上套上軛，帶著羞辱與痛苦把他拖向達馬萬德山。

passages.text: The tyrant writhed and yelled; the palace of the hundred columns shook, and Arnawaz asked what he had seen. He told them every whit, then counsel was given: call both the archmages and astrologers and see if the hand that threateneth thy life is that of fairy, div, or man. When the Lamp showed o'er the hills Zahhak brought the archimages and demanded his latter end on pain of being hung alive.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那暴君扭動身體、放聲大叫；百柱宮殿為之震動，阿爾納瓦茲問他看見了什麼。他把一切詳情都告訴了他們，隨後有人獻策：召來所有大祭司與占星師，看看那威脅你性命的手究竟屬於精靈、迪夫，還是人。當燈光顯現在山丘之上時，扎哈克召來大祭司們，以活活吊死相威脅，要求他們說出他的結局。

passages.text: Among them was a man wise, honest, and prescient, by name Zirak, chief of the band of archimages. Concerned but fearless, he addressed Zahhak: none is born except to die; if thou wert an iron wall yon heaven would grind thee. One will hereafter take thy throne and fling thy fortune to the ground; his name is Faridun, and he will be a royal heaven to earth. As yet he is not born, thy time of woe hath not arrived, but when his honoured mother hath borne him he will be a fruitful tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Zahhak sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們之中有一人智慧、誠實且能預見未來，名叫齊拉克，是大祭司們的首領。他憂心卻無所畏懼，對扎哈克說道：沒有人生來不是為了死去；即使你是一堵鐵牆，那蒼天也會把你碾碎。日後將有一人奪取你的王位，把你的命運拋擲於地；他的名字是法里頓，他將成為降臨大地的王者之天。他尚未出生，你的苦難之時還未到來，但當他尊貴的母親生下他時，他將成為一棵多結果實的樹。

title.en: The Hook in the Tail of the Fish
title.zh: 鉤住魚尾的預兆

region.en: Fishing ground off Manaia's village, Hawaiki (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哈瓦基馬納亞村外漁場（象徵性定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 15, The Emigration of Manaia (London 1855)

summary.en: While Manaia fishes for his spear-making workmen, they ravish his wife Rongotiki. A fish takes his hook in its tail - the traditional sign that a man's wife is being insulted - and he rows home without a word, ties the fish to a thwart for her to find, and turns his revenge crafty: he asks the offenders to make the spears large and strong, so that when he ambushes them their weapons will be too heavy. In the ambush his unknown last-born son Kahu-kaka-nui leaps out first crying his own name; his wife's incantation Tapuwae weakens the fleeing Tupenu, and the insult is paid for.
summary.zh: 馬納亞出海為造矛工匠捕魚，工匠卻趁機強暴其妻龍戈蒂基。一尾魚上鉤——鉤竟掛在魚尾！按毛利俗信，此兆主妻子受人欺辱。他一言不發收竿回村，將魚繫於船板讓妻子自己明白。報仇之道出奇：他囑工匠把矛造得又大又重——埋伏時敵人的兵器便難以招架。伏擊戰中，素未謀面的幼子卡胡卡卡努伊搶先出擊，自報姓名；其妻誦咒『塔普瓦埃』使逃亡的圖佩努腳軟乏力，恥辱終得清償。

sensitivity.note: Sexual-violence episode summarized, not dramatized; recorded here as the motive of a foundational legend.

passages.text: The cause which led Manaia to come here from Hawaiki was his being very badly treated by a large party of his friends and neighbours whom, according to the usual custom when a chief has any heavy work to be done, he had collected to make his spears for him. One day he determined to have his neighbours all warned to come to a great gathering for the purpose of making spears; the messenger arrived at the place of Tupenu, chief of the tribe living there, who encouraged his people to go in obedience to the message of Manaia. After some time it happened that Manaia felt a wish to go and catch some fish for his workmen, so he went off in his canoe with several of his people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 15 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬納亞之所以從哈瓦伊基來到此地，是因為他遭到一大群親友與鄰人的極惡劣對待——依照習俗，首領若有繁重工作要做，便會召集眾人前來；他當時正是召集了這群人為他製作長矛。有一天，他決定通知所有鄰人前來參加一場製作長矛的盛大聚會；傳信者抵達當地部落首領圖佩努之處，圖佩努鼓勵其族人順從馬納亞的傳召前往。過了些時日，馬納亞忽然想去為他的工匠們捕些魚，於是便帶著幾名族人乘獨木舟出海。

passages.text: After he had been gone for some time the workmen assaulted Rongotiki, the wife of Manaia, without any one knowing what they were doing. All this time Manaia, suspecting nothing, was paddling out to sea, and when he reached the fishing-ground they lay on their paddles. His people soon caught plenty of fish, but he had not even a single bite until at last, as they were on the point of returning, he felt a fish nibbling at his hook and gave a jerk to his line to pull it up; when he got the fish up to the side of the canoe, to his surprise he saw that the hook was not in the mouth of the fish, but fast in its tail - and as this had long been esteemed a sign that your wife was being insulted by somebody, he at once knew how his had been treated by his workmen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 15 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他離去一段時間後，工匠們竟在無人知曉的情況下侵犯了馬納亞的妻子龍戈蒂基。這段期間，馬納亞毫無察覺，一路划槳出海；到了漁場，眾人便放下槳歇息。他的族人很快便捕到許多魚，他卻連一次咬鉤也沒有，直到最後將要返航之際，他才感覺有魚在輕咬他的魚鉤，便猛地一扯釣線將魚拉起；當他把魚拉到獨木舟旁時，驚訝地發現魚鉤並不在魚嘴裡，而是牢牢鉤在魚尾上——長久以來，這一直被視為妻子遭人侮辱的徵兆，於是他立刻明白自己的妻子被工匠們如何對待了。

passages.text: Without waiting a moment longer he told his crew to heave up the anchor and return to the shore; whilst pulling in, he took the fish he had caught, with the hook still fast in its tail, tied it on to one of the thwarts of the canoe, and left it there, in order that when Rongotiki saw it she might know without his telling her that he was aware she had been badly treated. At home she was roasting fern-root and made signs to him by which he might know what had happened; but he knew it already from the manner in which his hook had caught in the tail of the fish. He sent her to fetch the fish, and said, 'That is the fish I meant you to bring, lest you should have said that I did not know what had taken place until you told me.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 15 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他片刻也不再等待，吩咐船員起錨返岸；划回岸邊的途中，他將捕到的那條魚——魚鉤仍牢牢鉤在魚尾上——綁在獨木舟的一根橫木上，留在那裡，好讓龍戈蒂基一看見便無須他開口也知道，他已明白她受了惡劣對待。在家中，她正烤著蕨根，並向他做出種種手勢，好讓他知道發生了什麼事；但他早已從魚鉤鉤住魚尾的方式得知了。他派她去取那條魚，並說道：「那就是我要你拿來的魚，免得你說我是直到你告訴我才知道發生了什麼事。」

passages.text: Manaia then turned over in his mind various plans for revenging himself, and before the fighting broke out he went to the people who had wronged his wife and told them he hoped they would make the spears large and strong, and not put him off with weak things - a mere piece of deceit, in order that when he attacked them their weapons might be too heavy readily to parry their enemies' blows. He lay in ambush with some of his people and nudged with his elbow his son Tu-ure-nui to rush in and kill the first man of the enemy; but being afraid to go he did not move, and whilst Manaia was encouraging him in vain, another young man, whose father had never been told him by his mother, rushed forward, slew the first of the enemy and cried out, 'The first slain of the enemy belongs to me, to Kahu-kaka-nui, the son of Manaia.' Then for the first time Manaia knew that this young man was his son, his last-born son, and pleased with his courage he loved him very much. The ambush followed the youth and slaughtered them; their chief Tupenu fled by the beach of Pikopikoi-whiti, and Manaia called to his wife Rongotiki to utter incantations to weaken his enemy; she repeated the incantation termed Tapuwae and rendered the flying warrior faint and feeble, so that Manaia rapidly gained on him, caught him, and slew him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 15 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬納亞隨後在心中盤算各種復仇之計；在戰事爆發之前，他前往那些虧待他妻子的人那裡，告訴他們，他希望他們把長矛做得又大又結實，不要拿脆弱的東西敷衍他——這純粹是欺騙之計，為的是當他攻擊他們時，他們的武器過於沉重，難以輕易格擋敵人的攻擊。他與一些族人埋伏起來，用手肘輕推他的兒子圖烏雷努伊，要他衝上前去殺死敵方的第一個人；但圖烏雷努伊心生畏懼，一動也不動；正當馬納亞徒勞地鼓勵他時，另一名年輕人——他的母親從未告訴過他父親是誰——衝上前去，殺死了敵方的第一人，並高喊：「敵方第一個被殺的人屬於我，屬於卡胡卡卡努伊，馬納亞之子。」這時馬納亞才第一次知道這名年輕人是他的兒子，是他最小的兒子；他對這份勇氣甚為欣喜，非常疼愛他。埋伏的人馬跟隨這名青年衝出，將敵人屠殺殆盡；他們的首領圖佩努沿著皮科皮科伊—惠蒂的海灘逃竄，馬納亞呼喚妻子龍戈蒂基唸誦咒語以削弱敵人；她唸誦名為「塔普瓦埃」的咒語，使那奔逃的戰士變得虛弱無力，於是馬納亞迅速追上他，將他擒住並殺死。

title.en: The Tokomaru and the Dog that Led to Land
title.zh: 托科馬魯號與引路的獵犬

region.en: Tongaporutu to Waitara, Taranaki coast, Aotearoa
region.zh: 紐西蘭塔拉納基海岸湯加波魯圖至懷塔拉

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 15, The Emigration of Manaia (London 1855)

summary.en: Driven from Hawaiki by relentless reprisals, Manaia refits his brother-in-law's canoe Tokomaru and tricks its owner into deep water as a sacrifice to the gods, then sails. Far out, his dog scents land, leaps overboard, and swims ahead howling; the canoe follows through the night and at dawn finds the dog beside a stranded whale. Another canoe lands there first but is beaten in the claim dispute by Manaia's earlier sheds, clearings and whale - until the newcomers produce a sacred place, and Manaia, conceding, coasts on to Taranaki, where the old inhabitants are destroyed and the country left for his descendants, the Ngati-Awa.
summary.zh: 復仇之火迫使馬納亞棄鄉遠走。他修好連襟的托科馬魯號，誘其涉入深水，以之祭神，揚帆出海。茫茫大洋上，獵犬嗅得陸地氣息，跳船在前，吠聲引航；破曉時分，犬立於擱淺巨鯨之側。後到的獨木舟亦抵此地，卻因馬納亞先建的棚屋、墾地與鯨魚而在爭執中落敗——直到對方出示先築的聖壇。馬納亞認輸讓地，沿海岸南行至塔拉納基，誅滅原住民，其子孫即納蒂阿瓦部落。

sensitivity.note: Founding legend includes the destruction of earlier inhabitants, reproduced as the record states it.

passages.text: Their army collected and started to avenge themselves on Manaia and his tribe, and to destroy them; they slew many of them, and continued from time to time to attack them, so that their numbers dwindled away, till at length Manaia began to reflect within himself: 'Ah, my warriors are wasting away, and by and bye perhaps I also shall be slain; rather than let this state of things continue, I had better abandon this country, and, removing to a great distance, seek a new one for myself and my people.' He began to repair a canoe and fit it for sea; the name of the canoe was Tokomaru, and it belonged to his brother-in-law.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 15 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們的軍隊集結起來，出發向馬納亞及其部落復仇，要將他們消滅；他們殺死了許多人，並一次又一次地持續攻擊，使馬納亞一方的人數日益減少，直到最後馬納亞開始在心中思量：「唉，我的戰士正日漸耗盡，不久之後或許連我也會被殺；與其讓這種情況持續下去，我不如捨棄這片土地，遠遷他方，為自己和族人另尋新地。」他開始修整一艘獨木舟，使之適於航海；這艘獨木舟名叫托科馬魯，本屬於他的妻舅。

passages.text: When the canoe was quite fit for sea they dragged it down to the water and hauled it in until it floated; then they brought down the cargo and stowed it away, and Manaia embarked with his wife, his children and his dependants. Then he said to some of his warriors, 'Let my brother-in-law now be slain as an offering for the gods, that they may prove propitious to this canoe of ours.' So he called to his brother-in-law, who was standing on the shore bidding him farewell: 'I say, wade out to me for one minute, that I may tell you something and take my last farewell, for I am going to part for ever from you.' The poor fellow began to wade out; at first the water hardly covered his ankles, next his knees, at last it came up above his loins, and he said, 'Shove the canoe in a little nearer the shore, I shall be under water directly'; but Manaia answered, 'Wade away, there is no depth of water', and to deceive him better kept pretending to touch the bottom with a stick. At length his feet could no longer touch the bottom, and he found himself swimming close to the canoe; then Manaia seized him by the head, and with one blow of his stone battle-axe clave it, and his brother-in-law perished. Having slain his victim, he caught up his dog which had swum out with its master, lifted it into the canoe, and sailed away to search for a new country for himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 15 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 獨木舟完全適於航海之後，他們將它拖到水邊，再拉入水中直到它浮起；接著他們把貨物搬下來堆放妥當，馬納亞便帶著妻子、兒女及部屬登船。然後他對幾名戰士說：「現在把我的妻舅殺死，作為獻給眾神的祭品，好讓眾神眷顧我們這艘獨木舟。」於是他呼喚站在岸上向他道別的妻舅：「喂，你涉水過來一下，我有話要對你說，並作最後的道別，因為我就要與你永別了。」那可憐的人便開始涉水而來；起初水只沒過他的腳踝，接著沒過膝蓋，最後沒過腰際，他說：「把獨木舟往岸邊推近一點，我馬上就要沒頂了」；但馬納亞回答：「繼續涉水過來吧，水並不深」，並且為了更好地騙他，還不斷假裝用棍子觸碰水底。最後他的腳再也踩不到底，發現自己正游在獨木舟旁；這時馬納亞抓住他的頭，用石斧一擊將它劈開，他的妻舅就此喪命。殺死祭品之後，他抓起那隻隨主人一同游出來的狗，將牠提上獨木舟，便揚帆而去，為自己尋找新的國度。

passages.text: He sailed on and on, and had proceeded very far from the land they had quitted, when one day the dog scented land and howled loudly, struggling to get loose and jump overboard into the water. The people said, 'We'd better let him go if he wishes it, and see what comes of it'; so they let the dog loose, and he jumped overboard and swam on ahead of the canoe, howling loudly as he went, till night fell, and they could only indistinctly hear the low faint howling; but the dog, after swimming for a long time, finally reached land. The canoe came following straight on the track the dog had taken, and when night ended and day began to break, they again heard the howling of the dog, which had landed close to the stranded carcase of a whale; they pulled eagerly to the shore, and there they landed on this island, on Aotea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 15 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他繼續航行，離開他們所離開的那片陸地已非常遙遠；有一天，那隻狗嗅到了陸地的氣息，便大聲嚎叫，掙扎著要脫身，跳下船去躍入水中。眾人說：『既然牠想去，我們不如放牠去，看看會有什麼結果。』於是他們放開了狗，牠便跳下船，游在獨木舟前頭，一邊游一邊高聲嚎叫，直到夜幕降臨，他們只能隱約聽見那低沉微弱的嚎聲；但那隻狗游了很久之後，終於抵達了陸地。獨木舟循著狗所走的路線直直跟隨而來，當夜色將盡、天色開始破曉時，他們又聽見了狗的嚎叫，原來牠已登陸，靠近一具擱淺的鯨魚屍體；他們奮力划向岸邊，就在那裡登上了這座島，登上奧特阿。

passages.text: First they allotted out equally amongst them the whale they had found; but Manaia addressed his men, 'We must now build a house to shelter us, and then we will cut up the whale.' Some of them cried 'Here is the best place for our village', others 'No, no, this is the best place', others further along 'Here, here, this is the best place we have yet seen' - thus all were led to wander a long way along the shore exploring the new country. Now there were some other canoes coming close after the Tokomaru, which presently made the land too, saw the marks on the sand and the sheds and cleared ground, and began to claim each one as his own. They disputed: 'When did you arrive here?' 'A long time ago.' 'And we also arrived a long time ago.' Manaia asked, 'What are the proofs you give to show when you arrived here?' - 'But what proofs have you?' - 'The proof I have to show when I arrived here is a whale of mine which I found upon the beach.' They all returned to the landing-place and inspected the sheds and clearings, but when Manaia demanded their sacred place they went together to see it, and when they saw it, Manaia believed them. He was sorely perplexed and abandoned the part of the country he had first reached, coasting right along the shores from Whangaparaoa, doubling the North Cape, making a direct course to Taranaki and making the land at Tongaporutu, between Parininihi and Mokau; they left the god they worshipped there, whose name was Rakeiora. At the river Mokau they left the stone anchor of their canoe - it is still lying near the mouth of the river on its north side, and the present name of the rock is the Punga-o-Matori. They explored the country to Pukearuhe, forded the river of Onaero, passed the plain of Motunui, and reached the river whose old name Manaia changed, calling it after his son Tu-ure-nui; at Kohutu, at the mouth of the river Waitara, they dwelt, and there they found people living, the native inhabitants of these islands; but Manaia and his party slew them, so that the country was left for himself and for his descendants, and for his tribe and their descendants. Manaia was the ancestor of the Ngati-Awa tribe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 15 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 起初他們把發現的那條鯨魚在眾人之中平均分配；但馬納亞對他的手下說：『我們現在必須蓋一間屋子來遮風避雨，然後再來切分鯨魚。』他們之中有些人喊道：『這裡是我們建村最好的地方』；另一些人說：『不，不，這裡才是最好的地方』；還有一些人沿著更遠處說：『這裡，這裡，這是我們至今所見最好的地方』——於是眾人都被引得沿著海岸走了很遠，去探察這片新土地。這時又有一些獨木舟緊跟在托科馬魯之後而來，不久也靠了岸，看見沙上的痕跡、棚屋和開墾過的土地，便開始各自聲稱那是自己的。他們爭辯道：『你們是什麼時候到這裡的？』『很久以前。』『我們也是很久以前到的。』馬納亞問道：『你們有什麼憑證能證明你們是何時到這裡的？』——『那你們又有什麼憑證？』——『我所能拿出證明我何時到這裡的憑證，就是我在海灘上發現的一條屬於我的鯨魚。』他們全都回到登陸之處，察看那些棚屋和開墾地，但當馬納亞要求看他們的聖地時，他們便一同前去觀看，馬納亞看了之後，便相信了他們。他十分困惑，便放棄了他最初抵達的那片地方，沿著海岸一路航行，從旺阿帕拉奧阿繞過北角，直航塔拉納基，在帕里尼尼希與莫考之間的湯加波魯圖登陸；他們在那裡留下了他們所崇拜的神，名叫拉凱奧拉。在莫考河，他們留下了獨木舟的石錨——它至今仍躺在河口北側附近，那塊岩石現在的名字叫蓬加奧馬托里。他們探察了皮凱阿魯赫一帶的地方，涉過奧納埃羅河，經過莫圖努伊平原，抵達一條河，馬納亞把它的舊名改掉，以他的兒子圖烏雷努伊命名；他們住在懷塔拉河口科胡圖的地方，在那裡他們發現有人居住，是這些島嶼的原住民；但馬納亞一行人把他們殺死，於是這片土地便留給了他自己、他的子孫，以及他的部族和他們的子孫。馬納亞是恩加蒂阿瓦部族的祖先。

title.en: Hine-moa Swims Lake Rotorua by the Sound of the Flute
title.zh: 希內莫阿循笛聲泳渡羅托魯瓦湖

region.en: Lake Rotorua and Mokoia Island, Aotearoa
region.zh: 紐西蘭羅托魯瓦湖與莫科亞島

period: Oral tradition; recorded 1855 (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 16, Hine-moa, the Maiden of Rotorua (London 1855)

summary.en: The low-born but beloved Tutanekai plays trumpet and pipe on a hillside balcony; across the lake the high-born Hine-moa listens nightly, each having secretly loved the other at the great assemblies. Guarded canoes force her to swim: with six dry gourds as floats she strikes out into the dark, steering only by the music, rests clinging to the sunken stump Hinewhata, and warms herself in the hot spring Waikimihia. Breaking Tutanekai's calabashes of water, she draws him to the bath; found under the ledges, 'as beautiful as the wild white hawk', she becomes his wife, and Tiki is comforted with Tutanekai's sister Tupa.
summary.zh: 出身寒微卻受寵愛的圖塔內凱在山坡高台上吹奏號角與竹笛；湖對岸高貴的希內莫阿夜夜傾聽，二人大會中早已暗生情愫。親友扣留舟船防她私奔，她便以六個乾葫蘆作浮漂，循著樂聲泳渡黑夜中的大湖，途中攀住沉木希內瓦塔歇息，又入溫泉瓦伊基米希亞取暖。她打碎圖塔內凱的水葫蘆，引他前來；熱泉岩下，她如白鷹般綽約起身，結為夫妻，笛友蒂基則娶得圖塔內凱之妹圖帕為慰。

sensitivity.note: Rotorua romance legend; place names (Kaiweka, Waikimihia, Hinewhata) anchored in the text.

passages.text: Rangi-Uru was the mother of a chief called Tutanekai; properly the wife of Whakaue-Kaipapa, the great ancestor of the Ngatiwhakaue tribe, she had at one time run away with a chief named Tuwharetoa, and from this affair sprang Tutanekai, who was an illegitimate child; but finally Whakaue and Rangi-Uru were united again, and Whakaue was very kind indeed to Tutanekai, treating him as if he was his own son, so they grew up on the island of Mokoia, Tutanekai and his elder brothers, until they attained to manhood. Now there reached them a great report of Hine-Moa, that she was a maiden of rare beauty as well as of high rank, for Umukaria was her father and her mother's name was Hine-Marii; and Tutanekai and each of his elder brothers desired to have her as a wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 16 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 朗吉烏魯是一位名叫圖塔內凱的酋長之母；她本是恩加蒂法卡烏埃部族的偉大祖先法卡烏埃凱帕帕的妻子，曾一度與一位名叫圖法雷托阿的酋長私奔，圖塔內凱便是由此而生，他是個私生子；但後來法卡烏埃與朗吉烏魯又復合了，法卡烏埃對圖塔內凱著實很好，待他如同己出，於是圖塔內凱和他的兄長們便在莫科亞島上長大，直到他們長大成人。這時，關於希內莫阿的盛名傳到了他們耳中，說她是一位容貌絕美、出身又高貴的少女，因為烏穆卡里亞是她的父親，她母親的名字叫希內馬里伊；圖塔內凱和他的每一位兄長都想要娶她為妻。

passages.text: Tutanekai built an elevated balcony on the slope of the hill called Kaiweka. He had contracted a great friendship for a young man named Tiki; they were both fond of music - Tutanekai played on the horn, and Tiki on the pipe - and they used to go up into the balcony and play on their instruments in the night; and in calm evenings the sound of their music was wafted by the gentle land-breeze across the lake to the village at Owhata, where dwelt the beautiful young Hine-Moa, the younger sister of Wahiao. Every night the two friends played in this manner, and Hine-Moa said to herself, 'Ah! that is the music of Tutanekai which I hear.' At the great assemblies of the people they had glanced each at the other, until in the breast of each there grew up a secret passion; Tutanekai could not tell whether he might venture to take her hand, and Hine-Moa's heart said to her, 'If you send one of your female friends to tell him of your love, perhaps he will not be pleased with you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 16 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 圖塔內凱在名叫凱韋卡的山坡上建了一座高起的露臺。他與一位名叫蒂基的年輕人結下了深厚的友誼；兩人都喜愛音樂——圖塔內凱吹號角，蒂基吹笛——他們常在夜裡登上露臺吹奏樂器；在風平浪靜的傍晚，他們的樂聲隨著輕柔的陸風飄過湖面，傳到奧法塔的村落，那裡住著美麗的年輕姑娘希內莫阿，她是瓦希阿奧的妹妹。兩個朋友每晚都這樣吹奏，希內莫阿自言自語道：『啊！我所聽見的，正是圖塔內凱的樂聲。』在眾人的盛大聚會上，他們曾彼此對望，直到各自胸中萌生出一份隱秘的愛慕；圖塔內凱不敢確定自己是否該冒昧去牽她的手，而希內莫阿的心對她說：『如果你派一位女伴去向他訴說你的愛意，也許他會不高興。』

passages.text: At last Tutanekai sent a messenger to tell of his love, and Hine-Moa said, 'Eh-hu! have we then each loved alike?' They had arranged the time at which Hine-Moa should run away to him, and when the maiden asked what should be the sign, he said, 'A trumpet will be heard sounding every night; it will be I who sound it, beloved - paddle then your canoe to that place.' So always about the middle of the night Tutanekai and his friend Tiki went up into their balcony and played; and Hine-Moa heard them, and desired vastly to paddle to Tutanekai; but her friends, suspecting something, had been careful with the canoes, leaving none afloat, but hauling them all up upon the shore. She reflected in her heart, 'How can I then contrive to cross the lake to the island of Mokoia?' Then soft measures reached her from the horn of Tutanekai, and the young and beautiful chieftainess felt as if an earthquake shook her to make her go to the beloved of her heart. She took six large dry empty gourds as floats, three of them for each side, went out upon the rock named Iri-iri-kapua and threw off her clothes and cast herself into the water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 16 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最後圖塔內凱派了一名使者去訴說他的愛意，希內莫阿說：『咦！那麼我們竟是彼此相愛嗎？』他們已約定好希內莫阿私奔到他那裡去的時間，當這少女問起以什麼為記號時，他說：『每晚都會聽見號角聲；吹號的就是我，心愛的人——到時你就划獨木舟到那個地方去。』於是每逢半夜時分，圖塔內凱和他的朋友蒂基便登上露臺吹奏；希內莫阿聽見了，極想划船到圖塔內凱那裡去；但她的親友們察覺到有些蹊蹺，便對獨木舟格外小心，一艘也不留在水上，全都拖上了岸。她在心中思量：『那我怎樣才能渡過湖面到莫科亞島去呢？』這時，圖塔內凱的號角傳來柔和的樂聲，這位年輕美麗的女酋長只覺得彷彿有地震在撼動她，催她奔向心上人。她取了六個乾燥的大空葫蘆作浮具，兩側各綁三個，走到名叫伊里伊里卡普阿的岩石上，脫下衣裳，縱身躍入水中。

passages.text: She reached the stump of a sunken tree which used to stand in the lake, called Hinewhata, clung to it with her hands and rested to take breath; whenever she was exhausted she floated with the current supported by the gourds, and swam on again; but she could not distinguish in which direction she should proceed from the darkness of the night - her only guide was the soft measure from the instrument of Tutanekai, and that was the mark by which she swam straight to Waikimihia, for just above that hot-spring was the village of Tutanekai. At the place where she landed there is a hot-spring separated from the lake only by a narrow ledge of rocks, and Hine-Moa got into it to warm herself, trembling all over from the cold and from modesty at the thought of meeting Tutanekai. He felt thirsty and sent his servant for water; the maiden called out in a gruff voice like that of a man, 'Whom is that water for?' - 'It's for Tutanekai.' - 'Give it here, then.' She drank and purposely broke the calabash; this happened repeatedly, and the enraged Tutanekai threw on some clothes, caught his club and came to the bath, crying, 'Where's that fellow who broke my calabashes?' Hine-Moa knew the voice of the beloved of her heart and hid herself under the overhanging rocks - not a real hiding, but a bashful concealing - whilst he went feeling about along the banks; at last he caught hold of a hand and cried, 'Hollo, who's this?' - 'It's I, Tutanekai.' - 'But who are you?' Then she spoke louder, 'It's I, 'tis Hine-Moa.' He threw garments over her and took her to his house, and thenceforth, according to the ancient laws of the Maori, they were man and wife. When the morning dawned a servant peeping into the house saw four feet, and all the village shouted, 'Oh! here's Hine-Moa, here's Hine-Moa with Tutanekai'; and his jealous elder brothers heard it and said, 'It is not true!' - until they saw her following him from the house. Tiki grieved that his friend had a wife and he none, and Tupa, Tutanekai's young sister, was given to him. The descendants of Hine-Moa and of Tutanekai dwell on the lake of Rotorua to this very day, and never yet have their lips forgotten to repeat tales of the great beauty of their renowned ancestress, and of her swimming over here.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 16 (1855); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她游到一截沉在水中的樹樁旁——那樹樁從前立在湖中，名叫希內法塔——雙手攀住它，歇下來喘口氣；每當她筋疲力盡，便靠著葫蘆的浮力隨水流漂浮，然後再繼續游；但夜色漆黑，她分辨不出該往哪個方向前進——她唯一的指引便是圖塔內凱樂器傳來的柔和樂聲，她就以那樂聲為標記，徑直游向懷基米希亞，因為圖塔內凱的村落就在那處溫泉的正上方。她上岸的地方有一處溫泉，與湖面只隔著一道狹窄的岩石邊緣，希內莫阿便進到泉中取暖，她渾身發抖，既是因為寒冷，也是因為想到要與圖塔內凱相見而羞怯。他覺得口渴，便派僕人去取水；那少女用粗啞如男子的聲音喊道：『這水是給誰的？』——『是給圖塔內凱的。』——『那就拿過來吧。』她喝了水，故意把葫蘆打碎；這樣的事接連發生了好幾次，圖塔內凱勃然大怒，披上些衣服，抓起他的棍棒來到浴池邊，喊道：『打碎我葫蘆的那傢伙在哪裡？』希內莫阿聽出那是心上人的聲音，便躲到懸垂的岩石底下——並非真的躲藏，而是羞怯地遮掩——他則沿著岸邊摸索；最後他抓住了一隻手，喊道：『喂，這是誰？』——『是我，圖塔內凱。』——『可你是誰？』於是她提高聲音說：『是我，是希內莫阿。』他把衣物披在她身上，帶她回到自己的屋裡，從此，依照毛利人的古老律法，他們便成了夫妻。天亮時，一名僕人往屋裡窺看，看見了四隻腳，整個村落都喊了起來：『哦！希內莫阿在這裡，希內莫阿和圖塔內凱在一起』；他那嫉妒的兄長們聽見了，說：『不會是真的！』——直到他們看見她跟著他從屋裡出來。蒂基因為朋友有了妻子而自己沒有，心中鬱鬱；圖塔內凱的妹妹圖帕便被許配給了他。希內莫阿與圖塔內凱的子孫至今仍住在羅托魯阿湖畔，他們的嘴唇從未忘記述說他們那位著名的女祖先何等美貌，以及她如何游到這裡來的故事。

title.en: Boyislav, Youngest of Twelve: The Black Island and the Taper
title.zh: 十二子中的幼子博伊斯拉夫：黑島與蠟燭

region.en: Bohemia (symbolic pin at Prague)
region.zh: 波希米亞（象徵性定位於布拉格）

period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'Boyislav, Youngest of Twelve'

summary.en: A dying king's dream sends his twelve sons to Black Island to free three princesses; Boyislav, the youngest, obeys a starving horse's strange instructions — eat, but let no princess kiss thee, and speak no word — until a taper's glow betrays him and his brothers cast him to the lions.
summary.zh: 病重國王之夢遣十二子赴黑島救三公主；幼子博伊斯拉夫依飢馬奇囑——可食而勿受公主之吻、全程禁語——直至燭光洩密，兄長們將他投入獅欄。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale.

passages.text: A king lies dying; three times a vision of three princesses on Black Island appears, promising 'Free us, and thou wilt recover; if not, thou wilt die.' The twelve sons draw lots and Boyislav, the youngest and most hated, wins the journey. On the black island he lifts a great hewn stone and descends into a glorious garden with three golden castles, where a famished horse greets him by name and teaches him the rule: in each castle eat, but let no princess eat with thee or kiss thee; take the leavings; and speak no word all the time — 'to thee 'tis a question of life or death.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'Boyislav, Youngest of Twelve'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位國王臥病將死；黑島上三位公主的幻象三度顯現，許諾道：「釋放我們，你便會康復；否則，你必死。」十二個兒子抽籤，最年幼、最受憎惡的博伊斯拉夫抽中了這趟旅程。在黑島上，他抬起一塊巨大的鑿石，下到一座有三位金色城堡的華美花園，那裡一匹飢餓的馬喚著他的名字迎接他，並教他規矩：在每座城堡裡進食，但不可讓任何公主與你同食或吻你；取走殘餘；並且全程一言不發——「對你而言，這是生死攸關之事。」

passages.text: He obeys in the three castles and gathers leavings for the horse, which brings him to the shore, and all three princesses are freed. On the homeward voyage the princess of White Island, coming at night to his cabin, quenches the light — Boyislav lights a taper to see her, and is seen; his brothers walled him into a lions' den and swore they had freed the princesses themselves. The princess demanded the liberator, and the false brothers were beheaded one by one when they could not answer her question about the taper.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他在三座城堡中一一遵行，並為那匹馬收集殘餘，馬將他帶到岸邊，三位公主皆獲釋放。在歸航途中，白島的公主夜裡來到他的艙房，熄滅了燈——博伊斯拉夫點起一支細燭想看她，卻被看見了；他的兄弟們把他砌進獅穴之中，並發誓說公主們是他們自己救出的。公主索求那位解救者，而那些假冒的兄弟在無法回答她關於細燭的問題時，便一個接一個被斬首。

passages.text: The old man who had saved Boyislav begged the king to open the den, and the princess's threat of turning the city to dust and ashes forced the truth out. Boyislav walked out with his taper and tablecloth, was recognized, and betrothed with a kiss. At the feast he asked for his trusty horse, who was starving on a cord of hay brought from Red Island, and at the horse's command cut off its head — whereupon a beautiful prince stood in its place, freed with the three princesses from the witch-queen's enchantment, and the land of Black Island shone again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 曾救過博伊斯拉夫的那位老人懇求國王打開獅穴，而公主揚言要把整座城化為塵土與灰燼，逼出了真相。博伊斯拉夫帶著他的細燭與桌布走了出來，被認出，並以一吻定下婚約。在宴席上，他索求他那匹忠誠的馬——那馬正因一束從紅島帶來的乾草而餓得奄奄一息——他依馬的命令砍下牠的頭，於是牠的位置上站著一位俊美的王子，他與三位公主一同從女巫王后的魔法中獲釋，黑島之地重放光明。

title.en: The Table, the Pack, and the Bag
title.zh: 餐桌、行囊與魔袋

region.en: Bohemia (symbolic pin at Brno)
region.zh: 波希米亞（象徵性定位於布爾諾）

period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'The Table, the Pack, and the Bag'

summary.en: Simple Yanek, beaten and left for dead by his gold-hungry brothers, serves giants for a table that feeds a king; two old grandfathers swap it for a pack of armies and a bag of castles — until the king who stole the table learns what war means.
summary.zh: 憨直的亞內克被貪金兄長毒打棄於林中；為巨人看守寶庫得國王餐台；兩位老祖父以召兵行囊與城堡魔袋易其台——直到竊取餐台的國王領教何謂戰爭。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale.

passages.text: Three brothers go into the world: Martin and Mihal fill their bags with food; Yanek, the youngest and simplest, takes nothing and is beaten with rage by both. In a castle of copper, silver, and gold they fill their bags and abandon Yanek for dead in the forest. He wakes and returns to the castle, where giants catch him and make him keeper of their treasures, granting him a little table: strike it three times and cry 'Food for a king!' and the table is covered with the daintiest dishes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'The Table, the Pack, and the Bag'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 三兄弟走入世間：馬丁與米哈爾把袋子裝滿食物；最年幼、最憨直的亞涅克什麼也沒帶，被兩人怒氣沖沖地打了一頓。在一座銅、銀、金的城堡裡，他們裝滿了袋子，把亞涅克棄於林中等死。他醒來後回到城堡，巨人們抓住他，讓他做他們財寶的看守，並賜他一張小桌子：敲它三下，喊道「給國王的美食！」，桌上便擺滿最精緻的菜餚。

passages.text: Tired of idleness Yanek walks home with the table on his back. An old grandfather begs food, eats his fill, and swaps the table for a pack out of which armies can be summoned; Yanek sends two hundred hussars after the old man and gets the table back. A second grandfather swaps it for a bag of castles — and Yanek sends three hundred Uhlans to fetch the table again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 亞涅克厭倦了閒散，背著桌子走回家。一位老翁乞求食物，飽餐一頓後，用一個能召出軍隊的背包換走了桌子；亞涅克派出兩百名驃騎兵追那老人，把桌子要了回來。第二位老翁又用一袋城堡換走了它——亞涅克便派出三百名槍騎兵再次取回桌子。

passages.text: In the capital his brothers, now great lords, feed him nothing; but each night Yanek raises a castle in the garden, guards it with fifty infantry, and sups like a king. The king borrows the table for three days and returns a counterfeit; Yanek declares war, marches armies out of the pack and castles out of the bag, and the king returns the true table — leaving Yanek richer than his brothers, with his mother beside him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在京城裡，他那如今做了大貴族的兄弟們什麼也不給他吃；但每到夜裡，亞涅克便在花園中升起一座城堡，以五十名步兵守衛，像國王一般用膳。國王借去桌子三天，卻還回一張贗品；亞涅克宣戰，從背包中開出軍隊、從袋中取出城堡，國王只得歸還真桌——亞涅克於是比他的兄弟們更為富有，母親也伴在他身旁。

title.en: The King of the Toads: The Frozen King and the Twig
title.zh: 蟾蜍王：冰凍國王與神枝

region.en: Bohemia (symbolic pin at Olomouc)
region.zh: 波希米亞（象徵性定位於奧洛穆茨）

period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'The King of the Toads'

summary.en: In a palace frozen into a lake, a king sits bound to his chair while his queen gathers frogs for the King of the Toads, who has promised her immortality; a wandering king with a boatman's magic twig freezes the queen, cheats the toad-king into restoring the kingdom, and hews him to pieces before the frogs devour their destroyer.
summary.zh: 王宮冰封為湖，國王縛於座椅；王后日日為蟾蜍王捕蛙，換取不死之諾；携舟子神枝的過路國王凍住王后，騙蟾蜍王還其國土，碎其身於劍下——群蛙遂吞其殘軀。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale.

passages.text: A wandering king, carried by a fisherman's boat across a strange lake, is warned of the sorceress-queen within and given a twig by the boatman. In the hall he finds an old king frozen to his chair, who tells his story: the King of the Toads crept into the place where his lake now is, turned his wife's heart, and promised her the eggs of the magic bird — 'thou wilt become immortal and ever young.' Cut in two by the king's sword, the toad grew together again and froze both king and kingdom; the lake where fish now swim is the king's own people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'The King of the Toads'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位流浪的國王被漁夫的船載著渡過一座陌生的湖，船夫警告他湖中有女巫女王，並給了他一根細枝。他在大廳裡發現一位凍結在椅子上的老國王，老國王講述了自己的故事：蟾蜍王潛入了如今是這片湖的地方，改變了他妻子的心，並向她承諾魔法之鳥的蛋——「你將變得永生不死、永遠年輕。」蟾蜍被國王的劍砍成兩半，卻又癒合在一起，並將國王與整個王國都凍結了；如今魚兒游弋的這片湖，正是國王自己的臣民。

passages.text: The queen returns at sunset and catches frogs for her lover; the visiting king strikes her three times with the twig, freezing her to her seat. Then, dressed in her garments, he goes in the dark to the King of the Toads, pretends to be his love, and begs him as her price to release the old king — so that he may 'fall to dust and ashes' — and to give the kingdom back its former shape.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 女王在日落時分歸來，為她的情人捕捉青蛙；來訪的國王用細枝打了她三下，將她凍結在座位上。隨後，他穿上她的衣裳，在黑暗中前往蟾蜍王處，假裝是他的愛人，並以自己為代價懇求他釋放老國王——好讓他「化為塵土與灰燼」——並讓王國恢復昔日的模樣。

passages.text: The toad-king consents, embraces his supposed love — and is struck three times with the twig, frozen to the earth. The king hews him into countless pieces and throws them into the water; frogs rush from every side with terrible croaking and greedily devour the bits of their destroyer's body. The lake drains away, trees rise from the water, and a splendid city stands where the spell had been; the old king gives the liberator his whole kingdom and dies at peace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蟾蜍王應允了，擁抱了他以為的愛人——卻被細枝打了三下，凍結在地上。國王將他砍成無數碎片，扔進水中；青蛙從四面八方湧來，發出可怕的呱呱聲，貪婪地吞食著它們毀滅者身體的碎塊。湖水退去，樹木從水中升起，一座壯麗的城市矗立在曾被施咒的地方；老國王將整個王國贈予了解救者，然後安然離世。

title.en: The Mouse-Hole and the Underground Kingdom
title.zh: 鼠穴與地下王國

region.en: Bohemia (symbolic pin at Pilsen)
region.zh: 波希米亞（象徵性定位於皮爾森）

period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'The Mouse-Hole, and the Underground Kingdom'

summary.en: The youngest prince shoots his arrow after a mouse and enters the underground kingdom through the mouse-hole: a white marble castle, twelve chambers, and a diamond pan under whose covers an ugly toad waits — the princess under a spell, waiting for a prince who will bathe her daily and carry her in his bosom.
summary.zh: 幼王子對鼠射箭、循箭入鼠穴，抵地下王國：白大理石城堡、十二重殿、鑽石鍋下伏一醜蟾蜍——受咒之公主，等一位日日為之沐浴、揣其於懷的王子。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale (frog-princess type).

passages.text: A king sends his three sons to travel for a year and bring back gifts from their chosen ones: the eldest aims east, the second west, and Yarmil, the youngest, lets fly after a mouse. The earth opens before the mouse-hole and he rides in to an open country where a white marble castle stands. A lady white as new snow gives him a white steed that flies him to a castle of gold, and in its twelfth chamber he finds only a diamond pan, written on: 'Whoever wishes to liberate me must carry me next to his body, and bathe me each day.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'The Mouse-Hole, and the Underground Kingdom'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位國王派他的三個兒子外出遊歷一年，並從他們各自選定的對象那裡帶回禮物：長子向東，次子向西，而最小的亞米爾則任憑一隻老鼠帶路。大地在鼠洞前裂開，他騎馬進入一片開闊之地，那裡矗立著一座白色大理石城堡。一位潔白如新雪的女士給了他一匹白馬，載他飛到一座黃金城堡，在它的第十二個房間裡，他只找到一個鑽石平底鍋，上面寫著：「凡願解救我的，必須將我貼身攜帶，並每日為我沐浴。」

passages.text: Under the covers Yarmil finds a great ugly toad, and such terror seizes him that he takes it out and puts it in his bosom; the more he washes it the uglier it grows. Invisible hands serve his meals; the year runs to its end, and a letter appears on his writing-table: 'I love thee unspeakably; but be thou patient, as I am patient. A gift for thy father thou hast in the pan; give it to him, but tarry not long at home. Put me back in the pan.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在被褥下，亞米爾發現一隻巨大醜陋的蟾蜍，恐懼攫住了他，他將它取出，放進自己的懷裡；他越是清洗它，它就越發醜陋。無形的手為他端上飯菜；一年將盡，他的寫字桌上出現一封信：「我無比地愛你；但請你忍耐，正如我忍耐一樣。平底鍋裡有你給你父親的禮物；把它交給他，但不要在家久留。把我放回鍋裡。」

passages.text: He returns home with the toad in the pan, is mocked by his brothers, and rides back to the castle, where after the year of patience the toad is washed into the most beautiful princess of the underground kingdom. The enchantment of the white castle is broken; Yarmil brings home a bride worth more than both his brothers' gifts, and the underground kingdom shines again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他帶著鍋裡的蟾蜍回到家中，遭到兄弟們的嘲笑，然後騎馬返回城堡，在那裡，經過一年的忍耐之後，蟾蜍被洗淨，變成了地下王國最美麗的公主。白色城堡的魔法被解除了；亞米爾帶回了一位比兩個兄弟的禮物都更珍貴的新娘，地下王國再次煥發光彩。

title.en: The Cuirassier and the Horned Princess
title.zh: 胸甲騎兵與長角公主

region.en: Bohemia (symbolic pin at Prague)
region.zh: 波希米亞（象徵性定位於布拉格）

period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'The Cuirassier and the Horned Princess'

summary.en: Twelve deserting cuirassiers take shelter in a sorceress's castle where nine die for opening forbidden caskets; the three survivors win a cap of invisibility, a mantle of flight, and a purse of gold — and pay back the card-playing princess who stole their gifts by selling her magic pears that grow horns, then curing her as a false physician.
summary.zh: 十二名逃亡胸甲騎兵夜宿女巫城堡，九人因啟禁閉之匣而亡；三名倖存者得隱形帽、飛行斗篷與金錢袋——而後以長角魔梨懲罰竊寶的嗜賭公主，再假扮醫師治癒她。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale.

passages.text: Twelve deserting cuirassiers ride to a great castle in wild mountains, where a table is laid for twelve and oats stand ready; the old sorceress feeds them but forbids anyone to look in the twelve unlocked caskets. Nine men's sinful curiosity costs them their lives; the three survivors are permitted to look and take what they find: a cap that makes its wearer invisible, a mantle on which a man can fly through the air, and a purse that yields ten ducats at every shake.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'The Cuirassier and the Horned Princess'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 十二名逃兵騎馬來到荒野群山間的一座大城堡，那裡已擺好供十二人用餐的餐桌，燕麥也已備妥；老女巫供他們吃喝，卻禁止任何人窺看那十二只未上鎖的箱子。九人因罪惡的好奇心而喪命；三名倖存者獲准觀看並取走他們所發現之物：一頂能讓戴者隱形的帽子、一件能讓人飛越空中的斗篷，以及一個每搖一次便吐出十枚達克特的錢袋。

passages.text: In a great town the princess, immeasurably fond of cards, outplays every comer and has the losers flogged from the castle. The three friends sit down to play her: the invisible man reads her cards, the purse pays her stake, and she loses all — then she has her servants steal the purse, the cap, and the mantle from the travellers, and has them flogged out of the town.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在一座大城裡，公主酷愛紙牌，勝過所有來客，並命人將輸家鞭打出城堡。三位朋友坐下與她對賭：隱形人看穿她的牌，錢袋替他們付賭注，於是她輸個精光——隨後她命僕人從旅人身上偷走錢袋、帽子和斗篷，並將他們鞭打出城。

passages.text: The avenger sells her pears so splendid that she cannot resist: with the first pear horns begin to grow on her head, and soon she cannot stand upright in the hall. Sawed by the doctors, the horns grow again; the king proclaims that whoever frees the princess shall marry her and have the kingdom. The disguised cuirassier, as a physician, first makes her return the stolen cap, mantle, and purse, then gives her quarters of a magic apple — and at the fourth quarter the horns fall off at a blow, and the freed princess marries her healer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 復仇者賣給她絕美的梨子，令她無法抗拒：吃下第一口梨，她頭上便開始長出角，很快她在大廳裡已無法直立。醫生鋸去角，角又再長出；國王宣告，誰能解救公主，便可娶她並得到王國。那名喬裝成醫生的胸甲騎兵，先讓她交還偷來的帽子、斗篷和錢袋，然後給她四分之一個魔法蘋果——吃到第四分之一時，角應聲脫落，獲救的公主便嫁給了她的醫治者。

title.en: The Treacherous Brothers
title.zh: 奸詐的兄長們

region.en: Bohemia (symbolic pin at Prague)
region.zh: 波希米亞（象徵性定位於布拉格）

period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'The Treacherous Brothers'

summary.en: Jalmir, the sickly youngest of seven sons, is healed by a white-bearded visitant and rides a miraculous horse to serve a foreign king for love of the golden-castle princess; his treacherous brothers set him one impossible task after another and finally perish when their slander is brought to light.
summary.zh: 七子中最孱弱的雅爾米爾得白髮訪客治癒，騎神馬為愛黃金城堡公主而效力他邦之王；奸詐兄長屢設險障，終因讒言敗露而自取滅亡。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale.

passages.text: Jalmir, youngest of seven sons, so weak he is still nursed like a child, is cured overnight by a venerable white-bearded man who thrice asks from the dark, 'Jalmir, art thou sleeping?' and commands him: go through the southern gate, mount the white horse under the old pear-tree, and ride after thy brothers. The horse speaks with a man's voice and carries him through the air.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'The Treacherous Brothers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 雅爾米爾是七個兒子中最年幼的，身體虛弱得仍像孩童般需人照料；一位白鬚的可敬老者一夜之間治好了他。老者三次在黑暗中問道：「雅爾米爾，你睡著了嗎？」並吩咐他：穿過南門，騎上老梨樹下的白馬，去追趕你的兄長們。那匹馬以人的聲音說話，並載著他飛越空中。

passages.text: His brothers, already grown great at another king's court, set him impossible tasks — the enchanted cask of wine from a sorceress's cellar, then the princess of the golden castle in the sea, her castle, her key, and last the waters of death, life, and youth. Each time the white steed instructs him, the animals he has helped repay him — a fish with a whistle, an eagle with a rescue — and each time the brothers read of the next toil in the castle books and laugh that little Jalmir will drown or run home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的兄長們在另一位國王的宮廷中已功成名就，卻派給他不可能的任務——先從女巫的地窖取來那隻施了魔法的酒桶，然後是海中金城堡的公主、她的城堡、她的鑰匙，最後是死亡之水、生命之水和青春之水。每一次，白馬都指點他，而他所幫助過的動物也回報他——一條魚送他一只哨子，一隻鷹救他一命——而每一次，兄長們都在城堡的書中讀到下一個苦役，並嘲笑小雅爾米爾將會溺死或逃回家去。

passages.text: On the dam to the waters' island the sea rises and swallows Jalmir; the eagle that owed him a quarter of beef dives, bears him to the island, and shows him the three springs. He returns to find his father dead of old age and the wedding set for that day: the princess, to make their marriage equal, rubs the king with the water of death, the water of youth — and by tragic error takes the flask of death for the water of life, so that the king is rubbed twice with death and can never live again. Jalmir revives the princess, is proclaimed king, and marries her; when his brothers whisper that the two poisoned the old king, the people, hearing his story of the six betrayals, seize the treacherous six and throw them into the flames of a straw-stack they themselves had set.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在通往眾水之島的堤壩上，海水漲起，吞沒了雅爾米爾；那隻欠他四分之一頭牛的鷹俯衝而下，將他帶到島上，並指給他看那三處泉水。他回來後發現父親已年老去世，而婚禮就定在當天：公主為了使他們的婚姻門當戶對，便用死亡之水、青春之水塗抹國王——卻因悲慘的差錯，把死亡之水的瓶子當成了生命之水，於是國王被死亡之水塗抹了兩次，再也無法復生。雅爾米爾救活了公主，被宣告為國王，並娶了她；當他的兄長們私下散布謠言，說這兩人毒死了老王時，民眾聽了他講述那六次背叛的經過，便抓住那六個背信之徒，把他們扔進他們自己點燃的稻草堆的火焰之中。

title.en: Huallallo Caruincho: One Child for the God, One for the Parents
title.zh: 瓦拉約·卡魯因喬:一孩獻神,一孩歸家

region.en: Province of Huarochiri, highlands above Lima (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 利馬高原瓦羅奇里省(象徵性標記)

period: Huarochiri manuscript collected by Francisco de Avila, 1608; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Francisco de Avila, 'A Narrative of the Errors, False Gods and other Superstitions... of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The most ancient tradition of Huarochiri tells of huacas called Yananamca Intanamca who, in an encounter with another huaca called Huallallo Caruincho, were conquered and destroyed; Huallallo remained Lord and God of the land. He ordered that no woman should bring forth more than two children, of which one was to be sacrificed for him to eat, and the other - whichever the parents chose - might be brought up. In those days all who died were brought to life again on the fifth day, and what was sown sprouted, grew and ripened on the fifth day; the three provinces were then a very hot country which the Indians call Yunca or Ande, with a great variety of beautiful birds, macaws and parrots. All this - the people, who led very evil lives, and the idol - came to be driven away to other Andes by the idol Pariacaca.
summary.zh: 瓦羅奇里最古的傳說講述名為「亞南亞姆卡-因坦亞姆卡」的瓦卡,與另一位瓦卡「瓦拉約·卡魯因喬」交戰而被征服毀滅;瓦拉約遂為該地之主神。他立規:婦女不得生多於二子,其一須獻祭給他吃,另一子——由父母自擇——可留養。彼時死者於第五日復活;播種之物第五日發芽、生長、成熟;三省之地氣候炎熱,印第安人稱之為「永卡」(溫熱之地),其間有金剛鸚鵡、鸚鵡等豔麗禽鳥。後來人民(相傳其行甚惡)連同該神,一併被瓦卡「帕里亞卡卡」逐往別處安第斯山林。

sensitivity.note: Huarochiri (Yauyos) tradition - Central Andean, pre-Inca; included in the Inca/Andean corpus as the classic Quechua myth text. Child-sacrifice rule recorded critically.

passages.text: It is a most ancient tradition that, before any other event of which there is any memory, there were certain huacas or idols, which, together with the others, must be supposed to have walked in the form of men. These huacas were called Yananamca Intanamca; and in a certain encounter they had with another huaca called Huallallo Caruincho, they were conquered and destroyed by the said Huallallo, who remained as Lord and God of the land.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 1 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一項極古老的傳統說：在記憶所及的任何其他事件發生之前，曾有某些華卡（huaca，即神像或偶像），與其他華卡一同，據信曾以人形行走於世。這些華卡名為亞納南卡·印塔南卡（Yananamca Intanamca）；在一次與另一名為瓦利亞柳·卡魯因丘（Huallallo Caruincho）的華卡交鋒時，他們被該瓦利亞柳擊敗並毀滅，瓦利亞柳遂成為此地的領主與神祇。

passages.text: He ordered that no woman should bring forth more than two children, of which one was to be sacrificed for him to eat, and the other - whichever of the two the parents chose - might be brought up. It was also a tradition that, in those days, all who died were brought to life again on the fifth day, and that what was sown in that land also sprouted, grew, and ripened on the fifth day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 1 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他下令任何婦女不得生育超過兩名子女，其中一名須獻祭供他食用，另一名——由父母從二者中擇一——則可撫養長大。另有一項傳統說：在那些日子裡，所有死去的人都在第五日復活；凡播種於該地之物，也在第五日發芽、生長並成熟。

passages.text: All these three provinces were then a very hot country, which the Indians call Yunca or Ande; and they say that these crops were made visible in the deserts and uninhabited places, such as that of Pariacaca; and that in these Andes there was a great variety of most beautiful and brilliant birds, such as macaws, parrots, and others. All this, with the people who then inhabited the land (and who, according to their account, led very evil lives), and the said idol, came to be driven away to other Andes by the idol Pariacaca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 1 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這三個省份當時是一片極為炎熱之地，印第安人稱之為雲卡（Yunca）或安第（Ande）；他們說，這些作物在荒漠與無人居住之地——如帕里亞卡卡（Pariacaca）之地——亦可見其生長；又說在這些安第斯之地有種類繁多、極為美麗燦爛的鳥類，如金剛鸚鵡、鸚鵡及其他種種。這一切，連同當時居住於該地的人們（據他們所述，這些人過著極其邪惡的生活），以及前述那尊偶像，最終都被偶像帕里亞卡卡驅逐至其他安第斯之地。

language: Spanish record of a Quechua tradition
canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Coniraya Viracocha in Rags: Terraces Raised by a Word
title.zh: 衣衫襤褸的庫尼拉亞·維拉科查:一語築田

region.en: Province of Huarochiri (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦羅奇里省(象徵性標記)

period: Huarochiri manuscript collected by Francisco de Avila, 1608; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Francisco de Avila, 'A Narrative of the Errors, False Gods and other Superstitions... of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: They say that in most ancient times Coniraya Uiracocha appeared in the form and dress of a very poor Indian clothed in rags, so that those who knew not who he was reviled him and called him a lousy wretch. He was the Creator of all things: by his word of command he caused the terraces and fields to be formed on the steep sides of ravines, and the sustaining walls to rise up and support them; he made the irrigating channels to flow by merely hurling a hollow cane, and went in various directions arranging many things. His great knowledge enabled him to invent tricks and deceits touching the huacas and idols of the villages he visited. He was invoked almost down to the arrival of the Spaniards: when the Indians worshipped him they said 'Coniraya Uiracocha, thou art Lord of all: thine are the crops, and thine are all the people'; in commencing any arduous undertaking they threw a piece of coca on the ground as an oblation, saying 'Tell me, O Lord Coniraya Uiracocha, how I am to do this?' - a custom which prevailed also among the weavers of cloths when their work was toilsome.
summary.zh: 相傳太古之時,庫尼拉亞·維拉科查以極貧印第安人之形現身,衣衫襤褸,不識其真身者皆唾罵他是骯髒的癩子。他卻是造物主:一言既出,溝壑陡坡上的梯田與擋土牆便平地而起;他只須擲出一根空心竹杖,灌溉水渠便自然暢流;他四處行走,安排諸事,還以其大智對所訪村落中的瓦卡與偶像戲弄百出。直至西班牙人到來之前,人們仍在呼求他:崇拜時說「庫尼拉亞·維拉科查,你是萬有之主:五穀屬你,萬民屬你」;凡遇艱難大事,先擲古柯葉於地為祭,說「主啊庫尼拉亞·維拉科查,告訴我當如何行事」;織工織造繁難花紋時亦行此俗。

sensitivity.note: The disheveled culture-hero of Huarochiri; the coca-divination custom is a living practice attested by the parish priest.

passages.text: They say that in most ancient times the Coniraya Uiracocha appeared in the form and dress of a very poor Indian clothed in rags, insomuch that those who knew not who he was reviled him and called him a lousy wretch. They say that this was the Creator of all things; and that, by his word of command, he caused the terraces and fields to be formed on the steep sides of ravines, and the sustaining walls to rise up and support them. He also made the irrigating channels to flow, by merely hurling a hollow cane, such as we call a cane of Spain; and he went in various directions, arranging many things. His great knowledge enabled him to invent tricks and deceits touching the huacas and idols in the villages which he visited.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 2 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們說，在極古老的時代，科尼拉亞·維拉科查（Coniraya Uiracocha）以一名衣衫襤褸、極其貧窮的印第安人的形貌與裝束出現，以致不認識他身份的人辱罵他，稱他為滿身蝨子的可憐蟲。他們說，此人乃萬物之造物主；他憑其命令之言，使梯田與田畝在陡峭的山谷兩側形成，並使支撐的牆壁升起以承托它們。他僅憑投擲一根空心蘆葦——即我們所稱的西班牙蘆葦——便使灌溉渠道流淌；他又往各處去，安排許多事物。他淵博的知識使他能就他所造訪之村落中的華卡與偶像，發明種種戲法與騙術。

passages.text: It is certain that it was invoked and reverenced almost down to the time when the Spaniards arrived in this land. For when the Indians worshipped it they said: 'Coniraya Uiracocha, thou art Lord of all: thine are the crops, and thine are all the people.' In commencing any arduous or difficult undertaking, they threw a piece of coca on the ground, as an oblation, and said: 'Tell me, O Lord Coniraya Uiracocha, how I am to do this?' The same custom prevailed among the weavers of cloths, when their work was toilsome and difficult.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, chs. 1-2 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 可以確定的是，幾乎直到西班牙人抵達此地之時，它仍受祈求與崇敬。因為當印第安人崇拜它時，他們說：「科尼拉亞·維拉科查，您是萬物之主：作物屬於您，所有人民也屬於您。」在著手任何艱鉅或困難之事時，他們會將一片古柯葉擲於地上作為祭品，並說：「請告訴我，科尼拉亞·維拉科查主啊，我該如何做成此事？」同樣的習俗也盛行於織布者之間，當他們的工作辛勞而困難之時。

language: Spanish record of a Quechua tradition
canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Lucma Fruit and the Crawling Child: Cavillaca's Virgin Conception
title.zh: 盧克瑪果與爬行的嬰孩:卡維利亞卡的處女感孕

region.en: Anchicocha, between Chorrillo and Huarochiri (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喬里略與瓦羅奇里之間的安奇科查(象徵性標記)

period: Huarochiri manuscript collected by Francisco de Avila, 1608; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Francisco de Avila, 'A Narrative of the Errors, False Gods and other Superstitions... of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: There was a woman who was a huaca, named Cavillaca, a most beautiful virgin sought after by all the principal idols, but she would never show favour to any. Once she sat down to weave a mantle at the foot of a lucma tree, when the wise Coniraya turned himself into a very beautiful bird, went up into the lucma tree, took some of his generative seed and made it into the likeness of a ripe and luxurious lucma, which he allowed to fall near the beautiful Cavillaca. She took it and ate it with delight, and was made pregnant without other contact with man. When nine months were completed she bore a son, herself remaining a virgin, and suckled the child for a whole year without knowing whose it was. When the child began to crawl, Cavillaca demanded that the huacas and principal idols should assemble, and that it should be declared whose son the child was. Each adorned himself in the richest clothes to appear brighter than the rest, that she might select him for her spouse. In the assembly at Anchicocha, in the lowest place of all, sat Coniraya Uiracocha in his beggar's rags. Cavillaca declared that as none would speak, she would let the child go, and his father would be the one to whom he crawls; she loosed the child, who, passing by all the others, went to Coniraya in his rags and dirt, rejoiced, laughed, and rested at his feet. Cavillaca, in shame - 'What disgrace is this, that a lady such as I am should be made pregnant by a poor and filthy creature' - snatched up the child and fled towards the sea-shore; Coniraya put on magnificent golden robes and pursued her crying loving words, his splendour illuminating the whole country; but the disdainful Cavillaca would not turn her head, calling him a creature so vile and filthy. She came to the sea coast of Pachacamac, entered the sea with her child, and was turned into a rock; the two rocks may still be seen, mother and child.
summary.zh: 當時有一位女性瓦卡,名卡維利亞卡,絕世美人,眾神皆求之,她卻一概不允。一日她在盧克瑪樹下織布,智者的庫尼拉亞化作美鳥飛上樹端,將自己的精液化作一顆熟透肥美的盧克瑪果,落到美人近旁。卡維利亞卡拾而食之,甘美異常,遂未經男女交接而感孕。十月期滿,處女生子,親自哺乳一年,不知其父為誰。孩子會爬之後,她召請諸瓦卡齊聚,宣告:誰是孩子的父親。諸神各梳洗盛裝,欲以最光鮮之姿被選為夫。在安奇科查的集會上,庫尼拉亞以乞丐襤褸之身坐在最末位。卡維利亞卡環視無人應答,便說:「你們既都不肯認,我便放了這孩子——他爬向誰,誰便是他的父親。」孩子爬過諸神,逕奔那襤褸骯髒的庫尼拉亞,嬉笑歡呼,依偎其足。卡維利亞卡羞憤交加:「我這般尊貴之身,竟為此卑賤污穢之物所孕!」抱起孩子轉身奔向海濱。庫尼拉亞忽换上燦然金袍,追她呼喚愛語,光輝照徹山野;美人卻頭也不回,罵他是穢物。她逃至帕查卡馬克海濱,抱子入海,化為礁石。至今海邊猶見兩石:母與子。

sensitivity.note: The Cavillaca cycle is the Huarochiri masterpiece; the conception scene is retold soberly as the source has it.

passages.text: At that time they also say that there was a woman who was a huaca. Her name was Cavillaca, and she was a most beautiful virgin, who was much sought after by the huacas, or principal idols, but she would never show favour to any of them. Once she sat down to weave a mantle at the foot of a lucma tree, when the wise Coniraya succeeded in approaching her in the following manner: he turned himself into a very beautiful bird, and went up into the lucma tree, where he took some of his generative seed and made it into the likeness of a ripe and luxurious lucma, which he allowed to fall near the beautiful Cavillaca. She took it and ate it with much delight, and by it she was made pregnant without other contact with man.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 2 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們又說，當時有一名女子是華卡。她的名字叫卡維利亞卡（Cavillaca），是一位極其美麗的處女，深受華卡即主要偶像們的追求，但她從不向其中任何一位示好。有一次，她坐在一棵盧克馬樹（lucma）下編織斗篷，機敏的科尼拉亞便以下述方式接近了她：他將自己變成一隻極美麗的鳥，飛上那棵盧克馬樹，在那裡取出自己的一些生殖之精，將其做成了一顆成熟而豐美的盧克馬果的模樣，並讓它落在美麗的卡維利亞卡近旁。她拾起它，滿心歡喜地吃了下去，因此便受孕，而未與男子有其他接觸。

passages.text: When the nine months were completed she conceived and bore a son, herself remaining a virgin; and she suckled the child at her own breast for a whole year without knowing whose it was. At the end of the year, when the child began to crawl, Cavillaca demanded that the huacas and principal idols of the land should assemble, and that it should be declared whose son was the child. Each one adorned himself in the best manner possible, combing, washing, and dressing in the richest clothes, each desiring to appear brighter and better than the rest in the eyes of the beautiful Cavillaca, that so she might select him for her spouse and husband.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 2 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 九個月期滿，她受孕生下一個兒子，自己仍保持童貞；她親自以母乳哺育這孩子整整一年，卻不知孩子的父親是誰。一年將盡，孩子開始爬行時，卡維亞卡要求全地的瓦卡與主要神像齊聚一堂，並要查明這孩子究竟是誰的兒子。每一位都盡其所能地盛裝打扮，梳頭、沐浴，穿上最華麗的衣裳，個個都希望在美麗的卡維亞卡眼中顯得比其餘人更為光鮮出色，好讓她選他為配偶與丈夫。

passages.text: They say that, in this assembly, in the lowest place of all, sat the god Coniraya Uiracocha in his beggar's rags. When she found that all were silent, she said: 'As none of you will speak, I shall let the child go, and doubtless his father will be the one to whom he crawls.' So saying, she loosed the child, who, passing by all the others, went to where was his father Coniraya in his rags and dirt, and when the child reached him, it rejoiced and laughed, and rested at his feet. This conduct caused Cavillaca great shame and annoyance, and she snatched up the child, exclaiming: 'What disgrace is this that has come upon me, that a lady such as I am should be made pregnant by a poor and filthy creature.' Then she turned her back and fled away towards the sea-shore.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 2 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說在這場聚會中，坐在最卑下位置的，正是身披乞丐破衣的孔尼拉亞·維拉科查神。她見眾人都默不作聲，便說道：「既然你們都不肯開口，我就放開這孩子，想必他爬向誰，誰就是他的父親。」說罷，她放開孩子，孩子越過其餘眾人，逕直爬向那身披破衣、滿身塵垢的父親孔尼拉亞所在之處；孩子一到他跟前，便歡喜發笑，依偎在他腳邊。這番情景令卡維亞卡深感羞恥與惱怒，她一把抱起孩子，驚呼道：「這是何等羞辱臨到我身上，像我這樣一位貴婦，竟被一個貧賤骯髒的傢伙弄大了肚子。」隨即她轉過身去，朝海濱方向逃走。

passages.text: Coniraya Uiracocha desired the friendship and favour of the goddess, so, when he saw her take her flight, he put on magnificent golden robes, and, leaving the astonished assembly of gods, he ran after her, crying out: 'O my lady Cavillaca, turn your eyes and see how handsome and gallant am I'; and they say that his splendour illuminated the whole country. Yet the disdainful Cavillaca would not turn her head, but rather increased her speed, saying she had been made pregnant by a creature so vile and filthy. She came to the sea coast of Pachacamac, where she entered the sea with her child, and was turned into a rock. They say that the two rocks may still be seen, which are mother and child.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 2 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 孔尼拉亞·維拉科查渴望得到這位女神的友誼與青睞，因此見她逃走，便換上華麗的金袍，離開那群驚愕的眾神，追趕上去，高聲喊道：「啊，我的卡維亞卡夫人，請回眸看看我有多麼俊美英挺。」據說他的光輝照亮了整個大地。然而高傲的卡維亞卡不肯回頭，反而加快腳步，說自己是被一個如此卑劣骯髒的傢伙弄大了肚子。她來到帕查卡馬克的海岸，帶著孩子走進海中，化作一塊岩石。據說至今仍可見到那兩塊岩石，便是母子二人。

language: Spanish record of a Quechua tradition
