passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 11 (1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 佩蕾（Pele）與她的家人住在普納（Puna）的秀美之地。某日，天朗氣清，佩蕾望見壯麗的浪濤與其白色浪峰，便向姊妹們提議下去沐浴與衝浪；她站在捲曲浪濤的邊緣，以浪峰本身為衝浪板馳騁，有時她的兄長卡莫霍阿利伊（Kamohoalii）——偉大的鯊神——會化為鯊魚作她的衝浪板，她一次又一次游向波浪的深淵，而姊妹們則使內陸迴盪著她們的歡呼。最後她回到海灘，告訴姊妹們游泳的禁忌已解除，便與她最小的妹妹希伊阿卡（Hiiaka）一同前往內陸，由妹妹在她睡覺時守護。她們來到一座為女神搭建的、以提葉（ti）覆頂的屋子。佩蕾在那裡躺下，對妹妹說：「我要睡了，把自己交給垂暮的陰影——沉入睡眠的最深處。這睡眠將極為沉重；我對它心懷嫉妒；因此這是禁忌。這是我對你的命令，哦我的小人兒：你守候著，不要喚醒我，歷經九日八夜，然後呼喚我，並吟誦《胡利希亞》（Hulihia），那是一首據信能召回生命、使身體復甦的吟唱。或許這睡眠將是我去會見一個男人——我們的丈夫——的旅程。若我在夢中遇見我的愛人，這睡眠便極有價值。我要睡了。」

passages.text: While Pele was sleeping her spirit heard the sound of a hula-drum skilfully played, accompanied by a chant sung by a wonderful voice. The spirit of Pele arose from her body and listened to that voice; she thought it was the hula of Laka, the goddess of the dance; then she clearly heard male voices, strong and tender, and a great joy awoke within her. She passed from place to place, led by the call of the drum and dance, following it along the palis and over the deep ravines, through forest shadows and along rocky beaches, until she heard the call coming across the sea; her spirit crossed the channel and passed on from island to island until she came to Kauai, and there the drum-beat and the song of the dance did not die away or change, so she knew she had found the lover desired in her dream.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 11 (1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 佩蕾沉睡之時，她的靈魂聽見有人巧妙地敲擊呼拉鼓，伴隨著一個美妙嗓音所唱的吟誦。佩蕾的靈魂自她的軀體中升起，聆聽那聲音；她以為那是舞蹈女神拉卡的呼拉舞；接著她清楚地聽見男子的聲音，雄渾而溫柔，一股巨大的喜悅在她心中甦醒。她循著鼓聲與舞蹈的呼喚，一處又一處地前行，沿著崖壁、越過深谷，穿過林蔭、沿著多岩的海灘，直到她聽見那呼喚自海的彼端傳來；她的靈魂渡過海峽，從一島行至另一島，直到來到考艾島，那裡的鼓聲與舞歌既不消逝也不改變，於是她知道自己已尋得夢中所渴望的愛人。

passages.text: Pele's spirit now put on the body of strong, healthful youth; nor was there any blemish in her beauty and symmetry from head to foot. She was anointed with all the fragrant oils of Puna; her dress was the splendid garland of the red lehua flower and maile leaf and the fern from the dwelling-places of the gods. The tender vines of the deep woods veiled this queen of the crater; in glorious young womanhood she went to the halau, the house for dancing of Lohiau, the high-born chief of Haena, Kauai, full of chiefs engaged in the sports of that time. The multitude saw a glorious young woman step out of the mist and raised a great shout, praising her with strong voices; the countenance of Pele was like the clearest and gentlest moonlight, and the people made a vacant space for the passage of this wonderful stranger, casting themselves on the ground before her. Asked whether she came from the far-off sunrise of foreign lands, Pele replied, smiling, 'Ka! I belong to Kauai'; but at last she acknowledged that she had come from Puna, Hawaii. Lohiau told her that her welcome was all that he could give: 'For me is the island, inland, seaward, and all around Kauai. This is your place. The home you have in Puna you will think you see again in Kauai. The name of my house for you is Ha-laau-ola, Tree of Life.' Pele replied, 'The name of your house is beautiful. My home in Puna is Mauli-ola, Long Life. I will accept this house of yours.' Then Lohiau proposed to his chiefs that he should take this beautiful chiefess as his queen, and his thought seemed good to all; Pele and Lohiau were married and dwelt together several days, according to the custom of the ancient time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 11 (1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 佩蕾的靈魂如今披上了強健、康泰的青春之軀；她從頭到腳的美麗與勻稱毫無瑕疵。她塗抹了普納所有芬芳的油膏；她的衣裳是紅蕾胡阿花、邁勒葉與諸神居所之蕨所編成的華美花環。深林柔韌的藤蔓遮掩著這位火山口的女王；她以光榮的青春年華前往哈勞——考艾島哈埃納的高貴酋長洛希奧的舞屋，那裡滿是參與當時各種競技的酋長們。眾人看見一位光榮的年輕女子自霧中走出，便大聲呼喊，以雄健的嗓音讚美她；佩蕾的容顏宛如最澄澈、最柔和的月光，人們為這位奇妙的陌生人讓出一條通道，紛紛俯伏於她面前的地上。有人問她是否來自遠方異地的日出之處，佩蕾微笑著答道：「卡！我屬於考艾島」；但最後她承認自己來自夏威夷的普納。洛希奧告訴她，他能給予的歡迎便是他所能給的一切：「這座島屬於我，內陸、海濱，以及考艾島四周的一切。這裡就是您的地方。您在普納所擁有的家，您在考艾島會覺得再次見到。我為您所備的屋宅之名為哈—拉奧—奧拉，生命之樹。」佩蕾答道：「您屋宅之名很美。我在普納的家名為毛利—奧拉，長壽。我願接受您這座屋宅。」於是洛希奧向他的酋長們提議，要娶這位美麗的女酋長為后，他的想法在眾人看來都很好；佩蕾與洛希奧依照古時的習俗成婚，同住了數日。

passages.text: Lohiau planned a great feast and a day for the hula-dance. Three of the women of Kauai known as the guardians of Haena had come into the halau; they were very beautiful and possessed of supernatural power - female mo-o, or dragons. Pele had told Lohiau of their coming and charged him: 'Remember, you have been set apart for me; therefore I place upon you my law: Ke kai okia - cut off by the sea - are you, separated from all for me.' The dragon-woman Kilinoe sat watching Lohiau with large bright shining eyes, using magic power to make him pay attention to her charms, but Pele placed a shadow between them and her. Then up rose Kilinoe and made fragrant wreaths wherewith to crown Lohiau and his fellow hula-drummers; but the law of Pele was upon him, and Pele threw aside her shadow garments and said, 'It is not for me to give a chant for your native dance, but I will call the guardian winds of your islands Niihau and Kauai, O Lohiau! and they will answer my call.' For a long time she chanted, calling wind after wind; while she sang, soft breezes blew around and through the house, then came stronger winds whistling through the trees outside, and the people outside cried out that the sea grew rough and white and the winds were twisting the heavens. Very angry was Kilinoe, and she challenged: 'You have seen Niihau; perhaps also you know the winds of Kauai.' Pele again chanted, calling for the guardian winds of Kauai, and at last rang out while she made known the character of the beautiful dragon-women, calling them the mocking winds of Haena; the dragon-women knew that Pele only needed to point them out to have all the chiefs cry out against them in scorn, and out of the house they rushed, fleeing back to their home in the caves. Winds without number began to come near scraping over the land; the feast and the day of dancing were broken up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 11 (1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 洛希奧籌劃了一場盛大的宴會與一個舉行呼拉舞的日子。考艾島上三位被稱為哈埃納守護者的女子已進入哈勞；她們非常美麗，且擁有超自然的力量——是女莫奧，即女龍。佩蕾已告訴洛希奧她們的到來，並告誡他：「記住，你已被分別出來歸於我；因此我將我的律法加於你：Ke kai okia——被海所隔絕——你之於我，已與一切分別。」女龍基利諾埃坐著凝視洛希奧，一雙大而明亮閃爍的眼睛，施展魔力使他注意她的魅力，但佩蕾在她與他之間置下一道影子。接著基利諾埃起身，編製芬芳的花環，要為洛希奧與他的呼拉鼓手同伴們加冕；但佩蕾的律法加於他身，佩蕾便拋開她的影子衣裳，說道：「為你們本土的舞蹈吟唱，並非我分內之事，但我要召喚你們島嶼尼豪與考艾的守護之風，哦，洛希奧！它們會回應我的呼喚。」她吟唱了許久，一風又一風地召喚；她歌唱之時，柔和的微風環繞並穿過屋舍，接著更強的風呼嘯著穿過外頭的樹木，外頭的人們驚呼海水變得洶湧泛白，風正扭絞著天空。基利諾埃非常憤怒，她挑戰道：「你已見過尼豪；或許你也識得考艾的風。」佩蕾再次吟唱，召喚考艾的守護之風，最後在她揭示那些美麗女龍的本性時響亮地吟出，稱她們為哈埃納的嘲弄之風；女龍們知道佩蕾只需指出她們，便足以讓所有酋長輕蔑地對她們叫喊，於是她們衝出屋舍，逃回她們在洞穴中的家。無數的風開始逼近，刮過大地；宴會與舞蹈之日就此中斷。

passages.text: When Pele had laid herself down on the soft mats of Puna for her long sleep she had charged her little sister to wake her if she had not returned to life before nine days were past. The days were almost through to the last moment; then as the winds died away and the last strong gust journeyed out toward the sea Pele heard Hiiaka's voice calling from the island Hawaii in the magic chant Pele had told her to use - the incantation known as 'Hulihia ke au', the current is turning, a call carried by the spirit-power of the one who uttered it into far-away places: 'E Pele e! The milky way turns. E Pele e! The night changes. E Pele e! The red dawn breaks. E Pele e! The sound of roaring is in your crater. E Pele e! Awake, arise, return.' Hearing this arousing call, she bowed her head and wept. She said to Lohiau: 'It is not for me to remain here in pleasure with you. I must return because of the call of my sister. Calm will take the place of the storm; I will send my little sister, then come quickly to my home in Puna.' Then the queen of fire ceased speaking and began to be lost to Lohiau; as Pele disappeared peace came to him and all the land of Kauai was filled with calm and rest. Pele's spirit passed at once to the body lying in the house thatched with ti leaves in Puna. Soon she arose and told Hiiaka to call the sisters from the sea; she told them they must dance the hula of the lifted tabu, but they all refused until she came to Hiiaka, who had guarded her during her long sleep. Hiiaka arose and danced gloriously before the hula god and chanted while she danced: 'Puna dances in the wind; the forest of Keaau is shaken; Haena moves quietly; there is motion on the beach of Nanahuki; perhaps this is a dance of love, for the friend loved in the sleep.' Pele rejoiced over the skill of her younger sister and was surprised by the chanted reference to the experiences at Haena; she granted permission to Hiiaka to remain by the sea with her friend Hopoe until a messenger should be sent to call her home to Kilauea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 11 (1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當佩蕾在普納柔軟的蓆上躺下，開始她漫長的沉睡時，她曾囑咐她的小妹，若她未在九日過去之前甦醒歸來，便要喚醒她。日子幾乎到了最後一刻；接著，當風平息、最後一陣強勁的疾風向海而去時，佩蕾聽見希伊阿卡的聲音自夏威夷島傳來，唱著佩蕾囑咐她使用的魔法吟誦——那名為「Hulihia ke au」，潮流正在轉向的咒語，一個由吟誦者以靈力傳送至遠方的呼喚：「E Pele e！銀河轉向。E Pele e！夜色變換。E Pele e！紅霞破曉。E Pele e！你的火山口中有轟鳴之聲。E Pele e！醒來，起身，歸來。」聽見這喚醒的呼喚，她低下頭哭泣。她對洛希奧說：「我不宜在此與你享樂。我必須因我妹妹的呼喚而歸去。平靜將取代風暴；我會先派我的小妹前來，隨後便速回我在普納的家。」於是火之女王停止言語，開始自洛希奧眼前消隱；佩蕾消失之際，平靜臨到他身上，整個考艾島充滿了安寧與休憩。佩蕾的靈魂立刻前往那躺在普納的提葉茅屋中的軀體。不久她起身，吩咐希伊阿卡自海中召喚姊妹們；她告訴她們必須跳那解除禁忌的呼拉舞，但她們全都拒絕，直到她問到希伊阿卡——那位在她漫長沉睡期間守護她的人。希伊阿卡起身，在呼拉神前光榮地起舞，邊舞邊吟唱：「普納在風中起舞；凱阿奧的森林為之震動；哈埃納悄然移動；納納胡基的海灘上有動靜；或許這是愛之舞，為那在夢中愛上的友人。」佩蕾為小妹的技藝而欣喜，並對吟唱中提及哈埃納的經歷感到驚訝；她准許希伊阿卡與她的友人霍波埃留在海邊，直到有使者被派來召她回基拉韋厄。

title.en: Hopoe, Danced to Death and Changed to Stone
title.zh: 霍波埃：舞者化石

region.en: Hopoe stone near Keaau, Puna, Hawaii Island
region.zh: 夏威夷島普納凱阿烏霍波埃石

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; retold 1916 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 12 (Chicago 1916)

summary.en: Near Keaau stands a great stone once so balanced that it moved at a touch. It was Hopoe, the graceful dancer of Puna who taught Hiiaka the oldest hulas and the making of leis, and who was beloved by the volcano goddess's sister. Sent to fetch Lohiau, Hiiaka lays a covenant on Pele: burn all else in Puna, but not my friend Hopoe. Pele's jealousy breaks the oath; the lava eats the hala groves, 'tumbling are Haena and Hopoe', and the goddess changes her rival's friend into a great block of lava balanced on the seashore - dancing to this day when the winds blow over it.
summary.zh: 凱阿烏附近立著一塊巨石，舊時觸之即搖。它就是霍波埃——普納最嫻雅的舞者，教會希阿卡最古老的胡拉舞與花環手藝。希阿卡奉命遠赴考愛接夫君，臨行與佩蕾立約：普納任你焚燒，唯霍波埃不可近。佩蕾妒火難抑，誓言成灰：熔岩吞沒露兜林地——『海納與霍波埃傾倒了』——女神將這位奪其所愛的少女化為海濱搖曳的熔岩石，永伴潮聲而舞。

sensitivity.note: Pele-cycle jealousy episode; the standing stone was overthrown by a 19th-century earthquake.

passages.text: On the southeastern seacoast of the island Hawaii, near a hamlet called Keaau, is a large stone which was formerly so balanced that it could be easily moved; one of the severe earthquake shocks of the last century overthrew the stone and it now lies a great black mass of lava rock near the seashore. This stone in the long ago was called by the natives Hopoe, because Hopoe, the graceful dancer of Puna who taught Hiiaka, the youngest sister of Pele, how to dance, was changed into this rock. Pele had come from the islands of the south seas and had found the Hawaiian Islands as they are at the present day; after visiting all the other islands she settled in Puna, on the large island Hawaii. There she had her long sleep in which she went to the island Kauai and found her lover Lohiau, whom she promised to send for that he might come to her home in the volcano Kilauea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 12 (1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在夏威夷島東南海岸，靠近一個名為凱阿奧的小村落，有一塊大石，昔日平衡得極易推動；上世紀一次強烈的地震震倒了這塊石頭，如今它作為一大塊黑色的熔岩石躺在海濱附近。這塊石頭在很久以前被當地人稱為霍波埃，因為霍波埃——普納優雅的舞者，曾教佩蕾最小的妹妹希伊阿卡跳舞——被變成了這塊岩石。佩蕾來自南海諸島，發現夏威夷群島正如現今的模樣；在遊歷了所有其他島嶼之後，她定居在大島夏威夷的普納。在那裡她進行了漫長的沉睡，沉睡中她前往考艾島，尋得她的愛人洛希奧，她承諾要派人召他前來，好讓他來到她在基拉韋厄火山的家。

passages.text: Pele called her sisters one by one and told them to go to Kauai, but they feared the uncertainty of Pele's jealousy and wrath and refused to go. At last she called for Hiiaka, but she was down by the seashore with her friend Hopoe, where in a beautiful garden spot grew the fine food plants of the old Hawaiians - ohias and the brilliant red feathery blossoms of the lehua trees, and the hala from which sweet-scented skirts and mats were woven. Hopoe was very graceful and knew all the dances of the ancient people; hour after hour she taught Hiiaka the oldest hulas known among the Hawaiians until Hiiaka excelled in all beautiful motions of the human form, and taught her how to make leis from the most fragrant and splendid flowers. Together they went out into the white-capped waves bathing and swimming and seeking the fish of the coral caves; thus they learned to have great love for each other, and the girl from the south seas promised to care for the Hawaiian girl whose home was in the midst of volcanic fires.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 12 (1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 佩蕾一一召喚她的姊妹們，吩咐她們前往考艾島，但她們畏懼佩蕾嫉妒與憤怒的無常，都拒絕前往。最後她召喚希伊阿卡，但她正與她的友人霍波埃在海邊，那裡有一處美麗的園地，生長著古夏威夷人的優良食糧作物——奧希亞樹，以及蕾胡阿樹鮮紅羽狀的繁花，還有用以編織芬芳裙裳與蓆子的哈拉樹。霍波埃非常優雅，通曉古人的所有舞蹈；她一小時又一小時地教希伊阿卡夏威夷人所知最古老的呼拉舞，直到希伊阿卡精通人體所有優美的動作，並教她如何以最芬芳、最絢麗的花朵編製花環。她們一同走入白浪翻湧的海中沐浴、游泳，尋覓珊瑚洞穴中的魚；如此她們學會了彼此深愛，而那位來自南海的姑娘承諾要照顧這位家園位於火山烈焰之中的夏威夷姑娘。

passages.text: To her came Hiiaka fresh from the clear waters of the sea and covered with leis made by her friend Hopoe; untwisting the wreaths one by one she danced until all the household seemed to be overcome by her grace and gladness. Pele alone looked on with scowling dissatisfied face. As soon as she could she said to Hiiaka: 'Go far away; go to Kauai; get a husband for us, and bring him to Hawaii. Do not marry him. Do not even embrace him. He is tabu to you. Go forty days only - no longer for going or coming back.' Hiiaka looked upon the imperious goddess of fire and said: 'That is right. I go after your husband but I lay my charge upon you: You must take care of my lehua forest and not permit it to be injured. You may eat all other places of ours, but you must not touch my own lehua grove, my delight. You will be waiting here; anger will arise in you; you will destroy inland; you will destroy toward the sea; but you must not touch my friend - my Hopoe. You will eat Puna with your burning wrath, but you must not go near Hopoe. This is my covenant with you, O Pele.' Pele replied, 'This is right; I will care for your forest and your friend. Go you for our husband.' As Pele had charged Hiiaka so had Hiiaka laid her commandment on Pele - this was ceremonial oath-taking between the two. Hiiaka rose to prepare for the journey, but Pele's impatience at every moment's delay was so great that she forced Hiiaka away without food or extra clothing, and Hiiaka slowly went forth catching only a magic pa-u, a skirt which had the death-dealing power of flashing lightning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 12 (1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 希亞卡剛從清澄的海水中出來，身上覆滿她的朋友霍波埃所編的花環，來到她面前；她一一解開花環，翩然起舞，直到全家似乎都被她的優雅與歡欣所傾倒。唯有佩蕾獨自看著，面色陰沉不悅。她一有機會便對希亞卡說：「去得遠遠的；到考艾去；為我們找個丈夫，把他帶回夏威夷。不要嫁給他。連擁抱他都不要。他對你是禁忌。只去四十天——去程與回程都不得更久。」希亞卡望著這位專橫的火焰女神說：「好。我去尋你的丈夫，但我對你立下囑咐：你必須照管我的雷胡阿森林，不許它受到傷害。我們其他的地方你都可以吃，但絕不可碰我自己的雷胡阿林，我的喜樂。你會在此等候；怒氣會在你心中升起；你會毀壞內陸；你會毀壞海邊；但你絕不可碰我的朋友——我的霍波埃。你會以灼熱的怒火吞噬普納，但你絕不可靠近霍波埃。這是我與你的約定，噢佩蕾。」佩蕾回答：「好；我會照管你的森林和你的朋友。你去為我們尋丈夫吧。」正如佩蕾囑咐希亞卡，希亞卡也對佩蕾立下誡命——這是兩人之間莊嚴的誓約。希亞卡起身準備上路，但佩蕾對每一刻延誤的急躁如此強烈，以致她迫使希亞卡未帶食物、未添衣物便離去，希亞卡只得緩緩前行，僅隨手抓起一條神奇的帕烏——一條具有閃電致命之力的裙裳。

passages.text: As Hiiaka went up to the highlands above the volcano she looked down over Puna; smoke from the volcano fell toward the sea, making dark the forest along the path to Keaau, where Hopoe dwelt. There had been many hindrances to the progress of Hiiaka on her way; meanwhile Pele became jealous, burning the forests which she had promised to protect, and Hiiaka chanted: 'Tumbling are Haena and Hopoe.' Hopoe was the last object of Pele's anger at her younger sister. The goddess went to the seashore where Hopoe waited death; she placed the garlands Hiiaka had given her friend around her own neck, that she might show the girl's tokens in the presence of Hiiaka, and changed Hopoe into a great block of lava and balanced it on the seashore - thus Hopoe was able to dance when the winds blew over it. Hiiaka fulfilled her mission patiently and faithfully, bringing Lohiau back to Hawaii, and was horrified beyond expression when she learned that Pele in her terrible wrath had brought death to Hopoe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 12 (1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當希亞卡登上火山上方的高地，她俯瞰普納；火山的煙朝海面飄落，使通往凱奧奧——霍波埃所居之處——沿途的森林一片昏暗。希亞卡途中曾遭遇許多阻礙；與此同時，佩蕾心生嫉妒，焚燒了她曾承諾保護的森林，希亞卡吟唱道：「哈埃納與霍波埃翻滾傾覆。」霍波埃是佩蕾對她妹妹怒氣的最後一個目標。這位女神來到海濱，霍波埃在那裡等待死亡；她將希亞卡贈予她朋友的花環掛在自己頸上，好在希亞卡面前展示那女孩的信物，並將霍波埃變成一塊巨大的熔岩，使它平衡地立於海濱——如此一來，當風吹過其上，霍波埃便能起舞。希亞卡耐心而忠實地完成了她的使命，將洛希奧帶回夏威夷，而當她得知佩蕾在可怕的怒火中使霍波埃喪命時，她驚駭得無法言喻。

title.en: Hiiaka's Battle with the Demons of Pana-ewa
title.zh: 希阿卡大戰帕納埃瓦妖群

region.en: Pana-ewa forest, Hilo, Hawaii Island
region.zh: 夏威夷島希洛帕納埃瓦林

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; retold 1916 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 13 (Chicago 1916)

summary.en: On the road to Kauai the fern-goddess Hiiaka meets the demon horde of Pana-ewa - lizard-bodied, ghost-form, mockers of her calm. He taunts: 'This is Hiiaka, who shall be killed by me'; she answers that her little rag of clothing is enough. Wrapped in fog bodies and thunder, the demon chief presses her almost to death, until she sweeps her lightning skirt against the fog, calls the heavens for rain, and the great thunderstorm of Pana-ewa - remembered for its floods - drowns the demon ranks in the valley she had fought through.
summary.zh: 赴考愛途中，蕨之女神希阿卡遭遇帕納埃瓦的妖群——蜥身鬼形、口吐譏嘲。魔首罵道：『這就是希阿卡，我要殺了她』；她答：『我這一小片衣裳足矣。』妖首以霧身纏她、以雷轟她，她幾乎力竭；終於她揮動綴滿閃電的裙裾劈開迷霧，又召來傾盆大雨——帕納埃瓦的大雷雨自那日起便名聞遐邇——洪流淹沒了谷中妖軍。

sensitivity.note: Hero-journey battle episode of the Hiilaka cycle.

passages.text: Hiiaka, the youngest sister of Pele, the goddess of fire, is the principal figure in the wonderful legends of the long journey from Hawaii to Kauai to find the lover Pele had found in her dream. Pele was impatient and angry at the slow progress of Hiiaka on her journey; at last the goddess of ferns, Pau-o-palae, made with a skirt of ferns which pleased Pele, and Pele ordered her to go with Hiiaka as her kahu, or guardian. Hiiaka's first test of patient endurance came in a battle with the demons of Pana-ewa - lizard-bodied, ghost-form, mockers of her calm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 13 (1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 希亞卡是火焰女神佩蕾最小的妹妹，是那些關於從夏威夷遠赴考艾、去尋找佩蕾在夢中所見情人的奇妙傳說中的主要人物。佩蕾對希亞卡旅途進展緩慢感到急躁而憤怒；最後，蕨類女神帕烏奧帕拉埃以蕨葉製成一條令佩蕾滿意的裙子，佩蕾便命她隨希亞卡同行，作她的卡胡，即守護者。希亞卡對耐心忍辱的第一次考驗，來自與帕納埃瓦群魔的一場戰鬥——那些魔物蜥蜴之身、幽靈之形，嘲弄她的沉靜。

passages.text: Hiiaka, entering the forest, threw aside her fern robes, revealing her divine powers; she heard the birds and laughed; then she chanted, and he heard the mocking call of the demon chief: 'This is Hiiaka, who shall be killed by me.' Hiiaka in her fog body, Kino-ohu, was thrown around by the demon's thick coils; she told her friend to hold fast to her girdle while she swiftly swept her lightning skirt up against the beat of the fog, and made incantations against the enchantments; the great thunderstorm swept down on Pana-ewa, and the floods drowned the demon ranks in the valley she had fought through.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 13 (1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 希亞卡進入森林，拋開她的蕨葉衣袍，顯露她的神力；她聽見鳥鳴而笑；接著她吟唱起來，而牠聽見魔物首領嘲弄的呼喚：「這就是希亞卡，將被我殺死。」希亞卡以她的霧身基諾奧胡，被魔物粗厚的盤繞所拋擲；她吩咐她的朋友緊抓她的腰帶，同時她迅速將閃電之裙掃起，迎擊霧氣的拍打，並念咒對抗那些魅惑；巨大的雷暴向帕納埃瓦傾瀉而下，洪水將魔物群眾溺斃於她曾奮戰穿過的山谷之中。

title.en: Hiiaka Catches a Ghost
title.zh: 希阿卡擒魂記

region.en: Forest above Hilo, Hawaii Island (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 夏威夷島希洛上林（象徵性定位）

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; retold 1916 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 15 (Chicago 1916)

summary.en: Camp rested, Wahine-omao sees a spirit wandering by the sea - a fisherman wrecked and drowned beside his shattered canoe. Hiiaka drives the ghost toward the house, thrusts out her 'strong hand of Kilauea', slaps the fleeing spirit back against the body and holds it while she chants the call of life; pouring fresh water upon the corpse she restores breath to the breast and sight to the eyes, and the healing power of the goddess of ferns restores the places wounded by coral and the sea.
summary.zh: 歇腳之際，瓦希內奧毛望見海邊遊蕩的幽魂——一位翻船溺亡的漁夫，獨木舟碎片狼藉。希阿卡驅魂回屋，伸出『基拉韋厄巨掌』將欲逃的魂魄拍回軀體，按住不放，口誦還生咒；再以清水澆淋屍身——胸膛起伏、雙目重張；蕨神之力還撫其被珊瑚與海水所傷之處。

sensitivity.note: Ghost-catching and revival record.

passages.text: Hiiaka, the sister of Pele, the goddess of ferns, and her friend Wahine-omao were hastening through the forests above Hilo. Hiiaka said: 'One of us will stop and eat; two of us will pass on, for we are not hungry.' So Wahine-omao stopped and ate, and saw that the girls were watching the sea; Hiiaka looked toward it and saw the spirit of a drowned man wandering, and hastened after the ghost and drove it toward the house. The people wept and began to beseech Hiiaka to bring him back to life; as she rose to pass out of the door the ghost leaped and disappeared, and Hiiaka rushed out and saw it run to the sea, where lay the broken pieces of the shattered canoe. She washed the ghost, thrust out her 'strong hand of Kilauea', slapped the ghost back against the body and told it to go in; then she uttered an incantation, and by the time the chant was ended Hiiaka had forced the ghost into the body.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 15 (1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 希亞卡是蕨類女神佩蕾的妹妹，她與朋友瓦希內奧毛正匆匆穿過希洛上方的森林。希亞卡說：「我們之中一人停下來吃；兩人繼續前行，因為我們不餓。」於是瓦希內奧毛停下來吃，並看見那些女孩正望著大海；希亞卡朝海望去，看見一個溺死者的亡魂在遊蕩，便急忙追趕那鬼魂，將牠趕向屋舍。人們哭泣起來，開始懇求希亞卡使他復生；當她起身要走出門時，那鬼魂一躍而消失，希亞卡衝了出去，看見牠奔向大海，那裡躺著破碎獨木舟的殘片。她洗淨那鬼魂，伸出她那「基拉韋厄的強健之手」，把鬼魂拍回身體，命牠進去；接著她念起咒語，而當咒語念畢，希亞卡已將鬼魂逼入身體之中。

passages.text: Then Hiiaka put forth her hand and took fresh water, pouring it upon the body, while she chanted 'Hiiaka is the prophet'; the healing power of Hiiaka restored the places wounded by coral and the sea; she told him to stand up, and putting out her strong hand she raised him; she called for the glory of a divine chief to shine around him, and knew that the ghost had gone back into the body and that the man was restored to life - breath returning to the breast and sight to the eyes by the skill of the goddess of ferns.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 15 (1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著希亞卡伸出手，取來清水，澆在身體上，同時吟唱「希亞卡是先知」；希亞卡的療癒之力修復了被珊瑚與海水所傷之處；她命他站起來，伸出她那強健之手將他扶起；她呼喚神聖首領的榮光環繞他，並知道鬼魂已回到身體之中，那人已復生——因蕨類女神的技藝，氣息重回胸膛，視覺重回雙眼。

title.en: Hiiaka Wrestles the Dragons of Haena for Lohiau's Spirit
title.zh: 希阿卡海納鬥龍奪魂

region.en: Caves of Haena, Kauai
region.zh: 考愛島海納龍窟

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; retold 1916 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 17 (Chicago 1916)

summary.en: Arriving in Kauai, Hiiaka finds Lohiau dead - the dragon-women of Haena have crushed the breath from his body. She fights her way through flying trees, dragons and storms to the cave where his body lies, hunts his small spirit voice along the shores, and charms it into a coconut calabash fastened tight. Waging incantation for nine days, she pours the spirit back into the body and he rises; but Pele's arriving flames take Lohiau's life a second time, and Hiiaka, crazed, fights fire and smoke until her faithfulness is confessed and Lohiau is restored to her forever.
summary.zh: 抵考愛，希阿卡得知洛希奧已死——海納的龍女們掐斷了他的呼吸。她穿越飛石、龍陣與風暴殺至藏屍之洞；沿岸追尋那細若游絲的魂音，將其咒入緊封的椰殼。九日祝禱之後，她把魂魄傾回軀體，酋長重新站起。然佩蕾之火隨後而至，二度奪其命；幾近瘋狂的希阿卡與火濃煙搏鬥，直至佩蕾承認背誓，洛希奧永屬於她。

sensitivity.note: Double-resurrection romance; spirit caught in calabash like Hiku's shell.

passages.text: The story of Hiiaka's journey over the seas which surround the islands is one of the legends which show how greatly the Hawaiians loved tales of the spirit world. As Hiiaka and her friend came near the island Kauai, Hiiaka told Wahine-omao that Lohiau was dead and that she saw the spirit of the chief wandering on the waters; the dragon-women of Haena had watched the life of Lohiau and compelled the breath to leave his body. The next day they made the house, and Hiiaka commanded that a door toward the east be opened, saying 'To-morrow let the tabu be lifted'; at sunrise they went on through the storm, and the small spirit voice of Lohiau called for help; Hiiaka chanted to Lohiau, telling him they would save him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 17 (1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 希亞卡渡越環繞群島之海的故事，是諸多傳說之一，顯示夏威夷人多麼喜愛靈界的故事。當希亞卡與她的友人接近考艾島時，希亞卡告訴瓦希內－歐瑪歐，洛希奧已死，她看見那位首領的靈魂在水面上遊蕩；哈埃納的龍女們曾窺伺洛希奧的性命，並迫使氣息離開他的身體。翌日，她們造好了屋子，希亞卡命人開一扇朝東的門，說道：「明日當解除禁忌」；日出時，她們穿過風暴前行，洛希奧微弱的靈魂之聲呼喚求助；希亞卡向洛希奧吟唱，告訴他她們必將救他。

passages.text: The dragons leaped down on Hiiaka trying to catch her and strike her with their tails; Hiiaka struck them with her magic skirt in which was the divine power of lightning; the dragons caught her, bending her over, catching her around the neck and arm, trying to press the life out of her - until she sent her power and took help of the forces of the forest, and the winds; at last Hiiaka shook her magic skirt and struck them again and again. The natives have for many years claimed that Hiiaka found the cave in the deep shadows where the body lay; she followed the spirit voice saying 'Moving, moving - you will find me in a small coconut calabash fastened in tight', and caught the spirit in the calabash fastened in tight, carrying it while she continued her necessary incantation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 17 (1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 群龍撲向希亞卡，試圖抓住她並以尾巴擊打她；希亞卡以她那蘊含雷電神力的魔法裙擊打牠們；群龍抓住了她，將她壓彎，纏住她的頸與臂，試圖將她的生命擠出——直到她施展自身的力量，借助森林之力與眾風之力；最後，希亞卡抖動她的魔法裙，一次又一次地擊打牠們。當地人多年來一直聲稱，希亞卡在幽深的陰影中找到了遺體所躺的洞穴；她循著那靈魂之聲前行，那聲音說道：「移動著，移動著——你會在一個緊緊封住的小椰殼葫蘆裡找到我」，於是她在緊緊封住的葫蘆裡捉住了那靈魂，帶著它，同時繼續她必要的咒語。

passages.text: Hiiaka said to her friend: 'You ask how the spirit can be restored to life; I am coming, I Hiiaka.' She poured the spirit back into the body and Lohiau rose from the cave of the wilderness, making with her a solemn promise; then Pele, arriving, would fling her scorching smoke and foul gas over Hiiaka's body and over the body of Lohiau - and a second time the breath left the chief. Hiiaka was crazed by the death of Lohiau; she had fought against Pele's fire and flames until Pele and her sisters were frightened. Pele called Wahine-omao and, conquered and full of self-blame, told her how to restore Lohiau; Wahine-omao went to Hiiaka and softly chanted by the side of the fire-pit, and Hiiaka turned from the pit and sought Lohiau; a second time Hiiaka had given life to Lohiau. Hiiaka and Lohiau went to Kauai, where, as chief and chiefess, they ruled the island; Lohiau had no longer any remnant of affection for Pele, for Hiiaka and Lohiau were now husband and wife, and Pele had lost forever the lover she had found in her long sleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 17 (1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 希亞卡對她的友人說：「你問靈魂如何能重獲生命；我來了，我希亞卡。」她將靈魂倒回身體之中，洛希奧便從荒野的洞穴中起身，與她立下莊嚴的誓約；隨後，佩蕾到來，將她灼熱的煙與惡臭的氣體噴灑在希亞卡的身上，也噴灑在洛希奧的身上——首領的氣息第二次離開了他。希亞卡因洛希奧之死而發狂；她曾與佩蕾的火焰與烈火搏鬥，直到佩蕾與她的姊妹們心生畏懼。佩蕾喚來瓦希內－歐瑪歐，帶著被征服與滿懷自責之心，告訴她如何使洛希奧復生；瓦希內－歐瑪歐來到希亞卡身旁，在火坑邊輕聲吟唱，希亞卡便轉身離開火坑，去尋找洛希奧；希亞卡第二次賦予了洛希奧生命。希亞卡與洛希奧前往考艾島，在那裡以首領與女首領的身分統治該島；洛希奧對佩蕾已不再存有任何一絲情意，因為希亞卡與洛希奧如今已是夫妻，而佩蕾則永遠失去了她在那漫長睡眠中所尋得的愛人。

title.en: God and the Devil Dive for Earth: The Baltic Creation
title.zh: 神與魔潛水取土：波羅的海創世

region.en: Lithuanian lakes (symbolic pin at Kaunas)
region.zh: 立陶宛湖泊（象徵性定位於考納斯）

period: Recorded 19th c. in Lithuanian and Latvian collections; documented by Vellius (1979)

source.work: Baltic diving cosmogony; documented in N. Vellius, Lithuanian Mythological Tales (1979) and Greimas, Of Gods and Men (1992)

license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain folk material; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: God, drifting on the endless water, sees the Devil swimming and sends him down for sand; the Devil hides a mouthful under his tongue, the blessed sand grows and swells in his mouth until he is forced to spit it out — and from the spitting come the mountains, the marshes, and the crooked places.
summary.zh: 神浮於無盡之水上，見魔游弋，命其潛底取沙；魔含沙於舌下私藏，受祝之沙在其口中不斷膨脹，被迫吐出——吐出之沙即成山嶺、沼澤與一切崎嶇之地。

sensitivity.note: The Baltic twin of the Slavic diving cosmogony (cross_ref slavic-god-devil-dive-creation); the Indo-European dualist creation.

passages.text: In the beginning there is only the endless water, with God drifting on it in his boat — and swimming beside him, the Devil. God looks at the water and tells the Devil to dive to the bottom and bring up a handful of sand, with the words 'In the name of God' in his mouth. The Devil dives twice and fails; the third time he brings the sand but forgets the holy words, and keeps a second mouthful hidden under his tongue.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Baltic diving cosmogony as documented in Vellius, Lithuanian Mythological Tales (1979), and Greimas (1992); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 起初只有無盡的水，上帝乘著他的船漂浮其上——而在他身旁游著的，是魔鬼。上帝望著水，吩咐魔鬼潛入水底，帶回一把沙，口中念著「以上帝之名」這句話。魔鬼潛了兩次都失敗；第三次他帶回了沙，卻忘了那句神聖的話語，並在舌下藏了第二口沙。

passages.text: God spreads the obedient sand on the water and blesses it: grow, thou earth — and it grows until it fills the sea. The stolen sand in the Devil's mouth also begins to grow, swollen by the blessing, until he must spit it out; the spitting becomes the mountains, the marshes, and all the crooked places of the world. The Baltic tale is the closest kinsman of the Slavic diving creation: one water, two divers, and a world double-authored.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the documented tale; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 上帝將那順服的沙撒在水面上並加以祝福：生長吧，大地——於是它生長起來，直到填滿了海洋。魔鬼口中偷來的沙也開始生長，因那祝福而膨脹，直到他不得不將其吐出；吐出的沙便成了山嶺、沼澤，以及世上一切崎嶇不平之處。波羅的海的這個故事，是斯拉夫潛水創世神話最親近的親屬：一片水，兩個潛水者，一個由雙方共同創作的世界。

title.en: The Sky That Holds the Earth
title.zh: 擎地之天

region.en: Lithuania (symbolic pin at Vilnius)
region.zh: 立陶宛（象徵性定位於維爾紐斯）

period: Recorded 19th-20th c.; documented by Vellius (1979)

source.work: Baltic sky-cosmology tales; documented in Vellius, Lithuanian Mythological Tales (1979)

license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain folk material; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: In the Baltic folk cosmology the sky is a lid over the world's dish: the earth floats and the sky leans down at its edges — held at the corners by great pillars, and so heavy that nothing sinful may climb to it, or the whole dish will spill.
summary.zh: 波羅的海民間宇宙論中，天如覆於世界之盤上的蓋：大地浮動，天沿邊傾垂——由四角巨柱所撐；其重無比，凡有罪者不可攀天，否則盤將傾覆。

sensitivity.note: Cosmological folk belief.

passages.text: In the tales recorded among the Lithuanians and Letts the world is a dish and the sky its cover: the earth floats on the primordial water, and the sky leans down at the edges of the world, resting at the corners on great pillars. Between the dish and its cover is all the room men will ever have.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Baltic sky-cosmology as documented in Vellius, Lithuanian Mythological Tales (1979); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在立陶宛人與拉脫維亞人所記錄的故事中，世界是一只盤子，天空是它的蓋子：大地漂浮在原始的水面上，天空在世界邊緣向下傾斜，在四角倚靠於巨大的柱子之上。盤子與其蓋子之間，便是人類所能擁有的全部空間。

passages.text: The pillars are so old that no one remembers setting them, and so necessary that the tales never let anyone knock one: the sinner who tries to climb to heaven is thrown down, for a man out of place upsets the dish. Under the same lid the sun has her road, the moon his, and the stars their fires — the Baltic sky is not empty space but a worked household, furnished by God and kept by his daughters.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the documented material; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那些柱子古老得無人記得是何時立下的，又不可或缺得使傳說從不讓任何人擊倒其中一根：妄圖攀上天國的罪人會被摔下，因為人若錯置其位便會打翻這盤菜。在同一片穹蓋之下，太陽有自己的道路，月亮有自己的道路，星辰有自己的火光——波羅的海的天空並非空無一物的空間，而是一戶操持有序的家宅，由上帝布置，由祂的女兒們看守。

title.en: God and the Devil as Brothers: Making the Animals
title.zh: 神魔為兄弟：造獸記

region.en: Lithuania (symbolic pin at Kaunas)
region.zh: 立陶宛（象徵性定位於考納斯）

period: Recorded 19th-20th c.; documented by Vellius (1979)

source.work: Baltic dualist creation tales; documented in Vellius, Lithuanian Mythological Tales (1979)

license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain folk material; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: God and the Devil work side by side like brothers in the first field: God creates the creatures that serve — the horse, the cow, the dog — while the Devil's hand makes the crooked ones, and every ill-shaped beast and bitter herb is his signature in God's new world.
summary.zh: 太初田中，神與魔如兄弟並肩勞作：神造服役之獸——馬、牛、犬；魔之手則造出歪斜之物——凡畸形之獸、苦澀之草，皆其在新世界中的落款。

sensitivity.note: Dualist creation tales, Christian-era in wording but pre-Christian in structure.

passages.text: In the Baltic tales God and the Devil create side by side, like two brothers at one plough. God makes the creatures that serve the household: the horse that carries, the cow that gives, the dog that guards. The Devil, jealous, makes his own creatures in the same field — the crooked, the stinging, the bitter — and wherever a beast is ill-shaped or a herb harsh, the tales say, that is the Devil's handiwork in God's world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Baltic dualist creation tales as documented in Vellius (1979); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在波羅的海的傳說中，上帝與魔鬼並肩創造，如同兩兄弟共扶一犁。上帝造出服侍家宅的生靈：負載的馬、供乳的牛、守護的狗。魔鬼心生嫉妒，在同一片田野上造出自己的生靈——歪斜的、蜇人的、苦澀的——凡有走獸形貌不正、凡有草木味道苦烈，傳說都說，那便是魔鬼在上帝的世界裡留下的手筆。

passages.text: The best-known example is the hare: the Devil made it, and God, passing by, saw that the creature was crooked and struck it across the mouth with the flat of his hand — the split lip of every hare since is the mark of that blow. So the animals' shapes and habits are read as the record of the two creators' argument: the straight and the crooked, the giving and the taking, walk together in the fields to this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the documented tales; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最為人熟知的例子是野兔：魔鬼造了牠，上帝路過，見這生靈歪斜不正，便用手掌摑過牠的嘴——此後每隻野兔的裂唇，都是那一摑留下的印記。於是動物的形貌與習性，都被讀作兩位造物者爭執的記錄：正直的與歪斜的、給予的與奪取的，至今仍在田野間同行。

title.en: Why the Hare's Lip Is Split
title.zh: 兔唇之由

region.en: Lithuanian field paths (symbolic pin at Kaunas)
region.zh: 立陶宛田間小徑（象徵性定位於考納斯）

period: Recorded 19th-20th c.; documented by Vellius (1979)

source.work: Etiological animal tales; documented in Vellius, Lithuanian Mythological Tales (1979)

license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain folk material; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: The Devil made the hare in God's field; God saw the crooked beast and struck it across the mouth — and the hare has carried the split lip ever since, running at the Devil's command through the fields God made.
summary.zh: 魔在神的田中造了兔；神見此歪獸，揮掌擊其口——兔自始帶著裂唇，依魔之令奔竄於神造的田野。

sensitivity.note: Etiological tale.

passages.text: The hare was the Devil's creature, made in God's field without God's leave. God walked by, saw the crooked beast, and struck it across the mouth with the flat of his hand; the lip split, and every hare born since carries the mark of the blow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the etiological tale as documented in Vellius, Lithuanian Mythological Tales (1979); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 野兔是魔鬼的生靈，未經上帝許可便造在上帝的田野裡。上帝走過，見這歪斜的走獸，便用手掌摑過牠的嘴；嘴唇裂開，此後出生的每一隻野兔都帶著那一摑的印記。

passages.text: In other tellings the blow falls when the hare betrays the work: the Devil's creature was set to spoil what God had planted, and the open lip is the brand that shows whose field it ran in. Children in the Baltic villages still say of a quick, crooked luck that it runs like a hare — the Devil's speed on God's ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the documented tales; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在其他的講述中，那一摑落在野兔敗露其行徑之時：魔鬼的生靈被派去糟蹋上帝所栽種之物，而那裂開的嘴唇便是烙印，表明牠曾跑在誰的田裡。波羅的海村莊的孩子至今仍說，迅疾而歪斜的運氣跑起來像野兔——那是魔鬼的速度，奔在上帝的土地上。

title.en: God's Dog: Why Dogs Guard the House
title.zh: 神之犬：犬守宅之由

region.en: Lithuanian homestead (symbolic pin at Vilnius)
region.zh: 立陶宛家宅（象徵性定位於維爾紐斯）

period: Recorded 19th-20th c.; documented by Vellius (1979)

source.work: Origin-of-dog tales; documented in Vellius, Lithuanian Mythological Tales (1979)

license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain folk material; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: When God made the first house he set his own dog at the gate to keep the Devil out; the dog sleeps when it should watch, the Devil slips in — and ever since, the tales say, the household dog barks at what men cannot see, doing God's watch as best a dog can.
summary.zh: 神造第一座宅時，親自置犬於門以拒魔；犬該守望時卻睡去，魔潛入——自此，故事說，家犬朝人所不見之物而吠，竭盡犬力代神守望。

sensitivity.note: Etiological tale; reconstructed framing flagged.

passages.text: When God made the first house he set his own dog at the gate, for the Devil walks abroad at night and a house unguarded is a house the Devil enters. The dog sleeps when it should watch, the Devil slips in and does his mischief in the dark — and when the owners wake, the loss is blamed on the dog's failure, not the Devil's cunning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the origin-of-dog tale as documented in Vellius, Lithuanian Mythological Tales (1979); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 上帝造第一座房屋時，便把自己的狗安置在門口，因為魔鬼夜間在外遊蕩，無人看守的房屋便是魔鬼得以進入的房屋。狗在本該守望時睡去，魔鬼便溜進來，在黑暗中行他的惡——而當主人醒來，損失總歸咎於狗的失職，而非魔鬼的狡詐。

passages.text: This is why, the tales say, a dog barks at what men cannot see: it remembers its first duty, standing where God stood it, and its bark at the empty yard is the oldest prayer of the household. (The framing of this record is reconstructed from the motif as documented in the collection; the tale's wording varies from teller to teller.)
passages.note: Paraphrase of the documented motif; framing reconstructed (Vellius 1979); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傳說因此說，狗之所以對著人看不見的東西吠叫，是因為牠記得自己最初的職責，站在上帝安置牠的地方；牠對著空蕩的庭院吠叫，是一戶人家最古老的祈禱。（本紀錄的框架係依據採集集中所載的母題重建；故事的措辭因講述者而異。）

title.en: The Swallow's Fiery Tail: How Fire Came to the House
title.zh: 燕子火尾：火入宅之由

region.en: Lithuanian farmhouse (symbolic pin at Vilnius)
region.zh: 立陶宛農舍（象徵性定位於維爾紐斯）

period: Recorded 19th-20th c.; documented by Vellius (1979)

source.work: Origin-of-fire tales; documented in Vellius, Lithuanian Mythological Tales (1979)

license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain folk material; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: The Devil hid fire at the bottom of the water; God sent the swallow, who dipped her tail into the flame and brought a spark back to the hearth — and ever since the swallow builds her nest by the chimney, for she is the bird that gave men fire.
summary.zh: 魔將火藏於水底；神遣燕子，其尾蘸入火焰，銜一火星歸於爐邊——自此燕於煙囪旁築巢，蓋其乃賜火於人之鳥。

sensitivity.note: Fire-in-water cluster parallel to Polynesian fire myths; framing partially reconstructed.

passages.text: In the beginning fire was hidden where no man could reach it — at the bottom of the water, where the Devil had sunk it. God sent the swallow, the bird that skims the wave-tops; she dove where the fire lay and dipped her tail in the flame, and flew back to the hearth with a spark burning in her feathers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the origin-of-fire tale as documented in Vellius, Lithuanian Mythological Tales (1979); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 起初，火被藏在無人能及之處——在水底，是魔鬼將它沉在那裡的。上帝派了燕子，那掠過浪尖的鳥；她潛入火所在之處，把尾巴浸入火焰，帶著在羽毛中燃燒的火星飛回爐邊。

passages.text: The fire burned the swallow's tail feathers to a fork — the shape every swallow's tail has kept since — and the spark went into the first hearth, where God set it to be kept and fed. Ever since, the tales say, the swallow builds her nest close to the chimneys of the houses, for she is the bird that brought men fire, and a house that lets her nest is a house that remembers its debt. (Segments of the framing are reconstructed from the motif as recorded in the collection.)
passages.note: Paraphrase of the documented motif; framing reconstructed (Vellius 1979); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 火把燕子的尾羽燒成了分叉——此後每隻燕子的尾巴都保持著這個形狀——那火星則進了第一座爐灶，上帝安置它在那裡，讓人守護、添薪。傳說自此以後，燕子總把巢築在房屋的煙囪近旁，因為她是為人類帶來火的鳥，而容她築巢的人家，是記得自己恩情的人家。（框架的部分內容係依據採集集中所載的母題重建。）

title.en: Žemyna, Mother Earth: The Kiss at Dawn
title.zh: 澤米娜，大地之母：黎明之吻

region.en: Lithuanian fields (symbolic pin at Vilnius)
region.zh: 立陶宛田野（象徵性定位於維爾紐斯）

period: Rite recorded by Lasicki (1582) and in 19th-c. collections; documented by Vellius (1979)

source.work: The cult of Žemyna; Lasicki, De diis Samagitarum (1582); documented in Vellius (1979) and Greimas (1992)

license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain material; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: Žemyna, the Lithuanian earth-mother, is kissed at dawn: the householder kisses the ground at sunrise and again when he goes to bed, at every spring blossom and every harvest — for the earth is the family's own mother and bears the family its daily bread.
summary.zh: 立陶宛大地母神澤米娜於黎明受吻：家主日出時親吻大地，就寢時再吻；每逢春花初綻、每次收割皆然——蓋大地乃一家之母，日日賜家以糧。

sensitivity.note: Earth cult; parallels Greek Gaia and Roman Tellus.

passages.text: Žemyna, the goddess of the earth, is the mother of the Baltic household: Lasicki's old register lists her among the Samogitian gods, and the folk custom kept her longest. At sunrise the householder kisses the ground and says a word of thanks; at the coming of every new blossom — the birch, the flax, the rye — he kisses the earth again, and at the harvest he kisses it last of all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Žemyna cult as documented in Lasicki (1582), Vellius (1979), and Greimas (1992); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大地女神熱米娜是波羅的海家戶的母親：拉西茨基的古老名錄將她列於薩莫吉提亞諸神之中，而民間習俗將她保存得最久。日出時，家主親吻土地，說一句感謝的話；每逢新花初綻——樺樹、亞麻、黑麥——他再親吻大地，到了收穫時，他最後親吻它。

passages.text: The rite is the oldest prayer of the field: not a petition but a greeting between kin. The earth is the mother who bears the family its bread, the dead return to her and the new-born are shown to her; a man who does not kiss Žemyna at dawn has forgotten whose household he belongs to.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the documented cult; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這儀式是田野最古老的祈禱：不是祈求，而是親族之間的問候。大地是為家庭生育麵包的母親，死者歸返於她，新生兒被抱來見她；不在黎明親吻熱米娜的人，已忘了自己屬於誰家。

title.en: Laima at the Cradle: The Spinner of One's Days
title.zh: 搖籃邊的萊瑪：紡人生之線者

region.en: Latvia and Lithuania (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞與立陶宛（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Belief recorded 19th c. (Biezais's studies; dainas); documented by Greimas (1992)

source.work: The goddess Laima; documented in the dainas and in A. J. Greimas, Of Gods and Men (1992)

license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain folk material; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: Laima comes to the cradle with her spindle and spins the length of the child's life; her sister dark Laima — Lauma gone bad — spins short, and the mothers of the Baltic sing to the spinner that she may measure kindly.
summary.zh: 萊瑪携紡錘臨於搖籃，紡出孩子一生的長度；其姊妹黑萊瑪——變壞的勞瑪——紡得短促；波羅的海的母親們向紡者歌唱，願她量度慈祥。

sensitivity.note: Fate goddess parallels the Moirai, Norns, and the Slavic Sudice.

passages.text: Laima, the dispenser of fate, comes to the lying-in room with her spindle: she spins the thread of the child's days, and what she has spun no one can re-spin. The dainas call her 'the spinner under the skies', and the household keeps her place — the clean bench, the spun flax — that she may find the room ready.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Laima belief as documented in the dainas and Greimas, Of Gods and Men (1992); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 命運的分配者萊瑪帶著她的紡錘來到產房：她紡出孩子歲月的線，而她所紡的，無人能再紡。達伊納稱她為「天空下的紡者」，家戶為她保留位置——潔淨的長凳、紡好的亞麻——好讓她發現房間已準備妥當。

passages.text: Beside her stands her dark sister, the Lauma gone bad, who spins short and laughs at what she has spun; between the two the whole fortune of the new-born hangs. A mother's song to Laima is the oldest Baltic cradle-hymn: spin long, spin kindly, and let the thread outlast the loom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the documented belief; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她身旁站著她黝黑的姊妹，即變壞的勞瑪，她紡得短，並嘲笑自己所紡之物；新生兒的全部命運就懸於這兩者之間。母親向萊瑪所唱的歌，是波羅的海最古老的搖籃聖歌：願你紡得長、紡得慈愛，讓這線比織機更長壽。

title.en: Māra: The Goddess of the Household and the Field
title.zh: 瑪拉：家宅與田野之女神

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Belief recorded in the dainas, 19th c.; documented by Greimas (1992)

source.work: The goddess Mara; documented in the dainas and in A. J. Greimas, Of Gods and Men (1992)

license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain folk material; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: Māra is the goddess of all that the hands touch — bread, linen, cattle, and the market — the third power of the dainas' sky beside Dievs and Saule; the dainas sing her as the bread-giver and the keeper of the household's linen chest.
summary.zh: 瑪拉乃手所觸一切之神——麵包、麻布、牛群與市集——達伊納斯天庭中僅次於季葉瓦斯與索列的第三位；歌中其為賜麵包者、家中麻箱之守。

sensitivity.note: Fertility and household goddess; Christian-era dainas often Christianize her as Mary — flagged.

passages.text: In the dainas the sky is governed as a household, and Māra is the goddess of its working parts: the bread that is baked, the linen that is spun, the cattle in the stall, and the goods that change hands. Beside Dievs, the father of the sky, and Saule, the sun, she completes the ruling trio of the Lettish songs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Māra belief as documented in the dainas and Greimas, Of Gods and Men (1992); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在達伊納斯中，天空如一個家戶般被治理，而瑪拉是其運作各部之神：所烤的麵包、所紡的亞麻、廄中的牲畜，以及易手的貨物。在天父迪耶瓦斯與太陽紹萊之旁，她補足了拉脫維亞歌謠中統治的三神。

passages.text: The Christian era gave her a new name in some songs — Māra and the Virgin Mary blur in the later dainas — but the older layer is clear: she is the bread-goddess, the goddess of the material world's fertility, invoked at the oven, the loom, and the market. A Latvian bride's song still wishes her 'Māra's luck in the linen chest'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the documented belief; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 基督教時代在某些歌中給了她一個新名字——在較晚的達伊納斯裡，瑪拉與童貞聖母瑪利亞模糊難分——但較古老的一層是清楚的：她是麵包女神，是物質世界豐饒的女神，在爐邊、織機旁與市集上受呼求。拉脫維亞新娘的歌至今仍祝她「在亞麻箱中得到瑪拉的好運」。

title.en: Medeina: The Huntress of the Lithuanian Woods
title.zh: 梅傑伊娜：立陶宛林中的女獵神

region.en: Lithuanian forests (symbolic pin at Trakai)
region.zh: 立陶宛森林（象徵性定位於特拉凱）

period: Recorded by Lasicki (1582) and in later chronicle material; documented by Greimas (1992)

source.work: The goddess Medeina; Lasicki, De diis Samagitarum (1582); documented in Greimas, Of Gods and Men (1992)

license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain material; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: In Lasicki's old register of the Samogitian gods stands Medeina, the forest huntress who runs with the wolves and will not be wed; the Lithuanian dukes hunted under her trees, and the huntsman who took more than his share answered to her.
summary.zh: 拉西茨基古神譜中有梅傑伊娜——與狼同奔、拒不受婚的林中女獵神；立陶宛大公於其樹下圍獵，獵取過甚者須向她交代。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary deity; interpretive reconstruction flagged.

passages.text: Medeina stands in Lasicki's sixteenth-century register of the Samogitian gods — the huntress of the woods, young and unwed, running with the wolves as their queen. The Lithuanian dukes' hunts were held under her protection, and the hunter's share was hers to set.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Medeina material as documented in Lasicki (1582) and Greimas, Of Gods and Men (1992); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 梅黛娜見於拉西茨基十六世紀的薩莫吉提亞諸神名錄——她是林中的女獵手，年輕而未嫁，與狼群一同奔馳，為群狼之后。立陶宛公爵們的狩獵在她的庇護下舉行，獵人所分得的份額由她定奪。

passages.text: She belongs to the same family of forest-rulers as the Slavic Leshy and the Greek Artemis: the wood is hers, the game is hers, and the huntsman is her guest. The sources give her only a name and a function — a goddess remembered by the enemies of her people — but the Lithuanian forest keeps her in every path where the wolves still run. (Interpretive reconstruction from fragmentary sources.)
passages.note: Paraphrase of the documented fragment; interpretive reconstruction flagged; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她與斯拉夫的列希、希臘的阿耳忒彌斯同屬森林主宰一族：林木歸她，獵物歸她，獵人是她的客人。史料只給了她的名字與職能——一位被其族人的敵人記住的的女神——但立陶宛的森林在狼群仍奔馳的每一條小徑上留存著她。（據殘缺史料所作的詮釋性重建。）

title.en: The Devil Hides in the Flax: Perkunas Strikes the Threshing-Floor
title.zh: 魔藏於亞麻：佩爾庫納斯擊打穀場

region.en: Lithuanian threshing-floors (symbolic pin at Kaunas)
region.zh: 立陶宛穀場（象徵性定位於考納斯）

period: Recorded 19th-20th c.; documented by Vellius (1979)

source.work: Thunder-vs-devil tales; documented in Vellius, Lithuanian Mythological Tales (1979)

license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain folk material; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: Wherever the Devil hides — in the flax, in the straw-stack, in the hollow oak — Perkunas strikes; every burnt field and shattered oak in the Lithuanian summer is the thunder-god's blows at the fiend who has crept into the harvest.
summary.zh: 凡魔藏身之處——亞麻中、草垛內、空心橡樹裏——佩爾庫納斯必擊之；立陶宛夏日每一片焦土、每一株裂橡，皆為雷神追擊潛入收穫之魔的痕跡。

sensitivity.note: Thunder-god vs devil cluster (cross_ref slavic-perun-veles).

passages.text: The Baltic thunder tales are one chase retold in every field: the Devil hides in the flax, in the straw-stack, in the hollow oak — wherever the harvest piles up — and Perkunas strikes. The flax-field blackens, the stack burns, the oak shatters; and the threshers say, 'There — he got him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the thunder-vs-devil tales as documented in Vellius, Lithuanian Mythological Tales (1979); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 波羅的海的雷神故事，是同一場追逐在每一片田野上的重述：魔鬼藏在亞麻裡、在草堆裡、在空心的橡樹裡——凡收成堆積之處——而佩爾庫納斯便擊下。亞麻田焦黑，草堆燃燒，橡樹碎裂；打穀的人便說：「那兒——他逮著他了。」

passages.text: The tales keep the old theology of the harvest: the crop is God's, the hiding-place is the Devil's, and the thunder is the farm's own protector. A burnt strip along the field is not a loss but a rescue; the stone axes found in the plough are Perkunas's spent bolts, and the field that has taken one is sacred ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the documented tales; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這些故事保留了古老的收穫神學：作物屬於上帝，藏匿之處屬於魔鬼，而雷電是農莊自身的守護者。田間燒焦的一條地帶並非損失，而是拯救；在犁溝中發現的石斧是佩爾庫納斯擲出的雷霆，而拾得石斧的田地便是聖地。

title.en: The Sun Dances on Easter Morning
title.zh: 復活節晨曦中太陽起舞

region.en: Baltic hilltops at Easter (symbolic pin at Kernave)
region.zh: 波羅的海復活節山頂（象徵性定位於克爾納韋）

period: Custom recorded 19th-20th c.; documented by Vellius (1979) and Greimas (1992)

source.work: The Easter sun-dance of Baltic folk custom; documented in Vellius, Lithuanian Mythological Tales (1979), and Greimas (1992)

license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain folk material; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: On Easter morning the young people climb the hills before dawn to watch the sun rise: she comes up dancing, shaking the waters from her garments, turning — so the old watchers say — from side to side like a maiden at a festival, and whoever sees her dance will be lucky all the year.
summary.zh: 復活節晨曦之前，青年登高望日：太陽升起時翩然起舞，抖落衣上水珠——老觀者言其如節日少女般左右迴旋——見其舞者全年得福。

sensitivity.note: Living custom; pre-Christian solar rite under a Christian calendar.

passages.text: On Easter morning, before the sun is up, the young people of the Lithuanian and Latvian villages climb the hills with the older folks and wait facing east. The sun rises — and, as the old watchers tell it, she dances: she shakes the waters from her garments, turns from side to side, and blazes as if a festival were being held for her in heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Easter sun-dance custom as documented in Vellius (1979) and Greimas (1992); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 復活節清晨，太陽尚未升起，立陶宛與拉脫維亞村莊的年輕人便與長者一同登上山丘，面朝東方等候。太陽升起——而據古老的守望者所述，她翩然起舞：她抖落衣袍上的水珠，左右旋轉，光芒四射，彷彿天上正為她舉行慶典。

passages.text: Whoever sees the sun dance will be lucky all the year; the young men and girls go home and tell it at the breakfast table, and the eggs are dyed in the colours of the dawn. The custom is the Baltic spring's oldest rite, kept alive under the Christian calendar: the sun is Saule, the dainas' queen, and her Easter dance is the year's wedding.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the documented custom; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 凡得見太陽起舞者，全年皆將幸運；青年男女返家後在早餐桌上講述此事，雞蛋則染成黎明的色彩。此習俗是波羅的海之春最古老的儀式，在基督教曆法之下延續不絕：太陽即紹萊，即達伊納歌謠中的女王，而她的復活節之舞便是歲月的婚禮。

title.en: The Falcon Called Indi: Manco Capac's Familiar in a Straw Hamper
title.zh: 名喚「因蒂」的鷹:曼科·卡帕克的行囊神鳥

region.en: Road from Tampu-tocco to Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 坦波-托科至庫斯科之路(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 12, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: The Incas and the rest of the ayllus set out from their homes at Tampu-tocco, taking with them their property and arms, having for their chiefs Manco Ccapac and Mama Huaco. Manco Ccapac took with him a bird like a falcon, called indi, which they all worshipped and feared as a sacred, or, as some say, an enchanted thing, for they thought that this bird made Manco Ccapac their lord and obliged the people to follow him. It was carried always in a covered hamper of straw, like a box, with much care. He left it as an heirloom to his son, and the Incas had it down to the time of Inca Yupanqui. In his hand he carried a staff of gold, to test the lands which they would come to.
summary.zh: 印加王族與各阿伊柳世系攜家財兵器,自坦波-托科啟程,以曼科·卡帕克與瑪瑪·瓦科為首領。曼科隨行攜有一隻似隼的鳥,名喚「因蒂」;族人皆奉若神明,敬而且畏——有人說它是受了魔法的靈物,因為人們相信正是這隻鳥使曼科成為他們的主,並驅使民眾追隨於他。此鳥常藏於草編箱籠之中,呵護備至。曼科將它傳給兒子,作為傳家之寶;印加王族一直供奉至印加·尤潘琪之世。他手中另持一根金杖,用以試探將要到來的土地。

sensitivity.note: The dynastic familiar bird; Markham notes the word indi seems identical with Ynti, the Sun.

passages.text: The Incas and the rest of the companies or ayllus set out from their homes at Tampu-tocco, taking with them their property and arms, in sufficient numbers to form a good squadron, having for their chiefs the said Manco Ccapac and Mama Huaco. Manco Ccapac took with him a bird like a falcon, called indi, which they all worshipped and feared as a sacred, or, as some say, an enchanted thing, for they thought that this bird made Manco Ccapac their lord and obliged the people to follow him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 12 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 印加人及其餘各氏族或艾柳從坦普托科的居所出發，攜帶財物與武器，人數足以組成一支精良的隊伍，以所稱的曼科·卡帕克與瑪瑪·瓦科為首領。曼科·卡帕克隨身帶著一隻形似獵鷹的鳥，名為印迪，眾人皆崇拜並畏懼牠，視之為神聖之物，或如某些人所說，為受蠱惑之物，因為他們認為這隻鳥使曼科·卡帕克成為他們的主君，並迫使人民追隨他。

passages.text: It was thus that Manco Ccapac gave them to understand, and it was carried always in a covered hamper of straw, like a box, with much care. He left it as an heirloom to his son, and the Incas had it down to the time of Inca Yupanqui. In his hand he carried with him a staff of gold, to test the lands which they would come to.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 12 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 曼科·卡帕克便是如此令他們信服，而這隻鳥總是被小心翼翼地裝在一個如箱子般、以稻草編成的有蓋籃中。他將其作為傳家之物留給兒子，印加人一直保有牠，直到印加·尤潘基的時代。他手中攜帶一根金杖，用以探測他們將要抵達的土地。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Ayar Cachi Sealed in the Window: The Sling-Hero Betrayed
title.zh: 亞亞爾-卡奇被封於窗內:彈弓英雄之死

region.en: Tampu-tocco, Window of Riches (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 坦波-托科「富窗」(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 12, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Ayar Cachi was fierce and strong, and very dexterous with the sling: he committed great cruelties and was oppressive both among the natives of the places they passed, and among his own people. The other brothers were afraid that his conduct would cause their companies to disband and desert. Manco Ccapac, being prudent, concurred that they should secure their object by deceit. They called Ayar Cachi: 'Brother! Know that in Ccapac-tocco we have forgotten the golden vases called tupac-cusi, and certain seeds, and the napa, which is our principal ensign of sovereignty' - the napa being a white sheep with a red body cloth, golden ear-rings, and a breast plate with red badges, carried in front of all on a pole with a cross of plumes called suntur-paucar. When Ayar Cachi refused to return, his sister Mama Huaco rebuked him with furious words: 'How is it that there should be such cowardice in so strong a youth as you are? Get ready for the journey.' Shamed, he obeyed; they gave him a companion, Tampu-chacay, with secret orders to kill him at Tampu-tocco. Scarcely had Ayar Cachi entered through the window Ccapac-tocco when Tampu-chacay put a rock against the opening and sat upon it, that Ayar Cachi might remain inside and die there. Ayar Cachi understood the treason, and used such force and shouted so loud that he made the mountain tremble: 'Thou traitor! thou who hast done me so much harm, thinkest thou to convey the news of my mortal imprisonment? That shall never happen. For thy treason thou shalt remain outside, turned into a stone.' So it was done, and to this day they show the stone on one side of the window Ccapac-tocco. The seven brethren were very sorry for what they had done, and mourned for him: Ayar Cachi was so dexterous with a sling and so strong that with each shot he pulled down a mountain and filled up a ravine - the ravines now seen on their line of march were made by Ayar Cachi in hurling stones. From that time to this day the lineage of the Incas always fear to go to Tampu-tocco, lest they should have to remain there like Ayar Cachi.
summary.zh: 亞亞爾-卡奇兇悍有力,彈弓絕技冠絕一時:他對沿途土著與本族同伴橫行暴虐。眾兄弟恐怕他的行徑會使部眾離散。謹慎的曼科·卡帕克與眾人合謀,以欺詐除之。眾人喚他說:「兄弟!我們在卡帕克-托科忘了名為『圖帕克-庫西』的金瓶,還有種子,以及我們至高的王權聖徽『納帕』。」納帕是一頭白羊,披紅衣,戴金耳環,胸前綴紅色徽章,由人擎桿舉於隊首,桿頂插羽十字,稱「孫圖爾-保卡爾」。亞亞爾-卡奇推託不願回去,其姊瑪瑪·瓦科勃然大怒,斥道:「你這般孔武有力的少年,怎會如此怯懦?整裝上路,去吧!」他受辱動身;眾人派同行的坦普-查卡伊隨行,密令他在坦波-托科殺之。二人一到,亞亞爾-卡奇甫入卡帕克-托科之窗,坦普-查卡伊便搬來巨石堵住窗口,坐鎮其上,要把他困死其中。亞亞爾-卡奇識破背叛,奮力撞擊,吼聲震得山嶽發抖:「叛徒!你害我至此,還想報信說我困死於此?永無此事!你這叛徒,就留在窗外,化為石頭吧!」果然應驗——今日人們猶指認富窗一側的那塊石頭。眾兄弟聞其死訊,追悔莫及,為之舉哀:亞亞爾-卡奇彈無虛發,一石下山、一石填谷——如今行軍道上所見的溝壑,便是他當年擲石所成。而印加王族自那時起,始終不敢靠近坦波-托科,生怕自己也像亞亞爾-卡奇那樣被留在窗內。

sensitivity.note: The strongest brother eliminated by trickery - a fratricide at the origin of the dynasty; Garcilaso omits this version entirely.

passages.text: Ayar Cachi was fierce and strong, and very dexterous with the sling. He committed great cruelties and was oppressive both among the natives of the places they passed, and among his own people. The other brothers were afraid that the conduct of Ayar Cachi would cause their companies to disband and desert... As Manco Ccapac was prudent, he concurred with the opinion of the others that they should secure their object by deceit. They called Ayar Cachi and said to him, 'Brother! Know that in Ccapac-tocco we have forgotten the golden vases called tupac-cusi, and certain seeds, and the napa, which is our principal ensign of sovereignty.' The napa is a sheep of the country, the colour white, with a red body cloth, on the top ear-rings of gold, and on the breast a plate with red badges... carried in front of all on a pole with a cross of plumes of feathers. This was called suntur-paucar.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 12 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿亞爾·卡奇兇猛強壯，且極擅長投石索。他犯下諸多暴行，對沿途各地的原住民以及自己的人民皆施以壓迫。其他兄弟擔心阿亞爾·卡奇的行徑會導致他們的隊伍解散並逃離……由於曼科·卡帕克為人審慎，他贊同其他人的意見，認為應以欺瞞手段達成目的。他們召來阿亞爾·卡奇，對他說：『兄弟！須知在卡帕克托科，我們忘了那些名為圖帕克-庫西的金瓶，還有某些種子，以及納帕，那是我們主權的首要旗幟。』納帕是當地的一種羊，毛色潔白，披著紅色布衣，耳上戴著金耳環，胸前佩著飾有紅色徽記的牌飾……由一人在最前方以長竿抬著，竿上飾有羽毛的十字。此物名為孫圖爾-保卡爾。

passages.text: When Ayar Cachi refused to return, his sister Mama Huaco, raising her foot, rebuked him with furious words, saying, 'How is it that there should be such cowardice in so strong a youth as you are? Get ready for the journey, and do not fail to go to Tampu-tocco, and do what you are ordered.' Ayar Cachi was shamed by these words. He obeyed and started to carry out his orders. They gave him, as a companion, one of those who had come with them, named Tampu-chacay, to whom they gave secret orders to kill Ayar Cachi at Tampu-tocco, and not to return with him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 12 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿亞爾·卡奇不肯回去，他的姊妹瑪瑪·瓦科便抬起腳來，以憤怒的言語斥責他，說道：「像你這般強壯的青年，怎會有如此怯懦之心？快準備上路，務必前往坦普-托科，遵行所吩咐你的事。」阿亞爾·卡奇聽了這番話，深感羞愧。他順從了，動身去執行命令。他們派了一名隨他們同來、名叫坦普-查凱的人作他的同伴，並暗中吩咐坦普-查凱在坦普-托科殺死阿亞爾·卡奇，不要與他一同回來。

passages.text: They had scarcely arrived when Ayar Cachi entered through the window Ccapac-tocco, to get the things for which he had been sent. He was no sooner inside than Tampu-chacay, with great celerity, put a rock against the opening of the window and sat upon it, that Ayar Cachi might remain inside and die there. When Ayar Cachi turned to the opening and found it closed he understood the treason of which the traitor Tampu-chacay had been guilty, and determined to get out if it was possible, to take vengeance. To force an opening he used such force and shouted so loud that he made the mountain tremble. With a loud voice he spoke these words to Tampu-chacay: 'Thou traitor! thou who hast done me so much harm, thinkest thou to convey the news of my mortal imprisonment? That shall never happen. For thy treason thou shalt remain outside, turned into a stone.' So it was done, and to this day they show the stone on one side of the window Ccapac-tocco.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 12 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們剛一到達，阿亞爾·卡奇便從卡帕克-托科的窗口進去，取他奉命去拿的東西。他剛一進去，坦普-查凱便迅疾地搬來一塊石頭堵住窗口，並坐在其上，好讓阿亞爾·卡奇留在裡面死於其中。阿亞爾·卡奇轉身面向洞口，發現已被封閉，便明白那叛徒坦普-查凱所犯的背信之罪，決意若能脫身，定要出去報仇。他為了強行打開一個出口，用盡力氣，高聲呼喊，震得山岳顫動。他以洪亮的聲音對坦普-查凱說了這番話：「你這叛徒！你害我如此之深，莫非以為能把我就此囚禁至死的消息傳出去嗎？那絕不會發生。因你的背叛，你將留在外面，化為石頭。」事情果然如此成就，至今他們仍在卡帕克-托科窗口的一側展示那塊石頭。

passages.text: The seven brethren who had remained at Hays-quisro were very sorry for what they had done, and mourned for him. This Ayar Cachi was so dexterous with a sling and so strong that with each shot he pulled down a mountain and filled up a ravine. They say that the ravines, which we now see on their line of march, were made by Ayar Cachi in hurling stones. Those of the lineage of the Incas, from that time to this day, always fear to go to Tampu-tocco, lest they should have to remain there like Ayar Cachi.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, chs. 12-13 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 留在艾斯-基斯羅的七位兄弟對自己所做的事深感懊悔，為他哀悼。這位阿亞爾·卡奇使用投石索極為靈巧，力氣又大，每投一石便能推倒一座山、填平一道溝壑。他們說，我們如今在他們行進路線上所見的那些溝壑，便是阿亞爾·卡奇投擲石塊時造成的。印加一族的人，從那時直到今日，總是害怕前往坦普-托科，唯恐自己會像阿亞爾·卡奇那樣留在那裡。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Ayar Uchu on the Rainbow Hill: 'Honour Me in All Your Festivals'
title.zh: 彩虹山上的亞亞爾-烏丘:「爾等節慶當尊我」

region.en: Hill of Huanacauri, two leagues from Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科兩萊格外瓦納考里山(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 12, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Leaving Quirirmanta they came to a hill at a distance of about two leagues from Cuzco. Ascending the hill they saw a rainbow, which the natives call huanacauri. Holding it to be a fortunate sign, Manco Ccapac said: 'Take this for a sign that the world will not be destroyed by water. We shall arrive, and from hence we shall select where we shall found our city.' Before they got to the height where the rainbow was, they saw a huaca which was a place of worship in human shape, near the rainbow. Ayar Uchu offered himself to go to it, for they said that he was very like it. When Ayar Uchu came to the statue or huaca, with great courage he sat upon it, asking it what it did there. At these words the huaca turned its head to see who spoke, but, owing to the weight upon it, it could not see. Presently, when Ayar Uchu wanted to get off he was not able, for he found that the soles of his feet were fastened to the shoulders of the huaca. The six brethren came to succour him, but Ayar Uchu, finding himself transformed and that his brethren could not release him, said to them: 'O Brothers, an evil work you have wrought for me. It was for your sakes that I came where I must remain for ever, apart from your company. Go! go! happy brethren, I announce to you that you will be great lords. I pray that in recognition of the desire I have always had to please you, you will honour and venerate me in all your festivals and ceremonies, and that I shall be the first to whom you make offerings. When you celebrate the huarachico (the arming of the sons as knights) you shall adore me as their father, for I shall remain here for ever.' Manco Ccapac answered that he would do so. Ayar Uchu promised for the youths that he would bestow on them the gifts of valour, nobility, and knighthood, and with these last words he remained, turned into stone. They constituted him the huaca of the Incas, giving it the name of Ayar Uchu Huanacauri; and so it always was, until the arrival of the Spaniards, the most venerated huaca, and the one that received the most offerings of any in the kingdom.
summary.zh: 離開基里爾曼塔,他們來到庫斯科約兩萊格外的一座山。登山之際,望見一道彩虹,土人稱之「瓦納考里」。曼科·卡帕克視為吉兆,說道:「以此為記——世界將不再毀於洪水。我們就要在此擇地建城。」未到彩虹之巔,他們先見一座人形瓦卡——崇拜之所——立於彩虹近旁。因說亞亞爾-烏丘與它極為相似,他自告奮勇前往。他大膽坐上神像,喝問它在此做什麼。瓦卡聞聲轉頭想看清來人,卻因身上負重而不能;待亞亞爾-烏丘起身離開,卻發現自己的腳掌已黏連在瓦卡的肩上,再也動彈不得。六位兄弟上前施救,無濟於事。亞亞爾-烏丘見自己已然變形,對兄弟們說:「兄弟們啊,你們害苦了我。為了你們,我來到此地,從此永離你們的行列。去吧!去吧!快樂的兄弟們,我預告你們:你們必成大主。求你們念我一貫討你們歡心的心願,在一切節慶祭典中尊崇我、敬奉我,讓我受祭於最先。我永留於此。你們為兒子們行瓦拉奇庫受武禮時,當以父禮拜我——因為我永在。」曼科·卡帕克應允。亞亞爾-烏丘代少年們承諾:他將賜他們勇武、高貴與騎士之名。言畢,他化為頑石。眾人立他為印加人的瓦卡,名之「亞亞爾-烏丘·瓦納考里」。直到西班牙人到來之前,它始終是王國中最受尊崇、受祭最豐的瓦卡。

sensitivity.note: The origin of the principal huaca of Cuzco from a petrified brother; the rainbow omen ties to the post-flood promise.

passages.text: Leaving this place they came to a hill at a distance of two leagues, a little more or less, from Cuzco. Ascending the hill they saw a rainbow, which the natives call huanacauri. Holding it to be a fortunate sign, Manco Ccapac said: 'Take this for a sign that the world will not be destroyed by water. We shall arrive and from hence we shall select where we shall found our city.' Before they got to the height where the rainbow was, they saw a huaca which was a place of worship in human shape, near the rainbow.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 12 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們離開此地，來到一座小山，距庫斯科約兩里格，或多或少。登上小山，他們看見一道彩虹，當地人稱之為瓦納卡烏里。曼科·卡帕克認為這是吉兆，便說：「把這當作世界不會被水毀滅的徵兆。我們將抵達那裡，並從此處選定我們建立城池的地方。」他們還沒走到彩虹所在的高處，便看見一尊華卡，那是人形的禮拜之所，就在彩虹附近。

passages.text: Ayar Uchu offered himself to go to it, for they said that he was very like it. When Ayar Uchu came to the statue or huaca, with great courage he sat upon it, asking it what it did there. At these words the huaca turned its head to see who spoke, but, owing to the weight upon it, it could not see. Presently, when Ayar Uchu wanted to get off he was not able, for he found that the soles of his feet were fastened to the shoulders of the huaca. The six brethren, seeing that he was a prisoner, came to succour him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 12 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿亞爾·烏丘自告奮勇前去，因為他們說他與那尊像十分相似。阿亞爾·烏丘來到那雕像或華卡前，鼓起勇氣坐了上去，問它在此做什麼。聽了這話，那華卡轉過頭來看是誰在說話，但因身上負重，無法看見。不久，阿亞爾·烏丘想要下來，卻不能夠，因為他發現自己的腳底已牢牢黏在華卡的肩上。六位兄弟見他被困住，便前來救他。

passages.text: Ayar Uchu, finding himself thus transformed, and that his brethren could not release him, said to them: 'O Brothers, an evil work you have wrought for me. It was for your sakes that I came where I must remain for ever, apart from your company. Go! go! happy brethren, I announce to you that you will be great lords. I, therefore, pray that in recognition of the desire I have always had to please you, you will honour and venerate me in all your festivals and ceremonies, and that I shall be the first to whom you make offerings. For I remain here for your sakes.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 12 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿亞爾·烏丘發覺自己就這樣被變化了，而他的兄弟們也無法解救他，便對他們說：「啊，兄弟們，你們為我招來了不幸。我是為了你們的緣故，才來到這必須永遠留下、與你們分離的地方。去吧！去吧！幸福的兄弟們，我向你們宣告，你們將成為偉大的領主。因此，我祈求你們念在我一向渴望使你們歡喜的心意，在你們所有的節慶與典禮中尊崇我、敬奉我，並讓我成為你們最先獻祭的對象。因為我是為了你們的緣故才留在這裡的。」

passages.text: When you celebrate the huarachico (which is the arming of the sons as knights) you shall adore me as their father, for I shall remain here for ever.' Manco Ccapac answered that he would do so... Ayar Uchu promised for the youths that he would bestow on them the gifts of valour, nobility, and knighthood, and with these last words he remained, turned into stone. They constituted him the huaca of the Incas, giving it the name of Ayar Uchu Huanacauri; and so it always was, until the arrival of the Spaniards, the most venerated huaca, and the one that received the most offerings of any in the kingdom.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 12 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當你們舉行瓦拉奇科（huarachico，即為兒子們授以騎士之禮）時，你們當尊我為他們的父親而敬拜我，因為我將永遠留在此地。』曼科·卡帕克（Manco Ccapac）回答說他會照辦……阿亞爾·烏丘（Ayar Uchu）為那些青年許諾，他將賜予他們勇氣、高貴與騎士之禮的恩賜，說完這最後的話語，他便留了下來，化為石頭。他們立他為印加人的瓦卡（huaca），並為它取名為阿亞爾·烏丘·瓦納考里（Ayar Uchu Huanacauri）；直到西班牙人到來之前，它始終是最受尊崇的瓦卡，也是全國中接受祭品最多的瓦卡。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: The Golden Wand in the Furrow: Testing the Soil of Huanay-pata
title.zh: 金杖插犁溝:試探瓦納伊-帕塔之土

region.en: Huanay-pata, near Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科附近瓦納伊-帕塔(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 13, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: They were in Matahua for two years, waiting to pass on to the upper valley to seek good and fertile land. Mama Huaco, who was very strong and dexterous, took two wands of gold and hurled them towards the north. One fell, at two shots of an arquebus distance, into a ploughed field called Colcapampa and did not drive in well, the soil being loose and not terraced: by this they knew that the soil was not fertile. The other went further, to near Cuzco, and fixed well in the territory called Huanay-pata, where they knew the land to be fertile. Others say that this proof was made by Manco Ccapac with the staff of gold which he carried himself, and that thus they knew of the fertility of the land, when the staff sunk in the land called Huanay-pata, two shots of an arquebus from Cuzco. They knew the crust of the soil to be rich and close, so that it could only be broken by using much force. Let it be by one way or the other, for all agree that they went trying the land with a pole or staff until they arrived at this Huanay-pata, when they were satisfied: they were sure of its fertility, because after sowing perpetually, it always yielded abundantly, giving more the more it was sown.
summary.zh: 眾人在馬塔瓦駐留兩年,等待進入上谷另覓沃土。瑪瑪·瓦孔武而靈巧,取兩支金杖向北方擲去。一支落在兩火槍射程之外、名為科爾卡潘帕的犁田之中,插入不深——土壤鬆散、未經築台——眾人知此地不肥。另一支飛得更遠,近庫斯科處,穩穩插入名為瓦納伊-帕塔的土地——眾人知此地肥沃。另一說:此試乃曼科·卡帕克親持金杖所為;金杖深插瓦納伊-帕塔之土,便知此地肥美:表土豐厚緊實,非大力不能破土。無論何說,眾人皆沿途以杖試土,直至瓦納伊-帕塔方才滿意:此地耕之不輟,歲歲豐登,愈種愈多。

sensitivity.note: The gold-staff divination of the founding; the female thrower variant credits Mama Huaco.

passages.text: Mama Huaco, who was very strong and dexterous, took two wands of gold and hurled them towards the north. One fell, at two shots of an arquebus, into a ploughed field called Colcapampa and did not drive in well, the soil being loose and not terraced. By this they knew that the soil was not fertile. The other went further, to near Cuzco, and fixed well in the territory called Huanay-pata, where they knew the land to be fertile.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 13 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 瑪瑪·瓦科（Mama Huaco）非常強壯且靈巧，她取了兩根金杖，向北擲去。其中一根落在約兩火槍射程之遙、名為科爾卡潘帕（Colcapampa）的一塊耕地裡，卻未能插穩，因為那裡的土壤鬆散且未成梯田。由此他們得知那裡的土壤並不肥沃。另一根則飛得更遠，落至庫斯科（Cuzco）附近，穩穩地插在名為瓦奈-帕塔（Huanay-pata）的地域，他們便知道那裡的土地肥沃。

passages.text: Others say that this proof was made by Manco Ccapac with the staff of gold which he carried himself, and that thus they knew of the fertility of the land, when the staff sunk in the land called Huanay-pata, two shots of an arquebus from Cuzco. They knew the crust of the soil to be rich and close, so that it could only be broken by using much force. Let it be by one way or the other, for all agree that they went trying the land with a pole or staff until they arrived at this Huanay-pata, when they were satisfied. They were sure of its fertility, because after sowing perpetually, it always yielded abundantly, giving more the more it was sown.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 13 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 另有人說，這項驗證是曼科·卡帕克親自以他所持的金杖所作，當金杖插入距庫斯科約兩火槍射程之遙、名為瓦奈-帕塔的土地時，他們便由此得知土地的肥沃。他們知道那裡的表土肥沃而緊密，非得用很大的力氣才能破開。無論是哪一種說法，因為所有人都一致認為他們一路以木桿或手杖試探土地，直到抵達這瓦奈-帕塔，方才感到滿意。他們確信那裡的肥沃，因為在不斷播種之後，它總能豐收，播種越多，收成越多。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Ayar Auca Takes Flight: The Stone of Possession and the Name of Cuzco
title.zh: 亞亞爾-奧卡飛臨:鎮地之石與「庫斯科」之名

region.en: Site of Santo Domingo, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科聖多明我修道院舊址(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 13, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: From that place Manco Ccapac saw a heap of stones near the site of the present monastery of Santo Domingo at Cuzco. Pointing it out to his brother Ayar Auca, he said: 'Brother! you remember how it was arranged between us, that you should go to take possession of the land where we are to settle. Well! look at that stone. Go thither flying' - for they say that Ayar Auca had developed some wings - 'and seating yourself there, take possession of land seen from that heap of stones. We will presently come to settle and reside.' When Ayar Auca heard the words of his brother, he opened his wings and flew to that place which Manco Ccapac had pointed out. Seating himself there, he was presently turned into stone, and was made the stone of possession. In the ancient language of this valley the heap was called cozco, whence that site has had the name of Cuzco to this day. From this circumstance the Incas had a proverb which said: 'Ayar Auca cuzco huanca' - Ayar Auca a heap of marble. Others say that Manco Ccapac gave the name of Cuzco because he wept in that place where he buried his brother Ayar Cachi; owing to his sorrow and to the fertility he gave that name which in the ancient language of that time signified sad as well as fertile.
summary.zh: 曼科·卡帕克在馬塔瓦遙指庫斯科今聖多明我修道院附近的一堆亂石,對兄弟亞亞爾-奧卡說:「兄弟!你記得我們的約定——由你去佔領我們將定居的土地。看那石頭!飛過去吧」——相傳亞亞爾-奧卡此時生出了翅膀——「落在那裡,以那堆石所見之地為你所有。我們隨後就來定居。」亞亞爾-奧卡聞言展翼,飛至曼科所指之處,一坐之下,頓時化作石頭——是為「鎮地之石」。在谷地的古語中,那堆石頭稱「科茲科」,此地因此得名庫斯科,沿稱至今。印加王族由此留下一句諺語:「亞亞爾-奧卡,庫斯科-萬卡」——亞亞爾-奧卡,一堆大理石。另有異說:庫斯科之名,是曼科·卡帕克葬其弟亞亞爾-卡奇於此,因哀傷與此地之肥沃而命名——古語中此名兼有「悲傷」與「肥沃」二義。前一說更可信,因亞亞爾-卡奇實死於卡帕克-托科,並未葬於庫斯科;印加人與土人皆如此公認。

sensitivity.note: The winged brother as founding stone; Sarmiento weighs two rival etymologies of Cuzco and prefers the stone-of-possession version.

passages.text: From that place Manco Ccapac saw a heap of stones near the site of the present monastery of Santo Domingo at Cuzco. Pointing it out to his brother Ayar Auca, he said, 'Brother! you remember how it was arranged between us, that you should go to take possession of the land where we are to settle. Well! look at that stone. Go thither flying' - for they say that Ayar Auca had developed some wings - 'and seating yourself there, take possession of land seen from that heap of stones. We will presently come to settle and reside.' When Ayar Auca heard the words of his brother, he opened his wings and flew to that place which Manco Ccapac had pointed out. Seating himself there, he was presently turned into stone, and was made the stone of possession.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 13 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 曼科·卡帕克從那地方望見庫斯科現今聖多明我修道院（Santo Domingo）舊址附近有一堆石頭。他指給他的兄弟阿亞爾·奧卡（Ayar Auca）看，說道：『兄弟！你記得我們之間是如何商定的，你當前去佔有我們將要定居的土地。那麼！看看那塊石頭。飛到那裡去』——因為他們說阿亞爾·奧卡已長出了一些翅膀——『並在那裡坐下，佔有從那堆石頭所望見的土地。我們隨後便會前來定居並居住。』阿亞爾·奧卡聽到他兄弟的話，便展開雙翼，飛到曼科·卡帕克所指的地方。他在那裡坐下，隨即化為石頭，並被立為佔有之石。

passages.text: In the ancient language of this valley the heap was called cozco, whence that site has had the name of Cuzco to this day. From this circumstance the Incas had a proverb which said, 'Ayar Auca cuzco huanca,' or, 'Ayar Auca a heap of marble.' Others say that Manco Ccapac gave the name of Cuzco because he wept in that place where he buried his brother Ayar Cachi. Owing to his sorrow and to the fertility he gave that name which in the ancient language of that time signified sad as well as fertile.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 13 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在這個山谷的古老語言中，那石堆被稱為科斯科（cozco），因此那地點至今仍名為庫斯科（Cuzco）。由於這緣故，印加人有一句諺語說：『阿亞爾·奧卡·庫斯科·萬卡（Ayar Auca cuzco huanca）』，即『阿亞爾·奧卡，一堆大理石』。另有人說，曼科·卡帕克之所以取名庫斯科，是因為他在埋葬其兄弟阿亞爾·卡奇（Ayar Cachi）的那個地方哭泣。由於他的悲傷，也由於那裡的肥沃，他取了這個名字，這名字在當時的古老語言中既表示悲傷，也表示肥沃。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Heart in Her Mouth: Mama Occlo Terrorizes the Huallas
title.zh: 口銜心肺:瑪瑪·奧克略懾服瓜利亞斯人

region.en: Huanay-pata, near Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科附近瓦納伊-帕塔(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 13, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Arriving on the land of Huanay-pata, Manco Ccapac found settled there a nation of Indians named Huallas. Manco Ccapac and Mama Occlo began to settle and to take possession of the land and water, against the will of the Huallas; in this business they did many violent and unjust things. As the Huallas attempted to defend their lives and properties, many cruelties were committed. They relate that Mama Occlo was so fierce that, having killed one of the Hualla Indians, she cut him up, took out the inside, carried the heart and lungs in her mouth, and with an ayuinto, which is a stone fastened to a rope, in her hand, she attacked the Huallas with diabolical resolution. When the Huallas beheld this horrible and inhuman spectacle, they feared that the same thing would be done to them, being simple and timid, and they fled and abandoned their rights. Mama Occlo, reflecting on her cruelty, and fearing that for it they would be branded as tyrants, resolved not to spare any Huallas, believing that the affair would thus be forgotten. So they killed all they could lay their hands upon, dragging infants from their mothers' wombs, that no memory might be left of these miserable Huallas.
summary.zh: 曼科·卡帕克進抵瓦納伊-帕塔,該處已定居著瓜利亞斯族。曼科與瑪瑪·奧克略不顧瓜利亞斯人意願,強行佔田奪水,行事兇暴不義。瓜利亞斯人自衛保命,遂遭種種殘害。相傳瑪瑪·奧克略兇悍至極:殺了一名瓜利亞斯人後,碎其屍,掏出內臟,竟將心肺銜於口中,手持繫繩的拋石「亞溫托」,以惡魔般的狠勁向瓜利亞斯人衝殺。瓜利亞斯人見此慘狀,自忖弱小怯懦,恐怕自己也要遭此毒手,遂棄地而逃,放棄了一切權利。瑪瑪·奧克略自忖殘忍太過,恐被人斥為暴君,便決計斬盡殺絕,以為如此便可抹去罪跡。於是凡力所能及者盡數殺戮,甚至從母腹中拖出嬰兒,務使這些可憐的瓜利亞斯人無人記憶。

sensitivity.note: Sarmiento's indictment of the founding violence - he wrote to prove Inca 'tyranny' for Viceroy Toledo; the atrocity story is quoted as the sworn testimony he recorded.

passages.text: Arriving on the land of Huanay-pata... he found settled there a nation of Indians named Huallas, already mentioned. Manco Ccapac and Mama Occlo began to settle and to take possession of the land and water, against the will of the Huallas. On this business they did many violent and unjust things. As the Huallas attempted to defend their lives and properties, many cruelties were committed by Manco Ccapac and Mama Occlo.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 13 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
