passages.zh: 抵達瓦奈-帕塔的土地後……他發現那裡已定居著一個名為瓦利亞斯（Huallas）的印第安民族，前文已提及。曼科·卡帕克與瑪瑪·奧克略（Mama Occlo）開始定居並佔有土地與水源，這違背了瓦利亞斯人的意願。在這件事上，他們做了許多暴虐而不義之事。由於瓦利亞斯人試圖保衛自己的生命與財產，曼科·卡帕克與瑪瑪·奧克略便犯下了許多殘酷的行徑。

passages.text: They relate that Mama Occlo was so fierce that, having killed one of the Hualla Indians, she cut him up, took out the inside, carried the heart and lungs in her mouth, and with an ayuinto, which is a stone fastened to a rope, in her hand, she attacked the Huallas with diabolical resolution. When the Huallas beheld this horrible and inhuman spectacle, they feared that the same thing would be done to them, being simple and timid, and they fled and abandoned their rights.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 13 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們講述，瑪瑪·奧克略（Mama Occlo）極為兇猛，殺死了一名瓦利亞（Hualla）印第安人之後，將他肢解，取出內臟，把心與肺含在口中，手持一根阿尤因托（ayuinto，即繫於繩上的石塊），以魔鬼般的決心攻擊瓦利亞人。瓦利亞人見此可怖而殘忍的景象，因生性單純怯懦，唯恐自己也遭同樣下場，便紛紛逃走，捨棄了自己的權利。

passages.text: Mama Occlo, reflecting on her cruelty, and fearing that for it they would be branded as tyrants, resolved not to spare any Huallas, believing that the affair would thus be forgotten. So they killed all they could lay their hands upon, dragging infants from their mothers' wombs, that no memory might be left of these miserable Huallas.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 13 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 瑪瑪·奧克略反省自己的殘酷，唯恐因此被人斥為暴君，遂決意不饒過任何瓦利亞人，認為如此一來此事便會被遺忘。於是他們殺盡所有能抓到的人，甚至從母親腹中拖出嬰兒，務使這些可憐的瓦利亞人不留半點記憶。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Copalimayta Stands: The Sinchi Who Was Erased
title.zh: 科帕利馬伊塔的抗爭:被抹去的辛奇

region.en: Cuzco valley (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科谷地(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 13, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Having done this Manco Ccapac advanced, and came within a mile of Cuzco to the S.E., where a Sinchi named Copalimayta came out to oppose him - a late-comer who had settled with the consent of the natives of the valley, incorporated in the nation of Sauaseray Panaca, natives of the site of Santo Domingo at Cuzco. Having seen the strangers invading their lands and tyrannizing over them, and knowing the cruelties inflicted on the Huallas, they had chosen Copalimayta as their Sinchi. He came forth to resist the invasion, saying that the strangers should not enter his lands or those of the natives. His resistance was such that Manco Ccapac and his companions were obliged to turn their backs. They returned to Huanay-pata, the land they had usurped from the Huallas; from the sowing they had made they derived a fine crop of maize, and for this reason they gave the place a name which means something precious. After some months they returned to the attack on the natives of the valley: they assaulted the settlement of the Sauaseras and captured Copalimayta, slaughtering many of the Sauaseras with great cruelty. Copalimayta, finding himself a prisoner and fearing death, fled out of desperation, leaving his estates, and was never seen again after he escaped. Mama Huaco and Manco Ccapac usurped his houses, lands and people. In this way Manco Ccapac, Mama Huaco, Sinchi Rocca and Manco Sapaca settled on the site between the two rivers, and erected the House of the Sun, which they called Ynti-cancha. They divided that position into four neighbourhoods or quarters, which they call cancha: Quinti-cancha, Chumpi-cancha, Sayri-cancha and Yarampuy-cancha.
summary.zh: 行此之後,曼科·卡帕克推進至庫斯科東南約一哩處,辛奇科帕利馬伊塔出而拒之。此人雖屬後來者,但經谷地土著同意入居,併入聖多明我舊址的薩瓦塞雷·帕納卡族。他們見外來者侵田凌民,又聞瓜利亞斯人慘遭荼毒,便推科帕利馬伊塔為辛奇。他起而抗侵入,聲言:「外人不得踏入我的土地、土著的土地!」其抵抗之烈,竟使曼科·卡帕克一夥敗退。他們退回從瓜利亞斯人手中奪來的瓦納伊-帕塔;所播玉米大豐,遂以「珍寶」之意為此地命名。數月後,他們捲土重來,再攻谷中土著:夜襲薩瓦塞拉斯聚落,俘科帕利馬伊塔,殘殺眾多族人。科帕利馬伊塔淪為囚徒,懼死而拼死出逃,棄其田宅,自此杳無音訊。瑪瑪·瓦科與曼科·卡帕克遂奪其屋、其田、其民。曼科·卡帕克、瑪瑪·瓦科、辛奇·羅卡與曼科·薩帕卡自此定居兩河之間,興建太陽之屋「因蒂-坎恰」;又將這片地方劃為四坊(坎恰):金蒂、瓊皮、賽里、亞蘭普伊。

sensitivity.note: The erased resister; Sarmiento's record is unusual in preserving the names of the dispossessed.

passages.text: Having done this Manco Ccapac advanced, and came within a mile of Cuzco to the S.E., where a Sinchi named Copalimayta came out to oppose him... Having seen the strangers invading their lands and tyrannizing over them, and knowing the cruelties inflicted on the Huallas, they had chosen Copalimayta as their Sinchi. He came forth to resist the invasion, saying that the strangers should not enter his lands or those of the natives. His resistance was such that Manco Ccapac and his companions were obliged to turn their backs.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 13 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 做完此事之後，曼科·卡帕克（Manco Ccapac）繼續前進，來到庫斯科（Cuzco）東南約一英里處，當地一位名為科帕利馬伊塔（Copalimayta）的辛奇（Sinchi）出來迎擊他……當地人見這些外來者侵入他們的土地、對他們施行暴政，又知曉他們對瓦利亞人所施加的種種殘酷行徑，便推舉科帕利馬伊塔為他們的辛奇。他挺身抵抗入侵，聲言這些外來者不得進入他的土地，也不得進入本地人的土地。他的抵抗十分頑強，以致曼科·卡帕克及其同伴不得不敗退。

passages.text: After some months they returned to the attack on the natives of the valley, to tyrannize over them. They assaulted the settlement of the Sauaseras, and were so rapid in their attack that they captured Copalimayta, slaughtering many of the Sauaseras with great cruelty. Copalimayta, finding himself a prisoner and fearing death, fled out of desperation, leaving his estates, and was never seen again after he escaped. Mama Huaco and Manco Ccapac usurped his houses, lands and people.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 13 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 數月之後，他們再度前來攻擊谷地的本地人，欲對其施行暴政。他們突襲了紹阿塞拉斯（Sauaseras）人的聚落，攻勢極為迅猛，竟俘獲了科帕利馬伊塔，並以極其殘酷的手段屠殺了许多紹阿塞拉斯人。科帕利馬伊塔發覺自己已成階下囚，又懼怕被殺，便絕望地逃走，捨棄了自己的產業，此後再也沒有人見到他。瑪瑪·瓦科（Mama Huaco）與曼科·卡帕克便霸佔了他的房屋、土地與人民。

passages.text: In this way Manco Ccapac, Mama Huaco, Sinchi Rocca, and Manco Sapaca settled on the site between the two rivers, and erected the House of the Sun, which they called Ynti-cancha. They divided all that position, from Santo Domingo to the junction of the rivers into four neighbourhoods or quarters which they call cancha. They called one Quinti-cancha, the second Chumpi-cancha, the third Sayri-cancha, and the fourth Yarampuy-cancha.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 13 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 就這樣，曼科·卡帕克、瑪瑪·瓦科、辛奇·羅卡（Sinchi Rocca）與曼科·薩帕卡（Manco Sapaca）定居於兩河之間的地帶，並建造了太陽之屋，他們稱之為因蒂坎查（Ynti-cancha）。他們將從聖多明各（Santo Domingo）至河流交匯處的整片地帶劃分為四個街區或分區，他們稱之為坎查（cancha）。他們將其一稱為金蒂坎查（Quinti-cancha），第二個稱為瓊皮坎查（Chumpi-cancha），第三個稱為薩伊里坎查（Sayri-cancha），第四個稱為亞蘭普伊坎查（Yarampuy-cancha）。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: The Two Lizards and the First Flute
title.zh: 二蜥蜴與第一支笛

region.en: Wamira coast, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉海岸（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Two Lizards'

summary.en: Nagari the lizard could whistle one sweet note and drew the women round him; plain-spoken Webubu, lonely, cut a slim piece of hollow bamboo and pierced holes in it — thus was the first duraio, the flute, born. His music drew the women one by one away from Nagari, until the platform of Webubu crashed under them all and the tioba trees have leaned earthward ever since.
summary.zh: 蜥蜴納加里會吹出甜美的『嗚——』聲，引得村中女子圍坐聽曲；言語笨拙的韋布布孤身無伴，忽得一計：他截一段空心竹、鑽上小孔——第一支杜拉伊奧（笛）由此而生。笛聲一起，女子們一個個借口離去，投奔笛聲，納加里獨坐原處。眾女湧上韋布布建在迪奧巴樹頂的樂台，不堪重負，轟然墜地——至今迪奧巴樹皆朝地面傾斜。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910), tales told to the author in Wedau and translated; Wamira heritage.

passages.text: In the old days there lived two lizards, Webubu and Nagari. Webubu was plain of speech, and moreover was unable to cry aloud, but Nagari, by stretching his long neck, could produce a sweet low sound, somewhat after the manner of a whistle. Nagari longed for companions, so he stretched his neck, and cried, 'U-u-u-u-u.' Then many women, hearing the sweet sound, flocked to where Nagari sat, and listened to his music. This pleased Nagari, and he continued to sound his long note, and the women sat so still, one might have thought them dead or sleeping.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Two Lizards' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古時候住著兩隻蜥蜴，韋布布（Webubu）與納加里（Nagari）。韋布布言語平淡，而且無法高聲鳴叫；但納加里伸長牠的長頸，便能發出一種甜美低沉的聲音，有點像吹哨。納加里渴望有伴，於是伸長脖子，叫道：「嗚——嗚——嗚——嗚——嗚。」許多婦女聽見這甜美的聲音，便成群結隊來到納加里所在之處，聆聽牠的樂音。這令納加里十分歡喜，牠便繼續發出那悠長的鳴聲，婦女們坐著一動也不動，旁人或許會以為她們已死或睡著了。

passages.text: Webubu, on the contrary, had no one to cheer him in his loneliness. 'What can I do,' he said, 'to draw women to me as Nagari has done? I have not a sweet voice as he has.' As he was speaking a thought grew up in his heart, and he began to act. He cut a slim piece of hollow bamboo, and pierced small holes in it. Thus was the first duraio or flute born. Webubu then built himself a platform high in a corkwood tree, which we call tioba, on the beach, and seating himself there, he began to play his duraio. High and sweet were the notes he sent forth; the listening women cried, 'Deafen us not with thine U, when we would fain hear this strange music!' Then one woman made bold to rise, and saying, 'I shall return,' went to seek the sweet music — and she lied, for she never returned. And so with each woman, until Nagari was left sitting alone as he had been at the beginning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Two Lizards' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 反之，韋布布在孤獨中無人為他歡呼。「我能做什麼，」他說，「才能像納加里那樣把女人們引到我身邊來呢？我沒有他那樣甜美的嗓音。」他正說著，心中便生出一個念頭，於是開始行動。他截下一段細長的空心竹子，在上面鑽了些小孔。第一支杜拉伊奧，也就是笛子，就這樣誕生了。接著，韋布布在海灘上一棵我們稱作蒂奧巴的軟木樹高處為自己搭了一座平台，坐在那裡，開始吹奏他的杜拉伊奧。他吹出的音符又高又甜；聽着的女人們喊道：「別用你那『嗚』聲震聾我們，我們正想聽這奇妙的音樂呢！」於是有一個女人壯起膽子站起身來，說了聲「我會回來的」，便去尋那甜美的音樂——她撒了謊，因為她再也沒有回來。每個女人都是如此，直到納加里像起初那樣獨自坐着。

passages.text: Now Webubu was still playing his duraio on the platform he had built in the tioba tree, when the women came in sight. He was alarmed for the safety of his frail platform, when he saw these many people advancing, and he cried, 'Come not up into the tree. Remain below, I beseech you, O women!' But the women were consumed with eagerness to be close to the music which had taken their hearts, and they climbed, all of them, until they were upon the platform of Webubu. Then straightway what he had feared came to pass, and Webubu, and his duraio, and the multitude of women fell crashing through the branches of the tioba to the ground beneath. And from that hour until now, all tioba trees lean towards the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Two Lizards' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這時，韋布布仍在他搭於蒂奧巴樹上的平台吹奏杜拉伊奧，女人們已進入眼簾。他見這許多人前來，擔心自己那脆弱的平台不保，便喊道：「不要上樹來。我求你們留在下面，女人們啊！」可是女人們一心只想靠近那奪了她們心魄的音樂，全都爬了上去，直到登上韋布布的平台。他所擔心的事立刻應驗了，韋布布、他的杜拉伊奧和那一大群女人一同嘩啦一聲穿過蒂奧巴的枝葉，墜落到下面的地上。從那一刻直到如今，所有的蒂奧巴樹都向着大地傾斜。

title.en: How the Turtle Got His Shell (Ker's Telling)
title.zh: 龜殼之由來（克爾傳本）

region.en: Wamira coast, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉海岸（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'How the Turtle Got His Shell'

summary.en: The Turtle and the Wallaby feasted in Binama the hornbill's garden; the wallaby leapt away, the turtle was caught for the feast, and won the children's help with soft words — crawling in their father's shell necklace, armlets, and a great wooden bowl. Diving from the stones of the pursuing birds, he lost armlets and necklace but the bowl never broke: all turtles carry Binama's bowl on their backs to this day.
summary.zh: 龜與袋鼠偷入犀鳥比納馬的園中飽食蕉蔗；袋鼠一躍而逃，龜被縛於架上待宰。他向看守的孩子們柔聲求情，借來父親最貴的貝殼項鍊、兩枚貝釧與一隻大木碗，披掛表演，逗得孩子們大笑。聽見大人回村，他直奔入海；群鳥沿岸擲石，先碎左釧，再碎右釧，又砸斷項鍊之繩；最後的大石紛紛落在木碗上，碗卻分毫無損。龜遠遁——至今龜背所負，仍是比納馬家中的木碗。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); cross-ref melanesian-bng-turtle-shell (Dixon recension).

passages.text: Long ago, our fathers have told us, the Turtle and the Wallaby were friends. Now on a certain day, the Turtle was hungry, and asked his friend to go with him to the beach and from thence to the hornbill's garden, where was much sugarcane and where bananas also were plentiful. This they did, and fed plentifully on all that was there. The Wallaby trod upon the stalks of the bananas and bowed them to the ground that his friend might eat. Thus did he also to the tall sugarcane and the orabu, the flowering rush. And they both did eat and their hunger was stayed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How the Turtle Got His Shell' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 很久以前，我們的父輩告訴我們，烏龜和袋鼠是朋友。有一天，烏龜餓了，便請他的朋友同他去海灘，再從那裡去犀鳥的園子，那裡有許多甘蔗，香蕉也很多。他們照做了，在那裡飽餐了一頓。袋鼠踩住香蕉的莖稈，把它們壓彎到地上，好讓他的朋友吃。他也照樣對待高高的甘蔗和奧拉布，也就是那開花的燈心草。他們倆都吃了，飢餓便止住了。

passages.text: Now while they were eating the birds were at work in their gardens, tilling the ground. When the work was finished they dug up much taro and returned to the village to cook their food. Then said Binama the hornbill, 'Let one of you go down to the beach and bring sea water that our food may be salted.' But his word bare no fruit, for one by one the birds made excuse, fearing lest an enemy lay in wait. At last the wagtail arose and ran to make ready. And as he went he leapt from side to side the better to avoid the foe, if foe there were. In a little he came to Binama's garden and saw the Turtle and Wallaby feeding. Their hearts trembled; nevertheless the Turtle made bold and said to the wagtail, 'Thy master has bidden us eat of his bananas that our hunger may be stayed.' Now the wagtail knew in his heart that they lied, but he answered never a word, but filled his bottles with sea water and ran back to the village by another way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How the Turtle Got His Shell' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們吃東西的時候，鳥兒們正在園子里幹活，翻耕土地。活兒干完后，他們挖了許多芋頭，回村去煮食物。這時犀鳥比納馬說：「你們派一個下海灘去取海水來，好給我們的食物加鹽。」可是他的話沒有結果，因為鳥兒們一個接一個地找借口推託，生怕有敵人埋伏。最後鷡鴒起身跑去準備。他一邊走一邊左右跳躍，好避開敵人，倘若真有敵人的話。不一會兒他到了比納馬的園子，看見烏龜和袋鼠正在吃東西。他們心裡發抖；然而烏龜壯起膽子對鷡鴒說：「你的主人吩咐我們吃他的香蕉，好止住我們的飢餓。」鷡鴒心裡知道他們撒了謊，卻一言不答，只把瓶子裝滿海水，從另一條路跑回村去。

passages.text: The Wallaby lifted up his head and seeing nought but enemies round about him, tarried not but leaped mightily and escaped. The Turtle could not jump, so he crawled with haste into a yam patch and hid himself under the leaves. But the birds hunted for him diligently and at last found him and dragged him forth, and tied him to a pole and thus carried him to Binama's house, where they laid him upon a shelf till the morrow. The next day Binama called his servants together and all went to dig food to make a feast when they should slay the Turtle. None were in the house but the children whom Binama had set to guard the captive. Then the Turtle made his voice soft, and called the children unto him. 'Loosen my bonds, O children,' quoth he, 'that we may play together.' Now the children knew not what was in the Turtle's mind, and they did as he bade them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How the Turtle Got His Shell' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 袋鼠抬起頭來，見四周無非是敵人，便不敢停留，奮力一跳逃走了。烏龜不會跳，只好急忙爬進一片芋頭地里，躲在葉子下面。可是鳥兒們仔細搜尋他，終於找到了他，把他拖了出來，綁在一根杆子上，就這樣抬到比納馬的家裡，放在架子上留到明天。第二天，比納馬召集他的僕人，大家一同去挖食物，準備在殺烏龜時設宴。屋裡只剩下比納馬派去看守俘虜的孩子們。於是烏龜放柔了聲音，把孩子們叫到跟前。「孩子們，解開我的綁繩吧，」他說，「好讓我們一起玩耍。」孩子們不知道烏龜心裡打的什麼主意，就照他的吩咐做了。

passages.text: He crawled down from the shelf, and stretched himself, for he was stiff and sore. Then he said to the children, 'Where are your ornaments? Leave the poor ones in the basket, and bring forth only the good ones, that I may see them.' The children ran to the place where Binama kept his ornaments, and brought forth a long necklace of shell money, also two shell armlets and a wooden bowl, and laid them before the Turtle. He forthwith wound the necklace many times round his neck, and put on both the shell armlets; moreover the bowl he fastened upon his back. The children laughed to watch his ungainly form decorated with their father's ornaments. But on a sudden he heard voices and knew the men were drawing near; then he ran swiftly to the sea, and hasted to dive. The birds called, 'Show thyself now. Lift up thine head.' This did the Turtle, and the angry birds cast great stones into the sea, and the left armlet which the Turtle wore was shattered. So he dived, but they called again, and a stone fell upon the right armlet and brake it into small pieces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How the Turtle Got His Shell' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他從架子上爬下來，伸了伸身子，因為他又僵又痛。然後他對孩子們說：「你們的飾物在哪兒？把那些差的留在籃子里，只把好的拿出來，讓我看看。」孩子們跑到比納馬存放飾物的地方，拿出一串長長的貝幣項鏈，還有兩隻貝殼臂環和一隻木碗，擺在烏龜面前。他立刻把項鏈在脖子上繞了好幾圈，戴上兩隻貝殼臂環；又把那隻碗綁在背上。孩子們看着他笨拙的身形佩戴着父親的飾物，都笑了起來。可是忽然他聽見人聲，知道男人們正走近；於是他飛快地向海邊跑去，急忙潛入水中。鳥兒們喊道：「現在露出你自己來。把你的頭抬起來。」烏龜照做了，憤怒的鳥兒們把大石塊扔進海里，烏龜戴的左臂環被砸碎了。於是他潛下水去，可是他們又喊，一塊石頭落在右臂環上，把它砸成了碎片。

title.en: The Man Who Left Heaven
title.zh: 離開天界之人

region.en: Wamira coast, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉海岸（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Man Who Left Heaven'

summary.en: Jealous companions cast out the man whose string of shell money outmeasured theirs; winds drove his lime-gourd boat to the foot of the mountains behind which the stars rise. Magamaia and Deboroia would not stay for him, but the morning star Maratomtom bore him up to heaven, where a damsel took him to husband. Seeing his own village's palms below, he let himself down to earth by a shell-money cord — and burned his faithless companions in the potuma, the club-house; their charred bodies clinging to the roof became the flying-foxes whose cry is the cry of a soul in pain.
summary.zh: 貝殼錢串最長的男人遭同伴嫉妒而棄於荒灘；他乘漂流的檳榔灰罐隨風至眾星之山。星星 Magamaia 與 Deboroia 都說『再等等』，只有晨星馬拉托姆托姆垂憐，攜他升天。天上佳人招他為夫，生子育女。一日父子以矛擲戲，矛落在地上他自家村中的椰樹頂上——他望鄉心切，以貝錢搓繩縋落人間（自此天上貝錢最美，人間的黯淡粗劣）。妻當他已死多年，見他歸來大喜。他設宴款待昔日負心之人，將他們關進男子會所，四面縱火；烈焰中他們攀附梁頂而亡，屍身化作狐蝠——至今棲於高處，其叫聲便是痛苦靈魂之聲。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: In a certain village lived some men who longed for strings of shell money. So they took counsel together and agreed to go to a far village and there barter store of betel nuts for what their souls desired. They set forth therefore, and in time reached the land where shell money was to be found. One of their number tarried with the canoe, while the others climbed the hill. In a little while a child came down to the beach near where the canoe lay, and to him spake the man; and he followed the child to his father's house, where he received much shell money. Then he coiled the strings of money in a water bottle, and went down to the canoe, where he awaited his companions. They were not long in coming, and glad were their voices as they spake of the long strings of money they had received. And all set out for their home. But on the way they were disputing whose string was the longest, and desired to land that they might know whose was the best.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man Who Left Heaven' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某村中住著一些渴望貝幣串的男子。於是他們一同商議，議定前往一座遠方的村落，在那裡以檳榔換取他們心中所渴望之物。他們於是動身，過了些時日便抵達了可尋得貝幣之地。他們之中有一人留守獨木舟，其餘的人則爬上山丘。不多時，一個孩子來到獨木舟停泊處附近的海灘，那男子便與他說話；他跟著那孩子到他父親的屋裡，在那裡得到了許多貝幣。於是他把貝幣串盤繞於一只水罐之中，下到獨木舟處，在那裡等候同伴。同伴們不久便來了，他們談起所得到的長長貝幣串，聲音裡滿是歡喜。眾人便一同啟程返家。然而途中他們爭論著誰的貝幣串最長，並想要靠岸，好知道誰的貝幣最好。

passages.text: It was a desolate shore on which they landed. A pandanus grew near, and one by one the men hung their strings of money over its branches and watched as they hung near the ground. And now it was the turn of the man who had stayed behind to measure his. But he hung his not on the branch of the pandanus, but on the top; and it lay upon the ground, and many coils were yet in the water bottle. When the men saw this and that their friend's money so far surpassed theirs, some of them were jealous, and some were sad, some others were angry, and many coveted it greatly. But on this were all of one mind. No longer should he travel with them. So they launched the canoe, and told the man with the long necklace that he might not go with them. The man sought for a way of escape, but found none. Then he bethought him of the lime gourd he carried over his shoulder.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man Who Left Heaven' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們靠岸的地方是一片荒涼的海岸。近處長著一棵露兜樹，眾人便一個接一個地把自己的貝幣串掛在它的枝條上，看著它們垂近地面。這下輪到那留守的男子量他的了。然而他不把貝幣掛在露兜樹的枝上，而是掛在樹頂；貝幣垂落於地，水罐裡卻還盤繞著許多圈。眾人見了，又見朋友的貝幣遠勝於自己的，有的心生嫉妒，有的悲傷，有的憤怒，還有許多人萬分覬覦。但在這件事上他們全都同心一致：他再也不能與他們同行了。於是他們把獨木舟推下水，告訴那戴著長項鍊的男子，他不得與他們同去。那男子尋求逃脫之法，卻一無所獲。這時他想起自己肩上所掛的石灰葫蘆。

passages.text: Night fell, and Magamaia rose above the sea. 'Stay but a moment,' cried the man, 'and let me hold thee and together we will mount.' But Magamaia answered, 'Tarry a little; our friend Deboroia will soon be here.' Then it was the turn of Deboroia. 'Stay but a moment,' cried the man again. But Deboroia answered even as had Magamaia, 'Tarry a little, for Maratomtom (the morning star) will soon be here.' The man's heart was hot within him for grief that no star would have pity on him in his sad plight, and he wept sore. But as he wept and lamented, Maratomtom rose and hearkened to his cry. The man held fast and Maratomtom and he rose together high into the heaven. The man let go his hold and lighted where much people were gathered together. The people of heaven marvelled greatly when the man showed himself unto them, and one damsel looking on him required that he should be her husband. So were they married, and for a time the man forgot the land which he had left. In due time a son was born to them, and grew and waxed strong.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man Who Left Heaven' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 夜幕降臨，馬加馬亞（Magamaia）升上海面。「且留片刻，」那男子喊道，「讓我抓住你，我們一同上去。」但馬加馬亞答道：「稍待一會兒；我們的朋友德博羅亞（Deboroia）馬上就來了。」接著輪到德博羅亞了。「且留片刻，」那男子又喊道。但德博羅亞也像馬加馬亞那樣答道：「稍待一會兒，因為馬拉通通（Maratomtom，即晨星）馬上就來了。」那男子心中因悲傷而灼熱，因為竟沒有一顆星在他這般悲慘的境遇中憐憫他，他便痛哭起來。然而就在他哭泣哀嘆之際，馬拉通通升起了，聽到了他的呼喊。那男子緊緊抓住，馬拉通通與他一同高高升入天際。那男子鬆了手，落在一處許多人聚集的地方。天上的人見那男子出現在他們面前，大為驚異，其中一位少女見了他，便要求他做她的丈夫。於是他們成了婚，有一陣子那男子忘卻了他所離開的那片土地。到了時候，他們生了一個兒子，這兒子漸漸長大，日益強壯。

passages.text: Now it fell upon a day that the lad cut many spears and brought them unto his father that he might sharpen them for him. This he did and the lad, seeing many coconuts far below him upon the earth, speared them from his home in the heaven. But the father was loth to make new darts, and said, 'Where are the ones I made thee?' Then he too looked down and saw upon the earth the tops of the palms of his own village. And his heart died at the sight, for he longed with an exceeding great longing to visit his land once more. So he took a long cord of pandanus and strung upon it the shell money which was not of the best; but the red and large and round he placed in a heap upon the ground, and commanded that it should be laid up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man Who Left Heaven' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 後來有一天，那少年削了許多矛，拿來給父親，好讓他為自己磨尖。父親磨好了，那少年望見下方大地上有許多椰子，便從天上的家中用矛擲取。但父親不願再做新的矛，說道：「我給你做的那幾支在哪裡？」於是他也往下望去，看見大地上自己村中棕櫚樹的樹梢。見此情景，他的心便死了，因為他懷著極其強烈的渴望，想再訪一次自己的故土。於是他取了一條長長的露兜樹繩，把不是最好的貝幣串在上面；至於那些又紅又大又圓的，他堆在地上，吩咐把它們收存起來。

title.en: The Feast in the Potuma and the Flying-Foxes
title.zh: 會所之宴與狐蝠之由

region.en: Wamira coast, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉海岸（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Man Who Left Heaven'

summary.en: Come down to earth after years in heaven, the man saluted his false companions with fair words, bade them to a feast, closed the doorways of the potuma and fired it at each corner. Their cries were stilled, and their charred bodies clinging to the roof became the flying-foxes which ever haunt high places, whose cry is the cry of a soul in pain. And a taboo on his coco palms had mourned him as dead all those years.
summary.zh: 男人自天上歸來，先向昔日棄他之人致以美言問候，並邀他們赴宴。宴備妥後，他自己不進會所，卻把 potuma（男子會所）的各門緊閉，再於四角縱火。火高煙濃，賓客遍尋出路不得；慘呼漸息，燒焦的屍體攀附在屋頂上——化作狐蝠。狐蝠至今棲居高處，其叫聲便是痛苦的靈魂之聲。而這些年裡，人間的妻子早把他當作亡夫服喪，連他名下的椰樹都被下了禁忌。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage. Second half of the Man Who Left Heaven cycle.

passages.text: Now, as the man was thus seated on high, it came to pass that the daughter who had been born to him upon earth came to gaze on her father's coconuts. She knew she might but look, and that to taste was forbidden, for her mother mourned her father as one long dead, and a taboo had been laid on all the coco palms which had been his. But, as she gazed, she discerned a man seated among the leaves, and, looking steadfastly on him, she knew him to be her father, and straightway ran to her mother and told her the tidings. But her mother answered, 'How can this be, my daughter? Thy father is dead, and I have mourned for him these many years. It is another man thou hast seen.' Nevertheless, at her daughter's word she went out and found even as she had said. Then was her heart glad, and she bade her husband come down and enter the house that she might make ready food for him to eat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man Who Left Heaven' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 且說那男子如此高坐之際，恰巧他在地上所生的女兒前來觀望父親的椰子。她知道只能看，品嘗是被禁止的，因為她母親哀悼她父親，如同他已死去多年，凡曾屬於他的椰子樹都已被列為禁忌。然而她觀望時，察覺有一人坐在葉間，定睛看他，認出那正是她的父親，便立刻跑到母親那裡，把這消息告訴她。但她母親答道：「這怎麼可能呢，我的女兒？你父親已經死了，我為他哀悼了這許多年。你所見的是另一個人。」儘管如此，聽了女兒的話，她還是出去，發現果然如女兒所說。於是她心中歡喜，吩咐丈夫下來進屋，好讓她備好食物給他吃。

passages.text: Being now refreshed, he minded him of the companions who had aforetime treated him evilly, and appeared unto them with many fair words and kindly greetings. He also bade them to a feast he was about to make. Much taro was boiled, and a pig was slain, and, all being made ready, the guests were gathered together in the potuma, which is the club-house. But the man himself did not enter, for he desired to take vengeance on his enemies. So he closed the doorways of the potuma and made them fast that no one might chance to escape, and then he set fire to each corner of the house. The flames rose high and thick smoke filled the potuma, as the feasters looked for a way of escape. But they looked in vain, and soon their cries were stilled, and their charred bodies clinging to the roof of the potuma were changed into flying foxes, which ever haunt high places, and whose cry is the cry of a soul in pain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man Who Left Heaven' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他如今精神恢復，便想起了從前惡待他的那些同伴，於是帶著許多好話和親切的問候去見他們。他也邀請他們赴他即將設下的宴席。許多芋頭煮好了，一頭豬也宰了，一切準備妥當，賓客們便聚集在「波圖馬」（potuma），也就是會所之中。但那男子自己並未進去，因為他想向仇敵報復。於是他把會所的出入口關上並牢牢封住，免得有人僥倖逃脫，然後在屋子的每個角落點起火來。火焰高高升起，濃煙充滿了會所，宴飲的人們尋找逃脫之路。但他們徒然尋覓，不久他們的呼喊便止息了，他們緊貼在會所屋頂上的焦黑屍身化作了飛狐，這種飛狐總是出沒於高處，其叫聲乃是受苦靈魂的哀鳴。

title.en: Dabedabe the Good and the Bones of His Mother
title.zh: 善人達貝達貝與母骨

region.en: Bou, hill country above Wamira, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉山地之布村（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'Dabedabe the Good'

summary.en: The sow that farrowed five pigs and one man-child was cooked for the workmen at her son Dabedabe's garden; he gathered her bones in a mat and carried them away to Qamana, and at the river's bank flung them on the stones — they became men and pigs in hundreds. With them he ransomed the captives bound for a Walaga cannibal feast, and from that day men are spared and pigs slain when a feast is made.
summary.zh: 布村一戶的母豬在林中產下五豬一男嬰；男孩達貝達貝被主人抱回撫養。他長成後請村人助墾新園，好養育豬母；主人卻殺了豬母款待助工。達貝達貝命人把骨頭盡數留在席布上，收拾進袋，離村遠行，直至不見母親村莊的卡馬納。他孤身住於洞穴，得一小童照料瘡傷。聞村人將開 Walaga 宴——以人為食——他怒而赴河邊，把袋中母骨奮力擲上石頭：骨化為人，立聽號令；再擲，化為成群之豬。他命新造之人砍桿縛豬，趕赴宴所，對宴主說：『放了你綁著的人，我把這些豬都給你。』宴主貪豬而從之。自那日起，巴布亞人開宴皆殺豬而不殺人——如無達貝達貝，講這故事的說書人也早被縛上木桿吃掉了。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage. The tale aitions the substitution of pigs for human victims at feasts.

passages.text: This is a tale of the men of Bou, which is in the hill country to the south of Wamira. A certain man had a pig, which left him and gave birth to her young in the bush. Now five of them were pigs like their mother, but the sixth was a man child, and him his mother loved best of all. Day by day did the six follow her as she sought their food in the bush, and after a time, their footprints being many, the men of Bou knew where they were hiding. So they took pig nets and set out to catch them. Now the owner of the old pig looked at the footprints, and seeing the footprints of a child among them said, 'Ye may keep the young pigs when they are caught, save only the one whose marks are these.' So the nets were made ready, and the five little pigs were soon caught. But the old mother, fearing danger, had hidden the man child, and he was not therefore caught in the net.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Dabedabe the Good' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這是關於瓦米拉以南丘陵地帶的布族人的故事。有一個人養了一頭豬，那豬離開了他，在叢林裡生下了豬崽。其中五頭像牠們的母親一樣是豬，但第六頭是個男孩，而牠母親最疼愛的就是他。日復一日，這六個孩子跟著母親在叢林裡覓食；過了些時日，由於牠們的足跡眾多，布族人便知道了牠們藏身何處。於是他們帶上捕豬網，出發去捕捉牠們。那頭老母豬的主人看了看足跡，見其中有一個孩子的腳印，便說：『你們捉到小豬後盡可留下，只除了腳印是這個的那一頭。』於是網子準備妥當，五頭小豬很快就被捉住了。但那老母親懼怕危險，早已把那個男孩藏了起來，因此他沒有落入網中。

passages.text: Now it came to pass when the boy was now grown that on a day he heard his mother crying for food, and he resolved to make a garden that he might grow food to give her when she was hungry. So he called to the men of the village, and asked them to help him make his garden; and the lad, whose name was Dabedabe, set out with many men for the plantation. Soon had they cleared the ground, and then they made a fence about it. Now while they were fencing the garden, the owner of the pigs went back to the village, and made ready food, that the men who had helped Dabedabe might eat in the evening when they returned. And as he desired that they should eat and be full he killed the old pig whose son was Dabedabe, and cooked her flesh with the taro. And when the men returned from the garden he said, 'Sit ye down and eat, for supper is ready.' Now Dabedabe watched while the man did this, and he said, 'What is the flesh in the pot?' 'It is pig's flesh, my son,' said the man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Dabedabe the Good' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 後來，男孩長大了，有一天他聽見母親因飢餓而哭泣，便決心開墾一座園子，好種出食物，在她餓時給她吃。於是他召喚村裡的男人們，請他們幫他開墾園子；這少年名叫達貝達貝，便帶著許多人前往園地。他們很快清好了地，接著在四周圍起了籬笆。就在他們圍園子的時候，那些豬的主人回到了村裡，準備好食物，好讓幫達貝達貝幹活的男人們傍晚回來時有得吃。他既希望他們吃得飽足，便宰了那頭老母豬——也就是達貝達貝的母親——把牠的肉和芋頭一起煮了。當男人們從園子回來時，他說：『你們坐下吃吧，晚飯預備好了。』達貝達貝在一旁看著那人做這些事，便問：『鍋裡是什麼肉？』那人說：『是豬肉，我的孩子。』

passages.text: Then Dabedabe went into the house and brought forth a mat, and spread it in the sight of all, saying, 'When ye eat throw no bone away, but lay all upon the mat which I have spread before you.' And they did even as he had said. Then when all had eaten Dabedabe wrapped up the bones of the pig, and slung the bundle on his shoulder, and said, 'Friends, we were to-day making a garden that I might have wherewithal to give my mother to eat when she hungered, but she hath been slain, and ye have eaten her, therefore I can no longer stay here, but must leave you. Farewell.' Thus he left the village, and journeyed until he came to Peubua; there he sat down, and would fain have remained there, but, turning himself, he saw his mother's village behind him, and his heart burned. Therefore he rose up, and journeyed until he came to Reborebo; and in like manner, on looking behind him, he could see his mother's village in the distance, and for grief at the sight he tarried not, but went on until he came to Doula.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Dabedabe the Good' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是達貝達貝走進屋裡，取出一張席子，當著眾人的面鋪開，說：『你們吃的時候，不要丟掉一根骨頭，要把所有的骨頭都放在我為你們鋪開的這張席子上。』他們便照他所說的做了。等大家都吃完，達貝達貝把豬骨包好，把包裹掛在肩上，說：『朋友們，我們今天開墾園子，本是為了我母親飢餓時有東西給她吃，但她卻被殺了，你們又吃了她，因此我不能再留在這裡，必須離開你們了。告辭。』他就這樣離開了村子，一路前行，來到佩烏布阿；他在那裡坐下，本願留在那裡，但回身一看，望見身後母親的村子，心中便如焚燒。於是他起身前行，來到雷博雷博；同樣地，他回頭一望，仍能望見遠處母親的村子，見此情景悲傷不已，便不停留，繼續前行，來到杜拉。

passages.text: But the men of Qamana would not suffer him to abide in their village, because his body was covered with noisome sores. Therefore, as the rain was heavy, he sought shelter in a cave, where he dwelt alone. And after not many days he called a child to him, who abode with him in the cave and dressed his sores, and cooked his food; so it was that his sores were healed and strength came back to him. Now it came to pass that, as he and the boy sat together in the cave, they heard the voice of a drum in the village. 'What meaneth the voice of the drum which I hear?' 'The men of Qamana are dancing because of the feast they are about to make.' 'On what are they going to feast?' 'On men,' quoth the boy, 'and the name of the feast is Walaga.' Dabedabe's heart grew hot within him at this word, and he went into the village and sought for the giver of the feast, and found him standing by a long row of poles on which burdens were strapped.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Dabedabe the Good' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但卡馬納的人們不肯讓他在他們的村裡住下，因為他渾身長滿惡臭的瘡。因此，由於雨下得很大，他便在一處山洞裡棲身，獨自住在那裡。不過多少日子之後，他喚來一個孩子，那孩子與他同住在洞裡，替他敷治瘡口，為他煮食；就這樣，他的瘡癒合了，力氣也恢復了。後來，他與那男孩一同坐在洞裡時，聽見村中傳來鼓聲。『我聽到的這鼓聲是什麼意思？』『卡馬納的人們正在跳舞，因為他們即將舉行宴會。』『他們要拿什麼來設宴？』『拿人，』男孩說，『這宴會名叫瓦拉加。』達貝達貝聽了這話，心中怒火中燒，便走進村裡，尋找設宴的人，見他站在一長排綁著重物的竿子旁。

title.en: The Ransom of the Walaga Feast
title.zh: 瓦拉加宴上之贖

region.en: Qamana, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞卡馬納（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'Dabedabe the Good'

summary.en: 'Do not this thing, I pray thee,' besought Dabedabe, 'but tarry a little while I go to the river.' There he flung his mother's bones violently upon a stone, and they became men and stood before him; again he flung the rest, and they became pigs, a great number. Bound to the poles they had cut, the pig-men came in a long line to the feast: 'Set free the men whom ye have bound, and I will give thee these pigs which thou seest.' From that day men are spared and pigs slain at feasts, and Qamana and Bou have abundance of pigs to this day.
summary.zh: 『求你莫行此事，』達貝達貝懇求道，『且稍等，我去去河邊便回。』他到河邊打開口袋，取母骨猛擲石上——骨化為人，立於面前聽令；他命他們入林砍桿，一砍再砍，直至夠數；又把餘骨擲上河岸之石，化作大群之豬。人們把豬縛上長桿，肩扛成行赴宴。達貝達貝對宴主說：『放了你綁著的那些人，我這些豬都給你。』宴主見豬心動，依言解縛。眾人歡宴，塗髮插羽，分食豬肉。自那日起直到如今，巴布亞人開宴殺豬而不殺人；卡馬納與布村至今豬群興旺。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); second half of the Dabedabe cycle.

passages.text: 'Do not this thing, I pray thee,' besought Dabedabe, 'but tarry a little while I go to the river. I shall return.' Then he hasted and returned to the cave, and took his bag in his hand, and went down to the river. There he opened the bag, and took from it some of his mother's bones which he had placed within it on the day that he took leave of his people at Bou. And he flung the bones violently upon a stone, and they became men, and stood before him to hear what he would say. Then said he to them, 'Go ye into the bush and cut many poles, and fetch them hither.' So they went and cut many poles, as he had said, but lo, when they brought them to Dabedabe he said, 'These are too few. Go ye and cut more.' Then they came again carrying more poles, but not yet were they enough, and he sent them forth a third time to fetch more, and now were there as many as he wanted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Dabedabe the Good' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 『我求你，不要做這件事，』達貝達貝懇求道，『且稍等片刻，我到河邊去一趟，就會回來。』於是他急忙趕回山洞，手裡拿著他的袋子，下到河邊。他在那裡打開袋子，從中取出一些母親的骨頭——那是他在布族與族人告別那天放進袋裡的。他猛地把骨頭擲在一塊石頭上，骨頭就變成了人，站在他面前聽他要說什麼。他對他們說：『你們到叢林裡去砍許多竿子，把它們帶到這裡來。』他們便照他所說的去砍了許多竿子，可是，當他們把竿子帶到達貝達貝面前時，他說：『這些太少了。你們再去砍些來。』於是他們又帶著更多竿子回來，但還是不夠，他又第三次派他們去取更多，這回數量才合他的意。

passages.text: He therefore took the rest of his mother's bones out of his bag and threw them violently upon the stones by the river's bank, and they became pigs, a great number. Then he bade the men who stood near bind the pigs to the poles they had cut, and he himself returned swiftly to the giver of the feast and cried, 'Cook now my gwada of plantains, and anoint it with coconut, for I and my men will soon be here.' When he had said this he returned to the river and bade the men carry the pigs, which had been bound to the poles, upon their shoulders to the feast. Thus did they, and many marvelled as they saw the long line of men, each bearing the end of a pole upon his shoulder, a pig being bound to each pole.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Dabedabe the Good' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他把袋子裡剩下的母親的骨頭取出來，猛力擲在河岸的石頭上，骨頭就變成了豬，為數眾多。然後他吩咐站在近旁的人們把豬綁在他們砍來的竿子上，自己則迅速回到設宴的人那裡，喊道：『現在把我的大蕉糰子煮好，澆上椰漿，因為我和我的人馬上就到。』說完這話，他回到河邊，吩咐人們把綁在竿子上的豬扛在肩上，帶到宴會去。他們便照做了，許多人看見那長長的一隊人，每人肩上扛著一根竿子的末端，每根竿子上都綁著一頭豬，都大為驚奇。

passages.text: Now when they reached the place set apart for the feast, Dabedabe said to his men, 'Set your burdens upon the ground,' and they did so. Then said he to the giver of the feast, 'Set free the men whom ye have bound, and I will give thee these pigs which thou seest.' And the giver of the feast, greatly desiring the pigs, did as Dabedabe had said, and unloosed the bonds of the men which lay upon the ground waiting to be slain. Then did all make merry, and tire their hair, and hang many ornaments of shell and feathers upon themselves, and did eat of the pigs which Dabedabe had given them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Dabedabe the Good' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 如今他們到了那為筵席分別出來的地方，達貝達貝對他的手下說：『把你們的擔子放在地上。』他們就照做了。於是他對設筵的人說：『把你們所捆綁的人釋放，我就把你看見的這些豬給你。』那設筵的人極其想要那些豬，就照達貝達貝所說的做了，解開那些躺在地上等著被殺之人的綁索。於是眾人都歡樂起來，梳理頭髮，在身上掛了許多貝殼和羽毛的飾物，又吃了達貝達貝所給他們的豬。

passages.text: And in truth if Dabedabe had not done this thing, we of Papua, yea, even I who tell the tale, would have been bound upon poles and eaten at the feasts of our enemies. But from that day even until now are men spared and pigs slain when a feast is made, and at Qamana as also at Bou are abundance of pigs to this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Dabedabe the Good' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 說實在的，倘若達貝達貝沒有做這件事，我們巴布亞人，是的，就連我這講述故事的人，也會被綁在木樁上，在我們仇敵的筵席上被吃掉。但從那日起直到如今，每逢設筵，人得以倖免，而豬被宰殺；在卡馬納如此，在布烏也如此，直到今日仍有豐盛的豬。

title.en: The Dancing Dame and the Drum of the Waves
title.zh: 盲嫗之舞與浪之鼓

region.en: Wamira coast, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉海岸（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Dancing Dame'

summary.en: A blind grandmother sent daily for salt water heard the waves beat on the coral cliffs and took it for the drum of a feast; she laid down her staff and danced on the beach. Her daughter-in-law set the child to spy, and mocked her — 'How loud is thy drum, O dame, seeing it is beaten by a thousand waves!' — and at the taunt and the cruel laughter the old woman grew cold with shame, fell to the earth, and her spirit left her. The loud beat of the waves is the voice of the blind woman's drum still.
summary.zh: 盲眼老嫗每日奉命下灘取鹹水，忽聞濤聲拍打珊瑚崖，誤以為是宴樂之鼓，便放下手杖在灘上獨舞至倦。媳婦疑其怠惰，遣幼子窺探；得知真相後母子大笑，嘲道：『你的鼓聲好響啊，老婆子——一千道浪替你打鼓！』老嫗聽了這嘲弄與殘忍的笑聲，羞愧徹骨，寒徹周身，倒地而亡。至今浪聲大作時，人們便說：『聽！那是盲嫗的鼓。』

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: In a certain village lived a woman and her little son, and with them dwelt an old woman, who was the child's grandmother, and she was blind. Now her daughter-in-law, not being willing that the dame should eat unless she also worked, bade her fetch salt water each day from the beach that the food might be salted. This did the old woman, and she went never astray, for there was but one path to the beach, and with her staff in her hand she went bravely. Now when her eyes were open in the old days, the dame lived ever upon the mountains, and thus had never seen the sea. And it came to pass that on a certain day when she went down to the beach, she heard the waves beating upon the coral cliffs and fancied it was the voice of the drum which she heard. So laying down her staff she fell to dancing, and ceased not until she was weary. Then filling the coconut water bottle with salt water she went back to the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Dancing Dame' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在某個村子裡住著一個女人和她的幼子，與她們同住的還有一位老婦人，就是那孩子的祖母，她是瞎眼的。她的媳婦不願讓這老婦人白吃而不幹活，便吩咐她每日從海灘取回鹹水，好讓食物有鹽味。老婦人照做了，從不迷路，因為通往海灘只有一條路，她手裡拿著拐杖，勇敢地走去。原來在從前她眼睛還看得見的日子，這老婦人一直住在山上，因此從未見過海。後來有一天，她下到海灘，聽見波浪拍打珊瑚崖壁，竟以為自己聽見的是鼓聲。於是放下拐杖，跳起舞來，直到疲倦才停止。然後她把椰子水瓶裝滿鹹水，回到屋裡。

passages.text: On the morrow did she the same as on the day before. Again the waves beat upon the coral, and again the dame thought it to be the voice of the drum. And this time she danced for so long that her daughter-in-law was very angry, and ceased not to scold her for not returning to the house until the night was nigh. And as the dame would not tell her for what cause she remained so long, she resolved to set a watch on her the next day. Therefore when the dame set out on the morrow her daughter-in-law said to her little son, 'Follow thy grandmother to the beach, and bring me word again why she tarrieth so long.' And the child did as his mother bade him, and sat down at a distance on the beach to see what the dame would do.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Dancing Dame' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 次日她又照前一日所做的做了。波浪再次拍打珊瑚，老婦人又以為那是鼓聲。這一回她跳得太久，她的媳婦非常生氣，不住地責罵她，說她直到天色將晚才回家。老婦人不肯告訴她為何逗留這麼久，媳婦便決意次日派人監視她。因此到了次日老婦人出門時，媳婦對她的幼子說：『跟著你祖母到海灘去，回來告訴我她為何逗留這麼久。』孩子照母親的吩咐做了，在海灘上遠遠地坐下，看那老婦人要做什麼。

passages.text: Then he saw her lay down her staff and dance to the sound of the waves which beat upon the coral. And when he had watched her for long, and saw that she ceased not to dance, he ran back to his mother and said, 'My grandmother is even now dancing alone upon the beach. There is no voice of drum, nor any people, but only the waves beating upon the coral.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Dancing Dame' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他看見她放下拐杖，隨著拍打珊瑚的波浪聲跳舞。他看了她許久，見她不住地跳，便跑回母親那裡說：『我祖母此刻正在海灘上獨自跳舞。沒有鼓聲，也沒有人，只有波浪拍打珊瑚。』

passages.text: Then the woman laughed for scorn that the dame should spend her time in such a manner, and when she returned bearing the sea water she cried, 'How loud is thy drum, O dame, seeing it is beaten by a thousand waves!' And she and her child laughed loudly at the blind woman. She heard the taunt and the cruel laughter, and grew cold with shame, and fell to the earth, and her spirit left her. And now when the waves beat loud upon the coral we say, 'Hark! it is the voice of the blind woman's drum.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Dancing Dame' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那女人便譏笑老婦人竟這樣消磨時光，等她帶著海水回來時，她喊道：『老婦人啊，你的鼓聲多麼響亮，竟有千重波浪在敲打它！』她和她的孩子大聲嘲笑那瞎眼的老婦人。她聽見了那譏諷和殘酷的笑聲，羞愧得渾身發冷，倒在地上，靈魂便離她而去。如今每逢波浪大聲拍打珊瑚，我們就說：『聽！那是瞎眼老婦人的鼓聲。』

title.en: Tabuikor's Flood: The Woman Who Made All Lands
title.zh: 塔布伊科爾洪水：造萬地之婦

region.en: Kababiai spring, New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛卡巴比亞聖泉（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by George Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, 1910, ch. XIV

source.work: George Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians: Their Life-Histories Described and Compared (London: Macmillan, 1910), ch. XIV 'History, Mythology'

summary.en: Tabuikor the woman made the land at Kababiai while her two sons worked it — until they caught her mingling her own water into their food. They ate her tainted tuba before her face, and in her anger she rolled away the stone that kept the sea confined: water poured out in a great flood, the origin of the sea. Then they sprinkled pieces of earth upon the waters and other islands came up; sprinkled them on the land and trees, and animals and men grew. Her sacred spring remains at Kababiai, where none dare bathe or drink, for an immense fish lives in it that will come when they call.
summary.zh: 婦人塔布伊科爾在卡巴比亞造地，兩個兒子耕作；她煮芋時竟以己溺調羹。二子察覺，商定計策，當面奪食她那摻了穢物的芋。她大怒，把一直鎮住海洋的那塊石頭推開——海水傾瀉而出，氾濫成災，海由此而生。二子又取地之碎塊撒於水上，別的島嶼隨之浮起；再撒於陸地，樹木、走獸與人類由此而生。卡巴比亞的聖泉至今猶在，村人不敢在其中沐浴或飲用——泉中住著一條大魚，喚之即來。

sensitivity.note: Missionary record (Brown 1910); New Britain heritage. Flood-cluster cross-ref.

passages.text: Tabui Kor was a woman, Tilik and Tarai were two men, her sons, whether born or not is not clear. They lived at Kababiai, where the sacred spring is, and from this they made the land (not yet the world). The woman made it and the two men worked it. The men worked whilst the woman cooked the tuba or cabbage. The two men, however, found out that their food tasted very nasty, and so one day they agreed that one of them should work with both axes so as to make the woman believe that they were both working, whilst the other went and hid so as to watch the cooking. He went and saw the woman make water into their cabbage, and put pure sea water into her own tuba. He said to himself, 'Alas indeed for us two if she continues doing that to our food.' He went and told his brother, and they agreed upon a certain action which they would take.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, ch. XIV (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 塔布伊·科爾（Tabui Kor）是一名女子，蒂利克（Tilik）與塔賴（Tarai）是兩名男子，即她的兒子，至於是否為她親生則不清楚。他們住在卡巴巴伊（Kababiai），即聖泉所在之處，並由此造出了陸地（當時尚未有世界）。女子造地，兩名男子則加以耕作。男子耕作之時，女子烹煮芋頭莖或甘藍菜。然而，兩名男子發現他們的食物味道極其難吃，於是有一天他們商定：其中一人以雙斧同時勞作，好讓女子以為他們兩人都在工作，另一人則躲起來窺看烹煮的過程。他去看了，見那女子把水尿進他們的甘藍菜裡，卻把潔淨的海水放進她自己的芋頭莖中。他暗自說道：「若她繼續這樣對待我們的食物，我們兩人可就慘了。」他去告訴了他的兄弟，兩人便商定要採取某項行動。

passages.text: When they came to dinner they took the woman's tuba while she was not looking and substituted theirs instead, which she had mixed with her urine because she was too lazy to go for sea water. They snatched away her food and ate it. She protested, but they ate it still. Then she got angry and went and rolled away the stone which had hitherto kept the sea confined, and the water and sea poured out in a great flood, and this was the origin of the sea. They afterwards took pieces of the earth and sprinkled them on the sea and other islands came up. Then they sprinkled this also on the land and trees, and animals and men grew.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, ch. XIV (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了用餐之時，他們趁女子不備，取走她的芋頭莖，換上他們自己的，因為她懶得去取海水，竟在其中攙了自己的尿。他們搶走她的食物吃了。她提出抗議，他們仍舊吃了。於是她發怒，前去滾開那塊迄今一直將海封閉住的石頭，海水便湧出，形成一場大洪水，這便是海的起源。之後他們取來一些泥土，撒在海面上，其他島嶼便浮現出來。接著他們又把泥土撒在陸地上，樹木、動物與人便生長出來。

passages.text: Kababiai have the spring yet, but they never bathe in it or drink of it, and were very frightened when our boys drank of it. They say that an immense fish lives in it which will come when they call it, but it failed to do so when our boys got them to call, though they called long and loudly enough. It will be seen from this that the belief in New Britain that the creator of all things was a woman was the same as that which is held in many other Melanesian groups. This Tabuikor seems to have had also the name of Ne Kidong; she was the woman who made all lands, and to whom the natives prayed when an eclipse of the sun or moon took place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, ch. XIV (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡巴巴伊至今仍有那處泉水，但他們從不在其中沐浴或飲用，當我們的男孩們喝了那泉水時，他們非常驚恐。他們說泉中住著一條巨魚，只要他們呼喚，牠便會出來，但當我們的男孩們讓他們呼喚時，牠卻沒有出現，儘管他們呼喚得夠久也夠響。由此可見，新不列顛島相信萬物的創造者是一名女子，這與許多其他美拉尼西亞族群所持的信仰相同。這位塔布伊科爾似乎另有名字叫作內·基東（Ne Kidong）；她就是造出一切陸地的女子，也是當地人在發生日食或月食時向其祈禱的對象。

title.en: To Kabanana the Good Workman and To Purgo the Bad
title.zh: 巧匠卡巴納那與拙工普爾戈

region.en: Duke of York Islands, New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛約克公爵群島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by George Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, 1910, ch. XIV

source.work: George Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians: Their Life-Histories Described and Compared (London: Macmillan, 1910), ch. XIV 'History, Mythology'

summary.en: In the New Britain mythology, To Kabanana was the first man and the maker of all things good and useful; To Purgo (on Duke of York) or To Purungo/To Purukelel (on New Britain) spoilt all the works of To Kabanana and was the author of all evil. Their names are used to this day: To Kabanana means a good workman, To Purgo a bad one — the local counterparts of Tagaro and Suqe of the northern New Hebrides.
summary.zh: 新不列顛神話中，卡巴納那為首人，造一切善物與有用之物；普爾戈（約克公爵島稱法；新不列顛島稱普魯恩戈或普魯克勒勒爾）專壞卡巴納那之功，乃一切禍惡之源。二人之名至今日常使用：稱能工為卡巴納那，稱拙工為普爾戈——恰與新赫布里底北部的塔加羅與蘇蓋相對應。

sensitivity.note: Missionary record (Brown 1910); cross-ref to-kabinana/to-karvuvu (Dixon recension of the same cycle).

passages.text: There were two other characters in their mythology, the one called To Kabanana, who was supposed to have been the first man, and the maker of all things good and useful; and another called on Duke of York To Pulgo, and on New Britain To Purungo or To Purukelel, who spoilt all the works of To Kabanana and was the author of all evil. The names of these two men are continually used to-day, the former meaning a good workman and the latter a bad one. It is interesting to note that these two personages have their counterparts in other Melanesian groups. In the northern New Hebrides, Tagaro and Suqe occupy the same relative positions. Tagaro wanted everything to be good, and would have no pain or evil; Suqe would have all things bad. At Whitsuntide Island whatever Tagaro did or made was right, Suqe was always wrong.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, ch. XIV (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們的傳說中還有另外兩個人物：一個名叫托·卡巴納納（To Kabanana），據信是第一個男人，也是所有美好有用之物的創造者；另一個在約克公爵島（Duke of York）稱為托·普爾戈（To Pulgo），在新不列顛島則稱為托·普倫戈（To Purungo）或托·普魯克萊爾（To Purukelel），他破壞了托·卡巴納納的一切作為，是一切邪惡的根源。這兩個人的名字至今仍不斷被使用，前者意指好工匠，後者意指壞工匠。值得注意的是，這兩個人物在其他美拉尼西亞族群中也有對應者。在新赫布里底群島北部，塔加羅（Tagaro）與蘇克（Suqe）佔據著相同的相對位置。塔加羅希望一切皆善，不願有痛苦或邪惡；蘇克則希望一切皆惡。在聖靈降臨節島（Whitsuntide Island），凡塔加羅所做或所造的都是對的，蘇克則總是錯的。

title.en: To Kadol, Limlimanawin, and the Head in the Water Hole
title.zh: 卡多爾、林利馬溫與水潭中的頭顱

region.en: New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by George Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, 1910, ch. XIV

source.work: George Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians: Their Life-Histories Described and Compared (London: Macmillan, 1910), ch. XIV 'History, Mythology'

summary.en: To Kadol found a little boy and girl who had run away from their angry mother and took them home; his wife Limlimanawin, jealous of the girl, feigned sickness, murdered the boy while the parents were away, ate part of the body and hid the head. Detected, she was burnt with her house — but the boy's head, thrown into a water hole, was visited again and again by the woman's spirit, who at last restored him to life, decked him with ornaments, took him back to To Kadol, and tried to prove her innocence.
summary.zh: 卡多爾拾得因偷芒果被母責罵而出逃的一對小兄妹，帶回家中；其妻林利馬溫嫉妒那女孩，佯裝生病留在家中，趁機殺害男孩、食其部分遺體、藏起頭顱。事發後，她連人帶屋被燒。男孩的頭被拋入水潭；那女人的魂靈卻一再回到潭邊探視，終於使他復活，為他披掛飾物，帶他回到卡多爾面前，並竭力為自己辯白無辜。

sensitivity.note: Missionary record (Brown 1910); New Britain heritage.

passages.text: To Kadol was a mythical person who found a little boy and girl who had run away from their mother in the plantation, because she was angry with them for having taken her mango. He took them home and his wife Limlimanawin wanted to eat the boy, and was very jealous of the girl who was watched by To Kadol. She pretended to be sick, stayed at home with the children, murdered the boy, ate part of the body, and hid the head. When detected she was burnt, together with the house in which she was. The boy's head was thrown into a water hole and was frequently visited by the spirit of the woman who eventually restored him to life, decked him out with ornaments, took him to To Kadol and tried to establish her innocence in the matter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, ch. XIV (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 托·卡多爾（To Kadol）是一個神話人物，他發現了一個小男孩和一個小女孩，他們因為母親惱怒他們摘了她的芒果，便從園圃中逃離了母親。他把他們帶回家，他的妻子利姆利馬納溫（Limlimanawin）想吃掉那個男孩，並且非常嫉妒那個受托·卡多爾看顧的女孩。她假裝生病，與孩子們留在家中，殺死了男孩，吃掉了部分屍體，並把頭藏了起來。被發現後，她連同她所在的房屋一起被燒死。男孩的頭被扔進一個水坑，那女子的鬼魂經常前去探訪，最終使他復活，為他戴上飾物，帶他去見托·卡多爾，並試圖證明自己在此事中無罪。

title.en: Ya Dapal on the Rising Tide
title.zh: 潮漲之巖上的雅達帕爾

region.en: New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛島（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by George Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, 1910, ch. XIV

source.work: George Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians: Their Life-Histories Described and Compared (London: Macmillan, 1910), ch. XIV 'History, Mythology'

summary.en: A mythical woman named Ia (or Ya) Dapal ran away from her jealous and angry husband to a rock in the sea. As the tide rose her husband entreated her to come on shore, but she refused unless he would come and escort her — even when she could only speak by springing up out of the water. Thus she died; and her name is now used, by those who know the tradition, for an obstinate woman, especially a runaway wife.
summary.zh: 神話女子雅達帕爾因丈夫嫉妒動怒而出逃，避居海上孤岩。潮水漲起，丈夫在岸上懇求她回來；她卻說除非他親自下海來接——哪怕那時她只能躍出水面方能開口。丈夫終究未去，她便溺亡於漲潮之中。知此傳說的人至今用『雅達帕爾』來稱呼固執的女子，尤其是私奔之妻。

sensitivity.note: Missionary record (Brown 1910); New Britain heritage.

passages.text: A mythical woman was named Ia (or Ya) Dapal who ran away from her jealous and angry husband to a rock in the sea. As the tide rose her husband entreated her to go on shore, but she refused to do so unless he would come and escort her even when she could only speak by springing up out of the water. Thus she died and her name is now used, by those who know the tradition, for an obstinate woman, especially if she be a runaway wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, ch. XIV (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一位名叫伊亞（Ia，或作雅 Ya）·達帕爾（Dapal）的神話女子，她逃離了嫉妒而憤怒的丈夫，躲到海中的一塊岩石上。潮水上漲時，她的丈夫懇求她上岸，但她拒絕，除非他前來接她，即使她只能從水中躍出才能說話。她就这样死了，如今知曉這一傳說的人，便用她的名字來指稱固執的女子，尤其是離家出走的妻子。

title.en: Kaia and Nara: Spirits of the Craters and the Eclipse
title.zh: 該亞與納拉：火山口之靈與日月蝕之禱

region.en: Mother and Daughters craters, Matupit, New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛馬圖皮特對面的『母與女』火山口（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by George Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, 1910, ch. XIV

source.work: George Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians: Their Life-Histories Described and Compared (London: Macmillan, 1910), ch. XIV 'History, Mythology'

summary.en: The Kaia is the evil omnipresent spirit of New Britain: he afflicts people with deformity and disease, causes earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and calamity, and lives in craters and dark places; To Lagulagu is the particular Kaia of the craters called the Mother and Daughters opposite Matupit. Against him stands Nara — 'the certain one' — the good omnipresent spirit to whom the people pray in earthquake and eclipse: 'Nara i tara dat,' Nara, who made us; and of the mountains, 'Nara ku i pami,' Nara alone he made them.
summary.zh: 新不列顛人的『該亞』乃遍在之惡靈：致人殘疾疾病，興地震、火山與災禍，居於火山口與幽暗之地；馬圖皮特對面『母與女』火山口中的該亞名為托拉古拉古。與之相對是善靈『納拉』（意謂『那一位』）：地震與日月蝕之時，人們向納拉祈禱——『Nara i tara dat』（納拉造了我們）；論及群山則說『Nara ku i pami』（唯納拉造了它們）。

sensitivity.note: Missionary record (Brown 1910); New Britain spirit-belief.

passages.text: The term Kaia (or Kaiya) was applied to an evil omnipresent and powerful spirit who afflicted people with deformity and diseases, was the cause of earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and other calamities, and lived in craters and dark places. The term was also applied to any evil spirit, a large snake or iguana that was much dreaded. To Lagulagu was the name of the particular Kaia who resided in the craters called the Mother and Daughters opposite the island of Matupit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, ch. XIV (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「Kaia」（或作 Kaiya）一詞，用以指稱一種邪惡、無所不在且強大的神靈，祂使人罹患畸形與疾病，是地震、火山爆發及其他災禍的成因，並棲居於火山口與幽暗之處。此詞亦用以泛指任何邪靈，以及一種令人極為畏懼的大蛇或鬣蜥。To Lagulagu 則是居於名為「母與女」的火山口中之特定 Kaia 之名，該火山口位於馬圖皮特島（Matupit）對面。

passages.text: There was also a good omnipresent and powerful spirit called Nara. This word means a certain one, or it may have come from two words na (mother) and ra (one). They prayed to this Nara during an earthquake and also at an eclipse. When asked the reason for this they always replied, 'Nara i tara dat,' i.e. Nara, who made us, or it may have meant he who made us. Speaking of the mountains on New Britain they said, 'Nara ku i pami,' i.e. Nara alone he made them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, ch. XIV (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 另有一種善良、無所不在且強大的神靈，名為 Nara。此詞意為「某一位」，亦可能源自 na（母親）與 ra（一）兩字。人們於地震時及日食時向此 Nara 祈禱。當被問及箇中緣由時，他們總是答道：「Nara i tara dat」，即「造我們的 Nara」，或可能意指「造我們的那一位」。談及新不列顛（New Britain）的群山時，他們說：「Nara ku i pami」，即「唯獨 Nara 造了它們」。

title.en: Pele Destroys Keoua's Army at Kilauea, 1790
title.zh: 一七九〇年佩蕾滅凱瓦阿軍

region.en: Kilauea crater path, Hawaii Island
region.zh: 夏威夷島基拉韋厄火山口旁通道

period: Historical eruption of November 1790; recorded by Dibble (1839) and Kamakau (Kuokoa 1867)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 18 (Chicago 1916), quoting Dibble and Kamakau

summary.en: Fleeing Kamehameha, the chief Keoua marches his army past Kilauea in three companies. A column of fire blazes higher than Mauna Kea and Mauna Loa, sand and ashes and great stones falling for days; the rear company, hurrying forward rejoicing at their escape, finds the central division all corpses - some lying, some sitting upright clasping wives and children and pressing noses in a final farewell, so lifelike that only touch proved them dead. A solitary hog alone survived. The people said Pele had taken Kamehameha under her protection.
summary.zh: 凱瓦阿為避卡美哈梅哈，率軍分三隊經基拉韋厄而行。火山噴出高過兩座大山的火柱，沙石灰石連日落降數日；殿後部隊慶幸脫險趕上前隊，卻見中路全軍已成屍骸——或臥或坐，有人還緊抱妻兒、鼻息相觸作永訣，栩栩如生，觸之方知已死；全隊唯餘孤豚一口生還。民間皆言：佩蕾已將卡美哈梅哈納入她的護佑。

sensitivity.note: Historic eruption read through Pele-worship; the Kilauea military fatality of 1790 is documented.

passages.text: Almost exactly thirty-four years before Kapiolani defied the worship of the fire-goddess Pele, Keoua, a high chief, lost a large part of his army near the volcano Kilauea. This was in November, 1790. Ka-lani-opuu had been king over the island Hawaii; when he died in 1782 he left the kingdom to his son Kiwalao, giving the second place to his nephew Kamehameha. War soon arose between the cousins; Kamehameha defeated and killed the young king, and Kiwalao's half-brother Keoua escaped to his district Kau. For some years the three factions practically let each other alone, although there was desultory fighting; then Keoua attacked Hilo, killed his uncle and ravaged Kamehameha's lands along the northeastern side of the island. Kamehameha quickly returned from Maui and made an immediate attack on his enemy; the chief was defeated and driven through forests along the eastern side of Mauna Kea to Hilo.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 18 (1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 幾乎恰在卡皮歐拉尼（Kapiolani）公然反抗火女神佩蕾（Pele）崇拜的三十四年前，一位高級酋長 Keoua 在基拉韋厄火山（Kilauea）附近損失了他軍隊的一大部分。時為一七九〇年十一月。Ka-lani-opuu 曾為夏威夷島之王；他於一七八二年去世時，將王國傳給其子 Kiwalao，並將次位給予其姪 Kamehameha。兩位堂兄弟之間旋即爆發戰爭；Kamehameha 擊敗並殺死了年輕的國王，而 Kiwalao 的同母異父兄弟 Keoua 則逃往其轄區 Kau。此後數年間，三派實際上彼此相安無事，雖有零星戰鬥；其後 Keoua 進攻希洛（Hilo），殺死其叔父，並蹂躪 Kamehameha 沿該島東北側的土地。Kamehameha 迅速自茂宜（Maui）返回，立即向其敵人發動攻擊；該酋長戰敗，被迫穿越冒納凱亞（Mauna Kea）東側的森林，逃往希洛。

passages.text: Keoua heard of an attack on his home district, gave the fish-ponds and fertile lands of Hilo to some of his chiefs, and hastened to cross the island with his army by way of a path near the volcano Kilauea, dividing his warriors into three parties and taking charge of the first in person. They passed the crater at a time of great volcanic activity. A native writer, probably Kamakau, in the native newspaper Kuokoa, 1867, describes the destruction of the central part of this army by an awful explosion from Kilauea: 'Thus was it done. Sand, ashes, and stones grew up from the pit into a very high column of fire, standing straight up. The mountains of Mauna Kea and Mauna Loa were below it. The people even from Ka-wai-hae saw this wonderful column with fire glowing and blazing to its very top. When this column became great it blew all to pieces into sand and ashes and great stones, which for some days continued to fall around the sides of Kilauea. Men, women, and children were killed. Mona, one of the army, who saw all this but who escaped, said that one of the chiefesses was ill and some hundreds of the army had delayed their journey to guard her and so escaped this death.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 18 (1916), quoting Kamakau; not verbatim.
passages.zh: Keoua 聽聞其家鄉轄區遭攻擊，便將希洛的魚池與肥沃土地賜予其部分酋長，並急忙率軍取道基拉韋厄火山附近的一條小徑橫越該島，將其戰士分為三隊，親自率領第一隊。他們在火山活動劇烈之際經過該火山口。一位原住民作家，或即 Kamakau，於一八六七年原住民報紙《Kuokoa》上，描述了這支軍隊中央部分因基拉韋厄一次可怕的爆發而覆滅的情形：「事情便是如此發生的。沙、灰與石自坑中升起，形成一根極高的火柱，筆直矗立。冒納凱亞與冒納羅亞（Mauna Loa）兩山皆在其下。甚至遠在 Ka-wai-hae 的人們也看見這根奇妙的火柱，火焰灼灼燃燒，直達其頂。當這火柱變得巨大時，它便爆裂四散，化為沙、灰與巨石，一連數日持續落於基拉韋厄四周。男人、女人與孩童皆被殺死。軍中之一員 Mona 目睹了這一切卻得以逃脫，他說有一位女酋長患病，軍中數百人因護衛她而延遲了行程，因而逃過此劫。」

passages.text: Dibble, the first among the missionaries to prepare a history of the islands, gave the following description of the event: 'The army of Keoua set out on their way in three different companies. The company in advance had not proceeded far before the ground began to shake and rock beneath their feet, and it became quite impossible to stand. Soon a dense cloud of darkness was seen to rise out of the crater, and almost at the same instant the electrical effect upon the air was so great that the thunder began to roar in the heavens and the lightning to flash; the whole region was enveloped and the light of day was entirely excluded. Soon followed an immense volume of sand and cinders which were thrown in high heaven and came down in a destructive shower for many miles around; some few persons of the forward company were burned to death by the sand and cinders and others were seriously injured. The rear body, which was nearest the volcano at the time of the eruption, seemed to suffer the least injury, and after the earthquake and shower of sand had passed over hastened forward to escape the dangers which threatened them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 18 (1916), quoting Dibble; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 迪布爾（Dibble）是傳教士中首位編纂群島歷史者，他對此事有如下描述：「Keoua 的軍隊分成三隊出發。前隊行進未遠，地面便開始在他們腳下震動搖晃，根本無法站立。不久，便見一團濃密的黑暗自火山口升起，幾乎在同一瞬間，空氣中的電效應如此強烈，以致天上雷聲轟鳴、閃電閃爍；整個地區被籠罩，日光完全被遮蔽。隨即而來的是巨量的沙與火山渣，被拋上高空，並在周圍數哩之內如毀滅性的驟雨般落下；前隊中有少數人被沙與火山渣燒死，另有人身受重傷。後隊在爆發時距火山最近，似乎受害最輕，待地震與沙雨過後，便急忙前進以逃避威脅他們的危險。

passages.text: But what was their surprise and consternation when, on coming up with their comrades of the centre party, they discovered them all to have become corpses. Some were lying down, and others sitting upright clasping with dying grasp their wives and children and joining noses (their form of expressing affection) as in the act of taking a final leave. So much like life they looked that they at first supposed them merely at rest, and it was not until they had come up to them and handled them that they could detect their mistake. Of the whole party, including women and children, not one of them survived to relate the catastrophe that had befallen their comrades; the only living being they found was a solitary hog, in company with one of the families which had been so suddenly bereft of life.' Keoua's prophets ascribed this blow from the gods to their high chief's gift of the fish-ponds, considered the favorite food-producers for offerings to Hiiaka, the youngest member of the Pele family. Kamehameha's prophets said this eruption was the favor of the gods on his temple building, and the people said it was proof that Pele had taken Kamehameha under her especial protection.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 18 (1916), quoting Dibble; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但當他們趕上中央隊伍的同伴時，發現他們全都已成了屍體，其驚愕與惶恐可想而知。有些人躺臥著，另有些人端坐著，以垂死的手緊抱妻兒，並鼻尖相觸（這是他們表達親愛的方式），彷彿正在作最後的告別。他們看起來如此栩栩如生，以致後隊起初以為他們只是歇息，直到走近觸碰他們，才發覺自己弄錯了。整隊人馬，包括婦女與孩童，無一倖存以述說降臨於他們同伴的災難；他們所找到的唯一活物，是一頭孤零零的豬，與其中一個驟然失去生命的家庭相伴。」Keoua 的預言者將這番來自神明的打擊歸咎於其高級酋長贈予魚池之舉，因為魚池被視為供養佩蕾家族最年幼成員希伊阿卡（Hiiaka）之祭品最受喜愛的食物來源。Kamehameha 的預言者則說，這次爆發是神明對他興建神廟的眷顧，而民眾則說，這證明佩蕾已將 Kamehameha 置於她特別的庇護之下。

title.en: Kapiolani Defies the Goddess of Kilauea, 1824
title.zh: 一八二四年卡皮歐拉尼挑戰火山女神

region.en: Kilauea crater rim, Hawaii Island
region.zh: 夏威夷島基拉韋厄火山口邊

period: Historical event of December 1824; recorded by Richards, Bingham and Alexander (19th c.)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 20 (Chicago 1916), quoting Richards, Bingham and Alexander

summary.en: Kapiolani, wife of the orator-chief Naihe, walks a hundred miles over sharp lava to Kilauea to break the worship of Pele. A rival priestess mumbles a 'letter from Pele'; Kapiolani reads back from her own book. At the crater's brink the berry-feeder warns 'You will die by Pele'; she answers 'I shall not die by your god; that fire was kindled by my God', descends several hundred feet, eats the consecrated ohelo berries, throws stones into the fire-pit, and prays. 'All the people saw that she was not injured and pronounced Pele to be powerless.'
summary.zh: 演說家酋長奈伊希之妻卡皮歐拉尼徒步百里，踏過鋒利熔岩前往基拉韋厄，誓破佩蕾之祀。途中女祭司展『佩蕾之信』喃喃咒罵；卡皮歐拉尼便朗讀自己識字課本中的經文相答。火山口畔，奉食者勸阻：『你必死於佩蕾。』她答：『我不會死於你們的神；這火是我神所點燃的。』她下行數百呎，食聖莓、擲石入火坑、同禱而返——『全境之民親見她毫髮無傷，皆稱佩蕾已無權能。』

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era event; retained as the historical end-point of Pele worship. Recorded with its Christian sources noted.

passages.text: The story of the high chiefess Kapiolani and her conflict with Pele, the goddess of Kilauea, in December, 1824, is historic. Kapiolani was the daughter of Keawe-mau-hili, the high chief of the district of Hilo. She became a tall, portly woman, with keen black eyes and an engaging countenance, a queen in appearance when with other chiefs or chiefesses; she was the wife of Na-ihe, the high chief of the district of Kona, said to be the national orator or best speaker on government affairs among the chiefs. Kapiolani, the-bending-arch-of-heaven, was very intelligent, quick-witted and fearless; both were so influential that they were chosen by Kamehameha as members of his council of chiefs. When the missionaries of the American Board arrived April 4, 1820, at Kailua Bay, Naihe and Kapiolani were among the first chiefs to welcome instruction and accept Christianity as far as they could understand it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 20 (1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 高級女酋長卡皮歐拉妮與基拉韋厄火山女神佩蕾之間的衝突，發生於一八二四年十二月，其事有史可考。卡皮歐拉妮是希洛地區高級酋長凱阿韋-毛-希利之女。她長成後身材高大豐腴，雙目烏黑銳利，面容動人，與其他酋長或女酋長並立時，儀態儼然如女王；她是科納地區高級酋長納伊赫之妻，據說納伊赫是全國的演說家，或酋長之中最善於議論政事者。卡皮歐拉妮——其名意為「天之彎拱」——極為聰慧，機敏而無所畏懼；夫婦二人皆極具影響力，因而被卡美哈美哈選為其酋長議會的成員。一八二〇年四月四日，美國海外傳道部的傳教士抵達凱盧阿灣時，納伊赫與卡皮歐拉妮是最先歡迎教誨、並在其所能理解的範圍內接受基督教的酋長之一。

passages.text: Priests of Pele were numerous on the island Hawaii; women were among those of highest rank in that priesthood, and many of the personal followers of Kapiolani were worshippers. When Kapiolani said she was going to prove the falsity of the worship of Pele there was a storm of heartfelt opposition; the priests and worshippers of Pele honestly believed divine punishment would fall on her, and those who were Christians were afraid some awful explosion might overwhelm the company, as a large body of warriors had been destroyed thirty-four years before. When Kapiolani left her home in Kona her people, with great wailing, attempted to persuade her to stay; the grief, stimulated by fear of things supernatural, was uncontrollable, and the people followed their chiefess some distance with prayers and tears. For more than a hundred miles she journeyed, usually walking, sometimes having to cross miles of the roughest, most rugged and sharp-edged lava on the island Hawaii.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 20 (1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 佩蕾的祭司在夏威夷島上為數眾多；其中女性位居該祭司階層的最高等級，而卡皮歐拉妮的許多隨從都是信奉者。當卡皮歐拉妮表示她要去證明佩蕾崇拜之虛妄時，激起了一片發自內心的反對之聲；佩蕾的祭司與信奉者真心相信神的懲罰會降臨於她，而那些已成為基督徒的人則害怕會有一場可怕的爆發吞噬眾人，因為三十四年前曾有一大隊戰士被毀滅。當卡皮歐拉妮離開科納的家時，她的人民號啕大哭，試圖勸她留下；這份因畏懼超自然之事而加劇的悲痛無法抑制，人們帶著祈禱與淚水跟隨他們的酋長走了一段路。她跋涉了一百多英里，通常步行，有時必須橫越夏威夷島上數英里最崎嶇、最險惡、邊緣銳利的熔岩。

passages.text: Toward the close of the day they crossed steaming cracks and chasms and drew nearer to the foul-smelling gaseous clouds of smoke which blew toward them from the great crater. Here a priestess of Pele of the highest rank came to meet the party and turn them away from the dominions of the fire-goddess unless they would offer appropriate sacrifices. This priestess was very haughty and bold, and forbade her to approach any nearer to the volcano on pain of death at the hands of the furious goddess Pele. 'Who are you?' asked Kapiolani. 'I am one in whom the God dwells.' 'If God dwells in you, then you are wise and can teach me. Come and sit down.' The priestess had seen printed pages or heard about them, so she drew out a piece of kapa and, saying that this was a letter from Pele, began to read or rather mumble an awful curse. The people with Kapiolani were hushed into a terrified silence, but she listened quietly until the priestess, carried beyond her depth, read a confused mass of jumbled words and unintelligible noises which she called the dialect of the ancient Pele. Then Kapiolani took her spelling-book, and a little book of a few printed hymns, and said: 'You have pretended to deliver a message from your god, but we have not understood it. Now I will read you a message which you can understand, for I, too, have a letter.' Then she read clearly the Biblical sentences printed in the spelling-book and some of the hymns; the priestess was silenced.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 20 (1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 時近傍晚，他們穿過冒著蒸氣的裂縫與深壑，愈來愈接近從大火山口朝他們吹來的、氣味惡臭的含氣煙雲。此時，一位地位最高的佩蕾女祭司前來迎接這一行人，要他們離開火之女神的領地，除非他們獻上適當的祭品。這位女祭司極為傲慢大膽，禁止她再靠近火山，違者將死於憤怒的女神佩蕾之手。「你是誰？」卡皮歐拉妮問道。「我是神所居於其中的人。」「若神居於你中，那麼你便有智慧，可以教導我。過來坐下吧。」那位女祭司曾見過印有文字的紙頁，或聽聞過這類東西，於是取出一片樹皮布，說這是佩蕾的書信，便開始誦讀，或者不如說含混地念出一段可怕的咒詛。與卡皮歐拉妮同行的人們陷入驚恐的沉默，但她靜靜地聽著，直到那位女祭司越出自身所能，讀出一堆雜亂無章、顛三倒四的詞語與不可解的聲響，並稱之為古佩蕾的方言。於是卡皮歐拉妮拿出她的拼字課本，以及一本印有幾首聖詩的小書，說道：「你假裝傳達你神的訊息，但我們並未聽懂。現在我要讀一段你能聽懂的訊息給你聽，因為我也有一封信。」接著她清晰地讀出拼字課本中所印的聖經文句以及若干聖詩；那位女祭司啞口無言。

passages.text: Kapiolani passed the priestess, went on to the crater, met Mr. Goodrich and was much affected by the effort he had made to aid her. Mr. Richards, a missionary, later wrote: 'Along the way to the volcano she was accosted by multitudes and entreated not to proceed. She answered, If I am destroyed, then you may all believe in Pele, but if I am not, you must all turn to the true writings.' Here in the large cones built up by leaping lava the natives said were the homes of the family of Pele; the roaring of the furnaces and crackling of flames was the music of drums beaten for the accompaniment of the household dances, and the red flaming surge was the surf wherein they played. Mr. Richards says: 'A man whose duty it was to feed Pele, by throwing berries and the like into the volcano, entreated her to go no farther. And what, said she, will be the harm? The man replied, You will die by Pele. Kapiolani answered, I shall not die by your god. That fire was kindled by my God. The man was silent and she went onward, descending several hundred feet, and there joined in a prayer to Jehovah. She also ate the berries consecrated to Pele, and threw stones into the volcano.' Bingham says: 'Then with the terrific bellowing and whizzing of the volcanic gases they mingled their voices in a solemn hymn of praise to the true God.' Alexander in the History of the Hawaiian People says, 'This has justly been called one of the greatest acts of moral courage ever performed.' Richards states that the leader of Kapiolani's party said to him: 'All the people of the district saw that she was not injured and have pronounced Pele to be powerless.' The influence of Kapiolani against this most influential form of idolatrous worship was felt throughout the whole nation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 20 (1916), quoting Richards, Bingham and Alexander; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡皮歐拉妮越過那位女祭司，繼續前往火山口，遇見古德里奇先生，並為他為援助她所作的努力而深受感動。傳教士理查茲先生後來寫道：「在前往火山的路上，許多人上前與她攀談，懇求她不要前行。她回答說：我若被毀滅，那麼你們盡可都去信奉佩蕾；但我若安然無恙，你們就都必須歸向真正的經文。」此處那些由噴湧的熔岩堆積而成的大錐體，當地人說是佩蕾家族的居所；熔爐的轟鳴與火焰的噼啪聲，是為伴隨家中舞蹈而擊鼓的樂聲，而那赤紅翻騰的浪湧，則是他們嬉戲其中的浪花。理查茲先生說：「有一個人的職責是餵養佩蕾，即把漿果之類投入火山之中，他懇求她不要再往前走。她說：那又有什麼害處呢？那人回答：你會死於佩蕾之手。卡皮歐拉妮答道：我不會死於你的神之手。那火是我的神所點燃的。那人默然不語，她便繼續前行，向下走了數百英尺，並在那裡一同向耶和華祈禱。她還吃了獻給佩蕾的漿果，並把石頭投入火山之中。」賓厄姆說：「於是，伴隨著火山氣體可怕的咆哮與嘶鳴，他們眾人的聲音交織成一首莊嚴的讚美詩，頌讚真神。」亞歷山大在《夏威夷民族史》中說：「此事被公正地稱為有史以來最偉大的道德勇氣之舉之一。」理查茲記述，卡皮歐拉妮一行人的領隊對他說：「該地區所有的人民都看見她毫髮無傷，並已宣告佩蕾毫無力量。」卡皮歐拉妮對這種最具影響力的偶像崇拜所施加的抵制，其影響遍及全國。

title.en: Maui Lifts the Fallen Sky
title.zh: 毛伊撐起坍塌的天穹

region.en: Kauwiki hill, Maui Island (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 毛伊島考維基山丘（象徵性定位）

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; retold 1910 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 3 (New York 1910)

summary.en: The heavens lay close on the earth; plants pushed them up inch by inch, and their leaves flattened forever. A man said to a woman: give me a drink from your gourd and I will push the heavens higher; drinking deep, Maui braced himself against the clouds, lifted them to the treetops, to the mountain summits, and thrust them into their place. A man who mocked the task was caught on the Lahaina coast and changed into a great black rock. Westervelt parallels the Samoa Tii-tii footprints, the serpent of Niue, and the Maori Tane straining sky from earth.
summary.zh: 昔日天穹低垂觸地；草木一寸寸頂天，葉片因此永遠攤平。一人向女子討水：『給我一口葫蘆水，我便把天舉高。』毛伊痛飲之後，抵住雲層奮力上舉——舉至樹梢、舉至山巔、終於撐定今日之位。譏笑者被追至拉海納海岸化作黑色巨石。桑加群島有蒂伊蒂伊六呎足印，紐埃島巨蛇碎身成島、血點為星，毛利人則說是塔內以足撐天——諸島同源。

sensitivity.note: Pacific-wide 'sky lifted' cluster; Westervelt's comparative notes summarized.

passages.text: Maui's home was for a long time enveloped by darkness. The heavens had fallen down, or, rather, had not been separated from the earth. According to some legends the skies pressed so closely and so heavily upon the earth that when the plants began to grow all the leaves were necessarily flat; according to other legends the plants had to push up the clouds a little, and thus caused the leaves to flatten out into larger surface so that they could better drive the skies back and hold them in place. Thus the leaves became flat at first and have so remained through all the days of mankind. The plants lifted the sky inch by inch until men were able to crawl about between the heavens and the earth, and thus pass from place to place and visit one another.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 3 (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 毛伊的家園長久以來為黑暗所籠罩。天已塌落，或者更確切地說，尚未與地分開。據某些傳說，天空如此貼近、如此沉重地壓在大地之上，以致植物開始生長時，所有的葉子都必然是扁平的；據另一些傳說，植物不得不把雲朵稍稍頂起，因而使葉子舒展成更大的表面，以便更好地把天空推回去並使之固定原位。於是葉子起初便成了扁平之狀，並在人類所有的日子裡一直如此。植物一寸一寸地頂起天空，直到人能夠在天與地之間爬行，從而往來各處，互相拜訪。

passages.text: After a long time, according to the Hawaiian legends, a man, supposed to be Maui, came to a woman and said: 'Give me a drink from your gourd calabash, and I will push the heavens higher.' The woman handed the gourd to him; when he had taken a deep draught he braced himself against the clouds and lifted them to the height of the trees; again he hoisted the sky and carried it to the tops of the mountains; then with great exertion he thrust it upwards once more and pressed it to the place it now occupies. Nevertheless dark clouds many times hang low along the eastern slope of Maui's great mountain, Haleakala, and descend in heavy rains upon the hill Kauwiki; but they dare not stay, lest Maui the strong come and hurl them so far away that they cannot come back again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 3 (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據夏威夷傳說，過了很久之後，一個男子——據信是毛伊——來到一個女人面前，說道：「從你的葫蘆瓢裡給我一點水喝，我便把天推得更高。」那女人把葫蘆遞給他；他深深飲了一口之後，便抵住雲朵，把它們舉到樹木的高度；他又一次舉起天空，把它托到山頂之上；接著他使出極大的力氣，再一次把它向上推去，並把它按壓到如今所在的位置。然而，烏雲仍屢屢低低地懸掛在毛伊那座大山哈萊阿卡拉東面的山坡上，並化作大雨降落在考維基山上；但它們不敢久留，唯恐力大無窮的毛伊前來把它們拋得遠遠的，再也回不來。

passages.text: A man who had been watching the process of lifting the sky ridiculed Maui for attempting such a difficult task; when the clouds rested on the tops of the mountains Maui turned to punish his critic. The man had fled to the other side of the island; Maui rapidly pursued and finally caught him on the sea coast, not many miles north of the town now known as Lahaina; after a brief struggle the man was changed into a great black rock which can be seen by any traveler who desires to localize the legends of Hawaii. In Samoa Tii-tii is the name of the one who braced his feet against the rocks and pushed the sky up; the foot-prints, some six feet long, are said to be shown by the natives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 3 (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個一直在旁觀看撐天過程的男子，嘲笑毛伊竟想嘗試如此艱難的任務；當雲朵停歇在山頂之上時，毛伊便轉過身來懲罰這個批評他的人。那人已逃到島的另一邊；毛伊迅速追趕，終於在海岸邊抓住了他，地點就在如今稱為拉海納的城鎮以北不過數英里處；經過短暫的搏鬥，那人被變成了一塊巨大的黑色岩石，任何想要為夏威夷傳說確定地點的旅人都能看見它。在薩摩亞，提伊提伊（Tii-tii）便是那個以雙腳抵住岩石、把天空推上去之人的名字；據說當地人至今仍展示著那雙腳印，長約六英尺。

passages.text: One of the Ellice group, Niu Island, says that as the serpent began to lift the sky the people clapped their hands and shouted 'Lift up! High! Higher!' but the body of the serpent finally broke into pieces which became islands, and the blood sprinkled its drops on the sky and became stars. The New Zealand Maoris say the six sons of heaven and earth discussed separating their parents; Rongo attempted to lift the sky but could not tear it from the earth, then Tangaroa failed, then Haumia and Tu struggled in vain; but Tane, the father of giant forests, pushed and lifted until he thrust the sky far up above him, and they discovered their descendants, the multitude of human beings concealed and crushed by the clouds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 3 (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 埃利斯群島中的紐島（Niu Island）傳說，當那條巨蛇開始撐起天空時，人們拍手高喊「撐起來！高些！再高些！」但巨蛇的身軀最終碎裂成塊，化作了島嶼，而牠的鮮血灑濺到天上，化作了星辰。紐西蘭的毛利人說，天與地的六個兒子商議要把父母分開；朗戈（Rongo）試圖撐起天空，卻無法將它從大地上扯開，接著坦加羅阿（Tangaroa）也失敗了，然後豪米亞（Haumia）與圖（Tu）徒勞地掙扎；但身為巨林之父的塔內（Tane）又推又舉，終於把天空高高推到自己頭頂之上，他們這才發現了自己的後裔——那被雲層遮蔽、壓迫的眾多凡人。

title.en: Maui Smites the Long Eel Tuna-roa
title.zh: 毛伊斬長鰻圖納羅阿

region.en: River bank near Kauiki (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 考伊基附近河岸（象徵性定位）

period: Hawaiian and New Zealand oral traditions; retold 1910 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 7 (New York 1910)

summary.en: Maui's wife Hina-a-te-lepo, drawing water at the river bank, is twice struck down and befouled by the tail of Tuna-roa, the long eel. Maui digs the 'sacred digging', a tabu ditch, across which he stretches a net, chants rain down, and floods the eel out of his deep pool; with his stone axe Ma-Tori-Tori, 'the severer', he cuts off the head and pieces the body. The tail becomes the conger-eel, the fresh-water parts the common eels, the head-hairs vines and creepers, and drops of blood mark birds red and make certain trees red-wooded - and from that day Maui's children eat eels freely.
summary.zh: 毛伊之妻希娜阿泰萊波河邊汲水，兩遭長鰻圖納羅阿尾擊、遍染黏污。毛伊掘『神聖之溝』——一條僅為擒鰻而設的禁溝——架網於上，誦咒召雨，洪水沖開深潭，將巨鰻沖入網中。他以石斧『瑪托里托里——斷絕者』一擊斷其首，碎其身：尾成大海鰻，淡水之部成尋常鰻，髮絲化藤蔓，血點染鳥羽成紅斑、入樹則木材盡赤——自此毛伊子孫恣食鰻魚。

sensitivity.note: Eel-slayer etiology; eel-trap chants origin.

passages.text: Maui sought Hina-a-te-lepo, daughter of the swamp, and secured her as his wife; she cared for his thatched house as any other Polynesian woman was in the habit of doing, and attempted the hurried task of cooking his food before he snared the sun and gave her sufficient daylight for her labors.
