They lived near the bank of a river from which Hina was in the habit of bringing water for the household needs. One day she went down to the stream with her calabash, entwined with wreaths of leaves and flowers as was the custom among Polynesian women; while she was standing on the bank, Tuna-roa, the long eel, saw her. He swam up to the bank and suddenly struck her and knocked her into the water and covered her with slime from the blow given by his tail. Hina escaped and returned to her home, saying nothing to Maui about the trouble; but the next day, while getting water, she was again overthrown and befouled by the slime of Tuna-roa. Then Hina became angry and reported the trouble to Maui, who decided to punish the long eel and started out to find his hiding place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 7 (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 毛伊尋訪沼澤之女希娜阿特萊波（Hina-a-te-lepo），並娶她為妻；她像其他玻里尼西亞婦女慣常所做的那樣，照料他的茅草屋，並在他套住太陽、給她足夠日光勞作之前，匆匆忙忙地為他烹煮食物。他們住在河岸附近，希娜習慣從那條河裡取水以供家用。有一天，她帶著她那纏繞著葉環與花環的葫蘆下到溪邊，這是玻里尼西亞婦女間的習俗；當她站在岸上時，長鰻圖納羅阿（Tuna-roa）看見了她。牠游到岸邊，猛然撞擊她，把她打落水中，並用尾巴一擊，將黏液塗滿她全身。希娜逃脫後回到家中，對毛伊隻字未提這樁麻煩；但第二天，她取水時又被圖納羅阿撞倒，並被牠的黏液弄得污穢不堪。於是希娜動了怒，把這樁麻煩告訴了毛伊，毛伊決定懲罰那條長鰻，便動身去尋找牠的藏身之處。

passages.text: Some of the New Zealand legends as collected by White state that Tuna-roa was a very smooth-skinned chief who lived on the opposite bank of the stream and, seeing Hina, had insulted her; when Maui saw this chief he caught two pieces of wood over which he was accustomed to slide his canoe into the sea, carried them to the stream and laid them from bank to bank as a bridge over which he might entice Tuna-roa to cross. Maui took his stone axe Ma-Tori-Tori, the severer, and concealed himself near the bank; when the long eel had crossed the stream Maui rushed out and killed him with a mighty blow of the stone axe, cutting the head from the body. Other legends say that Maui found Tuna-roa living as an eel in a deep water hole in a swamp on the sea-coast, or in the river near Maui's home; he saw that he could not get at his enemy without letting off the water which protected him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 7 (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 懷特（White）所搜集的若干紐西蘭傳說稱，圖納羅阿是一個皮膚非常光滑的酋長，住在溪流的對岸，他看見希娜後便侮辱了她；毛伊見到這位酋長時，找來兩塊他慣常用來把獨木舟滑入海中的木頭，把它們搬到溪邊，從一岸架到另一岸，作為一座橋，好引誘圖納羅阿走過來。毛伊拿起他那名為「馬托里托里」（Ma-Tori-Tori，意為「切割者」）的石斧，埋伏在岸邊附近；當長鰻渡過溪流時，毛伊衝了出來，以石斧猛烈一擊將牠殺死，把頭從身軀上砍了下來。其他傳說則說，毛伊發現圖納羅阿化身為鰻，住在海邊沼澤裡一個深水洞中，或住在毛伊家附近的河裡；他看出若不先放掉那保護牠的水，便無法接近他的敵人。

passages.text: Therefore into the forest went Maui, and with sacred ceremonies selected trees from the wood of which he prepared tools and weapons. Meanwhile, in addition to the insult given to Hina, Tuna-roa had caught and devoured two of Maui's children, which made Maui more determined to kill him. Maui made the narrow spade and the sharp spears with which to pierce either the earth or his enemy, consecrating them to the work of preparing a ditch by which to draw off the water protecting the long eel. The work of trench-making was accomplished with many incantations and prayers; the ditch was named the sacred digging, and was tabooed to all other purposes except that of catching Tuna-roa. Across this ditch Maui stretched a strong net, and then began a new series of chants and ceremonies to bring down an abundance of rain; soon the flood came and the overflowing waters rushed down the sacred ditch, the walls of the deep pool gave way and the long eel was carried down the trench into the waiting net. Then there was commotion - Tuna-roa was struggling for freedom. Maui saw him and hastened to grasp his stone axe, the severer; hurrying to the net he struck Tuna-roa a terrible blow and cut off the head; with a few more blows he cut the body in pieces. The head and tail were carried out into the sea: the head became fish and the tail became the great conger-eel; other parts of the body became sea monsters, but some parts which fell in fresh water became the common eels; from the hairs of the head came certain vines and creepers among the plants. After the death of Tuna-roa the offspring of Maui were in no danger of being killed and soon multiplied into a large family.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 7 (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是毛伊走進森林，以神聖的儀式挑選樹木，用其木材製作工具與武器。與此同時，除了對希娜的侮辱之外，圖納羅阿還捉住並吞食了毛伊的兩個孩子，這使毛伊更加決心要殺死牠。毛伊製作了窄鏟與銳矛，用以刺穿土地或他的敵人，並將它們奉獻於開鑿溝渠、引走保護長鰻之水的工作。開渠的工作在許多咒語與祈禱中完成；這條溝渠被命名為「神聖之掘」，並被禁忌用於除捕捉圖納羅阿之外的一切其他用途。毛伊在這條溝渠上張開一張堅固的網，然後開始一連串新的吟唱與儀式，以求降下豐沛的雨水；不久洪水來了，滿溢的水流沿著神聖的溝渠奔瀉而下，深潭的壁崩塌了，長鰻被沖下溝渠，落入等候的網中。接著便是一陣騷動——圖納羅阿正掙扎著想要脫身。毛伊看見了牠，急忙抓起他那名為「切割者」的石斧；他趕到網邊，給圖納羅阿猛烈一擊，砍下了牠的頭；又補了幾斧，把牠的身軀砍成碎塊。頭與尾被帶到海中：頭變成了魚，尾變成了巨大的海鰻；身軀的其他部分變成了海怪，但有些落入淡水中的部分則變成了普通的鰻魚；從頭上的毛髮中，長出了某些藤蔓與攀緣植物。圖納羅阿死後，毛伊的子嗣便不再有被殺的危險，很快繁衍成了一個大家族。

passages.text: Another New Zealand legend related by White says that Maui built a sliding place of logs over which Tuna-roa must pass when coming from the river, and made a screen behind which he could secrete himself while watching; he commanded Hina to come down to the river and wait on the bank to attract Tuna-roa. Soon the long eel was seen in the water swimming near to Hina; she went to a place back of the logs which Maui had laid down, and Tuna-roa came towards her and began to slide down the skids. Maui sprang out from his hiding place and killed Tuna-roa with his axe and cut him in pieces; the tail became the conger-eel, parts of his body became fresh-water eels; some of the blood fell upon birds and always after marked them with red spots, some was thrown into certain trees making this wood always red, and the muscles became vines and creepers. From this time the children of Maui caught and ate the eels of both salt and fresh water; eel traps were made, and Maui taught the people the proper chants or incantations to use when catching eels.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 7 (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 懷特所述的另一則紐西蘭傳說稱，毛伊用圓木鋪成一個滑道，圖納羅阿從河裡出來時必經此處，並在後方設了一道屏風，好讓自己藏身其後窺伺；他命令希娜下到河邊，在岸上等候，以引誘圖納羅阿。不久，便見那條長鰻在水中游近希娜；她走到毛伊所鋪圓木的後方一處，圖納羅阿朝她而來，開始沿著滑木滑下。毛伊從藏身之處躍出，用斧頭殺死了圖納羅阿，並把牠砍成碎塊；尾巴變成了海鰻，身軀的部分變成了淡水鰻；有些血濺到鳥兒身上，此後總在牠們身上留下紅斑，有些血被灑到某些樹上，使這種木材永遠呈紅色，而肌肉則變成了藤蔓與攀緣植物。從此以後，毛伊的子孫便捕捉並食用鹹水與淡水中的鰻魚；人們製作了捕鰻的陷阱，毛伊也教導人們在捕鰻時應使用何種適當的吟唱或咒語。

title.en: Hina-uri's Death Song and Chief Tini-rau
title.zh: 希娜烏里葬歌與酋長蒂尼勞

region.en: Sea drift from Aotearoa to Tini-rau's isle (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 自紐西蘭漂流至蒂尼勞之島（象徵性定位）

period: New Zealand oral tradition (White); retold 1910 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 8 (New York 1910)

summary.en: A New Zealand variant of the Irawaru cycle: Maui changes the brother-in-law into a dog by incantation while cleaning his hair in sleep. Hina-uri sings her death song to the steep billows and the ocean god, casts herself into the sea, and drifts many moons until two fishermen warm her body back to life; chief Tini-rau takes her as a wife, but his jealous other wives drive her away - the opening of the Tinirau cycle cut also from Grey's Rupe chapter.
summary.zh: 紐西蘭變體：毛伊趁替連襟理髮催眠之機施咒，將其化為犬。希娜烏里唱著葬歌向滔天巨浪與海神告別，投身大海，漂流多個月相，終被漁夫救起、以火溫暖還陽。酋長蒂尼勞娶她為妻；眾妒婦不容，將其逐出——此即蒂尼勞傳說之開端（另見魯佩篇）。

sensitivity.note: Variant record linking Grey's Hinauri/Ihungarupaea record and the Maori dog-cycle.

passages.text: The Tahu and Hau tribes of New Zealand tell a different story: Maui went to visit Ira-waru; together they set out on a journey. After a time they rested by the wayside and became sleepy. Maui asked Ira-waru to cleanse his head; this gave him the restful, soothing touch which aided sleep. Then Maui proposed that Ira-waru sleep, and taking the head in his hands put his brother-in-law to sleep; then by incantations he made the sleep very deep and prolonged. Meanwhile he pulled the ears and arms and limbs until they were properly lengthened; he drew out the under jaw until it had the form of a dog's mouth; he stretched the end of the backbone into a tail, and then wakened Ira-waru and drove him back when he tried to follow the path to the settlement. Hina-uri went out and called her husband; he came to her, leaping and barking; she decided that this was her husband, and in her agony reproached Maui and wandered away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 8 (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 紐西蘭的塔胡族與豪族流傳著另一個故事：毛伊前去拜訪伊拉瓦魯；兩人一同踏上旅程。走了一段路後，他們在路旁歇息，漸漸有了睡意。毛伊請伊拉瓦魯為他梳理頭部；這帶來了令人安適、撫慰的觸感，助人入睡。接著毛伊提議讓伊拉瓦魯睡下，便雙手捧住他的頭，使他的妻舅沉沉睡去；隨後又以咒語使這睡眠變得極深極長。趁此期間，他拉扯他的耳朵、手臂與四肢，直到它們被適當地拉長；他拉出他的下顎，直到它成了狗嘴的形狀；他將脊骨的末端拉長成一條尾巴，然後喚醒伊拉瓦魯，當他試圖循路返回聚落時，便把他趕了回去。希娜烏莉走了出來，呼喚她的丈夫；他跳躍著、吠叫著來到她身邊；她斷定這就是她的丈夫，在痛苦中責備了毛伊，便獨自離去。

passages.text: When Hina-uri saw the state of her husband she went into the thatched house by which Ira-waru had so often stood watching the hollow log in which she dried the fish and preserved the birds speared in the mountains. She bound her girdle and hala-leaf apron around her and went down to the sea to drown herself, that her body might be eaten by the monsters of the sea. When she came to the shell-covered beach she sat down and sang her death song: 'I weep, I call to the steep billows of the sea and to him, the great, the ocean god; to monsters, all now hidden, to come and bury me, who now am wrapped in mourning. Let the waves wear their mourning, too, and sleep as sleeps the dead.' Then Hina-uri threw herself into the sea and was borne on the waves many moons, at last drifting to shore, to be found by two fishermen. They carried the body off to the fire and warmed it back to life; they brushed off the sea moss and sea weeds and rubbed her until she awoke.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 8 (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 希娜烏莉見到丈夫的模樣後，走進那間茅草屋——伊拉瓦魯曾多少次站在屋旁，望著她用以曬魚、保存從山中以矛獵得的鳥兒的中空木頭。她將腰帶與哈拉葉圍裙繫在身上，走下海去，想投海自盡，好讓她的身體被海中的怪物吃掉。當她來到滿是貝殼的海灘，她坐了下來，唱起她的死亡之歌：「我哭泣，我呼喚那陡峭的海浪，呼喚他，那偉大的海洋之神；呼喚所有如今潛藏著的怪物，前來埋葬我，如今我正裹於哀悼之中。讓波浪也披上牠們的哀悼，並如死者般沉睡。」於是希娜烏莉投身入海，隨著波浪漂流了許多個月，最後漂到岸邊，被兩名漁夫發現。他們將屍體抬到火邊，把她暖回生命；他們刷去海苔與海草，揉搓她，直到她醒來。

passages.text: Soon they told their chief, Tini-rau, what a beautiful woman they had found in the sea. He came and took her away to make her one of his wives. But the other wives were jealous and drove Hina-uri away from the chief's houses - the opening of the Tinirau cycle of New Zealand legend, in which Rupe's descent to find his lost sister and the death of Kae in the house of Tinirau are told at length.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 8 (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久，他們便告訴他們的酋長提尼拉烏，他們在海中發現了一個多麼美麗的女子。他前來將她帶走，使她成為他的妻子之一。但其他的妻子心生嫉妒，將希娜烏莉趕出了酋長的屋舍——這便是紐西蘭傳說中提尼拉烏故事系列的開端，其中詳細講述了魯佩下凡尋找他失散的妹妹，以及凱在提尼拉烏屋中喪命之事。

title.en: Maui's Kite and the Winds of Waipio
title.zh: 毛伊放鳶與懷皮奧之風

region.en: Wailuku river, Hilo, Hawaii Island
region.zh: 夏威夷島希洛懷盧庫河

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; retold 1910 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 9 (New York 1910)

summary.en: Only Hawaiian myth gives kite-flying to a god. Maui builds a kite larger than any house, of kapa on a line of olona fibre, and calls the imprisoned winds from the calabash of the priest Kaleiioku in Waipio - 'O winds, winds of Waipio, come quickly, come with power'. The winds climb the heavens and attack the monster kite; the strain builds until the line breaks and the kite is tossed across the island to Kau. Leaping the mountains in half a dozen strides, Maui fetches it back - 'Maui the Swift' - and ever after the kite's floating means dry weather for drying kapa.
summary.zh: 夏威夷神話獨有：諸神亦放紙鳶。毛伊製巨鳶大於屋宇，以卡帕布為體、奧洛納纖維為線，召喚被囚於懷皮奧祭司卡萊伊奧庫風葫蘆中的群風——『懷皮奧之風啊，快來，挾威而來！』群風攀天撲擊巨鳶；線繃至極而斷，鳶被拋過全島落於考烏。毛伊六步跨越高山取回——人稱『飛毛腿毛伊』——從此鳶在，則天晴，百姓攤卡帕曬布，歡呼『毛伊的鳶在天上』。

sensitivity.note: Kite-weather etiology; petrified canoe and fishhook landmarks noted.

passages.text: The Hawaiian myths are perhaps the only ones of the Pacific Ocean which give to any of the gods the pleasure and excitement of kite flying. Maui, after repeated experiments, made a large kite for himself; it was much larger than any house of his time or generation. He twisted a long line from the strong fibers of the native plant known as the olona; he endowed both kite and string with marvelous powers and launched the kite up toward the clouds. It rose very slowly; the winds were not lifting it into the sky. Maui remembered that an old priest lived in Waipio valley, the largest and finest valley of the large island, Hawaii, on which he made his home. This priest had a covered calabash in which he compelled the winds to hide when he did not wish them to play on land and sea; the priest's name was Kaleiioku, and his calabash was known as ipu-makani-a ka maumau, the calabash of the perpetual winds. Maui called for the priest who had charge of the winds to open his calabash and let them come up to Hilo and blow along the Wailuku river; the natives say that the place where Maui stood was marked by the pressure of his feet in the lava rocks of the river bank as he braced himself to hold the kite against the increasing force of the winds which pushed it towards the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 9 (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 夏威夷神話或許是太平洋諸神話中，唯一賦予任何神明放風箏之樂趣與興奮者。毛伊經過反覆試驗，為自己造了一只大風箏；它比他那個時代或那一代人的任何房屋都要大得多。他用當地一種名為奧洛納的植物之強韌纖維搓出一條長線；他賦予風箏與線二者神奇的力量，並將風箏放上雲端。它升得極慢；風並未把它托上天空。毛伊想起一位老祭司住在懷皮奧谷——那是大島夏威夷上最大、最優美的山谷，他就在那裡安家。這位祭司有一只帶蓋的葫蘆，當他不願風在陸上與海上嬉戲時，便迫使風藏身其中；祭司名叫卡萊伊奧庫，他的葫蘆被稱為「伊普-馬卡尼-阿-卡-毛毛」，意即「永恆之風的葫蘆」。毛伊呼喚那位掌管風的祭司打開他的葫蘆，讓風升上希洛，沿著懷盧庫河吹拂；當地人說，毛伊站立之處，因他雙腳使勁撐住、以抵擋愈來愈強、把風箏推向天空的風力，而在河岸的熔岩石上留下了腳印。

passages.text: Then the priest lifted the cover of the calabash of the winds and let the strong winds of Hilo escape; along the sea coast they rushed until as they entered Hilo Bay they heard the voice of Maui calling - 'O winds, winds of Hilo, hasten and come to me.' With a tumultuous rush the strong winds turned toward the mountains; they forced their way along the gorges and palisades of the Wailuku river; they leaped into the heavens, making a fierce attack upon the monster which Maui had sent into the sky. The kite struggled as it was pushed upward by the hands of the fierce winds, but Maui rejoiced; his heart was uplifted by the joy of the conflict in which his strength to hold was pitted against the power of the winds to tear away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 9 (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是祭司掀開風之葫蘆的蓋子，放出希洛的強風；它們沿著海岸疾奔，直到進入希洛灣時，聽見毛伊呼喚的聲音——「噢，風啊，希洛的風啊，快快前來我這裡。」強風轟然翻湧，轉向群山；它們沿著懷盧庫河的峽谷與峭壁奮力前行；它們躍入天際，對毛伊送上天空的那隻巨物展開猛烈的攻擊。風箏在被強風之手推升之際奮力掙扎，但毛伊歡欣鼓舞；他的心因這場搏鬥的喜悅而昂揚——他撐持的力量，正與風撕扯的力量相抗衡。

passages.text: The kite had been made of the strongest kapa which Maui's mother could prepare; it was not torn, although it was bent backward to its utmost limit. Then the strain came on the strong cord of olona fibre; the line was stretched and strained as the kite was pushed back. Then Maui called again and again for stronger winds to come; the cord was drawn out until the kite was far above the mountains; at last it broke and the kite was tossed over the craters of the volcanoes to the land of the district of Kau on the other side of the island. Then Maui was angry and hastily leaped over the mountains, which are nearly fourteen thousand feet in altitude; in a half dozen strides he had crossed the fifty or sixty miles from his home to the place where the kite lay - his name was Maui-Mama, Maui the Swift.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 9 (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這只風箏是用毛伊的母親所能製出的最強韌的卡帕布製成的；它雖被向後彎到極限，卻沒有被撕裂。接著，那條奧洛納纖維製成的堅韌繩索承受了拉力；隨著風箏被往後推，線被拉緊、繃直。於是毛伊一次又一次地呼喚更強的風前來；繩索被拉長，直到風箏遠在高山之上；最後繩索斷了，風箏被拋過火山口，落到島另一側的考區之地。毛伊大怒，急忙躍過那高近一萬四千英尺的群山；只消六七步，他便從家鄉跨越了五、六十英里，來到風箏躺臥之處——他的名字叫毛伊-馬馬，意即「迅捷的毛伊」。

passages.text: When Maui returned with his kite he was more careful in calling the winds to aid him in his sport. The people watched their wise neighbor and soon learned that the kite could be a great blessing to them: when it was soaring in the sky there was always dry and pleasant weather; it was a day for great rejoicing; they could spread out their kapa cloth to dry as long as the kite was in the sky; they could carry out their necessary work without fear of the rain. Therefore when any one saw the kite beginning to float along the mountain side he would call out joyfully, 'E! Maui's kite is in the heavens.' Maui would send his kite into the blue sky and then tie the line to the great black stones in the bed of the Wailuku river. Time passed, and even the demi-god died; the fish hook with which he drew the Hawaiian Islands up from the depths of the sea was allowed to lie on the lava by the Wailuku river until it became a part of the stone; the double canoe was carried far inland and then permitted to petrify by the river side; the two stones which represent the double canoe now bear the name Waa-Kauhi, and the kite has fallen from the sky far up on the mountain side, where it still rests, a flat plot of rich land between Mauna Kea and Mauna Loa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 9 (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 毛伊帶著風箏回來後，更加謹慎地呼喚風來助他嬉戲。人們注視著他們睿智的鄰人，很快便明白風箏能帶給他們極大的福澤：當風箏翱翔天際時，天氣總是乾爽宜人；那是個值得大大歡慶的日子；只要風箏還在天空中，他們便可攤開樹皮布晾曬；他們可以安心從事必要的工作，不必擔心下雨。因此，任何人一看見風箏開始沿著山邊飄浮，便會歡喜地喊道：『噫！毛伊的風箏上天了。』毛伊會把風箏送入蔚藍的天空，然後將線繫在懷盧庫河床中巨大的黑石上。時光流逝，甚至這位半神也死去了；他用以從海底拉起夏威夷群島的魚鉤，被任其留在懷盧庫河畔的熔岩上，直到成為石頭的一部分；雙體獨木舟被帶往內陸遠處，隨後任其在河邊石化；代表雙體獨木舟的兩塊石頭如今名為瓦阿考希，而風箏已從天上墜落，落在山邊高處，至今仍安臥於此，成為毛納基亞與毛納羅亞之間一片平坦的沃土。

title.en: Hina of Hilo Beats Her Tapa by the Falls
title.zh: 希洛希娜瀑畔槌布

region.en: Wailuku river falls, Hilo, Hawaii Island
region.zh: 夏威夷島希洛懷盧庫河瀑布

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; retold 1910 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 12 (New York 1910)

summary.en: The Hina of Hilo is the true legendary Hina of all Polynesia, her stories transplanted by settlers to Hilo. In a cave under one of the Wailuku falls she pounded tapa with chants and incantations - round clubs and four-sided mallets, bark soaked and beaten day after day into sheets soft as silk. Days too short for drying, she grieved until Maui snared the sun for her. Her southern sisters beat out the glistening clouds: thunder when she throws aside the stones that hold them, lightning leaping from sheet to sheet.
summary.zh: 希洛的希娜即全波利尼西亞共尊的希娜女神；移民攜其傳說落籍希洛。她在懷盧庫瀑布下的岩穴中槌打樹皮布——浸皮、圓槌、方槌，伴著咒歌，日復一日捶出柔若絲綢的卡帕。日光太短、布無法晾乾，她鬱鬱寡歡，直到毛伊為她擒住太陽。南太平洋的姊妹希娜則在天上槌雲成布：擲開鎮布之石便是雷，雲層間閃跳之光便是電。

sensitivity.note: Moon-goddess Hina record; links to the kapa-origin and thunder-stone myths.

passages.text: Hina is not an uncommon name in Hawaiian genealogies; it is usually accompanied by some adjective which explains or identifies the person. In Hawaii the name Hina is feminine; this is also true throughout all Polynesia. The Hina of Hilo is the same as the goddess of that name most widely known throughout Polynesia - and yet her legends are located by the ancient Hawaiians in Hilo, as if that place were her only home; the legends are so old that the Hawaiians have forgotten their origin in other lands, and the stories were brought with the immigrants who settled on the Hilo coast, finding their final location with the families who brought them. There are three Hawaiian Hinas practically distinct from each other, although a supernatural element is connected with each one: Hina who was stolen from Hawaii by a chief of Molokai was an historical character; another Hina, the wife of Kuula, the fish god, was pre-eminently a local deity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 12 (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 希娜在夏威夷族譜中並非罕見的名字；它通常伴隨著某個形容詞，用以說明或辨識該人。在夏威夷，希娜這名字屬女性；這在整個玻里尼西亞亦然。希洛的希娜與玻里尼西亞各地最廣為人知的同名女神相同——然而她的傳說被古代夏威夷人定位於希洛，彷彿該地是她唯一的家鄉；這些傳說如此古老，以致夏威夷人已遺忘其源自其他土地的根源，而這些故事是隨著定居希洛海岸的移民帶來的，最終落腳於將其帶來的家族之中。夏威夷實際上存在三位彼此截然不同的希娜，儘管每一位都與超自然元素相關：被摩洛凱島某酋長從夏威夷擄走的希娜是歷史人物；另一位希娜，即魚神庫烏拉的妻子，則首要是一位地方神祇。

passages.text: The Wailuku river, which flows through the town of Hilo, is a series of waterfalls and rapids following the course of an ancient lava flow, sometimes forcing its way under bridges of lava, thus forming boiling pots, and sometimes pouring in massive sheets over the edges of precipices. By the side of this river Hina's son Maui had his lands. In the very bed of the river, in a cave under one of the largest falls, Hina made her own home, concealed from the world by the silver veil of falling water and lulled to sleep by the continual roar of the flood falling into the deep pool below.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 12 (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 流經希洛鎮的懷盧庫河，是一連串沿著古老熔岩流道而下的瀑布與急流，時而強行穿過熔岩橋下，形成沸騰之潭，時而化作大片水幕傾瀉於懸崖邊緣。希娜之子毛伊的領地便在這條河畔。就在河床之中、最大瀑布之一下方的洞穴裡，希娜為自己安了家，被垂落水流的銀色面紗遮蔽於世外，並在洪水不斷傾瀉入下方深潭的轟鳴聲中安然入睡。

passages.text: By the side of this river she pounded her tapa and prepared her food; here were the small graceful mamake and the coarser wauke trees from which the bark was stripped. The days were very short and there was no time for rest while making tapa cloth; as soon as the morning light reddened the clouds Hina would take her calabash filled with water and her little bundle of round clubs and her four-sided mallets and hasten to the sacred spot where, with chants and incantations, the tapa was made. Beautiful tapa, soft as silk, was made by adding pulpy mass to pulpy mass and beating it day after day until the fibres were lost and a sheet of close-woven bark cloth was formed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 12 (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在這條河畔，她捶打樹皮布並準備食物；這裡長著秀美的小瑪瑪凱樹與較為粗糙的瓦烏凱樹，樹皮便是從這些樹上剝下。製作樹皮布的日子十分短促，毫無休息的時間；晨光一染紅雲彩，希娜便會帶著盛水的葫蘆、一小捆圓形敲擊棒與四面木槌，趕往那神聖之地，在那裡以吟唱與咒語製作樹皮布。將一團團漿狀纖維層層疊加，日復一日地捶打，直到纖維消融、形成一片緊密交織的樹皮布，便製成了柔滑如絲的美麗樹皮布。

passages.text: The Hina of Hilo was grieved as she toiled because after she had pounded the sheets out so thin that they were ready to be dried she found it almost impossible to secure the necessary aid of the sun in the drying process; she would rise as soon as she could see and hasten to spread her tapa - until Maui snared the sun for her. The legends of the Southern Pacific Islands show more imagination: they say that Ina (Hina) was such a wonderful artist in making beautiful tapas that she was placed in the skies, where she beats out glistening fine tapas, the white and glorious clouds. When she stretches these cloud sheets out to dry she places stones along the edges, so that the fierce winds of the heavens shall not blow them away; when she throws these stones aside, the skies reverberate with thunder; when she rolls her cloud sheets of tapa together, the folds glisten with flashes of light and lightning leaps from sheet to sheet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 12 (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 希洛的希娜在勞作時深感苦惱，因為當她將布片捶打得薄到足以晾乾時，卻發現幾乎無法獲得晾曬過程中所必需的陽光之助；她會在天剛亮時起身，趕忙攤開她的樹皮布——直到毛伊為她套住了太陽。南太平洋群島的傳說更富想像力：他們說伊娜（希娜）是製作美麗樹皮布的絕妙藝術家，因此被安置於天上，在那裡捶打出閃耀的精緻樹皮布，即潔白而壯麗的雲彩。當她攤開這些雲之布片晾曬時，會沿邊緣放置石頭，以免天上的烈風將它們吹走；當她將這些石頭拋到一旁，天空便迴盪著雷聲；當她將雲之樹皮布捲攏在一起，褶皺便閃爍著光芒，閃電從一片布躍向另一片布。

title.en: Why the Moon Is Pale: The Looking-Glass of Night Water
title.zh: 月何以蒼白：夜水的鏡子

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Daina recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: When his spouse reproaches the Moon for his pale colour, he answers that while she shines for man by day, he can only look at himself by night in the water — the palest of the sky's lords is also its only mirror-user.
summary.zh: 當其妻責月之蒼白，月答曰：日間汝光照世人，而我唯夜以水自照——天庭諸君中最蒼白者，亦是唯一以鏡自照者。

sensitivity.note: Daina.

passages.text: In comparison with the sun the moon is a very minor figure in the dainas, and his chief importance is his connexion with her. When his spouse reproaches him for his pale colour, he replies that while she shines for man by day, he can only look at himself by night in the water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 與太陽相比，月亮在達伊納民歌中是個次要得多的角色，而其首要的重要性在於他與她的關聯。當他的配偶責備他膚色蒼白時，他回答說，她白天為人類照耀，而他只能在夜間的水中顧影自憐。

passages.text: He wears a mantle of stars, and — like the sun — is liable to be destroyed, that is, eclipsed, by dragons, serpents, and witches; the pale moon is the sky's bridegroom in exile, spending his nights at the water's edge where the reflection of his own light is the only face he has.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray (1918); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他披著星辰的斗篷，並且——如同太陽一般——可能被巨龍、蛇與女巫所毀滅，也就是被蝕去；那蒼白的月亮是天上的新郎，流放於外，在水邊度過他的夜晚，在那裡，他自己光芒的倒影是他唯一擁有的面容。

title.en: Saule's Housework: The Unswept Floor of Heaven
title.zh: 太陽的家務：天上未掃的地

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Daina recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: The Sun dwells on a mountain — the vault of heaven — and standing in mid-sky she reproves her daughters because one had not swept the floor and the other had failed to wash the table.
summary.zh: 太陽居於山上——即天穹——立於天心之時，她責備女兒們：一個未掃地，一個未洗桌。

sensitivity.note: Daina.

passages.text: She dwells on a mountain — the vault of heaven — and standing in mid-sky she reproves her daughters because one had not swept the floor, while the other had failed to wash the table. In the dainas heaven is not a throne-room but a working kitchen, and the Sun is the housewife of the day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她住在山上——即天穹——立於天空中央，她責備她的女兒們，因為一個沒有掃地，另一個則沒有擦桌子。在達伊納（dainas）中，天不是一個王座廳，而是一間幹活的廚房，而太陽是白晝的主婦。

passages.text: The daughters she scolds are the twilights; the floor of heaven unswept is a sky full of cloud. The song is sung at the loom and the wash-tub in the Latvian farmhouses, where the same scolding is given every morning to the daughters of the house — for the daughters of Saule and the daughters of the farm are one family in the songs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray (1918); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她所責罵的女兒們是暮光；未掃的天之地面是滿布雲彩的天空。這首歌在拉脫維亞農舍的織布機與洗衣盆旁唱起，在那裡，同樣的責罵每天早晨都施加於家中的女兒們——因為在歌中，掃爾（Saule）的女兒與農家的女兒同屬一家人。

title.en: God's Sons at the Solstice: Mending the Broken Sun
title.zh: 夏至時分的神之子：修補破碎之日

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Dainas recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: Life is not all love: after the summer solstice God's sons must band the broken solar orb; they heat the bath of dawn, mow the meadows of morning, and uproot the birch-forest of the last traces of day — then off to Germany to play games.
summary.zh: 生活非唯有愛：夏至之後，神之子須箍束破碎之日輪；燒熱黎明之浴、割平晨光之草、連根拔去白晝餘燼的樺林——而後遠赴『德意志』遊戲去了。

sensitivity.note: Daina.

passages.text: Both God's sons and the daughters of the sun have their tasks to perform. In Germany — the darkening west — the morning star must prepare a coat of samite, the rich hues of dawn; God's sons must band the broken solar orb after the summer solstice; they must heat the bath of dawn; and, as the workmen of Sun and Moon or the servants of Perkunas, they are reproved for not mowing the meadows — that is, for not preparing the day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 神的兒子們與太陽的女兒們都有各自的任務要完成。在德國——那漸暗的西方——晨星必須準備一件錦緞外衣，即黎明豐富的色彩；神的兒子們必須在夏至之後把破碎的太陽圓球箍合起來；他們必須燒熱黎明的浴水；而作為太陽與月亮的工作者或佩爾庫納斯（Perkunas）的僕役，他們因未割草——也就是未準備好白晝——而受到責備。

passages.text: After uprooting the birch-forest — dissipating the last traces of day — they go to Germany to play games. The Baltic year is a piece of workmanship perpetually in need of repair: the sun cracks at midsummer, the morning must be mowed and bathed into being, and the sons of God are the repairmen of the light.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray (1918); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在連根拔起樺樹林——驅散白晝最後的痕跡——之後，他們前往德國玩遊戲。波羅的海的一年是一件永遠需要修補的工藝品：太陽在仲夏裂開，清晨必須被割下並沐浴而成形，而神的兒子們是光的修理工。

title.en: The Absent Star: Why Morning Star Leaves the Sky
title.zh: 缺席之星：晨星離天之故

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Dainas recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: When all the other stars are visible, the morning star is absent: he has gone to woo the daughter of the sun, she hastens toward him, and they are wedded in Germany — beyond the sea, in the darkening west.
summary.zh: 眾星皆現之時，唯晨星缺席：他已去求婚日之女；她趨向他，二人成婚於『德意志』——海之外的暗沉西方。

sensitivity.note: Daina.

passages.text: When all the other stars are visible, the morning star is absent: he has gone to woo the daughter of the sun. She hastens toward him, and they are wedded in Germany — beyond the sea, in the darkening west.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當所有其他星辰都可見時，晨星卻不在：他已前去向太陽的女兒求愛。她急忙向他趕去，他們在德國——海的彼岸，那漸暗的西方——成婚。

passages.text: The song explains the plain fact of the sky — the morning star sets as the other stars appear — as a wedding journey: the brightest of the stars leaves the choir to meet the brightest of the daughters, and the Baltic poets, who read the sky as a farm, know exactly what such an absence means.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray (1918); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這首歌把天空的樸素事實——晨星在群星出現時落下——解釋為一趟婚禮旅程：群星中最明亮的一顆離開星群，去迎接眾女兒中最明亮的一位；而把天空讀作一座農場的波羅的海詩人，確切知道這樣的缺席意味著什麼。

title.en: Lovers' Quarrels: The Broken Sword and the Fished Ring
title.zh: 戀人之爭：斷劍與釣戒

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Dainas recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: Of course lovers quarrel: the daughter of the sun breaks the sword of God's son — dawn outshines the morning star — and in their turn God's sons deprive her of her ring, the solar disk, at evening, till they fish it up again at dawn.
summary.zh: 戀人自然有爭執：日之女折斷神之子的劍——曙光之輝壓過晨星——神之子們亦於日暮奪其環（即日輪），至黎明又自水中釣回。

sensitivity.note: Daina.

passages.text: Of course lovers occasionally quarrel: the daughter of the sun breaks the sword of God's son — for dawn surpasses the brightness of the morning star; and, in their turn, God's sons deprive her of her ring — the solar disk — at evening, though they presently fish it from the sea at dawn when it falls from her finger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 戀人當然偶爾會爭吵：太陽的女兒折斷神之子的劍——因為黎明勝過晨星的光輝；而輪到神之子們時，他們在傍晚奪走她的戒指——日輪——不過他們隨即會在黎明時分從海中把它撈起，那時它正從她的指間落下。

passages.text: But lovers' quarrels are love's renewal: since evening star and evening twilight, morning star and morning dawn, are inseparably associated, the quarrel ends where the day ends and begins again where the day begins. The whole mythology of the Latvian dawn is a courtship that renews itself by rule, twice a day, forever.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray (1918); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但戀人的爭吵是愛的更新：既然晚星與暮色、晨星與晨光密不可分地相連，爭吵便在白晝終結之處結束，並在白晝開始之處重新開始。拉脫維亞黎明的整套神話，是一場按規律自我更新的求愛，一日兩次，永無止境。

title.en: The Golden Cock on the Daugava: Waking the Sun's Spinner
title.zh: 道加瓦河畔金雞：喚醒太陽的紡者

region.en: River Daugava, Latvia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞道加瓦河（象徵性定位）

period: Dainas recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: On the edge of the Great Water the golden cock crows to rouse the sun's daughter, that she may spin the silver thread — the rays of the rising sun — for the day's weaving.
summary.zh: 偉大之水畔，金雞啼鳴以喚日之女，使其紡出銀線——即朝陽之芒——以織這一日。

sensitivity.note: Daina.

passages.text: As for the sun's daughter, the golden cock crows on the edge of the Great Water — the Daugawa — to rouse her that she may spin the silver thread, that is, the rays of the rising sun. Her chief task is to wash her golden jug — the solar disk — at evening; her morning task is the spinning of the silver thread on the golden wheel. Between cockcrow and sundown the daughter of the sun keeps the sky's household running: the cock, the spinner, and the washer are the three servants of the light, and the dainas give each his hour.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Gray (1918); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 至於太陽的女兒，金雞在大水——道加瓦河——的邊緣啼叫，喚醒她，好讓她紡出銀線，也就是初升太陽的光芒。她的主要任務是在傍晚洗滌她的金壺——日輪；她清晨的任務是在金輪上紡出銀線。從雞啼到日落，太陽的女兒維持著天空的家務運轉：公雞、紡者與洗滌者，是光的三個僕人，而達伊納斯歌謠為每一個都規定了時辰。

title.en: Little John Breaks the Golden Jug
title.zh: 小約翰打破金壺

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Dainas recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: When, in other dainas, the solar jug is broken by 'little John', it is the waning strength of the sun's rays after Midsummer Eve — St. John's night — that the song is telling: the feast that breaks the sun's vessel also begins the year's turning.
summary.zh: 其他達伊納中，日之金壺為『小約翰』所碎——此乃詠仲夏夜（聖約翰之夜）後日光之衰；打破太陽之壺的節日，亦正是歲序轉折之始。

sensitivity.note: Daina; Midsummer (Rasos/Jani) fire festival context.

passages.text: When, in other dainas, the solar jug is broken by 'little John', the song is telling the waning strength of the sun's rays after Midsummer Night's Eve — St. John's Eve, June 23. The longest day breaks the vessel of the light; from the morning after the feast the year declines.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當在其他達伊納斯歌謠中，日壺被「小約翰」打破時，這首歌所講述的是仲夏夜前夕——聖約翰節前夕，六月二十三日——之後太陽光芒的漸衰之力。最長的白晝打破了光的容器；從節慶之後的清晨起，一年便開始衰退。

passages.text: The Midsummer festival of the Baltic — with its fires, its oak-wreaths, and its fern-seed hunts — stands exactly on the hinge: the night when the golden jug breaks is the night when the greatest bonfires are lit to help the sun. John the Baptist keeps the festival in the Christian calendar, and 'little John' the breaker of jugs keeps it in the dainas — one saint, one season, two names for the same turning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray (1918); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 波羅的海的仲夏節慶——伴隨著它的篝火、橡樹花環與尋覓蕨籽——恰好立於這轉軸之上：金壺破碎的那一夜，正是點燃最盛大篝火以助太陽的那一夜。施洗約翰在基督教曆法中守護這個節慶，而打破壺的「小約翰」則在達伊納斯歌謠中守護它——同一位聖者，同一個季節，同一個轉折的兩個名字。

title.en: The Sun Who Watches the Wheat: 'Many Are My Gifts in Sooth'
title.zh: 守望麥田的太陽：『吾賜甚豐』

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Daina recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: Asked where she delays so long, the Sun — daughter of God — answers that beyond the sea she watches the wheat and shepherds: 'Many are my gifts in sooth'; Morning Star makes her fire and Evening Star prepares her couch, and 'many are my kin in sooth.'
summary.zh: 問其為何久留，太陽——神之女——答：海之外她守望麥田與牧人：『吾賜甚豐』；晨星為其生火，晚星為其鋪榻——『吾親甚眾』。

sensitivity.note: Daina.

passages.text: 'O thou Sun, daughter of God, where delayest thou so long, since thou hast from us withdrawn?' — 'O'er the sea, beyond the hills, wheat there is that I must watch, shepherds, too, that I must guard; many are my gifts in sooth.' 'Tending thee at morn and eve, who doth make for thee thy fire, who prepares thy couch for thee?' — 'Morning Star and Evening Star: Morning Star doth make my fire, Evening Star prepares my couch; many are my kin in sooth.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the daina as rendered by Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「哦，太陽啊，神的女兒，你為何遲遲不歸，既然你已從我們這裡離去？」——「在海上，在山的那一邊，有麥子我必須看守，也有牧人我必須守護；說真的，我的恩賜眾多。」「早晚侍奉你，誰為你生火，誰為你鋪床？」——「晨星與暮星：晨星為我生火，暮星為我鋪床；說真的，我的親族眾多。」

passages.text: The little song sets out the whole Baltic theology of the harvest in eight lines: the sun is God's own daughter, sent to watch the wheat and the shepherds beyond the sea — the under-world of the west where the year's riches ripen — and her gifts are counted as the household's wealth. The Baltic farmer's year begins and ends with the Sun's own account-keeping: she watches what she gives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray (1918); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這首短歌以八行道出了波羅的海關於收穫的整套神學：太陽是神自己的女兒，被派往海的那一邊看守麥子與牧人——那是西方的下界，一年之豐饒在此成熟——而她的恩賜被算作家庭的財富。波羅的海農民的一年，以太陽自己的記帳開始，也以之結束：她看守著她所賜予的一切。

title.en: Manco Capac, a Stone and a Half Tall: The Idol Found in 1559
title.zh: 半身高的石像:1559年尋獲的曼科遺石

region.en: Ynti-cancha and Bimbilla, near Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科因蒂-坎恰與賓比利亞村(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 14, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Feeling the approach of death, and fearing that his son might not retain the sovereignty because of the tyranny he had established, Manco Ccapac ordered the ten lineages that had come with him from Tampu-tocco to form a garrison to watch over his son and descendants, and to elect the successor nominated by the father. He left the bird indi in its cage, the tupac-yauri or sceptre, the napa and the suntur-paucar to his son Sinchi Rocca. Thus died Manco Ccapac, at the age of 144 years according to his lineage's accounts. They say that he was a man of good stature, thin, rustic, cruel though frank, and that in dying he was converted into a stone of a height of a vara and a half. The stone was preserved with much veneration in the Ynti-cancha until the year 1559, when the licentiate Polo Ondegardo being Corregidor of Cuzco found it and took it away from where it was adored and venerated by all the Incas, in the village of Bimbilla near Cuzco. From his time began the idols huauquis - an idol or demon chosen by each Inca for his companion and oracle which gave him answers; that of Manco Ccapac was the bird indi. He instituted the first ayllu, called Chima Panaca Ayllu; the members of this ayllu always adored the statue of Manco Ccapac. They carried it in their wars, thinking that it secured the victories they won; they also took it to Huanacauri for the huarachicos; Huayna Ccapac took it with him to Quito and Cayambis, and afterwards it was brought back to Cuzco with the dead body of that Inca.
summary.zh: 曼科·卡帕克自知死期將至,又恐因自己所行暴政,兒孫難以保住江山,便命自坦波-托科同來的十個世系結成衛隊,永遠護衛其子子孫孫,並在父王指定的繼承人死後負責推舉。他把籠中的「因蒂」鳥、圖帕克-亞烏里權杖、納帕聖羊與孫圖爾-保卡爾,一併傳給兒子辛奇·羅卡。曼科·卡帕克遂卒——按其世系所記,享年144歲。相傳他身量頎長,清瘦粗獷,兇殘而直率;死時化為一根半「瓦拉」高的石頭。此石供奉於因蒂-坎恰,備受印加王族崇敬;至1559年,庫斯科行政長官波羅·翁德加爾多在庫斯科附近的賓比利亞村將它尋出移走。自曼科之世起,歷代印加王各有「瓜烏基」神偶——選定的伴身偶像與神諭,能作答問;曼科的瓜烏基便是那隻「因蒂」鳥。他又立第一個阿伊柳,稱「奇馬·帕納卡」;此世系成員只拜曼科一人的石像。戰時他們抬著石像出征,相信它保佑勝利;行瓦拉奇庫禮時抬往瓦納考里;瓦伊納·卡帕克出征基多與卡揚比也帶著它,後來又隨王的遺體一同運回庫斯科。

sensitivity.note: The petrified founder as ancestral oracle; Polo's 1559 discovery is the archival moment when the mummy cult met the colonial state.

passages.text: They say that he was a man of good stature, thin, rustic, cruel though frank, and that in dying he was converted into a stone of a height of a vara and a half. The stone was preserved with much veneration in the Ynti-cancha until the year 1559 when, the licentiate Polo Ondegardo being Corregidor of Cuzco, found it and took it away from where it was adored and venerated by all the Incas, in the village of Bimbilla near Cuzco.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 14 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們說他身材高大，瘦削，質樸，殘酷卻坦率，又說他死時化作一塊一瓦拉半高的石頭。這塊石頭在印提坎查備受崇敬地保存著，直到一五五九年，執業律師波洛·翁德加多任庫斯科督撫時發現了它，並把它從眾人崇拜敬奉之處取走，那地方是庫斯科附近的賓比亞村。

passages.text: From this Manco Ccapac were originated the ten ayllus mentioned above. From his time began the idols huauquis, which was an idol or demon chosen by each Inca for his companion and oracle which gave him answers. That of Manco Ccapac was the bird indi already mentioned. The members of this ayllu always adored the statue of Manco Ccapac, and not those of the other Incas. They carried it in their wars, thinking that it secured the victories they won. They also took it to Huanacauri, when they celebrated the huarachicos of the Incas. Huayna Ccapac took it with him to Quito and Cayambis, and afterwards it was brought back to Cuzco with the dead body of that Inca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 14 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 前述的十個艾柳皆源自這位曼科·卡帕克。從他的時代起，便有了名為瓦烏基的偶像，那是每位印加為自己選作伴侶與神諭的偶像或惡魔，會給他答覆。曼科·卡帕克的瓦烏基便是前述的鳥印地。這個艾柳的成員始終崇拜曼科·卡帕克的雕像，而非其他印加的雕像。他們在戰爭中攜帶它，認為它確保了他們所贏得的勝利。當他們舉行印加的瓦拉奇科斯儀式時，也把它帶到瓦納考里。瓦伊納·卡帕克把它帶到基多與卡揚比斯，後來又隨那位印加的遺體被帶回庫斯科。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Do Not Be Sorrowful: The Sun Appears to the Childless Inca
title.zh: 勿憂傷:太陽顯現於無嗣的老王

region.en: Ynti-cancha, House of the Sun, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科太陽之屋因蒂-坎恰(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 16, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: One day Lloqui Yupanqui being very sad and afflicted, the Sun appeared to him in the form of a person and consoled him by saying: 'Do not be sorrowful, Lloqui Yupanqui, for from you shall descend great Lords'; also that he might hold it for certain that he would have male issue. For Lloqui Yupanqui was then very old, and neither had a son nor expected to have one. This having been made known, and what the Sun had announced to Lloqui Yupanqui having been published to the people, his relations determined to seek a wife for him. His brother Manco Sapaca, understanding the fraternal disposition, sought for a woman who was suitable for it. He found her in a town called Oma, two leagues from Cuzco, asked for her from her guardians, and, with their consent, brought her to Cuzco. She was then married to Lloqui Yupanqui. Her name was Mama Cava, and by her the Inca had a son named Mayta Ccapac.
summary.zh: 一日,利亞基·尤潘琪愁苦不已。太陽竟以人形顯現,安慰他道:「勿憂傷,利亞基·尤潘琪!你將有偉大的子孫。你必得男子之嗣,此為定數。」其時利亞基·尤潘琪已屆高齡,本以為無子可望。太陽之言傳布民間之後,親族們便決意為他尋一位妻子。其兄曼科·薩帕卡體察兄弟之意,在庫斯科兩萊格外一個名為奧馬的小鎮尋得合適女子,向其監護人求親,得其同意,攜歸庫斯科,嫁與利亞基·尤潘琪。她名喚瑪瑪·卡瓦;印加王由此得子,名「馬雅塔·卡帕克」。

sensitivity.note: Solar annunciation to a dynasty in crisis; the Sun as personal speaker within the royal cult.

passages.text: One day Lloqui Yupanqui being very sad and afflicted, the Sun appeared to him in the form of a person and consoled him by saying: 'Do not be sorrowful, Lloqui Yupanqui, for from you shall descend great Lords', also, that he might hold it for certain that he would have male issue. For Lloqui Yupanqui was then very old, and neither had a son nor expected to have one.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 16 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，略基·尤潘基十分悲傷痛苦，太陽以人的形貌向他顯現，安慰他說：「不要悲傷，略基·尤潘基，因為偉大的領主將出自你的後裔」，又說，好讓他確信自己將有男性子嗣。因為略基·尤潘基當時已十分年老，既沒有兒子，也不指望會有。

passages.text: This having been made known, and what the Sun had announced to Lloqui Yupanqui having been published to the people, his relations determined to seek a wife for him. His brother Manco Sapaca, understanding the fraternal disposition, sought for a woman who was suitable for it. He found her in a town called Oma, two leagues from Cuzco, asked for her from her guardians, and, with their consent, brought her to Cuzco. She was then married to Lloqui Yupanqui. Her name was Mama Cava, and by her the Inca had a son named Mayta Ccapac.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 16 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此事傳開之後，太陽向略基·尤潘基所宣告的話既已向民眾公布，他的親屬便決定為他尋妻。他的兄弟曼科·薩帕卡明白這份兄弟情意，便去尋找適合此事的女子。他在距庫斯科兩里格、名為奧馬的鎮上找到了她，向她的監護人求娶，並經他們同意，把她帶到庫斯科。她隨後便嫁給了略基·尤潘基。她的名字叫瑪瑪·卡瓦，印加與她生了一個兒子，名叫邁塔·卡帕克。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Born with Teeth After Three Months: Mayta Capac the Child-Hercules
title.zh: 三月而生、出生有齒:大力士馬雅塔·卡帕克

region.en: Cuzco valley (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科谷地(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 17, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Mayta Ccapac, the fourth Inca, is to those Indians what Hercules is to us, as regards his birth and acts, for they relate strange things of him. His father, when he was begotten, was so old and weak that every one believed he was useless, so that they thought the conception was a miracle. His mother bore him three months after conception, and he was born strong and with teeth; he grew at such a rate that in one year he had as much strength and was as big as a boy of eight years or more. At two years he fought with very big boys, knocked them about and hurt them seriously. The natives hold this to be so true that they would kill anyone who asserted the contrary. When he was of very tender years he was playing with boys of the Alcabisas and Culunchimas: he hurt many of them and killed some; one day, drinking or taking water from a fountain, he broke the leg of the son of a Sinchi of the Alcabisas. The Alcabisas, unable to endure longer the naughtiness of Mayta Ccapac, determined to regain their liberty and to venture their lives for it: they selected ten resolute Indians to go to the House of the Sun and enter it with the intention of killing Lloqui Yupanqui and his son. Mayta Ccapac was in the courtyard playing at ball; when he saw enemies entering with arms he threw one of the balls and killed one, did the same to another, and attacked the rest, so that they all fled wounded. The inhabitants of the valley united to make war on the Incas; there was a battle and the Alcabisas and Calunchimas were finally defeated. Again they challenged Mayta Ccapac: as they advanced such a hail storm fell over the Alcabisas that they were defeated a third time and entirely broken up; Mayta Ccapac imprisoned their Sinchi for the remainder of his life.
summary.zh: 第四位印加王馬雅塔·卡帕克,就其出生與行事而言,於印第安人猶如赫拉克勒斯之於我們——關於他的奇事甚多。相傳他父親年邁力衰,眾人皆以為已無生育之能,故此番受孕堪稱神蹟;其二,其母受孕三月便誕下他,他出生便強健有齒;其三,他生長神速,一歲之時,體格氣力已如八歲以上的孩童;兩歲便與大孩子角力,把他們摔打致傷。土人對此深信不疑,誰敢否認便要殺誰。他幼時與阿爾卡比薩、庫倫奇馬的男孩玩耍,傷人無數,甚至殺了幾個;一日從泉邊取水,竟折斷了阿爾卡比薩辛奇之子的腿。阿爾卡比薩人不堪其擾,決意以死爭回自由:選出十名悍勇之士,持械闖入太陽之屋,欲殺利亞基·尤潘琪父子。馬雅塔·卡帕克正在院中玩球;見敵持械入內,擲球殺一人,又殺一人,再驅其餘——來犯者帶傷而逃。谷中居民聯合討伐印加人,大戰一場,阿爾卡比薩與庫倫奇馬終被擊潰。他們再挑戰端:進軍之際,天降冰雹,專擊阿爾卡比薩軍,致其第三次慘敗潰散;馬雅塔·卡帕克將其辛奇終身監禁。

sensitivity.note: The three-month gestation hero-birth; Sarmiento explicitly compares him to Hercules.

passages.text: Mayta Ccapac, the fourth Inca, son of Lloqui Yupanqui and his wife Mama Cava, is to those Indians what Hercules is to us, as regards his birth and acts, for they relate strange things of him. At the very first the Indians of his lineage, and all the others in general, say that his father, when he was begotten, was so old and weak that every one believed he was useless, so that they thought the conception was a miracle. The second wonder was that his mother bore him three months after conception, and that he was born strong and with teeth. All affirm this, and that he grew at such a rate that in one year he had as much strength and was as big as a boy of eight years or more. At two years he fought with very big boys, knocked them about and hurt them seriously... they hold this to be so true that they would kill anyone who asserted the contrary.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 17 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 邁塔·卡帕克（Mayta Ccapac）是第四位印加王，為略基·尤潘基（Lloqui Yupanqui）與其妻瑪瑪·卡瓦（Mama Cava）之子；就出生與事蹟而言，他在那些印第安人心中，猶如赫拉克勒斯之於我們，因為他們為他講述了種種奇異之事。首先，他那一族的印第安人，以及所有其他印第安人普遍都說，他父親在孕育他時已年老體衰，人人都以為他已無用，因此他們認為這次受孕乃是奇蹟。第二件奇事是，他母親在受孕三個月後便生下了他，而且他出生時便強壯有力，且已長了牙齒。所有人都如此斷言，並說他成長極快，一年之內便已擁有相當的力氣，體格如同八歲或更大的男孩。兩歲時，他便與非常大的男孩搏鬥，將他們打倒在地，使他們受了重傷……他們認為此事千真萬確，誰若斷言相反，他們便會殺了他。

passages.text: They say of this Mayta that when he was of very tender years, he was playing with some boys of the Alcabisas and Culunchimas, natives of Cuzco, when he hurt many of them and killed some. And one day, drinking or taking water from a fountain, he broke the leg of the son of a Sinchi of the Alcabisas, and hunted the rest until they shut themselves up in their houses.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 17 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們說，這邁塔在年紀極幼時，曾與庫斯科原住民阿爾卡比薩人（Alcabisas）與庫倫奇馬人（Culunchimas）的一些男孩一同玩耍，當時他傷了他們許多人，還殺了幾人。有一天，他在泉邊飲水或取水時，打斷了阿爾卡比薩人一位辛奇（Sinchi）之子的腿，並追逐其餘的人，直到他們躲進自己家中。

passages.text: The Alcabisas, unable to endure longer the naughtiness of Mayta Ccapac, determined to regain their liberty and to venture their lives for it. So they selected ten resolute Indians to go to the House of the Sun where Lloqui Yupanqui and his son Mayta Ccapac lived, and enter it with the intention of killing them. At the time Mayta Ccapac was in the court yard of the house, playing at ball with some other boys. When he saw enemies entering the house with arms, he threw one of the balls he was playing with, and killed one. He did the same to another, and, attacking the rest, they all fled... There was a battle between the two armies and although it was doubtful for some time, the Alcabisas and Calunchimas were finally defeated by the troops of Mayta Ccapac. Again they challenged Mayta Ccapac to battle, which he accepted. As they advanced they say that such a hail storm fell over the Alcabisas that they were defeated a third time, and entirely broken up. Mayta Ccapac imprisoned their Sinchi for the remainder of his life.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 17 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿爾卡比薩人再也無法忍受邁塔·卡帕克的頑劣，決心重獲自由，並為此冒生命之險。於是他們挑選了十名果決的印第安人，前往略基·尤潘基與其子邁塔·卡帕克所居的太陽之屋，意圖進入其中將他們殺死。當時邁塔·卡帕克正在該屋的庭院裡與其他一些男孩玩球。當他看見敵人持械進入屋內，便將手中所玩的一顆球擲出，殺死一人。他又對另一人如法炮製，並攻擊其餘的人，他們便全都逃走了……兩軍交戰，雖然一時勝負未定，阿爾卡比薩人與卡倫奇馬人（Calunchimas）最終仍被邁塔·卡帕克的軍隊擊敗。他們再次向邁塔·卡帕克挑戰，他接受了。當他們前進時，他們說一場猛烈的冰雹落在阿爾卡比薩人頭上，使他們第三次被擊敗，並徹底潰散。邁塔·卡帕克將他們的辛奇囚禁終生。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: He Dared to Open the Hamper: The Oracle of the Bird Indi
title.zh: 敢啟箱籠者:因蒂神鳥的神諭

region.en: Ynti-cancha, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科因蒂-坎恰(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 17, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: They relate of Mayta Ccapac that he dared to open the hamper containing the bird indi. This bird, brought by Manco Ccapac from Tampu-tocco, had been inherited by his successors, the predecessors of Mayta Ccapac, who had always kept it shut up in a hamper or box of straw, such was the fear they had of it. But Mayta Ccapac was bolder than any of them. Desirous of seeing what his predecessors had guarded so carefully, he opened the hamper, saw the bird indi and had some conversation with it. They say that it gave him oracles, and that after the interview with the bird he was wiser, and knew better what he should do, and what would happen.
summary.zh: 相傳馬雅塔·卡帕克竟敢打開藏「因蒂」鳥的箱籠。此鳥乃曼科·卡帕克自坦波-托科攜來,歷代先王奉為傳家之寶;歷代諸王懼之甚深,始終將它鎖在草編箱籠之內。唯有馬雅塔·卡帕克膽氣過人:他急欲一睹先王守護如此之秘,遂啟箱籠,得見因蒂鳥,並與之交談。相傳神鳥向他降下神諭;自那番晤談之後,他變得更為明智,深知當行之事、將來之事。

sensitivity.note: The oracular bird as royal familiar; the taboo-breaking opening of the dynastic relic.

passages.text: They relate of him that he dared to open the hamper containing the bird indi. This bird, brought by Manco Ccapac from Tampu-tocco, had been inherited by his successors, the predecessors of Mayta Ccapac, who had always kept it shut up in a hamper or box of straw, such was the fear they had of it. But Mayta Ccapac was bolder than any of them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 17 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們講述他的事蹟說，他竟敢打開裝有印地鳥（indi）的籃子。這隻鳥由曼科·卡帕克（Manco Ccapac）從坦普-托科（Tampu-tocco）帶來，傳給了他的歷代繼承者，即邁塔·卡帕克的前任們，他們因對牠心懷畏懼，始終將牠關在草編的籃子或箱子裡。但邁塔·卡帕克比他們任何人都更為大膽。

passages.text: Desirous of seeing what his predecessors had guarded so carefully, he opened the hamper, saw the bird indi and had some conversation with it. They say that it gave him oracles, and that after the interview with the bird he was wiser, and knew better what he should do, and what would happen.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 17 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他渴望看看前任們如此小心守護的東西，便打開籃子，見到了印地鳥，並與牠交談了一番。他們說，牠向他賜下神諭，而與鳥會面之後，他變得更加睿智，更清楚自己該做什麼，以及將會發生什麼。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Inca Rocca Divides the Waters: The Birth of the Hanan-cuzcos
title.zh: 印加·羅卡分水:哈南庫斯科世系之立

region.en: Cuzco, upper and lower waters (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科上水與下水(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 19, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: When Ccapac Yupanqui died, Inca Rocca, his son by his wife Ccuri-hilpay, succeeded. This Inca Rocca showed force and valour at the beginning of his Incaship, for he conquered the territories of Muyna and Pinahua with great violence and cruelty, rather more than four leagues to the south-south-east of Cuzco. He killed their Sinchis Muyna Pancu and Huaman-tupac, though some say that Huaman-tupac fled and was never more seen. He did this by the help of Apu Mayta his nephew. He also conquered Caytomarca. He discovered the waters of Hurin-chacan and those of Hanan-chacan - the upper and lower waters of Cuzco - and led them in conduits, so that to this day they irrigate fields. While his ancestors had always lived in the lower part of Cuzco, and were therefore called Hurin-cuzcos, he ordered that those who sprang from him should form another party, and be called Hanan-cuzcos, the Cuzcos of the upper part. So from this Inca began the party of upper or Hanan-cuzcos, for he and his successors left their residence at the House of the Sun and established themselves in the upper part of the town, building palaces. Each Inca had a special palace in which he lived, the son not wishing to reside in the palace where his father had lived; it was left with servants, relations, ayllus or heirs that they might maintain it, and keep the edifices in repair.
summary.zh: 卡帕克·尤潘琪駕崩,其子印加·羅卡繼位。羅卡初登大位便顯示武力:以暴烈手段征服庫斯科東南偏南四萊格外的穆伊納與皮納瓦之地,誅其辛奇穆伊納·潘庫與瓜曼-圖帕克(一說瓜曼-圖帕克出逃,自此無蹤),其侄阿普·馬雅塔效力其間。他還征服了卡伊托馬爾卡。他又勘明庫斯科的「下水」與「上水」(烏林-查坎與哈南-查坎),鑿渠引水灌溉——至今其子孫猶受其利。其先祖世居庫斯科下城,故稱「烏林庫斯科」;他則下令:出自自己的子孫另立一支,稱「哈南庫斯科」——上庫斯科。自此,印加王族遷出太陽之屋,在城之上部營建宮室而居。每位印加王皆有專屬宮殿,子不居父宮;父王駕崩,宮殿原樣留存,由僕從、親族與阿伊柳子孫奉養修葺。

sensitivity.note: The Hanan/Hurin institutional split located in this reign; Sarmiento's version against those who date it to Pachacuti.

passages.text: This Inca Rocca showed force and valour at the beginning of his Incaship, for he conquered the territories of Muyna and Pinahua with great violence and cruelty. They are rather more than four leagues to the south-south-east of Cuzco. He killed their Sinchis Muyna Pancu, and Huaman-tupac, though some say that Huaman-tupac fled and was never more seen. He did this by the help of Apu Mayta his nephew... He also conquered Caytomarca. He discovered the waters of Hurin-chacan and those of Hanan-chacan, which is as much as to say the upper and lower waters of Cuzco, and led them in conduits; so that to this day they irrigate fields.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 19 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這位印加·羅卡（Inca Rocca）在其印加王位之初便展現了力量與勇武，因為他以極大的暴烈與殘酷征服了穆伊納（Muyna）與皮納瓦（Pinahua）的領地。這些地方位於庫斯科南南東方，距離略多於四里格。他殺死了他們的辛奇穆伊納·潘庫（Muyna Pancu）與瓦曼-圖帕克（Huaman-tupac），不過有人說瓦曼-圖帕克逃走了，此後再未被人見到。他是在其姪子阿普·邁塔（Apu Mayta）的幫助下做到這一切的……他還征服了凱托馬爾卡（Caytomarca）。他發現了烏林-查坎（Hurin-chacan）與哈南-查坎（Hanan-chacan）的水源，這兩個名稱意即庫斯科的上水與下水，並以渠道引導水流；因此時至今日，這些水仍灌溉著田地。

passages.text: While his ancestors had always lived in the lower part of Cuzco, and were therefore called Hurin-cuzcos, he ordered that those who sprang from him should form another party, and be called Hanan-cuzcos, which means the Cuzcos of the upper part. So that from this Inca began the party of upper or Hanan-cuzcos, for presently he and his successors left their residence at the House of the Sun, and established themselves away from it, building palaces where they lived, in the upper part of the town. It is to be noted that each Inca had a special palace in which he lived, the son not wishing to reside in the palace where his father had lived. It was left in the same state as it was in when the father died, with servants, relations, ayllus or heirs that they might maintain it, and keep the edifices in repair.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 19 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的祖先一向居住在庫斯科的下城區，因此被稱為「烏林-庫斯科」（Hurin-cuzcos）；他卻下令，凡出自他這一脈者，應另立一派，稱為「哈南-庫斯科」（Hanan-cuzcos），意即上城區的庫斯科人。於是，上城區或哈南-庫斯科這一派便自此印加開始；因為不久之後，他與其繼承者便離開太陽之屋的居所，遷居他處，在上城區建造宮殿居住。值得注意的是，每位印加都有專屬的宮殿供其居住，兒子不願住在父親曾居住的宮殿裡。那座宮殿便維持父親去世時的原狀，並留有僕役、親屬、艾尤（ayllu，即繼承者）以維持其運作，並修繕建築。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Eclipses of the Lights: Dragons, Serpents, and Witches
title.zh: 日月的蝕：龍、蛇與女巫

region.en: Baltic skies (symbolic pin at Riga)
region.zh: 波羅的海天空（象徵性定位於里加）

period: Belief recorded 19th c.; recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: Like the sun, the moon is liable to be destroyed — eclipsed — by dragons, serpents, and witches; the Baltic lights can be swallowed by the same powers that eat them in the rest of the Indo-European world, and the noise of the village rises to frighten the eater away.
summary.zh: 如日一般，月亦可能被龍、蛇與女巫所毀——即遭蝕；波羅的海的光明會被與整個印歐世界相同的吞噬者所食，村中喧聲齊起以嚇退吞者。

sensitivity.note: Eclipse-demon cluster; cross-tagged with Slavic vlkodlak and Norse wolf.

passages.text: The moon, in the dainas, wears a mantle of stars and — like the sun — is liable to be destroyed, that is, eclipsed, by dragons, serpents, and witches. Whatever darkens the lights above the Baltic village is read as an eater: the worm in the sky, the witch riding the wind, the serpent that has wound itself around the moon's silver wheel.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在達伊納（dainas）歌謠中，月亮披著星辰的斗篷，而且——如同太陽一樣——可能被龍、蛇與女巫毀滅，也就是被蝕。凡是使波羅的海村落上方之光變暗者，都被解讀為吞噬者：天空中的蟲、乘風而行的女巫、纏繞在月亮銀輪上的蛇。

passages.text: The remedy is as old as the belief: noise. Drums, bells, shouts, and shot-drive the eater away, as among the Slavs the vlkodlak who devours the sun is frightened off by the same uproar. The Baltic sky is a battlefield as well as a farm, and every eclipse is an alarm to be answered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray (1918); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 補救之法與此信仰同樣古老：噪音。鼓聲、鐘聲、呼喊與射擊——驅走吞噬者，正如斯拉夫人中吞噬太陽的沃爾科達拉克（vlkodlak）也被同樣的喧鬧嚇退。波羅的海的天空既是農田，也是戰場，每一次蝕都是一聲必須回應的警報。

title.en: Romowe and the Kriwe: The Baltic Pope and the Eternal Fire
title.zh: 羅莫沃與克里維：波羅的海教宗與長明火

region.en: Romowe shrine, Prussia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 普魯士羅莫沃聖所（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded by Simon Grunau (c. 1526) and later chroniclers; summarized in Machal 1918

source.work: The Romowe shrine as summarized in Mythology of All Races III (1918), plate and note, after Simon Grunau, Preussische Chronik

summary.en: At Romowe the eternal fire of oak-wood burned before the gods in the great evergreen oak, tended by the Kriwe — the 'Baltic pope', whose decrees ran as far as the flame's fame — with the Waidelots, the ordinary priests, in their houses round about, and a pot with a sacred serpent fed by the priests.
summary.zh: 羅莫沃聖所中，橡木長明火於常青巨橡之前燃燒，由克里維——『波羅的海教宗』，其令行於火之名所及之地——看管；普通祭司韋德洛特環列四周，並有祭司飼養的聖蛇一壺。

sensitivity.note: Grunau's accounts are treated critically by modern scholarship (Machal notes 'grave doubt'); flagged.

passages.text: The great centre of the cult of the ancient Prussians was at Romowe, a place of uncertain localization. There lived the head priest, the Kriwe, and there a perpetual fire was maintained — a fire of oak-wood which, once out, could be rekindled only by friction of the sacred wood. The Kriwe's authority ran through the whole Baltic world; his decrees, the sources say, were carried as far as the fame of the flame.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Romowe material summarized in Mythology of All Races III (1918), after Simon Grunau; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古普魯士人崇拜的一大中心在羅莫韋（Romowe），其確切位置不詳。首席祭司克里韋（Kriwe）住在那裡，那裡也維持著一團長明之火——一團橡木之火，一旦熄滅，便只能以聖木摩擦重新點燃。克里韋的權威遍及整個波羅的海世界；據史料記載，他的敕令所及之遠，一如那火焰的聲名。

passages.text: In the great oak, which remained green summer and winter and was screened from profane gaze, were the idols of the gods: a perpetual fire of oak before Perkunas, and a pot containing a serpent, carefully fed by the priests, before Potrimpo. In the open spaces lay piles of wood for the sacred fire, and the houses of the Waidelots — the ordinary priests — surrounded the whole. Modern scholarship doubts much of Grunau's picture; what is certain is that the Baltic religion kept a central fire, a central priest, and a sacred serpent in its own great sanctuary.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the plate-note material in Machal (1918); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在那棵冬夏常青、並遮蔽於凡人目光之外的大橡樹中，供著諸神的偶像：在佩爾庫納斯（Perkunas）面前是一團橡木長明火，在波特林波（Potrimpo）面前則是一只盛著蛇的罐子，由祭司悉心餵養。空地上堆放著供聖火使用的木柴，而瓦伊德洛特（Waidelots）——即普通祭司——的屋舍環繞著整個區域。現代學術界對格魯瑙（Grunau）的描述多有存疑；可以確定的是，波羅的海宗教在其自身的大聖所中，維持著一團中心之火、一位中心祭司，以及一條聖蛇。

title.en: The Prussian Triad: Perkunas, Potrimpo, and Patollo
title.zh: 普魯士三聯神：佩爾庫納斯、波特里姆波、帕托洛

region.en: Romowe, Prussia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 普魯士羅莫沃（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded by Simon Grunau (c. 1526); summarized in Machal 1918

source.work: The Prussian triad as summarized in Mythology of All Races III (1918), plate note, after Grunau's Preussische Chronik II

summary.en: In Grunau's old chronicle the Prussians worshipped a triad in the Romowe oak: Perkunas, god of thunder with the eternal fire; Potrimpo, god of rivers and springs, of vegetation and good fortune, with his sacred serpent; and Patollo, god of the underworld, before whom stood the heads of a man, a horse, and a cow.
summary.zh: 格勞瑙古編年史載普魯士人於羅莫沃橡中奉三聯神：掌長明火之雷神佩爾庫納斯；司河流泉源、豐饒與幸運之神波特里姆波，伴以聖蛇；以及冥界之神帕托洛，其前置人、馬、牛三首。

sensitivity.note: Grunau is a late and doubtful source (Machal's caveat); interpretive reconstruction flagged.

passages.text: According to the historian Simon Grunau, writing in the early part of the sixteenth century, a triad of gods received adoration at Romowe: Perkunas, deity of thunder, with his perpetual fire of oak; Potrympus, deity of rivers and springs — and hence of vegetation and good fortune — with a pot containing a serpent carefully fed by the priests; and Patollus, deity of the underworld.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the plate-note summary in Machal, Mythology of All Races III (1918), after Grunau; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據十六世紀初寫作的歷史學家西蒙·格魯瑙（Simon Grunau）所述，有三位一組的神祇在羅莫韋受到崇拜：佩爾庫納斯（Perkunas），雷電之神，配有橡木長明火；波特林普斯（Potrympus），河流與泉源之神——因而也是植物與好運之神——配有一只盛著蛇的罐子，由祭司悉心餵養；以及帕托盧斯（Patollus），冥界之神。

passages.text: Each god had his emblem in the evergreen oak: before Patollo stood the heads of a man, a horse, and a cow — the dead and the beasts he receives. We have, however, no certain evidence that the ancient Prussians possessed idols of their gods at all, and in many respects the statements of Grunau are open to grave doubt; the triad stands as the best-remembered shape of a religion recorded only by its destroyers. (Interpretive reconstruction flagged.)
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Machal (1918) caveat and material; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 每位神祇在常青橡樹上都有自己的標記：在帕托洛（Patollo）面前立著人、馬與牛的首級——那是他所接納的亡者與牲畜。然而，我們並無確切證據顯示古代普魯士人擁有其神祇的偶像，且在許多方面，格魯瑙（Grunau）的陳述都大有可疑；這三神組是這門宗教最為人所銘記的形態，而該宗教僅由其毀滅者所記載。（此為標註之詮釋性重建。）

title.en: Widewuto and Bruteno: The First Kings of the Prussians
title.zh: 維德武托與布魯特諾：普魯士的初代君王

region.en: Prussia, Romowe (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 普魯士羅莫沃（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded by Simon Grunau, Preussische Chronik (c. 1526); documented by later scholarship

source.work: Simon Grunau, Preussische Chronik (c. 1526), the legend of Widewuto and Bruteno; documented in Gray (1918) and Gimbutas, The Balts (1963)

license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain chronicle; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: Grunau's chronicle makes the Prussians descend from two brothers: Widewuto, the king, and Bruteno, the priest-king of the sacred grove; Widewuto's twelve sons gave their names to the lands of Prussia, and the old king ended his fifty-two years by burning himself, his wife, and his people's gifts in the pyre at Romowe.
summary.zh: 格勞瑙編年史謂普魯士人源自兩兄弟：國王維德武托與聖林祭司王布魯特諾；維德武托十二子之名分賜普魯士諸地；老王執政五十二年，於羅莫沃火葬堆中自焚其身、其妻與人民之獻禮。

sensitivity.note: Late legendary genealogy; flagged as unreliable by modern scholarship.

passages.text: The legend recorded by Simon Grunau makes the Prussian nation begin with two brothers: Widewuto the king, who gave the country its laws, its ploughing, and its names, and Bruteno the priest, lord of the sacred grove where the eternal fire burned. Widewuto reigned fifty-two years, dividing the land among his twelve sons, from whom — so the tale goes — the Prussian lands took their names.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Grunau's Preussische Chronik legend as documented in Gray (1918) and Gimbutas (1963); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 西蒙·格魯瑙（Simon Grunau）所記載的傳說，使普魯士民族始於兩兄弟：國王維德武托（Widewuto），他為這片土地制定了法律、農耕與名稱；以及祭司布魯特諾（Bruteno），他是聖林的領主，永恆之火即在那裡燃燒。維德武托在位五十二年，將土地分給他的十二個兒子，據傳說，普魯士各地的名稱便源自他們。

passages.text: When his time came Widewuto went to Romowe, the great sanctuary of his father's faith, laid himself on the pyre with his wife, and burned, as the law of his own founding required — the king who had given the fire to his people returning himself to it. The story is a late construction of a people remembering its freedom; but the two offices it names, the king and the priest of the fire, are the two pillars the Baltic religion truly kept. (Late and doubtful source; flagged.)
passages.note: Paraphrase of the legend with scholarly caveat; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他的時刻來臨，維德武托前往羅莫韋（Romowe）——他父輩信仰的偉大聖所——與妻子一同躺上火葬堆，依他自己所立之法焚燒而死：那位將火賜予其子民的國王，親自回歸於火。這故事是一個民族追憶其自由時的晚期建構；但其中所稱的兩種職分——國王與火的祭司——正是波羅的宗教真正持守的兩根支柱。（來源晚出且可疑；已標註。）

title.en: The First Man of Clay and the Devil's Spit
title.zh: 泥土初人與魔之唾

region.en: Lithuania (symbolic pin at Vilnius)
region.zh: 立陶宛（象徵性定位於維爾紐斯）

period: Recorded 19th-20th c.; documented by Vellius (1979)

source.work: Creation-of-man tales; documented in Vellius, Lithuanian Mythological Tales (1979)

license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain folk material; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: God made the first man of clay and set him in the sun to dry; the Devil, passing by, spat on him — and every illness and crookedness in the human body is the mark of that spitting, while what God made clean is the part of us that still obeys.
summary.zh: 神以泥土造初人，置於日下晾曬；魔經過時唾之——人體中一切疾病與歪斜皆為唾痕，而神所造之潔處，即人仍聽命之部分。

sensitivity.note: Clay-humans cluster (cross-tagged with Sumerian, Greek, Chinese parallels); framing reconstructed.

passages.text: God made the first man of clay and set him in the sun to dry. The Devil, walking by and jealous of the new creature, spat upon him; the spit dried into the body, and from that day the human frame has carried its crookedness and its sicknesses — every pain is the mark of the Devil's spitting, and every part that works well is the part God made.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the creation-of-man tale as documented in Vellius, Lithuanian Mythological Tales (1979); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 神用黏土造了第一個人，將他放在陽光下曬乾。魔鬼走過，嫉妒這新造的生物，便朝他吐唾沫；唾沫乾結成身體，自那天起，人的軀體便帶著它的歪曲與疾病——每一處疼痛都是魔鬼吐唾沫的痕跡，而每一處運作良好的部分，都是神所造的部分。

passages.text: The tale explains both the body and the medicine: what the doctors can mend, the tales say, is only the Devil's spitting scraped off again, for the clay God made was good. The record's framing is reconstructed from the motif as documented in the collection; the tellers' wording varies. (Reconstructed segments: the drying-in-the-sun scene; restored from the documented motif.)
passages.note: Paraphrase of the documented motif; framing reconstructed (Vellius 1979); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這則故事既解釋了身體，也解釋了醫術：故事說，醫生所能修補的，不過是再次刮去魔鬼的唾沫，因為神所造的黏土本是好的。此記載的框架是依據該集所記錄的母題重建而成；講述者的措辭各有不同。（重建段落：陽光下曬乾的場景；依據所記錄的母題復原。）

title.en: Why the Snake Bites: The Devil's Gift of Venom
title.zh: 蛇何以噬人：魔賜之毒

region.en: Lithuanian meadows (symbolic pin at Kaunas)
region.zh: 立陶宛草地（象徵性定位於考納斯）

period: Recorded 19th-20th c.; documented by Vellius (1979)

source.work: Etiological snake tales; documented in Vellius, Lithuanian Mythological Tales (1979)

license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain folk material; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: The snake was made gentle, but the Devil — or a jealous master — gave it venom; hence the house-snake is fed and honoured like a god, while the field-snake is feared as the Devil's beast wearing the same scales.
summary.zh: 蛇本溫馴，然魔（或忌妒者）賜其毒；故家蛇如神般受飼受敬，而田間之蛇則被視為披同鱗之魔獸而懼。

sensitivity.note: Etiological tale; framing reconstructed.

passages.text: In the beginning the snake was made gentle and harmless, a creature of the households — the same being the Lithuanians fed with milk as the guardian žaltys. But the Devil, envious of a beast so favoured, gave the field-snake its venom, and from that hour the same shape walked abroad in two fortunes: the house-snake honoured as a god, the field-snake feared as the Devil's beast.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the etiological tale as documented in Vellius, Lithuanian Mythological Tales (1979); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 起初，蛇被造得溫順無害，是家宅中的生物——立陶宛人餵以牛奶、奉為守護者的žaltys（家蛇），正是這同一種存在。但魔鬼嫉妒這般受寵的野獸，便賦予田間之蛇毒液，自那一刻起，同一形貌便以兩種命運行走於世：家蛇受尊為神，田蛇則被畏為魔鬼之獸。

passages.text: The tale explains why the same creature is worshipped and killed: it is not the scales that decide but the side of the creation the beast serves. The house-snake's milk-dish stands at the hearth to this day in the old stories, and the field-snake's bite is the Devil's signature — one animal, two creators, as in all the Baltic making. (Framing reconstructed from the motif as documented.)
passages.note: Paraphrase of the documented motif; framing reconstructed (Vellius 1979); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這個故事解釋了為何同一種生物既受崇拜又遭殺害：決定一切的不是鱗片，而是這頭野獸所侍奉的創世之方。在古老的故事中，家蛇的奶碟至今仍擺在爐邊；而田蛇的咬嚙則是魔鬼的印記——同一種動物，兩位創世者，正如波羅的海地區一切創世之事那般。（框架係依據所記載之母題重構而成。）

title.en: The Heir Sold for Peace: Titu Cusi Hualpa Stolen at Eight Years Old
title.zh: 以嗣子換和平:八歲的圖帕克·庫西·瓦爾帕遭擄

region.en: Paulo (Micocancha), Huayllacan country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦伊利亞坎的保羅鎮(米科坎恰)(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 20, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Those of Huayllacan had already promised to give Mama Micay, who was their countrywoman and very beautiful, in marriage to Tocay Ccapac, Sinchi of the Ayamarcas their neighbours. When the Ayamarcas saw that the Huayllacans had broken their word they were furious and declared war. While this war was being waged Mama Micay gave birth to her son Titu Cusi Hualpa. Both sides, seeing that they were destroying each other, agreed to come to terms: the Ayamarcas, who were the most powerful, requested those of Huayllacan to deliver the child Titu Cusi Hualpa into their hands, to do what they liked with him; on this condition they would desist from further hostilities. The Huayllacans, fearing this, accepted the condition, although they were uncles and relations of the child. To comply it was necessary to deceive the Inca: a brother of Inca Rocca, named Inca Paucar, asked Inca Rocca to send his nephew to his town of Paulo, that while still a child he might learn to know and care for his relations on his mother's side, who wanted to make him the heir of their estates. Believing these words, the Inca consented. When the child was in their town the Huayllacans made great feasts in honour of Titu Cusi Hualpa, who was then eight years old, his father having sent Incas to guard him. When the festivities were over, the Huayllacans sent to give notice to the Ayamarcas that, while they were occupied in ploughing their chacaras, they might come down on the town and carry off the child. The Ayamarcas came, and finding the child Titu Cusi Hualpa alone, carried it off; all the orejones who had come as a guard from Cuzco were slain.
summary.zh: 瓦伊利亞坎人早先把族中美貌女子瑪瑪·米卡伊許配給鄰邦阿亞馬爾卡之辛奇托卡伊·卡帕克;後來違約另嫁印加·羅卡,阿亞馬爾卡人憤然宣戰。戰火之中,瑪瑪·米卡伊產子圖帕克·庫西·瓦爾帕。兩邦相持數年,見彼此損耗殆盡,遂議和約——強大的阿亞馬爾卡人提出:交出圖帕克·庫西·瓦爾帕,任憑發落,否則戰至滅絕。瓦伊利亞坎人雖是孩子的舅家,懼於兵威,竟允其所請。為履行條約,必先誆騙印加王:印加·羅卡之弟印加·保卡爾遣使,請王將幼侄送至自己的保羅鎮,「好讓孩子自幼認識母族親人,繼承他們的家業」。印加·羅卡信以為真,允子前往。孩子入鎮,瓦伊利亞坎人大擺宴席——其時圖帕克·庫西·瓦爾帕年方八歲,其父另派印加衛士隨行護衛。宴罷,瓦伊利亞坎人密報阿亞馬爾卡人:趁他們下田耕作之際,可入鎮劫走孩子。阿亞馬爾卡人依約而至,見孩子獨處,便將他擄走;自庫斯科前來護衛的耳垂貴胄盡數被殺。

sensitivity.note: The child-kidnapping origin of the Yahuar-huaccac name; kinship betrayal at the heart of the succession myth.

passages.text: It has been related how the Inca Rocca married Mama Micay by the rites of their religion. But it must be understood that those of Huayllacan had already promised to give Mama Micay, who was their countrywoman and very beautiful, in marriage to Tocay Ccapac, Sinchi of the Ayamarcas their neighbours. When the Ayamarcas saw that the Huayllacans had broken their word, they were furious and declared war, considering them as enemies. War was carried on... both sides committing cruelties, inflicting deaths and losses, and causing great injury to each other. While this war was being waged, Mama Micay gave birth to her son Titu Cusi Hualpa.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 20 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 前文已述印加羅卡如何依其宗教儀式娶了瑪瑪·米凱。但必須明白，瓦伊利亞坎人早已承諾要將瑪瑪·米凱——她是他們的同鄉，且容貌極美——嫁給他們的鄰邦阿亞馬爾卡人的辛奇托凱·卡帕克。當阿亞馬爾卡人見瓦伊利亞坎人背棄諾言，便勃然大怒，宣布開戰，視他們為仇敵。戰爭持續進行……雙方皆行殘暴之事，造成死亡與損失，彼此造成極大傷害。正當這場戰爭進行之際，瑪瑪·米凱生下了她的兒子蒂圖·庫西·瓦爾帕。

passages.text: The Ayamarcas, who were the most powerful, requested those of Huayllacan to deliver the child Titu Cusi Hualpa into their hands, to do what they liked with him. On this condition they would desist from further hostilities, but if it was not complied with, they announced that they would continue a mortal war to the end. The Huayllacans, fearing this, and knowing their inability for further resistance, accepted the condition, although they were uncles and relations of the child. In order to comply it was necessary for them to deceive the Inca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 20 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最為強大的阿亞馬爾卡人要求瓦伊利亞坎人將孩子蒂圖·庫西·瓦爾帕交到他們手中，任憑他們處置。以此為條件，他們便停止進一步的敵對行動；但若不遵從，他們便宣告將進行一場至死方休的戰爭。瓦伊利亞坎人畏懼於此，又自知無力繼續抵抗，便接受了這個條件，儘管他們是這孩子的舅父與親屬。為了履行此約，他們必須欺騙印加。

passages.text: There was, in the town of Paulo, a brother of Inca Rocca and uncle of Titu Cusi Hualpa named Inca Paucar. He went or sent messengers to ask Inca Rocca to think well of sending his nephew Titu Cusi Hualpa to his town of Paulo in order that, while still a child, he might learn to know and care for his relations on his mother's side, while they wanted to make him the heir of their estates. Believing in these words the Inca Rocca consented... As soon as they had the child in their town the Huayllacans made great feasts in honour of Titu Cusi Hualpa, who was then eight years old. When the festivities were over, the Huayllacans sent to give notice to the Ayamarcas that, while they were occupied in ploughing certain lands which they call chacaras, they might come down on the town and carry off the child. The Ayamarcas, being informed, came at the time and to the place notified and, finding the child Titu Cusi Hualpa alone, they carried it off.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 20 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在保羅鎮上，有一位印加羅卡的兄弟、蒂圖·庫西·瓦爾帕的舅父，名叫印加·保卡爾。他親自前往或派遣使者去請求印加羅卡，好好考慮將他的姪兒蒂圖·庫西·瓦爾帕送到他在保羅的鎮上，好讓他在年幼之時便能認識並關照母系一方的親屬，因為他們想讓他成為他們產業的繼承人。印加羅卡聽信了這番話便應允了……瓦伊利亞坎人一將孩子接到他們的鎮上，便為蒂圖·庫西·瓦爾帕舉行了盛大的慶典，當時他年方八歲。慶典結束後，瓦伊利亞坎人便派人通知阿亞馬爾卡人：趁他們忙於耕種某些他們稱之為查卡拉的土地時，他們可以下山突襲該鎮並將孩子擄走。阿亞馬爾卡人得到消息後，便在所通知的時間與地點前來，發現蒂圖·庫西·瓦爾帕獨自一人，便將他擄走。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Tears of Blood: The Child's Curse on Tocay Ccapac
title.zh: 泣血之咒:幼童對托卡伊·卡帕克的詛咒

region.en: Ahuayro-cancha, Ayamarca country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿亞馬爾卡之阿瓦伊羅-坎恰(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 21, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: The Ayamarcas presented the child Titu Cusi Hualpa to Tocay Ccapac at the chief place of their province called Ahuayro-cancha, saying: 'Look here, Tocay Ccapac, at the prisoner we have brought you.' The Sinchi received his prize with great satisfaction, asking in a loud voice if this was the child of Mama Micay, who ought to have been his wife. Titu Cusi Hualpa, though but a child, replied boldly that he was the son of Mama Micay and of the Inca Rocca. Tocay was indignant when he had heard those words, and ordered those who brought the child as a prisoner to take him out and kill him. The boy, when he heard such a sentence passed upon him, was so filled with sadness and fright that he began to weep from fear of death. He began to shed tears of blood and with indignation beyond his years, in the form of a malediction he said to Tocay and the Ayamarcas: 'I tell you that as sure as you murder me there will come such a curse on you and your descendants that you will all come to an end, without any memory being left of your nation.' The Ayamarcas and Tocay attentively considered this curse of the child together with the tears of blood. They thought there was some great mystery that so young a child should utter such weighty words... They were in suspense divining what it portended. They revoked the sentence of death, calling the child Yahuar-huaccac, which means 'weeper of blood', in allusion to what had taken place. But although they did not wish to kill him then and with their own hands, they ordered that he should lead such a life as that he would die of hunger; they all said to the child that he should turn his face to Cuzco and weep over it, because those curses he had pronounced would fall on the inhabitants of Cuzco, and so it happened.
summary.zh: 阿亞馬爾卡人把圖帕克·庫西·瓦爾帕押到本省重鎮阿瓦伊羅-坎恰,獻與托卡伊·卡帕克:「瞧,托卡伊·卡帕克,我們給你帶來了俘虜!」辛奇大喜,高聲喝問:這可是本該嫁我的瑪瑪·米卡伊之子?孩子雖幼,卻昂然答道:我是瑪瑪·米卡伊與印加·羅卡之子!托卡伊聞言大怒,喝令將孩子拖出去處死。幼童聞此死刑判決,悲懼交加,竟泣出鮮血;又以超越年齡的憤慨,向托卡伊與阿亞馬爾卡人發出詛咒:「我告訴你們:你們若殺我,咒詛必臨到你們和你們的子孫——你們將滅絕殆盡,你們的國族將無人記起!」托卡伊與眾人反覆思量這孩子的泣血與詛咒:如此年幼竟出此重話,怕是藏著什麼天大的奧秘,便猜度這是否預兆此子將成大器。死刑遂被撤回;眾人因這件事稱他為「亞瓦爾-瓦卡克」——泣血者。他們雖不親手殺他,卻下令讓他過一種終將餓死的生活;臨行又對孩子說:把臉轉向庫斯科,對著它哭吧——你口中的詛咒,將應驗在庫斯科人身上。後來果然如此。

sensitivity.note: The name-giving curse episode; the tears of blood prefigure the dynastic bloodshed of the civil war.

passages.text: The Sinchi received his prize with great satisfaction, asking in a loud voice if this was the child of Mama Micay, who ought to have been his wife. Titu Cusi Hualpa, though but a child, replied boldly that he was the son of Mama Micay and of the Inca Rocca. Tocay was indignant when he had heard those words, and ordered those who brought the child as a prisoner to take him out and kill him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 21 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 辛奇極為滿意地收下了他的戰利品，高聲詢問這是否就是瑪瑪·米凱的孩子——那本該成為他妻子之人的孩子。蒂圖·庫西·瓦爾帕雖只是個孩子，卻大膽地回答說，他是瑪瑪·米凱與印加羅卡之子。托凱聽到這番話後勃然大怒，便命令那些將孩子作為俘虜帶來的人把他帶出去殺掉。
