passages.text: The boy, when he heard such a sentence passed upon him, was so filled with sadness and fright, that he began to weep from fear of death. He began to shed tears of blood and with indignation beyond his years, in the form of a malediction he said to Tocay and the Ayamarcas: 'I tell you that as sure as you murder me there will come such a curse on you and your descendants that you will all come to an end, without any memory being left of your nation.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 21 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這男孩聽到對自己宣判了這樣的刑罰，心中充滿了悲傷與驚恐，因懼怕死亡而開始哭泣。他開始流下血淚，並以超越其年齡的憤慨，以詛咒的形式對托凱與阿亞馬爾卡人說道：「我告訴你們，你們殺我之事千真萬確，必有一場災禍降臨到你們與你們的子孫身上，你們將全部滅絕，你們的族裔不會留下任何記憶。」

passages.text: The Ayamarcas and Tocay attentively considered this curse of the child together with the tears of blood. They thought there was some great mystery that so young a child should utter such weighty words, and that the fear of death should make such an impression on him that he should shed tears of blood. They were in suspense divining what it portended, whether that the child would become a great man. They revoked the sentence of death, calling the child Yahuar-huaccac, which means 'weeper of blood', in allusion to what had taken place. Before this they all said to the child that he should turn his face to Cuzco and weep over it, because those curses he had pronounced, would fall on the inhabitants of Cuzco, and so it happened.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 21 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿亞馬爾卡斯人與托凱一同仔細思量這孩子的詛咒，以及那血淚。他們心想，如此年幼的孩子竟能說出這般沉重的話語，其中必有某種重大的奧祕；而對死亡的恐懼竟在他身上留下如此深刻的印記，使他流下血淚。他們滿心懸疑，揣度這究竟預示著什麼，莫非這孩子將來會成為一位偉人。他們撤銷了死刑的判決，稱這孩子為亞瓦爾—瓦卡克，意即「泣血者」，以影射所發生之事。在此之前，他們都對這孩子說，他應當把臉轉向庫斯科，為庫斯科而哭泣，因為他所發出的那些詛咒將會落在庫斯科的居民身上，而事情果然如此應驗。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Chimpu Orma and the Race to the Hill: The Prince Freed by Anta
title.zh: 欽普·奧爾瑪與登山之賽:安塔人救出王子

region.en: Anta, three leagues from Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科三萊格外的安塔(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 22, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: The child Yahuar-huaccac was a year among the shepherds without leaving their huts, which served as a prison, well watched by the shepherds and other guards. But it so happened that there was a woman in the place called Chimpu Orma, native of the town of Anta, three leagues from Cuzco: she was a concubine of the Sinchi Tocay Ccapac, and for this reason she had leave to walk about and go into all parts as she pleased. She was the daughter of the Sinchi of Anta, and having given an account of the treatment of the child to her father, brothers, and relations, she persuaded them to help in his liberation. They came on a certain day and, with the pass given them by Chimpu Orma, arranged the escape. They stationed themselves behind a hill. Yahuar-huaccac was to run in a race with some other boys, to see which could get to the top of the hill first. When the prince reached the top, the men of Anta, who were hidden there, took him in their arms and ran swiftly with him to Anta. When the other boys saw this they quickly gave notice to the valiant guards, who ran after the men of Anta and overtook them at the lake of Huaypon, where there was a fierce battle; finally the Ayamarcas got the worst of it, for they were nearly all killed or wounded. In the town of Anta the boy remained a year, served with much love, but so secretly that his father did not know that he had escaped. At the end of a year those of Anta sent messengers to Inca Rocca; not feeling quite certain of the truth, he sent a poor man seeking charity to make enquiries at Anta, whether it was all true; the poor man ascertained that the child was certainly liberated, and returned with the news. Presently the Inca sent principal people of Cuzco with presents of gold, silver and cloth to the Antas, asking them to send back his son. The Antas replied that they did not want his presents, that they cared more that Yahuar-huaccac should remain with them; yet if Inca Rocca wanted his son he should be returned on condition that, from that time forwards, the Antas should be called relations of the orejones. Inca Rocca conceded what they asked, and brought his son to Cuzco, nominating him successor.
summary.zh: 亞瓦爾-瓦卡克被囚於牧人小屋整整一年,牧人與衛士嚴密看守,無人知其下落。其時營地有一女子,名欽普·奧爾瑪,乃庫斯科三萊格外安塔鎮人——托卡伊·卡帕克的妾,因此得以自由行走四方。她是安塔辛奇之女;她把幼童的遭遇告知父親、兄弟與親族,勸他們相助營救。某日,他們持欽普·奧爾瑪給的通行之權前來,預伏於一座山後。約定:亞瓦爾-瓦卡克將與其他男孩賽跑,看誰先登頂。王子一到山頂,潛伏的安塔人便將他攔腰抱起,飛奔而回安塔。同伴孩童見狀急報衛士;衛士狂追,在瓦伊蓬湖追上安塔人,一場惡戰——阿亞馬爾卡人幾乎全軍覆沒。王子在安塔鎮安居一年,備受愛戴,但行事極其隱秘,連其父印加·羅卡也不知他已脫身。一年之後,安塔人遣使報信;印加·羅卡尚不敢盡信,又派一名化緣的窮人往安塔查證。窮人證實王子確已獲釋,回報庫斯科,舉城再慶。印加王隨即遣重臣攜金銀布帛贈安塔人,求還其子。安塔人卻答:禮物不必了,他們更願意亞瓦爾-瓦卡克留居安塔,好讓他們侍奉王子父子;若印加王執意索回,須應一條件——自此以後,安塔人得稱為「耳垂貴胄」的親戚。印加·羅卡親赴安塔,允其所請,攜子回庫斯科,立為儲君。

sensitivity.note: The rescue that founded the Anta-Cuzco kinship pact - a founding charter narrated through a children's race.

passages.text: It so happened that there was a woman in the place called Chimpu Orma, native of the town of Anta, three leagues from Cuzco. She was a concubine of the Sinchi Tocay Ccapac, and for this reason she had leave to walk about and go into all parts as she pleased. She was the daughter of the Sinchi of Anta, and having given an account of the treatment of the child to her father, brothers, and relations, she persuaded them to help in his liberation.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 22 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 事情是這樣的：在一個名叫欽普·奧爾馬的地方，有一位女子，是距庫斯科三萊瓜之遙的安塔鎮的本地人。她是辛奇·托凱·卡帕克的妾室，因此得以獲准隨意走動，任意出入各處。她是安塔辛奇的女兒，她將這孩子所受的待遇告知了她的父親、兄弟與親族，並說服他們協助解救他。

passages.text: They came on a certain day and, with the pass given them by Chimpu Orma, the father and relations arranged the escape of Yahuar-huaccac. They stationed themselves behind a hill. Yahuar-huaccac was to run in a race with some other boys, to see which could get to the top of the hill first. When the prince reached the top, the men of Anta, who were hidden there, took him in their arms and ran swiftly with him to Anta. When the other boys saw this they quickly gave notice to the valiant guards, who ran after the men of Anta. They overtook them at the lake of Huaypon, where there was a fierce battle. Finally the Ayamarcas got the worst of it, for they were nearly all killed or wounded.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 22 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某一天，他們前來，憑著欽普·奧爾馬給他們的通行許可，父親與親族們安排了亞瓦爾—瓦卡克的逃亡。他們埋伏在一座山丘之後。亞瓦爾—瓦卡克要與其他幾個男孩賽跑，看誰能先跑到山頂。當王子抵達山頂時，藏身該處的安塔人將他抱入懷中，帶著他飛快地奔向安塔。其他男孩見狀，急忙通報那些勇猛的守衛，守衛們便追趕安塔人。他們在瓦伊蓬湖畔追上了安塔人，雙方展開了一場激烈的戰鬥。最終阿亞馬爾卡斯人落敗，因為他們幾乎全數陣亡或負傷。

passages.text: Not feeling quite certain of the truth of what he had been told, he sent a poor man seeking charity to make enquiries at Anta, whether it was all true. The poor man went, ascertained that the child was certainly liberated, and returned with the news to Inca Rocca... Presently the Inca sent many principal people of Cuzco with presents of gold, silver, and cloth to the Antas, asking them to receive them and to send back his son. The Antas replied that they did not want his presents which they returned... yet if Inca Rocca wanted his son, he should be returned on condition that, from that time forwards, the Antas should be called relations of the orejones. When Inca Rocca was made acquainted with the condition, he went to Anta and conceded what they asked for... For this reason the Antas were called relations of the Cuzcos from that time.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 22 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他對所聽聞之事無法完全確信，便派了一名乞討施捨的窮人去安塔打探，查明這一切是否屬實。那窮人前去，確知那孩子確實已獲解救，便帶著消息回到印加·羅卡那裡……不久，印加派遣了許多庫斯科的顯貴，帶著金、銀與布帛的禮物前往安塔人處，請他們收下禮物，並送回他的兒子。安塔人回答說，他們不要他的禮物，並將禮物退回……然而，倘若印加·羅卡想要回他的兒子，便應在這樣的條件下送回：自此以後，安塔人應被稱為大耳人的親族。當印加·羅卡得知這一條件後，便前往安塔，應允了他們所求……因此之故，安塔人自那時起便被稱為庫斯科人的親族。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: The Heir Killed in Paulo Again: The Huayllacans' Second Treason
title.zh: 保羅鎮再演弒儲:瓦伊利亞坎人的二次背叛

region.en: Paulo, Huayllacan country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦伊利亞坎的保羅鎮(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 23, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Yahuar-huaccac had by his wife Mama Chicya three legitimate sons: the eldest Paucar Ayllu; the second Pahuac Hualpa Mayta, chosen to succeed his father though he was not the eldest; the third Viracocha, who was afterwards Inca through the death of his brother. As the Huayllacans wanted Marca-yutu to succeed Yahuar-huaccac, because he was their relation, they determined to kill Pahuac Hualpa Mayta who was nominated to succeed. With this object they asked his father to let him go to Paulo. Forgetting their former treason, he sent the child to its grandfather Soma Inca with forty orejones of the ayllus of Cuzco as his guard. When he came to their town they killed him, for which the Inca, his father, inflicted a great punishment on the Huayllacans, killing some and banishing others until very few were left.
summary.zh: 亞瓦爾-瓦卡克與王后瑪瑪·奇西亞生三個嫡子:長子保卡爾·阿伊柳;次子帕瓜克·瓦爾帕·馬雅塔,雖非長子,卻被立為儲君;三子維拉科查,因兄長遇害而終得大位。瓦伊利亞坎人欲使自己親戚馬爾卡-尤圖繼位,便謀殺儲君帕瓜克·瓦爾帕·馬雅塔。他們請求印加王准孩子前往保羅;印加王忘卻舊恨,竟遣幼子赴外祖父索馬·印加處,並派庫斯科阿伊柳的四十名耳垂貴胄護衛。孩子一到鎮上,他們便將他殺害。印加王大怒,嚴懲瓦伊利亞坎人——或誅或逐,直至其族所剩無幾。

sensitivity.note: The second child-murder in the same town; the repetition is the point - the Huayllacan kinship is twice traitorous in this tradition.

passages.text: As the Huayllacans wanted Marca-yutu to succeed Yahuar-huaccac, because he was their relation, they determined to kill Pahuac Hualpa Mayta, who was nominated to succeed. With this object they asked his father to let him go to Paulo. Forgetting their former treason, he sent the child to its grandfather Soma Inca with forty orejones of the ayllus of Cuzco as his guard. When he came to their town they killed him, for which the Inca, his father, inflicted a great punishment on the Huayllacans, killing some and banishing others until very few were left.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 23 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 由於瓦伊利亞坎人希望由馬爾卡—尤圖繼承亞瓦爾—瓦卡克，因為他是他們的親族，他們便決意殺害被提名為繼承人的帕瓦克·瓦爾帕·邁塔。為此目的，他們請求他的父親讓他前往保洛。他忘卻了他們先前的背叛，將這孩子送往其外祖父索馬·印加處，並以四十名來自庫斯科各艾柳的大耳人作為護衛。當他來到他們的城鎮時，他們殺害了他，為此，他的父親印加對瓦伊利亞坎人施以嚴厲的懲罰，殺了一些人，流放了一些人，直到所剩無幾。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: The Night Apparition at Urcos: How Hatun Tupac Became Viracocha Inca
title.zh: 烏爾科斯夜現真神:哈頓·圖帕克改名維拉科查

region.en: Urcos, five leagues from Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科五萊格外烏爾科斯(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 24, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Once when Hatun Tupac Inca was in Urcos, a town a little more than five leagues S.S.E. of Cuzco, where there was a sumptuous huaca in honour of Ticci Viracocha, the deity appeared to him in the night. Next morning he assembled his orejones, among them his tutor Hualpa Rimachi, and told them how Viracocha had appeared to him that night, and had announced great good fortune to him and his descendants. In congratulating him Hualpa Rimachi saluted him: 'O Viracocha Inca.' The rest followed his example and celebrated this name, and the Inca retained it all the rest of his life. Others say that he took this name because, when he was armed as a knight and had his ears bored, he took Ticci Viracocha as the godfather of his knighthood. Be it as it may, all that is certain is that when a child, before he succeeded his father, he was named Hatun Tupac Inca, and afterwards, for the rest of his life, Viracocha Inca.
summary.zh: 哈頓·圖帕克·印加行至庫斯科東南偏南五萊格外的烏爾科斯鎮——那裡有一座供奉提基·維拉科查的豪華瓦卡——夜間,神祇向他顯現。次日清晨,他召集耳垂貴胄——其中包括他的師傅瓦爾帕·里馬奇——講述夜間維拉科查顯靈之事,以及神向他與其子孫預許的大福。師傅瓦爾帕·里馬奇賀道:「維拉科查·印加!」眾人隨之歡呼,共賀新名;印加王自此終身用之。另有異說:他之所以取此名,是因受武穿耳之時,拜提基·維拉科查為受武的教父。無論如何,可以確定的是:他繼位之前幼名哈頓·圖帕克·印加,此後終身名維拉科查·印加。

sensitivity.note: Royal theophany and renaming; the king takes the Creator's own name as his regnal title.

passages.text: Once when this Hatun Tupac Inca was in Urcos, a town which is a little more than five leagues S.S.E. of Cuzco, where there was a sumptuous huaca in honour of Ticci Viracocha, the deity appeared to him in the night. Next morning he assembled his orejones, among them his tutor Hualpa Rimachi, and told them how Viracocha had appeared to him that night, and had announced great good fortune to him and his descendants.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 24 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次，這位哈通·圖帕克·印加身在烏爾科斯，那是位於庫斯科南南東略多於五萊瓜處的一座城鎮，當地有一座供奉蒂克西·維拉科查的宏偉瓦卡，那位神祇在夜間向他顯現。翌日清晨，他召集了他的大耳人，其中包括他的導師瓦爾帕·里馬奇，告訴他們維拉科查那夜如何向他顯現，並向他及其子孫宣告了極大的福運。

passages.text: In congratulating him Hualpa Rimachi saluted him, 'O Viracocha Inca.' The rest followed his example and celebrated this name, and the Inca retained it all the rest of his life. Others say that he took this name, because, when he was armed as a knight and had his ears bored, he took Ticci Viracocha as the godfather of his knighthood. Be it as it may, all that is certain is that when a child, before he succeeded his father, he was named Hatun Tupac Inca, and afterwards, for the rest of his life, Viracocha Inca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 24 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 瓦爾帕·里馬奇向他道賀，稱他為「噢，維拉科查·印卡」。其餘的人也都仿效他，頌揚這個名號，而這位印卡終其餘生都保有它。另有人說，他之所以取這個名號，是因為當他受封為騎士、耳朵被穿孔時，他認蒂克西·維拉科查為他騎士封授的教父。不論實情如何，可以確定的是：他年幼時、尚未繼承父親之前，名叫哈通·圖帕克·印卡，此後終其餘生則名為維拉科查·印卡。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: The Old King Flees to Xaquixaguana: Gonzalo Pizarro Burns the Body
title.zh: 老王遁走夏基夏瓜納:皮薩羅焚屍索金

region.en: Caquia Xaquixaguana (Sacsahuana) (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 卡基亞-夏基夏瓜納(薩克薩瓦納)(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 25, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: As Viracocha was now very old, he nominated as his successor his bastard son Inca Urco, without regard to the order of succession, because he was very fond of his mother. This Inca was bold, proud, and despised others, so that he aroused the indignation of the warriors, more especially of the legitimate sons, and of the valiant captains Apu Mayta and Vicaquirau. These took order to prevent this succession, secretly setting their eyes on the third of the legitimate sons named Cusi, afterwards called Inca Yupanqui, because they believed that he was mild and affable, and showed signs of high spirit and lofty ideas. While they were consulting how it should be managed, the Chancas of Andahuaylas marched upon that city. Inca Viracocha, from fear of them, fled from Cuzco, and went to a place called Caquia Xaquixahuana, where he shut himself up, being afraid of the Chancas. Here he died after some years, deprived of Cuzco, of which his son Cusi had possession for several years before his father's death. This Inca was industrious, and inventor of cloths and embroidered work called Viracocha-tocapu, and amongst us brocade. He was buried in Caquia Xaquixahuana, and Gonzalo Pizarro, having heard that there was treasure with the body, discovered it and a large sum of gold; he burnt the body, and the natives collected the ashes and hid them in a vase. This, with the Inca's guauqui called Inca Amaru, was found by the Licentiate Polo, when he was Corregidor of Cuzco.
summary.zh: 維拉科查年事已高,不按繼位次序,竟立寵妃之子、庶出的印加·烏爾庫為儲。烏爾庫驕横傲慢,輕視他人,激起武人——尤其是嫡子們與猛將阿普·馬雅塔、維卡基勞——的憤慨。他們密謀阻止這樁繼承,暗中屬意三子庫西(即後來的印加·尤潘琪),因他溫和可親,又顯露出高遠之志。正當他們謀劃之際,安達瓦伊利亞斯的昌卡人進逼庫斯科。維拉科查懼敵,棄城而逃,退至卡基亞-夏基夏瓜納,閉門自守;數年後客死於斯,庫斯科早已在其子庫西手中。這位印加王勤於制作,是「維拉科查-托卡普」織金錦緞的發明者。他葬於夏基夏瓜納;貢薩洛·皮薩羅聞說隨葬有寶,掘墓得大批黃金,竟將遺體焚毀。土人收拾骨灰,藏於甕中;連同這位印加王的瓜烏基「印加·阿瑪魯」,一併被後來任庫斯科行政長官的波羅先生尋獲。

sensitivity.note: The flight that opened the way for Pachacuti; the body-burning by Pizarro is the conquest's violation of the ancestor cult.

passages.text: As Viracocha was now very old, he nominated as his successor his bastard son Inca Urco, without regard to the order of succession, because he was very fond of his mother. This Inca was bold, proud, and despised others, so that he aroused the indignation of the warriors, more especially of the legitimate sons... and of the valiant captains Apu Mayta and Vicaquirau. These took order to prevent this succession to the Incaship... They secretly set their eyes on the third of the legitimate sons named Cusi, afterwards called Inca Yupanqui.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 25 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 由於維拉科查此時已十分年老，他不顧繼承順序，指定他的私生子印卡·烏爾科為繼承人，因為他非常寵愛其母。這位印卡膽大、傲慢、輕蔑他人，因而激起戰士們的憤慨，尤其是諸位嫡子……以及英勇的隊長阿普·邁塔與維卡基勞。這些人著手阻止他繼承印卡之位……他們暗中屬意於第三位嫡子，名叫庫西，後來被稱為印卡·尤潘基。

passages.text: While they were consulting how it should be managed, the Chancas of Andahuaylas, thirty leagues from Cuzco, marched upon that city. Inca Viracocha, from fear of them, fled from Cuzco, and went to a place called Caquia Xaquixahuana, where he shut himself up, being afraid of the Chancas. Here he died after some years, deprived of Cuzco, of which his son Cusi had possession for several years before his father's death.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 25 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 正當他們商議該如何行事之際，距庫斯科三十里格的安達瓦伊拉斯昌卡人向該城進軍。印卡·維拉科查因畏懼他們，逃離庫斯科，前往一個名叫卡基亞·沙基沙瓦納的地方，因害怕昌卡人而閉門自守。數年後他死於此地，失去了庫斯科，而庫斯科在他死前數年便已由其子庫西佔有。

passages.text: He was buried in Caquia Xaquixahuana and Gonzalo Pizarro, having heard that there was treasure with the body, discovered it and a large sum of gold. He burnt the body, and the natives collected the ashes and hid them in a vase. This, with the Inca's guauqui, called Inca Amaru, was found by the Licentiate Polo, when he was Corregidor of Cuzco.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 25 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他被葬於卡基亞·沙基沙瓦納，貢薩洛·皮薩羅聽說遺體旁有財寶，便將其發掘出來，得了一大筆黃金。他焚燒了遺體，當地人收集骨灰，藏於一個瓶中。此物連同這位印卡的瓜烏基（神像），名叫印卡·阿馬魯，後來在波洛執事任庫斯科長官時被發現。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Kutiya Night: The Christmas Fortunes of the Village
title.zh: 庫提亞之夜：村莊的聖誕占卜

region.en: Russia, Christmas Eve (symbolic pin at Suzdal)
region.zh: 俄羅斯聖誕前夕（象徵性定位於蘇茲達爾）

period: Rite recorded 19th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part IV ch. 2

summary.en: On Christmas Eve the Russian farmer spreads hay under the cloth, hides behind the pot of kutiya to ask his wife 'Can you see me?', pours the first cup to the dead, and the girls read their marriages in the pudding — the whole year's fortune tried in one night of the old Koleda.
summary.zh: 聖誕前夕，俄羅斯農家在桌布下鋪乾草，家主藏於庫提亞鍋後問妻『可見我否』，先酹酒敬亡者，姑娘們以粥卜婚——一夕之間，以古柯列達之俗試盡全年運程。

sensitivity.note: Living rite; described ethnographically.

passages.text: Before the Christmas Eve supper the farmer walks the house carrying the kutiya, the ritual pudding of groats and honey, while his wife spreads hay over the table under the cloth — hay for the manger and for the beasts' luck. Grace is said with remembrance of the absent and the dead; the first cup of vodka is poured with a few drops falling on the cloth, and a portion of every dish is set aside for the deceased.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part IV ch. 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 聖誕夜晚餐之前，農夫捧著庫提亞——一種由麥粒與蜂蜜製成的儀式布丁——繞行屋內，他的妻子則在桌布下的桌上鋪撒乾草——乾草象徵馬槽，也象徵牲畜的福運。飯前祈禱時要追念不在場者與亡者；第一杯伏特加斟下時，有幾滴落在桌布上，而每道菜都留出一份給亡者。

passages.text: After supper all rise but the master, who keeps his seat hiding behind his pot of kutiya and asks his wife whether she sees him: 'No, I cannot' — 'I hope you may not see me next year either.' Prophecies of the harvest and the cattle are tried by the same art, and the girls tell their fortunes, the kutiya playing its part in every charm; the hay under the cloth is given to the animals of the house, and the hearth-fire is kept burning all night — the year renewed in one evening.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal (1918); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 晚餐後眾人皆起身，唯有主人仍坐著，藏在他的庫提亞罐後，問妻子是否看得見他：「不，我看不見。」——「但願明年你也看不見我。」收成與牲畜的預兆也以同樣的法術來試探，姑娘們則占卜自己的命運，庫提亞在每一道咒術中都扮演一角；桌布下的乾草餵給家中的牲畜，爐火整夜不熄——一個夜晚便使一年更新。

title.en: Oleg's Shield on the Gates of Constantinople, 907
title.zh: 奧列格之盾懸於君士坦丁堡城門，九〇七年

region.en: Constantinople, Golden Gate (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 君士坦丁堡金門（象徵性定位）

period: Event dated 907; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 907

summary.en: Oleg came to the Bosphorus with two thousand ships, put his men ashore and ordered the wheels taken off the boats so that the fleet sailed overland on the wind; the Greeks surrendered and paid tribute, and Oleg nailed his shield to the gates of Constantinople in sign of victory.
summary.zh: 奧列格率兩千艘船抵博斯普魯斯，令兵士上岸、卸下船輪，艦隊竟乘風陸行；希臘人乞和納貢，奧列格將己盾釘於君士坦丁堡城門，以誌勝利。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle legend; the land-sailing fleet is accepted as saga embellishment by historians.

passages.text: Oleg set out against the Greeks with his Varangians, Slavs, Chuds, and Krivichians — two thousand ships, the chronicle says — and came to the Bosphorus. He put his men ashore and commanded them to take the wheels off the boats; and when a fair wind had risen they spread sail on the land and bore the fleet overland to the Greeks — a marvel the Byzantine histories are silent on but the Russian chronicle keeps.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 907 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧列格率領他的瓦良格人、斯拉夫人、楚德人與克里維奇人出征希臘人——編年史說有兩千艘船——來到博斯普魯斯海峽。他命人登岸，並命令他們卸下船上的輪子；當順風興起時，他們在陸地上張帆，將艦隊由陸路載往希臘人處——這樁奇事，拜占庭史書隻字未提，俄羅斯編年史卻記載了下來。

passages.text: The Greeks sought peace and gave the tribute Oleg named — twelve hryvnas of silver for every oarsman of two thousand ships. He returned to Kiev with gold, silks, wines, and fruits of every kind, and as a sign of victory nailed his shield to the gates of Constantinople; the treaty of 911 that followed was sworn on the crossed arms of the envoys and sealed on Perun's hill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 907-912 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 希臘人求和，並獻上奧列格所索的貢賦——兩千艘船每名槳手十二格裡夫納銀。他帶著黃金、絲綢、葡萄酒與各式果品返回基輔，並將自己的盾牌釘在君士坦丁堡的城門上，作為勝利的標誌；其後於九一一年訂立的條約，則以使者們交叉的手臂起誓，並在佩倫山上加蓋印記。

title.en: The Storm of 860: Askold's Fleet Broken by the Theotokos' Robe
title.zh: 八六〇年風暴：阿斯科爾德艦隊為聖母衣所破

region.en: Constantinople, harbor of the Golden Horn (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 君士坦丁堡金角灣（象徵性定位）

period: Event dated 860; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 860

summary.en: Askold and Dir led two hundred ships against Constantinople while the Emperor was away at war; the Patriarch dipped the robe of the Theotokos in the sea, a storm burst at once and wrecked the raiders' boats, and only a few returned to Kiev to tell of the wind that came out of the church.
summary.zh: 阿斯科爾德與迪爾趁皇帝出征率二百船襲君士坦丁堡；牧首將聖母衣浸入海中，風暴驟起擊碎賊船；僅少數生還者返回基輔，述說那股出自教堂的狂風。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle legend; the robe-dipping rite of Blachernae is historical, the storm narrative is the Greek account retold.

passages.text: In the year 860, while the Emperor Michael was away at war against the Arabs, Askold and Dir came with a great host of Varangians — two hundred boats, the chronicle says — to Constantinople. The raiders ravaged the shores of the Bosphorus and besieged the city whose defences were stripped for the Emperor's campaign.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 860 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 八六〇年，正當米哈伊爾皇帝出征阿拉伯人時，阿斯科爾德與迪爾率領大批瓦良格人——編年史說有兩百艘船——來到君士坦丁堡。劫掠者蹂躪博斯普魯斯海峽沿岸，並圍攻這座因皇帝出征而防務空虛的城市。

passages.text: The Patriarch Photius, with the people, called upon the Theotokos, dipped her robe in the sea, and the weather that had been still and clear turned at once to a great storm; the waves rose and wrecked the boats of the raiders, so that only a few returned home to tell of the wind that had come out of the church. The chronicle counts the event as the first coming of the Rus to Constantinople — and the first lesson of what the city's Queen of Heaven could do.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 860; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 牧首佛提烏與民眾一同向天主之母祈求，將她的衣袍浸入海中，原本平靜晴朗的天氣頓時化為大風暴；波濤湧起，摧毀了劫掠者的船隻，以致只有少數人得以返鄉，述說那從教堂而來的風。編年史將此事記為羅斯人首次來到君士坦丁堡——也是這座城市的天上之后所能行之事的第一課。

title.en: Theodore and John: The First Martyrs of the Russian Land
title.zh: 狄奧多爾與約翰：俄羅斯土地的首批殉道者

region.en: Kiev (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基輔（象徵性定位）

period: Event dated 983; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 983

summary.en: Five years before Vladimir's baptism, when lots were cast for a human sacrifice to the idols, they fell on a Varangian Christian and his son; the father's answer — 'I have one God who made heaven and earth' — and their deaths at the mob's hands made them the first martyrs of the Russian land.
summary.zh: 弗拉基米爾受洗前五年，為神像擲籤擇人為祭，籤落於瓦良格基督徒父子；父親答『我有一位造天地之神』，父子二人死於暴民之手，成為俄羅斯土地的首批殉道者。

sensitivity.note: Hagiographic account; the lot-casting for sacrifice described critically, not endorsed.

passages.text: In 983, after a victory, Vladimir resolved to sacrifice men to the idols, and the elders and boyars cast lots: the lot fell on a Varangian whose name was Theodore; the Greeks called him such, but he was of the north country and a Christian. The crowd came to his house to take his son John, on whom the lot had fallen with his father.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 983 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 九八三年，弗拉基米爾在一次勝利之後，決意以人向偶像獻祭，長老與波雅爾們抽籤：籤落在一個名叫狄奧多爾的瓦良格人身上；希臘人如此稱呼他，但他來自北方之地，是一名基督徒。人群來到他家，要帶走他的兒子約翰，因為籤與他的父親一同落在了約翰身上。

passages.text: The father answered: 'This is not a god, but wood; today it stands, and tomorrow it rots. They do not eat, neither do they drink, nor hear nor see; there is one God only, who made heaven and earth.' The crowd burst in; the father stood at the entrance with John, and both were killed at the threshold by the pagans who yet knew not God. The chronicle sets their blood beside Olga's faith as the two beginnings of Russian Christianity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 983; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 父親回答說：『這不是神，而是木頭；今日它立著，明日便腐爛。它們不吃，也不喝，不聽也不看；只有一位神，就是創造天地的那一位。』人群闖了進來；父親與約翰站在門口，二人都在門檻處被那些還不認識神的異教徒殺害。編年史將他們的鮮血與奧爾加的信仰並列，視為俄羅斯基督教的兩大開端。

title.en: Svyatoslav's Word: 'The Dead Know No Shame'
title.zh: 斯維亞托斯拉夫之言：『死者無所謂恥辱』

region.en: Danube bank, 971 (symbolic pin at Dristra/Silistra)
region.zh: 多瑙河畔九七一年（象徵性定位於錫利斯特拉）

period: Event dated 971; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 971

summary.en: Hard pressed by the Greeks at the Danube, Svyatoslav called his men and said: 'Let us not disgrace the Russian land, but lie down here as dead men — for the dead know no shame; if we flee, disgrace will be upon us.' They fought again — and a peace was made that let the army go home.
summary.zh: 多瑙河畔為希臘人所困之際，斯維亞托斯拉夫召集部眾：『勿辱俄羅斯之土，寧臥屍於此——蓋死者無所謂恥辱；若逃，則恥加於我等。』眾人再戰——終訂和約，全軍得歸。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle oratory; Svyatoslav's 'the dead have no shame' became a Russian byword.

passages.text: Svyatoslav, the prince who slept on the ground with his saddle for a pillow and ate no cooked meat, was shut up by the Emperor John Tzimiskes at the Danube in 971, after three summers of war. His men were sick and hungry, and they begged him to make peace and go home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 971 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 斯維亞托斯拉夫是那位以馬鞍為枕、席地而睡、不食熟肉的親王；在歷經三個夏季的征戰之後，他於九七一年在多瑙河畔被皇帝約翰·齊米斯基斯圍困。他的部眾又病又餓，便懇求他議和返鄉。

passages.text: Svyatoslav called his men together and spoke: 'Let us not disgrace the Russian land, but lie down here as dead men — for the dead know no shame. But if we flee, disgrace will be upon us; so let us not scatter, but stand as one man.' The soldiers answered and fought again with desperate strength; and the Greeks, who had counted the Prince's army lost, offered peace, by which the Rus kept their ships and their heads and went home by the sea road.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 971; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 斯維亞托斯拉夫召集部眾，說道：「我們不可使羅斯之地蒙羞，而要在此如死者般倒下——因為死者不知羞恥。但若我們逃走，恥辱便會臨到我們身上；所以我們不要四散，而要如同一人般站立。」士兵們應聲再戰，以拼死之力奮勇廝殺；希臘人原以為親王的軍隊已全軍覆沒，此時卻提出議和，羅斯人遂藉此保住船隻與性命，經海路返鄉。

title.en: How the Flying Fish Lived First in a Tree
title.zh: 飛魚與樹中之海

region.en: Modaua, east of Wamira, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉以東之莫道阿（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'How the Flying Fish Lived First in a Tree'

summary.en: In the old days there was but dry land, for no man knew that the sea was pent up in a tree in the land of Modaua. A hungry dog found flying fish washed from a hole in the tree; the old wife Kemiana ate and slept sweetly; and when the Lavarata tribe felled the tree in envy of the Aurana men's feast, great waters rushed forth full of fish of all kinds — the sea itself, at first the colour of blood, blackened and salted by squeezed ebony scrapings.
summary.zh: 太古唯陸無海——海被封在莫道阿之鄉的一棵樹中。獵人尋犬，見犬食樹洞中漂出的銀白飛魚；老妻凱米亞娜食之酣睡，翌日精神煥發；眾人繼而日日取食。Lavarata 與 Aurana 兩部合力伐樹；奧臘納人砍累進食之際，拉瓦臘塔人暗中數斧將樹砍倒——巨水轟然而出，滿載百魚，直鋪到目力盡頭。水初呈血色；拉瓦臘塔人刮烏木屑入水擠汁，水轉灰黑，再擠，遂成湛藍而鹹——即今之海。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: In the old days there was but dry land, for no man knew that the sea was pent up in a tree in the land of Modaua, which is to the east of Wamira. It came to pass that a certain man had a wife, whose name was Kemiana, and she was old and therefore could not seek food for herself, but ever remained in the house, while her husband sought it for her. One day as he was thus hunting he called to his dog, which had been beside him. But the dog came not, and the man went to seek him. When he found him, the dog was under a tree eating greedily of some shining white things which lay upon the ground. Now, though he knew it not, the shining white things were flying fish which had been washed out of a hole in the tree by the waves of the sea inside; and some of the fish had lain there for long, and were evil smelling, while others were still alive.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How the Flying Fish Lived First in a Tree' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古時只有乾地，因為無人知道大海被囚禁在瓦米拉以東的莫道阿地方的一棵樹裡。後來有一個人，他的妻子名叫凱米亞娜，她年邁體衰，無法自行覓食，只得終日留在家中，由丈夫為她尋食。有一天，他正這樣外出打獵，便呼喚一直跟在他身旁的狗。但那狗沒有來，那人便去尋找牠。找到時，那狗正伏在一棵樹下，貪婪地吃著落在地上的一些閃著白光之物。原來，他並不知道，那些閃著白光的東西是被樹內海水的波濤從樹洞中沖出來的飛魚；有些魚已躺在那裡許久，散發著惡臭，另一些卻還活著。

passages.text: Now the man, doubting in his heart what this strange food might be, yet gathered some to take to Kemiana, saying, 'This truly is a strange food which I have brought thee. Yet thou art old, and if it bring death to thee the sooner what matter? It is better for thee to taste them than for a young person to do so.' Then Kemiana, being hungry, ate of the flying fish, and forthwith fell into a deep sleep. Nor did she wake in the morning when the sun rose, as did the others; therefore the children wondered if she were already dead that she yet slept when the sun was high in the heavens.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How the Flying Fish Lived First in a Tree' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那人心中疑惑這究竟是什麼奇怪的食物，卻仍舊拾了一些帶回去給凱米亞娜，說道：「我給你帶來的，真是一種奇怪的食物。不過你已年邁，倘若它使你早些死去，又有何妨？讓你嘗嘗它們，總比讓年輕人來嘗要好。」凱米亞娜因腹中飢餓，便吃了那飛魚，隨即陷入沉睡。次日太陽升起時，別人都醒了，她卻沒有醒來；因此孩子們心中納悶，不知她是否已經死去，否則為何太陽已高懸天上，她卻仍在沉睡。

passages.text: And they shook her until her eyes were opened. Then she said, 'Ah, what was this beautiful food which ye gave me, and which caused me to sleep so well?' Then the people having given her more, and seeing that she took no ill effect, ate of the flying fish also. And the people being many, the fish which the waves washed up each day were not sufficient. Therefore said the men, 'Let us cut down the tree, and so shall we eat in plenty of the fish.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How the Flying Fish Lived First in a Tree' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們搖晃她，直到她睜開眼睛。於是她說：「啊，你們給我吃的這美味食物究竟是什麼，竟使我睡得如此香甜？」眾人又給了她一些，見她並無不良反應，便也吃起飛魚來。由於人數眾多，每日被波浪沖上岸的魚並不夠吃。因此男人們說道：「我們把這棵樹砍倒吧，這樣我們就能有大量的魚可吃了。」

passages.text: The two tribes of Lavarata and Aurana set out to cut down the tree, and they took with them stone axes and food to eat when they were weary of their work. And first the Aurana tribe cut at the trunk of the tree while the Lavarata tribe made ready food, that they who laboured might eat when they were tired. Then the men of Aurana, having cut mightily into the trunk of the tree, sat down to eat. But as they ate the Lavarata tribe rose up secretly, and with few blows smote the tree until it fell. Then rushed forth great waters, and spread themselves forth as far as the eye could see, and they were full of fish of all kinds. And these waters were what men now call the sea. Now as the tree fell, it fell upon the men of Aurana who sat eating. And with such force did it smite them that they were rolled into the waters which surged before them, and thus they were carried far out into the sea, where they became the seafolk, Kuvokuvoe and Buabuaga, who dwell now amongst the floating spawn of the flying fish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How the Flying Fish Lived First in a Tree' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 拉瓦拉塔與奧拉納兩個部族動身去砍那棵樹，他們帶上了石斧，以及工作疲倦時要吃的食物。先是奧拉納部族砍伐樹幹，拉瓦拉塔部族則準備食物，好讓勞動的人疲倦時可以進食。後來奧拉納人奮力砍入樹幹之後，便坐下來吃東西。但就在他們進食之時，拉瓦拉塔部族悄悄起身，只砍了幾下便將樹砍倒。於是巨水奔湧而出，漫延至目力所及之處，水中滿是各種魚類。這水便是今日人們所稱的大海。那樹倒下時，正壓在坐著進食的奧拉納人身上。它擊打他們的力量如此之大，使他們被捲入眼前洶湧的水中，就這樣被帶到遼遠的海上，在那裡化為海族庫沃庫沃埃與布阿布阿加，他們如今棲居於飛魚漂浮的魚卵之間。

title.en: The Old Man Who Sent the Flying Fish to Sea
title.zh: 逐飛魚入海之叟

region.en: Wamira coast, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉海岸（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'How the Flying Fish Lived First in a Tree'

summary.en: When the sea burst from the tree the flying fish hid in the shore swamps, and the women fished them from dawn to dusk and left the gardens to choke with weeds. 'What shall be done that our women may leave this fishing?' said an old man. He went to the fish in the swamps: 'Only in your seasons shall ye be caught... If any search in vain for his food in the morning because the mouse hath eaten it, come ye not nigh unto him.' Then he cast a handful of broken coral at them and drove them into the heart of the sea — the marks of the coral are on a flying fish's head still.
summary.zh: 海自樹中迸出，飛魚躲入岸邊沼澤；婦人們自晨捕至暮，園圃荒蕪。老叟說：『怎樣才能叫女人們放下漁網、重操園務？我親自把這些魚送走，叫他們不再居於我們中間。』他到沼澤中對飛魚說：『你們到海中去吧。只在各自的季節方可被捕；若有人因鼠偷其食而無食下鍋，你們莫近他，叫他空尋一場。』說罷抓起一把碎珊瑚擲向飛魚，把它們驅入深海——至今飛魚頭上仍留著老人所擲珊瑚的痕跡。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: Now it came to pass that when the waters of the sea rushed forth, they carried many of the fish with them. But the flying fish hid in the swamps on the shore. There the women found them, and being thus nigh at hand they fished for them every day, and went never to the gardens to weed. Therefore weeds were many, and the men who went to work at the gardens, as of old, saw that soon the food would be choked. Yet still the women fished. When the first bird called to its mate they began to fish, and ceased not until the sun sank into the sea at even. Then said an old man, 'What shall be done that our women may leave this fishing and do their work once more? I, even I, will send these fish away that they be no longer in our midst.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How the Flying Fish Lived First in a Tree' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 後來，當海水湧流而出時，牠們帶著許多魚一同前來。但飛魚卻藏身於岸邊的沼澤之中。婦女們在那裡發現了牠們，因牠們近在眼前，便每日捕撈，從不去園中除草。因此雜草叢生，那些如往常一樣去園中工作的男人們，眼看食物不久便要被雜草掩沒。然而婦女們仍舊捕魚。當第一隻鳥呼喚其伴侶時，她們便開始捕魚，直到傍晚太陽沉入海中方才停止。於是有一位老人說道：『當如何行，才能使我們的婦女離開這捕魚之事，重新去做她們的工作呢？我，就是我，要將這些魚送走，使牠們不再留在我們中間。』

passages.text: Therefore he went to the flying fish who were yet in the swamps, and said to them, 'Go ye, and dwell in the midst of the sea. Only in your seasons shall ye be caught. If any be offended because he hath no fish, be not caught. Only if all share alike shall ye come into their nets. If any search in vain for his food in the morning because the mouse hath eaten it, come ye not nigh unto him. He shall search and shall not find.' Then he took a handful of broken coral from the ground and cast it upon the flying fish and drove them forth into the midst of the sea. And if thou wilt look at the head of a flying fish thou wilt see the marks of the coral which the old man cast at them when he sent them far from the land into the heart of the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How the Flying Fish Lived First in a Tree' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是，他走到仍留在沼澤中的飛魚那裡，對牠們說：『你們去吧，住在海的中間。只有在你們的季節裡，你們才會被捉。若有人因沒有魚而心懷不滿，你們就不要被捉。只有當眾人皆平均分享時，你們才進入他們的網中。若有人早晨尋找食物卻徒勞無獲，因為老鼠已將它吃掉了，你們就不要靠近他。他必尋找而尋不見。』然後他從地上取了一把碎珊瑚，投向飛魚，將牠們趕入海的中間。你若察看飛魚的頭，便會看見那老人將牠們從陸地遠遠送往海心時，向牠們投擲珊瑚所留下的痕跡。

title.en: The Talking Bananas
title.zh: 會說話的香蕉

region.en: Wamira coast, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉海岸（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Talking Bananas'

summary.en: Fishing parents hung a bunch of bananas in the house and bade them answer anyone who spoke, guarding their son against the hill-witch. Day by day the child called 'Au rava!' and the bananas answered 'U!' — until the day he ate the last banana, and silence betrayed him. The witch took his liver and left him wrapped in his mat; the father lured her down with fish and split her skull with his axe, then burned her house over her body.
summary.zh: 漁夫夫婦防山後食人巫婆加害幼子，切下一串香蕉掛在屋裡，囑它們替人應答。父母外出燻魚多日，孩子日日在杏樹鞦韆上吃蕉；巫婆窺探時問『有誰陪你？』孩子喊『Au rava（我的親人）！』屋內香蕉便應『嗯！』巫婆屢試皆然，不敢下手。直到孩子吃完了最後一根香蕉——巫婆再喚，屋內寂然。她撲上來取了孩子的肝，把屍體裹進小席放在屋角。父母歸來見兒身亡，父親磨利石斧，隔山喊『老太婆，給你魚來了』；巫婆貪魚下山探頭入門，一斧斃命；他背屍上山，砍倒屋柱，舉火焚屋，巫婆化為灰燼。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage. Cross-ref melanesian-sulka-tamus-pupal (abandoned-child cannibal motif).

passages.text: In the old days lived a man and his wife who had one little son. They dwelt in peace, and had but one fear. This was that some day the witch on the hill behind the house might come down and kill their little child. Now it fell on a day that the husband and wife desired to go fishing. To do thus they must needs leave their child behind. But they guarded against the witch by cutting a bunch of bananas, which they hung up in the house. Then they bade the bananas answer if anyone spake to them, and they set out. Fish were plentiful, therefore the man and woman built a little platform on which they smoked a great many of the fish they had caught. Now the smoking of fish cannot be hastened, so the little lad had many days to remain alone. Nevertheless he did not fret. There was a swing of jungle creeper hanging from the big almond tree in front of the house, and he spent most of the day there. Each day, too, he pulled a ripe banana from the bunch and ate it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Talking Bananas' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古時有一個人和他的妻子，他們有一個小兒子。他們安居度日，只有一樁恐懼。那就是有朝一日，屋後山上的女巫可能會下山來，殺害他們的小孩。後來有一天，夫妻二人想要去捕魚。如此一來，他們便不得不把孩子留在家中。但他們割下一串香蕉，掛在屋內，以防備那女巫。然後他們吩咐香蕉，若有人對它們說話，便要回答，隨後便出發了。魚很豐富，因此那男人和女人搭了一個小平台，在上面燻製了許多他們捕到的魚。燻魚之事無法加快，所以那小男孩有許多日子要獨自留下。然而他並不煩躁。屋前那棵大杏仁樹上垂著一條叢林藤蔓做的鞦韆，他大半天的時間都在那裡度過。每天他也從那串香蕉上摘一根熟了的來吃。

passages.text: Soon the witch, who often spied upon the child, began to think that he was alone. Then growing bolder, she crept down the hill and drew near to the swing where the child sat. 'Art alone, child?' she asked. 'Of a truth, no,' answered the child. 'Who are with thee, then?' 'Au rava (my kinsfolk),' answered he. 'I would fain hear their voices,' she said. 'Au rava!' called the child, and his voice was shrill. 'U!' answered the bananas from the house. Then the witch made haste back to her home on the hill, for she dared not harm the child if any grown persons were nigh. But the next day she thought upon it, and said in her heart that the voice might be that of a visitor. So, hungering for human flesh, she crept down the hill again. The child had been eating bananas every day, and there were but a few on the stalk. Yet they knew their work and fulfilled it. 'Who are with thee?' asked the witch once more. 'Au rava,' answered the child. 'I would fain hear their voices.' 'Au rava!' he called to the bananas.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Talking Bananas' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久，那常窺視孩子的女巫，開始覺得他是獨自一人。於是她愈發大膽，爬下山來，走近孩子所坐的鞦韆。『孩子，你獨自一人嗎？』她問道。『說真的，不是，』孩子回答。『那麼誰與你同在呢？』『Au rava（我的親族），』他回答。『我很想聽聽他們的聲音，』她說。『Au rava！』孩子喊道，他的聲音尖銳。『U！』屋裡的香蕉回答。於是女巫急忙回到山上她的住處，因為若有成年人在旁，她不敢傷害那孩子。但第二天她又思量此事，心中暗想那聲音或許是訪客的。於是，她渴望人肉，又爬下山來。孩子每天吃香蕉，那串上只剩下幾根了。然而它們仍知道自己的職責，並履行了。『誰與你同在？』女巫又問。『Au rava，』孩子回答。『我很想聽聽他們的聲音。』『Au rava！』他向香蕉喊道。

passages.text: Then alas! came an evil day. The little lad, being hungry, picked the last banana on the stalk, and ate it. When he had made an end of eating, he went out and sat on the swing under the almond tree. Not long was he there ere the witch came again, and asked the child who were with him. 'Au rava,' he made answer as was his custom. 'Then let me hear them speak,' said the witch. 'Au rava!' he called. But all was still, for there were no bananas left to speak. Then did the witch's eyes gleam, and she drew a little nearer, and said in a soft voice, 'Thy people may be sleeping. Call louder, child, that I may listen to their voices.' 'Au rava!' shouted the child. For a moment the witch stood and waited. But there was no sound. Then she knew that the child had lied, and that he was alone. Therefore she fell upon him straightway, and killed him, and took from his body his liver, which was what she had desired. Then she thrust leaves into the opening she had made, and closed the edges.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Talking Bananas' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然後，唉！不幸的日子來了。那小男孩因為餓了，便摘下那串上最後一根香蕉，吃了。他吃完之後，便出去坐在杏仁樹下的鞦韆上。他在那裡不久，女巫又來了，問孩子誰與他同在。『Au rava，』他照慣例回答。『那麼讓我聽聽他們說話，』女巫說。『Au rava！』他喊道。但一切寂然，因為已沒有香蕉留下來應答了。於是女巫眼中閃光，她稍稍靠近，用柔和的聲音說：『你的親人或許睡著了。孩子，再喊大聲些，好讓我聽聽他們的聲音。』『Au rava！』孩子大聲喊道。女巫站著等了一會兒。但沒有聲音。於是她知道孩子說了謊，他是獨自一人。因此她立刻撲向他，殺了他，從他身體中取出肝臟，那正是她所想要的。然後她把葉子塞進她所開的傷口，將邊緣合攏。

passages.text: Now it came to pass that in a little the child's father and mother returned from their fishing. 'Little son will like some fish,' said the father. 'Yea, truly,' answered his wife, as she went into the house. 'But look,' she cried, pointing to the mat in the corner, 'he is asleep.' Then did the woman gently shake the child by the shoulder, but he stirred not. 'Ah! lord,' she cried to her husband. 'Our child is cold and still. Come thou and waken him.' The man ran quickly and caught the child in his arms. But even then they saw the hole the witch had torn in his flesh, and they knew what had befallen him. The man gave the dead child to his mother, and went to get his stone axe. 'It is not sharp enough,' he said, and began to sharpen it until its edge was keen enough to cleave ebony. Then he called up the hill to the witch. 'Kaidurum (old woman), here is fish for thee,' he cried.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Talking Bananas' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 後來，不久孩子的父母捕魚歸來。『小兒子會喜歡吃些魚，』父親說。『是啊，真的，』他的妻子回答，一邊走進屋裡。『但你看，』她指著角落的墊子喊道，『他睡著了。』於是那女人輕輕搖了搖孩子的肩膀，但他一動也不動。『啊！夫君，』她對丈夫喊道。『我們的孩子冰涼而靜止不動。你來把他喚醒。』那男人趕快跑來，把孩子抱在懷裡。但就在那時，他們看見了女巫在他身上撕開的洞，便知道了他遭遇了什麼。那男人把死去的孩子交給他的母親，便去取他的石斧。『它不夠鋒利，』他說，便開始磨它，直到斧刃鋒利得足以劈開烏木。然後他向山上呼喚那女巫。『Kaidurum（老婦人），這裡有魚給你，』他喊道。

title.en: Kakukaku and Taureboga Swallow Their Necklaces
title.zh: 卡庫卡庫與陶雷波加吞錢赴死

region.en: Wamira district, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉地區（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'Kakukaku and Taureboga'

summary.en: Their widowed sister's careless word — 'thine uncles are but idly walking about' — shamed the brothers Kakukaku and Taureboga into seeking death. First they unthreaded their shell-money necklaces, mixed the coin with scraped coconut, and swallowed it so none should take it after them; then they went to war singing the death their sister begged them not to find.
summary.zh: 寡姊蕾柯塔一時氣話——『你兩個舅舅只會閒逛，哪會替你挖吃的』——深深羞辱了兩位兄弟。卡庫卡庫與陶雷波加商定赴死，卻先防人奪財：二人攀樹摘椰，刮肉盛碗，把貝錢串拆開與椰肉拌勻，全部吞下；又披掛戰飾，向甥兒留言『你母親的兄弟們聽了她的話，打仗赴死去了』。姊聞訊抱兒追來，喚他們回頭，又一同走向仇村，把孩子交託給樹下的老嫗。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: Kakukaku and Taureboga were brothers, and dwelt in one house with their sister Rekota, who was a widow. Now it fell on a day that the woman's little son, being alone in the house with his mother, cried to her for food, and Rekota, having none, said sharply, 'Hush thy cry! Thine uncles are but idly walking about. Dost think they would dig thy food?' And then, not wishing that the child should hunger, she took her pearl shell and string bag, and set out for the gardens to get food that her son might eat. Now while she was yet at the gardens Kakukaku and Taureboga returned to the house, and, seeing the child with tears on his cheeks, said, 'Why hast thou been crying, nephew?' Then the little boy, who could scarce speak plain, said, 'I cried for food, and Rekota said ye were walking about and would not dig to give me to eat. But she has gone herself and will bring us some.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Kakukaku and Taureboga' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡庫卡庫與陶雷博加是兄弟，二人與他們的姊妹蕾科塔同住一屋，蕾科塔是個寡婦。有一天，那婦人的小兒子獨自與母親在家，哭著向她要吃的，蕾科塔沒有食物，便厲聲說道：『別哭了！你的舅舅們只顧閒逛。你以為他們會去挖你的食物嗎？』隨後，她不願孩子挨餓，便拿起她的珍珠貝殼與網袋，動身前往園圃取食，好讓兒子有東西吃。正當她還在園圃之時，卡庫卡庫與陶雷博加回到了屋裡，見孩子臉上掛著淚，便問道：『外甥，你為什麼哭？』那小男孩話還說不清楚，答道：『我哭著要吃的，蕾科塔說你們只顧閒逛，不肯去挖東西給我吃。但她自己去了，會帶些回來給我們。』

passages.text: At these words the brothers' hearts grew hot within them, and taking counsel together they agreed to die, for who would care to live after being thus accused? But first they bethought them of their necklaces of shell money, and how they might see that none should take them after their death. To this end Kakukaku climbed a palm tree and plucked several young coconuts. One they gave to the child; the others they opened and scraped the flesh, heaping it in a wooden bowl. Then they unthreaded their necklaces, and mixed the shell money with the white flesh of the coconuts. This they ate, leaving none in the bowl. After they had thus done, they brought forth their war ornaments, and arrayed themselves as though they feared an enemy drew near, and they said to the child, 'Tell thy mother that her brothers, knowing of her words, have gone to die in battle.' And they laid spears on their shoulders, and set out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Kakukaku and Taureboga' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 聽了這番話，兄弟二人心中怒火中燒，彼此商議之後，決定赴死，因為受了這般責難之後，誰還願意活著呢？但他們先想到了自己的貝幣項鍊，尋思如何才能確保死後無人取走。為此，卡庫卡庫爬上一棵棕櫚樹，摘下幾顆嫩椰子。他們把一顆給了孩子；其餘的剖開，刮下椰肉，堆在木碗裡。接著他們拆下項鍊，把貝幣與潔白的椰肉拌在一起。他們把這些都吃了，碗裡一點不剩。做完之後，他們取出戰飾，裝扮起來，彷彿懼怕有敵人逼近，並對孩子說：『告訴你母親，她的兄弟們知道了她的話，已去戰死。』於是他們把長矛扛在肩上，動身離去。

passages.text: In a short space of time Rekota returned, and her son gave the message even as he had heard it. Her heart was sore when the news was told, and she threw down the bag of food, and ran out of the house with the child in her arms. The brothers had not gone far, and Rekota espied them as they began to go up a little hill. She called to them — 'Kakukaku ma Taureboga, Novumi Rekota; Matagei roboi' ('Kakukaku and Taureboga, I am your sister Rekota; Take your nephew in your arms').
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Kakukaku and Taureboga' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不多時，蕾科塔回來了，她的兒子便把聽到的話原樣轉告。消息傳來，她心如刀割，扔下裝食物的袋子，抱起孩子奔出屋外。兄弟二人尚未走遠，蕾科塔在他們開始登上一座小丘時望見了他們。她向他們呼喊——『卡庫卡庫與陶雷博加，我是你們的姊妹蕾科塔；把你們的外甥抱在懷裡吧』。

passages.text: Kakukaku, as he walked, said to his brother, 'Hark! That is our sister calling.' 'Nay,' replied Taureboga. 'It is now the softness of evening. It is but the kabaku singing ere it sleeps.' And they made as if to go on. But Rekota called again, and this time they knew it was the voice of Rekota, and waited for her to come to them, and Taureboga took the child into his arms and nursed it. Rekota said to her brothers, 'Whither go ye?' for she was much afraid when she saw the spears. 'We go to seek death, sister,' answered Kakukaku, sadly. 'Then will I go also,' quoth Rekota, and all went on together until they came to a large village. But though houses were many, men there were none. In the shade of a cycas palm sat an old woman, and round her played little children. Kakukaku asked them what had befallen the village that no men remained in it. 'Our fathers are working in the gardens,' said the children. 'Go then,' said the brothers, 'and tell them that Kakukaku and Taureboga and their sister are here, and have brought war!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Kakukaku and Taureboga' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡庫卡庫一邊走，一邊對兄弟說：『聽！那是我們的姊妹在呼喚。』『不，』陶雷博加答道，『如今正是黃昏的柔和時分。那不過是卡巴庫鳥在睡前鳴唱。』他們裝作要繼續前行。但蕾科塔又呼喚了一次，這回他們聽出那是蕾科塔的聲音，便停下來等她趕上，陶雷博加把孩子接過抱在懷裡撫慰。蕾科塔對兄弟們說：『你們往哪裡去？』她看見長矛，心中大為驚恐。『姊妹，我們去尋死，』卡庫卡庫悲傷地回答。『那我也去，』蕾科塔說道，於是一同前行，直到來到一座大村落。然而房屋雖多，卻不見一個男人。一株蘇鐵棕櫚的樹蔭下坐著一個老婦人，她身旁有孩童在玩耍。卡庫卡庫問他們，這村子遭了什麼事，竟無男人留下。『我們的父親們在園圃裡幹活，』孩子們說。『那麼去吧，』兄弟二人說，『告訴他們，卡庫卡庫與陶雷博加和他們的姊妹在此，帶來了戰爭！』

title.en: The Orphan's Revenge at Gavi's Burning
title.zh: 孤兒復仇與焚村

region.en: Wamira district, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉地區（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'Kakukaku and Taureboga'

summary.en: The brothers died as they sought, and the old woman, paid with 'what is found inside our bodies,' took back the shell money they had swallowed and raised the orphan. Years later a playmate's taunt told him whose fathers had killed his kinsfolk; and at night he closed every doorway of the village and set fire to the houses, sparing only hers.
summary.zh: 兄弟倆求死得死。老嫗向村人討『屍身內之物』為酬，收回二人所吞的貝錢，悉心撫養遺孤。孩子漸長，性情暴烈，常欺凌玩伴；一日有孩子反唇相譏：『你這是替死去的親人報仇麼？』他去問老嫗，得知殺他親人的正是玩伴們的父輩。當夜他潛回村中，關死每一道門，放火燒屋——只留老嫗所居那一間。全村盡燬，他心頭之恨方平。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage. Second half of the Kakukaku cycle.

passages.text: The children did as they were told, but on the path lay a fallen tree, and as they stepped over it the message they bore faded from their minds; and none that were with them could give answer. So they returned to the village and said to the brothers, 'Who are ye? We have passed over a fallen tree in the path, and cannot remember what ye gave us to say.' Then Kakukaku and Taureboga repeated the message, saying, 'Go, tell your fathers that Kakukaku and Taureboga and their sister Rekota are here, and have brought war! But when ye come to the fallen tree ye shall not all cross over at the same time, but let some of you tarry on the hither side, and repeat the words to those who have already stepped over.' Thus did the children; and when the men working there heard the message which had been sent to them, they seized their spears and hastened home to attack the strangers who had invaded their village.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Kakukaku and Taureboga' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 孩子們照著吩咐去了，但路上橫著一棵倒下的樹，他們跨過那樹時，所帶的口信便從腦中消散了；與他們同行的人也無人能作答。於是他們回到村裡，對兄弟二人說：『你們是誰？我們在路上跨過了一棵倒下的樹，記不得你們叫我們說什麼了。』卡庫卡庫與陶雷博加便把口信又說了一遍，說道：『去吧，告訴你們的父親們，卡庫卡庫與陶雷博加和他們的姊妹蕾科塔在此，帶來了戰爭！但你們來到那棵倒下的樹時，不要全都同時跨過去，讓你們中的一些人留在這一邊，把話複述給已經跨過去的人聽。』孩子們照此而行；在園圃裡幹活的男人們聽了傳給他們的信，便抓起長矛，急忙趕回家去，攻擊那些闖入他們村莊的陌生人。

passages.text: Kakukaku and Taureboga saw them coming, and Kakukaku said to the old woman sitting under the cycas palm, 'When we are dead save the child, and let him not be killed, and we will reward thee.' 'How may that be?' asked the dame, 'seeing that ye carry no goods or other payment?' 'Ask for what is found inside our bodies,' said Kakukaku quickly, for the men were close at hand. In a few moments all was over. The few spears the brothers had did not much harm, and death, which they had sought, came speedily to them and to their sister Rekota. But the old woman held the child firmly and yielded him up to none of those who would have taken his life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Kakukaku and Taureboga' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡庫卡庫與陶雷博加見他們來了，卡庫卡庫便對坐在蘇鐵棕櫚下的老婦人說：『我們死後，請保全這孩子，別讓他被殺，我們必報答你。』『這怎麼可能呢？』老婦問道，『你們既沒帶貨物，也沒帶別的報酬？』『向我們體內所藏之物求取吧，』卡庫卡庫急忙說道，因為那些人已近在咫尺。片刻之間，一切便結束了。兄弟二人僅有的幾支長矛並未造成多大傷害，他們所尋求的死亡迅速降臨到他們和他們的姊妹蕾科塔身上。但那老婦人緊緊護住孩子，不把他交給任何想要取他性命的人。

passages.text: It was now growing dark, and the bodies of the slain were soon cut up and made ready for the pot. The old woman said that she wished not for flesh to eat, but would fain have as her share what was found inside the men's bodies when they were cut up. The men gave her what she wanted, and she laid away carefully the shell money which the brothers had swallowed before setting out to meet their death. And she was faithful to her trust, and fed and cared for the little child left in her care until he was grown. Now as the child grew bigger, he grew also fierce and violent. Day by day, when playing with the village children, he would ever strive to be chief in the games, and desired that all should bend to his will. And it came to pass on a certain day, that he, as was his wont, was beating and stoning the children who pleased him not, and one bolder than the rest, cried, 'Why dost thou ever beat and ill-treat us? Is it thy vengeance for thy three kinsfolk who are dead?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Kakukaku and Taureboga' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此時天色漸暗，被殺者的屍體很快便被切開，準備下鍋。老婦人說她不要吃肉，只願分得眾人剖開屍體時在他們體內所發現之物。眾人便把她所要的給了她，她則小心收藏了那兩兄弟在動身赴死之前所吞下的貝幣。她忠於所託，餵養照料留給她照管的那個小孩，直到他長大。如今這孩子越長越大，性情也越發兇猛暴烈。他日日與村中孩童嬉戲時，總要爭做遊戲中的首領，且要眾人皆順從他的意願。某日，他照例毆打、以石擲向那些不合他意的孩子，其中一個較為膽大的喊道：『你為何總是打我們、虐待我們？莫非是為你那三個死去的親人報仇麼？』

passages.text: The boy was much perplexed to know what this saying might be, but he held his head high, and answered, 'It is no concern of thine. Hold thy peace.' Nevertheless, he hasted to the old woman who sat under the cycas palm, and asked, 'Dame, who killed my kinsfolk? Tell me, I pray thee.' And the old woman, ever ready to do his will, replied, 'The fathers of thy play-mates killed thy kinsfolk, my son.' When the child heard this he ran away from the village and laid a plan how he might avenge the deaths of his people. And at night he returned, and when all slept he closed every doorway, and set fire to the houses, sparing only the one wherein dwelt the old woman who had cared for him. So were all in the village destroyed, and the lad's heart cooled within him, for he had taken vengeance and was content.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Kakukaku and Taureboga' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那男孩聽聞此言，大為困惑，不知這話是何意思，卻仍昂首答道：『這不干你的事。住口。』然而他急忙趕到坐在蘇鐵棕櫚樹下的老婦人那裏，問道：『大娘，是誰殺了我的親人？請你告訴我。』那老婦人向來樂於順他的意，便答道：『我兒，是你玩伴們的父親殺了你的親人。』孩子聽了這話，便跑離村莊，謀劃如何為他族人的死報仇。到了夜裏他回來，趁眾人皆睡時堵住每一處門口，放火燒了房屋，只留下那照料他的老婦人所住的那一間。於是村中眾人盡皆毀滅，那少年的心也平靜下來，因為他已報了仇，心滿意足。

title.en: How Wakeke the Smallest Snake Defeated Arebo, King of the Sea
title.zh: 小蛇維克凱誅海王阿雷波

region.en: Wamira coast, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉海岸（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'How Wakeke Defeated Arebo'

summary.en: Arebo, King of the Sea, ate only betel nut and pepper leaf and rattled his lime gourd to boil any diver away. A man's sons begged a gourd and were refused — 'Would that I might eat your father's liver!' — so the father fed the snakes and led them to war. Given no portion, the smallest snake Wakeke was fed secretly by Motabawa; diving in the great snake's wake, he caught the falling sword, cut off Arebo's head, and rose with the liver in his mouth singing his spell — and the fish-host of Matamera was turned back by the cry of Toda the bower bird.
summary.zh: 海王阿雷波以檳榔與蔞葉為食，動輒以灰匙敲罐，使水沸騰，逼退潛者。有人遣二子討灰罐，遭拒且受辱——『恨不得吃你父親的肝！』父親怒而烹豬設宴，召群蛇助戰。最小的蛇維克凱未得分食，唯大蛇莫塔巴瓦偷偷以葉包食相贈。群蛇泛舟至海王上方，以椰漿平水窺其坐食；一蛇又一蛇潛下，皆被罐聲逼浮。輪到莫塔巴瓦，他囑維克凱隨後；維克凱乘其被氣泡上沖之際接住落劍，直撲海王，斬其首，剖其腹，口銜其肝浮出水面，唱起咒歌：『O korotoku Wakeke, Tiritiri remoremo!』群魚聞訊，由大魚馬塔美拉率領復仇而來；幸維克凱先已託 bower 鳥托達守候啼叫，魚群驚退——維克凱食其肝，如酋長般度過餘生。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: Arebo was fierce, and black, and great, and for his food ate only betel nut and pepper leaf, with which he took powdered coral lime out of a gourd by means of a long stick. One day, a man said to his two sons, 'Go down to the bottom of the sea to Arebo, and ask him to give you a gourd for me in which I may bestow my lime.' Therefore the lads went, as their father had told them, and dived to the bottom of the sea and sought for Arebo. And when they had found him, they told him their father's words. Then Arebo gave them a gourd and they returned to their father, and gave it to him. But he, looking on it, saw that it was poor, and he shook the lime stick backwards and forwards in it until it rattled loudly. And Arebo heard the sound and forthwith rattled his gourd also, under the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How Wakeke Defeated Arebo' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿雷波兇猛、黝黑而巨大，他的食物只吃檳榔與胡椒葉，並以一根長棒從葫蘆中取出珊瑚石灰粉佐食。有一天，一個人對他的兩個兒子說：『你們下到海底去找阿雷波，請他給我一個葫蘆，好讓我盛放我的石灰。』於是兩個少年照父親所吩咐的去了，潛到海底尋找阿雷波。他們找到他之後，便把他父親的話告訴了他。阿雷波便給了他們一個葫蘆，他們回到父親那裏，把葫蘆交給了他。但他一看，見那葫蘆粗劣，便拿著石灰棒在裏面前後搖晃，直到發出響亮的喀啦聲。阿雷波聽見那聲音，隨即也在海底搖響了他的葫蘆。

passages.text: Then said the man again, 'Go, my sons, and tell Arebo that he must give me a good gourd, for this one is but poor.' And the boys did so. But Arebo was very angry and said, 'Would that I might eat your father's liver!' Moreover, he gave them no gourd and drove them from him. Then was the man exceeding angry, and he thought how he might punish Arebo. So he killed a pig, and cooked it, and sent for the snakes that they might come and help him. And when they were come he fed them with the pig he had cooked and with taro. Now it befell that Wakeke, who is the smallest of the snakes, sat amongst the others, but was given no portion as were his fellows, for, said they, 'He is but small and needs no food.' Only Motabawa, the great snake, looking on him, pitied him and wrapped some food in a leaf and passed it to Wakeke when the others saw not the deed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How Wakeke Defeated Arebo' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是那人又說：『我兒，再去告訴阿雷波，他必須給我一個好的葫蘆，因為這一個實在粗劣。』兩個少年便照做了。但阿雷波非常憤怒，說道：『但願我能吃你父親的肝！』而且他沒有給他們葫蘆，反把他們趕走了。那人於是極為憤怒，思量著如何懲罰阿雷波。於是他殺了一頭豬，煮熟了，又召喚眾蛇前來幫他。眾蛇來到之後，他便以煮熟的豬肉和芋頭餵養牠們。恰巧瓦凱凱——眾蛇中最小的那條——也坐在眾蛇之中，卻不像同伴們那樣分得一份，因為牠們說：『牠那麼小，不需要吃東西。』唯有大蛇莫塔巴瓦看著牠，心生憐憫，用葉子包了些食物，趁其他蛇沒看見時遞給了瓦凱凱。

passages.text: When the eating was finished, the snakes arose and took wooden swords and launched their canoe, for they were about to fight Arebo. And Wakeke, fearing lest he might be forbidden, coiled himself upon the outrigger. Then did they paddle, and paddle, and paddle, until they floated over the place where dwelt Arebo at the bottom of the sea. And that they might better see him they squeezed coconut milk upon the water and made it calm, and so looked upon Arebo sitting below eating betel nut. Then one of the snakes took his sword and cast himself into the sea and sought to reach Arebo, that he might cut off his head. But as he was nigh unto him, Arebo rattled his lime spoon against the sides of his gourd and the water bubbled furiously around him, so that the snake was forced upwards and floated upon the sea again, having nothing done. Then did another try, and yet another, but Arebo ever drove them upwards by the rattling of his gourd, which caused the water to bubble.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How Wakeke Defeated Arebo' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 吃罷，眾蛇起身，拿起木劍，推舟下水，因為牠們將要與阿雷波交戰。瓦凱凱唯恐被禁止同行，便蜷身盤在舷外浮木上。於是牠們划呀、划呀、划呀，直到漂到阿雷波所居的海底之上。為了能更清楚地看見他，牠們把椰漿擠在水面上，使水面平靜，於是望見阿雷波坐在下方吃著檳榔。接著眾蛇中有一條拿起劍，投身入海，想接近阿雷波，好砍下他的頭。但當牠靠近他時，阿雷波以石灰匙敲擊葫蘆的邊緣，四周海水便猛烈翻騰冒泡，那蛇被迫向上浮起，又漂回海面，一無所成。接著又一條嘗試，再一條，但阿雷波總是以搖響葫蘆使海水翻騰冒泡，把牠們逼回上方。

passages.text: And now it was the turn of Motabawa. He said to Wakeke, 'Now is it my turn to try to kill Arebo. Do thou follow in my wake, and then will he have no time to drive thee upwards.' Now Wakeke had no sword as had the others, yet he feared not, and dived as Motabawa was sinking below the sea. Now as Motabawa was forced upwards by the great bubbles of water, Wakeke seized his friend's sword as he rose, and rushed upon Arebo and cut off his head. Nor did he then leave him, for he cut open his body and sought for his liver, which he held in his mouth as he rose. And as he floated on the water he sang his spell — 'O korotoku Wakeke, Tiritiri remoremo!' Then were the snakes confounded when they saw what so small a one as Wakeke had done, and they said nothing, but took up their paddles and set out for home, while Wakeke sat upon the canoe as a great chief.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How Wakeke Defeated Arebo' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 如今輪到莫塔巴瓦了。牠對瓦凱凱說：『現在輪到我試著去殺阿雷波了。你跟著我的蹤跡下來，這樣他就沒時間把你逼上去了。』瓦凱凱雖不像其他蛇那樣有劍，卻毫不畏懼，趁莫塔巴瓦沉入海下時也潛了下去。當莫塔巴瓦被巨大的水泡逼得向上浮起時，瓦凱凱在牠升起之際奪過朋友的劍，衝向阿雷波，砍下了他的頭。牠並未就此罷手，還剖開他的身體尋找他的肝，含在口中浮上水面。牠漂在水上時唱起咒語——『噢，科羅托庫瓦凱凱，蒂里蒂里雷莫雷莫！』眾蛇見瓦凱凱這般小的一條竟成就了此事，都驚愕不已，一言不發，拿起槳啟程返家，而瓦凱凱則如一位大首領般坐在獨木舟上。

title.en: The Wise Wagtail and the Five Wives
title.zh: 機警鶺鴒與五妻之厄

region.en: Wamira district, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉地區（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Wise Wagtail'

summary.en: A man whose throat was weary for lack of flesh meat lured his five wives one by one to the gardens to roast mourning-taro, and as each scraped it a wagtail sang from the bough — 'Takivim ke gibui! Scrape the food to be eaten with you!' — and each wife cried that the bird was singing she was to be eaten, and each was told 'Nay, woman; he doth but speak of the taro.' Thus he ate four, and came for the fifth.
summary.zh: 有夫五妻的男子久缺肉食，設計逐一誘妻赴園焙芋——喪儀之芋。每當妻子刮芋時，鶺鴒便落在樹枝唱道：『Takivim ke gibui!（刮那要配你們吃的東西！）』每個妻子都驚叫：『主人，鳥在唱我要被吃了！』丈夫每每撒謊：『莫怕，牠說的只是芋頭。』就這樣他吃了四個妻子，再喚最後一個同去。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage. Bird-oracle motif.

passages.text: In Papua a man may take many women to wife; this is therefore the tale of a man whose wives were five. Now it came to pass that on a day the man's throat was weary for lack of flesh meat, and he longed greatly for some. But the rains had not ceased, and the grass was yet green on the hunting ground, so he knew not how to gain that which his soul desired. Then in the night a thought was born, and he lay waiting for the dawn to break that he might do what he had planned. In the morning he arose, and called one of his wives, and bade her go with him to the gardens to weed the taro.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Wise Wagtail' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在巴布亞，一個男人可以娶許多女人為妻；因此，這便是關於一個有五個妻子的男人的故事。話說有一天，這男人的喉嚨因缺乏肉食而難耐，他極其渴望能吃些肉。然而雨尚未停歇，狩獵地上的草仍是一片青綠，因此他不知道該如何才能得到他心中所渴望之物。於是在夜裡，一個念頭油然而生，他躺著等待黎明破曉，好去實行他所謀劃之事。早晨他起身，喚來他的一個妻子，吩咐她與他同去園中為芋頭除草。

passages.text: This did she, and knew not what was in her husband's heart. But as she weeded, the man came to her, carrying ripe taro, which he bade her roast in the ashes of their fire. Now taro thus cooked is the food of those who mourn for the dead, and the woman wondered that her husband waited not to eat until the food was cooked in the pot at home. But she held her peace, and roasted the taro, as he desired.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Wise Wagtail' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她照做了，並不知道丈夫心中所想。但當她除草時，那男人來到她身邊，帶著成熟的芋頭，吩咐她將芋頭在他們火堆的灰燼中烤熟。須知如此烤熟的芋頭，乃是為死者哀悼之人的食物，那女人詫異丈夫竟不等食物在家中鍋裡煮熟再吃。但她默不作聲，照他所願烤了芋頭。

passages.text: And when it was cooked, she lifted a piece from the fire that she might scrape off the ashes and charred rind. As she did thus a wagtail flew to the tree in the shade of which she sat, and lighted on a bough over her head. And he sang, 'Takivim ke gibui! Takivim ke gibui!' ('Scrape the food to be eaten with you!') The woman hearkened to the song, and was much afraid, and cried to her husband, 'Dost hear, lord? The bird is singing that I am to be eaten.' 'Nay, woman,' lied the man; 'he doth but speak of the taro.' And then, being hungry, he called, 'Is the food ready for eating?' 'It is ready,' answered his wife. When he heard, therefore, that the food was cooked, he rose up and, taking his wooden sword in his hand, he drew near to the woman and severed her head from her body. Then, sitting down, he ate of her flesh, and with it the taro she had scraped after roasting it. Thus were the words of the wagtail fulfilled which he sang on the bough of the tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Wise Wagtail' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 芋頭烤熟後，她從火中取出一塊，好刮去灰燼與焦黑的皮。正當她這麼做時，一隻鶺鴒飛到她所坐之處蔭下的樹上，停在她頭頂的一根樹枝上。牠唱道：『Takivim ke gibui！Takivim ke gibui！』（『刮淨那要與你一同被吃的食物！』）那女人聽了這歌聲，大為恐懼，向丈夫喊道：『你聽見了嗎，主人？這鳥在唱說我要被吃了。』『不，女人，』那男人撒謊道，『牠不過是在說芋頭罷了。』接著，他因飢餓便喊道：『食物可以吃了嗎？』『可以了，』他的妻子答道。他聽聞食物已熟，於是起身，手持木劍，走近那女人，將她的頭從身上砍下。然後他坐下，吃她的肉，並配著她烤熟後刮淨的芋頭一同吃下。鶺鴒在樹枝上所唱的話，就此應驗了。

passages.text: Now the man, having eaten, would no longer work in the garden, and went home, saying to his wives that he was ill and for that cause he had returned while the sun was yet high in the heaven, but that the woman, who had set out with him, would sleep at the gardens that night. Then he bade them light a fire that he might warm himself and sleep. So well did he feign illness, that the women kept silence in the house and watched over him till morning. But on the morrow, he hungered once more for flesh meat, and called to his second wife that she should go with him to the gardens. She arose like unto the other, and the other women sent greetings by her to the first wife who, they thought, was yet alive. And at the gardens the man did even as he had done on the day before. Then came her husband, armed with his sword, and cut off her head and ate her flesh with the taro she had roasted. And after he had eaten, he returned home and told the same tale.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Wise Wagtail' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那男人吃罷，便不再在園中勞作，逕自回家，對他的妻子們說他病了，因此才在太陽仍高懸於天時便回來，而與他一同出門的那女人，今夜將在園中過夜。接著他吩咐她們生火，好讓他取暖睡覺。他裝病裝得極像，女人們在屋中默不作聲，守護他直到天明。但到了次日，他又渴求肉食，便喚他的第二個妻子與他同去園中。她像前一個那樣起身，其餘的女人託她向第一個妻子問候，她們以為她還活著。到了園中，那男人所做的與前一日完全相同。接著她的丈夫手持劍來了，砍下她的頭，並配著她烤熟的芋頭吃她的肉。他吃罷，便回家，說了同樣的一番話。

title.en: The Fifth Wife's Liver and the Falling Hills
title.zh: 五妻之肝與落山之咒

region.en: Wamira district, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉地區（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Wise Wagtail'

summary.en: The last wife knew her turn had come, and told her two children: 'If your father kills me my liver will travel until it reaches this house... Guard it carefully, for it will help you when you are in need.' It came rustling in the leaf wall; the children fled with it, and the hills fell at their cry — twice, thrice — until the third mountain buried their father and he perished in the heart of it. But in a perilous land they met the boar, and were devoured, strewing the ground with their bones.
summary.zh: 第五位妻子自知劫數難逃，囑咐一雙兒女：『你父親若殺了我，我的肝會一路游走回到這屋裡，你們會聽見它在葉牆中窸窣作響。好好保管，它會在你們危難時助你們。』肝果然遊回，被孩子收進木碗。兒女攜肝出逃；父親追至，孩子高舉肝臟呼喊『山啊，倒在追我們的人身上！』山應聲而倒，壓住父親；他掘土而出，再追；第二座山再倒；第三座大山傾覆，父親葬身山腹。可憐兄妹逃入險地，夜遇巨野豬，天明被其吞噬，白骨散落一地——亡母縱有靈肝，終未能救他們脫離獸境。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage. Second half of the Wise Wagtail cycle.

passages.text: Now this woman had two children, a boy and a girl, and when she was alone with them in the house she told them that she feared she had only one more night to live, for all her husband's wives were dead now save herself. Then she said, 'By this sign shall ye know that I am no more. If your father kills me my liver will travel until it reaches this house, and ye will hear it rustling in the leaf wall. Guard it carefully, for it will help you when you are in need.' The children wept bitterly at her words, but she bade them dry their tears ere their father should return, lest they should anger him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Wise Wagtail' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這女人有兩個孩子，一男一女。當她獨自與他們在屋中時，她告訴他們，她恐怕自己只剩一夜可活了，因為她丈夫的妻子們如今除了她以外都已死去。接著她說：『你們可憑這個徵兆知道我已經不在了。倘若你們的父親殺了我，我的肝會一路奔走，直到抵達這屋子，你們會聽見它在葉牆中窸窣作響。你們要小心守護它，因為它在你們有難時會幫助你們。』孩子們聽了這番話，痛哭不已，但她吩咐他們趁父親尚未回來時擦乾眼淚，免得惹他發怒。

passages.text: The next morning, she laid her face against the faces of her children, and bade them farewell, and set out with her husband to the gardens. And there it befell her as had befallen the other women. And also, her liver, even as she had said, went swiftly back to the house. The children sat waiting and fearing inside, and anon heard the low sound as of a lizard in the wall. They searched until they found what their mother had told them of, and laid the liver carefully in a wooden bowl.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Wise Wagtail' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 次日早晨，她將臉貼在孩子們的臉上，向他們道別，便與丈夫一同前往園中。在那裡，她的遭遇正如其他女人所遭遇的一般。而她的肝，也正如她所說的那樣，迅速回到了屋中。孩子們坐在屋裡等待，心中害怕，不久便聽見牆中傳來如蜥蜴般的低微聲響。他們尋覓，直到找到母親所告訴他們的那物，便小心地將肝放在一個木碗裡。

passages.text: Then the boy said to his sister, 'Our father will soon be back. It were well for us to fly far away, or he will kill us too.' The little girl rose up and made haste to leave the house, but she carried carefully the bowl in which they had placed the liver. Then they both sped quickly on the path which led to the hills. They had not gone far when their father came home, and sought for them that he might stay his hunger for flesh meat, but he could not find them. Then was he very wroth, and set out along the path to look for them. In a little space he saw them as they mounted a hill in front. So he made haste and drew near to them. But the children, turning as they reached the top of the hill, espied him below, and holding the liver in their hands, cried, 'O hill, fall upon the man who pursues us!' This did the hill, obeying the word of the children who held the liver in their hands. And the man was buried under much earth, and was like to be killed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Wise Wagtail' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是男孩對他的妹妹說：「我們的父親快要回來了。我們最好遠走高飛，否則他連我們也要殺掉。」小女孩起身，急忙離開屋子，但她小心翼翼地捧著他們放置肝臟的那個碗。接著兩人便沿著通往山丘的小路飛奔而去。他們還沒走多遠，父親就回家了，他尋找他們，想拿他們的肉來充飢，卻找不到他們。於是他勃然大怒，沿著小路出發去尋找他們。不多時，他看見他們正在前方攀上一座山丘。於是他加快腳步，逼近他們。但孩子們登上山頂時回頭一看，瞥見他在下方，便雙手捧著肝臟喊道：「山啊，壓在那個追趕我們的人身上吧！」山丘果然聽從了手捧肝臟的孩子們的話。那人被大量泥土掩埋，幾乎喪命。

passages.text: The children, when they saw that their father no longer pursued them, were glad, and their hearts cooled. But alas, they were in a perilous land. It was now towards evening, and they saw no house in the forest where they were. As they were about to lie down under a tree that they might sleep till the dawn, the boy sprang up from where he sat, and cried, 'See, sister, the boar, the boar!' Now the children knew it not, but the den of a fierce boar was but the cast of a stone from the tree in whose shade they sat, and it was time for the beast to enter his den there to pass the night. But there was now no time for them to run, for he was already rushing towards them, and his tusks were bare, and his bristles stood upright. Yet was there time to climb, and the boy and girl in great fear clung to the branches of the tree while the evil beast, with fearsome roaring, clawed below at the trunk.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Wise Wagtail' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 孩子們見父親不再追趕他們，便歡喜起來，心也平靜了。可是唉，他們身處險地。時近黃昏，他們在所處的森林裡看不到任何房屋。正當他們準備在一棵樹下躺下，睡到天亮時，男孩從坐著的地方一躍而起，喊道：「看哪，妹妹，野豬，野豬！」孩子們並不知道，一頭凶猛野豬的巢穴，就在他們乘涼的那棵樹投石之遙的地方，而此時正是那野獸進洞過夜的時候。可是他們已來不及逃跑，因為牠已朝他們衝來，獠牙裸露，鬃毛豎起。然而還來得及爬上去，男孩和女孩驚恐萬分，緊緊攀住樹枝，那凶惡的野獸在下方發出可怕的吼聲，用爪子抓著樹幹。

title.en: Why the Men of Gavi Will Not Eat Fish
title.zh: 加維人不食魚之由

region.en: Lake Wapogi, near Gavi, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞加維附近的瓦波吉湖（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'Why the Men of Gavi Will Not Eat Fish'

summary.en: The people of Gavi fished the teeming lake of Wapogi, not knowing that the magic eel Abaia lived at its bottom. One woman laid hold of the great eel and lost it; at the eel's word the young eels summoned the Water Spirits by night, and a dark rain-cloud rose and the lake drowned them all — save one old witch who had refused to eat, cast her fish-bone-eating dog into the flood, and read the depth of the water by her fire-stick's dying sparks. Up rose the feet of all her drowned people in the dancing waves; and from the survivors the Gavi people multiplied again — but they eat flesh, never fish, unto this day.
summary.zh: 加維村民在瓦波吉湖大肆捕魚，不知湖底潛有神鰻阿拜亞。一名婦人捉住大鰻又滑脫；夜裡，群小鰻奉鰻命召集水靈前來懲罰。黑雲聚頂，大雨傾盆，湖水暴漲，全村盡淹——唯一位老巫嫗得免：她早看出魚非尋常之物，拒而不食，把偷吞魚骨的狗拋入水中代罪，又以火把火花觸水即熄、觸葉復燃之法探知水退。翌晨她見波中忽然立起全村溺亡者的雙腳，方知族人盡歿。此後劫後餘種繁衍興旺，但加維人至今只食肉、不食魚——阿拜亞實在大，誰知魔法之力幾何。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira-region heritage. Local recension of the Abaia flood; cross-ref melanesian-massim-abaia-eel-flood.

passages.text: In the old days a man from that village went forth to hunt, and companion had he none save his dog. But though he walked far yet found he nought to kill save one wallaby. And it came to pass that as he walked he came upon a lake whose shores were round, and whose waters teemed with many fish. The name of the lake was Wapogi, and at the bottom lived the magic eel, Abaia. But this the man knew not, and when his dog reached the water and caught a fish in his mouth, the man feared not, but was glad to see so many fish. Yet he caught none himself, but, marking where the lake lay, he returned home. Then he roasted the wallaby and he and his people ate of it, and he told them not of what he had seen. But on the morrow he said to the people of Gavi, 'If ye will come with me I will show you where are many fish.' Then were the people glad, and they made ready to go with him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Why the Men of Gavi Will Not Eat Fish' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古時候，那個村子裡有一個人外出打獵，除了他的狗以外，他沒有別的同伴。可是儘管他走了很遠，卻什麼也沒打到，只獵得一隻小袋鼠。事情是這樣的：他走著走著，來到一座湖邊，湖岸圓整，湖水裡游滿了許多魚。這湖名叫瓦波吉，湖底住著魔法鰻魚阿巴亞。但這人並不知道，當他的狗到了水邊，嘴裡叼住一條魚時，這人並不害怕，反而高興見到這麼多魚。然而他自己一條也沒抓到，只記下了湖的位置，便回家去了。於是他烤了那隻小袋鼠，和族人一同吃了，卻沒有把所見之事告訴他們。到了第二天，他對加維的族人說：「你們若肯跟我來，我就指給你們看哪裡有許多魚。」族人聽了很高興，便準備跟他同去。

passages.text: When they were at the lake they laid down their food and bags in which were betel nut and lime gourds. Then women took their qadi, or hand nets, and began to fish. They caught many fish and prawns and eels, and as they caught them they laid them in heaps on the shore. And one woman, being more skilful than her fellows, laid hold on Abaia, the magic eel, but was not able to continue her hold, for Abaia, being very slippery, slid from out her hands. And now came the evening, when all rested. Yet had the eels not rested. All the small and young ones which were not caught, at the word of Abaia, carried the tidings of their foes to all the rivers, and led the Water Spirits to Wapogi as the night fell, that they might bring punishment upon the heads of the fishers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Why the Men of Gavi Will Not Eat Fish' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們到了湖邊，便放下食物，以及裝著檳榔和石灰葫蘆的袋子。接著婦人們拿起她們的卡迪，也就是手網，開始捕魚。她們捕到許多魚、蝦和鰻魚，一邊捕一邊把牠們堆在岸上。其中一個婦人比同伴更為靈巧，一把抓住了魔法鰻魚阿巴亞，卻沒能抓牢，因為阿巴亞非常滑溜，從她手中滑了出去。這時傍晚來臨，眾人都歇息了。然而鰻魚們卻沒有歇息。所有未被捕獲的小鰻和幼鰻，奉阿巴亞之命，把敵人來犯的消息傳遍各條河流，並在夜幕降臨時把水靈們引到瓦波吉，好讓牠們降罰於那些捕魚者的頭上。

passages.text: But it befell that a dark rain-cloud hung over their heads, and great and heavy was the rain which fell. And, moreover, as the rain fell so did the waters of the lake rise until the flood was over all the land, and the people of Gavi were drowned in the place where they fished. Nor did any of their number escape save one only, and she an old woman. And the cause of her life being spared was this. It so chanced that, being a witch, she had seen that the fish which had been caught were not common fish, but belonged to Abaia, the magic eel. Therefore she ate not, nor would she suffer her two dogs to eat. Nevertheless one struggled with her and snatched a fishbone from the ground, and swallowed it ere she could forbid him. Thus sat the dame under a tree at even, and watched the women as they fished.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Why the Men of Gavi Will Not Eat Fish' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不料一片烏黑的雨雲懸在他們頭頂，落下又大又密的雨。而且，隨著雨落，湖水也漲了起來，直到洪水淹沒了整片土地，加維的人們就在他們捕魚的地方溺死了。他們之中無一倖免，只有一人逃過，那是個老婦人。她得以保命的原因是这样的：她恰巧是個女巫，早已看出所捕的魚並非尋常之魚，而是屬於魔法鰻魚阿巴亞的。因此她不吃，也不許她的兩隻狗吃。然而其中一隻與她爭搶，從地上叼起一根魚骨，在她來得及阻止之前就吞了下去。於是這婦人傍晚時分坐在一棵樹下，看著婦人們捕魚。

passages.text: Now she knew that if the waters rose higher she must perforce be drowned, therefore she bethought her what she might do. And she remembered that one of the dogs had eaten a fish bone before she could hinder him, and she thought that for that reason perhaps the angry Abaia would cause her death. Therefore she cast the dog from her into the water below, and the flood rose no higher, for neither she nor the other dog had tasted of the fish of Wapogi. After a time the old woman knocked her fire stick again until sparks fell from it, and this time she knew that the waters were sinking, for the sparks fell on the leaves of Indian corn which grew below, and shone for a moment. And she waited and did as she had done before, and this time the sparks fell to the ground and died not at once. Therefore she knew that the flood was over. Yet she came not down from the tree until the day had fully dawned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Why the Men of Gavi Will Not Eat Fish' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這時她知道，若水再漲高，她勢必溺死，於是思量該怎麼辦。她想起有一隻狗在她阻止之前吃下了一根魚骨，便想也許正因如此，憤怒的阿巴亞會致她於死。於是她把那隻狗從身邊扔進下方的水裡，洪水便不再上漲，因為她和另一隻狗都沒有嘗過瓦波吉的魚。過了一會兒，老婦人再次敲擊她的取火棒，直到火星迸出，這一次她知道水正在退去，因為火星落在下方生長的玉米葉上，閃亮了一會兒。她等著，又照先前所做的一樣做了一次，這一次火星落在地上，沒有立刻熄滅。因此她知道洪水已經退了。然而她一直等到天完全亮了，才從樹上下來。

title.en: Vari, the Very Beginning, and Her Six Children
title.zh: 瓦里創世與其六子

region.en: The hollow of Avaiki, Mangaia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 曼加亞阿瓦伊基之殼（象徵性定位）

period: Hervey Islands oral tradition; recorded 1876 (Gill)

source.work: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, ch. 1, The Beginning of all Things (London 1876)
