passages.zh: 父親悲痛萬分，質問霍阿蘭尼為何如此羞辱地對待他的女兒，但水精為自己辯解，說是她執意要在月事剛過不久便下水沐浴，而他早已警告過她三次。父親身為皮艾（piai，巫醫），知道何處可尋得水精；他召集親族，告訴他們一聽見他吹響海螺，便須在所指之處挖掘。他潛入水精的地下洞穴，霍阿蘭尼就在那裡殺了他——但他在死前吹響了海螺；他的朋友聽見了，急忙挖掘，掘出這一人一精，殺死了水精，並把牠的骨骸棄於瓦卡波阿溪（Wakapoa Creek）任其腐爛。皮艾為何被殺？因為他不該獨自前往；人們展開這類行動時，總應有同伴相隨。

title.en: How Sickness and Death Came to the Warraus from the Water People
title.zh: 病與死自水族入瓦勞

region.en: Pomeroon River, Guyana (Warrau)
region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

period: Warrau oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XII 'Spirits of the Water', §190

summary.en: A fisherman wished for a wife from among the Ho-arännis; one appeared waist-high above the water and clambered into his corial. Her father below welcomed him on a live alligator bench — which is why the Warraus carve their benches in that likeness — and sent back a message: he must send his sister for the spirit's son. But the wife's one command was that at her moon-sickness she must stay in the hut, not be sent to the naibo-manoko: 'if I die, my father will have a spite against you, and send you sickness and death.' The Warrau women insisted on custom; she was found dead there the following morning. 'From now on sickness, accident, and death will come among your people from mine, and if any of your women-folk travel on water while moon-sick, my people will draw their shadows.' Before that time Warraus never had accidents or death; they had only moon-sickness. Later, forgetting the warning, he and his friends set out to sea in two big canoes; the Water People shot them down with round-knobbed arrows and unchained their sharks — for these people keep sharks as we keep dogs — which tore the drowned bodies to pieces. Thus the Water People punished the Warraus.
summary.zh: 漁者願娶水族之女；一女半身出水，登其舟。其父以活鱷為凳延客——瓦勞雕凳作鱷形由此始。妻誡曰：『吾經期毋送我出戶；若致死，吾父必遷怒於汝，降病與死。』族婦執舊俗送之出；翌晨已死。鬼父曰：『自今病、厄、死皆自我族入汝族；汝族婦人經期行水者，我必抽其影。』昔瓦勞無厄無死，惟有經期。後其人忘誡，與友泛海；水人以圓頭箭射沉二舟，縱鯊——彼等畜鯊如吾儕畜犬——碎溺者之屍。水人罰瓦勞如此。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: A man went fishing, and wished for a wife from among the Water People, the Ho-arännis. One day, while fishing, one put in an appearance waist-high above the surface and came quite close. 'Would you like to take me home with you?' was the first question she asked him; when he told her 'Yes', she clambered into his corial, and he took her home. She told him not to roast the morokot fish he had caught but to boil it, and impressed him that for the future he must never bring fish for her to eat, but only animals and birds.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §190; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有個男人去捕魚，想要從水族——即霍阿蘭尼——之中娶一個妻子。有一天，他正在捕魚時，一個水族現身於水面之上，齊腰露出，靠得極近。她問他的第一句話是：「你願意帶我回家嗎？」當他回答「願意」時，她便爬進他的獨木舟，他把她帶回了家。她告訴他，他捕到的莫羅科特魚（morokot）不可烤，而要煮；並囑咐他，今後絕不可再帶魚給她吃，只能帶獸類和鳥類。

passages.text: Next day she went with him in the corial, got into the water, and came up with a message from her father: he would be glad to welcome him below. The man was afraid, but she stood straight up in the water, which came to the level of her hips — 'Come along! Don't be frightened' — and he jumped in close by her side. She bent down, seized the head of a big water-camudi, clamped its jaws on the gunwale, and led the way below. He found himself in the house of his father-in-law, who gave him a bench to sit on which was really a large live alligator — this is how it has come to pass that we Warraus always use a bench carved in the likeness of that creature.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §190; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 翌日，她隨他乘獨木舟同行，進入水中，然後帶著她父親的口信浮上來：他很樂意在水下迎接他。那男人心生畏懼，但她直立在水中，水只及她的臀部——「來吧！別害怕」——他便跳入水中，緊隨她身旁。她俯身抓住一條大水卡穆迪（water-camudi）的頭，把牠的顎鉗在船舷上，領路往水下而去。他發現自己置身於岳父的屋中，岳父給他一張坐凳，那其實是一條活的大鱷魚——正因如此，我們瓦勞人（Warraus）至今總是用雕刻成那生物模樣的凳子。

passages.text: His wife warned him: when she was moon-sick he must not send her away to the naibo-manoko, but let her remain in the hut; if she died there, her father would send sickness and death. The Warrau women insisted on custom; she was found dead in the out-house the following morning. When the widower threw himself into the water and reached her father's house, the old man said: 'Why didn't you listen to my daughter? From now on sickness, accident, and death will come among your people from mine, and if any of your women-folk travel on water while they are moon-sick, my people will draw their shadows.' Before that time Warraus never had accidents or death. By and by, forgetting the warning, he and his friends started to sea in two big canoes: the Water People shot at them with round-knobbed arrows, both boats sank, and the Water People unchained their sharks — for these people keep sharks as we keep dogs — which tore the bodies of the drowned to pieces. Thus the Water People punished the Warraus.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §190; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的妻子警告他：當她月事來時，他不可把她打發到奈博馬諾科（naibo-manoko，經期小屋）去，而要讓她留在屋內；若她死在那裡，她的父親便會降下疾病與死亡。瓦勞婦女堅持遵行習俗；翌日清晨，她被人發現死在那間外屋裡。當那鰥夫投身入水，來到她父親的屋中時，老人說道：「你為何不聽我女兒的話？從今以後，疾病、災禍與死亡將從我的族人那裡降臨到你的族人身上；而你們族中若有婦女在月事期間行於水上，我的族人便會攝走她們的影子。」在那之前，瓦勞人從未有過災禍或死亡。後來，他忘卻了那警告，與朋友們分乘兩艘大獨木舟出海：水族以圓頭箭射向他們，兩艘船都沉了，水族又解開他們的鯊魚——因為這些人豢養鯊魚，如同我們養狗一般——鯊魚把溺死者的屍身撕成碎片。水族就這樣懲罰了瓦勞人。

title.en: The Bore on the River: Mother of Waters
title.zh: 河上怒潮：水之母

region.en: Berbice River bore, Guyana
region.zh: 蓋亞那伯比斯河怒潮

period: Arawak/Carib coastal tradition; recorded 19th-20th c., summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XII 'Spirits of the Water', §191

summary.en: The tidal wave, or bore, known as appapuru on the Berbice and other streams, is ascribed to the bad things of the deep: when the river becomes inconveniently low for them, they show their uneasiness by moving furiously about and thus agitate the river. The tribes on the coast usually give it some name signifying 'head of waters' or 'mother of waters', and in connection with this have many strange stories to tell of the Loku-kuyuha (people's spirit) mermaid, or 'watery mamma'. Wailak-paru, a creek on the right bank of the Potaro, is believed to be the home of Oriyu: the turbulence of the water as it runs into the Potaro is caused by water issuing from the body of that Spirit.
summary.zh: 伯比斯諸河之怒潮，土名阿帕普魯，皆歸於水中惡物：水淺不便其居，則狂動而撼河。濱海諸族名之曰『水首』『水母』，並有水靈洛庫庫雅（人鬼）人魚之異聞。波塔羅右岸之瓦伊拉克帕魯溪，相傳為奧里尤之居；其水入波塔羅之洶湧，即彼身中流出之水也。

sensitivity.note: Coastal Guiana tradition summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The tidal wave, or bore, known as appapuru on the Berbice and other streams, in certain of this colony's rivers is a case in point. Among the natives the popular explanation is that when this River becomes inconveniently low for the bad things of the deep, they show their uneasiness by moving furiously about, and thus agitate the river. The several tribes on the coast usually give it some name signifying 'head of waters' or 'mother of waters', and in connection with this have many strange stories to tell of the Loku-kuyuha (people's spirit) mermaid, or 'watery mamma' as they translate it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §191; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 潮波，或稱湧潮，在伯比斯河（Berbice）及其他溪流上稱為阿帕普魯（appapuru），在本殖民地某些河流中便是一例。在土著之間，流行的解釋是：當這條河低得令深處的惡物感到不便時，牠們便狂躁地游動以顯露不安，因而攪動了河水。沿海的幾個部族通常給它取一個意為「眾水之首」或「眾水之母」的名稱，並與此相關地流傳著許多關於洛庫庫尤哈（Loku-kuyuha，意即「人之靈」）美人魚的奇異故事，他們把牠譯作「水媽媽」。

passages.text: Wailak-paru, a creek on the right bank of the Potaro, is so called from a part of the human body, and is believed to be the home of Oriyu: the turbulence of the water as it runs into the Potaro is caused by water issuing from the body of that Spirit.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §191; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 瓦伊拉克-帕魯（Wailak-paru）是波塔羅河（Potaro）右岸的一條溪流，其名取自人體的一部分，據信是奧里尤（Oriyu）的居所：溪水流入波塔羅河時的洶湧湍急，乃是從那位神靈體內湧出的水所致。

title.en: Amanna and Her Talkative Husband
title.zh: 阿瑪納與多言之夫

region.en: Pomeroon district, Guyana (Carib)
region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍加勒比之地

period: Carib oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XII 'Spirits of the Water', §192

summary.en: Heated with the fumes and liquor of a big paiwarri feast, an Indian went to the pond to cool himself and was met by Amanna, one of the Okoyumo nation, who invited him into the water. Below the surface he saw houses, plenty of people, and many young women, and was offered drink; but Amanna took him straight to her old father, who welcomed him and instructed his daughter to look after him properly. His mother, tracing his tracks to the water's edge where they disappeared, mourned him a long time as dead. He visited her, went back to his water wife, visited again — and each time his little brother asked point blank whether he was living with the Okoyumo People. The third time, drunk, the brother pressed; 'Yes, I am!' replied the exasperated man, 'and this is my wife, Amanna, one of that nation.' Directly she heard this she made all haste to the waterside and jumped in, her husband in close pursuit; and as soon as he got below, her friends and relatives set on him and killed him for having mentioned her name and told people who she was.
summary.zh: 宴罷酒酣，一印第安人就池沐浴；遇奧庫尤莫族女阿瑪納，邀入水中。水下屋宇人群皆備；女引見其老父，父善遇之。其母循跡至水涯而絕，久以為溺死。夫三歸省；幼弟屢直問：『兄居奧庫尤莫族乎？』第三次弟醉而逼問；夫怒答：『然！此吾妻阿瑪納，其族之女也。』女聞言疾奔水邊躍入，夫追之；甫入水，其親族群起殺之——以其言其名、告人以其所自也。

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Heated with the fumes and liquor of a big paiwarri feast, an Indian succeeded in making his way to the pond where he intended bathing his skin and getting cool. On arrival there he was met by Amanna, one of the Okoyumo Nation, a very pleasant-spoken woman, who asked him to join her in the water. He demurred at first, but what with her repeated requests coupled with the attractiveness of her charms he ultimately consented, promised to be looked after, and went below: he saw a number of houses, plenty of people, and many young women, and felt quite content. Amanna would have none of the drink offered, and took him straight away to her old father, who gave him welcome and instructed his daughter to look after him properly.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §192; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一場盛大的派瓦里（paiwarri）宴會上，酒氣與酒液令他渾身燥熱，一名印第安人好不容易走到他打算洗淨身子、涼快一下的池塘。到了那裡，他遇見了阿曼娜（Amanna）——奧科尤莫族（Okoyumo）的一員，一位說話十分悅耳的婦人，她邀他一同下水。他起初推辭，但在她再三請求、加上她魅力動人的情況下，他終於應允，答應受人照料，便下到水中：他看見許多房屋、眾多的人、以及許多年輕女子，感到十分愜意。阿曼娜不肯沾半點奉上的酒，逕直帶他去見她的老父親，老人歡迎了他，並吩咐女兒好好照料他。

passages.text: In the meantime the man's mother had missed him from the convivial gathering and, following his tracks to the water's edge where they disappeared, mourned him a long time as dead. When at last he visited her he gave 'a walk-about' as his excuse, and on his second return found his mother and little brother drinking paiwarri; the latter questioned him point blank as to whether he was living with the Okoyumo People. 'How dare you ask me such a question?' — and back to the water he hurried, remaining longer than before. Amanna had in the meanwhile borne him three children; leaving them behind, he told his wife to accompany him on a visit to his mother.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §192; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 與此同時，這男人的母親在歡宴中發覺他不見了，循著他的足跡來到水邊，足跡卻在此消失，於是她哀悼他許久，以為他已死去。當他終於來探望她時，他以「四處走走」為藉口；第二次回來時，他發現母親與弟弟正在喝派瓦里酒；弟弟直截了當地問他，是否與奧科尤莫族人同住。「你竟敢問我這種問題？」——說完他便匆匆回到水中，這回待得比先前更久。阿曼娜在此期間已為他生下三個孩子；他把孩子留下，吩咐妻子隨他一同去探望他的母親。

passages.text: At the drinking party the little brother was absolutely drunk, and nothing would do but he must ask his elder brother as before whether he was living with the Okoyumo People. 'Yes, I am!' replied the exasperated man, 'and this is my wife, Amanna, one of that nation.' Directly the woman heard this she made all haste to the waterside and jumped into the water, her husband in close pursuit. As soon as he got below, her friends and relatives set on him and killed him for having mentioned her name and telling people who she was.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §192; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在飲酒聚會上，弟弟喝得酩酊大醉，非要像先前那樣再問哥哥，是否與奧科尤莫族人同住。「是的，我就是！」那惱怒的男人答道，「而這是我妻子阿曼娜，就是那一族的人。」那婦人一聽此話，便急忙趕往水邊，跳入水中，她丈夫緊隨其後。他剛下到水中，她的親友便一擁而上將他殺死，因為他道出了她的名字，還告訴別人她是誰。

title.en: Forbidden Words on the Water
title.zh: 行舟之禁語

region.en: Pomeroon-Moruca rivers, Guyana (Arawak)
region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍-莫魯卡河阿拉瓦克之地

period: Arawak oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XII 'Spirits of the Water', §194

summary.en: The surest way of offending the Water Spirits — and thereby getting caught in a storm, capsized, wrecked, or drowned — is to utter certain words strictly forbidden on a boat. Among the Arawaks of the Pomeroon and Moruca Rivers certain terms must never be employed but paraphrased: the gun becomes 'the foot', the dog 'the one with the teeth', the fowl 'load on the head', the horse 'round foot', the cow 'horn', the tiger 'the frothing one', the medicine-man 'the one with wisdom'. The Warraus had various words strictly taboo when traveling by boat; in Cayenne it is dangerous to name the streams and islands passed, even the medicine-men, on pain of rain, shipwreck, and some frightful monster rising from the deep to swallow the whole lot.
summary.zh: 冒犯水鬼最速之法，莫如舟中出禁語——立招風暴、翻覆、溺斃之罰。波默龍-莫魯卡之阿拉瓦克人行舟必諱言而易之：槍曰『足』，犬曰『有齒者』，雞曰『頂載』，馬曰『圓足』，牛曰『有角』，虎曰『沫吼者』，醫師曰『有智者』。瓦勞亦有舟中禁語；卡宴土人並忌呼所過川島之名，犯者降雨、覆舟，或有怪物自深淵出而盡吞之。

sensitivity.note: Arawak/Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The surest way of offending the Water Spirits, and thereby getting caught in a storm, and being capsized, wrecked, or drowned by way of punishment, is to utter certain words strictly forbidden under the circumstances. Thus, among the Arawaks of the Pomeroon and Moruca Rivers, there are certain terms which must never be employed when on a boat: they have to be paraphrased. The occupants of a corial will never be heard to use the term arcabuza (gun), but speak of a gun as kataroro (foot, referring to the stock); they talk of kariro (the one with the teeth) instead of perro (dog); of kanakara-shiro (load on the head, the cock's comb) instead of gallina (fowl); of akwadoa-kotiro (round foot) instead of caballo (horse); of kakwaro (horn) instead of vaca (cow); of chedoa (frothing, in reference to its snarling) instead of aroa (tiger); of katau-chi (the one with wisdom) instead of the medicine-man.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §194; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 要觸怒水靈，因而在暴風雨中遭殃，並作為懲罰而被掀翻、失事或溺斃，最穩妥的辦法莫過於在此等情況下說出某些嚴格禁忌的詞語。因此，在波梅隆河（Pomeroon）與莫魯卡河（Moruca）一帶的阿拉瓦克人（Arawaks）之中，有些詞語在船上絕不可用：必須換一種說法。獨木舟上的人從不會被聽見使用 arcabuza（槍）這個詞，而是把槍稱作 kataroro（腳，指槍托）；他們不說 perro（狗），而說 kariro（有牙的那個）；不說 gallina（家禽），而說 kanakara-shiro（頭上的負擔，即雞冠）；不說 caballo（馬），而說 akwadoa-kotiro（圓腳）；不說 vaca（牛），而說 kakwaro（角）；不說 aroa（虎），而說 chedoa（起白沫，指其咆哮）；不說巫醫，而說 katau-chi（有智慧的那個）。

passages.text: The Warraus also had various words strictly taboo when traveling by boat. The same holds good for Cayenne, where the superstitious Indians take care not to speak of several things by their right names: a rock must be described as 'that which is hard', a lizard as 'that which has a long tail'. It is dangerous also to name the streams and little islands passed en route; even the medicine-men may not be mentioned as such — infringement of this rule will cause at least rain to fall, besides exposing one to shipwreck and to the likelihood of some frightful monster rising from out the deep and swallowing the whole lot.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §194; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 瓦勞人（Warraus）在乘船出行時也有種種嚴格禁忌的詞語。卡宴（Cayenne）一帶亦然，那裡迷信的印第安人小心避免直呼若干事物的本名：岩石必須說成「堅硬之物」，蜥蜴必須說成「長尾巴之物」。說出沿途經過的溪流與小島之名同樣危險；甚至巫醫也不可直稱其名——違犯此規至少會招來降雨，此外還會使人面臨船難，並可能使某種可怕的怪物從深處升起，把整船人一併吞下。

title.en: Okohi's Last Journey: the Origin of the Sun's Warmth
title.zh: 奧科希末程：日光之暖所自

region.en: Pomeroon River, Guyana (Warrau)
region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

period: Warrau oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XIII 'Spirits of the Sky', §197

summary.en: At the water-side Waiamari's uncle's young wife tried to seduce him; he shouted 'Bilili! Kwahoro!' — 'Incest! Shame!' — and went to stay with his elder uncle Okohi, whose name among the Warraus means the hottest part of the day, the warmth of the sun. Accused and fought, the nephew was taken by Okohi on a long journey in a canoe painted with the sign of the Sun on the bows and a man and moon at the stern, across a big sea, to the house of Assawako, where the youth brought armadillo flesh and played the kahabassa beautifully. When uncle and nephew got back to their own country, old Okohi bathed, seated himself in his hammock, gathered all his family around and spoke: 'When I was young, I could stand traveling day after day, as I have just done; but I am old now, and this is my last journey.' So saying, his head burst, and out of it there came the Sun's warmth and heat.
summary.zh: 瓦伊阿馬里之嬸於水邊誘之；彼呼『亂倫！可恥！』而投長叔奧科希——其名即一日最熱之時，日之暖也。叔姪受誣而鬥；奧科希攜姪遠行，舟首畫日、尾畫人月，越大海至阿薩瓦科之舍，獵犰狳、奏卡哈巴薩之笛。既歸，老人沐浴坐吊床，聚家人而言：『昔我能日日行如今日；今老矣，此吾末程也。』言畢，頭裂，日光之暖與熱自中而出。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Waiamari was the name of a young fellow staying at the house of his uncle. One day he went down to the water-side to bathe; hearing a splash behind him he saw his uncle's young wife chasing him in the water. She whispered 'Don't you want me?' — but instead of replying quietly Waiamari loudly upbraided her by shouting 'Bilili! Kwahoro!' (Incest! Shame!), and the girl drew back. The couple got out of the water; the boy passed on to stay with his elder uncle, Okohi, at whose place he slept that night — for okohi among the Warraus means the hottest part of the day, referring to the warmth and heat of the sun.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §197; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 瓦亞馬里（Waiamari）是一個寄住在叔父家中的年輕小夥子的名字。有一天，他下到水邊洗澡；聽見身後有水花聲，他看見叔父的年輕妻子在水中追著他。她低聲說：「你不想要我嗎？」——但瓦亞馬里非但沒有輕聲回答，反而高聲斥責她，喊道：「比利利！夸霍羅！」（亂倫！可恥！），那姑娘便退了回去。這對男女從水中出來；那少年轉去與他的大伯父奧科希（Okohi）同住，當夜就睡在他那裡——因為在瓦勞人（Warraus）之中，okohi 意指一日之中最炎熱的時分，指的是太陽的溫暖與酷熱。

passages.text: The aunt's husband reproached his nephew for attempted improper conduct and fought him twice, being thrown down each time, until Okohi interfered: 'Boy! That will do.' To save further strife he took Waiamari away with him on his journey, and the youngster painted the sign of the Sun on the bows of the waija canoe, and at the stern a man and a moon — as the Indians' canoes were decorated even up to recent times. They crossed a big sea, the paddle-blades sweeping so that the water sang 'Wau-u! Wau-u!', and landed at the house of the pretty Assawako, where the youth shot a quakeful of armadillo flesh and played the kahabassa so beautifully it sang 'Waru-huru-tia'.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §197; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 嬸母的丈夫責備他的姪兒企圖行為不端，並與他打了兩次架，每次都被摔倒，直到奧科希出面干預：「孩子！夠了。」為了避免進一步的爭鬥，他帶著瓦亞馬里一同上路；那少年在瓦伊哈（waija）獨木舟的船首畫上太陽的記號，在船尾畫上一個男人和一個月亮——印第安人的獨木舟直到晚近時代仍是這樣裝飾的。他們渡過一片大海，槳葉划動，使水唱出「哇嗚！哇嗚！」之聲，最後在美麗的阿薩瓦科（Assawako）的屋子登岸；那少年在那裡射得一震（quakeful）的犰狳肉，又彈奏卡哈巴薩（kahabassa），彈得美妙極了，使它唱出「瓦魯胡魯提亞」（Waru-huru-tia）。

passages.text: When at last uncle and nephew got back to their own country, old Okohi bathed his skin, and after seating himself in his hammock gathered all his family around and spoke to them as follows: 'When I was young, I could stand traveling day after day, as I have just done, but I am old now, and this is my last journey.' So saying, his head burst, and out of it there came the Sun's warmth and heat.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §197; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當叔父與姪兒終於回到自己的國土時，老奧科希洗淨了自己的皮膚，坐進吊床之後，把全家人都召集到身邊，對他們這樣說道：「我年輕的時候，能夠經受一天又一天的旅行，就像我剛剛所做的那樣，但我現在老了，這是我最後一次的旅程。」說著，他的頭便裂開了，從中湧出了太陽的溫暖與酷熱。

title.en: How the Moon Got His Dirty Face
title.zh: 月之垢面何來

region.en: Pomeroon River, Guyana (Arawak/Warrau)
region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河阿拉瓦克-瓦勞之地

period: Arawak-Warrau oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XIII 'Spirits of the Sky', §198

summary.en: Long ago a brother and his sister were living by themselves. Every night after dark someone used to come and fondle and caress the sister — attentions she was far from averse to, but very curious to identify. She therefore blackened her hands with the soot from the bottom of the pepper-pot (the Warraus say with humatímba, the blue paint of the Caribs), and when her lover came that evening smeared her hands over his face. When day dawned she learned it was her own brother who had taken advantage of her. She abused him roundly and told the neighbors, who spread the story far and wide, till everybody shunned him. He is now the Moon, and the marks still recognizable on his face are those his sister imprinted with the soot years ago. Even to this day women do not trust him.
summary.zh: 昔兄妹獨居；每夜有人撫其妹，妹樂之而欲知其人。乃以椒釜底之煙墨手（瓦勞言加勒比人之藍 paint），夜抹其面。天明乃知亂之者即己兄。大罵而告鄰里，事播四方，眾皆棄之。彼今即月也，面上可辨之斑，即昔妹以煙所印者也。至今婦人不信之。

sensitivity.note: Arawak/Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically. Twin/incest-parallel to sky-body origin stories in other traditions.

passages.text: Long ago a brother and his sister were living by themselves. Every night after dark some one used to come and fondle and caress the sister, attentions which she was very far from being averse to, but she was very curious to discover who her unseen visitor was. She could never find out. She therefore blackened her hands one day with the soot from the bottom of the pepper-pot, and when her lover came that evening, she smeared her hands over his face.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §198; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 很久以前，一個哥哥和他的妹妹獨自住在一起。每天天黑之後，總有什麼人前來撫弄並愛撫那妹妹，而她對這些殷勤絕非不樂意，但她非常好奇，想知道她那看不見的訪客究竟是誰。她始終查不出來。於是有一天，她用胡椒罐底的煤煙把自己的手塗黑，當那天傍晚她的情人到來時，她便用雙手抹了他的臉。

passages.text: When day dawned she thus came to learn that it was her own brother who had taken advantage of her. She was extremely angry, abused him roundly, and told the neighbors, who in turn spread the story of his conduct far and wide. The result was that everybody shunned him, and he became at last so thoroughly ashamed of himself that he declared he would keep away from everyone and live by himself. He is now the Moon, and the marks which can still be recognized on his face are those which his sister imprinted with the soot years ago. Even to this day women do not trust him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §198; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天亮之後，她這才得知，佔了她便宜的竟是自己的哥哥。她極為憤怒，狠狠地辱罵他，又告訴了鄰居，鄰居們又把他的行徑四處傳揚開來。結果是人人見了他都避而遠之，他最後羞愧得無地自容，便宣稱要遠離所有人，獨自過活。他如今就是月亮，而他臉上至今仍可辨認的痕跡，就是多年前他妹妹用煤煙印上去的。直到今日，女人們仍不信任他。

title.en: The Legend of Bat Mountain
title.zh: 蝙蝠山傳說

region.en: Murapa-yeng, Pakaraima Range, Guyana
region.zh: 蓋亞那帕卡賴馬山脈穆拉帕山

period: Makusi tradition recorded by Schomburgk; summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XIII 'Spirits of the Sky', §203A

summary.en: A long, long while ago an immense Bat lived on Murapa-yeng — Bat Mountain — and spread fear and terror among the Makusis. As soon as the sun had sunk in the west the huge creature swept down upon the happy homes and carried off anyone found out of doors to be devoured; not a night passed without an abduction, and the tribe's entire annihilation seemed at hand. The medicine-man exorcised it in vain. To prevent the total destruction of her tribe an old woman arose and declared herself ready to sacrifice herself: stationing herself at night in the middle of the village with a covered fire-stick, she was seized by the creature's frightful claws and carried aloft — where she uncovered the fire-stick, and like the Sun throwing its rays backward (the Comet), the streak of light showed the people the direction of the creature's nest. Next morning the high flames from the burning nest upon the very mountain showed where to go; they succeeded in killing it, and even now immense heaps of bleached bones are to be found there.
summary.zh: 上古穆拉帕山有巨蝠，日沒即掠瓦勞人而出，夜夜擄人食之，族滅在即。醫師禳之無效。一老嫗自請犧牲：夜立村央，懷藏火棒；為蝠巨爪所攫，升空時揭棒——光芒如日之曳尾（即彗星），示人其巢之向。翌晨山巢烈焰騰空，眾尋至而誅之。至今山上有白骨巨堆。

sensitivity.note: Makusi tradition recorded by Schomburgk, summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: A long, long while ago an immense Bat lived on the mountain and spread fear and terror among the Makusis. As soon as the Sun had sunk in the west, the huge creature left its unknown dwelling, swept down upon the happy homes, and, swift as an arrow, pounced upon and carried off anyone whom it found out of doors: it carried the individual in its powerful claws up to its unknown nest and there devoured him. Not a night passed without an abduction, the tribe daily numbered less, and its entire annihilation seemed at hand. The medicine-man exorcised the Spirit; it returned again: the men went to discover the residence of the cursed murderer, but they did not find it — Makunaima was not with them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §203A (from Schomburgk); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 很久很久以前，一隻巨大的蝙蝠住在山上，在馬庫西人（Makusis）中間散布恐懼與驚駭。太陽一沉入西方，這龐然大物便離開它那不為人知的居所，撲向那些幸福的家庭，快如箭矢，猛撲向任何被它發現在戶外的人，將其攫走：它用強有力的爪子把那人帶上它那不為人知的巢穴，在那裡將他吞食。沒有一夜不發生擄人事件，部落的人數日日減少，全族的滅絕似乎近在眼前。巫醫驅逐了那精靈；它卻又回來了：男人們前去尋找那該死的兇手居住的地方，卻沒有找到——馬庫奈馬（Makunaima）沒有和他們在一起。

passages.text: To prevent the total destruction of her tribe an old woman arose and declared herself ready to sacrifice herself for the good of her nation. When night fell she stationed herself, with a covered fire-stick, in the middle of the village while the remainder of the people crouched in terror within their houses. The fluttering of the wings is heard, and the heroine, seized in the creature's frightful claws, is carried aloft to the charnel house. She now uncovers the fire-stick, which — like the Sun throwing its rays backward, the Comet — shows by the streak of light thus produced the direction that the people must follow to find the mortuary house of their brethren. The high flames of fire from the burning nest upon this very mountain showed the folk next morning where to go: they succeeded in killing the creature. History does not say whether the old woman lost her life in this heroic deed; but even now immense heaps of bleached bones are to be found there.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §203A (from Schomburgk); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 為了防止她的部落遭到徹底毀滅，一位老婦人挺身而出，宣告自己願意為了族人的福祉犧牲性命。夜幕降臨時，她帶著一根藏著火種的火棍，站到村子中央，其餘的人則驚恐地蜷縮在屋內。眾人聽見翅膀撲動的聲音，那位女英雄被那生物可怕的爪子攫住，高高帶往那座藏骨之屋。她這時揭開火棍——如同太陽向後投射光芒，如同彗星——藉由如此產生的那道亮光，指出族人必須遵循的方向，以找到他們同胞的停屍之所。就在這座山上，燃燒的巢穴所噴出的熊熊烈焰，翌日清晨向眾人指明了該往何處去：他們成功殺死了那生物。史載並未說明那位老婦人是否在這樁英勇事蹟中喪命；但即使到了今日，那裡仍可見到成堆巨大的白骨。

title.en: Okona-kura: the Morning Star Left in the Hole
title.zh: 奧科納庫拉：留在穴中之晨星

region.en: Pomeroon River, Guyana (Warrau)
region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

period: Warrau oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XIII 'Spirits of the Sky', §204

summary.en: The Warraus on the Pomeroon call the Morning Star Okona-kura. She it was who stuck in the hole when her people first came down from above the skies to populate the earth — the stout woman who closed the way home forever. The Makusis speak of the Evening Star as Kai-wono, wife of the Moon, because she is to be seen in his near neighborhood and shines more brightly than all the other stars. The Indians of the Casiquiare believed that the dew which falls by night was the spittle of the stars; the Caribs ascribed it to the urination of the stars.
summary.zh: 波默龍瓦勞人稱晨星曰奧科納庫拉。族人初自天下降而殖地時，即彼卡於穴中——絕其歸路之肥婦也。馬庫希人謂昏星為月之妻凱沃諾，以恆近月而光勝群星。卡西基亞雷土人謂夜露乃星之唾；加勒比人謂乃星之溺。

sensitivity.note: Guiana oral tradition summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically. Cross-reference to the Warau sky-descent record.

passages.text: The Warraus here on the Pomeroon call the Morning Star Okona-kura. She it was who stuck in the hole when her people first came down from above the skies to populate the earth. The Makusis speak of the Evening Star as Kai-wono, wife of the Moon, because she is to be seen in his near neighborhood, and also on account of her shining more brightly than all the other stars.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §204; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 波梅隆河畔的瓦勞人稱晨星為奧科納—庫拉。正是她，在她的族人最初從天上降下、繁衍於大地之時，卡在了那個洞裡。馬庫西人則稱晚星為凱—沃諾，即月亮之妻，因為人們總能在月亮近旁看見她，也因為她比所有其他星辰都更加明亮。

passages.text: According to Father Gili, the Indians of the Casiquiare believed that the dew which falls by night was the spittle of the stars, a belief similar to that reported of the Makusis. The Caribs ascribed it to the urination of the stars.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §204; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據希利神父所述，卡西基亞雷的印第安人相信，夜間降下的露水是星辰的唾液，這一信仰與據說馬庫西人所持的相似。加勒比人則將露水歸因於星辰的排尿。

title.en: The Sun and Moon Fight: Shouting at an Eclipse
title.zh: 日月相鬥：日蝕之呼

region.en: Guiana coast (Arawak)
region.zh: 圭亞那濱海阿拉瓦克之地

period: Arawak oral tradition; recorded 1883-1915 (im Thurn, Brett, Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XIII 'Spirits of the Sky', §§195-196

summary.en: On one occasion, during an eclipse of the sun, the Arawak men rushed from their houses with loud shouts and yells: a fight was going on between the Sun and the Moon, and they shouted to frighten and so part the combatants. Brett speaks of Oroan, the great Demon of Darkness, who causes eclipses: he seizes the Sun and strives to quench the fire, till scorched and blackened he retires, only to return another time. In Cayenne, eclipses upset the Indians a good deal: they think some frightful monster has come to devour the heavenly bodies, make a terrible noise, and shoot a volley of arrows into the air to chase it away — a total or short eclipse they consider a fatal thing.
summary.zh: 日蝕之時，阿拉瓦克男子自屋奔出，大呼大叫：日月方鬥也，呼以駭之使分。布雷特言黑暗大魔奧羅安致蝕：捉日而欲滅其火，灼黑而退，異日復來。卡宴土人謂怪獸欲吞日月，故大噪而向空發箭以逐之；全蝕或短蝕，皆視為凶。

sensitivity.note: Guiana oral tradition summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: It is said by im Thurn that on one occasion, during an eclipse of the sun, the Arawak men among whom he happened to be rushed from their houses with loud shouts and yells: they explained that a fight was going on between the Sun and the Moon, and they shouted to frighten and so part the combatants. Brett speaks of Oroan, the great Demon of Darkness, who causes eclipses: he seizes the Sun and strives to quench the fire, till scorched and blackened, he retires, only to return another time.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §196; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據伊姆·瑟恩所述，有一次日食期間，他恰好身處其間的阿拉瓦克男人們從屋裡衝出來，高聲呼喊叫嚷：他們解釋說，太陽與月亮之間正在交戰，他們呼喊是為了嚇退並藉此分開交戰的雙方。布雷特則提到奧羅安，那位造成日食的大黑暗惡魔：他抓住太陽，竭力撲滅其火焰，直到自己被灼燒發黑才退去，卻只是為了日後再來。

passages.text: In Cayenne, eclipses of the Sun and Moon upset the Indians a good deal: they think some frightful monster has come to devour these heavenly bodies. If the eclipse is total or of short duration, they consider it a fatal thing for them: they make a terrible noise, and shoot a volley of arrows into the air to chase away the monster.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §196; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在卡宴，日食與月食令印第安人十分不安：他們認為某個可怕的怪物前來吞噬這些天體。若食既或食的時間短暫，他們便視之為對他們而言的致命之事：他們製造可怕的喧鬧，並朝空中射出一陣箭雨，以驅趕那怪物。

title.en: Making the Moon a Field: Eclipse Rites on the Orinoco
title.zh: 為月墾田：奧里諾科蝕儀

region.en: Orinoco River (Lokeca, Saliva, Guayana, Otomac tribes)
region.zh: 奧里諾科河洛凱卡-薩利瓦-瓜亞納-奧托馬諸族

period: Orinoco tribal rites recorded by Gumilla; summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. XIII 'Spirits of the Sky', §201

summary.en: At an eclipse of the moon the Lokeca and Atabeca Indians believed it was about to die, and that all exposed fires would be extinguished if it did: their women, crying and yelling, seized glowing embers and hid them in the sand. The Salivas had other views: all the warriors stood in rows facing the Moon, offering their prowess, while the old men thrashed the young men with whips and the women bewailed the Moon's projected departure — their promises to fight in his favor allay his fears. As soon as the Guayanas recognized an eclipse, they took up their field implements, cut and dug, loudly proclaiming that the Moon had good reason for forsaking them since they had never made a field for him: they begged him not to go, now providing him a field to plant maize, cassava, and plantains — and there is no more working on the field in the Moon's behalf until the next eclipse!
summary.zh: 月蝕之際，洛凱卡-阿塔貝卡人以為月將死，露天之火將熄；婦人大哭，各取赤炭藏於沙中。薩利瓦戰士列隊向月，許以武勇；老者鞭笞青年，婦人泣別——戰士之許諾安其心，月遂不去。瓜亞納人見蝕即荷農具墾地，高聲曰：『吾儕未嘗為月墾田，月之去宜也；今為墾之，種玉蜀黍、木薯、香蕉，請勿去！』——蝕過即止，下次月蝕再為之。

sensitivity.note: Orinoco tribal rites recorded by Gumilla, summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Some of these nations believed that it [the moon] was about to die: others that it was angry with them, and that it would give them no more light. The Lokeca and Atabeca Indians held to the death theory and were under the conviction that if the Moon were indeed to die, all exposed fires would be extinguished. Their women, crying and yelling — an outburst in which the men joined — accordingly would each seize a glowing ember and hide it, either in the sand or underground. Moved by their tears and entreaties, the Moon however recovers, and the hidden fires are extinguished: but were he indeed to die, the concealed embers would remain alight.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §201 (from Gumilla); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這些民族中有一些相信它〔月亮〕即將死去：另一些則相信它對他們發怒，且不再賜予他們光明。洛凱卡與阿塔貝卡印第安人持死亡之說，並深信倘若月亮果真死去，所有露天的火都將熄滅。於是，他們的女人哭喊叫嚷——男人們也加入這陣喧鬧——各自抓起一塊熾熱的餘燼，藏進沙裡或地下。然而，月亮被她們的淚水與懇求所打動，終究恢復過來，而那些藏起的火便被熄滅：但倘若它果真死去，那些藏起的餘燼便會繼續燃燒。

passages.text: As soon as the Guayanas recognize an eclipse of the moon, they take up the implements used in cultivating their fields. With much talk and gesticulation, some cut the undergrowth, others clear it, and others again dig up the ground, all of them loudly proclaiming that the Moon has cause for being annoyed, and particularly good reason for forsaking them, considering that they had never made a field for him. They accordingly beg him not to go, because they are now providing him with a field, in which they propose planting maize, cassava, and plantains. With these promises and entreaties they continue at their task so long as the eclipse lasts; and, as soon as it is over, they return to their houses overjoyed — but there is no more working on the field in the Moon's behalf until the next eclipse takes place!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §201 (from Gumilla); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 圭亞那（Guayanas）人一察覺月蝕，便拿起耕作田地所用的器具。他們一邊議論紛紛、比手畫腳，有人砍除灌木，有人清理地面，又有人翻掘泥土，眾人皆高聲宣稱：月亮有理由感到惱怒，尤其有充分理由棄他們而去，因為他們從未為他開闢過田地。於是他們懇求他不要離去，因為他們如今正為他開闢田地，打算在其中種植玉米、木薯與芭蕉。他們一面許下這些承諾、一面苦苦哀求，持續勞作直到月蝕結束；月蝕一過，他們便歡天喜地地返回家中——然而，在下次月蝕來臨之前，他們再也不會為月亮動工開田了！

title.en: Sam Slays the Dragon of the Kashaf
title.zh: 薩姆誅卡沙夫河之龍

region.en: River Kashaf near Tus (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 圖斯附近卡沙夫河（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Minuchihr sec. 20

summary.en: In his letter to Minuchihr, Sam recounts his ordeal by a dragon haunting the river Kashaf, which made earth afoam from city to city and cleared sky of flying fowl and earth of beast of prey. Riding in God's strength with ox-head mace, bow, and shield, he pinned its tongue with three adamantine shafts, then smashed its skull like an elephant's, so that venom poured forth like the river Nile and Kashaf flowed like a stream of gall. There was no harvest in those parts for years, and Sam sickened many days with the venom.
summary.zh: 薩姆致米努奇赫爾書中自述：一條巨龍盤踞卡沙夫河畔，自城至城攪動大地，飛鳥絕跡、猛獸匿形。他奉神之力，持牛首狼牙棒、弓與盾出征，以三支金剛箭釘住龍舌，復如碎象顱般擊碎其頭，毒液如尼羅河般傾瀉，卡沙夫河水如膽汁流淌。其地多年無收成，薩姆亦因蛇毒病臥多日。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source. Dragon-slaying episode derived from Keresaspa's Avestan feats (Warner's note); cross-tradition serpent-slayer cluster. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Sam wrote to the Shah: there was a dragon haunting the Kashaf and making earth afoam. It reached from city to city and from hill to hill, the hearts of all were filled with panic; men kept watch both night and day. That dragon cleared the sky of flying fowl and earth of beast of prey. It scorched the vulture's feathers with its blast, set earth a-blazing where its venom fell, dragged from the water gruesome crocodiles, and swiftly flying eagles from the air.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 20 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 薩姆（Sam）寫信給沙阿（Shah）：有一條巨龍盤踞卡沙夫（Kashaf），攪得大地翻騰如沫。牠從一城蔓延至另一城，從一山蔓延至另一山，眾人之心盡皆充滿驚惶；人們日夜守望。那巨龍掃清了天空中的飛禽與大地上的猛獸。牠的吐息灼焦禿鷲的羽毛，牠的毒液所落之處令大地燃燒，牠從水中拖出猙獰的鱷魚，又從空中攫下疾飛的雄鷹。

passages.text: Seeing that none dared to lay hand upon it, in God's strength Sam banished terror from his heart, girt up his loins in His exalted name, and rode his elephantine steed, his saddle bearing the ox-head mace, his bow upon his arm and shield at his neck. He went forth like a savage crocodile. The dragon seemed a lofty mountain and trailed upon the ground its hairs like lassos; its tongue was like a tree-trunk charred, its eyes were like two cisterns full of blood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 20 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 薩姆見無人敢對牠動手，便憑上帝的力量驅除心中的恐懼，奉祂至高之名束緊腰帶，騎上他那如象般的駿馬，鞍上掛著牛頭錘，臂上挽著弓，頸上懸著盾。他如兇猛的鱷魚般出擊。那巨龍宛如一座高聳的山岳，牠的毛髮如套索般拖曳於地；牠的舌頭如燒焦的樹幹，牠的雙眼如兩口盛滿鮮血的水池。

passages.text: Like a gallant warrior Sam roared against that dragon and fitted to his bow a poplar arrow tipped with adamant, shooting it at the dragon's jaws to pin the tongue against the throat; the tongue lolled pinned. Again he shot, again he pierced the mouth; a third shaft went right adown its jaws and its heart's blood spouted seething. When it closed and pressed him hard he took his ox-head mace and, in the strength of God, smote the dragon's head: he smashed the skull as it had been a mighty elephant's, and venom poured forth like the river Nile.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 20 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 薩姆如英勇的戰士般向那巨龍怒吼，將一支以金剛石為鏃的楊木箭搭上弓弦，射向巨龍的咽喉，要把牠的舌頭釘在喉嚨上；那舌頭被釘住而垂落。他再射一箭，又刺穿牠的口；第三支箭直貫牠的下顎，牠心臟的鮮血沸騰般噴湧而出。當巨龍合攏下顎、緊緊壓迫他時，他取出牛頭錘，憑上帝的力量猛擊巨龍的頭：他將那頭顱砸得粉碎，宛如砸碎一頭巨象的頭骨，毒液如尼羅河般湧流而出。

passages.text: So struck he that the dragon rose no more, while earth was levelled to the hills with brains. Kashaf was flowing like a stream of gall and all was peace. The mountain-tops were thronged with folk who called down blessings on his head, because that dragon was a fearful bane. On this account men called him One-blow Sam, and all threw jewels o'er him; but he departed with all his shining body bare of mail and sickened with the venom many days, for there was no harvest in those parts for years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 20 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他這一擊，使巨龍再也無法起身，牠的腦漿將山丘夷為平地。卡沙夫如膽汁之流般流淌，一切歸於安寧。山巔擠滿了人群，他們為他的頭顱祈求祝福，因為那巨龍是可怕的禍害。因此之故，人們稱他為「一擊薩姆」，眾人紛紛將珠寶擲向他；然而他離去時，那光輝的身軀卻鎧甲盡失，且因中毒而病了许多天，因為那些地方多年來顆粒無收。

title.en: Zal Unmans the Archmages with Riddles
title.zh: 扎勒以謎語折服眾術士

region.en: Court of Minuchihr (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 米努奇赫爾王庭（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Minuchihr secs. 24-26

summary.en: Minuchihr, seeking to prove Zal, has the shrewd archmages question him on riddles veiled in mystery: twelve cypresses with thirty boughs each; two steeds, one crystal bright and one pitchy sable, that chase each other in vain; thirty riders who seem twenty-nine; a mower who cuts green and dry alike; two cypresses with a bird nesting on one at morning and the other at eve; a walled city whose memory will awake when earth quakes. Zal answers: the twelve moons of the year, night and day, the moon's phases, Time the mower, the sun flying between winter and summer, and this Wayside Inn against the city that is built on high. The company wonder and rejoice, and Zal's horsemanship and javelin feats are shown before the Shah.
summary.zh: 米努奇赫爾欲試扎勒，命術士以謎語考問：十二株三十枝之柏、追逐不休的黑白雙駿、視若二十九實為三十的騎者、青枯皆割的刈草人、晨昏棲於雙柏的神鳥、震後方為人憶的山城。扎勒一一答破：歲之十二月、晝與夜、月之盈虛、時間之鐮、飛行於冬夏之間的太陽，以及通往「高城」前的驛館人生。眾人驚嘆歡喜，扎勒更於王前顯露騎射絕技。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; riddle-contest episode. Tagged with wisdom-sacrifice interpretively (wisdom through ordeal); no living community restriction.

passages.text: The Shah called Zal to prove him by hard questions. The shrewd archmages and the men of lore sat in full conclave and examined him on many matters veiled in mystery. One asked: what are the dozen cypresses erect in all their bravery, each one of them with thirty boughs bedeckt? Another: what are those two steeds moving rapidly, as crystal bright is this one of the twain and that one sable as a pitchy sea, which gallop at their utmost speed and strain each one to catch the other but in vain? What are the thirty men who ride before their king and seem but twenty-nine to thee, but when thou countest them their number is complete?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 24 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 沙阿召來扎爾（Zal），要以難題考驗他。精明的首席祭司與博學之士齊聚一堂，就許多隱於奧祕之中的事考問他。一人問道：那十二株挺拔傲立、雄姿英發的柏樹是什麼？它們每一株都披掛著三十根枝條。另一人問：那兩匹疾馳的駿馬是什麼？二者之中，一匹晶瑩如水晶，另一匹漆黑如瀝青之海；牠們以極速奔馳，各自竭力追趕對方卻徒勞無功。那三十名騎在國王之前的男子又是什麼？在你眼中似只有二十九人，但當你細數之時，其人數卻完整無缺。

passages.text: What is the meadow-land to which a fierce man cometh with a scythe, sharp and long, who cutteth all the grass both green and dry, and if thou criest heareth not thy cry? What are those cypresses, a lofty pair, like reeds above a sea, and what bird nesteth on this at morning and on that at eve, the bird departing and the leaves turning pale, the bird arriving and they musk exhale? On a mountain I descried a city strongly fortified whose memory now hath gone; but some day suddenly the earth will quake, and remembrance of the city will awake.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 24 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那是什么草地，一个凶猛的人手持长而锋利的镰刀前来，割尽青草与枯草，纵使你呼喊，他也听不见你的哭声？那两株柏树是什么，一对高耸之物，如同海上的芦苇？又是什么鸟清晨栖于这一株、黄昏栖于那一株——鸟去而叶色转白，鸟来而叶散麝香？我在一座山上望见一座坚固设防的城，如今它的记忆已然消逝；但总有一天大地会突然震动，那城的记忆将会苏醒。

passages.text: Zal shook his plumage, spread his wings, and answered: the twelve cypresses are the twelve new moons of every year; the two chargers are night and day, the pulses of the sky; the thirty men are the phases of the moon, one night a phase from time to time eludeth sight. Time is the mower, and we are like the swath; the bird which flieth between the two cypresses is the sun; and the city built upon the mount is our long home, the scene of our account, while Thornbrake town is this Wayside Inn, at once our pleasure, treasure, pain and woe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 25 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 扎尔抖动羽饰，展开双翼，答道：那十二株柏树是每一年的十二轮新月；那两匹战马是昼与夜，是天穹的脉搏；那三十个人是月亮的月相，一夜一夜，月相时时隐去不见。时间就是那割草人，我们如同割下的草行；在两株柏树之间飞翔的鸟是太阳；建在山上的城是我们长久的归宿，是我们清算之所，而荆棘城便是这座路旁客栈，既是我们的欢乐、珍宝，也是我们的痛苦与悲哀。

passages.text: When Zal had thus expounded all the riddles the company both wondered and rejoiced, while Minuchihr cried well done. Then they exercised with mace, sword, shaft, and lance before the Shah, and never saw or heard of horsemanship like Zal's: he took his bow, urged on his steed, and pierced an ancient tree full in the centre with the royal shaft; he pierced three shields with his javelin and seized a famous cavalier from his saddle. The Shah said: none will see his peer; and he gave Zal a robe of honour that astonished all the chieftains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 26 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 扎尔如此解明了一切谜语，众人既惊异又欢喜，米努奇赫尔连声喝彩。随后他们在沙阿面前演练狼牙棒、剑、箭与长矛，从未见过或听说过像扎尔这样的骑术：他取弓策马，以王者的箭正中一棵古树的中心；他以标枪刺穿三面盾牌，又将一位著名的骑士从鞍上擒下。沙阿说：无人能见其匹敌；他赐给扎尔一件荣誉袍，令所有首领惊叹。

title.en: The Stars Foretell Rustam, Whom the Eagle Will Not Overlook
title.zh: 星辰預言魯斯塔姆

region.en: Court of Minuchihr (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 米努奇赫爾王庭（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Minuchihr sec. 23

summary.en: Minuchihr takes Sam's letter, is troubled yet resolved to grant Zal's wish, and commands the archimages and astrologers to read the stars. For three days they labour, then announce: no stagnant pool is here; there will arise from Sam's son and the daughter of Mihrab a hero full of prowess and fair fame, whose life will be prolonged for centuries, who will take the lion with his twisted lasso, roast whole onagers upon the fire, and make the air weep with his scimitar — the belted servant of the Shahs and shelter of the horsemen of Iran. The Shah charges them to disclose it to none.
summary.zh: 米努奇赫爾收薩姆來信，心雖不悅仍允扎勒所願，命術士占星三日，而後宣告：此非死水；薩姆之子與米赫拉布之女將誕生勇武聞名的英雄，其壽延數百年，能以套索擒獅、架野驢於火、以彎刀使蒼天垂淚——他將是列王的腰帶僕從、伊朗騎士的庇護。王命他們不得外洩。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: The Shah then took Sam's letter, read and smiled. Thou hast increased an ancient grief of mine, he said, yet for thy father's touching letter, although the matter hath much grieved my heart, I am resolved to think of it no more, and will perform and carry out thy wish, since that is all to thee; but tarry here while I deliberate on thine affairs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 23 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 沙阿于是接过萨姆的信，读罢微笑。他说：你加重了我旧日的悲伤；然而念及你父亲那封动人的信，虽然此事令我心中十分悲痛，我决意不再想它，并将实现和完成你的愿望，既然那对你便是全部；但你且留在此处，容我思量你的事。

passages.text: The Shah commanded that the archimages, the nobles, wise men, and astrologers should meet at his high throne and read the stars. They met and laboured for three days and then announced: we have perused the circling sky, and this is what the stars prognosticate: no stagnant pool is here. There will arise from Sam's son and the daughter of Mihrab a hero full of prowess and fair fame.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 23 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 沙阿命令大祭司、贵族、智者与占星家齐集于他的高座之前，解读星象。他们聚集起来，劳作了三日，然后宣布：我们已遍览旋转的天穹，星辰所预示的便是如此：此处并无停滞的死水。从萨姆之子与米赫拉布之女将诞生一位英雄，充满勇武与美名。

passages.text: His life will be prolonged for centuries; he will have strength, renown, and Grace, pluck, brains, and thews, and not a peer in fight or feast. Where'er his charger's coat shall run with sweat the liver of his foemen shall run dry. The eagle will not soar above his helm. He will take the lion with his twisted lasso, will roast whole onagers upon the fire, will make the air weep with his scimitar, will be the belted servant of the Shahs and shelter of the horsemen of Iran. Then said the exalted Shah: beware that ye disclose to none what ye have told to me.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 23 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的寿命将延绵数百年；他将拥有力量、声名与神恩，勇气、智谋与筋力，无论在战阵还是宴席之上都无人可匹。凡他的战马毛皮为汗水所浸之处，敌人的肝胆便将枯竭。鹰隼不能高翔于他的头盔之上。他将以盘绕的套索擒获雄狮，将整头野驴在火上烤炙，将使空气因他的弯刀而哭泣，将成为诸沙阿的束带仆从、伊朗骑士的庇护。于是那崇高的沙阿说：当心，切勿将你们对我所说之事泄露给任何人。

title.en: The Birth of Rustam by the Simurgh's Craft
title.zh: 西摩爾格神技助產魯斯塔姆

region.en: Zabulistan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 扎布勒斯坦（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Minuchihr sec. 29

summary.en: Rudaba's time comes but not deliverance; she lies sleepless, one would have said her skin is stuffed with stones. Zal burns a feather of the Simurgh; the bird swoops down, prophesies the lion-child that will fillip bricks two miles, and instructs a caesarean birth: bemuse the lady with wine, let a cunning man pierce her side, stitch up the gash, and dress it with a herb bruised with milk and musk, anointing it with the plume. The archimage delivers the babe uninjured; ten nurses suckle him, and Sam, receiving a silken effigy of his grandson in mail with mace and bridle, showers drachms till the heap is level with the messenger's head.
summary.zh: 魯達貝臨盆而不得娩，臥病不眠，皮膚如灌石。扎勒焚西摩爾格之羽，神鳥降至，預言「能擲磚兩里之獅子孩」，並授剖腹之法：以酒麻之，巧匠刺其側腹取出嬰孩，縫合傷口，以乳與麝香敷藥，再以神羽塗抹。術士順利娩出嬰兒；十乳母哺育之。薩姆收到身披甲冑、手執狼牙棒與韁繩的孫兒絲織像，喜而撒幣至信使頭頂。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Warner compares the anaesthetic to the Bundahishn account of Ohrmazd's healing fruits for the Primeval Ox. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Rudaba's time had come but not deliverance: by night and day she cried for help, sleepless and withered like a living corpse; one would have said her skin is stuffed with stones or iron. Then occurred a thought to Zal which eased him of his anguish: the plume of the Simurgh. He brought a censer, kindled fire, and burnt some of the plume; the air grew dark and that imperious bird swooped down, a cloud whose drops were pearls.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 29 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 魯達貝的時辰已到，卻仍不得解脫：她日夜呼救，無眠而枯槁，宛如一具活屍；人見了會說她的皮肉裡塞滿了石頭或鐵塊。這時扎爾心中忽然生出一念，解了他的憂苦：那便是西摩格的羽毛。他取來香爐，點起火，燒了一些羽毛；空氣頓時昏暗，那威嚴的巨鳥俯衝而下，如同一朵雲，而雲中滴落的盡是珍珠。

passages.text: From this moon-faced and silver-bosomed Cypress will come a noble babe, said the Simurgh: the mighty lion will kiss the dust upon his feet, no cloud will dare to pass above him. When he shouteth the pard will split its skin and gnaw its paws. This child will prove in counsels and in rede a weighty Sam, in height a cypress-tree, in wrath a lion, in strength an elephant, and fillip bricks two miles. His birth will not be natural, so willeth He who giveth good.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 29 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 西摩格說道：從這月面銀胸的柏樹之身，將誕生一位高貴的嬰孩；那雄獅將親吻他腳下的塵土，沒有雲朵敢從他上方經過。他一聲怒吼，豹子便會裂開自己的皮、啃咬自己的爪。這孩子在謀略與見識上將是沉穩的薩姆，在身量上是柏樹，在怒氣上是獅子，在力量上是大象，能將磚塊彈出兩哩之遠。他的降生不會循自然之途，此乃那賜福者的意旨。

passages.text: Bring a blue-steel dagger and seek a cunning man: bemuse the lady first with wine to ease her pain and fear, then let him ply his craft and take the Lion from its lair by piercing her waist while all unconscious, then stitch up the gash. Bruise with milk and musk a herb that I will show thee, dress and anoint Rudaba's wound, and rub o'er the wound my plume; its gracious shade will prove a blessing. There came an archimage, one deft of hand, who made the moon-faced dame bemused with wine, then pierced her side while she was all unconscious and delivered her uninjured.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 29 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 取來一把藍鋼匕首，尋一位巧手之人：先用酒使這位夫人昏沉，以減輕她的痛苦與恐懼，然後讓他施展技藝，趁她全然不省人事之際，刺穿她的腰側，將那獅子從巢穴中取出，再縫合傷口。用乳汁與麝香搗碎一種我將指示給你的草藥，敷裹並塗抹魯達貝的傷口，再將我的羽毛揉抹於傷處；它那仁慈的庇蔭將證實為一樁福佑。來了一位術士，手法靈巧，用酒使那月面夫人昏沉，趁她全然不省人事時刺穿她的身側，將她安然無損地接生下來。

passages.text: None had seen a thing so strange: the babe was like a lion, a hero tall and fair to look upon. They made of silk a herolet the size of that unsuckled Lion, stuffing it with sable's hair, with a mace in one hand and bridle in the other, and set the puppet on a chestnut horse to send to Sam, who looked thereon and said: this silken thing is just like me; if he is half this size his head will touch the sky. Ten nurses suckled Rustam, and being weaned he lived on bread and flesh, eating as much as five.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 29 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 無人見過如此奇異之事：那嬰孩宛如一頭獅子，是個高大俊美的英雄。他們用絲綢做了一個小英雄，大小與那尚未吮乳的獅子相仿，內裡塞滿黑貂之毛，一手持狼牙棒，一手執韁繩，將這人偶置於一匹栗色馬上，送去給薩姆；薩姆見了說道：這絲綢之物正與我一般模樣；若他只有這半個大小，他的頭便會觸及天空。十位乳母哺育魯斯塔姆，斷奶之後他便以麵包與肉為食，食量抵得上五人。

title.en: Rustam Slays the White Elephant in His Sleep
title.zh: 魯斯塔姆睡中斃白象

region.en: Garden of Zal, Sistan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 錫斯坦扎勒花園（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Minuchihr sec. 30

summary.en: During a garden revel the chiefs' white elephant breaks loose. The revelling boy Rustam runs forth with Sam's mace, splits the gate-keeper's skull when the keepers bar the way, smashes chains and bolts like wind, and, roaring like the sea at a mountain that bellowed, deals it one blow on the head: Mount Bisitun shook to its core and tumbled at one blow vile and strengthless. Thus it fell, and matchless Rustam went lightly to his place again and slept.
summary.zh: 花園宴飲之際，諸酋之白象掙脫而出。微醺的少年魯斯塔姆持薩姆狼牙棒衝出，守衛阻攔便擊碎其顱，如風般砸斷門鎖鏈栓，臨象怒吼如海，一擊擊其頭顱——比斯通山也為之震顫，白象一擊斃命。魯斯塔姆從容歸臥，酣然入睡。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: It came to pass that as they spent a day in revel in a garden with their friends, while harp-strings ran the gamut of sweet sounds and all the chiefs were one in merriment, they quaffed red wine from crystal cups until their heads were dazed, and then Zal bade his son make ready robes of honour for his warriors. So Rustam gave gold, many Arab steeds caparisoned and other gifts; Zal sought the bower, while Rustam reeled to his chamber, laid him down and slept.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 30 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 事情是這樣的：他們與友人在一座園中歡宴一日，琴弦奏遍甜美音階，眾首領同歡共樂，他們從水晶杯中暢飲紅酒，直至頭腦昏沉，隨後扎爾吩咐其子為他的勇士們備好榮譽之袍。於是魯斯塔姆賞賜黃金、許多披掛整齊的阿拉伯駿馬以及其他禮物；扎爾前往內室，而魯斯塔姆踉蹌回到自己的房間，躺下便睡。

passages.text: Shouts rose outside his door: the chiefs' white elephant hath broken loose, and folk are in its danger! He heard, and urged by hardihood ran forth, snatched up Sam's mace and made toward the street. The keepers of the gate opposed him; wroth at the speaker's words the matchless Rustam smote him on the nape, and his head rolled from him; the others fled the paladin, who boldly went up to the gate and smashed the chains and bolts with blows that well befitted one of such noble name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 30 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他門外響起呼喊：首領的白象掙脫了束縛，眾人正陷於危險之中！他聽見了，被剛勇所驅，奔了出去，抓起薩姆的狼牙棒，朝街上衝去。守門人攔阻他；無與倫比的魯斯塔姆因那說話者的言語而大怒，擊其後頸，那人的頭便滾落下來；其餘的人見了這勇士紛紛逃散，他則大膽走向城門，以與其高貴名聲相稱的重擊，砸碎了鎖鏈與門閂。

passages.text: He went forth like wind with shouldered mace excitedly, approached the mighty beast and roared out like the sea. He looked and saw a mountain bellowing, the ground beneath it like a boiling pot, and his own nobles fleeing in dismay like sheep that spy a wolf. Roaring like a lion he went courageously against the beast, which charged at him like a mountain and reared its trunk to strike, but Rustam dealt it a mace-blow on the head; the mountain-form stooped, Mount Bisitun shook to its core, and tumbled at one blow vile and strengthless. Thus it fell, and matchless Rustam went lightly to his place again and slept.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Minuchihr sec. 30 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他如風般奮勇前行，肩上扛著狼牙棒，興致勃勃地逼近那頭巨獸，如大海般咆哮。他放眼望去，只見一座山在怒吼，其下的大地宛如沸騰的鍋，而他自己的貴族們則驚惶逃竄，如同瞥見狼群的羊。他如獅子般咆哮，勇敢地迎向那頭巨獸；巨獸如高山般向他衝來，揚起象鼻欲擊，但魯斯塔姆一棒擊中牠的頭；那山形之軀彎伏下去，比西頓山震動至根基，一擊之下便頹然倒下，卑劣而無力。牠就這樣倒下了，無與倫比的魯斯塔姆則輕快地回到自己的位置，安然入睡。

title.en: Arawidi the Fisher: the Alligator Ransoms Himself with a Wife
title.zh: 漁者阿拉威迪：鱷以女贖罪

region.en: Arawak country, Guyana
region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地

period: Arawak oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §142

summary.en: Arawidi, the medicine-man, dammed a favorite stream to retain water and fish for later visits; the otters destroyed it, so he appointed the woodpecker as watchman. Warned by a loud tapping of an alligator's proximity, he hurried along and clubbed the reptile so unmercifully that it offered him a girl for wife if he would only stop. Arawidi accepted these terms — but to this day the alligator shows the marks of the thrashing on its battered head, and in the notches along its tail.
summary.zh: 醫師阿拉威迪築壩蓄水魚；水獺毀之，遂以啄木鳥為守望。鳥叩木示警鱷至；彼疾至而痛擊之。鱷求止，許以女為妻。約成；然鱷首傷痕與尾上齒痕，至今猶存。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Arawidi once, after fishing in a favorite stream, built a dam with the object of retaining both the water and the fish for use on subsequent visits. But the otters destroyed it, so he appointed the woodpecker to act as watchman. The latter warned him with a loud tapping of the proximity of an alligator: he hurried along and clubbed the reptile so unmercifully that it offered him a girl for wife if he would only stop. Arawidi accepted these terms, but to this day the alligator shows the marks of the thrashing on its battered head, and in the notches along its tail.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §142; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿拉維迪有一次在一條喜愛的溪流中捕魚之後，築了一道堤壩，目的是把水和魚都留住，以備日後再來時使用。但水獺毀了它，於是他指派啄木鳥充當看守。啄木鳥以響亮的啄擊聲警告他鱷魚正在逼近：他急忙趕去，毫不留情地用棍棒猛打那爬蟲，打得牠提出只要他肯停手，就獻上一個女孩給他為妻。阿拉維迪接受了這些條件，但直到今日，鱷魚那被打得傷痕累累的頭上，以及尾巴上的凹痕裡，仍留著遭痛打的痕跡。

title.en: The War of the Birds: How They Got Their Distinctive Markings
title.zh: 群鳥之戰：鳥羽之由

region.en: Arawak country, Guyana (after Brett)
region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地（據布雷特）

period: Arawak tradition recorded by Brett; summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §143

summary.en: An Arawak hunter captured a Vulture, daughter of Anuamima the carrion crow; she laid aside her feathers, appeared before him as a beautiful girl, and became his wife, bearing him above the clouds and persuading her father and family to receive him. When he wished to visit his aged mother they set him on a high thorn-covered tree; spiders spun cords and birds eased his descent. For years he strove to regain his wife until the birds espoused his cause, assembled their forces, and bore him as their commander above the sky — where at last he was slain by a valiant young warrior resembling him in person and feature: it was his own son. The legend ends with the conflagration of the house of the Royal Vultures: the kiskedee who shirked the war was sentenced to wear his white cotton bandage continually; the trumpeter, quarreling over the spoil, arose with patches of gray; and the Owl, finding in the spoil a package that contained Darkness only, has never been able to endure the light of day.
summary.zh: 獵者得禿鷲婦——食腐鴉阿努阿瑪之女也；彼脫羽為人妻，攜夫上雲端。夫省母，遂被棄於棘樹之巔；蛛結繩、群鳥扶之而降。經年謀復，群鳥舉之為帥，上戰於天；末為相似之少戰士所殺——乃其親子也。鷲宮焚毀。臨陣託病纏白布之提提鳥，被罰永纏；爭利之鶴得灰斑；鴞得暗一包，故畏日光。

sensitivity.note: Arawak tradition from Brett 1880, summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: An Arawak hunter captures a Vulture, daughter of Anuamima. She lays aside her feathers, appears before him as a beautiful girl, becomes his wife, bears him above the clouds, and after much trouble persuades her father and family to receive him. All then goes well until he expresses a wish to visit his aged mother, when they discard him and set him on the top of a very high tree, the trunk of which is covered with formidable prickles. He appeals to all the living creatures around: then spiders spin cords to help him and fluttering birds ease his descent, so that at last he reaches the ground in safety.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §143 (from Brett); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一名阿拉瓦克獵人捕獲了一隻禿鷲，她是阿努阿米瑪的女兒。她卸下羽毛，以美麗少女的模樣出現在他面前，成為他的妻子，帶他飛上雲端，並在諸多周折之後說服她的父親和家人接納他。一切原本都很順利，直到他表達了想探望年邁母親的願望，他們便拋棄了他，把他放在一棵極高的樹頂上，那樹幹佈滿了可怕的尖刺。他向周圍所有的生靈求助：於是蜘蛛紡出繩索來幫助他，拍翅的鳥兒緩和他的下降，使他最終安然無恙地到達地面。

passages.text: Then follow his efforts, extending over several years, to regain his wife. At length the birds espouse his cause, assemble their forces, and bear him as their commander above the sky. At last he is slain by a valiant young warrior resembling him in person and feature: it is his own son. The legend ends with the conflagration of the house of the Royal Vultures.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §143 (from Brett); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著便是他歷經數年、力圖尋回妻子的種種努力。最後鳥兒們擁護他的事業，集結兵力，並奉他為統帥，帶他飛上天空。最終他被一名英勇的年輕戰士所殺，那戰士的形貌與容貌都與他相似：那正是他自己的兒子。這則傳說以王家禿鷲之屋遭大火焚毀作結。

passages.text: The Kiskedee, though a valiant little bird, disliked the war, and bandaged his head with white cotton, pretending to be sick; but being detected, was sentenced to wear it continually. He is noted for his hostility to hawks and other large birds. The Warracaba, the trumpeter bird, and the kingfisher quarreled over the spoil and knocked each other over in the ashes: the former arose with patches of gray, while the other became gray all over. The Owl discovered among the spoil a package done up with care, which he found to contain Darkness only; he has never been able since to endure the light of day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §143 (from Brett); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 基斯克迪雖是勇敢的小鳥，卻厭惡這場戰爭，便用白棉花包紮頭部，假裝生病；但被識破後，被判罰永遠戴著它。他以敵視鷹和其他大鳥而聞名。瓦拉卡巴鳥、喇叭鳥和翠鳥為了戰利品爭吵，在灰燼中互相撞倒：前者起身時身上帶著灰色斑塊，後者則全身變灰。貓頭鷹在戰利品中發現一個仔細包紮的包裹，他發現裡面只有黑暗；自此以後，他再也無法忍受白晝的光。

title.en: The Deer and the Turtle Exchange Footwear
title.zh: 鹿與龜易履

region.en: Arawak country, Guyana
region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地

period: Arawak oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §143A

summary.en: The Deer met the Turtle one day while cleaning his hoofs — for in those days turtle wore hoofs and the deer had claws — and said: 'My friend, you have nice sandals. Let me have a trial of them.' The Turtle, very proud of them, handed them over, receiving in exchange the Deer's nails. When the Deer put on the hoofs he found he could walk ever so much quicker, and trotted off. The poor Turtle found his progress impeded, and stood still waiting every minute for the Deer to return — but he never did so.
summary.zh: 一日鹿遇龜理蹄——古時龜有蹄而鹿有利爪——曰：『友哉，汝履甚美，借吾一試。』龜愛其履而與之，易以鹿爪。鹿得蹄而行愈疾，遂逸去。龜步艱難，立而待其還——竟不返。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The Deer met the Turtle one day, while cleaning his hoofs — for in those days turtle wore hoofs and the deer had claws — and said: 'My friend, you have nice sandals. Let me have a trial of them.' The Turtle, who was very proud of them, said: 'Certainly. Why not?' and handed them over, receiving in exchange the Deer's nails. When the Deer now put on the hoofs, he found that he could walk ever so much quicker than before, and trotted off. The poor Turtle, however, found his progress impeded, and stood still, waiting every minute for the Deer to return — but he never did so.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §143A; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，鹿遇見正在清理蹄子的烏龜——因為那時候烏龜長著蹄子，而鹿長著爪子——便說：「我的朋友，你的涼鞋真好看。讓我試穿一下吧。」烏龜非常以它們為傲，說道：「當然。有何不可？」便把蹄子交了出去，換來鹿的爪子。這回鹿穿上蹄子後，發現自己走起路來比以前快得多，便小跑而去。可憐的烏龜卻發現自己寸步難行，只得站著不動，時時刻刻等著鹿回來——但鹿卻再也沒有回來。

title.en: The Unlucky Hunter and Black Tiger Tobe-horoanna
title.zh: 厄運獵人與黑皮虎

region.en: Pomeroon River, Guyana (Warrau)
region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

period: Warrau oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §144

summary.en: A man unlucky in hunting had two brothers-in-law who always brought home game; 'As he has no luck, we will lose him away.' They sent him on a route leading to the lair of Tobe-horoanna — an immense, cruelly savage beast, a tiger only when walking in the bush, at home 'like a man, people'. Chased round an immense tree, the man just managed to reach the animal's hindquarters and cut off both its heels; then he shot it through the neck and finished it with a knife. His brothers-in-law could hardly believe him until he boldly trampled on the carcass; the old father gave him another daughter, the brothers built him a bigger house, and he was henceforth recognized as chief of the settlement.
summary.zh: 一獵者屢空；二內兄常滿載，曰：『彼無運，吾儕當棄之。』乃導之行黑皮虎多貝霍羅安納之徑——巨獸也，行林則為虎，居家則如人。人繞巨樹而奔，伺其後而斷其雙踵；復射其頸，以刀了之。眾不信；彼直踐其屍。岳父以次女妻之，內兄為築大屋，遂為村長。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: There was once a man who had two brothers-in-law. While he was one of the unluckiest of mortals, they invariably returned home of an afternoon with plenty of game. They said: 'As he has no luck, we will lose him away.' So one day they took him into the bush, all three going in together, but soon told him to go in one direction while they went in another. The route the two wicked brothers instructed him to follow led to the lair of Tobe-horoanna — signifying in Warrau 'Tiger-black-skin', the name given to an immense, cruelly-savage beast believed to exist in the depths of the forest, a tiger only when it goes for a walk in the bush, at home 'like a man, people'.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §144; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個人，他有兩個姻親兄弟。他雖是凡人中最不幸的一個，他們卻總是在午後帶著豐富的獵物回家。他們說：「既然他沒有運氣，我們就把他丟掉吧。」於是有一天，他們帶他進入叢林，三人一同前往，但不久便叫他往一個方向走，而他們往另一個方向去。那兩個心懷惡意的兄弟指示他走的路線，通往托貝—霍羅安納（Tobe-horoanna）的巢穴——在瓦勞語（Warrau）中意為「黑皮虎」，這是人們給一種據信棲息於森林深處的巨碩而兇殘野獸所取的名字；牠只有在叢林中漫步時才是虎，在家時則「像人一樣，是人們」。

passages.text: He went on and on until, hearing a great rushing noise approaching, he saw the Tobe-horoanna coming and ran as fast as he could toward an immense tree, Black Tiger after him. Running round and round the trunk, the one after the other, the man just managed to reach the animal's hindquarters and cut off both its heels; Tiger sat down, for it could not walk at all now. Next the man shot it through the neck with his arrow, and after finishing the job with a knife went back home. His brothers-in-law never doubted they had seen the last of him — and were greatly surprised at his arrival, making excuses for their absence.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §144; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他走啊走，直到聽見一陣巨大的奔騰聲逼近，他看見托貝—霍羅安納來了，便拼命朝一棵巨樹跑去，黑虎緊追在後。他繞著樹幹一圈又一圈地跑，一個追一個，那人總算勉強夠到那野獸的後身，砍斷了牠的兩隻腳跟；虎坐了下來，因為牠現在根本無法行走。接著那人用箭射穿了牠的脖子，又用刀結果了牠，然後回家去了。他的姻親兄弟從不懷疑他們已見到他最後一面——對他的歸來大為驚訝，並為自己的不在場編造藉口。

passages.text: When he told them he had actually killed the Tobe-horoanna, the two brothers-in-law as well as their old father could hardly believe him, but insisted on being taken to the place. At a distance they saw Black Tiger on the ground; all except the man who had killed it were afraid to go near. To show them that he spoke true he boldly went up and trampled on the carcass — only then would the old man approach. On arrival home the old father-in-law gave him another daughter, so that he had two wives now; the brothers-in-law built him a bigger house, and he was henceforth recognized as Aijamo — chief, head-man of the settlement.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §144; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他告訴他們他確實殺死了托貝—霍羅安納時，那兩個姻親兄弟以及他們的老父親幾乎無法相信他，但堅持要帶他們去那個地方。他們遠遠地看見黑虎躺在地上；除了殺死牠的那人之外，所有人都害怕靠近。為了向他們證明他所言屬實，他大膽走上前去踩踏那具屍體——直到那時老人才肯靠近。回到家後，老岳父又給了他另一個女兒，因此他現在有了兩個妻子；姻親兄弟為他建了一座更大的房子，他從此被公認為艾哈莫（Aijamo）——首領，聚落的頭人。

title.en: Adaba the Tree-Frog Teacher of Hunters
title.zh: 樹蛙阿達巴：獵人之師

region.en: Arawak country, Guyana
region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地

period: Arawak oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §145

summary.en: Three brothers hunting far from home left their sister at the benab and brought back only a powis day after day. An Adaba tree-frog singing Wang! Wang! in a hollow tree nearby heard her complaint — 'Stop that noise and bring me some game to eat' — changed himself into a man, and returned with meat. He laughed at the fungus growing all over their arrows — 'So long as you do not remove this stuff your arrows will never shoot straight' — cleaned them, tied a fishing-line between two trees for target practice, and taught them his own trick of pointing the arrow into the sky so that in its descent it stuck into the creature's back. The brothers took him home as brother-in-law; but when his wife splashed him at the pond he turned back into a frog and hopped into the hollow tree, where he still is — and their luck went with him.
summary.zh: 三兄弟獵於遠處，留妹於棚，日惟得一鷸。棚側空心樹中樹蛙阿達巴聞其歎，化人出，攜肉而歸；見其箭遍生菌而笑：『不去此物，箭必不直。』為拭箭、懸釣線為的、教仰天射而落其背之秘。兄弟攜之歸為妹夫。後妻浴水潑之，蛙復本形而入空心樹，至今在焉；其運亦隨之去。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: There were once three brothers who went out to hunt, taking their sister with them. Far out in the bush they built a banab, where the sister was left all alone while they wandered about in search of game; every day the three brothers went hunting in all directions, but never brought back any meat except a powis. Now there was an Adaba [tree-frog] living in a hollow tree containing a little water close to the banab, and one afternoon he was singing his song 'Wang! Wang! Wang!' when the girl heard him. 'What are you holloing for?' she said; 'it would be much better if you stopped that noise and brought me some game to eat.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §145; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有三個兄弟外出打獵，帶著他們的妹妹同行。他們在叢林深處搭建了一座棚屋（banab），妹妹被獨自留在那裡，而他們四處遊蕩尋找獵物；三個兄弟每天往各個方向打獵，卻從未帶回任何肉，只帶回一隻鳥（powis）。話說有一隻阿達巴（Adaba，樹蛙）住在棚屋附近一棵積著少許水的空心樹裡，一天下午牠正唱著牠的歌「汪！汪！汪！」，那女孩聽見了牠。「你這樣叫喊是為了什麼？」她說；「你要是停止那噪音，帶些獵物給我吃，那會好得多。」

passages.text: So the Adaba stopped holloing, changed himself into a man, went away into the bush, and returned in about two hours with some meat for her. 'Cook this before your brothers come back: as usual they will return with nothing.' Adaba spoke truly. The brothers' surprise may be imagined when they saw their sister barbecuing plenty of meat and a strange man lying in one of their hammocks — a strange man indeed, with stripes all the way down his thin legs. He burst into a hearty laugh at the fungus growing everywhere on their arrows, saying that so long as they did not remove this stuff their arrows would never shoot straight; he cleaned them, tied a fishing-line between two trees, and had each brother's arrow stick into the very center of it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §145; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是阿達巴停止了叫喊，變成一個男人，走進叢林，大約兩小時後帶著一些肉回來給她。「在你兄弟回來之前把這個煮了：他們照例會一無所獲地回來。」阿達巴說的是實話。可以想像兄弟們看到妹妹烤著大量肉食，而一個陌生男人躺在他們的一張吊床裡時有多麼驚訝——那真是個陌生男人，細瘦的雙腿上從頭到尾都是條紋。他對他們箭上到處生長的黴菌放聲大笑，說只要他們不除去這東西，他們的箭就永遠射不準；他清理了那些箭，在兩棵樹之間綁了一條釣魚線，讓每個兄弟的箭都射中線的正中央。

passages.text: Adaba had a curious trick in shooting with his arrow: instead of taking aim at an animal direct, he would point the arrow up into the sky, so that in its descent it would stick into the creature's back. The brothers became such adepts that they never missed anything, took him home, and made him their brother-in-law. But one day his wife splashed water over him at the pond, and directly she put her hands on him he turned himself into a frog again and hopped away into the hollow tree, where he still is. The three brothers often went out hunting after that, but they never brought back anything like the quantity of game they used to get when Adaba was present.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §145; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿達巴射箭有個奇怪的竅門：他不直接瞄準動物，而是把箭朝天空射去，讓箭在落下時扎進那生物背上。兄弟們變得如此嫻熟，從未射失任何東西，他們把他帶回家，讓他做了他們的姻親兄弟。但有一天，他的妻子在水塘邊把水潑在他身上，她的手一碰到他，他便又變回一隻青蛙，跳進那棵空心樹裡，至今仍在那裡。此後三個兄弟仍常外出打獵，但他們再也沒有帶回像阿達巴在時那樣多的獵物。

title.en: Why Black Tiger Killed the Indians
title.zh: 黑皮虎戮人之由

region.en: Pomeroon River, Guyana (Warrau)
region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

period: Warrau oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §148

summary.en: Tobe-horoanna caught a young man in the bush, put him in the pot, and said: 'You must not be frightened. I do not intend killing, cooking, and eating you.' His captors fed him a whole bush-hog and a calabashful of cassiri, forcing him to drink until he vomited; his sister defended him, and when he returned from the bush with ten dried bush-hogs he won the tiger woman as wife. She bore him twin sons who growled like thunder — 'but the same row which the Black Tiger nation always made when they traveled in the bush'. Homesick, he visited his mother, who in drunken fury upbraided him for bringing home a tigress and slew him and his wife; the twin boys escaped, and their uncle Tobe-horoanna, hearing all, changed into a Black Tiger again, trotted off to the drinking-party, and killed everyone — mother, daughter, and all the guests.
summary.zh: 黑皮虎獲一青年，置之釜而曰：『毋懼，吾不烹汝。』令食全豚、盡飲一葫蘆之酒，嘔則再灌。其妹護之，許以女妻。婦生雙子，吼聲如雷——黑皮虎族行林之常聲也。夫省母；母醉怒，罵其娶虎婦，殺之並殺其妻。雙子遁歸；舅聞之，復化黑皮虎，奔至宴所，盡殺母、女與賓客。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: One day Tobe-horoanna caught a young man out in the bush and, dragging him home, put him inside the pot, saying: 'You must not be frightened. I do not intend killing, cooking, and eating you. You are going to live.' His brother and sister came home: 'Have you fed him? Well, give him a bush-hog, and if he does not finish the whole of it, we shall have to finish him.' The man did his best to eat, but by the time he had stowed away the two hind legs his belly could hold no more; they handed him a calabashful of cassiri, and when he vomited it, Black Tiger had his brother hold him while he should pour more down — until their sister told them to let the man alone, as she had taken a liking to him and wanted to live with him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §148; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，托貝-霍羅安納在灌木叢中抓到一個年輕人，把他拖回家，放進鍋裡，說道：「你不必害怕。我無意殺你、煮你、吃你。你要活下去。」他的弟弟和妹妹回到家：「你餵過他了嗎？好，給他一頭叢林野豬，要是他吃不完，我們就只好把他了結。」那人盡力去吃，可是等他吞下兩條後腿，肚子就再也裝不下了；他們遞給他一葫蘆卡西里酒，等他吐了出來，黑虎便叫弟弟按住他，好再往他嘴裡灌——直到他們的妹妹叫他們別再折騰那人，說她已經喜歡上他，想和他一起生活。

passages.text: They told him to go into the bush and hunt, so as to show them that he could support a wife; when he returned with ten dried bush-hogs, Tobe-horoanna said: 'All right! I am satisfied. You can have my sister.' Thus the man came to live a long time there with his Tiger wife, who ultimately bore him twin sons. As the children grew they growled and made a noise just like Naharani [thunder]; their mother told him it was nothing, 'but the same row which the Black Tiger nation always made when they traveled in the bush.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §148; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們叫他進灌木叢去打獵，好向他們證明他養得起妻子；當他帶著十頭燻乾的叢林野豬回來時，托貝-霍羅安納說：「好吧！我滿意了。你可以娶我妹妹。」於是那人便在那裡長住了下來，與他的虎妻一同生活，虎妻最終為他生下一對雙胞胎兒子。孩子們漸漸長大，咆哮起來，發出的聲音就像納哈拉尼〔雷〕一樣；他們的母親告訴他這沒什麼，「不過是黑虎族在灌木叢中行走時一向發出的那種聲響罷了。」

passages.text: Homesick, he visited his mother, who upbraided him for bringing home such a daughter-in-law — could he not see she was not 'a proper people' but a tigress, who would fall upon and destroy him some day? In her drunken fury she and her daughter killed him: his wife did her best to defend him, but they slew her also. His two boys managed to make good their escape and reached home in safety. Uncle Tobe-horoanna asked them where their father and mother were; hearing what had happened, he became very angry, changed himself into a Black Tiger again, trotted off to the place where they were all drinking, and killed everyone — mother, daughter, and all the guests.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §148; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他思鄉心切，回去探望母親，母親責罵他帶回這樣一個媳婦——難道他看不出她不是「正經人家」，而是一頭母虎，總有一天會撲上來把他毀掉嗎？在醉怒之下，她和她的女兒殺了他：他的妻子竭力護他，可她們把她也殺了。他的兩個兒子僥倖逃脫，平安回到家中。托貝-霍羅安納舅舅問他們父母在哪裡；聽說了發生的事，他勃然大怒，又變成一頭黑虎，小跑著趕到他們眾人飲酒的地方，把所有人殺光——母親、女兒，以及所有賓客。

title.en: Bravery Rewarded with a Wife: Sika-waka the Jigger-plenty
title.zh: 勇者得妻：多蚤之錫卡瓦卡

region.en: Pomeroon River, Guyana (Warrau)
region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

period: Warrau oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §147

summary.en: Some men out hunting found a dead mora tree overgrown with daiha creeper and went with their wives to strip the bark for apron-belts — a little boy along for company, climbing a manicole tree. The noise of their wooden staves drowned the roar of an immense Tiger, which appeared among them and killed every one except the boy, who slid down, jumped into the corial, and shoved off as Tiger, gorged with human flesh, came after him too late. Next morning he told the men; they found the mutilated bodies, and all but two turned cowards and climbed for safety — Tobe-akuba and Sika-waka, the latter half-lame with the jiggers in his feet, fought the tiger alone and destroyed it. Tobe-akuba taunted the tree-climbers, gave Sika-waka his daughter to wife, and the dogs needed twenty days to devour what a big brute he must have been.
summary.zh: 獵者與妻往取岱哈藤皮；小兒登棕上望。虎至而盡殺之；小兒滑下，解舟而遁。翌日告眾；眾尋屍，見妻胸被齧。群皆怯而登樹；惟多貝阿庫巴與足患沙蚤之錫卡瓦卡二人戰而斃虎。庫巴嘲之曰：『爾足無蚤而怯，彼殘而敢。』乃以女妻之。犬二十日方食盡虎肉——其巨可知。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Some men were out hunting, when they came across a dead mora tree that had a daiha creeper growing over it. So soon as they reached home they told their wives, who arranged to go next day to gather the bark for apron-belts. They took a little boy with them for company, and, having reached the spot, started removing the bark while the child amused himself by climbing into a manicole tree. The noise made by their wooden staves drowned the roar of an immense Tiger, which suddenly appeared among them and, without giving them a chance of escape, killed every one — all except the little boy, who could see everything that took place.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §147; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有些男人外出打獵，遇見一棵枯死的莫拉樹，上面爬滿了戴哈藤。他們一回到家就告訴了妻子們，妻子們便安排第二天去剝樹皮做圍裙帶。她們帶上一個小男孩作伴，到了那地方，便開始剝樹皮，孩子則爬上馬尼科勒樹玩耍。她們敲打木杖發出的聲響蓋過了一頭巨虎的咆哮，那虎突然出現在她們中間，不給她們逃脫的機會，把她們一個個都殺了——只有那個小男孩倖免，他把發生的一切都看在眼裡。

passages.text: He saw the Tiger eat a piece out of this body and a bit out of that, finally dragging the bodies into the bush. As soon as the coast was clear the child slid down the tree, ran to the landing, jumped into the corial and shoved off — only just in time, because Tiger was after him, but unable to catch up with him on account of being gorged with human flesh. Next morning he told the men everything, and how all their women had been killed. Going to the spot they saw only blood, and one after another the mutilated bodies.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §147; not verbatim.
