passages.text: To fight with Lions is my work, I match myself against Naudar, bragged Afrasiyab; now whatsoe'er my grandsire left undone of vengeance-seeking, fight, and stratagem is left for my sharp sword to execute; the time of turmoil is the time for me. When herbage made the plain like painted silk, an army marched forth from Turan and Chin with mace-men from the Western lands, a host without a middle or an end; and the fortune of Naudar was young no longer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Naudar secs. 2-3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 與獅子搏鬥乃我之業，我當與瑙達爾一較高下，阿弗拉西亞布誇口道；如今我祖父未竟之復仇、征戰與謀略，皆留待我鋒利之劍去執行；動盪之時正是我之時。當草木使平原宛如彩繪絲綢，一支軍隊自圖蘭與秦地開拔而出，帶著來自西方之地的持錘戰士，大軍無中無盡；而瑙達爾的福運已不再年輕。

passages.text: Afrasiyab surveyed them and despatched by night a cameleer to bear Pashang a letter: the expected good hath come; Naudar's whole host is as a quarry to us, and Sam is dead; I feared none in Iran but him. By this time Shamasas is in Nimruz enthroned and crowned. The armies fought, and while the javelins put the earth in shade defeat drew ever nearer to Naudar; upon the side where bold Shapur was stationed the ranks were broken and the troops dispersed, but he maintained his post till he was slain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Naudar secs. 3-6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿弗拉西亞布巡視他們，並於夜間派遣一名駱駝伕送信給帕尚：所期盼之善已至；瑙達爾全軍於我們如囊中之物，而薩姆已死；在伊朗我唯獨懼他。此時沙瑪薩斯已在尼姆魯茲登基加冕。兩軍交戰，當標槍將大地籠罩於陰影之中，敗勢日益逼近瑙達爾；在勇猛的沙普爾所駐守的一側，陣列被衝破，部隊四散，但他堅守崗位直至陣亡。

passages.text: Karan, moved with jealousy for the women of Iran, went with all his valiant men toward Pars, and slew Barman on the way, avenging his brother Kubad. Naudar, on hearing that Karan had gone, sped after him, all instant to escape the evil day. Afrasiyab gat tidings, collected troops, and followed as 'twere a lion. They fought all night till noonday, and at length the Shah was taken with twelve hundred nobles; strive as they might to flee they were ensnared within the net of bale, and Afrasiyab put into bonds the captured host and Shah.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Naudar secs. 6-7 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡蘭因對伊朗婦女心懷嫉妒，率其所有勇猛之士前往帕爾斯，途中誅殺巴爾曼，為其兄弟庫巴德復仇。瑙達爾聽聞卡蘭已去，便疾追其後，急欲逃離凶險之日。阿弗拉西亞布得悉消息，聚集兵馬，如獅般追擊。他們通宵激戰直至正午，最終沙阿與一千二百名貴族一同被擒；他們雖竭力欲逃，卻仍陷於災禍之網，阿弗拉西亞布將被俘的軍隊與沙阿一併捆縛。

title.en: Old Kubad Accepts Death and Falls to Barman
title.zh: 老將庫巴德赴死

region.en: Plain of Dahistan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 達希斯坦平原（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Naudar sec. 4

summary.en: Barman the Turkman shouts a challenge, and none responds but valiant old Kubad, Karan's brother, who knows the rolling sky hath given him enough: no mortal passeth into heaven alive; man is death's quarry. Make me a royal charnel in your love, he says, then sallies forth like a fierce elephant. The two contend from dawn till shadows lengthen; a dart through mail and buckle strikes his hip, and that ancient lion-heart falls headlong, leaving Karan to take up his blood-feud.
summary.zh: 突厥人巴爾曼陣前叫陣，應戰者唯有卡蘭之兄、老將庫巴德：「上天已給足我壽數；凡人無法活著進天堂，人皆為死之獵物。」他懇求弟弟日後為他築王家陵寢，便如猛象般出陣。二人自晨戰至日影斜長，一鏢穿甲扣中其臀，老獅之心轰然倒下——卡蘭從此背負血仇。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Barman pricked forth and shouted to Karan: in all the army of the famed Naudar hast thou a man who will contend with me? Karan looked round upon his mighty men for one to volunteer, but none responded save valiant old Kubad. The prudent chief was grieved and troubled when his brother spake, and wept for wrath, that with so many young to fight, one old man only volunteered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Naudar sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴爾曼策馬上前，向卡蘭喊道：在著名的瑙達爾全軍之中，你可有一人能與我交戰？卡蘭環顧他的勇士們，尋找一個自願應戰的人，但除了英勇的老庫巴德之外，無人回應。當他的兄弟開口時，這位審慎的統帥既悲傷又憂慮，並因憤怒而哭泣，因為有這麼多年輕人可以作戰，卻只有一個老人自願。

passages.text: The rolling sky hath given me enough, said Kubad in presence of the troops. Know, brother, that the body is for death; my head and neck were meant to wear a helm. No mortal passeth into heaven alive; man is death's quarry; one the scimitar destroyeth mid the mellay, and another's life is ended on his bed. Make me a royal charnel in your love, give musk, rose-water, camphor for my head, my body to the place of endless sleep; this do, live peacefully, and trust in God.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Naudar sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 庫巴德在軍隊面前說道：流轉的蒼天已給我足夠了。兄弟，你要知道，身體是為死亡而設的；我的頭和頸本是要戴頭盔的。沒有凡人活著進入天國；人是死亡的獵物；一個人在混戰中被彎刀毀滅，另一個人的生命則在床上終結。請在你的愛中為我造一座王家墓室，給我的頭塗上麝香、玫瑰水和樟腦，把我的身體交給無盡長眠之地；這樣做吧，平靜地活著，並信靠上帝。

passages.text: This said, he grasped his spear and sallied forth like some fierce elephant. The sky gave me my share long since, said he to Barman, and he whose hour hath come will have to die where'er he be: that time is not ill-timed at any time. He spake and urged his sable steed, denying his ardent heart all rest. The two contended from dawn till shadows lengthened; in the end the victory was Barman's, who as he rode hurled at Kubad a dart which struck his hip and pierced his belt. That ancient lion-heart fell headlong and so passed, and Karan, when Kubad was slain, drew out his army and attacked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Naudar sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 說完這話，他緊握長矛，像一頭兇猛的大象般衝了出去。他對巴爾曼說：蒼天早已給了我我的份額，而那個時辰已到的人，無論身在何處都必死：那個時刻在任何時候都不算不合時宜。他說完便催動他的黑色駿馬，不讓他那熾熱的心有片刻安寧。兩人從黎明爭鬥到影子拉長；最終勝利屬於巴爾曼，他騎馬時向庫巴德投出一支標槍，擊中他的臀部並刺穿他的腰帶。那顆古老的獅子之心一頭栽倒，就此逝去；庫巴德被殺後，卡蘭便率軍出擊。

title.en: Okonorote and the Pit into the Lower World (Warrau Version)
title.zh: 奧科諾羅特與通下界之穴（瓦勞版）

region.en: Pomeroon River, Guyana (Warrau)
region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

period: Warrau oral tradition; recorded 1883 (im Thurn)

source.work: Everard F. im Thurn, Among the Indians of Guiana (1883), ch. XVIII 'Folk-lore'

summary.en: The Warraus begin their story not with the manufacture of bodies but from a time when their ancestors lived in sky-land. There Okonorote, a famous hunter, followed a bird for many days; his arrow pierced it at last, but the game fell down into a deep pit — and looking down Okonorote saw daylight below, and discerned a land on which many kinds of four-footed animals were walking. With the help of his tribe he hung a long bush-rope down toward the earth and climbed down it. The Warraus who had remained in sky-land so appreciated the venison he brought home that they determined to move to the land below; after many had descended, a woman stuck in the hole and could never be moved — so those already on earth had to remain there, and those still in sky-land remained there. The True Caribs tell the story with one difference: their object in coming down was to clean the earth, which was evidently very dirty.
summary.zh: 瓦勞人言其祖居天上。獵人奧科諾羅特逐鳥多日，末射中之；鳥墮深穴。俯視見穴下有天光，更有大地，走獸成群。族人助之垂長藤而下。歸而携鹿肉；天上部族嘗之，皆願遷居下界。既降多人，一婦卡於穴口，推挽不動——已降者遂留人間，未降者留天上。真加勒比人則謂其下地之目的乃掃除大地之穢。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded by im Thurn 1883; archival record, read critically. Variant of the existing Warau sky-descent record.

passages.text: The Warraus, without troubling their minds as to the first manufacture of the bodily shapes which we see, begin their story from a time when their ancestors lived in sky-land. Up there one of their number, named Okonorote, was a famous hunter. On one occasion he followed a bird for many days without finding opportunity to shoot it. At length he succeeded, his arrow piercing the bird. But the game fell down into a deep pit, and was apparently lost.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 瓦勞人並不費心去探究我們所見的身體形態最初是如何製造的，而是從他們的祖先生活在天空之地的時代開始講述他們的故事。在那裡，他們中的一員名叫奧科諾羅特，是一位著名的獵人。有一次，他追蹤一隻鳥許多天，卻始終找不到射擊的機會。最後他成功了，他的箭射穿了那隻鳥。但獵物掉進了一個深坑，顯然就此失去了。

passages.text: Okonorote, looking down into the pit, saw daylight below, and before long was able to discern down below a land on which many kinds of four-footed animals were walking. With the help of his tribe he hung a long piece of bush-rope down toward the earth, and then climbed down this. After much successful hunting he climbed home again, taking with him some venison. The Warraus who had remained in sky-land, never having tasted such food before, appreciated it so highly that they determined to move to the land below.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧科諾羅特向坑中望去，看見下面有日光，不久便能辨認出下方有一片土地，許多種四足動物正在上面行走。在族人的幫助下，他朝地面垂下一長段叢林繩索，然後沿著它爬了下去。在多次成功的狩獵之後，他帶著一些鹿肉又爬回了家。留在天空之地的瓦勞人從未嘗過這樣的食物，對此極為讚賞，於是決定遷往下面的土地。

passages.text: After many had descended, a woman — who according to some was with child, according to others was very fat — stuck in the hole in sky-land, and though the other members of the tribe pushed and pulled from above and below, it was never possible to move her. So the Warraus who were already on earth had to remain there, and those who were still in sky-land remained there. The True Caribs have a story which differs from this of the Warraus only in that the former represent that their object in coming down from sky-land to earth was to clean the latter place, which was evidently very dirty.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在許多人降下之後，一個女人——有人說她懷著孕，有人說她非常肥胖——卡在天空之地的洞口，儘管部落的其他成員從上下又推又拉，卻始終無法移動她。於是，已經在地球上的瓦勞人只得留在那裡，而仍在天空之地的瓦勞人也留在了那裡。真正的加勒比人有個故事，與瓦勞人的這個故事僅在於前者聲稱，他們從天空之地降到地球的目的是清理後者，因為後者顯然非常骯髒。

title.en: Korobona and the Stump of the Pond
title.zh: 科羅波納與池中樹樁

region.en: Pomeroon swamps, Guyana (Warrau)
region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍沼地瓦勞之地

period: Warrau oral tradition; recorded 1883 (im Thurn)

source.work: Everard F. im Thurn, Among the Indians of Guiana (1883), ch. XVIII 'Folk-lore'

summary.en: The Warraus tell how the first Carib was born, and how the enmity between the two tribes began. There was a pond in which the Warraus feared to bathe; two women ventured into the water, and Korobona, touching the stump of a tree which rose over the surface, was seized by it and made his wife. Her brothers, jealous of their sister's honor, wished to kill her child; it soon died. A second child, a boy, she hid in the forest; the brothers shot their arrows into him and left him as dead, but the mother nursed and reared him. When he was a big boy they attacked him and cut his body in small pieces — and from the grave in which the mother buried him rose an Indian more powerful and more fierce than any Warrau had ever been. He was the first Carib, who, with his descendants, waged perpetual war on the Warraus and reduced them to their present miserable state.
summary.zh: 瓦勞人言首加勒比之生與二族之仇。池中有樹樁，人皆畏不敢浴；科羅波納觸之，樁攫之為妻。兄惡其辱，欲殺其嬰；嬰旋死。再生一男，匿於林中；兄射之而去，母育之得活。及長，兄攻而碎其體——母葬之，墓中起一勇士，猛逾瓦勞之任何男子。是為首加勒比；其子孫與瓦勞永戰，遂使瓦勞淪於今日之慘境。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded by im Thurn 1883; archival record, read critically. Variant cross-ref to Roth's origin-of-Caribs records.

passages.text: Once upon a time there was a pond in which, as is often the case, the Warraus feared to bathe. At last two Indian women ventured into the water. Presently one of the women, named Korobona, touched the stump of a tree which rose over the surface of the water, and immediately the stump seized her and made her his wife. Then Korobona returned home, where after some time a child was born. The brothers, jealous of their sister's honour, wished to kill it, but eventually consented to spare it. The child, however, soon died.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一處池塘，正如常見的情形那樣，瓦勞人不敢在其中沐浴。最後有兩名印第安婦女冒險下水。不久，其中一名名叫科羅博納的婦女觸到了露出水面的樹樁，那樹樁立刻抓住她，娶她為妻。後來科羅博納回到家中，過了些時日生下了一個孩子。她的兄弟們因顧惜姊妹的名譽，想要殺死這孩子，但最終同意饒他一命。然而這孩子不久便死了。

passages.text: Then Korobona went back to the pond, and again saw the stump. Once more a child was born, this time a boy. The mother, remembering her brothers' threats on the previous occasion, hid the child in the forest. But the brothers discovered their sister's secret, and, having shot their arrows into the boy, left him as dead. But the mother nursed her child, revived it, and succeeded in rearing it. It was not till the child was a big boy that the brothers discovered that he still lived. Then they attacked him, and cut his body in small pieces.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是科羅博納又回到池塘，再次見到了那樹樁。她又生下了一個孩子，這次是個男孩。母親記起兄弟們上一次的威脅，便把這孩子藏在森林裡。但兄弟們發現了姊妹的秘密，用箭射中了那男孩，把他丟下當作已死。然而母親照料自己的孩子，使他甦醒過來，並成功地將他撫養長大。直到這孩子長成一個大男孩時，兄弟們才發現他仍然活著。於是他們攻擊他，把他的身體切成小塊。

passages.text: From the grave in which the mother buried the victim rose an Indian more powerful and more fierce than any Warrau had ever been. He was the first Carib, who, with his descendants, waged perpetual war on the Warraus and reduced them to their present miserable state.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從母親埋葬死者的墳墓中，升起了一個比任何瓦勞人都更強壯、更兇猛的印第安人。他就是第一個加勒比人，他與他的後裔對瓦勞人發動了永無休止的戰爭，使他們淪落到如今悲慘的境地。

title.en: The Food-Tree and the Watchers (Carib Version)
title.zh: 食樹與窺者（加勒比版）

region.en: Carib country, Guyana
region.zh: 蓋亞那加勒比之地

period: Carib oral tradition; recorded 1883 (im Thurn)

source.work: Everard F. im Thurn, Among the Indians of Guiana (1883), ch. XVIII 'Folk-lore'

summary.en: The Caribs say that when they first arrived on earth from sky-land, cassava, plantains, and all useful vegetables grew on one huge tree. This tree was first discovered by a tapir, who grew fat on the fruits which fell from its branches. The Caribs, finding the new land a poor place without food, set the woodpecker to watch him — but the woodpecker, flying after the tapir, could not resist the temptation to tap the trees for insects, and the tapir, hearing the noise, knew he was followed and went another way. Then the Caribs sent a rat, who traced the tapir to his food-tree but, having agreed with the tapir to share the food quietly, persuaded the Caribs that he too had failed — until they found him asleep one day with corn still in his mouth, woke him and compelled him to show the tree. Each man took pieces of the felled tree and planted them in a field of his own; so from that day each Indian has had his own cassava-field.
summary.zh: 加勒比人言初至大地時，木薯、香蕉與百蔬皆生於一巨樹。貘先得之，食落果而肥。加勒比人饑而蹤之；啄木鳥窺之，忍不住叩木覓蟲，貘聞聲而遁。再遣田鼠；鼠與貘私約分食，詭言無所獲——後眾見其口含穀而睡，喚醒逼其指樹。伐而分之，各植於己田；自是印第安人各有薯田。

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded by im Thurn 1883; archival record, read critically. Variant of Roth's Allepdntepo record.

passages.text: The Caribs say that when they first arrived on earth from sky-land, cassava, plantains, and all useful vegetables grew on one huge tree. This tree was first discovered by a tapir, who grew fat on the fruits which fell from its branches. The Caribs, who as yet had found the new land a poor place and without food, were eager to find where the tapir fed. So they set the woodpecker to watch him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 加勒比人說，當他們最初從天空之地來到世上時，木薯、大蕉以及一切有用的蔬菜都長在一棵巨樹上。這棵樹最先被一頭貘發現，牠靠著從樹枝上落下的果實長得肥壯。加勒比人此時還覺得這片新土地貧瘠而沒有食物，急於找出貘在何處進食。於是他們派啄木鳥去監視牠。

passages.text: But the woodpecker as he flew through the forest after the tapir could not resist the temptation to tap the trees for insects, and the tapir, hearing the noise, knew he was followed, and went another way. Then the Caribs sent a rat, who stealthily succeeded in tracing the tapir to his food-tree; but the rat, having agreed with the tapir quietly to share the food, persuaded the Caribs that he too had failed in the quest. But the Caribs, finding the rat asleep one day with corn still in his mouth, woke him and compelled him to show the tree.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但啄木鳥在森林中追隨貘飛翔時，忍不住誘惑去啄樹尋蟲，貘聽見聲響，知道自己被跟蹤了，便改走另一條路。於是加勒比人派了一隻老鼠，牠悄悄地成功追蹤貘到了牠的食樹；但老鼠與貘私下約定共同分享食物，便哄騙加勒比人說牠也未能完成任務。然而加勒比人有一天發現老鼠睡著時嘴裡還含著穀物，便叫醒牠，強迫牠指出那棵樹。

passages.text: Then the Caribs took their stone axes, and after many months' hard work succeeded in felling it. Each man took pieces of the tree and planted them in a field of his own; so from that day each Indian has had his own cassava-field.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是加勒比人拿起石斧，經過數月的艱苦勞作，終於把樹砍倒。每個人都取了樹的碎片，種在自己的田裡；從那天起，每個印第安人便有了自己的木薯田。

title.en: The Flood from the Basket: the Howler's Throat and the Trumpeter's Legs
title.zh: 籃下洪水：吼猴之喉與鶴之脛

region.en: Ackawoi country, upper Mazaruni, Guyana
region.zh: 蓋亞那馬扎魯尼上游阿卡瓦之地

period: Akawai oral tradition; recorded 1883 (im Thurn)

source.work: Everard F. im Thurn, Among the Indians of Guiana (1883), ch. XVIII 'Folk-lore'

summary.en: The Ackawoi tell that the acourie was the original discoverer of the food-tree, and that one single man — their traditional ancestor — assisted by various animals cut it down. From the stump of the felled tree a flood began to flow out onto the land, but before much harm was done its flow was stopped by one man, who inverted an empty basket over the spring of water. For some time the water was confined under the basket; but at last the brown monkey, suspecting that something very good must be hidden under the carefully tended basket, cautiously raised it and peeped under. In an instant the flood rushed out, carrying away the monkey and overflowing the whole land. Then the man, with all manner of animals, took refuge up in a tall kokerite palm. Most of the fugitives remained patiently during the flood, but the red howling-monkey began to roar so loudly that his throat swelled and has remained extended ever since — that is the reason of the curious bony drum in the throat of this animal. The trumpet-bird flew down in such a hurry that he alighted in an ants' nest, and the hungry insects fastened on his legs, which had before been fairly thick, and gnawed them down to their present spindle-like size.
summary.zh: 阿卡瓦人言食樹乃刺鼠先得，其祖一人力伐之。樹樁湧泉成洪；一人倒置空籃於泉上而塞之。棕猴疑籃下藏美物，潛掀而窺之——洪即暴發，沖猴而去，盡沒大地。人與眾獸避於高柯基里棕。紅吼猴怒吼，喉腫而至今長存——故其喉中有骨鼓；鶴鳥急降蟻塚，脛為蟻齧細如今。

sensitivity.note: Akawai oral tradition recorded by im Thurn 1883; archival record, read critically. Flood-cluster record.

passages.text: The Ackawoi tell a tale which differs from the Carib story of the food-tree only in that they say that the acourie was the original discoverer of the food-tree, and that one single man, apparently their traditional ancestor, assisted by various animals, cut it down. From the stump of the felled tree a flood began to flow out on to the land, but before much harm was done the flow of water was stopped by one man, who inverted an empty basket over the spring of water and so stopped its flow.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿卡沃伊人講述的一則故事，與加勒比人的食樹故事只有一點不同：他們說阿庫里鳥才是食樹最初的發現者，而由一個單獨的人——顯然是他們傳說中的祖先——在各種動物的協助下將樹砍倒。從被砍倒的樹樁上，洪水開始湧出，漫向大地；但在造成大害之前，有一個人止住了水流，他將一隻空籃子倒扣在水源之上，就此堵住了水流。

passages.text: For some time the water was confined under the basket. But at last the brown monkey, curious, and suspecting that something very good must be hidden under the carefully tended basket, cautiously raised it and peeped under. In an instant the flood rushed out, carrying away the monkey, and overflowing the whole land. Then the man, with all manner of animals, took refuge up in a tall kokerite palm.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一段時間，水被拘禁在籃子底下。但最後，那隻褐猴心生好奇，猜想在這隻被小心看管的籃子底下必定藏著什麼極好的東西，便小心翼翼地將它掀起，往底下窺看。剎那之間，洪水奔湧而出，將猴子沖走，並淹沒了整片大地。於是，那個人帶著各種各樣的動物，逃到一棵高大的科克里特棕櫚樹上避難。

passages.text: Most of the fugitives remained patiently during the flood, but the red howling-monkey, getting excited, began to roar, and roared so loudly that his throat swelled, and has remained extended ever since — that is the reason of the curious bony drum in the throat of this animal. Meanwhile the trumpet-bird flew down in such a hurry that he alighted in an ants' nest, and the hungry insects fastened on his legs, which had before been fairly thick, and gnawed them down to their present spindle-like size.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大多數避難者在洪水期間都耐心地待著，但那隻紅吼猴卻興奮起來，開始吼叫，吼得如此響亮，以致喉嚨腫脹，自此便一直鼓脹著——這就是這種動物喉部長有那奇特骨質鼓膜的原因。與此同時，那隻喇叭鳥飛下來時太過匆忙，竟落在一處蟻巢上，飢餓的螞蟻便附上牠的腿——那腿原先相當粗壯——將牠啃得只剩下如今這般紡錘似的細小尺寸。

title.en: How the Alligator Lost His Tongue
title.zh: 鱷失舌記

region.en: Ackawoi country, upper Mazaruni, Guyana
region.zh: 蓋亞那馬扎魯尼上游阿卡瓦之地

period: Akawai oral tradition; recorded 1883 (im Thurn)

source.work: Everard F. im Thurn, Among the Indians of Guiana (1883), ch. XVIII 'Folk-lore'

summary.en: When the flood had subsided, the man began to rub two pieces of wood to make fire, and the first spark generated in this way is very small. The bush-turkey, at a moment when the man was looking away, swallowed this spark, mistaking it for a fire-fly, and then flew quickly away: the spark burned the bush-turkey's throat, and that is the reason why to this day those birds have a red wattle on their throats. Meanwhile the man, missing his spark, saw the alligator, who was then a gentle brute but ugly, standing near. Immediately the other animals, agreeing in their abhorrence of the ugliness of the alligator, raised a shout that it was he who had taken the spark. Whereupon the man, angry and impatient, tore out the tongue of the supposed culprit. And this is the reason why alligators have ever since had such very rudimentary tongues, and also why they wage perpetual war on other beasts.
summary.zh: 洪水既退，人始鑽木取火；初出之火星甚微。火雞誤為螢而吞之，喉灼成赤垂——至今猶然。人失火而見鱷——古性溫而貌醜——立於近旁。眾獸憎其醜，齊呼曰：『火乃鱷竊也！』人怒，拔其舌。故鱷之舌今甚短，且與百獸永戰不休。

sensitivity.note: Akawai oral tradition recorded by im Thurn 1883; archival record, read critically. Fire-theft cluster record.

passages.text: The others having descended more cautiously and safely, the man began to rub two pieces of wood to make fire. Now the first spark generated in this way is very small. The bush-turkey, at a moment when the man was looking away, swallowed this spark, mistaking it for a fire-fly, and then flew quickly away. The spark burned the bush-turkey's throat, and that is the reason why to this day those birds have a red wattle on their throats.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 其餘的動物較為謹慎、安全地下了樹，那個人便開始摩擦兩塊木頭來取火。這般取出的第一點火星非常微小。叢林火雞趁那人把目光移開的一刻，將這點火星吞了下去，誤以為牠是一隻螢火蟲，隨即迅速飛走。火星灼傷了叢林火雞的喉嚨，這就是為什麼這些鳥至今喉部仍長著紅色肉垂的原因。

passages.text: Meanwhile, the man missing his spark, saw the alligator, who was then a gentle brute, but ugly, standing near. Immediately the other animals, agreeing in their abhorrence of the ugliness of the alligator, raised a shout that it was he who had taken the spark. Whereupon the man, angry and impatient, tore out the tongue of the supposed culprit. And this is the reason why alligators have ever since had such very rudimentary tongues, and also why they wage perpetual war on other beasts. That is all that is known of the story.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 與此同時，那個人發現火星不見了，便看見鱷魚——牠當時還是性情溫順的畜生，只是醜陋——正站在近旁。其他動物立刻同聲憎惡鱷魚的醜陋，齊聲高喊說正是牠拿走了火星。於是，那個人又怒又急，便將這隻被認定的罪犯的舌頭扯了出來。這就是為什麼鱷魚自此以後舌頭都如此退化，也是為什麼牠們與其他野獸永世爭戰不休的原因。關於這個故事，所知的就是這些。

title.en: The Sun's Fish-Dam and the Alligator's Scales
title.zh: 日神之魚壩與鱷之鱗

region.en: Arawak country, Guyana (after Brett)
region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地（據布雷特）

period: Arawak tradition recorded by Brett; retold 1883 (im Thurn)

source.work: Everard F. im Thurn, Among the Indians of Guiana (1883), ch. XVIII 'Folk-lore'

summary.en: The Sun one day came down to fish. Like any other Indian, he built a dam across the mouth of a fish-haunted stream to retain the prey; but in his absence the otters broke his dam, and the fish escaped. Then the Sun rebuilt it and placed a woodpecker to watch it. One day the woodpecker tapped very loudly, and the Sun came to see what was the matter: this time it was the alligator who was trying to do damage. So the Sun drove him away by striking him again and again with a huge club — thus were made those marks which we think are scales, to be seen on the alligator to this day.
summary.zh: 一日日神下凡捕魚；如常人然，於多魚溪口築壩蓄之。日神不在，水獺毀壩，魚皆遁。日神重築，以啄木鳥守之。一日鳥叩甚急；日神至視之，乃鱷欲害也。遂以巨杖連擊而逐之——鱷身上所謂鱗者，即杖痕也。

sensitivity.note: Arawak tradition from Brett, retold by im Thurn 1883; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The Sun one day came down to fish. Like any other Indian, he built a dam across the mouth of a fish-haunted stream to retain the prey. But in his absence the otters broke his dam, and the fish escaped. Then the Sun rebuilt it and placed a woodpecker to watch it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，太陽下凡來捕魚。像任何其他印第安人一樣，他在一條多魚的溪流口築起一道堰壩，以留住獵物。但在他離開的時候，水獺弄破了他的堰壩，魚便逃走了。於是太陽重新築起堰壩，並派一隻啄木鳥看守。

passages.text: One day, the woodpecker tapping very loudly, the sun came to see what was the matter. This time it was the alligator who was trying to do damage. So the Sun drove him away by striking him again and again with a huge club. Thus were made those marks which we think are scales, which are to be seen on the alligator to this day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，啄木鳥啄得非常大聲，太陽便前來看看是怎麼回事。這一次是鱷魚在搗亂。於是太陽用一根巨大的棍棒一次又一次地打牠，把牠趕走。我們以為是鱗片的那些痕跡就是這樣留下的，至今仍可在鱷魚身上看到。

title.en: The King-Vulture Wife (im Thurn Version)
title.zh: 王鷲之妻（英特恩版）

region.en: Arawak country and sky-land
region.zh: 阿拉瓦克之地與天界

period: Arawak tradition recorded by Brett; retold 1883 (im Thurn)

source.work: Everard F. im Thurn, Among the Indians of Guiana (1883), ch. XVIII 'Folk-lore'

summary.en: A young Arawak chose as his wife a king-vulture; an Indian, when he marries, goes to live with his wife's father, so he went to sky-land and was well received by the vulture's people. But when after a time he announced his intention of paying a visit to his own people, the vultures were enraged, and set him on top of a tall awarra-palm whose trunk is covered with terrible thorns. There he remained until some spiders, feeling pity, spun a cord by which he descended. For many years he tried to get back to his wife, but the vultures would have nothing more to say to him; at last the other birds, taking compassion, carried him to sky-land and helped him to fight the vultures, whose settlement was burned over their heads. In the plundering the trumpet-bird and heron rolled each other in the ashes — the grey back and the all-grey — the owl opened a carefully-done-up package and out came the darkness; and the Arawak on whose behalf the war was waged fought with and was killed by his own son by his vulture wife.
summary.zh: 一阿拉瓦克少年娶王鷲為妻；依俗往岳家——即天界——鷲族善待之。後告歸省，鷲族怒，置之高阿瓦拉棕之巔，幹生惡刺。蛛憐之，結繩而下。經年求復，鷲不納；群鳥憫之，載之上天，助其伐鷲，焚其居。分贓之際，鶴與鷺滾於灰——一得灰背一得通灰；鴞啟密裹之包，黑闇出焉。而為之興師之阿拉瓦克，竟為其鷲妻所生之子所殺。

sensitivity.note: Arawak tradition from Brett, retold by im Thurn 1883; archival record, read critically. Variant of birds-markings-war record.

passages.text: A similar tale tells how a young Arawak chose as his wife a king-vulture. Now an Indian man, when he marries, goes to live with his wife's father. So the Arawak went to sky-land and was well received by the vulture's people. But when after a time he announced his intention of paying a visit to his own people, the vultures were enraged, and set him on top of a tall awarra-palm, the trunk of which is covered with terrible thorns. There he remained until some spiders, feeling pity, spun a cord by which he descended.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一個類似的故事，講述一名年輕的阿拉瓦克人娶了一隻王鷲為妻。當時，印第安男子結婚後便到妻子的父親家居住。於是這名阿拉瓦克人前往天空之地，受到鷲族人的善待。但過了一段時間，當他宣布打算回鄉探望自己的族人時，鷲族人大為震怒，把他放到一棵高大的阿瓦拉棕櫚樹頂上，那樹幹上長滿了可怕的荊棘。他就待在那裡，直到一些蜘蛛心生憐憫，紡出一根繩子，他才順著繩子下來。

passages.text: Then for many years he tried to get back to his wife, but the vultures would have nothing more to say to him. But at last the other birds, taking compassion on him, carried him to sky-land and helped him to fight the vultures. The latter having been driven into their own houses, their whole settlement was burned over their heads. The Arawak on whose behalf this war was waged fought with, and was killed by, his own son by his vulture wife.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此後許多年，他都試圖回到妻子身邊，但鷲族人再也不願理會他。不過最後，其他鳥兒憐憫他，把他帶到天空之地，並幫他攻打鷲族人。鷲族人被趕進自己的屋子後，他們整個聚居地就在他們頭頂上被燒毀了。這場戰爭所為之而戰的那名阿拉瓦克人，與他和鷲妻所生的親生兒子搏鬥，並被兒子殺死。

passages.text: Then the other birds began to quarrel over the plunder. The trumpet-bird and the heron got so angry that they fought and rolled each other in the ashes, which is the reason why the former bird has ever since had a grey back, and why the latter has been grey all over. Taking advantage of the confusion, the owl, prowling about, found a package so carefully done up that he thought it must contain something very valuable. So he opened it, and out came the darkness in which he has ever since had to live.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著，其他鳥兒開始為戰利品爭吵起來。喇叭鳥和蒼鷺氣得打了起來，在灰燼中互相翻滾，這就是為什麼前者從此背上呈灰色，而後者全身都是灰色的緣故。貓頭鷹趁著混亂四處徘徊，發現了一個包裹得如此仔細的包裹，牠心想裡面一定裝著非常珍貴的東西。於是牠打開包裹，從裡面出來的正是黑暗，自此牠便不得不生活在黑暗之中。

title.en: The Old Man Adrift over Kaieteur Fall
title.zh: 老人漂過凱厄圖爾瀑

region.en: Kaieteur Fall, Potaro River, Guyana
region.zh: 蓋亞那波塔羅河凱厄圖爾瀑

period: Ackawoi tradition recorded 1883 (im Thurn)

source.work: Everard F. im Thurn, Among the Indians of Guiana (1883), ch. XVIII 'Folk-lore'

summary.en: At the Kaieteur fall there is, in mid-stream a few hundred yards below the fall, a long narrow island shaped much like one of the wood-skins, the bark-boats used by the Ackawoi of that river; and at the side of the river close to the foot of the column of water is a curiously regular rectangular rock shaped like the pegall, the basket in which the Indian packs his properties. Once upon a time, say the Ackawoi, there was on the savannah above the fall an Indian settlement in which lived an old man so worn out and useless from age that in his feet the jiggers buried themselves unmolested — a scandal and a nuisance to his fellows. So they put the old man with his pegall into a woodskin, launched it on the river, and allowed it to drift over the fall. The old man was never seen again; but his woodskin became the island in the river below the fall, and his pegall turned to stone, and remains to this day.
summary.zh: 凱厄圖爾瀑下數百步，河中有狹長之島，形如阿卡瓦人之皮舟；瀑腳旁有方正之石，狀若印第安人裝物之皮籃。阿卡瓦人言：瀑上草原舊有村落，中有老翁，衰廢無用，足中沙蚤叢生，為眾所憎。眾遂置翁及其籃於皮舟，順流而下，任其墮瀑。翁遂不復見；其舟化為瀑下之島，其籃化石，至今猶存。

sensitivity.note: Ackawai tradition recorded by im Thurn 1883; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Once upon a time, say the Ackawoi, there was on the savannah above the fall an Indian settlement in which lived an old man so worn out and useless from age that in his feet the jiggers buried themselves unmolested. In short, the old man was a scandal and a nuisance to his fellows. So the latter put the old man with his pegall into a woodskin, which they then launched on the river and allowed to drift over the fall.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿卡沃伊人說，從前在瀑布上方的草原上有一個印第安人聚居地，那裡住著一位老人，他年老體衰、毫無用處，連沙蚤都肆無忌憚地鑽進他的腳裡。總之，這老人對他的同伴來說是個恥辱，也是個累贅。於是他們把老人連同他的籃子放進一隻獨木舟裡，然後把船放到河上，任它漂過瀑布。

passages.text: The old man was never seen again; but his woodskin became the island in the river below the fall, and his pegall turned to stone, and remains to this day a curiously regular rectangular rock at the side of the river, close to the foot of the column of water.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那老人從此再未被見到；但他的獨木舟變成了瀑布下方河中的島嶼，他的籃子變成了石頭，至今仍留在河邊，就在水柱腳下附近，是一塊形狀出奇規整的長方形岩石。

title.en: Fabled Peoples: the Night-Folk of Canakoo and the Hooronis
title.zh: 幻族：卡納庫夜民與呼魯尼人

region.en: Canakoo mountains and Pacaraima, Guyana
region.zh: 蓋亞那卡納庫山與帕卡賴馬

period: Guiana oral tradition; recorded 1883 (im Thurn)

source.work: Everard F. im Thurn, Among the Indians of Guiana (1883), ch. XVIII 'Folk-lore'

summary.en: Traveling round the Canakoo mountains, im Thurn was often told of a certain tribe who lived up among the highest rocks and never came down into the plain except by night; fires may sometimes be seen up in these mountains by night. The Hooronis are a tribe living beyond the Pacaraimas, men by night but fish by day: if an Indian of another tribe finds his way into a Hooroni house and tries to put one of the apparent fish over the fire to roast, all the fish change back into men and slay the intruder. Another tribe lives like ordinary Indians by day but retires into the water at night, sleeping standing with only their heads above water. On Roraima the Indians say there are huge white jaguars and huge white eagles; and the di-dis, beings in shape something between men and monkeys, live in the forests near the river banks — the being that suggested to Charles Waterton his famous nondescript.
summary.zh: 卡納庫山中有一族，居最高之巖，惟夜始下平原；夜間山上有火光。呼魯尼人者，居帕卡賴馬之外，晝為魚夜為人：他族人入其屋，見魚而烹之，則魚皆復為人而殺之。又有一族，晝如常人，夜入水而立眠，僅露其首。羅賴馬山有白虎白鷹之屬；迪迪者，形介人猴之間，居河畔之林——華特頓氏怪物標本，蓋本於此。

sensitivity.note: Guiana oral tradition recorded by im Thurn 1883; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: When travelling round the Canakoo mountains, im Thurn was often told by the Indians of a certain tribe of Indians who lived up among the highest rocks and who never came down into the plain except by night. Indians who have ventured up into the mountains have often heard sounds from the settlements of these people; and even from below one may often see their fires by night — an appearance as of fire to be seen sometimes up in these mountains.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當伊姆·瑟恩在卡納庫山脈一帶遊歷時，印第安人常向他提起某一支印第安部落，說他們住在最高的岩山之間，除了夜裡從不下到平原。曾冒險登上山去的印第安人常聽見這些人聚居處傳來的聲響；甚至從山下也常在夜間望見他們的火光——那景象彷彿有時能在這些山上望見火光一般。

passages.text: Other people of the same kind are the Hooronis, a tribe of Indians living beyond the Pacaraimas, who are men by night but fish by day: even by day they do not live in the water, but lie about their houses as do fish caught for food by ordinary Indians. But if by chance an Indian of another tribe finds his way into the house of a Hooroni, and, thinking it empty, helps himself to any of the apparent fish lying about, and tries to put this fish over the fire to roast, then all the fish change back into men and slay the intruder. Another favourite statement of the Indians is that there is another tribe who live like ordinary Indians by day, but retire into the water at night and sleep standing, with only their heads above water.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 與之同類的還有胡羅尼人，這是一支住在帕卡拉伊馬山之外的印第安部落，他們夜間為人，白晝為魚：即便在白晝，他們也不住在水中，而是橫陳於屋內，如同尋常印第安人捕來作食的魚一般。但倘若別族的印第安人偶然闖進某個胡羅尼人的屋子，以為屋中無人，便擅自取走那些看似橫陳的魚，並想把這魚放到火上烤，那麼所有的魚便都變回人形，將這闖入者殺死。印第安人另一常愛說的是，還有另一支部落，白晝像尋常印第安人一樣生活，夜裡卻退入水中，立著睡覺，只把頭露在水面之上。

passages.text: Again, any extraordinary or inaccessible rock is always said to be inhabited by monstrous animals: on Roraima the Indians say that there are huge white jaguars and huge white eagles. To this class probably belongs the di-dis, beings in shape something between men and monkeys, who live in the forests near the river banks — a being which has some literary interest as probably that which suggested to Charles Waterton the idea of constructing his famous nondescript.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 再者，凡是奇特或難以攀登的岩石，總被說成有巨怪棲居：關於羅賴馬山，印第安人說那裡有巨大的白美洲豹和巨大的白鷹。屬於這一類的，大概還有迪迪斯，即形貌介於人與猴之間的生物，住在河岸附近的森林裡——這種生物頗有些文學上的意趣，因為很可能正是它給了查爾斯·沃特頓靈感，使他構想出那著名的「非驢非馬」之物。

title.en: The Haiarri Root: Grown from a Son's Blood
title.zh: 海阿黎根：生於子血

region.en: Arawak country, Guyana (after Brett)
region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地（據布雷特）

period: Arawak tradition recorded by Brett; retold 1883 (im Thurn)

source.work: Everard F. im Thurn, Among the Indians of Guiana (1883), ch. XVIII 'Folk-lore'

summary.en: Once upon a time an Indian took his young son to bathe. Wherever the lad swam the fish died; and the father found by experiment that these fish were quite wholesome as food, so he made a practice of obtaining fish in this way. But after a time the fish, having taken counsel, chose a moment when the lad sat on a log just before plunging into the water — when, therefore, the fish could approach him safely — and then, all springing out of the water together, struck their spines into the lad. The wound made in this way by the sting-ray proved fatal. But as the father was carrying his dying son home, the blood dropped on to the ground, and wherever it fell there grew up a haiarri plant, which has ever since been used by Indians to poison the streams when they want to catch fish.
summary.zh: 昔一印第安人攜幼子浴於河；童所游處，魚皆斃，而其肉可食。父遂習以為常。魚會議定計：俟童坐木未下水之際，群躍出水，以刺螫之。魟之傷致命。父負垂死之子歸；血滴於地，滴處皆生海阿黎——印第安人至今以之毒水取魚。

sensitivity.note: Arawak tradition from Brett, retold by im Thurn 1883; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Once upon a time an Indian took his young son to bathe. Wherever the lad swam the fish died; and the father found by experiment that these fish were quite wholesome as food. So he made a practice of obtaining fish in this way.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前，有個印第安人帶他的幼子去洗澡。那少年游到哪裡，魚便死到哪裡；父親經過試驗，發現這些魚作為食物十分有益健康。於是他便慣用這種方法捕魚。

passages.text: But after a time, the fish having taken council, chose a moment when the lad sat on a log just before plunging into the water, when, therefore, the fish could approach him safely, and then, all springing out of the water together, struck their spines into the lad. The wound made in this way by the sting-ray proved fatal.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但過了些時日，魚群商議之後，選中一個時機：那少年正坐在一根木頭上，尚未躍入水中，因此魚可以安全地靠近他；於是所有的魚一齊躍出水面，把刺扎進少年身上。這樣造成的傷口，乃是由刺魟所刺，終於致命。

passages.text: But as the father was carrying his dying son home, the blood dropped on to the ground, and wherever it fell there grew up a haiarri plant, which has ever since been used by Indians to poison the streams when they want to catch fish.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但當父親把垂死的兒子抱回家時，血滴落在地上，凡血滴落之處，都長出一株海阿里里植物；自此以後，印第安人想捕魚時，便用它來毒害溪流。

title.en: The Arawaks against Meyanow and the Caribs
title.zh: 阿拉瓦克戰梅亞瑙與加勒比

region.en: Pomeroon River, Guyana (Arawak)
region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河阿拉瓦克之地

period: Arawak historical legend recorded 1883 (im Thurn)

source.work: Everard F. im Thurn, Among the Indians of Guiana (1883), ch. XVIII 'Folk-lore'

summary.en: The Arawaks say that their ancestors had first to fight a fierce tribe called Meyanow; and after they had exterminated these they were harassed by the Caribs, who came first from the islands and then settled on the mainland. Every year the Caribs from all quarters gathered round the Arawaks on the Pomeroon and attacked them. One year the Arawaks chose a chief, placed their men in ambush on each side of the path from the river to the settlement, and when the Caribs fell into it, exhausted their arrows on them and finished with war-clubs till the few survivors, their retreat cut off, were all slain. The next year the chief hid the women and children, laid a huge tree-trunk under water across the mouth of a side stream, and sent a light canoe to lure the enemy: the pursuing Caribs' heavy canoes struck the unsuspected barrier and were split, and the Arawaks rushed out and slew almost all. A third time the Caribs came, and were again overthrown; their chief, struck in the face by a three-pronged fish arrow, was captured alive — and the Arawaks determined to let him go unharmed; and this was the end of the feud between the tribes.
summary.zh: 阿拉瓦克人言其先戰梅亞瑙族而滅之；繼為加勒比所擾。歲歲加勒比合圍波默龍。一歲，阿拉瓦克擇酋設伏於河路兩側；敵入伏，箭盡而以戰棒斃之，無一得脫。次歲，匿婦孺，沈巨木於支流之口，以輕舟誘敵；敵舟疾追，觸暗木而裂；眾出而幾盡殲之。三歲又至，又敗；其酋面中三叉魚箭而被擒。阿拉瓦克縱之無傷——二族之仇，至此而終。

sensitivity.note: Arawak historical legend recorded by im Thurn 1883; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The Arawaks say that their ancestors had first to fight a fierce tribe called Meyanow; and after they had exterminated these they were harassed by the Caribs, who came first from the islands, but afterwards settled on the mainland and carried on an even more constant warfare. Every year the Caribs from all quarters gathered round the Arawaks on the Pomeroon and attacked them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿拉瓦克人說，他們的祖先起初必須與一個名為梅亞諾（Meyanow）的凶猛部族作戰；在他們消滅了這個部族之後，又遭到加勒比人的侵擾。加勒比人最初來自各島嶼，後來卻定居於大陸，並進行著更為持續不斷的戰爭。每年，來自各方的加勒比人都會聚集在波梅隆河（Pomeroon）一帶的阿拉瓦克人周圍，向他們發動攻擊。

passages.text: One year, when the Caribs were expected, the Arawaks chose a chief to lead them against the enemy. Having seen that large quantities of arrows had been provided, he placed his men in ambush, some distance from the river, at each side of the path leading from the river to the settlement. When the Caribs came they fell into the ambush: the Arawaks exhausted their arrows, fell upon the enemy with their war-clubs, and not a Carib of that whole party escaped.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一年，預料加勒比人將至，阿拉瓦克人便選出一位首領率領他們迎敵。他見已備妥大量箭矢，便將部下埋伏在離河一段距離、從河通往聚落的小路兩側。加勒比人來到時，正落入埋伏之中：阿拉瓦克人射盡了箭，便手持戰棍撲向敵人，那一整隊加勒比人無一逃脫。

passages.text: The next year the chief made all his men hide their women and children in safety in the forest, placed the huge trunk of a tree across the mouth of a side stream just under water, and sent a small boat of very light draught to lure the enemy: the pursuing Caribs' large and heavy canoes struck heavily against the unsuspected barrier and were split, and the Arawaks rushed out from their hiding-places and slew almost all. Yet a third time the Caribs came, and were again overthrown; their chief, struck in the face by a three-pronged fish arrow, was captured alive — and the Arawaks determined to let him go unharmed; and this was the end of the feud between the tribes.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 翌年，首領命所有部下將婦孺安全藏於森林之中，又將一截巨大的樹幹橫置於一條支流的河口，恰在水面之下，並派出一艘吃水極淺的小舟引誘敵人：追擊的加勒比人那又大又重的獨木舟猛烈撞上這意想不到的障礙，裂了開來，阿拉瓦克人便從藏身之處衝出，幾乎將他們盡數殺死。然而加勒比人第三次來犯，又再度被擊敗；他們的首領被一支三叉魚箭射中面部，活捉了去——阿拉瓦克人決定放他安然離去；兩部族之間的仇怨就此了結。

title.en: Manubada's Bride
title.zh: 魚鷹之新娘

region.en: Wamira coast, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉海岸（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'Manubada's Bride'

summary.en: Jealous companions marooned the fairest girl of the village on an island that the tide would cover; the mango stone she had thrown behind her sprouted into a tree that bore her above the waves. There Manubada, the great fish-hawk, took her to be his bride and brought her raw fish; her bird-child flew to the mainland in mourning garb's shadow and brought her grandfather with a cooking pot and fire. Restored to her people she married her old betrothed — and the faithful bird-lover stretched his wings into the night and was never seen again.
summary.zh: 眾女嫉妒村中最美的姑娘，藉捕魚之機把她丟在漲潮即沒的小島上。她拋在身後的芒果核竟一夜生根成樹，托她高於浪頭。大魚鷹馬努巴達飛至，傾心娶她為妻，日日啣魚來獻；她嫌生肉難嚥，鷹傷心不已。後來她生下一個會飛的兒子，囑他去大陸：『落在那棵 natu 樹上，等一個服喪的老人走過——那是你的外祖父，他在哀悼我。』鳥童依言相告；外祖父攜炊鍋、火種、芋頭與珠貝刀駕舟而來，父女團圓。歸村之夕，鳥童忽言：『你們是人，我只是鳥！』展翅入夜，一去不返。姑娘後來嫁給先前的未婚夫；而那癡心的鷹，從此無人再提起。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: In the old days there was a girl who was so fair to see that no man cared to look on any other when she was by. Her hair was curly, she was not too tall, and her eyes shone like stars. Her companions envied her, and they determined to rid themselves of her if it were possible. They therefore took counsel together and made a plan. 'Let us go fishing,' they said, 'and then we can leave our rival behind when we return.' They waited for a calm day, and when at last one dawned, they gathered their fishing baskets, took down their nets from where they hung in the house, and went down to the beach where the canoe lay. When they were come to the island, the girls asked their rival to tarry with the canoe, while they fished. 'We will take thy basket with us,' said they, 'and fill it for thee.' The girls were away for some time, and found plenty of fish, but they kept it all for themselves, and filled the basket of their rival with empty shells.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Manubada's Bride' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古時候有一個姑娘，生得十分美麗，只要她在場，就沒有男子願意再看別人一眼。她的頭髮捲曲，身材不太高，雙眼如星辰般閃耀。她的同伴們嫉妒她，決意若能辦到便將她除掉。於是她們一同商議，定下計謀。「我們去捕魚吧，」她們說，「這樣我們回來時就能把我們的對手丟在後頭。」她們等候一個風平浪靜的日子，當這樣的日子終於來臨，她們便收拾好魚籃，從屋裡掛著的地方取下漁網，下到海灘上獨木舟停泊之處。到了島上，姑娘們請她們的對手留在獨木舟旁等候，由她們去捕魚。「我們會帶上你的籃子，」她們說，「替你裝滿。」姑娘們去了好一陣子，捕到許多魚，卻全留給了自己，只把她們對手的籃子裝滿了空貝殼。

passages.text: The beautiful girl, who had cared for the canoe, looked into her basket as she sat, and found it was full of empty shells. Yet was she not angry, but said with gentle voice, 'Friends, will ye paddle back to the island for a little? I must get some fish ere I go home.' The girls nodded their heads kindly, for indeed this was what they had plotted, and their plan was working well. So they turned the canoe round, and went back once more to the island. The beautiful girl leapt lightly out, and ran along the beach looking for fish. In a little she found plenty, and hasted back to the landing place. But alas! there she found that the faithless maidens had deserted her, and she was alone on the desolate island. She sat down and wept until she was weary. Then she ate a mango which she had carried with her, and as she made an end of eating, she threw the stone behind her. After a time she saw that the tide was rising; moreover, she remembered that the island was covered at high tide.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Manubada's Bride' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那位看守獨木舟的美麗姑娘坐著往自己的籃子裡一看，發現裡面裝滿了空貝殼。然而她並不生氣，只是柔聲說道：「朋友們，你們可否划回島上去一會兒？我回家之前得弄些魚。」姑娘們和善地點了點頭，因為這正是她們所謀劃的，她們的計謀正進行得順利。於是她們把獨木舟掉轉頭，又一次回到島上。美麗的姑娘輕盈地跳上岸，沿著海灘跑去尋找魚。不一會兒她便找到許多，急忙趕回登岸之處。可是唉！她到了那裡，卻發現那些背信的姑娘們已將她拋棄，她獨自一人留在這荒涼的島上。她坐下來哭泣，直到哭得疲倦。然後她吃了隨身帶著的一顆芒果，吃完時，她把果核扔在身後。過了一會兒，她見潮水正在上漲；而且，她想起這座島在漲潮時會被淹沒。

passages.text: By and by came Manubada, the great fish hawk. He flapped his wings with joy when he saw the maiden in the tree. He had never looked on aught so fair before, and he took her to be his bride. Then did Manubada bring her fish, and she turned aside with loathing, saying, 'I cannot eat raw flesh.' But he had no fire to give her, and sorrow filled his heart that she ate not of his gifts. After a time a little son was born. As soon as he was grown his mother bade him fly to the mainland and bring her help. Quoth she, 'Little son, on the beach thou wilt see a natu tree. Perch on that and wait until a man in mourning garb passes under it. He is thy grandfather, and is mourning for me, his child. Do thou tell him where I am. Ask him also to give thee a cooking pot, a piece of burning wood, some taro, and a pearl shell with which to peel it.' The bird-child did even as his mother bade him, and perched on the natu tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Manubada's Bride' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久，大魚鷹馬努巴達（Manubada）來了。他看見樹上的少女，便歡喜地拍動翅膀。他從未見過如此美麗的事物，便娶她為妻。於是馬努巴達為她銜來魚，她卻厭惡地別過頭去，說道：「我不能吃生肉。」但他沒有火可以給她，見她不吃他的贈禮，心中充滿悲傷。過了些時，一個小兒子誕生了。他剛長大，母親便吩咐他飛往大陸為她求助。她說：「小兒子，你在海灘上會看見一棵納圖樹（natu）。停在樹上，等候一個身穿喪服的人從樹下經過。他是你的外祖父，正為我這個孩子服喪。你告訴他我在何處。也請他給你一個煮食的鍋、一塊燃燒的木頭、一些芋頭，以及一片用來削芋頭的珍珠貝殼。」這鳥兒孩子照母親的吩咐做了，停在納圖樹上。

passages.text: They reached the island, and the old man greeted his daughter with joy. Then he cooked taro for her, and she ate it and was filled. When the meal was now over, the old man helped his daughter into the canoe, and took her back to her old home, her little son flying overhead. In the evening all sat round the fire, and talked of what had befallen the girl. But while they were yet talking, little Manubada said on a sudden, 'Here we sit, but ye are people, and I am only a bird!' And having spoken he stretched his wings and departed into the night, nor did he ever return. As for Manubada's bride, her old lover, to whom she was betrothed before she left her village, was still faithful to her, and soon were they married. And no more was Manubada had in remembrance, the faithful bird-lover who had given all his heart to the maiden on the lonely island.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Manubada's Bride' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們抵達了那座島，老人歡喜地迎接女兒。接著他為她煮了芋頭，她吃了，吃飽了。飯食既畢，老人扶女兒上了獨木舟，把她送回她舊日的家，她的小兒子在上方飛翔。傍晚時分，眾人圍火而坐，談論那少女所遭遇的事。然而正當他們還在說話時，小馬努巴達忽然說道：『我們坐在這裡，但你們是人，我不過是一隻鳥罷了！』說完，他展開雙翼，沒入夜色而去，此後再也不曾回來。至於馬努巴達的新娘，她離開村莊之前與之訂婚的舊日情人，仍對她忠貞不渝，不久二人便成了婚。馬努巴達也再無人記念——那忠誠的鳥戀人，曾把全副心意都給了那孤島上的少女。

title.en: How the Twins Killed Manubada
title.zh: 雙生子誅馬努巴達

region.en: Wamira coast, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉海岸（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'How the Twins Killed Manubada'

summary.en: Kototabe and Kelokelo, twin sons of the man the great hawk Manubada had killed, watched the dracaena branch their mother held and set out for the eyrie. They dived on either side of the canoe as the hawk stooped; his beak pierced the wood and pinned him fast; they broke his wings and clubbed him to death — and the portions of the feast give the mountain people their bowed heads and the coast folk their sidestep against spears.
summary.zh: 孿生兄弟科托塔貝與凱洛凱洛的父親被大鷹馬努巴達所殺。二人長成後備好彈弓與棍棒出海尋仇，留下一枝龍血樹葉給母親：『葉動你可起舞；葉垂你當哭泣——我們就死了。』至崖下仰見鷹巢，他們發石挑戰。馬努巴達輕敵，展翅撲下；雙子分舟兩側跳水；鷹嘴來勢太猛，竟穿透舟板自釘其上；他掙扎不脫，力竭之際，雙子浮起，各折一翼，亂棍斃之。歸村之時，母親見龍血樹葉顫動，早已起舞迎子。全村分食鷹肉：山地人得頭，故今遇敵皆低頭避擊；海濱人得側身，故今飛矛臨身，側身即避——講這故事的人正是海濱人，征戰多次，未嘗受傷。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: Kototabe and Kelokelo were twin brothers whose father had been killed by Manubada, the great hawk. It came to pass that on a day they played with slings, and made as if to aim at the boys who were their companions. But they said, 'Hurt us not, O Kototabe and Kelokelo, but aim at the bird which killed your father.' The boys wondered much what this might mean, and ran home to ask their mother. The widow told them that it was true Manubada had killed their father, but she warned them that none might hope to fight with so great an enemy and yet prevail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How the Twins Killed Manubada' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 科托塔貝與凱洛凱洛是一對孿生兄弟，他們的父親為大鷹馬努巴達所殺。有一天，他們玩著投石索，裝作要向同伴的男孩們瞄準。但他們說：『科托塔貝、凱洛凱洛啊，別傷我們，去瞄準那隻殺了你們父親的鳥吧。』兩個男孩十分納悶，不知這是什麼意思，便跑回家去問母親。那寡婦告訴他們，馬努巴達確實殺了他們的父親，但她告誡他們，沒有人能指望與如此強大的敵人爭鬥而仍得勝。

passages.text: 'Nay, mother,' answered the children, 'but when we are bigger we shall slay him who hath slain our father.' The widow trembled much at these daring words, but held her peace. When Kototabe and Kelokelo were now grown they made ready for the journey to Manubada's eyrie. They took a strong canoe, and loaded it with slings and clubs. Then they gave to their mother a branch of dracaena leaves, and said, 'Watch these leaves, mother. When they wave thou mayest dance, but if they droop thou must weep, for we shall indeed be dead.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How the Twins Killed Manubada' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 『不，母親，』孩子們答道，『等我們長大了，就要殺掉那殺了我們父親的傢伙。』寡婦聽了這番大膽的話，顫抖不已，卻默然不語。如今科托塔貝與凱洛凱洛已長大成人，便準備踏上前往馬努巴達巢穴的旅程。他們取了一艘堅固的獨木舟，裝上投石索與棍棒。接著他們把一枝龍血樹葉交給母親，說道：『母親，看著這些葉子。葉子搖曳時，你便可起舞；但若葉子下垂，你就必須哭泣，因為那時我們當真已經死了。』

passages.text: Then set they forth to search for Manubada. Many times on the way they sent stones whizzing from their slings towards the mountains, but not so did they find Manubada. At last they came to the cliff where on high they could see his eyrie; and they sent a big stone flying towards it. Now Manubada was watching from above, and when he saw how few and feeble were the enemy who had come to attack him his fierce anger was aroused. He opened his broad wings, and soared high above Kototabe and Kelokelo in their little canoe below. Then he began to descend. The lads watched until he was now close to them. Then they slipped quickly into the water, one on each side of the canoe, and dived. Now Manubada in his wrath came down with such speed that he could not stop, and his mighty beak pierced the wood of the canoe, and made him fast to it. Then did he struggle with much force, and waves lashed and beat against the vessel. But it held firm, and Manubada having prevailed not, must perforce rest, that his strength might return to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How the Twins Killed Manubada' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他們出發去尋找馬努巴達。一路上他們屢次從投石索中射出石塊，呼嘯著飛向群山，卻都沒能藉此找到馬努巴達。最後他們來到一處峭壁，在高處可以望見他的巢穴；他們便射出一塊大石，朝那巢穴飛去。馬努巴達正在上方守望，當他看見前來攻擊他的敵人如此稀少孱弱，不禁勃然大怒。他展開寬闊的雙翼，高高翱翔於下方小舟中的科托塔貝與凱洛凱洛之上。接著他開始下降。兩個少年一直注視著，直到他已逼近他們。這時他們迅速溜入水中，一人一邊，潛了下去。馬努巴達盛怒之下疾速俯衝，收勢不及，他那巨大的喙刺穿了獨木舟的木頭，把自己牢牢釘在舟上。於是他奮力掙扎，波浪拍打衝擊著船身。但船身牢固不破，馬努巴達既不能得逞，只得暫且歇息，好讓力氣恢復。

passages.text: When this was done it was time to make for home. Manubada was heavy freight indeed, nevertheless at last they reached their village once more. Now it came to pass that ere they landed their mother had been to look at the branch of dracaena leaves, and found it was shaking and quivering as though a strong wind were blowing. Thereupon, never doubting her sons' word, the widow began to dance. 'What doest thou, O widow?' asked her neighbours. 'I do but rejoice since my sons have killed Manubada, who slew their father.' 'How then could two little lads have killed so great a bird?' mocked the villagers. But the widow gave them no heed, and danced on until the canoe came to the shore. Then did Kototabe and Kelokelo land, and they showed the spoil to the men who thronged about them. And Manubada was roasted and divided into joints, so that every tribe might have a share. The mountain people were given the head, and, when an enemy attacks them now, they bow the head that they may not be hurt.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How the Twins Killed Manubada' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此事既畢，該是返家的時候了。馬努巴達確是沉重的貨物，然而他們終於又回到了自己的村莊。卻說在他們登岸之前，他們的母親已去看過那枝龍血樹葉，發現它正搖曳顫動，彷彿有強風吹拂。於是寡婦毫不懷疑兒子們的話，便開始起舞。『寡婦啊，你在做什麼？』鄰人問道。『我只是歡喜，因為我的兒子們殺了馬努巴達，那殺了他們父親的傢伙。』『兩個小孩子怎麼殺得了這麼大一隻鳥？』村人們嘲笑說。但寡婦不理會他們，一直舞到獨木舟靠岸。於是科托塔貝與凱洛凱洛登了岸，把戰利品展示給簇擁而來的男人們看。馬努巴達被烤熟、分割成塊，好讓每個部族都能分得一份。山裡的人分得了頭，所以如今每當有敵人來犯，他們便低下頭，以免受傷。

title.en: The Crane That Swallowed the Runaways
title.zh: 吞下逃女的鶴

region.en: Wamira district, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉地區（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Crane'

summary.en: An elder sister misheard her mother's charge, slew the baby brother and cooked him; the wroth parents drove the girls into a desolate land, where a sore-covered old man caught them and set them to heavy toil. On the seventh day they fled with baskets of food — and when their master's running blood told him 'the children have fled,' the crane Uapanipani opened his mouth and swallowed them both, flying them home to the house under the white-fleshed coconut for the price of a cup of coconut shell.
summary.zh: 姐姐誤聽母命，竟殺幼弟煮食；父母大怒，把兩個女兒趕進荒野。飢寒之中，她們落入了滿身瘡痍的老人之手，日日重役。第七日，姐妹攜食而逃；老人割傷了自己的手，血涌不止——他試『這是巫術』、『是妖人所為』，血流如故；直到喊出『是孩子們逃了！』傷口才合。他狂追至灘；兩女向鶴呼救，鶴一口把她們吞進腹中，飛越老人頭頂，把她們放到『白肉椰』下自家屋門前，只收下一只椰殼杯作謝禮。父親本已備好喪宴的芋頭，見女兒自暗角落裡走出，悲憤盡消，摟她們入懷——苦難至此終了。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: There were once a man and his wife who had two daughters and one son, the youngest born, and he was but a baby. It fell on a day that the father and mother set out for the gardens and bade the girls bathe their little brother, and moreover to cook some food that he might eat. Now, when the children were left alone, the elder girl said to her sister, 'Our mother bade us slay our brother and cook his flesh, therefore let us obey her.' 'Nay, sister,' quoth the younger, 'our mother said not so.' But the elder girl would not hearken, and forthwith she slew the little child, and made ready his flesh, and cooked it in a pot over the fire. Presently came the man and his wife, and saw what had been done, and were very wroth with the children, and drove them forth into a desolate land, where was no house nor any food growing. Then were the hearts of the girls sad within them, and they wept sore. And afterwards they were an hungered, and sought for food, but found none.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Crane' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一對夫妻，生了兩個女兒和一個兒子，兒子是最小的，還是個嬰兒。有一天，父親和母親動身去園圃，吩咐兩個女孩給小弟弟洗澡，還要煮些食物給他吃。孩子們被單獨留下後，姐姐對妹妹說：『母親吩咐我們殺掉弟弟，把他的肉煮了，所以我們就照她的話做吧。』『不，姐姐，』妹妹說，『母親沒有這樣說。』但姐姐不肯聽，當下就殺了那小孩，整治了他的肉，放在火上的一口鍋裡煮。不久那男人和他的妻子回來了，看見所做的事，對孩子們大為震怒，把她們趕到一片荒涼之地，那裡沒有房屋，也不長任何食物。兩個女孩心中悲傷，痛哭不已。後來她們飢餓難耐，尋找食物，卻什麼也找不到。

passages.text: But the way was long, and their feet were weary, when at last they came upon a house in front of which sat an old man whose skin was covered with sores. The children watched him from afar, and feared greatly to draw nigh to him. Then the elder, being very hungry, was bold and walked to the house, and crept in past the old man, who spake not to her. She picked up a burning stick, and would have left the house, when the burning wood brushed against the old man, and as she hasted to escape, she trod upon his sore foot. 'Ah, little one, slay me not,' said the old man. His words were gentle, and the girl knew not that he was deceiving her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Crane' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但路途遥远，他们的双脚疲惫不堪，终于来到一间屋子前，屋前坐着一位老人，他浑身皮肤长满疮痍。孩子们远远地望着他，十分害怕走近他身旁。这时，年长的那个因为饥饿难耐，便壮起胆子走到屋前，从老人身边悄悄溜了进去，老人并没有对她说话。她拾起一根燃烧的柴枝，正要离开屋子，那燃着的柴枝却擦到了老人身上；她急忙逃开时，又踩到了他那生疮的脚。「啊，小家伙，别杀我。」老人说道。他的话很温和，女孩却不知道他正在欺骗她。

passages.text: Thus did they day by day, and it came to pass that on the seventh day the elder girl made a plan to escape, and told her little sister what she was about to do. Then in the softness of the day, she went near to the old man as he worked in the garden, and said, 'Thou art tired and hungry, O master. Bid me to go with my sister to the house that we may cook thy food.' Then did he bid her do as she had said, and the two girls made haste, and came to the house and cooked much of the food they had brought from the garden, but the rest they laid in a basket. And the two baskets, with food cooked and green, they hung by strings from their heads, and began to run along the beach. Now it fell out that the old man worked still on the hillside, and as he worked his digging stick became blunt. So he took his stone axe and began to sharpen it, but even as he did thus, the axe slipped and cut his hand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Crane' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她们就这样日复一日地行事。到了第七天，年长的女孩定下了一个逃跑的计划，并告诉了妹妹她将要做什么。于是在天气温和的时候，她趁老人在园中劳作，走近他身旁说道：「主人啊，你又累又饿。让我和妹妹回屋去为你做饭吧。」于是老人吩咐她照她所说的去做。两个女孩急忙赶回屋里，把他们从园中带来的食物煮了许多，剩下的则装进一只篮子。她们把煮熟的食物和生的食物分装两只篮子，用绳子系在头上，便开始沿着海滩奔跑。这时，老人仍在山坡上劳作，他挖土的木棍渐渐变钝了。于是他取出石斧来磨，可就在他磨斧的时候，斧头滑脱，割伤了他的手。

passages.text: The children were much afraid when they saw the old man so close to them, and ran the faster. Now, as they ran, they saw before them Uapanipani, the crane, and to him they cried, 'Ah, grandfather, canst thou save us from him who pursues us?' Then said Uapanipani, 'Fear not. With me ye are safe.' Nevertheless the old man was close upon them, and he cried to Uapanipani, 'Oh, Egubeda (Sharer of betel nut), take one child, but give me the other!' At this word the children feared greatly lest Uapanipani should do as he had been bidden. But he turned to them and asked of them whither they desired to go. 'Take us to our own land,' they cried, 'to the house under the white-fleshed coconut.' Now was the old man but a stone's cast from them, and would have laid hold on the girls, but Uapanipani opened his mouth and swallowed them, and flew far over the head of the man as he stood on the beach. Nor were his wings weary until he set the children side by side at the door of their father's house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Crane' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 孩子们见老人离得这么近，非常害怕，跑得更快了。她们跑着跑着，看见前面有只鹤，名叫乌阿帕尼帕尼，便向他喊道：「啊，爷爷，你能从追赶我们的人手中救我们吗？」乌阿帕尼帕尼说：「别怕，有我在，你们就安全。」然而老人已紧逼到她们身后，他向乌阿帕尼帕尼喊道：「哦，埃古巴达（槟榔的分享者），你带走一个孩子，把另一个给我！」听了这话，孩子们非常害怕，唯恐乌阿帕尼帕尼真照他吩咐的去做。但他转向她们，问她们想去哪里。「带我们回我们自己的家乡，」她们喊道，「回到那棵白肉椰子下的屋子去。」这时老人离她们只有一石之遥，正要抓住两个女孩，乌阿帕尼帕尼却张开嘴把她们吞了下去，远远飞过那站在海滩上的老人的头顶。他的双翅一直不曾疲倦，直到他把两个孩子并排放在她们父亲家的门口。

title.en: Toroa, the Song of the Dead
title.zh: 托羅亞：亡者之歌

region.en: Wamira, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'Toroa, the Song of the Dead'

summary.en: A man unknowingly married a witch, who went out nightly through the roof to work death. His sisters let him discover her for himself: one day the witches called down a ring of rain for a drum and danced singing Toroa, the Song of the Dead. He learnt it secretly against his wife's returns — and she, entering unannounced, caught him beating the tidoro and singing; she laid a spell on him that night, and he died. The dead sing Toroa still on the road to loloa, and in Wamira only Taukerobo has the song, to hand to his son.
summary.zh: 某人娶妻不知其為巫。妻子夜夜自屋頂穿洞而出，行邪法害人；還誣稱丈夫夜裡呻吟是被他姊妹們所魘。姊妹們不辯，只等他自己看個明白。一日，眾巫聚於圈地歌舞——她們召來環形之雨作鼓，唱起亡者之歌『托羅亞』。其夫正在榕蔭下縛蕉葉，姊妹引他傾聽，歌云：『Rerani gado, gado ai gado; Tubiri gado, gado ai gado. Koukou kana, bulame, bulame; Koukou kana, wagurare, wagurare.』他懼內，不敢明學，便借口看家帶娃，令妻子歸村前必先出聲招呼；每日她一去，他便抱娃低唱托羅亞。第三日妻子生疑，悄然而返，撞見他以竹筒擊地作雨聲、唱著那歌。她一言不發；當夜便對丈夫下了咒。不多日他死了——想必在通往 loloa 亡者之國的路上，他又唱起了托羅亞，因為那正是亡者還鄉路上所唱之歌。瓦米拉村中如今只有陶克羅波一人會唱，他得自父親，將傳給兒子。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage. Records a restricted inherited song.

passages.text: In the old days there was a man who married a woman, and she was a witch, but he knew it not. At night he lay across the doorway of their house, and his wife feared to go out by the door, for that she must needs draw near to her husband. Yet every night, being a witch, she desired to go forth to cause the death of men by her witchcraft. Therefore she climbed the wall, and went out through a hole in the roof. Now each night, as she climbed thus, her husband groaned in his sleep, and when in the morning he spake of it to his wife, she told him that he had been bewitched by his sisters. But when the sisters heard that they had been thus accused, they were very wroth. It is true that they were witches, but they had not wished harm to befall their brother, and they sought how they might cause him to know that his wife was a witch. 'If we say so to our brother,' they said, 'he will not believe us. We must wait till he can see for himself.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Toroa, the Song of the Dead' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古时候有一个人娶了一个女人，她是个女巫，但他并不知道。夜里他横卧在自家门口，他的妻子不敢从门口出去，因为她必须从丈夫身边经过。然而她既是女巫，每夜都想出去，用巫术致人于死。于是她爬上墙壁，从屋顶的一个洞钻了出去。每晚她这样爬出去时，她的丈夫便在睡梦中呻吟；早晨他把这事告诉妻子，妻子便说他是被自己的姐妹们施了巫术。姐妹们听说自己被这样指责，非常愤怒。她们确实是女巫，但并不想加害自己的兄弟，于是她们设法让他知道他的妻子是个女巫。「如果我们这样对兄弟说，」她们说，「他不会相信我们。我们必须等到他自己能亲眼看见。」

passages.text: It came to pass that on a certain day the man's wife and many other witches desired to dance. Therefore they caused rain to fall in a circle where they stood, in such a manner that they were in the middle and the rain was around them, and the drops falling fast were as a drum which is beaten by the hand. And as they danced thus they sang 'Toroa,' which is the Song of the Dead. Now, while they were thus dancing and singing, the man's two sisters sought their brother that they might show him his wife; and after they had sought for a long time, they found him mounted upon a notched stick, which leant against the stalk of a great plantain, and he was binding leaves about the fruit that it might ripen and that no birds might eat of it. Then said they to him, 'Thy wife hath accused us of bewitching thee. Look now where the rain is falling, and thou shalt see what thy wife herself is.' And the man above listened while they sang.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Toroa, the Song of the Dead' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 后来有一天，那人的妻子和许多别的女巫想要跳舞。于是她们让雨落在她们所站之处的四周，使她们处在中央，雨环绕着她们，急落的雨点如同用手敲击的鼓。她们这样跳着舞，唱起了「托罗阿」，也就是《亡者之歌》。正当她们这样跳舞唱歌的时候，那人的两个姐妹去寻找她们的兄弟，好让他看见自己的妻子；她们找了很久，终于发现他骑在一根带缺口的棍子上，那棍子靠着一株大芭蕉的茎，他正把叶子绑在果实周围，好让它成熟，也免得鸟儿来啄食。于是她们对他说：「你的妻子指责我们对你施了巫术。现在你看那落雨的地方，就会看见你的妻子自己是什么样子。」那人在上面听着她们唱歌。

passages.text: When they had made an end of singing, the rain ceased, and the witches went away. But the man in the plantain was afraid to come down from it until he knew they would not return. Then he too went away to his home, and thought on what he had seen and heard. And ever 'Toroa' rang in his ears, and he longed to sing it, that he might know it yet better. But he feared lest his wife should hear him, and so know that he had seen her as she danced with the witches. Therefore on the morrow he said to his wife, 'Go to-day to the garden and work. I shall stay at home and nurse our child. And when thou comest back in the evening call before entering the village, that I may know thou art returning.' Then the woman did as he bade her. And when she had gone the man took the child in his arms and sang 'Toroa' till the child slept, and the song was nearly learnt.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Toroa, the Song of the Dead' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她们唱完以后，雨停了，女巫们也都离去了。但那待在芭蕉上的人不敢下来，直到他确知她们不会回来。然后他也回了家，思索着自己所见所闻的一切。「托罗阿」的歌声不断在他耳边回响，他渴望唱它，好让自己更加熟悉它。但他又怕妻子听见，从而知道他看见了她与女巫们一同跳舞。于是第二天，他对妻子说：「今天你到园子里去干活吧。我留在家里照看我们的孩子。傍晚你回来时，进村之前先喊一声，好让我知道你要回来了。」那女人便照他吩咐的做了。她走后，那人把孩子抱在怀里，唱起「托罗阿」，直到孩子睡去，那首歌也几乎学会了。

passages.text: On the morrow he bade her go once more to the garden, and to call on returning, that he might know she was near. This she did, and again he ceased singing 'Toroa' before she could hear him. But on the next day, when he said the same words, the woman wondered in her heart what thing this might be that she was ever to call before coming into the village. Therefore she said to herself, 'What is this which my husband doeth secretly? I will not call out this time, but will come back quietly.' Then she went forth to weed, and the man took his child in his arms and began to sing. And when the child slept he laid it in the string bag, which was its bed, and sang on. And as he sang he beat with a hollow bamboo, which is tidoro, upon the ground, and drew it towards him, so that its voice was that of the rain drops which had fallen when the witches danced. Now, as he thus sang and beat with the tidoro, he saw not that his wife stood in the doorway watching him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Toroa, the Song of the Dead' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 翌日，他吩咐她再到園中去，並在歸來時呼喚一聲，好讓他得知她已近前。她照做了，而他又一次在她能聽見之前便停止了吟唱「托羅阿」。但到了第二天，當他說出同樣的話時，那婦人心裡暗自思忖：這究竟是怎麼一回事，竟要我在進村之前總得先呼喚一聲？於是她在心中對自己說：「我丈夫私下裡做的這是什麼事呢？這一回我不出聲呼喚，只悄悄地回來。」隨後她便出去除草，那男子則把孩子抱在懷中，開始吟唱。待孩子睡著，他便將孩子放進那作搖籃用的網袋裡，繼續吟唱。他一邊吟唱，一邊用一截空心的竹子——那便是提多羅——敲擊地面，並將它朝自己拖曳，使它發出的聲音宛如女巫起舞時落下的雨滴之聲。就在他如此吟唱、敲擊提多羅之際，他並未察覺他的妻子正站在門口望著他。

title.en: The King of the Fairies and the Waoi
title.zh: 仙王與瓦奧伊

region.en: Wamira district, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉地區（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The King of the Fairies'

summary.en: A man knotted grass on a young waoi to claim it; the King of the Fairies stole the knot, hid it in the grass, and tied an earth-worm in its place. When the man came to dig, the fairy's single call brought answering voices from grass, caves, valleys, and tree-tops; the man was bound with grass on a brittle aiumaumara pole that broke and broke again till dawn freed him. His revenge: torches around the fairy cave, where the fire left not one alive — and that is why men may eat waoi to this day.
summary.zh: 有人在林中看中一株嫩瓦奧伊，打草結為記；仙王路過，取走草結藏於草叢，另捉一條蚯蚓繫在瓦奧伊上。待男子前來掘取，仙王指蚯蚓為記，怒斥其撒謊；男子呼朋，山谷無應；仙王一呼，草間、洞穴、山谷、樹梢應聲四起。仙眾以草縛男子於 aiumaumara 脆木桿上，一路捆了斷、斷了捆，直到黎明仙眾遁入洞穴，男子掙脫自歸。翌日他率眾執矛秉炬圍攻仙穴，火起煙湧，仙眾一個不剩——自此凡人方能安心食用瓦奧伊，否則仙王必索人命為償。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: In the old days there lived a man, who one day as he journeyed found waoi, a jungle plant, which is good to eat. But it was still young and tender, so he tied a knot of grass upon it to show that it was his, and in order that no man should touch it. Then he departed, and made up his mind to return when the waoi should be ripe. Not many days after, the King of the Fairies chanced to pass that way. He also saw the waoi, and desired that it should be his. So he took the knot from off the stalk, and hid it in the grass. Then he caught an earth worm and tied it in a knot round the waoi, and went his way. Presently the man said in his heart, 'Now are the days of the waoi fulfilled. I will go and dig it up, and eat it this night.' So he journeyed until he reached the jungle, and there he found that the waoi was indeed ripe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The King of the Fairies' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古時候住著一個人，有一天他在旅途中發現了一株瓦奧伊，那是一種可食的叢林植物。但它尚且幼嫩，於是他便在它上面打了一個草結，以示此物歸他所有，並免得旁人觸碰。隨後他便離去，打定主意等瓦奧伊成熟時再回來。不過數日之後，仙王恰好路過此地。他也看見了那株瓦奧伊，想要據為己有。於是他把莖上的草結取下，藏進草叢裡。接著他捉來一條蚯蚓，把它打成結繫在瓦奧伊上，便自顧自走了。不久，那人在心中說道：「如今瓦奧伊成熟的日子到了。我要去把它挖出來，今晚就吃了它。」於是他一路前行，來到那片叢林，發現瓦奧伊果然已經成熟了。

passages.text: 'Thou speakest lies,' said the King of the Fairies angrily. Then he stooped and held up the earth-worm. 'Behold my knot. Where is thine?' 'I cannot tell,' answered the man. Then said the King of the Fairies, 'Stand aside while I pluck up my waoi.' 'That will I never do,' said the man. 'The waoi is mine, and thou darest not touch it.' The King of the Fairies was silent for a space, and then he said, 'Thou speakest boldly. Call thy men that I may see how many followers so great a chieftain owns.' The man called, though in truth he knew well that none of his friends could hear him. He called once more, and there was no sound. Then said the King of the Fairies, 'Now hold thy peace and I will call.' He lifted up his voice but once, and on a sudden, from the grass, from caves, from valleys, and from the tops of tall trees, came answering voices from the fairies. 'Dost hear?' asked the King of the Fairies of the man. 'These who answer me are my people. Where are thine?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The King of the Fairies' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「你說的盡是謊話，」仙王怒道。接著他俯身把蚯蚓舉了起來。「看哪，這是我的結。你的結在哪裡？」「我不知道，」那人答道。仙王便說：「站到一邊去，讓我拔起我的瓦奧伊。」「我絕不會這樣做，」那人說。「瓦奧伊是我的，你不敢碰它。」仙王沉默了片刻，然後說道：「你說話倒大膽。叫你的手下人來，好讓我看看這麼一位了不起的首領究竟有多少追隨者。」那人便呼喚起來，儘管他心裡清楚得很，他的朋友們沒有一個能聽見他。他又呼喚了一聲，依然毫無聲響。仙王於是說：「現在你且住口，讓我來呼喚。」他只揚聲一呼，剎那間，從草叢裡、從洞穴中、從山谷間、從高樹的頂梢，便傳來眾仙應答之聲。「你聽見了嗎？」仙王問那人。「這些應我之聲的便是我的子民。你的子民在哪裡？」

passages.text: The man answered never a word, but pulled the waoi from its hole. The King of the Fairies struggled with him for it, and fierce was the fight. Almost had the man won the day, when the King of the Fairies called again to his followers. They came from the grass, from caves, from valleys, and from the tops of tall trees, and seized the man, and held him while they waited to hear their lord's pleasure. The man, seeing he could not prevail by force, said to those who held him, 'If ye wish to bind me do so with grass upon a pole of aiumaumara.' (This wood, as the man knew, is brittle.) The fairies gave heed to his word, and bound him fast with grass upon a pole of aiumaumara, and set out for the cave where dwelt their master. They had gone but a little way when the bonds brake, and the man lay upon the ground. The fairies went to and fro seeking more grass, and being but silly folk, looked not for jungle creeper or the roots of pandanus. Then they bound the man again and set out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The King of the Fairies' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那人一言不發，只把瓦奧伊從土坑裡拔了出來。仙王與他爭奪起來，那場爭鬥甚是激烈。那人眼看就要得勝，仙王卻又呼喚起他的追隨者來。他們從草叢裡、從洞穴中、從山谷間、從高樹的頂梢趕來，抓住那人，將他按住，只等聽候他們主人的吩咐。那人見憑力氣無法取勝，便對按住他的人說：「你們若要捆我，就用草繩綁在艾烏毛馬拉的杆子上吧。」（這人深知，這種木頭是脆的。）眾仙聽了他的話，便用草繩把他牢牢綁在一根艾烏毛馬拉的杆子上，然後動身前往他們主人所居的洞穴。他們才走了沒多遠，繩索便斷了，那人跌倒在地。眾仙來回奔走，尋找更多的草，可他們本是些愚笨之輩，竟不去找叢林裡的藤蔓或露兜樹的根。接著他們又把那人捆了起來，重新上路。

passages.text: At last came the dawn, and the fairies fled with one accord to the cave, where their master awaited their coming, and sat at his feet in silence. But the man, who still lay where they had left him, brake his bonds in sunder and rose to his feet. Then, for there was none to let him, he went forth from the jungle to his own home. Then his anger being yet hot within him, he called his friends together, and bade them fetch spears and torches, and follow whither he should lead. They were obedient to his word, and ere long all were standing outside the cave where dwelt the fairies and their king. Inside were the fairies, waiting for the dusk that they might go forth once more. But suddenly flames were leaping round the opening of the cave, and rolling clouds of smoke poured in. 'Ai-gugugugu! Ai-gigigigi!' cried the fairies, but not for long were their voices heard, and the fire when it died left not one alive in the cave. Then was the man's heart glad, and he departed to seek his waoi. And that night many men ate of it, and were glad.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The King of the Fairies' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 終於天亮了，眾仙一齊逃回洞穴，他們的主人正在那裡等候他們歸來，他們便默默地坐在他腳邊。而那個人仍舊躺在他們丟下他的地方，掙斷了繩索，站起身來。此時既無人阻攔他，他便走出叢林，回到自己家中。他心中怒火仍未平息，於是召集了他的朋友們，吩咐他們帶上長矛和火把，跟隨他前往他所引領之處。他們聽從了他的話，不多時，眾人便都站在眾仙及其國王所居的洞穴之外了。洞裡是那些眾仙，正等著黃昏來臨，好再次出去。可是忽然間，火焰在洞口四周騰躍而起，滾滾濃煙湧了進去。「哎—咕咕咕咕！哎—嘰嘰嘰嘰！」眾仙叫喊起來，但他們的聲音沒能持續多久，大火熄滅之後，洞中無一活口。那人心裡這才歡喜起來，便動身去尋他的瓦奧伊。那一夜，許多人分食了它，皆大歡喜。

title.en: The Cockerel Kokorereko, Chief of the Birds
title.zh: 百鳥之王公雞科科雷雷科

region.en: Diriuna and Kaierara cape, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞迪魯納村與凱埃拉拉海角（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Cockerel'

summary.en: When the birds of Diriuna let their fire die, Kokorereko the cockerel flew many miles for a new brand, printing his feet in the rock where he rested. A girl by the cape loved him and pursued him by canoe past drum-villages to the stars' dance; at dawn she baited him with coconuts, and 'as he stooped, the basket was laid upon his head' — and since that sad day Kokorereko and his tribe live with the sons of men, while Diriuna itself is called Numa Pupu, Desolation.
summary.zh: 百鳥聚居迪魯納村。一夜狂歡，火種熄滅；晨起眾鳥哀鳴。公雞科科雷雷科自告奮勇飛行數百里取火，途中歇於岩上，雙爪嵌石——石上爪印至今猶存。凱埃拉拉海角有美人傾心於他，隨舟循『有鼓聲處』一路尋到迪魯納；破曉時分，百鳥逐一出巢，她連連搖頭——直至科科雷雷科緩步而出。她捧椰相誘，謊稱『我不能走到水邊』；大鳥猶豫再三，緩步近舟俯身之際，竹籃當頭罩下，天色未明，無人看清。他被運回海角。自此公雞一族與人雜居屋前腳下；迪魯納百鳥四散，犀鳥入空心樹，鵪鶉擇草而居，水雉赴海——那村至今名為『努馬普普』——荒墟。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: Long ago, in the old days, the birds all lived at Diriuna, which is at the foot of the hill country of Magavara. But of Diriuna nothing now remains, save only the circle of stones where the birds used to sit in council. One night they were all dancing, and in their pleasure saw not that their fire had died down until not a spark was left to glimmer in the ashes. In the morning, therefore, when they arose, they wept for their warm fire, which was now dead. But Kokorereko, the cockerel, when he was asked, promised to bring fresh fire that they might kindle it anew, and he set off, his strong wings cleaving the air. He flew, and flew, until he had covered many miles, and then alighted in the bush on a rock. With such force did he descend that his feet sank into the hard rock, and the mark of them remains to this day. Where he alighted he slept, and the next day he flew on once more until he reached Kaierara, the long cape which stretches into the sea. There he saw a beautiful girl sitting alone in a house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Cockerel' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 很久以前，在古時候，所有的鳥兒都住在迪里烏納，那地方位於馬加瓦拉山地腳下。可如今迪里烏納什麼也沒留下，只剩下那一圈石頭，那是鳥兒們昔日聚會議事時所坐之處。一天夜裡，他們全都在跳舞，一時盡興，竟沒察覺他們的火已漸漸熄滅，直到灰燼裡連一點閃爍的火星也不剩。因此到了早晨他們醒來時，便為那如今已然熄滅的溫暖之火而哭泣。可是當公雞科科雷雷科被問起時，他答應去取來新火，好讓他們重新點燃，於是便動身出發，強健的雙翅劈開長空。他飛呀飛，飛過了許多英里，然後落在一片灌木叢中的岩石上。他降落時力道之大，雙腳竟陷進了堅硬的岩石裡，那腳印至今仍在。他在落腳之處睡了一覺，第二天又繼續飛翔，一直飛到凱耶拉拉，那是伸入海中的一道長長的海角。在那裡，他看見一個美麗的姑娘獨自坐在一間屋裡。

passages.text: When the girl looked on the comely Kokorereko she loved him, and she tried to hold him that he might not leave her. But he picked up a burning brand from the fire, and turned to go. 'Ah, tell me then,' she cried, as he turned to go, 'tell me, at least, where thou livest.' 'Journey till the cape is rounded,' he answered as he spread his wings, 'and where the voice of drum and conch shell is heard in my village.' Alas! he had gone, and the girl shed many tears. But after a little her father and mother returned home, and she persuaded them by much weeping, to take her in their canoe to look for Kokorereko. They started soon. The little platform on the outrigger was laden with food for the journey. There were coconuts also to tempt Kokorereko, and a basket of plaited leaves in which to place him if he were caught. They paddled, and paddled, and they rounded the cape. Then the girl cried, 'Hark! do you not hear the voice of the drum?' They had reached the village of Lamogara, but that was not the home of Kokorereko.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Cockerel' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 少女見了俊美的科科雷雷科，便愛上了他，想抱住他，不讓他離去。但他從火中拾起一根燃燒的柴薪，轉身欲走。「啊，那麼告訴我吧，」當他轉身欲走時，她哭喊道，「至少告訴我，你住在何處。」「一直前行，直到繞過那海角，」他展開雙翼答道，「到了我的村落，那裡能聽見鼓聲與海螺號角之聲。」唉！他已離去，少女灑下許多眼淚。但過了一會兒，她的父母回到家中，她以許多哭泣勸服他們，帶她乘獨木舟去尋找科科雷雷科。他們不久便啟程。舷外浮桿上的小平台載滿了旅途的食物。還有椰子用以誘引科科雷雷科，以及一隻以葉片編成的籃子，若他被捉住便置於其中。他們划了又划，划過了那海角。於是少女喊道：「聽！你們沒聽見鼓聲嗎？」他們已抵達拉莫加拉之村，但那並非科科雷雷科的家。

passages.text: In truth they had at least reached Diriuna, and in the dim starlight they saw birds with waving wings dancing beneath the palms. The canoe floated outside till morning, for in that light who might know Kokorereko from another? At last 'Uba,' the cold morning wind, blew from off the mountain, and one by one the stars began to fade. Then far over Kaierara the dawn broke, and slowly, very slowly, the birds woke and came out from their sleeping chamber one by one. First came Binama, the hornbill. 'Is that thy lover?' asked the father. 'Nay, but that is another bird,' said the girl. And so in like manner with the parrot, the black cockatoo, and the wagtail. At last came the bird of paradise. 'Surely now I see him,' said the man. 'No,' replied his daughter proudly. 'My love is far more beautiful.' And now her long waiting met with its reward, for Kokorereko, the Chief of all the birds, came slowly forth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Cockerel' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 其實他們至少已抵達迪里烏納，在朦朧的星光下，他們看見鳥兒揮動雙翼，在棕櫚樹下起舞。獨木舟漂浮在外，直到天明，因為在那樣的光線下，誰能分辨科科雷雷科與別的鳥呢？終於，「烏巴」，那寒冷的晨風，從山那邊吹來，星辰一顆接一顆開始隱沒。接著，遠在凱耶拉拉之上，破曉了，鳥兒緩緩地、極其緩慢地醒來，一隻接一隻從牠們的睡處出來。最先出來的是比納馬，那犀鳥。「那是你的愛人嗎？」父親問道。「不，那是另一隻鳥，」少女說。於是鸚鵡、黑鳳頭鸚鵡與鶺鴒也同樣如此。最後出來的是天堂鳥。「這下我 surely 看見他了，」那人說。「不，」他的女兒驕傲地回答。「我的愛人遠比這美麗得多。」而如今她長久的等待得到了報償，因為科科雷雷科，眾鳥之首，緩緩地出來了。

passages.text: And now, ah, woe! Quickly, as he stooped, was the basket laid upon his head until it covered him completely. Then in the darkness he was placed upon the canoe, and taken swiftly to Kaierara once more.
