Since that sad day, Kokorereko and his tribe live ever with the sons of men in their dwellings and about their feet. But at Diriuna, where Kokorereko's followers were, great was the sorrow, and loud was the wailing which arose. 'Airake! our lord! Airake! our master!' cried all the birds. And no more was Diriuna a village. For Binama, the hornbill, fled to a hollow tree, where he remains even to this day. Iviki, the quail, chose the grass for her home. Kivivi, the plover, said, 'By the sea shall I dwell,' and all the other birds went far away into the jungle, and built their nests. And that is why Diriuna is no longer the Village of Birds, but is called Numa Pupu, or Desolation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Cockerel' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 而如今，唉，悲哉！當他彎下身時，籃子迅速罩上他的頭，將他完全蓋住。於是在黑暗中，他被放上獨木舟，迅速地被帶回凱耶拉拉。自那悲傷之日以後，科科雷雷科與他的族類便永遠與人類的子孫同住於他們的居所之中、他們的腳邊。但在迪里烏納，科科雷雷科的追隨者所在之處，悲傷甚大，哀號之聲大作。「艾拉凱！我們的主！艾拉凱！我們的主人！」眾鳥齊聲哭喊。迪里烏納不再是村落了。因為比納馬，那犀鳥，逃入一棵中空的樹中，至今仍留於彼處。伊維基，那鵪鶉，選擇草地為家。基維維，那鴴鳥，說：「我要住在海邊。」而所有其他的鳥都遠走叢林，築起牠們的巢。這就是為何迪里烏納不再是鳥之村，而被稱為努馬普普，即荒涼之地的緣故。

title.en: A Man Finds His Wife in the Land of the Dead
title.zh: 亡者之國尋妻記

region.en: Uruam river, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞烏魯阿姆河（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'How a Man Found His Wife in the Land of the Dead'

summary.en: Hunting a cuscus for the death feast, a mourner's dog followed the third one down a hole into loloa, the land of the dead — where all day the bones of the Dead lie on the ground, but at even each takes his own bones and lives till the dawn. His wife pinched his arm till the blood showed, hid him through the dancing night, and sent him away with a promise: come again after three nights. He lingered picking coconuts, scented herbs, and wild limes for the people of Uruam; the Dead seized them, he escaped with his life, and they closed the hole with a stone no man might lift. No one has found the way to loloa since.
summary.zh: 妻子亡故，丈夫備喪宴出獵樹袋熊。第三隻逃入地洞，犬也追了進去——原來那洞通往亡者之國 loloa。他掀開洞口巨石，望見洞底椰林，便也下去了。亡者之國晝日白骨橫陳，入夜各取己骨而活至天明。他亡妻捏他的手臂至見血，斷定他不是死人，便把他藏起——夜裡亡者各認其骨、擊鼓起舞，他躲在屋中膽戰心驚，卻因重見愛妻而忘卻恐懼。妻子催他回去，許諾三夜之後再來相會。他臨行貪採椰子、香草與野酸橙，欲帶回給烏魯阿姆鄉親開眼；亡者蜂擁而至，奪其手中之物，他僅以身免。等他三夜後重返，洞口已被巨石封死——從此無人再能找到通往 loloa 之路；若非那塊石頭，我們至今還能去見亡去的親人。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage. Descent-to-underworld cluster.

passages.text: When our dead leave us none knoweth whither they go, nor by much searching hath any man found the way to loloa, the land of the dead, save one, and of him will I tell thee. This man lived in the hills where riseth the Uruam, the river which flows into the sea between Wamira and Divari. It came to pass that the man's wife died, and he mourned for her many days. But when it was time for the death feast to be made for her, he went forth with his dog to hunt for a cuscus that it might be eaten at the feast. Now a cuscus sleeps all day, but in the softness of the evening it comes forth to seek its food. In a little he had found one, which he killed, and having no one with him who might carry it, he hung it upon a tree and went on. Once more he found one, which also he killed and hung on a tree. Then he saw a third, and the dog ran after it to catch it. But the cuscus ran also, and went down a hole in the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How a Man Found His Wife in the Land of the Dead' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當我們的死者離我們而去，無人知曉他們往何處去，也無人藉多方尋覓而找到通往洛洛阿——死者之地——的路，只有一人例外，我將向你講述他的事。這人住在烏魯阿姆河發源的山中，那河在瓦米拉與迪瓦里之間流入大海。事情是這樣的：這人的妻子死了，他為她哀悼了許多日子。但到了該為她舉行喪宴的時候，他帶著狗出去獵捕一隻袋貂，以便在喪宴上食用。袋貂終日沉睡，但在黃昏柔和之時便出來覓食。不久他便找到一隻，將其殺死，因身邊無人可替他搬運，便將牠掛在樹上，繼續前行。他又找到一隻，也將其殺死掛在樹上。接著他看見第三隻，狗便跑去追捕。但那袋貂也跑了，鑽入地中的一個洞裡。

passages.text: When the man reached the hole, he found that his dog had also gone down, and he feared lest it might lose its way and come not back to him. Therefore he rolled away the great stone which lay over the hole, and looked down. There far below he saw coconuts growing, so he said within himself, 'This is a village.' Then he too went down the hole far into the earth. His dog was before him, and he caught him in his arms. Now so it is in loloa that all the day the bones of the Dead lie on the ground, but at even each takes his own bones, and lives thus till the dawn. And as the man drew near, it was the time that the bones should live. It so befell that his wife was already walking, and was coming towards him. When she saw him, she said in her heart, 'My husband hath died on the earth, and hath come to me.' Then she went to him, and with her fingers pinched his arm until the blood showed on his skin. Then said she, 'Thou art not dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How a Man Found His Wife in the Land of the Dead' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當那人來到洞口，發現他的狗也下去了，他怕牠會迷路而不回到他身邊。因此他滾開覆在洞口的大石，向下望去。在遠遠的下方，他看見椰子生長，於是心中自語：「這是一個村落。」接著他也下到洞中，深入地下。他的狗在他前面，他將牠抱在懷中。原來在洛洛阿是這樣的：白日裡死者的骨骸躺在地上，但到了傍晚，各人取回自己的骨骸，如此活著直到天明。當那人走近時，正是骨骸該活起來的時候。恰巧他的妻子已在走動，正朝他走來。她見了他，心中說道：「我的丈夫已在地上死去，來到我這裡了。」於是她走向他，用指甲捏他的手臂，直到血顯現在他的皮膚上。於是她說：「你並沒有死。」

passages.text: Then she took him to her house and bade him lie still nor let the voice of the dog be heard, for it was now time for the Dead to arise. The man did as she bade him, and he watched as the Dead laid hold of each his own bones. 'This is my thigh,' and 'Here is my arm,' he heard them say. Now it was night, and the Dead began to dance, while some of them beat also upon drums. And the man was much afraid as he watched from the house. But his wife remained with him, and he cared not for fear nor any other thing while he had her with him once more. 'Ah, my wife,' he cried, 'how hot was my heart with grief till I found thee!' But his wife feared for him that the Dead would find him in their land and would work him some evil; therefore she said, 'Thou must not tarry here, for the Dead if they find thee will certainly fall upon thee.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How a Man Found His Wife in the Land of the Dead' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是她帶他到她的屋中，囑他靜靜躺著，也不要讓狗的叫聲被聽見，因為現在正是死者起身的時候。那人照她的吩咐做了，他觀看著死者各自抓住自己的骨骸。「這是我的大腿，」以及「這是我的手臂，」他聽見他們說道。如今是夜晚，死者開始跳舞，其中一些還擊鼓。那人在屋中觀看，十分害怕。但他的妻子留在他身邊，只要她再次與他同在，他便不在乎恐懼或任何其他事物。「啊，我的妻子，」他喊道，「在我找到你之前，我的心因悲傷而何等灼熱！」但他的妻子為他擔憂，怕死者會在他們的土地上發現他，並加害於他；因此她說：「你不能在此逗留，因為死者若發現你，必定會撲向你。」

passages.text: Then the man, after she had thus spoken, rose up to go. But on the way he stayed to pick coconuts, and scented herbs, and wild limes, that he might show them to the people of Uruam. And as he thus did, the Dead saw him and made haste after him in great numbers, and seized from his hands the coconuts, the scented herbs, and the wild limes, and he being beset by them could but escape with his life. And when he had come up to the face of the earth, the Dead closed the hole with a great stone that no man might lift. Therefore when the man returned after the three nights were past, he found no place where he might enter, and he saw his wife no more. Nor since that day have any found the way to loloa. But if the stone had not been placed over the hole we might even now have seen and talked with our dead after they had left us for their own land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How a Man Found His Wife in the Land of the Dead' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那男人聽了她這番話，便起身離去。但途中他停下來採摘椰子、香草和野檸檬，好拿給烏魯阿姆的人看。他正這樣做的時候，亡者見了他，便成群結隊地急忙追趕他，從他手中奪走了椰子、香草和野檸檬；他被他們圍困，只能僥倖逃得性命。當他回到地面之上時，亡者已用一塊無人能舉起的大石封住了那個洞口。因此，當那男人在三個夜晚過去之後回來時，他找不到可以進入的地方，也再見不到他的妻子。自那天以後，也再沒有人找到通往洛洛阿的路。但倘若那塊石頭不曾蓋在洞口之上，我們如今或許還能見到那些離開我們前往他們自己國度的亡者，並與他們交談。

title.en: Dakodako, the Man-Eater of Qamana Hill
title.zh: 食人者達科達科

region.en: Qamana hillside, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞卡馬納山坡（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'Dakodako, the Man Eater'

summary.en: Dakodako hungered for flesh that satisfied: a stranger's flesh left the drum faint and the dance weary; his friend's flesh the same. Only in war, feasting on a slain enemy of Qamana, did the drum sing sweet and his feet grow light — and crying 'what can compare with the flesh of an enemy?' he was turned to stone on the hillside with his victim, where they remain to this day.
summary.zh: 達科達科總嫌豬肉袋鼠肉不飽。他伏擊一名過路外鄉人，烹而食之，卻覺鼓聲不揚、舞步沉重；次日又殺了至交，仍是一樣。直到山民卡馬納人來犯，他於陣前飽食一名陣斃之敵——這回鼓聲悅耳，舞步輕快。他跨著敵屍高呼：『肉是好的，可哪有比敵人肉更美的？』話音未落，他與屍身一齊化作石頭，至今仍立在卡馬納山坡上，叫世人知道他是多麼『偉大』的一個人，他的話是多麼『真確』。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage. The tale moralizes on cannibalism's escalation.

passages.text: There was once a man named Dakodako, who ever hungered for flesh to eat. When the others ate pig or wallaby he ate, but was not satisfied as were they. And he daily bethought him where he might look for flesh meat which he might eat and therewith be filled. Thus it befell that one day he lay in wait on the path, and slew a man, a stranger passing to another village, as he walked. Then he took his body and cut it up, and laid the pieces in a great earthenware pot, and cooked them over the fire. When the flesh was cooked he sat down and ate of it till he could eat no more. Then rising up he said, 'I will beat upon the drum and dance, for that I have eaten flesh meat which satisfieth.' Therefore he did even as he had said. He beat upon the drum and danced, but not so was his heart glad. Then he cast his drum to the ground saying, 'How is it that, though I have eaten well, the voice of the drum pleaseth me not, and in the dance my feet grow weary?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Dakodako, the Man Eater' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個人名叫達科達科，他總是渴望吃肉。別人吃豬肉或袋鼠肉時他也吃，卻不像他們那樣滿足。他每天都思量著該到何處去尋肉吃，好藉此飽足。於是有一天，他埋伏在路上，殺了一個過路的陌生人，那人正走往另一個村子。然後他取了那人的屍體，切成塊，放進一個大陶罐裡，在火上烹煮。肉煮熟後，他坐下來吃，一直吃到再也吃不下。然後他站起身說：『我要擊鼓跳舞，因為我吃了能使人飽足的肉。』於是他就照自己所說的做了。他擊鼓跳舞，但他的心卻並不因此歡喜。於是他把鼓扔在地上說：『怎麼會這樣：我明明吃得很好，鼓聲卻不悅我耳，跳舞時我的腳也疲倦了？』

passages.text: As he marvelled at this he thought in his heart, 'It is because I have slain a man who is nought to me. But now, let me slay my friend, and surely his flesh will be good eating.' And it came to pass that on the morrow he sought for his friend, and slew him with his wooden sword. And his body he cooked in like manner to the body of the stranger. And he also ate of it, as he had done the other, and rose up to dance, beating upon the drum. But ere long he laid down the drum, and cried, 'What shall I do that I may find flesh to eat which will gladden my heart? Though I have slain and eaten my friend yet is the voice of the drum but faint in my ear, and my feet are heavy in the dance.' After a time the men of Qamana, in the hills, made them ready to fight the men of Dakodako's tribe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Dakodako, the Man Eater' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他對此感到驚異，心裡想：『這是因為我殺了一個與我毫無關係的人。如今且讓我去殺我的朋友，他的肉必定好吃。』到了第二天，他去找他的朋友，用木劍殺了他。他又照處理那陌生人屍體的方式烹煮了他的屍體。他也吃了那肉，如同吃前一個一樣，然後起身擊鼓跳舞。但沒過多久，他就放下鼓喊道：『我該怎麼做才能找到吃了能使我心歡喜的肉呢？我雖然殺了並吃了我的朋友，鼓聲在我耳中卻仍舊微弱，跳舞時我的腳也沉重。』過了些時候，山中的卡馬納人準備攻打達科達科族的人。

passages.text: Then was Dakodako glad, for he longed to slay men. Therefore he went forth and fell upon the men of Qamana, with his kinsfolk, and many of the hill men were slain, and the rest fled. Then Dakodako, being hungry, took the body of one of his foes whom he had slain, and made ready his flesh for the pot. And when it was cooked he sat down and ate of it until he could eat no more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Dakodako, the Man Eater' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 達科達科於是歡喜，因為他渴望殺人。因此他帶著親族出去，撲向卡馬納人，山中之人被殺死許多，其餘的都逃走了。達科達科因為飢餓，便取了他所殺的一個敵人的屍體，把他的肉準備好下鍋。肉煮熟後，他坐下來吃，一直吃到再也吃不下。

passages.text: And this time when he beat upon the drum its voice was pleasant in his ear, and his feet were light in the dance and grew not weary. Therefore he ceased, for he had found what he had sought for so long, and he stood over the body of a slain enemy, one foot being on either side of the body, and cried, 'Oh, my people, flesh meat is good indeed, but what can compare with the flesh of an enemy?' Then was he turned into stone, as also was the body of the slain man, and they remain to this day on the hillside of Qamana, that all men may know how great a man was Dakodako and how true are the words which he spake.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Dakodako, the Man Eater' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 而這一次他擊鼓時，鼓聲在他耳中悅耳動聽，跳舞時他的腳也輕快，並不疲倦。於是他停了下來，因為他終於找到了長久以來所尋求的東西；他站在一個被殺敵人的屍體上，一隻腳踏在一邊，喊道：『哦，我的族人啊，肉確實是好，但有什麼能比得上敵人的肉呢？』於是他變成了石頭，那被殺之人的屍體也變成了石頭，它們至今仍留在卡馬納的山坡上，好讓所有人都知道達科達科是何等偉大的人，他所說的話又是何等真實。

title.en: The Magic Almonds and the Coconut-Cup Witch
title.zh: 魔杏仁與製杯巫婆

region.en: Beach near Wamira, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉附近海灘（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Magic Almonds'

summary.en: Three ripe almonds rolled beneath a stripped tree, and on three days each turned into a young man. Two, simple, came down the coconut palm head-first as the old witch begged — 'Thy head should be first!' — and were killed and eaten. The third called back, 'Who ever came down with the head first?' seized the wooden sword, cooked the witch for her husband's supper, leapt palm to palm as the old man cut them down, and at the last became a gwagadogo crab burrowing in the sand — as his children do to this day, fleeing every human footstep.
summary.zh: 海灘杏仁樹被人們打果掃蕩殆盡，唯餘三枚熟杏仁落地。三日之內，三枚杏仁先後化作三個青年。頭兩個憨直，聽信老嫗『頭朝下爬下來』的話，雙雙摔死於其夫之木劍下，被烹而食。第三個卻不吃這一套：『誰是頭朝下爬下來的？』他滑下樹奪過木劍，把老嫗煮進鍋裡留給她丈夫『享用』，自己躲上檳榔樹頂。老漢歸來食『妻』，聞樹上人聲，怒而伐樹；青年一樹跳一樹，從檳榔到麵包果再到栗樹；老漢伐倒栗樹正要抓他，他竟化作一隻沙蟹鑽入沙中——那 gwagadogo 蟹族至今遍布沙灘，一聞人足音便竄入洞穴，怕是有人要替老嫗報仇。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: Long ago there grew on the beach an almond tree, which bare fruit plentifully. And men came and climbed the tree and shook its boughs, so that much fruit fell upon the ground. And the children underneath threw stones, and hit other of the almonds, which fell and were eaten. Thus was the almond tree spoiled of her fruit. But there still hung upon the tree a cluster of three almonds, and they remained until they were very ripe. Then they fell and lay beneath the tree. Now as they thus lay the largest began to move, and turned from side to side continually. On a sudden it was changed, and became a young man and stood upright. Then he made a fish spear for himself, and set out to catch fish that he might eat. He walked along the beach until he came to an inlet, where he caught a fish, and at another inlet he caught another, and further on yet another. Now, as he walked, he saw an old woman sitting near a coco palm making a cup of coconut shell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Magic Almonds' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 很久以前，海灘上長著一棵杏仁樹，結了許多果實。人們來爬上樹，搖動樹枝，於是許多果實落在地上。樹下的孩子們扔石頭，打中其他的杏仁，它們落了下來，被人吃掉。杏仁樹的果實就這樣被糟蹋了。但樹上仍掛著一簇三顆杏仁，它們一直留到熟透。然後它們落了下來，躺在樹下。它們這樣躺著的時候，最大的那顆開始動了起來，不停地從一邊轉到另一邊。忽然間它變了，變成一個年輕人，直立起來。然後他為自己做了一支魚叉，出發去捕魚好有得吃。他沿著海灘走，來到一個小灣，在那裡捕到一條魚；在另一個小灣又捕到一條；再往前又捕到一條。他走著走著，看見一個老婦人坐在椰子樹旁，用椰殼做杯子。

passages.text: Then said he, 'Yea, truly, mother, I will climb and pluck thy coconuts.' And he set about to make him ready to climb. When he had thrown down to the old woman as many coconuts as she desired, he started to come down. But she, hungering for his flesh, cried, 'Ah, little brother, why dost thou come down in this manner? Thy head should be first!' Then he, being but simple, did as the old woman bade him, and came down head first. And as he was now about to reach the ground, the dame beat upon his head with her husband's wooden sword, and killed him. And when she saw that he was dead, she cut up his body and cooked it, and in the evening she and her husband ate of the flesh and were full. It came to pass on the morrow that the second almond turned itself from side to side in like manner to the largest. And when it had now turned many times, it too became a young man, as had the other on the day before.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Magic Almonds' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他說道：「是的，母親，我這就去爬上樹，替你摘下椰子。」他便著手準備攀爬。當他把老婦人所要的那麼多椰子都扔下之後，便開始下來。但她垂涎他的肉，喊道：「啊，小兄弟，你為何這樣下來呢？你的頭應該先下才對！」他為人單純，便照老婦人所吩咐的去做，頭朝下地爬了下來。當他快要著地時，那婦人用她丈夫的木劍擊打他的頭，將他殺死。她見他死了，便把他的身體切碎煮熟，到了晚上，她與丈夫吃了那肉，吃飽了。到了次日，第二顆杏仁也同樣地從一邊翻到另一邊，就像最大的那顆一樣。當它翻轉了許多次之後，它也變成了一個青年，正如前一日另一顆所變成的樣子。

passages.text: On the third day it was the turn of the smallest almond. It lay under the tree, and turned from side to side continually, until it became a young man, and arose and stood upright. Then he did as had done his brothers. He speared fish, and then came to where the old woman sat making her cup. And she hailed him with joy, and when she had asked him the same favour she had his brothers, he climbed up at once. When he had thrown down the nuts he started to come down, and the dame cried, as she had done before, 'Ah, little brother, why dost thou come down in this manner? Let thy head be first!' But though the lad had been long in an almond shell yet was he not a fool, and he called back with a loud voice, 'Who ever came down with the head first?' and slipped quickly down and ran to the old woman, and seized the wooden sword from her hand and cut her head off.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Magic Almonds' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了第三天，輪到最小的那顆杏仁。它躺在樹下，不停地從一邊翻到另一邊，直到變成一個青年，起身直立。接著他照他兄長們所做的去做。他叉魚之後，來到老婦人坐著製作她的杯子的地方。她歡喜地招呼他，當她向他提出與他兄長們相同的請求後，他立刻爬了上去。當他把果子扔下之後，便開始下來，那婦人一如先前那樣喊道：「啊，小兄弟，你為何這樣下來呢？讓你的頭先下吧！」然而這少年雖在杏仁殼中待了很久，卻不是個傻瓜，他大聲回喊道：「有誰是頭先下來的？」隨即迅速滑下，跑到老婦人跟前，從她手中奪過木劍，砍下了她的頭。

passages.text: After a little the old woman's husband came home, and being hungry, he waited not to see if his wife would come, but began at once to eat what he found in the pot. While he was thus eating he heard a voice from the betel palm crying, 'It is thy wife whose flesh thou art eating!' Then, hearing a voice but seeing no one, he searched to see who this might be who called to him, and soon saw the lad seated in the betel palm above him. 'It is thou who hast killed my wife!' he cried, and ran into the house and sharpened his stone axe that he might cut down the palm and kill the lad. But as he cut it down the lad leapt to the next, and when that was cut down to yet another, and when that fell he climbed into a bread fruit tree and sat there. The old man had destroyed his betel palms, and now cut down the bread fruit tree, hoping to slay the lad who had killed his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Magic Almonds' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 過了一會兒，老婦人的丈夫回到家來，因為飢餓，他等不及看看妻子是否會回來，便立刻吃起他在鍋裡找到的東西。他正吃著的時候，聽見檳榔樹上傳來一個聲音喊道：「你吃的正是你妻子的肉！」他聽見聲音卻不見人影，便四下搜尋，看這呼喚他的究竟是誰，很快就看見那少年坐在他上方的檳榔樹上。「是你殺了我的妻子！」他喊道，隨即跑進屋裡磨利他的石斧，好砍倒那棵樹殺死少年。但當他砍樹時，少年跳到旁邊一棵，那棵被砍倒時又跳到另一棵，那棵倒下時他爬上一棵麵包樹坐在那裡。老人已毀了他的檳榔樹，如今又砍倒那棵麵包樹，希望能殺死那殺了他妻子的少年。

title.en: The Wife Who Became a Cassowary
title.zh: 化作鶴鴕之妻

region.en: Bush beyond Wamira, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉外叢林（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Cassowary'

summary.en: A husband brought no food from the gardens, day upon day, while his wife boiled pebbles and drank the water; the heap of stones grew in the doorway. She tied weeding-sticks to her legs, bound coconut-leaf bristles under her arms, pulled on a rough banana-leaf skirt, and escaped through a hole at the back of the house as he came empty-handed again — into the bush, where she became a cassowary: the bristles her quills, the skirt her feathers, the weeding-sticks the kick that can slay a man. For her sake no woman must eat cassowary flesh, or their children will have faces no man will love to look on.
summary.zh: 丈夫日日下園卻從不帶回食物；妻子煮鵝卵石、喝其湯度日，門口的石堆越堆越高。第三日她仍空盼；便把兩根除草棍綁上腿彎與腳踝，腋下束椰葉鬚，外罩香蕉葉粗裙，在屋後挖好逃洞。丈夫又空手歸來，她只留下一句：『你吃吧，看好孩子——我走了，永不回來。』便穿洞入林。丈夫怒極，抓起門前石塊連連擲去，皆未命中。她入林即化作鶴鴕：腋下鬚變為翼下翎羽——即戰時飾物；葉裙化為羽衣；綁棍的雙腿化作鶴鴕鐵腿，後踢一擊足以斃人。因她之故，女人至今不得食鶴鴕肉，否則生下的孩子面目可憎，無人願看。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: In the old days there were a man and his wife, and they had one child, a little baby. And the woman was not able to work at the gardens for that she had her child to care for. But the man went each day, and did the work which was to be done. Now, though the food was ripe, yet never brought he home any for his wife to eat. And she said to him, 'Why hast thou not brought food that I may cook it? What am I then to eat?' So he bade her wait till the morrow and he would bring her the food she asked of him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Cassowary' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古時候有一對夫妻，他們有一個孩子，是個小嬰兒。那婦人因為要照顧孩子，無法到園圃裡幹活。但男人每天前去，做該做的活計。然而，儘管食物已經成熟，他卻從不帶任何食物回家給妻子吃。她便對他說：「你為何不帶食物回來讓我煮呢？那我吃什麼呢？」於是他叫她等到明天，他會把她所要的食物帶給她。

passages.text: And, being hungry, she boiled pebbles and drank the water in which she had boiled them, and poured the stones out at the door in a heap. On the morrow the woman watched for her husband to return from the gardens and bring her food. But when he came he came empty, and she boiled pebbles once more, and drank the water in which she had boiled them. And now the heap of stones in the doorway was great indeed. Then she said again to her husband, 'Wilt thou never bring me food that I may eat?' 'Truly,' said the man, 'on the morrow thou shalt eat and be filled.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Cassowary' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她因為飢餓，便煮石頭，喝下煮石頭的水，又把石頭倒在門口，堆成一堆。到了次日，婦人盼著丈夫從園圃回來，帶食物給她。但他回來時卻空手而歸，她便又煮了一次石頭，喝下煮石頭的水。此時門口的石堆已經很大了。於是她又對丈夫說：「你難道永遠不帶食物回來給我吃嗎？」男人說：「真的，明天你就能吃飽。」

passages.text: But the woman trusted not his fair words, for he had already lied to her. She therefore prepared to leave him. When the sun was rising high in the sky she took two short sticks which women use for weeding tools, and tied them to her legs at the knees and the ankles. This was in order that she might be strong to travel far. Then she took bundles of coconut leaf bristles and fastened them under her arms, and she put on a rough skirt of banana leaf over her other skirts. Then she made a great hole at the back of the house wherein she sat, whereby to escape, and waited to see if her husband would bring her food or no. And even as she watched for him he came, and in his hand was no food at all. Then said the woman as he drew nigh, 'Eat thou of our food, and moreover nurse thou our child, for I go now, and will never more return.' So saying, she stooped and passed through the hole which she had made at the back of the house, and set out for the bush.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Cassowary' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但婦人不信他的甜言蜜語，因為他已經對她說過謊了。因此她準備離開他。當太陽升得高高的時候，她拿了兩根婦女用來除草工具的短棍，把它們綁在腿上的膝蓋和腳踝處。這是為了使她有力氣走遠路。接著她拿了幾束椰子葉的硬毛，綁在腋下，又在一層層裙子外面罩上一條粗糙的香蕉葉裙。然後她在自己坐著的屋子後面挖了一個大洞，以便逃走，並等著看丈夫會不會帶食物回來。就在她張望等候他時，他來了，手裡卻一點食物也沒有。當他走近時，婦人說道：「你吃我們的食物吧，而且撫養我們的孩子吧，因為我現在要走了，再也不會回來。」說著，她彎下身子，從她在屋後挖的洞裡穿了出去，動身往叢林去了。

passages.text: There was she changed, and became a cassowary. The bristles under her arms became the quills which are under the wings of the cassowary, and which we use for ornaments in the day of battle. Her rough skirt was turned into feathers, and her legs, to which she had fastened the weeding sticks, were now as strong and to be feared as are the legs of the cassowary, which with one kick to the rear can slay a man. And she remained ever in the bush, and for her sake no woman to this day must eat of the flesh of the cassowary, else will their children have faces on which no man will love to look. And this is bare truth I tell thee and no idle tale.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Cassowary' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她就在那裡起了變化，成了一隻食火雞。她腋下的硬毛化為食火雞翅下的羽管，我們在征戰之日便用它們作裝飾。她那粗糙的裙子變成了羽毛，她曾綁上除草棍的雙腿，如今也如食火雞的腿一般強壯可怖——食火雞只需向後一踢，便能致人於死。她從此永居叢林之中，為了她的緣故，至今沒有哪個女人可以吃食火雞的肉，否則她們的孩子臉上便會長出無人願意多看一眼的容貌。我對你說的乃是赤裸的實情，並非閒話。

title.en: Where the Coconut Came From
title.zh: 椰子之由來

region.en: Wamira coast, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉海岸（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'Where the Coconut Came From'

summary.en: In the days when no coconut grew, one fisher always came home with a full basket, alone and forbidding followers. A boy crept behind him through the long grass and saw the marvel: the man took off his own head, set it on the beach, and stood in the sea letting the fish rush down his open throat. The village punished him — one watcher flung the head far into the bush — and the headless man rushed into the sea and became a huge fish. Where the head had fallen grew a slender palm the like of which none knew, till a woman dared to eat its fruit: the coconut, our food and drink ever since — and look at a husked nut, and you see the face of the man whose head became the first coconut.
summary.zh: 無椰之世，村中有一人總是獨自捕魚、滿載而歸，且禁人跟隨。一少年藏身長草之後窺得怪狀：那人雙手摘下自家腦袋放在灘上，走入齊腰海水中，彎腰張喉——群魚爭相竄入！少年回村稟告，眾人噁心欲嘔，翌日群起伏擊：一人奪起那顆頭遠拋入叢林。無頭者摸不著頭，狂奔入海，化作一尾大魚。數日後少年去尋那顆頭，原地已長出一株細長的棕櫚，葉展如蓋，無人識得。果熟之時，眾人怕有毒不敢食；終有一婦大膽嘗果、以乳汁潤膚，非但無恙，反而更美。椰子從此成為眾人之食之飲——不信，剝開椰殼看看：那上面正是第一位椰主人的臉。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: There was a time, so our fathers have told us, when no coconut grew throughout the land, and in those evil days men drank water to quench their thirst, and ate taro upon which no coconut milk had been poured. Yet not knowing how good is the coconut, they were content that it should be so. Now in those days there was a certain village, and the men who dwelt there were for ever fishing. They went forth in the morning, and came back in the evening with the fish they had caught in long strings. And when the taro was cooked they sat round the pots and ate until none was left for the morrow. But one man, when he went to fish, went always alone, and in the evening he ever returned with a basket full of fish, for they were too many to thread upon grass. The men of the village wondered that this man should never return without many fish, and also that he always forbade any to follow him, and they took counsel together how they might discover what he did to capture so many fish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Where the Coconut Came From' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 我們的父輩告訴我們，曾有那麼一個時候，整個地方都不長椰子；在那困苦的日子裡，人們飲水解渴，吃那未曾澆過椰漿的芋頭。然而他們不知椰子有多好，也就安於如此。那時有一座村莊，住在其中的男人們終日捕魚。他們清晨出門，傍晚歸來，帶著用長串穿起的魚。芋頭煮熟之後，他們便圍著鍋子吃，直到一點也不剩給明日。可是有一個人，每逢去捕魚，總是獨自前往，傍晚歸來時總帶著滿滿一籃的魚，多得無法用草繩穿起。村裡的男人們覺得奇怪：這人為何從不空手而歸，還總是禁止任何人跟隨他；於是他們一同商議，要怎樣才能探明他究竟用了什麼法子捕到這麼多魚。

passages.text: So it came to pass that on the morrow the boy did even as he had said. The man set out along the path, and the boy followed through the grass. And sometimes, in his desire to see what would come to pass, the boy crept too near, and the rustling of his body made the man look round, and even cast a spear into the grass to kill the beast which he thought made the rustling sound. But the lad, seeing the spear coming, moved to one side, and went warily until the man reached the sea shore. Then the boy hid behind a corkwood tree, and from thence he saw this strange thing. The man laid down his basket and, putting both hands to his head, he pulled, and the head came off in his two hands. Then the man laid his head beside the basket on the beach, and walked into the sea, until the waters were about his middle. There he stood, and the boy's heart trembled for fear of what might next befall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Where the Coconut Came From' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是到了第二天，那男孩果然照他所說的做了。那人沿著小路出發，男孩便穿過草叢跟隨其後。有時他急於想看會發生什麼事，便爬得太近，身體的窸窣聲使那人回頭張望，甚至朝草叢裡擲出一支矛，要殺死他以為發出窸窣聲的野獸。但那少年見矛飛來，便閃向一旁，小心翼翼地跟著，直到那人來到海邊。於是男孩躲在一棵軟木樹後，從那裡看見了這樁怪事。那人放下籃子，雙手捧住自己的頭，一拉，那頭便落在他兩手之中。接著那人把頭放在海灘上籃子旁邊，走進海裡，直到海水沒過他的腰間。他就站在那裡，男孩的心因害怕接下來可能發生的事而顫抖。

passages.text: All this the boy saw from behind the tioba tree, where he lay hidden. And having seen he fled the place, for he feared the man who did such things as these. Now it came to pass that at supper that night all ate of the fish which had been caught, save only the boy. And though many asked him, 'Why eatest thou not? Art fasting?' he refused even to touch with his fingers the fish which the man had caught. After supper, therefore, certain of the men went apart with the boy and inquired of him for what cause he had not eaten the fish that night. Then the boy told them truly all that he had seen that day, and they in their turn were filled with loathing for the food which had been thus caught. They said, therefore, 'Let us all go on the morrow and punish the man who hath done us this wrong,' and to this all agreed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Where the Coconut Came From' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這一切，男孩都從他藏身的蒂奧巴樹後看得清清楚楚。看過之後，他便逃離了那地方，因為他害怕做出這等事的人。到了那天晚上吃晚飯時，除了那男孩，人人都吃了捕來的魚。雖然許多人問他：『你為何不吃？是在齋戒嗎？』他卻連用手指碰一碰那人捕來的魚都不肯。於是晚飯之後，有幾個男人帶著男孩走到一旁，問他那天晚上為何不吃魚。男孩便將他當日所見的一切據實告訴了他們，他們聽了，也對這樣捕來的食物心生厭惡。於是他們說：『明日我們大家一同前去，懲罰那對我們做了這等錯事的人。』眾人都同意了。

passages.text: Now it came to pass on the morrow that they did even as they had said, and as the man laid his head upon the beach, not one, but many, were watching from their hiding-place. And when he had bowed himself in the water and the watchers had seen the fishes which swam towards him that they might enter his throat, a man rose up and ran to where the head lay, and seizing it, flung it far from him into the bush. Then all waited to see what would happen. In a little the man, having fish enough, turned and came slowly back to the shore. There he shook out the fish as was his custom, and then he felt for his head with both hands. But lo, it was not there! The watchers saw that he crawled over the pebbles with his two hands outstretched, if haply he might so lay hold of his head. But it was in vain that he sought it, and suddenly he rose, and rushed into the sea again, and there, before their eyes, became a huge fish and dived out of their sight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Where the Coconut Came From' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了第二天，他們果然照所說的做了；當那人把頭放在海灘上時，從藏身之處觀看的已不是一人，而是許多人。當他在水中俯身，觀看的人看見魚兒游向他，好進入他的喉嚨；這時有一人起身，跑到那頭所在之處，一把抓起，遠遠地扔進叢林裡。於是眾人都等著看會發生什麼事。過了一會兒，那人捕夠了魚，便轉身慢慢回到岸邊。他在那裡照慣例把魚抖出來，然後用雙手去摸自己的頭。可是，唉，頭已不在那裡了！觀看的人見他伸出雙手在卵石上爬來爬去，或許這樣能摸到自己的頭。但他徒然尋覓，忽然間他站起身來，又衝進海裡，就在他們眼前變成了一條巨魚，潛入水中不見了。

title.en: Ighriras Spares the Captives and Dies for It
title.zh: 伊格里拉斯釋俘而亡

region.en: Sari to Rai (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩里至賴伊（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Naudar secs. 11-13

summary.en: After beheading Naudar in foul contempt, Afrasiyab would slaughter the captive host; virtuous Ighriras, his brother, pleads that slaying disarmed prisoners is base where we should look for magnanimity, and the captives are committed bound to his charge at Sari. When Zal swears a feud without rest, Ighriras agrees to quit Amul for Rai so the prisoners may escape the Dragon's clutch, and Kishwad frees them. At Rai Afrasiyab, raging like a mad elephant, cuts his merciful brother down: now shall the fortune of Afrasiyab be darkened, says Zal, and blows the trumpets for revenge.
summary.zh: 阿弗拉西亞卜無禮斬殺瑙達爾後欲屠戮戰俘；其弟伊格里拉斯進言：處決放下兵刃之囚有失王者仁厚。俘虜被縛交由他看守於薩里。扎勒立誓血仇不休，伊格里拉斯遂棄阿穆爾退往賴伊，基什瓦德救出俘虜。在賴伊，阿弗拉西亞卜如狂象般揮刀斬殺仁兄——扎勒聞言：「阿弗拉西亞卜的氣運將晦暗，其王座將荒蕪。」遂吹號復仇。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source. Warner notes Ighriras (Aghrera) is in the Bundahishn a good spirit rewarded for saving the Iranians. No living community restriction.

passages.text: They haled the other captives forth in shame, asking quarter. Virtuous Ighriras saw this and anxiously besought the king: to slay so many noble warriors and horsemen in cold blood, mere prisoners disarmed, is base, and base where we should look for magnanimity. Commit them bound to me and I will prison them within a cavern, well guarded; prison will restore their wits; but shed not blood. At Ighriras' request, perceiving his distress and earnestness, the monarch spared their lives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Naudar sec. 11 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們把其餘的俘虜羞辱地拖了出來，那些人正求饒。仁德的伊格里拉斯見此情景，焦急地向國王懇求：如此冷酷地殺害這麼多高貴的戰士與騎手，他們不過是手無寸鐵的俘虜，這是卑劣的，而在我們本應期待寬宏大量之處行此卑劣之事，更是卑劣。請把他們捆綁起來交給我，我將把他們囚禁在一處洞穴之中，嚴加看守；囚禁會使他們恢復理智；但請不要流血。國王聽了伊格里拉斯的請求，看出他的憂傷與懇切，便饒了他們的性命。

passages.text: When Zal heard the news of Naudar's beheading he rent all his raiment and sat down with lamentable outcries in the dust. My trenchant blade shall ne'er behold sheath till the Resurrection, my white charger shall be my throne, a spear mine only tree, my place a stirrup and a dusky helm the crown upon my head; there is no rest or slumber in this feud. When the captives heard that the Iranians were upon the march for vengeance they neither ate nor slept, and a message came to Ighriras: if prudent Ighriras see fit to free us we will disperse and make thanksgiving unto God for him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Naudar sec. 12 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 扎尔听闻瑙达尔被斩首的消息，便撕裂了所有衣裳，坐在尘土中发出悲恸的哀号。他说：「我的利刃在复活日之前绝不会入鞘，我的白马将是我的王座，长矛是我唯一的树木，马镫是我的居所，一顶暗色的头盔便是我头上的王冠；在这场仇怨中，既无安歇，也无睡眠。」被囚者听说伊朗人正行军前来复仇，便既不食也不眠，并有一道消息传到伊格里拉斯那里：倘若审慎的伊格里拉斯认为释放我们为宜，我们便各自散去，并为他向上帝献上感恩。

passages.text: Wise Ighriras replied: this human Ahriman would be incensed, and my brother may turn upon me in vengeance. If now Zal is keen for war and will advance to fight us at Sari, I will deliver you to him, myself evacuate Amul, forbear to fight, and bring to infamy my honoured head. He blew the brazen trumpets, marched away his troops and left the captives at Sari; when Kishwad arrived he found the key to loose their bonds and sped toward Zabul, while Zal took the loved ones within the city and gave them palaces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Naudar sec. 12 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 睿智的伊格里拉斯答道：「这个人间阿里曼必会震怒，而我的兄弟也许会转而向我复仇。倘若如今扎尔急于开战，要推进到萨里与我们交战，我便把你们交给他，我自己撤出阿穆尔，按兵不战，让我这受人尊敬的头颅蒙受耻辱。」他吹响铜号，率军离去，将俘虏留在萨里；基什瓦德抵达时，寻得了为他们解开束缚的钥匙，便疾驰前往扎布尔，而扎尔则把亲爱的人们接进城中，赐予他们宫室。

passages.text: When Ighriras went from Amul to Rai the king asked: wherefore hast thou mingled colocynth with honey? Tears and compassion are not wholly needless, he answered; when thou hast the power to harm, fear God and do it not, for crown and girdle see many like thee but are no man's own for ever. At his reply the chieftain, raging like an elephant gone mad, drew forth his scimitar and cut his brother down; that man of wisdom and goodness passed away. Zal heard, and said: now shall the fortune of Afrasiyab be darkened and his throne laid waste; he blew the trumpets, arrayed the army like the eye of chanticleer, and went toward Pars in anger and revenge.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Naudar sec. 13 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 当伊格里拉斯从阿穆尔前往赖伊时，国王问道：「你为何把苦西瓜与蜂蜜混在一起？」他答道：「眼泪与怜悯并非全然多余；当你拥有加害之力时，要敬畏上帝而不可行之，因为王冠与腰带见过许多像你一样的人，却从不永远属于任何人。」听了他的回答，那位首领如发狂的大象般暴怒，拔出弯刀将他的兄弟砍倒；那位智慧而善良的人就此逝去。扎尔听闻后说道：「如今阿夫拉西亚布的运势必将黯淡，他的王座必将荒废。」他吹响号角，将军队列阵如雄鸡之眼，怀着怒火与复仇之心向帕尔斯进发。

title.en: The Anganga and Pulotu, Land under the Ocean
title.zh: 靈魂安岡加與海底樂土普洛圖

region.en: Falealupo, west Savaii, and Pulotu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩瓦伊島法萊阿盧波與普洛圖（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1884 (Turner)

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 3 (London 1884)

summary.en: Samoans believed in a soul, the anganga, which at death left the body and went to the hadean regions under the ocean, called Pulotu, entered from the neighbourhood of Falealupo at the western point of Savaii. Birth placed every Samoan under an aitu - a god who appeared in some visible incarnation: eel, shark, turtle, dog, owl or lizard. To eat the incarnation of one's own god was death, for the god would dwell in the body of the offender and generate there the very thing he had eaten.
summary.zh: 薩摩亞人信有靈魂安岡加——人死離體，前往海底冥府普洛圖，其門戶在薩瓦伊島西端法萊阿盧波附近。人皆有守護神艾圖：或顯於鰻、鯊、龜、犬、鴞、蜥；若人食己神之化身，神便入其腹中孕育其所食之物，至死方休。

sensitivity.note: Samoan eschatology and totemic belief summarized.

passages.text: The Samoans believed in a soul or disembodied spirit, which they called the anganga. Anga means to go or come, according to the particle of direction suffixed; the reduplicated anganga is used to designate the soul as distinct from the body, which at death was supposed to go away from the body and proceed to the hadean regions under the ocean, which they called Pulotu. At his birth a Samoan was supposed to be taken under the care of some god, or aitu, as it was called: the help of several of these gods was probably invoked in succession on the occasion, and the one who happened to be addressed just as the child was born was fixed on as the child's god for life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 3 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 萨摩亚人相信有一种灵魂或脱离肉体的精灵，他们称之为「安甘加」（anganga）。「安加」（anga）意为去或来，视所附的方向助词而定；重叠形式的「安甘加」用来指称与肉体有别的灵魂，据信人死时灵魂便离开肉体，前往海底的冥界，他们称之为「普洛图」（Pulotu）。萨摩亚人出生时，据信会被置于某位神祇——即所谓的「艾图」（aitu）——的看护之下：在那一场合，人们大概会依次祈求好几位这样的神祇相助，而恰在孩子出生那一刻被祈求的那一位，便被定为这孩子终身的神祇。

passages.text: These gods were supposed to appear in some visible incarnation, and the particular thing in which his god was in the habit of appearing was to the Samoan an object of veneration - in fact, his idol, and he was careful never to injure it or treat it with contempt. One saw his god in the eel, another in the shark, another in the turtle, another in the dog, another in the owl, another in the lizard, and so on throughout all the fish of the sea, and birds, and four-footed beasts, and creeping things; in some of the shell-fish even, gods were supposed to be present. A man would eat freely of what was regarded as the incarnation of the god of another man, but the incarnation of his own particular god he would consider it death to injure or to eat. The god was supposed to avenge the insult by taking up his abode in that person's body, and causing to generate there the very thing which he had eaten, until it produced death. This class of genii, or tutelary deities, they called aitu fale, or gods of the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 3 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 这些神祇据信会以某种可见的化身显现，而某人的神祇惯于显现于其中的那种特定事物，对萨摩亚人而言便是崇敬的对象——事实上就是他的偶像，他小心翼翼地绝不伤害它，也绝不以轻蔑待之。有人在自己的神祇中看见鳗鱼，有人看见鲨鱼，有人看见海龟，有人看见狗，有人看见猫头鹰，有人看见蜥蜴，如此遍及海中一切鱼类、鸟类、四足兽与爬行之物；甚至在有些贝类之中，据信也有神祇存在。一个人可以随意食用被视为他人之神祇化身的东西，但若伤害或食用自己那位特定神祇的化身，他便会视之为致死之事。据信那神祇会以附入此人身体的方式来报复这一侮辱，使他所食之物在其体内滋生，直至致其死亡。这一类精灵或守护神，他们称之为「艾图法莱」（aitu fale），即家宅之神。

title.en: The Village God and the Oath of the Coconut Cup
title.zh: 村神與椰殼之誓

region.en: Samoan village temple (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩摩亞村廟（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1884 (Turner)

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 3 (London 1884)

summary.en: Every village had its god; every child born there was 'his property'. The temple might hold a conch shell blown to rouse the village to war, a sacred cup, or stones; the cup served in oaths - hands laid upon it: 'With my hand on this cup, may the god look upon me, and send swift destruction, if I took the thing which has been stolen' - and before this ordeal the truth was rarely concealed. Village gods were incarnate in owl, heron, bat or rainbow; a dead owl found on the road was wept over, the forehead beaten with stones till blood flowed, and the bird buried like a human body - while its flight in war was omen and command.
summary.zh: 各村皆有其神；村中新生嬰兒皆屬其所有。廟中或懸海螺——神欲開戰便吹之；或懸椰殼聖盃，用以起誓：『手按此盃，願神鑒察，若竊物者是我，願遭天誅。』臨此神判，真相極少能藏。村神或顯於鴞、鷺、蝠、虹；路遇死鴞，村民當場痛哭，以石擊額至血流，鄭重如葬人；而戰時鴞翔之向即進退之令。

sensitivity.note: Samoan communal religion; blood-mourning described as recorded practice.

passages.text: Another class of Samoan deities may be called gods of the town or village. Every village had its god, and every one born in that village was regarded as the property of that god: a woman would say on the birth of her child, 'I have got a child for so-and-so', and name the village god. There was a small house or temple also consecrated to the deity of the place; where there was no formal temple, the great house of the village, where the chiefs were in the habit of assembling, was the temple for the time being. Some settlements had a sacred grove as well as a temple, where prayers and offerings were presented.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 3 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 萨摩亚人的另一类神祇可称为城镇或村庄之神。每个村庄都有自己的神祇，凡在该村出生的人都被视为那位神祇的财产：妇人会在孩子出生时说：「我为某某生了一个孩子」，并说出村神的名字。村里还有一座奉献给当地神祇的小屋或神庙；在没有正式神庙的地方，酋长们惯于聚会的村中大屋便暂时充作神庙。有些聚落除神庙之外还有一片圣林，人们在那里献上祈祷与祭品。

passages.text: In their temples they had generally something for the eye to rest upon with superstitious veneration. In one might be seen a conch shell suspended from the roof in a basket made of cinnet network, and this the god was supposed to blow when he wished the people to rise to war; in another, two stones were kept; in another, something resembling the head of a man, with white streamers flying, was raised on a pole at the door of the temple on the usual day of worship; in another, a cocoa-nut shell drinking-cup was suspended from the roof, and before it prayers were addressed and offerings presented.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 3 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在他們的廟宇裡，通常總有些供人懷著迷信的敬畏凝視之物。在一座廟中，可見一只海螺殼懸於屋頂，盛在由椰殼纖維網編成的籃子裡，據說神明欲令眾人起而征戰時，便吹響此螺；在另一座廟中，供奉著兩塊石頭；又有一座廟中，於慣常的禮拜之日，廟門口的柱上高懸一物，狀似人頭，白色長幡飄揚；還有一座廟中，屋頂懸著一只椰殼製的飲杯，人們在其前祈禱並獻上供品。

passages.text: This cup was also used in oaths: if they wished to find out a thief, the suspected parties were assembled before the chiefs, the cup sent for, and each would approach, lay his hand on it, and say, 'With my hand on this cup, may the god look upon me, and send swift destruction, if I took the thing which has been stolen.' The stones and the shells were used in a similar way. Before this ordeal the truth was rarely concealed: they firmly believed that it would be death to touch the cup and tell a lie.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 3 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此杯亦用於立誓：若他們想查出竊賊，便將嫌疑之人召集於首領面前，取來此杯，眾人依次上前，把手放在杯上，說道：『我手按此杯，若我取了被竊之物，願神明鑒察我，速降毀滅於我。』石頭與貝殼亦以類似方式使用。在此神判之前，真相鮮少隱瞞：他們深信，觸碰此杯而說謊，必死無疑。

passages.text: The village gods, like those of the household, had all some particular incarnation: one was supposed to appear as a bat, another as a heron, another as an owl. If a man found a dead owl by the roadside, and if that happened to be the incarnation of his village god, he would sit down and weep over it, and beat his forehead with stones till the blood flowed - this was thought pleasing to the deity. Then the bird would be wrapped up and buried with care and ceremony, as if it were a human body; this, however, was not the death of the god, who was supposed to be yet alive, and incarnate in all the owls in existence. The flight of these birds was observed in time of war: if the bird flew before them, it was a signal to go on; but if it crossed the path, it was a bad omen and a sign to retreat. Others saw their village god in the rainbow, others in the shooting star; and in time of war the position of a rainbow and the direction of a shooting star were always ominous.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 3 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 村神如同家神，皆各有特定的化身：一說化為蝙蝠，一說化為蒼鷺，一說化為貓頭鷹。若有人在路旁發現一只死貓頭鷹，而它恰是其村神的化身，他便會坐下為它哭泣，並以石頭擊打自己的額頭直至血流——此舉被認為蒙神喜悅。隨後，這隻鳥會被包裹起來，以慎重的儀式安葬，如同對待人的遺體一般；然而這並非神明之死，人們認為神明仍然活著，化身於世間所有貓頭鷹之中。戰時會觀察這些鳥的飛翔：若鳥飛於前方，便是前進的信號；若鳥橫越道路，則是凶兆，是撤退的徵象。另有人從彩虹中、從流星中看見自己的村神；戰時，彩虹的位置與流星的方向，總被視為預兆。

title.en: Young Maui of Savage Island Steals the Fire
title.zh: 野島小毛伊竊火記

region.en: Savage Island (Niue) (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 紐埃島（象徵性定位）

period: Niue oral tradition; recorded 1884 (Turner)

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (London 1884)

summary.en: Three hundred miles south of Samoa, the natives of Savage Island have a somewhat similar tale about the origin of fire: instead of Talanga and Ti'iti'i they give the names of Maui the father and Maui the son; instead of going through a rock their entrance was down through a reed bush; and instead of a stipulation for the fire, the youth Maui, like another Prometheus, stole it, ran up the passage, and before his father could catch him had set the bush in flames in all directions. The father tried to put it out but in vain - and ever since the exploit of young Maui they have had fire and cooked food in Savage Island.
summary.zh: 薩摩亞以南三百里的紐埃島（野島）流傳著同源異文之火源神話：主人翁換作父子雙毛伊；入口不在岩縫而在蘆叢之下；取得之途亦非談判，而是竊取——小毛伊如另一普羅米修斯，攜火而逃，尚未被父追及便將蘆叢四處點燃；父親撲火無功。自從小毛伊這番功業之後，野島之人便有了火與熟食。

sensitivity.note: Fire-theft cluster: Niue Prometheus variant of the Ti'iti'i story.

passages.text: The natives of Savage Island, 300 miles to the south of Samoa, have a somewhat similar tale about the origin of fire: instead of Talanga and Ti'iti'i, they give the names of Maui, the father, and Maui, the son; instead of going through a rock, their entrance was down through a reed bush. And, instead of a stipulation for the fire, they say that the youth Maui, like another Prometheus, stole it, ran up the passage, and before his father could catch him, he had set the bush in flames in all directions. The father tried to put it out, but in vain; and they further add, that ever since the exploit of young Maui, they have had fire and cooked food in Savage Island.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 薩摩亞以南三百英里的野人島（Savage Island）原住民，對於火的起源有類似的故事：他們不說塔蘭加（Talanga）與蒂伊蒂伊（Ti'iti'i），而稱父毛伊（Maui）與子毛伊（Maui）；他們不是穿過岩石，而是從蘆葦叢中向下進入。而且，他們不說為火立約，而說年輕的毛伊如另一位普羅米修斯般偷了火，沿通道奔上，未待其父捉住他，他已將蘆葦叢四處點燃。父親試圖撲滅，卻徒勞無功；他們還進一步說，自小毛伊此舉之後，野人島便有了火與熟食。

title.en: The Wars of Stones, Grass and Trees
title.zh: 石草樹木之戰

region.en: Savaii uplands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩瓦伊島高地（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1884 (Turner)

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (London 1884)

summary.en: A golden age when all things spoke and warred: small stones beaten by grass, grass by bush-grass, bush-grass by trees, trees by creepers - 'and then began the wars of men'. The fish beat the birds in their first battle, fish becoming birds; the birds beat the fish in the second and have reigned ever since. The bat borrowed the rat's wings and never returned them; the banana family, beaten by the plantain, hangs its head in defeat - while the erect plantain remains the symbol of its own victory.
summary.zh: 太古黃金時代，萬物能言能戰：石敗於草，草敗於叢草，叢草敗於樹，樹敗於藤——『然後人類的戰爭開始了』。魚首戰勝鳥，魚化為鳥；再戰鳥勝，鳥遂永掌天翼。蝙蝠借鼠之翼而不還；芭蕉族敗於山蕉，從此垂首示敗——山蕉依然昂首，是自身勝利的標記。

sensitivity.note: Cosmogonic battle sequence; Turner's remark that these may encode inter-village wars noted.

passages.text: The Samoans have their stories of a golden age of intelligence long long ago, when all things material had the power of speech. They not only spoke, but they had evil natures as well, and quarrelled with each other and fought, very much like the races of mankind. To give it in their own words: 'The small stones fought with the grass, the stones were beaten and the grass conquered. The short grass fought with the strong weedy grass, the short grass was beaten and the strong grass conquered. The strong grass fought with the long grass of the bush, the strong grass was beaten and the bush grass conquered. The bush grass fought with the trees, the grass was beaten and the trees conquered. The trees fought with the creepers, the trees were beaten and the creepers conquered - and then began the wars of men.' The principle seems to be that whenever one thing prevails to excess above another thing, be it rock, stone, earth, grass or tree, we are sure to find some tradition of its battle and victory.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 薩摩亞人流傳著很久很久以前一個智慧黃金時代的故事，那時一切有質之物皆能言語。它們不僅能說話，還各有邪惡的本性，彼此爭吵、打鬥，與人類各族極為相似。用他們自己的話來說：『小石頭與草爭鬥，石頭被打敗，草得勝。短草與強韌的雜草爭鬥，短草被打敗，強草得勝。強草與叢林中的長草爭鬥，強草被打敗，叢林之草得勝。叢林之草與樹木爭鬥，草被打敗，樹木得勝。樹木與藤蔓爭鬥，樹木被打敗，藤蔓得勝——於是便開始了人類的戰爭。』其原則似乎是：每當一物勝過另一物而至於極盛，無論那是岩石、石頭、泥土、草還是樹，我們必能找到關於其爭鬥與勝利的某種傳說。

passages.text: A story is told of a battle between two trees - a Fijian Banian tree and the Samoan tree called Tatangia. A report reached Samoa that the trees of Fiji had fought with the Banian tree and that it had beaten them all; on this the Tatangia and another tree went off from Samoa in two canoes to fight the Fijian champion. They reached Fiji, went on shore, and there stood the Banian tree. 'Where is the tree which has conquered all the trees?' 'I am the tree', said the Banian. 'I have come to fight with you.' They fought: a branch of the Banian tree fell, but Tatangia sprung aside and escaped; another fell - ditto - the Tatangia; then the trunk fell, and again Tatangia darted aside unhurt. On this the Banian tree 'buried its eyes in the earth' and owned itself conquered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一則故事講述兩棵樹之間的戰鬥——一棵斐濟榕樹與一棵薩摩亞人稱為塔坦吉亞（Tatangia）的樹。有消息傳到薩摩亞，說斐濟的樹木曾與榕樹爭鬥，而榕樹擊敗了它們全部；於是塔坦吉亞與另一棵樹便乘兩艘獨木舟離開薩摩亞，前去與斐濟的冠軍一戰。它們抵達斐濟，上岸，榕樹便矗立在那裡。『那棵征服了所有樹木的樹在哪裡？』『我就是那棵樹，』榕樹說。『我來與你一戰。』它們打了起來：榕樹的一根樹枝落下，但塔坦吉亞閃身避開，安然無恙；又一根落下——塔坦吉亞同樣避開；接著樹幹倒下，塔坦吉亞再次閃身避開，毫髮無傷。於是榕樹『將雙眼埋入土中』，承認自己敗了。

passages.text: There were also accounts of battles fought by the birds on the one side and the fish on the other: the fish and the birds were in the habit of paying friendly visits to each other. The inanga, or small fry of a fresh-water fish, were offended at not being hospitably received on shore by the birds; on the other hand the birds despised the inanga for being so small. They fought, and the fishes conquered, and it ended in the fish becoming birds and the birds fishes - hence they say the back-bone of the inanga projects so much. But after that there was another battle, in which the fish were beaten and the birds conquered; and ever since the birds have had their wings, and their supremacy, and the right of going to the sea or the river as they please to pick up the fish which come within their reach.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 也有關於鳥類為一方、魚類為另一方交戰的記載：魚與鳥素來習慣互相友好往訪。inanga（一種淡水魚的幼魚）因在岸上未受鳥類殷勤接待而心生不滿；另一方面，鳥類又因inanga如此細小而輕視牠們。雙方交戰，魚類獲勝，結局是魚變成鳥、鳥變成魚——因此人們說inanga的背骨才如此突出。但此後又有一場戰役，魚類被擊敗，鳥類獲勝；自此以後，鳥類便有了翅膀、有了至高地位，並有權任意前往海中或河裡，啄食游到牠們搆得著的魚。

passages.text: They say that the rat had wings formerly, and that the large bat or flying fox at that time had no wings. One day the bat said to the rat: 'Let me try on your wings for a little, that I may see how I like flying.' The rat lent the bat his wings; off flew the bat with the wings and never came back to return them - hence the proverb applied to a person who borrows and does not return: 'Like the bat with the rat.' With the exception of the mountain plantain all the bananas have their bunches of fruit hanging downwards towards the earth like a bunch of grapes; the plantain shoots up its bunch of fruit erect towards the heavens. As the reason of this we are told that of old all the bananas held their heads erect, but they quarrelled with the plantain, fought, were beaten, and ever since have hung their heads in token of their defeat, whereas the plantain is erect still, and the symbol of its own victory.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 人們說老鼠從前有翅膀，而當時大蝙蝠（或狐蝠）沒有翅膀。有一天，蝙蝠對老鼠說：『讓我試戴一下你的翅膀，看看我喜不喜歡飛。』老鼠把翅膀借給了蝙蝠；蝙蝠戴著翅膀飛走，從此再沒回來歸還——因此有句諺語用來形容借物不還的人：『像蝙蝠借了老鼠的。』除了山蕉之外，所有香蕉的果串都朝地面下垂，像一串葡萄；山蕉則把果串筆直朝天挺立。關於箇中緣由，據說古時所有香蕉都昂首挺立，但牠們與山蕉爭吵、交戰、被擊敗，自此便垂頭以示敗績，而山蕉則依然挺立，成為自身勝利的象徵。

title.en: Tasi the Last Becomes First: The Owl, the Serpent, the Ten Brothers
title.zh: 貓頭鷹、蛇與十兄弟：末位成首位

region.en: Forest of Savaii (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩瓦伊島林間（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1884 (Turner)

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (London 1884)

summary.en: Ten brothers named after the numerals - Sefulu first, Tasi last - go to the forest for canoe timber and find an owl and a serpent fighting. Nine refuse the owl's plea; Tasi alone takes up his felling axe and kills the serpent. 'Well done, Tasi! To keep in remembrance your bravery, you shall stand foremost in everything that is numbered: Sefulu who has been first shall now be last, and you who have been last shall always be first.' So Samoan counting runs Tasi, Lua, Tolu... to Sefulu.
summary.zh: 十個以數字命名的兄弟入林伐舟材，遇貓頭鷹與蛇相鬥。九位兄長皆推卻鴞的求援；唯有末弟塔西掄斧斃蛇。鴞曰：『幹得好，塔西！為永誌你的勇氣，萬物計數你當居首：原為第一的塞福魯降居末位，而原居末位的你永為第一。』薩摩亞數數至今自塔西起、以塞福魯終。

sensitivity.note: Numeral-order etiology.

passages.text: A battle also between the owl and the serpent is noteworthy. There were ten brothers, whose names were Sefulu, Iva, Valu, Fitu, Ono, Lima, Fa, Tolu, Lua, and Tasi, and so named from the ten numerals, which in those days began with Sefulu as 1 and ended with Tasi as 10. These ten brothers went to the forest to cut wood for a large canoe; they came upon an owl and a serpent fighting. Sefulu was walking first, and to him the owl called out: 'Sefulu, you come and kill my enemy here, the serpent, and if you do you shall have a right to the Ifilele and Maota timber trees.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 貓頭鷹與蛇之間的一場戰鬥也值得一提。有十個兄弟，名字分別是Sefulu、Iva、Valu、Fitu、Ono、Lima、Fa、Tolu、Lua和Tasi，乃依十個數目字命名，當時的數目字以Sefulu為1，以Tasi為10。這十個兄弟到森林裡去砍伐造大獨木舟的木料；他們遇見一隻貓頭鷹與一條蛇在搏鬥。Sefulu走在最前頭，貓頭鷹便對他喊道：『Sefulu，你來把這裡我的敵人，那條蛇，殺掉，你若照做，就有權取用Ifilele與Maota這兩種木材樹。』

passages.text: 'No, let us pass on', said Sefulu, 'there are plenty of other trees which will answer our purpose.' Then the owl turned to Iva and all the others on to Lua, and implored help in killing the serpent, but each in turn answered as did Sefulu. Tasi, however, replied to the entreaty of the owl, and said, 'Yes, I will', and grasping his felling axe struck out at the serpent and killed it. 'Well done, Tasi!' said the owl, 'and to keep in remembrance for all time to come your bravery and respect for me, you shall stand foremost in everything that is numbered. Sefulu who has been first shall now be last, and you who have been last shall always be first.' And so it has continued to the present day - the first, Tasi, and the tenth, Sefulu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 『不，我們還是繼續走吧，』Sefulu說，『還有許多別的樹能合我們用。』於是貓頭鷹轉向Iva，又依次向其餘各人直到Lua懇求相助殺蛇，但各人輪流都像Sefulu那樣回答。然而Tasi回應了貓頭鷹的懇求，說道：『好，我來。』便握起砍伐的斧頭朝蛇砍去，把牠殺死了。『做得好，Tasi！』貓頭鷹說，『為了使你的勇敢和對我的敬重永世留作紀念，凡有數目排列之處，你都要居於最前。向來居首的Sefulu如今要居末，而向來居末的你則永遠居首。』此事一直沿襲至今——第一是Tasi，第十是Sefulu。

title.en: Toa and Pale: The Tree That Kept Rising
title.zh: 托阿與帕萊：砍而不倒的兄弟樹

region.en: Fiji bush (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 斐濟叢林（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1884 (Turner)

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (London 1884)

summary.en: Fleeing the cannibal king of Fiji, brothers Toa and Pale become trees. Pale takes the crooked creeper-covered shape and begs Toa to do the same; Toa stands erect as a handsome straight tree - and the king's carpenters, seeking a keel, choose him. Cut down, he is raised again by Pale; the cutting, falling and rising goes on till nightfall, when they give up. 'What a Toa I have been to you!' says the felled one - and Samoans still say, when one has been a burden to another, 'What a Toa it has been to you!'
summary.zh: 為避斐濟食人王，兄弟托阿與帕萊化為樹。帕萊化作纏藤的歪樹，勸弟從同；托阿偏要挺立如良材——造舟匠果然相中，揮斧砍伐；倒下即被帕萊扶起，砍倒又起，直至入夜作罷。托阿嘆道：『我真成了你的托阿（拖累）！』——至今薩摩亞人仍說：『你真是我的托阿。』

sensitivity.note: Proverb-origin fable; Samoa-Fiji link.

passages.text: The King of Fiji was a savage cannibal, and the people were melting away under him. Toa and Pale were brothers; they wished to escape being killed for the oven, and so fled to the bush and became trees. It was only the day before a party were to go to the woods to search for a straight tree from which to make the keel of a new canoe for the king. They knew this, and so Pale changed himself into a crooked stick overrun with creepers, that he might not be cut by the king's carpenters, and advised Toa to do the same; he declined, however, and preferred standing erect as a handsome straight tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 斐濟的國王是個殘暴的食人族，百姓在他治下日益凋零。Toa與Pale是兄弟；他們不願被殺去烤爐，於是逃入叢林，化成了樹。就在隔天，有一隊人要進林子去尋找一棵筆直的樹，用來為國王造新獨木舟的龍骨。他們知道此事，於是Pale把自己變成一株纏滿藤蔓的彎曲矮木，以免被國王的木匠砍伐，並勸Toa也照做；然而Toa不肯，寧願挺立成一棵俊秀筆直的樹。

passages.text: The party in search of a keel went to the very place, liked the look of Toa, and decided to cut it down. They cut, and Toa was felled to the ground, but Pale, who was close by, immediately raised him up again. The carpenters were confounded - cut again - but it was just the same. They persevered, and the cutting, falling, and rising again went on till night fell, when they gave it up. After they left Toa said to Pale, 'What a Toa (trouble) I have been to you!' - and hence the proverb to this day, when a person or thing has been a trouble to another, he says to the sufferer in a sympathising or apologetic tone: 'What a Toa it has been to you!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 尋找龍骨的那隊人來到正是那個地方，看中了Toa的模樣，決定把它砍下。他們砍了又砍，Toa被伐倒在地，但就在近旁的Pale立刻又把它扶立起來。木匠們大惑不解——再砍——結果依然如故。他們鍥而不捨，砍倒、扶起、再砍倒、再扶起，一直持續到夜幕降臨，他們才作罷。眾人離去後，Toa對Pale說：『我給你添了多大的Toa（麻煩）啊！』——因此至今有句諺語，當某人或某事給另一人添了麻煩時，便以同情或歉疚的口吻對受苦者說：『它給你添了多大的Toa啊！』

title.en: The Fowl and the Turtle at the Cool Spring
title.zh: 母雞與海龜爭泉

region.en: Rocks above a spring, Upolu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 烏波盧島泉邊岩（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1884 (Turner)

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (London 1884)

summary.en: The fowl claims the cool spring by the rock; the turtle, fresh from the hot salt sea, bathes and is driven off - 'Let whoever is first here in the morning have the spring'. The turtle toils all night up the river; the fowl, sure of one bound of her wings, roosts till sunrise - and finds the turtle before her. 'Here comes the fowl, the turtle is before you!' - the Samoan proverb for the lazy and the late.
summary.zh: 母雞霸佔清泉，海龜自滾熱鹹海而來只圖一浴，被逐出——『明晨誰先到，泉歸誰』。海龜連夜溯河而至；母雞自恃一躍即達，安睡至日出——泉邊早有海龜候著。諺云：『母雞來了，海龜卻已在前！』——薩摩亞人譏懶惰遲到者之辭。

sensitivity.note: Animal fable of proverb origin.

passages.text: Take the story of the fowl and the turtle. A fowl made her headquarters over a rock from which a cool spring of fresh water ran out into the adjacent stream. One day a turtle made its appearance; it was enjoying the cool fresh bath, and rising now and then to look about, when it was addressed roughly by the fowl: 'Who are you?' 'I am a turtle.' 'Where have you come from?' 'From the hot salt sea.' 'What are you doing here?' 'Bathing, and enjoying the fine cool fresh water.' 'Be off, this is my water.' 'No, it is mine as much as it is yours.' 'Well, then', said the fowl, 'let us decide in this way which of us will have it: let each of us go away, and whoever is first here in the morning shall have the right to the spring.' 'Let it be so', said the turtle, 'I'm off to the briny sea; you go away to the village.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 且說那隻雞與烏龜的故事。有一隻雞，把巢築在一塊岩石上，那岩石下湧出一股清涼的淡水泉，流入鄰近的溪中。有一天，一隻烏龜出現了；牠正享受著清涼的淡水浴，不時浮上水面四下張望，卻被那隻雞粗魯地喝問：「你是誰？」「我是烏龜。」「你從哪裡來？」「從炎熱的鹹海來。」「你在這裡做什麼？」「洗澡，享受這清涼的好淡水。」「滾開，這是我的水。」「不，這水是我的，也同樣是你的。」「那麼，」雞說，「我們就這麼決定這水歸誰：各自離開，明早誰先到這裡，誰就有權佔有這泉。」「就這麼辦，」烏龜說，「我回那鹹澀的海去；你回村裡去吧。」

passages.text: The turtle was back from the sea, up the river, and at the spring very early in the morning. The fowl thought there was no need to hurry, as she could with one bound on her wings be at the rock, and so she roosted till the sun was rising, and then flew over to the rock; but there was the turtle before her! 'You are there, I see', said the fowl. 'Yes, I am', replied the turtle, 'and the spring is mine.' And hence the proverb applied to the lazy and the late: 'Here comes the fowl, the turtle is before you!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 烏龜從海裡回來，溯河而上，一大清早就到了泉邊。雞心想不必著急，因為牠只要振翅一躍便能到那岩石上，於是便棲息著，直到太陽升起，才飛到岩石那邊；可是烏龜早已在那裡了！「我看見你在那兒了。」雞說。「是的，我在這兒，」烏龜回答，「這泉是我的了。」因此有句諺語，用來譏諷懶惰與遲到的人：「雞來了，烏龜已在你前頭！」

title.en: The Rat, the Octopus, and the Owls
title.zh: 鼠、章魚與群鴞

region.en: Coast of Savaii (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩瓦伊島海岸（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1884 (Turner)

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (London 1884)

summary.en: A rat, a snipe and a crab build a canoe; a squall upsets it, and the exhausted rat rides on the octopus's back, drinking salt water and secretly gnawing the neck of his rescuer. Ashore, the pain reveals the treachery; the octopus summons his friends the owls, who hunt down the rat and eat him - hardly a morsel each, they were so many. 'Do not be like the rat with the octopus: evil will overtake you if you do.'
summary.zh: 鼠、鷸、蟹同造獨木舟；風暴覆舟，力竭的老鼠攀上章魚之背，一邊飲鹹水解渴，一邊暗中啃咬恩人頸項。登岸後劇痛揭穿背叛；章魚召集盟友群鴞，追獵群鼠而食之——鼠眾太多，每鴞分得寥寥。諺云：『莫效章魚背上的老鼠——忘恩者必遭惡報。』

sensitivity.note: Gratitude-fable of proverb origin.

passages.text: There were three friends, a rat, a snipe, and a crab. They thought they would like to look about them on the sea, and so decided to build a canoe and go out on a short cruise. They did so, and when the canoe was ready off they went: the snipe pulled the first paddle, the crab the second, and the rat steered. A squall came on, and the canoe upset; the snipe flew to the shore, the crab sank and escaped to the bottom, and the rat swam. The rat was soon fatigued, but an octopus came along, and from it the rat implored help. 'Come on my back', said the octopus. The rat was only too happy to do so. By-and-by the octopus said: 'How heavy you are! my back is getting painful.' 'Yes', said the rat, 'I drank too much salt water when I was swimming there; but bear it a little longer, we shall soon be at the shore.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有三個朋友：一隻老鼠、一隻鷸和一隻螃蟹。牠們想到海上四處看看，於是決定造一隻獨木舟，出海作一趟短程航行。牠們照辦了，獨木舟造好後便出發：鷸划第一支槳，螃蟹划第二支，老鼠掌舵。忽然刮起一陣狂風，獨木舟翻了；鷸飛到岸上，螃蟹沉下去，逃到海底，老鼠則在水中游。老鼠很快就累了，這時一隻章魚游過來，老鼠向牠哀求幫助。「到我背上來吧。」章魚說。老鼠求之不得，便爬了上去。過了一會兒，章魚說：「你怎麼這麼重！我的背都痛起來了。」「是啊，」老鼠說，「我剛才在水裡游的時候喝太多海水了；不過再忍耐一會兒，我們馬上就到岸了。」

passages.text: When the octopus reached the shore off ran the rat into the bush. The octopus felt the pain still, however, and now discovered that the rat had been gnawing at the back of its neck. The octopus was enraged, called all his friends among the owls to assemble, and begged them to pursue and destroy the rat. They did so, caught it, killed it, and ate it, but there was hardly a morsel for each, they were so many. And hence the proverb in exhorting not to return evil for good: 'Do not be like the rat with the octopus, evil will overtake you if you do.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 19 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 章魚一到岸邊，老鼠便跑進灌木叢裡去了。可是章魚仍覺得疼痛，這時才發現老鼠一直在啃牠後頸的肉。章魚大怒，召集牠所有的貓頭鷹朋友聚在一起，懇求牠們去追捕並消滅那隻老鼠。牠們照辦了，捉住老鼠，把牠殺死吃掉，可是牠們數目太多，幾乎分不到一口。因此有句諺語，勸人不要以惡報善：「不要像老鼠對待章魚那樣，你若如此，惡必臨到你。」

title.en: The Four Sons of Pulotu and the First War
title.zh: 普洛圖四子與第一場戰爭

region.en: Pulotu to Papatea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 自普洛圖至帕帕特亞（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1884 (Turner)

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 20 (London 1884)

summary.en: At Pulotu lived Head of Day and Tail of Day, whose four children - Rain, Long-grass, Heavens and Story - visited Papatea in the east. Ua was struck on the neck (hence taua, to beat the neck, the word for war); Fan's neck was trodden; Langi was spat upon; Tala escaped. Elo, king of Pulotu, made the first war in history and swept Papatea clean: the refugees Tutu and Ila gave Tutuila its name, U and Polu that of Upolu, Sa and Vaila Savaii - islands born of a massacre's survivors.
summary.zh: 普洛圖住著『晝之首』與『晝之尾』夫婦，四子雨、長草、天與故事東訪帕帕特亞，遭毒打羞辱——烏阿被打頸（戰爭一詞tauua即『擊頸』之源），凡被踏頸、天被唾面，唯故事全身而退。普洛圖王埃洛怒而興師，史稱第一戰，掃滅帕帕特亞：逃亡者圖圖與伊拉合名圖圖伊拉，烏與普魯合名烏波盧，薩與瓦伊拉合名薩瓦伊——群島之名竟生於屠戮之餘燼。

sensitivity.note: Ethnogenesis legend naming the Samoan islands.

passages.text: Of the group generally it is said that a couple lived at Pulotu called Head of Day and Tail of Day; they had four children - Ua, or Rain; Fan, Long grass; Langi, Heavens; and Tala, or Story. The four went to visit Papatea. Pulotu is in the west, Papatea in the east. The Papateans heard of the arrival of the four brothers and determined to kill them: first Ua was struck on the neck, and hence the word taua, or beat the neck, as the word for war - this was the beginning of wars. Others stood on the neck of Fan, and hence the proverb in war: 'To-morrow we shall tread on the neck of Fan.' Others surrounded and spat on Langi, and hence the proverb for ill-usage or rudely passing before chiefs: 'It is spitting on Langi.' Tala was spared, and escaped uninjured.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 20 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 關於這一族群，一般說來，從前在普洛圖住著一對夫妻，名叫「日之首」與「日之尾」；他們有四個孩子——烏阿（即雨）、凡（即長草）、朗吉（即天）與塔拉（即故事）。這四人前去拜訪帕帕提亞。普洛圖在西，帕帕提亞在東。帕帕提亞人聽說四兄弟到來，便決意殺害他們：先擊打烏阿的脖子，因此「taua」這個詞，意即擊打脖子，便成了「戰爭」一詞——這就是戰爭的開端。另有人站在凡的脖子上，因此有句關於戰爭的諺語：「明日我們要踏在凡的脖子上。」又有人圍住朗吉，向牠吐唾沫，因此有句諺語，用於形容虐待或粗魯地從酋長面前走過：「這是在向朗吉吐唾沫。」塔拉則被放過，毫髮無傷地逃走了。

passages.text: Tala and Langi returned to Pulotu and told about their ill-usage. Then Elo, the king of Pulotu, was enraged and prepared to go and fight the Papateans; this was the first war in history. They went, they fought, they conquered, and made a clean sweep of Papatea - and hence the proverb: 'Like the rage of Elo.' All who fled to the bush were sought and killed; only those who fled to sea escaped: a man called Tutu and his wife Ila reached the island of Tutuila and named it so by the union of their names; U and Polu reached Upolu, hence the name of that island by uniting their names; Sa and Vaila reached Savaii, united their names also and, for the sake of euphony, made it Savaii instead of Savaila.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 20 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 塔拉與朗吉回到普洛圖，訴說他們所受的虐待。於是普洛圖的國王埃洛大怒，準備前去攻打帕帕提亞人；這是歷史上的第一場戰爭。他們去了，他們戰鬥，他們征服了，把帕帕提亞掃蕩一空——因此有句諺語：「如埃洛之怒。」所有逃入灌木叢的人都被搜出殺死；只有逃到海上的人倖免：一個名叫圖圖的男子與他的妻子伊拉抵達了圖圖伊拉島，並以二人名字的結合為該島命名；烏與波盧抵達了烏波盧，因此以二人名字結合而成該島之名；薩與瓦伊拉抵達了薩瓦伊，也結合了他們的名字，並為了音韻悅耳，把薩瓦伊拉改成了薩瓦伊。

title.en: The Two Brothers Who Weep January's Storms
title.zh: 一月風暴：哭泣的兩兄弟

region.en: Samoan sky (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩摩亞天空（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1884 (Turner)

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 18 (London 1884)

summary.en: January is Utu-va-mua, first yam-digging - or the two brothers Utuvamua and Utuvamuli, beaten in the war in heaven, who fled to earth bringing the January storms; or, escaping earth's wars to the skies, they look down on the hills - heaps of slain covered over with earth dug from the valleys - and their weeping and wailing and maddening exasperation occasion the storm and the hurricane. The Palolo worm swarms from the reefs three days a year, timed by the last quarter of the October moon.
summary.zh: 一月名『首掘薯』；又一說謂其源自烏圖瓦穆阿與烏圖瓦穆利兩兄弟：天界戰敗逃至人間，帶來一月風暴；或謂二兄避人間之戰而上天，俯瞰那些以谷土覆蓋的山丘——盡是陣亡者之墳——悲泣哀號、憤懣瘋狂，遂起風暴颶風。而每年有三天，帕洛洛蠕蟲自礁石湧出，其期由十月下弦月推定。

sensitivity.note: Calendar-month myth and palolo-worm season.

passages.text: This month, January, was called Utu va mua, first yam digging, and so named from their then digging wild yams before the cultivated ones were ripe. Others say that the origin of Utu va mua was in two brothers, the one called Utuvamua and the other Utuvamuli, who, when there was war in heaven, and their party beaten, fled to the earth and brought the January storms with them. A third account says that Utuvamua was the elder brother and Utuvamuli the younger, and that during a great war on earth they escaped to the heavens; that the hills are the heaps of slain covered over by earth dug up from the valleys, and that when the two brothers look down upon them their weeping and wailing and maddening exasperation occasion the storm and the hurricane. The month was also called Aitu tele, great god, from the principal worship of the month.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 18 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這個月，也就是一月，被稱為 Utu va mua，意為「首次掘薯」，此名源於他們當時在栽培薯尚未成熟之前先行挖掘野生薯。另有人說，Utu va mua 的起源在於兩兄弟，一個名叫 Utuvamua，另一個名叫 Utuvamuli；當天上發生戰爭、他們那一方戰敗時，二人逃到地上，並把一月的風暴一同帶來。第三種說法稱，Utuvamua 是兄，Utuvamuli 是弟，地上發生一場大戰時，他們逃到天上；那些山丘乃是陣亡者的屍堆，上面覆蓋著從山谷掘起的泥土；當兩兄弟俯視這些屍堆時，他們的哭泣、哀號與狂怒的激憤便造成了風暴與颶風。這個月也被稱為 Aitu tele，意為「大神」，因該月主要的崇拜對象而得名。

passages.text: July was called Palolo mua, the first of Palolo - the first month of the half year called the Palolo season. Palolo is that singular worm which swarms out from certain parts of the barrier reefs for three days in the course of a year, of which the natives are very fond, and all the more so from its rareness. If the last quarter of the moon is late in October, palolo is found the day before, the day of, and the day after, that quarter; if the last quarter of the moon is early in October, palolo does not come till the last quarter of the November moon. The middle day is the principal day for gathering these swarms of marine worms.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 18 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 七月被稱為 Palolo mua，意為「帕洛洛之始」——即被稱為帕洛洛季節的那半年的第一個月。帕洛洛是那種奇特的蠕蟲，一年之中有三天會從堡礁某些部分成群湧出；當地人非常喜愛牠，正因其罕見而更加珍視。若十月的最後四分之一月相來得晚，則帕洛洛會在该月相的前一天、當天及後一天出現；若十月的最後四分之一月相來得早，則帕洛洛要到十一月月相的最後四分之一時才會出現。中間那一天是採集這些海蟲群的主要日子。

title.en: Of the Supreme Being: Aiounun Kondi, Dweller in the Height
title.zh: 至高神艾奧蒙孔迪：高居者

region.en: Arawak country, Guiana coast
region.zh: 圭亞那濱海阿拉瓦克之地

period: Arawak oral tradition; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part I 'Legends of the Arawaks', 'Of the Supreme Being'

summary.en: There is a mighty One above, and like Him there is none: He sits on high, above the sky, where none can see His throne. He was there ere He made the world, with stars, and moon, and sun, and evermore He will be there. The Arawak tongue gives Him no proper name but titles more than one: 'Dweller in the Height' — Aiounun Kondi — since there He sits alone; the 'Great Our Father', though to Him for comfort none have gone; and 'Our Maker', Wamurreti-kwonci, of whom they oft speak but never call upon. Calm He sits above the sky; to Him for succour none can fly, He is so high above.
summary.zh: 至高者獨一無二；居於天上天，人莫見其座。造日月星辰與世界之先，彼已在；萬物運行之終，彼仍在。土語無其本名，惟多尊號：曰『高居者』艾奧蒙孔迪，以獨坐於高也；曰『大父』，然未嘗有求告者；曰『造者』瓦穆瑞提孔迪，常言之而不祈也。彼靜居高天，人莫能仰求——蓋其太高矣。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett in 1880 and versified by him; read critically — the hymnic form and titles are filtered through missionary interpretation, and im Thurn warned that such 'Supreme Being' passages may be colonial reflections.

passages.text: There is a mighty One above: and like Him there is none! He sits on high, above the sky, where none can see His throne. He was there ere He made the world, with stars, and moon, and sun; and evermore He will be there, when each its course has run.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Of the Supreme Being'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一位大能者居於上方：沒有誰能與祂相比！祂高坐於天之上，無人能見祂的寶座。在祂創造世界、星辰、月亮與太陽之前，祂已在那裡；當萬物各走完其路程之後，祂仍將永在那裡。

passages.text: Our tongue gives Him no proper name, but titles more than one: we call Him 'Dweller in the Height' — Aiounun Kondi — since there He sits alone; the 'Great Our Father', though to Him for comfort none have gone; and 'Our Maker' — Wamurreti-kwonci — of whom we oft speak, but never call upon. That Mighty Maker all things formed; 'tis He that made them move; and food for all things He bestows, which seems a proof of love. But calm He sits above the sky: to Him for succour none can fly — He is so high above!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Of the Supreme Being'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 我們的語言沒有給祂專名，卻有不止一個稱號：我們稱祂為「居於高處者」——Aiounun Kondi——因為祂獨自坐在那裡；稱祂為「偉大的我們的父」，雖然從沒有人到祂那裡尋求安慰；又稱祂為「我們的造物主」——Wamurreti-kwonci——我們常談論祂，卻從不呼求祂。那位大能的造物主造化了萬物；是祂使萬物運動；祂賜予萬物食物，這似乎是愛的明證。但祂安然坐在天之上：沒有人能飛到祂那裡求助——祂是如此高遠！

title.en: The Komaka Throne: Creation from the Silk-Cotton Tree
title.zh: 柯瑪卡座：木棉樹上之創造

region.en: Arawak country, Guiana coast
region.zh: 圭亞那濱海阿拉瓦克之地

period: Arawak oral tradition; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part I 'Legends of the Arawaks', 'Origin of Living Creatures'

summary.en: Old men told, beneath the sacred tree, how moon and sun, earth and sky, and wide-spread sea lay before the Mighty One. Still no life was in the land; nothing then was seen to move. Then His seat, the Komaka — the wondrous silk-cotton tree whose branches were mid the clouds, with earth and sea far below — He caused to grow. From that bright-green throne His hand scattered twigs and bark around: some in air, and some on land, some the sparkling waters found. Soon He saw with life abound water, air, and solid ground: shining fishes darted where the woody fragments fell; others sported through the air; beasts and reptiles moved on solid ground; and men and women stood upright, raised by their great Maker's hand. Wild fruits first were human food, and water man's sole drink; no bold hunters roamed the wood, none would take life away — beasts and birds would sport and play with young children day by day, until Wadili came, took the maidens for his wives, and taught hunting, fishing, and husbandry.
summary.zh: 老人們於神樹之下言：日月、天地、浩海初陳於至高者之前，而大地無生，萬物不動。乃令其座——神柯瑪卡木棉樹——生焉，枝在雲端，地海在下。自翠座之上，其手散枝皮於四方：入空者化鳥，入水者化魚，落地者化獸、化蟲、化男女——直立者，造物主之手所舉也。初民食野果，飲白水；無獵者，無殺生；鳥獸與孩童日日嬉戲。後瓦迪利至，娶其女，教以漁獵農耕之術。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880 in metrical form; paraphrased into prose and read critically.

passages.text: Here, beneath this sacred tree, old men told how moon and sun, earth and sky, and wide-spread sea lay before the Mighty One. Waves soft murmuring beat the strand, gentle breezes sighed above — still no life was in the land, no sweet birds sang songs of love; o'er the plain and through the grove nothing then was seen to move. Then His seat, the Komaka — the wondrous silk-cotton tree — He caused to grow: 'midst the clouds its branches were, earth and sea lay far below.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Origin of Living Creatures'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在這裡，在這棵聖樹之下，老人們講述月亮與太陽、大地與天空，以及廣闊的海洋，如何陳列在大能者面前。波浪輕聲低吟拍打著海岸，微風在上方嘆息——大地上仍無生命，沒有甜美的鳥兒唱著愛之歌；在平原上、樹林中，那時看不見任何移動之物。於是祂的座位，那神奇的吉貝樹 Komaka，祂使其生長：它的枝條在雲中，大地與海洋遠在下方。

passages.text: From that bright-green throne His hand scattered twigs and bark around: some in air, and some on land; some the sparkling waters found. Soon He saw with life abound water, air, and solid ground! Those which fell upon the stream found a pleasant shelter there — shining fishes dart and gleam where those woody fragments were; others sported through the air, bright with wings and feathers fair; moving on solid ground beasts and reptiles then were found, spreading thence to fill the land. Men and women upright stand, raised by their great Maker's hand.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Origin of Living Creatures'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從那翠綠的寶座上，祂的手向四周撒下細枝與樹皮：有些落在空中，有些落在地上；有些落入閃爍的水中。不久祂便看見水、空氣與堅實的大地都充滿了生命！那些落在溪流上的，在那裡找到了愉快的庇護所——閃亮的魚兒在那些木質碎片所在之處穿梭閃耀；其他的在空中嬉戲，長著明亮的翅膀與美麗的羽毛；在堅實的大地上，則出現了走動的野獸與爬蟲，從那裡蔓延開來，充滿大地。男人與女人直立而立，由他們偉大造物主的手所舉起。

passages.text: Wild fruits first were human food; water man's sole drink, they say. No bold hunters roamed the wood; none would then take life away — beasts and birds would sport and play with young children day by day. On this earth our sire then came, young and brave Wadili: he saw their maidens, felt love's flame, took them, fair, his wives to be, and taught the native arts you see — hunting, fishing, husbandry.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Origin of Living Creatures'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 野果最初是人类的食物；据说水是人唯一的饮品。那时没有大胆的猎人在林中游荡；当时无人会夺走生命——走兽与飞鸟日日与幼童嬉戏玩耍。我们的祖先随后降临此世，年轻而勇敢的瓦迪利：他见到她们的少女，感受到爱火，便娶她们为妻，美丽动人，并教导她们你所见的那些本土技艺——狩猎、捕鱼、耕作。

title.en: The Origin of the White Race: Wood Cast Upon the Sea
title.zh: 白人之起源：擲海之木

region.en: Arawak country, Guiana coast
region.zh: 圭亞那濱海阿拉瓦克之地

period: Arawak oral tradition; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part I 'Legends of the Arawaks', 'Origin of the White Race'

summary.en: Some addition has been made to that legend, grave and old, since our fathers surveyed steel-clad white men, strong and bold, who with blood-hounds, we are told, hunted men — and all for gold! 'Not from the Komaka tree sprang the whites,' our sages say: 'they, from wood cast on the sea, rose amidst wild ocean's spray, finding land on which to stay over the waters — far away.' 'If from wood our race has sprung, did it in these forests grow? Did it to green-heart belong, locust, or balata? Did its foliage ruddy glow with a mora's strength below? Ask no more, friend, you are wrong: those trees give us bark, gums, and timber strong — but the white man's stock, they say, good for nought, was cast away!' Smiles on every face appear; red men seated on the ground laugh to hear that satire old — a mild revenge which poor men found who escaped Spanish arcabuz and hound in the swamps around.
summary.zh: 自先祖見鋼甲白人以血犬獵人、專為掠金，古傳說遂增一篇。耆老言：『白人非自柯瑪卡樹出；乃擲海之木，起於怒濤之間，覓遠方之陸而居。』或問：『若吾族出自木，則此木生於此林乎？綠心木耶？洋槐耶？巴拉塔耶？』答曰：『毋多問，君誤矣。此諸樹日日賜我樹皮、樹膠、堅材；白人之材，無用而見棄者也！』紅人席地而笑——逃西班牙火銃與獵犬者之小復仇也。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880; a satire on the Spanish conquest embedded in the legend cycle, read critically.

passages.text: Some addition has been made to that legend, grave and old, since our fathers here surveyed steel-clad white men, strong and bold. They, with blood-hounds, we are told, hunted men — and all for gold! 'Not from the Komaka tree sprang the whites,' our sages say: 'they from wood cast on the sea rose amidst wild ocean's spray, finding land on which to stay over the waters — far away.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Origin of the White Race'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 自从我们的父辈在此见到身披钢铁的白人，强壮而大胆，这个古老而庄重的传说便增添了一些内容。据说他们带着猎犬猎捕人类——全为了黄金！我们的智者说：『白人并非源自科马卡树；他们是从被抛入海中的木头上，在狂野海洋的浪花中升起的，越过水面——在遥远之处——找到了可以停留的陆地。』
