Give us, I pray thee, the stopper of the water bottle that he may suck it and be refreshed.' 'Nay,' said the man fiercely. 'If ye want water ye should have brought it with you.' Then the children were silent, and paddled on once more. At last they came to a dreary place where no house was, and where food grew not. Then the man bade the children help him pull the canoe up on the beach, and they did so, and then ran to a pandanus tree which grew near and began sucking its fruit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man with the Open Throat' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 如今他們划著槳，太陽漸熱，孩子們也疲倦了。於是年長的孩子對祖父說：「我們口渴了。求你給我們一顆椰子，好讓我們喝。」那人說：「你為何不把椰子帶來呢？這裡沒有給你的。」孩子說：「那麼我們可以要一根甘蔗來吸嗎？」他的祖父問：「你的甘蔗在哪裡？你本該把它帶來的。」孩子又說：「祖父，我的弟弟非常口渴。求你給我們水瓶的塞子，讓他吸一吸，好得解渴。」那人兇狠地說：「不行。你們若要水，就該自己帶來。」於是孩子們沉默不語，又繼續划槳。最後他們來到一處荒涼之地，那裡沒有房屋，也不長食物。那人便吩咐孩子們幫他把獨木舟拖上海灘，他們照做了，隨後跑向附近長著的一棵露兜樹，開始吸食它的果實。

passages.text: The children wept bitterly, for they were much afraid to be alone in this strange place where no people were. But being hungry, they climbed into the pandanus tree, and sucked many of the fruit which they found. Now it came to pass that while they were thus doing, an old woman who was a witch dreamed that she saw two children in a lonely place sucking pandanus fruit. Therefore she arose and journeyed until she came to the place of which she had dreamed. There indeed she found them, but they knowing her to be a witch, feared to come down. Then said she to them, 'What do ye in the pandanus?' They said, 'Our grandfather brought us to this desolate land and left us here, saying that he would return in six days.' The witch hearing their tale, pitied them and said, 'Come down now to me, and let us see what may be done.' 'Nay,' said they, 'for if we do thou mayest kill us.' 'I will not harm you,' said the witch.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man with the Open Throat' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 孩子們痛哭起來，因為他們非常害怕獨自留在這陌生、無人煙的地方。但因飢餓，他們爬上露兜樹，吸食了許多找到的果實。事情就這樣發生了：正當他們如此做的時候，一個女巫老婦夢見自己在荒僻之地看見兩個孩子吸食露兜果。於是她就起身趕路，直到來到她夢中所見的地方。她果然在那裡找到了他們，但他們知道她是女巫，害怕下來。她便對他們說：「你們在露兜樹上做什麼？」他們說：「我們的祖父把我們帶到這荒涼之地，把我們留在這裡，說他六天後會回來。」女巫聽了他們的故事，憐憫他們，說：「現在下來到我這裡，讓我們看看能有什麼辦法。」他們說：「不行，因為我們若下來，你可能會殺了我們。」女巫說：「我不會傷害你們。」

passages.text: Now it came to pass on the sixth day, that the witch saw he was drawing nigh, and she bade the Sun burn him with its rays. And the Sun shone forth, and the old man was burned and thirsty. Then said the witch to the Rain, 'Rain upon this man.' And the Rain rained until the man was like to be drowned. Then the witch bade that the Sun should scorch him once more, and again the Rain that it should rain upon him, and then once more the Sun, that it should burn the man. Now he was close to the land, and he was very thirsty. Therefore he hasted to a little stream hard by, and stooped to drink. But the witch with her pearl shell had stopped the water from flowing, and only a few drops trickled. Therefore the man stooped low to drink what little was there, and at that moment the witch took away her pearl shell, and the water rushed mightily forward and down the man's throat, and choked him. So were the children delivered from their enemy who had wrought them much ill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man with the Open Throat' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了第六天，女巫見他漸漸接近，便吩咐太陽用光芒灼燒他。太陽照射出來，老人被灼燒而口渴。女巫便對雨說：「降雨在這人身上。」雨便下起來，直到那人幾乎要被淹死。女巫又吩咐太陽再灼燒他一次，又吩咐雨再降在他身上，然後再吩咐太陽灼燒那人。如今他已靠近陸地，非常口渴。於是他急忙趕到附近的一條小溪，彎腰喝水。但女巫用她的珍珠貝殼止住了水流，只有幾滴水珠滲出。因此那人彎低身子去喝那僅有的一點水，就在那一刻，女巫取走了她的珍珠貝殼，水便猛烈地向前奔湧，衝下那人的喉嚨，把他嗆死了。孩子們就這樣脫離了那加害他們甚多的仇敵。

title.en: Borevui and Her Three Brothers
title.zh: 波雷維伊與三兄弟

region.en: Mountain country, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞山地（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'Borevui and Her Three Brothers'

summary.en: On their mother's grave grew the red-leaved bush Borevui — their little sister, though they knew it not. She stepped down each day to cook for them, till the youngest caught her; when the brothers claimed her for a wife she told them she was their sister. Then a mountain man carried her off and killed each brother in turn as he came seeking — but Borevui saved each liver in a bowl of water, and at the last blew on the water until the three stood before her alive; her husband ate pig-food that night and was slain by the brothers he had cooked.
summary.zh: 母親墳上長出一株紅葉灌木——波雷維伊，實是化生的妹妹，兄長們卻不知。她日日下墳化身少女，為哥哥們備好飯食再化回灌木。最幼的弟弟藏於蔗堆後捉住她，兄長們爭相要以她為妻；她答：『我是你們的妹妹，願日日照料你們、為你們煮飯。』後來一個山人把她搶走成婚；三位哥哥先後尋妹而至，皆被妹夫殺死烹食。波雷維伊不哭不怨，只討得每人的肝，浸在椰殼水碗中。末了丈夫命她入山墾園，她攜重袋先行，回家吹拂那碗靜水——三兄弟漸漸成形，活生生站在她面前。她以熱飯款待兄弟，卻給丈夫備下豬食；他入門見豬食大怒欲毆，三兄弟聞聲而起，把這食人者剁碎燒屋。兄妹遂返故里，永世安泰。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: There was once a woman who had three sons but no daughters. After a time she died and was buried, and her sons mourned for her. And it came to pass that one day a little red-leaved plant sprung up on the woman's grave, and became a beautiful bush, called Borevui. The red leaves waved in the wind, and the lads saw that they were fair, but they knew not that it was their little sister who was there. One day they went hunting game, which was to be eaten at the death feast in honour of their mother. While they were all away Borevui stepped down from the grave and became a girl. Then she entered her brothers' house, and cooked some food for them. After she had done this, she ran back to the grave and became Borevui once more. Now the three lads were hungry when they came from their long day's hunting, and they found a big pot of food waiting for them. They turned to their old grandmother, who sat in the corner, and said, 'Grandmother, who cooked our food?' 'Who knows?' said the old woman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Borevui and Her Three Brothers' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個女人，生了三個兒子，卻沒有女兒。過了些時候，她死了，被埋葬了，她的兒子們為她哀悼。有一天，一株小紅葉植物在她墳上長了出來，長成一棵美麗的灌木，名叫博雷武伊。紅葉隨風搖曳，少年們看見它們很美，卻不知道那是他們的小妹妹在那裡。有一天，他們出去獵取野味，預備在為母親舉行的喪宴上吃。當他們全都外出時，博雷武伊從墳上走下來，變成了一個女孩。她走進哥哥們的屋子，為他們煮了些食物。做完之後，她又跑回墳上，重新變回博雷武伊。三個少年獵了一整天回來時餓了，發現一大鍋食物正等著他們。他們轉向坐在角落的老祖母，說：「祖母，是誰煮了我們的食物？」老婦人說：「誰知道呢？」

passages.text: When it was morning, the two elder brothers hid the youngest in a stack of sugar-cane, which they leaned against the wall. Then they left him, and it came to pass that the little sister came once more into the house to cook for her brothers. The youngest brother watched while she took a piece of taro and peeled it with a sharp pearl shell. Then he came quickly from his hiding-place, and laid hold of the girl. He saw how fair she was, and said, 'Aio, be my wife!' But the girl made answer, 'I cannot be thy wife, for I am thy sister.' Then the two brothers came home and saw the beautiful girl, and they said, 'She is to be my wife,' 'She is to be my wife.' But the girl told them that she was their sister, and would take care of them all and cook their food day by day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Borevui and Her Three Brothers' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了早晨，兩個哥哥把最小的弟弟藏在一堆甘蔗裡，那堆甘蔗靠在牆上。然後他們離開了他，事情就這樣發生了：小妹妹又一次進屋為哥哥們煮食。最小的弟弟看著她拿起一塊芋頭，用鋒利的珍珠貝殼削皮。於是他迅速從藏身之處出來，抓住了那女孩。他看見她多麼美麗，便說：「艾奧，做我的妻子吧！」但女孩回答說：「我不能做你的妻子，因為我是你的妹妹。」隨後兩個哥哥回到家，看見那美麗的女孩，便說：「她要做我的妻子。」「她要做我的妻子。」但女孩告訴他們，她是他們的妹妹，願意照顧他們所有人，天天為他們煮食。

passages.text: On the morrow the brothers went out hunting, as was their custom, and Borevui went to the spring to fill her coconut water bottles. Now as she was leaning over the spring, a man who was hiding there leapt out, picked her up in his arms, and carried her off to his home far in the mountains. After a time, when the brothers had waited in vain for Borevui to return, the eldest said that he would go and look for her. After searching for long, he found her at last, and was greeted by his sister and her husband. 'Go to the gardens,' said the man to Borevui, 'and bring food home and cook it, that our brother may eat.' The girl did as he bade her, and returned with some food, but, alas! she found that her brother had been killed by her husband, and that his flesh was to be eaten. But she did not cry out or reproach her husband.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Borevui and Her Three Brothers' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天，哥哥們照慣例出去打獵，博雷武伊則去泉邊裝滿她的椰子水瓶。正當她俯身向著泉水時，一個藏在那裡的男人跳了出來，把她抱在懷裡，帶回他遠在山中的家。過了些時候，哥哥們等博雷武伊回來卻白等了一場，長兄便說他要去找她。尋了許久，他終於找到了她，受到妹妹和她丈夫的迎接。那人對博雷武伊說：「到園子裡去，帶些食物回來煮，好讓我們的大舅子吃。」女孩照他的吩咐做了，帶著一些食物回來，可是，唉！她發現她的哥哥已被她的丈夫殺死，他的肉將要被吃。但她沒有哭喊，也沒有責備她的丈夫。

passages.text: The youngest brother, who was now at home alone with their grandmother, said, 'I must needs go to see why my brothers have not yet returned.' And he set out. But the same fate overtook him, and ere long his flesh was cooking over the fire. And Borevui could do nought but save the lad's liver, which she placed in the bowl of water where the others already lay. Then her husband bade her follow him to their mountain garden. There they toiled for long, and Borevui cut down a tree which was in the road, and helped her husband clear the ground for a great distance. At last he said, 'Go home now, when thou shalt have dug up some food, and cook it. I will follow thee.' Borevui obeyed and went home, carrying the heavy bag of food slung from her head. She cooked a great pot full, and then went to the bowl of water where lay the livers of her three brothers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Borevui and Her Three Brothers' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最小的弟弟這時獨自與祖母留在家中，說道：「我非得去看看哥哥們為何還沒回來不可。」於是便出發了。然而同樣的命運也降臨在他身上，不久他的肉便在火上烹煮。博雷武無計可施，只能保住這少年的肝，將它放入那盛水的碗中，其他幾個人的肝早已放在那裡。接著她的丈夫吩咐她隨他到他們山上的園子去。他們在那裡勞作了許久，博雷武砍倒了擋在路上的一棵樹，又幫丈夫清理了一大片地面。最後他說：「如今你挖些食物，煮熟了便回家去吧。我隨後就來。」博雷武遵命回家，把沉重的食物袋吊在頭上背著。她煮了滿滿一大鍋，然後走到那盛水的碗前，她三個兄弟的肝就放在那裡。

title.en: The Mud People and the House of Rei
title.zh: 泥屋與茅屋

region.en: Lake of Apogi, mountains, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞山區阿波吉湖（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Mud People'

summary.en: In the old days men dwelt in caves and holes, till two men agreed to build shelters on the face of the earth. One wove the long grass rei thickly over a frame of sticks; the other plastered mud over his. The mud-builder decried the rei — 'will not the sharp rei enter thine eye and blind thee?' — then besought the lake spirit Apogi for rain, which crumbled his own walls; and beaten upon the closed doorway he was answered with his own words, till the rain-builder's wife won shelter for the children. From that day mud is contemned and houses are built of rei.
summary.zh: 太古人穴居野處。有二人相約造屋：一個用長茅草『雷』密密編在木架上，滴水不漏；另一個只用泥漿糊在立木之上。泥屋主人先貶低茅屋：『茅草鋒利，怕不戳瞎你的眼？扎破你孩子的皮？』隨後他上阿波吉湖邊念咒求雨，大雨果然傾落——他的泥牆自己先塌了。一家人哭著奔向茅屋求收留，茅屋主人卻把他自己的話原樣擲回：『茅草鋒利，怕不戳瞎你的眼？』泥屋主人啞口無言；茅屋主人之妻心軟求情，才開門收留。雨過之後，泥屋主人羞愧難當，疾起仿建茅屋——自那日起泥屋為人所鄙，家家皆以茅草造屋，直到如今。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: In the old days men lived not in houses, but dwelt in caves and holes in the ground, for none knew how they might fashion a shelter which would keep out rain and sun. Now it came to pass that two men talking idly together agreed to attempt to build some shelter on the face of the earth where their families might dwell safe from sun and rain, and nevertheless live in the light of day and not in the dark earth as heretofore. They therefore arose and each went his way, neither did either see the face of other until the work was accomplished. Then came one and said to his fellow, 'Come, let us go now and I will show thee the house I have fashioned.' And they went both together until they came to where the man had built his house, and behold, it was a fair sight indeed. For the man had taken of the long grass which is called rei, and had woven it thickly upon a frame of sticks, so that no ray of sun nor drop of rain might pierce the roof or walls of his house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Mud People' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古時候人們不住在房屋裡，而是住在洞穴和地洞中，因為沒有人知道該如何造出一個能遮擋風雨和烈日的棲身之所。後來有兩個人閒談之間，相約要在地面上試著建造某種住所，好讓他們的家人安居其中，免受日曬雨淋，同時又能住在日光之下，而不像從前那樣住在黑暗的土裡。於是他們起身，各自分頭而去，彼此都不曾再見到對方的面，直到工程完成。然後其中一人來到同伴那裡，說道：「來吧，我們現在就去，我要把我造的屋子給你看。」兩人便一同前去，來到那人建造房屋的地方，看哪，那確實是悅目的景象。因為那人取了那叫做「雷伊」的長草，厚厚地編織在木架的框架上，使陽光與雨滴都無法穿透他房屋的屋頂或牆壁。

passages.text: But the other looking upon it saw that it was better than his own, and set about to decry it, that it might be worthless in the eyes of him who had built it. 'This then is thy shelter, brother,' quoth he. 'It were better for thee and thine to dwell therein than for me and mine. For I should fear greatly lest perchance the sharp rei should enter my eye, and so blind me. Moreover, it must needs be that it will prick thy skin and cause a rash to rise upon it. But come now,' he said, turning away, 'and I will show thee mine.' So they went together to see the other house. Now it was, in truth, but a sorry place, for its builder had taken handfuls and plastered it over the light sticks he had placed in the ground. And the man who had built his house of rei spake thus, saying, 'What wilt thou do, brother, when the rains come?' 'I fear no rain,' quoth the other proudly, and bade his family enter the mud house and dwell therein.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Mud People' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但另一人看著它，看出它比自己的更好，便著手貶損它，好讓它在建造者眼中變得一文不值。「那麼，兄弟，這就是你的住所了，」他說道。「你和你的家人住在裡面，總比我和我的家人住在裡面好。因為我會非常害怕，生怕那尖銳的雷伊草萬一刺進我的眼睛，把我弄瞎了。而且它必定會刺你的皮膚，使皮膚上長出疹子來。不過來吧，」他說著轉過身去，「我來把我的給你看。」於是兩人一同去看另一座房屋。那實在是個可憐的地方，因為它的建造者只取了幾把泥土，塗抹在他插在地上的細木棍上。那用雷伊草造屋的人便這樣說道：「兄弟，等雨來了，你要怎麼辦呢？」「我不怕雨，」那人傲然地說，並吩咐家人進入那泥屋，住在裡面。

passages.text: Not long had he to tarry, for the sun was yet high in the heaven when the rain clouds hid it from the eyes of men, and heavy was the rain which fell, and the man's heart was glad, for he knew that Apogi had done this. Now it had been but an idle vaunt of the man who dwelt in the house of mud that he feared no rain, for indeed his heart trembled within him as great drops fell and his walls began to crumble. Nevertheless he sat on and did not stir until his wife besought him to seek some place of shelter for their little ones, who were wailing at their mother's knees. Then he rose up, and taking his family with him he left the house, and it was now but a frame of sticks, for the mud lay upon the ground in a pool of water. And the children cried aloud as they followed after their father, who led them to the house which was built of rei.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Mud People' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他不必久等，因為太陽還高掛在天上時，雨雲便把它遮住，不讓世人看見，落下的雨極大，那人心裡歡喜，因為他知道這是阿波吉所為。那住在泥屋裡的人誇口說不怕雨，其實不過是空話，因為當大滴的雨水落下、他的牆壁開始崩塌時，他心裡著實發顫。然而他仍坐著不動，直到他的妻子懇求他為他們那些在母親膝前號哭的幼兒找個棲身之處。於是他站起身來，帶著家人離開那屋子，那時它只剩下一副木架，因為泥土已坍在地上，成了一窪水。孩子們大聲哭喊，跟在父親後面，父親把他們領到那座用雷伊草建造的屋子。

passages.text: Now it came to pass that the man who had built his house of rei looked forth and saw them as they drew nigh in the rain. And he hardened his heart, and closed the doorway of his house and waited to hear what the man who had trusted in mud would say. And he, having come, beat upon the closed doorway, and cried, 'Open to me, brother, and let us in, for the rain is great and my children weep without.' 'Nay, brother,' answered he from within the house. 'How may I dare to do such a thing? Will not the sharp rei enter thine eye and blind thee? Or perchance it will prick the skin of thy children and cause a rash to rise upon it.' Thus was the man met with his own words, and had nought wherewith to make answer. Sad was his plight and that of his wife and children as they turned away, and the wife of the man who had built the house of rei looking on them pitied them, and besought her husband to give them shelter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Mud People' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 後來，那用雷伊草造屋的人向外望去，看見他們在雨中走近。他硬起心來，關上屋門，等著聽那信賴泥土的人要說什麼。那人來到之後，拍打著緊閉的門，喊道：「兄弟，給我開門，讓我們進去，因為雨太大了，我的孩子們在外面哭呢。」「不行，兄弟，」他在屋裡回答。「我怎敢做這種事呢？那尖銳的雷伊草豈不是要刺進你的眼睛，把你弄瞎嗎？或許它還會刺你孩子們的皮膚，使皮膚上長出疹子來。」那人就這樣被自己的話堵住了，無言以對。他和妻兒轉身離去時，境況十分悲慘；那用雷伊草造屋之人的妻子看著他們，心生憐憫，便懇求丈夫給他們棲身之所。

title.en: Why the Wamirans Are Few
title.zh: 瓦米拉人少之由

region.en: Wamira and the rivers Magavara and Mai (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉與馬加瓦拉、邁河（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'Why Wamirans Are Few'

summary.en: An elder brother slew his younger in a game of spears at berries and hid him under the great pot Nau Oroto — the mother's own cut finger warned her, and the dripping blood told the rest. She drove the slayer west, and by the river Mai he broke a hollow bamboo out of which much people came forth: he who had taken one life repaid it by causing many persons to live. The Dimadima feasted them, and the west is many — but had the lad turned east when he set forth, we of Wamira should have been many and they few.
summary.zh: 兄弟倆以木矛投漿果為戲，弟弟百發百中，哥哥一無所中，惱羞成怒，一矛殺弟，把屍體藏在屋中大陶罐『瑙奧羅托』之下。母親在園中削芋時無故割傷手指，心生疑懼，急忙歸家——屋中滴答之聲引她揭開陶罐，見幼子屍身。母親驅逐長子；少年向西而逃，過馬加瓦拉河至邁河附近。時值迪馬迪馬人備宴，少年吩咐：『把食物全煮了，一半藏進叢林，一半設席。我去河裡沐浴，等我回來。』他在河灘尋得一截空心竹，折之——走出許許多多的人來！他曾取一命，如今以此還以眾命。迪馬迪馬人藏食自食，客人則飽餐大宴。故西方人丁興旺——倘若少年當日向東而去，瓦米拉人多、他們人少，也未可知。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: In the old days there lived in a certain village a woman who had two sons, and she left them behind while she went to the garden for food to cook that they might eat. Now the garden was far away from the village, for the reason that in the village pigs were many, and would be ever eating the taro if it were near. So the woman must needs be long away. The children desiring to play, made for themselves spears of wood, and picked some berries at which they aimed many times. Now it befell that the elder as he speared at no time speared the berries, whereas the younger each time pierced the mark. Then was the elder wroth with his brother, and turned upon him and slew him with his spear, and laid his body on a shelf in the house and covered it with Nau Oroto, the great earthenware pot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Why Wamirans Are Few' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古時候，某個村子裡住著一個婦人，她有兩個兒子，她留下他們，自己到園子裡去取食物回來煮給他們吃。那園子離村子很遠，因為村裡豬很多，若園子近了，豬便會不停地吃芋頭。所以那婦人不得不離家很久。孩子們想玩耍，便為自己做了木矛，又採了些漿果，朝著它投擲了許多次。後來事情是這樣：哥哥投矛時一次也沒刺中漿果，而弟弟卻每次都刺中目標。於是哥哥對弟弟發怒，轉身用矛將他殺死，把他的屍體放在屋裡的架子上，用那大陶罐「瑙·奧羅托」蓋住。

passages.text: Then fearing to be in the house with the dead, he went down to the sea-shore. The mother of the children at the garden dug up the taro she wanted, and then sat in the shade to make it ready to take home. She took each piece and with a sharp pearl shell scraped away the little roots and the earth which was upon them. Now as she thus scraped the pearl shell slipped and cut her finger, and she was much afraid, for she said in her heart, 'What hath befallen the lads that my blood is flowing?' And she made haste home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Why Wamirans Are Few' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他因害怕與死人同處一屋，便下到海邊去了。孩子們的母親在園中挖出她所要的芋頭，然後坐在陰涼處把它整理好，預備帶回家去。她拿起每一塊，用一枚鋒利的珍珠貝殼刮去上面的小根和泥土。正當她這樣刮著的時候，珍珠貝殼滑了一下，割破了她的手指，她大為驚恐，因為她心裡說：『我的血竟流了出來，莫非孩子們遭了什麼事？』於是她急忙趕回家去。

passages.text: When she entered the house she called to the children, and the elder came at her call from the beach where he was. Then said she to him, 'Where is now thy brother, child?' 'Who knoweth?' said he. 'I have not seen him.' The mother believing him to be playing alone, went in and peeled taro and made it ready for the evening meal. Now as she thus did the dead child's blood dripped upon the mat near to which she sat. And hearing the sound of the drops, she looked and saw it and rose up, saying, 'Whose blood is this?' And she lifted Nau Oroto and found the dead body of her little son. Then did grief make her heart hot, and she called for the elder child that he might tell her in what manner his brother had perished. 'We were spearing berries, mother,' said the lad, 'and my brother pierced many, whereas I had pierced none. Therefore I slew him with my spear.' At this word the woman arose and drove the lad from her, and he departed from the village and fled far away to the west.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Why Wamirans Are Few' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她進了屋子便呼喚孩子們，那大的聽見呼喚，就從他所在的海灘回來。她對他說：『孩子，你弟弟如今在哪裡？』他說：『誰知道呢？我沒有看見他。』母親以為他獨自玩耍去了，便進去剝芋頭，預備晚飯。正當她這樣做的時候，那死去的孩子的血滴在她所坐的席子旁邊。她聽見血滴的聲音，一看見了，就站起身來，說：『這是誰的血？』她掀起 Nau Oroto，發現了她小兒子的屍體。於是悲痛使她心中如焚，她便喚那大的孩子來，要他告訴她弟弟是怎樣死的。那少年說：『母親，我們在刺漿果，我弟弟刺中了許多，我卻一個也沒刺中。因此我用矛殺了他。』聽了這話，那婦人起來，把那少年趕了出去，他便離開村子，遠遠逃往西方去了。

passages.text: The lad went towards them and watched what they did. Then said he, 'Cook all the food which I see here. And when it is cooked hide some of it in the bush, and set forth the rest that men may eat. I go now to bathe at the river; tarry ye my coming.' The men of Dimadima did even as he had said, and waited for him to come to them again. Now the lad when he came to the river again searched until he found a hollow piece of bamboo which lay there. This he brake, and forthwith much people came forth and stood before him. Thus did he, who had taken one life, repay it by causing many persons to live. Then he bade them follow him to where the people of Dimadima awaited him, and they did so and did eat of the food which had been prepared. Yet though there was much food, they were so many in number that some after they had eaten were still hungry. But as for the men of Dimadima, they ate of the food which they had hidden in the bush, as the lad had bidden them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Why Wamirans Are Few' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那少年向他們走去，觀看他們所做的一切。然後他說：『把我所看見的這些食物全都煮了。煮好之後，藏一些在叢林裡，其餘的擺出來給人吃。我現在要到河裡去洗澡；你們等我回來。』Dimadima 的人就照他所說的做了，等他再回到他們那裡。那少年回到河邊時，四處搜尋，直到找到一截躺在那裡的空竹。他把竹子劈開，立刻有許多人出來，站在他面前。他曾經取去一條性命，如今便藉著使許多人得生來償還。然後他吩咐他們跟他到 Dimadima 的人等候他的地方去，他們就照做了，吃了所預備的食物。然而食物雖多，他們人數卻那麼眾多，有些人吃過之後仍然飢餓。至於 Dimadima 的人，他們照那少年所吩咐的，吃了藏在叢林裡的食物。

title.en: Waidudu, the Man Without Hands and Feet
title.zh: 無手無腳之人懷杜杜

region.en: Wamira district, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉地區（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Man Without Hands and Feet'

summary.en: Waidudu had neither hands nor feet, and his brothers fed him — until the leaf-decked spearsman Aidagagiogio came crying through the village and lent him hands and feet to climb for coconuts. At his brothers' word Waidudu carried a conch up the palm, and when Aidagagiogio stood below handless and footless, the blast brought the brothers who slew and burned him — and the hands and feet stayed with Waidudu, so that he was like other men.
summary.zh: 懷杜杜生來無手無腳，賴兩位哥哥供養。一日，頭戴樹葉、手持長矛的怪物艾達加焦焦闖進村中喝道：『人們都躲進屋裡，不然我用矛刺你們！』他卻命懷杜杜爬樹摘椰——『我借你手腳，快去。』懷杜杜被迫上樹摘果；怪物吸盡椰汁、吃完椰肉，把殼丟在門口而去。哥哥們教他下次攜法螺上樹。翌日怪物又來借手腳；懷杜杜上到樹頂便猛吹法螺。怪物失了手腳，逃不能逃、戰不能戰，只有連聲催促；兄弟聞螺而至，殺之焚之。懷杜杜下樹——手腳既歸他，便與常人無異了。兄弟三人歡喜不已。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: In a certain village lived a man whose name was Waidudu, and he had neither hands nor feet. But that mattered the less in that he had two brothers who brought him food each day, and cared for him in many other ways. Now it came to pass that one day they went forth to the gardens and left Waidudu alone in the village. And as he sat in the house alone he heard a terrible voice, which said, 'O ye sons of men, stay now in your houses, lest I spear you!' Waidudu looked forth, and saw the great and terrible Aidagagiogio, who was decked with leaves and who carried many spears. At this sight Waidudu's heart failed him, and he cried, 'I pray thee, spear me not!' Then said Aidagagiogio, 'Come out then and climb a coco palm that I may have dalo, young ones, to drink.' 'Alas, my lord,' said Waidudu, 'how may I do this thing, seeing I have neither hands nor feet?' 'Let not your heart get hot,' answered Aidagagiogio, 'but come out and I will give thee my hands and feet, and so shalt thou climb.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man Without Hands and Feet' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某村住著一個人，名叫 Waidudu，他既沒有手也沒有腳。但這倒無關緊要，因為他有兩個兄弟，每天給他送食物，又在許多別的事上照料他。有一天，他們到園子裡去了，把 Waidudu 獨自留在村中。他獨自坐在屋裡的時候，聽見一個可怕的聲音說：『你們這些人的子孫啊，如今都留在你們屋裡，免得我用矛刺你們！』Waidudu 向外張望，看見那又高大又可怕的 Aidagagiogio，他身披樹葉，帶著許多矛。Waidudu 一見這景象，心就慌了，喊道：『我求你，不要刺我！』Aidagagiogio 說：『那麼出來，爬上一棵椰子樹，好讓我有嫩椰子可喝。』Waidudu 說：『唉，我的主啊，我既沒有手也沒有腳，怎能做這事呢？』Aidagagiogio 回答說：『不要心裡發熱，出來吧，我把我的手腳給你，這樣你就能爬上去了。』

passages.text: Waidudu feared to disobey, and came forth trembling, and put on the hands and feet of Aidagagiogio which he gave him, and began to climb the coco palm. Then was he much afraid, for he had never tried to climb before, and he would have fain come down without going higher, but Aidagagiogio stood beneath with spears many and sharp, and Waidudu was forced to mount to the very top. There he picked many coconuts and threw them down to the ground, and came down himself. Then Aidagagiogio took back his hands and feet and set about taking the husk from the coconuts. The dalo he cracked, and clasping one in his hands held it high above his head and let the juice flow down his throat until the nut was empty, nor did he close his lips until he had drunk all the dalo which lay there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man Without Hands and Feet' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: Waidudu 害怕違抗，便顫抖著出來，穿上 Aidagagiogio 給他的手腳，開始爬那棵椰子樹。這時他大為害怕，因為他從未試過爬樹，他寧願不再往上爬就下來，可是 Aidagagiogio 帶著許多鋒利的矛站在下面，Waidudu 只得爬到最頂上。他在那裡摘了許多椰子，扔到地上，然後自己下來。Aidagagiogio 便收回他的手腳，動手剝去椰子的外殼。他把椰子砸開，雙手捧起一個，高高舉過頭頂，讓汁液流下喉嚨，直到椰子空了為止；他沒有合上嘴唇，直到把擺在那裡的所有椰子都喝光。

passages.text: Then he scraped the flesh of the nuts and ate until his hunger was stayed, and he flung the husks and shells of the coconuts in the doorway of Waidudu's house and departed. At even the brothers came home, and Waidudu told them what had befallen him. They took counsel together, and then said to Waidudu, 'If he comes again go up the tree as he bids thee, but take with thee a conch shell, and when thou art at the top of the tree blow upon it loudly, and we will come and slay this Aidagagiogio. He will not be able to harm thee, for thou wilt be in the tree and he will have no hands or feet wherewith to climb.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man Without Hands and Feet' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然後他刮下椰肉來吃，直到止住了飢餓，又把椰子的外殼和殼斗扔在 Waidudu 家的門口，便離去了。到了傍晚，兄弟們回到家裡，Waidudu 就把所遭遇的事告訴了他們。他們一同商議，然後對 Waidudu 說：『他若再來，你就照他所吩咐的爬上樹去，但要帶一隻海螺，等你到了樹頂，就大聲吹響它，我們便來殺掉這個 Aidagagiogio。他害不了你，因為你在樹上，而他沒有手腳可以爬上來。』

passages.text: So Waidudu did as his brothers had bidden him. On the morrow Aidagagiogio came even as he had done the day before, and called upon Waidudu to pick him dalo that he might drink. And he gave him his hands and feet wherewith to climb. When Waidudu reached the top of the tree he sat there and waited. And Aidagagiogio being very impatient, cried out, 'Why tarriest thou? Pick my dalo and throw them down, for I am thirsty.' 'Nay,' answered Waidudu, 'but I will cut them off, and throw them to thee.' But this he did not, for he blew loudly upon the conch shell he had brought with him, and waited for his brothers to come as they had promised. Aidagagiogio heard the voice of the conch shell and was much afraid, for he had neither feet wherewith to escape, nor hands wherewith to fight his enemies, and he called many times to Waidudu to come down and to give him his hands and feet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man Without Hands and Feet' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是瓦伊杜杜照著兄長們的吩咐去做了。翌日，艾達加吉奧吉奧一如前日那般前來，呼喚瓦伊杜杜為他採芋頭，好讓他飲用。他便把自己的雙手雙腳交給他，供他攀爬之用。瓦伊杜杜爬到樹頂後，便坐在那裡等候。艾達加吉奧吉奧極不耐煩，喊道：「你為何遲延？採我的芋頭扔下來，因為我渴了。」「不，」瓦伊杜杜回答說，「我要把它們砍下來，扔給你。」但他並沒有這麼做，而是大聲吹響他隨身帶來的海螺，等候兄長們如約前來。艾達加吉奧吉奧聽見海螺的聲音，大為恐懼，因為他既無雙腳可以逃遁，也無雙手可以與敵人搏鬥，於是他屢次呼喚瓦伊杜杜下來，把他的雙手雙腳還給他。

title.en: Gelaruru: The Boy Who Sailed North
title.zh: 飛魚卵：北航的男孩

region.en: Open sea north of Wamira (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉以北外海（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'Gelaruru'

summary.en: The unloved wife bore a son and waited for the day he would bring her gelaruru, the flying-fish spawn her husband kept for the other. The boy found a canoe, forgot his bailing-scoop, and steered not east or west but far north where no land is; he heaped the canoe with gelaruru till the east wind Kariwabu rose, and casting out his catch he sank with it. Lagina, the gentle sea breeze, pitied his searching mother and carried her canoe to his body — and the husband rushed down with spears crying 'Thou hast sent my son to his death!' That night all slept but her; she climbed a chestnut tree ere the first bird cried and cast herself down, and her heart was glad, for at the gate of the underworld her child tarried to greet her on the long path to loloa.
summary.zh: 失寵的妻子生下一子，日日盼著兒子長大替她撈取飛魚卵——丈夫從不把這美味留給她。男孩尋得一舟，忘了帶舀水的勺，也不朝東西兩岸，卻徑直向北——無陸之海劃去。他撈得滿船飛魚卵；東風卡里瓦布驟起，浪涌舟滿，他找不到水勺，只得把滿船魚卵倒回海中，舟輕而浪急，終究傾覆。他力竭而沉。傍晚家人遍尋不獲；母親知兒心事，次晨駕舟疾尋，正午尋得空舟，正欲絕望，和風拉吉娜憐她，送舟至兒子遺體之處。她抱屍吻面而歸；丈夫持矛奔下沙灘喊『是你害死了我兒子！』幸其父把她護送回家。當夜她獨坐至曉，趁第一聲鳥鳴之前爬上栗樹，一躍而下。她的心是歡喜的——因為在冥府之門，她的孩子正等著她，要陪她走上通往 loloa 的漫漫長路。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage. Contains a suicide narrative treated as mourning reunion in the source.

passages.text: There was once a man who had two wives, and one was very dear to him, but the other he loved not. So it came to pass that when he brought home gelaruru, which is the spawn of the flying fish, he fed with it the wife whom he loved, and laid by none for the other who had not taken his heart. When therefore she came home from the gardens and found that her portion of gelaruru had not been placed for her she became very angry, and her heart grew hot within her. And when upon another day her husband treated her so again, she fell upon the wife whom he loved, and would have slain her had not the man come between and parted them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Gelaruru' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個人娶了兩個妻子，其中一個他極為珍愛，另一個他卻不愛。於是事情便這樣發生：當他帶回蓋拉魯魯——也就是飛魚的魚卵——時，他便以此餵養他所愛的妻子，一點也不為那未得他心的另一個留下。因此，當她從園圃回家，發現自己那份蓋拉魯魯並未為她留好時，她大為憤怒，心中怒火中燒。又一日，她的丈夫再次如此待她，她便撲向那他所愛的妻子，若不是那男人從中攔阻、將她們分開，她早已將她殺死。

passages.text: Now it fell upon a day that the child sat alone in the house, and as he sat he bethought him of the gelaruru of which his mother had spoken. And he arose, and sought for a canoe, that he might go in search of some to make glad her heart. When therefore he had found one he set forth, taking with him a paddle, but forgetting a niutepo wherewith to bail out the water if the waves should grow big. Not to the east or the west did he steer, but far away to the north, where no land is. And as he paddled he gazed over the water seeking for gelaruru, and he found much and heaped it upon the canoe. Then he would have made for home, but Kariwabu, the strong east wind, blew upon the water, and caused great waves to beat against the canoe. The child looked at his feet for a niutepo that he might bail out the water, but found none. Then he cast the gelaruru into the sea; yet though the canoe was thus lightened, the waves filled it, and it sank.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Gelaruru' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 後來有一天，那孩子獨自坐在屋中，坐著坐著，他想起了母親所說過的蓋拉魯魯。於是他起身，尋覓一隻獨木舟，好讓他出海尋找一些來使她心中歡喜。他找到一隻之後便出發了，隨身帶了一支槳，卻忘了帶一只舀水用的尼烏特波，以備波浪變大時舀水。他既不向東也不向西，而是駛向遙遠的北方，那裡沒有陸地。他一邊划槳，一邊眺望水面尋找蓋拉魯魯，他找到了許多，堆在獨木舟上。隨後他本想返航回家，但強勁的東風卡里瓦布吹拂水面，掀起巨浪拍打獨木舟。孩子低頭看自己的腳邊，想找一只尼烏特波來舀水，卻找不到。於是他把蓋拉魯魯拋入海中；然而儘管獨木舟因此減輕了重量，波浪仍灌滿了它，它便沉沒了。

passages.text: In the evening the man and his two wives came home from the gardens and called to the child, but he gave no answer. Then with fear in their hearts they searched in many places, but found him not, and his mother sat upon the ground and wept till morning. Then, for she knew what was in the child's mind, she took a canoe and paddled swiftly over the sea in search of her son. Long was the search, and at noon she found the canoe in which the lad had started. She wept much at the sight, and forbore to paddle. Then Lagina, the gentle sea breeze, pitying her, blew on her canoe and carried her to where her son's body lay upon the waters. The woman raised it and kissed the face of her dead son. Then she lifted him into the canoe and covered him with her skirt, and paddled until she reached the shore. Her husband was told what she was bringing, and he rushed down to the beach with his spears that he might kill her. 'Thou hast sent my son to his death!' he cried.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Gelaruru' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傍晚，那男人和他的兩個妻子從園圃回家，呼喚那孩子，他卻不應。於是他們心中恐懼，在許多地方尋找，卻找不到他，他的母親坐在地上哭泣，直到天明。後來，因為她知道孩子心中所想，便乘上一隻獨木舟，迅速划過海面尋找她的兒子。尋覓良久，正午時分她找到了那少年出發時所乘的獨木舟。她見此情景痛哭不已，不忍再划槳。這時，溫柔的海風拉吉娜憐憫她，吹拂她的獨木舟，將她帶到她兒子屍身漂浮的水面。那婦人將他抱起，親吻她死去兒子的臉龐。然後她把他抬進獨木舟，用自己的裙子蓋住他，一路划槳直到抵達岸邊。她的丈夫得知她帶回什麼，便拿著長矛衝下海灘，想要殺她。「你害死了我的兒子！」他喊道。

passages.text: And that night all slept but the woman whose child was dead. In the early morning, ere the first bird cried to its mate, she arose and went silently out of the house. Under a chestnut tree she halted, and then climbed high into it. For a moment she tarried, and then cast herself down and her spirit fled from her. Then in her father's house great was the mourning and loud were the cries that arose as she was laid in the earth, which had but on the day before swallowed up her son. But the woman's heart was glad, for at the gate of the under world her child tarried for her to greet her as she travelled the long and weary path that leadeth to loloa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Gelaruru' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那一夜，人人都睡了，唯有那孩子已死的婦人未眠。清晨，在第一隻鳥呼喚伴侶之前，她便起身，悄悄走出屋外。她在一棵栗樹下停住，然後高高爬上樹去。她停留了片刻，隨即縱身躍下，她的魂魄便離她而去。於是在她父親的家中，哀悼之聲大作，當她被安葬入土時，哭喊之聲響亮而起——那土地前一日才剛剛吞沒了她的兒子。但那婦人的心卻是歡喜的，因為在陰間的門口，她的孩子正等候著迎接她，迎接她走完那通往洛洛亞的漫長而疲憊的路途。

title.en: The Three Sisters and the Snake by the Path
title.zh: 三姐妹與路旁之蛇

region.en: River path, Wamira district (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉河畔小徑（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Three Sisters'

summary.en: Three sisters walked single file to the river, and by the path lay a snake that begged each to chew a little food for him. The two elder refused — 'thou art only a snake' — but the youngest sat down and fed him. He gave her the word: 'When thou hearest a noise in the heavens, fish. But at the second noise climb the hill.' Thunder came; she fished her basket full, climbed at the second peal, and watched the flood sweep great trees down — and when she came home past the snake, her sisters had been swept out to sea. 'If they had fed me when I asked food of them they would be now not dead but living.'
summary.zh: 三姐妹魚貫而行去河邊捕魚，路旁臥著一條蛇，向每一個討一口嚼好的食物。大姐二姐都說『你只是條蛇』，拒而不予；最幼的妹妹卻坐下一口口喂他。蛇吃完指點她：『天上響第一聲時你去捕魚；響第二聲時立刻上山。』雷聲果然響起；妹妹筐中滿魚；第二聲雷動，她奔上山頂，眼睜睜看洪水把大樹沖走。歸途再過蛇旁，蛇問她的同伴哪裡去了——『唉，她們怕是被暴漲的河水捲到海裡去了。』蛇說：『若她們當日肯喂我，如今便不至於死。』妹妹把筐中大魚用綠葉包好奉蛇；蛇銜包而歸林中。（此蛇乃 bariawa 之屬，能作人言；卡瓦基奧的蛇會說兩次話；還有把火種賜予人類的杜博蛇——那些故事改日再講。）

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage.

passages.text: In a certain village there lived three sisters, and it fell on a day that they went a fishing. Now as they went they must needs walk along a narrow path until they reached the river, therefore they went in single file. By and by, the eldest, who walked first, saw a snake lying by the path. He said to her, 'I am an hungered. Wilt thou chew a little of the food in thy hand, and give it to me!' 'That will I never do,' quoth the girl. 'Thou art only a snake. My food is not for thee.' And she went her way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Three Sisters' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某個村子裡住著三姊妹，有一天她們去捕魚。她們前去時，必須沿著一條狹窄的小路走到河邊，因此她們排成一列而行。不久，走在最前頭的大姊看見一條蛇躺在路旁。牠對她說：「我餓了。你可願意嚼一點你手中的食物，給我吃嗎！」「我絕不會那麼做，」那女孩說。「你不過是一條蛇。我的食物不是給你的。」說罷她便逕自走了。

passages.text: Soon came by the second sister, and the snake seeing her, said, 'Wilt thou chew a little food for me? I am an hungered.' 'Nay, verily,' said the second sister. 'Thou art but a snake. Let me pass.' And she also went her way. Last of all came the third sister. The snake asked once more, 'Wilt thou chew some food for me because I am an hungered?' 'Yea, I will chew some for thee,' said she at once, and sat down beside the snake, fearing nought. Then she chewed the taro she held, and made it soft and fed him with it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Three Sisters' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久，二姐走了過來，蛇見了她，便說：「你可願意為我嚼一點食物？我餓了。」「不，真的，」二姐說，「你不過是條蛇罷了。讓我過去吧。」她也自顧自地走了。最後來的是三妹。蛇又問了一次：「你可願意為我嚼些食物，因為我餓了？」「好，我願意為你嚼一些，」她立刻說道，隨即毫無畏懼地在蛇身旁坐下。於是她嚼了手中所持的芋頭，把它弄軟，餵給他吃。

passages.text: After a space she said, 'Hast thou had enough?' 'It is enough,' he made answer. 'I am no longer hungry. Whither goest thou?' he asked. 'I go to the river to fish.' 'Then will I tell thee somewhat,' quoth he. 'When thou hearest a noise in the heavens, fish. But at the second noise climb the hill.' Then she bade him farewell and left him, wondering what his words might mean. Now when she reached the river she saw nought of her sisters, for they had not tarried for her. Then she heard the voice of thunder, of which the snake had spoken. She began therefore to fish, and soon the basket slung at her side was full. Then came the second peal, of which she had been warned. She fled up the side of the mountain, and watched while much rain fell and great trees were swept down by the flood, but she stirred not until the storm was over.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Three Sisters' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 過了一會兒，她說：「你吃飽了嗎？」「夠了，」他答道，「我不再餓了。你要往哪裡去？」他問。「我要去河邊捕魚。」「那麼我要告訴你一些事，」他說，「當你聽見天上傳來聲響時，就去捕魚。但到了第二聲響時，就爬上山去。」於是她向他道別，離開了他，心裡納悶他的話究竟是什麼意思。當她來到河邊時，卻不見她姊妹們的蹤影，因為她們並沒有等她。接著她聽見了雷聲，正是蛇所說的那個聲音。於是她便開始捕魚，不久，掛在她身側的籃子就裝滿了。隨後第二聲雷響來了，正是她曾被警告的那個。她逃上山坡，觀望著大雨傾盆而下，巨木被洪水沖走，但她一動也不動，直到暴風雨過去。

passages.text: Then she came down once more, and set out for home. On the path lay the snake, and he raised his head when he saw her coming. 'Well,' he said, 'where are thy companions?' 'Alas! where are they?' she made answer. 'They must have been swept out to sea when the river rose in flood.' 'No doubt,' quoth the snake. 'Yet if they had fed me when I asked food of them they would be now not dead but living.' Then the girl took from her basket fish which were large, and wrapped them in a green leaf and gave them to the snake. And he held the little bundle in his mouth, and crept away to his home in the bush. This then is the tale thou askedst of me, and if it seem folly for that snakes do not now hold converse with men, know that this snake of which I have told thee was bariawa, and spake even as a man. Moreover there is the snake of Kawakio, which spake twice, and Dubo, the snake which gave fire to the sons of men, but of them will I tell on another day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Three Sisters' (1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然後她又下山來，動身回家。蛇躺在路上，見她走來便抬起頭。「那麼，」他說，「你的同伴們在哪裡？」「唉！她們在哪裡呢？」她答道，「河水氾濫時，她們必定被沖到海裡去了。」「想必如此，」蛇說，「然而，倘若她們在我向她們討食時餵了我，她們如今就不會死，而是活著了。」於是女孩從籃中取出大魚，用綠葉裹好，交給蛇。他用嘴啣住那小包裹，爬回他在叢林中的家去了。這就是你向我問起的故事；若它顯得荒唐，只因如今蛇不與人交談，那麼你當知道，我所說的這條蛇乃是巴里亞瓦，說起話來就像人一樣。此外還有卡瓦基奧的蛇，它說了兩次話；以及杜波，那條把火賜給人類子孫的蛇；但這些我改日再講。

title.en: Pashang Disowns the Slayer of Ighriras
title.zh: 帕尚格否認弑弟者阿弗拉西亞卜

region.en: Turan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 圖蘭（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Garshasp sec. 1

summary.en: Garshasp, son of Zav, sits on the throne with majesty and Grace; when he too dies the throne of king of kings is void. Pashang, wild with grief for Ighriras, refuses month after month to greet Afrasiyab: whatever prince were on the throne, a friend like Ighriras would profit him, but thou art one to shed a brother's blood; thou shalt not look upon my face again. Only when Garshasp departs does the old king throw the stone: cross the Jihun and tarry not until yon throne be filled.
summary.zh: 扎夫之子加爾沙斯普以威嚴與天恩坐上王座；他死後「萬王之王之座空虛」。帕尚格因痛失伊格里拉斯，月復一月拒絕接見阿弗拉西亞卜：「無論何人登基，如伊格里拉斯之友皆是良助；你卻弑弟！休再見我。」直到加爾沙斯普去世，老王才擲下命令：「渡烏滸水，不得王座不止。」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Zav had a puissant son by name Garshasp who sat upon the throne and donned the crown; he ruled the world with majesty and Grace. But tidings reached the Turkmans: Zav hath gone and left an empty throne. Afrasiyab sent up the war-cry, launched his ships and made for Khar of Rai, but no one brought to him a greeting from Pashang, whose head was filled with hate, his heart with strife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Garshasp sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 扎夫有一個強盛的兒子，名叫加爾沙斯普，他登上王座，戴上了王冠；他以威嚴與神恩統治世界。但消息傳到了突厥人那裡：扎夫已經離去，留下空虛的王座。阿夫拉西亞布發出戰吼，調動船隻，向拉伊的哈爾進發，卻無人為他帶來帕尚的問候，帕尚滿腦子是仇恨，滿心是爭鬥。

passages.text: All wild with grief for Ighriras, of throne and crown he recked not, and would never look upon Afrasiyab; albeit messengers were sent to him month after month, he denied himself and said: whatever prince were on the throne, a friend like Ighriras would profit him, but thou art one to shed a brother's blood and flee before the nursling of a fowl. Thou shalt not look upon my face again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Garshasp sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他因伊格里拉斯之死而悲痛欲狂，全不顧王座與王冠，也絕不願見阿夫拉西亞布；儘管月復一月都有使者被派往他處，他仍閉門謝客，說道：無論哪位君王登上王座，像伊格里拉斯這樣的朋友都會對他有益，但你這人卻會流兄弟之血，在一隻禽鳥的雛兒面前逃竄。你再也別想見到我的面容。

passages.text: Thus matters fared awhile; at length the tree of bale bore colocynth. 'Twas in the year wherein Garshasp the son of Zav departed that evil showed itself, for tidings reached all ears: the throne of king of kings is void. There came a message to Afrasiyab, a stone flung by Pashang: cross the Jihun and tarry not until yon throne be filled. Between Jihun and plain of Sipanjab Afrasiyab arrayed his armaments, and thou hadst said: earth is a turning sky where Indian swords are shedding souls for rain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Garshasp sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 事情就這樣持續了一段時日；終於，災禍之樹結出了苦瓜。就在扎夫之子加爾沙斯普離去的那一年，邪惡顯露了出來，因為消息傳到了眾人耳中：萬王之王的主座空虛了。有一道訊息傳到阿夫拉西亞布那裡，是帕尚投來的一塊石頭：渡過吉渾河，不要停留，直到那王座有人填補。在吉渾河與西潘賈布平原之間，阿夫拉西亞布布下了他的軍隊，你定會說：大地成了一片旋轉的天穹，印度的刀劍正為降雨而傾灑靈魂。

title.en: Rustam Chooses the Steed Rakhsh
title.zh: 魯斯塔姆擇駿馬拉赫什

region.en: Herds of Zabul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 扎布勒馬群（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Garshasp sec. 2

summary.en: Zal gathers all the herds of horses for Rustam, who presses each steed's back until its belly reaches the ground. Among a herd of piebalds comes a colt as tall as his dam, dark-eyed, with hoofs of steel and pluck of lions bred on Mount Bisitun, who could discern the tiny emmet's foot on black cloth at night two leagues away. An old herdsman warns against him, but Rustam casts his lasso, tames the dam with one buffet on the withers, mounts the bay, and asks his price: if thou art Rustam, redress Iran upon his back; its broad champaign shall be his price.
summary.zh: 扎勒為魯斯塔姆聚攏馬群；英雄逐一按壓馬背，馬腹幾乎觸地。花斑馬群中走出一匹與母馬同高的雄駒：鋼蹄、獅膽（生於比斯通山）、夜間兩里之外能辨黑布上的蟻足。老牧人警告莫惹此龍，魯斯塔姆擲出套索，一掌擊退護駒的母馬，跨上花斑駿馬問價——「若你真是魯斯塔姆，就騎牠去為伊朗伸張正義吧。」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: When Zal had gathered all his herds of horses, and many from Kabul, the herdsmen drove them past Rustam, calling out the royal brands. Whenever Rustam caught a steed he pressed its back until its belly reached the ground. At length a herd of piebald steeds sped by, among them a grey mare short-legged and fleet, with lion's chest and ears like two steel daggers. Behind her came a colt as tall as she, dark-eyed and tapering, a piebald bay with belly hard and jet-black, hoofs of steel, spotted roan like roses spread upon a ground of saffron.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Garshasp sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當扎爾聚集了他所有的馬群，其中許多來自喀布爾，牧人們趕著牠們經過魯斯塔姆面前，喊出王家的烙印。每當魯斯塔姆攔住一匹駿馬，他便壓住牠的背，直到牠的腹部觸及地面。終於，一群花斑駿馬疾馳而過，其中有一匹灰母馬，腿短而迅捷，胸如獅，耳似兩把鋼匕首。牠身後跟著一匹與牠一般高的幼駒，黑眼而身形修長，是一匹花斑棗紅馬，腹部堅實而烏黑，蹄如鋼鐵，斑駁的雜色如玫瑰散布在番紅花色的底子上。

passages.text: He could discern the tiny emmet's foot upon black cloth at night two leagues away, had elephantine strength with camel's stature, and pluck of lions bred on Mount Bisitun. Now Rustam gazing on the mare observed that elephantine colt and coiled his lasso to catch it, but an ancient herdsman cried: forbear to take another's charger. We call him Rakhsh, a piebald bay, as good as water and as bright as fire; at the sight of noose and cavalier the dam is like a lion.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Garshasp sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他能在夜裡於兩里格外辨出黑布上螞蟻的細足，有象一般的力量、駱駝般的身量，以及生於比西通山的獅子般的膽魄。此時魯斯塔姆凝視那母馬，注意到那匹象一般的幼駒，便盤起套索要捕捉牠，但一位年老的牧人喊道：切勿奪取他人之馬。我們稱牠為拉赫什，一匹花斑棗紅馬，如水般良善，如火般明亮；一見套索與騎士，那母馬便如獅一般。

passages.text: The old man's sayings opened Rustam's eyes: he cast his royal lasso and entangled the piebald's head. Then like a furious elephant the dam advanced as she would tear off Rustam's head, who roared as savage lions roar and scared her, then with one buffet on the withers sent her all trembling to the ground. He mounted swift as wind and asked the Dragon's price. If thou art Rustam, said the herd, redress Iran upon his back; its broad champaign shall be his price, then thou wilt right the world. The hero's lips grew coral-like with smiles; he said: all good is God's, and saddled ruddy Rakhsh, bent on revenge.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Garshasp sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 老人的話打開了魯斯塔姆的眼界：他擲出王家的套索，纏住了那花斑馬的頭。於是那母馬如狂怒的象一般撲來，彷彿要撕下魯斯塔姆的頭；他如凶猛的獅子般咆哮，將牠嚇退，隨即一掌擊在牠的肩隆上，使牠渾身顫抖地倒在地上。他迅如風地跨上馬背，詢問這龍駒的代價。你若真是魯斯塔姆，那牧人說，便騎在牠背上匡扶伊朗；牠那廣闊的原野便是牠的代價，如此你將匡正世界。英雄的雙唇如珊瑚般綻出微笑；他說：一切美善皆歸於神，遂為赤紅的拉赫什備好鞍韉，一心復仇。

title.en: Rustam Brings Kai Kubad Down from Alburz
title.zh: 魯斯塔姆自阿爾布茲迎卡尤巴德

region.en: Mount Alburz (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿爾布茲山（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. I, Garshasp sec. 4

summary.en: With Garshasp dead and Afrasiyab across the Jihun, Zal harangues the host: we need a Shah of royal seed, and an archimage hath told me of valiant Kai Kubad of royal stature, a future Shah of Faridun's own line. Rustam rides for Alburz, breaks a Turkman outpost with his ox-head mace, and bears back the chosen king, on whom the royal Grace had already shown itself — the vision of sovereignty that appeared again as a ram before Ardashir Papakan.
summary.zh: 加爾沙斯普已死、阿弗拉西亞卜渡河而來，扎勒向大軍宣言：我們需要王室血脈之王；術士已告知阿爾布茲的勇武卡尤巴德——法里東一脈的未來之王。魯斯塔姆縱馬赴阿爾布茲，以牛首狼牙棒破突厥哨卡，迎回天恩早已眷顧的王者——那道王權異象，日後又在阿爾達希爾一世面前化為公羊重現。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; foundation of the Kaianian dynasty. No living community restriction.

passages.text: When Zav departed and his son was Shah the hands of evil men were kept from ill; now seeing that Garshasp hath passed away the world is Shahless and the army chiefless; a host hath crossed Jihun and men cannot see the sun for dust. Zal answered: since I girt the belt of manhood no rider like me hath bestridden steed; yet God be praised that from my root a glorious shoot hath sprung, whose head will reach the sky. But he must have a charger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Garshasp secs. 2-3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當扎夫離世、其子為王之後，惡人之手被阻於為惡；如今眼見加爾沙斯普已然逝去，世界無王，軍隊無首；一支大軍已渡過吉渾河，人們因塵土而看不見太陽。扎爾答道：自我束上男子漢的腰帶以來，從未有像我這樣的騎士跨上駿馬；然而讚美歸於神，從我的根上長出了一株榮耀的嫩枝，其頭將觸及天空。但他必須有一匹戰馬。

passages.text: Afrasiyab arose from banquet, rest, and slumber and marched toward Khar of Rai along the meadows among their streams and reeds. When the armies were two leagues apart Zal called the veterans and harangued them: we have arrayed us here an ample host; yet with no Shah upon the throne our toils lack purpose, and our troops a head. An archimage hath told me of valiant Kai Kubad of royal stature, a future Shah of Faridun's own line in whom Grace, height, and lawful claims combine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Garshasp sec. 3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿弗拉西亞布從宴飲、休憩與睡眠中起身，沿著草地、穿過溪流與蘆葦，向賴城的哈爾進發。當兩軍相距兩里格時，扎爾召集了老將們，向他們陳詞：我們在此列下了浩大的軍隊；然而王座上無王，我們的辛勞便失了目的，我們的軍隊也無首領。一位大祭司曾告訴我，有一位英勇的凱·庫巴德，具王者之姿，是未來的王，出自費里敦本人的血脈，在他身上，神恩、身量與合法的繼承權合而為一。

passages.text: Then glorious Zal spake unto Rustam: bestir thyself, take up thy mace, select the escort, go with speed to Mount Alburz, do homage unto Kai Kubad, and tell him: the soldiers long and deck the throne for thee; we see none fitted for the royal crown, O monarch, our defender, but thyself. When Zal had spoken matchless Rustam joyfully got on the back of Rakhsh and proudly rode in quest of Kai Kubad. A Turkman outpost held the road strongly, but he charged the foe as champion of the host, brandished the ox-head mace, and towering in his wrath raised his battle-cry; the Turkmans' hearts all failed and they had to flee the battle in the end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Garshasp sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是榮耀的扎爾對魯斯塔姆說：奮起吧，拿起你的狼牙棒，挑選護衛，速往阿爾布爾茲山，向凱·庫巴德致敬，並告訴他：士兵們渴望著你，正為你鋪設王座；哦，君主，我們的守護者，我們看不到有誰比你自己更適合王冠。扎爾說完，無與倫比的魯斯塔姆歡喜地跨上拉赫什的背，驕傲地騎行去尋訪凱·庫巴德。一支突厥人的前哨牢牢把守著道路，但他以全軍勇士之姿衝向敵人，揮舞著牛頭狼牙棒，在怒火中巍然屹立，發出戰吼；突厥人的心盡皆潰散，最終不得不逃離戰場。

title.en: The Maui Brothers Bring Fire from Pulotu
title.zh: 毛伊兄弟自普洛圖攜火而來

region.en: Pulotu to Tongatabu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 自普洛圖至湯加塔布（象徵性定位）

period: Tongan oral tradition; recorded 1924 (Gifford)

source.work: E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 21-23 (Honolulu 1924)

summary.en: The Maui brothers come from Pulotu bringing fire, for there is none on earth - wrapped in the loin-cloth of Maui Motua, where it smoulders. Their first work on earth is weeding; Maui Motua warns Maui Kisikisi not to look back lest the grass grow again, but the junior cheats, keeps looking back, and grass grows on forever. Quarrelling, Maui Kisikisi tears the fire-end from his brother's cloth and commands the fire to run into the different trees - where it is now - then flees to Pulotu with his brother chasing.
summary.zh: 毛伊諸兄弟自普洛圖而來，攜火入世——地上本無火，火裹在毛伊穆圖亞的纏腰布中陰燃。下界第一樁工作是鋤草；兄長囑弟勿回頭，否則草復生；弟作弊回望，草遂世世叢生。兄弟反目，毛伊基斯基斯基扯下藏火之布，喝令火遁入各種樹木——火至今猶在木中——隨即奔逃，兄長窮追至普洛圖。

sensitivity.note: Tongan fire-origin variant.

passages.text: The first thing was their coming from Pulotu: first Maui Motua, then Maui Kisikisi and Maui Atalanga, and another Maui whose other name I do not remember. And the thing that they brought with them was fire. It is said that there was no fire on earth; that is why they brought the fire. It was only brought to be taken back to Pulotu; it was wrapped in the end of Maui Motua's loin cloth, which smouldered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 21-23 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最初之事，是他們從普洛圖而來：先是毛伊·莫圖阿，接著是毛伊·基西基西與毛伊·阿塔蘭加，還有另一位毛伊，其別名我已不記得。而他們隨身帶來之物，便是火。據說當時地上並無火；正因如此，他們才帶來了火。這火只是被帶來，預備再帶回普洛圖；它被裹在毛伊·莫圖阿的腰布末端，悶燃著。

passages.text: It is said that the first work done on earth was to weed. Maui Motua told Maui Kisikisi, 'Don't look behind when you dig, lest the grass grow again. When the grass is first dug it will not grow again and no other bush or weed will grow forever, but the land will be clear forever.' But Maui Kisikisi cheated when he weeded, for he kept looking back. That is the reason why the grass keeps growing. While they were weeding Maui Motua felt his body pain him and he felt weak; then he turned and looked back, and behold all the weeds had grown where he had dug. Maui Kisikisi had kept looking behind as he weeded, and Maui Motua was very angry with him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 21-23 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說地上最早做的工作便是除草。毛伊·莫圖阿對毛伊·基西基西說：『你挖掘時不要回頭看，免得草又長出來。草一經掘起，便不會再長，別的灌木或雜草也永遠不會再生，土地將永遠潔淨。』但毛伊·基西基西除草時卻作弊，因為他頻頻回頭看。這便是草不斷生長的原因。他們除草時，毛伊·莫圖阿感到身體疼痛、虛弱無力；於是他轉身回頭看，只見他掘過之處雜草全都長了出來。毛伊·基西基西除草時一直回頭看，毛伊·莫圖阿對他大為惱怒。

passages.text: Maui Kisikisi tore off a piece of the loin cloth of Maui Motua that had the fire smouldering in it, and told the fire to run into the different trees - that is where it is now. After that Maui Kisikisi ran and Maui Motua chased him to Pulotu. That is the end of my poor story about Maui; please excuse me if it is wrong, for I am only of the present day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 21-23 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 毛伊·基西基西撕下毛伊·莫圖阿腰布的一塊，那布中悶燃著火，他命火奔入各樣的樹中——火如今就在那裡。此後，毛伊·基西基西奔逃，毛伊·莫圖阿追他追到普洛圖。我這可憐的毛伊故事到此結束；若有錯處，請原諒我，因為我不過是今世之人。

title.en: Maui Pushes Up the Teve-propped Sky
title.zh: 毛伊撐起芋菇所支之天

region.en: Tonga sky (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 湯加之天（象徵性定位）

period: Tongan oral tradition; recorded 1924 (Gifford)

source.work: E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 21-24 (Honolulu 1924)

summary.en: The boundary of the sky was a teve plant; Maui stood and pushed up the sky with a stick, so that we might walk upright under the sky. In Lavaka's account the sky was supported by teve plants, and it is Maui Kisikisi who raises it, not Maui Atalanga. In Moli's telling the elder Maui was preparing his earth oven when his poker got jammed in the sky; he reversed it and pushed the sky until it was very high - the reason the sky is black being that the end of Maui's oven stick was dirty.
summary.zh: 湯加傳說：天界之邊界曾是一株芋菇；毛伊以杖撐天，使世人得以直腰行走。拉瓦卡記述：天原由芋菇諸株承托，舉天者為毛伊基斯基斯基。莫利則說：長兄毛伊設灶時，灶箸卡進天底；他倒轉箸柄將天一推至極高——天空之所以發黑，只因毛伊的灶箸末梢沾了灶灰。

sensitivity.note: Sky-lifting cluster, Tongan recension.

passages.text: It is said that the boundary of the sky was a teve plant, that Maui stood and pushed up the sky with a stick for a confined woman, so that we might under the sky walk upright. In Lavaka's account, before the sky was pushed up to its present height it was supported by certain plants which were known as teve; in that account it is Maui Kisikisi who raises the sky, not Maui Atalanga.
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 21-24 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說天空的邊界是一株特維植物，毛伊為一名受困的婦人站立，用棍子把天空頂高，好讓我們能在天空下直立行走。在拉瓦卡的記述中，天空被頂到現今的高度之前，是由某些被稱為特維的植物支撐著；在那記述中，舉起天空的是毛伊·基西基西，而非毛伊·阿塔蘭加。

passages.text: Moli's version of the sky-raising is as follows: It is said that the sky was low in olden days. The elder Maui was preparing his earth oven; when he used his poker it got jammed in the sky. Then he reversed his poker and pushed up the sky until it was very high. They say the reason of the sky being black is because the end of Maui's oven stick was dirty. The poem adds that Maui lifted the eel from the hole of the cave in Kulukave, and that where he turned he shook the earth and did it again - the places Utukakai and Talaamohi, and Namalata which was very rough.
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 21-24 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 莫利關於舉起天空的說法如下：據說古時天空很低。年長的毛伊正在準備他的土窯；他用撥火棍時，棍子卡在天空裡。於是他把撥火棍倒轉過來，把天空頂高，直到它非常高。他們說天空之所以是黑的，是因為毛伊窯棍的末端很髒。詩中又說，毛伊從庫盧卡維洞穴的洞中舉起了鰻魚，他轉身之處震動了大地，又再做了一次——那地方是烏圖卡凱與塔拉阿莫希，以及十分崎嶇的納馬拉塔。

title.en: Maui Plants Food and Casts Two Sons into the Sea
title.zh: 毛伊墾地並將二子擲海成島

region.en: Ngaunoho, Utungake island, Vavau
region.zh: 瓦瓦烏群島烏通加凱恩加烏諾霍

period: Tongan oral tradition; recorded 1924 (Gifford)

source.work: E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 23-24 (Honolulu 1924)

summary.en: Maui resides at Ngaunoho in Utungake island, walking about all day while his wife and children weep - they are starving. He digs between the islands so hard that the land rocks and they cry out in fear; so he kills his two sons, Mosolahi and Mososii, and throws them into the sea, where they become two little islets that bear their names.
summary.zh: 毛伊居烏通加凱的恩加烏諾霍，終日閒遊，妻兒啼泣——因家無隔宿之糧。他遂往兩島之間奮力墾土，掘得大地撼搖，妻兒驚懼痛哭。於是他殺了兩個兒子莫索拉希與莫索希伊，擲入大海——二童化作兩座小島，島即以其名名之。

sensitivity.note: Child-sacrifice motif in the Tongan Maui cycle; recorded as in source.

passages.text: Maui resided at Ngaunoho in Utungake island, Vavau group, and lived there with his wife and children. Every day he only walked around, and his wife and children wept. He at last inquired of them the reason of their tears. So his wife replied: 'We are weeping because you always go away and leave us starving.' 'Very well', said Maui, 'I will go and plant something for us to eat.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 23-24 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 毛伊住在瓦瓦烏群島烏通加克島的恩高諾霍，與他的妻子兒女同住在那裡。他每天只是四處走動，他的妻子兒女則哭泣。他終於問他們流淚的原因。於是他的妻子回答：『我們哭泣，是因為你總是離去，留下我們挨餓。』『好吧，』毛伊說，『我去種些東西給我們吃。』

passages.text: He went between Ngaunoho and Utungake and started digging the soil there. He dug so hard that the land rocked and his children and his wife cried. Maui heard them and returned and asked them what was the matter and why they were crying. They told him: 'We are frightened.' And Maui said: 'You are frightened because I went to plant something to eat.' Then he killed his two sons and threw them into the sea. The names of the boys were Mosolahi and Mososii, and two little islets are called after them, because when the two boys were cast into the sea they were transformed into these two islets.
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 23-24 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他往來於恩高諾霍與烏通加凱之間，並開始在那裡挖掘泥土。他挖得如此用力，以致大地震動，他的孩子和妻子都哭了。毛伊聽見了他們的哭聲，便回來問他們發生了什麼事、為什麼哭泣。他們告訴他：「我們很害怕。」毛伊說：「你們害怕，是因為我去種植食物。」於是，他殺了自己的兩個兒子，把他們扔進海裡。這兩個男孩的名字是莫索拉希與莫索西伊，有兩座小島以他們命名，因為當這兩個男孩被拋入海中時，他們就化作了這兩座小島。

title.en: Ahoeitu, the Divine First Tui Tonga
title.zh: 阿霍埃圖：首任神裔湯加王

region.en: Popua and Holohiufi, Tongatabu
region.zh: 湯加塔布波普阿與霍洛希菲

period: Tongan oral tradition; recorded 1924 (Gifford, from Reiter 1907)

source.work: E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 25-29 (Honolulu 1924)

summary.en: The sky-god Tangaloa Eitumatupua descends the great casuarina of Toonangakava to the fisher-woman Ilaheva; their son Ahoeitu climbs the ironwood tree to the sky. Jealous celestial brothers tear him in pieces, cook and eat him, throwing his head into the hoi bush. Their father makes them vomit the flesh, gathers the head and bones in a bowl of water covered with nonuhaha leaves, and the boy sits up alive. He descends to become the first divine Tui Tonga; his brothers are distributed into the offices of the Tongan polity - 'Did he descend from the sky?' is still the test of a chief.
summary.zh: 天神坦加羅亞埃圖馬圖普瓦沿大木麻黃樹而下，與漁婦伊拉赫瓦生子阿霍埃圖。少年攀鐵木登天尋父；天上眾兄弟妒而肢解其身、烹而食之，頭顱擲入霍伊叢。父親命諸子嘔吐還肉，將頭骨納入水盆、覆以海蒲桃葉——死者竟於盆中坐起！阿霍埃圖下凡為首任神裔湯加王；其兄弟分任護衛執政——至今湯加人猶以『他是否自天而降？』考驗酋長之尊。

sensitivity.note: Founding legend of the Tui Tonga sacred line; cannibal revenge summarized.

passages.text: There first appeared on the earth the human offspring of a worm or grub, and the head of the worm became Tui Tonga; his name was Kohai and he was the first Tui Tonga in the world. A large casuarina tree grew on the island of Toonangakava, between the islands of Mataaho and Talakite in the lagoon of Tongatabu; this great casuarina tree reached to the sky, and a god came down from the sky by this great tree. This god was Tangaloa Eitumatupua. When he came down there was a woman fishing; her name was Ilaheva, and also Vaepopua. The god from the sky came to her and caught her, and they cohabited; their sleeping place was called Mohenga. The woman Ilaheva became pregnant and gave birth to a male child, and tended the child on earth while the god dwelt in the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 25-29 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大地上最先出現的是蟲或蛆的人類後裔，那蟲的頭成了圖伊・湯加；他的名字叫科海，他是世上第一位圖伊・湯加。在托納納卡瓦島上，即位於湯加塔布潟湖中馬塔阿霍島與塔拉基特島之間，長著一棵巨大的木麻黃樹；這棵巨大的木麻黃樹高聳入天，一位神祇便藉著這棵大樹從天而降。這位神祇是坦加洛阿・埃伊圖馬圖普阿。他降下時，有一個女人正在捕魚；她的名字叫伊拉赫瓦，又叫瓦埃波普阿。那位從天而降的神祇來到她身邊，抓住了她，二人便同寢；他們睡覺的地方叫做莫亨加。那女人伊拉赫瓦懷了孕，生下一個男嬰，並在大地上撫養這孩子，而那位神祇則住在天上。

passages.text: After a time the god returned and asked the woman about their child, and said, 'His name shall be Ahoeitu, Day-has-dawned.' He asked whether her soil was clay or sand, and, hearing that her place was sandy, said, 'Wait until I throw down a piece of clay from the sky, to make a garden for the boy Ahoeitu, and also a yam for the garden of our child.' So the god poured down the mount called Holohiufi, Pour-the-yam, and brought down the yam from the sky. The mother and son lived together until the child Ahoeitu was big; then he asked who his father was, and his mother told him his father was in the sky, named Eitumatupua, and that the great casuarina was the road to the sky. The boy climbed the great casuarina tree and reached the sky; he went along the big wide road, found the mound, and saw his father catching pigeons. When his father saw him approaching, he sat down because he was overpowered at seeing his son; they pressed noses and cried, and had kava and food.
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 25-29 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 過了一段時間，那位神祇回來了，向那女人問起他們的孩子，並說：「他的名字要叫阿霍埃伊圖，意為『白晝已破曉』。」他問她的土地是黏土還是沙土，聽說她那個地方是沙地，便說：「等我從天上扔下一塊黏土，為阿霍埃伊圖這孩子造一座園子，也為我們孩子的園子造一株山藥。」於是，那神祇傾倒下那座名叫霍洛希烏菲的山，意為「傾倒山藥」，並從天上帶下了山藥。母子二人一同生活，直到孩子阿霍埃伊圖長大；然後他問自己的父親是誰，他母親告訴他，他的父親在天上，名叫埃伊圖馬圖普阿，而那棵巨大的木麻黃樹就是通往天上的路。那男孩爬上那棵巨大的木麻黃樹，到達了天上；他沿著那條寬闊的大路走去，找到了那座土丘，看見他的父親正在捕捉鴿子。他父親看見他走近，便坐了下來，因為見到自己的兒子令他難以自持；他們互相碰鼻而哭，並一同享用卡瓦與食物。

passages.text: That day the celestial sons of Eitumatupua were having an entertainment, playing the game called sikaulutoa, played with a reed throwing-stick with a head of toa or casuarina wood. The god sent Ahoeitu to the entertainment of his brothers in the green. The people saw the lad and all gazed at him with one accord, for he was very handsome and well formed; his brothers were immediately jealous of him. They sprang upon and tore him to pieces, then cooked and ate him - some accounts say his flesh was eaten uncooked; his head was left over, so they threw it among the plants called hoi, which caused one kind of hoi to become bitter. After a little while Ahoeitu's father said to a woman, 'Go and seek the lad at the entertainment, so that he may eat.' They searched but could not find him. Eitumatupua suspected that Ahoeitu's brothers had killed the lad; therefore he sent a message for them to come and asked where the lad was. They lied, saying, 'We do not know.' Then their father said, 'Come and vomit.' A big wooden bowl was brought; they were told to tickle their throats so that they would vomit up the flesh of the lad and also the blood, in fact all the parts they had eaten; they all had their throats tickled and they vomited, filling the wooden bowl. They were asked where his head was; the murderers replied that they threw it into the bush, into the hoi bush.
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 25-29 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那天，埃伊圖馬圖普阿在天上的兒子們正在舉行一場娛樂活動，玩一種叫做西考盧托阿的遊戲，所用的是一根以托阿木或木麻黃木為頭的蘆葦投擲棒。那位神祇派阿霍埃伊圖到綠叢中他兄弟們的娛樂活動去。眾人看見這少年，全都一致地凝視著他，因為他非常俊美、體格勻稱；他的兄弟們立刻嫉妒他。他們撲上前去，把他撕成碎片，然後煮熟吃了他——有些說法說他的肉是生吃的；他的頭被留了下來，於是他們把它扔進叫做霍伊的植物叢中，這使得其中一種霍伊變苦了。過了一會兒，阿霍埃伊圖的父親對一個女人說：「去娛樂活動那裡找那少年，好讓他吃東西。」他們找了，卻找不到他。埃伊圖馬圖普阿懷疑是阿霍埃伊圖的兄弟們殺了那少年；因此他傳話叫他們來，問那少年在哪裡。他們撒謊說：「我們不知道。」於是他們的父親說：「來，吐出來。」一隻大木碗被拿了來；他們被吩咐去搔自己的喉嚨，好把少年的肉以及血，事實上把他們所吃下的一切部分都吐出來；他們全都搔了自己的喉嚨，嘔吐出來，裝滿了那隻木碗。他們被問到他的頭在哪裡；那些兇手回答說，他們把它扔進了灌木叢，扔進了霍伊叢中。

passages.text: Then the god Eitumatupua sent a messenger to seek the head of Ahoeitu; they also collected his bones and put them together with his head into the bowl and poured water on to the flesh and blood. Then were plucked and brought the leaves of the nonuhaha tree, whose leaves placed on a sick person possess the virtue of bringing immediate recovery, even if the person is nigh unto death. So the nonuhaha leaves were covered over the remains of Ahoeitu, and the bowl containing them was put behind the house; they visited the bowl continually, and after a time poured out the water - the flesh of his body had become compact. They visited the bowl again and again and at last found him sitting up in it. Then they told Eitumatupua that Ahoeitu was alive, and brought him into the house into the presence of his father, who spoke, ordering that the brothers of Ahoeitu, who ate him, be brought. 'You have killed Ahoeitu. He shall descend as the ruler of Tonga, while you, his brothers, remain here.' But the brothers loved Ahoeitu, as they had just realized that he was their real brother, and pleaded with their father to be allowed to accompany him; the plea was finally granted. Ahoeitu returned to earth and became Tui Tonga, the first divine Tui Tonga of the world; the Tui Tonga who originated from the offspring of the worm were displaced. The Tui Tonga and their families are of the highest rank, because Ahoeitu came originally from the sky; his divine origin makes his descendants real chiefs. In fact, it became customary to ask of one who is proud or thinks himself a chief: 'Is he a chief? Did he descend from the sky?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 25-29 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是，那位神祇埃伊圖馬圖普阿派了一名使者去尋找阿霍埃伊圖的頭；他們也收集了他的骨頭，把他的骨頭連同他的頭一起放進碗裡，並把水澆在肉和血上。然後他們採摘並拿來了諾努哈哈樹的葉子，這種樹的葉子放在病人身上，具有使人立刻康復的功效，即使那人已瀕臨死亡。於是，諾努哈哈的葉子被覆蓋在阿霍埃伊圖的遺骸上，裝著遺骸的碗被放在屋後；他們不斷地去看那隻碗，過了一段時間把水倒出來——他身體的肉已經凝合在一起了。他們一次又一次地去看那隻碗，最後發現他坐在碗中。於是他們告訴埃伊圖馬圖普阿，阿霍埃伊圖活了，並把他帶進屋裡，帶到他父親面前，他父親開口吩咐，把吃了阿霍埃伊圖的那些兄弟帶來。「你們殺了阿霍埃伊圖。他將下去作湯加的統治者，而你們，他的兄弟們，就留在這裡。」但兄弟們愛阿霍埃伊圖，因為他們剛剛才領悟到他是他們真正的兄弟，便懇求父親允許他們陪伴他；這懇求最終獲准了。阿霍埃伊圖回到大地，成為圖伊・湯加，世上第一位神聖的圖伊・湯加；源自蟲之後裔的圖伊・湯加被取代了。圖伊・湯加及其家族地位最為尊貴，因為阿霍埃伊圖原本來自天上；他的神聖出身使他的後裔成為真正的首領。事實上，這成了一種習俗：對於一個驕傲或自以為是首領的人，人們會問：「他是首領嗎？他是從天上降下來的嗎？」

title.en: Kavaonau: The Leper Girl and the First Kava Bowl
title.zh: 卡瓦奧瑙：痲瘋少女與第一碗卡瓦

region.en: Eueiki island, Tonga
region.zh: 湯加埃烏埃基島

period: Tongan oral tradition; recorded 1924 (Gifford, from Mrs. Rachel Tonga)

source.work: E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 71-72 (Honolulu 1924)

summary.en: Famine on Eueiki: Fefafa and Fevanga, attendants of the Tui Tonga, have only one great kape plant - which they cut while chief Loau sits beside it - and no meat, so they kill their daughter Kavaonau for the oven. Loau rebukes them and has her buried: from her head grows a great kava plant, from her intestines a great sugar-cane; a rat that chews the kava is partly paralysed, chewing the cane it recovers - showing cane must follow kava. Loau's instructions name the strainer, the bowl, the master of ceremonies and the banana-leaf cup: the kava ceremony of Tonga is born from the leper girl's grave.
summary.zh: 埃烏埃基島饑饉：僕夫婦費法法與費旺加只有一株大芋菇——趁洛奧酋長坐於其旁時砍倒作食——肉則以女兒卡瓦奧瑙充之。洛奧斥責並令安葬：頭上生出大卡瓦，腸中長出大甘蔗；老鼠嚼卡瓦則半身麻痺，嚼甘蔗則康復奔跳——故卡瓦必須配甘蔗同服。洛奧吩咐備濾纖維、制酒碗、設司儀、鋪蕉葉承盃——湯加的卡瓦儀式自此而生。

sensitivity.note: Human-sacrifice origin of the kava ceremony; retained as the record states it.

passages.text: Two persons called Fefafa and Fevanga dwelt at Eueiki; the man was an attendant of the Tui Tonga, and after continually going to visit the Chief at Mua he addressed him and asked him to sail over on a pleasure trip to the island. And Tui Tonga went to Eueiki at a time when there was a scarcity of food at the island. Only one big kape plant, a plant whose root is eaten but is very peppery, stood on the man's premises; and when they landed the gear of the vessel of the chiefs was taken and placed against the kape plant, and they went to see the man. The couple went and prepared the native oven, and desired earnestly to get the big kape plant against which Loau's canoe gear was resting. They asked Loau to go into the house so they might be at liberty to cut the big kape; after some time the chief went into the house, then they cut down the big kape and baked the food. But they had no meat, so they killed Kavaonau, their daughter, as meat for their oven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 71-72 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有兩個名叫費法法和費萬加的人住在埃烏埃伊基；那男人是圖伊・湯加的侍從，在不斷前往穆阿拜訪首領之後，他向首領進言，請他乘船到那座島上作一趟遊樂之行。圖伊・湯加在島上食物匱乏的時候去了埃烏埃伊基。那男人的住處只立著一株大卡佩植物，這種植物的根可以吃，但非常辛辣；當他們登陸時，首領們船上的器具被取下，靠在那株卡佩植物上，然後他們去見那男人。那對夫婦前去準備土窯，並極想得到那株洛奧的獨木舟器具所靠著的大卡佩。他們請洛奧進屋，好讓他們能自由地砍那株大卡佩；過了一會兒，首領進了屋，於是他們砍下那株大卡佩，烤好了食物。但他們沒有肉，於是他們殺了自己的女兒卡瓦奧瑙，作為他們窯中的肉。

passages.text: The food was cooked and brought to the Chief Loau, and he thanked them for preparing the food, but he said, 'Why did not know that it was a kava plant; have you destroyed your child?' Then he told them to take it away and bury it. They told their people to bury it at the rear of their house; but the intestines and head were buried separately. And for five nights they kept visiting the grave; after five nights there grew from the head a big kava plant, while from the intestines there grew a big sugar-cane. The kava plant grew big and also the sugar cane. It is said that a rat came and chewed the big kava and became partly paralysed; then it chewed the sugar cane and recovered and ran about. The rat continually did this, which showed that the sugar cane had to be eaten with the kava.
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 71-72 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 食物煮熟后，被送到首领洛奥（Loau）面前，他感谢他们准备食物，但他说：『你们为何不知道那是一株卡瓦（kava）？你们岂不是毁了自己的孩子？』于是他吩咐他们把尸体拿走埋葬。他们吩咐族人把它埋在屋后；但肠子和头颅则分开埋葬。此后连续五个夜晚，他们都去探访那座坟；五夜之后，从头颅长出一株大卡瓦，而从肠子长出一株大甘蔗。卡瓦长得高大，甘蔗亦然。据说有一只老鼠前来啃咬那株大卡瓦，身体便部分瘫痪；随后它啃咬甘蔗，便恢复过来，四处奔跑。老鼠不断这样做，这表明甘蔗必须与卡瓦一同食用。

passages.text: When the two plants were big Fefafa and Fevanga dug them up and took them to Loau. When they brought the plants to him, Loau saw them, and laughed and said: 'Chewing kava, a leper from Faimata in Eueiki, the child of Fevanga and Fefafa! Bring some coconut fiber to strain it, a bowl to contain it, some one as master of ceremonies, some young leaves of the banana as a receiver, and some one for the bowl to be turned to.' And they knew by this that it was kava and sugar cane. That is the origin of the kava: the shoots of the kava grow and split and become limy, or gray, like the skin of a leper, because the woman Kavaonau was a leper; and those that drink too much kava become scaly like a leper, because the kava grew out of the body of a woman that was a leper.
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 71-72 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 两株植物长大后，费法法（Fefafa）与费万加（Fevanga）将它们挖出，带到洛奥那里。当他们把植物带到洛奥面前时，洛奥见了，便笑着说：『咀嚼卡瓦吧，这是来自埃韦基（Eueiki）之法伊马塔（Faimata）的麻风病人，是费万加与费法法之子！拿些椰纤维来滤它，拿一个碗来盛它，找个人来当司仪，拿些香蕉嫩叶来作承接之物，再找个人来让碗转向。』他们由此便知道那是卡瓦与甘蔗。这就是卡瓦的起源：卡瓦的嫩芽生长、裂开，变得黏滑或灰白，如同麻风病人的皮肤，因为那女子卡瓦奥瑙（Kavaonau）是个麻风病人；而那些饮卡瓦过多的人会变得像麻风病人一样鳞屑斑斑，因为卡瓦是从一个患麻风病的女子体内长出来的。

title.en: Fetching the House of Hikuleo from Pulotu
title.zh: 自普洛圖迎取希庫萊奧之屋

region.en: Pulotu Tuumau, land of shades (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 冥府普洛圖圖毛（象徵性定位）

period: Tongan oral tradition; recorded 1924 (Gifford, from Heamasi Latu)

source.work: E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 171-174 (Honolulu 1924)

summary.en: A Tui Tonga sets his two patient servants impossible tasks: a reed fence, a rowing canoe of whale ivory, and last the house of Hikuleo, sovereign of Pulotu, constructed of human bones. Voyaging with the goddess Haelefeke - who swallows kava, ovens and a man-eating shark whole - they smash Hikuleo's own canoe, hide in the house posts, drink a hundred ovens and eight bowls dry, and knock loose the gods who sit upon the bone house to carry it home to Tongatabu.
summary.zh: 某代湯加王接連刁難兩位僕人：編蘆籬、造鯨牙大舟，最後竟要他們去冥府普洛圖搬回人骨造成之屋——希庫萊奧之居。女神哈埃萊費凱同行相助：一口吞盡八大碗卡瓦連碗帶濾網、整樹維果與食人鯊；他們撞碎冥主之舟、藏身屋柱、掀翻壓屋的諸神，最終把白骨之屋運回湯加塔布。

sensitivity.note: Pulotu journey; Hikuleo as sovereign of the shades.

passages.text: There was a Tui Tonga who annoyed his people considerably with irksome tasks. However, two men agreed that they would not be distressed by executing his errands, so they went and resided with the Tui Tonga and did his errands. The first order the Tui Tonga issued was that they build a reed fence around his plantation; after this was accomplished he ordered them to build a large rowing canoe of whale ivory. They constructed the canoe and executed many other orders besides; then the Tui Tonga said that there was still one more task to be done: to go to Pulotu and fetch Hikuleo's house, which was constructed of human bones. The two faithful servants set out from Tongatabu in the ivory canoe on their voyage to Pulotu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 171-174 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一位图伊·汤加（Tui Tonga）以烦人的差事颇令其子民苦恼。然而，有两个人约定，他们不会因执行他的差事而烦恼，于是他们前去与图伊·汤加同住，为他办事。图伊·汤加发布的第一道命令，是要他们在他的种植园周围筑一道芦苇篱笆；此事完成后，他又命令他们用鲸牙建造一艘大型划桨独木舟。他们造好了独木舟，还执行了许多其他命令；随后图伊·汤加说，还有一项任务要完成：前往普洛图（Pulotu），取回希库莱奥（Hikuleo）的房屋，那房屋是用人骨建造的。这两名忠仆乘着鲸牙独木舟从汤加塔布（Tongatabu）出发，航向普洛图。

passages.text: Upon reaching Haapai they noticed a woman standing on a beach waving a white fly whisk; they did not approach, but continued on their voyage to Vavau, where they again saw the same woman waving to them. Still they disregarded her signal and continued to Samoa, where the same woman was seen on a beach. The man who had been sitting near the bow suggested it would be well to discover what the woman wanted, as it was truly remarkable that she should beckon from so many places. When they reached her she spoke: 'I told you to come to me, because I want to know where you are going.' The two men took the woman aboard; she was really a goddess and her name was Haelefeke. So they all three voyaged in search of Pulotu, the road to which is guarded by the south and the north winds; usually the sea would be rough and the winds strong, but when the Tui Tonga's vessel went, the sea was neither rough nor the wind boisterous, and they arrived without mishap at Pulotu Tuumau, where a feast was being held at Pulotu Akaaka at which Hikuleo, the sovereign of Pulotu, was in attendance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 171-174 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 抵达哈阿派（Haapai）时，他们注意到一名女子站在海滩上，挥动着一柄白色拂尘；他们没有靠近，而是继续航行至瓦瓦乌（Vavau），在那里又看见同一名女子向他们招手。他们仍然不理睬她的信号，继续前往萨摩亚（Samoa），在那里又看见同一名女子站在一处海滩上。那个一直坐在船头附近的人提议，最好弄清楚那女子想要什么，因为她竟从这么多地方向他们招手，实在非同寻常。当他们来到她面前时，她说道：『我叫你们到我这里来，是因为我想知道你们要去哪里。』两人把那女子带上船；她其实是一位女神，名叫哈埃莱费凯（Haelefeke）。于是他们三人一同航行，寻找普洛图，通往那里的路有南风和北风把守；通常那里海面汹涌、风势强劲，但图伊·汤加的船经过时，海面既不汹涌，风也不狂暴，他们平安无事地抵达了普洛图·图乌毛（Pulotu Tuumau），当时普洛图·阿卡阿卡（Pulotu Akaaka）正在举行一场宴席，普洛图的君主希库莱奥也在场。

passages.text: Haelefeke ordered the two men to put their boat into the canoe shed, removing the one already there and throwing it down heavily outside; the canoe that rightfully belonged there was thrown out and broken, and the Tui Tonga's ivory canoe placed in its stead. The three entered Hikuleo's house while she was away; Haelefeke instructed the two men to each enter a house post and hide there, and she herself turned into a stone in the house. When Hikuleo heard the crash of her falling canoe she sent people to see what was the trouble; they saw that Hikuleo's canoe was smashed and that in its place was an ivory canoe. Hikuleo gave orders to be carried to Pulotu Tuumau and bade all the prophets and conjecturers assemble there to ascertain who had broken the canoe; they failed, so Hikuleo called out to the hidden intruders: 'Be so good as to show yourselves. If you are from the Tui Tonga, you may enter.' Thereupon Haelefeke arose, showing herself, and called the two men to come out of the posts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 171-174 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 哈埃莱费凯吩咐两人把他们的船放进独木舟棚里，将原本停在那里的那艘移开，重重地扔到外面；那艘本应停在那里的独木舟被扔了出去，摔坏了，图伊·汤加的鲸牙独木舟便取而代之。三人趁她不在时进入希库莱奥的房屋；哈埃莱费凯指示两人各自进入一根房柱中躲藏，她自己则化作屋内的一块石头。当希库莱奥听到她的独木舟坠落的巨响时，便派人去看出了什么事；他们看见希库莱奥的独木舟被砸碎，取而代之的是一艘鲸牙独木舟。希库莱奥下令把她抬到普洛图·图乌毛，并吩咐召集所有先知和占卜者到那里，查明是谁弄坏了独木舟；他们未能查明，于是希库莱奥向躲藏着的闯入者喊道：『请现身吧。如果你们是图伊·汤加的人，可以进来。』于是哈埃莱费凯起身现身，并叫那两人从柱子中出来。

passages.text: Hikuleo greeted them and ordered her people to prepare food for the reception of the chiefs from Tonga: the contents of one hundred ovens were brought and kava was made in eight bowls. Haelefeke told her two companions to drink from one bowl; they could not drain it, but Haelefeke drained all the bowls, swallowing them, the strainer, and the cups. She told her companions to eat of the baskets of food, but all they took was a liver, which they broke in two and ate and were satisfied; but Haelefeke ate all the food, crumbs, skins, baskets, the poles on which the baskets were carried, and everything appertaining to the feast. Next morning Hikuleo ordered them to consume entirely a huge vi tree heavily laden with fruit; the two plucked one fruit, divided it, and were satisfied, while Haelefeke changed herself into a great octopus stationed at the foot of the tree, and ate the fruit, then the whole tree and all the people thereon. She suggested they go to the sea for a surf ride, knowing full well there was a ferocious man-eating shark lurking near the surf; when they stranded on the beach for the third time the great shark was stranded with them, and Haelefeke swallowed the fish whole. Then she told the Tui Tonga's purpose; Hikuleo replied, 'Very well. Take the house with you.' The gods of Pulotu were sitting on the house so that it could not be lifted; Haelefeke smote the house and knocked off the people of Pulotu who were holding it down, and the house was carried to the beach and put aboard the vessel. The house was taken to the Tui Tonga and he thanked his faithful servants, telling them they had accomplished all that was necessary.
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 171-174 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 希库莱奥向他们致意，并吩咐她的人准备食物，以接待来自汤加的首领们：一百个烤炉里的食物被端了上来，卡瓦在八个碗中调制而成。哈埃莱费凯叫她的两个同伴共饮一碗；他们喝不完，但哈埃莱费凯把所有的碗都喝干了，连碗、滤器和杯子一并吞下。她叫同伴们吃那些篮中的食物，但他们只取了一块肝，把它掰成两半吃了，便饱了；而哈埃莱费凯吃光了所有食物，包括碎屑、皮、篮子、抬篮子的杆子，以及宴席上的一切相关之物。第二天早晨，希库莱奥吩咐他们吃光一棵果实累累的巨大维（vi）树；两人摘下一颗果子，分而食之，便饱了，而哈埃莱费凯则化作一只大章鱼，守在树脚下，吃掉了果子，接着吃掉了整棵树以及树上的所有人。她提议他们去海里冲浪，心里很清楚那冲浪处附近潜伏着一条凶猛的食人鲨；当他们第三次被冲上滩时，那条大鲨鱼也与他们一同搁浅，哈埃莱费凯便把那条鱼整个吞下。随后她说出了图伊·汤加的目的；希库莱奥回答说：『很好。把这座房屋带走吧。』普洛图的神祇们正坐在房屋上，使它无法被抬起；哈埃莱费凯击打房屋，把那些按住它的普洛图人打落，房屋便被抬到海滩，装上船。房屋被带到图伊·汤加那里，他感谢他的忠仆，告诉他们已完成了一切所需之事。

title.en: Tangaloa's Floating Fortress
title.zh: 坦加羅亞漂流的木堡

region.en: Fiji (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 斐濟（象徵性定位）

period: Tongan oral tradition; recorded 1924 (Gifford)

source.work: E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, p. 201 (Honolulu 1924)

summary.en: The god Tangaloa comes down from heaven with his son to sojourn in Tonga and build a fortress in Fiji so strong none could enter without consent. The jealous Fijians fight in vain until one of their gods commands a deluge of rain; the carpenters' water-tight wooden wall keeps the water in, and after hours of downpour the whole fort floats - scattering the builders to all parts of the world. For this reason carpenters may be found wherever you go.
summary.zh: 天神坦加羅亞攜子下凡，居湯加、赴斐濟築堡，堅不可摧。斐濟人妒而攻之，屢攻不克；後其神喚來傾盆暴雨——匠人木牆滴水不漏，水積堡中，數時之後整座堡壘浮起，匠人隨之漂散天涯海角——所以如今走到哪裡都能遇上木匠。

sensitivity.note: Deluge-parody explaining the diaspora of craftsmen.

passages.text: There was a god named Tangaloa, who came down from heaven in ancient times; he brought a son with him. After sojourning awhile in Tonga they went over to Fiji; there they built a strong fort for themselves, so strong that none could enter there without its occupants' consent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, p. 201 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古時有一位名叫唐加羅阿的神，從天而降；他隨身帶著一個兒子。他們在東加逗留了一段時日之後，便前往斐濟；他們在那裡為自己築了一座堅固的堡壘，堅固得若無堡中之人應允，誰也無法進入。
