passages.text: The Fijians were jealous of these carpenters and came and fought them. They tried and tried to take the fort, but without success. One day one of the gods of Fiji came down and told the Fijians to let him fight for them against the god Tangaloa and his carpenters. This Fijian god commanded the rain to pour down; the rain came down very hard on the carpenters' fort. The wooden wall, which the carpenters had built round the fort, was water tight; it excluded the water, and after many hours of downpour the fort floated. The carpenters were thus scattered to all parts of the world - for this reason you are now likely to find carpenters in any part of the world, wherever you may go.
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, p. 201 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 斐濟人嫉妒這些木匠，便前來與他們交戰。他們一次又一次地試圖攻下這座堡壘，卻始終未能成功。有一天，斐濟的一位神降下，吩咐斐濟人讓他替他們出戰，對抗唐加羅阿神和他的木匠們。這位斐濟神命令大雨傾盆而降；大雨猛烈地落在木匠們的堡壘上。木匠們圍繞堡壘所築的木牆滴水不漏；它將水擋在外面，然而經過好幾個時辰的傾盆大雨之後，整座堡壘竟漂浮了起來。木匠們就這樣被沖散到世界各地——正因如此，如今無論你走到哪裡，都可能在世界任何角落遇見木匠。

title.en: Tuavavau, the Virgin of Utungake
title.zh: 烏通加凱的貞女圖阿瓦瓦烏

region.en: Utungake island, Vavau
region.zh: 瓦瓦烏群島烏通加凱島

period: Tongan oral tradition; recorded 1924 (Gifford, from Fakatava)

source.work: E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 202-203 (Honolulu 1924)

summary.en: The most beautiful woman in the world, Tuavavau of Utungake, knows nothing of men. Chief Tui Lakepa comes snaring pigeons and falls in love; his friends follow until her hill is ringed with the houses of lovestruck chiefs. When she beckons Tui Lakepa and asks what they all want - her head, her feet, her arms? - he shows her, and she understands: 'Alas, I never knew that there was such a bad thing in the world as this, that a man should treat a woman as a rooster treats a hen. Such a world is not a good place for me.' She runs and leaps from the hilltop into the sea, and so dies.
summary.zh: 天下第一美人圖阿瓦瓦烏居烏通加凱，不解男女之事。酋長圖伊拉凱帕獵鴿至此墜入情網；眾友相繼而至，環山築屋圍住她的山丘。她喚圖伊拉凱帕問他們究竟要什麼——要她的頭、她的腳、她的手臂？酋長以身相示。她恍然長嘆：『世間竟有如此醜事，男子對待女子竟如公雞對待母雞——這樣的世界不配我居。』言罷奔上崖頂，縱身躍海而死。

sensitivity.note: Tragic legend; assault referenced obliquely as in the source narrative.

passages.text: Tuavavau was the most beautiful woman, not only in Vavau, but in the entire world. She lived at Utungake island with some maiden friends who shared her house; she was not the daughter of a chief, but her beauty made her respected and the recipient of many attentions from her maiden friends. The chief Tui Lakepa went to snare pigeons at Utungake; one day he saw the beautiful Tuavavau and fell in love with her, so he built his house close by where he could often see her. Many of his young chief friends, wondering at the continued absence of Tui Lakepa, went to search for him; when they found him they asked what he was doing there, and he answered that he was waiting to snare the fairest pigeon in all the world. When they saw the beautiful girl, they all fell in love with her; then each chief built himself a house near by until they entirely surrounded her house on the landward side.
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 202-203 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 圖阿瓦瓦烏是世上最美麗的女子，不僅在瓦瓦烏如此，在整個世界也是如此。她與幾位少女朋友一同住在烏通加凱島，她們與她同住一屋；她並非酋長之女，但她的美貌使她受人敬重，也令她的少女朋友們對她百般殷勤。酋長圖伊·拉凱帕前往烏通加凱設網捕鴿；有一天他看見了美麗的圖阿瓦瓦烏，便愛上了她，於是在她近旁建了自己的屋子，好能時常看見她。他許多年輕的酋長朋友們，對圖伊·拉凱帕久久不歸感到奇怪，便前去尋找他；他們找到他時，問他在那裡做什麼，他回答說他在等著捕捉全世界最美麗的一隻鴿子。當他們看見那位美麗的姑娘時，全都愛上了她；於是每位酋長都在近旁為自己建了一座屋子，直到他們從陸地那一側把她屋子團團圍住。

passages.text: Tuavavau had never been much among men and was entirely ignorant of all sex matters; when she saw all these chiefs camped about the mound upon which she lived she greatly wondered what they had come for. One day, as she looked out of the gate of the enclosure in which her house stood, she saw Tui Lakepa looking at her; she beckoned him to come up to her, and when he came, asked him what had brought all these men to live there. He answered that he could only speak for himself and that he was there because he liked her. 'What do you like about me?' she asked - 'My head, my feet, my arms?' He then told her that he wanted to sleep with her; not being able to understand this, Tuavavau asked him to come into the house and show her just what it was that he wanted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 202-203 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 圖阿瓦瓦烏向來很少與男人往來，對男女之事全然無知；當她看見這些酋長全都在她所居住的土丘四周紮營時，她十分納悶他們究竟是為何而來。有一天，她從自家屋子所在圍欄的大門向外望去，看見圖伊·拉凱帕正望著她；她招手要他上來，等他來了，便問他是什麼使這些男人都住到這裡來。他回答說他只能代表自己說話，他之所以在此，是因為他喜歡她。「你喜歡我什麼呢？」她問道——「我的頭、我的腳、我的手臂？」他於是告訴她，他想與她同眠；圖阿瓦瓦烏聽不懂這話，便請他進屋來，讓她看看他想要的究竟是什麼。

passages.text: So the chief followed her into the house and had his way with her. When he had finished she said to him, 'So that is what you chiefs have come for! Now go, and don't come here any more!' Then Tuavavau called her companions and said to them, 'Alas, I never knew that there was such a bad thing in the world as this, that a man should treat a woman as a rooster treats a hen. Such a world is not a good place for me.' So saying, she ran and leaped from the hill top over the steep precipice into the sea. So died Tuavavau.
passages.note: Paraphrase of E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales, pp. 202-203 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是酋長跟著她進了屋，對她為所欲為。事畢之後，她對他說：「原來你們這些酋長就是為這個而來的！現在走吧，別再來這裡了！」隨後圖阿瓦瓦烏喚來她的同伴，對她們說：「唉，我從不知道世上竟有這樣壞的事，一個男人竟像公雞對待母雞那樣對待女人。這樣的世界對我來說不是個好地方。」說罷，她奔跑起來，從山頂躍過陡峭的懸崖，投入海中。圖阿瓦瓦烏就這樣死了。

title.en: Okonorote and the Cotton Ladder (Brett Version)
title.zh: 奧科諾羅特與棉梯（布雷特版）

region.en: Sky-land above the Warau swamps
region.zh: 瓦勞沼地之上天界

period: Warrau oral tradition; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part II 'Legends of the Waraus', 'Legend of Okonorote'

summary.en: 'Say, Okonorote, thou archer so gay, whither away?' In that high abode, above the blue sky, were no living creatures save those that could fly, and the young Warau race, placed there by their Maker, the Wise and the Good. Pursuing a rare bird with lovely plumage, he transfixed it with a keen arrow — but arrow and bird were nowhere to be found, till he saw a deep pit and, approaching with care, saw daylight beneath him: far below he could see forests grow, wide plains and savannahs where rivulets flow, deer and peccary, the choice paca, and birds soaring near the sky. The tribe prepared a rope ladder of cotton — it took many months, and was lengthened till it grappled the trees of this lower ground. Okonorote ventured below, shot a young deer, kindled a flame, and found the venison excellent food. Ascending again with a portion of game, his words and its flavour put all in a glow: 'We cannot stay here!' So they came down the rope ladder to this world below — all reached the ground in safety save one poor woman, the last, who got wedged in the hole which the others had passed; she fills it up, and that is why the Waraus never can get a fair peep through the sky.
summary.zh: 瓦勞祖居天界，天上惟有飛鳥與瓦勞人。獵人奧科諾羅特射異鳥，鳥與箭俱失；覓至深穴，俯見穴下有天光：森林、平原、河流、鹿豚盡在。族人採棉為繩梯，歷數月乃成，延至下界之樹。彼下而射鹿，取火炙肉，攜歸示眾；眾皆願遷。遂相繼而下——惟末行一婦卡於穴口，推挽不動。彼塞穴口，故瓦勞人不得窺天之孔也。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880 in verse; paraphrased into prose. Variant of the Warau sky-descent records.

passages.text: He could only shoot birds, for above the blue sky were no living creatures, save those that could fly, and the young Warau race, who in that high abode had been placed by their Maker, the Wise and the Good. Pursuing a rare bird with its plumage so gay, he crawled within shot and transfixed the bright beauty with a keen arrow; but, searching all the ground, arrow and bird were nowhere to be found — till he saw a deep pit, and, the sides being steep, approached it with care. Gone was his arrow for ever and aye, gone too that bright bird; and he, fascinated, unable to move, saw daylight beneath him as well as above.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of Okonorote'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他只能射鳥，因為在藍天之上，除了那些能飛的生物之外，別無其他生靈，還有那年輕的瓦勞族——造物主，即那位智慧而善良者，將他們安置在那高處的居所。他追逐一隻羽毛豔麗的珍禽，匍匐爬行到射程之內，以一枝銳利的箭射穿了那明豔的美物；然而他搜遍了整片地面，箭與鳥卻遍尋不著——直到他看見一個深坑，因坑壁陡峭，便小心翼翼地靠近。他的箭永遠地消失了，那隻明豔的鳥也同樣消失了；而他被深深吸引，動彈不得，只見腳下與頭頂同樣都有天光。

passages.text: Far, far below he could see forests grow; wide plains, and savannahs, where rivulets flow. He could see there the deer and the peccary go, the choice paca, and others which now we all know, while birds which soar high, rising near to the sky, his clear vision could spy. 'Prepare a rope ladder; I must go below and see if those creatures are useful or no. If I lose my life, one man only is slain.' All to the woods, picking cotton, would go: it took many months, but the ladder they made — lengthened above when too short it was found, till it grappled the trees upon this lower ground.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of Okonorote'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在遠遠的下方，他能看見森林生長；遼闊的平原與稀樹草原，其間溪流蜿蜒。他能看見那裡的鹿與西貒走動，還有上選的無尾刺豚鼠，以及其他如今我們都知曉的動物；而那些高飛、幾乎升近天際的鳥兒，他清明的視力也能辨識。「準備一條繩梯；我必須下去看看那些生物是否有用。若我喪命，也只死一人而已。」眾人皆往林中採棉花去了：這花了許多個月，但他們終於造好了繩梯——發現太短時便在上方接長，直到它鉤住了這下方地面上的樹木。

passages.text: He shot a young deer, kindled a flame in the Indian style with two pieces of wood, and found the venison excellent food. Ascending again — oh, what labour and pain! — a portion of game he brought up from below, sufficient his people to show; his words (and its flavour) put all in a glow: 'Oh! we cannot stay here; animal food we know to abound on that lower ground which Okonorote for Waraus has found!' So they came down the rope ladder to this world below, all reaching the ground in safety, save one — a poor woman, the last, who got wedged in the hole which the others had passed. She fills up the hole; and that is why we never can get a fair peep through the sky!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of Okonorote'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他射殺了一頭幼鹿，用兩塊木頭以印第安人的方式生起火來，發現那鹿肉是極好的食物。再度攀爬而上——啊，何等辛勞與痛苦！——他從下方帶上來一部分獵物，足以向他的族人展示；他的話語（以及那肉的滋味）令眾人皆振奮起來：「哦！我們不能留在這裡了；我們知道那下方的地面上盛產動物之食，那是奧科諾羅特為瓦勞人所尋得的！」於是他們順著繩梯下到這下方的世界，全都平安落地，只除了一人——一個可憐的婦人，走在最後，被卡在其他人已通過的洞中。她堵住了那個洞；這就是為何我們永遠無法好好地窺見天空！

title.en: The Legend of the Drought: the Warau Prayers for Rain
title.zh: 旱魃之傳：瓦勞祈雨之辭

region.en: Warau swamps, Orinoco delta
region.zh: 奧里諾科三角洲瓦勞沼地

period: Warrau oral tradition; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part II 'Legends of the Waraus', 'Legend of the Drought'

summary.en: See the Warau race begin life in this new world below: with their bows the hunters won plenteous food, yet they felt within them grow anxious dread of future woe — savage beasts of prey abounded, reptiles coiled in trees around, and one thing filled all with fear: scanty water and unclean, for streamlets small in marshes green were then all that could be seen. 'Oh, where shall we water find, till the wished-for rain shall fall? Other woes we bear resigned, but this thirst consumes us all! Let us now, both great and small, on our mighty Maker call. O Karima (Father) Thou! We Thy place no more shall see. Ka-idamo (Master) Thou! All things are at Thy command. Must we perish beneath Thy hand, wretched, miserable band?' Kanonatu, throned on high — so Waraus the Maker call — heard, and from the darkening sky caused the welcome rain to fall, and made the rivers great and small which abundance bring to all; women filled their vessels to the brim, while the men saw joyfully glitt'ring fish in rivers swim.
summary.zh: 瓦勞人初居下界，獵者弓下得食甚豐；然猛獸毒蛇環伺，尤懼水之少且穢——溪流細小，皆在綠沼中。眾呼曰：『何處得水，以候甘霖？他苦可忍，此渴難支！請呼我造物主。卡里瑪（父也）！我等不復見爾之居。凱伊達莫（主也）！萬物皆在爾手。我儕將滅於爾掌乎？可憐之眾！』高居之卡諾納圖——瓦勞人之造者也——聞之，使甘霖自陰雲而降，成大小諸河；婦人滿其器，男子見銀鱗之魚游於川。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880. im Thurn explicitly suspected this 'prayer for rain' of being introduced under European teaching (Indians 'make no prayer'); the record is kept with that caution.

passages.text: See the Warau race begin life in this new world below: with their bows the hunters win plenteous food — no want they know; yet they feel within them grow anxious dread of future woe. Safety, which in heaven they had, here on earth cannot be found; good is mingled here with bad; savage beasts of prey abound. One thing then filled all with fear: scanty water and unclean — streamlets small, in marshes green, then were all that could be seen.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of the Drought'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 看哪，瓦勞族在這下方的嶄新世界中開始生活：獵人們以弓箭贏得豐足的食物——他們不知匱乏；然而他們內心卻生出對未來災禍的焦慮恐懼。他們在天上曾有的安穩，在這地上卻尋不著；善在此與惡相混；兇猛的野獸四處橫行。於是有一件事令所有人充滿恐懼：水源稀少且不潔——綠色沼澤中的細小溪流，便是當時所能見到的一切。

passages.text: 'Oh, where shall we water find, till the wished-for rain shall fall? Other woes we bear, resigned, but this thirst consumes us all! Let us now, both great and small, on our mighty Maker call. We forsook our Father-friend; we forsook His place on high; death by thirst He now will send. O Karima (Father) Thou! We Thy place no more shall see. Ka-idamo (Master) Thou! All things are at Thy command. Must we perish beneath Thy hand, wretched, miserable band?'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of the Drought'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「哦，在期盼的雨水降下之前，我們要到何處尋水？其他的苦難我們都忍受、順從，但這乾渴卻吞噬了我們所有人！如今讓我們，無論大小，都向我們大能的造物主呼求。我們背棄了我們的父友；我們背棄了祂在高處的居所；如今祂將以乾渴降下死亡。哦，卡里瑪（父）啊！我們再也見不到祢的居所。卡伊達莫（主）啊！萬物皆在祢的號令之下。我們這群可悲可憐的人，難道必須死在祢的手中嗎？」

passages.text: Kanonatu, throned on high (so Waraus the Maker call), heard, and from the darkening sky caused the welcome rain to fall; made the rivers great and small, which abundance bring to all. Women then, with happy glee, filled their vessels to the brim, while the men saw joyfully glitt'ring fish in rivers swim: strange it seemed, and, like a dream, food and drink in every stream!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of the Drought'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 高坐寶座上的卡諾納圖（瓦勞人如此稱呼造物主）聽見了，便從漸暗的天空降下可喜的雨水；使大小河流皆成，為眾人帶來豐足。婦人們於是滿心歡喜，將器皿盛得滿溢，而男人們則欣喜地看見閃爍的魚兒在河中游動：這一切看似奇異，恍如一場夢，每條溪流中皆有食物與飲水！

title.en: The Legend of the Great Waters: Eight Men and Six Women
title.zh: 大水之傳：八男六女

region.en: Warau swamps, Orinoco delta
region.zh: 奧里諾科三角洲瓦勞沼地

period: Warrau oral tradition; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part II 'Legends of the Waraus', 'Legend of the Great Waters'

summary.en: Years rolled on, and men, grown hateful, ceased their passions to restrain; they took their Maker's gifts, ungrateful, thanked Him not for sun and rain, and forsook Him once again when they ceased to suffer pain. Kanonatu, seeing slaughter, acts of rapine, deeds unclean, sent their punishment by water, which had once their blessing been: floods, obeying Him, were seen o'er the hills and valleys green. Eight poor men, in that disaster, with six women, trembling stood; pausing in His wrath, the Master saw their hearts still true and good, bade them take the bahbi wood, safe to float amidst the flood. Evil spirits of the waters saw them float past undrowned: they were saved that sons and daughters might again on earth be found, and from them mankind abound, fish, and hunt, and till the ground. He who saved them had provided land to which they might repair; streams appeared as floods subsided, one small lake shone bright and fair — yet of that He said: 'Beware! Shun its waters, bathe not there!' Well our sires obeyed the warning; ages pass, and no Warau goes where those waters calm repose.
summary.zh: 年久而人惡，縱欲不制；忘恩於日雨之賜，痛止則復棄主。卡諾納圖見殺戮掠奪諸穢行，乃以水罰之——水昔其恩賜也。洪過陵谷。八男六女，戰慄而存；主察其心尚善，命取巴巴木以浮。水鬼見之而不得溺。彼等得存，俾子孫再殖於地——漁獵耕種皆自此出。主備其土；水退川現，一小湖明澈——然主誡曰：『慎之！毋浴其中！』先祖謹遵；至今瓦勞人無敢近彼靜水者。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880 in verse; paraphrased into prose. Flood-cluster record.

passages.text: Years rolled on, and men, grown hateful, ceased their passions to restrain; took their Maker's gifts, ungrateful, thanked Him not for sun and rain; but forsook Him once again, when they ceased to suffer pain. Kanonatu, seeing slaughter, acts of rapine, deeds unclean, sent their punishment by water, which had once their blessing been: floods, obeying Him, were seen o'er the hills and valleys green.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of the Great Waters'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 歲月流逝，人們變得可憎，不再約束自己的情慾；他們領受造物主的恩賜卻不知感恩，不為陽光與雨水感謝祂；當他們不再受苦之時，卻又一次背棄了祂。卡諾納圖見殺戮、劫掠與不潔之行，便以水降下他們的懲罰——那水曾一度是他們的祝福：洪水順從祂，漫過青翠的山丘與谷地。

passages.text: Eight poor men, in that disaster, with six women, trembling stood. Pausing in His wrath, the Master saw their hearts still true and good, bade them take the bahbi wood, safe to float amidst the flood. Evil spirits of the waters saw them then float past undrowned. They were saved that sons and daughters might again on earth be found, and from them mankind abound, fish, and hunt, and till the ground.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of the Great Waters'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在那場災難中，八個窮苦的男子與六個女子，顫抖地站立著。造物主在盛怒中暫歇，見他們的心仍舊真誠善良，便吩咐他們取來巴赫比木，好讓它在洪水之中安然漂浮。水中的惡靈看見他們漂浮而過，竟未溺斃。他們因此得救，好讓兒女能再度在大地上出現，並使後世子孫繁衍，得以捕魚、狩獵、耕種土地。

passages.text: He who saved them had provided land, to which they might repair. Streams appeared as floods subsided, one small lake shone bright and fair. Yet of that he said: 'Beware! Shun its waters, bathe not there!' Well our sires obeyed the warning; some to guard that lake they chose, lest some bather, danger scorning, there should meet with deadly foes. Ages pass. No Warau goes where those waters calm repose!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of the Great Waters'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 拯救他們的那一位早已備妥土地，供他們前往安居。洪水退去後，溪流湧現，一座小湖閃耀著明亮而秀麗的光。然而論到那湖，他說：『當心！避開它的水，不可在那裡沐浴！』我們的祖先謹守這警告；有些人更自願守護那座湖，免得有沐浴者輕忽危險，在那裡遭遇致命的仇敵。歲月流逝。至今沒有瓦勞人敢去那平靜湖水安歇之處！

title.en: Korobona and the Rod of Charmed Wood
title.zh: 科羅波納與符木之杖

region.en: Waramuri, Barima River, Guyana (Warrau)
region.zh: 蓋亞那巴里馬河瓦拉穆里瓦勞之地

period: Warrau oral tradition; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part II 'Legends of the Waraus', 'Legend of Korobona' (1)

summary.en: Two Warau maidens sweetly sang of the waters calm and clear; though their brothers said, 'Beware, the lake is fatal, bathe not there!' they dared to venture nigh. Fair Korobona, the elder sister, led: 'We, by an idle threat restrained, from these clear waters have refrained; come, sister, bathe with me.' She plunged in and, diving and swimming, saw before her a rod of charmed wood — oh that some power had stayed her hand, and forced the maid to let it stand, her safeguard while it stood! But wild with glee she shook the rod and broke the mighty charm; they saw a man-like form arise, and Korobona was his prize, held by a powerful arm. (A water spirit, beneath the wave, lay bound by mightier power, till some one swimming in the lake should dare that charmed rod to shake: that was the destined hour.) 'O Warau maid!' the spirit said, 'thy sister there may go; but thee I hold: thou for a time my home must share, and come with me below.'
summary.zh: 二瓦勞女常至靜湖之畔而歌；兄誡曰：『彼湖致命，勿浴！』長姊科羅波納曰：『虛言何足懼，妹其偕我浴。』入水而游，見水中一符木之杖——惜乎！彼不持之，自毀其護符。杖折魅解；水中起一人形，強臂執之——蓋水鬼為大神所縛，待泳者搖杖之時而脫，此其注定之刻也。鬼曰：『瓦勞女！汝妹可去；汝則留，暫居吾水底之家。』

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880 in verse; paraphrased into prose.

passages.text: Two Warau maidens sweetly sang: 'O waters calm and clear! We love our happy walks to take by thy sweet margin, woodland lake, and find our pleasure here.' Those maidens, from the hills at first that guarded spot would spy; then, though their brothers said 'Beware, the lake is fatal, bathe not there!' they dared to venture nigh.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of Korobona'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兩名瓦勞少女甜美地唱著：『噢，平靜清澈的水啊！我們喜愛在你甜美的岸邊漫步，林間之湖，並在此尋得我們的歡樂。』起初，那些少女只是從山丘上窺望那守護之地；後來，儘管她們的兄長說『當心，那湖是致命的，不可在那裡沐浴！』她們仍斗膽靠近。

passages.text: At length fair Korobona said (the elder sister she): 'We, by an idle threat restrained, from these clear waters have refrained; come, sister, bathe with me. For what is here to do us harm? We maidens are alone.' Straight she plunged in, and both, through waters fair and clear, began to dive and swim. Before her Korobona saw a rod of charmed wood — oh that some power had stayed her hand, and forced the maid to let it stand, her safeguard while it stood!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of Korobona'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 終於，美麗的科羅博娜說道（她是姊姊）：『我們只因一句空言恫嚇，便一直遠離這些清澈的水；來吧，妹妹，與我一同沐浴。這裡有什麼能傷害我們呢？我們這些少女是獨自在此。』她當即躍入水中，兩人便在明淨秀麗的水中開始潛水與游泳。科羅博娜在她面前看見一根施了法術的木杖——噢，但願有某種力量能止住她的手，迫使這少女任它立著，因它立著時便是她的護佑！

passages.text: But, wild with glee, she shook the rod and broke the mighty charm. They saw a man-like form arise, and Korobona was his prize, held by a powerful arm. (A water spirit, 'neath the wave, lay bound by mightier power, till some one, swimming in the lake, should dare that charmed rod to shake: that was the destined hour.) 'O Warau maid!' the spirit said, 'Thy sister there may go; but thee I hold. O woman fair! Thou for a time my home must share, and come with me below.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of Korobona'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而她欣喜若狂，搖動那木杖，破除了強大的法術。她們看見一個似人的形體升起，科羅博娜成了他的獵獲，被一隻強壯的手臂抓住。（一個水靈被更強大的力量困在波濤之下，直到有人游入湖中，斗膽搖動那施法的木杖：那便是命定的時刻。）『噢，瓦勞少女！』那水靈說道，『你的妹妹可以離去；但你，我要留下。噢，美麗的女子！你必須暫時與我同住，隨我下到水底。』

title.en: Korobona's Son: the First Carib Rises from the Grave
title.zh: 科羅波納之子：首加勒比自墓而起

region.en: Waramuri, Barima River, Guyana (Warrau)
region.zh: 蓋亞那巴里馬河瓦拉穆里瓦勞之地

period: Warrau oral tradition; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part II 'Legends of the Waraus', 'Legend of Korobona' (3-4)

summary.en: The hapless Korobona now lives in the woods alone; another babe she hides from view, for if her fault her brothers knew, blood only could atone. One, passing by, heard the infant's cry and told her brethren hunting near; soon she saw the four appear, all wild with rage and shame: two dragged their sister home, two pierced the child through with an arrow and left him where he lay. But the care she gave revived that hapless child, who grew far more than other babes in wisdom and in size, shunning all eyes but hers. Her track, by small footprints shown, told each brother her secret; they hunted her through the woods, screened her from their arrows, and cut him into pieces small. She cursed their cruelty: 'Vile slayers of the innocent! The woes you fear will now be sent — and come through you, not me!' A mighty wonder happened then, for that great change which waits all men touched not the serpent child: the flower-decked heap began with life to heave, and a mighty warrior rose from the mound, white down adorning his short black hair, his skin like copper, his cheeks and brow besmeared with vermilion like blood — thus the first Carib stern arose. No Warau could his strength withstand; he slaughtered those who faced his club, forced the rest to flee, took their daughters for wives, and as his children increased they took the Warau's place.
summary.zh: 科羅波納獨居林中，再匿其子。兄四人怒而尋至；二人曳姊歸，二人以箭貫兒而棄之。母護而活之，其兒智體逾常，匿於密樹，惟母得見。足跡洩秘；眾追而射之，碎其體。母咒曰：『戮無辜者，禍將自爾出！』屍上花開，異變忽至：一切人皆有之死，不能加於蛇子之身。丘中有生，首肩漸起；偉武之人出焉——白絨飾短黑髮，膚如銅，頰額涂朱如血——首加勒比遂起。瓦勞莫能禦；其子孫繁衍，遂代瓦勞而興。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880 in verse; paraphrased into prose.

passages.text: The hapless Korobona now lives in the woods alone; another babe there hides from view, for if her fault her brothers knew, blood only could atone. One, passing by, the infant's cry heard, and upon her came; then told her brethren, hunting near, and soon she saw the four appear, all wild with rage and shame. Two of them dragged their sister home; two turned the child to slay: they with an arrow pierced him through, and left him where he lay.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of Korobona'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不幸的科羅博娜如今獨自住在林中；另一個嬰孩藏匿在那裡，不為人見，因為若她的兄長得知她的過錯，唯有流血才能贖罪。有一人路過，聽見嬰孩的哭聲，便朝她走來；隨後告訴了在附近狩獵的兄弟們，不久她便看見四人出現，個個滿懷狂怒與羞恥。其中兩人把妹妹拖回家去；兩人則轉身要殺那孩子：他們用箭將他射穿，棄於他倒臥之處。

passages.text: 'The child is dead,' the slayers said — but knew not that the care she gave revived that hapless child. He grew far more than other babes in wisdom and in size, and, still concealed in some thick tree, till he his mother's form could see, would shun all other eyes. With food she daily sought the woods where he was doomed to stay; but Korobona quite forgot that some her track might know — her track, by those small footprints shown. Each brother then, her secret known, prepared the shaft and bow; they screened her from his foes, cut him into pieces small, and she cursed their cruelty: 'Vile slayers of the innocent! The woes you fear will now be sent — and come through you, not me!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of Korobona'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「孩子已經死了。」殺手們說道——卻不知她所給予的照料，竟使那不幸的孩子復活了。他在智慧與體格上都遠勝其他嬰孩，並且仍舊藏身於某棵茂密的樹中，直到他能看見母親的身影，卻避開所有其他的目光。她每日帶著食物前往他註定棲身的那片樹林；但科羅博納全然忘了，或許有人能認出她的足跡——那由細小腳印顯露出來的足跡。於是每個兄弟在得知她的秘密之後，便備好箭與弓；他們替她擋開他的敵人，將他切成小塊，她便詛咒他們的殘忍：「你們這些殺害無辜者的惡徒！你們所畏懼的災禍如今將被送來——而且是經由你們，不是我！」

passages.text: A mighty wonder happened then, for that great change which waits all men touched not the serpent child. At length that heap, with flowers bedecked, began with life to heave; she seemed these words to hear: 'Thy son shall now avenge his murder done: O mother, cease to grieve!' And first a head and shoulders rose, slow growing from that mound: a mighty form appeared, well armed, with limbs complete and sound — white down adorned his short black hair, his skin like copper shone, more fair than with Waraus had been, his cheeks and brow besmeared with vermilion like blood. Thus the first Carib stern arose. No Warau could his strength withstand; he slaughtered those who dared his club, forced the rest to flee, took their daughters for wives, and as his children still increased, they took the Warau's place — invincible, from Wahma sprung.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of Korobona'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著發生了一樁巨大的奇蹟，因為那等待著所有人的重大變化，並未觸及那蛇之子。終於，那堆土上飾滿了花朵，開始隨著生命而起伏；她似乎聽見這些話語：「你的兒子如今將為他所遭的殺害復仇：哦，母親，別再悲傷了！」先是頭與肩升起，從那土堆中緩緩生長：一個巨大的形體出現了，裝備精良，四肢完整健全——白色的絨毛點綴著他短短的黑色頭髮，他的皮膚如銅般閃耀，比瓦勞人更為俊美，他的雙頰與額頭塗抹著如血般的朱紅。加勒比人的第一位嚴峻先祖就此崛起。沒有哪個瓦勞人能抵擋他的力量；他用棍棒屠殺那些膽敢抵抗的人，迫使其餘的人逃離，擄走他們的女兒為妻，而隨著他的子孫不斷繁衍，他們取代了瓦勞人的位置——所向無敵，出自瓦赫馬。

title.en: Warau Ideas Concerning Departed Souls
title.zh: 瓦勞亡魂之觀

region.en: Warau swamps and Trinidad
region.zh: 瓦勞沼地與特立尼達

period: Warrau oral tradition; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part II 'Legends of the Waraus', 'Warau Ideas of Departed Souls'

summary.en: When Waraus were oppressed by stronger foes, the fears which they through life had known beset them at its close. Each charged his children when he died to place his weapons at his side: 'Lay bow and arrows in my grave, that I may keep at bay the souls of foemen fierce and brave, and all who bar my way. My soul, thus armed, none dare withstand, to keep it from the spirit land.' How different was the legend told on Trinidad's fair isle, where Waraus gathered fruits of old and rested there awhile: there souls of good men they could find in glittering humming birds enshrined — those birds, like flashing jewels seen, bedecked each lovely bower; as ruby, topaz, emerald green, they kissed each fragrant flower, and saw fair hills and forests rise around their blissful paradise. But Chaymas dared those birds molest — then sank beneath the ground; and now, where happy souls had rest, the lake of pitch is found.
summary.zh: 瓦勞人受強鄰之迫，生時之懼臨終猶在。各遺命子孫置武器於其側：『以弓箭殉我，俾我魂禦仇魂之擊，無阻我歸靈土之路。』異哉，特立尼達島之傳：昔瓦勞人採果於彼，善者之魂棲於閃爍蜂鳥之身——如寶石之鳥，吻每朵香花，繞其極樂之丘林。然查馬人敢擾其鳥，遂陷地中；今善魂所棲之處，乃為瀝青之湖。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880; includes the Pitch Lake legend retold by Charles Kingsley, read critically.

passages.text: When Waraus were, as we have shown, oppressed by stronger foes, the fears which they through life had known beset them at its close. Each charged his children when he died to place his weapons at his side: 'Lay bow and arrows in my grave, that I may keep at bay the souls of foemen fierce and brave, and all who bar my way. My soul, thus armed, none dare withstand, to keep it from the spirit land!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Warau Ideas of Departed Souls'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當瓦勞人如我們所述，受到更強敵人的壓迫時，他們一生所知的種種恐懼，在生命終結時也纏繞著他們。每個人在死時都囑咐自己的孩子，將他的武器放在他身旁：「把弓與箭放進我的墳墓，好讓我能抵禦凶猛勇敢的敵人之魂，以及所有阻擋我道路者。我的靈魂如此武裝，便無人敢於抵抗，好使它得以進入靈界！」

passages.text: How different was the legend told on Trinidad's fair isle, where Waraus gathered fruits of old and rested there awhile: there souls of good men they could find in glittering humming birds enshrined. Those birds, like flashing jewels seen, bedecked each lovely bower; as ruby, topaz, emerald green, they kissed each fragrant flower, and saw fair hills and forests rise around their blissful paradise.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Warau Ideas of Departed Souls'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在特立尼達這座美麗的島嶼上，所流傳的傳說又是多麼不同啊，瓦勞人古時在那裡採集果實，並在那裡休憩片刻：他們能在閃爍的蜂鳥之中，尋得善人的靈魂。那些鳥兒，宛如閃耀的寶石，裝點著每一座可愛的涼亭；如紅寶石、黃玉、翠綠的祖母綠，牠們親吻每一朵芬芳的花，並看見美麗的山丘與森林，環繞著牠們的幸福樂園。

passages.text: But Chaymas dared those birds molest, and then sank beneath the ground; and now, where happy souls once had rest among the fragrant bowers, the lake of pitch is found: a wild Warau myth of ages past, told to English readers at last, and kept here as a record of how paradise can turn to bitumen in the telling.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Warau Ideas of Departed Souls'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但柴馬人竟敢侵擾那些鳥兒，於是便沉入地下；如今，在那些幸福靈魂曾於芬芳涼亭間安息之處，發現了瀝青湖：這是一則來自遠古的狂野瓦勞神話，終於講述給英語讀者，並保留於此，作為樂園如何在講述中化為瀝青的記錄。

title.en: Abore the Father of Inventions and Wowtah the Frog-Queen
title.zh: 發明之父阿博雷與蛙后瓦特

region.en: Barima River, Guyana (Warrau)
region.zh: 蓋亞那巴里馬河瓦勞之地

period: Warrau oral tradition; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part II 'Legends of the Waraus', 'Legend of Abore (the Warau Father of Inventions)'

summary.en: Abore the clever, Abore the brave, had served Wowtah's caprices like some household slave: bows, arrows, and such things he strove to improve, but she was most jealous lest aught he should love more than her, and sent him daily into the dense forests for bees' nests. A kind spirit met him at the root of a hollow tree and revealed the truth: 'Wowtah is a spirit, such also am I. Wowtah chose to be the great queen of the frogs; by day or by night it was her delight, with a terrible croak, other creatures to fright.' She told how as a boy he was seen by Wowtah and became her chief joy; how, in the form of a woman, she deceived his parents, who soon died — suspected by every Warau; how he had grown a tall youth through her mighty charms and would soon have to make her his bride. 'Seek not to slay! Having grown beneath her charm, still her slave thou must be, unless thou canst flee from her over the wide sea.' So Abore floated a gourd-half, then modelled a vessel from an oblong seed-pod, made a large vessel of wax, shaped till it was a woibka — canoe; his mistress broke the waxen craft; with a young cousin he worked in the bush, made paddles, strengthened the wax, lured Wowtah into a hollow tree after honey, drove a wedge fast, and launched: 'Ho, Waraus! This, this is the shape which your vessels must have. Make your woibakas so, friends; but make them of wood.' And the Warau land saw their last of Abore — they saw him no more.
summary.zh: 阿博雷智勇兼備，然如家奴之侍蛙后瓦特。彼思改良弓箭諸器，而瓦特妒之，日遣其入密林取蜜。一善靈語之曰：『瓦特乃鬼也，吾亦鬼。瓦特擇為蛙群之后，日夜以怖吼嚇百獸。』又述其幼時為瓦特所中，偽為婦人入其父母之家，父母旋死——眾皆疑之。『勿圖殺之！汝既為其術所困，非越大海不得脫。』阿博雷乃試葫蘆之半，繼以長莢為模，製蠟舟，形如今之所謂woibka（獨木舟也）。瓦特碎其蠟舟；遂與從弟匿林中製槳固蠟，誘瓦特入空心樹取蜜，緊楔其內，遂發舟曰：『瓦勞人乎！舟之形當如此；依此製之，然以木為之！』瓦勞之地，從此不復見阿博雷矣。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880 in verse; paraphrased into prose.

passages.text: Abore the clever, Abore the brave, had served her caprices like some household slave. To follow her wishes the youth was content, although his keen mind on inventions was bent: bows, arrows, and such things he strove to improve; but she was most jealous lest aught he should love more than her, and from all his works sent him away, to search the dense forests for bees, day by day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of Abore'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 聰明的阿博雷，勇敢的阿博雷，曾像家奴一般順從她的任性。這青年樂於追隨她的意願，儘管他敏銳的心思專注於種種發明：弓、箭之類的東西，他竭力加以改良；但她極為嫉妒，唯恐他喜愛任何事物勝過她，便把他從他所有的工作中打發走，日復一日地派他去茂密的森林裡尋找蜜蜂。

passages.text: When he saw, sitting down on the root of a tree, a young Indian maid — fair and graceful was she — he passed without notice, as good Indians do. But she said: 'Abore! Thy parents I knew. Wowtah is a spirit. Such also am I! We spirits assume any figure we please: some appear as bush-hogs, some as jaguars or dogs; while some, as large snakes, love the rivers and bogs — but Wowtah chose to be the great queen of the frogs. By day or by night it was her delight, with a terrible croak, other creatures to fright.' She told him how, when a young boy, he was seen by Wowtah and became her chief joy; how she, in the form of a woman, deceived his parents, and how his parents soon died — Wowtah suspected by every Warau.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of Abore'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他看見一位年輕的印第安少女坐在樹根上——她容貌秀麗、舉止優雅——便像規矩的印第安人那樣，不加理會地走了過去。但她說道：「阿博雷！你的父母我認識。沃塔是神靈。我也是！我們神靈能隨意化身為任何形貌：有的化為野豬，有的化為美洲豹或狗；有的化為大蛇，喜愛河流與沼澤——但沃塔選擇做青蛙的偉大女王。無論晝夜，她都樂於以可怕的呱呱之聲驚嚇其他生靈。」她告訴他，當他還是個小男孩時，如何被沃塔看見，成了她的心頭之樂；她如何化身為女人，欺騙了他的父母，他的父母又如何很快死去——每一個瓦勞人都懷疑是沃塔所為。

passages.text: 'O seek not to slay! But heed well what I say: 'twould be vain to shed blood, nor canst thou flee away. Having grown beneath her charm, still her slave thou must be, unless thou canst flee from her o'er the wide sea!' The half of a gourd he could readily float, but its shape would not do for a boat; from an oblong seed-pod his best model he drew. He formed a large vessel of wax, improved on its shape till our people might view what they call woibka, but others 'canoe'. His mistress came there, severely eyed, then broke it, and scattered the wax far and wide. With a young cousin he worked in the bush, lured Wowtah with a nest of fine honey deep in the heart of a large hollow tree, drove a great wedge tightly in — and launched: 'Ho, Waraus! This, this is the shape which your vessels must have. Make your woibakas so, friends; but make them of wood.' And thus they beheld, from the wild ocean shore, their last of Abore — they saw him no more!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Legend of Abore'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「啊，不要殺戮！但要好好聽我說：流血是徒勞的，你也逃不掉。你既在她的魔力下長大，就仍是她的奴隸，除非你能渡過廣闊的大海逃離她！」半個葫蘆他輕易就能浮起來，但它的形狀不適合做船；他從一個長形的種莢得到最好的模型。他用蠟造了一艘大船，不斷改進它的形狀，直到我們族人看到他們稱之為「沃伊布卡」、而別人稱之為「獨木舟」的東西。他的女主人來到那裡，嚴厲地看了一眼，然後把它打碎，將蠟撒得遠遠的。他帶著一位年輕的表親在叢林中勞作，用一棵大空心樹深處的一窩上等蜂蜜引誘沃塔，緊緊打入一根大楔子——然後下水：「喂，瓦勞人！這，這才是你們的船該有的形狀。朋友們，照這樣造你們的沃伊布卡；但要用木頭造。」於是他們從荒涼的大洋岸邊，見到了阿博雷的最後一面——他們再也沒有見到他！

title.en: The Sequel: Abore Among the White People
title.zh: 阿博雷後篇：居白人之間

region.en: Across the sea (Warrau modern tradition)
region.zh: 海外之地（瓦勞近世傳說）

period: Warrau oral tradition (modern addition); recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part II 'Legends of the Waraus', 'Sequel to the Ancient Legend'

summary.en: 'Waraus heard of Abore at last. He went over a smooth sea and, ere long, found land — some island — and landed upon that new strand. There, discarding the wax, he made a craft of wood, and visited places just as he thought good. At last he arrived where white people abound, whom poor and distressed above all men he found: they did support life, he could hardly tell how; far more wretched were they than the lowest Warau. When he saw them his heart with compassion flowed o'er, and he said, 'I will make my abode on this shore.' So he made up his mind the white people to raise: they, squalid and bare, had no garments to wear, till taught by Abore good clothes to prepare. He taught the white people to weave and to sew, to be skilful in wood and in iron, from a nail to a gun. To the whole world a friend, the good things he had made in large ships he would send; he improved the rough plan of his first waxen boat to the huge ships we see now — great monsters afloat — which bring you all things, from a pin to a coat. 'Tis said that Abore still lives: the magical power which, when he was young, that spirit imparted has made his life long; if he were to return she would claim him again, so he's forced in the white people's land to remain.'
summary.zh: 『瓦勞人終聞阿博雷之音。彼渡靜海，得一小島而登焉；棄蠟舟而製木舟，遍遊諸地。末至白人之國——見其窮困，更甚於最低之瓦勞——憫然曰：『吾將居此岸。』遂教白人織衣縫裳，授以木工鐵工，自鐵釘以至火銃。彼以大舟運其良器於天下；改良初之蠟舟而為今之巨舶——浮海之怪也——自衣針而至大氅，無所不載。相傳阿博雷今猶在世：靈所賦之力延其年壽；若返故里，瓦特必再索之，故終老於白人之邦。』

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880; an acknowledged modern addition to the ancient legend, read critically.

passages.text: 'He went o'er a smooth sea, and, ere long, he found land — some island — and landed upon that new strand. There, discarding the wax, he a craft made of wood, and visited places, just as he thought good. At last he arrived where white people abound, whom poor and distressed above all men he found. They did support life, he could hardly tell how; far more wretched were they than the lowest Warau. When he saw them his heart with compassion flowed o'er, and he said: I will make my abode on this shore.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Sequel to the Ancient Legend'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「他駛過一片平靜的海，不久便發現了陸地——某座島嶼——於是登上那片新的海岸。在那裡，他丟棄了蠟，用木頭造了一艘船，隨心所欲地遊歷各地。最後他來到白人眾多的地方，發現他們比任何人都貧窮困苦。他們勉強維持生計，他幾乎說不出他們是怎麼活的；他們比最卑下的瓦勞人還要悲慘得多。他見到他們時，心中充滿憐憫，說道：我要在這岸上安家。」

passages.text: 'So he made up his mind the white people to raise. They, squalid and bare, had no garments to wear, till taught by Abore good clothes to prepare. He taught the white people to weave and to sew, to be skilful in wood and in iron — from a nail to a gun. To the whole world a friend, the good things he had made in large ships he would send. He improved the rough plan of his first waxen boat to the huge ships we see now — great monsters afloat — which bring you all things, from a pin to a coat.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Sequel to the Ancient Legend'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「於是他下定決心要扶助白人。他們骯髒赤裸，沒有衣服可穿，直到阿博雷教他們製作好衣服。他教白人織布縫衣，精通木工與鐵工——從一根釘子到一桿槍。他對全世界都是朋友，他所造的好東西都用大船運送出去。他把自己第一艘蠟船粗糙的設計，改進成我們如今所見的巨船——漂浮的巨大怪物——為你們運來一切東西，從一根針到一件外套。」

passages.text: 'Tis said that Abore still lives, though no tree that grows in our woods can be older than he. The magical power which, when he was young, that spirit imparted has made his life long; if he were to return she would claim him again, so he's forced in the white people's land to remain. Knife and gun, ammunition, a cutlass and hoe, rum, needles and pins, with some coarse calico, were once freely given to each Warau — the price of assistance to Indians paid: when slavery ceased their help was not required, so the custom of annual presents expired.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Sequel to the Ancient Legend'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說阿博雷仍然活著，我們林中生長的樹木，沒有一棵比他更古老。他年輕時那神靈所賦予的魔力，使他長壽；倘若他回去，她便會再次佔有他，所以他被迫留在白人的土地上。刀與槍、彈藥、一把砍刀和鋤頭、朗姆酒、針和別針，還有一些粗棉布，曾一度免費發給每個瓦勞人——這是付給印第安人協助的代價：當奴隸制廢除後，不再需要他們的幫助，於是每年贈禮的習俗便終止了。

title.en: The Purucaya: Seven Dead Incas Enthroned in Gold
title.zh: 普魯卡亞:七位先王坐擁金座

region.en: House of the Sun, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科太陽之屋(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 31, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: He disinterred the bodies of the seven deceased Incas, from Manco Ccapac to Yahuar-huaccac, which were all in the House of the Sun, enriching them with masks, head-dresses called chuco, medals, bracelets, sceptres called yauri or champi, and other ornaments of gold. He then placed them, in the order of their seniority, on a bench with a back, richly adorned with gold, and ordered great festivals to be celebrated with representations of the lives of each Inca. These festivals, which are called purucaya, were continued for more than four months. Great and sumptuous sacrifices were made to each Inca at the conclusion of the representation of his acts and life. This gave them such authority that it made all strangers adore them and worship them as gods; these strangers, when they beheld such majesty, humbled themselves and put up their hands to worship or mucha. The corpses were held in great respect and veneration until the Spaniards came to this land of Peru.
summary.zh: 帕查庫提掘出七位先王的遺體——自曼科·卡帕克至亞瓦爾-瓦卡克——皆藏於太陽之屋。他為他們添置面具、「丘科」頭飾、徽章、鐲環、名為「亞烏里」或「昌皮」的權杖及諸般金飾,再按輩分次序,將他們安置在飾滿黃金的靠背長椅上;又下令舉行盛大節慶,搬演每位印加王的生平。這種節慶稱為「普魯卡亞」,歷時四個多月。每位先王的功業演畢,便為其獻上豐盛祭祀。此舉威儀赫赫,四方來客見之,無不折腰俯首、舉手行「穆恰」崇拜之禮,奉先王如神明。直至西班牙人到來,這些先王遺體始終備受尊崇。

sensitivity.note: The purucaya as state theatre of the ancestor cult; the living king staging his dead predecessors.

passages.text: He disinterred the bodies of the seven deceased Incas, from Manco Ccapac to Yahuar-huaccac, which were all in the House of the Sun, enriching them with masks, head-dresses called chuco, medals, bracelets, sceptres called yauri or champi, and other ornaments of gold. He then placed them, in the order of their seniority, on a bench with a back, richly adorned with gold, and ordered great festivals to be celebrated with representations of the lives of each Inca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 31 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他掘出了七位已故印加王的遺體，從曼科·卡帕克到亞瓦爾·瓦卡克，這些遺體都安放在太陽神廟中，他為它們配上金製的面具、稱為「丘科」的頭飾、獎章、手鐲、稱為「堯里」或「昌皮」的權杖，以及其他金飾。然後，他按輩分順序將它們安放在一張飾有大量黃金的靠背長凳上，並下令舉行盛大的慶典，以表演每位印加王的生平。

passages.text: These festivals, which are called purucaya, were continued for more than four months. Great and sumptuous sacrifices were made to each Inca, at the conclusion of the representation of his acts and life. This gave them such authority that it made all strangers adore them, and worship them as gods... The corpses were held in great respect and veneration until the Spaniards came to this land of Peru.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 31 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這些節慶稱為普魯卡亞（purucaya），持續舉行了四個多月。在每位印加的功業與生平事蹟表演完畢之後，都為他獻上盛大而奢華的祭品。這賦予了他們如此大的權威，使所有外邦人都崇敬他們，把他們當作神明來膜拜……這些遺體備受尊崇與敬奉，直到西班牙人來到這片秘魯土地為止。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: The Two-Headed Serpent Talisman: Chuqui Ylla, Guauqui of Pachacuti
title.zh: 雙頭蛇護符:帕查庫提的伴身神楚基·伊利亞

region.en: House of the Sun, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科太陽之屋(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 31, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Besides these corpses, Pachacuti made two images of gold. He called one of them Viracocha Pachayachachi: it represented the creator, and was placed on the right of the image of the Sun. The other was called Chuqui ylla, representing lightning, placed on the left of the Sun. This image was most highly venerated by all. Inca Yupanqui adopted this idol for his guauqui, because he said that it had appeared and spoken in a desert place and had given him a serpent with two heads, to carry about with him always, saying that while he had it with him, nothing sinister could happen in his affairs. To these idols the Inca gave the use of lands, flocks, and servants, especially of certain women who lived in the same House of the Sun, in the manner of nuns.
summary.zh: 帕查庫提另鑄兩尊金像:一尊名「維拉科查·帕查亞查奇」,代表造物主,置於太陽神像之右;另一尊名「楚基·伊利亞」,代表閃電,置於太陽神像之左,受萬眾至高崇敬。印加·尤潘琪將這尊神像收為自己的「瓜烏基」(伴身兄弟神):因為據他所言,此像曾在荒野現身、開口說話,並賜他一條雙頭蛇,命他隨身攜帶——只要此蛇在身,諸事便不會遭逢兇險。印加王撥給這些神像田地、畜群與僕役,尤其是那些住在太陽之屋、如修女般的女子。

sensitivity.note: The lightning-god as personal oracle-brother; the two-headed serpent talisman links to the amaru imagery.

passages.text: Besides these corpses, Pachacuti made two images of gold. He called one of them Viracocha Pachayachachi. It represented the creator, and was placed on the right of the image of the Sun. The other was called Chuqui ylla, representing lightning, placed on the left of the Sun. This image was most highly venerated by all.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 31 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 除了這些遺體之外，帕查庫提（Pachacuti）還製作了兩尊黃金神像。他將其中一尊命名為維拉科查·帕查亞查奇（Viracocha Pachayachachi）。它代表造物主，被安置在太陽神像的右側。另一尊名為丘基·伊利亞（Chuqui ylla），代表閃電，被安置在太陽神像的左側。這尊神像受到所有人極度的崇敬。

passages.text: Inca Yupanqui adopted this idol for his guauqui, because he said that it had appeared and spoken in a desert place and had given him a serpent with two heads, to carry about with him always, saying that while he had it with him, nothing sinister could happen in his affairs. To these idols the Inca gave the use of lands, flocks, and servants, especially of certain women who lived in the same House of the Sun, in the manner of nuns.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 31 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 印加·尤潘基（Inca Yupanqui）將這尊神像收為自己的瓜烏基（guauqui，守護神），因為他說它曾在一片荒野中顯現並開口說話，還賜給他一條雙頭蛇，讓他隨身攜帶，並說只要他帶著它，他的事務中就不會發生任何不祥之事。印加賜予這些神像土地、畜群和僕役的使用權，尤其是某些住在同一座太陽之屋中、過著修女般生活的婦女。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: 'I Tread on My Enemies': The Order of the Inca Triumph
title.zh: 「我腳踏仇敵」:印加凱旋儀典

region.en: Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 33, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: The triumph was after this manner. The warriors marched in order, in their companies, dressed in the best manner possible, with songs and dances, and the captives, their eyes on the ground, dressed in long robes with many tassels. They entered by the streets of the city, which were very well adorned to receive them. They went on, enacting their battles and victories, on account of which they triumphed. On reaching the House of the Sun, the spoils and prisoners were thrown on the ground, and the Inca walked over them, trampling on them and saying: 'I tread on my enemies.' The prisoners were silent without raising their eyes. This order was used in all their triumphs.
summary.zh: 凱旋儀式如下:戰士按部伍列隊而行,盛裝奏樂,載歌載舞;俘虜則身披綴滿流蘇的長袍,垂首不敢仰視,隨隊入城。街道妝點一新,以迎王師;隊伍且行且演,重現征戰得勝之狀。行至太陽之屋,戰利品與俘虜被拋擲於地;印加王從其上走過,踏踐而行,口誦:「我腳踏我的仇敵。」俘虜默然,不敢舉目。凡凱旋,皆循此儀。

sensitivity.note: The triumph liturgy as ritual humiliation; repeated verbatim formula in Sarmiento's war narratives.

passages.text: The triumph was after this manner. The warriors marched in order, in their companies, dressed in the best manner possible, with songs and dances, and the captives, their eyes on the ground, dressed in long robes with many tassels. They entered by the streets of the city, which were very well adorned to receive them. They went on, enacting their battles and victories, on account of which they triumphed.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 33 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 凱旋儀式是這樣的。戰士們按隊伍行進，盡可能盛裝打扮，伴隨著歌唱與舞蹈；俘虜們則目光垂地，身穿飾有許多流蘇的長袍。他們從城中街道進入，那些街道已裝飾得極為華美以迎接他們。他們一路行進，重演他們的戰鬥與勝利，正是為了這些勝利而舉行凱旋慶典。

passages.text: On reaching the House of the Sun, the spoils and prisoners were thrown on the ground, and the Inca walked over them, trampling on them and saying: 'I tread on my enemies.' The prisoners were silent without raising their eyes. This order was used in all their triumphs.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 33 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 抵達太陽之屋時，戰利品與俘虜被扔在地上，印加從他們身上走過，踐踏著他們說道：「我踐踏我的敵人。」俘虜們默不作聲，不敢抬眼。這一儀式用於他們所有的凱旋慶典。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: The Necromancer's Stone: Inca Rocca Slays Inca Urco in the River
title.zh: 巫師之石:印加·羅卡河畔誅烏爾庫

region.en: Yucay valley and rock of Chupellusca (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尤卡伊河谷與丘佩盧斯卡岩(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 33, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Pachacuti heard that his brother Urco was in a valley called Yucay, four leagues from Cuzco, and that he had assembled some people. Fearing that the movement was intended against him the Inca marched there with his army. His brother Inca Rocca went with him, who had the reputation of being a great necromancer. Arriving at a place called Paca in the said valley, the Inca went out against his brother Urco, and there was a battle between them. Inca Rocca hurled a stone which hit Urco on the throat. The blow was so great that Urco fell into the river flowing down the ravine where they were fighting. Urco exerted himself and fled, swimming down the river, with his axe in his hand. In this way he reached a rock called Chupellusca, a league below Tampu, where his brothers overtook him and killed him. From thence the Inca Pachacuti Yupanqui, with his brother Inca Rocca, marched with their troops to Caquia Xaquixahuana to see his father, who refused ever to speak with or see him, owing to the rage he felt at the death of Inca Urco. But Inca Rocca went in where Viracocha was and said: 'Father! it is not reasonable that you should grieve so much at the death of Urco, for I killed him in self defence, he having come to kill me... Think no more of it, for my brother Pachacuti Yupanqui is to be Inca, and I hold that you should favour him and be as a father to him.' Seeing the resolution of his son Inca Rocca, Viracocha did not dare to reply or to contradict him. At the end of a short time Inca Viracocha died of grief at the death of Inca Urco, deprived and despoiled of all honour and property. They buried his body in Caquia Xaquixahuana.
summary.zh: 帕查庫提聞報:其兄烏爾庫在庫斯科四萊格外的尤卡伊谷糾集人馬,恐其意在圖己,便提兵征討。其兄印加·羅卡隨行——此人素有「大巫師」之名。行至谷中名為帕卡之地,印加王與烏爾庫接戰。印加·羅卡擲石擊中烏爾庫咽喉;一擊沉重,烏爾庫墜入溝壑間奔流的河水。他掙扎逃生,手持戰斧,順流泅泳而下,漂至坦普下游一萊格處的名為「丘佩盧斯卡」的岩石旁——兄弟們追至,將他殺死。帕查庫提·尤潘琪與印加·羅卡遂率兵赴夏基夏瓜納探望父親;老王因烏爾庫之死怒不可遏,拒不與長子言語相見。印加·羅卡入見維拉科查,說道:「父親!烏爾庫之死,何足如此哀慟?他是來殺我的,我自衛而誅之。您兒子眾多,不必為一人如此傷心。忘了吧——帕查庫提·尤潘琪當為印加王;依我之見,您應扶持他,如父待子。」印加·羅卡意志堅決,維拉科查不敢反駁,只好說:「就依你所言,凡事聽你安排。」不久之後,印加·維拉科查因烏爾庫之死憂傷而死,生前已被奪去一切榮銜財產。遺體葬於夏基夏瓜納。

sensitivity.note: Fratricide in the river; the necromancer epithet attaches to Inca Rocca in this tradition.

passages.text: His brother Inca Rocca went with him, who had the reputation of being a great necromancer. Arriving at a place called Paca in the said valley, the Inca went out against his brother Urco, and there was a battle between them. Inca Rocca hurled a stone which hit Urco on the throat. The blow was so great that Urco fell into the river flowing down the ravine where they were fighting. Urco exerted himself and fled, swimming down the river, with his axe in his hand. In this way he reached a rock called Chupellusca, a league below Tampu, where his brothers overtook him and killed him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 33 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的兄弟印加·羅卡（Inca Rocca）與他同行，此人素有偉大巫師之名。抵達該山谷中一個名為帕卡（Paca）的地方時，印加出擊對抗他的兄弟烏爾科（Urco），雙方之間爆發了一場戰鬥。印加·羅卡擲出一塊石頭，擊中了烏爾科的喉嚨。這一擊如此沉重，以致烏爾科跌入了他們交戰之處那道溝壑中奔流的河裡。烏爾科奮力掙扎，手持戰斧順流游去而逃。他就這樣到達了一塊名為丘佩柳斯卡（Chupellusca）的岩石，該處位於坦普（Tampu）下游一里格處，他的兄弟們在那裡追上了他並將他殺死。

passages.text: Inca Rocca went in, where Viracocha was and said: 'Father! it is not reasonable that you should grieve so much at the death of Urco, for I killed him in self defence, he having come to kill me... Think no more of it, for my brother Pachacuti Yupanqui is to be Inca, and I hold that you should favour him and be as a father to him.' Seeing the resolution of his son Inca Rocca, Viracocha did not dare to reply or to contradict him. At the end of a short time Inca Viracocha died of grief at the death of Inca Urco, deprived and despoiled of all honour and property.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 33 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 印加羅卡走進去，維拉科查所在之處，說道：「父親！您實在不該為烏爾科的死如此悲傷，因為我是出於自衛才殺了他，他本是來殺我的……請不要再想這件事了，因為我的兄弟帕查庫提·尤潘基將成為印加，我認為您應當扶持他，待他如父。」維拉科查見其子印加羅卡的決心，不敢回話，也不敢反駁他。不久之後，印加維拉科查便因印加烏爾科之死而悲傷過度而逝，一切榮譽與財產皆被剝奪、劫掠一空。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: The Jar That Destroyed a Nation: The Potter of the Cuyos
title.zh: 一罐釀滅族之禍:庫約斯陶工擲器傷王

region.en: Cuyo-suyu, province of the Cuyos (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫約蘇尤庫約斯省(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 34, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: After this Inca Yupanqui took to wife a native of Choco named Mama Anahuarqui. For greater pleasure and enjoyment, away from business, he went to the town of the Cuyos, chief place of the province of Cuyo-suyu. Being one day at a great entertainment, a potter, servant of the Sinchi, without apparent reason, threw a stone or, as some say, one of the jars which they call ulti, at the Inca's head and wounded him. The delinquent, who was a stranger to the district, was seized and tortured to confess who had ordered him to do it. He stated that all the Sinchis of Cuyo-suyu, who were Cuyo Ccapac, Ayan-quilalama, and Apu Cunaraqui, had conspired to kill the Inca and rebel. This was false, for it had been extorted from fear of the torture, or, as some say, he said it because he belonged to a hostile tribe and wished to do them harm. But the Inca, having heard what the potter said, ordered all the Sinchis to be killed with great cruelty. After their deaths he slaughtered the people, leaving none alive except some children and old women. Thus was that nation destroyed, and its towns are desolate to this day.
summary.zh: 其後印加·尤潘琪娶喬科女子瑪瑪·阿納瓦爾基為后。為求逸樂、遠離政務,他前往庫約蘇尤省重鎮庫約斯鎮。一日大宴之上,辛奇家的一個陶工——外鄉人——無故向印加王擲出一塊石頭,或說擲出一只名為「烏爾蒂」的陶罐,擊傷其頭。兇手被擒,嚴刑拷打,逼問主使。他供稱:庫約蘇尤諸辛奇——庫約·卡帕克、阿揚-基拉拉馬、阿普·庫納拉基——曾密謀弒王作亂。此供實屬誣妄:或是刑求所迫,或是——如另一說——他本屬敵對部族,欲加害於人。然而印加王聞供大怒,命將諸辛奇盡數殘殺;隨後屠戮其民,僅留孩童與老婦。這一族便如此滅絕,其城邑至今荒蕪。

sensitivity.note: A thrown jar as the trigger of a massacre; Sarmiento flags the confession as extorted - preserved critically.

passages.text: Being one day at a great entertainment, a potter, servant of the Sinchi, without apparent reason, threw a stone or, as some say, one of the jars which they call ulti, at the Inca's head and wounded him. The delinquent, who was a stranger to the district, was seized and tortured to confess who had ordered him to do it. He stated that all the Sinchis of Cuyo-suyu, who were Cuyo Ccapac, Ayan-quilalama, and Apu Cunaraqui, had conspired to kill the Inca and rebel.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 34 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，在一場盛大的宴會上，一名辛奇（Sinchi）的僕人陶匠，毫無明顯緣由地朝印加的頭部擲出一塊石頭，或如某些人所說，擲出一個他們稱為烏爾提（ulti）的陶罐，將他打傷。這名罪犯是外地人，被抓住並遭嚴刑拷打，逼他供出是誰指使他這麼做的。他供稱，庫約蘇尤（Cuyo-suyu）的所有辛奇——即庫約·卡帕克（Cuyo Ccapac）、阿揚·基拉拉馬（Ayan-quilalama）與阿普·庫納拉基（Apu Cunaraqui）——曾共謀殺害印加並發動叛亂。

passages.text: This was false, for it had been extorted from fear of the torture, or, as some say, he said it because he belonged to a hostile tribe and wished to do them harm. But the Inca, having heard what the potter said, ordered all the Sinchis to be killed with great cruelty. After their deaths he slaughtered the people, leaving none alive except some children and old women. Thus was that nation destroyed, and its towns are desolate to this day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 34 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這是假的，因為那是在酷刑的恐懼下逼出來的；或者如某些人所說，他之所以這麼說，是因為他屬於敵對的部族，想加害他們。但印加聽聞陶匠所言之後，便下令以極其殘酷的方式處死所有辛奇。在他們死後，他又屠殺其人民，除了少數孩童與老婦之外，一個不留。那個民族就這樣被毀滅了，其城鎮至今荒蕪。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: The Head in Llasa-huasi: The Fall of Chuchi Ccapac
title.zh: 利亞薩-瓦西中的首級:喬奇·卡帕克之敗亡

region.en: Hatun-colla, Collao (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科利亞奧哈通-科利亞(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 37, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: The Sinchi of Collao was named Chuchi Ccapac or Colla Ccapac, who increased so much in power and wealth among the nations of Colla-suyu that he was respected by all the Collas, who called him Inca Ccapac. Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui determined to conquer him from a motive of jealousy. He sent a message to Chuchi Colla requesting him to serve and obey him or else to prepare for battle; Chuchi Colla replied proudly that he waited for the Inca to come and do homage to him, and that if the Inca did not choose to do so, he would prepare his head, with which he intended to drink in his triumph after the victory. In the battle, seeing that the Collas resisted so resolutely, Inca Yupanqui turned his face to his men saying in a loud voice: 'O Incas of Cuzco! conquerors of all the land! Are you not ashamed that people so inferior to you, and unequal in weapons, should be equal to you and resist for so long a time?' With this rebuke the troops pressed upon their enemies and broke them. Inca Yupanqui knew that the completion of the victory consisted in the capture of Chuchi Ccapac: seeing him in the midst of his people, the Inca attacked them at the head of his guards, took him prisoner. Chuchi Colla and the other Colla prisoners were placed before the Inca's litter dressed in long robes covered with tassels in derision; the captives and spoils were offered to the image of the Sun, and the Inca trod on all the spoils and captives. When the triumph was over, to give it a good finish, the Inca caused the head of Chuchi Ccapac to be cut off, and put in the house called Llasa-huasi with those of the other Sinchis he had killed. He caused the other Sinchis and captains of Chuchi Ccapac to be given to the wild beasts, kept shut up for the purpose, in a house called Samca-huasi - a prison for grave offences, into which serpents and toads were put with the delinquents.
summary.zh: 科利亞奧的辛奇名喬奇·卡帕克(亦稱科利亞-卡帕克),權勢財富日增,眾科利亞人尊之為「印加·卡帕克」。帕查庫提·印加·尤潘琪心生妒忌,決意征討。先遣使命其臣服,否則一戰;喬奇·科利亞傲然答道:等印加王來向他朝貢;若不然,他將備好自己的頭顱——勝利之後,好拿來盛酒慶功!大戰之中,見科利亞人頑強抵抗,印加·尤潘琪回首大喝:「庫斯科的印加人!大地的征服者!難道不羞愧嗎?武器遜於你們的下等之民,竟能與你們相持如此之久!」軍心受激,猛攻破敵。印加王深知全勝在於生擒喬奇·卡帕克,遂親率衛隊直搗敵陣,將其擒獲。凱旋之日,喬奇·科利亞與眾俘身披綴滿流蘇的長袍,以示羞辱,排列於印加王轎前;俘虜與戰利品獻於太陽神像之前,印加王踏踐其上。慶功既畢,為收全功之效,印加王命斬喬奇·卡帕克之頭,與所誅諸辛奇之首一同貯於「利亞薩-瓦西」(量屋)之中;喬奇帳下諸辛奇與將領,則被投入「桑卡-瓦西」——重罪囚犯之獄,獄中飼養毒蛇與蟾蜍,以飼猛獸之名,行生吞之實。

sensitivity.note: The Colla defeat cycle known also from Salcamayhua; here the prison with serpents and toads is a named institution.

passages.text: This message caused much heaviness to Chuchi Colla, but he replied proudly that he waited for the Inca to come and do homage to him like the other nations that had been conquered by him, and that if the Inca did not choose to do so, he would prepare his head, with which he intended to drink in his triumph after the victory which he would win if they should come to a battle.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 37 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這番話令丘奇·科利亞（Chuchi Colla）十分沉重，但他傲慢地回答說，他等著印加前來向他致敬，就像其他被他征服的民族一樣；倘若印加不願如此，他便要準備好他的頭顱，打算在勝利之後用那頭顱飲酒慶功——那勝利是他若開戰必將贏得的。

passages.text: Seeing that the Collas resisted so resolutely, and stood so firmly in the battle, he turned his face to his men saying in a loud voice: 'O Incas of Cuzco! conquerors of all the land! Are you not ashamed that people so inferior to you, and unequal in weapons, should be equal to you and resist for so long a time?' With this he returned to the fight, and the troops, touched by this rebuke, pressed upon their enemies in such sort that they were broken and defeated.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 37 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他見科利亞人抵抗得如此堅決，在戰鬥中站得如此穩固，便轉向他的部眾，高聲說道：「庫斯科的印加人啊！全地的征服者啊！你們難道不羞愧嗎？這些遠不如你們、兵器也不如你們的人，竟能與你們勢均力敵，抵抗這麼久？」說罷，他重返戰陣，士兵們受此責備所激，猛烈進逼敵人，終於將他們擊潰擊敗。

passages.text: When the triumph was over, to give it a good finish, the Inca caused the head of Chuchi Ccapac to be cut off, and put in the house called Llasa-huasi, with those of the other Sinchis he had killed. He caused the other Sinchis and captains of Chuchi Ccapac to be given to the wild beasts, kept shut up for the purpose, in a house called Samca-huasi.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 37 (Markham 1907); not verbatim; Markham's note glosses Samca-huasi as a prison where serpents and toads were put in with the delinquents.
passages.zh: 勝利結束之後，為使此事有個圓滿的了結，印加命人砍下丘奇·卡帕克的頭，放入一座名為利亞薩瓦西（Llasa-huasi）的屋子裡，與他所殺的其他辛奇的頭放在一起。他又命人將丘奇·卡帕克的其他辛奇與隊長們丟給為此特意關養的野獸，關在一座名為薩姆卡瓦西（Samca-huasi）的屋子裡。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Dengei the Great Serpent and the Flood on the Boat-Builders
title.zh: 大蛇恩蓋伊與舟匠之洪罰

region.en: Kau-vandra hill, Viti Levu, Fiji (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 斐濟維提島考萬德拉山（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Lorimer Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 1904

source.work: Lorimer Fison, Tales from Old Fiji (London: Alexander Moring, 1904), 'How the Fijians Learned to Build Their Canoes'

summary.en: The Great Serpent Dengei, who dwelt on the hill of Kau-vandra, chose the Boat-builders and taught them canoes, giving them the rule of Great Fiji; his closed eyes were night, his turning earthquakes, his opening eyes the morning, and his black dove on the banyan woke him. But proud Rokola and Kausambaria shot the dove — 'we fear you not, Great Serpent, though you be a god' — and the god's hurled club broke the clouds into a deluge that swept away war-fence, town, and people; the drowning Boat-builders floated on trees and rafts to the mountain-tops, to serve as canoe-builders in every kingdom, and the uprooted banyan made an island of Vatu-lele.
summary.zh: 大蛇恩蓋伊居考萬德拉山，揀選『舟匠部落』，授以造舟之術，並把大斐濟全境交其統治。牠閉眼即夜，翻身即震，睜眼即晨；黑鴿棲於榕樹，一聲『克魯克魯』便喚醒牠。舟匠漸驕漸惰，羅科拉與考桑巴里亞兄弟射殺神鴿，還隔谷叫囂：『我們不怕你，大蛇，哪怕你是神！』恩蓋伊擲杖上天，雲破而洪水傾瀉——浪高過戰柵，淹沒城池人民。倖存的舟匠攀樹乘筏漂上山頂，向各國求活；水退之後，他們成為各邦君主的造舟奴僕——斐濟人造舟之術，便是由此而來。被連根拔起的榕樹漂至瓦圖雷勒，樹根帶土成島，人遂居焉。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-anthropologist record (Fison 1904); iTaukei heritage. Flood cluster; Dengei = Ndengei.

passages.text: In the old times our fathers feared that spot, and reverenced it greatly, for there dwelt the Great Serpent whom they worshipped. In those days Bau was not the greatest kingdom in Fiji, as it is now. There were then no boat-builders among us, and our fathers made no canoes, for they knew not how to fashion them. They were living in a wretched way, each tribe dwelling apart in its own land; for there were no canoes wherewith to sail from one island to another. So the Great Serpent took pity upon them, and chose a tribe whom he called 'The Boat-builders,' and them he taught the art of canoe-building, giving them also the entire rule over Great Fiji, so that in those days they were a great and powerful people, and Bau was of little account. And indeed it was easy for them to become great, for they alone of all the dwellers in Fiji knew how to build canoes; so that men came from afar, begging to be taken as their servants.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 'How the Fijians Learned to Build Their Canoes' (1904); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在古時，我們的祖先畏懼那地方，並且極其敬重它，因為他們所敬拜的大蛇就住在那裡。在那個時候，包島還不是斐濟最強大的王國，不像如今這樣。那時我們之中沒有造船的人，我們的祖先也不會造獨木舟，因為他們不懂得如何製作。他們過著悲慘的生活，各部落分散居住在自己的土地上；因為沒有獨木舟可以從一個島航行到另一個島。於是那大蛇憐憫他們，揀選了一個部落，稱它為「造船者」，並教導他們造船的技藝，又將整個大斐濟的統治權賜給他們，使他們在那些日子成為偉大而強盛的民族，而包島則微不足道。事實上，他們要成為強大並不困難，因為在斐濟所有的居民中，唯有他們懂得造獨木舟；因此人們從遠方而來，懇求被收為他們的僕人。

passages.text: Now the Great Serpent dwelt on the hill of Kau-vandra, in Great Fiji; and when it was evening, the Great Serpent used to go to a cave in the hill of Kau-vandra, and there laid him down to sleep. When he closed his eyes then it was dark, and men said, 'Night is come over the land'; when he turned himself over in his sleep, the earth shook, and men said, 'It is an earthquake'; and at dawn of day, when he opened his eyes, then darkness fled away, and men said, 'It is morning.' Now there was a beautiful black dove, whose duty it was to awake him when it was morning. It slept always on a Baka (or banyan) tree, which grew hard by the mouth of the Great Serpent's cave, whence its voice, 'Kru, kru, kru, kru,' always roused him when it was time for the night to depart, and for the day to come over the land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 'How the Fijians Learned to Build Their Canoes' (1904); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那大蛇住在大斐濟的考萬德拉山上；每到傍晚，大蛇便前往考萬德拉山中的一個洞穴，在那裡躺下睡覺。當他閉上眼睛，天就黑了，人們便說：「黑夜已臨到大地」；當他在睡夢中翻身，大地便震動，人們便說：「這是地震」；到了黎明，當他睜開眼睛，黑暗便逃遁而去，人們便說：「天亮了。」那時有一隻美麗的黑鴿，牠的職責是在早晨喚醒他。牠總是睡在一棵榕樹上，那樹長在大蛇洞穴口旁，牠的叫聲「咕、咕、咕、咕」總是在黑夜該離去、白晝該降臨大地的時候喚醒他。

passages.text: So they took their bows and arrows, and crept beneath the banyan tree, where the dove was sleeping. Then said Rokola to his brother, 'I will shoot first. If I miss, then do you shoot'; and his brother replied, 'It is well. Shoot. I am ready.' So Rokola shot, and his arrow pierced the breast of the dove, so that it fell dead to the ground, and the two brothers fled away to their town. When the Great Serpent awoke from his sleep, he wondered that he did not hear the voice of his dove; so he came forth from his cave, and looked up into the banyan tree. Then, looking on the ground, he spied the dove, with the arrow sticking in her breast. Great was his grief for the dove, and great also was his rage; for he knew the arrow of Rokola, and, shouting across the valley with a terrible voice, he cried, 'Woe to you, Rokola, and unto you all, O Boat-builders, ungrateful ones, because you have killed my dove! Now is your kingdom taken away, and given to the children of Bau.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 'How the Fijians Learned to Build Their Canoes' (1904); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他們拿起弓箭，悄悄爬到那隻鴿子正在睡覺的榕樹下。羅科拉對他的兄弟說：「我先射。如果我射不中，那就由你來射」；他的兄弟回答說：「好。射吧。我準備好了。」於是羅科拉射了一箭，他的箭刺穿了鴿子的胸膛，鴿子便跌落地上死了，兩兄弟隨即逃回他們的城鎮。當大蛇從睡夢中醒來，他奇怪為何聽不到他鴿子的聲音；於是他走出洞穴，抬頭望向榕樹。接著，他朝地上看去，發現了那隻鴿子，箭還插在牠的胸膛上。他為鴿子悲痛萬分，同時也怒火中燒；因為他認得羅科拉的箭，便以可怕的聲音隔著山谷呼喊：「禍哉，羅科拉，也禍哉你們眾人，造船者啊，你們這些忘恩負義之徒，因為你們殺了我的鴿子！如今你們的王國已被奪去，賜給了包島的子民。」

passages.text: But the Boat-builders shouted back across the valley: 'We fear you not, Great Serpent. We are many, and you are but one, though you be a god. Come, let us fight together.' And they built a war-fence, strong, and wide, and high; whilst the Great Serpent sat on the hill of Kau-vandra, mocking them, and crying aloud, 'Build your fences strong. Carry them up to the sky; for a god is your enemy.' When they had finished, Rokola shouted across the valley, 'It is done. Come, let us fight, that our children may say in the days hereafter, Our fathers ate the Great Serpent, the god who lived on the hill of Kau-vandra.' Then the god arose in his wrath, and threw his club up into the sky; and the clouds were broken in pieces, and fell down to the earth in a deluge of rain. Many days did the rain continue — it was not like the rain which now falls upon the earth, but a great and terrible pouring out of waters — and the sea rose, flowing in over the land, a dreadful sight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 'How the Fijians Learned to Build Their Canoes' (1904); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但造船者隔著山谷呼喊回去：「我們不怕你，大蛇。我們人多，你只有一個，縱然你是神。來吧，讓我們一決勝負。」他們築起一道堅固、寬闊又高大的戰柵；而大蛇坐在考萬德拉山上，譏笑他們，高聲喊道：「把你們的柵欄築得堅固些。把它築到天上去吧；因為你們的敵人是神。」當他們完工後，羅科拉隔著山谷喊道：「完成了。來吧，讓我們一戰，好讓我們的子孫日後說：我們的祖先吞吃了大蛇，那住在考萬德拉山上的神。」於是那神在憤怒中興起，將他的棍棒拋向天空；雲層被擊成碎片，化作傾盆大雨降落到地上。雨持續下了許多天——那不像如今落在地上的雨，而是一場巨大而可怕的洪水傾瀉——海水漲起，漫過陸地，景象駭人。

title.en: The Sun-Child and the Red Pearl Shell
title.zh: 太陽之子與紅珠貝

region.en: Tonga as told in Fiji (symbolic pin: Lakemba)
region.zh: 湯加故事之斐濟傳本（象徵定位：萊凱姆巴）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Lorimer Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 1904

source.work: Lorimer Fison, Tales from Old Fiji (London: Alexander Moring, 1904), 'The Story of the Sun-Child'

summary.en: Begotten on a fence-enclosed bathing beauty by the Sun himself, the Sun-child was taunted as fatherless, sailed east and west until his father called up a cloud to slip down and greet him, and was sent to beg Melaia — not Monuia — from the Moon. Headstrong, he asked for Monuia, untied the wrapper before landfall, and held up a pearl shell of a shining red such as no man has seen since, while the whales and sharks and every kind of fish came leaping over the waters for it — and his canoe sank, and the sharks tore him to pieces.
summary.zh: 湯加酋長之女沐浴於海灘高欄之內，太陽在天上窺見而愛之，生下太陽之子。孩子遭同儕譏為無父野種，怒而別母出航尋父。他向東追不上初升之日，向西趕不上沉落之光；父親讚他機智——藏於雲後下海相見——卻囑咐：夜裡向姑姑月亮討『梅萊亞』而非『莫努亞』。任性的孩子偏討了莫努亞，月亮再三追問仍執拗不改；月亮暗驚，只得用布層層裹好、繩繞多道相贈，並囑：海上不得解封，抵岸方可展視。孩子行至第二日望見陸地，按捺不住，解繩展布——掌中是一枚紅光四射的珠貝，世所未見。他正自得意，忽聞海上水聲大作：鯨、鯊、海豚、海龜蜂擁而來，爭撲『莫努亞』；小舟頃刻沉沒，鯊群把他撕碎——太陽之子就此完了。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-anthropologist record (Fison 1904); told in Fiji of Tonga; iTaukei heritage.

passages.text: In the old days there was a great chief in Tonga, whose name has not come down to us; and he had a daughter whose name also has not been told us by our fathers, so that we always speak of her as the Mother of the Sun-child. Now this girl was beautiful exceedingly, and her father hid her from the eyes of men, so that none should look upon her; for he had never seen one whom he thought worthy to be her husband. Down on the sea-beach he built a fence, thick and strong and high, and this was where the Mother of the Sun-child used to go down and bathe. Every day she bathed herself in the salt water, till she grew wondrous fair; and amongst all the daughters of men there was not one so beautiful as the Mother of the Sun-child. After bathing it was her custom to lie down for a time upon the clean white sand within the fence, that she might rest for a while, and that her body might be dry.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 'The Story of the Sun-Child' (1904); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在古時，東加有一位偉大的酋長，他的名字沒有流傳下來給我們；他有一個女兒，她的名字我們的祖先也沒有告訴我們，所以我們總是稱她為太陽之子的母親。這女孩極其美麗，她的父親將她藏起來不讓男人看見，免得有人窺視她；因為他從未見過一個他認為配得上做她丈夫的人。他在海灘上築了一道厚實、堅固又高大的圍欄，太陽之子的母親常到那裡去沐浴。她每天在鹹水裡沐浴，直到出落得異常美麗；在所有人類的女兒中，沒有一個像太陽之子的母親那樣美麗。沐浴之後，她習慣在圍欄內潔白乾淨的沙上躺一會兒，好休息片刻，也讓身體晾乾。

passages.text: And the child grew up into a fine lad, comely and strong; proud, too, was he, and given to strike other children, like the son of a great chief. So one day, when all the town lads were playing together in the public square, some of them did something that was displeasing to the Sun-child, whereupon he beat them with a stick till his arm was weary and their bodies were sore. Then the lads rose up against him, saying, 'Who perchance, then, are you, child of the Sun? Why should you take upon yourself to beat us? We know who are our fathers; but you — you have no father: you are but a child of the path, a bastard!' Then was the boy eaten up by a devouring rage. Gladly would he have leaped upon them and killed them, but he could not stir, so great was his rage; his voice, too, was choked, and his eyes filled with angry tears. Thus he stood, glaring upon them, till, with a sudden cry, he turned and fled away to his home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 'The Story of the Sun-Child' (1904); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那孩子長成了一個俊秀的少年，相貌堂堂、身強體壯；他也十分驕傲，動輒打別的孩子，就像大酋長的兒子一般。於是有一次，城裡所有的少年都在公共廣場上一起玩耍，其中有些人做了些令太陽之子不高興的事，他便用棍子打他們，直到手臂痠軟、他們的身體傷痕累累。於是那些少年起來反對他，說：「那麼你到底是誰，太陽之子？你憑什麼擅自打我們？我們知道我們的父親是誰；可是你——你沒有父親：你不過是路邊的孩子，一個私生子！」那男孩聽罷，被一股吞噬人的怒火所充滿。他恨不得撲上去把他們殺死，卻動彈不得，因為他的怒氣太大了；他的聲音也哽住了，眼中滿是憤怒的淚水。他就這樣站著，怒視著他們，直到忽然一聲喊叫，轉身逃回家去了。

passages.text: 'Hush, my son,' said his mother. 'The boys of the town are liars. Let not your soul be small because of their words, for you are the child of a greater chief than they.' 'Who, then, is my father?' asked the lad once more, looking up with streaming eyes; and his mother laughed a scornful laugh as she answered. 'Who, then, are the boys of the town, that they should despise my son? They are the children of men, but you are the child of the Sun; he is your father.' And she told him all. Then was the heart of the Sun-child glad within him, and, dashing away his tears, he cried: 'I scorn them, these children of men! No more will I talk with them, or live with them. Good-bye, mother, for I am going to my father.' And, with a proud step, he went on his way, not even turning his head when his mother called after him; so she watched him going, till the forest hid him from her sight, and after that she saw him no more for ever.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 'The Story of the Sun-Child' (1904); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「別作聲，我的孩子，」他的母親說。「城裡的男孩們都是撒謊的人。不要因為他們的話就讓你的心靈變得渺小，因為你是一位比他們都更偉大的酋長之子。」「那麼，誰是我的父親？」少年又一次問道，抬起頭來，淚水直流；他的母親輕蔑地笑了一聲，回答說：「那麼，城裡的男孩們算什麼，竟該輕視我的兒子？他們是凡人的孩子，而你卻是太陽之子；他是你的父親。」於是她把一切都告訴了他。這時，太陽之子的心中充滿了歡喜，他抹去眼淚，喊道：「我鄙視他們，這些凡人的孩子！我再也不跟他們說話，也不再和他們住在一起了。再見了，母親，因為我要去找我的父親了。」於是他邁著驕傲的步伐上路了，甚至連母親在身後呼喚他時也沒有回頭；她就這樣望著他離去，直到森林把他從她的視線中遮住，此後她便再也沒有見到他了。

passages.text: It was morning when he hoisted his sail and steered towards the east, where the sun was rising; but, as he sailed along, it rose higher and higher above his head; and he shouted aloud, but his father heard him not. Then he tacked, and stood over to the west, whither the sun was hastening; but, though the wind was fair, he was too late, and his father dived down beneath the waters before he could come near enough to speak with him; so that he was left alone in the midst of the sea. Then he thought within himself: 'It is in the east that my father climbs up out of the water. I will now go back and wait for him there.' So he tacked again, sailing all night towards the east, and when morning dawned he saw the Sun close to him, and shouted aloud, just as it was rising above the waves, 'Father, father; here am I!' 'Who are you?' asked the Sun, still climbing up into the sky. 'I am the Sun-child,' cried the lad. 'You know me. I am your son, and my mother is left behind in Tonga.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 'The Story of the Sun-Child' (1904); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那時正是早晨，他揚起帆，朝著太陽升起的東方駛去；可是當他航行時，太陽在他頭頂上越升越高；他高聲呼喊，但他的父親沒有聽見他。於是他轉舵，朝太陽匆匆西沉的西方駛去；然而，儘管風向順遂，他還是太遲了，還沒等他靠近到能與父親說話，父親就已潛入水底；於是他就這樣被獨自留在海中央。這時他心裡想：「我的父親是從東方浮出水面的。我現在要回去，在那裡等他。」於是他又轉舵，整夜向東方航行，等到黎明破曉時，他看見太陽就在近旁，便趁它正從波浪上升起時高聲喊道：「父親，父親；我在這裡！」「你是誰？」太陽問道，一邊仍向天空攀升。「我是太陽之子，」少年喊道。「你認識我。我是你的兒子，我的母親留在東加（Tonga）了。」

title.en: The Doom of the Sun-Child
title.zh: 太陽之子之末日

region.en: Open sea between Tonga and Fiji (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 湯加與斐濟之間外海（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Lorimer Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 1904

source.work: Lorimer Fison, Tales from Old Fiji (London: Alexander Moring, 1904), 'The Story of the Sun-Child'

summary.en: The Sun's charge was 'Ask for Melaia, and she will give it to you; remember my words, for evil will assuredly befall you if you are disobedient' — but the headstrong boy asked for Monuia, and the Moon, musing, wrapped it in wrapper upon wrapper. 'Loose not the string, neither unfold the wrapper while you are at sea.' He held out till land was in sight, then untied string and cloth: a pearl shell of a shining red, such as no man has since beheld — and the whole sea came leaping for it, and there was an end of the Sun-child.
summary.zh: 太陽臨別贈言：『向月亮討梅萊亞，她便會給你。切記我的話，否則大禍必至。』孩子偏偏討了莫努亞。月亮喃喃自語：『莫非太陽恨這孩子，要害他性命？』終究遵兄之命，把莫努亞層層裹布、纏繩相贈，又囑：『海上莫解繩、莫展布；先掛帆駛回湯加，登岸再看。』孩子強忍一夜一日一夜，第二日晨望見陸地，再也忍不住，解繩展布——一枚紅光燦然的珠貝在手，前所未見。他正盤算掛在頸上回村炫耀，忽聽海上水聲大作：鯨鯊海豚海龜無數游魚爭先恐後撲向『莫努亞』，頃刻間小舟沉沒，鯊群撕碎了他——太陽之子就此完了。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-anthropologist record (Fison 1904); iTaukei heritage.

passages.text: At last he told him that he could stay no longer. 'And now, my son,' said he, 'listen to my words. Stay about here till the night comes over the waters, and then you will see your aunt, the Moon, my sister. When she begins to rise out of the sea, call out to her and tell her to give you one of the two things which she has in keeping. One of them is called Melaia, and the name of the other is Monuia. Ask her for Melaia, and she will give it to you. Remember now my words, and follow them, that it may be well with you; for know that evil will assuredly befall you if you are disobedient.' So the Sun leaped up above the black cloud, and the world was glad, but the children of men said one to another — 'Surely the Sun is climbing up into the sky more slowly to-day than on other days.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 'The Story of the Sun-Child' (1904); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最後他告訴他，自己不能再停留了。「現在，我的孩子，」他說，「聽我的話。就在這附近待到夜色降臨水面，然後你就會見到你的姑母，月亮，我的姊妹。當她開始從海中升起時，向她呼喊，叫她把她所保管的兩樣東西中的一樣給你。其中一樣叫做梅拉亞（Melaia），另一樣的名字是莫努亞（Monuia）。向她求梅拉亞，她就會給你。現在記住我的話，照著去做，好讓你一切順遂；因為你要知道，你若違命，災禍必定臨到你身上。」於是太陽躍上烏雲之上，世界為之歡欣，但凡人彼此說道——「今天太陽升上天空，確實比別的日子慢了些。」

passages.text: Then he woke up again and hoisted his sail, in readiness to hasten to the spot where he should first see the brightness of his aunt's face, so that he was close upon the Moon before she could rise above the waters; and she cried, 'Luff! Luff! child of the earth. Luff! or you will pierce my face with the sharp stem of your canoe.' But the Sun-child kept his canoe away a little with the steering-oar, so that he almost touched the Moon's face in passing; and then luffing suddenly into the wind, he shot up alongside of her, and caught her with a firm hold, saying, 'I am no child of the earth. The child of your brother, the Sun, am I. My name is the Sun-child, and you are my aunt.' 'Are you indeed the Sun-child?' asked the Moon in great surprise. 'Truly this is a wonderful thing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 'The Story of the Sun-Child' (1904); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然後他又醒來，揚起帆，準備趕往他最先望見姑母面容光輝之處，因此月亮還沒升出水面，他就已靠近了她；她喊道：「迎風轉舵！迎風轉舵！大地之子。迎風轉舵！不然你會用獨木舟尖銳的船首刺穿我的臉。」但太陽之子用舵槳把獨木舟稍稍偏開，以致經過時幾乎觸到月亮的臉；接著他忽然迎風轉舵，疾駛到她身旁，牢牢抓住她，說道：「我不是大地之子。我是你兄長太陽之子。我的名字是太陽之子，而你是我的姑母。」「你真的是太陽之子嗎？」月亮大為驚訝地問道。「這真是奇妙的事。」

passages.text: 'But what was it,' continued the Moon, 'that your father told you to ask of me?' Now the Sun-child had made up his mind not to act according to his father's words; for indeed it was his custom to be disobedient — a high-spirited, headstrong boy was he — so he said — 'My father told me to ask for Monuia.' 'For Monuia!' cried his aunt. 'Monuia! Do you not perhaps forget, my nephew, your father's words? Was it not Melaia that he told you to ask for?' 'Indeed it was not,' said the lad stoutly. 'He told me that Melaia was to stay with you, and that I should have Monuia.' 'Truly that is strange,' said the Moon musingly. 'Surely the Sun cannot hate the boy, and wish to kill him. Nevertheless I must obey his commands. You shall have Monuia, my nephew. See, it is but a little thing. It is here wrapped up in this piece of cloth. Now I wrap it in another wrapper, and fasten it with this string, winding it many times around, so that it cannot come loose of itself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 'The Story of the Sun-Child' (1904); not verbatim.
