passages.zh: 「可是，」月亮接著說，「你父親叫你向我求的是什麼呢？」這時太陽之子已打定主意不照父親的話去做；因為他本性的確慣於違命——他是個心高氣傲、固執任性的孩子——於是他说：「我父親叫我求莫努亞。」「求莫努亞！」他的姑母喊道。「莫努亞！我的姪兒，你莫非忘了你父親的話？他叫你求的不是梅拉亞嗎？」「的確不是，」少年堅定地說。「他告訴我梅拉亞要留在你這裡，而我該得到莫努亞。」「這真是奇怪，」月亮若有所思地說。「太陽斷不會恨這孩子，想要害死他。儘管如此，我必須服從他的命令。你會得到莫努亞的，我的姪兒。看，這不過是件小東西。它就在這裡，包在這塊布裡。現在我再用另一層包裹把它包起來，並用這根繩子繫緊，繞上許多圈，使它不會自己鬆開。」

passages.text: So she bade him farewell, and climbed up into the sky, whereupon all who were sailing in the midst of the waters shouted for joy, and said, 'There is our friend, the Moon. It is only we who go sailing by that know how good she is.' The girls also, and the boys in the towns, came running out of the houses, crying aloud, 'Here is the Moon; come, let us dance together in the public square.' And the Sun-child hoisted his sail and steered away for Tonga. All that night, and the next day, and the following night also went he sailing over the waters, till on the morning of the second day he saw the land. Then he could wait no longer, for the Sun-child was of a self-willed, impatient spirit; and so he lifted the parcel which his aunt had given him from the bottom of the canoe, and untied the string wherewith it was bound. Then he unrolled the cloth, fold after fold, till he held 'Monuia' in his hand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 'The Story of the Sun-Child' (1904); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是她向他道別，升上天空，於是所有在水中央航行的人都歡呼起來，說道：「那是我們的朋友，月亮。只有我們這些航行經過的人才知道她有多好。」城裡的女孩們和男孩們也從屋裡跑出來，高聲喊道：「月亮來了；來吧，讓我們一起在公共廣場上跳舞。」太陽之子揚起帆，朝東加駛去。那一整夜、第二天，以及接下來的一夜，他都在水上航行，直到第二天早晨他看見了陸地。這時他再也等不及了，因為太陽之子生性任性急躁；於是他從獨木舟底部拿起姑母給他的那個包裹，解開繫著它的繩子。然後他一層又一層地展開那塊布，直到「莫努亞」握在他手中。

title.en: The Fishing of Maui: Tonga Hauled from the Deep
title.zh: 毛伊垂釣：自深海拉起湯加

region.en: Bulotu to Tonga (symbolic pin: Tongatapu)
region.zh: 自布洛圖至湯加（象徵定位：湯加塔布）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Lorimer Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 1904

source.work: Lorimer Fison, Tales from Old Fiji (London: Alexander Moring, 1904), 'The Beginning of Death — The Fishing of Maui'

summary.en: Weary of kava-drinking eternity, Maui king of the gods sailed far from Bulotu — against the mockery of Hiku-leo the Tailed One and the warning of the Tree of Speech itself — and threw out an enormous fish-hook. The gods hauled in terror as smoke and thunder rose from the sea: mountain after mountain came up, seven of them, then Tonga all green and bursting with food; Maui trod four of his hills down, and Tonga he flattened into rich and fertile plains, on which, even as he trod, grass and flowers and trees sprang up, while the earth swelled into hillocks round his feet.
summary.zh: 神王毛伊厭倦了布洛圖日日飲卡瓦的死水生活，不顧長尾神希庫勒奧的譏誚與『言之樹』阿考萊亞的警示——『莫去！其禍大到你們無法想像』——率兩子與精選船員遠航。良久，他自甲板樓擲下巨鉤，慢慢放線；忽然海面冒煙轟鳴，神眾駭然拽拉：一座座山自波中升起，共七座，山谷平原俱全。『值得遠航！』毛伊跳上岸去，連踏四座高山，踏平填谷；再釣起湯加，把群山盡踏成沃野平原——他腳下處處冒出芋薯百糧，草木自生，眾神歡呼。湯加自海底被毛伊釣起，此事千真萬確。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-anthropologist record (Fison 1904); Fijian telling of the Tongan Maui cycle. Polynesian-stratum material within the Fiji corpus.

passages.text: In the beginning there was no land, save that on which the gods lived; no dry land was there for men to dwell upon; all was sea; the sky covered it above, and bounded it on every side. There was neither day nor night; but a mild light shone continually through the sky upon the waters, like the shining of the moon when its face is hidden by a white cloud. Thus it was in the beginning. The gods dwelt in Bulotu; but we cannot tell where that island is, though some say that the words which have come down from our fathers declare it to be where the sky meets the waters in the climbing-path of the sun. Here dwelt the gods, Maui, the greatest of them all, with his two sons and his brothers. A fine land is Bulotu, and happy are its people; for there, close to the house of Hiku-leo, is Vai-ola, the Water of Life, which the gods drink every day. Oh that we had it here on earth, for it will heal all manner of sickness!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 'The Beginning of Death' (1904); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 起初沒有陸地，只有眾神所居之地；沒有乾地可供人類居住；一切都是海；天空在上覆蓋著它，從四面環繞著它。那時既無白晝也無黑夜；只有一道柔和的光不斷穿過天空照在水面上，宛如月亮的面容被白雲遮蔽時所散發的光輝。起初便是如此。眾神住在布洛圖；但我們無法說出那座島在何處，雖有人說，從我們父輩傳下的話語宣稱，它位於天空與海水相接之處，即太陽攀升之路。眾神便住在此處，其中至大者為毛伊，與他的兩個兒子和兄弟們同住。布洛圖是塊美好的土地，其人民幸福安樂；因為在那裡，緊鄰希庫雷奧之屋的，便是生命之水瓦伊奧拉，眾神每日飲用。啊，但願我們在人間也能擁有它，因為它能治癒一切疾病！

passages.text: Here once upon a time they sat drinking kava; and after the bowl had gone round the circle, then outspake Maui, the king of them all — 'I am weary, ye gods,' he cried. 'I am weary of this life of ours. We eat, and drink, and sleep, and do nothing. My soul is stirred within me. Let my canoe float. Drag it down to the water, and let the crew get ready for sailing.' 'Whither are you going?' Hiku-leo asked in a mocking tone; for a saucy god was he; angry too, and evil of soul. 'What will you do? What do you want? This is a fool's business truly.' And he laughed a scornful laugh. 'Stay you behind, Hiku-leo,' answered Maui. 'We know you of old, how peevish are your ways. Stay therefore at home, and watch lest any of the boys should steal your tail.' For Hiku-leo was known among the gods by his tail, which had eyes in it, he alone of them all being thus adorned. But the Tailed One shook with rage; fierce was his anger. 'Go then!' he cried, 'and may evil go with you! May you never return!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 'The Beginning of Death' (1904); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一次，他們坐在這裡飲用卡瓦酒；酒碗在圈中傳過一輪之後，眾神之王毛伊開口說道——「我厭倦了，眾神啊，」他喊道。「我厭倦了我們這樣的生活。我們吃、喝、睡，什麼也不做。我的靈魂在我體內激盪。讓我的獨木舟下水吧。把它拖到水邊，讓船員們準備啟航。」「你要去哪裡？」希庫雷奧以嘲諷的語氣問道；因為他是個無禮的神；脾氣暴躁，心術邪惡。「你要做什麼？你想要什麼？這真是蠢人的行徑。」他發出輕蔑的笑聲。「你留在這裡吧，希庫雷奧，」毛伊回答。「我們早就認識你了，知道你的脾氣多麼乖戾。因此留在家中，看守著，免得哪個小子偷走你的尾巴。」因為希庫雷奧在眾神之中以他的尾巴聞名，那尾巴上長著眼睛，眾神之中唯有他如此裝扮。但有尾者氣得渾身發抖；他的怒火猛烈。「那就去吧！」他喊道，「願邪惡與你同行！願你永不歸來！」

passages.text: But before the two sons of Maui could say a word, there was a rustle and a stir among the leaves of the Tree of Speech, as if a sudden blast were sweeping through its branches; and all the gods kept silence, for they knew it was going to speak. 'Hear my words, Maui. Hear my words, Hiku-leo, and gods all. Go not! Evil will come to pass if you go — an evil so great and terrible, that you could not understand if I were to tell you what it is. I pray you not to go.' 'Let it come!' cried Maui, for his spirit was roused. 'Let those who are afraid stay with Hiku-leo. Come, my sons, both of you.' 'We are going,' they answered with a shout; and all the other gods clapped their hands, and cried, 'Good is the sailing!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 'The Beginning of Death' (1904); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但毛伊的兩個兒子還來不及說一句話，言語之樹的葉間便傳來一陣沙沙聲與騷動，彷彿一陣疾風掃過它的枝條；眾神都保持沉默，因為他們知道它要開口了。「聽我的話，毛伊。聽我的話，希庫雷奧，以及眾神。不要去！你們若去，邪惡必將降臨——那邪惡如此巨大可怖，即使我告訴你們那是什麼，你們也無法理解。我懇求你們不要去。」「讓它來吧！」毛伊喊道，因為他的精神已被激發。「那些害怕的人就跟希庫雷奧留在一起吧。來吧，我的兒子們，你們兩個都來。」「我們這就去，」他們高聲回答；其餘眾神都拍手叫好，喊道：「航行大吉！」

passages.text: For a long time they ran before the wind, and when the gods had sailed over a very great stretch of water, Maui ordered the sail to be lowered. The sail was soon lowered upon the deck, and made fast. Then Maui came down from his seat on the top of the deck-house, holding in his hand an enormous fish-hook, which he threw far away from him into the sea, paying out the line as the hook sank, and the gods looked on in wonder. 'Have we come all this way to fish?' cried Ata-longa. 'Are there no fish in the waters of Bulotu that we must sail thus far over the sea to catch them?' 'Wait and see,' answered Maui. And then the waters rose bubbling and foaming around the canoe, and smoke came from them with a thunderous rumble and roar, and the gods cried out in deadly fear. 'Haul away, my lads!' he cried. So they pulled and hauled with all their might, and presently the sea grew dark; and, looking down, they saw, as it were, a great black shadow beneath the waves. 'Fear not! Come back, little-livered cowards that you are!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 'The Beginning of Death' (1904); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們順風航行了好久，當眾神駛過一片極其遼闊的水域之後，毛伊下令降下帆來。帆很快便降落在甲板上，並被繫牢。接著毛伊從艙頂的座位上走下來，手中握著一隻巨大的魚鉤，他將它遠遠地拋入海中，隨著魚鉤下沉而不斷放出釣線，眾神驚奇地看著。「我們跑了這麼遠就是為了釣魚嗎？」阿塔隆加喊道。「布洛圖的水裡就沒有魚嗎，非得航行這麼遠過海來捕？」「等著瞧吧，」毛伊回答。接著海水在獨木舟四周翻騰冒泡，泛起泡沫，煙霧伴隨著雷鳴般的轟隆聲從水中升起，眾神在極度的恐懼中驚叫起來。「用力拉，小伙子們！」他喊道。於是他們使出全力又拉又拽，不一會兒海面變暗了；他們向下望去，看見波浪之下彷彿有一大片黑色的影子。「不要害怕！回來吧，你們這些膽小的懦夫！

title.en: The Death-Canoes: How Death Came Among the Gods
title.zh: 死亡之舟：神明之死與凡人之始

region.en: Tongatapu, Fiji telling (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 湯加塔布（斐濟傳本）（象徵定位）

period: Oral tradition; recorded by Lorimer Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 1904

source.work: Lorimer Fison, Tales from Old Fiji (London: Alexander Moring, 1904), 'The Beginning of Death — The Death-Canoes'

summary.en: Ata-longa stole his father's canoe and carried the younger gods to the plenty of Tonga, leaving behind the Water of Life — and one by one the cold crept up: a child on the sand shivering at the sight of a little canoe on the sea, a mother dim-eyed and drifting on a strong current, a husband smiling at canoes only he could see. Through the darkness came the voice of the Tree of Speech: 'Subject to disease and death! That is the doom of the disobedient ones who have left the Waters of Life. Bury the dead! Let the earth hide them!' — and Maui sent his son with sacred fire shut up in a tree, and stood beneath Tonga holding it up, where earthquakes are Maui nodding in his sleep.
summary.zh: 阿塔隆加竊父之舟，載一眾小神逃往富庶的湯加——卻把『生命之水』永遠留在了布洛圖。不久寒意漸至：沙灘上的小女孩望見海上一葉小舟便寒入骨髓；母親眼花耳語，自述如被激流裹挾而去；父親忽見眾人皆不可見的兩大一小三葉死亡之舟，妻女坐於其上向他招手微笑。眾神環立，忽有慘叫，一人倒地痙攣——『言之樹』的聲音穿過黑暗而來：『病與死纏身！這便是離棄生命之水者的厄運。埋葬死者吧，讓泥土掩蓋他們！你們都必如此。』眾神葬了菲菲塔一家，造舟回布洛圖求恕，卻從此再找不到那片仙島。毛伊念其未絕，遣子基吉基吉送來聖火封入樹中——兩木相搓，火即出。毛伊更潛入海底，以肩扛住下沉的湯加，至今仍扛著：地震便是他瞌睡點頭；眾人吶喊跺地擊杖，他便驚醒，大地也就不搖了。而希庫勒奧成了布洛圖之王，專門在死亡之舟靠岸處捉拿亡魂：有的做他奴隸，有的充當他籬笆的木樁。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-anthropologist record (Fison 1904); iTaukei heritage. Origin-of-death cluster; cross-ref Banks Islands and Ambrym death tales.

passages.text: Now Ata-longa's soul was very sore because of his father's words, which had put him to silence and shame before all the younger gods who had sailed with them. Great was his shame, great was his anger, and his soul grew ever darker and more evil towards Maui, as he thought upon his words on that day. At last he hatched a scheme by which he could at once vex his father and escape from under his control. He gathered together a number of the younger gods, his companions, and spoke to them of the tyranny of Maui; how they were checked and curbed by him, and how much better it would be for them to flee away, and to live in peace and plenty in the new land, where they would be free from the continual interference of tyrannical elders. 'Maui himself has made it easy, for he has fished up a beautiful land from the bottom of the sea. It is a land of plenty; no evil is there, and nothing good is wanting. Why then should we stay here in Bulotu, to be for ever snubbed by our elders?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 'The Beginning of Death' (1904); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 如今阿塔隆加的靈魂因父親的話而痛苦萬分，那些話在所有與他們同航的年輕眾神面前使他啞口無言、蒙受羞辱。他的羞恥之大，他的憤怒之大，當他回想那日毛伊所說的話時，他的靈魂對毛伊便愈發陰暗邪惡。最後他謀劃出一個計策，既能激怒父親，又能擺脫他的控制。他召集了一批年輕的眾神——他的同伴們——向他們訴說毛伊的暴政；訴說他們如何受他壓制與束縛，以及逃離此地、在那片新土地上和平富足地生活對他們來說該有多好，在那裡他們將擺脫暴虐長輩的持續干涉。「毛伊自己已經讓這件事變得容易了，因為他從海底釣起了一片美麗的土地。那是片富饒之地；那裡沒有邪惡，也沒有任何美好之物匱乏。那麼我們為何還要留在布洛圖，永遠受長輩們的冷落呢？」

passages.text: Merrily over the waters went Ata-longa in the stolen canoe with his crew of runaways. Pleasant was the breeze, and swiftly glided the canoe over the laughing waves, till Tonga rose out of the waters in their course; and they soon reached the shore, shouting aloud at the beautiful prospect before them. The gods were full of joy, and made the whole island ring with their merry laughter and shouts of glee, as they rambled about in companies, and found new beauties to admire, or more and more abundant food supplies, ripe and ready to their hands, yams and breadfruit, and coconuts in all stages of growth, with shoals of fish leaping out of the water here and there. The women sat on the seashore watching the children as they gambolled along the sands, some of them rushing into the water and spearing fish with their little spears. Fires were soon lit, food was baked, and all were full of delight. 'This is a better land than that we have left,' they said. 'Here will we stay. Never more will we return to Bulotu.' Little did they think what a fearful truth lay in those gladsome words!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 'The Beginning of Death' (1904); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿塔隆加乘著偷來的獨木舟，帶著他那群逃亡的船員，歡快地駛過水面。微風宜人，獨木舟在歡笑的波浪上輕快地滑行，直到湯加在他們的航程中從水中升起；他們很快便抵達岸邊，對著眼前的美景高聲歡呼。眾神滿心歡喜，成群結隊地四處漫遊，發現新的美景可供讚嘆，或找到越來越豐富的食物供應，成熟而唾手可得，有山藥、麵包果，以及各個生長階段的椰子，還有成群的魚兒不時從水中躍出。女人們坐在海邊看著孩子們在沙灘上嬉戲，其中一些孩子衝進水裡，用小魚叉叉魚。很快便生起了火，烤好了食物，所有人都滿心歡喜。「這是片比我們離開的那片更好的土地，」他們說。「我們要留在這裡。再也不回布洛圖了。」他們幾乎沒有想到，那些歡樂的話語中蘊含著多麼可怕的真相！

passages.text: Thus it came about. The fine young god, Fifita, came with him; he and his wife Moa, and their little girl, their only child. A loving couple were they, and dearly they loved their little one, the darling of their hearts. So it fell upon a day that Fifita, coming home from the fishing, wondered that his wife and his little daughter had not come down to the sea-shore to welcome him according to their wont. And, when he landed, he found his wife stretched upon the mats, with the child lying beside her. Languidly then his wife looked up at the sound of his voice; and Fifita saw that her eyes were dim — those eyes that were wont to sparkle so merrily. 'I know not,' she replied in a low tone and faint. 'It is to me as if I were drifting away on a strong current; but whither I know not, nor why. As I sat watching our little one at her play on the sand, she suddenly stopped; and shading her eyes with her hand, she looked out seaward.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 'The Beginning of Death' (1904); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 事情就這樣發生了。那位俊美的年輕神明菲菲塔與他一同前來；他與妻子莫阿，以及他們的小女兒，他們唯一的孩子。他們是一對恩愛的夫妻，也深愛著他們的小女兒，那是他們心頭的珍寶。於是有一天，菲菲塔捕魚歸來，詫異妻子和小女兒竟沒有照往常的習慣下到海邊來迎接他。而當他登岸時，發現妻子伸展著身子躺在席上，孩子躺在她身旁。他的妻子聽見他的聲音，便慵懶地抬眼望他；菲菲塔看出她的雙眼黯淡無光——那雙往常總是如此歡快地閃爍的眼睛。「我不知道，」她以微弱低沉的聲音答道。「我感覺自己彷彿被一股強勁的水流沖走；但要去往何處，我不知，也不知為何。我坐著看我們的小女兒在沙上玩耍時，她忽然停了下來；用手遮著眼睛，向海的那邊望去。」

passages.text: Her voice grew ever fainter as she spoke, till it died away in a low whisper; and Fifita sat by her side, holding her hand, with a sickening terror at his heart. Then, suddenly, she started, and raised her head. 'What is this?' she cried in a full-toned voice. 'How can this be? Is not this my child that I hold in my arms? How then do I see her yonder sitting on that little canoe? She smiles, Fifita, and beckons me away. There also is another canoe, larger than hers. Ah! I see it now! I am going. Farewell, my husband! I must leave you. I come, my child, I come!' Then, with a long-drawn sigh, her head sank again upon the mats, her eyes closed, and she was still. Suddenly, with a start, he raised his head, and turning quickly round, gazed out seaward, while there stole over his face a bewildered look, which brightened into a happy smile. 'Here now is a wondrous thing! Have I then been dreaming too? But how did you get there to the canoe?' 'What canoe, Fifita?' asked one of the gods. 'Here lies Moa, and here is her child.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fison, Tales from Old Fiji, 'The Beginning of Death' (1904); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她說話時聲音越來越微弱，直到化為一聲低低的細語而消逝；菲菲塔坐在她身旁，握著她的手，心中充滿令人作嘔的恐懼。接著，她忽然一驚，抬起頭來。「這是什麼？」她以飽滿的嗓音喊道。「這怎麼可能？我抱在懷裡的，不就是我的孩子嗎？那我怎麼又看見她坐在那邊那艘小獨木舟上？她微笑著，菲菲塔，還招手喚我過去。那裡還有一艘獨木舟，比她的更大。啊！我現在看見了！我要走了。別了，我的丈夫！我必須離開你了。我來了，我的孩子，我來了！」接著，隨著一聲長長的嘆息，她的頭又沉落在席上，雙眼闔上，便一動也不動了。忽然，他猛地一驚，抬起頭來，迅速轉身，向海的那邊凝望，臉上悄悄浮現一種困惑的神情，那神情又明亮起來，化作幸福的微笑。「這可真是件奇妙的事！難道我也一直在做夢嗎？可你是怎麼到那獨木舟上去的？」「什麼獨木舟，菲菲塔？」眾神中的一位問道。「莫阿就躺在這裡，她的孩子也在這裡。」

title.en: A Div in Minstrel's Guise Tempts Kai Kaus
title.zh: 魔化樂師誘惑卡烏斯

region.en: Pleasure-palace of Kaus (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 卡烏斯樂宮（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus secs. 2-3

summary.en: Sipping wine on a crystal-footed throne, Kai Kaus boasts that no Shah is worthy but himself — and a div in a minstrel's guise is admitted to sing of Mazandaran, its ever-blooming gardens and rose-water rivers. Enchanted, the Shah resolves to lead a host against the land of the divs; the nobles turn pale, send in haste to Zal, and Zal comes to counsel: that land is the home of warlock-divs and under spells which none hath power to loose. The Shah answers that he in courage, Grace, and treasure surpasses Jamshid and Faridun, and Zal, baffled, takes his leave with both sun and moon darkened in his eyes.
summary.zh: 卡烏斯坐於水晶足御座上飲酒自誇「無王配此座」，一名魔化樂師獲准入宮，彈唱馬贊德蘭的四季花園與玫瑰香河。王心醉神迷，決意征討魔國；群臣變色，急遣使請扎勒進諫：「那是術士魔怪的老巢，咒術無人能解。」王卻自稱勇武天恩勝過賈姆希德與法里東。扎勒無奈告退，眼中日月俱暗。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Kaus, succeeding to his father's throne with all the world to serve him, sat one day and quaffed delicious wine within a pleasure-palace arabesqued with gold, on the golden throne whose feet were crystal, master of the world, and spake on this wise: who is Shah but I, who worthy of the throne except myself? I rule the world with none to say me nay.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡烏斯繼承父王的王位，全世界都供他驅使，有一天他坐在一座飾有金色阿拉伯式花紋的遊樂宮殿裡，坐在那雙腳為水晶的黃金寶座上，暢飲美酒，身為世界之主，如此說道：除了我，誰還是沙阿？除了我自己，誰還配得上這王座？我統治世界，無人敢對我說個不字。

passages.text: The Shah was thus conversing in his cups, what while the captains wondered, when a div in minstrel's guise addressed the chamberlain: a native of Mazandaran am I, a noted bard. When his harp was tuned he sang a ditty of Mazandaran: may I forget my native land never; on its heights the hyacinth and tulip bloom, there is neither heat nor cold, but spring is ever present; as for the rivers thou wouldst say they run rose-water surely.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 沙阿就這樣在酒杯之間談論著，眾將領正暗自驚異，這時一個化作吟遊詩人模樣的迪夫對侍從長說道：我是馬贊德蘭的本地人，一位著名的歌者。當他的豎琴調好音，他便唱起一支馬贊德蘭的小曲：願我永遠不忘我的故鄉；那裡的高地上風信子與鬱金香盛開，既無酷熱也無嚴寒，春天常駐；至於那河流，你定會說它們流淌的真是玫瑰水。

passages.text: The words roused Kai Kaus, who resolved to lead a host against Mazandaran, and harangued his warriors: we have been too fond of feast; in fortune, Grace, and birth I pass Jamshid, Zahhak, and Kai Kubad, and must surpass them in prowess too. The nobles heard and liked it not, turned pale, and frowned, for no one wished to fight the divs, though daring not to say so openly; they met thereafter and sent a cameleer in haste to Zal: if now thy head be soiled stay not to wash it, but whet thy wits and let us see thy face.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus secs. 2-3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這番話激起了凱·卡烏斯，他決心率領大軍征討馬贊德蘭，並對他的戰士們慷慨陳詞：我們太過沉溺於宴飲了；在福運、靈恩與出身方面，我勝過賈姆希德、扎哈克與凱·庫巴德，在勇武上也必定要超越他們。貴族們聽了並不喜歡，面色發白，眉頭緊皺，因為沒有人願意與迪夫作戰，卻又不敢公開說出來；他們隨後聚會，急忙派一名駱駝伕去見扎爾：倘若如今你的頭上沾了塵土，別停下來洗，還是磨礪你的機智，讓我們見見你的面吧。

passages.text: Zal, attended by the lords, counselled the Shah: none of thy mighty predecessors thought of such a journey; Mazandaran is the home of warlock-divs and under spells which none hath power to loose; so give not thou men, wealth, and money to the winds. Kaus replied: nathless I in courage, Grace, and treasure surpass Jamshid and Faridun; I shall go thither, snare them all, then tax them heavily or leave all dead. Zal heard, and baffled answered: thou art Shah, and we are slaves who must move and breathe according to thy will; no one can root out death or sew up the eyes of destiny with needles. Grieved that the Shah would go, Zal took his leave in haste, and as he left the monarch's presence both sun and moon were darkened in his eyes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus secs. 3-4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 扎爾在眾領主的陪同下勸諫沙阿：你那些強大的先王中，沒有一個想過這樣的遠行；馬贊德蘭是術士迪夫的家園，受著無人有力解開的咒法所困；所以不要把你的將士、財富與金錢付諸東風。卡烏斯答道：儘管如此，我在勇氣、靈恩與財寶上都勝過賈姆希德與法里頓；我要到那裡去，把他們一網打盡，然後重重向他們徵稅，或者把他們全都殺光。扎爾聽了，無奈地答道：你是沙阿，我們是奴僕，必須依照你的意願行動與呼吸；沒有人能根除死亡，也沒有人能用針縫合命運的雙眼。扎爾為沙阿執意前往而憂傷，匆匆告辭；當他離開君王面前時，在他眼中，太陽與月亮都黯淡了。

title.en: The White Div's Tent of Pitchy Smoke
title.zh: 白魔的黑煙之幕

region.en: Mazandaran (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 馬贊德蘭（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus sec. 4

summary.en: Giv leads two thousand mace-wielders into Mazandaran, sacking and burning cities, and the Shah marvels at a land like Paradise. But the monarch of Mazandaran summons the White Div, who rises like a mountain, head level with the turning sky, spreads above the Iranian host a tent of pitchy smoke, and showers stones and darts from the sky. When day had come the ambitious Shah and most among his warriors were blind, his troops were prisoners, and his treasures pillaged: I was to blame for this, moans Kaus, and I alone.
summary.zh: 吉夫率兩千持錘武士蹂躪馬贊德蘭，燒殺擄掠；卡烏斯嘆此地如天堂。然而馬贊德蘭王急召白魔——其身如山、頂天立地——向伊朗軍頭頂張起黑煙之幕，自天撒下石鏢。天明時，驕狂之王與大部分將士皆盲，部眾被擄、財寶被劫。卡烏斯哀嘆：「此禍唯我一人之過。」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Warner identifies the White Div with the white daevas of the Avestan Dinkard tradition. No living community restriction.

passages.text: At dawn they woke and entered helmed and armed the presence of the Shah, who ordered Giv: choose from the warriors two thousand men, mace-wielders, to prepare for us a path Mazandanin-ward, slaughter young and old, fire all the settlements, turn day to night, and slay the warlocks ere they are aware. Giv girt him, reached Mazandaran, showered scimitars and maces; the women, children, and old men with staves received no quarter from his sword; he sacked and burned the cities.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 黎明时分，他们醒来，戴上头盔、披挂整齐，进入沙阿的御前。沙阿命令吉夫：从战士中挑选两千名持锤之人，为我们开辟一条通往马赞达兰的道路，无论老幼一概杀戮，焚毁所有聚落，使白昼化为黑夜，趁术士们尚未察觉便将他们诛灭。吉夫束装出发，抵达马赞达兰，弯刀与铁锤如雨而下；妇女、孩童与手持木杖的老者，在他的剑下皆未获宽宥；他洗劫并焚烧了那些城池。

passages.text: He lighted on a spot like Paradise, replete with all delights: the cattle were past count. They told Kaus the news, who cried: happy the man who said Mazandaran may match with Paradise. The Iranians plundered for one week, then ceased. The monarch of Mazandaran received the news; his heart was sad, his head was heavy, and there was a div named Sanja at the court, to whom the monarch said: go and tell the White Div there hath come a host out of Iran to spoil Mazandaran; without thy help we shall be all destroyed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他落在一处宛如天堂的地方，诸般欢愉应有尽有：牲畜多得不可胜数。他们把这消息禀报考斯，考斯高呼：说马赞达兰堪与天堂相比的人有福了。伊朗人劫掠了一周，方才罢手。马赞达兰的君主接到消息，心中悲苦，头颅沉重；宫中有一名唤作桑贾的迪夫，君主对它说：去告诉白迪夫，有一支大军从伊朗而来，要蹂躏马赞达兰；若无你的相助，我们必将尽数覆灭。

passages.text: The White Div answered: be not in despair, for I am coming with a mighty host to cut the Shah's foot from Mazandaran. He spake and like a mountain rose erect, his head level with the turning sky. Night came, a cloud involved the Iranian host, and the world grew like a negro's face for blackness. The White Div spread above their heads a tent of pitchy smoke; from the sky he showered stones and darts; the Iranian troops dispersed abroad, and many sought Iran heart-broken at the doings of Kaus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 白迪夫答道：不必绝望，我正率领一支雄壮的大军前来，要把沙阿的双脚从马赞达兰斩断。它说罢，便如高山般巍然立起，头颅与旋转的天穹齐平。夜幕降临，一片乌云笼罩了伊朗大军，世界因漆黑而变得如同黑奴的面庞。白迪夫在他们头顶张开一顶沥青般浓烟的帐篷；它从天上降下石块与飞镖；伊朗军队四散奔逃，许多人因考斯的所作所为而心碎，返回了伊朗。

passages.text: When day had come the ambitious Shah and most among his warriors were blind. The nobles were wroth with him, his troops were prisoners, his treasures pillaged, and his fortunes old. Now when the Shah perceived his plight he said: a prudent minister is more than treasure; alas that I accepted not the counsel of Zal the worldlord but misdoubted it. The White Div went back to his home as glorious as the sun, while Kai Kaus remained within Mazandaran to moan: I was to blame for this and I alone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 白昼来临之时，那野心勃勃的沙阿与他麾下大多数战士都已失明。贵族们对他满怀愤怒，他的军队成了俘虏，他的财宝遭人劫掠，他的运势也已衰颓。此时沙阿察觉了自己的处境，说道：一位审慎的宰相胜过财宝；唉，我竟未采纳世界之主扎尔的忠告，反而对它心存疑虑。白迪夫如太阳般荣耀地返回了自己的家园，而凯·考斯则留在马赞达兰境内哀叹：此事错在于我，且仅在于我。

title.en: The First Course: Rakhsh Fights the Lion While Rustam Sleeps
title.zh: 七關之一：拉赫什獅口搏命

region.en: Onager plain en route to Mazandaran (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 赴馬贊德蘭途中野驢平原（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus sec. 6 (First Course)

summary.en: Rustam makes a two days' journey into one, catches an onager with his royal lasso, roasts and eats it, slips off Rakhsh's bridle, and sleeps in a reed-bed that is fear's own door, for a lion's lair is in it. The lion resolves to maim the steed first; Rakhsh rages like fire, lashes out at its head, fixes his teeth in its back, and dashes the beast to pieces. Rustam wakes and scolds the foolish Rakhsh: hadst thou perished, could I have carried my helmet, tiger-skin, bow, lasso, sword, and massive mace to Mazandaran?
summary.zh: 魯斯塔姆兩日併作一日趕路，以套索獵野驢炙食，解下拉赫什韁繩，睡於蘆葦叢——那正是獅子的巢穴。獅子先撲駿馬；拉赫什如烈火般反抗，咬住獅背將其撕碎。英雄醒來斥責「愚馬」：你若死了，我怎能把頭盔虎皮弓索刀錘帶往馬贊德蘭？

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; first of the Haft Khan episodes. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Rustam, that world-brightening paladin, departed from his sire and, treating night like day, made two days' journey into one, not giving Rakhsh repose. Now as his body failed him through lack of food he reached a plain where onager abounded, and the Lion with his royal lasso caught a gallant onager and, striking sparks upon an arrow's point, enkindled fire with stubble, thorns, and wood to roast the beast; he ate the flesh and threw away the bones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 鲁斯塔姆，那照亮世界的圣骑士，辞别了父亲，把黑夜当作白昼，将两日的路程并为一日，不让拉赫什有片刻歇息。此时他因缺乏食物而体力不支，来到一片野驴成群的原野；那雄狮以他王者的套索捕获了一头矫健的野驴，又在箭尖上击出火星，用枯草、荆棘与木柴燃起火来烤炙那野兽；他吃了肉，把骨头丢弃。

passages.text: He spied some pasture, slipped off Rakhsh's bridle, turned him out loose upon the meadow-land, and made himself a couch within a reed-bed; he deemed it safe though it was fear's own door, for in it was a lion's lair. One watch passed, then the lion came boldly forth and was amazed to see an elephantine form among the reeds, reposing with a charger standing by. First, said the lion, I must maim the steed, then I can take the rider when I please.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他望见一片牧草，便解下拉赫什的缰绳，放它自由地在草地上游荡，自己则在芦苇丛中铺了一张卧榻；他以为那里安全，殊不知那正是恐惧之门，因为其中有一处狮穴。一更过去，那狮子便大胆地走了出来，惊愕地看见芦苇丛中有一个如大象般的身形正在歇息，旁边还立着一匹战马。狮子先说道：我必须先使这匹战马伤残，然后便可随心所欲地取那骑手。

passages.text: He sprang at glossy Rakhsh, who raged like fire and lashed out at the lion's head, then fixed his sharp teeth in its back and dashed the beast to pieces by a shift that made it shiftless. When Rustam, deft of hand, awoke and saw how earth was straitened to that ravening beast he said: O foolish Rakhsh! who bade thee fight a lion? Hadst thou perished 'neath its claws could I have carried to Mazandaran my helmet, tiger-skin, bow, lasso, sword, and massive mace? He slept and rested long, and when the sun rose o'er the darksome hills awoke still drowsy, rubbed down Rakhsh and saddled him, then prayed to God, the Author of all good, for aid.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他縱身撲向光澤的拉赫什，拉赫什如烈火般狂怒，猛踢獅子的頭，隨即將利齒咬進牠的背，憑一記使牠動彈不得的猛力，把那野獸擊得粉碎。當手腳靈巧的魯斯塔姆醒來，看見大地竟被那貪婪的猛獸逼得如此窘迫，便說道：噢，愚蠢的拉赫什！是誰叫你與獅子搏鬥的？倘若你喪命於牠的利爪之下，我還能將我的頭盔、虎皮、弓、套索、劍與沉重的狼牙棒帶到馬贊德蘭嗎？他睡了許久，也休息了許久；當太陽升上昏暗的群山之上，他醒來時仍帶著睡意，替拉赫什刷洗身子、備好馬鞍，然後向一切善的創造者上帝祈求援助。

title.en: The Second Course: The Ram that Led to Water
title.zh: 七關之二：引泉之羊

region.en: Scorched desert en route (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 赴馬贊德蘭途中焦漠（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus sec. 7 (Second Course)

summary.en: Rustam faces a waterless desert of intense heat that dried the birds to powder; his tongue fails, and the elephantine form falls on the burning dust. A well-fed ram passes by; the hero follows it till he sees the spring, and looking toward heaven says: the ram hath left no tracks about the spring — it is no desert-sheep of flesh and blood. He blesses the ram that rescued Rustam, roasts an onager, charges Rakhsh to fight nothing, and sleeps.
summary.zh: 魯斯塔姆陷入酷熱無水的荒漠，飛鳥成灰；他舌焦唇裂，如象之軀轟然倒於滾燙沙土。一頭肥羊經過；英雄強撑追隨至泉邊，仰望上蒼：「泉邊無羊蹄印——此非凡俗之羊！」他祝福引路的羊，烤食野驢，命拉赫什不得擅鬥，然後安然入睡。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the ram is read as a divine provision. No living community restriction.

passages.text: He had to face, all dizzy as he was, a desert waterless, a heat intense that dried the birds to powder; plain and waste were as they had been scorched. Rakhsh was exhausted, while his rider's tongue failed through the heat and drought, and Rustam, clutching a double-headed dart, went staggering like one bemused, and saw no means of safety. He looked up saying: O all-righteous Judge! Thou bring'st all toil and hardship on my head; I fare in hope that God will grant deliverance to the Shah, and that the Ruler of the world will free the Iranians from the clutches of the Div.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 7 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他儘管頭昏眼花，仍得面對一片無水的荒漠、酷烈得能把鳥兒曬成粉末的炎熱；平原與荒地彷彿都被燒焦了一般。拉赫什已精疲力竭，而牠的騎者因酷熱與乾渴連舌頭都不聽使喚；魯斯塔姆緊握一支雙頭標槍，像失神的人一般踉蹌而行，看不到任何脫險的辦法。他仰望天空說道：噢，至公的審判者！你將一切勞苦與艱難都加在我頭上；我此行懷著希望，盼上帝賜予沙阿解脫，盼世界的統治者使伊朗人脫離迪弗的魔掌。

passages.text: This said, that elephantine form became weak and distraught with thirst, and fell, with tongue all cracked and blistered, on the burning dust. Anon a well-fed ram passed by. The hero on seeing thought: where is its watering-place? In sooth God's mercy is extended to me! Then in the Worldlord's strength he rose to his feet and followed up the ram until he saw the spring, for thither went that stately ram. Then Rustam looked toward heaven and said: the ram hath left no tracks about the spring! It is no desert-sheep of flesh and blood!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 7 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 話一說完，那如象般魁梧的身軀便因乾渴而虛弱恍惚，舌頭盡皆乾裂起泡，倒在灼熱的塵土上。不久，一隻肥壯的公羊走了過去。這位英雄見了心想：牠的飲水處在何處？誠然，上帝的慈悲已施及於我！於是他憑著世界之主的力氣站起身來，跟隨那隻公羊，直到看見那處泉水，因為那隻雄偉的公羊正是往那裡去的。魯斯塔姆隨即仰望天空說道：那隻公羊在泉水四周竟未留下任何足跡！牠絕非血肉之軀的沙漠野羊！

passages.text: He blessed that ram and said: ne'er may mishap from circling heaven be thine; green be thy pastures; may cheetah never mark thee for its prey; snapped be the bow and dark the soul of him that shooteth at thee who hath rescued Rustam. His praises offered he unsaddled Rakhsh, washed him, and made him shining as the sun. Then Rustam much refreshed filled up his quiver, roasted an onager, feasted, and said to Rakhsh: fight not and make no friends; if any foe approacheth run to me, but venture not to counter divs and lions. He lay and slept, his lips in silence bound.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 7 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他為那隻公羊祝福，說道：願循環運轉的蒼天永不降禍於你；願你的牧場常青；願獵豹永不將你視為獵物；願向你放箭之人的弓折斷、靈魂昏暗——因為他救了魯斯塔姆。獻上這番讚頌之後，他卸下拉赫什的鞍，替牠洗刷，使牠光亮如太陽。魯斯塔姆精神大振，裝滿了箭囊，烤了一頭野驢，飽餐一頓，然後對拉赫什說：不要爭鬥，也不要結交朋友；若有敵人靠近，便跑到我這裡來，但切莫膽敢與迪弗和獅子較量。他躺下睡了，雙唇緊閉，默然無聲。

title.en: The Third Course: Rustam and the Dragon of the Waste
title.zh: 七關之三：荒漠巨龍

region.en: Haunted waste en route (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 赴馬贊德蘭途中魔地（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus sec. 8 (Third Course)

summary.en: A dragon comes from the waste whose haunt no div dared pass: no lions, divs, or elephants that went that way escaped its clutches. Rakhsh thrice rouses his sleeping master — and is twice chidden for it, threatened with the scimitar — till the Maker wills that the dragon be seen. The dragon boasts centuries of possession; Rustam names himself son of Zal and lays its head in dust, Rakhsh joining the fray, biting at its shoulders and tearing its hide; blood jets out in rivers, and the carcase hides the earth.
summary.zh: 荒漠巨龍現身——此地連魔怪也不敢擅越。拉赫什三度喚醒沉睡的主人，兩度遭斥，險些被劍斬首；直到造物主令龍現形。巨龍誇口盤踞數百年，魯斯塔姆自報家門「扎勒之子」，與龍搏鬥；拉赫什咬其肩、撕其皮，利劍斬下龍首，血如江河，龍屍蔽野。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; second Shahnama dragon-slaying of Rustam (cf. persian-sam-dragon-kashaf). No living community restriction.

passages.text: A dragon, such an one as no elephant could 'scape, came from the waste. Its haunt was there; no div dared pass thereby. It came, beheld the atheling asleep, a charger near him, and was wroth. It thought: what do I see? Who dareth to sleep here? Because no lions, divs, or elephants dared pass that way or, if they did, escaped not the clutches of that dragon fierce and fell, it turned on glossy Rakhsh, who ran to Rustam, stamped with his brazen hoofs upon the ground, whisked with his tail, and gave a thundering neigh.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 8 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一條連大象也逃不脫的巨龍從荒野而來。那裡是牠的巢穴；沒有哪個迪弗敢從此經過。牠來了，看見那位王子沉睡著，身旁有一匹戰馬，便勃然大怒。牠心想：我這是看見了什麼？誰敢在此睡覺？正因沒有獅子、迪弗或大象敢從那條路經過，即便經過，也逃不出那兇猛殘暴的巨龍的魔爪，牠便轉向光澤的拉赫什；拉赫什跑到魯斯塔姆身邊，以黃銅般的蹄子刨地，甩動尾巴，發出雷鳴般的嘶鳴。

passages.text: The hero woke up furious, perceived not that fell dragon, and wreaked his wrath on Rakhsh for waking him. He slept again; again the worm approached out of the gloom; Rakhsh ran to Rustam's couch and kicked the earth about. Thou canst not blink the darkness of the night, said the sleeper, yet wakest me again impatiently! If thou disturb me more I will behead thee with my sharp scimitar. Then for the third time with his tiger-skin upon his breast he set himself to sleep. The fearsome dragon roared and, thou hadst said, breathed fire; Rakhsh, o'ermastered by affection for his lord, rushed to Rustam's side and pawed upon the ground, till the Maker willed that the dragon should be seen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 8 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這位英雄怒氣沖沖地醒來，卻未察覺那兇惡的巨龍，反把怒氣發在喚醒他的拉赫什身上。他又睡了；那條巨蟲再度從幽暗中逼近；拉赫什跑到魯斯塔姆的臥榻旁，把泥土踢得四處飛揚。你躲不開這黑夜的昏暗，沉睡的人說道，卻又急躁地把我喚醒！你若再擾我，我便用鋒利的彎刀砍下你的頭。接著他第三次把虎皮覆在胸前，準備入睡。那可怕的巨龍咆哮起來，你定會說牠吐出了火焰；拉赫什因對主人的深情難以自持，衝到魯斯塔姆身旁刨地，直到造物主有意讓那巨龍顯露身形。

passages.text: Rustam unsheathed the keen sword at his girdle, thundered out like spring-clouds, and filled earth with battle-fire. Tell thy name, said he to the dragon; earth is no longer thine. The laidly dragon said: none escapeth me; for centuries this waste hath been my home, and mine its firmament; no eagle dareth to fly across or star to dream thereof. I am Rustam, he answered, sprung from Zal, the son of Sam and Nariman withal. The dragon closed with him, and Rakhsh, on seeing its might, laid his ears back, joined the fray, bit at the dragon's shoulders and tore its hide as though he were a lion; the paladin with keen glaive smote off the dragon's head, blood jetted out in rivers, and its carcase hid the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 8 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 魯斯塔姆拔出腰間鋒利的寶劍，聲如春雲般雷鳴，以戰火充滿大地。他對巨龍說：報上你的名來；大地已不再屬於你。那醜惡的巨龍說道：無人能逃脫我手；數百年來這片荒原便是我的家園，其蒼穹亦歸我所有；沒有鷹敢飛越，也沒有星辰敢於夢想此事。他答道：我乃魯斯塔姆，出自扎爾，扎爾乃薩姆與納里曼之子。巨龍與他纏鬥，拉赫什見其威勢，便將雙耳向後貼伏，加入戰團，咬向巨龍的肩膊，如獅子般撕扯其皮；那聖騎士以鋒利寶劍斬下巨龍之首，鮮血如江河般噴湧而出，其屍身遮蔽了大地。

title.en: The Fourth Course: The Witch in the Lasso
title.zh: 七關之四：繩中之巫

region.en: Sorcerers' spring (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 術士之泉（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus sec. 9 (Fourth Course)

summary.en: Rustam comes upon a desert laid out like a banquet-hall — a spring bright as pheasant's eyes, a golden bowl of wine, a roasted mountain-sheep, and a dainty lute — and sings to it of his toils: 'tis dragon, div, and desert, one perpetual engagement. The sound reaches a witch's ears; she makes her cheeks like spring and sits down by him, but when he names the Giver of all good her favour changes, she blackens at God's name, and Rustam, flinging his lasso quicker than the wind, ensnares a fetid hag all guile and wrinkle and cleaves her with his blade.
summary.zh: 魯斯塔姆行至術士布置的宴場——清泉、金盃美酒、烤羊與豎琴——彈唱自況：「終日所對者，唯龍、魔與荒漠。」琴聲入巫耳，巫女敷粉扮春，坐於其側；魯斯塔姆一念「施恩之神」之名，她容色驟變、聞神名而獰。英雄疾擲套索，套住一個滿面皺紋的醜巫，揮劍斬之。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Thanksgivings done, he harnessed rose-cheeked Rakhsh and mounting came in time where sorcerers dwelt. Long had he fared and saw, as Sol declined, trees, grass, and stream, the very spot for youth. There was a spring as bright as pheasant's eyes; beside it were a golden bowl of wine, a roasted mountain-sheep with bread thereon, and salts and sweetmeats. Rustam thanked the Lord for showing him a place so opportune. It was a sorcerers' meal, and when he came his voice had caused those divs to disappear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 9 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 致謝已畢，他為玫瑰色面頰的拉赫什備好鞍韉，騎乘而行，適時來到巫師們居住之地。他行路已久，正當太陽西沉之時，望見樹木、青草與溪流，正是少年人歇息的好地方。那兒有一泓清泉，明亮如雉雞之眼；泉旁有一隻盛酒的金碗、一隻烤好的山羊，其上放著麵包，還有鹽與甜食。魯斯塔姆感謝主讓他得見如此合宜之地。那是巫師們的餐食，當他到來時，他的聲音已使那些迪夫消失無蹤。

passages.text: He sat beside the rushy stream, brimmed a jewelled cup with wine, took up the lute, touched the chords, and sang: Oh! Rustam is an outcast still and hath no days of pleasure; his combatings are never done; 'tis dragon, div, and desert, one perpetual engagement. The sound of music reached a witch's ears; she made her cheeks like spring, although by rights she was not fair, and then, perfumed and decked, approached, saluted, and sat down by Rustam.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 9 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他坐在燈心草叢生的溪旁，以酒斟滿鑲寶石的杯盞，拿起魯特琴，撥動琴弦，唱道：啊！魯斯塔姆仍是個被放逐者，沒有歡樂的日子；他的征戰永無止息；巨龍、迪夫與荒漠，是一場永無休止的搏鬥。樂聲傳入一個女巫的耳中；她把自己的面頰裝扮得如春日一般，雖然按理她並不美麗，然後她薰香盛裝，走上前來，行禮致意，在魯斯塔姆身旁坐下。

passages.text: Not knowing that she was a wicked witch, an Ahriman beneath her bravery, he handed her a cup of wine, invoking the Giver of all good. Now when he named the Lord of love her favour changed; no soul had she for gratitude, no tongue for praise, but blackened at God's name, while Rustam, flinging his lasso quicker than the wind, ensnared her, and questioned her: what art thou? Speak and show thy proper favour. In the lasso's coils there was a fetid hag all guile and wrinkle, calamitous. He clave her with his blade and made the hearts of sorcerers afraid.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 9 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他不知她是個邪惡的女巫，那勇敢外表下的阿里曼，便遞給她一杯酒，同時呼求一切美善的賜予者。當他念出愛之主的名號時，她的面容驟變；她心中毫無感恩，口中毫無讚美，反而因神之名而面色發黑，而魯斯塔姆拋出套索，比風還快，將她擒住，並質問她：你是什麼？開口說話，顯出你的真面目。套索的纏繞之中，是一個惡臭的老嫗，滿是詭詐與皺紋，災禍臨身。他以刀刃將她劈開，使巫師們的心中生畏。

title.en: Kumulipo: The First Night of Corals and Shells
title.zh: 生命源起：第一夜的珊瑚與螺貝

region.en: Hawaiian chant sung at Honaunau (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 夏威夷霍瑙瑙誦唱地（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 18th c. for Ka-I-i-mamao; recorded by Queen Liliuokalani, translation 1897

source.work: The Kumulipo, Hawaiian creation chant, trans. Queen Lili'uokalani (San Francisco 1897); interlinear ed. M. W. Beckwith (1951)

summary.en: When the earth grew hot and the heavens turned about, and the sun was darkened that the moon might shine, there was nothing but night; night gave birth to Kumulipo, a male, and Po'ele, a female. From the darkness slip into light the first born of the sea: the coral polyp, the grub that heaps the earth, starfish, sea cucumbers, sea urchins, barnacles and pearl oysters, mussels and limpets, cowries and conch - each with its child. 'Born was man for the narrow stream, the woman for the broad stream; the god enters, man cannot enter.'
summary.zh: 地熱翻滾、天穹旋轉、日暗月明之際，唯有長夜；夜生男庫穆利波與女波埃萊。黑暗滑入光明，海中初生者次第而出：珊瑚蟲、掘地之蟲、海星、海參、海膽、藤壺珍珠貝、蚌螺之屬——各攜其子。經文反覆吟詠：『男屬細流，女屬寬流；神可入，人不可入。』

sensitivity.note: Genealogical chant of Hawaiian ali'i line; paraphrase of the Liliuokalani public-domain translation only.

passages.text: At the time when the earth became hot, at the time when the heavens turned about, at the time when the sun was darkened, to cause the moon to shine, the time of the rise of the Pleiades - the slime, this was the source of the earth. The source of the darkness that made darkness; the source of the night that made night. The intense darkness, the deep darkness; darkness of the sun, darkness of the night - nothing but night. The night gave birth: born was Kumulipo in the night, a male; born was Po'ele in the night, a female.
passages.note: Paraphrase of The Kumulipo, chant one (Liliuokalani 1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在大地變熱之時，在諸天旋轉之時，在太陽被遮蔽、使月亮得以照耀之時，在昴星團升起之時——那黏液，便是大地的本源。那使黑暗成為黑暗的黑暗之本源；那使夜成為夜的黑夜之本源。那濃重的黑暗，那深沉的黑暗；太陽的黑暗，夜晚的黑暗——除了夜，別無他物。夜誕生了：庫穆利波生於夜中，為男性；波埃萊生於夜中，為女性。

passages.text: Born was the coral polyp, born was the coral, came forth. Born was the grub that digs and heaps up the earth; born was his child, an earthworm. Born was the starfish, his child the small starfish came forth; born was the sea cucumber, his child the small sea cucumber; born was the sea urchin, and the short-spiked sea urchin, the smooth sea urchin with its child the long-spiked, the ring-shaped with its child the thin-spiked; born was the barnacle, his child the pearl oyster; born was the mother-of-pearl, his child the oyster; born was the mussel, his child the hermit crab; born was the big limpet, his child the small limpet; born was the cowry, his child the small cowry; born was the conch shell, his child the small conch shell; born was the nerita shellfish and the sand-burrowing shellfish; born was the fresh water shellfish, his child the small fresh water shellfish came forth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of The Kumulipo, chant one (Liliuokalani 1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 珊瑚蟲誕生了，珊瑚誕生了，湧現而出。掘土堆土的小蟲誕生了；他的孩子蚯蚓誕生了。海星誕生了，他的孩子小海星湧現而出；海參誕生了，他的孩子小海參；海膽誕生了，還有短刺海膽、光滑海膽及其孩子長刺海膽、環形海膽及其孩子細刺海膽；藤壺誕生了，他的孩子珍珠貝；珍珠母貝誕生了，他的孩子牡蠣；貽貝誕生了，他的孩子寄居蟹；大帽貝誕生了，他的孩子小帽貝；寶螺誕生了，他的孩子小寶螺；海螺殼誕生了，他的孩子小海螺殼；蜑螺與鑽沙貝誕生了；淡水貝誕生了，他的孩子小淡水貝湧現而出。

passages.text: Born was man for the narrow stream, the woman for the broad stream. Born was the Ekaha moss living in the sea, guarded by the Ekahakaha fern living on land; darkness slips into light; earth and water are the food of the plant. The god enters, man cannot enter. Born was the tough seagrass living in the sea, guarded by the tough landgrass living on land; born was the Ala'ala moss, guarded by the Ala'ala mint; born was the Manauea moss, guarded by the Manauea taro plant; born was the Ko'ele seaweed, guarded by the long-jointed sugarcane; born was the Puaki seaweed, guarded by the Akiaki rush living on land. Darkness slips into light; earth and water are the food of the plant; the god enters, man cannot enter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of The Kumulipo, chant one (Liliuokalani 1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 男人為窄流而生，女人為寬流而生。生出了生於海中的Ekaha苔蘚，由生於陸上的Ekahakaha蕨類守護；黑暗潛入光明；土與水是植物的食糧。神進入了，人不能進入。生出了生於海中的堅韌海草，由生於陸上的堅韌陸草守護；生出了Ala'ala苔蘚，由Ala'ala薄荷守護；生出了Manauea苔蘚，由Manauea芋頭植物守護；生出了Ko'ele海藻，由長節甘蔗守護；生出了Puaki海藻，由生於陸上的Akiaki燈心草守護。黑暗潛入光明；土與水是植物的食糧；神進入了，人不能進入。

title.en: The Second Night: Fish Born Swimming
title.zh: 第二夜：海中生靈齊誕

region.en: Hawaiian chant (symbolic pin, deep sea)
region.zh: 夏威夷祭歌（象徵性定位，深海）

period: Composed c. 18th c.; recorded by Queen Liliuokalani, translation 1897

source.work: The Kumulipo, Hawaiian creation chant, chant two, trans. Queen Lili'uokalani (San Francisco 1897); interlinear ed. M. W. Beckwith (1951)

summary.en: Born is a child to Po-wehiwehi, cradled in the arms of Po-uliuli, dweller in the land of Poho-mi-luamea - the sacred scent from the gourd stem proclaims itself, and the seven waters just float. Born is the child of the hilu fish and swims. Born is the porpoise in the sea there swimming; born is the shark and the goatfish; the eel and the crab; the octopus and the sting ray; the bonito and the albacore; mackerel, mullet - each born in the sea there swimming, while land creatures wait their pairing across the divided nights.
summary.zh: 波維希維希之子誕生，搖於波烏里烏里之懷，居於波霍米盧阿梅亞之境；葫蘆莖間聖香自陳，七水漂浮。希盧魚之子誕生而游。海中依次誕生：鼠海豚、鯊、山羊魚、鰻與蟹、章魚與魟、鰹與鮪、鯖與鯔——凡例皆『在海中游而誕』；陸上生靈則待各夜配對而生。

sensitivity.note: Chant-two catalogue paraphrase.

passages.text: Born is a child to Po-wehiwehi, cradled in the arms of Po-uliuli; a wrestler, a pusher; dweller in the land of Poho-mi-luamea. The sacred scent from the gourd stem proclaims itself; the stench breaks forth in the time of infancy; he is doubtful and stands swelling; he crooks himself and straddles. The seven waters just float; born is the child of the hilu fish and swims. The hilu fish rests with spreading tail-fin; a child of renown for Po-uliuli, a little one for Po-wehiwehi: Po-uliuli the male, Po-wehiwehi the female.
passages.note: Paraphrase of The Kumulipo, chant two (Liliuokalani 1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 為Po-wehiwehi生下一子，抱在Po-uliuli的臂彎中；一個摔跤者，一個推擠者；居於Poho-mi-luamea之地。葫蘆莖的神聖香氣自我宣告；惡臭在嬰兒時期迸發；他猶疑不定，站立而腫脹；他彎曲身子，跨立而踞。七道水只是漂浮；生出了hilu魚之子，游動起來。hilu魚張開尾鰭歇息；為Po-uliuli而生的一個有名望的孩子，為Po-wehiwehi而生的一個小傢伙：Po-uliuli是雄性，Po-wehiwehi是雌性。

passages.text: Born is the I'a, born the porpoise in the sea there swimming; born is the shark, born the goatfish, in the sea there swimming; born is the Mau and the Maumau; the Nana and the Mana; the Nake and the Make; the Napa and the Nala; the Pala and the Kala; the eel and the crab in the sea there swimming; born is the Kalakala and the Huluhulu sea slug; the Halahala and the Palapala; born is the octopus, born the sting ray in the sea there swimming; born is the Ao and the milkfish; born is the bonito, born the albacore in the sea there swimming; born is the mackerel and the Akule fish; born is the mullet and the Anae in the sea there swimming.
passages.note: Paraphrase of The Kumulipo, chant two (Liliuokalani 1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 生出了I'a，生出了海豚，在海中游動；生出了鯊魚，生出了山羊魚，在海中游動；生出了Mau與Maumau；Nana與Mana；Nake與Make；Napa與Nala；Pala與Kala；鰻魚與螃蟹，在海中游動；生出了Kalakala與Huluhulu海蛞蝓；Halahala與Palapala；生出了章魚，生出了魟魚，在海中游動；生出了Ao與遮目魚；生出了鰹魚，生出了長鰭鮪魚，在海中游動；生出了鯖魚與Akule魚；生出了鯔魚與Anae，在海中游動。

passages.text: Man for the narrow stream, woman for the broad stream - the refrain that opens each division of the chant: every sea creature born in its night has its counterpart born on land in a night to come, the pairing of sea and shore, water-thing and land-thing, running through sixteen chants until the human line of the chiefs appears. The Kumulipo sings the birth of the cosmos as a genealogy, so that the chief born at its end may claim the whole chain of life from the first darkness as his ancestors.
passages.note: Paraphrase of The Kumulipo, chant two and frame (Liliuokalani 1897; Beckwith 1951); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 男人為窄流，女人為寬流——這是吟唱每一段落開頭的反覆句：每一個在其夜晚出生的海中生物，都有一個在未來的某個夜晚生於陸上的對應者，海與岸、水中之物與陸上之物的配對，貫穿十六段吟唱，直到首領的人類世系出現。《Kumulipo》以譜系的形式吟唱宇宙的誕生，使在其末尾出生的首領得以宣稱，從最初之黑暗以來的整條生命之鏈都是他的祖先。

title.en: La'ila'i, the Woman of Nu'umealani, Mother of Men
title.zh: 神秘女子萊伊萊伊：人類之母

region.en: Nu'umealani, land of the gods (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 神居之地努烏梅阿蘭尼（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 18th c.; recorded by Queen Liliuokalani, translation 1897

source.work: The Kumulipo, Hawaiian creation chant, chants nine-ten, trans. Queen Lili'uokalani (San Francisco 1897); interlinear ed. M. W. Beckwith (1951)

summary.en: Still trembling stands the earth; hot, rumbling, split is the heaven - this woman ascends to heaven and the earth splits. The children of Ki'i sprung from the brain come out and fly to the heavens, marked by the ruddy tint. From the female fire-stick comes the fire that makes men; this woman dwelt in Nu'umealani, the land where the gods dwelt, stripped the dark leaves of the koa - a woman of mysterious body who lived with Ki'i, with Kane, with Kane of the time when men multiplied. She bore the Groping-one, the Dim-sighted, and last the Naked-one - part of the posterity from whom the chief's line is chanted.
summary.zh: 大地震顫而立；天穹轟裂如焚——神秘女子直上九天，大地為之坼裂。自奇伊腦髓迸出的子嗣飛昇於天，以紅暈為記。『女火棒迸出成人之火』：此女居神地努烏梅阿蘭尼，剝寇阿暗葉；身體莫測，與奇伊同居、與卡內同居、與人丁繁衍之世的卡內同居。她生下摸索者、昏昧者，最末生下赤裸者——酋長世系即自此女之後裔誦起。

sensitivity.note: The human-line opening of the Kumulipo; the female fire-stick image retained.

passages.text: Still, trembling stands earth; hot, rumbling, split is the heaven; this woman ascends to heaven, ascends right up to heaven; ascends up toward the forest. Tries to touch the earth and the earth splits up; children of Ki'i sprung from the brain came out, flew, flew also to the heavens; showed the sign, the ruddy tint by which they were known; showed the fine reddish hair at puberty; showed on the chin a reddish beard. The offspring of that mysterious woman - the woman of 'Iliponi, of within 'I'ipakalani.
passages.note: Paraphrase of The Kumulipo, chant nine (Liliuokalani 1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大地依然顫抖而立；天空炎熱、轟鳴、裂開；這女人升上天去，一直升上天去；升向森林。她試圖觸及大地，大地便裂開；從腦中迸出的Ki'i之子孫出來了，飛翔，也飛向諸天；顯示了記號，即他們藉以辨認的紅暈；顯示了青春期細紅的毛髮；顯示了下巴上紅色的鬍鬚。那神秘女人的後裔——'Iliponi的女人，'I'ipakalani之內的女人。

passages.text: From the female fire-stick comes the fire that makes men. That woman dwelt in Nu'umealani, the land where the gods dwelt; she stripped the dark leaves of the koa tree - a woman of mysterious body was this. She lived with Ki'i, she lived with Kane; she lived with Kane of the time when men multiplied; forgotten is the time of this multitude. A multitude, the posterity of the time of child-bearing; she returned again upward, dwelt in the sacred forest of the gods in Nu'umealani. Was pregnant there; the earth broke open; born was the woman Groping-one; born was Dim-sighted, a woman; last born was Naked-one, 'Olohelohe - part of the posterity of that woman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of The Kumulipo, chant nine (Liliuokalani 1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從女性的取火棒生出造人的火。那女人住在Nu'umealani，即諸神所居之地；她剝下koa樹的暗色葉子——這是一個身體神秘的女人。她與Ki'i同住，她與Kane同住；她與人類繁衍時代的Kane同住；這眾多者的時代已被遺忘。一個眾多者，生育時代的後裔；她再次向上返回，住在Nu'umealani諸神的神聖森林中。在那裡懷了孕；大地裂開；生出了女人Groping-one（摸索者）；生出了Dim-sighted（弱視者），一個女人；最後生出的是Naked-one（赤裸者），'Olohelohe——那女人後裔的一部分。

passages.text: Come hither, La'ila'i to the wall: Kane of Kapokinikini to the post; Ki'i be quiet. Born was La'i-olo-olo and lived at Kapapa; born was Kamaha'ina the first-born, a male; born was Kamamule, a male; Kamakalua the second child was a girl; came the child Po'ele-i, Midnight; came the child Po'ele-a, First-light; Wehi-wela-wehi-loa, opening-to-the-heat, opening wide. La'ila'i returned and lived with Kane - so the chant moves from the mysterious ancestress to the named generations through which the Kumulipo reaches the chief for whose birth the sixteen chants were composed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of The Kumulipo, chant ten (Liliuokalani 1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 前來吧，拉伊拉伊（La'ila'i）來到牆邊：卡波基尼基尼（Kapokinikini）的卡內（Kane）來到柱旁；基伊（Ki'i）安靜下來。拉伊奧洛奧洛（La'i-olo-olo）誕生了，住在卡帕帕（Kapapa）；卡馬哈伊納（Kamaha'ina）誕生了，是頭生的，是個男孩；卡馬穆萊（Kamamule）誕生了，是個男孩；卡馬卡盧阿（Kamakalua）是第二個孩子，是個女孩；波埃萊伊（Po'ele-i）這孩子來了，是午夜；波埃萊阿（Po'ele-a）這孩子來了，是初光；韋希韋拉韋希洛阿（Wehi-wela-wehi-loa），向著炎熱敞開，大大敞開。拉伊拉伊回去了，與卡內同住——於是這吟唱從那位神秘的女性祖先，轉向那些具名的世代，庫穆利波（Kumulipo）正是透過這些世代，抵達那十六首吟唱為其誕生而作的酋長。

title.en: Bretigny of Cayenne: the Governor the Caribs Slew
title.zh: 卡宴總督布雷蒂尼：加勒比人所誅之暴君

region.en: Cayenne, French Guiana
region.zh: 法屬圭亞那卡宴

period: Carib historical legend of the 17th c.; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part III 'Legends of the Caribs', 'Struggles with Early Colonists'

summary.en: Bretigny — man of evil fame — first Governor to Cayenne came. Stern his new ruler, harsh his deeds, for trifling acts the white man bleeds; most cruel was his sway — and the natives, too, he dared to oppress. Then Caribs vowed, in stern redress, that tyrant chief to slay. But Indian women often love the European far above their own red countrymen — and thus Bretigny came to know his danger in Cayenne: soon as, from female lips, he heard the Carib plan, he gave the word to seize all Caribs there. 'Each casts himself into the wave, and in a shark will find his grave, ere bondage he will bear.' The great canoe pursued the swimmers to the shore, and Bretigny, landing, searched until nightfall for an Indian cabin to remain. But the trees have eyes: all night the Carib warriors came noiselessly, and with morning light hundreds of painted warriors appeared, each with his bended bow. Wrapped in his cloak, Bretigny silently stood to meet his fate from Carib hands — by club and arrow there. They slew his guards, raged wherever colonists were found; the Frenchmen came again, but failed — 'tis twenty years ere they prevailed and settled in Cayenne.
summary.zh: 布雷蒂尼——聲名狼藉者——首任卡宴總督也。其治嚴酷，白人以小過見戮，土民亦遭其虐。加勒比人誓誅此暴君。然土女多愛歐人；布雷蒂尼自其口中聞謀，遂下令盡捕加勒比人。眾曰：『寧投波葬鯊腹，不為奴虜！』巨舟追至岸；總督搜至夜宿土屋。林中有目：加勒比戰士徹夜潛行，晨則彩繪武士數百執弓而至。總督裹氈默立，以待其命——棒與箭也。衛兵盡誅，白人村落俱焚；法人再至而不成——二十年後始得定居卡宴。

sensitivity.note: Carib historical legend recorded by the missionary Brett 1880; a colonial-era conflict narrative, read critically.

passages.text: Bretigny — man of evil fame — first Governor to Cayenne came. Frenchmen were there before, living as Indians there in peace, their wives and language Caribisce, thinking of France no more. Stern their new ruler, harsh his deeds, for trifling acts the white man bleeds; most cruel was his sway. The natives, too, he dared oppress. Then Caribs vowed, in stern redress, that tyrant chief to slay!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Struggles with Early Colonists'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布雷蒂尼（Bretigny）——惡名昭彰之人——是首位來到卡宴（Cayenne）的總督。此前已有法國人在此，像印第安人一樣在此和平生活，他們的妻子與語言皆為加勒比（Carib）式的，不再思念法國。他們的新統治者嚴酷，行事苛刻，白人因些微小事便流血；他的統治最為殘酷。他竟還敢壓迫原住民。於是加勒比人立誓，要嚴厲復仇，殺死那暴虐的酋長！

passages.text: But Indian women often love the European far above their own red countrymen — and thus Bretigny came to know his danger in Cayenne. Soon as, from female lips, he heard the Carib plan, he gave the word to seize all Caribs there. 'Each casts himself into the wave, and in a shark will find his grave, ere bondage he will bear.' Swim now, ye Caribs, for your lives! That great canoe can swiftly run; her crew have halberd, sword, and gun — all Frenchmen, strong and bold!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Struggles with Early Colonists'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但印第安婦女往往愛歐洲人遠勝於自己的紅種同胞——布雷蒂尼就這樣在卡宴得知了自己的危險。他一從女人口中聽到加勒比的計畫，便下令捉拿當地所有加勒比人。「他們寧可各自投身波濤，葬身鯊魚之腹，也不願忍受奴役。」如今，加勒比人啊，為活命而游吧！那大獨木舟能疾速行駛；船上的船員手持戟、劍與槍——全是法國人，強壯而勇敢！

passages.text: They gain the shore. Then, in pursuit, Bretigny lands, searches there, and finds an Indian cabin where he may all night remain. Ah! little does Bretigny know the tactics of an Indian foe: the trees have eyes to see where he abides, and all the night the Carib warriors, armed for fight, are coming noiselessly. With morning light they all appear, hundreds of painted warriors near, each with his bended bow. Wrapped in his cloak, he silent stands to meet his fate from Carib hands, by club and arrow there. They slay his guards, then rage around wherever colonists are found, destroying all white men. The Frenchmen come again, but fail; 'tis twenty years ere they prevail and settle in Cayenne.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Struggles with Early Colonists'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們上了岸。隨後布雷蒂尼登陸追擊，在那裡搜索，找到一間印第安人的小屋，可以在那裡過一整夜。啊！布雷蒂尼幾乎不知道印第安敵人的戰術：樹木有眼睛，能看見他待在何處，整夜裡加勒比戰士們武裝待戰，悄無聲息地前來。隨著晨光，他們全都出現，數百名塗繪的戰士逼近，人人手持彎弓。他裹著斗篷，默默站立，迎接來自加勒比人之手的命運，在那裡死於棍棒與箭矢。他們殺死他的衛兵，然後四處肆虐，凡有殖民者之處皆不放過，毀滅所有白人。法國人再度前來，卻失敗了；過了二十年他們才得勝，並在卡宴定居。

title.en: The Carib War Path
title.zh: 加勒比征途

region.en: From Marowijne to the Orinoco headwaters
region.zh: 馬羅維恩至奧里諾科上游

period: Carib historical legend; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part III 'Legends of the Caribs', 'Warlike Legends: The Carib War Path'

summary.en: The way they marched to all was known: custom had made that track their own. 'Twas to those rovers mere child's play to plunder there, sometimes to slay, and often to enslave. Their large canoes were often seen as they sailed round from Marowijne and Surinam to Corentyne, then towards that river's head; above the falls they cross Berbice, and march where all is perfect peace. That region they have swept quite bare, and all the people who lived there are captive, slain, or fled. O'er Essequibo then they go: plunder Macusis, or, below, sweep the Brazilian plain; or towards the Pacaraima chain bend their course. On rafts concealed they float near shore, with grass or branches covered o'er; sometimes on fallen trees they glide, such as come downward with the tide. Woe to the victims they surprise! All adults slain, each girl a prize must in their hands remain.
summary.zh: 加勒比人之征路，人所共知；沿俗而行，劫殺虜掠，如兒戲耳。巨舟自馬羅維恩、蘇利南至科倫丁，復溯其源；越灘而渡伯比斯，行於至靜之地——其地之民，或虜或戮或逃，蕩然無餘。復越埃斯塞基博，掠馬庫希，或南掃巴西之原，或向帕卡賴馬之山。藏筏草蔽而近岸；或乘浮木隨潮而進。遭其突者禍矣：成人盡戮，女子盡為戰利。

sensitivity.note: Carib raiding tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880; read critically — a colonizer's versification of intertribal warfare.

passages.text: The way they marched to all was known; custom had made that track their own. 'Twas to those rovers mere child's play to plunder there, sometimes to slay, and often to enslave; and all the peaceful tribes who dwelt around — the heavy hand had felt — of Caribs, fierce and brave. Their large canoes were often seen as they sailed round from Marowijne and Surinam to Corentyne, then towards that river's head. Above the falls they cross Berbice, and march where all is perfect peace.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Carib War Path'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們行軍的路線人人皆知；習俗已使那條路成為他們自己的。對那些遊蕩者而言，在那裡劫掠不過是兒戲，有時殺人，且常常擄人為奴；而周圍所有和平的部族——都感受過那沉重之手——感受過兇猛而勇敢的加勒比人。他們的大獨木舟常被看見，從馬羅韋訥河（Marowijne）與蘇里南（Surinam）繞行至科蘭坦河（Corentyne），再朝那條河的源頭而去。在瀑布之上他們橫越伯比斯（Berbice），行軍於一片全然和平之地。

passages.text: That region they have swept quite bare, and all the people who lived there are captive, slain, or fled. O'er Essequibo then they go: plunder Macusis, or, below, sweep the Brazilian plain; or towards those mountains bend their course where noble rivers have their source — the Pacaraima chain. On rafts concealed they float near shore, with grass or branches covered o'er; sometimes on fallen trees they glide, such as come downward with the tide. Woe to the victims they surprise! All adults slain, each girl a prize must in their hands remain.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Carib War Path'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那片地區已被他們掃蕩一空，所有住在那裡的人或被俘、或被殺、或已逃走。接著他們越過埃塞奎博河（Essequibo）：劫掠馬庫西人（Macusis），或在下游掃蕩巴西平原；或轉向那些山脈，那裡有壯麗的河流發源——帕卡拉伊馬山脈（Pacaraima）。他們乘著隱蔽的木筏靠近岸邊，上面覆以草或樹枝；有時他們乘著順潮而下的倒樹滑行。被他們突襲的受害者有禍了！所有成年人都被殺死，每個女孩都成了戰利品，必定留在他們手中。

title.en: The War on the Orinoco: the Cabres and the Ten Thousand
title.zh: 奧里諾科之戰：卡布雷與萬人之師

region.en: Caroni river and Orinoco cataracts
region.zh: 卡羅尼河與奧里諾科灘

period: Carib historical legend; recorded 1880 (Brett, after Humboldt)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part III 'Legends of the Caribs', 'The War on the Orinoco'

summary.en: Now when they reach Caroni's banks they find additions to their ranks — all come to fight the Cabre race, in Cabre blood wash out disgrace, and thus avenge their dead. By desultory fights enraged, both sides in earnest had engaged: the Cabres made their clans unite under one leader for that fight, and dealt a deadly blow — the Caribs, who till then believed themselves invincible, received a total overthrow. One who survived was forced to climb a tree that thence he might the better see the savage victors eat the slain, and there the wretch had to remain till morning; the chieftain Tep released him then, and bade him bring his countrymen for food some other day. Ah! better had the victors spared that horrid deed and taunt, which, heard, inspired with deadly hate their foe. They vowed, and had it in their power, their strength increasing every hour — allies by hundreds came — until ten thousand men, they say, the Caribs mustered for the fray to wipe away their shame. In deadly fight they met again; the Caribs victors were. Soon as that grim fight was done, extermination was begun: the conquering Caribs then could go where Orinoco's torrents flow — from those falls to ocean's wave, no living foe was found.
summary.zh: 加勒比至卡羅尼之岸，諸部來會——皆欲滅卡布雷之族，以血洗恥。卡布雷合諸部於一帥，大破加勒比——素以不敗自居者，竟全軍覆沒。一倖存者被迫登樹，目睹勝者食敵屍，竟夜不得下；晨，酋長特普釋之，且令他日再送族人為食。此暴行與譏言，激其死仇。盟友千百而至，末集萬人，以雪前恥。再戰，加勒比勝；戰罷即行滅族。其人遂可縱橫奧里諾科之灘——自灘至海，無一生敵。

sensitivity.note: Carib historical legend recorded by Brett 1880 after Humboldt; Brett notes the surviving Guiana Caribs deny cannibalism except as a threat, and Humboldt acquits the continental Caribs while blaming the Cabres — the record keeps both claims visible and read critically.

passages.text: Now when they reach Caroni's banks, they find additions to their ranks — all come to fight the Cabre race, in Cabre blood wash out disgrace, and thus avenge their dead. By desultory fights enraged, both sides in earnest had engaged. The Cabres made their clans unite under one leader for that fight, and dealt a deadly blow: the Caribs, who till then believed themselves invincible, received a total overthrow!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The War on the Orinoco'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 如今他們抵達卡羅尼河岸，發現隊伍中增添了生力軍——眾人皆來與卡布雷族交戰，以卡布雷之血洗刷恥辱，並為死者復仇。零星的戰鬥激起了雙方怒火，兩方終於認真交戰。卡布雷人為此戰團結各氏族，共推一位首領，並給予致命一擊：此前自認無敵的加勒比人，遭到了徹底的潰敗！

passages.text: But there is one who remembers well, who has been spared that he may tell of the succeeding night. He then was forced to climb a tree, that thence he might the better see the savage victors eat the slain; and there the wretch had to remain till morning, legends say. The chieftain, Tep, released him then, and bade him 'bring his countrymen for food some other day.' Ah! better had the victors spared that horrid deed and taunt, which, heard, inspired with deadly hate their foe, who vowed to strike a mortal blow.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The War on the Orinoco'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但有一人記憶猶新，他倖免於難，正是為了講述隨後那一夜之事。他當時被迫爬上樹，以便從高處更清楚地看見野蠻的勝利者吞食死者；據傳說，這可憐人只得在樹上待到天明。首領泰普隨後釋放了他，並命他「改日再帶同鄉來作食物」。啊！勝利者若未犯下那可怕的行徑與嘲弄該多好——那話傳出後，激起了敵人刻骨的仇恨，敵人發誓要給予致命一擊。

passages.text: At length ten thousand men, they say, the Caribs mustered for the fray, to wipe away their shame. In deadly fight they met again; each meant to conquer or be slain — the Caribs victors were. Their fury nothing could withstand; they fought, and perished there. Their warriors then in battle fell: and stern the fate, as legends tell, of all who bore their name. For, soon as that grim fight was done, extermination was begun. The conquering Caribs then could go where Orinoco's torrents flow — returning home, each Carib brave would pass by many a bloody grave: but, from those falls to ocean's wave, no living foe was found!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The War on the Orinoco'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說，加勒比人終於集結了一萬人馬前來廝殺，以洗刷恥辱。他們再度展開殊死戰鬥；雙方皆抱定不勝即死的決心——結果加勒比人獲勝。他們的怒氣無人能擋；他們奮戰，並葬身於此。他們的戰士隨後在戰鬥中倒下：據傳說，凡承其名號者，命運皆同樣嚴酷。因為那場慘烈的戰鬥一結束，滅絕便開始了。得勝的加勒比人此時可以前往奧利諾科河奔流之處——返鄉途中，每位加勒比勇士都會經過許多血染的墳墓：但從那些瀑布直到大海的波濤之間，已找不到一個活著的敵人了！

title.en: The First People: Mankind Descends to Cleanse the World
title.zh: 初民：下凡以淨世

region.en: Carib country, Guyana
region.zh: 蓋亞那加勒比之地

period: Carib oral tradition; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part III 'Legends of the Caribs', 'Mythological Legends of the Ancient World: The First People'

summary.en: From on high mankind descended: not, as some would say, for food; they came to cleanse this world intended, that it might be fair and good, bright and free from soil or stain, as the moon or starry train. While they toiled, the clouds receded which had borne them from on high; vainly for their help they pleaded — none restored them to the sky. Thus mankind remained below, in a world of toil and woe. As they wandered, pangs of hunger forced them clayey earth to take; which, that they might starve no longer, making fire, they tried to bake — but their cakes, when they were 'done', were like sand, or crumbling stone. Tamosi had there provided wild fruits, suiting beast or bird; by those creatures kindly guided to the trees which each preferred, men partook — but still would sigh for the food they left on high.
summary.zh: 初民自高天而降——非為覓食，乃欲滌此世，使如日月星辰之皎潔無瑕。方其勤作，載其下降之雲漸退；呼援無應，遂不得復歸於天。人間於是惟勤與苦。行乞於野，饑甚，採黏土燒之為餅；熟則如沙如礫。塔莫西已備野果，各宜其獸鳥；眾賴其引至各愛之樹而食——然猶思天上来之饌而歎焉。

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880 in verse; paraphrased into prose.

passages.text: From on high mankind descended; not (as some would say) for food: they to cleanse this world intended, that it might be fair and good, bright and free from soil or stain, as the moon, or starry train. While they toiled, the clouds receded, which had borne them from on high; vainly for their help they pleaded; none restored them to the sky. Thus mankind remained below, in a world of toil and woe.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The First People'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 人類自高處降臨；並非（如某些人所說）為覓食而來：他們意在潔淨這世界，使其美好良善，明亮無瑕，如月亮或繁星一般。當他們勞作時，曾載他們自高處而來的雲層退去了；他們徒然懇求雲層相助；再無任何力量將他們送回天空。於是，人類留在了下方，留在一個充滿勞苦與悲愁的世界裡。

passages.text: As they wandered, pangs of hunger forced them clayey earth to take; which, that they might starve no longer, making fire, they tried to bake. But their cakes, when they were 'done', were like sand, or crumbling stone. Tamosi had there provided wild fruits, suiting beast or bird; by those creatures kindly guided to the trees which each preferred, men partook: but still would sigh for the food they left on high.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The First People'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們流浪時，飢餓的煎熬迫使他們取來黏土；為了不再挨餓，他們生起火來試著烘烤。但他們的餅「烤好」之後，卻像沙子或碎裂的石頭。塔莫西在那裡備有野果，適合走獸與飛鳥；在那些生靈的善意引導下，人們來到各自偏愛的樹前，採食果實：但他們仍會為留在高處的食物而嘆息。

title.en: The First Cultivation: Tamosi Kabo-tano's Wondrous Tree
title.zh: 初耕：塔莫西卡博塔諾之神樹

region.en: Carib country, Guyana
region.zh: 蓋亞那加勒比之地

period: Carib oral tradition; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part III 'Legends of the Caribs', 'The First Cultivation'

summary.en: Tamosi, the Mighty Maker (whom no mortal eye can see) — Tamosi Kabo-tano, 'Ancient one of Heaven', the Supreme Being — made, that man might be partaker of His gifts, a wondrous tree. High o'er all its head uprearing, cloudlike mass of brilliant green; on its noble branches bearing fruits which none before had seen; each a different kind would bear. Lower down, its trunk surrounding, plantains grew, bananas sweet; golden maize waved its plumy tresses there; sweet cassava, with the bitter, beneath the fruits; yams, potatoes, every kind, where widely spread its mighty roots: there was found, in pristine state, all that men now cultivate. 'Twas Maipuri, the tapir, from the river's margin coming, who observed it first of all, daily through the forest stealing, devouring its fruits which fell, its existence still concealing. Men, who saw him fat and sleek, sent forth scouts the truth to seek: first Woodpecker, who kept tapping each old tree from long habit — shrewd Maipuri heard him rapping and went another way; but the Rat, with silent toil, tracked his steps, then shared the spoil — till some food, delicious, sticking to his lips was found, and mankind made him show that feeding ground. All exclaimed: 'O noble tree! Precious gift of Tamosi!' Then an oracle commanded: 'Cut it down!' — they wondered all; yet sharp stones, as fate demanded, caused it in ten months to fall; crashing, thundering to the ground, while they fly or tremble round. Then, a fair division making, for his field each man provides, slips and cuttings freely taking from its branches, roots, and sides: 'Gaining thus at once precious fruits and daily bread.'
summary.zh: 塔莫西卡博塔諾——『天上之古者』，至尊也——欲分其賜於人，乃造神樹。其冠如翠雲，高聳入雲；枝結人所未見之果，各各不同；樹幹四圍生蕉與甜薯，金黃玉蜀黍飄其穗；甘苦二薯、山藥、馬鈴薯，凡今人所耕者，皆具於其巨根之間。貘自河濱來，先見之；日日潛林食落果，秘而不宣。人見其肥，遣偵察之：啄木鳥叩木如常，貘聞聲而改道；田鼠無聲躡其跡，分其食——口黏美饌，眾乃逼其獻樹。眾呼曰：『偉哉此樹！塔莫西之珍賜也！』神諭令伐；以利石伐之，十閱月而樹仆。各取其枝、根、側之苗而分植——『果與日糧，一舉而兩得。』

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880 in verse; paraphrased into prose. Variant of the food-tree records.

passages.text: Tamosi, the Mighty Maker (whom no mortal eye can see), made, that man might be partaker of His gifts, a wondrous tree. Though on earth huge trees have grown, none like that was ever known. High o'er all its head uprearing, cloudlike mass of brilliant green! On its noble branches bearing fruits, which none before had seen: each a different kind would bear, beauteous clusters, high in air! Lower down — its trunk surrounding — plantains grew, bananas sweet: all choice plants were there abounding which we now in gardens meet.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The First Cultivation'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大能的造物主塔莫西（凡人之眼無法得見），為使人類能分享祂的恩賜，造了一棵奇樹。雖說地上曾長出巨樹，卻從未有誰聽聞過那樣的樹。它高高昂首於萬物之上，如雲般的燦爛綠冠！它高貴的枝條上結著前所未見的果實：每枝結出不同種類，美麗的果串高懸空中！較低處——環繞著樹幹——長著大蕉、甜美的香蕉：一切精選的植物都在那裡繁茂生長，正是我們如今在園中常見的。

passages.text: Golden maize, so fresh and fair, waved its plumy tresses there. Sweet cassava one might find there, with the bitter, 'neath the fruits; yams, potatoes, every kind, where widely spread its mighty roots. There was found, in pristine state, all that men now cultivate. 'Twas Maipuri, that way roaming (whom some white men 'tapir' call), from the river's margin coming, who observed it first of all — daily through the forest stealing, he devoured its fruits which fell, its existence still concealing: what he fed on none could tell.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The First Cultivation'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 金黃的玉米，如此鮮嫩美好，在那裡搖曳著它羽毛般的穗鬚。人們在那裡可以找到甜木薯，與苦木薯並列於果實之下；山藥、馬鈴薯，種類繁多，它強壯的根鬚廣為蔓延。在那裡，人們發現了原始狀態下的一切，即今日人們所栽培的所有作物。正是邁普里（Maipuri），那個四處遊蕩的傢伙（有些白人稱他為「貘」），從河岸邊走來，最先發現了它——他每日潛行穿越森林，吞食落下的果實，卻仍隱瞞著它的存在：他吃的是什麼，無人能知。

passages.text: Men, who saw him fat and sleek, sent forth scouts the truth to seek. First, Woodpecker: he kept tapping (from long habit) each old tree; shrewd Maipuri heard him rapping, and another way went he. But the Rat, with silent toil, tracked his steps — then shared the spoil — till some food, delicious, sticking to his lips was found, and mankind, become suspicious, made him show that feeding ground. All exclaimed: 'O noble tree! Precious gift of Tamosi!' Then an oracle commanded: 'Cut it down!' — they wondered all; yet sharp stones, as fate demanded, caused it in ten months to fall, crashing, thundering to the ground. Then, a fair division making, for his field each man provides, slips and cuttings freely taking from its branches, roots, and sides: 'Gaining thus at once precious fruits and daily bread.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The First Cultivation'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 人們見他肥壯光滑，便派出探子去探尋真相。首先是啄木鳥：他出於長久的習慣，不斷敲啄每一棵老樹；機敏的邁普里聽見他的敲擊聲，便改走另一條路。但老鼠以無聲的辛勞，追蹤了他的足跡——隨後分得了那份收穫——直到一些美味的食物黏在他的嘴唇上被發現，人類於是起了疑心，逼他交出那處進食之地。眾人驚呼：「啊，高貴的樹！塔莫西（Tamosi）的珍貴禮物！」接著，一道神諭命令道：「把它砍倒！」——眾人皆驚異不已；然而鋒利的石頭，正如命運所要求的那樣，使它在十個月後轟然倒下，雷鳴般地砸向地面。隨後，眾人公平分配，每人為自己的田地取用，自由地從它的枝條、根鬚和側邊取下插條與切段：「如此便一舉獲得珍貴的果實與每日的食糧。」

title.en: The Rock and the Wood: the Oracle, the Monkey, and the Flood
title.zh: 石與林：神諭、靈猴與洪水

region.en: Carib country, Guyana
region.zh: 蓋亞那加勒比之地

period: Carib oral tradition; recorded 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part III 'Legends of the Caribs', 'The Rock and the Wood'

summary.en: 'Neath the roots of that great tree some a sacred grot could see. Saw they there the Water-Mother bathing in her loved abode? That it was her form, none other, soon the swelling waters showed: men had all been swept away by a gushing flood that day — but a rugged rock, befriending, closed the fountain; and drew near that rock, which then gave forth oracles to men, saying: 'Though I from the waters save you, there may come a day when yourselves, your sons and daughters, in a flood will pass away. Listen, then, mankind, to me, that your years like mine may be. In yon wood are spirits dwelling, who will tempt you day by day. If you dread the waters swelling, answer not, whate'er they say! You are safe while you obey, heeding well your rock-stone grey. And if age bring evils on you — wrinkled skin and whitening hair — you at will may cast them from you, youth renewing, bright and fair: as the serpent glideth clear from the slough he scorns to wear!' Time has passed; deteriorating, men grow careless day by day, till their hearts, long hesitating, voices from the wood obey. From the grove comes, beguiling, Yarrekaru, the monkey; none prevent him while, alone, he undermines their guardian stone. From the grove come, mockingly, cries of 'Waters cover me!' They respond: 'O friend, we hear them!' laugh, and turn to slumber on — till the rush of waters near them terrifies the stoutest one. And these words, in solemn tone, issue from the outraged stone: 'Lo! the swelling floods before you; I no more your help can be. Yet had you but faithful been, death no man would e'er have seen!' Swell the mighty floods; yet to three or four is given safety till the floods subside, for a komoo palm surmounts the tide: all whom that tree does not save sink, as rocks, beneath the wave — and there is an episode of a cocorite palm whose top reached the heavens: a poor woman led the way halfway up, was turned into stone by terror and exhaustion, and all who tried to pass over her became rocks likewise.
summary.zh: 神樹根下有聖穴；見水母浴於其所居乎！水面暴漲，乃知其形。洪水將盡沒眾人——一巨石忽塞其泉，石遂出神諭：『我救爾於水，然爾與爾之子孫終有滅於洪之日。聽我言，可如我之長年。林中有鬼，日日誘爾；水漲之聲起，慎勿應答！守我灰石則安。老至而皺髮白者，可自脫之，復為青春——如蛇之蛻皮也！』久而人懈，聽林中之聲，忽其灰石。林中遣猴雅雷卡魯來，無人阻之，獨掘其守石。夜聞林中笑呼：『水沒我矣！』眾應曰：『友乎，我聞之矣！』笑而入睡——俄而水聲近，壯者亦懼。石憤而言：『洪水已至，我不能救；爾若忠信，世無見死之人！』洪水滔天；惟三四人攀天生之孔摩棕而免，餘者如石而沉——更有柯基里棕之插曲：其顛及天，一孕婦先登，半途驚疲化石，後攀者越之者亦皆化石。

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880 in verse; paraphrased into prose. Flood-cluster record.

passages.text: 'Neath the roots of that great tree some a sacred grot could see. Saw they there the Water-Mother bathing in her loved abode? That it was her form, none other, soon the swelling waters showed. Men had all been swept away by a gushing flood that day — but a rugged rock, befriending (by what power none can know), closed the fountain. They, attending, saw it stop the mighty flow; and drew near that rock, which then gave forth oracles to men, saying: 'Though I from the waters save you, there may come a day when yourselves, your sons and daughters, in a flood will pass away. Listen, then, mankind, to me, that your years like mine may be.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Rock and the Wood'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在那棵大樹的根鬚之下，有些人看見了一處神聖的洞穴。他們可曾見到水之母在她鍾愛的居所中沐浴？那正是她的身形，別無他人，不久便由漲起的洪水顯現出來。那一天，洶湧的洪水將所有人都沖走了——但一塊粗獷的岩石，出於友善（憑何種力量，無人能知），封住了泉眼。他們在一旁觀看，見它阻住了那巨大的水流；於是走近那塊岩石，它便向人們發出神諭，說道：「雖然我將你們從洪水中救出，但總有一天，你們自己、你們的兒女，將在洪水中逝去。那麼，人類啊，聽從我吧，好讓你們的歲月如同我的一樣。」

passages.text: 'In yon wood are spirits dwelling, who will tempt you day by day. If you dread the waters swelling, answer not, whate'er they say! You are safe while you obey, heeding well your rock-stone grey. And if age bring evils on you, wrinkled skin, and whitening hair, you at will may cast them from you, youth renewing, bright and fair: as the serpent glideth clear from the slough he scorns to wear!' Time has passed; deteriorating, men grow careless day by day, till their hearts, long hesitating, voices from the wood obey — they despise their rock-stone grey. From the grove then comes, beguiling, Yarrekaru, the monkey: none prevent, whilst he, alone, undermines their guardian stone.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Rock and the Wood'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「在那片樹林中住著精靈，他們將日復一日地誘惑你們。若你們畏懼洪水漲起，無論他們說什麼，都不要回應！只要你們聽從，好好聽從你們那灰色的岩石，你們便安然無恙。而若年歲給你們帶來種種苦惱，皺紋滿面、白髮蒼蒼，你們便可隨心所欲地將它們拋開，重獲青春，容光煥發：正如蛇從牠不屑穿戴的舊皮中清晰地滑出一般！」時光流逝；人類日漸墮落，一天天變得漫不經心，直到他們那長久猶豫的心，聽從了來自樹林的聲音——他們鄙棄了他們那灰色的岩石。於是，從樹林中來了那蠱惑人心的猴子亞雷卡魯（Yarrekaru）：無人阻攔，而他獨自一人，便掘毀了他們的守護之石。

passages.text: As the shades of night close o'er them, to their hammocks all repair; little reck they that before them stand grim death and dark despair. From the grove come, mockingly, cries of 'Waters cover me!' They respond: 'O friend, we hear them!' laugh, and turn to slumber on — till the rush of waters near them terrifies the stoutest one. And these words, in solemn tone, issue from the outraged stone: 'Lo! the swelling floods before you; see their waters cover me! Soon they will be closing o'er you; I no more your help can be.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Rock and the Wood' (with its footnote); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當夜幕籠罩他們之時，眾人皆回到吊床之上；他們毫不理會，那猙獰的死亡與黑暗的絕望正立在他們面前。從樹林中傳來嘲弄的呼喊：「洪水淹沒了我！」他們回應道：「啊，朋友，我們聽見了！」大笑一聲，便轉身入睡——直到逼近的洪水奔湧之聲，令最膽大的人也驚恐萬分。於是，這些話以莊嚴的語調，從那受辱的岩石中發出：「看哪！漲起的洪水就在你們面前；看它的水淹沒了我！不久它們便將合攏於你們之上；我再也不能幫助你們了。

passages.text: Yet had you but faithful been, death no man would e'er have seen!' Swell the mighty floods, prevailing — yet to three or four is given safety till the floods subside, for a komoo palm (by heaven made to grow) surmounts the tide: all whom that tree does not save sink, as rocks, beneath the wave. There is an episode, usually given here, of a cocorite palm whose top reached the heavens: a poor woman, not in a condition to climb, led the way, and halfway up was turned into stone by terror and exhaustion; none could help her, and all who tried to pass over her became rocks likewise.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Rock and the Wood' (with its footnote); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而，只要你們曾忠誠不渝，便無人會見到死亡！」巨大的洪水洶湧而上，勢不可擋——然而有三四人得以保全，直到洪水退去，因為一棵科莫棕櫚（由上天使其生長）高踞於潮水之上：凡那棵樹未能拯救的人，皆如石頭般沉入波濤之下。此處通常還插入一段情節，講的是一棵樹梢直達天庭的可可里特棕櫚：一個可憐的女人，因身體狀況無法攀爬，卻領頭而上，爬到半途時因恐懼與力竭而化為石頭；無人能幫助她，而所有試圖從她身上越過的人也都同樣化為了石頭。

narrative.en: The Carib cycle of Tamosi Kabo-tano — 'the Ancient One of Heaven', the Supreme Being — reaches its crisis in the legend of the Rock and the Wood. Under the roots of the wonderful tree from which all cultivated plants first came, some saw a sacred grotto, and in it the Water-Mother bathing in her loved abode; that it was her form none other, the swelling waters soon showed, for a gushing flood burst out that would have swept all mankind away — had not a rugged rock, by what power none can know, closed the fountain. The people drew near to their saviour, and the rock gave forth oracles: 'Though I from the waters save you, there may come a day when yourselves, your sons and daughters, in a flood will pass away. Listen, then, mankind, to me, that your years like mine may be. In yon wood are spirits dwelling, who will tempt you day by day. If you dread the waters swelling, answer not, whate'er they say! You are safe while you obey, heeding well your rock-stone grey. And if age bring evils on you — wrinkled skin and whitening hair — you at will may cast them from you, youth renewing, bright and fair, as the serpent glideth clear from the slough he scorns to wear.' Thus the rock offered both the covenant of safety and the serpent's gift of skin-renewal, the Guianese form of earthly immortality. Time passed; men grew careless, and their hearts, long hesitating, obeyed the voices from the wood. From the grove came Yarrekaru, the monkey, sent by man's malignant foes; none prevented him while, alone, he undermined their guardian stone.
