passages.zh: 當一名印第安人被殺，或一名孩童失蹤——而孩童若從家中失蹤，通常都歸咎於虎——便會請來巫醫，他著手查明，發現那是部落的敵人在暗中作祟，很可能是某個懷有敵意的巫醫的靈。在此情況下，虎須當作人類的敵人來對待：部落會組織一場大規模的狩獵，若獵物被擒獲，隨後便舉行一場虎肉盛宴，一場復仇的盛宴。印第安人在其他任何時候都不吃美洲豹的肉；虎皮則歸巫醫所有，因為他的法術如此勝過了對手的法術。

title.en: The Sun and His Wife the Moon, the Stars as Souls of Chiefs
title.zh: 日與其妻月，星為酋長之魂

region.en: Issa-Japura region
region.zh: 伊薩-哈普拉之地

period: Witoto-Boro oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Whiffen)

source.work: Thomas Whiffen, The North-West Amazons (1915), ch. XVII 'The Indians' Magico-Religious System'

summary.en: Finally, the tribes south of the Japura are concerned with the sun and the moon: these are venerated, the sun as a great and sympathetic spirit, but not an incarnation of the great Good Spirit; the moon as his wife, who is sent betimes by the sun into the heavens at night to prevent the evil spirits from depopulating the world. Of the stars these people seem to have the vaguest ideas, and only one Boro explained that they were the souls of the chiefs and of the great men of his tribe. The moon's inconstant appearances are accounted for by the suggestion that she is sent periodically by the sun her husband to drive away the evil spirits of the night that await the stray or heedless loiterers in the forest thickets — though this protective character is denied to the moon by other tribes, and some South American Indians will hide young infants lest the moon should injure them.
summary.zh: 哈普拉以南諸族尊日月：日為偉大仁慈之靈，非善靈之化身；月為其妻，夫遣之夜行於天，以阻惡靈之滅人。星則其識甚淺；一博羅人言星乃其族酋長與大人之魂也。月之隱現，蓋夫遣妻驅林間伺人之夜鬼——然他族不然，或有匿嬰以防月之害者。

sensitivity.note: Witoto-Boro beliefs recorded by Whiffen 1915; read critically.

passages.text: The tribes south of the Japura are concerned with the sun and the moon: these are venerated, the sun as a great and sympathetic spirit, but not an incarnation of the great Good Spirit; the moon as his wife, who is sent betimes by the sun into the heavens at night to prevent the evil spirits from depopulating the world. Of the stars these people seem to have the vaguest ideas, and only one Boro explained to me that they were the souls of the chiefs and of the great men of his tribe.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 雅普拉河以南的各部落崇奉太陽與月亮：二者皆受敬奉，太陽被視為一位偉大而慈悲的靈，但並非偉大善神的化身；月亮則是他的妻子，太陽不時派她於夜間上天，以防惡靈使世界人口滅絕。關於星辰，這些人似乎只有最模糊的概念，只有一位博羅人向我解釋說，星辰是他部落中酋長與偉人的靈魂。

passages.text: The moon's inconstant appearances are accounted for by the suggestion that she is sent periodically by the sun her husband to drive away the evil spirits of the night that await the stray or heedless loiterers in the forest thickets. But this protective character is denied to the moon by other tribes, and some South American Indians will hide young infants lest the moon should injure them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 月亮變化無常的出現，被解釋為：她是由她的丈夫太陽定期派去驅趕夜間的惡靈，那些惡靈正伺機等候在森林叢莽中迷途或漫不經心的逗留者。但其他部落卻否認月亮具有這種保護性質，有些南美洲印第安人會把幼嬰藏起來，唯恐月亮傷害他們。

title.en: The Camera That Stole Souls
title.zh: 竊魂之照箱

region.en: Boro-Witoto malokas
region.zh: 博羅-維托托大屋

period: Boro-Witoto beliefs; recorded 1915 (Whiffen)

source.work: Thomas Whiffen, The North-West Amazons (1915), ch. XVII 'The Indians' Magico-Religious System'

summary.en: Anything abnormal or unknown is regarded with suspicious dread; Whiffen's camera was naturally endowed by Indian imagination with magical properties, the most general idea among the Boro being that it was an infernal machine designed to steal the souls of those who were exposed to its baleful eye. The Indian was brought face to face with his naked soul, represented by the miniature of himself in the photographic plate: one glance, and one only, could he be induced to give; never again would he be privy to such magic. The Witoto women believed more material magic was afoot, and feared that, should they suffer exposure to the camera, they would bear resultant offspring to whom the camera — or the photographer — would stand in paternal relation.
summary.zh: 凡異常之物，皆疑而懼之。白人之照箱，博羅人以為地獄之器，凡受其凶目所照者，魂皆被竊。相版中縮小之影，即其赤裸之魂也；一見之後，永不復視。維托托婦人則懼其為形體之術：若受照，所產之子，當以照箱或照相者為父也。

sensitivity.note: Boro-Witoto beliefs recorded by Whiffen 1915; a colonial-era encounter, read critically.

passages.text: My camera was naturally endowed by Indian imagination with magical properties, the most general idea among the Boro being that it was an infernal machine, designed to steal the souls of those who were exposed to its baleful eye. The Indian was brought face to face with his naked soul, represented by the miniature of himself in the photographic plate: one glance, and one only, could he be induced to give — never again would he be privy to such magic.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 我的相機自然被印第安人的想像賦予了神奇的特性，博羅人中最普遍的看法是，它是一台陰險的機器，旨在竊取那些暴露於它邪惡之眼的人的靈魂。印第安人被帶到與自己赤裸的靈魂面對面的境地，那靈魂以他在照相底片上的縮小影像呈現：只能誘使他看一眼，僅此一眼——他再也不會去窺探這樣的法術了。

passages.text: The Witoto women believed that I was working more material magic, and feared should they suffer exposure to the camera that they would bear resultant offspring to whom the camera — or the photographer — would stand in paternal relation.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 維托托族的婦女相信我在施行更為物質性的法術，她們害怕若自己暴露於相機之下，便會生下由此而來的後代，而相機——或攝影師——將與那後代處於父子關係。

title.en: The White Indians Who Sleep by Day
title.zh: 晝眠之白印第安人

region.en: Upper rivers of Guiana and Amazonia
region.zh: 圭亞那與亞馬遜上游諸河

period: South American folk tradition; recorded 1915 (Whiffen)

source.work: Thomas Whiffen, The North-West Amazons (1915), ch. XVIII 'Myths'

summary.en: A story prevalent throughout South America tells of a race of white Indians who sleep in the daytime, and only go abroad at night. This tale was laughed at when repeated at a recent meeting of the Royal Geographical Society, but it is certainly in existence among the tribes; and Crevaux states that the Ouayana will not go near one river, 'à cause des singuliers habitants qui habiteraient près des sources... des Indiens aux chevaux blonds qui dorment le jour et marchent toute la nuit' — because of the strange dwellers near the sources, Indians with blond horses who sleep the day and march all night. Where tribal differentiation of colour is so marked it is only natural that tales should be told of some mythical 'white' folk.
summary.zh: 南美遍傳白印第安人之說：晝眠而夜行。皇家地理學會曾哂之，然土族中確有其傳。克雷沃言：瓦亞納人不近某河，『以河源有異民居之：白膚金髮之印第安人，晝眠而夜行也。』部落膚色既異，則幻設白人之族，固其宜也。

sensitivity.note: South American folk tradition recorded by Whiffen 1915; read critically.

passages.text: A story that is prevalent throughout South America tells of a race of white Indians who sleep in the daytime, and only go abroad at night. This tale was laughed at when repeated at a recent meeting of the Royal Geographical Society, but it is certainly in existence among the tribes; and Crevaux states that the Ouayana will not go near one river — because of the strange dwellers near the sources: Indians with blond horses who sleep the day and march all night.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Whiffen 1915, ch. XVIII (citing Crevaux); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個流傳於整個南美洲的故事講述一個白印第安人的種族，他們白天睡覺，只在夜間外出。這個故事在最近一次皇家地理學會的會議上被複述時遭到嘲笑，但它確實在各部落中流傳；而克雷沃則指出，瓦亞納人不會靠近某一條河——因為河源附近住著奇怪的居民：騎著金黃色馬匹的印第安人，他們白天睡覺，整夜行軍。

title.en: Cane Joints Full of Lice: The Tribute of the Disabled Poor
title.zh: 裝滿蝨子的竹節:貧弱者的貢賦

region.en: Villages of Ttahuantin-suyu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 大蘇尤各村(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: Another sort of tribute was imposed upon those who could not work, and were called poor: at certain intervals they had to deliver a specified number of cane joints full of lice to the governor of their village. They say that the Yncas imposed this tribute in order that no one (except those exempted from tribute) should contribute nothing, however poor he might be; and therefore from those who were disabled from paying tribute in personal service was exacted a tribute of lice. It was also said that the chief reason of the Yncas for requiring this tribute was a loving care for these poor people, that they might be obliged to clean themselves, and not become a prey to the lice. For such thoughtful care as this the Yncas were called the Friends of the Poor. The Decurions were expected to see that this tribute was paid.
summary.zh: 另一種貢賦加於不能勞作、被稱為「貧者」的人:他們須定期向村中長官繳交一定數量、裝滿蝨子的竹節。相傳印加王立此貢,是為使任何人——除非免貢之人——縱然赤貧,也不致一無所獻;故對無力以勞役納貢者,便徵「蝨貢」。又有一說:印加王設此貢,本出於對貧民的體恤,使他們不得不清潔自身,免遭蝨害。因有此等細緻入微的關懷,印加王被稱為「貧者之友」。十戶之長(十夫長)負責督察此貢的繳納。

sensitivity.note: Garcilaso's most tender anecdote of Inca social policy; read with his own apologetic purpose in mind.

passages.text: Another sort of tribute was imposed upon those who could not work, and were called poor; and this was that, at certain intervals, they had to deliver a specified number of cane joints full of lice to the governor of their village. They say that the Yncas imposed this tribute in order that no one (except those exempted from tribute) should contribute nothing, however poor he might be; and therefore from those who were disabled from paying tribute in personal service was exacted a tribute of lice.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 另有一種貢賦，是加於那些不能勞作、被稱為窮人的人身上的；那就是，每隔一定的時期，他們必須向本村的總督繳納一定數量的、裝滿蝨子的藤節。據說印加人徵收此項貢賦，是為了使任何人（除免徵貢賦者外）不論多麼貧窮，都不至於毫無貢獻；因此，對於那些因身體殘疾而無法以親身服役的方式繳納貢賦的人，便向他們徵收蝨子作為貢賦。

passages.text: It was also said that the chief reason of the Yncas for requiring this tribute was a loving care for these poor people, that they might be obliged to clean themselves, and not become a prey to the lice. For such thoughtful care as this, which the Yncas showed in all things, they were called the Friends of the Poor. The Decurions were expected to see that this tribute was paid.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 也有人說，印加人要求此項貢賦的主要緣由，是出於對這些窮人的關懷愛護，使他們不得不清潔自身，不至於淪為蝨子的犧牲品。正因為印加人在一切事上都表現出這般周到的關懷，他們被稱為「窮人之友」。十戶長有責任監督此項貢賦的繳納。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas (1871)

title.en: The Stones and Bushes Turned to Men: Garcilaso's Skeptical Pururaucas
title.zh: 石與灌木化為人形:加爾西拉索筆下的普魯勞卡斯

region.en: Yahuar-pampa, near Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科附近亞瓦爾-潘帕(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: The Yncas, being a people who strove to magnify their deeds by fables and false pretensions, seeing these new friends (the reinforcements), resolved not to lose the occasion, but to turn it to advantage as was their custom. They cried out that the very stones and bushes of the plain were turning into men, and coming to fight in the service of the Prince, because the Sun and the god Uiracocha had so ordered it. The Chancas, being a credulous people, were much amazed by this fable; and afterwards it was believed by all the common people throughout that empire, as Father Friar Geronimo Roman says: 'So that the field remained in the power of the Ynca. To this day all the Indians declare, in speaking of this famous battle, that the stones in the plain turned into men to fight for them, and that all this was done by the Sun to fulfil the promise that he had given to the brave Pachacuti Ynca Yupanqui.' Garcilaso, quoting Acosta's account, adds that from the time of that victory Uiracocha was held to be the universal lord; that the prince announced to his soldiers that they had not conquered their enemies, but that the victory had been gained by certain bearded men sent by the Uiracocha who were visible to none but himself, and that they had afterwards been turned into stones: they collected a great quantity of stones near the mountains which he selected, took them to the war with much devotion, holding that victory was certain with their assistance, and called them Pururaucas. Yet Garcilaso corrects the record: the Indians never had more than two gods, which were Pachacamac, who was invisible and unknown, and the Sun, who was visible and notorious; they held that Uiracocha and the other Yncas were children of the Sun.
summary.zh: 印加人素有以神話浮誇誇大戰功之風;見到援兵到來,便照例抓住時機,大肆利用。他們高喊:平原上的石頭和灌木叢都變成了人,奉太陽與維拉科查之命,來為王子助戰!昌卡人性喜輕信,聞之大駭;此後全帝國的平民也都信以為真——赫羅尼莫·羅曼神父記道:「至今所有印第安人談起這場著名會戰,仍說平原上的石頭化為人形為他們作戰,這一切都是太陽為履行他對英勇的帕查庫提·印加·尤潘琪的許諾而行的。」加爾西拉索又引阿科斯塔:自那場大捷之後,維拉科查被尊為至高之主;王子向將士宣布,此勝非人力所取,而是維拉科查所遣的、唯有王子能見的鬚髯神兵所建,戰後神兵化為石頭——人們於是拾取他所點的山邊巨石,奉為瓦卡,虔誠地抬上戰場,相信有神石相助則必勝,稱之為「普魯勞卡斯」。但加爾西拉索糾正道:印加人自來只有兩位神——隱而無名的帕查卡馬克,與顯而有名的太陽;維拉科查與歷代印加王,皆只是太陽的兒子。

sensitivity.note: The mestizo historian explicitly frames the pururaucas as an Inca propaganda invention while preserving the belief record - a uniquely critical native-voiced version.

passages.text: The Yncas, being a people who strove to magnify their deeds by fables and false pretensions, seeing these new friends, resolved not to lose the occasion, but to turn it to advantage as was their custom. They cried out that the very stones and bushes of the plain were turning into men, and coming to fight in the service of the Prince, because the Sun and the god Uiracocha had so ordered it. The Chancas, being a credulous people, were much amazed by this fable; and afterwards it was believed by all the common people throughout that empire.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 印加人是一個竭力以寓言和虛妄的託辭來誇大自己功業的民族，他們見到這些新來的朋友，便決心不放過這個機會，而要照他們的慣例加以利用。他們大聲宣稱，平原上的石頭和灌木正化為人，前來為王子效力作戰，因為太陽和神烏伊拉科查如此命令。昌卡人是一個輕信的民族的，被這則寓言大為驚詫；此後，這則寓言便被整個帝國的全體平民所相信。

passages.text: To this day all the Indians declare, in speaking of this famous battle, that the stones in the plain turned into men to fight for them, and that all this was done by the Sun to fulfil the promise that he had given to the brave Pachacuti Ynca Yupanqui. [Acosta quoted:] From the time of that victory Uiracocha was held to be the universal lord... As soon as he had gained the victory over the Chancas, he announced to his soldiers that they had not conquered their enemies, but that the victory had been gained by certain bearded men sent by the Uiracocha who were visible to none but himself, and that they had afterwards been turned into stones... They called them Pururaucas, and took them to the war with much devotion, holding that victory was certain with their assistance.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso quoting Roman and Acosta (Markham 1871); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 直到今日，所有印第安人在談及這場著名的戰役時都宣稱，平原上的石頭化為人為他們作戰，而這一切都是太陽所為，以履行他向勇敢的帕查庫蒂·印加·尤潘基所作的承諾。〔阿科斯塔引述：〕自那次勝利之時起，烏伊拉科查便被奉為宇宙之主……他一戰勝昌卡人，便向他的士兵宣佈，他們並未征服敵人，而是由烏伊拉科查派來的某些蓄鬚之人贏得了勝利，這些人除他本人外無人能見，而他們後來又化為了石頭……他們稱這些人為普魯勞卡斯，並懷著極大的虔誠帶他們出征，認為有他們的相助，勝利便穩操勝券。

passages.text: That they placed a statue of Uiracocha higher than that of the sun is a new invention of the Indians, to flatter the Spaniards... This was not so, for they never had more than two gods, which were Pachacamac, who was invisible and unknown, and the Sun, who was visible and notorious. They held that Uiracocha and the other Yncas were children of the Sun.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 至於他們把烏伊拉科查的雕像置於太陽雕像之上，那是印第安人為討好西班牙人而新編造出來的……事實並非如此，因為他們從來只有兩位神，即帕查卡馬克，他是不可見且不為人知的，以及太陽，他是可見且眾所周知的。他們認為烏伊拉科查和其他印加人都是太陽的子女。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas (1871)

title.en: The Field of Blood: Eight Hours at Yahuar-pampa
title.zh: 血野:亞瓦爾-潘帕八小時血戰

region.en: Yahuar-pampa, Chanca country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 昌卡地亞瓦爾-潘帕(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: The battle, having been so hardly won and having lasted for eight hours, was very bloody. The Indians declare that, besides the blood that was shed on the ground, a dry bed of a stream that crossed the plain also flowed with blood; hence the plain was called from that time forward Yahuar-pampa, which means 'the field of blood.' More than 30,000 Indians died, 8000 on the side of the Ynca, and the rest belonging to the nations Chanca, Hanco-huallu, Uruinarca, Vilca, Untun-sulla, and others. The two rebel masters of the camp, and the general Hanco-hualla, were made prisoners.
summary.zh: 此役得之極難,酣戰八小時,血染沙場。印第安人相傳:除了灑在地面上的鮮血,那片平原上乾涸的河床也流滿了血;自此這片平原便名為「亞瓦爾-潘帕」——血野。死者逾三萬:印加一方八千,餘者屬昌卡、安科-瓦尤、烏魯伊納爾卡、維爾卡、溫通-蘇利亞諸族。叛軍的兩位統帥與主將安科-瓦利亞俱被生擒。

sensitivity.note: Yahuar-pampa is the standard Garcilaso name for the decisive Chanca battlefield (Yuncaypampa in other sources).

passages.text: The battle, having been so hardly won and having lasted for eight hours, was very bloody. The Indians declare that, besides the blood that was shed on the ground, a dry bed of a stream that crossed the plain also flowed with blood; hence the plain was called from that time forward Yahuar-pampa, which means 'the field of blood.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這場戰役贏得如此艱難，持續了八個小時，傷亡極為慘重。印第安人宣稱，除了灑在地上的血之外，一條橫貫平原的乾涸河床也流著血；因此，從那時起，這片平原便被稱為「亞瓦爾潘帕」，意即「血之原野」。

passages.text: More than 30,000 Indians died, 8000 on the side of the Ynca, and the rest belonging to the Nations Chanca, Hanco-huallu, Uruinarca, Vilca, Untun-sulla, and others. The two rebel masters of the camp, and the general Hanco-hualla, were made prisoners.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 三萬多名印第安人死亡，其中八千人屬於印加一方，其餘則屬於昌卡、漢科瓦柳、烏魯因納爾卡、維爾卡、溫通蘇利亞等部族。營中兩名叛亂首領以及將軍漢科瓦利亞均被俘。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas (1871)

title.en: Drinking with the Sun: Evaporation as the God's Draught
title.zh: 與太陽對飲:蒸發即神飲

region.en: Temple of the Sun, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科太陽神廟(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: For these Yncas, although they held the Sun to be god, treated him as if he had been a man like themselves. Among other things that they did to him in his supposed character of a man was to drink with him, and they poured the Sun's drink into a half tinajon of gold, which they placed in the court where they held their festivals, or in the temple. They declared that what appeared to be gone had been drank by the Sun, and they said truly, for the Sun's heat had evaporated the liquor. They also put out plates of meat that the Sun might eat. And when a great event happened, like this victory, they sent a special messenger to tell the Sun what had happened, and to offer up thanks to him. In accordance with this ancient custom, the prince Uiracocha Ynca sent a messenger to the Sun with the news of the victory, and with orders to the priests to get together those who had fled, that they might offer up thanksgivings and make new sacrifices. He sent another messenger to the virgins dedicated to the Sun, with the news of the victory which had been granted in return for their prayers and merits.
summary.zh: 印加人雖奉太陽為神,卻像對待族人一般與他相處。其中一樁,便是與太陽對飲:他們把太陽的酒漿倒入一只半人高的金缸,安放在舉行節宴的庭院或神廟之中;眾人眼中「消失不見」的酒,便算是太陽飲下的——他們這話倒也不假,因為那正是太陽的熱力把酒蒸發了。他們還擺上肉盤,請太陽進食。凡遇大事——如這場大捷——便遣專使向太陽報喜致謝。照這古禮,維拉科查·印加王子遣使赴太陽神廟報捷,並命祭司召集逃散之人回來謝恩獻祭;另遣一使往太陽的貞女處報喜——說這場勝利是報答她們的祈禱與功德。

sensitivity.note: The famous evaporation anecdote - the most-quoted passage of Garcilaso; his rationalist wink inside the ritual description.

passages.text: For these Yncas, although they held the Sun to be god, treated him as if he had been a man like themselves. Among other things that they did to him in his supposed character of a man was to drink with him, and they poured the Sun's drink into a half tinajon of gold, which they placed in the court where they held their festivals, or in the temple. They declared that what appeared to be gone had been drank by the Sun, and they said truly, for the Sun's heat had evaporated the liquor. They also put out plates of meat that the Sun might eat.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 因為這些印加人雖然把太陽奉為神，卻待他如同與自己一樣的人。他們對待這位被視為人形的太陽所做的事之一，便是與他共飲：他們把太陽的酒倒進一只半大的金製提納洪（tinajon）中，置於他們舉行慶典的庭院裡，或放在神廟中。他們宣稱看似消失的酒已被太陽飲下，而他們所言不虛，因為太陽的熱力已將酒蒸發。他們還擺出盛肉的盤子，好讓太陽進食。

passages.text: When a great event happened, like this victory, they sent a special messenger to tell the Sun what had happened, and to offer up thanks to him. In accordance with this ancient custom, the prince Uiracocha Ynca sent a messenger to the Sun with the news of the victory... He sent another messenger to the virgins dedicated to the Sun, with the news of the victory which had been granted in return for their prayers and merits.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 每當發生大事，例如這次勝利，他們便派一名特別使者前去告訴太陽所發生之事，並向他獻上感謝。依照這古老的習俗，王子維拉科查·印加派了一名使者前往太陽處，報告勝利的消息……他又派了另一名使者前往奉獻給太陽的貞女處，告知這因她們的祈禱與功德而獲賜的勝利消息。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas (1871)

title.en: The Blood-Omen Fulfilled: The Dethroned King Keeps His Yellow Fringe
title.zh: 血兆應驗:廢王仍戴黃纓

region.en: Rumi-colca palace, between Muyna and Quespicancha (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 穆伊納與基斯皮坎恰之間的魯米-科爾卡宮(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: The prince returned to the city, put aside the yellow fringe, and adopted the red one. But though he wore the red fringe himself, he never would consent that his father should leave it off, caring little for the outward insignia, so long as he possessed the reality of dominion and power. As soon as the palace was finished it was supplied with servants and all other necessaries, so that, except the government of the kingdom, the Ynca Yahuar-huaccac was deprived of no other thing. The poor king passed the rest of his life in this solitude, deprived of his kingdom by his own son. The Indians say that this dethronement was prognosticated by the evil omen of his having wept blood in his childhood. They also say, reasoning amongst themselves and recalling the memory of past events, that if this Ynca, when he began to fear the disposition of his son, had resorted to the remedy of giving him a little poison (according to the custom of tyrants, which was practised by the sorcerers in some of the provinces of that empire) he would not have been dethroned. Others, defending the conduct of the prince, say that if his father had fallen into the hands of the enemy still worse would have befallen him. Others, who were held to be religious, said that even if the use of poison had been possible, all his predecessors would rather have died than have used it.
summary.zh: 王子回到城中,摘下黃纓,改用紅纓。然而他自己雖戴紅纓,卻始終不許父親摘下黃纓——在他看來,只要實權在握,外在的徽記無足輕重。宮殿一成,僕從用度俱全;除了失去國政,廢王亞瓦爾-瓦卡克別無所失。可憐的老王在這片幽居中度過餘生——江山斷送在親生兒子手上。印第安人說,這場廢立早有預兆:他幼年泣血的凶兆,如今應驗了。人們私下議論:這位印加王若在察覺兒子野心之初,便用上那劑小小的毒藥——暴君之間的慣技,帝國某些省份的巫師確曾使用——便不會遭此下場。另一些人為王子辯護:若老王落入敵手,下場只會更慘;棄城而逃者,性命、江山、子孫基業都將不保。還有些信教虔誠的人說:縱使毒計可行,歷代先王寧死也不肯用毒。

sensitivity.note: The wept-blood omen fulfilled; the fringe colours as rank semiotics; the poison debate is Garcilaso's moral commentary in native voices.

passages.text: The Ynca Uiracocha entered Cuzco on foot... put aside the yellow fringe, and adopted the red one. But though he wore the red fringe himself, he never would consent that his father should leave it off, caring little for the outward insignia, so long as he possessed the reality of dominion and power... The poor king passed the rest of his life in this solitude, deprived of his kingdom by his own son.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 印加維拉科查徒步進入庫斯科……摘下黃色流蘇，改戴紅色流蘇。然而，儘管他自己戴著紅色流蘇，卻始終不肯同意讓父親摘下黃色流蘇；只要他握有統治與權力的實質，便不太在意這外在的標誌……這位可憐的國王在這樣的孤寂中度過餘生，被自己的兒子奪去了王國。

passages.text: The Indians say that this dethronement was prognosticated by the evil omen of his having wept blood in his childhood. They also say, reasoning amongst themselves, and recalling the memory of past events, that if this Ynca, when he began to fear the disposition of his son, had resorted to the remedy of giving him a little poison (according to the custom of tyrants, which was practised by the sorcerers in some of the provinces of that empire) he would not have been dethroned. Others, who were held to be religious, and highly extolled the nobility and generosity of their Yncas, said that even if the use of poison had been possible, all his predecessors would rather have died than have used it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 印第安人說，這次廢黜早已由他幼年時哭泣流血的凶兆所預示。他們還說，他們彼此推論，並回想往事的記憶，認為倘若這位印加人在開始畏懼兒子的心性時，便採用給他少許毒藥的補救之法（這是暴君的慣例，該帝國某些省份的巫師曾如此施行），他就不會被廢黜了。另有一些被視為虔誠、且極力頌揚其印加人高貴與寬厚的人則說，即便使用毒藥可行，他所有的先王也寧可死去，也不願使用。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas (1871)

title.en: Tahmina Comes to Rustam by Night
title.zh: 塔米娜夜訪魯斯塔姆

region.en: Palace of Samangan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩曼甘王宮（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Suhrab secs. 3-4

summary.en: Rustam's Rakhsh is lassoed by Turkmen horsemen while he sleeps, and he tramps afoot to Samangan, where the king feasts him. At midnight a slave with an ambergris taper leads in a moon-faced girl: Tahmina, sole daughter of the king of Samangan, who has heard the romances of the man who fears not div and lion and has sacrificed her prudence to her passion, hoping God may lay upon her breast a child of his. They are wed by the usual rites, and Rustam, leaving at dawn, gives her his famous armlet as a token for the child: if a daughter, plait it in her hair; if a son, bind it round his arm, for he will be like Sam in stature and bring down soaring eagles.
summary.zh: 魯斯塔姆熟睡時拉赫什被突厥騎手套走，他徒步前往薩曼甘，受國王盛宴款待。半夜，一名手持龍涎香燭的侍女引來月貌少女——國王獨女塔米娜。她傾慕傳說中「不懼魔獅」的英雄，情勝理智，只盼真主在她懷中賜下他的孩子。二人依禮成婚；黎明分別時，魯斯塔姆解下名貴臂鐲相贈：「若是女兒，編入髮辮；若是兒子，繫於其臂——他將如薩姆一般雄偉，能擊落翱翔之鷹。」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the armlet is the recognition-token whose failure causes the tragedy. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Some Turkman horsemen chanced upon the plain and marked the tracks of Rakhsh. These they pursued beside the stream, surrounded him, and with their royal lassos essayed to take him. Rakhsh raged like a mighty lion: lashing out he laid two Turkmans low and with his teeth tore off another's head; at length the others threw from every side their lassos, caught him round the neck and took him. When Rustam woke and needed docile Rakhsh he looked about the mead but found him not, whereat in dudgeon and astound he hurried toward Samangan, thus armed with quiver, mace, helm, scimitar, and tiger-skin cuirass, and went in evil case and much discouragement.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab secs. 2-3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一些土庫曼騎兵偶然來到這片平原，發現了拉赫什的蹤跡。他們沿著溪流追蹤這些足跡，將他團團圍住，並用他們的王家用套索試圖將他擒獲。拉赫什如一頭雄獅般暴怒：他猛踢猛衝，擊倒兩名土庫曼人，又用牙齒撕下另一人的頭顱；最後其餘的人從四面八方拋出套索，套住他的脖子將他擒住。當魯斯塔姆醒來，需要溫順的拉赫什時，他環顧草地卻遍尋不著，於是又惱又驚，急忙趕往薩曼甘，身上配著箭袋、狼牙棒、頭盔、彎刀與虎皮胸甲，滿懷憂懼、灰心喪氣地離去。

passages.text: At noon of night, while Phosphor crossed the sky, there came mysterious whispers: Rustam's door was softly opened, and a slave who bare a taper savouring of ambergris walked stately toward the drunken sleeper's couch. Behind the slave there was a moon-faced girl sun-bright, all scent and hue, with arching eyebrows and locks that hung in tresses lasso-like, in stature like a lofty cypress-tree. The lion-hearted Rustam marvelled at her and asked: thy name? What seek'st thou midst the murk of night?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 夜半時分，啟明星劃過天際，忽有神秘的細語傳來：魯斯塔姆的門扉悄然開啟，一名手持散發龍涎香氣火炬的奴僕，儀態莊重地走向那醉臥者的床榻。奴僕身後跟著一位面如明月、燦若朝陽的少女，渾身芬芳、姿容絕豔，眉彎如弓，鬈髮如套索般垂落成辮，身形宛如一株高聳的柏樹。獅心魯斯塔姆見了她，驚異不已，問道：你叫什麼名字？在這夜色昏沉之中，你尋求什麼？

passages.text: She said: Tahmina; and thou well mayst say that mine affliction teareth me in twain. Sole daughter of the king of Samangan, there is no mate for me among the kings. Many and many a story have I heard of thee, just like romance: how div and lion, pard and crocodile thou fearest not; how eagles seeing thy naked sword dare not to swoop upon their quarry. God hath ordained thy sojourn in this city, and now if thou wilt have me I am thine, for I have sacrificed my prudence to my passion; haply God Almighty may lay upon my breast a child of thine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她說：我叫塔赫米娜；你大可說，我的苦痛正將我撕裂成兩半。我是薩曼甘國王唯一的女儿，在諸王之中，我找不到可相匹配的伴侶。我曾聽過關於你的許許多多故事，宛如傳奇一般：你如何不畏妖魔與猛獅，不懼豹與鱷魚；雄鷹見了你出鞘的寶劍，也不敢俯衝撲向獵物。上帝已註定你寄居於此城，如今你若願意接納我，我便屬於你，因為我已將我的謹慎獻祭給了我的熱情；或許全能的神會在我懷中賜下你的孩子。

passages.text: He bade an archimage go and demand the maiden from her sire. The king, that noble Cypress, was well pleased to be affined to Rustam and bestowed Tahmina on him with the usual rites. He wore an armlet, a famous one; that gave he to Tahmina, and said: keep this. If thou shalt bear a daughter then plait it in her hair; while if the stars vouchsafe to thee a son bind round his arm this token of his father. He will be like Sam son of Nariman in stature and bring down soaring eagles; the sun will scorch not him. Then homeward to Zabulistan he went, but no one heard him speak of this event.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他命一位占星術士前去向少女的父親求親。那位國王，高貴的柏樹，欣然願與魯斯塔姆結為姻親，並依循慣常的禮儀將塔赫米娜許配給他。他戴著一只著名的臂環；他將它贈予塔赫米娜，說道：留著這個。你若生下女兒，便將它編入她的髮辮；倘若星辰賜你一個兒子，便將這父親的信物繫在他的臂上。他將如納里曼之子薩姆一般高大，能射落高飛的雄鷹；烈日也灼不傷他。隨後他返回扎布利斯坦，但無人聽他提起此事。

title.en: The Birth and Boyhood of Sohrab
title.zh: 蘇赫拉布誕生

region.en: Samangan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩曼甘（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Suhrab sec. 5

summary.en: Nine months pass and a moon-like babe is born; thou wouldst have said 'tis elephantine Rustam or lion-Sam; and since the babe smiled and was bright of blee Tahmina gave to him the name Suhrab. He looked a year old in a month, his chest was like his sire's; at three he exercised in arms, at five he had a lion-heart, at ten none dared encounter him in fight. He bluntly asks his mother who his father is, and Tahmina, to keep the secret of her love, tells him that Rustam, son of Zal, is his father — and the boy's heart swells: I must go to Iran and set my father on the throne of Kai Kaus.
summary.zh: 九月期滿，誕下皎月般的嬰孩——「彷彿巨象般的魯斯塔姆，又如雄獅般的薩姆」；因嬰兒容光煥發，塔米娜為其取名蘇赫拉布（「光彩奪目」）。滿月如周歲，三歲習武，五歲膽壯，十歲無人敢與之角力。他直問母親生父是誰；塔米娜道出「扎勒之子魯斯塔姆」——少年壯志頓生：我要去伊朗，助父登上卡烏斯的王座！

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Nine months passed and a moon-like babe was born; thou wouldst have said: 'tis elephantine Rustam, or else: 'tis lion-Sam, or Nariman; and since the babe smiled and was bright of blee Tahmina gave to him the name Suhrab. He looked a year old in a month, his chest was like his sire's; at three he exercised in arms, at five he had a lion-heart, at ten none dared encounter him in fight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 5 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 九個月過去，一個如月般的嬰孩誕生了；你定會說：這是巨象般的魯斯塔姆，或者說：這是獅子般的薩姆，或是納里曼；由於這嬰孩面帶笑容、容光煥發，塔赫米娜便為他取名蘇赫拉布。他一個月大時看來已如一歲，胸膛如同他的父親；三歲時便習練兵器，五歲時已有一顆獅子般的心，十歲時無人敢與他交戰。

passages.text: He bluntly asked his mother once: now tell me, since none of my milk-fellows can compare with me, and my head reacheth to the sky, who is my sire? Tahmina, to keep the secret of her love, told him that Rustam, son of Zal, the hero of Zabul, was his father, and his heart swelled with the desire to go to Iran and set his father on the throne of Kai Kaus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 5 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次他直截了當地問母親：現在告訴我吧，既然我的同乳夥伴中無人能與我相比，而我的頭已觸及天空，那麼我的父親是誰？塔赫米娜為了保守她愛情的秘密，告訴他扎布利斯坦的英雄、扎爾之子魯斯塔姆便是他的父親，於是他心中湧起一股渴望，要去伊朗，將他的父親扶上凱·卡烏斯的王座。

title.en: Tuli Complains and Tangaloa Fishes Up the Land
title.zh: 鷸鳥啼訴：坦加羅亞釣起大地

region.en: Skies over Samoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩摩亞上空（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1897 (Stair)

source.work: John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (London 1897)

summary.en: Tangaloa of the Skies, principal god and creator, sent his son the plover Tuli down to the ocean's surface; finding no place to rest, Tuli returned to complain, and Tangaloa threw down a stone which became land - or fished one up from the bottom of the sea with his great fish-hook, raising it higher on a second cast when the waves still wetted Tuli's feet. The reclining rock gave place to the spreading, sitting and upright rocks, then earth and grass and conquering convolvulus - whose rottenness bred the two grubs out of which Ngai-tosi and Ngai-va'a-va'ai shaped the first two bodies of mankind, part by part named for Tuli.
summary.zh: 天主坦加羅亞遣其子——鷸鳥圖利——下探海面；無處棲身，鷸鳥啼訴於天，父乃擲下巨石化為陸地——或以神鉤自海底釣起山岩，浪濤仍濕其足，遂二次揚鉤升高陸地。臥岩讓位於蔓延岩、坐岩、立岩；其後泥土、青草、藤蔓相繼而出——腐藤之中化出兩條幼蟲，恩加伊托西與恩加伊瓦瓦艾將其塑為兩具人形，各部皆冠以圖利之名。

sensitivity.note: Samoan creation; fish-hook parallels the Maori Maui and Hawaiian creation.

passages.text: The Samoans had several superior divinities and a host of inferior ones, and they were also accustomed to deify the spirits of deceased chiefs. Of the primitive gods the chief place is assigned to Tangaloa, or, as he is sometimes called, Tangaloa-langi, Tangaloa of the Skies. He was always spoken of as the principal god, the creator of the world and progenitor of the other gods and mankind. In one tradition that gives an account of the formation of the earth mention is made of other divinities or helpers, Tangaloa-tosi, also styled Ngai-tosi (Ngai the marker), and Ngai-va'a-va'ai (Ngai the seer or beholder), also called Tangaloa-va'a-va'ai; these two helpers are introduced as being sent by Tangaloa to complete the formation of the bodies of the first two of mankind, and to impart life to them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 薩摩亞人有幾位高等神祇和一大群低等神祇，他們也習慣將已故酋長的靈魂奉為神明。在原始諸神之中，首要之位歸於坦加洛阿，或有時稱他為坦加洛阿-蘭吉，即「天空的坦加洛阿」。人們總將他稱為主神，世界的創造者，以及其他神祇與人類的始祖。在一則敘述大地形成的傳統傳說中，提到了其他神祇或助手，即坦加洛阿-托西，又名奈-托西（標記者奈），以及奈-瓦阿-瓦艾（先知者或觀看者奈），又名坦加洛阿-瓦阿-瓦艾；這兩位助手被描述為由坦加洛阿派遣，來完成人類最初兩人的身體構造，並賦予他們生命。

passages.text: The son of Tangaloa was the Tuli, a species of plover. Tuli went down from the heavens to the surface of the ocean, but found no place on which to rest, and returned to complain to his father. On this his father threw down a stone from the heavens, which became land. Another account of the origin of the earth states that, in answer to Tuli's complaint of want of a resting-place, Tangaloa fished up a large stone from the bottom of the sea with a fish-hook; having raised the stone to the surface, he gave it to his son for his dwelling-place. On going thither to take possession of his new home Tuli found that every wave or swell of the ocean partially overflowed it, which compelled him to hop from one part to another of the stone to prevent his feet being wetted by each succeeding wave; annoyed at this, he returned to the skies to complain to his father, who, by a second application of the mighty fish-hook, raised the land to the desired height. This version is also given by the inhabitants of other groups in Polynesia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: Tangaloa之子是Tuli，一种鸻鸟。Tuli从天界下到海面，却找不到可以歇息之处，便回去向父亲抱怨。于是父亲从天上掷下一块石头，石头化作了陆地。关于大地起源的另一种说法称：Tuli抱怨无处歇息，Tangaloa便用鱼钩从海底钓起一块大石；将石头举到海面后，他把它交给儿子作为居所。Tuli前往占有这新家时，发现海上的每一道波浪或涌浪都会部分漫过它，迫使他从石头的一处跳到另一处，以免双脚被接连而来的波浪打湿；他对此十分恼怒，便回到天界向父亲抱怨，父亲再次施展那有力的鱼钩，把陆地升到合意的高度。这一说法亦见于波利尼西亚其他群岛的居民之中。

passages.text: This tradition also gives the history of the worm of the earth. Popo-taoto, the reclining rock, was succeeded by Popo-sosolo, the spreading rock; Papa-sosolo was succeeded by Papa-nofo, the sitting rock; Papa-nofo was succeeded by Papa-tu, the upright rock. The rock was succeeded by the earth or mould, which was then spread over with grass; after this the fue (convolvulus) grew and overcame the grass. Tuli returned to his father, Tangaloa, having obtained his land, but there was no man to reside on it. His father said to him, 'You have got your land. What grows on it?' Tuli answered, 'The fue.' His father told him to go and pull it up, which he did, and on its rotting produced two grubs, which moved a little as Tuli looked upon them; he again returned to the skies to tell his father of their birth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 这一传说还记述了地虫的来历。Popo-taoto，即横卧之石，之后是Popo-sosolo，即蔓延之石；Papa-sosolo之后是Papa-nofo，即端坐之石；Papa-nofo之后是Papa-tu，即直立之石。石头之后是泥土或壤土，其上随即覆满青草；此后fue（旋花）生长起来，压过了青草。Tuli既已得到他的土地，便回到父亲Tangaloa那里，但地上无人居住。父亲对他说：『你已得到你的土地。地上长着什么？』Tuli答道：『fue。』父亲叫他去把它拔起，他照做了，fue腐烂后生出两条幼虫，Tuli看着它们时，它们微微蠕动；他又回到天界，把它们的诞生告诉父亲。

passages.text: Upon this Tuli was told to return to the earth and take with him Tangaloa-tosi, or Ngai-tosi, the marker, and Tangaloa-va'a-va'ai, the seer, who were told to operate upon the two grubs; on their arrival they began to form them into the shape of men, commencing at the head. When the head was completed Tuli said, 'Let my name be joined with that of the head', a portion of which was then named O le-tuli-ulu; they then proceeded to give sight by forming the eyes, when Tuli made the same request as before, upon which a portion of the eye was called O le-tuli-mata; the different members of the body were successively formed, each having the name of Tuli prefixed to the portion of the body as formed: as the elbow, O le-tuli-lima, and the knee, O le-tuli-vae.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 于是Tuli奉命回到地上，并带上Tangaloa-tosi，或称Ngai-tosi，即标记者，以及Tangaloa-va'a-va'ai，即预见者，他们奉命对那两条幼虫加以加工；他们到达后便开始把它们塑成人形，从头开始。头部完成后，Tuli说：『让我的名字与头部相连。』于是头部的一部分被命名为O le-tuli-ulu；接着他们造出眼睛使其有视觉，Tuli又提出同样的请求，于是眼睛的一部分被称为O le-tuli-mata；身体的各个部位依次成形，每成形一个部位，便在该部位之前冠以Tuli之名：如肘为O le-tuli-lima，膝为O le-tuli-vae。

title.en: The First Man Dies by the Little Fish Lo
title.zh: 初人之死：小魚羅致禍

region.en: New-formed Samoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新成之薩摩亞（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1897 (Stair)

source.work: John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (London 1897)

summary.en: The two shaped bodies lived, but were both males. One day, fishing with a net called the faamutu, one of them was injured by a small fish called the lo, which caused his death. Tuli returned to the skies and bewailed the loss of one of the inhabitants of his land; Ngai-tosi was directed by Tangaloa to proceed to the earth and reanimate the dead body, changing the sex of the deceased male to that of a female - and the two became man and wife, the parents of the human race.
summary.zh: 所塑的兩具身體活了，卻皆為男子。一日以『法阿姆圖圖』漁網捕魚，其一被小魚『羅』所傷而死。圖利上天空哀悼其民之喪；坦加羅亞遣恩加伊托西下界復活屍身——並將死者由男易女。二人遂結為夫婦，成為人類之父母。

sensitivity.note: Origin of death and of the human pair in the Stair recension.

passages.text: On the formation of the two bodies being complete they lived, but were both males, and dwelt on the land on which they were formed. One day, whilst fishing with a net called the faamutu, one of them was injured by a small fish called the lo, which caused his death. Upon this Tuli returned to the skies, and bewailed the loss of one of the inhabitants of his land to his father, when Ngai-tosi was directed by Tangaloa to proceed to the earth and reanimate the dead body; previously to which, however, he changed the sex of the deceased male to that of a female. The two then became man and wife, and the parents of the human race.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 两具身体成形完毕后，他们便活了起来，但二者皆为男性，居住在他们被造出的那片土地上。一天，他们用一张名为faamutu的网捕鱼时，其中一人被一种名叫lo的小鱼所伤，因而死去。于是Tuli回到天界，向父亲哀悼自己土地上一位居民的丧失，Tangaloa便命Ngai-tosi前往地上使那死去的身体复生；然而在此之前，他先把死者的性别由男变为女。二者于是成为夫妻，成为人类的父母。

passages.text: In connexion with this history of Tangaloa it may be mentioned that occasional visits are stated to have been made to the abode of the august Tangaloa by parties from the earth, who returned with some useful benefaction from the deity - as, for instance, Losi, who is reputed to have been the benefactor of his countrymen by bringing taro.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 与这段Tangaloa的传说相关，还可以提到：据说地上的人偶尔会前往威严的Tangaloa的居所，并带着神明所赐的某种有益恩惠返回——例如Losi，据传他为本族同胞带来芋头，因而成为他们的恩人。

title.en: The Leaping Stone and the Two Roads of the Dead
title.zh: 躍魂之石與亡者兩途

region.en: Falealupo, west point of Savaii (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩瓦伊島西端法萊阿盧波（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1897 (Stair)

source.work: John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (London 1897)

summary.en: The disembodied spirit retains the exact resemblance of its former self and immediately begins its solitary journey to the Fafa, westward of Savaii: from Manuka the ghost swims island to island to the west point of Savaii, where at the leaping-stone all spirits leap into the sea. There are two roads - O le Lua-loto-o-Alii, the deep hole of chiefs, to Pulotu the abode of the blest; and O le Lua-loto-o-tau-fanua, the deep hole of the common people, to Le nu'u-o-nonoa, the land of the bound, another name for the dreadful Sa-le-Fe'e. Natives have assured Stair that spirits passed them on the road and returned no answer.
summary.zh: 亡魂離體，貌如生前，即刻啟程獨行冥府法法——位於薩瓦伊之西：自毛卡出發的魂靈逐島泅渡，至薩瓦伊西端『躍魂之石』縱身入海。冥途有二：『酋長深穴』通往福地普洛圖；『平民深穴』通往『受縛者之鄉』——即可怖的薩勒費埃。斯泰爾親聞土人說：魂靈曾與他們同行於路，呼之而不應。

sensitivity.note: Samoan eschatology; two-roads parallel to Tongan Pulotu/Sa-le-Fe'e.

passages.text: O le Fafa, Sa-le-Fe'e, and Pulotu are places which occupy a prominent position in Samoan mythology, and seem in some manner to be connected the one with the other. O le Fafa (Hades) is alike the entrance to Sa-le-Fe'e, the Samoan Tartarus, or dread place of punishment, and also to Pulotu, the abode of the blest; the one entrance being called O le Lua-loto-o-Alii, or deep hole of chiefs, by which they passed to Pulotu; the other, O le Lua-loto-o-tau-fanua, or deep hole of the common people, by which they passed to Le nu'u-o-nonoa, or the land of the bound, which is simply another term for the much-dreaded Sa-le-Fe'e. The idea of the superiority of the chiefs over the common people was thus perpetuated, none but chiefs or higher ranks gaining entrance to the Samoan Elysium.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: O le Fafa、Sa-le-Fe'e与Pulotu在萨摩亚神话中占有显著地位，似乎以某种方式彼此相连。O le Fafa（冥界）既是通往Sa-le-Fe'e——萨摩亚的塔尔塔罗斯，即可怖的惩罚之地——的入口，也是通往Pulotu——蒙福者居所——的入口；其中一个入口名为O le Lua-loto-o-Alii，即酋长之深穴，酋长们经此前往Pulotu；另一个名为O le Lua-loto-o-tau-fanua，即平民之深穴，平民经此前往Le nu'u-o-nonoa，即被缚者之地，这不过是那令人深为畏惧的Sa-le-Fe'e的又一名称。酋长优于平民的观念由此延续下来，唯有酋长或更高等级者方能进入萨摩亚的极乐之境。

passages.text: The disembodied spirit was supposed to retain the exact resemblance of its former self, and immediately on leaving the body it was believed to commence its solitary journey to the Fafa, which was located to the westward of Savaii, the most westerly of the group, and towards this point disembodied spirits from all the islands bent their way immediately after death. Thus in case of a spirit commencing its journey at Manuka, the most easterly of the group, it journeyed on to the western end of that island from whence it started, where it dived into the sea and swam to the nearest point of Tutuila, where, having journeyed along the shore to the extreme west point of that island, it again plunged into the sea and pursued its solitary way to the next island, and thus onward throughout the entire group until it reached the extreme west point of Savaii, where it finally dived into the ocean and pursued its solitary way to the mysterious Fafa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說，脫離肉體的靈魂會保持其生前原貌，且人們相信它一離開軀體，便開始獨自踏上前往法法的旅程；法法位於薩瓦伊島以西，薩瓦伊島是群島中最西端的一座島，而所有島嶼的亡魂在死後都立刻朝這個方向前行。因此，若一個靈魂從群島最東端的馬努卡島啟程，它便一路行至該島的西端，從那裡潛入海中，游向圖圖伊拉島最近的一處海岸；接著，它沿著海岸行至該島最西端，再次躍入海中，獨自前往下一座島，如此一路行遍整個群島，直到抵達薩瓦伊島的最西端，最終潛入大洋，獨自踏上前往神祕法法的旅程。

passages.text: At the west point of Upolu the land terminates in a narrow rocky point, which is still known as O le fatu-osofia, the leaping-stone, from which all spirits were said to leap into the sea en route to the Fafa. This was a much-dreaded point, where the lonely travellers were said to be certainly met with, and their company was anything but desired. Many times natives have assured me that disembodied spirits have passed them on the road when travelling; when asked how they knew them, they answered, 'Why, we knew them personally, and spoke to them, but received no answer', which was quite sufficient in their estimation to determine the spiritual nature of the parties met, since it is the invariable custom of the Samoans to return an answer when accosted on a journey - to do otherwise being looked upon as an insult.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在烏波盧島的西端，陸地止於一處狹窄的岩石岬角，至今仍被稱為「O le fatu-osofia」，即「跳躍之石」；據說所有靈魂都從這裡躍入海中，踏上前往法法的路途。這是一處令人十分畏懼的地點，據說孤獨的旅人在此必定會遇見那些亡魂，而人們絕不願與之為伴。當地人曾多次向我保證，他們在旅途中曾與脫離肉體的靈魂擦身而過；當被問及如何辨認出它們時，他們答道：「哎呀，我們認得它們本人，還跟它們說過話，卻沒有得到任何回應。」在他們看來，這便足以斷定所遇者具有靈魂的本性，因為薩摩亞人有一項不變的習俗：旅途中若有人招呼，必定會回應——不這麼做會被視為一種侮辱。

passages.text: The priesthood, Taula-aitu (anchors of the spirits), were divided into four classes: priests of the war-gods, keepers of the war-gods, family priests, and prophets or sorcerers. The Taula-aitu-o-aitu-tau were important personages, being consulted upon all warlike occasions; this class invoked the assistance of various war-gods, but most of all Nafanua, a female deity who was reverenced by the entire population, and who in conjunction with Savea-se'u-leo may be considered the national gods of war. It was one of this class, the representative of Le Tamafainga, that usurped the regal power of the islands and reigned with great tyranny over the whole of Samoa until the year 1829, when he was slain by the people of A'ana - he was worshipped as combining both regal and divine attributes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 祭司階層「Taula-aitu」（意為「靈魂之錨」）分為四類：戰神祭司、戰神守護者、家族祭司，以及先知或巫師。Taula-aitu-o-aitu-tau 是重要的人物，凡有戰事皆會向他們請教；這一階層會祈求諸位戰神的協助，其中最常祈求的是女神納法努阿，她受到全體民眾的敬奉，與薩維亞塞烏萊奧一同可被視為國家的戰神。正是這一階層中的一員，即勒塔馬法因加的代理人，篡奪了群島的王權，以極其暴虐的方式統治整個薩摩亞，直到一八二九年他被阿阿納的人民殺死——他被當作兼具王權與神性者而受到崇拜。

title.en: Pachacamac, Whom No One Had Seen: Adoration Without Image
title.zh: 無人見過的帕查卡馬克:無像之拜

region.en: Valley of Pachacamac, coast below Lima (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 帕查卡馬克谷地（象徵性定位）

period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: The Yncas kings of Peru, with the light of nature which God had bestowed on them, had attained to a conception of the Maker of all things, whom they called Pachacamac, the word signifying the maker and sustainer of the universe. They said that Pachacamac was invisible, and that consequently they neither built temples nor offered sacrifices to him, as to the sun, but adored him inwardly with the greatest veneration, in accordance with the outward demonstrations they made with heads, eyes, arms, and body, when they used his name. Those who had adopted this belief before they were conquered by the Yncas were the ancestors of king Guismancu, who built a temple to Pachacamac and gave the same name to the valley where it stood. The Yuncas placed their idols in this temple, which were figures of fishes, and among them there was the image of a fox. The valley of Rimac, four leagues to the north, took its name from an idol there in the shape of a man, which spoke and gave answers to questions like the oracle of the Delphic Apollo: Rimac signifies 'He who speaks', and the city of Lima was founded in that valley.
summary.zh: 秘魯的印加諸王,憑上帝所賦的自然之光,已能體認造化萬物之主,稱之為「帕查卡馬克」——此名意即「宇宙的造就者與扶持者」。他們說帕查卡馬克隱而無形,故不像對太陽那樣為他建廟獻祭,只在內心以至高崇敬拜他;而每當提及他的名號,便以頭、眼、臂、身作出外在的敬意。此信仰廣布帝國;早在印加人到來之前便已信奉此道的,是庫伊斯曼庫王的先祖——他們為帕查卡馬克建了一座大神廟,並以其名命名所在的河谷。永卡人把偶像供在廟裡:是些魚形神像,其中還有一尊狐像。以北四萊格的利馬谷,則得名於一尊人形神像——它開口言事、有問必答,如德爾斐阿波羅的神諭;「里馬克」即「發言者」之意;今日利馬城便建於該谷。

sensitivity.note: Garcilaso's natural-theology reading of Pachacamac as an unimaged Creator - the classic passage on Andean henotheism.

passages.text: The Yncas kings of Peru, with the light of nature which God had bestowed on them, had attained to a conception of the Maker of all things, whom they called Pachacamac, the word signifying the maker and sustainer of the universe. They said that Pachacamac was invisible, and that consequently they neither built temples nor offered sacrifices to him, as to the sun, but adored him inwardly with the greatest veneration, in accordance with the outward demonstrations they made with heads, eyes, arms, and body, when they used his name.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 秘魯的印加諸王憑藉上帝賜予他們的自然之光，已領悟到萬物創造者的概念，他們稱之為帕查卡馬克，這個詞意指宇宙的創造者與維持者。他們說帕查卡馬克是無形的，因此他們既不為他建廟，也不像對太陽那樣向他獻祭，而是在提及他的名字時，以頭、眼、手臂與身體的外在動作，懷著最大的敬意在內心崇拜他。

passages.text: Those who more particularly had adopted this belief before they were conquered by the Yncas were the ancestors of king Guismancu, who built a temple to Pachacamac, and gave the same name to the valley where it stood. The Yuncas placed their idols in this temple, which were figures of fishes, and among them there was the image of a fox.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在印加人征服他們之前，尤其信奉這一信仰的，是國王圭斯曼庫的祖先；圭斯曼庫為帕查卡馬克建了一座神廟，並將神廟所在的山谷也命名為帕查卡馬克。尤恩卡人將他們的偶像安置在這座神廟中，那些偶像是魚的形狀，其中還有一尊狐狸的雕像。

passages.text: The valley of Rimac is four leagues to the north of Pachacamac. The word Rimac is the present participle, and signifies 'He who speaks.' The valley was so called from an idol there, in the shape of a man, which spoke and gave answers to questions, like the oracle of the Delphic Apollo and many others mentioned in the histories of the ancient heathens. So they called it 'He who speaks' because it talked, and the valley was given the same name.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 里馬克山谷位於帕查卡馬克以北四里格處。里馬克一詞是現在分詞，意為「說話者」。這座山谷因那裡的一尊偶像而得名，那偶像呈人形，能說話並回答問題，如同德爾斐的阿波羅神諭以及古代異教徒史書中提及的許多其他神諭一樣。他們之所以稱它為「說話者」，是因為它會說話，山谷也因此得了同樣的名字。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas (1871)

title.en: The Fox, the Ocean, and the Peace with Cuismancu
title.zh: 狐與海:與庫伊斯曼庫的和平之約

region.en: Valleys of Pachacamac and Rimac (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 帕查卡馬克與里馬克兩谷(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: The great lord Cuismancu replied that his people had no need of another lord; that the laws and customs he observed were those which had been received from his ancestors; that his people had no wish to put away their gods, for these gods were very powerful: among them was Pachacamac, whom they believed to be the creator and preserver of the universe, and therefore necessarily a greater god than the sun. They had built a temple to Pachacamac, where they offered up the best of everything they had, even sacrificing men, women and children; and such was the veneration in which they held him that they used not even to look upon his image, but the king and the priests entered the temple to worship, walking backwards, and went out so as to avoid raising their eyes. They also worshipped Rimac, a god that spoke and gave replies; their other objects of worship were the fox, which they respected for his cunning and sagacity, and the ocean, because it supplied them with fish. Cuismancu concluded by saying that these gods were sufficient for them: the sun less than any, as they needed no more heat than they already experienced. The Yncas resolved not to make war but to subdue the Yuncas by reasoning and kindness. A peace was concluded: the Yuncas agreed to worship the sun like the Yncas, and to build a separate temple; that no human sacrifices should be made, because to kill a man was contrary to the laws of nature, and the custom was to be entirely abolished; that the idols should be removed from the temple of Pachacamac, and that he should henceforth be worshipped in the heart, no statue being set up because no one had ever seen him; that a house of chosen virgins of the sun should be established, the two things the provinces most desired to possess being a temple of the sun and a convent of virgins, for by possessing these they resembled Cuzco; and the Yncas agreed to hold in high veneration the oracle Rimac.
summary.zh: 庫伊斯曼庫答道:他的子民不需要別的主;他的法度皆承自祖先;他們也無意拋棄自己的神——那些神威力無邊,其中有創造並扶持宇宙的帕查卡馬克,自然比太陽更偉大。他們為他建廟,獻上最好的所有,甚至人祭;崇敬之至,連神像也不敢仰視——王與祭司入廟禮拜,須倒退而行,出廟時亦不得抬眼。他們還拜里馬克——那尊會說話、有問必答的神;此外尊狐之狡智,敬海洋之賜魚。庫伊斯曼庫說:有這些神便夠了;太陽嘛,他們並不需要更多的熱。印加人聞言大喜,決定不以兵戎,而以理喻與善意收服永卡人。和平條款如下:永卡人奉拜太陽,另建太陽神廟;廢除人祭——殺人違逆自然之法;偶像盡出帕查卡馬克神廟——他既無形無像,自當「心拜」而不立像;並建太陽貞女之屋——各地最慕者,莫過太陽神廟與貞女院,有此二者便如庫斯科;印加人亦允崇奉里馬克神諭,令全境敬之。

sensitivity.note: A negotiated theology: Garcilaso presents the Inca conquest of the coast as a religious peace treaty; the fox-and-ocean cult detail is unique.

passages.text: He replied that his people had no need of another lord... that they had no wish to put away their gods, for these gods, he said, were very powerful. Among them was Pachacamac, whom they believed to be the creator and preserver of the universe, and therefore necessarily a greater god than the sun... such was the veneration in which they held him, that they used not even to look upon his image, but the King and the priests entered the temple to worship, walking backwards, and went out so as to avoid raising their eyes. They also worshipped Rimac, a god that spoke and gave replies to those who sought him. Their other objects of worship were the fox, which they respected for his cunning and sagacity, and the ocean, because it supplied them with fish... the sun less than any, as they needed no more heat than they already experienced.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他回答說，他的人民不需要另一位君主……他們也不願捨棄自己的神明，因為他說，這些神明極為強大。其中有帕查卡馬克，他們相信祂是宇宙的創造者與保存者，因此必然是比太陽更偉大的神……他們對祂如此崇敬，甚至連祂的像也不敢正視，唯有國王與祭司才進入神殿禮拜，且倒退而行，離去時也避免抬眼。他們也崇拜里馬克，那是一位會說話、並回答求問者的神。他們其他的崇拜對象還有狐狸，因其狡黠與機敏而受尊敬，以及海洋，因為海洋供給他們魚類……他們最不崇拜太陽，因為他們已無需比現今所感受更多的熱。

passages.text: The Yuncas agreed to worship the sun like the Yncas, and to build a separate temple... but that no human sacrifices should be made, because to kill a man was contrary to the laws of nature, and the custom was to be entirely abolished. It was agreed that the idols should be removed from the temple of Pachacamac... Pachacamac was henceforth to be worshipped in the heart, and no statue to him was to be set up; because, as no one had ever seen him, it was impossible to know his figure, or to make an image of him. It was also arranged, for the greater honour and glory of the valley of Pachacamac, that a house of chosen virgins of the sun should be established... The Yncas agreed to hold in high veneration the oracle Rimac.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 雲卡人同意像印加人一樣崇拜太陽，並另建一座神殿……但不可再行活人獻祭，因為殺人有違自然之法，此習俗應徹底廢除。眾人議定，應將偶像自帕查卡馬克神殿中移去……自此以後，帕查卡馬克當受心中之崇拜，不得為祂立任何雕像；因為既然從無人見過祂，便不可能知道祂的形貌，也無法為祂造像。眾人又議定，為增進帕查卡馬克谷地的榮耀與光榮，應設立一所精選的太陽貞女之院……印加人同意對神諭里馬克致以崇高的敬奉。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas (1871)

title.en: The Voice from the Corners of the Temple: Pachacamac's New Oracle
title.zh: 神廟角落的聲音:帕查卡馬克神諭的革新

region.en: Temple of Pachacamac (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 帕查卡馬克神廟(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: It is worthy of note that the Devil, as soon as he saw that the Yncas had subjugated the valley of Pachacamac, and that the temple was cleared of the numerous idols that it formerly contained, sought to make himself the special lord of it, in the character of the unknown god whom the Indians venerated so highly, so as to obtain worship in various ways, and to sell his lies at a higher price in some places than in others. With this object he began to speak from the corners of the temple to the priests of the highest position and character, saying that he wished to reply to their questions and inquiries, not when all were assembled, but to the most respected alone, because it was beneath his dignity to speak to men of low degree. He added that he could only condescend to converse with kings and great lords, but that he would order the idol Rimac, who was his slave, to speak to the common people, and to answer all their inquiries. From that time it was the rule to consult the oracle on matters of state in the temple of Pachacamac, and for the people to resort to that of Rimac. The latter idol thus had his name of 'Speaker' confirmed, for as he was obliged to answer all, he had to talk a great deal.
summary.zh: 值得注意的是:魔鬼一見印加人征服帕查卡馬克谷、神廟中原有的諸多偶像盡被清除,便趁機自封為此廟特別之主——假冒印第安人至為崇敬的那位「無名之神」,以便受人崇拜、把謊言賣得更貴。為此,他開始從神廟的角落向地位最高、品行最尊的祭司們講話:說他不願當眾作答,只肯對受尊崇者開口——向卑微之人說話有失他的尊嚴;還說他只肯屈尊與君王和大領主交談,至於平民的問詢,則命他的奴僕——里馬克神像——代答。自此以後,國家大事便到帕查卡馬克廟中問神,平民之事則赴里馬克廟求問;「發言者」之名就此坐實——因為他須有問必答,只好喋喋不休。

sensitivity.note: The missionary demonology of oracle differentiation: state cult vs popular cult, narrated in Garcilaso's inherited frame.

passages.text: The Devil, as soon as he saw that the Yncas had subjugated the valley of Pachacamac, and that the temple was cleared of the numerous idols that it formerly contained, sought to make himself the special lord of it, in the character of the unknown god whom the Indians venerated so highly, so as to obtain worship in various ways, and to sell his lies at a higher price in some places than in others.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 魔鬼一見印加人已征服帕查卡馬克谷地，且神殿中原有的眾多偶像已被清除，便想使自己成為此地特別的主宰，以印第安人所如此崇敬的那位未知之神的身份出現，好以各種方式取得崇拜，並在某些地方把他的謊言賣得比別處更高的價錢。

passages.text: He began to speak from the corners of the temple to the priests of the highest position and character, saying that he wished to reply to their questions and inquiries, not when all were assembled, but to the most respected alone, because it was beneath his dignity to speak to men of low degree... he would order the idol Rimac, who was his slave, to speak to the common people, and to answer all their inquiries. From that time, it was the rule to consult the oracle on matters of state in the temple of Pachacamac, and for the people to resort to that of Rimac.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Garcilasso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries (Markham 1871); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他開始從神殿的角落向地位與品格最高的祭司說話，說他願意回答他們的問題與求問，但不在眾人齊聚之時，而只對最受尊敬者一人作答，因為向低微之人說話有損他的尊嚴……他要命令那作他奴僕的偶像里馬克去向平民說話，並回答他們所有的求問。自此以後，便定下規矩：國事當在帕查卡馬克神殿求問神諭，而平民則往里馬克神殿求問。

canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas (1871)

title.en: Sohrab Chooses His Charger and Marches on Iran
title.zh: 蘇赫拉布擇駿出征

region.en: Herds of Samangan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩曼甘馬群（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Suhrab secs. 5-7

summary.en: Sohrab demands a charger swift of foot with hoofs of steel flint-shattering; his might breaks down many a noble steed until a warrior brings a colt of the breed of Rakhsh, in strength a lion and as fleet as wind, whose leap is like the lightning. Mounted, Sohrab appears like Mount Bisitun, his spear pillar-like, and asks his grandsire's leave to seek Iran and see his glorious sire. Afrasiyab, delighted, sends Barman and Human with twelve thousand troops and a secret policy: the father must not recognise his son, that matchless Rustam may be slain — and should the boy perish by his father's hand, that hero's heart will never cease to burn.
summary.zh: 蘇赫拉布索求鋼蹄碎石、疾如飛鳥的戰馬；他的神力折服諸多駿馬，直到有人獻上「拉赫什血統」的雄駒——力如獅、疾如風、躍如閃電。少年上馬如比斯通山聳立，向祖父請命赴伊朗「拜見生父」。阿弗拉西亞卜大喜，遣巴爾曼與胡曼率一萬二千人並授密計：務使父子互不相認，讓無敵的魯斯塔姆隕落；若少年死於父親之手，那位英雄之心將永燃悔恨之火。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Afrasiyab's intrigue is the tragic engine of the Sohrab story. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Thou shalt see my prowess, said Sohrab, but I must have a charger swift of foot with hoofs of steel flint-shattering, in strength like elephants, in flight like birds, in water like fish, and on the land like deer. His mother bade the herdsman bring his herds of horses for Sohrab to choose a charger; and when some large-limbed, lusty steed appeared Sohrab flung round its neck the leathern noose, then laid his hand upon the beast to prove it and made it grovel. Thus his might broke down full many a noble steed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蘇赫拉布說：你將見識我的勇武，但我必須有一匹駿馬，足如鋼鐵、能碎燧石，力如大象，奔如飛鳥，入水如魚，陸上如鹿。他母親吩咐牧人帶來他的馬群，讓蘇赫拉布挑選坐騎；每當出現一匹腿粗體壯的駿馬，蘇赫拉布便將皮索套上牠的頸項，然後伸手按在牠身上試其能耐，使牠伏倒在地。他的神力就這樣折服了許多良駒。

passages.text: At length a warrior approached the elephantine youth and said: I have a colt, one of the breed of Rakhsh, in strength a lion and as fleet as wind; beneath the stamping of his hoofs the Bull-fish quaketh; his leap is like the lightning; on the mountains he goeth like the raven, on the water like fish, upon the desert like shaft from bow. Sohrab laughed out for joy, both proved and approved it, saddled and mounted; he appeared like Mount Bisitun, his spear was pillar-like. Since I have gotten such a steed I must ride forth at once and turn the day of Kai Kaus to gloom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 終於有一位武士走近這如象般魁梧的少年，說道：我有一匹小馬，出自拉赫什的血統，力如雄獅，疾如風；牠蹄下踏動時，牛魚也為之顫抖；牠的躍起如閃電；在山間行如烏鴉，在水上如魚，在沙漠中如離弦之箭。蘇赫拉布歡喜得笑出聲來，既試過牠，也認可了牠，於是備鞍上馬；他看上去如比斯通山，他的長矛如柱。既然我已得此駿馬，我必須立刻馳騁而出，把凱考斯的日子化為陰霾。

passages.text: Afrasiyab had news: Suhrab hath launched his ship, a host hath gathered unto him; although his mouth still savoureth of milk his mind is set on shaft and scimitar. He chose two chiefs, Human and Barman, gave them twelve thousand valiant troops and said: be this your secret policy: the father must not recognise his son by any ties of instinct, love, or race; so, when the twain encounter, the matchless Rustam will be put to it; it may be that this lion-man will slay him. Then will we press Kaus and seize on Iran with Rustam gone; while should he perish by his father's hand, that hero's heart will never cease to burn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 7 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿夫拉西亞布得到了消息：蘇赫拉布已率船啟航，一支大軍已聚集到他麾下；雖說他口中仍帶著乳香，他的心卻已繫於箭矢與彎刀。他挑選了兩員大將，胡曼與巴爾曼，撥給他們一萬二千名勇猛的兵士，說道：你們的密計當是如此：做父親的絕不可因任何本能、親情或血脈的牽繫而認出自己的兒子；如此一來，當二人交鋒，無與倫比的魯斯塔姆必將陷入苦戰；或許這獅子般的人會將他殺死。那時我們便進逼卡烏斯，趁魯斯塔姆不在而奪取伊朗；倘若他死於親父之手，那位英雄的心也將永無止息地灼燒。

title.en: Gurdafrid Unmasks before White Castle
title.zh: 古爾達弗里德城堡前現真容

region.en: White Castle of Iran (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 伊朗白堡（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Suhrab secs. 8-11

summary.en: At White Castle veteran Hajir rides out against the boy and is thrown like a boulder to the earth; his daughter Gurdafrid, a woman ever famous in the fight, arms herself, conceals her tresses under her mail, and showers arrows on Sohrab, who abashed charges, rents her mail with a dart, and snatches off her helm — her hair escapes, her face shines like the sun: it is a girl! He lassoes her round the waist, but she bargains: chiefs should be wise, so let us keep it dark; our troops and stronghold are at thy command. Then from the ramparts she mocks him: when news shall reach the Shah, he will march forth with Rustam whom ye cannot stand against; woe is me that such a neck and shoulder should disappear within the maw of pards.
summary.zh: 白堡守將海吉爾出戰，竟被少年如巨石般摔落於地。其女古爾達弗里德——征戰聞名的巾幗英雄——披甲藏髮出戰，箭如飛蝗；蘇赫拉布慚愧而奮擊，一鏢撕裂其鎧甲，奪其盔——長髮飄散、面容如日：「原來是女子！」他以套索擒其腰；她卻與之講和：「智者不逞匹夫之勇，堡壘兵馬任憑差遣。」隨後在城頭譏笑他：等卡烏斯與魯斯塔姆大軍一到，你這等英偉的脖頸怕要葬身獅腹！

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Gurdafrid's taunt plants the fatal ambiguity of Sohrab's identity. No living community restriction.

passages.text: White Castle was a stronghold of Iran and veteran Hajir was castellan, a man of might and courage; for Gazhdaham was failing though still brave and venturesome. His daughter, who was proud, renowned, and malapert, bore arms and fought on horseback. As Sohrab approached, Hajir sped forth upon the field. Suhrab rushed from the host as 'twere a blast: what are thy name and lineage? She that bare will have to weep for thee.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 8 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 白色城堡是伊朗的一處要塞，老將哈吉爾為城主，此人勇力過人、膽識非凡；因為加茲達哈姆雖仍英勇好險，卻已日漸衰老。他的女兒驕傲、聲名遠播而又潑辣大膽，披甲執兵，騎馬征戰。蘇赫拉布逼近時，哈吉爾疾馳而出，奔上戰場。蘇赫拉布如一陣狂風般從軍中衝出：你姓甚名誰，出身何門？生你的那人將要為你哭泣。

passages.text: Hajir laughed out and charged; brave Sohrab, strong as an elephant, came on like fire upon his moving mountain of a steed. Hajir thrust at his waist; the spearpoint glanced. Sohrab struck with the butt his foe's waist lustily and threw him like a boulder to the earth, astound in heart and soul. Suhrab dismounted, sat on his foeman's breast; Hajir entreated quarter, was made fast in bonds, and sent to Human.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 8 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 哈吉爾放聲大笑，縱馬衝鋒；勇敢的蘇赫拉布力大如象，如火一般撲向他那移動如山巒的駿馬。哈吉爾刺向他的腰際；矛尖一滑而過。蘇赫拉布奮力以矛柄猛擊敵人的腰腹，將他如巨石般掀翻在地，令他心魂俱驚。蘇赫拉布翻身下馬，坐在敵人的胸膛上；哈吉爾求饒，被牢牢捆綁，送往胡曼處。

passages.text: A woman like some valiant cavalier was she and ever famous in the fight; her name was Gurdafrid, and none as yet had seen her match. Time pressed, she armed, concealed her tresses underneath her mail, secured her Ruman casque upon her head, and came down, like a lion, from the hold with girded waist upon a wind-foot steed. What lusty Crocodile is there among you to match himself with me in single combat? she cried in thunder-tones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 9 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她是一個宛如英勇騎士的女子，在戰陣中素來聞名；她名叫古爾達弗里德，至今尚無人見過能與她匹敵者。時機緊迫，她披掛整備，將髮辮藏於鎧甲之下，把羅馬頭盔牢牢戴在頭上，束緊腰帶，騎上一匹疾如風的駿馬，如獅子一般從堡中衝下。你們之中有哪一頭強健的鱷魚，敢與我單打獨鬥？她以雷鳴般的聲音喊道。

passages.text: He thrust a deadly dart with all his strength, struck Gurdafrid upon the belt and rent her coat of mail, but even as she reeled she drew her sword and clave the dart asunder; he pressed upon her, jostled her, and snatched her helm: her hair escaped, her face shone like the sun. It is a girl! he said amazed. He caught her round the waist, but she showed her face and said: chiefs should be wise, so let us keep it dark; our troops and stronghold are at thy command. Then, laughing, from the ramparts she mocked him: when news shall reach the Shah that a chief is leading an army from Turan, he will march forth with Rustam whom ye cannot stand against, and all thy host will perish; woe is me that such a neck and shoulder should disappear within the maw of pards.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab secs. 9-11 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他傾盡全力擲出一支致命的標槍，正中古爾達弗里德的腰帶，撕裂了她的鎖子甲，然而她雖身形搖晃，卻仍拔出劍來，將那標槍劈為兩段；他步步進逼，推擠著她，一把奪下她的頭盔：她的秀髮散落，面容燦爛如太陽。是個女子！他驚愕地說道。他攬住她的腰，她卻露出面容說道：首領當有智慧，此事且讓我們秘而不宣；我們的軍隊與要塞皆聽憑你調遣。隨後，她從城垛上笑著嘲弄他：一旦消息傳到沙阿耳中，說有一員大將正率軍自圖蘭而來，他便會與魯斯塔姆一同出征，那是你們抵擋不住的，你的全軍都將覆滅；可嘆我這般頸項與肩膊，竟要消失於豹子的咽喉之中。

title.en: Kana, Born a Rope, Grows into the Sky
title.zh: 繩形所生的巨人卡納

region.en: Piihonua, Hilo, Hawaii Island
region.zh: 夏威夷島希洛皮伊霍努阿

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; recorded 1916-1917 (Fornander Collection)

source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kana and Niheu (Honolulu 1916-1917)

license: Public domain (Bishop Museum Memoirs vol. IV, 1916-1917)

summary.en: Hakalanileo and Hina's first-born Kana is born as a piece of rope; grandmother Uli, famed sorceress, keeps it until it assumes human form and brings the child up at Piihonua in Hilo. His body grows so tall and terrible to behold that the house Halauoloolo must be lengthened from the mountain almost to the sea - the Jack-and-beanstalk growth of the Hawaiian hero who will one day reach the deep blue of the heavens.
summary.zh: 哈卡拉尼萊奧與希娜的長子卡納降生時竟是一段繩索，並無人形；祖母烏里——巫術界著名的女神——將其收藏，待其成人形後扶養於希洛皮伊霍努阿。其身軀猛長，可怖驚人，以致居屋哈勞洛洛不得不自山腳一延至海——這便是日後直上藍天的夏威夷英雄的傑克豆蔓式成長。

sensitivity.note: Kana is a figure of great antiquity in Hawaiian legendary lore; Uli the sorcerer-goddess.

passages.text: Hakalanileo was the father and Hina the mother of Kana, the first-born, and Niheu was the younger brother of Kana; Uli was the grandmother. Hamakualoa, Maui, was the land in which Kana was born, and Halauoloolo was the name of the house. At the birth of Kana he was in the form of a piece of rope; he had no human form. After the birth of Kana, Uli took and kept it until it assumed a human form, then she brought the child up. The place where Kana was brought up was in Piihonua, Hilo, Hawaii, a place lying to the east of Wailuku, where his house was built, called Halauoloolo.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kana and Niheu (1916-1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 哈卡拉尼萊奧是父親，希娜是母親，卡納是長子，尼赫烏是卡納的弟弟；烏利是祖母。卡納出生之地是毛伊島的哈馬庫阿洛阿，而哈拉烏奧洛奧洛是那房屋之名。卡納出生時是一段繩索的形貌；他並無人的形體。卡納出生之後，烏利將它取來保存，直到它化為人形，然後她將這孩子撫養長大。卡納被撫養長大之處，是在夏威夷希洛的皮伊霍努阿，那地方位於懷盧庫之東，他的房屋便建於該處，名為哈拉烏奧洛奧洛。

passages.text: In this legend it is said that the body of Kana grew to be very tall and large and was terrible to behold. While he was being brought up he grew so fast that the house had to be lengthened, so that it extended from the mountain until it was almost to the edge of the sea - such is the story as told of this house, Halauoloolo. Hina in this story has been called Hawaii's Helen of Troy; she has been a prolific inspiration of freaks and foibles in the folk-lore not only of these islands but throughout Polynesia, and Niheu was said to have special power, Sampson-like, through his long hair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kana and Niheu (1916-1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在這則傳說中，據說卡納（Kana）的身軀長得極其高大魁梧，令人望而生畏。在他被撫養長大的過程中，他長得太快了，以致房屋不得不加長，從山邊一直延伸到幾乎靠近海邊——關於這座名為哈勞歐洛洛（Halauoloolo）的房屋，流傳下來的故事便是如此。這則故事中的希娜（Hina）被稱為夏威夷的特洛伊海倫；她不僅在這些島嶼的民間傳說中，而且在整個玻里尼西亞的民間傳說中，都是層出不窮的怪異與荒誕故事的豐富靈感來源；而據說尼赫烏（Niheu）憑藉他的長髮，擁有如參孫一般的特殊力量。

title.en: Kana Snaps the Flippers of the Turtle Hill Haupu
title.zh: 卡納折斷龜山霍普之鰭

region.en: Haupu hill, Pelekunu, Molokai
region.zh: 摩洛凱島佩萊庫努霍普山

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; recorded 1916-1917 (Fornander Collection)

source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kana and Niheu (Honolulu 1916-1917)

license: Public domain (Bishop Museum Memoirs vol. IV, 1916-1917)

summary.en: The floating hill Haupu - in truth the great turtle Kahonunuimaeleka - carries off Hina to Molokai with chief Kapepeekauila. Uli's gods carry the double canoe Kaumaielieli down from Paliuli; Niheu fells the swordfish-man Keauleinakahi mid-channel and catches the hurled boulder in Kana's right hand. Fed at last by grandmother Uli, Kana towers over Haupu, makes eyes at it until it strains upward to meet him, then breaks the flippers right and left - the hill falls to pieces into the sea, leaving the Rocks of Kana at the mouth of Waikolu Valley.
summary.zh: 漂浮之山霍普——實為巨龜卡霍努努伊馬埃萊卡——攜走希娜至摩洛凱酋長卡佩佩考伊拉處。烏里之神眾自帕利烏里抬下雙舟考邁埃利埃利；尼赫烏中流斃劍魚勇士克勞萊納卡希，卡納右手接住山上擲來的巨石。祖母烏里以食慰之後，卡納拔身凌駕霍普之上，以目相逼——山將其鰭折斷，霍普頓失其力，崩落入海，遺下瓦伊科魯谷口的『卡納之岩』。

sensitivity.note: Molokai landmark legend; prophetic dream of priest Moi summarized in passages.

passages.text: Once upon a time this hill, Haupu, moved or floated to Mokuola in Hilo, Hawaii, carrying along the chief and the people and the things that grew on the hill. When Hina the mother of Kana and Niheu saw that the land was pleasant to the eye she climbed on up the hill with the idea of taking a look at the place; as soon as Hina was on the hill of Haupu it immediately moved back to Molokai, thus leaving Hakalanileo to mourn for her loss. When Hakalanileo saw that his wife was being carried away he tried to recover her but found it impossible to do so; after his failure he proceeded to Niheu and informed him that Hina had been taken away by the hill of Haupu. When Niheu heard this report from his father he said: 'I cannot get her; there is only one person who can do it, and that is Kana. You must go to him personally; don't be afraid of him and run away if he should turn and look at you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kana and Niheu (1916-1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前，這座名為豪普（Haupu）的山丘曾移動或漂浮到夏威夷希洛（Hilo）的莫庫歐拉（Mokuola），一路上載著首領、百姓以及山上生長的萬物。當卡納與尼赫烏的母親希娜看到這片土地賞心悅目時，她便爬上這座山丘，想看一看這個地方；希娜一踏上豪普山丘，山丘便立刻移回摩洛凱（Molokai），於是留下哈卡拉尼萊奧（Hakalanileo）為失去她而哀悼。當哈卡拉尼萊奧看到妻子被帶走時，他試圖把她奪回，卻發現無法做到；失敗之後，他便前往尼赫烏那裡，告訴他希娜已被豪普山丘帶走。尼赫烏聽完父親的這番話後說道：『我無法把她奪回；只有一個人能做到，那就是卡納。你必須親自去找他；不要害怕他，即使他轉過身來看你，也不要逃跑。』

passages.text: When Kana heard this he said to Hakalanileo: 'Go and issue a call that the people come together throughout Hawaii, and instruct the men to go and hew out canoes, by which we will get to Molokai and get back your wife.' With this the canoe hewers all around Hawaii came together and a large double canoe of ten fathoms in length was hewed out and made ready; but when Kana stretched out his hands and placed them on the canoe, the canoe sunk out of sight - the hands of Kana alone were too much for the canoe, and it too sunk out of sight, thus leaving them without a canoe to get to Molokai in. Therefore Hakalanileo went to the presence of Niheu, who said: 'You go to Uli and ask for a canoe; she has the canoe that will take you to Molokai, and she will direct you what to do.' Uli made reply: 'Yes, there is a canoe; it is in Paliuli; but you must go and call all the people together to go and drag down the canoes.' Hakalanileo did so and collected eight times forty men, and they proceeded to the uplands of Paliuli, where Uli prayed for a double canoe for Kana; after the people had all returned, the double canoe Kaumaielieli was lifted by the gods and carried down and placed in the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kana and Niheu (1916-1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡納聽到這番話後，對哈卡拉尼萊奧說道：『去發出號召，讓全夏威夷的人聚集起來，並吩咐男人們去砍削獨木舟，我們好乘著它前往摩洛凱，把你的妻子奪回來。』於是，夏威夷各地的獨木舟砍削匠都聚集起來，砍削出一艘長達十噚的大型雙體獨木舟並準備就緒；但當卡納伸出雙手放在獨木舟上時，獨木舟卻沉得無影無蹤——單是卡納的雙手就讓獨木舟承受不住，獨木舟也沉得無影無蹤，於是他們便沒有獨木舟可以前往摩洛凱了。因此，哈卡拉尼萊奧前去見尼赫烏，尼赫烏說道：『你去向烏利（Uli）求一艘獨木舟；她有一艘能載你前往摩洛凱的獨木舟，她會指點你該怎麼做。』烏利回答說：『是的，有一艘獨木舟；它在帕利烏利（Paliuli）；但你必須去把所有人召集起來，去把獨木舟拖下來。』哈卡拉尼萊奧照做了，聚集了八倍四十人，他們前往帕利烏利的高地，烏利在那裡為卡納祈求一艘雙體獨木舟；等眾人全都返回後，雙體獨木舟考邁埃利埃利（Kaumaielieli）被諸神舉起，搬運下來，安置在海中。

passages.text: While Kana and Niheu were making their preparations to sail on the double canoe Kaumaielieli to do battle with Kapepeekauila, the chief on the top of Haupu hill, Moi dreamed a dream - Moi was the priest to the chief Kapepeekauila, a very great priest, learned in his profession and all-powerful, his predictions always coming true. In the night of Kane he dreamed: 'A long man, a short man; a stunted youth, a male god. The eyes touched the heaven; the earth was overshadowed. Say Kamauhili, Ku is routed. Such is my dream, the priest.' After telling the dream Moi gave an interpretation of its meaning, but the chief would not believe it; seeing this Moi prophesied: 'If you are not going to take heed to my warning, you will surely be dispossessed. I saw a long man, and it was by him that the borders of Haupu were broken and the hill fell to pieces into the sea; therefore depart now while death is yet at a distance.' Kapepeekauila refused to take heed of this warning, saying: 'You are the one I shall cause to die, you deceiving priest. My hill of Haupu shall never be conquered. However, let it stand; if my hill is not conquered in the coming fight, I will kill you.' Moi then replied: 'Yes, well and good. The paths of the priests are narrow and can never be reached by crawling.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kana and Niheu (1916-1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 正當卡納與尼赫烏準備乘著雙體獨木舟考邁埃利埃利出航，去與豪普山頂的首領卡佩佩考伊拉（Kapepeekauila）交戰時，莫伊（Moi）做了一個夢——莫伊是首領卡佩佩考伊拉的祭司，一位極其偉大的祭司，精通本業、無所不能，他的預言總是應驗。在卡內（Kane）之夜，他夢見：『一個高個子，一個矮個子；一個矮小的青年，一位男神。雙眼觸及天際；大地被籠罩。說吧，卡毛希利（Kamauhili），庫（Ku）已被擊潰。這就是我的夢，祭司。』莫伊講完夢後，對其含義作了解釋，但首領不肯相信；見此情形，莫伊預言道：『如果你不聽從我的警告，你必將被逐出。我看見一個高個子，正是他攻破了豪普的邊界，使山丘崩裂墜入海中；因此趁死亡還遠，現在就離開吧。』卡佩佩考伊拉拒絕聽從這一警告，說道：『你就是我要處死的人，你這騙人的祭司。我的豪普山丘永遠不會被征服。不過，隨它去吧；如果在即將到來的戰鬥中我的山丘沒有被征服，我就殺了你。』莫伊於是回答說：『好，很好。祭司的道路狹窄，靠爬行永遠無法到達。』

passages.text: When the chief Kapepeekauila heard the words of Moi he sent his swiftest messengers, Kolea and Ulili, to fly and look for Kana and Niheu; when the two came to the harbor of Punahoa in Hilo they flew away up high so as to be out of the reach of Kana, and from up there called out to him. When Kana heard the call he reached up with his hands while still lying down, but did not catch them, though the wind of his hands made them swing away in haste, and in doing this they fell down on the hill of Haupu in Molokai. When the chief heard the report of the two birds he sent them to tell Keauleinakahi, his warrior who had charge of the ocean - a warrior who could thrust through a canoe with his snout. On the day when Kana and Niheu completed their preparations they boarded the canoe taking their father Hakalanileo, and set sail; Kana was wrapped up in the form of a large package placed on the platform, the length of the package extending the full length of the double canoe. While they had reached a point between Hawaii and Maui they were met by Keauleinakahi, who made an attack on the double canoe with the intention of breaking it to pieces with his sharp snout; while it was preparing for the attack Niheu stood up with his war club, Wawaikalani by name, and as Keauleinakahi made the attack Niheu struck it with his club, killing it. The voyage was resumed until they arrived at Waikolu, Molokai, near where the Haupu hill was standing, and here the canoe was moored; a large rock was rolled down from the hill aimed at the canoe, and as Kana was lying on the platform he heard the cry 'Say, there comes a large rock!
