passages.zh: 扎瓦拉立刻上前，传达了这番话；那位曾教苏赫拉布武艺的勇士如此答道：「是哈吉尔，那心怀恶意、挑起纷争之人，隐瞒了你们主帅之事；当苏赫拉布寻求父亲的凭证时，他闭口不言，只令其心陷于无知。哈吉尔的恶行给我们招来了这场灾祸。」随后鲁斯塔姆带着图斯、古达尔兹和古斯塔哈姆，匆匆赶向受伤的儿子；他抓起一把匕首欲自刎，却被众首领拦住，他们皆哭得心在滴血。

passages.text: Then Rustam called for an embroidered robe and, having laid the youth thereon, set off; but as he went one overtook him, saying: Sohrab hath passed from this wide world, and asketh no more a palace of thee but a bier. The father started, sighed, and groaning closed his eyes, then lighting swift as wind removed his helm and scattered dust upon his head, while all the great men also wept and wailed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 23 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 随后鲁斯塔姆命人取来一件绣花长袍，将少年安放其上，便启程离去；然而行至途中，有人追上他，说道：「苏赫拉布已辞别这广阔人世，不再向你求取宫殿，只求一具棺架。」父亲猛然一惊，叹息一声，呻吟着闭上双眼，随即迅疾如风地摘下头盔，将尘土撒在头上，而所有显贵也一同哭泣哀号。

passages.text: O warrior-youth exalted and a paladin by birth! the sun and moon, the breastplate and the helm, the crown and throne, will never see thy peer, he cried in mournful tones. Hath this that hath befallen me, to slay my son in mine old age, befallen another? The hero was distracted at the words of Human about Hajir; he quitted the battlefield and coming to Hajir laid hold upon his throat and threw him down, then drawing forth a dagger of bright steel was minded to behead him, but the nobles took part with him and saved him from death's door.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab secs. 23, 21 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「啊，尊贵的少年勇士，生来便是豪杰！日月、胸甲与头盔、王冠与宝座，都永不会见到与你匹敌之人。」他以悲怆的声调喊道。「我晚年弑子这等遭遇，可曾降临于他人身上？」这位英雄听闻胡曼关于哈吉尔的话，心神狂乱；他离开战场，来到哈吉尔跟前，一把掐住他的喉咙将他摔倒，随即抽出一把明晃晃的钢匕首，意欲斩其首级，但众贵族站在哈吉尔一边，将他从死亡之门救了出来。

title.en: Pava Fled from the Eye of Tangaloa
title.zh: 帕瓦逃避坦加羅亞之眼

region.en: South side of Upolu, Samoa
region.zh: 薩摩亞烏波盧島南岸

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1884 (Turner)

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (London 1884)

summary.en: Tangaloa, seeing the smoke of the children's fire, comes down from the heavens to Pava's house; a bowl of ava is upset by a creeping child, and in rage Tangaloa beats the child to death - then makes it live again. Pava in anger plucks a taro leaf, steps on it and goes off to Fiji, returning with the son of the king of Fiji; his emblem is the taro leaf, his people wear taro-leaf caps in battle, and he is seen in the rainbow. Another version has Pava fleeing from island to island, still pursued by the piercing eye of Tangaloa, until he reaches the district where the dreaded eye is no longer visible.
summary.zh: 坦加羅亞見孩童炊煙，自天而降至帕瓦家；孩童爬行間傾翻卡瓦碗，神怒而擊斃孩童——復又使之還生。帕瓦憤而摘芋葉踏之上天，往斐濟，後攜斐濟王子歸來；其神徽即芋葉，戰時其部眾皆戴芋葉之冠，彩虹即其所現。另一說謂帕瓦自一村一島輾轉逃避，坦加羅亞的利眼卻處處相隨，直至他抵達那無法再見神眼之地才得安居。

sensitivity.note: Deity legend; child-killing and revival recorded as in the tradition.

passages.text: This was the name of a war god on the south side of Upolu; it was originally the name of a man who came from the east end of the group. He and his wife went to work as usual in the bush and left their children in the house; the children kindled a fire to cook some food. Tangaloa, seeing the smoke, came down from the heavens; he found only the children, and inquired where their parents were - 'Gone to work', said they. 'Go and tell them I am here.' The children ran off and told them there was a chief in the house. Pava made haste home, found Tangaloa, and prepared a bowl of ava for him. A little child in creeping about the floor upset the ava; Tangaloa flew into a rage and beat the child to death; he again made it live, however, but Pava got up in anger, went out, plucked a taro leaf, stepped on to it and went off to Fiji. After a time he came back with a son of the king of Fiji, to the amazement of everybody, and when he died had a place in the Samoan pantheon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 这是乌波卢岛南侧一位战神的名称；它原本是一个人的名字，此人来自群岛东端。他和妻子如常去林中劳作，将孩子们留在家中；孩子们生火煮食。坦加洛阿见到炊烟，便从天而降；他只见到孩子们，便询问他们的父母何在——「去干活了」，他们说。「去告诉他们我在这里。」孩子们跑去告诉他们，说屋里有一位首领。帕瓦急忙赶回家，见到坦加洛阿，便为他备了一碗卡瓦酒。一个在地上爬行的小孩打翻了卡瓦酒；坦加洛阿勃然大怒，将那孩子打死；然而他又使孩子复活，但帕瓦愤然起身，走了出去，摘下一片芋叶，踏在其上，便前往斐济。过了一段时间，他带着斐济国王的一个儿子回来，令众人惊叹不已；他死后在萨摩亚万神殿中占有一席之地。

passages.text: His emblem was a taro leaf, and all his adherents in going to battle were known by taro leaf caps; the slain of that particular village were also known by the round leaf cap. Pava was seen in the rainbow: if it was clear and reflected down on the village, that was a good omen; but if it appeared far inland, the sign was bad, and a veto on any fighting for that day at least. Another story places the killing of the child in the east end of the group, and says that Pava fled from place to place, and from island to island, to get away from the presence of Tangaloa; as soon, however, as he reached a fresh place and thought of remaining there, he saw the terrible eye of Tangaloa looking down on him. Off he went to another village or another island, but still the piercing eye of Tangaloa followed him, until he reached the district to which I have referred, and where the dreaded eye was no longer visible.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的标志是一片芋叶，他所有的追随者出征时都以芋叶帽为记；那个特定村庄的战死者也以圆叶帽为记。人们能在彩虹中见到帕瓦：若彩虹清澈并映照在村庄之上，那是吉兆；但若它远远出现在内陆，便是凶兆，至少当日禁止任何战斗。另一个故事将那孩子的死置于群岛东端，并说帕瓦为躲避坦加洛阿的临在而四处逃亡，从一地到另一地，从一岛到另一岛；然而，他每到一个新地方，刚想留下，便见坦加洛阿那可怕的眼睛俯视着他。他动身前往另一个村庄或另一座岛屿，但坦加洛阿那锐利的眼睛仍追随着他，直到他抵达我所提及的那个地区，在那里那令人畏惧的眼睛才不再可见。

title.en: The Lizard and the Stone: Twin Gods of War Omens
title.zh: 蜥蜴與石：戰兆雙神

region.en: War villages of Upolu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 烏波盧戰村（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1884 (Turner)

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (London 1884)

summary.en: Pili ma le Maa, twin gods worshipped in war, famine and pestilence: a lizard darting across the road means turn back at once; running ahead means go on to meet the enemy. Cocoa-nut leaves are plaited over the middle post of the great house, and the chiefs watch - the lizard coming straight down the matting is good, zigzag is bad; the priest sprinkles each man with cocoa-nut juice, saying 'May the road I take flow with blood'. Smooth stones of the stream stand in a temple, one making yams and fruit, the other sending fish to the nets.
summary.zh: 『蜥蜴與石』——戰、饑、疫之時共祀的雙神。蜥蜴橫穿道路則立即回返；奔跑向前則可迎敵。眾酋以椰葉編席裹住大屋中柱守候觀察：蜥蜴直落席上為吉，曲折而下為凶；臨行祭司以椰汁灑身並誦『願我所行之路血流成河』。溪中光石奉於廟中——一石司薯芋果實，一石司漁網之魚。

sensitivity.note: War-omen ritual record.

passages.text: Pili ma le Maa were the names of twin gods, and worshipped at certain villages in time of war, famine, and pestilence. The month of May was a specially fixed time for prayers and food offerings. The lizard was the guiding incarnation, and carefully watched in times of war: if in going to battle a lizard was seen darting across the road they returned at once; if it ran ahead, however, they were cheered and went right on to meet the enemy. Another plan in searching for an omen was to plait cocoa-nut leaves and cover the middle post of the great house, from the floor to the ridge pole, and there the chiefs sat and watched: if a lizard from the roof came straight down on the matting that was a good sign, but if it came down zigzag the omen was bad, and fighting suspended. Before going to the fight they met and were sprinkled with cocoa-nut juice by the priest, each at the same time uttering the prayer, 'May the road I take flow with blood.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 皮利与马阿是两位孪生神祇的名字，在战争、饥荒与瘟疫之时于某些村庄受到崇拜。五月是专门固定的祈祷与献食之时。蜥蜴是引导的化身，在战时受到密切观察：若出征途中见蜥蜴横穿道路，他们便立刻返回；然而若它向前奔跑，他们便受到鼓舞，径直前去迎敌。另一种寻求预兆的方法是编织椰树叶，覆盖大屋的中柱，从地板直至屋脊，众首领便坐在那里观察：若蜥蜴从屋顶直落于席垫之上，那是吉兆；但若它曲折而下，预兆便凶，战斗即行中止。出战之前，他们聚集一处，由祭司以椰汁洒之，每人同时念诵祷词：「愿我所行之路血流成河。」

passages.text: Two unchiselled smooth stones of the stream were kept in a temple at one of the villages and guarded with great care; no stranger or over-curious person was allowed to go near the place, under penalty of a beating from the custodians of these gods. They represented good and not malicious death-causing gods: the one made the yams, bread, fruit and cocoa-nuts, and the other sent fish to the nets. Another stone was carefully housed in another village as the representative of a rain-making god: when there was over-much rain the stone was laid by the fire and kept heated till fine weather set in; in a time of drought the priest and his followers dressed up in fine mats and went in procession to the stream, dipped the stone and prayed for rain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 溪流中兩塊未經雕琢的光滑石頭，被供奉在其中一個村莊的神廟裡，受到極其小心的守護；任何陌生人或過於好奇的人都不許靠近該處，違者將遭這些神明的守護者鞭打。它們代表的是善良而非惡意致人死亡的神明：其一使山藥、麵包、果實與椰子生長，另一則將魚送入網中。另一塊石頭則被小心供奉於另一個村莊，作為一位降雨之神的代表：當雨水過多時，便將石頭置於火旁持續加熱，直到天晴為止；乾旱之時，祭司及其隨從身著精美的席墊，列隊前往溪流，將石頭浸入水中並祈求降雨。

title.en: The Petrified Coward and the Settling Stones
title.zh: 化石懦夫與決鬥之石

region.en: Road to the plantations, Samoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩摩亞墾道旁（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1884 (Turner)

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (London 1884)

summary.en: A stone in the road was said to have been a petrified coward: he and his brother covenanted to be brave in battle, praying that whichever fled should be changed into a stone; one turned before the enemy and was so changed by the god Fe'e - and every worker passing to the plantations kissed, or rather smelled, the stone, death being the penalty for neglect. Two boundary stones were two young men who killed each other in a quarrel - 'Go and settle it at the stones' being the standing order of two villages noted for peace and order.
summary.zh: 道旁之石乃化形的懦夫：兄弟倆立誓臨陣不退，並求神立約——臨陣脫逃者當化為石。戰日一到，其一轉身而逃，遂被神費埃當場石化；農人往來墾地皆親吻——毋寧說『嗅』——此石，怠慢者將遭橫死。村界處另立雙石，乃兩個相殺而亡的青年——『到石前解決去』成了兩村永享太平的口諭。

sensitivity.note: Stone-transformation and duel custom.

passages.text: In a road leading to village plantations a stone stood which was said to have been a petrified coward. He and his brother entered into compact that they would be brave in battle, and implored their god that if either fled that one should be changed into a stone. The day came, the battle was fought, but one of the brothers turned and fled before the face of the enemy, and so was changed into a stone there and then by the god Fe'e. All the people as they passed inland to work in their plantations kissed, or rather smelled, the stone, and in coming back did the same; death was supposed to be the consequence of the neglect of this mark of deference to the power of the Fe'e.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在一條通往村莊園圃的道路上，立著一塊石頭，據說曾是一個化為石頭的懦夫。他與兄弟立下約定，要在戰鬥中勇敢，並向他們的神祈求：若其中一人逃跑，那人便應化為石頭。日子到了，戰鬥打響，但兄弟之一在敵人面前轉身逃跑，於是當場被神明Fe'e化為石頭。所有人在前往內地園圃勞作時經過，都會親吻、或更確切地說是嗅聞這塊石頭，回來時也同樣如此；據信，若疏忽了這項對Fe'e之力的敬禮，便會招致死亡。

passages.text: At the boundary line between two villages there were two stones, said to have been two young men who quarrelled, fought, and killed each other on that very spot, and whose bodies were immediately changed into stones. If any quarrel took place in either of these two villages there was never any general disturbance: 'Go and settle it at the stones' was the standing order; and so all who were inclined to be demonstrative in any affair of honesty or honour went to the stones and fought it out. If either of the duellists was knocked down that was the final settlement; no one else interfered, and so, by common consent in such matters, these two villages were noted for peace and order.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在兩個村莊的交界處有兩塊石頭，據說曾是兩名青年，他們在此地爭吵、打鬥，互相殺死，屍體隨即化為石頭。若這兩個村莊中的任何一個發生爭執，從不曾演變成全面的騷亂：「去石頭那裡解決」是慣例的命令；於是，凡在任何涉及誠信或榮譽之事上想要有所表現的人，都前往石頭那裡一決勝負。若決鬥者中有一方被擊倒，那便是最終的了結；其他人概不干涉，因此，藉由在這類事情上的共同默契，這兩個村莊以和平與秩序著稱。

title.en: Salevao Becomes the Moon to Save Nonu
title.zh: 薩萊瓦奧化月救諾努

region.en: Court of the King of Tonga (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 湯加王庭（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1884 (Turner)

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (London 1884)

summary.en: Visiting the king of Tonga, the worshipper Nonu disputes with him over the age of the moon and stakes his life on his belief that the moon is visible in the morning. Salevao, his god, appears in the night: 'Nonu, you are wrong; the moon is not now seen in the morning. But, lest you should be killed, I will go and be the moon in the horizon to-morrow morning, and make the king believe you were right after all.' In the morning Salevao, as the moon, was seen, and Nonu was saved - adding alike to reverence for the god and to the treasury of the priest.
summary.zh: 諾努訪湯加王，因月亮晨間是否可見一事與王爭執，竟以性命作注。守護神薩萊瓦奧夜間顯現：『諾努，你錯了；晨間本無月。但為免你被殺，明日清晨我將化身為月掛在地平線，使王信你原是對的。』翌晨薩萊瓦奧果然以月形現身，諾努得救——神之靈驗與祭司之庫房因此兩皆增光。

sensitivity.note: Deity-loyalty tale.

passages.text: Salevao was a war god in a number of villages, and incarnate in a dog - a white one usually: when he wagged his tail, barked, and dashed ahead in sight of the troops of the enemy it was a good sign, but to retreat or howl was a bad omen. A story of his kindness to Nonu, one of his worshippers, relates that when Nonu was on a visit to the King of Tonga he and the king had a dispute about the age of the moon: Nonu maintained that it was then to be seen in the morning; the king held that it was not visible in the morning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: Salevao是許多村莊的戰神，並化身為一隻狗——通常是白色的：當牠搖尾巴、吠叫，並在敵軍眼前疾衝向前時，那是吉兆；但若退卻或嚎叫，則是凶兆。有一則關於他善待其信奉者之一Nonu的故事，講述當Nonu拜訪東加國王時，他與國王就月亮的年齡發生爭執：Nonu堅稱當時月亮在早晨可見；國王則認為早晨看不見月亮。

passages.text: Nonu said he would stake his life on it; and so it was left for the morning to decide. In the night Salevao appeared to Nonu and said to him: 'Nonu, you are wrong; the moon is not now seen in the morning. But, lest you should be killed, I will go and be the moon in the horizon to-morrow morning, and make the king believe you were right after all, and so save your life.' In the morning Salevao, as the moon, was seen, and Nonu was saved - such stories added alike to reverence for the god and to the treasury of the priest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: Nonu說他願以此賭上性命；於是便留待早晨來裁決。夜裡，Salevao向Nonu顯現，對他說：「Nonu，你錯了；月亮如今在早晨是看不見的。但為了不讓你被殺，我將前去，在明晨成為地平線上的月亮，使國王相信你終究是對的，從而救你一命。」到了早晨，Salevao化為月亮被看見了，Nonu因而得救——這類故事既增添了對神明的敬畏，也充實了祭司的財庫。

title.en: Le Sa Sends the Caterpillars to Forage
title.zh: 萊薩遣毛蟲代罰

region.en: Plantations of Upolu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 烏波盧墾地（象徵性定位）

period: Samoan oral tradition; recorded 1884 (Turner)

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (London 1884)

summary.en: In some places Le Sa was incarnate in an owl, more of an agricultural god who sent rain and abundance of food and was worshipped about April. He was prayed to and propitiated with offerings for the removal of caterpillars from the plantations, as they were thought to be servants under his orders to forage and punish; he was supposed to be fond of the bodies of thieves, and to go at once and devour them if prayed to do so. Bad-tempered parents frightened the children by saying they would call Le Sa to drink them up.
summary.zh: 萊薩或化身為鴞，主司農事賜雨豐穫，四月受祀；毛蟲侵田被視為神所遣之僕，藉以覓食懲罰，故須以祭品求其撤回。神尤喜食竊賊之身，一經祈求即往吞之；暴怒的父母以『叫萊薩來喝掉你』嚇唬孩童。

sensitivity.note: Agricultural deity record.

passages.text: In some places Le Sa was incarnate in an owl, was more of an agricultural god, who sent rain and abundance of food, and was worshipped about the month of April. He was prayed to and propitiated with offerings for the removal of caterpillars from the plantations, as they were thought to be servants under his orders to forage and punish. He was supposed to be fond of the bodies of thieves, and to go at once and devour them if prayed to do so; bad-tempered parents frightened the children by saying that they would call Le Sa to drink them up. In cases of sickness the patient went and weeded some piece of bush land as an offering to Le Sa; and the consequence was often a wonderful cure to the indolent dyspeptic!
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在某些地方，Le Sa化身為一隻貓頭鷹，更偏向是一位農業之神，掌管降雨與食物的豐足，約在四月前後受到崇拜。人們向祂祈禱，並以祭品討好祂，以求清除園圃中的毛蟲，因為人們認為這些毛蟲是奉祂之命前來覓食與懲罰的僕從。據信祂喜愛竊賊的屍體，若有人祈求，祂便會立刻前去吞食；脾氣暴躁的父母會嚇唬孩子，說要召喚Le Sa來把他們喝掉。遇有疾病時，病人會前去為某片灌木地除草，作為獻給Le Sa的祭品；其結果往往是對懶惰的消化不良者產生奇妙的療效！

passages.text: Le Sa in one place was a household god, and incarnate in the centipede: if any one was bitten by the reptile or otherwise ailing, an offering of a fine mat and a fan was presented, and the god entreated in some such words as: 'Lord! if you are angry, tell us the reason and send recovery.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 4 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某地的勒薩（Le Sa）是一位家神，並化身於蜈蚣之中：若有人被這爬蟲咬傷，或另有疾患，便獻上一張精美的蓆子和一把扇子，並以諸如此類的話向神祈求：『主啊！您若發怒，請告訴我們緣由，並賜下康復。』

title.en: A God Without a Name: Viracocha, Pachacamac, Vsapu
title.zh: 無名之神:維拉科查、帕查卡馬克與烏薩普

region.en: Peru (symbolic pin: Cuzco)
region.zh: 秘魯(象徵性標記:庫斯科)(象徵性標記)

period: Written by José de Acosta, publ. Hakluyt Society trans. 1880

source.work: José de Acosta, The Natural and Moral History of the Indies, vol. 2 (Books 5-7), ed. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1880

summary.en: They commonly acknowledge a supreme Lord and Author of all things, which they of Peru called Viracocha, and gave him names of great excellence, as Pachacamac, or Pachayachachic, which is the Creator of heaven and earth, and Vsapu, which is admirable. Him they did worship as the chiefest of all, whom they did honour in beholding the heaven. It hath caused great admiration in me, Acosta writes, that although they had this knowledge, yet had they no proper name for God: if we shall seek into the Indian tongue for a word to answer to this name of God, as in Latin Deus, in Greek Theos, in Hebrew Ii, in Arabike Alla, we shall not find any in the Cuscan tongues; such as preach use our Spanish name Dios. Yet in truth they had some little knowledge, and therefore in Peru they made him a rich temple, which they called Pachacamac, which was the principal sanctuary of the realm; and as this word is as much as to say the Creator, yet in this temple they used their idolatries, worshipping the devil and figures. They likewise made sacrifices and offerings to Viracocha, which held the chief place amongst the worships which the Kings Yncas made. Hereof they called the Spaniards Viracochas, for that they hold opinion they are the sons of heaven, and divine.
summary.zh: 秘魯土人素來承認有一位至尊之主、萬有之源,稱之為「維拉科查」,並以種種美名尊之:「帕查卡馬克」或「帕查亞查奇」——天地之造主;「烏薩普」——無比神奇者。他們奉他為至高,仰觀上天而致敬。阿科斯塔嘆道:奇哉,他們雖有此認知,卻無「神」的專名——在拉丁語中神名Dous,希臘語Theos,希伯來語Ii,阿拉伯語Alla;但在庫斯科語中竟找不到相當之詞!傳教士只能以西班牙語Dios稱之。然他們確有些微認知,故在秘魯為他建了一座富麗的神廟,名「帕查卡馬克」,為全國之首聖;只是廟中行的是偶像崇拜,拜的是魔鬼與雕像。他們也向維拉科查獻祭供奉,列印加諸王崇拜之首。西班牙人被稱為「維拉科查」,正因土人相信他們是「天之子、屬神之人」。

sensitivity.note: Acosta's argument from Acts 17 ('to the unknown God') is the classic missionary reading of Andean supreme-being religion; marked religious as a doctrinal record.

passages.text: They commonly acknowledge a supreme Lord and Author of all things, which they of Peru called Viracocha, and gave him names of great excellence, as Pachacamac, or Pachayachachic, which is the Creator of heaven and earth: and Vsapu, which is admirable. Him they did worship, as the chiefest of all, whom they did honour in beholding the heaven.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Acosta, Natural and Moral History, book 5 ch. 3 (Hakluyt Society 1880); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們普遍承認有一位至高無上的主、萬物的創造者，秘魯人稱之為維拉科查（Viracocha），並給他取了極為尊貴的名號，如帕查卡馬克（Pachacamac），或帕查亞查奇克（Pachayachachic），意即天地的創造者；又如烏薩普（Vsapu），意即可敬可佩者。他們崇拜他，視他為萬有之首，並藉由仰望蒼天來尊崇他。

passages.text: It hath caused great admiration in me, that although they had this knowledge, yet had they no proper name for God. If we shall seek into the Indian tongue for a word to answer to this name of God... we shall not find any in the Cuscan tongues. So as such as preach or write to the Indians use our Spanish name Dios... yet in truth they had some little knowledge, and therefore in Peru they made him a rich temple, which they called Pachacamac, which was the principal Sanctuary of the realm. And as it hath been said, this word of Pachacamac is, as much to say, as the Creator, yet in this temple they used their idolatries, worshipping the devil and figures.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Acosta, Natural and Moral History, book 5 ch. 3 (Hakluyt Society 1880); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 令我大為驚異的是，他們雖有這樣的認識，卻沒有為神取一個專有的名字。倘若我們要在印第安語中尋找一個對應於「神」這個名稱的詞……我們在庫斯科的語言中找不到任何一個。因此，向印第安人講道或著述的人，便使用我們西班牙語的「Dios」一名……然而他們實際上確有一點微薄的認識，所以在秘魯他們為他建了一座富麗的廟宇，稱之為帕查卡馬克，那是全國最主要的聖所。正如所說，帕查卡馬克這個詞，意思就等於「創造者」，然而在這座廟宇中，他們仍行其偶像崇拜，敬拜魔鬼與偶像。

passages.text: They likewise made sacrifices and offerings to Viracocha, which held the chief place amongst the worships which the Kings Yncas made. Hereof they called the Spaniards Viracochas, for that they hold opinion they are the sons of heaven, and divine.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Acosta, Natural and Moral History, book 5 ch. 3 (Hakluyt Society 1880); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們同樣向維拉科查獻祭與供物，這在印加諸王所行的崇拜中居於首位。因此之故，他們稱西班牙人為維拉科查，因為他們認為這些人是天之驕子，是神聖的。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, The Natural and Moral History of the Indies (Hakluyt Society, 1880)

title.en: Thunder as a Man with Sling and Mace: Chuquilla, Catuilla, Intiillapa
title.zh: 雷為持彈弓與權杖之人:楚基利亞、卡圖利亞、因蒂利亞帕

region.en: Cuzco and all Peru (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科與全秘魯(象徵性標記)

period: Written by José de Acosta, publ. Hakluyt Society trans. 1880

source.work: José de Acosta, The Natural and Moral History of the Indies, vol. 2 (Books 5-7), ed. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1880

summary.en: Next to Viracocha, or their supreme God, that which most commonly they have and do adore amongst the Infidels is the Sunne; and after, those things which are most remarkable in the celestial or elemental nature, as the moon, stars, sea and land. The Huacas, or Oratories, which the Yncas Lords of Peru had in greatest reverence next to Viracocha and the sun, was the thunder, which they called by three divers names, Chuquilla, Catuilla, and Intiillapa, supposing it to be a man in heaven, with a sling and a mace, and that it is in his power to cause raine, haile, thunder, and all the rest that appertains to the region of the aire, where the clouds engender. It was a Huaca generall to all the Indians of Peru, offering unto him many sacrifices; and in Cuzco, which is the Court and Metropolitan city, they did sacrifice children unto him, as to the Sunne. They did worship these three, Viracocha, the Sunne, and Thunder, after another manner than all the rest, as Polo writes: they did put, as it were, a gauntlet or glove upon their hands when they did lift them up to worship them. They did worship the earth, which they called Pachamama, as the Ancients did the goddess Tellus; and the sea likewise, which they call Mamacocha. Moreover they did worship the raine-bow, which were the arms and blazons of the Ynca, with two snakes stretched out on either side.
summary.zh: 繼維拉科查——他們的至尊之神——之後,秘魯土人最常拜的是太陽;其後則為天象與元素中最顯著者:月、星辰、海、大地。印加諸王崇敬次於維拉科查與太陽的瓦卡(聖所),便是雷霆——以三個名字稱之:楚基利亞、卡圖利亞、因蒂利亞帕。他們想象雷是一位身居天上的男子,手持彈弓與權杖;雨、雹、雷鳴,以及雲氣滋生的天空諸象,皆操於其手。此瓦卡為全秘魯印第安人所共奉,祭祀甚多;在都城庫斯科,人們像獻給太陽一樣,向他獻祭孩童。據波羅所述,他們拜維拉科查、太陽與雷時,別有一種禮節:舉手崇拜之際,手上要戴上如手套之物。他們拜大地「帕查瑪瑪」,如古人拜忒路斯;拜海洋「瑪瑪科查」。他們還拜彩虹——印加王的軍徽,兩側各伸出一條蛇。

sensitivity.note: Acosta's taxonomy of Peruvian cult (Polo's data); the gauntlet-worship detail is unique to this source.

passages.text: The Huacas, or Oratories, which the Yncas Lords of Peru had in greatest reverence next to Viracocha and the sunne, was the thunder, which they called by three divers names, Chuquilla, Catuilla, and Intiillapa, supposing it to be a man in heaven, with a sling and a mace, and that it is in his power to cause raine, haile, thunder, and all the rest that appertains to the region of the aire, where the cloudes engender. It was a Huaca generall to all the Indians of Peru, offering unto him many sacrifices; and in Cuzco... they did sacrifice children unto him, as to the Sunne.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Acosta, Natural and Moral History, book 5 ch. 4 (Hakluyt Society 1880); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 秘魯的印加諸王所最崇敬的華卡（Huacas，即神諭之所），僅次於維拉科查與太陽的，便是雷電，他們以三個不同的名字稱之：丘基利亞（Chuquilla）、卡圖伊利亞（Catuilla）與因蒂利亞帕（Intiillapa），認為它是天上的一個人，手持投石索與權杖，能隨意降下雨水、冰雹、雷電，以及一切與雲氣生成之空氣界域相關的事物。它是全體秘魯印第安人共有的華卡，人們向它獻上許多祭品；在庫斯科……他們如同對太陽一般，向它獻祭孩童。

passages.text: They did worship these three, Viracocha, the Sunne, and Thunder, after another manner than all the rest, as Polo writes, who had made triall thereof, they did put as it were a gauntlet or glove upon their hands when they did lift them up to worshippe them. They did worship the earth, which they called Pachamama, as the Ancients did the goddess Tellus; and the sea likewise, which they call Mamacocha. Moreover, they did worship the raine-bow, which were the armes and blazons of the Ynca, with two snakes stretched out on either side.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Acosta, Natural and Moral History, book 5 ch. 4 (Hakluyt Society 1880); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們崇拜這三位——維拉科查、太陽與雷電——的方式與其餘諸神不同，據波羅（Polo）所記，他曾親身驗證，當他們舉手崇拜這三位時，彷彿在手上戴了一隻手套或護手。他們崇拜大地，稱之為帕查瑪瑪（Pachamama），如同古人崇拜大地女神忒勒斯（Tellus）；也崇拜海洋，稱之為瑪瑪科查（Mamacocha）。此外，他們還崇拜彩虹，那是印加的紋章與標誌，兩側各伸展出一條蛇。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, The Natural and Moral History of the Indies (Hakluyt Society, 1880)

title.en: The Shepherd's Star and the Jaguar in Heaven: Astral Patrons of Beasts
title.zh: 牧人星與天上的美洲豹:畜群星辰守護者

region.en: Shepherd country of the Collao (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科利亞奧牧區(象徵性標記)

period: Written by José de Acosta, publ. Hakluyt Society trans. 1880

source.work: José de Acosta, The Natural and Moral History of the Indies, vol. 2 (Books 5-7), ed. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1880

summary.en: Amongst the stars they all did commonly worship that which they called Colca, and we here the little goats (the Pleiades). They did attribute divers offices to divers stars, and those which had need of their favour did worship them: as the shepherd did sacrifice to a star which they called vrcuchillay, which they hold to be a sheep of divers colours, having the care to preserve their cattle. It is understood to be that which the Astronomers call Lyra. These shepherds worship two other stars which walk near unto them: they call them Catuchillay and vrcuchillay, and they fain them to be an ewe and a lambe. Others worshipped a star which they called Machachuay, to which they attribute the charge and power over serpents and snakes, to keep them from hurting of them. They ascribe power to another star which they called Chuquinchincay (which is as much as jaguar), over tigers, bears, and lions; and they have generally believed that of all the beasts of the earth there is one alone in heaven like unto them, the which hath care of their procreation and increase. And so they did observe and worship divers stars, as those which they called Chacana, Topatorca, Alcimana, Mirco, Miquiquiray, and many others.
summary.zh: 星辰之中,人人共拜的便是他們稱為「科爾卡」的那顆——即我們所說的小山羊(昴星團)。他們把不同的職司派給不同的星:凡有求於某星者便拜某星。牧人向名為「烏爾庫奇利亞」的星獻祭——相傳那是一頭斑斕彩色的羊,專司保佑畜群;天文學家說那便是天琴座。牧人還拜在它近旁行走的兩顆星:卡圖奇利亞與烏爾庫奇利亞,把它們想象為一只母羊與一只羊羔。另有人拜名為「馬查丘艾」的星,派它掌管蛇蟲,不許它們傷人。還有一星名為「楚基欽卡伊」(意即美洲豹),掌虎、熊、獅之力;他們普遍相信:世上所有走獸,天上各有一位同類照管其繁衍增殖。此外他們還觀測、崇拜「查卡納」「托帕托爾卡」「阿爾西馬納」「米爾科」「米基基拉伊」等許多星辰。

sensitivity.note: The astral-patron system: Acosta's list of dark-cloud constellations is the earliest attestation; jaguar-star tagged with world-serpent for the beast-in-heaven topos.

passages.text: Amongst the starres they all did commonly worship that which they called Colca, and we here the little goates [the Pleiades]... as the shepheard did sacrifice to a star which they called vrcuchillay, which they holde to be a sheepe of divers colours, having the care to preserve their cattell. It is understood to be that which the Astronomers call Lyra. These shepheards worshippe two other starres, which walke neere vnto them, they call them Catuchillay and vrcuchillay; and they faine them to be an ewe and a lambe.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Acosta, Natural and Moral History, book 5 ch. 4 (Hakluyt Society 1880); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在眾星之中，他們普遍崇拜一顆他們稱為「科爾卡」（Colca）的星，我們此地則稱之為小山羊〔昴星團〕……牧人向一顆他們稱為「烏爾庫奇利亞伊」（vrcuchillay）的星獻祭，他們認為那是一頭雜色的綿羊，負有守護其牲畜之責。據了解，那便是天文學家所稱的天琴座。這些牧人還崇拜另外兩顆在近旁運行的星，他們稱之為「卡圖奇利亞伊」（Catuchillay）與「烏爾庫奇利亞伊」（vrcuchillay）；他們想像那是一頭母羊與一頭羔羊。

passages.text: Others worshipped a starre which they called Machachuay, to which they attribute the charge and power over serpents and snakes, to keepe them from hurting of them. They ascribe power to another starre, which they called Chuquinchincay (which is as much as jaguar), over tigros, beares, and lyons, and they have generally beleeved, that of all the beasts of the earth, there is one alone in heaven like unto them, the which hath care of their procreation and increase. And so they did observe and worship divers starres, as those which they called Chacana, Topatorca, Alcimana, Mirco, Miquiquiray, and many others.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Acosta, Natural and Moral History, book 5 ch. 4 (Hakluyt Society 1880); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 另有人崇拜一顆他們稱為「馬查丘艾」（Machachuay）的星，他們將掌管蛇類之責與權柄歸於它，使其不致傷害他們。他們又將權柄歸於另一顆星，稱之為「丘金欽凱」（Chuquinchincay，意即美洲豹），掌管虎、熊與獅；他們普遍相信，地上所有野獸之中，天上皆各有一與之相應者，負責其繁衍與增殖。於是他們觀察並崇拜諸多星辰，如他們稱為「查卡納」（Chacana）、「托帕托爾卡」（Topatorca）、「阿爾西馬納」（Alcimana）、「米爾科」（Mirco）、「米基基拉伊」（Miquiquiray）者，以及其他許多星辰。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, The Natural and Moral History of the Indies (Hakluyt Society, 1880)

title.en: Acllahuasi, the House of the Chosen: Virgins for Gods, Sacrifices and the Inca
title.zh: 阿克利亞瓦西「選者之屋」:侍神、獻祭與王之側室

region.en: Monasteries of virgins, one in every province of Peru (symbolic pin: Cuzco)
region.zh: 秘魯各省貞女院(象徵性標記:庫斯科)

period: Written by José de Acosta, publ. Hakluyt Society trans. 1880

source.work: José de Acosta, The Natural and Moral History of the Indies, vol. 2 (Books 5-7), ed. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1880

summary.en: There were in Peru many monasteries of Virgins (for there are no other admitted), at the least one in every Province. In these monasteries there were two sorts of women: one ancient, which they called Mamaconas, for the instruction of the young; and the other of young maidens, placed there for a certain time, and after they were drawn forth, either for their gods or for the Ynca. They called this house or monastery Acllahuasi, which is to say, the house of the chosen. Every monastery had his Vicar or Governour called Appopanaca, who had liberty and power to choose whom he pleased, of what quality soever, being under eight years of age, if they seemed to be of a good stature and constitution. These Virgins thus shut up were instructed by the Mamaconas in diverse things needeful for the life of man, and in the customs and ceremonies of their gods; and afterwards they took them from thence, being above fourteen, sending them to the Court, whereof some were appointed to serve the Guacas and Sanctuaries, keeping their virginities for ever; some others were for the ordinary sacrifices that were made of maidens, and other extraordinary sacrifices, they made for the health, death, or wars of the Ynca; and the rest served for wives and concubines to the Ynca, and unto other his kinsfolkes and captaines, unto whom he gave them, which was a great and honourable recompence: this distribution was used every year. Those monasteries possessed rents and revenues for the maintenance of these Virgins. It was not lawful for any father to refuse his daughters when the Appopanaca required them for the service of these monasteries; yea, many fathers did willingly offer their daughters, supposing it was a great merit to be sacrificed for the Ynca. If any of these Mamaconas or Acllas were found to have trespassed against their honour, it was an inevitable chastisement to bury them alive, or to put them to death by some other kind of cruel torment.
summary.zh: 秘魯各地——至少每省一所——廣設貞女院(院中只收女子)。院內女眾分兩類:一類是年長者,稱「瑪瑪庫納」,司教導幼女之職;一類是少女,入院有定期,期滿之後或獻於諸神,或獻於印加王。此院名「阿克利亞瓦西」,意即「選者之屋」。每院設院長一名,稱「阿波帕納卡」,有權自行選取八歲以下、體格健美的女子入院。入院後由瑪瑪庫納教以人生所需諸藝,並學習諸神的習俗禮儀;十四歲以上便被送往王庭:其中一部分奉派侍奉瓦卡與聖所,終身守貞;一部分備作尋常與非常之處女獻祭——為印加王的健康、喪亡或征戰而設;其餘則為印加王及其親族、將領的妻妾,由王分賜之——這是一種崇高榮寵的報償。此種分配,年年舉行。貞女院的開支由專項收入維持。阿波帕納卡索人之時,為父者不得拒絕其女入院;許多父親竟欣然獻女,以為「為印加王獻身乃大功德」。瑪瑪庫納或阿克利亞若犯失貞之罪,懲罰絕無可免:活埋,或以其他酷刑處死。

sensitivity.note: The Aclla institution in Acosta's terse administrative account; flagged as a system involving child selection and capital punishment - recorded as archival evidence.

passages.text: In these monasteries there were two sortes of women, one antient, which they called Mamaconias, for the instruction of the yong; and the other was of yong maidens, placed there for a certaino time, and after they were drawn forth, either for their gods or for the Ynca. They called this house or monastery Acllahuasi, which is to say, the house of the chosen. Every monastery had his Vicar or Governour called Appopanaca, who had liberty and power to choose whom he pleased, of what qualitie soever, being under eight years of age, if they seemed to be of a good stature and constitution.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Acosta, Natural and Moral History, book 5 ch. 15 (Hakluyt Society 1880); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在這些修道院中有兩類女子：一類年長，他們稱為「瑪瑪科尼亞」（Mamaconias），負責教導年幼者；另一類是年輕少女，安置於此一段時日，之後便被引出，或獻給其神明，或獻給印加（Ynca）。他們稱這座房屋或修道院為「阿克拉瓦西」（Acllahuasi），意即「被選者之屋」。每座修道院皆有其代理人或管理者，稱為「阿波帕納卡」（Appopanaca），他有自由與權力挑選任何合其心意者，無論其出身如何，只要未滿八歲，若其身材與體質看似良好即可。

passages.text: Afterwards they tooke them from thence, being above fourteen, sending them to the Court, whereof some were appointed to serve the Guacas and Sanctuaries, keeping their virginities for ever: some others were for the ordinary sacrifices that were made of maidens, and other extraordinary sacrifices, they made for the health, death, or warres of the Ynca: and the rest served for wives and concubines to the Ynca, and unto other his kinsfolkes and captaines, unto whom he gave them, which was a great and honourable recompence: This distribution was used every year.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Acosta, Natural and Moral History, book 5 ch. 15 (Hakluyt Society 1880); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 之後，待她們年滿十四歲以上，便將她們從那裡帶走，送往宮廷；其中有些被指派去服事「瓜卡斯」（Guacas）與聖所，終身守其童貞；另一些則用於以少女獻祭的常規祭祀，以及為印加的健康、死亡或戰爭而行的其他特別祭祀；其餘的則充作印加及其親族與將領們的妻子與妾室，印加將她們賜予這些人，這是一份重大而榮耀的獎賞。此種分配每年舉行一次。

passages.text: It was not lawfull for any father to refuse his daughters when the Appopanaca required them for the service of these monasteries. Yea, many fathers did willingly offer their daughters, supposing it was a great merit to be sacrificed for the Ynca. If any of these Mamaconas or Acllas were found to have trespassed against their honour, it was an inevitable chastisement to bury them alive, or to put them to death by some other kind of cruel torment.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Acosta, Natural and Moral History, book 5 ch. 15 (Hakluyt Society 1880); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當「阿波帕納卡」為這些修道院之服役而索求女兒時，任何父親皆不得拒絕。不僅如此，許多父親還心甘情願地獻出女兒，認為為印加而犧牲乃是一大功德。若這些「瑪瑪科納斯」（Mamaconas）或「阿克拉」（Acllas）中有人被發現有損其名節，則必受不可避免的懲罰：將其活埋，或以其他某種殘酷的刑罰處死。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, The Natural and Moral History of the Indies (Hakluyt Society, 1880)

title.en: Sudaba's Lust and Siyawush's Refusal
title.zh: 蘇達貝之慾與西亞瓦什之拒

region.en: Women's bower of Kaus (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 卡烏斯後宮（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Siyawush secs. 6-7

summary.en: Sudaba, the Shah's wife, beholds the peerless prince and grows distraught; her secret envoy is rebuffed — I am no chamberer, or given to romances and intrigues — so she beguiles Kaus into sending the youth to the women's bower to visit his sisters. She descends her golden throne, embraces him long and kisses his eyes, and Siyawush, knowing well what that love meant and that such fondness was not in the way of God, goes quickly to his sisters instead. When the Shah asks her judgment of Siyawush, her malice takes another turn.
summary.zh: 王后蘇達貝一見無雙王子便神魂顛倒；密使遭拒——「我非狎邪之徒」——她遂哄騙卡烏斯讓王子入後宮探望姐妹。她自金座降下，久久擁抱、吻其眉眼；西亞瓦什深知此情有悖神道，徑往姐妹處。當王問她對西亞瓦什的評價時，她的惡意另闢蹊徑。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the Potiphar's-wife motif. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Time passed, the Shah still joyed in Siyawush, till as they sat one day Sudaba entered, beheld the prince's face, and grew distraught. Her heart throbbed; she is wasted to a thread, thou wouldst have said, or ice before the fire. She bade one go by stealth to him and say: 'twould cause no wonder if thou shouldest visit the royal bower anon. The envoy went, but noble Siyawush was wroth and said: entice me not. I am no chamberer, or given to romances and intrigues.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Siyawush sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 時光流逝，沙阿仍以西亚瓦什（Siyawush）為樂，直到某日他們同坐時，蘇達巴（Sudaba）走了進來，凝視王子的面容，便心神恍惚。她的心怦怦跳動；你會說她已消瘦如線，或如火前的冰。她命人暗中前去對他說：你若不久後造訪王家的內室，也不足為奇。使者去了，但高貴的西亚瓦什卻發怒道：不要引誘我。我並非後宮之人，也不沉溺於風流韻事與私情。

passages.text: Another day at dawn Sudaba sought the Shah and said: the sun and moon have never seen thy peer or any like thy son. Send him to thy bower to see his sisters and thy favourites, whose hearts are full, whose cheeks are wet with yearning. The Shah replied: thou sayest right; thou hast a hundred mothers' love for him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Siyawush sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 又一日黎明，蘇達巴尋見沙赫，說道：日月從未見過與你匹敵之人，也未見過像你兒子這般的人。打發他到你的內宮去，見見他的姊妹與你的寵姬吧，她們的心滿懷思念，面頰為渴慕而濕潤。沙赫答道：你說得對；你對他懷有百位母親般的愛。

passages.text: The prince suspected that his father sought to prove him, for Kai Kaus was knowing and smooth-tongued, wise, shrewd of heart, and ready to distrust. But in the women's quarters of the Shah what shall I learn? Yet if so the Shah commandeth my custom henceforth is to visit them. When Hirbad held up the veil that hung before the door the mind of Siyawush foreboded ill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Siyawush secs. 6-7 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 王子疑心父親有意試探他，因為凱考斯見識廣博、言辭圓滑、明智、心思機敏，且易於生疑。但我在沙赫的后妃內院之中又能探知什麼呢？然而倘若沙赫如此吩咐，我往後便照例去探望她們。當希爾巴德掀起門前懸掛的帷幕時，西亞沃什心中已預感不祥。

passages.text: Now Siyawush on entering the bower beheld a brightly shining, golden throne where sat moon-faced Sudaba, like Paradise itself in hue and perfume. When Siyawush appeared within the veil Sudaba hastened to descend the throne, advanced with graceful gait, embraced him long, long kissed his eyes and face. Now Siyawush knew well what that love meant, and that such fondness was not in the way of God, and, since it was unseemly there, went quickly to his sisters, who enthroned him with many a blessing on a golden seat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Siyawush sec. 7 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 西亞沃什進入內宮，望見一座光輝燦爛的黃金寶座，座上坐著月貌的蘇達巴，其容色與芬芳宛如天園本身。西亞沃什出現在帷幕之內時，蘇達巴急忙走下寶座，以優雅的步態上前，久久擁抱他，久久親吻他的眼睛與面龐。西亞沃什深知那愛意意味著什麼，也知這般鍾情不合神道，且因於禮不合，便快步走向他的姊妹們，她們以連連祝福將他奉上黃金寶座。

title.en: Siyawush Passes Through the Fire
title.zh: 西亞瓦什過火之裁

region.en: Fire-ordeal plain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 過火平原（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Siyawush sec. 13

summary.en: To purge foul surmise, Kaus has a hundred caravans of camels gather firewood till two huge mountains rise on the plain, pours black naphtha over all, and has the heaps fired: the earth became more radiant than the sky. Siyawush comes forth in golden helmet and white raiment, sprinkles camphor over himself as bodies are prepared for burial, prays the Judge that hath no needs to grant him a passage through this mount of fire, and urges his black steed on like smoke. The flames close over his head; the noble hero reappears with rosy cheeks and smiles upon his lips — had flame been water he had not been wetted — and the people cry: God hath shown mercy to the innocent.
summary.zh: 為洗清誣告，卡烏斯令百隊駱駝運柴，壘成兩座柴山，澆以黑石腦油，點火焚天——大地比天空還亮。西亞瓦什金盔白衣、撒聖樟腦（如為身後事妝扮），祈求無所求的裁決者賜他穿越火山之路，縱黑駒如煙而入。烈焰吞沒其頂；英雄卻面頰緋紅、唇含笑意而現——火若為水，衣不沾濕——萬民歡呼：「神憐惜無辜者！」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the fire-ordeal is a Zoroastrian juridical motif. No living community restriction.

passages.text: He gave instructions to his minister to have a hundred caravans of camels brought from the plain. These went to gather firewood, while all the people of Iran looked on, till two huge mountains rose that might be seen two leagues away. They piled two mounts of firewood on the plain while all the folk looked on; a path was left such that a horseman armed might hardly pass between the piles. This done, the glorious Shah bade pour black naphtha over all the wood, and ten score men came to light and blow the fire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Siyawush sec. 13 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他吩咐大臣從平原調來百隊駱駝商隊。這些人去收集柴薪，全伊朗的百姓都觀看著，直到兩座巨大的山丘聳起，兩里格外都能望見。他們在平原上堆起兩座柴山，眾人皆在旁觀看；中間留出一條通道，僅容一名披甲騎手勉強通過兩堆之間。此事既畢，榮耀的沙赫命人將黑石腦油澆遍所有柴薪，二百人前來點火吹燃。

passages.text: When first they blew there was a mass of smoke, but presently the tongues of fire rose fast; the earth became more radiant than the sky, the people shouted and the flames ascended. All that were on the plain were scorched and wept to see the cheery face of Siyawush, who came before his sire with golden helmet and raiment all of white. His mien was tranquil, his face all smiles, his heart all hopefulness; his black steed's hoofs sent dust up to the moon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Siyawush sec. 13 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們初吹之時，濃煙滾滾，但不久火舌便迅速升騰；大地比天空更為輝耀，眾人呼喊，火焰高漲。平原上的人無不被灼烤，望見西亞沃什那爽朗的面容便為之哭泣，他頭戴金盔、身著全白衣袍，來到父親面前。他神態安詳，滿面笑容，心中滿懷希望；他那黑色駿馬的蹄子揚起塵土，直上明月。

passages.text: The prince then sprinkled camphor o'er himself, so bodies are prepared for burial, and lighting from his charger did obeisance. Be not discomfited, said Siyawush, that fortune taketh such a turn as this. I am dishonoured: such a state is ruin. If I am innocent I shall escape, while if in fault the Maker will not heed me; but by the power of God who giveth good I shall not feel the heat. As he drew near the flames he prayed the Judge that hath no needs: grant me a passage through this mount of fire, and free me from my sire's misprision.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Siyawush sec. 13 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 王子隨即將樟腦撒於己身，一如為安葬而備的遺體，並從坐騎上下來行禮。西亞沃什說道：不必因命運如此轉折而沮喪。我蒙受羞辱：這般境地便是毀滅。我若清白，自當脫險；我若有過，造物主便不會垂顧我；但憑那賜福的上帝之力，我必不覺灼熱。當他走近火焰時，他向那無所需求的裁判者祈禱：賜我穿越這座火山的通路，解我脫離父親的猜疑。

passages.text: Then urged he his black steed on like smoke; a wail ascended from the city and the waste. From every side the flames closed o'er his head, and none could see his helmet or his horse, while all the plain wept tears of blood. The noble hero nathless reappeared with rosy cheeks and smiles upon his lips; a roar went up as men caught sight of him: the young Shah cometh from the fire! Had flame been water he had not been wetted, his garments would have holden none of it, for when all-holy God doth so vouchsafe the breath of fire is even as the wind; there was universal joy, and each to other gave the gladsome tidings: God hath shown mercy to the innocent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Siyawush sec. 13 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他催動烏黑的駿馬，如煙般疾馳而去；城中與荒野間響起一片哀號。烈焰從四面八方合攏，罩住他的頭頂，無人能看見他的頭盔或他的坐騎，整片平原都泣下血淚。然而那位高貴的英雄再度現身，雙頰紅潤，唇邊含笑；眾人一看見他，便爆出震天的歡呼：年輕的沙赫從火中出來了！縱然火焰化為水，也沾不濕他分毫，他的衣袍也留不住半點火氣，因為當至聖的上帝如此恩准，火焰的氣息便如同微風一般；普天同慶，人人互相傳報這喜訊：上帝已向無辜者施恩。

title.en: Siyawush Begs Sudaba's Life, and Is Repaid in Sorcery
title.zh: 西亞瓦什為蘇達貝求情卻遭暗算

region.en: Court of Kai Kaus (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 卡烏斯王庭（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Siyawush sec. 14

summary.en: Kaus, ox-head mace in hand, condemns Sudaba to the gibbet for treacherously seeking his son's life and exposing him to fire. The Iranians say the punishment for her is death, but Siyawush pleads: pardon for my sake Sudaba's fault; she may be warned and walk advisedly — for if she perish by his hand he will be sorry for it in the end. The Shah grants mercy, Sudaba returns to the palace, and, by secret sorceries, works on Kaus to ruin Siyawush according to the evil of her nature; the Shah becomes mistrustful through her talk but speaks not aught thereof to any one.
summary.zh: 卡烏斯手持牛首錘，判蘇達貝絞刑——她陰謀害子、縱火試煉。群臣皆言當死，西亞瓦什卻代為求情：「饒她一命吧，願她引以為戒。」（他心想：若她死於父親之手，父親終將悔恨，反倒怨我。）王允其所請；蘇達貝重返後宮，暗中以妖術蠱惑王心圖謀害西亞瓦什；王漸生疑忌，卻不對任何人言明。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Kaus the fourth day sat upon the throne of kings; an ox-head mace was in his hand. Fierce in his wrath he had Sudaba summoned before him, told her what had passed, and said: thou art a shameless woman! What part is this that thou hast played throughout in treacherously seeking my son's life, in causing him to be exposed to fire? No excuses will now avail thee; thou art not fit to live.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Siyawush sec. 14 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡烏斯於第四日登上王座；他手中握著一柄牛頭錘。他滿懷怒火，將蘇達巴召到面前，告訴她所發生的一切，說道：你是個不知羞恥的女人！你從頭到尾扮演的是什麼角色，竟以奸計謀害我兒子的性命，使他被置於烈火之前？如今任何藉口都救不了你；你不配活著。

passages.text: The great Shah asked the Iranians: for the evil that she hath done by stealth, what shall I do? All did obeisance and said: the punishment for her is death; she ought to suffer for her evil deeds. He bade the deathsman: hang her in the street upon the gibbet and be pitiless. At her abandonment the women wailed, and Shah Kaus was sorrowful of heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Siyawush sec. 14 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 偉大的沙赫問伊朗人：她暗中犯下這等惡行，我該如何處置？眾人皆行禮說道：對她的懲罰便是死；她理應為自己的惡行受罰。他吩咐劊子手：將她吊在街上的絞架，毫不留情。她被棄置之時，婦人們哀哭，沙赫卡烏斯心中悲傷。

passages.text: Let not thy heart be troubled, said Siyawush, but pardon for my sake Sudaba's fault; she may be warned and walk advisedly. For, he thought, if she perish by his hand he will be sorry for it in the end, and see in me the author of his grief. The Shah, who had been seeking some excuse for mercy, answered him: I grant thee this because I see that right was on thy side.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Siyawush sec. 14 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 西亞武什說道：莫讓你的心憂煩，但看在我的份上，饒恕蘇達巴的過錯吧；她或可受到告誡，今後行事謹慎。因為他心想，若她死於他手，他終究會為此懊悔，並視我為他悲傷的根源。沙赫本就在尋求寬恕的藉口，便回答他：我准你所請，因為我看出理在你這一方。

passages.text: When Siyawush had kissed his father's throne he brought back Sudaba and escorted her home to the palace by the Shah's command. Now in time the heart of Shah Kaus so warmed to her that he could not forbear to eye her face in love, while, for her part, by secret sorceries she worked on him to ruin Siyawush according to the evil of her nature. The Shah became mistrustful through her talk, but spake not aught thereof to any one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Siyawush sec. 14 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 西亞武什親吻了父親的王座之後，便領回蘇達巴，奉沙赫之命護送她回宮。後來，沙赫卡烏斯的心對她漸生眷愛，忍不住以愛慕的目光凝視她的面容；而她那一方，則以其邪惡的本性，暗中施以巫術蠱惑他，圖謀毀掉西亞武什。沙赫因她的言語而生疑，卻未向任何人透露分毫。

title.en: Aiai Regains the Pearl Hook Kahuoi
title.zh: 埃埃重奪珍珠神鉤卡胡奧伊

region.en: Niolopa, Nuuanu, Honolulu, Oahu
region.zh: 瓦胡島檀香山努瓦努尼奧洛帕

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; recorded 1916-1917 (Fornander Collection)

source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Aiai (Honolulu 1916-1917)

license: Public domain (Bishop Museum Memoirs vol. IV, 1916-1917)

summary.en: Kuula and Hina, great fisher folk of Nuolopa, own the pearl hook Kahuoi, guarded by the bird Kamanuwai at Kaumakapili: every aku outside Mamala jumps into Kuula's canoe of its own accord. King Kipapalaulu steals the hook; the bird starves with closed eyes - hence the name Kaumakapili, roosting-with-closed-eyes. Their infant Aiai is cast into the stream, floats to the rock Nahakaipuami, and is reared by the king's daughter Kauaelemimo, whom he marries. Through her he tricks her father into producing the stolen hook from the fishermen's calabash, borrows a ten-fathom canoe, and fills it with aku that leap in of their own accord.
summary.zh: 庫拉與希娜居努瓦努尼奧洛帕，家藏珍珠神鉤卡胡奧伊，由神鳥卡馬努瓦伊守於考馬卡皮利：馬瑪拉外的鰆魚見鉤即自躍入舟。國王基帕帕勞盧竊鉤；神鳥閉目絕食——『考馬卡皮利』（閉目棲息）由此得名。嬰兒埃埃被擲入溪流，漂至巖巖納豪凱普阿米，為王女考埃萊米莫收養成婚。他借妻之手使父王自漁具葫蘆中取出竊鉤，再借十尋雙舟出海——鰆魚紛紛自躍入艙，滿載而歸。

sensitivity.note: Fish-god Kuula cycle; place-name etymologies Kaumakapili and Nahakaipuami retained.

passages.text: Kuula was the father and Hina was the mother of Aiai; they lived in Niolopa, Nuuanu. Kuula and his wife were great fisher folks, and they had in their possession a pearl fish-hook of great value called Kahuoi. This pearl fish-hook was in the keeping of a bird called Kamanuwai, and it was kept at Kaumakapili; this pearl fish-hook was so enticing that every time Kuula went out for aku, outside of Mamala, upon seeing the hook they would jump into the canoes of their own accord - this fish was the food which this bird lived on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Aiai (1916-1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 庫烏拉是父親，希娜是艾艾的母親；他們住在努烏阿努的尼奧洛帕。庫烏拉與他的妻子都是了不起的漁人，他們擁有一只名為卡胡奧伊、價值非凡的珍珠魚鉤。這只珍珠魚鉤由一隻名叫卡馬努瓦伊的鳥保管，存放在考馬卡皮利；這只珍珠魚鉤如此誘人，以致庫烏拉每次到馬馬拉外海捕撈鰹魚時，那些魚一見到魚鉤便自動跳進他們的獨木舟——這種魚正是這隻鳥賴以維生的食物。

passages.text: While Kuula was out for aku one day outside of Mamala, Kipapalaulu the king of Honolulu also went out fishing; and when he came near the place where Kuula was fishing he saw the aku jumping into the canoes of Kuula of their own accord. Upon seeing this he made up his mind to steal this fish-hook Kahuoi, which in due time was carried out; this act not only deprived Kuula of his favorite hook, but the bird also hungered from loss of its food - through this seizure of the pearl hook by Kipapalaulu the bird went without any food; it would fly on its roosting place and go to sleep. It was because the bird Kamanuwai closed its eyes from hunger that the place where it lived was called Kaumakapili, and the place is so called to this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Aiai (1916-1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，庫烏拉在馬馬拉外海捕撈鰹魚時，檀香山的國王基帕帕勞盧也出海捕魚；當他靠近庫烏拉捕魚的地方時，他看見鰹魚自動跳進庫烏拉的獨木舟裡。見到此景，他下定決心要偷走這枚魚鉤卡胡奧伊，此事後來果然付諸實行；這一行徑不僅使庫烏拉失去了他最鍾愛的魚鉤，那隻鳥也因失去食物而挨餓——由於基帕帕勞盧奪走了這枚珍珠魚鉤，那隻鳥便斷了食；牠會飛到棲息之處入睡。正因為那隻鳥卡馬努瓦伊因飢餓而閉上眼睛，牠所棲居的地方才被稱為考馬卡皮利，此地至今仍沿用此名。

passages.text: Some time after this Hina conceived and in due time gave birth to a male child who was called Aiai; at the birth of the child the parents threw it into the stream just below Kaumakapili. The water carried the child to a rock called Nahakaipuami just below the Haaliliamanu bridge, where it is seen to this day, where it floated. Kipapalaulu was at this time living at Kapuukolo, where his palace was situated, with his daughter Kauaelemimo by name; one day at noon she went in bathing with her maids and discovered Aiai by a large rock. Kauaelemimo took the child as her own and brought it up. When Aiai grew into manhood he was very handsome, so Kauaelemimo took him to be her husband.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Aiai (1916-1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此後過了些時日，希娜懷了孕，屆時產下一名男嬰，取名為艾艾；孩子出生時，父母將他丟進考馬卡皮利正下方的溪流中。溪水將孩子帶到哈阿利利亞馬努橋正下方一塊名為納哈凱普阿米的大石旁，孩子便漂浮在那裡，至今仍可見於該處。此時基帕帕勞盧住在卡普烏科洛，他的宮殿就設在那裡，與他同住的是他的女兒，名叫考阿埃萊米莫；有一天正午，她與侍女們一同下水沐浴，在一塊大石旁發現了艾艾。考阿埃萊米莫將這孩子據為己有並撫養長大。當艾艾長大成人後，他非常英俊，於是考阿埃萊米莫便收他為夫。

passages.text: After a while she conceived a child and began to have a longing for some fish; so Aiai went out rod fishing along the coast, and after catching a few took the fish home and gave them to his wife. After the lapse of some twenty or thirty days Kauaelemimo had a longing for aku, so she told Aiai to go out aku fishing. Aiai upon hearing his wife's request asked her to go to her father Kipapalaulu and ask him for a pearl fish-hook; the wife consented and went to her father, who gave her one. When Aiai saw the fish-hook he said, 'This pearl fish-hook is worthless; the fish will not bite it; it will weary one's body for nothing.' The wife then asked him where she could get another, and Aiai replied: 'You go to your father and tell him there is a pearl fish-hook that will enrich the fishermen; it is in the fishermen's calabash of fishing utensils.' By this the husband wished to get possession of the pearl fish-hook Kahuoi which had been stolen from his father by Kipapalaulu. Upon coming to her father she asked for another pearl fish-hook; Kipapalaulu refused, saying, 'There is none left to give; that was the last pearl fish-hook I had which I gave you.' Kauaelemimo said, 'Aiai told me you had another one; it is in the fishermen's calabash of fishing utensils.' 'Yes, certainly there is one; I now remember it for the first time.' The calabash was then brought to the king, and when he looked in it he found the hook which he gave to his daughter; the wife then returned with it to her husband. Aiai took it and said, 'My days of poverty are now over since you have come back.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Aiai (1916-1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 過了一段時日，她懷了孩子，並開始渴望吃些魚；於是艾艾便沿岸持竿釣魚，釣到幾條後便帶回家交給妻子。大約過了二、三十天，考阿埃萊米莫渴望吃鰹魚，便叫艾艾出海捕鰹魚。艾艾聽到妻子的要求後，要她去見她的父親基帕帕勞盧，向他討一枚珍珠魚鉤；妻子答應了，便去見父親，父親給了她一枚。艾艾見到那魚鉤時說：「這枚珍珠魚鉤毫無用處；魚不會上鉤；只會白白使人疲累。」妻子便問他何處可再取得另一枚，艾艾回答：「妳去見妳父親，告訴他有一枚能使漁人致富的珍珠魚鉤；它就在漁人裝漁具的葫蘆裡。」丈夫這麼說，是想取得那枚被基帕帕勞盧從他父親手中偷走的珍珠魚鉤卡胡奧伊。她來到父親面前，又討要另一枚珍珠魚鉤；基帕帕勞盧拒絕了，說：「已經沒有可給的了；那是我最後一枚珍珠魚鉤，我已經給妳了。」考阿埃萊米莫說：「艾艾告訴我您還有一枚；它就在漁人裝漁具的葫蘆裡。」「是的，確實還有一枚；我現在才第一次想起來。」於是那葫蘆被帶到國王面前，他往裡一看，找到了那枚魚鉤，便交給女兒；妻子於是帶著它回到丈夫身邊。艾艾接過它說：「既然你回來了，我貧困的日子如今結束了。」

passages.text: Aiai then said to his wife: 'Go back again to your father and ask him for a canoe; not one of five or eight fathoms in length, but get one that is ten fathoms in length; that is the size of the canoe that I want from your father.' When Kauaelemimo arrived in the presence of her father she asked for the canoe described by her husband; when the canoe ten fathoms in length was brought the father asked the daughter, 'Who will be able to paddle this canoe?' 'My husband will.' When Aiai heard the answer made by his wife he took the canoe and set out with the bird Kamanuwai, taking the pearl fish-hook Kahuoi along. When he arrived off of Mamala he took out the hook and began fishing; the aku began to come and jump into the canoe of their own accord until it was loaded down deep. The bird then ate some of the fish and was again restored to its former self. When Aiai came home his double canoe was loaded down deep with aku; upon arriving in the presence of his wife he gave her all the fish, but the pearl fish-hook was taken by the bird Kamanuwai, its guardian. This is the legend of Aiai.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Aiai (1916-1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 艾艾接著對妻子說：「再回去見妳父親，向他討一艘獨木舟；不是五尋或八尋長的那種，而要一艘十尋長的；我要向妳父親討的正是這種大小的獨木舟。」當考阿埃萊米莫來到父親面前，便討要她丈夫所描述的那艘獨木舟；當那艘十尋長的獨木舟被帶來時，父親問女兒：「誰能划得動這艘獨木舟？」「我丈夫能。」艾艾聽到妻子的回答後，便帶著那隻鳥卡馬努瓦伊，並帶上珍珠魚鉤卡胡奧伊，乘上獨木舟出發。當他抵達馬馬拉外海時，他取出魚鉤開始釣魚；鰹魚開始自動游來跳進他的獨木舟，直到舟身深深下沉。那隻鳥於是吃了一些魚，又恢復了原來的模樣。當艾艾回家時，他的雙體獨木舟滿載著鰹魚，深深下沉；來到妻子面前時，他把所有的魚都給了她，但那枚珍珠魚鉤則由守護牠的鳥卡馬努瓦伊取走。這就是艾艾的傳說。

title.en: Pupualenalena, the Dog Who Stole Awa and the Spirits' Shell
title.zh: 竊卡瓦與奪神螺的義犬普普阿萊納萊納

region.en: Puako to Waipio, Hawaii Island
region.zh: 夏威夷島普阿科至懷皮奧

period: Hawaiian oral tradition (reign of Hakau); recorded 1916-1917 (Fornander Collection)

source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Pupualenalena (Honolulu 1916-1917)

license: Public domain (Bishop Museum Memoirs vol. IV, 1916-1917)

summary.en: Pupualenalena, a dog of Puako, eats every fish his fisherman-master catches; the man bargains - eat away, if you bring me awa. Night after night the dog raids Hakau's awa field below the Puaahuku cliff in Waipio until the field is nearly gone and the king sets guards. Condemned with his master, the dog hears the king's price of pardon: the great shell Kuana, blown every night by the spirits above Waipio. At midnight it leaps the sleeping guards, hooks its head through the shell's loop and flees - one side striking a rock and breaking off, waking the spirits in vain chase. Master and dog become Hakau's favourites on a grant of land.
summary.zh: 普阿科的義犬普普阿萊納萊納食盡主人每尾漁獲；主人許諾——任你吃魚，只要為我取卡瓦。夜夜奔襲懷皮奧普瓦阿胡庫崖下的哈考王卡瓦田，直到田幾被掏空、國王設防。犬與主同判死刑；犬聽得王的赦免之價——懷皮奧上方群靈夜夜吹響的神螺庫阿納。午夜它躍過沉睡的守衛，頭穿螺繩而逃——螺觸巖缺角一聲，群靈驚起窮追不及。主犬終為哈考座上賓，得封地而居。

sensitivity.note: Animal-helper legend tied to Hakau (Umi's half-brother) cycle.

passages.text: Pupualenalena was a dog that once lived in Puako, Hawaii, with its own master. After a while his master was kidnapped by Kanikaa, a spirit, so the dog went and lived with another master; it was the usual thing for the new master to go out fishing, so he took the dog with him, making it sit behind him in the canoe. Every time a fish was caught the dog would eat it up, and as the dog kept on doing this for some time the master said: 'Yes, I have no objections to your eating the fish, if you can only supply me with my favorite drink, the awa, then it would be all right for you to eat the fish.' While the master was saying this the dog Pupualenalena understood him; in the evening the dog disappeared - this absence was because it went to steal awa down in the valley of Waipio. At this time Hakau the king was living at Waipio; he owned a large field of awa just at the foot of the Puaahuku cliff. This was the field where Pupualenalena came and got awa; at daybreak he would reach home with his awa, when his master would take it, cut it up and prepare some and drink it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Pupualenalena (1916-1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 普普阿萊納萊納是一隻狗，曾與自己的主人住在夏威夷的普阿科。過了些時日，牠的主人被一個名叫卡尼卡阿的精靈擄走，於是這隻狗便去與另一位主人同住；新主人慣常出海捕魚，因此帶著這隻狗同行，讓牠坐在自己身後的獨木舟裡。每當捕到一條魚，這隻狗就會把魚吃光，由於這隻狗持續這樣做了一段時日，主人便說：「是的，我不反對你吃魚，只要你能供給我愛喝的飲料——卡瓦酒，那麼你吃魚就無妨。」當主人說這番話時，那隻狗普普阿萊納萊納聽懂了；到了傍晚，這隻狗便消失了——牠之所以不見，是因為牠下到懷皮奧谷中去偷卡瓦酒。此時國王哈考住在懷皮奧；他在普阿阿胡庫崖正下方擁有一大片卡瓦田。普普阿萊納萊納就是來到這片田裡取得卡瓦酒；破曉時牠便帶著卡瓦酒回到家，主人便接過它，切碎、調製一些來喝。

passages.text: The master after this had all the awa he wanted and the dog kept him supplied for many days; the dog, however, went to the place so often that after a while very little of the field was left, so Hakau began to be suspicious and therefore set guards over the field. While the guards were watching one night the dog came to the field and began pulling up the awa; when he had a sufficient amount for a load he took up the load and returned home. The guards then were sure that a dog was pulling the king's awa, so they followed it; the dog being much faster than the guards it got away, but one fellow who was a good runner kept up the chase until Pupualenalena was finally tracked to Puako.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Pupualenalena (1916-1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此後主人便有了他所想要的卡瓦酒，這隻狗也持續供應了他許多天；然而這隻狗去那地方的次數太頻繁，過了一段時日，田裡所剩無幾，於是哈考開始起疑，便派守衛看守那片田。某夜守衛看守時，這隻狗來到田裡開始拔卡瓦；當牠拔足了一擔的量，便扛起那擔回家。守衛於是確信是一隻狗在拔國王的卡瓦，便跟蹤牠；這隻狗比守衛快得多，得以逃脫，但有一個跑得很快的傢伙一路緊追不捨，直到普普阿萊納萊納最終被追蹤到普阿科。

passages.text: When the guard saw the dog's master he was covered with scales from the constant use of awa; the guard then approached him and asked, 'Say, is this your dog?' The master replied, 'Yes.' The guard then said, 'You two have sinned against the king, Hakau; your dog has been stealing the awa which belongs to the king.' The guard then took the man and his dog and brought them to Hakau in the valley of Waipio; when they arrived in the presence of Hakau he asked, 'Is this your dog?' 'Yes, it is mine', answered the man. Hakau asked, 'Have you been drinking my awa then?' 'Yes, I have been drinking it. I thought that the awa came from some place nearer home; but I am mistaken, and he has been getting it from Waipio here.' Hakau replied, 'Yes, I am going to kill both of you for taking my awa.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Pupualenalena (1916-1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 守衛見到狗的主人時，他身上因長期飲用『阿瓦』而布滿鱗屑；守衛便走上前問他：『喂，這是你的狗嗎？』主人回答：『是的。』守衛於是說：『你們兩個都得罪了國王哈考；你的狗一直偷取屬於國王的阿瓦。』守衛隨即帶走那人與他的狗，把他們押到懷皮奧谷中的哈考面前；他們來到哈考跟前時，哈考問道：『這是你的狗嗎？』『是的，是我的。』那人答道。哈考問：『那麼，你一直在喝我的阿瓦嗎？』『是的，我一直在喝。我原以為那阿瓦是從離家較近的某處來的；但我錯了，牠一直是從這裡的懷皮奧取得的。』哈考回答：『不錯，我要把你們兩個都殺了，因為你們取了我的阿瓦。』

passages.text: During this time, in the reign of Hakau, there was a large shell used as a trumpet, called Kuana, that was owned by the spirits which lived above Waipio; this shell was blown every night and the sound from it made Hakau angry. So he said to the master of Pupualenalena: 'I will, however, save you and your dog if you will get me the shell owned by the spirits.' While Hakau was speaking Pupualenalena heard and understood the king's wish; that night the shell was again blown by the spirits. At midnight the king of the spirits retired, leaving the guards to keep watch; but later on they also fell asleep. Pupualenalena then stole in and jumped over the sleeping guards; seeing the shell hanging over the king it jumped over him, took the shell, stuck his head in through the loop of the string by which it was hung up and ran off with it. While in its flight and just as he was out of the house one side of the shell struck a rock and a piece of the shell was broken off; upon hearing the crack of the shell the spirits woke up and gave chase, but they were unable to catch the dog. When the dog arrived in the presence of Hakau with the shell he was so happy that he thereupon placed the master and his dog on a piece of land near by, and they became great favorites with Hakau.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Pupualenalena (1916-1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 就在這段時間，哈考在位期間，有一隻用作號角的大海螺，名叫庫阿納，為居住在懷皮奧上方的神靈所有；這隻海螺每晚都被吹響，其聲令哈考十分惱怒。於是哈考對普普阿萊納萊納的主人說：『不過，只要你替我取得神靈所有的那隻海螺，我就饒了你和你的狗。』哈考說話時，普普阿萊納萊納聽見了，也明白了國王的心願；那晚神靈又吹響了海螺。午夜時分，神靈之王退下歇息，留下守衛看守；但後來守衛們也睡著了。普普阿萊納萊納便潛入其中，躍過沉睡的守衛；牠見海螺懸掛在國王上方，便從國王身上躍過，取走海螺，把頭穿進懸掛海螺的繩圈裡，帶著牠跑了出去。牠在奔逃途中，剛出屋外，海螺的一側撞上一塊岩石，崩落了一片；神靈們聽見海螺的裂響便醒來追趕，卻沒能追上那隻狗。當狗帶著海螺來到哈考面前時，哈考大喜，隨即把主人與他的狗安置在附近的一塊土地上，他們從此成了哈考極為寵愛的人。

title.en: Mailelaulii and the Salt-pool Bridegroom
title.zh: 邁萊勞利伊與製鹽新郎

region.en: Kiholo to Kalahuipuaa, Kona, Hawaii Island
region.zh: 夏威夷島科納基霍洛至卡拉胡普瓦阿

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; recorded 1916-1917 (Fornander Collection)

source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kaulanapokii (Honolulu 1916-1917)

license: Public domain (Bishop Museum Memoirs vol. IV, 1916-1917)

summary.en: The five maile sisters of King Kaumalumalu sightsee down the Kona coast to Kalahuipuaa, where the perfectly formed Puako takes Mailelaulii to wife. At dawn the sisters see him hauling sea-water into salt-making pools and shrink from such lowly toil: 'If that is going to be your husband we will all be made weary' - and the marriage of the royal daughter to the salt-maker anchors the story of the salt ponds of Kalahuipuaa.
summary.zh: 國王考馬盧馬盧的五位邁蕾姊妹沿科納海岸遊歷至卡拉胡普瓦阿，遇上體貌完美的普阿科，長姊邁萊勞利伊與之成婚。翌日清晨姊妹們卻見他挑運海水灌注製鹽石池，頓生鄙意：『若要嫁這樣的丈夫，我們都得累死』——王室之女與製鹽人的這段姻緣，也就把卡拉胡普瓦阿鹽池的故事留在了島上。

sensitivity.note: Salt-pond etiology; sister-companions motif.

passages.text: Kaumalumalu was the father and Lanihau the mother who once lived in Holualoa, Kona, Hawaii, residing there as king and queen at that time: Mumu was their first-born, then came Wawa, then Ahewahewa, then Lulukaina and then Kalino, making five sons; then came Mailelaulii, Mailekaluhea, Mailepakaha, Mailehaiwale, and last came Kaulanapokii, making five daughters. After the children were grown up Mailelaulii asked her younger sisters, saying: 'Let us go sight-seeing hereabouts.' They then started out and went as far as Huehue, from which point Kohala can be seen; on beholding the white sands of Kiholo and Kapalaoa they were enticed to go on; when they arrived at Kapalaoa they thought they would keep on to Kalahuipuaa; upon arriving at Kalahuipuaa they met Puako.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kaulanapokii (1916-1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 考馬盧馬盧是父親，拉尼豪是母親，他們曾住在夏威夷科納的霍盧阿洛阿，當時在那裡身為國王與王后：穆穆是他們的長子，接著是瓦瓦，然後是阿赫瓦赫瓦，然後是盧盧凱納，然後是卡利諾，共五個兒子；接著是邁萊勞利伊、邁萊卡盧赫阿、邁萊帕卡哈、邁萊海瓦萊，最後是考拉納波基伊，共五個女兒。孩子們長大後，邁萊勞利伊對妹妹們說：『我們到附近去遊覽一番吧。』她們於是出發，一路走到胡埃胡埃，從那裡可以望見科哈拉；一見到基霍洛與卡帕拉奧阿的白色沙灘，她們便被吸引著繼續前行；到了卡帕拉奧阿，她們心想乾脆繼續走到卡拉胡伊普阿阿；抵達卡拉胡伊普阿阿時，她們遇見了普阿科。

passages.text: Puako was a very handsome man whose form was perfect; when he saw Mailelaulii he took her to be his wife, and that night they were covered with the same kapa. Very early the next morning the girls looked and saw Puako carrying sea water and filling pools for salt making; upon seeing this the sisters got disgusted and said to Mailelaulii: 'Say, if that is going to be your husband we will all be made weary' - the marriage of the royal daughter to the salt-maker anchoring the story of the salt ponds of Kalahuipuaa on the Kona coast.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kaulanapokii (1916-1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 普阿科是個非常英俊的男子，體態完美無瑕；他見到邁萊勞利伊便娶她為妻，那晚他們共覆同一張卡帕布。翌日清晨極早，女孩們望去，只見普阿科正挑著海水，注滿製鹽的鹽池；姐妹們見此心生嫌惡，對邁萊勞利伊說：『喂，若那人要做你的丈夫，我們可都要累壞了』——王室之女下嫁製鹽人，這則故事便成了科納海岸卡拉胡伊普阿阿鹽池的由來。

title.en: Laukiamanuikahiki Cast from the Cliff
title.zh: 被擲下懸崖的勞基亞馬努伊卡希基

region.en: Coast cliffs of Hawaii Island (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 夏威夷島海岸懸崖（象徵性定位）

period: Hawaiian oral tradition; recorded 1916-1917 (Fornander Collection)

source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Laukiamanuikahiki (Honolulu 1916-1917)

license: Public domain (Bishop Museum Memoirs vol. IV, 1916-1917)

summary.en: Hina, daughter of the man- and wife-eating Laamaomao, bears Laukiamanuikahiki in secret; the child is directed to the cliff and cast from it with a bamboo float, surviving as the 'bird-of-many-fares' of the legend's name. She is found and reared by her grandparents, who send her back to her father's house - the opening movement of a cycle in which Hina admits to her the fate of her father's victims.
summary.zh: 食人男女的勞毛毛之女希娜祕密產下勞基亞馬努伊卡希基；嬰兒被引至崖邊，縛著竹浮筒擲入海中——卻如其名『多程之鳥』般倖存。祖父母尋得並撫養她，後送返父家；循此開端，希娜終向她吐露父親食人的真相，展開整個傳說的循環。

sensitivity.note: Cannibal-parent theme recorded as in source.

passages.text: Hina admits to Laukiamanuikahiki of her father: she was the daughter of Laamaomao, who ate both men and wives, and rearers of Laukiamanuikahiki were her grandparents - Hina and Makiioeoe, whose daughter Laukiamanuikahiki was. Her grandmother directs her to the cliff, and the bamboo as her float: the child, given birth to in secret, was cast from the cliff with the bamboo, and like the bird-of-many-fares whose name she carries survived the fall, to be found and brought up by the grandparents and returned to her father's house - where Hina tells her the fate of the victims of her father's table.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Laukiamanuikahiki (1916-1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 希娜向勞基亞馬努伊卡希基吐露她父親的事：她是拉阿毛毛的女兒，那人既吃男人也吃妻子，而撫養勞基亞馬努伊卡希基的是她的祖父母——希娜與馬基伊奧埃奧埃，勞基亞馬努伊卡希基正是他們的女兒。她的祖母指點她前往那處懸崖，並以竹子作為她的浮具：這孩子是暗中生下的，連同竹子一起從懸崖上被拋下，如同她所承載其名的『多渡之鳥』一般，墜落後倖存下來，被祖父母尋獲並撫養長大，送回她父親的家中——在那裡，希娜告訴她那些淪為她父親餐桌上犧牲者的命運。

passages.text: The name Laukiamanuikahiki means the leaf of the bird that flies from island to island - 'many-fares' - and the legend makes her the child who escapes the cannibal father's practice by being cast into the sea and saved: Hina, her mother, suffered the same appetite in her own household, and the story runs that the grandmother Hina, who had been thrown from the same cliff in her own infancy and survived, taught her granddaughter the bamboo-float trick that saved the second generation of the family.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Laukiamanuikahiki (1916-1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 勞基亞馬努伊卡希基這個名字意為『往來於島嶼之間飛翔之鳥的葉子』——即『多渡』——傳說使她成為那個被拋入海中而獲救、因而逃脫食人父親習性的孩子：她的母親希娜在自己的家中也遭受同樣的貪慾，而故事說，祖母希娜在自己嬰兒時期也曾被從同一處懸崖拋下並倖存，她教會了孫女那套以竹子為浮具的訣竅，從而救了家族的第二代。

title.en: Three Eggs of Gold, Silver and Copper: Kings, Priests and Slaves
title.zh: 金銀銅三卵:王者、祭司與僕隸

region.en: Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科(象徵性標記)

period: Retold by Lewis Spence, 1913, from colonial chroniclers

source.work: Lewis Spence, The Myths of Mexico and Peru, London 1913

summary.en: Occasionally we find the sun acting as a kind of demiurge or sub-creator. He it is who in later legend founds the city of Cuzco, and sends thither three eggs composed of gold, silver, and copper, from which spring the three classes of Peruvians, kings, priests, and slaves.
summary.zh: 太陽有時儼然一位造化之神、次級創世者。後期傳說中,正是他建立了庫斯科城,並向城中送去金、銀、銅三枚卵;秘魯人的三個等級——王者、祭司與僕隸——便由這三卵中孕育而出。

sensitivity.note: Spence is a retelling compiler (1913); the egg-caste myth he cites matches the version reported by Cabello Valboa via later writers; period flagged as retold.

passages.text: Occasionally we find the sun acting as a kind of demiurge or sub-creator. He it is who in later legend founds the city of Cuzco, and sends thither three eggs composed of gold, silver, and copper, from which spring the three classes of Peruvians, kings, priests, and slaves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Spence, The Myths of Mexico and Peru (1913), Peru chapters; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 我們偶爾會見到太陽扮演某種造物主或次級創造者的角色。正是祂在後來的傳說中建立了庫斯科城，並遣送三枚分別由金、銀、銅構成的卵至該地，秘魯人的三個階級——國王、祭司與奴隸——便由此而生。

canonical_translation: Spence 1913 (reteller)

title.en: From His Teeth Grew Maize: The Son of the Sun Slain at Yarma
title.zh: 齒中生玉米:太陽之子在利馬谷遇害

region.en: Coastal valley of Rimac (Yarma), below Lima (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 利馬下方海岸利馬(亞爾馬)谷(象徵性標記)

period: Retold by Lewis Spence, 1913, from colonial chroniclers

source.work: Lewis Spence, The Myths of Mexico and Peru, London 1913

summary.en: In some of the more isolated valleys of Peru we discover local creation-myths. For example, in the coastal valley of Rimac Pachacamac was not considered to be the creator of the sun, but to be himself a descendant of it. The first human beings created by him were speedily separated, as the man died of hunger, but the woman supported herself by living on roots. The sun took compassion upon her and gave her a son, whom Pachacamac slew and buried. But from his teeth there grew maize, from his ribs the long white roots of the manioc plant, and from his flesh various esculent plants.
summary.zh: 秘魯較偏遠的一些河谷還保存著地方性的創世神話。例如在海岸的利馬谷,帕查卡馬克並非太陽的創造者,而是太陽的後裔。他所造的第一對人很快便天各一方:男子飢餓而死,女子靠食草根存活。太陽憐憫這女子,賜她一子;帕查卡馬克卻殺死此子,加以掩埋。然而,從孩子的牙齒裡長出了玉米,從肋骨間長出木薯修長的白根,從血肉中長出各樣可食的植物。

sensitivity.note: The Andean dismemberment cluster (crops from the slain body); Spence retells the Yarma/Pachacamac myth from Cabello Valboa's line of tradition. Cross-ref to Ymir/Pangu/Tiamat parallels.

passages.text: In the coastal valley of Rimac Pachacamac was not considered to be the creator of the sun, but to be himself a descendant of it. The first human beings created by him were speedily separated, as the man died of hunger, but the woman supported herself by living on roots.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Spence, The Myths of Mexico and Peru (1913), Peru chapters; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在里馬克的海岸谷地，帕查卡馬克並不被視為太陽的創造者，而被視為太陽本身的後裔。他所創造的第一批人類很快便分離了，因為那名男子死於飢餓，而那名女子則靠食用根莖維生。

passages.text: The sun took compassion upon her and gave her a son, whom Pachacamac slew and buried. But from his teeth there grew maize, from his ribs the long white roots of the manioc plant, and from his flesh various esculent plants.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Spence, The Myths of Mexico and Peru (1913), Peru chapters; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 太陽憐憫她，賜給她一個兒子，帕查卡馬克卻將他殺害並埋葬。然而，從他的牙齒長出了玉米，從他的肋骨長出了木薯植株長而白的根，從他的肉體則長出了各種可食的植物。

canonical_translation: Spence 1913 (reteller)

title.en: Intipampa, the Field of the Sun: Golden Trees and Mummified Kings
title.zh: 因蒂潘帕「日之田野」:金樹與環繞祭壇的王木乃伊

region.en: Coricancha, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科科里坎查(象徵性標記)

period: Retold by Lewis Spence, 1913, from conquistador testimonies

source.work: Lewis Spence, The Myths of Mexico and Peru, London 1913

summary.en: One of the most remarkable monuments of the Peruvian civilisation was the Coricancha (Town of Gold) at Cuzco, the principal fane of the sun-god. Its inner and outer walls were covered with plates of pure gold. Situated upon an eminence eighty feet high, the temple looked down upon gardens filled, according to the conquering Spaniards, with treasures of gold and silver. The animals, insects, the very trees, say the chroniclers, were of the precious metals, as were the spades, hoes, and other implements employed for keeping the ground in cultivation. Through the pleasances rippled the river Huatenay. Such was the glittering Intipampa (Field of the Sun). The interior displayed an ornate richness which impressed even the Spaniards: the gold-lust must have swelled within their hearts at sight of the great altar, behind which was a huge plate of the shining metal engraved with the features of the sun-god. The surface of this plate was enriched by a thousand gems, the scintillation of which was, according to eye-witnesses, almost insupportable. Around this dazzling sphere were seated the mummified corpses of the Inca kings, each on his throne, with sceptre in hand. Surrounding the Coricancha several lesser temples clustered, dedicated to the moon, to Cuycha the rainbow, and to Chasca the planet Venus. In the temple of the moon, the mythic mother of the Inca dynasty, a great plate of silver depicted the features of the moon-goddess, and around this the mummies of the Inca queens sat in a semicircle. In the rainbow temple of Cuycha the seven-hued arch was depicted by a great arc of gold. The colossal representation of the sun became the property of a certain Mancio Serra de Leguizano, a reckless cavalier and noted gambler, who lost it on a single throw of the dice.
summary.zh: 秘魯文明最壯麗的遺蹟之一,是庫斯科的科里坎查——「金城」,太陽神的主廟。內外牆壁皆覆純金之板。神廟踞於八十呎高地,俯瞰著征服者所說的滿園金銀的園林:據編年史家所言,園中的禽鳥、昆蟲乃至樹木,皆以貴金屬製成;耕作土地的鏟、鋤等農具亦然。瓦特納伊河流經園苑,粼粼生輝——這便是「因蒂潘帕」——日之田野。殿內窮奢極麗,連見多識廣的西班牙人也為之目眩:大祭壇之後懸著一塊巨大的金板,上鐫日神面容;板上鑲嵌千顆寶石,據目擊者言,其光芒幾乎令人不能逼視。圍繞這奪目的日盤,歷代印加王的木乃伊各據王座,手持權杖而坐。科里坎查四周簇擁著幾座小廟:月神廟——印加王族的傳說母親——供銀鑄月神面容之板,歷代王后的木乃伊如配偶一般在彼環坐成半圓;彩虹廟「庫伊查」以金弧呈七色長虹;金星廟奉「查斯卡」。至於那面巨大的太陽金盤,後來落入亡命賭徒曼西奧·塞拉·德·萊吉薩諾之手——他一擲骰子,便把它輸了個精光!

sensitivity.note: The Coricancha as described from conquistador loot-testimony; the dice anecdote (Mancio Serra) is a well-attested colonial story.

passages.text: The animals, insects, the very trees, say the chroniclers, were of the precious metals, as were the spades, hoes, and other implements employed for keeping the ground in cultivation. Through the pleasances rippled the river Huatenay. Such was the glittering Intipampa (Field of the Sun).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Spence, The Myths of Mexico and Peru (1913), Peru chapters; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 編年史家記載，動物、昆蟲，乃至樹木，皆由貴金屬製成，用以維持土地耕作的鏟、鋤及其他器具亦然。溪流瓦特奈蜿蜒流經這些園圃。這便是熠熠生輝的印蒂潘帕（太陽之田）。

passages.text: The surface of this plate was enriched by a thousand gems, the scintillation of which was, according to eye-witnesses, almost insupportable. Around this dazzling sphere were seated the mummified corpses of the Inca kings, each on his throne, with sceptre in hand... In the temple of the moon, the mythic mother of the Inca dynasty, a great plate of silver depicted the features of the moon-goddess, and around this the mummies of the Inca queens sat in a semicircle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Spence, The Myths of Mexico and Peru (1913), Peru chapters; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這塊圓盤的表面以千顆寶石增輝，據目擊者所言，其閃爍之光幾乎令人難以承受。在這耀眼的球體四周，端坐著印加諸王的木乃伊遺體，各居其王座之上，手持權杖……在月神廟中——月神是印加王朝的神話之母——一塊巨大的銀盤描繪出月神的容顏，而在其四周，印加諸后的木乃伊呈半圓形環坐。

passages.text: The colossal representation of the sun became the property of a certain Mancio Serra de Leguicano, a reckless cavalier and noted gambler, who lost it on a single throw of the dice! Such was the spirit of the adventurers who conquered this golden realm for the crown of Spain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Spence, The Myths of Mexico and Peru (1913), Peru chapters; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這尊巨大的太陽造像後來歸屬於某位名叫曼西奧·塞拉·德·萊吉卡諾的人所有，他是一名放蕩不羈的騎士，也是聲名遠播的賭徒，竟在一次擲骰中便將它輸掉了！為西班牙王冠征服這片黃金國度的冒險者們，其精神便是如此。

canonical_translation: Spence 1913 (reteller)

title.en: The Nun Who Broke Her Vow: Buried Alive, Her Village Razed
title.zh: 破誓的太陽貞女:活埋與夷村

region.en: Provinces of Ttahuantin-suyu (symbolic pin: Cuzco)
region.zh: 大蘇尤諸省(象徵性標記:庫斯科)

period: Retold by Lewis Spence, 1913, from colonial chroniclers

source.work: Lewis Spence, The Myths of Mexico and Peru, London 1913

summary.en: The legal code of the Incas was severe in the extreme. Murderers and adulterers were punished by death, and the unpardonable sin appears to have been blasphemy against the sun, or his earthly representative, the Inca. The Virgin of the Sun (or nun) who broke her vow was buried alive, and the village from whence she came was razed to the ground. Flogging was administered for minor offences. A peculiar and very trying punishment must have been that of carrying a heavy stone for a certain time.
summary.zh: 印加的法典嚴酷至極。殺人者與姦淫者皆處死刑;而不可赦之罪,似乎是褻瀆太陽——或其在世上的代表印加王。破誓的太陽貞女(修女)被活埋,她出生的村莊亦被夷為平地。輕罪處以鞭刑。還有一種奇特而難熬的刑罰:令罪犯負重石而行,歷時有定。

sensitivity.note: The collective punishment of the nun's home village - Spence's legal summary drawn from Garcilaso and Acosta.

passages.text: The legal code of the Incas was severe in the extreme. Murderers and adulterers were punished by death, and the unpardonable sin appears to have been blasphemy against the sun, or his earthly representative, the Inca. The Virgin of the Sun (or nun) who broke her vow was buried alive, and the village from whence she came was razed to the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Spence, The Myths of Mexico and Peru (1913), Peru chapters; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 印加人的法典極為嚴苛。殺人者與通姦者皆處以死刑，而最不可饒恕的罪過似乎是褻瀆太陽，或褻瀆其在人間的代表——印加王。違背誓願的太陽貞女（或稱修女）會被活埋，而她所來自的村莊則被夷為平地。

canonical_translation: Spence 1913 (reteller)

title.en: Siyawush Displays His Prowess Before Afrasiyab
title.zh: 西亞瓦什阿弗拉西亞卜前顯技

region.en: Polo-ground of Afrasiyab (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿弗拉西亞卜馬球場（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Siyawush sec. 33

summary.en: At polo Afrasiyab drives the ball up to the clouds and Siyawush smites it, or ever it could reach the ground, so stoutly that it disappears from sight; the Iranians play the Turanians, and Siyawush, displeased with his own people, cries in the olden Persian tongue: when ye are near the limits look aside and let the Turkmans have the ball for once. At archery Garsiwaz cannot bend the prince's royal bow, but Siyawush bends it sitting on his knees and splits the bull's-eye again and again: thy skill is witness to thy race, says the king, and heaped gifts are borne to Siyawush's house.
summary.zh: 馬球場上，阿弗拉西亞卜擊球沖天，西亞瓦什不待球落地便奮力一擊，球影頓消。伊朗隊與圖蘭隊較量，王子怕惹禍端，以古波斯語低喝：「靠近界線時讓讓突厥人吧！」比試神弓，加爾西瓦斯拉不開，王子跪地而拉、連中靶心——「你的技藝便是你血統的見證！」國王命人把成堆的賞賜送往西亞瓦什府邸。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Afrasiyab hit off and drove the ball up to the clouds just as it should be struck.
