passages.text: In the lake of Titicaca there are islands inhabited by people with large balsas, and another lord named Cari went to the islands, where he fought with the people insomuch that there were great battles between them, out of which the Cari came forth a conqueror. But he had no other object than to destroy the villagers and carry off plunder, without troubling himself to take prisoners. He returned to Chucuito, where he had established himself, and he had under his sway the towns of Ylave, Yuli, Zepita, Pomata, and others.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cieza de León, Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, ch. 41 (Markham 1883); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在的的喀喀湖中有一些島嶼，島上居民擁有大型蘆葦船；另一位名叫卡里（Cari）的領主前往這些島嶼，在那裡與居民交戰，雙方發生了許多大戰，卡里從中脫穎而出，成為征服者。但他別無他圖，只想毀滅村民、掠奪財物，並不在意俘虜敵人。他回到他已立足的丘庫伊托（Chucuito），將伊拉韋（Ylave）、尤利（Yuli）、塞皮塔（Zepita）、波馬塔（Pomata）等城鎮置於自己的統治之下。

passages.text: With the people he could collect, after having offered up great sacrifices to his gods, he determined to march to the province of the Canas. These men, when they heard of his approach, assembled together, came forth to meet him, and fought a battle in which they were defeated with much loss. After this victory Cari determined to continue his advance, and arrived at Luracachi, where it is said that he fought another battle, and was equally fortunate. With these victories Cari became very proud.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cieza de León, Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, ch. 41 (Markham 1883); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他向自己的神明獻上盛大祭品之後，便帶著所能召集的人馬，決意進軍卡納斯（Canas）省。這些人聽聞他逼近，便聚集起來，出迎與他交戰，結果大敗，損失慘重。取得這場勝利之後，卡里決意繼續推進，抵達盧拉卡奇（Luracachi），據說他在那裡又打了一仗，同樣幸運獲勝。憑著這些勝利，卡里變得非常驕傲。

passages.text: When Zapana, the lord of Hatun-colla, heard of it, he was very sad, and he assembled his friends and vassals to take the field and despoil Cari. But he could not do this so secretly as to prevent Cari from understanding the design of Zapana, and he retired in good order to Chucuito by an unfrequented road... And as the valour of the Incas, and the great power of Viracocha was spread abroad over all that region, each of these chiefs, desiring to obtain his friendship, sent ambassadors to Cuzco to secure his alliance and induce him to take part against the rival chief.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cieza de León, Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, ch. 41 (Markham 1883); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 哈通科亞之主薩帕納聞訊後極為悲傷，遂召集其友與附庸，欲出兵掠奪卡里。然其謀劃未能保密至令卡里無從察覺薩帕納之意圖，卡里乃循一條人跡罕至之路井然有序地退往丘庫伊托……而因印加之勇武與維拉科查之偉力已傳播於整個地區，此二酋長皆欲得其友誼，各自遣使前往庫斯科以求結盟，並勸其參與對抗敵對酋長。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, The Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru (Hakluyt Society, 1883)

title.en: Chin in Breast, Voice Loud: How the Oracles Were Consulted
title.zh: 垂首含胸、高聲傳話:神諭的問法

region.en: Temples of the Andes and the coast (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 安第斯與海岸諸廟(象徵性標記)

period: Written by Cieza de León, publ. Markham trans. 1883 (Second Part)

source.work: Pedro de Cieza de León, The Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, trans. and ed. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1883

summary.en: When the Inca determined to seek for an answer from the oracles, he sent for those who were accustomed to manage those things. The reply is sought by the priests in front of the idols: they bow down their shoulders, put their chins into their breasts, and begin to speak in loud voices. Occasionally I myself, with my own ears, have heard the Indians converse with the devil: in the province of Cartagena I heard the devil answer in a clear whistle, so loudly that a Christian more than half a league away heard the same whistle and was dismayed. On another day the Indians made great shoutings, publishing the reply of the devil. In some parts of these lands where they keep the dead in hammocks, the devils occasionally enter into the bodies and give answers: I heard a man named Aranda say that, in the island of Carex, he also saw one of these dead bodies speak, and the lies and nonsense they utter are laughable.
summary.zh: 印加王欲求神諭,便召慣司此事之人。祭司在偶像前求答:垂肩俯首,下巴抵胸,高聲傳話。塞薩自述:「我屢屢親耳聽過印第安人與魔鬼交談。」在卡塔赫納省的海港城巴亞伊雷,他聽見魔鬼以清晰口哨作答,聲聞半萊格之外,令一位在場基督徒惶然失措;另一日,印第安人高聲喧呼,宣告魔鬼的回復。在某些地方,人們把死者安置於吊床之中,魔鬼偶爾附體作答——有人名阿蘭達者說,他在卡雷克斯島親見一具死者屍體開口說話;那些謊言與胡話,聽來簡直可笑。

sensitivity.note: Cieza's rare first-person description of an oracle procedure (posture, voice, possession of hammock-kept dead); 'devil' is his frame, the procedure is the datum.

passages.text: This is done by the priests in front of the idols. They bow down their shoulders, put their chins into their breasts, and begin to speak in loud voices. Occasionally I myself, with my own ears, have heard the Indians converse with the devil.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cieza de León, Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, ch. 41 (Markham 1883); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此事由祭司在偶像前為之。他們俯下肩膀，將下巴抵於胸前，開始高聲言語。我本人偶爾亦曾親耳聽見印第安人與魔鬼交談。

passages.text: In some parts of these lands where they keep the dead in hammocks, the devils occasionally enter into the bodies and give answers. I heard a man named Aranda say that, in the island of Carex, he also saw one of these dead bodies speak, and the lies and nonsense they utter are laughable.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cieza de León, Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, ch. 41 (Markham 1883); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在此地某些區域，人們將死者置於吊床之中，魔鬼偶爾會進入其身體並作出回答。我聽一位名叫阿蘭達的人說，他在卡雷克斯島上亦曾見一具此類屍體開口說話，而它們所吐之謊言與胡言令人發笑。

passages.text: When the Inca determined to seek for an answer from the oracles, he sent for those who were accustomed to manage those things, and they say that the reply was that he should arrange to go to the Collao and seek the alliance of Cari.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cieza de León, Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, ch. 41 (Markham 1883); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當印加決定向神諭尋求答覆時，他召來慣於處理此類事務之人，據他們所言，答覆是他應安排前往科利亞奧，尋求與卡里結盟。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, The Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru (Hakluyt Society, 1883)

title.en: The Dinner of the Sun: Clay Cups Replaced with Gold
title.zh: 日神的晚餐:陶杯換金器

region.en: Coricancha, House of the Sun, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科太陽之屋科里坎查(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 36, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: After Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui had conquered the lands mentioned above and had triumphed over them, he came to visit the House of the Sun and the Mama-cunas or nuns who were there. He assisted one day to see how the Mama-cunas served the dinner of the Sun. This was to offer much richly cooked food to the image or idol of the Sun, and then to put it into a great fire on an altar. The same order was taken with the liquor: the chief of the Mama-cunas saluted the Sun with a small vase, and the rest was thrown on the fire; besides this many jars full of that liquor were poured into a trough which had a drain, all being offerings to the Sun. This service was performed with vessels of clay. As Pachacuti considered that the material of the vases was too poor, he presented very complete sets of vases of gold and silver for all the service that was necessary. To adorn the house more richly he caused a plate of fine gold to be made, two palmas broad and the length of the court-yard, and ordered it to be nailed high up on the wall in the manner of a cornice, passing all round the court-yard. This border or cornice of gold remained there down to the time of the Spaniards.
summary.zh: 帕查庫提·印加·尤潘琪征服諸邦、凱旋之後,親臨太陽之屋,查看瑪瑪庫納(貞女)侍奉日神晚餐的情形:眾女將精緻烹調的膳食供奉於太陽神像之前,然後投入祭壇上的烈火之中;酒漿亦然——瑪瑪庫納之首以小杯敬日神,其餘盡焚於火;此外又將滿罐奇恰酒傾入帶排水道的溝槽,盡為日神之祭。這些侍奉原用陶器。帕查庫提嫌器物卑陋,便賜下成套金銀器皿,以供全部所需。為使神屋更加輝煌,他又命人打造一塊兩掌寬、與庭院等長的純金薄板,釘於高牆之上作為簷飾,環繞庭院一周。這道金簷一直留存到西班牙人到來之日。

sensitivity.note: The daily liturgy of the Sun's meal as witnessed by the king; the gold cornice is the Coricancha's famous feature.

passages.text: He assisted one day, to see how the Mama-cunas served the dinner of the Sun. This was to offer much richly cooked food to the image or idol of the Sun, and then to put it into a great fire on an altar. The same order was taken with the liquor. The chief of the Mama-cunas saluted the Sun with a small vase, and the rest was thrown on the fire. Besides this many jars full of that liquor were poured into a trough which had a drain, all being offerings to the Sun.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 36 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某日他前去觀看瑪瑪庫納如何侍奉太陽之餐。此即向太陽之像或偶像獻上大量烹製精美的食物，然後將其置於祭壇上的大火之中。酒液亦依同樣程序處理。瑪瑪庫納之首領以小瓶向太陽致敬，其餘則傾入火中。除此之外，許多盛滿此種酒液之罐被倒入設有排水口之槽中，皆為獻給太陽之供品。

passages.text: As Pachacuti considered that the material of the vases was too poor, he presented very complete sets of vases of gold and silver for all the service that was necessary. To adorn the house more richly he caused a plate of fine gold to be made, two palmas broad and the length of the court-yard. He ordered this to be nailed high up on the wall in the manner of a cornice, passing all round the court-yard. This border or cornice of gold remained there down to the time of the Spaniards.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 36 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 帕查庫提認為瓶器之材質過於粗劣，遂呈獻整套金銀瓶器，以供一切必要之用途。為使屋宇更為富麗，他命人製作一塊純金板，寬二帕爾馬，長與庭院相等。他下令將其如簷口般高釘於牆上，環繞庭院一周。此金色邊飾或簷口一直留存至西班牙人到來之時。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Sixteen Visitors and the Road from Quito to Chile
title.zh: 十六位巡察使與從基多到智利的大道

region.en: Roads of the empire, Quito to Chile (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 帝國大道:基多至智利(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 45, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Seeing that the people were in greater fear at beholding the valour of Tupac Inca, Pachacuti determined to have a visitation of the land, and nominated 16 visitors, four for each of the four suyus or divisions of the empire: Cunti-suyu from Cuzco south and west as far as the South Sea, Chinchay-suyu from Cuzco to the north and west, Anti-suyu from Cuzco to the east, and Colla-suyu from Cuzco to the south. These visitors inspected, before all things, the work of the tucuyricos and the methods of their government; they caused irrigating channels to be constructed for the crops, broke up land where this had been neglected, built andenes or cultivated terraces, and took up pastures for the Sun, the Inca, and Cuzco; above all they imposed very heavy tribute on all the produce. The visitations occupied two years; when they were completed the visitors returned to Cuzco, bringing with them certain cloths descriptive of the provinces they had visited, and reported fully to the Inca all that they had found and done. The Inca also despatched other orejones as overseers to make roads and hospices on the routes of the Inca: they made roads, now called 'of the Inca', over the mountains and along the sea coast; those on the sea coast are all provided, at the sides, with high walls of adobe, wherever it was possible to build them. These roads go from Quito to Chile, and into the forests of the Andes.
summary.zh: 帕查庫提見民眾愈發畏懼圖帕克·印加之勇武,便決意巡查全境,任命十六位巡察使——四蘇尤各四位:昆蒂蘇尤(自庫斯科向南向西直至南海)、欽查蘇尤(向北向西)、安蒂蘇尤(向東)、科利亞蘇尤(向南)。巡察使首先督察各處「圖庫里科」官長的施政;又主持修築灌溉渠、墾闢荒田、建造安第斯梯田,並為太陽、印加與庫斯科劃定牧場;尤以加征重貢於一切出產為最。巡查歷時兩年;事畢,巡察使攜記述各省的彩布返回庫斯科,向印加王詳細復命。印加王另遣耳垂貴胄為監工,沿王路修築道路與驛館——即今所稱「印加道」——越山嶺、沿海岸;海岸一路,凡可築處皆以土坯砌高牆護道兩側。這些道路自基多直達智利,並深入安第斯森林。

sensitivity.note: The imperial visitation as administrative myth-history; the painted cloth reports echo the Pachacuti annals-library record.

passages.text: Seeing that the people were in greater fear at beholding the valour of Tupac Inca, he determined to have a visitation of the land, and nominated 16 visitors, four for each of the four suyus or divisions of the empire... These visitors each went to the part to which he was appointed, and inspected, before all things, the work of the tucuyricos and the methods of their government. They caused irrigating channels to be constructed for the crops, broke up land where this had been neglected, built andenes or cultivated terraces, and took up pastures for the Sun, the Inca, and Cuzco.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 45 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他見眾人目睹圖帕克·印加的英勇後更為恐懼，便決定巡察全國，任命了十六名巡察使，四個蘇尤（即帝國的四個分區）各派四人……這些巡察使各自前往所指派的地區，首先視察圖庫伊里科（tucuyricos）的工作及其治理方法。他們命人為農作物修築灌溉渠道，開墾先前荒廢的土地，建造安第內斯（andenes，即耕作梯田），並為太陽、印加與庫斯科劃定牧場。

passages.text: The visitations occupied two years. When they were completed the visitors returned to Cuzco, bringing with them certain cloths descriptive of the provinces they had visited. They reported fully to the Inca all that they had found and done. Besides these, the Inca also despatched other orejones as overseers to make roads and hospices on the routes of the Inca... These roads go from Quito to Chile, and into the forests of the Andes.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 45 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巡察歷時兩年。巡察完畢後，巡察使們返回庫斯科，帶回若干描繪所巡視各省的布匹。他們向印加詳細稟報所見所為。除此之外，印加還派遣其他奧雷洪（orejones）作為監督，在印加的道路上修築道路與驛館……這些道路從基多通往智利，並深入安地斯山脈的森林。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: 'O Father, Now Take Rest': The Obsequies of Pachacuti
title.zh: 「父王安息吧」:帕查庫提的葬禮

region.en: Cuzco great square (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科大廣場(象徵性標記)

period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 48, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: When Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui died, two orejones were deputed to watch the body, and to allow no one to enter or go out to spread the news of his death, until orders had been given. The other Incas and orejones went with Tupac Inca to the House of the Sun and then ordered the twelve captains of the ayllus of the Inca's guard to come. They came with 2200 men of the guard, fully armed, and surrounded the Yupanqui with the fringe, and gave him the other insignia of sovereignty, as he had now inherited and succeeded his father. Taking him in the midst of themselves and of the guards, they escorted him to the great square, where he was seated, in majesty, on a superb throne. All the people of the city were then ordered to come and make obeisance to the Inca on pain of death. Those who had come with the Inca went to their houses to fetch presents to show reverence and do homage to the new Inca; he remained with his guards only until they returned with presents, doing homage and adoring. This having been done, they approached the Inca and said: 'O Sovereign Inca! O Father! now take rest.' At these words Tupac Inca showed much sadness and covered his head with his mantle, which they call llacolla. He next went, with all his company, to the place where the body of his father was laid, and there he put on mourning. All things were then arranged for the obsequies, and Tupac Inca Yupanqui did everything that his father had ordered at the point of death.
summary.zh: 帕查庫提·印加·尤潘琪駕崩後,兩名耳垂貴胄奉命看守遺體:未奉諭旨,任何人不得出入、不得走漏死訊。其餘印加貴胄隨圖帕克·印加前往太陽之屋,召王之衛隊十二世系的隊長;他們率兩千二百名全副武裝的衛士趕到,為戴王纓的尤潘琪呈上其餘王權印信——蓋他已承襲父位。眾人將他簇擁於衛隊中央,護送至大廣場,威嚴地安置在華麗御座之上;旋即傳令全城百姓前來朝拜新王,違者處死。隨王前來之人各自回宅取獻禮,以示尊崇;新王獨留衛隊之中,待眾人攜禮而返,行禮致敬,一一祭拜。禮成之後,眾人趨前說道:「至尊的印加王!父王!如今請安息吧。」聞言,圖帕克·印加面現哀戚,以名為「利亞科利亞」的方氅掩面。繼而,他率全體扈從前往父親遺體安放之所,披麻戴孝。喪儀諸事一一安排;圖帕克·印加·尤潘琪遵照父王臨終遺命,辦理後事,無所遺漏。

sensitivity.note: Accession-by-obsequies: the new king crowned before the death news escapes; the formula 'now take rest' marks the transfer of care.

passages.text: When Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui died, two orejones were deputed to watch the body, and to allow no one to enter or go out to spread the news of his death, until orders had been given. The other Incas and orejones went with Tupac Inca to the House of the Sun... They came with 2200 men of the guard, under their command, fully armed, and surrounded the Yupanqui with the fringe, and gave him the other insignia of sovereignty, as he had now inherited and succeeded his father.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 48 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 帕查庫提·印加·尤潘基去世時，派了兩名奧雷洪看守遺體，不許任何人進出傳播他的死訊，直到下令為止。其餘的印加與奧雷洪隨圖帕克·印加前往太陽之家……他們率領麾下二千二百名衛兵，全副武裝，以流蘇圍繞尤潘基，並授予他其他主權象徵，因為他此時已繼承並接替了父親。

passages.text: All the people of the city were then ordered to come and make obeisance to the Inca on pain of death... This having been done, they approached the Inca and said: 'O Sovereign Inca! O Father! now take rest.' At these words Tupac Inca showed much sadness and covered his head with his mantle, which they call llacolla, a square cloak. He next went, with all his company, to the place where the body of his father was laid, and there he put on mourning.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 48 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隨後下令全城百姓前來向印加行禮，違者處死……行禮完畢後，他們走近印加說道：「哦，至尊的印加！哦，父親！如今請安息吧。」聞聽此言，圖帕克·印加顯得十分悲傷，以斗篷覆頭，他們稱之為利亞科利亞（llacolla），是一種方形斗篷。接著，他率領全體隨從前往安放父親遺體之處，在那裡服喪。

canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: The World-Tree and the Great Flood (Taulipang, Koch-Grünberg)
title.zh: 世界樹與大洪水（陶利潘格）

region.en: Mount Roroima, Taulipang-Arekuna country
region.zh: 羅羅伊馬山陶利潘格-阿雷庫納之地

period: Taulipang oral tradition; recorded 1911-12 (Koch-Grünberg), publ. 1924

source.work: Theodor Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roraima zum Orinoco, Bd. II: Mythen und Legenden der Taulipang- und Arekuna-Indianer (1924), Mythe 1-2

summary.en: Makunaima and his brothers suffered great hunger; Aküli the agouti always came home full-bellied, eating in secret the fruits of the wonderful tree Wazakä, which bears every good fruit. Makunaima, watching his lip, found a piece of banana between his teeth, and sent Kali after him. Against the elder brother's warning — 'If you fell the tree, there will be a great water' — the tree was felled with magic words that softened the wood: its stump is today the Roroima itself, and the felled trunks lie across the Caröni as the great falls. Makunaima covered the stump with a basket and let fish come out for the brooks, but lifted the basket a little too high: the water burst out with all its force and threw the basket aside — there was much water, and they could not cover it again. Each brother climbed an Inajä palm to escape the flood; and Aküli, who had hidden in the tree-hole with his fire, still has red hairs on his rump to this day.
summary.zh: 馬庫納伊瑪兄弟饑甚；阿庫利日日飽食而秘之——其私食者乃萬果之樹瓦薩卡也。窺其齒間得蕉，遣卡利隨之。兄誡曰：『伐樹則大水至！』眾以咒言軟其木而伐之——其樁今即羅羅伊馬山，倒木橫卡羅尼河為大灘。馬庫納伊瑪以籃覆樁，縱魚出；稍舉其籃，水暴發不可復塞。兄弟各登伊納雅棕避洪；阿庫利匿樹洞以火自暖，至今臀有赤毛。

sensitivity.note: Taulipang myth told by Aküli/Mayüluaipu to Koch-Grünberg 1911-12, publ. 1924; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Makunaima and his brothers suffered great hunger. Aküli came always home with a full belly: he ate the fruits of the tree Pupü, which he had found in the forest, and said nothing of it to the others; the others ate only the bad fruits of the Kaui-yeg. Makunaima watched him, lifted his lip while he slept, and found a piece of fruit between his teeth. Aküli hid the ripe fruits that lay on the ground in a hole in the trunk and stopped the hole with beeswax.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬庫奈馬（Makunaima）和他的兄弟們飽受飢餓之苦。阿屈利（Aküli）總是吃得飽飽地回家：他吃的是他在森林中發現的普普樹（Pupü）的果實，卻對其他人隻字不提；其他人只吃考伊耶格樹（Kaui-yeg）的壞果實。馬庫奈馬監視他，趁他睡覺時掀起他的嘴唇，發現他牙縫間夾著一塊果實。阿屈利把落在地上的熟果藏進樹幹的洞裡，並用蜂蠟封住洞口。

passages.text: The eldest brother gave his brothers the advice not to fell this tree again, but only to eat the fruits that fell; Makunaima however wanted to fell it with all his might. The tree Wazakä was tangled with lianas; Makunaima sent Kali up to cut them, but many wasps there stung him in the eyelids — hence they are swollen to this day. Makunaima hacked on one side of the trunk with his magic word and it grew ever softer, while the eldest brother hacked the other side with his, and it grew ever harder: the tree broke and fell — its stump is today the Roroima; the fallen trunks lie across the Caröni and form the high falls over which boats must be unloaded and hauled overland.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大哥勸兄弟們不要再砍倒這棵樹，只吃落下的果實；然而馬庫奈馬卻想竭盡全力把它砍倒。瓦扎卡樹（Wazakä）纏滿了藤蔓；馬庫奈馬派卡利（Kali）上去砍藤，但那裡有許多黃蜂蜇了他的眼皮——因此他的眼皮至今仍腫著。馬庫奈馬用咒語砍樹幹的一側，樹幹便越砍越軟；而大哥用他的咒語砍另一側，樹幹卻越砍越硬：樹終於斷裂倒下——它的樹樁就是今日的羅羅伊馬（Roroima）；倒下的樹幹橫跨卡羅尼河（Caröni），形成高聳的瀑布，船隻必須卸貨並從陸路拖運而過。

passages.text: The eldest brother covered the stump of Wazakä with a basket; out of the stump came many fish. When the stump was covered Makunaima said: 'Let a little more fish come out for these brooks; then we will cover the stump.' He lifted the basket a little — the water came with all its force and threw the basket quite aside: much water came out, and they could not cover it again. Makunaima stuck a very tall Inajä stem into the earth to save himself from the flood, and each brother climbed his own palm. Aküli had crawled into the hole of the trunk where he had hidden his bananas; he made a fire in the hole and warmed himself — the fire seized his rump and turned into red hairs: to this day Aküli has red hairs on his rump.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大哥用籃子蓋住瓦扎卡的樹樁；從樹樁裡出來了許多魚。樹樁被蓋住後，馬庫奈馬說：「讓再出來一些魚給這些小溪吧；然後我們就把樹樁蓋上。」他把籃子稍微抬起——水帶著全部的力量湧來，把籃子完全掀到一邊：大量的水湧了出來，他們再也蓋不回去了。馬庫奈馬把一根很高的伊納雅棕櫚莖插進土裡，以從洪水中自救，每個兄弟都爬上了自己的棕櫚樹。阿庫利曾爬進他藏香蕉的樹幹洞裡；他在洞裡生起火來取暖——火燒到了他的臀部，變成了紅色的毛髮：直到今天，阿庫利的臀部上還長著紅色的毛髮。

narrative.en: Among the Taulipang and Arekuna Carib-speaking peoples of the Roroima (Roraima) region, the cycle that explains the whole habitable world begins with hunger and ends with mountains. Makunaima — the youngest of a set of brothers but the craftiest — and his brothers are starving. Aküli, the agouti, comes home every evening with a full belly, and the brothers eat only the poor fruits of the Kaui-yeg tree. Makunaima's suspicion is proven in a small and vivid way: while Aküli sleeps he lifts his lip and finds a fragment of banana, Wazakä-püu, between his teeth. Spies are sent after the hoarder; wasps sting the eyelids of the first, Kali, whose swollen eyelids every one of his kind has carried since. At last the eldest brother brings back a full back-basket and confesses. Aküli, who is clever and knows everything beforehand, begs them to leave the great tree Wazakä standing: 'If you fell the tree, there will be a great water!' But the axe is guided by magic words — one brother chops a side soft, another chops his side hard, until the tree breaks. It falls toward the north, which is why the wild banana groves of that country belong not to men but to the Mauari, the mountain demons; and the standing stump is today the mountain Roroima itself, while the felled trunks lie across the Caröni river as its impassable cataracts. Out of the stump pours water and great fish. A basket is set over the stump to hold back the flood, but Makunaima, wanting a few more fish for the brooks, lifts it: the water bursts out with all its force and can never be stopped again. Each brother plants an Inajä palm-stem and climbs it as the world drowns; Aküli hides in the hollow of the trunk with his fire and warms himself — the fire catches his rump and turns to red hairs, which every agouti still wears. After the flood a second destruction follows, the Sinbrand or world-fire, and Makunaima then attempts the re-creation of mankind: first of wax, which melts in the sun, then of clay, which hardens in it — and from the hardened clay he transforms the people of to-day. The tale is told in one line or the other by the Arekuna shaman Aküli (mock-named for the agouti) and the Taulipang Mayüluaipu, who dictated it to Theodor Koch-Grünberg at camp-fires and on the river during his 1911-12 expedition, and stands as the Taulipang twin of the wider Guianese cycle of the wonderful tree whose stump becomes a mountain and whose waters become the flood.

functions: Explains the physical geography of the Pakaraima region: Roroima as the tree-stump, the Caröni falls as felled trunks, wild banana groves as the property of the mountain demons Mauari
Authorises the shaman's authority: the narrative is told by medicine-men, whose predecessors like Aküli 'know everything beforehand' and see the Mauari

Provides the calendar and subsistence frame: the flood explains the distribution of fish (abundant on the far side of the Roroima), and the cycle continues into fire, the making of people from clay, and the origin of hunting animals
Marks transgression: Aküli's concealment, Kali's disobedience, Makunaima's impatient lifting of the basket each leave permanent signs on the bodies of animals and men

variants.name: Arekuna version (Aküli)
variants.summary: The agouti found the tree Pupü first, and only later the great Wazakä; the brothers had no fire yet and took it from the small bird Mutüg by tying a cord to his tail; Aküli's rump reddens in the fire he lit inside the trunk-hole.

variants.name: Akawai version (Brett)
variants.summary: Makunaima's son rules the one-speech animals; the agouti Ahkoo finds the tree; the monkey Iwarreka, banished to fetch water, lifts the basket over the stump and releases the flood; the survivors climb a cocorite hill.

variants.name: Carib version (im Thurn)
variants.text_tradition: True Carib, recorded by im Thurn 1883
variants.summary: After descending from sky-land the Caribs find all food on one huge tree; the tapir discovers it, the woodpecker spoils the stalking, the rat leads to it; from the stump a flood flows and is stopped by an inverted basket — until the brown monkey raises it.

title.en: Ma'ndpe the Accursed Fells the World-Tree (Taulipang)
title.zh: 受咒者曼德佩伐世界樹

region.en: Mount Roroima, Taulipang country
region.zh: 羅羅伊馬山陶利潘格之地

period: Taulipang oral tradition; recorded 1911-12 (Koch-Grünberg), publ. 1924

source.work: Theodor Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roraima zum Orinoco, Bd. II: Mythen und Legenden der Taulipang- und Arekuna-Indianer (1924), Mythe 2

summary.en: In ancient time five brothers lived at the foot of the Roroima: Makunaima, Ma'ndpe, Anzikilan, Wakalaimbe and Anike. Aküli, then a human being, found deep in the forest the giant tree Wazakä, bearing every kind of banana, papaya, cashew, orange and maize, and told no one. Makunaima found the banana-fragment between his sleeping teeth; Kali stung by wasps came home with swollen eyelids; at last the eldest brother brought a full back-basket home and told everything. 'Tomorrow we will fell the tree!' said Ma'ndpe, the accursed. Aküli, who was very clever and knew everything beforehand, said: 'No, we will not fell it! If you fell the tree, there will be a great water!' But Ma'ndpe was stubborn, took an axe and hacked the trunk, saying the magic words that made the wood ever softer; Aküli warned again and again, taking every fruit-skin and beeswax to stop at once the holes Ma'ndpe hacked. The tree fell toward the other side of the Roroima, and many bananas fell there — that is why there are banana groves in the forest to-day that no one planted; they belong to the Mauari, the mountain demons, whose houses all the mountains there are, as the shamans say, who alone can see and speak with the Mauari. Much water pressed out of the tree, and many very great fish came out — but all went to the other side; there are still very many great fish there, and on this side only few and small.
summary.zh: 昔羅羅伊馬山下有五兄弟。阿庫利覓得巨樹瓦薩卡，百果具備而秘之。馬庫納伊瑪窺其齒；卡利為蜂螫而瞼腫；長兄負蕉滿筐而歸，盡告其事。曼德佩曰：『明日伐樹！』阿庫利豫知曰：『毋伐！伐則大水至！』曼德佩固執，以咒軟其木而斧之；阿庫利以果皮蜂蠟塞其斧穴。樹倒於山之彼側，蕉林遍布——今之野蕉林，皆屬山鬼毛阿利；薩滿獨能見之與言。水自樹出，巨魚隨湧——然皆往彼側；故彼處大魚極多，此側則稀而小。

sensitivity.note: Taulipang myth told by Mayüluaipu to Koch-Grünberg, publ. 1924; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: In ancient time five brothers lived at the foot of the Roroima: Makunaima, Ma'ndpe, Anzikilan, Wakalaimbe and Anike. These five brothers had great hunger and nothing to eat. Aküli, who in ancient time was a human being, found deep in the forest a giant tree, Wazakä, which bore every good fruit — all kinds of banana, papaya, cashew, orange, maize. He ate of it every day, but said nothing to the people.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古時候，五個兄弟住在羅羅伊馬山腳下：馬庫奈馬、曼德佩、安齊基蘭、瓦卡拉因貝和安尼克。這五個兄弟非常飢餓，沒有東西吃。阿庫利——古時候他還是個人——在森林深處發現了一棵巨樹瓦扎卡，樹上結著各種好果子——各種香蕉、木瓜、腰果、橙子、玉米。他每天都吃這樹上的果子，卻什麼也沒對人們說。

passages.text: Makunaima lifted Aküli's lip as he slept and found a piece of banana Wazakä-püu between his teeth. Kali climbed the tree against Aküli's warning and was stung in the upper eyelids by two wasps — since that time Kali has swollen eyelids. At last Ma'ndpe ate many bananas till his belly was full, filled his back-basket, and told his brother everything. 'Tomorrow we will fell the tree!' said Ma'ndpe, the accursed. Aküli, who was very clever and knew everything beforehand, said: 'No, we will not fell it! We will only gather fruits! If you fell the tree, there will be a great water!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬庫奈馬趁阿庫利睡著時掀起他的嘴唇，在他牙縫裡發現了一小塊瓦扎卡普烏香蕉。卡利不顧阿庫利的警告爬上了樹，被兩隻黃蜂蜇了上眼皮——從那時起，卡利的眼皮就腫著。最後，曼德佩吃了許多香蕉，直到肚子飽了，裝滿了他的背簍，然後把一切都告訴了他的兄弟。「明天我們就把樹砍倒！」被詛咒的曼德佩說。阿庫利非常聰明，事先什麼都知道，他說：「不，我們不砍倒它！我們只採果子！你們要是把樹砍倒，就會發大水！」

passages.text: But Ma'ndpe was stubborn, took an axe and hacked the trunk, saying the magic words; the wood became ever softer, and the axe bit ever deeper. Aküli warned still: 'Fell it not! Fell it not! Else comes much water!' He took all fruit-skins and beeswax and stopped at once all the holes Ma'ndpe hacked. The tree fell toward the other side of the Roroima, and many bananas fell there — therefore there are to-day banana groves in the forest which no one planted, and they belong to the Mauari (mountain demons): all the mountains there, Roroima and others, are their houses, so say the shamans, who alone can see the Mauari and speak with them. Much water pressed out of the tree, and many very great fish came out — but all went to the other side; there are still very many great fish there, and on this side only few and small.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但曼德佩很固執，他拿起斧頭砍向樹幹，念著咒語；木頭變得越來越軟，斧頭砍得越來越深。阿庫利仍然警告說：「別砍倒它！別砍倒它！不然會發大水！」他拿來所有果皮和蜂蠟，立刻堵住了曼德佩砍出的所有洞孔。樹朝羅羅伊馬山的另一邊倒去，許多香蕉落在那裡——所以今天森林裡有沒有人栽種的香蕉林，它們屬於毛阿里（山中的精靈）：那裡所有的山，羅羅伊馬山和其他山，都是他們的住所，薩滿們這樣說，只有薩滿能看見毛阿里並與他們交談。大量的水從樹裡壓出來，許多非常大的魚出來了——但全都去了另一邊；那邊至今仍有非常多的大魚，而這一邊只有少數的小魚。

title.en: Sinbrand: the Fire That Came After the Flood
title.zh: 天火：洪水之後焚世之焰

region.en: Taulipang country, Roroima
region.zh: 羅羅伊馬陶利潘格之地

period: Taulipang oral tradition; recorded 1911-12 (Koch-Grünberg), publ. 1924

source.work: Theodor Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roraima zum Orinoco, Bd. II: Mythen und Legenden der Taulipang- und Arekuna-Indianer (1924), Mythe 3-4

summary.en: After the great flood, when everything was dry, a great fire came. All the wild creatures slipped through a hole into the earth — no one knows where that hole stayed. It burned everything: the people, the mountains, the stones. The rivers dried up; therefore one still finds great pieces of coal in the earth. Makunaima made new people out of wax — but these melted quite away in the sun. Then he made people out of clay; these grew ever harder in the sun. Then he transformed them into human beings.
summary.zh: 大水之後，萬物既燥，天火至焉。百獸穿地穴而遁——穴在何處，無人知也。火焚一切：人、山、石皆燼；諸河盡涸——故地下至今猶得巨炭。馬庫納伊瑪以蠟造新人；日光之下盡融。乃以泥造人；日曬愈堅。遂化而為人。

sensitivity.note: Taulipang myth recorded by Koch-Grünberg, publ. 1924; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: After the great flood, when everything was dry, a great fire came. All the wild creatures slipped through a hole into the earth — no one knows where that hole stayed. It burned everything: the people, the mountains, the stones. The rivers dried up; therefore one still finds great pieces of coal in the earth.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 3; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大洪水之後，當一切都乾了的時候，來了一場大火。所有野生的生靈都從一個洞鑽進了地下——沒有人知道那個洞留在哪裡。火燒毀了一切：人、山、石頭。河流乾涸了；因此人們至今仍能在地下發現大塊的煤炭。

passages.text: After the great flood, when everything was dry, a great fire came. All the wild creatures slipped through a hole into the earth; no one knows where that hole stayed. The fire burned everything: the people, the mountains, the stones; the rivers dried up; therefore one still finds great pieces of coal in the earth to this day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 3; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大洪水之後，當一切都乾了的時候，來了一場大火。所有野生的生靈都從一個洞鑽進了地下；沒有人知道那個洞留在哪裡。火燒毀了一切：人、山、石頭；河流乾涸了；因此人們至今仍能在地下發現大塊的煤炭。

title.en: The Deeds of Makunaima: Men, Beasts, and the Singing Stone
title.zh: 馬庫納伊瑪之功業：人獸化石與鳴石

region.en: Surumü river country, Taulipang
region.zh: 蘇魯米河陶利潘格之地

period: Taulipang oral tradition; recorded 1911-12 (Koch-Grünberg), publ. 1924

source.work: Theodor Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roraima zum Orinoco, Bd. II: Mythen und Legenden der Taulipang- und Arekuna-Indianer (1924), Mythe 4-6

summary.en: Makunaima went to the other side of the Roroima, where he probably still lives to-day, and transformed men and women into rocks, as well as saüba ants, tapirs and wild swine: a rock near Koimelemong is a pig that sticks its head into the earth; at the Aruayä Mountains is a great pot with a basket inverted over it; at the Serra do Mel a hunting-bag turned to stone. A man had stolen a piece of urucü from Makunaima; Makunaima followed his trail, caught him, cut off his head, arms and legs, and transformed everything into stones, as one still sees them on a savanna of the Mairari Mountains — the savanna is called Anuntä-lemon, the 'urucü savanna'. There too stands a woman with her rump in the air, all parts visible. A Mutum bird is also to be seen close by: when a human being is going to die, the stone sings like a Mutum. Makunaima made all the hunting animals and fish. Then he met people who did not want to believe in the great water of which he had told them, and who wanted to go home: when they turned around he transformed them all into termite mounds, as many are still found on the side of the Mairari Mountains.
summary.zh: 馬庫納伊瑪越羅羅伊馬而居彼側，至今猶在。化男女為石，蟻、貘、野豬亦然：科伊梅勒蒙附近之石乃豬首入地者；阿魯雅揚山有大釜覆籃；賽拉多梅爾有石化獵囊。一人竊其烏魯庫；追而擒之，斬首截肢，盡化為石——其草原今名『烏魯庫草原』。又有婦石，臀翹而全形畢露。旁有穆通鳥之石：人將死時，石如穆通而鳴。凡獸與魚皆其所造。不信大水者，回首之頃盡化為白蟻塚。

sensitivity.note: Taulipang myth recorded by Koch-Grünberg, publ. 1924; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Makunaima went to the other side of the Roroima and probably still lives there to-day. He transformed there men and women into rocks, as well as saübas, tapirs and wild swine: a rock near Koimelemong is a pig that sticks its head into the earth; at the Aruayä Mountains is found a great pot over which a basket is inverted; at the Serra do Mel a hunting-bag transformed into stone.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 4; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬庫奈馬走到羅羅伊馬山的另一側，據說至今仍住在那裡。他在那裡把男男女女變成石頭，也把蟻木、貘和野豬變成石頭：科伊梅萊蒙附近的一塊石頭，是一頭把頭鑽進土裡的豬；在阿魯阿亞山有一口大鍋，上面倒扣著一只籃子；在梅爾山脈，有一只獵袋化成了石頭。

passages.text: A man had stolen a piece of urucü from Makunaima; Makunaima followed his trail, caught him, cut off his head, arms and legs, and transformed everything into stones, as one still sees them on a savanna of the Mairari Mountains — the savanna is called from it Anuntä-lemon, the 'urucü savanna'. There too is seen a woman with her rump in the air, all parts visible. A Mutum is also to be seen close by: when a human being is going to die, the stone sings like a Mutum.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 4; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一個人偷了馬庫奈馬的一塊烏魯庫；馬庫奈馬循著他的足跡追去，抓住他，砍下他的頭、手臂和腿，把一切都變成了石頭，人們至今仍可在邁拉里山的一片草原上看到它們——那片草原因此被稱為阿努塔-萊蒙，即「烏魯庫草原」。那裡還可以看到一個女人，臀部朝天，各部位都清晰可見。近旁還可以看到一隻穆圖姆鳥：當有人將要死去時，那塊石頭就會像穆圖姆鳥一樣鳴叫。

passages.text: Then he met the people who did not want to believe in the great water of which he had told them, and who wanted to go home. He said to them: 'Whither do you want to go?' When they turned around, he transformed them all into termite mounds, as many are still found on the side of the Mairari Mountains. Makunaima made all the hunting animals and fish.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 5; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著他遇到了那些人，他們不願相信他曾告訴他們的關於大洪水的事，想要回家去。他對他們說：「你們想往哪裡去？」當他們轉過身來時，他把他們全都變成了白蟻塚，至今在邁拉里山的一側仍可找到許多這樣的白蟻塚。馬庫奈馬造出了所有狩獵的動物和魚。

title.en: Makunaima the Aimarä Fish: the Stolen Fishing-Hook
title.zh: 馬庫納伊瑪化魚竊鉤

region.en: Roroima rivers, Taulipang
region.zh: 羅羅伊馬諸河陶利潘格之地

period: Taulipang oral tradition; recorded 1911-12 (Koch-Grünberg), publ. 1924

source.work: Theodor Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roraima zum Orinoco, Bd. II: Mythen und Legenden der Taulipang- und Arekuna-Indianer (1924), Mythe 5-6

summary.en: Then all the rivers dried up, and the fish stayed in the lakes and little brooks, and there was abundance of fish. Makunaima made fishing-hooks out of beeswax, but caught nothing, for when the fish bit they bit the hook in two. So he met a man who was fishing for Aimarä. 'What shall we do? We will steal his hook! I will transform myself into an Aimarä, and if he catches me and hauls me out I shall cheat him: when he strikes me on the head I shall make a mess and pretend to die. Brother, ask him for that fish to eat! I shall become the biggest Aimarä there is.' He sprang into the water, became the biggest Aimarä, and bit; the man hauled him out, struck him on the head, drew the hook from his mouth; the brother begged the fish, recognised it by its closed eyes, took it home — and it became Makunaima again. A second time he became a Piränya and snapped the hook away. When the man had gone off to work on the other side, the two brothers transformed themselves into crickets and sat in his back-basket, and so came over to the other side — where Makunaima and the eldest still live to-day. In the basket Makunaima conjured wounds upon his body, pulled them off, threw them on the path and transformed them into stones: 'Remain here! To all people who walk this path you shall cling!' — that is why people who walk this path suffer from wounds to this day.
summary.zh: 諸河既涸，魚聚湖沼，魚豐。馬庫納伊瑪以蜂蠟為釣鉤，無所得——魚齧即齧斷其鉤。乃化為大特拉希拉魚上鉤；人曳之出、擊其首，彼佯死；兄索魚而歸，魚復為馬庫納伊瑪。再化皮拉尼亞，齧斷其鉤。人往彼岸作工，兄弟化蟋蟀匿其背籃而同渡——至今居彼。籃中馬庫納伊瑪咒傷於身，摘而擲於道，化為石：『留此！凡行此道者，爾等附之！』故行此道者至今身多瘡傷。

sensitivity.note: Taulipang myth recorded by Koch-Grünberg, publ. 1924; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Then all the rivers dried up, and the fish stayed in the lakes and little brooks, and there was abundance of fish. Makunaima made fishing-hooks out of beeswax, but caught nothing, for when the fish bit, they bit the fishing-hook in two. So he met a man who was fishing for Aimarä.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 5; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著所有的河流都乾涸了，魚留在湖泊和小溪裡，魚多得數不勝數。馬庫奈馬用蜂蠟做魚鉤，卻什麼也沒釣到，因為魚一咬，就把魚鉤咬成兩截。於是他遇到一個正在釣艾馬拉魚的人。

passages.text: 'What shall we do? We will steal his hook! I will transform myself into an Aimarä and steal the hook from him. If he catches me and hauls me out, I shall cheat him: if he strikes me on the head, I shall make a mess and pretend to die. Brother, ask him for this fish to eat! I shall become the biggest Aimarä there is.' He sprang into the water, transformed himself into the biggest Aimarä and bit; the man hauled him out, struck him on the head, drew the hook from his mouth. The brother begged the fish, knew him by his closed eyes, took the fish with him — and it transformed itself again into Makunaima.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 5; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「我們該怎麼辦？我們去偷他的魚鉤！我要變成一條艾馬拉魚，從他手裡把魚鉤偷走。要是他抓住我、把我拖上岸，我就騙他：要是他打我的頭，我就裝死，弄得一團糟。兄弟，向他要這條魚來吃！我要變成世上最大的一條艾馬拉魚。」他跳進水裡，變成最大的一條艾馬拉魚，咬住了鉤；那人把他拖上岸，打他的頭，從他嘴裡取出魚鉤。兄弟討要這條魚，憑他緊閉的雙眼認出了他，把魚帶走——魚又變回了馬庫奈馬。

passages.text: The man went away to work on the other side, making manioc cakes for the journey. 'We will transform ourselves into crickets and sit in his back-basket!' They transformed themselves into crickets and sat in his basket, and so came to the other side, where Makunaima and the eldest brother still live to-day. In the basket Makunaima conjured wounds on his body and said: 'I am tired of these wounds! I will pull them off!' He pulled them off, threw them on the path and transformed them into stones: 'Remain here! To all people who walk this path you shall cling!' — that is why people who walk this path suffer from wounds to this day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 5; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那人到對岸去幹活，為旅途做木薯餅。「我們要變成蟋蟀，坐進他的背簍裡！」他們變成蟋蟀，坐進他的簍子，就這樣到了對岸，馬庫奈馬和大哥至今仍住在那裡。在簍子裡，馬庫奈馬在自己身上變出傷口，說道：「我受夠了這些傷口！我要把它們扯下來！」他把傷口扯下來，扔在路上，把它們變成石頭：「留在這裡！凡走這條路的人，你們都要纏住他！」——這就是為什麼走這條路的人至今仍受傷口之苦。

title.en: Akalapizeima and the Sun: Why We Grow Old
title.zh: 阿卡拉皮澤瑪與日神：人之所以老

region.en: Arekuna country, Caröni river
region.zh: 卡羅尼河阿雷庫納之地

period: Arekuna oral tradition; recorded 1911-12 (Koch-Grünberg), publ. 1924

source.work: Theodor Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roraima zum Orinoco, Bd. II: Mythen und Legenden der Taulipang- und Arekuna-Indianer (1924), Mythe 13

summary.en: In ancient time there was a very tall tree, which Walo'mä, the toad, climbed quite to the top. A man named Akalapizeima lurked every afternoon at the foot of the tree to catch her. 'If Akalapizeima catches me, I shall throw him into the sea!' She caught him by the hands, pushed him with her foot into the sea, loaded him on her back and swam with him to an island, where she left him under a tree on which carrion vultures sat; while he slept they covered him quite with their droppings. It was very cold on the island, and the man froze. The Morning Star would not take him up — 'you gave cassava cakes only ever to the Sun'; the Moon refused him too. Then came Wüi, the Sun, to whom he had given many cassava cakes: she took him into her boat, had him washed by her daughters, and wanted him for a son-in-law: 'You shall marry one of my daughters, but do not let yourself in with another woman!' Wüi stopped at a maloka; he went ashore anyway, met the daughters of the carrion vulture and fell in love with them. The daughters of the Sun scolded him; Wüi grew angry: 'Had you followed my counsel and married one of my daughters, you would have remained young and beautiful for ever like me. Now you remain young and beautiful only a short time; then you will grow old and ugly!' They slept; in the morning Wüi went away with his daughters and left Akalapizeima asleep: he found himself among the vultures, old and ugly, as Wüi had said. He married a daughter of the vulture and got used to the life. He was our forefather, the father of all Indians — that is why we remain young and handsome only a short time, and then become old and ugly.
summary.zh: 上古有巨樹；蟾蜍瓦洛瑪攀其顛。獵者阿卡拉皮澤瑪候樹下欲捕之；蟾言：『彼捕我，我必擲之於海！』遂執其手，以足踢入海，負之游至孤島，置於禿鷲樹下；鷲屎淋之。島寒甚。晨星不援——『爾薯餅惟供日也』；月亦拒之。日神惠伊至——彼薯餅多供於日——乃載之於舟，令諸女為之浴，欲妻以女：『娶我女，毋戀他女！』泊於屋而登岸；遇禿鷲諸女而戀之。日神怒曰：『若聽我言而娶我女，則恆如我之少且美；今爾美少不久，必老而醜！』晨惠伊攜女去；彼醒而處鷲群之中，老而醜矣。娶鷲女而安其生——彼即吾儕之祖，眾印第安人之父：故吾人少美不久，而老醌隨之。

sensitivity.note: Arekuna myth recorded by Koch-Grünberg, publ. 1924; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: In ancient time there was a very tall tree, which Walo'mä, the toad, climbed quite to the top. A man, named Akalapizeima, lurked every afternoon at the foot of the tree to catch Walo'mä. 'If Akalapizeima catches me, I shall throw him into the sea!' The man caught her; she seized him by the hands, pushed him with her foot into the sea, loaded him on her back, dove under and swam with him to an island. There she left him and swam back; she left him under a tree on which carrion vultures sat, which covered him quite with droppings while he slept.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 13; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古時有一棵極高的樹，蟾蜍瓦洛瑪（Walo'mä）一直爬到樹頂。有個名叫阿卡拉皮澤伊瑪（Akalapizeima）的男人，每天下午都埋伏在樹腳下，想捉住瓦洛瑪。「要是阿卡拉皮澤伊瑪捉住我，我就把他扔進海裡！」那男人捉住了她；她抓住他的雙手，用腳把他踹進海裡，把他馱在背上，潛入水下，帶著他游到一座島上。她把他留在那裡，又游了回去；她把他留在一棵樹下，樹上棲著食腐的禿鷲，他睡著時，禿鷲的糞便把他整個蓋住了。

passages.text: It was very cold on the island, and the man froze very much. Kaiuanög, the Morning Star, met him: 'I cannot take you up. You have given me nothing; you have only always given the Sun cassava cakes.' The Moon also refused him. Then came Wüi, the Sun. She took him into her boat, had him washed by her daughters and his hair cut, and made him beautiful again. Wüi wanted him for a son-in-law: 'You shall marry one of my daughters, but do not let yourself in with another woman!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 13; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 島上非常寒冷，那男人凍得厲害。晨星卡伊瓦諾格（Kaiuanög）遇見了他：「我不能帶你上去。你什麼也沒給過我；你一向只把木薯餅給太陽。」月亮也拒絕了他。接著太陽維伊（Wüi）來了。她把他帶上自己的船，命女兒們替他洗淨身子、剪去頭髮，使他重新變得俊美。維伊想招他做女婿：「你該娶我的一個女兒，但不可與別的女人廝混！」

passages.text: Wüi stopped at a maloka and went ashore with her daughters; he went ashore anyway, met some young girls, the daughters of the carrion vulture, and fell in love with them. The daughters of the Sun scolded him; Wüi grew angry: 'If you had followed my counsel and married one of my daughters, you would have remained always young and beautiful as I. Now you remain only a short time young and beautiful; then you will become old and ugly!' In the morning Wüi drove away with her daughters and left Akalapizeima sleeping; when he awoke he found himself among the vultures, old and ugly, as Wüi had said. He married a daughter of the vulture and got used to the life. He was our forefather, the father of all Indians. Therefore we live to-day in this condition: we remain only a short time young and handsome, and then become old and ugly.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 13; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 維伊在一座馬洛卡（maloka， communal house）前停下，帶著女兒們上了岸；他到底也上了岸，遇見幾個年輕姑娘，是食腐禿鷲的女兒，便愛上了她們。太陽的女兒們責罵他；維伊動了怒：「要是你聽了我的勸，娶了我的一個女兒，你就會像我一樣永遠年輕俊美。如今你只能年輕俊美一小段時日；過後你就會變得又老又醜！」早晨，維伊帶著女兒們驅船離去，留下阿卡拉皮澤伊瑪睡著；他醒來時，發現自己身在禿鷲中間，又老又醜，正如維伊所說。他娶了一個禿鷲的女兒，也習慣了這種生活。他是我們的先祖，是一切印第安人的父親。所以我們今日才落到這般境地：我們只能年輕俊美一小段時日，過後就變得又老又醜。

title.en: How the Moon Went Up to Heaven: the Liana Ladder and the Road of the Dead
title.zh: 月升天記：藤梯與亡者之路

region.en: Taulipang country, Roroima
region.zh: 羅羅伊馬陶利潘格之地

period: Taulipang oral tradition; recorded 1911-12 (Koch-Grünberg), publ. 1924

source.work: Theodor Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roraima zum Orinoco, Bd. II: Mythen und Legenden der Taulipang- und Arekuna-Indianer (1924), Mythe 14-15

summary.en: In ancient time Kapei, the Moon, was not in the sky but on the earth, and had a house here. He seized the soul of a child, put it into a pot and turned the pot upside down on the ground: the child fell sick, and a shaman was called to blow upon it in the night. Kapei hid in another great pot and bade his two grown daughters not betray where he was. The shaman forced into the house, smashed the pot, found the soul of the child, seized Kapei, thrashed him through, and drove him out: 'Stay here no longer! Go away from here!' Then Kapei thought where he should live. 'Cutia is eaten! Tapir is eaten! Wild swine is eaten! All the hunting animals are eaten! If I transform myself into a bird — a Mutüm? A Cujubim? They too are eaten! I go to heaven! It is better there than here! I will go, to shine for my brothers there below. Let us go, my daughters, to heaven!' They made a liana, Kapeyenkumä(x)pe, like a ladder, to climb up; a little bird from heaven carried one end up and tied it at the entrance of heaven; Kapei and his daughters climbed the liana into the sky. 'I remain here in heaven! Go higher, to light the way! I remain here to shine for my brothers below. You shall light the way for the people who die, so that the shadow may not remain in the dark!' He sent one daughter higher to another heaven, the other still higher to another heaven; he himself remained in the heaven above us — above our heaven, the Taulipang believe, are yet ten more heavens, one above the other.
summary.zh: 上古月神卡佩伊居地上，有屋焉。奪小兒之魂，納於釜而倒置之；兒病，召薩滿夜吹療之。卡佩伊匿於大釜，囑二女毋洩。薩滿破釜得魂，執卡佩伊痛毆而逐之：『毋復居此！去！』卡佩伊自思：『獸皆可食，鳥亦可食；天則勝此！吾往天，為吾兄弟下界而光。』乃結藤梯卡佩延庫馬佩，遣小鳥繫其端於天門；父女攀藤而升。『我居天！爾等升而照亡者之路，俾魂不滯黑暗！』遣一女更高之天，又遣一女更上之天；己居吾儕之上天——陶利潘格人言其上尚有十天，層層相疊。

sensitivity.note: Taulipang myth recorded by Koch-Grünberg, publ. 1924; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: In ancient time Kapei, the Moon, was not in the sky but on the earth. He had here a house. He seized the soul of a child, put it into a pot and turned the pot upside down on the earth: the child fell sick. Then they called a shaman and bade him blow upon the child in the night. Kapei was at enmity with the people. Kapei had two grown daughters; he hid in another great pot and bade his daughters turn the pot over him: 'Betray not where I am when the shaman comes! Betray not either where the child is!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 14; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古時月亮卡佩伊（Kapei）不在天上，而在地上。他在這裡有一所房子。他攫取了一個孩子的靈魂，把它放進一口鍋裡，又把鍋倒扣在地上：那孩子就病倒了。於是他們請來一位巫師，吩咐他在夜裡對孩子吹氣。卡佩伊與人們為敵。卡佩伊有兩個成年的女兒；他躲進另一口大鍋裡，吩咐女兒們把鍋扣在他身上：「巫師來時，不可洩露我在何處！也不可洩露孩子在何處！」

passages.text: The shaman came into the house and asked where the soul of the child was; the daughters did not betray it. He pressed into the house, smashed the pot with his club, then smashed the other pot too, and so found the soul of the child. He found also Kapei, who had hidden in the pot; he seized Kapei, thrashed him through, drove him out of the house and said: 'Stay here no longer! Go away from here!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 14; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巫師進了屋子，問孩子的靈魂在哪裡；女兒們沒有洩露。他擠進屋裡，用棍棒砸碎了那口鍋，接著又砸碎了另一口鍋，就這樣找到了孩子的靈魂。他也找到了躲在鍋裡的卡佩伊；他抓住卡佩伊，狠狠揍了他一頓，把他趕出屋子，說道：「不要再待在這裡！離開這裡！」

passages.text: Kapei thought where he should now live: 'Cutia is eaten! Tapir is eaten! Wild swine is eaten! All hunting animals are eaten! If I transform myself into a bird — a Mutüm? A Cujubim? They too are eaten! I go to heaven! It is better there than here! I will go, to shine for my brothers there below. Let us go, my daughters, to heaven!' They made a liana, Kapeyenkumä(x)pe, like a ladder to climb up; a little bird from heaven carried one end up and tied it at the entrance of heaven; Kapei and his daughters climbed the liana into the sky. 'I remain here in heaven! Go higher, to light the way! You shall light the way for the people who die, so that the shadow may not remain in the dark!' One daughter he sent higher to another heaven, the other still higher; he himself remained in the heaven above us — above our heaven are, the Taulipang believe, yet ten more heavens, one above the other.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 14; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡佩伊思量自己如今該住在何處：「刺豚鼠被人吃了！貘被人吃了！野豬被人吃了！一切獵物都被人吃了！要是我變成一隻鳥——穆圖姆鳥（Mutüm）？庫茹比姆鳥（Cujubim）？那些也被人吃了！我到天上去！那裡比這裡好！我要去，在那下面為我的兄弟們照耀。女兒們，我們上天去吧！」他們做了一條藤，名叫卡佩延庫瑪（x）佩（Kapeyenkumä(x)pe），像梯子一樣用來攀爬；一隻來自天上的小鳥把一端帶了上去，繫在天堂的入口；卡佩伊和女兒們順著藤爬進了天空。「我留在天上這裡！你們往更高處去，去照亮道路！你們要為死去的人照亮道路，好讓影子不至於留在黑暗裡！」他把一個女兒送到更高的另一重天，把另一個送得更高；他自己則留在我們頭上的這重天——陶利龐人（Taulipang）相信，在我們的這重天之上，還有十重天，一重疊著一重。

title.en: How the Moon Got His Dirty Face (Taulipang)
title.zh: 月面之垢（陶利潘格版）

region.en: Arekuna-Taulipang country
region.zh: 阿雷庫納-陶利潘格之地

period: Arekuna oral tradition; recorded 1911-12 (Koch-Grünberg), publ. 1924

source.work: Theodor Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roraima zum Orinoco, Bd. II: Mythen und Legenden der Taulipang- und Arekuna-Indianer (1924), Mythe 15

summary.en: Wüi and Kapëi, Sun and Moon, were in ancient time friends and went together. Kapëi was then very beautiful and had a clear face. He fell in love with a daughter of Wüi and consorted with her every night. But Wüi would not have it, and bade his daughter smear menstrual blood over Kapëi's face. Since that time they are enemies: Kapëi always goes far from Wüi, and is to this day quite dirty in the face.
summary.zh: 昔惠伊與卡佩伊相友而行。卡佩伊甚美，面明淨；戀惠伊之女，夜夜與之私。惠伊不許，命其女以經血塗卡佩伊之面。自此二人為仇：卡佩伊恆遠避惠伊，至今面垢如故。

sensitivity.note: Arekuna myth recorded by Koch-Grünberg, publ. 1924; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Wüi and Kapëi, Sun and Moon, were in ancient time friends and went together. Kapëi was then very beautiful and had a clear face. He fell in love with a daughter of Wüi and gave himself up with her every night. But Wüi would not have it, and bade his daughter smear menstrual blood over Kapëi's face. Since that time they are enemies: Kapëi always goes far from Wüi and is to this day quite dirty in the face.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 15; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 烏伊（Wüi）與卡佩伊（Kapëi），即太陽與月亮，在遠古時代是朋友，一同出行。卡佩伊當時非常俊美，面容潔淨。他愛上了烏伊的一個女兒，每夜都與她廝守。但烏伊不允許此事，便命女兒將經血塗抹在卡佩伊的臉上。自那時起，他們便成了仇敵：卡佩伊總是遠離烏伊，至今臉上仍十分骯髒。

title.en: The Moon and His Two Wives
title.zh: 月與其二妻

region.en: Taulipang country
region.zh: 陶利潘格之地

period: Taulipang oral tradition; recorded 1911-12 (Koch-Grünberg), publ. 1924

source.work: Theodor Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roraima zum Orinoco, Bd. II: Mythen und Legenden der Taulipang- und Arekuna-Indianer (1924), Mythe 16-17

summary.en: Kapëi, the Moon, has two wives, who are both called Kayuanög, one in the east, the other in the west — the two planets Venus and Jupiter. He is always with one wife: first he goes with the one who gives him much to eat, so that he grows ever fatter; then he leaves her and goes with the other, who gives him only little to eat, so that he grows leaner from day to day; then he meets the other again, who makes him fat again, and so on. The wife in the east quarrels with the Moon out of jealousy: 'Go to the other wife! Then you will grow fat again; with me you will not grow fat!' And he goes to the other. Therefore both wives are enemies and remain always far from each other. The wife who makes him fat said: 'This shall remain for ever the custom of these people!' — therefore many Taulipang and Makuschi have three or four wives. At sun- or moon-eclipse Olo'zän, who was formerly a human being and is now a demon in human form, strikes Wüi or Kapëi in the face with a club, so that blood flows over and the face darkens: it is a sign that there is war.
summary.zh: 月有二妻，皆名卡尤阿諾格，一東一西——即金星與木星也。月常與一妻偕：與肥妻則日胖；離而就瘦妻則日瘦；復遇肥妻而復胖，如是循環。東妻妒而詈曰：『往就彼妻！爾將復胖；於我則不能胖也！』月遂往。二妻因此為仇，永不相近。肥妻曰：『此俗當永為此人間之制！』故陶利潘格與馬庫希人多有三四妻。日月蝕之時，奧洛贊——昔為人今為人形之魔——以棍擊日或月之面，血流而面晦：此戰亂之兆也。

sensitivity.note: Taulipang myths recorded by Koch-Grünberg, publ. 1924; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Kapëi, the Moon, has two wives, who are both called Kayuanög, the one in the east, the other in the west. He is always with one wife: first he goes with the one who gives him much to eat, so that he becomes ever fatter; then he leaves her and goes with the other, who gives him only little to eat, so that he grows leaner from day to day; then he meets the other again, who makes him fat again, and so on. The wife in the east quarrels with the Moon out of jealousy: 'Go to the other wife! Then you will grow fat again; with me you will not grow fat!' And he goes to the other. Therefore both wives are enemies and remain always far from each other.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 16; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡佩伊，即月亮，有兩個妻子，都名叫卡尤阿諾格（Kayuanög），一個在東方，一個在西方。他總是與其中一個妻子在一起：起初他與給他許多食物吃的那個在一起，因此他變得越來越胖；然後他離開她，去與另一個只給他少許食物吃的妻子在一起，因此他一天天瘦下去；接著他又與另一個妻子相會，她又使他胖起來，如此循環不已。東方的妻子出於嫉妒與月亮爭吵：『去找另一個妻子吧！那樣你又會胖起來；跟我在一起你不會胖！』他便去找另一個。因此兩個妻子成了仇敵，彼此總是相隔遙遠。

passages.text: The wife who makes him fat said: 'This shall always remain custom for these people!' Therefore there are many Taulipäng and Makuschi who have three to four wives. At sun-eclipse or moon-eclipse Olo'zän, who was formerly a human being and is now a demon in human form, strikes Wüi or Kapëi with a club blows in the face, so that blood flows over it and the face darkens from it. It is a sign that there is war.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 16-17; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 使他變胖的那個妻子說：『這將永遠成為這些人的習俗！』因此有許多陶利潘人（Taulipäng）和馬庫希人（Makuschi）擁有三到四個妻子。在日食或月食時，奧洛贊（Olo'zän）——他從前是人，如今是化為人形的惡魔——用棍棒擊打烏伊或卡佩伊的臉，於是血流滿面，臉也因此變暗。這是發生戰爭的徵兆。

title.en: Tamekan, the One-Legged Man of the Pleiades
title.zh: 昴宿之獨腿人塔梅坎

region.en: Taulipang country (sky)
region.zh: 陶利潘格之地（天界）

period: Taulipang oral tradition; recorded 1911-12 (Koch-Grünberg), publ. 1924

source.work: Theodor Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roraima zum Orinoco, Bd. II: Mythen und Legenden der Taulipang- und Arekuna-Indianer (1924), Mythe 18-19

summary.en: Tamekän is a man with only one leg; the other was hacked off him on earth. Zilizoaibu had a wife, Wayülalë, who cared nothing for him but loved his handsome brother. Picking abacate-fruits up a tree, he was followed by his wife, who had secretly brought an axe: as he climbed down, halfway up the trunk, she hacked off his right leg. The little bird Koezäg sang to the brother in the plantation: 'His brother's leg his wife hacked off with the axe!' The brother ran home in fury; the wife wrapped him fast in the hammock so that he could not help, while the wounded man lay outside crying till midnight. Then the cripple raised himself at the doorpost, climbed the roof, and played on his reed flute 'tin-tin-tin'; and he spoke to his brother: 'Remain in the house! Raise good sons and good daughters! Good health and luck! I go away — but beware of the wife and mistrust her always!' — 'Whither goest thou?' — 'I go to heaven! I will be Tamekän, a body with one leg that remains behind!' The Pleiades are the head, the Aldebaran group the body, and Orion the leg that remained. When Tamekän went to heaven, always fluting 'tin-tin-tin', the wife released the brother; and he vowed revenge: catching her head in a hollow bee-tree, he thrust her in and sealed the hole — 'What you did to my brother you shall now pay me!' She cried for her children, made 'kenön-kenön' like an armadillo, and remained transformed into an armadillo. Later the father led his five children deep into the forest, burned the house behind them, and said: 'We will become Araiuäg, for these they do not kill and eat!' — and they vanished one behind the other into the forest; that is why the Araiuäg loves honey to this day, and fears no bees.
summary.zh: 塔梅坎者，獨腿人也；其腿在世為妻所斫。齊利佐伊布之妻惠雅拉勒不愛其夫而愛其弟。夫攀果樹，妻懷斧隨之；及降，半樹而斫其右腿。小鳥告其弟：『兄之腿，妻以斧斫之！』弟怒歸；妻裹之於吊床不得救，而傷者臥外哀號至半夜。傷者攀屋頂，吹葦笛『叮叮叮』，謂弟曰：『居家！育善子女！我往天，將為塔梅坎——獨腿之軀也！』昴宿乃其首，畢宿為其身，獵戶為其餘腿。妻聞笛而釋弟；弟復仇，誘妻首入空心蜂樹而封之——『爾所為吾兄者，今償於我！』妻呼其兒，作犰狳聲，遂化為犰狳。後父攜五子入深林，焚屋於後，曰：『吾儕將為阿拉伊瓦格——人不殺不食者也！』相繼隱於林；故阿拉伊瓦格至今嗜蜜而無懼於蜂。

sensitivity.note: Taulipang myth recorded by Koch-Grünberg, publ. 1924; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Tamekän is a man with only one leg; the other was hacked off him on earth. Zilizoaibu had a wife, Wayülalë, who cared nothing for him: he had a handsome brother whom she loved. Picking abacate-fruits, Zilizoaibu climbed the tree; she had secretly brought an axe, gathered the fruits he threw down, and waited only for the moment when he came down: as he was halfway up the trunk she took the axe and hacked off his right leg, as one still sees to-day. She returned to the house.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 18; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 塔梅坎（Tamekän）是一個只有一條腿的男人；另一條腿是在人間被砍掉的。齊利佐艾布（Zilizoaibu）有一個妻子，名叫瓦尤拉萊（Wayülalë），她對他毫不在意：他有一個英俊的兄弟，她愛的是那兄弟。齊利佐艾布為了採摘鱷梨果實而爬上樹；她暗中帶來一把斧頭，收集他扔下來的果實，只等他下來的時刻：當他下到樹幹半途時，她拿起斧頭砍掉了他的右腿，正如人們至今仍能看到的那樣。她回到了屋裡。

passages.text: The little bird Koezäg sang to the brother working in the plantation: 'Zilioai! Your brother's leg his wife hacked off with the axe!' The brother ran home in fury. Wayülalë lay in the hammock, gave him cassiri, and when night came wrapped him in the hammock so fast that he could not get out — not even to piss. The wounded man lay outside and cried with pain till midnight: 'O my brother, my leg is hacked off with the axe! Kill this woman!' But the wife did not let the brother out of the hammock.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 18; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 小鳥科埃察格（Koezäg）對在種植園裡幹活的兄弟唱道：『齊利佐艾！你兄弟的腿被他妻子用斧頭砍掉了！』那兄弟怒氣沖沖地跑回家。瓦尤拉萊躺在吊床裡，給他卡西里酒（cassiri），到了夜裡，她把他裹在吊床裡裹得那麼緊，使他無法出來——甚至連撒尿都不行。受傷的人躺在外面，痛苦地哭喊到半夜：『哦，我的兄弟，我的腿被斧頭砍掉了！殺了這個女人！』但妻子不讓那兄弟從吊床裡出來。

passages.text: The wounded man raised himself at the doorpost, climbed the roof and played on his reed flute 'tin-tin-tin'; he spoke to his brother: 'Remain in the house! Raise good sons and good daughters! Good health and luck! I go away. Raise a good family, but beware of the wife and mistrust her always!' — 'Whither goest thou?' — 'I go to heaven! I will be Tamekän, a body with one leg that remains behind!' The Pleiades are the head, the Aldebaran group the body, and Orion the leg that remained. Until this day Tamekän announces the winter: when he has gone to heaven there is much thunder and rain, the fish-shoals come, and you will eat many fish.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 18; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 受傷的人扶著門柱站起來，爬上屋頂，用他的蘆笛吹奏『叮—叮—叮』；他對兄弟說道：『留在屋裡吧！養育好兒子好女兒！健康與好運！我走了。養育一個好家庭，但要提防妻子，永遠不要信任她！』——『你去哪裡？』——『我去天上！我將成為塔梅坎，一個留在後面的獨腿之身！』昴星團是頭，畢宿星團是身體，獵戶座是留下來的那條腿。直到今日，塔梅坎預告著冬天：當他上了天，就會有許多雷鳴和降雨，魚群到來，你們將吃到許多魚。

passages.text: The younger brother remained with the wife, made house and plantation, and had with her five children. One day, going hunting, he found a bee-nest; leading her to it, he coaxed her to thrust her head into the hollow to gather the honey — and thrust her quite in with the piece of wood he had hewn out, sealing the hole. 'What you did to my brother you shall now pay me! You shall suffer what my brother suffered! I am very sorry for you, wife, but I can no longer bear what you did to my brother!' She cried at first aloud: 'My poor children! My poor children! Even if I am transformed into an armadillo, I shall always remember my children!' Then she cried ever softer, made 'kenön-kenön-kenön' like the armadillo, and remained transformed into an armadillo. Later the father led his five children deep into the forest, burned the house behind them, and said: 'We will become Araiuäg, for these they do not kill and eat!' — and they vanished one behind the other into the forest; therefore the Araiuäg loves honey to this day and has no fear of the bees.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 18; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 弟弟與那名妻子留了下來，建屋闢園，與她生了五個孩子。有一天，他外出打獵，發現一處蜂巢；他領她前去，哄她將頭探進樹洞裡去採蜜——隨即用他削出的那塊木頭把她整個推了進去，封住了洞口。「你對我哥哥所做的一切，如今要向我償還！你要受我哥哥所受的苦！妻子啊，我很為你難過，但我再也無法忍受你對我哥哥所做的一切了！」她起初放聲大哭：「我可憐的孩子們！我可憐的孩子們！即使我變成了犰狳，我也會永遠記著我的孩子們！」隨後她的哭聲越來越輕，發出「kenön-kenön-kenön」之聲，如同犰狳一般，就此化作了犰狳。後來，父親領著他的五個孩子深入森林，在身後燒了房子，說道：「我們要變成Araiuäg，因為他們不殺也不吃這種人！」——於是他們一個接一個地消失在森林之中；因此Araiuäg至今喜愛蜂蜜，也不懼怕蜜蜂。

title.en: Zilizoaibu and the Crystal Stones: the Origin of the Piranhas
title.zh: 齊利佐伊布與水晶石：皮拉魚之由

region.en: Arekuna country
region.zh: 阿雷庫納之地

period: Arekuna oral tradition; recorded 1911-12 (Koch-Grünberg), publ. 1924

source.work: Theodor Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roraima zum Orinoco, Bd. II: Mythen und Legenden der Taulipang- und Arekuna-Indianer (1924), Mythe 19

summary.en: The mother-in-law of Zilizoaibu gave her son-in-law Käliwaü fish to eat: she set an old calabash under herself and pressed her belly together, whereupon the fish came out of her uterus and fell into the calabash — that is why the Taulipang do not eat this fish to this day. The old woman bade him make a fish-trap, to make him believe she caught the fish with it; but the son-in-law, being a shaman, knew everything. He broke many crystal stones, such as are found at the Roroima, cut a leaf from the 'wild banana' and covered with it the stones at the river place where the old woman always went down and pressed the fish out of her uterus. When she went down to the landing she slipped on the stones and fell: the sharp stones cut her arms and legs and her whole body into little pieces, so that she died; the stones ate the flesh to the bones, then plunged into the river and transformed themselves into Arai — piranha fish — which eat people to this day. The liver of the old woman, cut by the stones, remained swimming on the water: one still sees it; the Taulipang call it Elima, the Brazilians Mureru brava — a water-plant with red leaves — and the heart of the old woman remained in the middle of the leaves: it is the heart-shaped seed of the plant.
summary.zh: 齊利佐伊布之岳母以卡利瓦伊魚饗其婿：置舊葫蘆於身下，壓其腹；魚自子宮出而落於葫蘆——故陶利潘格人至今不食此魚。老嫗令其婿製魚籠，詭稱以此捕魚；然婿為薩滿，盡知之。乃碎水晶石——羅羅伊馬所產也——以野蕉葉覆之於老嫗常臨之灘。嫻至灘而滑倒；利石碎其肢體，逐段食其肉，遂死；石飽而躍入河，化為皮拉尼亞——至今食人。其肝浮於水，至今可見：陶利潘格名之艾利馬，巴西人名穆雷魯布拉瓦——紅葉水草也——其心在葉心，即草之心形種子。

sensitivity.note: Arekuna myth recorded by Koch-Grünberg, publ. 1924; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The mother-in-law of Zilizoaibu gave her son-in-law Käliwaü-fish to eat: she took an old calabash, set it under herself and pressed her belly together, whereupon the fish came out of her uterus and fell into the calabash — that is why the Taulipang do not eat this fish to this day. The fish she gave to her son-in-law and to her daughter Wayülalë to eat; the latter knew nothing of it. But the son-in-law knew it, for he was a shaman.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 19; not verbatim.
passages.zh: Zilizoaibu的岳母把Käliwaü魚給她的女婿吃：她取來一隻舊葫蘆，置於自己身下，將腹部一擠，那魚便從她的子宮裡出來，落進葫蘆之中——這就是Taulipang人至今不吃這種魚的緣故。她把這魚給女婿和女兒Wayülalë吃；後者對此一無所知。但女婿卻知道，因為他是個巫師。

passages.text: The old woman bade him make a fish-trap: she wanted to make him believe she caught the fish with it. But the son-in-law knew everything. He broke many crystal stones, such as are found at the Roroima; then he cut a leaf from the 'wild banana' and covered with it the stones at the river place where the old woman always went down, pressed the fish out of her uterus, and washed them to make the son-in-law believe she drew the fish from the river.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 19; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 老婦人命他做一個魚簍：她想讓他相信她是用這魚簍捕到魚的。但女婿什麼都知道。他砸碎了許多水晶石，就是Roroima所產的那種；然後他從「野香蕉」上割下一片葉子，用它蓋住老婦人常去下水的那處河邊的石頭，把魚從她的子宮裡擠出來，又將它們洗淨，好讓女婿相信她是從河裡捕來的魚。

passages.text: When the old woman went down to the landing she slipped on the stones and fell: the sharp stones cut her arms and legs and her whole body into little pieces, so that she died. The stones ate the flesh to the bones, then plunged into the river and transformed themselves into Arai — piranha fish — which eat people to this day. The liver of the old woman, cut by the stones, remained swimming on the water; one still sees it: the Taulipang call it Elima, the Brazilians Mureru brava — a water-plant with red leaves — and the heart of the old woman remained in the middle of the leaves: it is the heart-shaped seed of the plant.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 19; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 老婦人下到碼頭時，在石頭上滑了一跤，跌倒了：那些鋒利的石頭把她的手臂、雙腿和整個身體割成碎塊，她就這樣死了。石頭把肉啃到只剩骨頭，隨後躍入河中，化作了Arai——食人魚——至今仍吃人。老婦人的肝被石頭割下，仍在水面上漂浮；人們至今仍能看見它：Taulipang人稱之為Elima，巴西人稱之為Mureru brava——一種長著紅葉的水生植物——而老婦人的心則留在葉片中央：那便是這植物心形的種子。

title.en: Kai Khusrau Takes the Throne and Rustam Does Homage
title.zh: 卡伊霍斯勞登基與魯斯塔姆朝賀

region.en: Throne of Iran (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 伊朗王座（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. III, Kai Khusrau secs. 2-3

summary.en: When Kai Khusrau acceded he sat upon the throne of king of kings, meted justice out to each, uprooting injustice from the earth: the moisture rained down from the clouds in spring and cleansed the face of earth from rust and sorrow, and the world was decked like Paradise by reason of his justice and his bounty. Rustam comes from Nimruz with Zal to offer homage, and the Shah descends from the throne to greet him: thou art the foster-sire of Siyawush and likewise of all men most wise and reticent. When Rustam marked the person of the Shah from head to foot the hero's cheek flushed up and his heart ached, so much reminded him of Siyawush: thou art the memory of thy sire.
summary.zh: 卡伊霍斯勞登基後執掌萬王之王寶座，剷除不義；春雲降雨，大地如天堂般因他的公義與慷慨而煥然一新。魯斯塔姆攜扎勒自尼姆魯茲前來朝賀；王親自下座相迎：「你是西亞瓦什的養父，也是最賢明謹慎之人。」魯斯塔姆端詳王的容貌，面頰漲紅、心中作痛——太像他的父親了：「您正是令尊在世間的化身。」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; accession of the avenger-king. No living community restriction.

passages.text: When Kai Khusrau acceded, and the world had been apprised, he sat upon the throne of king of kings and donned the crown of greatness. He meted justice out to each, uprooting injustice from the earth. He cultivated waste lands and freed the mourners' hearts from woe; the moisture rained down from the clouds in spring, and cleansed the face of earth from rust and sorrow; 'twas decked like Paradise with goodly havings by reason of his justice and his bounty. The world was full of happiness and peace, the hands of Ahriman were barred from ill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Khusrau sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當Kai Khusrau登基，天下皆知之後，他坐上了萬王之王的寶座，戴上了偉大的王冠。他對每個人施以公正，將不義從大地上連根拔除。他開墾荒地，使哀悼者的心從憂愁中解脫；春天，濕氣從雲中降下，洗淨了大地的面容，除去其鏽跡與悲傷；因著他的公正與慷慨，大地以美好的物產裝點得如同天堂。世界充滿了幸福與安寧，Ahriman的雙手被擋在了作惡之外。

passages.text: When Rustam's standard came in sight, and the host's dust mounted o'er the sun, shouts rose with sound of trump and kettledrum. Now when Khusrau beheld the elephantine warrior tears trickled from his eyelids down his cheeks; descending from the throne he greeted Rustam, who kissed the ground. The Shah said: Paladin! live ever glad and happy, for thou art the foster-sire of Siyawush and likewise art of all men most wise and reticent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Khusrau sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當Rustam的旗幟映入眼簾，大軍的塵土高揚於太陽之上，伴著號角與定音鼓之聲，呼喊四起。此時Khusrau望見那位象一般的勇士，淚水從他的眼瞼淌下，流過雙頰；他從寶座上下來迎接Rustam，Rustam則親吻了地面。沙阿說道：勇士啊！願你永遠歡欣幸福，因為你是Siyawush的養父，也是所有人中最為睿智、最為寡言之人。

passages.text: When Rustam marked from head to foot the person of the Shah, and how he sat, held converse, and advised, the hero's cheek flushed up and his heart ached, so much reminded him of Siyawush. He thus addressed the world's king: to the world thou art, O Shah, the memory of thy sire; I have not seen a king with Grace like thine, or one so like thy father.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Khusrau sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當魯斯塔姆從頭到腳打量沙阿的周身，看他如何端坐、如何交談、如何進言，這位英雄的雙頰漲紅，心中作痛，因為這一切都令他如此想起西亞沃什。他於是對這位世界之王說道：沙阿啊，對這世界而言，你便是你父王的遺念；我未曾見過一位君王有你这般的靈光，也未曾見過一人如此酷似其父。

title.en: The Div Akwan Offers Rustam His Choice
title.zh: 魔阿克萬令魯斯塔姆擇地而擲

region.en: Waste of Turan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 圖蘭荒原（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. III, Div Akwan sec. 4

summary.en: The Div Akwan sees Rustam sleeping and delves the turf about him, raising it skyward: take thy choice to fall upon the mountains or the waves. Rustam reasons that the div will do contrary to what he says — if I say 'throw me in the sea' he will dash me on the mountains — so he quotes a sage of Chin: whosoever is drowned his soul will never see Suriish in Paradise; let me not fall upon the ocean, but drop me on the mountains that lions may behold a brave man's hands. The trick works: the div, acting contrary, drops him upon the sea, and Rustam fights his way to the shore past the crocodiles.
summary.zh: 魔阿克萬見魯斯塔姆熟睡，便掘起他四周的土層拋上半空：「山與海，任你擇一。」魯斯塔姆料定此魔必反其道而行——「若說『擲入海中』，他必摔我於山岩」——便詐稱「溺水者靈魂不得見蘇魯什；請把我丟上山，好讓獅虎瞻仰勇士之手」。魔果然反其道，將他擲入大海；英雄揮劍破浪，擊退鱷群游上岸來。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the wise-fool inversion motif. No living community restriction.

passages.text: When from afar Akwan saw Rustam sleeping he came as swift as wind, delved round about the place where Rustam lay, and raised it skyward. When Rustam woke from sleep he woke to sorrow, and his wise head was filled with consternation: so this foul div hath laid for me a snare like this! Who will take vengeance on this curst div? No one will match him now. Then said Akwan to Rustam in his plight: now, elephantine chieftain! take thy choice to fall upon the mountains or the waves; so whither shall I fling thee far from men?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Div Akwan sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿夸恩遠遠望見魯斯塔姆睡著，便如風般疾馳而來，在魯斯塔姆躺臥之處四周挖掘，將那塊地高高舉向天空。魯斯塔姆從睡夢中醒來，醒來便是愁苦，他那睿智的頭腦充滿驚惶：這邪惡的迪弗竟為我設下這樣的陷阱！誰來向這可詛咒的迪弗復仇呢？如今再無人能與他匹敵了。阿夸恩於是對身陷困境的魯斯塔姆說道：如今，象一般的首領啊！你且選擇，是要我把你拋向群山，還是拋向波濤；那麼，我該把你遠遠拋離人煙，拋向何方呢？

passages.text: The elephantine hero communed thus: in every case naught bettereth artifice. He will do contrary to what I say; he will not recognise an oath or keep a pact. If I say, throw me in the sea, then will this evil-natured Ahriman fling me upon the mountains, dash me there to pieces, and destroy me. A sage of Chin hath spoken well: whosoever is drowned his soul will never see Suriish in Paradise; let me not therefore fall upon the ocean to make the fishes' maws my winding-sheet, but drop me on the mountains that the lions and tigers may behold a brave man's hands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Div Akwan sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這位象一般的英雄心中思忖：無論如何，智謀總勝過蠻力。他必會反其道而行我所說的；他不會認什麼誓言，也不會守什麼約定。倘若我說，把我拋進海裡，那麼這惡性子的阿赫里曼便會把我拋向群山，在那裡把我摔得粉碎，將我毀滅。中國的一位智者說得好：凡溺死者，其靈魂永不得在天園中得見蘇魯什；因此，別讓我落入大海，以魚腹為裹屍布，倒不如把我丟在山上，好讓獅虎得見勇士的雙手。

passages.text: Akwan at this roared like the sea and answered: now will I fling thee to the place wherein thou wilt be lost for ever to both worlds. And, acting contrary to Rustam's words, dropped him upon the sea. As Rustam fell he drew his sword, and when the crocodiles approached they turned aside from fighting him. He struck out with his feet and his left hand while with his right he fought his way along, and struggled bravely and reached the shore, and gave praises to the Maker who had delivered thus His slave from ill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Div Akwan sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿夸恩聞言，如大海般咆哮，答道：如今我要把你拋到那使你永世在兩界俱歸滅亡的地方。於是，他反其道而行魯斯塔姆所言，將他丟入海中。魯斯塔姆墜落時拔出寶劍，當鱷魚逼近，牠們便退避，不敢與他交戰。他以雙足與左手划水，右手則一路搏鬥前行，奮勇掙扎，終於抵達岸邊，並讚美那位如此將祂的僕人從災厄中拯救出來的造物主。

title.en: Rustam Dashes Out the Brains of the Div Akwan
title.zh: 魯斯塔姆擊碎阿克萬之首

region.en: Horse-plain of Afrasiyab (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿弗拉西亞卜牧馬場（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. III, Div Akwan sec. 5

summary.en: Afrasiyab speeds forth like a blast to inspect his herds, and finds single-handed Rustam bearing them off: he rained shafts from his bow and strokes from his steel sword till sixty gallant chiefs were overthrown, and taking up his mace slew forty more. The div Akwan again encounters him: art thou not surfeited with strife? The peerless hero flings his twisted lasso about the div's waist, turns in his saddle, raises his mace as 'twere the hammer of a smith, smites the div upon the head and smashes it, brains and neck, then cuts off the head with his blue steel sword and offers up thanksgivings.
summary.zh: 阿弗拉西亞卜疾馳巡視馬群，卻見單槍匹馬的魯斯塔姆驅群而去——箭如冰雹、刀光似雪，掀翻六十員戰將，又提錘再誅四十。魔阿克萬再度現身：「你殺夠了嗎？」英雄擲出套索纏其腰，鞍上回身，高舉巨錘如鐵匠之鎚，一擊碎其頭顱腦髓，再以青鋼劍斬落魔首，感謝造物主賜勝。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: It happened strangely that Afrasiyab had sped forth like a blast to view his steeds, and brought with him wine, harps, and warriors to merrymake upon the watered plain. The monarch on arriving saw them not. Then suddenly rose clamour, and Afrasiyab saw far away the dust of Rakhsh and other noble chargers. The ancient herdsman rushed up franticly in evil plight: though single-handed, Rustam hath borne off our horse-herds, killed no few of us, and gone!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Div Akwan sec. 5 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 事情發生得蹊蹺：阿弗拉西亞布如一陣疾風般奔出，前去察看他的馬群，並帶了酒、豎琴與戰士，要在水草豐美的平原上作樂。這位君王抵達時卻不見他們。忽然間喧聲四起，阿弗拉西亞布望見遠處拉赫什與其他高貴駿馬揚起的塵土。那年邁的牧人驚慌失措地奔來，身陷困境：魯斯塔姆雖隻身一人，卻已擄走我們的馬群，殺死我們不少人，然後離去了！

passages.text: The monarch with four elephants and troops went in pursuit of Rustam, who, when they had overtaken him, took from his arm his bow and charged against them furiously. He rained upon them, as the clouds rain hail, shafts from his bow and strokes from his steel sword; he dropped his arrows and his scimitar when sixty gallant chiefs had been overthrown, and taking up his mace slew forty more. Afrasiyab in dudgeon showed his back while Rustam took the four white elephants.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Div Akwan sec. 5 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這位君王帶著四頭大象與軍隊追擊魯斯塔姆；當他們追上他時，他從臂上取下弓，猛烈地向他們衝殺。他如雲降冰雹般向他們傾瀉弓上的箭與鋼刀上的劈砍；當六十名英勇的首領被擊倒後，他放下弓箭與彎刀，拿起狼牙棒又殺了四十餘人。阿弗拉西亞布惱怒地轉身而逃，魯斯塔姆則奪得了那四頭白象。

passages.text: The div Akwan again encountered him and said: art thou not surfeited with strife? Thou hast escaped the ocean and the claws of crocodiles; now shalt thou behold thy fate, for never shalt thou seek to fight henceforth. The peerless Rustam roared out like a lion of the fray, released his twisted lasso from its straps, flung it, and caught the div about the waist; then Rustam, turning in his saddle, raised his mace as 'twere the hammer of a smith, and smote the div like some mad elephant upon his head and smashed it, brains and neck; the hero lighted, drew his blue steel sword and cut the div's head off, then offered up thanksgivings to Almighty God through Whom he had achieved the victory that day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Div Akwan sec. 5 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那妖魔阿夸恩又遇見了他，說道：你難道還沒厭倦爭鬥嗎？你已逃過大海與鱷魚的利爪；如今你將看見自己的命運，因為從今以後你再也不能求戰了。無與倫比的魯斯塔姆如戰場上的雄獅般怒吼，從皮帶上解下他盤繞的套索，擲了出去，套住妖魔的腰際；接著魯斯塔姆在馬鞍上轉身，舉起他的狼牙棒，如同鐵匠的鎚子，像一頭發狂的大象般擊中妖魔的頭，將他的頭顱與脖頸砸得粉碎；這位英雄下馬，拔出他青鋼的寶劍，砍下妖魔的首級，然後向全能的神獻上感恩，因他當日正是藉著神才得勝。

title.en: Gurgin Beguiles Bizhan; Manizha's Tent
title.zh: 古爾金誘比讚；瑪尼札之帳

region.en: Pleasure-ground near Turan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 圖蘭近郊樂園（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. III, Bizhan and Manizha secs. 4-6

summary.en: Gurgin, jealous, spreads his nets upon the young man's path: there is a pleasure-ground two days' journey from Turan where Manizha, daughter of Afrasiyab, will set up her pavilion with a hundred fay-faced handmaids; now if we go toward that pleasure-ground we may bear off some of those damsels. Bizhan, the son of Giv, follows youthful fashion, some whiles pursuing fame and some whiles passion. He comes beneath a cypress by the fair's tent; her nurse is sent out — can it be Siyawush returned to life? — and Bizhan answers: I am not Siyawush or fairy-born, but from Iran, the country of the free. They feast three days, and when her time for going home arrives Manizha mingles a drug that maketh senseless with his draught and carries the sleeper veiled in a woman's wrapper into the palace of Afrasiyab.
summary.zh: 古爾金心生嫉妒，在少年途中布下羅網：「圖蘭兩日之外有樂園，阿弗拉西亞卜之女瑪尼札將攜百名侍女設帳於此——我們或可虜得仙姿侍女！」比讚（吉夫之子）年少心熱，循情逐名。他立於帳旁柏樹下；奶媽出帳相問——「莫非西亞瓦什復生？」比讚答：「我非西亞瓦什，亦非仙胎，乃自由之邦伊朗人。」三日歡宴後，返程之期已至，瑪尼札在他的酒裡摻入迷藥，將昏睡的他裹以女袍，秘密載入阿弗拉西亞卜的王宮。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Iran-Turan star-crossed lovers. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Gurgin for his own profit and renown spread out his nets upon the young man's path and said: O paladin, thou Heart of combat, and Soul of wisdom! There is a pleasure-ground not far away, and only two days' journey from Turan, where thou wilt see a plain all red and yellow. Manizha, daughter of Afrasiyab, will make that garden radiant as the sun, and with a hundred handmaids, perfect pictures, all daughters of the Turkmans, will set up her pavilion on yon meadows. Now if we go toward that pleasure-ground and hurry o'er the journey in one day, we may bear off some of those fay-faced damsels, and win the approbation of Khusrau.
