summary.zh: 波斯人不許立神像、建廟壇，斥其為愚妄——因神不具人形。他們登高山祭「宙斯」（即蒼穹之環），祭太陽、月亮、大地、火、水與風。獻祭者於潔淨之地呼神名、頭戴桃金娘冠冠冕，只為「全體波斯人與君王」祈福；煮肉陳於青草之上，由瑪術士誦唱神譜頌歌——無瑪術士在場，祭祀即屬非法。

sensitivity.note: Greek ethnographic account of Persian ritual (Zeus = Ahura Mazda, Mitra = Anahita?); read as classical witness. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Images and temples and altars they do not account it lawful to erect, nay they even charge with folly those who do these things; and this, as it seems to me, because they do not account the gods to be in the likeness of men, as do the Hellenes. But it is their wont to perform sacrifices to Zeus going up to the most lofty of the mountains, and the whole circle of the heavens they call Zeus: and they sacrifice to the Sun and the Moon and the Earth, to Fire and to Water and to the Winds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Herodotus 1.131 (Macaulay 1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們不認為立神像、建神廟、設祭壇是合法的，甚至斥責那些做這些事的人為愚妄；依我看來，這是因為他們不像希臘人那樣，認為諸神具有人的形貌。他們的習俗是登上最高的山向宙斯獻祭，並把整個天穹稱為宙斯；他們也向太陽、月亮、大地、火、水與風獻祭。

passages.text: When a man wishes to sacrifice to any one of the gods, he leads the animal for sacrifice to an unpolluted place and calls upon the god, having his tiara wreathed round generally with a branch of myrtle. For himself alone separately the man who sacrifices may not request good things in his prayer, but he prays that it may be well with all the Persians and with the king.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Herodotus 1.132 (Macaulay 1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當一個人想向諸神中的某一位獻祭時，他將用作祭品的牲畜牽到一處潔淨無穢之地，呼喚該神，頭上通常纏繞著一枝桃金孃。獻祭者不得在祈禱中單為自己祈求福祉，而是祈願全體波斯人和國王一切安好。

passages.text: And when he has cut up the victim into pieces and boiled the flesh, he spreads a layer of the freshest grass and especially clover, upon which he places forthwith all the pieces of flesh; and when he has placed them in order, a Magian man stands by them and chants over them a theogony, seeing that without a Magian it is not lawful for them to make sacrifices. Of all days their wont is to honour most that on which they were born; and to wine-drinking they are very much given.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Herodotus 1.132-133 (Macaulay 1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他將祭牲切成碎塊並把肉煮熟後，便鋪上一層最新鮮的草，尤其是三葉草，隨即把所有肉塊置於其上；待他排列整齊，便有一名麻葛（Magian）站在旁邊，對之吟誦神譜，因為沒有麻葛，他們便不得獻祭。在所有的日子中，他們的習俗是最尊崇自己出生的那一天；而他們也非常嗜好飲酒。

title.en: The Parsi Flight to Sanjan and the Sixteen Schloks
title.zh: 帕西人渡海至桑詹與十六讚頌

region.en: Sanjan, coast of Gujarat (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 古吉拉特桑詹海岸（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded 15th-17th century CE (Qissa-i Sanjan; Karaka translation 1884)

source.work: Qissa-i Sanjan, in D. F. Karaka, History of the Parsis, vol. I (1884), ch. I

summary.en: Fleeing Persia after the Arab conquest rather than abandon the faith of their fathers, the Parsis make themselves exiles for ever; in a storm at sea they offer up a prayer to the throne of the Most High, and the storm abates and a gentle gale carries them in safety to Sanjan, where they land about the year 716. The dastur explains their sufferings to the liberal chief Jadi Rana, and the most learned among them prepare sixteen schloks or distichs in which they briefly describe the tenets of their religion: we are worshippers of Ahura Mazda and the sun and the five elements; we wear the sacred garment, the sudra or shirt, the kusti or cincture for the loins.
summary.zh: 阿拉伯人征服波斯後，帕西人不肯背棄祖傳信仰，寧為萬世流亡。海上風暴中，他們向至高者禱告，風浪頓息，和風將船隊平安送抵桑詹（約公元716年）。祭司向寬仁的酋長賈迪·拉納陳情；族中賢者遂作十六聯頌詩概括其教義：「我們崇奉阿胡拉·馬茲達、太陽與五行；我們穿聖衣——聖衫與腰間聖帶。」

sensitivity.note: Living-tradition narrative (Parsi community charter myth); recorded respectfully from published 19th-century translation. No restricted content.

passages.text: Rather than abandon the faith they had inherited from their fathers, they had voluntarily made themselves exiles for ever from the land that gave them birth. In their helplessness they called to mind Him who is the author of all good, the Preserver, Supporter, and Cherisher of the poor and the distressed: deliver us, O Merciful Providence, from this trouble, and lead us to the right path, that we may escape from this sea to the shores of India; and we promise, O Lord, to kindle on high the flame sacred to Thee in grateful remembrance of Thy kindness and protection.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Qissa-i Sanjan, in Karaka, History of the Parsis I, ch. 1 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們寧可自願永遠流亡異鄉，也不願捨棄從父輩繼承下來的信仰，離開那生養他們的土地。在無助之中，他們想起了那位一切美善的根源，那窮苦與受難者的保存者、扶持者與撫育者：哦，慈悲的天意啊，求祢救我們脫離這患難，引我們走上正路，使我們能逃離這片大海，抵達印度的海岸；哦，主啊，我們許諾，為感念祢的恩慈與庇護，必在高處點燃獻給祢的聖火。

passages.text: We cannot doubt that this prayer of faith was heard, for the storm abated, and a gentle gale carried them in safety to Sanjan, some twenty-five miles south of Daman, where they landed about the year 716. The territory of Sanjan was then under the rule of a wise and liberal chief named Jadi Rana, to whom a venerable dastur or high priest of the Parsis was sent, with suitable presents, in order to ascertain from him the terms on which they would be permitted to land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Qissa-i Sanjan, in Karaka, History of the Parsis I, ch. 1 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 我們不能懷疑這出於信心的祈禱已被垂聽，因為風暴平息了，一陣和緩的微風將他們安然送抵桑詹（Sanjan）——此地約在達曼（Daman）以南二十五英里處——他們大約於公元716年在此登陸。當時桑詹的領地由一位明智而寬厚的首領賈迪·拉納（Jadi Rana）統治，他們派了一位德高望重的帕西人達斯圖爾（dastur，即大祭司）帶著合宜的禮物前去見他，以探明他們獲准登陸的條件。

passages.text: The most learned among them prepared sixteen schloks or distichs, in which they briefly described the tenets of their religion and their mode of worship: we are worshippers of Ahura Mazda and the sun and the five elements; we observe silence while bathing, praying, making offerings to fire, and eating; we wear the sacred garment, the sudra or shirt, the kusti or cincture for the loins, and the cap of two folds. Consequently, Sanjan became the adopted country of the Parsis.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Qissa-i Sanjan, in Karaka, History of the Parsis I, ch. 1 (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他们之中最有学问的人撰写了十六首什洛克（schlok）或对句，简要描述了其宗教的教义与崇拜方式：我们崇拜阿胡拉·马兹达、太阳与五大元素；我们在沐浴、祈祷、向火献祭与进食时保持静默；我们穿着神圣的衣物，即苏德拉（sudra）或衬衣、库斯提（kusti）或腰间束带，以及双褶帽。于是，桑詹便成了帕西人的定居之地。

title.en: Kais and Laili in the Schoolroom
title.zh: 凱斯與蕾莉同窗初戀

region.en: School of the Arab shaikhs (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿拉伯酋長學塾（象徵性定位）

period: Composed 12th century CE (Atkinson translation 1836)

source.work: Nizami, Laili and Majnun, trans. J. Atkinson (1836), Canto I

summary.en: In the school of the shaikhs of each tribe, Kais assiduously drew attainments and scattered pearls from lips of ruby hue; and there, of different tribe and gentle mien, a lovely maid of tender years was seen: her richly flowing locks were black as night, and Laili she was called. One single glance the nerves to frenzy wrought; and, when o'er Kais affection's blushing rose diffused its sweetness, from him fled repose. Love conquered both; they never dreamt to part; and, while the rest were poring o'er their books, they pensive mused, and read each other's looks: their only taste was love, and writing ghazels to each other's eyes.
summary.zh: 各族酋長的學塾中，凱斯勤學善辯、口吐珠璣；另有一位異族的窈窕少女——秀髮如夜，人稱蕾莉。「一瞥便令心神狂亂」；當愛情的玫瑰在凱斯心中綻放，安寧便棄他而去。二人相愛，從未想過分離；同窗苦讀時，他們只默默相視——「他們唯一的功課，就是為彼此的眼睛寫抒情詩。」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the Arab romance Persianised by Nizami. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Thence his attainments Kais assiduous drew, and scattered pearls from lips of ruby hue; and there, of different tribe and gentle mien, a lovely maid of tender years was seen: her mental powers an early bloom displayed. Her richly flowing locks were black as night, and Laili she was called, that heart's delight: one single glance the nerves to frenzy wrought; one single glance bewildered every thought.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Laili and Majnun (Atkinson 1836), Canto I; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 凯斯从此勤勉地汲取学识，自红玉般的唇间散落珍珠；在那里，一位性情温婉、出身异族的年幼可爱少女被人看见：她的心智才力早早绽放。她浓密飘逸的秀发黑如夜色，她名叫莱莉，那心之欢悦：一瞥便令神经狂乱；一瞥便使万念迷乱。

passages.text: Soon mutual pleasure warmed each other's heart; love conquered both, they never dreamt to part; and, while the rest were poring o'er their books, they pensive mused, and read each other's looks: while others various climes in books explored, both idly sat, adorer and adored. Science for them had now no charms to boast; their only taste was love, and love's sweet ties, and writing ghazels to each other's eyes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Laili and Majnun (Atkinson 1836), Canto I; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久，相互的欢愉温暖了彼此的心；爱情征服了两人，他们从未想过分离；而当其余人埋头苦读时，他们沉思默想，读着彼此的神色：当别人在书中探索各地风土时，两人却闲坐着，一个是爱慕者，一个是被爱慕者。学问对他们已无可夸耀的魅力；他们唯一的趣味是爱情、爱情甜蜜的纽带，以及彼此向对方的眼睛写下加扎勒（ghazel）。

passages.text: Immersed in love so deep, they hoped suspicion would be lulled asleep, and none be conscious of their amorous state; they hoped that none with prying eye, and gossip tongue invidiously, might to the busy world its truth relate. By worldly prudence uncontrolled, their every glance their feelings told; for true love never yet had skill to veil impassioned looks at will.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Laili and Majnun (Atkinson 1836), Canto I; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他们如此深陷爱河，便希望猜疑能安然入睡，无人察觉他们的情爱之状；他们希望无人以窥探之眼与搬弄是非之舌，心怀嫉恨地向忙碌的世人道出真相。他们不受世俗谨慎的约束，每一瞥都道出各自的情意；因为真正的爱情从来还没有本领随意遮掩炽热的目光。

title.en: Majnun in the Cave and His Father's Grave
title.zh: 瑪傑農穴居與亡父之墓

region.en: Rocky cave of Najd (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 納季德岩穴（象徵性定位）

period: Composed 12th century CE (Atkinson translation 1836)

source.work: Nizami, Laili and Majnun, trans. J. Atkinson (1836), Cantos V-VI

summary.en: To me the world is swallowed up: I see nothing but Laili, answers Majnun to his father's counsel in the cave; all is lost to me, save her bright image — father, mother, home, all buried in impenetrable gloom. Syd Omai, with unutterable grief, gazed on his son and parted from that dismal cave, wrapt in deepest anguish — but 'twas, alas, to his expected grave: gently he sank, by age and grief oppressed, from this vain world to that of endless rest. Majnun hears the sad tale, falls upon the earth insensible, and never rested night or day till he had reached the sad spot where lay his father's bones: his arms around the grave he flung, and to the earth delirious clung.
summary.zh: 岩穴中，父親勸子回頭；瑪傑農答：「世界於我已空無一物——除蕾莉倩影，父母家園盡埋於不透光的黑暗！」老父西德·歐邁悲不自勝，踉蹌離穴歸家——竟一臥不起，溘然長逝。噩耗傳來，瑪傑農撲地昏厥，日夜狂奔至亡父墳前，雙臂環抱墓碑、緊抓塵土，以懺悔之淚澆灑聖遺。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the mad lover's withdrawal (majnun = possessed). No living community restriction.

passages.text: Thy counsel, father, is the wisest, best, and I would gladly to thy wish conform: but what am I? a helpless wretch, a worm, without the power to do what I approve, enslaved, the victim of almighty love. To me the world is swallowed up: I see nothing but Laili; all is lost to me, save her bright image: father, mother, home, all buried in impenetrable gloom, beyond my feeling.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Laili and Majnun (Atkinson 1836), Canto V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 父亲啊，你的劝告最为明智、最为妥善，我本乐意遵从你的意愿：可我算什么呢？一个无助的可怜人，一条虫子，无力去做我所认可之事，被奴役着，成了全能爱情的牺牲品。对我来说，世界已被吞没：我除了莱莉什么也看不见；除她明亮的影像之外，一切都对我失去了意义：父亲、母亲、家，全都埋葬在无法穿透的幽暗之中，超出我的感受之外。

passages.text: Syd Omai, with unutterable grief, gazed on his son, whose sorrows mocked relief; and, hopeless, wretched, every thought resigned that once was balm and comfort to his mind. Then, showering blessings o'er his offspring's head, groaning, he parted from that dismal cave, and, wrapt in deepest anguish, homeward sped; but 'twas, alas, to his expected grave: gently he sank, by age and grief oppressed, from this vain world, to that of endless rest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Laili and Majnun (Atkinson 1836), Canto V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 赛义德·奥迈（Syd Omai）怀着难以言说的悲痛，凝望着他的儿子，儿子的忧伤使一切慰藉都成了徒劳；他绝望而凄苦，放弃了曾是他心灵慰藉与安慰的每一个念头。随后，他一边将祝福倾洒在儿子的头上，一边呻吟着离开那阴沉的洞穴，怀着最深的痛苦匆匆回家；然而，唉，那却是他预期中的坟墓：他被年老与悲伤所压，轻轻地从这虚妄的世界沉入无尽安息之境。

passages.text: He fell upon the earth insensible, and, grovelling, with a frantic air, his bosom beat, he tore his hair, and never rested, night or day, till he had, wandering far away, reached the sad spot where peaceful lay his father's bones. His arms around the grave he flung, and to the earth delirious clung; grasping the ashes of the dead, he cast them o'er his prostrate head, and, with repentant tears, bedewed the holy relics round him strewed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Laili and Majnun (Atkinson 1836), Canto VI; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他失去知覺，倒在地上，匍匐著，神情狂亂，捶打胸膛，撕扯頭髮，日夜不得安歇，直到他遠遊流浪，來到那淒涼之地，他父親的遺骨正安息於此。他雙臂環抱墳墓，神志昏亂地緊貼地面；他抓住亡者的骨灰，撒在自己俯伏的頭上，並以悔恨的淚水沾濕散佈於他四周的神聖遺骸。

title.en: The Fravashis Hold Up the World
title.zh: 弗拉瓦希守護世界

region.en: Sea Vouru-Kasha (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 烏魯卡沙海（象徵性定位）

period: Recorded in the Avesta, c. 6th-4th century BCE (Darmesteter translation 1883)

source.work: Farvardin Yasht (Zend-Avesta Part II), trans. J. Darmesteter, SBE 23 (1883)

summary.en: Through their brightness and glory, O Zarathustra! I maintain the wide earth made by Ahura, the large and broad earth, that bears so much that is fine, that bears all the bodily world, the live and the dead, and the high mountains rich in pastures and waters. Through their brightness and glory I maintain in the womb the child that has been conceived, so that it does not die from the assaults of Vidotu. Had not the awful Fravashis of the faithful given help unto me, those animals and men of mine would not subsist; strength would belong to the Druj, the dominion would belong to the Druj, the material world would belong to the Druj.
summary.zh: 憑弗拉瓦希（守護靈）之光輝榮耀——阿胡拉所造的寬廣大地、承載生者與亡者的高山草場才得以持立；胎中嬰兒才不致死於死神之手。若無忠信者的守護靈相助，牲畜與人類便不能存立——力量將歸惡魔德魯吉，王權將歸德魯吉，物質世界將歸德魯吉！

sensitivity.note: Avestan liturgical text; the Fravashis are the guardian-souls (Darmesteter compares the Hindu Pitrs). No living community restriction.

passages.text: Through their brightness and glory, O Zarathustra! I maintain the wide earth made by Ahura, the large and broad earth, that bears so much that is fine, that bears all the bodily world, the live and the dead, and the high mountains, rich in pastures and waters; upon which run the many streams and rivers; upon which the many kinds of plants grow up from the ground, to nourish animals and men, and to help the faithful.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Farvardin Yasht 9-10 (Darmesteter, SBE 23, 1883); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 啊，瑣羅亞斯德！藉著她們的光輝與榮耀，我維護由阿胡拉所造的廣闊大地，那遼闊而寬廣的大地，承載著如此多美好之物，承載著整個有形世界，生者與死者，以及那牧草與水源豐饒的高山；其上奔流著眾多溪流與江河；其上從地面生長出多種多樣的植物，以滋養牲畜與人類，並扶助信眾。

passages.text: Through their brightness and glory, O Zarathustra! I maintain in the womb the child that has been conceived, so that it does not die from the assaults of Vidotu, and I develop in it the bones, the hair, the entrails, the feet, and the sexual organs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Farvardin Yasht 11 (Darmesteter, SBE 23, 1883); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 啊，瑣羅亞斯德！藉著她們的光輝與榮耀，我在母腹中維護那已受孕的胎兒，使其不因維多圖的侵襲而死亡，並在其中培育骨骼、毛髮、內臟、雙足與生殖器官。

passages.text: Had not the awful Fravashis of the faithful given help unto me, those animals and men of mine, of which there are such excellent kinds, would not subsist; strength would belong to the Druj, the dominion would belong to the Druj, the material world would belong to the Druj. Between the earth and the sky the immaterial creatures would be harassed by the Druj; and never afterwards would Angra-Mainyu give way to the blows of Spenta-Mainyu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Farvardin Yasht 12-13 (Darmesteter, SBE 23, 1883); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 倘若信眾那可畏的弗拉瓦希未曾給予我援助，我那些種類如此優良的牲畜與人類便不能存續；力量將歸於德魯格，統治權將歸於德魯格，有形世界將歸於德魯格。大地與天空之間，無形諸造物將受德魯格侵擾；此後安格拉·曼紐便永遠不會屈服於斯彭塔·曼紐的打擊。

title.en: Nizami's Tale of Sikandar's Birth
title.zh: 尼扎米筆下的亞歷山大誕生

region.en: Roads of Rum (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 羅姆國土（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1200 CE (Clarke translation 1881)

source.work: Nizami, The Sikandar Nama e Bara, trans. H. Wilberforce Clarke (1881), Canto XV

summary.en: In this tale of Sikandar's birth are many disputes, says Nizami; from the sages of Rum thus it came: that of that land and clime, the wife of a devotee became helpless on the day of bringing forth; she deposited her burden in a desolate place and died, saying: I know not who will cherish thee; what wild beast will devour thee. King Faylikus, game-overthrowing, advanced toward that woman; he beheld a woman dead in that pathway, at her feet a child, head uplifted; from want of the mother's milk the child sucked its own finger. He took up the child from the dust of the road — and, by wisdom and judgment, King of the World he became, from Kaf to Kaf territory-conqueror.
summary.zh: 關於亞歷山大的誕生眾說紛紜，尼扎米取羅馬賢者之說：一位苦行僧之妻臨產無助，把嬰孩棄於荒野而亡，臨終悲呼：「誰來撫養你？哪只野獸會吞掉你？」英武的菲萊庫斯王行經此路，見產婦倒斃道上、腳邊嬰孩仰首吮指；他自塵埃抱起嬰兒——這孩子日後憑智慧與英斷，成為「自卡夫山至卡夫山」的征服者、天下之王。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Nizami's Iqbal-nama version of Alexander's birth legend. No living community restriction.

passages.text: In this tale of Sikandar's birth are many disputes: my ear is intent on everyone's speech. From the sages of Rum thus it came, that of that land and clime, the wife of a devotee became helpless on the day of bringing forth; she became a wanderer from her city and husband. When her time of burden-casting came near, the pang of delivery became strong upon her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Sikandar Nama (Clarke 1881), Canto XV; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在這則關於西坎達爾誕生的故事中，有許多爭議：我的耳朵專注於每個人的說法。出自魯姆的智者們如此傳說：在那片土地與地域，一位虔信者的妻子在分娩之日陷入無助；她離開了自己的城市與丈夫，成了漂泊之人。當她臨盆之期將近，分娩的劇痛便強烈地襲向她。

passages.text: She deposited her burden in a desolate place, and died; she suffered grief for the child and resigned her life to God, saying: I know not who will cherish thee; what wild beast will devour thee. Of this, news none heard, how the Omnipotent would cherish him in His bosom: what treasures He would draw within his load; what fortune He would draw into his bosom. When the woman died, that child remained friendless.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Sikandar Nama (Clarke 1881), Canto XV; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她在一處荒涼之地產下胎兒，隨即死去；她為孩子承受悲痛，將生命交託給神，說道：我不知誰會撫養你；什麼野獸會吞噬你。此事無人聽聞，全能者將如何把他抱在懷中撫養；祂將把何等寶藏納入他的負擔；祂將把何等福運引入他的胸懷。那婦人死後，那孩子便孤苦無依。

passages.text: From the enjoyment of the plain, King Faylikus advanced, game-overthrowing, towards that woman. He beheld a woman dead in that pathway: at her feet a child, head uplifted. From want of the mother's milk, the child sucked its own finger, and bit its own thumb in grief for its mother. He took up the child from the dust of the road — and, by wisdom and judgment, King of the World he became, from Kaf to Kaf territory-conqueror.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Sikandar Nama (Clarke 1881), Canto XV; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 法伊利庫斯王因平原之樂而前行，逐獵禽獸，朝那婦人而去。他見一婦人死於那條路上：她腳邊有一孩童，頭仰起。因缺乏母乳，那孩童吸吮自己的手指，又因思念母親而咬自己的拇指。他從道路的塵土中抱起那孩童——而他憑智慧與判斷，成了世界之王，從卡夫到卡夫，成為疆土征服者。

title.en: Darab's Son and Sikandar's Ambition
title.zh: 大流士與亞歷山大爭鋒

region.en: Field between Iran and Rum (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 伊朗與羅姆之間的戰場（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. VI, Dara secs. 1-6

summary.en: Dara harangued the chiefs and took order for the realm; and when Failakus died and Sikandar acceded to the throne of Rum, Sikandar went as his own ambassador to Dara, demanding tribute and submission. Dara fought with Sikandar and was worsted; the hosts fought a second time; and when Sikandar fought with Dara the third time, Dara fled to Kirman, his fortune sunk, the war-cry rising from both sides and the troops having little rest.
summary.zh: 大流士整軍經武；菲萊庫斯死後亞歷山大繼羅馬王位，竟親作使節赴波斯索貢。三度交鋒，大流士屢戰屢敗，終棄都奔往克爾曼——兩軍吶喊、征塵蔽日，士卒疲於奔命。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the Shahnama's Alexander-as-Persian-prince romance. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Sikandar went as his own ambassador to Dara, demanding tribute and submission; and Dara harangued the chiefs and took order for the realm. The two met in the field, and Dara fought with Sikandar and was worsted. Dara fought with Sikandar the second time; and when Sikandar fought with Dara the third time, and Dara fled to Kirman, the war-cry rose from both sides and the troops had little rest. Sikandar ranged his host, the air grew dark, earth viewless.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Dara secs. 1-4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Dara secs. 5-6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 西坎達爾作為自己的使節前往達拉處，要求貢賦與臣服；達拉則向首領們訓話，並為國度安排事務。二人在戰場相遇，達拉與西坎達爾交戰而敗北。達拉第二次與西坎達爾交戰；當西坎達爾第三次與達拉交戰，達拉逃往基爾曼時，雙方響起戰號，軍隊少有休息。西坎達爾布列其軍，天色轉暗，大地不可見。

title.en: Nizami on Dara's Murder and Sikandar's Victory
title.zh: 尼扎米詠大流士之弑

region.en: Night-camp of the two hosts (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 兩軍夜營（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1200 CE (Clarke translation 1881)

source.work: Nizami, The Sikandar Nama e Bara, trans. H. Wilberforce Clarke (1881), Canto XXX

summary.en: The representer of the verse of this history uttered words according to the manner of truthful ones: when the fire of the bright day passed away the vault swiftly revolving became full of the smoke of darkness. Both armies secretly prayer-uttering, saying: would that to-night had been long, perhaps its length would have made delay, the battle-day would have appeared with great delay. Then Dara's own officers abandoned the right due to favours of obligation to the king; they took up the pursuit of slaying the king — and when the thief took the ruby of the sun, the world pressed its foot in ruby-seeking: the murderer of Dara won no glory, and the kingdom passed to Sikandar.
summary.zh: 尼扎米寫道：白日之火熄滅、夜幕如煙籠罩穹廬；兩軍各自密禱：「但願今夜長些，好讓決戰之日遲些來臨！」然而大流士麾下重臣竟背棄君恩、陰謀弑主——「竊賊竊走紅寶石般的落日」——弑君者未得榮耀，江山終歸亞歷山大。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Nizami's moralising version of the regicide. No living community restriction.

passages.text: The representer of the verse of this history uttered words according to the manner of true ones, saying: when the fire of the bright day passed away, the vault swiftly revolving became full of the smoke of the darkness of night. Night established the ornament of the moon; the light of the moon in the dark shade of night was a wonderful thing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Sikandar Nama (Clarke 1881), Canto XXX; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這部歷史之詩的敘述者依循真誠者之方式說出話語，說道：當明亮白晝之火消逝，那迅速旋轉的穹蒼便充滿了黑夜暗影之煙。夜確立了月亮的裝飾；月光在夜的幽暗陰影中，是奇妙之事。

passages.text: Both armies secretly prayer-uttering, saying: would that to-night had been long; perhaps its length would have made delay; the battle-day would have appeared with great delay. By the coming and going of the watchman the night bird rested not; from fear of the raging elephant many a sleeper leaped from sleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Sikandar Nama (Clarke 1881), Canto XXX; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兩軍都暗自祈禱，說道：但願今夜漫長；或許其長度能使之延遲；戰鬥之日將以極大的延遲出現。因守夜人的來去，夜鳥不得安息；因懼怕那狂怒的大象，許多睡眠者從睡中驚起。

passages.text: They abandoned the right due to favours of obligation to the king; they took up the pursuit of slaying the king. When the thief took the ruby of the sun, the world pressed its foot in ruby-seeking; with theft of the sun they seized the moon, saying it took away that pure jewel, the setting sun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nizami, Sikandar Nama (Clarke 1881), Canto XXX; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們因對國王所負恩義之惠而捨棄正道；他們興起追殺國王之事。當盜賊取走太陽的紅寶石，世界便舉足尋求紅寶石；隨著太陽被竊，他們奪取了月亮，說它奪走了那純淨的寶石，即西沉的太陽。

title.en: How the World Began: Sky Woman's Fall and the Two Minds
title.zh: 世界之肇始：天女墜落與兩位心智

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin for Seneca oral tales)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（塞內卡口傳故事的採集定位）

period: Recorded 1900s-1922 from Seneca informants on the Cattaraugus Reservation (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. IV tale 1, 'How the World Began' (1923)

summary.en: In the sky world the Ancient One uproots the great tree at his dream's command and thrusts his pregnant wife through the hole; as she falls, the Fire Beast gives her corn, mortar, pot and pestle, and the water creatures receive her on the great turtle's back, where muskrat brings up earth. Her daughter dies giving birth to twins, and from her grave spring the beans, squash, corn and tobacco; Good Mind finishes the world, releases the animals from the bags of life, and seals his destructive brother Tawiskaron in the cave before molding the first men from clay.
summary.zh: 在天上世界中，遠古者依夢境之命連根拔起大樹，將懷孕的妻子推入洞中；她墜落時，火獸賜她玉米、臼、缽與杵，水中眾獸以巨龜之背承接她，麝鼠潛水取土。其女產下雙生而死，墓上生出豆、南瓜、玉米與菸草；善心者完成世界，自生命之袋釋出百獸，將其破壞之弟塔威斯卡隆封入洞穴，再以黏土捏塑最早的人類。

language: Seneca oral tradition told in English
canonical_translation: Arthur C. Parker's English text (1923)

narrative.en:
Parker's fullest Seneca account of creation opens above the sky. Beyond the dome is another world, a floating land where the great chief and his celestial people live around a central tree of light whose roots run in four directions and whose luminous blossom fills the air with the perfume of burning tobacco. Dreaming, the Ancient One desires a maiden and marries her; she conceives from his potent breath, and his anger at finding her already with child drives the plot. Another dream commands him to uproot the celestial tree; his people try and fail, he uproots it himself, and leads his wife Iagen'tci (the Sky Woman) to peer into the hole. Pushed through it in rage, she snatches as she falls a handful of seeds and the tobacco leaf, and drops through the crust of the sky world.

Below is an unformed sea. As she falls, a fire-emitting beast named Gaa'siohdie't'ha' hands her a small pot, a corn mortar, a pestle, a marrow bone and an ear of corn, with the grim promise that all who eat will one day see him last of all. The water creatures, among them the spirits of Wind, the Defending Face, Thunder and Heavy Night, take council: ducks interlace their wings to receive her, the great turtle rises from below to offer his back, and muskrat alone touches bottom, smearing a little earth on the shell, which grows until it is an island world. The woman shakes out the seeds and sets the root she held, and a new tree of light rises over the turtle island.

Her daughter grows up swinging on a vine, laughs as if embraced, and bears twins, one kind and one warty and savage who tears his way out through his mother's side, killing her. From the daughter's grave, tended by Good Mind, sprout the stringed potato, beans, squash, corn and tobacco: the Three Sisters and the sacred plant grow out of a death. Grandmother Sky Woman then names the animals when Good Mind releases them from the bags of life his father gave him after his four-fold ordeal on the mountain of the east (he casts the cliff, swims the cataract, wrestles Wind and endures flame), and anoints the fat ones in a pool of oil. His jealous brother Tawiskaron (Evil Mind, Flint) follows behind, breeding thorns, poison plants and slimes, and twice attacks Good Mind with cat-tail flags and deer horns. Good Mind wins the final fight and banishes him to the cave with all the enchanted beasts, where he still gives orders. The whirlwind Great Defender is mastered with the mountain-moving test and his bent, twisted face becomes the likeness carved for the False Face Society; Thunder is engaged to slay whatever escapes the cave. At last Good Mind molds men and women of clay in his own image, teaches them hunting, fishing and the incense of tobacco, and departs up the sky road with the first beings.

The story is the anchor record of the Haudenosaunee cosmos: a matrilineal world built downward from a violated marriage and upward from a grave, with the twin polarity (Good Mind / Flint) that the Maya Hero Twins, the Navajo Changing-Bear Twins and countless dual-creator systems share. Its ritual harvest is enormous: corn as milk, tobacco as speech to the Creator, the False Face masks as Defender's contract, the cave as the residence of the Destroyer.

functions: Cosmogony: explains the earth as Turtle Island built by co-operative water beings
Agricultural charter: corn, beans, squash and tobacco grow from the murdered daughter's grave
Ritual charter: tobacco incense, False Face carving and Thunder's pest-control all contracted in the tale
Dualistic ethics: Good Mind finishes and beautifies, Flint spoils; sickness and mischief trace to the cave

variants.summary: In another version the sky chief is killed and hidden in the tree's trunk; a rival chief marries his daughter, and it is the bride who demands the tree be uprooted to hunt for her father's body - Parker compares the Osiris motif.
