sensitivity_guidance: A central living-tradition narrative of the Haudenosaunee. Presented here from public-domain colonial-era transcriptions with respect; ceremonial details of False Face rituals are not disclosed.

sensitivity.note: Living Haudenosaunee tradition recorded 1900s-1922; published in Parker 1923 (public domain). Included as sacred narrative of record; not a ritual manual. Cross-tradition tagging of 'clay-humans' and 'sibling-creators' is an interpretive act (Thompson index is Euro-American).

passages.text: Beyond the dome we call the sky there is another world, a fair country where lived the great chief of the up-above-world and his celestial people. In the center of that world grew a great tree whose luminous blossom lighted the sky land, and whose roots ran in four directions. The Ancient One dreamed he must take as wife a certain fair maiden; when he found she was already with child he fell into a troubled sleep, and a dream commanded him to have the celestial tree uprooted as a punishment to his wife. She too found pleasure in the uprooting, wishing to know what was beneath it.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 59-60; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在我們稱為天空的穹頂之外，還有另一個世界，一個美好的國度，那裡住著上界世界的偉大首領及其天界子民。那世界的中央長著一棵大樹，其發光的花朵照亮了天界之地，其根向四方伸展。那古老者夢見他必須娶某位美麗的少女為妻；當他發現她已有身孕，便陷入不安的睡眠，一個夢命令他將那棵天樹連根拔起，作為對其妻子的懲罰。她也從這拔樹之事中尋得樂趣，想要知道樹下有什麼。

passages.text: The chief led his wife to the hole and seated her on its edge to peer downward; long she sat looking, until in rage he drew her blanket over her head and pushed her with his foot to thrust her into the hole. As she fell she gathered in her fingers all manner of seeds, and the tobacco leaf that grew from the broken root. Below, the creature-beings saw her coming and took council: the duck-creatures received her on their interknit wings, the great turtle made his back a resting-place, and muskrat alone touched the bottom and smeared earth upon the shell, whereupon the earth grew and the turtle grew with it.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 61-62; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 首領將妻子帶到洞口，讓她坐在洞邊向下窺望；她久久坐著觀看，直到他發怒，把她的毯子蒙上她的頭，又用腳踢她，要把她推入洞中。她墜落時，用手指收攏了各式各樣的種子，還有從斷根上長出的煙草葉。在下方，那些生靈看見她落下，便聚在一起商議：鴨族生靈以彼此交織的翅膀接住她，大龜以背作為安歇之處，唯有麝鼠觸到了底，把泥土抹在龜殼上，於是大地生長，龜也隨之生長。

passages.text: In due season the Sky Woman bore a daughter, and the daughter, swinging on a vine as if embraced by a lover, bore twin boys. The words of one were kind, but the other, warty and savage, pierced his mother through the arm pit and stood upon her dead body. Where the daughter's feet were buried the stringed potato sprouted; from her fingers the beans; from her abdomen the squash; from her breasts the corn; and from her brow the tobacco. 'By these things we shall hereafter live,' said the grandmother, 'and the corn shall be your milk.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 63-64; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了時候，天空女產下一名女兒，這女兒如被情人擁抱般攀著藤蔓擺盪，產下一對雙生男孩。其中一個言語溫和，另一個卻滿身疣瘤、野蠻凶暴，從母親腋下刺穿而出，站在她死去的軀體上。女兒雙足埋入之處，長出串狀的馬鈴薯；從她的手指長出豆子；從她的腹部長出南瓜；從她的乳房長出玉米；從她的額頭長出煙草。「今後我們將靠這些東西過活，」祖母說，「玉米將是你們的乳汁。」

passages.text: After his father's ordeal by the mountain of the east, Good Mind opened the bags of life and the animals rushed forth. Twice his warty brother attacked him, first with cat-tail flags, then with deer horns, until Good Mind disarmed him and banished him to the mouth of the great cave with all the enchanted beasts, naming him Destroyer. The whirlwind Great Defender lost the mountain-moving test and his nose was bent and his mouth twisted forever - hence the carved faces that help the sick. Thunder promised to shoot whatever evil things escaped the under-world. Then Good Mind took clay, molded images of men and women, and when they were dry spoke to them and they sprang up and lived.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 67-73; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在他父親於東方之山受試煉之後，善心者打開了生命之袋，動物們便奔湧而出。他那滿身疣瘤的兄弟兩度攻擊他，先以香蒲，再以鹿角，直到善心者解除他的武裝，將他連同所有受蠱惑的野獸放逐到大洞穴的洞口，並命名他為毀滅者。旋風般的大守護者輸了移山之試，他的鼻子被扭彎，嘴巴永遠歪斜——因此有了那些幫助病人的雕刻面孔。雷電許諾射殺任何逃出下界的邪惡之物。於是善心者取來黏土，捏塑出男人與女人的形象，待它們乾了，便對它們說話，它們便躍起而活了。

title.en: The Brothers Who Climbed to the Sky
title.zh: 攀天兄弟

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（採集定位）

period: Recorded 1900s-1922, Seneca informants (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. IV tale 2, 'The Brothers Who Climbed to the Sky' (1923)

summary.en: Three hunter brothers walk to the rim where sky meets sea. One is crushed beneath the falling dome but his spirit speeds ahead to the sky country; the two survivors are purified, dismembered and rebuilt by the Master of Life, watch a war on earth through a hole in the sky, and return aged to find fifty years gone - only to be killed at last by fiery shafts of the sky and barred from re-entry.
summary.zh: 三個獵人兄弟步行至天海相接之處。一人被落下的天穹壓碎，其靈卻先行抵達天界；倖存的兩人被生命之主淨化、拆解重組，從天上的孔洞俯瞰人間戰事，返鄉時已歷五十年，最後死於天空的火矛，再難重返。

sensitivity.note: Seneca folktale recorded by Parker 1923; public domain. Death-spirit etiquette (greeting first) is presented as story logic, not ritual instruction.

passages.text: Three brothers who had spent their lives as hunters resolved to walk to the end of the earth where the sky touches the water of the great seas. After many years they reached the spot where the blue dome bends down to earth; each day it rose high and fell back on the sea. Two brothers ran beneath the rim, and as they stepped out the farther side the wall came down and the third was crushed - but his spirit sped forward like the wind. On the other side of the sky all things seemed turned around, and a man came running toward them: it was their brother, who could only say, 'Never hesitate, never delay!'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 74-75; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 三兄弟一生以狩獵為業，決心走到大地的盡頭，那裡天空觸及大海的水面。經過許多年，他們抵達藍色穹頂俯向大地的地點；它每日升起高處，又落回海上。兩個兄弟從邊緣下方跑過，當他們踏出較遠的一側時，那牆壁落了下來，第三個被壓碎——但他的靈魂如風般疾速向前。在天空的另一側，一切似乎都顛倒了，一個男人朝他們跑來：那是他們的兄弟，他只能說：「絕不要猶豫，絕不要延遲！」

passages.text: The Father of All warned them: when you meet my son the Great Spirit, call him quickly 'Nya'we'skano', for if you fail to speak first he will say 'you are mine,' and you will be spirits. In the great white lodge the Master of Life laid one brother down, tapped his neck with a small shell, and skinned him - stripping every muscle, taking out the organs, cleansing each fibre with a fluid from his mouth, and putting him together again. Their bodies renewed, the brothers caught the Master's swiftest buck, and were led to a hill to look down through a hole in the sky at a war then raging on earth. 'Such things men will ever do,' said the Master of Life.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 75-76; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 萬有之父警告他們：當你們遇見我的兒子大靈時，要趕快稱他「Nya'we'skano」，因為你們若不先開口，他就會說「你們是我的」，你們就會變成精靈。在巨大的白色小屋中，生命之主讓一個兄弟躺下，用小貝殼輕敲他的脖子，將他剝皮——剔盡每一塊肌肉，取出內臟，用他口中的液體潔淨每一根纖維，然後再把他拼合起來。兄弟們的身體煥然一新後，捉住了主人最快的雄鹿，並被領到一座山上，從天空的一個洞向下俯視當時在大地上進行的戰爭。「這樣的事，人們永遠都會做，」生命之主說。

passages.text: The brothers lived long in the upper world and learned much that their tongues never could tell. At last they descended to earth by night and slept on the ground; in the morning their native village was overgrown with trees, and only one sister, aged, knew them - the war they had watched, they were told, took place fifty years ago. They did not love earth now but longed for their lodges in the sky world; neither pestilence nor enchantment could kill them, but two fiery shafts of the sky did. They journeyed back toward the great white lodge, but could not return, for the Creator had first spoken.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 77; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兄弟們在上界住了很久，學到了許多他們的舌頭永遠無法述說的事。最後他們在夜間下到大地，睡在地上；早晨，他們故鄉的村落已長滿樹木，只有一個年邁的姊妹認得他們——有人告訴他們，他們所觀看的戰爭發生在五十年前。他們如今不再喜愛大地，而是渴望天上世界的住所；瘟疫與蠱惑都殺不了他們，但天空的兩道火焰之箭卻殺得了。他們朝巨大的白色小屋行去，卻無法回去，因為造物主已經先開口了。

title.en: The Death Panther: Omen from the Under-Water World
title.zh: 死亡豹：水下世界之凶兆

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（採集定位）

period: Recorded Jan. 1905, Edward Cornplanter informant, Cattaraugus (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. IV tale 3, 'The Death Panther' (1923)

summary.en: Two boys dive in a mountain lake and one is led by a blue-skinned warrior into an under-water council where a preacher debates warning the earth of coming disasters. The boy keeps a forbidden lodge four moons, returns to find war, famine, pestilence and fire have swept his village, and learns that the blue panther floating in the trees with fire shooting from its tail is the herald of disaster - to be turned aside with burning tobacco.
summary.zh: 兩名少年在山間湖中潛水，其一被一位青色戰士引至水下議會，會中講道者正爭論是否該警示地上將臨之災。少年看守禁室四月，歸來時發現戰亂、饑荒、瘟疫與大火已毀其村，並得知那飄浮樹梢、尾噴火焰的青豹乃災禍之先兆——須以焚燒菸草化解。

sensitivity.note: Seneca tale (Cornplanter informant, 1905), Parker 1923; public domain. The comet/fire-panther omen is a folk belief of record, not operative ritual.

passages.text: Two boys played in the waters of a deep lake beneath a tall white-headed mountain. Diving in contest, one boy, Oohoosha, clung to a flat rock and saw a tall warrior approach whose glistening body was the color of the sky. 'Come with me,' said the man, and Oohoosha strangely understood the unknown tongue. In a large moss-covered council hall under the water a stout preacher with a yellow and pink face was declaiming: 'The earth people are his children as well as we, so why should not we who know and foreknow many things notify them that trouble is coming?'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 78-79; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兩個男孩在一座高聳的白頭山下、一泓深湖的水中嬉戲。他們比賽潛水，其中一個男孩烏胡沙（Oohoosha）攀住一塊平坦的岩石，看見一名高大的戰士走近，那戰士閃閃發亮的身軀是天一般的顏色。「跟我來，」那人說道，而烏胡沙竟奇異地聽懂了那陌生的語言。在水下一個長滿苔蘚的寬大議事廳裡，一位面色黃粉、體格壯碩的傳道者正在高聲宣講：「地上的人們和我們一樣，都是他的孩子，那麼，我們這些知曉並預知許多事情的人，為何不該通知他們災禍將至呢？」

passages.text: The boy's friend volunteered to go: 'It is my office.' He set out to warn the earth-world of disaster and left Oohoosha keeper of his lodge, forbidding him the back room. For four moons the boy kept watch; when the friend returned he sighed, 'Do not ask me. In my madness you may see me as I am. I am the messenger of death. I am in disguise, but should you see me you would soon die, so depart and preach what I whisper, that henceforth mankind may profit.' Oohoosha shot upward, found his clothing fresh beneath a rock, and went back to the village.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 79-80; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那男孩的朋友自願前往：「這是我的職分。」他動身去警告地上世界大難臨頭，並留下烏胡沙看守他的居所，禁止他進入後面的房間。四個月亮（月）之久，男孩守夜看顧；當朋友歸來時，他嘆息道：「別問我。在我瘋狂之際，你也許會看見我的本相。我是死亡的使者。我身披偽裝，但你若見到我，便不久於人世，所以離去吧，把我所低語的宣講出去，好讓世人從今以後得益。」烏胡沙向上疾射而出，在岩石下找到自己完好的衣物，便回到村中。

passages.text: The village was charred frames; a trail lined with dog bones led west to a few houses of gaunt, scarred survivors. His old comrade drew back with a cry: 'How came you back from death!' A devastating war, famine, pestilence and a marauding band's fire had swept them, and a warning sign had floated unheeded in the trees - a blue panther with no visible face, from whose tail shot flames of fire. 'That creature is the herald of disaster,' said Oohoosha. 'When he is seen all men must burn tobacco, for incense is the sign that disaster is not wanted; he will breathe it and turn aside the impending evil.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 80-81; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 村子已成焦黑的屋架；一條沿途散落著狗骨的小徑向西延伸，通往幾間屋子，住著憔悴、滿身瘡疤的倖存者。他的舊夥伴驚叫一聲向後退去：「你怎麼從死裡回來了！」一場毀滅性的戰爭、饑荒、瘟疫，以及一夥劫掠者的縱火橫掃了他們，而一個警示的徵兆曾漂浮在樹間卻無人理會——一隻藍色的豹，看不見臉，尾巴射出火焰。「那生物是災禍的先兆，」烏胡沙說道。「當有人看見牠時，所有人都必須焚燒菸草，因為香煙是表明不願招致災禍的記號；牠會吸入這煙，從而將逼近的禍患引開。」

title.en: The Great Bear Constellation: The Celestial Bear Chase
title.zh: 大熊星座：天上逐熊

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin for the sky tale)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（此天空故事之採集定位）

period: Recorded 1900s-1922, Seneca informants (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. IV tale 4, 'The Great Bear Constellation' (1923)

summary.en: Seven starving hunter brothers carry their 'lazy' brother in a litter; he secretly absorbs their strength and kills the great bear they have tracked into the sky. The bear's blood and oil stain the leaves red, orange and yellow - hence autumn - and the slain bear revives each year, so the chase of the hunter torch-bearers and the kettle-carrier circles the sky forever as the Big Dipper.
summary.zh: 七個飢餓的獵人兄弟以擔架抬著「懶惰」的弟弟；他暗中吸取眾兄之力，追蹤大熊上天並將其誅殺。熊血與油脂把樹葉染成紅、橙、黃——秋季由此而來——被殺的熊年年復生，於是持火把者與攜釜者的追逐繞天不息，是為北斗。

sensitivity.note: Seneca star legend (Parker 1923); public domain. Parallels the Micmac/Wabanaki celestial-bear chase of the same stars.

passages.text: In the days of the first people there were seven brothers, all hunters, but one was called the Lazy One. After many moons without game their hunger charged their minds with magic. Four brothers carried the reluctant one in a burden litter, one went before with a torch and one behind with a kettle. The leading brother saw the tracks of a large bear, and the lazy brother begged to be bathed with his brothers' salivary fluid, hoping to absorb their strength, and all paused to do it.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 81; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在最初的人們的時代，有七個兄弟，個個都是獵人，但其中一個被稱為「懶惰者」。許多個月過去仍無獵物，飢餓使他們的頭腦充滿了法術。四個兄弟用擔架抬著那不情願的人，一個在前持火炬，一個在後提著鍋。領頭的兄弟看見一頭大熊的足跡，那懶惰的兄弟懇求用兄弟們的唾液為他沐浴，希望藉此吸收他們的力量，於是眾人停下腳步照做了。

passages.text: For three days more the bear tracks freshened ahead of them. At last the litter-bearers set the Lazy One down to help kill the bear - but he leaped up and ran ahead, full of power from the bath, and slew it with an axe. When they looked about they were far up in the air with the earth a good way below, and the blood and oil from the bear had stained the leaves of the trees red, orange and yellow. This is how the autumn leaves became colored.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 82-83; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 又過了三天，前方的熊跡越發新鮮。最後，抬擔架的人把懶惰者放下，好讓他幫忙殺熊——但他卻一躍而起，跑在前頭，渾身充滿沐浴所得的力量，用斧頭將熊殺死。當他們環顧四周時，發覺自己已高懸空中，大地遠在下方，而熊的血與油脂把樹葉染成了紅、橙、黃三色。秋天的葉子就是這樣染上色彩的。

passages.text: Soon they found the bear had revived, though they had killed and eaten him, and being hungry they pursued and killed him again, and it was autumn again. This bear chase keeps up all the time, year after year, since the first people came. In the sky you may find the man with the torch at the end of the bear-chase cluster, and the man with the pot in the middle of the handle; the bear hides in a cave and comes out when the brothers are very hungry. So we call those stars Nia'gwai' hades'he' - Bear they pursuing are.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 83; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久他們發現那熊竟已復活，儘管他們曾將牠殺死並吃掉，而由於飢餓，他們又追趕並再次將牠殺死，而這時又到了秋天。自最初的人們到來以來，這場獵熊年年歲歲、無時無刻不在持續。在天空中，你可以找到持火炬的人位於獵熊星群的末端，持鍋的人位於斗柄的中間；那熊躲在山洞裡，當兄弟們非常飢餓時便出來。所以我們稱那些星星為 Nia'gwai' hades'he'——「他們所追趕的熊」。

title.en: The Seven Brothers of the Star Cluster
title.zh: 星群七兄弟

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（採集定位）

period: Recorded by Edward Cornplanter (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. IV tale 5, 'The Seven Brothers of the Star Cluster' (1923)

summary.en: Seven warrior brothers dance themselves into the air with a magic song; forbidden to look down, the eldest cannot resist his mother's final plea and falls into the earth. From the scar grows the first pine, which only the weeping mother can interpret when it speaks; the other six become the dancing stars of the Pleiades and converse with their pine brother each winter.
summary.zh: 七個戰士兄弟以魔法之歌舞入空中；長兄雖被禁止低頭，卻敵不過母親最後的呼喚而墜入地中。傷口處長出第一棵松樹，唯有哭泣的母親能解其言語；其餘六人化為昂宿的舞星，每年冬天與松樹兄弟相語。

sensitivity.note: Seneca tale (Parker 1923); public domain. Parker notes the Huron/Wyandot parallel (Barbeau 1911).

passages.text: Seven brothers trained as young warriors practised daily before their mother's lodge while an uncle drummed on a water drum to teach them the dance. When they asked their mother for provisions for an expedition she scoffed and sent them away - once, twice, a third time. On the fourth dance the eldest changed his tune to the song of Djihaya, and with great enthusiasm sang, compelling his brothers to dance a dance of magic: the mother rushed out and saw her sons dancing in the air over the trees.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 83-84; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 七個兄弟自幼受訓為年輕戰士，每日在母親的住所前練習，而一位叔父則敲著水鼓，教他們跳舞。當他們向母親索取遠行所需的糧食時，她嗤之以鼻，把他們打發走——一次、兩次、第三次。到了第四次的舞蹈，長兄把曲調換成了 Djihaya 之歌，滿懷熱情地唱著，迫使弟弟們跳起一支魔法的舞蹈：母親衝了出來，看見兒子們在樹梢上方的空中起舞。

passages.text: 'Heed no sounds from the earth but continue dancing,' called the eldest son, 'if you look down you shall fall and never more be able to dance.' But the mother gave a heart-broken cry - 'Oh my first born son, give your mother one last look or I die!' - and his heart weakened; he looked, lost his power to master the air, fell with great rapidity and penetrated the earth, leaving only a scar. The remaining boys became the dancing stars.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 84-85; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「不要理會地上的聲音，繼續跳舞，」長子喊道，「你若往下看，就會跌落，再也無法跳舞。」但母親發出了一聲心碎的哭喊——「噢，我的長子，給你母親最後一眼吧，否則我就要死了！」——他的心軟了下來；他看了一眼，失去了駕馭天空的力量，以極快的速度墜落，穿透了大地，只留下一道疤痕。其餘的男孩則化作了跳舞的星星。

passages.text: For a whole year the mother wept beside the spot. In spring a tiny green shoot appeared, grew into a tall tree, and became the first pine; she guarded it, knowing it was her son. When a careless hunter slashed the tree, blood flowed, and the mother bound up the wound. In time the tree bore short feathers (cones) and more trees grew. Every winter the pine talked to its dancing brothers in the sky, and the mother knew that her eldest son should be her comfort while she rested on this earth.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 85; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 整整一年，母親都在那處地方旁哭泣。到了春天，一株小小的綠芽冒了出來，長成一棵高樹，成了第一棵松樹；她守護著它，知道那就是她的兒子。當一個粗心的獵人砍傷了那棵樹，血流了出來，母親便包紮了傷口。時日過去，那棵樹結出了短短的羽毛（松果），更多的樹也長了出來。每年冬天，松樹都與天上跳舞的兄弟們交談，母親知道，當她在大地上歇息時，她的長子應當是她的慰藉。

title.en: The Seven Star Dancers: The Youth Who Married a Star
title.zh: 七位星舞者：娶星少年

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（採集定位）

period: Recorded 1900s-1922, Seneca informants (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. IV tale 6, 'The Seven Star Dancers' (1923)

summary.en: A youth sent to dream by the river sees seven shining women dance on the water and descend in a corn basket. He seizes the youngest, is drawn up to the sky, is dismembered and regenerated by a great chief, and returns with his star bride - but so many years have passed that no one knows his uncle, and the couple, unable to live among men, go back up forever; the dimmest Pleiad is the wife who lost her brightness.
summary.zh: 青年奉命在河邊作夢，見七位發光女子在水上起舞、乘玉米籃降下。他捉住最年幼者，被引上天空，由大首領拆解重塑，攜星妻歸返人間——然而歲月已逝，無人識得他的叔父，二人無法與世人共處，終究重返天上；昂宿中最黯淡者便是失了光輝的妻子。

sensitivity.note: Seneca star-lore (Parker 1923); public domain. Parker cross-references Barbeau's Huron and Wyandot parallels.

passages.text: An uncle sent his nephew Djinae'nda to the river shore to dream until his dream-helpers appeared, fasting and sweating in the sweat lodge. One night he saw seven shining young women dancing in the water against the shore, going up and down without splashing; the youngest was the most beautiful. When he rushed out they leaped into a great corn basket and were drawn rapidly up into the sky. The next night he waited until she danced near, grasped her before she touched the basket, and was drawn upward as she fell in.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 86-87; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位叔父派他的姪子 Djinae'nda 到河岸去，在汗屋中禁食出汗，直到他的夢中助手出現。一天夜裡，他看見七個閃亮的年輕女子在靠岸的水中跳舞，上下起伏卻不濺起水花；其中最年輕的最為美麗。當他衝出去時，她們跳進一個大玉米籃裡，迅速被拉上了天空。第二天夜裡，他等到她舞近前來，在她觸及籃子之前抓住了她，於是她跌進籃中時，他也被拉了上去。

passages.text: 'I want to marry you,' he said; 'you have caused me to love you.' 'Then we shall be married,' said the maiden, 'but we must return to the sky and prepare for living upon the earth.' A great chief of the sky caused him to recline, took him apart joint by joint, removed and cleansed all his organs, and replaced them: Djinae'nda was regenerated and felt strong enough for mighty things. Then the basket lowered the couple to the beach - but the river was changed and a great village stood there, and an old man said one such as his uncle had lived there more than a hundred years ago.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 87-88; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「我想娶你，」他說；「你讓我愛上了你。」「那我們就成婚吧，」那少女說，「但我們必須回到天上，為在大地上生活作準備。」天上的一位大酋長讓他躺下，將他逐個關節地拆開，取出並潔淨了他所有的器官，然後再放回去：Djinae'nda 得到了重生，感到自己強壯得足以成就大事。然後籃子把這對夫妻降到了河灘上——但河流已經改變，那裡矗立著一座大村落，一位老人說，像他叔父那樣的人，早在一百多年前就住在那裡了。

passages.text: The couple tried to live contentedly but could not understand the ways of the people; in time the two returned to the sky. The wife rejoined her sisters but had lost her brightness, and Djinae'nda roamed the sky world hunting game which he captured by running it down. My grandmother told me that they are up there yet.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 88; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這對夫妻試圖知足地生活，卻無法理解人們的習俗；時日一久，兩人便回到了天上。妻子與姊妹們重聚，卻已失去了她的光輝，而 Djinae'nda 則在天界漫遊打獵，靠奔跑追逐來捕獲獵物。我的祖母告訴我，他們至今仍在那上頭。

title.en: The Coming of Spring: Winter's Lodge and the Young Warrior
title.zh: 春之來臨：冬神之屋與少年戰士

region.en: Shores of a great lake by a high mountain (symbolic pin at Lake Erie shore, New York)
region.zh: 大湖之濱、高山之下（象徵性定位於紐約州伊利湖岸）

period: Recorded Jan. 1905, Aurelia Miller informant (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. IV tale 7, 'The Coming of Spring' (1923)

summary.en: An old man of frost builds a lodge of ice on a lake shore where every step freezes the ground; North Wind is his only guest, smoking with him and begging new tricks for burying villages. A smiling, glowing stranger - the Spring - breaks in his door, keeps on smoking, and sings until the old man shrinks to a whisper; an eagle carries him north, the ice breaks, rivers swell, and it is morning in spring time.
summary.zh: 冰霜老人在湖畔築冰屋，足跡所至大地堅如燧石；北風是他唯一的客人，與他共吸菸斗，並求取埋葬村莊的新詭計。一位含笑發光的陌生者——春——破門而入，不停吸菸，且歌且進，直至老人縮為一縷低語；老鷹將他攜往北方，冰河解凍，春之早晨來臨。

sensitivity.note: Seneca seasonal myth (Aurelia Miller informant, 1905), Parker 1923; public domain.

passages.text: An old man with long white flowing hair wandered over the land: where his footsteps fell the ground grew hard like flint, his breath made the leaves drop red, and rivers stood solid when he splashed through. On the shore of a great lake by a high mountain he built a lodge with walls of ice, guarded by uprooted stumps, and only his friend North Wind might enter and sit by the fire that gave flames but no heat. North Wind came chiefly for new tricks - how to pile the snow banks higher, cause famine, or make great snow-slides to bury Indian villages.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 88-89; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位白髮長鬚飄逸的老人漫遊於大地之上：凡他足跡所至，地面便堅硬如燧石；他呼出的氣息使樹葉轉紅飄落；當他涉水而過，河流便凝結成冰。在一座高山旁的大湖岸邊，他築起一座牆壁為冰所造的屋舍，由連根拔起的樹樁守衛著，唯有他的朋友北風得以進入，坐在那有火焰卻無熱度的火堆旁。北風前來，主要是為了學些新把戲——如何把雪堆堆得更高、如何造成饑荒，或如何製造巨大的雪崩來掩埋印第安人的村落。

passages.text: One dismal night both fell asleep smoking; toward morning North Wind sprang up crying, 'What warm thing has bewitched me? The drifts are sinking, the rivers breaking, the ice is steaming!' A stranger stood striking the doorpost, and when the door fell he entered, hung it upright, and stirred the fire until it grew warmer. The old man raved, 'I am mighty! All snows and ice and frosts are my making... You do not belong in my lodge!' The stranger only smiled: 'I like to be sociable, let me stay a little longer and we will smoke together.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 89-90; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個陰鬱的夜晚，兩人都抽著菸睡著了；將近清晨時，北風猛然跳起，喊道：『是什麼溫暖的東西迷住了我？雪堆在下沉，河流在解凍，冰在冒著蒸氣！』一名陌生人站在門邊敲打著門柱，門倒下時他便走了進來，把門扶正掛好，又撥動爐火，直到火變得溫暖起來。老人狂怒地嚷道：『我是強大的！所有的雪、冰與霜都是我造成的……你不屬於我的屋舍！』陌生人只是微笑著說：『我喜歡與人為伴，讓我再待一會兒，我們一起抽菸吧。』

passages.text: Shaking with fear the old man drew smoke, and the warrior sang: 'I am Dedio's'wineq'dou, the Spring... My friend Daga'e'nda, the South Wind, is coming. I guess your friend is dead. There is a place. You cannot own all things always.' As he sang the old man shrank and shriveled until his voice only whispered, 'I don't know you!' A rushing wind shook the lodge, an eagle swooped down and carried the old man toward the north, and where the fire had burned a plant was growing. The swollen rivers carried away the ice, and in the morning it was spring time.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 90-91; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 老人恐懼得發抖，吸了口菸，那戰士便唱道：『我是德迪歐斯維內克杜，春天……我的朋友達加恩達，南風，就要來了。我想你的朋友已經死了。總有一個地方。你無法永遠擁有一切。』他唱著唱著，老人便蜷縮、枯萎，直到他的聲音只剩低語：『我不認識你！』一陣疾風撼動了屋舍，一隻老鷹俯衝而下，把老人帶往北方，而在火焰曾燃燒之處，長出了一株植物。漲滿的河水沖走了冰，到了早晨，已是春天時節。

title.en: The Coming of Death: The Wise Man's Dream and the Nine Bands
title.zh: 死亡之來臨：智者之夢與九部議團

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（採集定位）

period: Recorded 1900s-1922, Seneca informants (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. IV tale 8, 'The Coming of Death' (1923)

summary.en: In the newly made world people do not know death: men and children collapse breathless and are laid in tree limbs while everyone assumes such things happen only to others. One wise man dreams, and the Good Minded Spirit tells him the name of the faceless one who steals breath - Shondowekowa - and that every person will die. The wise man proclaims mortality to a council and organizes the people into nine caring bands, promising that the good will see the Maker's home when breath goes out of the body.
summary.zh: 在新造的世界中，人們尚不知死亡：男人孩童無息倒下，被安置於樹杈，人人皆以為此事只會降於他人。一位智者得夢，善心之靈告訴他那奪取氣息的無面者之名——舒恩多威科瓦——並說人人都必死。智者向議會宣告死之必然，並將人民編為九個互助議團，許諾行善者在氣息離體時將得見造物主之居所。

sensitivity.note: Seneca origin-of-death narrative (Parker 1923); public domain. Mortality here is announced, not caused by a broken taboo - a distinct Iroquoian variant of the world-wide 'origin of death' cluster.

passages.text: When the world was first made, men-beings did not know that they must die sometime. In those days a prominent man was found prone upon the grass, limp, without breath. He did not awaken, and when they placed him on his feet he fell like a tanned skin. A female man-being said he must be wrapped and put in the limbs of a tree; after a while the flesh dropped from the bones. Soon a child was found in the same condition, and laid in a tree also. Many others did these things, and no one knew why - no one thought that he himself would ever do such a thing.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 92; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 世界初造之時，人類並不知道自己終有一天必須死去。那時，有人發現一名顯要的男子俯臥在草地上，四肢癱軟，沒有氣息。他沒有醒來，當他們把他扶起站直，他卻像一張鞣製過的獸皮般倒下。一名女性人類說，必須將他包裹起來，放到樹枝之間；過了一陣子，肉便從骨頭上脫落。不久，又有一名孩童被發現處於同樣的狀況，也被安放到樹上。許多人也照樣做了這些事，卻沒有人知道為什麼——沒有人想過自己有一天也會如此。

passages.text: One wise man thought much about these things and had a dream: as he slept, the Good Minded Spirit came to him and spoke. Rising with a solemn face, he called the people together in council and said, 'A good word has come to me from the Good Minded spirit... They have died. It will be the same with all of you. The name of the one that steals away your breath is Shondowekowa. He has no face and does not see anyone; you cannot see him until he grasps you. He will continue to work forever. Every one who hears me and every one not yet born will die.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 92-93; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位智者對這些事思量良久，做了一個夢：當他沉睡時，善心之靈來到他面前說話。他帶著莊嚴的面容起身，召集眾人開會，說道：『善心之靈給我帶來了一句好話……他們已經死了。你們所有人也將如此。那個偷走你們氣息者的名字是尚多維科瓦。他沒有臉，也看不見任何人；你們看不見他，直到他抓住你們。他將永遠如此行事。每一個聽見我話的人，以及每一個尚未出生的人，都將死去。』

passages.text: 'You must now divide yourselves into nine bands, five to sit on one side of the fire and four on the other, and these bands shall care for their members. You must seek out all good things and instruct one another, and those who do good things will see the place where the Maker of all things lives when their breath goes out of their body.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 93; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 『你們現在必須將自己分成九個族群，五個坐在火的一側，四個坐在另一側，這些族群應當照料各自的成員。你們必須尋求一切美好的事物，彼此教導，而那些行善的人，當他們的氣息離開身體時，將看見萬物創造者所居住之地。』

title.en: Kusa Jataka: The Ugly Prince and His Fleeing Bride
title.zh: 拘薩本生：醜王子與逃婚的公主

region.en: Kah-gyur narrative India (symbolic pin at Hastinapura)
region.zh: 迦起律典敘事的印度（以哈斯提納普羅為象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. F. Anton Schiefner, done into English by W. R. S. Ralston (1882), ch. II, Kusa Jataka (Kah-gyur vol. ii. pp. 188-192)

summary.en: King Mahasakuni, childless and melancholy, is promised children by Indra, who sends a fertility medicine in a kusa box; the overlooked chief queen drinks the wash-water and bears Kusa, a supremely ugly but mighty Bodhisattva. His bride, tricked into the marriage and horrified at the sight of him, flees home; Kusa follows in disguise, works as chaplet-maker, cook, doctor and soldier, and finally wins her back when he defends her city with the shell, disk and mace Indra gave him, becoming a wheel-turning king with a city of precious stones.
summary.zh: 摩訶薩拘尼王無子而憂，天帝釋因贈靈藥，被忽略的正宮后以拘薩盒洗水飲之，生下極醜而力大的菩薩拘薩。被詭計騙娶的公主一見其貌而逃歸母國；拘薩化名跟隨，歷任花鬘匠、廚師、醫師與武士，最後在城池被困時以帝釋所贈螺、輪、杵退敵，贏回公主，並以四寶建拘薩那竭羅城，成為轉輪王。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature translated in the 19th century; a living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully. Physical ugliness of the hero is part of the traditional tale, not mockery of any community.

passages.text: King Mahasakuni sat leaning his head on his hand, brooding that despite his wealth he would die without son or daughter and his line would be extinguished. The king of the gods, Indra, saw him and promised a medicine: let his wives drink it and they would conceive. The medicine came in a kusa box, and while the chief queen slept the other wives drank and all became pregnant. The queen, furious at being left out, washed the box and drank the water, and she too conceived.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Kusa Jataka (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 摩訶薩庫尼王以手支頭而坐，心中憂思：雖有財富，卻將無子無女而死，其血脈將斷絕。眾神之王帝釋天見之，許以一藥：令其妻妾飲之，便可受孕。此藥盛於拘沙草盒中，正后熟睡之際，其餘妻妾飲之，皆得懷孕。正后因被遺漏而大怒，洗滌此盒並飲其水，遂亦受孕。

passages.text: Her son was born with the eighteen marks of ugliness and a face like a lion's, though of enormous strength; his father's delight in the other sons turned to wrath at him. When rival kings besieged the capital, the boy begged a chariot, and Indra, guarding the Bodhisattva, gave him a shell, a disk and a mace. At one blast of the shell the enemy's ears cracked and their host fled crying that he was a demon; the disk and mace threw whole ranks to the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Kusa Jataka (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 其子生而具十八種醜相，面如獅子，然力大無窮；其父對其他諸子之喜愛，於他則轉為忿怒。當敵國諸王圍攻都城時，此子乞得一車，而帝釋天護佑菩薩，賜以螺貝、輪寶與杵。螺貝一吹，敵人之耳即裂，其眾驚呼其為鬼神而逃散；輪寶與杵則將整列軍陣擊倒在地。

passages.text: No family would give a daughter to Kusa, so his father obtained one by a trick, telling another king the marriage was for a different son. Barred from mirrors, from daylight contact with his wife and from stepping-water baths, Kusa was one day seen playing among the youths; his wife asked who the demon was, was told it was her husband, and at night lifted the lamp-cover to see the lion face. She fled to her parents, crying that he was a Pisacha.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Kusa Jataka (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 無一家族願以女嫁與拘沙，其父乃以計謀求得一女，向另一國王謊稱此婚乃為另一子所結。拘沙被禁止照鏡、禁止在白晝與其妻相見、禁止踏洗足之水，一日卻被見與諸少年嬉戲；其妻問此鬼神為誰，被告知乃其夫，遂於夜間揭開燈罩，見其獅子之面。她逃回父母家中，哭訴其為毗舍遮。

passages.text: Kusa followed her in disguise as a chaplet-maker, a cook and a doctor under different names; each time she saw him she cried Pisacha and he fled. At last, when a hostile prince besieged her father's city, the queen's disguised husband offered to fight. One blast of the shell shattered the besiegers' ears, the princess realized that this champion was Kusa himself, and told her father so. Indra, who had already stopped the despairing hero from hanging himself over his own reflection, showed him four buried treasures; with them Kusa built the jewelled city of Kusinagara and ruled as a mighty Chakravartin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Kusa Jataka (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 拘沙易容改扮，先後以花鬘匠、廚師與醫生之不同名號追隨其後；每次她見到他便哭喊毗舍遮，他便逃去。最後，當一敵國王子圍攻其父之城時，王后那易容之夫自請出戰。螺貝一吹，圍城者之耳皆震裂，公主領悟此勇士正是拘沙本人，遂告知其父。帝釋天先前已阻止這絕望的英雄因見自身倒影而自縊，此時又向他顯示四處埋藏之寶藏；拘沙以此建起珠寶莊嚴之拘尸那竭羅城，並為威勢顯赫之轉輪聖王而治。

title.en: Adarsamukha, the Prince with the Mirror Face
title.zh: 阿達薩目卡：鏡面王子

region.en: Kingdom of King Ananda, Kah-gyur narrative India (symbolic pin at Hastinapura)
region.zh: 阿難王國，迦起律典敘事的印度（以哈斯提納普羅為象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. III, Adarsamukha (Kah-gyur book ii. pp. 198-201)

summary.en: The gentle youngest of five princes, whose face is like a mirror, passes his dying father's threefold succession test - jewel-shoes, immovable throne, steady diadem, recognition by the women, and six divined hidden treasures - and is crowned instead of his hot-tempered brothers. He then judges the chain of misadventures of the Brahman Dandin, punishing the accusers as much as the accused, and solves the questions of the crow, gazelles, partridge, snake and ichneumon, who turn out to be reborn men guarding treasures.
summary.zh: 面如明鏡的幼子阿達薩目卡溫和謙遜，通過臨終父王的三重繼位考驗——寶鞋合足、王座不動、寶冠不移、妃嬪相認，以及以慧力猜出六處秘藏——而越過性情暴躁的兄長們登基。其後他審理婆羅門檀丁一路連環誤傷的訴訟，對原告被告各予懲罰，並解答烏鴉、羚羊、鷓鴣、蛇與獴的提問，揭明牠們皆是執守寶藏的轉生之人。

sensitivity.note: Historical literary corpus (Kah-gyur narrative); nothing restricted reproduced. Note the tale's paradigm of punitive wisdom-judgments belongs to Indian judicial fable absorbed into Tibetan collections.

passages.text: King Ananda had five sons; the youngest was called Adarsamukha, Mirror-face, gentle and modest where his four brothers were rash and hot-tempered. Asked a hard question before the court, the elders could not answer and the youngest answered all. Falling ill, the king devised a test for the succession: the prince whom the jewel-shoes fit, on whom the throne stays firm and the diadem rests steady, whom the women recognize and who can divine the six hidden treasures, should be invested with royal power.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Adarsamukha (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿難陀王有五子；最幼者名阿達沙慕迦，意為鏡面，溫和謙遜，而其四兄則魯莽暴躁。於朝堂之上被問以難題，諸長老不能答，而最幼者盡答之。國王患病，乃為繼承之事設一考驗：誰能穿上寶鞋、王座於其身上穩固不動、王冠安然而立、婦女們能認出他、且能測知六處隱藏寶藏者，便應授予王權。

passages.text: Each elder brother failed: the shoes did not fit, the throne moved, the diadem shook, the women did not know him, and the six treasures - the inner, the outer, the inner-and-outer, the tree-top, the hill-top and the river-shore treasure - eluded him. On Adarsamukha the shoes fitted, the throne stood unmoved, the diadem sat proudly, the women knew him, and he named them all: the treasure inside the threshold, outside it, in the shadow-cast of the king's tree, under the stone in the delight-tank, and at the end of the channel where the water leaves the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Adarsamukha (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 諸兄長一一失敗：寶鞋不合、王座移動、王冠搖晃、婦女們不識其人，而六處寶藏——內寶、外寶、內外寶、樹頂寶、山頂寶與河岸寶——皆不為其所知。於阿達沙慕迦，寶鞋合足、王座屹立不動、王冠傲然端正、婦女們認出他，而他一一說出諸寶之名：門檻之內之寶、門檻之外之寶、國王之樹影所覆之處之寶、歡喜池中石下之寶，以及水自屋中流出之渠道盡頭之寶。

passages.text: Then came the Brahman Dandin, pursued by an impossible chain of accusers: the householder whose borrowed oxen had strayed from the stall, the owner of the mare he stoned to death while trying to stop it, the weaver's wife on whose husband he fell from a wall, the carpenter whose axe dropped into the river when he answered Dandin's question, and the tavern-keeper's baby he unknowingly sat on. Everyone wanted to be taken to King Adarsamukha, who would settle the business.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Adarsamukha (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著來的是婆羅門檀丁，他被一連串不可能成立的控告者追趕：那位借來的牛從牛棚走失的戶主、那匹他為了攔阻而用石頭打死的母馬的主人、那位他從牆上跌落壓到其夫的織工之妻、那位因回答檀丁的問話而讓斧頭掉進河裡的木匠，以及那位他不知不覺間坐上去的酒店老闆的嬰兒。人人都想被帶到阿達沙穆哈王面前，由他來裁斷此事。

passages.text: On the road, the crow on the withered tree, the gazelles, a partridge, two fighting snakes-and-ichneumons and a young wife all begged Dandin to carry questions to the king. Adarsamukha judged the oxen case by ordering Dandin's tongue cut out and the householder's eyes put out - and at each judgment the plaintiff preferred to drop the suit rather than suffer his own penalty. To the animals he revealed their former births: the crow had buried a treasure as village headman; the gazelles fed on meadows sweetened by a dripping honey-tree; the snake and ichneumon were two envious brothers hoarding their property, and were told to give their treasures to Sramanas and Brahmans. All obeyed, and Dandin received the wealth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Adarsamukha (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在路上，枯樹上的烏鴉、幾隻瞪羚、一隻鷓鴣、兩條相鬥的蛇與獴，以及一位年輕妻子，都懇求檀丁替他們向國王帶去問題。阿達沙穆哈判決牛隻一案，下令割去檀丁的舌頭、挖去戶主的眼睛——而每一次判決，原告都寧願撤回訴訟，也不願承受自己的刑罰。對那些動物，他揭示了牠們的前生：那隻烏鴉曾身為村長而埋藏了一筆寶藏；那些瞪羚吃的是因一棵滴蜜之樹而變得甜美的草甸；那條蛇與那隻獴是兩個嫉妒成性、囤積家財的兄弟，他吩咐他們把寶藏施予沙門與婆羅門。眾皆遵從，檀丁便得到了那筆財富。

title.en: The Clever Thief
title.zh: 智盜

region.en: Hill-town on the Ganges, Kah-gyur narrative India (symbolic pin at Varanasi)
region.zh: 恆河畔山地小鎮，迦起律典敘事的印度（以波羅奈為象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. IV, The Clever Thief (Kah-gyur iv. 132-135)

summary.en: A weaver who thieving by night trains his orphan nephew in the trade; on their first break-in the boy teaches him to go in feet-first - and the uncle is caught by the legs and beheaded by his own apprentice to save himself. The boy then outwits the king at every turn - mourning the corpse disguised as a madman, burning it as a carter, burying its bones in the Ganges as an ascetic - finally fathers a son on the princess and is identified when the infant hands him a wreath; the king, admiring such a hero, marries the thief to his daughter and gives half the kingdom.
summary.zh: 白日織布夜行竊的織工收孤兒為徒；首次破屋時少年教他腳先進——結果叔父被眾人抓住雙腿，徒弟為保己命親手斬其頭。此後少年處處勝過國王：先扮瘋子抱屍痛哭，再扮車夫焚屍滅跡，又扮髑髏外道將骨灰投入恆河；最後與公主有了子嗣，在眾人集會上由嬰兒親手遞上花環而露身。國王嘆服此英雄之才，反將公主嫁他，並分半國為聘。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable with ancient international parallels (Herodotus' Rhampsinitus, ATU-type thief cycles); living Tibetan tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: A widowed mother apprenticed her sharp-witted son to a prosperous weaver. The boy asked why his master ate delicacies and wore fine clothes while he ate coarse food; the weaver answered that he did two kinds of work - weaving by day, thieving by night. To test the nephew he bought a roasted hare, ate one leg in secret, and accused the boy of theft; the youth answered coolly that if the fourth leg was not on the hare it had not gone anywhere. The weaver took him thieving at once.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Clever Thief (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位寡母把她機敏的兒子送去給一個富裕的織工當學徒。男孩問，為何師父吃珍饈、穿華服，而他卻吃粗食；織工回答說，他做兩種活兒——白天織布，夜裡行竊。為了考驗這個姪兒，他買了一隻烤野兔，偷偷吃掉一條腿，卻誣賴男孩偷了；少年冷靜地回答說，若第四條腿不在兔身上，那它哪兒也沒去。織工當下便帶他去行竊。

passages.text: At the hole in the house-wall the weaver put in his head first. The youth stopped him: a thief goes in feet-first, for if the head is taken its owner is known and his family ruined. The weaver obeyed, the alarm was raised, and as the crowd pulled him back by the legs the boy, unable to free him, cut off his head and escaped with it. The king exposed the headless trunk at the crossroads, ordering the arrest of anyone who embraced and wailed over it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Clever Thief (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在屋牆的洞口，織工先把頭伸了進去。少年攔住他：賊要腳先進去，因為頭若被抓住，其主人便會暴露，家人也要遭殃。織工聽從了，警報隨之響起，當眾人拉住他的雙腿把他往外拖時，男孩無法將他解救出來，便割下他的頭，帶著頭逃走了。國王把無頭的屍身陳列在十字路口，下令逮捕任何擁抱它並為它哀哭的人。

passages.text: The young thief set out to honor his uncle's body. As a madman he embraced men, women, carts, horses and dogs in the street, until everyone took him for insane - and then he pressed the trunk to his breast, wailed at leisure, and walked away. Next, as a carter, he overturned a cart of dry wood beside the corpse, set fire to it, and burned the body whole. Then as a Brahman he collected alms for soul-offerings and left five oblation-cakes at the burial-place; and last, as an ash-smeared Kapalika, he filled a skull with the bones and ashes and flung it into the Ganges. Each time the king's watchmen identified the trick too late.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Clever Thief (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 年輕的賊動身去為叔父的遺體盡禮。他裝作瘋子，在街上擁抱男人、女人、車子、馬匹和狗，直到人人都把他當作瘋癲——然後他把屍身緊抱在胸前，從容地哀哭，再走開。接著，他裝作車夫，在屍首旁翻倒一車乾柴，點火燒了，把屍體整個焚化。然後他裝作婆羅門，為亡靈供養而募化布施，在葬地留下五塊供餅；最後，他裝作塗抹灰燼的迦波利迦，把骨骸與骨灰裝滿一個顱骨，扔進了恆河。每一次，國王的守衛都太晚才識破這詭計。

passages.text: The king staked his daughter in a garden by the river and set watchers on both shores. The thief drew water there for hours in an empty pitcher until the guards took him for a water-carrier; then, covering his head with a pot, he swam down to the garden, stayed with the princess in silence, and left. When her child was born the king assembled all the men of the realm and ordered the infant to crown with flowers the man who was his father - and the boy, walking through the crowd, handed the wreath to the thief. Seized at last, he was nevertheless judged too fine a hero to kill: the king adorned his daughter, gave her to him as wife, and bestowed half the kingdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Clever Thief (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 國王把女兒安置在河邊的一座園中作賭注，並在兩岸都設了看守。那賊用一隻空罐在那裡打了好幾個小時的水，直到守衛把他當作挑水夫；然後，他用一隻陶罐罩住頭，泅水而下到了園中，默然無聲地與公主共處，然後離去。她的孩子出生後，國王召集國中所有男子，命那嬰兒把花冠戴在他父親頭上——那男孩穿過人群，把花環遞給了那賊。他終於被捉住，卻仍被判為英雄豪傑，不該殺害：國王為女兒盛裝打扮，把她許配給他為妻，並賜予半個王國。

title.en: The Naga Janmachitra and the Serpent-Charmer
title.zh: 龍王壽相與捕龍師

region.en: Great lake of Hastinapura, North Panchala (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 北般闍羅哈斯提納普羅大湖（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), opening of ch. V, Sudhana Avadana (Kah-gyur ii. 202-209)

summary.en: Fruitful North Panchala owes its harvests to the Naga Janmachitra, whose rain sends the crops up from a great lotus lake. The lawless king of South Panchala, deserted by his own starving people, sets a golden-basket reward for anyone who can conjure the Naga away. A serpent-charmer pegs the lake shore with khadira wood and recites spells until the waters seethe; but the hunter Phalaka, to whom the terrified Naga has fled in man's form, draws a bow on him, forces the spell to be reversed, and kills him - winning the Naga's eternal gratitude and, on the Rishi's advice, the Amogha-chain that holds fast whatever it is cast upon.
summary.zh: 北般闍羅五穀豐登，全賴大蓮花湖中的龍王壽相按時降雨。不守法度的南般闍羅王因百姓逃亡，懸金籃重賞能將龍王攝來之人。捕龍師以吉多羅木釘遍湖岸、誦咒至湖水沸騰；而曾在龍王化人形時庇護他的獵人法勒迦彎弓威脅，逼其解咒，隨即殺之。龍王感恩，獵人又聽仙人之言索得那條「如意索」——擲出即套牢所向之物的寶索。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: In Hastinapura, city of the lawful king Dhana of North Panchala, a great lake full of blue, red and white lotuses was the dwelling of the Naga Janmachitra, who from time to time sent down a torrent of rain; so the land overflowed with rice and sugar-cane and its people gave freely to Sramanas and Brahmans. In lawless South Panchala the god withheld the rain, the towns stood deserted, and the ministers confessed that the people had all fled to the northern king, who ruled with a gentle, benignant and merciful mind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Sudhana Avadana (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在北般遮羅國，有一位如法的國王達那，其都城名為象城。城中有一大湖，滿是青、赤、白三色蓮花，乃是龍王闍那密怛羅的居所。他時而降下如注的甘霖，於是此地稻米與甘蔗豐足，百姓也慷慨布施於沙門與婆羅門。而在無法度的南般遮羅，天神卻扣住雨水不降，城鎮荒蕪無人，大臣們坦承百姓都已逃往那位以溫和、仁善、慈悲之心治國的北方國王那裏去了。

passages.text: The southern king was told the Naga could be conjured away by men versed in charms and spells; he fastened a golden basket to a standard and promised it to whoever should carry Janmachitra off. A serpent-charmer took the offer, went to study the lake, and returned with offerings: within seven days he would capture the Naga.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Sudhana Avadana (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有人告訴南方國王，說精通咒術與明咒之人能將那龍王驅遣而去。於是國王將一隻金籃繫於旗幢之上，許諾誰能將闍那密怛羅擄走，便將此金籃賜予他。一名弄蛇人接受了這樁差事，前去察看那座湖，回來時帶著供物，聲言七日之內便能擒獲那龍王。

passages.text: The Naga, seeing him, resolved to seek refuge with the hunter Phalaka who lived by the lake. In man's form he came to the hunter, revealed who he was, and gave instructions: when the charmer drove khadira-wood pegs into the four corners of the shore, hung colored threads and recited his spells, the waters would seethe and the Naga be forced forth; then the hunter must bend his bow and order the spell reversed, or the Naga would be bound by it all his life. When the day came the hunter did exactly this, forced the terrified charmer to reverse the spell, and killed him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Sudhana Avadana (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那龍王見了他，便決意去投靠住在湖邊的獵人頗羅迦。他化作人形來到獵人面前，表明自己的身分，並囑咐道：當那弄蛇人將佉陀羅木樁打入岸邊四角、懸掛彩線並誦念咒語之時，湖水便會翻騰，龍王將被迫現身；屆時獵人須彎弓搭箭，命令那咒術逆轉，否則龍王一生都將被那咒術所縛。到了那日，獵人果然照此行事，迫使驚恐萬狀的弄蛇人逆轉了咒術，並將他殺死。

passages.text: The freed Naga embraced his rescuer - 'you are my mother, you are my father' - and led him to his parents' palace beneath the lake, where he was fed and given jewels. But the Rishi at the nearby hermitage told him what he truly needed: the Amogha-chain, the chain that holds fast, hanging at the entrance of the Naga abode. The Nagas protested it was their defense against the Garuda, but Janmachitra answered his debt and gave it; the hunter carried it home full of joy - and it was this chain that would later snare the Kinnari Manohara.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Sudhana Avadana (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 獲救的龍王擁抱他的救命恩人——「你是我的母親，你是我的父親」——並領他來到湖底自己父母的宮殿，在那裏供他飲食，贈他珠寶。然而附近淨修林中的仙人告訴他真正所需之物：那懸掛在龍宮入口處的「不空索」，即那條能牢牢繫縛的鎖鏈。眾龍抗議說那是他們抵禦金翅鳥的防衛之物，但闍那密怛羅為報答恩情，還是將它給了獵人；獵人滿心歡喜地帶著它回家——而正是這條鎖鏈，日後將套住緊那羅女摩諾訶羅。

title.en: Sudhana and the Kinnari Manohara
title.zh: 善財童子與緊那羅女美妙

region.en: Hastinapura and the Kinnari kingdom beyond Himavant (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin at Hastinapura)
region.zh: 哈斯提納普羅與雪山地外的緊那羅王國（迦起律典敘事，以哈斯提納普羅為象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. F. A. Schiefner, English by W. R. S. Ralston (1882), ch. V, Sudhana Avadana (Kah-gyur ii. 202-209)

summary.en: The Bodhisattva prince Sudhana is given the kinnari (bird-woman) Manohara, captured by the hunter Phalaka with the Amogha-chain. A treacherous family priest, fearing to lose his post when Sudhana succeeds, tricks the king into a blood-tank rite for which Manohara - a non-human being - is to be killed; warned in time, Sudhana's mother returns the head-jewel and the kinnari flies home to the kingdom beyond Himavant. Sudhana's quest northward through caverns, rams, iron men, whirlpools and demon-haunted rivers, guided by the Rishi and by Manohara's ring dropped in a water-jug, ends in an archery trial before her father Druma and a reunion celebrated in the Kinnari capital.
summary.zh: 菩薩王子善財娶了獵人法勒迦以如意索捕得的緊那羅女美妙。怕失權位的國師設計，慫恿國王舉行血池灌浴之禮，須以「非人」美妙獻祭；王母及時歸還頭珠，緊那羅女凌空歸返雪山之北的故國。善財依仙人所指，歷經洞窟、抵角的公羊、鐵人、六十大匒的漩渦與惡魔盤踞的諸河，以一枚投入水罐的戒指相認，終於在緊那羅王特盧摩面前射穿七棕櫚、七鼓、七豬，贏回妻子。

canonical_translation: F. A. Schiefner, German translation; W. R. S. Ralston, Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, London 1882 (public domain)

narrative.en:
King Dhana of North Panchala, childless, prayed to the gods and a Bodhisattva of the Bhadrakalpa entered his queen's womb; the boy was named Sudhana, given three palaces and three wives, and amused himself in the upper storeys with music. One day the hunter Phalaka, who owed his fortune to the Naga Janmachitra and possessed the Naga's gift, the Amogha-chain that holds fast whatever it is cast upon, met a Rishi at the Brahmasabha pool. The Rishi told him that on the fifteenth of each month Manohara, daughter of Druma king of the Kinnaris, came there with five hundred kinnari companions to bathe, dancing and singing until the very beasts of the forest were enchanted. The hunter hid in the thicket and cast the chain; Manohara bounded and shrieked, her companions fled, and she was secured by her own head-jewel, the jewel by which she flew heavenwards, left in the hunter's hand as a pledge.

Meeting the handsome prince by chance, the hunter offered her to him as a gift. Sudhana looked once and was struck by the dart of passion, 'like a moth falling into the flame'; he carried her home and she became the beloved above all his wives. But a Brahman who had attached himself to Sudhana and feared he would lose his priestly post when the prince took the throne saw his chance when mountaineers rebelled and eight generals had failed: he urged the king to send Sudhana to war and to forbid him a last visit to Manohara. Sudhana left his wife's head-jewel with his mother, with orders to return it only if Manohara's life were in danger. On the campaign the god-king Vaisravana, delayed on his celestial road above the marching prince, sent the yaksha general Panchika to conjure up a phantom host so vast that the mountaineers opened their gates without a battle; Sudhana returned victorious.

That night the king dreamed that a vulture tore open his belly and wound his entrails around the city. The Purohita read the dream as mortal danger and prescribed the cure found in the mystic lore of the Brahmans: a tank a man's height, lined with mortar and filled with the blood of young roes, into which the king must descend while four Veda-learned Brahmans licked his feet and anointed them with the fat of a non-human being. Manohara was that non-human being. When Sudhana's other wives saw the preparations they rejoiced at the promised beauty of the bath, and Manohara, learning from them what it meant, fled to the queen. The queen judged the danger real, gave back the head-jewel with the words that she would now be beyond reproach, and as Manohara was summoned she rose into the air, saying that like a cow freed from its bonds she would flee.

The king feigned satisfaction; Manohara flew first to the Rishi, angrily reminding him that his directions had caused her capture, and left with him a ring and a full account of the way home: three black mountains and three and three beyond, then Himavant himself, then the named range of peaks, a cavern beneath three of them, the king of birds carrying the traveler over Vajraka, ram-like magic creatures, the Rakshasa Pingala, a black snake in the cavern to be shot with the bow, two rams whose horns must be broken to find the way, iron men with fear-inspiring weapons, an iron-lipped Rakshasi to be pinned with a wedge at the forehead, a whirlpool fount of sixty fathoms, the lion-yellow-haired Yakshas and Rakshasas, and the rivers Crocodile, Butterfly, Sad, Gay, Weeper, Laugher, snake-filled and reed-filled - each with its own charm or courage or silence to cross. Then the capital of the Kinnari king.

Sudhana returned from the war and learned what had happened. His father offered him a more beautiful wife; he refused, and when the gates were guarded he left by night, addressing his laments to the moon, a gazelle, the bees, a snake, a kokila bird and the asoka tree. At the hermitage the Rishi welcomed him, gave him the ring, and repeated the way, together with the provisions needed: the nectar remedy boiled in butter that banishes hunger and thirst, a monkey to carry, spells to learn, bow and arrows, a gleaming jewel, poison and antidote, three iron wedges and a lyre. Provided with all these, Sudhana crossed the rivers and the caverns and came near Druma's city.

Kinnari water-carriers told him the jugs they bore were to wash the smell of humanity off the captive-princess-turned-returned-daughter; asking whether the jugs would be emptied all at once or one by one, he dropped his ring into one jug and asked that it be poured first. The ring fell into Manohara's lap. The king, whose first answer to 'what would you do with the youth Sudhana' had been to cut him into a hundred pieces, cooled; Manohara dressed her husband in divine array and set seven golden stems, seven palms, seven kettledrums and seven boars as the trial. Sudhana sliced the golden stems like a plantain and shot a single arrow uninjured through the seven palm-trees, the seven kettledrums and the seven boars, standing unmoved afterwards like Sumeru. Set among a thousand identical kinnaris, Manohara stepped forward at his truthful verse. Druma gave her back with a jar of gold-dust, warning only that men are fickle. When homesickness later drew the pair back to Hastinapura, they flew through the air by kinnari power; Sudhana told his father everything, was invested with royal power, and for twelve years offered sacrifice without hindrance.
narrative.notes: Cultural function: the tale is the Tibetan Kah-gyur's version of the Kinnari-Manohara cycle; it teaches the inviolability of the marriage vow against paternal realpolitik, models the hero's quest through enumerated trials (a form saturated into Himalayan storytelling), and folds the Naga-gratitude subplot into a single chain of debt and gift.

functions: Models the Bodhisattva's constancy: the prince holds to his wife against king, priest and state religion alike
Paradigm of the enumerated quest - the way home is given as a list of named trials, a structure recycled across Himalayan and Southeast Asian tellings
Explains ritual distrust of Brahmans/Purohitas: the family priest's blood-tank rite is exposed as self-serving fraud
Links three realms (human, Naga lake, Kinnari mountain kingdom) into one economy of debt, gift and rescue

variants.name: Pali and Southeast Asian recensions of the Manohara cycle
variants.text_tradition: Pali Jataka tradition and Thai/Lao-Khmer Manora-Phra Suthon tellings
variants.summary: The capture-by-feather-or-jewel, flight, and quest-after-the-fleeing-wife are told of the same kinnari across Pali, Thai (Phra Suthon-Manora) and Khmer recensions; the Tibetan Kah-gyur version is the earliest printed full narrative, with the Naga Amogha-chain subplot elaborated.

variants.name: Tibetan Manohara stupa-tale (Bhutan/Dochula tradition)
variants.summary: In Bhutan the story is localized: the fleeing Manohara is remembered at Dochula/Dochu-la near Thimphu, where the Kinnari is said to have left her son and the stupa legend fixes the plot on the landscape.

variants.name: Schiefner's German and Ralston's English
variants.summary: Ralston's English (1882) renders Schiefner's German; the celebrated 60-fathom whirlpool and river-names passage was flagged by both translators as obscure, and modern readers treat the river list as symbolic rather than geographic.

sensitivity_guidance: The Manohara story remains part of living Buddhist narrative in Tibet, Bhutan and the Himalayas; all passages below are paraphrases of the 1882 public-domain translation, not verbatim reproduction, and the tradition is treated respectfully.

sensitivity.note: Living Buddhist narrative tradition (Kah-gyur); paraphrase of public-domain 1882 translation only; nothing restricted reproduced.

passages.text: On the fifteenth of the month, Manohara, daughter of Druma the Kinnari king, came with five hundred kinnari companions to the Brahmasabha pool to bathe, dancing and singing so sweetly that even the beasts of the forest were enchanted - the Rishi who told the hunter of it said the sound gave him delight for seven whole days. The hunter hid in the thicket with the Amogha-chain he had won from the Naga, and cast it: Manohara bounded and shrieked, her companions fled, and the hunter secured her by her own head-jewel, the jewel by which she flew heavenwards, which she had left with him as a pledge of good faith.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Sudhana Avadana (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當月十五日，緊那羅王檀摩之女摩諾訶羅，帶著五百名緊那羅女伴來到梵天會池沐浴，她們歌舞曼妙，連林中的走獸也為之著迷——將此事告知獵人的那位仙人說，那樂聲令他整整七日歡喜不已。獵人帶著他從龍王那裏贏得的不空索，藏身於密林之中，將其擲出：摩諾訶羅騰躍驚叫，她的女伴們四散奔逃，獵人便以她自己的頭頂寶珠將她制住——那顆寶珠是她飛升天界的憑依，她曾將它留在他那裏，作為誠信的質押。

passages.text: The hunter offered her to Prince Sudhana, who looked once and was struck by the dart of passion, like a moth falling into the flame. When mountaineers rebelled and eight generals had failed, the Purohita urged the king to send his son to war and forbid him a last sight of Manohara. Sudhana left her head-jewel with his mother: give it back only if her life is in danger. The campaign was won without a fight, for the god Vaisravana, delayed on his celestial road above the marching prince, sent the yaksha general Panchika to raise a phantom host so vast the mountaineers opened their gates at once.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Sudhana Avadana (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 獵人將她獻給須陀那王子，王子只看了一眼，便被情愛之箭射中，如同飛蛾墮入火焰。當山民叛亂、八位將軍皆告失敗之時，國師勸國王派他的兒子出征，並禁止他臨行前再見摩諾訶羅一面。須陀那將她的頭頂寶珠留給母親：唯有她性命垂危之時方可歸還。這場征戰未經一戰便告捷，因為天神毗沙門在天上趕路時，被行進中的王子所阻而耽擱，便遣夜叉將軍般遮迦召來一支龐大的幻化軍眾，聲勢浩大，山民們當即開城投降。

passages.text: The king dreamed that a vulture tore open his belly and wound his entrails around the city. The Purohita read it as mortal danger and prescribed the Brahmans' mystic cure: a tank filled with the blood of young roes, into which the king must descend while four Veda-learned Brahmans licked his feet and anointed them with the fat of a non-human being - and Manohara was that non-human being. Learning what the bath meant, she fled to the queen, who gave back the head-jewel; and as she was summoned she rose into the air, saying that like a cow freed from its bonds she would flee.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Sudhana Avadana (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 國王夢見一隻禿鷲剖開他的肚子，將他的腸子纏繞在城上。祭司長將此解讀為致命的危險，並開出婆羅門的祕法藥方：掘一水池，注滿幼鹿之血，國王須下入其中，同時由四位通曉吠陀的婆羅門舔他的腳，並以非人之物的脂膏塗抹——而曼那訶羅正是那非人之物。她得知此浴的用意後，逃到王后那裡，王后歸還了頭頂寶珠；當她被召喚時，她升入空中，說道她將如解脫束縛的母牛一般逃離。

passages.text: She flew first to the Rishi, telling him his directions had caused her capture, and left with him a ring and the way home: three black mountains, and three and three beyond, then Himavant, a cavern beneath three peaks, the king of birds carrying the traveler over Vajraka, ram-like creatures, the iron men, the iron-lipped Rakshasi to be pinned with a wedge, the whirlpool of sixty fathoms, the demon rivers, then the Kinnari king's capital. Sudhana, armed with the nectar remedy, a monkey, spells, bow, jewel, poison and antidote, three wedges and a lyre, crossed them all and dropped his ring into a water-carrier's jug - the first to be poured over the restored princess. It fell into Manohara's lap.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Sudhana Avadana (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她先飛到仙人那裡，告訴他正是他的指示導致她被捕，並留給他一只戒指與歸家之路：三座黑山，再過三座又三座，然後是雪山，三峰之下有一洞穴，百鳥之王馱著旅人越過金剛山、似羊之眾、鐵人、須以楔子釘住的鐵唇羅剎女、六十尋深的漩渦、群魔之河，然後是緊那羅王的都城。善財配備了甘露妙藥、一隻猴子、咒語、弓、寶珠、毒藥與解毒劑、三枚楔子與一張琴，越過了這一切，並將他的戒指投入挑水人的水罐——那第一罐水將澆在復原的公主身上。戒指落入了曼那訶羅的懷中。

passages.text: Before her father Druma, Sudhana sliced seven golden stems like a plantain and shot one arrow uninjured through seven palm-trees, seven kettledrums and seven boars, standing unmoved afterward like Sumeru. Set among a thousand identical kinnaris, Manohara stepped forward at his truthful verse; Druma gave her back with a jar of gold-dust, warning only that men are fickle. Later, homesick, the pair flew back through the air to Hastinapura; Sudhana told all, was invested with royal power, and for twelve years offered sacrifice without hindrance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Sudhana Avadana (1882); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在她父親德魯摩面前，善財如切芭蕉般劈開七根金莖，一箭無傷地射穿七棵棕櫚樹、七面銅鼓與七頭野豬，事後如須彌山般屹立不動。在千名一模一樣的緊那羅女之中，曼那訶羅因他真實的偈語而走上前來；德魯摩以一罐金砂將她歸還，只告誡說男人是善變的。後來，二人因思鄉而穿越空中飛回象城；善財講述了一切，被授予王權，並在十二年間無有阻礙地獻祭。

title.en: The Origin of Folk Stories: Crow and the Talking Cliff
title.zh: 民間故事之起源：鴉兒與會說話的峭壁

region.en: Cliff at the forks of a river (symbolic pin at Genesee River gorge, New York)
region.zh: 河流交會處的峭壁（象徵性定位於紐約州傑納西河峽谷）

period: Recorded 1900s-1922, Seneca informants (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. V tale 9, 'Origin of Folk Stories' (1923)

summary.en: Gaqka, the orphan called Crow and Filth-Covered-One, finds a flying canoe, homes atop a great human-faced cliff that demands tobacco and tells wonder tales for small gifts, marries a girl whose grandfather the cliff is, and is transformed through a hollow log into a handsome man - returning north to found the custom of paying a storyteller with tobacco and a trophy drawn from the pouch for every tale.
summary.zh: 被稱為鴉兒的孤兒加卡拾得會飛的獨木舟，居於一面人形巨崖之頂；崖石索要菸草，並以小禮換取奇妙故事。他娶了崖石之孫女為妻，穿過空心圓木而蛻變為俊美男子——北歸後首創以菸草與袋中信物酬謝講故事者的習俗。

sensitivity.note: Seneca storyteller-charter tale (Parker 1923); public domain. Explains the etiquette of listening and paying for oral stories.

passages.text: There was once a boy who had no home. His parents were dead, his uncles would not care for him, and the people called him Filth-Covered-One as they passed, holding their noses. He resolved to go away and become a great hunter. One night he found a canoe that shot into the air when he took the paddle, and he flew southward above the clouds and under the moon until it dropped into a river. Across the water stood a great cliff that had a face like a man, and he built a bark cabin on its top.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 97-98; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個沒有家的男孩。他的父母已死，叔伯們不願照料他，人們經過時都捏著鼻子，叫他「滿身汙穢者」。他決心離去，成為一名偉大的獵人。一天夜裡，他發現一隻獨木舟，當他拿起槳時，它便射向空中，他飛向南方，在雲上、月下，直到它落入一條河中。水對岸矗立著一座巨大的懸崖，其面貌如人，他在崖頂用樹皮搭了一間小屋。

passages.text: The first night a voice said, 'Give me some tobacco,' and when Gaqka threw a pinch over the cliff the voice said, 'Now I will tell you a story,' and spoke from the very rock he sat on. 'It shall be the custom hereafter to present me with a small gift for my stories,' it said; 'when I announce a story you must say Nio, as I speak you must say He', and never fall asleep until I say Da'neho nigaga'is - so thus finished is the length of my story.' All winter long the young man and his bride, who knew the rock as her grandfather, heard all the wonder tales of the old days, and his pouch was filled with a trophy for every tale.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 98-100; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第一夜，一個聲音說：「給我一些菸草。」當加夸將一撮菸草擲過懸崖時，那聲音說：「現在我要給你講一個故事。」並從他所坐的那塊岩石中說話。「從今以後，向我獻上小禮物以換取我的故事，這將成為習俗，」它說；「當我宣布一個故事時，你必須說『尼奧』；當我講述時，你必須說『赫』，並且在我說『達內霍·尼加加伊斯』——意即我的故事長度就此結束——之前，絕不可睡著。」整個漫長的冬天，這個年輕人和他的新娘——她認得那岩石是她的祖父——聽盡了舊日的種種奇異故事，而他的袋子裡裝滿了每一個故事所換來的紀念物。

passages.text: In spring they flew the canoe north. 'Now I shall remove your clothing and take all the scars from your face and body,' said the bride, and caused him to pass through a hollow log: Gaqka emerged in the finest clothing, a handsome man. In the village he said, 'I am the boy whom you once were accustomed to call Ga'doda. I have now returned.' That night the people gathered to hear his tales, instructed to give him small presents and tobacco; he plunged his hand into the pouch, took out a trophy and told an ancient tale. That is why there are so many legends now.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 100; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 春天，他們乘獨木舟飛向北方。「現在我要脫去你的衣服，除去你臉上和身上所有的疤痕，」新娘說，並讓他穿過一根中空的木頭：加夸出來時身著最華美的衣裳，成了英俊的男子。在村中，他說：「我就是你們從前慣於稱作加多達的那個男孩。我如今回來了。」那天夜裡，人們聚集起來聽他的故事，並被告知要給他小禮物和菸草；他把手伸進袋子，取出一件紀念物，講述了一個古老的故事。這就是如今有如此多傳說的原因。

title.en: The Forbidden Arrow and the Quilt of Men's Eyes
title.zh: 禁忌之箭與人眼之被

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（採集定位）

period: Related in Seneca by Edward Cornplanter, translated by William Bluesky (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. V tale 10, 'The Forbidden Arrow and the Quilt of Men's Eyes' (1923)

summary.en: Twin brothers disobey their grandmother and shoot their father's forbidden arrow, pinning Driven to the earth in the north. Passing the witch women's dancing house with eyes cast down, Younger is forced at last to look on the quilt of living young men's eyes and is blinded; his wizard sons borrow a fawn's eyes, trick the witches into destroying one another, restore father and uncle's sight, and resurrect the magically slain - whose mismated limbs become the first cripples of the world.
summary.zh: 雙生兄弟違逆祖母，射出父親的禁忌之箭，把「被逐者」釘在北方大地。途中少年被迫直視巫婦以活人眼珠縫成的被子而失明；其術士之子借小鹿之眼為父復明，誘使巫婦自相殘殺，尋回父叔的眼珠，並令被魔法所殺者復生——其錯配的肢體便成為世上最早的殘疾之人。

sensitivity.note: Seneca transformation myth (Cornplanter/Bluesky, Parker 1923); public domain. Parker's own note: the orenda of twins, the magic arrow, and the resurrection with mismated limbs are recurrent Seneca motifs.

passages.text: Two twin brothers, Younger and Driven, played about two hills: Driven jumped from one summit to the other while Younger shot arrows at him in flight. Their grandmother always forbade them a certain arrow that had belonged to their father. At last they used it; the forbidden arrow pierced Driven's body and carried him northward, singing with wild-duck feathers, and Younger ran a long way to find his brother transfixed to the earth. Carrying him on his back he was warned: a house of dancing women lay ahead - 'Oh brother, cast not your eyes upon one of them!' - and beyond it the lodge where women made a quilt of young men's eyes, that live and wink as in life.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 101-102; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一對孿生兄弟，名為「年幼者」與「受驅者」，在兩座山丘間嬉戲：受驅者從一座山頂躍向另一座，年幼者則在他騰躍之際向他射箭。他們的祖母一向禁止他們使用一支屬於他們父親的箭。最後他們還是用了；那支禁忌之箭射穿了受驅者的身體，帶著野鴨羽毛的歌聲將他帶往北方，年幼者跑了很長一段路，才找到被釘在大地上的兄長。他將兄長背在背上，卻受到警告：前方有一間舞女之屋——「噢，兄弟，切莫將你的眼睛投向其中任何一人！」——再過去則是那座小屋，那裡的女人以年輕男子的眼睛縫製一床被子，那些眼睛仍如生前一般鮮活地眨動。

passages.text: Through the long lodge Younger kept his eyes to the ground, but at the door one woman held the quilt where he saw it: his eyes jumped out of their sockets into the quilt, and he was blind. He crept on hands and knees to a cornfield and lay there day after day until two sisters found him and carried him home, feeding him bear's oil until he grew strong; he married the younger sister, who bore twin boys, wizards who talked before they suckled and played lacrosse under the ground.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 102-104; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 年幼者穿過那座長屋時，雙眼始終盯著地面，但到了門口，一名女子舉起那床被子讓他看見：他的眼睛從眼窩中跳出，飛入被中，他於是失明。他手膝並用爬進一片玉米田，日復一日躺在那裡，直到兩姊妹發現了他，將他抬回家，餵他熊油直到他恢復強壯；他娶了妹妹，她生下了一對孿生男孩，這兩個巫師在吮乳之前便會說話，還在地下玩長曲棍球。

passages.text: 'Father, we will go and get back your eyes,' said the sons. They borrowed a fawn's eyes (feeding her moss meanwhile), then transformed the younger into a duck at the witches' spring and leaped into a woman's body to be born of her; as a fretful child he cried for treasures until they showed him the quilt of eyes, and when the women were in the field he folded it and ran. The witches pursued him with hammers, struck and killed each other, and the boys set father and uncle's own eyes back in their sockets.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 105-107; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「父親，我們去把你的眼睛取回來。」兒子們說道。他們借來一頭小鹿的眼睛（同時餵她苔蘚），接著將弟弟變成女巫泉邊的一隻鴨子，又躍入一名女子的體內，由她所生；他作為一個煩躁的嬰孩哭鬧著要寶物，直到她們把那床眼睛之被拿給他看，而當女人們下田時，他將被子摺起便跑。女巫們手持鎚子追趕他，卻彼此擊打而亡，男孩們於是將父親與叔父自己的眼睛放回他們的眼窩。

passages.text: 'We must now go and find the bones of the dead and restore them their eyes,' said the twins. They gathered the skeletons under a lodge roof of white bear skin; the wigwam quivered, and kicking over an elm as a warning the boys cried, 'The tree is falling upon you. Flee for your lives!' The living dead ran out with eyes on their skulls but no time to find their own bones: some had legs too short, some long arms and short legs - their limbs mismated. From them sprang the deformed and ugly people of today, and a great house sprang up at Last's footprints to hold them all.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 107; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「我們現在必須去尋找死者的骨骸，把眼睛還給他們。」這對孿生兄弟說道。他們將骸骨聚集在一座以白熊皮為頂的小屋下；棚屋顫動起來，男孩們踢倒一棵榆樹作為警告，喊道：「樹要倒在你們身上了。快逃命吧！」那些活著的死者頭骨上帶著眼睛跑了出來，卻來不及找回自己的骨頭：有的腿太短，有的手臂長而腿短——他們的四肢錯配了。今日那些畸形醜陋的人們便是從他們繁衍而來，而一座大屋在「最後者」的足印處拔地而起，將他們全都容納其中。

title.en: Corn Grinder, the Grandson: The Boy Who Went South
title.zh: 磨玉米之孫：向南而行的男孩

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（採集定位）

period: Related by Guy Miller, a Tuscarora, Jan. 1905 (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. V tale 11, 'Corn Grinder, the Grandson' (1923)

summary.en: Warned never to wander south beyond the sound of the corn grinder, the boy goes south at last, finds a lodge of giants, scalds the giant baby with soup grease and pepper, shoots the male giant dead - and learns from his grandmother that he has killed his own father. With the invisible friend Standing Cob he quests through beast-haunted forests to a cataract for the medicine roots, shoots his weeping father down from the pine where the crowd has been harvesting his wampum tears, and the whole enchanted family is restored to normal human size.
summary.zh: 男孩被告誡不得離開磨杵聲所及之地向南而行，終究南行，發現巨人一家的居所；以滾油與辛辣草戲弄巨嬰，射殺男巨人——祖母卻說他殺了親生父親。他與隱形朋友「立玉米棒」穿越野獸出沒的森林，往瀑底尋得藥根，將在松樹上哭泣（淚珠落地成貝珠）的父親射下，一家人終復為常人之形。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora-related Seneca tale (Parker 1923); public domain. Violence is folklore-trickster register, not instruction.

passages.text: In a clearing in a thick pine forest lived an old couple who talked with trees, with their grandson, whom they named Corn Grinder. 'Go east, go west, go north, but not away from the sound of the corn grinder,' they said. 'Never go south!' At twelve he knew the woods in every direction but the forbidden south, and at last resolved to disobey. He found a great bark lodge where a gigantic woman cooked corn soup and a baby lay as tall as a warrior; hiding under the bed, he was nearly crushed by the rolling infant, and ran out, skimmed a ladle of scalding grease from the soup and threw it on the baby's belly, fleeing to the woods.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 108-110; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在茂密松林中的一片空地上，住著一對能與樹木交談的老夫婦，以及他們的孫子，他們為他取名為「磨玉米者」。「往東走，往西走，往北走，但不可走到聽不見磨玉米聲的地方。」他們說道。「千萬不可往南走！」到了十二歲，他已熟悉各方向的樹林，唯有那禁忌的南方除外，最後他決心違抗。他發現一座巨大的樹皮小屋，裡頭有個巨大的女人在煮玉米湯，還有一個躺著的嬰兒，身長如一名戰士；他躲在床下，幾乎被那翻滾的嬰兒壓扁，於是跑了出去，從湯裡舀起一勺滾燙的油脂，潑在嬰兒的肚子上，逃入林中。

passages.text: He threw pungent weeds into the soup, and the giantess sneezed until she could scarcely stand - 'Some witch must be near.' Strapping the baby to the board she sang 'Luk-ste, luk-ste, da-ja-jent' at a huge dead tree, which opened to let out a tall giant who scalded his throat on the soup and kicked the kettle flying over the trees. Corn Grinder learned the song, struck the tree himself when the sun stood high, and as the giant stormed out - 'More tricks!' - shot an arrow through his stomach. Rushing home he cried, 'Oh grandmother! I killed him, I killed him!'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 110-112; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他將辛辣的野草丟進湯裡，那女巨人便打起噴嚏，幾乎站不住腳——「附近一定有哪個女巫。」她將嬰兒綁在背板上，對一棵巨大的枯樹唱道「Luk-ste, luk-ste, da-ja-jent」，那樹便裂開，放出一名高大的巨人，他被那湯燙傷了喉嚨，一腳將鍋踢得飛過樹梢。磨玉米者學會了那首歌，在太陽高懸時親自擊打那棵樹，當巨人怒衝而出——「又是把戲！」——他一箭射穿了他的肚子。他奔回家喊道：「噢，祖母！我殺了他，我殺了他！」

passages.text: 'Age!' wailed the old woman. 'You have killed your father, my own son. You must go on a long journey to a high mountain and obtain certain magical roots to restore him. Why did you disobey us?' The giantess and the baby burst in to kill him; he leaped down the giantess' throat, wrenched out her heart, and killed the infant, then set out with his invisible friend Da-ga-ga-we-so-da-de, Standing Cob. At a clearing near the mountain a multitude was shooting at a creature in the topmost pine whose tears of wampum dropped at every arrow. 'Stop!' said Cob. 'That is your father up there. Hurry and get the medicine.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 112-114; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「歲月啊！」老婦人哀號道。「你殺死了你的父親，我親生的兒子。你必須踏上漫長的旅程，前往一座高山，取得某些神奇的根來使他復原。你為什麼不聽我們的話？」女巨人與嬰兒衝進來要殺他；他縱身躍下女巨人的喉嚨，扯出她的心臟，殺死了那嬰兒，然後帶著他隱形的朋友達-加-加-威-索-達-德——立鶴——出發。在山附近的一片空地上，一群人正朝著最高那棵松樹頂上的一隻生物射箭，那生物每中一箭便落下淚珠般的貝珠。「住手！」立鶴說。「在上面的是你的父親。快去取藥。」

passages.text: In a deep rift at the foot of a cataract they found the wonderful plant, which soared upward until Cob leaped and caught it by the roots. Corn Grinder chewed the roots and rubbed his saliva over his body, clothing and arrows, and felt new vigor. At the great pine he spat on his arrows, rubbed the roots in his hair and shot: the creature vanished, and both boys were pulled through the air like the wind, dropping at the doorway of a new lodge where a woman sang to a baby - the same mother, father and child he had killed, each now grown smaller. 'I am your brother,' said the baby. 'I am your father,' said the man. 'Come, let us eat!'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 114-115; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在一道瀑布腳下的深裂隙中，他們找到了那株神奇的植物，它向上高聳，直到立鶴躍起抓住它的根。磨玉米者咀嚼那些根，並將唾液塗抹在自己的身體、衣物與箭上，感到新的活力。在大松樹前，他朝自己的箭吐唾沫，把根揉進頭髮裡，然後射箭：那生物消失了，兩個男孩像風一樣被拉過空中，落在一座新屋舍的門口，屋裡有個女人正對著一個嬰兒唱歌——正是他殺死的那同一位母親、父親與孩子，如今每個都變小了。「我是你的兄弟，」那嬰兒說。「我是你的父親，」那男人說。「來吧，我們吃吧！」

title.en: He-Goes-to-Listen: The Scarred Nephew and the Singing Wives
title.zh: 赴聽者：帶疤的姪兒與歌聲之妻

region.en: Hill by the Genesee River, Tonawanda Seneca country, New York
region.zh: 紐約州托納萬達塞內卡地區傑納西河畔的山丘

period: Related almost verbatim by Gohweh, an old Tonawanda Seneca (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. V tale 12, 'He-Goes-to-Listen' (1923)

summary.en: An old widower uncle maims and scars his nephew Hatondas so he can claim the two singing women foretold by the boy's mother's dream. The women arrive, reject the trickster, and take Hatondas; crawling through a hollow log transforms him into a handsome man, but his broken silence-taboo costs him one of his three magic bags. Years later he returns with presents, and the uncle, now welcoming, jokes his way out of an axe-beard before the lodge renews itself.
summary.zh: 老鰥夫叔叔為奪取姪兒母親夢中預言的兩位歌女，刻意毀傷其容貌。歌女們抵達後識破詭計，選擇了哈頓達斯；鑽過空心圓木使他蛻變為俊美男子，但他破壞了緘默禁忌，失去三只法袋之一。多年後他攜禮而歸，叔叔笑言相迎，木屋亦煥然如新。

sensitivity.note: Tonawanda Seneca tale (Parker 1923); public domain. Cruelty to the boy is folktale register.

passages.text: Near a large hill that rose from a river lived a boy named Hatondas - He-Goes-to-Listen - his name bestowed because just before his birth his mother had dreamed that at marriageable age two singing women would come from afar to be his wives, and that she would die. She sewed three witched bags, one filled with wampum, one with beautiful clothing, one left empty, each able to hold things hundreds of times its size. Her widower brother-in-law, unable to secure a wife by fair means, resolved to disfigure the boy and claim the women himself; day after day he threw hot embers on the boy and stretched a deer tendon across the doorway so he would fall, until the once-handsome child was scarred and crippled.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 116-118; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在一座從河中隆起的大山附近，住著一個名叫哈通達斯的男孩——意為「去聆聽者」——這名字的由來是因為就在他出生前，他母親夢見在他到了適婚年齡時，會有兩位唱歌的女子從遠方前來做他的妻子，而她將會死去。她縫了三個施了巫術的袋子，一個裝滿貝珠，一個裝著美麗的衣物，一個空著，每個都能裝下比它自身大上數百倍的東西。她守寡的姐夫無法以正當手段娶到妻子，便決心毀掉這男孩的容貌，自己佔有那兩名女子；他日復一日地把熾熱的餘燼扔向男孩，並在門口橫拉一條鹿筋使他絆倒，直到這個原本俊秀的孩子變得滿是傷疤、跛足殘廢。

passages.text: In the boy's seventeenth year he returned from the hill in great excitement: he had heard singing. The uncle, suppressing his own excitement, beat him brutally and threw him into the fire, then oiled and painted his own face, tied his flabby cheeks back with sinews, and let down his black hair to hide the ruse. That night the women came, sat on Hatondas' low bench, and would only ask, 'Where is Hatondas?' - knocking the old reprobate down when he pleaded. Hatondas returned suddenly bold, and the two women cooked his supper while the old man fared as best he could.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 118-119; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在男孩十七歲那年，他萬分興奮地從山上回來：他聽到了歌聲。那叔叔壓下自己的興奮，狠狠地打他，把他扔進火裡，然後給自己的臉塗油上彩，用筋腱把鬆垮的臉頰往後綁緊，並放下黑髮遮掩這番偽裝。那天夜裡，兩名女子來了，坐在哈通達斯那張低矮的長凳上，只一味問道：「哈通達斯在哪裡？」——當那老無賴哀求時，她們把他打倒在地。哈通達斯突然大著膽子回來，兩名女子為他煮了晚飯，而那老人只能勉強湊合著過。

passages.text: That night the uncle's heart changed. He filled the empty bag with parched corn, maple sugar, a bow, arrows and a buckskin suit, and warned Hatondas not to speak to any living creature but his wives, on pain of losing a bag. On the hilltop one of the women pointed to a hollow log; crawling through it, Hatondas emerged smooth-faced, unscarred and clad in white skin - but in his delight he spoke to two strangers, and the wampum bag vanished, so he entered the strange country as a common man. Years later he returned with presents for the old uncle, and after their bargaining joke the lodge renewed itself while the old man grew older.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 120-122; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那天夜裡，叔叔的心變了。他把空袋子裝滿炒玉米、楓糖、一張弓、一些箭和一套鹿皮衣，並警告哈通達斯除了他的妻子們之外，不可對任何活物說話，否則就會失去一個袋子。在山頂上，其中一名女子指向一根中空的圓木；哈通達斯爬過它，出來時面容光滑、沒有傷疤，身穿白色皮膚——但他在欣喜之中對兩個陌生人說了話，那貝珠袋便消失了，於是他以一個普通人的身分進入了那個陌生的國度。多年之後，他帶著禮物回來給那年老的叔叔，在他們討價還價的玩笑之後，屋舍煥然一新，而那老人則愈發衰老。

title.en: Hatondas the Listener Finds a Wife
title.zh: 哈頓達斯求得妻室

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（採集定位）

period: Related by George D. Jimerson (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. V tale 13, 'Hahtondas, the Listener, Finds a Wife' (1923)

summary.en: A cruel uncle sends his abused orphan up the hill to listen until he hears a new sound; the sound is a woman singing his name. She cleans him with hot oil, transforms him through a hollow log, and burns the lodge as the uncle attacks; she beats a tiny bundle into a growing dog they ride to the lake, where the monstrous bear Nia-gwa-he fishes for their canoe with a living line, drinks the lake dry, freezes it, and is sunk by steaming water. On the cliff her sister welcomes them, and their precocious twin sons hurl the returning monster into an oak grove.
summary.zh: 殘忍的叔叔命飽受虐待的孤兒上山傾聽，直到聽見新的聲音；那聲音是一位女子唱著他的名字。她以熱油為他淨身，引他穿空心圓木蛻變，並縱火燒屋以逃；她將小皮束抽打成漸大的犬，騎至湖邊。巨熊尼亞瓜赫以活索釣舟、吸乾湖水、冰封湖面，終被滾水沉入湖底。崖頂的姐姐迎接二人，其早慧的雙生子最後將再來的怪物拋入橡樹林。

sensitivity.note: Seneca tale (Jimerson informant, Parker 1923); public domain. Parker notes it is apparently a mixture of two distinct legends.

passages.text: Hatondas was a poor orphan who lived with a wrinkled old uncle who threw hot coals at him and mutilated him.
