passages.zh: 那人回到家中，開始行醫，治癒了許多疾病；他精於此道，能從那些被巫師吹入體內的人身上取出毛髮和蟲子。據說南方的南蒂科克人（Nanticokes），即斯考恩瓦托哈蒂霍克（Skaunvatohatihawk），最先創立了巫術：他們費盡心力取得蛇與根莖，用以製成毒害人們的藥物。巫師們組成一個秘密社團，夜間聚會；被發現時，他們會變成狐狸和狼，疾奔時帶著閃光，或變成火雞和大貓頭鷹，或變成石頭和腐爛的圓木。

title.en: The Origin of Witchcraft and the Witches Burned at Onondaga
title.zh: 巫術之起源與奧農達加焚巫

region.en: Near Fort Onondaga, New York
region.zh: 紐約州奧農達加堡附近

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: The Nanticokes of the south are said to have founded witchcraft: a secret society gathering by night, whose members turn into foxes, wolves, turkeys or great owls to go from town to town blowing hairs and worms into bodies, and into stones or rotten logs when discovered. About fifty persons were indicted as witches and burnt to death near Fort Onondaga by order of the national committee.
summary.zh: 據說南方納提科人首創巫術：一個夜間聚會的秘密社團，其成員化為狐、狼、火雞或巨鴞往來各鎮，向人體吹入毛髮與蠕蟲；被發現時則化為石頭或朽木。約五十人被控行巫，經國族委員會之命，於奧農達加堡附近焚死。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. Historicizes the Iroquois witch-belief that Parker's tales treat dramatically.

passages.text: It was supposed that the Skaunvatohatihawk, the Nanticokes in the south, first founded the witchcraft. Great pains were taken to procure the snakes and roots of which the stuff was made to poison the people. The witches formed into a secret society; they met in the night and consulted on various subjects respecting their engagements. When a person becomes a member of their society, he is forbidden to reveal any of their proceedings.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說南方的南蒂科克人（Nanticokes），即斯考恩瓦托哈蒂霍克（Skaunvatohatihawk），最先創立了巫術。他們費盡心力取得蛇與根莖，用以製成毒害人們的藥物。巫師們組成一個秘密社團；他們夜間聚會，就種種與其約定相關的事務商議。當一個人成為其社團的成員，便被禁止洩露他們的任何行事。

passages.text: In the night the witches would turn into foxes and wolves, and run very swift, attended with flashes of light; sometimes they turned into a turkey or big owl, and could fly very fast, going from town to town to blow hairs and worms into a person. If the witches were discovered by some person they turned into a stone or rotten log, entirely concealed in this situation. About fifty persons were indicted for being witches, and were burnt to death near the fort Onondaga, by order of the national committee.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 夜裡，女巫會變成狐狸與狼，奔跑極快，並伴隨著閃光；有時她們會變成火雞或大貓頭鷹，能飛得極快，從一鎮飛到另一鎮，把毛髮與蟲子吹進人的體內。若女巫被人識破，她們便會變成石頭或腐爛的木頭，完全隱藏於此形態之中。約有五十人因身為女巫而被起訴，並奉全國委員會之命，在奧農達加堡壘附近被燒死。

title.en: The Night in the Corpse House and the New Burial
title.zh: 屍屋之夜與新葬俗

region.en: Kaunehsuntahkeh, east of Oneida Creek, New York
region.zh: 紐約州奧奈達溪以東考內孫塔赫

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: Returning late from hunting, a man, his wife and another shelter overnight in a house where dead bodies are deposited. When the fire dies the room darkens and something gnaws; kindling the fire, he finds the third person dead, eaten by a ghost. Fleeing with his fainting wife toward the village light, they reach safety; next day the people burn the bodies, and the five nations change their mode of burying - faces set to the east - and later alter it again when still troubled.
summary.zh: 獵罷夜歸，一男攜妻與同伴投宿於停放屍體之屋。火熄屋暗之際，忽聞啃噬之聲；重新點火後，發現同伴已死——被鬼所噬。他攜昏弱的妻子奔向村中燈火而脫險；翌日族人焚屍，五族因而改變葬俗——面朝東而葬——其後仍有擾亂，葬俗再改。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. A burial-custom aition told as ghost-story.

passages.text: Near the village of Kaunehsuntahkeh a man and his wife and another person returned from hunting, but the night was getting late before they reached the village; they went into a house where dead bodies were deposited to stay over the night. They kindled a fire and went to sleep, but when the fire was out the room became dark, and the man heard something gnawing. Kindling the fire again, he discovered the person was dead, eaten by a ghost; he trembled with fright, told his wife to quit the room as soon as possible, and followed her out.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在考內順塔凱村附近，一名男子與他的妻子及另一人打獵歸來，但他們抵達村莊前夜色已漸深；他們走進一間停放死屍的屋子過夜。他們生了火便入睡，但火熄滅後屋內變得漆黑，那男子聽見有東西在啃咬。他再次生起火，發現那人已死，被鬼魂吃掉了；他嚇得發抖，叫妻子儘快離開屋子，自己跟在她後面出去。

passages.text: She became faint and could not run fast; they saw a light coming and supposed the ghost was chasing them, but fortunately gained the village. The next day the people went and burnt the dead bodies. This important event was soon made known among the five nations, and afterwards they changed their mode of burying, setting the posture face to the east; but again they were troubled with the dead bodies, and were compelled to make some alterations in burying.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她變得虛弱無力，跑不快；他們看見一道光逼近，以為是鬼魂在追趕他們，但幸運地抵達了村莊。翌日，人們前去焚燒那些死屍。這件重大事件很快在五族之間傳開，此後他們改變了埋葬的方式，讓死者面朝東方擺放；但他們又再次受到死屍的困擾，被迫在埋葬方式上再作一些改變。

title.en: Queen Yagowanea, the Betrayal, and the Fall of the Erians
title.zh: 亞格瓦尼亞女王：背叛與伊利人之傾覆

region.en: Fort Kauhanauka (Tuscarora) and the Genesee country, New York
region.zh: 考哈農卡堡（塔斯卡洛拉）與傑納西之地，紐約州

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: Queen Yagowanea of the Erians, 'mother of the Nations,' keeps a Peace House entertaining both warring parties. When two Canandaigua warriors are smoking with her she admits a party of Messissaugers and advises them to kill her guests. A woman slips away by canoe across Lake Ontario to warn the Governor Shorihowane; his three divisions ambush the Erians behind a bear-skin decoy and slay six hundred. The great war chief Shorihowane is killed at the siege of Fort Kauquatkay, and the Queen sues for peace.
summary.zh: 伊利人的亞格瓦尼亞女王為「諸族之母」，設「和平之屋」款待交戰雙方。兩名卡南代瓜戰士正與她吸和平之菸時，她放入麥西薩格人並唆使其殺害客人。一名女子駕獨木舟渡安大略湖報信給總督肖里豪恩；總督的三個分隊以熊皮誘敵設伏，殺敵六百。大戰士肖里豪恩攻考夸特凱堡時中箭陣亡，女王乞和。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. Cusick's Erian (Erie) war traditions.

passages.text: The Kanneastokaroneah or Erians sprung from the Senecas, becoming a numerous and powerful nation. A Queen named Yagowanea resided at the fort Kauhanauka; she had influence among the people and extended her authority over twelve forts. She lived outside the fort in a long house called a Peace House, entertaining the two parties who were at war with each other, and was called the mother of the Nations; each nation sent her a belt of wampum as a mark of respect. Where the Five Nations were engaged in the warfare she admitted two Canandaigua warriors into her house, and just as they began to smoke the pipe of peace, a small party of the Messissaugers came in - she betrayed her visitors, advising the Messissaugers to kill the warriors, which was soon executed.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡尼阿斯托卡羅尼亞人，即伊利人，源自塞內卡人，成為一個人口眾多、勢力強大的民族。一位名叫雅戈瓦尼亞的女王住在考哈瑙卡堡壘；她在民眾中頗具影響力，並將其權威擴及十二座堡壘。她住在堡壘外一棟稱為「和平之屋」的長屋中，款待彼此交戰的雙方，並被稱為「諸族之母」；每個民族都送她一條貝珠帶以示敬意。當五族捲入戰事時，她接納了兩名卡南代瓜戰士進入她的屋中，正當他們開始抽和平煙斗時，一小隊梅西索格人走了進來——她出賣了她的訪客，慫恿梅西索格人殺死那些戰士，此事隨即執行。

passages.text: During the Queen's absence a woman went privately, took a canoe, and proceeded on Lake Ontario toward Canandaigua as fast as possible, going through the woods to inform the Governor Shorihowane that the Erians were making preparations to destroy the people east of the Genesee river, and directed how to send the spies. Collecting fifteen hundred warriors besides the women and old men, the governor separated the people into three divisions and marched toward the Genesee river. A warrior was dressed in a bear skin and seated on the path; the enemy chased it, which brought them into the midst of the division - at once burst a most hideous yell, followed with a rattling of war clubs. After a severe contest the Erians fled, leaving six hundred warriors slain.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 趁女王不在時，一名女子私下取了一艘獨木舟，儘快駛上安大略湖前往卡南代瓜，並穿過森林去通知總督肖里霍瓦內，說伊利人正準備消滅傑納西河以東的人民，並指示該如何派出探子。總督集結了一千五百名戰士，另有婦女與老人，將人馬分為三隊，向傑納西河進發。一名戰士披著熊皮坐在路上；敵人追趕它，因而被引入隊伍中央——頓時爆發出一陣極其駭人的吶喊，緊接著是戰棍的噼啪聲。經過一場激烈的戰鬥，伊利人逃走了，留下六百名戰士陣亡。

passages.text: The King of the Five Nations ordered the great war chief Shorihowane, a Mohawk, to march with five thousand warriors to attack the fort Kauquatkay and extinguish the council fire of the enemy. During the siege, a shower of arrows flew from the fort and the great war chief was killed; his body was conveyed back to Genesee and buried in a solemn manner, but the siege continued for several days. The Queen sued for peace; the army ceased hostilities and left the Erians entire possession of the country.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 五族之王命令偉大的戰爭首領肖里霍瓦內——一位莫霍克人——率領五千名戰士進攻打垮考夸特凱堡壘，並撲滅敵人的議事火。圍城期間，一陣箭雨從堡壘中射出，偉大的戰爭首領被殺；他的遺體被運回傑納西，以莊嚴的方式安葬，但圍城仍持續了數日。女王求和；軍隊停止敵對行動，讓伊利人完全保有該地。

title.en: The Aged Visitor Among the Tuscaroras and the Prophecy of the Whites
title.zh: 塔斯卡洛拉的年邁訪客與白人預言

region.en: Tuscarora settlements, North Carolina (traditional)
region.zh: 塔斯卡洛拉聚落，北卡羅來納（傳統）

period: Written 1825 by David Cusick (Tuscarora)

source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Part III (1825/1848)

summary.en: An aged visitor, abused by the ball-players, throws one into a tree and vanishes; returning he releases the man, teaches the people to respect their dead and love their relations, tells them the whites beyond the great water have killed their Maker but he rose again, and prophesies that the whites will one day take the Big Island and the red children 'melt away like snow before the heat.' He dies, is buried - and some who visit the grave find he has risen, never to be heard of since.
summary.zh: 一位年邁訪客遭打球者欺侮，將一人擲上樹而消失；復返後釋放其人，教眾人敬重亡者、親愛族親，並說大洋彼岸的白人殺了他們的造物主——主卻復活——又預言白人終將佔有大島，紅皮子弟「將如雪遇熱而消融」。他死後下葬；有人往墓探視，發現他已復活，自此杳無音訊。

sensitivity.note: Tuscarora text, 1825; public domain. The Christianized prophecy is a colonial-era accretion Cusick records as tradition.

passages.text: The sixth family, the Tuscaroras, was visited by a person who went to see their amusements, but he was abused by some of the ball-players. He punished the offender by throwing him into a tree, and suddenly disappeared - but the person came again and released the fellow from the tree. The visitor appeared a very old man; he appeared among the people for a while and taught them many things: how to respect their deceased friends and to love their relations.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第六個家族，即塔斯卡羅拉族，曾有一位來訪者前去觀看他們的娛樂活動，卻遭到幾名球戲玩者的欺凌。他懲罰了那個冒犯者，把他拋進一棵樹裡，隨即消失無蹤——但那人又再度出現，把那個傢伙從樹上放了下來。這位來訪者看起來是個非常年邁的老人；他在眾人之中出現了一段時日，教了他們許多事情：如何敬重已故的親友，以及如何愛護自己的親屬。

passages.text: He informed the people that the whites beyond the great water had killed their Maker, but he rose again; and he warned them that the whites would in some future day take possession of the Big Island, and it was impossible to prevent it: the red children would melt away like snow before the heat. The aged man, becoming sick, told them to get different kinds of roots to cure diseases, and showed them the manner of mourning. He died among them and was buried; but soon after, some person went to the grave and found he had risen, and he was never heard of since.
passages.note: Condensed from Cusick 1825, Part III; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他告訴眾人，大海彼岸的白人殺害了他們的造物主，但造物主又復活了；他又警告他們，白人總有一天會佔據這座大島，而且無法阻止：紅皮膚的孩子們將如雪遇熱般消融。這位年邁的老人染了病，便吩咐他們去採集各種不同的根來治病，並向他們示範哀悼的方式。他死在他們中間，被埋葬了；但不久之後，有人去到墳前，發現他已復活，此後便再無人聽聞他的消息。

title.en: The Mantis's Son, the Baboons, and the Child's Eye
title.zh: 螳螂之子、狒狒與孩童之眼

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), '||Gaunu-tsaxau (the son of the Mantis), the Baboons, and the Mantis'

summary.en: |Kaggen sends his son ||Gaunu-tsaxau to fetch sticks for bows; the baboons mock the child's errand, break his skull and play ball with his eye. The Mantis dreams the crime, flies down, snatches the eye into his bag, and drops it into the water — and the boy rises from the pool, weak but alive.
summary.zh: 卡根遣子取木，狒狒譏其使命，碎其顱，以眼作球戲之。卡根夢知其事，飛下奪眼入囊，投之於水——孩童自池中復起，體弱而生。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings, not as permission to speak for living San communities.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore, ||Gaunu-tsaxau (the son of the Mantis), the Baboons, and the Mantis (Bleek & Lloyd 1911); not verbatim. ||Gaunu-tsaxau went to fetch sticks for his father, so that the Mantis might take aim at the people who sit upon their heels. An old baboon questioned him, and as the errand was passed from baboon to baboon with their chant 'First going I listen, to the child yonder,' the last of them cried that it was themselves the child was mocking. 'Ye shall strike the child with your fists.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), section I.—5.; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《布須曼民間故事樣本》的濃縮改述，||Gaunu-tsaxau（螳螂之子）、狒狒與螳螂（Bleek & Lloyd 1911）；非逐字照錄。||Gaunu-tsaxau 去為父親取木棍，好讓螳螂能瞄準那些蹲踞而坐的人。一隻老狒狒盤問他，隨著這差事伴著牠們的吟唱「我先走，我聽著，聽那邊那孩子」在一隻隻狒狒之間傳遞，最後一隻叫道，那孩子嘲弄的正是牠們自己。「你們要用拳頭打那孩子。」

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. They struck the child with their fists, breaking his head; another struck out his eye, and the eye rolled away. 'My ball! my ball!' they sang, and played at ball with the child's eye while the child lay still and died.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), section I.—5.; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改述，出處同上；非逐字照錄。牠們用拳頭打那孩子，打破了他的頭；另一隻打出了他的眼睛，那眼睛滾了出去。「我的球！我的球！」牠們唱著，拿那孩子的眼睛當球玩，而那孩子躺著不動，死了。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The Mantis lay dreaming that the baboons had killed his son and made a ball of his eye. He shut his tears in, slung his rattling quiver, ran to the game, caught the flying eye as it passed, and whirled it round. He threw the eye toward the baboons; it ascended, played in the sky, and sprang into the little bag tied beside his quiver.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), section I.—5.; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改述，出處同上；非逐字照錄。螳螂躺著做夢，夢見狒狒殺了他的兒子，還把他的眼睛做成了球。他把淚水忍在眼裡，背上他那格格作響的箭袋，奔到遊戲之處，趁那飛滾的眼睛經過時一把抓住，把它旋轉起來。他把眼睛朝狒狒擲去；它升上天空，在天上嬉戲，又跳進繫在他箭袋旁的小袋子裡。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. He put the child's eye into the water, saying: 'Thou must grow out, that thou mayest become like that which thou hast been.' The child grew again like its former self; the Mantis caught him as he basked by the water, anointed him with his scent, clothed him with the front kaross, and brought him home — while the young Ichneumon cried that the Mantis must have gone to put the eye into the water.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), section I.—5.; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改述，出處同上；非逐字照錄。他把孩子的眼睛放進水裡，說道：「你必須重新長出來，好讓你變得像你從前的樣子。」那孩子又長成了他原先的模樣；螳螂趁他在水邊曬太陽時抓住他，用自己的氣味為他塗抹，給他穿上前襟的斗篷，把他帶回家——而年幼的姬蜂叫嚷著說，螳螂一定是去把眼睛放進水裡了。

title.en: The Leopard Tortoise Traps the Hunters' Hands
title.zh: 豹龜困獵者之手

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡爾維尼亞北方卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by !Kweiten ta //Ken (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Story of the Leopard Tortoise'

summary.en: A sick woman of the early race asks passing hunters to rub her neck with fat; each man's hands decay to bare bone inside her neck. The leopard tortoise always seems about to die — she is the deceiver of the early race.
summary.zh: 早期之民病婦請過路獵者以脂膏擦頸；其手入頸即腐為枯骨。豹龜看似將死——實為早期之民的欺詐者。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by !Kweiten ta //Ken to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The people had gone hunting; she was ill; and she perceived a man who came up to her hut; he had been hunting around. She asked the man to rub her neck a little with fat for her; for, it ached. The man rubbed it with fat for her. And she altogether held the man firmly with it. The man's hands altogether decayed away in it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), section I.—7.B, p. 37 (public domain).
passages.zh: 人們都去打獵了；她病了；她看見一個男人朝她的小屋走來；他一直在附近打獵。她請那男人替她用油脂揉一揉脖子，因為脖子疼。那男人替她用油脂揉了。她便用那油脂把男人的手牢牢黏住。男人的雙手就在那裡面整個爛掉了。

passages.text: Again, she espied another man, who came hunting. And she also spoke, she said: 'Rub me with fat a little.' He sat, putting his hands behind him, when the other man came, taking them out from the Leopard Tortoise's neck. He showed the other one his hands; and the other one's hands were altogether inside the Leopard Tortoise's neck.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 37-39; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她又瞧見另一個男人，也是來打獵的。她也開口說道：「替我揉一點油脂吧。」他坐下來，把雙手背在身後，這時另一個男人來了，把他的手從豹龜的脖子裡拔出來。他把自己的手給另一個看；而另一個人的手卻整個陷在豹龜的脖子裡。

passages.text: He dashed the Leopard Tortoise upon the ground, while he desired that he should, by dashing it upon the ground, break the Leopard Tortoise. And the Leopard Tortoise held him fast. Then he returned home; and the people said: 'Art thou a fool? Did not thy parents instruct thee? The Leopard Tortoise always seems as if she would die; while she is deceiving us.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 39-41; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他把豹龜猛摔在地上，想藉著摔在地上把豹龜摔破。豹龜卻把他牢牢抓住。於是他回家去了；人們說：「你是傻子嗎？你的父母沒教過你嗎？豹龜總是裝得好像要死了；其實她是在騙我們。」

title.en: The Moon's Water: Why Game Must Not Be Looked At
title.zh: 月之水：不可注視獵物之故

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Moon is not to be looked at when Game has been shot'

summary.en: After shooting game the hunters may not look at the Moon: the beasts of prey will eat the dying animal. For the Moon's water — the honey-like dew — falls on game and makes it rise again; whoever looks at the Moon lets the game 'go along like the Moon,' away to a waterless place.
summary.zh: 射獲後不得仰月：獸將啖其獵物。月之水如蜜露，落於獸身使其復起；觀月者令獵物如月而行，引至無水之地。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: We may not look at the Moon, when we have shot game; for, we look, lowering our head, while we do not look up, towards the sky; while we are afraid of the Moon's shining. It is that which we fear. For, our mothers used to tell us about it, that the Moon is not a good person, if we look at him. For, if we look at him, when we have shot game, the beasts of prey will eat the game, when the game lies dying, if we look at the Moon.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), section II.—24, p. 67 (public domain).
passages.zh: 我們獵到獵物之後，不可以看月亮；因為我們看的時候是低著頭，不抬頭望天；因為我們怕月亮的光。我們怕的就是這個。因為我們的母親從前就告訴過我們這件事，說月亮不是個好東西，如果我們看他。因為如果我們獵到獵物之後看他，獵物躺著快死的時候，如果我們看月亮，猛獸就會把獵物吃掉。

passages.text: When the game does not die, the Moon's water is that which causes the game to live. For, our mothers used to tell us about it, that, the Moon's water yonder, (that) we see, which is on a bush, it resembles liquid honey. It is that which falls upon the game; the game arises, when it has fallen upon the game. It makes cool the poison with which we shot the game; and the game arises, it goes on... The Moon's water is that which cures it. And it lives, on account of it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 67-68 (public domain); minor elisions.
passages.zh: 獵物不死的時候，是月亮的水使獵物活著的。因為我們的母親從前就告訴過我們這件事，說那邊我們所看見的月亮的水，落在灌木上的，像液態的蜜。就是那東西落在獵物身上；那東西落在獵物身上之後，獵物就起來了。它使我們射獵物所用的毒冷卻下來；獵物就起來，繼續走……月亮的水就是治好它的東西。牠就因著它而活著。

passages.text: Therefore, our mothers did not wish us to be looking about, we should not look at the things which are in the sky... that the game which we had shot, would also go along like the Moon... he was not in the habit of going to a place near at hand, for, the day was used to break, while he was still going along. The game would also do the same, if we had looked at the Moon... we could go to die of thirst, while it, leading us astray, took us away to a place where no water was.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 68-69; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 所以，我們的母親不願我們東張西望，我們不該看天上的東西……免得我們所獵到的獵物也像月亮那樣一路走去……他不習慣去近處的地方，因為天常常要亮了，而他還在走。如果我們看了月亮，獵物也會這樣……我們可能走到渴死，而它卻把我們引迷了路，帶我們到沒有水的地方去。

title.en: The Mantis Throws His Shoe into the Sky: Origin of the Moon
title.zh: 螳螂擲鞋上天：月亮之源起

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §§ 3 and 16; Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), footnote to p. 53

summary.en: Piercing the eland's gall, the Mantis creates a darkness into which he springs. Grope-blind among the bushes, he snatches off his shoe — dust and all — and throws it into the sky: 'this my shoe shall verily become the Moon, which shines in the dark.' The Moon is cold because it is leather; it is red because of the dust of Bushmanland; and it dies and lives again like a shoe thrown up and falling away.
summary.zh: 螳螂刺破羚膽，造暗而躍入。摸索林中，急脫其鞋連塵擲天：「吾鞋必為月，暗中照耀。」月冷因皮革；月紅因桑人之塵；月死而復生，如鞋拋落復揚。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition from ||kabbo and Dia!kwain lines of the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: His thinking-strings quickly told him to take off his shoe and throw it up into the sky, for the shoe to light up the earth for him. So he quickly snatched off the shoe from his foot, with the dust on it, he quickly threw it up... Then he saw the Mierkats standing cutting up the Eland in the dark.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Mantis makes an Eland' (public domain).
passages.zh: 他的思緒之弦很快告訴他，要脫下他的鞋子，把它拋向天空，讓那隻鞋為他照亮大地。於是他迅速從腳上扯下那隻鞋，連同上面的塵土，他迅速把它拋了上去……接著他看見貓鼬們站在黑暗中，正切割著大羚羊。

passages.text: The Mantis said to them: 'You must hold a torch to light yourselves in cutting up the Eland, but my shoe stands up there in the sky where I have thrown it, to shine for me...' He said: 'I am the Mantis, and this my shoe shall verily become the moon which shines in the dark.' That is why the moon shines at night. That is why the moon is cold, because it is a shoe, it is leather. It is red, because it has earth on it, the dust in which the Mantis had walked.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924) (public domain).
passages.zh: 螳螂對牠們說：「你們切割大羚羊時，必須舉著火把照亮自己，但我的鞋立在那上方的天空中，就在我拋上去的地方，為我照耀……」他說：「我就是螳螂，而我的這隻鞋必將真正成為在黑暗中照耀的月亮。」這就是月亮在夜間照耀的原因。這就是月亮寒冷的原因，因為它是一隻鞋，是皮革做的。它是紅色的，因為它上面有泥土，就是螳螂曾走過的塵土。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the long version: he threw the feather up, he said: 'Thou must now lie up in the sky, thou must henceforth be the Moon. Thou shalt shine at night. Thou shalt by thy shining lighten the darkness for men, till the Sun rises to light up all things for men... Thou art the Moon, thou dost give light for men, then thou dost fall away, thou dost return to life, when thou hast fallen away.' That is what the Moon does.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 9-10; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 長版本的濃縮轉述：他把羽毛拋上去，他說：「你現在必須躺在那上方的天空中，你從今以後必須成為月亮。你將在夜間照耀。你將以你的照耀為人們照亮黑暗，直到太陽升起，為人們照亮萬物……你就是月亮，你為人們發出光，然後你便消減，當你消減之後，你又重返生命。」這就是月亮所做的事。

title.en: The Sun's Knife Cuts the Moon Away
title.zh: 日刀割月

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §§ 15-16; Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), pp. 50-53

summary.en: In astrological Bushman mythology the Moon is a man whom the Sun, jealous of his night light, stabs and cuts away with his knife of rays until one small piece is left — which the Moon piteously begs the Sun to spare for his children. From that backbone the Moon grows whole again, and the cutting begins again.
summary.zh: 桑人星象神話中，月本為人，因夜光遭日妒，被日以光芒之刀節節割削，僅餘小塊——月哀求日為其孩童留此脊椎。自小塊復長圓盈，割削復始。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The Sun comes, the Sun follows the darkness, the Sun takes away the moon, the moon stands, the Sun pierces it, with the Sun's knife, as it stands; therefore, it decays away on account of it. Therefore, it says: 'O Sun! leave for the children the backbone!' Therefore, the Sun leaves the backbone for the children; the Sun does so.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 51 (public domain).
passages.zh: 太陽來了，太陽追隨黑暗，太陽奪走月亮，月亮立著，太陽刺穿它，用太陽的刀，趁它立著的時候；因此，它因這緣故而衰減。因此，它說：「噢，太陽！把脊骨留給孩子們吧！」因此，太陽把脊骨留給孩子們；太陽如此行了。

passages.text: The Moon meant mankind to be like himself: dying, and then coming again living back... he again goes to become another moon, which is whole; he again lives... while he feels that he had seemed to die. Therefore, he becomes a new moon; while he feels that he has again put on a stomach; he becomes large; he comes, while he is alive. He goes along at night... while he feels that he is a shoe.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 52-53 (public domain), in the Sun-and-children narration.
passages.zh: 月亮本意是要人類像他自己一樣：死去，然後又活著回來……他再次去成為另一個月亮，一個完整的月亮；他再次活著……同時他覺得自己似乎曾經死去。因此，他成為一彎新月；同時他覺得自己又長出了肚子；他變大了；他前來，而他是活著的。他在夜間前行……同時他覺得自己是一隻鞋。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of W. H. I. Bleek's 1875 summary (§16): the Moon is looked upon as a man who incurs the wrath of the Sun, and is consequently pierced by the knife (rays) of the latter, until almost the whole of the Moon is cut away, and only one little piece left; which the Moon piteously implores the Sun to spare for his children. From this little piece the Moon gradually grows again until it becomes a full moon, when the Sun's stabbing recommences.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §16; not verbatim.
passages.zh: W. H. I. Bleek 於一八七五年所作摘要（§16）的濃縮轉述：月亮被視為一個人，他招致太陽的憤怒，因而被後者的刀（光芒）刺穿，直到月亮幾乎全部被切去，只剩下一小片；月亮可憐地懇求太陽為他的孩子們留下這一片。從這一小片，月亮又逐漸生長，直到成為滿月，此時太陽的刺戳又再度開始。

title.en: The Girl of the Early Race Who Made Stars
title.zh: 早期之民造星少女

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1873 by ||kabbo (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Girl of the Early Race, who made Stars'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §23

summary.en: In her seclusion hut a girl of the ancient race, angry that her mother gives her too few |hum roots, throws wood-ashes into the sky — they become the Milky Way — and the roots become the red and white stars, while the peel of her food becomes locusts. She was at last shot by her husband. This is the star-creation story of the |Xam.
summary.zh: 初潮隔離之少女，怨母予根少，擲灰上天成銀河；根化紅白之星；果皮化飛蝗。後為夫所射。此即|Xam造星之神話。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by ||kabbo to Bleek and Lloyd; girlhood seclusion customs are described; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

narrative.en:
The girl of the early race had reached the age when a Bushman girl is put into a tiny hut with a very small door, which her mother closes upon her. She must not look at the springbok, lest they grow wild; she must not look afar. Her mother brings her food. One day the mother gave her too little of the |hum, the scented root eaten raw, and the girl grew hungry and angry in her hut.

She took up wood-ashes and threw them into the sky, saying: 'The wood ashes which are here, they must altogether become the Milky Way; they must white lie along in the sky, that the stars may stand outside of the Milky Way.' The ashes became the glowing arch of the night, and the stars, she said, should sail along their footprints, standing brightly around, so that the people might find their way home by night, in the middle of the night.

Still angry, she threw up the roots of the |hum she had been given: the red old roots became the red stars and the white young roots the white stars. Then she threw up the peel of the |khissi root she was eating, and the peel became locusts. The Milky Way gently glows, it is said, because it feels that it is wood ashes; it lights a little, so that the people can return home.

But the myth closes darkly. The first girl of the early race acted ill, the narrators say; and she was at last shot by her husband. Girls who transgressed the seclusion rules could fix with their glance the people and things they looked at (§24 of Bleek's Brief Account records men turned into trees by a maiden's glance), and the star-maker's fate warns against the powers of the isolated girl. Her creation stands: every clear night the ashes still lie white along the sky, and the stars sail along behind them. The narrators add the frame: the \xwi-\na-ssho-\k'e, the people of the early race, were said to be stupid and not to have understood things well; their doings are retold so that the Flat Bushmen may know what the first inhabitants of the land did. The girl's ashes were the first light of the night road, and her angry root-throwing peopled the sky; the Milky Way must go round with the stars, lying as it goes, and when the sun turns back the stars also turn back to fetch the daybreak. Bushman children are shown the arch and told that it gently glows because it remembers being wood ashes; and mothers warn their daughters in the seclusion hut with the same story, so that the angry, hungry girl inside the little door is also the maker of the stars she may not stare at too long.

functions: Charter narrative for the Milky Way and the stars of the |Xam sky.
Teaches the girlhood seclusion rules: what a maiden must not eat, see, or do.
Links anger and hunger in the seclusion hut to cosmic creation.

sensitivity_guidance: Collected under colonial constraint (some informants were prisoners at the Breakwater); girls' rites appear here through male-colonial transcription — present with archival framing only.

passages.text: My mother was the one who told me that the girl arose; she put her hands into the wood ashes; she threw up the wood ashes into the sky. She said to the wood ashes: 'The wood ashes which are here, they must altogether become the Milky Way. They must white lie along in the sky, that the stars may stand outside of the Milky Way, while the Milky Way is the Milky Way, while it used to be wood ashes.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 73 (public domain).
passages.zh: 是我母親告訴我，那女孩起身了；她把手伸進木灰裡；她把木灰拋向天空。她對木灰說：「這裡的木灰，必須全部變成銀河。它們必須潔白地橫臥在天空中，好讓星辰能立在銀河之外，而銀河仍是銀河，儘管它從前是木灰。」

passages.text: The Milky Way lying comes to its place... that it may descend nicely... The Stars shall also stand nicely around. They shall sail along upon their footprints, which they, always sailing along, are following... The Stars had been setting; they had, again, been coming out; they had, sailing along, been following their footprints. They become white, when the Sun comes out.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 75 (public domain).
passages.zh: 橫臥的銀河來到它的位置……好讓它能美好地降下……星辰也將美好地環立四周。它們將沿著自己的足跡航行，那足跡是它們一直航行時所跟隨的……星辰曾一直西沉；它們又曾一直升起；它們曾航行著，跟隨自己的足跡。當太陽出來時，它們就變白了。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. She first gently threw up wood ashes into the sky, that she might presently throw up |hum roots; while she felt that she was angry with her mother, because her mother had not given her many |hum roots, that she might eat abundantly; for, she was in the hut. The red roots made red stars and the white roots white stars; the peel of the |khissi root she threw up became locusts. And the girl was at last shot by her husband.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 76-77; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同一段落的濃縮改述，非逐字照錄。她先輕輕地把木灰拋向天空，好讓她隨即拋上|hum根；當時她覺得自己對母親生氣，因為母親沒有給她許多|hum根，好讓她能吃得飽足；因為，她在那小屋裡。紅根變成紅星，白根變成白星；她拋上的|khissi根皮變成了蝗蟲。而那女孩最後被她的丈夫射殺。

title.en: \gaunu, the Great Star Who Named the Stars
title.zh: 大星加烏奴：命名眾星者

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Great Star, \gaunu, which, singing, named the Stars'

summary.en: \gaunu was once a great star; singing, he called out the names of all the stars, which is why the stars possess their names. The smallest, fine stars he made '\whai' — identified by the observatory with Altair and its neighbours — and the porcupine watches for them, for when they turn back it is dawn and he goes home.
summary.zh: 加烏奴昔為大星，唱而呼眾星之名，故眾星有其名。至小至細者，其名為'瓦海——經天文臺證為牛郎星（天鷹座α）。穿山甲候之：星回則天明，遂歸家。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; star identifications by Royal Observatory astronomers, 1873.

passages.text: \gaunu, he was formerly a great Star; therefore, his name is \gaunu, while he feels that he was the one who formerly spoke (called) the Stars' names; while he feels that he is a great one. Therefore, he called the Stars' names. Therefore, the Stars possess their names; while they feel that \gaunu was the one who called their names.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 79 (public domain).
passages.zh: \gaunu，他從前是一顆大星辰；因此，他的名字叫\gaunu，因為他覺得自己就是從前說出（呼喚）眾星辰名字的那一位；因為他覺得自己是一位偉大的存在。因此，他呼喚了眾星辰的名字。因此，眾星辰擁有它們的名字；因為它們覺得\gaunu就是呼喚它們名字的那一位。

passages.text: He formerly sang, while he uttered the Stars' names. He said '\whai' to (some) Stars which are very small; they are those of which he made '\whai'; their small, fine ones are those which are '\whai'. [The stars \whai-gwai and \whai-|pua were identified as Altair and neighbouring stars of Aquila.]
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 79 with editor's bracketed note (public domain).
passages.zh: 他從前歌唱，同時說出眾星辰的名字。他對（一些）非常小的星辰說「\whai」；它們就是他使之成為「\whai」的那些；它們那些細小的，就是「\whai」的那些。[星辰\whai-gwai與\whai-|pua被認定為河鼓二（牽牛星）及天鷹座鄰近的星辰。]

passages.text: Therefore, the porcupine, when these Stars have, sitting, turned back, he will not remain on the hunting ground; for, he knows that it is dawn, when '\whai' has, lying, turned back. He returns home; for, he is used to look at these Stars; they are those which he watches.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 81 (public domain).
passages.zh: 因此，當這些星辰坐著轉回時，豪豬就不會留在獵場上；因為，當「\whai」躺著轉回時，他知道天已破曉。他回家去；因為他習慣觀看這些星辰；它們就是他守望的那些。

title.en: What the Stars Say: 'Tsau!'
title.zh: 星之所言：「呲！」

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'What the Stars say, and a Prayer to a Star'

summary.en: On summer nights the stars cry 'Tsau! Tsau!' — they are cursing the shining eyes of springbok and the beasts of prey, which also gleam in the dark. The Bushman listens to the stars as a boy sleeping beside his grandfather, and learns their speech.
summary.zh: 夏夜星辰呼「呲！呲！」——詛咒羚羊與猛獸暗中閃耀之目。桑人童子偎祖父而眠，聆聽星語。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: They (the Bushmen) wish, that they may also perceive things. Therefore, they say that the Star shall take their heart, with which they do not a little hunger; the Star shall give them the Star's heart, — the Star's heart, — with which the Star sits in plenty. For the Star is not small; the Star seems as if it had food.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 81 (public domain).
passages.zh: 他們（布須曼人）希望自己也能感知事物。因此，他們說星星當取走他們的心，他們因這心而頗為飢餓；星星當賜予他們星星的心——星星的心——星星憑此豐足而坐。因為星星並不小；星星彷彿有食物。

passages.text: The Stars are wont to call, 'Tsau! Tsau!' therefore the Bushmen are wont to say, that the Stars curse for them the springboks' eyes; the Stars say, 'Tsau!' they say, 'Tsau! Tsau!' I am one who was listening to them. I questioned my grandfather, what things it could be that spoke thus. My grandfather said to me that the Stars were those who spoke thus.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 81-82 (public domain).
passages.zh: 星星慣於呼喚：『曹！曹！』因此布須曼人慣於說，星星為他們詛咒跳羚的眼睛；星星說：『曹！』它們說：『曹！曹！』我正是那聆聽它們的人。我問我的祖父，說話如此的究竟是何物。我的祖父對我說，說話如此的正是星星。

passages.text: The Stars said, 'Tsau! Tsau!' Summer is (the time) when they sound. Because I used to sleep with my grandfather, I was the one who sat with my grandfather, when he sat in the coolness outside. Therefore, I questioned him, about the things which spoke thus. He said, the Stars were those who spoke thus; they cursed for the people the springboks' eyes.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 82-83 (public domain).
passages.zh: 星星說：『曹！曹！』夏天正是它們作聲的時節。因為我常與祖父同睡，我便是那與祖父同坐的人，當他坐在外頭陰涼處時。因此，我問他，說話如此的究竟是何物。他說，說話如此的正是星星；它們為人們詛咒跳羚的眼睛。

title.en: The Prayer to Canopus for a Shooting Arm
title.zh: 向老人星求臂之祈禱

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'What the Stars say, and a Prayer to a Star'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §60

summary.en: When Canopus rises the old man speaks to the 'Bushman-rice' star: give me thy heart, take mine; give me thy stomach, take mine; give me thy arm, which never misses — for my arm misses its aim. He speaks the prayer sitting in the cool, wishing the arrow might hit the springbok for him.
summary.zh: 老人星升時，老者向「桑人之米」星祈曰：取我之心，予爾飽足之心；取我之臂——常失之臂——予爾百發百中之臂。坐於涼處誦禱，望箭中羚。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: My grandfather used to speak to Canopus, when Canopus had newly come out; he said: 'Thou shalt give me thy heart, with which thou dost sit in plenty, thou shalt take my heart, — my heart, — with which I am desperately hungry. That I might also be full, like thee. For, I hunger. For, thou seemest to be satisfied (with food); hence thou art not small. For, I am hungry.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 83 (public domain).
passages.zh: 我的祖父常對老人星說話，當老人星剛升起時；他說：『你當賜我你的心，你憑此豐足而坐；你當取走我的心——我的心——我因這心而極度飢餓。好讓我也能像你一樣飽足。因為我飢餓。因為你似乎飽足（於食物）；因此你並不小。因為我飢餓。』

passages.text: 'Thou shalt give me thy stomach, with which thou art satisfied. Thou shalt take my stomach, that thou mayst also hunger. Give thou me also thy arm, thou shalt take my arm, with which I do not kill. For, I miss my aim. Thou shalt give me thy arm. For, my arm which is here, I miss my aim with it.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 83 (public domain).
passages.zh: 『你當賜我你的胃，你憑此飽足。你當取走我的胃，好讓你也飢餓。你也當賜我你的手臂，你當取走我的手臂，我憑此不能獵殺。因為我射不中目標。你當賜我你的手臂。因為我這在此的手臂，我憑它射不中目標。』

passages.text: He desired that the arrow might hit the springbok for him; hence, he wished the Star to give him the Star's arm, while the Star took his arm, with which he missed his aim. He shut his mouth, he moved away, he sat down; while he felt that he wished to sit and sharpen an arrow.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 83-84 (public domain).
passages.zh: 他盼望箭能為他射中跳羚；因此，他願星星賜他星星的手臂，而星星取走他那射不中目標的手臂。他閉上嘴，他走開，他坐下；同時他感到自己想坐下磨一支箭。

title.en: Dawn's-Heart and the Lynx: The Star Husband's Wife
title.zh: 晨心星與天貓：星夫之妻

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), '\ko-g\nuih-tara, wife of the Dawn's-Heart Star, Jupiter'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §25

summary.en: Jupiter, the Dawn's-Heart star, married the Lynx, then a beautiful woman; the hyena, jealous, bewitched her with poisoned 'Bushman rice' so she became a lioness, and by night took her place in the hut. The star's eyes glowed like fires as he came home; he stabbed at the impostor, missed, and his wife, enticed from the reeds and stripped of her lion skin, could never eat Bushman rice again — she became the lynx that eats meat.
summary.zh: 晨心星（木星）娶天貓——其時為美婦；土狼妒之，以毒「桑人之米」巫化其為母獅，夜間代居其位。星目如火歸家；擲矛擊偽者不中；其妻自蘆葦被誘出，剝獅皮復為人——然終不復食桑人之米，遂為食肉之獰貓。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o (from his mother |xabbi-an) to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

narrative.en:
The Dawn's-Heart (Jupiter) had a beautiful wife of the early race and a younger sister-in-law, \xe-dde-yoe, who carried the digging-stick and minded the child. The Dawn's-Heart buried his child under the leaves of an edible root, hoping his wife would find it; other animals and birds arrived first and each proposed herself as mother, and the child mocked them until it recognized its own mother. Among the insulted animals were the Jackal and the Hyena, who plotted revenge.

They bewitched the Lynx with poisoned 'Bushman rice' — so-called ants' eggs — and she was transformed into a lioness. In the dark the Hyena tried to take her place in the hut when the Dawn's-Heart returned; but he noticed that the woman who sat with her back toward him was not his wife, and his sister-in-law told him of the imposture. He seized his assegai and stabbed at the place where the Hyena had been sitting; she sprang out, trod burning her foot in the fire, and fled, leaving the ornaments she had worn.

The bewitched wife had hidden in the reeds. Her sister called her at morning and again near sunset, and each time she came out to suckle the child, saying that her thinking-strings were falling, that she was forgetting. At last the sister brought goats, and the people hid around; when the wife sprang from the reeds to the goats, the Dawn's-Heart caught her and all the people held her fast. They cut open the goats, took out the contents of the stomachs and anointed her, rubbing off the lion hair; she asked that the hair on the tips of her ears be left, 'for in that manner I shall come to hear.'

She became a fair woman again; but because she had been bewitched by Bushman rice she could no longer eat it. She was changed into the lynx who eats meat, and the Dawn's-Heart, going home from hunting ever after, walked with an arrow on the bow and the assegai stuck in the ground, his eyes large like fires — for the hyenas had poisoned his wife, and his heart would never be quiet again. The discourses attached to this myth are long: the Dawn's-Heart talks to his daughter of their own history, of the lynx-mother, of the sun, moon and stars, and of the habits of lions and Bushmen, running at last into a whole account of the jackals' doings; and the fugitive hyena, her foot burnt in the fire, is followed home through long speeches with her mother and father about suitable marriages. In the second long piece the narrative of about seventy-two columns is followed by the hyena family's talk. The stars keep the story in the sky: Jupiter walks as the only Dawn's-Heart when his heart-daughter is swallowed, and precedes the Dawn's-Heart-child; the identification with Regulus was made at the Cape Observatory in the 1870s, on the narrators' pointing. The myth also fixes Bushman hut etiquette — the wife sits facing her husband, and the stranger who sits with her back to the door is the one to be suspected — and it teaches that poisoned food given in beauty is the most dangerous gift of all, for the Lynx ate what was offered to her and never tasted Bushman-rice again.

functions: Explains the lynx's diet and the tufts on its ears.
Charter for the woman 'sitting with her back' etiquette of the hut.
Links the planet Jupiter and his child-star to a domestic tragedy of the early race.

variants.summary: A short piece with the address of the younger sister to the transformed lioness-wife.

canonical_translation: Bleek & Lloyd translation, printed 1911

primary_sources.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore, '\ko-g\nuih-tara, wife of the Dawn's-Heart Star, Jupiter'
primary_sources.citation: London: George Allen & Co., 1911, pp. 84-97; manuscript L III.—30. 8393-8432

primary_sources.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts

secondary_sources.work: Lorna Marshall, The !Kung of Nyae Nyae
secondary_sources.citation: Marshall, L. 1976. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press.

secondary_sources.work: Megan Biesele, Women Like Meat: The Folklore and Foraging Ideology of the Kalahari Ju/'hoan
secondary_sources.citation: Biesele, M. 1993. Bloomington: Indiana University Press.

sensitivity_guidance: 19th-century colonial-era collection; identify star names as given by the narrators and the Royal Observatory, not as astronomical fact.

passages.text: And \kó-g\nuin-tdra exclaimed, she said to her younger sister: 'Thou shalt leave this |haken alone; I will be the one who eats it. For, thou art the one who shalt take care of the child. For, this |haken, its smell is not nice.' Therefore, as \kó-g\nuin-tdra sat, eating the |haken, the ornaments of themselves came off.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 86 (public domain).
passages.zh: 於是\kó-g\nuin-tdra 出聲說道，她對她的妹妹說：「這個|haken 你別管；我來吃它。因為，你才是要照顧孩子的人。因為，這個|haken，它的氣味不好。」因此，當\kó-g\nuin-tdra 坐著吃那|haken 時，那些飾物便自行脫落了。

passages.text: Then the Dawn's-Heart ran to the hyena; he took aim (with his assegai), he pierced the place where the hyena had been sitting, while the hyena sprang out, she trod, burning herself in the fire, while she sprang away; while the ornaments remained at the place where she had been sitting... And the Dawn's-Heart scolded his younger sister-in-law, why was it that his younger sister-in-law had not quickly told him about it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 92-93 (public domain).
passages.zh: 於是曙光之心奔向那鬣狗；他瞄準（以他的長矛），刺向鬣狗方才坐著的地方，而鬣狗躍出，她踩踏著，在火中燒傷了自己，同時躍開而去；而那些飾物則留在她方才坐著的地方……曙光之心責罵他的弟媳，為何他的弟媳不趕快把這事告訴他。

passages.text: They cut the goats open, they took out the contents of the stomach, they anointed \kó-g\nuin-tdra with the contents of the stomachs. They, taking hold, rubbed off the hair from her skin. Therefore, when she sat down, she said: 'Ye must, pulling, leave the hair on the tips of my ears; for, in that manner I shall come to hear; for, I do not feel as if I should hear.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 95-96 (public domain).
passages.zh: 他們把山羊剖開，取出胃裡的東西，用胃裡的東西塗抹\kó-g\nuin-tdra。他們抓住她，把她皮膚上的毛搓掉。因此，當她坐下時，她說：「你們拉扯時，務必把我耳尖上的毛留下；因為，那樣我才能聽得見；因為，我感覺自己好像聽不見。」

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's 1875 summary (§25): the mother of the Dawn's-Heart-child was the Lynx, who was then a beautiful woman; she was bewitched with poisoned Bushman rice and transformed into a lioness; her brothers pulled off the lion skin so that she became a fair woman again; but, in consequence of having been bewitched by Bushman rice, she could no longer eat that, and was changed into a lynx who ate meat.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §25; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布萊克一八七五年摘要（§25）的濃縮轉述：曙光之心之子的母親是猞猁，她當時是個美麗的女子；她被下了毒的布須曼米施了巫術，變成了一頭母獅；她的兄弟們把獅皮剝下，使她重新變回美麗的女子；但由於曾被布須曼米施了巫術，她再也吃不得那東西，於是被變成了一頭吃肉的猞猁。

title.en: The Dawn's-Heart Swallows His Child
title.zh: 晨心星吞其女

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 (Bleek archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §25; Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), p. 96 extract

summary.en: The Dawn's-Heart star has a daughter, his 'heart': he swallows her, walks alone as the only Dawn's-Heart, and when she is grown spits her out again. She becomes another female Dawn's-Heart and spits out another child which follows the pair — the recurring star-child that follows Jupiter across the sky.
summary.zh: 晨心星有一女，是其「心」：吞之，獨行為唯一晨心星；及長復吐出。女遂為另一晨心星，再吐新女隨行——即天上恆隨木星之 repeat 星子。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San star lore from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§25): the Dawn's-Heart (the star Jupiter) has a daughter, who is identified with some neighbouring star preceding Jupiter. Her name is the Dawn's-Heart-child, and her relation to her father is somewhat mysterious. He calls her 'my heart', he swallows her, then walks alone as the only Dawn's-Heart Star, and, when she is grown up, he spits her out again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §25; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布萊克摘要（§25）的濃縮轉述：曙光之心（木星）有一個女兒，她被認為是木星前方某顆鄰近的星。她的名字叫曙光之心之子，而她與父親的關係有些神秘。他稱她為「我的心」，他把她吞下，然後獨自前行，成為唯一的曙光之心之星，而當她長大後，他又把她吐了出來。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. She then herself becomes another female Dawn's-Heart, and spits out another Dawn's-Heart-child, which follows the male and female Dawn's-Heart. The Dawn's-Heart hid his first child under the leaves of an edible root, where he thought that his wife would come and find it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §25; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同一段落的濃縮轉述；並非逐字照錄。她隨後自己也成了另一個女性的曙光之心，並吐出另一個曙光之心之子，這孩子跟隨在男性與女性的曙光之心之後。曙光之心把他的第一個孩子藏在一種可食根莖的葉子下，他以為他的妻子會來那裡找到它。

title.en: The Son of the Wind Rolls the Ball
title.zh: 風之子滾球

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Son of the Wind'

summary.en: The Wind's child rolls a ball to |na-ka-ti, calling his name, but no one knows his; his mother warns |na-ka-ti to utter the name only when the hut is screened, and then run in — for the Wind will blow him away. |na-ka-ti shouts '\erriten-\kuan-\kuan!' and the storm flattens the boy and drives the huts apart; only the Wind's mother can raise him up. The Wind lies when it blows hard, and stands when it is still; and the Wind was once a man who became a bird that dwells in a mountain hole.
summary.zh: 風子滾球喚名，無人知其名；母囑：俟屏帳成方可呼其名，呼畢速入屋，防風捲走。名既出，颶風立至，掀屋倒童；唯風母扶之起。風猛吹時乃「臥」，靜時乃「立」；風本為人，化鳥棲山穴。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text:
The (son of the) Wind was formerly still. And he rolled (a ball) to 
a-ka-ti. He exclaimed: 'O 
a-ka-ti! There it goes!' And 
a-ka-ti exclaimed: 'O comrade! There it goes!' because 
a-ka-ti felt that he did not know his (the other one's) name.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 101 (public domain).
passages.zh:
風（之子）從前是靜止不動的。他把（一顆球）滾向 
a-ka-ti。他喊道：「哦，
a-ka-ti！球滾過去了！」
a-ka-ti 也喊道：「哦，夥伴！球滾過去了！」因為 
a-ka-ti 覺得自己不知道他（對方）的名字。

passages.text: His mother exclaimed: 'I will not utter to thee comrade's name. For, thou shalt wait; that father may first shelter for us the hut... And thou shalt, when I have uttered for thee comrade's name, thou must scamper away, thou must run home, that thou mayest come into the hut, whilst thou dost feel that the wind would blow thee away.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 102-103 (public domain).
passages.zh: 他的母親喊道：「我不會對你說出夥伴的名字。因為你得等著；讓父親先為我們把茅屋搭好……等我對你說出夥伴的名字之後，你就必須趕緊跑開，你必須跑回家，好讓你進到茅屋裡，同時你還要覺得風會把你吹走。」

passages.text: He beheld that his father had finished sheltering the hut, then he exclaimed: 'There it goes! O \erriten-\kuan-\kuan! There it goes! O \gau-\gaubu-ti! There it goes!' And he scampered away, he ran home; while the other one began to lean over, and the other one fell down. He lay kicking violently upon the vlei. Therefore, the people's huts vanished away, the wind blew, breaking their sheltering bushes, together with the huts.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 104-105 (public domain).
passages.zh: 他看見父親已經把茅屋搭好了，於是喊道：「球滾過去了！哦 \erriten-\kuan-\kuan！球滾過去了！哦 \gau-\gaubu-ti！球滾過去了！」他便趕緊跑開，跑回家去；而另一個人則開始彎下身子，另一個人倒了下去。他躺在窪地上猛烈地踢蹬。因此，人們的茅屋消失了，風吹起來，吹斷了他們用來遮擋的灌木叢，連同茅屋一起。

passages.text: His mother came out of the hut; his mother came, grasping (him), to raise him up... Therefore, the wind became still... Therefore, we who are Bushmen, we are wont to say: 'The wind seems to be lying down, for, it does not gently blow.' The Wind (the Wind's son) was formerly a man. He became a bird. And he was flying... he dwelt in a mountain (that is, in a mountain hole).
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 106-107 (public domain).
passages.zh: 他的母親從茅屋裡出來；他的母親走過來，抓住（他）要把他扶起來……因此，風靜了下來……因此，我們這些布須曼人常說：「風似乎躺下了，因為它不輕輕地吹了。」風（風之子）從前是一個人。他變成了一隻鳥。他飛著……他住在一座山裡（也就是一個山洞裡）。

title.en: \kagara and \haunu Fight with Lightning
title.zh: 卡加拉與哈烏奴雷電相鬥

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), '\kagara and \haunu, who fought each other with Lightning'

summary.en: \kagara the little bird-man rescues his sister from her husband \haunu, a Rain sorcerer. The brother-in-law sneezes blood and lightens at them; \kagara fends off the strokes and at last strikes back with the black lightning that kills, felling \haunu, who lies thundering. The grandmothers said these two fight in the east whenever the clouds stand like a mountain.
summary.zh: 小鳥人卡加拉自其妹夫——雨巫哈烏奴——處奪回妹妹。妹夫噴血閃電擊之；卡加拉揮臂格擋，終以「黑雷」反擊，擊倒哈烏奴，其臥而雷吼。祖母云：雲聚如山時，此二人在東方相鬥。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o (from his grandmother ≠kammi) to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: They formerly, \kagara formerly went to fetch his younger sister, he went to take her away; he went to take her away from \haunu; and he took (her) back to her parents. \haunu gave chase to his brother-in-law, he passed along behind the hill. The clouds came, clouds which were unequalled in beauty; they vanished away.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 113 (public domain).
passages.zh: 從前，\kagara 去接他的妹妹，他去把她帶走；他去把她從 \haunu 那裡帶走；他把她帶回她的父母身邊。\haunu 追趕他的妹夫，他從山丘後面繞過去。雲來了，那些美得無與倫比的雲；它們消失了。

passages.text: Then \haunu sneezed, on account of it; blood poured out of his nostrils; he stealthily lightened at his brother-in-law. His brother-in-law fended him quickly off, his brother-in-law also stealthily lightened at him. He quickly fended off his brother-in-law. His brother-in-law also lightened at him.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 115-116 (public domain).
passages.zh: 於是 \haunu 因此打了個噴嚏；血從他的鼻孔裡湧出來；他悄悄地朝他的妹夫打閃電。他的妹夫迅速擋開了他，他的妹夫也悄悄地朝他打閃電。他迅速擋開了妹夫。他的妹夫也朝他打了閃電。

passages.text: Then he stealthily lightened at his younger sister's husband with black lightning, he, lightening, whisked him up (and carried him to a little distance). His younger sister's husband, in this manner, lay dying; he, in this manner, he thundered, while \kagara bound up his head with the net, he, returning, arrived at home... they went along angry with each other.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 117 (public domain).
passages.zh: 接著，他暗暗以黑色閃電擊向他妹妹的丈夫，他，作為閃電，將他迅速捲起（並帶到不遠處）。他妹妹的丈夫就這樣躺著奄奄一息；他，就這樣，發出雷鳴，而 \kagara 用網綁住他的頭，他返回家中……他們彼此帶著怒氣同行。

passages.text: My grandmothers used to say: '\kagara and his companion are those who fight in the East, he and \haunu.' When the clouds were thick, and the clouds resembled a mountain, then, the clouds were lightening, on account of it. And my grandmothers used to say: 'It is \kagara, with \haunu.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 118 (public domain).
passages.zh: 我的祖母們常說：『\kagara 和他的同伴就是那在東方爭鬥的，他和 \haunu。』當雲層濃厚，雲層狀似山巒，那時，雲層正因它而閃電。我的祖母們常說：『那是 \kagara，與 \haunu 一起。』

title.en: The Hyena's Revenge on the Grudging Lion
title.zh: 土狼報復吝獅

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871 and 1875 (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Hyena's Revenge' (two versions); W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §27

summary.en: The lion grudges the hyena his meat; the hyena invites him home, ladles boiling soup into his mouth, jams the hot pot over his head, and beats him dead beneath it. In the second version the lion, who also eats people, has carried off an old woman, and the hyena strikes him down while his head is inside the pot.
summary.zh: 獅吝於予土狼肉；土狼邀其至家，以滾湯灌其口，覆熱釜其首，擊殺之。第二版中，食人之獅已擄一老嫗；土狼趁其首入釜時擊斃之。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The Hyena was the one who went to the Lion's house, then, he deceived the Lion; while he felt that the Lion had acted grudgingly towards him about the quagga's flesh; therefore, the Lion came to the Hyena's house, when the Hyena was boiling there in the Hyena's pot; the Hyena boiled ostrich flesh in it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 123 (public domain).
passages.zh: 鬣狗就是那去到獅子家中的人，於是，他欺騙了獅子；因為他覺得獅子曾因斑驢的肉而對他吝嗇；因此，獅子來到鬣狗家中，當時鬣狗正在鬣狗的鍋裡煮著；鬣狗在裡面煮鴕鳥肉。

passages.text: The Hyena gave soup to the Lion; therefore, the Lion took hold of the pot, while the pot was hot; the Hyena also grasped the pot with his hands; the Hyena said: 'O Lion! Allow me to pour soup into the inside of thy mouth.' The Hyena poured soup into the Lion's mouth; then, he put the mouth of the pot over the Lion's head, while the pot was hot.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 123 (public domain).
passages.zh: 鬣狗把湯給了獅子；因此，獅子抓住了鍋，當時鍋是熱的；鬣狗也用雙手抓住了鍋；鬣狗說：『哦，獅子！讓我將湯倒入你口中吧。』鬣狗把湯倒入獅子口中；接著，他把鍋口罩在獅子頭上，當時鍋是熱的。

passages.text: The soup was burning the Lion's eyes; the soup also burned the inside of his mouth. Then, he swallowed hot soup with his throat, he swallowed, causing himself to die with hot soup; he died, while his head was inside the pot. The Hyena took up the Hyena's stick, the Hyena was beating him with the stick, while his head was inside the pot; the Hyena was beating him; the Hyena struck, cleaving the pot asunder.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 123-124 (public domain).
passages.zh: 湯灼燒著獅子的眼睛；湯也灼燒了他口腔的內部。接著，他用喉嚨吞下熱湯，他吞了下去，以熱湯使自己致死；他死了，頭還在鍋裡。鬣狗拿起鬣狗的棍子，鬣狗用棍子打他，當時他的頭還在鍋裡；鬣狗打著他；鬣狗一擊，將鍋劈成兩半。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the second version: the Hyena said 'I am accustomed to pour soup into this child's mouth, I also pour soup into my wife's mouth' — and poured soup into the Lion's mouth, put the Lion's head into the pot, while he felt that he altogether put the Lion's head into the pot; that he might altogether kill the Lion with the soup's heat; and he carried off the old woman on account of it, and struck the Lion down while his head was inside the pot.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 126-127; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二版本的濃縮轉述：鬣狗說『我習慣把湯倒入這孩子的口中，我也把湯倒入我妻子的口中』——並把湯倒入獅子口中，將獅子的頭放進鍋裡，因為他覺得自己已將獅子的頭完全放進鍋裡；好讓他能以湯的熱度將獅子徹底殺死；他因此帶走了老婦人，並在獅子的頭還在鍋裡時將他擊倒。

title.en: The Lion Jealous of the Ostrich's Voice
title.zh: 獅妒鴕鳥之聲

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Lion jealous of the Voice of the Ostrich'

summary.en: The women praise the ostrich's booming; the jealous lion makes them stage a dance, kicks the ostrich's chest as he sings, tears it open, kills him and eats his lungs raw to boom like him. The ostrich's nail decayed from the kick — the scar on its chest is still the lion's nail — and boys must swallow the lungs whole and raw to keep the voice.
summary.zh: 婦人讚鴕鳥鳴聲；獅妒，令婦起舞，趁其鳴時踢其胸膛，撕裂殺之，生吞其肺以效其聲。鴕鳥之爪因踢而朽——胸上疤痕至今乃獅之爪痕。男孩須生吞整肺以存其聲。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The Lions conspired together that they might deceive the Ostrich; for, the women were wont, with regard to the Ostrich, they only praised the Ostrich for calling finely; the women did not praise them. And they (the Lions), speaking, said: 'In what manner shall we deceive?'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 128 (public domain).
passages.zh: 獅子們一同商議，想要欺騙鴕鳥；因為女人們對鴕鳥，向來只因鴕鳥叫得好聽而讚美牠；女人們並不讚美牠們（獅子）。牠們（獅子）便開口說道：『我們該用什麼法子來欺騙呢？』

passages.text: The other Lion answered, he said: 'The ostrich calls with his lungs; therefore, his throat sounds in this manner; his chest's front. Thou dost call with thy mouth; therefore, thou dost not call nicely.' The other Lion answered: 'Ye must make a (game of) \gebbi-ggu, that ye may kill the Ostrich, that ye may take out the Ostrich's lungs... and ye will call, sounding like the Ostrich, when ye have eaten the Ostrich's lungs.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 129-130 (public domain).
passages.zh: 另一隻獅子回答說：『鴕鳥是用肺來叫的；所以牠的喉嚨才發出這樣的聲音；是牠胸口的前面。你是用嘴來叫的；所以你叫得不好聽。』另一隻獅子回答說：『你們必須做一場（gebbi-ggu 的遊戲），好讓你們殺死鴕鳥，好讓你們取出鴕鳥的肺……等你們吃了鴕鳥的肺，你們叫起來就會像鴕鳥一樣響亮。』

passages.text: The Ostrich was still yonder at his house; the Lion called; the women did not applaud the Lion, because they felt that the Lion did not call well... And the Ostrich came; and the Ostrich called, sounding afar. And the women exclaimed: 'I do wish that the Lion called in this manner; for, he sounds as if he had put his tail into his mouth, while the Ostrich calls in a resounding manner.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 130-131 (public domain).
passages.zh: 鴕鳥還在那邊自己的家裡；獅子叫了；女人們並不為獅子喝采，因為她們覺得獅子叫得不好……後來鴕鳥來了；鴕鳥一叫，聲音傳得很遠。女人們便驚呼道：『我真希望獅子能這樣叫；因為牠叫起來，好像把尾巴塞進了嘴裡似的，而鴕鳥叫起來卻是響亮有餘。』

passages.text: He scratched, tearing it. And he called out: 'Is it a thing which calls sweetly?' while he kicked the Ostrich's chest. And the Ostrich also quickly turned back. And the Ostrich also kicked, tearing his chest... My grandfather also gave us the Ostrich's lungs to eat, that we might also resemble the Ostrich... our grandfather spoke... that we should not cook the Ostrich's lungs... we should not chew them, we should swallow them down, while they were whole.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 131-134 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 牠抓了抓，把它撕開。牠一面踢著鴕鳥的胸膛，一面喊道：『這可是個叫得甜美的東西嗎？』鴕鳥也很快地轉過身來。鴕鳥也踢了回去，撕開牠的胸膛……我的祖父也把鴕鳥的肺給我們吃，好讓我們也能像鴕鳥一樣……我們的祖父說過……我們不可把鴕鳥的肺煮熟……我們不可咀嚼它們，我們要把它們整塊吞下去，趁它們還是完整的時候。

title.en: The Resurrection of the Ostrich from a Bloody Feather
title.zh: 鴕鳥自血羽復生

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1871 by !A!kunta (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Resurrection of the Ostrich'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §34

summary.en: A hunter kills a male ostrich at its nest; a whirlwind lifts one blood-stained little feather into the sky, drops it into water, and there it becomes ostrich flesh, gains feathers, legs and bone, walks out of the water and returns to his wives as their regained husband. With the Moon and the male ostrich alone of mortal things, he dies and lives again.
summary.zh: 獵者於巢處殺雄鴕；旋風捲血羽上天，落入水中，漸成鴕肉，生羽生足生骨，出水而行，歸其妻為復得之夫。世間凡死不復生者眾，唯月與雄鴕，死而復生。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by !A!kunta to Bleek and Lloyd, c. 1871; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

narrative.en:
The Bushman kills an ostrich at its eggs and carries the bird home; the wife strips off the bloody short feathers and lays them on the bushes, and the family eats the meat. Then a little whirlwind comes, blows up one small bloodied feather, and lifts it into the sky. It whirls down, falls into the water, becomes wet — and becomes conscious. It lies in the water and becomes ostrich flesh.

In the water it puts on wings and gains its legs; then it walks out of the water and basks on the bank in the sun, for it is still a young ostrich with black quills. It dries its feathers lying on the water's bank, strengthening its feet, hardening its breastbone into bone, eating young bushes, growing. Its little feather it was which became the ostrich, blown up while the wind was a little whirlwind.

It thinks of the place where it scratched its nest; it lets itself grow first, then goes to its old house, to scratch there again, and calls its wives. Because he did die, he will marry three ostrich wives. He roars, hardening his ribs, that his ribs may become bone; he scratches out a house, and roars to call the females, that they may come to him. He meets them, runs round them, examines their feathers, drives them to the house to lay; he lies inside, guards the eggs against the jackal, and drives the jackal away with his feet — for his children are in the nest.

Bleek's summary adds the myth's frame: this idea of revival through a feather is compared to the Moon's revival; and, with the exception of the Moon and the male ostrich, all other mortal things die outright and do not come to life again — the myth is thus a twin to the Moon's monthly rebirth, and its denial is part of the death-decree world. Bleek's summary adds the myth's frame and its dialogue: the revived bird guards the nest against the attacks of the jackals and hyenas, who are thereby driven to seek for the nest of a she-ostrich who will not be fierce, and who runs away; and the flights of the two cowards are followed in a long, still unfinished dialogue between hyena and jackal. The idea of the revival of a dead male ostrich in and through one of its little feathers is also mentioned elsewhere and is compared to the coming to life of the Moon; whilst, with the exception of the Moon and the male ostrich, all other mortal things are said to die outright and not to come to life again. The hunter who told it had watched the whirlwind lift the plume, and the family stood at the water and saw the flesh come upon it; the myth is thus both an observation of the veld and a resurrection doctrine, for it grants to the ostrich the same monthly immortality as the Moon alone possesses among the old people's dead.

functions: Presents the single great exception to the finality of death.
Explains the male ostrich's nesting behaviour and fierceness at the nest.
Links avian resurrection to lunar resurrection in Bushman eschatology.

variants.name: Short 1875 version (B XII.1171-1213)
variants.summary: Brief outline of the feather's revival, ending with the ostrich guarding the nest and driving off jackals and hyenas.

variants.name: Moon's revival parallel (§16, §34)
variants.summary: The ostrich's return is explicitly compared with the Moon's monthly coming to life again.

canonical_translation: Bleek & Lloyd translation, printed 1911

primary_sources.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore, 'The Resurrection of the Ostrich'
primary_sources.citation: London 1911, pp. 136-143; manuscript B XII. 1171-1213

primary_sources.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts

secondary_sources.work: David Lewis-Williams, Believing and Seeing
secondary_sources.citation: Lewis-Williams, J. D. 1981. London: Academic Press.

secondary_sources.work: Megan Biesele, Women Like Meat
secondary_sources.citation: Biesele, M. 1993. Bloomington: Indiana University Press.

sensitivity_guidance: 19th-century colonial-era collection; presented as archive, not as living authority.

passages.text: The Bushman kills an Ostrich at the Ostrich's eggs; he carries away the Ostrich to the house... A little whirlwind comes to them; it blows up the Ostrich feathers. A little Ostrich feather that has blood upon it, it blows up the little feather into the sky. The little feather falls down out of the sky, it having whirled round falls down, it goes into the water, it becomes wet in the water, it is conscious, it lies in the water, it becomes Ostrich flesh; it gets feathers, it puts on its wings, it gets its legs, while it lies in the water.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 137-138 (public domain).
passages.zh: 布須曼人在鴕鳥蛋旁殺死一隻鴕鳥；他把鴕鳥帶回屋裡……一陣小旋風來到他們那裡；它把鴕鳥的羽毛吹了起來。一根沾著血的小鴕鳥羽毛，它把那根小羽毛吹上了天空。那根小羽毛從天上落了下來，它旋轉著落了下來，它落進水裡，它在水裡濕透了，它有了知覺，它躺在水裡，它變成了鴕鳥的肉；它長出羽毛，它披上翅膀，它長出雙腿，而它仍舊躺在水裡。

passages.text: It walks out of the water, it basks in the sun upon the water's edge, because it is still a young Ostrich... He dries (his feathers) lying upon the water's bank, that he may afterwards walk away... He swallows young plants which are small... His little feather it was which became the Ostrich, it was that which the wind blew up, while the wind was a little whirlwind.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 138-140 (public domain).
passages.zh: 它從水裡走了出來，它在水邊曬著太陽，因為它還是一隻小鴕鳥……牠躺在水岸上曬乾（羽毛），好讓自己之後能走開……牠吞下細小的嫩植物……正是牠的那根小羽毛變成了鴕鳥，正是那根被風吹起的羽毛，而那風是一陣小旋風。

passages.text: Because his breastbone is bone, he roars, hardening his ribs, that his ribs may become bone. Then he scratches (out a house)... he roaring calls the Ostrich wives, that the Ostrich wives may come to him... he meets them, that he may run round the females; for he had been dead; he dying left his wives.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 140-141 (public domain).
passages.zh: 因為他的胸骨是骨，他便咆哮，使肋骨變硬，好讓他的肋骨成為骨。接著他刨出（一個住處）……他咆哮著呼喚鴕鳥妻子們，好讓鴕鳥妻子們來到他身邊……他與她們相會，好讓他能繞著雌鳥奔跑；因為他曾經死去；他死去時留下了他的妻子們。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's 1875 summary (§34): a male ostrich is killed and carried home by a Bushman; one of its little feathers, stained with blood, is lifted up by a gentle whirlwind and falls into the water, where it gradually becomes an ostrich; it leaves the water as a young ostrich, grows up, and returns to its wives as their regained husband. This idea of revival is compared to the coming to life of the Moon; with the exception of the Moon and the male ostrich, all other mortal things die outright.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §34; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布萊克（Bleek）一八七五年摘要（§34）的濃縮轉述：一隻雄鴕鳥被一名布須曼人殺死並帶回家；牠的一根沾了血的小羽毛被一陣輕柔的旋風捲起，落入水中，在那裡漸漸變成一隻鴕鳥；牠以幼鴕鳥的形態離開水面，長大後回到牠的妻子們身邊，成為她們失而復得的丈夫。這種復生的觀念被比擬為月亮的復活；除了月亮與雄鴕鳥之外，其餘一切有死之物都徹底死去。

title.en: The Vultures, Their Elder Sister, and Her Husband
title.zh: 兀鷲、其姊與姊夫

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Vultures, their elder Sister, and her Husband'

summary.en: The vultures made a woman of the early race their elder sister and lived by her husband's kills; scolded for devouring the springbok, they fly up into the sky and look down, swooping only when game is sighted — and eating in such haste that they must leave the undercut for their sister.
summary.zh: 兀鷲以早期之民女子為姊，賴其夫所獵而活；因吞盡跳羚遭斥，乃飛上天空俯瞰，見獸方落，倉促啄食——須留「腹條」與其姊。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The Vultures formerly made their elder sister of a person; they lived with her. They, when their elder sister's husband brought (home) a springbok, they ate up the springbok. And their elder sister's husband cursed them, he scolded at them. And their elder sister took up the skin of the springbok, she singed it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 155 (public domain).
passages.zh: 禿鷲們從前把一個人當作她們的姊姊；她們與她同住。當她們姊姊的丈夫帶回一隻跳羚時，她們把那隻跳羚吃光了。於是她們姊姊的丈夫咒罵她們，責罵她們。她們的姊姊便拿起那張跳羚皮，用火燎去上面的毛。

passages.text: They said, this other one said: 'Thou shalt ascend, and then thou must come to tell us what the place seems to be like.'... a Vulture who was a little Vulture girl, she arose, she ascended... she went, disappearing in the sky, they no longer perceived her... Then, their younger sister descended from above out of the sky, she came and sat in the midst of them.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 159-160 (public domain).
passages.zh: 她們說，另一個她說：『你應當升上去，然後你必須回來告訴我們那地方看起來是什麼樣子。』……一隻禿鷲，一個年幼的禿鷲女孩，她起身，她升了上去……她去了，消失在天際，她們再也看不見她……接著，她們的妹妹從上方、從天空降下，她來坐在她們中間。

passages.text: And she said: 'There is nothing the matter with the place; for, the place is clear. The place is very beautiful; for, I do behold the whole place... the place seems as if we should perceive a springbok, if a springbok were lying under a tree; for the place is very beautiful.' Then, they altogether arose, all of them, they ascended into the sky.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 160-161 (public domain).
passages.zh: 她說：『那地方沒有什麼問題；因為那地方是清朗的。那地方非常美麗；因為我望見了整個地方……那地方看起來，彷彿若有跳羚躺在樹下，我們便能看見牠；因為那地方非常美麗。』於是，她們全體一同起身，全都升上了天空。

passages.text: They said: 'Ye must eat! ye must eat! ye must eat in great haste! for, that accursed man who comes yonder, he could not endure us.' And, they finished the springbok, they flew away, flew heavily away... Their elder sister said: 'Fie! how can ye act in this manner towards me? as if I had been the one who scolded you!'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 161-162 (public domain).
passages.zh: 她們說：『你們得吃！你們得吃！你們得趕緊吃！因為那個從那邊來的該死的人，他受不了我們。』於是，她們吃完了那隻跳羚，便飛走了，沉重地飛走了……她們的姊姊說：『呸！你們怎能這樣對待我？好像我才是責罵你們的那個人似的！』

title.en: Ddi-≠erreten, the Stone-Headed Man and the Lioness's Children
title.zh: 石頭人與母獅之子

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'Ddi-≠erreten, the Lioness, and the Children'

summary.en: A sick lioness gathers people's children to live with her at the water; Ddi-≠erreten — a man of the early race whose head is stone — sits in her house and sends the children home in batches, telling each that its people's fire burns at the head of this or that ravine. Returning, the lioness finds only the stone head; she bites it, shrieks at her broken teeth, and he goes home, telling her only: 'Our children were not.'
summary.zh: 病母獅聚人童同居水邊；石頭人Ddi-≠erreten入其屋，分批遣童歸家，告以各溝源處其族火所在。母獅歸，唯見石首；咬之，痛呼碎牙。石首唯答：「吾童本非爾有。」

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: Ddi-≠erreten, formerly, when the Lioness was at the water, dipping up water there, Ddi-≠erreten felt that the Lioness was the one who had gathered together the people's children, because the Lioness felt that she was an invalid on account of her chest; therefore, she gathered together the people's children, that the children might live with her, that the children might work for her.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 163-164 (public domain).
passages.zh: 迪-≠埃雷滕，从前，当母狮在水边舀水时，迪-≠埃雷滕觉得母狮就是那个把人们的孩子们聚集起来的人，因为母狮觉得自己因胸部而有病；因此，她把人们的孩子们聚集起来，好让孩子们与她同住，好让孩子们为她干活。

passages.text: Ddi-≠erreten said: 'O children sitting here! The fire of your people is that which is at the top of the ravine which comes down from the top (of the hill).' Therefore, two children arose, they went away to their own people. Ddi-≠erreten again said... 'The fire of your people is that which is below the top of the ravine which comes down on this side (of the hill).' And three children thus went.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 164-166 (public domain).
passages.zh: 迪-≠埃雷滕说：『哦，坐在这里的孩子们！你们族人的火，就是那在从（山）顶下来的山谷顶端的火。』于是两个孩子起身，离开回到他们自己的族人那里。迪-≠埃雷滕又说……『你们族人的火，就是那在从这一侧（山）下来的山谷顶端下方的火。』于是三个孩子就这样走了。

passages.text: And the Lioness came from the water, she thus returning came. She came along looking (at the house); she did not perceive the children. And she exclaimed: 'Why do the children not do so to me?... It must be this man who sits at the house; his head resembles Ddi-≠erreten.' And she became angry about it, when she perceived Ddi-≠erreten.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 166-167 (public domain).
passages.zh: 母狮从水边来了，她就这样回来。她一路走来（朝屋里）张望；她没有看见孩子们。她喊道：『孩子们为什么不对我这样？……一定是这个坐在屋里的人；他的头像迪-≠埃雷滕。』当她认出迪-≠埃雷滕时，她为此发怒了。

passages.text: The Lioness caught hold of his head. She exclaimed 'Growling' to the other one's head. And she exclaimed: 'Oh! Oh dear! my teeth! This must be why this cursed man's big head came to sit in front of my house!' While Ddi-≠erreten said: 'I told thee that our children they were not.'... And he arose, he returned home; while the Lioness sat in anger at her house... she did not a little love the children while she was doing so.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 168-169 (public domain).
passages.zh: 母狮抓住他的头。她对着另一个人的头喊『咆哮』。她喊道：『哦！哎呀！我的牙！一定是因为这个，这个该死的男人的大头才来坐在我的屋前！』而迪-≠埃雷滕说：『我告诉过你，我们的孩子不是。』……于是他起身，回家去了；而母狮怒气冲冲地坐在她的屋里……她这样做的时候，并非一点也不爱那些孩子。

title.en: The Mason Wasp Shoots His Wife
title.zh: 泥蜂射妻

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)
