title.en: Enlil and Sud: The Bridewealth of Nippur
title.zh: 恩利爾與蘇德：尼普魯的聘禮

region.en: Nippur, Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Enlil and Sud (ETCSL c.1.2.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Enlil, walking the street of Nippur, meets the young Sud at a woman's gate and proposes through her mother Nunbarshegunu. With proper bridewealth — a house, grain, and a mule — he wins her, and Enki names her Ninlil, lady of his city.
summary.zh: 恩利爾漫步尼普魯街巷，於一女宅門前遇少女蘇德，託其母努恩巴謝古努提親。以宅第、穀物與騾馬為聘，終得佳人；恩基為她命名寧利爾——其城之女主。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Enlil, the great lord, walks in the streets of Nippur in his splendor and sees the maiden Sud at the gate of her house. He greets her mother Nunbarshegunu with courtesy and asks for her daughter in marriage; the mother bargains with him like a real-world mother-in-law, requiring proper gifts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.2.2, courtship; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 恩利爾，偉大的主，以其榮光行走於尼普爾的街道上，看見少女蘇德在她家門前。他彬彬有禮地向她的母親農巴爾舍古努問候，並向她求婚；母親像現實中的岳母一般與他討價還價，要求合乎禮數的聘禮。

passages.text: Enlil sends the bridewealth: a house of his choosing, rations of grain, a mule to carry her, and the finest of everything for the household. Sud is bathed, anointed and adorned, and led to his house with the rites of a city bride.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.2.2, wedding gifts; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 恩利爾送來聘禮：一座由他選定的房屋、定量的穀物、一頭供她騎乘的騾子，以及家中一切最上乘之物。蘇德沐浴、塗油、盛裝打扮，並以城中新娘的禮儀被領往他的家。

passages.text: At the wedding Enki, lord of wisdom, gives the bride her new name: she shall be Ninlil, the lady of Enlil's city and of the grain; her breasts shall hold abundance for the land. The poem closes with blessings for the couple and for Nippur.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.2.2, naming and blessing; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在婚禮上，智慧之主恩基賜予新娘她的新名：她將名為寧利爾，是恩利爾之城與穀物之女主；她的雙乳將為大地蘊藏豐饒。詩篇以對這對佳偶與對尼普爾的祝福作結。

functions: Wedding myth and liturgy for the Enlil-Ninlil cult at Nippur
Mirror of real bridewealth negotiation and wedding rites
Etiology of Ninlil's name and her grain-abundance identity

title.en: Enlil's Command: The Hymn to the Lord of the Ekur
title.zh: 恩利爾之令：埃庫爾之主頌

region.en: Nippur, Ekur temple, Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯埃庫爾神殿（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A hymn to Enlil (ETCSL c.4.05.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The great hymn proclaims Enlil the enlil of all lands: his word makes heaven and earth obey, his shepherding staff rules the black-headed people, and his Ekur is the navel of the world. City by city, the hymn names the shrines that rise under his decree.
summary.zh: 偉大頌詩宣稱恩利爾為萬邦之恩利爾：其言一出，天地皆從；牧杖在手，統轄黑首之民；埃庫爾為世界之臍。頌詩逐一舉其敕命下興起的聖城。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Enlil's command reaches the ends of the earth: without him no city is built, no settlement founded, no stable of cattle raised. He is the shepherd of the black-headed people, and his word makes heaven itself, the great gods, obey.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.05.1, opening; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 恩利爾的號令直達大地盡頭：若無他，便無城可建，無聚落可立，無牛欄可興。他是黑頭之民的牧者，他的話語令諸大神乃至天本身也俯首聽命。

passages.text: The Ekur, his house on Nippur's hill, is called the navel of heaven and earth: its brickwork rises like a mountain of lapis and silver, its rites are deep as the Abzu. City by city the hymn names Urim, Eridug, Unug and the rest, founded and fed under his decree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.05.1, Ekur and city list; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 埃庫爾，他位於尼普爾山丘上的居所，被稱為天地之臍：其磚砌如青金石與白銀之山般聳立，其儀式深邃如阿普蘇。頌詩逐一唱名烏里姆、埃利都、烏努格等諸城，它們皆在他的敕令之下奠基並得滋養。

passages.text: The hymn closes by hailing Enlil as father and mother of the gods: when he looks kindly, a city prospers; when he turns away, its people scatter. His is the floodwind and the good wind alike, and his mouth is the year's fate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.05.1, closing; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 頌詩以稱頌恩利爾為諸神之父與母作結：當他垂顧恩慈，城邑便興旺；當他轉面不顧，其民便四散。洪水之風與和風同歸於他，他的口便是歲年的命運。

functions: Central liturgical hymn of the Ekur at Nippur
Theological charter of Enlil's primacy over cities and kings
Recited at the new year and at temple dedications

variants.summary: Kingship descends from heaven to Nippur in the king list, the prose counterpart of the hymn's claim.

title.en: The Marriage of Martu
title.zh: 瑪爾圖的婚事

region.en: Adab, Iraq
region.zh: 阿達布（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The marriage of Martu (ETCSL c.1.7.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Martu, god of the western tent-dwellers, sees the daughters of Adab dance at Uruk's festival and demands one of them in marriage. His friend rebukes him for wanting city customs — the Amorites know no house, no wife, no burial — but Martu wins the bride by serving a city feast and honoring the city's rites.
summary.zh: 西陲牧神瑪爾圖於烏魯克節慶見阿達布諸女起舞，執意求娶。友人譏其欲習城邦之俗——阿摩利人無宅、無妻、無葬禮——瑪爾圖卻以效勞城宴、恭謹循禮而終得佳偶。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth reflecting Sumerian prejudice toward nomads; included as literary-historical material, not endorsement.

passages.text: At the temple's great festival, the daughters of Adab dance in the courtyard. Martu, the god of the steppe, watches and declares: I will take one of these to wife. His companion mocks him — you are of the tent people, who know no honor of house or bride or grave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.7.1, opening; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在神廟的盛大慶典上，阿達布的女兒們在庭院中起舞。草原之神馬爾圖觀看著，宣告道：我要娶其中一人為妻。他的同伴嘲笑他——你是帳篷之民，不懂房屋、新娘或墳墓的體面。

passages.text: Martu answers with deeds: he serves at the banquet, portions the offerings, and conducts himself with the manners of a townsman. The young woman he chose, seeing his courtesy, agrees to marry him, and her mother consents. The marriage is performed with the full city rites — the bath, the anointing, the feast — and the poem closes praising Martu as lord of the west who has learned the ways of the city. The dialogue about nomad manners remains: his friend still says the Amorites eat their raw meat unmannered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.7.1, service and consent; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.7.1, wedding and closing debate; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬爾圖以行動作答：他在宴席上侍奉，分派供品，並以城鎮之人的禮儀行事。他所揀選的年輕女子見其彬彬有禮，便應允嫁他，她的母親也同意了。婚禮依全城之禮舉行——沐浴、塗油、設宴——詩篇最後讚頌馬爾圖為已習得城邑之道的西方之主。關於遊牧禮俗的對話仍留存：他的朋友仍說亞摩利人粗野地生食其肉。

functions: Charter for the integration of Amorite worshippers into city cult
Satirical mirror of Sumerian attitudes toward nomads
Marriage liturgy for the festival of a western god

title.en: Pabilsang's Journey to Nippur
title.zh: 帕比爾薩格赴尼普魯之行

region.en: Larsa, Iraq
region.zh: 拉爾薩（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Pabilsang's journey to Nibru (ETCSL c.1.7.8)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Pabilsang, the merchant's god of Isin, sails with his wife Nininsina from her city to Nippur to be blessed by Enlil, presenting gifts and earning the fates of prosperity for the barge, the crew and the journey.
summary.zh: 伊辛商人守護神帕比爾薩格攜妻寧寧西那自其城登舟，前往尼普魯求恩利爾賜福；獻禮獻牲，為舟、為舟子、為旅途求得繁盛之命。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn-narrative; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Pabilsang, the lord of Isin, prepares the barge and takes aboard his wife Nininsina, the queen of the city. The boat sails up the river to Nippur, and the city that receives them is adorned for the god's arrival. At the Ekur, Pabilsang presents his gifts to Enlil and asks the blessing of fates for the barge, its sailors, the cargo and the road; Enlil grants each in turn, and the god of merchants is confirmed in his office.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.7.8, voyage; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.7.8, blessing of fates; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊辛之主帕比爾桑備好平底船，將城中之后、他的妻子寧寧西娜接上船。船溯河而上，駛往尼普爾，迎接他們的城市為神明之到來而妝點一新。在埃庫爾，帕比爾桑向恩利爾獻上禮物，並為船隻、水手、貨物與道路祈求命運的祝福；恩利爾逐一應允，商人之神亦獲確認其職司。

functions: Blessing liturgy for merchant caravans and river trade
Journey hymn in the Nippur pilgrimage genre
Charter of Isin's tutelary cult

variants.name: Enki's journey to Nibru
variants.summary: The senior journey hymn of the same pilgrimage pattern.

canonical_translation: ETCSL team translation, Oxford, 2003-2006

primary_sources.citation: ETCSL c.1.7.8, trans. ETCSL team (2003-2006)

secondary_sources.work: Sumerian Mythology
secondary_sources.citation: Samuel Noah Kramer, Philadelphia, 1944

title.en: Ningishzida's Journey to the Netherworld
title.zh: 寧吉什茲達赴冥界之行

region.en: Girsu, Iraq (gateway of the netherworld, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 吉爾蘇（冥界之門，象徵性定位）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Ningiszida's journey to the nether world (ETCSL c.1.7.3)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Ningishzida, the vegetative god who dies with the year, is called down to the netherworld; the poem laments his departure and his wife's grief, and celebrates his kingship in the land below where he sits in judgment with the dead.
summary.zh: 歲末枯萎的草木神寧吉什茲達受冥界之召而去；詩篇哀其離別、其妻之慟，並頌其於冥土為王，與亡者同坐審判。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary literature; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Ningishzida is called to the netherworld as the year turns: the date palm's lord must go below when his greenery dies. The poem laments the journey — the boat that carries him, the road that leads him down — and the desolation of his city without him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.7.3, lament of departure; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 歲月流轉之際，寧吉什濟達被召往冥界：當其綠意枯死，棗椰之主必須下到地底。詩篇哀悼這趟旅程——載他而去的船、引他下行的路——以及他的城市因他離去而荒蕪。

passages.text: His wife's grief is described with the imagery of mourning women, and the netherworld receives him with honor: there he sits in judgment among the dead, a lord in the land of no return, where his decrees stand as law for the shades.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.7.3, netherworld enthronement; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他妻子的悲傷以哀悼婦女之意象描寫，而冥界以尊榮接待他：他在那裡與亡者同坐審判，為不歸之地的一位主，其諭令對幽魂而言即為律法。

functions: Seasonal death myth for the vegetation god of the date palm
Funerary lament liturgy used in mourning rites
Underworld theology: the dead land has legitimate kingship

variants.name: Dumuzid's dream and descent
variants.summary: The parallel seasonal death of the shepherd god Dumuzid.

canonical_translation: ETCSL team translation, Oxford, 2003-2006

primary_sources.work: Ningiszida's journey to the nether world
primary_sources.citation: ETCSL c.1.7.3, trans. ETCSL team (2003-2006)

secondary_sources.work: Death in Mesopotamia
secondary_sources.citation: papers of the XXIVe Rencontre assyriologique internationale, Copenhagen, 1980

title.en: |Nanna-sse: Respect for the Game
title.zh: 恩納瑟：敬重獵物

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'Certain Hunting Observances, called |nanna-sse'

summary.en: Hunters eat first the flesh of slow animals, never the springbok's, lest the game they have shot should rise and behave like what they ate; the boy who shot must not touch the meat, for his hands are full of springbok scent; and the springbok possess invisible magic arrows that pierce and fell people who play with its bones.
summary.zh: 獵者先食遲緩獸肉，勿食跳羚肉，免所射之獸起身如所食者而行；射者不得觸肉，因其手滿羚香；跳羚具無形魔箭，戲其骨者立仆。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San ritual instructions dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: When we show respect to the game, we act in this manner; because we wish that the game may die. For the game would not die if we did not show respect to it... a thing which does not run fast is that which we eat, when we have shot game; because we desire that the game should also do as it does.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 271 (public domain).
passages.zh: 當我們對獵物表示敬意時，我們便是如此行事；因為我們希望獵物能夠死去。因為若我們不對獵物表示敬意，獵物便不會死去……當我們射中獵物後，我們所吃的，正是跑得不快的東西；因為我們也希望獵物照牠本來的樣子行事。

passages.text: For the game is used to do thus, if we eat the flesh of a thing which is fleet, the thing (i.e. the game) arises; it does like that thing of whose flesh we did eat. Therefore, the old people are accustomed to give us the flesh of a thing which is not fleet. They do not give us all (kinds of) food.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 271-272 (public domain).
passages.zh: 因為獵物慣於如此行事：若我們吃了迅捷之物的肉，那東西（即獵物）便會興起；牠會仿效我們所吃其肉的那個東西。因此，老人們習慣給我們吃跑得不快的東西之肉。他們並不給我們所有種類的食物。

passages.text: Therefore, the old people fear to give us springbok's meat, because they feel that the gemsbok would not be willing to go to sleep, even at night... The springbok is wont to get into our flesh, and we become ill. And the springbok is inside of us and we become ill on account of it. Therefore, we do not play tricks with springbok's bones.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 272, 277 (public domain).
passages.zh: 因此，老人們害怕給我們吃跳羚的肉，因為他們覺得，即使到了夜裡，南非劍羚也不願入睡……跳羚慣於進入我們的肉體之中，我們便生病了。而跳羚就在我們體內，我們因牠而生病。因此，我們不拿跳羚的骨頭開玩笑。

passages.text: The women do not eat (the meat of) the springbok's shoulder blades, because they show respect for the men's arrows, so that the men may quietly kill... We are wont to be ill when we miss our aim... Therefore, we become ill. The springbok are in possession of (invisible) magic arrows. Therefore, we are ill on account of the springbok.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 277 (public domain).
passages.zh: 女人們不吃跳羚的肩胛骨（的肉），因為她們對男人的箭表示敬意，好讓男人能悄悄地獵殺……我們若射不中目標，往往就會生病……因此，我們就生病了。跳羚擁有（看不見的）魔法之箭。因此，我們因跳羚而生病。

title.en: Playing the Goura like ||kunh in the Thunderstorm
title.zh: 雷雨中效古恩彈琴

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Thunderstorm'

summary.en: Rain falling, the boy plays the goura like ||kunh — the rain sorcerer of !khai \ku who, when scolded, held back the rain. His mother rebukes him; he will not listen; and the lightning shivers the stone before the hut. She cries out in pain, says the rain tore her skin, and the boy learns that the rain had meant to kill them for his doings.
summary.zh: 雨落時，童效雨巫古恩（曾憤而止雨者）彈琴。母斥之不聽；雷電碎屋前之石。母痛呼：雷裂我膚。童乃悟：因己所為，雨欲殺其全家。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: When the rain fell upon us at night, I did thus, while the rain fell, I lay, playing the 'goura', like ||kun. And mamma said to me, did I not see how the rain was lightening; that I did like ||kun; did I not know that ||kun was a person who used, if people scolded him... to say to the people... that the people seemed to think that the rain would fall; but the rain would stand still, while the rain did not fall.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 321-322 (public domain).
passages.zh: 夜裡雨落在我們身上時，我就這樣做：雨落著，我躺著，彈著「goura」，像||kun一樣。媽媽對我說，難道我沒看見雨是怎麼變亮的嗎；說我就像||kun那樣行事；難道我不知道||kun是這樣一個人：若有人責罵他……他就對人們說……說人們似乎以為雨會落下來；但雨會停住不動，而雨並沒有落下來。

passages.text: When mamma rebuked me, I did not listen to her, for, I lay, playing the 'goura', like ||kun. And mamma became silent... And mamma lay down; I lay, playing the 'goura'. And the rain did thus, as I lay, playing the 'goura', the rain first seemed to shine into our eyes.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 322 (public domain).
passages.zh: 媽媽責備我時，我沒有聽她的話，因為我躺著，彈著「goura」，像||kun一樣。媽媽便沉默了……媽媽躺下了；我躺著，彈著「goura」。雨就這樣做：當我躺著彈「goura」時，雨起初彷彿照進我們眼裡。

passages.text: And the rain lightened, while our eyes felt green. And the rain, lightening, went over us; and the rain did as follows to a stone which stood outside, in front of our hut, the rain, lightening, shivered it. And mamma exclaimed: 'Nnnnn!'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 323 (public domain).
passages.zh: 雨變亮了，而我們的眼感到發綠。雨一邊變亮，一邊從我們上方掠過；雨對我們屋外、小屋前立著的一塊石頭這樣做：雨一邊變亮，一邊把它震碎了。媽媽驚呼：「Nnnnn！」

passages.text: And mamma told father about it, that the thing seemed as if the rain were tearing off her skin... And mamma said that we had wished to fall dead; it was our fault that we had not been willing to obey her when she rebuked us... I was the one who saw that the rain had intended to kill us, on account of my doings.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 324-325 (public domain).
passages.zh: 媽媽把這事告訴了父親，說那情形彷彿雨在撕她的皮……媽媽說我們本已想倒地而死；我們不肯在她責備我們時聽從她，這是我們的過錯……我就是那個看出雨因我的所作所為而有意殺死我們的人。

title.en: The Stone That Burns Bad Dreams
title.zh: 焚惡夢之石

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'Mode of getting rid of the evil Influence of Bad Dreams'

summary.en: Before digging, the mother plunges a stone into the fire-ashes crying '\kabbi-a yonder!', so that the evil dreamed of shall stay in the fire and not go out with her; for the Bushman rice knows the dreamer, and would not be favourable to her if she carried the dream.
summary.zh: 掘食前，母將石投入火灰，呼「卡比在那！」，令惡夢留於火中，勿隨身出；因桑人之米知夢者，若攜夢而行，則不賜食。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: My mother used to do in this manner, when she intended to go out to seek for food, when she was about to start, she took a stone; and as she plunged the stone into the ashes of the fire, she exclaimed: '\kabbi-a yonder!' while she wished that the evil things, about which she had been dreaming, should altogether remain in the fire; instead of going out with her.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 365 (public domain).
passages.zh: 我母親從前這樣做：當她打算出去尋找食物時，臨出發之際，她拿一塊石頭；當她把石頭投入火堆的灰燼中時，她驚呼：「\kabbi-a 在那邊！」同時她希望她所夢見的那些邪惡之物全都留在火裡，而不是隨她一同出去。

passages.text: That place to which she went would not be nice; while she knew that she had dreamt of evil things which were not nice. Therefore, she acted in this manner; because she was aware that, if she went out with the dream which she had dreamt, her going out would not be fortunate. The Bushman rice which she dug would not be favourable to her, because it was aware that she had dreamt evil things. Therefore, the Bushman rice would act in this manner about it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 365 (public domain).
passages.zh: 她所去的那個地方並不好；因為她知道她夢見了不好的事物。因此，她這樣行事；因為她明白，倘若她帶著自己所夢見的夢外出，她的外出便不會吉利。她所挖掘的叢林人米對她不利，因為它知道她夢見了不好的事物。因此，那叢林人米便會如此對待此事。

title.en: Concerning Two Apparitions on the Salt Pan
title.zh: 鹽沼二幽影

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1876 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'Concerning Two Apparitions'

summary.en: Crossing the salt pan after his wife's burial, Dia!kwain's family sees a small child sitting, wearing the cap of his dead wife. \ku-an explains: the sorcerers were taking her away, and what we saw was her outer skin, which still looks at us because she does not want to leave us. A second apparition — a shy child by a bush — frightens a hunter who concludes it is 'a different kind of thing'.
summary.zh: 葬妻後越鹽沼，見幼童坐，戴亡妻之帽。庫安解曰：巫者正攜其去，所見乃其外皮——因不欲離我們而回望。另影：灌木旁畏縮之童，獵者疑為「異物」。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San personal narrative dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1876; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: We buried my wife in the afternoon. When we had finished burying her, we returned to the home of my sister, \hai-ttu, and the other people... They had come to bury my wife with me; and we went away, crossing over the salt pan. And we perceived a thing which looked like a little child, as it sat upon the salt pan, seeming as if it sat with its legs crossed over each other.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 366-367 (public domain).
passages.zh: 我們在午後埋葬了我的妻子。我們埋葬完她之後，便回到我姊妹\hai-ttu以及其他人的家……他們曾與我一同來埋葬我的妻子；我們離去，越過了鹽沼。我們察覺到一個東西，看起來像個小孩，坐在鹽沼之上，彷彿盤著腿坐著。

passages.text: \ku-an spoke, she said: 'The old people used to tell me, that the angry people were wont to act thus, at the time when they took a person away, they used to allow the person to be in front of us, (so that) we might see it... she really had a very little child, therefore, ye should allow us to look at the thing which sits upon this salt pan; it strongly resembles a person.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 367 (public domain).
passages.zh: \ku-an開口說道：『老人們從前常告訴我，那些憤怒的人慣於如此行事，在他們把人帶走的時候，他們慣於讓那人走在我們前面，（好）讓我們能看見它……她確實有一個非常小的孩子，因此，你們應當讓我們看看坐在這鹽沼上的東西；它極像一個人。』

passages.text: For my mothers used to tell me that, when the sorcerers are those who take us away, at the time when they intend to take us quite away, that is the time when our friend is in front of us, while he desires that we may perceive him, because he feels that he still thinks of us. Therefore, his outer skin still looks at us... for he insists upon coming to us.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 368 (public domain).
passages.zh: 因為我的母親們從前常告訴我，當巫師是那些把我們帶走的人時，在他們打算把我們完全帶走的時候，那正是我們的朋友走在我們前面的時候，而他希望我們能察覺到他，因為他覺得自己仍在思念我們。因此，他的外皮仍在看著我們……因為他堅持要來到我們身邊。

passages.text: And he examined the child; as the child stood looking at him. He saw that it was a little girl; he saw that the child was like a person. In other parts of it it was not like a person... And he walked on, while the child stood looking from side to side. And the child, when she saw that he went away from it, came forward near the bush, it sat down.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 370-371 (public domain).
passages.zh: 他察看那孩子；那孩子站著看他。他看出那是個小女孩；他看出那孩子像個人。在它的其他部分，它並不像人……他繼續走著，那孩子站著左右張望。那孩子見他離它而去，便走上前靠近灌木叢，坐了下來。

title.en: The Jackal's Heart Not to Be Eaten
title.zh: 豺心不可食

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Jackal's Heart not to be eaten'

summary.en: A timid child becomes a coward if it eats the jackal's heart; the child eats the leopard's heart instead, which does not fear. Grandfather Tsatsi boils jackals only for his sons, saying: 'Thou dost seem to think that we eat jackals' hearts? for, we become cowards (if we do so).'
summary.zh: 童若食豺心則成懦夫；其當食豹心——豹不畏。祖特薩西煮豺僅予其子，曰：「爾以為吾等食豺心耶？食則懦矣。」

sensitivity.note: |Xam San custom dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: They (the Bushmen) feel that a little child is wont to be timid; therefore, the little child does not eat jackals' hearts; because the jackal is not a little afraid; for the jackal runs away. The leopard is the one whose heart the little child eats; it which is not afraid; for, a little child becomes a coward from the jackal's heart, it fears immoderately. Therefore, we do not give to a little child the jackal's heart; because we feel that the jackal is used to run away, when it has not even seen us.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 372 (public domain).
passages.zh: 他們（叢林人）覺得小孩子慣於膽怯；因此，小孩子不吃胡狼的心；因為胡狼並非稍有一點畏懼；因為胡狼會逃跑。豹才是小孩子吃其心臟的對象；牠並不畏懼；因為小孩子因胡狼的心而變得膽小，它畏懼過度。因此，我們不把胡狼的心給小孩子；因為我們覺得胡狼慣於逃跑，甚至連我們都還沒看見牠時便逃。

passages.text: Then my grandfather used to act in this manner, when he was boiling a jackal, he said: 'Thou dost seem to think that we eat jackals' hearts? for, we become cowards (if we do so).' Therefore, we did not eat the jackals' hearts. For, my grandfather used not to eat the jackal; he only boiled the jackal for his sons.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 374 (public domain).
passages.zh: 從前我祖父煮胡狼時，就是這般做法，他說：「你似乎以為我們吃胡狼的心？因為（若吃了）我們就會變成懦夫。」因此，我們不吃胡狼的心。因為我祖父從不吃胡狼；他只為他的兒子們煮胡狼。

title.en: The \tao Mine and the Sorcerers Who Dwell There
title.zh: 赭石礦與其居巫者

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'How \tao is obtained'

summary.en: The red \tao (haematite) lies in a mountain side where sorcerers dwell in mouse-hole houses. Diggers throw stones at the mine so the sorcerers will hide and let them work in peace; and they rub themselves with buchu before going, for they would be ill if the sorcerers saw them.
summary.zh: 赭石\tao藏於山腹，巫者居其間如鼠穴。採者先擲石於礦，令巫躲藏，方得安然掘取；且須先以布庫草擦身，否則被巫見則病。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: \tao is in the mountain, the \tao mine; the people say that the \tao mine is on the side of the mountain... The people are afraid of it, that is, of the sorcerers who live by the mine, because the people are aware that people are there (sorcerers). They (the sorcerers) make a house there.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 379 (public domain).
passages.zh: \tao 在山中，即 \tao 礦；人們說 \tao 礦在山的一側……人們懼怕它，也就是懼怕住在礦旁的巫師，因為人們知道那裡有人（巫師）。他們（巫師）在那裡造了一間屋子。

passages.text: And when they go to the \tao, they throw stones at the \tao mine, when they wish the sorcerers to hide themselves, that they may go undisturbed to work at the \tao, while they feel that the sorcerers dwell at the \tao mine. Therefore, they take up stones, they throw stones at the \tao mine, when they wish the sorcerers to hide themselves. Condensed paraphrase of the narrator's note: they would be ill, if the sorcerers saw them; the \tao mine is also in a different place, and the \hara mine [the black pigment] is in a different place again.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 379 (public domain). / Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 380 notes; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 而當他們前往 \tao 時，他們朝 \tao 礦扔石頭，當他們希望巫師們躲藏起來，好讓他們能不受干擾地前去採 \tao，因為他們覺得巫師們住在 \tao 礦。因此，他們撿起石頭，朝 \tao 礦扔石頭，當他們希望巫師們躲藏起來。對敘述者註解的濃縮轉述：若巫師們看見他們，他們就會生病；\tao 礦也在另一個地方，而 \hara 礦〔黑色顏料〕又在另一個地方。

title.en: The |xu: Four Pieces of Wood for Divining
title.zh: 克烏：占卜四木

region.en: Grootfontein district, Damaraland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 納米比亞達馬拉蘭格魯特方丹區（象徵定位）

period: |xu (!Kung-adjacent) San oral tradition; recorded 1880 by Inanni (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), Appendix: 'The |xu (four pieces of wood used for divining purposes)'

summary.en: The |kun women respect the |xu — four pieces of wood from the \ke tree, two male and two female — and will not touch it; a small girl child is told 'this thing thou must respect'. When the diviner's things fall, the mother asks water for her son; the fall of the |xu speaks, and the beating of the child with a \shana stick ends in the father taking aim at his wife with two arrows.
summary.zh: |昆婦女敬|克烏——\科樹之四木，二男二女——不敢觸之；母戒幼女「此物須敬」。卜者擲之落，其母為子索水；四木落地即言；以夏那枝杖笞子，終致父張弓雙箭向妻。

sensitivity.note: |xu San oral tradition dictated by Inanni to Bleek & Lloyd, 1880; contains domestic violence; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The \kun women respect these things, (they) do not take hold (of them). Men take hold (of them). A small \kun child, who is a little girl, does not take hold of this thing; for (she) respects (it). For, her mother says to her: 'This thing, thou must respect, my mother.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 425 (public domain).
passages.zh: \kun 的女人們敬重這些東西，（她們）不碰（它們）。男人們碰（它們）。一個 \kun 的小孩子，若是個小女孩，就不碰這東西；因為（她）敬重（它）。因為她的母親對她說：「這東西，你必須敬重，我的母親。」

passages.text: And the child listens, and respects the thing; but a little male child does not fear the thing, and takes hold of the thing, and carries, carries the thing to his father. And his father puts down the thing upon the ground... For his father objects to his looking on.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix pp. 425-426 (public domain).
passages.zh: 而那孩子聽從，並敬重這東西；但一個小男孩不怕這東西，碰這東西，並把這東西拿去、拿去給他的父親。而他的父親把這東西放在地上……因為他的父親反對他去觀看。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The child ran to his mother for water for the divination, dropped the vessel, cried that the water poured out; his father beat him with a \shana stick, the people took hold of the father, and he took aim at his wife with two arrows — one a \nublo and the other a \xu-\ta arrow.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix pp. 426-428; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮轉述，同一出處；非逐字。那孩子跑到他母親那裡，為占卜取水，失手掉了容器，哭喊著水灑了出來；他的父親用一根 \shana 棍打他，人們抓住那父親，而他以兩支箭瞄準他的妻子——一支是 \nublo，另一支是 \xu-\ta 箭。

title.en: Snakes, Lizards and Small Antelope Near Graves
title.zh: 墓旁之蛇、蜥與小羚

region.en: Grootfontein district, Damaraland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 納米比亞達馬拉蘭格魯特方丹區（象徵定位）

period: |xu San oral tradition; recorded 1881 by Inanni (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), Appendix: 'Certain animals, when seen near graves, to be respected'

summary.en: A snake near a grave is our dead person's snake — his spirit; a lizard that walks to our other person's place is followed, not killed; and the little antelope near a grave is not a mere antelope but the spirit antelope of the dead man, with small legs and male. All are respected and left alone.
summary.zh: 墓旁之蛇乃死者之蛇——其靈；蜥行至亡者之地則隨之而不殺；墓旁小羚非尋常羚，乃亡者之靈羚，腿小而為雄。皆敬而任之。

sensitivity.note: |xu San oral tradition dictated by Inanni to Bleek & Lloyd, 1881; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: A snake which is near a grave, we do not kill, for, (it) is our other person, our dead person's snake. And we do not kill (it); for (we) respect it. And (if, during) many days, we see it, we do not kill (it); looking (at it), (we) let it alone.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 429 (public domain).
passages.zh: 墳墓附近的蛇，我們不殺，因為（牠）是我們的另一個人，是我們死者的蛇。我們不殺（牠），因為（我們）敬重牠。若（一連）許多天我們看見牠，我們不殺（牠）；看著（牠），（我們）任牠去。

passages.text: Another day, (if) we see a lizard, we follow the lizard's spoor; (if) the lizard has gone to the earth (grave) of our other person, we respect the lizard, (we) do not kill the lizard, (we) let the lizard alone.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 429 (public domain).
passages.zh: 另一天，（若）我們看見一隻蜥蜴，我們循著蜥蜴的足跡；（若）那蜥蜴已去到我們另一個人的土裡（墳墓），我們敬重那蜥蜴，（我們）不殺那蜥蜴，（我們）任那蜥蜴去。

passages.text: (When) we see an antelope, an antelope (which is) near our other person's place... we respect the antelope; for, the antelope is not a mere antelope. Its legs seem small, it is the person who has died, and is a spirit antelope. It is a male antelope; it is not a female antelope.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 429 (public domain).
passages.zh: （當）我們看見一隻羚羊，一隻在我們另一個人所在之處附近的羚羊……我們敬重那羚羊；因為那羚羊不只是一隻羚羊。牠的腿看似細小，牠是那已死的人，是一隻精靈羚羊。牠是公羚羊；牠不是母羚羊。

title.en: The Snake That Lies Belly-Up to Announce a Death
title.zh: 腹朝天報喪之蛇

region.en: Grootfontein district, Damaraland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 納米比亞達馬拉蘭格魯特方丹區（象徵定位）

period: |xu San oral tradition; recorded 1881 by Inanni (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), Appendix: 'A certain Snake, which, by lying upon its back, announces a death in the family'

summary.en: The \hin, a long pale harmless serpent of the country, turns up its belly to warn of a death in the family; the frightened people go home crying, and tell the household. When it lies normally it may be killed and its skin given to the Makoba; but a snake that shows its belly must never be struck.
summary.zh: 長而色淡無毒之蛇辛，翻腹朝天以示家中將有喪事；眾懼而泣歸，告於家人。若其常臥，則可殺之，皮予馬科巴人；惟翻腹之蛇不可擊。

sensitivity.note: |xu San oral tradition dictated by Inanni to Bleek & Lloyd, 1881; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The \hin (is) a serpent of our country. (If, when) we strike it, it does in this manner with its belly, it gives us its belly, we fear it, and go away, and return home; while (we) do not kill it. For (we) let (it) alone; and it lies, lies, lies; arises, and goes away altogether.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix pp. 431-432 (public domain).
passages.zh: \hin 是我們國家的蛇。（若）我們打牠時，牠這樣用牠的腹部，牠把牠的腹部給我們，我們怕牠，便走開，回家去；而（我們）不殺牠。因為（我們）任（牠）去；牠躺著，躺著，躺著；起來，完全離去。

passages.text: Another day, (when) it sees us, (as) we approach it... (and) it gives us its belly, we are afraid, we do not kill it, we run away. Another day, we see it, (when) it is in the water — tree water — we are near it, we think that we will drink water, we see its body... it quickly goes out of the water, and lies upon the ground.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 432 (public domain).
passages.zh: 另一天，（當）牠看見我們，（當）我們走近牠……（而）牠把牠的腹部給我們，我們害怕，我們不殺牠，我們跑開。另一天，我們看見牠，（當）牠在水中——樹水——我們在牠附近，我們想我們要喝水，我們看見牠的身體……牠迅速從水中出來，躺在地上。

passages.text: If a woman comes and the woman sees it, (she) unloosens (her) skin necklace, and (gently) lays it down; and it turns, and lays its belly upon the earth. And the woman kills it, and throws it away. (If) another person dies, and we have not heard his news, and we see the \hin turning its belly towards us, we are afraid of the \hin, and cry. And (we) tell the people who are at home, and say: 'I saw a \hin, and struck the \hin; and the \hin objected, and gave me its belly; and I was afraid of the \hin...'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 433 (public domain). / Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 433 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 若一個女人來，那女人看見牠，（她）解開（她的）皮項鍊，（輕輕）放下；牠便轉身，把牠的腹部貼在地上。那女人便殺了牠，把牠丟棄。若另一個人死了，而我們尚未聽到他的消息，而我們看見 \hin 把牠的腹部轉向我們，我們便怕 \hin，並哭泣。而（我們）告訴在家的人，說：『我看見一條 \hin，打了那 \hin；那 \hin 反對，把牠的腹部給我；我怕那 \hin……』

title.en: Beating the Ground with a Stone
title.zh: 以石擊地

region.en: Grootfontein district, Damaraland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 納米比亞達馬拉蘭格魯特方丹區（象徵定位）

period: |xu San oral tradition; recorded 1880 by Tamme (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), Appendix: 'To beat the ground (with a stone)'

summary.en: Only women beat a stone upon the ground, crying 'Fall into the water! Fall into the water!' — and the thing (the lightning) falls into the water. Tamme's father's mother was N-\na; and a man does not do this rite.
summary.zh: 惟婦女擊石於地，呼「落入水中！落入水中！」——雷物遂落於水。塔米之祖母為恩那；男子不行此儀。

sensitivity.note: |xu San oral tradition dictated by Tamme to Bleek & Lloyd, 1880; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The \kun beat a stone upon the ground. My father's mother beat a stone upon the ground. She said: 'Fall into the water! Fall into the water!' And the thing (the lightning) fell into the water. A man does not beat a stone upon the ground. A woman beats a stone upon the ground. My (Tamme's) father's mother was N-\na. My mother's father was Little Tamme; and my mother's mother was \karo-\n'a. My father's father's father was Great Tamme.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 429 (public domain).
passages.zh: \kun 在地上敲石頭。我父親的母親在地上敲石頭。她說：「掉進水裡去！掉進水裡去！」那東西（閃電）就掉進水裡去了。男人不在地上敲石頭。女人在地上敲石頭。我（塔梅）父親的母親是 N-\na。我母親的父親是小塔梅；我母親的母親是 \karo-\n'a。我父親的父親的父親是大塔梅。

title.en: The Treatment of Thieves Among the |kun
title.zh: |昆部落對竊賊之處置

region.en: Grootfontein district, Damaraland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 納米比亞達馬拉蘭格魯特方丹區（象徵定位）

period: |xu San oral tradition; recorded 1881 by Inanni (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), Appendix: 'The Treatment of Thieves'

summary.en: A thieving woman is returned alive to her parents; a woman who returns to steal again is given to the wronged people, who shut her in a hut and burn her — and the husband whose heart aches may kill her with a \nublo arrow. Men thieves are shot with many arrows, not burned; children are only scolded. Those killed are feared for their spirits, and their names are not spoken.
summary.zh: 竊婦活還其親；再犯則交予被害者，閉屋焚之——心痛之夫可以努布羅箭殺之。男賊以群箭射殺，不焚；童賊僅訓斥。被殺者之靈可畏，其名不可言。

sensitivity.note: |xu San oral tradition dictated by Inanni to Bleek & Lloyd, 1881; describes capital punishment customs; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: If a \kun woman steals, her father and her mother being (still) there, we take hold of her, we give her to her mother and her father; and they all go away from their place... we say to the other person: 'My wife stole your thing which is here... And I have given back my wife to her father and her mother.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 417 (public domain).
passages.zh: 如果一個 \kun 女人偷東西，她的父親和母親（還）在，我們就抓住她，把她交給她的母親和父親；他們就全都離開他們的地方……我們對另一個人說：「我的妻子偷了你這裡的東西……而我已經把我的妻子交還給她的父親和母親了。」

passages.text: A female child, if her mother is dead and the female child is an only child, goes to another person's hut. Another day, if she steals, the other person into whose hut she went (to live) takes her, and gives her to the other person (from whom she stole), the other people kill her altogether; (they) put her into a hut, and burn, killing her with fire.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 420 (public domain).
passages.zh: 一個女童，如果她的母親死了，而這女童是獨生女，她就到別人的屋裡去。另一天，如果她偷東西，她（去住）的那間屋子的另一個人就抓住她，把她交給另一個人（她所偷的那個人），那些人就合力殺死她；（他們）把她放進一間屋裡，放火，用火燒死她。

passages.text: They say to the people... they (who) killed the girl... 'We have burning, killed the girl with fire, put the girl into a hut, and burning killed the girl. Leave off reproaching us about the girl.'... 'No; we are not scolding you; for, we object (to stealing)... we hear, and our hearts are glad.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 421 (public domain).
passages.zh: 他們對那些人說……那些殺死女孩的人……「我們放了火，用火燒死了女孩，把女孩放進一間屋裡，放火燒死了女孩。不要再為這女孩責備我們了。」……「不；我們不是在責罵你們；因為我們反對（偷竊）……我們聽見了，我們心裡歡喜。」

passages.text: If a man steals, we kill (him), we shoot, killing (him) with arrows, and do not put him into the fire; but, kill him altogether with arrows. It is only a woman (whom) we burn... If a child steals, we merely scold the child... Those persons whom we kill altogether, we fear their names; we do not utter their names.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 421 (public domain).
passages.zh: 如果一個男人偷東西，我們就殺（他），我們射，用箭殺（他），不把他放進火裡；而是用箭合力殺死他。我們只燒女人……如果一個孩子偷東西，我們只是責罵那孩子……那些我們合力殺死的人，我們畏懼他們的名字；我們不唸出他們的名字。

title.en: The Broken String: Lament for the Rain-Magician
title.zh: 斷弦：悼雨巫之歌

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Broken String'

summary.en: \xa-ttin's lament for his dead friend \kui-ten, the magician and rain-maker who died of a shot received while going about by night in the form of a lion. Now the string is broken, the sky's former ringing sound is heard no more, and the place does not feel as it used to feel.
summary.zh: 夏丁悼亡友庫伊滕——雨巫與術士，夜行獅形中槍而亡。弦既斷，昔日天際鳴響不復聞，此地亦不復如舊之感。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San lament dictated by Dia!kwain (heard from his father) to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: People were those who Broke for me the string. Therefore, The place became like this to me, On account of it, Because the string was that which broke for me. Therefore, The place does not feel to me, As the place used to feel to me, On account of it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 237 (public domain).
passages.zh: 是人們為我弄斷了那根弦。因此，這地方對我來說變成了這樣，因為它，因為那根弦就是為我弄斷的那根。因此，這地方對我來說不再有感覺，不像這地方從前對我的感覺那樣，因為它。

passages.text: For, The place feels as if it stood open before me, Because the string has broken for me. Therefore, The place does not feel pleasant to me, On account of it. Condensed paraphrase of the editor's note: the above is a lament, sung by \xa-ttin after the death of his friend, the magician and rain-maker, \kui-ten; who died from the effects of a shot he had received when going about, by night, in the form of a lion.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 237 (public domain). / Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 237 note; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 因為，那地方在我感覺彷彿是敞開在我面前的，因為那弦為我斷了。所以，那地方在我感覺並不愉快，就因為這個緣故。編者註的濃縮轉述：以上是一首哀歌，由\xa-ttin在其友人——魔法師兼祈雨者\kui-ten——死後所唱；此人因夜間化為獅形外出時中槍，因槍傷之效應而死。

title.en: !nuinumma-!kwiten: The White-Mouth Who Kills Crying Children
title.zh: 白嘴妖：專殺啼哭之童

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Song of !nuinumma-!kwiten'

summary.en: A beast of prey of the early race, his name 'White-Mouth' — he who gobbled eggs whole. Hearing a child cry he follows the sound, creeps to the hut, springs in, catches the child and swallows it. Grandfathers sang his song to frighten noisy children into silence.
summary.zh: 早期之民猛獸，名「白嘴」——吞蛋不嚼者。聞童啼即循聲潛至，躍入茅屋，擒童吞之。祖父輩唱其歌以懾鬧童。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San ogre-song dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text:
u
umma-\kwiten formerly said (sang) — 'Hn-n, hn; I kill children who cry; Hn-n, hn. I kill children who cry.' A beast of prey (he, 
u
umma-\kwiten) is. My grandfather used to say (that) 
u
umma-\kwiten formerly said — 'Hn-n, hn; I kill children who cry.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 239 (public domain).
passages.zh:
u
umma-\kwiten從前說（唱）道——「Hn-n，hn；我殺啼哭的孩子；Hn-n，hn。我殺啼哭的孩子。」牠是一頭猛獸（他，
u
umma-\kwiten）。我的祖父常說，
u
umma-\kwiten從前說——「Hn-n，hn；我殺啼哭的孩子。」

passages.text: The narrator gave the following explanation of \nu\numma-\kwiten's name: 'A man who eats great (pieces of) meat, he cuts them off, he puts them into his mouth. I think that eggs are white; therefore, I think that his name seems to be White-Mouth... Reference is here made to a man of the early race, who swallowed ostrich eggs whole, and is the chief figure in a legend related by \han≠kass'o (V.—56.).'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 239 note (public domain).
passages.zh: 講述者對\nu\numma-\kwiten之名的由來作了如下解釋：「一個吃大（塊）肉的人，他把肉切下來，放進自己嘴裡。我想蛋是白色的；因此，我想他的名字似乎是白嘴……此處所指是早期種族中的一個人，他將鴕鳥蛋整個吞下，並且是\han≠kass'o所講述的一則傳說（V.—56.）中的主要人物。」

passages.text: And (when) he hears a little child crying there, he follows the sound to it, while the little child is crying there, he, following the sound, goes to it, approaches it stealthily, approaching stealthily, reaches the hut, in which the little child is crying. He springs, springs into the hut. He catches hold of the little child, he springs, taking it away. He goes to swallow it down. He departs.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 241 (public domain).
passages.zh: 而（當）他聽見有個小孩在那裡啼哭，他便循聲而去，趁那小孩仍在那裡啼哭之際，他循著聲音走向它，悄悄接近它，悄悄接近，到達那小孩正在啼哭的茅屋。他躍起，躍入茅屋。他抓住那小孩，他躍起，把它帶走。他要去把它吞下。他離去了。

title.en: The Bustard's Head in the Fire: Why the Knorhaan Cries
title.zh: 鴇首入火：冠鴇啼聲之由

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Song of the Bustard'

summary.en: When the bustard (knorhaan, Brandkop) was still a man, his head was thrust into the fire by his brother-in-law, to punish him for having surreptitiously married a sister. Since then he is only a bustard: flushed red of head, crying 'wara \khau' when he flies and 'a wa, a wa' when he stands.
summary.zh: 冠鴇本為人；因偷娶其姊妹，遭妹夫將其頭按入火中。自兹為鴇：頭赤如火，飛時啼「瓦拉哈烏」，立時鳴「阿瓦」。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San song-legend dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: My younger brother-in-law, Put my head in the fire. My younger brother-in-law, My younger brother-in-law, Put my head in the fire. When we startle it up, it flies away; it (cries): 'Wara \khau, wara \khau, wara \khau...!' When it stands on the ground, it says: 'A wa, a wa, a wa, a wa!' when it stands on the ground.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 233 (public domain).
passages.zh: 我的小舅子，把我的頭放進火裡。我的小舅子，我的小舅子，把我的頭放進火裡。當我們驚起牠，牠便飛走；牠（叫道）：「Wara \khau，wara \khau，wara \khau……！」當牠站在地上，牠說：「A wa，a wa，a wa，a wa！」當牠站在地上。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the editor's note: when the 'Knorhaan Brandkop' was still a man, his head was thrust into the fire by his brother-in-law, in order to punish him for having surreptitiously married a sister. Since then he is only a bustard.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 233 note; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 編者註的濃縮轉述：當「Knorhaan Brandkop」還是人的時候，他的頭被他的小舅子推進火裡，以懲罰他偷偷娶了一個姊妹。自那時起，他就只是一隻鴇了。

title.en: The Cat's Song: Derided by the Lynx
title.zh: 貓之歌：為獰貓所嘲

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Cat's Song'

summary.en: The cat sings its own mockery — 'I am the one whom the Lynx derides, I am the one who did not run fast' — as it goes along doubling in flight; the cat talks with its tongue and sings with the upper part of its mouth.
summary.zh: 貓自唱其辱：「獰貓嘲我，我不善走」——且行且唱，逃時迴折而走；貓以舌語，以口上顎而歌。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San song dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: Ha ha ha, Ha ha, I am the one whom the Lynx derides, I am the one who did not run fast; For, the Lynx is the one who runs fast. It did foolish things; For, the Lynx is one who understands, The Cat does not understand. The Cat (nevertheless) is cunning. It had to be cunning. For, the Lynx is one who is cunning. Reference is here made to the Cat's way of doubling when pursued.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 221 (public domain). / Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 222 (public domain). / Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 222 with note (public domain).
passages.zh: 哈哈哈，哈哈，我就是那被猞猁所嘲笑者，我就是那跑得不快者；因为，猞猁才是跑得快者。牠做了愚蠢之事；因为，猞猁才是懂事者，貓卻不懂事。貓（儘管如此）仍狡黠。牠不得不狡黠。因為，猞猁才是狡黠者。此處所指的是貓在被追趕時折返繞行之法。

title.en: The Song of the Springbok Mothers
title.zh: 羚母搖籃歌

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Song of the Springbok Mothers'

summary.en: The springbok mothers sang, soothing their children — 'A-a hn, O Springbok Child! Sleep for me' — a lullaby from the fable of the Anteater, the young Springbok, the Lynx, and the Partridge.
summary.zh: 羚母哄幼而歌：「阿——哄，跳羚之童！為我安眠。」此歌出自食蟻獸、幼羚、獰貓與鷓鴣之寓言。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San lullaby dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The Springbok mothers sang (soothing their children) — 'A-a hn, O Springbok Child! Sleep for me. A-a hn, O Springbok Child! Sleep for me.' Condensed paraphrase of the editor's note: this song occurs in the fable of the Anteater, the young Springbok, the Lynx, and the Partridge (IV.—42.), in which the anteater carries away the young springbok and the mother sings to it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 235 (public domain). / Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 235 note; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 跳羚母親們唱著（安撫牠們的孩子）——「啊—嗯，哦跳羚孩子！為我睡吧。啊—嗯，哦跳羚孩子！為我睡吧。」編者註之節略轉述：此歌見於食蟻獸、幼跳羚、猞猁與鷓鴣之寓言（IV.—42.），其中食蟻獸叼走幼跳羚，母親便對牠歌唱。

title.en: The Old Woman's Song: The Hyena That Carried Her Off
title.zh: 老嫗之歌：負其而去之土狼

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871 and 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Old Woman's Song'

summary.en: Left in an old hut by her starving people, an old woman too weak to walk is carried off by the hyena; she springs aside, beats it, and the hyena kills itself casting itself on the pointed rock. From the hyena's flesh she grows strong enough to follow and reach her people while they are still starving.
summary.zh: 族人饑而遷，老嫗留於舊屋；土狼負之而去。她躍避擊之；土狼自投尖岩而死。食其肉，婦力復，追及飢困之族人。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San song-story dictated by !A!kunta and ||kabbo to Bleek and Lloyd; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The old Woman sings; goes singing along; sings as she goes; the old Woman sings as she goes along about the Hyena — 'The old she Hyena, Was carrying off the old Woman from the old hut; The old Woman in this manner, She sprang aside, She arose, She beat the Hyena. The Hyena, herself, The Hyena killed the Hyena.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 229 (public domain).
passages.zh: 老婦人唱著；一路唱著前行；邊走邊唱；老婦人一路唱著關於鬣狗之事——「那老母鬣狗，正把老婦人從舊茅屋裡叼走；老婦人這般，她閃身一旁，她起身，她痛打鬣狗。鬣狗，牠自己，鬣狗殺死了鬣狗。」

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's 1875 summary (§80): an old woman who was too weak to walk was left behind by her people, when they, to escape starvation, travelled to another part of the country. She was afterwards picked up by a hyena and carried off to the mountain on its back. But she contrived to kill it, and finding an old pot, she cooked and ate some of its flesh. From this, she became so strong that she followed her people, and arrived in good condition among them, while they were still starving.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §80; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布萊克一八七五年摘要（§80）之節略轉述：一名老婦人因過於衰弱而無法行走，被族人留下，當時他們為逃避饑荒而遷往國家的另一處。她後來被一隻鬣狗拾起，背在背上帶往山中。但她設法殺死了牠，並找到一只舊鍋，煮食了牠的一些肉。由此，她變得十分強壯，得以追隨族人，安然無恙地抵達他們中間，而他們當時仍在挨餓。

title.en: The Falling Star and the Hammerkop's Tidings
title.zh: 隕星與鎚頭鸛之訊

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1876 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'Death'

summary.en: When our heart falls, a star falls with it; the stars know the time at which we die. The hammerkop flies crying 'yha! yha!' to tell of a death; its story must be sunk in the Orange River, where the stars stand in the water like fires — for the water is a pool in which we see all things, even the dead whom the Rain has taken, become flowers.
summary.zh: 吾心墜時，星隨之墜；星知人死之時。鎚頭鸛飛啼「呀！呀！」以報喪；其訊須沉入奧蘭治河——星立水中如火。水乃映照萬物之池，包括雨所攜之少女——化為水中之花。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San death-lore dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1876; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The star does in this manner, at the time when our heart falls down, that is the time when the star also falls down; while the star feels that our heart falls over. Therefore, the star falls down on account of it. For the stars know the time at which we die. The star tells the other people who do not know that we have died.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 389 (public domain).
passages.zh: 星星便是這般行事，在我們的心墜落之時，那正是星星也墜落之時；而星星感覺到我們的心翻墜。因此，星星便因之而墜落。因為眾星知道我們死亡的時刻。星星告訴其他不知我們已死的人們。

passages.text: The people say: 'Did ye not hear the hammerkop, when the star fell? It came to tell us that our person is dead.' The people speak, they say that the hammerkop is not a thing which deceives, for it would not come to our home, if it did not know... it intends to come and tell us about it, namely, that our person has died.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 391 (public domain).
passages.zh: 人們說：『星星墜落之時，你們難道沒有聽見錘頭鸛嗎？牠是來告訴我們，我們的人死了。』人們說著，他們說錘頭鸛不是欺騙之物，因為牠若不知道……便不會來到我們的家；牠有意前來告訴我們此事，即我們的人已經死了。

passages.text: Mother and the others used, — if they heard a hammerkop, when it flew, going over us, — to say: 'Do thou go and plunge in, for I know that which thou earnest to tell me'; while mother and the others said that the story, which it came to tell, should go into the Orange River's water, where the stars stand in the water.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 391-392 (public domain).
passages.zh: 母親和其他人以往——若他們聽見錘頭鸛在我們上方飛過時——總會說：「你去潛入水中吧，因為我知道你前來要告訴我的是什麼」；而母親和其他人說，牠前來訴說的那個故事，應當進入橘河的水中，那兒有星星立在水裡。

passages.text: For, mother and the others used to tell us about it, that girls are those whom the Rain carries off; and the girls remain at that water, to which the Rain had taken them... The Rain lightens, killing them; they become stars, while their appearance has been changed... a girl, when the Rain has carried her off, becomes like a flower which grows in the water.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 393-395 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 因為母親和其他人以往常對我們講述此事，說女孩們就是被雨水帶走的人；而那些女孩留在雨水帶她們去的那片水邊……雨水發出閃電，將她們擊殺；她們便化作星星，而她們的形貌已被改變……一個女孩，當雨水將她帶走之後，就變得像一朵生長在水中的花。

title.en: The Rain's Thunderbolts and the Flower-Girls of the Water
title.zh: 雨之雷石與水中花女

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1876 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'Death', pp. 393-397

summary.en: Girls whom the Rain has killed become flowers standing in the water; we must not pick them, for when we go toward them they sink. And when the Rain lightens, we must quickly look at the place of the flash: our eye also shines like its thunderbolts, and the Rain fears our eye and passes over.
summary.zh: 為雨所殺之少女成為立於水中之花；不可摘之，近之則沉。雷起時，須速視其閃處：吾目亦如雷石而閃，雨畏吾目，遂掠頂而過。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San lore dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1876; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: Mother and the others used to tell us about it, that we ought not to go to the flowers which we see standing in the water, even if we see their beauty. For, they are girls whom the Rain has taken away, they resemble flowers; for they are the water's wives, and we look at them, leaving them alone.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 395-396 (public domain).
passages.zh: 母親和其他人以往常對我們講述此事，說我們不該走向我們所見立在水中的那些花，即使我們看見它們的美麗。因為它們是雨水帶走的女孩，它們形似花朵；因為它們是水的妻子，我們只觀看它們，任它們獨自留著。

passages.text: The flower — when it saw that we went towards it — would disappear in the water. We should think: 'The flowers which were standing here, where are they?'... It would disappear in the water, when it saw that we went towards it; we should not perceive it, for it would go into the water.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 396-397 (public domain).
passages.zh: 那花——當它看見我們朝它走去時——便會消失於水中。我們會想：「原本立在這兒的那些花，到哪兒去了？」……當它看見我們朝它走去時，它便會消失於水中；我們察覺不到它，因為它會進入水中。

passages.text: For they are afraid that the Rain also intends, lightening, to kill them. For the Rain is a thing which does in this manner when it rains here, it smells our scent, it lightens out of the place where it rains. It lightens, killing us at this place; therefore, mother and the others told us about it, that when the Rain falls upon us and we walk passing through the Rain, if we see that the Rain lightens in the sky we must quickly look towards the place where the Rain lightens.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 397 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 因為它們害怕雨水也打算發出閃電將它們擊殺。因為雨水就是這樣行事之物：當它在此降雨時，它嗅到我們的氣味，便從降雨之處發出閃電。它發出閃電，在此處將我們擊殺；因此，母親和其他人告訴我們此事，說當雨水落在我們身上、我們行走穿過雨中時，若我們看見雨水在天空發出閃電，我們必須趕快朝雨水發出閃電之處望去。

passages.text: The Rain, which intended to kill us by stealth... if its thunderbolts have come near us, (if) we look towards the place where it has lightened... we look, making its thunderbolts turn back from us; for our eye also shines like its thunderbolts. Therefore, it also appears to fear our eye... Therefore, it passes over us on account of it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 397 (public domain).
passages.zh: 那意圖暗中擊殺我們的雨水……若它的雷電已逼近我們，（若）我們朝它發出閃電之處望去……我們一望，便使它的雷電從我們身上折返；因為我們的眼睛也像它的雷電一樣閃耀。因此，它似乎也懼怕我們的眼睛……因此，它便因這緣故而從我們上方掠過。

title.en: Our Wind, Our Gall, and the Moon That Carries the Dead
title.zh: 吾風、吾膽與負死者之月

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Relations of Wind, Moon, and Cloud to Human Beings after Death'

summary.en: At death our own wind blows and makes clouds; the wind erases our footprints so the dead may not seem to live. Our gall sits green in the sky; our hair makes clouds. And the hollow moon carries the newly dead in its bowl — dying people are laid in it until it fills, then they descend and live again like the Moon, save that the Hare broke the bargain.
summary.zh: 死時吾風自吹而成雲；風抹吾跡，免似生者。吾膽懸碧於天；吾髮化雲。半月如匙，承載新死者——月盈而滿，死者下地復生如月；惟野兔毀約，死亡遂定。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San death-lore dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The wind does thus when we die, our own wind blows; for we, who are human beings, we possess wind; we make clouds, when we die. Therefore, the wind does thus when we die, the wind makes dust, because it intends to blow, taking away our footprints... our footprints, which the wind intends to blow away, would otherwise still lie plainly visible.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 397-398 (public domain).
passages.zh: 我們死時，風便如此這般；我們自己的風吹起；因為我們身為人，我們擁有風；我們死時，便造出雲來。因此，我們死時，風便如此這般；風造出塵土，因為它有意吹拂，帶走我們的足跡……我們的足跡，本是風有意吹散的，否則它們仍會清晰地留在那裡，清晰可見。

passages.text: And, our gall, when we die, sits in the sky; it sits green in the sky, when we are dead. Therefore, mother was wont to do thus when the moon lying down came, (when) the moon stood hollow... The hair of our head will resemble clouds, when we die, when we in this manner make clouds.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 398-400 (public domain).
passages.zh: 而我們的膽汁，在我們死時，便懸於天上；我們死後，它便綠綠地懸在天上。因此，母親慣常如此這般，當月亮躺下之時，（當）月亮空空洞洞地立著……我們死時，我們的頭髮將如同雲一般，當我們如此這般造出雲來。

passages.text: Mother spoke, she said: 'The moon is carrying people who are dead. For, ye are those who see that it lies in this manner; and it lies hollow, because it is killing itself (by) carrying people who are dead. This is why it lies hollow... A person is the one who has died, he whom the moon carries. Therefore, ye may expect to hear what has happened, when the moon is like this.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 399-400 (public domain).
passages.zh: 母親說道，她說：『月亮正載著死去的人們。因為，你們正是那些看見它如此這般躺著的人；而它空空洞洞地躺著，因為它正藉著載運死去的人們而殺死自己。這就是它為何空空洞洞地躺著……一個人便是那已死去的人，那月亮所載運的人。因此，當月亮這般模樣時，你們便可料想會聽到所發生之事。』

passages.text: We, who do not know, we are those who think in this manner, that (they) are clouds. We, who know, when we see that they are like this, we know that (they) are a person's clouds; that they are the hair of his head... while we feel that we seeing recognize the clouds, how the clouds do in this manner form themselves.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 400-401 (public domain).
passages.zh: 我們這些不知情的人，我們正是如此這般思想的人，以為（它們）是雲。我們這些知情的人，當我們看見它們這般模樣時，我們便知道（它們）是一個人的雲；它們是他頭上的頭髮……當我們覺得我們看見並認出那些雲時，那些雲是如何這般自行成形。

title.en: The Man Who Cut Open His Wife for Greed
title.zh: 疑妻貪食而剖之者

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1874 by !Kweiten ta //Ken (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §112

summary.en: A woman's darker mirror of faith: a man, believing his wife had been greedy, cut her open — and found, with great distress, that she was with child. He tried in vain to repair the harm by pinning her together with a stick, thinking she would live.
summary.zh: 男子疑妻貪食，剖其腹——惶然發現其有孕。以木針縫合，冀其能活，終不可救。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San tale dictated by !Kweiten ta //Ken to Bleek and Lloyd, 1874; contains domestic violence and pregnancy death; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§112): a man cut his wife open, because he believed that she had been greedy, and then discovering, with great distress, that she was with child, tried in vain to repair the harm he had done, by pinning her together with a stick, thinking that she would live.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §112; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布萊克摘要（§112）的濃縮轉述：一個男人剖開了他妻子的肚子，因為他相信她貪嘴，隨後他極其痛苦地發現她懷有身孕，便試圖用一根棍子把她釘合起來，以為她會活過來，卻徒勞無功，無法彌補他所造成的傷害。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the same locus: whilst the principal death-story of §112 touchingly illustrates an old man's conception of a woman's faithful nature, and her husband's trustfulness and charity, another tale shows a woman's idea of a man's stupidity and distrust of his wife.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §112; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同一段落的濃縮轉述：§112的主要死亡故事動人地闡明了一位老人對女子忠貞本性的理解，以及她丈夫的輕信與仁慈；而另一個故事則展現了一名女子對男子愚鈍的看法，以及她對丈夫的不信任。

title.en: Cutting the Little Finger, Piercing Ears and Nose
title.zh: 截小指、穿孔耳鼻

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) custom; recorded 1871 and 1884 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'Cutting off the Top of the Little Finger, and Piercing Ears and Nose'

summary.en: A boy has the top joint of the little finger of his shooting hand cut off — it is thought to make children live to grow up, and is done with a reed before they have sucked at all; the girl's left hand is cut for her female arm. Men pierce both ears; a woman with a pierced nose is handsome.
summary.zh: 男童截其射箭手小指之上節——俗信可保兒長成，以蘆葦為之，在吮乳之前；女童截左手，其女性之臂。男子穿雙耳；穿鼻之婦乃美。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San customs recorded by Bleek and Lloyd, 1871/1884; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: A little boy has this hand cut. A female child has this hand cut, because she is a little girl, therefore, she has the hand of her female arm cut; because this is her female hand. Thus, the boy has this arm cut, with which they intend him to shoot; therefore, he turns this (the right) hand, when he grasps the arrow, he turns this (the left) hand, when he grasps the bow.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 329 (public domain).
passages.zh: 有個小男孩的這隻手被切掉。有個女童的這隻手被切掉，因為她是個小女孩，所以，她被切掉的是她女性手臂的這隻手；因為這是她女性的手。因此，男孩被切掉的是這隻手臂，他們打算用這隻手臂讓他射箭；所以，他轉動這隻（右）手，當他握住箭時，他轉動這隻（左）手，當他握住弓時。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the 1884 account and note: the joint is cut off with a reed. It is thought to make children live to grow up. It is done before they suck at all. \xaben-an further explained that her father cut off the upper joint of his daughter Kaueten-an's little finger; and her husband cut off (the upper joint of) \kabbe-ttu's finger.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 330; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 對1884年記述與註釋的濃縮改述：關節是用蘆葦割下的。據信這能讓孩子活著長大。這是在他們吸吮之前就做的。\xaben進一步說明，她的父親切掉了他女兒Kaueten-an小指的上關節；而她的丈夫切掉了\kabbe-ttu手指的（上關節）。

title.en: |xue: The Doings of |xue Are Many
title.zh: 克烏：其行跡無數

region.en: Grootfontein district, Damaraland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 納米比亞達馬拉蘭格魯特方丹區（象徵定位）

period: |xu San oral tradition; recorded 1880 by Inanni (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), Appendix: 'The Doings of |xue are many'

summary.en: |xue is a being of countless transformations: by day a tree, by night himself; a Dui with green fruit, an Ovaherero, a \nayane, a ||gui tree, a fly. The wood pigeons ate him when he was \nayane; as a ||gui tree his wife tried to pick his fruit and he vanished into a fly, and she lay on the earth and cried — and died.
summary.zh: 克烏化形無數：日為樹，夜為己；化大伊（綠果樹）、化赫雷羅人、化內雅內、化巫桂樹、化蠅。為內雅內時木鴿食之；為巫桂樹時妻摘其果，他化蠅而遁；妻臥地而哭——而亡。

sensitivity.note: |xu San oral tradition dictated by Inanni to Bleek & Lloyd, 1880; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text:
The works of |xue are many, and were not one, but many; and my father's father, Karu, told me about doings, for |xue's works are numerous. (When) the sun rose, |xue was 
ayane; the birds ate |xue; |xue was 
ayane. The sun set, (and) |xue was |xue; and lay down and slept. The night fell, and |xue lay down, (he) slept; the place was dark; and the sun rose, and |xue was another (kind of) 
ayane, a large (kind of) 
ayane, which is a tree.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 405 (public domain).
passages.zh:
|xue的作為很多，並非只有一件，而是很多；而我父親的父親Karu向我講述了種種作為，因為|xue的作為眾多。（當）太陽升起時，|xue是
ayane；鳥兒吃了|xue；|xue是
ayane。太陽落下，（而）|xue是|xue；並躺下睡了。夜幕降臨，|xue躺下，（他）睡了；那地方一片漆黑；太陽升起，|xue是另一種
ayane，一種大的
ayane，那是一棵樹。

passages.text: And his wife saw the \gui, and went to the \gui, and went to take hold of a \gui fruit, and the \gui vanished; and |xue was a fly. And his wife laid herself upon the earth, and cried about the \gui, and died. And |xue was a fly, and settled upon the grass.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix pp. 406-407 (public domain).
passages.zh: 而他的妻子看見了\gui，便走向\gui，走上前去抓住一顆\gui果實，\gui便消失了；而|xue是一隻蒼蠅。他的妻子伏在地上，為\gui而哭，然後死了。而|xue是一隻蒼蠅，停落在草上。

title.en: |xue as Water: The Wood Pigeons and the Fire
title.zh: 克烏為水：木鴿與火

region.en: Grootfontein district, Damaraland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 納米比亞達馬拉蘭格魯特方丹區（象徵定位）

period: |xu San oral tradition; recorded 1880 by Inanni (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), Appendix: '|xue as Water and as other things. In his own form he rubs fire and dies'

summary.en: |xue becomes water under a tree; the wood pigeons come to drink, his reed-grass bites the bill of one, and he plucks its feathers and roasts it in the embers. Hearing Ovaherero coming he becomes a |nu-erre bird; his father finds him dead — and alive again, rubbing fire; each time he sees his father he dies, and his father cries that his child is |xue and no other.
summary.zh: 克烏化為樹下之水；木鴿來飲，其蘆草咬其一之喙；他拔其羽，於火燼中炙之。聞赫雷羅人至，化為小鳥；其父見之已死——又見其活，正鑽木取火。每見父則死；父哭曰：此我子克烏，非他人也。

sensitivity.note: |xu San oral tradition dictated by Inanni to Bleek & Lloyd, 1880; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: |xue was water; and the water was in the shadow of the tree. And the wood pigeons ate the fruit of the \ku. And |xue was a lizard, and lay in the dead leaves of the \ku. And (he) saw the wood pigeons, and was water. And the wood pigeons saw the water, and settled upon the water's edge.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix pp. 407-408 (public domain).
passages.zh: |xue是水；而那水在樹的陰影裡。斑鳩吃了\ku的果實。而|xue是一隻蜥蜴，躺在\ku的枯葉裡。（他）看見了斑鳩，便成了水。斑鳩看見了水，便停落在水邊。

passages.text: And |xue worked large grass, like reeds, and it took hold of a wood pigeon. And the wood pigeons came to drink water, and the grass came near, and bit the wood pigeon's bill, and the wood pigeon cried out; and the other wood pigeons flew away. And |xue was |xue, and rose up, and took hold of the wood pigeon, and plucked out the wood pigeon's feathers, and put the wood pigeon's feathers in his head, and lay upon the ground.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 408 (public domain).
passages.zh: 而|xue造出像蘆葦般的大草，那草抓住了一隻斑鳩。斑鳩們前來喝水，那草靠近，咬住斑鳩的喙，斑鳩便叫了起來；其餘的斑鳩飛走了。而|xue是|xue，起身，抓住那隻斑鳩，拔下斑鳩的羽毛，把斑鳩的羽毛插在自己頭上，然後躺在地上。

passages.text: And the Ovaherero came to search for him, to search for him, (and) did not see him. For (he) was little, and was a \nu-erre... he cried out. And the Ovaherero heard, and sought for him... and (he) flew away. And (he) flew, coming to his mother's country, and saw his father, and was not a \nu-erre, but was |xue, and died.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 410 (public domain).
passages.zh: 於是奧瓦赫雷羅人前來尋他，來尋他，（卻）沒有見到他。因為（他）很小，是個\nu-erre……他喊叫起來。奧瓦赫雷羅人聽見了，便尋他……而（他）飛走了。而（他）飛著，來到他母親的國度，見到了他的父親，不再是個\nu-erre，而是|xue，並且死了。

passages.text: It is my child, \xue! for it is not another person, but is my child; and (he) saw me, and died. And (he) was rubbing sticks to make fire... and saw me, and died; and is not another person, but is my child, and is |xue... I am afraid of my child, for my child is dead.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix pp. 411-412 (public domain).
passages.zh: 這是我的孩子，\xue！因為這不是別人，而是我的孩子；而（他）見到了我，便死了。而（他）正搓著木棍取火……見到了我，便死了；這不是別人，而是我的孩子，是|xue……我怕我的孩子，因為我的孩子死了。

title.en: Prayer to the Young Moon (|kun version)
title.zh: 向新月祈禱（|昆版）

region.en: Grootfontein district, Damaraland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 納米比亞達馬拉蘭格魯特方丹區（象徵定位）

period: |xu San oral tradition; recorded 1880 by Inanni (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), Appendix: 'Prayer to the Young Moon'

summary.en: 'Young Moon! Hail, Young Moon!... Thou must speak to me, that I may eat something. Thou must speak to me about a little thing, that I may eat. Hail, hail, Young Moon!' The prayer is sounded on the male antelope's horn when the new moon is seen.
summary.zh: 「新月啊！敬禮，新月！……須向我言，使我有食。以小事告我，使我得食。敬禮，敬禮，新月！」見新月即以雄羚之角吹奏此禱。

sensitivity.note: |xu San prayer dictated by Inanni to Bleek & Lloyd, 1880; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: Young Moon! Hail, Young Moon! Hail, hail, Young Moon! Young Moon! speak to me! Hail, hail, Young Moon! Tell me of something. Hail, hail! When the sun rises, Thou must speak to me, That I may eat something. Thou must speak to me about a little thing, That I may eat. Hail, hail, Young Moon! Condensed paraphrase of the note: when we see the moon, we say \kau-\karrishe; we sound the male antelope's horn. We call the small moon \ka-\karrishe; but women call it \ka-\karrihe.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 415 (public domain). / Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), Appendix p. 415 note; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 新月啊！萬歲，新月！萬歲，萬歲，新月！新月啊！對我說話吧！萬歲，萬歲，新月！告訴我些事情吧。萬歲，萬歲！當太陽升起時，你務必對我說話，好讓我吃些東西。你務必對我講一件小事，好讓我吃。萬歲，萬歲，新月！註解的濃縮轉述：我們看見月亮時，便說\kau-\karrishe；我們吹響雄羚羊的角。我們把小月亮叫作\ka-\karrishe；但女人們叫它\ka-\karrihe。

title.en: The Great Tortoise Deceives the Mantis
title.zh: 巨龜欺螳螂

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §7

summary.en: Following the Mantis's tricks with the Cat, the Great Tortoise turns trickster upon the trickster, feigning illness and helplessness as the Leopard Tortoise did to the hunters, and entangling the Mantis in his own devices.
summary.zh: 繼螳螂戲貓之後，巨龜反以其人之道還治其人：如豹龜詐病欺獵者一般，佯病佯弱，令螳螂自陷其詭計。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive (L II.—5. 565-624, 8. 811-882); presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§7): the first version of the myth of the Mantis and the Cat is followed by a story describing how the Mantis is tricked by the Great Tortoise (L II.—5. 565-624, 8. 811-882, of which only pp. 811-869 are translated). This is followed by a discourse upon the degrees of understanding possessed by various animals.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §7; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布萊克摘要（§7）的濃縮轉述：螳螂與貓的神話的第一個版本之後，接著是一個故事，描述螳螂如何被大烏龜所騙（L II.—5. 565-624，8. 811-882，其中僅第811-869頁被譯出）。其後是一篇論述，談各種動物所具備的種種理解程度。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The story of the Great Water Tortoise, who deceived men belonging to the early race of Bushmen by feigning illness (told by !Kweiten ta //Ken), appears to be a variation of the same myth.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §7; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同一出處的濃縮轉述；並非逐字照錄。大水龜的故事——牠裝病欺騙了屬於布須曼人早期族群的人們（由!Kweiten ta //Ken講述）——似乎是同一神話的變體。

title.en: The Two Pointer Lions, the Kori Bustard and the Blue Crane
title.zh: 南十字導星雙獅、鴇與藍鶴

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §§25-26

summary.en: The two Pointer stars of the Southern Cross were once men and lions, |gu and !khaue-ta-\khum. The lions kill and roast the kori bustard |gi and the blue crane \kao's husband; the crane, leaving her child behind, returns to the water and is eaten, while the kori, taking her child, is pulled up by the Crow and drops the pursuing lion into the fire. Revived, the greedy lion swallows a tortoise whole, which curses every pool dry and warns all game away until he starves.
summary.zh: 南十字導星二獅本為人——古烏與哈烏埃塔坤。二獅殺炙鴇吉與藍鶴考之夫。藍鶴棄其子返水而被食；鴇攜子，被烏鴉吊起，使追獅墜火。貪獅復活後整吞一龜，龜咒諸泉涸、萬獸逃，獅終餓斃。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San star-myth from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§26): the (two) Lions, which was the name given to us for the Pointers to the Southern Cross, were formerly men, and at the same time lions. One of them became a star, because a girl looked at him; and the other lion also became a star. They now stand silent, not far from the lionesses, who sit silent.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §26; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布萊克摘要（§26）的濃縮轉述：（兩頭）獅子——這是我們給南十字座指極星的稱呼——從前是人，同時也是獅子。其中一頭變成了星，因為一個女孩看了他；另一頭獅子也變成了星。他們如今靜立著，離那些靜坐著的母獅不遠。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The two husbands (the \gi and the \kao, 'Blue Crane') are killed and roasted by the lions; the \gi saw what the lions did and refused her husband's flesh, but the Blue Crane accepted some of the flesh of the \kao. Both birds went to fetch water; the Blue Crane, who had left her child behind, returned home from the water and was eaten by the lions.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §26; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同出處的濃縮改述，非逐字照錄。兩位丈夫（\gi 與 \kao，即「藍鶴」）被獅子殺死並烤熟；\gi 目睹獅子所為，拒絕吃丈夫的肉，但藍鶴接受了若干 \kao 的肉。兩隻鳥前去取水；藍鶴將孩子留在身後，取水歸來返家，卻被獅子吃掉。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The \gi, who had taken her child with her, went to the Crow's house on a thorn-tree and was pulled up by a gemsbok-skin thong; the Crow heated stones, the pursuing lion was pulled up with a rope of mouse's entrails, broke it, and fell into the fire, where he was roasted to death. The lions revived; the greedy lion swallowed a male tortoise whole, and the tortoise warned all game and dried every pool, so that the lions could get nothing, until \gu died of starvation.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §26; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同出處的濃縮改述，非逐字照錄。\gi 帶著孩子同行，前往荊棘樹上烏鴉的住處，被一條大羚羊皮帶拉了上去；烏鴉燒熱石頭，追來的獅子被一條以老鼠腸子編成的繩索往上拉，繩索斷裂，獅子跌入火中，被烤至死。獅子們復活；貪婪的獅子將一隻雄龜整隻吞下，烏龜警告所有獵物並使每個水塘乾涸，獅子因而一無所獲，直到 \gu 餓死。

title.en: The Man Who Brought Home a Lion's Cub as a 'Dog'
title.zh: 攜獅子歸謊稱為犬者

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §36

summary.en: One of the ancient people brings home a lion's cub, telling his wife it is a dog that kills gemsbok. She knows the roaring of its mother; he hunts with the growing 'dog', saved once only by his wife throwing fire, until the lion kills him and lays him under a thorn-tree. The widow flees with the children to her father-in-law, and the uncles find the spoor of seven lions.
summary.zh: 早期之人攜幼獅歸，謂其妻為殺大羚之犬。妻識母獅吼聲；夫攜「犬」獵大羚，唯妻擲火一次得免。獅長，殺其主，置屍荊樹下。寡婦攜子奔翁家；諸伯叔蹤七獅之跡。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San legend from the Bleek & Lloyd archive (L II.—26 to 31); presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§36): one of the ancient people preceding the Bushmen brought home a lion's cub, telling his wife that it was a dog which his younger brother had given him, and that it was the whelp of a dog which killed gemsbok. She, however, knew that it was the son of a lioness, whose voice was known to her of old, and who was now heard roaring for her lost cub.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §36; not verbatim.
