title.en: Shukaletuda's Crime in the Garden
title.zh: 舒卡萊圖達園中罪行

region.en: Gardens of Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克園圃（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Inana and Sukale-tuda (ETCSL c.1.3.3)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Shukaletuda, an ignorant gardener's son, plants a tree in the desert and tends it against all advice; a single leaf gives him shade. When the exhausted Inanna sleeps in the shade, he violates her; she wakes and vows to find him, and hides him no corner of the earth can keep.
summary.zh: 無知園丁之子舒卡萊圖達於荒漠植樹，不聽勸誡而悉心照料，僅得一片葉蔭。疲憊的伊南娜於蔭下沉睡，竟遭其玷污；她醒後立誓搜尋，普天之下無其藏身之處。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth of sexual violence; presented as literary-historical material without endorsement.

passages.text: Shukaletuda, son of a gardener, plants a tree in the desert where his father says nothing will grow. Against advice he waters it, and one leaf grows. When Inanna, weary from the me's great work, lies down to sleep in the tree's single shade, the fool takes her while she sleeps.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.3, the crime; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 園丁之子舒卡勒圖達在沙漠中種下一棵樹，他父親說那裡什麼也長不出來。他不聽勸告，為它澆水，於是長出了一片葉子。當伊南娜因「密」的偉大工作而疲憊，躺在那棵樹唯一的樹蔭下入睡時，那愚人趁她沉睡之際侵犯了她。

passages.text: Inanna wakes and sees what was done to her in her sleep. Like a flood she pours out her wrath: who has done this to me? She searches the earth for him, and to every animal, every city, every corner she puts the question.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.3, the wrath; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊南娜醒來，看見她在睡夢中遭受的所作所為。她如洪水般傾瀉出她的怒火：是誰對我做了這種事？她在大地上搜尋他，向每一隻動物、每一座城市、每一個角落提出質問。

functions: Morality tale of sacrilege and its inescapable punishment
Warning text about the goddess's honor and vigilance
Etiology of the gardener's low status in temple economy

variants.summary: Another offender destroyed by Inanna's wrath.

title.en: The Flight and Death of Shukaletuda
title.zh: 舒卡萊圖達逃亡與伏誅

region.en: Cities of Sumer, Iraq
region.zh: 蘇美諸城（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Inana and Sukale-tuda, second half (ETCSL c.1.3.3)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Shukaletuda flees from city to city; Inanna blights the crops to starve him out, freezes the birds on the wing, and hunts him across Sumer. Found at last, he begs only to see the sun; she grants the sight, then executes him on the spot.
summary.zh: 舒卡萊圖達一城又一城地逃亡；伊南娜摧毀莊稼斷其糧、凍凝飛鳥於半空，追索至蘇美全境。終被擒獲，他只求再看一眼太陽；她允其所請，隨即就地处決。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; execution imagery belongs to the mythic register.

passages.text: Shukaletuda runs from city to city, and Inanna follows him with curses on the land: she blights the grain in the fields, stops the cattle in their folds, freezes the birds in the air — all Sumer starves with him in hiding.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.3, pursuit; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 舒卡勒圖達從一座城市逃到另一座城市，伊南娜帶著對大地的詛咒追隨他：她使田間的穀物枯萎，使圈中的牛群止步，使空中的飛鳥凍僵——整個蘇美爾都隨他一同在藏匿中饑荒。

passages.text: At last found, Shukaletuda prays: let me at least see the sun before I die. Inanna answers with terrible justice — she grants the prayer and strikes him down in the sunlight. The poem closes hailing the goddess who leaves no outrage unavenged.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.3, capture and execution; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 終於被找到後，舒卡勒圖達祈禱：至少讓我在死前看一眼太陽。伊南娜以可怕的公正回應——她准許了這祈禱，並在陽光下將他擊倒。這首詩在結尾頌揚那位不讓任何暴行不受報復的女神。

functions: Culmination of the sacrilege-warning myth
Hymn to Inanna's justice performed in her cult
Etiology of blight as the goddess's pursuit made visible

title.en: Inanna and the River Monster Gudam
title.zh: 伊南娜與河怪古丹

region.en: Riverways of Sumer, Iraq
region.zh: 蘇美河渠（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Inana and Gudam (ETCSL c.1.3.4)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Gudam, a monstrous horned one who comes down the river devouring everything, defies Inanna; she cuts him down and his blood dyes the water. The short battle poem celebrates her as the slayer of the river's terror.
summary.zh: 河中巨怪古丹吞食萬物、公然挑釁伊南娜；她一刀斬之，其血染紅河水。短小的戰歌頌揚她為河川恐怖的誅除者。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Gudam, a horned monster of the river, comes down the waterways eating everything — trees, men, cattle — and defies the Lady of Heaven, challenging her power in her own city. Inanna seizes her weapons, strikes Gudam down, and his blood runs red in the river. The hymn ends with her praise as the terror of terrors, the power that keeps the waterways clean.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.4, the monster's defiance; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.4, the kill and closing hymn; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古丹，一頭長角的河怪，順著水道而下，吞噬一切——樹木、人、牛——並在天上女神的城中違抗她，挑戰她的權能。伊南娜抓起武器，擊倒古丹，他的血在河中染成一片赤紅。這首讚美詩以對她的頌揚作結：她是恐怖中的恐怖，是使水道保持潔淨的力量。

functions: Battle hymn of the Inanna cult
Etiology of the safe waterway and the slain river-demon

title.en: Inanna Takes Over Heaven
title.zh: 伊南娜接管天庭

region.en: E-ana temple, Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克埃安那神殿（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Inana and An (ETCSL c.1.3.5)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: An dwells in Inanna's house at Uruk and grows homesick for heaven; she seizes the chance — when he tries to leave, she demands the E-ana for herself, and heaven grants the ambitious goddess both temple and city in perpetuity.
summary.zh: 安居於烏魯克伊南娜神殿的安神思念上天；欲歸之際，伊南娜趁機索求埃安那神殿——天庭允之，野心之神遂永享殿宇與城池。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: An comes down from heaven to lodge in the E-ana, Inanna's temple at Uruk, and enjoys its beds and beer; but at night he misses heaven and longs to go back up. When An announces his departure, Inanna's people weep — for with An gone, no blessings remain. Inanna seizes the moment and demands the temple as her own; An, half in affection, half in haste to be gone, gives it to her with its destinies: the E-ana shall be Inanna's house forever. The poem ends with Inanna's glory: she has taken heaven's own residence for her city, and the gods serve her in it. Uruk's temple, the E-ana, becomes the meeting place of heaven and earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.5, An's visit; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.5, the transfer; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.3.5, closing hymn; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 安從天而降，棲居於烏魯克伊南娜的神廟埃安納，享受其中的床榻與啤酒；但到了夜裡，他思念天界，渴望重返天上。當安宣布離去時，伊南娜的子民哭泣——因為安一旦離去，便不再留有祝福。伊南娜抓住時機，要求將神廟歸於自己；安半是出於情意，半是急於離去，便將神廟連同其天命一併賜予她：埃安納將永遠是伊南娜的居所。詩篇以伊南娜的榮耀作結：她為自己的城奪取了天界自身的居所，眾神在其中服侍她。烏魯克的神廟埃安納，成為天與地交會之處。

functions: Founding charter of the E-ana temple at Uruk
Mythic projection of Uruk's cultic primacy
Performed at Inanna's festivals as the temple's legitimation

title.en: Inanna and the Huluppu Tree
title.zh: 伊南娜與胡盧普樹

region.en: Banks of the Euphrates, Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 幼發拉底河畔烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Gilgamesh, Enkidu and the Nether World, opening (ETCSL c.1.8.1.4)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: A willow pulled from the Euphrates is planted by Inanna in her garden and grows a crown; a serpent, an Anzu-bird and a ghost-maiden lodge in it. Gilgamesh drives them out, fells the tree, and from its wood makes Inanna's throne and bed — and a drum for himself.
summary.zh: 伊南娜自幼發拉底河拔得一株胡盧普樹植於園中；蛇、安祖鳥與魅女相繼棲於其內。吉爾伽美什逐之、伐之，以其木為伊南娜製御座與寢床，並為自己製鼓。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In those days, a single tree grew by the Euphrates; the south wind uprooted it, and Inanna walking by took it and planted it in her garden, watered it with her hand, waiting for it to grow into a throne and a bed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.4, opening; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在那些日子裡，幼發拉底河畔長著一棵孤樹；南風將它連根拔起，伊南娜走過時取走它，栽種在自己的園中，親手為它澆水，等待它長大成寶座與床榻。

passages.text: But at the tree's crown a serpent built its nest, the Anzu-bird set its young in the branches, and in its heart the dark phantom-maiden raised her house. Inanna wept — her tree was taken and she could not cut it down.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.4, the squatters; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但在樹冠之上，一條蛇築了巢；安祖鳥在枝頭安置幼雛；而在樹心之中，幽暗的幻影少女建起了她的居所。伊南娜哭泣——她的樹被佔據，她卻無法將它砍倒。

passages.text: Gilgamesh her brother came: he slew the serpent at the tree's base, drove out the bird and the maiden to their homes, felled the willow, and from its heartwood made Inanna's throne and bed; of the rest he made the drum for the young men of Uruk.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.4, the rescue and carpentry; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她的兄弟吉爾伽美什來了：他斬殺樹根處的蛇，將鳥與少女驅回各自的居所，砍倒柳樹，以它的心材製成伊南娜的寶座與床榻；其餘的木料，他做成了供烏魯克青年使用的鼓。

functions: Etiology of Inanna's throne and bed in the E-ana
Etiology of Gilgamesh's ceremonial drum
Miniature cosmogony introducing the netherworld poem

title.en: Enheduanna's Exaltation of Inanna
title.zh: 恩海杜安娜：頌揚伊南娜

region.en: Ur and Nippur, Iraq
region.zh: 烏爾與尼普魯（伊拉克）

period: Sargonic period poem, c. 2300 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A hymn to Inana: Nin-me-sara (ETCSL c.4.07.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The world's first signed author, Enheduanna, priestess of Nanna at Ur, praises Inanna as the power who turns An's own lesser gods from her and raises the exiled priestess back to her temple — the hymn ends with her restoration and Inanna's glory.
summary.zh: 世上第一位署名作者——烏爾月神祭司恩海杜安娜——頌揚伊南娜之權能：她能令安神座下諸神背離他人，亦能令被逐的祭司重返聖殿；頌詩以復位與神榮作結。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn by a named historical author; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Lady of all the me, radiant Inanna: you have taken up the great powers and turn the Anuna gods from whoever offends you. Before you, the great rites themselves grow silent; cities and temples obey your word. Enheduanna speaks in the first person: exiled from her temple by Lugalanne, driven from Ur and Nippur, she is made to walk the waste; her gifts rejected, her rites despised, she prays to Inanna — not to the moon god her father — to judge the rebels. Inanna hears and acts: the usurper is brought low, and the priestess returns to her temple. The hymn closes with the first signature in world literature: Enheduanna, en-priestess of Nanna, has composed this exaltation of Inanna.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.07.1, opening praise; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.07.1, the exile; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.07.1, restoration and signature; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一切me的女主人，光輝的伊南娜：你執掌了偉大的權能，使安努那諸神背離任何冒犯你的人。在你面前，偉大的儀典本身也歸於沉寂；城邑與神廟都聽從你的話語。恩赫杜安娜以第一人稱訴說：她被盧加蘭尼逐出自己的神廟，被逐出烏爾與尼普爾，被迫行走於荒原；她的獻禮遭拒，她的儀典遭鄙棄，於是她向伊南娜——而非她的父親月神——祈禱，求她審判那些叛亂者。伊南娜聽見並採取行動：篡位者被貶抑，女祭司重返她的神廟。這首讚美詩以世界文學中最早的署名作結：南納的en女祭司恩赫杜安娜，作了這篇對伊南娜的頌揚。

functions: Political hymn asserting Inanna's supremacy for the Akkadian dynasty
Autobiographical prayer of restoration used in the en-priestess cult
Foundational text of authored literature in world history

variants.summary: Mythic counterpart of the hymn's claim that even the sky god's realm yields to Inanna.

canonical_translation: ETCSL team translation, Oxford, 2003-2006

primary_sources.citation: ETCSL c.4.07.1, trans. ETCSL team (2003-2006), lines 1-137

title.en: Dumuzi and Enkimdu: Shepherd versus Farmer
title.zh: 杜穆茲與恩金姆杜：牧與農之爭

region.en: Steppe and canals near Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克近郊草原與運河（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Inana and Dumuzid: Dumuzid and Enkimdu (ETCSL c.1.4.x)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Two gods court Inanna: the noisy shepherd Dumuzi and the quiet farmer Enkimdu. Inanna's brother Utu advises her, the rivals trade boasts and insults, and the farmer, yielding, promises the shepherd grain, and the dispute ends in friendship.
summary.zh: 二神同求伊南娜：喧鬧的牧者杜穆茲與沉靜的農神恩金姆杜。兄長烏圖獻策，二神互相誇耀譏諷；農神終讓步許諾贈穀，爭端以友誼收場。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Inanna loves a man, and two gods come to court her: Dumuzi the shepherd, loud in his love-songs, and Enkimdu the farmer, lord of canals and plough. Inanna's brother Utu tells her to weigh them both, and the suitors fall to boasting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.2, the suitors; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊南娜愛上了一名男子，兩位神明前來向她求愛：牧人杜穆濟，他的情歌響亮；以及農夫恩金杜，他是運河與犁之主。伊南娜的兄長烏圖要她衡量二人，兩位求婚者便互相誇耀起來。

passages.text: Dumuzi taunts the farmer: what is your grain against my cream, your loaves against my milk and cheese? The farmer answers mildly: let him bellow — my gifts will come to his folds in good time. The contest ends in concord: Enkimdu promises Dumuzi his wheat, his flour and his beer, and the shepherd is given the bride. The poem closes with the marriage of Inanna to the shepherd, the farmer reconciled to the household.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.2, the contest of boasts; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.2, reconciliation and wedding; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 杜穆濟嘲弄農夫：你的穀物怎能比得上我的奶油，你的麵包怎能比得上我的奶與乳酪？農夫溫和地回答：任他咆哮吧——我的贈禮終會適時送到他的羊圈。這場較量以和睦收場：恩金杜許諾把他的小麥、麵粉與啤酒給杜穆濟，而牧人得到了新娘。詩篇以伊南娜嫁給牧人、農夫與這戶人家和解作結。

functions: Charter myth of the shepherd-farmer integration in the Uruk economy
Courtship narrative performed with the Inanna-Dumuzid songs
Etiology of the seasonal alternation of flocks and fields

variants.name: The debate between Grain and Sheep
variants.summary: The same shepherd-farmer rivalry as a personified debate judged by Enlil.

canonical_translation: ETCSL team translation, Oxford, 2003-2006

title.en: Dumuzi's Dream: The Omen of Capture
title.zh: 杜穆茲之夢：被擒之兆

region.en: Alaj ostrich-grove near Uruk, Iraq (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 烏魯克近郊鴕鳥林阿拉吉（象徵性定位）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Dumuzid's dream (ETCSL c.1.4.3)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Dumuzi dreams the reeds rise against him, a stirrup breaks, his sheep scatter — and Geshtinanna, his sister, reads the dream as the netherworld coming for him. He accepts: the dream is fate; only the hiding matters.
summary.zh: 杜穆茲夢見蘆葦崛起、馬鐙斷裂、羊群驚散——妹妹蓋什蒂南娜解夢：冥界將至。他認命：夢即天數，唯藏身之地尚可一搏。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Dumuzi, sleeping among the ostrich grove of Alaj, dreams: rushes rise in fire, one reed of the double reed splits, his stirrup shatters, his ewes and lambs scatter, his goats and kids tear at each other. He wakes in terror and tells his dream to Geshtinanna. She reads it: the rushes are the netherworld's henchmen rising to seize you; the broken stirrup and the scattered flocks are the desolation of your sheepfold after you are taken. My brother, the dream is fate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.3, the dream; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.3, the interpretation; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 杜穆濟在阿拉吉的鴕鳥林中沉睡，做了一場夢：蘆葦在火中升起，雙蘆葦中的一根蘆葦裂開，他的馬鐙碎裂，他的母羊與羔羊四散，他的山羊與小山羊互相撕咬。他在驚恐中醒來，把夢告訴了蓋什提南娜。她為他解夢：蘆葦是冥界的爪牙興起要捉拿你；碎裂的馬鐙與四散的羊群，是你被擄走後羊圈荒蕪的景象。我的兄長，這夢就是命運。

passages.text: Dumuzi answers calmly: in my youth my mother had me play at the dream's oracle; the dream is not kind, but let us not accept it. Let me hide in the Alaj grove — never tell the galla demons where I am.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.3, acceptance and resolve; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 杜穆濟平靜地回答：我年幼時，母親曾讓我演習解夢的神諭；這夢並不仁慈，但我們不要接受它。讓我躲進阿拉吉林中——千萬不要告訴加拉惡魔我在哪裡。

functions: Model dream-interpretation scene for the oracle craft
Seasonal myth of the vegetation god's approaching death
Performed with the Dumuzid laments in mourning liturgy

variants.summary: The goddess's descent narrative in which Dumuzid's takeover is foretold by his mourning.

title.en: The Hunt for Dumuzi
title.zh: 圍捕杜穆茲

region.en: Alaj grove to the sheepfold, Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 自鴕鳥林至羊欄，烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Dumuzid's dream, second half (ETCSL c.1.4.3)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The galla demons come up from the netherworld as gallows-spirits, enter no clean house, touch no clean man, and hunt Dumuzi. He flees grove to fold; the demons lure his shepherd, who betrays him; he is seized by the arms and dragged down to the great below.
summary.zh: 冥界鬼卒絞刑妖靈自冥土上來，不入潔室、不近潔人，專獵杜穆茲。他自樹林逃至羊欄；眾妖誘其牧人而得线索，遂擒其臂，拖入冥土。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The galla come up from the great below — small galla who take one, big galla who take all — spirits that enter no clean house and touch no clean man, that lurk on the roads and hunt one man only: Dumuzi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.3, the demons; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 加拉從深淵之下上來——捉一人的小加拉，捉盡一切的大加拉——這些鬼魂不進潔淨之家，不觸潔淨之人，潛伏於道路之上，只追獵一人：杜穆濟。

passages.text: Dumuzi flees from the Alaj grove to the old woman's house, from the house to the sheepfold, changing hiding places as the demons spread through the city; the demons speak sweetly to the shepherd and get from him the word that shows where the god is.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.3, pursuit and betrayal; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 杜穆濟從阿拉吉林逃到老婦人的屋中，又從屋中逃到羊圈，隨著惡魔遍佈城中而不斷變換藏身之處；惡魔們對牧人甜言蜜語，從他口中套出了指明神明所在的話語。

passages.text: They seize him by the arms, drag him by the hands, and carry him down; Geshtinanna runs through the city mourning her brother, and the shepherd god passes into the netherworld — his song of departure the model of the mourning liturgy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.3, the seizure; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們抓住他的手臂，拽著他的手，將他帶下去；革什提南娜跑遍城中哀悼她的兄長，牧神就此進入冥界——他離別之歌成了哀悼儀式的範本。

functions: Mourning liturgy text for the Dumuzid festival
Theology of the galla demons and their purity rules
Seasonal etiology of the summer decline of flocks

variants.name: Descent of Ishtar (Akkadian)
variants.summary: The Babylonian version in which Tammuz must descend for half the year.

canonical_translation: ETCSL team translation, Oxford, 2003-2006

primary_sources.citation: ETCSL c.1.4.3, trans. ETCSL team (2003-2006), lines 100-250

secondary_sources.work: Inanna, Queen of Heaven and Earth

title.en: Dumuzi and Geshtinanna: The Half-Year
title.zh: 杜穆茲與蓋什蒂南娜：半年之約

region.en: Uruk and the great below, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克與冥土（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Dumuzid and Geshtin-ana (ETCSL c.1.4.1.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The sister refuses to tell the demons where her brother hides and is tortured for it. Dumuzi's shade laments; Inanna weeps for her husband and decrees: for six months the sister serves in his place, for six months the husband — and thus the year turns.
summary.zh: 妹妹拒不出賣兄長藏身處，遭妖拷問。杜穆茲陰魂哀哭；伊南娜為夫垂淚，頒命：半年以妹代之，半年以夫代之——四季由是輪轉。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The galla press Geshtinanna for her brother's hiding place; she will not tell, and they torture her as they would a stranger. Dumuzi's shade, hearing of it, laments that his little sister suffered so for love of him. Inanna mourns her husband and goes to Ereshkigal to bargain. The decree is spoken: let the sister serve in the netherworld for the brother half the year, and the husband serve the other half — so the measure of the year is fixed. The poem closes with the ritual: on the day the shepherd returns, the dead man's sister rises, and the people of Uruk offer cream and beer to both. Whoever recites the song shall live long days.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.1.1, the loyalty test; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.1.1, the decree; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.1.1, closing rite; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伽拉鬼卒逼問革什提南娜她兄長的藏身之處；她不肯說，他們便像對待陌生人一樣折磨她。杜木茲的亡魂聽聞此事，哀嘆他的小妹竟為愛他而受此苦。伊南娜哀悼她的丈夫，前往埃列什基伽勒處交涉。詔令宣下：讓妹妹在冥界代兄服役半年，丈夫服役另半年——一年的尺度就此定下。詩篇以儀式作結：牧人歸來之日，亡者的妹妹升起，烏魯克的人們向二者獻上乳脂與啤酒。凡誦此歌者，必享長壽。

functions: Etiology of the seasonal exchange of Dumuzid and Geshtinanna
Liturgy of the return-day offerings in the Uruk calendar
Model of familial loyalty within the divine house

variants.summary: The Babylonian parallel granting Tammuz half the year.

variants.summary: The lament scene of Dumuzid in the netherworld with his two sisters.

title.en: Dumuzi in the Netherworld with His Sisters
title.zh: 杜穆茲冥界姊妹吟

region.en: The great below (symbolic pin at Uruk's underworld gate)
region.zh: 冥土（象徵性定位於烏魯克冥門）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Dumuzid and his sisters (ETCSL c.1.4.1.3)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Down in the land of no return, Dumuzi is visited by Geshtinanna, who brings comfort, and by the dark sister Amashilamma; the dialogue of lamentation shows the dead shepherd as a lord among shades, honored but grieving.
summary.zh: 冥土之中，蓋什蒂南娜攝慰藉而至，黑衣姊妹阿瑪什利拉瑪亦來；哀悼對話中，亡故的牧神為幽魂之王——受尊崇而亦哀傷。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary literature; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In the house of the land of no return, Dumuzi the shepherd sits among the dead; his sister Geshtinanna comes to him with comfort in her hands, and speaks to him as the living speak. The dialogue of the two sisters around the dead god teaches the manners of the underworld: the dark sister speaks of the customs of the shades, and Dumuzi answers as one who has learned them — the poem a manual of how the dead are treated and how the living should mourn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.1.3, the visit; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.1.3, the dialogue; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在無歸之地的屋中，牧人杜木茲坐在亡者之間；他的妹妹革什提南娜帶著慰藉前來，以生者之言對他說話。兩姊妹圍繞亡神的對話，教導了冥界的禮數：黑暗的妹妹講述亡魂的習俗，杜木茲則以習得者之姿作答——此詩乃一部關於如何對待亡者、生者當如何哀悼的指南。

functions: Mourning manual for the Dumuzid lament festival
Underworld etiquette: how the dead are addressed

variants.name: Dumuzid and Geshtin-ana
variants.summary: The half-year decree that ends the cycle.

canonical_translation: ETCSL team translation, Oxford, 2003-2006

primary_sources.citation: ETCSL c.1.4.1.3, trans. ETCSL team (2003-2006)

title.en: Inanna and Bilulu: The Vengeance at Dugrub
title.zh: 伊南娜與比利魯：杜格魯布復仇

region.en: Dugrub sheepfold, steppe of Sumer, Iraq
region.zh: 杜格魯布羊欄，蘇美草原（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Inana and Bilulu: an ulila to Inana (ETCSL c.1.4.4)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Traveling through the wilderness, Inanna finds the old woman Bilulu who holds her shepherd Dumuzi's herds; discovering in her the death of her husband, the goddess kills Bilulu, turns her son into a guardian spirit, and installs Bilulu as a mourning figure of the fold.
summary.zh: 伊南娜行經荒野，遇看守其夫杜穆茲羊群的老婦比利魯；察知其夫之死與她有關，女神殺之，化其子為守護神靈，令比利魯成為羊欄之哀悼化身。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Inanna walks the wilderness roads to find her shepherd; at the Dugrub sheepfold the old woman Bilulu keeps the herds, and in her Inanna recognizes the one who has caused Dumuzi's death. Inanna kills Bilulu and her son, then transfigures them: the old woman is made the mourning figure of the fold, whose laments will open the mourning rites; her son becomes the guardian spirit of the herds, so that the very house of the crime becomes its memorial. The song closes as an ulila, a mourning hymn for Inanna: the goddess who avenges her husband is praised, and the fold remembers both the crime and the mercy of transformation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.4, the discovery; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.4, vengeance and transformation; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.4.4, closing hymn; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊南娜行走於荒野之路，尋找她的牧人；在杜格魯布羊圈，老婦比魯魯看守著畜群，伊南娜從她身上認出了造成杜木茲之死的那個人。伊南娜殺死比魯魯和她的兒子，隨後將他們變形：老婦被化為羊圈的哀悼形象，她的哀號將開啟哀悼之禮；她的兒子則成為畜群的守護神，於是罪案發生之所本身成了它的紀念。歌以烏利拉——一首獻給伊南娜的哀歌——作結：為丈夫復仇的女神受到讚頌，羊圈則同時銘記那樁罪與變形的慈悲。

functions: Charter of the mourning figures used in the Dumuzid lament liturgy
Vengeance myth of Inanna performed as ulila hymn
Etiology of the guardian spirits of the sheepfold

variants.name: Dumuzid's dream
variants.summary: The parallel narrative of the shepherd's seizure by the galla.

canonical_translation: ETCSL team translation, Oxford, 2003-2006

primary_sources.citation: ETCSL c.1.4.4, trans. ETCSL team (2003-2006)

secondary_sources.work: The Harps that Once...

title.en: The Wedding of Inanna and Dumuzi
title.zh: 伊南娜與杜穆茲婚禮

region.en: Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Ur III cult song, c. 2000 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A balbale to Inana and Dumuzid (Dumuzid-Inana wedding songs, ETCSL c.4.08.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The bride's mother, brother and suitor speak in turn as the wedding is prepared; Dumuzi claims his bride with gifts of cream and dates, and the marriage bed of Uruk is blessed — the cult song performed at the hieros gamos rite.
summary.zh: 婚禮將備，母、兄、求婚者輪番陳辭；杜穆茲以乳酪與椰棗為聘迎娶，烏魯克的婚床受祝福——此即聖婚儀式所頌的祭歌。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cult song with sexual imagery in its ritual register; presented as literature, not endorsement.

passages.text: The wedding songs move between speakers: Inanna's mother tells her to bathe and anoint; her brother calls the shepherd's gifts good; Dumuzi offers cream and dates, his sheepfolds full, as bride-price for the lady of Uruk. Inanna consents in love-song: let the shepherd sleep beside me, let me caress the man. The bed is prepared with sweet oil and cedar, and the city rejoices at the union of the lady and the shepherd. The cult song ends with blessings for the city: through the sacred marriage Uruk's year is secured — grain, flocks and kingship renewed by the union performed annually in the temple.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.08.1, courtship exchange; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.08.1, wedding night; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.08.1, closing blessing; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 婚歌在諸多歌者之間交替：伊南娜的母親囑她沐浴塗油；她的兄長稱牧人的禮物為美善；杜木茲獻上乳脂與棗，羊圈滿盈，作為向烏魯克女主求親的聘禮。伊南娜以情歌應允：讓牧人睡在我身旁，讓我撫愛這男子。床榻以香油與雪松備好，全城為女主與牧人的結合而歡欣。祭儀之歌以對城市的祝福作結：藉由聖婚，烏魯克的年歲得以穩固——穀物、畜群與王權，皆因每年在神廟中舉行的結合而更新。

functions: Liturgy of the sacred marriage (hieros gamos) at Uruk
Wedding songs performed for royal participation in the rite
Charter of the city's annual renewal of fertility

title.en: Dumuzi's Waking Song
title.zh: 杜穆茲晨歌

region.en: Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Ur III cult song, c. 2000 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A balbale to Inana and Dumuzid (Dumuzid wakens, ETCSL c.4.08.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Dumuzi wakes beside Inanna and sings the morning of the lovers: the sleeping house, the sheep not yet stirred, the bed not yet cooled — the intimate liturgical morning-song of the sacred marriage cycle.
summary.zh: 杜穆茲在伊南娜身旁醒來，唱戀人的清晨：酣睡的屋宅、未動的羊群、尚溫的床榻——聖婚詩環中最親暱的晨間祭歌。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cult song; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The morning song opens on the sleeping house: the doors shut, the household asleep, the god rising beside the goddess while the city's fires are not yet lit. Dumuzi sings of the flocks still folded, the meadows unopened, the bed still warm — the shepherd's world paused around the lovers — and the song closes with the couple blessed in their union.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.08.2, the sleeping house; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.08.2, the paused world and blessing; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 晨歌自沉睡的屋中展開：門扉緊閉，家宅安睡，神明在女神身旁起身，而城中的火尚未點燃。杜木茲歌唱仍圈於欄中的畜群、尚未開啟的草場、仍帶餘溫的床榻——牧人的世界圍繞這對愛人而暫停——歌則以這對伴侶在其結合中蒙受祝福作結。

functions: Morning liturgy of the sacred marriage rite
Love-lyric performed in the Inanna-Dumuzid cult

title.en: The Mantis's Magic: Hartebeest Charm for Babies
title.zh: 螳螂之法：護嬰之麋羚符

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1874 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §13a; D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Hartebeest and the Eland'

summary.en: The Hartebeest and the Eland are things of the Mantis and have magic power: the hartebeest's head resembles his head. A mother with a young child must not eat hartebeest nor spring over its head, or the Mantis would press in the hollow of the child's head; she cuts a piece of hartebeest foot into a charm. When a man shoots an eland he stays away, ill, so the eland may smell no cooking.
summary.zh: 麋羚與大羚乃螳螂之物，具魔力：麋羚之頭似其頭。抱嬰之母不得食麋羚、不得跨其頭，否則螳螂壓陷兒之囟門；她截麋羚足一塊為符。射羚之獵者離家如病，使羚不嗅炊香。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San charm-lore from the Bleek & Lloyd archive (L V.—6. 4411-4434) and D. F. Bleek 1924; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Hartebeest and the Eland are things of the Mantis; therefore they have magic power. The Mantis is used to go with the Hartebeest when he walks about. Our parents used to ask us, Did we not see that the Hartebeest's head resembled the Mantis's head? It feels that it belongs to the Mantis: that is why its head resembles his head.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 10 (public domain).
passages.zh: 麋羚與大羚羊是螳螂之物；因此牠們具有魔力。螳螂走動時，慣常與麋羚同行。我們的父母常問我們：我們豈不是看見麋羚的頭像螳螂的頭嗎？牠自覺屬於螳螂：這就是牠的頭像牠的頭的原因。

passages.text: A woman who has a young child does not eat the Hartebeest, nor does she spring over the Hartebeest's head, for the Mantis would press down the hollow place on her child's head, and the child would die, if she did so. So our parents used to tell the women who had young children to cut out a piece of the Hartebeest's foot between the toes, to thread it upon a sinew and make a charm and put it on the little child.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 10 (public domain).
passages.zh: 有幼小孩子的婦人不吃麋羚，也不跨越麋羚的頭，因為若她這樣做，螳螂便會壓下她孩子頭上的囟門凹陷處，孩子就會死去。所以我們的父母常告訴有幼小孩子的婦人，要從麋羚腳趾之間割下一小塊腳，穿在筋上做成護符，戴在小孩子身上。

passages.text: When a man has shot an Eland with an arrow, he does not come home. He walks about as if he were ill; people carry him away as if he were ill, for he wants the Eland to act as he does... he goes to a place to windward, so that he may not smell the food the people are cooking at home. For if the Eland were to smell the scent of the food, it would arise and go away.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 10-11 (public domain).
passages.zh: 當一個人用箭射中一頭大羚羊後，他不回家。他像生病一樣四處走動；人們像對待病人一樣把他帶走，因為他要大羚羊也像他這樣……他走到上風處，以免聞到家中人們正在煮的食物氣味。因為大羚羊若聞到食物的氣味，就會起身離去。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's 1875 note (§13a): an account of the magic protection afforded by the Mantis to the Hartebeest and to the Eland, dictated in the Katkop dialect by Dia!kwain; the same informant mentions remarkable superstitions concerning the Hartebeest, whose head is said to resemble that of the Mantis, and a curious charm made from the foot of the Hartebeest, used by Bushman women for their children.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §13a; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布萊克1875年註釋（§13a）的濃縮轉述：記述螳螂給予麋羚與大羚羊的魔法保護，由Dia!kwain以Katkop方言口述；同一位講述者提及關於麋羚的奇特迷信，據說牠的頭像螳螂的頭，以及一種用麋羚腳製成的奇特護符，由布須曼婦人為其孩子使用。

title.en: How the Mantis Gave the Bucks Their Colours
title.zh: 螳螂賜羚羊之色

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'How the Mantis gave the Bucks their Colours'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §1

summary.en: The Gemsbok ate white liquid honey and is white; the Hartebeest ate the red comb of young bees and is red; the Eland ate wasps' honey and is dark; the Quagga ate small bees' honey and is dark; the Springbok drank the liquid from the red young bees' cells and is red. The Mantis squeezed each out for its animal.
summary.zh: 大羚食白蜜故白；麋羚食紅嫩蜂巢故赤；伊蘭羚食黃蜂蜜故暗；斑馬食小蜂蜜故暗；跳羚飲紅巢之液故赤。皆螳螂為之榨取。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San etiology from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Gemsbok once ate liquid honey which is white. This is why he is white. The Mantis once gave some of it to the Gemsbok. The Hartebeest was the one to whom the Mantis once gave some of the comb of young bees; that is why the Hartebeest is red, because the comb of young bees which he ate was red. So he became like the comb of young bees.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 10 (public domain).
passages.zh: 寶石羚曾吃過白色的液態蜂蜜。這就是牠呈白色的原因。螳螂曾把一些給寶石羚。麋羚是螳螂曾把一些幼蜂巢給牠的那一位；這就是麋羚呈紅色的原因，因為牠所吃的幼蜂巢是紅色的。於是牠變得像幼蜂巢一樣。

passages.text: The Eland was the one to whom the Mantis once gave some wasps honey; this is why he is dark, because he once ate wasps honey. The Quagga was the one to whom the Mantis once gave some of the small bees' honey; that is why he is dark... The Springbok was the one who once ate the liquid from the young bees' cells; that is why he is red. The Mantis squeezed it out for him and he drank.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 10 (public domain).
passages.zh: 大羚羊是螳螂曾把一些黃蜂蜂蜜給牠的那一位；這就是牠呈深色的原因，因為牠曾吃過黃蜂蜂蜜。斑驢是螳螂曾把一些小蜂蜂蜜給牠的那一位；這就是牠呈深色的原因……跳羚是曾吃過幼蜂巢中液體的那一位；這就是牠呈紅色的原因。螳螂為牠把液體擠出來，牠便喝了。

title.en: The Mantis and the Will-o'-the-Wisp
title.zh: 螳螂與鬼火

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Mantis and the Will-o'-the-Wisp'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §4

summary.en: The Mantis meets a smooth-headed being whose eyes are not in his head but between the toes of his feet; beaten the first time, he consults the Ichneumon, and the second time kicks dust into the eyes on his feet and breaks the will-o'-the-wisp's head.
summary.zh: 螳螂遇頭頂平滑之怪——其目不在首而在趾間。初戰敗北，商於小獴；再戰以塵揚其足間之眼，碎鬼火之頭。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Mantis caught sight of Will-o'-the-wisp walking about; he asked where Will-o'-the-wisp came from... he put down his quiver, he took out a knobkerry, he looked to see where Will-o'-the-wisp's eyes were. He looked him up and down, he walked all round him seeking his eyes. He asked Will-o'-the-wisp where his eyes might be. Will-o'-the-wisp said that his eyes were not anywhere.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 13 (public domain).
passages.zh: 螳螂瞥見鬼火四處走動；他問鬼火從何而來……他放下箭袋，取出圓頭棒，察看鬼火的眼睛在何處。他上下打量他，繞著他走了一圈，尋找他的眼睛。他問鬼火他的眼睛究竟在哪裡。鬼火說他的眼睛哪兒都不在。

passages.text: And Will-o'-the-wisp hit the Mantis's head and broke it, and hit it again. And the Mantis sprang aside and ran away, because he felt he could not bear it any longer. Then he called to the quiver and the shoes, that his things should follow him home.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 14 (public domain).
passages.zh: 鬼火擊中螳螂的頭，把它打破了，又再擊了一下。螳螂跳到一旁逃走了，因為他覺得再也受不了了。於是他呼喚箭袋和鞋子，叫他的東西跟著他回家。

passages.text: Kwammang-a told him that Will-o'-the-wisp's eyes ought to be on his feet between the great toe and the next... 'Then you must look at his feet and you will see the eyes peeping out between the toes. Then you must kick dust into his eyes, and while he sits rubbing his eyes there, you must keep hitting his head.'... And the Mantis sprang up and beat his head and broke it.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 14-15 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 夸曼加告訴他，鬼火的眼睛應該在他的腳上，位於大腳趾與第二趾之間……「那麼你必須看他的腳，就會看見眼睛從腳趾之間窺探出來。然後你必須把塵土踢進他的眼睛裡，趁他坐在那裡揉眼睛的時候，你必須不停地打他的頭。」……螳螂便跳起來打他的頭，把它打破了。

title.en: A Visit to the Lion's House
title.zh: 訪獅之家

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'A Visit to the Lion's House'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §5

summary.en: Kwammang-a and the Ichneumon visit the lions' home to eat quagga meat; the Mantis begs to come, hides in the bag, and whispers 'I should like to poke out your eye' to the little Lion, who runs crying to the Lioness. She stamps to crush him; the Mantis flies off with his calling shoes, then lies to the Dasse that both men were slain — until the Porcupine sees them coming laden.
summary.zh: 夸曼加與小獴訪獅家食斑馬肉；螳螂強要同行，藏於囊中，對小獅耳語「欲挖爾眼」。小獅啼告母獅；母獅欲踏殺之，螳螂展翅而遁，沿路呼其鞋。歸家謊報二人已死——豪豬卻見其滿載而歸。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Mantis said: 'O Ichneumon, put me into your bag!'... 'Quickly put me in, O Ichneumon, quickly put me in, so that the Lions do not see me! You must put in my legs, you must not tie up the mouth of the bag, for my head will stand above the bag's mouth... Just then the little Lion came in among Kwammang-a's people. The little Lion caught sight of him.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 16 (public domain).
passages.zh: 螳螂說：「噢，獴，把我放進你的袋子裡！」……「快把我放進去，噢，獴，快把我放進去，別讓獅子們看見我！你必須把我的腿放進去，你不必綁住袋口，因為我的頭會露在袋口上方……」就在這時，小獅子走進了夸曼加的人們中間。小獅子瞥見了他。

passages.text: The little Lion sprang back crying... As he stood by Kwammang-a's leg, he saw the Mantis. The Mantis shut one eye and winked at him, he whispered: 'I should like to poke out your eye.' The little Lion ran away crying; he went to his mother... She stood upon the Mantis to crush him. She said: 'Boo, what is this that is making the child cry, bringing me, the Lioness?' Then the Mantis jumped out of the bag and got feathers; he flew up into the sky.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 16 (public domain).
passages.zh: 小獅子哭喊著往後跳……當他站在夸曼加的腿旁時，他看見了螳螂。螳螂閉上一隻眼向他眨眼，低聲說：「我真想把你的一隻眼睛挖出來。」小獅子哭著跑走了；他跑到他母親那裡……她站在螳螂身上要壓死他。她說：「呸，這是什麼東西，竟把孩子弄哭，還把我這母獅引來？」於是螳螂從袋子裡跳出來，弄到一些羽毛；他飛上了天空。

passages.text: He went into the water... He stood on the bank above and said: 'O Hartebeest's children: wait for me!' O shoes, wait for me! O stick, wait for me! O bow, wait for me!... The Hartebeest-skin bag said: 'That man... now he speaks thus.' The shoes said: 'Let us go away and leave him... he is mocking us, he is deceiving us.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 17-18 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 他走進水裡……他站在上方的岸上說：「噢，狷羚的孩子們：等等我！」噢，鞋子，等等我！噢，手杖，等等我！噢，弓，等等我！……狷羚皮袋說：「那個人……現在他這樣說話。」鞋子說：「我們走吧，把他丟下……他在嘲弄我們，他在欺騙我們。」

passages.text: He sat down and said: 'O Dasse, we went to the Lion's house; the Lion slew Kwammang-a. He cheated the Dasse, he deceived her, because he is a liar. He also said: The Lion has swallowed the Ichneumon.'... The Porcupine got up and went out. She saw Kwammang-a's party coming laden with Quagga's meat... The Porcupine said: 'You sat there telling lies.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 18 (public domain).
passages.zh: 他坐下來說道：「哦，達塞啊，我們去了獅子的家；獅子殺了夸曼阿。他欺騙了達塞，他瞞騙了她，因為他是個騙子。他還說：獅子把鼬鼠吞了下去。」……豪豬起身走了出去。她看見夸曼阿一行人滿載著斑驢的肉歸來……豪豬說：「你坐在那裡說謊。」

title.en: The Mantis and the Cat
title.zh: 螳螂與貓

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Mantis and the Cat'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §6

summary.en: The Mantis attacks the Cat who sings of the Lynx's mockery; the cat buries its head in the ground and the Mantis can only strike its tail. The Ichneumon teaches him: feint at the head, watch where it hides, then strike breaking it — and the Mantis breaks the cat's head, boasting 'What man is our equal?'
summary.zh: 貓歌其為獰貓所嘲；螳螂攻之，貓首埋地，螳螂唯擊其尾。小獴教之：佯攻其首，觀其藏處，再擊碎之。螳螂破貓首，自詡「何人堪比吾儕？」

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: He met the Cat going along singing. The Cat sang that the Lynx mocked at him, because he could not run as fast as the Lynx did... The Cat said: 'Your eyes have warts on them. I will hit your head, I will break it.' The Mantis said: 'O Cat, hit my head, I will hit your head!'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 19 (public domain).
passages.zh: 他遇見貓正一路唱著歌走來。貓唱道，猞猁嘲笑他，因為他跑得不如猞猁快……貓說：「你的眼睛上長了疣。我要打你的頭，我要把它打碎。」螳螂說：「哦，貓啊，你打我的頭，我就打你的頭！」

passages.text: The Mantis struck at the Cat's head; the Cat drew back and hid his head in the ground. The Mantis hit the Cat's tail... The Cat hit the Mantis's head and broke it. The Mantis quickly got feathers, he flew away. He called to the Hartebeest-skin bag: 'O Hartebeest's children, leave here, we must fly.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 19 (public domain).
passages.zh: 螳螂朝貓的頭打去；貓往後一縮，把頭藏進了土裡。螳螂打中了貓的尾巴……貓打中了螳螂的頭，把它打碎了。螳螂急忙找來羽毛，飛走了。他對麋羚皮袋喊道：「哦，麋羚的孩子們，離開這裡，我們必須飛走。」

passages.text: The Ichneumon said: 'O Mantis, we always feint at the Cat's head, the Cat hides his head in the ground, we look to see where his head is, we strike, breaking it.'... He feinted at the Cat's head. The Cat quickly put his head into the ground, thinking that the Mantis would strike his tail again. The Mantis saw his head just above the ground; he struck at it and hit it.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 20-21 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 鼬鼠說：「哦，螳螂啊，我們總是虛晃一招，假意打貓的頭，貓便把頭藏進土裡，我們就看準他的頭在哪裡，打下去，把它打碎。」……他虛晃一招，假意打貓的頭。貓急忙把頭埋進土裡，以為螳螂又要打他的尾巴。螳螂看見他的頭正好露在地面之上；便朝它打去，打中了。

title.en: The Mantis and the Proteles: Roasted on His Own Fire
title.zh: 螳螂與土狼：自焚於己火

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Mantis and the Proteles'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §8

summary.en: Kwammang-a begs a lean little Proteles from his aunt's hole; the Mantis, greedy, goes back alone for another. The mother grips him with one arm and the little Proteles with the other and knocks him down on the fire he had made; he springs up crying 'O blisters!', flies to the water, and comes home moaning.
summary.zh: 夸曼加自姨母洞中求得小土狼一隻；螳螂貪心獨返再求。母土狼一臂抱幼獸、一臂擒螳螂，將其擲於自燃之火上。螳螂呼「燙泡矣！」，飛至水邊，歸家呻吟。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Kwammang-a said: 'O my Aunt! Come out and give me one, that I may put it to roast for myself.' Then the Mother Proteles came out... Then Kwammang-a said: 'I have begged you to give me one, that I may rub off the dust, for you see I am white with dust.' And the Mother Proteles said: 'O man, my children are not grown up yet, they are still little.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 21-22 (public domain).
passages.zh: 夸曼阿說：「哦，我的姑母啊！出來給我一個吧，好讓我拿去給自己烤。」於是土狼母走了出來……接著夸曼阿說：「我求過你給我一個，好讓我擦掉身上的塵土，因為你看，我滿身塵土，都白了。」土狼母說：「哦，人啊，我的孩子們還沒長大呢，他們還小。」

passages.text: The Mantis was greedy; therefore he turned back to the Proteles... He said: 'O my Aunt, come out, give me a little thing to cut up, that I may rub off the dust from myself.' Then the Proteles stuck out her head while her body was inside... she went in and took a little girl Proteles and pulled her out.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 22 (public domain).
passages.zh: 螳螂貪心；因此他又轉身回到土狼那裡……他說：「哦，我的姑母啊，出來吧，給我一點小東西切一切，好讓我擦掉自己身上的塵土。」於是土狼把頭伸了出來，身子卻還在裡面……她進去，抓起一隻小母土狼，把她拉了出來。

passages.text: Then the Proteles caught hold of the Mantis with one arm, she pulled the Mantis on to the fire, while she kept fast hold of the little Proteles. She knocked the Mantis down on the fire which he had shewn her. Then the Mantis said: 'O blisters! Hartebeest's children, you must go'... He descended when he saw the water was near... he popped into the water.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 22-23 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 土狼便一臂挾住螳螂，把她拖到火上，自己卻緊緊抓住小土狼。她把螳螂按倒在他指給她看的那堆火上。螳螂說：「燙死我了！狷羚的孩子們，你們得走了」……他一見水就在近旁便往下衝……撲通跳進了水裏。

title.en: Foulmouth, the Blue Crane and the Girls
title.zh: 穢口獸、藍鶴與少女

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'Foulmouth, the Blue Crane and the Girls'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §35a

summary.en: Foulmouth lies on an umbrella-top tree over the girls digging ants' eggs; the Blue Crane — Kaggen's sister — hiccough-hating, shields each girl with her own body, is stabbed, cut shoulder from shoulder and head from neck, and joins herself together again crying 'O Foulmouth, I am coming!' until, huts near, he flees.
summary.zh: 穢口獸臥於傘頂樹上，窺掘蟻卵之少女。藍鶴——卡根之姊——以身蔽各女，屢被刺；肩斷復續，首斷復續，呼「穢口，吾至矣！」直至茅屋相近，獸遁。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San tale from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; contains violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Foulmouth is a person; he was a man of the early race. The Blue Crane was also a person of the early race. She was the Mantis's elder sister. The girls were girls of the early race... One old woman used always to go out with the girls... Foulmouth lay upon an umbrella-top tree. The girls went to sit in the shade of the tree, for they wanted to sift ants' eggs.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 23 (public domain).
passages.zh: 髒嘴是一個人物，他是早期種族的一個男人。藍鶴也是早期種族的人物。她是螳螂的姐姐。那些女孩是早期種族的女孩……有一個老婦人總是陪女孩們出去……髒嘴躺在一棵傘頂樹上。女孩們到樹蔭下坐著，她們想篩蟻卵。

passages.text: Then Foulmouth hiccoughed, and the Blue Crane exclaimed: 'Humph, humph! Abominable! What decayed thing can be smelling here?' The girls were silent, because they saw Foulmouth up the tree... Then Foulmouth climbed down the tree while she was walking along. Then Foulmouth ran on past the Blue Crane.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 24 (public domain).
passages.zh: 髒嘴打了個嗝，藍鶴叫道：「哼，哼！可惡！這裏什麼東西爛了這麼臭？」女孩們都不作聲，因為她們看見髒嘴在樹上……藍鶴走開時，髒嘴爬下樹來。然後髒嘴從藍鶴身邊跑了過去。

passages.text: She covered the girl with her own body, and Foulmouth stabbed her. She lay as if dying upon her back... She arose behind Foulmouth's back... and she covered the girl. Foulmouth stabbed her back... Foulmouth grew angry and cut her. He cut off her shoulder and hurled it away... Her shoulders joined on again, she exclaimed: 'O Foulmouth! I am coming! I am coming!...'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 24-25 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 她用自己的身子護住那女孩，髒嘴刺了她一矛。她仰面倒下，像死了一般……她從髒嘴的背後起身……又去護那女孩。髒嘴又刺她的背……髒嘴惱怒起來，砍了她。他砍下她的肩胛，扔了出去……她的肩胛又長了回去，她喊道：「哦，髒嘴！我來了！我來了！……

passages.text: The Blue Crane rose up, she walked after him, she exclaimed: 'O Foulmouth, stab my heart!' Foulmouth walked on, for he felt angry. The Blue Crane said: 'O Foulmouth, stab me!... Then give me the spear and I will stab you.' Foulmouth snatched the spear away, when the Blue Crane caught at it in order to stab him... and she turned back and went home, while he went away.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 25 (public domain).
passages.zh: 藍鶴站起來，跟在他身後喊道：「哦，髒嘴，刺我的心吧！」髒嘴只顧走，他心裏動了怒。藍鶴說：「哦，髒嘴，刺我吧！……那把矛給我，我來刺你。」藍鶴伸手去抓矛要刺他，髒嘴把矛奪了過去……她轉身回家，他則走遠了。

title.en: The Blue Crane's Story: The Merrythought and the Two Star-Lions
title.zh: 藍鶴之故事：願骨與雙星獅

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Blue Crane's Story'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §26

summary.en: The Frog's husband sulks, flees into a stone at a beetle's flight, and the Blue Crane hunts his spoor till grief turns her to bones. Two lions — 'Belt' and 'Mat', now the Pointers to the Southern Cross — eat her; her merrythought springs from Belt's mouth. The Mantis finds it, sets it in the water, and she grows again; he clothes her, anoints her with his scent, and brings her home as his sister.
summary.zh: 蛙夫鬱而遁入石中；藍鶴尋其跡，悲瘦成骨。二獅「貝爾」與「馬特」——今南十字導星——食之；其願骨自獅口躍出。螳螂拾之，置於水中，鶴復生；為之製衣，以己汗塗面認親，攜之歸家。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San myth from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

narrative.en:
The Blue Crane's friend was the Frog. The Frog's husband sat and sulked because his wife would not speak to him; a beetle flew past his nose and he jumped up and ran into a flat stone. The Blue Crane searched for his spoor to catch him for her friend, and missed him; she grew lean with grief, she became bones.

The Lions heard her searching — two lions called 'Belt' and 'Mat', who are now the stars, the pointers to the Southern Cross. They stole up, killed and ate her. 'Mat' said: 'O Belt, I do not want this person's bone to spring out of your mouth'; and while they ate, the Blue Crane's merrythought sprang out of Belt's mouth and lay nearby. They could not find it and went away.

The Mantis sought his sister. He followed the lions' spoor to the killing-place and found the merrythought, which was big. He put it into the water and went home. When he returned, the Blue Crane jumped up and splashed into the water; he left her in peace. Again and again he came, saw her growing in the sun — she had grown — and turned back without startling her, and made clothes for her meanwhile. When she seemed a grown girl, he stole up, caught her as she tried to reach the water, rubbed her face with his perspiration, and said: 'It is I, the Tinderbox, your elder brother; leave off struggling and sit down.' He put the cap, kaross and skin petticoat on her, and took her home.

The myth knits three threads: the resurrection-by-water that also revives the ostrich feather and the Moon; the star-names of the two lions, who stand silent forever near their lionesses; and the Mantis's strange double role as sister-seeker and scent-anointing father. The myth is tied to the stars: 'Belt' and 'Mat' are the two male lions that stand as the Pointers to the Southern Cross, and the lionesses that sit silent near them are Alpha, Beta and Gamma Crucis; one of the lions became a star because a girl looked at him, and the other followed. In the longer version the kori bustard \gi and her child escape while the Blue Crane is eaten, and the surviving bird is pulled up by the Crow to a thorn-tree, where heated stones are made ready; the pursuing lion is drawn up with a rope of mouse's entrails, breaks it, and falls into the fire and is roasted; then the greedy lion swallows a male tortoise whole, and the tortoise curses every pool dry and warns all game away until he starves. The Mantis's recovery of his sister is therefore the quiet ending of a great star-myth: grief that turns the searcher to bones, the merrythought that springs from the eater's mouth, and the water that grows her again into the sister the Tinderbox clothes and carries home.

functions: Accounts for the Pointer stars of the Southern Cross as once-living lions.
Extends the resurrection-by-water complex to a bird of the early race.
Models kinship recognition by scent in Bushman social thought.

variants.name: Pointer-lions expanded version (§26, L II.—1/2)
variants.summary: A longer version in which the kori bustard \gi and her child escape while the Blue Crane is eaten, and the surviving bird drops the lion into a fire of heated stones.

canonical_translation: Bleek & Lloyd / D. F. Bleek translations, 1911 & 1924

primary_sources.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends, 'The Blue Crane's Story'
primary_sources.citation: London: George Allen & Unwin, 1924, pp. 26-28

primary_sources.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts

secondary_sources.work: David Lewis-Williams, Believing and Seeing
secondary_sources.citation: Lewis-Williams, J. D. 1981. London: Academic Press.

secondary_sources.work: Mathias Guenther, Tricksters and Trancers: Bushman Religion and Society
secondary_sources.citation: Guenther, M. 1999. Bloomington: Indiana University Press.

sensitivity_guidance: 19th-century colonial-era collection; presented as archive, not as living authority.

passages.text: The Blue Crane's friend was the Frog. The Frog was a person; her husband was a person; the Blue Crane was a person. They were people of the early race. The Frog's husband sat and sulked, because the Frog would not speak to him. And as he sat there, the Beetle came flying; the Beetle flew past his nose, and he jumped up, he ran away... he went into a stone, a flat stone.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 26 (public domain).
passages.zh: 藍鶴的朋友是青蛙。青蛙是一個人物；她的丈夫是一個人物；藍鶴也是一個人物。他們都是早期種族的人。青蛙的丈夫坐在那裏生悶氣，因為青蛙不肯理他。他正坐著，甲蟲飛來了；甲蟲從他鼻尖前飛過，他一躍而起，逃了……他鑽進一塊石頭，一塊扁平的石頭裏。

passages.text: And she grew lean, while she was searching there. Grief made her grow lean; she became bones. And the Lions heard her as she was searching there, two Lions: 'Belt' and 'Mat'. The Lions followed the sound to her... The Lions killed her and ate her... The Blue Crane's merrythought sprang out of 'Belt's' mouth and went and lay nearby. They tried to find it, but they could not see it, so they went away.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 26-27 (public domain). [These lions are now stars, the pointers to the Southern Cross. — D. F. Bleek's note]
passages.zh: 她在那裡尋覓時，漸漸消瘦了。悲傷使她消瘦；她成了一副骨頭。兩頭獅子聽見她在那裡尋覓，那是兩頭獅子：『腰帶』與『蓆子』。獅子循著聲音來到她那裡……獅子殺了她，把她吃了……藍鶴的胸骨從『腰帶』的口中彈了出來，落在一旁。他們想找它，卻看不見，於是便走了。

passages.text: Then the Mantis sought the Blue Crane... he caught sight of the merrythought lying there, for it was big. He picked it up and went and put it into the water... The Blue Crane jumped up and splashed into the water... Once more he went out to look. As he came up, he saw the Blue Crane sitting in the sun. She had grown. He turned back without startling her... he went to make things, clothes which he meant to give to the Blue Crane, when she grew up.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 27 (public domain).
passages.zh: 於是螳螂去尋找藍鶴……他瞥見那塊胸骨躺在那裡，因為它很大。他把它撿起來，拿去放進水裡……藍鶴跳了起來，濺入水中……他又一次出去察看。他走近時，看見藍鶴坐在陽光下。她已經長大了。他沒有驚動她，便轉身回去……他去製作東西，那是他打算等藍鶴長大後送給她的衣服。

passages.text: He caught hold of her; when she tried to get into the water, he held her fast and rubbed her face with his perspiration; he made her smell his scent. He told the Blue Crane that he was her brother. It was he, the 'Tinderbox', who was holding her... Then the Blue Crane sat down. He covered her with a cap which he had made for her, and with a kaross and a skin petticoat... Then he took the Blue Crane with him; they returned home.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 28 (public domain).
passages.zh: 他抓住了她；當她想鑽進水裡時，他緊緊抓住她，用自己的汗水抹她的臉；他讓她聞他的氣味。他告訴藍鶴，他是她的兄弟。正是他，『火絨盒』，抓著她……於是藍鶴坐了下來。他為她蓋上他為她做的一頂帽子，又蓋上一張皮斗篷和一條皮裙……然後他帶著藍鶴一起走；他們回家去了。

title.en: The Mantis and the Magic Bird's Eggs
title.zh: 螳螂與魔鳥之卵

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Mantis and the Magic Bird'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §9

summary.en: The Mantis robs the talking ostrich — the Magic Bird — whose eggs and brush-spoon stick to his mouth and whose load sticks to his back; he must carry them home until daybreak, when all falls off. Warned by the Ichneumon, he next takes only the little outside egg, then robs a real ostrich safely.
summary.zh: 螳螂劫會言之鴕——魔鳥；其卵與匙黏於其口，負荷黏於其背，直至天明方落。小獴戒之，此後只取巢外小卵；再向真鴕取卵，則安然無恙。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Mantis went out at daybreak. As he went he saw the Magic Bird sitting on her eggs. He shot at her; the arrow returned; the Mantis dodged it and said: 'Is this an Ostrich? She does not run away.' The Magic Bird said to the Mantis: 'You may take the little egg standing outside there and drink it.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 28 (public domain).
passages.zh: 螳螂在破曉時出門。他走著走著，看見魔鳥坐在她的蛋上。他朝她射箭；箭折了回來；螳螂閃身躲過，說道：『這是鴕鳥嗎？她都不逃走。』魔鳥對螳螂說：『你可以拿走外面立著的那顆小蛋，把它喝了。』

passages.text: He put the brush to his mouth. He pulled out his tongue with it and said: 'Is this an Ostrich? It is pulling out my tongue. My tongue is sticking to the brush.'... He took the yolk, he was silent, for the brush was in his mouth... He carried the eggs in the net. He returned home with an egg sticking to his mouth and the net sticking fast behind his back.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 28-29 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 他把刷子湊到嘴邊。他用它把舌頭拉了出來，說道：『這是鴕鳥嗎？它在拉我的舌頭。我的舌頭黏在刷子上了。』……他取了蛋黃，默不作聲，因為刷子在他嘴裡……他把蛋裝在網裡。他帶著一顆黏在嘴上的蛋、以及緊緊黏在背後的網，回家去了。

passages.text: The Ichneumon said to him: 'O Mantis, you must be carrying the Magic Bird's eggs! We always go and take the Magic Bird's little outside eggs... The Magic Bird talks, an Ostrich does not talk, for the Ostrich is afraid of us. The Magic Bird talks, because she is a different kind of Ostrich, the kind of Ostrich which talks.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 29 (public domain).
passages.zh: 姬蜂對他說：『哦，螳螂，你準是帶著魔鳥的蛋！我們總是去拿魔鳥放在外面的小蛋……魔鳥會說話，鴕鳥不會說話，因為鴕鳥怕我們。魔鳥會說話，因為她是另一種鴕鳥，是會說話的那種鴕鳥。』

passages.text: Then he grew nervous. He hoped that the brush would not stick fast... He put the brush away in the bag, he took the quiver and slung it on... He walked away, he went up to a real Ostrich... He felt that his hands were not sticking fast. He said to himself: 'Ah, I must have been mistaken...' Then he picked up the eggs, he loaded up quickly... He trotted quickly away.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 29-30 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 接著他緊張起來。他希望那刷子不要黏得太牢……他把刷子收進袋裡，取出箭袋掛在肩上……他走開，走向一隻真正的鴕鳥……他感覺自己的雙手並沒有黏住。他對自己說：「啊，我一定是弄錯了……」接著他撿起蛋，迅速裝好……他快步小跑離去。

title.en: The Mantis Takes Away the Ticks' Sheep
title.zh: 螳螂奪蜱人之羊

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Mantis takes away the Ticks' Sheep'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §10

summary.en: The black, bloody-handed Ticks hide in their sheep's wool and drop one by one on the visiting Mantis, beating him nearly to death. He flies to the water, dreams, and steals their whole kraal up into the sky: the sheep, houses, pots and knobkerries descend beside his own. Fireless, the Ticks must henceforth bite and suck blood raw.
summary.zh: 黑膚血手之蜱人藏於羊毛中，逐一落擊來訪之螳螂，幾斃之。他飛至水邊，夢而復仇：將其全欄羊群、屋舍、釜甑、棍棒自天而降置於己旁。蜱人失火，自茲惟有生啜血。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: They saw him; they said to each other: 'What man comes yonder?'... 'We will creep into the sheep's wool, that he may come to the house. This little child must stay; he shall look after the pots on the fire...' The Mantis walked up to the child. 'Am I like a fighting man, that the people have gone away in fear...?' The people listened in the sheep's wool.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 30 (public domain).
passages.zh: 他們看見了他；彼此說道：「那邊來的是什麼人？……」……「我們要鑽進羊毛裡，好讓他來到屋前。這個小孩必須留下；他得看守火上的鍋子……」螳螂走向那孩子。「我像個打仗的人嗎，竟讓人們嚇得逃走……？」那些人躲在羊毛裡聽著。

passages.text: A big young man Tick slipped down beside the Mantis; he sat holding the Mantis by the kaross. His other brother slipped down on the other side of the Mantis... Their father was still above, an old Tick... 'The Mantis slipped out of the kaross. The Ticks rushed together and struck at him... He went away first, his things followed him.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 30-31 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 一隻大個子的年輕壁蝨從螳螂身旁滑下來；他坐著，抓住螳螂的斗篷。他的另一個兄弟從螳螂的另一側滑下來……他們的父親仍在上面，是一隻老壁蝨……螳螂從斗篷裡溜了出來。壁蝨們一擁而上，朝他撲打……他先走了，他的東西跟著他。

passages.text: The Mantis sat down... he said: 'The people to whom I went must have been hidden, for I did not see them. They kept coming out from above, they kept sliding down... while the sheep were in the kraal.' The Ichneumon said: 'You went to the house to which people do not go... For those people are black; they are wont to beat a man to death because of those sheep.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 31-32 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 螳螂坐下來……他說：「我去找的那些人一定是躲起來了，因為我沒看見他們。他們不斷從上面出來，不斷滑下來……當時羊群就在圍欄裡。」獴說：「你去的是人們不去的屋子……因為那些人是黑人；他們常為了那些羊把人打死。」

passages.text: The sheep rise up, the sheep come and stand in front of his house... The sheep came out of the sky, they stood; the things also came out of the sky and sat down, while the people slept there... 'It seemed right to me, because those people attacked me... They shall now drink raw blood because they lack a fire... The old Tick shall always stand biting men's skins, he shall suck out blood, for he altogether lacks a knife.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 32-34 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 羊群起身，羊群過來站在他的屋前……羊群從天而降，站定了；那些東西也從天而降，坐了下來，而人們就在那裡睡著……「在我看來這是應該的，因為那些人攻擊了我……他們如今該喝生血，因為他們沒有火……老壁蝨該永遠站著咬人的皮，該吸出血來，因為他完全沒有刀。」

title.en: The All-Devourer: Swallowed and Cut Out Again
title.zh: 全吞者：吞噬與剖復

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Mantis and the All-devourer'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §10-11

summary.en: To punish the Ticks the Mantis summons |Khwa-hemm, the All-devourer — the Porcupine's real father, whose tongue is fire. He eats bushes, sheep, buckets, the hut, and finally the Mantis and Kwammang-a. The Porcupine burns her sons' ears with a hot spear to test who is fierce; the fierce ones cut the monster open, everything pours out alive, the world is set right, and the All-devourer utterly dies.
summary.zh: 為懲蜱人，螳螂召來全吞者——豪豬生父，舌如烈火。他食灌木、羊群、桶、屋，終吞螳螂與夸曼加。豪豬以熱矛燒其子之耳以試膽；勇者剖開巨怪，萬物盡出而復活，世界復原，全吞者遂滅。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San myth from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

narrative.en:
After the Ticks had beaten the Mantis and he had stolen their sheep, he wished for more: 'I want you, the Ichneumon, to catch some fat sheep, for father to cut up for us... The Man yonder shall come and eat with me of these sheep, because I have counted them and see they are plentiful.' The Porcupine warned him: 'Do you really want me to go to the Man who eats bushes? He will come and swallow all the sheep... we shall be swallowed with the sheep. A Man who devours things he is.'

She fetched her real father, the All-devourer. He followed her spoor, eating up the bushes as he came; his shadow glided over the Mantis's hut, and his red tongue was like a fire waxing. 'Is Father holding fire in his hand?' asked the Mantis. 'It is the Man coming there, whose tongue is red.'

The All-devourer arrived. The Mantis set meat before him, and the monster gulped it with the bushes it lay on. Buckets, water-bags, thorn-bushes, beds, the Porcupine's things — all vanished down the fire-tongue. The Mantis tried to hand him a bucket and his hands were scorched; he kept winking at the Dasse; the Ichneumon reminded him that no one invites this man. At last the All-devourer asked for 'the real food', burned the Mantis, and swallowed him — then Kwammang-a, with the bed he sat on. His stomach hung almost down to the earth.

The Porcupine reheated a spear and laid it burning on her younger son's temple, then in his nose: his tears gathered slowly, 'a mild person is this'. She laid it to the ear of young Kwammang-a, and his eyes stayed dry: 'Yes, a fierce man is this.' The children went out in wrath; each sat with spear arm outward, signed to one another, and cut the monster on both sides at once. They ran as their fathers poured forth — the sheep, the buckets, the pots, Kwammang-a on his bed. The All-devourer doubled up and died.

The children restored the world: 'O bushes, we have cut you out! You shall truly become bushes, you shall grow at your place... the place shall be right again and these sheep shall wander over it... that the people may get dry bushes and be able to warm themselves.' The young Mantis's speech came true. The Mantis himself drank a whole eggshell of water and fell; the Dasse beat his shin with a stick till he sat up. They moved away to a new home and left the monster lying before the old one, and lived in peace.

functions: World-renewal myth: the swallowed world is cut out and restored.
Charter for testing courage by endurance of burning.
Explains why the All-devourer-type being is never invited to share food.

variants.name: All-devourer's speech (B XXIII. 2161-2247)
variants.summary: The monster's speech to the Mantis and the Mantis's reply, recorded separately.

variants.name: Porcupine's warning version (L II.—32/33)
variants.summary: The connected version in which the Porcupine reluctantly fetches her father.

passages.text: The Porcupine said: 'Do you really want me to go to the Man who eats bushes? He will come and swallow all the sheep, as they stand in the kraal... A Man who devours things he is; he walks along eating up the bushes as he passes... The Mantis said to her: 'You must go to your other father, the All-devourer, that he may help me eat up these sheep, and drink this soup.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 34-35 (public domain).
passages.zh: 豪豬說：「你真要我去找那個吃灌木的人嗎？他會來把所有的羊都吞掉，就照牠們站在圍欄裡的樣子……他本就是個吞食萬物的人；他走過時一邊走一邊吃掉灌木……螳螂對她說：「你必須去找你的另一個父親，那吞食萬物者，好讓他幫我吃掉這些羊，喝掉這湯。」

passages.text: The All-devourer followed the Porcupine's spoor; as he went he ate up the bushes. He climbed up, finishing off the bushes, while his shadow glided up to the Mantis's hut. It fell upon the Mantis. The Mantis looked at the sun, he asked where the clouds were, for the sun seemed to be in clouds... 'Is Father holding fire in his hand, for a fire is waxing red yonder?' The Porcupine answered him: 'It is the Man coming there, whose tongue is red.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 35-36 (public domain).
passages.zh: 那吞噬一切者循著豪豬的足跡前行；他一邊走，一邊吃光了灌木叢。他攀爬而上，將灌木叢一一吃盡，而他的影子則滑向螳螂的茅屋。影子落在螳螂身上。螳螂望向太陽，問雲在哪裡，因為太陽似乎隱在雲中……「父親手中是否握著火？因為那邊有一團火正燒得通紅。」豪豬回答他：「是那個人來了，他的舌頭是紅的。」

passages.text: She heated the spear, she laid it burning hot to her son's ear-root; her son sat still. She heated the spear again, she said to her son: 'Remember, Grandfather's tongue is like this. You must sit firmly when you go to Grandfather.'... The All-devourer scorched the young Mantis's temple with his tongue... Young Kwammang-a looked hard at the other, he signed to him to hold his spear fast, and he held his own well.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 38-39 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 她燒熱了矛，將燒得熾熱的矛貼在她兒子的耳根上；她的兒子端坐不動。她又燒熱了矛，對兒子說：「記住，祖父的舌頭就是這樣。你去見祖父時，務必坐得穩當。」……那吞噬一切者用舌頭灼傷了小螳螂的太陽穴……小夸曼加-a 緊緊盯著對方，示意他握緊長矛，而他自己也握得穩穩的。

passages.text: They ran away, while their fathers poured forth; the sheep also poured forth, the buckets poured forth; his father sat on the bed; the pots poured forth; the things poured down. His Grandfather doubled up and died. The children said: 'O bushes, we have cut you out! You shall truly become bushes, you shall grow at your place... the place shall be right again and these sheep shall wander over it... that the people may get dry bushes and be able to warm themselves.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 39-40 (public domain).
passages.zh: 他們逃走了，而他們的父親們傾湧而出；羊群也傾湧而出，水桶傾湧而出；他的父親坐在床上；陶罐傾湧而出；萬物傾瀉而下。他的祖父彎下身來，死了。孩子們說：「哦，灌木叢，我們把你們砍出來了！你們必將真正成為灌木叢，你們要在自己的地方生長……那地方必將恢復如初，這些羊必將在其上漫遊……好讓人們能取得乾枯的灌木，得以取暖。」

title.en: The Elephant That Stole the Mantis's Springbok
title.zh: 象竊螳螂之跳羚

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1874 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Mantis and the Elephants'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §12

summary.en: Digging honey, the Mantis throws it up to his pet springbok; the elephant substitutes her calf, who answers 'Kurru!' The Mantis kills the impostor, tracks the herd, enters the mother at the navel, cuts her whole inside to pieces and comes out at her trunk with the child on his back as she falls dead.
summary.zh: 螳螂掘蜜擲予寵羚；母象以己子代之，答曰「庫魯！」。螳螂殺其偽者，追象群，自其臍入，碎其內臟，自其鼻而出，背負幼羚——母象倒斃。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Elephant carried off the little Springbok, while the Mantis was digging in the hole... The Mantis was digging out wild bees' honey and throwing it to the little Springbok. He said: 'Are you eating, as I am eating?'... Then the Elephant calf said: 'Kurru!' And the Mantis said: 'Listen! What is the matter? My child does not usually speak so that I cannot understand it.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 41 (public domain).
passages.zh: 大象擄走了小跳羚，當時螳螂正在洞裡挖掘……螳螂挖出野蜂的蜜，扔給小跳羚。他說：「你在吃嗎，就像我在吃一樣？」……接著大象幼崽說：「庫魯！」螳螂說：「聽！怎麼回事？我的孩子平常不會這樣說話，讓我聽不懂。」

passages.text: Then the Mantis got out of the hole; he found the Elephant calf sitting covered up with earth, he said: 'It must have been this person.'... This person must have been sitting here, his ears look like a mat lying there... And he killed the Elephant calf... He caught sight of the spoor of a troop of Elephants.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 41, 43 (public domain).
passages.zh: 於是螳螂從洞裡出來；他發現大象幼崽坐著，身上覆滿了泥土，他說：「一定是這個傢伙幹的。」……這傢伙一定曾坐在這裡，他的耳朵看起來像鋪在那裡的一張席子……於是他殺了大象幼崽……他瞥見了一群大象的足跡。

passages.text: Then the Elephants caught sight of him as he came over the hill, and the Mother Elephant arose and rushed out. She picked up the little Springbok and swallowed it... The Mantis said: 'I will get into your mouth.' And the Elephant replied that she would spit him out. Then the Mantis said he would get in under her fingernail... but he got into her navel, and the other Elephants stabbed at him with their spears as he went in.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 43-44 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 接著，當他翻過山丘而來時，大象們看見了他，母象起身衝了出去。她抓起小跳羚，吞了下去……螳螂說：「我要鑽進你的嘴裡。」大象回答說她會把他吐出來。於是螳螂說他要鑽進她的指甲底下……但他鑽進了她的肚臍，當他進去時，其他大象用長矛刺他。

passages.text: The Mantis cut the Elephant's whole inside to pieces, and while the Elephants were watching for him at the other Elephant's navel... he came out at the Elephant's trunk, came out above her head carrying the little Springbok on his back, while the Elephant fell down dead... he spoke as he flew away: 'Can you equal me? I am the Mantis... he is an enchanter, from whom you tried to steal his child.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 44 (public domain).
passages.zh: 螳螂把大象的整個內臟切成碎片，而當那些大象在另一頭大象的肚臍處守候他時……他從大象的象鼻處出來，背著小跳羚從她頭頂上方出來，而大象則倒地死去……他一面飛走一面說道：「你能比得上我嗎？我是螳螂……他是個巫師，你曾想從他那裡偷走他的孩子。」

title.en: The Kwai-kwai Bird, the Mantis and the Children
title.zh: 怪鴟、螳螂與孩童

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Kwai-kwai Bird, the Mantis and the Children'

summary.en: The Kwai-kwai, once a man, nets the children to kill them; the Mantis, dreaming it, stays home as their grown-up guard. When the bird comes, he has the children roast the Kwai-kwai on hot stones — 'for it is merely a Kwai-kwai' — and it screams 'I ought always to look where the Mantis is.'
summary.zh: 怪鴟本為人，網羅孩童欲殺之；螳螂夢而知之，留家守護。鴟至，螳螂令孩童以熱石炙之——「不過一怪鴟耳」。鴟號曰：「吾當常察螳螂何在。」

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; contains implied child-killing theme in a warning-fable frame; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Kwai-kwai bird was once a man. He put children into a net. Then the children sang about him... 'Mother, mother, The Kwai-kwai Is taking us to kill, Tho' we stayed at home!' Then Grandfather Mantis said: 'Call loudly, call, call loudly!'... Their mothers said: 'You must listen, our little ones are calling out!... The children speak with a small voice, while Grandfather speaks with a deep voice. Therefore I think he is walking, he is listening for us.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 45 (public domain).
passages.zh: 奎奎鳥從前是一個人。他把孩子們放進一張網裡。於是孩子們唱著關於他的歌……「母親，母親，奎奎要把我們帶去殺掉，儘管我們待在家裡！」接著螳螂祖父說：「大聲喊，喊，大聲喊！」……他們的母親們說：「你們必須聽，我們的小傢伙們在呼喊！……孩子們用細小的聲音說話，而祖父用低沉的聲音說話。因此我想他正在走動，他正在為我們傾聽。」

passages.text: The Mantis felt that he had been dreaming, that the Kwai-kwai had come in anger to the children... Therefore he, the Mantis, he who was wise would stay with the children at home, for children are ignorant... Then he spoke to the children, he said: 'Children, roast the Kwai-kwai, for it is merely a Kwai-kwai.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 45-46 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 螳螂覺得自己一直在做夢，覺得奎奎帶著怒氣來到孩子們那裡……因此他，螳螂，那位有智慧的，要和孩子們留在家裡，因為孩子們是無知的……接著他對孩子們說話，他說：「孩子們，把奎奎烤了，因為它不過是一隻奎奎罷了。」

passages.text: Then the children roasted the Kwai-kwai on hot stones, that is how they roasted him. And the Kwai-kwai screamed because of the burns... And the Kwai-kwai said: 'Vvvvvvv, I ought always to look where the Mantis is.' The Mantis said: 'I am the Mantis, I am here!... I am the one who is roasting you; I am the one who is clever!'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 46 (public domain).
passages.zh: 於是孩子們在滾燙的石頭上烤奎奎，他們就是這樣烤他的。而奎奎因為灼傷而尖叫……奎奎說：「嗚嗚嗚嗚，我應該時時留意螳螂在哪裡。」螳螂說：「我是螳螂，我在這裡！……我就是烤你的那一個；我就是聰明的那一個！」

title.en: The Dasse's Story and the Crow's Story
title.zh: 岩蹄兔與鴉之故事

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Dasse's Story and the Crow's Story'

summary.en: The Mantis's pranks bring falling stones down on Kwammang-a, who is hidden in a gambro hollow; the ring-necked crows sent out eat their neck-fat halfway home. The pied Crow flies on, and Kwammang-a's face and body are dug out — but Kauru must beg before they will take out her trickster husband, whom they drag roughly from the stones.
summary.zh: 螳螂戲耍致落石壓誇曼加，其藏於瓜布羅果洞中；環頸鴉半途食盡頸脂而返。白頸鴉飛達，誇曼加面體得掘出——唯卡烏魯哀求，眾方拔其夫，粗暴拖出。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Kwammang-a once went visiting. They were two, he and the Mantis, and they went to the Bees' house... Then a young Bee offered Kwammang-a his ostrich egg-shell... while a young Dasse offered the Mantis his ostrich egg-shell, into which he had put dirty water... When he tasted the Dasse's dirty water, he cursed the young Dasse.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 47 (public domain).
passages.zh: 夸曼加有一次出門做客。他們是兩個人，他和螳螂，他們去了蜜蜂的家……接著一隻年輕的蜜蜂把他的鴕鳥蛋殼遞給夸曼加……而一隻年輕的蹄兔把他的鴕鳥蛋殼遞給螳螂，他往裡面倒進了髒水……當他嘗到蹄兔的髒水時，他咒罵了那隻年輕的蹄兔。

passages.text: Then the Mother Dasse, who was on the hunting-ground, sneezed, and drops of blood came from her nostrils. Therefore stones rolled... Then the young Bee spoke to his Grandfather Kwammang-a... 'You get into it, for the Mantis was really with you, that man who has been teasing. Therefore hard things are falling upon you.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 47 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 接著，身在獵場上的蹄兔母親打了個噴嚏，血滴從她的鼻孔裡流出來。因此石頭滾落……接著年輕的蜜蜂對他的祖父夸曼加說……「你進去，因為螳螂其實是和你在一起的，就是那個一直在戲弄人的傢伙。因此堅硬的東西正落到你身上。」

passages.text: The people said: 'What can be the matter? You ought to send the ring-necked Crow, that it may go and see where the people are.' And the ring-necked Crow went; it had on its neck a little piece of fat which was very small. It went and ate up the fat half-way and it turned back. And the little piece of fat is that which sits white on its neck.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 47-48 (public domain).
passages.zh: 人們說：「這是怎麼回事？你們應該派環頸鴉去，讓牠去看看人們在哪裡。」環頸鴉便去了；牠脖子上帶著一小塊非常小的脂肪。牠去了，吃到一半就把那塊脂肪吃掉了，然後折返。而那塊小脂肪，就是牠脖子上那白色的東西。

passages.text: The Elephant and the Giraffe and the Rhinoceros were those who went to take out Kwammang-a's party... Then, when she saw that the people meant to leave the Mantis, she told the people to take the Mantis out for her, because he was her husband... Then the people took hold and uncovered the stones, and the people pulled the Mantis out roughly, hurting him.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 48-49 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 大象、長頸鹿和犀牛，就是那些去把克瓦曼加一夥人弄出來的人……後來，她看見人們打算拋下螳螂，便告訴人們替她把螳螂弄出來，因為他是她的丈夫……於是眾人動手揭開石頭，人們粗暴地把螳螂拉了出來，弄傷了他。

title.en: The Korotwiten: Why the Ground Must Be Shared
title.zh: 科羅蒂滕：大地必須分享

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Mantis and the Korotwiten'

summary.en: The Korotwiten, once a man, hovers and dives into ant-holes, carrying out a full kaross of Bushman-rice at another hole. The Mantis imitates him, breaks his bow, quiver and digging-stick, and scoops rice without sharing; the angry bird makes the ground hard, and the Mantis, plunging to enter an ant-hole, crashes on his brow bleeding. Share with the Korotwiten, Kwammang-a says, and the ground opens.
summary.zh: 科羅蒂滕本為人，翔而入蟻穴，自他穴拖出滿皮衣之蟻卵。螳螂仿之，折弓毀囊棄掘杖，取米而不分；鳥怒，令地變硬；螳螂撲穴，撞額流血。夸曼加曰：與科羅蒂滕分享，地自開。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San myth from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Korotwiten is a little bird; it is black; it has white feathers on its shoulders. It was once a man; it was one of the Early Race...
