The Korotwiten dropped down, he dived into a little ant-hole, while the Mantis stood looking at him. And lo! he carried out the kaross from another little ant-hole... a kaross full of 'Bushman rice'.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 50 (public domain).
passages.zh: 科羅特維滕是一隻小鳥；牠是黑色的；肩上長著白色的羽毛。牠從前是一個人；牠是「早期族類」的一員……科羅特維滕落了下來，牠鑽進一個小蟻穴，而螳螂站在那裡看著牠。瞧！牠從另一個小蟻穴裡搬出了一張斗篷……一張裝滿「布須曼米」的斗篷。

passages.text: The Mantis said: 'You must please anoint me, for you can do this, but I have to dig Bushman rice out with a stick. Therefore my hands are sore...' Then the Korotwiten spoke... 'You should go up to an ant heap... you should watch.' And the Mantis said: 'You can give me (the power) to see.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 50-51 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 螳螂說：「請你務必為我塗油，因為你能做這件事，而我卻得用棍子去挖布須曼米。所以我的手很疼……」於是科羅特維滕開口說……「你該到蟻丘上去……你該守著看。」螳螂說：「你可以賜我（能力）去看。」

passages.text: Then the Mantis broke the bow across his foot, he snapped the arrow in two, he tore up the quiver, he also struck and split the digging stone, he struck and broke the digging stick... Then he hovered and hovered in the air, he dived into a little ant-hole, and he verily carried out a karossful of Bushman rice at another place.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 51 (public domain).
passages.zh: 於是螳螂把弓在腳上折斷，把箭折成兩截，把箭袋撕破，他又擊打並劈裂了挖掘用的石頭，他擊打並折斷了挖掘用的棍子……接著他在空中盤旋又盤旋，他鑽進一個小蟻穴，果然在另一處搬出了一斗篷滿的布須曼米。

passages.text: And the Mantis woke up early... he went to hover above it. And he kept hovering there, he dropped down, he tried to dive in, he plunged on to his brow. And he cried with the pain in his brow... he again hovered above, he dropped down, he again crashed on to the front of his head, while blood flowed... 'Father wishes me to say, he told you to share with the Korotwiten, for the earth would be hard for us, if the Korotwiten were angry.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 53-54 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 螳螂早早醒來……他去到那上方盤旋。他不停在那裡盤旋，他落了下來，他試著鑽進去，他一頭栽到自己的額頭上。他因額頭的疼痛而哭喊……他又在上方盤旋，他落了下來，他又一頭撞上自己的前額，鮮血直流……「父親希望我來說，他吩咐你與科羅特維滕分享，因為若科羅特維滕發怒，這大地對我們就會很難熬。」

title.en: Ku-te-gaua and the Mantis: Cats Out of the Fire
title.zh: 庫特加瓦與螳螂：火中之貓

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'Ku-te-gaua and the Mantis'

summary.en: Ku-te-gaua sets wildcat lairs ablaze and steps into the fire unburnt, dragging out peerless cats, singing 'Ku-te-gaua, n bagen, bagen, gaua!' The Mantis imitates him and the fire feels cool — until he refuses Ku-te-gaua a share. Then the cats burn up and the fire scorches the Mantis: the fire is quiet only for those who give every other cat.
summary.zh: 庫特加瓦縱火焚野貓穴，裸步入火不傷，拖出無雙之貓，唱「庫特加瓦，恩巴根，巴根，加瓦！」。螳螂仿之，火覺清涼——直至拒予其一。貓盡焚，火灼螳螂：唯肯隔一予一者，火乃靜。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San myth from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Ku-te-gaua used once to set fire to the lairs of wildcats. Then he got into the fire and brought out the wild cats, and those cats had no equals in beauty... he would set fire to the lair, he would get into the fire, when the fire was burning, yet the fire would feel cool and not feel hot, because it felt that he was the one who owned the fire.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 54 (public domain).
passages.zh: 庫特加瓦曾有一次放火燒野貓的巢穴。然後他走進火中，把野貓帶了出來，而那些貓的美麗無與倫比……他會放火燒巢穴，他會走進火中，當火正燃燒時，火卻感覺涼爽而不覺得灼熱，因為火覺得他才是擁有火的那一位。

passages.text: Then the Mantis took a firebrand, he went up to a lair. He set fire to the lair, he sang again... for he imitated Ku-te-gaua... And he jumped into the fire, he dragged out cats, he laid them down... because he was glad that the fire did not burn him.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 55 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 接著螳螂拿了一根火把，他走向一個巢穴。他放火燒了巢穴，他又唱了起來……因為他模仿庫特加瓦……然後他跳進火中，他把貓拖了出來，他把牠們放下……因為他很高兴火沒有燒到他。

passages.text: Then Ku-te-gaua exclaimed: 'O Man! You shall give me a share of these cats, or else you will find out what the fire feels like; because you act like this, while we are wont to give to one another.'... 'Wait, you shall feel the fire to-morrow... those cats shall be burnt up, the fire shall burn you badly, when you try to enter the fire.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 56-57 (public domain).
passages.zh: 接著庫特加瓦喊道：「噢，人哪！你得分給我這些貓的一份，否則你就會知道火是什麼滋味；因為你這樣做，而我們向來是互相給予的。」……「等著吧，明天你就會感受到火……那些貓會被燒毀，當你試圖走進火中時，火會把你燒得很慘。」

passages.text: Then the Mantis set out, he reached a lair, he set fire to the lair, he sang again... Then he sprang into the fire, and he was scorched in the fire. He exclaimed: 'Hartebeest's children, you must go!' and he flew down, he popped into the water... Then Kwammang-a spoke... 'we are wont to do so, when we want the fire to be quiet and feel cool for us... For we are wont to give him every other cat.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 57-58 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 接著螳螂出發了，他到達一個巢穴，他放火燒了巢穴，他又唱了起來……然後他跳進火中，他在火中被燒焦了。他喊道：「狷羚的孩子們，你們必須走！」然後他飛落下來，他撲通一聲跳進水中……接著夸曼阿說話了……「我們向來這樣做，當我們想要火為我們安靜下來、感覺涼爽的時候……因為我們向來把其他的貓都給他。」

title.en: Why the Wildebeest Has a Light Tail
title.zh: 角馬尾之所以輕

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'Why the Wildebeest has a light Tail'

summary.en: The black wildebeest unties the Longnosed Mice's bowstrings, strings his own entrails on them, blunts their arrows, then tramples their hiding-screens as the quaggas stream past. The Mantis dreams the murders; the Striped Mouse mounts new strings and hidden arrowheads, builds an invisible screen, and shoots the wildebeest through the armpits as he gallops up.
summary.zh: 黑角馬解長鼻鼠之弓弦，以己腸代之，鈍其箭鏃，俟斑馬群奔時踏碎其隱屏。螳螂夢知其殺戮；條紋鼠換新弦、備隱箭、築不見之屏，於其飛馳時射穿其腋。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Black Wildebeest used once to do as follows: when the Longnosed Mice were sticking up ostrich-feather brushes on the hunting-ground to drive the Quaggas, he came up to a Mouse as it sat watching, he untied the Mouse's bowstring and swallowed it, and he strung on his own entrails for the Mouse; he blunted the Mouse's arrowheads.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 58 (public domain).
passages.zh: 黑角馬曾有一次這樣做：當長鼻鼠在獵場上豎起鴕鳥羽毛做的刷子來驅趕斑驢時，他走到一隻正坐著守望的鼠身旁，他解開那隻鼠的弓弦並吞了下去，他又用自己的腸子為那隻鼠上弦；他弄鈍了那隻鼠的箭頭。

passages.text: And he arose, he went to take a piece of (a certain) grass, he made a tail for himself of this grass... Whenever he wanted to kill a man... he turned himself into a Quagga (by means of this tail which was like theirs)... He ran up to it, he went and stamped on it, crushing the Mouse, as he trod it down.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 58-59 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 然後他起身，他去取了一片（某種）草，他用這草為自己做了一條尾巴……每當他想殺一個人……他就（藉助這條像牠們那樣的尾巴）把自己變成一頭斑驢……他朝牠奔去，他走過去踩在牠身上，把那隻鼠踩碎，當他踏下去的時候。

passages.text: The Striped Mouse took out a new bowstring, he untied and took off the entrails, he strung on the new bowstring. He took out arrowheads which were in the bag, he mounted them. He made a screen of bushes which was not small... He made a little screen of bushes which was not visible, which the Wildebeest did not see.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 59 (public domain).
passages.zh: 條紋鼠取出一根新弓弦，解開並取下腸線，把新弓弦裝上弓。他取出袋中的箭頭，將它們裝上。他做了一道不小的灌木屏障……他做了一道看不見的小灌木屏障，那牛羚並沒有看見。

passages.text: The Wildebeest ran on in front, he came looking as he ran, he saw the (larger) screen of bushes there. He ran up to it, and the Striped Mouse shot him right through the armpits. He snatched out the grass of which he had made himself a tail, he hurled it away, he went and lay down to die... The Striped Mouse made his people of the Longnosed Mice; he was strong, because he was clever. But the Mantis was the one who dreamt that that man had been killing the Longnosed Mice.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 59-60 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 牛羚跑在前頭，他一邊跑一邊張望，看見了那（較大的）灌木屏障。他朝它奔去，條紋鼠正中他的腋下射穿了他。他一把扯下自己做成尾巴的草，把它扔開，走去躺下等死……條紋鼠用長鼻鼠造出了他的族人；他強壯，因為他聰明。但做夢夢見那個人一直在殺長鼻鼠的，是螳螂。

title.en: The Lizard, the Mice and the Mantis
title.zh: 蜥蜴、群鼠與螳螂

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Lizard, the Mice and the Mantis'

summary.en: The Kogelman lizard sings on the thorn-tree, calls each Longnosed Mouse in 'to take out the bag for daughter-in-law', makes him shut his eyes as he comes out, and knocks him down with a stick, then roasts springbok for his daughter. The Mantis dreams the murders; the Striped Mouse comes calling, refuses the rotten water-bag, refuses to dive, and is handed the stick by the Lizard's own daughter — 'dzap-p' — and the mice revive.
summary.zh: 蜥蜴歌於荊樹，呼長鼻鼠入洞「為媳取袋」，令其閉眼而出，以杖擊之；炙羚肉予其女。螳螂夢知其殺；條紋鼠至，拒臭水囊，拒入洞；蜥蜴之女親授其杖——「啪」——鼠輩復甦。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The 'Kogelman' Lizard once sat upon a 'Driedoorn' tree. He lay singing on the thorntree... 'Oh, oh! The Lizard lies on the thorntree.' And his daughter heard a Longnosed Mouse come calling; he called, as he followed a wounded springbok.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 60 (public domain).
passages.zh: 「科赫爾曼」蜥蜴有一次坐在一棵「德利杜恩」樹上。他躺在荊棘樹上唱著歌……「哦，哦！蜥蜴躺在荊棘樹上。」他的女兒聽見一隻長鼻鼠前來呼喚；他一路呼喚著，跟在一隻受傷的跳羚後面。

passages.text: And he said: 'You must do like this, you must go in quickly, you must take out the bag for daughter-in-law.' And the Mouse went in. And he said: 'You must come turning your head back in this manner, as we do; you must shut your eyes, as you come out.'... The Mouse came out. He struck 'dzap-p', hitting the Mouse's face with the stick.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 60-61 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 他說：「你得這樣做，你得快快進去，你得把袋子取出來給媳婦。」那老鼠便進去了。他又說：「你得這樣把頭轉回來，就像我們這樣；你出來的時候，得閉上眼睛。」……老鼠出來了。他「札普」一聲打下去，用棍子打中老鼠的臉。

passages.text: The Striped Mouse said: 'If I go in, you will see that I cannot get in, for I shall stick fast, for the hole's mouth is not big enough for me to enter.'... The Lizard went in twisting about. The Girl went, she went to fetch the stick... She said: 'You will see your companions. This stick is the one with which he hit your companions.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 63-64 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 條紋鼠說：「要是我進去，你就會看到我進不去，因為我會卡住，因為洞口不夠大，我進不去。」……蜥蜴扭來扭去地進去了。那女孩去了，她去取那根棍子……她說：「你會見到你的同伴。這根棍子就是他打你同伴用的那根。」

passages.text: He shut his eyes coming out, and the Striped Mouse hit 'dzap-p', knocking him down at the hole's mouth. The Striped Mouse said: 'I am by myself killing to save my friends,' while the Longnosed Mice said: 'I am here, I am here!' and they lifted up their brushes, they waved their brushes.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 64 (public domain).
passages.zh: 他出來時閉著眼睛，條紋鼠「札普」一聲打下去，把他打倒在洞口。條紋鼠說：「我獨自殺戮，是為了救我的朋友。」而長鼻鼠們則說：「我在這兒，我在這兒！」他們舉起尾巴，揮動著尾巴。

title.en: The Striped Mouse and the Beetle
title.zh: 條紋鼠與甲蟲

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Striped Mouse and the Beetle'

summary.en: The Beetle, who was not strong but killed the Longnosed Mice for sport, throws his big stick 'habbu, pu, pu, pu'; the Striped Mouse throws back 'xet, te te te', knocks him down, and the dead mice come to life again, crying 'I am here!'
summary.zh: 甲蟲非強而以殺長鼻鼠為樂；擲巨棒「哈布噗噗噗」；條紋鼠擲回「克斯特特特特」，擊之倒地；死者群鼠復生，呼「我在此！我在此！」

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Longnosed Mice used to be people; they were not strong. Therefore the Beetle killed them. Then the Mantis dreamt about him... Then the wife of the Striped Mouse did this: when the Striped Mouse was a little way off, she sat up above there, sat sunning herself, because she was watching for her husband. Then she caught sight of the Beetle coming.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 65 (public domain).
passages.zh: 長鼻鼠從前是人；他們並不強壯。因此甲蟲殺了他們。後來螳螂夢見了他……接著條紋鼠的妻子這麼做：當條紋鼠離得稍遠時，她坐在那上頭，坐著曬太陽，因為她正守候著她的丈夫。然後她瞥見甲蟲走了過來。

passages.text: The Beetle said: 'Get out of the way, The Beetle is throwing.' And he threw 'habbu, pu, pu, pu, pu', hurling a stick, and the stick was not small. Then the Striped Mouse said: 'The Beetle is throwing, Get out of the way.' The Striped Mouse threw, 'xet, te te te te', letting fly back to the Beetle.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 65-66 (public domain).
passages.zh: 甲蟲說：『讓開，甲蟲要扔了。』他便扔出『habbu, pu, pu, pu, pu』，擲出一根棍子，那棍子可不小。接著條紋鼠說：『甲蟲要扔了，讓開。』條紋鼠扔出，『xet, te te te te』，把它飛擲回甲蟲那兒。

passages.text: And the striped Mouse threw, 'xet te te te, te', knocking the Beetle down. Then the Striped Mouse said: 'I am by myself, killing to save my friends.' Then the Longnosed Mice came to life again, those whom the Beetle had killed. They came to life. They kept saying: 'I am here, I am here,' as they jumped up.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 66 (public domain).
passages.zh: 條紋鼠扔出，『xet te te te, te』，把甲蟲擊倒。接著條紋鼠說：『我獨自一人，殺戮是為了救我的朋友。』於是長鼻鼠又活了過來，那些被甲蟲殺死的。他們活了過來。他們一邊跳起來，一邊不停說著：『我在這裡，我在這裡。』

title.en: The Colours in the Rainbow: Mantis Above, Kwammang-a Below
title.zh: 虹之色：上螳螂、下夸曼加

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Colours in the Rainbow'

summary.en: The rainbow is yellow above and red below, for the Mantis — who is also yellow — lies above and Kwammang-a below. Grown-ups call the rainbow Kwammang-a; and people say 'the Rainbow stands yonder and the rain will break.'
summary.zh: 虹上黃下赤：螳螂——其身亦黃——居上，夸曼加居下。長者稱虹為「夸曼加」；人曰「虹立於彼，雨將止」。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San lore from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Rainbow is yellow in that part which lies above; the piece which seems red lies below. For the Mantis, who is also yellow, lies above, and Kwammang-a lies below. For the Mantis is the one whose part above is yellow, and that part which lies below is red, while that part which is above is yellow. It is the Rainbow. Men call it Kwammang-a. Therefore we who are children say 'Kwammang-a' to it, because the grown-up people said Kwammang-a to it... Then people say: 'The Rainbow stands yonder and the rain will break.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 66 (public domain).
passages.zh: 彩虹在上面的那部分是黃色；看似紅色的那部分在下面。因為螳螂也是黃色的，位於上方，而Kwammang-a位於下方。因為螳螂就是上面那部分為黃色者，而下面那部分是紅色，上面那部分則是黃色。那就是彩虹。人們稱它為Kwammang-a。所以我們這些孩子稱它為『Kwammang-a』，因為大人們稱它為Kwammang-a……然後人們說：『彩虹立在那邊，雨就要下了。』

title.en: The Mantis Named the Places
title.zh: 螳螂命名諸地

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Names of Places'

summary.en: It was the Mantis who once called the places names: |hii/hoa is 'Rietfontein' because it once had many reeds; ||xu-||kum-we is 'Modder River'; and !xabbu is 'Zout Rivier'.
summary.zh: 命名諸地者，螳螂也：|希霍亞即「蘆葦泉」，因昔多葦；巫烏巫庫姆威即「泥河」；！阿布即「鹽河」。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San place-lore from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Bushmen say, it was the Mantis who once called the places names. |hii/hoa is 'Rietfontein', because it once had many reeds, while ||xu-||kum-we is 'Modder River'; that name is what white men call it. It was the Mantis who said: '|hii/hoa' and he also said ||xu-||kum-we. Then he said: '!xabbu' to 'Zout Rivier'.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 67 (public domain).
passages.zh: 布須曼人說，從前是螳螂給各地方取了名字。|hii/hoa是『Rietfontein』，因為它從前有許多蘆葦，而||xu-||kum-we是『Modder River』；那個名字是白人對它的稱呼。是螳螂說了：『|hii/hoa』，他也說了||xu-||kum-we。接著他對『Zout Rivier』說了：『!xabbu』。

title.en: How the Hare Got His Split Lip
title.zh: 兔子為何嘴唇豁裂

region.en: High mountain road above a Tibetan valley (symbolic pin in the Changtang highlands)
region.zh: 藏北高原山路（以羌塘高地為象徵定位）

period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story I

summary.en: A Tiger catches a Hare, who talks him into eating his own eyes on the promise they grow again, then leads the blind Tiger to a fire at the edge of a gulf until he falls; trapped on a tree-bough by his teeth, the Tiger is talked into saying 'Ah!' and dashed to the rocks. Next day the Hare engineers a whole morning of catastrophe - horses stampeded by ravens, sheep scattered by a wolf, a man skinning the dead Tiger - and watches it all from a hilltop, laughing until his upper lip splits, which it has remained ever since.
summary.zh: 虎捕兔，兔哄虎吃掉自己的雙眼（說會再生），再把失明的虎引到懸崖邊烤火，跌落深谷；虎齒咬住樹枝懸空，兔哄牠開口喊「啊」，虎便墜石而死。次日兔又接連撮合——烏鴉啄馬、狼逐羊、人剝虎皮——自己立於山頂旁觀，笑得前唇豁裂，至今如此。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected during a British diplomatic mission to Tibet (1906); treated respectfully as heritage of the Tibetan storytelling tradition.

passages.text: As they went along night began to fall, and when it was quite dark the Hare began smacking his chops as if he was eating something very nice. 'I am eating my eye, Uncle Tiger,' he replied; 'it is very nice, and it soon grows again.' The hungry Tiger scraped out his own eye and ate it; a little further on the Hare ate his other eye 'even better than the first', and the Tiger, quite blind, was led to the brink of a deep gulf and advised to sit down and rest while a fire was lighted in front of him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們走著走著，夜色開始降臨，當天完全黑下來時，野兔開始咂嘴，彷彿在吃什麼非常美味的東西。『我在吃我的眼睛，老虎叔叔，』他回答；『非常好吃，而且很快又會長出來。』飢餓的老虎挖出自己的眼睛吃了；又往前走了一點，野兔吃了他另一隻眼睛，『比第一隻還要好』，而老虎已完全瞎了，被領到一道深谷的邊緣，並被勸告坐下來休息，同時在他面前生起一堆火。

passages.text: As the blazing sticks came nearer the Tiger edged further and further back until he toppled over backwards into the gulf - and half-way down he seized a bough growing from a cleft with his teeth. Peeping over the edge, the Hare called out that he was afraid the Tiger must be badly hurt, and asked him to just say 'Ah!' so that he would know he was all right; the Tiger opened his mouth to say it and was instantly precipitated to the bottom, where he fell upon some rocks and was killed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當燃燒的柴枝越逼越近，老虎便一步一步往後退，直到仰面跌進深谷——跌到半途，他咬住一道裂縫裡長出的樹枝。野兔從崖邊探頭張望，高聲說他擔心老虎必定傷得不輕，請他只要應一聲「啊！」，好讓自己知道他安然無恙；老虎張開口正要應聲，登時便墜落谷底，摔在岩石上死了。

passages.text: Next morning the Hare offered a horse-driver the dead Tiger's skin, and while he skinned it set two Ravens to peck the sores on his unguarded horses; then he offered a shepherd-boy a raven's nest full of eggs, and while he climbed for them invited a Wolf down upon the unguarded sheep. From the top of a high hill the Hare surveyed the whole morning's work - the man stripping the Tiger, the horses careering with the ravens, the boy robbing the nest, the sheep scattered to the four quarters - and, leaning back on a stone, laughed so much that he split his upper lip, which has remained split to this very day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天早晨，野兔把死虎的皮送給一個趕馬人，趁他剝皮的時候，派了兩隻烏鴉去啄他無人看管的馬身上的瘡口；接著他又把一窩滿是蛋的烏鴉巢送給一個牧童，趁他爬上去取蛋的時候，引一頭狼撲向無人看管的羊群。野兔站在高崗頂上，把這一早上的成果盡收眼底——那人正剝著虎皮，馬群與烏鴉糾纏奔竄，牧童正搶著鳥巢，羊群四散各方——他往石頭上一靠，笑得合不攏嘴，竟把上唇笑裂了，那裂口直到今天還在。

title.en: The Tiger and the Man: The Dying Father's Warning
title.zh: 虎與人：臨終父訓

region.en: Jungle edge of a Tibetan valley (symbolic pin in the Kham hills)
region.zh: 康區山谷林緣（象徵定位）

period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story II

summary.en: A dying Father Tiger warns his three cubs that of all animals only Man is more powerful and cunning than the Tiger, and must never be hunted. The elder brothers obey; the youngest, proud of his stripes and claws, sets out to prove otherwise - and is lectured in turn by a scarred old Bullock and a goad-scarred old Elephant, both of whom Man served while strong and discarded when old. He finally meets the Woodcutter, who demonstrates the house - and when the boastful Tiger demands it, walks off locking him in to starve.
summary.zh: 臨終的虎父告誡三子：世間唯「人」比虎更強更狡，切不可獵。兩位兄長謹遵父命；幼虎仗著利爪斑紋，偏要證明父親錯了——路上先聽盡老牛與老象的控訴（年輕力壯時受寵，衰老即遭拋棄），最後遇見樵夫。樵夫演示了「房子」的妙處；幼虎強索此屋，被反鎖屋內活活餓死。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: Remember, my children, said the dying Father Tiger, that the Tiger is Lord of the jungle; but there is one animal against whom you must be on your guard, for he alone is more powerful and cunning than the Tiger. That animal is Man - I warn you solemnly before I die to beware of Man, and on no account to try to hunt or to kill him. The elder brothers confined themselves to deer and pigs; the youngest, of an independent and inquisitive disposition, chafed at the restriction.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「孩子們，要記住，」垂死的老虎父親說，「老虎是叢林之王；但有一種動物，你們必須提防，因為唯有他比老虎更強大、更狡猾。那動物就是人——我死之前鄭重警告你們，要提防人，無論如何都不要想去獵殺他。」年長的幾隻兄長只顧獵鹿和野豬；最小的那隻性情獨立又好奇，對這限制十分不耐。

passages.text: A worn-out pack-Bullock warned him with his own scars: while I was young and strong he cared for me, but as soon as I became old and weak and unable to do his work he turned me out to the jungle and gave no thought for me in my old age. An ancient Elephant said the same: Man made me his servant, put a saddle on my back and made stirrups of my ears, and used to strike me over the head with an iron goad - leave Man alone, or it will be the worse for you in the end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一頭筋疲力竭的馱牛指著自己身上的傷疤警告他：「我年輕力壯時，他照料我；可我一老弱、幹不動他的活兒，他就把我趕進叢林，對我晚年毫不掛心。」一頭年邁的大象也這麼說：「人把我當作他的僕役，在我背上架鞍，拿我的耳朵當馬鐙，還常用鐵刺棍敲我的頭——別去招惹人，否則到頭來吃虧的是你。」

passages.text: The Woodcutter, asked what sort of animal he was, showed the Tiger his timber house: you poor animals live in a hole in the forest exposed to wind, rain, cold and heat, while I build myself a fine house indifferent to the weather. The conceited Tiger flew into a passion - I am far more worthy than you of a house, come out at once and give it to me - and stalked in; the Man bolted the door outside and walked off with his axe, leaving the Tiger to starve to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 樵夫被問到他是什麼樣的動物時，便領老虎去看他的木屋：「你們這些可憐的畜生住在林中洞穴裡，任憑風吹雨打、受盡寒暑；我卻給自己蓋了一間好房子，不懼天候。」那自負的老虎勃然大怒——「我比你更配得上一間房子，立刻出來，把它讓給我」——便大步走了進去；那人從外頭閂上門，提著斧頭走了，留下老虎活活餓死。

title.en: The Story of Good Faith
title.zh: 信義的故事

region.en: Woodcutter's hut in a Tibetan forest (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 藏地林中樵夫小屋（象徵定位）

period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story III

summary.en: Trapped in the Woodcutter's hut, a starving Tiger promises a Musk Deer freedom if she unbolts the door - then seizes her, denying there is any such thing as good faith. They agree to refer the question to the first three living things they meet: the roadside Tree reports travellers who break his branches for whips; the Buffalo reports a calf that pushes its mother from the best pasture; the Hare, third judge, pleads ignorance of the story's details and walks the two back to the hut to demonstrate - where the Tiger shows how it was done, and the door is bolted on him for good.
summary.zh: 被困小屋的餓虎請麝鹿開門並許諾放生——出門即咬住她，還說世上根本沒有「信義」。雙方約定請三個活物評理：路邊大樹說旅人折其枝作鞭；水牛說牛犢長大便把母親趕出好草地；第三位裁判兔子裝糊塗，請二人回小屋現場演說——虎進屋演示，兔子與麝鹿把門栓上揚長而去，虎不久餓死屋中。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: When the Tiger seized the Deer and said he had no alternative but to eat her, she reproached him for breaking his faith, and he answered: Faith! I don't believe there is any such thing as good faith. So they made a bargain to ask the first three living things they met; the Tree, consulted first, gave shelter to man and beast on the highway and got broken branches for whips in return - my experience leads me to believe that there is no such thing as good faith in this world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 老虎抓住鹿，說自己別無選擇，只能吃掉她，鹿便責備他背信，他卻答道：「信義！我不信世上有信義這回事。」於是他們約定，去問他們遇到的前三樣活物；先問的是樹，樹在大路旁庇護人與獸，換來的卻是枝條被折去做鞭子——「憑我的經驗，我相信這世上根本沒有信義這回事。」

passages.text: The old Cow Buffalo, who stinted herself so her calf might have the best of everything, chewed the cud and gave the same verdict: as soon as the calf is big enough it will push me away from the places where I am grazing and drive me altogether from the pastures - my experience makes me believe there is no such thing as good faith. Downhearted, the Deer begged one more chance, the third and last judge.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那頭年老的母水牛，為了讓自己的犢牛樣樣都得到最好的，自己省吃儉用；牠反芻著，也下了同樣的判斷：等犢牛長得夠大了，牠就會把我從我吃草的地方推開，把我徹底趕出牧場——我的經驗讓我覺得，世上根本沒有什麼誠信可言。鹿灰心喪志，又求了一次機會，請第三位、也是最後一位裁判來評理。

passages.text: The Hare, hearing the strange story, professed himself unable to follow exactly who was shut up where, and proposed that all three adjourn to the scene of action. At the hut he had the Deer take her place at the stream and the Tiger take his inside; then, remarking that the door must have been shut like so, he shut it and bolted it, and he and the Deer went on their way safely, leaving the Tiger inside, where he shortly afterwards starved to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 野兔聽了這樁離奇的事，聲稱自己實在弄不明白究竟是誰被關在什麼地方，便提議三者一同前往事發之地。到了那間小屋，牠讓鹿站到溪邊自己原來的位置，讓老虎回到裡頭自己原來的位置；接著，牠說那扇門想必是這樣關上的，便順手把門關上、閂好，然後與鹿安然離去，把老虎留在裡頭，老虎不久便餓死了。

title.en: The Two Neighbours: Chamba and Tsering
title.zh: 兩位鄰居：強巴與次仁

region.en: Two houses side by side in a Tibetan village (symbolic pin in the Tsangpo valley)
region.zh: 藏南雅魯藏布谷地某村的兩戶人家（象徵定位）

period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story IV

summary.en: The generous poor man Chamba binds up a fallen sparrow's broken leg - the bird is a fairy in disguise - and is repaid with a grain that grows into jewel-bearing ears; the proud rich man Tsering drops a sparrow with chopsticks to manufacture the same luck, and his grain grows into a creditor apparition from a former existence, who seizes his whole property and makes him a slave. Reduced to want, Tsering embezzles the gold-dust his neighbour entrusts to him and refills the bag with sand - 'it has turned into this!' - and Chamba pays him back with a schooled monkey who cries 'worthy father, I am turned into this!' until the thief restores the gold to recover his own son.
summary.zh: 善良窮人強巴為摔傷的麻雀綁好斷腿（小鳥實為仙人化身），得珠粒為報；傲慢富人次仁用筷子把小麻雀摔下人造「善緣」，種出的卻是前世債主，被奪全部家產淪為奴僕。窮途末路的次仁又侵吞鄰人寄存的金沙、以沙充數，一句「變成這樣了！」——強巴便以一隻訓練過的猴子回敬「父親大人，我變成這樣了！」，直至他賠出金沙才領回親兒。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: The poor man bound up the young Sparrow's broken leg with thread and put it back in the nest; this Sparrow, although the poor man did not know it, was really a fairy in disguise, and when grown it flew in with its beak full of grain: this grain is in return for your kindness - plant it in your garden and see what comes up. The ears of corn contained valuable jewels instead of grain, and the poor man sold them for a large sum and found himself in comfort and prosperity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那窮人用線把小麻雀折斷的腿綁好，放回巢裡；這隻麻雀——雖然窮人並不知道——其實是仙女化身，等牠長大後，便啣著滿嘴的穀粒飛來：這穀粒是報答你的善心——把它種在你的園子裡，看看會長出什麼來。那些麥穗裡裝的不是穀粒，而是值錢的珠寶；窮人把它們賣了一大筆錢，從此過得安適富足。

passages.text: The rich man picked a young Sparrow out of the nest with a pair of chop-sticks and dropped it, bound up its leg, and got the same grain from a grateful-looking sparrow; but when he planted it in the richest part of his soil, there arose instead of barley a great fierce-looking man with a bundle of papers under his arm: I was a creditor of yours in one of your former existences. He seized the rich man's house, cattle, sheep and lands, and reduced him to a slave in his own household.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那富人用一雙筷子從巢裡夾出一隻小麻雀，把它摔下，綁好牠的腿，也從一隻看似感恩的麻雀那裡得到了同樣的穀粒；可是當他把穀粒種在自己最肥沃的田地裡時，長出來的卻不是大麥，而是一個相貌兇惡的魁梧大漢，腋下夾著一疊文書：我在你前世的某一世裡，是你的債主。他奪走了富人的房屋、牛、羊和土地，把富人貶為自己家中的奴僕。

passages.text: Entrusted with a bag of gold-dust, the impoverished Tsering spent it all and filled the bag with sand; Chamba, opening it, found sand instead of gold, and the dishonest neighbour could only say: my friend, it has turned into this! Then Chamba announced a free school for little boys, and while Tsering was away procured a tame Monkey taught to say 'worthy father, I am turned into this!' When the father demanded his son, the monkey repeated the words, and he decided it was better to pay up the stolen gold on condition of having his proper son restored.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 窮困的次仁受託保管一袋金沙，卻把它全花光了，往袋裡裝滿沙子；占巴打開一看，發現裡面是沙子而不是金子，那不老實的鄰居只能說：我的朋友，它變成這樣了！後來占巴宣布為小男孩開辦一所免費學堂，趁次仁不在時弄來一隻馴服的猴子，教牠說「可敬的父親，我變成這樣了！」當父親索要自己的兒子時，猴子便重複這句話，於是他認定，與其如此，不如把偷去的金子賠上，條件是換回自己真正的兒子。

title.en: The Cat and the Mice: The Procession Trick
title.zh: 貓與鼠：出巡之計

region.en: Great farm-house of a Tibetan village (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 藏地某村大農舍（象徵定位）

period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story V

summary.en: A Cat too old to hunt announces her repentance and asks the mice only to file past her twice daily in obeisance - and devours the last mouse of every procession. The two clever friends Rambe and Ambe counter with a roll-call: one always leads and one always trails, calling back and forth until all have passed. When at last the furious Cat leaps into the middle of the column, the warned mice scuttle to their holes, the room stands empty, and the Cat soon dies of starvation.
summary.zh: 老貓捕鼠無力，宣稱已悔過向善，只求鼠群一日兩次列隊打恭——隊尾的最後一隻總是被她吃掉。聰明的朋友然巴與安巴識破，以點名法破解：一隻永在隊首、一隻永在隊尾，一路互相唱和直至全體通過。老貓忍無可忍撲向隊伍中央，早有防備的鼠群四散入洞，房中頓空；老貓不久餓死。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: I have led a very wicked life, said the Cat to the assembled mice, and in my old age I repent; henceforth I shall give myself up to religious contemplation and no longer molest you - all I ask is that twice every day you file past me and each make an obeisance as a token of your gratitude. She took her seat on a cushion, the mice went by in single file, and as soon as the procession had passed with the exception of one little mouse she seized the last one and devoured it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 我這一生作惡多端，貓對聚集起來的老鼠們說，如今我老了，心生悔悟；從今以後，我要專心修行默想，不再騷擾你們——我只求你們每天兩次列隊從我面前經過，各自行一個禮，以示你們的感激。牠在墊子上坐定，老鼠們排成一列走過；等隊伍走完，只剩一隻小老鼠時，牠便抓住最後那隻，把牠吞吃了。

passages.text: The two friends agreed that Rambe was always to walk at the very front and Ambe bring up the rear, calling and answering at frequent intervals: Where are you, Brother Ambe? - Here I am, Brother Rambe. Twice the Cat dared not touch Ambe while his brother kept calling; the third evening she made a fierce leap right into the middle of the mice, who, thoroughly prepared, scuttled off in every direction, and before she could catch a single one the room was empty. After this the mice put no further trust in the treacherous Cat, who soon died of starvation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兩位朋友約定，讓冉貝永遠走在最前面，安貝殿後，並頻頻互相呼喚應答：安貝兄弟，你在哪裡？——我在這裡，冉貝兄弟。只要兄弟不斷呼喚，貓兒兩次都不敢碰安貝；第三個晚上，她猛地一躍，直撲鼠群中央，而老鼠們早有準備，四散奔逃，她一隻也抓不到，屋子便已空空如也。此後，老鼠們再也不信任那狡詐的貓，貓不久便餓死了。

title.en: The Foolish Young Mussulman: Grave, Jar and Shadow
title.zh: 糊塗回教青年：掘墓、油罐與樹影

region.en: Meadows and roads outside a large Tibetan trading town (symbolic pin at Gyantse)
region.zh: 藏地大商鎮郊野（以江孜為象徵定位）

period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story VI

summary.en: A simple young Mussulman is told that yellow soles mean he will die at once; he digs himself a shallow grave and lies down in it - and is recruited by a passing servant to carry the King's jar of oil for the price of a hen. Dreaming out the hen's eggs, the chickens, the cow, the house, the wife and the child's education, he stamps his foot at the naughty child and smashes the royal jar. Sent to his wedding through a shaded road, he hides his clothes to escape a pursuing shadow, climbs a poplar, and with one shout of 'I want my share too!' scares a caravan of thieves into leaving everything - a horse and garments - below.
summary.zh: 天真的回教青年聽信「腳底發黃必死」之言，自掘淺墓躺進等死；被王之僕半僱半哄背起御用油罐，換得「一隻母雞」的許諾。他一路盤算雞生蛋、蛋變雞、雞換牛、牛換屋、娶妻生子、管教兒子——想到要跺腳教訓，腳下一跺，油罐落地粉碎。成親路上他把衣衫脫下藏好以躲影子，爬上楊樹瞌睡；醒來一聲「我也要分一份！」嚇得路上那夥強人拋下馬匹衣物抱頭而逃。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: The soles of your feet are all yellow, called out a passing young man, and that is a sure sign you are going to die at once. The poor fellow dug himself a shallow grave and lay down in it to wait for death, and a King's Servant, passing with a jar of oil, recruited him for a hen; on the road he built up in his head the hen's eggs, the chickens, the cow and calf, the house, the wife and the child's education, and stamped his foot at the naughty imaginary child so violently that the jar of oil slipped off his back and was smashed to pieces on the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個路過的年輕人喊道：你的腳底全是黃的，這是你要立刻死去的確鑿徵兆。那可憐人替自己挖了一個淺墳，躺進去等死；一位帶著一罐油的國王的僕人僱他去趕雞；在路上，他在腦中盤算著母雞的蛋、小雞、母牛與小牛、房子、妻子以及孩子的教育，又對那個想像中調皮的孩子狠狠跺了一腳，結果那罐油從他背上滑落，在地上摔得粉碎。

passages.text: Sent off to his bride's wedding-feast, he was plagued on a shaded road by a shadow on whichever side he looked, so he stripped off his garments and hung them along the road, climbed into the upper branches of a poplar and fell asleep. A party of travellers collected the scattered garments and the grazing horse and stopped in the tree's shade to divide the spoil - and when the Boy woke and called out 'I want my share too!' they took him for a demon in the tree and fled, leaving the horse and all the clothes behind them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他被派去參加新娘的婚宴，在一條有蔭的路上，無論他朝哪邊看，都有影子困擾著他，於是他脫下衣服，沿路掛起，爬上白楊樹的高枝上睡著了。一群旅人收攏了散落的衣物和吃草的马，停在樹蔭下分贓——當那男孩醒來喊道「我也要分我的一份！」時，他們以為他是樹中的妖魔，便逃走了，把馬和所有衣服都丟在身後。

passages.text: At the wedding feast he saved dainties for his mother in a narrow-mouthed copper vessel and got his hand stuck fast in its neck; unable to eat, he was coaxed into telling his bride, who sent him down in the dark to beat the vessel against the white stone at the foot of the stairs - and he struck instead the grey head of his bride's father, asleep there from the feast. Terrified, he fled, slept on a honeycomb and then in a wool-shed, and waking white and woolly believed he had been turned into a sheep as punishment for killing his father-in-law.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在婚宴上，他把美味佳餚留給母親，裝在一個窄口的銅器裡，手卻牢牢卡在器頸中；他吃不了東西，被哄著告訴了新娘，新娘便打發他在黑暗中下樓，把銅器往樓梯腳下的白石上敲——他卻敲中了新娘父親那灰白的頭，老人因宴席睏倦，正睡在那裡。他嚇壞了，逃走了，睡在蜂巢上，隨後又睡在羊毛棚裡，醒來時渾身雪白、毛茸茸的，便相信自己因殺死岳父而被變成了一隻羊。

title.en: The Sheep in the Robbers' Hands and the Cat with the Lantern
title.zh: 強盜背上的「羊」與提燈的貓

region.en: Sheep-fold and inn on the road to India (symbolic pin at Phari)
region.zh: 通往印度的帕里羊圈與客棧（象徵定位）

period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story VI (continued)

summary.en: Believing himself a sheep, the honey-and-wool-covered youth joins a flock, and at midnight robbers pick him as the fattest; hoisted onto a back and laid down to have his throat cut, he breaks role and cries out, scaring them away. Later, trading to India, he is cheated of everything by an innkeeper who wins a bet that a cat will carry in the lantern at dusk - until his wife, disguised as a man, repeats the wager and has her husband release three mice in the courtyard: the trained cat drops the lantern at the third, the innkeeper loses house and goods, and the couple return home wealthy.
summary.zh: 塗滿蜂蜜羊毛的他自認變成了羊，混入羊群；夜裡強盜挑中他這「最肥的羊」，正要割喉，他忘了角色喊出人話，強盜抱頭而逃。後來他去印度經商，被店主以「貓能提燈」的賭局騙光全部財物——他的妻子扮作男商重下同樣賭注，再讓丈夫在院中連放三隻老鼠：訓練有素的貓在第三隻時丟下燈籠撲鼠，店主輸掉家業連同先前贏的財物，夫婦滿載而歸。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: At midnight robbers came to the fold and felt about for a good fat heavy one, finding the Boy the heaviest of them all; hoisted onto a back and laid on the ground to have his throat cut, this trial proved too much for his nerves, and forgetting his role of sheep he called out in a shrill voice: please don't kill me, kind robbers! They fled as fast as they could, and he returned to his bride's house, where the sorely hurt but not dead father-in-law freely forgave him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 午夜時分，強盜來到羊圈，摸索著要找一隻肥壯沉重的，發現那男孩是他們當中最重的；他被抬到背上，又放到地上準備割喉，這一試探超出了他的膽量，他忘了自己扮的是羊，尖聲喊道：好心的強盜們，請不要殺我！他們便拼命逃走，他則回到新娘家，那受了重傷卻未死的岳父寬宏大量地原諒了他。

passages.text: At a large house on the way to India the Landlord bet that when night fell a lantern would be carried into the room by a cat instead of by a servant - a regular trick, for the tame cat carried in a lighted lantern at dusk every evening, by which he secured unwary travellers' goods. The young Man forfeited all he possessed and stayed on as a servant.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在前往印度途中一座大宅裡，地主打賭說，夜幕降臨時，提燈進屋的會是一隻貓，而不是僕人——這是他慣用的把戲，因為那隻馴貓每天傍晚都會提著一盞點亮的燈籠進來，他藉此騙取不設防旅人的財物。那年輕人輸掉了所有財產，留下來當了僕人。

passages.text: His wife, disguised as a man with ponies laden with wool, repeated the wager, and privately told her Husband what he was to do: catch three mice and conceal them in a little box. At dusk, as the cat crossed the courtyard with the lantern in its mouth, one mouse, then a second, then a third were released - and at the third the cat dropped the lantern on the threshold and bounded after the mouse. The Landlord reluctantly owned his bet lost, and handed over not only his own property but the merchandise previously won from her Husband.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的妻子裝扮成男子，帶著馱滿羊毛的小馬，重提了那場賭約，並私下告訴丈夫該怎麼做：捉三隻老鼠，藏進一個小盒子裡。黃昏時分，當貓叼著燈籠穿過庭院，一隻老鼠、接著第二隻、然後第三隻被放了出來——到第三隻時，貓把燈籠掉在門檻上，縱身去追老鼠。地主不情願地認了賭輸，不僅交出自己的財產，還交出了先前從她丈夫那裡贏來的貨物。

title.en: The Kyang, the Fox, the Wolf and the Hare
title.zh: 野驢、狐、狼與兔

region.en: Upper Tibetan valley beyond cultivation (symbolic pin in the Changtang highlands)
region.zh: 藏地高寒無耕作的河谷上段（以羌塘為象徵定位）

period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story VII

summary.en: A young Kyang, too thin for a hungry Wolf, bargains for six months; in autumn the Wolf comes with a Fox and a Hare invited to share the spoil. The Hare proposes strangling the fat Kyang by rope instead of throat-biting, borrows a rope from a shepherd, rigs a big slip-knot for the Kyang and two smaller ones for the Wolf and Fox - and at the word 'pull' the Kyang simply walks forward, dragging his executioners, and gallops off; the two strangle themselves and the Hare trots home feeling he has done a good day's work.
summary.zh: 小野驢以「秋天再肥」哄走餓狼；秋日狼帶著狐與兔同來赴約分贓。兔獻策改咬喉為勒斃，向牧人借繩——大繩圈套野驢頸，狼與狐各把頭伸進兩個小繩圈，兔咬繩尾喊「拉」；野驢向前一走，拖著狼狐便跑，二獸自勒而死，野驢甩繩悠然吃草，兔自覺做了件好事。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: In spring the Kyang told the Wolf it was no good eating him then, thin after the hard winter, but that in autumn he would be twice as fat; the Wolf agreed to wait on condition that they meet on this very spot. In autumn he started for the appointment, picked up the Fox and the Hare to share the spoil, and found the Kyang very fat and sleek, licking his chops in anticipation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 春天裡，藏野驢對狼說，那時吃他沒什麼好處，熬過艱苦的冬天他瘦得很，但到了秋天他會肥上一倍；狼同意等待，條件是他們就在這同一個地方相會。秋天，他動身赴約，帶上狐狸和野兔一同分食獵物，發現藏野驢又肥又壯、毛色光潤，正饞得舔著嘴唇。

passages.text: The Hare suggested that strangling would save the blood a throat-seizure would waste, borrowed a rope from a shepherd's encampment, and rigged it: a large slip-knot over the Kyang's neck, two smaller loops for the heads of the Wolf and the Fox, himself holding the loose end with his teeth. At the word 'pull' the Kyang walked forward a few paces, the rope tightened on the executioners' necks, and when the Hare let go the Kyang galloped off dragging the Wolf and the Fox after him until both were strangled; the Hare scampered home feeling he had done a good day's work.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 野兔建議用勒死的方式，免得咬喉嚨白白浪費了血，便從一處牧人的營地借來一根繩子，佈置妥當：一個大活結套在藏野驢的脖子上，兩個小繩圈分別套住狼和狐狸的頭，他自己用牙齒咬住鬆著的繩頭。一聲「拉」，藏野驢向前走了幾步，繩子便勒緊了劊子手們的脖子；野兔一鬆口，藏野驢飛奔而去，拖著狼和狐狸跟在後面，直到兩者都被勒死；野兔蹦跳著回家，覺得自己這一天幹得不錯。

title.en: The Frog and the Crow
title.zh: 蛙與鴉

region.en: House roof and well in a Tibetan village (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 藏地村中屋頂與水井（象徵定位）

period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story VIII

summary.en: A Crow carries off a fat Frog to devour him on a roof; the Frog chuckles that his fierce Father lives on this very roof, then that a stronger Uncle lives in the gutter, until the Crow retreats to the ground. There the Frog admires her blunt bill and sends her to sharpen it on a flat stone - and dives into the well. Invited down to eat him there, the Crow's own advice traps her: 'the best thing would be for you to come down here.'
summary.zh: 鴉叼著肥蛙上屋頂欲食；蛙先笑言「猛父就住在這屋頂」，再言「更猛的叔父住在水槽」，鴉步步後退下到地面。蛙又贊其喙太鈍，勸牠去磨石上磨利；鴉一轉身，蛙跳井而逃。井邊鴉喚蛙上來受死，蛙答「我上不去，還是請你下來吃我吧」。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: As she alighted the Frog gave an audible chuckle: my Father lives close by here, on this very roof, and he is an exceedingly fierce, strong man who will certainly avenge my death. The Crow hopped to another corner; the Frog chuckled again that his Uncle, even stronger than his Father, lived in the very gutter; and the Crow, alarmed, flew down to the ground near the edge of a well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她一落下來，青蛙就發出一聲聽得見的輕笑：我父親就住在這附近，就在這屋頂上，他是個極其兇猛強壯的人，一定會為我的死報仇。烏鴉跳到另一個角落；青蛙又輕笑說，他的叔叔比他父親還要強壯，就住在這水溝裡；烏鴉一驚，飛落到地面，靠近一口井的邊緣。

passages.text: There the Frog observed that her bill seemed rather blunt, and advised her to strop it on a flat stone over there before beginning to eat; as soon as her back was turned the Frog gave one desperate jump and dived into the well. When the sharp-billed Crow called down for him to come up and be eaten, he replied that he could not get up the sides of this well - the best thing would be for you to come down here to eat me - and dived to the bottom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在那裡，青蛙看出她的嘴似乎相當鈍，便勸她先在那邊一塊平石上磨一磨，再開始吃；她的背剛一轉過去，青蛙便拼命一跳，潛入井中。當尖嘴的烏鴉朝下喊他上來受吃時，他回答說自己爬不上這井壁——最好的辦法是你下來這裡吃我——說罷便潛到了井底。

title.en: The Hare and the Lions
title.zh: 兔與獅子夫婦

region.en: Rocky den and stone tank on a Tibetan mountainside (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 藏地山腰石穴與石砌水池（象徵定位）

period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story IX

summary.en: A Hare caught by a Lion offers him a bigger meal: a fierce animal living in the valley pond. The Lion's own reflection, flattered and goaded by the Hare's running commentary, is attacked with a roar - and the masonry-sided tank drowns him. The Hare then boasts to the grieving Lioness that he gave her lord a free fight and left him dying in the valley, leads her at full gallop through the big end of a tapered hole in a ruined wall - and she wedges fast, to be pelted with stones until she starves.
summary.zh: 兔被獅擒，獻上「谷中水池中更強的猛獸」為食；獅向水面自己倒影狂吼撲擊，落入四壁光滑的石池溺斃。兔又對悲傷的母獅自誇「與你家老爺打了一架，他正垂死谷中」，引她狂追鑽入廢牆大口小尾的斜孔——母獅卡死其中，被兔投石辱罵，終至餓斃。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: The Hare begged the indignant Lion to be careful, promising an animal in the pond stronger than himself; at the square-built stone tank the Lion stalked to the edge and saw his own head reflected. Encouraged by the Hare to keep growling but on no account come to grips with the beast, he was goaded to desperation, sprang straight at the image, and being unable to climb the masonry sides, swam until, quite wearied out, he sank to the bottom and was drowned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 野兔懇請氣憤的獅子小心為妙，保證池中有一隻比他更強壯的動物；到了那座方形石砌的水池，獅子大步走到池邊，看見了自己的頭映在水中。野兔慫恿他繼續咆哮，但千萬不要與那野獸近身搏鬥，他被激得走投無路，直朝那影像撲去，又爬不上石砌的池壁，只得游著，直到筋疲力盡，沉到池底淹死了。

passages.text: Next morning the Hare told the perturbed Lioness that he and her lord had had a little argument and a free fight, and that he had been obliged to injure Mr. Lion rather severely before making him see reason; as she sprang at him he galloped off, made straight for the ruined wall, entered the breach at the large end and emerged at the small recess. The Lioness, blind with rage, rushed head-foremost into the opening and was wedged tightly in the tapering hole; the Hare cantered round and pelted her with stones and bad names, and she, unable to free herself, shortly afterwards starved to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天早晨，野兔告訴心緒不寧的母獅，說他與她的夫君曾有過一番小小的爭執和一場混戰，而他不得不在讓獅子先生明白道理之前，把他傷得相當嚴重；當她向他撲來時，他疾馳而去，直奔那堵殘破的牆，從大的一端進入缺口，再從小凹處出來。母獅怒不可遏，一頭衝進洞口，緊緊卡在逐漸收窄的洞裡；野兔繞著圈奔馳，向她投擲石塊、破口大罵，而她無法脫身，不久之後便餓死了。

title.en: The Sheep, the Lamb, the Wolf and the Hare
title.zh: 羊、羔、狼與兔

region.en: Migration road between the southern valley and the great northern plateau (symbolic pin in northern Tibet)
region.zh: 藏南谷地與藏北大高原之間的轉場路（象徵定位）

period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story X

summary.en: A Sheep and her Lamb, met by a Wolf on the road north, bargain for autumn; returning fat, they face the appointment in despair until a Hare rigs the scene - himself in fine robes with an ear-ring and a hat, pen behind his ear, mounted on the saddled Sheep with two bundles lashed on the Lamb. Hailing the Wolf in a sharp official tone as Lomden the Hare, deputed on a special mission by the Emperor of China with a commission of ten wolf-skins for the King of India, he writes a large figure 1 on his sheet of paper - and the Wolf flees ignominiously.
summary.zh: 母羊帶羔北遷遇狼，以「秋天再肥」訂約；歸來時兩代皆肥，赴約在即，兔挺身相救——自己穿上新袍、戴長耳環與時髦帽、耳後別筆，騎上被備鞍的母羊，並在羊羔身上縛好兩個小包袱。臨近狼時他以官腔喝問，自稱「奉中國皇帝特命出使印度的兔子羅木丹，正要向印度王進貢十張狼皮」，隨即在公文上寫下一個大大的「1」字——狼嚇得掉頭狂逃。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; the original collector notes this tale satirizes the arrogance of Tibetan and Chinese officials and the timidity of Tibetan peasants; treated respectfully as social satire of the period.

passages.text: The Hare dressed himself in his best clothes, a new robe of woollen cloth with a long ear-ring in his left ear and a fashionable hat, strapped a small saddle on the Sheep's back, prepared two bundles slung across the Lamb, took a large sheet of paper with a pen thrust behind his ear, and mounted. Soon after, at the appointed spot, the Wolf was waiting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 野兔穿上他最好的衣服，一件毛料的新袍子，左耳戴著一隻長耳環，頭戴一頂時髦的帽子，在綿羊背上繫好一副小鞍，備好兩個搭在羔羊身上的包裹，拿了一大張紙，耳後插著一支筆，然後騎了上去。不久之後，在約定的地點，狼正在等候。

passages.text: Called out to in a sharp tone of authority, the Wolf replied that he had come to eat the Sheep and its Lamb in accordance with a regular arrangement; the Hare answered that he was Lomden the Hare, deputed to India on a special mission by the Emperor of China, with a commission to bring ten wolf-skins as a present to the King of India - what a fortunate thing it is that I should have met you here; your skin will do for one, anyway. Producing his sheet of paper, he wrote down the figure 1 very large, and the Wolf, so frightened, turned tail and fled away ignominiously.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 狼被以嚴厲的權威口吻喝問，便回答說他是按照既定的約定前來吃綿羊和牠的羔羊的；野兔答道，他是野兔洛姆登，奉中國皇帝之命出使印度，受命帶十張狼皮作為送給印度國王的禮物——我竟在這裡遇見你，真是何等幸運；無論如何，你的皮總能湊上一張。他取出那張紙，把數字「1」寫得極大，狼嚇得掉頭鼠竄，狼狽而逃。

title.en: How the Hare Made a Fool of the Wolf
title.zh: 兔如何愚弄狼

region.en: Wolf's earth on a high pass (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 高口埡口的狼穴（象徵定位）

period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story XI

summary.en: Elated by the Hare's rescue, the Sheep and Goat camp at the mouth of the Wolf's earth, sharpening knives and collecting water to cook him in, until the Wolf bolts at the Sheep's nervous voice and kills her. The Goat flees, breaks his leg in a rock cleft, and dies promising his skin to the Fox for his young ones. The Fox meets the Hare, and together they lure the Wolf - found on a dead horse - to a wedding feast; each carries off provisions, and the Wolf, head through the handle of the wine jar, is made to sing before leaving: the men burst in, the jar is too broad for the window, and the Wolf is beaten to death with sticks and stones.
summary.zh: 羊與山羊自恃兔計得逞，蹲在狼穴口磨刀、備水「煮你」，狼卻聽出母羊聲音發抖，撲出將其咬死；山羊逃命跌斷腿，臨終託狐把皮送給孩子。狐遇兔，同往報仇：在喜宴人家偷吃飽喝，兔提議各自帶走食物——羊酪、冷雞、酒罈；狼把頭伸進罈柄，臨走兔又慫恿唱歌，屋內人一聽「屋裡有狼！」一擁而入，罈口太寬塞不過窗，狼被亂棒亂石打死。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: The Goat rubbed his horns on a stone - sharpening a knife to kill you with - and when rain fell answered that he was collecting the water to cook the Wolf in; but when the nervous Sheep took over the watch, the Wolf noticed the terrified sound of her voice, learned she was alone, dashed out, and slew her. Chasing the fleeing Goat, he lost him in rocky ground, where the Goat fell into a deep narrow cleft and broke his leg; the Wolf jumped over the crevice without seeing him, and the Goat died there, begging the passing Fox to strip off his skin for his young ones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 山羊在石頭上磨著角——是在磨刀要把你殺死——而當雨落下時，牠回答說自己是在收集雨水，好把狼煮了；但當膽怯的綿羊接過看守之責時，狼察覺到她聲音中的驚恐，得知她獨自一人，便衝了出來，把她殺死。狼追趕逃跑的山羊，在亂石地裡失去了牠的蹤跡，山羊在那裡跌進一道又深又窄的裂縫，摔斷了腿；狼跳過裂縫，卻沒有看見牠，山羊便死在那裡，懇求路過的狐狸為牠的幼崽剝下牠的皮。

passages.text: The Hare, hearing the Fox's errand, resolved not to let the Wolf kill his friends with impunity, and together they found him feeding on a dead horse and lured him to a wedding feast; through a narrow window they reached the unguarded larder and ate and drank their fill. The Hare advised each to carry off provisions - cheese for himself, cold fowl for the Fox, and the jar of wine for the Wolf, whose head he showed him how to slip through the handle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 野兔聽聞狐狸的差事，決心不讓狼肆意殺害他的朋友而不受懲罰，於是他們一同找到正在吃一匹死馬的狼，把他誘到一場婚宴上；他們穿過一扇窄窗，來到無人看守的食品儲藏室，盡情吃喝。野兔建議各自帶走些食物——給自己拿乳酪，給狐狸拿冷禽肉，給狼拿那罐酒，並教他如何把頭從提手間穿過去。

passages.text: As they were about to start the Hare proposed a song, and pressed the modest Wolf until he began to sing; at the first sound of his voice the men in the next room stopped their feasting, crying there is a Wolf in the house, and rushed towards the larder. The Hare and the Fox hopped quietly out of the window; the Wolf made a leap, but the great jar round his neck was too broad for the narrow opening, and he fell back - and was still jumping and falling when the people of the house rushed in and despatched him with sticks and stones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 正當他們要動身時，野兔提議唱首歌，並一再催促靦腆的狼，直到他開始唱起來；他的聲音一響，隔壁房間的人們便停止了宴飲，喊道屋裡有狼，並朝食品儲藏室衝去。野兔和狐狸悄悄從窗戶跳了出去；狼縱身一躍，但套在他脖子上的大罐子對那窄小的開口來說太寬了，於是他跌了回去——當屋裡的人衝進來用棍棒和石頭結果他時，他仍在跳著、跌著。

title.en: The Mouse's Three Children
title.zh: 母鼠的三個孩子

region.en: Kingdom of Nepal, by the King's palace (symbolic pin at Kathmandu)
region.zh: 尼泊爾王國王宮附近（以加德滿都為象徵定位）

period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story XII

summary.en: A Mouse prays for a strong child and bears a Tiger, for a beautiful child a Peacock, and for a wise, wealthy and powerful child a man-child whose hair turns to diamonds and whose nail-parings to turquoises. A greedy King, tipped off by a barber, tries to enslave the Boy with impossible demands - four Tigers for the gates, four Peacocks for the golden pinnacles, and finally that the Mouse herself fight the state Elephant - but the handfuls of hair and feathers summon a hundred Tigers and a sky full of Peacocks, and the poisoned Mouse runs up the Elephant's trunk into its brain and kills it. The King keeps his word: the daughter, half the kingdom, and in time the throne.
summary.zh: 母鼠求子：求強得虎、求美得孔雀、求智富權得人子——其髮落地成鑽石珍珠、指甲成綠松石。貪婪的國王聽理髮匠之言，連出難題——四虎守四門、四孔雀棲四金頂、母鼠單挑御象——但一把虎毛召來百虎，一把雀羽引來滿天孔雀；鼠抹毒鑽入象鼻直上象腦，毒斃巨獸。國王踐諾：嫁女、分半國，後傳位於他。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as heritage of the Nepal-Tibet storytelling borderlands.

passages.text: Praying that her offspring might be very strong, the Mouse bore a young Tiger, who left her a handful of his hair: go into yonder thicket, throw it into the air and call my name three times. The beautiful child was a Peacock, who left feathers with the same instruction; and the third child, prayed to become wise, wealthy and powerful, was a man-child.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 老鼠祈禱自己的孩子能非常強壯，於是生下一隻小虎，小虎留給她一把自己的毛：到那邊的密林裡去，把它拋向空中，呼喚我的名字三次。那美麗的孩子是一隻孔雀，也留下羽毛並作同樣的吩咐；第三個孩子，她祈禱他能變得智慧、富有且強大，是個男孩。

passages.text: A barber cutting the Boy's hair saw each hair fall as diamonds and pearls and each nail-paring as turquoises, and told the greedy King, who demanded four full-grown Tigers for the palace gates under threat of killing the mother; a handful of Tiger's hair summoned a great Tiger who opened his mouth with fearful roars until the whole jungle was full of hastening Tigers, and the Boy rode one's back to the throne. The Peacocks came the same way, four carrying the Boy to the King's courtyard, tails spread in rows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個理髮師在為那男孩理髮時，看見每根落下的頭髮都變成鑽石與珍珠，每片剪下的指甲都變成綠松石，便去告訴貪婪的國王；國王便以殺死母親相脅，索求四隻成年老虎看守宮門；一把虎毛召來一隻巨虎，牠張開大口發出可怕的吼聲，直到整片叢林滿是奔湧而來的老虎，男孩便騎在其中一隻背上登上王座。孔雀也以同樣的方式前來，四隻孔雀載著男孩飛到國王的庭院，尾羽成排展開。

passages.text: For the third trial the King demanded that Mother Mouse single-handed fight and destroy the state Elephant; she had herself smeared with poison and a long string tied to her tail, and carried in the Boy's sleeve. As the chained Elephant rushed bellowing, the Mouse hopped onto his foot and scuttled up the trunk into his brain, running round and round smearing poison; the Elephant fell stone dead, and the Boy, pulling the string, guided her out into the open air. The King gave him his daughter in marriage and half his kingdom, and on the King's death the Boy succeeded to the throne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第三次考驗，國王要求鼠媽媽獨自與國象搏鬥並將其消滅；她讓人把毒藥塗在自己身上，並在尾巴上繫了一根長繩，被藏在男孩的袖子裡帶去。當被鐵鍊鎖住的大象咆哮著衝來時，老鼠跳上牠的腳，疾速爬上象鼻鑽進牠的腦中，一圈又一圈地跑著塗抹毒藥；大象倒地而死，男孩拉動繩子，把她引到空曠處。國王將女兒嫁給他，並分給他半個王國；國王死後，男孩繼承了王位。

title.en: The Jackals and the Tiger
title.zh: 豺與虎

region.en: Thickest part of a Tibetan forest (symbolic pin in southeastern Tibet)
region.zh: 藏東南密林深處（象徵定位）

period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story XIII

summary.en: Driven from a village by too many dogs, a family of Jackals squats in a Tiger's den while he hunts. Father Jackal stations himself on the roof and raps a stone when the Tiger approaches, so that Mrs. Jackal can set the children crying for their supper of hot Tiger's meat; the terrified Tiger flees. An old Baboon laughs at him - you should eat the Jackals, not the Jackals you - and walks back with him, tail twisted round the Tiger's for support; but at the cry 'Brother Monkey, bring him along quickly - only one?' the Tiger bolts for good, dragging the Baboon through the thorns until only a broken bit of tail remains twisted round the Tiger's own.
summary.zh: 豺一家被村犬逼走，霸佔了虎穴。父豺守在穴頂，見虎歸來便敲石示意；母豺讓孩子們大哭「等虎肉晚餐」。虎嚇破膽逃走，遇白鬚老狒狒譏笑「該是你吃豺，不是豺吃你」，尾纏虎尾同行壯膽；穴頂一聲「猴兄，快帶他來——怎麼只帶一個？」，虎掉頭狂奔，把狒狒拖過荊棘叢，最後虎尾上只纏著一截斷落的猴尾。豺從此安居虎穴。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: Father Jackal arranged the stratagem: rapping with a loose stone on the roof of the den as the Tiger approached, he called out what are those children crying about, and was answered that they were very hungry and impatient for their supper; tell them they won't have long to wait now, he replied, the Tiger will probably be home very soon and we shall all be eating hot Tiger's meat before long. The Tiger thought what kind of strange animal can this be which has entered my den and is waiting to cook and eat me on my return - and turned tail and ran off through the forest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 豺爸爸定下計策：當老虎走近時，他用一塊鬆動的石頭敲打洞穴的屋頂，高聲喊道那些孩子哭什麼，得到的回答是他們非常飢餓，急著要吃晚飯；他回答說，告訴他們不用等太久了，老虎大概很快就會回家，我們大家不久就能吃到熱騰騰的老虎肉了。老虎心想，這是什麼奇怪的動物，竟闖進我的洞穴，還等著我回來把我煮了吃掉——於是掉頭穿過森林逃走了。

passages.text: An old Baboon with a fringe of white hair round his face laughed heartily: you should eat the Jackals, and not the Jackals you; come along with me and I will show you how to deal with people like that. Twisting his tail round the Tiger's to give him confidence, the Baboon walked with him toward the den - until Father Jackal called out, that is right, Brother Monkey, bring him along quickly; we are all half starved - but what do you mean by only bringing one of them? The Tiger fled precipitately, dragging the Baboon through the thickest and thorniest parts of the jungle until many miles away all he saw of the Monkey was a bit of its tail broken off and still twisted round his own.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一隻臉周圍長著一圈白毛的老狒狒開懷大笑：你該吃掉那些豺，而不是讓豺吃掉你；跟我來，我教你怎麼對付那樣的人。牠把自己的尾巴纏在老虎的尾巴上以給他信心，與他一同朝洞穴走去——直到豺爸爸喊道，這就對了，猴兄弟，快把他帶過來；我們都餓得半死了——可你只帶一隻來是什麼意思？老虎倉皇逃走，拖著狒狒穿過叢林中最密最荊棘叢生的地方，直到許多英里之外，他所看到的猴子只剩下一截斷掉的尾巴，仍纏在他自己的尾巴上。

title.en: The Three Thieves at the Court of the Emperor
title.zh: 三賊晉見中國皇帝

region.en: Palace court of the Emperor of China (symbolic pin at Beijing)
region.zh: 中國皇帝宮廷（以北京為象徵定位）

period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story XIV

summary.en: Three master-thieves meet at an inn - one can lift eggs from under a sitting hen, one can cut the soles off a walking man's boots, one can eat his fill off a man's plate unseen - and enter the Emperor's service by undoing, at a single audience, three scandals their own night's work created: the vanished peahen's eggs, the soleless Prime Minister imprisoned for a breach of etiquette, and the starving Emperor. For a final test the Emperor demands three Treasury pearls by next evening - and the thieves simply join the huge inventory party in official robes, each pocketing a pearl already entered on the list.
summary.zh: 三個絕技神偷在客棧相識——掏孵蛋母雞之卵、割行人之靴底、就席偷食他人盤中餐——為揚名於中國皇帝，各自「作案」：偷走御雉蛋、剝去宰相靴底、吃光御膳，再在公開召見時「物歸原主」救出被囚的宰相與御廚。皇帝最後一試：明晚六時前取出三顆內庫珍珠——他們只須混入清點寶庫的數百官員之中，點入清單後各藏一顆便大功告成。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as heritage of the Tibet-China storytelling borderlands.

passages.text: The first Thief had lifted the Emperor's pea-hen's eggs from under the sitting hen without her knowing; the second had cut the soles off the Prime Minister's new boots, so that when he knelt to kow-tow the Emperor, thinking the breach deliberate, imprisoned him for beheading unless the soles were produced; the third had taken the food from each dish as it was placed on the table until the Emperor, unable to make a satisfactory meal, had ordered the whole of his Cooks and Chamberlains imprisoned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第一個賊在孵蛋的母雞毫不知情的情況下，從牠身下偷走了皇帝的雌孔雀蛋；第二個賊割下了宰相新靴子的鞋底，因此當宰相跪下向皇帝叩頭時，皇帝認為這裂口是故意的，便將他囚禁起來，除非交出鞋底否則就要斬首；第三個賊在每道菜剛擺上桌時就取走食物，直到皇帝無法好好吃一頓飯，下令把他的所有廚師和侍從都關進監獄。

passages.text: At the public audience the three produced eggs, soles and dinner-plate in turn; the Emperor laughed heartily, released the Prime Minister and all the domestic officials, and then, before rewarding them, set a further test: three of the pearls from his Treasury, enclosed within a treble wall ten fathoms high and guarded by companies of soldiers, must be produced by six o'clock next evening, or the three should be put to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在公開覲見時，三人依次拿出蛋、鞋底和餐盤；皇帝開懷大笑，釋放了首相和所有宮廷官員，然後在獎賞他們之前，又設下另一項考驗：必須在次日傍晚六點前取出他國庫中的三顆珍珠，這些珍珠被圍在十噚高的三重牆內，並由數隊士兵看守，否則三人將被處死。

passages.text: The Thieves suggested a complete enumeration of the Treasury first, so the pearls could be proved missing; and when hundreds of palace officials were called in to inventory it section by section, the three, dressed in the complete robes proper for a palace official, mingled unnoticed in the crowd, were allotted sections, and each, after first placing a large pearl upon his list, secreted it. At six o'clock next day they laid three pearls on the steps of the throne; the Treasurer found three pearls missing, and the Emperor raised the Thieves to high rank with lands and money.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 盜賊們建議先對國庫進行一次徹底的清點，這樣才能證明珍珠失竊；當數百名宮廷官員被召來逐區清點時，三人穿著完整的宮廷官員禮服，混在人群中未被察覺，被分配到各區，每人先在自己的清單上記下一顆大珍珠，然後將它藏了起來。次日六點，他們將三顆珍珠放在王座的台階上；司庫發現少了三顆珍珠，皇帝便將盜賊們提升到高位，並賜予土地和金錢。

title.en: The Boy with the Deformed Head and the Fairy Bride
title.zh: 畸形頭少年與仙女妻

region.en: Small lake in a herding valley (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 牧谷中小湖（象徵定位）

period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story XV

summary.en: A cowherd boy born with a head deformed fore and aft watches a great white Drake circle the lake daily, catches him in a yaks'-hair rope-and-loop ring, and rejects his gold for the middle of his three daughters - for nine years only. The fairy wife raises a palace from magic, but on the last morning of the ninth year the Boy wakes on a bleak hillside with nothing but memory. Wandering, he saves three young Gryphons from a Dragon, and the grateful Gryphon carries him up through the golden gates to plead his case before the assembly of the gods - where the fairy bride rushes into his arms, the conclave consents, and she becomes mortal to return with him, the two living to a good old age.
summary.zh: 牛倌少年天生頭部前後突出、面貌醜陋。他日日觀看白鴨繞湖三匝，以犛牛毛繩圈套住牠；不要金銀珠寶，只求仙女的三女兒中的二女兒為妻——限九年。仙妻以法術建起華美宮殿，然而第九年最後一夜醒來，一切都消失了，只餘記憶。流浪途中他斬殺欲吞三隻幼獅鷲的巨龍；感恩的獅鷲馱他穿過金門直上神國，眾神震怒之際仙女新娘撲入他懷中；神議決定放行，但嫁凡人者須失去仙性。她欣然應允，二人重返人間白頭偕老。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: The Boy wove a long rope of yaks' hair big enough to encircle the lake, with fine horsehair loops floating in the water; the Drake, caught, revealed himself a fairy King who descended daily to amuse himself by swimming round and round, and offered gold, silver, jewels and coral. The Boy laughed: I do not care at all for your gold or your jewels, but what I really want is a wife - and chose the middle of the three daughters, accepting the condition that a fairy can live with a mortal only nine years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 男孩用犛牛毛編了一條足以環繞湖泊的長繩，並在水中漂浮著精細的馬尾毛圈；那隻公鴨被捉住後，顯露自己是一位仙王，每日下凡繞湖游泳取樂，並獻上金、銀、珠寶和珊瑚。男孩笑道：我對你的金子和珠寶毫不在意，我真正想要的是一個妻子——於是他選了三個女兒中的老二，並接受了仙人是只能與凡人共同生活九年的條件。

passages.text: The fairy wife erected a magnificent palace by her magic and furnished it luxuriously; but when the nine years ended the young Man awoke on a bleak hillside near the spot where he had first conversed with the Fairy King - his palace, his servants, his horses and, worst of all, his beautiful wife had all disappeared utterly, and nothing remained but a memory.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 仙女妻子用魔法建起了一座宏偉的宮殿，並將其佈置得奢華舒適；但九年期滿時，年輕人在他最初與仙王交談之處附近的一片荒涼山坡上醒來——他的宮殿、僕人、馬匹，以及最糟的是，他美麗的妻子全都消失得無影無蹤，只剩下回憶。

passages.text: Half distracted he wandered until he found three young Gryphons terrorized by an immense Dragon crossing the lake to devour them; drawing his sword he engaged the monster single-handed and severed its head from its neck. The grateful parent Gryphons carried him through the great golden gates to the country of the gods, where the assembly rose in wrath at the introduction of a human being - and where the fairy bride, hiding till then, rushed forward and threw herself into her husband's arms. The conclave decided that as she desired to return of her own free will she must take the consequence and become mortal; she joyfully agreed, and the two were deposited near their old home, where they grew to a good old age.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他半瘋似地遊蕩，直到發現三隻年幼的獅鷲正被一條巨大的龍嚇得驚恐萬分，那龍正渡湖來吞食牠們；他拔出劍，獨自與那怪物交戰，將牠的頭從頸上砍下。心懷感激的獅鷲父母載他穿過巨大的金色大門，來到眾神之國，在那裡，眾神因一個人類的到來而憤怒地起身——而一直躲藏著的仙女新娘衝上前來，投入丈夫的懷抱。眾神會議決定，既然她自願回去，就必須承擔後果，變為凡人；她欣然同意，兩人被安置在他們舊居附近，在那裡他們活到了高齡。

title.en: The Prince and the Ogre's Castle
title.zh: 王子與食人魔城堡

region.en: Ogre's castle in a valley below a high pass (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 啞口之下谷中的魔堡（象徵定位）

period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story XVI

summary.en: A childless King buys nine pills from a Lama who is really a man-eating Ogre: three children, three foals and three pups are born, and after three years the Ogre claims the youngest of each. At the castle the boy-Prince performs the first tasks unafraid - a bundle of straw turns to wolves devouring the goat, soaked grain to wild cats destroying the fowls - and finds in a glass room a Princess who sleeps under an enchanted flower: the Ogre eats men's hearts and gains power only over servants who disobey, while his own life depends on a hidden mascot. She coaches the counter-tricks: ask the Ogre to lead the way round the stove in the dark, then ask him to demonstrate the kow-tow - and when his face touches the ground the third time, the Prince's sword takes his head. In the vaults the mascot is a beautiful boy with a goblet of crystal liquid, each drop a man's life; the victims' hearts eaten, one drop each restores the scores of bodies in the back chamber.
summary.zh: 無子的國王從假扮喇嘛的食人魔處求得九丸仙藥：王后、母馬、母犬各生三子；三年後魔依約索走最年幼的三者。少年王子在魔堡不為怪事所懼——草束化三狼食羊、濕糧化三野貓盡毀雞群——並在玻璃室喚醒被魔花催眠的公主。公主道破魔的規則：只有僕人抗命他才能吃其心；其命則繫於密藏的「命石」。她教王子以計反制：請魔先行繞灶、請魔示範磕頭——魔額第三次觸地時，王子揮劍斬首。地窖深處「命石」乃一美童手捧水晶杯，杯中滴滴皆人命；以一滴復一人，後屋數十具無心之身盡數甦醒。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: The Ogre, disguised as a holy Lama, gave the King nine pills - three for the Queen, three for the mare, three for the dog - and after three months a child was born to each, followed by two others at intervals of one month; at the end of three years the Ogre returned to demand the youngest son, the youngest horse and the youngest dog.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那食人魔偽裝成一位聖潔的喇嘛，給了國王九顆藥丸——三顆給王后，三顆給母馬，三顆給狗——三個月後，每個都生下了一個孩子，隨後每隔一個月又各生下兩個；三年期滿時，食人魔回來索要最小的兒子、最小的馬和最小的狗。

passages.text: The tasks the Ogre set grew stranger: a bundle of straw became three great wolves who devoured the goat and fled, and a handful of soaked grain became three wild cats who destroyed the fowls. The Prince pushed open the castle door and found in a glass room a beautiful lady asleep with a flower behind her ear; taking away the flower woke her, and she explained that the Lama was a wicked Ogre who partakes of nothing but men's hearts, and gains power over a human being only when that being directly disobeys his orders.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 魔王所出的難題愈發古怪：一捆稻草化作三隻大狼，吞吃了山羊後逃去；一把浸濕的穀粒化作三隻野貓，毀盡了家禽。王子推開城堡的門，在一間玻璃房裡見到一位美麗的女子沉睡著，耳後簪著一朵花；取走那朵花便喚醒了她，她解釋說，那位喇嘛是個邪惡的魔王，除了人心之外什麼都不吃，唯有當一個人直接違抗他的命令時，他才能對那人取得掌控之力。

passages.text: Ordered to walk three times round the great stove in the dark kitchen, the Prince asked the Ogre to precede and show him the way; ordered to kow-tow three times, the Prince asked to be taught, and as the Ogre's face touched the ground the third time he delivered a violent blow and severed the Ogre's head from his body. The mascot - the beautiful boy in the ninth subterranean chamber with a goblet of crystal liquid, each drop a man's life - was slain, and one drop sprinkled on each of the scores of bodies in the back chamber restored the Ogre's victims, who thanked the Prince and Princess and returned to their own homes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 魔王命王子在漆黑的廚房裡繞著那座大爐灶走三圈，王子便請魔王先行帶路；又命他叩三次頭，王子便請魔王教他如何叩拜，而當魔王第三次以面觸地時，王子猛力一擊，將魔王的頭從身軀上砍了下來。那護符——第九間地下密室裡那個捧著水晶杯的俊美男孩，杯中每一滴皆是一條人命——也被殺死，並將一滴灑在後室裡那數十具屍體上，使魔王的受害者盡皆復活，他們向王子與公主道謝，各自返回家園。

title.en: The Stone Lion of the Hillside
title.zh: 山腰石獅

region.en: Wooded hillside by a well-cultivated valley (symbolic pin in the Nyang valley)
region.zh: 年楚河谷旁山林（象徵定位）

period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story XVII

summary.en: Turned out by his clever, selfish elder brother, the dull younger son and his mother settle in a hillside hut; he chops wood, and finding a life-sized Lion carved in stone takes it for the mountain's guardian deity and lights candles to it. The Lion speaks and vomits a bucketful of gold with the warning that no single piece must fall to the ground; mother and son grow rich. The elder brother demands the secret, buys the largest bucket, and shakes the gold down until a piece slips off - the stream stops, the largest piece sticks in the Lion's throat, and the jaws close on his arm. Only when his wife, sold down to the last scrap, comes weeping that they must all starve does the Lion laugh - ha, ha! - and in the open jaws the man wrenches himself free.
summary.zh: 能幹而自私的兄長趕走老實的弟弟；弟弟與母親在山腳茅屋落腳，砍柴度日，遇見山石上刻的等身石獅，供燭參拜。石獅開口，以口吐金，但嚴令「一粒也不可落地」。母子因此致富；兄長聞訊討教，買了全鎮最大的桶，還要把金子搖實多裝——一粒金落地，金流即止，最大一粒卡在獅喉，獅口合攏咬住其臂。直到他妻子變賣殆盡、哭訴「一家都快餓死」，石獅忍俊不禁「哈哈」開口大笑——他趁隙抽臂而逃。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: Finding himself face to face with a large life-sized Lion carved out of the stone, the boy took it for the guardian deity of the mountain, lit two candles before it, and prostrated himself for renewed good fortune. The Lion opened its mouth and asked what he was doing there; told to bring a large bucket, the boy held it under the Lion's mouth and caught a stream of gold pieces, informing the Lion before the bucket was quite full, as on no account must a single morsel of gold fall to the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那男孩發現自己面對著一頭與真人等大、由石頭雕成的巨獅，便把它當作這座山的守護神，在它面前點燃兩支蠟燭，俯身叩拜以求增添福運。石獅張開口，問他在那裡做什麼；男孩奉命取來一隻大桶，便將桶舉在石獅嘴下，接住一股湧出的金幣，並在桶尚未裝滿之前便告知石獅，因為無論如何都不能讓哪怕一小塊金子落在地上。

passages.text: The elder brother bought the largest bucket to be had and shook the bucket slightly from time to time to make the gold level, so as to obtain a larger quantity; overcome by greed he could not bring himself to warn the Lion until the bucket brimmed over and a piece of gold fell to the ground. The stream ceased, the Lion said hoarsely that the largest piece of all had stuck in his throat and asked him to put his hand in and pull it out - and closed his stone jaws on the arm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 哥哥買來所能買到的最大一隻桶，並不時輕輕搖晃桶身，使金子平整，以便多得一些；他為貪念所驅，遲遲不肯出聲提醒石獅，直到桶滿溢出、一塊金子落在地上。金流戛然而止，石獅沙啞地說，最大的一塊卡在了牠的喉嚨裡，要他伸手進去把它掏出來——隨即以石頭般的上下顎咬住了他的手臂。

passages.text: His wife brought him food daily while she grew poorer and sold her household goods, until one morning she came weeping up the hill: there is not a scrap left to eat anywhere, and now nothing remains but for us to starve to death. The Lion was so tickled that he could not refrain from laughing - ha, ha! - and opened his great jaws; as quickly as he could, before the Lion had time to close his mouth again, the man withdrew his arm, and the forgiving younger brother eventually supplied him with a small farm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的妻子日日前來送飯，自己卻愈發貧困，變賣了家中器物，直到某天早晨她哭著走上山來：到處都找不到一點可吃的東西了，如今除了我們餓死之外，再無別的出路。石獅被逗得忍俊不禁，哈哈大笑——哈，哈！——張開了牠的大嘴；那人趁石獅還來不及合上嘴，便以最快的速度抽回了手臂，而寬宏大量的弟弟最終供給了他一座小農場。

title.en: The Lama's Servant Rin-dzin
title.zh: 喇嘛的僕人仁增

region.en: Lonely hill-top hermitage in Tibet (symbolic pin in the Tsari region)
region.zh: 藏地扎日一帶的孤山修行處（象徵定位）

period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story XVIII

summary.en: The holy Lama's meat-abstaining diet starves his joker of a servant Rin-dzin, who rigs a slip-knot rope through the floor and talks the meditating Lama into 'holding a neighbour's sheep' while he poicks it into strangling itself below; several days of mutton follow, until the shepherd boy witnesses the trick and the Lama dismisses him. On the road Rin-dzin falls in with a thief who plants him behind a fresh corpse and passes himself off as the long-lost son - asking the corpse itself, and getting the sepulchral 'You are' - then decamps with a bag of gold; Rin-dzin overtakes him, drops two boots along the road, and while the thief trudges back for the pair, rides off with the gold.
summary.zh: 持齋的喇嘛讓饞肉的滑頭僕人仁增餓得發慌；仁增把繩圈穿過樓板，哄沉思的喇嘛「替鄰居拴羊」，自己在樓下捅羊致其勒斃，吃了幾天羊肉。放羊娃窺破告發，喇嘛將他逐出。路上他遇一賊，二人合謀：仁增藏於新亡人之柩旁扮鬼，賊冒認失散多年的「弟弟」，向屍體問話得到陰森的「你是」——騙走一大袋金子。仁增借馬追趕，沿路丟下兩隻新靴；賊為撿成一雙回頭取靴，仁增便馱金而走。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: The Servant caught a strayed sheep, hitched a slip-knot round its neck with a rope let down through a hole in the floor, and asked the meditating Lama to hold the rope while he went to inform the owner - and poked the sheep with a sharp stick below, until the tug-of-war strangled it. When he returned he informed the Lama that the sheep had died a natural death while he was away, and for several days the Servant was able to eat his fill of excellent mutton; but the shepherd boy had seen all that happened through the window, and the Lama, much incensed, dismissed him on the spot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 僕人捉住一隻走失的羊，用一根從地板洞中垂下的繩子打了個活結套在羊脖子上，請正在打坐的喇嘛替他拉住繩子，自己則前去通知羊主——並在下方用一根尖棍戳那隻羊，直到這場拔河把羊勒死。他回來後告訴喇嘛，說他不在時那隻羊已自然死亡，一連數日，僕人都能飽餐一頓上好的羊肉；但那牧童已從窗外看見了發生的一切，喇嘛大為震怒，當場將他辭退。

passages.text: The Thief's plan was ready-made: the owner of a great house had died awaiting burial, leaving one daughter, a son long lost - so Rin-dzin climbed in by the window and hid near the corpse, and the Thief told the mourning girl he was her long-lost brother and proposed to consult the corpse of her father on the matter. Are you there, father, said the Thief as he entered the darkened room, and Rin-dzin, in a sepulchral voice, replied, Ah - and to the question whether the Thief was his long-lost son, answered, You are.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 小偷的計畫早已現成：有一戶大戶人家的主人已死、正待下葬，留下一名女兒，還有一個失散多年的兒子——於是仁欽爬上窗戶潛入屋內，躲在屍體附近，小偷則對哀悼中的女孩說，自己就是她失散多年的兄長，並提議就此事請教她父親的遺體。父親，你在嗎？小偷一邊走進昏暗的房間一邊說道，而仁欽以陰森如墓的聲音回答：啊——而對於小偷是否就是他失散多年的兒子這個問題，他答道：你就是。

passages.text: Pretending urgent business that very night, the Thief made over the house and landed property to his 'sister' and took as his share a heavy bag of gold - leaving Rin-dzin behind. Borrowing a horse, Rin-dzin galloped after him and, dropping a new boot in the middle of the road and the fellow-boot further on, concealed himself; the Thief, finding one boot, thought it useless, and only at the second, nearly worn out, went back for the first - whereupon Rin-dzin emerged, picked up the bag of gold, strapped it to his saddle and rode on his way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 小偷假稱當夜有急事，把房屋與地產都轉讓給他的「妹妹」，自己則分得一大袋金子——把仁欽留在了後頭。仁欽借了一匹馬，疾馳追趕他，並把一隻新靴子丟在路中央，把另一隻丟在更遠處，然後躲藏起來；小偷撿到一隻靴子，覺得沒用，直到撿到第二隻、幾乎磨損不堪時，才回頭去撿第一隻——就在這時仁欽現身，撿起那袋金子，把它綁在馬鞍上，繼續趕路。

title.en: The Country of the Mice
title.zh: 鼠之國

region.en: Rice country with a great frontier river (symbolic pin in southern Tibet)
region.zh: 藏南有界河的產糧之地（象徵定位）

period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story XIX

summary.en: A famine year sends the King of the Mice to the human King with a silk thread in place of a ceremonial scarf, to borrow a barnful of grain against the next harvest; hundreds of thousands of mice empty the barn in one night and repay with interest. When a richer enemy musters an army across the river, the Mouse-King asks for a hundred thousand foot-long sticks laid on the bank - and his subjects sail them across by night, gnawing bowstrings, musket-slimgs, fuses, pigtails and provisions until the camp wakes to find itself stripped and flees at the first bugle. The King builds the flood dam they ask for, bans cats on pain of death, and sends both kingdoms a yearly barnful in thanks.
