region.zh: 世界邊緣群山（象徵性定位於東部山地）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Ninurta's exploits (ETCSL c.1.6.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Asag, demon of stone and disease, boils the land's edge with fever; Ninurta, prompted by his mace Sharur, storms the mountain and destroys the demon and his stone army, river after river of battle.
summary.zh: 石與疫病之魔阿薩格令大地邊緣沸騰；尼努爾塔受神杖沙魯爾之激，攻入群山，層層河戰，終誅魔神及其石軍。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Asag rises in the mountains: his heat makes the land's edge boil, fevers run from river to river, and the stones rally to him. Ninurta's mace Sharur flies to him and speaks: the master must fight, for the demon defies the gods' order. Ninurta meets Asag by the rivers, forty and more, each battle a separate river-name; Asag's mother, weary of her son's deformity, works against him too. The warrior god prevails and the demon falls.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.6.2, the summons; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.6.2, the battle of the rivers; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿薩格（Asag）在山中興起：他的灼熱使大地邊緣沸騰，熱病從一條河蔓延到另一條河，石頭也聚集到他那一邊。尼努爾塔（Ninurta）的權杖沙魯爾（Sharur）飛到他身旁說道：主人必須一戰，因為這惡魔公然違抗眾神的秩序。尼努爾塔在河邊與阿薩格交鋒，那裡的河有四十條還多，每一場戰鬥都以一條河的名字命名；阿薩格的母親厭倦了兒子的畸形，也與他作對。這位戰神最終得勝，惡魔就此倒下。

functions: Chaoskampf myth legitimating Ninurta's war cult
Etiology of the river names and the eastern mountain ranges
Performed at Ninurta's temple festivals in Nippur

variants.name: Enuma Elish: Marduk and Tiamat
variants.summary: The Babylonian parallel battle against chaos.

canonical_translation: ETCSL team translation, Oxford, 2003-2006

primary_sources.citation: ETCSL c.1.6.2, trans. ETCSL team (2003-2006)

secondary_sources.work: The Treasures of Darkness
secondary_sources.citation: Thorkild Jacobsen, New Haven, 1976

title.en: The Stones Become Mountains
title.zh: 群石化為山嶽

region.en: The hursag, highlands east of Sumer (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫爾薩格高地（象徵性定位）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Ninurta's exploits, second half (ETCSL c.1.6.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Victorious, Ninurta piles the defeated stones into the hursag, the mountain barrier that dams the rivers and makes Sumer's flood-land fertile; Ninmah reproves him for his pride, and he makes peace with her.
summary.zh: 大捷之後，尼努爾塔以敗亡之石堆成庫爾薩格山脈，攔住河流，令蘇美沖積平原沃野千里；寧瑪斥其傲慢，二神和解。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Ninurta heaps up the fallen stones into the hursag, the great mountain wall: it dams the floodwaters, holds back the waters of the deep, and turns the plain below into fertile flood-land for Sumer's fields. The stones themselves are praised in turn — each named for its new role, from flint to porphyry — as the spoils of chaos are organized into landscape. Ninmah, the mother goddess, rebukes the victor for the boastful massing of stones, and Ninurta makes peace, dedicating the hursag to her. The poem closes with the dedication: the mountain is Ninmah's seat, its produce her gift, and Ninurta returns to Nippur in triumph with the order of the world renewed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.6.2, the mountain-building; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.6.2, the stone catalogue and Ninmah's rebuke; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.6.2, dedication; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 尼努爾塔將倒下的石頭堆積成胡爾薩格（hursag），即那道巨大的山牆：它攔住洪水，擋住深淵之水，並將下方的平原變成肥沃的泛濫之地，供蘇美爾的田野之用。石頭本身也逐一受到讚頌——從燧石到斑岩，每一種都依其新的角色而被命名——混沌的戰利品就這樣被組織成地貌。母神寧瑪赫（Ninmah）責備這位勝利者誇耀般地堆積石頭，尼努爾塔遂與之和解，將胡爾薩格奉獻給她。詩篇以這奉獻作結：這座山是寧瑪赫的居所，其出產是她的贈禮，而尼努爾塔則帶著煥然一新的世界秩序，凱旋返回尼普爾（Nippur）。

functions: Etiology of the eastern mountain ranges and the flood-plain
Reconciliation myth of Ninurta and Ninhursag
Catalogue liturgy performed with the exploits at Nippur

variants.summary: The Babylonian parallel of building the world from the slain chaos-monster.

title.en: Ninurta's Return to Nippur
title.zh: 尼努爾塔凱旋尼普魯

region.en: Nippur, Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Ninurta's return to Nibru (ETCSL c.1.6.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Returning from battle, Ninurta stops at Nippur to be washed and blessed before entering the Ekur; his rituals of return — ablution, anointing, sacrifice — are narrated as the liturgy of the homecoming god.
summary.zh: 征戰歸來，尼努爾塔先於尼普魯受淨洗祝福，方入埃庫爾神殿；歸返禮儀——洗滌、敷油、獻祭——一一鋪陳，如凱旋神祇之禮書。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ritual narrative; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Ninurta, the warrior fresh from the mountains, halts outside the city; before entering the Ekur he must be purified: he is washed, anointed with fragrant oil, and dressed in clean linen. The city prepares his table: grain, cream and beer are offered, the Anuna gods praise him, and Ninurta decrees abundance for the fields and the house of Enlil as his gift of return. The hymn closes with the king's participation: the ruler who performs the warrior's return rites with Ninurta's zeal shall see the house of Enlil established and the year renewed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.6.1, purification; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.6.1, banquet and blessing; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.6.1, royal application; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 甫自山間歸來的戰士尼努爾塔，在城外止步；進入埃庫爾之前，他必須先行潔淨：他沐浴、塗抹香膏，並換上潔淨的亞麻衣。城中為他備妥筵席：獻上穀物、乳脂與啤酒，安努納諸神讚頌他，尼努爾塔則以其歸來之禮，為田野與恩利爾之家頒布豐饒。頌歌以國王的參與作結：凡以尼努爾塔之熱忱舉行戰士歸來儀式的君王，必見恩利爾之家得以建立、年歲得以更新。

functions: Return liturgy of the god and, by reflection, of the king
Charter of the purification rites before temple entry
Blessing text for abundance decreed by the war god

variants.name: Enki's journey to Nibru
variants.summary: The pilgrimage genre's senior member.

canonical_translation: ETCSL team translation, Oxford, 2003-2006

primary_sources.citation: ETCSL c.1.6.1, trans. ETCSL team (2003-2006)

secondary_sources.work: The Treasures of Darkness
secondary_sources.citation: Thorkild Jacobsen, New Haven, 1976

title.en: Ninurta and the Turtle: The Trick of Enki
title.zh: 尼努爾塔與龜：恩基之計

region.en: Marshes of the Abzu, Eridu, Iraq
region.zh: 埃利都阿卜祖沼澤（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Ninurta and the turtle (ETCSL c.1.6.3)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Ninurta, swollen with victory over Asag, schemes to seize the powers; Enki sets a great turtle in the marsh, which digs a pit behind the strutting god and grips his foot — the proud warrior is caught in a ditch and learns that craft outruns strength.
summary.zh: 誅阿薩格後志得意滿的尼努爾塔欲奪權柄；恩基於沼澤布一巨龜，在其身後掘陷坑、鉗其足——傲慢戰神陷於土坑，方悟智勝於力。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Ninurta, having destroyed Asag, schemes with his heart against Enki's household, coveting the powers. Enki hears of it and smiles; he sets a great turtle in the Abzu's marshes to wait for the god. Ninurta struts through the marshland of victory; behind him the turtle digs a pit, before him it grips his foot, and the god falls in and cannot get out, however he strains and struggles. Enki arrives and mocks the captor caught: who dug the ditch? who grips the foot? Ninurta, humiliated, is released only to sit silent; the tale closes with the triumph of craft over strength.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.6.3, the scheme and the trap; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.6.3, the pit; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.6.3, the mockery; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 尼努爾塔毀滅阿薩格之後，心中暗自圖謀恩基的家業，覬覦其神力。恩基聞之而笑；他在阿普蘇的沼澤中安置一隻巨龜，等候此神。尼努爾塔昂首闊步穿過勝利的沼澤地；巨龜在他身後掘坑，在他身前咬住他的腳，此神遂跌入坑中，任憑如何使勁掙扎也無法脫身。恩基來到，譏笑這被擒的捕者：是誰掘了溝渠？是誰咬住了腳？尼努爾塔受辱，獲釋後只能默然坐著；故事以巧智勝過蠻力作結。

functions: Comic check on the war god's cultic pride
Etiology of the turtle's cunning in exorcistic lore
Banquet recitation for Enki's festivals

variants.name: The heron and the turtle
variants.summary: A fable of the turtle's cunning in a natural setting.

title.en: Nanna-Suen's Journey to Nippur
title.zh: 南納-蘇恩赴尼普魯之行

region.en: Ur to Nippur by river, Iraq
region.zh: 烏爾至尼普魯河道（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Nanna-Suen's journey to Nibru (ETCSL c.1.5.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The moon god loads his barge at Ur and sails up the river to Nippur, pausing at five sanctuaries where each goddess blesses the boat; at the Ekur, Enlil gives the voyage prosperity, and Nanna returns with fat cattle and grain for his city.
summary.zh: 月神於烏爾裝載巨舟，溯河而上；沿途五聖所，各女神依次祝福。抵埃庫爾，恩利爾賜旅途昌盛；南納載肥牛佳穀歸城。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ritual narrative; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Nanna-Suen, lord of Ur, readies the barge: all kinds of goods are loaded, the crew assigned, and the god sails up the river past the marshes toward Nippur, stopping at five sanctuaries on the way. At each stopping place a goddess receives him — Ninmah, Ningal and the rest — and blesses the boat, the cargo and the road; the god offers sacrifices and continues north with his retinue. At the Ekur, Enlil receives his son and grants the fates of prosperity for the voyage; Nanna returns downriver to Ur with fat cattle and choice grain, and the city celebrates the moon god's advent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.5.1, departure and voyage; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.5.1, the five sanctuaries; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.5.1, arrival and return; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 烏爾之主南納—蘇恩備妥駁船：各類貨物裝載上船，船員分派妥當，此神便溯河而上，越過沼澤朝尼普爾前行，沿途在五處聖所停泊。每到一處停泊之地，皆有一位女神迎接他——寧瑪赫、寧加爾及其餘諸神——並祝福船隻、貨物與道路；此神獻上祭品，率隨從繼續北行。在埃庫爾，恩利爾迎接其子，並賜下航行順遂昌盛的命運；南納帶著肥壯的牛群與精選的穀物順流返回烏爾，全城慶祝月神的到來。

functions: Procession liturgy of the moon god's journey to Nippur
Charter of the Ur-Nippur river cult route
Blessing text for boats, cargo and travel

title.en: The Herds of Nanna
title.zh: 南納的牛群

region.en: Cattle pens of Ur, Iraq
region.zh: 烏爾牛欄（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The herds of Nanna (ETCSL c.1.5.x)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Nanna's great cattle-pens at Ur are catalogued — pen after pen of white-faced bulls and speckled cows — and the fattened herd is presented to Enlil: the moon god's wealth in livestock, praised as the glory of his city.
summary.zh: 烏魯克月神南納的牛欄一一點數：白面公牛、斑點母牛，欄欄相接；肥育之群獻於恩利爾——月神之畜產豐盈，譽為其城之榮光。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The herds of Nanna are praised pen by pen: the white-faced bulls of the moon's color, the speckled cows, the fattened steers — each pen with its name, its keeper and its tally. The chosen beasts are driven to Nippur and presented to Enlil as the moon god's tribute; the god of herds is thus the purveyor of the high temple's offerings, and Ur's wealth in cattle is celebrated as his gift.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.5.3, the cattle catalogue; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.5.3, the presentation; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 南納的畜群逐欄受到讚頌：月色的白面公牛、斑點母牛、肥育的閹牛——每一欄皆有其名、其牧人與其數目。精選的牲畜被趕往尼普爾，作為月神的貢品獻給恩利爾；畜群之神因而成為高廟祭品的供應者，烏爾牛群的富庶則被頌揚為他的恩賜。

functions: Festival liturgy of the moon god's herds
Administrative hymn of Ur's cattle economy
Tribute narrative for the Enlil offerings

title.en: The Song of the Hoe
title.zh: 鋤之歌

region.en: Nippur, Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The song of the hoe (ETCSL c.5.5.4)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Enlil forms the hoe from a lump of clay of heaven and earth and creates with it the first men, the rivers, the temples and the underworld's office — the humble tool celebrated as the instrument of all creation.
summary.zh: 恩利爾以天地之泥塑鋤，以之造出最初的人類、河流、神殿與冥界職司——卑微小器被頌為開天闢地之器。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Enlil takes a lump of the earth that was separated from heaven and shapes the hoe: he creates with it the first men, splits the canals, and founds the temples — the tool of the digger is the tool of the maker of the world. The hoe is praised as the builder of every city, the digger of every grave, the instrument of birth and burial alike: with it Enlil assigns the underworld its officers and the earth its inhabitants.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.5.4, the hoe's creation; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.5.4, the catalogue of works; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 恩利爾取來一塊自天分離而出的泥土，塑成鋤頭：他以此創造最初的人類，開鑿運河，奠定神廟——挖掘者之器，即世界創造者之器。鋤頭受讚為每座城市的建造者、每座墳墓的挖掘者、生與葬皆用的器具：恩利爾藉它為冥界指派官吏，為大地安置居民。

functions: Etiological hymn dignifying corvee labor as cosmogony
Creation text of the hoe as the first instrument
Performed with the tools' blessing rites at New Year

variants.name: Enki and Ninmah (creation from clay)
variants.summary: The parallel creation-from-clay myth.

canonical_translation: ETCSL team translation, Oxford, 2003-2006

primary_sources.citation: ETCSL c.5.5.4, trans. ETCSL team (2003-2006)

secondary_sources.work: The Harps that Once...
secondary_sources.citation: Thorkild Jacobsen, New Haven, 1987

title.en: Nungal in the Ekur: The Prison Goddess
title.zh: 寧嘎勒於埃庫爾：監獄女神

region.en: Prison-house of the Ekur, Nippur, Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯埃庫爾監獄（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Nungal in the Ekur (ETCSL c.4.28.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Nungal, daughter of Ereshkigal, is installed by Enlil in her prison-house at the Ekur: she tests the wicked in her dark house, humbles the guilty, and releases the true-hearted — a goddess of justice whose jail is an ordeal.
summary.zh: 埃列什基伽勒之女寧嘎勒，受恩利爾安置於埃庫爾監獄：於幽暗之殿驗證惡者、挫其驕氣、釋放真心之人——她的牢獄是正義的熔爐。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Enlil installs Nungal, daughter of Ereshkigal, in her house of judgment beside the Ekur: the prison-house where the guilty are held for trial, its gates dark, its records kept in her own hand. In her dark house she humbles the wicked and tests them as metal in fire; the true-hearted she releases with honor, the guilty she keeps for the day of reckoning — the prison an ordeal of the goddess's justice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.28.1, installation; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.28.1, the ordeal; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 恩利爾將埃列什基伽勒之女農加爾安置於埃庫爾旁她的審判之屋：那是囚禁罪人以待審判的牢獄，其門幽暗，其卷宗由她親手掌管。在她幽暗的屋中，她使惡人屈膝，如以火試煉金屬般考驗他們；她釋放心地純正者並予以尊榮，將有罪者留待清算之日——牢獄乃女神正義的試煉。

functions: Hymn and charter of the temple prison's judicial role
Ordeal theology: testing the heart in the goddess's house
Link between underworld lineage and city justice

variants.name: Nungal in the Ekur (Eanna version)
variants.summary: Later recensions locate her house at Uruk's Eanna.

canonical_translation: ETCSL team translation, Oxford, 2003-2006

primary_sources.citation: ETCSL c.4.28.1, trans. ETCSL team (2003-2006)

secondary_sources.work: Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia
secondary_sources.citation: Jeremy Black and Anthony Green, London, 1992, entry 'Nungal'

title.en: Utu the Sun Rises
title.zh: 烏圖日出頌

region.en: Larsa temple of the sun, Iraq
region.zh: 拉爾薩太陽神殿（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A hymn to Utu (Utu hymns, ETCSL c.4.32.x)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The sun god rises from his bedchamber: he lights the great heaven and earth, the underworld's gates and the traveler's road; he judges all and helps all — the hymn greets the dawn as the daily return of justice.
summary.zh: 太陽神自寢殿起身：照亮天地、冥門與旅人之路；裁斷萬物、庇護眾生——頌詩迎接黎明，如正義之每日重臨。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Utu rises from his bedchamber in the east: he puts on his crown of radiance, takes the decisive word, and lights the great heaven and earth — the eyes of the world open with him. His light reaches everywhere: the highways of the land, the waters below, the gates of the netherworld's river. He sees the deeds of men and gods and judges them; the orphan and the widow he watches over, and the traveler he guides.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.32.1, sunrise; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.32.1, the light's reach and judgment; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 烏圖自東方的寢室升起：他戴上光輝之冠，作出決斷之言，照亮了偉大的天地——世人的雙眼隨他一同睜開。他的光無所不至：境內的大道、下方的眾水、冥界之河的門戶。他看見人與神的作為並加以審判；孤兒與寡婦由他看顧，旅人由他引導。

functions: Morning liturgy of the sun cult at Larsa and Sippar
Charter of Utu's offices: light, judgment, protection of travelers
Oath text: the sun as witness in legal rites

variants.name: Shamash hymn (Akkadian)
variants.summary: The Babylonian sun god's hymn in the same judicial register.

canonical_translation: ETCSL team translation, Oxford, 2003-2006

primary_sources.citation: ETCSL c.4.32.1, trans. ETCSL team (2003-2006)

secondary_sources.work: The Treasures of Darkness
secondary_sources.citation: Thorkild Jacobsen, New Haven, 1976

title.en: A Hymn to Nergal of Kutha
title.zh: 庫薩內爾伽勒頌

region.en: Kutha, Iraq
region.zh: 庫薩（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A hymn to Nergal (ETCSL c.4.15.x)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Nergal, lord of the Meslam temple at Kutha, is praised as the fear of the land and the terror of the battlefield: his heat is the plague wind, his face the burning sun of noon, and the hymn petitions the dread god for mercy.
summary.zh: 庫薩梅斯拉姆神殿之主內爾伽勒，被譽為國之懼、戰場之怖：其熱為疫風，其容如正午烈日；頌詩向可畏之神祈求恩慈。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Nergal, lord of Meslam, is hailed as the fear of the land: his is the heat that withers the harvest, the plague wind, the sun of noon that no man withstands. Yet the hymn's petition is mercy: the lord who punishes can spare, the god of the battle's terror can guard his city, and his worshipers ask him to turn his face kindly upon Kutha.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.15.1, praise; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.15.1, petition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 涅伽爾，梅斯拉姆之主，被尊為全地之畏：枯焦收成的酷熱歸於他，瘟疫之風歸於他，無人能抵擋的正午之陽歸於他。然而頌歌所祈求的是慈悲：施罰之主能寬赦，戰慄之神能護衛其城，他的敬拜者求他慈顏眷顧庫塔。

functions: Appeasement liturgy of the plague and war god
Charter of the Meslam temple cult at Kutha

variants.name: Erra and Ishum
variants.summary: The Babylonian plague god's epic in the same fearsome register.

canonical_translation: ETCSL team translation, Oxford, 2003-2006

primary_sources.citation: ETCSL c.4.15.1, trans. ETCSL team (2003-2006)

secondary_sources.citation: Jeremy Black and Anthony Green, London, 1992, entry 'Nergal'

title.en: The Boy Who Set a Snare for the Sun
title.zh: 為太陽設網的男孩

region.en: Earth's eastern edge where the sun rises (symbolic pin at dawn horizon)
region.zh: 太陽升起的大地東緣（象徵性定位於黎明的地平線）

period: From the Odjibwa (Schoolcraft 1856); a myth of the origin of the dormouse

source.work: H. R. Schoolcraft, The Myth of Hiawatha, and Other Oral Legends (1856), 'The Sun-Catcher'

summary.en: When the animals reigned, a pygmy brother and sister are the last humans. The boy shoots snow birds for a coat, naps on a melted knoll, and wakes to find the hot sun has singed his bird-skin coat binding him fast; he fasts ten days on each side and then bids his sister make him a snare for the sun. Deer sinew will not do, her hair will not do - at last she twists a cord from her own body, which he draws through his lips, turning it into red metal. He snares the sun at the earth's rim so it does not rise; the animal council sends the dormouse - then the largest animal in the world, mountain-like - whose smoking back is burned to heaps of ashes as it cuts the cord; freed, the sun rises, and the dormouse has remained tiny ever since: men call it Kug-e-been-gwa-kwa, the blind woman.
summary.zh: 群獸統治大地時，一對侏儒姊弟是僅存的人類。弟弟射雪鳥製衣，在雪融的高丘小憩，醒來發現烈日把他的鳥皮衣烤得緊束其身；他兩側各齋戒十日，命姊姊為太陽設網。鹿筋不中用，頭髮不中用——最後她自身抽絲搓繩，弟弟以唇拉引，繩遂化為紅銅。他在大地邊緣縛住太陽，日遂不升；獸會遣當時世上最大的動物——鼯鼠——前去割繩，其背被烈日烤成灰燼之丘；太陽得釋而升，鼯鼠從此變得極小，人稱之為「盲婦」。

sensitivity.note: Odjibwa sun-snare myth (Schoolcraft 1856); public domain. Anchor record of the world-wide 'sun captured' cluster (cf. polynesian Maui).

passages.text: At the time when the animals reigned in the earth, they had killed all but a girl, and her little brother, and these two were living in fear and seclusion. The boy was a perfect pigmy, and never grew beyond the stature of a small infant, but the girl increased with her years, so that the labor of providing food and lodging devolved wholly on her. She made him a bow and arrows, and said to him one day, 'I will leave you behind where I have been chopping - you must hide yourself, and you will soon see the Gitshee-gitshee-gaun-ia-see-ug, or snow birds... Shoot one of them and bring it home.' He obeyed her, and at nightfall came in exultingly and threw down one of the birds which he had killed: 'My sister, I wish you to skin it and stretch the skin, and when I have killed more, I will have a coat made out of them.'
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 239-240; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當走獸統治大地之時，牠們殺盡了眾生，只餘一個女孩和她的幼弟，這兩人懷著恐懼、離群索居。那男孩是個十足的侏儒，始終長不過一個小嬰兒的身量，女孩卻隨年歲漸長，於是供給衣食的勞苦全落在她一人身上。她為他做了一張弓和幾支箭，有一天對他說：『我要把你留在我砍柴的地方——你得躲好，不久你就會看見吉奇—吉奇—岡—尼亞—西—烏格，也就是雪鳥……射下一隻帶回家來。』他照她的話做了，黃昏時分興高采烈地進來，扔下一隻他射殺的鳥：『姊姊，我要你把牠剝了皮、把皮撐開，等我多殺幾隻，我就要用牠們做一件外衣。』

passages.text: After walking a long time and meeting nothing, he became tired, and lay down on a knoll, where the sun had melted the snow. He fell fast asleep; and while sleeping, the sun beat so hot upon him that it singed and drew up his bird-skin coat, so that when he awoke and stretched himself, he felt bound in it, as it were. He flew into a passion, and upbraided the sun, and vowed vengeance against it. 'Do not think you are too high,' said he, 'I shall revenge myself.' He lay down as one that fasts, and did not stir for ten days, though she tried all she could to arouse him; at the end of ten days he turned over, and then lay ten days on the other side. When he got up, he told his sister to make him a snare, for he meant to catch the sun.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 240-241; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他走了很久，什麼也沒遇見，漸漸疲倦，便躺在一處太陽融了雪的小丘上。他沉沉睡去；睡著時，太陽炙熱地曬在他身上，把他那件鳥皮外衣烤得焦捲起來，以致他醒來伸展身子時，覺得自己彷彿被裹縛在衣中。他勃然大怒，責罵太陽，發誓要向它報仇。『別以為你高不可及，』他說，『我定要報復。』他像齋戒者那樣躺下，一連十天不動，任她千方百計想喚醒他；十天期滿，他翻了個身，又在另一側躺了十天。起身之後，他告訴姊姊為他做一個套索，因為他打算捕捉太陽。

passages.text: She said she had nothing; but finally recollected a little piece of dried deer's sinew, which she soon made into a string suitable for a noose; but the moment she showed it to him, he told her it would not do. She said she had nothing - nothing at all; at last she thought of her hair, and pulling some of it out of her head made a string; but he instantly said it would not answer. She went out of the lodge, and said to herself, while she was all alone, 'Now obewy indapin' - from my body I will take something. This she did, and twisting it into a tiny cord, she handed it to her brother. The moment he saw this curious braid he was delighted: 'It will do,' he said, and immediately put it to his mouth and began pulling it through his lips; and as fast as he drew it he changed it into a red metal cord, which he wound around his body and shoulders. He then prepared himself, and set out a little after midnight, that he might catch the sun before it rose: he fixed his snare on a spot just where the sun would strike the land, as it rose above the earth's disk; and sure enough, he caught the sun, so that it was held fast in the cord, and did not rise.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, p. 241; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她說她什麼也沒有；但終於想起一小段乾鹿筋，很快便把它搓成適合作套索的繩子；可是她剛拿給他看，他就說這不行。她說她什麼也沒有——什麼都沒有；最後她想到了自己的頭髮，從頭上拔下一些搓成繩子；但他立刻說這也不合用。她走出屋外，獨自一人時自言自語道：『Now obewy indapin』——我要從我身上取一樣東西。她果真如此做了，把它捻成一根細繩，遞給弟弟。他一看見這奇特的編繩便大喜：『這就行了，』他說，隨即把它放到嘴邊，從唇間抽拉過去；他抽得多快，它就變成一根紅色金屬的繩索，他把繩索纏繞在身上和肩上。隨後他準備妥當，在午夜剛過便出發，好在太陽升起之前捉住它：他把套索安在太陽升出地盤、恰好照臨地面的那一點上；果然，他捉住了太陽，太陽被繩索牢牢套住，無法升起。

passages.text: The animals who ruled the earth were immediately put into a great commotion. They had no light. They called a council to debate upon the matter, and to appoint some one to go and cut the cord - for this was a very hazardous enterprise, as the rays of the sun would burn whoever came so near to them. At last the dormouse undertook it - for at this time the dormouse was the largest animal in the world: when it stood up it looked like a mountain. When it got to the place where the sun was snared, its back began to smoke and burn with the intensity of the heat, and the top of its carcass was reduced to enormous heaps of ashes. It succeeded, however, in cutting the cord with its teeth, and freeing the sun, but it was reduced to a very small size, and has remained so ever since. Men call it the Kug-e-been-gwa-kwa - the blind woman.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 241-242; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 統治大地的走獸頓時陷入大騷動。牠們沒有了光。牠們召開會議商議此事，並指派一名前去割斷繩索——因為這是極其危險的差事，誰靠得那麼近，太陽的光芒就會灼傷誰。最後由睡鼠承擔此事——因為當時睡鼠是世界上最大的動物：牠站起來時宛如一座山。牠來到太陽被套住的地方，背脊因酷熱而開始冒煙燃燒，牠的身軀頂部化成了堆積如山的灰燼。然而牠終究用牙齒割斷了繩索，放出了太陽，但牠自己卻縮得極小，此後一直如此。人們稱牠為庫格—賓—瓜—夸——盲婦。

title.en: Eroneniera: An Indian Visit to the Great Spirit (Told by Pontiac, 1763)
title.zh: 伊羅尼埃拉：拜見生命之主（龐蒂亞克1763年所述）

region.en: Mountain of marvellous whiteness (symbolic pin in the upper Great Lakes)
region.zh: 奇白如雪的高山（象徵性定位於上大湖區）

period: Told by Pontiac to the assembled Indians in 1763, to enlist them against the English transfer of the country (recorded by Schoolcraft, 1856)

source.work: H. R. Schoolcraft, The Myth of Hiawatha, and Other Oral Legends (1856), 'Eroneniera; or, an Indian visit to the Great Spirit'

summary.en: An Indian resolved to see the Master of Life follows three paths for as many days, past fires issuing from the ground, until a mountain of marvellous whiteness rises before him, where a dazzling woman directs him to strip, wash in the river, and climb with left hand and foot only. Admitted through the gate by a man dressed all in white, he is seated on a gold-bordered hat by the Master of Life, who proclaims the moral laws - no drunkenness, one wife, no medicine song ('it is to the Manito that you speak') - commands the Indians to drive off the invaders, and gives him a written prayer to teach to all the Indians, morning and evening.
summary.zh: 一位印第安人立志面見生命之主，循三條路各行一日，經過地底噴火之處，終於望見一座奇白的高山；山上光豔的女子命他卸除衣裝、在河中淨身，僅以左手左足攀頂。白袍男子啟門引入，生命之主命他坐在鑲金的帽子上，宣布道德律令——戒酗酒、一夫一妻、禁唱藥歌（「你們是在對惡靈說話」）——並命印第安人驅逐入侵者，賜他一篇書寫的祈禱文，命他朝夕教授給所有印第安人。

sensitivity.note: Schoolcraft 1856; public domain. Schoolcraft notes Pontiac told this to the assembled Indians in 1763 to enlist resistance to the English - a political theophany of record.

passages.text: He walked a long time without being discouraged, having always a firm conviction that he should attain his aim. On the evening of the eighth day, at sunset, he stopped as usual on the bank of a brook, at the entrance of a little prairie, and perceived at the other end three very wide and well-beaten paths; the darker it grew, the more distinct were those paths, which surprised, nay, even frightened him. He remembered his dream, and thought that his only aim in undertaking his journey was to see the Master of Life. He left his encampment and fire, and took the widest of the paths; he followed it until the middle of the day, when he suddenly perceived a large fire coming from under ground, and, as it appeared to increase as he drew nearer, he was so overcome with fear that he turned back and took the widest of the other two paths - in which, after the same space of time, he perceived a similar spectacle, and was obliged to take the third path.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 252-253; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他走了很久，毫不气馁，始终坚定地相信他必能达成目的。到了第八天傍晚，日落时分，他照例在一处小溪岸边停下，那是在一片小草原的入口处，他望见草原的另一端有三条又宽又踩得结实的路径；天色越暗，那些路径就越发清晰，这令他惊讶，甚至使他害怕。他想起自己的梦，心想他踏上旅程的唯一目的就是去见生命之主。他离开自己的营地和火堆，走上最宽的那条路；他沿着它走到正午，忽然看见一团大火从地下冒出，而且随着他越走越近，那火似乎越发旺盛，他恐惧至极，便转身折回，走上另外两条路中最宽的一条——走了同样长的时间后，他又看见了同样的景象，于是不得不走上第三条路。

passages.text: All at once, a mountain of a marvellous whiteness burst upon his sight. At the foot he saw no signs of a road; looking on all sides he perceived a female seated upon the mountain, her beauty dazzling, and the whiteness of her garments surpassing that of snow. The woman said to him in his own language, 'You appear surprised to find no longer a path to reach your wishes... The way which leads to his abode is upon this mountain. To ascend it, you must undress yourself completely, and leave all your accoutrements and clothing at the foot... You will then go and wash yourself in the river which I am now showing you, and afterward ascend the mountain.' He asked how he was to accomplish it; she replied that if he really wished to see the Master of Life, he must, in mounting, only use his left hand and foot. When at the top he found himself alone, without a guide; three unknown villages were in sight, constructed on a different plan from his own, much handsomer and more regular.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 253-254; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 忽然间，一座奇异地洁白的山峦映入他的眼帘。山脚下他看不到任何道路的痕迹；他环顾四周，看见一位女子坐在山上，她的美貌令人目眩，她的衣裳比雪还要洁白。那女子用他自己的语言对他说：‘你似乎很惊讶，发现再也没有路径可以达成你的愿望了……通往他居所的路就在这座山上。要登上它，你必须把全身衣服脱去，把你所有的装备和衣物都留在山脚下……然后你要去在我此刻指给你看的河里洗净身子，之后登山。’他问该如何做到；她回答说，如果他真想去见生命之主，那么在登山时只可用左手和左脚。到了山顶，他发现自己孤身一人，没有向导；眼前有三座陌生的村落，其建造方式与他自己的村落不同，要漂亮、整齐得多。

passages.text: When about half way from the top of the mountain, he recollected that he was naked, and was afraid to proceed; but a voice told him to advance, and have no apprehensions. He proceeded to a place which appeared to be the gate of the village; the gate opened, and the Indian saw coming towards him a handsome man dressed all in white, who took him by the hand and said he was going to satisfy his wishes by leading him to the presence of the Master of Life. They arrived at a place of unequalled beauty. The Indian there saw the Master of Life, who took him by the hand and gave him for a seat a hat bordered with gold.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 254-255; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 当他大约走到离山顶一半路程时，他想起自己赤身裸体，便害怕再往前走；但有一个声音叫他继续前进，不要畏惧。他走到一处似乎是村落大门的地方；门开了，那印第安人看见一个身穿白衣的俊美男子朝他走来，那人牵起他的手，说他要满足他的愿望，带他去见生命之主。他们来到一处美得无与伦比的地方。那印第安人在那里见到了生命之主，主牵起他的手，给他一个镶着金边的帽子作座位。

passages.text: God said to him, 'I am the Master of Life, whom thou wishest to see... I am the Maker of Heaven and earth, the trees, lakes, rivers, men, and all that thou seest or hast seen on the earth or in the heavens; and because I love you, you must do my will... I hate you to drink as you do, until you lose your reason; I wish you not to fight one another; you take two wives, or run after other people's wives; you do wrong... When you go to war, you juggle, you sing the medicine song, thinking you speak to me; you deceive yourselves; it is to the Manito that you speak; he is a wicked spirit who induces you to evil. The land on which you are, I have made for you, not for others: wherefore do you suffer the whites to dwell upon your lands?... Drive them away; wage war against them. I love them not. They know me not... Here is a written prayer which I give thee; learn it by heart, and teach it to all the Indians and children... It must be repeated morning and evening.' His conductor then came, and leading him to the foot of the mountain, told him to take his garments and return to his village; having entered the village, he went immediately to the chief's wigwam and delivered to him the prayer and laws intrusted to his care by the Master of Life.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 255-257; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 神对他说：‘我就是生命之主，你渴望见的那一位……我是天地的创造者，是树木、湖泊、河流、人，以及你在地上或天上所见或曾见的一切的创造者；因为我爱你们，你们必须遵行我的旨意……我厌恶你们像那样饮酒，直到失去理智；我希望你们不要互相争斗；你们娶两个妻子，或追逐别人的妻子；你们做错了……当你们去打仗时，你们耍弄巫术，唱那药歌，以为是在对我说话；你们是在欺骗自己；你们是在对玛尼托说话；他是个邪恶的精灵，引诱你们作恶。你们所居的这片土地，是我为你们造的，不是为别人造的：那么你们为何容忍白人住在你们的土地上？……把他们赶走；向他们开战。我不爱他们。他们不认识我……这里有一篇写下的祷文，我赐给你；你要把它记在心里，并教导所有的印第安人和孩童……必须早晚诵念。’随后他的引路者来了，领他下山到山脚，叫他穿上衣服回到自己的村落；他进了村，立刻前往酋长的棚屋，把生命之主托付给他的祷文和律法交给了酋长。

title.en: The Six Hawks; or, Broken Wing: An Allegory of Fraternal Affection
title.zh: 六鷹：折翼——手足之情之喻

region.en: Northern woods where the falcons winter in a hollow tree
region.zh: 北地樹洞中越冬的鷹巢

period: An allegory of fraternal affection collected by Schoolcraft (1856)

source.work: H. R. Schoolcraft, The Myth of Hiawatha, and Other Oral Legends (1856), 'The Six Hawks'

summary.en: Both parent falcons are shot in one day, leaving six young birds. The eldest, Meeji-geeg-wona the Gray Eagle, feeds the brood until he breaks a wing pouncing on a swan; the brothers refuse the southern journey: 'If the climate kills you, it shall kill us.' They winter together in a hollow tree, two going south to lighten the store, until the Gray Eagle recovers and instructs them in hunting. The foolish Pigeon Hawk is robbed of every kill by a great white owl, which the Gray Eagle seizes; they counsel mercy - 'this will be a lesson to him not to tyrannize over any one who is weaker than himself' - and release the owl, which teaches what herbs will cure its wounds. The two southern nestmates return and all fly off to mate: 'these six birds only represent one of our impoverished northern families of children, who had been deprived of both their parents and the aid of their elder brother nearly at the same time.'
summary.zh: 雙親鷹一日之間雙雙被射殺，留下六隻幼鷹。長兄「灰鷹」米吉格格沃納哺育弟妹，直到撲殺天鵝時折損一翼；眾弟妹拒絕南飛：「若寒氣殺你，便連我們一起殺。」眾鷹同住樹洞過冬，兩隻南飛以省存糧；灰鷹傷癒後授以獵術。愚笨的鴿鷹屢被大白鴞劫掠獵物，灰鷹遂擒之；眾鷹勸以寬恕——「讓牠從此不敢欺凌弱小」——放鴞而去，並教牠治傷的草藥。南歸的二鷹返巢團聚，各擇佳偶飛入林中：「這六隻鳥，代表的正是我們北方那些同時失去雙親與長兄照拂的貧苦家庭。」

sensitivity.note: Schoolcraft 1856; public domain.

passages.text: There were six young falcons living in a nest, all but one of whom were still unable to fly, when it so happened that both the parent birds were shot by the hunters in one day. The young brood waited with impatience for their return; but night came, and they were left without parents and without food. Meeji-geeg-wona, or the Gray Eagle, the eldest, and the only one whose feathers had become stout enough to enable him to leave the nest, assumed the duty of stilling their cries and providing them with food, in which he was very successful. But, after a short time had passed, he, by an unlucky mischance, got one of his wings broken in pouncing upon a swan.
passages.note: Verbatim from Schoolcraft 1856, p. 258; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 有六只小隼住在一个巢里，除了一只以外，其余的都还不能飞，恰巧有一天，两只亲鸟都被猎人射杀了。这一窝幼雏焦急地等待它们归来；可是夜幕降临，它们失去了父母，也没有食物。米吉—吉格—沃纳，即灰鹰，是其中最年长的，也是唯一羽毛已长得足够结实、能够离巢的一只，便担起了止住它们的啼叫、为它们觅食的责任，而且做得非常成功。可是过了不久，他因一次不幸的意外，在扑击一只天鹅时折断了一只翅膀。

passages.text: 'Brothers,' he said, 'an accident has befallen me, but let not this prevent your going to a warmer climate. Winter is rapidly approaching, and you cannot remain here. It is better that I alone should die than for you all to suffer miserably on my account.' 'No! no!' they replied, with one voice, 'we will not forsake you; we will share your sufferings; we will abandon our journey, and take care of you, as you did of us... If the climate kills you, it shall kill us... Whether you live or die, we will live or die with you.' They sought out a hollow tree to winter in, and contrived to carry their wounded nestmate there; and, before the rigors of winter set in, they had stored up food enough to carry them through its severities. To make it last the better, two of the number went off south, leaving the other three to watch over, feed, and protect the wounded bird.
passages.note: Verbatim from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 258-259; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: ‘兄弟们，’他说，‘我遭遇了意外，但不要因此阻止你们前往更温暖的地方。冬天正迅速逼近，你们不能留在这里。我独自死去，总比你们大家为我而受苦要好。’‘不！不！’他们异口同声地回答，‘我们绝不抛弃你；我们要分担你的苦难；我们要放弃旅程，照顾你，就像你照顾我们一样……如果这气候要了你的命，那也要了我们的命……无论你活还是死，我们都与你同生共死。’他们找到一棵空心树过冬，设法把他们受伤的巢伴搬到那里；在严冬来临之前，他们已经储存了足够的食物，足以度过寒冬的严酷。为了使食物维持得更久，他们中有两只南飞而去，留下另外三只看护、喂养并保护那只受伤的鸟。

passages.text: Meeji-geeg-wona in due time recovered from his wound, and he repaid their kindness by giving them such advice and instruction in the art of hunting as his experience had qualified him to impart. The youngest, Peepi-geewi-zains, the Pigeon Hawk, always came back without anything: 'It is not my smallness or weakness of body... I kill ducks and other birds every time I go out; but, just as I get to the woods, a large Ko-ko-ko-ho robs me of my prey.' 'Well! don't despair, brother,' said Meeji-geeg-wona. 'I now feel my strength perfectly recovered, and I will go out with you to-morrow.' They went forth in company, and when the white owl claimed the pigeon hawk's prize, the Gray Eagle came up, and, fixing his talons in both sides of the owl, flew home with him.
passages.note: Verbatim from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 259-260; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 米吉-吉格-沃納適時從傷中復原，並以狩獵技藝方面的忠告與教導回報他們的恩情，因為他的經驗足以傳授這些。最小的皮皮-吉維-贊斯，即鴿鷹，每次回來都一無所獲：「這並非因為我身材小或體弱……我每次出去都能獵到鴨子和其他鳥類；但正當我走進樹林時，一隻大科-科-科-霍就搶走了我的獵物。」「好吧！別絕望，兄弟，」米吉-吉格-沃納說。「我現在覺得力氣已完全恢復，明天我跟你一起出去。」他們結伴出發，當白貓頭鷹來搶鴿鷹的獵物時，灰鷹上前，將爪子扎進貓頭鷹的兩側，帶著他飛回家去。

passages.text: The little pigeon hawk flew in the owl's face and vented his passion in abundance of reproachful terms. 'Softly,' said the Gray Eagle; 'do not be in such a passion, or exhibit so revengeful a disposition; for this will be a lesson to him not to tyrannize over any one who is weaker than himself for the future.' So, after giving him good advice, and telling him what kind of herbs would cure his wounds, they let the owl go. While this act was taking place, two visitors appeared at the hollow tree - the two nestmates who had just returned from the south; they were thus all happily reunited, and each one soon chose a mate and flew off to the woods. Spring had now revisited the north... 'But it is in vain,' said the old man who related this story, 'that spring returns, if we are not thankful to the Master of Life who has preserved us through the winter... These six birds only represent one of our impoverished northern families of children, who had been deprived of both their parents and the aid of their elder brother nearly at the same time.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 260-261; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 小鴿鷹飛到貓頭鷹臉上，盡情傾瀉滿腔的責罵之詞。「輕點，」灰鷹說；「別這麼動怒，也別顯出如此報復心切；因為這將成為一個教訓，使他今後不再欺壓任何比他弱小的人。」於是，他們給了他一番忠告，並告訴他何種草藥能治他的傷，然後便放了貓頭鷹。正當此事發生之際，兩位訪客出現在空心樹前——正是剛從南方歸來的兩位同巢夥伴；他們就這樣幸福地重聚了，每一個不久都選了配偶，飛向樹林。春天此時已重返北方……「但這是徒勞的，」講述這個故事的老人說，「春天歸來，如果我們不感謝那在整個冬天保全我們的生命之主……這六隻鳥僅僅代表了我們北方貧困家庭中的一群孩子，他們幾乎同時失去了雙親和長兄的幫助。」

title.en: Weeng, the Spirit of Sleep
title.zh: 溫格：睡眠之靈

region.en: Hunter's lodge and smoking pouch of the Odjibwa woods
region.zh: 奧吉布瓦林中的獵屋與菸草袋

period: Odjibwa personification recorded by Schoolcraft (1856)

source.work: H. R. Schoolcraft, The Myth of Hiawatha, and Other Oral Legends (1856), 'Weeng, the spirit of sleep'

summary.en: Sleep is personified by the Odjibwas under the name of Weeng, executed by gnome-like beings each armed with a tiny war-club, with which they nimbly climb up the forehead and knock the drowsy person on the head until the eyelids close. They hide in the smoking pouch of the hunter, ready to fly out when he sits down to light his pipe - and the game passes. Iagoo's tale: losing his dogs in a thicket, he found them asleep near Weeng's residence, and saw the Spirit of Sleep himself on a tree branch, a giant insect-like monetos with many wings making a low deep murmuring sound like distant falling water - 'but Iagoo himself, being a very great liar and braggart, but little credit was given to his narration.' Weeng is also the author of dulness: if an orator fails, he is struck by Weeng.
summary.zh: 奧吉布瓦人以「溫格」之名化身睡眠；其職司由一群手持小戰棒的精怪執行——牠們靈巧地爬上額頭，敲擊昏昏欲睡者的頭，直至眼瞼闔上。牠們藏在獵人的菸草袋中，待其坐下點菸時飛出施術——獵物便趁機逸去。亞古的故事：他在密林中丟了獵犬，尋見牠們睡在溫格居所附近；抬頭看見睡眠之靈坐在樹枝上——狀如多翼的巨蟲，發出如遠處流水般的低沉嗡鳴——「但亞古是出了名的吹牛大王，人們自然不大相信。」溫格還是沉悶之源：演說失敗，便說是被溫格擊中了。

sensitivity.note: Schoolcraft 1856; public domain.

passages.text: Sleep is personified by the Odjibwas under the name of Weeng. The power of the Indian Morpheus is executed by a peculiar class of gnome-like beings, called Weengs. These subordinate creations, although invisible to the human eye, are each armed with a tiny war-club, or puggamaugun, with which they nimbly climb up the forehead, and knock the drowsy person on the head; on which sleepiness is immediately produced. If the first blow is insufficient, another is given, until the eyelids close, and a sound sleep is produced. It is the constant duty of these little agents to put every one to sleep whom they encounter - men, women, and children. And they are found secreted around the bed, or on small protuberances of the bark of the Indian lodges.
passages.note: Verbatim from Schoolcraft 1856, p. 262; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 奧吉布瓦人將睡眠擬人化，稱之為「威恩格」。這位印第安摩耳甫斯的神力，由一類奇特的地精般的存在——稱為「威恩格們」——來執行。這些從屬的造物雖為肉眼所不能見，卻各自配備一根小小的戰棒，即「普加莫岡」，他們敏捷地爬上人的額頭，敲打昏昏欲睡者的腦袋；睡意便立刻產生。若第一擊不夠，便再擊一次，直到眼皮合上，酣睡隨之而來。這些小僕從的恆常職責，就是讓所遇到的每一個人入睡——男人、女人和孩子。人們發現他們藏匿在床鋪周圍，或印第安小屋樹皮上的小凸起處。

passages.text: They hide themselves in the Gushkeepitaugun, or smoking pouch of the hunter, and when he sits down to light his pipe in the woods, are ready to fly out and exert their sleep-compelling power. If they succeed, the game is suffered to pass, and the hunter obliged to return to his lodge without a reward. In general, however, they are represented to possess friendly dispositions, seeking constantly to restore vigor and elasticity to the exhausted body. But being without judgment, their power is sometimes exerted at the hazard of reputation, or even life... If an orator fails, he is said to be struck by Weeng. If a warrior lingers, he has ventured too near the sleepy god. If children begin to nod or yawn, the Indian mother looks up smilingly, and says, 'They have been struck by Weeng,' and puts them to bed.
passages.note: Verbatim from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 262-264; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 他們藏身於獵人的「古什基皮陶岡」，即煙袋之中，當獵人在林中坐下點煙斗時，他們便準備飛出，施展催人入睡的力量。若他們得逞，獵物便得以逃脫，獵人只得空手而歸，回到小屋。然而一般而言，他們被描述為性情友善，不斷設法使疲憊的身體恢復活力與彈性。但由於缺乏判斷力，他們的力量有時會冒著名譽甚至生命的危險而施展……若演說者失敗，人們便說他被威恩格擊中了。若戰士遲疑，便是他冒險靠睡眠之神太近了。若孩子開始打盹或打哈欠，印第安母親便含笑仰望，說道：「他們被威恩格擊中了」，然後把他們放上床。

passages.text: Most of what is known on this subject is derived from Iagoo, who related that going out one day with his dogs to hunt, he passed through a wide range of thicket, where he lost his dogs. He became much alarmed, for they were faithful animals... At length he came to a spot where he found them asleep, having incautiously run near the residence of Weeng. After great exertions he aroused them, but not without having felt the power of somnolency himself. As he cast his eyes up from the place where the dogs were lying, he saw the Spirit of Sleep sitting upon the branch of a tree. He was in the shape of a giant insect, or monetos, with many wings from his back, which made a low deep murmuring sound, like distant falling water. But Iagoo himself, being a very great liar and braggart, but little credit was given to his narration.
passages.note: Verbatim from Schoolcraft 1856, p. 263; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 關於此事所知的大部分，皆源自伊亞古，他講述道：有一天他帶著狗出去打獵，穿過一大片灌木叢，在那裡與狗失散了。他大為驚慌，因為牠們是忠實的動物……最後他來到一處，發現牠們睡著了，原來是不慎跑近了威恩格的居所。他費了好大勁才把牠們喚醒，但自己也感受到了昏睡之力的作用。當他從狗躺臥之處抬眼望去，看見睡眠之靈坐在一根樹枝上。他呈巨蟲或「莫內托斯」之形，背上長著許多翅膀，發出低沉深長的嗡鳴聲，宛如遠處的流水聲。但伊亞古本人是個十足的大騙子和吹牛者，因此他的敘述鮮少有人相信。

title.en: Addik Kum Maig: The Origin of the White Fish
title.zh: 白魚之起源

region.en: Rapids of Pauwateeg (Sault Ste. Marie), upper Great Lakes
region.zh: 保瓦提格急流（蘇聖瑪麗），上大湖區

period: Odjibwa aition collected by Schoolcraft (1856)

source.work: H. R. Schoolcraft, The Myth of Hiawatha, and Other Oral Legends (1856), 'Addik Kum Maig'

summary.en: A hunter's wife carries on a secret affair with a mysterious visitor who never walks the path nor carries food; warned by their sons, the father kills her with a war-club and buries her under the ashes of his fire. Her spirit and then her rolling skull haunt the sons down the shores of Lake Superior to the falls of Pauwateeg, where an aged crane ferries the persecuted brothers across - warning them not to touch the sore back of his head. The skull begs the same ferry, cannot resist touching the wound, and is thrown into the rapids: 'There... you shall now be changed into something for the benefit of your people, and it shall be called Addik Kum Maig.' As the skull floated from rock to rock the brains were strewed in the water, in a form resembling roes, which assumed the shape of a new species of fish possessing a whiteness of color and peculiar flavor.
summary.zh: 獵人之妻與一位不走路徑、不攜食物的神秘訪客私通；兒子們告知父親，他一棒擊斃妻子，葬於灶灰之下。她的魂魄與滾動的頭骨一路作祟，追著兒子們沿蘇必利爾湖岸逃至保瓦提格瀑布。一隻年邁的鶴渡二人過灘——囑咐切莫碰牠頭後的傷處。頭骨也求渡，卻忍不住碰了傷處，被擲入急流：「你生前毫無用處，如今化為造福你族之物，名為阿迪克庫梅格。」頭骨逐岩漂滾，腦髓散落水中，狀如魚卵，遂化作一種色白味美的新魚——白魚。

sensitivity.note: Schoolcraft 1856; public domain. Domestic violence is narrated as the crime's cause in story register.

passages.text: They noticed that a young man visited the lodge during their father's absence, and these visits were frequently repeated. At length the elder of the two said to his mother: 'My mother, who is this tall young man that comes here so often during our father's absence?' 'Bad boy,' said the mother, pettishly, 'mind your bow and arrows... Say not a word to him on the subject.' But as they grew older, and still saw the visits of this mysterious stranger, they resolved to speak again to their mother, and told her that they meant to inform their father of all they had observed, for they frequently saw this young man passing through the woods, and he did not walk in the path, nor did he carry anything to eat. At this the mother flew into a rage: 'I will kill you,' said she, 'if you speak of it.' They resolved at last to disclose the whole matter to their father. The result was such as might have been anticipated: the father, being satisfied of the infidelity of his wife, watched a suitable occasion, and with a single blow of his war-club dispatched her. He then buried her under the ashes of his fire, took down the lodge, and removed with his two sons to a distant position.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 265-266; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們注意到，在父親外出期間，有個年輕人來訪小屋，而且這些來訪頻繁重複。最後，兩個孩子中年長的那個對母親說：「母親，這個在我們父親外出時如此頻繁來訪的高個年輕人是誰？」「壞孩子，」母親不耐煩地說，「管好你的弓和箭……關於此事，一個字也別對他說。」但隨著他們長大，仍舊看到這個神秘陌生人的來訪，他們便決心再跟母親說一次，並告訴她，他們打算把所觀察到的一切都告訴父親，因為他們常看見這個年輕人穿過樹林，他既不走在路上，也不帶任何吃的東西。母親聽了大發雷霆：「你若說出去，」她說，「我就殺了你。」他們最終決心把整件事告訴父親。結果正如可以預料的那樣：父親確信妻子不忠，便窺伺一個適當的時機，一擊戰棒便結果了她。隨後他把她埋在火堆的灰燼之下，拆下小屋，帶著兩個兒子遷往遠處。

passages.text: But the spirit of the woman haunted the children, who were now grown up to the estate of young men. She appeared to them as they returned from hunting in the evening. They were also terrified in their dreams, which they attributed to her. Life became a scene of perpetual terrors. They resolved, together with their father, to leave the country, and commenced a journey toward the south. After travelling many days along the shores of Lake Superior, they passed around a high promontory of rock where a large river issued out of the lake, and soon after came to a place called Pauwateeg. They had no sooner come in sight of these falls than they beheld the skull of the woman rolling along the beach. They were in the utmost fear, and knew not how to elude her.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 266-267; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但那女子的亡魂卻糾纏著孩子們，他們如今已長大成人。每當他們傍晚打獵歸來，她便向他們顯現。他們在夢中也受驚嚇，並將此歸咎於她。生活成了一片永無止境的恐怖景象。他們與父親一同決意離開此地，啟程往南方去。他們沿著蘇必略湖岸走了許多天，繞過一座高聳的岩石岬角，那裡有一條大河從湖中流出，不久便來到一個名叫保瓦提格的地方。他們才剛望見這道瀑布，就看見那女子的頭骨沿著灘岸滾動。他們驚恐萬分，不知如何才能避開她。

passages.text: At this moment one of them looked out, and saw a stately crane sitting on a rock in the middle of the rapids. They called out to the bird, 'See, grandfather, we are persecuted by a spirit. Come and take us across the falls, so that we may escape her.' This crane was a bird of extraordinary size and great age... 'Be careful,' said the crane, 'that you do not touch the back part of my head. It is sore, and should you press against it, I shall not be able to avoid throwing you both into the rapids.' They were, however, attentive on this point, and were safely landed on the south shore of the river. The crane then resumed his former position in the rapids. But the skull now cried out, 'Come, my grandfather, and carry me over, for I have lost my children, and am sorely distressed.' The aged bird flew to her assistance, and carefully repeated the injunction...
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 267-268; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 就在此時，其中一人放眼望去，看見一隻雄偉的鶴棲在急流中央的一塊岩石上。他們向那鳥喊道：『看哪，祖父，我們正受一個亡魂迫害。請來把我們帶過瀑布，好讓我們逃離她。』這隻鶴體型非凡、年歲極高……鶴說：『小心，別碰到我後腦勺。那裡有傷，你若按壓到它，我就免不了把你們兩個都拋進急流裡。』然而他們在這一點上十分留意，便安然被送到河的南岸。鶴隨後回到急流中先前的位置。但那頭骨這時喊道：『來吧，我的祖父，把我帶過去，因為我失去了孩子，痛苦萬分。』這隻年邁的鳥飛去相助，又小心地重複了那番叮囑……

passages.text: She promised to obey, but soon felt a curiosity to know where the head of her carrier had been hurt... before they were half way over the rapids, she could not resist the inclination she felt to touch the affected part. Instantly the crane threw her into the rapids. 'There,' said he, 'you have been of no use during your life, you shall now be changed into something for the benefit of your people, and it shall be called Addik Kum Maig.' As the skull floated from rock to rock, the brains were strewed in the water, in a form resembling roes, which soon assumed the shape of a new species of fish, possessing a whiteness of color, and peculiar flavor, which have caused it, ever since, to be in great repute with the Indians.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 267-268; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她答應遵從，但不久便起了好奇心，想知道載她者的頭部是在何處受傷的……他們還沒渡過急流的一半，她就按捺不住想要觸碰那受傷之處的念頭。鶴立刻把她拋進急流之中。『好啦，』他說，『你生前毫無用處，如今要把你變成某樣東西，好造福你的族人，它將被稱為阿迪克·庫姆·邁格。』當頭骨從一塊岩石漂向另一塊岩石時，腦漿散落在水中，形狀宛如魚卵，不久便化作一種新魚的模樣，色澤潔白，風味獨特，自此以後便深受印第安人推崇。

title.en: The Enchanted Moccasins: Onwe Bahmondoong and the Sisters of the Tree Lodge
title.zh: 魔法鹿皮鞋：負球者與樹屋姊妹

region.en: Village of hunters with the smooth barkless tree, Odjibwa country
region.zh: 奧吉布瓦之地有光滑無皮大樹的獵村

period: Odjibwa tale collected by Schoolcraft (1856)

source.work: H. R. Schoolcraft, The Myth of Hiawatha, and Other Oral Legends (1856), 'The Enchanted Moccasins'

summary.en: Onwe Bahmondoong, He That Carries a Ball on His Back, seeks the village from which no person has ever returned. An old woman warns him of the tree lodge hung with the chief's two daughters - Azhabee, She Who Sits Behind, who makes the tree descend, and Negahnahbee, She Who Sits Before, who makes it shoot to the arch of heaven - and gives him the medicine-dance bones by whose magic he can penetrate any substance. Speaking only to the left-hand sister, he brings the tree down, clubs the death-dealing sisters, and flees the avenging brother Mudjikewis: into a moose skeleton whose enchanted moccasins walk 'to the end of the earth' to mislead the pursuit, then into the disguise of a feeble old man in a garden lodge, whose daughters feed the starving pursuer - breaking his fast, and so destroying his power - until Onwe Bahmondoong resumes his youthful form and ends him with one blow of the magic ball.
summary.zh: 「負球者」翁威巴蒙東前往那座從無人歸返的村子。老嫗警告他樹上吊著酋長兩個女兒的小屋——左手的「居後者」阿扎比能令樹降，右手的「居前者」內甘內比則令樹直升天穹——並授予醫舞之骨，憑其魔法可穿透萬物。他只與左手那位說話，使樹垂下，擊斃害人的姊妹，逃離復仇的兄長穆吉維斯：先化為駝鹿骸骨，讓魔法鹿皮鞋「走到大地盡頭」以誤導追蹤；再化身花園木屋中的衰邁老人，兩個女兒餵食瀕餓的追者——追者破齋，法力盡失——負球者恢復少年之形，一擊畢命。

sensitivity.note: Schoolcraft 1856; public domain.

passages.text: There once lived a little boy, all alone with his sister, in a very wild uninhabitable country... the opinion was formed that he had supernatural powers, and he was called Onwe Bahmondoong, or he that carries a ball on his back. As he grew up he was impatient to know whether there were other beings near them... Being now well grown, he determined to seek his fortune, and asked her to make him several pairs of moccasins to last him on the journey. He travelled on, not knowing exactly where he went. At last he came to a small wigwam, and, on looking into it, discovered a very old woman sitting alone by the fire. 'My poor grandchild, I suppose you are one of those who seek for the distant village, from which no person has ever yet returned... Be careful to provide yourself with the Ozhebahguhnun - the bones they use in the medicine dance - without which you cannot succeed.'
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 293-294; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有個小男孩，與他的姐姐孤零零地住在一個十分荒涼、不宜居住的地方……人們認為他具有超自然的力量，便稱他為翁威·巴蒙東，意即「背上帶著球的人」。他漸漸長大，急切地想知道附近是否還有別的生靈……如今他已長得健壯，便決心去闖蕩一番，並請姐姐為他做幾雙鹿皮鞋，好夠他旅途穿用。他一路前行，並不知道自己究竟要去哪裡。最後他來到一座小小的棚屋，往裡一看，發現一個很老的老婦人獨自坐在火邊。『我可憐的孫兒，我想你就是那些去尋找遠方村落的人之一吧，那村落至今還沒有人回來過……務必給自己備好奧澤巴古農——他們在藥舞中所用的骨頭——沒有它你便不能成功。』

passages.text: Before the door of the chief's lodge you will see a great tree, which is smooth and destitute of bark; on this tree, about the height of a man from the ground, a small lodge is suspended, in which the two daughters dwell. It is here so many have been destroyed. As often as he attempted to reach it, the tree began to tremble and soon shot up so that the lodge could hardly be perceived. He changed himself into a small squirrel and mounted the tree, thrusting one of the bones into the trunk as often as he became fatigued; but whenever he came near the lodge the tree would shoot up as before, until it had reached the arch of heaven and could go no higher. He entered the lodge and beheld the two sisters sitting opposite each other: the one on his left hand called herself Azhabee (one who sits behind), and the one on the right Negahnahbee (one who sits before). Whenever he addressed the one on his left hand, the tree would tremble and settle down to its former position; but when he addressed the one on his right hand, it would again shoot upward. Discovering this, he continued addressing the left-hand sister until the tree had resumed its former position; then seizing his war-club, 'You, who have caused the death of so many of my brothers, I will now put an end to' - and he laid them dead at his feet.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 294-296; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在酋長住所的門前，你會看見一棵大樹，樹身光滑，沒有樹皮；在這棵樹上，離地約一人高的地方，懸著一座小棚屋，那兩個女兒就住在裡面。許多人正是在這裡喪命的。每當他試圖接近那棚屋，樹便開始顫抖，隨即向上猛長，以致那棚屋幾乎看不見了。他把自己變成一隻小松鼠，爬上樹去，每逢疲倦就把一根骨頭插進樹幹；但每當他靠近棚屋，樹便又如先前一樣向上猛長，直到長到天穹，再也長不高了。他走進棚屋，看見兩姐妹相對而坐：他左手邊的那個自稱阿扎比（意即「坐在後面的人」），右手邊的那個叫內加納比（意即「坐在前面的人」）。每當他向左手邊的那個說話，樹便顫抖，落回原來的位置；但當他向右手邊的那個說話，樹便又向上猛長。他發現了這一點，便繼續對左手邊的姐姐說話，直到樹恢復了原來的位置；然後他抓起戰棒，說道：『你，害死了我那麼多兄弟，我現在要結束你』——於是他把她們打死，倒在他腳下。

passages.text: Learning that the sisters had a brother living with their father who would pursue him for the deed, he set off at random. Mudjikewis replied, 'The person who has done this must be the Boy that carries the Ball on his Back. I will pursue him... Above all, avoid tasting food till you succeed; for if you break your fast before you see his blood, your power will be destroyed.' The pursued climbed up into one of the tallest trees and shot forth his magic arrows; finding that his pursuer was not turned back, he transformed himself into the skeleton of a moose that had been killed, whose flesh had come off from his bones. He then remembered the moccasins which his sister had given him, which were enchanted. Taking a pair of them, he placed them near the skeleton: 'Go,' said he to them, 'to the end of the earth.' The moccasins then left him and their tracks remained; Mudjikewis followed the track he had long been pursuing till he came to the end of the earth, where he found only a pair of moccasins.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 296-297; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他得知兩姐妹有一個與她們父親同住的兄弟，會為此事追殺他，便漫無目的地動身離去。穆吉凱維斯答道：『幹下這事的人必定是那個背上帶著球的男孩。我要去追他……最重要的是，在成功之前切莫嘗食；因為你若在見到他流血之前就進食開齋，你的法力便會被毀。』被追者爬上一棵最高的樹，射出他的魔法之箭；他發現追者並未被逼退，便把自己變成一具被殺死的鹿的骸骨，其肉已從骨上脫落。他隨即想起姐姐給他的那些鹿皮鞋，它們是被施了魔法的。他取出一雙，放在骸骨旁邊，對它們說：『去吧，到天涯海角去。』鹿皮鞋便離開了他，足跡留了下來；穆吉凱維斯循著他追尋已久的足跡一路追去，直到天涯海角，卻只找到一雙鹿皮鞋。

passages.text: The other, finding he was closely pursued, now changed himself into a very old man, with two daughters, who lived in a large lodge in the centre of a beautiful garden, filled with everything that could delight the eye or was pleasant to the taste; he made himself appear so very old as to be unable to leave his lodge, and had his daughters to bring him food and wait on him. His pursuer continued on till he was nearly starved and ready to sink: 'Oh! I will forget the blood of my sisters, for I am starving'; but again he thought of the blood of his sisters, and again he resolved to pursue. At the beautiful garden the daughters invited him in, and boiled corn and prepared other savory food. Mudjikewis had no suspicion of the deception... he partook heartily of the meal, and in so doing was overcome: all at once he seemed to forget the blood of his sisters, and even the village of his nativity; he ate so heartily as to produce drowsiness, and soon fell into a profound sleep. Onwe Bahmondoong watched his opportunity, and as soon as he found his slumbers sound, resumed his youthful form; then he drew the magic ball from his back, which turned out to be a heavy war-club, with one blow of which he put an end to his pursuer, and thus vindicated his title as the Wearer of the Ball.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 297-298; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 另一個見自己被緊緊追趕，便將自己變成一個非常年老的人，帶著兩個女兒，住在美麗花園中央的一座大屋裡，園中滿是賞心悅目、可口宜人的一切；他讓自己顯得極其衰老，以致無法離開他的屋子，只得由女兒們為他送飯、侍奉他。追趕他的人繼續前行，直到幾乎餓死、快要倒下：「哦！我要忘掉我姊妹們的血，因為我快餓死了」；但他又想起姊妹們的血，便又決心追下去。在那美麗的花園裡，女兒們邀他進屋，煮了玉米，又備了其他美味的食物。穆吉凱維斯對這騙局毫無疑心……他盡情地吃了這頓飯，就在吃的當兒被制服了：他彷彿一下子忘掉了姊妹們的血，甚至忘掉了自己出生的村莊；他吃得太多，以致昏昏欲睡，很快便陷入了沉睡。翁威·巴蒙東窺伺時機，一發覺他睡得沉了，便恢復了年輕的形貌；接著他從背上取出那顆魔球，那球原來是一根沉重的戰棒，他一擊便結果了追趕他的人，從而維護了他「持球者」的稱號。

title.en: Leelinau: The Bride of the Fairy of Green Pines
title.zh: 莉莉娜：綠松仙子的新娘

region.en: Great sand dunes of Naigow Wudjoo (La Grandes Sables) and the manito wac, Spirit wood, Lake Superior
region.zh: 蘇必利爾湖畔奈戈伍吉大沙丘與「靈林」

period: A Chippewa tale collected by Schoolcraft (1856)

source.work: H. R. Schoolcraft, The Myth of Hiawatha, and Other Oral Legends (1856), 'Leelinau'

summary.en: At the great sand dunes of Naigow Wudjoo the Pukwudjininees, fairies of Lake Superior, are seen in moonlight, skipping over the hills and leaving footprints no bigger than a child's; they delight in mischief - stealing a fisherman's paddle, plucking the hunter's feathers, pilfering his game. From their sacred grove, the manito wac, they entice away a chief's pensive, sylph-like daughter, Leelinau, who pines for a land of no weeping, no cares, and no deaths, and deems the light little men emissaries from the Happy Land. Her mother matches her with a neighboring forester; dressed in her finest, with flowers in her hair, she asks one request - a farewell visit to the sacred grove before the nuptial bower. The bridegroom waits in vain: a fisherman conceives he saw her go off with one of the tall fairies known as the fairy of Green Pines, with green plumes nodding o'er his brows - and it is supposed she is still roving with him over the elysian fields.
summary.zh: 蘇必利爾湖畔奈戈伍吉大沙丘，是小人族「帕克伍吉尼內斯」的名居；月明之夜，漁人常見他們在丘間跳躍，沙上留下孩童大小的足印。他們頑皮搗蛋——偷漿、拔羽、竊獵物。自他們的聖林「靈林」，他們誘走酋長那位沉思如精靈的女兒莉莉娜——她渴望一個無淚、無憂、無死亡之地，把這些輕快的小人視作福地的使者。母親為她許配鄰近的獵人；婚禮之夜，她一身盛裝、髮插花朵，只求在入洞房前到仙林作別。新郎苦候無果：一位漁人自稱見她隨一位高大仙者而去——那人便是眉際綠羽點點的「綠松仙子」——相傳她至今仍在極樂原野與他雙雙漫遊。

sensitivity.note: Schoolcraft 1856; public domain.

passages.text: The Pukwudjininees, or fairies of Lake Superior, had one of their most noted places of residence at the great sand dunes of Naigow Wudjoo, called by the French La Grandes Sables. Here they were frequently seen in bright moonlight evenings, and the fishermen while sitting in their canoes on the lake often saw them playing their pranks, and skipping over the hills. There was a grove of pines in that vicinity called the manito wac, or Spirit wood, into which they might be seen to flee, on the approach of evening, and there is a romantic little lake on those elevated sand-hills, on the shores of which their tracks could be plainly seen in the sand. These tracks were not bigger than little children's footprints, and the spirits were often seen in the act of vanishing behind the little pine-trees. They love to dance in the most lonesome places, and were always full of glee and merriment.
passages.note: Verbatim from Schoolcraft 1856, p. 299; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 帕克伍德吉尼尼斯，即蘇必利爾湖的仙子，最著名的居所之一在奈戈·伍德朱的大沙丘，法國人稱之為「大沙」。這裡的人常在明亮的月夜看見她們，漁夫坐在湖上的獨木舟裡，也常看見她們嬉戲作樂、在山丘上跳躍。那一帶有一片松林，叫做「馬尼托瓦克」，即精靈之林，傍晚來臨時，可以看見她們逃進林中；在那些高聳的沙丘上還有一個幽美的小湖，湖岸的沙上可以清楚地看到她們的足跡。這些足跡並不比小孩子的腳印大，精靈們也常被看見正消失在小松樹後面。她們喜愛在最荒僻的地方跳舞，總是充滿歡欣與嬉鬧。

passages.text: These little men, the pukwudjininees, are not deeply malicious, but rather delighted in mischief and freaks, and would sometimes steal away a fisherman's paddle, or come at night and pluck the hunter's feathers out of his cap in the lodge, or pilfer away some of his game, or fish. On one occasion they went so far as to entice away into their sacred grove, and carry off a chief's daughter - a small but beautiful girl, who had been always inclined to be pensive, and took her seat often in these lonesome haunts. From her baby name of Neenizu, my dear life, she was called Leelinau, but she never attained to much size, remaining very slender, but of the most pleasing and sylph-like features, with very bright black eyes, and little feet.
passages.note: Verbatim from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 299-300; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 這些小人兒，即帕克伍德吉尼尼斯，並非心懷深重的惡意，而是喜愛惡作劇與捉弄，有時會偷走漁夫的槳，或夜裡來到獵人的棚屋，從他的帽子上拔去羽毛，或偷走他的一些獵物或魚。有一次她們甚至引誘一位酋長的女兒進入她們的神聖樹林，並把她帶走——那是個身材嬌小卻美麗的姑娘，素來性情憂鬱，常坐在這些荒僻的幽處。她幼時的名字叫尼尼祖，意為「我親愛的生命」，但她被喚作莉琳娜；她始終沒有長得多高大，一直十分纖細，卻有著最悅目、最輕盈如精靈般的容貌，一雙烏黑明亮的眼睛，和一雙小腳。

passages.text: She had imbibed ideas of a spiritual life and existence, which she fancied could only be enjoyed in the Indian elysium, and instructed as she was by the old story-tellers, she could not do otherwise than deem the light and sprightly little men who made the fairy footprints as emissaries from the Happy Land. For this happy land she sighed and pined. Blood, and the taking of life, she said, the Great Spirit did not approve... And she longed to go to a region where there was no weeping, no cares, and no deaths... She announced her willingness to accede to the matrimonial proposals, and the day was fixed. She dressed herself in the finest manner possible, putting flowers in her hair, and carrying a bunch of wild flowers, mixed with tassels of the pine-tree in her hand.
passages.note: Verbatim from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 300-301; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 她心中已接受了關於靈性生命與存在的種種觀念，她以為那只有在印第安人的極樂世界中才能享受；又因她受那些講古老人的教誨，她不由得把那些留下仙子足跡、輕盈活潑的小人兒看作來自幸福之地的使者。她為這幸福之地嘆息、憔悴。她說，大神並不贊同流血與殺生……她渴望去到一個沒有哭泣、沒有憂慮、沒有死亡的地方……她宣布願意接受婚事的提議，日子便定了下來。她盡可能打扮得最美，把花插在髮間，手裡拿著一束野花，夾著松樹的穗子。

passages.text: One only request she made, which was to make a farewell visit to the sacred grove of the fairies, before she visited the nuptial bower. This was granted, on the evening of the proposed ceremony, while the bridegroom and his friends gathered in her father's lodge, and impatiently waited her return. But they waited in vain. Night came, but Leelinau was never more seen, except by a fisherman on the lake shore, who conceived that he had seen her go off with one of the tall fairies known as the fairy of Green Pines, with green plumes nodding o'er his brows; and it is supposed that she is still roving with him over the elysian fields.
passages.note: Verbatim from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 300-301; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 她只提出一個請求，就是在進入新婚的洞房之前，先去向仙子的神聖樹林作一次告別。這請求在預定婚禮的那個傍晚得到了允許，當時新郎和他的朋友們聚在她父親的棚屋裡，不耐煩地等她回來。但他們等得徒然。夜色降臨，莉琳娜卻再也沒有被人看見，只有湖岸上的一個漁夫以為自己看見她跟一位高大的仙子走了，那仙子被稱為「綠松仙子」，綠色的羽飾在他眉上搖曳；據說她至今仍與他一同漫遊在極樂的原野上。

title.en: Gilgamesh and Aga: The Siege of Uruk
title.zh: 吉爾伽美什與阿伽：烏魯克之圍

region.en: Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Gilgamesh and Aga (ETCSL c.1.8.1.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Aga of Kish, once sheltered by Gilgamesh's council, marches on Uruk; the king refuses to surrender. The elders counsel submission, the young men counsel war, and on the wall Gilgamesh's face dazzles the besiegers; Aga's siege dissolves and Kish's yoke is broken.
summary.zh: 曾受吉爾伽美什庇護的基什王阿伽興兵圍城；國王拒降。長老主降，青年主戰。城頭上吉爾伽美什的面容使圍軍目眩，阿伽圍城遂解，基什之枷鎖碎。

sensitivity.note: Ancient legend; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Aga, king of Kish, sends envoys to Uruk: Gilgamesh once sheltered him in his council, and now Aga demands his city. Gilgamesh answers before the elders, who counsel surrender; before the young men, who counsel war — and Uruk will fight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.1, the summons and council; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 基什王阿伽遣使前往烏魯克：吉爾伽美什曾在他的議會中庇護過他，如今阿伽卻索要他的城。吉爾伽美什在長老們面前作答，長老們主張投降；他又在年輕人面前作答，年輕人主張開戰——烏魯克將要一戰。

passages.text: For ten days the siege of Uruk holds; the city's gates hold too. On the rampart Gilgamesh shows his face, and the dazzled besiegers cannot take aim; Birhurtura, sent out, is thrown down again and again by the lord's strength. Aga, disarmed by the man he once served under, releases the siege; the elders and the men of Kish bless the peace, and Uruk stands free — the poem closes praising the king whose face alone outdid an army.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.1, the siege; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.1, the release; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 烏魯克的圍城持續了十天；城門也依然堅守。吉爾伽美什在城牆上露面，目眩的圍城者無法瞄準；被派出的比爾胡爾圖拉，一次又一次被城主的力氣摔倒。阿伽被他曾在其麾下效力的人解除了武裝，解除了圍城；長老們與基什的人們祝福這和平，烏魯克自由屹立——詩篇在讚美那位僅憑面容便勝過一支軍隊的國王中結束。

functions: Founding legend of Uruk's independence from Kish
Charter of Gilgamesh's legitimacy as elected king
Performed with the Gilgamesh cycle at Uruk

title.en: Gilgamesh and the Bull of Heaven
title.zh: 吉爾伽美什與天牛

region.en: Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Gilgamesh and the Bull of Heaven (ETCSL c.1.8.1.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Inanna, spurned by Gilgamesh, demands the Bull of Heaven from An; the beast devours Uruk's pastures, and the heroes slay it — after which Inanna curses and is cursed, and the city feasts on the bull's horns' worth of oil.
summary.zh: 遭吉爾伽美什拒絕的伊南娜，向安神索要天牛；神獸吞食烏魯克牧場，二英雄合力誅之——事後伊南娜咒詛英雄，英雄亦回咒，全城以天牛之角熬油設宴。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Inanna comes to Gilgamesh with marriage offers; he refuses and taunts her lovers' fates. Furious, she climbs to heaven and demands of An the Bull of Heaven: without it, she swears, she will break the doors of the netherworld and let the dead outnumber the living.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.2, the demand; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊南娜帶著求婚的提議來到吉爾伽美什面前；他拒絕了，並嘲弄她諸位情人的命運。她勃然大怒，登上天界，向安索求天之公牛：她發誓，若得不到它，她就要打破冥界的門，讓死者多過生者。

passages.text: The Bull descends and drinks the Euphrates dry; at every snort a pit opens, and a hundred youths and fifty young men of Uruk fall in. Gilgamesh and Enkidu take the beast: Enkidu seizes its tail, and Gilgamesh stabs between neck and horns.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.2, the battle; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 公牛降下，把幼發拉底河飲乾；牠每噴一口氣便裂開一個坑，烏魯克的一百名青年與五十名壯士跌落其中。吉爾伽美什與恩奇都制服了這頭野獸：恩奇都抓住牠的尾巴，吉爾伽美什則刺向牠頸與角之間。

passages.text: Inanna mourns on the city wall; Gilgamesh curses her with her own deeds, tears off the bull's right thigh and throws it at her. The horns are made into vessels of oil, and the city feasts; the young men bless the heroes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.2, the aftermath; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊南娜在城牆上哀悼；吉爾伽美什以她自己的所作所為詛咒她，扯下公牛的右大腿朝她扔去。牛角被製成盛油的器皿，全城設宴歡慶；青年們祝福這兩位英雄。

functions: Battle myth of the Gilgamesh cycle performed at Uruk
Theology of Inanna's wrath and the hero's defiance
Etiology of the bull-horn oil vessels in temple use

title.en: Gilgamesh and Huwawa: Into the Cedar Forest
title.zh: 吉爾伽美什與胡瓦瓦：深入雪松林

region.en: Cedar forest of the Lebanon (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 黎巴嫩雪松林（象徵性定位）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Gilgamesh and Huwawa (version A, ETCSL c.1.8.1.5)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Gilgamesh asks Utu for help and leads fifty men into the cedar mountain where Huwawa keeps the auras of terror; the heroes chop trees by day and take the seven auras one by one until the guardian is powerless.
summary.zh: 吉爾伽美什求烏圖相助，率五十人入雪松山，直搗胡瓦瓦的七重恐懼光環；晝伐林木，逐一奪取光環，守衛者力竭。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Gilgamesh wants fame: there is no name to be won by staying home, so he asks Utu to open the way to the cedar mountain where Huwawa keeps his seven auras of terror. Fifty single men of Uruk are chosen for the road.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.5, the expedition's start; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 吉爾伽美什渴望名聲：留在家中無法贏得名號，於是他請求烏圖開闢通往雪松山的路，胡瓦瓦在那裡守著他那七道恐怖的靈光。烏魯克挑選了五十名單身男子同行。

passages.text: At the forest's edge the men fall asleep and one by one the auras of terror put them down like sleep; Gilgamesh alone fights on, chops cedar after cedar, and by chopping each aura out of its tree-house takes from Huwawa terror after terror until the guardian is stripped of his power.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.5, the auras; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在森林邊緣，眾人紛紛睡去，恐怖的靈光一道接一道把他們放倒，如同睡意；唯有吉爾伽美什繼續奮戰，砍倒一棵又一棵雪松，藉由將每一道靈光從其樹居之中砍出，從胡瓦瓦身上奪走一道又一道恐怖，直到這名守護者被剝奪了全部力量。

functions: Heroic charter of the Uruk expedition ethos
Etiology of the cedar trade to Sumer
Battle hymn performed with the Gilgamesh cycle

variants.summary: A rival telling in which Enkidu leads the ruse of the false friendship.

title.en: The Capture of Huwawa
title.zh: 胡瓦瓦之擒

region.en: Cedar forest of the Lebanon (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 黎巴嫩雪松林（象徵性定位）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Gilgamesh and Huwawa (version A, second half; ETCSL c.1.8.1.5)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Stripped of his auras, Huwawa weeps and offers his forest in vassalage; Gilgamesh's mercy wavers, but Enkidu — jealous or clear-eyed — strikes first, and the guardian's head is sent in a box to Enlil, who rebukes the killers.
summary.zh: 光環盡失的胡瓦瓦哭求饒命，願以雪松林稱臣；吉爾伽美什心生憐憫，恩奇都卻搶先出手斬之——首級裝匣送尼普魯，恩利爾嚴斥二人。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Stripped of terror, Huwawa weeps before Gilgamesh: my auras are gone, my trees are yours — take my forest in vassalage and let me live. Gilgamesh's heart is moved and he moves to bind him gently. Enkidu, angry — why does my lord pity the guardian of Enlil's trees? — strikes first and fells Huwawa; the head is cut off and sent to Nippur in a box of cedar.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.5, the plea; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.5, the kill; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 胡瓦瓦被剝去威懾之力，在吉爾伽美什面前哭泣：我的光輝已失，我的樹林歸你所有——收我的森林為藩屬，讓我活命吧。吉爾伽美什心生憐憫，正要溫和地將他捆綁。恩奇都卻憤怒了——我的主人為何要憐憫恩利爾樹林的守護者？——他率先出手，擊倒胡瓦瓦；頭被砍下，裝在雪松木箱中送往尼普爾。

passages.text: At the Ekur, Enlil, seeing the box, rebukes them: you have killed the guardian I appointed; his auras shall be smoke on the hearth, his hide the earth's rivers — and the heroes carry home a victory shadowed by the god's displeasure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.5, Enlil's rebuke; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在埃庫爾，恩利爾見到木箱，斥責他們：你們殺了我所任命的守護者；他的光輝將化為爐上的煙，他的皮將化為大地的河流——英雄們帶回家的勝利，籠罩著神的不悅。

functions: Moral centerpiece of the Uruk heroic cycle
Theology of mercy against dutiful violence
Etiology of the cedar tribute to Nippur

title.en: Huwawa (Version B): Enkidu's Ruse
title.zh: 胡瓦瓦（乙本）：恩奇都之計

region.en: Cedar forest of the Lebanon (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 黎巴嫩雪松林（象徵性定位）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Gilgamesh and Huwawa (version B, ETCSL c.1.8.1.5.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: In the second telling, Enkidu leads the strategy: the heroes offer Huwawa sister-wives and houses, playing on his loneliness; the auras are surrendered one by one, and when the guardian is powerless the friendship turns to blades.
summary.zh: 乙本敘事中恩奇都主導方略：眾英雄以姊妹為妻、宅第相許，誘其孤心；七光環逐一拱手，待其力竭，昔日賓主反目成仇。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In this telling Enkidu counsels the trick: they greet Huwawa as kin and promise him wives — elder and younger sisters — and houses with their goods, playing on the guardian's loneliness at the edge of the world. Huwawa, soothed, gives up his auras one by one as tokens of friendship; when the last is handed over, the heroes fall on him and bind him — the guardian betrayed by the friendship he believed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.5.1, the ruse; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.5.1, the surrender; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在此版本中，恩奇都獻上計策：他們以親人相稱問候胡瓦瓦，許諾給他妻子——姊姊與妹妹——以及連同財物一併奉上的房屋，利用這位守護者在世界邊緣的孤獨。胡瓦瓦被安撫，逐一交出他的光輝作為友誼的信物；當最後一道交出時，英雄們撲向他並將他捆綁——守護者被他所相信的友誼所背叛。

functions: Trickster variant of the guardian-slaying myth
Study text of narrative variants in scribal schools
Theology of betrayed friendship

title.en: Enkidu's Descent for the Ball
title.zh: 恩奇都為球入冥界

region.en: Uruk and the great below, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克與冥土（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Gilgamesh, Enkidu and the Nether World (ETCSL c.1.8.1.4)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Inanna's gift ball and malku-stick fall through a hole into the netherworld; a maiden sent to fetch them is caught there; Enkidu volunteers, is warned of the rules of the dead, breaks them all, and is held below until the sun god frees him as a ghost.
summary.zh: 伊南娜所贈之球與棍自地洞墜入冥界；遣去之少女亦被困；恩奇都自願下冥取物，卻將冥界禁忌一一觸犯，被困冥土；終由日神救出，然已成幽魂。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Inanna gives Gilgamesh the ball and stick; playing by the Euphrates, the young men drop both through a hole into the netherworld. The maiden sent down to fetch them never returns; Enkidu volunteers and descends through the hole. Gilgamesh warns him of the rules of the dead: do not put on clean clothes, do not anoint yourself, do not throw a stick, do not carry a bow, do not kiss your wife or strike her. Enkidu breaks every rule one by one — and is seized by the netherworld and held.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.4, the loss and descent; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.4, the broken rules; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊南娜把球與棍給了吉爾伽美什；在幼發拉底河畔嬉戲時，年輕人把兩樣東西都掉進一個洞裡，落入冥界。被派下去取回它們的少女一去不返；恩奇都自願從洞中下去。吉爾伽美什警告他亡者的規矩：不要穿上乾淨的衣服，不要給自己塗油，不要扔棍子，不要帶弓，不要親吻你的妻子，也不要打她。恩奇都逐一違反了每一條規矩——於是被冥界抓住並扣留。

passages.text: Gilgamesh begs Utu, the sun, who opens a hole: Enkidu comes up as a ghost, and the two friends talk until Enkidu must return — and the poem ends with Enkidu's report of the netherworld's customs, the famous catalogue of the fates of the dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.4, the ghost and the report; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 吉爾伽美什懇求太陽神烏圖，烏圖開了一個洞：恩奇都以幽靈之身升起，兩位朋友交談，直到恩奇都必須返回——詩篇以恩奇都講述冥界的習俗作結，即那著名的亡者命運名錄。

functions: Descent myth with the taboo list of the netherworld
Eschatological catalogue of the fates of the dead
Charter of funerary practice: remembrance as afterlife

title.zh: 吉爾伽美什之死

region.en: Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The death of Gilgamesh (ETCSL c.1.8.1.3)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Gilgamesh, having crossed the lands and seen everything, lies dying; a dream tells him he is taken. He decrees grave-goods for himself and burial offerings for his household, then descends to the assembly of the dead — and is made their king, judge of the shades.
summary.zh: 吉爾伽美什歷盡山河、見遍萬事後臥病垂死；夢兆示其將被接引。他自定隨葬之器、為家室定祭品，然後下至亡者會議——被立為亡者之王，幽魂之判官。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary literature; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Gilgamesh, the king who crossed the four quarters and saw everything, lies on his deathbed; a dream comes: he is seized and held in the great below. He wakes and knows the dream's meaning. He decrees his grave-goods — lapis and gold, weapons and vessels — and charges his household with the offerings that will feed him in the land of the dead; the burial is made as for a god. Descended among the dead, he is not lost but enthroned: the shades honor him as their king, and he sits in judgment over them — the last office of the hero who would not die and did.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.3, the death-dream; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.3, the grave-goods; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.1.3, enthronement among the dead; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 吉爾伽美什，這位走遍四方、見識萬物的國王，躺在臨終的床上；一個夢境降臨：他被抓住，扣留在大地之下。他醒來，明白夢的含義。他下令備辦陪葬品——青金石與黃金、武器與器皿——並囑咐家眷備好將在亡者之地供養他的祭品；葬禮按神的規格舉行。他下到亡者之中，並未消亡，而是登臨王座：亡魂尊他為王，他坐在他們之上審判——這是不願死去卻終究死去的英雄的最後職分。

functions: Funerary charter: grave-goods and offering obligations
Theology of the dead king's persistence as judge of shades
Royal burial liturgy performed for deceased rulers

variants.name: Gilgamesh epic Tablet X-XI
variants.summary: The living hero's quest that the death poem presupposes.

title.en: Lugalbanda Sick in the Mountain Cave
title.zh: 盧伽爾班達山中臥病

region.en: Highlands between Uruk and Aratta (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 烏魯克與阿拉塔之間山地（象徵性定位）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Lugalbanda in the mountain cave (ETCSL c.1.8.2.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Marching on Aratta, Uruk's army strains mountains like reed-bundles; Lugalbanda falls sick in the great Zabum hills and is left behind with provisions — alone between the armies of heaven and hell in the cave of the mountain.
summary.zh: 烏魯克大軍征伐阿拉塔，翻山如束葦；盧伽爾班達於扎布姆山中病倒，被留於後，獨伴乾糧——置身天兵與魔軍之間的山洞裡。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Uruk's army marches on Aratta, hauling its stones over mountains like bundles of reeds; in the high Zabum hills Lugalbanda, fifth of the brothers, falls sick with fever and cannot go on. His brothers leave him bread and water, an axe and a bow, and go on; Lugalbanda alone in the mountain cave is told in dream that he will be tested: whatever he meets — powers of heaven or of hell — he must honor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.2.1, the march and sickness; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.2.1, the abandonment and dream; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 烏魯克的軍隊向阿拉塔進發，將石塊如蘆葦束般越過山嶺搬運；在扎布姆高地，兄弟中排行第五的盧加爾班達染上熱病，無法前行。他的兄弟們留給他麵包與水、一把斧頭與一張弓，便繼續前進；獨自留在山洞中的盧加爾班達在夢中被告知，他將受到考驗：無論他遇見什麼——天上的神力或冥界的力量——他都必須予以敬奉。

functions: Quest myth of the Uruk-Aratta war cycle
Model of the tested solitary hero
Performed with the Enmerkar poems at Uruk

variants.summary: The sequel in which the sick hero meets the storm bird.
