title.en: Lugalbanda's Offerings in the Cave
title.zh: 盧伽爾班達洞中獻祭

region.en: Zabum mountain cave (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 扎布姆山洞（象徵性定位）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Lugalbanda in the mountain cave, second half (ETCSL c.1.8.2.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Recovered by dawn, Lugalbanda makes offerings to the gods of the cave — bread before Inanna and the river gods, unguents, libations — honoring every power he meets; his piety is the door through which the sequel's friendship with Anzud will open.
summary.zh: 黎明即癒的盧伽爾班達向山洞諸神獻祭——麵包供伊南娜與河神，敷油奠酒，所遇神靈無不致敬；其虔誠正是下一章與安祖結誼之門。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: At dawn Lugalbanda's fever breaks as if it had never been; he takes the rations his brothers left and prepares an offering table in the cave: bread before Inanna and the great river gods, unguent, libations of beer and water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.2.1, the offerings; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 黎明時分，盧加爾班達的熱病退去，彷彿從未發生過一般；他取來兄弟們留下的口糧，在山洞中備好一張供桌：在伊南娜與眾大河神面前擺上麵包、香膏，以及啤酒與水的奠祭。

passages.text: To every power of the mountain — the cave's lord, the river's god, the Anuna of the wild places — he presents his due, and none is slighted; the poem closes with the hero standing ready, his piety proven, for the meeting the mountains will now grant him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.2.1, the piety test passed; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 對山中的每一種力量——洞穴之主、河川之神、荒野之地的阿努納諸神——他都獻上應得之份，無一受到輕慢；詩篇以英雄挺身而立作結，他的虔敬已得證明，準備迎接群山如今將賜予他的相遇。

functions: Instruction in the offering rites of the wilderness
Piety test preparing the Anzud friendship
Liturgy for soldiers' camps and mountain marches

variants.summary: The reward of the tested piety.

title.en: Lugalbanda and the Nest of Anzud
title.zh: 盧伽爾班達與安祖巢

region.en: Nest on the mountain cliff (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 山崖鳥巢（象徵性定位）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Lugalbanda and the Anzud bird (ETCSL c.1.8.2.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Searching for his army, Lugalbanda finds the cliff-nest of Anzud, the storm bird whose face is the flood; he honors the fledglings with cream and ornaments and waits — praying not to be eaten — until the great bird returns and takes him as a guest, not prey.
summary.zh: 尋找大軍途中，盧伽爾班達發現安祖——面容即洪水的暴風鳥——的懸崖巢穴；他以乳酪與飾物敬奉雛鳥，虔誠等待，祈禱不被吞食；巨鳥歸來，以客相待而非獵物。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Lugalbanda, seeking his army, comes to the cliff where Anzud the storm bird nests — the bird whose face is the deluge and whose glance is lightning. He finds the nest with its single egg and its young, and he does them honor: cream, honey and ornaments laid before the fledglings. Waiting in the nest's shadow, the hero prays: let the great bird find me pleasing, not as prey. When Anzud returns and sees the offerings, he takes Lugalbanda into the nest as a guest and names him his son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.2.2, the nest; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.2.2, the adoption; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 盧加爾班達尋找他的軍隊，來到風暴之鳥安祖築巢的懸崖——那鳥的面容即是洪水，牠的目光即是閃電。他發現巢中有一枚獨卵與雛鳥，便向牠們致敬：將乳脂、蜂蜜與飾物陳放在雛鳥面前。英雄在巢影中等待，祈禱道：願巨鳥覺得我合牠心意，而非視我為獵物。安祖歸來，見到此番供獻，便將盧加爾班達當作賓客迎入巢中，並認他為子。

functions: Charter of guest-friendship with the powers of the wild
Etiology of the royal thunder-bird's cult at Uruk
Performed with the Aratta cycle at Uruk

variants.summary: The darker Babylonian myth of the same storm bird.

title.en: Anzud's Gift: The Speed of Light
title.zh: 安祖贈禮：疾行如光

region.en: Mountain heights to Aratta road (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 自山巔至阿拉塔之路（象徵性定位）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Lugalbanda and the Anzud bird, second half (ETCSL c.1.8.2.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Anzud grants Lugalbanda gifts of power: tires that never rest, the speed of light. Rejoining the army, the hero runs messages across mountains — and the queen-mother of Aratta's counsel is carried back to Uruk in a single day.
summary.zh: 安祖賜盧伽爾班達神力之禮：永不疲倦的雙足、疾行如光之速。歸隊後，他翻山傳訊——阿拉塔王太后之策，一日之間往返於烏魯克。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Anzud asks his guest what gift he would take; Lugalbanda asks for the tires that never tire and the speed of light. The bird grants them, and the hero can outrun the wind and outlast the day. He rejoins Uruk's army at the siege, runs messages through the mountains — to Aratta and back within a day — and the war's diplomacy is carried on his feet; the cycle's politics turn on the runner blessed by the storm bird.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.2.2, the gift; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.2.2, the service; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 安祖問他的賓客想要什麼禮物；盧加爾班達求取永不疲憊的雙腿與光的速度。此鳥應允了他，於是英雄能跑得比風更快，比白晝更持久。他在圍城之際重歸烏魯克的軍隊，翻山越嶺傳遞訊息——一日之內往返阿拉塔——戰爭的外交由他的雙腳承擔；此一詩組的政治，繫於這位受風暴之鳥祝福的奔跑者。

functions: Etiology of the messenger's divine speed
Plot device linking the Aratta cycle's poems
Cult myth of Lugalbanda as runner-god

title.en: Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta
title.zh: 恩美卡爾與阿拉塔之王

region.en: Uruk and Aratta (Aratta pin symbolic, eastern Iran)
region.zh: 烏魯克與阿拉塔（阿拉塔為象徵性定位，東伊朗）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Enmerkar and the lord of Aratta (ETCSL c.1.8.2.3)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Enmerkar demands Aratta's submission and tribute for the building of Uruk's temples; the two kings duel by riddle through a single exhausted messenger — the message grows so long that the lord of Uruk invents writing to defeat distance.
summary.zh: 恩美卡爾為建烏魯克神殿，向阿拉塔索貢索降；二王隔山以謎語交鋒，僅賴一名疲憊信使傳遞——訊息日長，烏魯克之王遂發明文字以勝距離。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Enmerkar, lord of Uruk, demands that Aratta build and bring the precious metals and stones for Inanna's temples; the lord of Aratta, also beloved of Inanna, refuses — the two kings argue through one exhausted messenger across seven mountains. The messages grow into riddling speeches: Enmerkar challenges with the shuttered grain and the shadow of seven years, and the messenger, worn out by the long recitations, cannot carry the speeches whole.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.2.3, the demand; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.2.3, the riddle duel; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 烏魯克之主恩美爾卡爾要求阿拉塔為伊南娜的諸神殿建造並送來貴金屬與寶石；同樣受伊南娜鍾愛的阿拉塔之主卻拒絕了——兩位君王隔著七座山，透過一名疲憊不堪的使者爭辯。這些訊息逐漸演變成謎語般的言辭：恩美爾卡爾以閉戶的穀物與七年之影相詰，而那名使者因冗長的誦述而筋疲力盡，無法將這些言辭完整傳達。

passages.text: Enmerkar's answer is civilization itself: he presses the words into wet clay with a reed — the first writing — so that the message can outlast the messenger. Aratta's lord, reading the tablet, is staggered: the Sumerian has defeated distance; the demand stands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.2.3, the invention of writing; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 恩美卡爾的回答正是文明本身：他以蘆葦將字句壓入濕泥——最初的書寫——使訊息得以比傳訊者更為長存。阿拉塔之主讀著這塊泥板，驚愕不已：蘇美人已戰勝了距離；要求依然成立。

functions: Founding myth of writing as an instrument of statecraft
Charter of Uruk's primacy and Aratta's tribute
Performed with the Aratta cycle in the scribal schools

title.en: The Land Unites Its Tongues
title.zh: 萬邦同聲之世

region.en: Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Enmerkar and the lord of Aratta, closing speech (ETCSL c.1.8.2.3)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: In Enmerkar's great prayer, the age before language-division is recalled: the whole world spoke to Enlil in one tongue; Enki confounded their speech — the Sumerian Babel — and the unity of mankind's tongue is prayed for at Uruk.
summary.zh: 恩美卡爾的偉大祈禱中追憶未分言之世：普天之下同以一語向恩利爾呼告；恩基亂其言語——蘇美的巴別故事——烏魯克遂祈願人類語言之重歸於一。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In his prayer Enmerkar recalls the age when the whole earth spoke to the lord of Nippur in one tongue — the one language of mankind, when no land was set apart. Then Enki, lord of wisdom and of the many tongues, confounded their speech in their mouths; the lands were set apart each with its own language — and the poem prays that the days return when all the lands praise Enlil in one tongue again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.2.3, the prayer; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.2.3, the confounding; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 恩美卡爾在祈禱中追憶那個時代：整個大地以同一種語言向尼普爾之主說話——那是人類唯一的語言，當時尚無任何土地被分隔開來。後來，智慧之主、掌管眾多語言的恩基，攪亂了他們口中的言語；各地被分隔開來，各有自己的語言——而這首詩祈願那樣的日子歸來：萬地再度以同一種語言讚頌恩利爾。

functions: Oldest attestation of the language-confusion myth
Political prayer for cultic unity under Enlil
Liturgical closing of the Aratta cycle performances

title.en: Enmerkar and Ensuhgirana: The Sorceress Duel
title.zh: 恩美卡爾與恩蘇赫吉拉那：巫師對決

region.en: Uruk and Aratta (Aratta pin symbolic)
region.zh: 烏魯克與阿拉塔（阿拉塔為象徵性定位）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Enmerkar and En-suhgir-ana (ETCSL c.1.8.2.4)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Aratta's lord claims seniority; the duel moves from boasts to magic — Aratta's sorcerer turns water into marble, but Uruk's old woman Sagburru counters every spell, and the challenger's severed head is thrown into the pit, ending the contest of cities.
summary.zh: 阿拉塔之王自誇居長；對決由言辭升級為法術——阿拉塔巫師化水為石，烏魯克老嫗薩格布魯逐一破解；挑戰者首級被擲入坑中，兩城之爭落幕。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The lord of Aratta writes to Uruk claiming seniority: his city held kingship before Enmerkar's line. The kings trade boasts and riddles until the duel turns to magic: Aratta sends a sorcerer, Uruk an old woman, Sagburru of the Eanna.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.2.4, the challenge; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿拉塔之主寫信給烏魯克，聲稱自己地位更尊：他的城在恩美卡爾一系之前便已握有王權。兩位君王互以誇耀與謎語相往來，直到這場較量轉為法術：阿拉塔派出一名巫師，烏魯克則派出一名老婦——埃安納的薩格布魯。

passages.text: The sorcerer throws fish spawn into the river and reads the future from them, turns water to marble and back; Sagburru answers spell for spell, spoils each marvel, and the challenger's head is struck off and thrown into the pit. Aratta yields.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.8.2.4, the contest; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那巫師將魚卵投入河中，藉此占卜未來，又將水化為大理石、再變回水；薩格布魯以咒還咒，一一破去他的奇術，挑戰者的頭被砍下，扔進坑中。阿拉塔於是屈服。

functions: Conclusion of the Uruk-Aratta rivalry cycle
Celebration of the craft of female ritual experts
School text for recitation and variant study

variants.summary: The earlier duel of words and the invention of writing.

title.en: Ziusudra and the Great Flood
title.zh: 祖蘇德拉與大洪水

region.en: Shuruppak, Iraq
region.zh: 舒魯帕克（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript (Nippur copy), c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The Flood story (ETCSL c.1.7.4)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The gods decide to destroy mankind; Ziusudra, the pious king of Shuruppak, hears in a dream the command to save the seed of mankind in a great boat, survives seven days of storm, and emerges to sacrifice — and is granted eternal life in Dilmun.
summary.zh: 眾神決議滅絕人類；舒魯帕克虔誠之王祖蘇德拉於夢中得令，造巨舟保存人類種子。風暴七日，倖存登岸獻祭——獲賜永生，居於迪爾蒙。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The great gods resolve to destroy mankind; the assembly of An and Enlil sends the flood. Ziusudra, the pious king of Shuruppak who stands each day with eyes and ears open to the gods, is warned in a dream: take apart the great boat, an old wall speaks to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.7.4, the decision and warning; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 眾大神決意毀滅人類；安與恩利爾的集會降下洪水。舒魯帕克虔敬的國王齊烏蘇德拉，日日睜著眼、豎著耳傾聽眾神，他在夢中受到警告：拆開那艘大船——一堵舊牆對他說話。

passages.text: The storm blows for seven days and seven nights; the flood covers the land, and the boat rides the waves. When the sun rises, Ziusudra opens a window, comes out, and offers sacrifice and libations before the rising sun. The king is granted life like a god's: An and Enlil breathe eternal life into him and set him in the land of Dilmun, the place where the sun rises — the first immortal, reward of the man who saved the seed of mankind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.7.4, the storm and sacrifice; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.7.4, the reward; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 風暴颳了七天七夜；洪水覆蓋大地，船乘著波浪而行。太陽升起時，齊烏蘇德拉打開窗戶，走了出來，在初升的太陽前獻上祭品與奠酒。這位國王獲賜如神一般的生命：安與恩利爾向他吹入永生之氣，將他安置在迪爾蒙之地，即太陽升起之處——他是第一位不死者，是拯救了人類種子之人的獎賞。

functions: Oldest flood myth: charter of the deluge tradition
Reward theology: piety saves the seed of mankind
Link between kingship, sacrifice and the sunrise land

title.en: Lahar and Ashnan: Grain and Sheep
title.zh: 拉哈爾與阿什南：五穀與羊群

region.en: The Dulkug, divine creation site (symbolic pin at Nippur)
region.zh: 杜爾庫格造物之地（象徵性定位於尼普魯）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The debate between Grain and Sheep (ETCSL c.5.3.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Created to give the Anuna gods their food, the sisters Lahar (cattle) and Ashnan (grain) brawl drunk at the banquet, breaking each other's gifts; Enlil and Enki must separate them and assign their stations.
summary.zh: 為供眾神飲食而造的姊妹——牛神拉哈爾與穀神阿什南——於宴上醉酒鬥毆，互毀所贈；恩利爾與恩基出面調停，各定其職。

sensitivity.note: Ancient debate poem; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The Anuna gods, still fed like men, know neither cloth to wear nor grain to eat; Enlil and Enki create in the Dulkug two sisters, Lahar the cattle goddess and Ashnan the grain goddess, to feed the gods and the great household.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.3.2, creation of the sisters; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 安努納諸神仍如凡人一般受供養，卻既無布可衣，也無穀可食；恩利爾與恩基在杜爾庫格造了兩姊妹——牛女神拉哈爾與穀女神阿什南——以餵養諸神與那龐大的家戶。

passages.text: But the two sisters, drunk at the gods' banquet, brawl in the dust: each destroys the other's gifts, the stalls and the fields suffer, and Enlil and Enki descend to separate them — cattle in its stall, grain in its field, each given its own decree of office.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.3.2, the brawl and settlement; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而這兩姊妹在諸神的宴席上醉倒，在塵土中扭打起來：各自毀壞對方的贈禮，畜欄與田地都遭了殃，恩利爾與恩基便下凡將她們分開——牛歸其欄，穀歸其田，各授其職分。

functions: Charter myth of the mixed cattle-grain economy
Etiology of the banquet brawl as the origin of abundance-limiting rules
Debate-poem liturgy performed at New Year

title.en: Winter and Summer Before the Judge
title.zh: 冬夏受審

region.en: Nippur, Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The debate between Winter and Summer (ETCSL c.5.3.3)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Enlil sows two seeds and begets two brothers, Enten the winter farmer and Emesh the summer builder; their boasts and quarrel come before Enlil, who judges in Enten's favor and names him the farmer of the gods — the origin of the agricultural year's order.
summary.zh: 恩利爾播下兩粒種子，生下二兄弟：農夫恩騰（冬）與建造者埃梅什（夏）。二人誇耀爭執，訴於恩利爾；恩利爾判恩騰勝，封其為眾神之農夫——農事年序由此而定。

sensitivity.note: Ancient debate poem; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Enlil begets two seeds in the earth: Enten, the winter, who digs canals, brings the flood-waters, and stocks the granaries, and Emesh, the summer, who builds houses, plants trees and raises the herds' abundance. The brothers quarrel over seniority before Enlil; each recites his works. Enlil judges: Enten is the farmer of the gods, and Emesh shall honor him; the brothers are reconciled with gifts, and the year's order is fixed — sowing and harvest each in its season.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.3.3, the two brothers; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.3.3, the judgment; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 恩利爾在大地中生出兩顆種子：冬神恩騰，開鑿溝渠、引來洪水、充實糧倉；夏神埃梅什，建造房屋、栽種樹木、使畜群繁盛。兄弟二人在恩利爾面前爭論誰為長；各自陳述自己的功業。恩利爾裁斷：恩騰是諸神的農夫，埃梅什當敬重他；兄弟二人以贈禮和解，一年的秩序就此定下——播種與收穫各依其時。

functions: Etiology of the agricultural calendar's two seasons
Judgment myth for the school recitation tradition
Charter of the farmer's seniority in the temple economy

title.en: The Debate between Bird and Fish
title.zh: 鳥魚之辯

region.en: Marshes and seashore of Sumer, Iraq
region.zh: 蘇美沼澤與海岸（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The debate between Bird and Fish (ETCSL c.5.3.5)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Bird boasts of sky and high places, Fish of the waters' depth; their quarrel comes before Enki, who judges both to have their places and assigns neither supremacy — a world where every element keeps its station.
summary.zh: 鳥誇天空與高地，魚誇深水之淵；二人爭執訴於恩基。恩基判定各安其位、無分高下——萬物各守其界的秩序。

sensitivity.note: Ancient debate poem; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Bird mocks Fish as the eater of filth; Fish answers that Bird nests in dirt and cannot enter the water's abundance. Each recounts its realm's gifts — the sky's wide reach, the sea's deep freight — and the quarrel grows bitter. Enki judges: each has its own place and its own plenty; neither shall rule the other. The mother of both waters their quarrel to peace, and the elements are assigned their bounds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.3.5, the debate; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.3.5, the judgment; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 鳥譏笑魚是吃穢物者；魚回答說鳥築巢於汙泥之中，進不了水的豐饒。各自細數其領域的贈禮——天空的遼闊、海洋的深藏——爭吵愈演愈烈。恩基裁斷：各有其位，各有其豐足；誰也不得統治誰。二者之母為他們的爭吵調停平息，諸元素各被劃定疆界。

functions: Debate liturgy on the bounds of the elements
School recitation text of the dispute genre

title.en: The Debate between Copper and Silver
title.zh: 銅銀之辯

region.en: Metalwork of the temples, Sumer (symbolic pin at Lagash)
region.zh: 神廟金工作坊（象徵性定位於拉加什）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The debate between Copper and Silver (ETCSL c.5.3.6)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Silver, the treasury's darling, mocks Copper as the smith's drudge; Copper answers with the tools and weapons that make civilization work. Enlil's judgment: the earth's metals are sisters, and Copper keeps its honor in use.
summary.zh: 國庫寵兒白銀譏銅為工匠之役；銅答以文明賴以運轉的工具與武器。恩利爾裁斷：大地諸金屬本為姊妹，銅在實用中自有其榮。

sensitivity.note: Ancient debate poem; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Silver boasts of the treasury and the bridal gifts; Copper answers that the axes, the ploughshares and the weapons that feed and defend the land are his work. Each catalogs the other's low uses. Enlil separates them in judgment: both are the earth's metals, each with its office — Silver for the temple's glory, Copper for the hand's work — and neither shall disown the other.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.3.6, the debate; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.3.6, the judgment; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 銀誇耀寶庫與聘禮；銅回答說，養育並保衛這片土地的斧頭、犁鏵與武器，都是他的功業。各自列舉對方的低賤用途。恩利爾在裁斷中將他們分開：二者皆是大地的金屬，各有其職——銀為神殿之榮耀，銅為雙手之勞作——誰也不得否認對方。

functions: Values debate on treasury wealth versus working metal
School recitation text of the dispute genre

title.en: The Debate between Date Palm and Tamarisk
title.zh: 椰棗與檉柳之辯

region.en: Gardens of Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克園林（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The debate between Date Palm and Tamarisk (ETCSL c.5.3.7)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The date palm, bread-tree of the south, and the tamarisk, wood of tools and temples, each claim the garden's crown; Enki judges the palm the more abundant — yet the tamarisk keeps the honor of the builder's timber.
summary.zh: 南國之糧椰棗樹與造器築殿之木檉柳，各爭園中之冠；恩基判椰棗豐產為勝——然檉柳仍享工匠之木的榮光。

sensitivity.note: Ancient debate poem; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The date palm catalogs its gifts: fruit, syrup, beer, ropes of fiber, shade for the garden. The tamarisk answers with its own: timber for tools, ploughs and temples, the wood that builds every house. Enki judges in the palm's favor for abundance — the south's bread-tree — while the tamarisk is honored as the builder's timber; both are praised and planted, each in its place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.3.7, the debate; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.3.7, the judgment; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 棗椰樹細數其贈禮：果實、糖漿、啤酒、纖維製的繩索、園中的蔭涼。檉柳以自己的相應作答：製作工具、犁與神殿的木材，建造每一座房屋的木料。恩基以豐饒為由判棗椰樹勝出——南方的麵包之樹——而檉柳則被尊為建造者的木材；二者皆受讚美、皆被栽種，各得其所。

functions: Botanical charter of the southern garden economy
School recitation text of the dispute genre

title.en: The Debate between Hoe and Plough
title.zh: 鋤犁之辯

region.en: Fields of Nippur, Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯田疇（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The debate between Hoe and Plough (ETCSL c.5.3.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The hoe claims the first dig of canals and graves, the plough the sowing that feeds the land; Enlil judges the plough the greater — and the hoe is honored for every task before and after the season of sowing.
summary.zh: 鋤自誇掘渠挖墓之先功，犁誇播種養民之本業；恩利爾判犁為大——然鋤在播種前後的一切勞作中仍享其榮。

sensitivity.note: Ancient debate poem; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The hoe boasts of the first works: digging the canals, opening the fields, digging the graves — the tool that starts and ends all labor. The plough answers with the sowing that feeds the land and the furrows of abundance. Enlil judges the plough the greater worker, and assigns the hoe its honor for every task around the season — the year's two tools reconciled to their offices.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.3.1, the debate; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.3.1, the judgment; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 鋤頭誇耀自己最先的功業：開鑿運河、開墾田地、挖掘墳墓——這工具是一切勞作的起始與終結。犁則以滋養大地的播種與豐饒的犁溝作答。恩利爾判定犁是更為偉大的勞作者，並為鋤頭在季節中每一項事務上分派其應得的尊榮——一年之中的兩件工具就此各安其職。

functions: Dignification of agricultural labor as divine work
School recitation text of the dispute genre

title.en: How Grain Came to Sumer
title.zh: 五穀入蘇美記

region.en: The Dulkug to Sumer's fields (symbolic pin at Nippur)
region.zh: 自杜爾庫格至蘇美田疇（象徵性定位於尼普魯）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: How grain came to Sumer (ETCSL c.1.7.6)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: In the Dulkug, Enlil lets barley sprout from the earth; Ninazu and Ninmada carry it from the mountains to Sumer so that the gods and men can have bread and beer — the origin of the south's staple.
summary.zh: 恩利爾於杜爾庫格使大麥自地中生出；寧阿祖與寧瑪達自山中將其引入蘇美，令諸神與人類得有麵包與啤酒——南方主食之起源。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In the Dulkug, Enlil lets barley rise from the earth's heart; but the grain lies in the mountains, unknown to Sumer's people and gods. Ninazu and Ninmada carry the grain down from the mountain to Sumer; with it come bread and beer, the gods' food and the people's — and the land of the south receives its staple.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.7.6, the sprouting; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.1.7.6, the transfer; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在杜爾庫格，恩利爾讓大麥從大地的心臟升起；然而穀物卻留在山間，不為蘇美的人與神所知。尼納祖與尼恩瑪達將穀物從山上帶下，帶到蘇美；隨之而來的是麵包與啤酒，既是神的食物，也是人的食物——南方之地就此領受了它的主食。

functions: Etiology of agriculture's arrival in southern Mesopotamia
Charter of bread and beer as divine gifts

title.en: The Home of the Fish
title.zh: 魚之居所

region.en: The marsh sea of the south, Iraq
region.zh: 南方沼海（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The home of the fish (ETCSL c.5.9.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: A catalog-poem of the fish and their stations: each fish named, its water, its catch and its place in the temple's fish-houses — a hymn to the marsh economy of the south.
summary.zh: 點數群魚及其居所之詩：一一具名，記其水域、捕獲與神廟魚舍中之位——南方沼澤經濟之頌歌。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The home of the fish is cataloged fish by fish: where each spawns, what each eats, which net takes it, which temple's fish-house keeps it — the marsh's economy set in verse. A catalog-poem of the fish and their stations: each fish named, its water, its catch and its place in the temple's fish-houses — a hymn to the marsh economy of the south.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.9.1, the catalogue; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 魚的家園被一尾一尾地編目記載：每一尾在何處產卵、吃什麼、由哪張網捕獲、由哪座神廟的魚庫收存——沼澤的經濟被寫成了詩。這是一首關於魚及其處所的目錄詩：每一尾魚皆有其名，有其水域、其捕獲之法，以及它在神廟魚庫中的位置——一首讚頌南方沼澤經濟的頌歌。

functions: Verse map of the marsh fishery economy
Hymn of Enki's watery kingdom

title.en: The Heron and the Turtle
title.zh: 鷺與龜

region.en: Marshes of the south, Iraq
region.zh: 南方沼澤（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The heron and the turtle (ETCSL c.5.9.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The heron, fish-hunter of the marsh, is lured by the turtle's promise of an easy catch; the turtle drags him into the water and drowns him — a fable of greed, patience and the marsh's justice.
summary.zh: 沼中捕魚之鷺為龜的易得之利所誘；龜將其拖入水中溺斃——貪婪、耐心與沼澤正義的寓言。

sensitivity.note: Ancient fable; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The heron hunts the marsh's fish; the turtle promises him an easy catch in the deep. The greedy bird follows — and the turtle grips his feet, drags him down, and drowns him in the water. The fable's moral is spoken by the marsh itself: the patient small one outwaits the greedy flyer; the one who hunts for ease is caught by the still one's cunning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.9.2, the fable; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.9.2, the moral; not verbatim.

title.en: A Man and His God
title.zh: 人與其神

summary.en: A righteous man who has done no wrong is stricken by his personal god; in his suffering he never curses, prays and weeps day and night — and his god, moved at last, restores him: the oldest righteous-sufferer poem.
summary.zh: 一位未曾作惡的義人遭其守護神降禍；苦難中他從不咒罵，日夜祈禱哭泣——其神終受感動，使他復原：最古老的義人受苦詩。

sensitivity.note: Ancient wisdom literature; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: A man who has done no wrong is stricken: sickness, loss and humiliation come from his own god, and no sin explains it. He does not curse; he weeps and prays day and night in the temple courts. His god, moved at last by the man's patient piety, turns and restores him: health, standing and prosperity return, and the poem closes blessing the man who did not curse his god in trouble.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.2.4, the suffering; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.2.4, the restoration; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個未曾行惡的人卻遭擊打：疾病、損失與屈辱皆來自他自己的神，而沒有罪愆能解釋這一切。他並不咒詛；他日夜在神廟的庭院中哭泣祈禱。他的神終於被這人恆忍的虔敬所感動，轉而復原了他：健康、地位與昌盛皆歸回，詩篇最後祝福這在患難中未曾咒詛其神的人。

functions: Founding poem of the righteous-sufferer genre

Temple liturgy of the penitent

title.en: The Poem of Early Rulers

region.en: Sumer's earliest cities, Iraq

summary.en: The poem recalls the lost age of the five ancient cities and their flood, the wisdom of Enmeduranki and the deeds of early kings — and teaches that the days of old were god-favored, and the present must labor to match them.
summary.zh: 詩篇追憶五古邦與洪水之前的年代、恩梅杜蘭基之智慧與先王的功業——教導昔日蒙神眷顧，今人當勉力追之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient wisdom literature; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In ancient times, the five cities before the flood — Eridug, Bad-tibira, Larsa, Sippar and Shuruppak — were given their fates, and the flood swept them; their kings were taken up to heaven. The poem names the wise of old — Enmeduranki who sat in the gods' assembly — and the rulers whose justice kept the land, teaching the present to match their piety: the days of old were long, the days of now are brief.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.2.5, the lost age; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.2.5, the wise and the teaching; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在遠古之時，洪水之前的五座城——埃利都、巴德提比拉、拉爾薩、西帕爾與舒魯帕克——被賦予了各自的命運，而洪水將它們沖走；它們的君王被接升上天。這首詩道出古時的智者——坐在眾神集會中的恩梅杜蘭基——以及以其正義維繫大地的統治者，教導今人以他們的虔敬為榜樣：古時的日子長久，如今的日子短促。

functions: Wisdom meditation on the antediluvian age

summary.en: Ludingira, far from home, writes to his mother at the house of Ur-Namma: do not be anxious — the courier is sound, the roads safe — a tender message-poem in which love of mother and the dangers of travel are set against the distance of empires.

sensitivity.note: Ancient letter-poem; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Ludingira, traveling far, writes to his mother at Ur-Namma's house: mother, do not be anxious for me — the courier is sound, the roads are safe, and your son thinks of you. The poem's tenderness is its theme: the mother's worry set against the son's reassurance, love measured across the distances of empire — the earliest letter-poem of family love in world literature.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.5.1, the message; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.5.1, the tenderness; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 盧丁吉拉遠行在外，寫信給烏爾納穆家中之母：母親，請勿為我憂慮——信使安然無恙，道路平安，您的兒子惦念著您。這首詩的溫柔即是其主題：母親的憂慮與兒子的寬慰相對，愛在帝國遼闊的距離間被丈量——世界文學中最早書寫親情之愛的書信體詩篇。

functions: Earliest letter-poem of family affection

title.en: Night and Darkness and Their Three Daughters
title.zh: 夜與暗之三女

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I: Mitologie en legendes (1919), No. 2

summary.en: Before sun, moon or stars there was only twilight. 'Ga (Night) and 'Gagen (Darkness) lived in a rock cave with three daughters, each wearing a magic rattle-string — of tortoise shells, of gourd shells, of springbok-ear bladders — forbidden ever to remove. 'Kaggen, the Mantis, watched their dances as a great buck; the father shot him; the quarters came alive, rejoined, and the 'Hotnotsgod' ran off. Then he sent three sons as suitors, and the girls, wed, became the mothers of plenty.
summary.zh: 日月星未生，天地僅餘微明。'加（夜）與'加根（暗）居石穴，育三女，各佩魔鈴串——龜殼、葫蘆殼、跳羚耳囊——戒令永不可解。螳螂卡根化大羚觀舞，父射之；肉塊復活，節節自合，卡根遁走。後遣三子求婚，三女既嫁，豐饒自茲始。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh from named Bushman narrators of the Hantam and Hartebeest rivers, 1870s-1880s; presented as an archival record.

narrative.en:
Von Wielligh's narrators were emphatic: everything was born from darkness. First it was evening, and then morning. In the old days there was only a dim twilight, like a heavy overcast day; it was cold, and the Sun, the Moon and the Stars did not yet shine. Old 'Ga (Night) and his wife 'Gagen (Darkness) lived in a rock cave. They had no sons, only three daughters.

When the three girls grew up, the mother made them rattling necklaces. For the eldest she took little tortoise shells, hollowed them, dropped pebbles inside so they would rattle, and strung them on a bobbejaan-skin thong; she forbade the girl ever to take it off, or the food in her belly would perish. For the second she strung little gourd shells filled with berry-seeds on a cord of inner bark; for the youngest she took springbok ears, made little bladders of the white inner pit, dried them with sand and filled them with the hard grains that lie inside springbok eyes, strung on springbok sinew. Each daughter wore her commandment: never remove the string.

The father and mother called the girls to dance before the people, and many came from far to see them; the young men were wary of the three dancers, for they held them to be witch-people. 'Kaggen — the Mantis, whom the narrators call the 'Hotnotsgod' — sat on a bush watching and listening day after day. To see better he changed himself into a great wild buck and came close. The old father seized his quiver and bow, stalked the great buck, shot and hit it; the buck ran a little way and fell — or rather, pretended to fall.

The family walked up to cut it up. The father carried a hindquarter and the skin, the mother the other hindquarter and the inner parts, the eldest daughter a forequarter, the second the other forequarter, and the youngest the head with the backbone. The head began to talk, to groan piteously, and to wink its eyes. Three times the youngest girl called out that the buck's head was still alive; the others laughed her off. At the third call the carriers stood still — and the four quarters turned on the carriers' heads. In terror they set them down on bushes; each quarter sprang up, ran to the backbone, and fastened itself to its place; the entrails crept back in; the skin folded itself around; and the buck stood again before them, calm. It gave a short gallop away and became the Mantis once more. So the old father and his family found that 'Kaggen had cheated them.

Not content, the Mantis after some days changed three of his sons into three young men and sent them to woo the three daughters. The girls fell in love with the fine young men and married them; they built huts of bushes and lived there, for game and veld food abounded — as their mother had foretold — so long as the daughters wore the rattle-strings. Other Bushmen came to live there and hunt, and the place became a place of pleasure: no quarrels, food and all needs in abundance. In one word, it was a lazy-sweet land.

functions: Cosmogony: night and darkness as the primal parents of the habitable world.
Explains the power of rattling necklaces (tortoise, gourd, springbok-ear) as life-giving amulets.
Reinforces the Mantis's role as undying deceiver even of Night's own family.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 2 (1919); not verbatim. In the old days there was only a dim twilight, like a heavily overcast day; it was cold, and the Sun, Moon and Stars did not yet shine. Old 'Ga (Night) and his wife 'Gagen (Darkness) lived in a rock cave; they had no sons, only three daughters.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此為馮·維利希（von Wielligh）第一卷第二則（1919年）之濃縮意譯，非逐字照錄。古時只有一片昏暗的微光，如同陰沉密雲之日；天寒，日月星辰尚未照耀。老「加」（'Ga，夜）與其妻「加亨」（'Gagen，黑暗）居於一岩洞中；他們沒有兒子，只有三個女兒。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. For the eldest daughter the mother strung riddling tortoise shells with pebbles inside on a bobbejaan-skin thong; for the second, little gourd shells with berry-seeds on inner-bark cord; for the youngest, bladders made from the white pit of springbok ears, filled with the hard grains from springbok eyes, on springbok sinew. Each was forbidden to remove her necklace, or the food in her belly would come to nothing.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同處之濃縮意譯，非逐字照錄。母親為長女以狒狒皮帶串起內藏卵石的龜殼；為次女以內樹皮繩串起裝著漿果籽的小葫蘆殼；為幼女以跳羚筋串起由跳羚耳白色耳骨製成的囊袋，內裝取自跳羚眼睛的硬粒。每個女兒都被禁止取下項鍊，否則腹中之食將化為烏有。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. 'Kaggen the Mantis, the 'Hotnotsgod', watched the three dancers from a bush, changed into a great wild buck to see better, and was shot by the girls' father. The head still talked and groaned; the youngest daughter warned three times; then the quarters turned about, sprang to the backbone, the entrails crept in, the skin folded round — and the buck stood whole, galloped off, and became the Mantis again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同處之濃縮意譯，非逐字照錄。螳螂「卡亨」（'Kaggen），即「霍特諾特神」（'Hotnotsgod），從灌木叢中觀看三名舞者，變為一頭巨大的野公鹿以便看得更清楚，卻被女孩們的父親射中。鹿頭仍能言語呻吟；幼女三次示警；隨後四足翻轉，猛然接上脊骨，內臟縮回，獸皮包攏——公鹿完好如初地立起，奔馳而去，又變回螳螂。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Then the Mantis changed three of his sons into young men and sent them to woo the daughters. The girls married them, built huts of bushes, and game and veld food abounded as the mother had foretold, so long as the daughters wore the rattle-strings; other Bushmen came to hunt there, and the place became a place of pleasure — a lazy-sweet land.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同處之濃縮意譯，非逐字照錄。隨後螳螂將自己的三個兒子變為青年，派他們去向三姊妹求婚。女孩們嫁給了他們，以灌木搭建小屋，獵物與野地食物如母親所預言般豐足，只要女兒們佩戴著響串；其他布須曼人前來此地狩獵，此地遂成歡樂之所——一片慵懶甜美的土地。

title.en: The Mountains Are the Eldest Daughter
title.zh: 山為長女

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I: Mitologie en legendes (1919), No. 3

summary.en: 'Kou, Night's eldest daughter, weds a son of the Mantis and grows tortoise-lazy; a bobbejaan demands her tortoise-shell necklace — made of his brother's skin — and returns with a commando. The Mantis changes his son into a great bird and the child into the Echo; the whirlwind fells the raiders, who swear to trample her grave and roll its stones forever. 'Kou sleeps and sleeps, and has become the mountains.
summary.zh: '口——夜之長女——嫁螳螂之子，因嗜龜肉而懶惰。狒狒索其龜殼鈴串——云係其兄弟之皮——率眾來襲。螳螂化子為巨鳥、化童為回聲；旋風摧敵，敗者誓踏其墓、永滾其石。'口長眠不醒，遂成群山。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

narrative.en:
'Kou, the eldest of Night's three daughters, married a son of the 'Hotnotsgod (the Mantis); they built huts of bushes. Never taking off her tortoise-shell necklace, she could catch tortoises as she pleased — but she grew so fond of tortoise flesh that she wanted nothing else, and, like the slow, lazy tortoise, she grew slow and lazy herself. A short walk to fetch tortoises took her nearly the whole day; she did nothing more for husband or child. Her husband scolded, then beat her — as well have scolded a tortoise, or rattled the pebbles in the shells. He had to do everything alone, even catch her tortoises.

One day, while he was away hunting, a bobbejaan came and asked the child where her mother was: he wanted the thong that bound the tortoise shells on her neck, for it was made of the skin of his brother. The child would not tell; the bobbejaan threatened to come next day and tear the necklace from 'Kou's neck by force. When the father came home the child begged him to stay; next day the bobbejaan came as promised, and the husband threatened him with bow and arrow. The bobbejaan warned that he would return with a commando of his brothers and break the huts to flinders.

The husband hurried out to gather food and made ready for the attack. As promised, the bobbejaan came with a great company of his family. The Mantis, watching quietly from a bush, changed his son into a great bird and the child into the Echo. The bird rose and made a great wind with its wings; thick dust arose, and the Echo made a great noise. As the bird wheeled, a terrible whirlwind arose, hurling stones and pieces of wood; here a bobbejaan took a stone on the head, there another a blow with a stick, and the sand and dust blinded them so that they scattered and fled.

From far off they called back: 'Wait, we will never leave 'Kou in peace — over her grave we will walk, and the stones of it we will turn and roll forever.' But they slunk away. And 'Kou grew lazier by the day: she fell asleep, and slept, and slept to this very day. In her sleep she became a great mountain, never to wake again. When the bobbejaans saw her become mountains they were only glad; in revenge they walk on the mountains and roll the stones, as they swore. 'Kou, the mountains, is not dead: she only rests in an eternal sleep.

functions: Origin of mountains as the sleeping body of Night's eldest daughter.
Explains the bobbejaan's habit of turning and rolling stones on high places.
Charter for the echo as a child-spirit that answers from the rocks.

The Mantis changed his son into a great bird and the child into the Echo; the bird's wings raised a great wind, and a terrible whirlwind hurled stones and sticks until the bobbejaans scattered and fled.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 3; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同段落的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。一隻狒狒索討那條以牠兄弟的皮製成的項鍊皮繩，並警告說牠會帶著一群兄弟組成的突擊隊回來搗毀茅屋。螳螂把他的兒子變成了一隻大鳥，又把那孩子變成了回聲；大鳥的翅膀掀起一陣大風，可怕的旋風拋擲石塊與木棍，直到狒狒們四散奔逃。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. In their flight they swore to walk over her grave and roll its stones for ever. But 'Kou grew lazier by the day, fell asleep, and slept until she became a great mountain, never to wake again; and the bobbejaans still walk on her and roll the stones of her grave.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 3; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同段落的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。牠們在奔逃中發誓要永遠走過她的墳墓，並翻動墓上的石頭。但「庫」一天比一天懶散，沉沉睡去，一直睡到化作一座大山，再也不會醒來；而狒狒們至今仍走在她身上，翻動著她墳墓的石頭。

title.en: The Wind and the Wind-Bird
title.zh: 風與風鳥

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 4

summary.en: 'Kou's husband, the Mantis's son, became the Wind-bird and dwells in a hole in the cliffs; near it no one goes. If angered he flings people down, whirls them into the sky, strips their huts and carries off the mats. He was once a man of the old race; now when he flaps slowly the wind blows soft, when he beats the ground a dust-storm rises. He is also the breath in living things: take away his wind and a person dies.
summary.zh: '口之夫——螳螂之子——化為風鳥，居於崖穴；近其穴者不得。怒則擲人於地、捲人上天、拆其屋掠其席。他本是古族之人；今其緩拍則微風，拍地則沙暴。又為萬物之氣息：奪其風者死。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 4 (1919); not verbatim. 'Kou's husband, the son of the 'Hotnotsgod, was changed into a bird, the Wind-bird, and went to live in a hole in a rock cliff. No one goes near the hole where the wind lives; out of it blows a violent wind that flings a person to the ground and fills his eyes with sand and dust — or the whirlwind lifts him up into the sky, carries him far away, and lets him fall from above.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 4; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 改寫自馮·維利希（von Wielligh）第一部第四號（1919年）的濃縮版本，非逐字照錄。「庫」的丈夫是「霍特諾茨神」之子，他被變成了一隻鳥，即風鳥，住到岩崖上的一個洞裡。沒有人敢靠近風所居住的那個洞；從洞中吹出猛烈的風，把人掀倒在地，並用沙土填滿他的眼睛——否則旋風便把他捲上天空，帶到遠方，再從高處把他摔下。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The Wind was first a man of the old race; he walked and played and hunted like the others. Now that he is a bird, when he flaps his wings slowly the wind blows gently; when he beats the ground with his feet and whips up the sand, the dust rises in banks, the trees bend and crack, and the storm flattens everything it touches.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 4; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同段落的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。風原本是古老族類中的一名男子；他像其他人一樣行走、嬉戲、狩獵。如今他成了一隻鳥，當他緩緩拍動翅膀時，風便輕輕吹拂；當他用雙腳蹬踏地面、揚起沙土時，塵土便成堆升起，樹木彎折斷裂，暴風雨所觸及的一切都被夷平。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The Wind-bird sends his wind into people and animals too; when he takes away the wind of a person or animal, that one dies, and no breath ever comes again into mouth and nostrils. So one must beware of naming the bird's name, or of speaking badly of him when he is near — two children who shot and threw stones at him were caught by the whirlwind, spun like tops, and driven fleeing from trees to rocks to a cave, until their mothers burned sweet-smelling bushes and strewed buchu into the wind, and sang it calm.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 4; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同段落的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。風鳥也把風送入人和動物體內；當他取走一個人或一隻動物的風時，那一個便死去，氣息再也不會回到口與鼻孔之中。因此，人必須小心，不可說出這隻鳥的名字，也不可在牠近旁說牠的壞話——有兩個孩子曾向牠射擊並投擲石塊，結果被旋風抓住，像陀螺般旋轉，從樹林被趕到岩石，再被趕到洞穴，直到他們的母親焚燒芬芳的灌木，把布枯（buchu）撒入風中，並唱歌使風平息。

title.en: The Echo, Daughter of the Mountains
title.zh: 回聲：山之女

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 5

summary.en: The Echo is the mountains' daughter; her father is the Wind speaking through her. Speelman, first inventor of music — kudu-horn trumpets, reed flutes, gut-stringed ramkies and a pot-drum — follows her singing into the kloofs, is lured apart voice by voice until lost among lions, wolves and jackals, escapes a lion by feigning death, and escapes the bobbejaans by blowing his horn till the cliffs thunder.
summary.zh: 回聲為山之女；其父乃風，借其口而言。斯皮爾曼——樂之始創者——聞其歌而入深谷，聲音漸分漸遠，迷失於獅、狼、豺之間；佯死脫獅，吹號震崖，驚走狒狒。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 5 (1919); not verbatim. The Echo, or Echo, is the daughter of the mountains — her father is the Wind, who speaks through her daughter. She is a mocker who is never tired: the one she teases will weary and grow angry, but the Echo never. She lives in the deep kloofs among the cliffs and precipices, and she sleeps never; when anyone calls, she answers at once — she is always awake.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 5; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 改寫自馮·維利希（von Wielligh）第一部第五號（1919年）的濃縮版本，非逐字照錄。回聲是群山之女——她的父親是風，風透過他的女兒說話。她是個從不疲倦的嘲弄者：被她戲弄的人會疲倦、會發怒，但回聲從不如此。她住在崖壁與峭壁之間幽深的峽谷裡，從不睡眠；任何人呼喚，她立刻回應——她永遠清醒。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The man who first invented music was named Speelman. He made trumpets from kudu horns, flutes from flute-reed, stringed instruments from the sinews of wild animals, and even a drum from a pot with a springbok skin stretched over it. Speelman could sing and play so beautifully that he sought for one who could sing and play as beautifully as he; and the people told him of a girl in the kloofs whose name was Echo.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 5; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同一段落的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。最早發明音樂的人名叫斯皮爾曼。他用捻角羚的角做成號角，用蘆葦做成笛子，用野獸的筋腱做成弦樂器，甚至用一口鍋繃上跳羚皮做成鼓。斯皮爾曼的歌聲與演奏美妙極了，於是他想找一個能唱得、奏得和他一樣美妙的人；人們便告訴他，峽谷裡有個姑娘名叫厄科。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. He blew his kudu horn and began to sing, and was astonished that the Echo sang more beautifully still, for an echo always sounds finer than the voice it answers. But the nearer he came the further the voices moved apart — one voice, then two, then three, then more — until he wandered into the gramadoelas, the wild mountains, lost. He escaped the bobbejaans by blowing his great horn till the kloofs thundered, the lion by playing dead while it carried him, and after long wandering he reached his home.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 5; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同一段落的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。他吹響捻角羚號角，開始歌唱，卻驚訝地發現厄科唱得更加美妙，因為回聲聽起來總比它所回應的聲音更動人。可是他越走近，那些聲音就分得越開——先是一個聲音，然後兩個，然後三個，然後更多——直到他誤入格拉馬多拉斯，那片荒山野嶺，迷失了方向。他吹響大號角，震得峽谷轟鳴，藉此擺脫了狒狒；他裝死，任獅子把他叼走，才逃過獅口；經過長久的流浪，他終於回到了家。

title.en: The Plains Are the Second Daughter
title.zh: 平原為次女

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 6

summary.en: 'Kaun, Night's second daughter, weds the Mantis's son and grows drowsy on her gourd-necklace of seeds; a Tree comes for the necklace strung on his brother's inner bark, then a whole wood. The Mantis changes his son into a great Fire and the child into the Mirage; the trees flee, swearing to root into her grave. 'Kaun sleeps and has become the plains, with bushes and grass rooted in her throat.
summary.zh: '昆——夜之次女——嫁螳螂之子，因葫蘆鈴串之籽而慵倦；樹來索其串——謂係其兄弟之內皮——後舉林而至。螳螂化子為烈火、化童為蜃景；群樹奔逃，誓根入其墓。'昆長眠成平原；灌木草芥根入其喉。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 6 (1919); not verbatim. The second daughter of 'Ga and 'Gagen, 'Kaun, went with her husband to live in huts of matjiesgoed; she was very clever at making mats. The bewitching necklace of gourd shells made many kinds of plants and fruits grow around her, so that there was plenty of mat-reed; but it took her appetite for meat away, and idleness came over her as over her eldest sister.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 6; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馮·維利赫《第一卷》第六則（1919年）的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。'Ga與'Gagen的次女'Kaun隨丈夫去住在用燈心草蓆搭成的棚屋裡；她非常擅長編蓆。那串用葫蘆殼製成的魔項鍊使她周圍長出各種植物和果實，因此編蓆用的蘆葦十分充足；但項鍊奪走了她的食肉之慾，懶惰也像降臨在她大姐身上那樣降臨到她身上。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. A Tree came asking for the necklace, whose cord was made of the inner bark of the trunk of his brother; the bare place on the trunk was rotting, and his brother wanted to die. Next day a whole wood came with him; the husband refused, and the trees grew riotous with a great noise. The 'Hotnotsgod changed the man into a great Fire and the child into the Mirage; the trees fled before the flames, swearing to root into her grave.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 6; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同一段落的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。一棵樹前來索要那串項鍊，項鍊的繩子是用它兄弟樹幹的內皮做成的；那樹幹上裸露的地方正在腐爛，它的兄弟想要死去。第二天，一整片樹林隨它而來；丈夫拒絕了，樹木便喧鬧騷動，發出巨大的聲響。'Hotnotsgod把男人變成一大團火，把孩子變成海市蜃樓；樹木在火焰前逃竄，發誓要在她的墳上扎根。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. 'Kaun grew lazier, felt a pain in her neck, and when she woke the seeds in the gourd shells had begun to grow and had sent their roots through her neck into her body. She became the plains and sleeps today; the trees, bushes and grass grow over her, thrusting their roots into the throat of the Earth — into 'Kaun's throat. As long as there is a world there will be plains, and as long as there are plains the bushes and grass will grow on them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 6; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同一段落的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。'Kaun越來越懶，感到脖子一陣疼痛，醒來時葫蘆殼裡的種子已經開始生長，根鬚穿過她的脖子伸進她的身體。她化作了平原，至今沉睡；樹木、灌木和青草在她身上生長，把根扎進大地的喉嚨——扎進'Kaun的喉嚨。只要世界還在，就會有平原；只要有平原，灌木和青草就會在上面生長。

title.en: Fire the Dancer and the 'Nu Feast
title.zh: 火焰舞者與'努之宴

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 7

summary.en: Danser, Fire, is a son of the Mantis; his head gives light in the sunless twilight world. At a great feast he teaches fire-drilling — soft wood, whirled stick, fine grass — and a blaze that the people worship; he draws two rings about the fire, one for roasting meat (for till then people ate raw like lions and jackals) and one beyond which is the outside world, and institutes the 'Ku-dance. He still hates the trees for rooting in his wife the Plains.
summary.zh: 丹瑟（火）為螳螂之子；無日之世界中，其頭放光。大宴之上，他教鑽木取火——軟木、旋桿、細草——烈焰起而眾人拜。他以二圈圍火：內圈炙肉（自此人類始食熟，免如獅豺生食），外圈之外乃外世；並立'庫之舞。彼至今恨樹根纏其妻（平原）。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 7 (1919); not verbatim. The Fire's name is Danser, but his wife 'Kaun has been changed into the plains. He is a son of the 'Hotnotsgod and first walked like a man, hunting and playing. He still walks about like a man, but mostly one cannot see him; like his brother the Wind he creeps everywhere. Strike stones together and fire leaps out; rub sticks together and the wood kindles; lightning-fire comes out of the sky too.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 7; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馮·維利赫《第一卷》第七則（1919年）的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。火的名字叫丹瑟，但他的妻子'Kaun已化作平原。他是'Hotnotsgod的兒子，起初像人一樣行走，打獵、嬉戲。他至今仍像人一樣四處走動，但大多時候人們看不見他；他像他的兄弟風一樣，到處潛行。把石頭相互敲擊，火便迸出；把木頭相互摩擦，木頭便燃起；閃電之火也會從天而降。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Fire has crept into people and animals and plants as well: if it goes out of a person or beast the flesh grows cold and they die. At a great feast Danser taught the people to make fire: he hollowed a soft stick, laid shavings in the hollow, put fine rubbed grass beside it, and whirled a thinner harder stick upright between his flat hands until the shavings took, the grass began, and a great fire burnt up; and the people sang and danced around it in wonder.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 7; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同出處的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。火也潛入了人、獸與草木之中：火若離開人或獸，血肉便會變冷，他們就死了。在一次盛大的宴會上，丹瑟教眾人取火：他將一根軟木挖空，把木屑放入凹槽，在旁放上細細搓揉過的乾草，再將一根較細較硬的木棍直立於兩掌之間搓轉，直到木屑著火、乾草引燃，熊熊大火便燒了起來；眾人驚奇地圍著火唱歌跳舞。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. He drew a wide ring about the fire and bade them bring the meat inside it to roast — for until then everyone ate raw food like the lion, leopard, wolf and jackal — and the people tasted that roast meat is sweeter than raw. Then he drew a second ring outside the roasting-ring, and between the two rings the people had to dance, sing and make music. From that day feasts were held and the 'Ku-dance was instituted.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 7; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同出處的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。他在火四周畫了一個大圈，吩咐眾人把肉帶進圈內燒烤——因為在此之前，人人都像獅子、豹、狼與胡狼一樣吃生食——眾人於是嘗到，烤過的肉比生肉更甘美。接著他又在烤肉圈外畫了第二個圈，眾人必須在兩圈之間跳舞、唱歌、奏樂。從那天起，便有了宴會，也創立了「庫舞」。

title.en: Antjie of the Plains: The Mirage Girl
title.zh: 平原姑娘：蜃景之女

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 8

summary.en: The mirage is the daughter of the Plains and of Fire, wordless but full of tricks, mother of dreams. When strangers overrun the Bushman country she dances above the flames — the chief's son follows and burns — then shows them glittering waters, woods and huts that shift and hang upside down, lulls them into dreams of plenty, and when they wake it is all gone and they are back where they began.
summary.zh: 蜃景乃平原與火之女，無言而多詭，夢之母。異族侵桑土，她於焰上起舞——酋長之子追之而焚——繼而現閃爍之水、林、屋，形影互易，倒懸於空；誘其入豐饒之夢；醒時萬象俱無，原地如故。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 8 (1919); not verbatim. Like the Echo, the Mirage is a mocker and lure of people in the field; she dazzles their eyes so that they see things that do not exist. The Mirage is the daughter of the Plains and of Fire; she has remained true to her parents and therefore still dances above the flame of Fire and on the Plains.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 8; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改寫自馮·維利希（von Wielligh）第一部第八則（1919年）；非逐字照錄。海市蜃樓與回聲一樣，是原野中戲弄並誘惑人的存在；她眩惑人的雙眼，使人看見並不存在的事物。海市蜃樓是平原之女、火之女；她對父母始終忠誠，因此至今仍在火焰之上、在平原之上起舞。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. She can speak with people through dreams, for she is the mother of Dreams. When the land of the Bushmen of the old race was overrun by strong strangers of another kind, Antjie of the Plains showed herself first as a beautiful girl; the son of the strangers' leader fell in love, and she bade him do as she did: she danced above the flames of the Fire — and he, who did not yet know fire, came into the flames and was burnt. The strangers rose in wrath to kill her people.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 8; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同出處的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。她能透過夢境與人交談，因為她是夢之母。當舊族的布須曼人（Bushmen）之地被另一種強悍的陌生人侵佔時，平原的安琪（Antjie）先以美麗少女的形貌現身；陌生人的首領之子愛上了她，她便吩咐他照她的樣子做：她在火焰之上起舞——而他尚不識火，走進火焰之中，被燒死了。陌生人勃然大怒，起身要殺害她的族人。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. She appeared to the weary pursuers in terror-filled dreams so they could not rest; she showed them in the distance a great pan of water, beautiful woods, houses and huts — but as they walked the shapes changed: the cliffs loosened, the trees hung head-down, trees grew in the air. They fell into despair and turned back; she let them fall asleep and showed them splendid dreams of fat game and fruit; when they woke they were standing again at their old dwelling-places. So the Mirage delivered her people.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 8; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同出處的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。她以充滿恐懼的夢境向疲憊的追兵顯現，使他們不得安歇；她在遠處向他們顯示一大片水塘、美麗的樹林、房屋與茅舍——但他們一路走去，景象卻變了樣：崖壁鬆動，樹木倒懸，樹木長在空中。他們陷入絕望，轉身折返；她讓他們入睡，向他們顯示肥美獵物與果實的華美夢境；他們醒來時，又站在自己舊日的居所前。海市蜃樓就這樣拯救了她的族人。

title.en: The Waters Are the Youngest Daughter
title.zh: 水為幼女

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 9

summary.en: 'Khwa, Night's youngest daughter, quick as a springbok by her ear-necklace, is demanded by a great Springbok who wants the sinew thong; he threatens to return with his brothers and trample her. The Mantis changes her husband into the great Rain-Beast and the child into the great Water-Snake with the shining stone on its head; mist and black rain-clouds burst, a flood drowns the raiders, and the girl becomes the restless Waters that never sleep — flowing to rivers, to the sea, and living also in men, beasts and plants.
summary.zh: '夸——夜之幼女——佩跳羚耳鈴，疾如羚；大羚索其筋弦，揚言率弟群踏之。螳螂化其夫為大雨獸、化其子為頂負閃石之大水蛇；黑雲迸發，洪水沒敵。'夸遂化為永不息之水——流為江河入海，且居於人獸草木之中。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

narrative.en:
'Khwa, the youngest daughter, differed from her sisters. The necklace of springbok ears made her as quick as a springbok; and because a springbok does not sleep by night, she too slept little and was always restless. The necklace gave her an overpowering craving for springbok flesh, and she took great pleasure in hunting the bucks herself. Her husband also hunted, so they always had plenty for themselves and their child.

One day the child was alone at home when a great Springbok came — one of the old race. He demanded the necklace of springbok ears bound on 'Khwa's neck with springbok sinew, and stood proud and wrathful. The child would not say where her mother was and begged him to go; he answered that he would go, but would return next day with a troop of his brothers to storm 'Khwa and trample her to death if she would not give up the string. When the father came home the child told him everything, and he stayed to prepare.

Next day the dust of the approaching springboks was seen, and they grew afraid. But the Mantis, watching from a bush, changed the man into a great Ox — the Water-Beast, also called the Rain-Beast — and the child into the great Water-Snake that wears the beautiful shining stone on its head. The Rain-Beast blew a thick bank of mist from his nostrils and heavy black rain-clouds into the sky, out of which a heavy downpour fell, and a great flood of water came; and the Water-Snake let streams of water bubble up out of the ground. The springboks had to swim out and flee for their lives; they were so frightened that springboks have drunk no water since that day.

When the Rain-Beast and the Water-Snake sought 'Khwa they found that she was what had become the Waters. Because she had had little rest and was always in motion, the Waters are so too: there is always stirring and restlessness in them, like the sea. The other people tasted them and found that water takes thirst away, and from that time they drank water. But some will not drink it — the springboks, hares, tortoises and insects drink another kind of water that does not make them soon thirsty; and they will never tell where that water is to be found.

'Khwa is now the wide and restless Waters. In streams she flows to the rivers, and the rivers flow into the restless sea; in rain she floats in the clouds through the sky; as misty weather — the breath of the Rain-Beast — she sweeps over mountains and plains; she never rests; she bubbles up from the ground in fountains. The Waters, like her sisters the Mountains and the Plains, are strong: they carry great weights, and heavy things float upon them. They live not only above and below the ground, but in people, animals and plants: if they go out of them, those die of thirst. Thus Water, Fire and Wind are what keep people alive; the three do not die, and as long as there is an Earth there will be Water, Fire and Wind. Sometimes the three fight with one another — a thunderstorm means 'today Water, Fire and Wind are quarrelling again' — but mostly they work together, for if they moved out of people and animals there would be no more friendship or quarrel among them.

functions: Origin of water, rivers, rain and springs through the youngest daughter's transformation.
Explains why springbok, hare, tortoise and insects do not drink standing water.
Frames weather as the quarrel and cooperation of Water, Fire and Wind.

variants.name: |Xam rain-maidens (Specimens)

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 9 (1919); not verbatim. 'Khwa, the youngest daughter, was made quick as a springbok by the necklace of springbok ears; because a springbok does not sleep by night she too slept little and was always in motion. A great Springbok of the old race came demanding the necklace strung on her neck with springbok sinew, threatening to return with a troop of his brothers to trample her to death.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 9; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改寫自馮·維利希（von Wielligh）第一部第九則（1919年）；非逐字照錄。最小的女兒「夸」（'Khwa）因戴上跳羚耳朵串成的項鍊，而變得如跳羚般迅捷；因為跳羚夜間不睡，她也睡得很少，總是動個不停。一頭舊族的巨大跳羚前來索討那條以跳羚筋串起、掛在她頸上的項鍊，並威脅要帶著一群兄弟回來把她踩死。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The 'Hotnotsgod changed the husband into a great Ox, the Water-Beast or Rain-Beast, and the child into the great Water-Snake with the shining stone on its head. The Rain-Beast blew thick mist from his nostrils and heavy black rain-clouds into the sky; a heavy downpour fell, a great flood came, and the Water-Snake let streams bubble up out of the ground; the springboks had to swim for their lives, and from that day springboks drink no water.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 9; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同出處的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。『霍特諾茨神』把丈夫變成一頭巨大的公牛，即水獸或雨獸，又把孩子變成一條巨大的水蛇，頭上頂著一顆發光的石頭。雨獸從鼻孔裡噴出濃霧，又向天空噴出厚重的黑色雨雲；大雨傾盆而下，洪水泛濫，水蛇讓溪流從地底湧出；跳羚只得拼命游泳逃命，從那天起，跳羚便不再喝水。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. They found that 'Khwa had become the Waters, restless like the sea, flowing in streams to the rivers and the rivers into the sea, floating in clouds, sweeping as mist over mountains and plains, bubbling up in fountains — never resting. The Waters live also in people, beasts and plants; when they leave them, those die of thirst. Water, Fire and Wind are what keep people alive; the three do not die, and as long as there is an Earth there will be Water, Fire and Wind.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 9; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同出處的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。他們發現『克瓦』已化作眾水，如大海般躁動不安，流成溪澗注入江河，江河又注入大海，浮於雲中，如霧般掠過山嶺與平原，從泉眼中湧出——從不歇息。眾水也活在人和獸與草木之中；當它們離去，那些便渴而死。水、火與風是維繫人命的東西；這三者不會死去，只要還有大地，就會有水、火與風。

title.en: The Rain-Beast and the Bobbejaan
title.zh: 雨獸與狒狒

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 10

summary.en: In drought the bobbejaan borrows the Rain-Beast as a milk-cow, then slaughters her for the udder. A burning thirst and hunger follow: every spring dries at his lips, the ostrich eggshell of water vanishes, shade retreats. He must return and cry 'Choro, Choro, live again!' — and when he also gives back the milk-pail, the Rain-cow revives at once and a flood with locusts afloat saves him.
summary.zh: 旱時，狒狒借雨獸為乳牛，繼而殺之以取乳器。焚渴與饑隨之：泉涸、蛋殼水消、樹影退避。須返而呼「卓羅，卓羅，復活！」——歸還乳器，雨牛頓活，洪水載蝗而救其命。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 10 (1919); not verbatim. The Rain-Beast is the great rain-maker of the Bushmen; his dwelling-place is beside the great waters. In drought the people fetch him, lead him round, and show him all the places where they want rain; to put him in a good mood they dance about him, clap hands, sing, praise him and beg him to let it rain so the fields may grow green and the game and honey-bees return. He is tame if no one vexes him, and changes himself into a cow so they can milk her.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 10; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馮·維利希第一卷第十號（1919年）的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。雨獸是布須曼人偉大的造雨者；他的居所就在大水之旁。乾旱時人們去請他來，領著他四處走，把他們想要降雨的地方一一指給他看；為了讓他心情愉快，他們圍著他跳舞、拍手、唱歌、讚美他，並懇求他降雨，好讓田野轉綠，讓獵物與蜜蜂歸來。只要無人惹惱他，他便溫順，還會把自己變成一頭母牛，好讓人擠她的奶。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Once there was drought in the mountains where the bobbejaans lived; their leader fetched the Rain-Beast, who changed into a cow so the bobbejaan could have milk on the journey, and was milked wherever he thirsted. After he had shown every dry place he brought the Rain-cow back, and everywhere it rained beautifully. But instead of thanking her, he killed her — only to get the milk-udder to take with him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 10; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同出處的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。有一次，狒狒居住的山中遭遇乾旱；他們的首領請來了雨獸，雨獸變成一頭母牛，好讓狒狒在旅途中能有奶喝，凡是他口渴之處便擠她的奶。他指遍了每一處乾旱之地後，便把雨牛帶了回來，所到之處都下起了好雨。然而他不但不感謝她，反而把她殺了——只為了取下那盛奶的乳房隨身帶走。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. A burning thirst and gnawing hunger seized him: the green karkoere dried to dust at his touch, the fountain dried as he bent to drink, the shade shifted away from him as he walked toward it, the eggshell of water vanished at his lips. The people bade him run back and cry 'Choro, Choro, live again as you were!' and then return the milk-udder; and the Rain-cow sprang up and at once let rain fall where they stood, a flood on which banks of locusts floated. The flood rose till he sat to his neck in a tree packed with locusts, and the Rain-Beast left him there until the next day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 10; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同出處的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。灼人的乾渴與難耐的飢餓攫住了他：青綠的卡爾庫里草一經他觸碰便枯成塵土，他俯身欲飲時泉水便乾涸，他朝蔭影走去時蔭影便移開，水蛋殼一到他唇邊便消失無蹤。人們叫他跑回去喊道：『喬羅，喬羅，照原樣活過來吧！』然後把盛奶的乳房還回去；於是雨牛躍起，立刻在他們所立之處降下雨來，洪水上漂浮著成群的蝗蟲。洪水越漲越高，直到他坐在一棵爬滿蝗蟲的樹上，水已沒到脖子，雨獸便把他留在了那裡，直到第二天。

title.en: The Great Water-Snake and Her Shining Stone
title.zh: 大水蛇與其閃石

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 11

summary.en: The great Water-Snake, daughter of the Waters and the Rain-Beast, wears a stone on her head whose light outshines the moon at noon. She hides it before bathing; whoever steals it unseen is showered with gifts while she wastes away — until the young thief, conscience-stricken and seeing the springs run dry, restores it and wins her lasting favour.
summary.zh: 大水蛇——水與雨獸之女——頂負寶石，其光於正午猶勝月。浴前必先藏石；竊者不為所覺則受贈而蛇枯——直至少年賊良心自譴，見諸泉涸竭，歸還寶石，遂得蛇之永恩。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 11 (1919); not verbatim. The great Water-Snake can make herself great or small as she pleases; swimming up or down a river she raises the water over the banks, and lying crosswise she dams the river far back. She wears a beautiful shining stone on her head; its gleam is visible at a great distance, flashing with rays of light that surpass the light of the Moon — it can be clearly seen at midday in the brightest sunshine.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 11; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馮·維利希第一卷第十一號（1919年）的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。巨大的水蛇能隨心所欲地變大或變小；她順河上下游動時，便使河水漫過兩岸，橫臥時則把河水遠遠地堵在上游。她頭上戴著一顆美麗的發光石頭；其光芒在很遠的地方就能看見，閃爍的光線勝過月光——即使在正午最明亮的陽光下也清晰可見。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. She prizes the stone: never will she venture into the water or drink without first hiding the stone in a safe place, and she is never at rest, glancing back toward it. Whoever finds someone near it she attacks, killing or maiming him for life. If anyone gets the stone without her knowing, he is for his whole life fortunate, loaded with presents; but if she finds the thief, his wife and children die the first day, all his goods vanish, and he wastes away and dies an agonising death.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 11; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同段落的濃縮意譯，非逐字照錄。她珍視那顆石頭：若不先將石頭藏於安全之處，她絕不涉水，也不飲水；她從不安歇，總要回頭張望那石頭。誰若被她發現靠近石頭，她便攻擊那人，將其殺死或使其終身殘廢。若有人在她不知情下取得石頭，那人便終身幸運，滿載贈禮；但她若尋得竊賊，其妻兒當日即死，所有財物盡皆消失，而他則日漸消瘦，最終痛苦而死。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. A young Bushman of the old race planned to rob the Water-Snake of her stone. He lay hidden under grass and bushes where she buried it, and while she went to bathe he wrapped the stone tight in many things, buried it where she could never find it, and ran home. The snake tracked his spoor to the huts and sniffed through everything; but he had smeared himself with buchu, and she found nothing. He grew rich with presents; but the snake wasted away, the springs ran dry, and he carried the stone back to its hiding-place and told her to come and help him seek for it — where they found it again with great joy. Both were happy thereafter, and the waters returned.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 11; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同段落的濃縮意譯，非逐字照錄。舊族中一名年輕的布須曼人謀劃竊取水蛇的石頭。他藏身於她埋石之處的草叢與灌木之下，趁她去沐浴時，將石頭緊緊裹於層層物件之中，埋在她永遠找不到的地方，然後奔回家中。水蛇循其足跡追至茅屋，嗅遍一切；但他身上塗了布枯（buchu），她什麼也沒找到。他因贈禮而致富；然而水蛇日漸消瘦，泉水乾涸，於是他將石頭帶回其藏匿之處，並叫她前來幫他一同尋找——他們再次尋得石頭，欣喜萬分。此後兩者皆歡喜，水亦復歸。

title.en: The Sun Is the Head of Danser the Fire-Man
title.zh: 太陽乃火人丹瑟之首

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 12

summary.en: The Fire-man's shining head lights the twilight world and takes the hunters' game; the women urge his death. As he crosses the water the arrows bring him down, and the children throw his head into the sky — where it becomes the Sun, seeking its body forever. The body, headless, rots into a crab and still walks the shores at dusk.
summary.zh: 火人明首照微明之世，且奪獵者之獲；婦人慫恿殺之。其涉水時箭下如雨；孩童擲其首上天——遂為日，永尋其軀。無首之軀朽化為蟹，至今黃昏沿岸而行。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

narrative.en:
Danser is the Fire-man, the fire-maker. He first walked as a man; light and warmth streamed from his head, for he was the one who placed fire in the stones, in the wood and in the clouds. Where he walked or went there was always light and warmth, so he always had a great company around him: the hunters in his neighbourhood could see where the game was, and those seeking veld food could find it by the light of Danser's head.

But sometimes he was too lazy to walk and sat at ease; when the hunters begged him to go further so they could see the game, he mocked them, asking why they did not go and make light themselves. He also had a way of taking the shot game from the hunters, and the hunters grew angry — for the women are discontented when their men come home without food and have nothing for the hungry children crying for it. So the women advised their men to kill Danser and carry his head round on a long pole, so that everyone might see.

One hunter who liked the women's talk said: 'Good, let us shoot Danser with poisoned arrows, to carry his head on a long pole so we can get warmth and light.' A second said: 'All very well; but whose eyes are tough enough to bear that strong light, and whose hands to cut off that warm head?' A third asked: 'And where do we get a pole that will not burn with the heat?' A fourth said: 'You are bad at making plans! I will tell you what to do: we wait till Danser walks through the water — something he does regularly — then we dart at him with poisoned arrows; if he falls into the water his light and warmth are gone.' A fifth answered: 'You think you are clever, but you are very stupid. Tell me, what good is it to us if Danser's light and warmth are put out? Then we sit in the same old darkness and cold.' But all cried: 'It is nothing! Once he is away from us he can plague and torment us no more.' Lion, leopard, wolf, jackal and cat — men of the old race — wanted nothing to do with the murder; they can see well enough in the dark.

The others kept to their plan. They watched Danser, and just as he stepped through the water they shot, all together; the arrows struck him, he fell forward into the water, and dead was the light and gone the warmth. They ran up, quickly cut off Danser's head under the water, dragged out the body and set the head down on the bank to see what would come of it. But the head and the body would not die: the head's eyes looked round and turned from side to side, and the body stood up and walked about without its head. The head could see and speak but could not move; the body could move but could not see, hear, smell or speak. The head called to the body, but the body did not hear; the body searched for the head but could not find it, and instead of coming nearer walked ever further away.

The murderers went away. Then a girl sent her children to throw the head of Danser into the air so that there should be light and warmth, warning them to beware of the headless body, which would murder them if it caught them. The children stepped carefully; the head was already drying and giving light, and it was so hot when they took hold of it that they threw it into the air at once. Then the mothers cried: 'Wind, Wind, come and take the head high into the blue sky, that we may have light and warmth!' A strong whirlwind came and carried the head above the clouds and let it stay there. The head of Danser the Fire-man became the Sun.

All the people rejoiced that there was now light and warmth over the whole earth: 'O Sun, stay there and give us light and warmth every day... Great is the Sun, who can see all people at once. Now there is light to forbid evil: whoever does evil, steals or murders will be seen, and the Sun will burn him with his heat.' But the head still plays one trick: it seeks for its body. In the morning it climbs, seeking, higher and higher at the mountains on the east side, and when it is high enough sinks again to the mountains on the west, and dives into the deep waters of the sea to seek there too — for the body wasted and rotted and has taken the shape of a Crab. And the body, still headless, walks up and down along the waters at evening, seeking its head.

functions: Cosmogony of the sun as the severed head of the fire-being.
Explains the crab's shape and its dusk patrolling of the shore.
Frames the day-night alternation as the head's endless search.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 12 (1919); not verbatim. Danser is the Fire-man; he first walked as a man, with light and warmth streaming from his head, for he was the one who placed fire in the stones, in the wood and in the clouds. But he sometimes sat lazy, mocked the hunters who begged him to walk further, and took their shot game; so the women advised their men to kill him and carry his head round on a long pole.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 12; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馮·維利希（von Wielligh）第一部第十二號（1919年）的濃縮意譯，非逐字照錄。丹瑟（Danser）是火之人；他最初以人形行走，光與熱自其頭部流溢而出，因為正是他將火置於石中、木中與雲中。但他有時懶散而坐，嘲弄那些懇求他繼續行走的獵人，並取走他們射得的獵物；於是婦女們勸她們的男人殺死他，並將他的頭顱穿在長竿上抬著走。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. They waited until Danser walked through the water, then shot him with poisoned arrows; he fell forward into the water, and dead was the light and gone the warmth. They cut off his head under the water; but head and body would not die: the head looked round, and the body stood up and walked about without it — the head could see and speak but not move, the body could move but not see, hear, smell or speak.

passages.zh: 同段落的濃縮意譯，非逐字照錄。他們等到丹瑟涉水而行時，便以毒箭射他；他向前倒入水中，光隨之而死，熱亦隨之而去。他們在水下割下他的頭顱；然而頭與身皆不肯死去：頭顱環顧四周，身體則無頭而立，四處行走——頭能視能言卻不能動，身體能動卻不能視、不能聽、不能嗅、不能言。

A girl sent her children to throw the head into the air, and the mothers cried: 'Wind, Wind, come and take the head high into the blue sky, that we may have light and warmth!' A strong whirlwind carried the head above the clouds and let it stay there: the head of Danser the Fire-man became the Sun. All the people rejoiced that there was now light and warmth over the whole earth, and that evil-doers could now be seen.

passages.zh: 同段落的濃縮意譯，非逐字照錄。一名女孩派她的孩子們將頭顱拋向空中，母親們喊道：「風啊，風啊，來吧，把頭帶上蔚藍的高空，好讓我們有光與熱！」一陣強烈的旋風將頭顱帶至雲端之上，讓它留於彼處：火之人丹瑟的頭顱化作了太陽。眾人歡欣，因為如今光與熱遍及大地，而作惡之人如今也能被看見了。

Morning after morning it climbs seeking at the mountains of the east, sinks again to the west, and dives into the sea to seek there too — for the body wasted and rotted and has taken the shape of a Crab, and the headless body still walks up and down along the waters in the evening, seeking its head.

passages.zh: 同段落的濃縮意譯，非逐字照錄。但那頭顱仍耍一個把戲：它尋找自己的身體。日復一日，它攀上東方的山巒尋找，又沉落於西方，並潛入海中在那裡尋找——因為那身體已腐朽消蝕，化作了螃蟹的形狀，而那無頭之身仍在傍晚沿著水邊來回行走，尋找它的頭。

title.en: The Moon Is the Shoe of the 'Hotnotsgod
title.zh: 月乃螳螂之鞋

region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）
