passages.text: Following the rishi's advice they took as wives sisters who were not of the same mother as themselves, and so had many children; the rishi marked out the town-site with golden sand mixed with water, and having given the soil of the place they called it the soil of Kapila, Kapilavastu. Later a deva pointed out another spot, where they built the town of Devadaha, and they made a law in general assembly that they should marry only one wife, and she of their own clan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們聽從仙人的建議，娶了與自己不同母的姊妹為妻，因而子孫眾多；仙人以摻水的金沙劃定城址，並將此地之土賜予他們，稱之為迦毗羅之土，即迦毗羅衛。後來一位天神又指出另一處地方，他們便在那裡建了提婆達訶城，並在大會中訂立法律：每人只娶一妻，且須出自本族。

passages.text: When Virudhaka thought one day of his comely sons and heard their adventures, he exclaimed 'the daring young men! the daring young men!' - and from this they became known as Shakyas. His descendants, fifty-five thousand in number, reigned in Kapilavastu down to Sinhahanu, whose sons were Shuddhodana and the uncles of the Blessed One.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，毗盧遮那迦想起自己俊美的兒子們，聽聞他們的種種經歷，便驚嘆道：『勇敢的年輕人！勇敢的年輕人！』——由此他們便得名為釋迦。他的後裔共五萬五千人，在迦毗羅衛治國，傳至師子頰，其子為淨飯王及世尊的諸位叔父。

title.en: The Birth of the Bodhisattva in the Lumbini Grove
title.zh: 藍毘尼園誕生

region.en: Lumbini grove near Kapilavastu (symbolic pin at Lumbini, Nepal)
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛附近的藍毘尼園（以尼泊爾藍毘尼為象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya vol. iii. f. 446ff.), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II, translated from the Dulva

summary.en: The future Buddha in the Tushita heaven makes the five preliminary examinations - family, country, time, race and woman - and enters Mahamaya's womb at midnight in the appearance of an elephant; she dreams of a six-tusked white elephant, of moving in space, of ascending a rocky mountain, of a multitude bowing down. Caught by labour in the Lumbini garden she seizes an ashoka tree while Shataketu (Indra) disperses the crowd, and the Bodhisattva takes seven steps to each of the cardinal points with a vow for each direction - then washings of cold and warm water fall on his head. On the same day the future kings Prasenajit, Bimbisara, Udayana and Pradyota are born with the world lit up, and at the temple the yaksha Shakyavardana bows at the child's feet: he is named All-fulfilled, Mighty One of the Shakyas, and God of gods.
summary.zh: 未來佛在兜率天作五觀察——族、地、時、種、女——於半夜化作白象入摩耶夫人胎中；夫人夢六牙白象入胎、凌空飛行、登上大山、眾人禮拜。藍毘尼園中臨盆，手攀無憂樹；帝釋化老嫗欲接聖嬰，被嬰遣回，隨即向四方各行七步，各發一願——「我將至最勝涅槃」「我將為一切眾生之首」「此為我最後之生」「我將渡生死之海」——頭上落下冷熱二水洗浴，誕生處湧出浴母之泉。同日世間四位未來國王誕生，而神殿中的夜叉像竟向嬰兒頂禮：得名「一切義成」「釋迦牟尼」「天人中尊」。

canonical_translation: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha, London 1884 (public domain)

narrative.en:
During King Sinhahanu's reign the Shakya country enjoyed peace; the future Buddha was in the Tushita heaven, and knowing that his time had come, made the five preliminary examinations - of the proper family, of the country, of the time, of the race, and of the woman - and having decided that Mahamayi was the right mother, in the midnight watch entered her womb under the appearance of an elephant. Then the queen had four dreams: she saw a six-tusked white elephant enter her womb, she moved in space above, she ascended a great rocky mountain, and a great multitude bowed down to her. The soothsayers predicted that she would bring forth a son with the thirty-two signs of the great man - if he stays at home he will become a universal monarch; but if he shaves his hair and beard and leaves his home for a homeless state, he will become a Tathagata, an arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha.

While visiting the Lumbini garden the pains of childbirth came upon her, and she seized hold of a wide-spreading ashoka tree. Then Shataketu - Indra - caused a violent rain to fall and a wind to blow that dispersed all the crowd of attendants, and assuming the appearance of an old woman went to receive the new-born child in his lap; but the Bodhisattva ordered him back, and took seven steps in the direction of each of the cardinal points. Looking to the east he said, 'I will reach the highest nirvana'; to the south, 'I will be the first of all creatures'; to the west, 'This will be my last birth'; to the north, 'I will cross the ocean of existence.' In accordance with what happens at the birth of every Buddha there fell on his head a stream of cold water and one of warm which washed him, and at the spot where he had been born there appeared a spring in which his mother bathed.

On the same day as the Buddha's birth, kings' sons were born with the world illuminated: Prasenajit of Shravasti, Bimbisara the son of queen Bimbi in Rajagriha, Udayana of Kaushambi, and Pradyota of Ujjayani. Many blessings came to the child's father, so the child was called Sarvarthasiddha, All-fulfilled; and as the Shakyas' custom was to make new-born children bow at the feet of the yaksha Shakyavardana, the king took the child to the temple - but the yaksha bowed down at his feet. On the way every one was struck with the infant's bold appearance, so he received the name of Shakyamuni, the mighty one of the Shakyas; and when the king saw the yaksha bow he exclaimed, 'he is the god of gods!', so the child was called Devatideva.
narrative.notes: Cultural function: the Tibetan Dulva nativity grounds the Buddha's birth in the same narrative economy as the four kings born the same day; the seven steps and four vows compress the whole career - nirvana, sovereignty, finality, crossing - into the infant's first movements.

functions: Nativity doctrine: the Bodhisattva chooses his mother by five examinations, so the birth is planned merit, not accident
The four cardinal vows compress the Buddha's whole future ministry into the seven steps of the new-born
Links the Buddha's birth-day with the birthdays of four royal patrons-to-be, the earthly framework of his later ministry
The temple-yaksha's bow transfers sacred authority from the old cult image to the child

variants.name: Lalita Vistara recension
variants.summary: The Lalita Vistara has seven steps east and seven west rather than the four-direction scheme of the Dulva, and develops the nativity pageantry at greater length; Rockhill notes the disagreement.

variants.name: Southern (Pali) nativity
variants.summary: The Pali account agrees on the dream and the steps but makes the bathing by two streams the devas' act and names the birth-tree plainly; the Tibetan text's detail of Indra disguised as an old woman receiving the child is distinctive.

primary_sources.citation: Tibetan Kangyur; English translation W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha, London 1884, pp. 14-18

secondary_sources.work: Philippe Edouard Foucault (Foucaux), Le Rgya tcher rol-pa, translation of the Lalita Vistara
secondary_sources.citation: Foucaux 1847-1862, Paris - comparator recension cited in Rockhill's notes.

secondary_sources.work: Erik Haarh, The Yar-lun Dynasty
secondary_sources.citation: Haarh 1969, Copenhagen - royal myth and the Tibetan use of Buddha-biography.

secondary_sources.work: Kurtis R. Schaeffer, The Culture of the Book in Tibet
secondary_sources.citation: Schaeffer 2009, New York: Columbia University Press - on Tibetan reading and transmission of the Buddha's life stories.

source_urls.description: Internet Archive scan of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884)

sensitivity_guidance: Canonical narrative still recited at Tibetan Buddhist festivals (esp. Lumbini and Saga Dawa); passages below are paraphrases of the public-domain 1884 translation.

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative of living tradition; paraphrase of public-domain translation only.

passages.text: Knowing that his time had come, the future Buddha in the Tushita heaven made the five preliminary examinations - of the proper family, the country, the time, the race, and the woman - and having decided that Mahamayi was the right mother, in the midnight watch entered her womb under the appearance of an elephant. The queen had four dreams: a six-tusked white elephant entering her womb, moving in space above, ascending a great rocky mountain, and a great multitude bowing down to her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 未來佛自知時機已至，在兜率天作了五種預察——察其應生的家族、國土、時節、種族與女子——斷定摩訶摩耶為合適的母親，便於中夜分現大象之形入其胎中。王后做了四個夢：一頭六牙白象入其胎中、在空中行走、登上一座大岩山，以及廣大群眾向她禮拜。

passages.text: In the Lumbini garden the pains of childbirth came upon her, and she seized a wide-spreading ashoka tree; Shataketu (Indra) dispersed the crowd with rain and wind and, as an old woman, went to receive the child in his lap - but the Bodhisattva ordered him back, and took seven steps toward each of the cardinal points: to the east, I will reach the highest nirvana; to the south, I will be the first of all creatures; to the west, this will be my last birth; to the north, I will cross the ocean of existence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在藍毗尼園中，分娩的陣痛向她襲來，她抓住了一棵枝葉繁茂的無憂樹；釋迦建陀（因陀羅）以風雨驅散眾人，並化作老婦，欲將嬰兒接於膝上——然而菩薩命他退下，隨即朝四方各邁七步：向東，我將證得至高涅槃；向南，我將為眾生之首；向西，此為我最後之生；向北，我將渡越存在之海。

passages.text: As at the birth of every Buddha, streams of cold and warm water fell on his head and washed him, and a spring appeared in which his mother bathed. On the same day kings' sons were born with the world illuminated at Shravasti, Rajagriha, Kaushambi and Ujjayani; and when the child was taken to the temple of the yaksha Shakyavardana, the yaksha bowed at his feet - so he was called All-fulfilled, the Mighty One of the Shakyas, and God of gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 如同每一位佛陀降生之時，冷暖水流自天而降，灌洗其頂，並湧出一泉，其母於其中沐浴。同日，舍衛城、王舍城、憍賞彌與鄔闍衍那皆有王子誕生，世界為之光明；當此嬰孩被帶往夜叉釋迦增長之廟時，夜叉俯伏於其足下——因此他被稱為「一切圓滿者」、「釋迦族之大力者」與「諸神之神」。

title.en: The Seer Asita and the Word Passed to Katyayana
title.zh: 阿私陀仙人預言

region.en: Sarvadhara mountain hermitage (symbolic pin at Kapilvastu)
region.zh: 一切護山仙人住處（以迦毘羅衛為象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: The mighty seer Asita of the Sarvadhara mountain comes with his nephew Nalada to see the new-born, takes him in his arms, and prophesies: at twenty-nine he will leave home, be an ascetic six years, then find the drink of the cessation of death. Dying soon after, Asita begs Nalada to join the young Shakya's order when the truth is found; Nalada studies mantras among five hundred Brahmans and, converted later by the Buddha, becomes Mahakatyayana, 'the great member of Katya's family.'
summary.zh: 一切護山的大仙人阿私陀偕姪那羅陀探望新生兒，抱之於懷而預言：二十九歲出家、苦行六年、得「不死之甘露」。臨終前囑咐姪兒待其證道後加入釋迦教團；那羅陀於五百梵志中學咒，後為佛陀所化，號大迦旃延。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: The two came to see the child, and Asita took him in his arms and asked what had been prophesied about him. He predicted that he would leave his home at twenty-nine, that he would be an ascetic for six years, and that then he would find the drink of the cessation of death. Shortly after, feeling his end approaching, he begged Nalada to enter the order of the young Shakya as soon as he should have found the truth, and then he died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 二人前來觀看此嬰孩，阿私陀將他抱於懷中，詢問關於他的預言。他預言此子將於二十九歲離家，修行苦行六年，其後將尋得斷滅死亡之飲。不久之後，他自覺死期將近，便懇求那羅陀，待其尋得真理之後，即刻加入年輕釋迦子的僧團，隨後便去世了。

passages.text: Nalada went to Varanasi and entered a company of five hundred mantra-studying Brahmans, and as he was of the family of Katya he became known as Katyayana; later on, having been converted by the Buddha, he was called Mahakatyayana, the great member of Katya's family.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那羅陀前往波羅奈，加入一個由五百名研習咒語的婆羅門所組成的團體；因他出身於迦旃延家族，故被稱為迦旃延；後來，他受佛陀度化，被稱為大迦旃延，即迦旃延家族之偉大成員。

title.en: Devadatta's Elephant and the Bodhisattva's Throw
title.zh: 提婆達多殺象與菩薩擲象

region.en: Road outside Kapilavastu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛城外大道（象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: The Licchavis of Vaisali send the Bodhisattva a magnificently jewelled elephant - and the envious Devadatta kills it with a blow of his fist; Nanda drags it aside, and the Bodhisattva, catching it by the tail, throws it over seven fences and ditches so hard it digs the 'elephant ditch', Hastigarta, where believers build a stupa. In the archery contest his arrow pierces every target and drives so deep into the ground it springs a well - and there too the faithful build a stupa.
summary.zh: 吠舍離離車族獻上寶飾大象；嫉妒的提婆達多一拳將象擊斃。難陀將屍體拖至路旁，菩薩抓住象尾擲過七重牆溝，落地成坑——「象坑」（虎多迦多）即由此得名，信眾於此建塔。比箭時菩薩之箭貫穿全部箭靶、深入土中湧出清泉，信眾又於彼處建塔。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: When they were near the town Devadatta noticed the jewelled elephant, and, filled with envy, killed it with a blow of his fist; Nanda, coming that way, threw the carcass to one side, but the Bodhisattva, taking it by the tail, threw it over seven fences and ditches, and it dug a great ditch in falling which became known as the elephant ditch, Hastigarta - and there the believing Brahmans and householders built a stupa which is reverenced to the present day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他們接近提婆達多城時，提婆達多注意到那頭飾以珠寶的大象，心生嫉妒，一拳將其擊斃；難陀途經此地，將屍體拋向一旁，然而菩薩抓住象尾，將其拋過七道圍欄與壕溝，大象墜落時砸出一道深溝，此溝遂被稱為「象溝」，即訶悉多迦多；信眾婆羅門與居家者於該處建起一座佛塔，至今仍受崇敬。

passages.text: And here it is said: Devadatta killed the mighty elephant, Nanda carried it seven paces, the Bodhisattva through space with his hand did cast it as a stone far away. After this the young Shakyas tried their skill at archery; the arrow of the Bodhisattva, after piercing all the targets, went so far into the ground that it caused a spring to rush forth - and there also the believers built a stupa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此處有言：提婆達多擊殺巨象，難陀將其拖行七步，菩薩則以手將其擲向遠方空中，如投石一般。此後，年輕的釋迦子們較量射藝；菩薩之箭射穿所有標靶後，深深沒入地面，以致湧出一泉——信眾亦於該處建起一座佛塔。

title.en: The Goose and the Arrow: Devadatta's First Quarrel
title.zh: 雁與箭：提婆達多結怨之始

region.en: Gardens on the banks of the Rohita river (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 羅希塔河畔林園（象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: Summoned to free the great tree blocking Kapilavastu's water, the prince is first tested in the gardens by Devadatta shooting a goose overhead; it falls in the Bodhisattva's garden, who extracts the arrow and binds the wound - and refuses to give up the bird: it belongs not to him who attempted to take its life, but to him who saved it. This was the first quarrel between the two.
summary.zh: 菩薩應召為城民移除堵水的大樹；途經園林，提婆達多一箭射落天上飛雁，雁落入菩薩園中。菩薩為其拔箭裹傷，並拒絕交出：雁屬於救其命者，不屬於欲害其命者——二人結怨由此而始。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: While they were still in the gardens Devadatta saw a goose flying overhead, so he shot it, and it fell in the Bodhisattva's garden; he took it, extracted the arrow and bound up its wound. Devadatta sent a messenger to claim the bird, but the Bodhisattva would not give it up, saying that it belonged not to him who had attempted to take its life, but to him who had saved it - and this was the first quarrel between these two.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他們還在那園林之中時，提婆達多看見一隻雁從頭頂飛過，便射了牠，雁落在菩薩的園中；他拾起雁，拔出箭並包紮了牠的傷口。提婆達多派人來索討這隻鳥，但菩薩不肯交出，說這鳥不屬於那個想奪牠性命的人，而屬於救了牠的人——這便是這兩人間的第一次爭執。

title.en: The Four Encounters on the Road
title.zh: 四門遊觀

region.en: Parks and roads of Kapilavastu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛城內園林道路（象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: Driving in the park, the prince sees an old man, and the charioteer Chhandaka must explain what old age is - all are subject to it; a dropsical, emaciated man teaches him disease; a torch-lit litter of many-coloured stuffs with wailing, dishevelled women is a corpse, and to this state all must come; and a deva of the pure abode, appearing as a shaven mendicant with an alms-bowl, shows him the man who has forsaken the world. Each time the prince turns back home pensively.
summary.zh: 太子出遊園林：先見老人，御者闡陀只能講明何為老——「無人能免」；再見浮腫枯瘦之病人，得知何為病；又遇火把簇擁的彩轎與披髮哀哭的婦女——那是屍體，「人人終將如此」；最後遇見化為剃度乞士的淨居天子，知世間另有「捨離在家」之人。太子每見一景，皆鬱鬱回宮。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: In the park he saw an old man, and the charioteer explained what old age was and how all were subject to it; deeply impressed, the prince turned back and went home. A short time after, out driving, he met a dropsical man, emaciated and weak, with faculties impaired, and Chhandaka told him what disease was - and again he turned back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在園中他看見一位老人，御者解釋了何謂年老，以及眾生皆難免於此；王子深受觸動，便折返回到家中。不久之後，他出遊時遇見一個患水腫的人，消瘦衰弱，諸根衰損，車匿告訴他何謂疾病——於是他又折返。

passages.text: Another time he came across a procession bearing along on a litter, with burning torches, something wrapped in many-coloured stuffs, the women accompanying it with dishevelled hair crying piteously: it was a corpse, Chhandaka told him, and to this state all must come. And yet on another occasion he met a deva of the pure abode who had assumed the appearance of a shaved and shorn mendicant bearing an alms-bowl, going from door to door - one who has forsaken the world, a righteous, virtuous man. Then pensively he drove back to the palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 又一次，他遇見一隊人抬著擔架前行，手持燃燒的火炬，抬著裹在種種彩色布帛中的東西，隨行的婦女披散著頭髮，哀切地哭泣：車匿告訴他，那是一具屍體，而眾生皆必歸於此狀。又有一次，他遇見一位淨居天的天神，化作剃髮持缽、挨家挨戶乞食的苦行者——那是一位捨棄世間的人，一位正直有德之人。於是他沉思著驅車返回宮中。

title.en: The Ploughmen and the Immovable Shade
title.zh: 觀耕與不動之蔭

region.en: Ploughed fields of a village near Kapilavastu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛近郊田疇（象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: Sent to divert himself watching the ploughmen, the prince finds the labourers hair erect, covered with sweat, and the oxen pricked with iron goads, bleeding at the mouth and nose, covered with gadflies. His tender heart freed them all - 'from today you are no longer slaves; go where you please and live in joy' - and the oxen to the sweetest grass and purest water; then, seated in meditation under a jambu-tree, he was found by his father, and lo! the shade had not moved from where he was.
summary.zh: 國王令太子散心觀耕；他見農夫汗流浹背、耕牛遭鐵刺傷口流血、蠅虻蔽體，大發悲心，當即釋放眾人「從今日起你們不再是奴隸」，牛亦得甘草淨水。隨後他在一株閻浮樹下入定沉思，父親尋來時——樹影竟然不移，始終覆在其身。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: He saw the labourers with hair erect, uncovered hands and feet, their bodies dirty and running with sweat, and the work-oxen pricked with iron goads, their backs streaming with blood, covered with gadflies and mosquitoes, the ploughshare wounding them. His tender heart was touched with compassion: to whom do you belong? - we are the king's property. From to-day you are no longer slaves; you shall be no longer servants; go where you please and live in joy. He freed also the oxen: from to-day eat the sweetest grass and drink the purest water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他看見那些勞工頭髮豎立，手腳裸露，身體污穢、汗流浹背，耕牛被鐵刺刺戳，背上鮮血直流，滿是牛虻與蚊蟲，犁頭割傷著牠們。他柔軟的心被悲憫所觸動：你們屬於誰？——我們是國王的財產。從今日起你們不再是奴隸；你們不再為僕役；隨你們所願而去，歡喜地生活吧。他也釋放了那些牛：從今日起吃最甘美的草，飲最清淨的水。

passages.text: Then, seeing a shady jambu-tree on one side, he sat down at its foot and gave himself to earnest meditation; and there his father found him - and lo! the shade had not moved from where he was. Through the lengthening afternoon the tree had kept its shelter over the absorbed prince as faithfully as an attendant, and the king, coming up at the edge of the furrows where the oxen had been freed that same day, stood silent before the unmoving shadow before he dared to wake his son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隨後，他看見一旁有一棵枝葉蔭蔽的閻浮樹，便坐在樹下，專心致力於禪思；他的父親就在那裡找到了他——看哪！那片樹蔭並未從他所在之處移開。整個漫長的午後，那棵樹始終如一地庇護著這位專注的王子，如同一位侍從般忠實；國王來到當日釋放耕牛的犁溝邊，在那靜止不動的樹蔭前默然站立，才敢喚醒他的兒子。

title.en: Gopa's Song and Mrigadja's Verse
title.zh: 喬波之贊與鹿女郎之偈

region.en: Terraces of Kapilavastu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛城頭（象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: Riding home from freeing the great tree, the prince is seen from her terrace by Gopa, daughter of the Shakya Kinkinisvara - they stop and gaze - and the king makes her his son's wife. Later, returning from the Rajagriha cemetery, he is met by Mrigadja's song from her window - 'happy is his mother, happy his father, happy she whose husband he shall be, that woman has gone beyond sorrow!' - and he throws her a necklace for her pretty words; the king hears of it and weds her too, seven days before the flight from home, with Yaśodhara and 60,000 attendant women.
summary.zh: 太子移樹歸城，麒麟獅王之女喬波自露臺見之，二人相視出神，國王遂以其為子媳。其後菩薩自王舍城屍林回城，鹿女郎（彌迦闍）自窗中唱偈：「其母有福！其父有福！將為其妻者，已出離憂苦！」菩薩擲一寶鏈酬其妙語；國王聞之又娶之為妃。故其妻有耶輸陀羅、喬波、鹿女等，侍女六萬，而鹿女入門僅七日，他便離家而去。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: Gopa saw him from the terrace of her house as he was riding home, and he also noticing her stopped his chariot to look at her; the people saw that they were fascinated with each other and told the king, who took Gopa and made her his son's wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 瞿波從她家中的露臺上看見他騎馬歸來，他也注意到了她，便停下馬車凝望她；眾人見他們彼此傾心，便稟告國王，國王便迎娶瞿波，使她成為他兒子的妻子。

passages.text: As he was going back to the city Mrigadja, the daughter of the Shakya Kalika, saw him from her window and sang: ah! happy is his mother; his father also, happy is he; ah! she whose husband he shall be, that woman has gone beyond sorrow! The Bodhisattva threw her a necklace to pay her for her pretty words, and the king, hearing of it, made her the Bodhisattva's wife - so his wives were Gopa, Mrigadja and 60,000 attendant women, and Mrigadja became his wife seven days before he left his home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他返回彌沙迦城時，釋迦族迦利迦之女從窗中望見他，便唱道：啊！他的母親真有福；他的父親也一樣有福；啊！將來作他妻子的人，那女子已超脫了憂悲！菩薩擲給她一串瓔珞，作為她美言的酬報；國王聽說此事，便將她許配給菩薩為妻——於是他的妻子有瞿波、彌沙迦，以及六萬名侍女，而彌沙迦在他離家前七日成了他的妻子。

title.en: The Flight from Kapilavastu
title.zh: 夜半踰城

region.en: Eastern gate of Kapilavastu and the night road (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛東門與夜路（象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: Guarded at four gates by his uncles, the Bodhisattva passes the night amid a sleeping harem that looks like the dead; Yaśodhara dreams he is abandoning her and asks to go wherever he goes. Indra and the gods exhort him; Chhandaka saddles Kanthaka, and the devatas of the palace weep like rain. At the eastern gate he greets his sleeping father - 'though I love thee, I must free myself from the fear of age and death' - passes Mahanaman's begging patrol, rides twelve yojanas, and sends his horse and charioteer home; his cut hair is carried by Shataketu to the Trayastrimcat heaven, and an old woman's legacy robe - the cotton garment of ten Pratyeka Buddhas - is exchanged with a hunter who is Indra in disguise.
summary.zh: 四門皆有叔父重兵把守；王宮後宮熟睡如死人，令菩薩心生厭離。耶輸陀羅夢他離去，求同行。帝釋率諸天相勸，闡陀備好神駒犍陟，宮中天人淚如雨下。東門外他向熟睡的父親告別：「我雖愛父，但須解脫老病死之怖。」又避開巡夜的難陀，一夜行十二由旬，隨即打髮馬與御者回城；剪下的頭髮被帝釋送往三十三天；又以「十辟支佛相傳、囑轉贈佛陀」之棉衣，換取帝釋所扮老獵人身上的粗衣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: On the night of the seventh day the Bodhisattva noticed all his sleeping harem, and the women looked so like the dead in their sleep that he was filled with loathing; on the same night Yaśodhara dreamt he was abandoning her, and awoke and told her lord of her dream: where'er thou goest, there let me go to. Cataketu (Indra) and the other gods came and exhorted him to flee the world, and told Chhandaka to saddle the treasure-horse Kanthaka.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第七日之夜，菩薩察覺他所有熟睡的嬪妃，那些女子在睡夢中看來宛如死人，令他心生厭惡；就在同一夜，耶輸陀羅夢見他拋棄了她，醒來便向夫君訴說她的夢：無論你往何處去，也讓我隨你同去。旃陀計都（即因陀羅）與其他諸天前來勸他出家，並吩咐車匿備好寶馬犍陟。

passages.text: The devatas inhabiting the palace commenced to cry, so that their tears fell like rain; at the eastern gate he perceived his sleeping father and cried, father, though I love thee, yet a fear possesses me and I may not stay - I must free myself from the fear of conquering time and death, of the horrors of age and death! Suddenly he came across Mahanaman patrolling the city, and though his cousin begged and cried aloud, telling him of all the sorrow he was bringing, he travelled that night twelve yojanas.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 住在宮中的諸天開始哭泣，淚水如雨般落下；他在東門望見熟睡的父親，便哭道：父親啊，雖然我愛你，然而有一種恐懼盤據我心，我不能再留——我必須從征服時間與死亡的恐懼中、從老與死的恐怖中解脫自己！忽然他遇見正在巡視城中的摩訶那摩，儘管他的堂弟苦苦哀求、高聲哭喊，向他訴說他將帶來的種種悲傷，他當夜仍行走了十二由旬。

passages.text: He stopped and told Chhandaka to return to the city with the horse and the jewels; the prince took his sword and cut off his hair, which he threw into the air, and Shataketu took it and carried it off to the Trayastrimcat heaven - there the faithful built the stupa of the taking of the hair and beard. Then, as a decrepit hunter wearing the cotton garment handed down through ten Pratyeka Buddhas for the son of Shuddhodana, Shataketu exchanged clothes with him, and the Bodhisattva went on to Rajagriha.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他停下來，吩咐車匿帶著馬與珠寶返回城中；太子取出劍來割下自己的頭髮，拋向空中，釋提桓因接住並帶往忉利天——在那裡，虔信者建起了奉納髮鬚的塔。隨後，釋提桓因化作一個衰朽的獵人，身穿歷經十位辟支佛傳下的棉衣，與淨飯王之子交換了衣服，菩薩便繼續前往王舍城。

title.en: Bimbisara's Offer on the Pandava Mountain
title.zh: 頻毘娑羅王靈鷲山相會

region.en: Pandava mountain near Rajagriha (symbolic pin at Gridhakuta)
region.zh: 王舍城外靈鷲山（以耆闍崛山為象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: Bimbisara, seeing the ascetic's noble bearing from his palace terrace, fills his bowl and follows him to the Pandava mountain, offering everything that makes life agreeable - women, riches, pleasures. The ascetic answers with the great renunciation-verses: the treasure I am seeking is that wisdom which knoweth no superior; and the king, 'when thou shalt have reached thy goal, teach it then to me,' receives the promise.
summary.zh: 頻毘娑羅王自宮中望見乞士風儀，令人布施、令人隨行，親登靈鷲山以財色諸樂相許。行者答曰：我屬釋迦日族，不慕世財；「我所求者，是無上智慧」；王曰「汝證道時，願以斯法教我」——王子允諾。此為日後王舍城弘法之伏筆。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: Bimbisara noticed the ascetic from the terrace of his palace, was struck with his noble bearing, sent some one to fill his bowl and another to see where he went; then he went to visit him on the Pandava mountain and offered him everything that makes life agreeable - women, riches and pleasures. I care not for this world's treasures; they cannot bring contentment, the ascetic answered, 'tis hard to cross the swamps of human passions - the treasure I am seeking is that wisdom which knoweth no superior. When thou shalt have reached thy goal, teach it then to me, said the king, and the Bodhisattva promised that he would.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 頻婆娑羅從宮殿的露臺上望見這位苦行者，為他高貴的儀態所打動，便派人為他盛滿缽盂，又派另一人察看他的去向；隨後他前往般荼婆山拜訪他，並供養他一切使生活愜意之物——美女、財富與享樂。我不貪戀這世間的財寶；它們不能帶來滿足，苦行者答道，要渡過人間情欲的沼澤實屬艱難——我所尋求的財寶，乃是那無有更上的智慧。當你達成目標時，請把它教給我，國王說道，菩薩便應允了他。

title.en: Six Years of Mortification
title.zh: 六年苦行

region.en: Bank of the Nairanjana river at Gaya (symbolic pin at Bodh Gaya)
region.zh: 恒河南岸尼連禪河畔（以菩提伽耶為象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: Surpassing all the ascetics of the Vulture's Peak, the Bodhisattva learns their goal is only Sakra-hood and moves on; refusing the gods' offer of miraculous feeding, he fasts to a single pea a day until his body is emaciated and blackish-red. Yaśodhara, hearing the reports, puts away her flowers and jewels and copies his mortifications until her father-in-law forbids anyone to speak of him. Seeing severe asceticism had not brought him nearer the truth, he takes food of an unpalatable kind and sleeps beside a corpse in the cemetery - where village girls throw dirt and stones at him, thinking him a flesh-eating fiend; his five attendants forsake him for Benares, where they become 'the Five.'
summary.zh: 他在靈鷲山苦行勝過一切仙人，知其所求不過帝釋之位，遂離去；諸天願以神力供養，他亦拒絕，日食一豆，身瘦如柴、色如黑紅。耶輸陀羅聞訊，棄珠花而同修苦行，直至公公下令不得再提其名。菩薩知苦行無益，食粗糲之物，臥屍林屍旁而眠——村女誤為啖人羅剎，投以泥土瓦礫；五侍者失望而去，往波羅奈鹿野苑，是為「五比丘」。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: He lived with the ascetics of the Vulture's Peak, surpassing them all in his mortifications, so that he became known as the great ascetic; but he finally learned from them that the object they had in view was to become Sakra or Brahma or even Mara, and knew that they were not in the right way. The gods offered to feed him miraculously and unknown to mankind, but he refused, and went on fasting until he reduced his food to a single pea a day, and his body was emaciated and of a blackish-red colour.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他與靈鷲山的苦行者同住，在苦行上超過他們所有人，因而被稱為大苦行者；但他最終從他們那裡得知，他們所追求的目標是成為帝釋或梵天，甚至魔王，便知道他們並非走在正道上。諸天願以神通之力、不為世人所知地供養他食物，但他拒絕了，繼續斷食，直到將食物減至每日一粒豌豆，身體消瘦，膚色呈黑紅色。

passages.text: Yaśodhara, greatly grieved, put away her flowers and jewels and performed the same mortifications which her husband was practising, until Shuddhodana, fearing for the child she bore, forbade any one to speak to her about the Bodhisattva. When he had obtained and eaten some very unpalatable food he wandered into the cemetery, and lying down beside a corpse went to sleep; the village girls saw him and thought he was a fiend seeking human flesh to devour, and threw dirt and stones at him - and his five attendants, forsaking him, started out for Benares and dwelt in the Mrigadava as the Five.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 耶輸陀羅悲痛至極，收起她的花鬘與珠寶，修持與她丈夫相同的苦行，直到淨飯王因憂慮她所懷的孩子，禁止任何人向她提起菩薩。當他取得並吃下一些極難下嚥的食物後，便遊蕩進入墓地，躺在一具屍體旁睡去；村中的女子看見他，以為他是尋求人肉吞食的鬼魅，便向他投擲泥土與石塊——而他的五位侍從捨棄了他，動身前往波羅奈，住在鹿野苑，成為五比丘。

title.en: The Milk-Soup of Nanda and Nandabala
title.zh: 難陀與難陀波羅的乳糜

region.en: Village of Senani near the Nairanjana (symbolic pin at Bodh Gaya)
region.zh: 尼連禪河畔舍那村（以菩提伽耶為象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: The headman's daughters Nanda and Nandabala, hearing of the Shakya prince foretold to be chakravartin or Buddha, prepare milk-soup for him; he takes it in a crystal vase brought by two devas of the Akanishta region, bathes in the Nairanjana, is handed out by an arjuna branch the devas bend down, and eats on the bank. His washed bowl, thrown into the river, is seized by the Nagas - until Shakra, as a garuda, dives and carries it to the Trayastrimcat heaven, where the gods build the stupa of the bowl. Asked what they seek by their gift, the sisters answer they wish to become his wives at his chakravartin rebirth - and he explains that could never be.
summary.zh: 舍那村長的兩個女兒難陀與難陀波羅聽聞釋迦太子將為轉輪王或佛陀，預備乳糜供養；他以光音天（阿迦膩吒天）二天子送來的水晶缽受食，入河沐浴——諸天彎下阿順那樹枝助其出水。飯畢洗缽擲於河中，龍王取之；帝釋化身大鵬入水奪缽，帶往三十三天建「缽塔」。二女問供養何求，答曰願其成轉輪王時為其妻；他為之解說此願不可得。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: Nanda and Nandabala had heard about the Shakya prince of the Kapilavastu Shakyas, and that it had been prophesied of him that he would become a universal monarch or a Buddha; so they had prepared for him a milk-soup, which the Bodhisattva took in a crystal vase adorned with jewels which two devas of the Akanishta region had brought him. Carrying the food with him he went to the Nairanjana river and bathed, and when he had finished the devas bent down the branches of an arjuna tree, which he seized to help him out of the water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 難陀與難陀婆羅曾聽聞迦毗羅衛城釋迦族的釋迦王子之事，並聽說曾有預言說他將成為轉輪聖王或成佛；於是他們為他備好乳糜，菩薩以兩位色究竟天的天神為他帶來的、飾以珠寶的水晶缽盛受了它。他帶著食物前往尼連禪河沐浴，沐浴完畢後，天神壓低了一棵阿順那樹的枝條，他抓住樹枝幫助自己出水。

passages.text: Having washed the bowl, he threw it into the river; the Nagas took it, but Shakra, assuming the form of a garuda, dashed into the river, seized the bowl and carried it off to the Trayastrimcat heaven, and there the gods built the stupa of the bowl. Asked what they sought by their gift, the sisters answered that the soothsayers had prophesied he would become a chakravartin monarch - may this seed of virtue make you become our husband at that time; he explained that this could never be, and they said, may you then quickly reach the highest wisdom and perfection.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 洗淨缽後，他將缽投入河中；龍族取走了它，但帝釋天化作金翅鳥之形，衝入河中，奪取此缽並將其帶往忉利天，眾神便在那裡建了缽塔。當被問及她們的供養所求為何時，姊妹們回答說，占相者曾預言他將成為轉輪聖王——願此功德種子使您在那時成為我們的丈夫；他解釋說這絕不可能，她們便說，願您於是迅速證得最高智慧與圓滿。

title.en: Mara's Defeat at the Bodhi Tree
title.zh: 菩提樹下降魔成道

region.en: Bodhi tree at Uruvilva (symbolic pin at Bodh Gaya)
region.zh: 閻浮提菩提樹下（以菩提伽耶為象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: Wading the river amid wondrous signs, the Bodhisattva takes from the grass-merchant Svastika - Shakra in disguise - a handful of grass for his seat under the Bodhi tree. Mara comes with the lie that Devadatta has crushed the Shakyas and apparitions of his wives and kinsmen, argues, sends his three daughters Desire, Pleasure and Delight with all their allurements - and the Bodhisattva changes them into old hags. The gods of the pure abode shower flowers on the conqueror and sing victory; reasoning within himself he sees the chain of causes and effects that brings existence, age and death - and becomes enlightened. Mara's bow and standard fall from his grasp, and a million and thirty-six thousand cohorts flee filled with dismay.
summary.zh: 菩薩涉河時異象頻現；帝釋化身賣草人婆藪陀，獻一把草為菩提樹下之座。魔王先以「提婆達多滅釋迦族」之謊、再以耶輸陀羅等親眷幻影、繼以雄辯、最後遣三女「欲、樂、喜」百般誘惑——菩薩不動，反令三女化為老嫗。淨居諸天雨花唱勝；菩薩於座上思維，徹見生死流轉之緣起，遂成正覺。魔王弓箭旗幟墜地，百萬三千六百魔軍驚惶潰散。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: Shakra took the shape of the grass merchant Svastika, and from him the Bodhisattva obtained a handful of grass out of which he made his seat at the foot of the Bodhi tree. Then Mara went to him and said, Devadatta has subdued Kapilavastu; he has seized the palace and crushed the Shakyas - why stay you here? He caused apparitions of Yaśodhara, of Mrigadja, of Gopa, of Devadatta and of the Shakyas who had escaped to appear before him, but the Bodhisattva remained unmoved.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 帝釋天化作賣草商人吉祥，菩薩從他那裡取得一把草，用以在菩提樹下鋪設座位。於是魔羅前來對他說：提婆達多已降伏迦毗羅衛城；他奪取了宮殿，摧毀了釋迦族——你為何還留在此處？他使耶輸陀羅、彌伽闍、瞿波、提婆達多以及逃脫的釋迦族人的幻象顯現在他面前，但菩薩依然不為所動。

passages.text: Then Mara called his three daughters, Desire, Pleasure and Delight, and they tried all their allurements in vain; the Bodhisattva changed them into old hags. Seeing all his devices fail, the gods of the pure abode showered down flowers on the conqueror and sang songs of victory; and reasoning within himself the Bodhisattva saw the cause of existence, of age, of death, and the way to free oneself of all this trouble - the concatenation of causes and effects which bring about existence and its cessation became known to him, and he became enlightened, a Buddha.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是魔羅召來他的三個女兒——愛欲、歡樂與喜悅，她們使盡一切誘惑皆徒勞無功；菩薩將她們變成老婦。眼見他的一切伎倆皆告失敗，淨居天的眾神向這位征服者灑下花朵，唱起勝利的歌；菩薩於自身中思惟，照見存在、衰老、死亡之因，以及解脫這一切煩惱之道——引生存在及其止息之因果相續為他所知，他於是開悟，成為佛陀。

passages.text: When all wisdom had been given him, Mara's bow and his standard fell from his grasp, and all his cohorts, a million and thirty-six thousand in number, fled filled with dismay. The rumour had reached Kapilavastu that the prince had died under the excess of his penances and all the court was in despair; then came the news that he had attained enlightenment, and great was the rejoicing everywhere.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當一切智慧皆已授予他時，魔羅的弓與旗幟從他手中墜落，他所有的部眾，數達一百零三萬六千，滿懷驚惶地逃散。消息傳到迦毗羅衛城，說王子因苦行過度而死，整個宮廷陷入絕望；隨後傳來他已成等正覺的消息，各處皆大歡喜。

title.en: Rahula on the Floating Stone
title.zh: 羅睺羅浮石驗子

region.en: Pond of Kapilavastu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛池畔（象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: On the day the enlightenment-news reaches Kapilavastu, Yaśodhara bears a son - and Rahu seizes the moon, so the eclipse marks the child: Rahula. The same day Amritodana's wife bears a son amid the city's rejoicing: All-joy, Ananda. But Shuddhodana doubts the child is his son's, and the mother, in great distress, sets the child on a stone and sinks both in the water: if the child be the Bodhisattva's, may it and the stone float! - and lo, it floats like a ball of cotton, and the people rejoice and take the young child out of the pond.
summary.zh: 證道之訊抵迦毘羅衛之日，耶輸陀羅產下一子；而當日「羅睺」蝕月，故子名羅睺羅。同日阿彌多陀那之妻亦生子，城中方大慶，遂名「一切喜」——阿難。淨飯王疑此子非其孫，母親大慟，將孩子置於石上同沉水中發願：「若真是菩薩之子，願子與石俱浮！」果然嬰兒浮於石上如棉團，眾人大喜，將孩子抱出。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: Just as the king was being told the news of the enlightenment, they came and told him that Yaśodhara had brought forth a son, and also that Rahu had seized the moon; so they called the child Rahula. On the same day the wife of Amritodana brought forth a son, and as the city was rejoicing greatly that day, they called him All-joy, Ananda.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 正当国王被告知成道的消息时，有人前来禀报他说，耶输陀罗生下了一个儿子，又说罗睺（Rahu）攫住了月亮；于是他们便给这孩子取名为罗睺罗（Rahula）。同一天，甘露饭王（Amritodana）的妻子也生下了一个儿子，而由于那一天全城上下都欢欣鼓舞，他们便给他取名为「一切欢喜」，即阿难（Ananda）。

passages.text: Shuddhodana thought that Yaśodhara's child could not be Shakyamuni's, and great was the mother's distress on hearing his suspicions; so she took the child to a pond, put it on a stone, and placed them together in the water with these words: if the child be the Bodhisattva's, may it and the stone float; if it is not, may it sink! And lo! the child floated on the stone as if it had been a ball of cotton, and the people rejoiced greatly and took the young child out of the pond.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 净饭王（Shuddhodana）心想，耶输陀罗的孩子不可能是释迦牟尼（Shakyamuni）的，而母亲听到他的猜疑后，心中极为痛苦；于是她带着孩子来到一个池塘边，把他放在一块石头上，将二者一同置于水中，并说了这样的话：倘若这孩子是菩萨的，愿他与石头一同浮起；倘若不是，愿他沉下去！看哪！那孩子竟浮在石头上，仿佛是一团棉花，众人欢欣不已，把那幼小的孩子从池中抱了出来。

title.en: The First Offering: Trapusha and Bhallika
title.zh: 初供養：提謂與波利

region.en: Bank of the Nairanjana under the Bo tree (symbolic pin at Bodh Gaya)
region.zh: 菩提樹下尼連禪河畔（以菩提伽耶為象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: Seven days after enlightenment two merchants, Trapusha and Bhallika, with five hundred waggons are led by a deva to offer honey-sweetened food; each of the four great kings of the cardinal points brings a bowl, and not wishing to offend any of them the Buddha takes the four and transforms them into one. He bids them go for refuge to the Buddha, the truth and the church that will hereafter exist - the first lay disciples - and whatever wish they made will be granted.
summary.zh: 證道七日後，商人提謂與波利率五百車隊，蒙天人指引獻上蜜和之食；四方四大天王各捧一缽前來，佛不欲偏捨，合四缽為一缽受之，並教二人皈依佛、法與「將來之僧」——是為最早的在家二弟子，且許諾「汝等所願皆得成就」。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: When the seven days were passed there came along two merchants, Trapusha and Bhallika, with five hundred waggons; and following the advice of a deva they came to the Buddha and offered him food sweetened with honey. Each of the four great kings of the cardinal points brought him a bowl in which to take the food, and not wishing to offend any of them he took the four bowls and transformed them into one. Then the Buddha said to the merchants, go for a refuge to the Buddha, to the truth and to the church that will hereafter exist; whatever wish you may have made when you made me this offering, it will be granted unto you.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 七日过后，来了两位商人，帝梨富娑（Trapusha）与跋梨迦（Bhallika），带着五百辆车；他们听从了一位天神的劝告，来到佛陀面前，献上以蜜调甜的食物。四方四大天王各献给他一个钵，以供他盛放食物，他因不愿得罪其中任何一位，便取了这四个钵，将它们化作一个。于是佛陀对两位商人说：去皈依佛陀、皈依真理，并皈依日后将存在的僧团；你们向我献此供养时所发的任何愿望，都将赐予你们。

title.en: Mara's Announcement and the Myrobalan Cure
title.zh: 魔王報死訊與訶子療疾

region.en: Bank of the Nairanjana (symbolic pin at Bodh Gaya)
region.zh: 尼連禪河畔（以菩提伽耶為象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: The honeyed food gives the Buddha colic, and Mara comes to announce that the time to die has come; but he answers that as long as his disciples have not become wise and of quick understanding, as long as the bhikshus, bhikshunis and lay disciples cannot refute their adversaries according to the Dharma, and as long as his moral teaching has not spread far and wide among gods and men, so long will he not pass away. Shakra brings an arura (myrobalan) fruit from Jambudvipa, and by it the Buddha is cured.
summary.zh: 蜜食令佛腹痛；魔王乘機來報「世尊，死期已至！」佛答：只要我的弟子尚未智慧猛利、四眾尚不能依正法折服論敵、正法尚未廣布天人世間——「我終不取滅度。」帝釋自閻浮提取一顆訶子（arura）來，佛因之而癒。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: The Buddha sat down on the bank of the Nairanjana and ate the food which the merchants had given him, but the honey gave him colic. Then the Evil one, seeing the pain he was enduring, came to him and said, Blessed One, the time to die has come! But he answered him, Mara, as long as my disciples have not become wise and of quick understanding, as long as the bhikshus, the bhikshunis and the lay disciples of either sex are not able to refute their adversaries according to the Dharma, as long as my moral teaching has not been spread far and wide among gods and men, so long will I not pass away. Then Shakra brought an arura fruit from a tree in Jambudvipa, and by it the Buddha was cured.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 佛陀在尼连禅河（Nairanjana）岸边坐下，吃了商人们给他的食物，但那蜜却使他腹中绞痛。于是那恶者见他忍受着痛苦，便来到他面前说：世尊，命终之时已到！但他回答他说：魔罗（Mara），只要我的弟子们尚未变得智慧而敏于领悟，只要比丘、比丘尼以及男女在家弟子尚不能依佛法驳倒他们的对手，只要我的戒律之教尚未在诸天与人间广泛传布，那么我便不会入灭。于是帝释天（Shakra）从阎浮提（Jambudvipa）的一棵树上取来一枚诃梨勒果（arura），佛陀借此得以痊愈。

title.en: Mutchilinda, the Serpent-King's Shelter
title.zh: 目支鄰陀龍王護佛

region.en: Abode of the Naga king Mutchilinda (symbolic pin near Bodh Gaya)
region.zh: 目支鄰陀龍宮（以菩提伽耶附近為象徵定位）

period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: After remaining under the Bo tree as long as pleased him, the Buddha went to where lived the Naga king Mutchilinda; wishing to protect him from the sun and rain, the serpent wrapped his body seven times around the Blessed One and spread out his hood over his head, and there the Lord remained seven days in thought.
summary.zh: 佛在菩提樹下隨意經行後，來到目支鄰陀龍王之處；龍王為其遮日避雨，以身繞佛七匝，展開傘蓋覆其頭頂——世尊在此思維七日。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: The Buddha went to where lived the Naga king Mutchilinda; and he, wishing to protect him from the sun and rain, wrapped his body seven times around the Blessed One, and spread out his hood over his head, and there the Lord remained seven days in thought.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 佛陀来到那伽王（Naga king）目支邻陀（Mutchilinda）所居之处；那伽王为保护他免受日晒雨淋，以自己的身躯绕世尊七匝，又将头罩展开覆于他头顶之上，于是世尊便在那里静思七日。

title.en: Glooskap Names the Animals and Forms His Family
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普為百獸命名並建立家室

region.en: Land of the Wabanaki, nearest to the sunrise (Maine and the Maritimes)
region.zh: 最接近日出的瓦巴納基之地（緬因與加拿大沿海）

period: Passamaquoddy tradition recorded by Charles G. Leland (1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'Of the Great Deeds which Glooskap did for Men'

summary.en: Glooskap comes over the sea in a great stone canoe, an island of granite covered with trees, and names the animals: the Bear fears man, the Squirrel - greater than the Bear in those days - is smoothed down to his present size and becomes Glooskap's dog, and the Moose and Beaver confess they would flee or run. Seeing that of all created beings the first and greatest was Man, he teaches men - who lived in darkness - how to hunt, build huts and canoes and weirs, the virtues of plants and roots, and the names of all the stars. He dwells with Noogumee his grandmother and Abistarnoock the Martin, who can change himself from baby to youth, and who wears the magic belt of endless strength when Glooskap lends it.
summary.zh: 格魯斯卡普乘巨石之舟——覆滿樹木的花崗岩島——渡海而來，為百獸命名：熊懼人，松鼠（彼時比熊還大）被他撫小至今日的模樣，成為其獵犬；麋鹿與河狸皆自承要逃。他見人是造物之首，便教導處於黑暗的人類狩獵、築屋、造舟結網、辨識草木之性，並為群星命名。他與「祖母」諾古米同住，又有能自由變身大小的貂弟阿比斯塔諾克，佩上主人的法帶便力大無窮。

sensitivity.note: Passamaquoddy tradition (Leland 1884); public domain. Leland prints the Indian-English manuscript with editorial notes.

passages.text: It is told in traditions of the old time that Glooskap was born in the land of the Wabanaki, which is nearest to the sunrise; but another story says that he came over the sea in a great stone canoe, and that this canoe was an island of granite covered with trees. When the great man, of all men and beasts chief ruler, had come down from this ark, he went among the Wabanaki. And calling all the animals he gave them each a name: unto the Bear, mooin; and asked him what he would do if he should meet with a man. The Bear said, 'I fear him, and I should run.' Now in those days the Squirrel (mi-ko) was greater than the Bear. Then Glooskap took him in his hands, and smoothing him down he grew smaller and smaller, till he became as we see him now.
passages.note: Condensed from Leland 1884, pp. 28-29; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古老的传说中讲道，格卢斯卡普（Glooskap）生于瓦巴纳基（Wabanaki）之地，那地方最靠近日出之处；但另一个故事则说，他是乘着一只巨大的石舟渡海而来的，而那石舟乃是一座覆满树木的花岗岩岛屿。当这位伟人——一切人与兽的主宰——从这方舟上下来之后，便来到瓦巴纳基人中间。他召来所有的动物，一一为它们取名：给熊取名为「mooin」；又问他若遇见人将如何行事。熊说：「我怕他，我会逃跑。」话说在那些日子里，松鼠（mi-ko）比熊还要高大。于是格卢斯卡普将它握在手中，把它抚平，它便变得越来越小，直到成为我们如今所见的样子。

passages.text: In after-days the Squirrel was Glooskap's dog, and when he so willed, grew large again and slew his enemies, however fierce they might be. But this time, when asked what he would do should he meet with a man, Mi-ko replied, 'I should run up a tree.' Then the Moose, being questioned, answered, standing still and looking down, 'I should run through the woods.' And so it was with Kwah-beet the Beaver, and Glooskap saw that of all created beings the first and greatest was Man.
passages.note: Condensed from Leland 1884, pp. 29-30; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 後來，松鼠成了格盧斯卡普的狗；只要他願意，牠便會再度變大，殺死他的敵人，無論那些敵人有多兇猛。但這一次，當被問到若遇見人會怎麼做時，米科回答：「我會爬上樹。」接著，駝鹿被問到時，站著不動、低頭答道：「我會穿過森林跑走。」海狸夸比特也是如此。於是格盧斯卡普看出，在所有受造之物中，最先也最偉大的是人。

passages.text: Before men were instructed by him, they lived in darkness; it was so dark that they could not even see to slay their enemies. Glooskap taught them how to hunt, and to build huts and canoes and weirs for fish. Before he came they knew not how to make weapons or nets. He, the Great Master, showed them the hidden virtues of plants, roots, and barks, and pointed out to them such vegetables as might be used for food, as well as what kinds of animals, birds, and fish were to be eaten. And when this was done he taught them the names of all the stars. He loved mankind, and wherever he might be in the wilderness he was never very far from any of the Indians: he dwelt in a lonely land, but whenever they sought him they found him.
passages.note: Condensed from Leland 1884, p. 30; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在人受他教導之前，他們生活在黑暗之中；那黑暗深得他們甚至看不見，無法殺死敵人。格盧斯卡普教他們如何狩獵，如何搭建小屋、造獨木舟、編魚梁。在他到來之前，他們不懂得製造武器或網。他，這位偉大的導師，向他們展示了植物、根與樹皮的隱藏功效，並指點他們哪些植物可作食物，以及何種走獸、鳥與魚可以食用。做完這些之後，他又教他們所有星辰的名字。他愛人類，無論他在荒野何處，他從不遠離任何一個印第安人：他住在荒僻之地，但每當他們尋求他，總能找到他。

passages.text: Glooskap was never married, yet as he lived like other men he lived not alone. There dwelt with him an old woman, who kept his lodge; he called her Noogumee, 'my grandmother.' With her was a youth named Abistarnoock, or the Martin. And Martin could change himself to a baby or a little boy, a youth or a young man, as befitted the time in which he was to act; for all things about Glooskap were very wonderful. This Martin ate always from a small birch-bark dish, and when he left this anywhere Glooskap was sure to find it, and could tell from its appearance all that had befallen his family. And Martin was called by Glooskap Uch-keen, 'my younger brother.' The Lord of men and beasts had a belt which gave him magical power and endless strength; and when he lent this to Martin, the younger brother could also do great deeds, such as were only done in old times.
passages.note: Condensed from Leland 1884, pp. 30-31; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 格盧斯卡普從未娶妻，然而他既像其他人一樣生活，便不是獨自一人。有一位老婦與他同住，為他照料住所；他稱她為努古米，意即「我的祖母」。與她在一起的還有一個少年，名叫阿比斯塔努克，即貂。而貂能隨意將自己變成嬰兒或小男孩、少年或青年，以配合他將要行事的那個時機；因為格盧斯卡普身邊的一切都奇妙非常。這貂總是用一隻樺樹皮小碟進食；無論他把碟子落在何處，格盧斯卡普都必定能找到，並能從碟子的模樣看出他家中發生的一切。格盧斯卡普稱貂為烏奇金，意即「我的弟弟」。這人與獸之主有一條腰帶，賦予他法力與無窮的力量；當他把腰帶借給貂時，這弟弟也能做出偉業，如同古時才有的作為。

title.en: Glooskap Pursues the Sorcerer Win-pe, and the Whale Smokes a Pipe
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普追捕巫師溫佩，鯨魚吸菸斗

region.en: From the St. John River to Newfoundland along the Wabanaki coasts
region.zh: 自聖約翰河沿岸至紐芬蘭的瓦巴納基海岸

period: Micmac tradition recorded by Leland (1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How Win-pe the Sorcerer... and how the Whale smoked a Pipe'

summary.en: The sorcerer Win-pe carries off Glooskap's grandmother and the Martin, and Glooskap rests seven years before pursuing. He sings the magic song the whales obey, rejects the small whale that sinks under one foot, and rides the mighty female toward the coast; she fears shoal water, and the Clams - his deadly enemies - sing to her to throw off and drown the rider, but Glooskap mistranslates their chant as 'hurry him along,' and she runs herself high on the shore. Singing her forgiveness he pushes her off with his bow, gives her an old pipe and tobacco, and stands on the shore watching the long low cloud that follows her until she vanishes in the far away.
summary.zh: 巫師溫佩擄走祖母與貂弟；格魯斯卡普獨居七年方启程追索。他高唱馭鯨之歌，先來的小鯨不堪其一足之重而遭遣回；得巨鯨負他渡海。鯨懼擱淺，而他的死敵蛤蜊在沙下合唱，教鯨把乘者甩下水去；格魯斯卡普卻把蛤歌「譯」作「快些趕路」，鯨遂全速衝上灘頭。主人唱起饒恕之歌，以弓輕推送她回深海，又賜老菸斗與菸草；他立於岸上，遠望她吐出的低雲伴她沒入天涯。

sensitivity.note: Micmac tradition (Leland 1884); public domain.

passages.text: In old times, in the beginning of things, men were as animals and animals as men... they could change to one or the other form; yet even as men there was always something which showed what they were. Now Glooskap lived on an island named Aja-lig-un-meehk, and with him were many Indians with the names and natures of animals and birds. These men, but most of all Pulowech, the Partridge, having acquired power themselves, became jealous of Glooskap, and made up their minds to depart when he was away, taking with them Martin and the grandmother... he returned home and found the old woman, whose name was Mooinarkw (Mrs. Bear), and Martin had been taken away. Following their tracks to the shore he saw one of his greatest enemies, a terrible sorcerer named Win-pe, just pushing off in his canoe. And with him were his wife and child and Dame Bear and Martin.
passages.note: Condensed from Leland 1884, pp. 31-32; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古時，在萬物之初，人如同獸，獸如同人……他們能變成彼此的形象；然而即便作為人，也總有某種東西顯露出他們本是什麼。那時，格盧斯卡普住在一個名叫阿賈利貢米克島的地方，與他在一起的還有許多印第安人，他們具有各種走獸與鳥類的名字和性情。這些人，尤其是最甚的鷓鴣普洛韋奇，自己獲得了力量之後，便嫉妒格盧斯卡普，決心趁他不在時離去，帶走貂和祖母……他回到家中，發現那名叫穆伊納克烏（熊夫人）的老婦和貂都已被帶走。他循著他們的足跡來到岸邊，看見他最強大的敵人之一——一個名叫溫佩的可怕巫師——正推著獨木舟離岸。與他在一起的還有他的妻兒、熊夫人和貂。

passages.text: But Glooskap rested seven years alone before he pursued the enemy, though some say it was seven months. And when the time had come, he took his dogs and went to the shore, and looked far out to sea over the waves, and sang the magic song which the whales obey. Soon there rose in the distance a small whale, who had heard the call, and came to Glooskap; but he was then very great, and he put one foot on the whale to test his weight, and the fish sank under him. So he sent it away. Then the lord of men and beasts sang the song again, and there came the largest, a mighty female, and she bore him well and easily over to Kes-poog-itk. But she was greatly afraid of getting into shoal water, or of running ashore.
passages.note: Condensed from Leland 1884, pp. 33-34; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但格盧斯卡普獨自歇息了七年才去追趕敵人，不過也有人說是七個月。時機到來時，他帶著他的狗來到岸邊，越過波浪遠望大海，唱起鯨魚聽從的魔法之歌。不久，遠處浮起一頭小鯨，牠聽到了召喚，來到格盧斯卡普面前；但他當時身形極大，便把一隻腳踏在鯨上試牠的承重，那魚便沉了下去。於是他把牠遣走。接著，這人與獸之主再次唱起歌，來了一頭最大的鯨，是一頭強壯的雌鯨，她穩穩地、輕鬆地把他載到凱斯普吉特克。但她非常害怕駛入淺水，或擱淺上岸。

passages.text: She saw shells below, and soon the water grew so shoal that she said in fear, 'Does not the land show itself like a bow-string?' And he said, 'We are still far from land.' Then the water grew so shoal that she heard the song of the Clams as they lay under the sand, singing to her that she should throw him off and drown him; for these Clams were his deadly enemies. But Bootup the Whale did not understand their language, so she asked her rider - for he knew Clam - what they were chanting to her. And he replied in a song: 'They tell you to hurry, to hurry, to hurry him along, over the water, away as fast as you can!' Then the Whale went like lightning, and suddenly found herself high on the shore. Then she lamented and sang: 'Alas, my grandchild, ah, you have been my death; I can never leave the land, I shall swim in the sea no more.'
passages.note: Condensed from Leland 1884, p. 34; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她看見下方有貝殼，不久水變得如此之淺，她害怕地說：「那陸地不就像弓弦一樣顯露出來了嗎？」他說：「我們離陸地還遠著呢。」接著水變得如此之淺，她聽見蛤蜊的歌聲，那些蛤蜊躺在沙下，唱著要她把背上的人甩下去、淹死他；因為這些蛤蜊是他的死敵。但鯨魚布圖普聽不懂牠們的語言，便問她背上的人——因為他懂蛤蜊語——牠們在對她唱什麼。他於是以歌聲回答：「牠們叫你快，快，快把他載過去，越過水面，盡你快地離去！」於是鯨魚如閃電般疾行，忽然發現自己高高地擱在岸上。於是她哀嘆著唱道：「唉，我的孫兒啊，唉，你害死了我；我再也離不開陸地，我再也不能在海中游泳了。」

passages.text: But Glooskap sang: 'Have no fear, noogumee, you shall not suffer, you shall swim in the sea once more.' Then with a push of his bow against her head he sent her off into deep water, and the Whale rejoiced greatly. But ere she went she said, 'Oh, my grandson, hast thou not such a thing as an old pipe and some tobacco?' He replied, 'Ah yes. You want tobacco, I behold you.' So he gave her a short pipe and some tobacco, and thereunto a light. And the Whale, being of good cheer, sailed away, smoking as she went, while Glooskap, standing silent on the shore, and ever leaning on his maple bow, beheld the long low cloud which followed her until she vanished in the far away.
passages.note: Condensed from Leland 1884, pp. 34-35; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但格盧斯卡普唱道：「不必害怕，努古米，你不會受苦，你將再次在大海中游弋。」接著他用弓頂了她的頭一下，把她送向深水，那鯨魚大喜。但她臨走前說：「哦，我的孫兒，你可有舊煙斗和煙草之類的東西嗎？」他答道：「啊，有的。你想要煙草，我看出來了。」於是他給了她一支短煙斗和一些煙草，還有一點火。那鯨魚心情愉快，一路航行而去，邊走邊抽著煙；而格盧斯卡普則靜立岸邊，始終倚著他的楓木弓，望著那長長的、低垂的雲跟隨著她，直到她消失在遠方。

title.en: The Evil Pitcher: Witch of the Enchanted Sausages and the Giant Flight
title.zh: 邪惡的罐婆：魔法香腸與巨人追逐

region.en: Grand Manan and the Wabanaki coast, Bay of Fundy
region.zh: 芬迪灣的格蘭馬南島與瓦巴納基海岸

period: Passamaquoddy tradition recorded by Leland (1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'Of the Dreadful Deeds of the Evil Pitcher'

summary.en: The witch Pook-jin-skwess, the Pitcher, falls in love with the young Glooskap and pursues him in giant form - like the wind chasing the cloud, the lightning chasing the thunder - until he leaps nine miles from the mainland to Grand Manan; her long pointed snowshoe-marks are seen deep in the rocks to this day. On his pursuit of Win-pe she guards the road as a filthy trembling hag crawling with devil-vermin; Glooskap picks each imp from her hair, turns them to porcupines and toads, crushes a cranberry for the noise, and lets her wake mocked. At the sorcerer's lodge her daughters offer enchanted sausages to string about his neck; his dogs - told 'Stop!' in a word they know as 'At them!' - tear the witches, and the master strangles the old man with his own sausage-links.
summary.zh: 巫婆「罐婆」坡吉斯奎絲愛上年輕的格魯斯卡普而化形追逐——如風逐雲、電逐雷——直至他從大陸一躍九里登上格蘭馬南島；她那尖長雪鞋的印痕至今深嵌岩石。格魯斯卡普追索溫佩途中，她扮作遍生魔鬼蟲的醜嫗守路；他逐一從她髮間拈出小鬼，使之化為豪豬與蟾蜍，捏碎蔓越莓裝作捏蟲，戲弄而過。在巫師屋中，其女以魔法香腸作項圈相贈；他的犬聽見他喊「住口」（犬卻聽成「撲上去」），撕碎眾巫，主人以香腸鏈絞殺老巫。

sensitivity.note: Passamaquoddy tradition (Leland 1884); public domain. Leland notes the witch may have given her name to Moll Pitcher of Lynn.

passages.text: When Glooskap came into the world it abounded in giants, monsters, sorcerers and witches, fiends and devils. Among the witches there was one whom the Passamaquoddy call Pook-jin-skwess, or the Pitcher. And they have a legend that she once fell in love with Glooskap when he was young and had not gained the power of his riper age. He fled before her, and she pursued him. It was a dreadful flight, since to make rapid steps both took the form of giants by their m'teoulin, or magic power. It was like an awful storm in winter, the wind chasing the cloud; it was like a frightful tempest in summer, the lightning chasing the thunder. As the snow lay deep, both had snow-shoes on. When they came to the shore Glooskap leaped from the main-land to the island of Grand Manan, and so escaped her. Now the snow-shoes of Glooskap were sumsook, or round, while those of Pook-jin-skwess were long and pointed, and the marks of them as they jumped are to be seen deep in the rocks to this day.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 36; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 當格盧斯卡普來到世上時，世間滿是巨人、怪物、巫師與女巫、惡魔與魔鬼。女巫之中有一個，帕薩馬科迪人稱之為普克金斯克維斯，即「水罐」。他們有一則傳說，說她曾愛上了格盧斯卡普，那時他還年輕，尚未獲得成熟之年的力量。他在她面前逃走，她則追趕他。那是一場可怕的奔逃，因為為了加快腳步，兩人都憑藉他們的姆特烏林，即魔法之力，化作巨人的形態。那就像冬日裡一場可怕的風暴，風追逐著雲；就像夏日裡一場駭人的暴風雨，閃電追逐著雷鳴。由於積雪很深，兩人都穿著雪鞋。當他們來到岸邊，格盧斯卡普從大陸躍到格蘭德馬南島，就此逃脫了她。如今格盧斯卡普的雪鞋是蘇姆蘇克，即圓形的，而普克金斯克維斯的雪鞋則是又長又尖的，他們跳躍時留下的印記，至今仍深深刻在岩石之中。

passages.text: And when he came to Ogumkeok he found a hut, and in it, seated over a fire, the ugliest old hag he had ever seen, trembling in every limb, as if near death, dirty, ragged, and loathsome in all ways. Looking up at him with bleared eyes, she begged him to gather her a little firewood, which he did. And then she prayed him to free her from the vermin with which she was covered, and which were maddening her with their bites. These were all devils in disguise, the spirits of foul poison, such as she deemed must kill even the Master. Now Glooskap, foreseeing all this, had taken with him, as he came, from a bog many cranberries. And bidding Pook-jin-skwess bend over, he began to take from her hair the hideous vermin, and each, as he took it, became a horrid porcupine or toad. Then the hag asked, 'Have you found one?' 'I have,' replied the Master. 'Crush it!' was her answer, and Glooskap crushed a cranberry; and she, hearing the noise, thought that he had done as she bid, and that the poison on his fingers would penetrate to his life.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 38-39; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 當他來到奧古姆凱奧克時，他發現了一間小屋，屋裡有一個他從未見過的、最醜陋的老巫婆坐在火邊，四肢顫抖，彷彿瀕臨死亡，骯髒、襤褸，處處令人作嘔。她抬起渾濁的眼睛望著他，求他替她拾些柴火，他便照做了。接著她求他替她清除滿身的蟲子，那些蟲子正咬得她發狂。這些蟲子全是偽裝的魔鬼，是惡毒之氣的靈，她以為這樣的毒物連大師也必死無疑。格盧斯卡普早已預見這一切，來時便從沼澤裡帶了許多蔓越莓。他吩咐普克金斯克維斯彎下腰，開始從她頭髮裡捉出那些可憎的蟲子，每捉出一隻，那蟲子便化作一隻可怕的豪豬或蟾蜍。接著那巫婆問道：「你找到一隻了嗎？」「找到了。」大師答道。「捏碎它！」她回答，於是格盧斯卡普捏碎了一顆蔓越莓；她聽到聲響，以為他照她的吩咐做了，以為他手指上的毒會滲透到他的性命之中。

passages.text: The girls came out greeting him with very pleasant glances, wooing softly and sweetly; they offered him a string of sausages... But these which the girls offered, as girls do, to show their love, by casting the string round the neck of the favored youth, were enchanted, and had they once put the necklace upon him he would have been overpowered. However, they knew not of this new magic which the Master had brought into the land, by which one can read the heart... When his dogs growled at them he cried, 'Cuss!' which means Stop! but which the dogs only knew as 'Hie, at them!' So they flew at the witches, and these flashed up like fire into their own dreadful forms of female fiends. Then there was a terrible tumult, for never before in the land of the Wabanaki had there been such a battle... Then he entered the wigwam where the old sorcerer sat, waiting for him as food. And the Master said, 'Are you hungry? Or do you love sausages? Here they are!' Instantly casting the links around his neck, he was taken, and Glooskap slew him with one blow.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 40-41; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 姑娘們出來迎接他，向他投以十分愉快的目光，柔聲而甜美地求愛；她們獻給他一串香腸……但姑娘們所獻的這些東西——正如姑娘們慣常所為，把那串東西繞在所中意青年的脖子上以示愛意——是被施了魔法的，一旦她們把這項鍊掛到他身上，他便會被制伏。然而，她們並不知道大師帶到這片土地上的這種新魔法，憑此可以看透人心……當他的狗對她們低吼時，他喊道：「庫斯！」意思是「停下！」但狗只把它聽作「上，咬他們！」於是牠們撲向那些女巫，女巫們便如火焰般騰起，現出她們自身那可怖的女性惡魔形態。接著便是一場可怕的騷亂，因為在瓦巴納基人的土地上，從未有過這樣的戰鬥……接著他走進那間棚屋，老巫師正坐在那裡，等著把他當食物。大師說：「你餓了嗎？還是你愛吃香腸？這裡有！」他立刻把那串香腸繞到老巫師的脖子上，老巫師便被制住了，格盧斯卡普一擊將他殺死。

title.en: Pook-jin-skwess and the Black Cats: The Birth of the Mosquito
title.zh: 罐婆與黑貓族：蚊蟲之誕生

region.en: Black Cat village and Bar Harbor, Maine coast
region.zh: 黑貓族村與緬因州的巴港

period: Passamaquoddy version told by Noel Josephs, recorded by Leland (1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How the Story of Glooskap and Pook-jin-skwess is told by the Passamaquoddy Indians'

summary.en: In a village of Black Cats, the chief Pogumk (Glooskap) feeds all the people; the witch Pitcher - a Black Cat, man or woman as she willed - strands him on an egg-gathering island and paddles home singing 'I shall be the chief of the Fishers now.' The Fox, hearing his magic song from beyond the mountains, swims him home with the warning to hold his tail in good faith; the chief, of little faith, opens an eye - and ten feet become ten miles against Pitcher's storm. Back in camp he has Sable burn the witch's babe; as she pursues like a starving wolf, he confronts her and magically pins her back against a tree, where the Black Cats mock her all night as she chops herself free. Fleeing to Bar Harbor she wishes to become something to torment all men - and becomes the mosquito.
summary.zh: 黑貓族村中，酋長波恭克（格魯斯卡普）養活全族；女巫罐婆——同族、可男可女——把他騙上採蛋的荒島，划舟而歸，且行且歌：「今後我便是漁者之酋。」狐聽見他遠山的魔法歌，泅水來渡；囑他閉眼抱尾、信之勿疑；酋長心存疑慮偷眼一開——十呎化作十里，逆著罐婆掀起的风暴。回村後他命貂弟焚巫婆之嬰；罐婆如餓狼追來，他迎面現身，以法術將她釘在樹上，黑貓族人徹夜譏笑她劈木自脫。她逃至巴港，咒願化為折磨眾人之物——便成了蚊子。

sensitivity.note: Passamaquoddy version (Leland 1884); public domain. The infanticide is villain-vs-villain story register.

passages.text: There was a village of Indians who were all Black Cats, or Po'gum'k. One of them, the cleverest and bravest, went forth every day with bow and arrow, tomahawk and knife, and killed moose and bear, and sent meat to the poor, and so he fed them all... Pook-jin-skwess, the Witch, was a Black Cat. She was a woman or a man as she willed to be; but in these days she was a man. And she, being evil, hated the chief, and thought long how she could kill or remove him, and take his place. Now, one day when all the camp had packed what they had, being about to travel, Pitcher asked the chief to go with him... down to the water-side to gather gulls' eggs. And then they went far out in a canoe... till they came to an island, and there they landed, and while Pogumk (who was Glooskap) sought for eggs, the false-hearted Pitcher stole away in the canoe, and as she paddled she sang a song: 'I have left the Black Cat on an island, I shall be the chief of the Fishers now!'
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 44-45; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 有一個印第安人的村落，村民全是黑貓，即波古姆克。其中有一人，最聰明也最勇敢，每天帶著弓和箭、戰斧和刀出去，獵殺駝鹿和熊，把肉送給窮人，就這樣養活了所有人……女巫普克金斯克維斯是一隻黑貓。她隨心所欲地或為女人或為男人；但在那些日子裡，她是男人。她心懷邪惡，憎恨首領，長久盤算著如何殺死他或除掉他，取而代之。有一天，整個營地的人都收拾好行裝，準備啟程，水罐便邀首領與他同行……下到水邊去拾海鷗蛋。於是他們乘獨木舟划向遠方……直到來到一座島，便在那裡上岸；正當波古姆克（即格盧斯卡普）尋找鳥蛋時，那心懷奸詐的水罐偷偷划著獨木舟離去，一邊划一邊唱道：「我把黑貓留在了一座島上，如今我將成為漁人的首領了！」

passages.text: Now on the thirtieth day the chief remembered his friend the Fox, who had m'teoulin, or magic power. And he sang a song, and the Fox heard it, although he was miles away, beyond forests and mountains. And thus knowing all, he went to the shore and swam to the island, where he found the chief... The Fox said, 'Close thine eyes and hold fast to my tail as tightly as thou canst, and be of good faith, oh, my elder brother, and we shall soon gain the shore.' Saying this, he swam away and his friend followed. And it went well with them, but the chief grew weary, and he opened one eye a little, and saw that they were not ten feet from the shore. And being of little faith he thought, 'We shall never get to land.' But the Fox replied, 'Do not believe it.' But the journey lasted long, for what seemed to Pogumk to be ten feet was ten miles, and the wind was high and the waters were wild, for Pitcher had called forth a storm. So they swam all day and all the evening before they landed.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 46-47; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 到了第三十天，首領想起了他的朋友狐狸，狐狸擁有姆特烏林，即魔法之力。於是他唱起一首歌，狐狸聽到了，儘管他遠在數英里之外，隔著森林與群山。狐狸就此明白了一切，便走到岸邊，游向那座島，在那裡找到了首領……狐狸說：「閉上眼睛，盡可能緊緊抓住我的尾巴，要心懷信念，哦，我的兄長，我們很快就能到達岸邊。」說完，他便游了出去，他的朋友跟在後面。他們一路順利，但首領漸漸疲倦，便微微睜開一隻眼，看見他們離岸不到十英尺。他信心不足，心想：「我們永遠到不了陸地了。」但狐狸回答：「別這麼想。」然而這趟旅程漫長得很，因為在波古姆克看來是十英尺的距離，其實是十英里，而且風大浪急，因為水罐喚起了一場風暴。於是他們游了一整天，又游了整整一晚，才終於上岸。

passages.text: And the chief bade Sable run to the camp. 'And when you are there, build up a great fire of hemlock bark, and take Pitcher's babe, even the babe which she loves, and which you tend, and throw it into the fire, and run to me as fast as you can... And as he commanded it was done; and when the fire was hot, Sable threw the babe into it, and it was burned to death. And Pitcher, being, as one may well believe, maddened at such a sight, pursued him as a starving wolf pursues a rabbit... And at that word Pogumk stepped forward and confronted her, and said, 'Truly, she need not run so far.' And seeing him and hearing this, fear came upon her; but she laughed aloud to hide it... Then, as his magic had come to him, he used his power, and put Pitcher with her back against a tree; and there she stayed, stuck to it, unable to get away. But the chief and Sable went to the camp. Now Pitcher had a hatchet and wedge, and with much ado she cut herself away, and the Black Cats heard her pounding and chopping all night long. And in the morning she came to them, and there was a great piece of wood sticking to her back, and they laughed her to scorn.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 47-48; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 首領吩咐賽博跑回營地。「你到了那裡，就用鐵杉樹皮燃起一堆大火，把皮徹的嬰孩，就是她所疼愛、由你照看的那個嬰孩，丟進火裡，然後盡快跑回我這裡來……於是照他所吩咐的做了；火燒旺了，賽博便把嬰孩丟進去，嬰孩就被燒死了。皮徹見了這般景象，想必是氣得發狂，像餓狼追兔子一般追趕他……這話一出，波古姆克便上前迎著她，說道：『說真的，她不必跑那麼遠。』她見了他、又聽了這話，心中便生出恐懼；卻大聲笑起來，以掩飾懼意……這時他的法力已臨到他身上，他便施展本領，把皮徹背靠一棵樹定住；她就待在那裡，黏在樹上，脫身不得。首領和賽博則回營地去了。皮徹有一把斧頭和一個楔子，費了好大的勁才把自己砍脫，黑貓們整夜都聽見她敲敲砍砍的聲音。到了早晨，她來到他們面前，背上還黏著一大塊木頭，他們便譏笑她，把她嘲笑了一番。

passages.text: Now Pitcher the Witch, being mad with shame and spite, fled from the face of man, and ran through the woods like a wild wolf. And so she came to Bar Harbor, and sat down on a log, and said, with her heart full of bitterness and malice, 'I would that I could become something which should torment all men.' And as she said this she became a mosquito (T'sis-o), and so it came to pass that mosquitoes were made. And to this day men see that wherever the Black Cat is, there too is the Sable not far away.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 49; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 皮徹這女巫又羞又恨，氣得發狂，便逃離人面，像野狼一般在林中奔竄。她就這樣來到巴港，坐在一根圓木上，滿心苦毒與惡意地說道：『但願我能變成什麼東西，去折磨所有的人。』她話音剛落，就變成了一隻蚊子（T'sis-o），蚊子便是這樣來的。直到今日，人們都看得出，黑貓所在之處，賽博也總在不遠處。

title.en: Glooskap and the Loons: His Faithful Messengers
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普與潛鳥：忠實的信使

region.en: Lakes of Newfoundland (Uktukamkw)
region.zh: 紐芬蘭（烏克圖坎庫）的湖泊

period: Micmac tradition recorded by Leland (1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How Glooskap became friendly to the Loons'

summary.en: Pursuing Win-pe, Glooskap sees from afar the Loons flying over water, circling the lake thrice as if seeking something; their chief would be his servant and friend. Glooskap teaches him a strange long cry like the howl of a dog, to be uttered when the loons need him; and in Newfoundland he comes to a town of Loons in human form who rejoice to see their lord, and he makes them his huntsmen and messengers. Whence to this day, when the Indians hear the cry of the Loon, they say, 'Kwemoo el-komik-too-ujul Gloocapcil' - He is calling upon Glooskap.
summary.zh: 追索溫佩途中，格魯斯卡普遠望潛鳥在水上盤旋三匝，似有所求；鵝首自願為其僕友。格魯斯卡普授牠一種如犬吠般的奇異長鳴，有需則呼。其後他在紐芬蘭來到一座全是化形潛鳥的城鎮，眾鳥歡迎其主；他便立牠們為自己的獵手與信使。故至今印第安人聞潛鳥長鳴，便說：「牠在呼喚格魯斯卡普。」

sensitivity.note: Micmac tradition (Leland 1884); public domain.

passages.text: When Glooskap was pursuing Win-pe, he one day on Uktukamkw saw from afar flying over water the Kwe-moo, or Loons. And thrice did their chief make the circle of the lake, coming near to the land of men and beasts every time, as if he would fain seek somewhat. Then Glooskap asking him what he wanted, Kwe-moo replied that he would be his servant and friend. So Glooskap taught him a strange long cry like the howl of a dog, and when the loons were in need of him or would pray to him they were to utter this cry.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 50; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 格盧斯卡普追趕溫佩時，有一天在烏克圖卡姆克遠遠望見水面上飛著奎穆，也就是潛鳥。他們的首領繞著湖飛了三圈，每一圈都靠近人與獸的陸地，彷彿很想尋求什麼。格盧斯卡普問他要什麼，奎穆回答說願做他的僕人和朋友。於是格盧斯卡普教他一種奇特的長鳴，像狗的嚎叫，此後潛鳥們若需要他或向他祈禱，便發出這叫聲。

passages.text: And it came to pass that when he was in Newfoundland he came to an Indian town, and they who dwelt therein were all Kwee-moo-uk, or Loons. And they, as men, were exceeding glad to see their lord, who had blessed them as birds, and did their best to please him. So he made them his huntsmen and messengers, and in all the tales of Glooskap the Kwee-moo ever appears as faithful to him. Whence to this day, when the Indians hear the cry of the Loon, they say, 'Kwemoo el-komik-too-ujul Gloocapcil' (He is calling upon Glooskap).
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 50-51; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 後來他在紐芬蘭時，來到一座印第安人的城鎮，住在其中的全是奎穆克，也就是潛鳥。他們既為人，見到自己的主便歡喜不盡，因為他曾賜福使他們成為鳥，於是盡力討他歡心。他便立他們為自己的獵人和使者，在所有關於格盧斯卡普的故事裡，奎穆總是顯得對他忠心耿耿。因此直到今日，印第安人聽見潛鳥的叫聲，便說：『Kwemoo el-komik-too-ujul Gloocapcil』（他在呼喚格盧斯卡普）。

title.en: Glooskap Makes a Great Man of His Uncle Mikchich the Turtle
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普使龜叔米基奇成為偉人

region.en: Piktook (Pictou), Nova Scotia, and its lake
region.zh: 新斯科舍的皮克托及其湖泊

period: Micmac and Passamaquoddy traditions compiled from six versions by Leland (1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How Glooskap made his Uncle Mikchich the Turtle into a Great Man'

summary.en: Poor, lazy, not very clever old Mikchich the Turtle bears all his wants with such good nature that Glooskap resolves to make of him a mighty man: with the magic belt he becomes young and comely, marries the loveliest daughter of the chief of Piktook, and is warned that the jealous young men will trample him at the ball game - jump the lodge twice, but the third time is terrible. Caught on the tent-poles in the smoke, he is smoked into his hard shell and made the sogmo, great chief of the Tortoises, able to roll through flame, live on land or water, and survive his own severed head for nine days. Thrown into a fire he sleeps and calls for more wood; begged-and-prayed not to be drowned, he fights them lustily - is thrown in the lake - and next noon is found basking on a rock, saying 'Good-by,' and rolling over plump into the water, where he is living to this day; and in memory of Glooskap's jest the Turtle layeth eggs even to this day.
summary.zh: 貧窮懶惰、其貌不揚的龜叔米基奇性情溫厚，格魯斯卡普決意使他成為偉人：繫上法帶他便年少俊美，娶得皮克托酋長最美的小女兒，又受警在球賽中會被妒忌的少年踐踏——跳屋兩次可脫，第三次必有凶險。他第三次果然被帳頂煙霧中的椽木掛住；主人以菸將他薰成堅殼，立他為龜族大酋長——可穿火而行、水陸兩棲、斷首九日不死。投之於火，他酣睡醒來討柴；眾人商議溺斃，他佯作驚恐苦苦哀求——被拋入湖中——次日正午卻見他曝於岩上，說聲「再見」，翻身撲通入水，至今仍在；為紀念此趣，龜自那日起產卵至今。

sensitivity.note: Leland 1884; public domain. Totem-origin story of the Tortoise, highest rank among the Algonquin clans.

passages.text: And this was not because this man, whose name in Micmac is Mikchich and in Passamaquoddy Chickwe-notchk, meaning the Turtle, was great, or well favored, or rich. For truly he was none of these, being very poor and lazy, no longer young, and not very clever or wise in any way. It is said that he was indeed Glooskap's uncle, but others think that this was by adoption. However, this old fellow bore all his wants with such good nature that the Master, taking him in great affection, resolved to make of him a mighty man... Glooskap, being a very handsome, stately man, with the manner of a great chief, was much admired, and that not a little by all the women, so that every one wished to have him in the house. Yet he gave them all the go-by, and dwelt with his old uncle, in whose quaint ways and old-time stories he took great delight.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 52-53; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 這並不是因為這人——他在米克馬克語中名叫米克奇奇，在帕薩馬科迪語中名叫奇克韋諾奇克，意即烏龜——有什麼了不起，或相貌出眾，或富有。因為說實在的，他這些一樣也沒有，既十分貧窮又懶惰，已不年輕，也並不怎麼聰明或有智慧。據說他其實是格盧斯卡普的叔父，但也有人認為那是收養的關係。然而這老頭兒安於自己的一切匱乏，性情如此和善，大師便十分疼愛他，決意要使他成為一個了不起的人……格盧斯卡普是個十分英俊、氣度不凡的人，舉止有如偉大的首領，深受眾人仰慕，尤其為所有婦女所傾慕，人人都想把他留在家中。然而他對她們一概不理，只與他的老叔父同住，對他那古怪的作風和古老的故事甚為喜愛。

passages.text: 'Truly, if that be all, uncle,' replied Glooskap, 'I trow I can turn tailor and fit you to a turn... for to him who knows how, 't is as easy to make a man over as a suit of clothes.' 'Yes; but, nephew,' said Mikchich, 'how say you as to making over the inside of a mortal?' 'By the great Beaver!' answered the Master, 'that is something harder to do, else I were not so long at work in this world. But before I leave this town I shall do that also for you; and as for this present sport, do but put on my belt.' And when he had done that, Mikchich became so young and handsome that no man or woman ever saw the like... So Mikchich went to the feast. Now the chief of Piktook had three beautiful daughters, and the youngest was the loveliest in the land. And on her he cast his eyes, and returning said, 'I have seen one whom I want.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 53-54; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 「說真的，叔父，若只是這樣，」格盧斯卡普答道，「我想我能當個裁縫，把你裁得恰到好處……因為對懂得門道的人來說，重造一個人就像重做一套衣服一樣容易。」「是啊；可是，姪兒，」米克奇奇說，「你說把一個凡人的內裡也重造一番，又當如何？」「憑大狸！」大師答道，「那可就難辦些了，不然我也不會在這世上忙這麼久了。但在我離開這座城鎮之前，我也要為你把那件事辦成；至於眼前這場玩樂，你只管把我的腰帶繫上。」他繫上之後，米克奇奇就變得又年輕又英俊，無論男女都從未見過這般模樣……於是米克奇奇赴宴去了。皮克圖克的首領有三個美麗的女兒，最小的那個是全國最可愛的。他看中了她，回來便說：『我見到了一個我想要的人。』

passages.text: All this happened as he foretold; for the young men indeed tried to take his life, and to escape them Mikchich jumped over the lodge, so that he seemed like a bird flying. But the third time he did this he was caught on the top of the tent-poles, and hung there dangling in the smoke which rose from below. Then Glooskap, who was seated in the tent, said, 'Uncle, I will now make you the sogmo, or great chief of the Tortoises, and you shall bear up a great nation.' Then he smoked Mikchich so long that his skin became a hard shell, and the marks of the smoke may be seen thereon to this day... And he cried aloud, 'Miloohs! My nephew, you will kill me!' But the nephew replied, 'Not so. I am giving you great life. From this time you may roll through a flame and never feel it, and live on land or in the water. And though your head be cut off, it will live for nine days, and your heart, even, shall beat as long when taken from your body.' So Mikchich rejoiced greatly.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 55-56; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 這一切都如他所預言的那樣發生了；因為那些年輕人確實想要取他性命，米克奇奇為了逃開他們，便躍過小屋，看起來就像一隻飛鳥。但當他第三次這麼做時，卻被帳篷的柱子頂端掛住了，就那樣懸在那裡，晃蕩在從下方升起的煙霧之中。這時，坐在帳篷裡的格盧斯卡普說道：「叔父，我現在要立你為索格莫，也就是龜族的大酋長，你將要承載一個偉大的民族。」於是，他抽著米克奇奇抽了很久，久到他的皮膚變成了一層堅硬的殼，而那煙熏的痕跡至今仍可在其上見到……他大聲喊道：「米盧斯！我的姪兒，你會殺了我的！」但那姪兒回答說：「不會的。我是在賜給你偉大的生命。從今以後，你可以滾過火焰而毫不覺得灼熱，並且無論在陸上或水中都能存活。即使你的頭被砍下，它也會活上九天，甚至你的心，從身體裡取出之後，也同樣會跳動那麼久。」於是米克奇奇大大地歡喜。

passages.text: And they seized him and threw him into a great fire, but he turned over and went to sleep in it, being very lazy; and when the fire had burnt out he awoke, and called for more wood, because it was a cold night. Then they seized him yet again, and spoke of drowning. But, hearing this, he, as if he were in mortal dread, begged them not to do this thing. And he said they might cut him to pieces, or burn him, as they would, but not to throw him into the water. Therefore they resolved to do so, and dragged him on. Then he screamed horribly and fought lustily, and tore up trees and roots and rocks like a madman; but they took him into a canoe and paddled out into the middle of the lake, and, throwing him in, watched him sink as he vanished far down below. So they thought him dead, and returned rejoicing. Now the next day at noon there was a hot sunshine, and something was seen basking on a great rock, about a mile out in the lake... And when they came to the edge of the rock... there lay Mikchich sunning himself; but seeing them coming to take him, he only said, 'Good-by,' and rolled over plump into the water, where he is living to this day. In memory whereof all turtles, when they see any one coming, tip-tilt themselves over into the water at once.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 56-57; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 他們抓住他，把他扔進一堆大火裡，但他翻了個身，就在火裡睡著了，因為他非常懶惰；等火燒盡之後，他醒了過來，還要人添更多的柴，因為那是個寒冷的夜晚。於是他們又再次抓住他，說要把他淹死。但他聽見這話，便裝作極度恐懼的樣子，求他們千萬不要這麼做。他說他們可以隨意把他剁成碎片，或者燒了他，但就是不要把他扔進水裡。因此他們便決意這麼做，把他拖了過去。於是他發出可怕的尖叫，拼命地掙扎，像瘋子一樣把樹木、樹根和石頭都連根拔起；但他們把他帶上一艘獨木舟，划到湖中央，把他扔了進去，看著他沉下去，遠遠地消失在深處。於是他們以為他死了，便歡歡喜喜地回去了。到了第二天正午，陽光熾熱，有人看見有個東西在湖中約一英里外的一塊大岩石上曬太陽……當他們來到岩石邊上……米克奇奇就躺在那裡曬著太陽；但他看見他們過來要抓他，只說了聲「再見」，便撲通一聲翻滾進水裡，至今仍住在那裡。為了紀念這件事，所有的烏龜一看見有人過來，就會立刻翻身滾進水裡。

title.en: Glooskap Vanquishes a Sorcerer by Smoking Tobacco
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普以吸菸鬥敗巫師
