region.en: The Wabanaki land where tobacco was once raised
region.zh: 曾種菸草的瓦巴納基之地

period: Told by John Gabriel, Passamaquoddy (Leland 1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'Of Turtles' Eggs, and how Glooskap vanquished a Sorcerer by smoking Tobacco'

summary.en: The great Glooskap was a right valiant smoker; in all the world was no man who loved a pipe of good tobacco so much as he. In those days the summers were longer, the sun was warmer, and the Indians raised tomawe (tobacco). An evil-minded magician, believing himself greatest in all things, sought to appall Glooskap by outdoing him at something at which he excelled - for a fish is frightened when another swims faster, but not till then. The sorcerer sat down to smoke with an exceeding long pipe with a great bowl, but that of Glooskap grew much greater; the sorcerer burnt his out at one pull and blew all the smoke from his nose at one puff. Glooskap, whose pipe held ten times as much tobacco, did the same, and blowing it out split the rocky ground, so that a great chasm opened before them. 'If you can do that you may kill me.' But he could not, and went back with shame to those who had sent him.
summary.zh: 偉大的格魯斯卡普是出了名的老菸槍，普天之下無人比他更愛一斗好菸。那時夏天更長、日頭更暖，印第安人種著菸草。一位自詡天下第一的惡巫想在他最擅長的事上壓倒他——魚只有在別人游得更快時才會驚惶。巫師以超長大斗菸對坐較量，格魯斯卡普的菸斗卻脹得更大；巫師一口吸盡、一鼻噴盡；格魯斯卡普的菸斗容得十倍之菸，如法炮製，噴氣之間竟劈裂岩地，一道深壑在他們面前裂開。「你能如此，便可以殺我。」巫師做不到，羞慚而返。

sensitivity.note: Leland 1884; public domain.

passages.text: The great Glooskap was a right valiant smoker; in all the world was no man who loved a pipe of good tobacco so much as he. In those days the summers were longer in the land of the Wabanaki, the sun was warmer, and the Indians raised tomawe (tobacco), and solaced themselves mightily therewith. And there came to Glooskap a certain evil-minded magician, who sought to take his life, as the Master very well knew, for he read the hearts of men as if they had been strings of wampum. And this m'teoulin, believing himself to be greatest in all things, thought to appall Glooskap by outdoing him at first in something at which he excelled; for a fish is frightened when another swims faster, but not till then.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 58-59; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 偉大的格盧斯卡普是個十足的煙癮君子；普天之下再沒有誰比他更愛抽一斗好菸草了。在那個年代，瓦巴納基人的土地上夏天更長，陽光更暖，印第安人種植托馬威（菸草），並以此大大地慰藉自己。有一個心懷惡意的巫師來到格盧斯卡普面前，想要取他性命，而這位大師對此一清二楚，因為他看透人心，就像看一串串貝珠帶一樣。這個巫師自以為在一切事上都最為高明，便想先在格盧斯卡普擅長的事情上勝過他，以此來嚇倒他；因為一條魚只有在另一條魚游得更快時才會害怕，在那之前是不會怕的。

passages.text: And the man sat down to smoke with an exceeding long pipe with a great bowl, but that of Glooskap grew to be much greater. Then, having filled his pipe, the sorcerer exhausted and burnt it out at one pull, and then blew all the smoke out of his nose at one puff. So he sat and looked at the Master. But Glooskap, whose pipe held ten times as much tobacco, did the same, and blowing it out split the rocky ground, so that a great chasm opened before them. Then they were silent awhile, till the Master said, 'If you can do that you may kill me.' But he could not, and so went back with shame to those who had sent him.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 59; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 那人坐下來抽菸，用的是一根極長的菸斗，斗缽很大，但格盧斯卡普的菸斗卻長得更大。接著，那巫師裝滿他的菸斗，一口氣就把它抽盡燒光，然後一下子把所有的煙從鼻子裡噴了出來。於是他坐在那裡看著大師。但格盧斯卡普的菸斗裝的菸草有十倍那麼多，他也照樣做了，並且把煙噴出來時竟把岩石地面都震裂了，以致在他們面前裂開了一道巨大的深淵。於是他們沉默了一會兒，直到大師說：「你要是能做到那個，或許就能殺了我。」但他做不到，於是便羞愧地回到派他來的人那裡去了。

title.en: Glooskap Sails Through the Great Cavern of Darkness
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普舟渡黑暗巨洞

region.en: Mighty river that runs beneath the earth into the night
region.zh: 奔流地底、貫入黑夜的大河

period: Micmac tradition recorded by Leland (1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How Glooskap sailed through the Great Cavern of Darkness'

summary.en: Seven neighbors of Glooskap, so many different animals, steal away his family, and he follows them to Newfoundland. Finding Marten alone he arms the boy with his belt, and the Crow spreads the news that Marten is drying meat - so a great fear falls on the town and all await death; but the Master, laughing, forgives them and gives venison, then leaves them. In a canoe with Marten and Dame Bear he sails down a mighty river: great cliffs gather round and close over them, and the river runs underground, deeper and deeper, dashing into rapids and cataracts so horrible that death seems to come and go with every plunge; Marten and the woman die of fear, but the Master sits with silent soul singing the songs of magic, passes into the night, and comes forth again into sunlight, where 'Numchahse! arise!' restores them, and Glooskap has gained the greatest power.
summary.zh: 格魯斯卡普的七位鄰居——皆為異獸——擄走其家人，他一路追至紐芬蘭。他為孤留的貂弟繫上法帶；烏鴉傳播貂弟曬肉的消息，全城大恐以待死；主人卻大笑赦免，並賜鹿肉，隨後離去。他與貂弟、熊嫗乘舟順巨流而下：絕壁合攏罩頂，大河潛入地底，愈行愈深，撞入灘石與駭人的懸瀑，每一下傾跌都似死生之交；貂弟與嫗驚懼而斃，主人卻靜坐吟唱魔法之歌，穿過長夜重見天光，一聲「起來！」喚醒二人——自此他獲得至高的力量。

sensitivity.note: Micmac tradition (Leland 1884); public domain. Leland compares the passage-underground to shamanic initiation and to the Norse river Ifing.

passages.text: Now it is told in another tradition - and men tell even this differently - that in these old times Glooskap's seven neighbors, who were all so many different animals, took away his family, and that he followed them, even as it has been written, unto Newfoundland. And when he came there it was night, and, finding Marten alone, he took him forth into the forest to seek food, putting his belt on the boy, which gave him such power that he hunted well and got much meat. So it came to pass that the next morning Dame Kah-kah-gooch, the Crow, observed that Marten was drying meat on his wigwam. And this she spread abroad. But when the people learned that the child had done this, a great fear came upon them all, and they sat every man in his lodge and awaited death, for they knew that the Master had come.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 60; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 如今在另一個傳說裡記載著——而人們連這件事也說得各不相同——說在這遠古的時代，格盧斯卡普的七個鄰居，他們都是各種不同的動物，把他的家人帶走了，而他便追隨他們，正如所記載的那樣，一直追到紐芬蘭。當他到達那裡時，天色已晚，他發現只有馬滕一個人在，便帶他到森林裡去尋找食物，把腰帶繫在那男孩身上，這腰帶給了他如此大的力量，使他狩獵順利，獲得了許多肉。於是到了第二天早晨，烏鴉夫人卡卡古奇就注意到馬滕正在他的棚屋上晾曬肉。她便把這件事傳揚開來。但當人們得知這孩子做了這件事時，一種巨大的恐懼降臨到他們所有人身上，他們每個人都坐在自己的小屋裡等待死亡，因為他們知道大師已經來了。

passages.text: And he indeed came; but when he saw them all as frightened as rabbits before the wild-cat, he laughed aloud and forgave them, for he was noble and generous. And as they were hungry - for he had come in hard times - he gave them much venison, and sorrow departed from their wigwams. But as they had left him of old, he now left them. When they knew him not they left him to die; now that they knew him they feared lest they should perish without him. But he turned his steps towards other paths.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 61-62; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 而他確實來了；但當他看見他們全都像兔子見了野貓一樣驚恐時，他放聲大笑，並原諒了他們，因為他高貴而寬厚。又因為他們正飢腸轆轆——他是在艱難的時節來的——他便給了他們許多鹿肉，憂愁也就離開了他們的小屋。但正如他們從前離棄了他，如今他也離棄了他們。從前他們不認識他時，便任他死去；如今他們認識了他，卻又害怕自己會失去他而滅亡。但他卻轉過腳步，走向別的道路去了。

passages.text: Now having made a canoe, the Master, with Marten and Dame Bear, went upon a mighty river. As the story says, it was broad and beautiful at first, and so they sailed away down towards its mouth. Then they came to great cliffs, which gathered round and closed over them. But the river ran on beneath these, and ever on far underground, deeper and deeper in the earth, till it dashed headlong into rapids, among rocks and ravines, and under cataracts which were so horrible that death seemed to come and go with every plunge of the canoe. And the water grew narrower and the current more dreadful, and fear came upon Marten and the woman, so that they died. But the Master sat with silent soul, though he sang the songs of magic, and so passed into the night, but came forth again into sunlight. And there was a lonely wigwam on the bank, into which he bore Marten and the grandmother, and saying, 'Numchahse! arise!' lo, they arose, and deemed they had only slept. And now Glooskap had gained the greatest power.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 61-62; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 大師造好獨木舟後，便與貂及熊婆婆一同駛上一條大河。據故事所說，那河起初寬闊而秀美，於是他們順流而下，朝河口而去。不久，他們來到巨大的崖壁之前，那崖壁合攏過來，將他們籠罩其中。然而河水仍在崖下奔流，且一直流向極深的地底，愈下愈深，直至猛然衝入急流，穿行於岩石與峽谷之間，又從瀑布之下流過；那瀑布可怖至極，獨木舟每一下顛簸，彷彿死亡便來去一回。水勢漸窄，水流愈發可怖，恐懼臨到貂與那婦人身上，他們便死了。大師卻靜默著心靈端坐，雖唱著法術之歌，就這樣進入了黑夜，卻又再度出來，重見天光。岸上有一座孤零零的棚屋，他將貂與祖母抱了進去，說道：『Numchahse！起來！』看哪，他們便起來了，只覺得自己不過睡了一覺。至此，格盧斯卡普已獲得了最大的力量。

title.en: The Great Works of Glooskap: The Boar's Back, Beaver Dam, and Five Islands
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普的偉蹟：豬背道、河狸壩與五島

region.en: Minas Basin and Cape Blomidon, Nova Scotia
region.zh: 新斯科舍的米納斯盆地與布洛米頓角

period: Micmac, Passamaquoddy and Penobscot traditions (Leland 1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'Of the Great Works which Glooskap made in the Land'

summary.en: Over all the land of the Wabanaki there is no place which was not marked by the hand of the Master. The great causeway from Cwesowralegek to Parrsborough - Ou-wokun, the Causeway, or the Boar's Back - was cast up over bogs and streams for his weary companions. The monstrous Beavers of the old time had dammed from Cape Blomidon across the Annapolis valley; Glooskap cut the great dam, and the rush of many waters swung westward and lodged with a great split - Cape Split, Pleegim, the opening of a beaver dam - while the pond left behind is the Basin of Minas. To scare the Beaver he threw handfuls of earth east of Partridge Island, which became the Five Islands; and, the Beaver having gone over the Grand Falls, he hurled a rock a hundred and fifty miles after it, which remaineth there even to this day.
summary.zh: 瓦巴納基全境無一處不見主人之手跡。自哈德伍德角至帕斯伯勒的大道——印第安名「堤道」，白人稱「豬背」——是他為疲乏的同伴在沼澤溪流之上堆起的長崗。上古巨河狸自布洛米頓角築壩攔斷安納波利斯河谷；格魯斯卡普斬開巨壩，洪水西衝，壩端留下大裂口——即「普利吉姆」、河狸壩之開口，今之斯普利特角；餘水成湖，便是米納斯盆地。為驚走河狸，他把幾把土拋到鷓鴣島以東，化作五島；河狸經大瀑而逃，他擲出一百五十里外的飛石以嚇之——此石至今猶在。

sensitivity.note: Leland 1884; public domain. Place-myth cluster of the Bay of Fundy tides and landforms.

passages.text: Over all the Land of the Wabanaki there is no place which was not marked by the hand of the Master. And it is to be seen on hills and rivers and great roads, as well as mighty rocks, which were in their day living monsters. For there is a very wonderful highway from Cwesowralegek to Parrsborough, running parallel with the river now called Hebert, and this road is called by Indians Ou-wokun, the Causeway, but by white men, or the Iglesmani, the Boar's Back. For it is said that he meant to visit Partridge Island and Cape Blomidon, but they who were with him had got tired of the sea, and wished to cross over by land. And while they were resting and getting ready for their trip across, the Master, raising his magic power to a great deed to be spoken of forever, went away a little time, and cast up a great and beautiful level ridge, throwing it over bogs and streams; and on this they traveled, rejoicing, and, having reached the island, awaited him.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 62-63; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 在整個瓦巴納基人的土地上，沒有一處不留下大師手印的痕跡。山丘、河流、大道之上皆可見其遺跡，還有那些巨大的岩石，它們在當年本是活生生的怪物。因為從克韋索瓦拉格克到帕斯伯勒有一條極其奇妙的大道，與如今稱為赫伯特河的那條河平行，這條路印第安人稱之為「烏沃昆」，意即堤道，而白人，或稱伊格萊斯馬尼人，則稱之為「野豬背」。據說他本打算去訪帕特里奇島與布洛米登角，但隨他同行的人已厭倦了海路，想要由陸路過去。正當他們歇息、準備渡陸之行時，大師施展法力，成就一樁必將永世傳頌的偉業；他離開片刻，築起一道又大又美的平坦山脊，橫跨沼澤與溪流；眾人便在上面歡歡喜喜地行走，到了那島上，等候著他。

passages.text: And yet again the Master did a mighty deed. It came to pass in those days that the Beavers had built a dam across from Utkoguncheek, or Cape Blomidon, to the opposite shore, and thereby made a pond that filled all the valley of Annapolis. Now in those times the Beavers were monstrous beasts, and the Master, though kind of heart, seems to have had but little love for them ever since the day when Qwah-beetsis, the son of the Great Beaver, tempted Malsum to slay his brother. Now the bones of these Beavers may be found to this day, and many there are on Oonamahgik, and their teeth are six inches across, and there are no such quah-beet to-day. And these are the remains of the Beavers who built the dam at Cape Blomidon and forded the Annapolis Valley.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 63-64; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 大師又成就了一樁偉業。話說那些日子裡，河狸們從烏特科貢奇克，即布洛米登角，築起一道堤壩，直通對岸，因而造出一個池塘，淹沒了整個安納波利斯谷地。那時河狸乃是龐然巨獸，而大師雖心地仁厚，自從大河狸之子夸比齊斯引誘馬爾蘇姆殺害其兄的那一天起，似乎對牠們便少有喜愛。如今這些河狸的骨骸至今仍可尋見，烏納馬希吉克島上便有許多，牠們的牙齒寬達六英寸，今日已沒有這樣的夸比了。這些便是當年在布洛米登角築壩、並在安納波利斯谷地涉水而行的河狸所留下的遺骸。

passages.text: Now Glooskap would have a hunt and do a deed which should equal the great whale-fishing of Kitpooseaginow. So he cut the great dam near the shore, and bade Marten watch; for he said, 'I mistrust that there is a little Beaver hiding hereabouts.' And when the dam was cut from where it joined the shore there was a mighty rush of many waters, so that it swung round to the westward, yet it did not break away from the other shore. Therefore the end of it lodged with a great split therein when the flood had found a free course, and the whole may be seen there still... and this point, or Cape Split, is called by the Micmacs Pleegim, which, being interpreted, means the opening of a beaver dam. Then, to frighten the Beaver, Glooskap threw at it a few handfuls of earth, and these, falling somewhat to the eastward of Partridge Island, became the Five Islands. And the pond which was left was the Basin of Minas.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 64; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 格盧斯卡普想要打一場獵，成就一樁足以媲美基特普塞阿吉諾捕巨鯨的偉業。於是他掘開近岸處那道大堤，命貂看守；因為他說：『我疑心這附近藏著一隻小河狸。』當堤壩從與岸相連處被掘開，眾水便洶湧奔騰，以致堤身向西擺去，卻並未與對岸斷開。因此堤的末端擱在那裡，其上裂開一道大口，洪水便尋得了自由的水道，那堤至今仍可看見……而這個岬角，即斯普利特角，米克馬克人稱之為普利吉姆，意譯過來，便是河狸堤的開口。接著，為嚇唬那河狸，格盧斯卡普朝牠擲去幾把泥土，這些泥土落在帕特里奇島稍東之處，便成了五島。而留下的那個池塘，便是米納斯灣。

passages.text: And yet another tradition tells that, after cutting the dam, Glooskap sat and watched, but no beaver came out; for Qwah-beet had gone out of a back door. So he took a rock and threw it afar - one hundred and fifty miles - to scare the Beaver back again; but the Beaver had gone over the Grand Falls, and the stone remaineth there even to this day.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 65; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 又有一則傳說說，掘開堤壩之後，格盧斯卡普坐著守望，卻沒有河狸出來；因為夸比已從後門逃走了。於是他取來一塊石頭，遠遠擲去——擲了一百五十英里——要把那河狸嚇回來；但那河狸已越過大瀑布而去，那石頭至今仍留在那裡。

title.en: Glooskap Leaves the World: The Beasts Lose One Tongue
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普離世：群獸失其同語

region.en: Great Lake Minas, where the feast was held before his departure
region.zh: 他辭世前設宴的米納斯大湖

period: Micmac tradition recorded by Leland (1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How Glooskap, leaving the World, all the Animals mourned for him'

summary.en: Glooskap had freed the world from the mighty monsters of an early time - giants, the cullo, the dreadful Chenoo of the North - and taught men the arts which made them happier; but they were not grateful, and though they worshiped him they were not the less wicked. When the ways of men and beasts waxed evil they greatly vexed Glooskap, and he made a rich feast by the shore of the great Lake Minas; when the feast was over he got into a great canoe, and the beasts looked after him till they saw him no more, still hearing his voice as he sang, fainter and fainter - and then deep silence fell, and the beasts, who had till now spoken but one language, were no longer able to understand each other, and fled each his own way. Until the day when Glooskap shall return to restore the Golden Age all Nature mourns: the Great Snowy Owl repeats to the night 'Koo-koo-skoos!' - Oh, I am sorry! - and the Loons go restlessly up and down through the world seeking vainly for their master.
summary.zh: 格魯斯卡普已為世間清除上古的巨怪——巨人、庫洛巨鳥、北方可怖的食人鬼——並教人技藝使其安樂；然人心不感其恩，雖崇拜他卻依然作惡。當人獸之行日益敗壞，主人再也忍受不住，便在米納斯大湖畔設下盛宴。宴罷他登上巨舟，群獸目送他直至不見；歌聲漸遠漸微，終歸死寂——而一直同語的群獸從此再聽不懂彼此，各自四散奔逃。直到格魯斯卡普歸來、重開黃金時代的之日，萬物皆哀：大雪鴞入林夜啼「庫庫斯庫斯！」——唉，我難過！——而忠於他的潛鳥們在世上往復徘徊，尋主不獲，悲鳴不已。

sensitivity.note: Micmac tradition (Leland 1884); public domain. A Babel-style ending and a millennial return prophecy.

passages.text: Now Glooskap had freed the world from all the mighty monsters of an early time: the giants wandered no longer in the wilderness; the cullo terrified man no more, as it spread its wings like the cloud between him and the sun; the dreadful Chenoo of the North devoured him not; no evil beasts, devils, and serpents were to be found near his home. And the Master had, moreover, taught men the arts which made them happier; but they were not grateful to him, and though they worshiped him they were not the less wicked.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 66-67; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 至此，格盧斯卡普已使世界擺脫了遠古時代一切強大的怪物：巨人不再在荒野中遊蕩；庫洛不再驚嚇人，牠展翅如雲，橫在人與太陽之間；北方可怕的切努不再吞噬人；人的家園附近再也找不到邪惡的野獸、魔鬼與毒蛇。大師還教會了人們種種使他們更為幸福的技藝；然而他們並不感激他，雖敬拜他，卻並不因此少些邪惡。

passages.text: 'Now when the ways of men and beasts waxed evil they greatly vexed Glooskap, and at length he could no longer endure them, and he made a rich feast by the shore of the great Lake Minas. All the beasts came to it, and when the feast was over he got into a great canoe, and the beasts looked after him till they saw him no more. And after they ceased to see him, they still heard his voice as he sang; but the sounds grew fainter and fainter in the distance, and at last they wholly died away; and then deep silence fell on them all, and a great marvel came to pass, and the beasts, who had till now spoken but one language, were no longer able to understand each other, and they fled away, each his own way, and never again have they met together in council. Until the day when Glooskap shall return to restore the Golden Age, and make men and animals dwell once more together in amity and peace, all Nature mourns.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 67-68; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 「後來，人與獸的行徑日益敗壞，他們大大地煩擾了格魯斯卡普，他終於再也無法忍受，便在大湖米納斯畔設下豐盛的筵席。眾獸皆來赴宴，筵席既畢，他登上一艘大獨木舟，眾獸目送他遠去，直到再也看不見他。而在再也看不見他之後，他們仍聽見他歌唱的聲音；但那聲音在遠處越來越微弱，最後終於完全消逝；於是深沉的寂靜降臨在他們眾人身上，一樁極大的奇事發生了，那些直到此時只說一種語言的眾獸，再也無法彼此聽懂，於是他們各自逃散，各走各的路，此後再也不曾一同聚會商議。直到格魯斯卡普歸來、恢復黃金時代，使人和動物再度和睦平安地同住的那一日，整個自然都在哀悼。」

passages.text: And tradition says that on his departure from Acadia the Great Snowy Owl retired to the deep forests, to return no more until he could come to welcome Glooskap; and in those sylvan depths the owls even yet repeat to the night 'Koo-koo-skoos!' which is to say in the Indian tongue, 'Oh, I am sorry! Oh, I am sorry!' And the Loons, who had been the huntsmen of Glooskap, go restlessly up and down through the world, seeking vainly for their master, whom they cannot find, and wailing sadly because they find him not. But ere the Master went away from life... he bade it be made known by the Loons, his faithful messengers, that before his departure years would pass, and that whoever would seek him might have one wish granted, whatever that wish might be.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 68-69; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 而傳說有言，他離開阿卡迪亞之時，那隻大白鴞退隱到幽深的森林裡，不再復返，直到他能前來迎接格魯斯卡普為止；而在那些林間深處，貓頭鷹至今仍對著夜色反覆鳴叫『咕—咕—斯庫斯！』，這在印第安語中便是說：『哦，我好難過！哦，我好難過！』而那些曾為格魯斯卡普獵手的潛鳥，則不安地走遍世界，徒然地尋找他們的主人，卻尋他不著，並因尋他不見而悲傷哀鳴。但在主人離世之前……他吩咐由潛鳥——他忠實的使者——傳告：在他離去之前，歲月將會流逝，而凡願意來尋他的人，都可以得到一個願望的實現，無論那願望是什麼。

title.en: The Three Seekers: The Magic Pipe, the Bag of Women, and the Root
title.zh: 三位求願者：魔法笛、女人之袋與奇根

region.en: The long road to Glooskap's dwelling, and Old Town, Maine
region.zh: 通往格魯斯卡普居所的長路，與緬因老鎮

period: Told in the tent of John Gabriel, Passamaquoddy (Leland 1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'Of other Men who went to Glooskap for Gifts'

summary.en: When all men heard that Glooskap would grant a wish to any one who would come to him, three Indians - a Maliseet and two Penobscots - resolved to try, and were seven years on the road. The honest bad hunter receives the magic pipe that persuades every animal to follow its player; the second, whose heart is set on the love of many women, receives a tightly tied bag with the warning not to open it till home - he opens it in the woods, and hundreds of beautiful girls, wild with passion, swarm about him until, panting and crying for breath, he perishes; and the foolish merry fellow who wants the marvelous laughing-sound eats the magic root on the road - it answers perfectly, in the woods and among the people - until he grows weary of himself, goes into the woods and slays himself, and Bumole, the evil spirit of the night-air, bears him away to Lahmekqu, the dwelling place of darkness.
summary.zh: 傳聞格魯斯卡普許願於來訪者，三位印第安人（一米克馬利特、二佩諾布斯科特）踏上七年長路。誠實而拙於狩獵者得魔法笛——笛聲所至，百獸相隨；求「女人越多越好」者得一繫緊的袋子，囑其到家再開——他半路啟袋，數百黑眸長髮的美女如白鴿湧出，熱情擁吻，愈聚愈多，他喘息求饒不得，終被窒息而死；求「奇妙笑聲」的輕浮少年半路吞下魔法之根——聲響妙極，卻在獵鹿時不受控制地爆出，嚇走獵物；族人漸厭，他厭倦自己，入林自盡——夜氣之惡靈布穆勒自雲端降下，攜他往黑暗的居所。

sensitivity.note: Passamaquoddy tale (Leland 1884); public domain.

passages.text: When all men had heard that Glooskap would grant a wish to any one who would come to him, three Indians resolved to try this thing; and one was a Maliseet from St. John, and the other two were Penobscots from Old Town. And the path was long and the way was hard, and they suffered much, and they were seven years on it ere they came to him. But while they were yet three months' journey from his dwelling, they heard the barking of his dogs, and as they drew nearer, day by day, it was louder. And so, after great trials, they found the lord of men and beasts, and he made them welcome and entertained them. But, ere they went, he asked them what they wanted.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 69-70; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 當所有人都聽說格魯斯卡普會賜予任何前來尋他的人一個願望時，有三個印第安人決心一試此事；其中一個是來自聖約翰的馬利西特人，另外兩個是來自老鎮的佩諾布斯科特人。那路途漫長，道路艱難，他們受盡苦楚，走了七年才來到他面前。但當他們距他的居所尚有三个月路程時，他們便聽見他獵犬的吠聲，而隨著他們日復一日地靠近，那吠聲也越發響亮。於是，歷經重重艱難之後，他們找到了這人和獸的主宰，他歡迎他們，並款待了他們。但在他們離去之前，他問他們想要什麼。

passages.text: And the eldest, who was an honest, simple man, and of but little account among his people, because he was a bad hunter, asked that he might excel in the killing and catching of game. Then the Master gave him a flute, or the magic pipe, which pleases every ear, and has the power of persuading every animal to follow him who plays it. Now the second Indian, being asked what he would have, replied, The love of many women... At hearing this the Master seemed displeased, but, smiling anon, he gave him a bag which was tightly tied, and told him not to open it until he had reached his home. Now the third Indian was a gay and handsome but foolish young fellow, whose whole heart was set on making people laugh; and he said that it would please him most to be able to make a certain quaint and marvelous sound or noise... And to him Glooskap was also affable, sending Marten into the woods to seek a certain mystical and magic root, which when eaten would make the miracle the young man sought. But he warned him not to touch the root ere he got to his home, or it would be the worse for him.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 70-71; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 那最年長的，是個誠實純樸的人，因他是個拙劣的獵人，在族人中無足輕重，便求能精於獵殺與捕捉獵物。於是主人給了他一支笛子，或稱魔笛，它能取悅每一隻耳朵，並有力量使每一隻動物都跟隨吹奏它的人。那第二個印第安人被問及想要什麼時，回答說：許多女人的愛……主人聽了似乎不悅，但隨即微笑，給了他一個紮得緊緊的袋子，並囑咐他在到家之前不可打開。那第三個印第安人是個快活英俊卻愚蠢的年輕人，他滿心只想逗人發笑；他說最令他稱心的是能夠發出某種古怪而奇妙的聲音或聲響……格魯斯卡普對他也同樣和藹，派貂入林去尋找某種神秘而具魔力的根，吃了它便能成就這年輕人所求的奇蹟。但他警告他，在到家之前不可碰那根，否則他就要遭殃了。

passages.text: It had taken seven years to come, but seven days were all that was required to tread the path returning to their home, that is, for him who got there. Only one of all the three beheld his lodge again... But he who loved women, and had never won even a wife, was filled with anxious wishfulness. And he had not gone very far into the woods before he opened the bag. And there flew out by hundreds, like white doves, swarming all about him, beautiful girls, with black burning eyes and flowing hair. And wild with passion the winsome witches threw their arms about him, and kissed him as he responded to their embraces; but they came ever more and more, wilder and more passionate. And he bade them give way, but they would not, and he sought to escape, but he could not; and so panting, crying for breath, smothered, he perished. And those who came that way found him dead, but what became of the girls no man knows.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 71-72; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 來時花了七年，但走回他們家鄉的路，只需七天便可走完，也就是說，對於那個真正到達的人而言。三人之中只有一人重見了自己的小屋……但那愛戀女人、卻連一個妻子也未曾娶得的人，心中充滿了焦切的渴望。他還沒走進林中多遠，便打開了袋子。於是成百上千地飛出，像白鴿一般，成群地繞著他飛舞，那是美麗的姑娘，有著烏黑灼亮的眼睛和飄逸的長髮。那些迷人的女巫狂熱地摟住他，在他回應她們的擁抱時親吻他；但她們來得越來越多，越來越狂野，越來越熱烈。他命她們退開，她們卻不肯，他想逃，卻逃不掉；於是氣喘吁吁、呼喊著要呼吸、被悶得窒息，他就這樣死了。那些經過那條路的人發現他死了，但那些姑娘去了何處，無人知曉。

passages.text: Now the third went merrily onward alone, when all at once it flashed upon his mind that Glooskap had given him a present, and without the least heed to the injunction... drew out the root and ate it; and scarce had he done this ere he realized that he possessed the power of uttering the weird and mystic sound to absolute perfection. And as it rang o'er many a hill and dale... he felt that it was indeed wonderful. So he walked on gayly, trumpeting as he went, over hill and vale, happy as a bird. But by and by he began to weary of himself. Seeing a deer he drew an arrow and stealing silently to the game was just about to shoot, when despite himself the wild, unearthly sound broke forth like a demon's warble. The deer bounded away, and the young man cursed! And when he reached Old Town, half dead with hunger, he was worth little to make laughter, though the honest Indians at first did not fail to do so... But as the days went on they wearied of him, and, life becoming a burden, he went into the woods and slew himself. And the evil spirit of the night-air, even Bumole, or Pamola, from whom came the gift, swooped down from the clouds and bore him away to Lahmekqu, the dwelling place of darkness, and he was no more heard of among men.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 71-72; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 那第三個人獨自快活地繼續前行，忽然他心中一閃，想起格魯斯卡普給了他一件禮物，於是全然不顧那告誡……掏出那根吃了下去；他剛一吃下，便發覺自己已能將那怪異而神秘的聲音發揮得淋漓盡致。當那聲音響遍許多山丘與溪谷……他覺得那真是奇妙極了。於是他快活地走著，一路吹奏著，越過山丘與溪谷，像鳥兒一樣快樂。但漸漸地，他開始厭倦了自己。他看見一頭鹿，便搭上箭，悄悄潛近獵物，正要放箭，那狂野、非人間的聲音卻不由自主地迸發出來，像惡魔的囀鳴。鹿跳開逃走了，那年輕人咒罵起來！當他抵達老鎮時，已餓得半死，實在沒什麼逗人發笑的價值了，儘管那些誠實的印第安人起初倒也不免笑了一場……但日子一久，他們便厭倦了他，生活成了負擔，他便走進林中自盡了。而那夜氣的惡靈，正是布莫勒，或稱帕莫拉，這份天賦便是從他那裡來的，他從雲端俯衝而下，把他帶到拉赫梅克庫——那黑暗的居所，此後人們便再也沒聽聞過他。

title.en: The Crow's Humiliation
title.zh: 鴉之屈辱

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II: Dierstories (1920), No. 26

summary.en: The Crow finds a sick springbok he cannot kill; he begs help from vulture, lion, wolf, jackal and baboon in turn, quarrelling with each under his boast 'My name is Hunter Straightshot' — until only the snake, bought with a mouse, can bite the buck; and lion, jackal and wolf eat everything while he screams 'It is my buck I shot!'
summary.zh: 鴉遇病羚而不能殺；求兀鷲、獅、狼、豺、狒狒——皆因自詡「吾名直射獵手」而起爭執——終以鼠換蛇噬羚；而獅豺狼食盡其獲，他唯呼「此吾所射之羚！」

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 26 (1920); not verbatim. The Crow felt hungry and saw a sick springbok lying under a bush; but he saw no chance to kill the sick animal, and tried to peck out its eyes — yet the springbok was not so sick, and butted the Crow away with its horns every time.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 26; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馮·維利希《第二部》第26號（1920年）之濃縮改述；非逐字照錄。烏鴉感到飢餓，看見一隻病弱的跳羚躺在灌木叢下；但牠找不到殺死這隻病獸的機會，便試圖啄出牠的眼睛——然而跳羚並沒有那麼病重，每次都用角把烏鴉頂開。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. He went for help, but quarrelled with the Vulture ('why are you so dirty?'), the Lion ('your eyes sit behind on the heels of your feet'), the Wolf ('you carry your eyes in your belly'), the Jackal ('you eat so much gum your eyelashes are glued together') and the Baboon, until he caught a mouse and bought the Snake's help with it; but the snake swallowed the mouse and lay still for a long time digesting.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 26; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改述，出處同上；非逐字照錄。牠前去求助，卻先後與禿鷲（「你怎麼這麼髒？」）、獅子（「你的眼睛長在腳後跟上」）、狼（「你把眼睛裝在肚子裡」）、胡狼（「你吃太多樹膠，睫毛都黏在一起了」）和狒狒爭吵起來，直到牠捉到一隻老鼠，用牠買通了蛇的幫助；但蛇吞下老鼠後，便躺著不動，消化了很久。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. By the time the Crow came back the buck was too weak to fight; he picked out the eyes and tongue while it still lived. The Lion smelled the blood and came and ate; the Jackal gnawed the sinews; the Wolf gnawed the bones; and each time the Crow screamed from the tree: 'Who is there? Let go: it is my springbok that I shot for myself!' The Lion answered: 'If you had not been so insolent with me, I would have left you something; but now nothing!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 26; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改述，出處同上；非逐字照錄。等烏鴉回來時，那隻羚羊已虛弱得無力抵抗；牠趁牠還活著時啄出了牠的眼睛和舌頭。獅子聞到血味趕來吃了；胡狼啃食筋腱；狼啃食骨頭；而每一次烏鴉都從樹上尖叫：「誰在那裡？放開：那是我為自己射到的跳羚！」獅子回答：「要不是你對我如此無禮，我本會留些東西給你；但現在什麼也沒有了！」

title.en: The Vultures: The Lover Who Became a Bird
title.zh: 兀鷲：化鳥之戀人

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 27

summary.en: A young Bushman madly in love changes into a vulture to fly over the mountains to his girl; that very night lions fall on her parents' huts and eat everyone but the three sisters sleeping in the walled-up rock cave. He opens it, changes all three into vultures, marries her — and the greedy cliff-vultures strip every kill his household makes, so they must fly away and live with the vultures who hunt together.
summary.zh: 少年戀人化兀鷲飛山赴其愛人；當夜獅群襲其父母之屋，食盡眾人，唯三姐妹於封石之穴得免。他啟穴，化三人皆為兀鷲，娶之——而貪婪之崖鷲食盡其獵獲，遂不得不飛離，與群獵之兀鷲同居。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 27 (1920); not verbatim. A young Bushman was madly in love with a young Bushman girl; but her father and his had constant quarrels, and her father moved away beyond the mountains. Every night the young man dreamed he could fly over the mountains to where the girl's parents lived, and woke with a sore heart; until one day he managed to change himself into a vulture, for he was one of the Bushmen of the old race.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 27; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馮·維利希《第二部》第27號（1920年）之濃縮改述；非逐字照錄。一個年輕的布須曼人瘋狂地愛上了一個年輕的布須曼姑娘；但她的父親和他的父親爭吵不斷，她的父親便搬到山那邊去了。每天晚上，年輕人都夢見自己能飛越群山，到姑娘父母居住的地方，醒來時心痛不已；直到有一天，他設法把自己變成了一隻禿鷲，因為他屬於古老種族的布須曼人。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. He flew over the mountains, found the place, and sat near her; when she raised a stone to throw he changed himself into a Bushman. He meant to change her into a vulture too, so that their parents could not know them; but that night lions attacked the huts and ate all that slept there — only the three girls in the little rock cave, which the parents walled up every night, survived.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 27; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改述，出處同上；非逐字照錄。他飛越群山，找到了那個地方，坐在她附近；當她舉起石頭要扔時，他變回了布須曼人。他打算把她也變成禿鷲，好讓雙方的父母認不出他們；但那天夜裡獅子襲擊了茅屋，吃掉了所有睡在那裡的人——只有岩洞裡的三個姑娘倖存，因為父母每晚都用石頭把洞口封起來。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. In the morning he flew over the huts, saw what had happened, opened the rock-house for the three sisters, changed them into vultures — for they also belonged to the old race — took the girl for his wife, and they flew to the mountains to live with the other cliff-vultures, who were also Bushmen of the old race. But the other cliff-vultures grew lazy and ate up every kill; so at last the man and his wife flew away to live with vultures who seek food together.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 27; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改述，出處同上；非逐字照錄。早晨他飛過茅屋，看見了發生的事，為三姐妹打開了岩屋，把她們變成禿鷲——因為她們也屬於古老種族——娶了那個姑娘為妻，然後他們飛往群山，與其他崖上的禿鷲同住，那些禿鷲也是古老種族的布須曼人。但其他崖上的禿鷲變得懶惰，把每一次獵物都吃光；所以最後那男人和妻子飛走了，去與一同覓食的禿鷲同住。

title.en: Aardvark, Warthog and Zebra
title.zh: 土豚、疣豬與斑馬

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 28

summary.en: The toothless, day-shy aardvark marries a warthog woman and orders her to empty her kaross of its back-skin for his ants' eggs; she refuses thrice, he tears the skin half off her back, and the zebra beats him off. Since then warthogs and zebras graze together, the aardvark wanders solitary by night, and no bush-pig girl will have him.
summary.zh: 無齒畏晝之土豚娶疣豬女，命她脫背皮以盛蟻卵；三拒之，他撕其背皮半幅，斑馬擊退之。自兹疣豬與斑馬同牧；土豚夜行孤獨，林豬之女無一肯嫁。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; contains domestic violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 28 (1920); not verbatim. Aardvark took a wife from the warthogs. He has no front teeth and is ashamed, fearing the others will mock him; so he seeks his food by night. His wife, Warthog, seeks hers by day and at first would not marry him: 'I work in the day, but by night I want to sleep.' He answered: 'In the day I will not walk about, for they laugh at my big ears and mock me because I have no teeth; but come with me, and I shall teach you to see well by night, for we both belong to the old race.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 28; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馮·維利希（von Wielligh）第二部第28則（1920年）之濃縮改述；非逐字照錄。土豚從疣豬那裡娶了一個妻子。他沒有門牙，為此感到羞愧，害怕其他動物會嘲笑他；因此他只在夜間覓食。他的妻子疣豬則在白天覓食，起初她不願嫁給他：「我白天勞作，但到了夜裡我想睡覺。」他回答說：「白天我不會四處走動，因為他們嘲笑我的大耳朵，又因我沒有牙齒而譏笑我；但跟我來吧，我會教你在夜裡看得清楚，因為我們都屬於古老的一族。」

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. When his knapsack was full of Bushman-rice he ordered her to bring her back-kaross to pour the rice on; three times she refused — 'we warthogs never walk without our back-skin kaross; bury the rice in the ground.' Then Aardvark flew at her and tore the skin half off her back with his great claws, and her entrails came out; she wept, and the zebra fought, kicked and drove him away. Her mother fetched her home sick.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 28; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改述，出處同上；非逐字照錄。當他的背袋裝滿了布須曼米時，他命令她把她背上的斗篷拿來，好把米倒上去；她三次拒絕——「我們疣豬從不離開背上的皮斗篷行走；把米埋進地裡吧。」於是土豚撲向她，用他的大爪子把她背上的皮撕掉了一半，她的內臟也流了出來；她哭了，斑馬則與他搏鬥、踢打，把他趕走。她的母親把她病著接回了家。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. From then on the warthogs and the zebras graze together. Aardvark repented his attack on his wife, wandered about helpless, and tried to take a bush-pig girl for a wife; but because they can see well by night and know what he did, they would not have him and all mocked him, so that the aardvark wanders to this day as a solitary wanderer by night, still gathering Bushman-rice — but they took his knapsack away, and now he must eat everything he digs up.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 28; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改述，出處同上；非逐字照錄。從那時起，疣豬和斑馬便一同吃草。土豚悔恨自己對妻子的攻擊，無助地四處遊蕩，並試圖娶一頭叢林豬姑娘為妻；但因為她們在夜裡看得清楚，也知道他做了什麼，她們不願接納他，全都嘲笑他，所以土豚至今仍作為夜間孤獨的遊蕩者四處漂泊，仍在採集布須曼米——但他們拿走了他的背袋，如今他挖到什麼就得吃什麼。

title.en: Hare, Tingtinkie and Owl
title.zh: 野兔、亭亭雀與梟

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 29

summary.en: The lazy dancing Hare teases the little Tingtinkie all night, shaking his nest until the bird bolts in the dark; then he confesses it was the Owl all along. The birds torment the Owl by day — though the truth is that Hare was the boy who strove with the Moon; Tingtinkie stayed child-size from eating forbidden fruit; and the Owl was a sorcerer whose power was broken, but who still knows what will happen within a month.
summary.zh: 懶舞之兔徹夜捉弄亭亭雀，搖其巢令其黑暗中亂撞；後自認乃梟所為。眾鳥晝擾梟——其實兔即昔日與月相爭之少年；亭亭雀因食禁果而不長；梟本巫者，法力被奪，然仍知一月內將發生之事。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 29 (1920); not verbatim. Hare was always a fellow who looked out for showing off; of hunting he never was fond, but dancing was his vocation: he rattled about the whole night, and by day, when one must hunt, he slept his body out... Because he was too lazy to fetch water, the dew and the sap of juicy plants were enough to quench his thirst.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 29; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馮·維利希第二部第29則（1920年）之濃縮改述；非逐字照錄。野兔向來是個愛賣弄的傢伙；他從不喜愛打獵，但跳舞才是他的天職：他整夜嘩啦作響，到了白天，該打獵的時候，他卻睡個夠……因為他太懶，不肯去取水，露水和多汁植物的汁液就足以解他的渴。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. That Hare now lives so withdrawn he himself is to blame; for earlier he was the swaggering fellow who dared to strive with the Moon and to contradict her that all would come alive again after they had died a while; for this they hated him, and even his wife and children do not live with him. Tingtinkie was in his childhood disobedient and ate of the veld-fruits his parents had forbidden; the poison in those fruits made that he grew no more, so he kept the size of a child, however old he became.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 29; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改述，出處同上；非逐字照錄。野兔如今過得如此孤僻，是他自己的過錯；因為早先他是那個狂妄的傢伙，竟敢與月亮爭辯，反駁她說眾生死後過些時日都會重新活過來；為此他們恨他，甚至他的妻子兒女也不與他同住。廷廷基（Tingtinkie）小時候不聽話，吃了父母禁止他吃的野地果實；那些果實中的毒使他不再長大，所以無論他變得多老，都保持著孩童的身量。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Night after night Hare shook Tingtinkie's hanging nest, till the bird got the convulsions of all the fright; then Hare said with a laugh that it was not he but the Owl who had frightened him. Tingtinkie told all the birds that it was the Owl with his great eyes who chased death onto their bodies by night; the birds believed it, left Hare, and plagued and teased the Owl in the day. The Owl was an old sorcerer, but a greater and mightier sorcerer broke his power and took it from him — yet to tell things beforehand they could not take from him: the Owl still knows what goes on far away and what will happen within a month.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 29; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改述，出處同上；非逐字照錄。一夜又一夜，野兔搖晃廷廷基懸掛的巢，直到那鳥因驚嚇過度而抽搐；然後野兔笑著說，嚇他的不是自己，而是貓頭鷹。廷廷基告訴所有的鳥，是那雙大眼睛的貓頭鷹在夜裡把死亡驅趕到他們身上；鳥兒們信了，離開野兔，並在白天糾纏、戲弄貓頭鷹。貓頭鷹是個老巫師，但一個更偉大、更強大的巫師破了他的法力，奪走了它——然而預言事物的能力，他們卻奪不走：貓頭鷹至今仍知道遠方發生的事，以及一個月內將要發生的事。

title.en: The Bushman and the Lion Meet in a Cave
title.zh: 桑人與獅會於穴中

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 30

summary.en: The lion makes rain so dark that a lost Bushman creeps into the very cave where the lion waits; feeling the hairy ribs, he tiptoes out, swims the torrent the lion's own rain has raised, takes the lion's glowing eyes for a fire, hides in a rock-slit that opens on a second chamber where two armed Bushmen sleep, and the three keep the fire till dawn — for the lion fears burning brands more than assegais.
summary.zh: 獅降雨蔽天，迷途桑人誤入獅候之穴；觸其毛肋，踮足而出，泅渡獅雨所漲之洪，誤認獅目為火光，匿入石縫——縫通暗室，內有二持弓桑人。三人守火至旦：獅畏燃柴甚於矛。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 30 (1920); not verbatim. The Lion got a plan one evening, when the sun went down, to make rain; he let the sky grow so dark that one could not see one's hands before one's eyes, and it rained as if old maids and knobkerries were falling out of the sky together. One Bushman quite lost his way; he knew he was near a cave, but where exactly it was he could not say.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 30; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這是對馮·維利希（von Wielligh）第二部第30則（1920年）的濃縮改述，並非逐字照錄。某天傍晚太陽西下時，獅子心生一計，要讓天下雨；祂把天空弄得一片漆黑，黑得人連自己眼前的手都看不見，雨下得彷彿老處女和圓頭棒一同從天上落了下來。有個布須曼人完全迷了路；他知道自己離一個洞穴不遠，但洞穴究竟在哪裡，他卻說不上來。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The Lion noticed the Bushman seeking the cave, ran ahead in the rain and cold, and curled up waiting inside. The Bushman crept in feeling his way, heard someone breathing hard — too hard for a man — and laid his hand softly on a hairy something: it was none other than the Lion, a perfect giant! Softly as a cat he crept back and tiptoed out.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 30; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這是同一段落的濃縮改述，並非逐字照錄。獅子注意到那個布須曼人在尋找洞穴，便冒著雨和寒風搶先跑去，在洞裡蜷起身子等著。布須曼人摸索著悄悄爬進去，聽見有誰在沉重地喘氣——那喘氣聲太重，不像是人——便輕輕把手放在一個毛茸茸的東西上：那正是獅子，一個十足的龐然大物！他像貓一樣輕手輕腳地退回去，踮著腳尖溜了出去。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. He knew the lion would get his scent and follow, so he swam a stream — for the lion is a little averse to running water, which its own rain had filled. In the dark he saw a fire glowing and thought it was the lion's eye; a rock-slit received him, and it opened on another chamber where two lost Bushmen slept by a fine fire, bows and arrows ready. 'Push out that man who dared to plague me in my house!' roared the lion; 'Come and fetch him out yourself if you are man enough,' they answered — and they kept up the fire till daylight, when the lion slunk away, for he will not attack men in clear daylight.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 30; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這是同一段落的濃縮改述，並非逐字照錄。他知道獅子會嗅到他的氣味追上來，於是游過一條溪流——因為獅子對流水有些忌憚，而那條溪已被祂自己降的雨漲滿了。黑暗中他看見一團火光，還以為是獅子的眼睛；一道岩縫接納了他，岩縫通向另一個洞室，那裡有兩個迷路的布須曼人正睡在一堆旺火旁，弓箭都已備好。「把那個膽敢在我屋裡騷擾我的人推出來！」獅子吼道；「你有種就自己進來把他帶出去，」他們回答——他們一直把火燒到天亮，獅子便悄悄溜走了，因為祂不願在光天化日之下攻擊人。

title.en: Snake and Tortoise Are Brothers
title.zh: 蛇與龜為兄弟

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 31

summary.en: Two old Bushmen each have a son: the good one, whose arms and legs a jealous father cuts off, becomes the great field tortoise; the second, beheaded by the sorcerer father of the first, is split lengthwise — and when the Jackal comes to eat the pieces, the Moon drops her dew on them and each piece stretches into a long field snake. Snake and Tortoise never quarrel to this day.
summary.zh: 兩老桑人各有一子：善者被妒父斷其四肢，化為大草原龜；次子被首者被縱剖為二——豺來食之，月滴露其上，每片伸長為長蛇。蛇與龜至今不相爭。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; contains graphic violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 31 (1920); not verbatim. There were two old Bushmen of the old race; each had a son. But the son of the one was a good-for-nothing, and the son of the other was clever at hunting, and could dance beautifully and play the ramkie; this made jealousy between the two fathers.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 31; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這是對馮·維利希（von Wielligh）第二部第31則（1920年）的濃縮改述，並非逐字照錄。從前有兩個屬於古老族類的老布須曼人；各有一個兒子。但其中一人的兒子是個一無是處的廢物，另一人的兒子則擅長打獵，舞跳得極美，還會彈拉姆基琴（ramkie）；這便在兩位父親之間種下了嫉妒。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. One day the father of the good-for-nothing caught the good son alone in the veld; he took him by treachery, cut off his arms and legs, took his beautiful knitted kaross and gave him a piece of hard old buffalo hide in exchange. The good son, with neither arms nor legs to hunt, dance or make music, crawled about and became the great field tortoise.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 31; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這是同一段落的濃縮改述，並非逐字照錄。有一天，那個廢物的父親在草原上撞見了好兒子獨自一人；他使詐將他擒住，砍去他的雙臂雙腿，奪走他那件漂亮的針織卡羅斯皮披（kaross），換給他一塊又硬又舊的水牛皮。好兒子既無手臂也無腿，不能打獵、跳舞或奏樂，只能四處爬行，後來就成了大草原龜。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The sorcerer father next bewitched his own stout son into a gorgeous bird, waited till the tortoise's young brother crept near, sprang down as an old Bushman, cut off the boy's head and split him from below upwards into two pieces, each with an arm and leg. When the sun went down and the moon came out, the Jackal came to eat the pieces; but the Moon, who comes alive again month after month, poured her dew on the two pieces, the arm and leg of each stretched out, and each piece became a long field snake. The father found the great field snakes but did not know them; and Tortoise knew they were his brothers, so Snake and Tortoise never quarrel to this day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 31; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這是同一段落的濃縮改述，並非逐字照錄。那位巫師父親接著又把自己那肥壯的兒子施法變成了一隻華美的鳥，等到龜的弟弟爬近時，便化身為一個老布須曼人跳下來，砍下那男孩的頭，又從下往上把他劈成兩半，每一半各帶著一條手臂和一條腿。太陽西下、月亮升起時，豺狼前來吃那兩半；但月亮月復一月地死而復生，便將她的露水澆在那兩半上，每一半的手臂和腿都伸展開來，各自變成了一條長長的草原蛇。父親找到了那些大草原蛇，卻不認得牠們；而龜知道牠們是自己的兄弟，所以蛇與龜直到今日從不爭吵。

title.en: Lion, Wolf and Jackal
title.zh: 獅、狼與豺

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 32

summary.en: At a zebra kill the lioness scatters the pack while cubs bellow; Wolf whimpers 'how-hoo' and Jackal laughs 'ha-ga-ga!' with a dry tongue; when they circle back for scraps the lion slides in beneath them and rakes them both. Wolf learns to eat at the meat, Jackal to beg with one eye on the vulture and one on Wolf — because they too were once Bushmen.
summary.zh: 斑馬獲處，母獅驅散獸群，幼獅怒吼；狼泣「霍霍」，豺乾舌而笑「哈嘎嘎」；二人回頭覓食，獅潛其下抓傷二獸。狼學得就肉而食，豺學得一日視鷲、一日視狼而乞——因彼等本亦是桑人。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 32 (1920); not verbatim. Lion also belongs to the old race; therefore he is Lion. His hunting mates walk about little. Wolf can also hunt... but where Lion still stands and says 'Dare to come near!', Wolf has long since thrown down the reins and run till he grew small. Of Jackal there is nothing to say! He is a beggar, bolts at the smallest rustle.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 32; not verbatim.
passages.zh: von Wielligh 第二卷第三十二號（1920年）的濃縮改述；並非逐字照錄。獅子也屬於古老的一族；因此牠就是獅子。牠的狩獵夥伴們很少四處走動。狼也能狩獵……但當獅子還站在那裡說「敢靠近試試看！」時，狼早已扔下韁繩逃跑，跑到身子都變小了。至於豺狼，根本沒什麼好說的！牠是個乞丐，一點風吹草動就竄逃。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. When the sun went down Lion stood up, sniffed against the wind: 'Aha, wife, I smell zebras — they are here near; come with the children behind me as soon as I have the zebra down.' The lioness rounded the zebras, her mate sprang, held the prey with teeth behind the neck... The two eldest cubs tore strips from the skin to make eating-places for the little ones.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 32; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改述，同一段落；並非逐字照錄。太陽下山時，獅子站起身，迎著風嗅了嗅：「啊哈，老婆，我聞到斑馬了——牠們就在這附近；等我把斑馬撲倒，你就帶著孩子們跟在我後面來。」母獅繞到斑馬後方，牠的伴侶縱身一躍，用牙齒咬住獵物後頸……兩隻最大的幼獅從皮上撕下條狀的肉，為小傢伙們弄出進食的地方。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Wolf and Jackal drew near at the smell of blood. 'Please, Lion, give me also a piece,' begged Wolf; 'and me too,' begged Jackal. 'Wau! Haau!' was all Lion said, as he tried how deep he could drive his claws into Wolf's hide; Wolf wept and fled... but when they saw the lioness eating again, they came foot for foot nearer — until Lion slid in unawares under the two quarrel-makers: Jackal got a few scratches and Wolf enough to make his hair fly.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 32; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改述，同一段落；並非逐字照錄。狼和豺狼聞到血腥味便湊了過來。「拜託，獅子，也給我一塊吧，」狼乞求道；「我也要，」豺狼也乞求道。「哇！哈！」獅子只說了這些，一邊試著把爪子往狼的皮裡扎得有多深；狼哭著逃走了……但當牠們看見母獅又開始吃時，便一寸一寸地越靠越近——直到獅子冷不防地從兩個爭吵者底下滑進來：豺狼挨了幾下抓，狼則被抓得毛都飛了起來。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Wolf then saw it paid him better to look after his body at the meat and marrowbones than to keep Jackal from it; and Jackal knows it does not become him to eat too near Wolf: he sits, head in the air, tongue out, crying out his heart in sorrow — one eye on the meat, the other on Wolf. That they are so clever is because they too were once Bushmen, who have now become Lion, Wolf and Jackal.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 32; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改述，同一段落；並非逐字照錄。狼於是明白，守著肉和骨髓骨來照顧自己的身體，比阻止豺狼靠近更划算；而豺狼也知道，吃得太靠近狼並不合適：牠坐著，頭仰向空中，舌頭伸在外，悲痛地哭訴著心事——一隻眼睛盯著肉，另一隻眼睛盯著狼。牠們之所以這麼機靈，是因為牠們從前也是布須曼人，如今變成了獅子、狼和豺狼。

title.en: The Baboons, the Apes and Little Jantjie
title.zh: 狒狒、猿與小揚奇

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 33

summary.en: Jantjie, a Bushman child taken by white hunters, runs away stuffed with stolen flour and tobacco; the apes — old Korannas — and the baboons — old Bushmen — want his bundle, and the children cry 'kill him and give us the nice grains'. At the river he bangs his tin pail like a thousand-pound cannon and the apes bolt; in the rocks he cannot, so he mocks their flat overhanging foreheads, cries 'Boer, bring your gun!' and escapes over the kranses.
summary.zh: 小揚奇為白獵者所擄之桑童，攜競得之粉與煙逃亡；猿（古科蘭人）與狒狒（古桑人）欲奪其包，幼者呼「殺之予我香粒！」。河邊他敲錫桶如千磅巨炮，猿群奔逃；岩間不能敲，遂譏其平懸之額，呼「布爾人，帶槍來！」，越崖而遁。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; colonial-era setting; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 33 (1920); not verbatim. Hunters from the sunset side (from the sea side) once came and caught a Bushman child and took it home with them; the hunters were white people, and they named the little Bushman Jantjie... He made a plan to run away, and days beforehand packed food quietly in his knapsack: bread, meal, wheat, meat, fish and whatever he could get hold of sneakily — especially tinderboxes and firesteels, knives and tobacco.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 33; not verbatim.
passages.zh: von Wielligh 第二卷第三十三號（1920年）的濃縮改述；並非逐字照錄。來自日落之方（來自海那一方）的獵人曾來抓走一個布須曼人的孩子，帶回家去；那些獵人是白人，他們給這個小布須曼人取名為揚基……他謀劃逃跑，並在數日前悄悄把食物裝進背包：麵包、粗粉、小麥、肉、魚，以及他能偷偷弄到手的一切——尤其是火絨盒和火鐮、刀子和菸草。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The land he had to flee through was inhabited by apes and baboons. The apes lived along a great river and were said to be old Korannas that became apes; and the baboons farmed in the ridge-country and were said to be old Bushmen changed into baboons, now living on veld-food and insects. At the river the apes said: 'Let us go for the man: he carries goods; let us kill him and take the goods.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 33; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改述，同一段落；並非逐字照錄。他必須逃經的那片土地住著猿和狒狒。猿住在一條大河沿岸，據說是變成猿的老科蘭納人；狒狒則在山脊地帶耕作，據說是變成狒狒的老布須曼人，如今以野地食物和昆蟲為生。在河邊，猿說：「我們去對付那個人吧：他帶著貨物；我們殺了他，把貨物拿走。」

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Jantjie got the thought that apes fear a great noise. He mocked them — 'why are your bottoms so black? just above your eyes the skin is still white if you roll your eyes back' — till they stormed him; then he banged on the tin pail and made a thousand-pounder noise; the apes were frightened and flew off, the children wailed, the old ones roared from above and fled into the high trees. At the baboons' rocks the pail was full of water and useless, so he mocked their foreheads — 'like a krans at the front of a ridge' — and cried: 'Boer, boer, bring your gun! Here are the ugly ones you seek!' and while they fled to the cliffs he made off home.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 33; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同處的濃縮改述；並非逐字照錄。揚提耶想到猿猴害怕巨大的聲響。他嘲弄牠們——「你們的屁股為什麼這麼黑？只要把眼睛往上翻，眼睛上方的皮膚還是白的」——直到牠們朝他撲來；於是他猛敲錫桶，發出千磅巨響；猿猴受驚飛逃，孩子們號哭，老猿從高處咆哮，逃入高樹之中。到了狒狒的岩地，桶裡裝滿了水，派不上用場，於是他又嘲弄牠們的額頭——「像山脊前頭的崖壁」——並喊道：「布爾人，布爾人，帶上你的槍！你要找的醜東西就在這裡！」趁牠們逃向峭壁時，他抽身回家。

title.en: The Sunbeetles and the Crickets
title.zh: 日甲蟲與蟋蟀

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 34

summary.en: A father shoots a lion that carried off his baby; later a water-spirit pulls his daughter into a pool and the mother fights her way out with her. Years on, the two children are lost in the veld; the father and sons seek by day, the mother and daughters by night, calling, until worn to skin and bone they become the sunbeetles (doringbesies) that sing and seek by day, and the crickets that sing and seek by night.
summary.zh: 父射殺奪嬰之獅；後水靈曳其女入池，母搏鬥救出。多年後二子失於原野；父與子晝尋、母與女夜尋，呼號不輟，直至形銷骨立——化為晝歌晝尋之日甲蟲，與夜歌夜尋之蟋蟀。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 34 (1920); not verbatim. An old Bushman and his wife had one little boy; they went to dig Bushman-rice, and the child fell asleep on the mother's back-kaross under a bush. A lion that had eaten its fill at a hartebeest picked up the kaross with the child and lay down near by to watch what the parents would do. The father climbed a bobbejaan-tou, shot the lion with his last poisoned arrow in the open throat, and brought home meat.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 34; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馮·維利希第二卷第三十四號（1920年）的濃縮改述；並非逐字照錄。一個老布須曼人和他的妻子有一個小男孩；他們去挖布須曼米，孩子在一叢灌木下、母親的背毯上睡著了。一頭在麋羚旁吃飽了的獅子叼起裹著孩子的背毯，在附近躺下，觀望這對父母會怎麼做。父親爬上一條猴繩，用最後一支毒箭射中獅子敞開的喉嚨，帶回了肉。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Years passed; a girl child came, and when she could play about, the mother was cutting matjiesgoed by the fountain. The child picked reeds too near the pool; the water-spirit came out and drew the child in; the mother leapt into the water, wrestled with the water-spirit at great risk of her life, saved her child and swam out, exhausted and half dead.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 34; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同處的濃縮改述；並非逐字照錄。多年過去；一個女孩出生了，當她能四處玩耍時，母親正在泉邊割取墊草。孩子在水潭太近處採蘆葦；水精出來把孩子拉了進去；母親跳入水中，冒著極大的生命危險與水精搏鬥，救回了孩子，筋疲力盡、半死不活地游了出來。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The father played the violin and the mother the ramkie beautifully, and the two children danced before them; they spent many a pleasant evening and night by the veld-fire. One day the two children were sent for veld-food and never came back: the parents sought and called and played violin and ramkie, but no answer came; the father asked the Hammerkop, who sees all in the water, and the mother the Owl, whose dolosse stood still. So father and sons seek by day, mother and daughters by night — and worn out with grief they became the sunbeetles and the crickets, the one singing and seeking by day, the other by night.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 34; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同處的濃縮改述；並非逐字照錄。父親拉小提琴，母親彈拉姆基琴，都十分動聽，兩個孩子在他们面前跳舞；他們在草原篝火旁度過了許多愉快的夜晚。有一天，兩個孩子被派去採集草原食物，卻再也沒有回來：父母尋找、呼喚，拉小提琴、彈拉姆基琴，卻沒有回音；父親去問錘頭鸛，牠能看見水中一切；母親去問貓頭鷹，牠的卜骨靜止不動。於是父親和兒子們白天尋找，母親和女兒們夜裡尋找——最後他們因悲傷而憔悴，化作了太陽甲蟲和蟋蟀，一個白天鳴唱尋找，另一個夜裡鳴唱尋找。

title.en: Lion and Wolf Eat Over and Over
title.zh: 獅與狼反覆相食

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 35

summary.en: The stingy Lion palms off two sucked marrowbones on the begging Wolf; Wolf invites him to ostrich soup, pretends to feed wife and children from a cold pot, then pours the boiling one over the lion's head and claps it tight — and brains him with his kierie. So a mean deed always comes back on a man's own head.
summary.zh: 吝獅以兩根吮盡之髓骨欺乞食之狼；狼邀其飲鴕湯，假作以冷釜飼妻兒，實傾沸釜於獅首而扣緊——復以短杖擊斃之。故刻薄之行，終返其人之首。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; graphic violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 35 (1920); not verbatim. Wolf was out the whole night on the hunt without luck; near daybreak he came on Lion's spoor and followed it, for he knows Lion is a lucky fellow who always gets food. Lion had caught a zebra and eaten his fill... 'And there lies more than half a zebra still,' noted Wolf. 'Yes, but that I must keep for my wife and children,' said Lion, and went and fetched a marrowbone whose marrow he had sucked out himself: 'There, eat.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 35; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馮·維利希第二卷第三十五號（1920年）的濃縮改述；並非逐字照錄。狼整夜在外打獵，一無所獲；近黎明時他發現了獅子的足跡，便跟了上去，因為他知道獅子是個幸運的傢伙，總能弄到食物。獅子捕到一匹斑馬，吃了個飽……「那兒還剩下半匹多斑馬呢，」狼說道。「不錯，但那是我要留給老婆孩子的，」獅子說，然後去取來一根髓骨，骨髓是他自己吸乾的：「喏，吃吧。」

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Wolf took the bone, gave it a few licks, and asked to be allowed to lick the sops by the zebra; Lion said he himself was so fond of soup he would not give away a drop. Wolf asked for a bone to take home, and got another cleaned-out one: 'There, take it; you beggar. Now go!'... 'Now I ask you, brother Lion, to come and eat at my place to-morrow.' On the way home Wolf caught an ostrich and ate his fill of it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 35; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同處的濃縮改述；並非逐字照錄。狼接過骨頭，舔了幾下，請求允許他去舔斑馬旁的湯汁；獅子說他自己太愛喝湯了，一滴也不肯讓。狼討一根骨頭帶回家，又得到一根啃乾淨的：「喏，拿去；你這叫花子。現在滾吧！」……「那麼我請你，獅子兄弟，明天到我那兒去吃。」回家路上，狼捕到一隻鴕鳥，吃了個飽。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Next day he cooked the ostrich flesh, poured the cold soup into another pot, and kept the fresh one boiling; when Lion came he pretended to feed his wife and children soup by the mouthful — then set the empty pot down and took up the boiling one: 'Now it is our turn; we have time and can drink at our ease — you first, then I.' He turned the pot of boiling soup over Lion's head and pressed the hot pot fast over it; Lion's eyes, mouth and throat were scalded; he dropped to the ground, and Wolf took his kierie and battered him dead. So a mean deed always comes back on a man's own head.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 35; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同處情節的濃縮改述，非逐字照錄。翌日他煮了鴕鳥肉，把冷湯倒進另一口鍋，讓新煮的那鍋繼續滾沸；獅子來時，他假裝一口一口餵妻子兒女喝湯——然後放下空鍋，端起滾沸的那鍋：「現在輪到我們了；我們有時間，可以從容地喝——你先，然後我。」他把那鍋滾湯翻倒在獅子頭上，又將熱鍋緊緊按住；獅子的眼睛、嘴和喉嚨都被燙傷；他倒在地上，狼拾起他的木棍把他打死。所以，卑劣的行徑總會回到作惡者自己頭上。

title.en: The Ostrich Comes Alive Again
title.zh: 鴕鳥復活

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 36

summary.en: The hunter Raakskiet is trampled senseless by a bewitched ostrich; thirsting for water, he crawls to the pool and drowns. His family find him, lay him in the sun, and kill the boy's pet hare 'for the hare brought death into the world'. As they mourn, Raakskiet revives in the sun. Later a whirlwind carries one bloody plume into the pool where he drowned, and it becomes a little ostrich that grows and returns to his wives.
summary.zh: 獵者直射者遭妖鴕踏暈；渴極爬至池邊而溺斃。家人置屍日下曝之，並殺其子之寵兔「因兔帶死亡入世」。眾方哀哭，直射者日下復甦。後旋風捲一血羽入其溺斃之池，化為小鴕，漸長而歸其妻。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 36 (1920); not verbatim. Raakskiet (Straightshot) was known as one of the best hunters of his time... He felt sick and decided to turn back home; an ostrich cock came behind him, blew mightily and wanted only to kick and trample him. He lay flat; the bird sat on him with its sharp breastbone and kneaded him as if it would press him flat like a foot-sole; the string of his bow broke under the kicks.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 36; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馮·維利希（von Wielligh）第二部第36號（1920年）的濃縮改述，非逐字照錄。拉克斯希特（Raakskiet，意為「直射」）被公認為他那個時代最出色的獵人之一……他感到不適，決定折返回家；一隻公鴕鳥從他身後趕來，猛烈地鼓氣，一心只想踢他、踩他。他平躺在地；那鳥以銳利的胸骨坐壓在他身上，像要把他的腳掌壓平似地揉搓他；他弓上的弦在踢踏之下斷了。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. He bound himself over with twigs so that he looked like a bush and so escaped home, took to his bed, and lay sick. Thirsting for water he crawled to the pool and fell forward into the water and was drowned. The family found him in the water dead, rolled him on the ground, and laid him in the sunshine by the pool to get warm; and the mother killed the boy's pet hare, for the hare is food with which one may not play, and death came into the world through a hare.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 36; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同處情節的濃縮改述，非逐字照錄。他用細枝把自己捆綁起來，使自己看起來像一叢灌木，就這樣逃回家中，臥床不起，病倒在床。他渴求水，爬到水潭邊，一頭栽進水裡，溺死了。家人發現他死在水裡，把他翻滾到地上，又將他安置在水潭邊的陽光下取暖；母親殺死了男孩心愛的野兔，因為野兔是不可拿來戲耍的食物，而死亡正是經由野兔進入世界的。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. But just then his father Raakskiet came alive again; he raised himself, sat in the sunshine, grew better with every breath, and stood up lacking nothing. Later a mighty whirlwind came and whirled all the plumes away; one feather heavy with blood could not whirl so high, came down, and fell into the pool in which Raakskiet had drowned the day before, and swam on the water: while they watched, that bloody feather changed into a little ostrich. The little creature took its down-feathers; they grew; it stepped with weak legs out of the water, sat basking in the sun, grew stronger and stronger — and an adult bird, black and white, trotted off straight to its own home to tell its wives it still lived.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 36; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同處情節的濃縮改述，非逐字照錄。但就在那時，他的父親拉克斯希特又活了過來；他撐起身子，坐在陽光下，每呼吸一次就好一些，最後站了起來，毫髮無傷。後來一陣猛烈的旋風颳來，把所有羽毛都捲走了；一根沾滿血的重羽毛捲不了那麼高，落了下來，掉進拉克斯希特前一天溺死的那個水潭裡，在水面上漂浮：正當他們觀看時，那根血羽毛變成了一隻小鴕鳥。這小東西長出絨羽；羽毛漸長；牠邁著虛弱的腿從水裡走出來，坐在陽光下取暖，越來越強壯——最後成了一隻黑白相間的大鳥，直奔自己的家，去告訴牠的妻子們牠還活著。

title.en: The Lion Grows Jealous
title.zh: 獅生妒心

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 37

summary.en: The lionesses praise Ape's springing, Gemsbok's speed and Ostrich's booming; the jealous lions stage a feast, scratch ape's rump, score gemsbok's face, strip ostrich's rump feathers, and stalk off — but hunt ostriches for their lungs till they boom from the chest. The wives learn the value of their providers; and one wife's mockery costs the lionesses their long manes forever.
summary.zh: 母獅讚猿之躍、大羚之疾、鴕鳥之吼；妒獅設宴，抓猿臀、劃羚面、拔鴕臀羽，揚長而去——然轉而獵鴕取肺，直至吼自胸膛。妻等始知供養者之貴；而一妻之譏笑，令母獅自此失其長鬣。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; contains domestic violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 37 (1920); not verbatim. The lions often come together in company, and then their wives always praise the apes for their nimbleness, the gemsbok for their speed, and the ostriches for their beautiful booming voice. This did not please the male lions at all, and they grew jealous about it and gave their dissatisfaction to their wives in full company; but the lionesses held that they were right.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 37; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馮·維利希第二部第37號（1920年）的濃縮改述，非逐字照錄。獅子常成群結伴而來，那時牠們的妻子總是誇讚猿猴的靈巧、大羚羊的迅捷，以及鴕鳥那美妙的低鳴聲。這讓雄獅們大為不悅，牠們因此心生嫉妒，當著全體同伴的面把不滿發洩在妻子身上；但母獅們堅持認為自己說得對。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The wives made a feast and dance and invited Ape, Gemsbok and Ostrich; the lionesses clapped hands and cheered Ape and Gemsbok and Ostrich, but not their own men. One lion scratched the hair off Ape's seat, another sprang on Gemsbok and scored marks in his face, the third stripped all the feathers off the Ostrich's rump; and the three males walked away and left their wives with the little children.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 37; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同處情節的濃縮改述，非逐字照錄。妻子們設宴跳舞，邀請了猿猴、大羚羊和鴕鳥；母獅們拍手為猿猴、大羚羊和鴕鳥喝采，卻不為自己的丈夫喝采。一頭獅子抓掉了猿猴臀部的毛，另一頭撲向大羚羊，在他臉上抓出傷痕，第三頭則把鴕鳥臀部上的羽毛全部拔光；三頭雄獅就此離去，拋下妻子和年幼的孩子。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The lions went and hunted ostriches only to eat their lungs, so that they could boom as beautifully as the ostrich out of the forechest; and after they had eaten many ostrich lungs they no longer boomed as if they had tails in their mouths or bones in their throats. The wives sought their providers out again and promised to do better; and from then on, when Ostrich booms, they clap no more hands; but when their own men boom they feel grand and praise them, for it is harder than any other voice. Yet one wife began again to mock her man's mane; he grew so angry that he dragged her round by the head-hair and plucked her so bald that her head-hair never grew so long again; the other lionesses cut theirs off in fear — that is why their manes are not so long as the males' to this day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 37; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同一段落的濃縮改寫，並非逐字照錄。那些獅子前去獵捕鴕鳥，只為了吃牠們的肺，好讓自己也能像鴕鳥那樣，從前胸發出美妙的轟鳴；而牠們吃了許多鴕鳥肺之後，再發出轟鳴時，就不再像是嘴裡含著尾巴、喉嚨裡卡著骨頭了。妻子們再次尋找她們的供養者，並承諾會做得更好；從那時起，當鴕鳥轟鳴時，她們不再拍手；但當她們自己的男人轟鳴時，她們感到威風，並讚美他們，因為那比任何其他聲音都更難發出。然而有一個妻子又開始嘲笑她男人的鬃毛；他氣得抓住她的頭髮把她拖來拖去，把她拔得光禿禿的，以致她的頭髮再也沒能長得那麼長；其他的母獅因恐懼而剪掉了自己的鬃毛——這就是為什麼至今她們的鬃毛不如公獅那麼長。

title.en: The Saucy Indians Who Became Rattlesnakes
title.zh: 無禮的印第安人化為響尾蛇

region.en: Passamaquoddy country before the Great Flood
region.zh: 大洪水之前的帕薩馬科迪之地

period: Passamaquoddy tale related by an old woman to Mrs. W. Wallace Brown (Leland 1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How Glooskap changed Certain Saucy Indians into Rattlesnakes'

summary.en: Long time ago the Rattlesnakes were saucy Indians - they had too much face, and could not be put down by much, and they got up for very little. When the great Flood was coming Glooskap told them about it; they said they did not care. 'The Flood will come and drown you all' - then these Indians hurrahed again, got their rattles made of turtle-shells fastened together and filled with pebbles, and had a grand dance. The rain began to fall, but they danced; the thunder roared, and they shook their rattles and yelled at it. Then Glooskap was angry: he did not drown them in the Flood, but changed them into rattlesnakes. Nowadays, when they see a man coming, they lift up their heads and move them about - that's the way snakes dance - and they shake the rattles in their tails just as Indians shake their rattles when they dance.
summary.zh: 很久以前，響尾蛇原是一群無禮的印第安人——架子極大，軟硬不吃，動輒起鬨。大洪水將至，格魯斯卡普勸告他們，他們卻說毫不在乎。「洪水將至，要淹死你們全體！」——這些印第安人再次歡呼，取來龜殼串成、內填碎石的老式響鈴，跳起大舞。大雨落下，他們照舞；雷霆轟鳴，他們搖鈴吼叫以對。格魯斯卡普怒了——他不在洪水中淹死他們，而是把他們化為響尾蛇。如今蛇見人來，便昂首擺動——那是蛇的舞蹈——尾鈴搖動，正如印第安人跳舞時搖鈴一般。

sensitivity.note: Passamaquoddy tale (Leland 1884); public domain. A flood-and-transgression aition in the NE Woodlands register.

passages.text: You know At-o-sis, the Snake? Well, the worst of all is Rattlesnake. Long time ago the Rattlesnakes were saucy Indians. They were very saucy. They had too much face. They could not be put down by much, and they got up for very little. When the great Flood was coming Glooskap told them about it. They said they did not care. He told them the water would come over their heads. They said that would be very wet. He told them to be good and quiet, and pray. Then those Indians hurrahed. He said, 'A great Flood is coming.' Then they gave three cheers for the great Flood. He said, 'The Flood will come and drown you all.' Then these Indians hurrahed again, and got their rattles, made of turtle-shells, in the old fashion, fastened together, filled with pebbles, and rattled them and had a grand dance.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 110-111; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 你知道阿托西斯，也就是蛇嗎？嗯，最壞的要數響尾蛇了。很久以前，響尾蛇是些無禮的印第安人。他們非常無禮。他們太不要臉了。很難壓制住他們，而他們為了一點小事就發作。當大洪水將要來臨時，格盧斯卡普告訴了他們。他們說他們不在乎。他告訴他們水會淹過他們的頭頂。他們說那會很濕。他叫他們要乖、要安靜，並祈禱。於是那些印第安人歡呼起來。他說：『一場大洪水要來了。』於是他們為大洪水歡呼三聲。他說：『洪水會來把你們全都淹死。』於是這些印第安人又歡呼起來，拿出他們用龜殼按舊法製成的響環，串在一起，裝滿小石子，搖晃起來，跳了一場盛大的舞。

passages.text: Yes, they had a great dance. The rain began to fall, but they danced. The thunder roared, and they shook their rattles and yelled at it. Then Glooskap was angry. He did not drown them in the Flood, however, but he changed them into rattlesnakes. Nowadays, when they see a man coming, they lift up their heads and move them about. That's the way snakes dance. And they shake the rattles in their tails just as Indians shake their rattles when they dance. How do you like such music?
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 111; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 是的，他們跳了一場盛大的舞。雨開始下起來，但他們照樣跳舞。雷聲轟鳴，他們就搖晃響環，對它大喊大叫。於是格盧斯卡普生氣了。不過他並沒有在洪水中淹死他們，而是把他們變成了響尾蛇。如今，當他們看見有人走來，就抬起頭來，左右擺動。那就是蛇跳舞的方式。他們搖動尾巴上的響環，就像印第安人跳舞時搖晃他們的響環一樣。你喜歡這樣的音樂嗎？

title.en: Glooskap Binds Wuchowsen, the Great Wind-Bird
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普縛住風鳥伍喬森

region.en: Great rock at the end of the sky, far to the North
region.zh: 北方天際盡頭的巨岩

period: Passamaquoddy manuscript collection by Louis Mitchell (Leland 1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How Glooskap bound Wuchowsen, the Great Wind-Bird'

summary.en: The Indians believe in a great bird called Wochowsen or Wuchowsen, meaning Wind-Blow, who lives far to the North and sits upon a great rock at the end of the sky; whenever he moves his wings the wind blows. When it blew a tempest so that Glooskap could not go out at all, he sought the Bird-giant: 'You take no compassion on your Koosesek, your grandchildren. You have caused this wind and storm; it is too much. Be easier with your wings!' 'I have been here since ancient times... mine was the first voice, and I will ever move my wings as I will.' Then Glooskap rose in his might to the clouds, took the Great Bird-giant as though he were a duck, tied both his wings, and threw him down into a chasm between deep rocks. The Indians could now go out in their canoes all day long - but with that all the waters became stagnant, so thick that Glooskap could not paddle. Then he raised Wuchowsen, who is immortal, put him on his rock again, and untied one of his wings; since then the winds have never been so terrible as in the old time.
summary.zh: 印第安人信奉大鳥伍喬森——「吹風者」——居極北，坐在天際盡頭的巨岩上；牠一振翅，風便吹起。暴風大到格魯斯卡普無法出舟時，他前去尋這鳥中巨人：「你竟不憐惜你的孫兒們。這風暴皆你所致，太過分了！收斂些翅膀吧！」「自太古我便在此……最初的聲音便出於我翅，我永遠要隨心振翅。」格魯斯卡普躍上雲端，如提鴨般拎起巨鳥，縛其雙翅，擲入深岩之隙。此後印第安人終日泛舟——然而天下之水皆成死水，濃稠得連舟都划不動。主人便再扶起不朽的伍喬森，放回岩上，解其一翼——自那以後，風再沒有上古時那樣狂暴。

sensitivity.note: Passamaquoddy tale (Leland 1884); public domain. Leland compares Wuchowsen to the Norse Hraesvelg and stresses he is a wind-bird, not the western thunder-bird.

passages.text: The Indians believe in a great bird called by them Wochowsen or Wuchowsen, meaning Wind-Blow or the Wind-Blower, who lives far to the North, and sits upon a great rock at the end of the sky. And it is because whenever he moves his wings the wind blows they of old times called him that. When Glooskap was among men he often went out in his canoe with bow and arrows to kill sea-fowl. At one time it was every day very windy; it grew worse; at last it blew a tempest, and he could not go out at all. Then he said, 'Wuchowsen, the Great Bird, has done this!' He went to find him; it was long ere he reached his abode. He found sitting on a high rock a large white Bird.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 111-112; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 印第安人相信一隻大鳥，他們稱之為沃喬森或烏喬森，意思是「吹風」或「吹風者」，牠住在極北之地，坐在天邊的一塊大岩石上。正因為每當牠移動翅膀就會起風，古時的人們才這樣稱呼牠。格盧斯卡普在人間時，常帶著弓和箭乘獨木舟出去獵捕海鳥。有一段時間，天天都刮大風；風越刮越猛；最後竟刮起了暴風雨，他根本無法出門。於是他說：『這是那大鳥烏喬森幹的！』他去尋找牠；過了很久才到達牠的居所。他發現一隻巨大的白鳥坐在高岩上。

passages.text: 'Grandfather,' said Glooskap, 'you take no compassion on your Koosesek, your grandchildren. You have caused this wind and storm; it is too much. Be easier with your wings!' The Giant Bird replied, 'I have been here since ancient times; in the earliest days, ere aught else spoke, I first moved my wings; mine was the first voice - and I will ever move my wings as I will.' Then Glooskap rose in his might; he rose to the clouds; he took the Great Bird-giant Wuchowsen as though he were a duck, and tied both his wings, and threw him down into a chasm between deep rocks, and left him lying there.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 112-113; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 『祖父啊，』格盧斯卡普說，『你對你的庫西塞克，你的孫兒們，毫不憐憫。這場風和暴風雨是你引起的；這太過分了。對你的翅膀溫柔些吧！』那巨鳥回答說：『我自古以來就在這裡；在最早的時代，在別的任何東西開口之前，我就最先動了我的翅膀；第一個聲音是我的——而我將永遠隨心所欲地動我的翅膀。』於是格盧斯卡普奮起他的神力；他升到雲端；他抓住那巨鳥巨人烏喬森，就像抓一隻鴨子一樣，把牠的雙翅都綁起來，扔進深岩之間的裂隙裡，讓牠躺在那裡。

passages.text: The Indians could now go out in their canoes all day long, for there was a dead calm for many weeks and months. And with that all the waters became stagnant. They were so thick that Glooskap could not paddle his canoe. Then he thought of the Great Bird, and went to see him. As he had left him he found him, for Wuchowsen is immortal. So, raising him, he put him on his rock again, and untied one of his wings. Since then the winds have never been so terrible as in the old time.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 113; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 印第安人現在可以整天乘獨木舟出去了，因為一連好幾個星期、好幾個月都風平浪靜。隨之而來的是，所有的水都變得停滯不動。水濃稠得讓格盧斯卡普無法划動他的獨木舟。於是他想起了那隻大鳥，便去看牠。他發現牠仍是他離開時的樣子，因為烏喬森是不死的。於是，他把牠扶起來，重新放回牠的岩石上，並解開了牠的一隻翅膀。從那時起，風就再也不像古時那樣可怕了。

title.en: The Great Bull-Frog: The River Made Flesh and the First Water Creatures
title.zh: 巨牛蛙：化為血肉的大河與最初的水族

region.en: Mountain village on a brook, and the up-country dam
region.zh: 溪畔的山村與上游的水壩

period: Told by Tomah Josephs, Passamaquoddy (Leland 1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How Glooskap conquered the Great Bull-Frog'

summary.en: A village by a brook - the only water in all the country round - watches the stream dry to a dead bone. Upstream a monster chief, immense, bloated, with yellow eyes stuck out like pine-knots and a mouth from ear to ear, has dammed the rivulet for nothing, and bellows 'Do as you choose... If you want water, go somewhere else.' Glooskap comes among the honest villagers dressed terribly ferocious - ten feet high, a hundred feathers, clam-shells at each ear - bade them be of good cheer, and at the monster's town demands water: thrusting a spear into his belly, there gushed forth a mighty river, even all the water which should have run on while in the rivulet, for he had made it into himself. Glooskap crumpled his back with a mighty grip - it was the Bull-Frog, whose back bears the prints to this day - and hurled him into the stream. Meanwhile, in the hour when all wishes are granted, the simple villagers had wished themselves into the soft mud, the diving rocks, the rippling waves and the water forever: the first became a Leech, the second a Spotted Frog, the third a Crab, and the fourth a Fish - for ere this there had been in all the world none of the creatures which dwell in the water.
summary.zh: 山村傍溪而居——四野僅此一水——卻眼看溪水枯竭如死骨。上游的怪酋巨大臃腫、黃眼如松節、口裂至耳，平白築壩攔水，咆哮著「隨你們便……要水，另找去」。格魯斯卡普氣勢駭人地來到村中——身高十呎、頂插百羽、耳掛蛤殼——安慰村民，直搗怪酋之城索水；一矛刺入其腹，滔滔大河傾瀉而出——原來整條溪水都被他吞化於己身。主人如握巨松般捏彎其背——正是牛蛙，其背至今留著那可怕的指痕——隨手擲入溪流。同時，在「萬願得償」的那個時辰，純樸的村民許願入軟泥、躍岩潛水、隨波起伏、永居水中：第一人化為水蛭，第二人化為斑蛙，第三人化為螃蟹，第四人化為魚——在此之前，世上從無棲水之物。

sensitivity.note: Passamaquoddy tale (Leland 1884); public domain. Leland notes the bull-frog is the river incarnate - the ice of winter pierced by the spear of the sun.

passages.text: Of old times, there was an Indian village far away among the mountains, little known to other men... The town was by a brook, and except in it there was not a drop of water in all the country round, unless in a few rain-puddles. No one there had ever found even a spring. But after a time they began to observe that the brook was beginning to run low, and that not in the summer time, but in autumn, even after the rains. And day by day it diminished, until its bed was as dry as a dead bone in the ashes of a warm fire. Now it was said that far away up in the land where none had ever been there was on this very stream another Indian village; but what manner of men dwelt therein no one knew.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 114-115; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 古時，在遠方的群山之間有一座印第安村落，外人對它知之甚少……這座城鎮臨著一條小溪，而除了這條溪之外，周遭整片土地上再無一滴水，除非是幾處雨後的水窪。那裡從沒有人找到過哪怕一眼泉水。但過了些時日，他們開始察覺溪水漸淺，而且不是在夏天，而是在秋天，甚至是在雨季之後。它一天比一天減少，直到河床乾得像暖火灰燼裡的一根枯骨。當時有傳言說，在這條溪流上游極遠處、從無人踏足的地方，還有另一座印第安村落；但那裡住著什麼樣的人，卻無人知曉。

passages.text: And after he had traveled three days he came to the place; and there he found that a dam had been raised across the rivulet, so that no water could pass, for it was all kept in a pond. Then asking them why they had made this mischief, since the dam was of no use to them, they bade him go and see their chief, by whose order this had been built. And when he came to him, lo, there lay lazily in the mud a creature who was more of a monster than a man, though he had a human form. For he was immense to measure, like a giant, fat, bloated, and brutal to behold. His great yellow eyes stuck from his head like pine-knots, his mouth went almost from ear to ear, and he had broad, skinny feet with long toes, exceeding marvelous. The messenger complained to this monster, who at first said nothing, and then croaked, and finally replied in a loud bellow: 'Do as you choose... If you want water, go somewhere else.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 115-116; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
