passages.zh: 他走了三天之後，來到了那個地方；到了那裡，他發現有人在小溪上築起了一道堤壩，使水無法流過，全都蓄在一個池塘裡。於是他問他們為何要造這樣的禍害，既然這堤壩對他們毫無用處；他們便叫他去見他們的酋長，說這堤壩是奉酋長之命築起的。當他來到酋長面前，瞧，泥裡懶洋洋地躺著一個與其說是人、不如說是怪物般的東西，雖有人形。因為他身形巨大，量起來像個巨人，肥胖、臃腫，面目粗野。他那雙黃色的大眼睛像松節一樣從頭上凸出，嘴巴幾乎從一隻耳朵咧到另一隻耳朵，還長著寬大而瘦削的腳，腳趾細長，奇異至極。使者向這怪物訴苦，怪物起初一言不發，接著呱呱叫了幾聲，最後以響亮的吼聲答道：『隨你怎麼辦……你要水，就到別處去。』

passages.text: Then Glooskap, who was much pleased with all this, for he loved a brave man, came among them looking terribly ferocious; in all the land there was not one who seemed half so horrible. For he appeared ten feet high, with a hundred red and black feathers in his scalp-lock, his face painted like fresh blood with green rings round his eyes, a large clam-shell hanging from each ear, a spread eagle, very awful to behold, flapping its wings from the back of his neck... 'Give me to drink, and that of the best, at once, thou Thing of Mud!' But the chief reviled him, and said, 'Get thee hence, to find water where thou canst.' Then Glooskap thrust a spear into his belly, and lo! there gushed forth a mighty river; even all the water which should have run on while in the rivulet, for he had made it into himself. And Glooskap, rising high as a giant pine, caught the chief in his hand and crumpled in his back with a mighty grip. And lo! it was the Bull-Frog. So he hurled him with contempt into the stream, to follow the current. And ever since that time the Bull-Frog's back has crumpled wrinkles in the lower part, showing the prints of Glooskap's awful squeeze.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 117-118; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 於是格盧斯卡普——他對這一切甚為滿意，因為他喜愛勇敢的人——來到他們中間，神情兇猛可怖；全地之上，沒有一個看起來有他一半那麼可怕。因為他顯出十英尺高的身形，額髮上插著一百根紅黑相間的羽毛，臉上塗得如鮮血一般，眼睛周圍畫著綠色圓環，每隻耳朵上掛著一片大蛤殼，脖頸後背上有一隻展翅的鷹，拍打著翅膀，令人望而生畏……『給我水喝，要最好的，立刻，你這泥巴東西！』但那酋長辱罵他，說道：『滾開，到你能找到水的地方去找吧。』於是格盧斯卡普把一支矛刺進他的肚子，瞧！一條大河噴湧而出；正是那本該在溪中流淌的全部水量，因為他已把它盡數納入自己體內。格盧斯卡普高高升起，如同一棵巨大的松樹，一手抓住酋長，以強勁的一握把他的背捏得皺縮起來。瞧！那正是牛蛙。於是他帶著鄙夷把他扔進溪流，隨波而去。自那時起，牛蛙的背部下半截便有了皺縮的紋路，顯出格盧斯卡普那可怕一握的印痕。

passages.text: Then he returned to the village; but there he found no people - no, not one. For a marvelous thing had come to pass during his absence, which shall be heard in every Indian's speech through all the ages. For the men, being, as I said, simple, honest folk, did as boys do when they are hungry, and say unto one another, 'What would you like to have, and what you?' Even so these villagers had said, 'Suppose you had all the nice cold, fresh, sparkling, delicious water there is in the world, what would you do?' And one said that he would live in the soft mud, and always be wet and cool. And another, that he would plunge from the rocks, and take headers, diving into the deep, cold water, drinking as he dived. And the third, that he would be washed up and down with the rippling waves, living on the land, yet ever in the water. Then the fourth said, 'Verily, you know not how to wish, and I will teach you. I would live in the water all the time, and swim about in it forever.' Now it chanced that these things were said in the hour which, when it passes over the world, all the wishes uttered by men are granted. And so it was with these Indians. For the first became a Leech, the second a Spotted Frog, the third a Crab, which is washed up and down with the tide, and the fourth a Fish. Ere this there had been in all the world none of the creatures which dwell in the water, and now they were there, and of all kinds. And the river came rushing and roaring on, and they all went headlong down to the sea, to be washed into many lands over all the world.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 118-119; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 然後他回到村裡；但他在那裡找不到人——一個也沒有。因為在他離去期間發生了一件奇事，這將在千秋萬代所有印第安人的言語中流傳。因為那些人，正如我所說，是純樸誠實的百姓，他們就像飢餓的孩子那樣，彼此問道：『你想要什麼，你呢？』這些村民也正是這樣說的：『假設你擁有世上所有清涼、新鮮、冒泡、美味的水，你會做什麼？』一個說他願住在柔軟的泥裡，永遠濕潤涼爽。另一個說他願從岩石上躍下，頭朝下扎進深而冷的水中，一邊潛水一邊飲水。第三個說他願隨著漣漪的波浪被沖上沖下，住在陸上，卻總在水裡。接著第四個說：『說真的，你們都不懂得怎麼許願，我來教你們。我願一直住在水裡，永遠在其中游來游去。』恰巧這些話是在那樣一個時辰說出的：當它掠過世界之時，人所許的一切願望都會實現。這些印第安人便是如此。因為第一個變成了水蛭，第二個變成了斑蛙，第三個變成了螃蟹，隨潮水被沖上沖下，第四個變成了魚。在此之前，全世界從未有過任何棲息水中的生靈，如今它們出現了，而且種類繁多。那條河奔騰咆哮而下，它們全都一頭衝向大海，被沖散到全世界的許多地方。

title.en: Glooskap and the Mighty Wasis: The Invincible Baby
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普與偉大的瓦西斯：不敗的嬰兒

region.en: The sunny lodge floor where Wasis sits
region.zh: 瓦西斯安坐的向陽屋地

period: Told by Maria Saksis, Penobscot (Leland 1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How the Lord of Men and Beasts strove with the Mighty Wasis'

summary.en: When Glooskap had conquered all his enemies - the giants and sorcerers, the magicians, Pamola the evil spirit of the night air, all manner of ghosts, witches, devils, cannibals and goblins - he wondered if his work was at an end. 'Not so fast, Master, for there yet remains One whom no one has ever conquered... It is the mighty Wasis, and there he sits; and I warn you that if you meddle with him you will be in sore trouble.' Now Wasis was the Baby, and he sat on the floor sucking a piece of maple-sugar. The Master smiled sweetly, spoke terribly, and at last had recourse to magic - used his most awful spells, and sang the songs which raise the dead and scare the devils. And Wasis sat and looked on admiringly, and seemed to find it very interesting, but all the same he never moved an inch. So Glooskap gave it up in despair, and Wasis went goo! goo! and crowed. And to this day when you see a babe well contented, going goo! goo! and crowing, and no one can tell why, know that it is because he remembers the time when he overcame the Master who had conquered all the world. For of all the beings that have ever been since the beginning, Baby is alone the only invincible one.
summary.zh: 當格魯斯卡普降服了所有敵手——巨人與巫者、術士、夜氣惡靈帕莫拉，以及一切鬼魅巫妖——他自問功成之業是否已畢。「莫急，主人。尚有一位從未被任何人降服者……那便是偉大的瓦西斯；他就坐在那裡。我警告你，若去招惹他，你必大吃苦頭。」瓦西斯就是嬰兒，正坐在地上含著一塊楓糖。主人先是甜笑柔聲，繼而疾言厲色，最後動用法術——唸起最可畏的咒語，唱起能喚死者、懾鬼魅之歌。瓦西斯只是饒有興味地看著，寸步不動。格魯斯卡普只得絕望作罷；瓦西斯坐在陽光裡「咯咯」而笑。至今嬰兒無故咯咯而笑時，那是他記起了戰勝「征服全世界之主」的那一刻——自開天闢地以來，唯有嬰兒是無敵的。

sensitivity.note: Penobscot tale (Leland 1884); public domain. Leland calls its Indian author 'a genius' and dates the tale ancient because it explains the unaccountable crowing of babies.

passages.text: Now it came to pass when Glooskap had conquered all his enemies, even the Kewahqu, who were giants and sorcerers, and the m'teoulin, who were magicians, and the Pamola, who is the evil spirit of the night air, and all manner of ghosts, witches, devils, cannibals, and goblins, that he thought upon what he had done, and wondered if his work was at an end. And he said this to a certain woman. But she replied, 'Not so fast, Master, for there yet remains One whom no one has ever conquered or got the better of in any way, and who will remain unconquered to the end of time.' 'And who is he?' inquired the Master. 'It is the mighty Wasis,' she replied, 'and there he sits; and I warn you that if you meddle with him you will be in sore trouble.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 120-121; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 話說格盧斯卡普征服了他所有的敵人——包括凱瓦庫，那些巨人和巫師；包括姆特烏林，那些魔法師；包括帕莫拉，那夜間空氣中的惡靈；以及形形色色的鬼魂、女巫、魔鬼、食人者和小妖精——之後，他回想自己所做的一切，思忖自己的事業是否已到盡頭。他把這話對一個女人說了。但她回答：『別這麼快下結論，主人，因為還剩下一位，從來沒有人征服過他，也從未有人以任何方式勝過他，他將直到時間的盡頭都未被征服。』『他是誰？』主人問道。『是強大的瓦西斯，』她回答，『他就坐在那裡；我警告你，你若去招惹他，必將陷入大麻煩。』

passages.text: Now Wasis was the Baby. And he sat on the floor sucking a piece of maple-sugar, greatly contented, troubling no one. As the Lord of Men and Beasts had never married or had a child, he knew naught of the way of managing children. Therefore he was quite certain, as is the wont of such people, that he knew all about it. So he turned to Baby with a bewitching smile and bade him come to him. Then Baby smiled again, but did not budge. And the Master spake sweetly and made his voice like that of the summer bird, but it was of no avail, for Wasis sat still and sucked his maple-sugar. Then the Master frowned and spoke terribly, and ordered Wasis to come crawling to him immediately. And Baby burst out into crying and yelling, but did not move for all that.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 121; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 瓦西斯就是那個嬰兒。他坐在地板上吮著一塊楓糖，十分滿足，不擾任何人。由於這人和獸之主從未娶妻生子，他對照料孩子之道一無所知。因此他十分確信——這正是此類人的習性——自己對此無所不知。於是他轉向嬰兒，帶著迷人的微笑，叫他到自己跟前來。嬰兒又笑了笑，卻一動不動。主人甜言蜜語，把聲音弄得像夏日的鳥兒一般，但毫無用處，因為瓦西斯坐著不動，只管吮他的楓糖。於是主人皺起眉頭，厲聲喝令瓦西斯立刻爬到他跟前來。嬰兒放聲大哭大叫，卻依然一動不動。

passages.text: Then, since he could do but one thing more, the Master had recourse to magic. He used his most awful spells, and sang the songs which raise the dead and scare the devils. And Wasis sat and looked on admiringly, and seemed to find it very interesting, but all the same he never moved an inch. So Glooskap gave it up in despair, and Wasis, sitting on the floor in the sunshine, went goo! goo! and crowed. And to this day when you see a babe well contented, going goo! goo! and crowing, and no one can tell why, know that it is because he remembers the time when he overcame the Master who had conquered all the world. For of all the beings that have ever been since the beginning, Baby is alone the only invincible one.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 121-122; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 接著，大師既然只能再做一件事，便求助於魔法。他施展最可怖的咒語，唱起能令死者復生、令魔鬼驚懼的歌。瓦西斯坐著觀看，滿懷欽佩，似乎覺得十分有趣，但儘管如此，他始終紋絲不動。於是格魯斯卡普絕望地放棄了，而瓦西斯坐在陽光下的地板上，發出「咕！咕！」的聲音，咿呀歡叫。直到今日，當你看見一個心滿意足的嬰兒發出「咕！咕！」的聲音、咿呀歡叫，而沒有人能說出箇中緣由時，你要知道，這是因為他記得自己曾制伏那位征服了整個世界的大師。因為自太初以來所有曾經存在的生靈之中，嬰兒是唯一不可戰勝的。

title.en: The Lament for Ur
title.zh: 烏爾哀歌

region.en: Ur, Iraq
region.zh: 烏爾（伊拉克）

period: Isin-Larsa period composition, c. 2000 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The lament for Urim (ETCSL c.2.2.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: When the storm god's wind is unleashed against Ur, the moon god's city falls: the temple desecrated, the people scattered as slaves, mothers and children dying of hunger — and at last Nanna mourns to Enlil and the city is promised restoration.
summary.zh: 暴風之神之風襲向烏爾，月神之城傾覆：神殿被瀆，民眾被虜為奴，母與子飢餓而死——南納終向恩利爾哀告，城池蒙許復興。

sensitivity.note: Ancient city lament; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: On the day the storm's order was given, Ur was smitten: its temple looted, its people herded away as captives, its cattle and grain carried off — the city that knew no enemy is stripped bare. The lament's heart is hunger: mothers shut their doors against their children, the river runs with bodies, and Nanna, the moon god, has wrapped his city in silence and gone by boat to another place. Nanna mourns before Enlil; the god of the storm answers that the decree was his, and Ur shall be restored: kingship returns to the city, the temple rebuilt, the people regathered — mourning becomes prophecy of return.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.2, the destruction; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.2, the hunger; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.2, the restoration promise; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在風暴之令下達的那一日，烏爾遭受打擊：其神廟遭劫掠，其人民被驅趕為俘虜，其牲畜與穀物被奪走——這座從不識敵人的城市被洗劫一空。哀歌的核心是飢餓：母親們閉門不顧自己的孩子，河流漂滿屍體，而月神南納將他的城市裹入寂靜，乘船前往他方。南納在恩利爾面前哀悼；風暴之神回答說，這道詔令出自他手，烏爾必將復興：王權回歸此城，神廟重建，人民重聚——哀悼化為復歸的預言。

functions: Memorial liturgy for the fall of Ur III
Prototype of the city-lament genre
Prophecy text of restoration tied to royal ideology

variants.summary: The wider lament over the whole land's fall.

variants.summary: The same genre for Enlil's city.

primary_sources.citation: ETCSL c.2.2.2, trans. ETCSL team (2003-2006), lines 1-436

title.en: The Lament for Sumer and Ur
title.zh: 蘇美與烏爾哀歌

region.en: Sumer, southern Iraq
region.zh: 蘇美，南伊拉克

period: Isin-Larsa period composition, c. 2000 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The lament for Sumer and Urim (ETCSL c.2.2.3)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The whole land is visited by the flood-storm: city after city falls — Uruk, Lagash, Umma, Shuruppak — the temples emptied, the land made a wilderness, until the gods restore Sumer and the cities sing again.
summary.zh: 洪水暴風席捲全境：烏魯克、拉加什、烏瑪、舒魯帕克相繼陷落，神殿空虛，大地化為荒野——直至眾神復興蘇美，諸城再啟歡歌。

sensitivity.note: Ancient city lament; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The flood-storm comes on the land by the gods' decree: city after city is named and smitten — Uruk, Lagash, Umma, Shuruppak — temples emptied, houses burned, the black-headed people scattered like sheep. The lament catalogs each city's ruin, then turns: the gods restore Sumer, kingship returns to Ur, and the land is promised the days of abundance again — the lament closes in blessing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.3, the storm over the land; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.3, restoration; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 洪水風暴依諸神之詔降臨大地：一座又一座城市被點名並遭受打擊——烏魯克、拉格什、烏瑪、舒魯帕克——神廟被清空，房屋被焚燒，黑頭之人如羊群般四散。哀歌逐一記述各城的毀滅，隨後轉折：諸神復興蘇美，王權回歸烏爾，大地再度被許以豐饒之日——哀歌以祝福作結。

functions: Widest city lament: memorial of the land's fall
Restoration prophecy embedded in liturgy
Performed in the lament festivals of the Isin restoration

variants.name: The lament for Urim
variants.summary: The single-city lament of the same fall.

primary_sources.work: The lament for Sumer and Urim
primary_sources.citation: ETCSL c.2.2.3, trans. ETCSL team (2003-2006), lines 1-397

title.en: The Lament for Nippur
title.zh: 尼普魯哀歌

region.en: Nippur, Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian composition, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The lament for Nibru (ETCSL c.2.2.4)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The storm reaches even Enlil's own city: the Ekur defiled, its rites silenced, the shepherd's flock scattered — and Enlil, whom no city may accuse, must be petitioned to restore his own house.
summary.zh: 暴風竟及恩利爾之城：埃庫爾被瀆、祭儀止息、牧群四散——無人可責之神，須被懇求復興其殿。

sensitivity.note: Ancient city lament; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The storm visits even Nippur: the Ekur defiled, its hymns silenced, its priests scattered; Enlil's own city learns what ruin is. The petition to Enlil is unique in the genre: no god may be accused, so the lament asks the offended lord himself to remember his house — and the restoration of the Ekur restores the world's axis.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.4, the ruin; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.4, the petition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 風暴甚至降臨尼普爾：埃庫爾遭褻瀆，其讚歌沉寂，其祭司四散；恩利爾自己的城市也領略了何謂毀滅。向恩利爾的請願在此類文體中獨樹一幟：不得控告任何神祇，因此哀歌懇求這位受冒犯的主宰親自記念他的居所——而埃庫爾的復興即恢復世界的軸心。

functions: Lament for the sanctuary of sanctuaries
Theology of petition without accusation

variants.summary: The lament of the oldest city.

title.en: The Lament for Eridu
title.zh: 埃利都哀歌

region.en: Eridu, Iraq
region.zh: 埃利都（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian composition, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The lament for Eridug (ETCSL c.2.2.6)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The oldest city, Enki's own, is smitten: the Abzu defiled, wisdom's house emptied — and the lament mourns the first city as mourning one's own mother.
summary.zh: 最古老的城、恩基之城遭劫：阿卜祖被瀆，智慧之殿空虛——哀歌以悼母之情悼第一城。

sensitivity.note: Ancient city lament; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Eridu, the first of cities, Enki's own seat, is smitten by the storm: the Abzu defiled, wisdom's house emptied, the rites of the oldest temple silenced. The lament mourns the first city as a mother; its restoration is the renewal of the world's beginning — when Eridu lives again, the order of things is re-founded.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.6, the ruin; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.6, the restoration; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 埃利都，眾城之首，恩基自己的居所，遭受風暴打擊：阿普蘇遭褻瀆，智慧之屋被清空，最古老神廟的儀式沉寂。哀歌如母親般哀悼這第一座城；它的復興即是世界之始的更新——當埃利都重獲生機，萬物的秩序便重新奠定。

functions: Lament for the first city and its sanctuary
Restoration theology anchored in origins

title.en: The Lament for Unug
title.zh: 烏魯克哀歌

region.en: Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian composition, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The lament for Unug (ETCSL c.2.2.5)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The city of Inanna and Gilgamesh falls to the storm; the Eanna is defiled and its people scattered — the lament petitions the goddess herself to restore her own city, and Uruk's renewal is promised.
summary.zh: 伊南娜與吉爾伽美什之城遭暴風之劫：埃安那被瀆，民眾四散——哀歌向女神本身祈求復興其城，烏魯克之新生蒙許。

sensitivity.note: Ancient city lament; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The storm falls on Unug, city of Inanna and Gilgamesh: the Eanna defiled, its people scattered, the city of the great wall emptied by decree. The lament petitions the lady of the city herself — she who was smitten must smite back the ruin — and Unug's renewal is promised with her restoration of the Eanna.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.5, the ruin; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.5, the petition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 風暴降臨烏努格，伊南娜與吉爾伽美什之城：埃安納遭褻瀆，其人民四散，這座擁有偉大城牆的城市依詔令被清空。哀歌向這座城市的女主本人請願——遭受打擊的她必須反擊毀滅——而烏努格的更新被許諾，伴隨她對埃安納的復興。

functions: Lament of the Inanna city
Liturgical petition to the city goddess

title.en: The Sumerian King List: Kingship from Heaven
title.zh: 蘇美王表：王權自天而降

region.en: Nippur (compilation site), Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯（編纂地，伊拉克）

period: Compiled OB, based on older lists, c. 1800 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The Sumerian king list (ETCSL c.2.1.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Kingship was lowered from heaven: in the five cities before the flood, eight kings reigned fantastic reigns of tens of thousands of years until the flood swept them; afterwards kingship came again to Kish and passed through the dynasties down to Isin.
summary.zh: 王權自天而降：洪水之前五城八王，在位動輒數萬年；洪水掃盡其後，王權復臨基什，歷經諸朝，傳至伊辛。

sensitivity.note: Ancient historiographical myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: When kingship was lowered from heaven, it was in Eridug: Alulim reigned 28,800 years, Alalgar 36,000 — five cities, eight kings, five sars and more, until the flood swept over the land and kingship was taken to heaven. After the flood kingship came again from on high, to Kish first: long reigns shorten through the dynasties — Kish, Uruk, Ur, Akkad, and again Uruk and Ur — each dynasty named, each king given his years, until the list closes with the kings of Isin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.1.1, antediluvian section; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.1.1, postdiluvian dynasties; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當王權自天而降時，它位於埃里杜格：阿魯利姆在位二萬八千八百年，阿拉爾加在位三萬六千年——五座城、八位王、五個薩爾有餘，直到洪水漫過大地，王權被帶回天上。洪水之後，王權再度自高處降下，首先來到基什：漫長的統治在諸王朝間逐漸縮短——基什、烏魯克、烏爾、阿卡德，又再度是烏魯克與烏爾——每個王朝皆被具名，每位王皆被賦予其年數，直到名單以伊辛的諸王作結。

functions: Political charter: kingship as heaven-given office
Historiographical frame linking flood, dynasties and legitimacy
Reference text for scribal schools and chronicles

variants.summary: The Babylonian priest's version of the antediluvian reigns.

variants.summary: The longest surviving manuscript of the list.

title.en: The Rulers of Lagash
title.zh: 拉加什諸王

region.en: Lagash, Iraq
region.zh: 拉加什（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian compilation of Ur III-Isin records, c. 1800 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The rulers of Lagas (ETCSL c.2.1.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: A dynastic list in which Lagash's rulers — Ur-Nanshe's line, Gudea's house, the soldier kings of the Gutian interlude — are remembered with their deeds, buildings and wars: city history as sacred memory.
summary.zh: 拉加什王朝記：烏爾南什之系、古蒂亞之家、庫提人插曲中的戰士王——以功業、建築與戰事載入記憶：城邦史即神聖記憶。

sensitivity.note: Ancient chronicle; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The rulers of Lagash are remembered dynasty by dynasty: Ur-Nanshe who built the temples, Gudea who saw his god in a dream, the kings who warred with Umma over the boundary — each reign measured by deeds and buildings. The list closes with the restoration kings, whose piety returned Lagash's worship to its gods — city history told as a sacred ledger of justice and building.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.1.2, the dynasties; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.1.2, the close; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 拉格什的統治者按王朝被銘記：興建神廟的烏爾南舍，於夢中得見其神的古地亞，為邊界與烏瑪交戰的諸王——每一朝皆以其事蹟與建築來衡量。名單以復興諸王作結，他們的虔敬使拉格什的崇拜復歸於其諸神——城的歷史被述說為一部關於正義與營建的聖帳。

functions: City dynastic chronicle
Charter of Lagash's temple-building legitimacy

variants.name: Gudea cylinders A and B
variants.summary: The narrative expansion of Gudea's reign.

primary_sources.citation: ETCSL c.2.1.2, trans. ETCSL team (2003-2006)

title.en: The Death of Ur-Namma
title.zh: 烏爾納瑪之死

region.en: Ur, Iraq
region.zh: 烏爾（伊拉克）

period: Ur III composition, c. 2100 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The death of Ur-Namma (ETCSL c.2.4.1.x)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Ur-Namma, the king who built the ziggurat and gave the land its laws, dies in battle; his son mourns him, and the king descends to the netherworld where the dead come out to greet him as their lord — a royal descent poem of consolation.
summary.zh: 建神塔、定律法之王烏爾納瑪戰場殞身；其子哀悼，國王下冥，亡者出迎其主——一首慰藉性的王室冥界詩。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary literature; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Ur-Namma, who built the temple and gave the land its measures and laws, falls in battle; his son Shulgi mourns: the shepherd is taken, the city's father is gone. The king descends to the netherworld, and the dead come out to greet him as their lord: he is given his seat among the shades, and his offerings are appointed — the king in the land of the dead keeps his kingdom's order.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.4.1.2, the death; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.4.1.2, the descent; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 烏爾南瑪，興建神廟並為大地立下度量與律法者，戰死沙場；其子舒爾吉哀悼：牧者被奪去，城之父已逝。王降入冥界，亡者出來迎接他為其主：他在幽影之間獲賜其座，其祭品亦被規定——身處亡者之地的王仍維繫其王國的秩序。

functions: Royal funerary liturgy of the Ur III founder
Theology of the dead king's netherworld reign
Charter of continuing royal offerings

variants.summary: The heroic prototype of the dead king's enthronement.

title.en: Shulgi's Run from Nippur to Ur
title.zh: 舒爾吉尼普魯烏爾長跑

region.en: Nippur to Ur, Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯至烏爾（伊拉克）

period: Ur III composition, c. 2100 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A hymn to Inana (Shulgi cycle, ETCSL c.2.4.2.x)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Shulgi boasts that in one day he ran from Nippur to Ur — a hundred miles through the storm — to bring offerings on the New Year; the self-deified king measures his kingship in feats: the run, the writing, the justice.
summary.zh: 舒爾吉自誇一日之間自尼普魯奔至烏爾——穿越風暴的百里之程——為新年奉上祭品；自神化的國王以功業丈量王權：長跑、書寫、正義。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Shulgi, king of Ur, boasts: I ran in the storm from Nippur to Ur in a single day, through the teeming rain, and brought the offerings of the New Year with my own hands. The king's litany of feats continues: I learned the scribal art from the tablet-house, I know the songs and the games, I judge the land's cases with justice — the deified king as the complete man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.4.2.2, the run; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.4.2.2, the litany; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 烏爾之王舒爾吉誇口：我在風暴中一日之內從尼普爾奔至烏爾，穿過滂沱大雨，親手帶來新年的祭品。王的事蹟連禱繼續：我從書板之家習得書吏之藝，我通曉歌謠與競技，我以正義裁斷大地之訟——被奉為神的王作為完備之人。

functions: Manifesto of royal deification in the Ur III state
Charter of the New Year offering journey
School text of the royal-hymn genre

variants.name: Shulgi A (the self-praise)
variants.summary: The companion hymn of the king's praise.

title.en: Shulgi the Learned King
title.zh: 博學之王舒爾吉

region.en: Ur, Iraq
region.zh: 烏爾（伊拉克）

period: Ur III composition, c. 2100 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A praise poem of Shulgi (Shulgi cycle, ETCSL c.2.4.2.x)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Shulgi praises himself as the son of Ninsun's line: learned in every scribal art, master of music and games, judge of the land — the king as literate demi-god whose praise was copied in schools for centuries.
summary.zh: 舒爾吉自頌為寧蓀後裔：通曉書吏百藝、精於樂藝棋戲、審判全土——身為有學半神之王的讚歌，為校中傳抄數百年。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Shulgi, king of Ur, claims the pedigree of heroes: born of the line of Ninsun, nourished by Ninlil, he is the lord whom the great gods raised to shepherding the land. His learning is the boast of a new age: from the tablet-house he learned the scribal art entire — Sumerian and the foreign tongue, the songs and the calculations — and the schools copied his praise for centuries after his death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.4.2.1, pedigree; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.4.2.1, the learning; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 烏爾之王舒爾吉自稱承襲英雄的血統：出身於寧松之系，由寧利爾哺育，他是偉大諸神擢升以牧養大地的主。他的學識是新時代的誇耀：他從書板之家習得書吏之藝的全部——蘇美爾語與外邦之語、歌謠與計算——而在他死後數百年間，學校仍抄錄對他的讚頌。

functions: Canonization of the deified king in school curricula
Ideology of the literate king

variants.summary: The companion hymn of the king's feats.

title.en: Iddin-Dagan's Bride of the New Year
title.zh: 伊丁達甘的新娘慶典

region.en: Isin, Iraq
region.zh: 伊辛（伊拉克）

period: Isin dynasty composition, c. 1900 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A hymn to Inana for Iddin-Dagan (Iddin-Dagan A, ETCSL c.2.5.3.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The morning of Inanna's festival: the goddess bathed and perfumed takes the hymn's stage — her assembling of the land, the sacred marriage bed prepared, the king blessed — the great liturgy of the goddess as bride of the city.
summary.zh: 伊南娜慶典之晨：沐浴敷香的女神登台——她召集全境、備妥聖婚之床、祝福國王——女神身為城邦新娘的偉大祭儀。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cult hymn with sexual imagery in ritual register; presented as literature.

passages.text: On the morning of the festival, Inanna bathes and perfumes herself and takes her seat; the land assembles to her, the stars bow to the morning star, and the city is dressed for her advent. The bed is prepared with the king: the goddess claims her lord for the night of the sacred marriage, and through the union the year's abundance is secured for Isin — the rite sung as the goddess's bride-gift to the land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.5.3.1, the advent; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.5.3.1, the marriage; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 節慶之晨，伊南娜沐浴並以香膏塗身，然後就座；大地向她聚集，眾星向晨星俯首，城邑為她的蒞臨而盛裝。床榻與王一同備妥：女神為聖婚之夜認取其主，藉此結合，伊辛得以確保一年的豐饒——此儀式被歌詠為女神獻予大地的聘禮。

functions: Liturgy of the sacred marriage at Isin
Charter of the year's abundance through the royal union
Masterpiece of cult love-lyric

variants.summary: The Uruk cult song of the same rite.

title.en: Gudea's Dream of Ningirsu
title.zh: 古蒂亞夢見寧吉爾蘇

region.en: Lagash, Iraq
region.zh: 拉加什（伊拉克）

period: Gudea Cylinder A, c. 2100 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Gudea Cylinder A (ETCSL c.2.3.2.x)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: In a dream a giant stands by Gudea's bed — a winged storm bird at his feet, a woman with a stylus, a youth with a cornerstone — and the dream is read: Ningirsu orders his temple built, and the ruler obeys to the letter.
summary.zh: 夢中巨神立於古蒂亞榻旁——足下振翅的暴風鳥、執書板的女子、持奠基石的少年——夢解為命：寧吉爾蘇命其建殿，統治者依夢而行。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal inscription narrative; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In his dream a giant stands by Gudea's bed, head to heaven; at his feet a winged storm bird, beside him a woman holding a lapis stylus and tablet, and a youth holding a cornerstone slab — the ruler wakes troubled and seeks the dream's meaning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.3.2.1, the dream; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在他的夢中，一名巨人立於古迪亞的床邊，頭頂及天；在他腳邊有一隻帶翼的風暴之鳥，在他身旁有一名女子手持青金石筆與泥板，還有一名青年手持奠基石板——這位統治者醒來後心神不寧，尋求此夢的意涵。

passages.text: Nanshe, lady of divination, reads it: the giant is Ningirsu, who orders his temple built; the storm bird is his weapon; the woman is Nisaba who will draw the plan. Gudea obeys: the temple Eninnu is begun exactly as the dream showed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.3.2.1, the interpretation; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 占卜女神南舍為他解讀此夢：巨人是寧吉爾蘇，他命令為其興建神廟；風暴之鳥是他的武器；女子是將繪製圖則的尼薩巴。古迪亞遵從：神廟埃寧努便完全按照夢中所現開始興建。

functions: Charter of royal building as obedience to dream revelation
Detailed liturgy of temple construction
Cult myth of Ningirsu's Eninnu at Girsu

title.en: Gudea's Temple Completed and Consecrated
title.zh: 古蒂亞建殿功成

region.en: Girsu, Iraq
region.zh: 吉爾蘇（伊拉克）

period: Gudea Cylinder B, c. 2100 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Gudea Cylinder B (ETCSL c.2.3.2.x)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The temple Eninnu rises: materials gathered from every land, the foundations laid on the morning of propitious days, the god installed with a seven-day festival — and the land rests in abundance, the year of the temple's dedication blessed.
summary.zh: 埃寧努神殿落成：建材自萬邦匯聚，擇吉晨奠基，七日慶典迎神入殿——國土休養生息，獻殿之年受福。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal inscription narrative; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Materials come from every land for the Eninnu: cedar from the mountains, gold and lapis from far countries, and the foundations are laid on the propitious morning the omens chose. Ningirsu is installed with a seven-day festival; the land rests, taxes are remitted, and the temple's year is blessed — Gudea's piety rewarded with abundance for Lagash.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.3.2.2, the building; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.3.2.2, the consecration; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 為埃寧努而來的材料來自各地：山中的雪松、遠方的黃金與青金石，而地基則在徵兆所選定的吉晨奠定。寧吉爾蘇以七日慶典安座；土地休養，賦稅豁免，神廟之年蒙受祝福——古迪亞的虔敬為拉格什換來了豐饒。

functions: Consecration liturgy of the Eninnu temple
World-renewal theology of temple dedication
Charter of the pious builder king

title.en: A Hymn to Inana for Hammurabi
title.zh: 漢謨拉比之伊南娜頌

region.en: Babylon, Iraq
region.zh: 巴比倫（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian composition, c. 1750 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A hymn to Inana for Hammu-rabi (ETCSL c.2.8.2.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The Babylonian dynasty's king is praised in Sumerian: Inana, lady of battle, is hymned in her thunder and beauty, and Hammurabi named her favorite — the old south's language put to work for a new empire's king.
summary.zh: 巴比倫王朝之王以蘇美語受頌：戰爭女神伊南娜之雷霆與美麗入詩，漢謨拉比列名其寵——舊邦之語，為新帝之王所用。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Inana is hymned in her double nature: the terror of battle whose heart is storm, and the beauty whose grace fills the temples — the goddess of both war and desire. The hymn names Hammurabi her chosen: the king of Babylon, beloved of the lady, under whose justice the land finds order — Sumerian sung for a new empire's ruler.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.8.2.1, the goddess; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.8.2.1, the king; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊南娜以其雙重本性受頌讚：既是心懷風暴、令人畏懼的戰鬥，也是優雅之美充盈神廟——她既是戰爭女神，也是慾望女神。頌歌稱漢摩拉比為她所選：巴比倫之王，受這位女士所鍾愛，在他的正義之下，土地得享秩序——這是一首為新帝國統治者而唱的蘇美爾之歌。

functions: Royal legitimacy hymn in the old language
Continuity of the Inanna hymn genre under Babylon

variants.summary: The Isin dynasty's hymn of the same goddess.

title.en: The Kes Temple Hymn
title.zh: 克什神殿頌

region.en: Kes, Iraq
region.zh: 克什（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The Kes temple hymn (ETCSL c.4.80.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The house of Ninhursag at Kes is praised as the mother-temple of the land: the birthplace of kingship's blessings, its rites deep as the Abzu — the hymn copied as a school masterpiece for a thousand years.
summary.zh: 克什的寧鬍爾薩格神殿被頌為國土之母殿：王權祝福的誕生地，其祭儀深如阿卜祖——千年間為校中傳抄之名篇。

sensitivity.note: Ancient temple hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The house of Kes, great house of Ninhursag, is praised: the mother-temple where the land's blessings are born, whose rites are deep as the Abzu and whose brickwork rises like the hills. The hymn closes with the temple's charter: whoever honors the house of the mother goddess is blessed with kingship's favor — a school masterpiece copied for a millennium.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.80.2, the temple's praise; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.80.2, the close; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 凱什之屋，寧胡爾薩格的大屋，受到頌讚：這是大地祝福誕生的母神廟，其儀式深如阿普蘇，其磚砌如丘陵般聳立。頌歌以神廟的憲章作結：凡敬奉母神之屋者，必蒙王權之恩寵——這是一部被抄傳千年的學校傑作。

functions: Classic of the temple-hymn genre
Charter of the mother goddess's sanctuary

title.en: The Temple Hymns of All Sumer
title.zh: 蘇美諸神殿頌

region.en: From Eridu to Nippur and Lagash, Iraq
region.zh: 自埃利都至尼普魯與拉加什（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript of an older cycle, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The temple hymns (ETCSL c.4.80.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Forty-two temples from Eridu's Abzu shrine to Nippur's Ekur and Lagash's Eninnu are praised in order: a liturgical map of the land's sanctuaries, city by city, god by god.
summary.zh: 自埃利都阿卜祖神殿至尼普魯埃庫爾、拉加什埃寧努，四十二座神殿依序受頌：一座聖所的禮儀地圖，城以城計、神以神名。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn cycle; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The cycle praises forty-two temples in order: Eridu's house on the Abzu, Nippur's Ekur the navel of the land, Uruk's Eanna, Ur's house of Nanna, Girsu's Eninnu — city by city, god by god. The map's order is theological: the temples are sung as stations of the world's order, each house holding its god's portion of the land's life — a liturgical geography of Sumer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.80.1, the cycle; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.80.1, the geography; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這組頌歌依次讚頌四十二座神廟：埃利都位於阿普蘇之上的屋宇、尼普爾的大地之臍埃庫爾、烏魯克的埃安納、烏爾的南納之屋、吉爾蘇的埃寧努——一城接一城，一神接一神。這幅地圖的次序是神學性的：諸神廟被歌頌為世界秩序的站點，每一座屋宇承載其神祇在大地生命中的一份——這是蘇美爾的禮儀地理。

functions: Liturgical map of Sumer's sanctuaries
Charter of each temple's cultic identity

variants.name: The Kes temple hymn
variants.summary: The most celebrated single member of the cycle.

primary_sources.citation: ETCSL c.4.80.1, trans. ETCSL team (2003-2006), lines 1-310

title.en: The Ekur: House of the Mountain
title.zh: 埃庫爾：山之殿

region.en: Nippur, Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A hymn to the Ekur (ETCSL c.4.80.4)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Enlil's temple is praised as the bond of heaven and earth: its foundations in the underworld, its crown in the sky, the place where the fates are decreed — the world's axis in brick and song.
summary.zh: 恩利爾之殿被頌為天地之紐帶：根基入冥界，頂冠接天穹，命運裁定之所——以磚石與頌歌築成的世界之軸。

sensitivity.note: Ancient temple hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The Ekur is praised as the bond of heaven and earth: its foundations reach the underworld, its crown touches the sky, and within it the fates of the land are decreed. The hymn names the temple the place of Enlil's speech: what he says in the Ekur stands — the world's axis sung in brick and ritual.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.80.4, the praise; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.80.4, the decree; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 埃庫爾被頌讚為天地之紐帶：其地基直達冥界，其頂冠觸及蒼穹，境內諸般命運皆在其中裁定。此頌歌稱此神廟為恩利爾言語之所：他在埃庫爾所言者皆立定不移——以磚石與儀式歌詠而出的世界軸心。

functions: Theology of the Ekur as world axis
Liturgical praise of the fates-decreeing house

variants.summary: The god's hymn matching the temple's.

title.en: The Instructions of Shuruppak
title.zh: 舒魯帕克訓言

region.en: Shuruppak, Iraq
region.zh: 舒魯帕克（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript of an older text, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The instructions of Suruppag (ETCSL c.5.6.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The antediluvian sage Shuruppak teaches his son Ziudsura the maxims of life — do not buy a wild ass, do not locate a field on the road, do not curse — the oldest instruction text, father to the wisdom books of the whole Near East.
summary.zh: 洪水前的賢者舒魯帕克訓其子祖蘇德拉處世箴言——勿購野驢、勿於路旁置田、勿咒罵——最古老的訓言文獻，近東智慧書之祖。

sensitivity.note: Ancient wisdom literature; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Shuruppak, son of Ubar-Tutu, speaks to his son Ziudsura: the instructions of the father to the son — a name to be given, a mouth to be held, a heart not to be trusted to strangers. The maxims follow: do not locate a field on the road; do not buy a wild ass; do not swear; do not revile; do not lie in the assembly — the practical wisdom of the antediluvian sage that schools copied for two millennia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.6.1, the frame; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.6.1, the maxims; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 舒魯帕克，烏巴爾—圖圖之子，對其子齊烏蘇德拉說道：父對子的教誨——當受之名，當守之口，不可將心託付於陌生人。格言隨之而來：勿在路旁置田；勿買野驢；勿妄立誓；勿出惡言；勿在集會中說謊——此乃洪水前賢者的實用智慧，學校抄習達兩千年之久。

functions: Oldest wisdom instruction text
Ancestor of the Near Eastern instruction genre
School curriculum masterpiece

title.en: The Farmer's Instructions
title.zh: 農夫訓言

region.en: Fields of Sumer, Iraq
region.zh: 蘇美田野（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The farmer's instructions (ETCSL c.5.6.3)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The god of agriculture instructs a farmer through the year: plough at the right time, let the flood come, guard the seed, harvest before the storm — the complete agronomy of Sumer in the form of a god's advice.
summary.zh: 農耕之神訓誡農夫一年之事：適時犁地、候洪水至、守種防鳥、風暴前收割——以神諭形式寫成的蘇美農學全書。

sensitivity.note: Ancient instruction text; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The agricultural god instructs the farmer through the year: plough when the land is ready, let the flood-water come, keep the seed from the birds, harvest before the storms of the year's end. The text closes with blessing: the farmer who follows the instructions shall fill the temple's granaries — agronomy taught as divine advice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.6.3, the instruction; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.6.3, the close; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 農神教導農夫一年之中的耕作：土地就緒時便犁耕，任洪水漫來，護種子免受鳥啄，於歲末風暴之前收割。全文以祝福作結：遵循教誨的農夫必將裝滿神廟的穀倉——農學以神聖勸誡的形式傳授。

functions: Agronomy in instruction form
School text linking farming and liturgy

title.en: The Three Ox-Drivers from Adab
title.zh: 阿達布三趕牛人

region.en: Adab, Iraq
region.zh: 阿達布（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The three ox-drivers from Adab (ETCSL c.5.6.5)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Three ox-drivers from Adab dispute over one ox — each claims it — and the case is argued with proverb and precedent until the beast is shared: an early literature of dispute settled by wit.
summary.zh: 阿達布三名趕牛人爭一頭牛，各執一詞；以諺語與先例相辯，最後分牛了事——以機智了結爭端的早期文學。

sensitivity.note: Ancient humor text; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Three ox-drivers of Adab each claim the same ox; their dispute is argued in proverbs and precedents, each man proving his right with a saying of the fathers. The case is settled by division rather than victory — the ox shared — and the tale closes laughing at the wit that ends what strength could not: an early literature of dispute settled by cleverness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.6.5, the dispute; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.6.5, the settlement; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿達布的三名趕牛人各自聲稱擁有同一頭牛；他們的爭執以諺語與先例辯論，各人以父輩的格言證明自己的權利。此案以分配而非勝負了結——牛由眾人共享——故事最後嘲笑那以機智終結力量所不能終結之事者：這是早期以聰慧平息爭端的文學。

functions: Humorous dispute tale of legal wit
School text of proverb argumentation

title.en: The Elegy for Nannaya
title.zh: 南納雅輓歌

region.en: Nippur, Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: An elegy on the death of Nannaya (ETCSL c.5.5.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Nannaya, young scribe of the tablet-house, is taken by the underworld's fate; the elegy mourns him at the funeral — the bier, the mourning women, the procession — and consoles with the memory of his learning and love.
summary.zh: 書屋少年書記南納雅被冥界奪去；輓歌於葬禮哀悼——靈床、哭喪婦、送葬行列——以其學問與情愛之憶為慰。

sensitivity.note: Ancient elegy; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Nannaya, the young scribe of the tablet-house, is taken by fate; the elegy mourns him at the funeral procession — the bier carried, the mourning women keening, the friends following. The consolation is memory: his learning, his love, his brightness among the students — and the underworld addressed as the household that now receives him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.5.2, the mourning; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.5.2, the consolation; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 南納亞，書板館的年輕書吏，被命運奪去；輓歌在送葬行列中哀悼他——棺架抬行，哀哭的婦女悲號，友人們隨行其後。慰藉在於記憶：他的學識、他的仁愛、他在學生之間的聰慧光采——而冥界則被稱作如今接納他的家戶。

functions: Personal elegy of the scribal world
Liturgical model of funeral mourning

title.en: The Elegy for Nawirtum
title.zh: 娜薇爾圖姆輓歌

region.en: Nippur, Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: An elegy on the death of Nawirtum (ETCSL c.5.5.3)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Nawirtum, the beloved of the poem's speaker, is taken young; the elegy mourns her with the imagery of the barren house and the wedding song now silenced — love's grief in the voice of the tablet-house.
summary.zh: 詩人的心上人娜薇爾圖姆早逝；輓歌以空寂之宅與戛然而止的婚歌哀悼她——書屋之聲裡的愛之慟。

sensitivity.note: Ancient elegy; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Nawirtum is taken young, and the elegy mourns her in the imagery of the silenced wedding song: the house barren, the bed unslept, the streets she graced now empty. The speaker's grief answers the underworld directly — why was she taken before her time? — and the consolation offered is the memory of love: she is not forgotten while the song is sung.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.5.3, the mourning; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.5.3, the grief; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 納維爾圖姆英年早逝，輓歌以婚歌沉寂的意象哀悼她：屋舍空寂，床榻無人共眠，她曾增輝的街道如今空蕩。說話者的悲痛直接質問冥界——為何她未及天年便被奪去？——所給予的慰藉是愛的記憶：只要歌聲仍唱，她便不被遺忘。

functions: Love-elegy of the scribal world
Liturgical model of mourning a beloved

title.en: An Axe for Nergal
title.zh: 獻內爾伽勒之斧

region.en: Kutha, Iraq
region.zh: 庫薩（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: An axe for Nergal (ETCSL c.5.7.3)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: A votive text presenting a new axe to the dread god: the smith's work praised, the god's terror described, and the offering's purpose spelled — appeasement of the lord of plague through gift.
summary.zh: 向可畏之神獻新斧之還願文：讚頌工匠之作、描摹神之威怖、陳明獻禮之意——以禮物撫慰瘟疫之主。

sensitivity.note: Ancient votive text; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: A new axe is presented to Nergal: the smith's work praised in its cutting edge and weight, the god's terror named — lord of the plague wind and the battle's heat. The offering's purpose is spelled: appease the dread lord, turn his face from the city, keep the plague away — gift as negotiation with the god of misfortune.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.7.3, the gift; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.7.3, the purpose; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一把新斧被呈献给涅伽尔：颂扬铁匠的工艺，赞其锋刃与重量，并道出这位神祇的威怖之名——瘟疫之风与战火之热的主宰。献祭的目的被明言：安抚这位可畏之主，使他的脸转离此城，令瘟疫远离——以献礼与这位厄运之神交涉。

functions: Votive offering text of appeasement
Document of the plague god's cult logic

title.en: A Dog for Nintinuga
title.zh: 獻寧提努加之犬

region.en: Nippur, Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A dog for Nintinuga (ETCSL c.5.7.2)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: A votive text presenting a dog to the healing goddess: the animal as guardian of the sick-room and image of the goddess's own protective hounds — healing offered through symbol.
summary.zh: 向療癒女神獻犬之還願文：犬為病室之衛、女神護犬之像——以象徵奉獻療癒。

sensitivity.note: Ancient votive text; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: A dog is presented to Nintinuga, the healing goddess whose hounds guard the sick-room; the votive text praises the animal as image of the goddess's own protective pack. The offering asks the goddess to guard her suppliant as her dogs guard the sick — healing mediated by symbol and pack.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.7.2, the gift; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.7.2, the petition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一只狗被呈献给宁提努伽，这位治愈女神，她的猎犬守护着病房；这篇还愿铭文赞颂此兽为女神自身护佑之群的写照。献祭祈求女神守护她的祈求者，一如她的犬守护病人——以象征与群体为中介的治愈。

functions: Votive text of the healing cult
Document of the goddess's hound iconography

title.en: The Wasp and His Wife
title.zh: 馬蜂與其妻

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 38

summary.en: A bragging mother offers her daughter to the best singer, dancer, archer, and best-dressed suitor in turn, and the girl laughs them all off — until the Wasp's glittering blue kaross wins her. He feeds her on spiders and grubs; when she mocks his thin body, he shoots her dead on the spot. So the mother got the payment for all her parading.
summary.zh: 誇口之母輪流以「最善歌者」「最善舞者」「最善射者」「最美衣者」許嫁其女，女皆笑而拒之——直至馬蜂之閃爍藍裘得之。他以蛛與蛹飼妻；妻譏其瘦軀，他即射殺之。母之炫燿，報應如此。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; contains domestic violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 38 (1920); not verbatim. The mother's greatest amusement was to praise her children in their faces before others... she offered the girl to the one who could sing the most beautifully. Cricket came singing, Sunbeetle came singing, Owl came singing, Wolf and Jackal came singing; but the girl, to the great consternation of the mother, burst out laughing and mocked the singers to their faces.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 38; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 据 von Wielligh 第二卷第38号（1920年）压缩转述；非逐字照录。母亲最大的乐事，便是在他人面前当面夸赞自己的孩子……她提出将女儿许给唱得最美的人。蟋蟀唱着来了，太阳甲虫唱着来了，猫头鹰唱着来了，狼与豺唱着来了；可那女孩却令母亲大为惊愕地放声大笑，当面嘲弄这些歌者。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Another time she offered the girl to the one who danced the most finely: Frog danced, Springbok, Hare, Snake, Partridge, Tortoise — and again the girl sat and laughed the whole lot of dancers in their faces. Then again: the one who could shoot the neatest with an arrow should have her; and Honeybee shot, Mosquito shot, Gnat, Blindfly and Flea shot — and the company scattered with smarting eyes.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 38; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 压缩转述，同一出处；非逐字照录。又一次，她提出将女儿许给舞得最精妙的人：青蛙舞了，跳羚、野兔、蛇、鹧鸪、乌龟——而那女孩又一次坐着，当面把这一整群舞者都笑了。接着又是：能以箭射得最精准的人便可得她；蜜蜂射了，蚊子射了，蚋、盲蝇与跳蚤射了——众人便揉着刺痛的眼睛四散而去。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Then the mother said the one with the most beautiful kaross could have her daughter: Moth came with his, Mouse, Lizard, Sugarbird, Zebra, Mongoose — and Wasp with his; and they opened their karosses to show how beautiful they were — only Wasp did not. The girl promised solemnly not to laugh, and her choice fell on the glittering blue kaross of Wasp; they went together to his clay house with its many chambers. But he caught only caterpillars, worms and spiders; when she saw his thin body and laughed 'so that is why you never took your kaross off!', he shot her dead on the spot.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 38; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 压缩转述，同一出处；非逐字照录。接着母亲说，拥有最美 kaross（皮披）的人可得她的女儿：飞蛾带着他的来了，老鼠、蜥蜴、食蜜鸟、斑马、獴——还有黄蜂带着他的；他们纷纷展开各自的 kaross 以显其美——唯独黄蜂没有。女孩郑重许诺不笑，她的选择落在了黄蜂那件闪亮的蓝色 kaross 上；他们一同前往他那有许多房间的泥屋。可他只捕毛虫、蠕虫与蜘蛛；当她看见他瘦削的身体，笑道「原来这就是你从不脱下 kaross 的缘故！」，他当场将她射死。

title.en: Mother Lion and the Stolen Children
title.zh: 母獅與被擄之童

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 39

summary.en: The old lions catch Bushman children alive at the water-pool; a decoy 'woman' dancing under a tree lures father Lion to his death by poisoned arrows. Mother Lion raises the stolen children, feeding them a forgetful fruit, hunting with them in the night; a brave Bushman feeds them charm-wood, and each remembers: 'Your parents' fire burns under that krans — see the smoke!' She weeps her grey age; the parents spring out of their skins for joy.
summary.zh: 老獅於池邊活捕桑童；假「婦人」於樹下起舞誘雄獅至，毒箭斃之。母獅養被擄之童，飼以忘憂之果，夜率其獵。勇桑人以巫木飼之，眾童記憶復甦：「爾父母之火燃於彼崖下——見煙乎！」。母獅泣其灰老；父母見子復歡騰。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 39 (1920); not verbatim. The old Father Lion and Mother Lion grew old and toothless; they could no longer hunt well, and began to catch among the Bushmen — especially the old maids who went to seek veld-food — and to catch the children alive and carry them home to live and play under their trees by the great rocks. The Bushmen made an old pop of skins and stuffed it with grass so that it looked at a distance like a real Bushman; two hunters climbed a tree and pulled the string so the pop danced.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 39; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 据 von Wielligh 第二卷第39号（1920年）压缩转述；非逐字照录。年老的狮父与狮母渐老而无齿；他们再也无法好好狩猎，便开始在布须曼人中间捕猎——尤其是那些外出寻觅野地食物的老处女——并活捉孩子们，带回家中，让他们在大岩石旁他们的树下生活嬉戏。布须曼人用兽皮做了一个老翁像，里面塞满草，使它在远处看来像个真正的布须曼人；两名猎人爬上树拉动绳子，那草像便跳起舞来。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Father Lion thought it was an old maid who could not climb a tree; he stalked the pop, the hunters made a noise above, and as he opened his mouth wide they shot poisoned arrows straight into it, and after a few moments Father Lion was a carcass, never again to catch old maids and children. Mother Lion had watched the murder of her old man all the time; she armed the Bushman children she kept with knobkerries and went with them by night to hunt.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 39; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同出處的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。獅子爸爸以為那是一個爬不上樹的老婦人；他悄悄潛近那棵楊樹，獵人在上方弄出聲響，當他張大嘴巴時，他們把毒箭直射進他口中，過不多時獅子爸爸就成了一具屍體，再也不能抓老婦人和小孩了。獅子媽媽自始至終目睹了老伴被殺；她把自己收養的布須曼小孩用圓頭棒武裝起來，帶著他們趁夜去打獵。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. By her house grew a great dark-green tree with delicious fruit: as soon as the children ate of it they forgot everything that had happened before, so that they quite forgot they had Bushmen for parents... One day a brave Bushman heard the children playing and laughing under Mother Lion's tree. He had 'houtjies' in his knapsack — wood-chips his sorcery-doctor had given him — and let all the children chew of it, and their former understanding came back.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 39; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同出處的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。她家旁長著一棵深綠色的大樹，結著美味的果子：孩子們一吃下果子，就忘了先前發生的一切，以致完全忘了自己的父母是布須曼人……有一天，一個勇敢的布須曼人聽見孩子們在獅子媽媽的樹下玩耍嬉笑。他的背包裡有一些「小木片」——是巫醫給他的木屑——他讓所有孩子都嚼一嚼，他們先前的理解力便恢復了。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. 'You two that sit there, your parents' fire burns under that krans; do you see the smoke shooting out there?' And the two children sprang up and ran home to their parents' house; and so, child by child, all ran off. Mother Lion came back with the water, out of breath, and wept bitterly: 'You have taken the children from here. They were so contented here... Can you not see I am growing grey and old?'... And the parents of the children wanted to spring out of their skins for joy when they saw their children again playing round them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 39; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同出處的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。「坐在那兒的你們兩個，你們父母的火在那座崖壁下燒著；你們看見那兒冒出的煙了嗎？」那兩個孩子便跳起來，跑回父母的家；就這樣，一個接一個，全都跑掉了。獅子媽媽提著水回來，氣喘吁吁，痛哭道：「你們把孩子從這兒帶走了。他們在這兒多麼安樂……你們看不出我正變得灰白衰老嗎？」……而孩子們的父母看見自己的孩子又在自己身邊玩耍，高興得簡直要從皮裡蹦出來。

title.en: The Lion in the Hut by the Child
title.zh: 屋中之獅與孩童

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 41

summary.en: A girl who cries all night for Bushman-rice brings the lion into the hut's doorway; while the parents lie rigid under their skins, the child tickles the lion with a stick — 'Ek 'tieke jou!' — and at last stuffs a burning brand into his long mane. The lion bolts with the veld aflame behind him and drops dead; and the parents give the child a whole eggshell of Bushman-rice, for she saved them from death.
summary.zh: 夜哭索蟻卵飯之女引獅入屋門；父母僵臥皮褥之下，孩童以小枝撓獅——「我騷你！」——終以燃柴塞入其長鬣。獅火焚原野而逃，終倒斃；父母酬以滿蛋殼之蟻卵飯，因其救全家於死。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 41 (1920); not verbatim. A Bushman and his wife had only one girl child who had just begun to talk... they dug Bushman-rice, shot a springbok on the way home, roasted and boiled and ate straight through; and late in the night they went to sleep under their skins — but the child not: she sat crying at the fire for Bushman-rice, and would not stop, till she began to cry loudly.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 41; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馮·維利希第二卷第四十一號（1920年）的濃縮改寫；非逐字照錄。一個布須曼人和他的妻子只有一個剛開始說話的女兒……他們挖了布須曼米，回家路上射了一隻跳羚，又烤又煮，一口氣吃了個精光；夜深時他們鑽到皮褥下睡了——但那孩子沒有：她坐在火邊哭著要布須曼米，怎麼也不肯停，直到放聲大哭起來。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Lion heard the child and came creeping; he saw the child alone by the fire while the parents lay under their skins... Lion came and sat in the doorway of the big hut; now nobody could flee. He meant to eat the parents and not the child, so he began sedately to play with the child: he put out his paw, took hold of her and played like a cat with her.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 41; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同出處的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。獅子聽見孩子的哭聲，便悄悄爬過來；他看見孩子獨自坐在火邊，而父母躺在皮褥下……獅子來到那間大茅屋的門口坐下；這下誰也逃不掉了。他打算吃掉父母而不吃孩子，於是便不慌不忙地跟孩子玩起來：他伸出爪子，抓住她，像貓一樣逗她玩。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The parents wanted to die of anguish, but scarcely drew breath; yet the child found this play of Lion's very fine; she laughed at it and said every time: 'Ek 'tieke jou! Ek 'tieke jou!' while she tickled and pricked Lion with a little stick. At last the child gripped a burning brand with a little flame from under the pot and stuffed the flame into the long mane-hair of Lion; the hair caught fire, and the more Lion shook his head the more the flames roared. He took to his heels, and as far as he ran he set the veld alight; then the parents first looked out from under the skins... they saw the veld burn, Lion running about in full flame, and at last drop dead to the ground.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 41; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同出處的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。父母痛苦得想死，卻幾乎不敢喘氣；然而孩子覺得獅子這般玩耍十分有趣；她笑了起來，每次總說：「Ek 'tieke jou！Ek 'tieke jou！」一邊用小棍子搔癢、戳弄獅子。最後，孩子從鍋底下抓起一根帶著小火焰的燃燒柴薪，把火焰塞進獅子長長的鬃毛裡；鬃毛著了火，獅子越搖頭，火焰就燒得越旺。他拔腿就跑，跑過之處把草原都點燃了；這時父母才從皮褥下探出頭來……他們看見草原在燃燒，獅子渾身是火地四處奔竄，最後倒地而死。

title.en: Wolf and His Two Wives
title.zh: 狼與其二妻

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 42

summary.en: The gluttonous Wolf eats his neighbours bare and is burnt out of three bush-houses; he lodges in holes, woos a girl for his second wife, and to fetch her necklace from a rock-slit enlists the dung-beetle — 'you roll your ball backwards because you can see the whole world round about you' — to hook it out with its horn. He wins the girl and two wives, and the neighbours' proverb is born: 'Give him two wives.'
summary.zh: 饞狼食盡鄰人、三度茅屋被焚；匿居穴中，另聘一女為二房；取岩縫中之項鍊時求助於糞金龜——「汝倒推糞球，因可環顧四周」——以角鉤出項鍊。既得二妻，鄰人諺語遂生：「予其二妻。」

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 42 (1920); not verbatim. Wolf was, and is to this day, a quick hunter; but he eats a great deal, and it takes a big knapsack of meat to silence his hunger... When the neighbours heard him coming they hid the food away; but his scent is good, and he begged and insisted so shamelessly that at last they gave him something to eat.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 42; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 改寫自馮·維利希（von Wielligh）第二部第42號（1920年）之節縮釋義；非逐字照錄。狼在過去、乃至今日，都是敏捷的獵手；但他食量極大，要填飽他的飢腸，得用上一大背包的肉……鄰人們聽見他來，便把食物藏了起來；但他的嗅覺靈敏，又厚著臉皮苦苦哀求、糾纏不休，最後他們只好給他一些吃的。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. At last they set fire to his bush-houses — one after another — till he moved quite to another place, and lived in holes, for ground- and rock-houses cannot be set alight. Wolf and his wife each went their own way so far that they never came to the same place... One evening he went courting and saw a young girl after his own heart, and told his tales of hunting and strength; three evenings later she said: 'Go and seek my necklace and bring it here, then I shall take you.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 42; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同處之節縮釋義；非逐字照錄。最後他們放火燒了他的灌木屋——一間接一間——直到他索性搬到別處，住進洞穴裡，因為地面屋與岩屋是燒不著的。狼與他的妻子各走各的路，走得如此之遠，以致他們從未到過同一個地方……某天傍晚，他去求偶，看見一個合他心意的年輕姑娘，便向她講述自己打獵與力氣的故事；三個傍晚之後，她說：「去把我的項鍊找來，帶到這裡，我就接納你。」

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. He lay downwind and heard where she had hidden it: in the rock-slit by the 'norra-karee tree, in the ear of a kudu. He hooked with a stick but the mice had eaten the ear's underpoint, and the necklace slipped deeper than he could reach. Then came Mistkruiwer (the dung-beetle) rolling a ball of clay backwards; Wolf mocked him as a fool, and the beetle answered: 'I am not so stupid: if I push the ball behind-foremost I can see the whole world round about me... I am strong and can push far bigger pieces of clay than this!' Wolf wagered him the necklace; the beetle stepped into the slit, hooked it out with its horn, and threw it down before Wolf. So Wolf got his second wife — and the neighbours said the best punishment was: 'Give him two wives.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 42; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同處之節縮釋義；非逐字照錄。他臥在下風處，聽見了她把項鍊藏在哪裡：在「norra-karee」樹旁的岩縫裡，藏在一隻捻角羚的耳朵中。他用棍子去勾，但老鼠已把耳朵的下端咬掉了，項鍊滑得比他搆得到的更深。這時，米斯特克魯維爾（Mistkruiwer，即蜣螂）滾著一顆泥球倒退著走來；狼嘲笑他是個傻瓜，蜣螂答道：「我可不那麼笨：我若把球倒著推，就能看見四周的整個世界……我力氣大，能推動比這大得多的泥塊！」狼拿項鍊與他打賭；蜣螂鑽進岩縫，用角把它勾了出來，丟在狼的面前。於是狼得到了他的第二個妻子——而鄰人們說，最好的懲罰就是：「給他兩個妻子。」

title.en: The Leopard Is Displeased with the Sun
title.zh: 豹不滿於日

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 43

summary.en: The leopard, of the old race and a hater of the new Sun's heat, scolds all day, is ringed by his own burning veld, and leaps blind through the flames that singe his coat bonter. He dens in a cool cave, kills an old hartebeest in drizzle, and — pretending to be a weary traveller — creeps into the Bushmen's thorn-kraal by night; the sharp-eyed maid sees his feet, lures the family out with a tale of ostrich eggs, and the archers shoot him through the chinks.
summary.zh: 豹本古族，恨新日之炎，終日咒罵；野火自焚其境，閉目躍過烈焰，毛色愈斑。遂居涼穴；細雨中殺老公羚；夜間佯為倦旅混入桑人之荊欄。利眼侍女見其足，以「鴕蛋」謊語誘全家出，弓手自隙射之，豹斃於欄中。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; graphic violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 43 (1920); not verbatim. The Leopard built his house there on the plain among tall grass and bushes. He is also one of the old race, who walked about when there was as yet no Sun; therefore he is Leopard. He was only angry at the children who threw the Sun's head into the sky to make it so bright by day and cause such unbearable heat; therefore he never had a good word for the Sun, but scolded the Sun the whole day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 43; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 改寫自馮·維利希第二部第43號（1920年）之節縮釋義；非逐字照錄。豹在平原上高草與灌木之間為自己蓋了房子。他也是古老族類的一員，那時還沒有太陽，他們便已四處行走；因此他才是豹。他只對那些把孩子們把太陽的頭拋上天空、使白晝如此明亮、並造成這般難以忍受的酷熱的孩子們發怒；因此他從不對太陽說一句好話，而是整天責罵太陽。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. One day it was very hot; the Sun set the veld ablaze with his great heat, and when the Leopard smelt the fire and heard it crackle he sprang out, ringed on all sides by flames; there was nothing else for it but to shut his eyes and leap straight through the roaring flames — that singed and burnt the hair of his spotted kaross so that it became only the more spotted. He found a beautiful koppie with a rock cave shaded by great trees and took up his dwelling there, for 'the Sun cannot shoot his warm arrows through the great rocks.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 43; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同處之節縮釋義；非逐字照錄。有一天非常炎熱；太陽以他巨大的熱力把草原燒得一片火海，豹聞到火味、聽見火的噼啪聲，便跳了出來，四周盡是火焰環繞；別無他法，他只能閉上眼睛，逕直穿過那咆哮的火焰跳過去——火焰燒焦、灼壞了他那斑點毛皮斗篷的毛，使它變得更加斑斑點點。他找到一座美麗的小丘，那裡有巨樹遮蔭的岩洞，便在那裡安了家，因為「太陽的暖箭射不穿那些巨大的岩石。」

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. In drizzle he caught an old hartebeest, and while he lay on an overhanging branch the Jackal's begging betrayed him. When he came back the Bushmen had hedged the hartebeest in with a thorn-kraal, waiting for him. So he wrapped himself tight in his kaross, walked up and said he was a traveller who wanted only a sleeping-place, no food, and had a heavy headache — and sat in a dark corner. A maid's stone-knife slipped and fell near his feet; as she sought it she saw the Leopard's two feet sticking out under the kaross. Without a sound she cried: 'We are roasting meat here and forgetting a nest full of ostrich eggs! Come, it is dark; let us all go and fetch the eggs' — and she winked her husband out with the family. Then the three men drew their bows and shot at the Leopard through the branches; he could not flee, for the little gate was shut behind them — and so the Leopard met his end inside the kraal.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 43; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同處之節縮釋義；非逐字照錄。在細雨中，他捕到一頭老麋羚，當他躺在一根橫伸的樹枝上時，胡狼的乞討洩露了他的行蹤。等他回來時，布須曼人已用荊棘圍欄把那頭麋羚圈了起來，正等著他。於是他把自己緊緊裹在毛皮斗篷裡，走上前去，說自己是個旅人，只想要個睡覺的地方，不要食物，而且頭痛得厲害——然後坐在一個黑暗的角落裡。一個女僕的石刀滑落，掉在他腳邊；她尋找石刀時，看見豹的兩隻腳從斗篷下伸了出來。她一聲不響地喊道：「我們在這裡烤肉，卻忘了滿窩的鴕鳥蛋！來吧，天黑了；我們大家一起去把蛋取回來」——她一面眨眼示意，讓丈夫帶著全家溜了出去。接著那三個男人拉開弓，穿過枝葉向豹射去；他逃不了，因為那小門在他們身後關上了——豹就這樣在圍欄裡喪了命。

title.en: Porcupine and Bat: The Orphans' Night-Sight
title.zh: 豪豬與蝙蝠：孤兒之夜眼

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 44

summary.en: A cruel stepmother starves her stepchildren; the dead mother sends the Owl, who plays father, leads them to his cliff, changes the boy into a porcupine — his arrows become quills in his kaross — and the girl into a bat, giving them fireflies so they can see by night. Their mother becomes a second owl that visits them; and the porcupine's sleep-charm quills can be dodged by the knowing.
summary.zh: 惡繼母餓其繼子；亡母遣梟假扮父親，引二子至崖居，化子為豪豬——其箭化為裘上之刺——化女為蝙蝠，並賜螢火使其夜能視。亡母化為另一梟夜夜探望；豪豬之催眠刺，知情者可避。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 44 (1920); not verbatim. In the old days there was an old Bushman and his old wife who belonged to the old race, and they had a little boy and a little girl as their only children. When the mother died the girl was still very young; now they were orphans. The father took another wife — a young woman who did not care for other people's children, and her two stepchildren did not have it good under her.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 44; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馮·維利希《第二卷》第44號（1920年）之濃縮改述；非逐字照錄。古時候有一位老布須曼人和他的老妻，屬於古老種族，他們只有一個小男孩和一個小女孩這兩個孩子。母親去世時，女孩還很小；如今他們成了孤兒。父親另娶了一個年輕女子，她不疼愛別人的孩子，兩個繼子女在她手下過得不好。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. For the little boy she deliberately had springbok skins laid out to play on, and smeared the bow his father had made for him with springbok fat, so that the spirit of the springboks drew into the boy and his bow, and all the springboks in the veld feared him and never gave him a chance to come near... For the little girl the stepmother neglected everything, and the poor child lived mostly on little insects and flies.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 44; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改述，出處同上；非逐字照錄。她特意為小男孩鋪開跳羚皮讓他玩耍，又用跳羚油脂塗抹他父親為他做的弓，於是跳羚的靈氣便注入男孩和他的弓中，草原上所有的跳羚都懼怕他，從不給他靠近的機會……至於小女孩，繼母對一切都不聞不問，這可憐的孩子大多靠小蟲和蒼蠅過活。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. One evening the dead mother of the two children sent the Owl to them. The Owl is a sorcerer and can change himself into a man or an owl; and he played himself before them as their own father. He took them to the rock kranses where he lived, gave them veld-food and veld-fruit, changed the boy into a Porcupine — his arrows, of which there were many, he changed into quills that stuck fast in the kaross of the boy, so that nobody dared touch him — and the girl he changed into a Bat, which lives on insects to this day; and he gave them fireflies to eat, so that they could see well in the dark. From then on they can only see by night and are blind in the day when the sun shines.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 44; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改述，出處同上；非逐字照錄。一天傍晚，兩個孩子死去的母親派貓頭鷹來到他們身邊。貓頭鷹是巫師，能把自己變成人或貓頭鷹；他在他們面前裝作他們的親生父親。他把他們帶到他居住的岩崖，給他們草原上的食物和野果，把男孩變成豪豬——他的箭為數眾多，他把它們變成牢牢插在男孩皮斗篷上的刺，誰也不敢碰他——又把女孩變成蝙蝠，蝙蝠至今仍以昆蟲為食；他給他們螢火蟲吃，使他們在黑暗中也能看得清楚。從那以後，他們只能在夜間視物，在太陽照耀的白天則目不能見。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Their mother, changed into another kind of owl, visits them by night; the porcupine knows all the tricks of porcupine-hunters, whose eyelids grow heavy under his sleeping-charm, and when he is found first he shoots his quills and is off — but the Bushmen know all his tricks.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 44; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改述，出處同上；非逐字照錄。他們的母親變成另一種貓頭鷹，夜間來探望他們；豪豬熟知獵豪豬者的種種伎倆，那些人在他的催眠魔力下眼皮沉重，而當他先被發現時，便射出身上的刺逃之夭夭——但布須曼人熟知他所有的伎倆。

title.en: Two in One Shot
title.zh: 一箭雙鵰

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 45

summary.en: A maid who has eaten a jackal's heart dreams a lion is biting her and wakes the whole camp; her dream is laughed off. Next morning the tickling behind her man's back means gemsbok blood; the children spy the herd, the hunters creep out — and one finds himself a stone's throw from a lion stalking the same gemsbok. He climbs, shoots, and kills gemsbok and lion with one arrow.
summary.zh: 食豺心之侍女夢獅噬己，驚醒全營；其夢遭眾人訕笑。翌晨其夫背後之癢意味大羚之血；孩童窺得羚群，獵者潛出——其中一人發現自己與伺羚之獅近在咫尺。他攀樹射之，一箭連斃羚與獅。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; graphic violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 45 (1920); not verbatim. One of the maids had set the liver and heart of the jackal for herself in a little pot on the fire, for the children may not eat of this — especially not the heart. A jackal is very timid, and if children eat its heart they grow up as cowards and bolt at the smallest rustle; therefore the Bushmen never give the jackal's heart to their children.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 45; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馮·維利希《第二卷》第45號（1920年）之濃縮改述；非逐字照錄。其中一名女僕把胡狼的肝和心放在火上的一隻小罐裡留給自己，因為孩子們不能吃這個——尤其是心。胡狼非常膽小，孩子若吃了它的心，長大後便會成為膽小鬼，一點風吹草動就逃之夭夭；因此布須曼人從不把胡狼的心給孩子吃。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. When all was quiet and everyone snored aloud, the maid had a ghastly dream, and she began to scream as if she were being murdered: 'Here is a lion! He is biting me! Help, help!' The men searched with bows and assegais and found nothing, and her husband laughed: 'O, I know what it is: it is the heart of the jackal that now comes to frighten you!' — 'Dreams lie!' — 'Wait, you shall see that this dream that came to warn me is not for nothing.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 45; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 濃縮改述，出處同上；非逐字照錄。當一切歸於寂靜、人人都大聲打鼾時，那女僕做了個可怕的夢，她開始尖叫，彷彿正被人殺害：「這裡有隻獅子！牠在咬我！救命，救命！」男人們拿著弓和長矛搜尋，什麼也沒找到，她的丈夫笑道：「哦，我知道是怎麼回事：是胡狼的心現在來嚇唬你了！」——「夢是騙人的！」——「等著吧，你會看到，這個來警告我的夢並非無緣無故。」

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Next morning over the meat her husband sat suddenly still and said: 'I feel my flesh creep on my back; that means a gemsbok is scratching its back with its horn near here... it means we shall shoot gemsbok and carry them home, for it is their blood that runs down behind my back.' He sent the children to climb the koppie and look; the children whispered back: gemsbok lay just below. The hunters crept out, and the man who had felt the creeping hid behind a thick tree-stem — and saw, a little before him, a giant of a lion also stalking the gemsbok. He climbed, shot as the lion seized the buck, and the arrow struck the lion in the flank; so the tree-climber got a gemsbok and a lion with one arrow-shot.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 45; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同段落的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。翌日清晨，丈夫在吃肉時忽然靜坐不動，說道：「我覺得背上的肉在發麻；這表示有一隻南非劍羚正在附近用角搔牠的背……這表示我們將射到南非劍羚並把牠們扛回家，因為正是牠們的血沿著我的背流下。」他打發孩子們爬上小山丘去看；孩子們低聲回報：南非劍羚就躺在下方不遠處。獵人們悄悄出去，那個感到背肉發麻的人躲在一根粗大的樹幹後面——他看見前方不遠處，有一頭巨大的獅子也在悄悄逼近那些南非劍羚。他爬上樹，趁獅子撲住那隻羚羊時放箭，箭射中了獅子的側腹；於是這個爬樹的人一箭便得到了南非劍羚和獅子。

title.en: The Hammerkop and the Swallows: Children of the Moon
title.zh: 鎚頭鸛與燕：月之子

region.en: Transvaal (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非德蘭士瓦（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; told by a Transvaal Bushman in 1885 to G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 46

summary.en: Swallows are the children of the Sun: murdered Bushman children who lie dead in the hollow moon until it waxes, then drop from the sky as swallows and build their crescent nests under the krans. The Hammerkop warns of a Kaffir raiding party; the first kraal that stoned the birds is massacred, the second, warned by the old wise man, shoots the raiders from the rocks. The black raiders become the mieland-raiding crows.
summary.zh: 燕為日之子：被殺之桑童屍月之空匙，月盈則自天墜為燕，於崖下築半月之巢。鎚頭鸛預警科薩劫掠隊；第一村擲石驅鳥者遭屠，第二村中老智者得警，據石射殺掠者。黑掠者化為劫米田之烏鴉。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; colonial-era interethnic violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 46 (1920); not verbatim. The swallows (krans-swallows) make their little houses under the overhanging rock; their nests look like the moon with its two horns standing up... for the Hammerkop told them to build them so. Now, the moon, when it makes a bowl upward, carries the bodies of people who have only just died; and the swallows are dead little children come alive again. When the moon becomes half again the hollow vanishes, and then there is no more place for the children; so they fall out of the sky and become swallows.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 46; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馮·維利希（von Wielligh）第二卷第四十六號（1920年）的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。燕子在懸岩下築起牠們的小屋；牠們的巢看起來像一輪月亮，兩隻角朝上豎起……因為錘頭鸛吩咐牠們這樣築巢。話說，月亮在向上彎成碗狀時，載著剛剛死去之人的身體；而燕子則是死去的小孩子重新活過來。當月亮又變成半邊時，那凹處便消失了，於是再也沒有孩子們容身的地方；他們便從天上掉下來，變成了燕子。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. One evening the Hammerkop saw in the water that a great murdering band of long black people was on the march. He flew out at once and called the Owl, and the two flew to warn the Bushmen. At the first kraal they were clapped at and stoned and flew away grieved; at the second kraal an ancient Bushman, who was wise, bade the others be still and listen: 'the two birds come to warn us that a murdering band is coming and the little kraal's folk must be ready.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 46; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同段落的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。一天傍晚，錘頭鸛在水中看見一大隊殺人的黑色長人正在行軍。牠立刻飛出去，叫來貓頭鷹，兩隻鳥便飛去警告布須曼人。在第一個村落，人們拍手驅趕、向牠們扔石頭，牠們便傷心地飛走了；在第二個村落，一位年邁而睿智的布須曼人叫其他人安靜下來聽：「這兩隻鳥是來警告我們，有一隊殺人的人馬正前來，小村落的人必須做好準備。」

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. That evening many little stars shot; the swallows feared the fire-lights; but the Hammerkop looked and saw: 'Now the great black ones are murdering out the little brown ones... at the first kraal, where the Owl and I were yesterday; they there would not believe us.' Later in the night more stars with long tails shot: 'Be at rest; the great black ones are now attacking at the second kraal, where the Bushmen sit armed in a stone hedge and shoot the great black ones dead in heaps — I can see in the water how they roll over.'... When the Moon's hollow had grown level again the bodies dropped from the Moon, and the Sun sent the brown children of the Bushmen alive to the Hammerkop: they became swallows. And the great black ones the Sun changed into black crows, which make such a noise as the raiders did; and so the black folk departed and plague the mielie-lands to this day, while the Hammerkop and the Sun's children, the swallows, dwell together in love in the kranses.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 46; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同段落的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。那天傍晚，許多小星星劃過天際；燕子害怕那些火光；但錘頭鸛看了看，說道：「現在那些黑色的大人正在屠殺那些棕色的小人……就在第一個村落，昨天我和貓頭鷹去過的地方；那裡的人不肯相信我們。」夜裡稍晚，更多拖著長尾的星星劃過：「安心吧；那些黑色的大人現在正攻打第二個村落，那裡的布須曼人手持武器坐在石籬中，把那些黑色的大人成堆射死——我能從水中看見他們如何翻倒。」……當月亮的凹處又變得平坦時，那些身體便從月亮上掉落，太陽把布須曼人的棕色孩子活著送給錘頭鸛：他們變成了燕子。而那些黑色的大人，太陽把他們變成了黑烏鴉，牠們發出的喧鬧聲正如那些劫掠者一般；於是那些黑人離去了，至今仍為害玉米田，而錘頭鸛與太陽的孩子——燕子——則相親相愛地一同住在岩壁之間。

title.en: The Clouds: Hair, Feathers and the Whirlwind That Carries the Dead
title.zh: 雲：髮、羽與負屍之旋風

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 47

summary.en: The storm-wind is the breath of the Great Bird that dwells in a mountain hole. A dead person's hair becomes clouds; the whirlwind lifts the corpse — even buried — and lays it gently in the bowl between the horns of the new moon; the mist-cloud covers the rising dead so none see them; and the rocks, which cursed wind and cloud, can never wake again.
summary.zh: 暴風乃居山穴之大鳥之氣息。死者之髮化為雲；旋風捲屍（縱已葬）輕置於新月雙角之空匙；霧雲掩護復起之死者使其不見；詛咒風雲之岩石則永不復醒。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 47 (1920); not verbatim. All the clouds are not of one kind: there are clouds that pour out rain, and others that are dry; there are thunder-clouds that hold water, fire and thunder-stones; and there are those that hold only hair, feathers and wind. The wind is the breath of everything that lives; so the storm-winds are the breath of the Great Bird, which lives in a hole in the mountains, can hide itself in clouds, and flies to the sea to fetch rain.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 47; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馮·維利希第二卷第四十七號（1920年）的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。雲並非只有一種：有的雲傾瀉雨水，有的雲則是乾的；有的雷雲蘊含水、火與雷石；還有的雲只蘊含毛髮、羽毛與風。風是一切活物的氣息；因此暴風便是大鳥的氣息，那大鳥住在山中的一個洞裡，能藏身於雲中，並飛往海邊取雨。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. When a person dies his hair becomes clouds; when a bird dies its feathers also become clouds. But such clouds give no rain, for they are only hair and feathers without water; they come and vanish without letting fall a drop. If a person has died, his footprints still stand fresh in the sand as if he lived; therefore the storm-wind comes and blows the footprints of the dead level with the sand.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 47; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同段落的濃縮改寫，非逐字照錄。人死後，他的頭髮變成雲；鳥死後，牠的羽毛也變成雲。但這樣的雲不下雨，因為它們只是毛髮和羽毛，沒有水；它們來了又消失，一滴也不落下。若有人死去，他的腳印仍清晰地留在沙上，彷彿他還活著；因此暴風前來，把死者的腳印吹得與沙面齊平。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. When a corpse lies dead on the earth, the wind makes a strong whirlwind; and it takes the corpse up — even though buried under the ground — and carries it to the hollow bowl between the two standing horns of the new moon, and lays it gently therein. Therefore the Bushmen bury a corpse in a sitting posture: it must at any time be ready to stand up. Before Death came into the world through the Hare, people and animals slept only till new moon, and then came alive again like the moon; but now they must sit long in their graves before they will one day come alive again. Then the person's cloud comes down and drifts like a heavy mist over the grave to cover the rising one, so that the others cannot see that the dead has come alive again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 47; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同處的濃縮改述，非逐字照錄。當一具屍體僵臥於地上，風便捲起猛烈的旋風；它將屍體托起——縱然屍體埋在地下——帶到新月兩隻立角之間的空凹處，輕輕安放其中。因此布須曼人以坐姿埋葬屍體：它必須隨時準備起身。在死神藉野兔進入世界之前，人與動物只睡到新月，然後便像月亮一樣重獲生命；但如今他們必須在墳墓中久坐，日後才會有一天重獲生命。接著，那人的雲降下，如濃霧般飄過墳墓，遮住那正在升起者，使其他人看不見死者已重獲生命。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim.
