region.en: The otherworld of Plato's Republic, compared by Evans-Wentz (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 柏拉圖《理想國》之他世（伊文思溫茲並觀，象徵定位）

period: Plato, Republic, Bk. X (4th century BC), compared by Evans-Wentz 1927 with the Sidpa Bardo

source.work: The Tibetan Book of the Dead, ed. W. Y. Evans-Wentz (1927), Introduction, quoting Plato's Republic, Bk. X

summary.en: Evans-Wentz's great cross-cultural comparison: Er, son of Armenius, slain in battle, found uncorrupted, returned to life on the funeral pile on the twelfth day and told what he had seen - a mysterious place with two openings in the earth and two in the heaven, judges seated in the intermediate space, the just ascending by the heavenly way on the right and the unjust descending on the left, bearing the symbols of their deeds - and then the choosing of lives: Orpheus taking the swan, Ajax the lion, Agamemnon the eagle, Atalanta the athlete, Epeius the cunning woman, Therites the monkey, and Odysseus, disabused of ambition, the neglected life of a private man who had no cares.
summary.zh: 伊文思溫茲的大跨文化對照：厄爾戰歿而屍身不腐，第十二日於火葬堆上復生，述其所見——地有二口、天有二口之秘境，中間坐著審判者，善者由右天路而升，惡者由左下道而降，背縛其業跡；繼而眾魂擇生：奧菲斯取天鵝，埃阿斯取獅，阿伽門農取鷹，阿塔蘭忒取力士，厄珀俄斯取巧女，特西忒斯取猿——而厭倦了野心的奧德修斯，取那被眾人遺忘的「無憂平民之生」。

sensitivity.note: Comparative material from Evans-Wentz's edition; paraphrase only.

passages.text: Er, the son of Armenius, a Pamphylian by birth, was slain in battle, and ten days afterwards, when the bodies of the dead were taken up already in a state of corruption, his body was found unaffected by decay, and carried home to be buried; and on the twelfth day, as he was lying on the funeral pile, he returned to life and told them what he had seen in the other world. He said that when his soul left the body he went on a journey with a great company, and they came to a mysterious place at which there were two openings in the earth, and over against them two other openings in the heaven above; in the intermediate space there were judges seated, who commanded the just, after they had given judgement on them, to ascend by the heavenly way on the right hand, and the unjust to descend by the lower way on the left, these also bearing the symbols of their deeds fastened to their backs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jowett's Plato as quoted in Evans-Wentz's edition (1927); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿爾米紐斯之子厄爾，生於潘菲利亞，戰死沙場，十日後，當死者之屍體被收殮時已腐敗，其屍體卻被發現未受腐朽影響，遂運回家中安葬；至第十二日，當他躺在火葬堆上時，竟復活過來，並告訴眾人他在另一世界之所見。他說，當其靈魂離開肉體時，他與一大群同行者踏上旅程，來到一處神秘之地，那裡地上有兩個開口，其對面天上另有兩個開口；在中間地帶坐著判官，他們於判決後命公正者由右手天之道路上升，命不公正者由左手下之道路下降，後者亦背負其行為之標記。

passages.text: Most curious was the spectacle - sad and laughable and strange; for the choice of the souls was in most cases based on their own experience of a previous life: the soul which had once been Orpheus choosing the life of a swan out of enmity to the race of women; Ajax refusing to be a man, remembering the injustice done him in the judgement about the arms, chose the life of a lion; Agamemnon took the life of an eagle; Atalanta, seeing the great fame of an athlete, was unable to resist the temptation; Epeius passed into the nature of a woman cunning in the arts; the jester Therites was putting on the form of a monkey - and Odysseus, the mutabilities of human life having disabused him of ambition, went about for a considerable time in search of the life of a private man who had no cares, and, finding it lying about and neglected by everybody else, said he would have done the same had his lot been first instead of last, and was delighted to have it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jowett's Plato as quoted in Evans-Wentz's edition (1927); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最奇特的是那景象——既可悲又可笑又怪异；因为灵魂的选择大多基于其前世的经验：曾为俄耳甫斯的灵魂，出于对女性族类的敌意而选择了天鹅的生命；埃阿斯拒绝成为人，因记得在关于武器的裁决中遭受的不公，选择了狮子的生命；阿伽门农取了鹰的生命；阿塔兰忒见一位运动员享有盛名，无法抗拒诱惑；厄培俄斯转生为精于技艺的女子之性；丑角忒耳西忒斯披上了猴子的形貌——而奥德修斯，因人类生活的无常已使他摒弃了野心，四处游荡了相当长的时间，寻找一种无忧无虑的平民生活，发现它被所有人弃置一旁、无人问津，便说若他的签运排在最先而非最后，他也会作同样的选择，并为得到它而欣喜。

title.en: !Gauwa's Invisible Arrows: Illness and Death
title.zh: 高瓦之隱箭：疾病與死亡

region.en: Nyae Nyae (Tsumkwe district), Namibia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 納米比亞尼亞尼亞（欽韋區）（象徵定位）

period: Ju/'hoansi (!Kung) oral tradition; recorded 1950s-1960s by Lorna Marshall and John Marshall, published 1976

source.archive: Harvard University Press (book); ethnographic film archive
source.work: Lorna Marshall, The !Kung of Nyae Nyae (1976); John Marshall, films of the Ju/'hoansi

license: Paraphrase for educational use; underlying recordings remain with the Marshall family and Ju/'hoan community

summary.en: Among the Ju/'hoansi illness and death come from !Gauwa, the great god who shoots people with invisible arrows from ambush or sends ghosts to do it. The arrows lodge unseen in the body; sickness grows as they fester; and only the trancing healers, who die and rise within the dance, can see and draw them out. !Gauwa owns the eland and all the big game, and men plead with him for animals as they plead for health.
summary.zh: 朱霍安西人中，疾病與死亡皆出於大神高瓦：他自埋伏處以隱形之箭射人，或遣鬼為之。箭匿體內，病隨之發；唯入迷之醫者——於舞中死而復生者——能見之拔之。高瓦掌大羚與群獸；獵者為獸如為健康而懇求於他。

sensitivity.note: Modern Ju/'hoan religious knowledge recorded by ethnographers with community cooperation; presented as documented paraphrase, not as community speech.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall, The !Kung of Nyae Nyae (1976), chs. on religion and illness; not verbatim. The Ju/'hoansi hold that !Gauwa (|Gauwa), the great god, shoots people with invisible arrows — from his own hand, or through the ghosts of the dead which he sends. The arrows enter the body unseen and lie there; the sickness grows as they work, and a person dies when !Gauwa has shot him finally, or when a ghost has come to take him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lorna Marshall, The !Kung of Nyae Nyae (1976); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 据马歇尔《尼亚埃尼亚埃的!Kung人》（1976）宗教与疾病诸章的浓缩转述；非逐字引用。朱/'霍安西人认为，大神!Gauwa（|Gauwa）以无形的箭射人——或出自他亲手，或经由他差遣的死者鬼魂。箭无形地进入身体并留驻其中；随着箭的作用，疾病渐长，当!Gauwa最终射中某人，或当鬼魂前来带走他时，人便死去。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same work; not verbatim. Ghosts (the spirits of dead Ju) are blamed for many deaths; they belong to !Gauwa and do his shooting. A sick person may say that a ghost came to him at night, or that !Gauwa has shot him; the family debates which of the two it was, for the treatment — and the blame — differ. Only the healers (n/um k’iaosi, 'owners of n/um') can see the arrows.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同一著作的浓缩转述；非逐字引用。鬼魂（死去的朱人的灵魂）被归咎于许多死亡；它们属于!Gauwa，并执行他的射箭。病人可能会说某夜有鬼魂来找他，或说!Gauwa射中了他；家人会争论究竟是二者中的哪一种，因为治疗——以及归咎——有所不同。只有疗者（n/um k’iaosi，“n/um的拥有者”）才能看见那些箭。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Katz, Boiling Energy (1982); not verbatim. In the great medicine dances the healers trance, die for a moment, and rise to lay hands on the sick: they see !Gauwa's arrows glittering in the patient's body, seize them, and pull them out, flinging them back toward the darkness. !Gauwa also owns the eland and the big game; hunters who fail say he has hidden his animals, and plead with him as they plead for health.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Richard Katz, Boiling Energy: Community Healing among the Kalahari !Kung (1982); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 据卡茨《沸腾的能量》（1982）的浓缩转述；非逐字引用。在盛大的医药舞中，疗者进入恍惚，短暂地死去，然后起身把手按在病人身上：他们看见!Gauwa的箭在病人体内闪烁，便抓住它们，将其拔出，掷回黑暗之中。!Gauwa也拥有大羚羊与大型猎物；失败的猎人说他把他的动物藏了起来，并像祈求健康那样向他恳求。

title.en: The !Gauwasi: Ancestors Who Shoot from the Dark
title.zh: 高瓦西：暗處射人之祖靈

region.en: Dobe area, Kalahari (Botswana/Namibia border) (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喀拉哈里多貝地區（波札那與納米比亞交界）（象徵定位）

period: Ju/'hoansi oral tradition; recorded 1963-1973 by Richard B. Lee, published 1979

source.work: Richard B. Lee, The !Kung San: Men, Women, and Work in a Foraging Society (1979); Lorna Marshall (1976)

summary.en: The Ju dead become !Gauwasi, spirits of the dead who live in holes in rocks and trees and are subject to !Gauwa. They shoot the living with invisible arrows, they frighten lonely travellers, and they are treated with name-avoidance and gifts: their names are never spoken again, food is left at the grave, and the dead person's belongings are broken so no ghost may come for them.
summary.zh: 朱人死者成為高瓦西——居於岩石樹洞之祖靈，受高瓦轄制。彼等以隱箭射生者，嚇孤旅；人們避其名、獻食於墓、毀其遺物，以免其魂來尋。

sensitivity.note: Modern Ju/'hoan belief recorded by ethnographers; presented as documented paraphrase.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Lee, The !Kung San (1979), ch. 9 (Religion and Healing); not verbatim. The !Kung hold that the dead turn into ghosts (!Gauwasi) who dwell in the holes of rocks and baobab trees and are ruled by the great god !Gauwa. The ghosts are feared rather than loved: they are believed to shoot the living with invisible arrows, and to come for the dying.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lee (1979); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 据李《!Kung桑人》（1979）第九章（宗教与疗愈）的浓缩转述；非逐字引用。!Kung人认为死者化为鬼魂（!Gauwasi），居于岩洞与猴面包树的洞中，受大神!Gauwa统治。鬼魂令人畏惧而非令人爱戴：人们相信它们以无形的箭射活人，并前来带走将死之人。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same work; not verbatim. The name of a dead person is never spoken again by his kin; if the name is that of a common object or animal, the word itself is changed or replaced — so closely is the living tied to the dead. The dead person's hut, bow, mats and cooking gear are broken and burned so that no part of him remains for a ghost to come back for; food is sometimes left at the grave.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lee (1979) and Marshall (1976); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同一著作的浓缩转述；非逐字引用。死者的名字绝不再被其亲属说出；若该名字是某常见物品或动物的名称，则该词本身会被更改或替换——生者与死者之间的联系竟如此紧密。死者的茅屋、弓、席子和炊具被砸毁焚烧，使他没有任何部分留存下来供鬼魂回来索取；有时会在坟前留下食物。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim. A widow or widower is smudged and rubbed with ash and medicines to drive off the ghost of the spouse, who is thought to hover close; the mourners wail a formula that sends the dead away to !Gauwa's country, for the dead who linger too long begin to shoot the living.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 改寫自馬歇爾（1976）的濃縮版本；並非逐字引用。寡婦或鰥夫會被煙燻，並以灰燼和藥草搓揉身體，以驅趕配偶的鬼魂——人們認為那鬼魂正徘徊在近處；哀悼者哀號著一段咒語，把亡者送往 !Gauwa 的國度，因為逗留過久的亡者會開始射擊生者。

title.en: Boiling Energy: The Ju/'hoan Trance Dance
title.zh: 沸騰之力：朱霍安西迷舞

region.en: Dobe / Nyae Nyae, Kalahari (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喀拉哈里多貝／尼亞尼亞（象徵定位）

period: Ju/'hoansi religious practice; recorded 1950s-1980s by Lorna Marshall, Richard Katz and Megan Biesele

source.work: Richard Katz, Boiling Energy: Community Healing among the Kalahari !Kung (1982); Lorna Marshall, The !Kung of Nyae Nyae (1976)

summary.en: Around the night fire, women in file sing and stamp the giraffe songs while the men — the owners of n/um, a boiling energy at the base of the spine — dance in a half-circle. The n/um heats, climbs the spine, and the dancers trance: they die for an instant, cross into !Gauwa's country, and rise to draw !Gauwa's arrows out of the sick with their hands, feet, and the smell of burning herbs.
summary.zh: 夜火之畔，女列隊而歌而踏長頸鹿之歌；男者——脊柱基部沸騰之n/um之主——半環而舞。n/um發熱，沿脊上行，舞者入迷：剎那而死，越入高瓦之境，復起以手、足與焚草之氣拔出病者體內高瓦之箭。

sensitivity.note: Ju/'hoan healing practice documented with community participation; paraphrase only, not ritual instruction.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Katz, Boiling Energy (1982), chs. 1-3; not verbatim. The trance dance (n/um tchai or the giraffe dance) is the central religious institution of the Ju/'hoansi. Women sit in file around the fire singing and clapping the medicine songs — the giraffe song is the great one — while the men dance around them; the singing and the drumming of feet feed the n/um, the medicine power, in the dancers.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Katz (1982); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 改寫自卡茨《沸騰的能量》（1982）第一至三章的濃縮版本；並非逐字引用。出神之舞（n/um tchai，或稱長頸鹿之舞）是 Ju/'hoansi 人核心的宗教制度。婦女們圍著火堆成排坐著，唱著並拍手打著藥歌——長頸鹿之歌是最重要的一首——而男人們在她們周圍跳舞；歌聲與腳踏的節奏滋養著舞者體內的 n/um，即藥力。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same work; not verbatim. As n/um boils up from the base of the spine, some dancers enter kia, the trance state: they say they die for a moment, that their thoughts travel to !Gauwa's place, and that they come back with the sight to see !Gauwa's arrows in the sick. They lay trembling hands on chests and backs, suck and blow, and pull the arrows out, sometimes staggering and falling; the others steady them and keep them from the fire.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Katz (1982); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同一著作的濃縮改寫；並非逐字引用。當 n/um 從脊椎底部沸騰而上，有些舞者便進入 kia，即出神狀態：他們說自己死去片刻，說自己的思緒前往 !Gauwa 之地，又說自己帶著視見歸來，能看見病者身上的 !Gauwa 之箭。他們將顫抖的雙手按在病者的胸膛與背上，吸吮並吹氣，把箭拔出，有時踉蹌跌倒；其他人則扶穩他們，使他們不致跌入火中。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim. The dance goes on through the night until the sick sleep and the arrows are out; in the morning the camp says who was healed and who was shot too deeply. The dance is also the meeting-place of the whole waterhole group — the social and religious centre of Ju/'hoan life.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 改寫自馬歇爾（1976）的濃縮版本；並非逐字引用。舞蹈徹夜持續，直到病者入睡、箭被拔出；到了早晨，營地裡的人會說誰被治癒了、誰被射得太深。這舞蹈也是整個水塘群體的聚會之所——Ju/'hoan 人生活裡的社會與宗教中心。

title.en: Eland Potency: The Rock-Art Reading
title.zh: 大羚之力：岩畫之解

region.en: Drakensberg escarpment, South Africa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非德拉肯斯堡山（象徵定位）

period: Southern San rock art (last painted before c. 1900); interpreted 1981-2000 from 19th-century |Xam records

source.archive: Published scholarship drawing on Bleek & Lloyd archive
source.work: David Lewis-Williams, Believing and Seeing: Symbolic Meanings in Southern San Rock Paintings (1981); Lewis-Williams & Dowson, Images of Power (1989)

summary.en: The eland is the great reservoir of n/um potency: in |Xam thought its blood and fat are medicine, and shamans enter trance 'dying' like wounded eland. Lewis-Williams reads the painted eland and the crossed, half-human dancers beside them as the record of the trance dance — potency rising, shamans bleeding from the nose, and the dance-floor of the rock wall.
summary.zh: 大羚為n/um之力之巨庫：|Xam觀念中其血其脂皆藥，薩滿入迷時如傷羚『垂死』。路易斯-威廉斯解讀岩壁之大羚與交叉半人舞者，為迷舞之記——力上升、薩滿鼻血、岩面即舞場。

sensitivity.note: Interpretive archaeology built on the |Xam archive; the eland remains ritually central to San-descended communities.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Lewis-Williams, Believing and Seeing (1981), chs. on eland and potency; not verbatim. In |Xam accounts the eland is the embodiment of !gi (potency): its fat and blood are the strongest medicines, and the shaman in trance is said to 'die' and behave like a wounded eland, standing with lowered head, shaking, and bleeding from the nose.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lewis-Williams (1981); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 改寫自路易斯-威廉斯《相信與看見》（1981）中論大羚羊與效力諸章的濃縮版本；並非逐字引用。在 |Xam 人的記述中，大羚羊是 !gi（效力）的化身：牠的脂肪與血液是最強效的藥，而處於出神狀態的薩滿據說會「死去」，舉止像一頭受傷的大羚羊，低著頭站立、顫抖，並從鼻子流血。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Lewis-Williams & Dowson, Images of Power (1989); not verbatim. Paintings of eland surrounded by elongated, bent-forward human figures with crossed arms and white potency spots are read as shamans dancing around the reservoir of power in trance, their ritual killing of the eland paralleling the trance death. The rock face itself is the veil of the spirit world; the dance is danced against it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lewis-Williams & Dowson (1989); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 改寫自路易斯-威廉斯與道森《力量之像》（1989）的濃縮版本；並非逐字引用。大羚羊的畫像被細長、前傾、雙臂交叉、身上帶有白色效力斑點的人形圍繞，這些畫被解讀為薩滿在出神狀態中繞著力量之庫起舞，他們儀式性地殺死大羚羊，與出神之死相互對應。岩壁本身即是靈界的帷幕；舞蹈正是對著它而跳。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the same scholarship drawing on Vinnicombe (1976); not verbatim. The eland's blood, spilled in the first-kill rites, is believed to make the hunter who eats of it strong and calm; the eland dance at a girl's first menstruation marks her as the eland's bride, and the potency of the animal passes into the band.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lewis-Williams (1981) and Vinnicombe (1976); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 依據維尼康布（Vinnicombe, 1976）同一學術研究的濃縮改寫；非逐字引用。人們相信，在初次獵殺儀式中灑出的伊蘭羚羊之血，能使食其肉的獵人變得強壯而沉靜；女孩初經時舉行的伊蘭羚羊之舞，標誌著她成為伊蘭羚羊的新娘，而這動物的力量便流入整個群體之中。

title.en: The Lion Outside the Body: Ju/'hoan Astral Shamans
title.zh: 體外之獅：朱霍安西離體薩滿

region.en: Nyae Nyae / Dobe, Kalahari (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喀拉哈里尼亞尼亞／多貝（象徵定位）

period: Ju/'hoansi oral tradition; recorded 1950s-1990s by Lorna Marshall, Katz and Guenther

source.work: Lorna Marshall, The !Kung of Nyae Nyae (1976); Mathias Guenther, Tricksters and Trancers (1999); Katz (1982)

summary.en: Powerful healers are said to leave their bodies in trance (k’ebu) and travel to far camps, to the dead, or into lions: dying !Gauwa-men become lions, and a lion met on the path may be a shaman out walking. The lion's roar at night may be a sorcerer's spirit calling; the healer who brings his k’ebu back tells where he has been.
summary.zh: 力大之醫者入迷時（克布）離體遠行——至遠村、至死者處、或入獅身：垂死之高瓦之人化為獅，途遇之獅或為外遊之薩滿。夜吼之獅或為巫靈之喚；攜克布歸之醫者能述其所至。

sensitivity.note: Documented Ju/'hoan belief; paraphrase only.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976), religion chapters; not verbatim. The !Kung say that a man with strong n/um can, in trance, send his k’ebu — his spirit or shadow-self — out of his body to travel far away, to see what is happening at other waterholes, or to visit !Gauwa and the dead; his body lies as if asleep while his k’ebu is abroad.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 依據馬歇爾（Marshall, 1976）宗教諸章的濃縮改寫；非逐字引用。!Kung人說，擁有強大n/um的男子能在出神狀態中將其k’ebu——即他的靈魂或影子自我——送出體外，遠行至他處，去看其他水坑邊發生了什麼事，或去拜訪!Gauwa與亡者；當他的k’ebu在外遊歷時，他的身體則如沉睡般躺著。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Guenther, Tricksters and Trancers (1999); not verbatim. Lions are intimately linked with trancers: a dying shaman becomes a lion, and a lion met in the bush may be a trance-traveller in lion form; the roar heard at night is sometimes taken for the voice of a !Gauwa-man calling. When a healer returns from trance he tells of his journey — where he went, what he saw, whom he fought.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guenther (1999); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 依據金瑟（Guenther）《騙徒與出神者》（Tricksters and Trancers, 1999）的濃縮改寫；非逐字引用。獅子與出神者關係密切：瀕死的薩滿會化為獅子，而在灌木叢中遇見的獅子，可能正是以獅子形貌出遊的出神旅人；夜裡聽到的吼聲，有時被當作!Gauwa之人呼喚的聲音。當療者從出神中返回，他會講述自己的旅程——去了何處、看見了什麼、與誰搏鬥。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Katz (1982); not verbatim. In the dance a healer may announce that he has been among the ghosts, or that he has pulled a lion out of a sick person — that the illness was a !Gauwa-man in lion form lodged inside; the extraction and the story together close the case of the illness.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Katz (1982); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 依據卡茨（Katz, 1982）的濃縮改寫；非逐字引用。在舞蹈中，療者可能宣告自己曾置身於亡靈之間，或宣告自己從病人體內拉出了一頭獅子——即那疾病乃是化為獅子形貌、盤踞於體內的!Gauwa之人；取出病根與講述故事，二者合而了結了這樁疾病。

title.en: The Name That Must Not Be Spoken
title.zh: 不可言之名

region.en: Dobe / !Kangwa, Kalahari (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喀拉哈里多貝／坎瓜（象徵定位）

period: Ju/'hoansi custom; documented 1963-1973 by Richard B. Lee, published 1979

source.work: Richard B. Lee, The !Kung San (1979), ch. 9; Lorna Marshall (1976)

summary.en: After death a Ju/'hoan's name is tabooed forever; kin may not speak it, and if it is an everyday word — 'honey', 'zebra', 'fire' — the word is replaced in the language of that band. The name-taboo follows the ghost into the naming of children and even of jokes, so that the dead are honoured by silence.
summary.zh: 朱人逝者之名永為禁忌；親屬不得言，若其名為常用詞——『蜜』『斑馬』『火』——該詞於其群之語中即遭替換。名諱隨鬼魂延及兒名與戲言；死者以緘默受尊。

sensitivity.note: Documented Ju/'hoan custom; paraphrase only.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Lee (1979), ch. 9; not verbatim. The names of the dead are avoided absolutely: a kinsman will not speak his dead father's or mother's name, and people related by the name-link (children named after the dead) avoid it too. Where the dead person's name was an ordinary word, the band replaces the word — a new word is coined for 'honey' or 'zebra' — so that the name never has to be said again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lee (1979); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 依據李（Lee, 1979）第九章的濃縮改寫；非逐字引用。亡者的名字被絕對避諱：親屬不會說出已故父親或母親的名字，而因名字連結而相關的人（以亡者命名的孩子）也同樣避諱。若亡者的名字本是一個普通詞彙，群體便會替換該詞——為「蜂蜜」或「斑馬」另造新詞——如此一來，那個名字便永遠不必再被說出口。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim. The name-taboo is part of the fear and honour owed to the !Gauwasi: speaking the dead person's name invites the ghost, as does handling his belongings. Children named for the dead are said to carry the dead person's 'shade' and must be watched.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 依據馬歇爾（Marshall, 1976）的濃縮改寫；非逐字引用。名字禁忌是對!Gauwasi所懷的敬畏與尊崇的一部分：說出亡者的名字會招來鬼魂，觸碰他的遺物亦然。以亡者命名的孩子據說帶有亡者的「影子」，必須加以看顧。

title.en: The Eland Bull Dance at First Menstruation
title.zh: 初潮之大羚牛舞

region.en: Nyae Nyae, Namibia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 納米比亞尼亞尼亞（象徵定位）

period: Ju/'hoansi rite; recorded 1950s-1980s by Lorna Marshall and John Marshall

source.work: Lorna Marshall, The !Kung of Nyae Nyae (1976); John Marshall, films of the Ju/'hoansi (N!ai, 1978)

summary.en: At a girl's first menstruation the camp performs the eland dance: women and men file around her, stroke her arms and shoulders 'the way an eland's mane is stroked', singing the eland songs, so that the potency of the eland bull — !Gauwa's favourite animal — enters her body and makes her strong, fat, and fruitful.
summary.zh: 少女初潮時，營地行大羚之舞：眾人列隊繞之，如撫羚鬣般撫其臂肩，歌大羚之歌——使高瓦至愛之動物大羚牛之力入其身，使其強壯、豐腴、多產。

sensitivity.note: Documented Ju/'hoan puberty rite; paraphrase only, no ritual instruction.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976), ch. on the eland ceremony; not verbatim. When a girl menstruates for the first time the band holds the eland ceremony: the people form a line and dance around her, singing the eland songs; they touch and stroke her arms, shoulders and back — as one strokes the mane of an eland bull — so that the eland's potency enters her.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 改寫自馬歇爾（1976）關於大羚羊儀式一章的濃縮釋義；非逐字引文。當女孩初次月經來潮時，營隊會舉行大羚羊儀式：眾人排成一列，圍著她跳舞，唱大羚羊之歌；他們觸摸並撫摩她的手臂、肩膀與背部——如同撫摩大羚羊公牛的鬃毛一般——好讓大羚羊的靈力進入她體內。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same work; not verbatim. The eland is !Gauwa's great animal, the reservoir of n/um; the dance is held so that the girl will be strong, that her blood will flow well, and that she will grow fat and bear children well. The rite ends with feasting on eland meat if the hunters have been lucky, and the girl is said now to be 'like an eland'.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同一著作的濃縮釋義；非逐字引文。大羚羊是!Gauwa的偉大動物，是n/um的貯藏之所；舉行此舞，是為了讓女孩強健、讓她的血順暢流動，並讓她長得豐腴、善於生育。若獵人運氣好，儀式便以享用大羚羊肉的盛宴作結，而人們說這女孩如今「像一頭大羚羊」。

title.en: The Giraffe Song: The Great Medicine of the Dance
title.zh: 長頸鹿之歌：舞之大藥

region.en: Dobe, Kalahari (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喀拉哈里多貝（象徵定位）

period: Ju/'hoansi medicine songs; recorded 1950s-1980s by Marshall, Katz and Biesele

source.work: Richard Katz, Boiling Energy (1982); Megan Biesele, Women Like Meat (1993); Lorna Marshall (1976)

summary.en: The giraffe song is the strongest of the Ju/'hoan medicine songs: sung at the night dance, its long rising phrases pull the n/um up the dancers' spines and open the deepest trances. The giraffe, like the eland, is an animal of !Gauwa; to sing the giraffe is to call the biggest medicine into the circle.
summary.zh: 長頸鹿之歌為朱霍安西醫歌之至強者：夜舞中其悠揚上揚之句牽動舞者脊中之n/um，開最深之迷。長頸鹿與大羚同為高瓦之獸；唱長頸鹿即召至大之藥入環。

sensitivity.note: Documented Ju/'hoan medicine song; paraphrase only.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Katz (1982); not verbatim. The giraffe dance is the most powerful of the Ju/'hoan medicine dances; the women's song of the giraffe, with its long, rising, circling phrases, is said to pull the n/um hardest up the men's spines, and the deepest trances are entered under this song.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Katz (1982); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 改寫自卡茨（1982）的濃縮釋義；非逐字引文。長頸鹿之舞是朱／霍安醫藥之舞中最強有力的一種；據說婦女們的長頸鹿之歌——以其悠長、上揚、迴旋的樂句——最能將n/um沿著男人們的脊椎往上拉，而最深的出神狀態便是在這首歌之下進入的。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Biesele, Women Like Meat (1993); not verbatim. Medicine songs belong to the animals of !Gauwa — eland, giraffe, gemsbok — and each song is 'owned' by the line of healers who inherited it; the songs are the animals' gifts, and singing them correctly is itself a form of hunting the animal's power into the camp.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Biesele (1993); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 改寫自比塞爾《如肉般的女人》（1993）的濃縮釋義；非逐字引文。醫藥之歌屬於!Gauwa的動物——大羚羊、長頸鹿、南非劍羚——而每一首歌都由繼承它的治療者世系所「擁有」；這些歌是動物的贈禮，而正確地唱這些歌，本身便是一種將動物的力量獵入營地的方式。

title.en: Dreams as Visits from the Dead
title.zh: 夢為亡者之訪

region.en: Nyae Nyae, Namibia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 納米比亞尼亞尼亞（象徵定位）

period: Ju/'hoansi oral tradition; recorded 1950s-1970s by Lorna Marshall

source.work: Lorna Marshall, The !Kung of Nyae Nyae (1976); Lorna Marshall, Nyae Nyae !Kung Beliefs and Rites (1999)

summary.en: Dreams are taken literally: to dream of a dead kinsman is to be visited by his !Gauwasi, who may come in kindness or to shoot. The dreamer wakes the camp, tells the visit, and the healers check the sick list; dreams of !Gauwa himself foretell the deaths he is planning.
summary.zh: 夢境被視為實事：夢見亡親即其高瓦西來訪——或善或射。夢者醒而告營眾，醫者檢視病者名單；夢見高瓦本人者，預示其所謀之死。

sensitivity.note: Documented Ju/'hoan belief; paraphrase only.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976/1999); not verbatim. The Ju/'hoansi treat dreams as real events: the dead come in dreams because it is the way the !Gauwasi visit; a dream of a dead kinsman may mean he came in kindness, to look at his people, or that he has come to shoot someone in the camp.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 改寫自馬歇爾（1976／1999）的濃縮釋義；非逐字引文。朱／霍安人將夢視為真實的事件：亡者會在夢中出現，因為那是!Gauwasi來訪的方式；夢見已故的親屬，可能意味著他善意來訪、來看看自己的人們，也可能意味著他來是要射殺營地中的某個人。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same works; not verbatim. A dream of !Gauwa is the gravest: he is said to sit counting his arrows in the dreamer's dream, and each arrow counted is a death he has decided on. In the morning the camp debates the dream, and the healers keep watch over the person the arrows seemed to point at.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同一批著作的濃縮釋義；非逐字引文。夢見!Gauwa是最嚴重的：據說他會在作夢者的夢中坐著數他的箭，而每數一支箭，便是他所決定的一樁死亡。到了早晨，營隊會議論這個夢，而治療者們則守望著那些箭似乎所指的人。

title.en: Naro Trickster Tales: The Dassie's Council
title.zh: 納羅詭計故事：蹄兔之議

region.en: Ghanzi district, Botswana (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波札那甘茲區（象徵定位）

period: Naro (Central Kalahari) oral tradition; recorded 1980s-1990s, published in Guenther 1999

source.work: Mathias Guenther, Tricksters and Trancers: Bushman Religion and Society (1999); Guenther, The Naron Bushmen (1986 field corpus)

summary.en: In Naro storytelling the trickster world of Kaggen's descendants lives on: animal tales in which the weak outwit the strong — the dassie's council on the rock, the jackal's feints, the lion fooled at his own kill — carry the same message as the old myths: that the small, the hungry and the cunning survive in a world ruled by !Gauwa's arrows and the big game's whims.
summary.zh: 納羅敘事中，卡根後裔之詭計世界猶存：弱者智勝強者之獸故事——岩上蹄兔之議、豺之佯攻、獅受騙於己獲——承古神話之訊：在高瓦之箭與巨獸任性統治之世，唯小者、飢者、狡者得存。

sensitivity.note: Modern Naro oral tradition recorded with community collaboration; paraphrase only.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Guenther, Tricksters and Trancers (1999), chs. on Naro folklore; not verbatim. Naro animal tales continue the Kaggen cycle's logic: the trickster is small and vulnerable, and his tricks are responses to hunger and threat; the dassie's council on the rock, the jackal's endless feints, and the lion outwitted at his own kill all teach that the weak survive by cunning.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guenther (1999); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 改寫自 Guenther《Tricksters and Trancers》（1999）中關於納羅（Naro）民間傳說之章節的濃縮釋義；非逐字翻譯。納羅的動物故事延續了卡根（Kaggen）循環的邏輯：搗蛋者身形渺小且脆弱，而他的種種伎倆皆是對飢餓與威脅的回應；岩上蹄兔的議會、豺狼無止盡的佯攻，以及獅子在自己的獵物前被智取，在在教導人：弱者憑藉機巧而得以存活。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same work; not verbatim. The trickster tales are told at night around the fire and are explicitly entertainment as well as instruction — a Naro speaker says the old stories and the new ones are the same talk, only the animals change; and behind them all stands the same dangerous world of !Gauwa and his arrows.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guenther (1999); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同一著作的濃縮釋義；非逐字翻譯。搗蛋者的故事於夜間圍著火堆講述，既是娛樂，也明確具有教誨之意——一位納羅語使用者說，古老的故事與新的故事是同一種話語，只是動物換了；而在這一切背後，矗立著同一個由 !Gauwa 及其箭矢所構成的危險世界。

title.en: Scaring the Ghost: Fire, Ash and the Widower
title.zh: 驅鬼之火：灰燼與鰥夫

region.en: !Kangwa, Botswana (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波札那坎瓜（象徵定位）

period: Ju/'hoansi rite; documented 1963-1973 by Richard B. Lee

source.work: Richard B. Lee, The !Kung San (1979), ch. 9; Lorna Marshall (1976)

summary.en: After a death the widow or widower is smudged with ash and medicine smoke, the belongings of the dead are broken, and the camp lights fires at the path so the ghost will not follow the living home. The mourners call the formula that sends the !Gauwasi to !Gauwa's country, and the first nights are kept loud and bright.
summary.zh: 喪禮之後，以灰與藥煙熏寡婦鰥夫，碎毀亡者之物，於歸途燃火，使鬼不隨生者歸家。哀者誦送魂之辭，遣高瓦西赴高瓦之境；初夜喧亮不輟。

sensitivity.note: Documented Ju/'hoan mourning rite; paraphrase only.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Lee (1979), ch. 9; not verbatim. After the burial the dead person's hut and belongings are broken up and burned; the widowed spouse is smoked and rubbed with ash and medicines to drive off the spouse's ghost, which is thought to hover around and to be able to shoot the survivor with !Gauwa's arrows.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lee (1979); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 改寫自 Lee（1979）第九章的濃縮釋義；非逐字翻譯。葬禮之後，死者的屋舍與物品被拆毀並焚燒；喪偶的一方被煙燻，並以灰燼與藥草塗抹，以驅逐配偶的亡魂，據信那亡魂會在其四周徘徊，並能以 !Gauwa 的箭射擊生還者。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim. Fires are kept burning on the paths at night so the ghost will not follow the living home; the mourners wail the words that send the dead away to !Gauwa's country, and the camp keeps loud and bright for the first nights, for a quiet dark camp is where a ghost can walk.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 改寫自 Marshall（1976）的濃縮釋義；非逐字翻譯。夜間在小徑上維持火堆燃燒，使亡魂不會跟隨活人回家；哀悼者哀號著那些將死者送往 !Gauwa 之國的話語，而營地在最初幾夜保持喧鬧與明亮，因為安靜黑暗的營地正是亡魂得以行走之處。

title.en: The Hare Reverses the Message (Katkop/Hottentot Version)
title.zh: 野兔逆轉訊息（卡茲科普／霍屯督版）

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition (Katkop dialect); recorded 1875 by !khusin (Bleek & Lloyd); English redaction in Honey 1910

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (1875), §18; James A. Honey, South-African Folk-Tales (1910), 'The Origin of Death'

summary.en: In the messenger form of the myth the Moon sends the Hare to men with the message of the renewal of life; but the Hare reverses it into a message of death. The angered Moon heats a stone and burns the Hare's mouth, causing the harelip — the told-three-times Katkop version recorded by Bleek, and the English redaction printed by Honey.
summary.zh: 訊使版神話中，月遣野兔赴人類報『復生』之訊；野兔反轉為『死亡』之訊。月怒，燒石烙其口，兔唇由此而來——此為布萊克三度採錄之卡茲科普版，亦為霍尼1910年英譯所本。

sensitivity.note: The narrator !khusin's father was Hottentot; Bleek doubts whether this form is original Bushman. Flagged as a border-version of the origin-of-death cluster.

passages.text: The Moon, it is said, sent once an Insect to Men, saying, 'Go thou to Men, and tell them, As I die, and dying live, so ye shall also die, and dying live.' The Insect started with the message, but whilst on his way was overtaken by the Hare, who asked: 'On what errand art thou bound?'... With these words he ran off, and when he reached Men, he said, 'I am sent by the Moon to tell you, As I die, and dying perish, in the same manner ye shall also die and come wholly to an end.'
passages.note: Quote from James A. Honey, South-African Folk-Tales (1910), 'The Origin of Death' (public domain; the tale derives from Bleek 1875 §18).
passages.zh: 據說，月亮曾派遣一隻昆蟲去見人類，說道：「你去到人類那裡，告訴他們：正如我死去，卻在死去中活著，你們也將同樣死去，並在死去中活著。」昆蟲帶著這訊息出發，然而在途中被野兔追上，野兔問道：「你奉命去辦什麼事？」……說完這些話，他便跑走了，當他抵達人類那裡時，說道：「我是受月亮派遣來告訴你們：正如我死去，卻在死去中消亡，你們也將以同樣的方式死去，並徹底歸於終結。」

passages.text: Then the Hare returned to the Moon, and told her what he had said to Men. The Moon reproached him angrily, saying, 'Darest thou tell the people a thing which I have not said?' With these words she took up a piece of wood, and struck him on the nose. Since that day the Hare's nose is slit.
passages.note: Quote from Honey (1910), public domain.
passages.zh: 於是野兔回到月亮那裡，告訴她他對人類所說的話。月亮憤怒地責罵他，說道：「你竟敢告訴人們一件我未曾說過的事？」說著，她拿起一塊木頭，擊中他的鼻子。自那天起，野兔的鼻子便是裂開的。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§18): the veritable Hottentot myth of the 'Origin of Death' is told in the Katkop dialect by !khusin, whose father was a Hottentot; although the narrator says he heard the story from his mother \xa-\kho, a Bushwoman, its Hottentot origin can hardly be doubted. Here the Moon sends the Hare to men with the message of the renewal of life, but it reverses it into a message of death; the angered Moon then heats a stone and burns the Hare's mouth, causing the harelip. !khusin told this story three times.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §18; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布里克（Bleek）摘要（§18）的濃縮改述：真正的霍屯督（Hottentot）「死亡起源」神話，由!khusin以卡特科普（Katkop）方言講述，其父為霍屯督人；儘管講述者說他是從母親\xa-\kho（一名布須曼婦女）那裡聽來這個故事，其霍屯督起源仍幾乎無可置疑。在此，月亮派野兔帶著生命更新之訊息去見人類，但野兔卻將它顛倒為死亡之訊息；被激怒的月亮於是燒熱一塊石頭，燙傷野兔的嘴，造成兔唇。!khusin講述這個故事三次。

title.en: Padmasambhava Tames the Demons of Tibet
title.zh: 蓮花生降伏吐蕃諸魔

region.en: The road of the Guru's march across Tibet (symbolic pin at Samye)
region.zh: 蓮師入藏之路（以桑耶寺為象徵定位）

period: Legendary life of Padmasambhava (Guru Rimpoche), 8th century; Waddell's summary 1895

source.work: L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism (1895), ch. II-IV

summary.en: The Tibetans, beset on every side by malignant devils, warmly welcomed the Guru from Udyana as the bringer of deliverance: arriving in 747 AD he vanquished all the chief devils of the land, sparing most of them on their consenting to become defenders of his religion while he guaranteed that in return they would be duly worshipped and fed. His weapons were the vajra and spells extracted from the Mahayana gospels; his twenty-five disciples each performed a grotesque magical feat - mounting the sunbeams, driving iron bolts into rocks, reviving the slain, making water run upwards, taming wild yaks - and each was instructed in making magic circles for coercing demons and exorcism.
summary.zh: 吐蕃人四面受惡魔擾害，故熱烈歡迎來自鄔仗那的蓮花生大師，視之為解脫者。公元747年入藏後，他降伏境內諸大魔鬼——多數答應充當佛法護衛，大師則保證令其受供養享祭祀。其法器為金剛杵與《摩訶衍那》諸經之咒；二十五位弟子各顯神通：踏日而行、以鐵釘釘入巖石、令死者復生、使水逆流、馴服野犛牛……並各授結界鎮魔之術。

canonical_translation: L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism, London 1895 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The founder of Lamaism, Saint Padma-sambhava, 'the Lotus-born one,' usually called by the Tibetans Guru Rimpoche or 'the precious Guru', was a native of Udyana, famed for the proficiency of its priests in sorcery, exorcism and magic: Hiuen Tsiang, writing a century previously, said of Udyana that the people practise the art of using charms and the employment of magical sentences is with them an art and a study. The Tibetans, steeped in superstition which beset them on every side by malignant devils, warmly welcomed the Guru as he brought them deliverance from their terrible tormentors.

Arriving in Tibet in 747 AD at the invitation of King Thi-Sron Detsan, he vanquished all the chief devils of the land, sparing most of them on their consenting to become defenders of his religion, while he on his part guaranteed that in return for such services they would be duly worshipped and fed. Thus, just as the Buddhists in India, in order to secure the support of the semi-aborigines of Bengal, admitted into their system the bloody Durga and other aboriginal demons, so on extending their doctrines throughout Asia they pandered to the popular taste by admitting within the pale of Buddhism the pantheon of those new nations they sought to convert. The Guru's most powerful weapons in warring with the demons were the Vajra (Tibetan, dor-je), symbolic of the thunderbolt of Indra, and spells extracted from the Mahayana gospels, by which he shattered his supernatural adversaries.

Under the zealous patronage of the King he built at Sam-yas in 749 AD the first Tibetan monastery, said to be modelled after the Indian Odantapura of Magadha and entitled the 'Self-sprung immovable shrine', believed to be based on immovable foundations of adamantine laid by the Guru; and there, assisted by the Indian monk Shanta-rakshita - made first abbot - he instituted the order of the Lamas. The leading events of his march through Tibet and his subjugation of the local devils indicate the original habitats of several of the pre-Lamaist demons; each of the demons of the indigenous Bon-pa religion was assigned its proper place in the Lamaist pantheon, and primitive Lamaism may be defined as a priestly mixture of Sivaite mysticism, magic and Indo-Tibetan demonolatry overlaid by a thin varnish of Mahayana Buddhism.

Padma-sambhava had twenty-five disciples, each credited with magical power, mostly of a grotesque character: Nam-k'a s'in-po mounted the sunbeams; San-gye-ye-se drove iron bolts into rocks; Gyal-wa-ch'og-yan changed his head into a horse's and neighed thrice; K'ar-ch'en Ch'o-gyal revived the slain; Pal-ki-ye-se overcame three fiendesses; Pal-ki-Sen-ge enslaved demons, nymphs and genii; Vairocana obtained the five heavenly eyes of knowledge; Dorje-Dun Jem travelled invisibly as the wind; Ye-se-Nan visited the fairy world; Shu-bu-pal-sen made water run upwards; Gyal-wai-Lodoi raised ghosts and converted the corpse into gold; Ten-pai-nam-k'a tamed wild yaks of the northern desert; 'Odan-Wan-p'yug dived into water like a fish; Ma-t'og rin-ch'en crushed adamant to powder and ate it like meal; Pal-kyi Dor-je passed through rocks and mountains; and Lan-dod Kon-ch'og wielded and repelled thunderbolts. And these disciples he instructed in the way of making magic circles for coercing the demons and for exorcism.

The Guru's departure from Tibet was as miraculous in character as his life: addressing the king he said that in Jambudvip were five Raksha countries crowded with men-eating devils who, if not conquered, would depopulate the whole world of Jambudvip, and except me none other can subdue them - thither must I now go. Accompanied by the king and nobles and his two fairy wives, he went to the Gung-thang La on the northern confines of Tibet, and there, after giving farewell advice to keep the doctrine and the revelations hidden in caves throughout the land, he was enveloped in a glorious rainbow-halo within which appeared the four great heroes of the world, who assisted him in mounting the celestial horse-car named Ialaha, in which he was borne away through the sky in a south-westerly direction amid heavenly music and showers of flowers. The assembled multitude remained transfixed as if dead, and after twenty-five days and nights could still see the Guru's celestial party, like a shooting star, sailing away through the sky till lost to sight. He reached Singala after about two days' journey, penetrating the iron palace, entered the body of the Raksha king named 'He of the Skull rosary', and preached the doctrine to the thousand daughters of the Raksha; at the capital Sando-pal-ri, abstracting the life of the demon-king Yaksha Me-wal and entering his body, the Guru reigns there supreme over the Rakshas even up till the present day, and in perpetual youth is preaching there the doctrine of Lamaism in a paradise which rivals that of Amitabha's western heaven of Sukhavati. And notwithstanding his grotesque charlatanism and uncelibate life, he is deified and worshipped as the 'second Buddha', his image under 'The eight worshipful Forms' found in every Tibetan temple of the old sect.
narrative.notes: Cultural function: the demon-taming legend is the charter of the Nyingma order and of the whole Tantric apparatus of Tibetan religion - every protective deity and every exorcistic rite traces itself to the Guru's bargain with the local gods, and the landscape of Tibet is mapped as the sequence of his subjugations.

functions: Charter of the Nyingma (Old School): the local demons of the Bon are converted into 'defenders of the faith' under contract of worship
Explains the Tibetan religious landscape: each demon's original habitat is remembered as a stage of the Guru's march
Authorizes exorcistic rites: the twenty-five disciples' feats and the magic circles are the pedigree of the sorcerer's craft
Establishes the terma doctrine - the revelations hidden in caves throughout the land, to be 'discovered' by later saints

variants.name: The legendary life of the Guru
variants.text_tradition: Padma bka'-thang and later Nyingma hagiographies
variants.summary: The full hagiographies add the princess Mandarava, a sister of Shanta-rakshita, whom the Guru married, and the birth-legend from a lotus; Waddell's summary here follows the standard compiled tradition.

variants.name: The historical view
variants.text_tradition: Rockhill's Life of the Buddha, ch. VII
variants.summary: Rockhill's sober account has Shantarakshita advising the king to invite Padma Sambhava of Udyana after his own teachings met opposition; the demon-taming belongs to the later legendary accretion.

primary_sources.citation: Tibetan Padma bka'-thang tradition; English summary L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism, London 1895, ch. II-IV, pp. 25-33

secondary_sources.work: René de Nebesky-Wojkowitz, Oracles and Demons of Tibet
secondary_sources.citation: Nebesky-Wojkowitz 1956, The Hague - the demon classes tamed by the Guru in living ritual.

secondary_sources.work: Geoffrey Samuel, Civilized Shamans
secondary_sources.citation: Samuel 1993, Washington: Smithsonian - the tantric shamans' frame for the Padmasambhava cult.

secondary_sources.work: Kurtis R. Schaeffer, The Culture of the Book in Tibet
secondary_sources.citation: Schaeffer 2009, New York: Columbia - the terma ('rediscovered text') economy to which the Guru's hidden revelations gave rise.

source_urls.description: Internet Archive scan of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism (1895)

sensitivity_guidance: Padmasambhava is a living devotional centre of Tibetan Buddhism; passages below are paraphrases of the 1895 public-domain summary, not verbatim liturgy, and the tradition is treated respectfully.

sensitivity.note: Living devotional tradition; paraphrase of public-domain 1895 summary only. Waddell's own 'charlatanism' verdict is a colonial-era judgment, reported as part of the source's framing.

passages.text: The Tibetans, steeped in superstition which beset them on every side by malignant devils, warmly welcomed the Guru as he brought them deliverance from their terrible tormentors. Arriving in Tibet in 747 AD, he vanquished all the chief devils of the land, sparing most of them on their consenting to become defenders of his religion, while he on his part guaranteed that in return for such services they would be duly worshipped and fed; the leading events of his march through Tibet and his subjugation of the local devils indicate the original habitats of several of the pre-Lamaist demons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 藏人深陷於迷信之中，四周盡受惡魔侵擾，當蓮華生（Guru）為他們帶來對可怕折磨者的解救時，他們熱烈地歡迎他。他於公元747年抵達西藏，降伏了當地所有主要的惡魔，其中大多數因同意成為其宗教的護法而被饒恕，而他這一方則保證：作為此類服務的回報，他們將受到應有的崇拜與供養；他行經西藏並降伏當地惡魔的主要事蹟，顯示了若干前喇嘛教時期惡魔的原初棲息地。

passages.text: The Guru's most powerful weapons in warring with the demons were the Vajra, symbolic of the thunderbolt of Indra, and spells extracted from the Mahayana gospels, by which he shattered his supernatural adversaries. Under the zealous patronage of King Thi-Sron Detsan he built at Sam-yas in 749 AD the first Tibetan monastery, the 'Self-sprung immovable shrine', believed to be based on immovable foundations of adamantine laid by the Guru, and there instituted the order of the Lamas with Shanta-rakshita as first abbot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蓮華生與惡魔爭戰時最強大的武器是金剛杵（Vajra），象徵因陀羅（Indra）的雷霆，以及取自大乘福音的咒語，他藉此擊碎其超自然的對手。在赤松德贊（Thi-Sron Detsan）王的熱心護持下，他於公元749年在桑耶（Sam-yas）建造了第一座西藏寺院「自成不動寺」，據信其奠基於蓮華生所鋪設、堅不可摧的金剛地基之上，並在那裡創立喇嘛僧團，以寂護（Shanta-rakshita）為首任住持。

passages.text: Padma-sambhava had twenty-five disciples, each credited with magical power, mostly of a grotesque character: one mounted the sunbeams, one drove iron bolts into rocks, one revived the slain, one made water run upwards, one raised ghosts and converted the corpse into gold, one tamed wild yaks of the northern desert, one crushed adamant to powder and ate it like meal, and one wielded and repelled thunderbolts - and these disciples he instructed in the way of making magic circles for coercing the demons and for exorcism.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蓮華生（Padma-sambhava）有二十五位弟子，各被認為具有神通法力，多屬怪誕之性質：一人乘日光而行，一人將鐵釘打入岩石，一人使死者復活，一人使水向上流，一人召喚鬼魂並將屍體化為黃金，一人馴服北方荒漠的野犛牛，一人將金剛石碾成粉末如麵粉般食之，一人操縱並擊退雷霆——而他教導這些弟子製作魔法圈以制伏惡魔及驅邪之法。

passages.text: Addressing the king, the Guru said that in Jambudvip were five Raksha countries crowded with men-eating devils who, if not conquered, would depopulate the whole world - except me none other can subdue them. Enveloped in a glorious rainbow-halo within which appeared the four great heroes of the world, he mounted the celestial horse-car named Ialaha and was borne away through the sky in a south-westerly direction amid heavenly music and showers of flowers; after twenty-five days and nights the multitude could still see the Guru's celestial party, like a shooting star, sailing away through the sky till lost to sight. Reaching the Raksha capital Sando-pal-ri, he abstracted the life of the demon-king Yaksha Me-wal, entered his body, and reigns there supreme over the Rakshas even up till the present day, in perpetual youth preaching the doctrine of Lamaism in a paradise which rivals that of Amitabha's western heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蓮華生對國王說道，在閻浮提（Jambudvip）有五個羅剎（Raksha）國，擠滿了食人惡魔，若不加以征服，將使整個世界人煙絕跡——除我之外，無人能降伏他們。他籠罩於輝煌的彩虹光暈之中，光暈內顯現世間四大英雄，他騎上名為Ialaha的天馬車，在天樂與花雨之中，被載往西南方向穿越天空；經過二十五晝夜，眾人仍能看見蓮華生的天界隊伍，如流星般航行於天際，直至消失無蹤。抵達羅剎都城Sando-pal-ri後，他抽取了魔王夜叉（Yaksha）Me-wal的性命，進入其身體，直至今日仍在那裡作為羅剎的至尊統治者，永保青春，在一座可與阿彌陀佛西方極樂世界相媲美的樂園中宣講喇嘛教義。

title.en: Vairocana Banished and the Red Rahula She-Devil
title.zh: 毗盧遮那流放與「紅羅睺羅魔女」

region.en: Eastern province of Kham (symbolic pin at Chamdo)
region.zh: 藏東康區（以昌都為象徵定位）

period: Reign of Thi-Sron Detsan (8th century); Waddell 1895

source.work: L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism (1895), ch. II

summary.en: The most learned of the young Lamas, Vairocana, translated many Sanskrit works into Tibetan, but his usefulness was interrupted by the Tibetan wife of Thi-Sron Detsan, who, in bitter opposition to the King's reforms and instigated by the Bon-pa priests, secured the banishment of Vairocana to the eastern province of Kham by a scheme similar to that practised by Potiphar's wife. But, on her being forthwith afflicted with leprosy, she relented, and the young Bairo-tsana was recalled and effected her cure - she is still handed down to history as the 'Red Rahula she-devil', while Vairocana is made an incarnation of Buddha's faithful attendant and cousin Ananda.
summary.zh: 青年僧中最博學的毗盧遮那譯經甚多，卻遭赤松德贊的藏籍王妃阻撓——她受苯教僧唆使、堅決反對王的改革，以「波提法之妻」之計將毗盧遮那貶至東部康區。然王妃隨即染癩，悔悟之下迎回毗盧遮那，並由他醫癒其疾——她從此被史書稱為「紅羅睺羅魔女」，而毗盧遮那則被奉為佛陀近侍阿難之化身。

sensitivity.note: Historical-legendary material; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: The most learned of these young Lamas was Vairocana, who translated many Sanskrit works into Tibetan, though his usefulness was interrupted for a while by the Tibetan wife of Thi-Sron Detsan; who in her bitter opposition to the King's reforms, and instigated by the Bon-pa priests, secured the banishment of Vairocana to the eastern province of Kham by a scheme similar to that practised by Potiphar's wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這些年輕喇嘛中最博學的是毗盧遮那（Vairocana），他將許多梵文著作譯成藏文，然而他的效用曾一度因赤松德贊（Thi-Sron Detsan）的藏族妻子而中斷；她激烈反對國王的改革，並在苯教（Bon-pa）祭司的慫恿下，以類似波提乏之妻所用的計謀，使毗盧遮那被放逐至東部的康區（Kham）。

passages.text: But, on her being forthwith afflicted with leprosy, she relented, and the young Bairo-tsana was recalled and effected her cure; she is still, however, handed down to history as the Red Rahula she-devil, while Vairocana is made an incarnation of Buddha's faithful attendant and cousin Ananda - and on account of his having translated many orthodox scriptures, he is credited with the composition and hiding away of many of the fictitious scriptures of the unreformed Lamas, which were afterwards discovered as revelations.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而，她隨即染上痲瘋病，於是心生悔意，年幼的貝若札那被召回並治癒了她；儘管如此，她至今仍以「紅羅睺羅女魔」之名流傳於史冊，而毗盧遮那則被視為佛陀忠實侍者兼表弟阿難的化身——由於他翻譯了許多正統經典，人們便將許多未改革派喇嘛的偽造經典之撰寫與藏匿歸功於他，這些經典後來被當作啟示而發現。

title.en: The Black-Hat Devil-Dancer Who Shot the King
title.zh: 黑帽咒師刺王記

region.en: Below the king's palace at Lhasa (symbolic pin at the Jokhang, Lhasa)
region.zh: 拉薩王宮之下（以大昭寺為象徵定位）

period: Assassination of Ralpachen's successor-era king, c. 899-925 AD; Waddell 1895

source.work: L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism (1895), ch. II

summary.en: Ralpachen's devotion to Buddhism led to his murder at the instigation of his younger brother Lan Darma - the so-called Julian of Lamaism - who then persecuted the Lamas, desecrated the temples, burned many of their books and forced many to become butchers. But the persecution was short-lived: Lan Darma was assassinated in the third year of his reign by a Lama of Lha-lung named Pal-dorje, who to effect his purpose assumed the guise of a strolling black-hat devil-dancer and hid in his ample sleeves a bow and arrow; his dancing below the king's palace attracted the king, who summoned the dancer to his presence - where the disguised Lama shot him with the arrow, which proved almost immediately fatal. In the resulting tumult the Lama sped away on a black horse tethered near at hand, and riding on plunged through the Kyi river on the outskirts of Lhasa, whence his horse emerged in its natural white colour, as it had been merely blackened by soot - and this murderous incident forms a part of the modern Lamaist masquerade.
summary.zh: 赤祖德贊因崇佛而遇弒，其弟朗達瑪繼位——人稱「藏傳之朱利安」——毀廟焚經，強僧操刀為屠。然迫害未及三年：拉龍貝吉多傑扮作遊方黑帽咒舞者，袖藏弓箭，於王宮下起舞；王召見之，趁机放箭，王中箭立斃。亂中貝吉多傑騎近旁之黑馬疾馳，渡拉薩河——馬出水面竟復原為白色，蓋其黑乃煙熏所致——此刺殺之舞至今仍是藏歷新年跳神之程式。

sensitivity.note: Historical-legendary material; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: Lan Darma ascended the throne after Ralpachen's murder and at once commenced to persecute the Lamas and did his utmost to uproot the religion; he desecrated the temples and several monasteries, burned many of their books, and treated the Lamas with the grossest indignity, forcing many to become butchers. But Lan Darma's persecution was very mild for a religious one, and very short-lived.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 朗達瑪在熱巴巾被謀殺後登上王位，隨即開始迫害喇嘛，並竭力根除佛教；他褻瀆寺院和數座僧院，焚燒其中許多書籍，並以最粗鄙的侮辱對待喇嘛，強迫許多人成為屠夫。但朗達瑪的迫害就宗教迫害而言相當溫和，且極為短暫。

passages.text: He was assassinated in the third year of his reign by a Lama of Lha-luh named Pal-dorje, who has since been canonized by his grateful church, and this murderous incident forms a part of the modern Lamaist masquerade. This Lama, to effect his purpose, assumed the guise of a strolling black-hat devil-dancer, and hid in his ample sleeves a bow and arrow; his dancing below the king's palace attracted the attention of the king, who summoned the dancer to his presence - where the disguised Lama seized an opportunity while near the king to shoot him with the arrow, which proved almost immediately fatal. In the resulting tumult the Lama sped away on a black horse tethered near at hand, and riding on, plunged through the Kyi river on the outskirts of Lhasa, whence his horse emerged in its natural white colour, as it had been merely blackened by soot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他在位第三年被一位名叫帕爾多傑的拉隆喇嘛刺殺，此人後來被心懷感激的教會封為聖者，而這起謀殺事件成為現代喇嘛教化裝舞會的一部分。這位喇嘛為達成目的，裝扮成遊方的黑帽跳神者，並在寬大的袖子裡藏了弓箭；他在國王宮殿下跳舞引起了國王的注意，國王召喚舞者上前——偽裝的喇嘛趁靠近國王時抓住機會以箭射他，幾乎立即致命。在隨之而來的騷亂中，喇嘛騎上繫在近處的一匹黑馬疾馳而去，繼續前行，衝過拉薩郊外的吉曲河，他的馬從河中出來時恢復了天然的白色，因為牠只是被煙灰染黑了。

title.en: Pehar in the Box: The State Oracle of Nechung
title.zh: 寶盒中的白哈爾：乃瓊護法

region.en: Nechung temple, near Drepung, west of Lhasa (symbolic pin at Nechung)
region.zh: 哲蚌寺附近的乃瓊寺（以乃瓊寺為象徵定位）

period: Nechung oracle tradition (mediaeval to 19th century); Waddell 1895

source.work: L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism (1895), ch. on Sorcery and Necromancy

summary.en: The demon-king Pehar, originally a god of the Turki tribes named 'The White Overcast Sky', was brought to Tibet by Padmasambhava and made religious guardian of the first monastery, Sam-ya. Centuries later his spirit transferred itself to Ts'al-gun-t'an and said to a Lama named Z'ari, 'Let us go to Udyana' - whereupon the Lama shut up the possessed man in a box and flung it into the river Kyi; the abbot of Depung, who had prophesied the previous day that a box would float down the river, had his pupils seize it, and when they opened it a great fire came out and disappeared into a tree, and a dead man's body was found within. By the abbot's prayers the spirit consented to return to the body, and the resuscitated corpse, refusing to enter the pure monastery of Depung on the plea of being uncelibate, requested to be granted 'a small dwelling' where he stood - hence the name of the place Na-ch'un, 'the small dwelling'; and the identical tree is still to be seen there.
summary.zh: 護法神白哈爾本為突厥部落之神「陰天白」，由蓮花生攜入吐蕃，任桑耶寺首座護法。數百年後其神識遷至拉薩近郊，向喇嘛扎日言「我們去鄔仗那吧！」——喇嘛遂將被附身者鎖入木箱，拋入吉曲河。哲蚌寺住持前日已預言「河上將漂來一箱」，弟子們截住之；開箱時火焰騰起沒入一株樹中，箱內只餘一具死屍。經住持祈請，神魂重返屍身；復活者自言不守淨戒、不肯入哲蚌大寺，只求在立足處賜「一小居」——乃瓊（意為「小居」）之名由此而來，那株樹至今猶在。

sensitivity.note: Living oracle tradition; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: This demon-king was originally a god of the Turki tribes, and named The White Overcast Sky, and on account of his Turki descent the popular epic of the famous prince Kesar, who had conquered the Turki tribes, is not permitted to be recited at Depung, under whose aegis the Na-ch'un oracle resides, for fear of offending the latter. He was brought to Tibet by Padma-sambhava in Thi-Sron Detsan's reign, and made the Ch'o-Kyon or religious guardian of the first monastery, Sam-ya.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這位魔王原為突厥部落的神祇，名為「白陰天」，由於他的突厥血統，著名的凱薩王子史詩——他曾征服突厥部落——不被允許在哲蚌寺誦唱，因為那春神諭就駐於該寺庇護之下，唯恐冒犯後者。他在赤松德贊在位期間被蓮花生大士帶到西藏，並被立為第一座寺院桑耶寺的護法神。

passages.text: The legend states that the spirit of Pehar entered into a resident of Ts'al-gun-t'an, and said to a Lama named Z'ari, Let us go to Udyana; the Lama then shut up the possessed man in a box, which he flung into the river Kyi. Now the abbot of De-pung had prophesied the previous day to his pupils, saying, a box will float down the river, go find it and seize it; the pupils found the box and brought it to the spot where the Na-ch'un temple now stands, and there they opened it, and lo! a great fire came out and disappeared into a tree, and the dead body of a man was found in the box; but by the prayers of the abbot the spirit consented to return to the body. And the resuscitated corpse, refusing to enter the pure monastery of De-pung on the plea of being uncelibate, requested to be granted a small dwelling where he stood - hence the name of the place Na-ch'un, the small dwelling; and the identical tree is still to be seen there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傳說記載，白哈爾的神靈進入了一位察貢丹居民的身中，並對一位名叫札里的喇嘛說：我們去烏仗那吧；喇嘛於是將這被附身的人關進一個箱子，投入吉曲河。話說哲蚌寺的住持前一天曾向弟子們預言說：一個箱子會順流漂下，去找它並抓住它；弟子們找到了箱子，帶到如今那春寺所在之處，在那裡打開它，瞧！一團大火冒出，消失於一棵樹中，箱中發現一具男子的屍體；但藉著住持的祈禱，神靈同意返回那具屍體。而這復活的屍體以自己未守獨身為由，拒絕進入純淨的哲蚌寺，請求在他所站之處賜予一間小屋——因此該地得名那春，意為「小屋」；而那棵同樣的樹至今仍可在該處見到。

title.en: The Necromancer-in-Ordinary to the Government
title.zh: 政府御用占卜師乃瓊神巫

region.en: Nechung temple and the Jo-wo temple at Lhasa (symbolic pin at Lhasa)
region.zh: 乃瓊寺與拉薩大昭寺（以拉薩為象徵定位）

period: State-oracle tradition, organized by the fifth Grand Lama (17th century); Waddell's observations 1895

source.work: L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism (1895), ch. on Sorcery and Necromancy

summary.en: The chief wizards are called Defenders of the Faith, and the highest of these, Na-ch'un, is the government oracle, consulted on all important state occasions; he was made a Lama of the yellow sect and state-oracle by the fifth Grand Lama, the reason alleged being that he frustrated an attempt of the Newar merchants of Lhasa to poison the tea-cistern at the great festival by driving a knife through the vessel. Once a year he proceeds in great pomp to Lhasa, is accommodated in a special temple close to the east of the great Jo-wo temple, and prophesies the events of the year; the applicant's request must be presented in writing, and when a sufficient number have accumulated the augur is disclosed in a wildly ecstatic state - he throws rice at the applicants, and becoming more inflamed by fury, falls down in convulsions and then replies to questions, the replies noted by attendant scribes and sealed by the sorcerer himself on his recovery.
summary.zh: 眾巫之首稱「護法」，其極者乃瓊，即政府占卜之神諭，凡國家大事皆諮之。五世達賴將其納入黃教僧籍、立為國師神巫——相傳因其挫敗拉薩尼泊爾商人在大法會中下毒茶池之謀（一劍刺穿茶缸）。歲首次日，神巫儀仗入拉薩，宿於大昭寺東之專廟，預言一年之事；求示者須以書面呈請，積至相當數量，神巫狂迷而出——向請示者擲米，愈舞愈狂，癲倒抽搐，方才作答；回答由侍立書記記錄，事後由神巫蘇醒時親自鈐印。

sensitivity.note: Living oracle tradition; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: The chief wizards are called Defenders of the Faith, and the highest of these, namely Na-ch'un, is the government oracle, and is consulted on all important state occasions and undertakings. The chief of these necromancers was first brought into the order of the Lamas by the fifth Grand Lama, who seems to have felt, like the Roman governors, the necessity for placing the divination for government service under the control of the priests, and he admitted the augur of Na-ch'un to the brotherhood and made him the state-oracle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 主要的巫師被稱為護法者，其中最高者，即那春，是政府神諭，所有重要的國家場合與事務都會諮詢他。這些巫師之首最初是由第五世達賴喇嘛引入喇嘛教團的，他似乎像羅馬總督一樣，感到有必要將為政府服務的占卜置於僧侶的控制之下，於是他接納那春的占卜師入教團，並立其為國家神諭。

passages.text: This state-sorcerer proceeds in great pomp to Lhasa once a year, attended by the magistrate of De-pung, and is accommodated in a special temple close to the east of the great Jo-wo temple, where he prophesies the events of the year. The applicant to the oracle must have his request presented in writing, and when a sufficient number of applications have accumulated, the augur is disclosed in a wildly ecstatic state; he throws rice at the applicants, and becoming more inflamed by fury, he falls down in convulsions and then replies to questions addressed to him. The replies are noted down by attendant scribes, and the document is afterwards sealed - it is said by the sorcerer himself on his recovery - and the utterances are often couched in poetry or allegory, with the brevity and ambiguousness of an oracular response.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這位國師每年都會在德彭地方官的陪同下，以極大的排場前往拉薩，並被安置在大昭寺東側附近的一座特別寺院中，在那裡預言一年中的種種事件。向神諭請示者必須以書面呈遞其請求，當累積了足夠數量的請示之後，降神者便會在狂亂恍惚的狀態中顯露；他向請示者投擲米粒，並愈發狂怒，繼而痙攣倒地，然後回答向他提出的問題。這些答覆由隨侍的書記記錄下來，事後再將文件封存——據說是由巫師本人在恢復神智後親自封存——而其言語往往以詩歌或寓言的形式表達，具有神諭答覆特有的簡潔與含糊。

title.en: Gesar Among the Suitors of the Chinese Princess
title.zh: 求娶文成公主的格薩爾王

region.en: The epic world of Ling, northeastern Tibet (symbolic pin in Kham)
region.zh: 嶺國史詩世界——康區（以康區為象徵定位）

period: Gesar epic (oral, earliest written recensions mediaeval); Waddell's notice 1895

source.work: L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism (1895), ch. on The Scriptures and Literature

summary.en: The best-known of Tibetan tales is that of Ge-sar - 'Czar or Caesar' - described as a mighty war-like king of northern Asia, who is made to figure as a suitor for the hand of the Chinese princess before her marriage with Sron Tsan Gampo, although it is evident the legendary accounts of him must be more ancient; the epic is so identified with the Turki enemies of the oracle-god Pehar that its recitation is forbidden at Depung, under whose aegis the Na-ch'un oracle resides, for fear of offending the latter.
summary.zh: 藏地最著名的故事是格薩爾——「愷撒」之音——被描寫為北亞驍勇之王，甚至被編入文成公主求婚者的行列（其傳說實遠早於此）。因格薩爾征服突厥部落，而突厥正乃護法白哈爾之敵，故哲蚌寺——乃瓊神諭所寄之寺——禁誦此史詩，以免觸怒護法。

sensitivity.note: Living epic tradition (still recited across the Tibetan culture area); paraphrase of public-domain notice.

passages.text: The best known of these tales is that of Ge-sar, who is described as a mighty war-like king of northern Asia, and who is made to figure as a suitor for the hand of the Chinese princess before her marriage with Sron Tsan Gam-po, although it is evident the legendary accounts of him must be more ancient. And on account of his Turki descent the popular epic of the famous prince Kesar, who had conquered the Turki tribes, is not permitted to be recited at De-pung, under whose aegis the Na-ch'un oracle resides, for fear of offending the latter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這些故事中最著名的是格薩爾的故事，他被描述為北亞一位強大的好戰國王，並被安排成在中國公主與松贊干布成婚之前向她求婚的人物，儘管顯而易見，關於他的傳說記載必定更為古老。而由於他出身突厥，那位曾征服突厥諸部落的著名王子凱薩爾的民間史詩，便不被允許在德彭誦唱，因為納春神諭即駐於德彭的庇護之下，此舉是唯恐冒犯後者。

title.en: The Creation: Sky Woman, Turtle Bearer, and the Twin Spirits
title.zh: 創世：天女、負地之龜與雙靈

region.en: The floating island in the cloud sea (symbolic pin above the Seneca country)
region.zh: 雲海中的浮島（象徵性定位於塞內卡之地上空）

period: Collected by Harriet Maxwell Converse over 22 years among the Seneca, ed. A. C. Parker (1908)

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (NY State Museum Bulletin 125, 1908), 'Creation'

summary.en: By Iroquois mythology the earth was the thought of the Indian Ruler of a great island which floats in space. When the Great Ruler bade the council tree be uprooted and bade the pregnant Sky Woman look down, he wrapped around her a great ray of light and sent her down to the cloud sea. The animals counseled in alarm: the Beaver dived and never returned, the Duck floated dead, until the Muskrat - knowing the way - brought up a portion of the oeh-da (earth) in his paw. The Turtle bore it on his hard shell and became the Earth Bearer; when he stirs, the seas rise in great waves, and when restless and violent, earthquakes yawn and devour. On the island the Sky Woman bore twin lives - one peaceful, one restless and vicious, the latter thrusting himself through under his mother's arm - and Hah-gweh-di-yu, Spirit of Good, shaped the sky with the palm of his hand, creating the Sun from his dead mother's face, the Moon and Stars from her breast, giving the Earth her body as Great Mother; while Hah-gweh-da-et-gah set Darkness in the west sky, sundered the mountains, gnarled the forests, and led monsters to the sea. When the Good Mind had pulled up the tree of light he beheld his face in the pool beneath and, molding images in red clay, transformed them into living beings: thus did the human race take origin.
summary.zh: 易洛魁神話說：大地原是至高主宰對一座浮於太空的巨島的意念。主宰命拔起議事樹，令懷孕的天女俯視深淵，以光包裹她，送她降向雲海。眾獸驚慌聚議：河狸潛水不返，鴨浮屍而上，直至識途的麝鼠以爪捧上一撮「奧達」（土）。龜以硬殼負之，成為「負地者」——牠一動，海起巨浪；牠暴怒翻騰，地震裂谷。島上，天女生下雙生——一者安寧，一者暴躁邪惡（自母腋下硬擠而出）；善靈哈格威迪尤以掌成天，自亡母之面造太陽、自其胸造月與星，把大地認作大母親；惡靈則在西方天際布下黑暗，裂山毀林、縱獸入海。善靈拔起光之樹後，於樹下水池中照見己容，遂以紅黏土捏像而賦生——人類由此起源。

sensitivity.note: Converse/Parker 1908; public domain. Parker annotates the moral-dualism evolution from Ioskeha/Tawiscara (1636) to the Good and Evil Minds.

passages.text: In the far away days of this floating island there grew one stately tree that branched beyond the range of vision. Perpetually laden with fruit and blossoms, the air was fragrant with its perfume, and the people gathered to its shade where councils were held. One day the Great Ruler said to his people: 'We will make a new place where another people may grow. Under our council tree is a great cloud sea which calls for our help. It is lonesome. It knows no rest and calls for light. We will talk to it. The roots of our council tree point to it and will show the way.' Having commanded that the tree be uprooted, the Great Ruler peered into the depths where the roots had guided, and summoning Ata-en-sic, who was with child, bade her look down. Ata-en-sic saw nothing, but the Great Ruler knew that the sea voice was calling, and bidding her carry its life, wrapped around her a great ray of light and sent her down to the cloud sea.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 32-33; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 在這浮島的遠古歲月裡，生長著一棵參天大樹，其枝幹伸展到視野之外。樹上常年結滿果實與花朵，空氣中瀰漫著它的芬芳，人們聚集到它的樹蔭下，在那裡舉行議事。有一天，偉大的統治者對他的子民說：「我們要造一個新的地方，讓另一個民族可以在那裡生長。在我們的議事樹下，有一片巨大的雲海，正呼喚著我們的幫助。它很孤寂。它不得安寧，呼喚著光明。我們要去與它交談。我們議事樹的根指向它，會指出道路。」偉大的統治者下令將樹連根拔起，然後凝視樹根所指引的深處，並召來懷有身孕的阿塔恩西克，命她向下看。阿塔恩西克什麼也沒看見，但偉大的統治者知道那海的聲音正在呼喚，便命她承載它的生命，將一道巨大的光芒裹在她身上，把她送下雲海。

passages.text: Dazzled by the descending light enveloping Ata-en-sic, there was great consternation among the animals and birds inhabiting the cloud sea, and they counseled in alarm. 'If it falls it may destroy us,' they cried. 'Where can it rest?' asked the Duck. 'Only the oeh-da (earth) can hold it,' said the Beaver, 'the oeh-da which lies at the bottom of our waters, and I will bring it.' The Beaver went down but never returned. Then the Duck ventured, but soon its dead body floated to the surface. Many of the divers had tried and failed when the Muskrat, knowing the way, volunteered to obtain it and soon returned bearing a small portion in his paw. 'But it is heavy,' said he, 'and will grow fast. Who will bear it?' The Turtle was willing, and the oeh-da was placed on his hard shell. Having received a resting place for the light, the water birds, guided by its glow, flew upward, and receiving the woman on their widespread wings, bore her down to the Turtle's back. And Hah-nu-nah, the Turtle, became the Earth Bearer. When he stirs, the seas rise in great waves, and when restless and violent, earthquakes yawn and devour.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 33; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 那降下的光芒籠罩著阿塔恩西克，令居住在雲海中的飛禽走獸目眩，牠們驚惶失措，紛紛商議。「它若掉下來，可能會毀了我們。」牠們喊道。「它能安放在哪裡呢？」鴨子問道。「只有奧赫達（大地）才能承載它，」河狸說，「就是我們水域底下的奧赫達，我去把它取來。」河狸下去了，卻再也沒有回來。接著鴨子冒險一試，但不久牠的屍體便浮上了水面。許多潛水者都嘗試過而失敗，這時麝鼠知道路徑，自告奮勇去取，很快便用爪子帶著一小塊回來了。「但它很重，」牠說，「而且會長得很快。誰來承載它呢？」烏龜願意一試，於是奧赫達便被放在牠堅硬的龜殼上。光明有了安放之處後，水鳥們循著它的光芒向上飛去，用牠們展開的雙翼接住那女人，將她帶到烏龜的背上。於是哈努納，那隻烏龜，便成了大地承載者。當牠動一動，海洋便掀起巨浪；當牠躁動狂暴時，地震便裂開大口吞噬一切。

passages.text: To her solitude two lives were coming, one peaceful and patient, the other restless and vicious. The latter, discovering light under his mother's arm, thrust himself through, to contentions and strife, the right born entered life for freedom and peace. These were the Do-ya-da-no, the twin brothers, Spirits of Good and Evil. At the birth of Hah-gweh-di-yu his Sky Mother, Ata-en-sic, had died, and the island was still dim in the dawn of its new life when, grieving at his mother's death, he shaped the sky with the palm of his hand, and creating the Sun from her face, lifted it there, saying, 'You shall rule here where your face will shine forever.' But Hah-gweh-da-et-gah set Darkness in the west sky, to drive the Sun down behind it. Hah-gweh-di-yu then drew forth from the breast of his Mother, the Moon and the Stars, and led them to the Sun as his sisters who would guard his night sky. He gave to the Earth her body, its Great Mother, from whom was to spring all life.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 33-34; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 在她的孤寂中，有兩個生命即將降臨，一個平和而堅忍，另一個躁動而邪惡。後者發現了母親臂下的光亮，便強行鑽出，帶來爭鬥與紛爭；先出生的那個則為自由與和平而進入生命。這些便是多雅達諾，那對雙生兄弟，善與惡的靈。哈格韋迪尤誕生時，他的天空母親阿塔恩西克已經死去，島嶼仍在新生命的黎明中昏暗不明，他因母親之死而悲傷，便用手掌塑造天空，從她的面容造出太陽，將它舉到那裡，說道：「你要在這裡統治，你的面容將永遠照耀。」但哈格韋達埃特加卻把黑暗安置在西天，要把太陽驅趕到它背後。哈格韋迪尤於是從母親的胸中取出月亮與星辰，將它們引到太陽那裡，作為守護他夜空的姊妹。他將自己的身體賜予大地，即大地之母，一切生命都將從她而生。

passages.text: When the earth was completed and Hah-gweh-di-yu had bestowed a protecting Spirit upon each of his creation, he besought Hah-gweh-da-et-gah to reconcile his vicious existences to the peacefulness of his own, but Hah-gweh-da-et-gah refused, and challenged Hah-gweh-di-yu to combat, the victor to become the ruler of the earth. Hah-gweh-da-et-gah proposed weapons which he could control, poisonous roots strong as flint, monster's teeth, and fangs of serpents. But these Hah-gweh-di-yu refused, selecting the thorns of the giant crab-apple tree, which were arrow pointed and strong. With the thorns they fought. The battle continued many days, ending in the overthrow of Hah-gweh-da-et-gah. Hah-gweh-di-yu, having now become the ruler, banished his brother to a pit under the earth, whence he can not return. The first beings of earth were a race of gods who returned to the sky world when the Good Mind created men-beings. After the Good Mind had pulled up the tree of light he beheld his face in the pool of water in which it had grown. This gave him the idea of molding images in red clay which he afterward transformed into living beings. Thus did the human race take origin.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 36 and footnote; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 當大地完成，哈格韋迪尤為他所造的每一樣都賦予了一位守護之靈後，他懇求哈格韋達埃特加讓他那些邪惡的存在與自己那和平的存在相調和，但哈格韋達埃特加拒絕了，並向哈格韋迪尤挑戰決鬥，勝者將成為大地的統治者。哈格韋達埃特加提議使用他能操控的武器——堅如燧石的毒根、怪物的牙齒和毒蛇的獠牙。但哈格韋迪尤拒絕了這些，選擇了巨山楂樹的荊刺，它們如箭般尖銳而堅硬。他們以荊刺交戰。戰鬥持續了許多天，最終以哈格韋達埃特加被擊敗告終。哈格韋迪尤如今成了統治者，便將他的兄弟放逐到地底的一個深坑，從那裡他再也無法回來。大地最初的存在是一族神靈，當善心創造了人類之後，他們便回到了天空世界。善心拔起那棵光之樹後，在它曾生長的水池中看見了自己的面容。這給了他用紅泥塑造形象的想法，他隨後將其轉化為活生生的存在。人類便由此發源。

title.en: Naming the Winds: Bear, Panther, Moose, and Fawn
title.zh: 為四方之風命名：熊、豹、麋與幼鹿

region.en: Ga-oh's lodge in the north sky, and the four gates of the sky
region.zh: 北天風神之居與天的四門

period: Converse (1908)

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'Naming the Winds'

summary.en: When, in the creation of the earth, Hah-gweh-di-yu limited the duties of the powerful Ga-oh to the sky, assigning to him the governing of the tempests, he blew a strong blast that shook the whole earth to trembling, and summoned his assistants to a council. Ga-oh chose his aids from the terrestrial because of their knowledge of the earth: the bulky Bear Ya-o-gah, who had battled the boisterous winds as he came pushing mountains from his path, is bound and leashed into the north sky - 'you can freeze the waters with your cold breath; in your broad arms you can carry the wild tempests... You shall be North Wind'; the gentle Fawn Ne-o-ga walks with the summer sun and rules the flock of summer winds in the south; the ugly, fierce Panther Da-jo-ji, with a sound as of great claws tearing the heavens into rifts, carries the whirlwind on his strong back and is leashed to the west, 'where even the Sun will hurry to hide when you howl your warning to the night'; and the Moose O-yan-do-ne, whose horns spread wide to push back the forests and whose breath blows the mist and leads the cold rains, takes the east. Thus, with his assistants, does Ga-oh control his storms. When the north wind blows strong, the Iroquois say, 'The Bear is prowling in the sky.'
summary.zh: 創世之時，善靈把風神加奧的力量限定於天界，令其執掌風暴。加奧轟然一嘯，大地震顫，召集助手議事——他選擇地上的獸，因其識得大地：笨重的熊亞奧加一路推開群山而來，被縛上北天的韁繩——「你能以寒息凍結水面；你能以巨臂擁抱狂飆……你就是北風」；溫柔的幼鹿內奧加與夏日同行，執掌南天的夏日風群；兇惡的黑豹達喬吉撕天裂雲而至，背負旋風，被縛往西天——「你一長嘯，連太陽也要急急躲藏」；麋鹿奧揚多內角闊如犁、氣息引雨，領東方之風。自此四風各司其方：北風起時，易洛魁人便說「熊在天上巡行」。

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. The four winds as four beast-wardens is the Iroquois signature of the cardinal-direction myth.

passages.text: When, in the creation of the earth, Hah-gweh-di-yu limited the duties of the powerful Ga-oh to the sky, assigning to him the governing of the tempests, he blew a strong blast that shook the whole earth to trembling, and summoned his assistants to a council. Ga-oh chose his aids from the terrestrial because of their knowledge of the earth; and when his reverberating call had ceased its thunderous echoes, he opened his north gate wide across the sky and called Ya-o-gah, the Bear. Lumbering over the mountains as he pushed them from his path, Ya-o-gah, the bulky bear, who had battled the boisterous winds as he came, took his place at Ga-oh's gate and waited the mission of his call. Said Ga-oh, 'Ya-o-gah, you are strong, you can freeze the waters with your cold breath; in your broad arms you can carry the wild tempests, and clasp the whole earth when I bid you destroy. I will place you in my far north, there to watch the herd of my winter winds when I loose them in the sky. You shall be North Wind. Enter your home.' And the bear lowered his head for the leash with which Ga-oh bound him, and submissively took his place in the north sky.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 38; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 當大地初創之時，哈格威迪尤將強大的加奧的職責限定於天空，指派他掌管暴風雨；加奧吹出一陣強烈的氣息，震得整個大地顫抖，並召集他的助手們前來議事。加奧從陸地生物中挑選助手，因為牠們熟知大地；當他那迴盪的呼喚停止了雷鳴般的回聲之後，他在天空中大大敞開他的北門，召喚熊——雅奧加。雅奧加這頭笨重的熊，一路將山巒推離自己的道路、蹣跚地越過群山，牠來時曾與喧囂的狂風搏鬥，如今在加奧的門前就位，等待召喚所賦予的使命。加奧說：『雅奧加，你強壯，你能以寒息凍結眾水；在你寬闊的雙臂中，你能承載狂野的暴風雨，當我命令你毀滅時，你能緊抱整個大地。我要將你安置在我遙遠的北方，當我在天空中放出我的冬風之群時，你就在那裡看守牠們。你將成為北風。進入你的家吧。』那熊低下頭，接受加奧用以束縛牠的韁繩，順從地在北方的天空中就位。

passages.text: In a gentler voice Ga-oh called Ne-o-ga, the Fawn, and a soft breeze as of the summer crept over the sky; the air grew fragrant with the odor of flowers, and there were voices as of babbling brooks telling the secrets of the summer to the tune of birds, as Ne-o-ga came proudly lifting her head. Said Ga-oh, 'You walk with the summer sun, and know all its paths; you are gentle, and kind as the sunbeam, and will rule my flock of the summer winds in peace. You shall be the South Wind. Bend your head while I leash you to the sky, for you are swift, and might return from me to the earth.' And the gentle fawn followed Ga-oh to his great gate which opens the south sky.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 38-39; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 加奧以較為溫和的聲音召喚小鹿——尼奧加，一陣如夏日般的柔風掠過天空；空氣中瀰漫著花朵的芬芳，並有彷彿潺潺溪流的聲音，伴著鳥兒的曲調向夏天訴說秘密，此時尼奧加驕傲地昂首走來。加奧說：『你與夏日的太陽同行，知曉它所有的路徑；你溫和，如陽光般仁慈，將平安地統領我的夏風之群。你將成為南風。低下你的頭，讓我將你繫於天空，因為你敏捷，或許會從我這裡返回大地。』那溫順的小鹿跟隨加奧來到他那敞開南方天空的巨門前。

passages.text: Again Ga-oh trumpeted a shrill blast, and all the sky seemed threatening; an ugly darkness crept into the clouds that sent them whirling in circles of confusion; a quarrelsome, shrieking voice snarled through the air, and with a sound as of great claws tearing the heavens into rifts, Da-jo-ji, the Panther, sprang to the gate. Said Ga-oh, 'You are ugly, and fierce, and can fight the strong storms; you can climb the high mountains, and tear down the forests; you can carry the whirlwind on your strong back, and toss the great sea waves high in the air, and snarl at the tempests if they stray from my gate. You shall be the West Wind. Go to the west sky, where even the Sun will hurry to hide when you howl your warning to the night.' And Da-jo-ji, dragging his leash as he stealthily crept along, followed Ga-oh to the furthermost west sky.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 39; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 加奧又吹響一陣尖銳的號聲，整個天空似乎都充滿威脅；一片醜惡的黑暗潛入雲中，使它們在混亂的漩渦中旋轉；一個好爭吵、尖嘯的聲音在空中咆哮，伴隨著彷彿巨大的爪子將天穹撕裂成裂隙般的聲響，豹——達喬吉——躍至門前。加奧說：『你醜陋、兇猛，能與強烈的風暴搏鬥；你能攀上高山，能撕倒森林；你能以強壯的背承載旋風，將巨大的海浪拋向高空，若暴風雨偏離我的門，你還能對牠們咆哮。你將成為西風。前往西方的天空，當你向黑夜吼出警告時，連太陽也會急忙躲藏。』達喬吉拖著韁繩，悄悄地匍匐而行，跟隨加奧來到最遙遠的西方天空。

passages.text: Yet Ga-oh rested not. The earth was flat, and in each of its four corners he must have an assistant. One corner yet remained, and again Ga-oh's strong blast shook the earth. And there arose a moan like the calling of a lost mate, the sky shivered in a cold rain, the whole earth clouded in mist, a crackling sound as of great horns crashing through the forest trees dinned the air, and O-yan-do-ne, the Moose, stood stamping his hoofs at the gate. Said Ga-oh, as he strung a strong leash around his neck, 'Your breath blows the mist, and can lead the cold rains; your horns spread wide, and can push back the forests to widen the path for my storms as with your swift hoofs you race with my winds. You shall be the East Wind, and blow your breath to chill the young clouds as they float through the sky.' Thus, with his assistants, does Ga-oh control his storms. When the north wind blows strong, the Iroquois say, 'The Bear is prowling in the sky'; if the west wind is violent, 'The Panther is whining.' When the east wind chills with its rain, 'The Moose is spreading his breath'; and when the south wind wafts soft breezes, 'The Fawn is returning to its Doe.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 39; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 然而加奧並未歇息。大地平坦，在其四個角落的每一處，他都必須有一位助手。尚餘一個角落，加奧強烈的氣息再度震動大地。於是響起一聲如失偶之獸呼喚般的哀鳴，天空在冷雨中顫抖，整個大地籠罩在霧中，一陣彷彿巨角衝撞林中樹木的劈啪聲響徹空中，麋鹿——奧揚多內——站在門前跺著蹄子。加奧一邊將一條強韌的韁繩套上牠的脖子，一邊說：『你的氣息吹起霧靄，能引來冷雨；你的角寬闊展開，能推開森林，為我的風暴拓寬道路，同時你以迅捷的蹄子與我的風競逐。你將成為東風，當年輕的雲朵飄過天空時，吹出你的氣息使牠們寒冷。』加奧就這樣與他的助手們一同掌控他的風暴。當北風強勁吹起時，易洛魁人說：『熊正在天空中徘徊』；若西風狂暴，則說：『豹正在哀鳴』。當東風帶著雨寒冷吹拂時，說：『麋鹿正在散播牠的氣息』；而當南風送來柔和的微風時，說：『小鹿正回到牠的母鹿身邊』。

title.en: He-no, the Thunderer: The Niagara Serpent and the Horseshoe Fall
title.zh: 雷神希農：尼亞加拉巨蛇與馬蹄瀑

region.en: Behind the great falls at Niagara
region.zh: 尼亞加拉大瀑之後

period: Converse (1908), with Esquire Johnson's account recorded 1876

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'He-no, the Thunderer'

summary.en: As guardian of the heavens, He-no is intrusted with the thunder, the voice of admonition, which can be heard above the turmoil of the tempests; it is also his duty to direct the rain for refreshing the earth. As a human being he wears in his hair a magic feather which renders him invulnerable to the attacks of Evil. In his celestial travels He-no carries on his back a great basket containing boulders of the chert rock, which he hurls at evil spirits whenever he discovers them in the sky; sometimes the evil spirits evade these boulders and they fall to the earth enveloped in fire. Before He-no was transferred to the skies, he dwelt behind the great falls at Niagara, where he controlled the roaring of its waters. 'I can wash the world if you want me to,' he told God, in Esquire Johnson's telling. During his terrestrial life the Iroquois were terrified by the annual visits of a hideous serpent that lived in a cave near the Niagara cataract: toward the spring this creature would emerge, enter the burial places of the Iroquois, feed on the dead, and poison the land with pestilence. He-no pursued it, and overtaking it as it wound through Buffalo creek threw a terrific thunderbolt upon it; in its writhings the monster pushed the shores of the creek into the bends which yet remain. Slowly dying, it floated down the Niagara river to the verge of the great cataract where, in a final death throe, its bulky body arched backward in a semicircle extending from shore to shore; the dead body restrained the rushing waters for a time, but finding an opening through the rocks they dashed on, sundering the ledge - and thus was formed the Horse Shoe fall of the great cataract.
