summary.zh: 作為天界守護者，希農執掌雷霆——高過風暴喧囂的警世之聲；他亦司降雨潤土。他化人形時髮間插著一根使其不受邪惡所傷的魔法羽毛。他在天上行旅時背負巨筐，內裝燧石巨礫，見邪靈在天空出現便擲石擊之；邪靈偶或閃避，石塊裹火墜地。希農上天之前住在尼亞加拉大瀑之後，掌管瀑聲。老酋約翰遜的講述裡，他對神說：「若你願意，我能洗淨整個世界。」他尚在人間時，一條棲於瀑旁岩洞的醜蛇年年為患：春水初漲，此物出洞鑽入易洛魁人的墓地吞食死者，歸途毒化大地，疫病流行。希農追之，在水牛溪畔以巨雷擊中；怪物掙扎間把溪岸擠出至今猶存的河曲。它垂死順尼亞加拉河漂向瀑口，最後的掙扎使龐軀向後彎成跨岸的半環；屍身一度攔住奔流，水自岩隙破峽而出，掀翻岩棚——馬蹄瀑由此而成。

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. The Thunderer hates witches, underwater people and False Faces - he must be soothed with tobacco incense.

passages.text: As guardian of the heavens, He-no is intrusted with the thunder, the voice of admonition, which can be heard above the turmoil of the tempests. It is also his duty to direct the rain for refreshing the earth. In the planting season, He-no has supervision of the seeds, and in the growing time renders beneficent aid in ripening the fruits and maturing the harvest. He-no can assume the form of a human being and, as such, dressed as a warrior, he wears in his hair a magic feather, which renders him invulnerable to the attacks of Evil. On these occasions he is invested with authority to inflict dire punishment upon evil doers, and is dreaded as the avenger of vice. In his celestial travels, He-no carries on his back a great basket containing boulders of the chert rock, which he hurls at evil spirits whenever he discovers them in the sky. Sometimes the evil spirits evade these boulders and they fall to the earth enveloped in fire.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 39-40; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 作為天界的守護者，赫諾受託掌管雷電——那告誡之聲，能在暴風雨的喧囂之上被聽見。他的職責還包括引導雨水以滋潤大地。在播種的季節，赫諾監管種子；在生長之時，他施予仁慈的助力，使果實成熟、收穫圓滿。赫諾能化為人形，如此裝扮時，他如戰士一般，髮間插著一根神奇的羽毛，使他免受邪惡的攻擊。在這些場合，他被授予對作惡者施以嚴厲懲罰的權柄，並作為惡行的復仇者而令人畏懼。在天界巡行時，赫諾背上背著一個大籃子，裡面裝著燧石岩的巨石，每當他發現天空中的惡靈，便向牠們投擲。有時惡靈躲過這些巨石，巨石便裹著火焰墜落大地。

passages.text: Sometime afterward God met a man walking about by himself and addressing him in a pleasant way, asked him what he was looking for. He said he was amusing himself looking around the world, that he had a great many grandchildren not far off, that he was in fact the Thunderer and had many grandchildren near and loved them much. Moreover, that he wished to be set about some great work and asked God to give him something to do. God said to him, 'What can you do?' He said, 'I can wash the world if you want me to.' 'Very well,' said God, 'that would be a good work for you to do and I will employ you to do that work for me. You can make it rain and wash the earth often.' (Taken verbatim from the manuscript notes of Mrs Asher Wright, a missionary who interviewed Johnson in 1876.)
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, footnote; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 此後某時，上帝遇見一個獨自走動的人，以和悅的方式向他打招呼，問他在尋找什麼。他說他正自娛自樂地環顧世界，說他在不遠處有許多孫兒，說他實際上就是雷神，在附近有許多孫兒且深愛著他們。此外，他希望被委派一些偉大的工作，並請求上帝給他一些事做。上帝對他說：『你能做什麼？』他說：『如果你願意，我能洗滌世界。』『很好，』上帝說，『那對你來說會是一件好工作，我要雇用你為我做那件工作。你可以造雨，時常洗滌大地。』（逐字錄自阿舍·賴特夫人的手稿筆記，她是一位傳教士，於一八七六年採訪了約翰遜。）

passages.text: During the terrestrial life of He-no, the Iroquois people were terrified by the annual visits of a hideous serpent that lived in a cave near the Niagara cataract. Toward the spring, when the rivers were loosing themselves and pouring their torrents into Lake Erie, this creature would emerge from its cave, and entering the burial places of the Iroquois, feed on the dead; and in the sinuous paths of its return, would poison the land with a pestilence to which large numbers of the people fell victims.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 42-43; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 在赫諾於人間生活的期間，易洛魁人年年都為一條猙獰巨蛇的來訪而驚恐不已，那蛇棲居在尼亞加拉瀑布附近的洞穴中。每逢春季，河水解凍、洪流傾注伊利湖時，這怪物便會出洞，潛入易洛魁人的墓地，以死者為食；而在牠蜿蜒歸返的途中，還會以瘟疫毒害大地，大批族人因而喪命。

passages.text: He-no pursued it, and overtaking it as it wound through the De-gi-ya-goh (Buffalo creek) threw a terrific thunderbolt upon it, and in its writhings to escape, the monster pushed the shores of the creek into the bends which yet remain. Slowly dying, it floated down the Niagara river to the verge of the great cataract where, in a final death throe, its bulky body arched backward in a semicircle extending from shore to shore. The dead body restrained the rushing waters for a time, but finding an opening through the rocks, they dashed on, sundering the ledge which shelved over the river as they tumbled down the abyss in a riotous roar. And thus was formed the Horse Shoe fall of the great cataract.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 42-43; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 赫諾追趕牠，在牠蜿蜒穿過德吉亞戈（水牛溪）時追上，向牠擲下一道可怖的雷霆；怪物在掙扎逃竄之際，把溪岸推擠成至今仍存的那些彎曲。牠緩緩死去，順著尼亞加拉河漂流到大瀑布的邊緣，在那裡作最後的垂死掙扎，龐大的身軀向後拱起，形成一道由一岸延伸至對岸的半圓。死屍一時阻住了奔騰的河水，但水流在岩石間找到缺口，便猛衝而下，把懸在河上的岩臺撕裂，轟然喧囂地墜入深淵。大瀑布的馬蹄瀑便是這樣形成的。

title.en: Gun-no-do-yah, the Thunder Boy, and the Human Snake
title.zh: 雷童貢諾多亞與人形蛇

region.en: Lake Ontario and the Thunderers' sky
region.zh: 安大略湖與雷族的天空

period: Converse (1908)

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'Gun-no-do-yah, the Thunder Boy, and the Human Snake'

summary.en: He-no had hurled down a terrific rain storm which had flooded the land and overflowed the lakes and rivers, and, in pity for Earth, sent down one of his aids to pacify the waters. Passing over a canton of the Senecas he heard a voice wailing in great distress, and descending found a small child floating in the flood that had carried its parents away. Recognizing the child as Gun-no-do-yah, the son of a chief, he determined to save it, and carrying it to his home in the sky laid it to rest on a strong black cloud. He-no, who had been out drilling his Thunderers, upon returning overheard the boy grieving the loss of his parents and, deciding to adopt him, transformed him into a Thunder Hunter: 'There dwells in a lake a human monster that no mortal has been able to kill; my Thunderers, not being of earth, have sought him in vain... Gun-no-do-yah, having been human, can follow the trails of the earth.' For many months the hunt was in vain until, under the black clouds of Lake Ontario, the monster beckoned him to come closer: 'I know your strong arrows; they can not reach me. He-no, your master, I fear not; I scorn his thunder... Come with me. I will guide you to my home in the rocks deep below which the sun never sees. Come and comb my long mane, it is tangled with fish and is heavy.' As Gun-no-do-yah drew his bow with all his strength the string snapped; seizing him in its hissing mouth the monster carried him down to the bottom of the lake. He-no was sleeping when the boy appeared to him in a dream; the Thunderers ploughed through the deep caves under the water, found the monster sleeping, drew it from its hiding place and carried it to He-no, who slew it and drew from its body the life of Gun-no-do-yah. Lake Ontario is noted for its violent winds, and when they drive the canoe high on the waves, the Indians know that the spirit of the snake is there 'twisting the water' in its revenge; and when the lightning darts quick across the sky, they whisper in awe, 'Gun-no-do-yah is chasing it!'
summary.zh: 希農擲下暴雨，大水泛濫成災；他憐惜大地，遣一名助手下凡安撫洪水。助手飛過塞內卡人的村社時，聽見哭喊，降落水面，發現一個漂在洪水中的孩子——他的父母已被水沖走。這正是酋長之子貢諾多亞；助手把孩子抱上雲端安放於黑雲之上。希農聽聞男孩哀悼雙親，決定收養他，把他變成「雷獵手」：「湖中住著一個人形怪物，凡人殺之不得；我的雷族非地上之身，遍尋無果……貢諾多亞曾是凡人，能踏地上的蹤跡。」數月無功。一個烏雲壓湖之夜，怪物喚他近前：「我認得你的神箭，但箭到不了我身；我不怕你的主子，我鄙視他的雷霆……來吧，我領你去我太陽照不到的深岩之家。來替我梳理長鬣——裡面纏滿魚，重得很。」貢諾多亞張弓用力，弓弦啪然崩斷；怪物張開嘶嘶的大口把他拖入湖底。希農在夢中聽他陳情，大怒，遣最勇的雷戰士犁遍水下深穴，把熟睡的怪物拖出，殺之，自其軀中取出貢諾多亞的性命。安大略湖以狂風著稱——風把獨木舟掀上浪尖時，印第安人知道那是蛇靈在「攪水」復仇；閃電疾掠長空時，他們便敬畏地低語：「貢諾多亞在追牠！」

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. The underwater people (Jo-di'kwa-do') are great sorcerers; their daughters especially beautiful - landmen who don the shining snake-skin suits become forever horned serpents.

passages.text: He-no, the Thunderer, had hurled down a terrific rain storm which had flooded the land and overflowed the lakes and rivers, and, in pity for Earth, sent down Ha-de-ne-no-da-on, one of his aids, to pacify the waters. As Ha-de-ne-no-da-on was passing over a canton of the Senecas, he heard a voice wailing in great distress, and descending, found a small child floating in the flood that had carried its parents away. Recognizing the child as Gun-no-do-yah, the son of a chief whom on his earth visits he had frequently seen, and who was a great warrior, he determined to save it, and carrying it to his home in the sky, laid it to rest on a strong black cloud and returned to earth on his peace mission. He-no, who had been out drilling his Thunderers, upon returning overheard the boy grieving the loss of his parents and, deciding to adopt him, transformed him into a Thunder Hunter.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 42-43; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 雷霆者赫諾曾擲下一場可怖的暴雨，洪水淹沒大地，湖泊與河流皆漫溢而出；他憐憫大地，便遣下他的一名助手哈德內諾道安去平息眾水。哈德內諾道安經過塞內卡人的一處村落時，聽見一個聲音在極度的痛苦中哀號，便降下察看，發現一個小孩漂浮在沖走了其父母的洪水中。他認出這孩子是岡諾多亞，乃是一位酋長之子——他造訪人間時常見到這位酋長，其人是一員偉大的戰士——便決意救他，把他帶到天上的家中，安置在一朵堅實的黑雲上，然後重返人間執行他平息的使命。赫諾外出操練他的雷霆眾，回來時聽見這男孩為失去雙親而悲傷，便決定收養他，把他化為一名雷霆獵手。

passages.text: Said He-no, 'He has been sent to me; he is a human and knows all the paths of the earth, and can render me great service. There dwells in a lake a human monster that no mortal has been able to kill; my Thunderers, not being of earth, have sought him in vain; and he defies me and my thunderbolts while he ravages the lake of its fish, and frightening the fishers away deprives the people of their food. Gun-no-do-yah, having been human, can follow the trails of the earth. I will make him powerful, and give him a strong bow and arrow, and he shall follow my storms when my black clouds shadow the lakes, and hunt the monster to its death.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 43; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 赫諾說道：『他被送到我這裡來了；他是人，熟知大地上的一切路徑，能為我立下大功。有一湖中住著一頭人形的怪物，沒有哪個凡人能殺得了牠；我的雷霆眾既非大地之物，尋牠也是徒勞；牠蔑視我和我的雷霆，一面蹂躪湖中的魚，一面把漁人嚇走，奪去族人的食物。岡諾多亞既曾為人，便能追循大地的蹤跡。我要使他強大，賜他強弓利箭，當我的黑雲遮蔽湖泊時，他將隨我的風暴而行，把那怪物追殺至死。』

passages.text: But one night when the Thunderers were savagely hurling their bolts over the lake which the clouds obscured in their blackness, and the fish swam deep in fear of the reverberating echoes, Gun-no-do-yah went boldly into the lake, and encountering the snake again drew his bow, when the snake beckoned to him to come closer and listen; and then it began to speak. 'Come closer,' it said, 'and fear me not. I know you well, and I know your strong arrows; they can not reach me. He-no, your master, I fear not; I scorn his thunder, the lightning passes by me. Your task is useless and you need not serve him. I am your friend and will teach you how to shoot the fish in the night. I will reveal to you all the secrets of the waters. Come with me. I will guide you to my home in the rocks deep below which the sun never sees. Come and comb my long mane, it is tangled with fish and is heavy.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 43-44; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 然而有一夜，雷霆眾正兇猛地向湖上擲下雷霆，烏雲以其漆黑遮蔽了湖面，魚兒因畏懼迴盪的雷聲而游向深處；岡諾多亞卻大膽走入湖中，再度遭遇那蛇，便拉開弓，那蛇卻向他招手，要他靠近細聽；隨後牠開口說話。『靠近些，』牠說，『不要怕我。我很了解你，也知道你那強勁的箭；它們射不到我。你的主人赫諾，我不怕；我蔑視他的雷霆，閃電從我身旁掠過。你的任務徒勞無功，你不必為他效勞。我是你的朋友，會教你如何在夜裡射魚。我會向你揭示水中所有的秘密。跟我來。我會帶你到我深居岩下的家，那裡太陽從不曾看見。來吧，替我梳理我長長的鬃毛，它纏著魚，沉重得很。』

passages.text: Gun-no-do-yah would not listen, he came to kill; but as he drew his bow with all his strength, the string snapped, the dead arrow fell to the water, and he was powerless. Raising its head high in the air, the monster opened its hissing mouth, and seizing Gun-no-do-yah, carried him down to the bottom of the lake. He-no was sleeping, when Gun-no-do-yah appeared to him in a dream and related his misfortune... Diligently they ploughed through the deep caves under the water, where they found the monster sleeping; and drawing it from its hiding place carried it to He-no, who slew it and drew from its body the life giving Gun-no-do-yah. And great was the rejoicing of the Thunderers and warriors. Now, that Gun-no-do-yah had been saved, He-no would never permit him to revisit the earth... Lake Ontario is noted for its violent winds, and when they drive the canoe high on the waves, the Indians know that the spirit of the snake is there 'twisting the water' in its revenge and when the lightning darts quick across the sky, they whisper in awe, 'Gun-no-do-yah is chasing it!'
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 44-45; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 岡諾多亞不肯聽從，他來是為了誅殺；但當他竭盡全力拉開弓時，弓弦斷了，那支未發的箭落入水中，他變得毫無力量。怪物把頭高高舉向空中，張開嘶嘶作響的嘴，抓住岡諾多亞，把他帶到湖底。赫諾正在沉睡，岡諾多亞在夢中向他顯現，訴說了自己的不幸……他們勤奮地犁過水下的深穴，在那裡發現怪物正在沉睡；他們把牠從藏身之處拖出，帶到赫諾面前，赫諾殺了牠，並從牠體內取出賦予生命的岡諾多亞。雷霆眾與戰士們歡欣鼓舞。如今岡諾多亞既已獲救，赫諾便再也不許他重返人間……安大略湖以狂風猛烈著稱，當狂風把獨木舟推上高高的浪頭時，印第安人便知道那是蛇的靈魂在那裡『攪動水面』以圖報復；而當閃電迅疾劃過天際，他們便敬畏地低聲說道：『岡諾多亞正在追它呢！』

title.en: O-se-ha-da-gaar, the Dew Eagle: The Lake of Dew on His Back
title.zh: 露鷹奧塞哈達加爾：背上的露水之湖

region.en: Lodge far beyond the west sky
region.zh: 西天之外的鷹巢

period: Converse (1908)

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'O-se-ha-da-gaar, the Dew Eagle'

summary.en: In the myth lore of the Iroquois, where everything animate or inanimate is endowed with supernatural powers, the myths relating to the sun have special significance. But there are Spirits of Evil who roam the Earth and defying the Sun seek to overthrow its beneficent power: the Fire Spirit may summon his Flame Bearers and, descending to Earth, burn and destroy the harvests. At the coming of the Fire Spirit, mountains shrink down, the thirsting valleys suck dry the streams and springs, night pales her stars, and all Earth faints. In vain Ga-oh searches the heavens for his hiding winds; in vain He-no hunts his thunderbolts to hurl at the Flame Bearers. But to this desolation comes O-se-ha-da-gaar, a great bird whose lodge is far beyond the west sky and who carries a lake of dew in the hollow of its back, faithfully guarded by a band of Listeners, great birds who fly far above the Sun, hear every sound and know every voice in the heavens. When the Fire Spirit suffocates the Earth, they speed to her voice and bear it to the Dew Eagle, who hears, and pluming for flight pushes the skies far apart, obscuring the Sun with his vast spreading wings as they dip to the east and the west fanning gentle breezes, and mist veils the skies as through his fluttering wings he sifts down from his lake the dews to refresh the famishing Earth. Then all nature revives, the Fire Spirit flees, and her harvests rise to new life.
summary.zh: 易洛魁神話中萬物皆有靈性，而關於太陽的神話尤具深意。但也有邪靈在地上橫行、公然挑戰太陽的恩澤——火靈可召其火焰使者下凡焚燬莊稼。火靈一至，山嶽萎縮，乾渴的谷地把溪泉吸盡，夜色掩星，大地昏厥。風神遍尋不見藏匿的風，雷神遍尋不見可擲的雷石，一切似已無望。此時，露鷹奧塞哈達加爾自西天之外的巢居而來——牠背上馱著一泓露水之湖；一群「傾聽者」巨鳥飛翔在太陽之上，聽盡天上的聲音。火靈窒息大地時，眾鳥把她的呼聲送到露鷹耳中；鷹展翅高飛，把天穹推向兩旁，雙翼遮日、自東而西扇起微風；霧靄垂天，牠篩下的露水滋潤飢渴的大地。於是萬物復甦，火靈遁逃，田疇重煥生機。

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. Parker notes the Dew Eagle has been stripped of the thunder power other races gave the Thunder Bird - Hi'no took that office, and the Eagle labors faithfully when Hi'no fails to come. A legend says an enormous white eagle from the east ocean will battle with the Dew Eagle until he dies; then the Ongweh'owe will no longer have woods and fields but dry desert places where they will starve.

passages.text: In the myth lore of the Iroquois, where everything animate or inanimate is endowed with supernatural powers either evil or good, the myths relating to the sun, so fecund with life-giving power, have special significance. Although never wandering from his path across the sky, the Sun controls his broad dominion through his assistants. Serving Spirits, whom he endows with various powers and sends down to Earth to fulfil his missions... But there are others, Spirits of Evil, who roam the Earth, and defying the Sun, seek to overthrow its beneficent power. Among these is the Fire Spirit who, malevolently jealous of the Spirits of Good, may summon his Flame Bearers and, descending to Earth, burn and destroy the harvests. At the coming of the Fire Spirit, mountains shrink down, the thirsting valleys suck dry the streams and springs. Night pales her stars, and all Earth faints.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 45-46; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 在易洛魁人的神話傳說中，一切有生命或無生命之物皆被賦予或善或惡的超自然力量，因此，與太陽——這般充滿賦生之力者——相關的神話具有特殊的意義。太陽雖從不偏離其橫越天空的路徑，卻透過其助手們掌控著遼闊的領地。那些服侍的靈，他賦予牠們種種力量，並派遣牠們下凡人間以完成他的使命……但還有另一些靈，即邪惡之靈，牠們漫遊於大地，違抗太陽，力圖推翻其仁慈的力量。其中之一便是火靈，牠心懷惡意地嫉妒善靈，可能召來牠的持焰者，降臨大地，焚燒並毀壞收成。火靈一到，山岳退縮，乾渴的谷地吸乾溪流與泉源。黑夜使群星黯淡，整個大地昏厥。

passages.text: In vain Ga-oh searches the heavens for his hiding winds. In vain He-no hunts his thunderbolts to hurl at the Flame Bearers, and all seems hopeless and lost. But to this desolation comes O-se-ha-da-gaar, a great bird, whose lodge is far beyond the west sky, and who carries a lake of dew in the hollow of its back. O-se-ha-da-gaar is wise, and does not listen to every call. He knows his power and waits. He is faithfully guarded by a band of Listeners, great birds who fly far above the Sun and can see all that passes below. They hear every sound and know every voice in the heavens, and watch the soft winds which waft the summer clouds to gather the showers; and when the Fire Spirit suffocates the Earth, they speed to her voice, and bear it to O-se-ha-da-gaar who waits in his lodge.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 46-47; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 加奧（Ga-oh）徒然在天上搜尋他藏匿的風。赫諾（He-no）徒然尋覓他的雷霆以投向持焰者，一切似乎都絕望而無望。然而，就在這片荒蕪之中，奧塞哈達加爾（O-se-ha-da-gaar）來了，那是一隻巨鳥，其巢穴遠在西天之外，牠的背脊凹陷處載著一湖露水。奧塞哈達加爾睿智，不聽從每一聲呼喚。牠深知自己的力量，靜候時機。牠由一群「諦聽者」忠實守護，這些巨鳥飛翔於太陽之上極高處，能看見下方發生的一切。牠們聽見每一個聲響，知曉天上每一個聲音，並守望那吹送夏日雲朵以聚積陣雨的柔和之風；而當火靈令大地窒息時，牠們便疾奔至她的聲音處，將其帶給在巢中等待的奧塞哈達加爾。

passages.text: Then O-se-ha-da-gaar hears; and pluming for flight, pushes the skies far apart, obscuring the Sun with his vast spreading wings as they dip to the east and the west fanning gentle breezes, and mist veils the skies as through his fluttering wings he sifts down from his lake the dews to refresh the famishing Earth. Then all nature revives, the Fire Spirit flees; the parching Earth bares her broad breast to the falling dews; her glad rivers and lakes rejoice, and her harvests rise to new life. At the Harvest Feast of the Iroquois, the Creator is thanked for having bestowed upon the people the guarding vigilance of He-no, and is implored not to withdraw from them his power, which controls the gentle rains in the seedtime and the dews in the ripening.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 47; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 於是奧塞哈達加爾聽見了；牠理羽準備飛翔，將天穹遠遠推開，當牠巨大的雙翼向東與向西低垂、扇起輕柔的微風時，遮蔽了太陽，而當牠透過撲動的雙翼從湖中篩下露水以滋潤枯竭的大地時，霧氣籠罩了天空。於是萬物復甦，火靈逃遁；焦渴的大地袒露寬闊的胸膛迎接落下的露水；她歡欣的河流與湖泊喜悅起來，她的收成重獲新生。在易洛魁人的豐收節上，人們感謝造物主賜予族人赫諾的守護警覺，並懇求他不要從他們那裡收回他的力量——那掌控播種時節的甘霖與成熟時節的露水的力量。

title.en: Sais-tah-go-wa: How the Rainbow Was Made from a Sea Serpent
title.zh: 賽斯托瓦：彩虹由海蛇化成

region.en: The arc of the sky between east and west
region.zh: 橫跨東西天空的彩弧

period: Converse (1908)

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'O-ga-nyo-da and Sais-tah-go-wa, the Rainbow and the Serpent'

summary.en: In the creation of the earth the Sky Woman gave birth to the twins, Hah-gweh-di-yu and Hah-gweh-da-et-gah; and with their birth Good and Evil came upon the Earth, for between the brothers there was continual strife. Hah-gweh-di-yu created beautiful rivers and planted high hills to guard their peaceful flow through the valleys, which enraged Hah-gweh-da-et-gah, who brought forth Sais-tah-go-wa, a sea monster, directing him to enter and destroy them. Accustomed to the freedom of the broad seas, Sais-tah-go-wa was furious when restricted by the banks of the streams, and viciously strove to rend them apart, writhing his way through the waters and hurling great rocks upon them as they fled to the sea. Hastening to their rescue, Hah-gweh-di-yu caused the monster, dreading his power, to seek escape: being unable to return through the rivers he had destroyed, he fled to the sky. The Sun was peacefully tracking its trail across the heavens when Sais-tah-go-wa appeared, and upon learning what the monster had done, determined that it should never return to the earth to injure the creations of Hah-gweh-di-yu, and throwing him across the sky, clasped him down to the east and the west. It chanced at this time that He-no, the Thunderer, was passing on his way through a storm, and admiring the beautiful colors of Sais-tah-go-wa as he stretched across the sky, picked him up, saying, 'My Lightning Hunter needs this for his bow,' and straightway carried him up to his lodge. Sais-tah-go-wa is restless in his captivity, and when He-no is busy directing his storms, endeavors to escape; but the ever watchful Sun detects him, and again bending him across the sky, paints him with his brightest colors that he may be discovered by He-no. In summer showers the red man sees Sais-tah-go-wa in the resplendent hues that arch the sky, and as they fade away and the sun comes forth, he exclaims, 'The rain is past! - Sais-tah-go-wa tried to escape, but He-no has taken him back to his lodge!'
summary.zh: 天女生下雙生兄弟，善惡二靈自此同居於世，鬥爭不休。善靈闢出美麗的河流、植下高山以護其安流，惡靈大怒，遣出海怪賽斯托瓦入河毀壞。慣於遼闊大海的海怪被溪岸所拘，狂怒地扭身撕裂河川、投石阻流。善靈趕來相救；海怪懼其神威，既無法經由自己毀掉的河道返回，便逃往天空。太陽正沿天路安行，見此情景，決不許怪物再回大地傷害善靈的造物，便把他橫拋過天、按定於東西兩端。恰逢雷神希農穿風而過，讚賞海怪橫天的美色，便拎起他說：「我的追雷獵手正需要這個做弓弦。」隨即把他帶回天屋。賽斯托瓦被囚不安，趁希農忙於指揮風暴時企圖逃脫；但日輪明察，再次把他彎橫天際、塗上最豔的彩繪，好讓希農認出捉回。夏日驟雨之後，紅人望見橫天的絢爛虹彩漸褪、日頭重現，便歡呼：「雨過了！——賽斯托瓦想逃跑，希農又把他押回去了！」

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. A rainbow-from-serpent aition unique in the corpus.

passages.text: In the creation of the earth, which the Turtle bears upon its back, the Sky Woman gave birth to the twins, Hah-gweh-di-yu, and Hah-gweh-da-et-gah; and with their birth, Good and Evil came upon the Earth; for Hah-gweh-da-et-gah was bad minded, and between the brothers there was continual strife. Hah-gweh-di-yu, the Good Minded, was ever striving to create all things beautiful, which angered Hah-gweh-da-et-gah, who sought only to disfigure and destroy. Hah-gweh-di-yu created beautiful rivers, and planted high hills to guard their peaceful flow through the valleys, which enraged Hah-gweh-da-et-gah, who brought forth Sais-tah-go-wa, a sea monster, directing him to enter and destroy them.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 47; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 在大地的創生中——大地由烏龜背負——天空女子生下了雙胞胎哈格韋迪尤（Hah-gweh-di-yu）與哈格韋達埃特加（Hah-gweh-da-et-gah）；隨著他們的誕生，善與惡降臨大地；因為哈格韋達埃特加心懷惡念，兄弟之間爭鬥不斷。哈格韋迪尤，即善心者，始終致力於創造一切美好之物，這激怒了哈格韋達埃特加，他只想毀壞與破壞。哈格韋迪尤創造了美麗的河流，並植下高丘以守護它們穿越谷地的平靜流淌，這激怒了哈格韋達埃特加，他召來了賽斯塔戈瓦（Sais-tah-go-wa），一頭海怪，指使牠進入並摧毀它們。

passages.text: Sais-tah-go-wa, accustomed to the freedom of the broad seas, was furious when restricted by the banks of the streams, and viciously strove to rend them apart, writhing his way through the waters and hurling great rocks upon them as they fled to the sea. Hearing the loss of his rivers should they be engulfed in the deep seas and his high lands and valleys perish from thirst, Hah-gweh-di-yu hastened to their rescue, whereupon, Sais-tah-go-wa, discovering his approach and dreading his power, sought to make his escape, and being unable to return through the rivers he had destroyed, fled to the sky.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 47-48; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 賽斯塔戈瓦習慣於廣闊海洋的自由，當被河岸所限時便暴怒不已，兇猛地力圖將它們撕裂，蜿蜒穿行於水中，並在它們逃向大海時向它們投擲巨石。哈格韋迪尤聽聞他的河流若被深海吞沒便將失去，他的高地與谷地也將因乾渴而消亡，便急忙前去營救；於是，賽斯塔戈瓦發現他逼近，畏懼他的力量，企圖逃脫，卻因無法經由牠所毀壞的河流返回，便逃向天空。

passages.text: The Sun was peacefully tracking its trail across the heavens when Sais-tah-go-wa appeared, and upon learning what the monster had done, determined that it should never return to the earth to injure the creations of Hah-gweh-di-yu, and throwing him across the sky, clasped him down to the east and the west. It chanced at this time that He-no, the Thunderer, was passing on his way through a storm, and admiring the beautiful colors of Sais-tah-go-wa as he stretched across the sky, picked him up, saying, 'My Lightning Hunter needs this for his bow,' and straightway carried him up to his lodge.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 48; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 太陽正平靜地循其軌跡橫越天際，賽斯塔戈瓦出現了；太陽得知這頭怪物所行之事後，決意牠絕不應再返回大地傷害哈格韋迪尤的造物，便將牠擲過天空，把牠扣鎖於東與西之間。恰在此時，雷霆者赫諾正穿越一場風暴而行，他讚賞賽斯塔戈瓦橫展天際時那美麗的色彩，便將牠拾起，說道：「我的閃電獵人正需要這個作他的弓」，隨即把牠帶上他的居所。

passages.text: Sais-tah-go-wa is restless in his captivity, and when He-no is busy directing his storms, endeavors to escape; but the ever watchful Sun detects him, and again bending him across the sky, paints him with his brightest colors that he may be discovered by He-no, who quickly comes and carries him back to his lodge. In summer showers the red man sees Sais-tah-go-wa in the resplendent hues that arch the sky, and as they fade away and the sun comes forth, he exclaims, 'The rain is past! - Sais-tah-go-wa tried to escape, but He-no has taken him back to his lodge!'
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 48; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 賽斯-塔-戈-瓦在囚禁中躁動不安，趁赫諾忙於指揮他的風暴時，竭力想要逃脫；但永遠警覺的太陽察覺了他，再次將他彎曲橫跨天際，以自己最明亮的色彩將他塗染，好讓赫諾能發現他，赫諾便迅速趕來，將他帶回自己的小屋。在夏季的陣雨中，紅人從橫跨天際的絢爛色彩裡看見賽斯-塔-戈-瓦，而當色彩褪去、太陽現身時，他驚呼：『雨過去了！——賽斯-塔-戈-瓦試圖逃走，但赫諾已將他帶回自己的小屋了！』

title.en: Ska-hai-we, Indian Summer: The Sun Smokes His Peace Pipe
title.zh: 印第安夏：太陽吸起和平之菸

region.en: The south sky where the Sun rests through the winter solstice
region.zh: 太陽冬至休憩的南天

period: Converse (1908)

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'Ska-hai-we, Indian Summer'

summary.en: When in the late autumn the Sun 'walks crooked,' he is on his way to the south sky where during the winter solstice he rests, leaving his sleep spirit on guard during his absence. Previous to his departure he smokes the ah-so-qua-ta (peace pipe) to veil the earth as he councils with the Great Mother. 'Earth, Great Mother, holding your children close to your breast, hear my power! Listen. The days of my glowing are passed. I glare and I burn and I scorch no more. I am lighting my fire from you to kindle my ah-so-qua-ta, the pipe of my sleep. In the haze of my Indian summer I wrap you to silence while Ga-oh holds fast on your pillowing hills the flock of his jealous clouds... Soon I will travel my crooked sky trail. I hurry. I have heard the swift blast of Go-ho-ne's voice... When I sleep in my South, Go-ho-ne is bold, when I open my eyes, Go-ho-ne flies, and He-no grows frightened and still! I am A-deka-ga-gwaa! I reign, and I rule all your lives!... When I come again my warriors will battle throughout the skies; Ga-oh will lock his fierce winds; He-no will soften his voice; Go-ho-ne will fly, and tempests will war no more!'
summary.zh: 深秋時節，太陽「斜行」——那是他趕往南天冬眠的路上，留下「睡靈」代為守夜。臨行前他點燃「阿索誇塔」和平菸斗，以煙靄罩地，與大母親議事。「大母親啊，把你懷中的孩子摟緊，聽我的權能！我發光的時日已盡；我不再灼烤大地。我正從你身上引火，點燃我安眠的菸斗。印第安夏的煙靄把你裹入寧靜，風神在他的雲群中按住你的丘陵……我將沿著斜斜的天路趕路。我聽見冬神戈霍內的疾呼了……我在南方沉睡時，戈霍內便猖狂；我一睜眼，戈霍內便逃，雷神也嚇得啞然！我是太陽阿德卡加瓜！我統御、我掌管你們所有生命！……我再來時，我的戰士將遍戰諸天；風神將鎖住狂風，雷神將柔聲，冬神將奔逃，風暴止息！」

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain.

passages.text: When in the late autumn the Sun 'walks crooked,' he is on his way to the south sky where during the winter solstice he rests, leaving his 'sleep spirit' on guard during his absence. Previous to his departure he smokes the ah-so-qua-ta (peace pipe) to veil the earth as he councils with the Great Mother. 'Earth, Great Mother, holding your children close to your breast, hear my power! Listen. The days of my glowing are passed. I glare and I burn and I scorch no more. I am lighting my fire from you to kindle my ah-so-qua-ta, the pipe of my sleep. In the haze of my Indian summer I wrap you to silence while Ga-oh holds fast on your pillowing hills the flock of his jealous clouds. The smoke of my ah-so-qua-ta must not be driven back. Soon I will travel my crooked sky trail. I hurry. I have heard the swift blast of Go-ho-ne's voice, and am flocking the fearing clouds of the Ska-hai-we closer together as they feather the stem of my ah-so-qua-ta.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 48-49; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 當深秋時節太陽「歪斜而行」，他正前往南方的天空，在冬至期間於彼處歇息，離去時留下他的「睡眠之靈」看守。啟程之前，他抽著阿-索-夸-塔（和平煙斗），在與大母商議時以此籠罩大地。『大地，大母啊，將你的孩子緊抱於胸前，聽我的力量！聽吧。我熾燃的日子已然過去。我不再灼耀、不再燃燒、不再炙烤。我從你身上點燃我的火，以燃起我的阿-索-夸-塔，我睡眠的煙斗。在我印第安夏日的薄霧中，我將你裹入寂靜，而加-奧則將他那群嫉妒的雲牢牢拘於你如枕的群山之上。我的阿-索-夸-塔之煙絕不可被驅回。不久我將踏上我歪斜的天路。我匆匆而行。我已聽見戈-霍-內之聲的疾風，正將斯卡-海-韋那群驚懼的雲聚攏得更緊，它們如羽般附於我阿-索-夸-塔的莖上。』

passages.text: 'See! Ga-oh floats gentle winds to the smoke of my ah-so-qua-ta. The north, east, south and west must smoke my peace pipe. I rule the sky! I summon An-da, and she watches my fields. I call Se-oh and she sends forth her stars to guard my dark paths. When He-no, the Thunderer, pours down his rain, I warn as I paint my O-ga-nyo-da to hang on the falling clouds, and He-no hushes his voice... Your mountains will wake when I come again, your mountains will wake, your rivers run fast, and lakes cradle low. Go-ho-ne will flee, I will burn his thongs. Your heart will hear my calling voice. Your seeds will climb to my waiting glow, and your breast flow swift to nourish your young.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 49-50; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 『看哪！加-奧將柔和的風吹向我阿-索-夸-塔的煙。北方、東方、南方與西方都必須抽我的和平煙斗。我統治天空！我召喚安-達，她看守我的田野。我呼喚塞-奧，她放出她的星辰守護我黑暗的路徑。當雷霆者赫諾傾下他的雨，我以描繪我的奧-加-尼奧-達懸於落雲之上作為警示，赫諾便壓低了他的聲音……當我再度歸來，你的群山將甦醒，你的群山將甦醒，你的河流將奔流迅疾，湖泊將低低搖盪。戈-霍-內將逃遁，我將燒斷他的皮索。你的心將聽見我呼喚的聲音。你的種子將攀向我等待的光輝，你的胸膛將迅速湧流以哺育你的幼子。』

passages.text: 'Great Mother, listen! I am A-deka-ga-gwaa, the Sun! I rule the skies! I govern An-da. I chase Go-ho-ne. I frighten the shriek of the Thunderer's voice when he furrows my paths with his storms; but when I touch the wings of his flying clouds, they fold the rains fast and sift dews to your thirsting vales. I scorch and I burn, and I kill! I turn my face, and the tempests come. When I sleep in my South, Go-ho-ne is bold, when I open my eyes, Go-ho-ne flies, and He-no grows frightened and still! I am A-deka-ga-gwaa! I reign, and I rule all your lives!... As I sleep down to my dreams, the paths of my sky land slant crooked and small; the breath of my ah-so-qua-ta grows slow, its panting fire dies black, its ashes are pale, the trails grow dark, and my sleep spirit watches near!'
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 50-51; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 『大母啊，聽吧！我是阿-德卡-加-瓜，太陽！我統治天空！我管轄安-達。我追逐戈-霍-內。當雷霆者以風暴犁開我的路徑時，我驚散他那聲音的尖嘯；但當我觸及他飛雲的翅膀，它們便將雨緊緊收攏，並篩下露水滋潤你乾渴的谷地。我炙烤、我燃燒，我殺戮！我轉過臉去，暴風雨便至。當我在南方沉睡，戈-霍-內便大膽妄為；當我睜開雙眼，戈-霍-內便逃遁，赫諾也變得驚懼而沉寂！我是阿-德卡-加-瓜！我君臨，我統治你們所有的生命！……當我沉入夢鄉，我天空之地的路徑便歪斜而細小；我阿-索-夸-塔的氣息漸緩，它喘息的火焰化為黑燼，它的灰燼蒼白，小徑漸暗，而我的睡眠之靈在近旁守望！』

title.en: Deh-oh-niot, the Evil Soul Gatherer
title.zh: 魂收集者德奧尼奧特

region.en: The pathway of spirits (the Milky Way) and the treetops
region.zh: 精靈之路（銀河）與樹梢

period: Converse (1908)

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'Deh-oh-niot, the Evil Soul Gatherer'

summary.en: Sky color is the Deh-oh-niot, who haunts the tall tree tops and the high mountain crests. With the face of a wolf, the wings of a vulture, the body of a panther and claws like a hawk, the Deh-oh-niot wanders in the pathway of spirits - the Milky Way - and is one of the emissaries Death sends to the earth to gather souls. The sick fear him, the dying hear him clawing at the door, where he whines like a cat if the spirit is departing, or barks like a wolf if it is not ready to travel. By the law of Death, Deh-oh-niot can seize only the evil of a spirit which enters his domain; should he capture but a small portion of a soul, he may convey it to Death and be rewarded for his service. If, in a fierce struggle, the spirit should gain its freedom, Deh-oh-niot will have revenge by transforming it into a 'fire stone' and throwing it down to the earth where it may be eternally imprisoned. When a 'fire stone' (meteor) flames through the sky, 'Deh-oh-niot is gathering souls'; and should it fall to the earth, 'Deh-oh-niot has pushed a soul from its trail.' When a comet appears in the heavens, Deh-oh-niot is spreading his tail.
summary.zh: 德奧尼奧特通身天色，出沒於高樹之巔與山峰之脊。牠有狼的面孔、兀鷹的翅膀、豹的身軀與鷹的利爪，遊走於精靈之路——銀河——是死神差往大地收集魂魄的信使之一。病人懼牠，垂死者聽見牠在門外抓撓：魂將離去時牠如貓般哀鳴，魂未就緒時牠如狼般吠叫。依死亡之律，牠只能捕取進入其疆域之魂的惡的部分；即使只攫得魂的一小角，也可上交領賞。若魂在惡鬥中掙脫，牠便化之為「火石」擲回大地，永世囚禁。流星劃空，是「德奧尼奧特在收集魂魄」；流星墜地，是「德奧尼奧特把一個魂推下了它的軌道」；彗星現於天空，是德奧尼奧特在舒展長尾。

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain.

passages.text: Sky color is the Deh-oh-niot, who haunts the tall tree tops and the high mountain crests. With the face of a wolf, the wings of a vulture, the body of a panther and claws like a hawk, the Deh-oh-niot wanders in the 'pathway of spirits,' and is one of the emissaries Death sends to the earth to gather souls. The sick fear him, the dying hear him clawing at the door, where he whines like a cat if the spirit is departing, or barks like a wolf if it is not ready to travel.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 51; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 天空之色即德-奧-尼奧特，他出沒於高聳的樹梢與高山之巔。德-奧-尼奧特長著狼的面孔、禿鷲的翅膀、黑豹的身軀，爪如鷹隼，遊蕩於「神靈之路」，是死神派往大地收集靈魂的使者之一。病者畏懼他，將死者聽見他在門上抓撓，若靈魂正將離去，他便如貓般哀鳴；若靈魂尚未準備好啟程，他便如狼般吠叫。

passages.text: By the law of Death, before whom all departing spirits must pass on their journey, Deh-oh-niot can seize only the evil of a spirit which enters his domain, and even then it may escape him if, in its earth existence, good has predominated. Yet, should Deh-oh-niot be able to capture but a small portion of a soul, he may convey it to Death, and be rewarded for his service. If, in a fierce struggle, the spirit should gain its freedom, Deh-oh-niot will have revenge by transforming it into a 'fire stone,' and throwing it down to the earth where it may be eternally imprisoned. Were Deh-oh-niot any other than sky color, there might be escape from his power; but he can sit on a tree where its top blends with the sky, and there no one can see him.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 51-52; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 依死神之律——所有離去的靈魂在旅途中都必須從他面前經過——德-奧-尼奧特只能攫取進入其領域之靈魂的邪惡部分，即便如此，若該靈魂在世時善佔優勢，仍可能從他手中逃脫。然而，只要德-奧-尼奧特能捕獲靈魂的一小部分，便可將其帶給死神，並因這份效勞而獲得獎賞。若在一場激烈的搏鬥中靈魂獲得了自由，德-奧-尼奧特便會將其變成一塊「火石」拋落大地，作為報復，使其永遠被囚禁於彼處。倘若德-奧-尼奧特不是天空之色，或許還有逃脫其力量的可能；但他能坐在樹上，樹梢與天空融為一體，在那裡無人能看見他。

passages.text: To hear the voice of Deh-oh-niot is an evil omen, and some dire calamity will follow those who have listened to it. If Deh-oh-niot appears to a person who is not ill, his death will soon follow... When a 'fire stone' (meteor) flames through the sky, 'Deh-oh-niot is gathering souls'; and should it fall to the earth, 'Deh-oh-niot has pushed a soul from its trail.' When a comet appears in the heavens, Deh-oh-niot is spreading his tail.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 52; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 聽見德-歐-尼歐特（Deh-oh-niot）的聲音是不祥之兆，聽過這聲音的人必將遭遇可怕的災禍。若德-歐-尼歐特現身於一個沒有生病的人面前，那人的死期便不遠了……當「火石」（流星）劃過天際燃燒時，便是「德-歐-尼歐特正在聚集亡魂」；倘若它墜落於地，則是「德-歐-尼歐特把一個亡魂推離了它的軌跡」。當彗星出現在天上時，便是德-歐-尼歐特在展開他的尾巴。

title.en: Od Je-so-dah and Ji-hen-yah: The Dancing Stars and the Sky Witches
title.zh: 舞星與天巫

region.en: The Pleiades over the council house at New Year
region.zh: 新年時議屋上空的昂宿

period: Converse (1908)

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'Od Je-so-dah and Ji-hen-yah, the Dancing Stars and the Sky Witches'

summary.en: An Indian hunter was teaching his eleven sons the secrets of the forest when, as night shadowed the trees, soft singing voices floated through the stillness till they awakened Hai-no-nis, the eldest. Charmed by the weird chanting, he aroused his brothers to listen, and they followed as it led through bewildering paths to a large tree where under its branches a great circle widened its moon shadows. The song resumed in a quicker strain that tuned them to swift dancing till in the frenzy of its measure they could not cease; delirious with motion, they danced onward and upward till they had left the earth far beneath in their skyward flight. Day after day the brothers danced; the pitying Moon, thinking to quiet them, left her path and led them to her procession of stars, but their ceaseless dancing set the stars whirling till the Moon, frightened at the confusion, transformed them to a group of fixed stars and assigned them the charge of the New Year of the red man, commanding that forevermore they must dance over the council house during the ten days of his New Year's feast. When Hai-no-nis left his brothers he followed the voices - the Ji-hen-yah, the Sky Witches - and promised that if they would not further torment his brothers, they should dance forever in their honor. These Sky Witches frequently descend to the earth in the darkness in search of victims for their sky feasts.
summary.zh: 獵人正教十一個兒子森林的奧秘；夜色籠林之際，柔緩的歌聲飄來，喚醒了長兄海諾尼斯。他被奇異的歌聲迷住，喚醒弟弟們循聲而去，穿過迷離小徑，來到一株大樹下月光圈出的圓地。歌聲再起，節奏轉急，眾兄弟不由自主地旋轉起舞，神志迷離，愈舞愈高，直把大地拋在遙遠的下方。他們晝夜不休地舞著；慈心的月亮離開自己的軌道，領他們加入星辰的行列——但他們不停的舞步把眾星攪得團團轉，月亮驚慌，便把他們化為一群定星，並委以紅人新年的職守：永遠在議屋上空、於新年十日祭期中起舞。海諾尼斯則循聲尋去，發現那是「天巫」吉亨雅；他與她們約定：若不再折磨他的弟弟們，眾星便永遠以舞向他們致敬。這些天巫至今仍常在黑夜降臨大地，為她們的天上盛宴獵取人牲。

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. Parker's footnote version: the chief sang the Ji-ha-ya (the witch) song and bade them dance and look upward; one who looked down fell.

passages.text: An Indian hunter was teaching his eleven sons the secrets of the forest, and had led them into its innermost density where game strode unafraid in its stillness... As they slept, soft singing voices floated through the still trees, nearer and nearer approaching till they awakened Hai-no-nis, the eldest of the eleven brothers. Charmed by the weird chanting, he aroused his brothers to listen to the sorcerous song, and they followed as it led through bewildering paths to a large tree where under its branches a great circle widened its moon shadows. For a time the voices ceased, but as the brothers waited, the song was resumed in a quicker strain that tuned them to swift dancing till in the frenzy of its measure, they could not cease. They implored the Night Wind to guide them back to their father, but it passed heedlessly by, and the voices led the brothers still further as, delirious with motion, they danced onward and upward till they had left the earth far beneath in their skyward flight.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 53; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 有一位印第安獵人正在教他的十一個兒子森林的奧祕，並領他們進入森林最深密之處，那裡的獵物在寂靜中毫不畏懼地闊步而行……當他們睡著時，柔和的歌聲飄過靜止的樹林，愈來愈近，直到喚醒了十一個兄弟中的長兄海-諾-尼斯（Hai-no-nis）。他被那怪異的吟唱所迷，便喚醒兄弟們一同聆聽這魔幻之歌，他們隨著歌聲前行，穿過令人迷亂的小徑，來到一棵大樹下，樹枝下一個大圓圈展開了它的月影。歌聲一度停歇，但當兄弟們等待時，歌聲又以更急促的曲調重新響起，使他們隨之起舞，愈舞愈快，直到在樂曲的狂熱中再也無法停下。他們懇求夜風引領他們回到父親身邊，但夜風毫不理會地掠過，歌聲仍引領兄弟們繼續前行，他們因舞動而神志恍惚，一路舞著、向上，直到在飛向天際的途中把大地遠遠拋在腳下。

passages.text: Day after day the brothers danced, and day after day the troubled Sun glanced after them but could not reach them. Night after night the stars grew dizzy as the dancers swirled round the sky, when Hai-no-nis disappeared and the song-voices fainted far away. Yet the dancers could not rest, and the pitying Moon, thinking to quiet them, left her path and led them to her procession of stars which was marching across the night sky. But their ceaseless dancing set the stars whirling till the Moon, frightened at the confusion, transformed them to a group of fixed stars and assigned them the charge of the New Year of the red man, commanding that forevermore they must dance over the council house during the ten days of his New Year's feast.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 53-54; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 兄弟們日復一日地舞著，憂心的太陽日復一日地瞥視他們，卻無法觸及他們。夜復一夜，星辰隨著舞者在天空中旋轉而眩暈，此時海-諾-尼斯消失了，歌聲也遠遠地微弱下去。然而舞者們仍無法停歇，心生憐憫的月亮想使他們安靜下來，便離開了自己的軌道，領他們加入她正行過夜空的星辰行列。但他們無休止的舞蹈使星辰旋轉不已，月亮驚懼於這混亂，便將他們變為一組固定的星辰，並指派他們掌管紅人的新年，命令他們從此必須在紅人新年慶典的十天期間，在議事屋上方舞蹈。

passages.text: When Hai-no-nis left his brothers he followed the voices, and discovering them to be the Ji-hen-yah (Sky Witches), promised that if they would not further torment his brothers, they should dance forever in their honor. And so the brothers continue to dance, ever obeying the Moon, which sometimes sends them to return wandering stars that may have lost their way in the darkness. These Sky Witches frequently descend to the earth in the darkness in search of victims for their sky feasts which they are ever celebrating. In the astronomical lore of the paleface, this celestial group of dancing brothers is known as the Pleiades, the brilliant constellation in the neck of Taurus.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 54; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 海-諾-尼斯離開兄弟們後，跟隨那些聲音而去，發現它們是吉-亨-雅（Ji-hen-yah，天空女巫），便許諾若她們不再折磨他的兄弟，她們便可永遠為紀念他們而舞蹈。於是兄弟們繼續舞蹈，始終聽從月亮的吩咐，月亮有時派他們去領回那些可能在黑暗中迷途的遊星。這些天空女巫常在黑暗中降臨大地，為她們不斷舉行的天空盛宴尋找犧牲者。在白人的天文學知識中，這組舞蹈的兄弟星辰被稱為昴宿星團，即金牛座頸部那明亮的星座。

title.en: O-so-ah, the Tall Pine, Speaks
title.zh: 高松奧索阿之言

region.en: Forest pines whose top branches point east and west
region.zh: 頂枝分指東西的森林高松

period: Converse (1908)

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'O-so-ah, the Tall Pine, Speaks'

summary.en: The spirit of the pine was once a brave war chief who led his warriors to victory till captured by his enemies and burned at the stake. In the metempsychosis of the Iroquois, the liberated spirit of the chief entered the pine, where it will remain forever the forest guide of the Indian people. It is a fact that the two topmost branches of the pine point to the east and the west, thus furnishing a compass for the red man when lost in the woods. These branches also symbolize the 'deer horns,' the insignia that ranks a chief. The legend relates that the chief of the skyward dancing party hearing the cries of his mother looked down: his act was a fatal one, for he immediately fell like a stone into soft clay, and disappeared. The mother mourned and watched over his grave spot for a year, and when springtime came again she saw a tiny green shoot springing above the sod. When the years passed by, it became a lofty evergreen tree and the people called it O'-so'-a. It was the first of its kind and the soul and blood and body of the chief were in it: this the people knew for they heard it sighing and moaning to its mates in the heavens at night. A thoughtless warrior slashed its bark with his knife and red blood poured out, and it was human blood. 'After many years,' says the story-teller, 'the feathers that dropped from the wide branches sprang up into the pine trees and these have thick sticky blood, but it is good for many things, canoes, ropes and medicines. So it's a good thing he looked down.'
summary.zh: 松樹之靈原是一位勇猛的戰爭酋長，屢戰屢勝，終被敵人所俘，縛上火刑柱燒死。依易洛魁的轉生之說，酋長解脫的魂魄進入了松樹，永為印第安人的林中嚮導。松樹最高的兩根頂枝分指東西，正是紅人迷途時的羅盤；這兩枝也象徵酋長的徽記「鹿角」。傳說說：升天舞隊的首領聽見母親的哭喚而低頭一望，此舉即是死期——他如石墜入軟泥，隨即沒入土中。母親守墓哀哭一年；翌年春天，草土間冒出一莖新綠。歲月流轉，長成參天常綠之樹，人稱「奧索阿」——此樹為其類之首，酋長的魂、血與身皆在其中：人們夜裡聽見它向天上的兄弟嘆息呻吟，便知端的。一個莽撞的戰士以刀割樹皮，樹中流出的竟是人的鮮血。「多年之後，」講故事的人說，「寬枝上落下的羽毛長成了松林，松脂黏稠如血，卻能用來造舟、搓繩、製藥。所以說，他當年低頭一望，倒是件好事。」

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. Companion to Parker's Seven Brothers of the Star Cluster.

passages.text: The spirit of the pine was once a brave war chief who led his warriors to victory till captured by his enemies and burned at the stake. In the metempsychosis of the Iroquois, the liberated spirit of the chief entered the pine, where it will remain forever the forest guide of the Indian people. It is a fact that the two topmost branches of the pine point to the east and the west, thus furnishing a compass for the red man when lost in the woods. These branches also symbolize the 'deer horns,' the insignia that ranks a chief.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 54; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 松樹之靈曾是一位勇敢的戰酋，他率領戰士們屢獲勝利，直到被敵人俘虜並綁在火刑柱上燒死。在易洛魁人的靈魂轉世信仰中，這位酋長解脫的靈魂進入了松樹，將永遠留駐其中，成為印第安人的森林嚮導。事實上，松樹最頂端的兩根枝條分別指向東方與西方，因而為在林中迷路的紅人提供了指南針。這兩根枝條也象徵著「鹿角」，即標示酋長身分的徽記。

passages.text: The legend relates that the chief of the skyward dancing party hearing the cries of his mother looked down. His act was a fatal one for he immediately fell like a stone into soft clay, for when he struck the earth he entered it and disappeared. The mother mourned and watched over his grave spot for a year and when springtime came again she saw a tiny green shoot springing above the sod. When the years passed by, it became a lofty evergreen tree and the people called it O'-so'-a (pine). It was the first of its kind and the soul and blood and body of the chief were in it. This the people knew for they heard it sighing and moaning to its mates in the heavens at night. A thoughtless warrior slashed its bark with his knife and red blood poured out, and it was human blood. 'After many years,' says the story-teller, 'the feathers that dropped from the wide branches sprang up into the pine trees and these have thick sticky blood, but it is good for many things, canoes, ropes and medicines. So it's a good thing he looked down.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, footnote; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 傳說講述，那位向天舞蹈的首領聽見母親的呼喊便向下望去。這一舉動為他招來致命的後果，因為他立刻像石頭般墜入柔軟的泥土中，當他觸及地面時便沒入其中消失了。母親哀悼不已，守護著他的墳地一年，當春天再度來臨時，她看見一株小小的綠芽從草皮中冒出。歲月流逝，它長成一棵高大的常綠樹，人們稱之為歐-索-阿（O'-so'-a，即松樹）。它是同類中的第一棵，酋長的靈魂、血液與身體都在其中。人們知道這一點，因為他們聽見它在夜間向天上的同伴嘆息呻吟。一個魯莽的戰士用刀割開它的樹皮，紅色的血便湧了出來，那是人血。「許多年後，」講述者說，「從寬大枝條上掉落的羽毛長成了松樹，這些松樹有著濃稠黏滯的血液，但這血對許多事物都有益處——獨木舟、繩索和藥材。所以他向下望了那一眼，倒是件好事。」

title.en: The Oppression of Uruk and the Making of Enkidu
title.zh: 烏魯克暴政與恩奇都之造

region.en: Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Standard Babylonian, c. 1200 BCE, Nineveh recension (Wilson/Muss-Arnolt translation 1901)

source.work: Babylonian and Assyrian Literature, 'The Epic of Ishtar and Izdubar', trans. Muss-Arnolt (1901)

summary.en: Gilgamesh, two-thirds god, no rival — no son to his father, no bride to her groom — wears out the young men of Uruk. The gods hear the people's cry and Aruru kneads a match for him: Enkidu, a strong bone of the earth.
summary.zh: 三分之二為神的吉爾伽美什無人能敵——不許父親有子、不許丈夫有妻——耗盡烏魯克的年輕人。眾神聞民之泣，阿魯魯以泥塑造其對手：恩奇都，大地強壯之骨。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Gilgamesh, two-thirds god and one-third man, leaves no son to his father, no bride to her groom; the shepherds of Uruk complain, and the walls themselves protest: the king's strength has no rival. The gods hear the cry and charge Aruru: create the double. She kneads a pin of clay from the earth's heart — Enkidu, the strong bone, covered with hair like grain, who eats grass with the gazelles and fills the waterholes with the wild herd.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gilgamesh epic, Tablet I (Wilson/Muss-Arnolt 1901); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Gilgamesh epic, Tablet I; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 吉爾伽美什三分之二是神、三分之一是人，他不留兒子給父親，不留新娘給新郎；烏魯克的牧人們抱怨，城牆本身也抗議：國王的力量無人能敵。眾神聽見了呼喊，吩咐阿魯魯：造出他的對偶。她從大地之心揉捏出一塊黏土——恩奇都，堅強的骨骼，渾身覆毛如穀物，與瞪羚同食草，與野獸群一同填滿水塘。

functions: Opening charter of the epic's social theme
Creation of the double as check on royal power
Frame narrative of the wall and the tablet-box

title.en: Enkidu Tamed
title.zh: 恩奇都被馴化

region.en: Steppe and Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 草原與烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian tablet 2 (Langdon translation 1917)

source.work: The Epic of Gilgamish, trans. Stephen Langdon (1917)

summary.en: The hunter's nets are useless against the beast-man; a temple courtesan is sent out, and a week of love civilizes Enkidu — the gazelles flee him — and Shamhat teaches him the bread, the beer and the counsel of Uruk.
summary.zh: 獵人無法以網捕捉獸人；神廟聖妓出草原，七日歡愛使恩奇都開化——羚羊棄他而去——沙姆哈特教他吃麵包、飲啤酒、聽烏魯克的智言。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; sexual content in ritual register.

passages.text: The hunter's snares catch nothing: the beast-man fills the pits with earth and frees the herd. The hunter sends for Shamhat, the temple's woman, and she takes Enkidu for six days and seven nights. When Enkidu rises, the gazelles flee him; his strength is doubled but his home is gone. Shamhat teaches him the bread men eat and the beer men drink, and he becomes as a man — she leads him to Uruk to meet the king.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gilgamesh, OB Tablet 2 (Langdon 1917); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Gilgamesh, OB Tablet 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 獵人的陷阱什麼也捕不到：那獸人用土填滿坑洞，放走了獸群。獵人派人去請神廟的女子沙姆哈特，她與恩奇都共度六天七夜。恩奇都起身之後，瞪羚見他而逃；他的力量倍增，但他的家園已失。沙姆哈特教他吃人吃的麵包、喝人喝的啤酒，他便成了如人一般——她領他前往烏魯克，去見國王。

functions: Allegory of civilization's threshold
Charter of the temple courtesan's civilizing office

variants.name: SB Tablet I-II
variants.summary: The Nineveh recension's version of the taming.

primary_sources.citation: Tablet 2, trans. Stephen Langdon (1917)

title.en: The Door of the Wedding: Gilgamesh Meets Enkidu
title.zh: 婚門之戰：吉爾伽美什遇恩奇都

region.en: Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian (Jastrow & Clay translation 1920)

source.work: An Old Babylonian Version of the Gilgamesh Epic, trans. Jastrow and Clay (1920)

summary.en: Enkidu bars the wedding door where Gilgamesh is to claim the first night; they wrestle through the street and doorway until the king conquers, and the conquered wild man becomes his friend — the friendship the epic will die of.
summary.zh: 恩奇都攔於婚門之前，阻吉爾伽美什行初夜之權；二人自街頭扭打到門檻，國王終勝；敗者反成摯友——史詩將為此誼而死。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Enkidu bars the door of the wedding chamber where Gilgamesh is about to claim the bride's first night; the two wrestle through the street and shatter the doorpost until Gilgamesh conquers. The defeated wild man declares his admiration: you are the strongest of men, and the friendship is sealed — the partnership the gods intended, against which Enlil later decrees one of them must die.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gilgamesh, OB tablets (Jastrow & Clay 1920); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Gilgamesh, OB tablets; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 恩奇都擋住婚房的門，吉爾伽美什正要在此佔有新娘的初夜；兩人在街上扭打，撞碎了門柱，直到吉爾伽美什取勝。戰敗的野人宣告他的欽佩：你是人中最強者，友誼就此締結——這是眾神所安排的夥伴關係，日後恩利爾卻判定他們之中必有一人死去。

functions: Founding scene of the friendship theme
Social critique of the lord's first night embedded in the duel

primary_sources.work: An Old Babylonian Version of the Gilgamesh Epic

title.en: Gilgamesh's Dreams and Ninsun's Adoption
title.zh: 吉爾伽美什之夢與寧蓀認子

region.en: Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian tablet 2 (Langdon translation 1917)

source.work: The Epic of Gilgamish, trans. Stephen Langdon (1917)

summary.en: Gilgamesh dreams a star falls like a meteor on him and an axe all love him; Ninsun interprets — a friend, mighty as a star of heaven, will be given you — bathes, prays to Shamash, and adopts Enkidu as her own.
summary.zh: 吉爾伽美什夢見流星墜身、神斧眾人爛愛；寧蓀解夢——天降摯友，力大如星——沐浴祈禱於沙瑪什，認恩奇都為己子。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Gilgamesh dreams a star falls on him like a gift of heaven, and a mighty axe that all the land loves; he brings the dream to his mother Ninsun, who reads it: a mighty friend shall be given you — the star is Enkidu, the axe his strength. Ninsun bathes, prays to Shamash, and adopts Enkidu as her own son; the two heroes are bound by the mother's blessing before they ever fight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gilgamesh, OB Tablet 2 (Langdon 1917); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Gilgamesh, OB Tablet 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 吉爾伽美什夢見一顆星如天賜之物落在他身上，又夢見一柄全地所愛的巨斧；他將夢帶給母親寧松，她解讀道：必有一位強大的朋友賜給你——那星是恩奇都，那斧是他的力量。寧松沐浴，向沙馬什祈禱，並收恩奇都為自己的兒子；兩位英雄在尚未交手之前，便已因母親的祝福而結為一體。

functions: Oracle model of the epic's dream readings
Adoption rite binding the heroes as brothers

title.en: The Yale Tablet: Toward the Cedar Forest
title.zh: 耶魯泥板：奔赴雪松林

region.en: Uruk to the cedar mountain (symbolic pin at the Lebanon range)
region.zh: 自烏魯克至雪松山（象徵性定位於黎巴嫩山脈）

period: Old Babylonian (Jastrow & Clay translation 1920)

source.work: An Old Babylonian Version of the Gilgamesh Epic, Yale tablet, trans. Jastrow and Clay (1920)

summary.en: The elders counsel against the journey — who has ever reached the cedar forest? Gilgamesh weeps and prays; Enkidu's lost gate-blade dreams are read; and the two set out with fifty picked men.
summary.zh: 長老勸阻此行——何人曾抵雪松林？吉爾伽美什泣而祈禱；恩奇都門扉之夢被解讀；二人遂率五十精兵出發。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The elders of Uruk counsel against the road: who, my king, has climbed the cedar mountain and kept his life? Gilgamesh weeps to Shamash and the journey is blessed. Enkidu dreams his gate-blade broken — the omen of his own end — and the dreams are read as tokens of the battle to come; the two friends set out with fifty picked men of the city.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gilgamesh, OB Yale tablet (Jastrow & Clay 1920); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Gilgamesh, OB Yale tablet; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 烏魯克的長老們勸阻這趟旅程：我的王啊，誰曾登上雪松山而保住性命？吉爾伽美什向沙馬什哭泣，旅程遂得祝福。恩奇都夢見他的門閂之劍折斷——那是他自己終局的徵兆——這些夢被解讀為即將到來的戰鬥之兆；兩位朋友帶著城中五十名精選的勇士出發。

functions: Preparation scene of the quest for fame
Dream-omen of Enkidu's death

variants.summary: The Nineveh recension's fuller march.

title.en: The Slaying of Humbaba
title.zh: 誅胡姆巴巴

region.en: Cedar forest of the Lebanon (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 黎巴嫩雪松林（象徵性定位）

period: Standard Babylonian, c. 1200 BCE (Wilson/Muss-Arnolt translation 1901)

source.work: Babylonian and Assyrian Literature, 'The Epic of Ishtar and Izdubar', trans. Muss-Arnolt (1901)

summary.en: The seven auras of Humbaba are taken from him one by one; the giant, stripped and caught, begs for his life and offers vassalage. Enkidu — or Gilgamesh's own resolve — strikes, and Humbaba's head is cut off and carried to Enlil.
summary.zh: 胡姆巴巴七道光環逐一被奪；巨人被擒後哭求饒命、願稱臣納貢。恩奇都（或吉爾伽美什之決心）搶先出手，胡姆巴巴首級被斬下獻於恩利爾。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The seven terrors of Humbaba are stripped from him one by one as the friends attack; caught in the net of his own auras, the giant weeps and offers his forest in vassalage, and Gilgamesh's mercy moves. Enkidu insists — kill him before Shamash's anger changes to aid — and the guardian's head is struck off and packed for Nippur; the cedar falls, and the friends carry home a victory that the god's rebuke will darken.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gilgamesh epic, Tablet V (Wilson/Muss-Arnolt 1901); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Gilgamesh epic, Tablet V; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 朋友們進攻時， Humbaba 的七種恐怖被逐一剝除；巨人困在自己光環的網中，哭泣著獻出他的森林為臣屬，吉爾伽美什的憐憫為之動搖。恩奇都堅持——趁沙馬什的怒氣尚未轉為援助之前殺了他——守護者的頭被砍下，打包送往尼普爾；雪松倒下，朋友們帶著勝利返家，而神的責備將使這勝利蒙上陰影。

functions: Central moral crisis of the quest for fame
Etiology of the cedar trade and the road to the west

title.en: Ishtar Rebuffed
title.zh: 伊什塔爾受辱

region.en: Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Standard Babylonian, c. 1200 BCE (Wilson/Muss-Arnolt translation 1901)

source.work: Babylonian and Assyrian Literature, 'The Epic of Ishtar and Izdubar', trans. Muss-Arnolt (1901)

summary.en: Ishtar, washing and adorning herself after the cedar victory, offers Gilgamesh marriage with all its gifts — the recitation of her ruined lovers is his answer; the goddess, shamed before heaven, demands the Bull of Heaven.
summary.zh: 雪松大捷後，伊什塔爾沐浴敷粉、妝點自身，向吉爾伽美什求婚，許以百般榮華——他卻歷數其情郎的下場作答。蒙羞的女神上告天庭，索要天牛。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Ishtar washes, dresses and comes to Gilgamesh with an offer of marriage: come, be my husband, and I will give you the lapis chariot, the golden wheels, the tribute of lands. Gilgamesh answers with her catalogue of ruined lovers — the shepherd turned to wolf, the gardener to spider. Shamed, the goddess climbs to heaven and demands the Bull of Heaven; Anu warns that the demand means seven years of famine, and she has the stores laid up first — the Bull descends.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gilgamesh epic, Tablet VI (Wilson/Muss-Arnolt 1901); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Gilgamesh epic, Tablet VI; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊絲塔沐浴、更衣，來到吉爾伽美什面前，向他求婚：來吧，做我的丈夫，我便賜你青金石戰車、黃金車輪，以及各邦的貢賦。吉爾伽美什卻以她那一串被毀的愛人作答——牧人化為狼，園丁化為蜘蛛。女神受辱，登上天界，索求天之公牛；安努警告說，此求將帶來七年饑荒，於是她先囤積了糧食——公牛便降臨了。

functions: Confrontation of hero and goddess
Catalogue of the goddess's ruined lovers as satire of the Ishtar cult

variants.name: Gilgamesh and the Bull of Heaven (Sumerian)
variants.summary: The earlier Sumerian version of the confrontation.

canonical_translation: Muss-Arnolt, 1901

primary_sources.citation: Tablet VI, trans. Muss-Arnolt (1901)

secondary_sources.work: The Epic of Gilgamesh
secondary_sources.citation: Andrew George, London, 1999

title.en: The Bull of Heaven Descends
title.zh: 天牛降世

region.en: Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Standard Babylonian, c. 1200 BCE (Wilson/Muss-Arnolt translation 1901)

source.work: Babylonian and Assyrian Literature, 'The Epic of Ishtar and Izdubar', trans. Muss-Arnolt (1901)

summary.en: The Bull drinks the Euphrates dry; at each snort a pit swallows a hundred men. Gilgamesh and Enkidu slay it — Enkidu taunts the weeping goddess with the beast's haunch — and Anu, the fates, and Enlil confer: one of the two must die.
summary.zh: 天牛吸乾幼發拉底河；每噴一次鼻息，便有一百人墮入地坑。二英雄合力誅之——恩奇都以牛後腿擲向哭泣的女神——安努、命運與恩利爾合議：二人之中必有一死。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The Bull of Heaven drinks the Euphrates dry and opens pit after pit with each snort; a hundred youths fall in. The heroes take it: Enkidu seizes the tail, and Gilgamesh drives the blade between neck and horns. Ishtar mourns on the wall; Enkidu throws the severed haunch at her — you demanded this death — and the gods confer: for the Bull and Humbaba, one of the two friends must die.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gilgamesh epic, Tablet VI (Wilson/Muss-Arnolt 1901); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Gilgamesh epic, Tablet VI end; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天之公牛飲乾幼發拉底河，每噴一口鼻息便裂開一個又一個坑洞；百名青年墜入其中。兩位英雄迎戰：恩奇都抓住牛尾，吉爾伽美什將刀刺入牛頸與牛角之間。伊絲塔在城牆上哀悼；恩奇都將割下的牛腿擲向她——這死是你所求的——眾神商議：因公牛與洪巴巴之故，兩位摯友之中必有一人死去。

functions: Catastrophe mechanism of the epic
Theology of hubris priced in a friend's life

variants.name: Gilgamesh and the Bull of Heaven (Sumerian)
variants.summary: The Sumerian version of the same battle.

canonical_translation: Muss-Arnolt, 1901

primary_sources.citation: Tablet VI, trans. Muss-Arnolt (1901)

secondary_sources.work: The Epic of Gilgamesh
secondary_sources.citation: Andrew George, London, 1999

title.en: Enkidu's Dream and Curse
title.zh: 恩奇都之夢與詛咒

region.en: Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Standard Babylonian, c. 1200 BCE (Wilson/Muss-Arnolt translation 1901)

source.work: Babylonian and Assyrian Literature, 'The Epic of Ishtar and Izdubar', trans. Muss-Arnolt (1901)

summary.en: Enkidu dreams the assembly of heaven condemns him to die in his friend's place; he curses the door, the hunter and the harlot — then, at Shamash's rebuke, blesses the woman who made him human — and lies down to die.
summary.zh: 恩奇都夢見天庭會議判其替友而死；他咒罵門扉、獵人與聖妓——經沙瑪什斥責後，轉而祝福使其成人的女子——隨即臥床待死。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Enkidu dreams the assembly of the great gods: for the Bull and Humbaba, one must die — it is Enkidu, taken in his friend's place. He curses the door he made, the hunter who trapped him, and Shamhat who civilized him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gilgamesh epic, Tablet VII (Wilson/Muss-Arnolt 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 恩奇都夢見眾大神的集會：因公牛與洪巴巴之故，必有一人死去——那人便是恩奇都，代其摯友而死。他詛咒自己造的那扇門、設陷阱捉住他的獵人，以及使他開化的沙姆哈特。

passages.text: Shamash rebukes him from the sky: it was Shamhat who gave you bread fit for a god and the counsel of men. Enkidu relents and blesses her — kings and priests will court her memory — and lies down, fevered, to die.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gilgamesh epic, Tablet VII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 沙馬什從天上責備他：正是沙姆哈特給你配得上神明的麵包，以及人的勸誡。恩奇都回心轉意，為她祝福——君王與祭司都將追念她——隨後臥倒，發著高熱，走向死亡。

functions: Judgment dream of the divine assembly
Curse-blessing turn as the epic's humanist core

variants.name: Death of Gilgamesh (Sumerian)
variants.summary: The consolation theology of the hero's own death.

canonical_translation: Muss-Arnolt, 1901

primary_sources.citation: Tablet VII, trans. Muss-Arnolt (1901)

secondary_sources.work: The Epic of Gilgamesh
secondary_sources.citation: Andrew George, London, 1999

title.en: The Lament over Enkidu
title.zh: 哭恩奇都

region.en: Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Standard Babylonian, c. 1200 BCE (Wilson/Muss-Arnolt translation 1901)

source.work: Babylonian and Assyrian Literature, 'The Epic of Ishtar and Izdubar', trans. Muss-Arnolt (1901)

summary.en: Gilgamesh touches his friend and cannot believe: shall I lie like him, and never rise? He commissions a statue of gold and lapis, lays Enkidu on a bed of the forest's gold, and keeps vigil until the worm falls from the nose.
summary.zh: 吉爾伽美什撫友而泣：我也要如此躺下，永不復起？他命人以黃金青金石造像，使恩奇都臥於雪松林之金床，守靈至屍蟲自其鼻落下。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Gilgamesh weeps over his friend: may I not die like you — my heart will not believe it. He veils the face, touches him, and the friend does not lift his head. A statue of gold and lapis is made; Enkidu is laid on a bed of the cedar forest's gold; the vigil is kept until the worm falls from his nose — and Gilgamesh, terrified by his friend's death, turns his face to the road of Utnapishtim.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gilgamesh epic, Tablet VIII (Wilson/Muss-Arnolt 1901); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Gilgamesh epic, Tablet VIII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 吉爾伽美什為摯友哀哭：願我不像你那樣死去——我的心不肯相信。他蒙住友人的臉，觸碰他，友人卻不再抬起頭來。一尊黃金與青金石的雕像被造了出來；恩奇都被安放在雪松林黃金所製的床上；守靈持續到蟲子從他鼻中落下——而吉爾伽美什，因摯友之死而驚懼，轉而面向通往烏特納匹什提姆的道路。

functions: Grief liturgy of the epic
Pivot from the fame quest to the immortality quest

variants.name: Death of Gilgamesh (Sumerian)
variants.summary: The hero's own death poem with grave-goods.

canonical_translation: Muss-Arnolt, 1901

primary_sources.citation: Tablet VIII, trans. Muss-Arnolt (1901)

secondary_sources.work: The Epic of Gilgamesh
secondary_sources.citation: Andrew George, London, 1999

title.en: Through the Tunnel of the Sun
title.zh: 穿越太陽隧道

region.en: Mount Mashu (symbolic pin in the eastern highlands)
region.zh: 瑪舒山（象徵性定位於東部山地）

period: Standard Babylonian, c. 1200 BCE (Wilson/Muss-Arnolt 1901)

source.work: Babylonian and Assyrian Literature, 'The Epic of Ishtar and Izdubar', trans. Muss-Arnolt (1901)

summary.en: Gilgamesh comes to the twin peaks of Mashu where the sun enters and leaves; the scorpion-people bar him, hear his grief, and let him pass: twelve hours of dark — then a garden of jewels with trees of carnelian and lapis bearing fruit.
summary.zh: 吉爾伽美什抵瑪舒雙峰——日出日入之處；蠍人守門，聞其哀慟而放行：黑暗十二時辰——隨後是寶石花園，瑪瑙與青金石之樹結滿果實。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Gilgamesh comes to Mount Mashu, twin peaks where the sun enters and leaves the world; the scorpion-people, male and female, bar the way — a mortal has never come here — until his grief moves them: go, and may the road bring you back safe. Twelve hours of darkness; then light. Before him spreads a garden of jewels: trees of carnelian and lapis bearing fruit of pearl, a grove that no sorrow has touched.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gilgamesh epic, Tablet IX (Wilson/Muss-Arnolt 1901); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Gilgamesh epic, Tablet IX; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 吉爾伽美什來到馬什山，那是太陽出入世界的雙峰；蠍人一男一女把守道路——凡人從未來過此地——直到他的悲傷打動了他們：去吧，願道路使你平安歸來。十二個時辰的黑暗；然後是光明。他面前展開一座寶石花園：紅玉髓與青金石之樹結出珍珠的果實，一片從未受過憂傷觸碰的樹林。

functions: Otherworld passage of the immortality quest
Vision of the jewel garden as the epic's image of paradise

variants.name: Nergal and Ereshkigal
variants.summary: The underworld journey genre's god-version.

canonical_translation: Muss-Arnolt, 1901

primary_sources.citation: Tablet IX, trans. Muss-Arnolt (1901)

secondary_sources.work: The Epic of Gilgamesh
secondary_sources.citation: Andrew George, London, 1999

title.en: Siduri's Counsel and the Ferryman
title.zh: 西杜里之諫與擺渡人

region.en: Tavern at the sea's edge (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 海邊酒館（象徵性定位）

period: Standard Babylonian, c. 1200 BCE (George Smith translation 1876)

source.work: The Chaldean Account of Genesis, 'Siduri and Sabitu. Nes-Hea the pilot. Water of death', George Smith (1876)

summary.en: At the world's edge the tavern-keeper Siduri bars her gate against the wild man and gives him the poem's great counsel: eat, drink, love — the gods kept eternal life for themselves. Then the ferryman Urshanabi is found: cross the waters of death, but not without breaking his stone things.
summary.zh: 在世界盡頭，酒館女掌櫃西杜里拒野人於門外，卻道出史詩中最偉大的忠告：食、飲、愛——永生乃神明自留之物。隨後尋得船夫烏爾沙納比：欲渡死亡之水，須先碎其石偶。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Siduri, the tavern-keeper at the sea's edge, bars her gate against the man who has destroyed her jars; hearing his grief — Enkidu, my friend, is clay — she counsels: eat your bread, wash your head, enjoy the child at your knee; the gods kept eternal life for themselves. She names the ferryman Urshanabi and his stone things; Gilgamesh, in fury, shatters them — and must now pole the boat himself across the waters of death with Urshanabi, the longest crossing in literature.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gilgamesh epic, Tablet X (George Smith 1876; SB recension); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Gilgamesh epic, Tablet X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 西杜里是海邊的酒館女主人，她關上大門，不讓那個毀壞她酒罈的人進來；聽了他的悲嘆——我的朋友恩奇都已成泥土——她勸告道：吃你的麵包，洗你的頭，享受膝上的孩子；眾神把永生留給了他們自己。她說出擺渡人烏爾沙納比與他的石物之名；吉爾伽美什一怒之下將它們砸碎——如今他必須親自與烏爾沙納比一同撐船渡過死亡之水，這是文學中最漫長的一次渡越。

functions: Philosophical counsel of the epic (carpe diem)
Threshold passage to Utnapishtim

variants.name: The song of the tavern (OB 'Gilgamesh, Enkidu and the netherworld' frame)
variants.summary: The earlier wisdom framing of death.

canonical_translation: George Smith, 1876

primary_sources.citation: Tablet X, trans. George Smith (1876), Siduri chapter

secondary_sources.work: The Epic of Gilgamesh
secondary_sources.citation: Andrew George, London, 1999

title.en: The Test of Sleep and the Plant of Youth
title.zh: 沉睡之試與青春仙草

region.en: Dilmun at the mouths of the rivers (symbolic pin at Bahrain)
region.zh: 兩河口之迪爾蒙（象徵性定位於巴林）

period: Standard Babylonian, c. 1200 BCE (Budge translation 1920)

source.work: The Babylonian Story of the Deluge and the Epic of Gilgamesh, E. A. Wallis Budge (1920)

summary.en: Utnapishtim tests the king with sleep — six days and seven the hero sleeps — then grants him the thorn-plant of youth; Gilgamesh bathes, and the serpent, rising from the pool, eats it and sloughs its skin: why death is now forever and the snake renews itself.
summary.zh: 烏特納皮什提以沉睡試探——英雄一睡七日——隨後賜予青春之刺草；吉爾伽美什沐浴之際，池中巨蛇竄出吞草、蛻去舊皮：死亡從此永駐，蛇卻得以新生。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Utnapishtim tests the claim that death can be defeated: sit, and do not sleep. Gilgamesh sleeps — six days and seven — and wakes with the fresh loaves counted against him: you cannot even conquer sleep; how will you conquer death?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gilgamesh epic, Tablet XI (Budge 1920); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 烏特納匹什提姆考驗「死亡可被戰勝」這一主張：坐下，且不要睡。吉爾伽美什卻睡了——六天又七天——醒來時，新鮮的麵包已在他面前一一數過：你連睡眠都無法征服，又怎能征服死亡？

passages.text: Yet Urshanabi reveals the thorn-plant of the deep: it restores youth. Gilgamesh brings it up, and while he bathes in the pool, the serpent rises from the water, eats the plant, and sloughs its skin. The hero weeps: for whose benefit have my hands labored? — and the answer of the epic is silence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gilgamesh epic, Tablet XI; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而烏爾沙納比揭示了深處的荊棘之草：它能使人恢復青春。吉爾伽美什將它取上來，而當他在池中沐浴時，蛇從水中升起，吃下那草，蛻去了皮。英雄哭泣道：我的雙手究竟為誰而勞作？——而史詩的回答是沉默。

functions: Etiology of the serpent's sloughing and mankind's mortality
Philosophical close of the immortality quest

variants.name: Etana and the plant of birth
variants.summary: The parallel plant-quest of the Kish king.

canonical_translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, 1920

primary_sources.citation: Tablet XI, trans. E. A. Wallis Budge (1920)

title.en: The Ghost of Enkidu
title.zh: 恩奇都之魂

region.en: Uruk, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克（伊拉克）

period: Standard Babylonian Tablet XII (translation of a Sumerian poem), c. 1200 BCE (Wilson/Muss-Arnolt 1901)

source.work: Babylonian and Assyrian Literature, 'The Epic of Ishtar and Izdubar', Tablet XII, trans. Muss-Arnolt (1901)

summary.en: The appended twelfth tablet returns to the netherworld: Enkidu goes down for the ball and stick, breaks the taboos, is held, and rises as a ghost to tell his friend the rules of the dead — the man with many sons sits at ease, the man with none weeps, the unburied has no rest.
summary.zh: 附錄第十二泥板重返冥界：恩奇都為球與棍下冥土，觸犯禁忌被困，化為幽魂升還，向摯友講述亡者之規——多子者安然坐，無子者啼哭，未葬者不得安息。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Enkidu descends for the fallen ball and stick and is held below; Gilgamesh begs the sun god, who opens a hole, and Enkidu rises as a ghost — the only living friend allowed a visit from the dead. The ghost's report is the underworld's law: the man with many sons sits at ease, the man with one weeps, the man with none burns his hand on bread he cannot eat; the man hung in the field has no rest, and the one whose corpse no one buried lies hungry in the street.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gilgamesh epic, Tablet XII (Wilson/Muss-Arnolt 1901); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Gilgamesh epic, Tablet XII; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 恩奇都為那落下的球與棍而下到冥界，卻被扣留於下；吉爾伽美什懇求太陽神，太陽神開了一個洞，恩奇都便以鬼魂之身升起——他是唯一獲准受亡者探訪的生前摯友。鬼魂的陳述便是冥界的法則：多子之人安然而坐，僅有一子之人哭泣，無子之人則在無法進食的麵包上灼燒自己的手；被懸於田野之人不得安息，而無人埋葬其屍者則在街頭飢餓地躺著。

functions: Eschatological instruction of the ghost visit
Charter of funerary remembrance as the dead's sustenance

variants.name: Gilgamesh, Enkidu and the Nether World (Sumerian)
variants.summary: The original Sumerian poem of which this is a translation.

canonical_translation: Muss-Arnolt, 1901

primary_sources.citation: trans. Muss-Arnolt (1901)

secondary_sources.work: The Epic of Gilgamesh
secondary_sources.citation: Andrew George, London, 1999, on Tablet XII

title.en: The Eagle, the Serpent and the Oath
title.zh: 巨鷹、巨蛇與盟誓

region.en: A great tree on the plain, Kish region, Iraq
region.zh: 平原巨樹，基什附近（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian and Neo-Assyrian versions (George Smith translation 1876)

source.work: The Chaldean Account of Genesis, 'The Story of the Eagle and Etana', George Smith (1876)

summary.en: An eagle and a serpent nest in one tree and swear the great oath of friendship by Shamash — whoever fails, his own reward shall fail. The eagle, greedy, eats the serpent's young; the betrayed one prays to the sun and takes its revenge in the pit.
summary.zh: 鷹與蛇同棲一樹，向沙瑪什立下友誼大誓——背誓者必遭天譴。鷹貪食蛇之子；被欺者祈於日神，在坑中復仇。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: An eagle and a serpent nest in the same great tree and swear the oath of Shamash: friendship and loyalty, and may the reward of the oath-breaker fail him. The eagle, flying high, sees the serpent's young and eats them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Etana legend, Tablet I (George Smith 1876); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一隻鷹與一條蛇在同一棵大樹上築巢，並向沙馬什立誓：友誼與忠誠，願背誓者的回報落空。鷹飛上高空，看見蛇的幼崽，便將牠們吃掉了。

passages.text: The serpent, betrayed, prays to Shamash; the sun's counsel is to lie hidden in the belly of a slain wild ox — and when the eagle comes to feed, the serpent seizes him by the wings, breaks them, and casts him into the pit to die of hunger and thirst.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Etana legend, Tablet I; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蛇遭背叛，向沙馬什祈禱；太陽神的建議是躲藏在一頭被殺的野牛腹中——當鷹前來進食時，蛇抓住牠的翅膀，折斷它們，將牠拋入坑中，讓牠死於飢渴。

functions: Fable of oath-breaking under the sun god's justice
Frame of the Etana ascent story

variants.name: Etana's ascent on the eagle
variants.summary: The sequel in which the pit-cured eagle carries the king to heaven.

canonical_translation: George Smith, 1876

primary_sources.citation: Tablet I, trans. George Smith (1876), 'Story of the Eagle and Etana'

secondary_sources.work: The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria
secondary_sources.citation: Morris Jastrow Jr., Boston, 1898, on Etana

title.en: Etana Rides the Eagle to Heaven
title.zh: 埃塔納乘鷹升天

region.en: Pit in the plain to the gates of Anu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 自平原深坑至安努之門（象徵性定位）

period: Old Babylonian and Neo-Assyrian versions (Jastrow translation 1898)

source.work: The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria, the Etana legend, Morris Jastrow (1898)

summary.en: Shamash sends Etana to the pit-bound eagle; the king nurses it back to flight and asks the plant of birth. Up they climb: a league high, the land a hill; two leagues, the land a garden; three, the sea a bucket — and at the gate of Anu the eagle can rise no more, and they fall back to earth.
summary.zh: 沙瑪什遣埃塔納至深坑救鷹；國王餵養之使其復飛，求生育仙草。步步攀升：一程山丘、二程園林、三程大海如桶——至安努之門，鷹力竭難升，二者墜回大地。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Shamash sends Etana to the pit: nurse the eagle and he will carry you. The king feeds the bird until its wings are healed, and asks for the plant of birth — for without an heir, his house will fail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Etana legend (Jastrow 1898); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 沙瑪什將埃塔納送往坑中：餵養那隻鷹，牠便會載你上去。國王餵養此鳥，直到牠的雙翼痊癒，並求取那株生育之草——因為若無繼承人，他的家業便將斷絕。

passages.text: The ascent: one league up and the land is a hill; two and it is a garden; three and the sea is a bucket. At the gate of Anu the eagle falters — higher yet, my friend, cries Etana — and they fall; the bird is restored, and the king gains his heir Balih.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Etana legend (Jastrow 1898); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 上升之途：升上一里格，大地便成一座山丘；升上兩里格，便成一座園圃；升上三里格，大海便成一只水桶。到了安努之門，那鷹卻躊躇不前——再高些，我的朋友，埃塔納喊道——於是他們墜落；此鳥得以復原，國王也得了他的繼承人巴利赫。

functions: First attested ascent-to-heaven narrative
Charter of the sacred kingship of Kish and its heir
Model of the shrinking-landscape ascent imagery

variants.summary: The parallel quest for a plant of life.

title.en: Adapa at the Gate of Heaven
title.zh: 阿達帕於天門

region.en: Eridu to the gate of Anu, Iraq
region.zh: 自埃利都至安努之門（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian (Amarna and Nineveh copies), c. 1500-700 BCE (Rogers translation 1912)

source.work: Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, 'The Myth of Adapa', trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

summary.en: Ea's priest breaks the south wind's wing; summoned to heaven, he is warned to refuse the bread and water of death — but they are the bread and water of life, and Anu's gate lets mortality win: mankind loses immortality for obedience.
summary.zh: 埃亞的祭司折斷南風之翼；被召上天，受誡勿食死之麵包、勿飲死之水——然那實為生命之食；安努之門令死亡獲勝：人類因聽話而失去永生。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Adapa, Ea's priest of Eridu, fishing in the quiet water, breaks the south wind's wing; summoned to Anu's gate for the crime, he is warned by his lord: they will offer you bread and water of death — do not eat, do not drink; mourn, and you will be sent home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Adapa myth (Rogers 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿達帕，埃亞在埃利都的祭司，在靜水中捕魚，折斷了南風之翼；因這罪過被召至安努之門時，他的主警告他：他們會獻給你死亡之餅與死亡之水——不要吃，不要喝；哀悼吧，你便會被遣送回家。

passages.text: But the bread and water offered are of life: Anu, having heard how wise he is, means to make him immortal. Adapa obeys his lord and refuses — Tammuz and Gishzida mourn with him at the gate — and mortality is fixed for mankind: wisdom he won, eternal life he lost.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Adapa myth (Rogers 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而所獻上的餅與水乃是生命之餅與生命之水：安努既已聽聞他何等智慧，便有意使他長生不死。阿達帕聽從他的主而拒絕了——坦木茲與吉什齊達在門前與他一同哀悼——於是死亡之命便為人類定下：他贏得了智慧，卻失去了永生。

functions: Etiology of human mortality through misplaced obedience
Charter of the priestly craft's wisdom
Parallel to the lost-paradise motif cluster

variants.summary: The first half of the tale as a separate telling.

variants.summary: The biblical parallel of the lost immortality.

title.en: The Descent of Ishtar
title.zh: 伊什塔爾下冥界

region.en: Gate of the land of no return, Kutha (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 無歸之地之門，庫薩（象徵性定位）

period: Old Babylonian and Neo-Assyrian versions (Rogers translation 1912)

source.work: Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, 'Ishtar's Descent to Hades', trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

summary.en: Ishtar goes down to the land of no return; at each of the seven gates a garment is stripped until she stands naked before Ereshkigal, and the goddess of the dead strikes her with every disease — the world above ceases: nothing mates. Ea's cunning creature wins her release for a price — Tammuz must go down half the year.
summary.zh: 伊什塔爾下至無歸之地；七門過處，衣飾盡褪，赤身立於埃列什基伽勒面前；冥后以其百病擊之——陽間因此絕育：萬物不再交合。埃亞的智造者以金古之命贖她——代價：塔穆茲半年居冥。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Ishtar, daughter of Sin, sets her mind on the house of darkness, the land of no return; at each of the seven gates a garment is stripped from her, and naked she comes before Ereshkigal, queen of the dead, who strikes her with every disease and holds her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ishtar's Descent (Rogers 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊什塔爾，辛之女，立意前往黑暗之屋、不歸之地；在七道門的每一道門前，都有一件衣物從她身上被剝去，她赤裸著來到死者之后埃列什基伽勒面前，后者以種種疾病擊打她，並將她扣留。

passages.text: With the goddess of fertility below, nothing mates above: bull does not mount cow, ass does not cover mare, the young man does not approach the girl in the street. Papsukkal's report sends Ea's cunning creature, who wins her release — but the price is named: Tammuz shall go down for half the year, and his sister serve the other half.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ishtar's Descent (Rogers 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 生育女神既在下方，上方便無所交合：公牛不跨母牛，公驢不覆母驢，青年男子不在街上走近少女。帕普蘇卡爾的稟報引來埃亞那狡黠的造物，贏得了她的釋放——但代價已被指明：坦木茲須下去半年，而他的姊妹須服侍另外半年。

functions: Fertility-cycle theology of the underworld visit
Charter of the Tammuz mourning rites
Model of the stripped-seven-gates descent

variants.name: Inana's Descent to the Nether World (Sumerian)
variants.summary: The Sumerian twin narrative.

variants.summary: The underworld queen's other mythic visitor.

primary_sources.citation: trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

title.en: Tammuz Restored to Life
title.zh: 塔穆茲復生

region.en: Uruk and the land below, Iraq
region.zh: 烏魯克與冥土（伊拉克）

period: Neo-Assyrian epic section (Wilson/Muss-Arnolt translation 1901)

source.work: Babylonian and Assyrian Literature, 'Tammuz Restored to Life', trans. Muss-Arnolt (1901)

summary.en: When Ishtar comes up from the land of no return, Tammuz meets her — the shepherd husband who never mourned her going — and she decrees his share: half the year below, half above, and the rites of his return are fixed in the calendar of the summer month.
summary.zh: 伊什塔爾自無歸之地歸來，塔穆茲迎之——這位牧神丈夫未曾為她的下降哀悼——女神判其份額：半年居冥、半年居陽，其歸返之祭遂定於夏日曆法。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cult narrative; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Tammuz comes out to meet the returning goddess and does not mourn her descent as her women do; Ishtar decrees his fate in turn: for half the year he serves below, and for half he is restored to the upper world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of 'Tammuz Restored to Life' (Muss-Arnolt 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 塔穆茲出來迎接歸返的女神，並不似她的婦女們那般為她的降入冥界而哀悼；伊什塔爾接著定下他的命運：半年他在地下服役，半年他復歸於上界。

passages.text: The women of the city weep for the shepherd in his month below and rejoice at his rising — the mourning liturgy fixed in the summer calendar, the myth of the dying husband's return kept by the rites of wailing and rejoicing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of 'Tammuz Restored to Life' (Muss-Arnolt 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 城中的婦女在他下界的月份為這牧者哭泣，又為他的升起而歡欣——那哀悼的儀式固定於夏季的曆法之中，那垂死丈夫歸返的神話，藉由哀號與歡慶的儀節而得以保存。

functions: Cult charter of the Tammuz wailing month
Dying-and-rising god theology of the seasons

variants.summary: The Sumerian half-year decree.
