title.en: Nergal and Ereshkigal: The Long Descent
title.zh: 內爾伽勒與埃列什基伽勒：長途下行

region.en: Gate of the netherworld, Kutha (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 冥界之門，庫薩（象徵性定位）

period: Amarna and Sultantepe versions, c. 1400-700 BCE (Rogers translation 1912)

source.work: Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, 'Nergal and Ereshkigal', trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

summary.en: Namtar's message finds no one to rise at the gate of heaven; Ereshkigal's rudeness must be answered — Nergal is sent down and warned to leave at once, but stays; the queen of the dead demands him back as her husband, and he descends forever — king in the land below.
summary.zh: 納姆塔爾傳信至天門，無人起身相迎；埃列什基伽勒的失禮必須回應——內爾伽勒奉命下冥、囑其即刻返回，他卻滯留不去；冥后索之為夫，他遂永駐冥土——成為下界之王。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Namtar, messenger of the netherworld, comes to the assembly and no one rises at his gate; Ereshkigal has no messenger above. Nergal is sent down to punish the rudeness and is warned: return before you eat, drink, wash or rest below.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nergal and Ereshkigal (Rogers 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 冥界的使者南塔爾來到集會，卻無人在他的門前起身；埃列什基伽勒在上界沒有使者。涅伽爾被遣下界去懲罰這無禮之舉，並受告誡：在下界飲食、沐浴或歇息之前，務必歸返。

passages.text: But Nergal stays — seven days of love with the queen of the dead — and leaves at dawn; Ereshkigal, weeping her loss, demands him back as husband, and the hero descends for good: king in the land of no return.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nergal and Ereshkigal (Rogers 1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而涅伽爾留了下來——與亡者之后共度七日的恩愛——直至黎明方才離去；埃列什基伽勒哀泣其失，要求他歸來為夫，這英雄便就此永下：成為不歸之地的君王。

functions: Marriage myth of the netherworld's royal couple
Etiology of Nergal's shared rule of the dead
Charter of the Meslam cult at Kutha

variants.name: Sultantepe version (the fourteen plagues)
variants.summary: The later recension with the disease-demons detail.

canonical_translation: Robert W. Rogers, 1912

primary_sources.citation: Amarna recension, trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

secondary_sources.work: The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria
secondary_sources.citation: Morris Jastrow Jr., Boston, 1898, on Nergal and Allatu

title.en: The Fourteen Doors of the Underworld
title.zh: 冥界十四門

region.en: Netherworld gates, Kutha (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 冥界諸門，庫薩（象徵性定位）

period: Sultantepe recension, c. 700 BCE (Jastrow retelling 1898)

source.work: The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria, retelling of Nergal and Allatu, Morris Jastrow (1898)

summary.en: In the Sultantepe recension, Ereshkigal's dance with the fourteen plague-demons sends Nergal down in disgrace; his second descent, with the demons of disease as his escort, makes him the underworld's master — the darker telling of the same marriage.
summary.zh: 蘇爾坦特佩本中，埃列什基伽勒與十四瘟疫妖靈起舞令內爾伽勒蒙羞下行；其二次下冥，以疫病群魔為儀仗，遂成冥土之主——同一婚事的更陰鬱版本。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Ereshkigal's dance with her fourteen plague-demons puts Nergal to shame in the first descent; he goes down again with the demons of disease as his escort, and the queen of the dead is won by force of presence. The marriage closes the tale: the war god and the death queen rule the land below together, and the disease-demons take their station at the gates — the underworld's staff named.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sultantepe recension as retold by Jastrow (1898); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Sultantepe recension (Jastrow 1898); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 埃列什基伽勒與她那十四個瘟疫魔共舞，令初次下界的涅伽爾蒙羞；他再度下界，以疾病之魔為其扈從，亡者之后終因他凜然的威儀而被征服。這樁婚事為故事作結：戰神與死亡之后共同統治下界之地，疾病之魔則各就其位守於門前——冥府的班列於此具名。

functions: Exorcistic variant of the underworld marriage
Catalogue of the disease-demons of the gates

variants.name: Amarna version
variants.summary: The gentler telling of the same myth.

canonical_translation: Morris Jastrow Jr., 1898 (retelling)

primary_sources.citation: as retold in Jastrow, Religion of Babylonia and Assyria (1898)

secondary_sources.work: Myths & Legends of Babylonia & Assyria
secondary_sources.citation: Lewis Spence, London, 1916

title.en: Shamash the Judge of All
title.zh: 沙瑪什：萬民之判官

region.en: Sippar temple of the sun, Iraq
region.zh: 西帕爾太陽神殿（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian hymns, c. 1800 BCE (Jastrow 1898)

source.work: The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria, the Shamash hymns, Morris Jastrow (1898)

summary.en: The sun god rises over the world: his light touches every road and every deed; the orphan and the widow he watches, the false witness he sees — the hymns to Shamash ground the law's theology of the witnessed oath.
summary.zh: 日神升臨世界：其光照臨每條路、每件事；孤兒寡母得其護佑，偽證者無所遁形——沙瑪什頌詩為律法之「見證誓言」奠定神學基礎。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Shamash rises over the world: his light reaches the roads, the fields, the deep; nothing is hidden from the sun of judgment. He watches the orphan and the widow, sees the false witness and the bribe-taker, and upholds the traveler on the road — the theology of the witnessed oath on which the law of Hammurabi's stele stands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Shamash hymns (Jastrow 1898); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 沙馬什升起於世界之上：他的光芒遍及道路、田野與深淵；在審判的太陽之前，無物得以隱藏。他看顧孤兒與寡婦，察見偽證者與受賄者，並扶持路上的旅人——此即受見證之誓的神學，漢摩拉比石碑上的律法正立於其上。

functions: Theology of the witnessed oath and the law
Liturgical hymn of the Sippar and Larsa sun cults

variants.name: Hammurabi stele prologue
variants.summary: The law's own invocation of Shamash.

canonical_translation: Morris Jastrow Jr., 1898

primary_sources.citation: as quoted in Jastrow, Religion of Babylonia and Assyria (1898)

secondary_sources.work: Babylonian and Assyrian Laws, Contracts and Letters
secondary_sources.citation: C. H. W. Johns, New York, 1904

title.en: Anzu Steals the Tablet of Destinies
title.zh: 安祖竊取天命泥板

region.en: Bathing-house of the gods, Nippur (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 眾神浴所，尼普魯（象徵性定位）

period: Old Babylonian and Standard Babylonian versions (Spence retelling 1916)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Babylonia & Assyria, 'The Legend of Zu', Lewis Spence (1916)

summary.en: Anzu, the lion-headed storm bird set to guard the bathwater, watches Enlil strip off his Tablet of Destinies; while the god washes, the bird seizes it — his word now commands the fates — and the whole world's order hangs on a theft.
summary.zh: 獅首暴風鳥安祖受命看守浴水；窺見恩利爾卸下天命泥板，趁其沐浴時搶走——從此一言可定天下命運——世界秩序懸於一竊。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Anzu, the lion-headed storm bird, is set to guard the bathwater of Enlil; he watches the god take off his raiment and the Tablet of Destinies with it, and while the god washes, the bird seizes the tablet and flies with it to his mountain. With the tablet on his breast, Anzu's word commands the fates: whoever goes against him dissolves — his cry uncreates. The gods convene in terror: the thief must be met by one whose fate the tablet cannot touch.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Anzu legend (Spence 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 獅首的風暴之鳥安祖奉命看守恩利爾的沐浴之水；他看著這位神祇脫下衣袍，連同天命泥板一併卸下，趁神沐浴之際，這隻鳥奪走泥板，帶著它飛回自己的山。泥板佩於胸前，安祖的話語便能號令命運：凡與他作對者皆化為烏有——他的呼喊能令萬物歸於無有。眾神驚恐地集會商議：必須派出一位天命泥板無法觸及其命運者，前去迎戰這名竊賊。

functions: Coup myth of the Tablet of Destinies
Theology of the fates-bearing word

variants.name: Enuma Elish: Qingu bears the tablets
variants.summary: The tablet motif in the creation epic.

variants.name: Lugalbanda and the Anzud bird (Sumerian)
variants.summary: The gentler Sumerian myth of the same bird.

title.en: Ninurta Recovers the Destinies
title.zh: 尼努爾塔奪回天命

region.en: Mountains of the thief, Nippur region (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 竊賊之山，尼普魯地區（象徵性定位）

period: Old Babylonian and Standard Babylonian versions (Spence retelling 1916)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Babylonia & Assyria, 'The Legend of Zu', Lewis Spence (1916)

summary.en: Ea's stratagem is preached: call Anzu's bride, unmoralize him mid-battle — when his wings are stripped by arrows as he chants the tablet's power, Ninurta's wind cuts through and the bird falls; the tablet is returned to Enlil's breast, and Ninurta is honored.
summary.zh: 埃亞獻策：喚其新婦、戰中蠱惑其心——當安祖誦念泥板之力時，以箭破其翼，風切而入；巨鳥墜落，泥板歸還恩利爾胸前，尼努爾塔受尊崇。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The champions sent fail; Ea preaches the stratagem: shake Anzu's bride at him and confuse his wits in battle — for the tablet's word can dissolve any named foe unless his mind is scattered. Ninurta meets the bird; as Anzu chants the tablet's power, arrows strip his feathers, the wind cuts through, and the thief falls. The Tablet of Destinies returns to Enlil's breast, and Ninurta is honored in the assembly — kingship's champion proven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Anzu legend (Spence 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 派出的勇士皆告失敗；埃阿獻上計策：在安祖面前搖動他的新娘，使他在戰鬥中心神迷亂——因為泥板之言能令任何被點名的敵手化為烏有，除非其心智被攪散。尼努爾塔迎戰此鳥；正當安祖吟誦泥板之力時，箭矢剝去他的羽毛，風貫穿而過，竊賊就此墜落。天命泥板重歸恩利爾胸前，尼努爾塔在集會中受尊崇——王權的護衛者由此得證。

functions: Restoration of legitimacy by the war god
Warfare of wits against magical power

variants.name: Ninurta's exploits (Sumerian)
variants.summary: The same god's earlier chaos-battle.

canonical_translation: Lewis Spence, 1916 (retelling)

title.en: Erra Wakes
title.zh: 埃拉醒來

region.en: Esagila, Babylon, Iraq
region.zh: 埃薩吉拉神殿，巴比倫（伊拉克）

period: Composed c. 800 BCE (Spence retelling of the Dibarra legend, 1916)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Babylonia & Assyria, the Erra (Dibarra) legend, Lewis Spence (1916)

summary.en: Erra, lord of plague and fire, wakes with a lust for battle; his weapons — seven personified terrors — complain of rust, and their master answers: only war will keep us sharp. Ishum, his herald, pleads for the cities; Erra refuses: the Suteans are due their fate.
summary.zh: 瘟火之主埃拉帶著嗜戰之渴醒來；七位人格化的恐怖武器抱怨刀劍生鏽，其主答道：唯有戰爭能使其鋒利。傳令官伊舒姆為城邦哀求；埃拉拒之：蘇特人命該如此。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Erra wakes with a hunger for war; his seven weapons, personified terrors, complain that they are rusting in idleness, and their master answers: only war keeps us sharp. Ishum, the herald, pleads for the cities — who will serve the gods if Babylon burns? — but Erra refuses: the Suteans are due their fate, and the weapons roar like lions.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Erra epic (Spence 1916 retelling); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Erra epic (Spence 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 埃拉醒來，滿懷對戰爭的饑渴；他那七件擬人化的恐怖武器抱怨自己在閒置中生鏽，而它們的主人答道：唯有戰爭能使我們保持鋒利。傳令者伊舒姆為眾城求情——若巴比倫焚毀，還有誰來侍奉眾神？——但埃拉拒絕：蘇泰人理當承受其命運，武器如獅群般咆哮。

functions: Apotropaic recitation against plague
Theology of war as divine restlessness
Crisis-period charter of destruction and restraint

title.en: Marduk Leaves His Throne
title.zh: 馬爾杜克離其御座

region.en: Esagila, Babylon, Iraq
region.zh: 埃薩吉拉神殿，巴比倫（伊拉克）

period: Composed c. 800 BCE (Spence retelling 1916)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Babylonia & Assyria, the Erra (Dibarra) legend, Lewis Spence (1916)

summary.en: Marduk's regalia lie dark in the temple — the god has left his throne for the smith's house to have his emblems refitted — and Erra walks into the vacant seat: the cities of the land are given to the sword while the king of the gods is away.
summary.zh: 馬爾杜克的神權象徵幽暗塵封於神殿——原來神明離座前往工匠之處整修其徽記——埃拉遂坐入空位：眾神之王離席之際，舉國城池盡付刀兵。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The regalia of Marduk lie dark; the god has left his throne — gone to the smith to have his emblems refitted — and in the vacant seat Erra takes the government of the world. While the king of the gods is away, the cities of the land are given to the sword: Sippar, Uruk, Babylon, Dilmun — every name is sung as Erra's harvest, and the temples stand silent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Erra epic (Spence 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬爾杜克的王權標誌黯淡無光；這位神祇已離開他的王座——前往鐵匠處重整他的徽記——而在空懸的座位上，埃拉接管了世界的統治。趁眾神之王外出之際，大地上的城邑盡付刀劍：西帕爾、烏魯克、巴比倫、迪爾蒙——每一個名字都被歌詠為埃拉的收成，神廟一片死寂。

functions: Theodicy of the era's collapse: the absent king
City-catastrophe catalogue as memorial

title.en: Ishum's Plea and Erra's Peace
title.zh: 伊舒姆之勸與埃拉之安

region.en: Esagila, Babylon, Iraq
region.zh: 埃薩吉拉神殿，巴比倫（伊拉克）

period: Composed c. 800 BCE (Spence retelling 1916)

source.work: Myths & Legends of Babylonia & Assyria, the Erra (Dibarra) legend, Lewis Spence (1916)

summary.en: Ishum keeps arguing — the temples are ash, the gods unfed — until Marduk returns to his throne; Erra, satiated, hands back the world: let him who recites this song be spared from plague and war — the epic's own apotropaic promise.
summary.zh: 伊舒姆不斷進諫——神殿成灰、眾神乏祀——直至馬爾杜克重歸御座；埃拉饜足而返還天下：凡誦此歌者，疫與戰皆不能近身——此即史詩自帶的護身之諾。

sensitivity.note: Ancient epic; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Ishum argues through the burning cities — the temples are ash, the gods unfed, mankind in chains — until Marduk returns to his throne and Erra, satiated, hands back the government of the world. The epic's own close is its use: let him who recites this song be spared from plague and war — the poem an incantation against the destruction it narrates.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Erra epic (Spence 1916); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊舒姆穿越焚燒的城邑力陳——神廟化為灰燼，眾神無所供奉，人類身陷枷鎖——直到馬爾杜克重返王座，饜足的埃拉才交還世界的統治。史詩自身的結語即是其用途：願吟誦此歌者得免於瘟疫與戰爭——這首詩是一道咒語，用以對抗它所敘述的毀滅。

functions: Apotropaic promise of the recitation
Resolution theology of restraint over destruction

title.en: The Seven Evil Demons
title.zh: 七惡魔

region.en: Roads and thresholds of the land, Iraq
region.zh: 大地道路與門檻（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian bilingual incantation (Wilson/Muss-Arnolt translation 1901)

source.work: Babylonian and Assyrian Literature, 'The Accadian Poem on the Seven Evil Spirits', trans. Muss-Arnolt (1901)

summary.en: Seven are they, seven are they: spirits of the flame and the flood, knowing no mercy, that burst in at the door like the flood at night — the bilingual incantation names the seven demons and drives them from the sick man's house.
summary.zh: 彼等有七，其數為七：火焰與洪水之靈，全無憐憫，夜半如洪水破門而入——雙語咒文一一具名七魔，驅之於病者宅外。

sensitivity.note: Ancient incantation; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Seven are they, seven are they: in the vault of heaven, in the deep of earth, spirits that know no father or mother, that burst in at the door like the flood at night. The incantation names each — the fever, the fiend, the flood-spirit — and drives them from the house: the exorcist's craft in its oldest poetic form, the demons that walk ahead of death's business made nameable and expellable.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the bilingual poem on the seven evil spirits (Muss-Arnolt 1901); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the bilingual poem (Muss-Arnolt 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們是七個，他們是七個：在天穹之中，在大地深處，那些不知有父不知有母的靈，如夜間的洪水般破門而入。咒語逐一喚出他們之名——熱病、惡魔、洪水之靈——並將他們逐出家門：這是最古老詩歌形式中的驅邪之術，那些行走於死亡事務之前的惡魔，就此變得可以指名、可以驅逐。

functions: Exorcistic naming and expulsion of the demons
Foundation text of the udug-hul anti-demon corpus

title.en: Lamashtu and the Demon of the Wind
title.zh: 拉瑪什圖與風之魔

region.en: Birth houses of Babylon, Iraq
region.zh: 巴比倫產房（伊拉克）

period: Neo-Assyrian demonology (Jastrow 1898)

source.work: The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria, the Labartu demoness, Morris Jastrow (1898)

summary.en: Lamashtu, the daughter of Anu, creeps into the birth-house: seven are her names, seven her deeds — she snatches the infant from the nurse's lap and drinks his blood. Against her the amulet is set, with Pazuzu, demon of the plague wind, standing guard.
summary.zh: 安努之女拉瑪什圖潛入產房：其名有七、其行有七——從乳母膝上奪嬰、飲其血。人們設置護符抵禦之，以瘟疫風魔帕祖祖立於其位守護。

sensitivity.note: Ancient demonology; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Lamashtu, daughter of Anu, creeps into the house of birth: seven are her names and seven her deeds — she snatches the infant from the nurse's lap and drinks his blood, she with the lion's head and the eagle's talons. Against her the amulet is set: Pazuzu, demon of the plague wind, her own terror set as her guard, the bronze heads hung over the bed of mother and child — the demon managed by the demon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Labartu (Lamashtu) demonology (Jastrow 1898); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Lamashtu demonology (Jastrow 1898); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 拉瑪什圖，阿努之女，潛入分娩之屋：她的名字有七個，她的行徑也有七樁——她從乳母膝上奪走嬰兒，飲其鮮血，她生著獅首與鷹爪。人們在她面前設下護符：帕祖祖，瘟疫之風的惡魔，以她自身的恐懼充作她的守衛，青銅頭像懸於母子床榻之上——以惡魔制馭惡魔。

functions: Charter of the infant-protection amulet
Theology of the demon managed by the demon

title.en: Maqlu: The Burning of the Witches
title.zh: 瑪克盧：焚巫之儀

region.en: Crossroads of Babylon, Iraq
region.zh: 巴比倫十字路口（伊拉克）

period: Kassite-Neo-Assyrian series, c. 1400-700 BCE (Jastrow 1898)

source.work: The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria, the Maklu (Maqlu) series, Morris Jastrow (1898)

summary.en: The witch works her image by night; the sufferer, led by the exorcist, burns her effigy at the crossroads — eight tablets of the Maqlu series recited until dawn, the fires of dawn completing the burning: the witchcraft is undone by daylight.
summary.zh: 女巫夜間以偶人施術；受苦者由驅邪師引領，於十字路口焚其草人——瑪克盧八卷咒文誦至黎明，晨曦之火完成焚燒：巫術在白晝中瓦解。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ritual literature; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The witch works her image by night, binding the sufferer's name in wax and flour; the exorcist leads the counter-rite: the effigy of the witch is burned at the crossroads while the eight tablets of the Maqlu series are recited. The fires of dawn complete the burning: the witchcraft is undone by daylight, and the closing incantation returns the sufferer's name to the protection of Shamash — witchcraft defeated by the sun of justice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Maqlu series (Jastrow 1898); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 女巫在夜間製作她的形象，以蠟與麵粉束縛受害者的名字；驅邪祭司主持對抗之儀：女巫的肖像在十字路口被焚燒，同時誦讀《馬克盧》系列的八塊泥板。黎明之火完成焚燒：巫術為日光所破除，結尾的咒語將受害者的名字交還沙馬什的庇護——巫術為正義之太陽所擊敗。

functions: Anti-witchcraft liturgy of the night-and-dawn rite
Theory of image-magic and its remedy

title.en: Shurpu: The List of Sins
title.zh: 舒爾普：罪目清單

region.en: Temple of purification, Babylon, Iraq
region.zh: 巴比倫淨化神殿（伊拉克）

period: Kassite-Neo-Assyrian series (Jastrow 1898)

source.work: The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria, the Shurpu series, Morris Jastrow (1898)

summary.en: Whether he has sinned knowingly or unknowingly, offended god or goddess — the Shurpu series lists every sin that could have brought the sickness, that the purification may name it and burn it away.
summary.zh: 無論其明知或誤犯、觸怒男神或女神——舒爾普系列一一列出可致疾病之諸罪，使淨化儀式得以指名並焚除之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ritual literature; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Whether he has sinned knowingly or unknowingly, offended god or goddess, sworn falsely or cursed in the assembly — the Shurpu series lists every sin that could have brought the sickness upon the sufferer. The named sin is then burned away: the purification rite completes the diagnosis — the liturgy that turned guilt into a curable condition.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Shurpu series (Jastrow 1898); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 無論他是明知而犯罪或不知而犯罪，冒犯了神或女神，妄發假誓或在集會中詛咒——〈舒爾普〉系列列舉了每一樁可能招致疾病降於受害者之身的罪。被指名的罪隨後被焚除：淨化之儀完成了診斷——那套將罪咎轉化為可醫治之狀況的禮儀。

functions: Diagnostic liturgy of sin and purification
Catalogue of ethical values in cult practice

title.en: Sirius and Canopus: The Grandmother's Rejoicing Song
title.zh: 天狼與老人星：祖母之歡歌

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'Sirius and Canopus'

summary.en: Ttuai-an used to rejoice about Canopus when it rose, singing 'Sirius! Sirius! Winks like Canopus! Canopus winks like Sirius!' — while she felt that food was abundant; the stars' winking back and forth is the sign of the good season.
summary.zh: 圖亞安每於老人星升時歡慶，歌曰「天狼！天狼！眨眼如老人星！老人星眨眼如天狼！」——其時她覺食物豐盈；二星互眨乃豐季之兆。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San song dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: My (step)grandmother, Ttuai-an, was the one who used to rejoice about Canopus. She said — 'Sirius! Sirius! Winks like Canopus! Canopus Winks like Sirius!... Sirius Winks like Canopus!' while my grandmother felt that food was abundant. Condensed paraphrase of the editor's notes: we are wont to say \hu, when food is abundant; the two stars are called by name as they rise, and the song is one of the old people's rejoicing at the beginning of the good season.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 231-233 (public domain). / Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 233 notes; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 我的（繼）祖母圖阿伊安，正是從前常為老人星而歡欣的那一位。她說——『天狼星！天狼星！像老人星一樣閃爍！老人星像天狼星一樣閃爍！……天狼星像老人星一樣閃爍！』而我的祖母覺得食物豐足。編者註解的濃縮轉述：當食物豐足時，我們慣常說 \hu；這兩顆星升起時被呼喚其名，這首歌是老人們在美好季節開始時的歡欣之歌。

title.en: The Song Sung by the Star \gaunu and by Bushman Women
title.zh: 星加烏奴與桑婦之歌

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'A Song sung by the Star \gaunu, and especially by Bushman Women'

summary.en: 'Does the \garraken flower open? The +ku-yam is the one which opens. Dost thou open? The +ku-yam is the one which opens.' The star \gaunu sings it, and Bushman women sing it especially as they dig bulbs; the riddling call is the star's question and the women's answer.
summary.zh: 「加拉克花開否？開者乃+庫雅姆。爾開否？開者乃+庫雅姆。」此歌星加烏奴唱之，掘球根之桑婦尤歌之；謎語之呼喚，乃星之問與婦之答。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San song dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: Does the \garraken flower open? The +ku-yam is the one which opens. Dost thou open? The +ku-yam is the one which opens. Condensed paraphrase of the notes: the \garraken are bulbs, which the Bushmen dig out; \ku-yam is the daisy-like flower in blossom at Mowbray in August; the star \gaunu sings this song, and Bushman women especially sing it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 231 (public domain). / Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 231 notes; not verbatim.
passages.zh: \garraken 花可曾綻放？+ku-yam 才是綻放的那一個。你可曾綻放？+ku-yam 才是綻放的那一個。註解的濃縮轉述：\garraken 是球莖，布須曼人將其掘出；\ku-yam 是八月間在莫布雷盛開的菊狀花；星 \gaunu 唱這首歌，而布須曼婦女尤其唱它。

title.en: The Song of the Caama Fox: Crosser of the Spoor
title.zh: 狐之歌：踏跡者

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1873 by !A!kunta (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Song of the Caama Fox'

summary.en: The caama fox sings 'Crosser of the Spoor! Crosser of the Spoor!' — for it avoids the dog nicely when the dog chases it, turning suddenly to run back across the dog's spoor while the dog races on in front, thinking to catch the fox.
summary.zh: 狐自歌「踏跡者！踏跡者！」——因犬逐之，牠巧妙避讓，急轉回越犬之跡；而犬奔於前，自以為能捕之。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San song dictated by !A!kunta to Bleek and Lloyd, 1873; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Crosser of the Spoor, Crosser of the Spoor, Crosser of the Spoor, Crosser of the Spoor! Condensed paraphrase of the narrator's note: the Caama Fox is called 'Crosser of the Spoor', because it avoids the dog nicely when the dog chases it, and, turning suddenly, runs back, crossing the dog's spoor behind it, while the dog is racing on in front, thinking to catch the Caama Fox by so doing.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 223 (public domain). / Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 223 note; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 踏跡橫越者，踏跡橫越者，踏跡橫越者，踏跡橫越者！敘述者註解的濃縮轉述：卡馬狐被稱為『踏跡橫越者』，因為當狗追逐牠時，牠巧妙地避開狗，並突然轉身往回跑，從狗的身後橫越狗的足跡，而狗卻在前方疾奔，以為如此便能捉住卡馬狐。

title.en: The Songs of the Blue Crane
title.zh: 藍鶴之歌

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1879 (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Songs of the Blue Crane'

summary.en: The Blue Crane — once a person of the early race and the Mantis's sister — sings about her shoulder, where the krieboom berries lie; she sings 'a splinter of stone which is white' as she runs from a man, sings the walk of peace as she leaves, and sings 'scrape the springbok skin for the bed' as she flaps her wings.
summary.zh: 藍鶴——本為早期之民，螳螂之姊——歌其肩上之克裏布姆漿果；奔逃時歌「白色石片」，離去時歌和平之步，振翅時歌「刮羚皮為床」。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San songs dictated by ||kabbo and /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: It is the Blue Crane's story which it sings; it sings about its shoulder, namely, that the 'krieboom' berries are upon its shoulder; it goes along singing — 'The berries are upon my shoulder, The berries are upon my shoulder, The berry it is upon my shoulder.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 225 (public domain).
passages.zh: 牠所唱的，正是藍鶴自己的故事；牠唱著自己的肩膀，也就是說，那「krieboom」的漿果正落在牠的肩上；牠一路走一路唱——「漿果落在我的肩上，漿果落在我的肩上，那漿果就落在我的肩上。」

passages.text: 2. (When running away from a man.) 'A splinter of stone which is white, A splinter of stone which is white.' 3. (When walking slowly, leaving the place — walk of peace.) 'A white stone splinter.' 4. (When it flaps its wings.) 'Scrape the springbok skin for the bed.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 226-227 (public domain).
passages.zh: 2.（當牠逃離人時。）「一片白色的碎石，一片白色的碎石。」3.（當牠緩步而行、離開原地時——即平安之步。）「一片白色的碎石。」4.（當牠拍動雙翼時。）「刮一刮那跳羚皮，好鋪床。」

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the notes: the Blue Crane was formerly a person of the early race; the crane sings about its head, which is shaped like a stone knife and has white feathers; the Bushmen make beds from springbok and goat skins.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 224-227 notes; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 註釋的濃縮轉述：藍鶴從前是早期種族的一個人；這鶴唱著自己的頭，那頭形如石刀，長著白色的羽毛；布須曼人以跳羚皮和山羊皮鋪床。

title.en: ||kabbo's Song on the Loss of His Tobacco Pouch
title.zh: 卡布失煙袋之歌

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), '||kabbo's Song on the Loss of his Tobacco Pouch'

summary.en: 'Famine it is, Famine is here' — the old man's song on his tobacco-hunger: a hungry dog named Blom had come in the night and carried off his pouch, and he woke in the dark and missed it; the little song turns hunger into verse.
summary.zh: 「飢也，飢在此」——老人失煙袋之歌：名布隆之餓犬夜來奪袋；他暗中醒覺，尋而不得；小歌化飢為詩。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San song dictated by /Han≠kass'o (for ||kabbo) to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Famine it is, Famine it is, Famine is here. Famine it is, Famine it is, Famine is here. Famine ['tobacco-hunger' is meant here] — he did not smoke, because a dog had come in the night and carried off from him his pouch. And he arose in the night, he missed his pouch. And then he again lay down, while he did not smoke. And we were early seeking for the pouch. We did not find the pouch.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 235-236 (public domain). / Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 236 (public domain).
passages.zh: 是饑荒啊，是饑荒啊，饑荒就在這裡。是饑荒啊，是饑荒啊，饑荒就在這裡。饑荒〔此處指的是「菸癮」〕——他沒有抽菸，因為夜裡來了一隻狗，把他的菸袋叼走了。他夜裡起身，發覺菸袋不見了。於是他又躺下，始終沒有抽菸。我們一早就去找那菸袋。我們沒有找到那菸袋。

title.en: Stories That Float Like the Wind: ||kabbo's Return
title.zh: 如風漂至之故事：卡布之歸

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1873-1875 by ||kabbo (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), '||kabbo's intended Return Home'

summary.en: Waiting for the moon to turn back for him, ||kabbo plans to go home to listen to the stories: 'I am one who listens behind me... a story is like the wind; it comes from a far-off quarter, and we feel it.' Our names float to places our bodies cannot; the people at home visit each other's huts to sit smoking and hear the histories.
summary.zh: 卡布待月回圓以歸家聽故事：「我乃於背後傾聽者……故事如風，自遠方而來，吾等感之。」吾名能漂至軀體不能至之地；鄉人相訪各屋，對坐吸煙而聽史。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San personal narrative dictated by ||kabbo to Bleek and Lloyd, 1873-1875; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Thou knowest that I sit waiting for the moon to turn back for me, that I may return to my place... That I may listen to all the people's stories, when I visit them... They are those which they thus tell, they are listening to them; while the other \xe-ssho-\kui (the sun) becomes a little warm, that I may sit in the sun.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 299-301 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 你知道我坐著等月亮為我回轉，好讓我回到我的地方……好讓我去拜訪眾人時，聽他們所有的故事……那些就是他們這樣講述的，他們正聽著那些故事；而另一邊那\xe-ssho-\kui（太陽）漸漸暖和起來，好讓我坐在陽光裡。

passages.text: I am here; I do not obtain stories; because I do not visit, so that I might hear stories which float along... For, I am wont to listen, watching for a story, which I want to hear; while I sit waiting for it; that it may float into my ear. These are those to which I am listening with all my ears; while I feel that I sit silent. I must wait (listening) behind me, while I listen along the road; while I feel that my name floats along the road.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 302-303 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 我在這裡；我得不到故事；因為我不去拜訪，好讓我聽見那些漂浮而來的故事……因為我慣於傾聽，守候著一個我想聽的故事；我坐著等它；等它漂浮進我的耳裡。這些就是我全神貫注傾聽的故事；而我覺得自己靜靜坐著。我必須在身後等候（傾聽），同時我沿著道路傾聽；而我覺得我的名字正沿著道路漂浮。

passages.text: While I feel that a story is the wind. It (the story) is wont to float along to another place. Then, our names do pass through those people; while they do not perceive our bodies go along. For, our names are those which, floating, reach a different place... [||kabbo explains that] a story is 'like the wind, it comes from a far-off quarter, and we feel it.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 304-305 with editor's note (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 而我覺得故事就像風一樣。它（故事）慣於飄向另一個地方。於是，我們的名字便穿過那些人；而他們並未察覺我們的身體也隨之而去。因為，正是我們的名字，飄著抵達了另一個地方……［||卡布解釋說］故事「像風一樣，它來自遙遠的某處，而我們能感覺到它。」

title.en: How /Han≠kass'o's Pet Leveret Was Killed
title.zh: 恩卡索之寵兔之死

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'How \Han≠kass'o's pet Leveret was killed'

summary.en: Tsatsi caught a leveret for the boy, who played with it while it ran; his mother wished him to kill and roast it, he would not, so she sent him to fetch water and killed it while he was gone. They calmed his crying by telling him the lizard's song — the story of the Death of the \khau.
summary.zh: 察特西為少年捕幼兔；兔奔而童追之戲；母欲其殺而炙之，他不從，母遂遣其取水，趁其離去殺兔。眾以蜥蜴之歌——哈之死之故事——安其啼。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San personal memory dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Tsatsi was the one who caught hold of and took up a leveret on the hunting-ground; and, he brought it home alive, he came and gave it to me. And I played with it; I set it down, it ran; I also ran after it... |xabbi-an wished that I should leave off playing with the leveret, that I should kill it, that I should lay it to roast. I was not willing to kill the leveret.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 318-319 (public domain).
passages.zh: 是察齊在獵場上抓住並拾起了一隻小野兔；他把它活著帶回家，走過來把它交給了我。我便與它玩耍；我把它放下，它便跑；我也追著它跑……｜沙比安希望我別再與那小野兔玩耍，希望我殺了它，希望我把它放去烤。我不願殺那小野兔。

passages.text: I was not willing to kill the leveret, because I felt that nothing acted as prettily as it did, when it was gently running, gently running along... Then they told me to fetch water; for I was one who quickly came away from the water... And I went to fetch water; then, they killed my leveret for me, while I was at the water.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 320 (public domain).
passages.zh: 我不願殺那小野兔，因為我覺得沒有什麼比它更可愛了，當它輕輕地跑著、輕輕地跑著的時候……然後他們叫我去取水；因為我是個很快就能從水邊回來的人……我便去取水；接著，趁我在水邊時，他們替我殺了我的小野兔。

passages.text: Then I came and cried, about it; because I had thought that they would let my leveret alone... They had killed it for me. Therefore, I came and cried... They said, that we should not again get another leveret... Therefore, they soothingly calmed me with the (story of the) lizard; while they wished that I might quietly listen to them.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 320-321 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 然後我回來，為它哭泣；因為我本以為他們會放過我的小野兔……他們替我殺了它。因此，我回來哭了……他們說，我們不會再得到另一隻小野兔了……於是，他們用（那則關於）蜥蜴的（故事）來撫慰我，使我平靜；而他們希望我能靜靜地聽他們說。

title.en: The Bushmen's Letters Are in Their Bodies
title.zh: 桑人之書信在體內

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1873 by ||kabbo (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'Bushman Presentiments'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §99

summary.en: 'The Bushmen's letters are in their bodies. They speak, they move, they make their bodies move.' The tapping of the flesh tells of visitors coming (an old wound taps at the place where the wounded man walks), of springbok behind the Brinkkop, of blood soon to flow down the hunter's calves; only fools disobey the body's letters — such as get killed by lions.
summary.zh: 「桑人之書信在其體內。彼等言、動、令其體而動。」肉之搏跳告知來客（舊傷在彼行處而跳）、告知布林山後之羚、告知獵者腿肚將流之血；愚者不從體信者遭獅噬。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San presentiment-lore dictated by ||kabbo to Bleek and Lloyd, 1873; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Bushmen's letters are in their bodies. They (the letters) speak, they move, they make their (the Bushmen's) bodies move. They order the others to be silent; a man is altogether still, when he feels that his body is tapping (inside). A dream speaks falsely, it is (a thing) which deceives. The presentiment is that which speaks the truth.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 331 (public domain).
passages.zh: 布須曼人的文字在他們的身體裡。它們（那些文字）會說話，會移動，會使他們（布須曼人）的身體移動。它們命令其他人安靜；當一個人感覺自己的身體（在裡面）敲擊時，他便全然靜止不動。夢會說假話，它是（一種）欺騙人的東西。預感才是說真話的那個。

passages.text: The beatings tell those who understand them, which way they are not to go, and which arrow they had better not use, and also warn them, when many people are coming to the house on a wagon. They inform people where they can find the person of whom they are in search, i.e., which way they must go to seek him successfully.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 331 with editor's quote of Bleek 1875 §99 (public domain).
passages.zh: 那些敲擊告訴懂得它們的人，他們不該往哪個方向去，他們最好不要用哪一支箭，並且也警告他們，何時有許多人乘著牛車前來家中。它們告知人們何處能找到他們所尋找的人，也就是說，他們必須往哪個方向去尋，才能成功地找到他。

passages.text: With regard to an old wound, a Bushman feels a tapping at the wound's place, while the tapping feels that the man (who has the old wound) walks, moving his body... he says to the children: 'Look ye around, for grandfather, for grandfather seems to be coming; this is why I feel the place of his body's old wound.'... He feels a tapping at his ribs; he says to the children: 'The springbok seem to be coming... Climb ye the Brinkkop standing yonder, that ye may look around at all the places. For I feel the springbok sensation.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 332-333 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 關於一處舊傷，布須曼人會感到舊傷之處有敲擊之感，而那敲擊之感則覺得那（帶著舊傷的）人正在行走、正在移動他的身體……他對孩子們說：「你們向四周看看吧，看看祖父，因為祖父似乎要來了；這就是為什麼我感覺到他身上舊傷之處。」……他感到肋骨處有敲擊之感；他對孩子們說：「那些跳羚似乎要來了……你們爬上立在那邊的布林克山，好讓你們能向四周眺望所有的地方。因為我感覺到了跳羚的感應。」

passages.text: I am wont to feel thus, I feel a sensation in the calves of my legs when the springbok's blood is going to run down them. For I always feel blood, when I am about to kill springbok... The other agrees with him (saying): 'Yes, my brother.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 334-335 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 我慣於有這樣的感覺，當跳羚的血即將順著我的小腿流下時，我便在小腿肚上感到一種感應。因為每當我即將殺死跳羚時，我總是感覺到血……另一個人同意他的話（說道）：「是的，我的兄弟。」

title.en: The Earth Thrown Up by a Fainting Man
title.zh: 昏者擲塵之訊

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'A Bushman, becoming faint from the Sun's heat when returning home, throws earth into the air'

summary.en: The sun-killed hunter, too spent to reach home, throws earth into the air; the watching wife sees the dust, and the people run out crying 'His heart is that for which he throws up earth; the sun is killing him; give him water quickly!' He sits in the water's coolness while the sun's darkness is removed from his face.
summary.zh: 為日所殺之獵者，力竭難歸，乃據地擲塵上天；守望之妻見之，眾人奔出呼曰「彼擲塵為其心；日殺之；速予水！」。坐於水涼處，日之暗影遂離其面。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San practice-lore dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: A man is wont, when returning home, when he feels as if he should not reach home, he throws up earth (into the air), because he wishes that the people at home may perceive the dust... She stands up, she looks around. And, as she stands looking around, she perceives the dust, she exclaims: 'A person seems to be throwing up earth there!'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 385-386 (public domain).
passages.zh: 一個人慣於在回家途中，當他覺得自己似乎到不了家時，便將泥土（向空中）揚起，因為他希望家中的人能看見那塵土……她站起身來，向四周張望。而當她站著向四周張望時，她看見了那塵土，便驚呼道：「那邊似乎有人正在揚土！」

passages.text: And the people run, run out of the house, exclaiming: 'His heart is that on account of which he throws up earth. Ye must run quickly, that ye may go to give him water quickly; for, it is his heart; the sun is killing him... Ye must quickly go to give him water.'... They go, pouring (water), to cool the man with water. And he first sits up, to remove the darkness from his face; for, the sun's darkness resembles night.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 386-387 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 於是眾人奔跑起來，跑出屋外，驚呼道：「他的心就是使他揚土的原因。你們必須快跑，好讓你們快去給他水喝；因為，這是他的心；太陽正在殺他……你們必須快去給他水喝。」……他們前去，傾倒（水），用水使那人涼快下來。而他先坐起身來，好除去臉上的黑暗；因為，太陽的黑暗宛如黑夜。

title.en: The Treatment of Bones: Tsatsi's Way
title.zh: 骨之處置：察特西之法

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), '|Nanna-sse. Second Part: the Treatment of Bones'

summary.en: Gnawed bones are poured down at a heap opposite the hut's mouth; the women may not eat the springbok's shoulder blades, for they respect the men's arrows; the dogs may not crunch the bones of the man who shot, or his first finger will be wounded when he shoots; and Tsatsi sews his first finger into a cover to pull the string.
summary.zh: 啃畢之骨傾於屋門前之堆；婦女不得食跳羚肩胛，以敬男子之箭；犬不得嚼射者之骨，否則其食指於射時受傷；察特西縫食指於皮套以挽弓弦。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San custom dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: They (the Bushmen) put the things' bones nicely aside, while they do not throw them about. They put down the bones opposite to the entrance to the hut... they go, they pour down the bones at it. Therefore, they call it, 'The heap of meat bones.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 274 (public domain).
passages.zh: 他們（布須曼人）把獵物的骨頭整齊地放到一旁，而不把它們四處亂扔。他們把骨頭放在茅屋入口的對面……他們前去，把骨頭倒在它上面。因此，他們稱它為「肉骨堆」。

passages.text: The women do not eat (the meat of) the springbok's shoulder blades, because they show respect for the men's arrows, so that the men may quietly kill... Therefore, we do not allow the little children to play upon the springbok skin. For the springbok is wont to get into our flesh, and we become ill.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 277 (public domain).
passages.zh: 女人們不吃（跳羚）肩胛骨的（肉），因為她們對男人的箭表示敬意，好讓男人們能安然地獵殺……因此，我們不允許小孩子在跳羚皮上玩耍。因為跳羚慣於進入我們的肉裡，我們便會生病。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the narrator's account of Tsatsi: my grandfather put away in the sticks of the hut the upper bones of the fore leg, the shoulder blades and the springbok's \khuru-\khuruken, because the first finger of the shooting hand gets a wound when we shoot if the dogs eat the springboks' bones; we sew the first finger into a cover, which the wife cuts out and sews for us, and then we pull the bow-string while we feel that our finger is inside.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 282-283; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 對敘述者關於察齊（Tsatsi）之記述的濃縮轉述：我的祖父把前腿的上部骨頭、肩胛骨以及跳羚的\khuru-\khuruken收進茅屋的木棍之間，因為若狗吃了跳羚的骨頭，我們射箭時，持弓手的第一根手指就會受傷；我們把第一根手指縫進一個套子裡，這套子由妻子剪裁並為我們縫製，然後我們一邊拉弓弦，一邊感覺我們的手指在裡面。

title.en: The \goih-\goih: Bullroarer for the Bees and the Night Dance
title.zh: 牛鳴器與夜舞

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The use of the \goih\goih, followed by an Account of a Bushman Dance'

summary.en: The \goih-\goih is beaten so the bees may grow abundant and drift into other people's places, that honey may be cut; the men bring the honey to the hungry women at home, the women make the drum, and the dance goes round till sunrise — the men dancing and the women clapping, the drum-dust rising upon every face.
summary.zh: 擊牛鳴器使蜂繁衍、飄入他家之域，以得割蜜；男子攜蜜歸予飢餓之家婦；婦製鼓，眾舞至日出——男舞女拍，鼓塵揚於眾面。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San practice-lore dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The people beat the \goih\goih, (in order) that the bees may become abundant for the people, (in order) that the bees may go into the other people's places, that the people may eat honey... And the people take honey to the women at home. For, the women are dying of hunger, at home... that the women may go to eat... while they wish that the women may make a drum for them, so that they may dance, when the women are satisfied with food.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 353-355 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 人們敲擊\goih\goih，（為的是）讓蜜蜂為人們變得繁多，（為的是）讓蜜蜂進入其他人的地方，讓人們有蜂蜜可吃……而人們把蜂蜜帶回家中的女人那裡。因為女人們在家中正餓得要死……為的是讓女人們前去吃……同時他們希望女人們為他們做一面鼓，好讓他們跳舞，當女人們吃飽食物而滿足時。

passages.text: Then, the sun rises, while they are dancing there, while they feel that they are satisfied with food... Therefore, the sun shines upon the backs of their heads; while the women get the dust of the drum... their foot's dust covers the women's faces; because they have danced strongly... Therefore they sleep, letting the sun set; because they are tired when they have been dancing there.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 355-357 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 然後，太陽升起，而他們還在那裡跳舞，同時他們感到自己吃飽食物而滿足……因此，太陽照在他們的後腦上；而女人們沾上鼓的灰塵……她們腳上的塵土覆蓋了女人們的臉；因為她們跳得很用力……因此她們睡覺，任憑太陽落下；因為她們在那裡跳了舞之後累了。

title.en: \hara and \tao: The Black Head of the Handsome Young Man
title.zh: 赫拉與陶：美男之黑髮

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), '\hara and \tao'

summary.en: \hara is black and anoints the head; \tao is red and rubs the body. The head anointed with \hara shimmers; and the old women say of a youth: 'That man, he is a handsome young man, on account of his head's blackness, which is surpassingly beautiful with the \hara's blackness — his head is like the \khi tree.'
summary.zh: 赫拉為黑，塗於首；陶為赤，擦於身。以赫拉塗之首閃爍；老嫗謂少年曰：「此人因首之黑而為美男——其黑至美；其首如克希樹。」

sensitivity.note: |Xam San practice-lore dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: \hara is black; the people having mixed it with fat anoint their heads with it; while \tao is red, and the people rub their bodies with it, when they have pounded it... They anoint their heads very nicely, while they wish that their head's hair may descend. And it becomes abundant on account of it... wishing that the hair may grow downwards, that their heads may become black with blackness.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 375 (public domain).
passages.zh: \hara是黑色的；人們把它與脂肪混合後塗抹頭部；而\tao是紅色的，人們把它搗碎後用它塗抹身體……他們把頭部塗抹得非常漂亮，同時他們希望頭上的頭髮能夠垂下。於是頭髮因此變得濃密……希望頭髮向下生長，希望他們的頭因這黑色而變黑。

passages.text: \hara sparkles; therefore, our heads shimmer, on account of it... Therefore, the Bushmen are wont to say, when the old women are talking there: 'That man, he is a handsome young man, on account of his head, which is surpassingly beautiful with the \hara's blackness.' They say, 'Handsome young man' to him, 'His head is surpassingly beautiful; for, his head is like the \khi tree.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 376-378 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: \hara閃閃發光；因此，我們的頭因它而泛光……因此，布須曼人常說，當老婦人們在那裡談話時：『那個男人，他是個英俊的年輕人，因為他的頭，那頭因\hara的黑色而美得超乎尋常。』他們對他說『英俊的年輕人』，『他的頭美得超乎尋常；因為他的頭像\khi樹一樣。』

title.en: Doings of the Springbok: Mothers, Kids and the Hunter's Warning
title.zh: 跳羚之為：母子與獵者之警

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'Doings of the Springbok'

summary.en: The mother springbok grunts 'a, a, a' as she trots with her kid, and the kid bleats 'me, me, me'; the herd makes a resounding noise because they are many. The hunter, lying hidden, warns: 'O beast of prey! thou art the one who hearest the place behind — the male springbok which stand around will go along, passing behind you; because I am lying down, and they do not perceive me.'
summary.zh: 羚母負子而行，喉中作「阿，阿，阿」；幼者啼「米，米，米」；群聲迴響，因其眾多。匿伏獵者警曰：「猛獸啊！爾所聞者乃身後之地——周圍之公羚將自爾身後經過；因我臥伏，彼等不見我。」

sensitivity.note: |Xam San observation-lore dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The mother springbok is wont to do thus, as she trots along, when she has a springbok kid which is little, she grunts, as she trots along; she says — 'a, a, a'... while the springbok kids also cry (bleat), while their mothers cry (grunt). Their mothers say — 'a, a, a,' the springbok kids say — 'me, me, me'... Therefore, we are wont to say: 'O beast of prey! thou art the one who hearest the place behind, it is resonant with sound.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 244-246 (public domain), minor elisions.
passages.zh: 母跳羚常這樣做，當她小跑前行時，若她有一隻幼小的跳羚崽，她便一邊小跑一邊發出咕嚕聲；她說——『啊，啊，啊』……而跳羚崽也叫（咩咩叫），同時它們的母親也叫（咕嚕叫）。它們的母親說——『啊，啊，啊』，跳羚崽說——『咩，咩，咩』……因此，我們常說：『哦，猛獸啊！你就是那聽見後方之地者，那地方迴響著聲音。』

passages.text: For these male springbok which stand around, are those which will go along, passing behind you; because I am lying down, and they do not perceive me; they will have to go along, passing behind you, when ye have gone behind the hill... while the place is resonant with sound.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 246 (public domain).
passages.zh: 因為這些站在四周的公跳羚，正是那些會一路前行、從你身後經過的；因為我正躺著，牠們沒有察覺我；當你們繞到山丘後方之後，牠們就必須一路前行、從你身後經過……而那個地方正迴盪著聲響。

title.en: Lhamo, the Goddess Who Rode on Her Son's Skin
title.zh: 吉祥天母：以兒皮為鞍的女神

region.en: Mountain Olkhan in the district Olgon, beyond the ocean Muliding (symbolic pin in the north-east)
region.zh: Muliding大洋彼端奧爾袞之奧爾堪山（以東北方為象徵定位）

period: Paldan Lhamoi kang shag (Confession before the venerated Lhamo); Schlagintweit's English 1863

source.work: Emil Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863), ch. X

summary.en: The goddess Lhamo was married to Shinje, king of the Dudpos, who at the time of the marriage had assumed the form of the king of Ceylon; she had made a vow either to soften her husband's notoriously wild and wicked manners, and make him favourably disposed towards the religion of Buddha, or, failing, to extirpate a royal race so hostile to his creed by killing the children that might issue from the marriage. Unable to improve the king's evil ways, she flayed her own beloved son alive during his father's absence, drank the blood from out his skull, ate his flesh, and using the skin as a saddle for the king's best horse, set out for her northern home. The king shot a poisoned arrow after her with a terrible incantation; she neutralized the imprecation, took out the deadly weapon, and uttered her curse-blessing: 'May the wound of my horse become an eye large enough to overlook the twenty-four regions, and may I myself extirpate the race of these malignant kings of Ceylon!' - and traversing India, Tibet, Mongolia and part of China in great haste, finally settled in the mountain Olkhan surrounded by deserts and the ocean Muliding.
summary.zh: 吉祥天母嫁與辛傑王（時化身為錫蘭王），曾誓：若不能感化此暴虐之王信奉佛法，便絕其惡王血統——親手誅其所生之子。她於夫王外出之際，活剝親生愛子，以顱飲血、啖其肉，以子皮為鞍乘王之駿馬北歸。王以毒咒射出毒箭，箭透馬背；天母破其咒，拔出利鏃，發願曰：「願馬背之傷化為巨眼，足以遍觀二十四域；願我親手絕滅錫蘭惡王之族！」遂疾馳印度、吐蕃、蒙古與中原，定居於 Muliding 大洋環抱之奧爾堪山。

canonical_translation: Emil Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet, London 1863 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The goddess Lhamo was married to Shinje, the king of the Dudpos, who at the time of the marriage had assumed the form of the king of Ceylon. The goddess had made a vow, either to soften her husband's notoriously wild and wicked manners, and make him favourably disposed towards the religion of Buddha, or, failing in her praiseworthy endeavours, to extirpate a royal race so hostile to his creed by killing the children that might issue from the marriage. Unfortunately it was beyond her power to effect an improvement in the evil ways of the king, and, accordingly, she determined to kill their son, who was greatly beloved by his father because in him he had hoped to put a complete end to Buddhism in Ceylon.

During a temporary absence of the king, the goddess put her design in execution: she flayed her son alive, drank the blood from out his skull, and even ate his flesh. She then left the palace and set out for her northern home, using her son's skin as a saddle for the king's best horse. On his return, seeing what had happened, the king at once seized a bow, and, with a terrible incantation, shot off a poisoned arrow after his dreadful wife. The arrow pierced the horse's back, in which it stuck fast; but the queen, neutralizing the efficacy of the imprecation, took out the deadly weapon and uttered the following sentence: 'May the wound of my horse become an eye large enough to overlook the twenty-four regions, and may I myself extirpate the race of these malignant kings of Ceylon!'

The goddess then continued her journey towards the north, traversing in great haste India, Tibet, Mongolia and part of China, and finally settling in the mountain Olkhan, in the district Olgon, which is supposed to be situated in Eastern Siberia. This mountain is said to be surrounded by large, uninhabited deserts, and by the ocean Muliding. In a prayer addressed to this goddess she is invoked as Rimate - the present legend is related in the book Paldan Lhamoi kang shag, 'to perform confession before the venerated Lhamo', a treatise read when offerings are presented to this goddess, and a copy in Tibetan and Mongolian is in the library of the St Petersburg university, the Mongolian edition containing some details in Kalmuck which are not met with in the Tibetan.

The legend explains, in one stroke, the iconography and the office of Tibet's chief protectress: the flayed-skin saddle is the mule's pad she rides, the skull-cup of blood is the offering she drinks, the eye on the horse's rump is the wound of the poisoned arrow grown into the all-seeing eye that overlooks the twenty-four regions, and her permanent campaign against the malignant kings of Ceylon is the vow still operative whenever she is summoned from the north-eastern region surrounded by the ocean Muliding - by the blue letter Hum traced upon the suppliant's heart, spreading with its iron hook a beam of light, as the prayer has it. Schlagintweit identifies her with the goddess Okkin Tangri of the Mongolians, and with the Chammo or Lchamu of Pallas; her portrait, he notes, is found added to the picture of the thirty-five Buddhas of confession, and in Pallas's plates she stands beneath the central figure, sometimes without the staff and the skull-cup.
narrative.notes: Cultural function: the legend explains the goddess's terrifying iconography - the flayed-skin saddle, the skull-cup of blood, the eye on her horse's rump - and her function as the wrathful protector who executed a dynastic vow to save Buddhism in Ceylon; she is identical with the goddess Okkin Tangri of the Mongolians.

functions: Explains the iconography of Lhamo's wrathful form: the mule's eye, the skin-saddle, the skull-cup of blood
Charter of theProtectress' vow: dynastic filicide committed to save the Buddhist dispensation
Localizes the goddess beyond the ocean Muliding, in the deserts of the north-east, from which she is summoned by prayer
The Paldan Lhamoi kang shag confession text is read when offerings are presented to her

variants.name: The Mongolian Okkin Tangri
variants.summary: Lhamo is identical with the goddess Okkin Tangri of the Mongolians, and with the Chammo or Lchamu of Pallas; the Mongolian edition of the confession contains some details in Kalmuck not met with in the Tibetan.

sensitivity_guidance: Palden Lhamo is the state protectress of Tibet and a living devotional focus; passages below are paraphrases of the 1863 public-domain translation for study, not ritual use.

sensitivity.note: Living devotional tradition; paraphrase of public-domain 1863 translation only. The filicide belongs to the traditional tale, reported factually and without endorsement.

passages.text: The goddess Lhamo was married to Shinje, the king of the Dudpos, who at the time of the marriage had assumed the form of the king of Ceylon; she had made a vow either to soften her husband's notoriously wild and wicked manners and make him favourably disposed towards the religion of Buddha, or, failing in her praiseworthy endeavours, to extirpate a royal race so hostile to his creed by killing the children that might issue from the marriage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 女神拉莫嫁給了杜德波（Dudpos）之王辛傑（Shinje），成婚之時，辛傑化為錫蘭王之形；她曾立下誓願：或要感化丈夫那惡名昭彰的狂野邪惡習性，使他對佛陀之教心懷善意；倘若她這番值得稱許的努力失敗，便要殺死這段婚姻所生的子女，以根除這個如此敵視其教法的王族。

passages.text: During a temporary absence of the king, the goddess flayed her son alive, drank the blood from out his skull, and even ate his flesh; she then left the palace and set out for her northern home, using her son's skin as a saddle for the king's best horse. On his return the king seized a bow and, with a terrible incantation, shot off a poisoned arrow after his dreadful wife; the arrow pierced the horse's back, but the queen, neutralizing the efficacy of the imprecation, took out the deadly weapon and uttered her sentence: may the wound of my horse become an eye large enough to overlook the twenty-four regions, and may I myself extirpate the race of these malignant kings of Ceylon!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 趁國王暫時外出之際，女神活剝了兒子的皮，從他的頭骨中飲血，甚至吃下他的肉；隨後她離開王宮，動身前往北方的家鄉，並以兒子的皮作為國王最好那匹馬的鞍韉。國王歸來後，抓起一張弓，念出可怕的咒語，朝他那駭人的妻子射出一支毒箭；箭射穿了馬背，但王后化解了咒語的效力，拔出那致命的武器，說出她的判詞：願我這匹馬的傷口化作一隻足以俯瞰二十四境的大眼，願我親自根除這些錫蘭邪惡國王的族裔！

passages.text: The goddess then continued her journey towards the north, traversing in great haste India, Tibet, Mongolia and part of China, and finally settled in the mountain Olkhan, in the district Olgon, said to be situated in Eastern Siberia and surrounded by large uninhabited deserts and by the ocean Muliding; in a prayer addressed to this goddess she is invoked as Rimate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 女神隨後繼續向北行進，匆匆穿越印度、西藏、蒙古及中國部分地區，最後定居於奧爾汗山（Olkhan），位於奧爾貢（Olgon）地區，據說地處西伯利亞東部，四周環繞著大片無人居住的荒漠與穆利丁海（Muliding）；在向她祈禱的禱文中，她被尊稱為里瑪特（Rimate）。

title.en: Tsangpa (Brahma) Tricked and Sworn
title.zh: 梵天受誘與立誓

region.en: Forest hermitage of Tsangpa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 梵天隱修之林（象徵定位）

period: Drimed shel phreng (Spotless Garland of Crystals); Schlagintweit's English 1863

source.work: Emil Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863), ch. X

summary.en: Tsangpa, a follower of the Buddha who had retired into the woods, was on the point of discovering the secrets of the Buddha doctrine by extraordinary meditation and the practice of virtues, when a Dudpo appeared before him in the shape of a beautiful woman who offered him exquisite delicacies; Tsangpa incautiously partook of them, was soon drunk, and in his phrensy killed the ram upon which the demon had ridden. By this savage act he lost the merits of the good works which he had accumulated with so much pain and perseverance, and attained no higher degree than that of a common follower, or Upasaka - filled with rage towards the evil spirits, he took an awful oath in the hands of the Buddha Vajradhara, vowing to do his utmost to extirpate the pernicious race through which he had lost his position.
summary.zh: 梵天（Tsangpa）本為精修佛法之隱士，將以禪定與持戒窺得佛道之秘；一魔忽化作美婦，獻上珍饈。梵天誤食而醉，狂亂中殺死魔所乘之羊——由此暴行，盡喪苦修功德，僅得「近事男」（優婆塞）之位。他憤而於金剛持佛前立下重誓：必竭力翦滅使其失位之惡魔之族。

sensitivity.note: Living pantheon tradition; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: Tsangpa, a follower of the Buddha who had retired into the woods, was on the point of discovering the secrets of the Buddha doctrine by extraordinary meditation and the practice of virtues, when a Dudpo appeared before him in the shape of a beautiful woman, who offered him exquisite delicacies; Tsangpa incautiously partook of them, was soon drunk, and in his phrensy killed the ram upon which the demon had ridden. By this savage act he lost the merits of the good works which he had accumulated with so much pain and perseverance, and attained no higher degree than that of a common follower, or Upasaka.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 倉巴（Tsangpa）是一名退隱林中的佛陀信徒，正要以非凡的禪定與修德之功參透佛陀教法的奧祕，此時一名杜德波化作美女現身於他面前，獻上精美可口的食物；倉巴不察，吃了下去，隨即醉倒，在狂亂之中殺死了那惡魔所騎的公羊。由於這野蠻的行徑，他失去了以如此艱辛與毅力所積累的善業功德，最終只達到普通信徒，即優婆塞（Upasaka）的境地。

passages.text: Tsangpa was now filled with rage towards the evil spirits, and took an awful oath in the hands of the Buddha Vajradhara, vowing to do his utmost to extirpate the pernicious race through which he had lost his position - a myth Schlagintweit cites to explain why the Bodhisattva Manjushri assumed the dreadful form of Yamantaka of his own free will, in consequence of a similar snare laid for him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 倉巴此時對那些惡靈滿懷怒火，在佛陀金剛持（Vajradhara）面前立下可怕的誓言，誓願竭盡全力根除那使他失去地位的害人之族——施拉金特魏特（Schlagintweit）引用這則神話，以解釋菩薩文殊師利為何因遭逢類似的陷阱，而自願化現為可怖的大威德金剛（Yamantaka）之形。

title.en: Chakdor and the Thief of the Water of Life
title.zh: 金剛手與偷飲不死甘露者

region.en: Mount Meru and the ocean of milk (cosmic, symbolic pin at the meridian of Meru)
region.zh: 須彌山與乳海（宇宙圖景，以須彌山為象徵定位）

period: Drimed shel phreng (Spotless Garland of Crystals); Schlagintweit's English 1863

source.work: Emil Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863), ch. X

summary.en: The Buddhas met on the top of Mount Meru to procure the water of life, Dutsi, concealed at the bottom of the deep ocean, as a powerful antidote against the poison Hala-hala the evil demons were using against mankind; they churned the ocean with the mountain Meru, and delivered the water of life to Vajrapani to secure safely. But the monster Rahu, a Lhamayin, watched his movements, seized his absence to drink the water of life - and voided his water deliberately into the vessel. Fleeing past the sun and moon, whom he menaced with vengeance should they betray him, he was betrayed by the candid moon, overtaken, and struck by Vajrapani's sceptre so that his body was split in two, the legs blown off; forced by the Buddhas to drink the fouled water as punishment, his fair yellow complexion turned dark, and the Buddhas made a horrible monster of him: his legs replaced by the tail of a dragon, nine different heads formed from his broken one, the principal wounds made into an enormous throat and the lesser ones into so many eyes. His rage turned especially against the sun and the moon: he overshadows them trying to devour them, and thus causes eclipses - but owing to Vajrapani's unceasing vigilance he cannot succeed in destroying them.
summary.zh: 諸佛會於須彌山頂，欲取深海之底所藏的不死甘露，以解諸魔施於人間的劇毒「黑哈利」；遂攪乳海，令甘露上浮，交金剛手菩薩（Chakdor）看管。怪物羅睺（Lhamayin）窺其行止，乘其不在，偷飲甘露，更故意向缽中小解。逃遁時他威嚇日月不得告密；月亮直言相告，羅睺旋即被追及——金剛手一杵擊下，其身斷為兩截，雙腿飛散。諸佛又命他飲下被污之水作為懲罰，其金黃膚色遂變為黝黑；諸佛更將其化為怪物：雙腿代以龍尾，殘首化為九頭，主傷成巨喉，餘創化為眾眼。自此羅睺專仇日月，每欲吞之——是為日月蝕之由；然因金剛手時時警衛，終不能滅。

canonical_translation: Emil Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet, London 1863 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Once upon a time the Buddhas all met together on the top of Mount Meru, to deliberate upon the means of procuring the water of life, Dutsi, which lies concealed at the bottom of the deep ocean. In their benevolence they intended, as soon as they obtained possession of the water of life, to distribute it amongst the human race as a powerful antidote against the strong poison Hala-hala, which the evil demons, at this period, had been using with such mischievous effect against mankind. In order to procure the antidote they determined to churn the ocean with the mountain Meru, and so cause the water of life to rise to the surface of the sea. This they did, and delivered the water of life to Vajrapani, with orders to secure it safely until a future meeting, when they would impart it to living beings.

But the monster Rahu, a Lhamayin, happened to hear of this precious discovery, and having carefully watched Vajrapani's movements, seized an opportunity, in the absence of the latter, to drink the water of life; not satisfied with this act, he even voided his water deliberately into the vessel. He then hurried away as fast as possible, and had already proceeded a great distance, when Vajrapani came home, and having perceived the theft, instantly set out in pursuit of the culprit. In the course of his flight Rahu had passed the sun and the moon, whom he menaced with vengeance should they venture to betray him to Vajrapani. His searches proving fruitless, Vajrapani betook himself to the sun, and asked him about Rahu; but the sun replied evasively, saying that he had certainly seen somebody passing a long time ago, but had paid no particular attention as to who it was. The moon, on the other hand, returned a candid answer, only requesting that Vajrapani would not repeat it before Rahu. Upon this information Rahu was shortly afterwards overtaken, when he got such a terrible blow from Vajrapani's sceptre that, besides receiving many wounds, his body was split into two parts, the lower part of the body with the legs being entirely blown off.

The Buddhas once more held a meeting, in which they deliberated upon the best means of disposing of Rahu's urine: to pour it out would have been most dangerous for living beings, as it contained a large quantity of the poison Hala-hala; they therefore determined that Vajrapani should drink it, in just punishment for the carelessness through which the water of life had been lost. Accordingly he was forced to do so, when his fair, yellow complexion was changed by the effects of this dangerous potion into a dark one. Vajrapani conceived, from his transfiguration, a most violent rage against all evil demons, and in particular against Rahu, who, notwithstanding his deadly wounds, was prevented from dying by the water of life. This powerful water, however, dropped from his wounds and fell all over the world, numerous medicinal herbs springing up on the spots where it touched the soil. A severe punishment was also inflicted upon Rahu by the Buddhas themselves: they made a horrible monster of him, replaced his legs by the tail of a dragon, formed nine different heads from his broken one, the principal wounds were made into an enormous throat, and the lesser ones changed into so many eyes. Rahu became, after this transformation, more dreadful than he was before; his rage was turned especially towards the sun and the moon, who had betrayed him. He is constantly trying to devour them, particularly the moon, who displayed the most hostile disposition towards him; he overshadows them whilst trying to devour them, and thus causes eclipses, but owing to Vajrapani's unceasing vigilance he cannot succeed in destroying them.
narrative.notes: Cultural function: the Tibetan redaction of the Hindu churning-of-the-ocean, transformed into an etiology of eclipses and of Vajrapani's dark complexion; Schlagintweit notes it derives almost without alteration from Hindu tales, where Vishnu severed Rahu's head and the nectar secured his immortality.

functions: Etiology of eclipses: Rahu, unable to die because of the amrita, forever pursues sun and moon in revenge
Charter of Vajrapani's dark form and his permanent office as guardian against the sun-devourer
Explains medicinal herbs as the drops of life-water fallen from Rahu's wounds all over the world
Demonstrates the rule that the gods who cause existence simultaneously bring its destructive power into action

variants.name: The Hindu churning of the ocean
variants.summary: In the Hindu versions the amrita was also procured by churning the ocean; Rahu, a monster with a dragon's tail, disguised himself like one of the gods and received a portion; his fraud discovered by the sun and moon, Vishnu severed his head, but the nectarean fluid secured his immortality.

variants.text_tradition: Singhalese books (Spence Hardy's Manual of Buddhism)
variants.summary: Rahu is 76,000 miles high, 19,000 broad across the shoulders, his head 14,500 miles round, his mouth 3,200 miles in size - and with one finger he can cover the sun or moon so as to obscure their light.
