passages.text: The Buddhas all met together on the top of Mount Meru to deliberate upon the means of procuring the water of life, Dutsi, concealed at the bottom of the deep ocean, intending to distribute it amongst the human race as a powerful antidote against the strong poison Hala-hala which the evil demons had been using against mankind; they churned the ocean with the mountain Meru, and delivered the water of life to Vajrapani with orders to secure it safely until a future meeting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 諸佛齊聚於須彌山頂，商議如何取得深藏於深海之底的甘露（Dutsi，生命之水），打算將其分予人類，作為對抗邪惡鬼神用以加害世人的劇毒哈拉哈拉（Hala-hala）的強效解藥；他們以須彌山攪動大海，並將生命之水交付金剛手（Vajrapani），命其妥善守護，直至下次集會。

passages.text: The monster Rahu, a Lhamayin, having watched Vajrapani's movements, seized his absence to drink the water of life, and even voided his water deliberately into the vessel; fleeing past the sun and the moon, whom he menaced with vengeance should they betray him, he was betrayed by the candid moon and overtaken, and got such a terrible blow from Vajrapani's sceptre that his body was split into two parts, the lower part with the legs being entirely blown off.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 羅睺（Rahu）這隻名為拉瑪因（Lhamayin）的妖魔，窺伺金剛手的行動，趁其不在時偷飲生命之水，甚至故意將自己的尿液排入容器之中；他逃經太陽與月亮時，威脅若他們告發他必將報復，卻被坦率的月亮告發而被追上，並遭金剛手權杖重擊，身體被劈成兩半，帶著雙腿的下半身完全被打飛。

passages.text: The Buddhas determined that Vajrapani should drink the fouled water in just punishment for his carelessness, whereupon his fair, yellow complexion was changed into a dark one, and he conceived from his transfiguration a most violent rage against all evil demons. The life-water dropped from Rahu's wounds fell all over the world, numerous medicinal herbs springing up where it touched the soil; and the Buddhas made a horrible monster of Rahu - his legs replaced by the tail of a dragon, nine different heads formed from his broken one, the principal wounds made into an enormous throat and the lesser ones changed into so many eyes. His rage was turned especially towards the sun and the moon, who had betrayed him: he overshadows them whilst trying to devour them, and thus causes eclipses, but owing to Vajrapani's unceasing vigilance he cannot succeed in destroying them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 諸佛裁定，金剛手應飲下被汙染的水，作為對其疏忽的公正懲罰；於是，他原本白皙的黃色膚色變為深色，並因自身的轉變而對一切邪惡鬼神生起極其猛烈的怒火。羅睺傷口滴落的生命之水灑遍全世界，凡觸及土壤之處皆長出無數藥草；諸佛又將羅睺造成一頭可怕的怪物——他的雙腿被龍尾取代，破裂的頭顱化成九個不同的頭，主要傷口變成巨大的喉嚨，較小的傷口則化為同樣眾多的眼睛。他的怒火特別轉向出賣他的太陽與月亮：他遮蔽它們，試圖吞噬它們，因而造成日食與月食，但由於金剛手不懈的警覺，他終究無法毀滅它們。

title.en: The Dragsheds, the Cruel Hangmen
title.zh: 屠吏尊：懲惡之神

region.en: Pantheon of protective deities (symbolic pin at Lhasa)
region.zh: 護法神殿（以拉薩為象徵定位）

period: Tibetan pantheon compendia; Schlagintweit's English 1863

source.work: Emil Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863), ch. X

summary.en: To subdue the evil spirits is one of the most important duties of the gods and genii, and they assume a horrible aspect when fighting with them, becoming highly inflamed with rage; a particular class have especially devoted themselves to the extirpation of evil spirits, further confirmed by an awful oath deposited in the hands of the Buddha Vajradhara - these are called Dragsheds, 'the cruel hangmen', and their anger against the evil spirits, so the legends relate, arose in consequence of the innumerable tricks that had been played off upon them by the latter. Amongst the Dragsheds the one called Yab yum chudpa, 'the father embracing his mother', is in addition able to deliver man from his sins if he sincerely repents and confesses them prostrate before his image - representations showing him with a female tenderly clasped round his body.
summary.zh: 降伏惡靈乃神祇之要務，臨陣時彼等現可怖之相，怒焰熾燃；有一類神專司翦滅惡靈，更於金剛持佛前立下重誓——是稱「Dragshed」，意為「兇殘之劊子手」。傳說其憤怒之由，乃因惡靈曾以千般詭計戲弄於彼。其中有名「父母相擁」（Yab yum chudpa）者，不僅能拒惡靈於外，亦能赦人之罪——只要人真心悔罪、於其像前伏地懺悔。其像皆作男女相擁狀。

sensitivity.note: Living pantheon tradition; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: To subdue the evil spirits is one of the most important duties of the gods and genii, and they assume a horrible aspect when fighting with the evil spirits, becoming highly inflamed with rage during these dreadful encounters; a particular class have especially devoted themselves to the extirpation of evil spirits, further confirmed by an awful oath deposited in the hands of the Buddha Vajradhara - these gods are called Dragsheds, the cruel hangmen, and their anger against the evil spirits arose, so the legends relate, in consequence of the innumerable tricks that had been played off upon them by the latter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 降伏惡靈是諸神與神靈最重要的職責之一，他們在與惡靈爭戰時會現出可怖之相，在這類駭人的交鋒中怒火熾盛；其中有一特定類別尤其致力於根除惡靈，並以存放在金剛持佛（Buddha Vajradhara）手中的可怕誓願加以確認——這些神被稱為「札謝」（Dragsheds），即殘酷的劊子手；據傳說，他們對惡靈的怒火，是因後者對他們施加了無數詭計而起的。

passages.text: The one called Yab yum chudpa, the father embracing his mother, in addition to his power of successfully keeping off a legion of evil spirits, is also able to deliver man from his sins, if the latter sincerely repents and confesses them prostrate before his image; these representations show them in a curious position, with a female tenderly clasped round their bodies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 名為「雅雍秋巴」（Yab yum chudpa，即擁抱其母的父尊）者，除了擁有成功驅退成群惡靈的力量之外，若有人在其像前虔誠懺悔、俯伏認罪，他也能使人脫離罪孽；這些造像以奇特的姿態呈現他們，身上溫柔地緊抱著一名女性。

title.en: The Dudpos and the Prolonged Bardo
title.zh: 辛傑之吏與延長的中陰

region.en: Region Paranirmita-Vasavartin, highest of the desire-worlds (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 他化自在天（欲界之頂，象徵定位）

period: Tibetan doctrinal compendia; Schlagintweit's English 1863

source.work: Emil Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863), ch. X

summary.en: The Dudpos, the assistants of Shinje the judge of the dead, inhabit the region Paranirmita Vasavartin, the highest in the world of desire; they try to hinder the depopulation of the world by supporting man in evil desire, and by keeping off the Bodhisattvas from attaining the Bodhi - it is they who disturb the devoutness of assembled Buddhists, and put an end to steady meditation by assuming the shape of a beautiful woman, or by suggesting ludicrous ideas, asserting that those who do not enjoy the pleasures of life shall be re-born in hell. But they are also those spirits who, when the time of death has arrived, seize the released soul and bring it before Shinje to be tried and sentenced according to its works. That death is considered untimely which, in opposition to the ordinary course of nature, is accelerated by the evil spirits; as a consequence the Bardo - the middle state between death and rebirth - is prolongated, and the wretched souls seized by the spirits appear to men as a raw, shapeless piece of meat, a vision considered unlucky, boding illness and even death.
summary.zh: 辛傑（閻魔）之吏「Dudpo」居於欲界之頂他化自在天；他們助長人的惡欲、阻菩薩證道，擾亂僧眾的誠敬，又化作美婦、出以諧謔，令修定者失其正念——並謂「不享人生之樂者將生地獄」。而人命終之時，亦是彼等抓住離體之魂，押至辛傑王前依業受審。凡為惡靈所催而違乎自然之壽，謂之「橫死」；橫死者中陰延長——此即死後與轉生之間的中間態；為靈所執之魂現於人前，狀如一塊無形生肉，見者大凶，主疾病乃至死亡。

sensitivity.note: Living doctrinal tradition; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: The Dudpos, the assistants of Shinje the judge of the dead, inhabit the region Paranirmita Vasavartin, the highest in the world of desire; they try to hinder the depopulation of the world by supporting man in evil desire, and by keeping off the Bodhisattvas from attaining the Bodhi - it is they who disturb the devoutness of assembled Buddhists, and put an end to steady meditation by assuming the shape of a beautiful woman, or by suggesting ludicrous ideas, by asserting that those who do not enjoy the pleasures of life shall be re-born in hell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 杜波（Dudpos）是亡者判官辛傑（Shinje）的助手，居於帕拉尼爾米塔·瓦薩瓦爾丁（Paranirmita Vasavartin），即欲界最高處；他們藉由助長人的邪欲，並阻撓菩薩證得菩提（Bodhi），試圖阻止世界人口減少——正是他們擾亂聚集信眾的虔誠，化為美女之形，或提出荒謬的念頭，或宣稱不享受人生樂趣者將轉生地獄，以此斷絕穩定的禪修。

passages.text: They are also those spirits who, when the time of death has arrived, seize the released soul and bring it before Shinje their King, to be tried and sentenced according to its works; that is considered an untimely death which, in opposition to the ordinary course of nature, is accelerated by the evil spirits, and as a consequence of premature decease the Bardo, the middle state between death and the new rebirth, is prolongated - the soul existing during this interval without any shape whatever, and the wretched ones seized by the spirits appearing to men as a raw, shapeless piece of meat, a vision considered unlucky, boding illness and even death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們也是那些在死亡時刻到來時，攫取解脫之靈魂並將其帶到他們的國王辛傑面前，依其業行受審判與判決的鬼靈；這被視為一種非時之死，此死違逆自然常軌，由惡靈所加速，而由於早夭，中陰——即死亡與新轉生之間的中間狀態——便延長了——靈魂在此期間以毫無任何形貌的方式存在，而那些被鬼靈攫取的悲慘眾生顯現於人前時，如同一塊生肉、無形無狀，此景象被視為不祥，預示疾病乃至死亡。

title.en: Om Mani Padme Hum: The Six-Syllable Prayer
title.zh: 六字真言：唵嘛呢叭咪吽

region.en: Prayer-wheels and walls of all Tibet (symbolic pin at Lhasa)
region.zh: 全藏轉經筒與嘛呢牆（以拉薩為象徵定位）

period: Six-syllable formula attributed to Padmapani; Schlagintweit's notice 1863

source.work: Emil Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863), ch. X

summary.en: Om mani padme hum - O the Jewel in the Lotus, Amen - is an invocation of Padmapani, who is believed to have delivered it to the Tibetans; it is the most frequently repeated of all prayers, and to each syllable is attributed a special magical faculty. In a prayer cylinder which Schlagintweit opened he found the sentence printed in six lines and repeated innumerable times upon a leaf 49 feet long and four inches broad; when Baron Schilling de Canstadt visited the temple Subulin in Siberia the Lamas were preparing 100 millions of copies of this prayer to be put into a prayer cylinder, and accepted his offer to have the necessary number executed at St. Petersburg - presenting him in return with an edition of the Kanjur of about 40,000 sheets. When engraved upon the slabs resting on prayer walls the letters are often so combined as to form an anagram, called in Tibetan Nam chu vangdan, 'the ten entirely powerful', and the power of the sacred sentence is supposed to be increased by its being written in this form.
summary.zh: 「唵嘛呢叭咪吽」——觀音（蓮華手）親授藏人之六字真言，為最常誦之咒。每字皆具別持神力。施拉金特魏特所開轉經筒中，六字凡四十九英尺長之紙上重複無數；希林伯爵在布里亞特寺院見僧眾備一億份以裝經筒，遂允代製，寺方回贈《甘珠爾》全藏（約四萬頁）。嘛呢石上六字常合為一個「十相自在」（Nam chu vangdan）符形，云其力更增。

sensitivity.note: Living liturgical formula; paraphrase of public-domain notice.

passages.text: Om mani padme hum, O the Jewel in the Lotus, Amen, is an invocation of Padmapani, who is believed to have delivered it to the Tibetans; it is the most frequently repeated of all prayers, and has on this account excited the curiosity of the earliest visitors to Tibet. To each syllable of the prayer is attributed a special magical faculty, and in a prayer cylinder which I had the opportunity of opening I found the sentence printed in six lines and repeated innumerable times upon a leaf 49 feet long and 4 inches broad.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 嗡嘛呢叭咪吽，即「蓮花中的珍寶」，阿們，是對蓮花手（Padmapani）的祈請，據信是他將此祈請傳授給藏人；這是所有祈禱文中被最頻繁誦念的一句，也因此激起了最早造訪西藏者的好奇。此祈禱文的每一個音節都被賦予一種特殊的法力，而在我有幸打開的一個祈禱輪中，我發現這句話印成六行，並在一張長四十九英尺、寬四英寸的葉片上重複了無數次。

passages.text: When Baron Schilling de Canstadt paid a visit to the temple Subulin in Siberia, the Lamas were just occupied with preparing 100 millions of copies of this prayer to be put into a prayer cylinder; his offer to have the necessary number executed at St. Petersburg was most readily accepted, and he was presented, in return for the 150 millions of copies he forwarded to them, with an edition of the Kanjur, the sheets of which amount to about 40,000. When engraved upon the slabs resting on the prayer walls, the letters are often so combined as to form an anagram, called in Tibetan Nam chu vangdan, the ten entirely powerful, and the power of this sacred sentence is supposed to be increased by its being written in this form.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當施林·德·坎施塔特男爵造訪西伯利亞的蘇布林寺時，喇嘛們正忙於準備一億份此祈禱文的抄本，以放入祈禱輪中；他提出在聖彼得堡製作所需數量的建議被欣然接受，而作為他轉送給他們的一億五千萬份抄本的回報，他獲贈了一部《甘珠爾》，其散頁總數約達四萬頁。當刻於祈禱牆上的石板時，字母往往被如此組合，以構成一個字母重排詞，藏語稱之為「南楚旺丹」（Nam chu vangdan），意為「十全具力」，而此神聖語句的力量被認為會因以這種形式書寫而增強。

title.en: The Lion, the Jackal and the Eland (Katkop Version)
title.zh: 獅、豺與大羚（卡茲科普版）

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by !khusin (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §29

summary.en: A fable somewhat similar to the Hottentot one of the Lion and the Jackal who went to shoot elands: the jackal cheats the lion of the kill by tricks of the hunt — the Katkop version recorded from !khusin and from his mother.
summary.zh: 寓言近似霍屯督版獅豺共獵大羚：豺以獵中之詭計騙取獅之獲物——布萊克自庫辛及其母所錄之卡茲科普版。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§29): a fable, somewhat similar to the Hottentot one of the Lion and the Jackal who went to shoot elands ('Reynard the Fox in South Africa', p. 3), was told in the Katkop dialect by !khusin; from whose dictation another beginning of the same fable has also been written down. A slightly different version, likewise given by !khusin, has only been hurriedly taken down in English.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §29; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布里克摘要（第29節）的濃縮轉述：一則寓言，與霍屯督人關於獅子與豺去射獵大羚羊的故事（《南非的列那狐》，第3頁）略為相似，由!khusin以卡特科普方言講述；亦已根據他的口述記錄下同一寓言的另一個開頭。另一個版本略有不同，同樣由!khusin提供，僅以英文倉促記下。

title.en: The Doings of a Family of Lions
title.zh: 獅族之言行

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §30

summary.en: An account of the doings of a family of lions — apparently a continuation of the Ichneumon's speeches in the myth of the Mantis — giving a good deal of conversation of such a description as might naturally be ascribed by Bushmen to lions.
summary.zh: 獅族言行之記述——似為螳螂神話中小獴言語之續篇——含桑人歸於獅類之自然對話。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§30): an account of the doings of a family of lions (apparently a continuation of one of the Ichneumon's speeches, in the myth of the Mantis), gives a good deal of conversation of such a description as might naturally be ascribed by Bushmen to lions (L II.—10. 1051-1170).
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §30; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布里克摘要（第30節）的濃縮轉述：一段關於一個獅子家族所作所為的記述（顯然是螳螂神話中某篇獴演說的續篇），其中包含大量此類性質的對話，即布須曼人自然會歸於獅子的那種對話（L II.—10. 1051-1170）。

title.en: The Jackal's Tower
title.zh: 豺之塔

region.en: Zak River, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省扎克河（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §31a

summary.en: The 'Jackal's Tower' — still visible as a spitzkop on the other side of the Zak River — gives rise to a Jackal and Hyena fable told to Dia!kwain by his mother: the jackal's standing-place of stones, from which he watched and was watched.
summary.zh: 「豺之塔」——至今仍為扎克河彼岸之尖丘——由此生豺與土狼之寓言，戴亞寬自其母所聞：豺之石壘瞭望所，觀人亦為人所觀。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§31a): the 'Jackal's Tower' (still visible as a 'spitzkop' on the other side of the Zak River) gives rise to a 'Jackal and Hyena' fable, told to Dia!kwain by his mother ≠kamme-an (L V.—4. 4231-4265).
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §31a; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布里克摘要（第31a節）的濃縮轉述：「豺之塔」（至今仍可見為扎克河對岸的一座「尖頂山」）引出了一則「豺與鬣狗」的寓言，由Dia!kwain的母親≠kamme-an講述給他聽（L V.—4. 4231-4265）。

title.en: The Ichneumon Disputes the Eland with the Mierkats
title.zh: 小獴與狐獴爭大羚

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by !khusin (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §32

summary.en: A Katkop fable (told to !khusin by his mother \xa-\kho) relates how the Ichneumon came to the mierkats (suricats) who were cutting up an eland one of them had shot, and how he disputed the prey with them, but unsuccessfully — a fable belonging to the series of myths of the Mantis.
summary.zh: 卡茲科普寓言（庫辛自其母舍夸所聞）：小獴至正分剖其群所射大羚之狐獴處，與之爭獲而不果——此屬螳螂神話之系列。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§32): a fable, in the Katkop dialect (told to !khusin by his mother \xa-\kho), relates how the Ichneumon came to some mierkats, or suricats, who were cutting up an eland which one of them had shot, and how he disputed the prey with them, but unsuccessfully. This is evidently a fable belonging to the series of myths of the Mantis.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §32; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布萊克摘要（§32）的濃縮轉述：一則卡托普方言的寓言（由他的母親 \xa-\kho 講給 !khusin 聽），敘述一隻埃及獴如何來到幾隻貓鼬（或狐獴）那裡，牠們正在切割其中一隻所射殺的一頭大羚羊，以及牠如何與牠們爭奪這份獵物，卻未能成功。這顯然是屬於螳螂神話系列的一則寓言。

title.en: The Vicious Water-Tortoise and the Charitable Katel
title.zh: 惡水龜與善蜜獾

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §32a

summary.en: A fable related to Dia!kwain by his mother: the vicious water-tortoise and the charitable katel (ratel or Mellivora), the giver, outdone in trickery and generosity.
summary.zh: 戴亞寬自其母所聞之寓言：惡水龜與善施之蜜獾，詐與施之相較。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§32a): the vicious Water-tortoise and the charitable Katel (Mellivora), a fable related to Dia!kwain, by his mother (L V.—5. 4265-4291, partly translated). A fable related to Dia!kwain by his mother: the vicious water-tortoise and the charitable katel (ratel or Mellivora), the giver, outdone in trickery and generosity.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §32a; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布萊克摘要（§32a）的濃縮轉述：兇惡的水龜與仁慈的卡泰爾（蜜獾），一則由 Dia!kwain 的母親講給他聽的寓言（L V.—5. 4265-4291，部分翻譯）。一則由 Dia!kwain 的母親講給他聽的寓言：兇惡的水龜與仁慈的卡泰爾（拉特爾或蜜獾），那位施予者，在狡詐與慷慨上都被比了下去。

title.en: The Anteater's Laws: The Springbok, the Lynx and the Partridge
title.zh: 食蟻獸之法：羚、獰貓與鷓鴣

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §33

summary.en: The anteater inquires of each springbok ewe whether her child is female; a foolish ewe confesses, the anteater springs into a hole with the kid, and lays down the law about the proper food and proper marriages of every animal. The lynx repeats her words, and later steals the daughter back, unlooses her bowstring on the anteater's head, and becomes the springbok-eating lynx, marrying a lynx.
summary.zh: 食蟻獸逐一詢問母羚其子性別；愚母吐實，食蟻獸攜羔入穴，並立萬獸飲食與婚配之法。獰貓復述其言，後又盜回其女，解弓弦於食蟻獸之首，遂成食羚之獰貓，並娶獰貓為妻。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San myth-fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§33): the Anteater inquires from a flock of springbok ewes, one after another, whether her child is a female. Each mother answers that hers is a male, until, at last, a foolish springbok confesses that her child is a daughter. The anteater offers to hold the child, so that the springbok should eat some of the anteater's food. The latter then springs into a hole with the kid.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §33; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布萊克摘要（§33）的濃縮轉述：食蟻獸向一群跳羚母羊逐一詢問，牠的孩子是不是雌性。每一位母親都回答自己的孩子是雄性，直到最後，一隻愚蠢的跳羚承認自己的孩子是女兒。食蟻獸提出代為抱那孩子，好讓那隻跳羚吃一些食蟻獸的食物。食蟻獸隨後便帶著小羊躍入一個洞中。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The male springbok scolds his wife for having lost their child. The anteater then lays down the law with regard to the proper food for different animals, and that their marriages should be suitable. They all listen to the anteater, and also to the lynx, who repeats to them the anteater's words... in the directions given about marriage, some animals marry wives, others husbands — a trace, Bleek notes, of a former grammatical gender in Bushman.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §33; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同一段落的濃縮轉述；並非逐字照錄。雄性跳羚責罵妻子弄丟了牠們的孩子。食蟻獸接著就不同動物應有的食物立下法則，並規定牠們的婚姻應當相配。牠們全都聽從食蟻獸，也聽從猞猁，猞猁向牠們複述食蟻獸的話……在關於婚姻的指示中，有些動物娶妻，有些動物嫁夫——布萊克指出，這是布須曼語中昔日語法性別的一絲痕跡。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. In another version the daughter of the springbok, \khauko, is stolen away by the lynx, who marries her. The anteater, told of this by the partridge, follows them underneath the ground; whereupon the lynx unlooses his bowstring and throws it down, the anteater's head is caught in it, and the lynx orders her to become altogether an anteater and live in a hole. Then he takes back the young springbok to her mother, becomes the lynx who eats springbok, and marries a lynx.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §33; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同一段落的濃縮轉述；並非逐字照錄。在另一個版本中，跳羚的女兒 \khauko 被猞猁偷走，猞猁娶了她。食蟻獸從鷓鴣口中得知此事，便在地底下追隨牠們；於是猞猁鬆開弓弦並將其擲下，食蟻獸的頭被弓弦套住，猞猁命令她徹底變成一隻食蟻獸，住在洞裡。接著牠把年幼的跳羚帶回牠母親身邊，成為吃跳羚的猞猁，並娶了一隻猞猁。

title.en: The Quagga Who Fed Her Child Her Own Liver
title.zh: 以己肝哺子之母斑馬

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1874 by !Kweiten ta //Ken (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §35

summary.en: The quagga, who fed her hungry child with a piece of her own liver, died by her husband's doing: the jackal put poisoned pieces of sharp bone into her bed because his relations said that he had married 'meat'. Her death was avenged by her own family.
summary.zh: 母斑馬以己肝一片哺飢兒；死於夫手：豺因親屬譏其娶「肉」為妻，置毒骨碎屑於其褥。其死由母族復仇。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; contains poisoning; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§35): the quagga, who fed her hungry child with a piece of her own liver, and whose death was caused by her husband, the jackal, who put poisoned pieces of sharp bone into her bed, because his relations said that he had married 'meat'. Her death was avenged by her own family — in the Katkop dialect, by !Kweiten ta //Ken (L VI.—1. 3898-3915).
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §35; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布萊克摘要（§35）的濃縮轉述：那隻斑驢用自己肝臟的一塊餵養牠飢餓的孩子，而牠的死是由牠的丈夫胡狼造成的，因為胡狼的親屬說牠娶了「肉」，胡狼便把帶毒的尖骨塊放進牠的床鋪。牠的死由牠自己的家族報了仇——在卡托普方言中，是由 !Kweiten ta //Ken 所講（L VI.—1. 3898-3915）。

title.en: The Bushman Woman Who Became a Lion
title.zh: 化獅之桑婦

region.en: Cape colonial frontier (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 開普邊境（象徵定位）

period: San oral tradition; told by Sir J. Alexander, translated by !A!kunta (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §37a

summary.en: The legend of a Bushman woman who transformed herself into a lion — told by Sir James Alexander and translated through Dutch by !A!kunta; a second version is preserved in the notebooks.
summary.zh: 桑婦自化為獅之傳說——詹姆士·亞歷山大爵士所述，由阿昆塔經荷語轉譯；筆記中另存第二版。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San legend from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§37a): the Hottentot legend of a Bushman woman who transformed herself into a lion, as told by Sir J. Alexander, was translated, through the medium of the Dutch, by !A!kunta (B I. 161-167); we have also a second version of this translation (L I.—1. 114-118).
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §37a; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布萊克摘要（§37a）的濃縮改述：霍屯督人關於一名布須曼女子化身為獅的傳說，由亞歷山大爵士所述，經由荷蘭語中介，由!A!kunta譯出（B I. 161-167）；我們另有此譯文的第二個版本（L I.—1. 114-118）。

title.en: The Lion's Name Not to Be Spoken by Children
title.zh: 童不得言獅之名

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §74a

summary.en: Children may not speak the lion's name; another version of the warning warns that a full-grown Bushman was punished by a lion for having eaten forbidden portions of the lion's prey as a child.
summary.zh: 童不得言獅名；另一版警語云：成年桑人因幼時曾食獲物中禁食之部，遭獅所懲。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San taboo-lore from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§74a): the name of the Lion not to be spoken by children — in the Katkop dialect, by Dia!kwain, from ≠kamme-an (L V.—7. 4526, 8. 4527-4562); another version of this warning by the same (L V.—8. 4563-4573). Condensed paraphrase, same locus (§74b): a full-grown Bushman, whom the narrator knew, punished by a lion for having eaten forbidden portions of the lion's prey, as a child — told by Dia!kwain (L V.—8. 4574-4617).
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §74a; not verbatim. / Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §74b; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布萊克摘要（§74a）的濃縮改述：孩童不得說出獅之名——以卡特科普方言，由Dia!kwain所述，出自≠kamme-an（L V.—7. 4526，8. 4527-4562）；同一人所述此警告的另一版本（L V.—8. 4563-4573）。同一出處（§74b）的濃縮改述：一名敘述者認識的成年布須曼人，因年幼時吃了獅子獵物的禁食部分而受獅子懲罰——由Dia!kwain所述（L V.—8. 4574-4617）。

title.en: The Bushman Doctor and the Old Sorceress
title.zh: 桑人醫者與老巫嫗

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §105

summary.en: The Bushman doctor or sorcerer cures by medicines, charms and magic; Dia!kwain reports two cures performed upon himself, the first including a speech made by the sorceress, the second how she cured him when injured by a Kafir; and an old sorceress, a relative who befriended his family, had the power of turning herself into a lioness and kept a pet springbok.
summary.zh: 桑人醫者以藥、符、術治病；戴亞寬自述兩次被醫——其一含巫嫗之言，其二為其遭科薩人傷後之救。另有一親戚老巫嫗能自化為母獅，且畜寵羚。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San healer-lore from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§105): the Bushman Doctor or Sorcerer (L II.—1. 273-275); an account of these people was also given in the Katkop dialect by Dia!kwain, from whom we besides have two reports of cures performed upon himself. The first includes a speech made by the sorceress; the second relates how she cured him when injured by a Kafir. Condensed paraphrase, same locus (§105b): an old sorceress (a relative who befriended the narrator's family), her power of turning herself into a lioness, her pet springbok, etc. — by Dia!kwain (L V.—10. 4707-4743).
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §105; not verbatim. / Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §105b; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布萊克摘要（§105）的濃縮改述：布須曼醫生或巫師（L II.—1. 273-275）；關於這些人的記述亦由Dia!kwain以卡特科普方言提供，我們另外還有兩份關於他本人所受治療的報告。第一份包括女巫所說的一段話；第二份敘述她如何在他被卡菲爾人傷害後治癒他。同一出處（§105b）的濃縮改述：一名老女巫（一位善待敘述者家人的親屬）、她化身為母獅的能力、她的寵物跳羚等——由Dia!kwain所述（L V.—10. 4707-4743）。

title.en: Sho-loii: The Medicine of the Snakes
title.zh: 紹洛伊：蛇之藥

region.en: Orange River mountains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 奧蘭治河山區（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §§107-108

summary.en: Sho-loii, a Bushman vegetable medicine and charm, grows in the mountains near the Orange River; men fight after rubbing their hands with it and heal each other after. An ignorant digger of sho-loii was found speechless among serpents; a skilled application drove the snakes away — taking the harmful scent with them — and restored him.
summary.zh: 紹洛伊為桑人草木藥與符，生於奧蘭治河近山；鬥者先以此擦手，戰後再以之互醫。一無知掘者被發現無言僵坐群蛇之中；善用此藥者驅蛇——連其惡嗅同去——並救醒之。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San medicine-lore from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§107): \slo-loii, a Bushman vegetable medicine, used also as a charm (L II.—36. 3242-3261). How one man fights with another, having previously rubbed his own hands with \slo-loii; and how he afterwards restores the man with whom he fought by means of a fresh application. The sho-loii in general use is not found upon the flats, but in the mountains near the Orange River; when dug out, the Bushmen replant part of it with a small piece of the root.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §107; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布萊克摘要（§107）的濃縮改述：\slo-loii，一種布須曼植物藥，亦用作護符（L II.—36. 3242-3261）。一人如何先以\slo-loii搓手，然後與另一人搏鬥；以及他後來如何藉由重新施用而治癒與他搏鬥之人。一般使用的sho-loii不在平地上，而在奧蘭治河附近的山中；挖出後，布須曼人會連同一小塊根重新栽種其中一部分。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus (§108): an ignorant man having gone to dig up sho-loii is discovered speechless and motionless, sitting among serpents, by the hole where he had been digging. By a skilful application the snakes are driven away, taking with them the scent which had injured the man, and the man is restored to speech and motion.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §108; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同一出處（§108）的濃縮改述：一名無知之人前去挖掘sho-loii，被人發現坐在他挖掘的洞旁蛇群之中，不能言語、不能動彈。經由巧妙的施用，蛇被驅走，並帶走了傷害此人的氣味，此人遂恢復言語與行動能力。

title.en: What a Maiden Must Eat and Avoid
title.zh: 少女之食與戒

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §106

summary.en: A new maiden must eat and avoid certain foods, must not look on young men's game lest the arrows cool, and treats herself with a red stone; and maidens and young men must not say or do certain things to avoid the wrath of the Water.
summary.zh: 新入潮之少女須食與戒特定之食，不得視青年之獵以免箭冷，並以紅石自療；少女與少年須言行有戒，以避水之怒。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San puberty rules from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§106): what a Maiden must eat and avoid (L II.—28. 2520-2524); how a new Maiden is treated, told in the Katkop dialect by !Kweiten ta //Ken (L VI.—2. 3997-4003), who also narrates the use made by Bushman Maidens of a kind of red stone (L VI.—1. 3970-3974). Condensed paraphrase, same locus (§106a): what Maidens (and young men) must not say or do, to avoid the wrath of the Water — by Dia!kwain (L V.—6. 4377-4407).
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §106; not verbatim. / Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §106a; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布萊克摘要（§106）的濃縮改述：少女必須吃什麼、避免什麼（L II.—28. 2520-2524）；新少女如何受到對待，由!Kweiten ta //Ken以卡特科普方言所述（L VI.—2. 3997-4003），她亦敘述布須曼少女使用某種紅石的情形（L VI.—1. 3970-3974）。同一出處（§106a）的濃縮改述：少女（及年輕男子）不得說什麼或做什麼，以免招致水之怒——由Dia!kwain所述（L V.—6. 4377-4407）。

title.en: The Dying Man's Last Speech and the Widow's Lament
title.zh: 臨終之言與寡婦之泣

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1873 by ||kabbo (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §112

summary.en: Wounded by a companion's arrow while hunting springbok, a man begs that they speak gently, not angrily, to the shooter — for unlucky shots come from the remissness of wives, children playing on beds; he gives his widow advice, and she cries that she would like to cry herself to death and will not eat, and will not marry again for fear of a lesser husband.
summary.zh: 獵羚時為同伴之箭所傷，其人求眾人對射者溫言勿怒——因失準之射乃由婦人怠慢、孩童戲床所致。他留遺言於寡妻；妻泣欲哭至死、不食、不再嫁——恐遇不及故夫之良人。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San death-narrative from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§112): a man is accidentally wounded by another, when they were both hunting springbok. Dialogue, in which the wounded man begs them to speak gently, not angrily, to the one who shot him. Unfortunate shots are believed to be due to such causes as the children at home playing on a man's bed, etc., and are ascribed to the remissness of the wives.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §112; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布里克摘要（§112）的濃縮轉述：一名男子在與另一人一同獵捕跳羚時，意外被對方所傷。對話中，受傷的男子懇求他們對開槍傷他的人溫言相勸，而非怒言相向。不幸的槍傷被認為源於諸如此類的原因，例如家中的孩子在人床上玩耍等等，並被歸咎於妻子們的疏怠。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The dying man's last speech to his wife, in which he gives her advice. The widow's lament, in which she says that she should like to cry herself to death, and does not want to eat food; her mother-in-law comforts her. After the burial the widow returns home to her father, where her brothers receive her very well; she expresses her intention not to marry again, for fear of meeting with a husband who had not the good qualities of the deceased.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §112; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同一出處的濃縮轉述，並非逐字照錄。瀕死男子對妻子的最後一番話，他在其中給予她勸告。寡婦的哀悼，她說自己恨不得哭死，也不想進食；她的婆婆安慰她。葬禮之後，寡婦回到父親家中，她的兄弟們待她極好；她表示無意再嫁，唯恐遇到一個不具亡夫那般美德的丈夫。

title.en: The Hyena Defends Her Gemsbok from the Lion
title.zh: 土狼衛其大羚以抗獅

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 by !A!kunta (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §63

summary.en: The hyena, defending from a lion the game (a gemsbok) which she is carrying home for her children, bites his thigh, so that he retires in pain — told by !A!kunta from the personal experience of his maternal grandfather \kui-\go, who was still living when his grandson left Bushmanland.
summary.zh: 土狼衛其負歸哺子之大羚以抗獅，咬其股，獅負痛而退——阿昆塔自其外祖父古伊果親歷所述；外祖父猶存於孫離布什曼蘭之時。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§63): the Hyena, in defending from a Lion the game (a gemsbok) which she is carrying home for her children, bites his thigh, so that he retires in pain — by !A!kunta, from the personal experience of his maternal grandfather \kui-\go (B V. 591-645).
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §63; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布里克摘要（§63）的濃縮轉述：鬣狗為保護牠正帶回家給孩子們的獵物（一頭南非劍羚）而抵禦一頭獅子，咬傷了獅子的大腿，使牠負痛退去——由 !A!kunta 所述，出自其外祖父 \kui-\go 的親身經歷（B V. 591-645）。

title.en: The Knorhaan Who Married His Sister
title.zh: 娶其妹之冠鴇

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §35b

summary.en: The Knorhaan (Brandkop bustard) who married his sister — told to Dia!kwain by his mother; apparently a version of the fable embedded in the Anteater's Laws, in which the bustard's head was thrust into the fire for the incestuous marriage.
summary.zh: 娶其妹之冠鴇——戴亞寬自其母所聞；似為食蟻獸之法中所嵌寓言之一版：因近親婚配，其首被按入火中。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§35b): the Knorhaan (Brandkop) who married his sister — told to Dia!kwain by his mother (L V.—5. 4292-4320); apparently a version of the fable embedded in the Anteater's Laws (§33). The Knorhaan (Brandkop bustard) who married his sister — told to Dia!kwain by his mother; apparently a version of the fable embedded in the Anteater's Laws, in which the bustard's head was thrust into the fire for the incestuous marriage.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §35b; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布里克摘要（§35b）的濃縮轉述：娶了自己姊妹的納氏鴇（Brandkop）——由 Dia!kwain 的母親講述給他聽（L V.—5. 4292-4320）；顯然是嵌於〈食蟻獸之法〉（§33）中那則寓言的另一版本。娶了自己姊妹的納氏鴿（布蘭德科普鴇）——由 Dia!kwain 的母親講述給他聽；顯然是嵌於〈食蟻獸之法〉中那則寓言的另一版本，其中這隻鴇因亂倫婚姻而被把頭按進火裡。

title.en: The Lion Who Exchanged His Chest with the Field-Mouse
title.zh: 與田鼠互換胸膛之獅

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 by !A!kunta (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §28

summary.en: A fable in which the lion exchanged his chest (breast) with the field-mouse — which !A!kunta had from his mother Ttoaken-an, as yet unfinished in the notebooks.
summary.zh: 獅與田鼠互換胸膛之寓言——阿昆塔自其母圖奧坎安所聞；筆記中未完。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§28): the fable of the lion who exchanged his chest (breast) with the field-mouse (which !A!kunta had from his mother Ttoaken-an) is as yet unfinished (B XIX. 1778-1789). A fable in which the lion exchanged his chest (breast) with the field-mouse — which !A!kunta had from his mother Ttoaken-an, as yet unfinished in the notebooks.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §28; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布里克摘要（§28）的濃縮轉述：獅子與田鼠交換胸膛（胸部）的寓言（!A!kunta 得自其母親 Ttoaken-an）至今尚未完成（B XIX. 1778-1789）。一則寓言，其中獅子與田鼠交換了胸膛（胸部）——!A!kunta 得自其母親 Ttoaken-an，在筆記本中尚未完成。

title.en: The Mani Walls: Prayers Built into the Landscape
title.zh: 嘛呢牆：以石砌經祈禱

region.en: Mani walls of eastern Tibet, near Kanze (symbolic pin at Kanze, Kham)
region.zh: 康區甘孜一帶的嘛呢牆（以甘孜為象徵定位）

period: Observed by W. W. Rockhill, 1889-1891

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Land of the Lamas (1891)

summary.en: The Tibetans have another way of showing their religious feelings, that love of mankind dear to Buddhism: this is, in multiplying for the weal of sentient creation written or sculptured copies of the mani prayer. It is no uncommon thing to pass a family established under a tent in a locality where shaly stones are abundant, every member busily occupied incising on slabs of rock the sacred formula, and building up after months, perhaps years, of labor a 'mani wall', each stone in it having the prayer sculptured on it and frequently carefully painted; walls a hundred yards and more long and eight or ten feet high. Others will shape the letters composing the prayer with blocks of white stone on some far-seen mountain side, giving them such huge dimensions that they can be read four or five miles away.
summary.zh: 藏人以另一方式表達宗教情懷——佛教所珍視的「愛眾」之心：為一切有情之福，不斷雕刻、書寫六字真言。常見一家人支帳於頁巖豐富之地，全家日日於石片上刻經；積數月乃至數年之功，壘成「嘛呢牆」——每塊石上皆刻經文且常加彩繪，牆長可逾百步、高八九英尺。更有以白色石塊於遠望可見的山坡上砌出咒字，其大可於四五里外誦讀。

sensitivity.note: Living devotional practice; paraphrase of public-domain travel record.

passages.text: It is no uncommon thing to pass a family established under a tent in a locality where shaly stones are abundant, every member busily occupied incising on slabs of rock the sacred formula, and building up after months, perhaps years, of labor a mani wall, each stone in it having the prayer sculptured on it and frequently carefully painted; I have seen these walls a hundred yards and more long, and eight or ten feet high. Others will shape the letters composing the prayer with blocks of white stone on some far-seen mountain side, giving them such huge dimensions that they can be read four or five miles away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Land of the Lamas (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在盛產片岩的地方，一家人安頓在帳篷裡，每個成員都忙著在石板上刻鑿神聖的咒語，經過數月、或許數年的勞作，砌成一道瑪尼牆，這並非罕見之事；牆上每一塊石頭都雕有祈禱文，且往往經過精心彩繪；我見過這樣的牆長達一百碼有餘，高達八到十英尺。另有一些人則在遠處可見的山坡上，用白色石塊拼出組成祈禱文的字母，其尺寸之巨，使人在四五英里之外都能辨讀。

passages.text: Small stones on which this prayer is sculptured are continually offered to one by beggars, who are paid for them by a handful of tsamba or a little tea; and a person of any respectability never dreams of refusing to buy all offered to him, placing them along the walls of his house, or else on the nearest mani wall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Land of the Lamas (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 刻有這祈禱文的小石塊，不斷有乞丐向人兜售，人們以一把糌粑或一點茶葉作為報酬；稍有體面的人，從不會想要拒絕買下所有向他兜售的石塊，而是把它們沿著自家房屋的牆壁擺放，或者放到最近的瑪尼牆上。

title.en: The Hairy Savages of the Northern Desert
title.zh: 北漠毛人

region.en: Desert of northern Tibet, on the caravan road (symbolic pin in the Changtang)
region.zh: 藏北高原商路（以羌塘為象徵定位）

period: Tibetan travellers' tales, collected by W. W. Rockhill, 1891

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Land of the Lamas (1891)

summary.en: An old lama from Rewang gomba described most graphically the journey of the caravan he had joined through the desert of northern Tibet, and the attacks made on it by small parties of brigands; several times, he said, his party had met hairy savages, with long, tangled locks falling around them like cloaks, naked, speechless beings, hardly human, who threw stones at the travellers but, having no arms, could do but little harm. This story of hairy savages Rockhill had often heard from Tibetans while at Peking, and was convinced that it has its origin in travellers seeing bears standing erect - in northern Tibet these brutes are numerous and large, and their tracks, especially those of the hind paws, have some resemblance to those made by men with naked feet.
summary.zh: 一位自拉薩返鄉的老喇嘛，繪聲繪色講述其商隊穿越藏北荒漠、屢遭小股強人（果洛）襲擊的經歷；又說途中數遇「毛人」——長髮披散如氅、赤身無言、幾非人類之物，向旅人投石，因無兵器故難以傷人。羅克漢在北京時已屢聞此說，認為其實起於旅人望見直立的熊：藏北熊多而巨，其足印（尤後掌）與赤足人跡極為相似。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief recorded by a 19th-century traveller; treated respectfully as heritage of Tibetan travel-lore. The 'Yeti' identification with bears is Rockhill's own rationalist note, reported as such.

passages.text: An old lama from Rewang gomba, some five days' journey south of Lusar, stopped at my inn on his way home from Lhasa; he described most graphically the journey of the caravan he had joined, through the desert of northern Tibet, and the attacks made on it by small parties of brigands. Several times, he said, his party had met hairy savages, with long, tangled locks falling around them like cloaks, naked, speechless beings, hardly human, who threw stones at the travellers, but who, having no arms, could do but little harm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Land of the Lamas (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位來自熱旺寺（Rewang gomba）的老喇嘛，該寺位於盧薩（Lusar）以南約五日路程處，他在從拉薩返鄉途中投宿於我的客棧；他極為生動地描述了所加入的商隊穿越藏北沙漠的旅程，以及小股強盜對商隊的襲擊。他說，他的隊伍曾數次遇到長毛野人，牠們長而糾結的髮辮如斗篷般披垂周身，赤身裸體、不會言語，幾乎算不上是人，牠們向旅人投擲石塊，但因沒有武器，所能造成的傷害甚微。

passages.text: This story of hairy savages I had often heard from Tibetans, while at Peking, and I was interested at hearing it again; from many things that happened later, on my journey, I am convinced that this story has its origin in travellers seeing bears standing erect. In northern Tibet these brutes are numerous and large, and people who are in constant dread of meeting brigands take the bears, seen probably at a distance, for them; this notion is further strengthened by the sight of their tracks, which, especially those of the hind paws, have some resemblance to those made by men with naked feet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Land of the Lamas (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 關於長毛野人的這個故事，我先前在北京時就常聽藏人說起，如今再次聽到，頗感興趣；從我後來在旅途中發生的許多事情來看，我確信這個故事源於旅人看見直立而立的熊。在藏北，這些野獸數量眾多且體型龐大，而時常害怕遭遇強盜的人們，便把大概是在遠處看見的熊當成了強盜；見到牠們的足跡，尤其是後掌的足跡，與人赤腳留下的足跡有幾分相似，更進一步加深了這種想法。

title.en: The Story-Tellers and the Ripa Mummers
title.zh: 說書人與麗巴假面戲

region.en: Village squares of eastern Tibet (symbolic pin at Ta-chien-lu)
region.zh: 康區打箭爐等地村落（以打箭爐為象徵定位）

period: Observed by W. W. Rockhill, 1891

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Land of the Lamas (1891)

summary.en: Besides the very large religious literature extant in Tibet there are a number of works of a semi-biographical nature, called nam-t'ar, histories, and translations of Chinese standard works; also books of songs and a few of pure fiction, these latter of Chinese origin and published probably by Chinese enterprise. The nam-t'ar are the favourite compositions, just as the historical novel is the most popular literature throughout China, and quite a numerous class of men earn their livelihood by giving readings of these books; these story-tellers afford the nearest approach the people have to theatrical representations, if we except the Ripa or itinerant mummers (mostly boys) who with hideous masks over their heads perform a grotesque dance to the music of their song, whose burden was a courting of one's expected generosity, becoming fulsome praise when one gave them anything.
summary.zh: 除浩繁宗教典籍外，藏地尚有半傳記性之「南木特爾」（聖者傳）、史書、漢文譯本、歌集，以及少數純虛構之書（多源於漢地）。南木特爾最為風行，一如歷史演義之於中國；賴此為生之說書人自成一行，於市井誦講——他們是藏人最接近戲劇的存在，若不算那些頭戴猙獰面具、邊歌邊舞的流浪「麗巴」（多為男孩），其歌辭之核心不外乎討賞，得賞則讚不絕口。

sensitivity.note: Living performance tradition; paraphrase of public-domain travel record.

passages.text: The nam-t'ar are the favourite compositions, however, just as the historical novel is the most popular literature throughout China, and quite a numerous class of men earn their livelihood by giving readings of these books; these story-tellers afford the nearest approach the people have to theatrical representations, if we except the Ripa or itinerant mummers (mostly boys) who with hideous masks over their heads perform a grotesque dance to the music of their song.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Land of the Lamas (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而，nam-t'ar（傳記故事）才是最受喜愛的著作，正如歷史小說在整個中國是最受歡迎的文學一樣，而有相當多的一類人以朗讀這些書為生；這些說書人可說是民眾所能接觸到的最接近戲劇表演的形式，如果我們不算那些里帕（Ripa）即流動的戲班子（多為男孩）的話——他們頭戴猙獰的面具，伴著歌聲的樂曲跳著怪誕的舞蹈。

passages.text: There are in this country certain festivals, but of a religious character and performed by the lamas, such as the Chamba ch'u-k'or, or Procession of the god Chamba (Maitreya) around the temples, to drive away demons, the festivities of the Lu-gon gyabo dung-dri, or Expulsion of the Prince of Devils, etc., which present much analogy to the mediaeval mystery plays - but these are not given for the amusement of the people, and form no part of their life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Land of the Lamas (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這個國家有一些節慶，但都帶有宗教性質，並由喇嘛主持，例如強巴卻科爾（Chamba ch'u-k'or），即強巴神（彌勒）繞寺巡行，以驅逐惡魔；又如魯袞嘉波東哲（Lu-gon gyabo dung-dri），即驅逐魔王節等等，這些與中世紀的神秘劇頗有相似之處——但這些並非為供民眾娛樂而舉行，也不構成他們生活的一部分。

title.en: The Evening Prayer and the Juniper Smoke
title.zh: 暮禱與柏煙

region.en: Villages of the Horba states, eastern Tibet (symbolic pin at Kanze)
region.zh: 康區霍爾巴諸部村落（以甘孜為象徵定位）

period: Observed by W. W. Rockhill, 1891

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Land of the Lamas (1891)

summary.en: The most pleasing ceremony noted among them is the evening prayer, observed by nearly every one in the larger villages and towns: as night falls lamps are lit on the altars of every Buddhist temple, and a short service is chanted, while lamas seated on the porch play a rather mournful hymn on long copper horns and clarinets. This is the signal for the housewives to light bundles of aromatic juniper boughs in the ovens made for the purpose on the roofs of their homes, and as the fragrant smoke ascends to heaven they sing a hymn or litany in which the men of the house often join, the deep voices of the latter and the clear high notes of the former blending most agreeably with the distant music in the lamaseries; in the morning juniper boughs are again burnt, with offerings - bowls of water, wine, milk, or butter lamps - placed before the household gods.
summary.zh: 藏人家最動人者，莫過暮禱：夜幕垂落，寺中佛壇燃燈，僧眾誦短經，廊下喇嘛以長銅號與單簧管奏哀婉之曲——這是主婦們的號令：於屋頂專設的爐中點燃香柏枝，青煙裊裊上達於天，婦女們唱起讚美詩或連禱文，男子亦常隨聲相和，低沉男聲與清亮女聲，與遠處寺院的樂音交融無間。晨間復焚柏枝，以水、酒、乳、酥油燈供於家神之前。

sensitivity.note: Living household devotion; paraphrase of public-domain travel record.

passages.text: As night falls lamps are lit on the altars of every Buddhist temple, and a short service is chanted, while lamas seated on the porch play a rather mournful hymn on long copper horns and clarinets; this is the signal for the housewives to light bundles of aromatic juniper boughs in the ovens made for the purpose on the roofs of their homes, and as the fragrant smoke ascends to heaven they sing a hymn or litany in which the men of the house often join, the deep voices of the latter and the clear high notes of the former blending most agreeably with the distant music in the lamaseries.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Land of the Lamas (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 夜幕降臨時，每座佛寺的祭壇上都會點起燈盞，並誦唱一段簡短的祈禱儀式；與此同時，喇嘛們坐在門廊上，以長銅號和單簧管吹奏一首頗為哀傷的聖歌。這便是信號，讓主婦們在自家屋頂上為此目的而設的爐灶裡點燃一束束芳香的杜松枝；當芬芳的煙霧升向天空時，她們便唱起一首聖歌或連禱文，家中的男子也常加入其中，男子低沉的聲音與女子清亮的高音，與遠處寺院裡的樂聲交融得極為悅耳。

passages.text: It is a universal custom among this people, before eating or drinking anything, to dip the forefinger of the right hand in it and scatter a little of the contents towards the four cardinal points, reciting a short prayer the while; this and the mumbling of the mani prayer are practically the only religious observances of the people. And they have another way of showing their religious feelings, that love of mankind dear to Buddhism - this is, in multiplying for the weal of sentient creation written or sculptured copies of the mani prayer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Land of the Lamas (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這個民族有一個普遍的習俗：在吃喝任何東西之前，先將右手食指蘸入其中，把少許內容物向四方灑散，同時誦念一段簡短的祈禱文；此舉與喃喃誦念嘛呢祈禱文，實際上便是人們僅有的宗教儀式。他們還有另一種表達宗教情感的方式，即佛教所珍視的對人類之愛——那就是為眾生的福祉而大量製作嘛呢祈禱文的書寫或雕刻複本。

title.en: The Wheel of Life: Buddha's Pictorial Universe
title.zh: 生命之輪：佛之宇宙圖

region.en: Doorways of Tibetan temples, where the Wheel is painted (symbolic pin at Samye)
region.zh: 藏地寺門所繪之輪（以桑耶寺為象徵定位）

period: Pictorial Wheel of Life (Bhavacakra); Tibetan copy attributed to the Indian monk Bande Yeshe, 8th century; Waddell 1895

source.work: L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism (1895), ch. on Metaphysics

summary.en: The Tibetan Wheel of Life is a disc symbolizing the endless cycle of existence, of which each rebirth is a revolution, held in the clutches of a monster who represents the hideousness of the Clinging to Life; the broad tire is occupied by the Causal Nexus, and the nave by the three vices - the Daughters of Desire, Raga, Dvesa, Moha, lust, ill-will and stupidity - figured as a dove, serpent and pig; outside the wheel is a figure of Buddha, showing that he has escaped from the cycle, pointing the way of escape. The six regions of rebirth - gods, Titans, men, beasts, tantalized ghosts and hell - are shown in the middle whorl, demarcated by rainbow-coloured cordons, and the twelve links round the rim follow the chain of causation from Unconscious Will to Decay and Death.
summary.zh: 藏式生命之輪是一圓盤，象徵生死無盡的輪迴——每一次轉生即一週轉；輪為怪獸利爪所攫，喻「戀生」之可怖；輪輞為十二因緣，輪轂為三毒——貪、瞋、癡，即「欲之三女」，畫作鴿、蛇、豬；輪外立佛像，示其已出離此輪，並指解脫之道。中輪畫六道——天、非天（阿修羅）、人、畜、餓鬼、地獄——以虹色界線相隔，而輪輞十二環節由「無明」至「老死」次第相續。

sensitivity.note: Living iconographic tradition; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: The Tibetan form of the picture should be studied with its Key; it is a disc or wheel, symbolizing the endless cycle of Life, of which each re-birth is a revolution. The wheel is held in the clutches of a monster, who represents the hideousness of the Clinging to Life; the broad tire is occupied by the Causal Nexus, and the nave by the three vices or delusions, the Daughters of Desire - lust, ill-will, stupidity - which lie at the core of re-birth, and are figured here as a dove, serpent and pig, appropriately coloured red, green and black; while outside the wheel is a figure of Buddha, showing that he has escaped from the cycle, to which he is represented as pointing the way of escape.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 藏式此圖應連同其圖解一併研讀；它是一個圓盤或輪，象徵生命的無盡輪迴，每一次再生即為一轉。輪被握在一隻怪物的爪中，這怪物代表對生命執著的醜惡；寬闊的輪胎部分為因果鏈所佔據，輪轂則為三種惡習或妄念，即欲望之女——貪欲、惡意、愚癡——它們位於再生之核心，此處分別以鴿、蛇、豬為形象，並恰如其分地著以紅、綠、黑三色；而在輪之外則有一尊佛像，表明他已脫離輪迴，圖中並繪他指向解脫之道。

passages.text: The various regions of re-birth, the Gati, are pictorially represented in the drawing called The Wheel of Life; they are given as six, and are thus enumerated in the order of their superiority: the Gods, the Titans, Man, the Beasts, the Tantalized Ghosts, and Hell. Existence in the first three worlds is considered superior or good, and in the last three inferior or bad; the six regions of re-birth are shown in the middle whorl, demarcated from each other by rainbow-coloured cordons representing the atmospheric zones that separate the different worlds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 再生的各個區域，即「趣」（Gati），在名為《生命之輪》的圖中被形象地描繪出來；它們被列為六道，並按其優劣次序如此列舉：天神、阿修羅、人、畜生、受折磨的餓鬼、地獄。前三界中的存在被視為優越或善，後三界則為低劣或惡；六道再生繪於中圈，彼此以彩虹色的帶狀線分隔，代表區隔不同世界的氣層。

passages.text: In the picture the phases of life are depicted: birth in a cottage; children at play; village scenes with people drinking wine under the shade of a tree; labour by sweat of brow; a man and horse falling into a river; two men fighting, one under trial before the judge; the king and his ministers; decrepit old people; a physician feeling the pulse of a patient; a corpse with a Lama feeling whether breath be extinct and relatives weeping; and funeral ceremonies, a corpse being carried off to the funeral pyre on the top of a hill preceded by a Lama blowing a thigh-bone trumpet and rattling a hand-drum - he also has hold of the end of a white scarf affixed to the corpse, the object of which is to guide the soul by the white path to the pyre so that it may be disposed of in the orthodox manner, have the best chance of a good re-birth, and may not stray and get caught by outside demons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 圖中描繪了生命的各個階段：在茅屋中出生；孩童嬉戲；村莊景象，人們在樹蔭下飲酒；汗流浹背地勞作；一人一馬墜入河中；兩人爭鬥，其中一人在法官面前受審；國王與其大臣；衰朽的老人；醫生為病人診脈；一具屍體，一位喇嘛在探其氣息是否已絕，親屬在哭泣；以及葬禮儀式，一具屍體被抬往山頂的火葬堆，前面有一位喇嘛吹著脛骨號、搖著手鼓——他還握著繫於屍體上的一條白巾末端，其目的是以白色之路引導亡魂至火葬堆，使其得以按正統方式處理，獲得善趣再生的最佳機會，而不致迷失並被外來的惡魔捉住。

title.en: The Twelve Nidanas: Buddha's Chain of Causation
title.zh: 十二因緣

region.en: Under the Tree of Wisdom at Gaya (symbolic pin at Bodh Gaya)
region.zh: 菩提伽耶智慧樹下（以菩提伽耶為象徵定位）

period: Chain of Causation formulated by the Buddha; Tibetan picture attributed to Bande Yeshe, 8th century; Waddell 1895

source.work: L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism (1895), ch. on Metaphysics

summary.en: Buddha formulated his view of life into a twelve-linked closed chain called the Wheel of Life or of 'Becoming', or the Causal Nexus, which he is represented in the Vinaya scripture itself to have thought out under the Tree of Wisdom; the way in which the narrative is couched leads to the impression that it was precisely the insight into this Wheel of Life which constituted his Buddhahood and distinguished him from the other Arhats. The twelve links round the rim follow in evolutionary fashion: Unconscious Will (Avidya), Conformations (Samskara), Consciousness (Vijnana), Self-consciousness (Nama-rupa), Sense-surfaces and Understanding (Shadayatana), Contact (Sparsha), Feeling (Vedana), Desire (Trishna), Indulgence (Upadana), Fuller Life (Bhava), Birth of heir (Jati), Decay and Death (Jaramarana) - and passing from Death to Re-birth, the chain closes back on Unconscious Will.
summary.zh: 佛陀將其人生觀結為十二環節之封閉鎖鏈——「有輪」或「緣起」；經藏中言其於智慧樹下思得此輪——敘事之筆，令人覺得正是洞見此「生命之輪」，方成其佛覺，而異於其他阿羅漢。輪輞十二環節次第為：無明、行、識、名色、六入、觸、受、愛、取、有、生、老死——而由死轉生，復歸無明，閉環不已。

sensitivity.note: Living doctrinal tradition; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: Buddha formulated his view of life into a twelve-linked closed chain called the Wheel of Life or of Becoming, or the Causal Nexus; which he is represented, in the Vinaya scripture itself, to have thought out under the Tree of Wisdom. The way in which the narrative is couched leads, indeed, to the impression that it was precisely the insight into this Wheel of Life which constituted his Buddhahood, and distinguished him from the other Arhats; he gave it a very leading place in his philosophy, so that the stanza recounting its utterance - Of all objects which proceed from a Cause, the Tathagatha has explained the cause, and he has explained their cessation also; this is the doctrine of the great Samana - is the most frequent of all Buddhist inscriptions.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 佛陀將其生命觀構造成一條十二環節的封閉鏈條，稱為生命之輪或存在之輪，或稱因果鏈；在《毗奈耶》經典本身中，他被描述為在智慧樹下思考出這一鏈條。敘述的措辭方式確實給人這樣的印象：正是對這生命之輪的洞見構成了他的成佛，並使他區別於其他阿羅漢；他在其哲學中賦予它極為重要的地位，因此敘述其宣說的那首偈頌——「諸法從因生，如來皆說其因，亦說其滅；此即大沙門之教」——是所有佛教銘文中最为常見的。

passages.text: The introduction of the pictorial details is ascribed to the great Indian monk Nagarjuna, who lived in the second century AD; these pictorial details, however, are alleged to be objective representations of the self-same similes used by Buddha himself, who constantly used homely similes and allegories to illustrate his doctrines. The Tibetan picture which supplements the Ajanta painting is alleged to be a copy of one brought to Tibet by the Indian monk Bande Yeshe in the eighth century AD, and now at Sam-yas monastery.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這些圖像細節的引入，被歸功於偉大的印度僧人龍樹，他生活在公元二世紀；然而，這些圖像細節據稱是對佛陀本人所用之同一比喻的客觀再現，佛陀經常使用樸素的比喻和寓言來闡釋他的教義。補充阿旃陀壁畫的這幅西藏畫作，據稱是公元八世紀印度僧人班德·耶謝帶到西藏的一幅畫的複製品，現存於桑耶寺。

title.en: The Jataka Tales and the Wheel of Karma
title.zh: 本生譚與業力之輪

region.en: The 550 births of the Buddha (symbolic pin at the Indian mission fields)
region.zh: 佛陀五百五十生（以印度傳教場域為象徵定位）

period: Jataka tradition (Buddha's births numbered at 550); Waddell 1895

source.work: L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism (1895), ch. on Karma and Palingenesis

summary.en: In this way Buddha explained all the acts and events of his life, his joys and sorrows, his success and failures, his virtues and weaknesses, as results of things done by him in previous states of life, which he recalled to mind as occasion arose for teaching purposes; and thus those anecdotes of the antecedent lives of the Buddha - the so-called Jataka tales - with the moral lessons derived from them, came to be among the most cherished items of Buddhist belief. Buddha's births are usually numbered at 550, of which the latter and more important are called 'the Great Births'.
summary.zh: 佛陀如是解說自己一生的一切行止與際遇——其樂與憂、其成與敗、其德與弱——皆是宿世所作之果；每當教化之需，他便憶念宣說。由此，佛陀前世之軼事——所謂「本生譚」——及其道德教訓，遂成為佛教信仰中最受珍視的篇章。佛陀之生通常計為五百五十，其中後期而重要者稱「大生」。

sensitivity.note: Living narrative tradition; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: In this way Buddha explained all the acts and events of his life, his joys and sorrows, his success and failures, his virtues and weaknesses, as results of things done by him in previous states of life, which he recalled to mind as occasion arose for teaching purposes; and thus those anecdotes of the antecedent lives of the Buddha - the so-called Jataka tales - with the moral lessons derived from them, came to be among the most cherished items of Buddhist belief. Buddha's births are usually numbered at 550, of which the latter and more important are called the Great Births.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 佛陀就這樣把他一生的一切行為與事件、他的歡樂與悲傷、他的成功與失敗、他的美德與弱點，都解釋為他在前世所作之事的結果；每當有教化的需要時，他便會回想起這些前世之事。於是，那些關於佛陀前世事蹟的軼事——即所謂的本生故事——連同從中引申出的道德教訓，便成了佛教信仰中最受珍視的內容之一。佛陀的轉生通常計為五百五十次，其中較晚且較為重要的被稱為「大生」。

title.en: The False Face's Bargain: The Contest of the Two Mountains
title.zh: 假臼者的交易：雙山較力

region.en: Grand River reserve, Ontario (related by David Boyle)
region.zh: 加拿大安大略格蘭德河保留地（大衛波義耳講述）

period: Related by David Boyle on the Grand River, printed in W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922)

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore, gathered from the Six Nations of New York (1922), 'False Faces and Creation'

summary.en: After the making of the world and its people by Rawen Niyoh (Hawenneyu), he was one day walking through an open place, following the sun and examining the ground where the people were going to live, when his eye caught a strange, long-haired figure coming in the opposite direction, the face red and twisted, the mouth pulled up at the left corner. 'I am the real owner of this world. I was here before you.' To prove strength the False Face ordered one of two mountains to come nearer, and it moved close to them; Rawen Niyoh ordered the other mountain to approach, which it did, the two remaining so nearly together that they had hardly room to get out. Each was satisfied with this exhibition of power, and Rawen Niyoh said, 'I think it would not be well for you to be seen by the people who are coming to this place, because you are so ugly.' The False Face agreed to hide on condition that he should claim the new people as his grandchildren and be called Grandfather, 'I will help all I can to drive away sickness from among the new people, and I am able to protect them from storms by causing the winds to go up high into the sky.' 'They shall be your grandchildren and you their Grandfather. They must observe a dance - the False Face Dance - at the Long House forever. Now we make this bargain, which shall last as long as you and I, and the people and the world shall last.' In other stories the False Face fails to move the mountain.
summary.zh: 造物主哈威尼尤造好世界與人民之後，一日沿日而行，視察將有人煙的地土，迎面遇見一個奇異的長髮身影——紅面歪扭，嘴角向左上吊。「我才是這世界的真主，我比你先在。」為較力，假臼者命兩座山之一靠近，山果然移來；哈威尼尤命另一山前進，兩山幾乎相擠，二人險無容身之地。彼此服其神力；哈威尼尤說：「你如此醜陋，不宜讓將來的人們看見。」假臼者應允隱匿，條件是認新人類為孫、被稱作「祖父」，「我當盡力驅除人間疾病，又能使風暴高飛天空以護他們。」於是二人立約：人民行「假臼之舞」於長屋，直到永遠。另一些故事裡，假臼者移山失敗。

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922 (Boyle informant); public domain. The False Face bargain is a living covenant of the medicine societies; no ritual details disclosed.

passages.text: After the making of the world and its people by Rawen Niyoh, he left it for a time, but when he returned he was one day walking through an open place, following the sun, overlooking his own work and examining the ground where the people were going to live, when his eye caught a strange, long-haired figure coming in the opposite direction. The face of this figure was red and twisted, the mouth being pulled up at the left corner. Rawen Niyoh (Hawenneyu) said to him: 'Where did you come from?' to which the False Face replied: 'I am the real owner of this world. I was here before you.' Rawen Niyoh said, 'I think I am the owner of this place, because I made it.' 'That may be quite true,' the False Face assented, 'but I have been here a long time, and I have a good claim to it, and I am stronger than you are.' 'Show me how you can prove this,' demanded Rawen Niyoh.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 12-13; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 在拉文·尼約創造世界及其人民之後，他離開了一段時間；但當他歸來時，有一天他正循著太陽的方向走過一片開闊之地，俯瞰自己的作品，察看人們將要居住的土地，這時他的目光瞥見一個長髮的怪異身影正從對面走來。這身影的臉是紅色的，扭曲著，左邊嘴角向上扯起。拉文·尼約（哈文尼尤）對他說：「你從哪裡來？」假面回答說：「我是這世界的真正主人。我在你之前就在這裡了。」拉文·尼約說：「我認為我是這地方的主人，因為是我創造了它。」「那也許完全屬實，」假面贊同道，「但我已在這裡很久了，我對它有充分的權利，而且我比你更強壯。」「讓我看看你如何證明這一點，」拉文·尼約要求道。

passages.text: The False Face suggested that they should retire to a valley not far from two high mountains. The False Face ordered one of the mountains to come nearer, and it moved close to them. Rawen Niyoh was very much surprised at the result, on which he ordered the other mountain to approach, which it did - the two remaining so nearly together that Rawen Niyoh and the False Face had hardly room to get out. Each was satisfied with this exhibition of power on the part of the other, and Rawen Niyoh said, 'I think it would not be well for you to be seen by the people who are coming to this place, because you are so ugly, for every one would follow you to look at you.' Ak-on-wa-rah (the False Face) agreed to this on condition that he should be allowed to claim the new people as his grandchildren, and they were to call him Grandfather. 'I will help all I can,' said he, 'to drive away sickness from among the new people, and I am able to protect them from storms by causing the winds to go up high into the sky.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 13-14; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 假面建議他們退到離兩座高山不遠的一個山谷裡。假面命令其中一座山靠近，那山便移近到他們身旁。拉文·尼約對這結果大為驚訝，於是命令另一座山靠近，那山也照做了——兩座山靠得如此之近，以致拉文·尼約和假面幾乎沒有容身的空間。雙方都對對方展示的力量感到滿意，拉文·尼約說：「我認為讓那些即將來到此地的人看見你並不好，因為你如此醜陋，人人都會跟著你去看你。」阿克翁瓦拉（即假面）同意這一點，條件是允許他把這些新來的人認作自己的孫輩，而他們要稱他為祖父。「我會盡我所能，」他說，「幫助驅除新來的人中間的疾病，我還能讓風升上高空，從而保護他們免受風暴之害。」

passages.text: Rawen Niyoh replied, 'I am sure you have much power to help the people, and you must keep this power as long as they live. We will make a bargain. They shall be your grandchildren and you their Grandfather. They must observe a dance - the False Face Dance - at the Long House forever. Now we make this bargain, which shall last as long as you and I, and the people and the world shall last.' Akonwarah replied, 'It is well.' In other stories the False Face fails to move the mountain.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 14; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 拉文·尼約回答說：「我相信你有很大的力量幫助人們，只要他們活著，你就必須保有這力量。我們來立一個約定。他們將是你的孫輩，你則是他們的祖父。他們必須在長屋永遠舉行一種舞蹈——假面舞。現在我們立下這個約定，它將持續到你和我、以及人民和世界終結之時。」阿孔瓦拉回答說：「很好。」在其他故事中，假面未能移動那座山。

title.en: The Terrible Skeleton of the Adirondack Cabin
title.zh: 阿迪朗達克木屋中的可怕骸骨

region.en: Hunting camp in the Adirondacks, from the Onondaga reservation
region.zh: 奧農達加獵隊在阿迪朗達克的營屋

period: Told by Albert Cusick (Sa-go-na-qua-de), published 1888; reprinted by Beauchamp 1922

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), 'The Terrible Skeleton'

summary.en: An Onondaga hunting party once went off with an old man, his daughter and her husband, and their little boy; the boy accidentally went the other way with his uncle. Late in the day the three found an empty cabin in a clearing and resolved to stay the night. When the fire became low and it grew dark, the young people were aroused by a sound like a dog gnawing a bone - it was a terrible skeleton, feeding on the old man. The wife slipped away to 'the spring,' the husband followed a little later, and as the fire went down the skeleton found both gone and started in chase. That night the Onondagas had a great dance: the fugitives heard the drum far away, turn-turn, turn-turn, and shouted; their friends heard the distress-hallo and came with all their arms, and the skeleton fled. A council sent the warriors to the dreadful spot: in the loft was a bark coffin with the skeleton of a man left unburied by his friends. Fuel was gathered and fire applied; the fire grew hot, the cabin fell in, and out of the flames rushed a fox with red and fiery eyes, dashed through the ranks and disappeared in the forest. The dead hunter was seen no more. 'But what had the little boy to do with all this?' 'O, that is to show it was well he went the other way.'
summary.zh: 奧農達加獵隊遠行，同行的有老人、其女與女婿，還有小男孩——男孩卻誤隨舅父走了另一條路。三人在空曠地的空屋過夜。火弱天黑之際，年輕夫婦聽見如犬啃骨的聲響——原來是一具可怕骸骨，正在啃食老人。妻子藉口「口渴去泉邊」先溜，丈夫稍後藉口尋妻而逃；火滅之後骸骨見二人皆走，隨後狂追。當夜奧農達加正舉行大舞：逃者遠聞鼓聲「轉—轉、轉—轉」，邊跑邊喊；族人聞救命呼聲持械而至，骸骨遁走。戰士們奉議前往：閣樓上有具樹皮棺，內是一具被族人棄而不葬的骸骨。眾人堆柴縱火；火旺屋塌，一隻紅眼的火狐自焰中竄出，穿陣而逃。死者從此不再現形。「那小男孩與這事有何相干？」「噢，那正是要說明：他走另一條路，走對了。」

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922 (Albert Cusick informant); public domain. Cusick's grandfather David Cusick briefly related the same tale - a burial-custom aition.

passages.text: In old times the Onondagas lived on a much larger reservation than now - a great land - but they made hunting parties to the Adirondacks. A party once went off in which were an old man, his daughter and her husband, and their little boy. They went one day and camped, and another day and camped, and then separated... late in the day found an empty cabin in a clearing... they resolved to stay for the night. They gathered plenty of fuel, stripping long pieces from the shag-bark hickory, built a fine fire, spread their deerskins on the rude bedsteads, and then went to sleep - the old man on one side, and the man and his wife on the other.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 13-14; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 古時候，奧農達加人居住的保留地比現在大得多——是一片廣大的土地——但他們會組織狩獵隊前往阿迪朗達克山區。有一次，一支狩獵隊出發了，其中有位老人、他的女兒和女婿，以及他們的小男孩。他們走了一天，紮了營；又走了一天，又紮了營，然後便分開了……當天傍晚，他們在一片林中空地上發現一間空無一人的小屋……他們決定留下過夜。他們收集了充足的燃料，從山核桃樹上剝下長條的樹皮，生起一堆旺火，把鹿皮鋪在簡陋的床架上，然後便睡下了——老人睡在一邊，那男人和他的妻子睡在另一邊。

passages.text: When the fire became low and it grew dark in the cabin, the young people were aroused by a sound like a dog gnawing a bone. They stirred about and the noise ceased, but was followed by something like rattling bones overhead. They arose and put on more fuel, and were going back to bed when they saw a dark stream from the other couch. It was blood and the old man was dead. His clothes were torn open and his ribs broken and gnawed. They covered him and lay down again. The same thing happened the second time, and this time they saw it was a terrible skeleton, feeding on the dead man. They were frightened and in whispers devised a plan of escape. They made a greater fire, and the wife said to her husband, 'I am so thirsty; I must go to the spring and have a long drink.' She went quietly out, but a little way off ran with all her might toward her own country. When her husband thought she had a good start he made a very big fire, to last a great while, and then he said, 'What has become of my wife? I am afraid she is drowned in the spring. I must go and see.' So he went out, and a little way off he, too, ran with all his might.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 14; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 當火勢漸弱、小屋裡暗了下來時，年輕人被一陣像是狗啃骨頭的聲音驚醒。他們動了動，聲音便停了，但接著又傳來像是骨頭在頭頂上喀啦作響的聲音。他們起身添了些柴火，正要回去睡時，看見另一張床榻上流出一道暗色的液體。那是血，老人已經死了。他的衣服被撕開，肋骨被折斷、啃咬過。他們替他蓋好，又躺了下來。同樣的事第二次發生，這回他們看見那是一個可怕的骷髏，正在吃那死人。他們害怕極了，低聲商議逃走的計策。他們把火燒得更旺，妻子對丈夫說：『我好渴；我必須去泉邊好好喝個夠。』她悄悄走出去，但走沒多遠便使出全力朝自己的家鄉奔去。丈夫估量她已跑出一段距離，便燃起一堆極大的火，好讓它燒很久，然後說：『我妻子怎麼了？我怕她淹死在泉裡了。我得去看看。』於是他走了出去，走沒多遠，他也使出全力跑了起來。

passages.text: By and by the fire went down, the skeleton came again, and when he found both were gone he started in chase. Soon they heard him howling terribly behind them and ran the faster for this. It happened that night that the Onondagas had a great dance and it now drew near morning. The fugitives heard the drum far away, turn-turn, turn-turn, and ran faster and shouted, but the skeleton did the same... Their friends heard the distress-hallo and came with all their arms. The skeleton fled. The fugitives fainted and did not regain their senses for four hours.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 14-15; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 漸漸地，火熄了下去，骷髏又來了，當他發現兩人都跑了，便開始追趕。不久他們聽見他在身後可怕地嚎叫，因此跑得更快。那一夜恰巧奧農達加人舉行盛大的舞蹈，此時已近清晨。逃亡的人遠遠聽見鼓聲，咚—咚，咚—咚，便跑得更快、放聲呼喊，但那骷髏也照樣做……他們的朋友聽見求救的呼喊，便帶著所有武器趕來。骷髏逃走了。逃亡的人昏了過去，過了四個時辰才恢復知覺。

passages.text: A council was held and the warriors started for the dreadful spot. They found the hut and a few traces of the old man. In the loft were some scattered articles and a bark coffin. In this was the skeleton of a man left unburied by his friends. It was determined to destroy everything. Fuel was gathered and fire applied. The warriors stood around with bended bows and raised hatchets. The fire grew hot, the cabin fell in, and out of the flames rushed a fox with red and fiery eyes, dashed through the ranks and disappeared in the forest. The dead hunter was seen no more. 'But what had the little boy to do with all this?' 'O, that is to show it was well he went the other way.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 15; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 他們召開議會，戰士們出發前往那可怕的地方。他們找到那間小屋，以及老人留下的一些痕跡。閣樓上有幾件散落的物品和一口樹皮棺材。裡面是一具被親友棄置未葬的骸骨。眾人決定把一切銷毀。他們聚攏柴薪，點上了火。戰士們圍立四周，彎弓搭箭、舉起戰斧。火燒得熾熱，小屋塌陷，一隻雙眼赤紅如火的狐狸從火焰中衝出，穿過隊伍，消失在森林裡。那死去的獵人再也沒有出現。『可那小男孩跟這一切有什麼關係呢？』『噢，那是要說明他走了另一條路是件好事。』

title.en: The Hunter Whose Friend Married the Big Serpent
title.zh: 與巨蛇成婚的朋友：雷族的誘殺

region.en: Group of lakes at Tully, Onondaga country (perhaps Crooked Lake and Round Lake)
region.zh: 奧農達加塔利湖群（或即克湖與圓湖）

period: Told at Onondaga Castle by an old Oneida, related by Albert Cusick (published 1888; Beauchamp 1922)

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), the serpent-wife tale told by Sa-go-na-qua-de

summary.en: Two young men, close friends, hunt far from home; the handsome one returns gameless day after day until his friend follows him: he plunges into the lakes, swims across 'like a snake,' and confesses he is going to be married - to the big serpent in the lake - and must leave his friend alone, though he may call him to the shore with fresh Indian tobacco and clean clay pipes laid on new bark, saying to the lake, 'I want to see my friend.' A youth dressed in white with white feathers on his head comes to the lonely hunter: 'My chief has sent me to invite you to our council' - eight chiefs in white feathers, whose plan is to destroy the serpent and his silver-shining wife, and who will come 'in the form of a cloud; on the lake, not in the sky.' The hunter lays the offering, calls his friend, is asked to lead the pair away from the lake into the woods - then runs; a great cloud comes at once over everything, and terrible thunder and lightning follow where they had sat, with rain everywhere. A big and a little serpent lie dead on the ground - the serpent woman and his friend. The eight chiefs cut up both serpents, making eight equal bundles, each chief carrying one, and go off in Indian file, seeming to step higher and higher until they went up to the sky, in a great thunder storm - for the chiefs were the Thunderers. The sorrowing hunter is adopted by his friend's mother and has two mothers.
summary.zh: 兩位親密的朋友遠行打獵；俊美者日日空手而歸。朋友跟蹤他：他竄入湖中「如蛇般」游過，坦白說他將成婚——娶湖中的大蛇為妻——並教朋友日後以新樹皮墊著新鮮菸草與潔淨陶管置於岸邊，對湖說「我想見我的朋友」。一日一位白衣白羽的青年來到孤獨的獵人門前：「我的首領派我來請你入議。」八位白羽酋長的計策是誅殺蛇夫婦；他們將「化為一片雲——在湖面上，而非天上」。獵人如言設供、喚友，並邀蛇夫婦離湖入林——隨後脫身而逃；烏雲立時罩天，雷電暴雨盡落二人坐處。湖畔躺著一大一小兩條死蛇——蛇妻與他的朋友。八位酋長把蛇切成八份，各背一份，列隊而去，步履漸高，升天而去——雷聲大作，因為他們就是雷族。悲傷的獵人被朋友的母親收養，從而有兩位母親。

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922; public domain. Beauchamp notes the tale is unique though with features peculiar to thunder-god stories.

passages.text: A long time ago, in an Indian settlement, were two wigwams not far apart, and in these lived two squaws who were very good friends. They had two children of about the same age, who played together... They were now young men and good hunters. One of them, being handsome and kind, was very much liked by the women and some of the maidens would have married him, but he refused all offers. At last his friend talked with him, and told him he had better marry, or something might happen for which he would be sorry. This troubled him, and he said he would soon choose a wife, but first they would have a long hunt together. They got ready for this, telling their mothers they were going away on a great hunt, far from their village, and might be gone many days. So their mothers took some corn and roasted it, and then pounded this into meal in their wooden mortars. The young men filled their sacks, took their bows, and went to their hunting ground.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 15-16; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 很久以前，在一個印第安人的聚落裡，有兩座相距不遠的棚屋，裡面住著兩個非常要好的女人。她們各有一個年紀相仿的孩子，常在一起玩耍……如今他們已是年輕男子，也都是好獵手。其中一個相貌俊美、心地善良，很受女人們喜愛，有些少女本願意嫁給他，但他拒絕了所有提親。最後他的朋友與他談話，告訴他最好娶妻，否則可能會發生令他後悔的事。這話使他心煩，他說他很快就會挑選一個妻子，但首先他們要一起去打一場長獵。他們為此做了準備，告訴母親們說他們要離村到很遠的地方去打一場大獵，也許會去很多天。於是母親們取了些玉米烤熟，再用木臼把它搗成粉。年輕男子裝滿了袋子，帶上弓，前往他們的獵場。

passages.text: After this they hunted every day, and one was lucky and brought home a great deal of game, but the one whom the girls liked came home without any, and said very little. Every morning they went to hunt in opposite directions, and one day his friend thought he would follow him and see what he did. He soon saw him running very fast through the woods and hurried after him, calling to him to stop, but he did not. They ran till they came to a lake, and the first one plunged into the water and swam across, while his friend went around the shore... As the swimmer entered the other jumped out and caught him, asking what was the matter and why he acted so strangely. At first the young man could say nothing and seemed to know nothing, but soon came to his senses. He told his friend that he was going to be married and must leave him all alone, for he could not go back to his home. If he wished to see him at any time, he might come to the lake, bringing fresh Indian tobacco and clean clay pipes. These things he must lay on bark just from the tree, and must then say to the lake, 'I want to see my friend.' So he went off another way and married the big serpent in the lake.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 16-17; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 此後他們天天打獵，其中一人運氣好，帶回許多獵物，但那個受少女們喜愛的人卻空手而歸，話也說得很少。每天早上他們往相反的方向去打獵，有一天他的朋友想跟著他，看看他究竟在做什麼。他很快看見他飛快地在林中奔跑，便急忙追上去，喊他停下，但他不肯。他們一直跑，跑到一座湖邊，前面那人便跳入水中游了過去，而他的朋友則繞著湖岸走……游水的人一上岸，另一個人便跳出來抓住他，問他怎麼了、為何舉止如此古怪。起初那年輕人什麼也說不出，似乎什麼也不知道，但不久便恢復了神智。他告訴朋友說他就要結婚了，必須撇下他獨自一人，因為他不能回到自己的家。若他什麼時候想見他，可以到湖邊來，帶上新鮮的印第安菸草和乾淨的陶土菸斗。這些東西他必須放在剛從樹上剝下的樹皮上，然後對湖說：『我想見我的朋友。』於是他就往另一條路去了，娶了湖中的大蛇。

passages.text: When he turned around a young man stood in the doorway, dressed in white and with white feathers on his head. The visitor said, 'You seem to be in trouble, but for all that you are the only one that can help us. My chief has sent me to invite you to our council.' Then he gave him wampum, to show that he brought a true message... Going in, he saw eight chiefs sitting quietly on the ground. All had white feathers on their heads, but the principal chief had larger feathers than the rest... 'Your friend has married the big serpent in the lake, whom we must kill... When your friend comes you must ask to see his wife. She will want to know if the sky is clear. When she comes you must take them a little way from the lake and talk to them there. The chiefs will come in the form of a cloud; on the lake, not in the sky.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 17-18; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
