title.en: How Turkey Boy Squeezed the Hearts of a Sorcerer and His Seven Sisters
title.zh: 火雞童捏心記：巫師與其七姊妹之亡

region.en: Lonely lodge of the old grandmother, and the strawberry clearing to the east
region.zh: 老祖母的孤屋與東方草莓林間空地

period: Recorded 1900s-1922, Seneca informants (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. VI tale 23, 'Turkey Boy Squeezed the Hearts of Sorcerers' (1923)

summary.en: An old woman and her grandson Turkey live alone in an old lodge, all their people killed by the monster wizard Deadoehdjadse' who lives to the east near a bed of strawberries as large as hearts. In the forbidden room Turkey finds the drum and the lacrosse ball, and learns the secret from Skin Man, the dried human skin swinging on a pole: he borrows a mole's coat, burrows underground, buys the mysteries with wampum beads stained with berry juice, and learns that the lives of the sorcerer and his seven sisters are secure, their hearts being concealed under the wing of a loon that swims in a pool under a bed in the lodge. Made up to look exactly like Deadoehdjadse' and chewing a strawberry, he eats the human flesh his sisters set before him, then - when Skin Man cries that the deer are in the strawberries - lifts the bed, commands the loon, grabs the eight hearts and runs: 'I am Turkey, and I've got your hearts.' Squeezing each heart as the sisters close with their deer-clubs, he fells them one by one and cracks every heart open on the flat killing-stone like flint. The Skin Man taunts the returning sorcerer - 'Turkey has your heart' - and his own heart breaks on the rock; patted all over, Skin Man is restored to his normal form: Turkey's own brother, held by sorcery. From the bones strewn on the flat rock they raise a host of quarreling people with mismatched limbs, pacify them, and with the grandmother's people build a new village by the strawberries, where they live to this day.
summary.zh: 老嫗與孫兒火雞相依為命，族人盡喪於東方巫魔迪多耶茲之手。禁室裡，火雞偷擊鼓、偷玩袋棍球，又借鼴鼠之皮鑽地而行，以染莓汁的貝珠向「皮人」購得奧秘：巫魔與七姊妹的心藏在屋中一張床下的水潭裡、由一隻潛鳥挾於翼下看守。火雞幻化成巫魔模樣，嚼著草莓吐汁，吞下姊妹們奉上的人肉；待皮人高呼「鹿進草莓地了」引開眾女，他掀床、令潛鳥、奪得八顆心臟奔出：「我是火雞，你們的心都在我手裡！」眾女持鹿棒追來，他便一顆顆捏心使其昏厥，再把心臟逐一摔在殺人石上，如燧石般迸裂。歸來的巫魔被皮人嘲弄——「火雞拿了你的心」——心石俱碎；皮人經他遍體拍撫復原，竟是受妖術所制的親哥哥。二人拾骨堆山，踢倒山核桃樹喊「散骨之眾，趁樹未倒快起！」——眾人肢體錯配、爭吵不休；火雞安撫之後，偕祖母一家在草莓地旁重建新村，安居至今。

sensitivity.note: Seneca tale (Parker 1923); public domain. Cannibalism is the villain's own trait, narrated at story distance.

passages.text: The lodge was old and very large, but only the two lived in it, for all others had been killed by sorcerers. Winter was coming on and the old woman was busily engaged each day in gathering firewood for the winter's store. Every day she would cry as she started on her journey and when she returned she would cry again... 'All of our people are dead. They have been destroyed by a monster wizard who eats human flesh. His lodge is to the east and near it is a great bed of strawberries. Oh, they are as large as hearts. Once there was a good village of our tribe there, but the people were killed and the houses have now fallen down.' Turkey now said, 'My grandmother, now is the time for me to go... Make me some moccasins. I am going east.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 200-202; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這座小屋很古老，也非常大，但只有她們兩人住在裡面，因為其他人都被巫師殺害了。冬天將至，老婦人每天忙著拾柴，以備過冬之需。每天她出門時都會哭泣，回來時又會再哭一場……「我們族人都死了。他們被一個吃人肉的怪物巫師毀滅了。他的小屋在東邊，附近有一大片草莓。噢，那些草莓大得像心臟一樣。那裡曾經是我們部落一個美好的村落，但人們都被殺了，房屋如今也已倒塌。」火雞男孩這時說：「我的祖母，現在是我該出發的時候了……替我做一些鹿皮鞋。我要往東去。」

passages.text: Turkey was cautious and crept along through the underbrush until he came to a clearing where he saw a dried human skin fastened by a cord to a tall pole. It swung around in the wind and watched the clearing. He was very crafty and knew that he could not approach the Hadjoqda (dried skin) without being seen and reported to its masters. Looking about he saw a mole and made a bargain with it to borrow its coat. Shrinking himself by magic he entered the mole skin and then burrowed underground until he was directly under the skin, when he broke a little root into beads and stained them with berry juice. He called to the skin and offered to give it wampum if it would talk for a while... He learned that the master sorcerer was Deadoehdjadse', and that the seven sisters cooked human flesh for him, grinding it in a corn mortar with white corn meal... Then he learned that the lives of the sorcerer and his sister were secure, for they could not be killed, their hearts being concealed under the wing of a loon that swam in a pool under a bed in the lodge.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 202-203; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 火雞男孩十分謹慎，沿著灌木叢潛行，來到一片空地，看見一張乾枯的人皮用繩子繫在一根高竿上。它在風中轉動，監視著這片空地。他非常狡猾，知道自己無法接近那張乾皮（Hadjoqda）而不被發現、不被通報給它的主人。他環顧四周，看見一隻鼴鼠，便與牠談妥條件，借來牠的皮毛。他施法縮小自己，鑽進鼴鼠皮中，然後在地下挖掘，直到正好來到那張皮的正下方，接著他把一小段根莖掰成珠子，用漿果汁染色。他向那張皮呼喚，說若它願意說一會兒話，就送它貝珠串……他得知那巫師首領名叫 Deadoehdjadse'，而七姊妹為他烹煮人肉，把肉和白玉米粉一起在玉米臼裡磨碎……接著他又得知，那巫師和他姊妹的性命十分穩固，因為他們殺不死，他們的心臟藏在一隻潛鳥的翅膀下，那潛鳥游在小屋裡一張床底下的水池中。

passages.text: Then he used magic to make himself appear exactly like Deadoehdjadse', and strode boldly into the clearing, chewing a strawberry and spitting the juice. This gave him great power. He drew near the lodge and called for food, but one sister was suspicious and offered him corn, then meat, then fish, but Turkey refused them all and roared that he was Ongwe I'as and wanted his accustomed dinner. This they put before him and he ate it all, satisfying the women that he was indeed their brother. Suddenly Skin Man began to call and the women all ran out of the lodge, for Skin Man was crying that the deer were in the strawberries. When the sisters were out of sight, Turkey noticed a small dog watching one of the beds. He threw a piece of meat to the dog and then lifted up the bed. Beneath was a pool of water and a loon swimming about. 'Give me the hearts,' commanded Turkey... This time the loon lifted its right wing and beneath were the eight hearts. Turkey grabbed them and ran out crying, 'I am Turkey, and I've got your hearts.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 203; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他施法讓自己看起來和 Deadoehdjadse' 一模一樣，大膽地大步走進空地，嚼著一顆草莓，吐出汁液。這給了他強大的力量。他走近小屋，呼喚要食物，但其中一個姊妹起了疑心，先後端上玉米、肉和魚，火雞男孩全都拒絕，還咆哮說自己是 Ongwe I'as，要吃他慣常的晚餐。她們便把晚餐擺到他面前，他全部吃光，讓那些女人相信他確實是她們的兄弟。突然，皮人開始呼喊，女人們全都跑出小屋，因為皮人正叫嚷著說鹿跑進草莓地裡了。趁姊妹們離開視線，火雞男孩注意到一隻小狗正盯著其中一張床。他丟了一塊肉給那隻狗，然後掀起那張床。底下是一池水，一隻潛鳥在水中游動。「把心臟給我。」火雞男孩命令道……這一次，潛鳥抬起了右翅，底下是八顆心臟。火雞男孩一把抓住它們，跑出去大喊：「我是火雞，我拿到了你們的心臟。」

passages.text: When the sisters saw Turkey with the hearts they began to chase him with the clubs which they used on the deer, but as each assailant approached Turkey squeezed her heart, causing her to faint... By this time the women were at the flat rock where their brother killed his victims. Turkey now threw their hearts one by one on the stone and each cracked open like a flint stone. 'Turkey has your heart, Turkey has your heart,' sang the Skin Man in derision. The monster sorcerer then rushed into the clearing where he saw Turkey dancing about the flat stone. He rushed upon him, but Turkey threw the heart upon the rock and broke both heart and rock. Then he patted Skin Man all over the body and restored him to his normal form. To his surprise he found him to be his own brother, who had been held by sorcery to obey the commands of the wizard and his sisters. Together they gathered many bones that were strewn about the flat rock. When all were piled up Turkey kicked over a pig-nut tree and called out, 'Disjointed bones, arise before this tree falls upon you!' The tree fell and before it hit the ground a great host of people arose and all were quarreling, for all had portions of the others' bodies. Turkey pacified them... and there they built a new village, and there they live to this day.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 203-204; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 姊妹們看見火雞男孩拿著心臟，便舉起她們用來打鹿的棍棒追趕他，但每當一個攻擊者逼近，火雞男孩就捏緊她的心臟，使她昏倒……此時女人們已來到那塊平坦的岩石旁，也就是她們的兄弟殺害受害者之處。火雞男孩這時把她們的心臟一顆一顆扔到石頭上，每一顆都像燧石一樣裂開。「火雞拿到了你的心，火雞拿到了你的心。」皮人嘲弄地唱著。那怪物巫師隨即衝進空地，看見火雞男孩正繞著那塊平石跳舞。他朝他撲去，但火雞男孩把心臟扔到岩石上，心臟和岩石一同碎裂。接著他拍遍皮人的全身，使他恢復原形。令他驚訝的是，他發現那竟是自己的親兄弟，被巫術控制，不得不聽從巫師和他姊妹們的命令。他們一同收集了散落在平石四周的許多骨頭。當所有骨頭都堆好後，火雞男孩踢倒一棵山核桃樹，喊道：「散開的骨頭啊，在這棵樹壓到你們身上之前起來吧！」樹倒了下來，還沒落地，一大群人便站了起來，而且全都爭吵不休，因為每個人都帶著別人身體的一部分。火雞男孩安撫了他們……他們就在那裡建起了一座新村落，至今仍住在那裡。

title.en: Corn Rains into Empty Barrels: The Bride from the Far South
title.zh: 玉米如雨入空桶：南國來的新娘

region.en: The hilltop of bark-eaters, and the far south land of corn
region.zh: 食樹皮者的山丘與南方的玉米之鄉

period: Recorded 1900s-1922, Seneca informants (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. VI tale 24, 'Corn Rains into Empty Barrels' (1923)

summary.en: At one time there was nothing to eat on all the earth: nearly all the people had starved to death, and a few that remained gathered together on a high hill and lived on boiled bark. There was a certain young man who kept saying all the time, 'It will be better after a while,' while his brother tortured him with sharp stones. After a while he heard footsteps, as if on a clean path; he listened for the span of a moon and then heard them running - but nobody believed him. One morning while he sat in the doorway with his head down on his knees a young woman stood before him, smiled and handed him a basket of bread: 'My mother sent me to this lodge to find a young man. My mother wants me to marry him... I have come from the far south. There is plenty of food there.' 'My mother sent me to bring food to you. Let everybody take off the tops of their corn barrels and then enter the lodge and cover their faces' - and soon they heard a sound like corn falling into their barrels; the barrels were full of shelled corn, and everybody ate and all were satisfied. But the younger brother threw his food into the fire and said he wanted game; the young wife's food was rejected, and speaking thereby the dissatisfaction of all the people she returned to her home - the barrels scraped bare overnight. The husband found her on a high mound covered with corn plants, her body burned and scarred where the thrown corn had struck her; and after living in the south several months the couple returned to find the people again starving. The young wife ordered them to open their corn barrels and hide their faces once again, and shelled corn fell like rain into the barrels filling them to the top. Then the young wife told the people that corn must never be wasted or thrown away, for it is food and if destroyed will cause the crops to be poor and the corn to cease to yield.
summary.zh: 大地上曾經顆粒無存：幾乎人人餓死，倖存者聚於高丘以煮樹皮為生。有個青年總是念叨「過一陣就會好起來」，他的弟弟卻用利石折磨他。他聽見乾淨小徑上的腳步聲，守了一個月才聽見奔跑之聲——卻無人信他。一日清晨，一位少女立在他門前，微笑著遞上一籃麵包：「我母親派我來此地找一個青年，要我嫁他……我自遙遠的南方來，那裡食物充足。」她命眾人打開玉米桶的桶蓋、進屋矇住面孔——頃刻間桶中傳來玉米落下的沙沙聲，桶桶皆滿，人人吃飽。但小叔把食物丟進火裡說要吃獵物；新娘的食物遭拒，便代表全族的嫌棄回娘家去了——當夜玉米桶被刮得精光。丈夫在長滿玉米株的高丘上尋見她，她的身子被丟棄的玉米灼燒得傷痕累累；南國數月之後夫妻重返，族人又在挨餓。新娘再命他們開桶矇面，玉米如雨般落滿桶中。她告誡眾人：玉米萬不可糟蹋拋棄——它是糧食，糟蹋它便會歉收絕產。

sensitivity.note: Seneca tale (Parker 1923); public domain. A food-taboo charter: wasted corn = the corn maiden's burns.

passages.text: At one time there was nothing to eat on all the earth. Nearly all the people had starved to death, and a few that remained gathered together on a high hill. They lived on boiled bark. There was a certain young man who kept saying all the time, 'It will be better after a while.' Nobody believed him because things were getting worse each day. His brother used to torture him with sharp stones and say harsh things to him. The young man, however, kept thinking that something would happen soon. After a while he heard footsteps, as if on a clean path. He listened for the span of a moon and then heard them running. He told the people but nobody believed him.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, p. 205; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 有一段時期，整個大地上都沒有東西可吃。幾乎所有人都餓死了，剩下來的少數人聚集在一座高丘上。他們靠煮樹皮維生。有一個年輕人一直不停地說：「再過一陣子就會好起來的。」沒有人相信他，因為情況一天比一天糟。他的兄弟常用尖石折磨他，對他說些刻薄的話。然而那年輕人始終認為，不久就會有事發生。過了一陣子，他聽見腳步聲，彷彿走在乾淨的小徑上。他傾聽了一個月的時間，然後聽見腳步聲在奔跑。他告訴了人們，但沒有人相信他。

passages.text: One morning while he sat in the doorway of his lodge with his head down on his knees, a young woman stood before him. He heard her breathe and looked up. She smiled and handed him a basket of bread. 'My mother sent me to this lodge to find a young man,' she said. 'My mother wants me to marry him... I have come from the far south. There is plenty of food there.' So the young man ate the bread and was married to the young woman from the south. Then the young wife said, 'My mother sent me to bring food to you. Let everybody take off the tops of their corn barrels and then enter the lodge and cover their faces.' The sun had now come up and it was hot. The people did not like their faces covered, but soon they heard a sound like corn falling into their barrels. After a time the noise ceased and the young wife said, 'It is finished now.' Out into the shed went the people of the lodge and found the barrels full of shelled corn. Everybody ate and all were satisfied.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, pp. 205-206; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 一天早晨，他坐在小屋門口，頭伏在膝上，一個年輕女子站到了他面前。他聽見她的呼吸聲，便抬起頭來。她微笑著遞給他一籃麵包。「我母親派我到這間小屋來找一個年輕人，」她說。「我母親要我嫁給他……我從遙遠的南方來。那裡食物充足。」於是那年輕人吃了麵包，娶了那位來自南方的年輕女子。接著年輕的妻子說：「我母親派我來給你們送食物。讓每個人都打開玉米桶的蓋子，然後進屋去遮住自己的臉。」這時太陽已經升起，天氣炎熱。人們不喜歡遮住臉，但不久他們就聽見一種聲音，像玉米落進他們的桶裡。過了一會兒，聲音停止了，年輕的妻子說：「現在完成了。」小屋裡的人們走到棚屋外，發現桶裡裝滿了去殼的玉米。每個人都吃了，全都吃飽了。

passages.text: But the younger brother threw his food into the fire and said he wanted game... When the husband returned he found his wife crying and when he asked her what was troubling her she said, 'Your younger brother has spoiled everything. He has rejected my food (speaking thereby the dissatisfaction of all the people). I shall now return to my home.'... During the following night there was a sound of scraping in the corn barrels and in the morning when the women went for their corn it was all gone, and with it the bride had vanished... He came to a region of great corn fields and after a while saw a high mound covered with corn plants. On this mound he found his wife and her mother.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, pp. 206-207; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 但弟弟把食物扔进火里，说他想吃肉……丈夫回来时，发现妻子在哭泣，便问她为何烦恼，她说：『你弟弟把一切都毁了。他拒绝了我的食物（以此道出了所有人的不满）。我现在要回我的家去了。』……在接下来的夜里，玉米桶中传来刮擦之声，到了早晨，妇女们去取玉米时，玉米已全部不见，新娘也随之消失……他来到一片广阔的玉米田，过了一会儿看见一座覆盖着玉米植株的高丘。在这座丘上，他找到了他的妻子和她的母亲。

passages.text: His wife showed him her body and it was burned and scarred. 'This is what your brother did to me,' she said, 'when he threw the corn into the fire. He would have killed me had I remained.' After living in the south for several months the couple returned and found the people again starving. The young wife ordered them to open their corn barrels and hide their faces once again. They did so and shelled corn fell like rain into the barrels filling them to the top. Then the young wife told the people that corn must never be wasted or thrown away for it is food and if destroyed will cause the crops to be poor and the corn to cease to yield.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, pp. 206-207; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 他的妻子给他看她的身体，那身体被烧伤，满是疤痕。『这就是你弟弟对我做的事，』她说，『当他把玉米扔进火里的时候。若我留下来，他会杀了我。』这对夫妇在南方住了几个月后返回，发现人们又在挨饿。年轻的妻子吩咐他们打开玉米桶，并再次遮住脸。他们照做了，剥好的玉米粒便如雨般落入桶中，装得满满的。随后，年轻的妻子告诉人们，玉米绝不可浪费或丢弃，因为它是食物，若被毁坏，就会导致庄稼歉收，玉米不再结穗。

title.en: Twentgowa and the Mischief Maker: Powers Granted Twice
title.zh: 特溫特瓜瓦與搗蛋鬼：只賜兩次的法力

region.en: Lazy man's mossy rock by the river, and the hidden bark house of S'hodie'onskon'
region.zh: 河畔懶人的青苔岩與搗蛋鬼的隱形木屋

period: Related by Edward Cornplanter, 1905 (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. VI tale 25, 'Twentgowa and the Mischief Maker' (1923)

summary.en: Twentgowa the lazy man dreams on a mossy rock by the river of killing big game if he only had a chance, until a friend appears: 'I have good things in my place of abode and there is plenty to eat and much game hanging on my rafters.' In the bark house that only appears from his bed the friend conjures the loathly mess into steaming pudding - 'Djiskwengo' - and throws the pot of food right through the wall of Twentgowa's abdomen. But the power fails at home - all that is produced is a terrible mess that drives his family out of the house - for the friend is none other than S'hodie'onskon', the mischief maker. Each gift is granted only twice: the pumpkin from the head of the war club - Twentgowa's third try whacks his own big toe and he faints; the shins whittled to bone knives to strike the fish - his second home attempt bleeds him into a faint until the friend heals the wounds with salivary fluid; the elm-bark cords and fish-bladder nose for hunting ducks underwater - on his third try the ducks he has tied draw him up into the air over the forest and drop him into an enormous hollow stub, where his drumming and song 'Djii-ha-ha' make the wood-gathering damsels dance until an axe reveals only a man with his clothes torn off. The wife gives him a terrible scolding, and the friend says: 'Twentgowa must not go to the woods any more to the spot where he has been accustomed to recline. He may not come to my house any more. Henceforth he must hunt like other men.'
summary.zh: 懶漢特溫特瓜瓦總在河畔青苔岩上空想著「若有机會必獵大獸」，直到一位朋友現身：「我家好吃好喝，梁上掛滿獵物。」只在他躺臥處才顯形的木屋裡，朋友一聲「迪斯克文戈」便把腥臭的糊漿化為香噴噴的熱布丁，還把食盆連食物隔牆送入他的腹中。可回到家法力盡失——只變出一團惡臭，把妻兒都熏出屋去——原來這位朋友正是搗蛋鬼肖迪恩斯康。每次法力只賜兩次：戰棒頭裡滾出南瓜——他第三次揮槌砸中自己的大腳趾，昏死過去；把小腿削成骨刀插水刺魚——第二次自家試法血流如注，昏倒溪邊，虧得朋友以唾液療傷；以榆皮繩與魚鰾鼻潛水獵鴨——第三次嘗試時鴨群振翅把他拖上天空、拋進巨大空樹樁，他的鼓聲與歌聲「吉—哈—哈」引得拾柴的姑娘們翩翩起舞，直到斧聲揭穿——樹洞裡不過是個衣衫被刮光的漢子。妻子把他痛罵一頓；朋友也言明：「特溫特瓜瓦不得再往河畔的青苔岩去，也不許再來我家。從今往後，他得像別的男人一樣打獵。」

sensitivity.note: Seneca tale (Cornplanter informant, 1905, Parker 1923); public domain.

passages.text: There was once a very lazy man named Twentgowa. He had a wife and several children. Twentgowa was always giving excuses to his wife as to why he did not hunt game more often like other men. Twentgowa often went into the deep woods and had a mossy rock near a river where he would lie and dream of the things he would like to do and how he would kill big game animals if he only had a chance... One evening a man came to the lodge where Twentgowa lived. He stood in the doorway and said: 'I am your friend. I have visited you before but this is the first time you have seen me. I have known your name for a long time. Now you must come often and see me. I have good things in my place of abode and there is plenty to eat and much game hanging on my rafters.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, p. 208; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 从前有一个非常懒惰的人，名叫特温特戈瓦。他有一个妻子和几个孩子。特温特戈瓦总是向妻子找借口，解释自己为何不像别的男人那样常去打猎。特温特戈瓦常走进密林深处，在河边有一块长满苔藓的岩石，他躺在那里，梦想着自己想做的事，以及只要有机会，他将如何猎杀大猎物……一天傍晚，一个人来到特温特戈瓦居住的棚屋。他站在门口说：『我是你的朋友。我以前拜访过你，但这是你第一次见到我。我早就知道你的名字。现在你必须常来看我。我的住处有好东西，食物充足，椽子上挂着许多猎物。』

passages.text: When he had lain there a short time he looked up and saw a large bark house, with very fine poles as supports and over the door a head of some animal he could not identify... 'Come in,' said his friend, 'This is where I live... Now it is time to eat. Be seated here on a mat and let us eat together.' Thereupon the friend went to an upper shelf and took down a bowl into which he placed a loathly mess of substance that had the odor of a fish a long time dead. 'Djiskwengo,' exclaimed the friend, and the bowl filled up with steaming pudding of most enticing odor. So the two friends ate the food and relished it greatly... 'My friend, there is no need of that,' said the householder. 'I will give you power to do as I have done.' So Twentgowa stood at the back of the lodge and his friend threw the pot of food into him right through the wall of his abdomen. It vanished through magic and power was within Twentgowa.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, pp. 209-210; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 他在那里躺了不久，抬头一看，看见一座大树皮屋，支撑的柱子非常精美，门上方挂着某种他认不出的动物头颅……『进来吧，』他的朋友说，『这就是我住的地方……现在是吃饭的时候了。坐在这张席子上，我们一起吃吧。』于是朋友走到上层架子旁，取下一只碗，往里面放了一团令人作呕的东西，散发着死去很久的鱼的气味。『吉斯克温戈，』朋友喊道，碗里便盛满了热气腾腾、香气极为诱人的布丁。两位朋友于是吃了这食物，吃得津津有味……『我的朋友，不必那样，』屋主说。『我会赐你力量，让你能像我一样做。』于是特温特戈瓦站在棚屋后方，他的朋友把那一锅食物朝他扔去，径直穿过他腹部的皮肉。那食物借魔法消失，力量便进入了特温特戈瓦体内。

passages.text: He kept thinking of his newly acquired power and thought it might be well to test it. So he sat down on a log and used his magical word, 'Odjiskwagoh.' As he did this a great pile of steaming pumpkin pudding formed on the ground... He placed in it the loathly substance like unto a dead fish and then conjured it until it overflowed... His wife was very angry and would not touch the food but scolded him, for instead of real food all that was produced was a terrible mess that drove her and the children out of the house... 'Do not go to the lodge of that man any longer. He is none other than S'hodie'onskon', whom we know as a mischief maker. He will make your mind abnormal and what is bad he will make you think is good.' The second gift: pumpkins from the head of the war club - 'I will give you power to so produce twice... Stand, swing your war club until it comes whack against the head of my club' - and at home Twentgowa lifted up his foot upon the bench and whacked his big toe: it was a terrible and resounding whack, but no pumpkin rolled forth; Twentgowa fell off the bench like a dead man.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, pp. 210-212; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 他不断想着自己新获得的力量，觉得不妨试一试。于是他坐在一根圆木上，念出他的咒语：『奥吉斯克瓦戈。』念罢，地上便形成了一大堆热气腾腾的南瓜布丁……他把那像死鱼一样令人作呕的东西放进去，然后施法，直到它溢出来……他的妻子非常生气，不肯碰那食物，反而责骂他，因为变出来的不是真正的食物，而是一团可怕的东西，把她和孩子们赶出了屋子……『不要再去找那个人的棚屋了。他不是别人，正是什奥迪翁斯孔，我们所知的捣蛋鬼。他会让你的心智失常，会把坏的东西让你以为是好的。』第二件礼物：从战棍头上变出南瓜——『我会赐你力量，让你能这样变出两次……站好，挥动你的战棍，直到它啪地一声打中我棍子的头』——而在家里，特温特戈瓦把脚抬到长凳上，啪地一声砸在自己的大脚趾上：那是一声可怕而响亮的拍击，却没有南瓜滚出来；特温特戈瓦像死人一样从长凳上摔了下来。

passages.text: So saying he went out and strode down to the creek where he removed his leggings. He took out his knife and passed it through his lips, moistening it. Then he began to whittle the meat off his shins so that the bone stood out sharp like a long knife. 'Now, my friend,' said he, 'I will wade swiftly through the water and strike the fishes before they can move to one side.'... Coming ashore he put down his basket and then began to moisten his shins with salivary fluid. They quickly were restored and did not bleed at any time... At length, despairing of causing him harm in this manner... Twentgowa tried his new power and caught many fish which he left with his friend... At home As he cut the flesh blood flowed out and he was in great pain... She dragged him to the lodge and then called upon her dog to go and fetch S'hondie'onskon', the magical friend, to come and heal the husband... Then said the friend, 'I gave you power twice, but further than that I did not give you. You have cheated and wasted your power.' The last gift was duck-hunting under water with elm bark cords and a fish's air-bladder touched to his nose: at home, into the lake he went for he saw upon its surface a great flock of ducks swimming closely together... Upward flew the ducks with such impetus that Twentgowa was drawn up into the air and over the forest. When the ducks had flown a short way the string which he was holding broke and down he fell and into the top of an enormous hollow stub... Twentgowa then sang 'Djii-ha-ha, djii-ha-ha!' many times, and the damsel danced... He took an axe and chopped down the tree... and there inside was a man with his clothes torn off. The wife scolded him for making the damsels dance... Then the friend came out of the bushes where he was hiding and he said, 'Twentgowa must not go to the woods any more to the spot where he has been accustomed to recline. He may not come to my house any more. Henceforth he must hunt like other men.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, pp. 213-216; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 说着，他走出去，大步来到溪边，脱下绑腿。他取出刀，把刀从唇间穿过，沾湿它。然后他开始削自己小腿上的肉，直到骨头像一把长刀一样尖利地凸出来。『现在，我的朋友，』他说，『我要迅速涉水而过，趁鱼还来不及游开就击中它们。』……上岸后，他放下篮子，然后开始用唾液润湿自己的小腿。它们很快便复原了，而且始终没有流血……最后，对用这种方式加害于他感到绝望……特温特戈瓦试了他的新力量，捕到许多鱼，留给了他的朋友……在家里，他切肉时血流了出来，他痛苦万分……她把他拖到棚屋，然后唤她的狗去把那位有魔法的朋友什翁迪埃翁斯孔请来医治丈夫……于是朋友说：『我两次赐你力量，但除此之外我并没有给你。你欺骗并浪费了你的力量。』最后一件礼物是：用榆树皮绳和一只鱼鳔贴在鼻子上，在水下猎鸭：在家里，他看见湖面上有一大群鸭子紧挨着游动，便跳进湖里……鸭子向上飞起，冲力如此之大，竟把特温特戈瓦拽上空中，越过森林。鸭子飞了不远，他手中握着的绳子断了，他跌落下来，掉进一根巨大的空心树桩顶部……特温特戈瓦于是多次唱道：『吉——哈——哈，吉——哈——哈！』那少女便跳起舞来……他拿起斧头砍倒了那棵树……里面竟是一个衣服被撕破的人。妻子因他让少女们跳舞而责骂他……这时，朋友从藏身的灌木丛中走出来，说道：『特温特戈瓦不可再去林中他惯常躺卧的地方。他不可再来我家。从今以后，他必须像其他男人一样打猎。』

title.en: Nanshe, Lady of the Fish
title.zh: 娜姆舍：魚群女主

region.en: Nina and the marsh lagoon, Iraq
region.zh: 妮娜與沼澤潟湖（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A hymn to Nanshe (Nanshe A, ETCSL c.4.14.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The daughter of Enki is praised as lady of fish and birds, interpreter of dreams and patron of the orphan: on New Year's day she judges the land, weighing the widow's case — the goddess of social justice and the lagoon's wealth.
summary.zh: 恩基之女被頌為魚鳥之主、解夢之師、孤兒之護：新年之日她審理天下，為寡婦秉公裁斷——兼具社會正義與湖沼財富的女神。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Nanshe, daughter of Enki, is praised as lady of the fish and the birds of the lagoon, whose own mother was born of the water's plenty. She is the interpreter of dreams and the patron of the orphan and the widow: on New Year's day she holds court, weighing the cases of the poor with the water's justice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.14.1, opening praise; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.14.1, the New Year court; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 南舍（Nanshe），恩基（Enki）之女，被讚頌為潟湖魚鳥之女主，其生母乃誕於水之豐饒之中。她是夢的解釋者，也是孤兒與寡婦的守護者：於新年之日，她開庭審理，以水之正義權衡窮人的案件。

functions: Charter of the marsh administration and its justice
Dream-interpretation patroness liturgy

variants.summary: The narrative companion of the hymn.

title.en: Nanshe and the Birds
title.zh: 娜姆舍與群鳥

region.en: Lagoon of Nina, Iraq
region.zh: 妮娜潟湖（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: Nanshe and the birds (Nanshe C, ETCSL c.4.14.3)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The birds of the marsh dispute their stations before their mistress; each is named, its cry described and its place assigned — a comic catalogue of the lagoon's citizens judged by the goddess.
summary.zh: 沼澤群鳥於女主之前爭論職位；逐一具名、摹其啼聲、各定其位——潟湖公民的喜劇目錄，由女神親裁。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The birds of the marsh come before their mistress Nanshe to dispute their stations; each is named, its cry described, its feathers and habits catalogued — a comic assembly of the lagoon's citizens. The goddess assigns each bird its place, and the dispute is settled with her own wit — the marsh given its constitution in verse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.14.3, the assembly; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.14.3, the settlement; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 沼澤之鳥來到其女主人南舍面前，爭論各自的地位；每一隻皆被指名，其鳴聲被描述，其羽毛與習性被編錄——一場潟湖居民之滑稽集會。女神為每一隻鳥指派其位置，爭端以她自身的機智平息——沼澤於詩句中獲其憲章。

functions: Comic catalogue of the marsh's birds
Naturalization of the dispute genre

variants.summary: The formal debate counterpart.

title.en: Nisaba, the Grain and the Stylus
title.zh: 妮莎芭：五穀與書筆

region.en: Eresh, Iraq
region.zh: 埃雷什（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A hymn to Nisaba (Nisaba A, ETCSL c.4.16.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The goddess of grain is praised as the scribe of the gods: she who measures the harvest on her lapis tablet, who lends her name to every school exercise — the patron of the writing that makes order.
summary.zh: 穀物女神被頌為眾神之書記：於青金石泥板上量度收成，以其名冠於每份校習之卷——使秩序得以成立的書寫之守護者。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Nisaba is praised as the grain goddess and the scribe of the gods: the one who measures the harvest on her lapis tablet and counts the years. She lends her name to every school exercise, and the closing prayer asks her for the art of writing perfected — the patroness of the craft that makes order out of accounts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.16.1, opening praise; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.16.1, the school prayer; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 尼薩巴（Nisaba）被讚頌為穀物女神與諸神的書吏：那位在其青金石板上丈量收成、計算年歲者。她將其名借予每一則學校習作，而結尾的祈禱向她求取臻於完善的書寫之藝——那使帳目化為秩序的技藝之守護神。

functions: Patroness liturgy of the scribal schools
Theology of accounting as divine order

title.en: Ninlil, Lady of the Grain-Filled City
title.zh: 寧利爾：穀滿之城女主

region.en: Nippur, Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯（伊拉克）

period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: An adab to Ninlil (Ninlil A, ETCSL c.4.24.1)

license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Enlil's consort is praised as the lady whose presence fills the granaries: the queen of Nippur whose word with her lord's decides the year — the adab hymn of the city's mother.
summary.zh: 恩利爾之妻被頌為使倉廩充盈之女主：尼普魯王后，其言與其主之命共同裁決歲事——城邦之母的阿達卜頌詩。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Ninlil is praised as the lady whose presence fills the granaries: the queen of Nippur, whose word with her lord's decides the year's plenty. The adab's refrain asks her intercession: through the lady, the lord's anger is softened — the queen as the land's advocate before the storm god.

passages.text: In the proverb collections the fox is the sly one: the fox who set a snare for others is caught in his own — the collections' repeated moral on cunning's price. The school texts used the fox tales to teach scribal wit and its limits: the animal fable teaching what the debate poems argued — the ancestor of the trickster fable in world literature.

passages.text: Before Babylon's god was Marduk he was Asarluhi of Kuara: the Sumerian hymns praise the exorcist's god, the mace that talks, the wise man's helper. Enuma Elish would give his name to Marduk as the first of the fifty: the old god absorbed by the new — the theological engineering of Babylon's rise, already visible in the Sumerian liturgy.

title.en: The Good Hunter and the Great Medicine
title.zh: 善獵人與大藥之起源

region.en: Battlefield where the good hunter fell, Seneca and Tuscarora country
region.zh: 善獵人倒下的戰場，塞內卡與塔斯卡洛拉之地

period: Oldest version in Doty's History of Livingston County from an old Seneca via Mr. Horsford; ampler Tuscarora form in Elias Johnson 1881; transcribed by Beauchamp 1922

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), 'The Good Hunter and the Great Medicine'

summary.en: In ancient times a war broke out between two tribes. On the one side the forces were jointly led by a great warrior and a noted hunter - the good hunter, noted for kindness and generosity to all, even to beasts and birds, and considered their protector. The battle was going against his side, and as he turned to quit the field a heavy blow felled him; on recovering he found that he could as easily pass through as over the great tree that lay across his path, and at home his friends would not talk with him - he had been killed, and was present in spirit only. On the field lay his mortal part quite dead, and its scalp gone. A fox raised the death lament and called all the beasts together; they came by hundreds, vainly trying to revive their friend; the bear was asked to speak as the nearest relative and best friend of man, and appealed to each and all for medicine, but none did any good. The oriole called a council of the birds, from the eagle to the wren: the white-headed eagle said the dead would not revive unless the scalp was restored. The fox searched every bird's nest and every hen-roost in vain; the pigeon hawk flew too swiftly; the white heron stopped to feed on wild beans; at last the crow - whom the warrior with the scalp did not fear, for he was accustomed to her - saw the scalp stretched on its hoop to dry in the smoke above his cabin, and carried it off. But so dry and warped had it become that it would not fit, until the great eagle plucked one of his long feathers, dipped it in the mountain dew that had collected on his back, and applied it to the scalp. The scalp was placed on the head, to which it closely adhered; the hunter revived and recovered his strength, and they gave him the compound which had restored him, as the gift of the Great Spirit.
summary.zh: 上古兩族交戰，一方由大戰士與著名獵人共同統率——那「善獵人」對飛禽走獸無不仁慈，被視為它們的保護者。戰事失利，他轉身欲退，卻被重擊斃命；魂魄歸家，親友竟視而不見——他已身死，唯魂尚在。戰場上他的遺體橫陳，髮皮已被割去。狐哀號召集群獸，數以百計的野獸趕來相救而無效；熊以人類至親之名求眾獸獻藥，仍無一靈驗。金鶯又召百鳥之會，自鵰至鷦鷯雲集；白頭的老鵰說：除非尋回髮皮，死者不能復生。狐遍尋鳥巢雞舍無果；隼飛得太快；白鷺貪食野豆誤事；最後是烏鴉——割皮戰士素來不怕她——看見髮皮繃在籠上、懸於屋煙之上晾曬，便趁機攜走。但皮已乾翹不合頭顱；白頭鵰自背上凝結的山露中拔一根長羽蘸露敷之，髮皮遂潤而貼合。獵人復甦，恢復氣力；眾獸將救他的合藥作為大神之賜贈予他。

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922 (Seneca via Horsford/Doty; Tuscarora via Elias Johnson 1881); public domain. Leland compares this to the Jesuit Relation's Ononhara feast of 1636; the panther (Ontarraoura) revived the good hunter 'in the midst of a good feast'.

passages.text: In ancient times a war broke out between two tribes. On the one side the forces were jointly led by a great warrior and a noted hunter. The latter had killed much game for the skins, the remains being left for beasts and birds of prey. The battle was going against his side, and he saw that, to save his own life, he must quit the field. As he turned, the body of a great tree lay across his path. He came up to it, when a heavy blow felled him. On recovering he found, strangely enough, that he could as easily pass through as over the obstruction. Reaching home, his friends would not talk with him; indeed they seemed quite unaware of his presence. It now occurred to him that he, too, had been killed, and was present in spirit only, human eyes not seeing him. He returned to the place of conflict, and there, sure enough, lay his mortal part quite dead, and its scalp gone.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 31-32; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 上古之時，兩個部落之間爆發了戰爭。一方由一位偉大的戰士與一位著名的獵人共同率領。後者為取皮毛而獵殺了大量獵物，殘骸則留給野獸與猛禽。戰局對他那方不利，他看出若要保住性命，必須離開戰場。當他轉身時，一棵大樹的樹幹橫在他的路上。他走到樹前，卻被一記重擊擊倒。醒來後，他驚奇地發現，自己竟能同樣輕易地穿過這障礙，如同越過它一般。回到家中，朋友們都不與他交談；事實上，他們似乎完全沒有察覺他的存在。這時他想到，自己其實也已死去，只是以靈魂之身存在，凡人的眼睛看不見他。他回到交戰之地，那裡果然躺著他已然死去的肉身，而其頭皮已被取走。

passages.text: A pigeon hawk, flying by, recognized the disembodied hunter, and gratefully offered to restore his scalp; so, stretching away in its flight to the retiring victors, he plucked it from the bloody pole. The other birds had, meantime, prepared a medicine which soon united the scalp to the head, when bears and wolves gathered around and joined in the dance. The hunter got well and lived many years, his experience strengthening their religious faith, and teaching them how to use the remedies so strangely acquired, which, to this day, are among the most efficacious known to the Indians.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 31-32; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 一隻鴿鷹飛過，認出了這脫離肉身的獵人，便感激地提出要為他取回頭皮；於是牠振翅飛向撤退中的勝利者，從那血淋淋的杆上將頭皮取下。與此同時，其他鳥兒已備好一劑藥，很快便將頭皮與頭顱接合，此時熊與狼聚集而來，一同加入舞蹈。獵人痊癒了，又活了許多年；他的經歷堅定了他們的宗教信仰，並教會他們如何使用這般奇異獲得的療方——這些療方至今仍是印第安人所知最有效的藥方之一。

passages.text: A fox came along when the conflict was over, and recognized this friend of bird and beast lying lifeless on the field. Shocked by the sight he raised the death lament, and called all the beasts together. Their cries were heard in the forest; they came by hundreds to the spot and tried to revive their friend. Vain were all their efforts, and he remained lifeless... Then the bear was asked to speak, as being the nearest relative and best friend of man. He appealed to each and all for medicine, but though each had his own, none did any good... This sad lament brought the oriole to the spot. He was told of their sad plight, and in turn went and called a council of the birds. There was a flapping of wings everywhere, and all came, from the eagle to the wren, in response to the call... The eagle's head had become white in his long and wise life... This white-headed sage said that the dead would not revive unless the scalp was restored.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 32-33; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 戰事結束後，一隻狐狸走來，認出這位鳥獸之友正毫無生氣地躺在戰場上。牠見此情景大為震驚，發出死亡的哀悼，並召喚所有野獸聚集。牠們的哭聲在森林中迴響；牠們成百地來到此地，試圖救活牠們的朋友。牠們的一切努力都徒勞無功，他依然毫無生氣……於是牠們請熊發言，因為熊是人最近的親屬與最好的朋友。牠向每一位懇求藥方，然而儘管每一位都有自己的藥，卻無一奏效……這悲傷的哀悼引來了黃鸝。牠被告知了牠們悲慘的處境，於是輪到牠前去召集鳥類的議會。到處都是振翅之聲，所有鳥兒都應召而來，從鷹到鷦鷯……鷹的頭因漫長而智慧的一生而變得雪白……這位白頭的智者說，除非取回頭皮，否則死者不會復生。

passages.text: At last the crow took up the mission. The warrior who had the scalp knew of the council, but feared nothing when he saw the crow flying near, for he was accustomed to that. She saw the scalp stretched on its hoop, to dry in the smoke above his cabin. Her chance came and she carried it off. Great was the rejoicing at her successful return. At once they put the scalp on his head, but so dry and warped had it become that it would not fit... Then the great eagle said that on the high rocks where he lived far above all other birds, the mountain dew had collected on his back, and perhaps this might serve. He plucked one of his long feathers, dipped it in this dew, and applied it to the scalp. It worked finely and the scalp was moist again... The scalp was placed on the head, to which it closely adhered. The hunter revived and recovered his strength. They gave him the compound which had restored him, as the gift of the Great Spirit, and there was then a pattering of feet and a rustle of wings as the council dispersed. The good hunter returned to his lodge in peace.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 33-34; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 最後，烏鴉接下了這項任務。持有頭皮的那位戰士知道有這場會議，但當他看見烏鴉飛近時卻毫不畏懼，因為他早已習慣了。她看見那張頭皮被撐在圓環上，在他小屋上方的煙霧中晾乾。她的機會來了，便把它叼走了。她成功歸來，眾人歡欣鼓舞。他們立刻把頭皮放回他頭上，但它已變得又乾又扭曲，怎麼也戴不合……於是巨大的老鷹說，在他居住的高岩上，遠在所有其他鳥類之上，山間的露水積聚在他的背上，或許這能派上用場。他拔下自己的一根長羽，蘸了這露水，塗在頭皮上。效果極佳，頭皮又濕潤了……頭皮被放回頭上，緊緊貼合。獵人甦醒了過來，恢復了力氣。他們把他用來復原的藥劑交給他，作為偉大神靈的贈禮，隨後便響起一陣腳步的啪嗒聲與翅膀的窸窣聲，會議就此散去。善良的獵人平安地回到了他的小屋。

title.zh: 自癒之草：循歌聲覓得的藥

period: Tuscarora chief Elias Johnson, Legends, Traditions and Laws of the Six Nations (1881), via Beauchamp 1922

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), 'The Medicine' (Elias Johnson's second medicine)

summary.en: One day a hunter heard the sweetest music in the woods, but thorough search did not reveal its source. Charmed by the sound he went again and again, but with no better success. Not a note was heard. At last the Great Spirit came to him in a dream and told him what to do. He was to purify himself before seeking it, and this he at once did. The forest path was taken, the charming strain fell upon his ear, and he listened attentively till he could sing every note himself. Then he drew nearer. A tall green plant stood before him, with long and tapering leaves. This he cut down, but it was immediately healed and became as before. He did this repeatedly with the same results, and then knew it as medicine especially good for wounds. Rejoicing in his great discovery, he took part of the plant home, where it was dried and pulverized. Then he touched it to a bad wound which a man had received, and it was healed at once. Thus did the Great Spirit give this great medicine to men, and very grateful were they for it.
summary.zh: 一日，獵人在林中聽見世上最甜美的樂聲，遍尋卻不見其源；他一再去聽，依舊一無所獲，連一個音符也聽不見。最後大神入夢指點：須先潔淨己身再去尋覓。他如儀淨身，重入林徑，仙樂入耳，他凝神諦聽直至自己能唱出每個音符。漸漸走近，一株高挑的綠草立在眼前，葉長而尖。他把它割倒，它卻立時癒合如初；屢割屢合，他這才知道這正是專治創傷的靈藥。他喜不自勝，取其一部分回家曬乾研末；觸於一處重傷之上，傷口立時癒合。大神便如此把這大藥賜給了人們。

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922 (Johnson 1881); public domain. The plant's self-healing on being cut is the sign of its virtue.

Not a note was heard. At last the Great Spirit came to him in a dream and told him what to do. He was to purify himself before seeking it, and this he at once did. The forest path was taken, the charming strain fell upon his ear, and he listened attentively till he could sing every note himself. Then he drew nearer. A tall green plant stood before him, with long and tapering leaves.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 34; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The False Faces at the Onondaga Medicine Dance
title.zh: 奧農達加醫舞中的假臼者

region.en: Onondaga council house at the midwinter feast
region.zh: 奧農達加隆冬祭的議屋

period: Observed by De Cost Smith, Jan. 26, 1883, at Onondaga; printed by Beauchamp 1922

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), 'False Faces' (De Cost Smith's account of the medicine dance)

summary.en: Though there have been medicine men of local reputation among the Onondagas, the False Faces have taken their place here in ceremonies for the sick. The members wear large wooden masks, the faces grotesquely carved and painted, the eyes adorned with brass or tin, and with horse hair for long flowing locks. If one dreamed he was a False Face, he related his dream to a proper person, and as Iroquois dreams must be fulfilled, he gave a feast and was initiated. All are males except one woman, who is Mistress of the Band - Go-go-sa Ho-nun-na-tase-ta, Keeper of the False Faces - who has charge of the regalia. The dance of Thursday, January 26th [1883] was a medicine dance, in which the Hon-do-i were not asked to help the people against the witches, but were expected, in view of the honor shown them, to withdraw the sickness for which they themselves were responsible. The head devil pushed open the door suddenly and entered with a bound to see if the feast were ready; when the food was declared cooked, the whole band of dancers entered and took seats near the middle of the room; the head chief threw tobacco into the fire, and lifting off the pot full of food gave it to the head devil, who took it and walked out, followed by the others; benches were arranged in a semi-circle in front of the women's stove, and those who were suffering from disease seated themselves to the number of thirty or forty; the False Faces ran their hands through the ashes on the hearth and, in single file around the half-circle of benches, each Hon-do-i in turn rubbing ashes upon the head of each of the sick persons - the action consisting in rubbing the hands quickly on the head, and then blowing upon it two or three times; a woman somewhat beyond middle age led out one of the sick women, while a man led forth one of the devils to dance with the patient, until each sick woman had danced with one of the devils.
summary.zh: 在奧農達加，為病人行禮的主事的已是「假臼者」社團。社員戴著巨大的木製面具，面相怪誕、塗繪斑斕，眼嵌銅錫，髮披馬鬃。凡夢見自己成為假臼者者，須把夢告知執禮之人——易洛魁之夢必須應驗——設宴而受入社禮。社中皆男子，唯有一位婦女為「假臼之守」戈戈薩霍南納塞塔，掌管法器。1883年1月26日的舞蹈是一場醫舞：不是請假臼者助人驅巫，而是他們受此尊崇之後，應自行收回其所致的疾病。大鬼猛地推門躍入查看宴席是否備妥；食物煮熟後，全隊入屋就座；大酋長向火中投菸草，舉起滿鍋食物交給大鬼，鬼隊隨之而出；病者三四十人列坐於弧形長凳，假臼者們以手攪動灶灰，列隊繞弧而行，逐一為病者以灰抹頭——其法為急搓頭頂兩三下、隨後向之吹氣；一位中年婦人引病婦出列，另一人引一位假臼者與病人對舞，直到每位病婦都與一位假臼者共舞一圈。

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922 (De Cost Smith, JAFL 1888); public domain. An outside observer's 1883 ethnographic description of a living healing society; no ritual formulas disclosed.

passages.text: Though there have been medicine men of local reputation among the Onondagas, the False Faces have taken their place here in ceremonies for the sick. The members wear large wooden masks, the faces grotesquely carved and painted, the eyes adorned with brass or tin, and with horse hair for long flowing locks. Doorkeepers wear corn-husk masks here, but in Canada these form a distinct society. In the N. Y. Regents' Report for 1850, Mr. Lewis H. Morgan gives an account of them. The actual False Faces were properly evil spirits with supernatural powers, and without bodies or limb - really the traditional Flying Heads. They frequented solitary places, starting from tree to tree, paralyzing men and bringing storm and pestilence.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 36; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 雖然奧農達加人中曾有過在當地頗有名望的醫藥人，但如今在為病人舉行的儀式中，假面人已取代了他們的位置。成員們戴著巨大的木製面具，面孔雕刻與彩繪得怪誕離奇，眼睛飾以黃銅或錫，並以馬鬃作為長長的飄逸髮綹。守門人在此戴著玉米穗殼面具，但在加拿大，這些面具構成了一個獨立的社團。在一八五○年紐約州董事會報告中，路易斯·H·摩根先生對他們有所記述。真正的假面人本應是擁有超自然力量、卻無身無肢的惡靈——實際上就是傳統中的飛頭。他們常出沒於僻靜之地，從一棵樹跳到另一棵樹，使人麻痺，並帶來風暴與瘟疫。

passages.text: As a society they appear in all Iroquois villages, having secret initiations, ceremonies and dances. If one dreamed he was a False Face, he related his dream to a proper person, and as Iroquois dreams must be fulfilled, he gave a feast and was initiated. If he dreamed he ceased to be a member, he gave a feast and withdrew. The dream governed throughout. When they appear in public as such, they all wear masks. All are males except one woman, who is Mistress of the Band. She is called Go-go-sa Ho-nun-na-tase-ta, or Keeper of the False Faces. She has charge of the regalia, and is the only organ of communication with the members, whose names are supposedly unknown.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 36; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 作為一個社團，他們出現在所有易洛魁村落中，有秘密的入會儀式、典禮與舞蹈。若有人夢見自己是假面人，他便向適當的人講述自己的夢，而由於易洛魁人的夢必須實現，他便設宴並接受入會。若他夢見自己不再是成員，他便設宴並退出。一切皆由夢主宰。當他們以此身分公開露面時，全都戴著面具。除了一名女子之外，所有成員皆為男性，她是這個團體的女主人。她被稱為Go-go-sa Ho-nun-na-tase-ta，即假面人的守護者。她掌管全套法器，並且是與成員之間唯一的溝通管道，而成員的姓名據說是不為人知的。

passages.text: The dance of Thursday, January 26th, was more interesting, but was, properly speaking, a 'medicine dance,' in which the Hon-do-i were not asked to help the people against the witches, but were expected, in view of the honor shown them, to withdraw the sickness for which they themselves were responsible... During the early part of the day the dancers went from house to house, dancing for the cure of those who could not leave home. In the afternoon, toward three o'clock, the people gathered in the council house to await the coming of the Hon-do-i... the 'head devil' would push open the door suddenly and enter with a bound, to see if the feast were ready. When this had happened several times the food was declared cooked, and the whole band of dancers entered and took seats near the middle of the room.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 38-39; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 一月二十六日星期四的舞蹈更為有趣，但嚴格說來，那是一場「醫藥舞」，其中Hon-do-i並未被請來幫助人們對抗女巫，而是由於他們所受的尊崇，被期望收回他們自己應負責的疾病……當天早些時候，舞者們挨家挨戶地跳舞，為那些無法離家的人治病。下午將近三點時，人們聚集在議事廳中，等候Hon-do-i的到來……「首魔」會突然推開門，一躍而入，看看宴席是否已備妥。這樣發生過幾次之後，食物便宣告煮好了，整隊舞者於是進入，在房間中央附近就座。

passages.text: The head chief then stood up and addressed the dancers as A-gwe-ge, 'All.' Then proceeding to the stove, he threw tobacco into the fire, and lifting off the pot full of food gave it to the 'head devil,' who took it and walked out, followed by the others... On this semi-circle of benches those who were suffering from disease or sickness now seated themselves to the number of thirty or forty. When the devils had eaten the food they returned to the council house, and all save one... went to the stove, and with a great deal of grunting and groaning, 'Han-han, han-han,' ran their hands through the ashes on the hearth, and then started in single file around the half-circle of benches, each Hon-do-i in turn rubbing ashes upon the head of each of the sick persons. The action consists in rubbing the hands quickly on the head, and then blowing upon it two or three times... a man led forth one of the devils to dance with the patient. The pair, having danced facing each other to the other end of the row of benches, resumed their seats... until each sick woman had danced with one of the devils.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 38-39; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 接著，首領站起來，向舞者們致辭，稱他們為 A-gwe-ge，意即「全體」。隨後他走向火爐，把菸草投入火中，並取下盛滿食物的鍋子，交給「首魔」，首魔接過鍋子便走了出去，其餘的人跟隨在後……此時，那些患病或身體不適的人，共約三十至四十名，便在這半圓形的長凳上坐下。眾魔用畢食物後，回到議事堂，除了一人之外……全都走向火爐，一邊發出「漢—漢，漢—漢」的哼哼唧唧與呻吟聲，一邊把手伸進爐床上的灰燼裡，然後排成單列，繞著那半圓形的長凳行進，每個 Hon-do-i 輪流把灰燼抹在每一位病人的頭上。這個動作是把雙手在頭上快速搓揉，然後朝頭上吹兩三口氣……一名男子領著其中一個魔鬼出來，與病人共舞。這一對面對面跳著舞，直到長凳行列的另一端，然後各自回到座位……直到每一位患病的婦女都與其中一個魔鬼跳過舞為止。

title.en: The Stone Giant of Cardiff and the Covered Pitfall
title.zh: 卡迪夫的石巨人與陷坑之計

region.en: Near Cardiff, a little south of the Onondaga reservation
region.zh: 奧農達加保留地以南的卡迪夫附近

period: Onondaga local tradition printed by Beauchamp 1922

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), 'Stonish Giants'

summary.en: The Onondagas have a local but different story. They say that a Stone Giant lived near Cardiff, a little south of their reservation. He was once like other men, but was a great eater, became a cannibal, and increased in size. His skin became hard and changed into scales, which alone would turn an arrow. Every day he came through the valley, caught and devoured an Onondaga, a fearful toll. The people were dismayed but formed a plan. They made a road in the marsh with a covered pitfall, decoyed the giant through the path and down he went and was killed. Of course when the Cardiff Giant was 'found' it did not astonish the Onondagas that he was of stone.
summary.zh: 奧農達加人另有一個本地故事：石巨人住在保留地以南不遠的卡迪夫附近。他本與常人無異，因為饕餮無度而食人，身軀日漸巨大；皮膚硬化成鱗，唯鱗甲能彈開箭矢。他每日穿谷而來，捉食一名奧農達加人，代價慘重。族人驚恐之餘定下計策：在沼澤中闢一條路，暗設覆草的陷坑，誘巨人循路而行——他一腳踏空，墜坑被誅。後來「卡迪夫石巨人」出土時，奧農達加人一點也不驚訝他竟是石頭做的。

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922; public domain. The famous 1869 Cardiff Giant hoax is here folded into Onondaga tradition.

passages.text: The Onondagas have a local but different story. They say that a Stone Giant lived near Cardiff, a little south of their reservation, which is by no means their early home. He was once like other men, but was a great eater, became a cannibal, and increased in size. His skin became hard and changed into scales, which alone would turn an arrow. Every day he came through the valley, caught and devoured an Onondaga, a fearful toll.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 40-41; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 奧農達加人則有一個地方性的、與眾不同的故事。他們說，有一位石巨人住在卡迪夫附近，也就是他們保留地以南不遠處，而那裡絕非他們早年的家園。他曾經和常人無異，但食量極大，後來成了食人者，身軀也日益壯大。他的皮膚變得堅硬，化為鱗片，單是這些鱗片就能擋開箭矢。他每天都穿過山谷，抓走並吞食一名奧農達加人，真是可怕的傷亡。

passages.text: The people were dismayed but formed a plan. They made a road in the marsh with a covered pitfall, decoyed the giant through the path and down he went and was killed. Of course when the Cardiff Giant was 'found' it did not astonish the Onondagas that he was of stone.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 41; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 族人驚恐萬分，但仍定下計策。他們在沼澤中開出一條路，並設下一個有遮蓋的陷阱，把巨人誘入那條路徑，他便掉了下去，被殺死了。當然，當卡迪夫巨人被「發現」時，奧農達加人並不驚訝他是石頭的。

title.en: The Stone Giant's Race at Green Pond and the Bone Pointer
title.zh: 綠池賽跑與骨指針

region.en: Green Pond hollow west of Jamesville, where the rocks rise 200 feet on three sides
region.zh: 詹姆斯維爾以西的綠池窪地，三面絕壁高二百呎

period: Onondaga local tradition (Beauchamp 1922); 'one of the oldest Stone Giant stories, closely resembling one told by David Cusick'

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), 'Stonish Giants' (the Jamesville race)

summary.en: The Onondagas have also a story of a Stone Giant's race with a man near Jamesville. He ran the man into the hollow at Green Pond, west of that village, where the rocks rise 200 feet above the water on three sides. On the south side the precipice can be ascended by a natural stairway at one spot, and the man was far enough ahead to reach the top before the other. He lay down and looked from the rocks to see what the other would do. The latter came and looked around. Not seeing the man he took out of his pouch what seemed a finger, but was really a pointer of bone. By means of this he could find any object he wished, and so it was always useful in hunting. As he climbed the rocks the man reached down and took away the pointer before the other saw him. The giant begged him to restore it: if he would do this he was promised good luck and long life for himself and friends. Though he begged so piteously the man ran home with it to show his friends, leaving him there helpless, unable to find his way. His friends interceded, telling him to accept the giant's good offer and not incur his enmity. So they went back and found him still at the lake. He received his pointer, promising to eat men no more, and good luck followed the man.
summary.zh: 奧農達加人還有一則石巨人與人在詹姆斯維爾附近賽跑的故事。巨人把那人追進村西的綠池窪地——三面絕壁高二百呎；南壁有一處天然石階，那人領先足以先登頂。他伏在岩上俯視對手的動靜。巨人尋人不見，便自囊中取出一物，看似手指，其實是骨製的指針：憑它可尋得任何物件，打獵時最是有用。他攀岩之際，那人俯身奪走指針。巨人苦苦哀求歸還：若肯還他，他允諾賜那人及其親友福壽綿長。那人不顧哀告，攜針跑回家向朋友誇示，把巨人丟在原地無路可尋。親友勸他莫結仇怨、領受巨人的好意；眾人折返，見巨人仍在湖邊。他交還指針，巨人允諾從此不再食人；福運自此伴隨那人。

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922; public domain. Same pointer motif as Cusick's Stonish Giant tale and Parker's Animated Finger.

passages.zh: 奧農達加人還有一個故事，說一位石巨人在詹姆斯維爾附近與一名男子賽跑。他把那男子一路追進該村以西綠塘的窪地，那裡三面岩石高出水面兩百英尺。南面有一處峭壁，可經由一道天然的階梯攀登而上，那男子領先得夠遠，得以在對方之前抵達頂端。他趴下身子，從岩石間窺看對方會怎麼做。那巨人來到，四下張望。他沒看見那男子，便從袋中取出一個看似手指、實則為骨製指針的東西。憑著這個指針，他能找到任何他想要的目標，因此在狩獵時總是派得上用場。

He received his pointer, promising to eat men no more, and good luck followed the man.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 41; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 當巨人攀爬岩石時，那男子伸手向下，趁對方還沒看見他，就把指針取走了。巨人苦苦哀求他歸還。若他肯歸還，便許諾他本人及其友人好運與長壽。儘管巨人哀求得很可憐，那男子還是帶著指針跑回家去向朋友們炫耀，把巨人留在那裡，無助地找不到路。他的朋友們從中調解，勸他接受巨人的善意條件，不要招來他的敵意。於是他們回去，發現巨人仍在湖邊。他取回了指針，並承諾不再吃人，而那男子此後便交了好運。

title.en: The Pigmy Feast and the Dance in Darkness
title.zh: 小人祭宴與黑暗中的舞蹈

region.en: Caves in rocky places of the Grand River country
region.zh: 格蘭德河之地岩穴中的小人族

period: Related by David Boyle (Grand River, Canada), printed by Beauchamp 1922

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), 'Indian Fairies' (Boyle's account of the pigmy dance)

summary.en: A race of small people is believed to inhabit caves in rocky places. These people did not appear till long after the creation of the Indians, and are quite different from them in disposition, as well as in size and appearance. Scarcely more than three feet high and of a pale yellow color, they dressed 'all over,' even in summer time, differing in this respect from the Indian. They are not credited with any mischievous tendencies, but were rather disposed to assist the hunter in pursuit of his game. To secure the good offices of the pigmies, however, it was necessary that a feast should be given in their honor: in the old days the custom was to kill the first deer for this purpose, and as the pigmies were particularly fond of corn soup, this dish formed a prominent feature of the feast. Thirty-six songs are peculiar to this ceremony, during the first part of which, these, with four exceptions, are sung in accompaniment to the women's dance, in perfect darkness. Wherever a pigmy feast is given, all these songs must be sung, one-half of them by the men and one-half by the women. No rattle is employed in these dances, but a drum in the hands of a man is constantly in use... At the conclusion of this second part the room is lighted and the remaining four songs are sung by the women, who dance by moving in a circle in the usual way, while the dance engaged in when the room was dark consisted of a slight alternate shuffle forwards and backwards. My informant gave it as his opinion that the portion of the ceremony performed in darkness referred to the doubt and difficulty connected with an unsuccessful hunt, while the lighting up symbolized the capture of game.
summary.zh: 相傳有一族小人居於岩穴之中。他們在印第安人受造之後很久方才出現，性情、身量、外貌皆與印第安人迥異：身高不足三呎、膚色淡黃，連盛夏也「全身」著衣。他們並無惡作劇之名，反而樂於助獵人追捕獵物。要得小人相助，須為他們設祭：古俗是射殺的第一頭鹿即為此用；小人最愛玉米湯，此菜為祭宴之主。這場儀式專有三十六首歌：前半段除四首外皆伴女子之舞於全黑之中唱出；凡舉小人祭，三十六歌必須全唱，男女各半；舞不用鈴，唯男子執鼓不輟。第二段結束時屋內點燈，餘下四首由女子唱出，她們如常繞圈起舞——黑暗中的舞步只是前後輕輕挪移。講述者以為：黑暗中行禮，喻獵之無獲與艱難；點燈之時，喻獵物到手。

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922 (Boyle); public domain. The Mohawks call the pigmies Yagodinenyoyaks, Stone Throwers.

passages.text: A race of small people is believed to inhabit caves in rocky places. These people did not appear till long after the creation of the Indians, and are quite different from them in disposition, as well as in size and appearance. Scarcely more than three feet high and of a pale yellow color, they dressed 'all over,' even in summer time, differing in this respect from the Indian. They are not credited with any mischievous tendencies, but were rather disposed to assist the hunter in pursuit of his game. To secure the good offices of the pigmies, however, it was, as a matter of course, necessary that a feast should be given in their honor. In the old days the custom was to kill the first deer for this purpose, and as the pigmies were particularly fond of corn soup, this dish formed a prominent feature of the feast.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 42; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 據信有一族矮小的人居住在多岩石之處的洞穴裡。這族人直到印第安人被創造之後很久才出現，他們的性情與印第安人截然不同，身材與外貌也大不相同。他們身高幾乎不超過三英尺，膚色淡黃，全身都穿著衣物，即使在夏天也是如此，這一點與印第安人不同。他們並不被認為有任何作惡的傾向，反而樂於協助獵人追捕獵物。然而，要獲得這些矮人的幫助，理所當然必須為他們舉辦一場盛宴。往昔的習俗是為此獵殺第一頭鹿，而由於矮人特別喜愛玉米濃湯，這道菜便成了宴席上的一大特色。

passages.text: Thirty-six songs are peculiar to this ceremony, during the first part of which, these, with four exceptions, are sung in accompaniment to the women's dance, in perfect darkness. Wherever a pigmy feast is given, all these songs must be sung, one-half of them by the men and one-half by the women. No rattle is employed in these dances, but a drum in the hands of a man is constantly in use. After the men have sung their sixteen songs, the women do their half of the singing, continuing to dance at the same time. At the conclusion of this second part the room is lighted and the remaining four songs are sung by the women, who dance by moving in a circle in the usual way, while the dance engaged in when the room was dark consisted of a slight alternate shuffle forwards and backwards, the dancers remaining in one place. The pigmy dance requires about an hour and a half, and is usually held in the house of the man or woman who gives the feast.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 42; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 有三十六首歌為此儀式所專有；在儀式的前半段，除四首之外，其餘各首皆在漆黑之中伴隨婦女之舞而唱。凡舉行矮人宴之處，這些歌都必須唱，其中一半由男子唱，一半由女子唱。這些舞蹈不用搖響器，但男子手中之鼓則不斷使用。男子唱完他們的十六首歌之後，便由女子唱她們的那一半，同時繼續跳舞。這第二部分結束時，室內點亮，其餘四首歌由女子唱，她們照常繞圈移動而舞；至於室內黑暗時所跳的舞，則是輕輕地前後交替拖步，舞者留在原地。矮人舞約需一個半小時，通常在那位設宴的男女家中舉行。

passages.text: My informant gave it as his opinion that the portion of the ceremony performed in darkness referred to the doubt and difficulty connected with an unsuccessful hunt, while the lighting up symbolized the capture of game. In accordance with the Mohawk myth, as held by some, the pigmies are fond of playing pranks by throwing stones, hence the name - Yagodinenyoyaks, Stone Throwers.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 42-43; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 我的報導人表示，他認為儀式中在黑暗裡進行的部分，指的是狩獵不順所帶來的疑慮與困難，而點亮則象徵獵獲獵物。依照某些人所持的莫霍克神話，矮人喜歡擲石惡作劇，因此得名——Yagodinenyoyaks，即「擲石者」。

title.en: The Little Old Woman and the Three Gifts
title.zh: 小老嫗與三件禮物

region.en: Between Mohawk and Palatine Bridge, Mohawk Valley
region.zh: 莫霍克與帕拉廷橋之間的莫霍克河谷

period: Told by Rev. Thomas La Fort, Onondaga Wesleyan minister, 1899 (Beauchamp 1922)

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), 'Indian Fairies' (La Fort's tale of the stone-throwers)

summary.en: By our forefathers it has been related that long, long ago, there lived between Mohawk and Palatine Bridge very little folks. They lived by themselves and were called 'stone-throwers.' I, Thomas La Fort, saw such a one about thirty years ago, when I was traveling on the road to Albany; he sat on top of a hill and looked down on the road. These little men could appear and disappear whenever they wished. About 200 years ago there was a poor man, running around hunting in the woods, but unable to kill a deer. So he was feeling very badly and very hungry, when suddenly he saw a very little old woman standing before him, who said she had been waiting for him and could make him very happy. She offered him three different things: (1) He could find precious gold; (2) He could find bright silver; (3) He could kill as many deer as he wished, having the power to call the animals to him. Then she told him he would enjoy the venison which he would find on the shelves of his wigwam. It happened as the little woman had said, he could shoot the deer without trouble, for they came to him when he called.
summary.zh: 祖先相傳：很久很久以前，莫霍克與帕拉廷橋之間住著一群小小的人。他們自成一部，人稱「擲石者」。我托馬斯拉福特約三十年前赴奧爾巴尼途中親見其一——他坐在山頂俯望大路。這些小人可隨意隱現。約二百年前，有個窮苦的獵人在林中奔走卻獵不到鹿，又餓又難過。忽然一位極矮小的老嫗立在他面前，說已等候多時，能叫他快活起來。她許他三樣東西任選：一、可以尋得貴重的黃金；二、可以尋得閃亮的白銀；三、可以隨心所欲地獵鹿——有呼獸即至的本領。她又說他將在自家棚架上看見掛好的鹿肉。果如小老嫗所言，他喚鹿鹿至，射之不費吹灰之力。

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922 (La Fort 1899); public domain.

passages.text: By our forefathers it has been related that long, long ago, there lived between Mohawk and Palatine Bridge, very little folks. They lived by themselves and were called 'stone-throwers.' I, Thomas La Fort, saw such a one about thirty years ago, when I was traveling on the road to Albany; he sat on top of a hill and looked down on the road. These little men could appear and disappear whenever they wished.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 43; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 據我們的祖先相傳，很久很久以前，在莫霍克與帕拉廷橋之間，住著一些非常矮小的人。他們獨自居住，被稱為「擲石者」。我，托馬斯·拉福特，大約三十年前在前往奧爾巴尼的路上旅行時，曾見過這樣一個；他坐在一座山丘頂上，俯視著道路。這些小人兒能隨心所欲地出現和消失。

passages.text: About 200 years ago there was a poor man, running around hunting in the woods, but unable to kill a deer. So he was feeling very badly and very hungry, when suddenly he saw a very little old woman standing before him, who said she had been waiting for him and could make him very happy. She offered him three different things: (1) He could find precious gold; (2) He could find bright silver; (3) He could kill as many deer as he wished, having the power to call the animals to him. Then she told him he would enjoy the venison which he would find on the shelves of his wigwam. It happened as the little woman had said, he could shoot the deer without trouble, for they came to him when he called.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 43; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 大約兩百年前，有一個窮人，在林中四處奔走打獵，卻獵不到鹿。因此他心情非常低落，也非常飢餓，忽然他看見一個非常矮小的老婦人站在他面前，她說她一直在等他，能使他非常快樂。她向他提出三樣不同的東西：(1) 他能找到珍貴的黃金；(2) 他能找到明亮的白銀；(3) 他能隨心所欲地獵殺鹿，並有呼喚動物前來的能力。接著她告訴他，他會享用他將在自己棚屋架上找到的鹿肉。事情正如那矮小婦人所說的那樣發生了，他能毫不費力地射鹿，因為他一呼喚，鹿就來到他面前。

title.en: The Bone Comb: Do Not Look Back
title.zh: 骨梳之戒：切莫回頭

region.en: The road where the little woman met the grandmother and child
region.zh: 小老嫗遇祖孫二人的大路

period: Told by Rev. Thomas La Fort (Beauchamp 1922)

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), 'Indian Fairies' (the bone comb tale)

summary.en: When I was a boy my grandmother told me that she had a grandchild who once was walking with her great grandmother on a road, the grandchild going ahead. Suddenly there appeared a strange-looking little woman, who spoke to her and said, 'You are feeling unhappy because you cannot walk as steadily as in your younger days, and yet you may become young again, providing you will do as I tell you. Tell your grandchild to walk straight ahead, and not to look back until I give her permission.' The grandmother did as she was bidden, and the little woman took a bone comb out of her pocket and said, 'Comb your hair with this as far as your hands can extend.' The old woman noticed that her hair was lengthening as far as she could reach, at the same time her skin changed color rapidly, when suddenly the grandchild looked back, and her grandmother, saying, 'My dear child you have destroyed me,' fell down dead.
summary.zh: 我幼時聽祖母講過：她的孫女曾與曾祖母同行，孫女在前。忽然一位模样奇異的小婦現身對老太太說：「你正為步履不再穩健而鬱鬱；但只要你照我說的做，便可重返青春。叫你的孫女一直朝前走，未經我允許不可回頭。」老太太依言行事；小婦自囊中取出一把骨梳：「用它梳頭，梳到你手能伸到之處。」老太太只覺秀髮隨梳而長，膚色瞬息轉變——孫女卻忽然回頭。老太太說聲「我的孩子，你害了我」，倒地而亡。

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922 (La Fort); public domain.

passages.text: The grandmother did as she was bidden, and the little woman took a bone comb out of her pocket and said, 'Comb your hair with this as far as your hands can extend.' The old woman noticed that her hair was lengthening as far as she could reach, at the same time her skin changed color rapidly, when suddenly the grandchild looked back, and her grandmother, saying, 'My dear child you have destroyed me,' fell down dead.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 44; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 祖母照著吩咐做了，那小婦人從口袋裡取出一把骨梳，說道：「用這把梳子梳你的頭髮，能梳多遠就梳多遠。」老婦人發覺她的頭髮隨著她所能觸及的範圍不斷變長，同時她的皮膚迅速變了顏色，忽然那孫女回頭看，她的祖母說了聲「我親愛的孩子，你把我毀了」，便倒地而死。

title.en: The Invisible Fingers and the Twelve Pairs of Moccasins
title.zh: 看不見的手與十二雙鹿皮鞋

region.en: Lone lodge where the sick youth lay while the village was sugar-making
region.zh: 村人熬糖時病童獨臥的孤屋

period: Told by Rev. Thomas La Fort not long before his death (Beauchamp 1922)

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), 'Indian Fairies' (La Fort's moccasin-maker tale)

summary.en: While all the Onondagas were once off sugar-making, a young man remained at home alone because he was ill. While lying on his couch he felt fingers stroking his forehead. Then they patted his shoulders, but no one was seen. Then they came down his arm, and a small arm appeared, but no body. He seized the arm with all his might, but could not hold it, and received a blow upon his head. Then all was still. His mother came home and he told her all this. 'O, my son,' said she, 'You have done very wrong. You have driven away your best friend, but I will try to make amends. To-night I will take a good deer's hide and cut it in pieces for twelve pairs of moccasins. This I will put in a convenient place, and lay with it beads, thread and colored moose hair.' This she did. At midnight the young man heard a noise and felt the fingers, as before, but kept still. Then the fingers went away and he heard a sound where the deer-skin lay. In the morning all was gone. The next night came and nothing was heard, but in the morning there stood a pair of moccasins, beautiful beyond anything Onondaga had ever seen. The sick youth was soon well.
summary.zh: 奧農達加人傾村熬糖之時，一個生病的青年獨自留守家中。他臥在榻上，覺得有手指撫弄他的額頭；接著拍他的肩，卻不見人影；又順著他的手臂而下，現出一條小臂，卻沒有身子。他用力去抓，卻抓不住，反捱了一記腦門。此後一片寂靜。母親回來聽了原委：「兒啊，你錯了。你把最好的朋友趕走了；讓我設法補救。今夜我取一張好鹿皮，裁成十二雙鞋料，連同珠子、線和染色駝鹿毛一併放在方便之處。」她如言備齊。半夜青年又聞響動、覺得手指拂來，這回他屏息不動；手指離去，鹿皮處沙沙作響。清晨皮料盡失。次日夜裡無聲無息，晨起卻立著一雙鹿皮鞋——精美絕倫，奧農達加前所未見。病青年的病也很快好了。

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922 (La Fort); public domain. Such things, La Fort said, used to be frequent in the old times; since Christianity prevailed they had disappeared.

passages.text: While all the Onondagas were once off sugar-making, a young man remained at home alone because he was ill. While lying on his couch he felt fingers stroking his forehead. Then they patted his shoulders, but no one was seen. Then they came down his arm, and a small arm appeared, but no body. He seized the arm with all his might, but could not hold it, and received a blow upon his head. Then all was still.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 44; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 有一次，當所有的奧農達加人都外出熬製糖漿時，一個年輕人因為生病而獨自留在家中。他躺在臥榻上時，感覺有手指撫摸他的額頭。接著那些手指又拍了拍他的肩膀，卻不見任何人影。然後它們沿著他的手臂而下，一條細小的手臂顯現出來，卻沒有身體。他用盡全力抓住那條手臂，卻抓不住，頭上還挨了一擊。隨後一切歸於寂靜。

passages.text: His mother came home and he told her all this. 'O, my son,' said she, 'You have done very wrong. You have driven away your best friend, but I will try to make amends. To-night I will take a good deer's hide and cut it in pieces for twelve pairs of moccasins. This I will put in a convenient place, and lay with it beads, thread and colored moose hair.' This she did. At midnight the young man heard a noise and felt the fingers, as before, but kept still. Then the fingers went away and he heard a sound where the deer-skin lay. In the morning all was gone. The next night came and nothing was heard, but in the morning there stood a pair of moccasins, beautiful beyond anything Onondaga had ever seen. The sick youth was soon well.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 44; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
passages.zh: 他的母親回到家，他把這一切都告訴了她。「噢，我的兒子，」她說，「你做了一件大錯事。你把你最好的朋友趕走了，不過我會設法補救。今晚我要拿一張上好的鹿皮，把它裁成片，做十二雙莫卡辛鞋。我會把這些放在一個方便取用的地方，並在旁邊擺上珠子、線和彩色的駝鹿毛。」她便照此做了。午夜時分，年輕人聽見一陣聲響，又感覺到那些手指，一如先前，但他保持不動。接著那些手指離去，他聽見鹿皮所在之處傳來聲響。到了早晨，一切都不見了。第二夜來臨，什麼也沒聽見，但到了早晨，那裡擺著一雙莫卡辛鞋，其精美遠超奧農達加人所曾見過的任何事物。那生病的年輕人不久便痊癒了。

title.en: The First Stage: Asfandiyar and the Two Wolves
title.zh: 阿斯凡迪亞爾七關之一：雙狼

region.en: Road to the Brazen Hold (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 通往銅堡之路（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. V, Seven Stages sec. 2

summary.en: Gurgsar warns: two wolves, each like a lusty elephant, a male and female, having horns like stags and all a-gog to make a fight of lions, broad in the neck and breast and thin of flank, with monstrous elephants' tusks, first will confront thee. The prince commits the host to Bishutan and rides to the First Stage; the wolves beheld his breast and neck and his iron mace, and like grim elephants made at him; the hero strung his bow, roaring like a rending lion, and rained arrows down upon those Ahrimans; the steel-tipped shafts disabled both the beasts, and he unsheathed his watered glaive, charged, and hacked their heads, and made the dust mire with their blood.
summary.zh: 古爾格薩爾示警：「首關有雙狼——雄雌各一，大如壯象，鹿角獠牙，獅膽豹心！」王子把大軍託付比舒坦，獨騎赴關；雙狼見其胸膛與鐵錘，如巨象般撲來；英雄獅吼彎弓，箭如暴雨，鋼鏃俱中；他拔出大馬士革利劍衝鋒，斬下狼首，鮮血染塵如泥。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the Seven Stages (Haft Khan) of Asfandiyar. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Two wolves, each like a lusty elephant, a male and female, having horns like stags and all a-gog to make a fight of lions, broad in the neck and breast and thin of flank, with monstrous elephants' tusks, first will confront thee, said Gurgsar. Asfandiyar bade lead back Gurgsar bound as he was in miserable plight, and blithe himself assumed his Kaian casque.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古爾格薩爾說道：兩隻狼，每一隻都像一頭強壯的大象，一公一母，長著雄鹿般的角，蠢蠢欲動要與獅子搏鬥，頸與胸寬闊而脅腹瘦削，生著巨象般的獠牙，牠們會先來迎擊你。阿斯凡迪亞爾吩咐把仍身處悲慘境地的古爾格薩爾綁著帶回去，自己則欣然戴上他的凱揚頭盔。

passages.text: The chief, when he had drawn anigh the wolves, sat firmly like a mighty elephant. The wolves beheld his breast and neck, his waist, his warrior-handgrip, and his iron mace, and like grim elephants and keen for fight made at him from the plain. The hero strung his bow and, roaring like a rending lion, rained arrows down upon those Ahrimans.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那首領逼近群狼時，如一頭雄偉的大象般穩穩坐定。群狼見了他的胸膛與頸項、他的腰身、他那戰士般的握持，以及他的鐵錘，便如猙獰的大象般、渴求一戰地從平原上向他撲來。那英雄張弓上弦，如撕裂的獅子般咆哮，向那些阿赫里曼傾瀉箭雨。

passages.text: The steel-tipped shafts disabled both the beasts, and neither could approach unscathed. With joy Asfandiyar perceived them growing weak and sore distressed, unsheathed his watered glaive, and charged. He hacked their heads and made the dust mire with their blood, lit from his noble steed, acknowledging his helplessness to God, and washed the wolves' gore from his arms and person, then sought a spot that had not been defiled upon the sand and, turning toward the sun, exclaimed: O righteous Judge! Thou hast bestowed upon me strength, Grace, process.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 鋼尖的箭矢使兩頭野獸都失去戰力，誰也無法毫髮無傷地靠近。阿斯凡迪亞爾欣喜地察覺牠們漸趨衰弱、痛苦不堪，便拔出他那水紋寶劍，發起衝鋒。他砍擊牠們的頭顱，使塵土被牠們的血染成泥濘，從他那高貴的駿馬上躍下，向上帝承認自己的無力，洗去手臂與身上狼的血污，隨後在沙地上尋了一處未被玷污的地方，轉向太陽，高聲說道：噢，公正的審判者！你已賜予我力量、恩典、進境。

title.en: The Second Stage: The Lion and the Lioness
title.zh: 七關之二：獅與牝獅

region.en: Second Stage of the road (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 七關第二段（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. V, Seven Stages sec. 3

summary.en: Upon the next stage lions will assail thee, such as no crocodile would dare encounter; the lusty eagle, valiant though it be, will fly not in their path. There were a lion and a lioness, and bravely both came forth to fight with him, the lion first: he smote it with his sword; its face grew coral-hued; 'twas cloven from head to midriff, which appalled the lioness, yet, like her mate, she came on savagely. The chieftain smote her on the head, which fell and rolled upon the sand; her paws and breast were tulip-hued with blood. He bathed himself and, looking to all-holy God alone as his Protector, said: O righteous Judge! Thou hast destroyed these creatures by my hand.
summary.zh: 第二關有雙獅——「鱷魚不敢近其身、雄鷹不敢掠其頂」！雄獅先撲；他一劍從頭劈至胸膈，獅面如珊瑚綻裂；牝獅不懼，仍凶猛撲上，一錘擊碎其首，頭顱滾落沙中，爪胸染血如鬱金香。英雄沐浴淨身，獨向聖神祝禱：「公義的審判者啊，是祢借我的手誅了這對猛獸！」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Upon the next stage lions will assail thee, such as no crocodile would dare encounter; the lusty eagle, valiant though it be, will fly not in their path, said Gurgsar. Tomorrow thou shalt see a valiant man address the lion with the scimitar, answered Asfandiyar.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古爾格薩爾說道：到了下一關，獅子會來攻擊你，那是連鱷魚也不敢與之相遇的獅子；那強壯的雄鷹雖勇猛，也不會飛到牠們的路上。阿斯凡迪亞爾答道：明日你將看見一位勇武之人手持彎刀迎向那獅子。

passages.text: There were a lion and a lioness, and bravely both came forth to fight with him, the lion first. He smote it with his sword; its face grew coral-hued; 'twas cloven from head to midriff, which appalled the lioness, yet, like her mate, she came on savagely. The chieftain smote her on the head, which fell and rolled upon the sand; her paws and breast were tulip-hued with blood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一隻雄獅與一隻母獅，兩者都勇猛地前來與他搏鬥，雄獅先行。他以劍擊之；其面遂成珊瑚之色；自頭至腹被劈為兩半，母獅見之驚駭，卻仍如牠的伴侶一般兇猛地撲上前來。那位首領一擊正中其頭，頭顱落地，滾於沙上；牠的爪與胸皆染血而成鬱金香之色。

passages.text: He bathed himself and, looking to all-holy God alone as his Protector, said: O righteous Judge! Thou hast destroyed these creatures by my hand. Meanwhile the troops came up, and Bishutan surveyed the lions' breasts and limbs while all acclaimed Asfandiyar.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他沐浴淨身，唯以全聖之神為其庇護者，說道：啊，公正的裁判者！你已藉我之手毀滅了這些生靈。其時大軍趕到，比舒坦察看獅子的胸與四肢，眾人皆為阿斯凡迪亞爾歡呼。

title.en: The Fourth Stage: The Witch of the Water-side
title.zh: 七關之四：水畔妖巫

region.en: Fourth Stage of the road (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 七關第四段（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. V, Seven Stages sec. 5

summary.en: When thou alightest tomorrow at the stage a witch will come to greet thee; she hath looked on many a host, but quailed at none: she turneth waste to sea at will and maketh sunset at mid-day; men call her Ghul. Asfandiyar takes goblet and lute to battle, dight as for a feast, and sings by the fountain's marge; the witch, foul, wrinkled, and malevolent, plies her magic arts amid the gloom and grows beauteous as a Turkman maid, and draws anear with roses in her breast. He possesses a goodly chain of steel which Zarduhst brought down from Paradise for Shah Gushtasp: he flings it around her neck, her strength is gone, she takes a lion's form; within the chain there was a fetid hag, calamitous, and with trenchant sword he smote her on the head.
summary.zh: 第四關的妖巫「古爾」能令沃土化海、白日作暮。王子偏攜酒盃與琵琶赴險，泉邊自歌自飲；巫嫗施法變作麗姝，捧花而至。他早藏著扎爾杜什特自天堂攜來的聖鐵鏈——一鏈套頸，妖力頓消、現出獅形；鏈中蜷伏的仍是那個滿頭白髮、黑面可憎的醜嫗。他揮劍斬其首級，日月為之晦暗。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; pairs with Rustam's witch (persian-rustam-course-witch). No living community restriction.

passages.text: When thou alightest tomorrow at the stage a witch will come to greet thee; she hath looked on many a host, but quailed at none: she turneth waste to sea at will and maketh sunset at mid-day. Men call her Ghul, O Shah! Face not her toil in these thy days of youth. The atheling replied: tomorrow, knave! thou shalt recount my prowess, for I will break the warlocks' backs and hearts, so will I maul that witch.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 5 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 明日你抵達那驛站時，將有一女巫前來迎你；她曾見過許多軍旅，卻不曾對任何一支退縮：她能隨意將荒野化為大海，令正午變成日落。人們稱她為食屍鬼，啊，沙阿！在你這青春年華，切勿直面她的凶險。那位王子答道：明日，你這惡徒！你將述說我的英勇，因為我要打斷那些巫師的脊背與心膽，我也要如此撕碎那女巫。

passages.text: Foul, wrinkled, and malevolent she plied her magic arts amid the gloom and grew as beauteous as a Turkman maid, with cheek as 'twere brocade of Chin and musk-perfumed, of cypress-height, a sun to look upon; her cheeks like rosaries, she drew anear Asfandiyar, with roses in her breast.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 5 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她醜陋、滿面皺紋、心懷惡意，在幽暗中施展魔法，繼而變得如突厥少女般美貌，面頰宛如中國錦緞，散發麝香之氣，身如柏樹之高，望之如日；她的面頰如念珠，她走近阿斯凡迪亞爾，胸中藏著玫瑰。

passages.text: Now he possessed a goodly chain of steel which he had kept concealed from her. Zarduhst, who brought it down from Paradise for Shah Gushtasp, had bound it about the prince's arm. Asfandiyar flung it around her neck; her strength was gone; she took a lion's form. Within the chain there was a fetid hag, calamitous, with head and hair like snow, and black of face; with trenchant sword he smote her on the head, which with her body came down to the dust; sight failed, so loured the sky when that witch died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 5 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此時他有一條精良的鋼鏈，一直對她隱藏不露。扎爾杜什特曾為沙阿古什塔斯普自天堂將它帶下，並將它纏繞於王子臂上。阿斯凡迪亞爾將它擲套於她的頸上；她的力量盡失；她化為獅形。鏈中乃是一醜惡的老嫗，災禍之源，頭與髮白如雪，面黑如墨；他以利劍擊其頭，頭與身一同落於塵土；目光失明，當那女巫死去時，天色亦如此陰沉。

title.en: The Sixth Stage: Snow, a Spear's Length Deep
title.zh: 七關之六：深可及矛之雪

region.en: Sixth Stage of the road (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 七關第六段（象徵性定位）

period: Composed c. 1010 CE (Warner translation 1905)

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. V, Seven Stages sec. 7

summary.en: Thou wilt take no thought of mace or bow or sword, and see no opening for fight, no way of flight, for snow, a spear's length deep, will come upon thee, warns Gurgsar. With that there came a fierce blast from the mountains: all the world became like ravens' plumes, and none knew plain from upland; from that dark cloud descended showers of snow; the earth was filled with snow and raging blast, and o'er the desert for three days and nights the fury of the wind was measureless. The tents were soaked through, and not a man could stand or stir for cold; the chief, resourceless, called to Bishutan: make supplication, all of you, to God — and thereon a gentle breeze arose which bare the clouds away and heaven became serene.
summary.zh: 第六關的試煉不是刀兵，而是天災：「雪深及矛、大軍將沒！」和暖春日裡，山間驟起狂飆——天地如烏鴉之羽、不辨丘壑，黑雲瀉雪三日三夜；帳幕浸透、士卒僵立難動。王子束手，命比舒坦率全軍向神祈禱；忽有和風驅散愁雲、天色復明——「真主之門已為我們敞開！」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Thou wilt take no thought of mace or bow or sword, and see no opening for fight, no way of flight, for snow, a spear's length deep, will come upon thee, said Gurgsar; a crisis will confront thee, thou with all thy famous army wilt be lost therein.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 7 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 古爾格薩爾說道：你將無暇顧及狼牙棒、弓或劍，也看不到任何可戰之機、可逃之路，因為深達一矛之長的雪將降臨於你；一場危機將臨到你面前，你與你那赫赫有名的全軍都將在其中覆沒。

passages.text: With that there came a fierce blast from the mountains, and sore dismayed him. All the world became like ravens' plumes, and none knew plain from upland. From that dark cloud descended showers of snow; the earth was filled with snow and raging blast, and o'er the desert for three days and nights the fury of the wind was measureless. The tents and tent-enclosure were soaked through, and not a man could stand or stir for cold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 7 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隨著這一陣猛烈的狂風自山間襲來，令他驚恐萬分。整個世界變得如同烏鴉的羽毛般漆黑，無人能分辨平地與高地。從那片黑雲中降下陣陣大雪；大地被積雪與狂暴的風所覆蓋，沙漠之上，狂風的怒號連續三晝夜無休無止。帳篷與營帳圍欄盡皆濕透，無人能因寒冷而站立或動彈。
