When Tugto's wandering wife, herself a greater wizard than her husband, was asked to magic away the blocking ice, she called a bear and a walrus as helping spirits, was carried out over the floes in their jaws, fought and groomed an old woman of the undersea, and returned with scratched cheeks; only when her sores healed did the wind loose the ice, and no one might hunt until five days had passed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Qujavarssuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在一個饑荒的時節，來訪者聽說了庫亞瓦蘇克（Qujavarssuk），便來到他的土地上。來人中有兩位老巫師，是他母親的親族，他們被以漁獲中最好的部分款待——但其中一人因被告知他開始從海豹錯誤的一側吃起而動怒，唯恐獵人的運氣就此斷絕。那位憤怒的親族在歸途上滿載禮物，決心造一個圖皮拉克（Tupilak）來吃掉庫亞瓦蘇克。圖格托（Tugto）那四處遊蕩的妻子，本身是比丈夫更強大的巫師，當她被請來以法術驅走阻擋的冰時，她召來一頭熊和一隻海象作為助靈，被牠們的顎骨帶著作越過浮冰，與海底的一位老婦搏鬥並為她梳理，歸來時雙頰被抓傷；直到她的傷口癒合，風才鬆開了冰，而在五天過去之前無人得以狩獵。

passages.text: The Tupilak paddled after Qujavarssuk, but each time he stepped into his kayak he vanished from its sight, and each evening he came home with two seals. Starving, it went on land — and struck its head on ground that had become a sheer cliff with Qujavarssuk standing plain on top; a great stone broke its rib; a black bird bit a hole above its flipper. Turning in fury on the man who had made it, the Tupilak coloured the water red with his blood — then, ashamed that all other Tupilaks would call it shameful to kill one's maker, it swam far out into the open sea and was never seen again. Qujavarssuk later moved to Amerdloq, out-hunted its champion, harpooned a whale that came in toward his house as he said the beasts he struck always did, and at last went home south and died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Qujavarssuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 圖皮拉克划槳追趕庫亞瓦蘇克，但每當他踏進皮划艇，它便從其視野中消失，而每個傍晚他都帶著兩隻海豹回家。圖皮拉克饑餓難耐，便上了陸地——卻把頭撞在已變成陡峭懸崖的地面上，而庫亞瓦蘇克就清清楚楚地站在崖頂；一塊巨石砸斷了它的肋骨；一隻黑鳥在牠的鰭肢上方啄出一個洞。圖皮拉克滿懷怒火轉向造出它的那人，用他的血把海水染紅——隨後，因羞愧於所有其他圖皮拉克都會斥其殺死造物主為可恥，它游向遠方的大海，從此再未被見到。庫亞瓦蘇克後來遷往阿梅德洛克（Amerdloq），狩獵勝過那裡的冠軍，用魚叉刺中一頭朝他屋前游來的鯨，正如他所說他擊中的野獸總是如此，最後回到南方家鄉死去。

title.en: Kunigseq's Flight Down to the Underworld
title.zh: 庫尼格塞克下行冥界記

region.en: Godthaab (Nuuk), West Greenland
region.zh: 西格陵蘭努克

period: Inuit oral tradition (Godthaab, West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Kunigseq', eBook #28932

summary.en: The wizard Kunigseq flies through the floor down to the underworld, where the dead live in a land of sun and smooth seas. His dead mother and brother welcome him but warn him against eating, lest he never return; he promises to send them ice for their thirst and comes back to earth. When his son then dies, Kunigseq eats guillemot and raven — the eaten spirit-food of farewell — and rows out to sea to die.
summary.zh: 巫師庫尼格塞克穿地飛降冥界，死者居於有太陽平海之鄉。亡母亡弟相迎，卻誡其勿食，否則不得歸返；他允諾送冰解冥界之渴，重返人間。其子病亡後，庫尼格塞克先後吞食海鳩與渡鴉——死亡之食——遂乘皮艇出海而逝。

sensitivity.note: Godthaab district angakok (shaman) spirit-flight narrative recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. The angakok seance is described as historical practice; presented as archival record.

passages.text: Kunigseq the wizard prepared a descent to the underworld: the floor was swilled with salt water to drive away the smell that might frighten his helping spirits. Calling them, he passed downward through the floor without moving his body. On the way a weed-covered reef was too slippery to pass until his helping spirit lay down beside it and he walked over on the spirit's back. Far down, the land is level, the hills are small, and there is sun and a sky like that on earth. He heard a cry: 'Here comes Kunigseq,' and saw children fishing for greyfish by a little river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kunigseq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巫師庫尼格塞克（Kunigseq）準備下往冥界：地板用鹽水沖洗，以驅散可能驚嚇其助靈的氣味。他召喚助靈，身體不動便穿過地板向下而去。途中有一處覆滿海草的礁石滑得無法通過，直到他的助靈在旁伏下，他踩著助靈的背走了過去。在深處，土地平坦，山丘低矮，有太陽，也有如同地上一般的天空。他聽見一聲呼喊：「庫尼格塞克來了」，並看見孩子們在一條小河邊釣灰魚。

passages.text: Before reaching the houses he met his dead mother, who had gone out gathering berries; she tried again and again to kiss him, but his helping spirit thrust her aside — 'He is only here on a visit.' When she offered berries the spirit warned him: 'If you eat of them, you will never return.' He caught sight of his dead brother; his mother urged him to stay — look at the great stores of dried meat, the smooth sea, no snow, a beautiful open sea where two kayaks rowed and laughed, darting birds. 'I will come again when I die,' said Kunigseq. On a little island lay the drying kayaks of men who had just lost their lives at sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kunigseq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在到達那些房屋之前，他遇見了已故的母親，她外出採集漿果去了；她一次又一次想親吻他，但他的助靈把她推開——「他只是來此造訪。」當她遞上漿果時，助靈警告他：「你若吃了這些，就永遠回不去了。」他瞥見了已故的兄弟；母親勸他留下——看看那堆積如山的乾肉、平靜的海面、沒有雪、一片美麗的開闊海面，兩隻皮划艇划著、笑著，鳥兒疾飛。「等我死後我會再來，」庫尼格塞克說。一座小島上晾著那些剛在海上喪命之人的皮划艇。

passages.text: The people of the underworld asked that when he returned to earth he send them ice, 'for we thirst for cold water down here.' Back on earth, his son soon fell sick and died; Kunigseq no longer cared to live, having seen what the underworld was like. He caught a guillemot, then a raven, ate them one after the other, and died — and they threw his body out into the sea. The tale encodes the angakok seance in which the shaman visits the land of the dead and returns as messenger for his people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kunigseq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 冥界的子民請求他回到地上後給他們送去冰，「因為我們在下面渴望冷水。」回到地上後，他的兒子不久便病倒死去；庫尼格塞克見識了冥界的模樣，便不再想活下去。他捉了一隻海鳩，又捉了一隻渡鴉，一隻接一隻吃下，然後死去——他們把他的屍體拋入海中。這個故事編碼了巫師降神會，其中薩滿造訪亡者之地，並作為其子民的使者歸來。

title.en: The Woman Who Had a Bear as a Foster-Son
title.zh: 養熊為子的老嫗

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The woman who had a bear as a foster-son', eBook #28932

summary.en: An old woman thaws a frozen bear cub and raises it on blubber, teaching it human speech and hunting manners; with a plaited-sinew collar as its mark, it becomes an unbeatable seal-hunter that men can recognize and spare. After it hauls home the corpse of the one man who would not spare it, the foster-mother sends her bear away to its own kin, and far north, when bears are abroad, an iceberg-sized bear with a black smudged spot on its side is still seen.
summary.zh: 老嫗將凍僵的熊崽置於晾架解凍，以脂油哺育，教以人言與獵禮；頸繫筋辮項圈為記，成為無人能勝的海豹獵手，見圈者皆放行。熊拖回不肯留情者之屍後，養母泣遣其返北地親族。自今北境熊群出沒時，猶有巨如冰山、脅染黑漬之熊現身。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo (Inughuit) tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Includes killing of a reckless outsider hunter as told in the source; presented as archival narrative.

passages.text: An old woman lived nearest the shore and was fed by the hunters above. They brought home a whole bear, and its killer's wife asked through the window whether she would like the cub. She warmed the frozen cub on the drying frame, fed it on greaves and melted blubber, and it lay beside her at night and grew fast. Talking to it in human speech, she gave it a human mind: when it wanted food it sniffed. The children played with it — 'Little bear, remember to sheathe your claws' — until it grew stronger than grown men and the hunters took it out to find seal, telling it to keep down wind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The woman who had a bear as a foster-son'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位老婦人住在最靠近海岸的地方，由上方的人們供養。他們帶回一整頭熊，殺熊者的妻子隔著窗問她是否想要那隻幼崽。她在晾曬架上把凍僵的幼崽暖過來，用油脂渣和融化的鯨脂餵牠，牠夜裡躺在她身旁，長得很快。她用人類的語言對牠說話，賦予牠人的心智：當牠想吃東西時便嗅一嗅。孩子們與牠玩耍——「小熊，記得把爪子收起來」——直到牠長得比成年男子還強壯，獵人們便帶牠出去尋找海豹，囑咐牠要待在下風處。

passages.text: Hunters from the north nearly killed the bear; its rescuers begged the old woman to give it a mark by which it might be known, and she made it a collar of plaited sinews as broad as a harpoon line. Thenceforth it never failed to catch seal, stronger than the strongest hunter and never staying home even in the worst weather, though never bigger than an ordinary bear. All the villages knew the collar, and though hunters sometimes came close, they let it go on sight. When men from beyond Angmagssalik vowed to kill the uncatchable bear, the elders forbade it: the foster-mother could ill manage without its help.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The woman who had a bear as a foster-son'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 北方的獵人幾乎殺死了那頭熊；牠的救命恩人懇求老婦人給牠一個可供辨認的記號，她便用搓編的筋腱為牠做了一條項圈，寬如一條魚叉繩。自此以後，牠捕海豹從不失手，比最強壯的獵人還要強健，即使天氣最惡劣也從不待在家裡，然而牠從不比一頭尋常的熊更大。所有村落都認得那條項圈，儘管獵人有時會靠近，卻一見牠便放牠走。當安馬格薩利克以外的人發誓要殺死那頭無法捕獲的熊時，長老們禁止了此事：那養母若無牠的幫助，實在難以度日。

passages.text: One stormy evening the bear came home and sprang to its bench, and the old woman found outside the body of a dead man it had hauled home — the man from the north, who had run so fast he had thrown off his furs; his comrades, said the report, had urged the bear to resist him, because he would not leave it alone. Long after, the old foster-mother told the bear it must leave her, or it would be killed, and wept as she said it; the bear pressed its muzzle to the floor and wept too. One morning with no cloud as big as a hand in the sky, she smeared oil and soot on her hands and stroked its side unseen. It sniffed at her and went. Far to the north, when many bears are abroad, there sometimes comes a bear as big as an iceberg, with a black spot on its side.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The woman who had a bear as a foster-son'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個風暴的傍晚，那頭熊回到家，躍上牠的長凳，老婦人在外頭發現了一個被牠拖回家的死人——那是來自北方的男子，他跑得太快，連毛皮衣物都甩脫了；據說他的同伴曾慫恿那頭熊抵抗他，因為他不肯放過牠。很久以後，那年老的養母告訴那頭熊，牠必須離開她，否則會被殺死，說時不禁哭泣；那頭熊把口鼻貼在地上，也哭了。一天早晨，天上連一片巴掌大的雲也沒有，她將油和煤煙抹在手上，趁人不見時撫摸牠的側腹。牠嗅了嗅她，便走了。在遙遠的北方，當許多熊出沒時，有時會來一頭大如冰山的熊，側腹上帶著一塊黑斑。

title.en: Imarasugssuaq, Who Ate His Wives
title.zh: 食妻者伊馬拉舒亞克

region.en: South-East Greenland (Ammassalik district)
region.zh: 東南格陵蘭（阿馬薩利克一帶）

period: Inuit oral tradition (South-East Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Imarasugssuaq, who ate his wives', eBook #28932

summary.en: The fattener-of-wives Imarasugssuaq feeds each bride nothing but salmon and no water, until she is too heavy to flee and he kills and eats her. His newest wife, Misana, sister of many brothers, licks drifted snow to thin herself, stuffs her clothes into a dummy that shrieks when harpooned, and escapes through a hole behind the house; changing herself into a piece of wood by amulet, she evades his knife and reaches her brothers, who hold him fast so she may kill him.
summary.zh: 食妻者伊馬拉舒亞克每娶新婦，僅以鮭肉飼之，滴水不予，待其肥重難逃，便殺而食之。新妻米薩納——眾兄弟之妹——趁夫外出舐雪瘦身，以衣絮充假人騙其魚叉，又唸護身符化為木塊避刃，逃歸兄弟之家。眾人縛住那食妻者，讓她親手復仇。

sensitivity.note: South-East Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Domestic-violence and cannibalism motifs presented as told in the archival source.

passages.text: The great Imarasugssuaq was wont to eat his wives. He fattened them, giving them nothing but salmon to eat and nothing at all to drink. Once when he had lost a wife in the usual way, he took Misana, the sister of many brothers, and began fattening her as usual. One day, grown so fat she could hardly move, she managed to tumble down from the bench, crawl to the entrance, and lick the snow that had drifted in; licking and licking, she felt herself lighter. Whenever her husband was out in his kayak she licked up snow, until she could once more move about freely.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Imarasugssuaq, who ate his wives'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 偉大的伊馬拉蘇格蘇阿克慣於吃掉自己的妻子。他把她們養肥，只給她們吃鮭魚，什麼也不給她們喝。有一次，他以慣常的方式失去了一個妻子之後，便娶了米薩娜——有許多兄弟的姊妹——並照例開始把她養肥。有一天，她胖得幾乎動彈不得，卻設法從長凳上滾下來，爬到門口，舔食飄進來的雪；舔著舔著，她覺得自己輕了些。每當丈夫划著皮艇外出，她就舔雪，直到她又能自由行動。

passages.text: One day she stuffed out her breeches and tunic until they looked like a real human being behind the lamp, and instructed the dummy: when my husband comes and tells you to come out, answer 'I cannot move because I am grown so fat'; and when he comes in and harpoons you, shriek as if in pain. She dug a hole at the back of the house and crept in. The husband returned, harpooned the dummy wife with his great bird-spear, heard it shriek and fall — but found no blood, only stuffed-out clothes. Searching, he chased the fleeing woman; seeing him closing, she said 'Now I remember, my amulet is a piece of wood,' and changed into wood at once. He stabbed the piece once or twice; she felt only a stinging pain. When he left to fetch his axe, she changed back and fled to her brothers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Imarasugssuaq, who ate his wives'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，她把褲子和上衣塞得鼓鼓的，使那東西在燈後看起來像個真人，並吩咐那假人：我丈夫回來叫你出來時，你就回答「我胖得動不了了」；當他進來用魚叉刺你時，你就裝作痛苦地尖叫。她在屋後挖了一個洞，鑽了進去。丈夫回來，用他那支捕鳥的大矛刺向假妻子，聽見它尖叫倒地——卻找不到血，只有塞得鼓鼓的衣物。他四處搜尋，追趕那逃跑的女人；眼看他要追上，她說「我現在想起來了，我的護符是一塊木頭」，隨即變成了一塊木頭。他朝那木頭刺了一兩下；她只感到一陣刺痛的疼。當他離開去取斧頭時，她變回原形，逃到她的兄弟們那裡。

passages.text: Hiding behind the skin hangings at her brothers' house, she heard her husband approach, weeping over his lost wife. In the evening the many brothers sang mockery at him — 'Men say that Imarasugssuaq eats his wives' — and she answered from behind the hangings: 'I said it, and I ran away because you tried to kill me.' The brothers fell upon him and held him fast so that his wife might kill him. She took her knife, but each time she tried to strike it only grazed his skin, for her fingers lost their power. While she stood there trying in vain to stab him, they saw that he was already dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Imarasugssuaq, who ate his wives'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她躲在兄弟家的皮簾後面，聽見丈夫走近，為失去的妻子哭泣。傍晚，那許多兄弟唱著嘲弄他的歌——「人們說伊馬拉蘇格蘇阿克吃自己的妻子」——她從簾後答道：「是我說的，我逃走是因為你想殺我。」兄弟們撲向他，把他牢牢按住，好讓他的妻子殺他。她拿起刀，但每次她想刺下去，刀只擦過他的皮，因為她的手指失去了力氣。當她站在那裡徒勞地想刺他時，他們看出他早已死了。

title.en: Qalaganguase, Who Passed to the Land of Ghosts
title.zh: 入幽靈之地的卡拉康瓦塞

region.en: South-East Greenland (Ammassalik district)
region.zh: 東南格陵蘭（阿馬薩利克一帶）

period: Inuit oral tradition (South-East Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Qalaganguase, who passed to the land of Ghosts', eBook #28932

summary.en: Lame and orphaned, Qalaganguase is left behind when the village goes hunting — and the ghosts come in to play: wrestling, telling stories, drinking from the water tub, even his dead sister among them. Promised his strength again if he tells no tales, he blurts out the visit to the returning hunters and the strength drains away. At last his dead parents lead him out of the house to the land of ghosts, and he passes over, becoming (so it is said) a woman among the dead.
summary.zh: 跛足孤兒卡拉康瓦塞被村人棄於屋中——幽靈成群而入，角力講古、舀水而飲，亡姊亦在其中。幽靈允諾守秘者可復得氣力；他向歸獵者吐實，氣力隨之流逝。最後亡父亡母引他出屋，渡往幽靈之地；據云他化為女子，村人自此不復見之。

sensitivity.note: South-East Greenland ghost-land narrative recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Gender transformation of the dead presented as told in the source.

passages.text: Qalaganguase's parents ate seaweed and died of it; then his one sister died, and only strangers looked after the boy, whose lower body was dead so that he could not walk. Left alone while the village hunted, he heard a sound and dragged himself, in great pain, into the next house to hide behind the skin hangings. In walked a ghost — 'Ai! There are people here!' It drank from the water tub, emptying the dipper twice, thanked the thirsty one for the drink as it used to drink when it lived on earth, and went out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Qalaganguase, who passed to the land of Ghosts'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡拉甘瓜塞的父母吃了海藻，因此而死；接著他唯一的姊妹也死了，只有陌生人照料這男孩，他的下半身已死，無法行走。村裡人外出打獵時，他獨自被留下，聽見一個聲響，便忍著劇痛拖著身子爬進隔壁的屋子，躲在皮簾後面。一個鬼走了進來——「哎！這裡有人！」它從水桶裡喝水，把水瓢喝空了兩次，像它生前喝水時那樣，向那口渴的人道謝賜飲，然後走了出去。

passages.text: Another day, left alone again, he heard the walls and frame of the house shake, and a crowd of ghosts came tumbling in, one after the other — the last one his sister, dead but a little time before. The ghosts sat on the floor and played: they wrestled, told stories, laughed all night. At first afraid, Qalaganguase found the company pleasant. When the hunters were heard returning, the ghosts hastened away: 'Now mind you do not tell tales; if you do as we say, you will gain strength again, and there will be nothing you cannot do.' His sister could hardly slip out because her brother's touch stayed her — the hunters could just see a pair of vanishing feet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Qalaganguase, who passed to the land of Ghosts'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 又一天，他再次獨自被留下，聽見屋子的牆壁與樑架震動，一群鬼魂接連翻滾而入——最後一個是他的妹妹，死去才不久。鬼魂們坐在地上嬉戲：他們角力、說故事、整夜歡笑。起初害怕的卡拉克安瓜塞，發覺有這群伴兒倒挺愉快。當聽見獵人歸來的聲音，鬼魂們急忙離去：「現在切記，你萬萬不可說出去；你若照我們說的做，就會重新獲得力氣，屆時沒有什麼是你做不到的。」他的妹妹幾乎脫不了身，因為哥哥的觸碰留住了她——獵人們只瞥見一雙正在消逝的腳。

passages.text: 'The house has been full of people, and they made the night pass pleasantly for me,' said Qalaganguase, already feeling his strength return — but hardly had he spoken when the strength slowly left him. The villagers tied the lame boy to a frame post and let him swing, trying to beat the drum, and then went off to a singing contest, leaving him behind. There his dead mother and father came in and asked why he was alone. 'I am lame,' he said, 'and they left me behind.' 'Come away with us.' 'It is better so, perhaps,' said the boy, and they bore him to the land of ghosts. It is said he became a woman when they changed him to a ghost, and his fellow-villagers never saw him again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Qalaganguase, who passed to the land of Ghosts'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「屋裡滿是人，他們讓我的夜晚過得愉快，」卡拉克安瓜塞說道，已感覺力氣正在回復——但話剛出口，力氣便緩緩離他而去。村人把這跛腳的男孩綁在樑柱上，讓他懸盪，試著敲鼓，隨後便去參加歌唱比賽，把他留在後頭。就在那裡，他死去的母親與父親進來，問他為何獨自一人。「我是跛腳的，」他說，「他們把我留下了。」「跟我們走吧。」「或許這樣也好，」男孩說道，他們便將他帶往鬼魂之地。據說當他們把他變成鬼魂時，他成了女人，而他的村人此後再沒見過他。

title.en: Isigaligarssik and the Wizard Who Took His Wife
title.zh: 伊西加利加舒克與奪妻之巫

region.en: South-East Greenland (Ammassalik district)
region.zh: 東南格陵蘭（阿馬薩利克一帶）

period: Inuit oral tradition (South-East Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Isigaligarssik', eBook #28932

summary.en: The wifeless strongman Isigaligarssik weds the widow's daughter during a spirit-calling, but the jealous wizard banishes the marriage by the ritual of drying her shoes on the frame. When Isigaligarssik finally answers the taunt 'what of you who took my wife away?', the wizard stabs him; the wound heals the moment his childhood dress, dipped in water, touches it. In the bow-duel he shrinks himself to a nodding head, breaks the wizard's arrows, and kills him as he creeps into his passage way.
summary.zh: 無妻壯漢伊西加利加舒克在降靈夜娶得寡婦之女，妒巫卻以晾鞋之術斷其姻緣。他終於回罵『你奪我妻又如何』，巫師以刀重創其身；小時舊衣浸水觸傷即癒。弓箭決鬥中，他縮得只剩點動的頭顱，折斷巫箭，待其彎身入甬道時一箭射殺，奪回妻子。

sensitivity.note: South-East Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Spirit-calling seance described as historical community practice.

passages.text: Isigaligarssik, a wifeless man and very strong, was taken to live with a house of brothers who were fond of him. The village wizard's custom at spirit-callings was to call through the window, 'Only the married men may come and hear,' so the little widow, her daughter, and Isigaligarssik always stayed behind. One evening the daughter whispered to her mother, who said: 'This little girl would like to have you.' Before the others returned they were man and wife. Next evening the rule reversed: 'Let only those who have wives come and hear' — and the great wizard, calling Isigaligarssik's wife to him, took off her shoes and hung them on the drying frame, a rite of banishment. After the calling he told Isigaligarssik: 'Go away now; you will never have this dear little wife of yours again.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Isigaligarssik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊西加利加爾西克是個沒有妻子卻非常強壯的男人，被帶去與一戶喜愛他的兄弟同住。村裡的巫師在召靈時的慣例是隔著窗戶喊道：「只有已婚的男子可以來聽，」因此那小寡婦、她的女兒和伊西加利加爾西克總是留在後頭。一天傍晚，女兒向母親低語，母親便說：「這小姑娘想要你。」還沒等其他人回來，他們已成夫妻。翌日傍晚，規矩反了過來：「只讓有妻子的人來聽」——那大巫師把伊西加利加爾西克的妻子喚到跟前，脫下她的鞋子掛在晾曬架上，這是放逐的儀式。召靈之後，他對伊西加利加爾西克說：「現在走吧；你再也得不到你這親愛的小妻子了。」

passages.text: Every spirit-calling the wizard mocked him: 'Ho, what are you doing here, you who have no wife?' Anger grew slowly, and the village warned him — 'if you answer him, he will kill you.' One evening he answered: 'Ho, and what of you who took my wife away?' The wizard stood up at once, and as Isigaligarssik bent to creep out of the entrance, stabbed him with a great wound. Run home, he bade his wife's mother fetch from the chest the dress he wore when little, so small it hardly looked like a dress, and dip it in the water bucket; wet, it stretched enough to put on, and when the lacing thong at its hem touched the wound, it healed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Isigaligarssik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 每次召靈，巫師都嘲弄他：「嘿，你在這裡做什麼，你這沒有妻子的人？」怒氣慢慢積聚，村人警告他——「你若回他嘴，他會殺了你。」一天傍晚，他回嘴道：「嘿，那你這奪走我妻子的人又怎麼說？」巫師立刻站起，正當伊西加利加爾西克彎身要從入口爬出去時，狠狠刺了他一道大傷口。他奔回家，吩咐妻子的母親從箱子裡取出他小時候穿的衣服，那衣服小得幾乎不像件衣裳，把它浸入水桶；濕了之後，它便撐大到足以穿上，而當衣襬的繫帶觸及傷口時，傷便癒合了。

passages.text: His house-fellows, following the blood spoor after the calling, found him inside without a single wound and rejoiced. Next day he took from his chest a bow so small it could hardly be seen in his hands, challenged the wizard to a shooting match by the little river, and when the man aimed at him he made himself so small that only his head could be seen nodding. Twice the wizard shot and missed; Isigaligarssik stood, broke the arrow across, and said: 'Go home; you cannot hit.' And when the wizard, glancing back many times, bent to his passage way, Isigaligarssik aimed and shot — the little arrow doubled him up through the entrance, and he fell dead in the passage. So Isigaligarssik won his wife again and lived with her until death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Isigaligarssik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的同屋人循著召靈後的血跡跟來，發現他在屋內毫髮無傷，欣喜不已。翌日，他從箱子裡取出一把弓，小得在手中幾乎看不見，向巫師挑戰到小河邊比射箭；當那人瞄準他時，他把自己縮得極小，只看得見他的頭在點動。巫師射了兩次都沒中；伊西加利加爾西克站起，把箭折成兩段，說道：「回家去吧；你射不中的。」而當巫師頻頻回頭張望、彎身要鑽進他的通道時，伊西加利加爾西克瞄準射去——那支小箭穿過入口把他射得蜷成一團，他倒在通道裡死了。於是伊西加利加爾西克重新贏回妻子，與她同住直到死去。

title.en: The Insects That Wooed a Wifeless Man
title.zh: 向無妻者求愛的蟲群

region.en: South-East Greenland (Ammassalik district)
region.zh: 東南格陵蘭（阿馬薩利克一帶）

period: Inuit oral tradition (South-East Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The Insects that wooed a wifeless man', eBook #28932

summary.en: A chronically sleepy wifeless man saves a capsized kayaker — one of the Noseless Ones from beneath the earth — who grants him a single seal each dawn and forbids him ever to tell. Prosperity brings him a wife, but her questioning breaks the taboo; his luck dies, she leaves him through a rock crevice, and blowfly, fly, cranefly, centipede, and gnat each crawl out to woo him in turn. Reclaiming her, he is put under a sleeping spell and wakes to a summer-aged world: his kayak rotted through, years gone by.
summary.zh: 貪睡的無妻男子救起翻艇呼救者——地底無鼻族人——後者許其一晨一豹，且誡之不可外泄。富足為他娶得嬌妻，然而妻子追問破禁忌，獵運即盡；妻子自石隙離去，蒼蠅、大蚊、蜈蚣、蚊子逐一出洞求偶。他重新娶妻，卻陷入沉睡咒術，醒來時夏色滿地、皮艇朽爛，多年已逝。

sensitivity.note: South-East Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. The Noseless Ones are an otherworld people of Greenlandic oral cosmology.

passages.text: There was once a wifeless man — so every story begins — who was too sleepy to hunt, waking only at sunset when the kayakers came home with their catch. Rowing out one evening anyway, he heard a man crying that his kayak had upset, righted him, and saw he was one of the Noseless Ones, the people from beneath the earth. Refusing the reward of ornamented hide thongs — 'the only thing I cannot overcome is my miserable sleepiness' — he was led to land by the Fire Man, who announced him as the saviour of his life and laid down the terms: one beast and one only may you choose on your homeward way; be careful never to tell what you have seen, or it will go ill with your hunting hereafter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Insects that wooed a wifeless man'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有個沒有妻子的男人——每個故事都這樣開頭——他太貪睡而無法打獵，只在日落時分、划皮艇的人帶著漁獲歸來時才醒。某天傍晚他還是划了出去，聽見有人喊叫說自己的皮艇翻了，便幫他扶正，發現他是「無鼻者」之一，即來自地下的人。他拒絕了以飾紋皮革繩索為報酬——「我唯一克服不了的，就是我那可悲的貪睡」——火人領他上岸，宣告他是自己性命的救命恩人，並立下條件：歸途上你只可挑選一頭野獸，僅此一頭；千萬小心，絕不可說出你所見之事，否則你日後的狩獵將大為不利。

passages.text: Thenceforth the wifeless man went out before sunrise and came home with three seals while his fellows were still preparing to launch. The young girls who had once run from him now vied for his favour, laughing, and he chose the best of the flock. But his wife wearied of the endless cutting-up of seals and kept asking why he caught such a terrible lot. 'The seals come of themselves, and I catch them — that is all,' he said, until at last he told her everything: the capsized kayaker, the Noseless One, the gift. From that time forward he lost his power of hunting; the old sleepiness came over him, and he lost all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Insects that wooed a wifeless man'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從那以後，這無妻之人在日出前便出門，當同伴們還在準備下水時，他已帶著三隻海豹回家。那些曾從他身邊逃開的年輕姑娘如今爭相討他歡心，笑語盈盈，他便從這群姑娘中挑了最好的。但他的妻子卻厭倦了無休無止地剖切海豹，不斷追問他為何捕到這麼多可怕的海豹。「海豹自個兒來的，我把它們捉住——如此而已，」他說，直到最後他把一切都告訴了她：那翻覆皮艇的人、那無鼻者、那饋贈。從那時起，他便失去了狩獵的本領；昔日的睏倦又襲上他身，他失去了一切。

passages.text: Without even skins enough for her clothes, his wife ran away through a crevice in the rocks he could scarcely pass, and lay in wait inside. Out crawled a blowfly — 'Take me' — but he refused her: 'You pick your food from the muck-heaps.' Then a fly ('You lay your eggs about anyhow, and your eyes are quite abominably big'), a cranefly ('Your legs are too long'), a centipede ('Far too many legs... your eyes are simply nasty'), and a gnat ('No thanks, you bite') — each laughed and went back inside with the report. At last his wife bade him in, since he would have none of the others; he squeezed through the crack, took her to wife again, and asked her to comb his hair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Insects that wooed a wifeless man'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的妻子連做衣裳的皮子都不夠，便從一道他幾乎擠不過去的岩縫中逃走，在裡面潛伏等候。一隻綠頭蒼蠅爬了出來——「娶我吧」——但他拒絕了她：「你從糞堆裡揀食吃。」接著是一隻蒼蠅（「你隨處亂下卵，眼睛又大得著實可惡」）、一隻大蚊（「你的腿太長了」）、一隻蜈蚣（「腿多得不得了……你的眼睛簡直噁心」），還有一隻蚊蚋（「多謝了，你會咬人」）——每一個都笑著回到裡面，帶回了回話。最後，既然他誰都不要，他的妻子便喚他進去；他擠過那道裂縫，重新娶她為妻，並請她為他梳理頭髮。

passages.text: Combing, she sang over him: 'Do not wake until the fulmar begins to cry; sleep until we hear a sound of young birds.' He fell asleep — it was winter when he crawled in through the crack — and when he awoke the earth was blue with summer and the fulmar cried noisily on the bird cliff. His kayak down on the shore was rotted through with age. And he reached home, the teller says, and now sits scratching himself at ease. The tale folds the spirit-gift, the broken secrecy taboo, and the stolen time of the sleeping enchantment into one comic warning about a wifeless man and the wives of the insect world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Insects that wooed a wifeless man'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 梳理時，她在他頭頂唱道：「莫醒來，直到暴風鸌開始啼叫；睡吧，直到我們聽見雛鳥的聲響。」他沉沉睡去——他爬過裂縫進來時還是冬天——待他醒來，大地已是一片夏日的青藍，暴風鸌在鳥崖上喧鬧地啼叫。他擱在岸邊的皮艇已因年歲而朽爛透穿。講述者說，他回到了家，如今正悠閒地撓著癢。這則故事將神靈的饋贈、被打破的守秘禁忌，以及沉睡魔法所竊走的時光，編織成一則關於無妻之人與昆蟲世界諸妻的滑稽警示。

title.en: The Very Obstinate Man Who Drove to the Moon
title.zh: 倔強人駕犬行月記

region.en: South-East Greenland (Ammassalik district)
region.zh: 東南格陵蘭（阿馬薩利克一帶）

period: Inuit oral tradition (South-East Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The very obstinate man', eBook #28932

summary.en: No one could be as obstinate as the Obstinate Man, who forces his mourning wife to sew his kayak cover — and the sewing raises a sea-monster dog, whose owner is the Moon Man. Wrestling the Moon Man nearly dead, he releases him only at the threat 'there will never be dawn or daylight again,' then follows the Moon Man's dog-team through the naked air. Warned to pass the great rock by its shady side, he goes by the sunny side and a knife-whetting old woman tears out his heart; retrieved and restored at the Moon, he watches his wife's evil thoughts rise as smoke, harpoons forbidden walrus from the sky, and comes home cured of his obstinacy.
summary.zh: 倔強無人能敵的男子強迫服喪中的妻子縫皮艇，縫線之聲竟喚出海中犬形怪物；其主乃月人。他扼喉幾乎勒死月人，直至對方喊出『再無黎明白晝』才罷手。他隨月人犬隊驅入長空，卻違囑繞行大石向陽一面，被磨刀老嫗挖去心臟；月人為其復心，又教他俯瞰人間——妻子惡念化煙——禁不住誘惑而叉獵天池海象。歸來後，他終於不再倔強。

sensitivity.note: South-East Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Moon Man (tarraq) as sky regulator of tides and daylight is standard Greenlandic cosmology.

passages.text: There was once an Obstinate Man — no one in the world could be as obstinate as he, and no one dared come near him. When his wife lost her little child and sat idle at home in mourning, as the custom of the time required, he ordered her to sew the skin of his kayak down on the shore. Sewing, her thread began to make a sound, the sound a muttering, the muttering louder — and a monster in the shape of a dog rose out of the sea: 'Why are you sewing, you who are still in mourning?' The mighty dog sprang ashore upon the husband, but the Obstinate One would get his own way and killed the dog in the fight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The very obstinate man'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個固執之人——世上再沒有誰能像他那樣固執，也沒有人敢靠近他。他的妻子失去了年幼的孩子，依照當時的習俗，在家閒坐守喪，他卻吩咐她到岸邊去縫補他皮艇的皮子。縫著縫著，她的線開始發出聲響，那聲響化作喃喃低語，低語又愈發響亮——一頭狗形的怪物從海中升起：「你還在守喪，為何縫補？」那巨犬躍上岸撲向丈夫，但固執之人偏要遂自己的意，在搏鬥中殺死了那狗。

passages.text: The dog's owner appeared — the Moon Man — and the Obstinate One fell upon him in turn, catching him by the throat, clenching until the Moon Man was nearly strangled. 'There will be no more ebb-tide or flood if you strangle me,' he cried; the Obstinate One clutched tighter. 'The seal will never breed again if you strangle me.' Tighter still. 'There will never be dawn or daylight again if you kill me' — at that the Obstinate One hesitated, for he did not like the thought of living in the dark forever, and let him go. The Moon Man called his dog to life, cast his team one by one up into the air until the whole sledge team hovered there, cracked his whip, and drove off through the naked air — but he invited the Obstinate One to visit him in the Moon, warning him: when you see a great rock in your way, drive round behind it; do not pass it on the sunny side, for your heart will be torn out of you.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The very obstinate man'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 狗的主人出現了——月人——固執之人又撲向他，扼住他的喉嚨，越扼越緊，直扼得月人幾乎窒息。「你若扼死我，便再也不會有退潮和漲潮了，」他喊道；固執之人扼得更緊。「你若扼死我，海豹便再也不會繁衍了。」扼得更緊。「你若殺了我，便再也不會有黎明和日光」——聽到這話，固執之人猶豫了，因為他不願永遠生活在黑暗之中，便放開了手。月人喚活了他的狗，把他的雪橇隊一隻一隻拋向空中，直到整隊雪橇犬都懸浮在那裡，他甩響鞭子，驅車穿過赤裸的虛空而去——但他邀請固執之人到月亮上拜訪他，並警告他：當你見到一塊擋路的巨石時，要繞到它後面去；不要從向陽的一側經過，否則你的心會被掏出來。

passages.text: The Obstinate One washed his dirt-caked dogs in the sea and cast them into the air until they stayed aloft, made a sledge, and drove off. At the rock he said to himself, 'Why should I drive round a rock at all? I will go by the sunny side.' Up alongside he heard a woman singing drum songs and whetting her knife, the steel humming; he tried to overpower the old woman and lost his senses, and when he came to himself, his heart was gone. Going round by the shady side, he came to the moon and told how he had lost it; the Moon Man laid him on his back on a black sealskin and stuffed the heart in again. From a lifted stone he looked down on the earth and saw his wife on the bench plaiting sinew before her mourning was passed, thick smoke — the smoke of her evil thoughts — rising from her body, and grew angry, forgetting that he himself had bidden her work.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The very obstinate man'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 固執之人把他滿身泥垢的狗在海裡洗淨，拋向空中，直到它們懸停不落，又造了一架雪橇，驅車而去。到了那塊岩石前，他自言自語道：「我憑什麼要繞著岩石走？我要從向陽的一側過去。」他沿著岩石上行，聽見一個女人唱著鼓歌，磨著她的刀，鋼刃嗡嗡作響；他試圖制服那老婦，卻失去了知覺，待他回過神來，他的心已不見了。他繞到背陰的一側，來到月亮上，訴說自己如何失去了心；月人讓他仰面躺在一張黑海豹皮上，又把心塞了回去。他從一塊舉起的石頭上俯瞰大地，看見他的妻子在守喪期未滿之前便坐在長凳上編搓筋線，濃煙——她那邪念的煙——從她身上升起，他不禁動怒，忘了正是他自己吩咐她幹活的。

passages.text: Later the Moon Man opened a stone in the entrance and let him look down on a place full of walrus, lying one on top of another — 'It is a joy to catch such beasts.' Forbidden to harpoon, promised only a share of the Moon Man's own catch, the Obstinate One would not be content: he took harpoons from the store and, being a man of very great strength, killed one walrus on the line and then another. After his return from the Moon Man's place he left off being obstinate, and never again forced his wife to work while she was in mourning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The very obstinate man'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 後來，月亮人打開入口處的一塊石頭，讓他俯視一個滿是海象的地方，那些海象一隻疊著一隻躺著——「能捕到這樣的野獸真是樂事。」他被禁止用魚叉，只被許諾分得月亮人自己捕獲的一份，但那個固執的人卻不肯滿足：他從儲藏處取出魚叉，憑著極大的力氣，用繩索先殺了一隻海象，接著又殺了一隻。從月亮人的地方回來之後，他就不再固執了，也再不曾強迫妻子在服喪期間勞作。

title.en: The Dwarfs of the Deep Fjord
title.zh: 深峽灣中的矮人族

region.en: South-East Greenland (Ammassalik district)
region.zh: 東南格陵蘭（阿馬薩利克一帶）

period: Inuit oral tradition (South-East Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The Dwarfs', eBook #28932

summary.en: A kayaker befriends a timid dwarf, carries up a seal with one hand to the amazement of the little folk, and wins the dwarf's mighty daughter in marriage. When the mixed family returns to the world of real people, a great black-and-white-faced dog devours the dwarf child in the passage; the terrified little folk flee from village to village, the old man hauling his tent-skins ashore to ask 'Are there any dogs here?' until the skin is worn from his forehead — and he calms a storm with a magic song about crested clouds in the clearing east.
summary.zh: 皮艇客結識羞怯的矮人，單手提豹上岸令小族驚為巨人，娶得矮人力大無窮的女兒。混居人間後，一隻黑白天面的大狗在甬道中吞食矮人幼兒；小族驚懼四逃，老翁每到一村便背著帳皮登岸問『此地有狗否？』，額頭皮膚為之磨穿——他更以一段『東天霽雲』的咒歌使怒海復平。狗吠聲起，他又倉皇登舟，飄然不知所終。

sensitivity.note: South-East Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. The storyteller performs the dwarf's part in a hurried jerky manner, per the source's note — performance convention documented here as context.

passages.text: A man out in his kayak rowed up to another kayak far off and found the paddler a very little man, a dwarf, plainly troubled and afraid. The dwarf said he was hunting a little fjord seal he could not hit; the stranger took his throw and struck it between the shoulder-blades — 'Ai, ai, what a throw!' cried the dwarf in astonishment. Rowing in company, the little one mumbled out his story in jerks: he had a daughter, very beautiful, whom many men wanted and could not take by force because she was too strong — even for her own father. 'Might perhaps do for you... you could manage her... what?' 'Let us first see her,' said the man, and they rowed into a great deep fjord.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Dwarfs'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個男人划著皮划艇出海，划近遠處另一艘皮划艇，發現那划槳的人是個非常矮小的男子，一個侏儒，顯然心煩意亂、滿懷恐懼。那侏儒說他正在追獵一隻他打不中的小峽灣海豹；那陌生人替他擲出魚叉，正中它的兩肩之間——「哎，哎，好一擲！」侏儒驚愕地喊道。兩人結伴划行，那小個子斷斷續續地咕噥著說出自己的遭遇：他有個女兒，非常美麗，許多男人都想要她，卻無法強奪，因為她太強壯了——甚至連她自己的父親也敵不過。「也許她還配得上你……你能制得住她……怎麼樣？」「讓我們先見見她吧，」那男人說，於是他們划進了一道又大又深的峽灣。

passages.text: In the house of the little old man the guest's catch was cut up with heroic labour — the two women and the old man together could not drag the little seal up from the shore until the stranger carried it by one flipper; to the dwarfs, cutting it up was like cutting up a huge walrus, and each guest received a breastbone so large it reached to the ground. An old hag made herself agreeable and was frightened off with a loud whistle. Up in the other house the guest munched dried foxes' liver as if it were fresh meat while the dwarfs worked and could not cut it through. But the old man's daughter was the most beautiful, and he said he would have her to wife, and they lived happily and soon had a child.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Dwarfs'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在那矮小老人的屋裡，客人的獵物被以極大的力氣切開——那兩個女人和老人合力也無法把小海豹從岸邊拖上來，直到那陌生人抓住一隻鰭足把它提了起來；對這些侏儒來說，切開它就像切開一頭巨大的海象，每位客人都分到一塊大得垂到地面的胸骨。一個老巫婆上前來討好，卻被一聲響亮的哨音嚇跑了。在另一座屋裡，客人嚼著乾狐狸肝，彷彿那是鮮肉，而侏儒們忙著幹活，卻怎麼也切不開它。但老人的女兒是最美的，他說他要娶她為妻，他們幸福地生活在一起，不久便有了一個孩子。

passages.text: When the man longed for his own kin, the whole dwarf family went with him to visit the world of real people, who were astonished to find their old comrade alive. The dwarf folk forgot to be afraid among the real men — until the little dwarf grandmother, sitting at the passage opening with the child, dropped it, and a great dog with a black face on one side and white on the other lay in the passage and ate it up on the spot. 'Nothing is left but a little smear on the ground,' she cried. The horror-stricken dwarf folk gathered their belongings and set out, and at every village the old man went ashore with his tent-skins on his back, asking first thing, 'Are there any dogs here? Is there a great beast with a black-and-white face?' — and at every yes he was back in his boat before anyone could turn round, until the skin was worn quite away from his forehead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Dwarfs'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當那男人思念自己的親族時，整個侏儒家族便隨他一同去探訪真人們的世界，那些人驚訝地發現他們的老夥伴還活著。侏儒們在真人中間忘了害怕——直到那矮小的侏儒祖母坐在通道口抱著孩子時失手把孩子掉了下去，一隻一邊黑臉一邊白臉的大狗躺在通道裡，當場把它吃掉了。「地上只剩下一點點印漬了，」她哭喊道。驚恐萬狀的侏儒們收拾起自己的東西便動身了，每到一個村子，那老人就背著帳篷皮上岸，頭一件事便問：「這裡有狗嗎？有一隻黑白臉的大野獸嗎？」——而每一次得到肯定的回答，他都在任何人來得及轉身之前就回到了船上，直到他額頭上的皮都磨得精光。

passages.text: One day, lying-to as a north wind began to blow, the old man groaned and asked his question — but heard the barking of the dogs themselves, and fled to his boat. The seas frothed white; then the old dwarf stood up in his boat and cried: 'The sky is clearing to the east with crested clouds.' It was a magic song: the sea was calm and bright at once, so great was the power of his words. But for all that he had no peace, by reason of the dogs, and went on his way again — and whither he came at last, the teller does not know.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Dwarfs'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，北風開始吹起，他們頂風停泊著，那老人呻吟著問出他的問題——卻聽見了狗自己的吠叫聲，便逃回他的船上。海面泛起白沫；接著那老侏儒在船上站起身來喊道：「東方的天空正隨著峰狀雲放晴。」那是一首有魔力的歌：海面立刻平靜而明亮，他言語的力量竟如此之大。然而儘管如此，因為那些狗，他仍不得安寧，於是又繼續上路——至於他最後到了何處，講述者並不知道。

title.en: The Boy from the Bottom of the Sea
title.zh: 海底之童

region.en: South-East Greenland (Ammassalik district)
region.zh: 東南格陵蘭（阿馬薩利克一帶）

period: Inuit oral tradition (South-East Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The Boy from the Bottom of the Sea', eBook #28932

summary.en: A beaten, pregnant wife walks straight out into the sea and survives, building a house on the bottom; there she bears a son with jellyfish eyes, seaweed hair, and a mussel for a mouth. Grown strong from lifting stones, the boy visits the world above with his mother — who warns him to look as angry as he can — and one thrust of his monstrous head at a doorway frightens every person inside to death, a vengeance on the household where his mother once fled her husband's beatings.
summary.zh: 受虐孕婦徑直走入海中不死，於海底築屋安身；所生之子，眼為水母、髮為海藻、口如蚌殼。少年力大，能舉箱大之石。母子重返人間，母親囑其入屋時要裝出最怒的面容；他把怪頭一伸門口，屋內之人全數嚇死——那正是母親昔日逃家避打的人家。

sensitivity.note: South-East Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Domestic-violence frame presented as told in the archival source.

passages.text: It was the usual thing: the Obstinate One had taken a wife and beat her, and when he wanted to make it an extra special beating he took a box and banged her about with that. One day, nearly at her time, she ran away and walked straight out into the sea; nearly drowned, she came to herself at the bottom of the sea, and there built herself a house. While she was down there the child was born — so ugly she nearly died of fright: its eyes were jellyfish, its hair seaweed, its mouth like a mussel. And these two lived down there together.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Boy from the Bottom of the Sea'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 事情一如既往：那個固執的人娶了妻子又打她，而當他想把這頓打變得格外特別時，他就拿來一個箱子，用那箱子把她打得東倒西歪。有一天，她臨產在即，卻逃了出去，徑直走進海裡；她幾乎淹死，卻在海底甦醒過來，並在那裡為自己蓋了一座房子。她在那下面時，孩子出生了——醜得她幾乎嚇死：眼睛像水母，頭髮像海草，嘴巴像貽貝。於是這兩個便一同住在那下面。

passages.text: The boy grew up able to hear the children playing on the earth above, and said he would like to go up and see. 'When you have grown stronger, then you may go,' said his mother, and he practised with stones until he could pick up stones as big as a chest and carry them into the house. One dark evening, when the children above cried out 'Iyoi-iyoi-iyoi' with all their might, she agreed to go with him — but he must not enter the houses nearest the shore, for there she had often fled in when his father would have beaten her, and there she had suffered much evil. 'When you thrust in your head, be sure to look as angry as you can.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Boy from the Bottom of the Sea'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 男孩長大後，能聽見上方陸地上的孩子們嬉戲的聲音，便說他想上去看看。「等你長得更強壯些，就可以上去，」他母親說。於是他用石頭練習，直到能撿起像箱子那麼大的石頭，並把它們搬進屋裡。一個昏暗的傍晚，上方的孩子們用盡全力喊著「伊喲伊—伊喲伊—伊喲伊」，她便同意與他同去——但他不可進入最靠近海岸的那些屋子，因為從前他父親要打她時，她常逃進那裡，也在那裡受過許多苦。「你探頭進去時，務必裝出盡可能憤怒的樣子。」

passages.text: Two houses stood on the shore, one a little way above the other. When the mother saw her son heading for the lower one — the very house where she had always run from her husband's fists — she cried out to him to go to the one above. The boy made his face fierce and thrust his head in at the doorway, and all those inside fell down dead with fright. He would have beaten his father, but his father had died long since. Then he went down again to the bottom of the sea. When day dawned, the people of the lower house came out and marvelled at footprints all full of seaweed; following them to the upper house, they found that all inside had died of fright.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Boy from the Bottom of the Sea'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 岸上立著兩座屋子，一座比另一座稍高一些。母親見兒子朝較低的那座走去——那正是她一向為躲避丈夫拳頭而奔逃的屋子——便大聲喊他，叫他去上面那座。男孩板起凶狠的面孔，把頭探進門口，裡面所有人全都嚇得倒地而死。他本想揍他父親，但他父親早已死去多年。隨後他又下到海底。天亮時，較低那座屋子的人們走了出來，驚異地看著滿是海草的腳印；他們循著腳印走到上面那座屋子，發現裡面的人全都嚇死了。

title.en: Makite and the Lone-Dweller's Candles
title.zh: 馬基特與獨居者的蠟燭

region.en: West Greenland coast
region.zh: 西格陵蘭沿岸

period: Inuit oral tradition (West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Makite', eBook #28932

summary.en: A unsuccessful hunter abandons his seal-rich in-laws to live alone in the hills, sleeps in a lone-dweller's house hung with reindeer and fox skins, and learns by threat where the candle-like treasures grow — on the farther of two blue hills in the south. Surviving his host's midnight bow, he kills the pursuer with a backward-thrust harpoon, witnesses the dwarfs' wave-war with the inland-dwellers, and returns home to hang the candle-things from the high hill in his own house.
summary.zh: 獵運不濟的馬基特拋下多豹的妻族，獨自入山居住。他借宿獨居者之屋——牆掛馴鹿狐皮，屋內有如蠟燭之物——逼問得其所來：在南天兩座藍山中較遠的山頂。夜半避過主人的弓，又反手一叉殺了追兵；其後目擊矮人與內陸人鬥水成浪之戰，歸家後取回山頂蠟燭之物，懸掛屋中直至終老。

sensitivity.note: West Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s; lone-dweller (tornit/inlander) narratives are a major cycle of Greenlandic oral literature.

passages.text: Makite took to wife the sister of many brothers, but he never managed to catch a seal in his kayak while his wife's brothers caught them in great numbers. Hearing that his wife would leave him because he never caught anything, he resolved in his grief to go up into the hills and live there all alone. When darkness fell he set off; his wife's father saw him go and cried to the house, 'Go after him' — but Makite made his steps longer and longer until the brothers gave up the pursuit. At dawn he came to a house with hangings of nothing but reindeer and foxes' skins, and went in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Makite'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬基特娶了有許多兄弟的女子為妻，但他始終沒能在皮划艇裡捕到一隻海豹，而他妻子的兄弟們卻捕到許多。他聽說妻子因為他什麼也捕不到而要離開他，便在悲痛中決意上山，獨自住在那裡。天黑時他動身出發；他妻子的父親見他離去，便朝屋裡喊道：「去追他」——但馬基特把步子邁得越來越大，直到那些兄弟放棄了追趕。黎明時他來到一座屋子，屋裡掛的全是馴鹿皮和狐狸皮，他便走了進去。

passages.text: The door hinge creaked and the house shook; the lone-dweller, its master, came in and offered food, but Makite would eat nothing until he learned what those candle-like things in front of the window were. 'That is no concern of one who is not himself a lone-dweller,' came the answer — until Makite threatened to kill him. Then the lone-dweller told: on the nearer of the two great blue hills away south you will find nothing, but he who climbs the farther hill and reaches the top will find such things there; but this cannot be done by one who is not a lone-dweller. During the night Makite caught the host quietly stringing his bow to kill him in his sleep, feigned waking, and at dawn slipped out; pursued, he ran three times round a big rock and thrust his harpoon out behind him without turning, striking the pursuer in the side and killing him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Makite'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 門軸吱嘎作響，屋子也震動起來；獨居者，也就是這屋的主人，走了進來，奉上食物，但馬基特什麼也不肯吃，除非弄明白窗前那些像蠟燭的東西究竟是什麼。「這不關一個自己不是獨居者的人的事，」對方答道——直到馬基特威脅要殺了他。於是獨居者說道：在南邊兩座藍色大山中較近的那座上，你什麼也找不到；但誰若爬上較遠的那座山並到達山頂，就會在那裡找到這樣的東西；然而這不是一個自己不是獨居者的人所能做到的。夜裡，馬基特察覺主人悄悄拉開弓，想趁他睡夢中殺他，便假裝醒來，黎明時溜了出去；被追趕時，他繞著一塊大石跑了三圈，頭也不回地把魚叉向身後刺出，刺中追趕者的肋側，將他殺死。

passages.text: Wandering at hazard he came to a great plain with something like a house in the middle: the house of a dwarf, crowded with folk streaming in and out, too small even to put his foot in the passage until told to heave up the passage way with his back. The old creature warned him as he went out: look towards the west, the inland-dwellers are coming. The dwarfs went out to fight, posting themselves on the plain in two silent lines; when the inlanders' dog gave a great bark, a mighty wave rolled up to the dwarfs — and shrank to nothing close by them. Then the dwarfs' dog barked, their own wave rose and washed right over the inland folk, drowning all but a few. Makite built himself a house, fetched some of the candle-like things from the high hill, hung them up in his house, and lived there until he died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Makite'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他漫無目的地遊蕩，來到一片大平原，平原中央有個像屋子的東西：那是一個矮人的屋子，裡面擠滿了人，進進出出，川流不息，那通道小得他連腳都伸不進去，直到有人叫他用自己的背把通道撐起來。那老東西在他出去時警告他：朝西看，內陸的居民來了。矮人們出去迎戰，在平原上排成兩列沉默的隊伍；當內陸人的狗發出一聲響亮的吠叫，一道巨浪朝矮人們湧來——卻在他們近旁縮小得無影無蹤。接著矮人的狗吠叫起來，他們自己的浪湧起，直直漫過內陸人，除了少數幾個，全都淹死了。馬基特給自己蓋了一座屋子，從高山上取來一些像蠟燭的東西，掛在屋裡，便住在那裡，直到死去。

title.en: Asaloq: The Strength Trial and the Magic Songs
title.zh: 阿薩洛克：角力試煉與咒歌

region.en: West Greenland coast
region.zh: 西格陵蘭沿岸

period: Inuit oral tradition (West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Asaloq', eBook #28932

summary.en: Searching for his vanished foster-brother in a three-layered umiak, Asaloq passes a black ripple of sea-lice that eats one skin layer and a ripple of sea-serpents that eats another, to land among strangers whose squint talebearer-boy betrays his presence. Summoned before their strong man, he eats until the food falls out of his stomach and pulls arms until the skin is worn from his own — leaving strongest of all — then hides on an island and sings magic songs until the pursuing umiaks give up and row home.
summary.zh: 阿薩洛克乘三層皮大舟尋找失蹤的結拜兄弟，途經海虱黑浪（蝕去一層皮）與海蛇黑浪（再蝕一層），抵達異鄉；斜眼傳話童洩其蹤。彼族力士召他比武——他大吃至腹中之物盡吐，又拉臂拉到自身皮開肉綻，終以最強者離場。北來大舟搜捕之際，他立於山頂高唱咒歌，直到追兵放棄返航。

sensitivity.note: West Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Sea-lice and sea-serpent passages are cosmological hazards of the Greenlandic kayak world.

passages.text: Asaloq had a foster-brother who disappeared one day while he was out in his kayak. Finding him nowhere, Asaloq built a big umiak covered with three layers of skins and rowed south with his wife. A black ripple appeared on the sea ahead: the sea-lice, which ate away the outermost layer of skins before they got through. Another black ripple: the sea-serpents, which cost them a second layer. With one layer left they rowed in fear, rounded a point, and came in sight of a place with many houses, where the strangers caught hold of their boat and hauled it up for them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Asaloq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿薩洛克有一個義兄弟，有一天他乘皮划艇外出時失蹤了。阿薩洛克到處都找不到他，便造了一艘蒙著三層皮的大划艇，帶著妻子向南划去。前方海面上出現一道黑色的漣漪：那是海蝨，在他們穿過之前就啃掉了最外面的一層皮。又一道黑色漣漪：那是海蛇，使他們又損失了一層皮。只剩一層皮時，他們滿懷恐懼地划著，繞過一個岬角，望見一個有許多屋子的地方，那裡的外鄉人抓住他們的船，替他們把船拖了上去。

passages.text: The place had a strong man in its midst, and a squinting talebearer boy who, in spite of being set up behind the lamp, slipped out and ran to tell. Faces filled the window: 'We are sent to bid the stranger come.' In the crowded house the strong man called from the far end of the bench, 'Let us have a wrestling match'; a skin was spread on the floor and food brought in — Asaloq ate till there was no more left, and when he rose, all he had eaten fell out of his stomach. Then the pulling of arms: he pulled at the arms of all the men until the skin was worn from his own arm, the flesh almost bare. Straightening out every arm in the house, he went out strongest of all and rowed south with his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Asaloq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這個地方有個力大無窮的人，還有一個瞇著眼的搬弄是非的男孩；這男孩雖然被安置在燈後，卻仍溜了出去，跑去報信。窗口擠滿了臉孔：「我們奉命來請那位陌生人過來。」在擁擠的屋裡，那壯漢從長凳的遠端喊道：「我們來比一場角力吧。」地上鋪開一張獸皮，食物也端了進來——阿薩洛克一直吃到再沒有東西剩下；當他起身時，他吃下的一切都從胃裡掉了出來。接著是較量臂力：他與所有男人較臂力，直到他自己手臂上的皮都磨掉了，肉幾乎裸露。他把屋裡每個人的手臂都扳直之後，以最強者的身分走了出去，帶著妻子向南划去。

passages.text: On a little island they pitched their tent on the sunny side; from the hilltop Asaloq saw many umiaks coming from the northward, which camped on the shady side, searching carefully about — 'He can hardly be on such a little island.' Asaloq sang magic songs over them from the top of the hill until he heard them say, 'We may as well go home again.' Not until they were out of sight did he row on south, and at last they reached Aluk, where their bones still rest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Asaloq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在一座小島上，他們把帳篷搭在向陽的一側；阿薩洛克從山頂望見許多烏米亞克（umiak，大型皮艇）從北方駛來，那些人把營地紮在背陰的一側，仔細四處搜尋——「他不可能在這麼小的一座島上。」阿薩洛克從山頂對他們唱起魔法之歌，直到他聽見他們說：「我們還是回家去吧。」直到他們消失不見，他才繼續向南划去，最後他們抵達阿盧克，他們的遺骨至今仍安息在那裡。

title.en: Ukaleq: Killed by the Magic Bear, Raised by His Mother
title.zh: 烏卡萊克：魔熊之殺與母親之復生

region.en: West Greenland coast
region.zh: 西格陵蘭沿岸

period: Inuit oral tradition (West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Ukaleq', eBook #28932

summary.en: Ukaleq, who never failed to kill whatever game he chased, dies at last to a Magic Bear whose teeth whisper his killing to the comrades who find him. His mother, keeping the dress he wore as a little child, hushes it in her carrying bag through five days without food or drink until it begins to crawl — and as it springs out the dead man begins to breathe and sit up, restored. At a great spirit calling, an old wifeless man's question shames the woman who owned the Magic Bear so that she dies on the spot; Ukaleq goes home and never hunts bears again.
summary.zh: 從不失手的獵手烏卡萊克終為魔熊所殺——熊齒低語向同伴揭露真相。其母藏著他幼時舊衣，將之抱於行囊中如哄嬰兒，絕食絕飲五日，直到囊中之物蠕動欲出；舊衣一躍而出，屋搖震動，死者開始呼吸、坐起，復活如初。大降靈會上，無妻老人一句質問，令養魔熊的老嫗羞死當場；烏卡萊克從此再不獵熊。

sensitivity.note: West Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Magic Bear (a tupilak-like created bear) and child's-dress resurrection beliefs documented as told in the source.

passages.text: Ukaleq was a strong man who had only to go out after whatever game was heard of, even a great bear, to kill it. One winter, hunting on the new ice, he found the bear not easily brought down; it sighted him and turned to pursue, and though he wounded it now and again as he fled, he was killed himself at last — at the same moment the bear fell dead. When his comrades came to look at it, its teeth began to whisper, and then they knew Ukaleq had been killed by a Magic Bear. They took the dead man home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Ukaleq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 烏卡萊克是個強壯的人，只要聽說有什麼獵物，哪怕是一頭大熊，他只需出去便能將牠殺死。有一年冬天，他在新結的冰上打獵，發現那頭熊不容易被擊倒；熊看見了他，便轉身追來，他一面逃一面不時將牠刺傷，最後自己卻被殺死了——就在同一刻，那頭熊也倒地而死。當他的同伴前來察看那頭熊時，牠的牙齒開始低聲細語，他們這才明白烏卡萊克是被一頭魔法熊殺死的。他們把死者帶回了家。

passages.text: His mother had kept the dress he wore as a little child. She had him laid in the middle of the floor on a skin, put the dress in her carrying bag, went out to the cooking place in the passage, and said: 'For five days I will neither eat nor drink.' Then she began hushing the dress in the bag as if it were a child, hushing on and on until it began to move — and just then someone came out saying Ukaleq was beginning to quiver. She hushed still harder; the thing in the bag tried to crawl out as someone called that Ukaleq had begun to breathe and was sitting up. The bag's occupant sprang out and made the whole house shake. They made up a bed on the side bench; after five days without eating or drinking he came to himself, and commenced to go out hunting once more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Ukaleq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的母親一直保存著他小時候穿的那件衣服。她讓人把他放在地板中央的一張獸皮上，把那件衣服放進她的背袋裡，走到通道裡的炊煮處，說道：「五天之内，我既不吃也不喝。」然後她開始在袋中像哄孩子一樣哄著那件衣服，哄了又哄，直到它開始動了起來——就在那時，有人出來說烏卡萊克開始顫動了。她哄得更用力了；袋裡的東西試圖爬出來，同時有人喊道烏卡萊克已經開始呼吸，並且坐了起來。袋中之物跳了出來，震得整座屋子都搖晃。他們在側邊的長凳上鋪了一張床；五天不吃不喝之後，他恢復了神智，又開始外出打獵了。

passages.text: Next winter, when the ice had formed, the villages held their spirit callings and visited one another. Ukaleq went with his family to a big calling in a house with three windows, crowded with folk. Midway, an old woman sitting cross-legged on the bench turned and said: 'We heard last autumn that Ukaleq had been killed by a Magic Bear.' An old wifeless man turned to her at once: 'Was it by any chance your Magic Bear that killed him?' She answered, 'Mine? Now where could I have kept such a thing?' — but after saying that she did not move; she even forgot to breathe, for shame at having been discovered, and died on the spot. Ukaleq went home and never went out hunting bears again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Ukaleq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二年冬天，冰結成之後，各村舉行了招魂聚會，彼此往來拜訪。烏卡萊克帶著家人去參加一場在一座有三扇窗戶的屋裡舉行的大型聚會，屋裡擠滿了人。聚會進行到一半，一個盤腿坐在長凳上的老婦人轉過身來說：「我們去年秋天聽說烏卡萊克被一頭魔法熊殺死了。」一個沒有妻子的老人立刻轉向她：「殺死他的，該不會正好是妳的魔法熊吧？」她回答：「我的？唉，我能把那種東西藏在哪裡呢？」——但說完這話之後，她一動也不動；她甚至忘了呼吸，因為被人識破而羞愧，當場就死了。烏卡萊克回了家，此後再也不出去獵熊了。

title.en: Raja Suran Descends to the Sea-Kingdom in a Glass Chest
title.zh: 蘇蘭王乘玻璃櫃潛入海底王國

region.en: Southern Java Sea (symbolic pin — the open sea crossed between Kling and Tamsak)
region.zh: 爪哇南部海域（象徵性定位：克林與淡馬錫之間的公海）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. I (Raja Suran's descent), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Wishing to see the wonders of God's creation, Raja Suran seals himself in a locked glass chest lowered by a golden chain into the sea. He lands in the submarine realm of Zeya, marries the sea-king's daughter Putri Mahtab-al-Bahri, fathers three sons, and escapes upward on a flying, swimming sea-horse named Sambrani — the Malay Annals' charter myth of the dynasty's descent from the world under the water.
summary.zh: 蘇蘭王欲一睹上帝造化之奇，乃自封於玻璃櫃中，繫以金鏈沉入海底。抵水下之境澤亞，娶海王之女瑪赫塔布，生三子；後騎能飛能泳之海馬桑布拉尼上歸人世——《馬來紀年》以此為王族出自水下世界之憲章神話。

sensitivity.note: Literary dynastic chronicle (Sejarah Melayu); Malaysian and Indonesian Malay communities hold the heritage; the text itself is public domain. Cross-cluster: descent to the otherworld parallels Inanna/Ishtar and Izanagi.

passages.text: Raja Suran, considering that he had now become acquainted with the contents of the land, wished to acquire information concerning the nature of the sea. For this purpose he ordered a chest of glass, with a lock in the inside, and fixed it to a chain of gold. Then, shutting himself up in this chest, he caused himself to be let down into the sea, to see the wonders of God Almighty's creation. At last the chest reached a land, denominated Zeya, when Raja Suran came forth from the chest and walked about to see the wonders of the place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蘇蘭王（Raja Suran）心想自己如今已熟知陸地上的種種事物，便希望獲知關於海洋性質的種種情報。為此，他命人打造一隻玻璃箱，內側裝有鎖，並把它繫在一條金鏈上。然後，他把自己關在這隻箱子裡，命人將他縋入海中，以便觀看全能真主所造萬物的奇觀。最後，箱子抵達了一片名為澤亞（Zeya）的陸地，蘇蘭王便從箱中出來，四處走動，觀看這地方的奇觀。

passages.text: In Zeya he found a people so numerous that God alone could know their numbers, and their king, Aktab-al-Arz, seated him upon his own throne and gave him his daughter, Putri Mahtab-al-Bahri, in marriage; by her he had three sons. At length Suran reflected what advantage it was to stay so long below the earth, and how he might carry his sons' line upward, for it would be a great disadvantage to cut off the line of Secander Zulkarneini.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在澤亞，他發現一個人口眾多到唯有真主才能知其數目的民族；他們的國王阿克塔布-阿爾-阿爾茲讓他坐上自己的王座，並將自己的女兒普特麗·馬赫塔布-阿爾-巴赫里許配給他為妻；他與她生了三個兒子。後來，蘇蘭思忖，長久留在地下究竟有何益處，又該如何將子孫的血脈向上延續，因為斷絕塞坎德·祖爾卡爾奈尼的血脈將是極大的不利。

passages.text: His father-in-law furnished him with a sea-horse named Sambrani, which could fly through the air as well as swim in the water. Suran mounted amid the lamentations of his spouse; the steed quickly cleared the nether atmosphere and rapidly traversed the upper ocean, where his followers perceived him, and by presenting a mare on the shore they lured Sambrani to land and recovered their king. Suran then commanded that the account of his descent be inscribed on a stone monument for posterity, to be found by one of his descendants who should reduce all the rajas under the wind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的岳父為他備了一匹名為桑布拉尼的海馬，此馬既能飛越空中，亦能游於水中。蘇蘭在妻子的哀泣聲中跨上馬背；這匹駿馬迅速穿出下層的大氣，疾速橫越上方的海洋，他的追隨者在那裡望見了他，並在岸上牽出一匹母馬，將桑布拉尼誘上岸來，從而尋回了他們的國王。蘇蘭隨後下令，將他下海的經過銘刻於石碑之上，以傳後世，留待他的一位後裔——那位將使所有羅闍皆屈從於風之下者——發現。

title.en: The Rusty Needles: China Cheats the Conqueror
title.zh: 生鏽的鐵針：中國以計退敵

region.en: Tamsak (Singapore), Malay Annals geography
region.zh: 淡馬錫（今新加坡一帶，《馬來紀年》地理）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. I (the ruse of the mantri of China), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: When Raja Suran's immeasurable host threatens China, a sagacious mantri loads a prow with old, toothless sailors, seeds of bidara trees, and iron bars thick as an arm, all rusted over, and sends it to Tamsak. The 'traders' explain that they left China as children and have grown old on the voyage — so vast is the distance. Believing the world's measure, Suran turns back without a battle.
summary.zh: 蘇蘭王大軍將犯中國，中國一賢臣獻計：以滿載老邁無齒水手、巴旦樹種與粗如臂之鐵條（皆已鏽蝕）之船駛至淡馬錫，訛稱自幼離華、行旅經年、樹已結實、鐵已鏽細——蘇蘭王信路途無涯，遂罷兵而返。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle fiction; an episode of ruse-warfare in the Malay Annals' Alexander-derived prehistory.

passages.text: It was reported in the land of China that Raja Suran was advancing with an innumerable army and had arrived at Tamsak. The raja of China was alarmed and said to his mantris and chieftains: 'If the Kling raja approach, the country will be inevitably ruined; what method do you advise to prevent his approach?' Then a sagacious mantri said: 'Lord of the world, your slave will fall on a device.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 中國之地有傳聞說，羅闍·蘇蘭正率領無數大軍推進，已抵達塔姆薩克。中國的羅闍大為驚恐，對他的曼特里斯與首領們說道：『倘若克林羅闍逼近，此國必將毀於一旦；你們有何計策可阻止他前來？』於是，一位睿智的曼特里斯說道：『世界之主啊，您的奴僕將獻上一計。』

passages.text: He ordered a prow filled full of fine needles but covered with rust, planted with seeds of the casamak and bidara trees, and selected a party of old and toothless people to sail to Tamsak. When Suran's men asked how far it was to China, the Chinese replied: 'When we set sail we were all young, about twelve years of age, and we planted these seeds; now we have grown old and lost our teeth, and the seeds we planted have become trees which bore fruit before our arrival here.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他命人備好一艘船，船中裝滿上好的針，卻覆以鐵鏽，並種上卡薩馬克樹與比達拉樹的種子，又挑選了一隊年老無牙之人，揚帆駛往塔姆薩克。當蘇蘭的人問起此地距中國尚有多遠時，那些中國人答道：『我們啟航之時，皆尚年少，約十二歲，並種下這些種子；如今我們已年老，牙齒盡落，而我們所種的種子已長成大樹，且在我們抵達此地之前便已結果。』

passages.text: They took out some of the rusty needles and showed them, saying: 'When we left China these bars of iron were thick as your arm; now they have grown thus small by the corrosion of rust.' If the account were true, said Suran, the land of China must be at an immense distance — when should they ever arrive? All the champions assented, and Raja Suran turned back his host without a battle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們取出一些生鏽的針展示出來，說道：『我們離開中國時，這些鐵條粗如你們的手臂；如今因鏽蝕而變得這般細小。』蘇蘭說道，倘若此言屬實，則中國之地必定遙遠至極——他們何時才能抵達？所有勇士皆表贊同，羅闍·蘇蘭便未經一戰即率軍折返。

title.en: The Fall of Gangga Nagara: Suran and Ganggi Shah Juana
title.zh: 剛迦王國之陷落：蘇蘭對剛吉沙朱阿納

region.en: Gangga Nagara on the river Dinding, Perak (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 霹靂州丁丁河畔剛迦城（象徵性定位）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. I (conquest of Gangga Nagara and Glang Kiu), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: On his march, Raja Suran breaks the steeps of Gangga Nagara with his chacra and duels its raja on elephant-back: Ganggi Shah Juana's arrow fells Suran's huge elephant, but Suran springs up and cuts off the defender's head. He marries the dead king's sister and rides on to destroy Glang Kiu and its raja Chulan in a mêlée of amokas — the Annals' grand old-war set piece.
summary.zh: 蘇蘭王征途之中，以查克羅擊碎剛迦陡城之門，與守王於象背決鬥：剛吉沙朱阿納一箭射倒蘇蘭巨象，蘇蘭躍起拔劍斬其首。娶其妹剛迦公主，續而破翡翠之地格蘭基烏，陣斬朱蘭王——此乃《紀年》古戰史之壯闊段落。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle battle-legend; Perak (Malaysia) place-myth recorded within the shared Malay chronicle tradition.

passages.text: Raja Suran mounted his huge elephant and approached the gate of the fortress, notwithstanding the showers of spears and arrows with which he was assailed; he smote the gate with his chacra, and it immediately tumbled down, while the raja entered the fort with all his champions.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 羅闍·蘇蘭騎上他那頭巨象，逼近堡壘的城門，儘管矛與箭如雨般向他襲來；他以恰克拉擊打城門，城門當即倒塌，而這位羅闍便率領他所有的勇士進入堡壘。

passages.text: Raja Ganggi Shah Juana seized his bow and smote the elephant of Raja Suran on the forehead, which instantly fell down. Raja Suran quickly sprang up and drew his sword, and smote off the head of Raja Ganggi Shah Juana; after the raja's death all his subjects submitted, and Suran married Putri Gangga, the beautiful sister of the slain king.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 岡吉沙胡阿納王抓起他的弓，射中蘇蘭王那頭大象的前額，大象當即倒地。蘇蘭王迅速躍起，拔出劍來，砍下岡吉沙胡阿納王的頭；這位羅闍死後，他所有的臣民都歸順了，蘇蘭便娶了被殺國王那位美麗的妹妹普特麗岡加為妻。

passages.text: At Glang Kiu the place of the emerald, raja Chulan met him with a host like the sea rough with waves; elephants rushed against elephants, horses bit horses, and the dust ascended to the heavens till the day was darkened like an eclipse. Suran and Chulan charged each other on their elephants roaring like thunder; Chulan's spear pierced Suran's elephant from side to side, and Suran's arrow struck Chulan on the breast and pierced him to the back, and Chulan fell dead on his elephant. Suran took to wife his daughter, Putri Onang-kiu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在翡翠之地格朗基烏，朱蘭羅闍率領著如波濤洶湧的大海般的軍隊與他相遇；象衝向象，馬咬著馬，塵土升上天空，直到白晝昏暗如日蝕。蘇蘭與朱蘭騎著象彼此衝殺，咆哮如雷；朱蘭的長矛將蘇蘭的象從一側刺穿到另一側，蘇蘭的箭射中朱蘭的胸膛，穿透到背後，朱蘭便死在他的象上。蘇蘭娶了他的女兒普特麗奧南基烏為妻。

title.en: Bichitram Shah Abandons His Kingdom for the Sea
title.zh: 比奇特蘭沙棄國出海

region.en: The sea of Silbou (symbolic pin, western Malay world)
region.zh: 西爾布之海（象徵性定位，馬來世界西部）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. I (Bichitram Shah's fleet), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Angry that his father Raja Suran gave him only a small territory while his brothers received kingdoms, Bichitram Shah embarks with twenty war-vessels to conquer the maritime lands. After taking scores of countries he reaches the sea of Silbou, where a hurricane scatters his fleet: half returns to Chandukani, the fate of the other half is unknown — the Annals' template of the sea-faring prince from whom the Palembang line will later descend.
summary.zh: 父王蘇蘭僅予小邑，比奇特蘭沙憤而率二十艘戰船出海，征服海上諸邦；至西爾布海遇風暴，船隊四散——半數歸于昌杜卡尼，半數下落不明。《紀年》以此為海上王侯漂泊之母題，日後巴鄰旁王系即出其後。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle legend; fine as a comparative 'hero on the sea' motif record.

passages.text: On his eldest son Bichitram Shah, Raja Suran only conferred a territory of small extent; and the young prince being displeased at this measure, resolved to abandon his country. He embarked with twenty vessels fitted out with all the apparatus of war, determining to conquer all the maritime districts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蘇蘭王只把一小片領地封給他的長子比奇特拉姆沙；這位年輕的王子對此心懷不滿，決意離開自己的國家。他帶著二十艘配備齊全戰具的船隻出海，決心征服所有沿海地區。

passages.text: After conquering several scores of countries, he at last reached the sea denominated Silbou, where, being caught in a dreadful hurricane, his fleet was dispersed, and the half of them returned to the country of Chandukani, but the fate of the other half is unknown. The adventures of this prince were very numerous, but they are only alluded to briefly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在征服了幾十個國家之後，他終於到達了名為西爾布的海洋；在那裡，他遭遇了一場可怕的颶風，艦隊被吹散，其中半數返回了昌杜卡尼國，而另一半的命運則無人知曉。這位王子的冒險經歷極為繁多，但此處僅簡略提及。

title.en: The Rice That Turned to Gold on the Mountain of Belidung
title.zh: 勿里洞山上化金之稻

region.en: Mount Sagantang Maha Miru, near Palembang (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 巴鄰旁附近薩甘當摩訶米魯山（象徵性定位）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. II (Wan Ampu and Wan Malin), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Two rice-cultivating women of Belidung, Wan Ampu and Wan Malin, see their fields gleam like fire in the night. At dawn the grain has become gold, the leaves silver, the stalks brass — and on the golden ground stand three young men: Bichitram Shah's heir as Sang Sapurba on a white steer, with Nila Pahlawan and Karana Pandita holding sword and lance. The Annals' founding apparition of the Palembang dynasty, and the origin of the Awang and Dara castes.
summary.zh: 勿里洞二女萬阿木普與萬馬林耕稻於薩甘當山上，夜見田如火光；晨起視之，穀化金、葉化銀、稈化銅——金土之上立三少年：白牛背上的王儲（後稱三保爺·三蘇爾巴），持劍執矛二侍從立於兩側。此即巴鄰旁王系之顯聖神話，亦阿旺、達拉二姓之由來。

sensitivity.note: Dynasty-foundation apparition; Palembang and Minangkabau communities hold the heritage; public-domain source.

passages.text: There were two young women of Belidung, Wan Ampu and Wan Malin, employed in cultivating rice on this mountain, where they had large and productive rice-grounds. One night they beheld their rice-fields gleaming and glittering like fire; 'It is some great snake or naga,' said Malin, and they lay quiet for fear. When it was daylight they went to see what it was, and found the grain of the rice converted into gold, the leaves into silver, and the stalks into brass.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伯利東有兩個年輕女子，萬安普與萬馬林，在這座山上種稻，她們在那裡有大片而豐產的稻田。一天夜裡，她們看見自己的稻田閃爍發光，如同火焰一般；「準是某條大蛇或那伽，」馬林說道，她們便因害怕而靜靜躺著。天亮時她們前去查看究竟是什麼，發現稻穀變成了金子，葉子變成了銀子，稻稈變成了黃銅。

passages.text: On the ground which had assumed this golden colour they saw three young and handsome men: one in the dress of a raja mounted on a bull white as silver, the others holding a sword and a spear. Asked whether they were Jins or Peris, the centre one answered that they were of the race of men, descendants of Raja Secander Zulkarneini and offspring of Raja Suran, whose crown was the evidence of their descent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在那片染上這金色的大地上，她們看見三個年輕英俊的男子：一個身穿羅闍的服飾，騎著一頭白如銀子的公牛，其餘兩人手持劍與矛。問他們是精靈還是仙人，中間那人回答說他們屬於人類，是塞坎德爾祖爾卡內尼羅闍的後裔、蘇蘭羅闍的子孫，他們的王冠便是其出身的明證。

passages.text: The girls invited them home and cut the paddy for their food; the prince's name was changed to Sang Sapurba. The bull vomited foam, from which emerged a man named Bat'h, with an immense turban, who began to recite the prince's praises in the Sanscrit language, giving him the title Sang Sapurba Trimarti Tribhuvena. From Bat'h descend the original reciters of the cheritras; Nila Pahlawan and Karana Pandita married the two women, and their male offspring were called Baginda Awang and the female offspring Baginda Dara — hence the origin of all the Awangs and Daras.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那些女子邀請他們回家，並割下稻穀作為他們的食物；王子的名字被改為桑·薩普爾巴。那頭公牛吐出泡沫，從泡沫中出現了一個名叫巴特的人，頭戴巨大的頭巾，開始用梵語歌頌王子的功德，賜予他桑·薩普爾巴·特里馬爾蒂·特里布韋納的稱號。巴特是切里特拉諸吟誦者的始祖；尼拉·帕拉萬與卡拉納·潘迪塔娶了那兩名女子，他們所生的男性後裔被稱為巴金達·阿旺，女性後裔被稱為巴金達·達拉——所有阿旺與達拉的起源便由此而來。

title.en: The Thirty-Nine Leprous Brides of Sang Sapurba
title.zh: 三蘇爾巴王的三十九位痲瘋新娘

region.en: Mount Sagantang Maha Miru, Palembang (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩甘當山，巴鄰旁（象徵性定位）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. II (the leprosy of the low-born brides), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: When the heaven-descended prince Sang Sapurba wishes to marry, local rajas bring their daughters — but thirty-nine brides of unsuitable rank are stricken with leprosy 'as with a plague sent as a curse' the moment they join him. Only Wan Sundaria, daughter of the Palembang raja Damang Lebar Dawn, of sufficiently noble blood, escapes untouched — the Annals' mythic warning that kingship of divine descent must be matched with royal blood.
summary.zh: 天降王子三蘇爾巴欲娶親，諸邦獻女——然門第不配者，一與王合即患痲瘋，凡三十九人，如遭天譴。惟巴鄰旁王女萬蘇達莉亞出身高貴，獨免於災——《紀年》以此警示：神裔之王必配王族之血。

sensitivity.note: Royal-hypogamy taboo in the Annals; flagged as interpretive — the leprosy curse encodes caste/royal endogamy rules.

passages.text: It was soon noised over the whole country that a descendant of Raja Secander Zulkarneini had descended on the mountain Sagantang Maha Miru, and all the rajas of the neighbouring countries came with rich presents to pay their respects to him. As he wanted to marry, they all brought him their daughters; but as they were not of proper rank for such a noble prince, as soon as they associated with him they were stricken with a leprosy, as with a plague sent as a curse, to the number of thirty-nine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久，全國上下便傳聞拉惹·塞坎德·祖爾卡爾內尼的後裔降臨於薩甘唐·馬哈·米魯山上，鄰近各國的拉惹們都帶著豐厚的禮物前來向他致敬。由於他想要成婚，他們都把自己的女兒帶來獻給他；但因為她們的門第不足以匹配如此高貴的王子，所以一旦與他結合，便染上了痲瘋病，如同上天降下詛咒的瘟疫一般，人數多達三十九人。

passages.text: The raja of Palembang had a daughter of extreme beauty, Wan Sundaria. Sang Sapurba sent to ask her in marriage; her father excused himself, alledging that she would probably be struck with sickness, and would only resign her on certain conditions. After the marriage it was found that she had escaped the curse of leprosy which had afflicted his former wives, to the raja's great satisfaction, and Damang Lebar Dawn came in great haste, rejoiced to find her in excellent health.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴鄰旁（Palembang）的拉惹有一個容貌極美的女兒，名叫萬·孫達里亞。桑·薩普爾巴派人前去求婚；她的父親婉言推辭，聲稱她很可能也會染上疾病，並表示只有在某些條件下才願將她許配。婚後發現她並未染上困擾他前幾位妻子的痲瘋詛咒，拉惹大為滿意，達芒·勒巴爾·道恩也急忙趕來，欣喜地發現她身體極為健康。

title.en: The Covenant of Damang Lebar Dawn: Why a Malay Raja May Not Shame His People
title.zh: 達萬·勒巴爾道恩之盟約：馬來王何以不可羞辱其民

region.en: Palembang, Sumatra
region.zh: 蘇門答臘巴鄰旁

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. II (the marriage conditions), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Before giving his daughter to Sang Sapurba, Damang Lebar Dawn imposes conditions binding both lines forever: his descendants shall serve the raja's line, but shall never be bound, shamed, or reviled — great faults punished only by death under law; while the raja's line shall never suffer treason from his people's descendants, on pain of heaven 'turning their authority upside down.' The Annals presents this mythic oath as the constitutional origin of Malay kingship and its corresponding loyalty.
summary.zh: 達萬·勒巴爾道恩嫁女之前與三蘇爾巴立盟：其後裔世奉王室，然永不受縛、不受辱、不受詈——重罪唯依法處死；而王系永不受其民後裔之叛，違者天罰顛覆其權。《紀年》以此神話之誓為馬來君權與臣忠之憲政起源。

sensitivity.note: Charter-myth of Malay constitutional custom (adat); the Annals states this oath as the origin of the no-shaming rule.

passages.text: The conditions were that on Sangsapurba marrying his daughter, all the family of Damang Lebar Dawn should submit themselves to him; but that Sangsapurba should engage, both for himself and his posterity, that they should receive a liberal treatment — that when they committed faults they should never be exposed to shame nor opprobrious language, but if their faults were great, that they should be put to death according to the law.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 條件是：桑薩普爾巴娶其女兒之後，達芒·勒巴爾·道恩的全族應歸順於他；但桑薩普爾巴須為自己及其後代承諾，他們應受到寬厚的對待——當他們犯下過錯時，絕不應使他們蒙受羞辱或遭受辱罵之言，但若他們的過錯重大，則應依法處死。

passages.text: Sangsapurba requested in his turn that the descendants of Damang Lebar Dawn should never move treasonable practices against his descendants, even though they should become tyrannical. 'Very well,' said Damang Lebar Dawn, 'but if your descendants break your agreements, probably mine will do the same.' These conditions were mutually agreed to, and the parties swore to perform them, imprecating the divine vengeance to turn their authority upside down who should infringe these agreements.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 桑薩普爾巴則反過來要求，達芒·勒巴爾·道恩的後代絕不應對他的後代圖謀叛亂，即使他們變得暴虐無道亦然。『很好，』達芒·勒巴爾·道恩說道，『但若你的後代違背你們的約定，我的後代大概也會如此。』這些條件經雙方相互同意，各方並發誓履行，並祈求神明降罰，使違背這些約定者權位傾覆。

passages.text: From this condition it is that none of the Malay rajas ever expose their Malay subjects to disgrace or shame; they never bind them, nor hang them, nor give them opprobrious language; for whenever a raja exposes his subjects to disgrace, it is the certain token of the destruction of his country: hence also it is that none of the Malay race ever engage in rebellion, or turn their faces from their own rajas, even though their conduct be bad.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 正因這一條件，馬來諸拉惹從不使其馬來臣民蒙受恥辱或羞辱；他們從不捆綁他們，從不吊死他們，也從不對他們說辱罵之言；因為每當一位拉惹使其臣民蒙受羞辱，那便是其國家滅亡的確定徵兆：因此，馬來族人也從不參與叛亂，或背棄自己的拉惹，即使他們的行為不端亦然。

title.en: The Bathing-House of Seven Stories: Installation of Sang Sapurba
title.zh: 七層浴殿：三蘇爾巴的即位大典

region.en: Palembang, Sumatra
region.zh: 蘇門答臘巴鄰旁

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. II (the royal bath), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: To celebrate the marriage that escaped the leprosy curse, Damang Lebar Dawn builds the seven-storied bathing-house Pancha Presadha, and for forty days and nights the country feasts until 'the heaps of half-burnt rice lay like hillocks' and buffalo heads float in seas of rice-broth like islands. The royal couple then circles the bath seven times, bathes on its highest story, and ascends the golden throne — the Annals' fullest picture of royal installation ritual.
summary.zh: 為慶婚姻之成，達萬·勒巴爾道恩建七層浴殿『五重寶』；四十晝夜大宴，燒半之米堆積如丘，牛首浮於米湯如島。王與后繞殿七匝，登最高層共浴，後易禮服登金座鳴鼓即位——此為《紀年》所載最詳之王室即位儀注。

sensitivity.note: Royal installation ritual narrative; the bath rite (bersalin) persisted in Malay courts.

passages.text: After his return to Palembang, Damang Lebar Dawn ordered a splendid bathing-house to be constructed, and the architect was the aforesaid Bat'h. This bathing house was named Pancha Presadha, and it had seven stories, and terminated in five towers on the roof. A public festival was then made for the space of forty days and forty nights, attended by all the inferior rajas, mantris, eunuchs, bantaras, champions, and commons in general.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 達曼·勒巴爾·道恩返回巴鄰旁後，下令建造一座華美的浴場，建築師即為前述之巴特。此浴場名為潘查·普雷薩達，共有七層，屋頂以五座塔樓作結。隨後舉行為期四十晝夜的公眾慶典，所有下級拉者、曼特里、宦官、班塔拉、勇士及一般平民皆出席參與。

passages.text: The heaps of half-burnt rice rejected lay like hillocks, and the skimming of the foam of the rice-broth stood in little seas, in which floated the heads of buffaloes and goats like so many islands. After the completion of the forty days and nights, the bathing water was introduced with all kinds of music and an immense concourse of people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 棄置的半焦米飯堆積如小丘，米湯浮沫撇出後積成小海，其中漂浮著水牛與山羊的頭顱，宛如眾多島嶼。四十晝夜屆滿後，沐浴之水在各種音樂與龐大人群的簇擁下被引入。

passages.text: The husband and wife, with a great multitude, seven times encircled the bathing-house, and afterwards bathed in the highest story, Bat'h officiating at the bath. After bathing they changed their garments — Sangsapurba arraying himself in the derapata deremani and the queen in the burudaimani — then mounted the golden throne of authority, and the state drums were beat; Bat'h inserted the Panchawa Panchara on the temples of the royal pair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 夫婦二人偕同大批人眾，繞行浴場七圈，隨後於最高層沐浴，由巴特主持沐浴之禮。沐浴之後，二人更換衣袍——桑薩普爾巴著德拉帕塔·德雷馬尼，王后著布魯達伊馬尼——繼而登上黃金權座，邦國鼓聲響起；巴特將潘查瓦·潘查拉飾於王室夫婦的鬢角。

title.en: Putri Tunjong Bui, the Princess Born of a Foam-Bell
title.zh: 泡沫之鐘公主：敦戎布伊

region.en: River of Palembang, Sumatra
region.zh: 蘇門答臘巴鄰旁河

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. II (Putri Tunjong-bui), trans. John Leyden 1821
