Gathering bones of all sorts of animals, he fashioned it so it could take the shape of different animals, birds as well as seals, and having stirred them into life, let it loose with orders to persecute Kujavarsuk. Diving into the sea it appeared in the shape of a seal, but he was already on his way home drawing his kayak on the shore — the same on the second and third day. It then determined to pursue him to his house and frighten him to death: transforming itself into a toogdlik (the great northern diver), it commenced shrieking outside the house; Kujavarsuk went out but could not be brought to look at it, so the charm would not work. Going underground to pop up into the room, it succeeded no better; rising at the back of the house, just as it was about to climb up the roof it met his own amulet-bird, which at once set about picking and scratching its face. Turning desperate — 'Why did this miserable fool of a man ever make me!' — in the height of its wrath it turned against its maker: diving into the water near his fishing-place, it emerged right beneath his kayak, fairly upsetting it, and devoured him on the spot, then fled far away out on the roaring ocean. Kujavarsuk afterwards remained unmolested and died at a very old age.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 13 'The Barren Wife'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，他的妻子們只留下一塊背部的肉，而沒有為他母親的兄弟留下胸肉，那人本預計當晚稍晚回家；他因這份欠缺體貼而心生不滿，決意藉助巫術，為庫亞瓦爾蘇克造一個圖皮拉克。他收集各種動物的骨頭，將其塑造成能化為不同動物——鳥類與海豹皆可——的形貌，並使之活轉過來，然後放它出去，命它去迫害庫亞瓦爾蘇克。它潛入海中，化為海豹之形出現，但他早已在歸家途中，正把皮划艇拖上岸——第二日、第三日亦然。它於是決意追到他家中，將他嚇死：它變身為圖格德利克（大北方潛鳥），開始在屋外尖聲啼叫；庫亞瓦爾蘇克走了出去，卻怎麼也不肯看它一眼，因此咒術無法生效。它鑽入地下，想從屋內冒出，也未能得逞；它從屋後升起，正當它要爬上屋頂時，遇上了他自己的護身鳥，那鳥立刻啄抓它的臉。它走投無路——「這可憐的蠢人為何要造出我來！」——在盛怒之下，它轉而對付造它的人：它潛入他捕魚處附近的水中，正好從他的皮划艇底下冒出，將艇徹底掀翻，當場把他吞食，然後遠遁到咆哮的大洋之上。庫亞瓦爾蘇克此後再未受侵擾，活到極老才去世。

title.en: The Two Brothers and the Supernatural Boat
title.zh: 兩兄弟與幽靈之舟

region.en: Fiord mouth, sunny and shady shores, West Greenland
region.zh: 西格陵蘭峽灣口的陽岸與陰岸

period: Inuit oral tradition; compiled from four manuscripts, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 14 'The Two Brothers', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A servant-girl, frozen speechless by the sight, watches an umiariak — a supernatural boat manned with fabulous beings — land glittering-sworded people who spear a tent through from all sides and leave all its inmates dead; the seals move out to sea with the water foaming. The surviving brother suspects her until he sees the pierced tent, then has an angakok spy the enemies far inland; guided by a one-eyed inlander whose shouts conjure three bears and then a multitude of archers, he hides behind his protector until the arrows abate, overtakes and kills the whole enemy party, and is repaid with renowned white-streaked reindeer skins carried home faster than he can follow.
summary.zh: 僕女目睹幽靈之舟——奇異生物駕駛、閃刀者登岸——將帳篷四面戳穿、殺盡居民，海豹隨泡沫奔海。倖存的弟弟起初疑心僕女行兇，見了洞穿的帳篷才釋疑；遂請巫師遙望，敵蹤遠在內陸。獨眼內陸人引路，一聲呼喚召出三熊、再呼喚召出弓箭大軍；弟弟藏於其身後，箭雨漸歇，二人追殺敵眾至一個不留。獨眼人看中他的魚叉，以斑紋白鹿皮相易；小婦人負皮疾奔，先他而抵，把鹿皮置於屋頂——他從此心安。

sensitivity.note: Rink's note: the umiariak is the avenging boat of seals overkilled; the inlanders may echo the Loucheux ('squint-eyes') Indians, described as arrow-proof by a movement of the eyes. Killed household recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Two brothers lived in the mouth of a fiord, the elder on the sunny side of the inlet, the other on the shady side. One night the servant of the younger brother, going behind the house, suddenly perceived something bright glittering out on the sea, and detected a boat that seemed to grow in size as it approached — an umiariak, a supernatural boat manned with fabulous beings. She wanted to run but was not able to stir; she tried to call out but could not utter a sound, and so must needs keep quiet. She saw a number of people land, all carrying glittering swords, walk straight up to the tent, and stick their spears through it from all sides; loud cries were heard from within, and the foreigners rushed down to their boat. She saw the water foaming and a multitude of seals moving out seawards, and was not able to rise till they were quite out of sight. Then she went to the tent, where she found all the inmates killed, and the earth covered with blood; though it was still dark she could not wait, but set off at once and wandered ever so far round the whole bay to reach the opposite shore where the other brother lived, and told him all her housemates had been put to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 14 'The Two Brothers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兩兄弟住在一個峽灣的灣口，兄長住在水灣向陽的一側，弟弟住在背陰的一側。一天夜裡，弟弟的僕人走到屋後，忽然看見海面上有東西閃閃發亮，並發現一隻船隨著靠近似乎越變越大——那是一艘烏米亞利亞克，一艘載著神話生靈的超自然之船。她想跑，卻動彈不得；她想呼喊，卻發不出半點聲音，只得默不作聲。她看見一群人上了岸，個個手持閃亮的刀劍，徑直走向帳篷，從四面把長矛刺進帳中；裡面傳出響亮的叫喊，那些外來者便衝回他們的船上。她看見海水翻騰，一大群海豹向海外游去，直到它們完全消失不見，她才得以起身。隨後她走到帳篷，發現裡面的人全被殺死，地上滿是血跡；雖然天還黑著，她卻等不下去，立刻動身，繞著整個海灣走了極遠的路，才到達對岸另一兄弟居住的地方，告訴他所有同屋的人都被殺害了。

passages.text: Somehow he got suspicious, believing she herself had killed them; seeing this, she merely said, 'First go and look for thyself, and afterward thou mayst kill me if thou likest.' He went across to his brother's station, and when he had seen the tent pierced from all sides he was reassured with regard to the servant, and only thought of finding out the enemies. He bespoke an angakok to come and point them out to him: at night, lamps extinguished, the angakok spoke, 'Look there; far away in the interior of the land, I espy them.' The next day the surviving brother paddled to the fiord head, left his kayak, and walked inland armed only with his spear until he discovered a house; stealing to the window he beheld a man with only one eye busily carving some implement out of wood, who caught sight of the stranger and invited him in — motioning him off a little, 'Don't sit quite so close to me; I might happen to cut thee.' A loud peal of laughter followed, and from beneath the ledge emerged a lot of narrajut (big-bellied), the only womankind of his household, returning with great quantities of meat, chiefly reindeer flesh and tallow. 'To-morrow I will go with thee and help thee to find out thy enemies, but now thou must lie down to rest here; thou hast nothing to fear.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 14 'The Two Brothers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不知怎的，他起了疑心，認為是她自己殺了那些人；見此情形，她只說道：「你先自己去看看吧，之後你若願意，盡可殺我。」他渡過水灣到兄弟的住處，當他看到帳篷四面被刺穿，便對那僕人放了心，只想著要找出那些敵人。他請來一位安加科克，請他為自己指出敵人的所在：夜裡，燈火熄滅，那安加科克說道：「看那邊；在陸地深處很遠的地方，我瞧見了他們。」第二天，那倖存的兄弟划槳到峽灣盡頭，留下皮划艇，只帶著長矛徒步深入內陸，直到發現一座房屋；他悄悄走到窗邊，看見一個只有一隻眼睛的人正忙著用木頭雕刻某件器具，那人瞧見了這陌生人，便邀他進屋——同時稍稍示意他退開些，「別坐得離我這麼近；我可能會不小心割到你。」接著響起一陣大笑，從壁架下鑽出一大群納拉尤特（大肚者），那是他家中僅有的女眷，帶著大量肉食歸來，主要是馴鹿肉和油脂。「明天我跟你一起去，幫你找出你的敵人，但現在你得在這裡躺下歇息；你沒什麼好怕的。」

passages.text: Next day the one-eyed man followed him, taking a large bunch of arrows fitted up in a skin cover, walking so quickly his companion could hardly keep up. Stopping, he put his arrows on the ground and said, 'Turn thy face towards the interior and give a shout'; the brother cried out aloud without knowing why, and three large bears instantly appeared — the one-eyed man aimed his bow and killed them all. 'Turn round and call as before!' — and a multitude of people appeared, armed with bows and arrows. Dreadfully frightened, he was told, 'Go and hide behind me; but mind, as soon as thou puttest forth thy head they'll shoot thee,' and sheltering behind his protector, trembling all the while, he saw the arrows flying right and left, decreasing in number, and finally abating altogether — the enemies having discharged all their arrows had taken flight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 14 'The Two Brothers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天，那獨眼人跟隨他同行，帶著一大捆裝在皮套裡的箭，走得極快，他的同伴幾乎跟不上。他停下來，把箭放在地上說道：「把臉轉向內陸，大喊一聲」；那兄弟不知為何便放聲大喊，三隻大熊立刻出現——獨眼人瞄準他的弓，把它們全都射死。「轉過身去，像剛才那樣呼喊！」——於是一大群人出現了，個個手持弓箭。他嚇得要命，卻被告知：「去躲到我身後；但記住，你一探出頭，他們就會射你。」他躲在他的保護者身後，一直渾身發抖，看著箭矢左右飛射，數目漸減，最後完全止息——那些敵人射光了所有的箭，便逃走了。

passages.text: The one-eyed man took up his bow, the still revengeful brother his spear, and both set off in pursuit, overtaking and killing the whole of them. On the way home the inlander noticed his companion's weapon, questioned him, never having seen the like before, and told him he would like very much to purchase it — and because of his handsome behaviour he had his wish. On their return they went together to his storehouse, and he was repaid with the renowned sea-hare skin (white reindeer skins with black streaks), one of the little women called to take them down: she put the bundle on her stomach and ran so fast with it that the visitor could not keep pace with her. Reaching home, he found them put on the roof of his house, and from that time his mind was at rest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 14 'The Two Brothers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 獨眼人拿起他的弓，那仍懷復仇之心的兄弟拿起他的長矛，兩人一同出發追擊，追上並殺光了他們所有人。歸途中，那內陸人注意到同伴的武器，便問起他，因為他從未見過這樣的東西，並告訴他自己非常想買下它——由於他為人慷慨得體，他如願以償。他們回來後，一同前往他的儲藏屋，他以著名的海兔皮（帶黑色條紋的白色馴鹿皮）作為回報，其中一個小婦人被喚來把這些皮取下來：她把那捆皮放在肚子上，跑得飛快，那訪客怎麼也跟不上她。回到家中，他發現那些皮已被放到他屋頂上，從那時起，他的心便安定了下來。

title.en: Mula Jadi Na Bolon: The Batak Creation and the Naga Padoha Beneath
title.zh: 穆拉·賈迪·納·波隆：巴塔克創世與地下那伽

region.en: Toba Batak country and Mount Pusuk Buhit, North Sumatra
region.zh: 北蘇門答臘多巴巴塔克之地與普素·布希山

period: Batak cosmogonic tradition recorded by H. N. van der Tuuk (J.R.A.S., N.S. vol. XIII, 1860s) and later ethnography

source.work: Batak cosmogonic tradition (Mula Jadi Na Bolon; Batara Guru's raft; Naga Padoha), as recorded in van der Tuuk's Batak studies

summary.en: In the beginning was Mula Jadi Na Bolon, 'the origin of becoming,' alone in the void; he creates the three levels of the world and three sons to rule them. The middle world is spread as dry land over the primeval waters — supported, the Toba Batak say, on the raft Batara Guru made at the creation, and held upon the back of the underworld serpent Naga Padoha, whose stirrings are the earthquakes.
summary.zh: 太初有『形成之源』穆拉·賈迪·納·波隆，獨存於虛空；他造世界三層，並生三子以分掌之。中界乃鋪於原水之上之乾土——多巴巴塔克人說：大地枕於巴塔拉·古魯創世時所造之筏上，臥於地下巨蛇那伽·帕多哈之背；蛇之一動，即為地震。

sensitivity.note: Batak cosmogony; the raft detail is cited by Skeat (1900) from the J.R.A.S. Batak material; paraphrase of the standard telling.

canonical_translation: Based on the standard Batak cosmogonic account (van der Tuuk tradition); paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The Batak cosmogony recorded in the great Batak studies of the nineteenth century tells how the world rests on agreements made in the deep past — and on a serpent who never agreed to them.

BEGINNING: THE ALONE ONE. Before everything was Mula Jadi Na Bolon, 'the origin of becoming,' alone in space, without companion or material. From his own substance he brings forth the framework of the cosmos in three levels — the upper world of the gods, the middle world of men, and the underworld of the dead and the powers below — and then three sons, to whom he allots these levels: Batara Guru in the highest, Sori Deak in the middle, and Mangalabulan below.

MIDDLE: THE RAFT AND THE SERPENT. The middle world is made habitable by spreading dry earth over the primeval waters; the earth rests, in the standard telling, on a raft which Batara Guru made for its support at the creation (the detail Skeat quotes from the J.R.A.S. Batak material). Beneath everything lies Naga Padoha, the great serpent of the underworld, on whose back the world-raft rides; when the serpent stirs — cramped, offended, or simply tired — the earth shakes, and the Batak offerings must remind him of his charge.

END: THE GRANDDAUGHTER'S DESCENT. To people the middle world, the line of the high god descends: Batara Guru's daughter (in the standard account the granddaughter of Mula Jadi Na Bolon) is sent down to the middle world and becomes the ancestress of mankind there; her descendants people the Toba highlands around the great lake, and the first of them, Si Raja Batak, is born on the holy mountain Pusuk Buhit. The three-level cosmos thus becomes a genealogy: the Batak live between the gods above and the serpent below, related to both.

FUNCTIONS. The cosmogony (1) explains the vertical order of the Batak universe and the places of ritual speech; (2) etiologizes earthquakes as the serpent's movement beneath the raft; (3) grounds the clans (marga) in a divine descent tied to Pusuk Buhit; and (4) supplies the world-serpent cluster's Sumatran highland form. The serpent's office is the cosmology's hinge: Naga Padoha is not a rebel to be defeated but a bearer to be maintained, and the Batak ritual address to him is contractual — offerings remind the serpent of the charge accepted at the creation, and earthquakes are read as arrears. The raft, likewise, is not merely a platform but a covenant-object: the world sits on something made, and made things can be renegotiated. To people the middle world, Batara Guru's daughter descends, and the genealogy that follows is the Batak system in miniature: the clans of the Toba country trace their marga to Si Raja Batak, born on the holy mountain Pusuk Buhit beside the lake, so that the cosmology's vertical levels — gods above, serpent below — are connected by a family tree running through the mountain's slopes. The story is told at both weddings and funerals, where the two directions of the vertical axis are invoked in turn.
narrative.zh: 十九世紀巴塔克研究記錄之創世論講述世界如何依遠古之約而安——以及一條從未應約之蛇。開篇：先有『形成之源』穆拉·賈迪·納·波隆，獨存無伴無材；自其本質生出三層宇宙（神之上界、人之中界、亡者與下方之力之下界），並生三子分掌：巴塔拉·古魯居最高，梭裏·迪亞克居中，芒加拉布蘭居下。中段：以乾土鋪於原水而使中界宜居；標準敘述云：地枕於巴塔拉·古魯創世時所造之筏（斯凱特引自J.R.A.S.巴塔克材料）；而萬物之下，臥著下界巨蛇那伽·帕多哈，世界之筏騎於其背；蛇一動（或拘、或怒、或倦），大地便震，巴塔克之祭品須提醒它記其職守。結尾：神裔降中界生民：巴塔拉·古魯之女（標準敘述中為穆拉之孫女）受遣下凡，成為人類之祖；其後裔繁於大湖周圍之多巴高地，其首者西·拉賈·巴塔克生於聖山普素·布希。三層宇宙於是成為譜系：巴塔克人上承諸神、下繫巨蛇，與兩界皆有血緣。功能：釋宇宙縱序與儀式語言之位、釋地震為筏下之蛇之動、以神裔繫氏族於聖山、並為世界蛇母題供給蘇門答臘高地之形態。

functions: Explains the three-level vertical cosmos of Batak ritual speech
Etiologizes earthquakes as the stirring of Naga Padoha beneath the world-raft
Grounds the Batak clans (marga) in divine descent tied to Mount Pusuk Buhit
Sumatran highland form of the world-serpent motif cluster

variants.name: Karo and Simalungun tellings
variants.summary: Neighbouring Batak peoples tell parallel creations with differing names and offspring orders.

variants.name: Comparative world-serpent myths
variants.text_tradition: Norse Jormungand; Hindu Shesha; Malay Ular Naga
variants.summary: The serpent beneath (or around) the world; the Batak Naga Padoha uniquely carries the earth-raft as a burden that can be renegotiated by offerings.

primary_sources.work: Batak cosmogonic tradition (Mula Jadi Na Bolon)
primary_sources.citation: Recorded in H. N. van der Tuuk's Batak studies (J.R.A.S., N.S. vol. XIII) and subsequent ethnography; paraphrased.

secondary_sources.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (note on the Batak raft)
secondary_sources.citation: Skeat 1900, London: Macmillan — note citing J.R.A.S. N.S. vol. XIII: the raft made by Batara Guru for the support of the earth at the creation.

source_urls.description: Internet Archive scan of Marsden, History of Sumatra (1784) — Batak country context

sensitivity_guidance: Living Batak religious tradition; paraphrase respectfully, avoid publishing ritual detail out of context.

passages.text: In the beginning was Mula Jadi Na Bolon, the origin of becoming, alone in the void; from his own substance he brings forth the three levels of the world and three sons — Batara Guru in the upper world, Sori Deak in the middle, Mangalabulan below.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the standard Batak cosmogonic account; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 起初，唯有穆拉·賈迪·納·博隆，即「生成之源」，獨處於虛空之中；他從自身的實體中生出世界的三個層次和三個兒子——上界的巴塔拉·古魯、中界的索里·德阿克、下界的曼加拉布蘭。

passages.text: The middle world is spread as dry earth over the primeval waters, resting on the raft which Batara Guru made for its support at the creation; beneath all lies the underworld serpent Naga Padoha, on whose back the raft rides, and whose stirrings are the earthquakes that offerings must soothe. The daughter of Batara Guru descends to people the middle world, and her line culminates in Si Raja Batak, born on the holy mountain Pusuk Buhit — the Batak living related to the gods above and the serpent below.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the standard Batak account (raft detail as cited in Skeat 1900 from the J.R.A.S. Batak material); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the standard Batak account; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 中間世界如乾燥的陸地般鋪展於原初之水上方，安放在巴塔拉·古魯於創世時為支撐它所造的筏上；一切之下伏著冥界巨蛇納迦·帕多哈，筏便行於其背上，而牠的翻動即是地震，必須以獻祭安撫。巴塔拉·古魯之女降臨以繁衍中間世界，其血脈終結於聖山普蘇克·布希特上所生的西·拉賈·巴塔克——巴塔克人因此與上方的諸神及下方的巨蛇皆有親緣。

title.en: The Origin of Lake Toba: The Fisherman Who Broke the Taboo
title.zh: 多巴湖之由來：破禁的漁夫

region.en: Lake Toba and Samosir island, North Sumatra
region.zh: 北蘇門答臘多巴湖與沙摩西島

period: Toba Batak oral legend; recorded in 19th-20th century collections

source.archive: Indonesian oral tradition (Toba Batak legend cycle)
source.work: The legend of the origin of Lake Toba (Toba Batak oral tradition)

summary.en: The fisherman who casts his hook into the Toba valley catches a golden fish that becomes a woman; he marries her on one condition — that he never tell anyone she was once a fish. Years later, in anger at his son, he breaks the promise; that night the sky darkens, the rains fall without end, the valley sinks, and the wife returns to the water: the drowned valley is Lake Toba, and the island where she set down her son in the flood is Samosir.
summary.zh: 漁夫在多巴谷地垂釣，釣上一尾化為女子之金魚；他娶之，唯一條件：永不可對人言其曾為魚。多年後，他怒於其子而破誓；當夜天昏雨瀉不止，谷地下陷，妻子歸水——被淹之谷是多巴湖，而她在洪水中放下兒子之處，便是沙摩西島。

sensitivity.note: Best-known Toba Batak legend; taboo-broken-flood cluster.

canonical_translation: Based on the Toba Batak oral legend; paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The origin legend of Lake Toba is the Toba Batak's great taboo-broken catastrophe story, told to explain the largest volcanic lake on earth and the island in its middle.

BEGINNING: THE GOLDEN FISH. A fisherman works the small rivers of the Toba valley and one day hooks a fish of golden shine; it speaks, and becomes a woman of great beauty. He marries her on her one condition: that he never tell anyone where she came from — that she was a fish of the water. They live well, and she bears a son.

MIDDLE: THE BROKEN SECRET. The boy grows hungry and greedy at meals, and one day the father, exhausted and furious, shouts the secret at him: 'You eat like the child of a fish — for your mother was a fish!' The word is out; the fish-wife hears it and grieves, for the promise that kept the world ordered is broken.

END: THE FLOODING OF THE VALLEY. That night the sky closes; rain falls without pause, and the waters rise from the earth as well as the sky. The wife returns to the water that made her, taking to safety the son she sets on the high ground that will become the island of Samosir; the father's valley floods entire. What had been fields and villages becomes Lake Toba, and the headland opposite Samosir keeps the father's name in the local tellings — the taboo's price still visible in the landscape.

FUNCTIONS. The legend (1) etiologizes Lake Toba and Samosir island; (2) polices the marriage-tell-no-origin taboo that governs many Batak affinity relationships; (3) supplies the Malay-world flood cluster with its highland Sumatran form; and (4) ties the landscape's topography to a moral memory told on every school trip to the lake. The legend's landscape is precise and checkable: Lake Toba fills a vast volcanic caldera, and Samosir is the island in its middle; the tellings align the boy's refuge with Samosir's high ground and keep the father's memory in the headland opposite. The moral architecture is equally exact: the fish-wife's single condition is the classic affinity taboo of the Batak world, in which a marriage partner's origin must not be named, and the father's breach is not mere anger but the public unmaking of the marriage's fiction — the word spoken aloud costs the world its surface. Village tellings distribute the blame variously: in some the son provokes the outburst, in others neighbours demand the secret, in others the father boasts; the flood follows the word, not the speaker. As comparative material, the legend belongs to the taboo-broken-flood cluster — Deucalion's flood, the sinking-village tales of Sundanese Situ Bagendit — with the distinctive feature that the survivor is the child of the taboo-breaker and the flood the return of the tabooed parent to her element.
narrative.zh: 多巴湖由來傳說乃多巴巴塔克最大之破禁災變故事，用以解釋世上最大火山湖及其中央之島。開篇：漁夫於多巴谷小河垂釣，一日釣得金光之魚；魚能言，化為美貌女子。他娶她，但只有一個條件：永不說出她的來歷——她本是水中之魚。二人生活美滿，得一子。中段：兒子進餐貪饞；一日父親疲憊憤怒，衝口而出：『你吃得像魚之子——因你母親本是魚！』誓言既破，魚妻聞言而悲——維持世界秩序的承諾已斷。結尾：當夜天閉，雨瀉不止，水自地中亦湧；妻子歸於其所從來之水，攜子置於高地——即日後之沙摩西島；父親的谷地盡沒。昔日田舍化為多巴湖，沙摩西對岸之岬在當地敘述中仍保留父親之名——禁忌之價，至今顯於山水。功能：釋多巴湖與沙摩西島、規訓巴塔克姻親之『勿言來歷』禁忌、為馬來世界洪水母題群供給蘇門答臘高地之形態、並將地貌與道德記憶繫於湖畔之講述。

functions: Etiology of Lake Toba and the island of Samosir
Policing the tell-no-origin taboo that governs Batak affinity marriages
Sumatran highland form of the flood cluster
Topography as moral memory in the landscape of the lake

variants.name: Samosir-mother variants
variants.summary: Village tellings vary in who hears the broken secret — son, neighbours, or the father's boast — and in the fate of the father.

variants.name: Comparative taboo-flood myths
variants.text_tradition: Genesis flood; Greek Deucalion; sinking-village tales
variants.summary: The flood that answers a broken promise; compare the Sundanese Situ Bagendit sinking-village tale.

primary_sources.work: Origin of Lake Toba (Toba Batak oral legend)
primary_sources.citation: Oral legend of the Toba Batak around Lake Toba, North Sumatra; recorded in modern Batak and Indonesian collections; paraphrased.

secondary_sources.work: William Marsden, The History of Sumatra
secondary_sources.citation: Marsden 1784, London — the Batta country and its great lake as the legend's setting.

source_urls.description: Internet Archive scan of Marsden, The History of Sumatra (1784)

sensitivity_guidance: Living legend with an active tourist site; paraphrase respectfully.

passages.text: The fisherman hooks a golden fish that speaks and becomes a woman; he marries her on the single condition that he never tell anyone she was once a fish of the water. In fury at his hungry son the father shouts the secret: 'You eat like the child of a fish — your mother was a fish!' The promise is broken, and the fish-wife hears it and grieves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Toba Batak legend of Lake Toba; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Toba Batak legend; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 漁夫釣起一尾會說話的金魚，牠化作一名女子；他娶了她，唯一的條件是他絕不向任何人吐露她曾是一尾水中之魚。父親因飢餓的兒子而大怒，喊出了那秘密：「你吃起來像魚的孩子——你母親是條魚！」誓言就此破裂，魚妻聽見了，悲痛不已。

passages.text: That night the rains fall without pause and the waters rise from the earth; the wife returns to the water, setting her son on the high ground that becomes the island of Samosir, and the drowned valley is Lake Toba — the taboo's price still visible in the landscape.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Toba Batak legend; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那一夜大雨不止，水從地中湧起；妻子回到水中，將兒子安置於高地，那高地便成了沙摩西島，而被淹沒的山谷即是多巴湖——禁忌的代價至今仍顯現於地景之中。

title.en: Si Raja Batak: Born on the Holy Mountain
title.zh: 西·拉賈·巴塔克：生於聖山

region.en: Mount Pusuk Buhit, Toba Batak country, North Sumatra
region.zh: 北蘇門答臘普素·布希山，多巴巴塔克之地

period: Toba Batak ancestral tradition

source.archive: Indonesian oral tradition (Toba Batak legend cycle)
source.work: The tradition of Si Raja Batak (Toba Batak ancestry)

summary.en: All the Toba Batak clans trace themselves to Si Raja Batak, the first man of the middle world, born on the holy mountain Pusuk Buhit beside Lake Toba. From his sons descend the great marga (clans) of the Batak country; the mountain remains the place where oaths are strongest and the oldest clan-songs return.
summary.zh: 多巴巴塔克諸氏族皆自『西·拉賈·巴塔克』——中界第一人——追溯血統；他生於多巴湖畔之聖山普素·布希。巴塔克大地之各大marga（氏族）皆其諸子之後；聖山至今為誓言最重之地，氏族最古之歌皆歸於此。

sensitivity.note: Clan-ancestry charter; careful with living clan claims, kept at tradition level.

passages.text: The Toba Batak clans trace their descent to Si Raja Batak, the first man of the middle world, born on the holy mountain Pusuk Buhit beside Lake Toba; from his sons descend the great marga of the Batak country. Pusuk Buhit remains the mountain of strongest oaths and the oldest clan-songs: genealogy, law and landscape are one in the Batak telling of the first man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Toba Batak ancestral tradition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 多巴巴塔克諸氏族追溯其血統至西·拉賈·巴塔克，即中間世界的第一人，生於多巴湖旁的聖山普蘇克·布希特；巴塔克地方的各大瑪爾加皆出自其諸子。普蘇克·布希特至今仍是立最重誓言之山，也是最古老氏族歌謠之山：在巴塔克人關於第一人的敘述中，譜系、律法與地景合而為一。

title.en: The Batak Ordeals: Rice That Turns to Stone
title.zh: 巴塔克神判：化為石頭的米

region.en: Batak country, North Sumatra
region.zh: 北蘇門答臘巴塔克之地

period: Customs observed by Marsden 1784, History of Sumatra

source.work: William Marsden, The History of Sumatra (1784), the oath-ordeals of the Batta people

summary.en: A person accused of a crime who asserts innocence may be acquitted by solemn oath, or by ordeal: a cock's throat is cut, and the accused, putting rice in his mouth, wishes it may turn to stone if he is guilty; or, holding up a musket bullet, wishes to be shot in that case. In weightier matters a small leaden or tin image is set in a dish of rice garnished with musket bullets, and the kneeling man prays that his crop may fail and his cattle die — and that he may never taste salt — if he lies.
summary.zh: 被控而自稱無辜者，可經莊嚴宣誓或神判而獲釋：割開公雞之喉，被告含米於口，祝曰若有罪則米化為石；或持火槍彈在手，祝曰若有罪則為彈所斃。重案則以鉛或錫小像置於撒有槍彈之米盤中，跪者禱曰：若吾說謊，願田禾絕收、牛群盡死、終身不得嘗鹽。

sensitivity.note: Eighteenth-century ethnography of Batak oath-law; the salt-curse remains a living idiom of oath-taking.

passages.text: A person accused of a crime who asserts innocence is in some cases acquitted by solemnly swearing to it, and is sometimes obliged to go through a kind of ordeal: a cock's throat is cut, the accused puts a little rice into his mouth and wishes it may become a stone if he is guilty of the crime charged.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Marsden, History of Sumatra (1784); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 被控犯罪而自稱無辜者，在某些情形下可藉莊嚴宣誓而獲開釋，有時則須經受一種神判：割斷公雞的喉嚨，被告將少許米放入口中，並祈願若他確犯所控之罪，那米便化為石頭。

passages.text: In more important instances they put a small leaden or tin image into the middle of a dish of rice garnished with musket bullets, and the man, kneeling down, prays that his crop of paddy may fail, his cattle die, and that himself may never taste salt — which is regarded as necessary to existence — if he does not declare the truth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Marsden (1784); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在更重大的案件中，他們將一枚小小的鉛製或錫製神像置於一盤以火槍彈丸點綴的米飯中央，男子跪下祈禱：若他不說出真相，願他的稻作歉收、牲畜死亡，且他本人永不嘗到鹽——鹽被視為生存所必需。

title.en: The White Buffalo's Entrails: War Augury of the Batak
title.zh: 白牛之腸：巴塔克戰卜

region.en: Batak country, North Sumatra
region.zh: 北蘇門答臘巴塔克之地

period: Customs observed by Marsden 1784, History of Sumatra

source.work: William Marsden, The History of Sumatra (1784), the war-divination of the Batta people

summary.en: Before going to war the Batak kill a perfectly white buffalo or fowl and judge the fortune of the campaign from the motion of the intestines. The priest who performs this ceremony 'had need to be infallible,' Marsden notes: if he predicts contrary to the event he is sometimes put to death for want of skill.
summary.zh: 出兵之前，巴塔克人宰殺純白之水牛或家禽，觀腸之動以判戰之吉凶。行此禮之祭司『必須無誤』——馬爾斯登記曰：若其預言與事實相反，有時即因『術之不精』而被處死。

sensitivity.note: Historical ethnography of sacrificial divination; noted as custom, not prescription.

passages.text: Before they go to war they kill a buffalo or a fowl that is perfectly white, and by observing the motion of the intestines they judge of the good or ill fortune that will attend them. The priest who performs this ceremony had need to be infallible, for if he predicts contrary to the event he is sometimes put to death for his want of skill — the augur's life staked with the army's fortune.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Marsden, History of Sumatra (1784); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Marsden (1784); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們出征之前，會宰殺一頭水牛或一隻純白的家禽，並藉由觀察其腸子的蠕動，來判斷此行將遭遇的是吉是凶。主持此儀式的祭司必須萬無一失，因為若他的預言與結果相違，有時便會因技藝不精而被處死——占卜者的性命，與全軍的命運同繫一線。

title.en: The Months-Long Funeral: Dancing Round the Coffin, Fleeing the Fiend
title.zh: 經月之葬：繞棺之舞與逐鬼之奔

region.en: Batak country, North Sumatra
region.zh: 北蘇門答臘巴塔克之地

period: Rites observed by Marsden 1784, History of Sumatra

source.work: William Marsden, The History of Sumatra (1784), the funeral rites and ceremonies of the Batta people

summary.en: When a raja or person of consequence dies, the funeral may take up several months: the corpse is kept unburied in a hollowed gomuti-tree coffin sealed with dammar, a bamboo tube draining into the ground. When the relatives and creditors assemble, each woman brings a biscuit of rice and dances round the coffin; the priest, in robes cut like birds and beasts and painted various colours, swings buffalo flesh, kills a fowl over the body, then seizes a cocoanut-fibre broom and sweeps furiously about as if to chase away an evil spirit — at which four appointed men lift the coffin and run with it as if escaping the fiend, the priest sweeping after it for some distance before the grave is closed and buffalo horns nailed to the posts.
summary.zh: 拉賈或顯要亡故，葬禮常歷時數月：屍身不葬，置於鏤空之糖棕木棺，以達瑪脂封之，棺底插竹管入地排水。親友債主齊集之日，每位婦女攜米餅近屍，繞棺而舞歡飲；祭司身著鳥獸形彩衣，揮舞水牛肉、殺雞瀝血於棺，繼而抓起椰纖之帚狂掃四週如逐惡鬼——四名指定之人立時抬起棺木疾奔，如逃離魔掌，祭司追掃甚遠；墓既封，水牛之角釘於柱上，眾人乃安然散歸。

sensitivity.note: Historical ethnography of Batak funerary rite (as observed 1784); the modern rite differs — noted to avoid antiquarian fixity.

passages.text: When a raja or person of consequence dies, the funeral usually takes up several months: the corpse is kept unburied in a coffin of the hollowed gomuti tree well covered with dammar, a bamboo tube inserted below carrying away the matter into the ground till the bones alone remain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Marsden, History of Sumatra (1784); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當一位拉者或有地位的人去世時，葬禮通常要持續數月之久：遺體不入土，而是安放在一具以挖空的戈穆蒂樹製成的棺木中，棺外密密塗滿達瑪樹脂，下方插入一根竹管，將滲出的液體導引至地下，直到僅剩骨骸為止。

passages.text: When the people assemble each woman brings a biscuit of rice and places it near the corpse; they dance round it and make merry, killing buffaloes or horses for the feast. The priest, whose robes are cut into the shape of birds and beasts and painted of different colours, takes a piece of buffalo's flesh, swings it about in violent attitudes, and eats it voraciously; he kills a fowl over the dead body, letting the blood run upon the coffin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Marsden (1784); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 眾人聚集之時，每個婦人都帶來一塊米製的餅，放置在遺體近旁；她們繞著它跳舞作樂，並宰殺水牛或馬匹以供宴饗。祭司的袍服裁成鳥獸之形，並塗上種種不同的顏色；他取來一塊水牛肉，以激烈的姿態揮舞擺盪，再狼吞虎嚥地吃下；他又在死者遺體上方宰殺一隻家禽，任鮮血淌流在棺木之上。

passages.text: He then takes a broom of cocoanut fibres and sweeps furiously about him as if to chase away some evil spirit; when suddenly four men appointed for the purpose lift up the coffin and run quickly off with it, as if escaping from the fiend, the priest continuing to sweep after it for some distance. It is then buried; the horns of the buffalos killed on the occasion are nailed to the posts, and the people depart in peace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Marsden (1784); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著，他取來一把椰纖製成的掃帚，在自己四周猛烈地揮掃，彷彿要驅趕某種惡靈；忽然間，四名為此指派的人員抬起棺木，迅速奔逃而去，好似在躲避那惡魔一般，祭司則繼續在後追掃了一段距離。隨後棺木入土；當日所宰水牛的角被釘在柱上，眾人便安然散去。

title.en: The Skull at the Raja's Door: Marsden's Testimony on the Old Feast
title.zh: 王邸門前之顱：馬爾斯登之證言

region.en: Batak country, North Sumatra (eighteenth century)
region.zh: 北蘇門答臘巴塔克之地（十八世紀）

period: Recorded by Marsden, History of Sumatra (1784), from the accounts of residents and travellers

source.work: William Marsden, The History of Sumatra (1784), the Batta customs section (skull trophy and feast accounts)

summary.en: Marsden records, from the converging testimony of English residents at Natal and Tappanooly, the old Batak custom of the prisoner's feast: Charles Miller's journal notes a man's skull hanging in the raja's hall 'placed there as a trophy, it being the skull of an enemy they had taken prisoner, whose body, according to the custom of the Battas, they had eaten about two months before' — a rite of absorbing the enemy's strength, Marsden argues, attested by old writers and recent witnesses alike.
summary.zh: 馬爾斯登據納塔爾與塔帕努利英國居民之一致證言，記錄巴塔克俘虜之宴古俗：查爾斯·米勒日記見拉賈廳中懸一人顱——『作為戰利品懸於此；此乃所擒之敵之顱，依巴塔克之俗，其身於約兩月前已食』——馬爾斯登論曰：此乃吸收敵力之儀，古書近證皆相合。

sensitivity.note: Historical ethnography of a discontinued rite; presented as eighteenth-century testimony, framed within its colonial context of reporting. No present-day community is accused.

passages.text: Charles Miller, in the journal quoted by Marsden, writes: 'In the house where the raja receives strangers we saw a man's skull hanging up, which the raja told us was placed there as a trophy, it being the skull of an enemy they had taken prisoner, whose body, according to the custom of the Battas, they had eaten about two months before.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the testimony quoted in Marsden, History of Sumatra (1784); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 查爾斯·米勒在馬斯登所引述的日誌中寫道：「在拉者接待外人的那間屋裡，我們看見一顆懸掛著的人頭骨；拉者告訴我們，那是作為戰利品而掛在那裡的，是一名被他們俘虜的敵人的頭骨，而其屍身則依巴塔人的習俗，已在大約兩個月前被他們吃掉了。」

passages.text: Marsden gathers the converging accounts of the residents of Natal and Tappanooly and concludes that the experience of later days agrees with the uniform testimony of old writers — presenting the practice as a rite of the period, framed within the colonial context of its reporting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Marsden (1784); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬斯登彙集了納塔爾與塔帕努利兩地居民彼此吻合的記述，並斷定後世的經驗與舊時作家眾口一致的證詞相符——將此習俗呈現為當時的一種儀式，並置於其記述所處的殖民脈絡之中。

title.en: Giviok: The Voyage Past Whirlpool, Sea-Lice, and the Tail-Hag
title.zh: 吉維奧克：漩渦、海虱與斷尾老嫗之間

region.en: Open sea and other shore, Greenland voyage
region.zh: 格陵蘭外海與彼岸

period: Inuit oral tradition; chiefly from a single manuscript, well known all over Greenland, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 15 'Giviok', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Unable to abandon his motherless son, Giviok at last flees when the boy cries that his dead mother is walking outside with a stranger — the resurrected wife he then kills a second time and stacks in her stone grave. Paddling on, he cheats the whirlpool, feeds the sea-lice with gloves till his paddle-blades are sheathed, sleeps on a raft of sea-weed, and squeezes through two closing icebergs that bruise his stern. Warned by rowed-up human heads and a glittering tail, he foils the man-killing hag Usorsak with a flat stone on his chest — breaking her tail — kills her shrieking daughter, then wintered with two kindly halibut-haunting women whose bladders he fetches back through the tide. Coming home he finds his abandoned child a grown whale-hunter standing on a whale's back.
summary.zh: 吉維奧克不忍拋下喪母的幼子；直到孩子哭喊『死去的母親正與陌生人同行』，他二度殺妻，疊屍石墓，終於駕艇出走。途中他逃過漩渦，以手套餵飽海虱，睡於海藻浮筏，從合攏的冰山夾縫中擠過，艇尾被擠傷。借人頭堆與閃亮尾巴識破食人老嫗烏索薩克，以胸前置石使其斷尾斃命，再叉殺其女。後與兩位善良的大比目魚漁婦同住，為她們追回漂流的大魚。歸鄉之日，當年拋下的幼兒已是立於鯨背的偉大獵手。

sensitivity.note: Rink notes slight traces of the Hiawatha tale type. Killing of the resurrected wife and of the hag's daughter recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Giviok, it is told, lost his wife and was about to leave his child and the place where she was buried, in despair. He only waited till the boy had gone to sleep, then let himself down from the ledge to the floor; but when the child began crying he again lay down beside him. Once he was all ready, stooping to get out of the entrance, but went back unable to leave his son. One day the little boy passionately entered the room, saying, 'My mother is walking outside with a stranger.' 'Thy mother is not here; she is lying under the big stones yonder.' 'Look for thyself, then' — and when Giviok did look out of the window, he actually saw his wife in the arms of another man. At this he got into a great rage, went out, killed them, and put them on top of each other into the stone grave. Father and son went to rest; but when the boy slept the father carried out his intention of taking flight, and passing through the doorway — this time resisting the cries of the boy — got into his kayak and hastened away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 15 'Giviok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說，吉維奧克失去了妻子，在絕望之中，他正打算拋下孩子，離開她所埋葬的地方。他只等到男孩睡著，便從高台溜到地面；但孩子一哭，他又躺回他身旁。有一次他已準備妥當，彎下身要從入口出去，卻又折返，無法離開兒子。有一天，小男孩激動地衝進屋裡，說：「我母親正和一個陌生人在外面走著。」「你母親不在這裡；她躺在那邊的大石頭底下。」「那你自己看吧。」——吉維奧克從窗戶望出去，果真看見妻子在另一個男人的懷裡。他因此勃然大怒，走出去殺了他們，把他們疊在一起放進石墓裡。父子倆去歇息；但男孩睡著後，父親便實行他逃跑的打算，穿過門口——這回不再理會男孩的哭喊——上了他的獨木舟，匆匆離去。

passages.text: He paddled on and on across the wild sea; he came to the whirlpool and was nearly drawn into it, but somehow escaped. Then he got among the villainous sea-lice: first he tried to keep them back by striking at them with his kayak-stick, but that was soon devoured; then he threw out his sealskin gloves, and seeing they lasted a little longer, covered his paddle-blades with a pair of old gloves, lest the beasts should attack his paddle before he could slip away — and managed to get past them. Continuing his voyage, he saw a long black line: sea-weed, so compact he got out and slept on it, then pushed himself and his kayak across with his hands. He paddled until he came in sight of two icebergs with a narrow passage between them, alternately opening and closing; paddling round outside them, they always kept ahead of him, so at length he ventured between — pushing on with great speed, he had just passed when the bergs closed together and the stern-point of his kayak got bruised between them. At last he caught a glimpse of something dark, and soon reached a great stretch of land looming ahead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 15 'Giviok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他划了又划，橫越狂野的大海；他來到漩渦，幾乎被捲了進去，但總算設法逃脫。接著他闖進了兇惡的海蝨群中：起初他試著用獨木舟的槳棍擊退牠們，但那槳棍很快就被啃光了；於是他扔出他的海豹皮手套，見它們撐得稍久一些，便用一雙舊手套裹住槳葉，免得那些野獸在他還來不及溜走之前就攻擊他的槳——他總算設法通過了牠們。繼續航行，他看見一道長長的黑線：是海草，密實得他索性走上去睡了一覺，然後用手把自己和獨木舟推過去。他划著，直到望見兩座冰山，中間有一道狹窄的通道，時而張開、時而閉合；他繞著冰山外側划，它們卻總是在他前頭，於是他終於冒險從中間穿過——他飛快地推進，剛一通過，兩座冰山便合攏起來，他獨木舟的船尾尖端被夾傷了。最後他瞥見一團黑影，不久便抵達一片在前方隱約浮現的廣闊陸地。

passages.text: 'If this country be inhabited, I will be sure to find a bare rock' — and such a one he found, then a house by the smoking chimney. He went straight to it, upset the funnel, and hid; a female came rushing out — 'I wonder if any one upset it?' — put it to rights, perceiving Giviok, quickly re-entered, and as quickly returned: 'Thou art invited to step inside.' Inside lay a hideous old hag beneath a coverlet, who ordered her daughter to fetch berries; she returned with a great quantity profusely mixed with fat. 'They are really delicious,' remarked Giviok. 'No wonder; the fat is of quite a young fellow,' rejoined Usorsak, the name of the old hag — but Giviok answered, 'Fie! anything of that kind I cannot eat,' and stooping down noticed a lot of human heads all in a row beneath the ledge; and when the hag uncovered herself a little and turned her back towards him, he saw something glittering close behind her. When all were ready to go to rest, Giviok went outside and soon found a flat stone to cover his breast with, then lay down on the ledge beneath the window. No sooner did he seem to be sleeping than the daughter said, 'Now he is sound asleep,' and the old hag came jumping down from the main ledge — but on his feigning not to be quite asleep she cautiously returned; when he had become quiet, lying on his back with his breast exposed, the daughter said again, 'He surely sleeps now,' and the mother let herself down even quicker, jumping up where he lay and sitting down with all her weight upon his chest, crying out 'Oh dear!' — and instantly tumbled down. 'What a pity!' cried the daughter; 'Usorsak has broken her tail; she provided so nicely for all of us.' Giviok got up from his couch, let fall the stone, and escaped through the door, the daughter shouting after him, 'Thou rascal! wouldn't I like to have had a taste of thy fine cheeks!' — but he was already in his kayak, where he was nearly upset; rising again he broke out, 'Shouldn't I like to harpoon her!' and so saying killed her on the spot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 15 'Giviok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「若這地方有人居住，我一定能找到一塊裸露的岩石」——他果然找到了這樣一塊，接著又找到一間煙囪冒著煙的屋子。他徑直走過去，掀翻煙囪管，躲了起來；一個女人衝了出來——「不知是不是有人把它掀翻了？」——她把煙囪管扶正，察覺到吉維奧克，便迅速回到屋裡，又同樣迅速地出來：「請你進來。」屋裡，一個醜陋的老巫婆躺在被單底下，她吩咐女兒去採漿果；女兒帶回一大堆，裡面拌了大量油脂。「真是美味，」吉維奧克說。「難怪；那油脂可是個年輕小夥子的，」老巫婆烏索爾薩克答道——但吉維奧克回答：「呸！那種東西我可吃不下，」他彎下身，注意到高台底下整齊排著一大排人頭；而當老巫婆稍稍掀開被單、背對著他時，他看見她背後緊貼著什麼閃閃發亮的東西。當大家都準備就寢時，吉維奧克走到外面，很快找到一塊扁石頭蓋住自己的胸口，然後躺在窗下的高台上。他才剛像是睡著，女兒便說：「現在他睡熟了，」老巫婆從主高台上跳下來——但因為他假裝還沒完全睡著，她又小心翼翼地退了回去；等他安靜下來，仰面躺著、胸口露出來時，女兒又說：「他這會兒一定睡著了，」母親便更迅速地縱身而下，跳到他躺著的地方，用全身重量坐到他胸口上，大叫一聲「哎喲！」——隨即滾落下來。「真可惜！」女兒喊道；「烏索爾薩克把尾巴摔斷了；她本來為我們大家都安排得那麼好。」吉維奧克從臥處起身，丟下石頭，從門口逃了出去，女兒在他身後喊道：「你這壞蛋！我多想嘗嘗你那漂亮的臉頰啊！」——但他早已上了獨木舟，在那裡他差點翻船；重新坐穩後，他脫口而出：「我多想用魚叉叉她！」說著便當場把她殺了。

passages.text: Continuing his journey he again reached a bare rock, landed, went up to a house, upset the chimney-funnel, and hid himself; when the woman emerged and re-entered, he heard them wondering at the chimney having been upset, there being no wind. Invited inside, he observed the walls covered all over with hunting-bladders, the inmates a mother and daughter. The mother spoke: 'It will soon be low-water; it is a bad job for us that we have no one to haul in our draught when we have harpooned and fixed the bladders to the fishes.' 'I have my kayak close by, and have just come from the bad women yonder, both of whom I have killed.' 'Then thanks to thee!... We, too, have had men in our house, but these monsters put all of them to death; but now thou hadst better stay here with us.' To-morrow there would be low-water: when he heard a roaring noise he must hasten back, for then the high tide set in. He was sound asleep when awakened by the roaring waters and saw the daughter glide through the house-passage; hastening down to the shore, he was only in time to finish off a few of the halibut lying high and dry on the beach when the rising waters rolled great waves over him, and he had a narrow escape to the coast. The harpooned fish, floating by their bladders, drove across to the opposite shore; Giviok fetched them back in his kayak, for which the women were very thankful, and he remained with them for some time. After a while the memory of his son haunted him — 'My poor little son! what a pitiful thing it was to hear him cry when I went away! Some day I must go and see him' — and travelling back past all the dangers, he reached the opposite country and heard people singing: a great many boats tugging a whale along, on which stood a vigorous man. He did not recognise him; but this was his son, and he had been catching the whale. The father left him a weeping child, and now beheld him a great hunter, standing on a whale's back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 15 'Giviok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他繼續旅程，又抵達一塊裸露的岩石，上了岸，走向一間屋子，掀翻煙囪管，躲了起來；當那女人出來又進去後，他聽見她們納悶煙囪管怎麼會被掀翻，明明沒有風。他被邀進屋內，看見牆上掛滿了獵囊，屋裡住著一對母女。母親開口說：「很快就要退潮了；我們沒有幫手，等我們用魚叉叉中魚、把獵囊綁上去之後，沒人替我們把獵物拖進來，這對我們可是件麻煩事。」「我的獨木舟就在附近，我剛從那邊的壞女人那兒來，她們兩個都被我殺了。」「那真要感謝你！……我們屋裡也曾有過男人，但那些怪物把他們全都弄死了；如今你最好留在這裡和我們一起。」明天就要退潮：當他聽見轟隆聲時，就必須趕緊回來，因為那時漲潮就要開始。他正睡得沉，被水聲驚醒，看見女兒滑過屋子的通道；他急忙趕到岸邊，只來得及把幾條擱在灘上乾處的大比目魚收拾掉，漲起的水便掀起大浪朝他湧來，他險些才逃回岸上。那些被魚叉叉中、靠獵囊漂浮的魚，漂到了對岸；吉維奧克划著獨木舟把它們取了回來，母女倆為此非常感激，他便在她們那裡待了一段時日。過了些時候，對兒子的思念纏上了他——「我可憐的小兒子！我離開時聽他哭，真是讓人心酸！總有一天我得去看看他」——於是他一路回去，經過所有危險，抵達對岸的地方，聽見人們在唱歌：許多船正拖著一頭鯨魚，鯨背上站著一個健壯的男人。他認不出他；但那正是他的兒子，是他捕到了那頭鯨魚。父親離開他時，他還是個哭泣的孩子，如今卻見他成了偉大的獵人，站在鯨魚背上。

title.en: Tiggak: The Sorcerer Who Sang the Sea and Ate the Brains
title.zh: 提加克：唱海、食腦的巫師

region.en: Ice fields and the enemy country beyond the isthmus
region.zh: 冰原與地峽彼端的敵邦

period: Inuit oral tradition; abstract from three varying Greenland copies, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 16 'Tiggak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: The lazy sorcerer Tiggak shames his brothers-in-law by hauling in two seals through a snowstorm, then prophesies their storm from drifting sea-weed, sings his one song of ocean foam to land them on a driving iceberg, and sings water out of its centre. Taken to a giant-house where his brother-in-law is hoisted through the ceiling to be flensed alive, Tiggak feigns defeat to kill the wrestler, answers his own 'Haul away!' to flense the flensers, calls down his blood-stained amulet from the boat-pillars to avenge them all, then eats the served-up brains, hands, and feet of his victim with shut eyes and turns the dish on the hag — who goes raving mad and dies. Sliding into the sea as a bear, he leads the whole party home transformed, the snow-bunting boy flying between their ears.
summary.zh: 懶散的巫師提加克風雪中拖回兩頭海豹，令內兄弟們羞愧；又憑漂向岸邊的海藻預言風暴，以一首海沫之歌將眾人引上漂流的冰山，再唱出冰心湧泉解渴。在巨人屋中，眼看內兄被吊上天花板活剮，他詐敗反殺摔跤巨人，學其聲音喊『拉繩』、『割吧』，讓屋上剮人者自剮其主；再呼血染的護身符復仇，閉眼吃下被殺內兄的腦漿手足，把菜盤一翻——老嫗發狂而死。滑入海中化為熊，他領眾人化熊泅渡歸鄉；雪鳥化身的養子飛倦了，便歇在熊耳之間。

sensitivity.note: Rink abstracted three Greenland copies; Labrador traces of the same tale exist. Cannibalism and killing recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Tiggak was a famous angakok and sorcerer who married a girl with a number of brothers, and after this grew neglectful of his duties and gave up hunting: when the brothers-in-law left home in the morning they could not persuade him to follow, and sometimes he even slept till the first of the kayakers returned, doing nothing but keep his wife company and dawdle the time away. This offended the other men. When one of the brothers ordered boiled briskets, he said to Tiggak as they were served up, 'Do eat some meat — that is easy work'; Tiggak took a considerable quantity and ate away without giving any answer. In midwinter a gale from the north set in; the brothers lived solely upon stored-up provisions until these came to an end, and one day, when they could not even go out in the kayak, Tiggak was missing. Towards evening they looked about for him in a terrible snow-drift, and late at night heard a call and saw him approaching, dragging two seals along with him. From that time he rose in their estimation; he now had the briskets served up and addressed the brothers: 'Now come and fall to; the meat is boiled and served up, and eating it is easy work.' They all ate, but nobody spoke; and all the winter he continued providing for the others, in summer letting his brothers-in-law undertake the task themselves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 16 'Tiggak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蒂加克是著名的安加科克（巫師）與術士，他娶了一個有許多兄弟的姑娘，此後便疏於職責，不再打獵：妻舅們早晨離家時，怎麼也勸不動他同行，有時他甚至睡到第一批划獨木舟的人回來，什麼也不做，只陪著妻子，虛度時光。這惹惱了其他男人。有一次，其中一個兄弟吩咐煮牛胸肉，肉端上來時，他對蒂加克說：「吃點肉吧——那可是輕鬆活兒」；蒂加克拿了相當多，埋頭吃著，一句話也不答。隆冬時節，北面颳起大風；兄弟們全靠儲存的糧食過活，直到糧食吃盡，有一天，他們連獨木舟都出不了海，蒂加克卻不見了。傍晚時分，他們在猛烈的風雪中四處找他，深夜聽見一聲呼喚，見他拖著兩隻海豹走來。從那時起，他在他們心目中的分量提高了；這回輪到他吩咐端上牛胸肉，並對兄弟們說：「來吧，動手吃吧；肉煮好了、端上來了，吃它可是輕鬆活兒。」大家都吃了，卻沒人作聲；整個冬天他都繼續供養其他人，到了夏天，便讓妻舅們自己擔起這差事。

passages.text: Subsequently Tiggak adopted a boy as his son. Once more it was winter, the sea covered with ice as far as the eye could see, and Tiggak the only one to roam about upon the ice, looking out for the haze and seeking the open holes where sea animals resort to breathe. One cloudless, windless day he turned to his adopted son: 'To-day thou mayst come with us and try thy hand at seal-catching.' At the remotest islets he made an opening in the ice to examine the waters beneath: 'I believe it will come to pass; the sea-weed seems to be drifting landwards: just look' — the current setting towards land was stronger than usual, and he said, 'We shall have a gale presently; let us make all haste for the shore.' Though they could hardly credit his words, the weather being so calm, they left their seals behind and followed him quickly; then the snow was seen foaming on the mountain-peaks, and when they had only reached the first row of islets the storm burst strong and fierce and broke up the ice. Tiggak took his son's hand, running and leaping across the clefts, until a very broad one near the land: all jumped over but the son, who kept running to and fro along the edge; Tiggak took pity and returned to him — and then they all drifted away seawards, the waves washing over the floe, and they grew silent with fear. 'It is said that Tiggak is learned in magic art, and we are drifting out to the wild sea.' 'I only know a short song treating of the ocean foam' — and at once he began singing; they saw an iceberg close in front of them, watched their chance against its driving up and down, and Tiggak jumped first and got sure footing, the others following. Drifting further out, one remarked they would perish of thirst unless Tiggak knew some charm: 'I only know this one little song to get water' — and a little spring bubbled forth from the centre of the iceberg, which he tasted first, permitting them to drink only then, so it could not change.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 16 'Tiggak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 後來，蒂加克收養了一個男孩作兒子。又到了冬天，海面結冰，一望無際，只有蒂加克一個人在冰上遊走，察看霧氣，尋找海獸前來呼吸的冰洞。一個無雲無風的日子，他對養子說：「今天你可以跟我們一起來，試試你的身手捕海豹。」在最遠的小島上，他在冰上開了一個洞，察看底下的水：「我相信會應驗的；海草似乎正往陸地方向漂：你瞧」——流向陸地的水流比平常更強，他說：「馬上就要起大風了；我們趕快全都回岸上去。」雖然天氣如此平靜，他們幾乎不信他的話，還是把海豹丟下，快步跟著他走；接著便看見山頂上雪花翻騰，他們才剛到第一排小島，暴風便猛烈地襲來，把冰都打碎了。蒂加克牽著兒子的手，在冰縫間奔跑跳躍，直到靠近陸地的一道極寬的裂縫：大家都跳了過去，只有兒子沒跳，沿著邊緣來回奔跑；蒂加克心生憐憫，折回去找他——於是他們全都隨著浮冰漂向海裡，海浪沖刷著冰塊，他們因恐懼而沉默下來。「據說蒂加克精通法術，而我們正漂向狂野的大海。」「我只會一首講海洋泡沫的短歌」——他立刻唱了起來；他們看見一座冰山就在正前方，趁著它上下浮動的時機，蒂加克先跳上去站穩了腳，其他人跟著跳上。再往外漂，有人說除非蒂加克懂得什麼咒語，否則他們會渴死：「我只會這一首取水的小歌」——冰山中央便湧出一小股泉水，他先嘗了嘗，然後才准他們喝，這樣水就不會變質。

passages.text: Drifting a long time, they came in sight of an extensive country; Tiggak warned that whoever leaped ashore must not look towards the sea so long as any were behind, otherwise their place of refuge would break up and be annihilated. One by one they jumped ashore without looking round; when the last had safely landed, Tiggak turned and exclaimed, 'Behold our place of refuge!' — and lo, nothing remained of it but a heap of foam. Crossing an isthmus they came in sight of many houses and were invited into one, hanging their outer garments on the boat-pillars; during the meal a squint-eyed youth with a shaggy head appeared in the doorway: 'The strangers from the east are hereby invited to pay a visit.' The host said, 'Since he presses you so ardently, you will be obliged to go.' In the other house a disagreeable giant-like man sat on the main ledge, beside him a similar old woman gnawing at a big shoulder-bone; pulling forth a seal-skin and spreading it on the ground, the huge man exclaimed in a deep voice, 'Now come on for a wrestling-match!' The brothers whispered Tiggak to take the first turn — 'Not so; you go down first, then I'll follow' — the other guests were ordered away, and the old hag fastened the door with the shoulder-blade. One of the brothers hooked his arm into the giant's; unable to vanquish him, he was obliged to give in, the strong man catching hold of his lower parts, falling over him, and with a deep groan crushing him to death. A rope was let down through the ceiling, the dead man's body fastened and hoisted to the roof of the house, where a sound of knives was presently heard, and one cried out, 'Here is his eye; let it be kept for our master.' Tiggak thought, 'In this manner I shall soon lose all my brothers-in-law,' and whispered to him who was going to stand forward, 'Just let me take a turn with him!' Hooking arms, the giant took a pull in good earnest, nearly hauling Tiggak's arm across; pausing a minute, Tiggak feigned to have been overcome, then suddenly threw him down and leapt upon him, the brothers coming to his aid and putting him to death in the same way he had treated their brother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 16 'Tiggak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們漂流了許久，望見一片廣闊的陸地；提加克警告說，凡是跳上岸的人，只要後面還有人未上岸，就絕不可朝海的方向看，否則他們的避難之所就會崩裂、化為烏有。他們一個接一個跳上岸，都沒有回頭看；當最後一人安然登岸後，提加克轉過身來喊道：「看哪，我們的避難之所！」——豈料那地方只剩下一堆泡沫。他們穿過一道地峽，望見許多房屋，並受邀進入其中一間，把外衣掛在船柱上；用餐時，一個斜眼、頭髮蓬亂的青年出現在門口：「謹此邀請來自東方的陌生人前去拜訪。」主人說：「既然他如此殷切相邀，你們就不得不去了。」在另一間屋裡，一個令人不快的巨人般的男子坐在主炕上，身旁是一個與他相仿的老婦，正啃著一根大肩胛骨；那巨人取出一張海豹皮鋪在地上，用低沉的聲音喊道：「來吧，來角力一場！」兄弟們低聲要提加克先上場——「不行；你先下去，我隨後就來」——其餘的客人被喝令離去，那老妖婆用肩胛骨把門閂上。兄弟之一與巨人挽起手臂；他無法取勝，只得認輸，那壯漢抓住他的下身，撲倒在他身上，隨著一聲深沉的呻吟把他壓死。一條繩子從天花板垂下來，死者的屍體被綁住吊上屋頂，隨即傳來刀子的聲響，有人喊道：「這是他的眼睛；留著給我們的主人。」提加克心想：「這樣下去，我很快就要失去所有的姻親了」，便對那個正要上前的人低聲說：「就讓我跟他較量一番吧！」兩人挽起手臂，巨人著實用力一拉，幾乎把提加克的手臂扯過身去；提加克停頓片刻，假裝已被制伏，隨即猛然把他摔倒，躍身壓上，兄弟們前來相助，用他對待他們兄弟的同樣方式把他殺死。

passages.text: Imitating the voice of the other, Tiggak now called out, 'A rope, a rope!' which instantly appeared and was made fast round the giant's neck; 'Haul away!' — once more the sound of knives was heard, until one cried out, 'Are we not flensing our own master? We'll make them perish down below!' — and they commenced pouring water down upon them. No means of escape appearing, Tiggak remembered that his amulet was sewed up in the lining of his outer jacket, left on the boat-pillars on their arrival, and called out, 'Bring me my coat that lies outside; I want it for a shroud!' Contrary to his anticipations it was instantly thrown down; catching hold of it, he loosened his amulet from within the fur-lining, put it into his mouth, and after saying 'Revenge us!' took it out again. Voices outside cried, 'He is falling! — and he too! — and there is another one!' — and after a while the amulet returned, covered with blood. Well wiped and cleaned, the owner again threw it out and cried, 'All of them!'; the next time no sound was heard outside. Pushing forward from a corner of the ledge they found their way out, saw no person alive, and went back to the first house to their meal — but the silly-looking youth again appeared: 'I'll tell you what — Apiak is now doing her very worst: she is cooking the brains, hands, and feet of her son.' Tiggak could not understand him, until a brother explained: it was the brains, hands, and feet of the one killed up yonder, and his mother probably intended to regale him with a dish made of them. When asked to go he would perceive an oblong dish right in front of the entrance, filled with brains nicely served up; taking hold of it quickly, standing erect with his face turned towards her and his eyes shut, he must eat it all up — if with open eyes, he would go mad and die — then turn the dish upside down, put it back in its place, open his eyes, and sit down beside the lamp. She would turn her gaze upon him and he would remain unchanged; when she took the dish and turned it round, the contents would be all restored, and he should say, 'Now, please, eat something thyself, as I have done. While she is eating, with her looks turned upon thee, just see what becomes of her!' Tiggak walked up to the house of the old hag and acted exactly as he had been told; having eaten, the wicked old woman turned raving mad and died. 'I have killed the old hag, but they will go on in this manner if we stay here; so we had better leave the place altogether and make for our home again.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 16 'Tiggak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 提加克模仿另一個人的聲音喊道：「繩子，繩子！」繩子立刻出現，並在巨人脖子上繫緊；「拉！」——刀子的聲響再度傳來，直到有人喊道：「我們豈不是在剝我們自己主人的皮嗎？我們要叫他們在下面喪命！」——於是他們開始往下面倒水。眼見無路可逃，提加克想起他的護身符縫在外套的襯裡中，而那件外套在他們到來時留在了船柱上，便喊道：「把我放在外面的外套拿來；我要用它作裹屍布！」出乎他的意料，外套立刻被扔了下來；他抓住外套，從毛皮襯裡中解下護身符，放進嘴裡，說了聲「為我們報仇！」之後又取了出來。外面有聲音喊道：「他倒下了！——他也倒了！——還有一個！」——過了一會兒，護身符回來了，沾滿了血。主人把它擦拭乾淨，又把它扔了出去，喊道：「全部！」下一次外面便聽不到任何聲響了。他們從炕的一角擠出去，找到出路，不見一個活人，便回到第一間屋子繼續用餐——但那傻頭傻腦的青年又出現了：「我告訴你們——阿皮亞克現在正使盡她最狠毒的手段：她正在煮她兒子的腦子、手和腳。」提加克聽不懂他的意思，直到一個兄弟解釋：那是上面被殺那人的腦子、手和腳，他母親大概打算用它們做一道菜來款待他。當他被要求前去時，他會看見入口正前方有一隻長方形的盤子，盛著精心調製的腦子；他必須迅速端起盤子，挺直站立，面朝她、閉上眼睛，把它全部吃光——若睜著眼睛，他就會發瘋而死——然後把盤子倒扣，放回原處，睜開眼睛，在燈旁坐下。她會把目光轉向他，而他會保持原樣不變；當她拿起盤子把它轉一圈時，盤中的東西會全部復原，而他應該說：「現在，請你自己也吃一點吧，就像我剛才那樣。趁她吃著、目光轉向你時，且看她會怎樣！」提加克走到那老妖婆的屋前，完全照吩咐行事；吃完之後，那邪惡的老婦人發瘋而死。「我已經殺死了那老妖婆，但我們若留在這裡，他們還會這樣繼續下去；所以我們最好徹底離開這個地方，動身回家。」

passages.text: At a snow-covered hill sloping to the water's side Tiggak asked each brother what amulet he had taken when he had to make his choice — all answered a small piece of bear-skin: 'That's all right; you will all do very well.' But the adopted son could only answer, 'I don't know indeed,' and pressed, confessed: 'When I was able to judge for myself, I got a snow-bunting for my amulet.' Tiggak became silent and shook his head; after a while he remarked, 'And yet it may do; thou must perch down on us.' He let himself slide down the hill right into the sea, disappeared, and reappeared in the shape of a bear, shaking the water from his ears: 'Now follow me all of you' — and they were all transformed into bears. When the son's turn came he had not the courage, but at last went gliding slowly down and grew a snow-bunting, as such able to fly; meanwhile all the others were swimming homewards, and when the little snow-bunting got tired he took a rest between their ears. They landed a little to the north of their old homestead; climbing up the shore, Tiggak shook himself well and his bear-skin glided off, the rest all doing the same — and when the son's turn came, he shook off the snow-bunting's skin, and thus all of them marched home, except the one who had been killed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 16 'Tiggak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在一座向水邊傾斜的積雪小山旁，提加克逐一問每個兄弟，當他們必須作出選擇時取了什麼護身符——大家都回答是一小塊熊皮：「那就好；你們都會一切順利的。」但那養子只能回答：「我實在不知道」，被追問之下才承認：「當我能自己作主時，我拿了一隻雪鵐作護身符。」提加克沉默不語，搖了搖頭；過了一會兒他說：「不過這也許行得通；你得棲在我們身上。」他讓自己順著山坡滑下，直入海中，消失了，又現身時已是一頭熊的模樣，抖落耳邊的水：「現在你們全都跟我來」——於是他們全都變成了熊。輪到那養子時，他沒有勇氣，但最後還是緩緩滑了下去，變成了一隻雪鵐，因此能夠飛翔；與此同時，其他人都向家游去，當小雪鵐疲倦時，便在他們的耳朵之間歇息。他們在舊居以北不遠處登陸；爬上岸後，提加克好好抖了抖身子，他的熊皮便滑落下來，其餘眾人也照樣做——輪到那養子時，他抖落了雪鵐的皮，於是他們全都一同走回家去，只有那個被殺的人除外。

title.en: The Kayan Creation: The Tree from the Sun, the Creeper from the Moon
title.zh: 加揚創世：日生之樹與月生之藤

region.en: Upper Baram river country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸巴蘭河上游之地（象徵性定位）

period: Kayan creation myth, sung in rhymed blank verse; recorded by Hose and McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), vol. II, the Kayan creation myth

summary.en: In the beginning there was a barren rock; rains bred moss, and worms aided by dung-beetles made soil by their castings. A sword-handle came down from the sun and became a great tree; from the moon came a creeper that hung from the tree and was mated with it through the action of the wind — and from this union were born the first human beings, Kaluban Gai and Kalubi Angai, incomplete, lacking legs and the lower half of their trunks, their entrails hanging loose and exposed.
summary.zh: 太初唯荒岩一塊；雨生苔蘚，蟲類得糞甲蟲之助，以其排洩物造土。一柄劍柄自太陽而降，化為大樹；自月亮來一藤蔓，懸於樹上，因風而與樹交合——由是誕生最早之人類卡魯班·該與卡魯比·安該；二形不完備，缺足與下半身，臟腑懸露於外。

sensitivity.note: Kayan creation myth recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912); colonial-era collection flagged; Bornean communities hold the heritage — paraphrase only.

canonical_translation: Hose & McDougall 1912 (English); paraphrase

narrative.en:
The Kayan creation myth, sung in rhymed blank verse by all branches of the Kayan people, is the great cosmogony of interior Borneo, recorded by Hose and McDougall in the opening years of the twentieth century.

BEGINNING: THE ROCK AND THE SOIL. In the beginning there was a barren rock. On this the rains fell and gave rise to moss, and the worms, aided by the dung-beetles, made soil by their castings — creation begins not with a god but with weather and the small labour of the lowliest creatures.

MIDDLE: THE TREE FROM THE SUN. Then a sword-handle (Haup Malat) came down from the sun and became a large tree; from the moon came a creeper, which hanging from the tree became mated with it through the action of the wind. From this union were born Kaluban Gai and Kalubi Angai, the first human beings, male and female — but they were incomplete, lacking the legs and the lower half of their trunks, so that their entrails hung loose and exposed. The world fills around them: leaves falling from the tree became the species of birds and winged insects; from the fallen fruits sprang the four-footed beasts; and resin oozing from the trunk gave rise to the domestic pig and fowl — two species distinguished, the myth says, by their understanding of matters that remain hidden from all others, even from human beings.

END: THE COMPLETION AND THE PEOPLES. The incomplete first humans produced Pengok Ngai and Katira Murei; Katira Murei bore a son, Batang Uta Tatai, who married Ajai Avai and begot the five ancestors of the existing peoples — Sijau Laho, Oding Lahang, Pabalan, Pliban and Tokong. Oding Lahang is claimed as ancestor by the Kayans and also by the Kenyahs and some Klemantan tribes; Tokong by the Sebops and the Punans — the genealogy of the myth is thus the charter of the interior's ethnic map.

FUNCTIONS. The myth (1) makes humanity's completion a process, not an event (the legless first pair); (2) ties the human body to the tree and the sun-moon pair; (3) grants pigs and fowls a special secret knowledge that explains their use in divination; and (4) distributes the living peoples among five named ancestors. The myth's botany is deliberate: the sun supplies the tree, the moon the creeper, and the wind supplies the act of union, so that the first humans are the child of all three — solar stock, lunar climbing, and the breeze's joining. The incompleteness of Kaluban Gai and Kalubi Angai is the myth's signature: the first pair lack legs and the lower half of the trunk, their entrails exposed, and completion comes only through their descendants — humanity is finished by descent, not delivered ready-made. The same generative logic fills the world: leaves become birds and winged insects, fallen fruits become the four-footed beasts, and the resin of the trunk becomes the domestic pig and fowl, the two creatures credited with understanding what remains hidden from others — a charter, the recorders noted, for their use in divination. The genealogy then distributes the interior's peoples among the five sons of Batang Uta Tatai, so that the myth is at once a cosmogony and the ethnic map of Borneo sung in blank verse.
narrative.zh: 加揚創世神話以押韻之素體詩吟唱，流行於加揚諸支，由霍斯與麥克杜格爾於二十世紀初記錄。開篇：太初唯荒岩；雨生苔，蟲與糞甲蟲以其排洩物造土——創世始於天氣與至微生物之勞作，而非神明。中段：日降劍柄化大樹；月來之藤因風與樹交合，誕生首對不完備之人類（缺足與下半身，臟腑外露）。周遭世界隨之而生：落葉化為鳥與有翅之蟲，落果生四足獸，樹脂育出家豬與家雞——神話言此二者通曉連人類也隱而不知之事。結尾：不完備的首對人類生彭奧克·恩蓋與卡蒂拉·穆雷；其子巴當·烏塔·塔泰娶阿賈伊·阿瓦伊，生五支現存民族之祖——西兆·拉霍、奧丁·拉航、帕巴蘭、普利班、托貢。加揚人、肯雅人與部分克勒曼丹人奉奧丁·拉航為祖；塞博普人與普南人奉托貢為祖——神話之譜系即婆羅洲內陸族群地圖之憲章。功能：以『未完之人』立人性之漸成、以身體繫於樹與日月、以豬雞之秘知解釋占卜之用、以五祖分派現存民族。

functions: Makes human completion a process: the first pair lacks legs and lower trunks
Ties the human body to the sun-tree and the moon-creeper union
Grants pigs and fowls secret knowledge, explaining their use in divination
Distributes the living Bornean peoples among five named ancestors

variants.name: Kenyah variants
variants.summary: The Kenyahs claim Oding Lahang within a parallel genealogy headed by the supreme Bali Penylong, identified with the Kayan Laki Tenangan.

sensitivity_guidance: Colonial-era collection (1912); Bornean Dayak communities hold the heritage — paraphrase only, no verbatim ritual text.

passages.text: In the beginning there was a barren rock. On this the rains fell and gave rise to moss, and the worms, aided by the dung-beetles, made soil by their castings. Then a sword-handle came down from the sun and became a large tree. From the moon came a creeper, which hanging from the tree became mated with it through the action of the wind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Kayan creation myth in Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 起初只有一塊光禿的岩石。雨水落在其上，生出了苔蘚，而蠕蟲在蜣螂的幫助下，以其排泄物造出了土壤。接著，一個劍柄從太陽降下，變成了一棵大樹。從月亮來了一條藤蔓，它懸掛在樹上，藉著風的作用與樹交合。

passages.text: From this union were born Kaluban Gai and Kalubi Angai, the first human beings, male and female; these were incomplete, lacking the legs and lower half of their trunks, so that their entrails hung loose and exposed. Leaves falling from the tree became the various species of birds and winged insects, and from the fallen fruits sprang the four-footed beasts; resin oozing from the trunk gave rise to the domestic pig and fowl, distinguished by their understanding of matters hidden from all others.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Kayan creation myth; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 由這結合生出了卡魯班·蓋與卡魯比·安蓋，即最初的人類，一男一女；他們並不完整，缺少雙腿和軀幹的下半部，以致內臟鬆垂外露。從樹上落下的葉子變成了各種鳥類和有翅昆蟲，從落下的果實中生出了四足野獸；從樹幹滲出的樹脂生出了家豬和家禽，牠們因通曉其他一切生物所不知的隱秘之事而與眾不同。

passages.text: The incomplete first humans produced Pengok Ngai and Katira Murei; Katira Murei bore Batang Uta Tatai, who married Ajai Avai and begot the five progenitors of the existing peoples — the Kayans, Kenyahs and some Klemantans claiming Oding Lahang, the Sebops and Punans claiming Tokong.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Kayan creation myth; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那不完整的最初人類生出了彭戈克·蓋與卡蒂拉·穆雷；卡蒂拉·穆雷生了巴唐·烏塔·塔泰，他娶了阿賈伊·阿瓦伊，生出了現存各民族的五位始祖——卡揚人、肯雅人和一些克萊曼坦人自稱出自奧丁·拉杭，塞博普人和普南人則自稱出自托孔。

title.en: The Frog's Advice: Tokong and the Charter of Head-Hunting
title.zh: 青蛙之諫：托貢與獵首之憲章

region.en: Upper Baram river country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸巴蘭河上游之地（象徵性定位）

period: Kayan/Klemantan myth recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the Tokong story

summary.en: Preparing to attack a village, Tokong is hailed by a frog crying 'cut through the neck.' The people, who had taken only their enemies' hair to adorn their shields, scoff — until the frog decapitates a small frog to demonstrate, and promises prosperity of every kind. Tokong carries away the heads of his enemies, and as the party returns home the padi grows from knee-high to full ears; head-hunting is adopted from that day as the rite that makes the crops and the household prosper.
summary.zh: 托貢正欲攻村，一蛙呼曰：『斬其頸！』眾人素來只取敵髮飾盾，皆嘲笑之——直至青蛙斬一小蛙以示範，並許諸般繁榮。托貢遂取敵首而歸；歸途經過田中，稻穀自膝高驟長至穗滿。自此獵首成為使莊稼興旺、家宅昌盛之禮。

sensitivity.note: Historical headhunting charter-myth, recorded 1912; presented as ethnographic record of a discontinued practice, framed with care.

passages.text: Once upon a time, when Tokong and his people were preparing to attack a village, he was addressed by the frog, who called out words meaning in the Sebop language 'cut through the neck.' At first the people, who hitherto had taken only the hair of their enemies to adorn their shields, scoffed at this advice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Tokong story in Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前，當托孔（Tokong）與他的族人正準備攻打一座村莊時，青蛙向他開口說話，在塞博普語（Sebop）中喊出意為「砍穿脖子」的話語。起初，族人向來只取敵人的頭髮來裝飾盾牌，對這番建議嗤之以鼻。

passages.text: But the frog assured them that the taking of heads would bring prosperity of every kind, and demonstrated the procedure by decapitating a small frog. Tokong carried away the heads of his enemies, and this was followed immediately by increased prosperity: as the party passed through their fields the padi grew very rapidly, from knee-high to full ears before they had passed through. The words of the frog thus came true, and Tokong and his people continued the new practice, and from them it was learned by others — the charter of the head-hunting rite and its promise of the harvest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Tokong story; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但青蛙向他們保證，獵取人頭會帶來各式各樣的興旺，並以小青蛙為例，示範了斬首的過程。托孔帶走了敵人的頭顱，隨即而來的便是日益興旺：當一行人穿過他們的田地時，稻禾生長得極快，在他們尚未走出田地之前，便已從及膝之高長成飽滿的稻穗。青蛙的話於是應驗了，托孔與他的族人繼續奉行這項新習俗，其他人又從他們那裡學得此舉——這便是獵頭儀式的起源，以及它對豐收的許諾。

title.en: Lafaang in the Sky: The Bridegroom Who Lost His Arm
title.zh: 拉方上天：失臂的姐夫

region.en: Upper Baram river country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸巴蘭河上游之地（象徵性定位）

period: Long Kiput (Klemantan) star myth recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the story of Lafaang (Orion)

summary.en: The daughter of Palai (the constellation Pegasus) loves the Long Kiput youth Lafaang and brings him to the sky. Sky custom defeats him at every turn: food taken with fingers instead of a needle, trees that fall when the axe is merely laid at their feet — until a tree felled carelessly cuts off Lafaang's left arm, the very arm missing in the constellation Orion. Disgusted and homesick, he is let down to earth by a creeper with sugar-cane tops and banana roots, hears his newborn child cry as he descends, and plants the gifts in soil instead of throwing them — which is why, the myth says, cane and banana remain inferior wherever they grow, and why Orion still moves overhead, one-armed.
summary.zh: 帕拉伊（飛馬座）之女愛上隆基普青年拉方，引他上天。天界之俗處處敗他：以指代針取食、斧置樹腳樹即自倒——直到一棵粗心砍伐之樹墜落，斬斷拉方左臂——正是獵戶座所缺之臂。他厭倦思鄉，由藤蔓縋回地面，懷中帶著甘蔗梢與香蕉根；下降之際聽見新生兒啼哭而求回頭被拒。他將贈物種入土中而非擲地——神話言：故甘蔗香蕉至今低劣；而獵戶座仍缺臂巡天。

sensitivity.note: Star-myth with bride-taken-to-sky structure; Orion's missing arm fixed etiologically.

passages.text: The daughter of Palai fell in love with a Long Kiput youth, Lafaang, and invited him to ascend to the heavens, warning him that the customs of her celestial home were very different from those of earth. He found it difficult to conform: he put food into his mouth with his fingers instead of using a needle, and felled trees by chopping, when he was merely to lay the axe at their feet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Lafaang story in Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 帕萊（Palai）的女兒愛上了一位隆基普特（Long Kiput）青年拉法昂（Lafaang），並邀他升上天界，同時警告他，她天界家鄉的習俗與人間大不相同。他發現自己難以遵從：他用手把食物送進嘴裡，而不用針；他砍伐樹木，而按規矩他只須把斧頭放在樹腳下即可。

passages.text: This breach of custom was punished by the fall of a tree that cut off Lafaang's left arm — the arm wanting in the constellation. Disgusted by these incidents, he made up his mind to return to his own people; his wife let him down to earth by a long creeper, giving him sugar-cane tops and banana roots previously unknown to men, and he heard the cry of his new-born child as he descended but was not allowed to return.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Lafaang story; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這違反習俗之舉招致了懲罰：一棵樹倒下，砍斷了拉法昂的左臂——那正是星座中所缺的那條手臂。他對這些遭遇深感厭惡，決心回到自己的族人那裡；他的妻子用一條長藤把他放回人間，給了他人類前所未見的甘蔗梢與香蕉根，他在下降途中聽見自己新生兒的哭聲，卻不被允許回去。

passages.text: Told to throw the gifts on the ground, he planted them carefully in soil instead; the plants grew up inferior, and such they have remained wherever they have spread. Lafaang died among his own people on earth, but the bright constellation that bears his name and shape still moves across the heavens, reminding men of his journey to the world above the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Lafaang story; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他被告知要把這些禮物扔在地上，他卻仔細地將它們栽入土中；這些植物長得低劣，此後無論傳播到何處，它們都一直如此。拉法昂死於人間自己的族人之中，但那以他的名字與形貌命名的明亮星座，仍舊運行於天際，提醒著人們他曾踏上前往天外世界的旅程。

title.en: Usaï the Giant: Why the Sky Is Far Away
title.zh: 巨人烏賽：天何以高遠

region.en: Baram river country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸巴蘭河流域（象徵性定位）

period: Klemantan myth recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the story of Usaï

summary.en: At one time the sky was close to the earth; but one day Usaï, a giant working sago with a wooden mallet, accidentally struck his mallet against the sky, and since then the sky has been far out of man's reach. The rest of the myth follows the giant's grief down the Baram: the dammed river that drowns his wife, the weeping stations that name every rapid, his cut-down death at Miri with 'my brains are sago, my liver is tobacco,' and the mosquitoes of his day, big as fowls, hewn small by the people.
summary.zh: 昔天低近地；一日巨人烏賽舂西谷米，木杵誤擊於天——自此天高而人不可及。神話續敘巨人順巴蘭江而下之悲：築壩引水而妻溺亡；沿江哭泣之處各成灘名；至米里被伐如樹而亡——遺言曰『吾腦為西谷、吾肝為菸草』；其世之蚊大如雞，為眾人斬小。

sensitivity.note: Sky-lifting motif (cf. Maui, Reushi); landscape etiology of the Baram rapids.

passages.text: At one time the sky was close to the earth, but one day Usaï, a giant, when working sago with a wooden mallet accidentally struck his mallet against the sky; since which time the sky has been far up out of the reach of man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Usaï story in Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 曾經有一段時期，天空離大地很近，但有一天，巨人烏賽（Usaï）在用木槌製作西米時，不慎將木槌撞到了天空；自那時起，天空便高高在上，遠非人力所能觸及。

passages.text: Building a dam to catch a prawn for his wife, Usaï saw the dam give way and his wife drowned in the rush of water; he waded weeping down the Baram, and his stations of grief gave the river its named rapids — weeping anew at every bend where he found her coat, her waist-cloth, or nothing at all, until the sea was only knee-deep to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Usaï story; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 烏賽為了替妻子捕捉一隻蝦而築了一道堰，卻見堰潰決，妻子溺斃於奔湧的水流之中；他泣著涉水順巴南河而下，他每一處哀悼駐足之地，便使這條河有了那些以之為名的急灘——他在每一個河灣重新痛哭，那裡他尋見她的外衣、她的腰布，或什麼也尋不著，直到海水於他只及膝深。

passages.text: At Miri the people took him for a great tree and hewed him down; blood poured from his foot, and he spoke: 'I am about to die. My brains are sago, my liver is tobacco. Where my head falls there the people will have much knowledge, where my feet lie will be the ignorant ones.' He fell with a mighty crash, head toward the sea; a thousand Miris were killed by the fall, and the mosquitoes of his day, big as fowls, were hewn into small pieces — so that now they are the smallest of animals, but their bite is still painful.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Usaï story; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在美里，人們把他當作一株大樹，將他砍倒；血從他的腳湧出，他說道：「我將要死了。我的腦髓是西米，我的肝是菸草。我的頭落下之處，那裡的人們將擁有許多知識；我的腳躺臥之處，將是那些無知的人。」他隨著一聲巨響倒下，頭朝向大海；千人因這一倒而喪命，而他那一日如家禽般巨大的蚊子，被砍成了小塊——所以如今牠們是最微小的動物，但牠們的叮咬依然疼痛。

title.en: Simpang Impang and the Wind-Spirit: The Flood, the Half-Man, the Compensation
title.zh: 半身人與風靈：洪水、半人與賠償

region.en: Batang Lupar country, Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲巴唐盧帕爾流域（象徵性定位）

period: Iban (Sea Dayak) myth recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the Iban story of Simpang Impang

summary.en: Men who cut up a python for cooking bring on a deluge; all the land is covered and only the peak of Tiang Laju stands above the flood, with one woman, a dog, a rat and a few small animals. The woman, taking a hint from a creeper warmed by friction, produces fire by rubbing wood; lacking a husband she takes the creeper as mate and bears a son who is only half a human being — one arm, one leg, one eye: Simpang Impang. When the wind-spirit scatters the rat's padi the half-boy demands compensation at the house of the wind, outlasts the spirit's ordeal contests with the help of fish, swift and ant, burns the wind-house with his father the fire-drill, and wins the price: 'I'll make you a whole man with two arms and two legs and two eyes.'
summary.zh: 人們誤斬巨蟒而炊，招致大洪水；大地盡沒，唯蒂昂·拉尤峰出於水面，一婦人攜犬、鼠及小獸登峰。婦人見藤蔓摩擦生暖而悟，鑽木取火；無夫，遂以藤為伴，產下半身之子——一臂一腿一目：半身人辛邦·因邦。風靈吹散鼠之稻穀，半身人前往風之居所索償；得魚、雨燕、螞蟻之助連勝神判，再以生父鑽火器焚風屋——風靈終允賠償：『我讓你成為完人，兩臂兩腿兩目。』

sensitivity.note: Iban composite myth (flood + quest + fable); Hose notes its heterogeneous, fun-loving character.

passages.text: Some people came upon a huge python in the jungle and, taking it for a log, sat on it and wounded it; heavy rain fell for days and days, till all the land was covered with water and only the top of Tiang Laju stood out above the flood, with one woman, a dog, a rat and a few small animals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Iban story of Simpang Impang in Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有些人於叢林中遇見一條巨蟒，誤以為是一段木頭，便坐在其上，並將牠弄傷；大雨連日連夜落下，直到整片土地都被水淹沒，唯有蒂昂拉朱的頂端露出洪水之上，還有一名女子、一隻狗、一隻鼠和幾隻小動物。

passages.text: The woman, taking the hint from a creeper warmed by friction against a tree, rubbed the creeper hard on a piece of wood and so for the first time produced fire; having no husband she took the creeper for her mate, and gave birth to a son who was but one-half of a human being — one arm, one leg, one eye — Simpang Impang.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Iban story; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那女子從一條因與樹摩擦而發熱的藤蔓得到啟示，將藤蔓在一塊木頭上用力摩擦，於是第一次生出了火；她沒有丈夫，便以那藤蔓為配偶，生下一個兒子，而這兒子只是人的一半——一臂、一腿、一目——即辛龐英龐。

passages.text: When the wind-spirit scattered the padi grain in dispute with the rat, Simpang Impang demanded his corn back at the house of the wind; helped by the fish, the swift and the ant through the spirit's contests of diving, jumping and blow-pipe, and armed at last with his father the fire-drill, he burned the wind-spirit's house, and the spirit paid compensation — 'I'll make you a whole man with two arms and two legs and two eyes' — and did as asked for the tree and the lake that had sent messages with him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Iban story; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當風靈因與鼠爭執而吹散了稻穀，辛龐英龐便在風的屋中索回他的穀物；他藉著魚、迅捷者與螞蟻之助，通過了風靈的潛水、跳躍與吹箭種種較量，最後以他的父親火鑽為武器，燒了風靈的屋子，風靈便付出補償——「我要使你成為一個完整的人，有兩臂、兩腿和兩目」——並照所求的，為那曾隨他傳訊的樹與湖而行。

title.en: The Mouse-Deer and the Tortoise: 'Please Throw Me in the River'
title.zh: 鼠鹿與水龜：『請把我丟進河裏』

region.en: Baram river country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸巴蘭河流域（象徵性定位）

period: Kenyah fable recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the Kenyah fable of the mouse-deer and the tortoise

summary.en: The mouse-deer Plandok gives the tortoise Kelap a leg up the fruit-tree and abandons him; caught by the household as the thief, Kelap begs for each punishment — fire ('last time they left one side untouched'), the cane-press ('last time they squeezed only one side') — and weeps only at the river. Thrown in, he surfaces: 'That's alright, this is my home.' The villagers try to poison the water with tuba, but one man uses the tortoise's back for a stone, and Kelap sinks his back little by little until they think the river is rising and give up.
summary.zh: 鼠鹿普蘭多克扶水龜柯拉普上果樹而棄之；柯拉普被屋中人當賊擒獲，對各種刑罰皆討饒求之——火刑（『上次只燒了一面』）、蔗壓（『上次只壓了一面』）——唯獨怕被丟入河中而啼哭。眾人將其拋入河中，他浮出水面：『沒錯，這就是我的家。』村民欲以毒藤毒水，一人竟以其背為砧杵搗毒藤；柯拉普讓背慢慢下沉，眾人以為河水漲了，只好作罷。

sensitivity.note: Classic trickster fable (punishment-inversion type); also performed as social parable among the Kenyahs.

passages.text: Plandok the mouse-deer gives Kelap the tortoise a leg up the laden fruit-tree; Kelap throws down all the fruit, cannot get down, and is caught by the people of the house as the thief. Brought to punishment, Kelap begs for every fate but the river: 'please put me in the fire; last time they only half did the thing and left one side untouched'; 'please squeeze me in the press; last time they squeezed only one side of me.' So they throw him into the river, and he surfaces calling that this is his home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Kenyah fable in Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Kenyah fable; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 鼠鹿普蘭多克托了烏龜克拉普一把，助牠爬上結滿果實的果樹；克拉普把果實全都扔了下來，卻下不了樹，被那屋裡的人當作賊捉住。被帶去受罰時，克拉普懇求除了河以外的每一種命運：「請把我放進火裡吧；上次他們只做了一半，留下一邊沒碰」；「請把我壓在壓榨器裡吧；上次他們只壓了我的一邊。」於是他們把他扔進河裡，他浮出水面，喊著說這裡才是他的家。

passages.text: The people resolve to poison the water with tuba; one man, taking Kelap's back for a stone, beats his tuba upon it, and Kelap sinks his back lower and lower till the water covers it — 'the water's rising, it's no good trying to poison the river' — and the people go home defeated.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Kenyah fable; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 眾人決意以魚藤毒水；一人誤將克拉普的背當作石頭，把魚藤往他背上捶打，克拉普便將背越沉越低，直到水淹沒了它——「水漲起來了，想毒這條河是沒用的」——眾人只得敗興而歸。

title.en: Laki Tenangan: The Fatherly God Above All Departments
title.zh: 拉基·特南安：超越諸職司的慈父之神

region.en: Kayan country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸加揚之地（象徵性定位）

period: Kayan religious tradition recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the gods of the Kayans
