passages.zh: 舜問乎丞曰：「道可得而有乎？」曰：「汝身非汝有也，汝何得有夫道？」舜曰：「吾身非吾有也，孰有之哉？」曰：「是天地之委形也。生非汝有，是天地之委和也。性命非汝有，是天地之委順也。子孫非汝有，是天地之委蛻也。故行不知所往，處不知所持，食不知所味。天地之強陽氣也，又胡可得而有邪？」

title.en: The TAO Is in the Ant, the Tare, the Potsherd, and the Ordure (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 莊子曰：無所不在，在螻蟻、在稊稗（莊子）

region.en: Tung Kuo Tzŭ's questioning (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 東郭子問莊子（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 22, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 22

summary.en: Tung Kuo Tzŭ demands one place where the TAO is. It is in the ant, answers Chuang Tzŭ; in a tare; in a potsherd; in ordure — until the questioner makes no reply. Then comes the instruction to reach the palace of Nowhere and carry discussions into the infinite, and the great doctrine: TAO causes fulness and emptiness, but it is not either.
summary.zh: 東郭子問莊子曰：所謂道，惡乎在？莊子曰：無所不在——在螻蟻；在稊稗；在瓦甓；在屎溺。道在屎溺：每下愈況。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the pantheistic descent is Zhuangzi's most-quoted answer on the Tao's location. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Tung Kuo Tzŭ asked Chuang Tzŭ, saying, "What you call TAO,--where is it?" "There is nowhere," replied Chuang Tzŭ, "where it is not." "Tell me one place at any rate where it is," said Tung Kuo Tzŭ. "It is in the ant," replied Chuang Tzŭ. "Why go so low down?" asked Tung Kuo Tzŭ. "It is in a tare," said Chuang Tzŭ. "Still lower," objected Tung Kuo Tzŭ. "It is in a potsherd," said Chuang Tzŭ. "Worse still!" cried Tung Kuo Tzŭ. "It is in ordure," said Chuang Tzŭ. And Tung Kuo Tzŭ made no reply.
passages.zh: 東郭子問於莊子曰：「所謂道，惡乎在？」莊子曰：「無所不在。」東郭子曰：「期而後可。」莊子曰：「在螻蟻。」曰：「何其下邪？」曰：「在稊稗。」曰：「何其愈下邪？」曰：「在瓦甓。」曰：「何其愈甚邪？」曰：「在屎溺。」東郭子不應。

passages.text: "Sir," continued Chuang Tzŭ, "your question does not touch the essential. When Huo, inspector of markets, asked the managing director about the fatness of pigs, the test was always made in parts least likely to be fat. Do not therefore insist in any particular direction; for there is nothing which escapes. ... Try to reach with me the palace of Nowhere, and there, amidst the identity of all things, carry your discussions into the infinite. ... TAO causes fulness and emptiness, but it is not either. It causes renovation and decay, but it is not either. It causes beginning and end, but it is not either."
passages.zh: 莊子曰：「夫子之問也，固不及質。正獲之問於監市履豨也，每下愈況。……嘗相與游乎無何有之宮，同合而論，無所無窮。……道使物盈虧，而盈虧非道也；使物消息，而消息非道也；使物終始，而終始非道也。」

title.en: The TAO Cannot Be Heard, Seen, or Spoken (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 道不可聞，聞而非也（莊子）

region.en: The dialogue of the Empyrean (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 泰清之問（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 22, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 22

summary.en: The Empyrean asks Without-end, Inaction, and No-beginning whether TAO can be known. No-beginning answers: not to know is profound, to know is shallow; TAO cannot be heard — heard, it is not TAO; seen, it is not TAO; spoken, it is not TAO. That which imparts form to forms is itself formless; therefore TAO cannot have a name.
summary.zh: 泰清問乎無窮，無始曰：道不可聞，聞而非也；道不可見，見而非也；道不可言，言而非也——知形形之不形乎！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The Empyrean asked Without-end, saying, "Do you know TAO?" "I do not," replied Without-end; whereupon the Empyrean proceeded to ask Inaction. "I do know TAO," said Inaction. "Is there any method," asked the Empyrean, "by which you know TAO?" "There is," replied Inaction. "I know," answered Inaction, "that TAO may honour and dishonour, bind and loose. That is the method by which I know TAO."
passages.zh: 光曜問乎無有曰：「夫子有乎？其無有乎？」光曜不得問，而孰視其狀貌，窅然空然，終日視之而不見，聽之而不聞，搏之而不得也。「於是乎無有矣，惡乎至此哉？」

passages.text: "Not to know," replied No-beginning, "is profound. To know is shallow. Not to know is internal. To know is external. ... TAO," said No-beginning, "cannot be heard. Heard, it is not TAO. It cannot be seen. Seen, it is not TAO. It cannot be spoken. Spoken, it is not TAO. That which imparts form to forms is itself formless; therefore TAO cannot have a name." ... "To ask a question which cannot be asked is vain. To answer a question which cannot be answered is unreal. And one who thus meets the vain with the unreal is ... unfit alike to roam over the K'un-lun peak or to soar into the Supreme Void."
passages.zh: 無始曰：「道不可聞，聞而非也；道不可見，見而非也；道不可言，言而非也。知形形之不形乎！道不當名。……有問不問者，答之者亦無憑；以無憑答無問，其內外不可相與遊乎崑崙之虛，遊乎太虛之上也。」

title.en: Light Asks Nothing (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 光曜問乎無有（莊子）

region.en: The colloquy of Light and Nothing (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 光與無有之對話（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 22, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 22

summary.en: Light asks Nothing whether he exists; getting no answer, Light watches for the appearance of Nothing all day long — looks but cannot see it, listens but cannot hear it, grasps at but cannot seize it. Bravo! cries Light. I can get to be nothing, but I cannot get as far as the absence of nothing.
summary.zh: 光曜問乎無有曰：夫子有乎？其無有乎？無有弗應也。光曜視之，無見也；聽之，無聞也；摶之，不可得也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Light asked Nothing, saying, "Do you, Sir, exist, or do you not exist?" But getting no answer to his question, Light set to work to watch for the appearance of Nothing. Hidden, vacuous,--all day long he looked but could not see it, listened but could not hear it, grasped at but could not seize it. "Bravo!" cried Light. "Who can equal this? I can get to be nothing, but I cannot get as far as the absence of nothing. Assuming that Nothing has an objective existence, how can it reach this next stage?"
passages.zh: （承前）光曜問乎無有，無有不得問而孰視之：窅然空然——「於是乎無有矣。吾得無為而為無有矣，而未得乎無無也。使無有者有形乎，則曷至此哉？」

title.en: The Sword-Forger of Eighty Years (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 大馬之捶鉤者，年八十矣（莊子）

region.en: The Minister of War's forge (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 司馬之冶（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 22, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 22

summary.en: The man who forged swords for the Minister of War is eighty years of age, yet never makes the slightest slip in his work. It is concentration, he answers: when twenty years old he took to forging swords and cared for nothing else — if a thing was not a sword, he did not notice it, availing himself of whatever energy he did not use in other directions.
summary.zh: 大馬之捶鉤者，年八十矣，而不失豪芒。曰：是守之也——於物無視也，非鉤無察也；是用之者，假不用者也以長得其用。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The man who forged swords for the Minister of War was eighty years of age. Yet he never made the slightest slip in his work. The Minister of War said to him, "Is it your skill, Sir, or have you any method?" "It is concentration," replied the man. "When twenty years old, I took to forging swords. I cared for nothing else. If a thing was not a sword, I did not notice it. I availed myself of whatever energy I did not use in other directions in order to secure greater efficiency in the direction required. Still more of that which is never without use;--So that there was nothing which did not lend its aid."
passages.zh: 大司馬家有捶鉤者，年八十矣，而不失豪芒。大司馬曰：「是子之巧歟？有道歟？」曰：「臣有守也。臣之年二十而好捶鉤，於物無視也，非鉤無察也。是用之者，假不用者也以長得其用。用之者，假乎於有，所得者無為也——而況有不賴其用者也乎！」

title.en: Life as a White Horse Passing a Crack (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 人生天地之間，若白駒之過郤（莊子）

region.en: Confucius's hall (Qufu, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 夫子之堂（今山東曲阜）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 22, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 22

summary.en: Jen Ch'iu asks Confucius whether we can know the time before the universe existed; Time was of old precisely what it is now, is the answer. Life and death are correlates; what there was before the universe was TAO — TAO makes things what they are, but is not itself a thing. And man passes through this sublunary life as a white horse passes a crack: the bow-sheath is slipped off, and in the confusion the soul wings its flight on the great journey home.
summary.zh: 冉求問於仲尼：未有天地可知邪？孔子曰：可——古猶今也。人生天地之間，若白駒之過郤，忽然而已。已化而生，又化而死。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Jen Ch'iu asked Confucius, saying, "Can we know about the time before the universe existed?" "We can," replied Confucius. "Time was of old precisely what it is now." At this rebuff, Jen Ch'iu withdrew. Next day he again visited Confucius and said, "Yesterday when I asked you that question and you answered me, I was quite clear about it. To-day I am confused. How is this?" "Your clearness of yesterday," answered Confucius, "was because my answer appealed direct to your natural intelligence. Your confusion of to-day results from the intrusion of something other than the natural intelligence. There is no past, no present, no beginning, no end.
passages.zh: 冉求問於仲尼曰：「未有天地可知邪？」仲尼曰：「可。古猶今也。」冉求失問而退。明日復見，曰：「昔者吾問『未有天地可知乎』，夫子曰『可，古猶今也』。昔日吾昭然，今日吾昧然。敢問何謂也？」仲尼曰：「昔之昭然也，神者先受之；今之昧然也，又且為不神者求邪？無古無今，無始無終。

passages.text: What there was before the universe, was TAO. TAO makes things what they are, but is not itself a thing. Nothing can produce TAO; yet everything has TAO within it, and continues to produce it without end. "Man passes through this sublunary life as a white horse passes a crack. Here one moment, gone the next. ... Living creatures cry out; human beings sorrow. The bow-sheath is slipped off; the clothes-bag is dropped; and in the confusion the soul wings its flight, and the body follows, on the great journey home!"
passages.zh: 未有天地，自古以固存。物物者非物，物出不得先物也，而猶其有物也無已。……人生天地之間，若白駒之過隙，忽然而已。……生物哀之，人類悲之。脫其桎梏，解其囊橐，魂魄將往，身乃隨之，此乃大歸乎！」

title.en: Kêng Sang Ch'u Refuses to Be a Tutelary God (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 庚桑楚居畏壘之山（莊子）

region.en: The Wei-lei mountains in the north (symbolic pin: Yimengshan, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 畏壘之山（象徵定位：山東沂蒙山）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 23, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 23

summary.en: Kêng Sang Ch'u, the only disciple of Lao Tzŭ to attain his TAO, lives on the Wei-lei mountains, dismissing clever and charitable attendants — and in three years the district is greatly benefited. The villagers ask to honour him as a tutelary god; he turns his face south in shame, and prophesies that a thousand ages hence man will be feeding upon man.
summary.zh: 老聃之役有庚桑楚者，偏得老聃之道，北居畏壘之山；居三年，畏壘大壤。相與言曰：庶幾其聖人乎——胡為乎尸祝而社稷之乎？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); Keng-sang became a canonized immortal of the Zhuangzi's first 'outer' chapter. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Among the disciples of Lao Tzŭ was one named Kêng Sang Ch'u. He alone had attained to the TAO of his Master. He lived up north, on the Wei-lei Mountains. Of his attendants, he dismissed those who were systematically clever or conventionally charitable. The useless remained with him; the incompetent served him. And in three years the district of Wei-lei was greatly benefited.
passages.zh: 老聃之役，有庚桑楚者，偏得老聃之道，北居畏壘之山。其臣之畫然知者去之，其妾之絜然仁者遠之。擁腫之與居，鞅掌之為使。居三年，畏壘大穰。

passages.text: One of the inhabitants said in conversation, "When Mr. Kêng Sang first came among us, we did not know what to make of him. Now, we could not say enough about him in a day, and even a year would leave something unsaid. Surely he must be a true Sage. Why not pray to him as to the spirits, and honour him as a tutelary god of the land?" On hearing of this, Kêng Sang Ch'u turned his face to the south in shame, at which his disciples were astonished. But Kêng Sang said, "What cause have you for astonishment? The influence of spring quickens the life of plants, and autumn brings them to maturity. In the absence of any agent, how is this so? It is the operation of TAO.
passages.zh: 畏壘之民相與言曰：「庚桑子之始來，吾洒然異之。今吾日計之而不足，歲計之而有餘。庶幾其聖人乎！胡不相與尸而祝之，社而稷之乎？」庚桑楚聞之，南面而不釋然。弟子異之。庚桑子曰：「弟子何異於予？夫春氣發而百草生，正得秋而萬寶成。夫春與秋，豈無得而然哉？天道已行矣。

passages.text: "A beast big enough to swallow a cart, if it wanders alone from the hills, will not escape the sorrow of the snare. A fish big enough to gulp down a boat, if stranded on the dry shore will become a prey to ants. Therefore it is that birds and beasts love height, and fishes and turtles love depth. And the man who cares for himself hides his body. He loves the occult. ... If the virtuous are honoured, emulation will ensue. If knowledge be fostered, the result will be theft. ... I tell you that the root of this great evil is from Yao and Shun, and that its branches will extend into a thousand ages to come. A thousand ages hence, man will be feeding upon man!"
passages.zh: 「吾聞至人，尸居環堵之室，而百姓猖狂不知所如往。今以畏壘之細民而竊竊焉欲俎豆予於賢人之間，我其杓之人邪？是以老聃之言：函車之獸，介而離山，則不免於網罟之患；吞舟之魚，碭而失水，則蟻能苦之。故鳥獸不厭高，魚鱉不厭深。夫全其形生之人，藏其身也，不厭深眇而已矣。……舉賢則民相軋，任知則民相盜。……大亂之本，必生於堯舜之間，其末存乎千世之後。千世之後，其必有人與人相食者也！」

title.en: Nan Yung Ch'u's Seven Days' Journey to Lao Tzŭ (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 南榮趎南見老子（莊子）

region.en: Lao Tzŭ's abode (symbolic pin: Ku county, Bozhou, Anhui, China)
region.zh: 老子之居（象徵定位：安徽亳州苦縣）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 23, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 23

summary.en: Nan Yung Ch'u carries provisions on a seven days' journey to Lao Tzŭ with three dilemmas: if I do not know, men call me a fool; if I do know, I injure myself; and charity injures both others and myself. The sage teaches the art of preserving life — to be as a child, crying all day without becoming hoarse — and warns that there is no weapon so deadly as man's will.
summary.zh: 南榮趎贏糧，七日七夜至老子之所。老子曰：衛生之經——能抱一乎？能勿失乎？一純素之道，惟神是守。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the classic teaching-scene of the 'art of preserving life'. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: So Nan Yung took some provisions, and after a seven days' journey arrived at the abode of Lao Tzŭ. "Have you come from Kêng Sang Ch'u?" said the latter. "I have," replied Nan Yung. "But why," said Lao Tzŭ, "bring all these people with you?" Nan Yung looked back in alarm, and Lao Tzŭ continued, "Do you not understand what I say?" Nan Yung bent his head abashed, and then looking up, said with a sigh, "I have now forgotten how to answer, in consequence of missing what I came to ask."
passages.zh: 南榮趎贏糧，七日七夜，至老子之所。老子曰：「子自楚之所來乎？」南榮趎曰：「唯。」老子曰：「何偕眾人之眾多也？」南榮趎懼然顧其後。老子曰：「子不知吾所謂乎？」南榮趎俯而慚，仰而嘆，曰：「吾忘吾答，而失吾所問。」

passages.text: If I do not know," replied Nan Yung, "men call me a fool. If I do know, I injure myself. If I am not charitable, I injure others. If I am, I injure myself. If I do not do my duty to my neighbour, I injure others. If I do it, I injure myself. My trouble lies in not seeing how to escape from these three dilemmas.
passages.zh: 曰：「不知乎？人謂我朱愚。知乎？反愁我軀。不仁則害人，仁則反愁我身。不義則傷彼，義則反愁我己。我安逃此而可？此三言者，我所患也。

passages.text: "The art of preserving life," replied Lao Tzŭ, "consists in being able to keep all in ONE, to lose nothing, to estimate good and evil without divination, to know when to stop, and how much is enough, to leave others alone and attend to oneself, to be without cares and without knowledge,--to be in fact as a child. A child will cry all day and not become hoarse, because of the perfection of its constitutional harmony. ... "There is no weapon so deadly as man's will. Excalibur is second to it. There is no bandit so powerful as Nature. In the whole universe there is no escape from it. Yet it is not Nature which does the injury. It is man's own heart."
passages.zh: 老子曰：「衛生之經，能抱一乎？能勿失乎？能無卜筮而知吉凶乎？能止乎？能已乎？能舍諸人而求諸己乎？能翛然乎？能侗然乎？能兒子乎？兒子終日嗥而嗌不嗄，和之至也。……夫外韱者不可繁而捉，將內揵；內韱者不可繆而捉，將外揵。夫外韱內揵者，道德不能持。……最莫毒焉：人自作孽，猶可活也；天作孽者，孰能逃之？然傷者非天也，人之心也。」

title.en: Hsü Wu Kuei Judges of Dogs and Horses (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 徐無鬼見魏武侯：相狗相馬（莊子）

region.en: The Wei court (Anyang region, Henan, China)
region.zh: 魏廷（今河南安陽一帶）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: The hermit Hsü Wu Kuei, sympathising with the prince rather than being pitied himself, cheers the melancholy ruler by telling how he judges dogs — the highest class as though they had parted with their own individuality — and horses: the horses of the State run to line and arc, but the horses of the Empire move as though they had lost the way, and outstrip all competitors over the unstirred dust, out of sight.
summary.zh: 徐無鬼見魏武侯，相狗相馬之術——直者中繩，曲者中鉤，此國家之馬也；若此者，絕塵弭轍，若喪其一，此天下之馬也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); tagged oracle-divination for the judge-of-horses topos (interpretive). Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: "It is I who should sympathise with your Highness, not your Highness with me," answered Hsü Wu Kuei. "If your Highness gives free play to passion and yields to loves and hates, then the natural conditions of your existence will suffer. ... The Prince was too astonished to reply; and after a while Hsü Wu Kuei continued, "I will try to explain to your Highness how I judge of dogs. The lowest in the scale will eat their fill and then stop, like a cat. Those of the middle class are as though staring at the sun. The highest class are as though they had parted with their own individuality.
passages.zh: 「不若我，而相于人君也，」徐無鬼對魏武侯曰。「君獨為萬乘之主，以苦一國之民，以養耳目鼻口……夫神者不自許也。將以良狗為喻：下等之狗，飽食而止；中之等，若視日；上等之狗，若喪其形者。

passages.text: "But I do not judge of dogs as well as I judge of horses. I judge of horses as follows. Their straightness must be that of a line. Their curve must be that of an arc. Their squareness, that of the square. Their roundness, that of the compasses. These are the horses of the State. They are not equal to the horses of the Empire. The horses of the Empire are splendid. They move as though anxious to get along, as though they had lost the way, as though they had parted with their own individuality. Thus, they outstrip all competitors, over the unstirred dust, out of sight!"
passages.zh: 「若夫執鞭之人，則又不如相狗矣。吾相馬：直者中繩，曲者中鉤，方者中矩，圓者中規，是國馬也。而未若天下馬也。天下馬有成材，若卹若失，若喪其一。若是者，超軼絕塵，不知其所由也！」

passages.text: The Prince was greatly pleased and smiled. ... "Have you not heard," said Hsü Wu Kuei, "of the outlaw of Yüeh? After several days' absence from his State, he was glad to meet any one he had known there. After a month, he was glad to meet any one he had even seen there. And after a year, he was glad to meet any one who was in any way like to his fellow-countrymen. ... Long it is, I ween, since his Highness has heard the voice of a pure man at his side!"
passages.zh: 武侯大說而笑。徐無鬼曰：「嘗語君，吾相狗又不若相馬也。……不亦聞夫越之流人乎？去國數日，見其所知而喜；去國旬月，見所嘗見於國中者喜；及期年也，見似人者而喜矣。……不亦去人滋久、思人滋深乎！夫逃虛空者……聞人足音跫然而喜矣，又況乎昆弟親戚之謦欬其側者乎！」

title.en: The Divine Teacher Boy Who Governed the Empire as He Kept His Horses (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 黃帝襄城之野遇牧馬小童（莊子）

region.en: The wilds of Hsiang-ch'êng, beyond the known world (symbolic pin: Xiangcheng, Henan, China)
region.zh: 襄城之野（象徵定位：河南襄城）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: The Yellow Emperor rides to seek the Tao upon the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain with six sage companions, and all seven lose their way in the wilds of Hsiang-ch'êng. A boy grazing horses tells them where the mountain is and where the TAO abides — and how to govern the empire: just the same as I look after my horses. See that no harm comes to the horses, that is all! The Emperor prostrates himself before the boy, addressing him as Divine Teacher.
summary.zh: 黃帝將見大隗乎具茨之山——七聖皆迷，無所問塗；適遇牧馬童子。小童曰：夫為天下者，亦奚以異乎牧馬者哉？亦去其害馬者而已矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the seven-sages-lose-the-way myth and the Divine-Teacher boy. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: When the Yellow Emperor went to see TAO upon the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain, Fang Ming was his charioteer, Ch'ang Yü sat on his right, Chang Jo and Hsi P'êng were his outriders, and K'un Hun and Hua Chi brought up the rear. On reaching the wilds of Hsiang-ch'êng, these seven Sages lost their way and there was no one of whom to ask the road. By and by, they fell in with a boy who was grazing horses, and asked him, saying, "Do you know the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain?" "I do," replied the boy. "And can you tell us," continued the Sages, "where TAO abides?" "I can," replied the boy.
passages.zh: 黃帝將見大隗乎具茨之山，方明為御，昌寓驂乘，張若、謵朋前馬，昆閽、滑稽後車。至於襄城之野，七聖皆迷，無所問塗。適遇牧馬童子，問塗焉，曰：「若知具茨之山乎？」曰：「然。」「若知大隗之所存乎？」曰：「然。」

passages.text: "This is a strange lad," cried the Yellow Emperor. "Not only does he know where the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain is, but also where TAO abides! Come tell me, pray, how would you govern the empire?" "I should govern the empire," said the boy, "just the same as I look after my horses. What else should I do? "When I was a little boy and used to live within the points of the compass, my eyes got dim of sight. An old man advised me to mount the chariot of the sun and visit the wilds of Hsiang-ch'êng. My sight is now much better, and I continue to dwell without the points of the compass. I should govern the empire in just the same way. What else should I do?"
passages.zh: 黃帝曰：「異哉小童！非徒知具茨之山，又知大隗之所存。請問為天下。」小童曰：「夫為天下者，亦若此而已矣，又奚事焉！予少而自遊於六合之內，予適有瞀病，有長者教予曰：『若乘日之車而遊於襄城之野。』今予病少痊，予且復遊於六合之外。夫為天下亦若此而已，又奚事焉！」

passages.text: The boy declined to answer, but on being again urged, cried out, "What difference is there between governing the empire and looking after horses? See that no harm comes to the horses, that is all!" Thereupon the Emperor prostrated himself before the boy; and addressing him as Divine Teacher, took his leave.
passages.zh: 黃帝曰：「夫為天下者，則誠非吾子之事。雖然，吾願聞於子。」小童辭。黃帝又問。小童曰：「夫為天下者，亦奚以異乎牧馬者哉！亦去其害馬者而已矣！」黃帝再拜稽首，稱天師而退。

title.en: Lu Chü's Two Lutes and the Twenty-Five Jangled Strings (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 魯遽調瑟，二十五弦皆動（莊子）

region.en: The hall and adjoining room (symbolic pin: Qufu, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 堂與室之瑟（象徵定位：山東曲阜）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: A disciple of Lu Chü boasts he can do without fire in winter and make ice in summer; Lu Chü answers by tuning two lutes, one in the hall and one in the adjoining room, so that the struck note sounds in both — then, changing one string out of the octave, he strikes it and all the twenty-five strings jangle together. There was sound as before, but the influence of the key-note was gone.
summary.zh: 魯遽曰：是直以陽召陽，以陰召陰——於是乎為之調瑟；廢一於堂，廢一於室；鼓宮宮動，鼓角角動。於是乎為之改調，一於宮宮，五音不比，二十五弦皆動。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: "Thereupon he tuned two lutes, and placed one in the hall and the other in the adjoining room. And when he struck the Kung note on one, the Kung note on the other sounded; when he struck the chio note on one, the chio note on the other sounded. This because they were both tuned to the same pitch. But if he changed the interval of one string, so that it no longer kept its place in the octave, and then struck it, the result was that all the twenty-five strings jangled together. There was sound as before, but the influence of the key-note was gone. Is this your case?"
passages.zh: 於是為之調瑟，廢一於堂，廢一於室，鼓宮宮動，鼓角角動，音律同矣。夫或改調一弦，於五音無當也，鼓之，二十五弦皆動，未始異於聲，而音之君已。……是其言之所主乎！」

title.en: The Stone-Mason and the Scab No Thicker Than a Fly's Wing (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 匠石斲郢人之鼻堊（莊子）

region.en: Ying, capital of Ch'u (Jingzhou, Hubei, China)
region.zh: 郢都（今湖北荊州）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: At Hui Tzŭ's grave, Chuang Tzŭ recalls the man of Ying whose nose bore a scab no thicker than a fly's wing: the stone-mason chipped it off with his adze while the patient sat unmoved, the nose uninjured. Summoned by the prince of Sung to try the same, the stone-mason answers that his material has long since perished — and I too, ever since he perished, have been without my material, having no one with whom I can speak.
summary.zh: 郢人堊漫其鼻端若蠅翼，使匠石斲之；匠石運斤成風，聽而斲之，盡堊而鼻不傷。臣嘗能之矣，雖然，臣之質死久矣！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Chuang Tzŭ was once attending a funeral, when he passed by the grave of Hui Tzŭ. Turning to his attendants, he said, "A man of Ying who had his nose covered with a hard scab, no thicker than a fly's wing, sent for a stone-mason to chip it off. The stone-mason plied his adze with great dexterity while the patient sat still and let him chip. When the scab was all off, the nose was found to be uninjured, the man of Ying never having moved a muscle.
passages.zh: 莊子送葬，過惠子之墓，顧謂從者曰：「郢人堊慢其鼻端若蠅翼，使匠石斲之。匠石運斤成風，聽而斲之，盡堊而鼻不傷，郢人立不失容。

passages.text: When Yüan, prince of Sung, heard of this, he summoned the stone-mason and said, 'Try to do the same for me.' "'I used to be able to do it Sire,' replied the stone-mason, 'but my material has long since perished.' "And I too, ever since he perished, have been without my material, having no one with whom I can speak."
passages.zh: 宋元君聞之，召匠石曰：『嘗試為寡人為之。』匠石曰：『臣則嘗能斲之。雖然，臣之質死久矣。』自夫子之死也，吾無以為質矣，吾無與言之矣。」

title.en: Kuan Chung's Deathbed Advice: It Must Be Hsi P'êng (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 管仲有病，屬國於隰朋（莊子）

region.en: The Ch'i court (Linzi, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 齊廷（今山東臨淄）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: Dying Kuan Chung refuses Duke Huan's choice of Pao Yü — pure, incorruptible, he will not associate with those unlike himself — and names instead Hsi P'êng, who forgets the authority of those above him, grieves over those not the peers of himself, and hears not the things in the State he should not hear. There is no alternative; it must be Hsi P'êng.
summary.zh: 管仲有病，公曰：鮑叔牙可乎？管仲曰：不可——其為人也，潔廉善士也，其於不己若者不比之。其於國也，有不聞也；其於家也，有不見也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Kuan Chung being at the point of death, Duke Huan went to see him. "You are ill, venerable Sir," said the Duke, "really ill. You had better say to whom, in the event of your getting worse, I am to entrust the administration of the State." "Whom does your Highness wish to choose?" enquired Kuan Chung. "Will Pao Yü do?" asked the Duke. "He will not," said Kuan Chung. "He is pure, incorruptible, and good. With those who are not like himself, he will not associate. And if he has once heard of a man's wrong-doing, he never forgets it. If you employ him in the administration of the empire, he will get to loggerheads with his prince and to sixes and sevens with the people.
passages.zh: 管仲有病，桓公往問之曰：「仲父病，可謂至矣。屬諸其族，以寡人之疾病也，言微有讓者。」管仲曰：「公誰欲相？」公曰：「鮑叔牙可乎？」管仲對曰：「不可。其為人潔廉，善士也；其於不己若者不比之；又一聞人之過，終身不忘。使之治國，上且鉤乎君，下且逆乎民。其得罪於君也，弗可久已矣。

passages.text: "There is no alternative," replied Kuan Chung; "it must be Hsi P'êng. He is a man who forgets the authority of those above him, and makes those below him forget his. Ashamed that he is not the peer of the Yellow Emperor, he grieves over those who are not the peers of himself. To share one's virtue with others is called true wisdom. To share one's wealth with others is reckoned meritorious. To exhibit superior merit is not the way to win men's hearts. To exhibit inferior merit is the way. There are things in the State he does not hear; there are things in the family he does not see. There is no alternative; it must be Hsi P'êng."
passages.zh: 管仲曰：「必不得已也，其隰朋乎！其為人也，忘其身以及於上者，忘其親以及於下者，忘其慚而忘其榮者，於天下弗如者也。以賢臨人，未有得人者也；以賢下人，未有不得人者也。其於國有不聞也，其於家有不見也。勿已，其隰朋可乎！」

title.en: The Showing-Off Monkey of Monkey Mountain (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 吳王狙猴之技（莊子）

region.en: Monkey Mountain of Wu (symbolic pin: Zhenjiang, Jiangsu, China)
region.zh: 吳之猨山（象徵定位：江蘇鎮江）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: The monkeys of Monkey Mountain flee from the prince of Wu's shooting-party — except one which flaunts its skill and catches the flying arrow in its hand, to be killed by the guards' cloud of arrows. Beware! says the prince: do not flaunt your superiority in the faces of others. Yen Pu I goes home and studies under Tung Wu, and in three years his praise is in everybody's mouth.
summary.zh: 吳王浮於江，登乎狙之山；眾狙見之，恂然棄而逃——有一狙焉，見巧乎王；王射之，敏給搏捷矢。王命相者趨射，狙執死。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The prince of Wu took a boat and went to the Monkey Mountain, which he ascended. When the monkeys saw him, they fled in terror and hid themselves in the thicket. One of them, however, disported himself carelessly, as though showing off its skill before the prince. The prince took a shot at it; but the monkey, with great rapidity, seized the flying arrow with its hand. Then the prince bade his guards try, the result being that the monkey was killed.
passages.zh: 吳王浮於江，登乎狙之山。眾狙見之，恂然棄而逃，逃於深蓁。有一狙焉，委蛇攫搔，見巧乎王。王射之，敏給搏捷矢。王命相者趨射之，狙執死。

passages.text: Thereupon the prince turned to his friend Yen Pu I, and said, "That monkey flaunted its skill and its dexterity in my face. Therefore it has come to this pass. Beware! Do not flaunt your superiority in the faces of others." Yen Pu I went home, and put himself under the tuition of Tung Wu, with a view to get rid of such superiority. He put aside all that gave him pleasure and avoided gaining reputation. And in three years his praise was in everybody's mouth.
passages.zh: 王謂其友顏不疑曰：「之狙也，伐其巧，恃其便，以敖予，以至此殛也。戒之哉！嗟乎，無以汝色驕人哉！」顏不疑歸而師董梧，以鋤其色，去樂辭顯。三年而國人稱之。

title.en: Chiu Fang Yin Examines the Eight Sons (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 子綦八子，九方歅相之（莊子）

region.en: The father's hall (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 父之堂（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: Tzŭ Chi summons the physiognomist Chiu Fang Yin to examine his eight sons; K'un will be the fortunate one — he will eat at the table of a prince — and the father weeps, for every uncanny effect must be preceded by some uncanny cause. Shortly afterwards K'un is captured by brigands, his feet cut off, and sold as door-keeper to Duke Chü — with meat to his dinner for the rest of his life.
summary.zh: 子綦有子八人，屬諸九方歅：楣也，必與國君同食以終其身。俄而楣到於燕，盜得之於道，刖而鬻之於齊——適為渠公之街，然食肉終身。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Tzŭ Chi had eight sons. He ranged them before him, and summoning Chiu Fang Yin, said to him, "Examine my sons physiognomically, and tell me which will be the fortunate one." "K'un," replied Chiu Fang Yin, "will be the fortunate one." "In what sense?" asked the father, beaming with delight. "K'un," said Chiu Fang Yin, "will eat at the table of a prince, and so end his days." Thereupon Tzŭ Chi burst into tears and said, "What has my son done that this should be his fate?"
passages.zh: 子綦有八子，陳諸前，召九方歅曰：「為我相吾子，孰為祥？」九方歅曰：「梱也為祥。」子綦瞿然喜曰：「奚若最乎？」曰：「梱也，將與國君同食以終其身。」子綦索然出涕曰：「吾子何為以至於是極也！」

passages.text: "My sons and I do but roam through the universe. With them I seek the joys of heaven; with them I seek the fruits of earth. With them I engage in no business; with them I concoct no plots; with them I attempt nothing out-of-the-way. ... Every uncanny effect must be preceded by some uncanny cause. Alas! my sons and I have done nothing. It must be the will of God. Therefore I weep."
passages.zh: 子綦曰：「吾與吾子幾為樂矣。未嘗為人之事，未嘗為人之謀，未嘗與人為怪。……凡有怪徵者，必有怪行。殆乎！非我與吾子之罪，殆天之為也。吾是以泣也。」

passages.text: Shortly afterwards, when K'un was on his way to the Yen State, he was captured by brigands. To sell him as he was, would be no easy matter. To sell him without his feet would be easy enough. So they cut off his feet and sold him into the Ch'i State, where he became door-keeper to Duke Chü and had meat to his dinner for the rest of his life.
passages.zh: 未幾，梱使於燕，盜見之，以其為可貨也，遂劫而刖之，將以屬齊。既至齊，梱為渠公之閽，而終身飫膏焉。

title.en: Hsü Yu Runs Away from Yao (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 嚙缺遇許由，遁堯（莊子）

region.en: The hermit's path (symbolic pin: Jishan, Henan, China)
region.zh: 隱者之塗（象徵定位：河南箕山）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: Asked where he is going, Hsü Yu answers: away from Yao — who thinks of nothing but charity, and will become a laughing-stock of the world until future ages eat one another. Love and profit are born of charity and duty to one's neighbour; those who ignore them are few, those who make capital out of them are many.
summary.zh: 齧缺遇許由曰：子將奚之？曰：將逃堯——夫堯畜畜然仁，吾恐其為天下笑；後世其人與人相食與！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Yeh Ch'üeh meeting Hsü Yu, said to him, "Where are you going?" "Away from Yao!" replied the latter. "What do you mean?" asked Yeh Ch'üeh. "Yao," said Hsü Yu, "thinks of nothing but charity. I fear he will become a laughing-stock to the world, and that in future ages men will eat one another.
passages.zh: 齧缺遇許由，曰：「子將奚之？」曰：「將逃堯。」曰：「奚謂邪？」曰：「夫堯，畜畜然仁，吾恐其為天下笑。後世其人與人相食與！

passages.text: "There is no difficulty in winning the people. Love them and they will draw near. Profit them and they will come up. Praise them and they will vie with one another. But introduce something they dislike, and they will be gone. ... Love and profit are born of charity and duty to one's neighbour. Those who ignore charity and duty to one's neighbour are few; those who make capital out of them are many. ... Yao knows that good men benefit the empire. But he does not know that they injure it. Only those on a higher level than good men know this."
passages.zh: 「夫民，不難聚也，愛之則親，利之則至，譽之則勸，致其所惡則散。……愛利出乎仁義，捐仁義者寡，利仁義者眾。……堯知賢人之利天下也，而不知其賊天下也。夫唯外乎賢者知之矣。」

title.en: The Two Kingdoms on the Snail's Horns (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 蝸角觸蠻之爭（莊子）

region.en: The Liang court (Kaifeng, Henan, China)
region.zh: 梁廷（今河南開封）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: On a snail's left horn there is a kingdom called Aggression and on its right horn another called Violence, constantly fighting for territory — corpses by the thousands, pursuers away for fifteen days. Descend from boundless space to a kingdom with fixed boundaries, and in it is Wei, in Wei the city of Liang, and in Liang a prince — in what does he differ from Violence? Whew! cried the prince. Then Hui Tzŭ's tube-note: Yao and Shun, compared with Tai Chin Jen, are but whssh.
summary.zh: 有國於蝸之左角者曰觸氏，有國於蝸之右角者曰蠻氏；時相與爭地而戰，伏尸數萬——君之與蠻氏，亦猶是也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the snail-horn kingdoms are Zhuangzi's most-cited satire on war. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Prince Hui of Wei had made a treaty with prince Wei of Ch'i, which the latter broke. Thereupon prince Hui was wroth, and was about to send a man to assassinate him. When Hui Tzŭ heard of the ministers' war-plans, he introduced Tai Chin Jen to the prince. "There is a creature called a snail," said Tai Chin Jen. "Does your Highness know what I mean?" "I do," replied the prince. "There is a kingdom on its left horn," continued Tai Chin Jen, "ruled over by Aggression, and another on its right horn, ruled over by Violence. These two rulers are constantly fighting for territory. In such cases, corpses lie about by thousands, and one party will pursue the other for fifteen days before returning."
passages.zh: 惠子聞而見之魏王，引戴晉人。戴晉人曰：「有所謂蝸者，君知之乎？」「然。」「有生於左角者，曰觸氏，有生於右角者，曰蠻氏。時相與爭地而戰，伏屍數萬，逐北旬有五日而後反。」

passages.text: "Sire," replied Tai Chin Jen, "I beg you to regard it as fact. Does your Highness recognise any limit to space?" "None," said the prince, "It is boundless." "When, therefore, the mind descends from the contemplation of boundless space to the contemplation of a kingdom with fixed boundaries, that kingdom must seem to be of dimensions infinitesimally small?" "Of course," replied the prince. "Well then," said Tai Chin Jen, "in a kingdom with fixed boundaries there is the Wei State. In the Wei State there is the city of Liang. In the city of Liang there is a prince. In what does that prince differ from Violence?" "There is no difference," said the prince.
passages.zh: 君曰：「噫！其虛言與？」曰：「臣請為君實之。君以意在四方上下有窮乎？」君曰：「無窮。」曰：「知遊心於無窮，而反在通達之國，若存若亡乎？」君曰：「然。」曰：「通達之中有魏，於魏中有梁，於梁中有王，王與蠻氏有辯乎？」君曰：「無辯。」

passages.text: Thereupon Tai Chin Jen took his leave, and the prince remained in a state of mental perturbation, as though he had lost something. When Tai Chin Jen had gone, Hui Tzŭ presented himself, and the prince said, "Our friend is truly a great man. Sages are not his equal." "If you blow through a tube," replied Hui Tzŭ, "the result will be a note. If you blow through the hole in a sword-hilt, the result will be simply whssh. Yao and Shun have been belauded by mankind; yet compared with Tai Chin Jen they are but whssh."
passages.zh: 客出而君惝然若有亡也。客出，惠子見。君曰：「客，大人也，聖人不足以當之。」惠子曰：「吹管，其聲倊；吹劍首者，吷而已矣。堯舜，人之所譽也；道堯舜於戴晉人之前，譬猶一吷也。」

title.en: The Sage Under a Menial's Garb on Mount I (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 孔子之楚，舍於蟻丘之漿（莊子）

region.en: The wine-shop of Mount I, Ch'u (Yicheng, Hubei, China)
region.zh: 蟻丘之漿（象徵定位：湖北宜城）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: Stopping at a wayside wine-shop on Mount I, Confucius sees a servant climb onto the roof: a Sage under the garb of a menial, who has drowned himself on dry land — I think 'tis I Liao of Shih-nan. Sent to call him, Tzŭ Lu finds the house empty; the hidden one has scorned the toady's words.
summary.zh: 孔子之楚，舍於蟻丘之漿。其鄰有夫妻臣妾登極者——是陸沉者也。是其言也，猥以人乎！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: When Confucius went to Ch'u, he stopped at a restaurant on Mount I. The servant to a man and his wife who lived next door, got up on top of the house. "Whatever is he doing up there?" asked Tzŭ Lu. "He is a Sage," replied Confucius, "under the garb of a menial. He buries himself among the people. He effaces himself at the wayside. Fame, he has none; but his perseverance is inexhaustible. Though his mouth speaks, his heart speaks not. He has turned his back upon mankind, not caring to abide amongst them. He has drowned himself on dry land. I think 'tis I Liao of Shih-nan."
passages.zh: 孔子適楚，次於莫山下。鄰人之婢僕有登桅然在屋者，子路問之曰：「是攫攫何為者也？」孔子曰：「是聖人僕也。是自埋於民，自藏於畔。其聲銷，其志無窮。其口雖言，其心未嘗言。方且與世違，而心不屑與之俱。是陸沉者也。是其市南宜僚邪？」

passages.text: Tzŭ Lu asked to be allowed to go and call him; but Confucius stopped him, saying, "No. He knows that I know what he is. He knows that I have come to Ch'u to recommend him to the prince. And he looks on me as a toady. Under the circumstances, as he would scorn to hear the words of a toady, how much more would he scorn to see him in the flesh! How could you keep him?" Tzŭ Lu went to see, but the house was empty.
passages.zh: 子路請往召之。孔子曰：「已矣！彼知丘之著於己也，知丘之適楚也，以丘為必使楚王之故人也至也，彼且以丘為佞人也。夫如是，其於佞人也羞聞其言，而況親見其身乎！而何以為存？」子路往視之，其室虛矣。

title.en: Poh Chü Asks Lao Tzŭ to Wander the World (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 柏據學於老聃，請遊天下（莊子）

region.en: Lao Tzŭ's retreat (symbolic pin: Ku county, Bozhou, Anhui, China)
region.zh: 老聃之居（象徵定位：安徽亳州苦縣）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: The disciple Poh Chü begs Lao Tzŭ to wander the world with him. The world is just as you see it here, replies the Sage. Poh Chü explains that he would begin in Ch'i, viewing the dead bodies of malefactors, pushing them to make them rise, crying to God and bemoaning their lot — for honour and disgrace were set up, and evil followed; wealth was accumulated, and contentions began.
summary.zh: 柏據曰：請之齊，見其辜，推而強之，解其朝服而幕之——噫嘻！夫子亦知古之所謂亂者乎？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Poh Chü was studying under Lao Tzŭ. "Let us go," said he, "and wander over the world." "No," replied Lao Tzŭ, "the world is just as you see it here." But as he again urged it, Lao Tzŭ said, "Where would you go to begin with?" "I would begin," answered Poh Chü, "by going to the Ch'i State. There I would view the dead bodies of their malefactors. I would push them to make them rise. I would take off my robes and cover them. I would cry to God and bemoan their lot, as follows:--'O sirs, O sirs, there was trouble upon earth, and you were the first to fall into it!'
passages.zh: 柏矩學於老聃，曰：「請之天下遊。」老聃曰：「已矣，天下猶是也。」又請之，老聃曰：「汝將何始？」曰：「始於齊。」至齊，見辜人焉，推而僵之，解朝服而幕之，號天而哭之，曰：「子乎！子乎！天下有大菑，子獨先離之。」

passages.text: "I would say, 'Perhaps you were robbers, or perhaps murderers?'... Honour and disgrace were set up, and evil followed. Wealth was accumulated, and contentions began. Now the evil which has been set up and the contentions which have accumulated, endlessly weary man's body and give him no rest. What escape is there from this?"
passages.zh: 曰：「莫為盜，莫為殺人。榮辱立，然後睹所病；貨財聚，然後睹所爭。今立人之所病，聚人之所爭，窮困人之身，使無休時，欲無至此，得乎？」

title.en: The Stone Coffin Under Sha-ch'iu: Duke Ling's Tomb Inscription (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 沙丘石槨銘（莊子）

region.en: Sha-ch'iu, the Wei burial ground (symbolic pin: Guangzong, Hebei, China)
region.zh: 沙丘（象徵定位：河北廣宗）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 25, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 25

summary.en: When Duke Ling died, divination showed it auspicious to bury him at Sha-ch'iu; digging several fathoms deep, the workmen found a stone coffin bearing the inscription: Posterity cannot be trusted. Duke Ling will seize this for his tomb. As a matter of fact, Duke Ling had been named Ling long before.
summary.zh: 靈公葬於沙丘而得石槨之銘：不馮其子，靈公奪而里之——靈公之為靈也久矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); tagged oracle-divination for the divinatory burial and prophetic inscription. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Confucius asked the historiographers Ta T'ao, Poh Ch'ang Ch'ien, and Hsi Wei, saying, "Duke Ling was fond of wine and given up to pleasure, and neglected the administration of his State. He spent his time in hunting, and did not cultivate the goodwill of the other feudal princes. How was it he came to be called Ling?" "The Duke," said Poh Ch'ang Ch'ien, "had three wives. He was having a bath together with them when Shih Ch'in, summoned by his Highness, entered the apartment. Thereupon the Duke covered himself and the ladies. So outrageously did he behave on the one hand, and yet so respectful was he towards a virtuous man. Hence he was called Ling."
passages.zh: 孔子見大史伯玉、史鰍曰：「衛靈公飲酒湛樂，不聽國家之政；田獵畢弋，不應諸侯之際。其所以名為靈公者何邪？」大史鰍曰：「是因是也。」伯常騫曰：「夫靈公有妻三人，同濫浴而史鰍奉御而進所，搏幣而扶翼。其慢者也，而其於賢者也，此其所以為靈公也。」

passages.text: "When the Duke died," said Hsi Wei, "divination showed that it would be inauspicious to bury him in the old family burying-ground, but auspicious to bury him at Sha-ch'iu. And upon digging a grave there, several fathoms deep, a stone coffin was found, which, being cleaned, yielded the following inscription:--Posterity cannot be trusted. Duke Ling will seize this for his tomb. As a matter of fact, Duke Ling had been named Ling long before. What should these two persons know about it?"
passages.zh: 狶韋氏曰：「夫靈公之死也，卜葬於故墓不吉，卜葬於沙丘而吉。掘之數仞，得石槨焉，洗而視之，有銘焉，曰：『不馮其子，靈公奪而里之。』夫靈公也，而久矣，而二子何足以知之！」

title.en: The Stickleback in the Cart-Rut (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 涸轍之鮒（莊子）

region.en: The road to the prince of Chien-ho (symbolic pin: Kaifeng, Henan, China)
region.zh: 監河侯之途（象徵定位：河南開封）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 26, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 26

summary.en: Poor Chuang Tzŭ borrows corn and is offered three hundred ounces of silver after the revenue is collected. He answers with the stickleback stranded in a cart-rut who begs a pint of water, and is promised the west river after a journey south to Wu and Yüeh: you might as well put me in a dried-fish shop at once.
summary.zh: 莊周家貧，往貸粟於監河侯。周顧視車轍中，有鮒魚焉——我，東海之波臣也；君豈有斗升之水而活我哉？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the dried cart-rut fish is a proverbial image of delayed relief. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Chuang Tzŭ's family being poor, he went to borrow some corn from the prince of Chien-ho. "Yes," said the prince. "I am just about collecting the revenue of my fief, and will then lend you three hundred ounces of silver. Will that do?" At this Chuang Tzŭ flushed with anger and said, "Yesterday, as I was coming along, I heard a voice calling me. I looked round, and in the cart-rut I saw a stickleback. "'I am a denizen of the eastern ocean,' replied the stickleback. 'Pray, Sir, a pint of water to save my life.'
passages.zh: 莊周家貧，故往貸粟於監河侯。監河侯曰：「諾。我將得邑金，將貸子三百金，可乎？」莊周忿然作色曰：「周昨來，有中道而呼者。周顧視，車轍中有鮒魚焉。周問之曰：『鮒魚來，子何為者邪？』對曰：『我，東海之波臣也。君豈有斗升之水而活我哉？』

passages.text: "'Yes,' said I. 'I am just going south to visit the princes of Wu and Yüeh. I will bring you some from the west river. Will that do?' "At this the stickleback flushed with anger and said, 'I am out of my element. I have nowhere to go. A pint of water would save me. But to talk to me like this,--you might as well put me in a dried-fish shop at once.'"
passages.zh: 周曰：『諾。我且南遊吳越之王，激西江之水而迎子，可乎？』鮒魚忿然作色曰：『吾失我常與，我無所處。吾得斗升之水然活耳。君乃言此，曾不如早索我於枯魚之肆！』」

title.en: Jên Kung Tzŭ's Hook Baited with Fifty Oxen (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 任公子大鉤巨緇五十犗（莊子）

region.en: Kuei-chi and the eastern ocean (Shaoxing bay, Zhejiang, China)
region.zh: 會稽東海之上（今浙江紹興灣）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 26, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 26

summary.en: Jên Kung Tzŭ baits a huge hook on a big line with fifty oxen, squats at Kuei-chi and casts into the eastern ocean; a year passes without a catch. Then a great fish swallows the bait, plunges, and shakes the deep with a noise like so many devils; and from Chih-ho eastwards and Ts'ang-wu northwards there was none but ate his fill of that fish.
summary.zh: 任公子為大鉤巨緇，五十犗以為餌，蹲乎會稽，投竿東海——已而大魚食之，牽巨鉤，鎅沒而下；白波若山。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Jên Kung Tzŭ got a huge hook on a big line, which he baited with fifty oxen. He squatted down at Kuei-chi, and cast into the eastern ocean. Every day he fished, but for a whole year he caught nothing. Then came a great fish which swallowed the bait, and dragging the huge hook dived down below. This way and that way it plunged about, erecting the dorsal fin. The white waves rolled mountain high. The great deep was shaken up. The noise was like that of so many devils, terrifying people for many miles around.
passages.zh: 任公子為大鉤巨緇，五十犗以為餌，蹲乎會稽，投竿東海，旦旦而釣，期年不得魚。已而大魚食之，牽巨鉤，銘沒而下，鶩揚而奮鬐，白波若山，海水震蕩，聲侔鬼神，憚赫千里。

passages.text: But when Jên Kung Tzŭ had secured his fish, he cut it up and salted it. And from Chih-ho eastwards, and from Ts'ang-wu northwards, there was none but ate his fill of that fish. Even among succeeding generations, gobemouches of the day recounted the marvellous tale. To take a rod and line, and go to a pool, and catch small fry is a very different thing from catching big fish.
passages.zh: 任公子得若魚，離而臘之，自制河以東，蒼梧已北，莫不厭若魚者。已而後世輕才諷說之徒，皆驚而相告也。夫揭竿累，趣灌瀆，守鯢鮒，其於得大魚難矣。

title.en: Day Is Breaking: The Confucianists and the Mouth-Pearl (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 儒以詩禮發冢（莊子）

region.en: The tomb being opened (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 發冢之地（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 26, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 26

summary.en: Some Confucianists open a grave in accordance with their Canons of Poetry and Rites; the master shouts 'Day is breaking,' and the apprentice reports a pearl in the mouth. Seizing the corpse's brow, they tap its cheeks with a metal hammer to make the jaws open gently and not injure the pearl — the satire: they quote the greenest corn that grows over graves even as they rob.
summary.zh: 儒以詩禮發冢——口中有珠。詩固言之曰：青青之麥，生於陵陂；生不布施，死何含珠為？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: When some Confucianists were opening a grave in accordance with their Canons of Poetry and Rites, the master shouted out, "Day is breaking. How are you getting on with the work?" "Not got off the burial-clothes yet," answered an apprentice. "There is a pearl in the mouth."
passages.zh: 儒以詩禮發冢，大儒臚傳曰：「東方作矣！事之何若？」小儒曰：「未解裙襦，口中有珠。」

passages.text: So seizing the corpse's brow with one hand, and forcing down its chin with the other, these Confucianists proceed to tap its cheeks with a metal hammer, in order to make the jaws open gently and not injure the pearl!
passages.zh: 詩固有毒也！曰：「生不布施，死何含珠為？」接其鬢，壓其顱，儒以金椎控其頤，徐別其頰，無傷口中珠。

title.en: Lao Lai Tzŭ Rebukes the Sorrowing Confucius (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 老萊子之弟子出薪遇仲尼（莊子）

region.en: The fuel-wood path of Ch'u (Jingmen, Hubei, China)
region.zh: 楚薪樵之塗（象徵定位：湖北荊門）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 26, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 26

summary.en: A disciple of Lao Lai Tzŭ, gathering fuel, meets a long-bodied, short-legged, round-shouldered man sorrowing over mankind — Confucius himself. Lao Lai Tzŭ bids him get rid of his dogmatism, and asks whether the wounds of one generation being too much, you would take to yourself the sorrows of all time. Better than extolling Yao and cursing Chieh is oblivion of both.
summary.zh: 老萊子曰：丘！去汝躬矜與汝容知，斯為君子矣——不忍一世之傷，而鰲萬世之患。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: A disciple of Lao Lai Tzŭ while out gathering fuel, chanced to meet Confucius. On his return, he said, "There is a man over there with a long body and short legs, round shoulders and drooping ears. He looks as though he were sorrowing over mankind. I know not who he can be." "It is Confucius!" cried Lao Lai Tzŭ. "Bid him come hither."
passages.zh: 老萊子之弟子出薪，遇仲尼，反曰：「有人於彼，修上而趨下，末僂而後耳，視若營四海，不知其誰氏之子。」老萊子曰：「是丘也，召而來。」

passages.text: When Confucius arrived, Lao Lai Tzŭ addressed him as follows:--"Ch'iu! Get rid of your dogmatism and your specious knowledge, and you will be really a superior man." ... "The wounds of one generation being too much," answered Lao Lai Tzŭ, "you would take to yourself the sorrows of all time. Are you not weary? Is your strength equal to the task? "Better than extolling Yao and cursing Chieh is oblivion of both, keeping one's praises to oneself."
passages.zh: 仲尼至，曰：「丘！去汝躬矜與汝容知，斯為君子矣。」老萊子曰：「是汝服也。……忍一傷，以濟萬世之患邪？則固不忍終身之醜乎？施於人者，又不如自施者之賢。」

title.en: Prince Yüan Dreams of the Divine Tortoise (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 宋元君夜半夢人被髮窺阿門（莊子）

region.en: The Sung court (Shangqiu, Henan, China)
region.zh: 宋宮（今河南商丘）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 26, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 26

summary.en: Prince Yüan of Sung dreams that a man with dishevelled hair peeps through a side door: I am a marine messenger attached to the staff of the River God, and a fisherman named Yü Ch'ieh has caught me. The divine tortoise is slain for divination, and out of seventy-two omens not a single one proves false — wisdom has its limits; spirituality, that which it cannot reach.
summary.zh: 宋元君夢神龜——予，江河之靈也；漁者豫且得予。乃芻龜而卜，七十二鑽而無遺筴。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the River-God messenger dream is a landmark oracle-divination narrative. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Prince Yüan of Sung dreamed one night that a man with dishevelled hair peeped through a side door and said, "I have come from the waters of Tsai-lu. I am a marine messenger attached to the staff of the River God. A fisherman, named Yü Ch'ieh, has caught me." When the prince awaked, he referred his dream to the soothsayers, who said, "This is a divine tortoise."
passages.zh: 宋元君夜半夢人被髮窺阿門，曰：「予自宰路之淵，予為清江使河伯之所，漁者余且得予。」元君覺，使人占之，曰：「此神龜也。」

passages.text: Being told there was such a fisherman, the prince gave orders for his appearance at court. "I have netted a white tortoise," replied the fisherman, "five feet in semi-circumference." "Bring your tortoise," said the prince. But when it came, the prince could not make up his mind whether to kill it or keep it alive. Thus in doubt, he had recourse to divination, and received the following response: Slay the tortoise for purposes of divination and good fortune will result. So the tortoise was despatched. After which, out of seventy-two omens taken, not a single one proved false.
passages.zh: 君曰：「漁者余且，余且也。」余且網得白龜，圓五尺。君曰：「獻若之龜。」龜至，君再欲殺之，再欲活之。疑而卜之，曰：「殺龜以卜，吉。」乃刳龜，七十二鑽而無遺筴焉。

passages.text: "A divine tortoise," said Confucius, "can appear to prince Yüan in a dream, yet it cannot escape the net of Yü Ch'ieh. Its wisdom can yield seventy-two faultless omens, yet it cannot escape the misery of being cut to pieces. Truly wisdom has its limits; spirituality, that which it cannot reach. In spite of the highest wisdom, there are countless snares to be avoided; If a fish has not to fear nets, there are always pelicans. Get rid of small wisdom, and great wisdom will shine upon you."
passages.zh: 仲尼曰：「神龜能見夢於元君，而不能避余且之網；知能七十二鑽無遺筴，而不能避刳腸之患。如是，則知有所困，神有所不及也。雖有至知，萬人謀之。魚不畏網而畏鵜鶘。去小知而大知明。」

title.en: The Fish-Trap, the Rabbit-Snare, and Where to Find One to Converse With (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 得魚忘筌，得意忘言（莊子）

region.en: The dialogue's end (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 問答之末（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 26, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 26

summary.en: The raison d'être of a fish-trap is the fish; when the fish is caught, the trap may be ignored. The raison d'être of language is an idea to be expressed; when the idea is expressed, the language may be ignored. But where shall I find a man to ignore language, with whom I may be able to converse?
summary.zh: 筌者所以在魚，得魚而忘筌；言者所以在意，得意而忘言。吾安得忘言之人而與之言哉！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the fish-trap and rabbit-snare became the classic image for scripture as a means. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: The raison d'être of a fish-trap is the fish. When the fish is caught, the trap may be ignored. The raison d'être of a rabbit-snare is the rabbit. When the rabbit is caught the snare may be ignored. The raison d'être of language is an idea to be expressed. When the idea is expressed, the language may be ignored. But where shall I find a man to ignore language, with whom I may be able to converse?
passages.zh: 荃者所以在魚，得魚而忘荃；蹄者所以在兔，得兔而忘蹄；言者所以在意，得意而忘言。吾安得忘言之人而與之言哉！

title.en: Shan Chüan Declines the Empire and Hides in the Mountains (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 舜讓天下於善卷（莊子）

region.en: Shan Chüan's farm in the wilds (symbolic pin: Songshan, Henan, China)
region.zh: 善卷之田（象徵定位：河南嵩山）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: Shun offers Shan Chüan the empire; he answers that he is a unit in the sum of the universe — fur in winter, grass-cloth in summer, ploughing in spring, rest in autumn — and declines, subsequently hiding himself among the mountains, nobody knew where.
summary.zh: 舜以天下讓善卷。善卷曰：余立於宇宙之中，冬日衣皮毛，夏日衣葛絺；春耕種，形足以勞動；秋收斂，身足以休食——逍遙於天地之間而心意自得。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Shun offered to resign the empire to Shan Chüan. Shan Chüan said, "I am a unit in the sum of the universe. In winter I wear fur clothes. In summer I wear grass-cloth. In spring I plough and sow, toiling with my body. In autumn I gather in the harvest, and devote myself to rest and enjoyment. At dawn I go to work; at sunset I leave off. Contented with my lot I pass through life with a light heart. Why then should I trouble myself with the empire? Ah, Sir, you do not know me." So he declined, and subsequently hid himself among the mountains, nobody knew where.
passages.zh: 舜以天下讓善卷，善卷曰：「余立於宇宙之中，冬日衣皮毛，夏日衣葛絺。春耕種，形足以勞動；秋收斂，身足以休食。日出而作，日入而息，逍遙於天地之間，而心意自得。吾何以天下為哉！悲夫，子之不知余也。」遂不受，於是去而入深山，莫知其處。

title.en: The Labourer of Shih Hu Goes Off to the Sea (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 舜以天下讓石戶之農（莊子）

region.en: The sea-coast of exile (symbolic pin: Qingdao, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 海上（象徵定位：山東青島）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: Shun offers the empire to a friend, a labourer of Shih Hu. Sire, you exert yourself too much, says the labourer — the chief thing is to husband one's strength. Then husband and wife, bearing away their household gods and taking their children with them, went off to the sea and never came back.
summary.zh: 舜以天下讓其友石戶之農。石戶之農曰：捲捲乎后之為人，葆力之士也——於是夫負妻戴，攜子以入於海，終身不反也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Shun offered the empire to a friend, a labourer of Shih Hu. "Sire," said the latter, "you exert yourself too much. The chief thing is to husband one's strength;"--meaning that in point of real virtue Shun had not attained. Then, husband and wife, bearing away their household gods and taking their children with them, went off to the sea and never came back.
passages.zh: 舜以天下讓其友石戶之農。石戶之農曰：「捲捲乎，后之為人也，葆力之士也。」於是夫負妻戴，攜子以入於海，終身不反也。

title.en: T'ai Wang Shan Fu Abandons Pin to the Savages (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 太王亶父居邠，讓地於狄（莊子）

region.en: Pin, and the new state at the foot of Mount Ch'i (Binxian/Qishan, Shaanxi, China)
region.zh: 邠地與岐山之下（今陝西彬州／岐山）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: Attacked by savages who want his territory, T'ai Wang Shan Fu refuses to fight: to live with a man's elder brother and slay his younger brother I could not bear to do. He takes his staff and goes off, his people all following him, and they found a new State at the foot of Mount Ch'i.
summary.zh: 太王亶父居邠，狄人攻之；事之以皮帛而不受——與人之兄居而殺其弟，與人之父居而殺其子，吾不忍也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the migration-legend of the Chou royal ancestors, told by Zhuangzi. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: When T'ai Wang Shan Fu was occupying Pin, he was attacked by savages. He offered them skins and silk, but they declined these. He offered them dogs and horses, but they declined these also. He then offered them pearls and jade, but these too they declined. What they wanted was the territory. "To live with a man's elder brother," said T'ai Wang Shan Fu, "and slay his younger brother; to live with a man's father and slay his son,--this I could not bear to do. Make shift to remain here. To be my subjects or the subjects of these savages, where is the difference?"
passages.zh: 大王亶父居邠，狄人攻之。事之以皮帛而不受，事之以犬馬而不受，事之以珠玉而不受。狄人之所求者土地也。大王亶父曰：「與人之兄居而殺其弟，與人之父居而殺其子，吾不忍也。子皆勉居矣！為吾臣與為狄人臣，奚以異哉！」

passages.text: Thereupon he took his staff and went off. His people all followed him, and they founded a new State at the foot of Mount Ch'i. Now T'ai Wang Shan Fu undoubtedly had a proper respect for life. And those who have a proper respect for life, if rich and powerful, do not let that which should nourish injure the body.
passages.zh: 且吾聞之，不以所用養害所養。因策杖而去之。民相連而從之，遂成國於岐山之下。夫大王亶父，可謂能尊生矣。能尊生者，雖貴富不以養傷身，雖貧賤不以利累形。

title.en: Shou of Yüeh Smoked Out of the Hills (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 越王子搜逃乎丹穴（莊子）

region.en: Tan Hsüeh cave in Yüeh (Kuaiji, Zhejiang, China)
region.zh: 丹穴（今浙江會稽）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: Three successive princes of Yüeh have been murdered, so the heir Shou flees to the cave of Tan Hsüeh; the people smoke him out with moxa, have a royal carriage ready, and as he seizes the cord to mount he looks up to heaven and cries: Oh! ruling, ruling, could I not have been spared this?
summary.zh: 越人三世弒其君，王子搜患之，逃乎丹穴；越人薰之以艾——若敖之為君乎，不以國傷生。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: In three successive cases the people of Yüeh had put their prince to death. Accordingly, Shou, the son of the last prince, was much alarmed, and fled to Tan Hsüeh, leaving the State of Yüeh without a ruler. Shou was at first nowhere to be found, but at length he was traced to Tan Hsüeh. He was, however, unwilling to come forth, so they smoked him out with moxa. They had a royal carriage ready for him; and as Shou seized the cord to mount the chariot, he looked up to heaven and cried, "Oh! ruling, ruling, could I not have been spared this?"
passages.zh: 越人三世弒其君，王子搜患之，逃乎丹穴，而越國無君。求王子搜不得，從之丹穴。王子搜不肯出，越人薰之以艾，乘以王輿。王子搜援綏登車，仰天而呼曰：「君乎，君乎，獨不可以舍我乎！」

title.en: Yen Ho the Ox-Herd Vanishes Before the Messenger's Return (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 顏闔守陋閭，布衣帶索（莊子）

region.en: The hovel of Lu (Qufu, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 魯之陋閭（今山東曲阜）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: Hearing that Yen Ho has attained the TAO, the prince of Lu sends messengers with presents. I fear you have made a mistake, says the man in coarse grass clothes who tends oxen — go back and make sure. When they return there is no trace of Yen Ho, and the saying follows: the best part of TAO is for self-culture, the surplus for governing a State, and the dregs for governing the empire.
summary.zh: 顏闔將傅衛靈公太子——魯君聞顏闔得道之人也，使人以幣先焉；闔對曰：恐聽謬而遺使者罪——而顏闔已亡矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The prince of Lu, hearing that Yen Ho had attained to TAO, despatched messengers with presents to open communications. Yen Ho lived in a hovel. He wore clothes of coarse grass, and occupied himself in tending oxen. When the messengers arrived, Yen Ho went out to meet them; whereupon they enquired, "Is this where Yen Ho lives?" "This is Yen Ho's house," replied the latter. The messengers then produced the presents; but Yen Ho said, "I fear you have made a mistake. And as you might get into trouble, it would be as well to go back and make sure."
passages.zh: 魯君聞顏闔得道之人也，使人以幣先焉。顏闔守陋閭，苴布之衣，而自飯牛。魯君之使者至，顏闔自對之。使者曰：「此顏闔之家與？」顏闔對曰：「此闔之家也。」使者致幣。顏闔對曰：「恐聽者謬而遺使者罪，不若審之。」

passages.text: This the messengers accordingly did. When however they returned, there was no trace to be found of Yen Ho. Thus it is that men like Yen Ho hate wealth and power. Wherefore it has been said that the best part of TAO is for self-culture, the surplus for governing a State, and the dregs for governing the empire.
passages.zh: 使者還反審之，復來求之，則不得已。故若顏闔者，惡富貴也。故曰：道之真以治身，其緒餘以為國家，其土苴以治天下。

title.en: Lieh Tzŭ Declines the Prime Minister's Food (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 子陽遺粟，列子辭之（莊子）

region.en: The State of Chêng (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 鄭國（今河南鄭州）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: Poor Lieh Tzŭ, hungry-faced, is offered food by the prime minister Tzŭ Yang on the strength of what others said — and bows twice and declines. His wife beats her breast; but the men of Chêng presently rise in trouble and Tzŭ Yang is slain. His Excellency did not know me personally, answered Lieh Tzŭ: if men were to speak ill of me, he would also act upon it.
summary.zh: 子列子窮，容貌有飢色；客言之於鄭子陽。子列子笑謂其妻曰：君非自知我也，以人之言而遺我粟也——至於罪我者，又且以人之言。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Lieh Tzŭ was poor. His face wore a hungry look. A visitor one day mentioned this to Tzŭ Yang of Chêng, saying, "Lieh Tzŭ is a scholar who has attained to TAO. He lives in your Excellency's State, and yet he is poor. Can it be said that your Excellency does not love scholars?" Thereupon Tzŭ Yang gave orders that Lieh Tzŭ should be supplied with food. But when Lieh Tzŭ saw the messengers, he bowed twice and declined.
passages.zh: 列子窮，容貌有飢色。客有見之於鄭子陽者，曰：「列禦寇蓋有道之士也，居君之國而窮，君無乃為不好士乎？」鄭子陽令官遺之粟數十秉。列子見使者，再拜而辭。

passages.text: When the messengers had gone, and Lieh Tzŭ went within, his wife gazed at him, and beating her breast said, "I have heard that the wife and children of a man of TAO are happy and joyful. But see how hungry I am. His Excellency sent you food, and you would not take it. Is not this flying in the face of Providence?" "His Excellency did not know me personally," answered Lieh Tzŭ with a smile. "It was because of what others said about me that he sent me the food. If then men were to speak ill of me, he would also act upon it. For that reason I refused the food." Subsequently, there was trouble among the people of Chêng, and Tzŭ Yang was slain.
passages.zh: 使者去，列子入，其妻望而拊心曰：「聞為有道者之妻子，皆得佚樂。今有飢色，君過而遺先生食，先生不受，豈非命也哉！」列子笑謂之曰：「君非自知我也，以人之言而遺我粟也。至其罪我也，又且以人之言，此吾所以不受也。」其卒，民果作難而殺子陽。

title.en: The Butcher Yüeh Refuses to Be Made a Minister (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 楚昭王屠羊說辭三旌（莊子）

region.en: The restored court of Ch'u (Jingzhou, Hubei, China)
region.zh: 楚復國之廷（今湖北荊州）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: When Prince Chao of Ch'u lost his kingdom, his butcher Yüeh followed him into exile; on restoration Yüeh declines every reward — I recovered my office and salary, what need for further reward? — and refuses audience by the laws of Ch'u itself, until the prince orders him made a San Ching; and he still refuses, begging to go back to his butchery.
summary.zh: 楚昭王失國，屠羊說從；反國，將賞從者，及說——說曰：大王失國，說失屠羊；大王反國，說亦反屠羊。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: When Prince Chao of the Ch'u State lost his kingdom, he was followed into exile by his butcher, named Yüeh. On his restoration, as he was distributing rewards to those who had remained faithful to him, he came to the name of Yüeh. Yüeh, however, said, "When the prince lost his kingdom, I lost my butchery. Now that the prince has got back his kingdom, I have got back my butchery. I have recovered my office and salary. What need for further reward?"
passages.zh: 楚昭王失國，屠羊說走而從於昭王。昭王反國，將賞從者。及屠羊說。屠羊說曰：「大王失國，說失屠羊；大王反國，說亦反屠羊。臣之爵祿已復矣，又何賞之有！」

passages.text: When the prince heard this answer, he commanded Yüeh to be brought before him. But Yüeh said, "The laws of the Ch'u State require that a subject shall have deserved exceptionally well of his prince before being admitted to an audience. Now my wisdom was insufficient to preserve this kingdom, and my courage insufficient to destroy the invaders. When the Wu soldiers entered Ying, I feared for my life and fled. That was why I followed the prince. And if now the prince wishes to set law and custom aside and summon me to an audience, this is not my idea of proper behaviour on the part of the prince." ... "I must beg to decline. Let me go back to my butchery." And he adhered to his refusal.
passages.zh: 王曰：「見之。」說曰：「楚國之法，得主車者，大夫之尊也；今臣之知不足以存國，而勇不足以死寇。吳軍入郢，說畏難而避寇，非故隨大王也。今大王欲廢法毀約而見說，此非臣之所以聞於天下也。……臣不敢受，復反其屠羊。」

title.en: Yüan Hsien's Mud Hut with a Jar-Mouth Window (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 原憲居魯，環堵之室（莊子）

region.en: The mud hut of Lu (Qufu, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 魯之環堵（今山東曲阜）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: Yüan Hsien dwells in Lu in a mud hut with grass-grown roof and a jar-mouth window closed by a wad of old clothes, sitting gravely there playing the guitar when Tzŭ Kung drives up in a fine chariot. Good gracious! cries Tzŭ Kung; whatever is the matter with you? I am merely poor, answers Yüan Hsien; I have nothing the matter with me.
summary.zh: 原憲居魯，環堵之室，茨以生草，蓬戶不完，桑以為樞而甕牖——上漏下濕，匡坐而弦歌。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Yüan Hsien dwelt in Lu,--in a mud hut, with a grass-grown roof, an apology for a door, and two mulberry-trees for door-posts. The windows which lighted his two rooms were no bigger than the mouth of a jar, and were closed by a wad of old clothes. The hut leaked from above and was damp under foot; yet Yüan Hsien sat gravely there playing on the guitar. Tzŭ Kung came driving up in a fine chariot, in a white robe lined with purple; but the hood of the chariot was too big for the street.
passages.zh: 原憲居魯，環堵之室，茨以生草；蓬戶不完，桑以為樞而甕牖；二室，褐以為塞，上漏下濕，匡坐而弦歌。子貢乘大馬，中紺而表素，不容於巷。

passages.text: "Good gracious!" cried Tzŭ Kung, "whatever is the matter with you?" "I have heard," replied Yüan Hsien, "that he who is without wealth is called poor, and that he who learns without being able to practise is said to have something the matter with him. Now I am merely poor; I have nothing the matter with me." Tzŭ Kung was much abashed at this reply; upon which Yüan Hsien smiling continued, "To try to thrust myself forward among men; to seek friendship in mutual flattery; to learn for the sake of others; to teach for my own sake; to use benevolence and duty to one's neighbour for evil ends; to make a great show with horses and carriages,--these things I cannot do."
passages.zh: 子貢曰：「嘻！先生何病？」原憲應之曰：「憲聞之，無財謂之貧，學道而不能行者謂之病。今憲，貧也，非病也。」子貢逡巡而有愧色。原憑笑曰：「夫希世而行，比周而友，學以為人，教以為己，仁義之慝，輿馬之飾，憲不忍為也。」

title.en: Tsêng Tzŭ Sings the Sacrificial Odes in Threadbare Coat (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 曾子居衛，曳縱而歌商頌（莊子）

region.en: The State of Wei (Anyang region, Henan, China)
region.zh: 衛國（今河南安陽一帶）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: Tsêng Tzŭ in Wei wears a wadded coat with no outside cloth, hands horny hard, three days without fire; yet slipshod he sings the Sacrificial Odes of Shang, his voice filling the whole sky as though it had been some instrument of metal or stone. The Son of Heaven could not secure him as a minister; the feudal princes could not secure him as a friend.
summary.zh: 曾子居衛，縕袍無表，顏色腫噲，手足胼胝；三日不舉火，十年不製衣——正冠而纓絕，捉衿而肘見。曳縱而歌商頌，聲滿天地，若出金石。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Tsêng Tzŭ lived in the Wei State. His wadded coat had no outside cloth. His face was bloated and rough. His hands and feet were horny hard. For three days he had had no fire; no new clothes for ten years. If he set his cap straight the tassel would come off. If he drew up his sleeve his elbow would poke through. If he pulled up his shoe, the heel would come off. Yet slipshod he sang the Sacrificial Odes of Shang, his voice filling the whole sky, as though it had been some instrument of metal or stone.
passages.zh: 曾子居衛，縊袍無表，顏色腫噲，手足胼胝，三日不舉火，十年不製衣。正冠而纓絕，捉衿而肘見，納屨而踵決。曳縱而歌《商頌》，聲滿天地，若出金石。

passages.text: The Son of Heaven could not secure him as a minister. The feudal princes could not secure him as a friend. For he who nourishes his purpose becomes oblivious of his body. He who nourishes his body becomes oblivious of gain. And he who has attained TAO becomes oblivious of his mind.
passages.zh: 天子不得臣，諸侯不得友。故養志者忘形，養形者忘利，致道者忘心矣。

title.en: Yen Hui Declines Official Life (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 孔子謂顏回：回何不仕？（莊子）

region.en: The hall of Lu (Qufu, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 魯之堂（今山東曲阜）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: Confucius urges the poor and lowly Yen Hui into official life; Yen Hui declines — fifty acres beyond the walls for food, ten more for clothes, the lute for amusement, the study of the doctrines for happiness. Bravo! cries Confucius with beaming countenance: only now, that I have seen Yen Hui, am I conscious of the realisation of these words.
summary.zh: 孔子謂顏回曰：回！來！家貧居卑，胡不仕乎？顏回對曰：不愿仕——郭外有五十畝足以給飦粥；郭內十畝足以為絲麻。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: "Come hither," said Confucius to Yen Hui. "Your family is poor, and your position lowly. Why not go into official life?" "I do not wish to," replied Yen Hui. "I have fifty acres of land beyond the city walls, which are enough to supply me with food. Ten more within the walls provide me with clothes. My lute gives me all the amusement I want; and the study of your doctrines keeps me happy enough. I do not desire to go into official life."
passages.zh: 孔子謂顏回曰：「回，來！家貧居卑，胡不仕乎？」顏回對曰：「不願仕。回有郭外之田五十畝，足以給飦粥；郭內之田十畝，足以為絲麻；鼓琴足以自娛；所學夫子之道者，足以自樂也。回不願仕。」

passages.text: "Bravo! well said!" cried Confucius with beaming countenance. "I have heard say that those who are contented do not entangle themselves in the pursuit of gain. That those who have really obtained do not fear the contingency of loss. That those who devote themselves to cultivation of the inner man, though occupying no position, feel no shame. Thus indeed I have long preached. Only now, that I have seen Yen Hui, am I conscious of the realisation of these words."
passages.zh: 孔子愀然變容，曰：「善哉回之意！丘聞之：知足者，不以利自累也；審自得者，失之而不懼；行修於內者，無位而不怍。丘誦之久矣，今於回而後見之，是丘之得也。」

title.en: Tzŭ Lu Dances with a Shield in the Starvation Camp (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 陳蔡之間，子路抗然執干而舞（莊子）

region.en: Between Ch'ên and Ts'ai (Zhoukou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 陳蔡之間（今河南周口一帶）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: Seven days without proper food between Ch'ên and Ts'ai, Confucius sings to his guitar; Tzŭ Lu and Tzŭ Kung grumble that whoever kills him is to be held guiltless. The superior man who succeeds in TAO has success, answers Confucius — it is the chill winter weather, it is frost, it is snow, which bring out the luxuriance of the pine and the fir. Tzŭ Lu hastily seizes a shield and dances to the music, and Tzŭ Kung owns he had no idea of the height of heaven and the depth of earth.
summary.zh: 孔子窮於陳蔡之間，七日不火食；藜羹不糝。子路曰：夫子逐於魯，削跡於衛——弦歌鼓琴未嘗絕音，豈君子之無恥也若此乎？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: When Confucius was caught between the Ch'êns and the Ts'ais, he went seven days without proper food. He ate soup of herbs, having no rice. He looked very much exhausted, yet he sat within playing his guitar and singing to it. Yen Hui was picking over the herbs, while Tzŭ Lu and Tzŭ Kung were talking together. One of them said, "Our Master has twice been driven out of Lu. They will have none of him in Wei. His tree was cut down in Sung. He got into trouble in Shang and Chou. And now he is surrounded by the Ch'êns and the Ts'ais. Whoever kills him is to be held guiltless. Whoever takes him prisoner is not to be interfered with. Yet all the time he goes on playing and singing without cease. Is this the right thing for a superior man to do?"
passages.zh: 孔子窮於陳蔡之間，七日不火食，藜羹不糝，顏色甚憊，而弦歌於室。顏回擇菜，子路、子貢相與言曰：「夫子再逐於魯，削跡於衛，伐樹於宋，窮於商周，圍於陳蔡。殺夫子者無罪，藉夫子者無禁。弦歌鼓琴，未嘗絕音，君子之無醜也若此乎？」

passages.text: "The superior man who succeeds in TAO, has success. If he fails in TAO, he makes a failure. Now I, holding fast to the TAO of charity and duty towards one's neighbour, have fallen among the troubles of a disordered age. What failure is there in that? ... It is the chill winter weather, it is frost, it is snow, which bring out the luxuriance of the pine and the fir. I regard it as a positive blessing to be thus situated as I am." Thereupon he turned abruptly round and went on playing and singing. At this Tzŭ Lu hastily seized a shield and began dancing to the music, while Tzŭ Kung said, "I had no idea of the height of heaven and of the depth of earth."
passages.zh: 「君子通於道之謂通，窮於道之謂窮。今丘抱仁義之道，以遭亂世之患，其何窮之為！……天寒既至，霜雪既降，吾是以知松柏之茂也。陳蔡之隘，於丘其幸乎！」孔子削然反琴而弦歌。子路扢然執干而舞。子貢曰：「吾不知天之高也，地之下也。」

title.en: Pien Sui and Wu Kuang Drown Themselves Rather Than Take T'ang's Throne (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 湯將伐桀，卞隨務光自投（莊子）

region.en: The rivers Chou and Lu (symbolic pin: Tongbai, Henan, China)
region.zh: 桐水盧水之濱（象徵定位：河南桐柏）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: T'ang consults the hermits Pien Sui and Wu Kuang about attacking Chieh — It is not a matter in which I can help you, say both — then attacks and vanquishes, and offers each in turn the empire. To depose a ruler is not to do one's duty to one's neighbour, answers Wu Kuang; to slay the people is not charity — and one after another they take a stone on their backs and jump into the river.
summary.zh: 湯遂伐桀，克之；因讓卞隨、務光——廢上非義也，而殺民非仁也。乃負石自沈於廬水。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: When T'ang was about to attack Chieh, he went to consult with Pien Sui. "It is not a matter in which I can help you," said the latter. "Who can?" asked T'ang. "I do not know," replied Pien Sui. T'ang then went to consult with Wu Kuang. "It is not a matter in which I can help you," said the latter. "Who can?" asked T'ang. "I do not know," replied Wu Kuang.
