So T'ang took I Yin into his counsels. They attacked Chieh, and vanquished him.
passages.zh: 湯將伐桀，因卞隨而謀。卞隨曰：「非吾事也。」湯曰：「孰可？」曰：「吾不知也。」湯又因瞀光而謀。瞀光曰：「非吾事也。」湯曰：「孰可？」曰：「吾不知也。」湯曰：「伊尹何如？」曰：「勉力哉！吾弗能也。」湯遂與伊尹謀伐桀，剋之。

passages.text: Then T'ang offered to resign the empire in favour of Pien Sui. But Pien Sui declined, saying, "When your Majesty consulted with me about attacking Chieh, you evidently looked on me as a robber. Now that you have vanquished him, and you offer to resign in my favour, you evidently regard me as covetous. I was born indeed in a disordered age. But for a man without TAO to thus insult me twice, is more than I can endure." So he drowned himself in the river Chou.
passages.zh: 以讓卞隨，卞隨辭曰：「后之伐桀也，謀乎我，必以我為賊也；勝桀而讓我，必以我為貪也。吾生乎亂世，而無道之人再來謾我以行，吾不能堪數矣。」乃自投稠水而死。

passages.text: Then T'ang offered to resign in favour of Wu Kuang, saying, "The wise plan, the brave execute, the good rest therein,--such was the TAO of the ancients. Why, Sir, should not you occupy the throne?" But Wu Kuang declined, saying, "To depose a ruler is not to do one's duty to one's neighbour. To slay the people is not charity. For others to suffer these wrongs, while I enjoy the profits, is not honest. I have heard say that one should not accept a wage unless earned in accordance with right; and that if the world is without TAO, one should not put foot upon its soil, still less rule over it! I can bear this no longer." Thereupon he took a stone on his back and jumped into the river Lu.
passages.zh: 湯又讓瞀光，曰：「知者謀之，武者遂之，仁者居之，古之道也。吾子胡不立乎？」瞀光辭曰：「廢上，非義也；殺民，非仁也；人犯其難，我享其利，非廉也。吾聞之曰：非其義者，不受其祿；無道之世，不踐其土。況尊我乎！吾不忍久見也。」乃負石而自沉於廬水。

title.en: Poh I and Shu Ch'i Starve on Mount Shou-yang (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 伯夷叔齊餓於首陽（莊子）

region.en: Mount Shou-yang (Shouyangshan, Shanxi, China)
region.zh: 首陽山（今山西永濟）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: At the rise of the Chou dynasty the two scholars Poh I and Shu Ch'i go west to see men in possession of TAO, and are offered a treaty of emoluments sealed with blood and buried. Troops are mobilised to protect prestige; victims are slaughtered to give good faith to a treaty — the empire is now in darkness. They flee north to Mount Shou-yang, where they starve themselves to death.
summary.zh: 昔周之興，有士二人處於孤竹——虞暴亂以相誅，伐以要利——遂北至於首陽之山，遂餓死焉。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: At the rise of the Chou dynasty there were two scholars, named Po I and Shu Ch'i, who lived in Ku-tu. One of these said to the other, "I have heard that in the west there are men who are apparently in possession of TAO. Let us go and see them." When they arrived at Ch'i-yang, Wu Wang heard of their arrival and sent Shu Tan to enter into a treaty with them. They were to receive emoluments of the second degree and rank of the first degree. The treaty was to be sealed with blood and buried.
passages.zh: 昔周之興，有士二人處於孤竹，曰伯夷叔齊。二人相謂曰：「吾聞西方有偏有其人，似有道者，試往觀焉。」至於岐陽，武王聞之，使叔旦往見之，與盟曰：「加富二等，就官一列。」為血牲而埋之。

passages.text: At this the two looked at each other and smiled. "Ah!" said one of them, "this is strange indeed. It is not what we call TAO. When Shên Nung ruled the empire, he worshipped God without asking for any reward. ... But now that the Chous, beholding the iniquities of the Yins, have taken upon themselves to govern, we have intrigues above and bribes below. Troops are mobilised to protect prestige. Victims are slaughtered to give good faith to a treaty. A show of virtue is made to amuse the masses. Fighting and slaughter are made the means of gain. Confusion has simply been exchanged for disorder.
passages.zh: 二人相視而笑，曰：「嘻，異哉！此非吾所謂道也。昔者神農之有天下也，時祀盡敬而不祈喜。……今周見殷之亂而遽為政，上謀行而下阻，兵馳兵行，牲牲約信，揚行以說眾，殺伐以要利，是推亂以易暴也。

passages.text: "I have heard tell that the men of old, living in quiet times, never shirked their duties; but lighting upon troublous times, nothing could make them stay. The empire is now in darkness. The virtue of the Chous has faded. For the empire to be united under the Chous would be a disgrace to us. Better flee away and keep our actions pure." Accordingly, these two philosophers went north to Mount Shou-yang, where they subsequently starved themselves to death.
passages.zh: 「吾聞古之士，遭乎治世不避其任，遇乎亂世不為苟存。今天下闇，周德衰，其並乎周以塗吾身也，不如避之以絜吾行。」二子北至於首陽之山，遂餓而死焉。

title.en: Robber Chê and the Liver Stew: The Harangue of the Great Brigand (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 盜跖怒斥孔子（莊子）

region.en: The robber-camp south of Mount T'ai (Shandong, China)
region.zh: 泰山之陽盜寨（今山東泰安南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 29, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 29

summary.en: With a band nine thousand strong, Robber Chê ravages the empire, and Confucius — charioteered by Yen Hui — goes to convert him, finding the brigand eating a dish of minced human liver. Chê's harangue turns every table: Yao and Shun got the empire, yet their descendants have not territory enough to insert an awl's point; you are the biggest thief I know of — if the world calls me Robber Chê, it most certainly ought to call you Robber Ch'iu. Confucius three times misses the reins, having cauterized himself without being ill and very nearly got into the tiger's mouth.
summary.zh: 孔子與柳下季為友；柳下季之弟名曰盜跖。孔子往見之，盜跖乃方休卒徒太山之陽，膾人肝而餔之——若以利惑其真而強反其情性，詩書發塚！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the spurious-but-canonical Robber Chê dialogue is Zhuangzi's great trickster-narrative. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Robber Chê had a band of followers nine thousand strong. He ravaged the whole empire, plundering the various nobles and breaking into people's houses. He drove off oxen and horses. He stole men's wives and daughters. Family ties put no limit to his greed. He had no respect for parents nor for brothers. He neglected the worship of his ancestors. Wherever he passed, the greater States flew to arms, the smaller ones to places of safety. All the people were sore distressed.
passages.zh: 盜跖從卒九千人，橫行天下，侵暴諸侯。入室，驅人之牛馬，取人之婦女。貪得妄親，不顧父母兄弟，不祭先祖。所過之邑，大國守城，小國入保，萬民苦之。

passages.text: The latter had just encamped to the south of T'ai-shan, and was engaged in devouring a dish of minced human liver. Confucius alighted from his chariot, and advancing addressed the doorkeeper as follows:--"I am Confucius of the Lu State. I have heard of the high character of your captain." When Robber Chê heard who it was, he was furious. His eyes glared like stars. His hair raised his cap from his head as he cried out, "What! that crafty scoundrel Confucius of Lu? Go, tell him from me that he is a mere word-mongerer. That he talks nonsense about Wên Wang and Wu Wang. That what he says is mostly rhodomontade. That he consumes where he does not sow, and wears clothes he does not weave. That his lips patter and his tongue wags. Tell him that he deserves the worst, and that if he does not take himself off his liver shall be in my morning stew."
passages.zh: 孔子往見盜跖。盜跖乃方休卒徒大山之陽，膾人肝而餔之。孔子下車而前，見謁者曰：「魯人孔丘，聞將軍高義。」盜跖大怒，兩展其足，案劍瞋目，聲如乳虎，曰：「丘前來！夫可規以利而可諫以言者，皆愚陋恆民之謂耳。今丘，修文武之道，掌天下之辯，以教後世。縫衣淺帶，矯言偽行，以迷惑天下之主，而欲求富貴焉。盜莫大於子。天下何故不謂子為盜丘，而乃謂我為盜跖？」

passages.text: "Ch'iu! come here," cried Robber Chê in a great rage. "There is no State bigger than the empire. Yao and Shun both got this, yet their descendants have not territory enough to insert an awl's point. T'ang and Wu Wang both sat upon the Imperial throne, yet their posterity has been obliterated from the face of the earth. Was not this because of the very magnitude of the prize? ... And now you come forward preaching the old dogmas of Wên Wang and palming off sophistries without end, in order to teach future generations. You are the biggest thief I know of; and if the world calls me Robber Chê, it most certainly ought to call you Robber Ch'iu.
passages.zh: 盜跖曰：「丘來前！夫所謂大者，莫若天下。堯舜有天下，子孫無置錐之地；湯武立為天子，而後世絕滅。非以其利大故邪？……今子修文武之道，掌天下之辯，以教後世。縫衣淺帶，矯言偽行，以迷惑天下之主，而欲求富貴焉。盜莫大於子。天下何故不謂子為盜丘，而乃謂我為盜跖？」

passages.text: "Ch'iu! all your teachings are nothing to me. Begone! Go home! Say no more! Your doctrine is a random jargon, full of falsity and deceit. It can never preserve the original purity of man. Why discuss it further?" Confucius made two obeisances and hurriedly took his leave. On mounting his chariot, he three times missed hold of the reins. His eyes were so dazed that he could see nothing. His face was ashy pale. ... "He did," said Confucius. "I am a man who has cauterized himself without being ill. I hurried away to smooth the tiger's head and comb out his beard. And I very nearly got into the tiger's mouth."
passages.zh: 「丘之所言，皆吾所棄也。亟去走歸，無復言之！子之道，狂狂汲汲，詐巧虛偽事也，非可以全真也，奚足論哉！」孔子再拜趨走，出門上車，執轡三失，目茫然無見，色若死灰。……孔子曰：「然。丘所謂無病而自灸也。疾走料虎頭，編虎鬚，幾不免虎口哉！」

title.en: Nest-Builders, the Provident, and the War Whose Blood Flowed a Hundred Li (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 有巢氏、知生氏與涿鹿之戰（莊子）

region.en: Chŏ-lu, the battlefield of the Yellow Emperor and Ch'ih Yu (Zhuolu, Hebei, China)
region.zh: 涿鹿之野（今河北涿鹿）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 29, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 29

summary.en: In Robber Chê's mouth, the great cultural myths are turned into an indictment: in olden times birds and animals outnumbered man and he built his domicile in trees — hence the name Nest-builders; the people did not know how to make clothes and warmed themselves by fire — hence the name Provident; in Shên Nung's days a man knew his mother but not his father and lived among the wild deer. Then the Yellow Emperor fought with Ch'ih Yu at Chŏ-lu, and blood flowed for a hundred li — ever since T'ang and Wu Wang we have had none other than disturbers of the peace.
summary.zh: 古者禽獸多而人民少，於是民皆巢居以避之；晝拾橡栗，暮棲木上，故命之曰有巢氏之民。古者民不知衣服——故命之曰知生之民。黃帝不能致德，與蚩尤戰於涿鹿之野，流血百里。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the Robber Chê version of China's culture-hero sequence — Nest-builders, fire-warming providents, Shên Nung's age of perfect virtue. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: "I have also heard that in olden times the birds and animals outnumbered man, and that the latter was obliged to seek his safety by building his domicile in trees. By day he picked up acorns and chestnuts. At night he slept upon a branch. Hence the name Nest-builders.
passages.zh: 盜跖曰：「古者禽獸多而人少，於是民皆巢居以避之。晝拾橡栗，暮棲木上，故命之曰有巢氏之民。

passages.text: "Of old, the people did not know how to make clothes. In summer they collected quantities of fuel, and in winter warmed themselves by fire. Hence the name Provident. "In the days of Shên Nung, they lay down without caring where they were and got up without caring whither they might go. A man knew his mother but not his father. He lived among the wild deer. He tilled the ground for food. He wove cloth to cover his body. He harboured no thought of injury to others. These were the glorious results of an age of perfect virtue. "The Yellow Emperor, however, could not attain to this virtue. He fought with Ch'ih Yu at Chŏ-lu, and blood flowed for a hundred li. Then came Yao and Shun with their crowd of ministers. Then T'ang who deposed his sovereign, and Wu Wang who slew Chou. After which time the strong took to oppressing the weak, the many to coercing the few. In fact, ever since T'ang and Wu Wang we have had none other than disturbers of the peace."
passages.zh: 古者民不知衣服，夏多積薪，冬則煬之，故命之曰知生之民。神農之世，臥則居居，起則于于。民知其母，不知其父，與麋鹿共處。耕而食，織而衣，無有相害之心，此至德之隆也。然而黃帝不能致德，與蚩尤戰於涿鹿之野，流血百里。堯舜作，立其臣；湯放其主，武王殺紂。自是以後，以強陵弱，以眾暴寡。湯武以來，皆亂人之徒也。」

title.en: Chieh Tzŭ T'ui's Slice of Thigh and the Bridge-Assassin Wei Shêng (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 介子推割股，尾生抱柱（莊子）

region.en: The drowned assignation beneath the bridge (symbolic pin: Qufu, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 橋下之約（象徵定位：山東曲阜）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 29, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 29

summary.en: Robber Chê's catalogue of the world's 'virtuous': Chieh Tzŭ T'ui cut a slice from his thigh to feed Wên Wang, then grasped a tree and was burnt to death; Wei Shêng made an assignation with a girl beneath a bridge, the water rose, he grasped a buttress and died; Poh I and Shu Ch'i died of starvation on Mount Shou-yang, their corpses deprived of burial — these four differed in no way from dogs and pigs going about begging to be slaughtered.
summary.zh: 介子推至忠也，自割其股以食文公；尾生與女子期於梁下——水至不去，抱梁柱而死。此四子者無異於磔犬流豕。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Among those whom the world calls virtuous were Poh I and Shu Ch'i. They declined the sovereignty of Ku-chu and died of starvation on Mount Shou-yang, their corpses deprived of burial. "Pao Chiao made a great show of virtue and abused the world in general. He grasped a tree and died. "Shên T'u Ti, when no heed was paid to his counsels, jumped into the river with a stone on his back and became food for fishes.
passages.zh: 世之所謂賢士，伯夷叔齊。伯夷叔齊辭孤竹之君，而餓死於首陽之山，骨肉不葬。鮑焦飾行非世，抱木而死。申徒狄諫而不聽，負石自投於河，為魚鱉所食。

passages.text: "Chieh Tzŭ T'ui was truly loyal. He cut a slice from his thigh to feed Wên Wang. Afterwards, when Wên Wang turned his back upon him, he retired in anger, and grasping a tree, was burnt to death. "Wei Shêng made an assignation with a girl beneath a bridge. The girl did not come, and the water rose. But Wei Shêng would not leave. He grasped a buttress and died. "These four differed in no way from dogs and pigs going about begging to be slaughtered. They all exaggerated reputation and disregarded death. They did not reflect upon their original nature and seek to preserve life into the old age allotted."
passages.zh: 介子推至忠也，自割其股以食文公。文公而後背之，介子推怒而去，抱木而燔死。尾生與女子期於梁下，女子不來，水至不去，抱梁柱而死。此六子者，無異於磔犬流豕、操瓢而乞者，皆離名輕死，不念本養壽命者也。

title.en: The Three Swords: Of the Son of Heaven, of the Princes, and of the People (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 說劍：天子之劍、諸侯之劍、庶人之劍（莊子）

region.en: The court of Wên Wang of Chao (Handan, Hebei, China)
region.zh: 趙文王之廷（今河北邯鄲）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 30, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 30

summary.en: Wên Wang of Chao loves sword-play, with three thousand swordsmen bouting yearly and a hundred killed; Chuang Tzŭ, engaged by the Heir Apparent, enters dressed as a fencer and offers three swords. The sword of the Son of Heaven — the stone wall of Yen-ch'i its point, the mountains of Ch'i its edge, enclosed in the four hordes, wrapped in the four seasons — cleaves the floating clouds above and cuts through the density of earth below; one flash and the princes of the empire submit.
summary.zh: 趙文王喜劍，劍士夾門三千餘人。莊子入殿門不趨——天子之劍：以燕谿石城為鋒，齊岱為鍔；包以四夷，裹以四時；上決浮雲，下絕地紀。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Of old, Wên Wang of Chao loved sword-play. Swordsmen thronged his halls, to the number of three thousand and more. Day and night they had bouts before the prince. In the course of a year, a hundred or so would be killed or wounded. Yet the prince was never satisfied. Within three years, the State had begun to go to rack and ruin, and other princes to form designs upon it.
passages.zh: 昔趙文王喜劍。劍士夾門而客三千餘人，日夜相擊於前，死傷者歲百餘人，好之不厭。如是三年，國衰，諸侯謀之。

passages.text: "What is the sword of the Son of Heaven?" asked the prince. "The stone wall of Yen-ch'i is its point," replied Chuang Tzŭ. "The mountains of Ch'i are its edge. Chin and Wei are its back. Chou and Sung are its hilt. Han and Wei are its sheath. It is enclosed in the four hordes of barbarians, wrapped in the four seasons, surrounded by the great ocean. It is made of the five elements. It is the arbiter of punishment and reward. It operates under the influence of the Yin and the Yang. In spring and summer it is at rest. In autumn and winter it moves abroad. Push it, it does not advance. Raise it, it does not go up. Lower it, it does not go down. Whirl it around, it does not change position. Above, it cleaves the floating clouds; below, it cuts through the density of earth. One flash of this blade, and the princes of the empire submit. Such is the sword of the Son of Heaven."
passages.zh: 王曰：「天子之劍何如？」曰：「天子之劍，以燕谿石城為鋒，齊岱為鍔，晉魏為脊，周宋為鐔，韓魏為夾；包以四夷，裹以四時，繞以渤海，帶以常山；制以五行，論以刑德；開以陰陽，持以春夏，行以秋冬。此劍一用，匡諸侯，天下服矣。此天子之劍也。」

passages.text: "The sword of the People," replied Chuang Tzŭ, "has dishevelled hair hanging over its temples. It wears a slouching cap with coarse tangled tassel, and a short-tailed coat. It glares with its eyes and talks in a fierce tone. When it engages in conflict, above, it cuts off head and neck; below, it smites liver and lungs. Such is the sword of the People. It is like a game-cock. One day, its life is cut short, and it is of no more use to the State. Now you, great prince, wield sovereign power, and yet you devote yourself to this sword of the People. I am truly ashamed of it." After this the prince did not quit his palace for three months, while the swordsmen, submitting to the new order of things, died in their own homes.
passages.zh: 曰：「庶人之劍，蓬頭突鬢垂冠，曼胡之纓，短後之衣，瞋目而語難。相擊於前，上斬頸領，下決肝肺。此庶人之劍，無異於鬥雞，一旦命已絕矣，無所於國事。今大王有天子之位，而好庶人之劍，臣竊為大王薄之。」王乃牽而登殿，不出宮三月，劍士皆服斃其處也。

title.en: The Old Fisherman of the Apricot Altar (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 杏壇漁父（莊子）

region.en: The Apricot Altar in the Black Forest of Ch'u (Huaiyin, Jiangsu, China)
region.zh: 緇帷之林杏壇（象徵定位：江蘇淮陰）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 31, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 31

summary.en: Travelling in the Black Forest, Confucius rests at the Apricot Altar, playing and singing, until a snowy-bearded fisherman steps out of his boat and asks what the man is doing. The old man tells of the eight blemishes and four obstructions, and of the man who fled his shadow and died of running; the original purity is the perfection of truth unalloyed, given from God — ceremonial is the invention of man. Confucius waits until the ripples have smoothed down and the punt-pole's sound died away before he ventures to get up.
summary.zh: 孔子遊乎緇帷之林，休坐乎杏壇之上；弟子讀書，孔子絃歌鼓琴。漁父曰：真者，所以受於天也，自然不可易也——法天貴真，不拘於俗。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the Apricot Altar of this chapter became the legendary site of Confucius's teaching. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Confucius, travelling in the Black Forest, rested awhile at Apricot Altar. His disciples sat down to their books, and he himself played upon the lute and sang. Half way through the song, an old fisherman stepped out of a boat and advanced towards them. His beard and eyebrows were snowy white. His hair hung loose, and he flapped his long sleeves as he walked over the foreshore. Reaching firm ground, he stood still, and with left hand on his knee and right hand to his ear, listened.
passages.zh: 孔子遊乎緇帷之林，休坐乎杏壇之上。弟子讀書，孔子弦歌鼓琴。奏曲未半，有漁父者下船而來，鬚眉交白，被髮揄袂，行原以上，距陸而止，左手據膝，右手持頤以聽。

passages.text: "There was once a man who was so afraid of his shadow and so disliked his own footsteps that he determined to run away from them. But the oftener he raised his feet the more footsteps he made, and though he ran very hard his shadow never left him. From this he inferred that he went too slowly, and ran as hard as he could without resting, the consequence being that his strength broke down and he died. He was not aware that by going into the shade he would have got rid of his shadow, and that by keeping still he would have put an end to his footsteps. Fool that he was!
passages.zh: （問「何謂真」之前，漁父說）畏影惡跡者，舉足愈數而跡愈多，走愈疾而影不離身，自以為尚遲，疾走不休，絕力而死。不知處陰以休影，處靜以息跡，愚亦甚矣！

passages.text: "Our original purity," replied the fisherman, "is the perfection of truth unalloyed. Without this, we cannot influence others. Hence, those who weep to order, though they mourn, do not grieve. Those who assume anger, though violent, do not inspire awe. Those who affect friendship, though they smile, are not in unison. "Real mourning grieves in silence. Real anger awes without expression. Real friendship is unison without the aid of smiles. Our emotions are dependent upon the original purity within; and accordingly we hold the latter in esteem. "Ceremonial is the invention of man. Our original purity is given to us from God. It is as it is, and cannot be changed."
passages.zh: 真者，精誠之至也。不精不誠，不能動人。故強哭者雖悲不哀，強怒者雖嚴不威，強親者雖笑不和。真悲無聲而哀，真怒未發而威，真親未笑而和。真在內者，神動於外，是所以貴真也。……禮者，世俗之所為也；真者，所以受於天也。自然不可易也。

passages.text: Thereupon he pushed off his boat, and disappeared among the reeds. Yen Yüan then brought up the chariot, and Tzŭ Lu offered the hand-cord to Confucius. But the latter paid no attention. He waited until the ripples on the water had smoothed down and the sound of the punt-pole had died away, before he ventured to get up. "Master, I have been in your service now for a long time, yet never did I see you treat any man like this. ... Yet before this old fisherman, leaning on his punt-pole, you cringe and bow and prostrate yourself twice before answering."
passages.zh: 客去，遂操舟而去。顏淵還車，子路授綏，孔子不顧，待水波定，不聞拏音而後敢乘。子路旁車而問曰：「由得為夫子久矣，未嘗見夫子遇人如此其威也。……萬乘之主，千乘之君，見夫子未嘗不分庭伉禮，夫子猶有倨敖之容。今漁父杖拏逆立，而夫子曲要磬折，再拜而應，得無太甚乎！」

title.en: The Courtyard Full of Boots: Lieh Tzŭ's Relapse (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 列子反齊，門庭充盈（莊子）

region.en: The road to Ch'i and back (symbolic pin: Linzi, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 適齊之道（象徵定位：山東臨淄）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 32, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 32

summary.en: Lieh Tzŭ turns back halfway to Ch'i in fear, for five out of ten restaurants would take no payment — conquer men's hearts by force of the external and trouble follows. Later his courtyard is filled with visitors' boots; the Master Poh Hun Wu Jen stands facing the north, cheek wrinkled on his staff, then departs without a word, crying: It is all over! Exerting influence unduly over others, you are by them influenced in turn.
summary.zh: 列子行食於十家，五家先逆——驚恐而返。居於鄙，人舍者將見之——見其客而歎曰：戶庭之閒，其人弗睹也！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: When Lieh Tzŭ went to Ch'i, half way there he turned round and came back. Falling in with Poh Hun Wu Jen, the latter said, "How is it you are so soon back again?" "I was afraid," replied Lieh Tzŭ. "Out of ten restaurants at which I ate," said Lieh Tzŭ, "five would take no payment. ... A restaurant keeper is one who lives by retailing soup. When his returns are counted up, his profit is but small, and his influence is next to nothing. But if such a man could act thus, how much more the ruler of a large State? ... That is what I was afraid of."
passages.zh: 列子出行，遇伯昏瞀人。伯昏瞀人曰：「何方而反？」曰：「吾驚焉。」「惡乎驚？」「吾食於十漿，而五漿先饋。」……夫漿人特為食羹之貨，無多餘之贏，其為利也薄，其為權也輕，而猶若是，而況於萬乘之主乎！身勞於國而知盡於事，彼將任我聽我，此吾所以驚也。

passages.text: Shortly afterwards Poh Hun Wu Jen went to visit Lieh Tzŭ, and lo! his court-yard was filled with boots. Poh Hun Wu Jen stood there awhile, facing the north, his cheek all wrinkled by resting it on his staff. Then, without a word, he departed. Upon this being announced to Lieh Tzŭ, he seized his shoes and ran out barefoot. When he reached the outer gate, he called aloud, "Master! now that you have come, will you not give me medicine?" "It is all over!" cried Poh Hun Wu Jen. "I told you that the world would gather around you. It is not that you can make people gather around you. You cannot prevent them from doing so. Of what use would my instruction be? Exerting influence thus unduly over others, you are by them influenced in turn. You disturb your natural constitution, and are of no further account.
passages.zh: 伯昏瞀人往見列子，見其門外之屨滿矣。伯昏瞀人北面而立，頓杖而頤，已而辭去。賓者以告列子，列子提屨跣而走，暨乎門，曰：「先生既來，曾不發藥乎？」曰：「已矣！吾固告汝，眾人保之，而莫使然也。汝何得以拒之？……非汝能使人保也，而汝固使人保也，吾何為任汝！」

title.en: Huan's Suicide and the Dream of the Autumn Pine (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 鄭人緩也呻吟裘氏之地（莊子）

region.en: Ch'iu-shih, in the Chêng State (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 裘氏之地（今河南鄭州）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 32, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 32

summary.en: Huan of Chêng graduates as a Confucianist in three years and sends his younger brother to study as a Mihist; when the father takes the Mihist's side, Huan commits suicide — and appears in a dream: It was I who caused your son to become a Mihist. Why give all the credit to him who is but as the fruit of an autumn pine? Verily God does not reward man for what he does, but for what he is.
summary.zh: 鄭人緩也呻吟裘氏之地，祗三年而緩為儒；其父以為墨者。緩於十年自殺；其父夢之曰：使而子為墨者，予也——秋柏之實者。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: There was a man of the Chêng State, named Huan. He pursued his studies at a place called Ch'iu-shih. After three years only, he had graduated as a Confucianist; and like a river which fertilises its banks to a distance of nine li, so did his good influence reach into three families. He caused his younger brother to graduate as a Mihist. But inasmuch as in the question of Confucianism versus Mihism, the father took the side of the Mihist, at the end of ten years Huan committed suicide.
passages.zh: 鄭人緩也呻吟裘氏之地，祗三年而緩為儒。河潤九里，澤及三族，使其弟墨。儒墨相與辯，其父助翟。十年而緩自殺。

passages.text: Then the father dreamed that Huan appeared to him and said, "It was I who caused your son to become a Mihist. Why give all the credit to him who is but as the fruit of an autumn pine?" Verily God does not reward man for what he does, but for what he is. ... Whereas a man who should regard his distinctive abilities as of his own making, without reference to his parents, would be like the man of Ch'i who dug a well and then wanted to keep others away from it.
passages.zh: 其父夢曰：「使而子為墨者，予也。闔胡嘗視其良，既為秋柏之實矣？」……夫造物者之報人也，不報其人而報其人之天。……彼且乘人而無天，則是掘井而謂之塞人矣。

title.en: Chu P'ing Man Learns to Slay Dragons (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 朱泙漫學屠龍於支離益（莊子）

region.en: The school of Chih Li I (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 支離益之門（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 32, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 32

summary.en: Chu P'ing Man spends a large patrimony learning under Chih Li I how to kill dragons. By the end of three years he is perfect — but there is no direction in which he can show his skill. TAO cannot be put into practice.
summary.zh: 朱泙漫學屠龍於支離益，單千金之家；三年技成，而無所用其巧。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the dragon-slaying vanity is proverbial. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Chu P'ing Man spent a large patrimony in learning under Chih Li I how to kill dragons. By the end of three years he was perfect, but there was no direction in which he could show his skill. The true Sage regards certainties as uncertainties; therefore he is never up in arms.
passages.zh: 朱泙漫學屠龍於支離益，單千金之家，三年技成而無所用其巧。……聖人以必不必，故無兵。

title.en: Ts'ao Shang's Hundred Carriages and the Licker of Piles (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 曹商得車，舐痔之譏（莊子）

region.en: The court of Ch'in (Xianyang, Shaanxi, China)
region.zh: 秦廷（今陝西咸陽）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 32, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 32

summary.en: Ts'ao Shang, the Sung envoy, returns from Ch'in with a hundred carriages and taunts the sandal-making Chuang Tzŭ. The physician who opens a boil gets one carriage; the man who licks his piles gets five — the more degrading the work, the greater the number of carriages. You, Sir, must have been attending to his piles to get so many carriages. Begone with you!
summary.zh: 宋人有曹商者，為宋王使秦；其往也，得車數乘；秦王有疾，舐痔者得車五乘——所治愈下，得車愈多。子豈治其痔邪？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: A man of the Sung State, named Ts'ao Shang, acted as political agent for the prince of Sung at the court of the Ch'in State. When he went thither, he had a few carriages; but the prince of Ch'in was so pleased with him that he added one hundred more. On his return to Sung, he visited Chuang Tzŭ and said, "As for living in poverty in a dirty hovel, earning a scanty subsistence by making sandals, with shrivelled face and yellow ears,--this I could not do. Interviewing a powerful ruler, with a retinue of a hundred carriages,--that is my forte."
passages.zh: 宋人曹商，為宋王使秦。其往也，得車數乘；王說之，益車百乘。反於宋，見莊子曰：「夫處窮閭阨巷，困窘織屨，槁項黃馘者，商之所短也；一悟萬乘之主而從車百乘者，商之所長也。」

passages.text: "When the prince of Ch'in is sick," replied Chuang Tzŭ, "and he summons his physician to open a boil or cleanse an ulcer, the latter gets one carriage. The man who licks his piles gets five. The more degrading the work, the greater the number of carriages given. You, Sir, must have been attending to his piles to get so many carriages. Begone with you!"
passages.zh: 莊子曰：「秦王有病召醫，破癰潰痤者得車一乘，舐痔者得車五乘，所治愈下，得車愈多。子豈治其痔邪，何車之多也？子行矣！」

title.en: The Pearl Under the Sleeping Dragon's Nose (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 驪龍頷下之珠（莊子）

region.en: Ho-Shang, the riverside hamlet (symbolic pin: Zhenjiang, Jiangsu, China)
region.zh: 河上之家（象徵定位：江蘇鎮江）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 32, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 32

summary.en: A man presented with ten chariots by the prince of Sung puts on airs before Chuang Tzŭ, who tells of the poor plaiter of rushes whose son dived into the river and got a pearl worth a thousand ounces — from under the nose of the dragon, which must have been asleep. The prince of Sung is fiercer than a dragon: to get these chariots you must have caught him asleep, and when he wakes you will be ground to powder.
summary.zh: 河上有家貧恃緯蕭而食者；其子沒於淵，得千金之珠——必在九重之淵而驪龍頷下，子能得珠者，必遭其睡也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the black dragon's pearl became a classic image of perilous gain. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: A man who had been to see the prince of Sung and had been presented with ten chariots, was putting on airs in the presence of Chuang Tzŭ. "At Ho-Shang," said the latter, "there was a poor man who supported his family by plaiting rushes. One day his son dived into the river and got a pearl worth a thousand ounces of silver. The father bade him fetch a stone and smash it to pieces, explaining that he could only have got such a pearl very deep down from under the nose of the dragon, which must have been asleep. And he said he was afraid that when the dragon waked, the boy would have a poor chance.
passages.zh: 人有見宋王者，錫車十乘，以其十乘驕稚莊子。莊子曰：「河上有家貧恃緯蕭而食者，其子沒於淵，得千金之珠。其父謂其子曰：『取石來鍛之！夫千金之珠，必在九重之淵而驪龍頷下。子能得珠者，必遭其睡也。使驪龍而寤，子尚奚微之有哉！』

passages.text: "Now the State of Sung is deeper than a deep river, and the prince of Sung is fiercer than a dragon. To get these chariots, you must have caught him asleep. And when he wakes, you will be ground to powder."
passages.zh: 今宋國之深，非直九重之淵也；宋王之猛，非直驪龍也。子能得車者，必遭其睡也。使宋王而寤，子為齏粉夫！」

title.en: The Sacrificial Ox Would Gladly Change Places with a Neglected Calf (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 莊子釣於濮水，龜曳尾；犧牛之喻（莊子）

region.en: Some prince's court (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 聘使之廷（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 32, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 32

summary.en: Invited to enter a prince's service, Chuang Tzŭ replies to the envoy: Sir, have you ever noticed a sacrificial ox? It is bedecked with ribbons and fares sumptuously — but when it comes to be slaughtered for the temple, would it not gladly exchange places with some neglected calf?
summary.zh: 或聘於莊子；莊子應其使曰：子見夫犧牛乎？衣以文繡，食以芻菽——及其牽而入於太廟，雖欲為孤犢，其可得乎！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); quoted by Sima Qian in his biographical notice of Zhuangzi. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Some prince having invited Chuang Tzŭ to enter his service, Chuang Tzŭ said in reply to the envoy, "Sir, have you ever noticed a sacrificial ox? It is bedecked with ribbons and fares sumptuously. But when it comes to be slaughtered for the temple, would it not gladly exchange places with some neglected calf?"
passages.zh: 或聘於莊子，莊子應其使曰：「子見夫犧牲乎？衣以文繡，食以芻菽。及其牽而入於太廟，雖欲為孤犢，其可得乎！」

title.en: Heaven and Earth for My Coffin: Chuang Tzŭ's Death-Bed (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 莊子將死，以天地為棺槨（莊子）

region.en: The death-bed in Sung (Shangqiu, Henan, China)
region.zh: 宋之病榻（象徵定位：河南商丘）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 32, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 32

summary.en: When Chuang Tzŭ was about to die, his disciples wished to give him a splendid funeral. With Heaven and Earth for my coffin and shell; with the sun, moon, and stars as my burial regalia; and with all creation to escort me to the grave, are not my funeral paraphernalia ready to hand? And when they fear the carrion kite: above ground I shall be food for kites; below I shall be food for mole-crickets and ants — why rob one to feed the other?
summary.zh: 莊子將死，弟子欲厚葬之。莊子曰：吾以天地為棺槨，以日月為連璧，星辰為珠璣，萬物為齎送——吾葬具豈不備邪？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the classic statement of the cosmic funeral. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: When Chuang Tzŭ was about to die, his disciples expressed a wish to give him a splendid funeral. But Chuang Tzŭ said, "With Heaven and Earth for my coffin and shell; with the sun, moon, and stars as my burial regalia; and with all creation to escort me to the grave,--are not my funeral paraphernalia ready to hand?"
passages.zh: 莊子將死，弟子欲厚葬之。莊子曰：「吾以天地為棺槨，以日月為連璧，星辰為珠璣，萬物為齎送。吾葬具豈不備邪！何以加此？」

passages.text: "We fear," argued the disciples, "lest the carrion kite should eat the body of our Master"; to which Chuang Tzŭ replied, "Above ground I shall be food for kites; below I shall be food for mole-crickets and ants. Why rob one to feed the other? ... Those who trust to their senses become slaves to objective existences. Those alone who are guided by their intuitions find the true standard."
passages.zh: 弟子曰：「吾恐烏鳶之食夫子也。」莊子曰：「在上為烏鳶食，在下為螻蟻食，奪彼與此，何其偏也！……以俗觀之……無私，故能致其私。」

title.en: The Great Yü Drains the Flood: The Mihist Hero-Model (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 大禹治水：墨者之榜樣（莊子）

region.en: The nine divisions of the drained empire (symbolic pin: Yuzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 九洲通流之地（象徵定位：河南禹州）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 33, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 33

summary.en: Mih Tzŭ's followers take for their model the Great Yü, who drained off the flood of waters, causing rivers and streams to flow through the nine divisions of the empire — three hundred great rivers, three thousand branches, and streams without number. With his own hands he plied the bucket and dredger until his calves and shins had no hair left upon them; the wind bathed him, the rain combed him — and ages of Mihists wear short serge jackets and straw sandals, toil day and night, and make self-mortification their end and aim.
summary.zh: 昔者大禹湮洪水，疏九河，瀹濟漯而注諸海——腓無胈，脛無毛；沐甚雨，櫛疾風，置萬國。後世之墨者，多以裘褐為衣，以跂蹻為服，日夜不休，以自苦為極。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the Mihist retelling of Yü's flood-labour within Zhuangzi's survey chapter, cross-linked to the flood cluster. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Mih Tzŭ argued in favour of his system as follows:--Of old, the great Yü drained off the flood of waters, and caused rivers and streams to flow through the nine divisions of the empire and the parts adjacent thereto,--three hundred great rivers, three thousand branches, and streams without number. With his own hands he plied the bucket and dredger, in order to reduce confusion to uniformity, until his calves and shins had no hair left upon them. The wind bathed him, the rain combed him; but he marked out the nations of the world, and was in very truth a Sage.
passages.zh: 墨子稱道曰：昔者禹之湮洪水，決江河而通四夷九州也。名山三百，支川三千，小者無數。禹親自操橐耜而九雜天下之川，腓無胈，脛無毛，沐甚雨，櫛疾風，置萬國。禹大聖也，而形勞天下也如此。

passages.text: And because he thus sacrificed himself to the commonwealth, ages of Mihists to come would also wear short serge jackets and straw sandals, and toil day and night without stopping, making self-mortification their end and aim, and say to themselves, "If we cannot do this, we do not follow the TAO of Yü, and are unworthy to be called Mihists."
passages.zh: 使後世之墨者，多以裘褐為衣，以跂蹻為服，日夜不休，以自苦為極。曰：不能如此，非禹之道也，不足謂墨。

title.en: Hui Tzŭ's Ten Paradoxes: Feathers in an Egg, a Nail with a Tail (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 惠施多方，其書五車（莊子）

region.en: The schools of Sung and Liang (Shangqiu, Henan, China)
region.zh: 宋梁之辯（象徵定位：河南商丘）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 33, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 33

summary.en: Chuang Tzŭ's survey of Hui Tzŭ, whose learning filled five carts: the sun at noon is the sun setting; southwards there is no limit and yet there is a limit; one can reach Yüeh to-day and yet be there before; the middle of the world is north of Yen and south of Yüeh; there are feathers in an egg; a nail has a tail; fire is not hot; wheels do not press down the ground; the shadow of a flying bird does not move — a great philosopher and very subtle dialectician.
summary.zh: 惠施多方，其書五車；歷物之意曰：至大無外，謂之大一；至小無內，謂之小一——卵有毛；雞三足；郢有天下；犬可以為羊；馬有卵；丁子有尾；火不熱；目不見。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: That the sun at noon is the sun setting. That when an animal is born, it dies. That the likeness of things partly unlike is called the lesser likeness of unlikes. That the likeness of things altogether unlike is called the greater likeness of unlikes. That southwards there is no limit, and yet there is a limit. That one can reach Yüeh to-day and yet be there before. That joined rings can be separated. That the middle of the world is north of Yen and south of Yüeh.
passages.zh: 惠施多方……其舛駁：天與地卑，山與澤平。日方中方睨，物方生方死。大同而與小同異，此之謂小同異；萬物畢同畢異，此之謂大同異。南方無窮而有窮。今日適越而昔來。連環可解也。我知天下之中央，燕之北、越之南是也。

passages.text: He said that there were feathers in an egg. That a fowl had three feet. That Ying was the world. That a dog could be a sheep. That a mare could lay eggs. That a nail has a tail. That fire is not hot. That mountains have mouths. That wheels do not press down the ground. That the eye does not see. That the finger does not touch. That the uttermost extreme is not the end. That a tortoise is longer than a snake. That a carpenter's square is not square. That compasses will not make a circle. That the shadow of a flying bird does not move. That there is a moment when a swiftly-flying arrow is neither moving nor at rest. That a dog is not a hound. That a bay horse and a dun cow are three.
passages.zh: 氾愛萬物，天地一體也。惠施以此為大觀於天下而曉辯者。雞三足；郢有天下；犬可以為羊；馬有卵；丁子有尾；火不熱；山出口；輪不蹍地；目不見；指不至；至不絕；龜長於蛇；矩不方，規不可以為圓；鑿不圍枘；飛鳥之影未嘗動也；鏃矢之疾而有不行不止之時；狗非犬；黃馬驪牛三。

title.en: The Tao That Can Be Trodden: The Nameless Beginning (Tao Te Ching 1)
title.zh: 道可道，非常道（道德經第一章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 1

summary.en: The opening cosmogony of the classic of the Way: the Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao; the Nameless is the origin of Heaven and Earth; the Named is the mother of all things — both secrets, doubly profound, the door from which issued the secret of the way of life.
summary.zh: 道可道，非常道；名可名，非常名。無名，天地之始；有名，萬物之母。玄之又玄，眾妙之門。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. The Tao which can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao; the name which can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name. 2. (Conceived of as) having no name, it is the Originator of Heaven and Earth; (conceived of as) having a name, it is the Mother of all things.
passages.zh: 第一章：道可道，非常道；名可名，非常名。無名，天地之始；有名，萬物之母。

passages.text: 3. Always without desire we must be found, if its deep mystery we would sound; and if ever we are need desire, its outer fringe is all that we shall see. 4. Under these two aspects, it is really the same; but as development takes place, it receives the different designations. 5. Together we may call them the Mystery. 6. Where the Mystery is the deepest is the gate of all that is subtle and wonderful.
passages.zh: 故常無欲，以觀其妙；常有欲，以觀其徼。此兩者，同出而異名，同謂之玄。玄之又玄，眾妙之門。

title.en: The Honoured Ancestor of All Things (Tao Te Ching 4)
title.zh: 吾不知誰之子，象帝之先（道德經第四章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 4

summary.en: The Tao is like the emptiness of a vessel, deep and unfathomable, as if it were the Honoured Ancestor of all things — I do not know whose son it is: it might appear to have been before God (the Lord of Heaven).
summary.zh: 道沖而用之，或不盈；淵兮似萬物之宗——吾不知誰之子，象帝之先。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. The Tao is (like) the emptiness of a vessel; and in our employment of it we must be on our guard against all fulness. How deep and unfathomable it is, as if it were the Honoured Ancestor of all things!
passages.zh: 第四章：道沖，而用之或不盈。淵兮，似萬物之宗。

passages.text: 2. We should blunt our sharp points, and unravel the complications of things; we should attemper our brightness, and bring ourselves into agreement with the obscurity of others. How pure and still the Tao is, as if it would ever so continue! 3. I do not know whose son it is. It might appear to have been before God.
passages.zh: 第四章：挫其銳，解其紛，和其光，同其塵。湛兮似或存。吾不知誰之子，象帝之先。

title.en: Straw Dogs and the Bellows of Heaven and Earth (Tao Te Ching 5)
title.zh: 天地不仁，以萬物為芻狗（道德經第五章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 5

summary.en: Heaven and earth do not act from any wish to be benevolent; they deal with all things as the dogs of grass are dealt with — and the space between heaven and earth is like a bellows: 'tis emptied, yet it loses not its power; 'tis moved again, and sends forth air the more.
summary.zh: 天地不仁，以萬物為芻狗；聖人不仁，以百姓為芻狗。天地之間，其猶橐籥乎——虛而不屈，動而愈出。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition; the straw dog (ch'u-kou) is the funeral-sacrifice image echoed in Zhuangzi's ch. 14. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: 1. Heaven and earth do not act from (the impulse of) any wish to be benevolent; they deal with all things as the dogs of grass are dealt with. The sages do not act from (any wish to be) benevolent; they deal with the people as the dogs of grass are dealt with.
passages.zh: 第五章：天地不仁，以萬物為芻狗；聖人不仁，以百姓為芻狗。天地之間，其猶橐籥乎？

passages.text: 2. May not the space between heaven and earth be compared to a bellows? 'Tis emptied, yet it loses not its power; 'Tis moved again, and sends forth air the more. Much speech to swift exhaustion lead we see; Your inner being guard, and keep it free.
passages.zh: 虛而不屈，動而愈出。多言數窮，不如守中。

title.en: The Valley Spirit Dies Not: The Mystery of the Female (Tao Te Ching 6)
title.zh: 谷神不死，是謂玄牝（道德經第六章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 6

summary.en: The valley spirit dies not, aye the same; the female mystery thus do we name. Its gate, from which at first they issued forth, is called the root from which grew heaven and earth.
summary.zh: 谷神不死，是謂玄牝；玄牝之門，是謂天地根。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition; the 'mysterious female' (hsüan-p'in) became a core inner-alchemy image. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: The valley spirit dies not, aye the same; The female mystery thus do we name. Its gate, from which at first they issued forth, Is called the root from which grew heaven and earth. Long and unbroken does its power remain, Used gently, and without the touch of pain.
passages.zh: 第六章：谷神不死，是謂玄牝。玄牝之門，是謂天地根。綿綿若存，用之不勤。

title.en: The Thirty Spokes and the Empty Nave (Tao Te Ching 11)
title.zh: 三十輻共一轂（道德經第十一章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 11

summary.en: The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; clay is fashioned into vessels; doors and windows are cut out to form an apartment — but it is on the empty space that their use depends. What has positive existence serves for profitable adaptation, and what has not that for actual usefulness.
summary.zh: 三十輻共一轂，當其無，有車之用；埏埴以為器，當其無，有器之用——故有之以為利，無之以為用。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty space (for the axle), that the use of the wheel depends. Clay is fashioned into vessels; but it is on their empty hollowness, that their use depends. The door and windows are cut out (from the walls) to form an apartment; but it is on the empty space (within), that its use depends. Therefore, what has a (positive) existence serves for profitable adaptation, and what has not that for (actual) usefulness.
passages.zh: 第十一章：三十輻共一轂，當其無，有車之用。埏埴以為器，當其無，有器之用。鑿戶牖以為室，當其無，有室之用。故有之以為利，無之以為用。

title.en: The Equable, the Inaudible, and the Subtle: The Form of the Formless (Tao Te Ching 14)
title.zh: 視之不見名曰夷（道德經第十四章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 14

summary.en: We look at it and do not see it, and name it the Equable; we listen and do not hear it, the Inaudible; we try to grasp it and do not get hold of it, the Subtle. These three blended obtain The One — we meet it and do not see its Front; we follow it and do not see its Back. When we can lay hold of the Tao of old to direct the things of the present day, this is called unwinding the clue of Tao.
summary.zh: 視之不見名曰夷，聽之不聞名曰希，摶之不得名曰微——迎之不見其首，隨之不見其後；執古之道，以御今之有。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. We look at it, and we do not see it, and we name it 'the Equable.' We listen to it, and we do not hear it, and we name it 'the Inaudible.' We try to grasp it, and do not get hold of it, and we name it 'the Subtle.' With these three qualities, it cannot be made the subject of description; and hence we blend them together and obtain The One.
passages.zh: 第十四章：視之不見，名曰夷；聽之不聞，名曰希；搏之不得，名曰微。此三者不可致詰，故混而為一。

passages.text: 2. Its upper part is not bright, and its lower part is not obscure. Ceaseless in its action, it yet cannot be named, and then it again returns and becomes nothing. This is called the Form of the Formless, and the Semblance of the Invisible; this is called the Fleeting and Indeterminable.
passages.zh: 其上不皦，其下不昧。繩繩不可名，復歸於無物。是謂無狀之狀，無物之象，是謂惚恍。

passages.text: 3. We meet it and do not see its Front; we follow it, and do not see its Back. When we can lay hold of the Tao of old to direct the things of the present day, and are able to know it as it was of old in the beginning, this is called (unwinding) the clue of Tao.
passages.zh: 迎之不見其首，隨之不見其後。執古之道，以御今之有。能知古始，是謂道紀。

title.en: Return to the Root: The Unchanging Rule (Tao Te Ching 16)
title.zh: 致虛極，守靜篤（道德經第十六章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 16

summary.en: All things alike go through their processes of activity, and then we see them return to their original state; when things in the vegetable world have displayed their luxuriant growth, each of them returns to its root — the regular, unchanging rule whose knowledge is intelligence; he who is king-like goes on to be heaven-like, and possessed of the Tao he endures long.
summary.zh: 致虛極，守靜篤；萬物並作，吾以觀其復——夫物芸芸，各復歸其根；歸根曰靜，是謂復命。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. The (state of) vacancy should be brought to the utmost degree, and that of stillness guarded with unwearying vigour. All things alike go through their processes of activity, and (then) we see them return (to their original state). When things (in the vegetable world) have displayed their luxuriant growth, we see each of them return to its root. This returning to their root is what we call the state of stillness; and that stillness may be called a reporting that they have fulfilled their appointed end.
passages.zh: 第十六章：致虛極，守靜篤。萬物並作，吾以觀復。夫物芸芸，各復歸其根。歸根曰靜，是謂復命。

passages.text: 2. The report of that fulfilment is the regular, unchanging rule. To know that unchanging rule is to be intelligent; not to know it leads to wild movements and evil issues. The knowledge of that unchanging rule produces a (grand) capacity and forbearance, and that capacity and forbearance lead to a community (of feeling with all things). From this community of feeling comes a kingliness of character; and he who is king-like goes on to be heaven-like. In that likeness to heaven he possesses the Tao. Possessed of the Tao, he endures long; and to the end of his bodily life, is exempt from all danger of decay.
passages.zh: 復命曰常，知常曰明。不知常，妄作凶。知常容，容乃公，公乃王，王乃天，天乃道，道乃久，沒身不殆。

title.en: I Alone Am Different: Carried About as on the Sea (Tao Te Ching 20)
title.zh: 絕學無憂，眾人熙熙（道德經第二十章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 20

summary.en: The multitude look satisfied, as if enjoying a full banquet, as if mounted on a tower in spring; I alone seem listless and still, like an infant which has not yet smiled, carried about as on the sea, drifting as if I had nowhere to rest — I alone am different from other men, but I value the nursing-mother, the Tao.
summary.zh: 眾人熙熙，如享太牢，如春登臺；我獨泊兮其未兆，如嬰兒之未孩——乘乘兮若無所歸。我獨異於人，而貴食母。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The multitude of men look satisfied and pleased; as if enjoying a full banquet, as if mounted on a tower in spring. I alone seem listless and still, my desires having as yet given no indication of their presence. I am like an infant which has not yet smiled. I look dejected and forlorn, as if I had no home to go to.
passages.zh: 第二十章：眾人熙熙，如享太牢，如春登台。我獨泊兮其未兆，如嬰兒之未孩；儽儽兮，若無所歸。

passages.text: Ordinary men look bright and intelligent, while I alone seem to be benighted. They look full of discrimination, while I alone am dull and confused. I seem to be carried about as on the sea, drifting as if I had nowhere to rest. All men have their spheres of action, while I alone seem dull and incapable, like a rude borderer. (Thus) I alone am different from other men, but I value the nursing-mother (the Tao).
passages.zh: 眾人皆有餘，而我獨若遺。我愚人之心也哉，沌沌兮！俗人昭昭，我獨昏昏。俗人察察，我獨悶悶。澹兮其若海，飂兮若無止。眾人皆有以，而我獨頑且鄙。我獨異於人，而貴食母。

title.en: The Grandest Forms of Active Force Come from the Tao (Tao Te Ching 21)
title.zh: 孔德之容，惟道是從（道德經第二十一章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 21

summary.en: The grandest forms of active force from Tao come, their only source — eluding sight, eluding touch, the forms of things all in it crouch; profound it is, dark and obscure; things' essences all there endure. Now it is so; 'twas so of old. Its name — what passes not away.
summary.zh: 孔德之容，惟道是從；道之為物，惟恍惟惚——窈兮冥兮，其中有精；其精甚真，其中有信。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The grandest forms of active force From Tao come, their only source. Who can of Tao the nature tell? Our sight it flies, our touch as well. Eluding sight, eluding touch, The forms of things all in it crouch; Eluding touch, eluding sight, There are their semblances, all right. Profound it is, dark and obscure; Things' essences all there endure. Those essences the truth enfold Of what, when seen, shall then be told. Now it is so; 'twas so of old. Its name--what passes not away; So, in their beautiful array, Things form and never know decay.
passages.zh: 第二十一章：孔德之容，惟道是從。道之為物，惟恍惟惚。惚兮恍兮，其中有象；恍兮惚兮，其中有物。窈兮冥兮，其中有精。其精甚真，其中有信。自今及古，其名不去，以閱眾甫。吾何以知眾甫之狀哉？以此。

title.en: The Things Which from of Old Have Got the One (Tao Te Ching 39)
title.zh: 昔之得一者：天得一以清（道德經第三十九章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 39

summary.en: The things which from of old have got the One: heaven which by it is bright and pure, earth rendered firm and sure, spirits with powers by it supplied, valleys kept full throughout their void, all creatures which through it do live, princes and kings who from it get the model which to all they give. If heaven were not thus pure, it soon would rend.
summary.zh: 昔之得一者：天得一以清，地得一以寧，神得一以靈，谷得一以盈，萬物得一以生，侯王得一以為天下正——天無以清將恐裂。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. The things which from of old have got the One (the Tao) are-- Heaven which by it is bright and pure; Earth rendered thereby firm and sure; Spirits with powers by it supplied; Valleys kept full throughout their void All creatures which through it do live Princes and kings who from it get The model which to all they give.
passages.zh: 第三十九章：昔之得一者：天得一以清，地得一以寧，神得一以靈，谷得一以盈，侯王得一以為天下貞。其致之也，謂天無以清，將恐裂；地無以寧，將恐廢；神無以靈，將恐歇；谷無以盈，將恐竭；侯王無以貞，將恐蹶。

passages.text: 2. If heaven were not thus pure, it soon would rend; If earth were not thus sure, 'twould break and bend; Without these powers, the spirits soon would fail; If not so filled, the drought would parch each vale; Without that life, creatures would pass away; Princes and kings, without that moral sway, However grand and high, would all decay.
passages.zh: 故貴以賤為本，高以下為基。是以侯王自謂孤、寡、不穀。此非以賤為本邪？非乎？故致數輿無輿。是故不欲琭琭如玉，珞珞如石。

title.en: The Movement of the Tao by Contraries Proceeds (Tao Te Ching 40)
title.zh: 反者道之動（道德經第四十章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 40

summary.en: The movement of the Tao by contraries proceeds; and weakness marks the course of Tao's mighty deeds. All things under heaven sprang from It as existing (and named); that existence sprang from It as non-existent (and not named).
summary.zh: 反者道之動，弱者道之用；天下萬物生於有，有生於無。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. The movement of the Tao By contraries proceeds; And weakness marks the course Of Tao's mighty deeds. 2. All things under heaven sprang from It as existing (and named); that existence sprang from It as non-existent (and not named).
passages.zh: 第四十章：反者道之動；弱者道之用。天下萬物生於有，有生於無。

title.en: The Three Ministers of Life and the Three Ministers of Death (Tao Te Ching 50)
title.zh: 出生入死，十有三（道德經第五十章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 50

summary.en: Men come forth and live; they enter again and die. Of every ten, three are ministers of life and three of death; three in every ten whose aim is to live but whose movements tend to the land of death — while he who is skilful in managing his life travels without having to shun rhinoceros or tiger, for there is in him no place of death.
summary.zh: 出生入死。生之徒十有三，死之徒十有三——陸行不遇兕虎，入軍不被甲兵；兕無所投其角，虎無所措其爪，兵無所容其刃。夫何故？以其無死地。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition; the 'no place of death' doctrine grounds later invulnerability claims. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: 1. Men come forth and live; they enter (again) and die. 2. Of every ten three are ministers of life (to themselves); and three are ministers of death. 3. There are also three in every ten whose aim is to live, but whose movements tend to the land (or place) of death. And for what reason? Because of their excessive endeavours to perpetuate life.
passages.zh: 第五十章：出生入死。生之徒，十有三；死之徒，十有三；人之生，動之於死地，亦十有三。夫何故？以其生生之厚。

passages.text: 4. But I have heard that he who is skilful in managing the life entrusted to him for a time travels on the land without having to shun rhinoceros or tiger, and enters a host without having to avoid buff coat or sharp weapon. The rhinoceros finds no place in him into which to thrust its horn, nor the tiger a place in which to fix its claws, nor the weapon a place to admit its point. And for what reason? Because there is in him no place of death.
passages.zh: 蓋聞善攝生者，陸行不遇兕虎，入軍不被甲兵。兕無所投其角，虎無所措其爪，兵無所容其刃。夫何故？以其無死地。

title.en: The Mother of All Under the Sky (Tao Te Ching 52)
title.zh: 天下有母，可以為天下母（道德經第五十二章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 52

summary.en: The Tao which originated all under the sky is to be considered as the mother of them all; when one knows that he is his mother's child, and proceeds to guard the qualities of the mother that belong to him, to the end of his life he will be free from all peril.
summary.zh: 天下有母，以為天下母；既得其母，以知其子——沒身不殆。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. (The Tao) which originated all under the sky is to be considered as the mother of them all. 2. When the mother is found, we know what her children should be. When one knows that he is his mother's child, and proceeds to guard (the qualities of) the mother that belong to him, to the end of his life he will be free from all peril.
passages.zh: 第五十二章：天下有母，以為天下母。既得其母，以知其子；既知其子，復守其母，沒身不殆。

passages.text: 3. Let him keep his mouth closed, and shut up the portals (of his nostrils), and all his life he will be exempt from laborious exertion. Let him keep his mouth open, and (spend his breath) in the promotion of his affairs, and all his life there will be no safety for him. 4. The perception of what is small is (the secret of) clear-sightedness; the guarding of what is soft and tender is (the secret of) strength.
passages.zh: 塞其兌，閉其門，終身不勤。開其兌，濟其事，終身不救。見小曰明，守柔曰強。

title.en: Nothing Softer Than Water Attacks the Strong (Tao Te Ching 78)
title.zh: 天下莫柔弱於水（道德經第七十八章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 78

summary.en: There is nothing in the world more soft and weak than water, and yet for attacking things that are firm and strong there is nothing that can take precedence of it — he who accepts his state's reproach is hailed therefore its altars' lord; words that are strictly true seem to be paradoxical.
summary.zh: 天下莫柔弱於水，而攻堅強者莫之能勝——受國之垢，是為社稷主；受國不祥，是為天下王。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. There is nothing in the world more soft and weak than water, and yet for attacking things that are firm and strong there is nothing that can take precedence of it;--for there is nothing (so effectual) for which it can be changed.
passages.zh: 第七十八章：天下莫柔弱於水，而攻堅強者莫之能勝。以其無以易之。

passages.text: 2. Every one in the world knows that the soft overcomes the hard, and the weak the strong, but no one is able to carry it out in practice. 3. Therefore a sage has said, 'He who accepts his state's reproach, Is hailed therefore its altars' lord; To him who bears men's direful woes They all the name of King accord.' 4. Words that are strictly true seem to be paradoxical.
passages.zh: 柔之勝剛，弱之勝強，天下莫不知，莫能行。是以聖人云：受國之垢，是謂社稷主；受國不祥，是為天下王。正言若反。

title.en: The Creative Principle Which Is Itself Uncreated (Liezi)
title.zh: 有生不生，有化不化（列子天瑞篇）

region.en: Lieh Tzŭ's plot of ground in Chêng (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 鄭國圃田（今河南鄭州）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book I (Cosmogony)

summary.en: Lieh Tzŭ repeats Hu Ch'iu Tzŭ-lin's teaching: there is a Creative Principle which is itself uncreated, a Principle of Change which is itself unchanging; the Uncreated is able to create life, the Unchanging to effect change — self-engendered and self-evolved, it would be a mistake to call it by any one of its names.
summary.zh: 有生不生，有化不化；不生者能生生，不化者能化化——自生自化，自形自色。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Taishang zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: There is a Creative Principle which is itself uncreated; there is a Principle of Change which is itself unchanging. The Uncreated is able to create life; the Unchanging is able to effect change. That which is produced cannot but continue producing; that which is evolved cannot but continue evolving. Hence there is constant production and constant evolution. The law of constant production and of constant evolution at no time ceases to operate. So is it with the Yin and the Yang, so is it with the Four Seasons.
passages.zh: 有生不生，有化不化。不生者能生生，不化者能化化。生者不能不生，化者不能不化。故常生常化。常生常化者，無時不生，無時不化。陰陽爾，四時爾。

passages.text: That, then, which engenders all things is itself unengendered; that by which all things are evolved is itself untouched by evolution. Self-engendered and self-evolved, it has in itself the elements of substance, appearance, wisdom, strength, dispersion and cessation. Yet it would be a mistake to call it by any one of these names.
passages.zh: 不生者疑獨，不化者往復。往復其際不可窮；疑獨其道不可盡。……自生自化，自形自色，自智自力，自消自息。謂之生化形色智力消息者，非也。

title.en: Heaven and Earth Engendered Out of Nothing (Liezi)
title.zh: 天地安從生：渾淪與清濁（列子天瑞篇）

region.en: The Great Change before substance (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 太易之初（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book I (Cosmogony)

summary.en: The Liezi's great cosmogonic sequence: the Great Change, the Great Origin, the Great Beginning, the Great Primordial Simplicity — until substance, form, and essential qualities still blended together is called Chaos. Then the purer and lighter elements, tending upwards, made the Heavens; the grosser and heavier, tending downwards, made the Earth; and substance, harmoniously proportioned, became Man.
summary.zh: 太易、太初、太始、太素——形質混而不離，謂之渾淪；清輕者上為天，重濁者下為地，沖和氣者為人。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; a priority Creation & Cosmology narrative — the tai-chi sequence that later Cosmological Daoism systematised. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: The inspired men of old regarded the Yin and the Yang as the cause of the sum total of Heaven and Earth. But that which has substance is engendered from that which is devoid of substance; out of what then were Heaven and Earth engendered? They were engendered out of nothing, and came into existence of themselves.
passages.zh: 夫有形者生於無形，則天地安從生？故曰：有太易，有太初，有太始，有太素。

passages.text: Hence we say, there is a great Principle of Change, a great Origin, a great Beginning, a great Primordial Simplicity. In the great Change substance is not yet manifest. In the great Origin lies the beginning of substance. In the great Beginning, lies the beginning of material form. In the great Simplicity lies the beginning of essential qualities.
passages.zh: 太易者，未見氣也；太初者，氣之始也；太始者，形之始也；太素者，質之始也。氣形質具而未相離，故曰渾淪。

passages.text: When substance, form and essential qualities are still indistinguishably blended together it is called Chaos. Chaos means that all things are chaotically intermixed and not yet separated from one another. The purer and lighter elements, tending upwards, made the Heavens; the grosser and heavier elements, tending downwards, made the Earth. Substance, harmoniously proportioned, became Man; and, Heaven and Earth containing thus a spiritual element, all things were evolved and produced.
passages.zh: 渾淪者，言萬物相渾淪而未相離也。清輕者上為天，濁重者下為地，沖和氣者為人。故天地含精，萬物化生。

title.en: Why the Dead Are Called 'Men Who Have Returned' (Liezi)
title.zh: 鬼者，歸也（列子天瑞篇）

region.en: Lieh Tzŭ's plot of ground in Chêng (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 鄭國圃田（今河南鄭州）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book I (Cosmogony)

summary.en: The spiritual element in man is allotted by Heaven, the corporeal frame by Earth; when the spirit parts from the body each returns to its proper place — that is why disembodied spirits are called kuei, which means 'returning,' returning to their true dwelling-place. And the Yellow Emperor said: If my spirit returns through the gates whence it came, where does the Ego continue to exist?
summary.zh: 精神者天之分，骨骸者地之分——精神離形，各歸其真，故謂之鬼；鬼，歸也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the kuei=returning etymology is the aition of the Chinese word for ghost. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: The spiritual element in man is allotted to him by Heaven, his corporeal frame by Earth. The part that belongs to Heaven is ethereal and dispersive, the part that belongs to Earth is dense and tending to conglomeration. When the spirit parts from the body, each of these elements returns to its proper place. That is why disembodied spirits are called kuei, which means "returning," that is, returning to their true dwelling-place.
passages.zh: 精神者，天之分；骨骸者，地之分。屬天清而散，屬地濁而聚。精神離形，各歸其真，故謂之鬼。鬼，歸也，歸其真宅。

passages.text: The Yellow Emperor said: "If my spirit returns through the gates whence it came, and my bones go back to the source from which they sprang, where does the Ego continue to exist?" Between his birth and his latter end, man passes through four chief stages of development:--infancy, adolescence, old age and death. In infancy, the vital force is concentrated, the will is simple, and the general harmony of the system is perfect. ... In death, he comes to his rest, and returns to the Absolute.
passages.zh: 黃帝曰：「精神入其門，骨骸反其根，我尚何存？」人自生至終，大效有四：嬰兒也，少壯也，老耄也，死亡也。……死也，止也，歸於本真。

title.en: The Old Man in Deerskin Who Was Happy Three Ways (Liezi)
title.zh: 泰山之叟，被裘擊壤（列子天瑞篇）

region.en: The wilds of Mount T'ai (Shandong, China)
region.zh: 泰山之野（今山東泰安）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book I (Cosmogony)

summary.en: Over Mount T'ai Confucius finds an aged man in a deerskin girded with rope, singing as he plays on a lute — happy for three grounds: it has fallen to his lot to be a man, the noblest of God's creations; to be a male; and to have walked the earth for ninety years. Poverty is the normal lot of the scholar, death the appointed end for all human beings.
summary.zh: 孔子遊於泰山，見裘公聲然操琴——天生萬物，唯人為貴；既得為人，是一樂也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Confucius was travelling once over Mount T'ai when he caught sight of an aged man roaming in the wilds. He was clothed in a deerskin, girded with a rope, and was singing as he played on a lute. "My friend," said Confucius, "what is it that makes you so happy?" The old man replied: "I have a great deal to make me happy. God created all things, and of all His creations man is the noblest. It has fallen to my lot to be a man: that is my first ground for happiness. Then, there is a distinction between male and female, the former being rated more highly than the latter. Therefore it is better to be a male; and since I am one, I have a second ground for happiness.
passages.zh: 孔子泰山遊，見榮啟期鹿裘帶索，鼓琴而歌。孔子問曰：「先生所以樂，何也？」對曰：「吾樂甚多：天生萬物，唯人為貴，而吾得為人，是一樂也；男女之別，男尊女卑，故以男為貴，吾既得為男矣，是二樂也。

passages.text: Furthermore, some are born who never behold the sun or the moon, and who never emerge from their swaddling-clothes. But I have already walked the earth for the space of ninety years. That is my third ground for happiness. Poverty is the normal lot of the scholar, death the appointed end for all human beings. Abiding in the normal state, and reaching at last the appointed end, what is there that should make me unhappy?" "What an excellent thing it is," cried Confucius, "to be able to find a source of consolation in oneself!"
passages.zh: 人生有不見日月、不免襁褓者，吾既已行年九十矣，是三樂也。貧者，士之常也；死者，人之終也。處常得終，當何憂哉？」孔子曰：「善乎！能自寬者也。」

title.en: Great Indeed Is Death: Tzŭ Kung Yearns for Rest (Liezi)
title.zh: 大哉死乎：子貢厭學（列子天瑞篇）

region.en: The graves in the wilds (symbolic pin: Qufu, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 原野之墳（象徵定位：山東曲阜）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book I (Cosmogony)

summary.en: Tzŭ Kung, tired of philosophy, yearns for rest; Confucius points to all the graves, vaults, tombs, and funeral urns. Great indeed is Death! exclaims Tzŭ Kung — it gives rest to the noble-hearted and causes the base to cower. Men feel the joy of life, but do not realise its bitterness; they think of the evils of death, but not of the repose which it confers. And the dead are men who have returned.
summary.zh: 子貢倦於學，告仲尼曰：願有所息——大哉死乎！君子息焉，小人休焉。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Tzu Kung was tired of philosophy, and confided his feelings to Confucius, saying: "I yearn for rest." Confucius replied: "In life there is no rest." "Is rest, then, nowhere to be found?" "Oh, yes!" replied Confucius; "look at all the graves in the wilds, all the vaults, all the tombs, all the funeral urns, and you may know where rest is to be found." "Great, indeed, is Death!" exclaimed Tzu Kung. "It gives rest to the noble-hearted, and causes the base to cower." "You are right," said Confucius. "Men feel the joy of life, but do not realise its bitterness. They feel the weariness of old age, but not its peacefulness. They think of the evils of death, but not of the repose which it confers."
passages.zh: 子貢倦於學，告仲尼曰：「願有所息。」仲尼曰：「生無所息。」子貢曰：「然則賜息無所乎？」仲尼曰：「有焉耳。望其壙，睪如也，宰如也，墳如也，鬲如也，則知所息矣。」子貢曰：「大哉死乎！君子息焉，小人休焉。」

passages.text: The ancients spoke of the dead as kuei-jen (men who have returned). But if the dead are men who have returned, the living are men on a journey. Those who are on a journey and think not of returning have cut themselves off from their home. Should any one man cut himself off from his home, he would incur universal reprobation. But all mankind being homeless, there is none to see the error.
passages.zh: 古人謂死人為歸人。夫言死人為歸人，則生人為行人矣。……行人而不歸者，則離家久矣。……在生而怨不歸者，眾人也；其知歸者，君子也。

title.en: The Man Who Feared the Sky Would Fall (Liezi)
title.zh: 杞人憂天（列子天瑞篇）

region.en: The State of Ch'i (Linzi, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 杞國（今河南杞縣）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book I (Cosmogony)

summary.en: A man of Ch'i is so afraid the universe will collapse and fall to pieces that he can neither sleep nor eat. Heaven is only an accumulation of ether, says his enlightener; the sun, moon and stars are bright lights within that mass; the earth is an agglomeration of matter filling the four corners of space — why be afraid? And Ch'ang Lu Tzŭ laughs at both: Heaven and earth must of necessity pass away, but neither will revert to destruction apart from the other.
summary.zh: 杞國有人憂天地崩墜，身亡所寄，廢寢食者——天，積氣耳；亡處亡氣。地，積塊耳；充塞四虛。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the 'worry of Ch'i' (Ch'i-jen yu-t'ien) became a proverb for needless alarm. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: There was once a man in the Ch'i State who was so afraid the universe would collapse and fall to pieces, leaving his body without a lodgment, that he could neither sleep nor eat. Another man, pitying his distress, went to enlighten him. "Heaven," he said, "is nothing more than an accumulation of ether, and there is no place where ether is not. Processes of contraction and expansion, inspiration and expiration are continually taking place up in the heavens. Why then should you be afraid of a collapse?" "It is true that Heaven is an accumulation of ether; but the sun, the moon, and the stars -- will they not fall down upon us?" "Sun, moon and stars are likewise only bright lights within this mass of ether. Even supposing they were to fall, they could not possibly harm us by their impact."
passages.zh: 杞國有人憂天地崩墜，身亡所寄，廢寢食者。又有憂彼之所憂者，因往曉之，曰：「天，積氣耳，亡處亡氣。若屈伸呼吸，終日在天中行止，奈何憂崩墜乎？」其人曰：「天果積氣，日月星宿不當墜耶？」

passages.text: "But what if the earth should fall to pieces?" "The earth," replied the other, "is merely an agglomeration of matter, which fills and blocks up the four corners of space. There is no part of it where matter is not. All day long there is constant treading and tramping on the surface of the earth. Why then should you be afraid of its falling to pieces?" Thereupon the man was relieved of his fears and rejoiced exceedingly. But Ch'ang Lu Tzu laughed at them both, saying: "Knowing these facts, who can say that they will never be destroyed? Heaven and earth must of necessity pass away, but neither will revert to destruction apart from the other. Who, having to face the day of disruption, would not be alarmed?"
passages.zh: 曉之者曰：「日月星宿，亦積氣中之有光耀者，只使墜，亦不能有所中傷。」其人曰：「奈地壞何？」曉者曰：「地，積塊耳，充塞四虛，亡處亡塊。若躇步跐蹈，終日在地上行止，奈何憂其壞？」其人捨然大喜，曉之者亦捨然大喜。長廬子聞而笑之曰：「謂天地不壞者誠謬，謂天地果壞者亦妄也。

passages.text: The Master Lieh Tzu heard of the discussion, and smiling said: "He who maintains that Heaven and earth are destructible, and he who upholds the contrary, are both equally at fault. Whether they are destructible or not is something we can never know. The living and the dead, the going and the coming, know nothing of each other's state. Whether destruction awaits the world or no, why should I trouble my head about it?"
passages.zh: 列子聞之，笑曰：「言天地壞者亦謬，言天地不壞者亦謬。壞與不壞，吾所不能知也。雖然，彼一也，此一也。故生不知死，死不知生；來不知去，去不知來。壞與不壞，吾何容心焉？」

title.en: Mr. Kuo the Good Thief of Heaven and Earth (Liezi)
title.zh: 齊國國氏善為盜（列子天瑞篇）

region.en: The road from Sung to Ch'i (Shangqiu to Linzi, China)
region.zh: 宋適齊之道（商丘至臨淄）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book I (Cosmogony)

summary.en: Mr. Hsiang the poor man asks Mr. Kuo the rich for the secret of his prosperity: it is because I am a good thief — stealing the riches of Heaven and earth each in their season, the fertilising rain-water from the clouds, the natural products of mountain and meadow. The literal thief climbs walls and is stripped of all he has; Tung Kuo the learned explains that we are all thieves of the harmony of the Yin and Yang in order to keep alive.
summary.zh: 國氏曰：吾善為盜——盜天之時，盜陰陽之和，若耳目鼻口；向氏踰垣鑿室而盜，被殘而歸。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The latter travelled from Sung to Ch'i and asked the other for the secret of his prosperity. Mr. Kuo told him. "It is because I am a good thief," he said. "The first year I began to be a thief, I had just enough. The second year, I had ample. The third year, I reaped a great harvest. And, in course of time, I found myself the owner of whole villages and districts." Mr. Hsiang was overjoyed; he understood the word "thief" in its literal sense, but he did not understand the true way of becoming a thief. Accordingly, he climbed over walls and broke into houses, grabbing everything he could see or lay hands upon. But before very long his thefts brought him into trouble, and he was stripped even of what he had previously possessed.
passages.zh: 齊國氏大富，宋國氏向氏自宋往齊，問其所以致富者。國氏曰：「吾善為盜。始吾為盜也，一年而給，二年而足，三年大穰。自此以往，施及州閭。」向氏大喜，然真以為盜言也，遂逾垣鑿室，手目所及，亡不探也。……不數年，則誅贓逮考，資財俱亡。

passages.text: Now let me put you on the right track. We all know that Heaven has its seasons, and that earth has its riches. Well, the things that I steal are the riches of Heaven and earth, each in their season -- the fertilising rain-water from the clouds, and the natural products of mountain and meadow-land. Thus I grow my grain and ripen my crops, build my walls and construct my tenements. From the dry land I steal winged and four-footed game, from the rivers I steal fish and turtles. There is nothing that I do not steal. For corn and grain, clay and wood, birds and beasts, fishes and turtles are all products of Nature. How can I claim them as mine?
passages.zh: 國氏曰：「若為盜若何？」……向氏曰：「吾為盜夫子之教也。夫子善為盜，而不使人知為盜之方。若使耳可聽、目可得，則非盜也。……吾竊天道以盡天時地利：雲雨之滂潤，山澤之產育，以生吾禾，殖吾稼，築吾垣，建吾舍。陸盜禽獸，水盜魚鱉，亡非盜也。夫禾稼土木禽獸魚鱉，皆天之所生，豈吾之所有？」

title.en: Turtle's Escape from the Pot
title.zh: 龜脫鍋之計

region.en: Bog, Westmoreland, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加西摩蘭博格

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 41 'Turtle's Escape' (told by Henry Spence, Bog, Westmoreland)

summary.en: Caught for dinner, Turtle warns his cook that his fat will mash if the pot boils — so Anansi must lift him out at every bubble. A blow of the turtle's nose raises the water, Anansi sets him by the pan-side to cool, and the dinner slides back into the pond.
summary.zh: 龜被捕入鍋，先行告誡：水一沸，肥肉必爛，須隨時提起。龜以鼻息鼓水，蜘蛛人驚慌之下把他移到鍋邊『降溫』——晚餐便滑回了池塘。
