sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Turtle fooled Anansi one day. Anansi went out and caught one turtle, quite glad of the turtle. When he got home, Turtle knew Anansi was going to eat him and said, 'Brar Anansi, you know me fat? When you put me on, as the water boils up you take me off, 'cause fat will mash.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 41 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，烏龜把阿南西耍了一回。阿南西出去捉了一隻龜，高興得很。回家路上，烏龜知道阿南西要吃他，便說：「阿南西老弟，你看我肥不肥？你把我放到鍋裏，水一滾開就要把我拿出來，肥肉會化掉的。」

passages.text: So when the water got warm, Turtle blew his nose to make the water boil up. Anansi got frightened, said the turtle would mash! So he laid him down at the pan-side to let the fat cool so he would not mash — and Turtle ran away into the pond. Anansi lost his dinner.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 41, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 水一熱起來，烏龜就用鼻子吹氣，讓水大滾。阿南西嚇壞了，說龜要化掉了！便把他擱在鍋邊，讓油脂涼一涼免得化掉——烏龜卻逃回池塘裏去了。阿南西的晚飯落了空。

title.en: Fire Burns Out the Spider's House
title.zh: 火焚蛛宅

region.en: Bog, Westmoreland, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加西摩蘭博格

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 42 'Fire and Anansi' (told by Henry Spence, Bog, Westmoreland)

summary.en: Fire, unable to walk, requires a road of dry bush laid to his host's door. Anansi's wife, the Ground Dove, warns against the visit — he will burn the house and everyone in it — but the spider lays the trash anyway, and Fire, arriving in a great jump, burns Anansi, his house and everything except his wife.
summary.zh: 火不能行走，須沿乾柴鋪路來訪。蜘蛛人之妻地面鴿力勸莫邀——他必焚屋焚人——蜘蛛人不聽，照舊鋪柴；火到門前猛然一躍，焚蜘蛛人、焚其屋、焚盡一切，唯獨留下他的妻子。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; fire-as-personage tale linking to fire clusters. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi and Fire were good friends. Anansi came and saw Fire and they had dinner; then he invited Fire to come and see him. Fire told him he could not walk — from his house, Fire said, his host must lay a path of dry bush, and he would walk on top of the dry bush.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 42 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿南西和火是好朋友。阿南西去看火，兩人吃了一頓飯；然後他邀火去他家做客。火說自己不會走路——從火家出來，東道主必須鋪一條乾灌木的路，火才能踩著乾灌木走過去。

passages.text: Anansi was married to Ground Dove, who told him no: he must not invite Fire, who would burn his house and burn him out. Anansi would not hear what his wife said and laid the trash on. Fire burned from his house, and when he came near Anansi's house he made a big jump, burned Anansi, burned his house, burned everything but his wife. Fire fooled Anansi!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 42, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿南西娶的是地鳩，地鳩告訴他不行：不能邀火，火會燒掉他的房子，把他也燒了。阿南西不聽妻子的話，把柴草鋪上了。火從他家燒過來，快到阿南西家時一個大跳，燒了阿南西，燒了他的房子，燒了一切，只留下他的妻子。火把阿南西耍了！

title.en: The Suit of Maggot-flies
title.zh: 蛆蠅裁成的衣裳

region.en: Lacovia, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加拉科維亞

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 43a 'Tailors and Fiddlers' (told by David Roach, Lacovia)

summary.en: At the ball the tailor Quit-quit's fiddle outdraws the spider's until Anansi's 'Me nyam-nyam taya' wins the girls. Quit-quit retorts that 'taya' is nothing; Anansi demands a suit of clothes that cannot be matched, and the tailor cuts it from maggot-flies — which, smelling the dinner meat at the ball's end, run off and leave the fiddler naked.
summary.zh: 舞會上裁縫的琴聲起初蓋過蜘蛛人，直到蜘蛛人奏出『我吃了肉泥』贏得姑娘們。布特布特反唇相譏；蜘蛛人便索要一套『無人能及』的衣裳，裁縫便以蛆蠅裁成——宴罷肉香一起，蛆蠅四散，琴師當眾裸身。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; fiddle-contest type. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi and Lizard went to a ball. Anansi was a fiddler, Lizard a tailor; Quit-quit was the fiddler's rival. Anansi played 'turn, turn, turn' and all the girls went round Brar Quit-quit; then Anansi played 'Me nyam-nyam taya!' — and it pleased the people, all the girls crowding round Brar Anansi. Brar Quit-quit said, 'Taya no somet'ing!' Anansi came in with his music — 'Me nyam de somet'ing! If taya no somet'ing, whe' are de somet'ing?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 43a (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿南西和蜥蜴去參加舞會。阿南西是琴師，蜥蜴是裁縫；確確是琴師的情敵。阿南西奏「轉呀，轉呀，轉呀」，姑娘們都圍著確確老弟轉；接著阿南西奏「我嘗呀嘗得甜！」——大受歡迎，姑娘們都擁向阿南西老弟。確確老弟說：「甜可不是個東西！」阿南西用琴聲接上——「我把那東西嘗了！甜既然不是東西，那東西在哪裏？」

passages.text: Brar Anansi then said the tailor must make him a suit of clothes that could not be matched; Brar Quit-quit told him it must be made out of maggot-fly. After the ball they went to dinner — and when the maggot-flies smelled the meat, they ran off and left him naked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 43a, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿南西老弟又提出，裁縫必須給他做一套無與倫比的衣服；確確老弟說，那必須用蛆蠅來做。舞會之後他們去吃飯——蛆蠅一聞到肉味，就跑光了，留下他一絲不掛。

title.en: Spider Marries Monkey's Daughter
title.zh: 蜘蛛人娶猴家女

region.en: Newmarket, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加紐馬克特

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 44 'Spider Marries Monkey's Daughter' (told by May Ford, Newmarket)

summary.en: Monkey scorns Spider as too fast a suitor; Green-lizard's counter-plan is a guessing riddle — 'Miss Nennan-kennan-wid-a-turn-down-gown' — which only the spider, tipped off by the same lizard, can answer. Married with a baby in his arms, Anansi sings his own secret — 'A me cunnie mak me get yo' mama' — while the wife is at the pond; Monkey, arriving to hear it, grabs away the baby and kills Spider, and the baby drops dead from his hand. So never kill a spider: whatever you have in hand will surely break.
summary.zh: 猴嫌蜘蛛人太輕浮，綠蜥蜴獻策：以謎語婚試——『穿下垂裙的南南肯南小姐』——唯蜘蛛人得蜥蜴泄題而答中。婚後抱嬰獨守，蜘蛛人自鳴得意唱出機密：『全憑我機智娶到你媽』；猴子聞歌而至，奪嬰殺蛛，嬰兒亦墜地而死。故曰：莫殺蜘蛛——手中之物必隨之而碎。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; hidden-name riddle marriage links to Yoruba hidden-name traditions (cross-ref motif family).

passages.text: Bredder Monkey had a daughter whom Bredder Spider wanted to marry. Monkey did not want Spider to marry his daughter, thinking him too fast and beneath him — he only kept Spider company because he found him useful. He jumped to Bredder Green-lizard: 'Fancy! Bredder Spider want to marry me daughter! I don't want to hurt his feelings, as he is useful to us, so help me to get out of it.' Green-lizard answered, 'I tell you a way, man. Call her Miss Nennan-kennan-wid-a-turn-down-gown, and whoever guesses her name marries her — for Bredder Spider never can guess that!' Then the lizard went direct and told Bredder Spider the name to say.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 44 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 猴子老弟有個女兒，蜘蛛老弟想娶她。猴子不想讓蜘蛛娶自己的女兒，嫌他太輕浮、配不上——他只是覺得蜘蛛有用才跟他做伴。他去見蜥蜴老弟：「你想想！蜘蛛老弟竟想娶我的女兒！可我又不想傷他的面子，他對我們有用，你幫我想個法子擺脫掉。」蜥蜴答道：「我給你出個主意。叫她『垂裙奈寧肯南小姐』，誰猜中她的名字誰娶她——蜘蛛老弟是永遠猜不到的！」然後蜥蜴直接跑去把這個名字告訴了蜘蛛老弟。

passages.text: Monkey sent out word to all the gentlemen who wanted to marry his daughter to come and guess her name. Not one could tell it until Bredder Spider came and said, 'Miss Nennen-kennan-wid-a-turn-down-gown.' So Bredder Spider got the daughter and married her. When his wife had a baby, she left the pickney with Spider and went to the pond; and Spider, thinking her gone, started to sing, 'Hush, me pickney, hush me baby — a me cunnie mak me get yo' mama!' His wife turned back — 'What is that you sing?' — and he answered only, 'Hush, me pickney! Hush, me baby! It's a good t'ing marry yo' mama?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 44, middle (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 猴子放出話來，叫所有想娶他女兒的先生們來猜她的名字。誰都猜不出，直到蜘蛛老弟來了，說：「垂裙奈寧肯南小姐。」蜘蛛老弟便得到了女兒，娶了她。妻子生了孩子，把孩子留給蜘蛛，去池塘去了；蜘蛛以為她走了，唱起來：「睡吧我的寶貝，睡吧我的娃娃——是靠我的機靈才得到你媽媽的！」妻子折了回來：「你在唱什麼？」他只答：「睡吧我的寶貝！睡吧我的娃娃！娶到你媽媽真是件好事？」

passages.text: Bredder Monkey had been coming to see him and heard what Bredder Spider was singing. 'So that is how you got my daughter!' — and he grabbed away the baby and killed Spider. And as he killed Spider, the pickney dropped out of his hand dead. So never kill a spider, as whatever you have in hand will be sure to break.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 44, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 猴子老弟本來就來看他，聽見了蜘蛛老弟唱的話。「原來你就是這樣得到我女兒的！」——他一把奪過孩子，殺死了蜘蛛。他殺蜘蛛的時候，嬰兒也從他手中掉下摔死了。所以永遠不要殺蜘蛛：你手裏握著的東西必定會碎。

title.en: The Chain of Victims
title.zh: 受害者之鏈

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山區

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924 (published 1924)

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 45 'The Chain of Victims' (told by Richard Morgan, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Anansi borrows a dollar from Hog, Dog, Monkey, Tiger and Lion — each 'repayable tomorrow at twelve'. Next day the creditors arrive one by one, and the spider sends each successive guest into the back room with a warning to kill the one before: Hog kills nothing, Dog is sent after Hog, Monkey after Dog, Tiger after Monkey, and Lion finally kills Tiger. Anansi then calls Lion out to a deep hole by the kitchen 'to put on hot water', and the lion breaks his neck in it — leaving the spider alone with five creditors' bones to crack at night.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人向豬、狗、猴、虎、獅各借一元，約定『明日十二時來取』。翌日債主逐一登門，蜘蛛人卻把每位客人送進後屋，並囑其殺掉前一位；獅子終於殺了老虎。隨後蜘蛛人喚獅子到廚房邊深坑旁『燒熱水』——獅子墜坑折頸。蜘蛛人獨得五份『骨頭』，夜裡慢慢敲。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale (debt-chain / ogre-kill type). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi saw Brar Hog and said, 'Brar Hog, lend me a dollar — tomorrow, twelve o'clock, come for it.' He saw Brar Dog and said the same; Brar Monkey, the same; Brar Tiger, the same; and Brar Lion, the same. Next day he heard a knock at the door — 'Me, Brar Hog' — and Hog came in and stayed talking until another knock.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 45 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿南西看見豬老弟，說：「豬老弟，借我一塊錢——明天十二點來取。」他看見狗老弟也這樣說；猴老弟同樣；虎老弟同樣；獅老弟同樣。第二天他聽見敲門——「是我，豬老弟」——豬進來聊著，直到另一聲敲門。

passages.text: 'Me, Brar Dog.' Anansi told Brar Hog to run into that room, for Dog was too bad — if he caught him he would kill him. When Dog came in they talked until Monkey knocked, and Anansi sent Dog into the room, telling him that when he went in he would see Brar Hog under the bed — kill him. Monkey and Anansi talked until Tiger knocked: 'Brar Monkey, run into that room and hide, or Tiger catch you!' When Brar Tiger came in they talked until Lion knocked, and Anansi sent Tiger in with the same instruction about Monkey.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 45, middle (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「是我，狗老弟。」阿南西叫豬老弟躲進那間屋，說狗太兇——被捉住會殺了他。狗進來聊著，直到猴子敲門；阿南西把狗支進那間屋，說他進去會看見豬老弟躲在床下——殺了他。猴子和阿南西聊著，直到老虎敲門：「猴老弟，快躲進那間屋，不然老虎要抓住你！」虎老弟進來後他們聊著，直到獅子敲門；阿南西照樣把老虎支了進去。

passages.text: As Lion came in, Anansi told him: 'Look here! Plenty of meat. Brar Tiger gone in there; you are going to kill him!' Lion went in and killed Tiger. Meanwhile Anansi went out the kitchen door, dug a deep hole, and called, 'Brar Lion, run come here! We go put on little hot water to clean up those fellahs!' As Lion jumped out of the house, feeling so glad, and galloped to the kitchen, he got down into the hole and broke his neck. Anansi said, 'You brute! Look how much money I borrowed from you, and I have all your bones to crack tonight!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 45, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 獅子進來時，阿南西對他說：「瞧！好多肉。虎老弟進去了；你要去殺他！」獅子進去殺了老虎。同時阿南西從廚房門溜出去，挖了一個深坑，喊道：「獅老弟，快過來！咱們燒點熱水，把那幾個傢伙收拾乾淨！」獅子滿心歡喜地跳出院子，直奔廚房，一頭栽進坑裏摔斷了脖子。阿南西說：「你這個畜生！我從你那裏借了那麼多錢，今晚我可以把你的骨頭一根根敲碎了！」

title.en: Why Tumble-bug Rolls in the Dung
title.zh: 推糞蟲何以滾糞

region.en: Dry River, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加雞窩地乾河

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 46 'Why Tumble-bug Rolls in the Dung' (told by William Forbes, Dry River)

summary.en: The king offers his daughter to whoever brings a jar of money. Tumble-bug fills his jar with coin; Anansi fills his with cow- and horse-dung. At a wayside shop the two jars are swapped during a bread errand, and before the king Anansi's jar showers true silver while Tumble-bug's flings dung — 'Take it up, take it up, you nasty fellow, carry it out of the missis yard!' — which is why Tumble-bug rolls in filth to this day.
summary.zh: 國王懸賞：獻上一罐錢者可娶公主。推糞蟲罐中是錢，蜘蛛人罐中填牛馬之糞。途中兩罐在商店被調換；國王面前，蜘蛛人的罐子金幣嘩嘩傾瀉，推糞蟲的罐子滾出糞便——『撿起來！撿起來！你這骯髒的傢伙，把髒物帶出小姐的院子！』推糞蟲至今在穢物中打滾，便是由此而來。

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There was a young lady, the king's daughter; her father said whoever came with a jar of money would get her to marry. Tumble-bug got a jar of money. Anansi got a jar and could get no money to put in it, so he got some cow dung and some horse dung and filled up the jar. As the two were going up to the young lady, they stopped at a shop, and the two jars favored one another. Anansi said, 'Brar Tumble-bug, let we go in the shop and get a drink' — and, sending him out for bread, took up Tumble-bug's jar and left his own.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 46 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一位少女是國王的女兒；她父親說，誰帶來一罐錢就娶她。蜣螂弄到一罐錢。阿南西也有個罐子，卻弄不到錢裝，便弄了些牛糞馬糞把罐子填滿。兩人去見少女的路上，在一家店鋪前停下，兩個罐子彼此相像。阿南西說：「蜣螂老弟，咱們進店喝一杯吧」——支他出去買麵包，拿起蜣螂的罐子，留下了自己的。

passages.text: Up in the king's yard Anansi said, 'Massa, must bring a clean sheet to throw the money out of the jar!' and he threw out money — wa-a-a-a-a! As Tumble-bug threw, he threw out horse-dung and cow-dung. Anansi said, 'Take it up, take it up, you nasty fellow, carry out the missis yard!' That is why you see Tumble-bug roll in filth until today.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 46, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在國王的院子裏，阿南西說：「老爺，得拿一塊乾淨的布把罐裏的錢倒出來！」他把錢倒出來——嘩啦啦！蜣螂一倒，倒出來的是馬糞牛糞。阿南西喊：「撿起來，撿起來，你這髒傢伙，把它端出去！」——這就是為什麼你今天還看見蜣螂在糞裏滾。

title.en: Why John-crow Has a Bald Head
title.zh: 兀鷲何以禿頂

region.en: St. Ann's Bay and Bog, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖安灣與博格

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 47 'Why John-crow Has a Bald Head' (a, Margaret Brown, St. Anne's Bay)

summary.en: Anansi, nursing his grudge against John-crow for stealing his nests, invites the crow alone to a wedding feast — then stages a 'baptism' that uses nothing but boiling water: every guest dips his head into the copper. The scalded crow, in the paired dance version, receives a ladle of hot pop flung on his head for dancing too neatly — and no John-crow in this world has had a feather on his head since.
summary.zh: 兀鷲屢偷蛛巢，蜘蛛人懷恨在心。他獨邀兀鷲赴婚宴，宴後舉行『洗禮』——洗禮用的除了滾水別無他物：每位客人把頭浸入大銅鍋。另一版本：兀鷲舞步太過出色，蜘蛛人以滾粥一瓢潑頂，把那顆頭上的羽毛燒個精光——從此世間兀鷲再無一羽覆頂。

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale. The 'baptism' frame is folk-comic use of a church term. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi always had a grudge against John-crow: whenever he made his nest, the Crow flew on it and caught it up, and he could never keep a nest. So he said he was going to marry, and he was going to invite no one but Crow; and he had a big dinner, and no one was at the table but Crow. After the eating and drinking were done, he said he was going to have a baptism — but he did not baptize with anything but boiling water. After the water boiled, he took it off, ordered Crow to sit round the copper, and dipped every one's head into the water — and that is why Crow has a bald head today.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 47a (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿南西一直跟烏鴉結仇：他每次做窩，烏鴉都飛上去抓走，他從來保不住一個窩。於是他說他要成親，卻只請烏鴉一個；他備下豐盛的宴席，桌上只有烏鴉一個客人。吃喝完畢，他說要辦洗禮——可他用什麼洗禮呢？用的是滾水。水燒開後端下來，他吩咐烏鴉圍著大銅鍋坐好，把每個人的頭浸進水裏——這就是為什麼烏鴉今天有個光禿禿的頭。

passages.text: In the paired telling, Anansi and John-crow had a ball one night, and dinner was found for all the dancers. John-crow was a great stepper and could step better than Anansi; finding John-crow danced neater than he, Anansi got vexed. After the dinner, when the pop was hot, he told John-crow he must dance up to the pop — and just to be rid of John-crow that night, he took a ladle and dashed the hot pop right up on his head, and all John-crow's head stripped off. All the John-crows in this world never have had a feather on their heads since: Anansi burned them off with hot pop.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 47b 'The Dance' (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 配對的講法裏，阿南西和烏鴉一夜共舞，還給所有的舞者備了飯。烏鴉跳得極好，比阿南西強；見烏鴉跳得比自己漂亮，阿南西惱了。飯後，鍋一熱，他叫烏鴉必須跳到鍋跟前——只為把烏鴉擺脫掉，他拿起長勺，把滾熱的鍋汁兜頭澆在烏鴉頭上，烏鴉的頭毛全掉了。這世上所有的烏鴉從此頭上再也沒有長出一根羽毛：都被阿南西用熱汁燙掉了。

title.en: Why Dog Is Always Looking
title.zh: 狗為何總盯著人吃飯

region.en: Mandeville, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加曼德維爾

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 48 'Why Dog Is Always Looking' (told by Moses Hendricks, Mandeville)

summary.en: Scouting land to rent, Anansi and Dog both fall for the same field. The spider boasts that his father once planted yams on that very spot — yams that bore 'big like me leg!' — and Dog, whose legs are worth more than thread, walks off to look round instead: which is why, when you are eating, a dog is sure to be looking at you.
summary.zh: 尋地租耕，蜘蛛人與狗同時相中一塊好地。蜘蛛人誇稱父親曾在彼處種薯，結的薯『大得像我這條腿』——而蜘蛛人的腿細如線。狗兒寧可去處處張望也不願與他合夥——所以如今你吃飯時，狗總在一旁盯著看。

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi and Dog were friends. They wanted to go into cultivation, so both of them went out in search of good land to rent and came across a nice bit of land; Anansi fell in love with the spot, and Dog fell in love with the spot too. Anansi said to Dog he remembered when he was a little boy his father planted yams on that very spot — 'and the yams did bear.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 48 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿南西和狗是朋友。兩人想一起墾殖，便一起出去找好地租，遇上一塊好地；阿南西看中了那塊地，狗也看中了。阿南西對狗說，他記得小時候父親就在那塊地上種過山藥——「山藥還真結得好。」

passages.text: Dog asked how big they bore. Anansi said, 'Brar Dog, they bear big — big like me leg!' (Anansi's leg is just like a thread.) Brar Dog said, 'Before I work and plant yam, and the yam not bigger than your leg, I sooner walk round and look!' That is the reason why, when you are eating, a dog is sure to be looking at you.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 48, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 狗問結得有多大。阿南西說：「狗老弟，結得大——跟我這腿一樣粗！」（阿南西的腿跟一根線似的。）狗老弟說：「要我出力種山藥，結出來還不如你腿粗，我倒不如先四處看著！」——這就是為什麼你吃飯的時候，狗總盯著你看。

title.en: Why Rocks at the River Are Covered with Moss
title.zh: 河石何以生苔

region.en: Bog, Westmoreland, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加西摩蘭博格

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 49 'Why Rocks at the River Are Covered with Moss' (told by Sarah Vassel, Bog, Westmoreland)

summary.en: Eating at the river-side, Anansi refuses a begging rock-stone a share of his meal — and when he tries to rise the stone holds him fast until a hidden passerby hauls him up, leaving half his skin on the stone: moss grows on the rocks at the river-side, and Anansi's skin grows there.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人在河邊進食，乞食的岩石討不到一口，便在他起身時死死攥住他；藏在林中窺伺的路人最後將他拔起——蜘蛛人半張皮留在了石上：河邊的石頭上長苔，那是蜘蛛人的皮。

sensitivity.note: Etiological landscape tale (origin of river-stone moss). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi was going out one day and stopped at the river-side eating. A rock-stone begged him, and he would not give it any. After he had eaten his fill and wanted to get up, the rock-stone held him and he could not get up — and began to bawl.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 49 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿南西一天出門，在河邊停下吃飯。一塊石頭求他分一些，他不肯。他吃得飽飽的想起身，那塊石頭卻把他按住，他起不來了——便大聲哭喊起來。

passages.text: A man was coming past at the same time and asked, 'Bredder Anansi, who has been crying here?' Anansi said he did not know; the man went inside the bush and hid. Anansi hollered, and the man came out and caught him by his two hands and drew him right up — half of his skin left on the stone. Moss grows upon the rock-stones at the river-side: Anansi's skin grows there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 49, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 恰巧有人經過，問：「阿南西老弟，這裏是誰在哭啊？」阿南西說他不知道；那人便躲進灌木叢裏。阿南西又喊，那人出來，抓住他的兩隻手把他往上拔——他的皮有一半留在了石頭上。河邊的石頭上長著青苔：那就是阿南西的皮。

title.en: Why Ground-dove Complains
title.zh: 地面鴿何以哀鳴

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山區

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924 print), tale 50 'Why Ground-dove Complains' (told by Simeon Falconer, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Tiger hires Dove to help watch his corn by night; Dove keeps the watch while Tiger sleeps — and by day destroys the corn himself. When Tiger, tipped to the scheme, dodges in the ground and catches the raiding gang, he slaps the traitor on the ears; the dove has been singing 'Me ears! me ears!' ever since.
summary.zh: 虎雇鴿子夜間守玉米；虎睡覺，鴿守夜——白天卻親自毀田。虎識破奸計，白日伏於地中擒獲劫掠的鴿群，摑其耳光；地面鴿自此哀唱『我的耳朵！我的耳朵！』至今。

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Tiger was planting corn, and birds and everything were destroying the corn, so he got Dove to help him watch who was destroying it. After they sat up the whole night watching the corn, the next day Tiger went to sleep. Bredder Dove went back in the day and destroyed the corn himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 50 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 老虎種玉米，鳥兒等等來糟蹋，便請地鳩幫他看守是誰在毀。他們守了一整夜的玉米，第二天老虎去睡覺了。地鳩老弟白天回去，自己把玉米毀了。

passages.text: So the next day Tiger went in the day and dodged in the ground. Bredder Dove had a gang, and Tiger was slapping him on the ears as the gang was caught — and he sang out, 'Me ears! me ears! me ears!' And from that day to this the dove sings, 'Me ears!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 50, ending (2024); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天老虎白天去躲在地裏。地鳩老弟帶著一群同夥來，老虎抓到同夥便打地鳩的耳朵——他喊了起來：「我的耳朵！我的耳朵！我的耳朵！」——從那天直到今天，鴿子唱的都是「我的耳朵！」

title.en: Why Hog Is Always Grunting
title.zh: 豬為何總在哼哼

region.en: Harmony Hall, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加和諧堂

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 51 'Why Hog Is Always Grunting' (told by Norman Hilton, Harmony Hall)

summary.en: Bathing with Dog by the river-side, Hog takes off his mouth for the diving contest — and Dog, surfacing first, swims away with it. The mouthless hog surfaces grunting for his missing face, and has grunted ever since.
summary.zh: 豬與狗在河邊同浴，豬為比賽潛水卸下嘴巴；狗先冒頭，叼起豬嘴泅走。失去嘴的豬浮出水面，尋不著自己的嘴，只能哼哼作聲——豬的哼哼自那日起再未停過。

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale (detachable-mouth motif). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Brar Hog and Brar Dog lived close by the river-side, and Brar Dog said to Brar Hog, 'Come! we get a bathe!' Brar Hog agreed, took off his mouth, and Brar Dog and Brar Hog jumped into the water. Brar Dog said, 'Come! let us see who can dive longer than the other.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 51 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 豬老弟和狗老弟住在河邊相鄰，狗老弟對豬老弟說：「來！咱們洗個澡！」豬老弟答應了，卸下自己的嘴，狗老弟和豬老弟跳進水裏。狗老弟說：「來！咱們比比誰潛得久。」

passages.text: The two of them dived underneath the water. Brar Dog came up, jumped out of the water, took Brar Hog's mouth and went away with it. When Brar Hog came out of the water searching for his mouth and could not find it, he said, 'Humph! Brar Dog take a me mouth!' That is why Brar Hog is always grunting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 51, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兩個都潛到了水下。狗老弟先上來，跳出水面，抓起豬老弟的嘴跑掉了。豬老弟出水找他的嘴找不到，說：「哼！狗老弟拿了我的嘴！」——這就是為什麼豬老弟至今總在哼哼。

title.en: Why Toad Croaks in the Wild Pine
title.zh: 蟾蜍何以在野松中呱呱

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山區

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 52 'Why Toad Croaks' (told by Richard Morgan, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: The axe-magic bride contest — cut the cotton tree that fastens back its own chips — is won by Toad, who flings a pocketful of ashes at every flying chip until the tree falls. At the celebration 'washing', a great pot of boiling water is overturned over the stripped bridegroom-to-be, who jumps into the wild pine; every night to this day you hear him cry out, 'Kwoka soaka!'
summary.zh: 砍不斷自己復合的棉木樹——婚試之謎被蟾蜍破解：每有木屑飛回，他便撒一把懷中灰燼，砍倒大樹。慶功『淨身』時，一大鍋滾水被傾覆在剝光的準新郎身上；蟾蜍跳入野松，至今夜夜聽他哀叫『誇卡索卡！』

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale; axe-magic contest links to worldwide 'impossible task' cycle. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: One man had a daughter. He said, 'There is a cotton tree; the man who cuts down that cotton tree marries my daughter.' Every man went to cut it, and soon the cut chips fastened back, so they could not get the girl to marry. Toad said he would fell it. Toad filled his pocket with ashes, and every chop he chopped he flung the ashes upon the tree when the chips flew — and they could not fasten. So Toad did and did until he felled the cotton tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 52 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個人有個女兒。他說：「那裏有棵木棉樹；砍倒那棵樹的人娶我的女兒。」人人都去砍，砍下的木屑很快又粘回去，誰也娶不成姑娘。蟾蜍說他來砍。蟾蜍口袋裏裝滿灰，每砍一下，木屑飛起時他便把灰撒到樹上——木屑就粘不住了。他砍啊砍，終於砍倒了木棉樹。

passages.text: The master had a long barbecue and told him, 'Now you must go down there and strip yourself, and I will pour on the water to let you skin.' All this time a big pot of hot water was boiling on the fire; so they turned over the pot of hot water and said, 'Brar Toad, water come! Take your rubbing cloth.' And Toad jumped into the wild pine; up to this day, every night you hear him cry out, 'Kwoka soaka!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 52, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 主人搭了長長的燒烤架，吩咐他：「你下去脫了衣服，我倒水來幫你褪皮。」這時一大鍋滾水正在火上燒著；他們把那鍋滾水一傾，說：「蟾蜍老弟，水來了！拿好你的搓澡布。」蟾蜍跳進了野松林；直到今天，每天夜裏你都聽見他叫「瓜哭——索卡！」

title.en: Why Woodpecker Bores Wood
title.zh: 啄木鳥為何啄木

region.en: Maroon Town, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 53 'Why Woodpecker Bores Wood' (told by Samuel Wright, Maroon Town)

summary.en: A dying mother's wish to be buried in stone proves impossible: Woodpecker bores and bores and returns confessing failure, and lays her in wood instead — which is why the woodpecker bores the wood.
summary.zh: 垂死的母親願葬於石中；啄木鳥啄石不成，回來認罪，改葬母親於木中——啄木鳥啄木之習，便由此而來。

sensitivity.note: Etiological tale with filial-piety frame. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There was a bird called Woodpecker who promised his mother to bury her in a stone, and went all about telling all his friends that he was going to bury his mother in a stone. The mother was poorly unto death, and he went to bore a stone — then turned back and said, 'Mother, I try the stone but I can't bore it. I'll bury you in a wood.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 53 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一隻鳥叫啄木鳥，答應母親要把她葬在石頭裏，便到處告訴朋友們說要把母親葬進石頭。母親病得要死，他便去鑿一塊石頭——鑿不動，回頭對母親說：「媽媽，我試了石頭鑿不動。我把你葬在木頭裏吧。」

passages.text: And he bored the wood with his bill, working it wider and deeper day by day, until it was fit to receive her. After the death of his mother, he buried her in a wood, in the hole he had bored. That is the reason the woodpecker bores the wood, and bores it to this day, making the little round doors and windows of the dry trees for the dead of his kind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 53, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他便用嘴鑿那木頭，一天比一天鑿得又寬又深，直到可以把母親安放進去。母親死後，他把她葬在木頭裏，葬在他鑿好的洞中。這就是啄木鳥啄木的緣故，他啄到今天，為同類的死者在乾枯的樹上開出小小的圓門圓窗。

title.en: Why Crab Is Afraid after Dark
title.zh: 螃蟹何以夜間驚惶

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山區

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 54 'Why Crab Is Afraid after Dark' (told by Richard Morgan, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Promised a head by God tomorrow, Crab sings and dances his gratitude all night until he muddies the water; God refuses him the head — 'if you get a head you will do worse' — and decrees he shall carry his head on his shoulders all the days of his life, trusting no shadow after dark lest he be picked up and thrown into someone's basket.
summary.zh: 螃蟹得神應許明日賜頭，歡歌狂舞至攪渾河水；神怒而拒賜——『得了頭你會更壞』——並判他終生以肩負首，入夜後不敢信任何影子，唯恐被人拾起扔進籃中。

sensitivity.note: Etiological tale. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Crab went to God to give him a head. God told him he must go back: 'Tomorrow come, I will give you a head.' After Crab was going home he rejoiced in himself, singing, 'Tank God, tomorrow God a'mighty gi' me head! Tank God, tomorrow God a'mighty gi' me head!' He danced until he muddied the water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 54 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 螃蟹去見上帝討一個頭。上帝說他必須先回去：「明天來，我給你一個頭。」螃蟹回家路上自我歡喜，唱著「感謝上帝，明天全能的上帝要給我頭啦！感謝上帝，明天全能的上帝要給我頭啦！」他跳著舞，把水都攪渾了。

passages.text: Next day he went to God a'mighty to get his head. God told him, 'Stop! Before you have gotten a head, you go and muddy the water; then if you get a head you will do worse. So you must carry your head upon your shoulder all the days of your life.' So when Crab was returning home, when he got to Orange Bay and stood there, he would not trust a shadow after dark, for he does not know when they will pick him up and throw him into a basket.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 54, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天他去全能的上帝那裏領頭。上帝說：「站住！頭還沒拿到，你倒先把水攪渾了；真給了你頭，你還要幹出更壞的事。所以你這輩子都把頭夾在肩膀上走好了。」於是螃蟹回家去的時候，一到橙灣站定，天黑之後連影子也不敢信——因為他不知道什麼時候會被人撿起來扔進籃子裏。

title.en: Why Mice Are No Bigger
title.zh: 老鼠何以不再長大

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山區

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 55 'Why Mice Are No Bigger' (told by Richard Morgan, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Robin Mice-rat wants to 'turn big man'. The Saviour sets him the test of killing his oldest uncle; the first night he only strikes him, and the blabbing uncle — boasting of the temple-blow that would have finished him — shows the very spot to the disguised nephew, who returns and kills him there. The Saviour refuses promotion: 'You little bit of man, go kill your oldest uncle, then if I let you turn bigger you will do worse!' — and mice stay small.
summary.zh: 老鼠羅賓想『變成大人』。救主設考：去殺大伯。第一夜他只是打了一下；大伯事後炫耀『幸而只中此處』，指點太陽穴位置——化裝歸來的姪兒依言補上一擊，將他打死。救主拒其升格：『你這點小人，殺了大伯還想變大？只會更壞！』——老鼠便再未長大。

sensitivity.note: Etiological tale with violent folkloric content, recorded as folk narrative. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There is a man named Robin Mice-rat going to his uncle's house. He and the uncle stayed in the dark the whole time; when he was going away, he said good-by, took a stick and struck his uncle. At this time he went to our Saviour and said he wanted to turn big man; the Saviour told him that if he wanted to turn big man he must go and kill his oldest uncle. So, as the uncle never died, he went back the next night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 55 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一個人叫羅賓鼠鼠，去舅舅家。他和舅舅一直在黑屋子裏待著；臨走告別時，他拿起一根棍子打了舅舅。這時他去見我們的救主，說他想變成大人；救主說，想變大人就必須去殺掉你最年長的舅舅。可是舅舅一直沒死，第二天夜裏他又去了。

passages.text: Talking with his uncle, he heard the account: 'That fellow Robin came here last night; when he was going away, he took a stick and struck me on the head. But if he had caught me here (pointing to the temple), the fellow would have got me.' So as the uncle showed him the place, when he got up he met his uncle at the said place and killed him stiff dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 55, middle (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他和舅舅說話時聽見這番話：「昨天晚上羅賓那傢伙來過；走的時候拿棍子打了我的頭。可他要是打中這裏（指著太陽穴），那傢伙就得手了。」舅舅指給他看位置，他第二天照著那個位置殺了舅舅，殺得死死的。

passages.text: Next day he went to his Saviour to be turned into a big man. The Saviour said to him, 'You little bit of man, go kill your oldest uncle — then if I let you turn bigger, you will do worse!' So from that day, that is the reason you see mice don't grow bigger, to this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 55, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天他去見救主要變成大人。救主對他說：「你這麼一丁點的人，去殺你最年長的舅舅——我要是讓你再變大些，你還要幹更壞的事！」所以從那天起，這就是為什麼你今天看見老鼠永遠長不大。

title.en: Rat's Wedding and the Burnt Rice
title.zh: 老鼠婚宴與焦飯

region.en: Harmony Hall, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加雞窩地和諧堂

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 56 'Rat's Wedding' (told by Thomas Williams, Harmony Hall)

summary.en: At his own wedding feast Rat remembers the burnt rice he loves to scrape. Halfway home with his bride he invents a forgotten treasure, leaves her on the water-table, and sneaks to the kitchen — where the burnt-rice pot, disturbed, turns over and traps his head. Craping away in the dark, he is found, lifted, and killed by the cook's helpers: which is why there are so many widows in the world — their husbands died and left them.
summary.zh: 老鼠在自己的婚宴上惦記著愛刮的焦飯。半路撇下新娘，謊稱遺忘貴重之物，溜回廚房——焦飯鍋被碰翻，罩住了他的頭。黑暗中刮飯作響的鼠被廚娘逮個正著，一鍋抬起，當場斃命——世上寡婦之多，正因丈夫死了撇下她們。

sensitivity.note: Folk animal tale with comic ending. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Rat got married, and rice and peas were provided for the dinner. It was so richly cooked and so much that it got burnt. Rat remembered that the rice burnt in the pot, and Rat liked scrapping; while he was going home with his wife in the way, when he got part way he said to her, 'I forget something very valuable in the wedding house — have to go back for it!' She agreed, and he set the buggy out on the water-table and ran back to the wedding house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 56 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 老鼠成親了，酒席備了米飯和豌豆。做得太豐盛、太多了，結果燒糊了。老鼠記得鍋裏的米燒糊了，老鼠又愛刨東西；跟妻子回家的路上，走到半路他對她說：「我把一件很值錢的東西忘在婚宴的房子裏了——得回去取！」她同意了，他把小車停在路邊水溝沿上，跑回婚宴的房子。

passages.text: He never went in where everybody was merrying himself; he went to the kitchen. The pot with the burnt rice was leaning up by the side of the wall. He went to the pot, troubled it, and the pot, instead of rolling away, turned over and covered him underneath. When he found he could not come out he said, 'Chut! What about that? I wouldn't give a biscuit for a man who can't lose his night rest!' — and he began to scrape the burnt part, kur-ur-rup, krup, krup, krup.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 56, middle (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他不去大家作樂的地方，去了廚房。盛著糊米的鍋靠在牆邊。他去動那口鍋，鍋沒有滾走，反倒翻過來把他扣在了底下。他發現出不來了，說：「呸！這叫什麼事？一個人連一夜安穩覺都保不住，一文錢也不值！」——便開始刮那些燒糊的部分，咯嚕嚕，咔嚓，咔嚓，咔嚓。

passages.text: His wife was calling now, 'Mr. Rat! Mr. Rat!' — 'Me head fasten in pot-o!' — and he turned back scraping, scraping. The cook heard the noise, went out to the kitchen, found it was Rat underneath the pot, called out for help; they came out, lifted up the pot and killed him. That is why there are so many widows in the world — because their husbands died and left them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 56, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 妻子在喊了：「鼠先生！鼠先生！」「我的頭卡在鍋裏啦！」——他回過頭來又刮又刮。廚師聽見響動，走到廚房，發現是老鼠在鍋底下，喊人來幫忙；眾人出來，掀起鍋，把他打死了。這就是世上寡婦這麼多的緣故——丈夫死了，把她們撇下了。

title.en: The Cock's Breakfast
title.zh: 公雞的早餐

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山區

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 57a 'Cock's Breakfast' (told by Richard Morgan, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Cockroach twice eats Cock's breakfast under the promise of a return meal with an Anansi-style noise-signal that never comes. Creeping back at last with his fiddle — 'Ring a ting ting, me know nigger fe nigger!' — he is heard inside a gourd, cornered, picked up and swallowed; and from that day not a cockroach walks into a fowl yard any more.
summary.zh: 蟑螂兩次吃掉公雞的早餐，又以『無聲即開飯』的暗號耍賴不還席。最後他拉琴潛返——『叮叮響，我知黑吃黑！』——卻在葫蘆中被聽破，被公雞堵住、拾起、吞下；自那天起，蟑螂再也不敢踏進雞院半步。

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale (cockroach/fowl-yard proverb). Beckwith's source text contains period racial idiom in song; paraphrase avoids it.

passages.text: One day Cockroach said to Cock, 'Brar Cock, get a little breakfast, so I will come and have breakfast with you.' Cock said yes. Cockroach came, Cockroach ate; when he had done, he said, 'Brar Cock, when you know my breakfast is ready, come.' — 'How must I know?' — 'I will give you a sign: when you hear me make noise, don't come; but when you hear me stay still in the yard, you must come.' When Cock went, he did not find Cockroach, and returned back to his yard.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 57a (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一天蟑螂對公雞說：「雞老弟，備一點早飯，我來陪你吃。」公雞答應了。蟑螂來了，蟑螂吃了；吃完說：「雞老弟，你知道我的早飯好了，就來。」「我怎麼知道？」「我給你個信號：你聽見我弄出動靜，別來；你聽見我在院子裏安安靜靜的，就來。」公雞去了，找不見蟑螂，回到自己的院子。

passages.text: The second day Cockroach came and said, 'O Brar Cock! from the time I left you, pain all over my skin, so I went and lay down; but today you can come.' Cock did the same, went to the yard, did not find him, and returned back. When he got halfway, he heard in Cockroach's house — 'Ring a ting ting!' Cock took time, tiptoed along, and heard Cockroach inside a gourd. Cock took his bill and licked him at the gourd; Cockroach ran out, Cock picked him up and swallowed him. So from that day, not a cockroach walks into a fowl yard any more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 57a, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天蟑螂來說：「哦雞老弟！自從離開你，我渾身疼得躺下了；今天你可以來了。」公雞照樣去了院子，找不見他，回來了。走到半路，他聽見蟑螂家裏——「叮叮咚咚！」公雞踮著腳悄悄走近，聽見蟑螂在一個葫蘆裏。公雞伸嘴在葫蘆上舔他；蟑螂跑出來，公雞一把抓住吞了。所以從那天起，一隻蟑螂也不敢再走進雞的視線。

title.en: The Drum of Borrowed Skins
title.zh: 借皮製鼓

region.en: Harmony Hall, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加和諧堂

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 57c 'The Drum' (told by Mrs. Matilda Hall, Harmony Hall)

summary.en: Dog, Monkey, Tiger, Puss and Cockroach, hearing music everywhere at Christmas and having none, agree to cut little bits of their own skin to make a drum. Roach claims to have no skin, is driven from the company into a banana tree — and vows to be the first to play the finished drum. On Christmas eve the friends, three-quarters of a mile off at market, hear it sounding under Roach's feet; Puss finds him and kills him, and Puss has eaten Roach until this day.
summary.zh: 聖誕將至，狗、猴、虎、貓與蟑螂聽遍四方音樂而自己一無所有，遂約定各割少許皮來蒙鼓。蟑螂自稱『無皮』，被逐出夥伴、躲進芭蕉樹——卻揚言要第一個敲響此鼓。聖誕前夕，眾友在市集上三哩外便聽見鼓聲——是蟑螂以足擊鼓；貓尋聲而至殺之，貓吃蟑螂之習至今未改。

sensitivity.note: Etiological tale (why cat eats cockroach). Skin-cutting frame is folkloric; no ritual instruction. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Once there were Dog, Monkey, Tiger, Puss and Cockroach. Christmas was coming and they heard music played all about, and they had none. They said, 'We have to make up to make a drum — how will we manage?' And they said, 'The only way is to cut a little of our skin to make a drum.' The Roach said, 'I have none' — so they drove him out of the company and he got into a banana tree to live; then he turned round to them and said, 'I first will play that drum!' — 'How will you get it to play?' they asked him, and he said, 'I first will play it!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 57c (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有狗、猴子、老虎、貓和蟑螂。聖誕節快到了，聽見處處有樂聲，他們卻沒有。他們說：「我們得做一面鼓——怎麼辦呢？」有人說：「唯一的辦法是割一點我們的皮來做鼓。」蟑螂說「我沒有皮」——便被趕出夥伴，鑽進一棵香蕉樹裏住下；然後他回頭對他們說：「我要頭一個打那面鼓！」「你怎麼能讓它響呢？」他們問，他說——

passages.text: They fitted up the drum with the skins and hung it up to get cured. Christmas eve fell; going to the market to buy up all the things, about three quarters of a mile off they heard the drum playing — 'Biddy bwoy! who is playing our drum?' It was Roach, who had taken down the drum, put it between his feet and begun to play, singing his song. The Puss came and saw him and killed him, and Puss has eaten Roach until this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 57c, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們把鼓蒙好皮，掛起來晾乾。聖誕夜到了；去市場採買東西的路上，約四分之三哩之外他們聽見鼓響——「天哪！誰在打我們的鼓？」是蟑螂，他把鼓取下來，夾在兩腳之間打起來，唱著他的歌。貓來了，看見了他，把他殺了；貓吃蟑螂一直吃到今天。

title.en: Hunter, Guinea-hen and Fish
title.zh: 獵人、珠雞與魚

region.en: Harmony Hall, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加雞窩地和諧堂

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 58 'Hunter, Guinea-hen and Fish' (told by Thomas Williams, Harmony Hall)

summary.en: A hunter's clearing is also Guinea-hen's feeding ground, and the two unwitting strangers — one by day, one by night — keep thanking each other for the work. When harvest comes, Guinea-hen calls Fish with a trombone, trades a loan of her wing for his help, and harvests the field with him; at dawn she borrows the wings back 'to catch a butterfly' and sails away, leaving Fish in the furrow. The hunter finds the trembling borrower, is offered a song instead of death, carries the tub of water singing to the sea — and the Fish rides the first big wave home; which is why we always have to catch fish at sea.
summary.zh: 獵人墾的地恰是珠雞的食場——晝人夜禽，互不謀面，卻各自感謝『幫工』。收穫在即，珠雞以號角喚魚，借翼交易同往收穫；天亮前又借『捉蝴蝶』之名收回翅膀遠遁，拋下田中的魚。獵人擒住顫抖的借宿者，魚以歌換命，載歌載舞至海邊，乘巨浪而歸——所以我們總得到海裡才能捕到魚。

sensitivity.note: Etiological tale (why fish live at sea). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: The Hunter was always hunting, and he met up with a splendid piece of rich land and thought to cultivate it, beginning the same day to cut bush. The piece of land was Guinea-hen's feeding ground; Guinea-hen comes out at night and does not walk in the day. 'Massa is good — he knows this is my feeding ground and begins to clean it, so I can get my pullings clear! Let me help myself,' and she made a little chopping herself too.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 58 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 獵人一直在打獵，遇上了一塊極肥美的地，想耕種，當天就動手砍灌木。那塊地是珠雞的覓食場；珠雞夜裏出來，白天不走路。「主人心好——他知道這是我的覓食場，先替我清理了，我就能白撿了！讓我自己也幫一手吧，」她也自己砍了一小片。

passages.text: The old man came in the morning: 'Hi! thankful! I commenced work yesterday, and massa helped me!' — and did a little more. The third day he burned what he cut — 'Hi! thankful! massa burned the balance!' — and Guinea-hen came at night and gave thanks and cleaned up the balance of what the old man left. Then he planted peas and corn, and Guinea-hen came in the night and said, 'Massa is good! I don't need to plant any' — and began to eat what the old man planted. The old man came in the morning, saw the damage — 'Hi! what insect did this?' — and planted some more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 58, middle (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 老人早上來了：「嗨！多謝！我昨天開了工，主人都幫我幹了！」——又多幹了一點。第三天他燒了砍下的灌木——「嗨！多謝！主人把剩下的都燒了！」——珠雞夜裏來道謝，把老人留下的也清理乾淨。然後他種了豌豆和玉米，珠雞夜裏來說：「主人心好！我一棵也不用種了」——開始吃老人種下的。老人早上來，看見損失——「嗨！

passages.text: It went on until the peas began to ripen, about eight weeks. The old man said, 'Going to gather it in tomorrow.' Guinea-hen heard and went to the sea and called the Fish with her trombone: 'I planted a bit of corn and peas, getting ripe, and the old man is coming tomorrow; I want to gather it in tonight before he comes.' Fish accepted — but could neither walk nor fly; Guinea-hen lent her wing and they flew and dropped, and ran, till they came to the ground. 'Here is my own field; gather and eat as much as you like.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 58, middle-b (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 就這樣過了八個星期，豌豆快熟了。老人說：「明天來收割。」珠雞聽見了，去海邊用她的長號叫魚：「我種了一點玉米和豌豆，快熟了，老人明天來；我要今晚他來之前收完。」魚答應了——可她既不會走也不會飛；珠雞借出翅膀，她們便飛一陣、落一陣，跑一陣，直到來到那塊地。「這是我自己的田；隨便收、隨便吃。

passages.text: When day commenced to light, Guinea-hen saw the old man coming and said it was a butterfly jumping about — 'Lend me your wings, I go catch it for you' — and sailed away quietly out of the field. The old man grumbled, picked what he could, and came to where the Fish was. 'O Fish! is it you who did this damage all this time?' — 'No, not I! Don't kill me and I will sing you some songs.' The old man liked music, put him in a tub of water to sing and dance; Fish said, 'Take me to the nearest sea-side you have.' The old man carried the tub on his head, dancing as the Fish sang, until a big wave came and the Fish aimed for it and went along with it. The old man stayed dancing, not knowing the Fish was gone; he ran home for hook and line and threw it into the sea to catch Fish — and that is why we always have to catch fish at sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 58, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天色剛亮，珠雞望見老人來了，說那是一隻蝴蝶在跳來跳去——「把翅膀借我，我去替你捉它」——悄悄飛出了田外。老人嘟囔著，能撿的撿了，走到魚那裏。「哦魚！一直是你幹的這些破壞？」——「不是我！別殺我，我給你唱幾首歌。」老人愛音樂，把他放進一桶水裏唱歌跳舞；魚說：「把我送到最近的海邊去吧。」老人

title.en: Brer Rabbit and the Tar-pole
title.zh: 兔子哥哥與柏油樁

region.en: Mandeville, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加曼德維爾

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 59a 'The Tar Baby' (told by Rennie Macfarlane, Mandeville)

summary.en: The classic sticky capture, Jamaican style: Fox's tar-pole ignores Rabbit's commands until fist, foot and head are fast. Offered the choice of burning, drowning, hanging or dashing over the bramble-patch, the captured rabbit begs for anything but the brambles — and the satisfied Fox hurls him there, to the freedom cheer of 'Oh, what a fool!'
summary.zh: 黏捉經典的牙買加版：福克斯的柏油樁不理兔子的喝令，直到拳、腳、頭逐一粘牢。火燒、溺斃、吊死、拋過荊棘叢——任選其一？被擒的兔子哀求『千萬別拋荊棘』；得意的福克斯便把他拋過荊棘叢——兔子落地歡呼：『哎呀，真是個蠢貨！』

sensitivity.note: Brer Rabbit tar-baby episode (Jamaican variant); cross-tradition cluster with Anansi tar-baby (Tale 21) and US plantation versions.

passages.text: When Brer Fox tried to catch Brer Rabbit, he could not catch him. He stuck up a tar-pole in his common, and when Brer Rabbit came and saw it, he said, 'Come out of Brer Fox's place, or I kick you!' And the tar-pole wouldn't come out. And he kicked it and his foot fastened. 'Let go foot, else I kick you with the other one!' — and he kicked it with the other one and the other foot fastened. And he boxed it and his hand fastened. 'Let go me, else I box you!' — he boxed it with the other hand and his hand fastened. 'Let it go, else I buck you!' — he bucked it and his head fastened. 'Let me go, else I bite you!' — and when he bit it, his mouth fastened, and he couldn't move or talk.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 59a (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 狐狸老弟想捉兔子老弟，卻捉不到。他在自家空地上立了一根瀝青柱；兔子老弟來了看見它，說：「從狐狸老弟的地裏出去，不然我踢你！」瀝青柱不出來。他踢了它，腳粘住了。「放開我的腳，不然我用另一隻踢！」——他用另一隻踢，另一隻腳也粘住了。他用拳打它，手粘住了。「放開我，不然我用另一隻拳打你！」——他用另一隻手打，手也粘住了。「放

passages.text: And Brer Fox said, 'Think I couldn't catch you! Burning you, and drowning you, and hanging you, and dashing you over the bramble — which one would you rather?' He said, 'Do anything you like, but don't dash me over that bramble!' And Brer Fox took him and dashed him over the bramble — and he said, 'Oh, what a fool!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 59a, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 狐狸老弟說：「以為我捉不到你！燒了你，淹了你，吊了你，把你摔過黑刺莓叢——你挑哪樣？」他說：「隨你便，只是別把我摔過那黑刺莓叢！」狐狸老弟便拿起他摔過黑刺莓叢——他喊道：「哦，好個傻瓜！」

title.en: Rabbit's Grace: Bless and Blind Us
title.zh: 兔子哥的禱文：賜福且致盲

region.en: Mandeville, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加曼德維爾

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924 print), tale 59b 'Saying Grace' (told by Rennie Macfarlane, Mandeville)

summary.en: Captured again, Rabbit asks Fox for a pre-execution prayer — clasp your hands and repeat after me: 'O God, bless and blind us!' Fox, hearing only 'bless and help us', closes his eyes to say it devoutly; the rabbit runs away, and they never see him again.
summary.zh: 兔子再遭擒獲，請求臨刑前做個禱告——『合掌跟著我念：啊上帝，賜福且致盲於我們！』福克斯只聽成『賜福並庇佑』，虔誠閉眼誦念；兔子趁機逃走，從此再無人見過他。

sensitivity.note: Prayer-trick amusement tale; folk-comic use of prayer, not devotional material. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Brer Fox caught Brer Rabbit again, and was going to kill him. Brer Rabbit said, 'Do, Brer Fox — as you are going to kill me, have prayers.' And he said, 'Clasp your hands and say what I say: O God, bless and blind us!' But Brer Fox thought he said 'Bless and help us,' and he said it, eyes shut — and Rabbit ran away, and they never saw him again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 59b (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 狐狸老弟又捉住了兔子老弟，要殺他。兔子老弟說：「求你了，狐狸老弟——你要殺我，先做個禱告吧。」他說：「合起手來，照我說的念：哦上帝，保佑並弄瞎我們！」狐狸老弟聽成「保佑並幫助我們」，便閉著眼念了——兔子跑掉了，從此再沒有人見過他。

title.en: The Funeral That Wiggled
title.zh: 會動的葬禮

region.en: Mandeville, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加曼德維爾

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924 (published 1924)

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 59c 'Pretending Dead' (told by Rennie Macfarlane, Mandeville)

summary.en: Bear comes to Rabbit's yard with news that Fox is dead and needs burying. Rabbit dresses for the funeral — bonpon hat, coatie, spectacles — sits in the rocking-chair and observes that folks who fall down dead always cock a foot in the air and say 'Pooh!' The corpse, taking direction, cocks its foot and says 'Pooh!' — and Rabbit goes away saying a man like that never died yet.
summary.zh: 熊來報喪：福克斯死了，須抬去埋葬。兔子盛裝赴喪——鐵罐高帽、外套、眼鏡——端坐搖椅批評道：『人死倒地，總該翹腳喊一聲噗！』屍體依言翹腳喊了一聲『噗！』——兔子拂袖而去：『你這樣的人，還沒死透呢！』

sensitivity.note: Feigned-death amusement tale (ATU 'pretend dead' cycle). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: When Brer Fox wanted to get Brer Rabbit again, he and Bear made up to catch him. Brer Bear went to Brer Rabbit's yard and told him that Brer Fox was dead and he must help to bury him, for he and Brer Fox were friends. When he got to Brer Fox's yard, he saw Brer Fox lying down. Brer Rabbit put on his bonpon hat and coatie and spectacles, sat up in a rocking-chair and said, 'I never see it so! What a style! What a funniness! I think that when folks fall down dead, they always cock up their foot in the air and make pooh!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 59c (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 狐狸老弟又想捉兔子老弟，便和熊約定一起抓他。熊老弟去兔子老弟的院子，告訴他狐狸老弟死了，他得去幫忙安葬，因為他和狐狸老弟是朋友。到了狐狸老弟的院子，他看見狐狸老弟直挺挺地躺著。兔子老弟戴上他的bonpon帽子、穿上外衣、戴上眼鏡，坐在搖椅上說：「我從沒見過這樣的事！好大的架勢！多有趣！我想人們倒斃的時候，總是要把一隻腳翹到空中，做出那個姿勢——

passages.text: And Brer Fox cocked up his foot in the air and said, 'Pooh!' — and Brer Rabbit went away and said, 'A man like you never dead yet!' — for a dead man does not take instruction, and the corpse that takes it is only playing. He went home whistling, and the bear and the fox were left to bury nobody, the funeral breaking up over a wooden grave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 59c, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 狐狸老弟把一隻腳翹到了空中，說「呸！」——兔子老弟走開了，說「像你這樣的人永遠死不了！」——因為死人不會聽從教導，聽從教導的屍體只是在裝死。他吹著口哨回家了，留下熊和狐狸誰也埋不成，一場葬禮在一座木頭墓前散了場。

title.en: The Animal Race: Horse and Turtle
title.zh: 動物賽跑：馬與龜

region.en: Maroon Town, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924 (published 1924)

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 60a 'The Animal Race: Horse and Turtle' (told by Alfred Williams, Maroon Town)

summary.en: Horse bets Turtle he will reach Kingston first; Turtle stations one of his children at every mile-post with the same travelling-song, the last at the Kingston wharf-house. All night Horse gallops, reining and spurring mile-post to mile-post, each one answering soft and sweet — until at the last post, riding into Kingston, he drops down dead.
summary.zh: 馬與龜賭賽先到京斯頓；龜在每個里程碑各埋伏一個孩子，同唱旅途之歌，最後一個守在碼頭倉房。馬整夜疾馳、勒韁加鞭，每一里程碑都『軟甜』應答——直到最後一站，衝進京斯頓的馬倒地而亡。

sensitivity.note: Hare/tortoise race cycle (ATU 275) in Jamaican form; family relay trick. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Horse bet Turtle that he would get to Kingston before him. Turtle bet him he would get to Kingston first, Brar Horse. Turtle took up one of his pickney and dropped them at every mile-post, and dropped the last one in at Kingston at the wharf-house, telling them they were going for a sack of salt. The night when they started, as Brar Horse caught up to the first mile-post he sang out in a harsh note — and Turtle answered quite yonder, soft and sweet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 60a (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬跟烏龜打賭，說自己會先到金斯頓。烏龜跟他打賭自己先到金斯頓。烏龜帶上自己的一個孩子，每個里程碑丟下一個，最後一個丟到金斯頓的碼頭倉庫，告訴他們說是去背一袋鹽。起跑那夜，馬老弟追上第一個里程碑，粗聲喊了一聲——烏龜在遠處柔聲甜聲地應了。

passages.text: Horse said, 'Well! Brar Turtle gone!' Gallop, draw rein, and spur; as he got to the next mile-post he heard the same answer. Gallop and gallop till he got to the next mile-post, and the same song, and at every mile-post the answer soft and sweet from quite yonder — until, as Horse caught to that last mile-post going into Kingston, he dropped down dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 60a, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬說：「好傢伙！烏龜老弟跑在前頭了！」飛奔，勒韁，加鞭；到下一個里程碑又聽見同樣的回答。飛奔再飛奔到下一個里程碑，又是同樣的歌聲，每個里程碑的回答都柔聲甜聲從遠處傳來——直到馬追到進金斯頓的最後一個里程碑，倒地死了。

title.en: The Animal Race: Pigeon and Parrot
title.zh: 動物賽跑：鴿與鸚鵡

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山區

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 60b 'The Animal Race: Pigeon and Parrot' (told by Julia Gentle, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Courting the same girl — first into the house in the morning wins — slow-flying Parrot subcontracts a faster cousin: one goes ahead to sit in the tree by her door while the other follows Pigeon behind, answering every taunting call, until the Pigeon, believing Parrot has beaten him in the air, lands beaten outside a house where Parrot is already inside, married to the girl.
summary.zh: 二鳥同追一位姑娘——清早誰先進屋便嫁誰。慢飛的鸚鵡另雇一隻同族：一隻先去她門前樹上候著，一隻跟在鴿子身後應答挑釁之語，直到鴿子以為空中已敗，落在一座鸚鵡早已入內成婚的房子外面，只得留守門外。

sensitivity.note: Race-cycle variant. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Pigeon and Parrot were courting one girl, and she said whichever came first into the house in the morning she would marry. Parrot could not fly very fast; he made a bargain with another Parrot — one went before and left the other to follow Pigeon behind, and the first went near to the girl's house and sat down in a tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 60b (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 鴿子和鸚鵡同追一位姑娘，她說誰先在早晨飛進屋就嫁誰。鸚鵡飛不快，便跟另一隻鸚鵡立約——一隻先去，把那姑娘家的樹占了位，另一隻跟在鴿子後面，先頭那隻便在姑娘家附近的樹上落下。

passages.text: Pigeon called, 'Come on, me pretty Poll!' — and Parrot answered behind, 'Go on, me pretty Pigeon!' Pigeon sailed again and called again; Parrot answered again. When Pigeon nearly caught the house he called again in the same tune — and Parrot answered before him now. Pigeon said, 'Stop! all the while Parrot was behind; how has Parrot got before?' When Pigeon went to the house, Parrot was in the house; Pigeon had to stay outside, and Parrot married the girl.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 60b, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 鴿子喊「跟上啊，我漂亮的波莉！」——鸚鵡在後面應「飛吧，我漂亮的鴿子！」鴿子再飛再喊；鸚鵡再應。鴿子快飛到家門時又照原調喊——鸚鵡這回搶在他前頭應了。鴿子說：「慢著！鸚鵡明明一直在我後面；怎麼鸚鵡跑到我前頭了？」鴿子到屋子時，鸚鵡已在屋裏；鴿子只好留在屋外，鸚鵡娶了那位姑娘。

title.en: Man Is Stronger
title.zh: 人是更強者

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山區

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 62 'Man Is Stronger' (told by Simeon Falconer, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Tiger boasts no one beats their strength; Lion knows there is a little something called 'Man'. The hunter misfires on his first reconnaissance — Tiger flattens a ram-goat, mistaking horns for guns, his belly-scar for a ram-rod, the scrotum for a shot-bag — but the true Man answers Tiger's challenge with a single shot, blood flying all through his body, and Lion gets his 'I told you' over the carcass.
summary.zh: 老虎自誇無人敵得過獅虎之力；獅子深知有個叫『人』的小東西更強。初探時，虎錯把公羊當人——角當槍、腹疤當槍栓、陰囊當彈袋——一掌拍倒。真的人只以一槍應答，血透全身；獅子對著虎屍說：『早跟你說過，如今信了吧！』

sensitivity.note: Animal tale on human supremacy (cf. woodland tradition parallels). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: The Lion and the Tiger were very good friends. Tiger said, 'No one beats us in strength!' Lion said, 'No, my friend — somebody is stronger than we.' Tiger could not believe it; Lion said there was a little something called Man that was stronger. Tiger said he would have to find that something called Man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 62 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 獅子和老虎是極好的朋友。老虎說：「論力氣沒有誰勝得過我們！」獅子說：「不，我的朋友——有一個比我們更強的。」老虎不信；獅子說有一個叫「人」的小東西更強。老虎說他非要把那個叫人的東西找出來。

passages.text: He went hunting the Man and bucked up Mr. Ram-goat, asked if his name was Man — and whether the two things up here (the horns) were called gun, whether that long scar on his belly was called ram-rod, and whether that bag he had was called shot-bag. Goat said yes. Tiger walked up and licked him flat on the ground, and Goat hollered 'Wi-i! wi-i-i!' Tiger went back to Lion and said he had found something called Man and laid him dead with a single lick. Lion said, 'No, me friend! dat no Man — Man has two feet, and what you tell me has four legs.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 62, middle (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他去尋找人，撞上了山羊先生，問他是不是叫人——頭上那兩樣（角）是不是叫槍，肚子上那道長疤是不是叫推彈桿，那個袋子是不是叫火藥袋。山羊說是。老虎走上前把他一舔舔平在地上，山羊喊「危！危！」老虎回到獅子那裏，說他找到了叫人的東西，一舔就把他撂死了。獅子說：「不，我的朋友！那不是人——人有兩隻腳，而且

passages.text: He went out again seeking Man, and a Hunter was out. Tiger saw him — 'Now this yah must be Man!' — and as he went up to the man, the Hunter was aiming for him with the gun. Tiger asked if his name was Man, and the Hunter drove at him with the gun. He ran back to Lion and could only say, 'I find Man, and him single answer — him answer me, blood fly all through me body!' — and he died. Lion said, 'I tell you; you no believe me; but you believe me now!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 62, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他又出去找人，一個獵人正好在。老虎看見他——「這回這個一定是人了！」——他走向那人時，獵人正用槍瞄著他。老虎問他是不是叫人，獵人朝他開了槍。他跑回獅子那裏，只能說：「我找到了人，他單獨一個人就回答了我——他回答我，血從我全身飛出！」——說完就死了。獅子說：「我告訴過你；你不信我；現在信了吧！」

title.en: The Yellow Emperor Dreams of the Kingdom of Hua-hsü (Liezi)
title.zh: 黃帝夢遊華胥國（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: The kingdom of Hua-hsü, tens of thousands of miles away (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 華胥之國（夢中異域；象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: The Yellow Emperor, worn out by three months of fasting in heart after abandoning his schemes, dreams of the kingdom of Hua-hsü beyond the reach of ship or vehicle, where the people have no desires, feel neither joy in life nor abhorrence of death, and bestrode the air as though treading on solid earth. Waking on his throne, he knows the Perfect Way is not to be sought through the senses — and for twenty-eight years there was great orderliness in the Empire.
summary.zh: 黃帝晝寢而夢遊於華胥氏之國——其民無嗜慾，不知樂生，不知惡死；乘空如履實，寢虛若處牀。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the Hua-hsü dream is the classic Taoist utopia-vision, tagged otherworld-voyage for the dream-journey cluster. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: For three months he abstained from personal intervention in government. Then he fell asleep in the daytime, and dreamed that he made a journey to the kingdom of Hua-hsü, situated I know not how many tens of thousands of miles distant from the Ch'i State. It was beyond the reach of ship or vehicle or any mortal foot. Only the soul could travel so far.
passages.zh: 黃帝即位十有五年，喜天下之戴己，養正命，娛耳目，供鼻口，焦然肌色皯黣，昏然五情爽惑。又二十有八年，天下大治，幾若華胥氏之國。……晝寢而夢，遊於華胥氏之國。華胥氏之國在弇州之西，台州之北，不知斯齊國幾千萬里。蓋非舟車足力之所及，神遊而已。

passages.text: This kingdom was without head or ruler; it simply went on of itself. Its people were without desires or cravings; they simply followed their natural instincts. They felt neither joy in life nor abhorrence of death; thus they came to no untimely ends. They felt neither attachment to self nor indifference to others; thus they were exempt from love and hatred alike. They knew neither aversion from one course nor inclination to another; hence profit and loss existed not among them.
passages.zh: 其國無師長，自然而已。其民無嗜無欲，自然而已。不知樂生，不知惡死，故無夭殤；不知親己，不知疏物，故無愛憎；不知背逆，不知向順，故無利害：都無所愛惜，都無所畏忌。

passages.text: All were equally untouched by the emotions of love and sympathy, of jealousy and fear. Water had no power to drown them, nor fire to burn; cuts and blows caused them neither injury nor pain, scratching or tickling could not make them itch. They bestrode the air as though treading on solid earth; they were cradled in space as though resting in a bed. Clouds and mist obstructed not their vision, thunder-peals could not stun their ears, physical beauty disturbed not their hearts, mountains and valleys hindered not their steps. They moved about like gods.
passages.zh: 入水不溺，入火不熱。斫撻無傷痛，指擿無痟癢。乘空如履實，寢虛若處床。雲霧不硋其視，雷霆不亂其聽，美惡不滑其心，山谷不躓其步，神行而已。

passages.text: When the Yellow Emperor awoke from his dream, he summoned his three Ministers and told them what he had seen. ... Now I know that the Perfect Way is not to be sought through the senses. This Way I know and hold within me, yet I cannot impart it to you. For twenty-eight years after this, there was great orderliness in the Empire, nearly equalling that in the kingdom of Hua-hsü.
passages.zh: 黃帝既寤，怡然自得，召天老、力牧、太山稽，告之曰：「朕閒居三月，齋心服形，思有以養身治物之道，弗獲其術。……朕知至道之不可求於外矣。朕知之矣，朕得之矣，而不能以告若矣。」又二十有八年，天下大治，幾若華胥氏之國。

title.en: Riding Home on the Wings of the Wind: Lieh Tzŭ's Nine Years (Liezi)
title.zh: 列子御風而行，九年之後（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: Nan-kuo, Lieh Tzŭ's home in Chêng (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 南郭（今河南鄭州）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: Lieh Tzŭ, having mastered the system of Lao Shang and Po Kao Tzŭ, rides home on the wings of the wind. His nine-year apprenticeship passes from silence about right and wrong, through the Master's smile, to the seat beside him, until his mind was frozen, his body in dissolution, and he was borne this way and that on the wind like dry chaff or leaves falling from a tree — I knew not whether the wind was riding on me or I on the wind.
summary.zh: 列子師老商子，友伯高子，進二子之道，乘風而歸——九年之後：心凝形釋，骨肉都融；不知風乘我邪？我乘風乎？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the wind-riding motif paralleled in Zhuangzi ch. 1 (skipped to avoid duplication with the chinese record). Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Lieh Tzu had Lao Shang for his teacher, and Po Kao Tzu for his friend. When he had fully mastered the system of these two philosophers, he rode home again on the wings of the wind. At the end of nine years my mind gave free rein to its reflections, my mouth free passage to its speech. Of right and wrong, profit and loss, I had no knowledge, either as touching myself or others. I knew neither that the Master was my instructor, nor that the other man was my friend. Internal and External were blended into Unity. After that, there was no distinction between eye and ear, ear and nose, nose and mouth: all were the same. My mind was frozen, my body in dissolution, my flesh and bones all melted together.
passages.zh: 列子師老商氏，友伯高子；進二子之道，乘風而歸。……九年之後，橫心之所念，橫口之所言，亦不知我之是非利害歟，亦不知彼之是非利害歟，亦不知夫子之為我師、若人之為我友：內外進矣。……

passages.text: I was wholly unconscious of what my body was resting on, or what was under my feet. I was borne this way and that on the wind, like dry chaff or leaves falling from a tree. In fact, I knew not whether the wind was riding on me or I on the wind.
passages.zh: 心凝形釋，骨肉都融。不知形之所倚，足之所履，隨風東西，猶木葉干殼。竟不知風乘我邪？我乘風乎？

title.en: Shang Ch'iu K'ai Walks Through Fire for the Pearl (Liezi)
title.zh: 商丘開下地投水赴火（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: Tzŭ Hua's hall in Chin (Taiyuan, Shanxi, China)
region.zh: 晉國范氏之門（今山西太原）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: The starving old man Shang Ch'iu K'ai, jeered by a sorcerer's disciples, is tricked into leaping off a cliff — and is wafted down like a bird, not a bone hurt; into the river for the pearl — and comes up holding it; into a great fire — and returns with his garments unsoiled and his body unsinged. Secret I have none, he answers: my mind was simply One, and material objects thus offered no resistance.
summary.zh: 餓夫商丘開，為幻術之徒所弄；一躍而下，身若飛鳥；入水得珠，赴火不燎——吾心一也，外物不能梗。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; tagged faith-trial for the ordeal sequence (interpretive). Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: So, by way of a jest, they took the old man with them to the top of a cliff, and the word was passed round that whosoever dared to throw himself over would be rewarded with a hundred ounces of silver. There was an eager response, and Shang Ch'iu K'ai, in perfect good faith, was the first to leap over the edge. And lo! he was wafted down to earth like a bird on the wing, not a bone or muscle of his body being hurt. Mr. Fan's disciples, regarding this as a lucky chance, were merely surprised, but not yet moved to great wonder.
passages.zh: （范氏之黨）因謂之曰：「吾能為汝懸崖也。」眾皆駭然。商丘開先處黑而有怯色，眾指之曰：「能投茲崖者，賞以百金。」商丘開遂投之，飛鳥之翼若雲者，實無所傷。范氏之黨以為偶然，未肯謂之奇也。

passages.text: Then they pointed to a bend in the foaming river below, saying: "There is a precious pearl at the bottom of that river, which can be had for the diving." Shang Ch'iu K'ai again acted on their suggestion and plunged in. And when he came out, sure enough he held a pearl in his hand. Then, at last, the whole company began to suspect the truth, and Tzu Hua gave orders that an array of costly viands and silken raiment should be prepared; then suddenly a great fire was kindled round the pile. "If you can walk through the midst of these flames," he said, "you are welcome to keep what you can get of these embroidered stuffs." Without moving a muscle of his face, Shang Ch'iu K'ai walked straight into the fire, and came back again with his garments unsoiled and his body unsinged.
passages.zh: 又指其水曲曰：「彼水中有珠，泳之可取。」商丘開又從而泳之。既出，果得珠焉。眾防同疑，子華昉令昉食，衣文縑之衣，乘高軒。俄而范氏之藏大火。子華曰：「若能入火取錦者，從所得多少賞若。」商丘開往，無難色，入火往還，埃不漫，身不焦。

passages.text: "Secret I have none," replied Shang Ch'iu K'ai. "Even in my own mind I have no clue as to the real cause. ... I knew not what part of space my body occupied, nor yet where danger lurked. My mind was simply One, and material objects thus offered no resistance. That is all. But now, having discovered that your disciples were deceiving me, my inner man is thrown into a state of doubt and perplexity, while outwardly my senses of sight and hearing re-assert themselves. When I reflect that I have just had a providential escape from being drowned and burned to death, my heart within me freezes with horror, and my limbs tremble with fear. I shall never again have the courage to go near water or fire."
passages.zh: 商丘開曰：「吾亡道。雖吾之心，亦不知所以然而然。……昔以為眾人皆詐我，是以恐懼，恐懼之心存於中者未篤。今日知其不然也，恐慮釋然，是以無傷。……夫內外之情一，則水火不能害。」

title.en: The Tiger-Feeder Who Was Neither Antagonistic Nor Compliant (Liezi)
title.zh: 梁鴦養虎：不逆不順（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: King Hsüan's park-enclosure (symbolic pin: Xi'an, Shaanxi, China)
region.zh: 周宣王之囿（象徵定位：陝西西安）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: Liang Yang, skilled in the management of wild birds and beasts, feeds tigers and wolves, eagles and ospreys in King Hsüan's park without one clawing or biting another. His method: avoid giving live animals or whole carcasses, time their hunger and repletion, and be neither antagonistic nor compliant, so that the animals regard me as one of themselves.
summary.zh: 周宣王之牧正有役人梁鴦者，能養野禽獸——養虎之法：不逆其怒，不順其喜；虎可與遊者，必順其性也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; paralleled in Zhuangzi ch. 19 tiger-passage. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: The Keeper of Animals under King Hsüan, of the Chou dynasty, had an assistant named Liang Yang, who was skilled in the management of wild birds and beasts. When he fed them in their park-enclosure, all the animals showed themselves tame and tractable, although they comprised tigers, wolves, eagles and ospreys. Male and female freely propagated their kind, and their numbers multiplied. The different species lived promiscuously together, yet they never clawed nor bit one another.
passages.zh: 周宣王之牧正有役人梁鴦者，能養野禽獸，委食於園庭之內，雖虎狼鵰鶚之類，無不柔馴者。雄雌在前，孳尾成群；異類雜居，不相搏噬也。

passages.text: In feeding tigers, then, I avoid giving them either live animals or whole carcasses, lest in the former case the act of killing, in the latter the act of tearing them to pieces, should excite them to fury. Again, I time their periods of hunger and repletion, and I gain a full understanding of the causes of their anger. Tigers are of a different species from man, but, like him, they are docile with those who treat them kindly, though they will show fight when their lives are attacked.
passages.zh: （梁鴦曰）「夫食虎者，不敢以生物與之，為其殺之之怒也；不敢以全物與之，為其碎之之怒也。時其飢飽，達其怒心。虎之與異類殊，然亦順於養己者，逆其心則怒。……

passages.text: Hence it is my aim to be neither antagonistic nor compliant, so that the animals regard me as one of themselves. Thus it happens that they walk about the park without regretting the tall forests and the broad marshes, and rest in the enclosure without yearning for the lonely mountains and the dark valleys. Such is the effect of using one's common sense.
passages.zh: 吾所憎憎者，亦不敢逆其所憎憎，亦不敢順其所順。夫然後虎視眈眈，其心已矣；故不逆不順，使之若己。故游於園庭者，不念林澤之高廣；寢於檻者，不念巖谷之幽深：此顺適之理也。

title.en: The Sailor and the Sea-Gulls That Would Not Alight (Liezi)
title.zh: 海上之人好鷗鳥者（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: The sea-shore (symbolic pin: Yantai, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 海濱（象徵定位：山東煙臺）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: The sailor swam daily in the sea-gulls' midst, a hundred gulls and more flocking about him — until his father asked him to catch one or two for pets. The next day the gulls only wheeled about in the air and would not alight.
summary.zh: 海上之人有好漚鳥者，每旦之海上，從漚鳥遊；漚鳥之至者百住而不止。其父曰：吾聞漚鳥皆從汝遊，汝取來吾玩之。明日之海上，漚鳥舞而不下也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the 'birds dance but will not descend' (ou-wu-wu-hsia) became a proverb for self-conscious scheming. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: There was once a man, a sailor by profession, who was very fond of sea-gulls. Every morning he went into the sea and swam about in their midst, at which times a hundred gulls and more would constantly flock about him. One day his father said to him: "I am told that sea-gulls swim about with you in the water. I wish you would catch one or two for me to make pets of." On the following day, the sailor went down to the sea as usual, but lo! the gulls only wheeled about in the air and would not alight.
passages.zh: 海上之人有好鷗鳥者，每旦之海上，從鷗鳥遊，鷗鳥之至者百住而不止。其父曰：「吾聞鷗鳥皆從汝遊，汝取來，吾玩之。」明日之海上，鷗鳥舞而不下也。

title.en: The Man Who Came Out of the Rock and Walked Through Fire (Liezi)
title.zh: 趙襄子率徒狩山中，石中生人（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: The Central Mountains of Chao (Hengshan, Shanxi, China)
region.zh: 趙之中山（象徵定位：山西恆山）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: Hunting with a hundred thousand men in the Central Mountains, Chao Hsiang Tzŭ's party fire the forest, and a man appears, emerging from a rocky cliff to hover in the air amidst flames and smoke. What do you mean by rock? what do you mean by fire? he asks — I know nothing of them. Tzŭ Hsia tells Marquis Wên that the Master is able to do these things, but he is also able to refrain from doing them.
summary.zh: 趙襄子率徒十萬狩於中山，藉芿燔林——有一人從石壁中出，隨煙火上下，若無所傷。襄子曰：石？火？其人曰：不知也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; tagged faith-trial for the fire-ordeal. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Chao Hsiang Tzu led out a company of a hundred thousand men to hunt in the Central Mountains. They dropped sparks in the undergrowth, which set fire to the whole forest, and the glow of the flames was visible for a hundred miles around. Suddenly a man appeared, emerging from a rocky cliff, and was seen to hover in the air amidst the flames and the smoke. Everybody took him for a disembodied spirit. When the fire had passed, he walked quietly out, and showed no trace of having been through the ordeal.
passages.zh: 趙襄子率徒十萬狩於中山，藉芻燎林，扑火百世。有一人從石壁中出，隨煙燼上下，眾謂鬼物。火過，徐行而出，若經歷乎水火者也。

passages.text: So the prince inquired what secret power it was that enabled him to dwell in rock and to walk through fire. "What do you mean by rock?" replied the man; "what do you mean by fire?" "What you just now came out of is rock; what you just now walked through fire." "I know nothing of them," replied the man.
passages.zh: 襄子怪而留之，徐而察之，形色七竅，人也；氣音聲，人也；投石超距，亦人也。問之：「何道而能處石？何道而能入火？」其人曰：「奚物而謂石？奚物而謂火？」襄子曰：「嚮之所出者石也，嚮之所涉者火也。」其人曰：「不知也。」

passages.text: "From what I have heard the Master say," replied Tzu Hsia, "the man who achieves harmony with Tao enters into close unison with external objects, and none of them has the power to harm or hinder him. Passing through solid metal or stone, walking in the midst of fire or on the surface of water— all these things become possible to him." ... "The Master," replied Tzu Hsia, "is able to do these things, but he is also able to refrain from doing them." Which answer hugely delighted the Marquis.
passages.zh: （子夏答魏文侯曰）「吾聞之夫子：和於大道，則外物不傷。涉金石，蹈水火，皆可也。」……「夫子能之，而能不為者也。」魏文侯大說。

title.en: P'ao Hsi, Nü Kua, and Shên Nung with Serpents' Bodies (Liezi)
title.zh: 庖犧氏女媧氏神農氏，蛇身人面（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: The demi-gods of remote antiquity (symbolic pin: Tianshui, Gansu, China)
region.zh: 上古神人（象徵定位：甘肅天水）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: Outward form is no criterion: P'ao Hsi, Nü Kua, Shên Nung and Hsia Hou had serpents' bodies, human faces, ox-heads and tigers' snouts — their forms were not human, yet their virtue was of the saintliest; while Chieh and Chou, in all external respects like other men, had the minds of savage brutes.
summary.zh: 庖犧氏、女媧氏、神農氏、夏后氏，蛇身人面，牛首虎鼻——此有非人之狀，而有大聖之德。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the demi-god catalogue cross-linked to the chinese tradition's Nüwa records. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: P'ao Hsi, Nil Kua, Shen Nung and Hsia Hou had serpents' bodies, human faces, ox-heads and tigers' snouts. Thus, their forms were not human, yet their virtue was of the saintliest. Chieh of the Hsia dynasty, Chou of the Yin, Huan of the Lu State, and Mu of the Ch'u State, were in all external respects, as facial appearance and possession of the seven channels of sense, like unto other men; yet they had the minds of savage brutes.
passages.zh: 包犧氏、女媧氏、神農氏、夏后氏，蛇身人面，牛首虎鼻：此有非人之狀，而有大聖之德。夏桀、殷紂、魯桓、楚穆，狀貌七竅，皆同於人，而有禽獸之心。

title.en: The Yellow Emperor's Beast-Army and K'uei's Musical Stone (Liezi)
title.zh: 黃帝熊羆貔貅貙虎前驅，夔擊石拊石（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: The field of P'an-ch'üan (Banquan, Hebei/Shanxi, China)
region.zh: 阪泉之野（今河北／山西阪泉）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: When the Yellow Emperor fought with Yen Ti on the field of P'an-ch'üan, his vanguard was composed of bears, wolves, panthers, lynxes and tigers, his ensign-bearers eagles, ospreys, falcons and kites. And when K'uei tapped the musical stone in varying cadence, all the animals danced to the sound; the strains of the Shao on the flute brought the phœnix itself flying down to assist.
summary.zh: 黃帝與炎帝戰於阪泉之野，帥熊羆狼豹貙虎為前驅——堯使夔典樂，擊石拊石，百獸率舞；簫韶九成，鳳凰來儀。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the beast-army of the Yanhuang war, retold from Liezi. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: When the Yellow Emperor fought with Yen Ti on the field of P'an-ch'iian, his vanguard was composed of bears, wolves, panthers, lynxes and tigers, while his ensign-bearers were eagles, ospreys, falcons and kites. This was forcible impressment of animals into the service of man. The Emperor Yao entrusted K'uei with the regulation of music.
passages.zh: 黃帝與炎帝戰於阪泉之野，帥熊、羆、狼、豹、貙、虎為前驅，鵰、鶚、鷹、鳶為旗幟——此以力使禽獸者也。堯使夔典樂。

passages.text: When the latter tapped the musical stone in varying cadence, all the animals danced to the sound of the music. When the strains of the Shao were heard on the flute, the phœnix itself flew down to assist. This was the attraction of animals by the power of music. In what, then, do the minds of birds and beasts differ from the minds of men?
passages.zh: 擊石拊石，百獸率舞；簫韶九成，鳳凰來儀——此以聲致禽獸者也。然則禽獸之心，奚為異人？

title.en: Sarabha-miga-Jātaka (The Stag That Saved the King)
title.zh: 鹿王本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Benares and the royal hunting forest
region.zh: 波羅奈與王家獵林

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: A hunting king, mocked by his courtiers for missing a stag, chases it alone into the forest and falls into a sixty-cubit pit; the stag he hunted hauls him out without a thought of malice and teaches him the Five Virtues. When Sakka tests the king by tempting him to shoot the stag that appears at his target, the king refuses—'this very stag saved me from hopeless woe'—and Sakka reveals himself and blesses his mercy.
summary.zh: 王獵鹿不中，為群臣所笑，遂單身逐鹿入林，墮六十肘深坑；所逐之鹿不念舊惡，援王出坑，並教以五戒。後帝釋化樹靈試王，誘其射鹿，王言「此鹿嘗救我於絕境」，堅拒之；帝釋現身讚其仁而賜福。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living Buddhist tradition; freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: The Master told this in the Hall of Truth to show Sāriputta's wisdom, after the miracle at Sāvatthī where a mango stone planted at the city gate grew before the crowd's eyes into a tree a hundred cubits tall; the quarrelsome sectarians were confounded, and the Teacher, ascending to the Heaven of the Thirty-three for the rains, returned by a stairway of gems, silver and gold at Sankassa, and there, by a ladder of graded questions, made known before all men and gods the greatness of the Captain of the Faith. "This is not the first time," said he, "that Sāriputta answered at large a question briefly put." Of old, when Brahmadatta was king of Benares, the Bodhisatta lived in the forest as a stag; the king delighted in hunting and reckoned no other man worthy of the name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 483 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 導師在真諦殿中講此生，以彰顯舍利弗的智慧——那是在舍衛城的神變之後：一顆種在城門口的芒果核在眾人眼前長成百肘高樹，好辯的外道們啞口無言；導師上三十三天度雨安居，經由金銀寶石三重階梯於僧迦舍城降臨，以階梯般的層層提問，當著天人顯明教法之主的偉大。「這不是如來第一次顯現奇蹟——往昔他作為六牙之鹿也曾如此。」往昔梵授王統治波羅奈，菩薩生為一頭叫沙羅奔彌迦的金色奔鹿。

passages.text: One day in the hunt the king declared that whoever let a deer pass should be punished, and the courtiers, posting him at the end of a path, drove a great covert toward him. Our stag was first to be put up; seeing men in an unbroken ring on every side, he saw his only chance where the king stood, and rushed at him with eyes dazzling like flung sand. The king shot and missed—the deer are clever to dodge arrows—and the stag, swift as the wind, broke through the circle. The courtiers made sport of their king without stint: "He has hit the ground!" Stung by their mockery, the king girded up his loins and chased the stag on foot, sword in hand, for three leagues.
