The stag sniffed the smell of water in a sixty-cubit pit hidden under weeds and swerved aside; the king went straight on and fell in. Hearing no footsteps, the stag turned, saw his peril, and pitied rather than hated him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 483 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一天打獵，國王宣布放走一頭鹿者必受罰，臣子們把他安置在路徑的末端，把大片的樹林朝他驅趕。我們的鹿第一個被驅出；見四面人牆連成一環，他看出唯一的生路在國王站立的地方，便目光如擲沙般刺目地向國王衝去。國王射箭未中——鹿是躲箭的行家——那鹿快如疾風，破環而出。臣子們無情地取笑他們的國王，連連哀嘆與猛獸結盟的代價；獵手們追下去，看見鹿跳進了一個石坑。

passages.text: "Fear nothing, O king, for I will deliver you from your distress," cried the stag from the pit's edge, and with an effort as earnest as though he were saving his own beloved son he braced himself on the rock and hauled the king out of the deep pit, set him on his back, and carried him forth from the forest. There he admonished the king and established him in the Five Virtues; the king begged him to come to Benares and rule it, but the stag answered that he was one of the animals and wanted no kingdom—let the king keep the precepts he had taught, and teach them to his subjects. The king went home weeping to remember the stag's nobility, proclaimed by the drum of the Law that all the city should observe the five virtues, and at daybreak sat cross-legged and chanted his aspiration in six stanzas—"Hope on, O man, if thou be wise..." The chaplain, come thus early to enquire after the king's welfare, overheard the chant and deduced the whole adventure as clearly as a face in a polished mirror, and told it back to the astonished king, who gave him a rich present.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 483 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「大王，不要害怕，我要救你脫離苦難，」鹿在坑邊喊道，然後以救自己愛子一般的努力，撐著岩石把國王從深坑中拉了出來，讓他趴在自己背上，馱他出了森林。他在那裏勸誡國王，為他建立五戒；國王請他去波羅奈統治王國，鹿答道他是畜類，不欲王國——讓國王堅守正法就好。

passages.text: One day the king went into the park with the chaplain to shoot at a mark, and Sakka, perceiving how the king's virtue was filling heaven with new sons and daughters of the gods, resolved to try him. By his power he made the stag appear at the target, and entering the chaplain's body urged him: let fly the shaft, for the stag is meat for monarchs. "I am grateful for a service done, and therefore hold my hand from killing now," the king replied. Then Sakka threatened: kill it, a Titan, not a stag, and thou shalt be king of the gods; refuse, and thou and wife and children shall descend to death's cold river. "So be it," answered the king; "by my hand this stag shall not be slain. That very stag saved me from hopeless woe—how can I wish my benefactor dead?" Sakka left the chaplain's body and stood in the air in his own shape, blessing the true and faithful friend—"comfort with truth and goodness this domain, and thou shalt reign as Indra amid the gods"—then returned. Of that time Ananda was the king, Sariputta the chaplain, and the Master the stag.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 483 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一天國王與國師入園射靶；帝釋見國王的德行正使天界添滿新的兒女，決意試探他。他以神力使那鹿出現在靶前，又入國師之身催他放箭，說鹿肉正是王侯之食。「我受人恩惠，所以現在手不殺生，」國王答道。帝釋便威脅：殺了它，那不是鹿而是阿修羅，你就能保住王位——國王拒絕了，帝釋顯出真身，賜福於他，並預言那鹿將成佛。那鹿就是我。

title.en: Canda-Kinnara-Jātaka (The Kinnara Couple)
title.zh: 緊那羅本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Mountain of the Moon (Canda-pabbata) in the Himalaya (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 雪山月山（象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: The Bodhisatta, born a kinnara or woodland fairy, and his wife Canda live in loving song on the Mountain of the Moon. A king on a solitary hunting trip shoots the fairy out of lust for his wife; Canda curses the king, refuses his offer of queenship, and laments over her dying mate until her grief's power heats Sakka's throne, and the god, as a brahmin, heals the wound with heavenly water and bids the pair keep to their mountain.
summary.zh: 菩薩生為山林精靈緊那羅，與妻月女居月山，以歌相娛。王獨自狩獵，貪其妻之美，射傷緊那羅。月女咒詛王，拒其后位之誘，抱垂死之夫哀泣，悲慟之力熱帝釋座；帝釋化婆羅門以天水愈其傷，囑二神自此勿下山。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this in the palace of Rāhula's mother, praising her constancy: she had clothed herself in yellow at the news of his ordination, given up garlands, and refused the gifts of other kings. "Not now only, but even when born as an animal, she was faithful and mine alone." Of old, when Brahmadatta was king in Benares, the Great Being was born a fairy or kinnara in the Himalaya, and his wife was named Canda; the two dwelt together on a silver mountain called Canda-pabbata, the Mountain of the Moon. The king of Benares had committed his government to his ministers and gone alone into the Himalayas in yellow robes, armed with the five weapons. There the kinnaras came down for the hot season, crowned with flowers and clothed in flower-gauze, singing in honey voices.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 485 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 導師在羅睺羅母親的宮中講此生，讚歎她的堅貞：他出家消息傳來之日她便披上黃衣，捨棄花鬘，拒絕了別國國王的聘禮。「不只是如今，即便生為畜類時，她也是貞潔的、只屬於我的。」往昔梵授王統治波羅奈之時，菩薩生為喜馬拉雅山中一位緊那羅（樂神），妻子名叫旃陀；二人在一座銀山——月山——上比鄰而居。國王獵至山中，見他們

passages.text: On a sandy spot white as a silver plate they spread a couch of flowers, and the fairy played upon a piece of bamboo and sang while Canda waved her soft hands and danced beside him, singing too. The king caught the sound, stole close, and stood watching from a hiding place; he fell in love with the female fairy and resolved to shoot the husband and live there with the wife. He shot the fairy Canda, who lamented in four stanzas as his blood flowed and his breath went—yet each stanza turned not on his own pain but on his yearning for her sorrow. Lying upon his couch of flowers he lost consciousness; the king stood where he was. Canda, rapt in her own delight, did not know he was wounded till she saw the blood oozing from the wound's mouth; then, unable to bear the pain of sorrow, she cried out loud, and the king came out and showed himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 485 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在一片銀盤般潔白的沙地上，他們鋪了一張花床；樂神吹著一段竹管而歌，旃陀揮著柔軟的手在他身旁起舞，也唱著。國王聽見了歌聲，悄悄靠近，藏在暗處觀看；他愛上了那仙女，決意射殺她的丈夫，與她同住。他射中了樂神旃陀；樂神血流氣絕之際以四偈悲嘆——每一偈都不說自己的痛，只掛念妻子的去留。

passages.text: Thinking him the brigand who had slain her husband, she fled trembling to the hill-top and denounced the king in five stanzas, praying that the woe that wrung her heart be repaid upon his mother and his wife, who would mourn her lord and son for this deed done for lust. "Weep not nor grieve: the woodland dark has blinded you, I ween; a royal house shall honour thee, and thou shalt be my queen," the king answered. "No! I will surely slay myself! thine I will never be, who slew my husband innocent and all for lust of me," she roared like a lion; and his passion left him, and he let her go to the Himalaya. Then she came down, embraced the Great Being, carried him to the hill-top, and laid his head on her lap, making her moan in twelve stanzas over every hill and glen and flower that would see her no more; and taunting the gods for leaving a righteous world ungoverned, she so wrought on them that Sakka's throne grew hot with the power of her pain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 485 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她以為殺夫的正是強盜，戰慄著逃上山頂，以五偈譴責國王，祈願那撕裂她心的悲苦報在他的母親和妻子身上——她們將為這一樁因欲而起的惡行哀悼她們的主與子。「不要哭，不要悲傷：想必是幽暗的林子迷了你的眼；王家的殿宇將尊榮你，你當為我的王妃，」國王答道。「不！我必定自盡！你永遠得不到我——你無辜地殺了我的丈夫，只為欲樂！」

passages.text: Sakka, pondering, discovered the cause, and in the form of a brahmin approached with a water-pot and sprinkled the Great Being with water. On the instant the poison ceased to act, his colour returned, and he knew not so much as where the wound had been: the Great Being stood up quite well. Canda fell at the brahmin's feet and sang his praise for restoring her well-loved husband with the elixir of life; Sakka bade them go no more down from the Mountain of the Moon among the paths of men, and returned to his own place. And Canda said to her husband, "Why stay here in danger, my lord? come, let us go to the Mountain of the Moon, where the lovely rivers flow, all o'ergrown with flowers; there for ever, while the breeze whispers in a thousand trees, charm with talk the happy hours." The Master identified the Birth: Anuruddha was the king, Rāhula's mother was Canda, and the fairy was himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 485 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 帝釋思量其故，化作婆羅門，持水缽前來，以水灑在菩薩身上。毒立即失效，膚色復原，連傷口在哪裏都不知道了：菩薩好好站了起來。旃陀拜倒在婆羅門腳前，歌頌他以長生之藥救回她親愛的丈夫；帝釋命他們不要再從月山到人間來。

title.en: Dasabrahmana-Jātaka (The Ten Kinds of Brahmins)
title.zh: 十婆羅門本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Indapatta, capital of the Kuru kingdom, and Mount Nanda in the Himalaya (symbolic pin for the mountain)
region.zh: 俱盧國因陀羅波達城；雪山楠達山洞（山為象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: King Koravya's lavish almsgiving profits him nothing, for every recipient is wicked; his wise minister Vidhura catalogues ten kinds of men who are brahmins in name only—herb-sellers, bell-ringing servants, importunate beggars, wood-cutters, traders, cattle-dealers, sacrificers who slaughter, caravan guards, hunters, and scapegoats beneath the royal bed—and finds the only worthy recipients in five hundred Silent Buddhas of Mount Nanda, whom the king feasts for seven days.
summary.zh: 憍羅耶王廣行布施而無所得，蓋受者皆無德。賢臣毘提羅歷數十種徒有其名之婆羅門——賣藥者、鳴鈴僕役、強乞者、樵夫、商販、賣女者、殺生祭司、護商者、獵人、代王受垢者——並指唯有楠達山洞中五百獨覺佛堪受供養。王齋供七日，所施衣物隨之凌空而返。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this at Jetavana of a gift incomparable, given by the king of Kosala with discrimination to the holiest of the Brethren; "wise men of old, ere yet the Buddha had arisen, even they gave with discrimination." Of old, in the kingdom of Kuru and the city of Indapatta, reigned king Koravya, whose adviser in things temporal and spiritual was the wise Vidhura. The king's great almsgiving set all India in commotion, yet among all who received and enjoyed his gifts not one kept so much as the Five Virtues—all were wicked to a man—and the king's giving brought him no satisfaction. Desiring to give to the virtuous, he took counsel with Vidhura: seek me brahmins good, in whom much wisdom lies, men free from deeds of evil lust, that they may eat my food.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 495 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 導師在祇園說起憍薩羅王以分別之心、把無與倫比的供養施給最聖潔的比丘——「古人甚至在佛陀出世之前，便已能分別而行布施。」往昔俱盧國因陀波吒城中，科羅比耶王在位，他世俗與宗教兩方面的顧問是智慧的智尊。國王的布施震動了全印度，然而受享其供養者之中沒有一個真正值得的。

passages.text: "'Tis hard to find such holy men," answered Vidhura, and in question and answer with the king he distinguished ten kinds who are brahmins in name only: some carry sacks of healing herbs, bathe, and recite magic spells—physician-like; some ring bells before the king and drive his chariot—servant-like; some with waterpot and crooked staff follow towns crying for gifts—importunate as tax-men; some, long-nailed and dirty, hew wood—mere hewers; some traffic in fruit and honey—merchants; some follow trade and sell their daughters in marriage—like Vessa; some as chaplains tell fortunes and slaughter many beasts at village invitations—like butchers; some stand armed with sword and shield before merchants' caravans—like bandits; some trap fish and hare in woodland huts—hunters; and some lie beneath the royal bed at the soma-sacrifice to catch the washing of the king's sins—like barbers. "These have no right to such a name: lost is their brahminhood," said the king to each in turn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 495 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「這樣的聖者難得，」智尊答道，並與國王一問一答，區分十種徒有婆羅門之名者：有的扛著藥囊，沐浴誦咒，如醫師；有的為國王鳴鑼駕車，如僕役；有的持水罐與曲杖沿街乞施，如催租人；有的留長甲、骯髒不堪地劈柴，只是樵夫；有的販賣果實與蜂蜜——如商販。

passages.text: But there are brahmins, too, said Vidhura, men very wise and good, free from the deeds of evil lust, who eat one meal of rice and never touch strong drink—they dwell in the further Himalaya, in a cave of Mount Nanda. Then Vidhura bade the king proclaim through the city that all should adorn it, give alms, keep the holy-day vows, and pledge themselves to virtue; and himself, taking the vows, cast eight handfuls of flowers into the air, calling to mind the virtues of the Silent Buddhas: let the five hundred Pacceka Buddhas of the cave of Mount Nanda to-morrow partake of our food. The flowers fell upon them in their far dwelling; they understood, judged Vidhura no mean creature—one having the seed of a Buddha within him, to be a Buddha in this very cycle—and accepted the invitation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 495 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但也有真正的婆羅門，智尊說，那些極其賢明善良、遠離邪淫之行、日食一餐、滴酒不沾的人——他們住在極遠的喜馬拉雅山中，難陀山的洞裏。於是智尊請國王向全城宣告：人人妝點都城，廣行布施，受持齋願，自誓於戒；他自己也受持諸願，向空中拋撒八把花，憶念靜默諸佛之德。

passages.text: Next day they flew through the air from Lake Anotatta and descended in the royal courtyard; the king and Vidhura received their bowls, seated them on the terrace, gave them the gift-water, and served them with delightful food for seven days, presenting many gifts; on the seventh day he gave them all the requisites, and they gave thanks and flew back to their cave, the requisites going with them. Of that time Ananda was the king, and the wise Vidhura was the Master himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 495 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 次日他們自阿耨達池凌空而來，降落在王庭；國王與智尊接了缽，請他們坐在露台上，獻上施水，七天以美味飲食供養，獻上許多禮物；第七天他把一切資具盡數奉上，他們致謝後凌空飛回洞中，資具隨行。那時的阿難即國王，智慧的智尊即導師本人。

title.en: Haṃsa-Jātaka (The Golden Goose and the Faithful Friend)
title.zh: 天鵝本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Benares and Mount Cittakūṭa (symbolic pin for the mountain)
region.zh: 波羅奈與質多羅山（山為象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: Queen Khema dreams of hearing a Golden Goose preach the Law, and the king builds a lake to snare one; the goose-king Dhatarattha is caught, and his captain Sumukha, though free, returns to share his prisoner's fate, 'I'll not leave you... will either live or die.' The moved hunter frees and heals the royal bird, and the goose preaches all night to the king until the queen's craving is appeased, then flies home.
summary.zh: 吉祥王后夢聞金鵝說法，王遂鑿湖設網捕鵝。鵝王法螺賢落網，其部屬善友雖可脫身仍返相伴，誓同生共死。獵人感動，縱之療傷；鵝王入宮為王說法通宵，王后願足，雙鵝飛還山中。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this in the Bamboo Grove of Elder Ananda's renunciation of his life for the Teacher's sake—"not the first time." Of old, in Benares reigned a king named Bahuputtaka, Father of Many Sons, and his queen consort was Khema. The Great Being then dwelt on Mount Cittakūṭa, chief of ninety thousand wild geese, come to life as a golden goose. The queen dreamed a dream and told the king she had conceived a woman's craving to hear a Golden Goose discourse of the Law; told that such creatures lived on Cittakūṭa, the king made a lake which he called Khema, planted it with all manner of food-corn, had immunity proclaimed daily in the four quarters, and sent a hunter to catch the geese. In a snare set among the crops the Great Being was caught; the goose flock fled in three divisions, but Sumukha their chief captain, missing his king, came back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 502 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 導師在竹林精舍說起阿難長老為導師捨身之事——「這不是第一次。」往昔波羅奈有一位王，名叫多子王，王后是基瑪。菩薩那時住在支提山，是九萬雁群的王，身為金色之鵝。王后做了一個夢，告訴國王她懷了女人聽金色之鵝說法的癡念；國王

passages.text: Hanging in the noose, the goose-king tested his friend: "There go the birds, the ruddy geese, all overcome with fear: O golden-yellow Sumukha, depart! what want you here? ... Fly, noble bird! with prisoners no fellowship can be." "No, I'll not leave you, Royal Goose, when trouble draweth nigh: but stay I will, and by your side will either live or die," Sumukha answered, sitting on the mud. "'Twas but to put you to the test I bade you fly away," said the king of the geese. Up came the huntsman at top speed; Sumukha flew to meet him and declared the virtues of the royal bird, and the hunter's heart was softened. Asked how the birds, treading unfooted ways, had failed to spy the snare, the Great Being answered, "When life is coming to an end, and death's hour draws anigh, though you may close upon it come, nor trap nor snare you spy." Asked why, though free, he stayed with a prisoner, Sumukha said, "He is my comrade, friend, and king, dear as my life is he: forsake him—no, I never will, until death calls for me."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 502 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 懸在套索中的鵝王試探他的朋友：「你看那些鳥，赤鵝們，都嚇破了膽：金色的善容啊，走吧！你在這裏做什麼？……飛吧，高貴的鳥！囚徒沒有伴侶。」「不，我不丟下你，鵝王，當災禍臨頭之時：我要留下，與你同生共死，」善容答道，坐在泥中。「我不過是試探你，才叫你飛走，」雁王說。

passages.text: The hunter thought that if he harmed such virtuous creatures the earth would gape and swallow him—what care he for the king's reward?—and set them free, drawing the royal bird from the stick, washing the blood from him, and setting the dislocated sinews, so that by the Great Being's perfections the foot became whole on the instant and not a mark showed. The goose-king chose rather to go to the town: the hunter would be rewarded, the queen's craving appeased, Sumukha's friendship made known, and by his wisdom he should receive the lake Khema as a free gift. So the hunter carried them on his carrying-pole to the king, who placed both geese on a golden perch, fed them with honey and fried grain, and held out his hands, praying them to speak of the Law. The goose catechised the king on his health, wealth, righteous rule, unblemished court, far-off foes, queen, and sons—"sons I have of fame, five score and one; tell them their duty: they'll not leave your good advice undone"—and then admonished him in five stanzas.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 502 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 獵人心想，若傷害這樣有德的生靈，大地會裂開把他吞了——他哪在乎國王的賞賜？——便放了他們，把雁王從棍子上解下，洗去血跡，把脫臼的筋復位，憑菩薩的波羅蜜，那隻腳頃刻復原，不留一痕。鵝王寧願進城：獵人得賞，王后的癡念得慰，善容的友誼得全。

passages.text: "He that puts off until too late the effort to do good, though nobly bred, with virtue dowered, yet sinks beneath the flood; his knowledge fades... as one moonblind at night sees all things swollen twice their size with his imperfect sight. Who sees the truth in falsity no wisdom gains at all, as on a rugged mountain-path the deer will often fall. If any strong courageous man loves virtue, follows right, though but a low-born churl, he burns like bonfires in the night. By using this similitude all wisdom's truths explain: cherish your sons till wise they grow, like seedlings in the rain." So the Great Being discoursed to the king the livelong night; the queen's craving was appeased, and by sunrise, having established the king in the virtues of kings and exhorted him to vigilance, the goose flew out of the northern window with Sumukha and away to Cittakūṭa. The Master identified the Birth: the huntsman was Channa, Sāriputta the king, Ānanda was Sumukha, and he himself was the Goose King.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 502 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「遲遲不肯行善的人，縱然出身高貴、德性具足，終將沉於洪流；他的智慧消逝……如夜盲者看什麼都漲大兩倍。把假當真的人得不到智慧，如鹿在崎嶇山路上常常跌倒。若有勇毅之人愛德行正，縱然出身低微，也如黑夜中的火炬。」

title.en: Aḷambusā-Jātaka (The Nymph and the Young Ascetic)
title.zh: 阿蘭浮沙天女本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Himalaya hermitage and Indra's heaven (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 雪山精舍與天界（象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: The ascetic Isisinga, born of a doe that drank water mixed with a brahmin's seed, is warned by his dying father against women, yet the sheer power of his austerity so heats Sakka's throne that the god sends the nymph Aḷambusā to break his virtue. Her praise-song lures him to seize her in flight, and he lies lost in her arms three years; waking, he laments his broken vows, resumes his meditation, forgives her, and she begs a boon never to tempt a saint again.
summary.zh: 獨覺之子伊 西 行伽 乃母鹿飲仙人之水而孕所生；父臨終誡勿近女色，然其苦行威德熱帝釋座，神遣天女阿蘭浮沙誘之。天女讚歌相誘、佯逃相引，仙人執其髮而失定，沉眠其懷三年。醒後慟悔，重入禪定，赦其罪；天女求得「永不誘聖者」之願。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka paralleling the Rishyasringa episode of the Hindu Ramayana and the Barlaam-and-Josaphat tradition; retold freely as scripture of a living tradition; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this of a Brother tempted to discontent by the wife of his unregenerate days—owing to her, said the Master, he once fell from mystic meditation and lay three years lost and distracted. Of old, in the reign of Brahmadatta in Benares, a doe ate grass and drank water mingled with a brahmin ascetic's seed, became enamoured, and bore him a man child, Isisinga, whom the ascetic reared with a father's affection, admitted to holy orders, and warned: "In this Himalaya country are women as fair as these flowers: they bring utter destruction on all that fall into their power." Soon after he was destined for the Brahma world; but the son, indulging in mystic meditation with all his senses mortified, became an ascetic so severe that the abode of Sakka was shaken, and Sakka, fearing to be displaced, searched the twenty-five millions of his handmaids for one equal to the task of breaking the saint's virtue, and found none but Aḷambusā.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 523 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 導師說起一位被前妻動搖了道心的比丘——因她，導師說，他曾在禪定中墮落，三年迷失恍惚。往昔梵授王統治波羅奈時，一隻母鹿吃了摻著婆羅門苦行者精種的水草，動了情，生下一個男嬰，名叫獨角仙人；苦行者以父愛撫育他，為他授戒，並警告他：「在這喜馬拉雅山中，女人是極可怕的，

passages.text: "Go, Temptress, ever dog his steps, for holy sage is he, and, seeking ever highest bliss, still triumphs over me," said Sakka; Aḷambusā asked why she alone of all the nymphs of Nandana, and feared the hell that waits on wrongs to saints, yet went at the god's behest. At break of day, before the sun was astir, she drew near to Isisinga as he swept out his cell. The ascetic questioned her—"Who art thou, like to lightning flash, or bright as morning star?"—and sang her praises from head to foot: slender waist, eyes like guñja berries, teeth like pearls, the triple line on her neck. While he spoke she was silent, and reading how disturbed his state of mind had grown, she answered, "Heaven bless thee, Kassapa, my friend, the time is past and gone for idle questions such as these—for are we not alone?—come let us in thy hermitage embracing haste to prove the thousand joys well known to all the votaries of love."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 523 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「去吧，誘惑者，緊跟他的腳步；他是聖哲，常求至高的福樂，總是勝過我，」帝釋說；阿蘭婆薩問為何偏是她，天女千萬為何獨選她，並害怕冒犯聖者要墮地獄，卻還是奉命前往。天將破曉、太陽未起之時，她走近正在打掃僧房的獨角仙人。苦行者問她——「你是誰，像閃電，像晨星？」——以偈讚歎她

passages.text: Then, with a woman's cunning, she made as if to run away; the ascetic cried "She is off," intercepted her with motion swift as air, and seized her by the hair. Just where he stood the lovely maid embraced him in her arms, and his virtue fell before the magic of her charms; in thought she flew to Indra's throne in Nandana afar, and the god sent a golden car with trappings spread. There the saint lay in her arms for many a long day: three years passed over his head as though it were a moment's space. At last he woke, saw the green trees and the cuckoo-crying groves, and wept bitterly: "I make no offering, raise no hymn; no sacrifice is here. Who can my tempter be, who by foul practice has overcome all sense of right in me, even as a ship with precious freight is swallowed in the sea?" Told that she was sent by king Sakka, he called to mind his father's warning—"Women are fair as lotus flower; beware, good youth, their subtle power"—and lamented that he had let his wise old father's words pass unheeded.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 523 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她便使出女人的狡計，假裝要跑；苦行者喊「她逃了」，以疾如風的身法攔住她，抓住她的頭髮。就在他站立之處，那可愛的少女把他擁入懷中；他的戒行在妖媚之前瓦解了；她心思一動便飛到了遠方難陀那園帝釋的寶座，天神遣來一輛裝飾華美的金車。聖者便在她懷中過了許多漫長的日子：三年如一轉瞬。

passages.text: "Accursed be the life of old: henceforth I'll do as I am told; far better death itself to face, than be again in such a case." So he forsook sensual desire and entered upon mystic meditation; and Aḷambusā, seeing his steadfast power and courage return, became terrified and asked his forgiveness, kneeling to embrace his feet: "A mighty work I wrought, when heaven itself and gods of fame trembled with fear to hear thy name." "I pardon thee, fair lady; go, as thou wilt," he said, blessing the Thirty-three and her; and saluting him, she mounted the golden car and sped away like blazing torch or lightning flash. Sakka, glad at heart, cried "No boon can I deny," and Aḷambusā asked but this: "Let me ne'er tempt a saint again to violate his vow." Of that time the nymph was the Brother's former wife, Isisinga the backsliding Brother, and the great saint his father the Master himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 523 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「衰老的生命該詛咒：從今我聽命而行；寧可直面死亡，不再落入這樣的境地。」於是他捨棄情欲，重新入定；阿蘭婆薩見他的定力與勇氣復原，大為恐懼，跪抱其足求恕：「我成就了一件大事，連天界與諸天聽見你的名字也發抖。」「我饒恕你，美人；去吧，隨你意，」他說。

title.en: Saṅkhapāla-Jātaka (The Serpent King's Fast)
title.zh: 海螺龍王本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Rajagaha in Magadha; river Kannapennā and the naga palace
region.zh: 摩竭陀王舍城；迦那奔那河與龍宮

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: Prince Duyyodhana of Magadha, coveting the glory of the naga king Saṅkhapāla who visits his ascetic father, gives alms and keeps the holy days until reborn as a serpent king—then, finding the naga world no place for purity, keeps fast-days on an ant-heap, offering his body to all comers. Sixteen hunters stake and drag him; the landowner Āḷāra buys him free, is rewarded with a year in the naga palace, and returns to preach the vanity of desires to the king of Benares.
summary.zh: 摩竭陀王子睹龍王榮耀而生欣羨，廣行布施、持齋布薩，感生龍界為王；然悟龍身非清淨之地，遂於蟻垤持齋，自許其身任人取用。十六獵人戳刺拖曳；地主阿羅以牛與金贖之，獲龍宮一年之報，歸而向波羅奈王宣說欲之無常。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master, expressing approval of lay folk who kept holy days, told them that wise men of old gave up the great glory of the Naga world to observe those vows. Of old, a king of Magadha reigned in Rajagaha, and the Bodhisatta, born as prince Duyyodhana, was installed in the kingdom while his father took up the religious life in the park. Thrice daily the son visited the father, whose honor and profit thus grew so great that the old king could not even prepare for mystic meditation, and stole away without a word beyond the borders, to a hut by Mount Candaka at the bend of the river Kannapennā, where it issues from lake Saṅkhapāla. There the naga king Saṅkhapāla, issuing from the river with his company, would visit the ascetic and hear the Law. The son, seeking his father, came upon the serpent's departing magnificence and conceived a longing for the Naga world; ever after he kept the moral law and the holy days, gave alms at the four gates, and at his death was reborn in the Naga world as king Saṅkhapāla.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 524 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 導師稱許在家持齋的人，告訴他們古人曾捨棄龍界的大榮華來守持這些誓願。往昔一位摩揭陀王在王舍城為王，菩薩生為太子婆藪耶丹那，被立為國，父親退居林苑修行。兒子一日三次探望父親，父親的名望與利養因此大到無法安坐禪修。

passages.text: In time he grew sick of that magnificence and longed to be born as a man, for dwelling in the Naga world his observance of the holy days was not a success and he deteriorated in morals. Leaving the Naga world he coiled round an ant-hill between the high road and a narrow path, resolved to keep the holy day, saying, "Let those that want my skin or want my skin and flesh, let them, I say, take it all," and lay there on the fourteenth and fifteenth of the half-month, returning to the palace on the first day of each fortnight. One day sixteen men of a neighboring village, hunting in vain for flesh, saw him and resolved to kill and eat the snake-king; fearing his size, they took stakes, and the Bodhisatta made his body big as a trough-shaped canoe, beautiful as a jasmine wreath, and tucked his head into his hood, resolved that when they struck him he would not open his eyes or regard them with anger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 524 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久他厭倦了那榮華，渴望生為人身，因為住在龍界他的齋戒不得圓滿，德行也退失了。他離開龍界，盤繞在大路與小徑之間的一座蟻丘上，決意守齋，說「凡想要我的皮、想要我的皮肉者，儘管全拿去」，在半月的十四、十五兩日臥在那裏，

passages.text: They seized him by the tail, dragged him, wounded him in eight places with sharp stakes and thrust black bamboo sticks, thorns and all, into the open wounds; strung him by cords through eight piercings; and when his head drooped, pierced his nostrils with a slender stake and raised his head by a cord. Never once from the moment of the first wound did he open his eyes or look on them with anger. Then Āḷāra, a landowner of Mithila journeying with five hundred wagons, gave all sixteen an ox apiece, a handful of golden coins, garments, and ornaments for their wives, and so got them to release him. The Bodhisatta returned to the Naga palace, issued forth with a great retinue, took Āḷāra with him, and for a whole year satisfied him with heavenly delights, three hundred naga maidens serving, until Āḷāra asked instead for the requisites of the ascetic life and departed to the Himalaya.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 524 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們抓住他的尾巴拖拽，以尖樁在八處戳傷他，把黑竹籤連刺帶扎釘進創口；以繩穿過八處穿孔把他吊起；他一垂頭，便以細簽刺其鼻孔、用繩把頭吊起。從第一處創傷起，他一次也沒有睜眼，一次也沒有以怒目視他們。後來彌提羅一位率五百車出行的地主阿羅邏傾其所有

passages.text: In time the ascetic came to Benares and lodged in the king's park; charmed, the king asked why one of such noble presence had renounced earth's joys. Alara told him how on a trading venture he had met the captured snake, bought him with oxen and gold, and been led to a dwelling of gold and gems thronged with nymphs; and how the serpent-king, questioned, confessed that the mansion was owed to his own good actions as king Duyyodhana of Magadha—he supplied meat and drink religiously, and made his house an inn where sages refreshed themselves—and that he had suffered hurt on the holy days by no overmastering dread but in the cause of goodness, whose bounds like the seashore are never transgressed: "Nowhere but in the world of men, I ween, may purity and self-restraint be seen: if only once midst men I draw my breath, I'll put an end to further birth and death." The king vowed to perform all deeds of piety; the ascetic passed to the Brahma heaven, and the Master identified the Birth: the father-ascetic was Kassapa, the king of Benares was Ananda, Alara was Sariputta, and Sankhapala was himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 524 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 苦行者後來來到波羅奈，住在王家的園林；國王為之傾倒，問這樣尊貴的人為何捨棄世間之樂。阿羅邏告訴他，自己經商途中遇見被捉的蛇，以牛與黃金贖了他，被引到一座天女環繞的金寶之宮；龍王被問起時，坦承那宮殿歸功於他作摩揭陀王婆藪耶丹那時的善行——他供養飲食、守持正法。

title.en: Cūḷa-Sutasoma-Jātaka (The Grey Hair)
title.zh: 小蘇達沙摩本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Sudassana city (the Benares of that birth) and the Himalaya hermitage
region.zh: 須達沙城（彼世之波羅奈）與雪山精舍

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: King Sutasoma, whose face is glorious as the full moon, orders his barber to tell him when a grey hair appears—and on receiving that single grey hair renounces his vast kingdom over the wailing of his mother, father, seven hundred wives and his pregnant queen. He bribes the nurse to take his clinging seven-year-old son away, cuts his top-knot on the Palace of Flowers before the people, and leads a company covering twelve leagues to a hermitage built for him by Sakka's command.
summary.zh: 蘇達沙王面如滿月，命理髮師見白髮即告；得一莖白髮遂捨大國。母、父、七百妃與懷孕王后皆泣勸不果，並賄乳母抱走其七歲稚子；於花宮頂當眾斷髮髻，率十二由旬之眾往帝釋所命營建之精舍。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this concerning the perfect exercise of self-abnegation. Of old, what is now Benares was a city called Sudassana, and king Brahmadatta's chief consort bore the Bodhisatta, whose face was glorious as the full moon, so that he was named Somakumāra, and from his fondness for soma juice, Sutasoma. Educated at Taxila, he ruled a vast dominion with sixteen thousand wives, Candadevī at their head, and a numerous family. But he grew discontented with domestic life and told his barber, "When you see a grey hair on my head, you are to tell me." In time the barber, with golden tweezers, laid a grey hair in his hand. "My body is a prey to old age," cried the king, and descending from the terrace he seated himself on a throne before the people, summoned his eighty thousand councillors and sixty thousand brahmins, and announced, "A grey hair has appeared on my head; I am an old man, and you are to know that I am become an ascetic."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 525 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 導師說起捨身的圓滿修行。往昔今日的波羅奈曾是一座名叫善見的城，梵授王的正妃生下菩薩，容顏如滿月般光輝，取名蘇摩童子；因他喜飲蘇摩汁，人稱須陀須摩。他在呾叉始羅受業，統治廣大的疆土，有一萬六千位王妃，以旃陀提毗為首，家族繁盛。但他漸生厭離之心，

passages.text: Each counsellor felt the arrow quiver in his heart: remember thy seven hundred wives, O king—what will become of them? "Their sorrows soon another will console, for they are young in years and fair to see; but I am bent upon a heavenly goal." His mother came in hot haste lamenting the day that hailed her mother of such a son; his father asked what Law led him to quit kingdom and home with old parents left alone; and he, for answer, showed them the Law and held his peace. His seven hundred wives threw themselves at his feet weeping that his heart must break or pity unknown; "My heart in sorrow may not break, though I feel pity for your pain, but holy orders I must take, that I may heavenly bliss attain." His queen consort, heavy with child and near her time, begged him stay till the babe was born; "The hour of thy delivery is nigh; until the babe is born, I'll stay with thee; then will I leave the royal imp and fly far from the world a holy monk to be."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 525 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 每位大臣都覺得那支箭扎在自己心裏：大王，還有你的七百位妻子——她們怎麼辦？「她們的悲傷自有別人安慰，她們年輕貌美；我的心卻繫於天界之目標。」他的母親聞訊趕來，哭喊那個立她為如此之子之母的日子；他的父親問什麼樣的法讓他拋下王國與家、留下年邁的雙親；他以法相答，默然無言。

passages.text: His elder son asked whom he must impiously slay for his mother's tears; but the younger, seven years old, comforted them both, and coming down from the tower clasped his father by the neck: "I too will hold thee by the hand, nor let thee go against our will." "This child is a source of danger to me," thought the Bodhisatta, and looking at the nurse, "Good nurse, behold this jewel ornament: this is yours: only take away the child, that he be not a hindrance to me." She took the bribe and led the boy away. His commander offered the subdued world; the rich merchant Kulavaddhana offered wealth beyond reckoning; his brother Somadatta begged to follow him into the hermit's cell, and was refused. "Like water through a sieve, our day so brief alas! fast slips away," the Great Being taught the weeping people, and then, on the topmost storey of the Palace of Flowers, cut off his top-knot with a sword and cried, "I am now nothing to you; choose ye a king of your own," casting turban and all into the crowd, who rolled on the ground in lamentation under the rising dust-cloud.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 525 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 長子問自己該不孝順地殺誰來止住母親的眼淚；七歲的幼子卻安慰了他們兩人，從塔上走下來摟住父親的脖子：「我也要拉住你的手，不讓你違著我們的心意走。」「這孩子是我的障礙，」菩薩心想，看向乳母，「好乳母，看這寶石瓔珞：歸你了；只求你把孩子帶走，別讓他攔我。」她把孩子

passages.text: A barber shaved his hair and beard; he fastened an earthen bowl on his shoulder, took the mendicant's staff, and stepped out into the street unrecognised; his wives found only the bundle of his adornments, and the city cried, "King Sutasoma, sad to tell, has left his throne for hermit cell, and, clad in yellow, goes his way like some lone elephant astray." The people followed him and the whole city emptied, until the company covered twelve leagues. Sakka ordered Vissakamma to build a hermitage thirty leagues long and five broad; the Great Being entered by the path, was first ordained, admitted the rest to orders until a space of thirty leagues was filled, and if any false thought arose in any mind he would come through the air and admonish them: "Call not to mind love's sports of yore... indulge without or stint or stay good will to men by night and day, so shall ye win the angel home." The saints abiding by his admonition were destined to the Brahma world; the elder son was Sariputta, the younger Rahula, prince Somadatta was Ananda, and king Sutasoma was the Master.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 525 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 理髮匠剃了他的鬚髮；他把陶缽繫在肩上，拿起乞食之杖，走到街上無人認出；妻子們只找到他妝飾的包袱，全城哭喊「須陀須摩王，悲哀啊，捨了王座入草庵，披著黃衣去了，像迷途的孤象」。民眾跟隨他，全城走空，隊伍綿延十二由旬。帝釋命毗首羯磨

title.en: Nalinikā-Jātaka (The Princess in Ascetic's Dress)
title.zh: 天女誘仙本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Benares and the Himalaya hermitage
region.zh: 波羅奈與雪山精舍

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: Sakka stops the rain for three years to break the austere virtue of the young ascetic Isisinga, and tells the starving king of Benares that only his daughter Nalinikā can do it. Sent into the forest with ministers and elephants, the princess disguises herself as an ascetic youth playing with a ball that always returns to her hand, seduces the innocent boy, and slips away before his father returns; the rain falls that very day, and the father's rebuke restores his son's meditation.
summary.zh: 帝釋為破伊 西 行伽 少年仙人之淨行而止雨三年，語飢困之波羅奈王：唯王女娜律尼迦能成此事。公主隨眾入山，偽裝仙人少年，弄一手擲必回之球誘惑天真的小仙人，旋即遁去；當日雨降。父歸斥其為妖變所惑，其禪定復得。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this of a Brother tempted by the wife of his unregenerate days—of old it was owing to her that he fell from mystic meditation and was mightily destroyed. Of old, a brahmin of the North, trained in all the arts, became an ascetic in the Himalayas; exactly as in the Aḷambusā Birth a doe conceived by him and brought forth a son called Isisinga. His father admitted him to holy orders, had him instructed in the rites inducing mystic meditation, and the youth soon enjoyed the bliss of ecstasy, an ascetic of such severe austerity that the abode of Sakka was shaken. Sakka discovered the cause, and for three years stopped the rain over the kingdom of Kāsi: the country was scorched, no crops came to perfection, and the people gathered in the palace yard to reproach the king, who, though he took the moral vows and fasted, could bring down no rain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 526 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 導師說起一位被前妻動搖的比丘——往昔正是因她，他在禪定中墮落，受到大損。往昔北方一位通曉諸藝的婆羅門在喜馬拉雅山出家苦行；正如阿蘭婆薩本生那樣，一隻母鹿感其精而孕，生下名叫獨角的兒子。父親為他授戒，教他引發禪定的儀軌，少年很快證得

passages.text: At midnight Sakka stood in mid-air in the illuminated royal chamber and told the king that in the Himalaya dwelt the ascetic Isisinga, who constantly, when it began to rain, looked up at the sky in a rage, and so the rain ceased. "Should his virtue be broken down, it will rain." "But who is able to overcome his virtue?" "Your daughter, Sire, Nalinikā can do it." Though these were things not to be spoken of in words, the king, for the protection of his realm, talked with his daughter and sent her away with his ministers, elephants and footmen. Pitching camp at the frontier, they had the princess conveyed by foresters' paths to the edge of the hermitage; and while the Bodhisatta was gone into the forest for wild fruits, they surrounded the cloister, disguised the princess as an ascetic youth in a beautiful bark garment with all manner of ornaments, and sent her in playing with a painted ball tied to a string, while they stood on guard without.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 526 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 午夜，帝釋立在放光的王寢上空，告訴國王喜馬拉雅山中住著獨角仙人，每逢下雨他便對天發怒，雨就停了。「若破了他的德行，就會下雨。」「誰能勝過他的德行？」「大王，您的女兒那利尼迦可以。」這些本不是能用言語說的事，但為了國土的安寧，國王還是與女兒商議了。

passages.text: Isisinga, seeing her come, was terrified and hid in his hut; but she played with her ball at the door, her lovely limbs exposed to his gaze, and when he broke forth asking what fruit of what tree this might be that however far 'tis tossed still returns again and never more is lost, she answered falsely of Mount Gandhamādana, whose trees bear such fruit. Believing her an ascetic, he offered seat and food; and being an ingenuous youth who had never seen a woman before, he was led to believe her extraordinary story, and through her seductions his virtue was overcome and his meditation broken off. When he asked by what road she had come, she described her hermit cot by the Kāusikī north of the Himalayan snows; but fearing his father's return, she planned her escape—"Alas! I fear I may no longer stay, but many a royal saint lives on the way: ask one of them to point you out the road"—and left the youth wistfully looking after her. That very day Sakka, delighted, caused rain to fall throughout the whole kingdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 526 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 獨角見她來了，嚇得躲進草舍；她卻在門口拋著球玩耍，美妙的身姿映入他的眼簾；他忍不住問，這是什麼樹的什麼果，拋得多遠總會回到手中、再也不會丟失——她謊稱是香醉山上的果子，那裏的樹結這樣的果。他信她是個女苦行者，讓座供食；他是個從未見過女人的天真少年，便被引誘了。

passages.text: But directly she had left, a fever seized the boy, and he lay groaning in his hut where his returning father found him. Then the boy poured out his lovesick lament over the fair youth—the smoothed dark hair, the curvéd rings at either ear, the voice softer than the cuckoo's—and begged to be told where this holy youth dwelt, or he would lie down and die at the door. The Great Being knew at once that through some woman his son had lost his virtue, and rebuked him: friendships exist and then they cease; just as a flood sweeps off the ripened corn, so will the power of virtue be overborne by such a meeting—"Demons there be that through the wide earth run in varied form disguised. Beware, my son!" The terrified youth thought, "She was a female yakkha, he says," and asked his father's pardon, promising never to leave the spot; his father comforted him and proclaimed the four Perfect States, and the son walked therein and once more developed mystic meditation. Of that time the wife of his unregenerate days was Nalinika, the backsliding Brother was Isisinga, and the Master was the father.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 526 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但她一走，少年便害了熱病，躺在草舍裏呻吟，回來的父親看見了他。少年傾吐對那位美貌少年的相思——那柔滑的烏髮，兩耳的環形，比杜鵑更柔的嗓音——懇求告知這位聖者住處，否則便倒在門前死去。菩薩立刻明白兒子因某個女人失了德行，斥責道：友誼一旦建立在幻象上便完了。

title.en: Sonaka-Jātaka (The Crow on the Carcass)
title.zh: 蘇那迦本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Rajagaha, Benares royal park and palace
region.zh: 王舍城；波羅奈御苑與王宮

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: King Arindama forgets his friend Sonaka for forty years, singing his reward song through all Benares, while Sonaka, a withered sal-leaf falling before him, becomes a Silent Buddha. Fifty years on he teaches the reward-song's refrain to a wood-gathering boy, who sings it back before the king; led to the park, the king insults the shaven recluse and is rebuked, then hears the parable of the crow that feasted on a floating carcass until the Ganges swept it to the sea, and renounces his throne the same day.
summary.zh: 阿林達摩王四十年來遍唱「見我故友者賞千頂冠」之歌，而蘇那迦見落葉悟無常，已成獨覺佛。後教拾柴小兒續唱其歌詞；王循歌至御苑，斥剃髮行者為可憐蟲而遭反詰；聞「烏鴉食浮屍隨流至海」之喻，當日捨王位。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this concerning the Perfection of Renunciation: "not now only, but of old also the Tathāgata verily left the world and made the Great Renunciation." Of old, the Magadha king reigned in Rajagaha, and on the day the Bodhisatta was born to his chief queen as prince Arindama, a son was born to the royal chaplain and named young Sonaka. The two boys grew up alike as twins and studied at Taxila; wandering to Benares they lodged in the royal park, and at a brahmins' almsgiving the seats assigned them—white cloth for one, red woollen rug for the other—told Sonaka that that day his friend would be made king of Benares and would offer him the post of commander-in-chief. On the seventh day after the king's death the festal car stopped at the park gate for any worthy man to mount; the chaplain sprinkled the Bodhisatta king on the spot and led him into the city with a vast escort, and in the greatness of his glory the king forgot all about Sonaka.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 529 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 導師說起出離波羅蜜：「不只是如今，往昔如來也真實地離世而出家。」往昔摩揭陀王在王舍城為王，菩薩生為其正妃之子王子阿林陀摩那天，同日王家祭司得一子，取名少年蘇那迦。兩個孩子如孿生兄弟一般長大，同在呾叉始羅求學；遊學至波羅奈，住在王家園林，在一次婆羅門的集會上

passages.text: But when the king was gone, Sonaka sat again on the stone seat, and a withered leaf of a sal tree fell from its stalk in front of him. "Even as this leaf, so will my body fall into decay," he cried, and acquiring supernatural insight by reflecting on the impermanence of all things he attained that instant to the state of a Silent Buddha—his layman's marks vanishing, the ascetic's appearing—and set out for the cave of Nandamūla. The king, after forty years, remembered Sonaka, and offered a thousand pieces to whoever should see him with his own eyes and a hundred to whoever should hear of him, singing his aspiration: "A thousand crowns for one that sees my friend and playmate dear; a hundred lo! I give if one of Sonaka should hear." The song passed from mouth to mouth through harem, city and country till all sang it. Fifty years on, Sonaka, moved by the king's longing, came back through the air and taught the refrain to a seven-year-old boy gathering sticks in the park.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 529 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 國王離去之後，蘇那迦又坐回石座，一片乾枯的娑羅樹葉從枝頭落在他面前。「如這片葉，我的身體也將壞滅，」他喊道，觀察萬事無常而得神通慧，當下證得獨覺佛位——在家人的標記消失，苦行者的標記顯現——便動身往難陀慕羅洞去。四十年後國王想起蘇那迦，

passages.text: Bathed and dressed in his best, the boy had a drum beaten through the city, and before all the people the king sang first and the boy—five tangled locks he wore—answered: "The thousand give to me who saw, who heard a hundred more: I'll tell thee news of Sonaka, thy playfellow of yore. Within this realm, in thine own park is many a big sal tree... and at their foot lo! Sonaka in meditation lies, filled with the Arhat's holy calm, when human passion dies." The king started in full force and found his friend at rest, passionless and saintly; but given up to evil passion, he insulted him without saluting: "His parents dead, with shaven head, clad in monk's robe I see, a wretched Brother in a trance, stretched here beneath this tree." "He is no wretched wight who in his every action, Sire, has aye attained to right; nay rather wretched those who right neglect and practise ill, for evil doer evil doom is destined to fulfil."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 529 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 少年沐浴盛裝，擊鼓巡城；國王在眾人面前先唱，少年——他梳著五絡亂髮——應答：「千萬人所見所聞，我告訴你蘇那迦的消息：你舊日的遊伴。在你國中你自己的園林裏有許多大娑羅樹……樹下看哪，蘇那迦正在禪坐，充滿阿羅漢的聖寂，人間的激情止息之處。」國王大驚，

passages.text: Proving himself king of Kasi, Arindama asked if the sage had met with anything deserving blame, and Sonaka told the eight blessings of the homeless monk; but the king cut him short: "I have no need of monkish blessings... how to gain both worlds at once, to me, I prithee, tell." Then came the parable: a foolish crow, seeing a vast carcass floating past on the Ganges' tide, boarded it for goodly store of food and stayed eating and drinking till the river swept him headlong to the sea, where the monster fish came ravening round and devoured him. "So thou and all that greedily pleasures of sense pursue are deemed as wise as was this crow, till ye all lusts eschew." "In pity once, nay even twice, utter the warning word, but keep not on repeating it like a slave before his lord"—and the sage vanished through the air. The king resolved, "To-morrow one may die, who knows? I'll be ordained to-day," gave his sixty thousand villages, elephants, horses, cars and maidens to his son Dighavu, and was destined for the Brahma world; of that time the son was young Rahula and the king the Master.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 529 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 證明自己是迦尸之王后，阿林陀摩那問聖者可有可指責之處，蘇那迦講了無家者的八種福；國王卻打斷他：「我不需要沙門的福……如何在兩世同時得福，請你告訴我。」於是來了那個譬喻：一隻愚蠢的烏鴉，見恒河潮水漂來巨大的屍體，便落在上面貪圖豐盛的食物，邊吃邊喝，直到河水把他席捲著沖向

title.en: Mahāsutasoma-Jātaka (The Ogre-King and the Four Verses)
title.zh: 大蘇達沙摩本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Indapatta in the Kuru country and the man-eater's forest (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俱盧國因陀羅波達與食人者之林（象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: The king of Benares, given corpse-meat by his cook, conceives an incurable craving for human flesh, is exposed by his commander and banished, and becomes a man-eater who captures a hundred and one kings to sacrifice to the tree-nymph who healed his wound. Warned by that nymph, he seizes prince Sutasoma, his old teacher; released to hear four stanzas worth a hundred pieces each, Sutasoma returns under oath and wins four boons—life for the man-eater, the kings' lives, their release, and the end of cannibalism—till gods and men applaud the conversion.
summary.zh: 波羅奈王誤食人肉而生難遏之嗜，事發遭逐，成為食人魔王；為償樹神愈傷之願，捕一百零一王以祭。樹神勸其先擄舊師蘇達沙摩王子；釋之令聽四偈，王子誓言既立乃返，索四願——魔王長壽、諸王不死、各歸其國、戒食人肉——天人同聲喝采。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka containing cannibalism and vivid hell-threats; retold freely as scripture of a living tradition; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: The Master told this concerning the Elder Angulimala, the blood-stained robber whom he converted without violence: "I also tamed him when I was living in a previous stage of existence." Of old, king Koravya reigned in Indapatta of the Kuru country, and the Bodhisatta was born his son, Sutasoma, sent with one hundred and one princes to the same world-famed teacher; Sutasoma, senior pupil, took prince Brahmadatta of Benares for his private pupil, and on parting bade them all keep the Uposatha vows and abstain from taking life on the new- and full-moon days. But the king of Benares never ate his rice meal without meat; when the palace dogs ate the meat kept for a fast-day, the cook, fearing death, served flesh cut from a corpse in the cemetery, and the king, thrilled to the seven thousand nerves of taste—human flesh had been his food as a yakkha in the birth before—commanded the cook to furnish it always: first from the prisons, then by a baited purse of a thousand pieces, then by murdering passers-by at the night-watches. Caught at last with his basket of flesh, the cook accused his master before commander-in-chief Kalahatthi, and the king confessed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 537 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 導師說起阿闍世那人長老——那個他不假暴力便度化的血腥強盜：「我前世為畜生時也馴服過他。」往昔俱盧國因陀波吒的科羅比耶王在位，菩薩生為其子須陀須摩，與一百零一位王子同在舉世聞名的老師門下求學；須陀須摩為首席弟子，把波羅奈的婆羅多王子收作私淑弟子，臨別時囑咐大家守

passages.text: "Sire, do not this thing; eat not the flesh of men... if you do not cease from it, you will destroy both yourself and your realm." The commander told him of the monster fish Ananda, who tasted one of the fish that paid him court and then devoured his subjects until, madness and hunger driving him, he seized his own tail and was eaten piecemeal by the fish he had spared; but the king answered with his own examples—the lad who died for want of a third rose-apple, the brahmin's son ruined by a first taste of liquor, the gentleman who pined away crying for an Apsarā—and the golden geese who, eating the eggs, goslings and flesh of their own kin through a five-month rain, grew so feeble that the cave-spider sucked their blood one by one till their family was extinct. The citizens rose and would hear nothing: "Have him expelled from his kingdom." The king begged only his sword, his cooking vessel and his cook, and went into the forest, where he waylaid travellers, crying "Here am I, the man-eating robber!"—till he killed even the cook who failed him, and lived alone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 537 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「大王，不要做這件事；不要吃人肉……你若不止，你將毀了自己與你的王國。」大將軍告訴他巨魚阿難陀的故事：牠嘗了一尾來朝拜的魚，便吞食自己的臣民，直到瘋狂與飢餓驅使下咬住自己的尾巴，被牠饒過的魚群分食；但國王卻以自己的例子作答——那個為等第三顆蘋果而死的孩子，婆羅門的

passages.text: A wealthy brahmin's caravan paid for convoy through the forest, yet the man-eater seized him from his white-oxen carriage and carried him off head downward, lamed by an acacia splinter. At the foot of his banyan tree he prayed the tree-nymph: heal my wound within seven days and I will sacrifice the blood and inwards of a hundred and one princes of all India. His wound healed, his old comrade of yakkha days taught him a spell of strength and wind-swift speed, and within seven days he found and captured a hundred and one kings, hanging them by cords through their pierced palms on the banyan tree. But Sutasoma he spared—"Sutasoma was my private teacher: let not India be altogether desolate"—and when he lit the fire and sat sharpening the stake, the tree-nymph, fearing the coming slaughter, sought the Four Great Kings and Sakka, who could not stop him but named the one who could: prince Sutasoma of Indapatta. Disguised as an ascetic, she let herself be chased three leagues, stood fast at the word "Stand!"—"I am standing; do you too try and stand"—revealed herself blazing in the sky, and counseled: bid him first bring Sutasoma, then offer his sacrifice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 537 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位富婆羅門的商隊出錢僱他護送穿過森林，食人者卻從他的白牛車上把婆羅門抓走，倒懸而去，他被相思木刺所傷。在榕樹下他向樹神祈願：七日之內治好我的傷，我便以全印度一百零一位王子的血與內臟獻祭。傷癒之後，夜叉時代的老朋友教了他一個力大如風快的咒，七天之內

passages.text: Learning by the stars when Sutasoma would bathe in the royal tank, the man-eater lurked in the water and took him from the midst of his army. "I weep not for myself or wife or child or realm," said the prince, "but for a promise: once to a brahmin I my word did plight; that word I fain would keep, and then, my honour saved, return to thee." "No man escaped from death returns to his foe," laughed the robber, till Sutasoma swore a kshatriya's oath and the man-eater let him go. Sutasoma heard the four stanzas the brahmin Nanda had brought from Kassapa Buddha, and went back with death written on his forehead. Awestruck, the man-eater begged to hear them, and offered a boon for each stanza; the prince chose: long life for the man-eater himself; the hundred kings not eaten; each king restored to his realm; and abstinence from human flesh. The ogre wept and yielded at last, bowing at the prince's feet and taking the five moral laws at his hands; the deities of earth roared applause, and the man-eater went with Sutasoma and loosed the kings. Of old the Master, as Sutasoma, tamed this man-eater.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 537 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他以星象推知須陀須摩將到王家水池沐浴，便藏身水中，從千軍之中把他抓走。「我不是為自己哭，不是為妻子兒女或王國哭，」王子說，「是為一個承諾：我曾向一位婆羅許下諾言；我願守約，然後，保全了名節，回到你這裏來。」「沒有人從死裏逃出還回到敵人那裏的，」強盜大笑，直到須陀須摩以剎帝利之誓起誓，食人者才放他走。

title.en: The Tree-wife and the Spitting Trail
title.zh: 樹妻與唾沫之徑

region.en: Maroon Town, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (1924), tale 67 'The Tree-wife' (told by Thomas White, Maroon Town)

summary.en: A childless hunter wishes a pretty Jessamy tree into a wife, clothes her, and lives with her until another man inveigles her away. Fleeing, she spits at every half-mile of the two-mile road; the abandoned husband sings the Maroon Koromanti death-song at each spitting-place, the spits answer him, and the trail of answers leads him to the door where he takes his wife home again.
summary.zh: 無子的獵人許願美麗的素馨樹化為妻子，為其穿衣、成家；後被他人誘拐。逃亡路上，她在兩哩間每半哩吐一口唾沫；被棄的丈夫在每一處唾沫地唱起馬倫人的科羅曼蒂喪歌，唾沫竟一一應聲——循聲而至，他把妻子領回了家。

sensitivity.note: Wonder tale; the Koromanti death-song (Maroon burial song) is quoted in the source as sung at burials — noted here as cultural context, not reproduced verbatim.

passages.text: It was a man who had no wife and was a hunter-man; he hunted in the bush all day. One day he went into the bush and shot, and coming home he saw a pretty tree called Jessamy — 'O me biddy boy, that is a pretty tree!' He said, 'If this tree could turn a wife to me, I would like to be married to her!' And so it was: the tree turned a wife for him. The woman was naked; he left her at the spot, went home, got clothing for her, dressed her up nicely and carried her home to his house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 67 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一個人沒有妻子，是個獵人；他整天在叢林裏打獵。一天他進林子射獵，回家的路上看見一棵叫茉莉的漂亮樹——「哦我的寶貝，那棵樹真漂亮！」他說：「這棵樹若能變個妻子給我，我就娶她！」事情果然如此：那棵樹為他變出了一個妻子。那女子一絲不掛；他把她留在原地，回家取來衣服，把她打扮得漂漂亮亮，帶回自己的家

passages.text: He and the woman stayed a long time, until one day he went out to the bush to shoot and slept out; another man came and inveigled his wife and took her away to his house. When the poor man came home from the bush the next day, he could not find his wife. The frightened woman, leaving one house for the next about two miles off, spat all the way until she got to the other man's house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 67, middle (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他和女人過了很長時間，直到一天他進林子打獵在外過了夜；另一個男人勾引了他的妻子，把她帶到自己家。可憐的人第二天從林子回來，找不到妻子了。受驚的女人從一座房子搬到兩哩外的下一座，一路吐口水，直到她到了那個男人的家。

passages.text: The man was in a rage that he could not find his wife and did not know what to do. He sang the Koromanti death-song, the song always used by the Maroons at a burial — 'Jesta be-yo, eh, eh, eh, o! Jesta be-yo, a wi' die-o...' — and at every place where the woman spat, the spit answered him. He went and stood at each stopping-place of half a mile until the two miles were passed; and just as the woman heard the voice of the man, she stood at the door-mouth and saw that the man was coming. The man took his wife and carried her right back to the home yard. Jack man dora, choose none!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 67, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 男人找不到妻子，憤怒之下不知所措。他唱起科羅曼蒂的喪歌——馬隆人葬禮上永遠唱的那支——「耶斯塔備喲，哎，哎，哎，哦！耶斯塔備喲，我們要死了喲……」——女人吐口水的地方，口水都回答了他。他一處一處地站，每半哩一站，直到兩哩走完；女人聽見男人的聲音，正站在門口，看見那個男人

title.en: Sammy the Comferee Melted on the Iron Rod
title.zh: 康菲里小哥在鐵桿上熔盡

region.en: Maroon Town, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 68 'Sammy the Comferee' (told by Thomas White, Maroon Town)

summary.en: Sammy's stray arrow lands in Massa Jesus's yard; the wife detains the beautiful boy all day until rain soaks the Master's washing, and scolds her husband that Sammy is prettier than the Maker of him. Massa Jesus heats an iron rod red-hot and orders the boy to climb it; Sammy melts leg by leg, singing his farewell song — 'Ah, me Sammy de Con-fa-ri-a-e-ro, Gi-ra no, ah, in din ro' — and all the pretty men born into the world thereafter get some of his fat; the ugly ones get none.
summary.zh: 小哥的箭誤落耶穌先生院中；其妻扣留美少年整日，直到大雨淋濕晾曬的衣物，還向丈夫抱怨小哥比自己造物者更俊。耶穌先生把鐵桿燒得通紅，命其攀爬；小哥一節節熔化，唱著告別之歌——『啊，我是康菲里小哥，吉拉諾……』——此後世上所有俊美的男子都分得他的一點脂膏；醜陋者分毫不沾。

sensitivity.note: Wonder tale with syncretic Christian frame ('Massa Jesus'); folk-comic use of scripture names, transcribed from named tellers.

passages.text: A woman had one son, a boy very unruly, who had nothing to do but fire bow and arrow all day. One day he fired the arrow and it dropped into Massa Jesus's yard. He went in to pick it up; Massa Jesus was gone out, but the wife was in the yard, and all the clothes were sunning out of doors. She detained the boy in the yard the whole day until the rain came and wet up all Massa Jesus's clothes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 68 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個女人只有一個兒子，非常調皮，整天只會拉弓射箭。一天他射出一支箭，落進了耶穌老爺的院子。他進去撿箭；耶穌老爺出去了，夫人在院子裏，所有的衣服都晾在外面。她把男孩留在院子裏一整天，直到下雨把耶穌老爺的衣服全淋濕了。

passages.text: When Massa Jesus came in wet, wanting dry clothes and finding none, he asked his wife what she had been doing all day. She answered that as Sammy the Comferee was in the house, that was why the clothes got wet — and when Massa Jesus pressed her, she replied that if he had been as pretty as Sammy the Comferee, she would have done more. 'I know I made Sammy the Comferee,' said Massa Jesus, 'and if Sammy the Comferee is prettier than me, I will see about it.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 68, middle (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 耶穌老爺淋著雨回來，要乾衣服卻找不到，問妻子一天都在幹什麼。她答道，康菲里的薩米在屋裏，所以衣服淋濕了——耶穌老爺再逼問，她答道，他要是長得像康菲里的薩米那麼俊，她還會做得更多。「我知道是我造了康菲里的薩米，」耶穌老爺說，「康菲里的薩米若比我俊，我倒要看看。」

passages.text: Massa Jesus put up an iron rod, hot as fire, hot until it was red, and sent for Sammy the Comferee. He ordered the boy to climb the iron rod, and Sammy commenced to melt away, singing — 'Ah, me Sammy de Con-fa-ri-a-e-ro, Gi-ra no, ah, in din ro!' — he melted off to his leg, sang again, melted to his middle, to his hand, to his neck, and sang again until he melted off to nothing. When you look at the iron rod, a whole heap of fat is heaped up about it: all the pretty men that come into the world get some of Sammy the Comferee's fat, but the ugly ones don't get none of it. Jack man dory, me story done!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 68, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 耶穌老爺立起一根火紅滾燙的鐵棒，把康菲里的薩米叫來，命他爬上鐵棒；薩米開始融化，唱著——「啊，我薩米是康法里——哎——羅，吉拉——喏，啊，因丁——羅！」——融到腿上，又唱，融到腰上，融到手，融到脖子，再唱，直到融化得乾乾淨淨。你去看那根鐵棒，旁邊堆著一大堆油脂：所有俊俏的男人

title.en: Grandy Beard-o and the Bull Who Didn't Care
title.zh: 大奶奶碧兒多與無畏的公牛

region.en: Mandeville, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加曼德維爾

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 69a 'Grandy-Do-an'-Do' (told by Moses Hendricks, Mandeville)

summary.en: The rich witch Grandy Beard-o feeds no one who cannot name her. A hungry captive girl is sent for water past each separated pasture; cow, mule and horse fear to speak, but the mighty bull bawls the name aloud. Fed and freed, the girl inherits the estate when the old lady, tracking the telltale pasture by pasture, is tossed leg by leg, arm by arm, and finally by the neck into the air — which is why the land goes from hand to hand in legacy up to today.
summary.zh: 富有的女巫大奶奶碧兒多只餵能道出她名字的人。被扣的飢餓女孩穿過一座座隔離牧場去取水；牛、騾、馬皆不敢言，唯公牛大聲吼出其名。女孩吃飽獲釋；老太婆逐場追問洩密者，卻被公牛一次次拋向空中——先斷雙腿，再斷雙臂，最後斷頸——所以至今田產仍一代代易手相傳。

sensitivity.note: Wonder tale (hidden-name witch type, ATU 500-linked). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There was an old woman, a witch, very wealthy, who lived quite to herself — plenty of stock, horses, cows, sheep, mules, each kind kept in a separate pasture. The old lady's name was Grandy Beard-o, but nobody knew that name. She wanted someone to sup with her, took home a little girl, prepared a meal — and said, 'Unless you tell me my name, I will not give you anything to eat.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 69a (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一個老婦人，是個巫婆，非常富有，自己一個人住——家畜成群，馬、牛、羊、騾，各類牲口分開圈養。老太太名叫鬍子婆婆，卻沒有人知道這個名字。她想找個伴吃飯，帶回家一個小女孩，備了一頓飯——卻說：「除非你能說出我的名字，否則一點吃的也不給你。」

passages.text: She sent the girl out to fetch water through all the pastures, and the girl went along crying, being hungry. In the cow-pasture the cow asked what was the matter, and heard it — the old lady would give nothing to eat unless the girl could tell her name — but Cow was afraid to tell her. The mule wouldn't tell her; the horse wouldn't tell her. In the bull pasture, Bull said, 'Cho! when you go home, tell her her name, Grandy Beard-o' — Bull was a mighty man; he didn't care!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 69a, middle (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她叫女孩穿過所有的牧場去打水，女孩一路哭著走，肚子餓著。牛圈裏母牛問怎麼回事，聽說了——老太太不說出名字就不給吃的——可母牛不敢告訴她。騾子不肯告訴；馬也不肯告訴。公牛圈裏，公牛說：「呸！你回去就告訴她，她的名字叫鬍子婆婆」——公牛是條好漢；他不怕！

passages.text: The girl hastened home glad to get food at last: 'Your name is Grandy Beard-o, ma'am.' The old lady, indignant, gave her a good feed, then started to find who told her — cow, horse: 'A ring ding ding, mamma, ring ding ding; no me tell.' In the bull pasture Bull confessed — 'Damme, me tell 'm!' She gripped the bull and tossed him in the air; he dropped unhurt. The bull tossed her now; she dropped, one leg broken. Toss for toss, her legs, then her arms broke, until the last toss the bull made — her neck broke. That was the end of her. The girl became mistress of all she possessed, and that is why the land goes from hand to hand in legacy up to today.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 69a, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 女孩趕緊回家，高興總算有飯吃了：「您的名字是鬍子婆婆，夫人。」老太太大怒，還是給了她一頓好飯，然後去查是誰告訴的——牛、馬都說「叮叮咚咚，媽媽，叮叮咚咚；不是我說的。」公牛圈裏公牛坦白了——「該死，是我告訴她的！」她抓住公牛，把他拋到空中；他落下毫髮無傷。公牛這回拋她；她掉下來，摔斷了一條腿。一拋換一拋，腿斷了，胳膊斷了，直到公牛最後一拋——她的脖子斷了。這就是她的下場。女孩成了她一切財產的主人，這就是為什麼

title.en: Grandy Do-an'-Do and the Singing Crab
title.zh: 大奶奶杜安杜與唱歌的螃蟹

region.en: Malvern, Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山莫爾文

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 69b (told by Julia Gentle, Malvern, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: A very bad woman sends her only daughter for river water with a name-riddle death-threat. The forgetful girl is returned empty twice; the second time the Crab tells her to sing the answer all the way home — 'Your name is Grandy-do-an-do' — and the maddened witch travels the pastures interrogating Cow, Sheep, Horse, Duck and Crab, machete in hand. The Crab owns the truth, sinks into his hole, and stays in the hole till now.
summary.zh: 惡婆遣獨女取水，以名字之謎相威脅。健忘的女孩兩度空手而回；第二次螃蟹教她一路唱回家——『你叫大奶奶杜安杜』。惡婆大怒，持彎刀遍訪牛、羊、馬、鴨、蟹追問洩密者；螃蟹認下實情，沉入洞中，至今仍在洞裡。

sensitivity.note: Wonder tale, paired variant of the hidden-name cycle. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: A very bad woman had only one daughter, and said, 'Go to the river for water, and when you come back, if you cannot tell my name, I will destroy you.' Going for water she saw Crab, who asked where she was going: 'Grandy sent me to the river for water and said when I come back, if I cannot tell his name, she will kill me.' The Crab told her, 'When you go, tell her that her name is Grandy Do-an-do.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 69b (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個非常惡毒的女人只有一個女兒，說：「去河邊打水，回來之後，你若說不出我的名字，我就毀了你。」去打水的路上她遇見螃蟹，螃蟹問她去哪裏：「鬍子婆婆叫我來河邊打水，說我回來若說不出她的名字，她要殺了我。」螃蟹告訴她：「你回去就告訴她，她的名字叫東安東婆婆。」

passages.text: When she came back she had forgotten the name, and the old woman dashed away the water and sent her back. Going again, the Crab said, 'Sing it all the way!' So the girl went back singing, 'You name Grandy-do-an-do! You name Grandy-do-an-do!' The woman, mad when she heard it, traveled and met Cow — 'You Cow, did you tell the girl my name Grandy Do-an-do?' — 'No, no, me tell him so, you name Grandy Do-an-do!' Sheep said the same; Horse said the same; Duck said the same.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 69b, middle (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她回來時忘了名字，老婦把水潑了，叫她再去。再去的路上，螃蟹說：「一路唱著去！」女孩便一路唱回去：「你的名字叫東安東婆婆！你的名字叫東安東婆婆！」老婦聽見了氣瘋了，去問母牛——「你牛，是不是你告訴女孩我的名字東安東婆婆？」——「不，不是，我告訴她的是，你叫東安東婆婆！」羊這樣說；馬這樣說；鴨子這樣說。

passages.text: She met Crab: 'You Crab, did you tell the girl my name Grandy Do-an-do?' — and Crab said, 'Yes, it is me who told him your name is Grandy Do-an-do!' She took the machete and chopped after the Crab, and Crab sank into the hole and stayed in the hole till now.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 69b, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她遇見螃蟹：「你螃蟹，是不是你告訴女孩我的名字東安東婆婆？」——螃蟹說：「是我，是我告訴她你的名字叫東安東婆婆！」她拿著大砍刀追著螃蟹砍，螃蟹沉進洞裏，直到今天還住在洞裏。

title.en: Jack and Harry: Four Kind Strangers and the Boy Who Ruins Them
title.zh: 傑克與哈利：四位恩人與敗事的孩子

region.en: Dry River, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加雞窩地乾河

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (1924), tale 70 'Jack and Harry' (told by William Forbes, Dry River)

summary.en: In the cool morning the brothers beg coffee from an old man in the watch-house — Jack drinks the host's own cup and both flee. Hen, poor lady, and carencro each shelter them in turn; at each rescue Jack ruins it — popping the hen's wing, choking the lady, popping the carencro's wing — until the brothers knock themselves senseless, meet a land turtle, and Jack cuts off the head that Harry had called out of its shell.
summary.zh: 清早兄弟倆向守屋老人討咖啡——傑克卻把主人那杯也喝了，二人被追而逃。母雞、老婦、兀鷹先後施救；每次傑克都親手毀局——彈雞翅、掐老婦、彈鷹翅——直到二人摔得昏迷。醒來遇陸龜；哈利剛喚出其頭，傑克一刀斫下。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale (ungrateful-brother type). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Jack and Harry were going out for a walk. The morning was cool, and they came to an old man in a watch-house. Harry said, 'Old Massa, beg you a little coffee if you have any.' He said, 'Yes, me pickney!' and gave Jack a cup of coffee and Harry a cup. The old man had not drunk his own coffee yet when Jack said, 'Harry, I gwine drink the old man's coffee.' Harry said no; Jack took the old man's coffee and drank it, and the old man took his stick after them and they ran.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 70 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傑克和哈利出門散步。清晨涼爽，他們遇見一個守望所裏的老人。哈利說：「老爺爺，求您一點咖啡吧，若您有的話。」老人說：「有的，我的孩子！」給傑克一杯咖啡，哈利一杯。老人自己的咖啡還沒喝，傑克就說：「哈利，我要把老爺爺的咖啡喝了。」哈利說不行；傑克拿了老人的咖啡喝了，老人拿起棍子追他們，他們跑了。

passages.text: Running, they saw a hen with some chickens. 'Do, me good hen, cover me with your wing!' — and she covered them like her own chicks; the old man came after, saw nothing, turned back. 'I gwine pop the hen wing,' said Jack, and popped it — the hen fluttered after them. They ran to a poor lady standing in the way, who covered them with her coat; Jack said, 'I gwine choke the old lady' — and as he choked her, she shook them out and ran after them. Then a carencro (crow) took them both up on its wing, flying right up into the sky — 'I gwine pop the carencro wing, mek him drop' — and as they dropped, they knocked themselves out of their senses.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 70, middle (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 跑著跑著，他們看見一隻母雞帶著小雞。「求求你，好母雞，用翅膀蓋住我們！」——她把他們當自己的小雞蓋住；老人追來，什麼也沒看見，折回去了。「我要折母雞的翅膀，」傑克說，折了——母雞撲扇著追他們。他們跑到一位站在路上的可憐婦人那裏，婦人用外衣蓋住他們；傑克說「我要掐這老太太」——他一掐，婦人把他們抖出來追他們。然後一隻兀鷹把他們倆都馱在翅膀上，直飛上天——「我要折兀鷹的翅膀，讓他們掉下來」——他們掉下來時，

passages.text: When they came to themselves, a land turtle was coming. Harry called to it kindly, and as it shoved out its head, Jack cut off the head with his knife — so the two boys, who had spoiled every kindness shown them on the road, ended the day by taking the one quiet stranger that offered no shelter and asking nothing back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 70, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們清醒過來時，一隻陸龜正爬過來。哈利和氣地喚它，它一伸出頭，傑克就用刀把頭砍了下來——這兩個把一路上所有的好意都糟蹋了的孩子，最後把唯一一個不給他們庇護、也不求回報的安靜陌生人，也照樣糟蹋了。

title.en: Pea-fowl as Messenger
title.zh: 孔雀傳信

region.en: Maroon Town and Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮與聖克魯斯山

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 71 'Pea-fowl as Messenger' (a, Matilda Hall; b, Oliver D. Witter)

summary.en: Summoned to a lying-in, the midwife auditions the household for a messenger able to sing a man's name — cock, dog and puss fail; the pea-fowl, paid a quart of corn, flies miles singing 'You John Studee, for me master!' until the gambler hears his name from a house-top and rides home, hanging his gold chain on the bird's neck — which is why the peacock wears golden feathers there. In the paired tale the same errand ends in pecked baldness for Bra Peacock and a lump of gold for a head.
summary.zh: 產婦臨盆喚夫，接生婆逐一試鳥——雞、狗、貓皆不能名；孔雀受賄一夸脫玉米，飛行數哩高唱『約翰·斯圖迪，我主人在哪！』賭徒聞名歸家，把金鏈掛上鳥頸——孔雀頸上金羽由此而來。另一版本：同一差事卻以孔雀被啄禿頭、頭頂金塊收場。

sensitivity.note: Etiological bird tales. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: The husband and wife were married people, and the husband a great gambler, never at home with the wife — until the wife was going to have a baby, and the ninth month came. They sent for the midwife; when she came there was no husband in. She wanted someone to go call the husband, John Studee. She called for the fowl, a cock: 'What will you say to call the husband?' The cock crew 'Ko ku ru ku-u-u!' — 'You won't do.' The dog said 'Hoo-oh!' — 'No, won't do.' Puss said 'Me-oo!' — 'Won't do.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 71a (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 夫妻倆結了婚，丈夫是個大賭徒，從不在家陪妻子——直到妻子要生孩子，第九個月到了。他們去請接生婆；她來時丈夫不在家。她想找個人去叫丈夫約翰·斯圖迪。她叫家禽，一隻公雞：「你去叫丈夫，要說什麼？」公雞打鳴「科咕嚕咕——！」——「你不行。」狗說「嗚——哦！」——「不行。」貓說「喵——！」——「不行。」

passages.text: Then she called for the pea-fowl and provided a quart of corn, asking what he would say. Pea-fowl sang, 'You John Studee, you John Studee, fe me master John Studee! There's a pretty gal from Silo, there's a handsome gal from Silo, want the care of a new John bwoy — it almost deh!' — 'Yes, you'll do!' When the pea-fowl flew miles off and did not see the master, he took up the quart of corn and flew away; then he pitched on a house-top and sang his song again. The people said John Studee had been there but had just gone away — that great gambler! He flew another mile off and sang from another great house-top, and John Studee came: 'Who calls my name?' He took up the fowl, got the buggy in haste, took the gold chain from his neck and put it on the pea-fowl — the pea-fowl has the golden feathers round his neck on account of that chain. When the feather came home, the baby was born and named John Studee after him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 71a, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然後她叫孔雀，備了一夸脫玉米，問他要說什麼。孔雀唱道：「你的約翰·斯圖迪，你的約翰·斯圖迪，我的主人約翰·斯圖迪！有位漂亮的姑娘從錫羅來，有位俊俏的姑娘從錫羅來，要照顧一個新生的小約翰——就快啦！」——「行，就你了！」孔雀飛出好幾哩沒看見主人，便叼起那夸脫玉米飛走了；然後落在一家屋頂上又唱了一遍。人們說約翰·斯圖迪來過又剛走——那個大賭徒！他又飛一哩，從另一個屋頂唱

passages.text: In the paired version, Miss Nancy's husband Contavio locked her up when he went to market. Hungry, she begged Sheep, then Billy-goat, to call him for a lump of gold — 'No, my dear, that will not do.' Then Bra Peacock flew right away until he saw Contavio, pecked him in his head and picked off all the feathers, and spurred him the whole way home until all Bra Peacock's spurs dropped off. When he got Contavio home, Miss Nancy flung the lump of gold on Bra Peacock's head — that is why the feathers on a peacock's head look like gold, why it has no spurs, and why a crow has no feathers on its head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 71b 'Contavio' (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 配對的版本裏，南茜小姐的丈夫康塔維奧上集市時把她鎖在家裏。她餓了，先求羊、再求山羊去叫他，許一塊金子——「不行，親愛的，那不行。」孔雀老弟卻直飛出去，直到看見康塔維奧，啄他的頭，拔掉他所有的羽毛，一路用距刺著他回家，直到孔雀的距刺全掉光了。他把康塔維奧弄回家，南茜小姐把那塊金子扔在孔雀老弟的頭上——所以孔雀頭上的羽毛像金色，為什麼它沒有距刺，而烏鴉頭上沒有毛。

title.en: The Barking Puppy and the Phinney Man
title.zh: 吠叫的小狗與菲尼人

region.en: Maroon Town, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (1924), tale 72 'The Barking Puppy' (told by Alfred Williams, Maroon Town)

summary.en: An old lady's nightly visitor is driven off by the barking puppy; she burns the dog in a big fire — and the ashes bark. Thrown into the river, they bark in the river; thrown into the sea, they hush. At last the gentleman comes in, draws a chair — 'So long I couldn't come on account of Dick and Dandy!' — says he is coming to marry her, sings back her own Phinney-man song, and tears her up to inch pieces: 'sometime shadow come back.'
summary.zh: 老婦的夜訪者屢被吠叫的小狗嚇退；她把狗燒了——灰燼卻仍吠。投入河中，河裡也吠；投入海中，方才安靜。紳士終於登門，拉椅而坐：『這麼久來不了，都是因為迪克和丹迪！』自稱要娶她，還回唱她的菲尼人之歌——隨後把她撕成碎片：影子，有時是會回來的。

sensitivity.note: Duppy-romance tale with violent ending, told as wake-night entertainment. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There was an old lady living at home with one little puppy, and every night a gentleman came to pay her a visit; but the little puppy snapped and barked, and he had to turn back. The old lady caught the puppy and made up a big fire and burned the puppy. Next night the gentleman came back again, and the old lady sang her song — 'Heah, heah, Phinney man, heah, oh, heah, Phinney man; nobody heah, Phinney man, Dick and Dandy heah!' — and the ashes barked as the puppy. The old lady got up, took up the ashes and dashed them in the river, saying the gentleman was going to pay her a visit and could not, because the ashes barked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 72 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位老婦人獨自在家養著一隻小狗，每天夜裏有位紳士來看她；可小狗又咬又叫，他只好折返。老婦抓住小狗，燃起大火，把小狗燒了。第二天夜裏紳士又來了，老婦唱起她的歌——「來吧，來吧，芬尼漢子，來吧，哦來吧，芬尼漢子；沒有人在家，芬尼漢子，迪克和丹迪在呢！」——灰燼學著小狗叫了起來。老婦起身，捧起灰燼倒進河裏，說紳士要來看她了，不會再

passages.text: Next night the gentleman came back again and hollered 'Hulloo!'; the old lady sang, and the puppy ashes barked in the river — and the gentleman would not come. The old lady took the river water and dashed it in the sea to hinder Dick and Dandy from barking. Next night the gentleman came back for the last time; the old lady raised up and sang her song while the gentleman danced, came in now, drew a chair and said, 'So long I couldn't come on account of Dick and Dandy!' — and said, 'I coming to marry you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 72, middle (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天夜裏紳士又來，喊「喂！」；老婦唱起歌，小狗的灰在河裏叫起來——紳士不肯來了。老婦舀了河水倒進海裏，不讓迪克和丹迪再叫。第二天夜裏紳士最後一次回來；老婦起身唱她的歌，紳士跳著舞，這回進來了，拉了把椅子說：「這麼久來不了，都是因為迪克和丹迪！」——並說，「我是來娶你的。」

passages.text: The old lady said yes, but did not know but a dog shadow had come — sometime a shadow comes back. She sang her song again, and the gentleman caught the old lady and tore her up to inch pieces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 72, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 老婦答應了，卻不知道是不是狗的影子回來了——有時影子會回來。她又唱起她的歌，紳士抓住老婦，把她撕成了碎片。

title.en: The Singing Bird and the Well
title.zh: 會唱歌的小鳥與水井

region.en: Maroon Town, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (1924), tale 73 'The Singing Bird' (a, Alfred Williams, Maroon Town)

summary.en: The waiting-boy Collin pitches his master into a well at the water-stop and drives home alone with the buggy, reporting visits and delays. A little bird in the tree by the house sings the crime to the mistress — 'Fine waiting boy, fine waiting boy, throw his master into a well' — a sensible person is called to interpret the whistling, the well is searched, the body found, and Collin is hanged.
summary.zh: 車伕科林在取水處把主人推入井中，獨自驅車回家，謊稱主人訪友未歸。屋前樹上的小鳥把罪行唱給女主人聽——『好車伕，好車伕，把主人拋進井裡』——請來通鳥語者解其哨音，井中尋得屍身，科林被處絞刑。

sensitivity.note: Murder-revelation ballad-tale (singing bone type, ATU 780). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: A gentleman had his servant, and one day he said to the servant, 'Collin, go and look about the horse harness, my buggy.' Collin harnessed the master's horse and put it in the buggy; the master drove on till he got to a well and said he wanted some water. 'Massa, there is a well down before.' While the massa sat against the well-side, Collin pitched his master into the well, turned back, and went halfway home with the buggy; when he got home the missus asked where the master was, and Collin said he was going to pay a visit and coming tomorrow — the buggy going to meet him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 73a (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位紳士有個僕人，一天他對僕人說：「科林，去看看馬具，我的馬車。」科林套好主人的馬，裝上馬車；主人一直趕到一口井前說想喝水。「老爺，前面就有口井。」老爺倚著井邊坐下時，科林把主人推下井去，折回來，趕著馬車走到半路；回到家，夫人問主人在哪裏，科林說他訪友去了，明天才回——馬車要去接他。
