passages.text: Collin went the next day with the buggy; back at the house again, the missus asked once more where the master was — 'Gone to pay a visit, won't be back till tomorrow.' When Collin was gone, another servant in the yard said, 'Missus, hear what the little bird is singing?' The missus came to the doorway and listened, and heard the little bird whistling: 'Fine waiting boy, fine waiting boy — throw his master into a well! Collin, Collin, no ben see dat little bird upon tree so long?' She could not understand it, called a sensible person to interpret the bird, went and searched the well, found the master's body — and took Collin and hanged him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 73a, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天科林又趕著馬車去；回到宅子，夫人又問主人在哪——「訪友去了，明天才回。」科林走後，院子裏另一個僕人說：「夫人，聽聽小鳥在唱什麼？」夫人來到門口聽，聽見小鳥在啭：「好聽話的僕人，好聽話的僕人——把主人扔進井裏！科林，科林，那棵樹上的小鳥你看見這麼久了嗎？」她聽不明白，請了一位明白人來解鳥語，去井邊搜尋，找到了

title.en: Miss Grace, My Fair Lady
title.zh: 葛蕾絲小姐，我的美人

region.en: Maroon Town, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 2024 (published 1924)

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 74 'Two Sisters' (told by Margaret Morris, Maroon Town)

summary.en: Servant Miss Grace marries her mistress-sister's Busha and bears his baby; the jealous Miss Wheel lures her to pick peas by the sea-ball and shoves her in, taking the baby as her own. Nights on, the dead woman returns to the lying Busha's doorstep, and only the little dog answers her litany — hand me my baby, my bowl, my comb, my clo'es — until the neighbors' pail-of-milk-and-hot-water trap revives her in the sheet, her testimony is heard, and Miss Wheel goes down the hill-side in a barrel bound for the lime-kiln fire.
summary.zh: 女僕葛蕾絲嫁給姐姐侍奉的監工，生下一子；善妒的惠爾小姐誘她到海蝕洞邊摘豌豆，把她推入水中，抱走嬰兒據為己有。此後夜夜，亡魂回到昏睡的丈夫門前，只有小狗應她的連禱——把我的孩子、我的碗、我的梳子、我的衣裳拿來——直到鄰居以奶桶與滾水之計在白布下還魂；她道出真相，惠爾小姐被裝桶滾下坡，送入石灰窯的火中。

sensitivity.note: Murdered-sister revenant tale (ATU 780-linked 'Two Sisters' type). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Two sisters stayed in a house. One sister was servant to a Busha (overseer) in one pen, and arranged for the Busha to marry the other sister — Miss Grace, my fair lady; the older sister, Lady Wheel, served her sister. The Busha went to his work and never came back till midnight. One day when he was out, Miss Wheel called Miss Grace to go pick peas; taking a basket and the baby — Miss Grace my fair lady's baby — they picked peas around the sea-ball, where Miss Wheel made Miss Grace take off her dress and shoved her into the hole. She picked up the peas, came home, washed her breast with water, took the baby for herself, and when night came, suckled it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 74 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兩姐妹住在一座房子裏。妹妹在一處農莊給監工（布沙）做僕人，安排布沙娶姐姐——格蕾絲小姐，我美麗的小姐；姐姐惠爾女士伺候妹妹。布沙去上工，不到半夜不回家。一天他外出時，惠爾女士叫格蕾絲小姐去摘豌豆；帶著籃子和嬰兒——美麗小姐格蕾絲的嬰兒——她們在海邊草球周圍摘豌豆，惠爾女士讓格蕾絲小姐脫下裙子，把她推進坑裏。她撿起豌豆回家，用水擦了胸膛，

passages.text: The Busha came home midnight and was given dinner, but never noticed his wife at all; three days he kept coming and never noticed. When he asked for the servant he was told she was sent out to the common and would soon come. Warned by a neighbor that harm had been done in his house — told not even to drink cold water in the house that night — the Busha lay down at midnight seeming to doze, but not asleep. There was a little dog called Doggie, and Dog saw when the dead woman came.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 74, middle (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 布沙半夜回家，有人端上飯，他卻一點也沒注意到妻子；三天他照常回家從未察覺。問起僕人，他們說被打發去公共草地了，很快就回來。鄰居提醒他家中出了禍事——叮囑他那晚連冷水也不要喝——布沙半夜躺下，假裝打盹，其實醒著。家裏有一隻小狗叫狗狗，狗狗看見了死去的女人什麼時候來。

passages.text: The gentleman heard every word; the lady said it was nothing, not wanting the Busha to hear. The last night, the neighbors put up a pail of milk and a pail of hot water at the doorway covered with a sheet; the dead woman came and called out the same litany, took the baby and put it to bed, stepped in the hot water, pitched into the milk covered with the white sheet, was taken out and wrapped up — and she looked up with her eyes fixed. 'What do you, me dear?' — 'My sister shoved me down in the ball. She called me to go pick peas and shoved me in there.' When the gentleman found out his wife had been dead, he took Miss Wheel, built a lime-kiln, shipped her into a barrel, pitched it down the hill-side and rolled it into the fire. Jack man dora!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 74, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 先生聽見了每一句話；那位女士說沒什麼，不想讓布沙聽見。最後一夜，鄰居們在門口擺了一桶牛奶和一桶熱水，蓋著一張白布；死去的女人來了，念出同樣的禱詞，抱起嬰兒放回床上，踏進熱水，撲進蓋著白布的牛奶裏，被拉出來裹起——她抬起頭，眼睛直直的。「你做了什麼，親愛的？」——「我的姐姐把我推進了球坑。她叫我去摘豌豆，把我推了進去。」先生查明妻子被殺之後

title.en: Asoonah, the Big-Skinned Thing
title.zh: 阿蘇那：大皮怪

region.en: Mandeville, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加曼德維爾

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 75 'Asoonah' (told by Philipp Brown, Mandeville)

summary.en: Asoonah, a big-skinned thing that sinks a whole yard, invades the house daily in the mother's absence, interrogating the children — where is your mother, where the pretty little one, where the house with the guinea corn, where's the mortar — until the father guns it down in the gully. The king offers three hundred pounds to name the monstrous skin brought to his gate; the little boy lifts it — 'Eh! no Asoonah 'kin?' — and everybody, frightened, comes right out, and the boy works again with plenty of clothes.
summary.zh: 大皮怪阿蘇那能陷沒整座院落，趁母親外出日日光臨，盤問孩子們——你母親何在、漂亮的小的何在、有玉米的房子何在、石臼何在——直到父親在溝壑中一槍擊斃。國王懸賞三百鎊辨認那張拖到王門前的巨皮；小男孩一舉——『咦！這不就是阿蘇那的皮？』——眾人嚇得四散，男孩得賞，穿新衣重操舊業。

sensitivity.note: Monster-slayer tale. 'Asoonah' is an unidentified large animal in Beckwith's cycle (cf. tale 75 note). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Asoonah is a big-skin thing; when it comes into your yard it will sink the whole place. One day the lady left her three children out and went to work; this Asoonah came in every day, and the children knew what time it was coming — and it asked the small one, 'Where is your mother?' — 'Gone a washing-day.' — 'Where is the pretty little one?' — 'Inside the room.' — 'Where the house with the guinea corn?' and it hollered, 'Where is the mortar?' — 'Inside the kitchen.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 75 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿蘇納是個大皮囊的怪物；它一進你的院子，能把整個地方壓塌。一天太太把三個孩子留在外面去上工；這阿蘇納天天來，孩子們都知道它來的時辰——它問最小的：「你媽媽在哪裏？」——「去洗衣日了。」——「漂亮的那個呢？」——「在屋裏。」——「種玉米的房子在哪裏？」它大喊，「石杵在哪裏？」——「在廚房裏。」

passages.text: One day when the mother came, the children said, 'Every day a big thing comes in here and can't tell what is what.' The mother said to the husband, 'You better stop and see what comes here in the daytime.' He got the gun and went up into the kitchen loft and sat; when he saw Asoonah come, it was so big he got frightened and dodged behind the door, but as it reached the gully he fired the gun and Asoonah fell down in the gully and broke its neck.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 75, middle (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一天母親回來，孩子們說：「天天有個大東西進來，分不清它是什麼。」母親對丈夫說：「你最好停下來，看看白天來的是什麼。」他拿了槍，爬上廚房的閣樓坐著；看見阿蘇納來了，那東西大得他嚇壞了，躲到門後，等它走到水溝時開了槍；阿蘇納跌進水溝，摔斷了脖子。

passages.text: The king heard about this Asoonah but couldn't tell what it was; he said anybody who could come in and tell what it was would get three hundred pounds. The little boy heard about it and was so torn up about it. The old lady keeping a jooty at the king's gate said, 'What way is Asoonah 'kin going to be brought in here today?' When the king asked everybody and nobody could tell, he called up the little boy; the boy went to take it up, and the king asked him if he knew what it was. He held it up like this and said, 'Eh! no Asoonah 'kin?' Everybody got frightened and came right out, and the king offered the boy three hundred pounds, gave him plenty of clothes, and got the boy to work again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 75, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 國王聽說了這隻阿蘇納卻分不清它是什麼；他宣布誰能進來說出它是什麼，就賞三百鎊。小男孩聽說了，激動得要命。在國王門口打雜的老婦說：「今天阿蘇納那個傢伙要怎麼抬進來呢？」國王問遍了所有人，誰也說不出，便叫來小男孩；男孩去搬它，國王問他知不知道那是什麼。他把它舉了一點

title.en: The Greedy Child at the Devil's Ford
title.zh: 貪心孩子與魔鬼渡口

region.en: Mandeville and Maroon Town, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加曼德維爾與馬倫鎮

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (1924), tale 76 'The Greedy Child' (a, George Barrett; b, Philipp Brown)

summary.en: The old ferryman takes breakfast from every child he carries but one — and drowns the refuser, singing up and down the rising water until the mother pays two pounds. In the paired Devil tale, the safe pass-phrase is 'no one go s'y, no two go s'y, no three go s'y, but it go s'y for him mamma' — and the greedy little sister, stuffing herself with the ferryman's plantain, repeats it wrong, is caught over the hill, carried to the river and killed; from that day the Devil's hair came off at the sea-side, and the sea got moss.
summary.zh: 老渡工向每個渡河的孩子討早飯，唯獨一個不給——他便淹死她，任水位隨歌聲一寸寸上漲，直到母親付兩鎊。魔鬼篇：通關口訣是『沒有一個過路、沒有兩個過路、沒有三個過路，只有他為媽媽過路』——貪嘴的小妹吃了渡口的芭蕉，把口訣念岔，被捉過山、拖到河邊殺害；從那天起，魔鬼在海邊掉了頭髮，海裡便生了苔。

sensitivity.note: Paired cautionary tales (river-toll and password types). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: The children were going to school, and every day the old man took them over the river. The old man asked some of them for breakfast; all the children gave him some but one. He appointed a day to come, and said he wanted something from her, and she would not give it. When she was coming back, the river came down; he took over the rest of the children and would not take over that one. The little boy sang, 'Mudder Galamo, I gwine dead today!' — and every time he sang, the water came up a little higher, while the mother was coming. The old man said, 'I must have two pounds'; she said all right, and took him over — and from that day he offered the old man breakfast every day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 76a 'Crossing the River' (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 孩子們上學去，每天老人送他們過河。老人向其中一些人討早飯；所有孩子都給了，只有一個不給。他定下一個日子再來，說想要她一樣東西，她不肯給。她回來的時候，河水漲了；他把其餘的孩子都送過去，偏不渡那一個。小男孩唱道：「加拉莫媽媽，我今天要死了！」——他每唱一次，水就漲高一點。

passages.text: Every night the Debbil went out; coming in he said, 'Wife, I scent fresh blood!' — 'No, me husband, no fresh blood here!' It was the wife's sisters who came looking for her. Every night when the Debbil was coming in, the wife knew and put the sister into a barrel. At daylight he went back over the river; the sister was given a plantain and told that when she reached the hill she would see the Debbil sitting right over it, and he would say, 'Go s'y (go your way), madame?' — and she must say, 'No one go s'y, no two go s'y, no three go s'y, but it go s'y for him mamma,' and the Debbil would let her pass.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 76b 'The Plantain' (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 惡魔夜夜出門；回來時他說：「妻子，我聞到新鮮的血了！」——「沒有，我的丈夫，這裏沒有新鮮的血！」原是妻子們的姐妹來找她。惡魔夜裏進門時妻子都知道，便把姐妹裝進一隻桶裏。天一亮他回河那邊去；姐妹得了一根芭蕉，還被告知走到山岡就會看見惡魔坐在上面，他會說「走你的路吧，太太？」——而她必須答「不是

passages.text: There was a little small sister, and she was greedy. When the Debbil came in the night he smelled fresh blood; the wife denied it. At daylight the sister sent the little girl away and gave her a plantain; on the hill the Debbil said, 'Go s'y?' — and the little girl, so greedy now, said, 'No, go s'y for mamma, no one go s'y...' — and the Debbil caught her over the hill, carried her right over to the river and killed her. And from that day the Debbil's hair came off at the sea-side; and from that, the sea got moss.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 76b, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一個小小的妹妹，她貪吃。惡魔夜裏進來聞到新鮮的血；妻子否認。天亮時姐姐打發小姑娘走，給了她一根芭蕉；在山岡上惡魔說：「走你的路吧？」——小姑娘貪心到了極點，答道：「不是，替媽媽走你的路吧，沒有人走你的路……」惡魔便在山岡上抓住了她，把她一直帶到河邊殺了。從那天起，惡魔的毛髮在海邊脫落了；從那時起，

title.en: Alimoty and Aliminty: the Swapped Frocks
title.zh: 阿莉莫蒂與阿莉明蒂：調換的衣裳

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山區

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (2024), tale 77 'Alimoty and Aliminty' (told by Julia Gentle, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Jealous of the beloved niece Alimoty, the aunt contracts Lion to kill the girl in the red frock — and each night the frocks are swapped by the girls themselves, so Lion kills the aunt's own daughter, twice, until there are none. Sent to Lion's yard to be killed, Alimoty passes her dead mother's grave, drops the bottle of milk left there, and sings her fate — until the hunter Aliminty hears the voice, comes to the Lion's yard, and kills the Lion.
summary.zh: 嬸母妒忌人人喜愛的姪女阿莉莫蒂，約獅子誅殺穿紅裙者——女孩們夜夜自己調換衣裳，獅子兩次殺的都是嬸母的親生女兒，直至無女可殺。被送赴獅穴途中，阿莉莫蒂經過亡母墳前，失手跌落墓前留下的奶瓶，唱起自己的命運——獵人阿莉明蒂聞聲辨人，趕到獅穴誅獅。

sensitivity.note: Killed-through-swap tale (cruel stepmother type). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: One day a lady had two daughters, but her sister had one; the sister's daughter was named Alimoty, and everybody loved Alimoty but nobody loved the lady's daughters. She went to the Lion and told him he must kill Alimoty for her. The Lion said she must put a red frock on Alimoty and a blue frock on her own daughter when they went to bed. After going to bed, the girl said, 'Cousin Alimoty, your red frock doesn't fit you; let us swap!' — and they swapped, and the Lion killed the lady's daughter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 77 (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一天，一位太太有兩個女兒，她的妹妹卻只有一個；妹妹的女兒叫阿利莫提，人人都愛阿利莫提，卻沒有人愛太太的女兒。她去見獅子，叫他為她殺掉阿利莫提。獅子說她必須在她們睡覺時給阿利莫提穿上紅裙子，給自己的女兒穿上藍裙子。睡下之後，姑娘說：「阿利莫提表妹，你的紅裙子不合身；我們換一換吧！」——她們換了，獅子殺死了太太的女兒。

passages.text: Then the lady told the Lion to kill Alimoty, whom everybody loved. 'Tonight you must sew the red frock on Alimoty and the blue frock on your daughter, and I come and kill her tonight.' When they went to bed they swapped again, and the Lion killed the lady's daughter — she had none now. The Lion said, 'Tomorrow send Alimoty to my yard; I will kill her.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 77, middle (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 太太便叫獅子去殺人人喜愛的阿利莫提。「今晚你要在阿利莫提身上縫上紅裙子，在你女兒身上縫上藍裙子，我今晚來殺她。」她們睡下時又換了一次，獅子又殺死了太太的女兒——她一個女兒也沒有了。獅子說：「明天把阿利莫提送到我的院子來；我要殺她。」

passages.text: Alimoty was going from the yard and her dead mother gave her a bottle of milk, which she dropped, and she ran off singing — 'Poor me, Alimoty, poor Alimoty, a me Dickie sahnie o-o, see me go long a wid two.' Aliminty was a hunter and heard the singing: 'That is Alimoty's voice!' He came to the Lion's yard and killed the Lion.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 77, ending (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿利莫提離開院子時，死去的母親給了她一瓶奶，她失手掉了，便一路唱著走開——「可憐的我，阿利莫提，可憐的阿利莫提，是我迪奇薩尼哦哦，看我一路走來還有兩個。」阿利敏提是個獵人，聽見歌聲：「那是阿利莫提的聲音！」他來到獅子的院子，殺死了獅子。

title.en: King Mu and the Sky-Palace of the Western Magician (Liezi)
title.zh: 周穆王西極化人，天上宮闕（列子周穆王篇）

region.en: The magician's palace above the clouds (symbolic pin: Mount Tianshan, Xinjiang, China)
region.zh: 雲雨之上化人之宮（象徵定位：新疆天山）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book III (Dreams)

summary.en: A magician from the far west, who could pass through fire and water and ride on thin air, treats King Mu of Chou to a flight up to his own palace of gold, silver, pearls and jade towering above clouds and rain — then to a region where neither sun nor moon could be seen. When the King begs to return, the magician gives him a shove, and he wakes on his throne with the wine still full of sediment: we were only wandering about in the spirit.
summary.zh: 周穆王時，西極之國有化人來，入水火，貫金石，乘虛不墜——王與之同遊；化人宮中，金銀珠玉之府；覺而坐其所坐之處，酒未清，肴未朒。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the King Mu flight is the classic Taoist otherworld-voyage, cross-linked to the chinese tradition's Mu Wang record. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: In the time of King Mu of Chou, there was a magician who came from a kingdom in the far west. He could pass through fire and water, penetrate metal and stone, overturn mountains and make rivers flow backwards, transplant whole towns and cities, ride on thin air without falling, encounter solid bodies without being obstructed. There was no end to the countless variety of changes and transformations which he could effect; and, besides changing the external form, he could also spirit away men's internal cares.
passages.zh: 周穆王之時，西極之國有化人來。入水火，貫金石；反山川，移城邑；乘虛不墜，觸實不硋。千變萬化，不可窮極。既已變物之形，又且易人之慮。

passages.text: So the King clutched the magician's sleeve, and soared up with him higher and higher into the sky, until at last they stopped, and lo! they had reached the magician's own palace. This palace was built with beams of gold and silver, and incrusted with pearls and jade. It towered high above the region of clouds and rain, and the foundations whereon it rested were unknown. It appeared like a stupendous cloud-mass to the view. The King verily believed that he was in the Halls of Paradise, tenanted by God Himself, and that he was listening to the mighty music of the spheres.
passages.zh: 王執化人之袪，騰而上者，中天乃止。暨及化人之宮。構以金銀，絡以珠玉；出雲雨之上，而不知下之所據，望之若屯雲焉。王自以為居數十百年，不思其國也。……王俯而視之，其宮榭若累塊積蘇焉。王自以居數十年不思其國也。

passages.text: When he awoke to consciousness, he found himself sitting on his throne just as before, with the selfsame attendants round him. He looked at the wine in front of him, and saw that it was still full of sediment; he looked at the viands, and found that they had not yet lost their freshness. ... "Your Majesty and I," replied the magician, "were only wandering about in the spirit, and, of course, our bodies never moved at all. What essential difference is there between that sky-palace we dwelt in and your Majesty's palace on earth, between the spaces we travelled through and your Majesty's own park?"
passages.zh: 既寤，所坐猶曩者之處，侍御猶曩者之人。視其前，則酒未清，餚未暍。……王問所從來。曰：「王與吾同遊，形不動也，況厥宮居與吾同者乎，何所殊異哉？」

title.en: Life Is Really Illusion, Death Is Really Evolution (Liezi)
title.zh: 生者，假借也；死者，歸人也（列子周穆王篇）

region.en: The venerable Yin Wen's inner apartment (symbolic pin: Qi, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 尹文先生之室（象徵定位：齊，今山東）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book III (Dreams)

summary.en: Lao Ch'êng Tzŭ studies magic under the venerable Yin Wen for three years; the old teacher quotes Lao Tzŭ's western journey: all that has the breath of life is mere Illusion — only one who knows that Life is really Illusion and Death is really Evolution can begin to learn magic from me. Returning home, Lao Ch'êng Tzŭ gains the power of appearing or disappearing at will but never makes public display of his art.
summary.zh: 老成子學幻於尹文先生——盡幻者之數——窮神知化，德之盛也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Long ago, when Lao Tzu was setting out on his journey to the West, he addressed me and said: 'All that has the breath of life, all that possesses bodily form, is mere Illusion. The point at which creation begins, the change effected by the Dual Principles -- these are called respectively Life and Death. That which underlies the manifold workings of Destiny is called Evolution; that which produces and transforms bodily substance is called Illusion. The Creator's ingenuity is mysterious, His operations secret and profound. In truth, He is inexhaustible and eternal.
passages.zh: 昔老聃之徂西也，顧而告予曰：有生之氣，有形之狀，盡幻也。造化之所始，陰陽之所變者，謂之生，謂之死。窮數達變，因形移易者，謂之化，謂之幻。造物者其巧妙，其功深。

passages.text: Only one who knows that Life is really Illusion, and that Death is really Evolution, can begin to learn magic from me. You and I are both illusions. How are we, then, to make a study of the subject? ... Lao Ch'eng Tsu returned home, and for three months pondered deeply over the words of the Venerable Yin Wen. Subsequently, he had the power of appearing or disappearing at will; he could reverse the order of the four seasons, produce thunderstorms in winter and ice in summer, make flying things creep and creeping things fly. But to the end of his days he never made any public display of his art.
passages.zh: 故知幻化之不異生死也，始可與學幻矣。吾與汝亦幻也，奚須學哉！……尹文先生歸，三月不廢。從而學幻，遂能隱形現形，冬起雷，夏造冰，飛者走，走者飛。

title.en: King by Night, Slave by Day (Liezi)
title.zh: 尹氏老役夫，晝為僕，夜為君（列子周穆王篇）

region.en: Mr. Yin's estate in Chou (symbolic pin: Luoyang, Henan, China)
region.zh: 周尹氏之莊（象徵定位：河南洛陽）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book III (Dreams)

summary.en: The old servant of Mr. Yin, worked mercilessly all day, dreams every night that he is a king enthroned in authority — my happiness is beyond compare, so what have I to grumble at? Mr. Yin himself, full of worldly cares, dreams every night that he is another man's servant, until his friend explains the proper balance in human destiny.
summary.zh: 周之尹氏大治產，其下趣役者侵晨昏而弗息——役夫曰：吾晝為人僕，吾夜為人君；樂樂孰加焉？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: There was one old servant in particular whose physical strength had quite left him, yet his master worked him all the harder. All day long he was groaning as he went about his work, and when night came he was reeling with fatigue and would sleep like a log. His spirit was then free to wander at will, and every night he dreamt that he was a king, enthroned in authority over the multitude, and controlling the affairs of the whole State. He took his pleasure in palaces and belvederes, following his own fancy in everything, and his happiness was beyond compare.
passages.zh: （役夫）晝則呻吟即事，夜則昏愈而熟寐。精神荒散，昔昔夢為人君，居人民之上，總一國之事。遊燕宮觀，恣意所欲，其樂無比。覺則復役人。

passages.text: In the daytime I am only a slave, it is true, and my misery cannot be gainsaid. But by night I am a king, and my happiness is beyond compare. So what have I to grumble at?" ... Every night he dreamt that he was another man's servant, running about on menial business of every description, and subjected to every possible kind of abuse and ill-treatment. ... "If at night you dream that you are a servant and exchange ease for affliction, that is only the proper balance in human destiny. What you want is that your dreams should be as pleasant as your waking moments. But that is beyond your power to compass."
passages.zh: 「晝為僕，苦則苦矣；夜為人君，其樂無比。何所怨哉！」……（尹氏之役夫）昔昔夢為人僕，趨走作役，無不為也；數罵杖撻，無不至也。眠中啽呓呻呼，徹旦息焉。……「若夜夢為僕，勞與苦易之，此命之相也。汝何所欲哉！」

title.en: The Wood-Cutter, the Dream-Deer, and the Magistrate (Liezi)
title.zh: 鄭人獲鹿，薪者夢鹿（列子周穆王篇）

region.en: The fuel-wood path of Chêng (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 鄭國薪樵之塗（今河南鄭州）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book III (Dreams)

summary.en: A wood-cutter kills a deer, hides it in a dry ditch, and forgets the spot — becoming convinced it was all a dream. A hearer finds the deer; his wife declares it must be his own dream that has come true. The wood-cutter, dreaming that night of the real hiding-place, recovers it, and the magistrate divides the deer between them: you began by really killing a deer, but wrongly thought it was a dream.
summary.zh: 鄭人有薪於野者，遇駭鹿，御而擊之，斃之；藏諸隍中——遽而失其處，遂以為夢。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the dream-deer lawsuit became the classic Chinese dream-paradox tale. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: A man was gathering fuel in the Cheng State when he fell in with a deer that had been startled from its usual haunts. He gave chase, and succeeded in killing it. He was overjoyed at his good luck; but, for fear of discovery, he hastily concealed the carcass in a dry ditch, and covered it up with brushwood. Afterwards, he forgot the spot where he had hidden the deer, and finally became convinced that the whole affair was only a dream. He told the story to people he met as he went along; and one of those who heard it, following the indications given, went and found the deer.
passages.zh: 鄭人有薪於野者，遇駭鹿，御而擊之，斃之。恐人見之也，遽而藏諸隍中，覆之以蕉，不勝其喜。俄而遺其所藏之處，遂以為夢焉。順塗而詠其事。路人有聞之者，因取之。

passages.text: "Once upon a time," he said to his wife, "a wood-cutter dreamt that he had got a deer, but couldn't remember the place where he had put it. Now I have found the deer, so it appears that his dream was a true dream." "On the contrary," said his wife, "it is you who must have dreamt that you met a wood-cutter who had caught a deer. Here you have a deer, true enough. But where is the wood-cutter? It is evidently your dream that has come true."
passages.zh: （薪者）告其室人曰：「向薪者夢得鹿而不知其處；吾今得之，彼直夢矣。」室人曰：「若將是夢得鹿與薪者？今真得鹿，是夢與鹿不異也。」

passages.text: So the next morning, in accordance with his dream, he went to seek him out in order to recover the deer. A quarrel ensued, and the matter was finally brought before the magistrate, who gave judgment in these terms: "You began by really killing a deer, but wrongly thought it was a dream. Then you really dreamt that you had got the deer, but wrongly took the dream to be a reality. ... Meanwhile, here is the deer itself in court, and you had better divide it between you." The question was referred to the Prime Minister: "If you want to distinguish between waking and dreaming, you would have to go back to the Yellow Emperor or Confucius. But both these sages are dead, and there is nobody now alive who can draw any such distinction."
passages.zh: 薪者歸，不甘失鹿，並以夢徵之於人，遂致訟於士師。士師曰：「若初真得鹿，妄謂之夢；真夢得鹿，妄謂之實。……嘿而得鹿，聊以分之。」遂以聞之鄭君。鄭君曰：「嘻！士師將復夢分人鹿乎？」

title.en: Yang-li Hua-tzŭ's Blessed Amnesia (Liezi)
title.zh: 秦人逢氏子有忘疾，楊里華子（列子周穆王篇）

region.en: The Sung State (Shangqiu, Henan, China)
region.zh: 宋國（今河南商丘）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book III (Dreams)

summary.en: Yang-li Hua-tzŭ of Sung is afflicted in middle age by amnesia; fortune-tellers, wizards, and physicians all fail, until the learned professor from Lu shuts himself up seven days alone with the patient — whereupon the disease disappears. And Hua-tzŭ flies into a rage: preservation and destruction, gain and loss, sorrow and joy have begun to throw out their myriad tentacles to invade my peace — oh! if I could but recapture a short moment of that blessed oblivion!
summary.zh: 宋陽里華子，中年病忘——魯儒生能治之；既愈，大怒曰：曩吾忘也，蕩蕩然——今往事之是非，哀樂嗜欲得喪，相與繆刺之若此。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Yang-li Hua-tzu, of the Sung State, was afflicted in middle age by the disease of amnesia. Anything he received in the morning he had forgotten by the evening; anything he gave away in the evening he had forgotten the next morning. Out-of-doors, he forgot to walk; indoors, he forgot to sit down. ... Fortune-tellers were summoned, but their divinations proved unsuccessful; wizards were sought out, but their exorcisms were ineffectual; physicians were called in, but their remedies were of no avail.
passages.zh: 宋陽里華子中年病忘，朝取而夕忘，夕與而朝忘；在塗則忘行，在室則忘坐。……史卜占之而不中，巫禱禳之而弗效，扁鵲曰：「是固非吾所能治也。」

passages.text: Then, one fine morning, the treatment came to an end, and, wonderful to relate, the disease of so many years' standing had entirely disappeared! No sooner had Hua-tzu regained his senses, however, than he flew into a great rage, drove his wife out of doors, beat his sons, and, snatching up a spear, hotly pursued the professor through the town. "Lately, when I was steeped in forgetfulness, my senses were so benumbed that I was quite unconscious of the existence of the outer world. But now I have been brought suddenly to a perception of the events of half a lifetime. Preservation and destruction, gain and loss, sorrow and joy, love and hate have begun to throw out their myriad tentacles to invade my peace. Oh! if I could but recapture a short moment of that blessed oblivion!"
passages.zh: 一旦儒生以術彌，歷七年而疾愈。華子既悟，乃大怒，黜妻罰子，操戈逐儒生。……曰：「曩吾忘也，蕩蕩然不覺天地之有無。今頓識既往數十年來存亡得失哀樂好惡，擾擾萬緒起矣。

title.en: The Old Man of Yen Who Wept for a Hoaxed Homeland (Liezi)
title.zh: 燕人生於燕，長於楚（列子周穆王篇）

region.en: The road from Ch'u to Yen (symbolic pin: Beijing, China)
region.zh: 楚適燕之塗（象徵定位：北京）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book III (Dreams)

summary.en: A man born in Yen and brought up in Ch'u returns to his native country in old age; his fellow-travellers hoax him through the Chin State — the capital of Yen! your village altar! your ancestors' tomb! — until he weeps aloud, then they laugh: this is only the Chin State. When he really does see the city and altars of Yen, his emotion is much less acute.
summary.zh: 燕人生於燕，長於楚，及老而還本國——過晉國，同行者誑之：此燕國之城、先人之廬、先人之壟——燕人大哭；眾人皆大笑。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: There was once a man who, though born in Yen, was brought up in Ch'u, and it was only in his old age that he returned to his native country. On the way thither, as they were passing through the Chin State, his fellow-travellers played a practical joke on him. They pointed to the city and said: "Here is the capital of the Yen State;" whereupon the old man flushed with excitement. Pointing out a certain shrine, they told him that it was his own village altar, and he heaved a deep sigh. They showed him a house, and said: "This is where your ancestors lived;" and the tears welled up in his eyes.
passages.zh: 燕人生於燕，長於楚，及老而還本國。過晉國，同行者誑之，指城曰：「此燕國之城。」其人愀然變容。指社曰：「此若里之社。」乃喟然而嘆。指舍曰：「此若先人之廬。」乃涓然而泣。

passages.text: Finally, they brought him in front of a mound and said: "This is the tomb where your ancestors lie buried." The old man could control himself no longer, and wept aloud. But his fellow-travellers burst into roars of laughter. "We have been hoaxing you," they cried; "this is only the Chin State." Their victim was greatly mortified; and when they arrived at their journey's end, and he really did see before him the city and altars of Yen, with the actual abode and tombs of his ancestors, his emotion was much less acute.
passages.zh: 指壟曰：「此若先人之冢。」其人自哭失聲。同行者啞然大笑，曰：「昔予誑若，此晉國耳。」其人大慚。及至燕，真見燕國之城社，真見先人之廬冢，悲心更微。

title.en: Confucius and the True Sage in the West (Liezi)
title.zh: 西方之人有聖者焉（列子仲尼篇）

region.en: The court of the Shang minister (symbolic pin: Anyang, Henan, China)
region.zh: 商太宰之廷（象徵定位：河南安陽）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book IV (Confucius)

summary.en: A high official from Shang quizzes Confucius on the sages — the Three Kings, Five Emperors, Three Sovereigns — and gets the same 'I do not know that they were sages.' Confucius changes countenance: among the people of the West a true sage dwells — he governs not, yet there is no disorder; he speaks not, yet he is naturally trusted; so great and incomprehensible is he that the people can find no name to call him by.
summary.zh: 商太宰問於孔子：三王、五帝、三皇皆聖乎？孔子曰：西方之人有聖者焉——不治而不亂，不言而自信，不化而自行，蕩蕩乎民無能名焉。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the 'true sage in the West' passage later attracted the Jesuit reading as an allusion to Christ. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: A high official from Shang paid a visit to Confucius. "You are a sage, are you not?" he inquired. "A sage!" replied Confucius. "How could I venture to think so? I am only a man of extensive learning and moral culture." The Minister then asked: "Were the Three Kings sages?" "The Three Kings," replied Confucius, "were great in the exercise of wisdom and courage. I do not know, however, that they were sages." "What of the Five Emperors? Were they not sages?" "The Five Emperors excelled in the exercise of altruism and righteousness. I do not know that they were sages." "And the Three Sovereigns: surely they were sages?" "The Three Sovereigns excelled in the virtues that were suited to their age. But whether they were sages or no I really cannot say."
passages.zh: 商太宰見孔子曰：「丘聖者歟？」孔子曰：「聖則丘何敢，然則丘博學多識者也。」商太宰又問：「三王孰聖？」孔子曰：「三王善任智勇者，聖則丘弗知。」又問：「五帝孰聖？」孔子曰：「五帝善任仁義者，聖則丘弗知。」

passages.text: The expression of Confucius' countenance changed, and he replied after a pause: "Among the people of the West a true sage dwells. He governs not, yet there is no disorder. He speaks not, yet he is naturally trusted. He makes no reforms, yet right conduct is spontaneous and universal. So great and incomprehensible is he that the people can find no name to call him by. I suspect that this man is a sage, but whether in truth he is a sage or is not a sage I do not know." The Minister from Shang meditated awhile in silence. Then he said to himself: "Confucius is making a fool of me!"
passages.zh: 三皇孰聖？曰：「三皇善任時力者，聖則丘弗知。」商太宰大駭曰：「然則孰者為聖？」孔子動容有間，曰：「西方之人有聖者焉，不治而不亂，不言而自信，不化而自行，蕩蕩乎民無能名焉。丘疑其為聖，弗知真為聖歟，真不聖歟？」商太宰默然心計曰：

title.en: The Repulsive-Looking Nan-kuo Tzŭ (Liezi)
title.zh: 南郭子貌陋而心虛（列子仲尼篇）

region.en: Nan-kuo, Lieh Tzŭ's neighbourhood (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 南郭（今河南鄭州）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book IV (Confucius)

summary.en: Nan-kuo Tzŭ, Lieh Tzŭ's next-door neighbour of twenty years with whom no visit passed, turns out to be a repulsive-looking creature who gazes blankly, body and soul seeming not to belong together — yet he fraternises with the hindmost row of disciples. He who has reached the stage of thought is silent; he who uses silence in lieu of speech really does speak.
summary.zh: 子列子學於壺丘子林——南郭子貌陋，形若槁木；迎見而語——見同者形骸之外，不以鏡之於形骸。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Nan-kuo Tzu was his next-door neighbour, but for twenty years no visit passed between them, and when they met in the street they made as though they had not seen each other. ... Accordingly, forty of the disciples went with him to call on Nan-kuo Tzu, who turned out to be a repulsive-looking creature. He made no show of receiving his guests, but only gazed blankly at Lieh Tzu. Body and soul seemed not to belong together, and to be unable to respond to the stimuli of the external world.
passages.zh: 南郭子貌充，與列子為友二十年，不相聞問；遇於道，目若不見。……及歸，以告壺丘子，壺丘子曰：「盍與之來乎？」四十弟子皆往見之。南郭子見其形容枯槁，形若槁木，不與賓客酬酢，唯列子目之而已。

passages.text: Their Master Lieh Tzu said to them: "He who has reached the stage of thought is silent. He who has attained to perfect knowledge is also silent. He who uses silence in lieu of speech really does speak. He who for knowledge substitutes blankness of mind really does know. Without words and speaking not, without knowledge and knowing not, he really speaks and really knows. Saying nothing and knowing nothing, there is in reality nothing that he does not say, nothing that he does not know."
passages.zh: 列子曰：「至其去也，默而正之；至言者不言，至知者不知。夫無言無言，故無聲響之中而實言；無知無知，故冥然坐忘而實知。」

title.en: Lung Shu's Hollow Square Inch of Heart (Liezi)
title.zh: 龍叔謂文摯：心有七孔（列子仲尼篇）

region.en: The physician's chamber (symbolic pin: Linzi, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 文摯之室（象徵定位：山東臨淄）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book IV (Confucius)

summary.en: Lung Shu tells the master of cunning arts that praise and disgrace, gain and loss, life and death, riches and poverty excite him nothing — what disease is this? Wen Chih, facing the light, sees that a good square inch of Lung Shu's heart is hollow, six of its orifices open and only the seventh blocked: you are mistaking for a disease that which is really divine enlightenment.
summary.zh: 龍叔謂文摯曰：吾疾——譽不以為榮，毀不以為辱；得而不喜，失而弗憂——文摯曰：見子之心矣，方寸之地虛矣；幾聖人也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: "I hold it no honour," said Lung Shu, "to be praised in my native village, nor do I consider it a disgrace to be decried in my native State. Gain excites in me no joy, and loss no sorrow. I look upon life in the same light as death, upon riches in the same light as poverty, upon my fellow-men as so many swine, and upon myself as I look upon my fellow-men. I dwell in my home as though it were a mere caravanserai, and regard my native district with no more feeling than I would a barbarian State. Afflicted as I am in these various ways, honours and rewards fail to rouse me, pains and penalties to overawe me, good or bad fortune to influence me, joy or grief to move me."
passages.zh: 龍叔謂文摯曰：「子之術微矣！吾有疾，子能已乎？」文摯曰：「唯命所聽。然先言子所病之證。」龍叔曰：「吾鄉譽不以為榮，吾國毀不以為辱；得而不喜，失而弗憂；視生猶死，視富猶貧；視人猶豕，視吾猶人。宅如逆旅，視吾鄉黨如蠻夷之國。

passages.text: Wen Chih replied by asking Lung Shu to stand with his back to the light, while he himself faced the light and looked at him intently. "Ah!" said he after a while, "I see that a good square inch of your heart is hollow. You are within an ace of being a true sage. Six of the orifices in your heart are open and clear, and only the seventh is blocked up. This, however, is doubtless due to the fact that you are mistaking for a disease that which is really divine enlightenment. It is a case in which my shallow art is of no avail."
passages.zh: 文摯乃命龍叔背明而立，文摯自後向之而望焉，曰：「嘻！吾見子之心矣。方寸之地虛矣。幾聖人也！子心六孔流通，一孔不達。今以聖智為疾者，或由是乎！非吾淺術所能攻也。」

title.en: Teng Hsi's Herd of Swine and the Retort of the Vassals (Liezi)
title.zh: 鄧析難伯豐子，如犬彘乎（列子仲尼篇）

region.en: Tung-li, in the Chêng State (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 鄧里（今河南鄭州）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book IV (Confucius)

summary.en: Teng Hsi the sophist greets the vassals of Po Feng Tzu with the sneer that those who receive sustenance from others through inability to support themselves are in the category of dogs and swine. One of the company retorts: it is really we who may be said to employ the Government authorities — only when there is a combination of technical knowledge and power can co-operative service exist. Teng Hsi could think of nothing to say in reply.
summary.zh: 鄧析顧其徒曰：為若受——子不能自給，受養於人，犬豕之類也。伯豐子之從者曰：齊楚之處士多為工焉——吾實謂役使君之臣者。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Teng Hsi then turned to Po Feng Tzu. "Are you acquainted with the true theory of Sustentation?" he inquired. "To receive sustenance from others, through inability to support oneself, places one in the category of dogs and swine. It is man's prerogative to give sustenance to other creatures, and to use them for his own purposes. That you and your fellows are provided with abundant food and comfortable clothing is due to the Government. Young and old, you herd together, and are penned up like cattle destined for the shambles: in what respect are you to be distinguished from dogs and swine?"
passages.zh: 鄧析謂伯豐子曰：「汝知養養之義乎？受人養而不能自養者，犬豕之類也；養萬物則人之為也。汝曹飽食暖衣，厚養以待，長幼相聚而為牢蒭乎！」

passages.text: One of his company, disregarding the rules of precedence, stepped forward and said: "Has your Excellency never heard of the variety of craftsmen in Ch'i and Lu? Some are skilled potters and carpenters, others are clever workers in metal and leather; there are good musicians, trained scribes and accountants, military experts and men learned in the ritual of ancestor-worship. All kinds of craftsmanship are there fully represented. Now, if there were no division of ranks and duties, mutual co-operation would be impossible. ... It is really we who may be said to employ the Government authorities. Why then should you pity us?" Teng Hsi could think of nothing to say in reply.
passages.zh: 伯豐子之從者越次而進曰：「大夫不聞齊魯之多機乎？有善治土木者，有善冶金革者，有善作聲樂者，有善書數者，有善軍旅者，有善宗廟祭祀者。群才備也。而無位無尊者，事之不相資也。……居上位者，豈不能用人哉！」

title.en: T'ang Asks Hsia Ko Whether Things Existed in the Beginning (Liezi)
title.zh: 殷湯問於夏革：古初有物乎？（列子湯問篇）

region.en: The court of T'ang of Yin (Anyang, Henan, China)
region.zh: 殷湯之廷（今河南安陽）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book V (The Questions of T'ang)

summary.en: In the beginnings of antiquity, did individual things exist? asks T'ang of Yin. If things did not exist then, how could they be in existence now? replies Hsia Ko — to the beginning and end of things there is no precise limit; beginning may be end, and end may be beginning; but when it comes to something outside matter in space or anterior to events in time, our knowledge fails us.
summary.zh: 殷湯問於夏革曰：古初有物乎？夏革曰：古初無物，今惡得物——物之始終，初無極已；始或為終，終或為始。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; a priority Creation & Cosmology dialogue. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: T'ANG of Yin questioned Hsia Ko, saying: "In the beginnings of antiquity, did individual things exist?" "If things did not exist then," replied Hsia Ko, "how could they be in existence now? Or will the men of future ages be right in denying the existence of things at the present time?" "Things in that case," pursued T'ang, "have no before nor after?" Hsia Ko replied: "To the beginning and end of things there is no precise limit. Beginning may be end, and end may be beginning. How can we conceive of any fixed period to either?
passages.zh: 殷湯問於夏革曰：「古初有物乎？」夏革曰：「古初無物，今惡得物？後之人將謂今之無物，可乎？」湯曰：「然則物無先後？」曰：「物之終始，初無極已。始或為終，終或為始，惡知其紀？」

passages.text: But when it comes to something outside matter in space, or anterior to events in time, our knowledge fails us." "Then, upwards and downwards and in every direction space is a finite quantity?" Ko replied: "I do not know." T'ang asked the question again with more insistence, and Ko said: "It may be that space is infinite, or it may be that it is limited. How can I tell? But beyond infinity there must again exist non-infinity, and within the unlimited again that which is not unlimited.
passages.zh: 然自物之外，自事之先，朕所不知也。……湯曰：「然則上下八方有極乎？」革曰：「不知也。」湯固問。革曰：「無則無極，有則有盡，朕何以知之？然無極之外復無無極，無盡之中復無無盡。

title.en: The Outer Shell That Encloses Heaven and Earth (Liezi)
title.zh: 四海之外，六合之外（列子湯問篇）

region.en: The lands beyond the Four Seas (symbolic pin: Yantai, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 四海之外（象徵定位：山東煙臺）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book V (The Questions of T'ang)

summary.en: What is there beyond the Four Seas? Just what there is here in the province of Ch'i — Hsia Ko travelled east to Ying and west to Pin and found the inhabitants nowise different. The lesser is always enclosed by a greater without ever reaching an end: heaven and earth, which enclose the myriad objects, are themselves enclosed in some outer shell that is infinite and immeasurable.
summary.zh: 四海之外奚若？曰：猶齊州也——大猶含小，終無窮已；天地含物之體，亦自含於太虛。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: T'ang continued his inquiries, saying: "What is there beyond the Four Seas?" Ko replied: "Just what there is here in the province of Ch'i." "How can you prove that?" asked T'ang. "When travelling eastwards," said Ko, "I came to the land of Ying, where the inhabitants were nowise different from those in this part of the country. I inquired about the countries east of Ying, and found that they, too, were similar to their neighbour. Travelling westwards, I came to Pin, where the inhabitants were similar to our own countrymen. ... That is how I know that the regions within the Four Seas, the Four Wildernesses and the Four Uttermost Ends of the Earth are nowise different from the country we ourselves inhabit.
passages.zh: 湯又問曰：「四海之外奚有？」革曰：「猶齊州也。」湯曰：「汝奚以實之？」革曰：「朕東行至營，人民猶是也。問營之東，復猶營也。西行至豳，人民猶是也。問豳之西，復猶豳也。

passages.text: Thus, the lesser is always enclosed by a greater, without ever reaching an end. Heaven and earth, which enclose the myriad objects of creation, are themselves enclosed in some outer shell. Enclosing heaven and earth and the myriad objects within them, this outer shell is infinite and immeasurable. How do we know but that there is some mightier universe in existence outside our own? That is a question to which we can give no answer.
passages.zh: 朕以是知四海、四荒、四極之不異是也。故大小相含，無窮極也。含萬物者，亦如含天地；含萬物也故不窮，含天地也故無極。朕亦焉知天地之表不有大天地者乎？則吾亦不知也。

title.en: Nü Kua's Five-Coloured Stones and Kung Kung's Snapped Pillar (Liezi)
title.zh: 女媧鍊五色石補天，共工觸不周山（列子湯問篇）

region.en: Mount Pu-chou and the leaning heavens (mythic NW; symbolic pin: Jiayuguan, Gansu, China)
region.zh: 不周山（神話西北；象徵定位：甘肅嘉峪關）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book V (The Questions of T'ang)

summary.en: Heaven and earth are themselves only material objects, and therefore imperfect: Nü Kua of old fashioned many-coloured blocks of stone to repair the defective parts, and cut off the legs of the Ao to support the four corners of the heavens. Later, Kung Kung fought with Chuan Hsü for the throne and blundering in his rage against Mount Pu-chou, snapped the pillar which connects Heaven and earth — that is why Heaven dips downwards to the north-west, and why all rivers roll to the south-east.
summary.zh: 天地亦物也——女媧氏鍊五色石以補其闕，斷鼇足以立四極；共工氏與顓頊爭為帝，怒而觸不周之山，折天柱，絕地維。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the Nü Kua repair-myth cross-linked to the chinese tradition's Huainanzi record of the same story. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Heaven and earth, then, are themselves only material objects, and therefore imperfect. Hence it is that Nii Kua of old fashioned many-coloured blocks of stone to repair the defective parts. He cut off the legs of the Ao and used them to support the four corners of the heavens.
passages.zh: 天地亦物也。物有不足，故昔者女媧氏煉五色石以補其闕；斷鼇之足以立四極。

passages.text: Later on, Kung Kung fought with Chuan Hsu for the throne, and, blundering in his rage against Mount Pu-chou, he snapped the pillar which connects Heaven and earth. That is why Heaven dips downwards to the north-west, so that sun, moon and stars travel towards that quarter. The earth, on the other hand, is now not large enough to fill up the south-east, so that all rivers and streams roll in that direction.
passages.zh: 其後共工氏與顓頊爭為帝，怒而觸不周之山，折天柱，絕地維。故天傾西北，日月星辰就焉；地不滿東南，水潦塵埃歸焉。

title.en: The Exchange of Hearts Performed by Pien-ch'iao (Liezi)
title.zh: 扁鵲換心（列子湯問篇）

region.en: The clinic of the great physician (symbolic pin: Zhengzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 扁鵲之診（象徵定位：河南鄭州）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book V (The Questions of T'ang)

summary.en: Kung-hu of Lu and Ch'i-ying of Chao both fall ill and are cured by Pien-ch'iao — who then offers to grapple with each man's congenital disease: your mental powers are strong but your character is weak, says he to Kung-hu; his are weak while his character is strong. A potion of medicated wine throws them into a three-day death-like trance, and each man's heart is placed in the other's body — leading to a lawsuit between the two families.
summary.zh: 魯公扈趙齊嬰俱疾，扁鵲遂飲二人毒酒，迷死三日；剖胸探心，易而置之——辭而歸，則公扈反齊嬰之室。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the heart-exchange tale is a landmark of Chinese medical myth. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Pien-ch'iao turned to Kung-hu. "Your mental powers," he said, "are strong, but your character is weak. Hence, though fruitful in plans, you are lacking in decision. Ch'i-ying's mental powers, on the other hand, are weak, while his character is strong. Hence there is want of forethought, and he is placed at a disadvantage by the narrowness of his aim. Now, if I can effect an exchange of hearts between you, the good will be equally balanced in both."
passages.zh: 扁鵲遂飲二人毒酒，迷死三日，剖胸探心，易而置之，投以神藥。既悟如初，各辭而歸。……公扈反齊嬰之室，齊嬰反公扈之室，妻子不相識。

passages.text: So saying, Pien-ch'iao administered to each of them a potion of medicated wine, which threw them into a death-like trance lasting three days. Then, making an incision in their breasts, he took out each man's heart and placed it in the other's body, poulticing the wounds with herbs of marvellous efficacy. When the two men regained consciousness, they looked exactly the same as before; and, taking their leave, they returned home. Only it was Kung-hu who went to Ch'i-ying's house, where Ch'i-ying's wife and children naturally did not recognise him, while Ch'i-ying went to Kung-hu's house and was not recognised either. This led to a lawsuit between the two families, and Pien-ch'iao was called in as arbitrator. On his explaining how the matter stood, peace was once more restored.
passages.zh: 扁鵲謂公扈曰：「汝志強而氣弱，故足於謀而寡於斷。齊嬰志弱而氣強，故少於慮而傷於專。若換汝之心，則均於善矣。」

title.en: The Three Magic Swords and the Blood-Feud That Could Not Kill (Liezi)
title.zh: 孔周三劍：含光、承影、宵練（列子湯問篇）

region.en: The house of K'ung Chou of Wei (Anyang region, Henan, China)
region.zh: 衛孔周之家（象徵定位：河南安陽一帶）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book V (The Questions of T'ang)

summary.en: Lai Tan, whose body is slight but whose spirit is fierce, seeks the blood of Hei Luan and borrows one of K'ung Chou's three Yin-Emperor swords — Light-absorber, Shadow-container, Night-tempered. He cuts clean through Hei Luan's body in three places, but the victim is quite unconscious of it; the son laughs that he is merely motioning in a silly way with his hand — the improper use of divine weapons only leads to discomfiture.
summary.zh: 來丹請於衛孔周，得宵練之劍；三斬黑卵之頸——黑卵不覺；其子曰：汝以指揮吾手何也？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the sword allegory satirises the vendetta. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: This Hei Luan was the most ferocious character of his day, and in brute strength he was a match for a hundred men. His bones and sinews, skin and flesh were cast in superhuman mould. He would stretch out his neck to the blade or bare his breast to the arrow, but the sharp steel would bend or break, and his body show no scar from the impact.
passages.zh: 黑卵最驍悍絕倫，力抗百夫。筋骨皮肉，非人間有。挺頸承刃，披胸受矢，鋩摧鐵折，曾無痕皪。

passages.text: "I have three swords," replied K'ung Chou, "but with none of them can you kill a man. You may choose which you like. First, however, let me describe their qualities. The first sword is called 'Light-absorber.' It is invisible to the eye, and when you swing it you cannot tell that there is anything there. Things struck by it retain an unbroken surface, and it will pass through a man's body without his knowing it. The second is called 'Shadow-container.' ... The third is called 'Night-tempered,' because in broad daylight you only see its shadow and not the brightness of its blade, while at night you see not the sword itself but the dazzling light which it emits.
passages.zh: 孔周曰：「吾有三劍，唯其所擇。一曰含光，視之不可見，運之不知有。其所觸也，泯然無際，經物而物不覺。二曰承影，……三曰宵練，……」

passages.text: Grasping his new weapon, Lai Tan now sought out his enemy, and found him lying in a drunken stupor at his window. He cut clean through his body in three places between the neck and the navel, but Hei Luan was quite unconscious of it. ... And happening to meet Hei Luan's son at the door, he struck at him three times with his sword. But it was like hitting the empty air. Hei Luan's son laughed and said: "Why are you motioning to me in that silly way with your hand?" Thus, the improper use of divine weapons only leads to discomfiture.
passages.zh: 來丹遂執劍以尋黑卵，見其醉臥於牖下，自頸及腰三斬之，黑卵不覺。……遇黑卵之子於門，擊之三下，如投虛。其子嘻曰：「汝何怪而三招予？」以此知無所覺。

title.en: Effort and Destiny Argue the Case (Liezi)
title.zh: 力謂命曰：若之功奚若我哉（列子力命篇）

region.en: The debate between human striving and fate (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 力命之辯（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VI (Effort and Destiny)

summary.en: Effort claims power over length of life, success, rank, and wealth; Destiny answers with the catalogue of misallotments — P'êng Tsu's wisdom did not exceed Yao and Shun's, yet he lived eight hundred years; Yen Yüan's ability was not inferior, yet he died at thirty-two; Po I and Shu Ch'i starved at Shou-yang while Chi Shih waxed rich. When the way is straight, I push on; when it is crooked, I let be.
summary.zh: 力謂命曰：若之功奚若我哉？命曰：彭祖之智不出堯舜之上，而壽八百；顏淵之才不出眾人之下，而壽十八——窮聖而達逆，賤賢而貴愚。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: EFFORT said to Destiny: "Your achievements are not equal to mine." "Pray what do you achieve in the working of things," replied Destiny, "that you would compare yourself with me?" "Why," said Effort, "the length of man's life, his measure of success, his rank, and his wealth, are all things which I have the power to determine." To this, Destiny made reply: "P'êng Tsu's wisdom did not exceed that of Yao and Shun, yet he lived to the age of eight hundred. Yen Yüan's ability was not inferior to that of the average man, yet he died at the early age of thirty-two. The virtue of Confucius was not less than that of the feudal princes, yet he was reduced to sore straits between Ch'en and Ts'ai.
passages.zh: 力謂命曰：「若之功奚若我哉？」命曰：「汝奚功於物而欲比朕？」力曰：「壽夭窮達，貴賤貧富，我力之所能也。」命曰：「彭祖之智不出堯舜之上，而壽八百；顏淵之才不出眾人之下，而壽十八。

passages.text: Chi Cha would not accept the overlordship of Wu, while T'ien Hêng usurped sole power in Ch'i. Po I and Shu Ch'i starved to death at Shou-yang, while Chi Shih waxed rich at Chan-ch'in. If these results were compassed by your efforts, how is it that you allotted long life to P'êng Tsu and an untimely death to Yen Yüan; that you awarded discomfiture to the sage and success to the impious, humiliation to the wise man and high honours to the fool, poverty to the good and wealth to the wicked?" ... "When the way is straight, I push on; when it is crooked, I let be. Old age and early death, failure and success, high rank and humble station, riches and poverty -- all these come naturally and of themselves. Of their ultimate causes, I am ignorant; how could it be otherwise?"
passages.zh: 「……季札無爵於吳，田恆專有齊國；夷齊餓於首陽，季氏富於展禽。若是汝力之所能，奈何壽彼而夭此，窮聖而達逆，賤賢而貴愚，貧善而富惡邪？」……命曰：「既謂之命，奈何有制之者邪？」

title.en: Chi Liang's Deathbed and the Three Doctors (Liezi)
title.zh: 季梁之疾，三醫並進（列子力命篇）

region.en: Yang Chu's friend's sick-room (symbolic pin: Kaifeng, Henan, China)
region.zh: 楊朱友人病榻（象徵定位：河南開封）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VI (Effort and Destiny)

summary.en: Yang Chu chants to his weeping friend's sons that over his destiny man has no control. Three doctors diagnose in turn: the origin is traceable to disordered appetites — you are only one of the common ruck, says Chi Liang; it is incurable — you are a good doctor; lastly Dr. Lu: it was already fore-ordained in the mind of Providence when you were endowed with this bodily form at birth — you are a heaven-born physician indeed! Not long after, his illness disappeared of itself.
summary.zh: 楊朱歌曰：天其弗識，人胡能覺？——汝疾非由天，非由人，亦非鬼神；命之所制也。季梁曰：天醫也！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Yang Chu then chanted the following words: "How should men possess the knowledge which God Himself has not? Over his destiny man has no control, and can look for no help from God. You and I know this for truth, but our knowledge is not shared by sorcerers and quacks." The sons, however, did not understand, and finally called in three physicians, Dr. Chiao, Dr. Yü and Dr. Lu.
passages.zh: 楊朱曰：「天其弗知，人其弗知。吾與汝知之，巫醫勿知。」其子不曉，乃延三醫：曰嬌、曰俞、曰盧。

passages.text: Lastly, Dr. Lu said: "Your illness is attributable neither to God, nor to man, nor to the agency of spirits. It was already fore-ordained in the mind of Providence when you were endowed with this bodily form at birth. What possible good can herbs and drugs do you?" "You are a heaven-born physician indeed!" cried Chi Liang; and he sent him away laden with presents. Not long after, his illness disappeared of itself.
passages.zh: 盧醫曰：「汝疾不由天，亦不由人，亦不由鬼。稟生受形，既有制之者矣，亦有知之者矣。藥石其如汝何？」季梁曰：「神醫也！」重貺遣之。俄而季梁之疾自瘳。

title.en: Duke Ching Weeps on the Ox-Mountain and Yen Tzŭ Smiles (Liezi)
title.zh: 齊景公遊於牛山，北臨其國城而流涕（列子力命篇）

region.en: The Ox-mountain north of Linzi (Niushan, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 牛山（今山東臨淄南）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VI (Effort and Destiny)

summary.en: Duke Ching of Ch'i, gazing from the Ox-mountain at his lovely kingdom, weeps that some day he must die and leave it; two fawning ministers weep too. Yen Tzŭ smiles: if the worthy ruler were to remain in perpetual possession, Duke T'ai and Duke Huan would still be exercising their sway — condemned to a hard life on earth, you would have had no time for brooding over death. The Duke fines himself two cups of wine.
summary.zh: 齊景公遊於牛山，北臨其國城而流涕曰：美哉國乎！若何滂滂去此而死乎！晏子獨拊心大笑。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Duke Ching of Ch'i was travelling across the northern flank of the Ox-mountain in the direction of the capital. Gazing at the view before him, he burst into a flood of tears, exclaiming: "What a lovely scene! How verdant and luxuriantly wooded! To think that some day I must die and leave my kingdom, passing away like running water! If only there were no such thing as death, nothing should induce me to stir from this spot." Two of the Ministers in attendance on the Duke, taking their cue from him, also began to weep.
passages.zh: 齊景公遊於牛山，北臨其國城而流涕曰：「美哉國乎！鬱郁芊芊。若何滾滾去此而死者乎！使古無死者，則寡人將去此而何往矣？」史孔梁丘據皆從而泣曰：「然臣賴君之賜，疏食惡肉可得而食，駑馬柴車可得而乘也，猶且嫌死者之先立，不亦哀乎！」

passages.text: Yen Tzu replied: "If the worthy ruler were to remain in perpetual possession of his realm, Duke T'ai and Duke Huan would still be exercising their sway. If the bold ruler were to remain in perpetual possession, Duke Chuang and Duke Ling would still be ruling the land. But if all these rulers were now in possession, where would your Highness be? Why, standing in the furrowed fields, clad in coir cape and hat! ... And are you alone going to weep and lament over this order of things? That is unmanly. It was the sight of these two objects -- an unmanly prince and his fawning attendants -- that was affording me food for laughter just now."
passages.zh: 晏子獨笑於旁。公雪涕而顧晏子曰：「寡人今日之遊悲，孔與據皆從寡人而泣，子之獨笑何也？」晏子對曰：「使賢者常守之，則太公、桓公將常守之矣；使勇者常守之，則莊公、靈公將常守之矣。數君者將守，則吾君安得位焉？……古而無死，其樂若何？吾是以見其為大不義也。」

title.en: Tung-men Wu Does Not Mourn His Son (Liezi)
title.zh: 魏有東門吳者，其子死而不憂（列子力命篇）

region.en: The State of Wei (Anyang region, Henan, China)
region.zh: 魏國（今河南安陽一帶）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VI (Effort and Destiny)

summary.en: Tung-men Wu of Wei testifies no grief when his son dies. There was a time when I had no son, he answers his house-steward; during the whole period that elapsed before my son was born, I never had occasion to grieve. Now that my son is dead, I am only in the same condition as I was before I had a son — what reason have I, then, to mourn?
summary.zh: 魏有東門吳者，其子死而不憂。其室家曰：子之愛子，天下無有；今子死不憂，何也？東門吳曰：吾嘗無子，無子之時不憂。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; paralleled in Zhuangzi's drum-on-basin mourning scenes. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: There was once a man, Tung-men Wu of Wei, who when his son died testified no grief. His house-steward said to him: "The love you bore your son could hardly be equalled by that of any other parent. Why, then, do you not mourn for him now that he is dead?" "There was a time," replied Tung-men Wu, "when I had no son. During the whole period that elapsed before my son was born, I never had occasion to grieve. Now that my son is dead, I am only in the same condition as I was before I had a son. What reason have I, then, to mourn?"
passages.zh: 魏人有東門吳者，其子死而不憂。其相室曰：「公之愛子，天下無有。今子死不憂，何也？」東門吳曰：「吾嘗無子，無子之時不憂。今子死，乃與嚮無子同。吾何憂哉？」

title.en: Do You Know Why You Hit the Target? (Liezi)
title.zh: 列子學射中矣，請於關尹子（列子說符篇）

region.en: Kuan Yin Tzŭ's archery-ground (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 關尹子之射場（象徵定位：河南靈寶函谷關）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: Lieh Tzŭ learns archery and, able to hit the target, asks Kuan Yin Tzŭ's opinion. Do you know why you hit the target? No. Then you are not good enough yet. Three years of practice later: Yes, I do — hold that knowledge fast and do not let it slip.
summary.zh: 列子學射中矣，請於關尹子。尹子曰：子知子之所以中乎？對曰：弗知也——三年，又以報關尹子。曰：可矣，守而勿失也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Lieh Tzü learned archery and, when he was able to hit the target, he asked the opinion of Kuan Yin Tzü on his shooting. "Do you know why you hit the target?" said Kuan Yin Tzü. "No, I do not," was the reply. "Then you are not good enough yet," rejoined Kuan Yin Tzü. Lieh Tzü withdrew and practised for three years, after which he again presented himself. Kuan Yin Tzu asked, as before: "Do you know why you hit the target?" "Yes," said Lieh Tzü, "I do." "In that case, all is well. Hold that knowledge fast, and do not let it slip."
passages.zh: 列子學射中矣，請於關尹子。尹子曰：「子知子之所以中者乎？」對曰：「弗知也。」關尹子曰：「未可。」退而習之，三年，又以報關尹子。尹子曰：「子知子之所以中乎？」列子曰：「知之矣。」關尹子曰：「可矣，守而勿失也。」

title.en: Three Years to Carve a Mulberry Leaf in Jade (Liezi)
title.zh: 宋人以玉為楮葉（列子說符篇）

region.en: The Sung court (Shangqiu, Henan, China)
region.zh: 宋宮（今河南商丘）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: A man of Sung carves a mulberry leaf out of jade for his prince; it takes three years, and imitates Nature so exquisitely that it cannot be distinguished from real leaves in a heap. Lieh Tzŭ hears of it: if it took the Creator three years to make a single leaf, there would be very few trees with leaves on them — the Sage will rely not so much on human science and skill as on the evolution of Tao.
summary.zh: 宋人有為其君以玉為楮葉者，三年而成；列子曰：使天地三年而成一葉，則物之有葉者寡矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: There was once a man in Sung who carved a mulberry leaf out of jade for his prince. It took three years to complete, and it imitated Nature so exquisitely in its down, its glossiness, and its general configuration from tip to stem, that, if placed in a heap of real mulberry leaves, it could not be distinguished from them. This man was subsequently pensioned by the Sung State as a reward for his skill. Lieh Tzu, hearing of it, said: "If it took the Creator three years to make a single leaf, there would be very few trees with leaves on them. The Sage will rely not so much on human science and skill as on the evolution of Tao."
passages.zh: 宋人有為其君以玉為楮葉者，三年而成。鋒殺莖柯，毫芒繁澤，亂之楮葉中而不可別也。此人遂以巧食宋國。列子聞之，曰：「使天地三年而成一葉，則物之有葉者寡矣。」

title.en: The Two Sons of Mr. Shih and Mr. Meng (Liezi)
title.zh: 魯施氏二子，孟氏同業（列子說符篇）

region.en: The courts of Ch'in and Wei (Xianyang and Anyang, China)
region.zh: 秦廷與衛廷（咸陽、安陽）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: Mr. Shih's two sons, scholar and soldier, rise through Ch'i and Ch'u; his poor neighbour Mr. Meng's sons apply the same formula and come to grief — castrated in Ch'in, feet cut off in Wei. Success consists in hitting off the right moment, answers Mr. Shih; nothing in the ordering of this world is either at all times right or at all times wrong.
summary.zh: 魯施氏有二子，其一好學，其一好兵；孟氏同業而不同得——秦王宮刑之，衛侯刖之。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Mr. Shih of Lu had two sons, one of whom was a scholar and the other a soldier. The former found in his accomplishments the means of ingratiating himself with the Marquis of Ch'i, who engaged him as tutor to the young princes. The other brother proceeded to Ch'u, and won favour with the King of that State by his military talents. The King was so well pleased that he installed him at the head of his troops. Thus both of them succeeded in enriching their family and shedding lustre on their kinsfolk.
passages.zh: 魯施氏有二子，其一好學，其一好兵。好學者以齊侯處之，為諸公子之傅；好兵者之楚，以法干楚王，王以為軍正。二子祿，爵其家。……而施氏之鄰孟氏有子同焉，以其所為於施氏，而折兵於秦，刖而歸。

passages.text: The eldest son immediately set off for Ch'in, hoping that his moral culture would recommend him to the King of that State. But the King said: "At the present moment all the feudal princes are struggling to outbid one another in power, and the great essential is to keep up a large army. If I tried to govern my State on the lines of altruism and righteousness, ruin and annihilation would be the outcome." So saying, he had the unfortunate man castrated, and turned him away. The second son, meanwhile, had gone to Wei ... so, without more ado, he cut off his feet and sent him back to Lu.
passages.zh: 孟氏之一子之秦，以仁義干秦王。秦王曰：「今諸侯以力相競，兵革是務。若以仁義治吾國，是滅亡之道也。」遂宮而逐之。其一子之衛，以權干衛侯。衛侯曰：「吾弱國也，攝乎大國之間。以法治齊，以固吾圉，可也。」

passages.text: Mr. Shih, however, said: "Success consists in hitting off the right moment, while missing it means failure. Your method was identical with ours, only the result was different. That is not due to any flaw in the action itself, but simply because it was not well timed. Nothing, in the ordering of this world, is either at all times right or at all times wrong. What formerly passed current may nowadays be rejected; what is now rejected may by and by come into use again."
passages.zh: 施氏曰：「凡得時者昌，失時者亡。子道與吾同，而功與吾異，失時者也，非行之謬也。且天下理無常是，事無常非。先日所用，今或棄之；今之所棄，後或用之。」

title.en: The Duke's Laugh: the Silkworm-Tender and the Escorted Wife (Liezi)
title.zh: 晉文公將伐衛，公子鉏仰天而笑（列子說符篇）

region.en: The army of Chin on the march (Houma, Shanxi, China)
region.zh: 晉師之途（今山西侯馬）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: Duke Wên of Chin marches to attack the Duke of Wei; Tzŭ Ch'u throws his head back and laughs — recalling the neighbour who escorted his wife to her family and stopped to court a silkworm-tending woman, only to find his own wife receiving the attentions of an admirer. The Duke saw the point and turned home — before an invading force had already crossed his northern frontier.
summary.zh: 晉文公出，將伐衛；公子鉏仰天而笑——郊有蠶婦——見其妻之受非望之遇也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Duke Wen of Chin put an army into the field with the intention of attacking the Duke of Wei, whereat Tzŭ Ch'u threw his head back and laughed aloud. On being asked the reason of his behaviour, he replied: "I was thinking of the experience of a neighbour of mine, who was escorting his wife on a visit to her own family. On the way, he came across a woman tending silk worms, who attracted him greatly, and he fell into conversation with her. Happening to look up, what should he see but his own wife also receiving the attentions of an admirer! It was the recollection of this incident that made me laugh." The Duke saw the point, and forthwith turned home with his army. Before he got back, an invading force had already crossed his northern frontier!
passages.zh: 晉文公出，會欲伐衛，公子鉏仰天而笑。公問何笑。曰：「臣笑鄰之人有送其妻之私家者，道見桑婦，悅而與言。然顧視其妻，亦有招之者矣。臣竊笑此也。」

title.en: Ch'i Yung, Who Could Tell a Robber by His Face (Liezi)
title.zh: 晉之郗雍能視盜（列子說符篇）

region.en: The robber-infested Chin State (Houma, Shanxi, China)
region.zh: 晉國盜藪（今山西侯馬）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: In the robber-infested Chin State, Ch'i Yung could tell a robber by his face and read his inmost thoughts; the Marquis delights in him — until the robbers band together and murder him. Wen Tzŭ of Chao has foretold it, quoting the Chou proverb: search not the ocean-depths for fish — and prescribes promoting the worthy to office instead; all the robbers flee to Ch'in.
summary.zh: 晉侯曰：吾有一人，逐盜而獲之。文子曰：以察伺盜，盜不盡矣——周諺有言：察見淵魚者不祥。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: In the Chin State, which was infested with robbers, there lived a certain Ch'i Yung, who was able to tell a robber by his face; by examining the expression of his eyes he could read his inmost thoughts. The Marquis of Chin employed him in the inspection of hundreds and thousands of robbers, and he never missed a single one. The Marquis expressed his delight to Wen Tzu of Chao, saying: "I have a man who, single-handed, is ridding my whole State of robbers." Wen Tzu replied: "If your Highness relies on a detective for catching robbers, you will never get rid of them. And what is more, Ch'i Yung is certain sooner or later to meet with a violent end."
passages.zh: 晉國苦盜，有郗雍者，能視盜之貌，察其眉睫之間而得其情。晉侯使視盜，千百無遺一焉。晉侯大喜，告趙文子曰：「吾得一人，而一國盜為盡矣，奚用多為？」文子曰：「吾子恃窺盜而盡之，是無已時也。

passages.text: Meanwhile, a band of robbers were plotting together. "Ch'i Yung," they said, "is the enemy who is trying to exterminate us." So one day they stole upon him in a body and murdered him. ... "In Chou," replied Wen Tzu, "we have a proverb: 'Search not the ocean-depths for fish: calamity comes upon those who pry into hidden mysteries.' If you want to be quit of robbers, the best thing your Highness can do is to promote the worthy to office." The Marquis then appointed Sui Hui to be Prime Minister, and all the robbers fled to the Ch'in State.
passages.zh: 郗雍必死。俄而群盜曰：「吾所窮者，郗雍也。」乃共取而刲之。……文子曰：「周諺有言：察見淵魚者不祥。若欲不逢盜，莫若舉賢而任之。」晉侯乃舉隨會為政，而群盜奔秦焉。

title.en: Chiu-fang Kao and the Superlative Horse (Liezi)
title.zh: 秦穆公九方皋相馬（列子說符篇）

region.en: The court of Duke Mu of Ch'in (Xianyang, Shaanxi, China)
region.zh: 秦穆公之廷（今陝西咸陽）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: Po Lo recommends the fuel-and-vegetable hawker Chiu-fang Kao, who returns after three months with a steed at Sha-ch'iu — a dun-coloured mare, he says, though it turns out a coal-black stallion. Much displeased, the Duke summons Po Lo, who heaves a sigh of satisfaction: what Kao keeps in view is the spiritual mechanism — in making sure of the essential, he forgets the homely details. When the horse arrived, it turned out indeed to be a superlative horse.
summary.zh: 秦穆公謂伯樂：子之年長矣——九方皋相馬：牝而驪——得其精而忘其粗，在其內而忘其外。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the judge-of-horses topos paralleled in Zhuangzi ch. 24. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: "You are now advanced in years. Is there any member of your family whom I could employ to look for horses in your stead?" Po Lo replied: "A good horse can be picked out by its general build and appearance. But the superlative horse -- one that raises no dust and leaves no tracks -- is something evanescent and fleeting, elusive as thin air. The talent of my sons lies on a lower plane altogether: they can tell a good horse when they see one, but they cannot tell a superlative horse. I have a friend, however, one Chiu-fang Kao, a hawker of fuel and vegetables, who in things appertaining to horses is nowise my inferior."
passages.zh: （秦穆公謂伯樂曰）「子之年老矣，子姓有可使求馬者乎？」伯樂曰：「良馬可形容筋骨相也。天下之馬者，若滅若沒，若亡若失，若此者絕塵弭踵。臣之子皆下才也，可告以良馬，不可告以天下之馬也。臣有所與共擔纆薪菜者，有九方皋，此其於馬，非臣之下也。

passages.text: However, on some one being sent to fetch it, the animal turned out to be a coal-black stallion! Much displeased, the Duke sent for Po Lo. "That friend of yours," he said, "whom I commissioned to look for a horse, has made a nice mess of it. Why, he cannot even distinguish a beast's colour or sex!" Po Lo heaved a sigh of satisfaction. "Has he really got as far as that?" he cried. "Ah, then he is worth a thousand of me put together. What Kao keeps in view is the spiritual mechanism. In making sure of the essential, he forgets the homely details; intent on the inward qualities, he loses sight of the external. So clever a judge of horses is Kao, that he has it in him to judge something better than horses." When the horse arrived, it turned out indeed to be a superlative horse.
passages.zh: 馬至，果雄牝而黃色。穆公不說，召伯樂曰：「敗矣，子所使求馬者！毛物牝牡尚弗能知，又何馬之能知也？」伯樂喟然太息曰：「一至於此乎！是乃其所以千萬臣而無數者也。若皋之所觀，天機也。得其精而忘其粗，在其內而忘其外。

title.en: The Dead Rat Dropped by the Kite (Liezi)
title.zh: 白頷之鴞腐鼠（列子說符篇）

region.en: The rich man's balcony over the high road (symbolic pin: Kaifeng, Henan, China)
region.zh: 梁富人北宮之上（象徵定位：河南開封）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: A lucky throw of the dice evokes a burst of merriment from Mr. Yü's gambling party above the main road; precisely at that moment a kite sailing overhead drops the carcass of a rat among the young gallants below, who take it for an insult and exterminate every member of the family. Pride and extravagance lead to calamity and ruin in more ways than one.
summary.zh: 虞氏富樂無比——梁上有鴞，墮其腐鼠於中——虞氏之患以驕奢故也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Mr. Yü was a wealthy man of the Liang State. It was his custom to have banquets served, to the accompaniment of music, in a high upper hall overlooking the main road; there he and his friends would sit drinking their wine and amusing themselves with bouts of gambling. One day, a party of young gallants happened to pass along the road. In the chamber above, play was going on as usual, and a lucky throw of the dice, which resulted in the capture of both fishes, evoked a loud burst of merriment from the players.
passages.zh: 虞氏，梁之大富人也。家充殷盛，錢帛無量，財貨無訾。登高樓，臨大路，設樂陳酒，擊博樓上。俠客相隨而行，樓上博者射，明瓊張龍，下指兩魚，以為笑譚。

passages.text: Precisely at that moment, it happened that a kite which was sailing overhead dropped the carcass of a rat in the midst of the company outside. The young men held an angry consultation on the spot: "This Mr. Yü has been enjoying his wealth for many a long day, and has always treated his neighbours in the most arrogant spirit. And now, although we have never offended him, he insults us with this dead rat. ... Let us summon up our utmost resolution, and combine with one accord to wipe him and his family out of existence!" The whole party signified their agreement, and when the evening of the appointed day had come, they collected, fully armed for the attack, and exterminated every member of the family.
passages.zh: 適有飛鳶墜腐鼠於其上，而虞氏之尪。其徒曰：「虞氏富樂之日久矣，而常輕易人。吾嘗不辱其人，而彼辱我以死鼠。……請與若戮力協心，誓必滅其家。」

title.en: The Honest Man Who Could Not Eat a Robber's Gruel (Liezi)
title.zh: 東方有士曰爰旌目，食於盜者（列子說符篇）

region.en: The hungered road of the east (symbolic pin: Linyi, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 東方之塗（象徵定位：山東臨沂）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: Yüan Ching Mu, overcome by hunger on the road, is fed with a bowl of rice-gruel by the robber Ch'iu of Hu-fu; after three mouthfuls he learns his benefactor's name, cries: I am an honest man and cannot eat your food — and clutches the ground with both hands, retching and coughing to bring it up again.
summary.zh: 爰旌目曰：嘻！汝非盜邪？胡為而食我？吾義不食子之食也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: In the east of China there was a man named Yuan Ching Mu, who set off on a journey but was overcome by hunger on the way. A certain robber from Hu-fu, of the name of Ch'iu, saw him lying there, and fetched a bowl of rice-gruel in order to feed him. After swallowing three mouthfuls, Yuan Ching Mu opened his eyes and murmured, "Who are you?" "I am a native of Hu-fu, and my name is Ch'iu." "Oh misery!" cried Yuan Ching Mu, "are not you the robber Ch'iu? What are you feeding me for? I am an honest man and cannot eat your food." So saying, he clutched the ground with both hands, and began retching and coughing in order to bring it up again.
passages.zh: 中國之東有袁精睦者，出遊而飢於道。狐父之丘之盜丘見其臥地，取一盂粥以飼之。袁精睦三咽而後能視，曰：「子何為者也？」曰：「我狐父之丘人丘也。」「嘻！汝非盜邪？胡為而食我？吾義不食子之食。」

title.en: Timbo Limbo: the Fish-husband
title.zh: 廷波林波：魚郎

region.en: Maroon Town, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 78a 'Timbo Limbo' (told by Thomas White, Maroon Town)

summary.en: Overworked Lydia, sent alone with a jug heavier than herself, is heard crying at the river by a Jack-fish, Timbo Limbo, who offers to help if she will be his wife; their song summons him each morning. The spying half-sibling betrays the secret, the father calls the fish out with the stolen song and shoots him, and a single scale flies two miles to fall on Lydia's breast. Learning the truth, she sings three times at the river — the water turns blood — and drowns herself where her husband's body was not.
summary.zh: 重役之下的莉迪亞獨負巨壺至河邊啜泣； Jack 魚廷波林波聞聲相助，許以婚約，並以歌相召。同父異母的妹妹窺探告密，父親用偷學的歌聲喚魚出水槍殺之；一片魚鱗飛行兩哩落在莉迪亞胸前。她知情後三次臨河而歌——河水化血——最後在丈夫不在的水中投河自盡。

sensitivity.note: Wonder tale (fish-husband/animal-bridegroom type). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: A man had one daughter named Lydia. His wife died and he married another woman, who had children for the man and liked her own children more than the daughter-in-law — mostly it was the daughter-in-law she imposed the work on. She sent Lydia for water, giving her a big jug heavier than Lydia's weight, and would not send any of her own children to help Lydia up. When Lydia got to the river-side she was crying that the jug was too heavy and she could get no one to help her up; a Jack-fish in the river heard the lament, came up, and said that if she would be a wife to him he would help her up whenever she came to the river-side. Lydia consented, filled her jar, and the Jack-fish helped her up and she went to the yard.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 78a (1924); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個人有個女兒叫莉迪亞。妻子死了，他又娶了一房，後妻為他生了孩子，更疼自己的孩子——重活多半都壓在繼女身上。她叫莉迪亞去打水，給她的罐子比莉迪亞還重，又不派自己的孩子去幫她抬。莉迪亞到了河邊，哭著說罐子太重，她舉
