summary.zh: 一九一八年蔗季，海地美糖公司懸賞招工；一天清晨，科隆比耶的老工頭小約瑟夫帶著一隊衣衫襤褸、目光呆滯如夢行者般的『工人』前來登記，問其姓名皆不應答。那不是活人，是可憐的還魂屍——約瑟夫與妻子克魯瓦昂絲把他們從安息的墳墓裡拖出，為其在烈日下作奴；眾所周知還魂屍絕不可沾鹽與肉，故克魯瓦昂絲另起一鍋，其食淡而無味。

sensitivity.note: The canonical modern zombie narrative (Seabrook 1929, event of 1918); presented as legend told by a named informant. The sensationalist frame of the source is noted; no recipes or practical details beyond the folklore.

passages.text: The spring of 1918 was a big cane season, and the factory, which had its own plantations, offered a bonus on the wages of new workers; soon heads of families and villages from the mountain and the plain came trailing their ragtag little armies — men, women, children trooping to the registration bureau and thence into the fields. One morning an old black headman, Ti Joseph of Colombier, appeared leading a band of ragged creatures who shuffled along behind him, staring dumbly, like people walking in a daze. As Joseph lined them up for registration they still stared, vacant-eyed like cattle, and made no reply when asked to give their names.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook, The Magic Island, ch. 'Black Sorcery' (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 1918年的春天是大甘蔗季，工廠自己有種植園，對新工人的工錢給了津貼；不久，山區與平原的家長和村長便拖著他們破衣爛衫的小軍隊前來——男男女女、孩子們成群擁向登記處，再擁向田間。一天早晨，一個黑皮膚的老村長，哥倫比埃的蒂·約瑟夫，帶

passages.text: Joseph said they were ignorant people from the slopes of Morne-au-Diable, a roadless mountain district near the Dominican border, who did not understand the creole of the plains; they were frightened, he said, by the din and smoke of the great factory, but under his direction they would work hard in the fields — and the farther they were sent away from the noise and bustle of the railroad yards, the better. Better indeed: for these were not living men and women but poor unhappy zombies whom Joseph and his wife Croyance had dragged from their peaceful graves to slave for him in the sun — and if by chance a brother or father of the dead should see and recognize them, Joseph knew that it would be a very bad affair for him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 約瑟夫說他們是惡魔山山坡上無知的百姓，那是一片無路的山區，臨近多米尼加邊境，不懂平原的克里奧爾話；他說，大工廠的嘈雜與煙氣嚇著了他們，但在他的指導下他們會在田裏努力幹活——把他們派得離鐵路調車場的喧囂越遠越好，

passages.text: So they were assigned to distant fields beyond the crossroads, and camped there, keeping to themselves like any proper family or village group; but in the evening, when other little companies gathered each around its one big common pot of savory millet or plantains generously seasoned with dried fish and garlic, Croyance would tend two pots upon the fire — for as every one knows, the zombies must never be permitted to taste salt or meat. So the food prepared for them was tasteless and unseasoned; and as the zombies toiled day after day dumbly in the sun, Joseph sometimes beat them to make them move faster, but Croyance began to pity the poor dead creatures who should be at rest — and pitied them in the evenings when she dished out their flat, tasteless bouillie.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是他們被派到十字路口之外的遠處田裏，在那裏安營，像任何像樣的家庭或村社一樣自成一群；但到了傍晚，別的小隊各自圍著一大鍋撒了乾魚與蒜調味的美味小米或芭蕉聚餐時，克魯瓦揚斯卻要燒兩口鍋——因為人人皆知，還屍必須

title.en: Salted Tablettes: the Zombies Remember Their Graves
title.zh: 加了鹽的花生糖：還魂屍歸墳

region.en: Cul-de-Sac cane fields and Morne-au-Diable, Haiti
region.zh: 海地庫爾德薩克蔗田與魔難山

period: Haitian legend, event of 1918; recorded 1927-1929; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: William B. Seabrook, 'The Magic Island' (1929), ch. 'Black Sorcery' — the Fete-Dieu ending of the Hasco story

summary.en: On the day of the great feast Croyance, pitying her dead drudges once more, bought tablettes — 'not salted or seasoned, they are sweet, and can do no harm just this once.' But the baker had salted the pistache nuts before stirring them into the rapadou; and as the zombies tasted the salt, they knew that they were dead, made a dreadful outcry, arose, and turned their faces toward the mountain. No one dared to stop them, for they were corpses walking in the sunlight; and at their own village in the twilight they shuffled past fathers, wives, mothers who screamed and begged them to stay, up the path to the graveyard, and each before his own empty grave clawed the stones and earth to enter it again — and as their cold hands touched the earth of their own graves, they fell and lay there, rotting carrion.
summary.zh: 大節之日，克魯瓦昂絲再度憐憫這些亡者苦工，買來花生糖——『沒鹽沒料，是甜的，就這一次無妨』。誰知糖販在拌入糖漿前先給花生加了鹽；還魂屍一嘗到鹽，便知自己已死，發出可怖的哀號，起身轉向群山。無人敢攔——那是行走在日光下的屍體。薄暮時分，他們踏著碎步經過認出親人、哭喊挽留的村人，走上通往墓園的小徑，在各自空墳前刨掘石土欲入；冰冷的手觸到自家墳土的一刻，他們倒下，橫陳為腐肉。

sensitivity.note: Sequel of the Hasco narrative; the salt-taste rule is folklore-level. Source is Seabrook's popular-ethnography; the melodrama is his, the folk logic (salt releases the dead) is the tellers'.

passages.text: As Croyance sat with her savory dried herring and biscuit baked with salt and soda, and her provision of clairin in the tin cup by her side, she pitied the zombies who had worked so faithfully for Joseph in the cane fields and who now had nothing, while all the other groups around were feasting; and as she pitied them a woman passed, crying, 'Tablettes! Tablettes pistaches! Trois pour dix cobs!' — tablettes are a sort of candy, in shape and size like cookies, made of brown cane sugar, sometimes with pistaches, which in Haiti are peanuts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook, The Magic Island, ch. 'Black Sorcery' (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 克魯瓦揚斯坐著，面前是美味的乾鯡與鹽鹼烤餅，身旁的錫杯裏備著白酒，可憐那些在甘蔗田裏為約瑟夫忠實幹活、如今一無所有的還屍，周圍各隊都在大吃大喝；她憐憫他們的當口，一個女人走過，喊著「糖片！開心果糖片！十庫卜三片！」——

passages.text: And Croyance thought, 'These tablettes are not salted or seasoned, they are sweet, and can do no harm to the zombies just this once.' So she untied the corner of her kerchief, took out a coin — a gourdon, the quarter of a gourde — and bought some of the tablettes, which she broke in halves and divided among the zombies, who began sucking and mumbling them in their mouths. But the baker of the tablettes had salted the pistache nuts before stirring them into the rapadou, and as the zombies tasted the salt, they knew that they were dead, and made a dreadful outcry, and arose and turned their faces toward the mountain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 克魯瓦揚斯心想：「這些糖片沒有加鹽也沒有加味，是甜的，就這一次對還屍無害。」於是她解開頭巾的一角，取出一枚錢——一個古爾登，四分之一古爾德——買了一些糖片，掰成兩半分給還屍，還屍們開始吮著含著它們。但那糖片的烘焙

passages.text: No one dared to stop them, for they were corpses walking in the sunlight, and they themselves and all the people knew that they were corpses; and they disappeared toward the mountain. When later they drew near their own village on the slopes of Morne-au-Diable — these dead men and women walking single file in the twilight, with no soul leading them or daring to follow — the people of their village, holding their hamboche in the market-place, saw them drawing closer, and recognized among them fathers, brothers, wives and daughters whom they had buried months before. Most of them knew at once the truth, that these were zombies who had been dragged dead from their graves; but others hoped that a blessed miracle had taken place on this Fete Dieu, and rushed forward to take them in their arms and welcome them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 沒有人敢攔他們，因為他們是在陽光下行走的屍體，他們自己和所有人也都知道他們是屍體；他們朝山裏消失了。後來他們走近自己惡魔山坡上的村莊——這些死去的男女在暮色中列成單行行走，沒有靈魂領著，也沒有靈魂敢跟著——村裏的人

passages.text: But the zombies shuffled through the market-place, recognizing neither father nor wife nor mother; and as they turned leftward up the path leading to the graveyard, a woman whose daughter was in the procession of the dead threw herself screaming before the girl's shuffling feet and begged her to stay — but the grave-cold feet of the daughter and the feet of the other dead shuffled over her and onward. As they approached the graveyard they began to shuffle faster and rushed among the graves, and each before his own empty grave began clawing at the stones and earth to enter it again; and as their cold hands touched the earth of their own graves, they fell and lay there, rotting carrion.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 還屍們卻踉蹌著穿過市場，既不認父親，也不認妻子母親；他們左轉沿通往墓園的小路而上時，一個女兒在死者的隊伍裏的母親扑倒在她女兒拖沓的腳前尖聲哀求她留下——但女兒那墓穴一樣冰冷的腳與其他死者的腳從她身上拖沓著踏過，繼

title.en: Why the Peasants Build Tombs: Polynice's Apology
title.zh: 為何農人築石墓：波利尼斯的辯白

region.en: Grande Source district, Haiti
region.zh: 海地大泉區

period: Haitian funerary practice; recorded 1927-1929; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: William B. Seabrook, 'The Magic Island' (1929), ch. 'Black Sorcery' (Constant Polynice on tombs, graves beside the road, and the night-watch with shotguns)

summary.en: Polynice, the rationalist friend, would not call it superstition: why do you suppose that even the poorest peasants, when they can, bury their dead beneath solid tombs of masonry? Why do they bury them so often in their own yards, close to the doorway? Why, so often, do you see a tomb set close beside a busy road where people are always passing? It is to assure the poor unhappy dead such protection as we can — and for his own brother, killed as everyone knew, he and Osmann kept four nights of watch in the peristyle with shotguns, until they were sure the body had begun to rot.
summary.zh: 理性友人波利尼斯不肯稱之迷信：為何連最窮的農人也要把亡者葬入堅固的石砌墓穴？為何常葬在自家院中、緊挨門口？為何墓塚總立於行人絡繹的大路旁？——這是為那些可憐而不幸的死者盡我們所能的保護。至於他那位死因眾人皆知的弟弟，他與奧斯曼在祭亭持獵槍守了四夜，直到確信屍身已開始腐爛為止。

sensitivity.note: Haitian funerary-protective practices described by a named informant; the watch described is a protective vigil, recorded as folkloric fact from the published source.

passages.text: The zombie, Polynice's neighbors said, is neither a ghost nor yet a person who has been raised like Lazarus from the dead: the zombie is a soulless human corpse, still dead, but taken from the grave and endowed by sorcery with a mechanical semblance of life — a dead body which is made to walk and act and move as if it were alive. People who have the power to do this go to a fresh grave, dig up the body before it has had time to rot, galvanize it into movement, and make of it a servant or slave, occasionally for the commission of some crime, more often simply as a drudge around the habitation or the farm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook, ch. 'Black Sorcery' (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 波利尼斯的鄰居們說，還屍既不是鬼魂，也不是像拉撒路那樣從死裏復活的人：還屍是沒有靈魂的人屍，仍是死的，卻從墳墓裏被取出，由巫術賦予一種機械的生命表象——一具被弄得行走行動如活的死屍。有這種能力的人到一座新墳，掘出

passages.text: Seabrook asked Polynice to tell him something of the zombie superstition, that he might get at some idea of how it originated. His rational friend was deeply astonished, and put his hand in protest on his knee: 'Superstition? But I assure you that this of which you now speak is not a matter of superstition. Alas, these things — and other evil practices connected with the dead — exist. They exist to an extent that you whites do not dream of, though evidences are everywhere under your eyes.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 西布魯克請波利尼斯給他講一講還屍的迷信，好對它的起源有個概念。他那位理性的朋友深深驚愕，抗議地把手按在膝上：「迷信？但我向你保證，你現在說的這件事不是迷信的事。唉，這些事——還有與死者相關的其他惡行——是存在的。它們存在

passages.text: 'Why do you suppose that even the poorest peasants, when they can, bury their dead beneath solid tombs of masonry? Why do they bury them so often in their own yards, close to the doorway? Why, so often, do you see a tomb or grave set close beside a busy road or footpath where people are always passing? It is to assure the poor unhappy dead such protection as we can.' He would take Seabrook in the morning to see the grave of his brother, killed as everyone knew: open space all round it, close beside the trail which everybody passes — and through four nights Polynice and Osmann had watched in the peristyle with shotguns, for at that time both his dead brother and he had bitter enemies, until they were sure the body had begun to rot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook (1929); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「你以為為什麼連最窮的農夫，只要力所能及，都把死者葬在結實的磚石墳墓裏？為什麼他們這麼常把死者葬在自己的院子裏，就在門口近旁？為什麼你這麼常看見一座墳或墓立在繁忙的大路或小徑旁，人們時時走過？那是為了給可憐而不幸的死者我們所能給的保護。」他會帶著西布魯克在

title.en: King and Queen of the Vaudoux: Moreau de Saint-Méry's Account
title.zh: 伏都之王與后：聖梅里的記述

region.en: Western Saint-Domingue (Haiti)
region.zh: 法屬聖多明各（今海地）西部

period: Recorded c. 1790 (Moreau de Saint-Méry); republished by St. John 1884

source.work: Sir Spenser St. John, 'Hayti; or, The Black Republic' (1884), ch. V, reproducing Moreau de Saint-Méry's description of the Vaudoux (1790s)

summary.en: According to the Arada negroes, the true sectaries of the Vaudoux, the word signifies an all-powerful and supernatural being on whom depend all the events which take place in the world: the non-venomous serpent, through whose grand priest and high priestess — the King and Queen, or Master and Mistress, or the touching titles of Papa and Mama — all its knowledge of the past, the present and the future is communicated. The two delegates, chiefs for life of the great family of the Vaudoux, keep the serpent in its box upon the altar; petitioners bring their vows of eternal love or maledictions against a rival; the Queen, mounted on the sacred ark, is seized by the spirit and the oracle speaks by her mouth; and the offerings gathered in a covered hat pay the expenses of the meetings and give aid to absent or needy members — a secret society that functioned, in part, as a burial-and-relief fund.
summary.zh: 據真正的伏都教眾阿爾達黑人所言：『伏都』意即一位全能超凡之存在——無毒之蛇——世上諸事皆繫於它；其神諭只借大祭司與女大祭司之口而傳——人稱王與后、主與母、或親暱的爸爸媽媽。二位終身執掌伏都大家族，蛇靈伏於祭壇木匣之中；祈願者帶來永恆之愛的誓詞或詛咒情敵的惡語；王后立於神匣之上，神靈附體，神諭借其口而出；以蓋帽收下的獻金支付聚會開支，並接濟遠行或困乏的會友——這個秘密結社，實亦兼作互助與喪葬金會。

sensitivity.note: 18th-century colonial description (Moreau de Saint-Méry) reproduced through St. John's late-19th-century hostile framing. The society's relief-fund function is in the source text itself; the record preserves the balance between the source's sensationalism and its documentary detail. Living religion: liturgy not reproduced.

passages.text: According to the Arada negroes, who are the true sectaries of the Vaudoux in the colony, and maintain its principles and its rules, Vaudoux signifies an all-powerful and supernatural being, on whom depend all the events which take place in the world. This being is the non-venomous serpent, and it is under its auspices that all those assemble who profess this doctrine. Acquaintance with the past, knowledge of the present, prescience of the future, all appertain to this serpent, that only consents to communicate his power and prescribe his will through the organ of a grand priest, whom the sectaries select, and still more by that of the negress whom the love of the latter has raised to the rank of high priestess.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, Hayti, ch. V, reproducing Moreau de Saint-Méry (1884/1790s); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 照阿拉達的黑人所說——他們才是殖民地裏伏都教的真正教徒，維持著它的原則與規矩——伏都意指一位全能而超自然的存在，世上所發生的一切事件都倚靠於他。這存在是無毒的蛇，凡奉此教的人都聚在牠的庇佑之下。認識過去，

passages.text: These two delegates, who declare themselves inspired by their god — or in whom the gift of inspiration is really manifested in the opinion of their followers — bear the pompous names of King and Queen, or the despotic ones of Master and Mistress, or the touching titles of Papa and Mama. They are during their whole life the chiefs of the great family of the Vaudoux, and they have a right to the unlimited respect of the sectaries.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, ch. V (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這兩位使節自稱蒙神感召——或在信眾看來感召之恩確實顯現在他們身上——頂著「國王與女王」的堂皇名號，或「主人與主母」的專制名號，或「爸爸與媽媽」的親切頭銜。他們終身是伏都大家族的首領，有權不受懲

passages.text: A young one solicits eternal love, or she repeats the maledictions that hate dictates against a preferred rival; there is not a passion which does not give vent to its vow. At each of these invocations the King of the Vaudoux appears absorbed in thought; the spirit seizes him, and suddenly he takes hold of the box in which the serpent is confined, places it on the ground, and commands the Queen to get on it. As soon as the sacred ark is beneath her feet, the new Pythoness is filled by the spirit of their god; she trembles, all her body is in a state of convulsion, and the oracle speaks by her mouth — now she flatters and promises happiness, now she bursts into reproaches, dictating as decrees without appeal everything she is pleased to prescribe in the name of the serpent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, ch. V (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位少女祈求永恆的愛，或她複誦仇恨針對一個受寵的情敵所口授的咒詛；沒有一種激情不發出它的誓願。每一次這樣的呼求，伏都之王都現出沉思之狀；靈附了他，他忽然抓住關蛇的箱子，放在地上，命女王

passages.text: After the questions have received their answers, they form a circle and the serpent is again placed on the altar; his followers bring as tribute the objects they think most worthy, and that no jealous curiosity may raise a blush the offerings are placed in a covered hat. The King and Queen promise the offerings shall be accepted by their god. It is from this collection that the expenses of the meetings are paid, that aid is afforded to absent members, or to those present who may be in want, or to others from whom the society may expect something in favor of its glory or renown — and a fresh oath engages each one to be silent as to what has passed, sometimes sealed by the warm blood of a goat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, ch. V (1884); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 問題得到回答之後，他們圍成一圈，蛇又被放上祭壇；信眾把他們認為最配得上的物件作為貢禮帶來，為免嫉妒的好奇心使人臉紅，祭品放在一頂有蓋的帽子裏。國王與女王允諾祭品必蒙他們的神收納。聚會的開銷便出自這份收集，

title.en: The Initiation Circle and the Monter-Vaudou in Old Saint-Domingue
title.zh: 聖多明各的入會圈與『上伏都』

region.en: Western Saint-Domingue (Haiti)
region.zh: 法屬聖多明各（今海地）西部

period: Recorded c. 1790 (Moreau de Saint-Méry); republished 1884

source.work: Sir Spenser St. John, 'Hayti; or, The Black Republic' (1884), ch. V — the dance of the Vaudoux and the admission of new candidates

summary.en: The fete begins with the admission of the candidate: the King traces a large circle with some black substance and places the novice within it, a packet of herbs, horsehair, pieces of horn and other trifling objects in his hand; lightly touching his head with a wooden wand, he thunders forth an African song repeated in chorus around the circle — then the new member begins to tremble and to dance, which is called to practise Vaudoux. If excess of excitement makes him leave the circle the song stops, the King and Queen turn their backs to avert the evil omen; he re-enters, trembles, drinks, and arrives at so convulsive a state that the King stops him with a touch of the wand — and from that moment he belongs to the sect.
summary.zh: 慶典以收徒開場：王以黑物畫一大圈，置新會者於圈中，手捧藥草、馬鬃、獸角諸物；木杖輕點其頂，朗聲唱起非洲古調，圈眾應聲而和——於是新會者顫慄起舞，是謂『行伏都』。若狂喜過度而跨出圈外，歌聲立止，王與后背身轉向以避凶兆；其人回圈再顫、復飲，終至痙攣之境，王以杖點其頂止之——自那一刻起，他便屬於這個教團。

sensitivity.note: 18th-century colonial description; the same ceremony reappears in the 1904 Cuban record (cross_ref: afroatlantic-louisiana-voodoo-rites, afroatlantic-vaudoux-king-queen). Living religion: initiation liturgy not reproduced.

passages.text: After these ceremonies commences the dance of the Vaudoux. If there should be a new candidate, it is by his admission that the fete commences. The King of the Vaudoux, with some black substance, traces a large circle, and in this the novice is placed; and in his hand he puts a packet of herbs, horsehair, pieces of horn, and other trifling objects.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, Hayti, ch. V (1884/1790s); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這些儀式之後，伏都之舞開始了。若有新的候選人，慶典便以他的入會開始。伏都之王以某種黑色的物料畫一個大圈，新手便置於圈中；他手裏放上一包草藥、馬鬃、角片與其他瑣碎之物。

passages.text: Then lightly touching him on the head with a slight wooden wand, he thunders forth an African song, which is repeated in chorus by those who stand around the circle; then the new member begins to tremble and to dance, which is called to practise Vaudoux. If, unhappily, excess of excitement makes him leave the circle, the song immediately ceases, the King and Queen turn their backs to avert the evil omen. The dancer recollects himself, re-enters the circle, again trembles, drinks, and arrives at length at so convulsive a state that the King orders him to stop by striking him lightly on the head with his wand. He is taken to the altar to swear, and from that moment he belongs to the sect.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, ch. V (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The 1864 Trial and the Empty Graves
title.zh: 一八六四年審判與空墳之謎

region.en: Port-au-Prince, Haiti

period: Historical event of 1864, described in a hostile colonial account (St. John, 1884)

source.work: Sir Spenser St. John, 'Hayti; or, The Black Republic' (1884), ch. V — the trial at which the author was present, and the disappearances after execution

summary.en: The eight convicts of the 1864 sorcery trial were executed in white robes on a market-day for solemnity — and the Vaudoux priests gave out that although the deity would permit the execution, he would only do it to prove his power by raising them all again from the dead. Piquets of troops were placed round the burial place to prevent the bodies being carried away in the night; but in the morning three of the graves were found empty — the bodies of the two priests and the priestess had disappeared; superstitious fear had probably unmanned the sentries, and as most of the troops belonged to the sect, they probably connived at rather than prevented the exhumation.

Modern scholarship reads these trial narratives skeptically as colonial sensationalism; the record preserves the documented elements (trial, executions, claim of resurrection, empty graves) without reproducing gore, and flags the source bias. This is not representative of Vodou, a living religion.

narrative.en: In Haitian Vodou the creator, Bondye — a Kreyol rendering of the French Bon Dieu, the Good God — stands at the apex of the cosmos, and stands there as a distant power. He set the world in motion, established its moral order, and then withdrew from the direct management of human affairs. The peasant adage that this distance is precisely why the lwa matter runs through the whole theology: Bondye is too great, too high, too occupied with the ends of things to be troubled with every small case of a farmer's child or a fisherman's boat, and so prayer is properly addressed to the intermediaries. The intermediaries are the lwa — the ancestral and cosmic powers, many of them named individuals with histories, tastes, tempers, and whole biographies of marriage and feud — a crowded pantheon carried across the Middle Passage from Fon, Yoruba, Kongo and other African sources and renewed generation by generation by Haitian experience. Some are old African gods in Kreyol dress; some are the spirits of revolutionary heroes; some are powers of the road, the sea, the market, the graveyard — the in-between places where the living and the dead trade. The cosmos itself is mapped as a system of roads. Between the world of the living and the world of the dead runs the Grand Chemin, the great road; the dead travel it under the care of Baron Samedi and the Gede, and the living send word along it by service, song and sacrifice. Every ceremony dramatizes a journey: the processionals that enter the peristyle from the mystery house, the tracing of vèvè signs on the ground, the poteau-mitan center-pole up which the lwa are called to descend. The peristyle floor is a map; the dance is a form of travel; the drummer is a driver of the road. Syncretism in this system is structural, not accidental. Bondye merges with the Christian God and shares his distance; the lwa wear Catholic faces — Legba with Saint Peter or Saint Lazarus, Ezili with the Mater Dolorosa, Ogou with Saint James — and the Catholic calendar of saints' feasts, Good Friday and All Souls organizes the Vodou year. Leslie Desmangles reads this double registry as a theology in its own right rather than a camouflage: the African powers wearing Catholic faces made the religion survivable under the Code Noir, and in time the two registers fused into one grammar in which the same power is known by two names and honored at two altars. The cultural function of the whole structure is to make the African gods governable in a colony and a republic that burned them: the distant creator keeps the state's God out of the way of the ancestors' business, and the roads keep every petition answerable in this world. The Grand Chemin deserves its own close attention, because it is the image that most distinguishes this cosmology from its Old World sources. In the African homelands the worlds of the living and the dead are adjacent villages, connected by boundaries that are tended — the sacred grove, the river crossing, the family tomb inside the compound wall. In Haiti the crossing became the road: a long, dangerous, traveled distance, made by the Middle Passage and renewed by the regime of mobility that the plantation imposed — the forced march of the coffle, the flight of the maroon along the mountain paths, the constant traffic of the dead in a colony where death was everywhere at work. The road-cosmos is therefore a historical cosmology: it maps the specific geography of survival in Saint-Domingue, in which everyone, living or dead, was a traveler between two worlds, and in which every ceremony was a way-station. The Comparative value for the Motif Atlas is that this image joins the descent-myths and underworld-roads of the Greek, Sumerian, Norse and Maya traditions with an ocean-crossing account of the same structure: the road between the worlds is the Middle Passage itself, remembered cosmologically, and every ritual journey on it is at once a liturgy and a history lesson.

summary.en: Ezili Freda Dahomey is the lwa of love, beauty and luxury — perfumed, jeweled, quarrelsome, cursed to love and never to be satisfied. Her menage of three husbands (Ogou, Damballa, Danbala's rival Ti-Jean) is a marriage-romance of jealousy; her sign is the weeping heart pierced by a sword; her service demands perfume, sweets and white things, and no tobacco smoke or pork. narrative.en: Ezili Freda Dahomey is the lwa of love, beauty and luxury: perfumed, jeweled, pale in the iconography, quarrelsome — and cursed never to be satisfied in love. Her very name carries her origin: Freda Dahomey, the lady from Dahomey, and Karen McCarthy Brown reads in her the creolized memory of a Dahomean noblewoman of the slave-trade era, a woman who may once have owned slaves herself and who in Haiti was enslaved. The luxury of her cult is her remembered station — perfume, sweets, lace, white rum, the finest white and pink things in the household — and her tears are her remembered fate: she weeps, the tradition says, because she is destined always to love and never to be loved enough. Her mythic biography is a romance of jealousy, played out among the pantheon's most powerful men: she is the wife or lover of three rivals — the iron soldier Ogou, the serpent Damballa, and the mortal trickster Ti-Jean, who won her for a single night and lost her forever. The triangle is the engine of her service-songs, which recount her fits of pique, her errands of vengeance against rival women, her shopping for the finest cloth in the market of heaven. Her emblem is the heart pierced by a sword — the emblem that Catholic Haiti knows as the Mater Dolorosa — and her day is Thursday, her color white and pink, her posture fainting elegance. Those who serve her keep her altar immaculate: she cannot abide tobacco smoke, and above all she cannot abide the smell of pork, which the tradition reads as the smell of the suffering of her people — the smell of the ship, the smell of the cane. She has her dark twin, and the pair makes a single theology of love. Ezili Danto is black, scarred, the warrior-mother who fights with a child strapped to her back and a knife in her teeth, her speech folded with the hard bends of a rough life; where Freda weeps at romance gone wrong, Danto aches for the children of Haiti; where Freda's service is a garden of white things and sweet perfumes, Danto's is a dark kitchen of iron, pepper and machete. Together they are the two faces of love — the longing and the labor — and the devotee who serves one learns to serve both, for the same heart wears both faces in a country that has known both the fantasy of luxury and the discipline of survival. The ritual economics of her cult make the theology legible. Ezili is the most expensive of the lwa to serve: her perfumes, her white cakes, her imported lace, her pink and white candles — the altar of a rich Ezili house in Haiti is a small museum of the dream of luxury, and the poor devotee who buys one candle for her is buying, consciously, a share in the fantasy. Brown's ethnography shows the other side with equal care: in the Brooklyn apartment altar of Mama Lola, Ezili Freda's things stand beside Ezili Danto's machete and the family's Ogou flags, and the three of them constitute a single statement about love and iron and survival — the fantasy, the labor and the fight, each with its own price. In the comparative grid Ezili stands with the Aphrodite-and-Ares pair of the Greek cycle and with the Mesopotamian Inanna in her modes of desire and war; the Haitian particularity is that the pair are two names of one goddess, and that the history of slavery is written into the seam between them. For the Motif Atlas the record anchors the cluster of love-goddess-with-war-goddess and supplies the Afro-Atlantic case in which the split is explained by history rather than by theology.

title.en: Ogou Feray: the Iron Soldier Who Made a Revolution
title.zh: 奧貢·菲雷：鑄成革命的鐵之軍人

summary.en: Ogou Feray (Ogun Ferraille) is the soldier-lwa of iron: machete, flag, and the hard labor of revolution. In Haitian memory he is the spirit of the warriors of 1791-1804; his shrine holds machetes crossed and an iron bar beaten by a horseshoe; when he comes in service he moves like a soldier on parade, drinks rum straight, smokes, and demands payment for his work. He is also the healer of iron's wounds — the worker's lwa as much as the warrior's.

narrative.en: Ogou Feray — Ogun Ferraille, Ogun of the Irons — is the lwa of iron and war in Haitian Vodou, the Yoruba road-opener and blacksmith-god carried to Saint-Domingue and fused there with the iron-powers of the Fon and Kongo ancestors. His emblems are a machete crossed on his shrine, an iron bar, the red flag; his colors are red and blue, his animal the red rooster, his Saint the warrior-saint James in his iconography of battle. In the Haitian telling he is pre-eminently the spirit of the warriors of the revolution of 1791 to 1804 — the power that marched with the maroons and the freedmen of the North Plain, that stood beside Dessalines at the crack of independence — and at the same time the workers' lwa of forge, field and factory: the same iron that fights also feeds, the same blade that harvests cane also harvests enemies. When he comes in service he arrives like a soldier: standing at attention in the doorway of the peristyle, drinking rum neat, smoking a cigar, his voice hoarse with command, his feet planted. He demands payment for his work — a small coin, a splash of rum, a cigar — and he keeps accounts: the Haitian proverb that Ogou is owed remembers every unpaid debt of the revolution's dead, and the service-song that lists his battles is a ledger of national memory. But he is also a healer, and the two offices are one: iron's own medicine for iron's own wounds, the cuts and fevers of labor treated with heated blades, cauterizing iron, the red steel laid on red flesh. Brown's telling makes the politics of this explicit and personal. In Mama Lola's family Ogou is the ancestor-spirit of a lineage of rebel men — a great-grandfather who fought in the cacos, a grandfather who died under the American occupation — and the family service to him is at once a remembering and an accounting: what was promised to the men, what was owed to the lwa, what has been paid and what remains. The iron soldier of the revolution lives on in the iron of the household, and the household keeps his books. The comparative grid confirms how much of this is old iron in new hands: the Yoruba Ogun of the homeland is the hunter and road-opener who first cleared the paths with his blade, the blacksmith whose forge civilized the forest, the orisha who insists on being fed before any serious work begins; the Haitian Ogou keeps every one of these offices and adds the political one, because in Saint-Domingue and after, iron was the metal of the slaves — the machete that cut cane and cut masters, the chains that had to be broken, the tools that were forbidden and were seized. In the Petro register of the hot rites he appears as Ogoun Badagris, the bloody dreadful one whose voice is thunder, and in the Rada register he is the cooler soldier of the calendar saint; the two registers share a single shrine and a single ledger. For the corpus of comparative myth he supplies the Afro-Atlantic form of the culture-hero of iron: the first clearers of the road, the smiths of the social contract, the warriors whose pay is always partly owed.

summary.en: Damballa Wedo is the ancient serpent-lwa of the Fon pantheon carried to Haiti: old, slow, white, speechless — he can only hiss. Where he moves in service, the waters tremble: he is the lwa of rain, rivers and the primal waters from which the world was made; his wife Ayida Weddo is the rainbow that bridges sky and earth, and their union is the movement of creation itself. The colonial sources record the serpent in its box on the altar; the living religion records a far older and quieter power.

narrative.en: Damballa Wedo is the serpent-lwa of Haitian Vodou, and he is old — the oldest in the ritual order of the Rada rites. Ancient, slow, white, and speechless, he does not speak in service: he hisses, and his horse — the possessed celebrant — moves like a great snake along the ground, slithering rather than walking, tasting the air. He is the power of the waters: rain, rivers, the primal sea from which the world was made; in the Fon mythology he descends from the creator pair Mawu-Lisa, and in Haiti he keeps that seniority. He is served first among the Rada lwa, with the whitest and coolest offerings — white flour, white eggs, cool water, white sheets — because heat is not his element and the coolness of the deep water is. His wife, or co-wife in different tellings, is Ayida Weddo, the rainbow: the serpent that bridges the sky to the earth and carries the waters home. Where Damballa is the still deep water, Ayida is the arc of color that the water makes climbing back to the sky, and their union is the movement of creation itself — the water falling and returning, the world breathing. Their paired emblem — two serpents about the center-pole — is one of the oldest signs of the religion, drawn first on the floor of every service. The colonial record preserves the same deity under the name of the Vaudoux serpent. Moreau de Saint-Méry, writing in the 1790s, describes the non-venomous serpent kept in a box upon the altar of the sect, before which the King and Queen take their oath and the whole community swears by the serpent's power; the serpent in the box is, in the living theology, the same power that made the world — a god too old to argue, kept near at hand in a small wooden ark. The continuity is exact and documentable: the Arada serpent of 1790 and the Damballa of the present-day peristyle are one lineage, and the colonial archive itself — hostile as it is — becomes evidence of survival. What the colonial eye read as superstition is the memory of a cosmology in which the world itself was made by the serpent and the rainbow, and in which every rain is the old agreement renewed. In the comparative grid Damballa and Ayida stand with the world-serpents of every mythology — the Midgard serpent beneath the sea, the Chinese Yinglong and the coiling dragons of the flood-tales, the Rainbow Serpent of Australia and Melanesia — but with a Haitian particularity: the world-serpent here is not a threat to be fought but a peace to be kept. The waters that he governs are the waters of origin, and his service is a renewal of the original calm rather than a defeat of chaos; the rainbow that Ayida spans is the sign that the flood has an end. The colonial sources, seeing only the box and the oath, could not read this; the living liturgy reads it every time the paired serpents are drawn on the floor of the peristyle and the oldest drums begin to cool the air of the yard. For the comparative corpus the Haitian serpent supplies the one case in which the world-serpent is both creator and comforter, and in which the oldest god is the quietest one in the room.

title.en: The Marassa: Sacred Twins of Vodou
title.zh: 瑪拉薩：伏都的雙生聖童

summary.en: The Marassa — the sacred twins, Marassa Twims, Marasa Etwa Dosa — are children-lwa, the most childlike and most dangerous of the powers: fed first at every ceremony, from the twin-plates and twin-spoons no other lwa may use, served on the ground like children and treated with the tender terror reserved for something too close to the divine. In Africa they are the Ibeji of the Yoruba and the hohovi of the Fon; in Haiti they are the memory of the twin birth as a cosmic event.

passages.text: The Marassa are the lwa of twins — and, by extension, of every doubled and sacred childhood. They are served first at every ceremony, from twin-plates and twin-spoons that no other lwa may touch, on the ground like children at a picnic; their offering is the simplest food of the compound. They are petulant, easily offended, prone to strike the household with the childhood diseases — and so tenderly feared that the whole service pauses until they are fed and pleased.

The Haitian Marassa carry this memory whole: the twin-plates, the first-served portion, the childish fury — a theology in which twinship is the nearest human image of the divine doubling of the world.

passages.text: In the Afro-Atlantic grid the Marassa stand with the Yoruba Ibeji, the Maya Hero Twins, and every tradition's doubled founders: the twin as creator, twin as trickster, twin as omen. The Haitian form is distinct — children, not heroes — but the structural rhyme is exact: two born together, honored with doubled things, feared with doubled fear.

passages.zh: 在跨大西洋的譜系裏，瑪拉薩與約魯巴的伊貝吉、瑪雅的英雄雙子、以及每一個傳統的成雙的創立者並立：作為創造者的雙子，作為惡作劇者的雙子，作為徵兆的雙子。海地的形式有其獨特之處——是孩子，不是英雄——但結構上的押韻是嚴絲合縫的：一同出生的二，以成雙之物尊崇，以成雙的畏懼畏懼。

narrative.en: The Marassa are the lwa of twins in Haitian Vodou — Marasa Twims, Marasa Etwa Dosa, the sacred doubled children — and they are served first at every ceremony, from twin-plates and twin-spoons that no other lwa may touch, seated on the ground like children at a picnic and offered the plainest food of the compound. Their theology is the theology of double birth: twins are not ordinary children but spirits walking among mortals, close to the source of things, dangerous to cross and glorious to please. They are petulant, easily offended, prone to strike a household with the childhood diseases when slighted, and so tenderly feared that the whole service pauses until they are fed and pleased. In the Fon-Yoruba homeland the same powers are the Ibeji of the Yoruba and the hohovi of the Fon: twin-births as miracles or calamities, twin-deaths not as ends but as returns to the wild twin-country from which the children came, twin-cults of little paired figures carved, fed, and kept on the family shelf. The Haitian Marassa carry this memory whole across the Middle Passage: the twin-plates, the first-served portion, the childish fury, the small chairs set for guests who are always invisible and always expected. In the Afro-Atlantic comparative grid the Marassa stand with the Yoruba Ibeji, with the Hero Twins of the Maya Popol Vuh, and with every tradition's doubled founders: the twin as creator, twin as trickster, twin as omen. The Haitian form is distinct — children rather than heroes, hunger rather than conquest — but the structural rhyme is exact: two born together, honored with doubled things, feared with doubled fear. Their ritual function in the diaspora is a social one as much as a cosmic one: to serve the Marassa is to serve every doubled and divided household in a society created by forced separations, to honor the sibling pair as the smallest unit of survival, and to keep the first portion of every feast for the smallest and most easily wounded of the powers. The ritual technology of the cult is precisely calibrated to its theology: twin-plates that no single food may be served on, twin-spoons, twin-cups, two small chairs, two portions of everything, and the rule that the Marassa are fed before any other lwa — the first portion of the first dish, on the ground, with the house children standing around as if at the feeding of real children. When the twins are angry, the whole household knows it at once: the children sicken, the food spoils, the services stall, and the remedy is a double feast as quickly as it can be cooked. The Marassa therefore function as the household conscience of the religion — the lwa whose displeasure is immediate, domestic, and repairable, and whose cult teaches the primary Afro-Atlantic ethic that the doubled and the divided must be honored together. In the corpus of world myth they stand with every sacred-twin tradition, from the Ashanti twins to the Popol Vuh, supplying the Haitian case in which twinship is treated not as a heroic epoch but as a permanent domestic arrangement that must be kept in good order at every meal.

title.en: Gede and Baron Samedi: the Cemetery Masters
title.zh: 蓋德與星期六男爵：墓園之主

source.work: Alfred Métraux, 'Voodoo in Haiti' (1959); Karen McCarthy Brown, 'Mama Lola' (1991)

summary.en: The Gede family — Baron Samedi, Baron La Croix, Gede Nibo, Gede Frey — are the lwa of death and fertility, of the cemetery and the party that laughs at it: top hats over skull-faces, black coats, filthy songs, a cane and a rum bottle, and an obscene dance that makes the dead laugh. They guard the graves and the unborn alike; they are petitioned to cure the dying child and to open the gates for the dying adult; they are the comic and terrible masters of the crossing.
summary.zh: 蓋德家族——星期六男爵、十字男爵、尼博蓋德、弗雷蓋德——是死亡與豐育、墓園與訕笑死亡之宴的羅阿：骷髏面上頂高帽、黑外套、污穢的歌、手杖與朗姆瓶，還有一支令亡者發笑的猥褻之舞。他們既護墳墓也護未生者；人們求他們醫治垂死的孩童、為垂死的成人開門；他們是渡口滑稽而可怖的主人。

sensitivity.note: Deep record from published paraphrase only; Gede cult is living practice.

passages.text: The Gede are the lwa of the cemetery and of everything that crosses it: Baron Samedi, the top-hatted master of the dead; Baron La Croix, keeper of the cross at the tomb's head; Gede Nibo, the young dandy of the cemetery paths; Gede Frey, the great protector of children. They come in service with skull-painted faces, black coats and sunglasses, a cane in one hand and a rum bottle in the other; they sing the filthiest songs in the peristyle and dance the banda, the obscene two-step that makes the whole yard laugh — because the Gede know how the story ends and know how it does not.

narrative.en: The Gede family are the lwa of the cemetery and of everything that crosses it: Baron Samedi, the top-hatted master of the dead; Baron La Croix, keeper of the cross at the tomb's head; Gede Nibo, the young dandy of the cemetery paths, patron of those who die young and unshriven; Gede Frey, the great protector of children; and the Gede as a laughing, swarming crowd behind them. They come in service with skull-painted faces, black coats, dark glasses, a cane in one hand and a rum bottle in the other; they sing the filthiest songs in the peristyle and dance the banda, the obscene two-step that makes the whole yard laugh — because the Gede know how the story ends and know how it does not, and their laughter is the laughter of those who have read the ledger. Their work is double. They guard the graves of the dead, and they superintend the fertility of the living — the same power over the gates of entry and exit: a dying child is carried to the Gede; a woman who cannot conceive petitions the Baron; the funeral is negotiated with the cross at the tomb's head, the price discussed, the gate opened or kept shut. They are the psychopomps and the gynecocrats of the Afro-Atlantic crossing, and their cult, in the Kongo-inflected rites, preserves the African grammar of the land of the dead as a crowded village just beyond the fence. Brown's telling holds the two moods together. At her altar-service the Gede arrive drunk, obscene, pinching the guests, demanding cigarettes and rum and telling the sort of jokes that no other lwa would tell; and then, when the serious work begins, the same figures make the most sober contracts of all: who shall live, who shall die, who shall be remembered and how. The cemetery's laughter is not denial; it is the professional manner of the only specialists who deal daily with the crossing, and who insist that the crossing be conducted with style — a top hat, a good song, a fair price, and a laugh at the gate. The Gede's festival season is a study in this doubleness: on the feasts of the dead — All Souls and the days of the cemetery — the peristyle fills with black-clad, skull-faced dancers, and the services run all night, part funeral and part carnival, with the banda danced until the drums give out. The economics of the cult are equally explicit: the Gede are paid for everything — a coin for a prayer, a bottle for an audience, a substantial fee for the contract at the tomb — and they are famous for collecting; a service without payment is a service the Baron will remember. In the comparative grid they stand with every psychopomp of world mythology — Hermes, the Egyptian Anubis and Osiris, the Norse Hel — but with the Afro-Atlantic particularity that the lord of the dead is also the patron of the unborn, and that his cult is the one place in the religion where death and fertility are negotiated at the same table. For the corpus of comparative myth the Haitian Gede supply the fullest case of death as a professional service: contracted, priced, celebrated, and always, in the end, laughed with rather than at.

title.en: Bois Caïman, 1791: the Ceremony That Opened the Revolution

summary.en: In August 1791, on a wooded height called Bois Caïman near Cap-Français, the planners of the great slave rising met in ceremony: according to the planter Dalmas's account, a pig was sacrificed and the participants swore an oath over its blood to destroy the whites. Out of that night came the insurrection of the Northern Plain — and Bois Caïman became the founding scene of Haitian memory: the oath, the blood, the storm, the first nation born of a slave revolution.

narrative.en: The earliest written account of the ceremony at Bois Caïman is that of Antoine Dalmas, a planter of the Northern Plain, who wrote within a few years of the events he described: on the night of August 14, 1791, the principal leaders of the rising — Boukman Dutty among them — gathered in a wooded place called Bois Caïman near Cap-Français, where a pig was sacrificed and an oath taken over its blood to destroy the power of the whites. Dalmas wrote as an enemy of the revolution, and his account was meant to horrify; but his testimony that such a meeting took place is not seriously doubted, and every later source builds on his report or quarrels with it. What the ceremony actually contained — the exact liturgy, the deity invoked, the share of each participant — is beyond recovery, and honest scholarship keeps the uncertainty open. What is certain is what followed. A week later the Northern Plain was in flames: the insurrection that began the Haitian Revolution — the only successful slave revolution in modern history — took its order and its courage from the networks of vodou priests and Congolese and Arada elders who had organized it. The rising was coordinated across plantations by runners and by drum, and its leadership was thick with ritual specialists; the plantation world's secret assembly was the school of its politics. Boukman's speech, as remembered in the oral tradition, casts the theology of the rising: the God of the whites demands crime, but our God asks only good works; and the remembered storm that broke that night — rain that covered the first fires — is read in the tradition as the ancestors themselves answering. In Haitian memory Bois Caïman functions as a founding scene on the order of a covenant: the oath over blood, the first fires of the North, and the birth of a nation whose independence in 1804 declared that the color question had been answered in favor of the enslaved. Historians debate the details — Geggus doubts the pig, Fick doubts the planter's numbers, and the oral tradition keeps its own counsel — but the memory has never been in doubt, and the oath, the storm and the covenant are rehearsed in song on the revolution's anniversaries to this day. For the comparative corpus Bois Caïman supplies the Afro-Atlantic form of the covenant scene: the oath sworn over blood in the wood, the divine sanction claimed by the weakest party, and the fire that follows as the sign that the covenant has been accepted. Parallels are exact and instructive — the covenant of the Hebrew exodus, the Maccabean oath at Modin, the secret oath-societies of the Kongo and the Anjelo coast that the slave-trade carried to the Caribbean — and the Haitian case is the only one that succeeded all the way to statehood. The sensitivity of the material is proportionate to its importance: Bois Caïman is invoked by Haitians as the nation's baptism, contested by scholars as a planter's story, and claimed by the living religion as proof that the ancestors were present at the founding; the honest record keeps all three claims in view and adds none of its own. In the Motif Atlas the record anchors the cluster of oath-over-blood foundings and links the Haitian revolution to the worldwide grammar of covenant and exodus.

Thompson reads it as Kongo writing — cosmic graphs drawn in the old homeland on the ground, the bodies of initiates and the walls of tombs — carried to Haiti and made the choreography of the ceremony: the dance is danced on the signature.

narrative.en: Every Vodou ceremony begins with writing. On the peristyle floor, in flour or cornmeal or ash, the celebrant traces the vèvè of the lwa to be called — the signature-script of Legba's crossroads, Damballa's paired serpents, Ezili's pierced heart, the boat of Agoué, the crossed iron of Ogou. The sign is the invitation: until it is drawn, the ground is ordinary ground; once it is drawn, the ground is the spirit's address, and the drums that follow are read by the spirits who arrive to find their names written. The practice is described by Métraux in his classic account as the technical heart of the service — a liturgy of drawing, singing and rhythm in which the visual, the verbal and the musical are one act. Robert Farris Thompson traces the practice to Kongo. In the old homeland, cosmic graphs are drawn on the ground, on the bodies of the initiated, on the walls of tombs — writing that makes a place a crossing of worlds; the Kongo cosmogram, the diamond-with-cross that maps the living and the dead on the four quarters of a single field, is the master-sign of this art. In Haiti the Kongo sign-writing fused with the Fon and Yoruba emblem-languages and became the choreography of the ceremony: the dance is danced on the signature, the singers sing the signature into voice, and the signature is erased before the service ends — the writing is for the moment of the crossing, not for the museum, and the same hand that draws it sweeps it away. The vèvè belongs to the grammar of the road-cosmos: each emblem is a door, and the ceremony is a sequence of doors opened in order. Legba's is drawn first, that the other gates may open; the paired serpents next, that the oldest powers may come cool; the crossed iron of Ogou, that the work may be done; the boat of Agoué, that the crossing may be made. To read a vèvè is to read the itinerary of a service, and the liturgy of drawing is thus the written liturgy of the religion — the part of the sacred that leaves a mark, and the part that leaves none, both at once. The pedagogy of the vèvè is worth stating plainly, because it explains why the practice survives so tenaciously: a vèvè can be learned by watching a hand draw it, without books, without literacy, without any of the institutions of writing that the colony denied the enslaved; it is a script designed by and for a population from whom reading was forbidden. The flour that carries it is food; the ash that carries it is the residue of the fire; both are humble materials, renewed every service, and the ephemerality is doctrinal — the writing belongs to the moment of contact between worlds and must not outlast it. In the comparative grid the practice stands with the ground-drawings of the Kongo, the sand-figures of West African divination (the sikidy of Madagascar, the Ifá marks of the Yoruba), and the chalk diagrams of European cunning-folk; the Haitian vèvè is the point at which all of these stream together into one liturgical art. For the Motif Atlas the record anchors the cluster of sacred sign-writing — the diviner's marks, the cosmograms, the signatures of the gods — and gives the Afro-Atlantic case in which writing itself is a rite of hospitality: the gods arrive because someone took the trouble to spell their names on the floor.
